profile: A 67-year-old man with Fitzpatrick skin type IV presented with a 1-year history of an asymptomatic cutaneous eruption on the hands. His medical history included gout, hypothyroidism, hypertension, and dyslipidemia; medications were allopurinol, levothyroxine, losartan, and rosuvastatin. On examination, there were multiple, discrete, well-circumscribed, smooth, somewhat flat-topped, erythematous-to-violaceous papules on the bilateral dorsal hands. A skin biopsy showed an increased number of vascular channels, fibrohistiocytic cells, and large angulated multinucleate cells within a collagenous stroma in the papillary and mid dermis.

An 82-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation, surgically treated small bowel carcinoid tumor (15 years prior), latent tuberculosis, hypothyroidism, and hypertension was transferred for progressive bilateral lower-extremity weakness and frequent falls. Over the past four months she had three prior admissions for similar symptoms without a diagnosis. 

On the first admission, she had seven days of vertical and horizontal diplopia, mild vertigo, right-eye ptosis, left facial droop, decreased right hemi-body sensation to light touch, and right lower-extremity weakness. Laboratory tests, including thyroid function, vitamin B12, folate, inflammatory markers, and creatine phosphokinase, were within normal limits. Brain CT and MRI showed no acute findings.

During the second admission, she experienced severe bilateral leg weakness with back pain on ambulation and a left facial droop. MRI of the head, neck, and lumbar spine revealed only advanced degenerative disk disease and moderate spinal stenosis without acute pathology.

On the third admission, she presented after multiple falls associated with presyncope. She developed diarrhea and was treated for campylobacteriosis. She again had a left facial droop; repeat head CT and CTA were negative for ischemia. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed hypoglycorrhachia, elevated protein, and lymphocytic pleocytosis without oligoclonal bands or malignant cells. CSF culture grew Propionibacterium acnes, and she received two weeks of ampicillin without improvement.

A third lumbar puncture revealed a positive QuantiFERON-TB Gold and elevated β-(1,3)-D-glucan but negative CSF PCR for herpes simplex virus I and II, varicella, West Nile virus, and tuberculosis; negative fungal and acid-fast bacillus stains and cultures; negative VDRL; and negative cryptococcal antigen and brucella titers. Serum tests were negative for brucella, coxsackie, and HIV. CSF Lyme IgG and IgM were elevated. Autoimmune and paraneoplastic antibody panels, complement levels, and thyroid studies were unremarkable. Screening for recurrent carcinoid (24-h urine 5-HIAA, serum serotonin, chromogranin A, gastrin, and vasoactive intestinal peptide) and abdominal imaging were normal. She underwent penicillin desensitization and completed a course of IVIG without clinical response.

A 68-year-old man with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and coronary artery disease presented with a 5-year history of left knee swelling, pain, and progressive limitation of motion. He denied any history of trauma. Initial treatment with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and rest provided no relief, and knee mobility declined over time, substantially affecting daily activities.

On examination, the left knee had flexion limited to 90° and extension to 20°, with visible swelling but no erythema or warmth.

Plain radiographs of the left knee showed degenerative changes and a large, irregular calcific mass extending from below the patella into the suprapatellar region. A CT scan demonstrated multiple popcorn-like calcifications beneath the quadriceps tendon and within the Hoffa fat pad, along with a moderate joint effusion and bicompartmental osteoarthritis. MRI revealed an enlarged suprapatellar recess containing multiple focal lesions with osteocartilaginous signals: central marrow-like signal surrounded by a hyperintense peripheral ring on T2-weighted and T2 FATSAT sequences, along with degenerative changes in the patella and edematous femoral condyles and tibial plateau.

An 81-year-old Asian woman with no prior medical history presented with one week of progressive shortness of breath and bilateral leg swelling. Vital signs: heart rate 130 b.p.m., respiratory rate 24 /min, blood pressure 127/92 mmHg, SpO₂ 92% on room air. Examination revealed jugular venous distension, bilateral crackles (more pronounced at the right base), and Grade III pitting edema of both lower extremities; cardiac auscultation was unremarkable. Intravenous diuretics produced symptomatic improvement. Chest radiography showed bilateral pleural effusions. Laboratory tests were notable for a lactate dehydrogenase level of 1228 U/L (normal 100–250); all other studies were within normal limits. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a large, mobile homogeneous mass filling the right atrium and protruding into the right ventricular inflow tract, along with a separate large extracardiac mass compressing the right heart. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen revealed an 8.4 × 8.9 × 9.1 cm ill-defined enhancing soft-tissue mass extending from the pericardial cavity into the right atrium and ventricle, with multiple lobulated enhancing epicardial fat masses abutting the left ventricle; there was right pleural effusion and enlarged lower paratracheal and right hilar lymph nodes without hepatosplenomegaly or abdominal lymphadenopathy. Pleural fluid cytology was negative for malignancy. Transjugular cardiac biopsy under imaging guidance yielded limited tissue showing spindle to round neoplastic cells. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated expression of ERG and Fli-1, whereas AE1/AE3, EMA, CD31, and CD34 were all negative.

A 67-year-old woman presented after a collapse and was found to be hyponatremic. She had a history of hypertension, a remote femoral neck fracture, bilateral cosmetic breast implants, and a 50-pack-year smoking history (quit 6 months ago). She reported several months of fatigue and a 2-kg weight loss but denied cough or hemoptysis. Physical examination was unremarkable. Chest radiography revealed a large soft-tissue density lesion in the right hemithorax. CT of the chest showed a predominantly cystic mass (attenuation 14 HU) in the right upper lobe, extending from the hilum and communicating with dilated subsegmental bronchi, producing a “finger-in-glove” appearance; there was focal mural enhancement adjacent to the hilum. Bronchoscopy demonstrated a soft-tissue lesion in the right upper lobe bronchus resembling granulation or necrotic tissue. A provisional diagnosis of complex bronchocele was made. PET-CT showed focal FDG uptake (SUV 4–5) in the medial aspect of the mass, with no other sites of abnormal activity, suggesting malignant pathology.

A 3-month-old girl was referred for evaluation of a left retro-auricular mass that had been noted on postnatal day 5 and slowly enlarged over 3 months. There was no history of trauma, infection, or systemic symptoms, and her family history was unremarkable. On examination, the lesion measured approximately 3 cm in its long axis, was firm, non-tender, and without overlying erythema or warmth. A temporal bone MRI demonstrated an oval 3-cm subcutaneous mass in the left retro-auricular region with moderately intense, heterogeneous enhancement on post-contrast T1-weighted, fat-saturated sequences. A lymphangioma was suspected.

A 16-year-old female presented with a 7-year history of a lump on her left upper lip. She was in good general health, with no systemic disease, no regular medications, and no smoking history. The lesion had grown slowly since its initial appearance. On clinical examination, there was a 1.5 × 3 cm sessile mass of soft consistency, skin-colored and painless, that was freely mobile within the lip. A diascopy test was negative. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy yielded erythrocytes, lymphocytes, and macrophages, with no evidence of malignancy.

An 80-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes mellitus presented with a 4-month history of progressive exertional dyspnea. He appeared well. Blood pressure was 120/70 mmHg, pulse 90 bpm. Cardiac examination was unremarkable. Breath sounds were absent over the inferior two thirds of the right lung. He had a small-volume ascites, and his lower limbs were without edema.

Laboratory results showed a normal hemogram, mildly decreased renal function, and hyperkalemia (5.8 mEq/L; reference range, 3.7–5.0). Liver enzymes and gamma-glutamyl transferase were normal.

Chest radiography demonstrated a right-sided pleural effusion. Thoracentesis yielded 1800 mL of bloody fluid; cytology studies and pleural biopsy did not reveal malignant cells. Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal cardiac chambers, normal left ventricular systolic function, and normal valves; an echo-dense mass measuring 3.4 × 2.4 cm was noted in the right atrium extending from the intrahepatic inferior vena cava.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the thorax and abdomen confirmed the right atrial and inferior vena cava mass, showed ascites, cystic hypoattenuated areas in the left kidney, and a heterogeneous mass in segment VII of the right hepatic lobe obliterating the right hepatic vein. Splenomegaly was present. The patient had no history of viral hepatitis or alcohol use.

A 49-year-old woman noted a palpable lump in her right breast 3 months earlier. Two years ago, she had fibroadenomas and cysts in the left breast confirmed on biopsy. Her medical history includes hypothyroidism (on levothyroxine) and use of oral contraceptives. Her paternal aunt had breast cancer at age 20. 

On examination, two right-breast masses (40 mm at 12-o’clock, 20 mm at 3-o’clock; both scored S3) were palpable. Mammography with tomosynthesis showed dense breast tissue, scattered calcifications, a new smooth density in the medial right breast inferiority, and an architectural distortion in the upper outer left breast. Ultrasound confirmed multiple cysts and a 1.2 cm hypoechoic area of distortion at 2-o’clock in the left breast. 

A stereotactic biopsy of the left lesion revealed a fibroepithelial lesion without atypia but with an irregular stromal interface. Six months later, ultrasound again showed a 1.2 cm oval hypoechoic lesion at 12-o’clock in the left breast. Core biopsy demonstrated bland spindle‐cell proliferation, focal hemosiderin deposition, no cytological atypia or increased mitotic activity, and features of fibrocystic disease. On this basis, a B3 designation was assigned and wire-guided excision was performed.

Excision revealed a 7.2 mm intracanalicular fibroadenoma adjacent to an irregular pale 14.1 mm spindle‐cell proliferation. The spindle cells showed focal extension to the margin, occasional mitotic figures but no cytological atypia, and an irregular interface with lobules and adipose tissue. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated that the spindle cells were strongly positive for vimentin and negative for muscle‐specific actin, S100 protein, and pan-cytokeratins. The Ki-67 proliferation index was 2%.

A 21-year-old woman presented with right hip pain of several months’ duration without trauma. Examination showed normal hip range of motion but pain on weight bearing. Laboratory tests were within normal limits. Plain radiographs and CT revealed an osteolytic lesion of the right ilium and acetabulum with cortical destruction, marginal sclerosis, slight pseudotrabeculation, and bone expansion. MRI demonstrated a large iliac lesion with low signal intensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images relative to muscle. Because of severe acetabular destruction, malignant tumors such as low-grade fibrosarcoma and malignant transformation of fibrous dysplasia were considered. An open biopsy showed proliferation of spindle cells in an abundant collagenous matrix involving the bone cortex, without cellular atypia or mitotic figures. The specimen comprised mature bone tissue rather than the C-shaped woven bone of fibrous dysplasia. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for cytoplasmic vimentin and smooth muscle actin. Low-grade fibrosarcoma was not definitively excluded, and close radiologic follow-up was planned. Bisphosphonate therapy was initiated, and weight bearing was permitted.

An 18-year-old boy presented with progressively worsening dull aching pain in the lower back and both lower limbs for several weeks, accompanied by loss of appetite and malaise. He had localized tenderness over the D7–D8 vertebral region. On examination, he was thin, with mild pallor. Neurologic assessment revealed bilateral lower-limb weakness (muscle power 3/5) and decreased sensation to light touch below the level of D8; other findings were normal.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL, white-cell count 8200 cells/mm3 (70% neutrophils, 26% lymphocytes), and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 60 mm in the first hour. Urinalysis and bone-marrow examination were unremarkable, and a tuberculin test was negative. A chest radiograph was normal.

Computed tomography of the spine demonstrated an expansile lytic lesion of the posterior element of the D7 vertebra, with a heterogeneously enhancing soft-tissue component extending from D7 to D9, involving the thecal sac, lamina, and spinous process, and causing anterior displacement of the spinal cord. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed an expansile lesion of the D7 posterior elements with a 67 × 32 × 18 mm enhancing soft-tissue mass in the posterior paraspinal region, extending into the epidural space at D6–7 and D7–8 levels, compressing the spinal cord and producing severe central canal stenosis (anteroposterior diameter ~2 mm).

A previously healthy 7-year-old girl presented with a 3-month history of headache and vomiting. On examination, she was conscious, oriented, and had bilateral papilledema; there were no focal neurologic deficits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head revealed a large enhancing lesion occupying the bilateral lateral ventricles. MRI of the brain showed that the lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images and predominantly isointense to hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with a few hyperintense areas within the mass. No other lesions were identified on the initial neuroimaging.

A 27‐year‐old man reported a slowly enlarging right breast mass that he first noticed about 10 years earlier. He had no significant medical history, took no medications, and had normal secondary sexual characteristics; his serum hormone profile was within normal limits. On examination, there was diffuse enlargement of the right breast consistent with gynecomastia. In the lower inner quadrant of the right breast, a mobile, lobulated, firm mass measuring 4 × 2 cm was palpated; it was not fixed to skin or underlying fascia, and there was no axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. The left breast was unremarkable.  
Breast ultrasonography showed diffuse thickening of the right mammary gland and an oval hypoechoic mass with a well‐defined border measuring 41 × 12 mm in the lower inner quadrant. Contrast‐enhanced chest CT demonstrated diffuse right breast swelling and a lobulated nodule with gradual enhancement in the same region. Fine‐needle aspiration cytology revealed a biphasic population composed of spindle stromal cells and ductal cells; naked nuclei, myoepithelial cells, and apocrine metaplastic cells were also identified.

A 73-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive abdominal distension, severe epigastric pain radiating to her back (worse with eating, partially relieved by rest), and early satiety. She reported feeling feverish for 1 week. There was no nausea, vomiting, hematemesis, per rectal bleeding, or weight loss. Her past medical history included hypertension, gout, and recurrent cystitis. She consumed six units of alcohol per week and was a lifelong nonsmoker; there was no family history of gastrointestinal malignancy.

On admission she was afebrile but tachycardic (104 bpm) and otherwise hemodynamically stable. Abdominal examination revealed a large, firm, mildly tender mass measuring approximately 10 × 15 cm in the left side of the abdomen, extending into the umbilical and epigastric regions. By day 3 she had persistent tachycardia and developed a temperature of 38.5 °C, meeting criteria for systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS).

Laboratory studies showed white blood cell count 30.8 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 366 mg/L, hemoglobin 107 g/L, platelets 234 × 10^9/L, bilirubin 14 µmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 380 U/L, ALT 71 IU/L, amylase 42 U/L, and estimated GFR 52 mL/min/1.73 m^2. Blood and urine cultures were negative; chest radiograph showed no consolidation. Initial differential diagnoses included a left renal or adrenal mass, splenic flexure tumor, pancreatic neoplasm, or pheochromocytoma. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a large (17 × 16 × 17 cm) cystic lesion occupying the left upper and central abdomen with calcification in the wall, most likely arising from the pancreas or left adrenal gland, with low-grade malignancy in the differential. Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics were started and stopped after 7 days because no infectious source was identified. A 24-hour urine catecholamine collection was negative.

After multidisciplinary discussion, surgical exploration was undertaken. At laparotomy a giant cystic tumor was found to arise from the left adrenal gland, displacing the stomach, spleen, pancreas, left kidney, and colon. The lesion weighed 3 kg. The patient recovered uneventfully.

Histologic examination showed an extensively necrotic adrenal neoplasm composed of dense sheets of small, immature mononuclear cells with occasional blasts and multilobated nuclei. There was no adipose tissue or other marrow elements. Neoplastic cells stained positive for myeloperoxidase, CD45, and lysozyme, and were negative for broad-spectrum cytokeratins, melanocytic markers, and neuroendocrine markers. The principal histological differential diagnosis lay between a myelolipoma and a myeloid malignancy (granulocytic sarcoma/acute myeloid leukemia), and the absence of adipose tissue argues against a myelolipoma.

A 4-year-old girl was brought for evaluation of a swelling in the maxillary anterior region present since 6 months of age and gradually enlarging. The swelling has been asymptomatic, with no pain or discharge. Her parents also noted delayed eruption of her primary teeth; there was no history of trauma. Medical and family histories were noncontributory. On extraoral examination, findings were unremarkable. Intraorally, a diffuse swelling measuring approximately 1 × 2 cm was observed above the gingival margin in the region of the right maxillary primary central incisor, lateral incisor, and canine. The swelling was nontender and bony hard on palpation. A periapical radiograph of the area showed multiple radiopacities of densities equal to or greater than tooth structure, arranged irregularly and each separated and surrounded by a thin radiolucent capsule; above these calcifications lay a developing permanent tooth bud.

An 8-month-old female infant with a history of anorectal malformation and rectovestibular fistula (status post colostomy) presented with a vestibular mass that had protruded for 4 months. The mass was painless, nonbleeding, with an uneven surface and ruddy mucosa without skin covering. Other congenital anomalies included hemivertebrae and thumb hypoplasia. Serum creatinine was 0.54 mg/dL. Renal and bladder ultrasonography showed normal kidneys without hydronephrosis and no cystic dilatation at the ureterovesical junction. Voiding cystourethrography demonstrated complete bladder filling without vesicoureteral reflux or bladder prolapse. Under general anesthesia, cystoscopy and vaginoscopy revealed smooth bladder neck, bladder mucosa, and vaginal mucosa with no intraluminal masses. A reddish polypoid mass measuring 2.0 × 1.5 × 1.0 cm on a 0.5-cm stalk was identified arising from the outer wall of the urethra, 1.5 cm from the urethral meatus. The mass was excised completely, and hemostasis was achieved without complications. A catheter was left in place for 14 days and then removed. The excised specimen was sent for pathological examination.

A 16-year-old girl presented with a mass protruding from her vaginal introitus that she had first noticed 3 years earlier. She reported no associated pain or systemic symptoms.

On examination, a 6-cm pedunculated polyp arose from the cervix; it had a smooth, glistening, “grape-like” appearance with focal hemorrhage.

A pelvic CT scan was initially requested but declined for financial reasons. She underwent examination under anesthesia and a cervical polypectomy.

Histologic examination of the excised polyp showed it to be covered by squamous and endocervical mucosa. The underlying tumor consisted of small, rounded cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and atypical nuclei. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated tumor cells that were strongly positive for desmin and showed nuclear reactivity to myogenin in less than 50% of nuclei, while staining was negative for cytokeratin.

A staging CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a residual mass at the cervix measuring approximately 4.5 cm in greatest dimension and no evidence of metastatic disease.

A 51-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of painful urination and right flank pain associated with gross hematuria. He had a history of smoking and multiple treatments for schistosomiasis and urinary tract infections. Examination revealed a weak, wasted man with temperature 36.2 °C, blood pressure 130/87 mm Hg, pulse 80 beats/min, and respiratory rate 20 breaths/min. Abdominal examination showed a fixed, tender, palpable suprapubic mass. Laboratory studies demonstrated a platelet count of 53×10^3/µL and hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL; renal function, white-cell count, and electrolytes were normal. An intravenous urogram CT scan showed a heterogeneous 5.5×4.5 cm mass at the right superolateral bladder wall with ipsilateral hydronephrosis and hydroureter. A bone scan was unremarkable. Clinically, urothelial carcinoma was considered most likely. Cystoscopic evaluation revealed a solid mass with necrotic areas on the anterior bladder wall, and an incisional biopsy was obtained. Histological evaluation showed a high-grade malignant mesenchymal tumor composed of oval to spindle cells with osteoid formation in many areas; no definite carcinomatous component was appreciated.

A 36-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension presented with a three-month history of gradual, painful diminution of vision in her left eye. She denied any trauma, surgery, tobacco use, or alcohol consumption. On examination, there was swelling of the left hemiface with tenderness anterior to the left maxillary sinus. Ophthalmologic evaluation demonstrated a painful left exophthalmos with opalescent cornea, chemosis, complete ophthalmoplegia, and strabismus involving the abducens nerve. Visual acuity in the left eye was reduced to light perception only, and fundus examination revealed a greyish retina. Anterior rhinoscopy showed a friable, bleeding tumor mass filling the left superior nasal cavity; the right nasal cavity was normal. Computed tomography of the brain and orbits demonstrated a large heterogeneous mass occupying the left nasal fossa with extension into the left maxillary, ethmoid, frontal, and sphenoid sinuses, invasion of the left orbit, bone lysis at the skull base, and endocranial extension. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed these findings and further showed involvement of the left temporal and frontal lobes, cavernous sinuses, sella turcica, and parapharyngeal, masticatory, and submandibular spaces, with grade III axial exophthalmos.

A 38-year-old man with a 20–pack-year smoking history presented with several weeks of progressive right nasal obstruction, right facial numbness, persistent right-sided headache, intermittent right orbital pain, and recurrent right-sided epistaxis. He underwent septoplasty three months earlier; his symptoms began shortly afterward. 

On nasal endoscopy, a mass filled the right nasal cavity; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. 

A CT scan of the paranasal sinuses showed opacification and expansion of the right sphenoidal sinus by a poorly defined soft-tissue mass that extended into the nasal cavity and eroded the inferior bony wall of the sphenoid sinus. 

MRI of the facial region demonstrated a large, contrast-enhancing, destructive mass involving the sphenoid, posterior ethmoid, and right maxillary sinuses, extending posteriorly into the nasal cavity and laterally into the right infratemporal fossa; a large right retropharyngeal lymph node also enhanced after intravenous contrast. 

A PET scan revealed moderate fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the right nasal cavity and in a right level-3 jugular–digastric lymph node; there was no evidence of distant metastatic disease in the chest, abdomen, pelvis, or skeleton. 

Tumor grading was T4N2M0, stage IVa.

A 70-year-old man with dyslipidemia presented with a 5-month history of recurrent vertebral compression fractures and back pain. Five months earlier, he developed acute back pain while changing his clothes and was treated for T11 and L3 compression fractures. Two months later, after slipping down stairs, he sustained L2 and L4 compression fractures. Five days before referral, he experienced back pain while sneezing and had difficulty walking.

Spine bone densitometry at prior visits showed osteopenia. Lumbar MRI revealed multiple compression fractures with inconspicuous retropulsion of the cortex into the canal. T-L spine X-rays showed degenerative changes and compression fractures at T12 and L1–L3; pelvic X-rays confirmed osteopenia. A bone scan demonstrated an L1 compression fracture, post-traumatic rib changes, and degenerative changes in T9–L5 and both hips.

Laboratory tests revealed normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 11.0 g/dL), a normal serum calcium level (8.9 mg/dL), and normal renal function (creatinine 0.78 mg/dL). There was no evidence on labs or imaging of osteoporosis, metabolic bone disease (including hyperparathyroidism or Paget disease), or an obvious tumor.

Serum protein electrophoresis showed normal immunoglobulin levels and gamma globulin fractions. Urine protein electrophoresis revealed no monoclonal protein.

A 69-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, and prior radioiodine ablation of the thyroid underwent routine abdominal ultrasonography, which revealed a pancreatic mass. She had no abdominal symptoms and had lost 4 kg on a diabetic diet. On examination, her body mass index was 32.2 kg/m2. Laboratory tests were normal except for an elevated cholesterol level; cholestatic enzymes and CA 19-9 were within reference ranges.  
Abdominal ultrasound showed a 45-mm homogeneous hypoechoic mass in the head of the pancreas with well-defined margins and no blood flow on Doppler. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a homogeneous, encapsulated mass in the pancreatic head and uncinate process with fat‐density attenuation (–30 to –120 HU) and no contrast enhancement; the main pancreatic duct proximal to the mass was dilated to 4 mm. MRI revealed that the mass was isointense to subcutaneous fat on T1- and T2-weighted images and showed homogeneous signal suppression on fat-suppressed T2-weighted sequences. The upper portion of the mass indented the extrahepatic biliary tree without causing dilation, and the lower portion displaced the duodenum. Imaging also disclosed several perihilar and periportal lymph nodes measuring 10–13 mm in diameter. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed no evidence of duodenal compression or infiltration.

A 24-year-old woman with no prior illness presented with vomiting and melena. On examination, she was tachycardic, and her hemoglobin level was 6.3 g/dL. She received 10 units of packed red cells and was transferred for further evaluation. Emergency upper endoscopy showed active bleeding from an ulcer on the surface of an elevated lesion in the lower stomach along the greater curvature; bleeding was controlled with local sclerosis therapy. Two days later, repeat endoscopy revealed a 30 mm, well-circumscribed, soft submucosal mass with a small nonbleeding ulcer on its mucosal surface; no biopsy was performed because of bleeding risk. Endoscopic ultrasonography demonstrated a well-demarcated, hypoechoic mass arising from the third and fourth gastric wall layers. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a lesion in the gastric wall with dense homogeneous enhancement in both early and delayed phases, suggesting abundant blood supply and intact overlying mucosa.

A 63-year-old Hispanic man with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, and right nephrectomy eight years earlier presented with a three-month history of urinary obstructive symptoms. On digital rectal examination, the prostate was enlarged with a soft nodule in the left lobe. The prostate-specific antigen level was 3.4 ng/mL. He underwent a suprapubic prostatectomy. 

Grossly, the 4.5 × 4.0 × 2.0 cm gland (27 g) was multinodular and elastic, with a well-circumscribed, blackish area measuring 1.4 cm in the left lobe. Microscopic examination demonstrated nodular hyperplasia with acute inflammation and a proliferation of spindle-shaped stromal cells containing abundant melanin pigment. Histochemical stains were positive with Masson-Fontana and negative with iron, and immunohistochemistry showed S-100–positive pigmented stromal cells.

A newborn girl was referred for evaluation of a vulvar mass that had been identified prenatally. On examination, there was a soft, poorly mobile 2.5×4.0-cm mass in the right labia majora; urinary and bowel function were normal, and there was no relevant family history. Pelvic ultrasonography showed a homogeneous, hypoechoic lesion with well-defined borders; the uterus and ovaries appeared normal. Contrast-enhanced pelvic CT demonstrated a well-circumscribed, hyperenhancing vulvar mass measuring 2.5×4.0 cm without evidence of invasion into adjacent structures.

A 69-year-old multiparous woman, postmenopausal for 20 years, presented with a 3-month history of foul-smelling vaginal discharge, intermittent bleeding, and lower abdominal pain. She had never undergone cervical cancer screening. On examination she was pale and tachycardic; other vital signs were stable and BMI was 23.4 kg/m2. Speculum examination revealed a cauliflower-like cervical mass measuring 8 × 6 cm involving the upper vagina; bilateral parametria were not involved and the rectal mucosa was free. Clinical FIGO stage was IIA2.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis showed a 9 × 6 × 5 cm heterogeneously enhancing lesion arising from the cervix and lower uterine segment, abutting but not invading the rectal wall posteriorly and the bladder wall anteriorly, with no lymphadenopathy. Punch biopsy of the cervical mass revealed sheets of spindle cells with moderate pleomorphism and interspersed glands lined by benign endocervical-type epithelium. Immunohistochemical studies showed positivity in the epithelial component for cytokeratin and weak immunoreactivity of the spindle cells for SMA, CD10, P53, and P63, with negativity for desmin, P40, S-100, and ER; the Ki-67 index was 20–30%.

A 42-year-old man presented to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain. His temperature was 36.4°C, heart rate 84/min, respiratory rate 16/min, and blood pressure 130/90 mmHg. The abdomen was rigid with diffuse tenderness. Laboratory studies showed WBC 7,220/mm3 (57.5% neutrophils), hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL, platelets 299,000/mm3, AST 25 IU/L, ALT 21 IU/L, total bilirubin 0.81 mg/dL, total protein 6.4 g/dL, albumin 3.5 g/dL, BUN 8 mg/dL, creatinine 0.65 mg/dL, glucose 97 mg/dL, LDH 580 IU/L, ESR 41 mm/hr, and CRP 6.84 mg/L.  
He had been diagnosed with HIV in 2010; in November 2014 his CD4+ count was 355 cells/mm3 and viral load 156,000 copies/mL. He started HAART (abacavir/lamivudine/darunavir/ritonavir) in April 2015. One week before this admission he had mild abdominal pain; endoscopy at that time showed an acute gastric ulcer and biopsy was performed. Over the next week, pain persisted and he returned to the ED.  
A plain abdominal radiograph showed multiple air–fluid levels and dilated small-bowel loops consistent with obstruction. Abdominopelvic CT revealed multiple “bowel-within-bowel” configurations in the jejunum, indicating several sites of intussusception.

A 37-year-old woman was admitted in September 2020 with a sudden onset of fever to 39 °C and mild discomfort over her transplanted kidney. She had end-stage renal disease from IgA nephropathy and received a deceased-donor kidney transplant at age 29, with induction basiliximab and maintenance tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisolone. Three years posttransplant, recurrent IgA nephropathy was confirmed on biopsy. The graft subsequently failed, and she initiated peritoneal dialysis in April 2020, at which time tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisolone were tapered. Two months later she developed intermittent gross hematuria and worsening anemia (hemoglobin 6.3 g/dL from a baseline of 9.7 g/dL), which transiently improved with increased immunosuppression but recurred with tapering. 

On examination at admission, she was febrile (39 °C) and had tenderness over the graft site without lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies showed WBC 4.9×10^3/μL, hemoglobin 5.5 g/dL, total protein 5.0 g/dL, albumin 3.0 g/dL, BUN 54 mg/dL, creatinine 8.5 mg/dL, LDH 1453 IU/L, high-sensitivity CRP 187 mg/L, transferrin saturation 31%, and ferritin 1080 ng/mL. A peripheral smear demonstrated normochromic normocytic anemia with poikilocytosis. Both urine and blood cultures were negative. EBV serologies showed VCA IgM negative and VCA IgG positive. Contrast-enhanced CT of the transplanted kidney revealed graft swelling and multiple low-attenuated areas with calyceal dilatation. 

We promptly initiated antibiotic treatment. However, the patient's fever did not subside, and her condition weakened compared to her prehospitalization state.

A 64-year-old Indian man with coronary artery bypass graft surgery, congestive heart failure, and diabetes mellitus presented with 2 weeks of progressive shortness of breath. He denied fever, weight loss, and had normal urinary output. On examination, he was obese (BMI 38 kg/m2), pulse 95/min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, and afebrile. Cardiovascular findings included a midline sternotomy scar, displaced apex beat, and diminished heart sounds without murmurs; fine crepitations were heard at both lung bases and there was no organomegaly. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 13 g/dL, leukocytes 7.4×10^9/L, platelets 159×10^9/L, creatinine 90 μmol/L, ALT 15 IU/L, and urinalysis revealed microscopic hematuria. Chest X-ray demonstrated cardiomegaly, and ECG showed sinus rhythm with nonspecific T-wave inversion in the lateral leads. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed an ejection fraction of 40% and a large, highly mobile, “thumb-like” mass in the right atrium extending through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle each systole; tricuspid valve function was normal. Abdominal MRI demonstrated a heterogeneous lobulated 6.8×8.4×4.2 cm mass in the upper and mid pole of the right kidney with tumor thrombus extending from the right renal vein into the infrahepatic, intrahepatic, and suprahepatic inferior vena cava and into the right atrium.

A 72-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 1-year history of a right nasal lesion that he found cosmetically bothersome. He reported mild nasal obstruction, mild pain at the lesion site, and nasal congestion but denied ulceration, bleeding, or drainage. His medical history was notable for allergic rhinitis, macular degeneration treated with intravitreal ranibizumab, glaucoma, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. He took pitavastatin, losartan, amlodipine, omeprazole, naproxen, and ranibizumab. He had no tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drug use. 

Vital signs were normal. Examination revealed a single, well-circumscribed, flesh-colored, dry, mildly tender, crateriform lesion on the anterosuperior portion of the right anterior nasal septum. No ulceration, drainage, regional lymphadenopathy, or other similar lesions were noted; cranial nerve function was intact.

The lesion was excised under local anesthesia with a 0.6 × 0.3 cm specimen containing a centrally located 0.3 × 0.3 × 0.2 cm ovoid papule. The specimen was submitted for histopathological analysis.

A 15-year-old girl presented with a 2-year history of right shoulder pain and progressive swelling. The pain had gradually worsened over time despite trials of antiinflammatory medications and physical therapy. There was no personal or family history of rheumatologic disease or comorbid conditions, and she was not on chronic medications. On examination, the right shoulder showed diffuse enlargement, globally decreased range of motion—especially in elevation—and pain on passive mobilization. Plain radiographs of the shoulder were unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right shoulder demonstrated intense, diffuse synovial thickening localized to the subacromial bursa with grouped nodular images and abundant bursal fluid but no intra-articular involvement.

A 31-year-old male teacher of African origin presented with a four-year history of an intensely pruritic rash on the face, trunk, and limbs. The rash began as 2–3 macules and papules on the trunk and gradually progressed over months to involve the limbs, buttocks, face, and nearly the entire trunk. Lesions eventually ulcerated. From 2017 to 2020, he received multiple topical treatments (steroids and moisturizing creams) for presumed eczema without response. He denied prior similar illness, chronic diseases, exposures to chemicals or radiation, family history of atopy, alcohol or tobacco use, fevers, night sweats, weight loss, or arthralgia; he did report intermittent diarrhea.

On examination, he was afebrile with blood pressure 137/81 mmHg, pulse 87/min, respiratory rate 15/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air; ECOG performance status was 1. Skin exam showed multiple well- to ill-defined hyperpigmented erosive plaques, nodules, and tumors on the trunk, all limbs, and face, covering more than 95% of the body surface area, including non–sun-exposed sites. Lesions ranged from 2 cm to 6 cm; there was an 8×10 cm ulcer on the left knee and a 2×3 cm ulcer on the left elbow. There was no significant peripheral lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Neurologic, cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed WBC 8.67×10^9/L, hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL, hematocrit 26.4%, MCV 58.6 fL, neutrophils 6.39×10^3/µL, platelets 656×10^3/µL; ALT 47.5 IU/L; AST 21.8 IU/L; creatinine 84.2 µmol/L; HIV-1 serology negative. Chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasound were normal.

The initial differential diagnoses included atopic dermatitis, chronic eczema, and psoriasis.

An 18-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of a tender swelling over her left mid-arm. The lesion had gradually increased in size and measured 3 × 2 cm on examination. The overlying skin exhibited atrophic changes and focal hypopigmentation. On palpation, the mass was firm to hard, tender, mobile, and situated in the subcutaneous plane. Fine-needle aspiration cytology was performed. The smears showed a cell-rich aspirate composed predominantly of basaloid cells in tight clusters with scattered squamous cells and anucleate squames; numerous shadow (ghost) cells; plentiful multinucleated giant cells; and focal areas of calcification.

A 63-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of vague, colicky epigastric pain radiating to the interscapular region, associated with anorexia and malaise. The pain was relieved by changes in sitting position and worsened by eating. There was no history of alcohol use, abdominal trauma, or pancreatitis. Routine laboratory studies showed thrombocytosis (platelet count >1 000 000/µL) and elevated blood urea. Aspirin (80 mg daily) was initiated for presumed essential thrombocytosis. 

An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a cystic lesion in the head of the pancreas. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a well-circumscribed, 11.8 cm cystic mass in the pancreatic head, without invasion of adjacent organs or lymphadenopathy. The serum CA 19-9 level was within the normal range. 

On physical examination, vital signs were normal. The abdomen was soft and non-distended, with mild epigastric tenderness on deep palpation but no rebound or rigidity. There were no signs of portal hypertension or history of prior abdominal surgery.

A 34-year-old man with no systemic disease presented with a 3-month history of intermittent left otorrhea, described as yellowish, pus-like discharge. He also reported mild tinnitus, hearing loss, and occasional headache but denied fever, dizziness, or ear pain. An initial diagnosis of chronic otitis media was made, and topical antibiotic eardrops were prescribed without improvement.

Three months later, he experienced acute-onset vertigo and unsteady gait that lasted several hours and was nonpositional. On presentation to the emergency department, extraocular movements were normal but horizontal nystagmus was noted. Otoscopic examination revealed redness and scaling of the left external auditory canal, a thickened tympanic membrane coated with brownish discharge, and turbid middle-ear effusion. Pure-tone audiometry showed a mixed hearing loss with an air–bone gap of 20–30 dB.

A contrast-enhanced temporal CT scan demonstrated a well-defined, 5.6-cm mass in the left middle cranial fossa with both enhancing solid components and nonenhancing cystic areas, associated with bony erosion of the adjacent skull base and continuity with the middle-ear space. A subsequent gadolinium-enhanced brain MRI showed an extra-axial lesion over the left middle cranial fossa with mixed signal intensity on T2-weighted and FLAIR images, multiloculated cystic components, and rim enhancement. The lesion appeared to originate from the skull base, and the differential diagnosis included aneurysmal bone cyst with internal hemorrhage, neurogenic tumor, and pigmented villonodular synovitis.

A 33-year-old man was referred after a cystic mass near his pancreas was found during a routine health examination 4 days earlier. He had no abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, weight loss, or changes in bowel habits. His medical history was unremarkable, and he was taking no medications.

On examination, his vital signs were within normal limits, and the abdominal examination revealed no tenderness, masses, or organomegaly.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, metabolic panel, liver function tests, and serum tumor markers, were all within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed a 5.6 × 4.5 cm well-circumscribed, low-density lesion with internal calcifications at the interface between the tail of the pancreas and an adjacent intestinal loop. The cystic lesion had a CT attenuation of approximately 13 HU, and the cyst wall showed partial enhancement (suggestive of a calcified cystic mass in the left upper quadrant, abutting but not invading pancreatic tissue).

A 44-year-old man with a history of alcohol abuse presented with 2 days of right upper-quadrant abdominal pain and vomiting and had one episode of hematemesis before arrival. He was pale, diaphoretic, hypotensive and confused. Initial hemoglobin was 10.1 g/dL, falling to 5.3 g/dL. An arterial blood gas showed pH 7.03 and lactate 11 mmol/L. A massive transfusion protocol was initiated along with vasopressors. Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma (FAST) was positive for fluid in the right upper quadrant. Computed tomography angiography of the chest, abdomen and pelvis revealed hemoperitoneum anterior to the left lobe of the liver, a 5.2 × 8.1 cm para-aortic and aortocaval mass with peripheral enhancement suggestive of neoplastic adenopathy, and a complex septated lesion in the right scrotum. The patient underwent emergency exploratory laparotomy, which showed active bleeding from two lesions in the left lateral liver segment; hemostasis was achieved, and an incisional biopsy was performed. On postoperative day 1, scrotal ultrasound confirmed a 6 cm complex cystic mass in the right testis. Laboratory studies showed a β-hCG of 130,985 mIU/mL, lactate dehydrogenase of 581 U/L and α-fetoprotein of 2 ng/mL.

A 38-year-old Mediterranean man presented with a 7-month history of recurrent headaches, left eye pain, blurred vision, and left-sided facial weakness. Over this period he lost 15 kg and experienced recurrent strokes characterized by right-sided weakness, dysarthria, and confusion.

On examination, he had left eye exophthalmos and a mass occupying the left nasal cavity. Neurologic findings included horizontal nystagmus on rightward gaze, an absent gag reflex, right-sided extremity weakness with hypertonia, and a positive Babinski sign.

High-resolution CT of the head demonstrated bilateral basal ganglia hypodense areas suggestive of chronic ischemia and a separate hypodense region in the left basal ganglia indicative of subacute ischemia. A coronal CT scan revealed an iso-dense expansile soft tissue lesion with internal calcifications centered in the anterior left ethmoid sinus, protruding into the left orbital apex, displacing the medial rectus muscle laterally, and obliterating the left frontal sinus.

Brain MRI with FLAIR sequence showed an abnormal hyperintense signal in the left cavernous sinus and a mass in the left ethmoid sinus extending toward the cavernous sinus.

An extensive vasculitis work-up was inconclusive.

An 81-year-old Caucasian woman was hospitalized for treatment of a deep vein thrombosis of the right leg.  
Abdominal CT showed a 7.5 × 6 × 6 cm inhomogeneous mass in the right pelvis, thought to arise from the right ovary, lying on the external iliac artery and infiltrating adjacent pelvic wall musculature; there was no ascites or distant metastasis.  
Her medical history included hypertension, Hashimoto thyroiditis, and pernicious anemia; she had no prior surgeries and no family history of malignancy. She denied pain or vaginal bleeding.  
On examination her vital signs were normal; abdominal and gynecologic examinations were unremarkable except for a palpable right pelvic mass.  
Transvaginal ultrasound confirmed an irregular right adnexal mass measuring 10 × 6 × 8 cm; endometrial and cervical imaging were normal.  
Serum CA 125 was elevated at 133 U/mL (normal < 35 U/mL).  
Because the pattern of spread was atypical for ovarian carcinoma, a CT-guided biopsy of the adnexal mass was performed and showed a solid neoplasm infiltrating ovarian stroma and resembling urothelial carcinoma.  
Immunohistochemical studies revealed CK7 positive, CK5 positive, CK20 negative, estrogen receptors negative, and p63 positive.  
Diagnostic cystoscopy and pyelography excluded a primary urinary tract neoplasm, and an exploratory laparotomy was planned.

A 75-year-old man presented with a few days of intermittent gross hematuria. He denied systemic symptoms. He quit smoking 21 years ago and has used smokeless tobacco for 16 years. Cystoscopy at the referring institution revealed a bladder tumor. Biopsy showed high-grade urothelial carcinoma with >80% clear cell differentiation, severe necrosis, and invasion into the muscularis propria. Renal ultrasound demonstrated a large bladder mass without extravesical disease and mild right hydronephrosis. Serum creatinine was 1.6 mg/dL; chemotherapy was deferred, and the patient underwent radical cystoprostatectomy. 

Gross examination revealed a 5.5 × 5.0 × 2.3 cm fungated hemorrhagic mass arising from the right lateral wall, nearly obliterating the right ureteral orifice, and invading through the detrusor into perivesical fat. 

Microscopically, the tumor consisted of sheets and nodules of rounded to polygonal malignant cells with enlarged nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant clear cytoplasm (>90% clear cell differentiation). No glandular differentiation or hobnail cells were seen. The tumor invaded through the full thickness of the muscularis propria into perivesical adipose tissue, with extensive necrosis, acute inflammation, lymphovascular invasion, and focal carcinoma in situ in adjacent urothelium.

A 7-year-old previously healthy boy presented with a 1-day history of “poking” epigastric pain that radiated in a band to his right upper quadrant and worsened with movement. He had one episode of non-bloody emesis and had experienced poor appetite, decreased energy for 1 week, and recent dyspnea on exertion. On arrival, his heart rate was 144 bpm. Examination revealed right-sided abdominal tenderness with guarding. Initial laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 15.1×10^9/L with a left shift, mild hypochloremia, and hypocalcemia. An abdominal ultrasound was normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a partially visualized, large, heterogeneously enhancing mass centered in the middle mediastinum, concerning for malignancy. Dedicated chest CT confirmed a middle mediastinal origin of the mass, which infiltrated the right lung parenchyma, encased the right pulmonary and hilar vessels, suprahepatic IVC, esophagus, and encased the trachea with occlusion of the bronchus intermedius. Given its CT appearance and location, initial differential diagnoses included NUT midline carcinoma, lymphoma, metastatic disease, and fibrosing mediastinitis. Upon transfer for further evaluation, additional laboratory tests showed an alpha-fetoprotein level of 167 ng/mL (normal <8.4), lactate dehydrogenase of 665 U/L, and a minimally elevated β-hCG.

A 67-year-old right-hand-dominant man presented with a 3-year history of a swelling on the volar aspect of the right middle fingertip without antecedent trauma. Over the preceding 3–4 months the mass had enlarged slowly, become tender, and had bled intermittently from superficial abrasion. His medical history included Grave’s disease, atrial fibrillation, and a perforated gastric ulcer. Examination revealed a 2.0 × 1.5 cm mass at the distal pulp and hyponychium of the right middle finger, with mild tenderness and a central area of superficial ulceration. The digit was neurovascularly intact, had normal range of motion, and showed no erythema, inflammation, or discoloration. The working differential diagnosis following initial consultation included glomus tumour, ganglion cyst, and haemangioma, and the patient was scheduled for excisional biopsy without prior imaging.

A 56-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a recurrent skin lesion on the dorsum of his right thumb. He reported a four-year history of a lesion at that site, for which a partial amputation of the thumb was performed in December 2016. In August 2017, the lesion reappeared at the distal aspect of the thumb stump. He had no significant medical history and took no medications. On examination, there was a 1.8 × 1.3 cm well-circumscribed, firm, non-tender, indurated lesion over the dorsum of the right thumb stump that was mobile over the deep structures. No palpable lymphadenopathy was noted. A metastatic workup—including CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and a bone scan—revealed an enlarged ipsilateral axillary lymph node presumed to represent metastatic disease. The patient was scheduled for a wide local excision with amputation at the level of the distal interphalangeal joint and fine-needle aspiration of the axillary node.

A 45-year-old man presented with an 8-month history of thoracic back pain. His medical history was unremarkable. On examination, his neurological status was normal. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging of the thoracic spine revealed a dumbbell-shaped enhancing lesion spanning the T4–T6 vertebral levels, with compression of the spinal cord. The mass extended through the right T4–T5 neural foramen into the paraspinal muscles. On MRI, the lesion demonstrated homogeneous signal intensity and mild enhancement after gadolinium administration.

An 84-year-old woman presented with an expanding, pigmented lesion in the left nasal canthus that had grown rapidly over 5 months. She first noted the lesion incidentally during an optometry exam 14 months earlier, with no change until the recent size increase. She denied vision loss, eye pain, redness, foreign body sensation, discharge, or bleeding. Ocular history was notable only for bilateral cataract surgery 13 years prior, with no history of trauma, eye disease, malignancy, chemotherapy, or toxic exposures. Her medical history included well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and cardiac arrhythmia; family history was noncontributory. Visual acuity was 6/6 in the right eye and 6/6-2 in the left; intraocular pressures were 8 mm Hg in each eye. On anterior segment examination, there was a raised, homogeneous, pigmented region overlying the left caruncle and involving the plica semilunaris, without scleral extension. There were no hairs, feeder vessels, cysts, or satellite lesions, and the surrounding tissue appeared healthy. Dilated fundus examination was unremarkable bilaterally.

A 66-year-old woman presented for evaluation of a left renal mass found on ultrasound two months earlier. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a 3.3-cm heterogeneously enhancing exophytic mass arising from the left renal interpole, suspicious for renal cell carcinoma. Incidentally, CT revealed a 4.5-cm ill-defined right retroperitoneal mass inseparable from the right adrenal gland, with mild enhancement of multiple soft-tissue nodules and possible infiltration of adjacent retroperitoneal fat. The central soft-tissue component measured 4.1 × 3.0 × 4.5 cm; including the infiltrative portions, the lesion extended to approximately 10 cm. The mass had lobulated lateral margins, ill-defined medial and anterior borders, and displaced the inferior vena cava anteriorly. The left adrenal gland appeared normal. The patient reported right flank pain and had tenderness on examination. Her history included hypothyroidism and hyperlipidemia managed medically. Vital signs were within normal limits.

A 57-year-old right-handed woman presented with 5 months of left wrist pain that worsened with ulnar deviation, accompanied by swelling and erythematous change. She denied trauma, sports activities, and had no other joint symptoms or significant medical history.  
On examination, there was swelling and tenderness over the left distal radioulnar joint and the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon insertion near the pisiform. Active left wrist range of motion was 50° extension, 50° flexion, 5° ulnar deviation, and 20° radial deviation (right wrist: 70° extension, 80° flexion, 20° ulnar, 30° radial). Pain was elicited with resisted ulnar deviation and wrist flexion and with passive wrist extension and radial deviation. Aching pain was noted around the distal radioulnar joint during active wrist flexion and ulnar deviation. Neurovascular testing, including electromyography, nerve conduction studies, and Tinel’s sign at Guyon’s canal, was normal.  
Plain radiographs showed diffuse soft-tissue swelling and widening of the pisotriquetral joint without calcified bodies. MRI revealed multiple masses around the pisiform and triquetral bones with perilesional soft-tissue swelling.

A 52-year-old man presented with a painful lump in his left lateral abdominal wall. He reported that a small nodule had appeared about one year earlier and had gradually increased in size. He denied any history of abdominal trauma or other medical problems. On palpation, there was a 4×5 cm nodular mass protruding through the left upper lateral abdominal wall; it was firm, tender, and not fixed to the overlying skin. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 32×45 mm cystic lesion located between the external and internal oblique muscles. Abdominal MRI revealed a well-circumscribed 4×5 cm cystic mass in the abdominal wall that was hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and fat-suppressed sequences suggested cystic degeneration. Clinical appearance and radiologic findings were nonspecific. A chronic haematoma and a cystic tumour of the abdominal wall were considered in the differential diagnosis.

A 54-year-old woman with a history of severe obesity, myocardial infarction, hypertension, and prior uterine fibroid resection presented with progressive epigastric and right subcostal pain for 1 year. She denied tobacco or alcohol use. On examination, vital signs were normal; there was localized tenderness on peri-umbilical palpation without other abnormalities. Laboratory studies showed no infectious syndrome; the electrocardiogram was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed gallstones. A routine chest radiograph demonstrated an opacity in the right costophrenic angle. 

A subsequent thoraco-abdominopelvic CT scan showed a heterogeneous right pleural-based mass containing both fatty and soft-tissue components, without calcification and without apparent invasion of adjacent structures or the chest wall. Chest MRI confirmed an antero-inferior right subpleural heterogeneous mass with fat and tissue elements, with no signs of adjacent-organ or chest-wall invasion, and was reported as suggestive of liposarcoma. An 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET scan showed low metabolic activity in the lesion (SUV 1.8) and no other sites of abnormal uptake.

A 41‐year‐old man presented with a mass in his right knee that had slowly enlarged over the past 15 years. He reported mild tenderness but no mechanical locking or instability. On examination there was a 2‐cm, solid, glossy, mobile swelling at the lateral upper pole of the patella, mildly tender to palpation. Routine radiographs of the knee were negative. MRI demonstrated a well‐demarcated, oval lesion measuring 1.5 cm in diameter in the soft tissues abutting the lateral upper pole of the patella. The lesion was isointense to muscle on T1‐weighted and STIR T1 sequences, slightly hyperintense on T2‐weighted and STIR T2 images, and its edge was heterogeneously enhanced on contrast‐enhanced T1‐weighted images. MRI interpretation was that the lesion represented a loose body or other benign process, and hemangioma was not excluded.

A 20-year-old woman presented with sudden, severe, non-colicky upper abdominal pain. She had no history of trauma or prior similar episodes; appetite and bowel habits were normal. On examination, she was in painful distress but hemodynamically stable; there was a smooth, firm, tender epigastric mass extending from the rib cage to the umbilicus. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a multiloculated cyst in the upper abdomen extending over the pancreas and suggested a pancreatic pseudocyst. Her pain improved with analgesics. One week later, contrast-enhanced CT showed a multiseptated cystic retroperitoneal mass with homogeneous fluid located below the liver, extending over the pancreas and the medial right and left kidneys, pushing the stomach superiorly and abutting the anterior abdominal wall; there was no evidence of acute hemorrhage. MRI demonstrated a multicystic, uniformly dense mass with long signal intensity extending just below the anterior abdominal wall, separate from major organs, and without features of hemorrhage.

A 74-year-old woman presented with a 4-year history of a gradually enlarging vulvar lump on the mons pubis. The lesion measured 15 cm in diameter, was ulcerated, painful, and pink in color. Her medical history was notable only for a 12-year history of hypertension; she had no family history of malignancy, no prior surgeries, and no known allergies. On examination, the remainder of the physical exam was unremarkable and there was no lymphadenopathy. Pelvic ultrasound was within normal limits. A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed a 2 × 3 cm cystic lesion at the umbilicus, a hypodense lesion in segment IV of the liver, collapse of the T9 vertebral body with slight retraction of its posterior edges, and degeneration with sclerosis of the pubic symphysis; there was no lymphadenopathy or evidence of distant metastasis.

A 20-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 2-month history of a visible mass in the left parotid region. She had no significant past medical or surgical history. Physical examination revealed a 3-cm, oval, semi–tense-elastic, painless mass adherent to deep planes, covered by intact skin, without facial nerve dysfunction. Routine blood tests, including complete blood count and liver and kidney panels, were normal. Neck ultrasound demonstrated a large, solid nodular lesion with regular margins and internal areas of colliquation at the lower pole of the left parotid gland, along with reactive bilateral cervical lymph nodes. MRI of the neck revealed an oval-shaped lesion with lobulated margins, intermediate to low intensity on T1-weighted images, high intensity on T2-weighted and STIR sequences, and marked homogeneous enhancement after contrast administration. Fine-needle aspiration cytology was not performed. On the basis of location, epidemiology, and imaging characteristics, the leading preoperative diagnosis was pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland.

A 79‐year‐old woman was admitted after a fall at home. The admitting doctor noted a large ulcer on her lower back measuring approximately 20 × 32 cm. The patient had first seen her general practitioner 6 months earlier, who deemed the lesion benign. It progressed gradually as she delayed care. She was otherwise healthy, with no significant medical history or medications. 

On examination, the differential diagnoses included pyoderma gangrenosum, cutaneous vasculitis, infection, and malignancy. A 4-mm punch biopsy from the edge of the lesion was reported as an invasive basal cell carcinoma. Routine blood tests and a vasculitis screen were unremarkable, and wound swabs did not show any significant growth. Clinicopathological correlation was not consistent with a morphoeic basal cell carcinoma, so a repeat incisional biopsy was performed. This showed a large, endophytic tumour displaying both basaloid and squamoid areas. This unusual finding could represent either a ‘collision’ tumour or a BCC with some squamous differentiation, as in BsC.

A 30-year-old man presented with a six-month history of progressive neck swelling and sore throat. He had no significant past medical history. On examination, there was a 4-cm, hard mass in the right anterior neck. Thyroid function tests (T4, free T3, TSH) and other laboratory studies were within normal limits.  
   
Contrast-enhanced CT showed a heterogeneous mass at the level of the hyoid bone (35 × 47 × 38 mm) that expanded the cortical bone of the hyoid and contained a central solid component with calcification as well as a marginal cystic component; left submental lymphadenopathy was also noted. The thyroid gland appeared normal in its usual paratracheal position.  
   
MRI demonstrated that the solid portion of the lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images, slightly hypointense on T2-weighted images, and showed marked enhancement on contrast-enhanced fat-suppressed T1-weighted images; the cystic areas were T1 hypointense and T2 hyperintense.  
   
Fine-needle aspiration of the mass revealed papillary carcinoma.

A 42-year-old white woman with a history of neurofibromatosis type 1 diagnosed in 1989 presented for elective open myomectomy due to symptomatic uterine fibroid and chronic anemia. Despite iron and folic acid supplementation, her hemoglobin remained as low as 6.5 g/dL, and she received 2 units of red cells and 1 unit of plasma the evening before surgery, raising her hemoglobin to 8.9 g/dL. She had no allergies, took no regular medications, was a non-smoker, and had undergone prior surgeries under general anesthesia without complications. Preoperative examination was unremarkable: blood pressure 140/70 mmHg, heart rate 102 bpm, and airway assessment Mallampati I with good cervical mobility.

On arrival in the operating room, standard monitors and two large-bore IV lines were placed. Her blood pressure was 180/100 mmHg, heart rate 110 bpm, and SpO₂ 99%. She received midazolam 2 mg and fentanyl 100 μg without change in blood pressure. An arterial line was placed. Induction with fentanyl 100 μg, etomidate 20 mg, and rocuronium 50 mg was administered. During bag-mask ventilation, her blood pressure rose to 220/120 mmHg and heart rate to 135 bpm. To exclude inadequate anesthesia, propofol boluses totaling 150 mg were given, and a glyceryl trinitrate infusion was started. Given persistent hypertension and tachycardia, the surgical procedure was postponed. A laryngeal mask airway was placed, and anesthesia was maintained with sevoflurane (MAC 0.8), nitrous oxide, and oxygen. After neuromuscular reversal with sugammadex, removal of the airway device again precipitated a blood pressure rise to 220/110 mmHg, which was controlled with increased nitroglycerin. She was extubated with blood pressure 150/80 mmHg and heart rate 80 bpm, and postoperative blood pressures remained elevated. The surgery was cancelled for further evaluation.

A 54-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a slowly enlarging mass in her right thigh. She first noted the lesion 34 years earlier. Her medical history was significant for chronic renal failure on hemodialysis for 2 years. 

On examination, there was a non-tender, firm, rubbery, mobile, melon-sized mass on the anterior distal thigh. Routine radiographs showed a large soft-tissue mass with irregular calcifications in the distal femoral region. 

Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-defined 17 × 11 × 9 cm mass beneath the quadriceps muscle. On T1-weighted images, the lesion had irregular areas of low signal intensity; on T2-weighted images, it was heterogeneously hyperintense and hypointense. The adjacent femoral cortex and marrow appeared normal.

The tumor was excised. Grossly, it was a well-circumscribed, lobulated, firm mass with a yellowish-white fibrous-to-myxoid cut surface and no hemorrhage or necrosis. 

Microscopically, the lesion showed a sharp border, nodular architecture with intervening hypocellular collagenous stroma, and a biphasic pattern of fibrous and myxoid areas. The cells were small, bland, spindle-shaped fibroblasts with minimal pleomorphism, low to moderate cellularity, and a swirling, whorled growth pattern. The background matrix ranged from fibromyxoid to densely fibrous.

Immunohistochemical studies revealed diffuse strong positivity for vimentin and negativity for cytokeratin, smooth muscle actin, S-100 protein, and neuron-specific enolase.

A 31-year-old Arabian man, with a history of acute biphenotypic leukemia treated with chemoradiation followed by allogeneic stem cell transplant 4 years earlier, was referred for evaluation of a 1-month history of sore throat that did not respond to two courses of oral antibiotics. He denied fever, chills, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. His medical history also included controlled essential hypertension, treated hepatitis B infection, and prior mandibular mucormycosis during transplant.

On oropharyngeal examination, there was a 3×2 cm granular mass arising from the right lateral pharyngeal wall, reaching the midline and pushing the uvula contralaterally; the contralateral tonsil appeared normal. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy and the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed normal hemoglobin, platelet, and white-cell counts; normal coagulation profile, liver enzymes, and electrolytes. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck showed a homogeneous, nonenhancing enlargement of the right tonsillar region measuring 2.7×2.3 cm, without lymphadenopathy or other abnormalities.

A 58-year-old man was referred for evaluation of bilateral sudden hearing loss unresponsive to initial treatment with antibiotics, pseudoephedrine, and nasal corticosteroids. His past medical history was notable for asthma, sicca symptoms, IgG4‐related autoimmune pancreatitis, and features of Mikulicz's disease. He had no prior hearing loss and no family history of hearing impairment. 

On first audiometry, the right ear was deaf and the left ear showed severe sensorineural hearing loss (pure-tone averages, 69/107 dB). Physical examination of the upper respiratory tract and otomicroscopy were normal. Methylprednisolone (64 mg daily) was initiated. 

One week later, his hearing declined to bilateral deafness (pure-tone averages, 120/103 dB). On examination, vesicular blisters were noted on the lips, tongue, and oral mucosa. The head‐thrust test was positive to the left, and spontaneous nystagmus beat to the right. Ramsay–Hunt syndrome was suspected; valaciclovir and hyperbaric oxygen therapy were added, and methylprednisolone was continued (32 mg daily). 

Within another week, he developed left facial nerve palsy and vertigo and was admitted; methylprednisolone was increased to 64 mg daily. Brain MRI demonstrated T2 hyperintense lesions adjacent to the genu of the corpus callosum, fornix, and temporal lobe on the left, as well as a similar lesion in the right cerebellum. Contrast enhancement involved the left facial (VII) and vestibulocochlear (VIII) nerves and the right VII–VIII nerves at the porus acusticus.

Neurology and rheumatology consultation raised suspicion for CNS involvement of IgG4‐related disease after serum IgG4 was found to be elevated at 2.71 g/L (reference, 0.08–1.4 g/L). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed a leukocyte count of 22 × 10^6/L (reference, 0–5 × 10^6/L) and total IgG of 55 mg/L (reference, 13–36 mg/L). Pulse methylprednisolone (1 g daily) was administered without improvement. A repeat MRI one week later showed progression of the intracranial lesions.

A 28-year-old woman presented with several weeks of progressive abdominal pain, severe anorexia, and recurrent vomiting, occasionally bloody. She had no significant past medical history or systemic symptoms. Physical examination was unremarkable. Upper endoscopy revealed a 5 cm × 6 cm submucosal mass with central umbilication in the gastric antrum causing gastric outlet obstruction. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed a hypodense mass along the anterior wall of the antrum with pyloric stenosis, luminal obstruction, and dilation of the gastric body and fundus.

A 32-year-old Asian woman was referred for evaluation of an incidental chest radiographic abnormality. A well-defined mass at the cardiac apex increased in diameter from 34 mm to 64 mm over one year. The patient was asymptomatic, a non-smoker, and had a history of hyperthyroidism treated with thiamazole but was medication-free at presentation. She had no history of pregnancy or childbirth, no relevant family history, and no occupational exposures. Vital signs, physical examination, and neurologic examination were unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including blood cell counts, liver and renal function tests, urinalysis, and serology, were within normal limits. Chest CT revealed a pear-shaped, homogeneous mass measuring 80 mm between the pericardium and left lung, with attenuation values of 23–32 HU; it was expansile and showed no invasion of adjacent structures. MRI demonstrated a uniformly low signal on T1-weighted images and a low, heterogeneous signal on T2-weighted fat-saturation images, with no fat intensity within the lesion. Based on these findings, a benign anterior mediastinal tumor or thymoma was suspected.

A 58-year-old man presented with a 45-year history of recurrent, asymptomatic red papules on his arms, thighs, and trunk. Each crop of lesions healed spontaneously in 2 to 4 weeks, leaving minimal scarring. He denied weight loss, night sweats, or fevers. On examination, there were scattered erythematous to violaceous edematous papules, some with an overlying collarette of scale and crust, on the dorsal hands, arms, thighs, and trunk. There was no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. 

A punch biopsy showed a wedge-shaped perivascular and interstitial infiltrate extending from the papillary dermis to the deep reticular dermis, composed primarily of small and medium-sized lymphocytes with occasional scattered large lymphocytes and focal small- and large-vessel destruction. Immunohistochemical studies revealed CD3+ lymphocytes from the epidermis to the deep dermis, loss of CD7 expression, a 10:1 CD4-to-CD8 ratio, and 75% CD30+ lymphocytes. T-cell receptor β gene rearrangement was positive. Staining for Epstein–Barr virus and anaplastic lymphoma kinase 1 was negative.

A 30-year-old African woman presented with a 2-year history of progressive abdominal distension associated with early satiety, easy fatigability on walking, increased urinary frequency, and nonspecific lower abdominal pain. She also reported difficulty conceiving and a history of recurrent abortions. Menarche was at age 14, cycles were every 28 days with 5–6 days of heavy, painful menstruation requiring four fully soaked pads per day. She denied contraceptive use or prior cervical cancer screening. Her medical, surgical, and family histories were unremarkable. On examination, her vital signs were normal. The abdomen was grossly distended, moving with respiration, with a fundal height of 30/37 weeks; suprapubic scar marks were noted. Pelvic examination revealed right adnexal tenderness; the speculum examination was normal. A pregnancy test was negative. Laboratory studies, including CBC, electrolytes, liver function tests, hepatitis serologies, urinalysis, and stool studies, were within normal limits. Chest radiography was normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed splenomegaly. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 25.8 × 25.9 × 14.3 cm cystic mass with enhancing solid components and thickened septa, displacing intraperitoneal organs, with the uterus displaced to the left and bladder compressed; the impression was a right adnexal complex cystic mass.

An 80-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of a slightly painful swelling on the left side of his face. His medical history was notable only for type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with oral agents. He denied any history of trauma. On examination, there was facial asymmetry due to a firm, nonfluctuant swelling of the left mandible; the overlying skin and gingival mucosa appeared normal and there was buccal and lingual cortical bulging. The patient had no trismus or sensory deficits. Laboratory studies, including white blood count with differential, platelet count, and hemoglobin level, were within normal limits. Panoramic radiograph revealed a unilocular, radiolucent lesion in the body of the left mandible from tooth 35 to 33, causing anterior displacement of tooth 34. Three-dimensional CT confirmed a unilocular, expansile, radiolucent lesion in the same region with thinning of both cortical plates and anterior displacement of tooth 34.

A 45-year-old Japanese woman was evaluated preoperatively for cochlear implant surgery. During COVID-19 screening, a CT scan of the chest and upper abdomen incidentally revealed a left upper abdominal mass. She denied abdominal pain, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. Her medical history was notable for bilateral sensorineural hearing impairment, pulmonary artery stenosis, type 1 diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, and short stature (height, 142 cm); her mother had a similar history of hearing impairment and type 1 diabetes. She had no known adrenal disease.

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits, and the abdomen was soft and nontender without palpable masses. Laboratory studies showed mild hyperglycemia, an elevated HbA1c level, and an increased dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate concentration; other routine blood tests were unremarkable.

A noncontrast CT scan of the abdomen demonstrated a 7-cm, well-circumscribed mass in the left adrenal region that was isodense to muscle with a small central hypodense area and no calcifications. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen (early arterial, late arterial, and 5-minute secretory phases) showed inhomogeneous enhancement: the dorsal portion of the lesion reached peak enhancement in the late arterial phase and subsequently washed out, whereas the ventral portion enhanced progressively. The absolute enhancement washout at the secretory phase was 55%. On MRI, the lesion was almost isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images with lower signal in the dorsal region than the ventral region and a central area of high signal intensity, and demonstrated restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted images with a lower ADC value dorsally. A capsular structure was seen on T2-weighted imaging, and chemical shift imaging showed no fat within the lesion.

A 14-year-old girl presented with intermittent right flank pain, recently worsened and accompanied by fever. Examination revealed right lumbar tenderness and guarding; temperature was 40°C. Laboratory testing was consistent with a urinary tract infection, and intravenous ceftriaxone was initiated.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 173 × 67 × 59 mm well-defined, lobulated, hypodense mass in the right retroperitoneum with delayed, low-level enhancement. MRI showed heterogeneous high signal on T2-weighted images, iso- to hypointense signal on T1-weighted images, and delayed heterogeneous contrast enhancement with septations and necrotic areas. The lesion abutted the abdominal aorta, inferior vena cava, and right renal pedicle, extended toward the liver and right diaphragmatic crus, and compressed the right kidney and ureter, resulting in ureterohydronephrosis and cortical thinning. The adrenal glands appeared normal.

Obstructive pyelonephritis from extrinsic compression by a retroperitoneal mass was suspected. Differential diagnoses included neuroblastoma, ganglioneuroblastoma, germinal tumor, and paraganglioma. Alpha-fetoprotein and methoxylated catecholamine–derivative levels were normal.

A 58-year-old African American man with a 15–pack-year smoking history and stage IIC (cT1cN0M0) high-risk prostate adenocarcinoma treated with 6 months of androgen-deprivation therapy and ongoing intensity-modulated radiotherapy presented with a 2-week history of a rapidly enlarging, painful left groin nodule. Four weeks after initiating radiotherapy (41.4 Gy delivered of a planned 77.4 Gy), he noted a tender, erythematous, 3-cm nodule with central erosion and purulent, malodorous drainage. He denied constitutional symptoms.

A shave biopsy was performed. Histologic examination revealed clusters and sheets of small basaloid cells with fine stippled chromatin, minimal cytoplasm, nuclear molding, crush artifact, frequent mitoses and apoptotic figures, and areas of ulceration with necrosis. Immunohistochemical staining showed that tumor cells were negative for S100, MelanA, CD45, and CDX2; negative for prostate markers PSA, PSAP, PSMA, and NKX3.1; and positive for AE1/AE3 cytokeratins, synaptophysin, and thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1). CK20 staining was negative, and Ki-67 labeling approached 100%.
