A whole-body 18-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT scan demonstrated multiple FDG-avid sites, including an 8.2 × 5.2 cm soft-tissue mass in the left lung hilum, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, a 5.8 × 5.2 cm pancreatic body mass, multiple hepatic lesions, an intramuscular focus in the right posterior neck, and a subcutaneous focus in the left proximal thigh. Laboratory studies showed a normal PSA level (0.2 ng/mL), elevated lactate dehydrogenase (308 U/L; reference <240 U/L), leukopenia (0.5 k/µL; reference 1.0–4.8 k/µL), and monocytosis (0.7 k/µL; reference 0.3–0.5 k/µL).

A 53-year-old man presented with several weeks of frequent nocturnal urinary urgency but no hematuria. He was an occasional smoker and had no other significant medical history. An ultrasound of the urinary tract showed a thickened bladder wall, which was confirmed by computed tomography. A transurethral resection of the bladder lesion (and simultaneous prostate chips for presumed benign prostatic hyperplasia) was performed. 

Histologic examination of the bladder specimen revealed gray-brown tissue fragments with a spray-like discohesive infiltration of neoplastic cells forming small irregular nests and cords. There were erosions of the urothelium, widening of the suburothelial stroma with tumor cells penetrating the muscularis mucosae and splintering bladder wall muscle. On hematoxylin and eosin staining, the tumor cells exhibited eccentric nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm, occasional multinucleated “rhabdoid” cells, and intracytoplasmic vacuoles; lymphatic invasion was present. Small superficial areas of urothelial carcinoma in situ were also noted. Similar tumor infiltrates were identified in the prostatic tissue.

The patient underwent cystoprostatectomy with lymphadenectomy and construction of an ileal conduit. Pathology confirmed the same high-grade tumor in the bladder, isolated tumor cells in lymph nodes and at the margin, and an incidental low-grade prostatic adenocarcinoma.

Eight months later, he developed upper abdominal discomfort and vomiting of dark red-brown to greenish material. Gastroesophageal biopsies showed only erosive inflammation, and standard therapy was ineffective. A CT scan revealed acidic fluid in the abdominal cavity and ductal ectasia of the intrahepatic bile ducts but no mass in the pancreas or biliary tree. During endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography, the duodenum appeared distorted and bluish, and the papilla of Vater could not be identified. Four duodenal biopsy pieces were obtained.

Histologically, most biopsies showed normal villous architecture with mild inflammation. In one fragment, the submucosa contained sparse interspersed atypical cells with enlarged nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and partial plasmacytoid morphology presenting as single cells among normal tissue.

An 18-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of pain in the right mandibular body. On clinical examination, there was discrete facial asymmetry, bone expansion in the vestibular sulcus, tenderness on palpation, slight extrusion of tooth 46, and a positive pulp-vitality test. Panoramic and periapical radiographs revealed a well-circumscribed radiopaque mass approximately 1.5 mm in diameter, surrounded by a thin radiolucent halo, attached to the apex of the distal root of tooth 46. Initial management consisted of occlusal reduction, but the pain persisted after 30 days. The patient then underwent endodontic therapy of tooth 46 followed by surgical excision of the lesion with removal of the apical third of the root. The excised lesion was a firm, rounded mass measuring 1.3 mm. Histopathologic examination showed calcified tissue with superimposed lamellae and dentin united to cementoid material; centrally, a cementoid structure with blood vessels and basophilic lamellae; and peripherally, irregular fibrous tissue resembling cementoid tissue with vascularity.

A 39-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of persistent oral erosions and skin vesicles on his left forearm. He also reported voice changes, a foreign body sensation in his eyes, and unintentional weight loss. On examination, he had multiple erosions on the lips, hard palate, and buccal mucosa with hemorrhagic crusts on the lips and a single resolving vesicle on the left forearm. Nikolsky’s and bulla signs were negative, and there was no lymphadenopathy. A perilesional lip biopsy for direct immunofluorescence showed a fishnet pattern of IgG deposition in the lower third of the epidermis and coarse granular C3 deposition along the basal keratinocytes; IgA and IgM were negative. He was treated with prednisolone and azathioprine for one month without improvement. A chest radiograph revealed a right hilar mass. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax demonstrated a 6 × 3.8 cm, densely enhancing mass in the anterior and middle mediastinum.

A 46-year-old woman presented with 6 months of progressive abdominal distention, slight vaginal bleeding, poor appetite, early satiety, and constipation. She had no history of toxin exposure, chemotherapy, or radiotherapy. On examination, she was ECOG performance status 1, with a large, nonmobile abdominopelvic mass extending to the epigastrium; no lymphadenopathy was noted. Gynecologic examination revealed a collapsed cervix obscured by the mass; parametrium evaluation was limited. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL and normal serum CA-125, CA 19-9, and CEA levels. Transabdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a >30-cm solid mass with mixed echogenicity and cystic components occupying the abdomen and pelvis; there was no ascites. Contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 31.4-cm heterogeneous mass displacing the intestinal loops anteriorly and superiorly, surrounding and lifting the uterine body with a normal myometrium and homogeneous 6-mm endometrium; no metastatic lesions were seen. Chest CT was unremarkable. Colonoscopy showed extrinsic compression of the left colon; esophagogastroduodenoscopy was normal.

A 62-year-old Malay man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and ischemic heart disease presented with a 6-month history of a painless lump over his left upper back and unintentional weight loss. Preoperative magnetic resonance imaging of the trunk revealed an aggressive, infiltrative soft-tissue mass involving the spleen, left kidney, pancreas, descending colon, ribs, and paravertebral muscles. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis showed an ill-defined mass in the left retroperitoneum and paracolic gutter measuring 15.5 cm by 12.3 cm, extending beyond the posterior abdominal wall, with no evidence of distant metastases. Core-needle biopsy demonstrated a low- to intermediate-grade spindle cell tumour; the main diagnostic considerations were liposarcoma and desmoid tumour.

A 56-year-old man presented with left flank pain.  
Abdominal ultrasound revealed an 8 × 10 cm round mass in the mid–lower pole of the left kidney.  
Contrast-enhanced CT showed an 11 cm lower-pole renal mass with poor vascularization, a large central collapsed area, infiltration of perirenal fat and the perirenal fascia, and several small (<1 cm) mesenteric lymph nodes.  
In the arterial phase, the lesion exhibited rapid peripheral enhancement with wash-out.  
There was no evidence of involvement of the renal vascular pedicle or distant metastases on CT and bone scan.  
The patient had one episode of gross hematuria after imaging.  
To reduce intraoperative bleeding, he underwent preoperative left renal artery embolization.  
He then underwent an open radical nephrectomy with hilar and para-aortic lymph node dissection, removal of perirenal fat, ipsilateral adrenal gland, a segment of ureter, and a portion of psoas muscle.  
Postoperative recovery was uneventful.

A 35-year-old woman presented with one month of lower-abdominal pressure and a palpable midline mass. Physical examination revealed a large, soft, non-tender mass extending above the umbilicus. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 10.9×10^9/L and a red-cell count of 4.86×10^12/L; thyroid profile, FSH, LH, prolactin, testosterone, hCG, and CA125 levels were all within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a centrally cystic and necrotic pelvic mass measuring 10×13×16.5 cm, with a small amount of free fluid in the presacral space. At laparotomy, a 16 cm torted right ovarian mass was identified; a right salpingo-oophorectomy and omental biopsy were performed. Grossly, the ovary harbored a 15×10×5 cm lobulated mass with an intact capsule; the cut surface was pale yellow, nodular, solid, with scattered cystic areas and regions of hemorrhage up to 6 cm. Microscopically, the tumour showed multiple nodules with predominantly diffuse architecture, focal nested and corded areas, cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, largely uniform nuclei with occasional markedly atypical nuclei, multiple small foci of necrosis, and significant mitotic activity (several mitoses per high-power field); there was no lymphovascular invasion. Immunohistochemical staining revealed diffuse strong positivity for calretinin, CD99, and inhibin; focal positivity for cytokeratin 7; occasional MNF116 and EMA positivity; and negativity for WT1, PAX8, and GATA3. Reticulin staining showed fibers encircling nests of tumour cells and individual cells.

A 40-year-old man noted a right-sided neck swelling that had gradually enlarged over 5 years. He denied hoarseness, cough, or light-headedness but reported difficulty swallowing and limited neck movement. On examination, there was a firm, immobile, non-tender, nonpulsatile 10 × 10 cm mass on the right neck, extending from behind the sternocleidomastoid muscle across the midline and from the hyoid bone to the clavicle. No bruit was heard. The mass displaced the carotid artery; cranial nerves were intact. No other neck swellings or lymphadenopathy were palpable. Cervical X-ray showed no tracheal narrowing and slight mediastinal widening. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and chest revealed a well-defined hypodense mass in the right carotid space extending to the upper mediastinum, measuring up to 4.2 × 5.4 cm in cross-section and 17.8 cm craniocaudally, with poor contrast enhancement and a few mildly enhancing internal components. The lesion displaced and separated the carotid arteries and internal jugular vein and shifted the trachea and larynx leftward without erosion or infiltration. Thyroid scintigraphy showed normal thyroid uptake and a cold nodule in the right lobe; FNA of that nodule revealed a benign colloid nodule. FNA of the neck mass was inconclusive. Routine blood, renal, and thyroid tests were normal. The patient was then scheduled for surgical resection.

An 80-year-old man with hypertension and benign prostatic hypertrophy reported several weeks of mild, non-specific abdominal discomfort without weight loss, appetite change, melena, or hematochezia. He had no personal or family history of malignancy. On examination his abdomen was soft, non-tender, and without masses.

He underwent esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) for evaluation of symptoms, which revealed a 1.5 cm subepithelial lesion along the greater curvature approximately 10 cm from the pylorus. He was started on twice-daily proton-pump inhibitor therapy and referred for endoscopic ultrasound (EUS). Repeat EGD confirmed benign-appearing gastric antral mucosa with the same 1.5 cm lesion. EUS showed a 1.6 × 1.3 cm isoechoic, homogeneous mass with small calcifications in the subepithelial layers of the gastric antrum abutting the left hepatic lobe.

An EUS-guided fine-needle biopsy using a 25-gauge needle was performed. Histologic evaluation demonstrated neoplastic cells, and immunohistochemical staining of the specimen was diffusely positive for smooth muscle actin, vimentin, patchy muscle-specific actin, and focal synaptophysin. Stains were negative for pancytokeratin, desmin, CD117, DOG1, S100, CK7, CDX-2, Pax-8, HepPar1, and CD34. There were no cytologic atypia or mitotic figures.

A 37-year-old man with tuberous sclerosis complex and a history of childhood seizures underwent evaluation of his liver. He was asymptomatic without abdominal pain, gastrointestinal symptoms, jaundice, or palpable mass. Skin examination showed facial tubers and angiofibromas. Liver function tests, renal function, and electrolytes were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed hepatomegaly (cranio-caudal length 17 cm) and a large, ill-defined, nonencapsulated mass involving segments I, IVa, IVb, VII, and VIII, measuring 123 × 124 × 138.9 mm. On noncontrast images, the lesion contained both fat and soft-tissue components. During the arterial and venous phases, it showed heterogeneous enhancement with internal vascular structures arising from the hepatic artery and portal venous branches. The mass spared the biliary hilum. The portal and hepatic veins were patent, and the biliary ducts were not dilated.

A 70-year-old Caucasian man with no significant medical history presented with sudden-onset jaundice and weight loss. He had no prior history of jaundice or hepatitis, denied alcohol use, exposure to arsenic, vinyl chloride, Thorotrast, or hepatotoxic/herbal medications, and reported a maternal history of undiagnosed liver disease. On examination, he was jaundiced and alert with no encephalopathy or focal neurologic deficits; he had bilateral pedal edema and hepatomegaly without other stigmata of chronic liver disease. Laboratory studies at the referring hospital showed: total bilirubin 203 µmol/L (normal 5–17), AST 52 IU/L (normal 4–44), alkaline phosphatase 170 IU/L (normal 67–213), albumin 2.0 g/dL, PT 22 seconds, APTT 51 seconds, and platelets 113,000/mm^3. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated hepatomegaly with marked parenchymal alteration. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed gross replacement of the liver with tumor tissue suggestive of a primary liver process. On transfer to our center two days later, laboratory studies showed further deterioration: total bilirubin 401 µmol/L, AST 132 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 370 IU/L, and INR 2.1.

A 35-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a three-year history of a painful lump in the right breast, anatomically close to the nipple. The pain was severe, squeezing in nature, radiated into the nipple and deep into the breast, and was not relieved by regular analgesics. The lump had slowly increased in size since first noted, and the patient attributed its onset to a traumatic abrasion of the nipple incurred during breastfeeding. She is a mother of twins, takes combined oral contraceptives (ethinylestradiol and cyproterone acetate), and is a heavy smoker. 

On examination, there was a firm, tender, pink, cauliflower-shaped lump, approximately 1 cm in diameter, located just superior to the right nipple. The lesion appeared fixed to underlying tissues, with no nipple discharge, no translumination, and no regional lymphadenopathy. 

A screening mammogram showed bilateral dense breasts with minimal fatty replacement.

A 61-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of a bumpy, non-tender, mildly pruritic rash on her right lateral shoulder that had gradually increased in size. She denied trauma, insect bites, fever, night sweats, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. Her medical history was notable for biopsy-proven left-sided primary breast diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (germinal center–like; BCL2+, BCL6+, MYC+, Ki-67 90%) diagnosed 10 months earlier with negative staging PET and bone marrow biopsy. She achieved remission following rituximab-based immunochemotherapy; a PET scan 6 months after diagnosis showed no evidence of disease. Additional history included rheumatoid arthritis, hypertension, and a 40-pack-year smoking history (quit 15 years ago). On examination, there was a 2.5 × 1.9 cm pink to mildly erythematous, non-scaly, indurated plaque with asymmetric borders on the right lateral shoulder. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. Differential diagnoses included granuloma annulare, cutaneous lymphoma, and annular elastolytic granuloma. Two 4-mm punch biopsies were performed, and the patient was referred for a staging PET scan.

A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a 1-month history of increasing abdominal fullness and dyspnea. She had no significant past medical or surgical history. On examination, there was marked abdominal distension but no evidence of pleural effusion. 

Laboratory studies showed a serum CA-125 level of 220.5 U/mL (normal ≤35 U/mL) and normal levels of carcinoembryonic antigen and CA 19-9. 

Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed massive ascites and a heterogeneous mass measuring 15×14×13 cm in the lower abdomen. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a well-defined solid pelvic mass with cystic components arising from the left adnexa, measuring 15×14×13 cm, without evidence of lymphadenopathy or distant organ involvement. 

An ^18F-FDG PET/CT scan demonstrated low peripheral FDG uptake in the pelvic mass (SUVmax, 2.1) and no abnormal uptake elsewhere.

A 29-year-old man presented with a 40-day history of dry cough, afternoon fevers (up to 38.7 °C), shivering, and left flank pain. He had lost approximately 5 kg since symptom onset. His medical history was notable for acute lymphoblastic leukemia treated with allogeneic stem-cell transplantation in 2007; he had no prior renal disease. Initial laboratory studies revealed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein; urinalysis showed hematuria and proteinuria. He received successive courses of metronidazole, penicillin, and levofloxacin without clinical improvement, and his flank pain worsened.

On admission, his temperature was 37.7 °C, pulse 107 beats/min, and physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory results included a white-cell count of 12.3 × 10^9/L (63.7% neutrophils), hsCRP 125.2 mg/L, ferritin 1421 ng/mL, ESR 104 mm/h, serum creatinine 97 μmol/L, and BUN 9.04 mmol/L. Six subsequent routine urinary tests showed no evidence of infection. Doppler ultrasound of the left kidney demonstrated a 3.8 × 3.7 cm hypoechoic mass with distinct borders and dot or strip-like flow signals in the upper pole. Percutaneous biopsy showed only scant necrosis.

Despite intravenous imipenem (later changed to meropenem), indomethacin, and levofloxacin, fever persisted. A PET/CT scan revealed a 4.7 × 5.7 × 5.1 cm lesion in the upper pole of the left kidney (early SUVmax 14.5; delayed SUVmax 21.7) with thickening and occlusion of the upper ureter. On hospital day 20, laboratory studies showed WBC 14.22 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 8.45 × 10^9/L, ALT 152 U/L, hsCRP 146 mg/L, ESR 121 mm/h, creatinine 61 μmol/L, and BUN 5.78 mmol/L. Antibiotics were discontinued, and a renal malignancy was suspected.

A 43-year-old man presented with a 3-week history of right-sided headache and photophobia, unrelieved by paracetamol. He had no visual symptoms, nausea, or constitutional complaints. His medical history included untreated dyslipidemia and a 20-pack-year smoking history. Physical examination was unremarkable, and routine blood tests were normal. Noncontrast CT of the brain was normal, and MRI of the brain showed only mild paranasal sinus inflammation.  

Two months later, he developed rapidly progressive visual loss in the left eye and a temporal hemianopsia in the right eye. Confrontation testing confirmed a right temporal field defect, and there was a left relative afferent pupillary defect. Urgent sellar MRI revealed a 33.3 × 44.1 × 47.3 mm lobular, isointense, heterogeneous sellar and suprasellar mass extending along the third ventricular floor, abutting both internal carotid arteries without cavernous sinus invasion, with marked superior displacement of the optic chiasm. A 5 mm nodular enhancing lesion was also seen at the gray–white matter junction of the right cerebellar hemisphere. CT with contrast showed erosion of the sellar floor and dorsum, suggesting aggressive behavior.

A 12-year-old boy presented with a 2-month history of limp and bone pain localized to the left knee. He had no prior medical history and denied constitutional symptoms initially. On examination, left knee flexion was limited; there was no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, MCV 86 fL, WBC 10 000/µL, platelet count 275 000/µL, and an ESR of 35 mm/hr; other biochemical tests were unremarkable. Radiographs of the left knee revealed a lytic–sclerotic lesion in the proximal tibia; a bone scan demonstrated a single focus of increased uptake in that region. An open biopsy of the tibial lesion showed a mixture of Langerhans cells and eosinophils, and a diagnosis of eosinophilic granuloma was made. 

Over the next four months, without specific treatment, the patient developed weight loss, persistent limp, worsening knee pain, and on examination had generalized lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly. A thoracoabdominal CT scan revealed mediastinal, cervical, right axillary, and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, multiple pulmonary nodules, and hepatic and splenic involvement.

A 27-year-old woman without significant past medical history presented with a 1-year history of lower back pain. She denied hypertension, headaches, palpitations, diaphoresis, muscle weakness, bruising, menstrual irregularities, acne, or hirsutism. Physical examination was unremarkable, with a blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg and no orthostatic hypotension.  

An ultrasound performed for back pain revealed a 46 × 40 mm hypoechoic solid lesion in the left adrenal gland. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 50 × 42 mm well-circumscribed, homogeneous, solid mass in the left adrenal gland with a spontaneous density of 46 Hounsfield units and enhancement after contrast administration.  

Routine laboratory studies, including CBC, urinalysis, BUN, and creatinine, were within normal limits. Early follicular-phase hormonal studies at 8 am fasting showed total testosterone 0.9 ng/mL (0.1–0.8 ng/mL), DHEA-S 2735.3 ng/mL (201–4142), androstenedione 3.3 ng/mL (0.5–2.7), 17-hydroxyprogesterone 3.1 ng/mL (0.3–1.0), aldosterone 11 ng/dL (1.2–16), plasma renin activity (PRA) 0.2 ng/mL/h (0.5–2.6), sodium 141 mmol/L (135–145), potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5–5.3), plasma cortisol 16.2 μg/dL (5–25), and ACTH <10 pg/mL (<54). Late-night salivary cortisol was 9.3 nmol/L (0.7–5.0), urinary free cortisol 73.2 μg/24 h (<100), adrenaline 4.7 μg/24 h (0–6.2), noradrenaline 14.2 μg/24 h (11.3–74.3), and VMA 3.8 mg/24 h (<8.5). Repeat late-night salivary cortisol was 5.1 nmol/L (0.7–5.0). An overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test yielded a morning cortisol of 16.3 μg/dL (<1.8).  

Endogenous hypercortisolism of adrenal origin was confirmed, along with biochemical features of hyperandrogenism and an elevated aldosterone/PRA ratio.

A 37-year-old woman, with a 10–pack-year smoking history and no other comorbidities, noted dull pain and occasional lameness in her right thigh for 10 years. Five years after symptom onset, radiographs showed a 6-cm, septated, cystic-appearing lytic lesion of the mid-diaphysis of the right femur; the cortex was thinned but intact, with no periosteal reaction or soft-tissue mass. MRI revealed a 71×42×42-mm compartmentalized lesion with fluid-fluid levels after gadolinium, involving the inner cortex with intramedullary extension and surrounding muscle reaction but sparing major vessels. Core-needle biopsy showed lamellar bone trabeculae separated by blood-filled spaces lined by flattened endothelial cells and osteoclast-type giant cells. The Mirels score was 9, and one year later the patient underwent intralesional curettage, autologous bone grafting, and plate fixation. Radiographs at 3 and 6 months postoperatively appeared stable. Fifteen months after surgery, she developed increasing thigh pain, swelling, and required a cane; radiographs demonstrated recurrence of the cystic lesion around the hardware. A repeat biopsy (7 years after symptom onset) showed hemorrhagic cavities without an endothelial lining within solid regions composed of mononuclear and multinucleated osteoclast-type cells; the mononuclear cells had ovoid nuclei, fine chromatin, and no atypia, with foci of reactive osteogenesis. Immunohistochemistry for MDM2 was negative.

A 48-year-old Caucasian man presented with an 18-month history of progressive right-sided otalgia, nonpulsatile tinnitus, episodic vertigo, and unilateral hearing loss. He denied recurrent otitis media, exposure to ototoxic medications or loud noise, and chemotherapy. On examination, the right external auditory canal was narrowed and inflamed, and palpation elicited tenderness over the mastoid without fluctuant swelling. The tympanic membrane was not visible through the inflamed canal. No cervical lymphadenopathy was noted.

A dedicated CT scan of the temporal bones demonstrated diffuse opacification throughout the right temporal bone with coalescent airspaces and lytic destruction of the mastoid cortex, surrounded by thickening and sclerosis of the mastoid air cells, and soft-tissue thickening causing near-complete stenosis of the external auditory canal. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain revealed a right mastoid lesion with dural thickening adjacent to the petrous temporal bone, minor enhancement at the inferior skull base, enhancement along the vestibular aqueduct extending to involve adjacent dura, and a hypoenhancing soft-tissue plug in the medial external auditory canal abutting the tympanic membrane.

An initial trans-external-canal biopsy was nondiagnostic. An open mastoid biopsy showed a lymphohistiocytic infiltrate surrounding residual bony trabeculae. The histiocytes had abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm and ovoid nuclei; nucleoli were inconspicuous, the mitotic rate was low, and no necrosis was identified. Immunohistochemical staining of the histiocytic component demonstrated positivity for CD68 and S100 and negativity for CD1a.

A 48-year-old Pakistani woman presented with a 2-year history of intermittent vomiting, right upper-quadrant pain, and a sensation of fullness on the right side of the abdomen. She denied urinary symptoms or changes in bowel habits. Her medical history was notable for heavy menstruation and iron deficiency anemia managed with oral iron for over 10 years. On examination, there was fullness of the right upper quadrant with a large, firm, palpable mass with a rounded surface and ill-defined borders. Laboratory studies revealed chronic microcytic anemia with hemoglobin levels ranging from 6 to 10 g/dL on different occasions. Hemoglobin electrophoresis demonstrated beta-thalassemia trait.  
Abdominal ultrasonography showed a well-defined hyperechoic heterogeneous mass in the right upper quadrant measuring approximately 16.6 × 8.9 cm with a smooth outline and minimal vascularity. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a well-defined, encapsulated retroperitoneal lesion of mostly fat density with internal areas of soft-tissue density in the hepatorenal space measuring 11.2 × 9.7 × 14.4 cm; it displaced the right kidney inferiorly and displaced the inferior vena cava, duodenum, and pancreatic head without evidence of invasion, and the right adrenal gland was not visualized separately. MRI confirmed a large right retroperitoneal predominantly fatty mass in the location of the right adrenal gland measuring 15.6 × 11.7 × 10.4 cm, extra-renal in location, with soft-tissue nodular and linear strand-like areas showing mild enhancement on post-contrast images and no definite infiltration of adjacent organs.

A 51-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of verrucous lesions in her oral cavity. She reported that these lesions had been present since birth and exhibited slow, painless growth over the left hemipalate and the bilateral superior labiogingival sulcus. On examination, verrucous papules involved the nasal columella, upper lip, soft and hard palate, and oropharynx, with complete preservation of the facial midline. 

Her medical history was notable for a myxoid tumor of the left parotid gland at age 16, treated with partial parotidectomy; the tumor recurred two years later, requiring reoperation with resultant ipsilateral facial nerve paralysis and subsequent radiotherapy. Neither the patient nor her family recalled any change in the oral lesions before or after these treatments.

An incisional biopsy of the palatal lesion was performed. Histopathological examination revealed stratified cornified epithelium with severe hyperplasia and mild chronic inflammatory infiltration. There were no signs of malignancy or infection by external agents (eg, Candida spp., human papillomavirus).

A 37-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 10-year history of a slowly growing, bilateral palatal mass that was causing difficulty breathing. She had no significant medical history and denied trauma. Dental history was notable only for extraction of the upper right first and second premolars. On intraoral examination, two firm, pedunculated lesions, each about 5 × 2 cm, were present on the hard palate under normal mucosa. The patient reported no pain. Initial differential diagnoses included peripheral giant cell granuloma, odontogenic myxoma, neurofibroma, minor salivary gland tumor, and desmoid tumor. Radiographic imaging showed no invasion of the underlying bone.

A 24-year-old G3P3 breastfeeding woman presented with 2 weeks of nausea and vomiting without vaginal bleeding. She had three prior cesarean deliveries, the most recent one year ago, and no known drug allergies. On examination, her blood pressure and heart rate were within normal limits. Initial laboratory studies revealed a serum β-hCG of 984,240.8 mIU/L, a suppressed TSH of 0.013 UI/mL, and an elevated free T4 of 2.9 ng/dL. Four days later, β-hCG had risen to 1,083,832 mIU/L. Pelvic transabdominal ultrasound showed an intrauterine mass occupying most of the uterus composed of numerous small cystic structures with high-velocity, low-impedance flow and no fetal parts. Contrast-enhanced CT of the brain, chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated an enlarged uterus containing a 12 × 9 cm heterogeneous cystic mass, with no evidence of metastases.

A 62-year-old Macedonian woman, gravida 2 para 2, presented with a 2-year history of unexplained pain in the left iliac fossa and pain radiating down the left leg on walking. She was 15 years postmenopausal with no use of hormone replacement therapy, and she denied abnormal vaginal bleeding or urinary and bowel symptoms. Her medical, surgical, and family histories were unremarkable. The family physician had attributed her symptoms to lumbar canal stenosis and treated her conservatively with analgesics without significant relief.

On examination, vital signs were normal. The abdomen showed minimal tenderness in the left lower quadrant. A speculum examination revealed postmenopausal atrophy. Bimanual pelvic examination demonstrated a non-tender, mobile mass in the left adnexal region without other signs of malignancy.

Laboratory testing revealed a CA-125 level of 5 U/mL (reference range 0–35 U/mL). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a well-defined solid mass in the left adnexa; the liver, pancreas, spleen, and adrenal glands were normal, and no ascites or lymphadenopathy were noted. Imaging also confirmed lumbar canal stenosis at L4–L5, more severe on the right than on the left. Pelvic ultrasound demonstrated a 9.0 × 6.3 × 4.9 cm solid mass in the left adnexal region.

A 20-year-old man with high-risk Philadelphia chromosome–negative pre–B acute lymphoblastic leukemia and an MLL rearrangement had achieved a second complete remission with positive minimal residual disease after FlaG-Ida salvage chemotherapy and was awaiting an urgent allogeneic bone marrow transplant. Five days before the initiation of conditioning, he noted visual loss in his left eye. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/100 in the left eye. Optical coherence tomography of the left eye showed a serous subfoveal detachment. Two days later, the right eye became involved; visual acuity was 20/100 OD and 20/400 OS, and OCT revealed bilateral macular detachments. Enhanced-depth imaging OCT demonstrated markedly increased subfoveal choroidal thickness (836 μm OD and 1036 μm OS; normal average, 310 μm). Two lumbar punctures with cytologic studies, flow cytometry, and opening-pressure measurements showed no evidence of central nervous system involvement. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits revealed only slight peripheral optic nerve enhancement. Optic neuritis was ruled out by OCT nerve-fiber imaging. Fluorescein angiography disclosed multiple, diffuse pinpoint leakage points in the macular areas of both eyes.

A 61-year-old man presented with acute painless urethral bleeding and lower urinary tract symptoms, predominantly voiding obstruction. His history included hypertension, dyslipidemia, and two episodes of acute urethral bleeding 20 years earlier, at which time glans-penile haemangiomas were diagnosed and sutured. On examination, several haemangiomas were visible in the glandular urethra at the submeatal level when the meatus was gently spread. Scrotal haemangiomas and prominent bilateral leg varicose veins were also noted. Digital rectal examination revealed a nonsuspicious, medium-sized adenomatous prostate. Uroflowmetry yielded no measurable values due to low voiding volume. A retrograde urethrogram and voiding cystourethrogram demonstrated a short proximal bulbar urethral stricture and contrast extravasation into peribulbar veins. Urethroscopy confirmed a stricture ring near the external urinary sphincter. After discussion, an internal urethrotomy under direct vision was performed. During the procedure, glans haemangiomas and small haemangiomas in the prostatic urethra—unrelated to the stricture—were identified. There was no hemorrhagic event, and the catheter was removed five days later without complications.

A 41-year-old woman presented with a history of regular menstrual cycles until age 36, when oligomenorrhea progressed to amenorrhea. She also reported headaches and blurred vision. MRI of the sellar region revealed a 43 × 40 × 29 mm pituitary mass. Visual field testing showed bilateral temporal hemianopia. Initial pituitary hormones were: TSH 1.9 μIU/mL, FT4 7.2 pmol/L, T3 1.3 nmol/L, LH 2.6 mIU/mL, FSH 7.3 mIU/mL, estradiol 14.4 pg/mL, prolactin 20.0 ng/mL, ACTH 15.0 pg/mL, cortisol 12.4 μg/dL, and IGF-1 53.8 ng/mL. Central hypothyroidism was treated with levothyroxine. In August 2013, she underwent transsphenoidal resection; immunostaining of the tumor was positive for FSH and LH. Postoperatively, visual fields improved but amenorrhea persisted. In 2015, visual fields deteriorated; repeat labs showed FSH 6.31 mIU/mL, LH 2.20 mIU/mL, and estradiol 135 pg/mL. Surgical reintervention was planned but delayed. In March 2016, MRI showed tumor remnant growth without further visual change; estradiol had risen to 394.5 pg/mL with FSH 6.19 mIU/mL and LH 1.98 mIU/mL, while amenorrhea remained.

A 41-year-old Caucasian man with neurofibromatosis type 1 since age 21 noted a slow-growing, painless swelling of his left forearm for 1.5 years. He had no trauma or inflammation. His family history was notable for bowel carcinoma in his father and grandmother. On exam, he had generalized cutaneous neurofibromas and oral papillomas. Local examination revealed a hard, lemon-sized, nonmovable mass on the ventral aspect of the left mid-forearm. The overlying skin was normal, and forearm and wrist motion were full.

X-ray of the forearm showed a soft-tissue tumor without bone involvement. Ultrasonography demonstrated a 91 × 52 × 50 mm inhomogeneous, condensed tumor with a well-defined border. Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed a 95 × 55 × 49 mm well-defined, highly inhomogeneous mass with liquid- and fat-equivalent components displacing surrounding tissues. Radiologic criteria suggested malignancy, and an open biopsy of the central region was performed.

Microscopic examination showed a heterogeneous tumor: one area with myxoid ground matrix and parallel, elongated spindle-shaped cells with hyperchromatic nuclei; another with enlarged clear-cytoplasm cells with deformed hyperchromatic nuclei; multiple apoptoses, mitoses, necrosis, and thrombosed capillaries. Better-differentiated regions contained lipoblasts with polylobulated hyperchromatic nuclei and cytoplasmic vacuoles. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated S100 protein positivity in lipoblast cells of the well-differentiated component, whereas the solid regions were S100-negative.

A 23-year-old otherwise healthy man presented with multiple elevated skin lesions on his left upper extremity and upper chest for 5 years. The lesions initially appeared on the left palm as multiple horny elevations and subsequently developed over the entire left upper extremity and left side of the chest in a linear fashion. The condition was stable for 3 years and was accompanied by mild itching. The patient's past medical and family history were unremarkable, and topical treatments provided no benefit. On examination, there were skin-colored to brownish, discrete verrucous papules, nodules, and plaques in a linear configuration following Blaschko's lines over the left forearm, arm, and the left side of the upper chest, strictly respecting the midline. There were also multiple small keratotic and pitted papules linearly arranged along the medial border and central portion of the left palm, some coalescing into plaques, along with numerous punctate pits. The rest of the mucocutaneous and systemic examination was normal. Routine laboratory tests, serum chemistry panel, and HIV serology were within normal limits.

A 45-year-old woman with no history of breast cancer or chest radiotherapy noted a slow-growing palpable nodule in her left breast. Initial mammography showed a well-defined opacity, and ultrasound demonstrated a corresponding 5 cm hyperechoic lesion that was deemed consistent with a lipoma. One year later, she returned with the same lesion, now described on examination as a hard, fixed, painless mass. Mammography revealed asymmetric enlargement of the left breast with a large heterogeneous mass. Ultrasound showed a confluent 10 cm lesion causing structural distortion, with increased color-Doppler vascular signal and multiple large anechoic fluid areas. 

A first free-hand core biopsy (14-G) yielded necrosis and fibrin-leukocyte tissue (B1). A second free-hand core biopsy again showed necrosis without epithelial cells (B2). Two weeks later, after the development of a cutaneous fistula, a third ultrasound-guided core biopsy (14-G) revealed necrotic and fibrin-hemorrhagic material with fibro-adipose fragments and small foci of atypical vascular proliferation; immunohistochemical staining was CD31+/–, CD34+, FLI1+, Factor VIII+/–, and MIB1 20%.

A 59-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of suprapubic pain and gross hematuria without fever or dysuria. He had end-stage renal disease secondary to diabetes and hypertension, had been on hemodialysis for 3 years, and received a deceased-donor kidney transplant 5 years earlier. His immunosuppression regimen consisted of tacrolimus and mycophenolate sodium. His medical history also included a 30-pack-year smoking history (quit 10 years prior), morbid obesity, hepatitis C–related stage II cirrhosis, hypertension, and long-standing diabetes mellitus. 

On examination, he had suprapubic tenderness without costovertebral angle tenderness. An abdominal ultrasound showed a normal-appearing renal allograft but did not visualize the native kidneys well. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen revealed a 6.0 × 5.5 × 7.3 cm heterogeneous mass in the left native kidney. MRI confirmed these findings and raised concern for renal malignancy; no distant metastases were identified. He underwent a hand-assisted laparoscopic radical nephrectomy of the native left kidney.

Grossly, the kidney contained an ill-defined gray–tan solid mass measuring 7.5 × 6.5 × 5.0 cm in the mid–lower pole, with extension into the renal sinus and perinephric fat and involvement of a regional lymph node. Histologic examination showed a widely infiltrative high-grade adenocarcinoma with variable architectural patterns, including solid nests and linear single-cell infiltration with prominent desmoplasia. The tumor cells exhibited marked nuclear pleomorphism, a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, prominent nucleoli, and brisk mitotic activity. The tumor was assigned Fuhrman nuclear grade 4.

A 21-year-old man with no past medical or surgical history presented with a tender, palpable mass in his left buttock that he had noticed for several years but which had rapidly enlarged over the previous six months. He also reported recent onset of constipation and numbness of the left lower extremity, worsened by sitting. He denied any drainage, redness, fever, or systemic symptoms. He took no medications and had no family history of cancer.

On examination, a 4 × 4 cm tender mass was palpated in the left perineum without overlying skin changes. Neurologic examination showed hypoesthesia in the L5–S4 distribution on the left with intact motor function; the right lower extremity was normal. Abdominal and digital rectal examinations were unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis revealed a well-defined, nonenhancing, unilocular hypodense cystic lesion anterior to the rectum measuring 7.0 × 9.0 cm, as well as a separate 4.4 × 4.7 cm cyst in the left perineum. On contrast-enhanced MRI, both lesions appeared homogeneous, T1 hypointense, T2 hyperintense, and showed no wall enhancement. The cysts were distinct from the bladder, urethra, prostate, and rectum, and were suggested to have a narrow neck traversing the pelvic floor near the pudendal canal.

A 71-year-old Caucasian woman with chronic right hip pain and intermittent medical care presented after a mechanical fall. She had COPD with active smoking, periodontal disease, sick sinus syndrome with a permanent pacemaker, urinary frequency, and newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes and congestive heart failure. In the ED, examination revealed a large (6.1 × 5.5 cm) fungating right shoulder mass. Pelvic radiographs showed a pathologic fracture of the right iliac wing. CT scans disclosed a lytic lesion with pathologic fracture of the right iliac wing, additional pelvic lytic lesions in the sacrum, right inferior pubic ramus, and left iliac wing, and lytic lesions in the right mandibular condyle, left occipital condyle, left posterior rib, right third rib, and L2 vertebral body. The CT abdomen/pelvis also showed left renal parenchymal irregularity suspicious for malignancy and bilateral adrenal nodules concerning for metastases. On hospital day 1, dermatology performed a shave biopsy of the shoulder mass. The pathology returned as nodular, ulcerated basal cell carcinoma extending to the base of the sections.

A 61-year-old woman with a history of malignant thymoma (Masaoka–Koga stage III) treated in 2013 with neoadjuvant chemotherapy, surgical resection (including wedge lung resection and SVC graft), and adjuvant radiotherapy presented in January 2020 with a several-week history of dry cough and exertional dyspnea. She had declining pulmonary metastases on prior surveillance imaging and had declined further chemotherapy. 

On restaging CECT of the brain, thorax, abdomen, and pelvis, there was evidence of progressive lung nodules consistent with known metastases and incidentally noted right breast lumps. She denied breast pain or nipple discharge.

Examination of the breasts revealed two mobile, non–tethered right breast masses measuring 5 cm × 5 cm (upper mid quadrant) and 2 cm × 1 cm (upper outer quadrant) without overlying skin changes. The left breast and bilateral axillae were unremarkable.

Mammography demonstrated two well-circumscribed, round, high-density lesions in the right breast without microcalcifications. Complementary breast ultrasound showed two well-defined heterogeneous lesions corresponding to the mammographic findings and assigned BI-RADS category 4b. There were no suspicious axillary lymph nodes on imaging.

A 65-year-old man presented with a 6-week history of fatigue, jaundice, pale stools, and right upper quadrant pain. Eighteen months earlier, he underwent orthotopic liver transplantation for fulminant autoimmune hepatitis, complicated by primary graft nonfunction and a second transplant one week later. One month before this presentation, he reported similar symptoms; his local hepatologist attributed them to late graft rejection in the setting of self-reported immunosuppression disruption and elevated liver enzymes, and he was started on high-dose oral glucocorticoids in addition to tacrolimus and mycophenolate.

On admission, laboratory studies showed: total bilirubin 6.9 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 1465 U/L, AST 109 U/L, ALT 86 U/L, CA 19-9 419 U/mL, and an EBV viral load of 1075 IU/mL. Liver ultrasound revealed an ill-defined, heterogeneously hypoechoic mass along the inferior margin of the left lobe with vascular involvement. MRI of the abdomen demonstrated a 7.3 cm infiltrative mass in segments II, III, and the caudate lobe, causing intrahepatic biliary ductal dilatation and features concerning for high-grade stenosis.

Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography was consistent with a benign post-transplant biliary anastomotic stricture. Following balloon dilation, a fully covered metal stent was placed. Brush cytology of the stricture was negative for cholangiocarcinoma in situ.

A 28-year-old Thai man with a known history of neurofibromatosis type 1 presented with four months of progressive left supraclavicular swelling, unintentional weight loss, and night sweats. Two months before admission, he developed hoarseness of voice, ptosis of the left eyelid, and diplopia.

On examination, there was left-sided ptosis, miosis, and facial anhidrosis consistent with Horner’s syndrome. His skin showed multiple well-defined café au lait macules on the abdomen, areolae, arms, back, and buttocks; axillary freckling; and soft, movable cutaneous nodules on the left thigh, forearm, and back. Slit-lamp examination revealed multiple Lisch nodules. His father had similar cutaneous lesions. A large (15×10 cm), non-tender, rubbery mass was palpable in the left supraclavicular region; there were no other palpable lymph nodes.

Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 14.5 g/dL, leukocyte count 8.2×10^9/L (70% neutrophils, 22% lymphocytes, 8% monocytes), platelet count 280×10^9/L, lactate dehydrogenase 525 U/L (normal 225–450), and uric acid 13.4 mg/dL (normal 2.4–7). Liver function tests were normal.

Chest radiography demonstrated a large anterior mediastinal mass. CT of the neck revealed matted lymphadenopathy on the left side extending along the carotid vessels into the thoracic inlet. CT of the chest showed a 10.9×9.7×18 cm lobulated, heterogeneous, enhancing mass with central necrosis in the anterior and middle mediastinum, extending into the left neck, encasing the aortic arch, left subclavian artery, left jugular vein, trachea, left main bronchus, and left pulmonary artery. Multiple small mediastinal nodes, a left pleural effusion, and adjacent atelectasis of the left lower lobe were also noted.

A 7-year-old girl presented with a 1-month history of constant pain and food impaction in the lower back teeth bilaterally, worsened by chewing. Clinical examination revealed carious lesions in the mandibular molars on both sides. In the left mandibular primary first molar region, there was an unusual tooth-like structure: the coronal portion was surrounded circumferentially by a white globule of tooth material extending below the gingival margin, with adjacent gingival inflammation and edema. The patient reported that this tooth-like structure had been slowly growing and erupting over the past 6 months. An orthopantomogram showed a radiopaque mass overlapping the crown of the primary first molar, imparting an irregular shape, while the underlying permanent premolar tooth bud appeared normal.

A 67-year-old man presented with a 4-week history of dizziness, dysesthesia, and ataxia. His medical history was notable for hypertension and melanoma in situ excised 2 months earlier. Neurologic examination revealed mild gait ataxia, subtle right-sided dysmetria, saccadic intrusion during ocular pursuit, and right facial numbness in the trigeminal V1 distribution; there was no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Brain MRI showed a 13×10×10 mm enhancing lesion in the right brachium pontis. CT of the chest revealed multiple pulmonary nodular opacities with consolidation, ground-glass change, and cavitation; on FDG-PET, the pulmonary lesions were not FDG-avid, whereas the brainstem lesion showed mild FDG uptake. CSF analysis, including cytology, microbiology, flow cytometry, and oligoclonal bands, was unrevealing. CT-guided biopsy of a pulmonary nodule demonstrated nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with predominantly CD3+ lymphocytes and short septate fungal hyphae on methenamine silver staining, but fungal cultures and PCR were negative. Despite 10 weeks of antifungal therapy with oral voriconazole and IV liposomal amphotericin, his clinical and radiologic findings progressed.

A woman in her mid-thirties was referred after an incidental pelvic mass was found. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. Vital signs were normal. Physical examination revealed a nonpainful, mobile, hard mass about 6 cm in diameter in the left adnexal region; the remainder of the abdomen, pelvic exam, and laboratory tests were unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed a 7.3 cm × 4.2 cm × 5.8 cm mixed cystic and solid mass in the left adnexa with multiple irregular septa and solid components; color Doppler imaging revealed strip-like blood flow within the septa and a resistance index of 0.37. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a 7.6 cm × 5.2 cm mixed cystic/solid lesion attached to the left uterine wall. The solid component was iso- to slightly hyperintense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images with >50% of the lesion showing a strong T2 signal, and exhibited restricted diffusion. No enlarged lymph nodes were seen.

A 28-day-old boy was referred for evaluation of a mass on the anterior ventral surface of the tongue extending to the floor of the mouth. The mass had been present since birth and had gradually increased in size, causing posterior displacement of the tongue, difficulty feeding, and episodes of cyanosis when crying. The infant was the product of a fourth gestation, born full term by cesarean delivery with normal Apgar scores, weighing 3.87 kg and measuring 51.5 cm in length. Prenatal supplementation included folic acid and iron.  
On admission, laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 16.2 g/dL, white blood cell count 12,500/mm3 (62.9% lymphocytes, 17.8% neutrophils), total bilirubin 4.4 mg/dL (direct 0.4 mg/dL, indirect 4.0 mg/dL), phosphorus 6.0 mg/dL, prothrombin time 10.3 s, and partial thromboplastin time 38.3 s.  
Computed tomography of the neck revealed a midline cystic mass measuring 3.6 × 3 × 2.2 cm in the floor of the mouth and ventral tongue, following the path of the sublingual gland with an approximate volume of 12 cc. In the sagittal view, the lesion extended above the mylohyoid muscle. The initial radiologic interpretation suggested a ranula of the sublingual gland.

A 63-year-old Caucasian woman presented with several months of progressive left-ear hearing loss and nasal congestion unresponsive to antibiotics, decongestants, and intranasal steroids. Medical history included nonallergic rhinitis, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and morbid obesity. On examination, she had conductive hearing loss from a left middle ear effusion, but her cranial nerves were intact. Sinonasal endoscopy revealed an excoriated mass in the posterior nasopharynx and nasal turbinates.  
Biopsy of the mass showed intermediate-sized blastic cells that stained positive for myeloperoxidase, CD68 (dim), CD99, and CD117 (dim), consistent with granulocytic sarcoma. A complete blood count, serum chemistries, and liver enzymes were normal. Peripheral blood flow cytometry was unremarkable, and PCR studies for BCR-ABL and JAK2 mutations were negative. Bone marrow biopsy demonstrated normal trilineage hematopoiesis with no evidence of acute myeloid leukemia or myeloproliferative neoplasm; karyotype was 46,XX. Whole-body PET-CT showed only modest inflammation localized to the nasopharyngeal region.

A 40-year-old gravida 3, para 2 woman presented with a 1-year history of changes in bowel habits and bright-red rectal bleeding. She had undergone a subtotal abdominal hysterectomy for uterine leiomyoma 3 years earlier and a right ovarian cystectomy. She denied prior symptoms of endometriosis and had never received hormone‐replacement therapy. On digital rectal examination, a firm, fixed mass was palpated, and there was blood on the examining finger. Laboratory studies were notable only for moderate anemia; serum carcinoembryonic antigen was within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT showed thickening of the rectal wall with inhomogeneous enhancement and a 4-cm soft-tissue mass involving the rectum and left ovary; there was also right hydronephrosis and hydroureter. Colonoscopy revealed a protruding lesion in the rectum with segmental stenosis of the rectosigmoid lumen. An endoscopic biopsy demonstrated tubular adenoma and proliferation of spindle cells at the edge of the tissue.

An 82-year-old Japanese man with a 10-year history of rheumatoid arthritis presented with a 1-week history of fever and malaise. His rheumatoid arthritis had been treated for 9½ years with methotrexate (currently 12 mg weekly; total dose 3454 mg), prednisolone (2.5 mg daily), and bucillamine. He had no alcohol use, a remote 20–pack-year smoking history, and no family history of malignancy. On examination, he was alert, febrile (39.2 °C), and hemodynamically stable; joints showed chronic RA changes but no acute synovitis; there was no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies showed:  
• Elevated C-reactive protein (6.66 mg/dL) and soluble interleukin-2 receptor (4090 U/mL)  
• Mildly elevated AST (89 IU/L), ALT (76 IU/L), GGT (82 IU/L), ALP (608 IU/L)  
• Rheumatoid factor 490.8 U/mL and anti-CCP antibody 118.1 U/mL  
• Tumor markers: CA19-9 130.9 U/mL, SLX 54.7 U/mL, NSE 16.6 ng/mL  
• EBV serology: VCA-IgG 1:320, VCA-IgM <1:10, EBNA 1:20  
• Hepatitis B and C serologies negative  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen demonstrated multiple hypovascular nodules in the lungs, liver, spleen, and para-aortic region.

A 65-year-old Hispanic man with a history of hypertension, obesity, dyslipidemia, and diabetes mellitus presented with a 1-month history of progressive frontal and biparietal headache associated with photophobia, diplopia, decreased visual acuity, right eye ptosis, nausea, and vomiting. He also reported an unintentional 32-lb weight loss over 2 months. On examination, he had an internuclear ophthalmoplegia, a pupil-sparing right third nerve palsy, and a left sixth nerve palsy; no other cranial nerve deficits were noted. He denied any personal or family history of malignancy and had a 20 pack-year smoking history with daily alcohol use. MRI of the brain revealed a 3.1×3.2×4.4 cm heterogeneous, contrast-enhancing mass originating in the clivus and sella, displacing the pituitary gland cephalad, slightly shifting the infundibulum leftward, and insinuating into the cavernous sinus. Laboratory studies showed normal levels of prolactin, thyroid-stimulating hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone, and adrenocorticotropic hormone. In view of the lack of hormonal activity, the leading diagnoses included a nonfunctioning pituitary adenoma, meningioma, chordoma, and metastasis.

A 59-year-old woman was referred after two nodules in her right breast were detected on annual mammography. She had a history of hypothyroidism on levothyroxine and no family history of malignancy. On examination, there was a slightly palpable, painless, mobile  lump in the superior-middle right breast and bulky left axillary lymphadenopathy. The overlying skin was intact without retraction, peau d’orange, or nipple discharge. A red-brown itchy plaque was noted on the scalp. No other peripheral nodes were palpable and there were no fevers, night sweats, or weight loss.

Laboratory tests showed normal blood counts, thyroid function, complement levels, inflammatory markers (CRP), autoantibodies (ANA, RF), and virology; CA 15-3 was 33 U/mL, LDH was mildly elevated at 290 U/L, and uric acid was 5.8 mg/dL. Mantoux, Coombs, and hepatitis serologies were negative.

Digital mammography showed two radiopaque masses in the right breast without microcalcifications and prominent left axillary lymph nodes. Breast ultrasound confirmed two mixed echogenicity lesions with irregular borders and increased vascularity. Chest and abdominal CT revealed mild hepatomegaly with fatty infiltration; gastroscopy and colonoscopy were unremarkable except for gastritis and diverticulosis.

A 45-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of progressively worsening headaches, right-sided weakness, and speech difficulties, and one generalized tonic-clonic seizure. On examination he had papilledema, expressive aphasia, and right hemiparesis (MRC grade 4/5). He had no history of intravenous drug use, radiation exposure, or other comorbidities. Routine laboratory studies were within normal limits, and serologic tests were negative for HIV, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, and Epstein–Barr virus. Noncontrast and contrast-enhanced head CT showed a heterogeneously enhancing left temporo-parietal mass extending into the basal ganglia, with extensive perilesional edema and midline shift. Brain MRI revealed a 5.9 × 4.4 × 5.2 cm heterogeneous solid and cystic lesion that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and demonstrated heterogeneous gadolinium enhancement, with massive surrounding edema and mass effect. Preoperative chest radiography and abdominal ultrasound were normal. The differential diagnosis included high-grade glioma or atypical meningioma.

An 82-year-old woman underwent abdominal CT screening, which revealed a 15 mm mass in the lower pole of the left kidney. She had a history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and dyslipidemia but no stigmata of tuberous sclerosis. Urinalysis was normal, and urinary cytology was negative. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a homogeneously hyperdense mass with early-phase enhancement and late-phase washout; there was no evidence of metastasis. The lesion was clinically staged as cT1aN0M0. Her performance status was 100%, and she elected to undergo curative surgery.  

Laparoscopic partial nephrectomy was performed via a retroperitoneal approach, and the tumor was excised with a small rim of normal parenchyma. On gross examination, the lesion was 15 mm in diameter, yellowish-white, solid, and poorly circumscribed.  

Microscopically, the tumor arose within the renal parenchyma without adherence to the capsule. It was composed almost exclusively of spindle-shaped cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm, ovoid to elongated nuclei with mild atypia, and a fascicular growth pattern; a few blood vessels were present, and no adipocytes were identified.

A 57-year-old man was referred for treatment of acute appendicitis. During his evaluation, an incidental renal mass was detected on computed tomography. The patient was asymptomatic with no clinical signs, and routine blood tests were normal. 

Plain CT demonstrated a 30 × 28 × 25 mm, homogeneously slight hyperattenuating renal mass (CT number 49 HU). Dynamic contrast-enhanced CT showed slight, gradual, and homogeneous enhancement in the mass without fat, calcification, or cystic elements. 

On MRI, the mass was located in the renal medulla and showed homogeneous low signal intensity on T2-weighted images and fat-suppressed T2-weighted images, with internal areas of mildly high signal intensity but no obvious capsular structure. Diffusion-weighted imaging revealed homogeneous low signal intensity, and the apparent diffusion coefficient map showed high signal intensity. Dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI again demonstrated slight, gradual, and homogeneous enhancement of the mass.

A 26-year-old nulligravid Hispanic woman presented with 4 months of dysfunctional uterine bleeding that persisted despite oral contraceptives. Transvaginal ultrasound showed an enlarged uterus with a 5.7 × 7.0 × 7.0 cm homogeneous mass in the lower uterine segment and an enlarged right ovary. An endometrial biopsy demonstrated endometrial tissue with possible small-cell neuroectodermal differentiation. At referral, repeat endometrial biopsy revealed a high-grade malignant tumor infiltrating endometrial and cervical tissue. Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed a uterine width of 8.2 cm with a 5.8 × 4.2 cm intramyometrial mass, a 4.1 cm cystic lesion in the right adnexa, ascites, a left pleural effusion, and mildly enlarged para-aortic lymph nodes.

A 68-year-old man presented with a one-month history of a gradually enlarging growth in the lower right posterior oral cavity associated with cheek biting and difficulty eating. The lesion was mildly painful, aching in quality, and not associated with any discharge. His medical history was notable for hypertension managed with medication; dental and family histories were noncontributory.

On extraoral examination, the face was bilaterally symmetrical, the temporomandibular joints were normal, and no cervical lymphadenopathy was palpable. Intraoral inspection revealed a nonhealing, ulceroproliferative, sessile growth measuring 5.0 cm × 3.5 cm in the right mandibular buccal mucosa extending from the region of the lower right first molar to the retromolar area. Palpation showed the mass to be tender, firm, nonreducible, noncompressible, and nonfluctuant; no purulent discharge was noted. The lesion extended into both the labial and lingual vestibular mucosa adjacent to the alveolar mucosa.

A provisional diagnosis of malignancy of the alveolobuccal complex was made, with a differential that included squamous cell carcinoma, tuberculosis, rhabdomyosarcoma, and fibrosarcoma. Routine blood and biochemical investigations were within normal limits. Panoramic radiography demonstrated generalized horizontal bone loss in the regions corresponding to the lower right first and second premolars.

An incisional biopsy yielded multiple firm, brownish soft-tissue fragments (largest, 3.5 cm × 2.2 cm; smallest, 0.5 cm × 0.4 cm). Histologic examination of hematoxylin-and-eosin–stained sections showed, at low power, a fibrinopurulent membrane overlying connective tissue consistent with surface ulceration. Intermediate magnification revealed spindle-shaped and ovoid neoplastic cells arranged in storiform and fascicular patterns with focal myxoid areas. High-power views demonstrated marked cellular and nuclear pleomorphism, multiple nucleoli, an increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and atypical mitotic figures.

The histopathologic differential diagnoses included fibrosarcoma, pleomorphic sarcoma, desmoplastic melanoma, leiomyosarcoma, and synovial sarcoma.

A 67-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of a painful, rapidly enlarging swelling of the left mandible following extraction of tooth #38. He denied trauma, radiation exposure, HPV infection, and family history of malignancy.  
On examination, there was left facial asymmetry and a soft-to-firm, tender swelling in the lower third of the face with paresthesia in the distribution of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve; no neck lymphadenopathy was found.  
Intraorally, a 3 cm × 3 cm, well-defined, flesh-colored mass occupied the left molar and retromolar regions; it was soft to firm, non-bleeding, and without trismus.  
Panoramic radiograph showed a poorly defined, multiloculated radiolucent lesion extending from the left first premolar to the mandibular angle.  
CT scan demonstrated a large expansile lytic lesion with irregular margins and cortical breaches of the left posterior mandible, without obvious soft-tissue extension.  
A previous biopsy had been interpreted as fibroma.  
Based on the clinical and radiographic features, intraosseous carcinoma of the left retromolar area was tentatively diagnosed; central giant cell lesions and osteosarcoma were also considered.

A 27-year-old previously healthy man presented after an episode of chest pain with syncope during exercise. He reported several days of exertional chest discomfort, exercise intolerance, and cold sweats. On arrival to the critical care unit he was alert and in no acute distress. His heart rate was 112 beats per minute and irregular, blood pressure was 112/77 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation was 94% on 2 L of oxygen by nasal cannula. A palpable pulsus paradoxus was noted. Laboratory studies were normal except for a mildly elevated creatinine. Given the clinical presentation, he received therapeutic enoxaparin for a presumptive pulmonary embolism. A chest radiograph showed cardiomegaly. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology, and contrast-enhanced CT of the chest confirmed the pericardial effusion. Cardiothoracic surgery was consulted, and the patient was scheduled for a pericardial window the next morning.

A 12‐year‐old girl was referred to a dental office for pain and swelling of the right buccal vestibule and palate of the maxilla. Her medical history was notable for a right kidney transplant 5 years earlier, for which she takes chronic immunosuppressive medication. She had been diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia 6 months ago and completed a 6-month course of chemotherapy (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, and prednisolone) with no detectable abnormalities on follow-up complete blood counts. On examination, there was a firm, nonerythematous swelling of the right maxillary vestibule extending to the palate, associated with localized tenderness. Given the persistent lesion, an incisional biopsy was planned.

A 10-year-old healthy Indian boy presented with a 10-day history of a small swelling on the roof of his mouth, noticed spontaneously with no trauma. The lesion was associated with minor bleeding and mild pain on chewing. He denied nasal obstruction or epiphora. His past medical, social, family, and environmental histories were noncontributory. 

On examination, vital signs were normal. Intraoral inspection revealed a well-circumscribed, approximately 2 cm diameter, dark purple growth along the midline of the posterior hard palate, with an irregular surface and an overlying whitish-yellow pseudomembrane. On palpation the lesion was sessile, soft-to-firm, and tender; diascopy produced mild blanching; manipulation did not provoke bleeding. Neurologic examination was normal.

Initial clinical differential diagnoses included hemangioma/vascular malformation, pyogenic granuloma, and angina bullosa hemorrhagica. Laboratory evaluation (complete blood count, coagulation profile, renal function) was within normal limits; serologies for HIV and hepatitis B were nonreactive.

Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging of the oral lesion showed a well-encapsulated mass with thinning of the floor of the nasal cavity, suggestive of a vascular lesion. On the basis of the clinical and radiologic findings, the differential was broadened to encapsulated vascular lesions and palatal minor salivary gland tumors. 

The patient underwent complete surgical excision of the lesion under general anesthesia. The specimen was submitted for histopathological examination.

A 38-year-old gravida 3 para 2 woman at 29 weeks of gestation was referred for evaluation of a vaginal mass. The lesion was first noted at 24 weeks during routine prenatal care; she had sensed perineal discomfort prior to pregnancy but its origin was unclear. She had no significant past medical history. Family history was notable only for gastric cancer in a grandmother and lung cancer in a grandfather. 

On pelvic examination, there was an elliptical, nontender, approximately 5 cm mass arising from the posterior vaginal wall, projecting into the vaginal canal; it was easily palpable and mobile. Rectal examination revealed intact mucosa. 

Transvaginal ultrasound showed a 51.7 × 32.5 mm hypervascular mass. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a 52 × 37 × 35 mm lesion in the rectovaginal septum, isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with well-defined borders and no apparent invasion of the rectum or vaginal mucosa. No metastatic lesions were identified.

A 40-year-old man presented with a sudden episode of hematemesis. He had no prior medical history, did not smoke or drink alcohol, and denied use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.  
On examination, his vital signs were stable. The abdomen was soft and non-distended, with no organomegaly. Rectal examination was negative for melena. Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin level of 11 g/dL (baseline 13 g/dL).  
Upper endoscopy revealed a 4 cm yellowish submucosal mass in the gastric antrum with an ulcerated surface and a positive pillow sign on compression.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a well-circumscribed, hypodense submucosal gastric mass without lymphadenopathy.  
Endoscopic ultrasound confirmed a 4 cm, homogeneous, hyperechoic lesion arising from the third layer of the gastric wall, with no perigastric lymphadenopathy.  
Mucosal biopsy of the lesion was negative.

A 27-year-old woman (G0P0) presented with a 1-year history of progressive abdominal girth enlargement and a 1-month history of a large pelvic mass. She noted minimal vaginal spotting for 2 days after menses but denied abnormal discharge or changes in menstrual volume or cycle length. She had no hormone therapy or prior gynecologic procedures. Serum tumor markers, including CA 19-9, CA 125, CA 153, CA 742, CEA, AFP, LDH, HE4, and NSE, were all within normal limits.

On pelvic examination, a large tender pelvic mass measuring approximately 15 × 17 cm was palpated protruding about 3 cm into the vagina; the vaginal walls were smooth, and the cervix was displaced laterally. Transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a heterogeneous cystic-solid mass (17 × 11.7 × 8.7 cm in the extraperitoneal pelvis; 3.6 × 6 cm in the vaginal wall) displacing bladder, uterus, and cervix posteriorly and to the right. The solid areas were hypoechoic with multiple cord-like anechoic bands. Color Doppler showed low vascular flow, and pulsed-wave Doppler revealed an arterial resistive index of 0.57. Three-dimensional ultrasound identified a 3.5 cm defect in the anterior vaginal wall connecting the pelvic and vaginal components.

MRI confirmed a well-circumscribed, calabash-shaped cystic-solid tumor with a thick fibrous capsule, involving the extraperitoneal pelvis (18 × 7.2 × 11.5 cm) and the anterior vaginal wall (6.5 × 2.6 × 6.2 cm) through a 1.3 × 2.9 cm defect. Peripheral cystic areas were hypointense on T1-weighted images, mixed hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and nonenhancing postcontrast. Central solid components near the vagina showed low T2 signal, intermediate T1 signal, and intense contrast enhancement similar to the uterus. The lesion displaced but did not invade the vaginal mucosa, which remained intact. Diffusion-weighted imaging showed no restricted diffusion, with a mean ADC of 1.492 × 10^−3 mm^2/s. Intravenous urography revealed displacement of the left ureter toward the midline.

An 82-year-old Caucasian man presented with progressive left-sided nasal obstruction and occasional epistaxis. He also noted dysphagia, post-nasal drip with red blood streaks, and long-standing snoring with nocturnal apnea. His medical history included type 2 diabetes, hypertension, gastroesophageal reflux, hepatic steatosis, colon polyposis, and a 190–pack-year smoking history. Nasal endoscopy revealed a unilateral polypoid mass with irregular, friable margins in the left nasal fossa that bled easily, precluding visualization beyond the anterior third of the inferior turbinate. CT of the facial bones showed left turbinate hypertrophy with non-specific subtotal obliteration of the ipsilateral nasal cavity. MRI demonstrated a polypoid lesion that was isointense on T1, mildly hyperintense on T2 and STIR sequences, occupying the left middle meatus and partially obstructing the maxillary sinus ostium; there was no enhancement after gadolinium administration. Laboratory tests were within normal limits, and PET imaging was negative for distant metastases. Because of the lesion’s morphology and unilaterality, the differential diagnosis included neoplastic lesions such as an inverted papilloma and squamous cell carcinoma, whereas foreign body insertion was deemed unlikely given a negative history.

A 54-year-old woman with a history of acute myeloid leukemia in remission for 4 years underwent a routine CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis, which demonstrated a large pelvic mass arising from the uterus. She was asymptomatic. Laboratory studies showed:  
• Serum CA125, 89.2 U/ml (normal 0–35)  
• Lactate dehydrogenase, 540 IU/l (219–480)  
• Immunoglobulin M, 314 mg/dl (40–230)  
• Serologic tests negative for HBsAg, HIV, hepatitis C virus, HBsAb, HBeAb, and HBcAb  
• Immunofixation electrophoresis of serum and urine negative  

18F-FDG PET/CT revealed:  
• A large, intensely hypermetabolic uterine mass involving the cervix and right pelvic side wall (SUV max 37.1), suggestive of a uterine malignancy  
• Multifocal hypermetabolic bone lesions (spines C2, T4, T6, T8, L3; SUV max 8.0–11.9)  
• Hypermetabolic lymph nodes in the neck, mediastinum, presacral, and intrapelvic regions (SUV max 6.2–18.5)  
• Diffuse peritoneal hypermetabolism, consistent with peritoneal seeding

A 66-year-old woman presented in August 2020 with mild motor weakness of the right lower extremity and gait disturbance. She had no personal or family history of von Hippel-Lindau disease. Neurologic examination revealed mild right-sided hemiparesis of the lower limb (manual muscle test 4/5). Brain MRI showed a well-circumscribed solid mass in the left frontal lobe that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted and FLAIR images, hyperintense on diffusion-weighted imaging, and homogeneously and strongly enhanced after gadolinium administration; there was no cystic change. Noncontrast CT showed no calcification, and a CT scan performed in 2012 did not reveal any lesion in the same area. Cerebral angiography demonstrated intense tumor staining supplied by the bilateral middle meningeal arteries and the left anterior cerebral artery, with patency of the superior sagittal sinus. The leading preoperative diagnosis was a parasagittal meningioma.

A patient was referred to the hospital in March 2022 with a leukocyte count of 105×10^9/L. Initial laboratory assessment showed normal to slightly increased levels of C-reactive protein and procalcitonin and markedly increased lactate dehydrogenase. Tests for autoimmune disease were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography and computed tomography revealed a spleen measuring 14 cm, normal liver size, and no lymphadenopathy. A peripheral blood smear showed proliferative myelopoiesis with a pathologic left shift and a myelocyte peak; basophilic and eosinophilic granulocytes were underrepresented. Bone marrow puncture revealed hypercellularity, dominating granulopoiesis left shifted with myelocyte predominance, a blast count of 15%, underrepresentation of basophilic and eosinophilic granulocytes (<2%), erythroid precursors comprising 27–31% of hematopoiesis, and trilinear dysplasia. Conventional cytogenetic analysis demonstrated a normal male karyotype (46,XY). PCR analysis of BCR::ABL1 major and minor breakpoints and fluorescence in situ hybridization were negative.

A 19-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with bulging of the left eye and progressively blurred vision over the past few months. He had no fever, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms, and there was no family history of cancer or known exposure to chemicals or radiation. Six months earlier, an orbital lesion of approximately 3 cm in diameter had been noted but not further evaluated because of the COVID-19 pandemic. More recently, the lesion enlarged rapidly and began bleeding, prompting evaluation.

On MRI, there was a 60 × 44 × 50 mm mass in the extraconal space of the left orbit. The lesion was isointense to extraocular muscle on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on STIR sequences, and showed heterogeneous enhancement after contrast administration. No internal cysts or calcifications were seen. The borders with the medial rectus muscle and the adjacent ethmoid sinus wall were ill-defined. The mass compressed and deformed the globe but did not invade the eyeball, the intraconal compartment, or extend intracranially. Diffusion-weighted imaging demonstrated strong restricted diffusion with a minimum apparent diffusion coefficient of 0.7 × 10⁻³ mm²/s.

A systemic workup—including complete blood count, urinalysis, serum electrolytes, bone marrow aspiration, lumbar puncture, bone scintigraphy, cervical and abdominal ultrasonography, and CT scans of the abdomen and chest—was unremarkable.

A 73-year-old Caucasian man with a family history of prostate and breast cancer presented with a 6-month history of a right upper medial thigh mass. There was no trauma history; the mass was nontender and had not changed in size. He denied fevers, night sweats, weight loss, nausea, or malaise and had no history of immunocompromise.  
On examination, he had a firm, nonmobile, irregular 4 cm subcutaneous mass on the right upper outer thigh without inguinal lymphadenopathy. The abdomen was soft and nontender, with no hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. Strength and range of motion in the affected leg were normal.  
Laboratory studies showed a WBC count of 7.9×10^3/μL (normal 4.8–10.8), an RBC count of 5.84 M/μL (4.70–6.10), a hematocrit of 50.7% (42.0–52.0), and a platelet count of 243×10^3/μL (164–446). Electrolytes and liver and renal function tests were normal.  
Ultrasound of the thigh revealed a vascularized heterogeneous subcutaneous mass measuring 5.9×3.8×1.3 cm, suggesting a primary soft-tissue or metastatic tumor. MRI of the right lower extremity showed a 5.4×3.4×1.5 cm T2-hyperintense, slightly T1-hyperintense lesion with uniform contrast enhancement, superficial to the rectus femoris without invasion; several small inguinal nodes were within normal limits. Findings raised concern for a soft-tissue sarcoma or metastasis.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated bilateral axillary lymphadenopathy, multiple enlarged gastrohepatic lymph nodes (up to 5×3 cm), and mildly prominent retroperitoneal nodes (up to 10 mm), with otherwise unremarkable solid organs. Differential diagnosis included metastatic adenopathy and lymphoma.

A 59-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with a 4-month history of gradually enlarging masses in both parotid regions. The enlargement was painless, non–meal related, and without facial weakness.
