Examination revealed tender, well-defined masses in both parotid glands (left 3.5×4 cm; right 3×2 cm) with normal overlying skin, no cervical lymphadenopathy, and normal salivary flow from Stensen’s ducts. Ultrasound showed multiple hypoechoic lesions in both parotid glands, up to 27 mm on the left and 18 mm on the right. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the face and neck demonstrated bilateral nonhomogeneous gland enlargement with multiple well-defined nodules (largest 35×28 mm on the left) that were hypointense on T1 and T2 sequences with intense gadolinium enhancement. Based on these imaging features, metastatic lymph nodes and lymphoma were thought most likely. Fine-needle aspiration cytology was performed and was inconclusive.

A 64-year-old man with hypertension and a history of myelodysplastic syndrome was referred for evaluation of a splenic mass identified incidentally on ultrasonography. He was asymptomatic. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 15.0 g/dL, white blood cell count 5.54×10^3/μL, and platelets 78,000/μL. Liver enzymes were modestly elevated (AST 38 IU/L; ALT 79 IU/L; ALP 291 IU/L; γ-GT 441 IU/L); soluble interleukin-2 receptor was within normal limits.  
Ultrasonography revealed splenomegaly (10.8×6.6 cm) with a solid, hypoechoic mass measuring 8.0×7.0 cm; Color Doppler ultrasound demonstrated blood flow within the mass.  
Abdominal CT showed an isodense splenic mass on noncontrast images, with heterogeneous enhancement in the arterial phase and isodensity to splenic parenchyma in the portal phase on contrast-enhanced CT.  
PET-CT showed no significant FDG accumulation within the mass.  
The differential diagnosis included splenic hamartoma, splenic hemangioma, splenomegaly due to extramedullary hematopoiesis, and malignant tumor (including solitary splenic metastasis). A laparoscopic splenectomy was performed given the possibility of malignancy, the presence of thrombocytopenia, and the risk of splenic rupture.

A 31-year-old man was incidentally found to have a moderate, asymptomatic pericardial effusion on echocardiography in early 2017. A subsequent CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated aortic, mediastinal, and pericardial thickening, bilateral pleural effusions, and a soft-tissue mass encasing the bilateral ureters and extending around the thoracic and abdominal aorta. Blood tests showed a white blood cell count of 14.5×10^9/L, neutrophils 9.99×10^9/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 16 mm/h, and CRP 9.45 mg/L. Antinuclear and ANCA antibodies were negative; IgG4 level, liver, and renal function were normal. Physical examination revealed distant heart sounds, no palpable lymphadenopathy or masses. 

Based on imaging and inflammatory markers, the patient was diagnosed with retroperitoneal fibrosis (RPF) and treated with intravenous methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisone and tamoxifen; cyclophosphamide was added later. Despite 6 months of therapy, repeat CT showed no reduction in the retroperitoneal mass, and the periaortic soft tissue encircled the aorta completely—findings atypical for RPF, which usually involves only the anterior and lateral aorta.

A 50-year-old woman with a 3-month history of progressive, dull, diffuse headache presented with nausea and dizziness on the day of admission. She had no focal neurologic deficits and normal cerebellar testing. Noncontrast CT of the brain revealed a 4.1×3.3 cm hypodense cystic lesion in the fourth ventricle and cerebellum. MRI showed a cystic lesion in the inferior cerebellar vermis with signal intensity identical to CSF on T1- and T2-weighted images; T2 imaging confirmed CSF-like content. Contrast-enhanced T1 images demonstrated a tiny enhancing mural portion at the right inferior cyst wall, suggestive of a mural nodule. Cerebral angiography revealed no definitive vascular abnormality or staining. On the basis of a T2-hyperintense cyst in the posterior fossa with an enhancing mural nodule, the lesion was clinically diagnosed as a cystic hemangioblastoma with a small nodule.

A 37-year-old woman presented with acute onset of lower abdominal pain that began one week earlier and intensified over the previous four hours. She had a history of a submucosal uterine myoma, stable in size on annual ultrasound over the past 10 years, with only occasional mild pelvic pain. She had two prior full-term vaginal deliveries and no other significant medical history.  

On examination, she had signs of peritoneal irritation with positive rebound tenderness. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 16,000/mL (80.1% neutrophils) and a C-reactive protein level of 2.1 g/dL. Transabdominal ultrasound demonstrated a large submucosal uterine mass exceeding 10 cm in diameter and free fluid in the pelvis.  

Contrast-enhanced CT scan revealed a heterogeneously enhancing pelvic mass measuring approximately 5 × 15 cm arising from the uterus and extending toward both ovaries (predominantly on the right), with reactive fluid in the pouch of Douglas and Morrison’s pouch and small (≈1 cm) retroperitoneal lymph nodes. The radiologist’s impression was a myomatous uterus with high suspicion for malignancy.  

A plan was made for total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. The patient, wishing to preserve fertility, consented to resection of the uterus and only the left ovary unless intraoperative frozen section indicated endometrial cancer. At laparotomy, a uterine mass was noted along with multiple lesions suggestive of adenomyosis and cord-like extensions from the uterus to the left ovary. Frozen-section biopsy of uterine tissue was negative for malignancy, and the surgeon proceeded with hysterectomy and left oophorectomy.

A 49-year-old premenopausal nulliparous woman presented with a longstanding history of severe constipation and intermittent abdominal pain since childhood. She reported bowel movements every 7 to 10 days, often requiring laxatives. One year earlier, she underwent exploratory laparotomy for ileus; the report noted extensive dilation and elongation of the colon with massive fecal impactions that were removed without other findings.

On current evaluation, laboratory tests and tumor markers were within normal limits. Anal manometry demonstrated basal waves and a normal rectosphincteric reflex. A barium enema revealed dilation of the entire colon, and colonic transit time was prolonged. Colonoscopy showed normal mucosal structure, and defecography was unremarkable.

Because of refractory chronic constipation, she underwent a subtotal colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis. Intraoperatively, the colon was markedly elongated and dilated. Gross examination of the resected distal ileum, cecum, ascending, transverse, and sigmoid colon revealed multiple hard, elastic nodular and polypoid formations in the mesenteric adipose tissue, up to 10 × 4 × 2.5 cm in size, either spherical-ovoid or irregularly shaped, connected to the bowel wall by thin fibrous bands. Cut surfaces were gray-white and fibrous. The colonic mucosa appeared normal, but the bowel wall was hardened and partially thickened (approximately 1.5 cm). The parietal and pelvic peritoneum, small-intestinal mesentery, uterus, and ovaries were grossly normal.

A 34-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a rash on the right side of her face. She first noticed multiple skin-colored, firm papules at age 5. The lesions have been asymptomatic but cosmetically bothersome, and there is no family history of similar lesions. Her medical history is otherwise unremarkable.

On examination, there are numerous 2–8 mm smooth, firm, nontender, skin-colored papules localized to the mid-forehead, right eyebrow, eyelids, right cheek, and right nasolabial fold; no lesions are present elsewhere.

Contact polarized dermatoscopy of the papules reveals an ivory-white background with bright white linear streaks and scattered yellow and light-brown dots and clods.

A 62-year-old woman presented with a two-month history of weight loss, fever, night sweats, and increasing abdominal size. Her medical history included rheumatoid arthritis treated with chloroquine and methotrexate, and untreated chronic non-replicating hepatitis B virus infection (HBsAg positive, HBeAg negative, HBV DNA 10^4 IU/ml). HIV and HCV serologies were negative. On examination, she appeared emaciated and pale, with massive splenomegaly, no hepatomegaly, and no lymphadenopathy. CT imaging confirmed subtle hepatomegaly and marked splenomegaly without lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.8 g/dl, platelet count 124 ×10^9/l, and total leukocyte count 6.18 ×10^9/l. Peripheral smear revealed that 21% of lymphoid cells had a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, loose chromatin, a small clear nucleolus, and thin cytoplasmic projections. Immunophenotyping of peripheral blood lymphocytes demonstrated positivity for CD19, CD20, FMC7, CD22, CD23, strong CD79b and CD25, weak surface IgM, partial CD5 expression, and negativity for CD200, CD10, CD11c, and CD103; monoclonality was confirmed by kappa light-chain restriction. Bone marrow biopsy showed intrasinusoidal infiltration by small B lymphoid cells.

A 60-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of painless swelling on the right side of his face, associated with progressive facial asymmetry. His medical history was noncontributory. On examination, there was a large, purple, fluctuant mass overlying the right posterior mandibular body and ramus without cranial nerve deficits. Soft-tissue sonography showed a hypoechoic mass measuring 49 × 22 × 40 mm on the right mandible with cortical plate disruption. MRI revealed an expansile lytic lesion in the right posterior mandibular body and ramus with cortical erosion, extraosseous extension between the masseter and pterygoid muscles (without muscle invasion), infiltration of the mandibular condyle, extension into the oral floor, and lymphadenopathy in levels Ib and II; post-contrast images demonstrated homogeneous enhancement with small nonenhancing necrotic areas. A 17 × 10 mm lymph node anterior to the right submandibular gland and a 21 × 12 mm enhancing lesion in the right cerebellopontine angle cistern were also noted. Under ultrasound guidance, a core biopsy of the mandibular mass was performed. Microscopic examination revealed two separate populations of neoplastic cells displaying prominent cellular atypia, nuclear pleomorphism, and numerous mitotic figures.

A 65-year-old man with no past medical history, HIV negative, was diagnosed with mixed superficial spreading and desmoplastic melanoma of the left elbow (Breslow thickness 3 mm, non-ulcerated, mitotic rate 3/mm2). He underwent lymphoscintigraphy for sentinel node mapping prior to wide excision. Ultrasound identified a 40 × 11 × 20 mm solid hypoechoic mass in a left axillary lymph node. The patient was asymptomatic with no systemic signs. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the node showed normal lymphoid cells with admixed macrophages and no malignant cells. Because of ongoing concern for metastatic involvement, ultrasound-guided FNA was repeated three months later and again showed no malignant cells.

A 51-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of progressive nasal obstruction, intermittent epistaxis, headaches, decreasing visual acuity, and diplopia. She denied nausea, vomiting, or seizures. On examination, she had left-eye strabismus due to abducens-nerve palsy; there were no sensory or motor deficits in the extremities, and the rest of her examination was unremarkable. Computed tomography of the head showed a large, heterogeneous, expansile lesion measuring 75 × 54 mm, centered on the sphenoid bone and clivus, with erosion of adjacent bone and extension into the nasal cavity and nasopharynx. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a lobulated mass in the sphenoidal region with heterogeneous signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images, abutting the optic nerve and internal carotid arteries.

A 60-year-old man presented with one month of night sweats and malaise and one week of increasing exertional dyspnoea. He had a history of congenital aortic stenosis treated with aortoplasty at age 17, mechanical aortic-valve replacement at age 35, and aortic stenting at age 58. He was taking losartan and warfarin, and his self-monitored INR had fluctuated between below 2 and above 5 over the prior five weeks. On examination, he was dyspnoeic at rest, blood pressure was 92/66 mmHg, there was a holosystolic murmur in the left second intercostal space, bibasal crackles, and mild peripheral oedema. Laboratory tests showed haemoglobin 9.2 g/dL, LDH 260 U/L, and CRP 129 mg/L. The ECG demonstrated normal sinus rhythm, left axis deviation, and poor R-wave progression. Chest X-ray revealed pulmonary congestion, Kerley B lines, and bilateral pleural effusions. Transthoracic echocardiography showed large masses in the left atrium causing functional mitral stenosis (mean gradient 13 mmHg) and protruding into the left ventricle causing an aortic outflow gradient of 130 mmHg; tricuspid regurgitation gradient was 50 mmHg. Transoesophageal echocardiography confirmed massive masses in the left atrium and ventricle perforating the mitral valve and extending into the left ventricular outflow tract, resulting in functional obstruction. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a mass in the left atrium and ventricle, pulmonary congestion, and enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes; the mass had a radiodensity of 50 Hounsfield units. PET/CT showed strong metabolic activity of the masses in the left atrium, left ventricle, and septum. All mediastinal lymph nodes lacked significant uptake and were thought to be benign.

A 58-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of swelling and pain of the right upper posterior gums. Two months earlier he had undergone an uneventful tooth extraction in the same region after noticing a loosening tooth. He reported epistaxis and blood-tinged sputum over the past month.  

On examination, there was mild right facial swelling. Intraorally, a single large noduloproliferative growth was noted on the right maxillary ridge, extending from the second premolar to the tuberosity and onto the mid-palate, not crossing midline. The lesion was firm, sessile, tender, and covered by reddish-pink mucosa. No regional lymphadenopathy was palpable.  

Panoramic radiography showed loss of the right maxillary antral bone with ragged borders extending to the orbital floor, destruction of the right alveolar bone, and a soft-tissue shadow over the ridge. A paranasal sinus view demonstrated destruction of the superior, lateral, and facial walls of the right maxillary antrum, lateral expansion of the right malar bone, medial involvement of the middle and inferior nasal conchae, destruction of the right infraorbital margin, and bilateral antral haziness.  

Routine blood tests, urinalysis, chest radiograph, and serologic tests for HIV and hepatitis B virus were all normal or negative.  

Incisional biopsy revealed squamous mucosa with underlying diffuse, uniform proliferation of small round cells with large dark nuclei, scant eosinophilic cytoplasm, loose fibrocellular stroma, and comedo necrosis, suggestive of a lymphoproliferative disease.  

Immunohistochemical staining showed that the tumor cells were positive for CD45 and negative for CD20.

A 55-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of left-sided ear pain, diminished hearing, and pulsatile tinnitus in the same ear. Otoscopic examination revealed a purple, ovoid, nonpulsatile, exophytic lesion on the superior quadrant of the left tympanic membrane, with a pedicle at the manubrium of the malleus. A temporal-bone CT scan demonstrated a smooth, round, 3-mm mass on the external surface of the tympanic membrane and showed no evidence of bone erosion or middle-ear extension. Pure-tone audiometry revealed a mixed hearing loss in the left ear, with a 20–30 dB air–bone gap at frequencies of 250–1000 Hz.

A 14-year-old girl with no prior medical history noted a lump in her left breast that had rapidly increased in size over the preceding two months. On examination, there was a well-demarcated, painless, mobile mass in the inner quadrant of the left breast and the overlying skin was unremarkable. Breast ultrasound showed a 79 × 53.5 mm ovoid mass with lobulated contours and mixed echogenicity (hypo-, iso-, and hyper-echoic areas), no internal vascularity on Doppler, and no calcifications, causing a mass effect on adjacent tissue. Considering the patient’s age, rapid growth, and ultrasound appearance, the leading considerations were giant juvenile fibroadenoma and phyllodes tumor.

A 42-year-old woman was admitted with a 1-month history of headaches, nausea, and vomiting. She had lost 2 kg and experienced diplopia, bilateral orbital pain, and gaze disturbances. On examination, she had bilateral third and sixth cranial nerve palsies. Laboratory tests revealed alpha-fetoprotein 1665 ng/mL, carcinoembryonic antigen 1493 ng/mL, and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 695 U/mL; other studies were normal. CT of the brain showed a bulging bony mass destroying the clivus and involving the sphenoid and cavernous sinuses. MRI demonstrated a 2.7 × 1.6 × 2.0 cm sellar mass in the upper clivus with cystic change and heterogeneous enhancement, extending into the cavernous sinuses, both internal carotid arteries, and the optic chiasm, with destruction of the clivus and sphenoid corpus. Abdominal CT suggested gastric cancer with liver and multiple lymph node metastases. Endoscopic evaluation confirmed advanced poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma at the cardia. Chest CT showed left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. A lumbar puncture yielded clear fluid, normal opening pressure, and no malignant cells.

A 65-year-old man with type II diabetes mellitus and a history of distal sigmoid colorectal adenocarcinoma presented with acute onset of left ankle pain. Six years earlier, he had undergone Hartmann’s procedure for a pT4N0M0 Dukes B tumour, end colostomy, lung nodule resection (confirmed colorectal metastasis), and adjuvant chemotherapy; subsequent surveillance for five years included normal CEA levels and unremarkable CT scans of chest, abdomen, and pelvis, as well as negative rectal stump biopsies. On this presentation, antero-posterior and lateral ankle radiographs revealed only mild degenerative changes of the tibio-talar and mid-tarsal joints with a small plantar calcaneal spur. He was treated conservatively, but ankle pain persisted and swelling increased. A diagnosis of Charcot’s joint was made in keeping with his diabetes. Other differentials included ankle fracture, osteomyelitis, arthritis, and bony metastasis.

A 34-year-old woman presented with an eight-month history of episodic abdominal pain accompanied by nausea and vomiting. Over several weeks, she visited the emergency department four times for migrating abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting and was treated empirically for gastroenteritis and irritable bowel syndrome. Each time, evaluations including urine studies, abdominal ultrasound, and CT of the abdomen and pelvis were unrevealing apart from incidentally noted physiologic ovarian cysts. Because her symptoms persisted, she underwent exploratory laparoscopy. On the day after surgery, she developed progressive neurological deterioration. Noncontrast cranial CT demonstrated hydrocephalus. On examination, she was obtunded, moaning in response to painful stimuli, moving all four extremities spontaneously, and had large sluggishly reactive pupils. She underwent emergent ventriculostomy and returned to her neurologic baseline within 24 hours. Subsequent MRI of the brain demonstrated a nonenhancing cystic mass near the caudal fourth ventricle, with obstructive hydrocephalus and brainstem compression.

A 53-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with low back pain and acute right foot drop. She had a history of chronic low back pain radiating to both legs for over a year; a lumbar CT performed two months earlier had shown an L5–S1 disc protrusion. She noted an exacerbation of her back pain over the past week and, for the 48 hours before presentation, a sensation of heaviness in her right leg with subjective weakness of dorsiflexion. There was no history of trauma, fever, weight loss, incontinence, or constitutional symptoms.  

Medical history was notable for psoriasis and inflammatory arthritis in remission on sulfasalazine; she was an active smoker (20 pack-years) and worked as a housekeeper.  

On examination, upper-limb strength and reflexes were normal. The left lower limb was normal. In the right lower limb, iliopsoas and quadriceps strength were slightly decreased; tibialis anterior and toe extensor strength were nearly absent. Foot plantar flexors and intrinsic foot muscles were intact. Sensation was reduced over the L5 and S1 dermatomes on the right. The right straight-leg raise test was positive; deep tendon reflexes were normal; plantar responses were flexor. Peripheral pulses were normal.  

Given presumed lumbar radiculopathy, a repeat lumbar CT showed the known central and right L5–S1 disc protrusion with degenerative and sclerotic changes, unchanged from prior imaging. A gadolinium-enhanced lumbar MRI confirmed right L5–S1 foraminal stenosis but showed no central canal stenosis or cord abnormality. A pelvic and hip CT scan was unremarkable for any mass or osseous lesion.

A 40-year-old previously healthy Puerto Rican man presented with 3 months of diffuse, cramping abdominal pain, nausea, loose brown stools, and a 9-kg unintentional weight loss. He denied anorexia, travel, dietary changes, or sick contacts. He had no prior surgeries, medications, or family history of gastrointestinal disease. On examination, his abdomen was soft, distended, and diffusely tender without peritoneal signs.

Initial laboratory studies were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed marked wall thickening of the transverse and proximal descending colon with dilation of the ascending colon. Colonoscopy showed mucosal edema, inflammation, and luminal stenosis from 30 cm to the distal transverse colon. Multiple biopsies demonstrated mild acute and chronic inflammation without evidence of dysplasia or malignancy.

He was treated with ciprofloxacin and metronidazole for presumed infectious colitis, with mild symptomatic improvement, and discharged. One month later, he returned with persistent symptoms; stool studies for infectious pathogens and a celiac panel were negative, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was normal. Magnetic resonance enterography (MRE) demonstrated right colon dilation, transverse colon thickening, and adjacent fat stranding. He improved transiently with bowel rest, prednisone (60 mg daily), and mesalamine (800 mg three times daily) for presumed inflammatory bowel disease.

At 1-month follow-up, intermittent symptoms persisted. Repeat CT showed severe transverse colitis with proximal dilation. Infliximab therapy was initiated for presumed refractory IBD. One month later, he was readmitted with ongoing pain and nausea; imaging was unchanged. Repeat colonoscopy revealed segmental colitis with a stricture in the transverse colon, pseudopolyps, and small aphthous ulcers in the terminal ileum, concerning for Crohn’s disease. Biopsies again showed mild acute and chronic inflammation without granulomas, dysplasia, or malignancy.

Reluctant to restart anti–tumor necrosis factor therapy, he was discharged on azathioprine (100 mg daily) in addition to prednisone and mesalamine. One month later, he presented with obstructive symptoms unresponsive to bowel rest and high-dose intravenous steroids. C-reactive protein was elevated at 32.7 mg/L. Repeat MRE showed persistent thickening of the transverse colon without mesenteric stranding. Given ongoing obstruction and refractory disease, he was taken for total colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis.

A 9-year-old boy presented with a 3-week history of dull, persistent, positional headaches localized to the left side of his skull, accompanied by nausea and vomiting for 7 days that were refractory to antiemetic therapy. His past medical history was unremarkable. On examination he was alert (GCS 15), with normal vital signs; pupils were equal and reactive, cranial nerves intact, deep tendon reflexes 2+ throughout, and muscle strength 5/5 in all extremities. During hospitalization he developed altered mental status and experienced a focal seizure. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed a 5 × 3 × 1 cm mass in the right temporal lobe. He underwent a right temporal craniotomy with gross total excision of the tumor.

A 72-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of pain and discomfort in the right posterior mandibular region. He had undergone root canal therapy on the right mandibular second molar without relief. His history was notable for total thyroidectomy 3 years earlier, with pathology showing a follicular adenoma in the left thyroid and an adenomatous goiter in the right thyroid; he took levothyroxine 75 µg daily. On examination, the right face was mildly swollen; a hard, tender bony mass (~3 cm × 3 cm) was palpable at the right mandibular angle. The right mandibular second molar was mobile (Grade II), the right lower lip was numb, and intraoral mucosa was unremarkable. Cone-beam CT of the mandible demonstrated severe resorption and disorganization of bone from the right second molar region to the angle, with ill-defined, rough margins, needle-like periosteal bone formation, and obliteration of the mandibular canal. Biopsy of the lesion yielded epithelioid-derived tumor tissue; immunohistochemistry showed CK5/6 (–), CK7 (focally +), CD14 (–), S-100 (–), Ki-67 < 3%, NSE (–), chromogranin A (–), synaptophysin (–), and P63 (focally +), with detection of suspected thyroid tissue components.

A 24-year-old man with a 3-year history of Crohn’s disease in remission underwent routine surveillance colonoscopy. He was asymptomatic, with no abdominal pain, weight loss, or change in bowel habits. He had no significant medical or family history, did not smoke, and drank alcohol only occasionally.

Vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination was unremarkable. Testicular examination revealed no masses.

Colonoscopy identified a single 25 mm polypoid, sessile, friable, ulcerated lesion in the caecum. No other lesions were seen. Mucosal biopsy showed fragments of an ulcerating tumour comprising nests, small dyshesive clusters, and poorly formed tubules within desmoplastic stroma; intravascular tumour emboli were present. Adjacent large-bowel mucosa exhibited villous accentuation, hypermucinosis, and patchy neutrophilic infiltrates.

Immunohistochemical staining of the biopsy was diffusely positive for glypican 3 and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). Serum AFP was elevated at 2145 IU/ml; carcinoembryonic antigen and human chorionic gonadotropin levels were normal.

Scrotal ultrasound showed no testicular masses. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed no pineal or suprasellar lesions. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography demonstrated increased fluorodeoxyglucose uptake confined to the caecal lesion and adjacent mesenteric lymph nodes.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 6-year-old girl presented with chronic white lesions of the oral mucosa that first appeared at age 2. There was no parental consanguinity and no family history of similar lesions. The lesions had been treated as mucosal candidiasis for more than 3 years without improvement. The patient was asymptomatic except for occasional burning when eating acidic or spicy foods. On examination, there were bilateral, symmetric, well-defined, irregular, white plaques on the buccal mucosa. The mucosa was not erythematous, and the plaques could not be scraped off with a tongue blade. A periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) stain for fungal elements was negative.

A 52-year-old woman was readmitted with a wound infection 2 weeks after mastectomy for breast cancer. She had received antibiotics for presumed infective endocarditis after transthoracic echocardiography showed a 1.0 cm mobile, spherical mass attached to the anterior mitral leaflet. Because the size of the cardiac mass had not changed despite 2 weeks of antibiotics, she was referred for further evaluation. Her blood pressure, pulse, and respiratory rate were within normal limits; temperature was 37.5 °C. Laboratory evaluation showed a leukocyte count of 15,700/mm3, platelet count of 3,251,000/mm3, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 53 mm/h. Results of urinalysis, blood chemistry, and electrolytes were normal. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed a mass >1.0 cm in size, mobile, attached to the atrial aspect of the anterior mitral leaflet, and round with a homogeneously speckled surface; there was moderate-to-severe mitral regurgitation.

A 75-year-old man was referred for evaluation of erythrocytosis discovered during follow‐up for cerebral arteriosclerosis. He appeared sanguineous; his oxygen saturation on room air was 96%. He had a history of hypertension and cerebral arteriosclerosis treated with aspirin and atorvastatin. He denied dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, smoking, high-altitude residence, and there was no family history of polycythemia or myeloproliferative disorders.

Laboratory studies showed: hemoglobin 175 g/L, hematocrit 54.7%, mean corpuscular volume 101 fL, lactate dehydrogenase normal, blood urea nitrogen 10.05 mmol/L, creatinine 143.2 µmol/L. Serum erythropoietin level was 53.9 mIU/mL (reference 1.48–31.88). Mutation analysis for JAK2 (V617F and exons 12–15), MPL, CALR, and CSF3R was negative. BCR::ABL1 transcripts were negative. Serum protein studies revealed a monoclonal IgA-λ spike of 5.65 g/L; IgA was elevated at 7.63 g/L (normal 0.82–4.53 g/L), with normal IgG and IgM levels. Abdominal ultrasound showed no masses or organomegaly, and spinal MRI showed no bone lesions.

A 27-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of diffuse, colicky abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. The pain began in the right lower quadrant, became generalized, and was associated with abdominal distension. She had bilious vomiting and was unable to tolerate oral intake for 24 hours. She initially had loose stools but reported no bowel movements or flatus for 2 days. Her surgical history was notable only for a previous cesarean delivery.

On examination, she was tachycardic, tachypneic, hypotensive, and afebrile. The abdomen was distended with generalized tenderness and diffuse guarding. Bowel sounds were exaggerated with borborygmi. Rectal examination revealed an empty rectal vault with suprapubic ballooning.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 16 × 10^9/L (neutrophils 89.3%), a C-reactive protein level of 286 mg/L, and a serum lactate of 2.4 mmol/L. A plain abdominal radiograph demonstrated dilated small-bowel loops with multiple air-fluid levels and a collapsed large bowel. Chest radiography showed no free air under the diaphragm.

An urgent CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a prominent “target sign” in the right lower quadrant, consistent with a long-segment ileocolic intussusception. Within the intussuscepted loop was a well-defined, predominantly fatty lesion with enhancing septations, suggestive of an intestinal lipoma serving as the lead point. There was upstream dilatation of the small bowel and stomach with collapse of the colon distal to the hepatic flexure.

A 42-year-old Caucasian woman was referred for evaluation of a large, pedunculated, painless mass on the anterior thoracic wall. She reported that the lesion had been present for approximately 22 years and had been incompletely resected twice, with subsequent locoregional recurrence. Over the past 3 months she also experienced fatigue and weakness. 

On examination, the mass was exophytic, pseudolobulated, and tan-pink, measuring 18 × 10 cm, with multiple hemorrhagic foci, areas of yellow and black necrosis, and localized infection with purulent exudate. No regional lymphadenopathy was noted.

Laboratory studies showed hypochromic microcytic anemia with a hemoglobin level of 5.2 mg/dL, which improved after transfusion of two units of packed red blood cells.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the chest revealed a highly vascular soft-tissue mass infiltrating the chest wall without involvement of bone or cartilage. A chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasound showed no evidence of metastatic disease. To reduce intraoperative bleeding, a preoperative selective embolization of the right internal thoracic artery was performed.

A 37-year-old woman with sporadic Peutz–Jeghers syndrome (intestinal hamartomatous polyposis status-post small bowel resection, prior ovarian sex cord tumor treated by bilateral oophorectomy) presented with two months of metrorrhagia, profuse watery vaginal discharge, low abdominal pain, and vaginal bleeding. Gynecologic examination showed an enlarged cervix with normal-appearing mucosa. Transvaginal ultrasound revealed a poorly vascularized, heterogeneous submucosal cervical lesion and fluid accumulation in the endometrial cavity due to cervical stenosis. Endocervical curettage cytology was nondiagnostic. Pelvic MRI demonstrated:
• A 65×32×30 mm cervical mass that was isointense on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images  
• The lesion comprised more than 20 microcysts (≤5 mm diameter, smooth walls) and a solid component deeply infiltrating the right cervical stroma (less on the left), suggesting parametrial extension; the solid part also invaded the lower uterine body, isthmus, and upper vagina  
• Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images showed enhancement of the lesion  
• On diffusion-weighted imaging (b = 800), both cystic and solid components were hyperintense, but there was no diffusion restriction on the ADC map

A 53-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with a two-year history of vague, paroxysmal abdominal pain localized to the right hypochondrium, occurring throughout the day. She denied fever, vomiting, or jaundice but reported a 10-kg weight loss over this period. Her general condition was well preserved; vital signs were stable. On abdominal examination, a fixed, well-limited 4-cm mass was palpable in the right hypochondrium; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including liver and renal function, were within normal limits. Six months earlier, an abdominal ultrasound had shown no abnormalities. A contrast-enhanced CT scan revealed a heterogeneous, lobulated soft-tissue mass arising from the anterior wall of the inferior vena cava, measuring 50 × 37 × 46 mm, with invasion of the right renal vein. On MRI, the lesion was of low signal on T1, T2, and diffusion sequences, demonstrated intraluminal extension, and showed enhancement after gadolinium injection. The mass abutted the duodenum, pancreatic head, and hepatic pedicle without definite invasion. No lymphadenopathy or metastatic lesions were identified.  
Differential diagnoses of a retroperitoneal mass affecting the inferior vena cava included cruoric thrombus, leiomyosarcoma, intimal sarcoma, gastrointestinal stromal tumor, adrenal tumors (such as pheochromocytoma) extending into the IVC, and paraganglioma. However, all the radiological findings were highly suggestive of a leiomyosarcoma of the inferior vena cava according to the opinion of the vascular and digestive surgery teams and radiologists.

A 31-year-old woman (gravida 0, para 0) presented with a 1-year history of a progressively enlarging pelvic mass and heavy menstrual bleeding. On pelvic examination, the uterus was enlarged to approximately the size of a 5-month pregnancy, with an uneven surface and limited mobility. Hysteroscopic evaluation showed a bulging anterior uterine wall but no distinct fibroid nodules. Transabdominal ultrasound revealed multiple heterogeneous intrauterine masses measuring up to 10.0 × 8.8 × 7.4 cm. Hemoglobin was 80 g/L.

She underwent uterine myomectomy. Intraoperatively, the masses were soft, round, finger-like, and cord-like, with no clear boundary between the lesions and adjacent pseudo-envelope. Frozen-section pathology indicated degenerated leiomyoma; permanent pathology confirmed uterine leiomyoma. Postoperatively, she received 3 months of GnRH-agonist therapy. One month after therapy, her menstruation resumed with heavy bleeding similar to baseline, and ultrasound again demonstrated uterine fibroids. Over the next 3 years, fibroids gradually enlarged, and she developed severe anemia requiring intermittent transfusions.

In July 2020, she was readmitted for severe anemia. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis demonstrated the uterine mass extending into the left iliac vein, the common iliac vein, and the inferior vena cava, with evidence of intraluminal tumor.

A 61-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidemia presented with a left upper abdominal wall mass that began as a tiny nodule and gradually enlarged over 15 years. The lesion caused intermittent pain, bloody discharge, and skin changes around the mass. She denied fever, weight loss, trauma, or a family history of cancer. On examination, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Local inspection revealed a brown, mobile, pedunculated polypoid mass with an irregular border, measuring approximately 3.0 cm × 2.0 cm, on the left upper abdomen. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated an anterior left upper abdominal wall, skin-based, pedunculated soft-tissue nodule with a large stalk, measuring 1.8 cm × 3.6 cm × 3.6 cm, without evidence of invasion into deeper soft tissues. Surgical excision was planned for definitive diagnosis and treatment.

A 60-year-old woman presented with acute-onset dyspnea and palpitations. Her oxygen saturation was 66% on room air, heart rate 145 beats/min, and respiratory rate 40 breaths/min. Four weeks earlier she had developed unilateral left lower-leg edema, erythema, and pain. Over the preceding week her functional class had declined from New York Heart Association grade I to III. With supplemental oxygen her saturation improved to 88%, and pulmonary embolism was suspected. CT pulmonary angiography showed acute pulmonary emboli in lobar branches, deep-vein thrombosis of the left leg, and a 10 cm multicystic, septated pelvic mass in the left adnexal region.  
On examination she had jugular venous distention and a positive hepatojugular reflux. NT-proBNP was >25 000 pg/mL, troponin I 186.8 pg/mL, and lactate 4.3 mmol/L. She underwent thrombolysis with alteplase and was intubated for respiratory failure. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a markedly dilated right ventricle with systolic dysfunction, a dilated right atrium, global right-ventricular hypokinesia, and severe tricuspid regurgitation.  
She then developed persistent hypotension, fever, and clinical signs of septic shock. Empiric antibiotics were started; blood cultures later grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Despite fluids and vasopressors, she deteriorated. Given the adnexal mass, an oncologic workup with abdominal ultrasound and CT was performed, revealing multiple hepatic lesions suggestive of metastases. Over the next days she evolved to multi-organ failure and died.

A 51-year-old woman with a history of right shoulder melanoma excised seven years earlier presented with chest pain and palpitations. Emergency medical services recorded a wide-complex tachycardia that terminated after vagal maneuvers. On admission, her vital signs and physical examination were normal. Laboratory studies showed a peak high-sensitivity troponin I of 935 ng/L (normal < 49 ng/L), with normal blood counts and metabolic panel. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. The arrhythmia was diagnosed as monomorphic ventricular tachycardia based on right bundle-branch–block morphology not present in sinus rhythm, a monophasic R wave in V1, and an R:S ratio < 1 in V6. Coronary angiography revealed normal coronary arteries. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging was performed to evaluate for scar or infiltration and demonstrated a left ventricular mass, prompting transfer for further evaluation.

Transthoracic echocardiography with contrast showed a small LV chamber without outflow or intracavitary obstruction, mild mitral regurgitation, and a non-mobile mass in the mid-to-basal septum and inferior walls with mild contrast enhancement. There was normal biventricular systolic function and no regional wall-motion abnormalities.

Outside-hospital CMR (1.5 T) confirmed a 5.9 × 4.4 × 2.6 cm mass in the mid-to-basal inferoseptal and inferior walls with eccentric mitral regurgitation due to restricted posterior leaflet motion. On CMR:
• T2-weighted fat-suppressed images showed hyperintense signal in the mass compared with myocardium.  
• T1-weighted images showed hyperintense signal in the mass relative to myocardium.  
• Inversion-recovery steady-state images (IR 600 ms) showed the mass to be isointense to myocardium.  
• T1 mapping demonstrated elevated T1 relaxation times in the mass.  
• First-pass perfusion imaging showed significant perfusion of the mass.  
• Delayed myocardial enhancement sequences showed diffuse enhancement throughout the mass.

Contrast-enhanced chest, abdomen, and pelvis CT did not identify any extracardiac primary malignancy. The mass lacked calcification and measured 74 Hounsfield units, inconsistent with fat or fluid.

On the basis of imaging, the differential included secondary metastatic tumour or a primary malignant tumour such as angiosarcoma or rhabdomyosarcoma, while benign primary tumours (haemangioma, myxoma) were deemed less likely.

A 79-year-old Black man with type 2 diabetes mellitus was referred after a routine diabetic eye exam identified a choroidal mass in the left eye. He was asymptomatic, with no history of cancer or neurofibromatosis. His visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally, without a relative afferent pupillary defect or visual field deficit. Slit-lamp examination was unremarkable except for mild nuclear sclerotic cataracts. Fundus examination of the right eye showed extramacular drusen without diabetic retinopathy. In the left eye, there was a 12.0 × 11.0 × 3.9 mm pigmented choroidal lesion abutting the optic nerve from 7:00 to 1:00, with an amelanotic central portion and overlying retinal pigment epithelial hyperplasia. Standardized ocular echography (B-scan) revealed a dome-shaped choroidal lesion measuring 3.9 mm in thickness with irregular internal reflectivity and no internal vascularity. Posterior to the globe, there was a 3.8 mm thick dome-shaped area concerning for extraocular extension, also low reflective and avascular. Optical coherence tomography over the lesion showed a dome-shaped elevation with chronic-appearing cystoid intraretinal fluid and retinal pigment epithelial atrophy at the apex.

A 17-year-old Syrian adolescent presented with a 6-month history of pain and swelling over the anterior aspect of the left leg. The pain was constant, worsened with activity, and improved with rest. There was no history of trauma or other medical conditions. On examination, there was a 3 cm × 2 cm bony-hard, immobile swelling over the anterior left tibia; the overlying skin was warm but not tethered. 

A plain radiograph of the left tibia demonstrated an intracortical, oval radiolucent lesion in the diaphysis. CT of the left tibia showed an intracortical, isodense lesion in the anterior cortex of the midshaft. MRI T1-weighted and T2-weighted sequences revealed a focal lesion of increased signal intensity involving the anterior cortex of the midshaft of the tibia.

A 68-year-old man presented with vague right flank pain and a history of nephrolithiasis. CT of the abdomen revealed a large heterogeneous left upper-quadrant mass. MRI confirmed a 16 × 9 cm lesion with cystic and solid components arising from the gastric wall, causing mass effect on the pancreas but without lymphadenopathy or metastases. Endoscopic ultrasound showed a submucosal lesion with intact mucosa. Fine-needle aspiration cytology demonstrated a paucity of bland spindle cells. On cell block, the lesional cells stained strongly for CD34 and failed to stain for DOG1 and CD117; PDGFR and succinate dehydrogenase testing could not be performed due to limited material. Despite these equivocal results, a GIST was favored based on morphology and location. Given extensive tumor necrosis, the patient began imatinib therapy rather than undergo repeat biopsy. After 4 weeks of imatinib, imaging showed no significant regression.

A 3-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a 6-month history of dysphagia and repeated oral bleeding. On examination, there was a soft, painful, reddish-blue, immobilized mass measuring approximately 3 cm in its greatest dimension on the mid-dorsum of the tongue extending toward the base, without cervical lymphadenopathy. Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI showed a 3.3×1.9×2.0 cm hypervascular mass obstructing the pharyngeal inlet, initially interpreted as a hemangioma. Under general anesthesia, an incisional biopsy was performed; histopathology was reported as a benign capillary hemangioma by both the treating institution and a specialized vascular anomalies center. The patient received systemic corticosteroids and interferon alpha-2a, but over the next six months the mass continued to enlarge, leading to partial airway obstruction. He underwent tracheostomy and wide local excision of the lesion; review at a pediatric tumor center again favored hemangioma.

A 24-year-old man presented with a 10-day history of thoracic back pain radiating to his right shoulder, associated with increased sweating over his right upper body and face and decreased sensation in his right chest. On examination, he had right thoracic pain, gait disturbance, right-sided hypoesthesia, hemi-hyperhidrosis, a positive right Babinski sign, increased reflexes in the right arm and leg, and ataxia consistent with posterior-column involvement. Cranial nerves were intact, there were no motor deficits or meningism, and bladder function was preserved. MRI of the spine showed a large intramedullary lesion extending from C5 to T7 with multiple contrast-enhancing lesions at the craniocervical junction and throughout the spinal cord, as well as heterogeneous vertebral signals suggestive of osseous involvement. Brain MRI demonstrated multiple periventricular contrast-enhancing lesions. CT of the thorax and abdomen revealed diffuse osseous metastases of the entire spine and sternum but no lesions in other organs. Lumbar-puncture CSF analysis revealed atypical cells concerning for leptomeningeal spread, although the cell count was too low for immunohistochemical studies.

A 17-year-old boy presented with a 10-month history of gradually increasing severe, continuous low back pain radiating along the L5 and S1 distributions, unrelieved by analgesics. He noted new lower extremity weakness and pain on walking in the days before presentation. There was no history of trauma or prior medical problems. On examination, strength in the proximal and distal left leg was 3/5, the Mingazzini sign was positive on the left, and he had difficulty standing for prolonged periods. The remainder of the physical examination and laboratory studies were unremarkable. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar and sacral spine revealed a large soft-tissue mass that was isointense on T1-weighted images and heterogeneous on T2-weighted images, with peripheral enhancement. The mass was centered at the L5 level, showed an “hourglass sign” through a widened foramen, and had an intradural extramedullary component extending from L4 to S2, displacing neural elements and causing posterior scalloping and cortical lysis of lumbar and sacral vertebrae. The lesion extended through the left S1 foramen (which was widened and lysed) into the left sacrum—most notably at S1—where there were small T2-hyperintense foci and more heterogeneous enhancement. It also extended through the left S2 and S3 foramina with nerve enlargement and infiltrated the left piriformis muscle. There was prevertebral extension displacing abdominal contents anteriorly, and invasion of the bilateral longissimus thoracis and left psoas muscles.  

Computed tomography of the lumbosacral spine confirmed significant destruction of the S1 vertebral body.

A 63-year-old woman was found to have a new right breast mass on routine screening. Mammography revealed a 35-mm lobular, densely calcified lesion in the medial right breast. Ultrasound showed an irregular 11.1 × 20.1 mm mass. On examination, a firm, golf-ball-sized lesion was palpable at the 6- to 9-o’clock position; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable, and her only comorbidity was hypertension.

In July 2009, a core needle biopsy demonstrated ductal hyperplasia with metaplastic ossification; no malignant cells were identified. The findings were reviewed by two pathologists, and metaplastic carcinoma was considered in the differential. Complete excision with standard margins was performed in October 2009, confirming metaplastic ossification with tumor-free margins. No adjuvant therapy was given, and she underwent clinical follow-up every 3–6 months for 2 years.

Three years after the excision, she returned with a rapidly enlarging right breast mass measuring approximately 150 × 80 × 70 mm, extending into the axilla with overlying skin ulceration. PET-CT and staging studies revealed no evidence of metastatic disease.

A 71-year-old woman presented with painful nodules on her frontal-parietal scalp. MRI and CT scans showed frontal bone and adjacent subgaleal soft-tissue abnormalities without involvement of the brain parenchyma. In January 2010, she underwent a frontal bone craniotomy and dural biopsy, which revealed a malignant spindle and epithelioid cell neoplasm that was focally positive for smooth muscle actin and negative for cytokeratins, EMA, CD34, desmin, GFAP, and S100. Focal necrosis was present, and mitotic figures numbered up to 5 per 10 high-power fields, leading to a diagnosis of an unclassified high-grade sarcoma. A PET scan showed FDG uptake only in the scalp, and her CBCs were within normal limits. She began temozolomide and radiation therapy; temozolomide was discontinued after one month due to thrombocytopenia, and radiation continued for three months. Five months later, PET imaging showed new FDG-avid lesions in both kidneys, with no residual uptake at the calvarium or in the brain. A biopsy of a renal lesion demonstrated an epithelioid neoplasm with a prominent infiltrative pattern between renal tubules. Immunohistochemistry showed nuclear reactivity for PAX8 but was negative for cytokeratins, EMA, CD34, RCC antigen, smooth muscle actin, and desmin. Although PAX8 is commonly used to confirm renal epithelial neoplasms, the infiltrative growth pattern, cytologic features, and absence of other markers typical of renal primaries raised the possibility of a B-cell lymphoma.

A 62-year-old woman presents with 24 hours of fever, left-sided flank pain, and foul-smelling urine. Five years earlier she underwent bilateral lung transplantation for severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (FEV1 15%). Her past medical history is notable for hypertension and a 70–pack-year smoking history. Immunosuppressive therapy consists of prednisone and tacrolimus; mycophenolate mofetil was discontinued for leukopenia. Prophylactic antimicrobial therapy includes trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, itraconazole, and valganciclovir (continued for detectable CMV viremia). On examination she is febrile but otherwise unrevealing. Laboratory studies show a leukocytosis of 20,000 per µL (neutrophils 18,150 per µL) and hyponatremia (122 mEq/L). Urinalysis is positive for leukocyte esterase, nitrites, and white blood cells. Blood and urine cultures grow Escherichia coli; she is initially treated with vancomycin and piperacillin–tazobactam and then de-escalated to ceftriaxone. CT of the abdomen and pelvis reveals a non-obstructing right nephrolithiasis and irregular, nodular thickening of the bladder wall, suspicious for neoplasm.

A 23-year-old man presented with a grotesque overgrowth of soft tissue on his left lower extremity, first noted around age 16. He has no family history of similar lesions. On examination, there was a bulging soft mass from the distal third of the thigh to the ankle measuring approximately 90 × 50 × 10 cm, with associated swelling of the heel and dorsum of the foot and ipsilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. He ambulated with difficulty due to the weight of the mass. Multiple café-au-lait macules and smaller cutaneous and subcutaneous nodules were present on his trunk. Routine laboratory studies were within normal limits, and he had no neurologic symptoms. MRI of the left leg demonstrated a soft-tissue mass infiltrating the gastrocnemius, soleus, and peroneal muscles with marked hypervascularization and large feeding vessels in close proximity to the popliteal and peroneal arteries. A preoperative plan was made for arterial embolization followed by serial surgical excision and biopsy of the lesion.

A 6-month-old boy, previously healthy, was brought in for progressive protrusion of the left upper quadrant and irritability. His mother noted an enlarging abdominal mass. 

An initial abdominal ultrasound showed a large (91 × 72 mm), septate cystic lesion on the left side causing hydronephrosis of the left kidney. 

On examination he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Abdominal examination revealed a palpable left-sided mass. 

Laboratory studies demonstrated a C-reactive protein level of 67 mg/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 21 mm/h, and a white-blood-cell count of 13,000 per μL. Blood urea nitrogen and creatinine were normal. Urinalysis showed an alkaline pH with specific gravity 1.005. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 90 × 88 × 118 mm left retroperitoneal mass with both cystic and solid components, containing areas of fat density and calcification. The mass displaced the pancreas anteriorly, deviated the left kidney laterally, compressed the left ureter, and caused moderate hydronephrosis with reduced enhancement of the left kidney.

A 72-year-old Hispanic woman was brought to the emergency department by family for 3 days of worsening confusion, urinary incontinence, and difficulty ambulating after an unwitnessed fall. She had been noted to be mildly altered at home 3 weeks earlier but remained independent in activities of daily living. Over the past 3 days, she developed rapid neurologic decline, inability to perform ADLs, urinary incontinence, and echolalia.

Her medical history was significant for breast cancer diagnosed 4 years earlier on screening mammogram. She underwent bilateral mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection, which revealed invasive lobular carcinoma of the left breast (estrogen-receptor positive, progesterone-receptor positive, HER-2 negative) with nodal metastases (pathologic stage T2N2M0) and ductal carcinoma in situ of the right breast. She received 12 cycles of paclitaxel, external beam radiation to the left axilla, and daily anastrozole for 3 years.

In the ED, noncontrast CT of the head showed mild hydrocephalus with transependymal CSF resorption and no intracranial hemorrhage, mass, infarction, or fracture. Brain MRI demonstrated enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles, T2 hyperintensity consistent with transependymal CSF spread, and no abnormal gadolinium enhancement or mass. EEG was negative for seizure activity.

Lumbar puncture revealed CSF with lymphocytic pleocytosis (25 cells/µL), elevated protein (365 mg/dL), elevated glucose (91 mg/dL), and normal opening pressure. She became febrile to 101 °F and was started empirically on antibiotics, antivirals, and antifungals. CT of the chest showed bilateral pleural effusions, right basilar consolidation, and intraluminal filling defects in the right pulmonary arteries. She was admitted to the ICU for acute hypercapnic respiratory failure requiring intubation; CT angiography confirmed a pulmonary embolism, and heparin was initiated.

CSF studies showed a positive quantiferon gold test, but acid-fast bacilli smears were negative on three occasions. CSF assays were negative for herpes simplex virus, varicella zoster virus, and coccidioidomycosis. MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine showed no metastatic lesions. A CA 27-29 assay was negative.

A 17-month-old girl was referred for evaluation of a mass on her right ankle. There was no significant past medical or family history. Her parents first noticed a medial ankle swelling at approximately 10 months of age. On examination, there was a soft, partly solid subcutaneous tumor over the anterior aspect of the right ankle. 

Ultrasonography demonstrated a 2-cm heterogeneous echogenic lesion with an indistinct border. Plain radiographs revealed a slightly increased density corresponding to the soft-tissue mass. 

Magnetic resonance imaging showed a 22 × 10 mm ill-defined, irregular mass anterior to the ankle joint. On axial T1-weighted images, the lesion was isointense to muscle. On T2-weighted images, it demonstrated heterogeneous high signal intensity with small foci of low signal intensity.

A 6-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of recurrent acute tonsillitis and a mass on the left palatine tonsil. She had six episodes of tonsillitis over the past year, each presenting with sore throat, odynophagia, and fever, resolving with oral antibiotics. A pedunculated mass on the left palatine tonsil had been present for 1 year. Birth, development, and family histories were unremarkable; she had a history of partial seizures but no other surgeries or hospitalizations.

On examination, she was well-appearing and in no respiratory distress. Otologic and nasal examinations were normal. Both tonsils appeared symmetrical in size. A smooth, mucosa-covered, pedunculated lesion measuring approximately 8 mm × 3 mm arose from the superomedial pole of the left palatine tonsil without obstructing the oropharynx. The remainder of the oral cavity and neck examination was unremarkable.

A 14-year-old girl presented with a lump in her right breast. Her medical and family history were unremarkable. On examination, a circumscribed soft mass 30 mm in diameter was palpable in the inner aspect of the right breast without axillary lymphadenopathy. Ultrasonography showed a 40 mm irregular mass with mixed low and high internal echoes. A PET-CT scan showed high FDG uptake (SUVmax, 5.05) in the right breast and no abnormal uptake elsewhere. Ultrasound-guided needle biopsy revealed diffuse infiltration of atypical lymphoid cells with irregular nuclear membranes and discohesive features. Malignant lymphoma was suspected, but a definitive diagnosis could not be made because of crushing artifact in the biopsy specimen.

A 73-year-old woman, hospitalized for unrelated medical issues, developed a continuous headache, nausea, and vertigo. Noncontrast brain CT revealed a 4 × 3 cm calcified lesion at the left cerebellopontine angle with erosion of the mastoid bone around the facial and semicircular canals. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI showed a rim-enhancing mass with surrounding edema and central necrosis. Diffusion-weighted imaging did not demonstrate the restricted diffusion typical of an abscess. Given her remote history of otitis media and CT evidence of a passage between the middle ear and posterior cranial fossa, a chronic brain abscess was initially suspected. The patient underwent burr‐hole trephination and attempted abscess drainage; when no purulent material was obtained, a biopsy was performed. The pathological diagnosis on that specimen was fibrous meningioma. One week later, she developed aspiration pneumonia secondary to unilateral vocal cord palsy, and MRI demonstrated indentation of the pons and medulla consistent with low cranial nerve palsies. She then underwent a lateral suboccipital craniotomy. The lesion was noted to be stony hard peripherally with a yellowish-gelatinous central core, and a subtotal resection was achieved.

A 77-year-old woman with bronchiectasis, ulcerative colitis, immune thrombocytopenia (platelet count 105 000/μL), and rheumatoid arthritis presented in 2012 with a transient ischaemic attack. Transoesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a right atrial mass measuring 2.5 × 2.4 cm without a patent foramen ovale. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging suggested a probable myxoma. The patient declined surgical removal, was started on anticoagulation, and was followed with serial imaging. Surveillance transoesophageal echocardiography in 2022 revealed that the mass had grown to 4 cm, was mobile, and appeared attached to the lateral wall of the right atrium near the superior vena cava ostium. The patient again declined surgery and was referred for percutaneous extraction.

A 38-year-old white man initially presented 2 years ago with intermittent sharp left eye pain. At that time, brain MRI was reported as normal, but on retrospective review showed multiple small stippled foci throughout the basioccipital clivus that were iso- to hypointense on T1-weighted imaging, hypointense on T2-weighted imaging, and demonstrated minimal post-gadolinium enhancement. Two years later, he developed bilateral eye discomfort without headache, vision changes, seizures, or difficulty chewing or swallowing. Neurologic examination was unremarkable.

Repeat MRI of the brain demonstrated a mildly expansile clival lesion that was isointense on T1-weighted imaging, heterogeneous but predominantly hypointense on T2-weighted imaging, avidly enhancing after gadolinium administration, and showed no diffusion restriction. The lesion extended to the left occipital condyle and left jugular tubercle. Although T2 hypointensity was atypical for chordoma, the diagnosis of chordoma was suggested.

Subsequent CT of the head revealed a sharply demarcated, well-circumscribed, mildly expansile marrow-replacing lesion of the clivus without cortical disruption, erosion, or periosteal reaction. Metastatic disease and multiple myeloma were also considered. Endoscopic endonasal biopsy was offered, and the patient sought a second opinion.

A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, and a history of chronic tobacco smoking presented with a 3-week history of gradually worsening dry cough, dysphagia, and cough provoked by any oral intake. He reported an unintentional 30-pound weight loss over 3 months. On examination, he was afebrile, his respiratory rate was 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation was 91% on room air. He appeared in no acute distress, with nonlabored breathing, no palpable liver or spleen, and no superficial lymphadenopathy. Initial laboratory tests revealed a white blood cell count of 21 900/μL (5% bands, 81% neutrophils, 5% lymphocytes, 8% monocytes), a lactate dehydrogenase level of 223 U/L (reference range 135–225 U/L), normal liver and renal function tests, and a negative HIV assay. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed mid-esophageal wall thickening with enhancement, a fistulous connection between the membranous trachea and anterior mediastinum, nonspecific mediastinal lymph node enlargement, and bilateral ground-glass opacities in the upper and lower lobes. CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated multiple lytic lesions in the pelvic bones, mild hepatic steatosis, a normal spleen, and no intraabdominal or pelvic lymphadenopathy. He was started on levofloxacin for presumed aspiration pneumonia. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a large fungating, ulcerating mass in the middle third of the esophagus causing partial obstruction, with a tracheoesophageal fistula in the same region. Bronchoscopy confirmed a 3 cm fistula in the trachea and a 1.5 cm bronchoesophageal fistula in the left mainstem bronchus.

A 65-year-old woman with a 10-year history of hypertension and newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with 2 months of painless hematuria (without clots) and right thoracolumbar pain. She denied weight loss or fevers. Her body mass index was 22 kg/m2, and blood pressure was within normal limits. On abdominal examination, a palpable mass was noted in the right hemiabdomen. Laboratory evaluation showed hemoglobin 12.7 g/dL, hematocrit 39%, glucose 100 mg/dL, urea 43.9 mg/dL, creatinine 0.72 mg/dL, normal clotting times, and normal calcium levels. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a 15.4 × 10.5 cm right renal mass arising from the upper pole, crossing the interpolar line, infiltrating the renal sinus, and containing a hypodense center suggestive of extensive necrosis. There was no lymphadenopathy or distant metastatic disease.

A 17-year-old male sustained a hyperflexion injury of his right knee while playing soccer. Immediately after the injury, he developed a tense hemarthrosis and underwent knee aspiration elsewhere, yielding a significant amount of blood. Ligamentous injury was suspected, and MRI was obtained 2–3 weeks later. The patient reported persistent pain and limitation of knee motion, particularly with squatting. On examination, right knee range of motion was 0° to 110° (left 0° to 140°), with mild tenderness posteriorly and no palpable effusion or mass. MRI of the right knee showed a lobulated, 3.3 × 1.7 × 1.9 cm mass in the posteromedial joint space adjacent to the posterior cruciate ligament and posterior joint capsule, with cortical involvement of the posteromedial femoral condyle (1.1 × 0.9 cm). There was a moderate joint effusion and synovial enhancement. The lesion was isointense on T1-weighted images except for a small T1-hyperintense superior portion and was heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images. At this point, the preoperative differential diagnosis included a nodular form of pigmented villonodular synovitis, ganglion, and synovial chondromatosis.

A 71-year-old man with a history of midline hernia repair presented with two months of right lower quadrant, nonfeverish pain and chronic constipation. He was afebrile, alert, and had a soft abdomen with maximal tenderness in the right iliac fossa. Laboratory studies showed microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL; reference, 12–17) and an elevated C-reactive protein level of 25 mg/dL (reference, <0.2); other studies were within normal limits. An abdominal ultrasound was non‐diagnostic because of bowel gas. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 5-cm segment of cecal wall thickening, with maximum thickness of 7 mm, extending into the terminal ileum, with surrounding fat infiltration but no regional or distant metastases. Colonoscopy confirmed parietal thickening of the cecum approximately 20 mm from the ileocecal valve, and multiple biopsies showed nonspecific chronic colitis.

A 2-year-old boy presented with a 6-day history of a left auricular mass that did not respond to 3 days of amoxicillin–clavulanate. There was no history of trauma, fever, pain, or other signs of infection. On examination, a painless, smooth, rubbery mass in the left postauricular area was pushing the conchal cartilage anteriorly and obstructing the external ear canal. Computed tomography of the temporal bone showed a 23×12 mm solid soft-tissue mass in the postauricular region with regular margins, homogeneous hypodensity, and canal obstruction.

A 25-year-old primigravida at 28 weeks of gestation presented with new‐onset facial acne and abdominal and facial hirsutism that began at 23 weeks. On examination, her Ferriman–Gallwey score was 18, and she had early clitoromegaly and a deepening of her voice. Ultrasound imaging showed a single viable fetus appropriate for gestational age and a 12 × 9 cm right adnexal mass with areas of necrosis and low color Doppler flow; the left adnexa appeared normal. Laboratory studies revealed mildly elevated transaminases, negative serum tumor markers, and markedly elevated androgen levels: total testosterone 6270 ng/dL (normal 0.4–4.1), SHBG 689.6 nmol/L (normal 18–114), androstenedione ≤200 ng/dL (normal 0.4–4.1), and DHEAS 645.9 μg/dL (normal 98.8–340). Magnetic resonance imaging was recommended but declined by the patient. Over the following weeks, her hirsutism and virilization progressed despite conservative management, and severe right hydronephrosis developed. At 34 weeks, because of worsening laboratory findings, symptom progression, suspected ovarian malignancy, and incomplete antenatal evaluation, a cesarean delivery with unilateral oophorectomy was performed.

A 33-year-old woman with a five‐year history of occasional right lower extremity pain presented with a one‐month history of pain, numbness, and muscle weakness from the posterior aspect of her right hip to her lower extremity after lifting a heavy object. Her medical history was unremarkable except for a cesarean section. She did not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. Medications included pregabalin and brotizolam. On examination, she had a right‐sided limp, was afebrile, and had normal vital signs; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including tumor markers, were within normal limits.

Plain radiographs of the sacrum showed an indistinct first sacral hiatus and osteosclerosis from the upper edge of the right S1 vertebral body to the lower edge of the S2 sacral foramen. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 7.0×2.5×3.0 cm lobular intraspinal mass within the sacral canal with scalloping of the S1 and S2 vertebral bodies. The mass was inhomogeneously hyperintense on T1‐weighted imaging; regions that were hyperintense on T1 showed signal loss on fat‐suppressed T1, compatible with fat. It demonstrated avid heterogeneous contrast enhancement. On T2‐weighted imaging, there were areas of intermediate signal intensity with flow voids and areas of high signal intensity. The apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) of the mass was 0.875×10⁻³ mm²/s. Dynamic contrast‐enhanced CT showed arterial hypervascularity within the lesion and areas of hypodensity suggesting fat components. The leading imaging differential consideration was schwannoma.

A 76-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of fatigue, intermittent abdominal cramps, swelling in the left lower quadrant, and a 5-kg weight loss. Physical examination showed pallid mucous membranes and no palpable lymphadenopathy; her performance status was ECOG 1. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL, hematocrit 24.6%, and a white-cell count of 9300/µL (72% neutrophils, 20% lymphocytes); other blood chemistries, lactate dehydrogenase, and HIV serology were normal. A myelogram was normal. Colonoscopy demonstrated multiple polyps in the rectum, sigmoid colon, descending colon, and both colic flexures. A rectal biopsy showed lymphomatous infiltration of the intestinal wall, and the pathologic diagnosis was primary colorectal lymphoma. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed no extraintestinal disease and normal liver and spleen. Thoracic CT was unremarkable. Gastroduodenoscopy showed no significant abnormalities. Owing to the large size of the polypoid masses narrowing the colonic lumen, the patient developed acute intestinal obstruction and was referred for laparotomy.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of a nonhealing ulcer on the left lower posterior gingiva, associated with intermittent pain and burning on ingestion of spicy or hot foods, and with continuous severe burning and pain for the past week. She had no relevant medical, dental, occupational history or known habits. 

On initial intraoral examination, there was a solitary, firm, ulcerative lesion measuring 2 × 2 cm on the left buccal alveolar mucosa near the premolar region, surrounded by clinically healthy mucosa. Retraction of the cheek revealed a retained tooth root impinging on the lesion. No other intraoral lesions were observed. The tooth root was extracted under local anesthesia, and at a 15-day postoperative follow-up the lesion had completely resolved and symptoms had abated.

Three months later, she returned with recurrence of pain and severe burning at the same site. Examination revealed a nodular, proliferative ulcerative growth measuring 3 × 2 cm on the left alveolar mucosa in the premolar–molar region, with focal areas of white spots. She was prescribed topical 2% acyclovir for one week without regression. Routine blood tests were normal. An incisional biopsy was advised, and the preliminary differential diagnosis included focal epithelial hyperplasia, traumatic fibroma, verruciform leukoplakia, verruca vulgaris, verrucous carcinoma, and ulcerative squamous cell carcinoma.

An 87-year-old man presented with a two-week history of edema and erythema of the distal phalanx of the left fourth digit. He had received oral antibiotics followed by intravenous antibiotics for presumed infection without improvement. On examination, the fingertip was erythematous, edematous, and tender. Radiographs of the left hand showed no bony abnormalities. An incisional biopsy of the soft tissue was performed. Histologic examination revealed small lobules, cords, and single epithelial cells set within a desmoplastic stroma. Immunohistochemical stains were strongly positive for cytokeratins CK7 and CK AE1/3, and negative for cytokeratins CK20, TTF-1, prostate-specific antigen, synaptophysin, chromogranin, p63, and S-100. To evaluate for a possible metastatic source, MRI of the left upper extremity and computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis were obtained. Imaging demonstrated a 5.1 × 4.2 cm solid heterogeneous right upper lobe hilar mass with irregular margins, an enlarged right axillary lymph node, multiple mediastinal lymph nodes, and an enlarged right paratracheal lymph node. A chest radiograph obtained one year earlier had been normal.

A 62-year-old man with a 14-year history of chronic myeloid leukemia treated sequentially with imatinib and dasatinib presented with several weeks of multiple painful, firm subcutaneous nodules on the forearms, left buttock, and knee. The nodules developed circumferential purplish discoloration and surrounding hematoma. He also reported worsening dyspnea, low-grade fever, and arthralgias. He admitted to recent irregular adherence to dasatinib. There was no history of trauma, travel, infection, or new medications.

On examination, he was afebrile. Chest and joint examinations were unremarkable. Skin examination revealed multiple tender, firm, subcutaneous nodules with peripheral hematoma.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL; white-cell count 199.3×10^9/L with 5% blasts; neutrophils 93.05×10^9/L; lymphocytes 7.18×10^9/L; monocytes 24.32×10^9/L; platelets 389×10^9/L; C-reactive protein 18.7 mg/L; haptoglobin <10 mg/dL; creatinine 1.32 mg/dL; lactate dehydrogenase 7268 U/L; uric acid 12.4 mg/dL. Coagulation tests were consistent with disseminated intravascular coagulation (D-dimer 23 077 ng/mL; fibrinogen 1.07 g/L; prothrombin ratio 40%). Blood cultures and serologic assays for HIV, HCV, Rickettsia, and syphilis were negative.

Given the leukocytosis, there was concern for recurrence of CML or progression to acute myeloid leukemia. Bone marrow aspiration demonstrated a hypercellular marrow with proliferation of the granulocytic lineage, dysplasia in erythroid and megakaryocytic lines, and 3.9% blasts.

An 11-year-old girl presented with a 6-month history of an asymptomatic swelling on the left lower border of the mandible, noted to enlarge slightly over the past 2 months. Extraoral examination revealed mild facial asymmetry with a firm, nontender nodular mass and normal overlying skin. Intraoral examination showed a full permanent dentition except for the missing left mandibular first molar (tooth 36), with an intact buccal vestibule and normal mucosa. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated a large radiodense mass surrounded by a radiolucent rim in the left posterior mandible, lying in the eruption path of an unerupted tooth 36 and acting as a barrier to its eruption; the permanent mandibular second molar (tooth 37) was also absent.

A 72-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of progressive upper thoracic spine pain radiating to her left arm and leg. She had no functional deficits and did not respond to analgesics. Her medical history was notable only for multi-segmental degenerative changes in the cervical and lumbar spine, and she took no medications. On examination, she had localized tenderness over the upper thoracic vertebrae but no neurologic deficits. Routine blood tests were unremarkable. Chest magnetic resonance imaging showed a 2.7 × 2.0 × 1.2 cm para-vertebral mass in the left hemithorax at the T2–T3 level that extended into the neural foramina, contacted the dural sac, had smooth contours, and displayed no bony destruction. The differential diagnosis included neurogenic tumours (e.g., schwannomas, neurofibromas, parasympathetic ganglion tumours, sympathetic chain tumours) and non-neurogenic tumours (e.g., chordoma, chondrosarcoma, Ewing’s sarcoma).

A 43-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of gradually increasing, painless swellings on the anterior chest wall and left mandibular region. Physical examination revealed multiple subcutaneous nodules measuring 1.0–3.0 cm, with normal overlying skin; the nodules were nontender, without warmth or itch, soft to firm, freely mobile, and not fixed. General examination was otherwise unremarkable. Routine hematological and biochemical tests were within normal limits; viral markers and VDRL serology were nonreactive. Based on the clinical appearance and investigations, the working differential diagnoses included lipomatous lesion, benign neural sheath tumour, fibroblastic/fibrohistiocytic lesion, adnexal tumour, and amelanotic melanoma. Fine-needle aspiration cytology was performed from multiple sites, yielding serosanguinous material. Smears showed dispersed cells of variable size and shape—predominantly oval and spindloid to plasmacytoid—with mild anisokaryosis, small inconspicuous nucleoli, and “salt and pepper” chromatin; the cytoplasm was eosinophilic with fine pink granularity, and focal amyloid-like material was noted. The cytological opinion was in favour of subcutaneous deposits of a “neuroendocrinal” lesion. On reevaluation, the patient reported intermittent flushing episodes. A provisional diagnosis of a neuroendocrine lesion arising from the gastrointestinal tract, lungs, or thyroid was made. Further history revealed thyroid surgery 5 years earlier, confirmed by a fine scar in a neck crease. A working diagnosis of cutaneous metastatic deposits of medullary thyroid carcinoma was suggested, and histopathology of a cell block and radiologic studies were ordered.

A 16-year-old male with a history of headaches presented with two weeks of progressively worsening frontal headaches, decreased visual acuity, and subjective diplopia on lateral gaze. He was transferred after resection of a left frontal dural meningioma. On transfer, he endorsed persistent headaches, poor visual acuity, and diplopia, but denied any history of epistaxis. Noncontrast CT demonstrated a large expansile, irregular destructive mass centered in the sphenoid sinus with obliteration of the sinus cavity, involvement of the clivus, pterygopalatine fossa, and sphenopalatine foramen, and erosion of the planum sphenoidale, floor of the sella, and optic canal. No bowing of the posterior maxillary sinus wall was noted.
