MRI showed an avidly, heterogeneously enhancing lesion with multiple cystic and necrotic areas without fluid levels, involving the central skull base and extending into the planum sphenoidale, posterior ethmoid sinus, nasal cavity, and nasopharyngeal soft tissues, with encasement of the internal carotid arteries and optic nerves but no prominent flow voids. Based on clinical presentation and radiographic characteristics, a preliminary diagnosis of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma was made. Aneurysmal bone cyst and giant cell tumor were felt to be less likely possibilities. Preoperative angiography demonstrated a hypervascular blush from the left internal maxillary artery.

A 73-year-old Caucasian man with a history of a left orchiectomy at age 59 for a 4.2 cm encapsulated testicular Leydig cell tumor without lymphovascular invasion or extratesticular involvement presented with two months of progressive lower back pain. MRI of the thoracic and lumbar spine demonstrated lesions at the L1 and L5 vertebral levels concerning for osseous metastatic disease. An L5 vertebral body biopsy showed a lesion composed of polygonal, plump cells with abundant cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli. Immunohistochemical studies revealed that the tumor cells were positive for calretinin, α-inhibin, synaptophysin, melan-A, chromogranin, and vimentin, with a Ki-67 proliferative index of 7%, and were negative for CK AE 1/3, AFB, CK 20, CK 7, EMA, S100, WT1, arginase-1, SALL-4, and SOX10.

An 11-year-old Caucasian boy was referred for progressive swelling on the right side of the mandible. The swelling had been present for 18 months and had gradually enlarged; the patient reported intermittent tenderness but no pain. His medical history was unremarkable and there was no history of trauma. 

On extraoral examination, there was diffuse swelling from the right oral commissure to the angle of the mandible and from the oral commissure to the lower border of the jaw. The overlying skin and soft tissue appeared normal, and there was a pink-purplish area over the right upper lip. No lymphadenopathy was noted.

Intraorally, a firm, non-tender bony swelling of the right buccal cortex measured about 3–4 cm, extending from the right first premolar to the distal aspect of the right second molar. The overlying mucosa was normal, teeth were vital, non-mobile, and there was no paresthesia.

Cone-beam CT showed an expansile ill-defined mixed lesion from the mesial aspect of the right first premolar to the periapical region of the right first molar, with thinning and disruption of both buccal and lingual cortices, alveolar crest erosion, inferior displacement of the inferior alveolar canal, and root divergence of the second premolar and first molar without root resorption.

Noting a port-wine stain on the right upper lip and lumen-like radiolucencies in a radiopaque background, computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the neck with contrast was obtained. CTA revealed a 20 × 35 mm expansile mixed lytic lesion in the right mandibular body with no significant vascularity. Catheter angiography showed normal findings in the carotid arteries and jugular veins; reactive cervical lymph nodes were present. The CTA impression was intraosseous hemangioma (low flow), with other provisional diagnoses of fibrous dysplasia and osteoblastoma.

A 59-year-old morbidly obese woman with a 10-year history of essential hypertension and known hypothyroidism was referred to urology after an incidental finding on imaging. She reported no abdominal pain, weight loss, palpitations, flushing, or other symptoms suggestive of adrenal overactivity. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory evaluation, including 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines, was within normal limits. A pre- and postcontrast abdominal CT scan revealed a large (approximately 16 × 15 × 10 cm) heterogeneous solid mass in the left adrenal region, containing internal calcifications and areas of central low attenuation consistent with necrosis. On postcontrast images, the lesion demonstrated peripheral nodular and discontinuous enhancement. The mass displaced the left kidney inferiorly but showed no overt signs of local invasion.

A 9-year-old boy presented with right-sided sciatica and a gradually enlarging swelling in the right buttock of 6 months’ duration. His pain was constant and unrelated to activity, with no constitutional symptoms. On examination, there was a mildly tender, firm-to-hard, fixed mass measuring 8.5 × 7.5 cm in the outer upper part of the right buttock; no other lesions were noted. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. MRI of the right gluteal region showed a relatively well-defined mass measuring 5.5 × 7.5 × 8.5 cm involving the gluteus maximus, medius, and minimus muscles and infiltrating the piriformis; the lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense with marked heterogeneity on T2-weighted images, abutting but not eroding the iliac blade. Fine-needle aspiration cytology was reported as a benign spindle cell lesion with a differential diagnosis of proliferative fasciomyositis and desmoid tumor.

A 36-year-old nulliparous woman presented with 11 years of primary infertility, progressive hirsutism since age 25, recent secondary amenorrhea, deepening voice, clitoral enlargement, and male-pattern baldness. She had no medication use or relevant family history. On exam, BMI was 21 kg/m2, blood pressure normal, Ferriman-Gallwey score was 22, and clitoromegaly was noted. Laboratory studies showed total testosterone 1.71 ng/mL (normal 0.3–0.75), androstenedione 4.1 ng/mL (normal 0.4–3.5), normal dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate, prolactin, cortisol, TSH, and hCG. A 17-hydroxyprogesterone level was normal after ACTH stimulation. Serum CA 125, CEA, CA 19-9, CA 15-3, and AFP were within normal limits. Transvaginal ultrasound showed no adnexal masses. Laparoscopic ovarian biopsy and drilling were nondiagnostic, and postoperative testosterone rose to 10 ng/mL. A follow-up pelvic ultrasound showed a right ovarian cyst measuring 42 × 34 mm. MRI demonstrated multiple ovarian cystic formations and no adrenal mass.

A 63-year-old Chinese man presented with a one-year history of swelling and intermittent pain in the right scrotum. He had previously undergone surgery for a left testicular hydrocele but had no significant exposures or family history of malignancy. Examination revealed normal vital signs and intact scrotal skin without redness, swelling, or tenderness. The left testis and epididymis were normal. In the right scrotum, there was a hard, poorly mobile 4 cm × 4 cm nodule in the upper-posterior epididymal region without tenderness. Scrotal ultrasound showed an irregular cystic mass in the right epididymal area, tightly adherent to the testis, with an uneven mixed echogenic appearance and unclear borders, measuring approximately 4 cm × 3 cm × 2 cm. MRI of the scrotum demonstrated that the right epididymis was enlarged, containing a 2.6 cm × 2.8 cm × 2.1 cm lesion with mixed cystic and solid signal intensity and an irregular, poorly defined margin. CT scans of the chest and retroperitoneum showed no abnormalities. Serum alpha-fetoprotein was 3.6 ng/mL, human chorionic gonadotropin 0.3 mIU/mL, and lactate dehydrogenase 220 IU/L (all within normal limits).

A 29-year-old woman presented with progressive bilateral lower-extremity edema and months of vulvar discomfort. She had a history of May–Thurner syndrome diagnosed in childhood, with placement of a left iliac vein stent 23 years earlier (revised once) and ongoing antithrombotic therapy. Despite decompressive therapy and compression garments, she had persistent nonpitting lymphedema of both legs. She noted a rash on her labia majora, which she initially attributed to an allergic reaction. During a recent cesarean delivery, her obstetrician observed bilateral verrucous papular lesions of the labia and referred her for further evaluation. 

On gynecologic examination, there was marked induration and multiple wart-like papules along the labia majora and minora, extending into the mons pubis bilaterally and sparing the clitoris. Speculum and bimanual examinations were unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed mass effect of the right common iliac artery compressing the left common iliac vein against the L4 vertebral body, with narrowing of the anteroposterior diameter despite an existing vascular stent. 

MRI of the pelvis revealed a 7.5-cm, T2-hyperintense, lobulated, multicystic, subcutaneous lesion in the left vulva (greater than right), with T2 fat-suppressed edema and no demonstrable contrast enhancement.

A 29-year-old woman, 6 weeks pregnant, was referred for evaluation of an asymptomatic intraabdominal mass that had been present for ~2 years and had enlarged over the prior month. Initial ultrasonography confirmed an intrauterine pregnancy and identified a right upper quadrant mass appearing cystic. MRI of the abdomen showed a thin-walled, unilocular cystic lesion measuring 17×16×12 cm in the right upper quadrant; it had no septations, floating membranes, soft-tissue components, fat-fluid levels, or daughter cysts and was separable from the IVC, aorta, liver, right kidney, and right psoas muscle. The patient had no significant medical or surgical history. On examination she had a smooth, non-tender right upper quadrant mass of ~10×12 cm inseparable from the liver; there was no jaundice or pallor. Laboratory tests revealed a negative hepatitis screen, negative HIV test, and normal liver function; echinococcus serology was pending. She was scheduled for elective open cystectomy during pregnancy. Before that date, she presented after blunt abdominal trauma with acute right upper quadrant pain; she remained hemodynamically stable, with normal laboratory results and a viable intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound. Emergency laparotomy revealed a large benign-appearing liver tumour with evidence of rupture (bleeding had ceased) adherent to the posterior gallbladder. The surgical team performed tumour excision with cholecystectomy; the patient recovered well postoperatively.

A 34-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with a 2-month history of progressively worsening morning headaches associated with nausea and vomiting, which did not fully resolve with analgesics. He later noted numbness, tingling, and weakness in both upper extremities, and intermittently experienced blurred or double vision, vertigo, and a clumsy gait. On neurologic examination, he had both vertical and horizontal nystagmus and gait ataxia; cranial nerve function was otherwise normal.

Noncontrast head CT demonstrated a mildly hypodense, 30 × 40 × 40 mm mass lesion centered in the fourth ventricle region of the posterior fossa, without contrast enhancement or calcifications, and with surrounding brain edema and obstructive hydrocephalus. T2-weighted brain MRI confirmed a well-demarcated, relatively homogeneous mass filling the fourth ventricle, causing effacement of the fourth-ventricle outlets, cerebellar compression, and tonsillar herniation.

A 69-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 6-month history of a single lesion on the inner right calf that had enlarged threefold over the past month. He reported discomfort but no pain, bleeding, discharge, odor, pruritus, or color change. On examination, the lesion was a firm, violaceous, erythematous, eroded nodule measuring 3.5 × 3.5 × 1.5 cm with sharp margins, adherent to skin, and with a pigmented papillomatosis surface. Vital signs were normal, and there was no weight loss or systemic symptoms. His past history included basal cell carcinoma and seborrheic keratosis of the face; he had no history of smoking, alcohol use, or family history of skin disease or malignancy.

An excisional biopsy (2 × 3 mm with a 1 cm margin) showed an orthokeratotic epidermis and sheets of cells in the dermis with a high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio, hyperchromatic pleomorphic nuclei, and mitotic figures, infiltrating collagen bundles and subcutaneous fat, consistent with a small round cell tumor.

A 68-year-old Japanese man underwent robot-assisted laparoscopic distal gastrectomy with D1+ lymph node dissection and Roux-en-Y reconstruction for a poorly differentiated gastric adenocarcinoma (pT1aN0M0, stage IA). His early postoperative course was uncomplicated, and no adjuvant therapy was given. Two years later, surveillance CT showed a 38×36 mm soft-tissue mass on the greater-curvature side of the residual stomach; retrospective review of the 1-year scan revealed mild wall thickening at the same location. Tumor markers were within normal limits (CEA 1.8 ng/mL; CA 19-9 8.5 U/mL; soluble IL-2 receptor 396 U/mL). FDG-PET/CT demonstrated moderate uptake in the mass (SUVmax 5.25) with no other abnormal foci. Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed a heterogeneous high signal on T2-weighted images, low signal on T1-weighted images, and a slow, progressive contrast effect. Upper endoscopy of the remnant stomach showed no mucosal lesion. EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration of a 43×30 mm borderline oligo-hypoechoic mass in the splenic hilum yielded spindle-shaped cells; immunostaining for CD34, c-kit, desmin, S-100, and β-catenin showed no significant positivity. The working differential diagnoses included recurrent gastric cancer, regional lymph node metastasis, gastrointestinal stromal tumor, leiomyoma, schwannoma, and desmoid tumor. Because malignancy could not be ruled out, diagnostic surgical resection was planned.

A 53-year-old woman presented with right groin pain radiating to the thigh, present for 4 years. The pain began insidiously as an aching groin and thigh discomfort, worsened with daily activities, and was severe at night. Early in her course, aspirin and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs provided significant relief. For approximately 3 years before the correct diagnosis, she was treated unsuccessfully for bursitis, tendonitis, and muscle strain. 

Six months after percutaneous radiofrequency ablation of a presumed intraarticular lesion in the right hip, she experienced recurrence of similar symptoms in the second month post-treatment. On examination, the right hip had moderately reduced range of motion in all planes with end-range pain, and a mild antalgic Trendelenburg gait. Neurologic examination was normal. Complete blood count and biochemical profile were within reference ranges.

A plain radiograph of the right hip showed an oval nidus surrounded by a radiolucent ring at the femoral neck proximal to the femoral head. CT and MRI of the right hip demonstrated a 0.7-cm intramedullary lesion at the posterior cortex of the femoral neck with increased sclerosis and central lucency.

A 15-year-old boy presented with a six-month history of voiding difficulties characterized by sudden interruption of urination and prolonged micturition time. He denied haematuria. His medical and family histories were unremarkable, with no exposure to tobacco, chemicals, or drugs. Physical examination findings were normal.  
Renal-bladder ultrasonography revealed a 1.4 cm × 1.3 cm well-defined mass arising near the internal urethral orifice in the bladder, with internal vascular flow on Doppler imaging. Cystoscopy demonstrated a spherical mass with a broad pedicle at the bladder neck at the 1 o’clock position.

A 39-year-old Japanese man presented with a 3-month history of numbness on the left side of his face. Over the preceding month the numbness had become painful, and he sometimes found that he could not chew on the left side. Treatment with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and muscle relaxants had no effect, and carbamazepine provided only slight relief. He reported no clicking sounds. 

On examination there was decreased sensation in the distribution of the left trigeminal nerve and dyskinesia of the left masticatory muscles; facial expression was symmetrical at rest. His medical history included acute gastritis, duodenal ulcer, and depression managed with brotizolam, flunitrazepam, and paroxetine. 

Panoramic radiography showed no dental pathology and slight restriction of movement of the left temporomandibular joint. An MRI scan of the temporomandibular region was inconclusive for temporomandibular disorder, so imaging was extended to the brain. Axial T1-weighted images showed a 10-mm homogeneously hyperintense lesion in the left Meckel’s cave compared with gray matter, and axial T2-weighted images showed it to be hypointense and exerting pressure on the trigeminal nerve. Unenhanced CT of the head confirmed a well-defined, homogeneously hyperdense mass in Meckel’s cave without calcification.

A 50-year-old woman presented with vague right upper abdominal pain of several weeks’ duration. On examination, she had a firm, palpable mass in the right hypochondrium. Laboratory studies showed a normal haemogram and normal liver-function tests. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 9 × 8 cm mass in the gallbladder fossa with loss of a clear interface with the liver and evidence of gallstones. Biphasic computed tomography of the abdomen showed a grossly distended gallbladder containing a soft-tissue mass with multiple large intraluminal projections, findings suggestive of a polypoidal gallbladder malignancy in the setting of cholelithiasis. A provisional diagnosis of carcinoma of the gallbladder was made.

A 38-year-old woman (gravida 4, para 4) presented with irregular vaginal bleeding for two months and a desire for elective tubal ligation. Physical examination, including pelvic and digital rectal examinations, was unremarkable. Routine hematology and chemistry were normal. Tumor markers—carcinoembryonic antigen, cancer antigen 125, and cancer antigen 19-9—were within normal limits; cancer antigen 15-3 was elevated at 30.33 U/mL (normal 0–25 U/mL). Transvaginal ultrasonography revealed a 46×42 mm heterogeneous cystic mass with a thick wall and intense internal fluid in the left ovary; the right ovary appeared normal. Given the sonographic appearance and tumor-marker profile, the mass was presumed benign. At laparotomy via a Pfannenstiel incision, a 5 cm coarse adnexal mass with a solid component was found in the left ovary; the right adnexa and peritoneal surfaces were normal, and no ascites was present. A left salpingo-oophorectomy was performed. Initial microscopic examination of the specimen showed a malignant tumor that was suspicious for undifferentiated carcinoma.

A 42-year-old right-handed man was referred with generalized epileptic seizures, bilateral limb weakness, gait instability, and headache. He had a history of recurrent seizures since childhood managed with phenobarbital and valproic acid. He was a heavy smoker with dyslipidemia and an amoxicillin allergy; 2 years earlier he had right hip surgery with retained screws. On examination, he had increased reflexes in the left leg; otherwise neurologically intact. 

Noncontrast CT of the brain showed a right parietal-occipital lesion. Contrast enhancement revealed a 7.5×2×4.6 cm heterogeneous mass, a 1 cm midline shift, and elevation of the right occipital horn. After removal of hip hardware, MRI confirmed a solitary lesion adjacent to the right occipital horn that appeared compatible with a low-grade glioma. Ophthalmologic evaluation was normal. Routine blood tests were unremarkable, and CT of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no extracranial disease.

The patient underwent stereotactic biopsy, which was inconclusive. Given his age and lesion accessibility, an occipital craniotomy with neuronavigation and intraoperative monitoring was performed, and the tumor was resected. Postoperative MRI confirmed subtotal excision, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed no abnormalities.

A 7-year-old girl presented with 8 months of mild, non–activity-related pain and progressive swelling in the left distal third of the forearm. There was no history of trauma, fever, or weight loss. On examination, a 5 × 2 cm fusiform swelling over the diaphysis of the radius was firm, tender, and continuous with the bone; the overlying skin was normal, and there was no neurovascular deficit. Pronation and supination of the forearm were painfully restricted; finger movements were intact.  
Preoperative radiographs showed a well-defined, lytic, expansile lesion measuring approximately 4 × 2 cm in the diaphyseal region of the radius, with cortical thinning but no breach. MRI confirmed a sharply marginated intramedullary lesion without soft-tissue extension.

A 63-year-old Caucasian man with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma diagnosed 5 months earlier and receiving systemic chemotherapy and external radiotherapy to the right hip underwent a routine eye examination. He was asymptomatic. Best-corrected visual acuities were 20/32 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Intraocular pressures were 15 mmHg in the right eye and 17 mmHg in the left eye. Slit-lamp examination showed moderate nuclear sclerosis bilaterally. Fundus examination of the right eye revealed a well-circumscribed whitish retinal lesion measuring 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 mm located along the inferotemporal vascular arcade, without apparent vitreous or choroidal involvement; the left eye was normal. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography of the right eye demonstrated a hyperreflective dome-shaped lesion in the inner retinal layers with a few hyperreflective dots in the posterior vitreous, compression of the outer retina, and partial choroidal shadowing but no evidence of choroidal infiltration. Fundus autofluorescence imaging showed that the lesion was hypofluorescent. Fluorescein angiography revealed early hyperfluorescence of the lesion, late staining, and no leakage. B-scan ultrasonography showed a flat, nonmeasurable lesion. Brain magnetic resonance imaging was unremarkable.

A 66-year-old man presented with 2 months of recurrent fever, chills, fatigue, anorexia, malaise, and a 15-kg weight loss. Initial evaluation at an outside hospital revealed elevated inflammatory markers, pyuria, progressive serum creatinine elevation, proteinuria, and hematuria. Despite 1 week of antibiotic therapy, only transient improvement occurred. 

On admission, temperature was 36.6°C, blood pressure elevated, and oxygen saturation was 98% on room air. Examination showed pale conjunctiva, scattered crackles at lung bases, mild lower-extremity edema, and no palpable lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. 

Laboratory studies revealed:  
• Urine protein 3+; 24-h urine protein 2.97 g/day; glomerular hematuria (8–10 RBCs/HPF)  
• BUN 10.74 mmol/L (3.6–9.5); serum creatinine 128.2 µmol/L (57–111)  
• Albumin 26.2 g/L (40–55); globulin 37.5 g/L (20–30)  
• WBC 9.36×10^9/L (3.5–9.5); Hgb 96 g/L (130–175); platelets 250×10^9/L (125–350)  
• Progressive normocytic anemia; normal reticulocyte count  
• Ferritin 615.3 ng/mL (23.9–336.2); transferrin saturation 45%  
• No GI bleeding symptoms; tumor markers negative  
• Outside bone marrow biopsy and PET/CT showed no malignancy  
• Direct antiglobulin test positive  

On hospital day 4, fever recurred with chills; WBC, IL-6, CRP, and ESR rose, while procalcitonin was 0.16 ng/mL. Serum creatinine fell with renewed antibiotics. Chest CT showed bilateral pneumonia, mild interstitial edema, and pleural effusions, which improved on follow-up imaging. Urine next-generation sequencing detected Candida; targeted antifungal therapy improved creatinine and proteinuria. 

Further immunologic studies showed:  
• Serum protein electrophoresis: γ-globulin 21.6% (9–16%)  
• IgA 497 mg/dL (82–453); IgG and IgM normal  
• Immunofixation: positive IgA and λ light chain; κ/λ ratio 0.26 (0.26–1.65)  
• Urine protein electrophoresis negative  
A bone marrow biopsy was repeated and showed no evidence of multiple myeloma. Ultrasound revealed multiple small lymph node–like nodules in the left neck, right axilla, and left inguinal region, the largest measuring 9.5×5.0 mm.

A 55-year-old woman from a mountainous region of northern Morocco presented with a 2-month history of a painless enlarging cervical mass. She had no prior radiation exposure, no personal or family history of thyroid disease, and no history of smoking, alcohol, or drug use. On examination, there was a marked enlargement of the left thyroid lobe with a palpable nodular lesion, and a separate skin lesion located adjacent to the thyroid bed. Thyroid ultrasonography revealed a multinodular, plunging, compressive goiter of the left lobe (TI-RADS 6). Chest CT showed multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules suggestive of metastatic disease. Thyroid function tests were within normal limits. Two weeks after presentation, the patient underwent a total thyroidectomy, and a biopsy of the skin lesion was taken; both specimens were submitted for histopathological evaluation.

An 18-year-old man was referred for evaluation of splenic lesions found incidentally on routine follow-up imaging for treated Burkitt’s lymphoma. Seven years earlier, he had gastric Burkitt’s lymphoma treated with chemotherapy for one year, with no evidence of recurrence on serial examinations. He reported no abdominal pain, fever, or weight loss. His past medical and family histories were otherwise noncontributory.

Vital signs were normal. The abdomen was soft, nontender, and without palpable organomegaly. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and liver-function tests, were within normal limits.

Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a 24 mm hyperechoic mass and a 9 mm cystic lesion in the splenic parenchyma. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed several adjacent cystic lesions up to 18 mm in the anterosuperior spleen and a 24 mm subcapsular hypoattenuated lesion with faint contrast enhancement, findings described as “suggestive of lymphomatous infiltration.”

A 38-year-old man was admitted with 5 days of lower-limb fatigue and soreness that worsened over 2 days, leading to difficulty rising. Initial evaluation at another hospital showed a serum potassium of 2.27 mmol/L. Thyroid-stimulating hormone was 0.01 mIU/mL (0.27–4.2), and free thyroxine was 34.2 pmol/L (12–22). Despite potassium supplementation, his serum potassium remained below 2.8 mmol/L, and his symptoms did not improve.

On transfer, vital signs were temperature 36.2 °C, pulse 98 beats/min, respirations 20 breaths/min, and blood pressure 146/96 mmHg. The thyroid gland was not enlarged or tender. Neurologic examination revealed muscle strength graded 3/5 in the upper limbs and 1/5 in the lower limbs, normal tone, normal biceps and triceps reflexes, and diminished knee and Achilles reflexes.

Laboratory tests confirmed suppressed TSH, elevated T3 and T4, and negative thyroid-peroxidase, thyroglobulin, and thyrotropin-receptor antibodies. Thyroid ultrasound showed focal calcification in the right lobe and a hypoechoic region in the left lobe. A 2-hour radioactive iodine uptake was 8.9% (5–20%) and 24-hour uptake was 2.9% (20–50%), consistent with subacute thyroiditis.

The patient developed tawny urine, marked elevations of myoglobin and creatine kinase, and was diagnosed with rhabdomyolysis. He received aggressive hydration, alkali, and potassium replacement, with gradual normalization of muscle enzymes. Twenty-four-hour ambulatory monitoring showed loss of nocturnal blood-pressure dipping and elevated daytime and nighttime pressures. Funduscopic examination revealed arteriovenous tortuosity, arterial thinning, and arteriosclerotic changes in both eyes. Arterial blood gas showed a pH of 7.52, bicarbonate of 31.8 mmol/L, and serum potassium 2.5 mmol/L. A simultaneous 24-hour urine collection revealed potassium excretion of 110.6 mmol.

A 90-year-old man was referred for extraction of a dual-chamber pacemaker implanted 2 years earlier for sinus-node dysfunction and a prolonged PR interval. A few months before referral, he noticed an ulceration directly over the pacemaker pocket that failed to heal and evolved into an exophytic mass draining yellow purulent fluid. He was treated with oral cephalexin. He had no fevers, no leukocytosis, and blood cultures were negative, and he denied any systemic symptoms.

Because of his age, transportation barriers, and caregiving responsibilities, the initial consultation was via telemedicine. Given the chronic draining lesion contiguous with the device pocket, a device infection was presumed, and he was scheduled for system extraction. His device was reprogrammed locally to VVI 30 bpm to assess intrinsic function, which showed a ventricular pacing burden of less than 0.1% but provoked fatigue; his native PR interval was over 450 ms.

On the day of the planned extraction, examination revealed a crusted, nonhealing mass with a small rim of erythema and scant drainage over the pacemaker site. Surprisingly, the skin overlying the lesion was freely mobile with no adherence to the underlying pacemaker or leads. There was no erythema, warmth, pain, or fluid collection in the device pocket itself.

A 65-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of progressive, atraumatic pain and swelling of her right ankle. Physical examination revealed a palpable mass over the anterolateral aspect of the lower leg without overlying skin changes. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the ankle showed multiple extra-muscular soft tissue masses within the lower leg. The largest lesion measured 4.5 cm and involved the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis; smaller lesions were present at the level of the distal tibial metaphysis and within the ankle joint. All masses were encapsulated and internally heterogeneous. On MRI they were predominantly T1 iso- to hyperintense, SPAIR hyperintense, and demonstrated heterogeneous post-contrast enhancement. There was trace perilesional edema.

A 54-year-old Japanese woman presented with one month of swelling in the inner region of her left cheek. On examination, there was a 1.0 × 0.75 cm mobile, well-circumscribed, non-tender mass of normal-appearing mucosa on the left buccal mucosa, clinically thought to be benign, and it was excised under local anesthesia. Histopathological examination of the excised tumor unexpectedly showed acinic cell carcinoma with positive margins, and further resection was recommended. Two months later, she was asymptomatic. Bilateral level 1B lymph nodes were palpable, bean-sized, mobile, elastic, and soft. Intraorally, there was a 7 mm surgical scar on the left buccal mucosa without tenderness on palpation. Her history was significant for right breast ductal carcinoma in situ (TisN0M0) treated by excision and 57 Gy of radiotherapy five months earlier. Imaging studies, including head and neck CT, contrast-enhanced MRI, and ultrasonography, showed no abnormalities, and PET-CT revealed no evidence of distant metastasis. The resection margins were then removed under general anesthesia and sent for histopathological examination.

A 29-year-old pregnant woman at 38 weeks’ gestation with gestational diabetes mellitus was admitted awaiting delivery. Initial laboratory studies showed platelets 73×10^9/L, fibrinogen 0.667 g/L, antithrombin III 108.2%, and D-dimer 6.68 mg/L. Her ISTH DIC score was 5, and after intravenous fibrinogen her fibrinogen level rose to 1.9 g/L; she subsequently delivered a healthy infant. One hour postpartum, her blood pressure was 180/110 mmHg. 

On examination: temperature 36.8 °C; pulse 92 beats/min; respirations 20 breaths/min; BP 180/110 mmHg; no edema; normal heart and lung sounds. Laboratory tests revealed LDH 654 U/L, platelets 71×10^9/L, fibrinogen 0.719 g/L, and +1 proteinuria. She received plasma, coagulation factors, and fibrinogen. Magnesium sulfate was administered for seizure prophylaxis. Her blood pressure stabilized, coagulation improved, but she required continuous oxygen. Chest X-ray demonstrated pulmonary edema. She had noted a persistent cough and exertional dyspnea for 4 weeks prior to admission.

Six days later, platelets 96×10^9/L; fibrinogen 1.784 g/L; D-dimer 9.51 mg/L; PT, APTT, and ATIII were normal. She remained hypoxemic on 33% oxygen. Tumor markers were elevated: CEA 24.4 ng/mL; CA 19-9 >1000 U/mL; CA 72-4 >300 U/mL. Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal chamber sizes, left ventricular ejection fraction 55%, moderate tricuspid regurgitation with peak velocity ~3.56 m/s, and estimated pulmonary artery pressure ~56 mmHg. Venous Doppler studies of the legs were normal.

An 11-year-old girl presented with pain in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen of recent onset. On examination there was minimal tenderness in that region. Urinalysis and plain abdominal radiographs were unremarkable. Serum levels of α-fetoprotein and β-chorionic gonadotropin were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a 37 mm × 32 mm solid lesion with lobular margins in the medial inferior pole of the spleen that was slightly isoechoic with echogenic areas. Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen revealed a 37 mm lesion in the anterior spleen that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and contained a prominent contrast-enhancing nodule. As radiological findings were in agreement with a hemangioma, daily oral administration of propranolol at 1 mg/kg was initiated.

An 8-year-old girl presented with one week of spasmodic, nonlocalized abdominal pain without fever, vomiting, diarrhoea, or constipation. There was no significant past medical or surgical history. On examination, she had mild tenderness in the right hypochondrium; the remainder of the general and systemic examination was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 3.2×2.0 cm echogenic mass in the right subhepatic region. Short-term dicyclomine relieved her pain. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a well-defined intraperitoneal mass in the right subhepatic region containing fat-density areas interspersed with higher-density soft-tissue areas, with mild enhancement of the capsule and intrinsic soft-tissue components and no calcification or invasion of adjacent structures. T2-weighted fat-suppressed MRI confirmed the presence of fat along with other soft tissues within the lesion. Laboratory investigations were within normal limits.

A 32-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of painless jaundice. He had undergone prior evaluation with contrast-enhanced CT, which showed a distal common bile duct (CBD) stricture. Endoscopic ultrasound revealed dilation of the CBD and multiple enlarged periportal and periductal lymph nodes. An EUS-guided fine-needle biopsy of a periductal lymph node was performed. Subsequent ERCP with placement of a plastic biliary stent relieved the obstruction, and his bilirubin normalized within one week.

Histopathological staining on the biopsy specimen showed:
– Positive cytokeratin 7; negative cytokeratin 17 and cytokeratin 20.  
– Positive alpha fetoprotein and glypican-3.  
– Positive sal-like protein 4 (SALL4); negative hepatocyte paraffin-1 (HepPar-1) and arginase-1 (Arg-1).

A 3-month-old full-term female infant was evaluated for a 3-month history of curvilinear and linear palpable hyperpigmented papules and plaques. The lesions developed shortly after birth and were asymptomatic. Her parents denied any skin trauma prior to the appearance of the lesions. On skin examination, there were hyperpigmented papules on the scalp, chest, and legs and a sharply demarcated curvilinear plaque on the left distal forearm. A 4-mm punch biopsy of a curvilinear lesion on the left arm was performed. Histologic evaluation showed epidermal melanosis and intraepidermal histiocytes with few eosinophils. Immunohistochemical staining revealed S100 positivity in the epidermis and focally in the dermis. The papillary dermis stained positively for CD68 and was negative for CD34.

An 8-year-old boy presented with progressive shoulder pain for 1 year. The pain was worse at night and improved with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. He denied radiation of pain, sensory or motor deficits, or any history of trauma, and there was no family history of musculoskeletal disorders. On examination, there was mild swelling over the anterior shoulder and clavicular area without limitation of active movement or neurovascular compromise.  
Plain radiographs demonstrated thickening of the coracoid process and adjacent scapular bone. Magnetic resonance imaging showed marked bone marrow edema in the coracoid, cortical thickening of the anterior scapula, soft tissue swelling, and an intra-articular effusion. A computed tomography scan revealed a small lesion at the base of the coracoid process with surrounding cortical thickening and reactive sclerosis.

A 41-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of asthenia, anorexia, fever, abdominal pain, early satiety, and diarrhea. She reported intermittent migratory pruritic maculopapular rash and mild flushing over past years. On examination, she was febrile and had a dark tongue spot; a slightly pruritic brownish maculopapular rash predominantly on upper limbs; hepatomegaly (left lobe to epigastrium, right lobe 4 fingers below costal margin); and splenomegaly (5 fingers below costal margin). No lymphadenopathy was noted.

Laboratory studies showed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 11.0 g/dL; platelets 16×10^9/L; WBC 4.25×10^9/L with 7.0% neutrophils, 6% blasts, and 20% circulating cells with metachromatic granules initially classified as basophils). Serum lactate dehydrogenase was elevated at 369 U/L. Liver tests revealed a cholestatic pattern (alkaline phosphatase 731 U/L; γ-glutamyl transferase 638 U/L), with hypoalbuminemia (32 g/L) and hypogammaglobulinemia. Serum tryptase was markedly elevated at 184 μg/L (normal <13 μg/L). Renal function, calcium, phosphate, and coagulation tests were normal; viral serologies were negative.

Bone marrow aspirate showed 24% myeloperoxidase-positive blasts, 17% promyelocytes, and 16% toluidine blue–positive morphologically abnormal mast cells. No eosinophilia or dysplasia was observed. Flow cytometry of bone marrow detected populations of CD45^low CD117^+ CD34^+ myeloid blasts, CD45^low CD117^+ CD34^− mast cell precursors coexpressing CD25, and aberrant promyelocytes with maturation arrest. KIT D816V mutation was detected in marrow mast cells and other progenitor populations; cytogenetics revealed a normal 46,XX karyotype. Computed tomography showed hepatomegaly (18.5 cm), mild splenomegaly (13 cm), small hypodense nodules in the liver, and retroperitoneal adenopathy.

A 72-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of an insidiously progressive swelling in front of his left ear. He reported no pain, no changes during meals, and no history of trauma, infection, or salivary complaints. He had a 20-year history of beedi smoking and social alcohol use; no other comorbidities or family history of similar lesions were noted.

On examination, there was a diffuse, non-tender left parotid swelling that was predominantly cystic with some firm areas and was fixed to the underlying structures. A distinct hard nodule was palpable at the anterosuperior aspect, adherent to the skin, though the overlying skin appeared normal. Facial nerve function was intact. Intraoral, neck, ear, and nasal examinations were unremarkable.

High-resolution ultrasonography suggested a pleomorphic adenoma. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology indicated salivary gland neoplasia of uncertain malignant potential, with “cellular basaloid neoplasm/myoepithelial neoplasm” in the differential. Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed multiple lobulated lesions in the superficial and deep lobes of the left parotid gland with heterogeneous enhancement, concerning for a malignant process.

A 29-year-old woman presented with mild chronic right upper-quadrant pain of several years’ duration, which had worsened over several days. She also reported constipation and mild dyspepsia. Her medical history included scoliosis and exercise-induced asthma. On examination, vital signs were normal and abdominal examination revealed no abnormalities. Routine laboratory tests were unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound showed a 5.6 cm cystic lesion adjacent to the gallbladder. Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI demonstrated a multiloculated cyst measuring approximately 28 × 33 × 46 mm in the head and neck of the pancreas with multiple thin septa. Endoscopic ultrasound confirmed a 5 × 5 cm multiloculated cyst with clear borders, without nodules, calcifications, or perilesional lymphadenopathy; the cyst contained micro- and macrocystic anechoic components. EUS-guided aspiration with a 22G needle yielded milky fluid, but biochemical analysis revealed low triglyceride levels (<10 mg/dL). Three months later, repeat EUS-FNA again produced milky fluid and low triglycerides (<10 mg/dL). Cytological examination showed a hypocellular specimen with only rare lymphocytes and neutrophils, no epithelial cells, and no features of malignancy. Measurement of carcinoembryonic antigen in the cyst fluid was negative.

A 58-year-old woman with a history of bronchial asthma since childhood, well controlled without hospital admission or physician review for over 10 years, was admitted with 2 days of worsening dyspnoea associated with mild wheezing and cough. She denied weight loss or chest pain. On examination, she was tachypnoeic but speaking in sentences, with diffuse wheeze on chest auscultation and no stridor. There was no salivary gland or lymph node enlargement. She was treated as an asthma exacerbation but did not improve and remained hypoxic despite therapy. To exclude pulmonary embolism, a CT pulmonary angiogram was obtained, which showed:  
• A 12 mm mass protruding into the posterior aspect of the trachea with enlarged pre-carinal and subcarinal lymph nodes  
• Complete collapse of the left lower lobe and right middle lobe  
• A right upper lobe pulmonary embolism  
She was also noted to have difficulty clearing tracheal secretions despite initial measures.

An 18-year-old primigravida at 37 weeks’ gestation was referred for evaluation of a placental mass noted on prenatal sonography. First-trimester aneuploidy screening was low-risk with normal nuchal translucency; maternal PAPPA was 0.99 MoM and beta-hCG 1.46 MoM. She had been briefly treated for mild diastolic blood-pressure elevations with methyldopa and aspirin but self-reported normal pressures thereafter. 

At the mid-trimester anatomy scan, a 54-mm cystic placental lesion with multiple septations and internal echoes was reported; the patient then missed follow-up until 33 weeks, when ultrasound showed a 70×76-mm cystic structure with septations and calcifications on the fetal surface near the cord insertion (no Doppler assessment documented). Fetal echocardiography revealed septal hypertrophy >6 mm and mild ventricular discrepancy.

At 37 weeks, ultrasound estimated fetal weight at 2930 g, amniotic-fluid index 10 cm, and the complex placental mass measured 91×87 mm. Color Doppler revealed a small feeding vessel with low-resistance, pulsatile indices. Middle cerebral-artery peak systolic velocity was 68.9 cm/s (1–1.3 MoM); umbilical-artery Dopplers were normal; fetal four-chamber view again showed mild septal hypertrophy. 

According to the characteristics of the tumor on sonography, two main differential diagnoses were chorioangioma and, less probably, placental teratoma, and not just a simple placental cyst.

A 36-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with a 4-year history of diffuse bone pain around the knees and elbows and intermittent generalized pruritus. Over the past 2 months, his bone pain worsened and he developed blurred vision, bilateral exophthalmos, and difficulty walking. Previous workups at multiple centers were nondiagnostic; he had been treated intermittently with analgesics, vitamin D, topical steroids, and antihistamines.

On admission, he appeared well and was hemodynamically stable. Laboratory studies showed:
• White-cell count and differential: normal  
• Hemoglobin: normal  
• Platelet count: mild thrombocytosis (120 × 10^9/L)  
• Renal and liver function tests: normal  
• Tumor markers and autoimmune serologies: negative  
• C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate: mildly elevated  

Radiographic studies demonstrated:
• Knee radiographs: bilateral symmetric sclerotic changes of the distal femora and proximal tibiae  
• Humeral radiographs: intramedullary sclerosis of the distal humeri  
• Forearm radiographs (lateral view): sclerosis of the proximal ulnae and radii without fracture  

Nuclear and cross-sectional imaging revealed:
• 99mTc bone scintigraphy and FDG-PET: bilateral symmetric uptake in long bones, right clavicle, and mandible, with uptake in subcutaneous and muscle tissues of the lower limbs  
• CT and MRI of the lower limbs: multifocal intramedullary sclerosis of the femora and tibiae  
• MRI of the brain: enhancing lesions in the pituitary gland and retrobulbar soft tissues  
• PET/CT of the brain: corresponding FDG-avid lesions  
• CT and PET/CT of the abdomen: bilateral perinephric soft-tissue thickening with FDG uptake  

A CT-guided biopsy of the left proximal tibia showed diffuse infiltration by foamy histiocytes and fibrosis with rare Touton-like giant cells. Immunohistochemical staining of the histiocytes was positive for CD68, CD163, and factor XIIIa, and negative for CD1a, S100, and langerin; no granulomas or malignant cells were identified.

A 38-year-old woman presented with 2 months of abdominal distension and a palpable, firm, nonmobile lower abdominal mass. She denied pain, diarrhea, dyspepsia, or significant weight loss. Her past medical history was unremarkable; there was no personal or family history of malignancy. Vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, a 10-cm hard mass was palpated in the lower abdomen without other abnormalities.

Laboratory studies revealed serum CA19-9 of 489 U/mL and CA125 of 179 U/mL; routine blood count, biochemistry, and coagulation tests were unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound showed solid-cystic lesions in both ovarian regions and a 3-cm solid lesion in the pancreatic tail. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a hypo-enhancing pancreatic mass with areas of necrosis and vascular invasion, and bilateral multilocular cystic-solid ovarian masses measuring up to 15.4×18.3 cm, highly suggestive of malignancy. PET-CT further showed a cystadenocarcinoma in the pancreatic tail invading the celiac trunk, with multiple lesions implanted in the pelvic region.

At this point, the differential diagnosis included a primary ovarian tumor, primary pancreatic cancer with ovarian metastases, or synchronous primary tumors.

A 28-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of back pain that had worsened over 8 months. Over the preceding 3 months, she developed progressive weakness of the lower extremities, worse on the left, and became unable to ambulate independently in the week before admission. She denied bladder or bowel incontinence, fever, trauma, or known malignancy. On examination, upper-extremity strength was normal. Lower-extremity strength was 4+/5 on the right and 4–/5 on the left, with left ankle dorsiflexion 0/5 and plantar flexion 3/5. Sensation was intact except for decreased sensation over the dorsum of the left foot. Knee reflexes were +3 bilaterally, ankle reflexes +2 on the right and 0 on the left; plantar responses were equivocal on the left and downward on the right. Blood tests were within normal limits. Chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasonography were normal. Sagittal T1-weighted MRI of the thoracolumbar spine showed an intramedullary mass from T8 to T12 that was peripherally isointense and centrally hypointense, with an associated proximal syrinx. On T2-weighted images, the mass was peripherally isointense and centrally hyperintense. Gadolinium enhancement demonstrated intense peripheral enhancement with a multiloculated central cystic component. MRI also revealed extensive vertebral body destruction from T9 to T12 and thoracolumbar scoliosis. CT of the spine confirmed multiple lytic areas with sclerotic borders and decreased vertebral height at T9–T12.

A 53-year-old woman who suffered an ischemic stroke 13 days earlier was transferred for neurologic care. She had persistent light-headedness, left hemiparesis, aphasia, and cognitive impairment. Her medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, supraventricular tachycardia, and coronary artery disease; she was taking a beta-blocker and hydralazine. On transfer, her blood pressure was 220/120 mm Hg. CT angiography showed hemorrhagic conversion of a left anterior and middle cerebral artery infarct with edema and midline shift. Continuous EEG monitoring revealed poor function over the infarcted hemisphere without seizures.

On hospital day 1, a nicardipine infusion (2.5 mg/hour) and labetalol (200 mg every 8 hours) were started, but she remained hypertensive (178/81 mm Hg) and developed an episode of supraventricular tachycardia treated with hydralazine (10–20 mg as needed) and metoprolol (5 mg as needed). By day 3, increasing labetalol to 300 mg every 8 hours and nicardipine to 5 mg/hour reduced her blood pressure to 153/56 mm Hg. An abdominal CT scan obtained for constipation incidentally revealed a right adrenal mass measuring 5.0 × 5.7 cm. Endocrinology consultation generated a differential diagnosis of pheochromocytoma versus adrenal cortical carcinoma, and beta-blockade was discontinued.

Biochemical analysis showed total urinary metanephrine levels of 34,297 μg/day (upper limit of normal, 832 μg/day), free plasma normetanephrine of 45 nmol/L (normal, <0.90 nmol/L), and free plasma metanephrine of 31 nmol/L (normal, <0.50 nmol/L).

A 10-year-old otherwise healthy prepubertal girl was referred for evaluation of a dark spot in her right eye, first noted 3 years earlier and recently noted to be enlarging. She had no systemic complaints and was on no chronic medications. On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 OU and intraocular pressures were 17 mm Hg bilaterally. Slit-lamp examination of the left eye and dilated fundus examination OU were normal. In the right eye, there was a well-demarcated, minimally elevated, irregularly pigmented brown-black conjunctival lesion measuring 1.2 × 1.4 mm, mobile over the sclera, encroaching the limbus without corneal involvement and without visible intralesional cysts. AS-OCT through the lesion demonstrated a homogenous deep conjunctival stromal mass with intense hyperreflectivity and posterior shadowing, intact overlying epithelium, and no scleral invasion. The working differential diagnosis included primary acquired melanosis, atypical conjunctival nevus, and, less likely, malignant conjunctival melanoma. Observation was elected. 
At 6 months, the lesion measured 1.1 × 1.5 mm with a new focus of darker episcleral pigmentation; AS-OCT showed corresponding hyperreflectivity and back shadowing. Observation continued.  
At 1 year, the lesion exhibited further radial elongation of dark pigmentation reaching the peripheral cornea, with 0.5 mm of subepithelial corneal pigmentation; AS-OCT confirmed deeper stromal involvement with focal hyperreflectivity and shadowing and still no cysts. Given progression, corneal involvement, and absence of cysts, the decision was made to perform an excisional corneal, conjunctival, and partial lamellar scleral biopsy.

A 4-year-old girl presented with a 2-year history of a gradually enlarging swelling in the left preauricular region. She had no history of trauma, surgery, fever, lymphadenopathy, or weight loss. On examination, there was a painless, firm, nonfluctuant 2.5-cm mass palpable in the area of the left parotid gland; facial nerve function was intact. Ultrasonography revealed a well-defined, homogenous, round, hypodense mass situated within the superficial lobe of the parotid gland, appearing encapsulated. MRI showed that the lesion abutted but did not infiltrate surrounding tissues, was adjacent to the external auditory canal, was hyperintense on T2-weighted images, intermediate on T1-weighted images, and did not enhance with contrast. No pathological lymph nodes were detected. Given the lack of imaging criteria for malignancy, no fine-needle aspiration cytology was performed, and the patient underwent a partial superficial parotidectomy under facial nerve monitoring.

A 6-day-old female neonate was admitted with skin lesions, bleeding, and jaundice. She was born at 38 weeks’ gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery, birth weight 3.5 kg, to consanguineous parents; pregnancy and family history were unremarkable. The parents noted three lesions present at birth on the left lower extremity: a 14×8 cm blue-red lesion with a coarse, nodular surface and pale-pink halo on the anterolateral thigh extending to the calf, and two smaller similar lesions on the dorsum of the left foot. Three hours before presentation, bleeding began from a ruptured telangiectatic nodule of the large lesion. On examination she was lethargic; rectal temperature 34.9°C; respiratory rate 68/min; heart rate 170/min; blood pressure 50/30 mm Hg with unpalpable radial pulses; capillary refill 4 seconds; cold extremities; weak reflexes; jaundice to palms and soles; pale conjunctiva; and pulse oximetry 74% on room air. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 9 g/dL, WBC 9000/mm3, platelets 317 000/mm3, reticulocyte count 2%, C-reactive protein 0.4 mg/dL, blood glucose 89 mg/dL, total bilirubin 16 mg/dL (indirect 15 mg/dL); coagulation profile, liver enzymes, thyroid and renal function were normal; infant and mother were both A Rh-positive. She was diagnosed with hypovolemic shock, neonatal anemia, and indirect hyperbilirubinemia, and received 35 mL IV normal saline over 20 minutes, oxygen, and 70 mL packed red cells over one hour, after which vital signs and feeding normalized.

A 43-year-old man with a history of former smoking and diabetes presented with recurrent fever and progressive dyspnea of one year’s duration. One year earlier, he had been evaluated for fever of unknown origin and hypoxemia (ABG on room air: pH 7.41; PaCO₂ 36.6 mmHg; PaO₂ 65.0 mmHg), with mildly elevated procalcitonin (0.26 ng/mL), C-reactive protein (22.5 mg/L), and ferritin (910 ng/mL). Comprehensive screening for infection, autoimmune disease, and malignancy was negative. Chest CT and pulmonary angiography were normal despite an elevated D-dimer (1902 ng/mL) and abnormal V/Q scan; empirical anticoagulation resolved his symptoms.

On current presentation he again had fever and dyspnea. ABG on room air showed pH 7.46; PaCO₂ 32.0 mmHg; PaO₂ 44.0 mmHg. Initial blood counts, liver enzymes, and bilirubin were normal. Two weeks of broad-spectrum antibiotics yielded no improvement. On referral, he had mild anemia (hemoglobin 112 g/L) and marked elevations of CRP (313 mg/L), ESR (111 mm/h), procalcitonin (3.4 ng/mL), IL-6 (404 pg/mL), ferritin (1356 ng/mL), LDH (557 IU/L), and direct bilirubin (24.1 μmol/L). Microbiologic and autoantibody tests remained negative.

Abdominal CT showed splenomegaly (approximately seven rib units); PET-CT revealed slight splenic uptake (SUVmax 4.1). Echocardiography disclosed no structural heart disease but high cardiac output (10.56 L/min; heart rate 110 bpm; estimated pulmonary artery pressure 32.6 mmHg). Pulmonary function testing demonstrated normal volumes but a reduced DLCO (47% predicted). With no evidence of parenchymal lung disease or pulmonary embolism, a 100% oxygen inhalation test showed a shunt fraction of 47% (normal <5%), and transthoracic contrast echocardiography detected substantial delayed right-to-left shunting without evidence of a patent foramen ovale.

A 2-month-old males infant, born at term by spontaneous vaginal delivery, was brought for evaluation of a left upper-quadrant abdominal lump noted by his parents. On examination, there was an approximately 8×12 cm firm, semi-mobile, non-tender mass in the left hypochondrium extending into the left lumbar and epigastric regions. Abdominal ultrasonography confirmed a retroperitoneal mass. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen revealed a well-defined heterogeneous lesion in the left upper quadrant displacing bowel loops and major abdominal vessels. The lesion contained soft tissue, fat, fluid, and multiple bone fragments, including structures resembling a spine, ribs, facial bones, scapula, and upper and lower limbs.

A 27-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with a 2-month history of progressive dyspnea, biphasic (inspiratory and expiratory) stridor, and hoarseness. On examination by otolaryngology, she had significant hoarseness and biphasic stridor. Flexible laryngoscopy revealed marked swelling of the right false vocal cord extending into the subglottis, with immobility of the right vocal cord and approximately 90% reduction in airway caliber. MRI of the larynx with contrast demonstrated a 2.0 × 1.8 × 3.0 cm right-sided transglottic submucosal mass invading the right paraglottic space, cricoid and thyroid cartilage, and extending into adjacent soft tissues of the neck; two ipsilateral level-IV lymph nodes were enlarged. Diffusion-weighted imaging showed restricted diffusivity with an apparent diffusion coefficient of 0.7–0.8 × 10⁻³ mm²/s. FDG-PET/CT revealed intense uptake in the laryngeal mass (maximum standardized uptake value, 9.7) and three abnormal lymph nodes. Concerned about airway obstruction and possible malignancy, the patient underwent direct laryngoscopy with laser debulking to restore the airway and obtain tissue. Histologic examination of the debulked specimen showed a mixed inflammatory infiltrate composed predominantly of lymphocytes, plasma cells, neutrophils, and fibrosis. Histology and immunohistochemistry ruled out lymphoma, carcinoma, and sarcoma, but failed to provide a definitive diagnosis.

A 52-year-old woman noted a rapidly enlarging right breast mass over 2 months. She had no family history of breast cancer and no history of hormone use. An outside US-guided core needle biopsy described a spindle sarcomatous tumor with focal osteoid formation, necrosis, and osteoclast-like giant cells. The initial differential diagnosis included metaplastic carcinoma, sarcoma with heterologous metaplastic elements, and malignant phyllodes tumor. 

On referral, physical examination revealed a large, firm, mobile mass in the upper inner quadrant of the right breast, tethered to the overlying skin with mild lymphedema of the nipple–areolar complex. A soft, movable lymph node was palpated in the right axilla. 

Mammography showed a 7 cm high-density mass with a partially indistinct margin and clustered coarse and amorphous calcifications in the right upper inner breast. Breast ultrasound revealed a heterogeneous, partly cystic and partly solid irregular mass measuring 6.4 × 4.7 × 7.3 cm abutting but not invading the skin, with internal calcifications and peripheral vascular flow (BI-RADS 6). A 1.4 cm right axillary node had low-suspicion features; fine-needle aspiration yielded an acellular specimen.

Breast MRI demonstrated a 7.2 × 6.5 × 7.4 cm irregular, multicystic mass with perilesional edema, an iso- to hypointense solid component on T1 and T2 sequences showing diffusion restriction, heterogeneous rim and septal enhancement on postcontrast images, and a predominantly persistent kinetic pattern. There was skin thickening without definite invasion (BI-RADS 6).

A 65-year-old Syrian woman was referred for a 2-month history of a painless, rapidly enlarging mass in her right cheek. Six years earlier, she had undergone lumpectomy, axillary lymph-node dissection, adjuvant cyclophosphamide–methotrexate–5-fluorouracil chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and 5 years of letrozole for stage I right breast invasive ductal carcinoma, with no recurrence. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender, 2-cm mass at the inferior pole of the right parotid gland at the angle of the mandible. The right corner of the mouth was asymmetric at rest and worsened with movement, consistent with a mandibular branch facial nerve palsy. No cervical, supraclavicular, or axillary lymphadenopathy was palpable, and flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy was normal. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the neck showed a 2-cm ill-defined mass in the inferior portion of the right parotid gland that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, mildly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and enhanced moderately with gadolinium; there was no cervical lymphadenopathy.

A 62-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a rapidly growing, non-ulcerated swelling in the left retromolar trigone that had appeared about 15 days earlier and was causing difficulty chewing and mouth closure. He reported no pain but noted recent onset numbness of the left upper and lower lip on the side of the lesion. His history was notable for a B3 thymoma (WHO 2015) diagnosed in 2019, treated by thymectomy in 2020, and a lymph node metastasis of the thymoma in the left supraclavicular area confirmed by biopsy in February 2022. He had no history of smoking, alcohol use, or other comorbidities.

On examination, there was non-tender swelling of the left hemiface. Intraorally, a 3 cm × 2 cm × 2 cm bluish, hard-elastic, epithelium-covered mass was seen at the left mandibular angle in the retromolar area. 

Orthopantomography showed a large radiolucent area in the left mandibular angle. A CT dentascan confirmed a sizable osteolytic lesion in the posterior left mandible. Under local anesthesia, a needle aspiration biopsy yielded mainly sero-hematic fluid, followed by intralesional sampling of gelatinous tissue. As the lesion continued to enlarge, it was excised with a diode laser and submitted for pathologic analysis.

A 46-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with 3 weeks of progressive dyspnea, chest pain, dysphagia, facial and trunk cyanosis, and distended superficial veins. She denied tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drug use. On examination, breathing sounds were decreased with dullness to percussion at the right lower lung field and diffuse wheezing over the right hemithorax. Laboratory studies showed normal blood counts, electrolytes, and coagulation. A chest radiograph demonstrated widening of the anterosuperior mediastinum. Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed a 78 × 40 mm mediastinal mass with right-sided pleural effusion and compression of the superior vena cava and pulmonary artery trunk. No distant metastases were apparent. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy showed bronchial wall infiltration at the carina and right main bronchus, but bronchial biopsies were nondiagnostic. Mediastinoscopy and biopsy of a right laterotracheal lymph node revealed an undifferentiated malignant tumor composed of large round cells with prominent nucleoli, inflammatory cell infiltration, and extensive necrosis. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated diffuse p40 positivity with some vimentin reactivity; tumor cells were negative for cytokeratins, epithelial membrane antigen, and lymphocyte surface markers.

A 50-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a painful sensation when chewing with his lower anterior teeth. He reported no fever or weight loss. Physical examination revealed a 4.0 × 3.5 cm red, hard, and non-tender swelling over the left mandible. His oral hygiene was poor; several teeth in the region had caries and grade II mobility. There was no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. His medical history was notable only for long-term betel nut chewing. 

A maxillofacial CT scan demonstrated a soft-tissue mass with bone destruction in the median alveolar region of the left mandible, without evidence of fracture.

A 15.8-year-old boy was referred for severe back pain and evaluation of low bone mass. Five days after starting deflazacort for autoimmune hepatitis in November 2020, he developed lumbar spine pain that became constant. On May 7, 2021, DXA revealed low bone mass (Z-score spine −4.2, Z-score total body less head −1.9). In June 2021, while still on steroids, he was admitted for further evaluation. 

He was the second child of nonconsanguineous parents, born at term with normal anthropometrics. He had intermittent vitamin D supplementation in infancy. There was no family history of bone disease. Physical examination showed short stature without dysmorphic features. His weight was 47.4 kg (3rd–10th percentile), height 162 cm (<3rd percentile), BMI 18.1 kg/m2 (10th–25th percentile), Tanner pubarche stage 4, and testicular volume 10–12 mL bilaterally. Growth charts showed deceleration from age 11.

Laboratory studies showed normal serum calcium, phosphorus, PTH, and 25(OH)D. Twenty-four–hour urine calcium was mildly increased. Bone age was 15 years. Peak spontaneous nocturnal GH, thyroid function tests, gonadotropins, and androgens were appropriate for puberty.

Spine radiographs revealed compression fractures of T5–T9 and upper endplate depression of L4–L5; MRI of the spine confirmed multilevel vertebral fractures. Osteoporosis was diagnosed. The parents declined bisphosphonate therapy, and he received calcium and cholecalciferol.

Given his growth retardation, endocrine testing of the cortisol axis was performed. Late-night serum cortisol at 24:00 was elevated (10.7 µg/dL). An overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test showed a morning cortisol of 3.4 µg/dL (unsuppressed), whereas a low-dose dexamethasone regimen (0.5 mg every 6 h for 48 h) normalized the 8:00 cortisol to 1.0 µg/dL. Pituitary MRI demonstrated a poorly demarcated 2.0×3.5×5.0 mm area in the anterior lobe.

Deflazacort was discontinued on October 1, 2021. In January 2022, repeat diurnal ACTH and cortisol measurements showed persistent nocturnal elevation without a normal rhythm. A repeat overnight dexamethasone suppression test and low-dose dexamethasone test again failed to suppress cortisol, whereas a high-dose dexamethasone test (1.5 mg every 6 h) achieved suppression.

A 40-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a retroperitoneal mass discovered incidentally during preoperative CT for umbilical hernia repair. She had a 3-year history of hypertension on antihypertensive therapy and complained of a mild headache. Vital signs were unremarkable except for elevated blood pressure.  

Abdominal CT showed a 4×3×3 cm homogenous round mass located just below the left renal vein, with gradual, weak enhancement beginning in its peripheral area. MRI demonstrated low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and very high signal intensity on T2-weighted images.  

Laboratory studies revealed a plasma norepinephrine level of 702 pg/mL (normal, 100–450), with normal plasma epinephrine and dopamine levels. A 24-hour urine collection showed a slight increase in normetanephrine. However, ^123I-metaiodobenzylguanidine scintigraphy did not show uptake in the tumor.

A 56-year-old man presented with several weeks of dull pain and localized swelling over the right posterior thoracic wall. He was otherwise healthy and active, with a history of a simple fracture of the right ninth rib sustained one year earlier. On examination, there was a firm, nonerythematous swelling over the right lower back without respiratory distress or systemic symptoms. A chest radiograph revealed a shadow in the lower right hemithorax. Computed tomography of the thorax showed an 8×4-cm heterogeneous mass arising from the right chest wall, destroying the ninth rib and extending into two adjacent intercostal spaces while sparing the lung parenchyma and muscular layers. Lung windows demonstrated bilateral micronodular infiltrations up to 5 mm in diameter and a solitary 1 cm nodule in the right lower lobe; mediastinal lymph nodes were not enlarged. The radiologist concluded that this likely represented a malignant chest-wall tumor with pulmonary metastases and recommended biopsy. Through a small posterior thoracotomy, frozen-biopsy specimens were obtained from five pulmonary nodules and the chest-wall mass; none contained malignant cells.

A 61-year-old man presented after a 3-meter fall at a construction site with chest pain. He had a history of frequent alcohol use and prior trauma. On examination, he had tenderness of the right chest wall, right periorbital swelling, and a laceration on the right foot. The abdomen was soft and non-tender. Laboratory studies showed creatine kinase 637 IU/L, AST 143 IU/L, and total bilirubin 1.8 mg/dL. Chest CT revealed multiple right rib fractures and a right hemopneumothorax, as well as an incidental mass posterior to the liver. Subsequent contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed a 10 cm ovoid, low-density mass in the retroperitoneum posterior to the liver, compressing and displacing the inferior vena cava anteriorly. The mass demonstrated mild peripheral enhancement, internal fluid–fluid levels, and septa-like structures in its superior aspect.

A 59-year-old man with stage IVB salivary duct carcinoma of the right submandibular gland (pT3, pN3, bcM0), treated surgically followed by 5-fluorouracil/cisplatin and later docetaxel/trastuzumab for bone metastases, presented one year after initiation of chemotherapy with postprandial nausea. Physical examination was unremarkable: blood pressure 136/92 mmHg, heart rate 105 beats/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, temperature 36.4 °C. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, metabolic panel, tumor markers (CEA, SCC), and Helicobacter pylori IgG, were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT and PET-CT demonstrated rapid, diffuse thickening of the gastric-body wall with intense FDG uptake. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed diffuse mucosal thickening with exudate and luminal narrowing in the oxyntic stomach, resembling scirrhous gastric carcinoma. Multiple biopsy specimens showed densely proliferating neoplastic cells with pleomorphic hyperchromatic large nuclei arranged in sheets.

A 28-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of ill-defined, noncolicky right flank pain. She had no known hypertension, diabetes, or significant personal or family history. On examination, her vital signs were normal, and she had no stigmata of Cushing’s syndrome. Abdominal examination revealed a soft, nondistended, nontender abdomen.

An abdominal ultrasound showed a large heterogeneous mass between the right kidney and liver containing both hyperechoic and hypoechoic areas. A contrast-enhanced CT scan revealed a well-demarcated, homogeneous 7 × 5.5 cm mass arising from the right adrenal gland with a few foci of necrosis. The lesion enhanced to 50 HU after contrast administration and showed no calcification, surrounding tissue invasion, or adenopathy.

Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood count, electrolytes, and renal and liver function tests. A serum cortisol at 0800 h was 360 nmol/L (normal 171–536 nmol/L) and suppressed to 30 nmol/L after 1 mg dexamethasone. A 24-hour urinary collection showed metanephrine 111.6 μg (normal ≤131 μg) and normetanephrine 157.1 μg (normal ≤177 μg).

A 43-year-old woman presented with a painful hemorrhagic umbilical swelling that appeared during her menstrual period and was associated with dysmenorrhea. She had no prior abdominal surgeries. On examination, there was a 3-cm firm, tender, irreducible subcutaneous mass in the umbilicus without overlying skin changes. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 20×20-mm nonvascularized subcutaneous mass at the umbilicus, confirmed by Doppler ultrasonography.

A 40-year-old woman, one month postpartum, with no significant past medical history, presented with three weeks of left chest pain, dry cough, and progressive dyspnea (mMRC grade III) in a context of general health deterioration. On examination, she had signs of a left pleural effusion. A posteroanterior chest radiograph showed a homogeneous opacity occupying the entire left hemithorax with mediastinal shift to the right. Serial thoracenteses produced approximately 2 L of serous fluid every three days. Thoracic ultrasonography confirmed a large pleural effusion; an ultrasound-guided pleural biopsy was non‐diagnostic. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a 104 × 102 × 141 mm mediastino-pulmonary mass in the left upper lobe contacting the subclavian artery and lateral border of the aorta and encasing a branch of the left pulmonary artery, with a large ipsilateral pleural effusion. Bronchoscopic examination showed an endobronchial lesion in the left upper-lobe bronchus, but endobronchial biopsies were non‐contributory on two occasions.

A 57-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented after several falls without head trauma. Neurologic examination revealed moderate left hemiparesis (grade 3 on the Medical Research Council scale) without sensory deficits or cranial nerve abnormalities. Routine laboratory tests, chest radiography, and electrocardiography were unremarkable.

Noncontrast CT of the head showed a bilateral extra-axial frontoparietal mass measuring approximately 55 × 70 × 18 mm. The lesion was slightly hyperdense relative to cortex, caused hyperostotic reaction of the adjacent calvarium, and encased the middle third of the superior sagittal sinus. Prominent vasogenic edema of the right frontal lobe and corpus callosum was present, with sulcal effacement and ventricular buckling.

MRI demonstrated the lesion to be isointense on T1-weighted images, hypointense on T2-weighted images, lacking restricted diffusion, and showing relatively homogeneous enhancement after gadolinium. The superior sagittal sinus was occluded. The adjacent calvaria exhibited T1 and T2 hypointensity with enhancement on postcontrast fat-suppressed T1-weighted images.

A 50-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of fatigue. Physical examination revealed a palpable abdominal mass. Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin level of 6.8 g/dL, a white-cell count of 8.9 × 10^3/µL, a C-reactive protein level of 6.0 mg/dL, and an albumin level of 2.7 g/dL. Serum tumor markers, including CEA, CA19-9, and sIL-2R, were negative.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the pelvis identified a highly lobulated, hypervascular submucosal mass measuring approximately 5 cm in diameter in the distal ileum, with circumferential wall thickening, ulceration, and early venous return to the mesenteric vein. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated intermediate signal intensity on T1-weighted images, moderate hypointensity on T2-weighted images with internal hyperintense areas suggesting cystic degeneration, and marked diffusion restriction on diffusion-weighted imaging (average ADC value, 0.8 × 10^−3 mm^2/s).

Although the highly lobulated morphology and marked diffusion restriction were atypical, a gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) was considered the most likely diagnosis. No lymph node enlargement or distant metastases were evident.

A 45-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of generalized, mildly dull headaches without fever, nausea, visual symptoms, seizures, focal deficits, or immunosuppression. Neurologic examination was unremarkable.  
Brain MRI showed solid lesions in the bilateral lateral ventricles and fornix that were isointense on T1-weighted images, hypointense on T2-weighted images, and demonstrated homogeneous enhancement and hyperperfusion on postcontrast and arterial spin-labelling perfusion sequences. Diffusion-weighted imaging showed no diffusion restriction. The bilateral thalami and splenium of the corpus callosum exhibited symmetric swelling and T2 hyperintensity, and susceptibility-weighted imaging showed prominent veins adjacent to the thalami and ventricular surfaces.  
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed 42 white cells (normal <4×10^6/L), protein 1773 mg/L (normal 80–430 mg/L), IgG 235 mg/L (normal 0–34 mg/L), and cytology demonstrated malignant cells. Flow cytometry of CSF showed a CD19+ B-cell population (50.8%). Tests for syphilis, HIV, and hepatitis C were negative. Bone marrow biopsy, thoracic/abdominal CT, and ophthalmologic examination showed no evidence of systemic lymphoma.

A 17-year-old girl presented in November 2016 with multiple palpable masses in her left breast. She denied anorexia, fever, weight loss, skin ulceration, or nipple discharge. There was no family history of breast disease. On examination, five well-defined, mobile masses measured 9, 8, 5, 3, and 2 cm; there was no axillary lymphadenopathy. Blood tests were normal. Excision and histology showed fibrous tissue surrounding acinar and cystically dilated ducts without atypia, leading to a diagnosis of multiple juvenile fibroadenomas.

One year later, she returned with six breast masses (one in the right breast, five in the left) measuring 2.5, 8, 7, 6, 5, and 4 cm. Excision revealed multiple cellular fibroadenomas without atypia. Follow-up was recommended.

A few months later, she developed a lobulated 15 cm mass in the left breast. Excision confirmed a giant cellular fibroadenoma without atypia.

Six months later, she noted rapid enlargement of her left breast. Clinical examination found several lobulated masses, and she underwent lumpectomies. Grossly, multiple well-circumscribed masses measured a total of 20 × 15 × 16 cm, the largest being 8 cm in diameter. Computed tomography showed no visceral or lymph node metastases.

A 70-year-old woman with hypothyroidism and a remote history of pemphigus presented with a one-month history of progressively worsening nonproductive cough. She had a 25 pack-year smoking history. On examination, crackles were heard bilaterally. Initial laboratory tests showed a WBC count of 6610/μL with lymphocytopenia (1000 lymphocytes/μL), hematocrit 47.4%, and platelet count 208,000/μL; biochemical tests were within normal limits. Chest CT demonstrated lymphadenopathy up to 13 mm and diffuse ground-glass opacities with superimposed interlobular septal thickening (crazy paving pattern). Inflammatory markers were ESR 10 mm/hr, CRP 0.39 mg/dL, SACE 7 U/L, and ANA were negative. EBUS bronchoscopy revealed a BAL with 58% lymphocytes (CD4/CD8 ratio 1.91) without clonal populations, and neither cytologic examination of washing and TBNA nor pathologic examination of sampled nodes showed malignancy. Cultures for aerobes, anaerobes, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis were negative.

Fifteen days later, she developed acute dyspnea and was found to have an oxygen saturation of 83% on room air. Laboratory tests showed WBC 13,870/μL (90% neutrophils) and CRP 4.40 mg/dL; she was treated empirically with broad‐spectrum antibiotics and oseltamivir. Neck ultrasound revealed bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy up to 24 mm. Repeat chest CT showed bilateral lower-lobe infiltrates, persistent ground-glass opacities, right pleural effusion, and multiple enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes. Despite escalation of antibiotics and addition of corticosteroids, respiratory status worsened, and she was intubated. New sputum studies were negative for bacterial pathogens and P. jirovecii. A repeat bronchoscopy BAL was positive for coronavirus by PCR. Chest CT again showed bilateral lower-lobe consolidations, pleural effusions, and lymphadenopathy.

A 13-year-old boy presented with a 1-week history of right facial swelling and cellulitis. He reported noticing a mass in his right maxillary molar area 6 months earlier. On examination, there was a hard swelling over the right maxilla with an associated intraoral calcified mass and missing right maxillary molar teeth. No sensory nerve deficits were noted. Plain radiographs and computed tomography demonstrated an extensive, well-demarcated, dense amorphous irregular calcified lesion in the right maxilla, extending to the infraorbital rim.
