A 48-year-old woman presented with palpable masses in both parotid regions that had been slowly enlarging over 6 months. She had no pain, facial weakness, constitutional symptoms, or relevant medical or family history. On examination, bilateral firm, mobile tumors were noted in the parotid areas, measuring 2.0×1.5 cm on the right and 3.0×3.5 cm on the left; no salivary duct discharge or lymphadenopathy was found, and facial nerve function was normal. Two fine-needle aspiration attempts yielded non-diagnostic results. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the parotids included T1- and T2-weighted, diffusion-weighted, and dynamic contrast-enhanced sequences. Three well-defined lesions were identified: one in the superficial lobe of the left parotid (3.6×3.2×3.7 cm), one in the inferior superficial lobe on the right (2.9×2.6×3.0 cm), and a second in the deep lobe on the right extending into the parapharyngeal space (4.8×3.6×4.0 cm). All three tumors were heterogeneous with central cystic areas (some with high protein or hemorrhagic content) and peripheral solid components. The time-intensity curves demonstrated continuous contrast uptake suggestive of adenomas, and none of the lesions showed diffusion restriction (apparent diffusion coefficient, ~1.48×10⁻³ mm²/s).

A 21-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 4-month history of dysphagia due to mobile teeth and sleep disturbance. He had a prior gingivectomy in 2018 for presumed “pyogenic granuloma,” with equivocal pathology. On examination, he had generalized dark-red gingival enlargement, most pronounced on palatal and lingual aspects, extending over incisal edges and occlusal surfaces, with nonpurulent periodontal pockets, bleeding on palpation, and tooth mobility with a “floating in air” appearance. Multiple nodular masses were noted on labial and palatal gingiva (#6–11, #18–21) with surface erosion. Extraorally, a firm, well-demarcated 2.5 × 1.5 cm nodular lesion was palpated on the left shoulder; the patient declined biopsy of that lesion. Panoramic radiography showed ill-defined multilocular radiolucencies in the maxilla and mandible, erosion of the lamina dura, generalized bone loss beyond the middle third of the roots, and punched-out lesions with periosteal reaction along the mandibular inferior border. Karyotype was normal. Bone marrow flow cytometry revealed mild granulocytic deficiency and erythroid proliferation without aberrant immunophenotypes. A gingival biopsy demonstrated histiocyte aggregates, multinucleated giant cells including Touton giant cells, scattered lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils, and focal calcifications. Immunohistochemical staining showed LCA(+), Vimentin(+), CD68(+); and negative staining for Langerin, CD1a, S-100, CD35, CD21, MyoD1, CD138, CD34, Myogenin, CD38, SMA, and cytokeratin.

A 37-year-old man presented with a 10-year history of slow-growing, painless grouped lesions on the scrotum. He reported no fever, weight loss, prior surgery, or sexually transmitted infection. Family history was negative for similar lesions. On examination, multiple grouped vesicles involved nearly the entire scrotal skin. Dermoscopy showed grouped flesh-colored to slightly erythematous nodules with translucent yellow lacunae and occasional linear vessels. Laboratory studies—including blood biochemistry, serum lactate dehydrogenase levels, and serologic tests for sexually transmitted diseases—were normal, and there was no peripheral eosinophilia. Detailed physical examination, serology, and the absence of eosinophilia excluded filariasis.

A 71-year-old woman with a history of cholecystectomy, appendectomy, and hysterectomy presented with a 1-month history of asthenia and weight loss, and 1 day of nausea and lower abdominal pain. On examination, her abdomen was tender, and a firm mass was palpable in the lower abdomen. Routine blood tests were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed a 9 × 7 × 4 cm mass within the small-bowel mesentery near its root, with several adjacent lymph nodes and no other lesions.

A 3-week-old female neonate presented with progressive abdominal distention but no vomiting or constipation; she passed small, well-formed stools regularly. On examination, her abdomen was markedly distended, soft, and non-tender. Multiple café-au-lait spots were noted on her skin. Laboratory studies were normal. Five days later, she returned with severe abdominal distention, absolute constipation, and vomiting. Abdominal radiographs showed markedly dilated bowel loops with multiple air–fluid levels. An emergency laparotomy revealed a severely dilated ileum with volvulus; de-rotation relieved the obstruction, and no Ladd’s bands were identified. An elective appendectomy was performed. Postoperative recovery was initially good, but seven days later she again developed severe distention and signs of obstruction. A second laparotomy showed an adhesion between the appendiceal stump and ileum causing internal herniation; multiple biopsies of the colon and ileum showed no diagnostic abnormality. A diverting ileostomy was created, and her condition improved. Three months later, she presented in extremis with recurrent obstruction. Contrast studies via anus and stoma confirmed small-bowel obstruction. A computed tomography scan demonstrated a transition zone 4 cm distal to the stoma, a 3-cm segmental stricture with a 4-mm–thickened bowel wall, and malrotation indicated by reversal of the superior mesenteric artery and vein, but no evidence of a discrete bowel mass.

A 48-year-old woman, originally from Brazil and residing in Portugal, was referred to plastic surgery for evaluation of a slow-growing, asymptomatic mass on her right foot. She had a history of epilepsy (not on medication), no tobacco or alcohol use, and no family history of cancer. Physical examination revealed a single, 1 × 1 cm mass on the fibular aspect of the dorsum of the second toe. The lesion was solid, rubber-hard, and immobile relative to deeper tissues. There was no pain, and the mass did not interfere with walking. No palpable lymph nodes were detected in the popliteal or inguinal regions. Given the firm, indurated nature of the lesion, the initial differential diagnosis included soft-tissue sarcoma and osteosarcoma. An incisional biopsy of the mass was performed.

A 67-year-old Japanese man with a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and myocardial infarction treated by percutaneous coronary intervention and anticoagulant therapy presented with sputum production. Chest radiography demonstrated consolidation in the left middle to lower lung field. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed consolidation with a CT angiogram sign in the S3 and lingular segments of the left lung, and PET–CT showed corresponding increased uptake. Sputum culture and cytology were negative. Serum carcinoembryonic antigen and Sialyl Lewis X-i levels were slightly elevated at 9.4 ng/mL (normal 0–5.0) and 52 U/mL (normal ≤38), respectively, whereas squamous cell carcinoma antigen and cytokeratin 19 fragment (CYFRA) were within normal limits. Flexible bronchoscopy with radial endobronchial ultrasonography performed in the left B4 bronchus revealed snowball-like hyperechoic nodules floating on a hypoechoic background. Bronchial wash and brushing specimens were obtained, and cytological examination did not demonstrate malignancy.

A 72-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of a painless, progressively enlarging mass in the right preauricular area. She had no smoking or alcohol history. Her past medical history included mechanical aortic and mitral valve replacements for rheumatic disease, atrial fibrillation, hysteroannexectomy for uterine fibroids, and stage III papillary thyroid cancer treated with radical thyroidectomy and radioiodine. Physical examination revealed a 2 cm firm mass in the right parotid region without overlying skin changes or palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the face and neck showed an ill-defined 19×22×23 mm mass in the right parotid gland infiltrating the ipsilateral masseter muscle. The patient underwent right parotidectomy with facial nerve dissection. Grossly, the specimen contained a 35×25×15 mm well-circumscribed mass. Microscopically, the tumor comprised monotonous small round cells arranged in cords and nests with monomorphic nuclei, infiltrating skeletal muscle, perisalivary soft tissue, and demonstrating angioinvasion and perineural invasion; margins were negative. Initial immunohistochemistry showed tumor-cell positivity for CD56 and occasional synaptophysin, leading to a diagnosis of poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma. On further review, tumor cells were positive for CD99, CK8/18, and focally for p63 and p40, and negative for NUT, CK7, TTF1, S100, and androgen receptor; the Ki-67 index was 60%.

A 28-day-old girl, born at term after an uneventful pregnancy, was noted at birth to have bluish, palpable nodular lesions (0.5–1 cm) on her face. At 21 days of age, she presented with irritability and progressive abdominal distention. On examination, she was pale and had 13 visible and 6 palpable skin nodules on her face, thorax, and extremities, along with massive hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. Initial blood tests showed mild anemia and thrombocytopenia. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed multiple nodular lesions throughout the enlarged liver. 

After transfer to a tertiary care center, her anemia and thrombocytopenia worsened (platelet count, 4,000–18,000/mm3; hemoglobin, 7.5–11.3 g/dL), but her leukocyte count remained normal. Serologic studies for HIV, cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, and Toxoplasma were negative, and serum tumor markers (alpha-fetoprotein, human chorionic gonadotropin, and carcinoembryonic antigen) were negative. Electrolytes showed persistent hyponatremia (124–133 mEq/L); renal function and potassium were within normal limits. 

Three days after admission, she developed anasarca. Liver function tests showed hypoalbuminemia (1.4 g/dL), coagulopathy (INR, 2.52), elevated aminotransferases (AST, 11–325 U/L; ALT, 1.1–55 U/L), hyperbilirubinemia (2.59–8.75 mg/dL), low alkaline phosphatase (38.5 U/L), and elevated C-reactive protein (47.7 mg/L). Serum immunoglobulins were IgG 169 mg/dL, IgM 14 mg/dL, IgA 3 mg/dL, and IgE 0.71 U/mL. Serologic testing for syphilis was negative. A repeat abdominal ultrasound showed retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy and ascites; the kidneys appeared normal. Radiographs demonstrated elevated diaphragms and intestinal distention. 

On hospital day 4, a limited bone marrow aspirate showed no abnormal infiltrate or hemophagocytosis, and an excisional skin biopsy was performed. The patient died on day 5 from respiratory distress syndrome.

A 37-year-old man presented with a 5-year history of intermittent thoracic back pain and gradually worsening gait disturbance, associated with pain and numbness predominantly in his right lower extremity. He had no prior medical consultations or imaging studies. He had no significant past medical history. Neurologic examination revealed spastic paraparesis with muscle weakness, brisk reflexes, and extensor plantar responses in both lower limbs, proprioceptive deficits, and myoclonus of the right lower limb.

MRI of the thoracic spine was performed with T1- and T2-weighted sequences, fat suppression, and post–gadolinium imaging in multiple planes. There was an intramedullary bilocular lesion at T2–T5 measuring 8.5 × 2.1 × 1.5 cm, causing canal expansion and obliteration of subarachnoid and epidural spaces. On T1 and T2 images, the lesion was hyperintense; on fat-suppressed images, both compartments were hypointense. Susceptibility-weighted images showed minor blooming, likely from hemosiderin. After contrast, there was no nodular enhancement, only faint, incomplete, linear peripheral enhancement including the mid-septum separating the two compartments. The findings were compatible with intramedullary lipoma. The differential diagnosis included lipomyelomeningocele and dermoid cyst.

A 63-year-old man with a history of poorly differentiated prostate adenocarcinoma (clinical stage T3a, Gleason score 4+4=8) had been treated with bicalutamide and goserelin, achieving a PSA nadir of 0.2 ng/mL. Five years later, despite a persistently low PSA (0.036 ng/mL), he was found to have local extension into the bladder and a metastasis to the S1 vertebra. He also noted a gradually enlarging, painless mass in the first web space of his right hand that impaired thumb motion and caused sensory disturbance. 

On examination, there was a well-circumscribed, elastic, nonmobile mass measuring 5 × 4 × 3 cm between the right thumb and index finger, with overlying skin discoloration. Laboratory tests showed an elevated alkaline phosphatase level. 

Radiographs of the right hand demonstrated enlargement of the first metacarpal interspace without bony destruction. MRI revealed a well-defined mass adjacent to the first metacarpal with iso- to low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, heterogeneous high signal on T2-weighted images, peripheral contrast enhancement, and central nonenhancement suggestive of necrosis. Thallium scintigraphy showed marked uptake in the right hand only. CT of the body confirmed a lytic and sclerotic lesion of the sacrum. 

Based on these findings, the differential diagnosis included a primary malignant soft tissue tumor (such as myxoid liposarcoma or myxofibrosarcoma) versus a metastatic lesion of prostate adenocarcinoma.

A 15-year-old previously healthy female noted a right breast mass several months ago on self-examination. She denied pain, nipple discharge, or overlying skin changes and had no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. On examination, there was a firm, mobile 3-cm mass in the right upper outer quadrant without axillary lymphadenopathy. Breast ultrasound showed a solitary, solid 3.0 × 2.1 × 2.2-cm mass at the 10 o’clock position with no Doppler vascularity and was interpreted as most consistent with a fibroadenoma.

A 62‐year‐old man with no personal or family history of malignancy noted a mass in his right parotid region. On examination, there was a poorly mobile, 5.0×5.0 cm mass in the right parotid gland. Contrast‐enhanced CT showed a 5.1×5.0 cm irregular tumor with calcifications, a low‐density area, and indistinct margins in the right parotid gland. A malignant tumor was suspected, and the mass was resected with lymph node dissection. On gross examination, the cut surface was yellow–white with hemorrhage and necrosis, and the tumor boundary was ill‐defined. Histopathologic examination revealed three distinct neoplastic cell types: 
• Atypical cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm, large nuclei and prominent nucleoli forming duct‐like, glandular, and solid patterns (consistent with salivary duct carcinoma).  
• Atypical spindle‐to‐epithelioid cells with clear cytoplasm forming trabecular, tubular, and solid patterns with hyalinized stroma (consistent with myoepithelial carcinoma).  
• Atypical duct‐like structures composed of an inner layer of cuboidal cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and an outer layer of cells with clear cytoplasm (consistent with epithelial‐myoepithelial carcinoma).  
These three tumor types invaded surrounding tissues and were intermixed with areas of reciprocal cell transfer.

A 55-year-old perimenopausal woman presented after a syncopal episode. She reported three days of progressively worsening bruising over her right lower abdomen. Her medical history was notable only for hypertension, and she had undergone a cesarean section 18 years earlier, complicated postoperatively by a persistent incision-site mass thought to be a seroma, which had remained unchanged.  

On presentation, CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a 6.5 cm lobulated soft-tissue mass in the right anterior abdominal wall, associated 4–5 cm masses along the right pelvic sidewall, and a 3.4 cm enhancing mass in the right inguinal region; no other pelvic or abdominal organ abnormalities were noted. A PET scan confirmed high FDG uptake in these lesions (SUV max 3.3–21.4) without identifying a clear primary site. Tumor markers were within normal limits (CA125 17.2 U/mL, CEA 2.0 ng/mL, CA19-9 26.9 U/mL).  

A percutaneous biopsy of the anterior abdominal wall lesion demonstrated malignant cells positive for CK7, PAX-8, WT-1, p53 (strong and diffuse), ER, and PR; morphology and immunoprofile were read as “high-grade adenocarcinoma, favor high-grade serous carcinoma of ovarian, fallopian tube, primary peritoneal origin, or endometrial serous carcinoma.”

A 12-year-old girl presented with a 3-month history of a growth on the mandibular gingiva between tooth #31 and #32. The lesion measured 1.0 × 1.5 cm, was firm, adherent to the gingiva but not fixed to underlying structures, and the overlying mucosa appeared normal. An intraoral periapical radiograph showed drifting of teeth #31 and #32 without alveolar bone erosion. Clinically and radiographically, a pyogenic granuloma was provisionally diagnosed.

The lesion was completely excised and curetted under local anesthesia. Grossly, the specimen was a soft-to-firm, grayish-white pedunculated mass. Microscopically (H&E), the tissue was well circumscribed and separated from the overlying epithelium by fibrous tissue. The lesion consisted of a relatively acellular, loose myxoid stroma containing scattered spindle-to-stellate cells and many delicate proliferating capillaries, with minimal collagen.

Toluidine blue staining highlighted numerous mast cells. Reticulin staining was strongly positive, and alcian blue staining demonstrated alcinophilia. Immunohistochemical studies showed vimentin positivity and S-100 negativity.

A 45-year-old African-American man presented with a 3-year history of well-circumscribed, scaly plaques on his back, abdomen, groin, and axillae. The lesions began in the right groin, spread to his back within 2 weeks, and gradually increased in size and number. He reported only pruritus and denied systemic symptoms.

Six months after onset, a skin biopsy was nondiagnostic, and he was treated for presumed plaque psoriasis with apremilast, then guselkumab for 6 months, and subsequently secukinumab; the plaques continued to increase in number, became scalier, and developed fissures despite these therapies.

A Wood’s lamp examination revealed fluorescence of the lesions, and he received oral terbinafine and antifungal topical agents, with decreased scale for 2 weeks but progression of pruritus and new lesions by 6 weeks. Antifungals were discontinued, and he was placed on oral and topical corticosteroids plus hydroxyzine, without lasting benefit.

After 3 years of unsuccessful treatments by multiple providers, he was referred for further evaluation of his treatment-refractory “psoriasis.”

A 40-year-old Moroccan woman presented with a 2-year history of a slowly enlarging swelling on the right side of her neck. She reported mild dysphagia and dyspnea but denied dysphonia, fever, syncope, or other compressive symptoms. Physical examination revealed a firm, oblong, nonpulsatile, nontender mass measuring approximately 10 × 10 cm in the right carotid triangle. Oropharyngeal examination showed a bulge in the right tonsillar region; indirect laryngoscopy demonstrated mobile vocal cords, and cranial nerve and nasal endoscopic examinations were normal.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a well-defined mass measuring 110 × 100 × 147 mm in the right carotid triangle extending into the superior mediastinum. The mass was heterogeneous and pushed the carotid artery and internal jugular vein anteriorly, displacing the larynx, trachea, and thyroid gland outward. Contrast dye showed late peripheral enhancement with an isodense center. No cervical lymph nodes were identified. Fine-needle aspiration of the mass was nondiagnostic.

A 43-year-old woman underwent pelvic MRI for evaluation of uterine myoma, which incidentally revealed a 4.6 × 2.8 cm soft-tissue mass in the right perineal area. She had no anal pain, bleeding, or change in bowel habits. Physical examination was unremarkable. Rectal endoscopy demonstrated a submucosal tumor just above the anal canal on the right side. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. FDG-PET/CT showed intense uptake in the anorectal mass (SUVmax = 17.9). Aspiration cytology and needle biopsy were inconclusive.

A 43-year-old Indian man with no significant past medical history presented with a lesion on his right groin. He noted a painless nodule at that site four years earlier, which had gradually grown. Approximately four months before evaluation, the lesion became tender and began to exude pus. He denied systemic symptoms, radiation exposure, weight loss, or a family history of cancer. On examination, there was a firm, fixed, tender, erythematous nodule measuring 2 × 3 cm on the right groin, with superficial erosion and purulent discharge. No regional lymphadenopathy or other skin lesions were observed. An incisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia for histopathologic assessment.

A 4-month-old infant presented with an enlarging mass on the right thigh that had been present at birth and exhibited rapid growth over several months. The cutaneous lesion had a vinous coloration. The patient’s history was notable for abnormal bleeding associated with vaccine inoculation. On examination, there was a large, warm, and tender vinous mass on the right thigh with ipsilateral thigh and leg edema and bilateral leg petechiae. Laboratory evaluation revealed anemia, thrombocytopenia, and hypofibrinogenemia. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right thigh showed a large infiltrative soft-tissue lesion with poorly defined margins. The central portion was isointense on both T1- and T2-weighted images, whereas the peripheral portion demonstrated significant hyperintensity on both sequences. After intravenous contrast, the lesion exhibited diffuse heterogeneous enhancement. The mass measured approximately 7 × 7 × 9 cm and involved all muscle compartments of the thigh, most prominently the medial compartment. It extended into the subcutaneous tissue with diffuse enhancing cutaneous thickening. There was diffuse soft-tissue edema with reticular stranding in the subcutaneous fat perpendicular to the skin surface, showing avid enhancement after gadolinium administration. Dilated femoral and external iliac veins were noted. The arteries and the underlying femur appeared normal. Subcutaneous edema of the leg was also present.

A 34-year-old woman was admitted with massive upper gastrointestinal bleeding. She complained of epigastric pain, nausea, weakness, and five episodes of melena over three days. On arrival she was hypotensive (70/40 mmHg), tachycardic, pale, cyanotic, and confused. Her abdomen was soft and non-distended, with slight epigastric tenderness; a rectal examination confirmed melena. Hemoglobin was 5.8 g/dL. She was resuscitated with intravenous fluids and three units of packed red blood cells. Emergency upper endoscopy revealed active bleeding from an elevated, ulcerated lesion on the greater curvature of the upper stomach, which was controlled with local sclerosis. Four days later, repeat endoscopy showed mild, diffuse esophagitis, a small sliding hiatal hernia, and at the cranial part of the gastric corpus a 5 cm, well-circumscribed reddish submucosal mass with a small fibrin-covered ulcer. Multiple biopsies demonstrated histological features of a smooth muscle tumor. Abdominal CT scan confirmed a 4.9 × 4.4 cm submucosal lesion arising from the muscularis propria with strong contrast enhancement and no hepatic metastases or lymphadenopathy. With a preoperative diagnosis of gastric leiomyoma, she was referred for elective surgical resection.

An 81-year-old man presented with 4 months of progressively worsening dyspnea on exertion. His medical history included chronic kidney disease and coronary artery disease status post coronary artery bypass grafting. On examination, his blood pressure was 138/82 mm Hg, heart rate 76 beats per minute, and respiratory rate was normal. An electrocardiogram was unremarkable. Chest radiography revealed a rounded mass measuring approximately 8 cm in the left lower lung zone. A noncontrast CT scan of the chest showed an enhancing soft-tissue mass along the left aspect of the pericardium, measuring 6.2 × 5.3 cm. At that time, the differential diagnosis included pericardial cyst, teratoma, lymphangioma, and branchial cyst. A dedicated CT heart angiogram demonstrated a 6.9 × 5.4 cm mass in the left inferior mediastinum with a stalk-like connection to the pericardium. A biopsy of the mass was performed.

A 72-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a lesion in the right seventh rib, initially noted as an abnormal chest shadow on screening at age 50 and followed intermittently by a general physician.  
He was asymptomatic, and physical examination findings were unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies showed an elevated alkaline phosphatase level of 706 U/L; other values were within normal limits.  
Pulmonary function testing revealed a mild restrictive pattern (percent vital capacity, 78.8%).  
Chest radiography demonstrated a well-defined radiopaque mass measuring 12 × 9 × 18 cm arising from the right seventh rib, which had enlarged progressively over 22 years.  
Computed tomography revealed an extraosseous, calcified mass with cortical destruction of the right seventh rib, a similar small lesion on the right ninth rib, and lesions in the ninth thoracic vertebral body.  
Magnetic resonance imaging showed low signal intensity relative to muscle on T1-weighted images, heterogeneous low and high signal on T2-weighted images, and enhancement in the lower-intensity T2 regions.  
Bone scintigraphy and PET/CT demonstrated increased uptake in the right seventh and ninth ribs and the ninth thoracic vertebral body, with a maximum standardized uptake value of 7.67 in the seventh rib.

A 61-year-old man presented with gross hematuria and intermittent right pelvic pain. His medical history included hypertension, psoriasis, treated pulmonary tuberculosis, and a 60–pack-year smoking history. Urinalysis revealed microscopic hematuria; biochemical tests were normal. Renal ultrasound and cystoscopy showed no abnormalities. Intravenous urography demonstrated a tubular filling defect with partial obstruction of the right mid ureter. Retrograde ureteropyelography confirmed a 5 cm long tubular mass in the mid ureter proximal to the iliac vessels. Flexible ureteroscopy revealed a pedunculated ureteral tumor with a vulnerable surface. Urine cytology and endoscopic biopsy of the lesion and renal pelvis were negative for malignancy. A staging CT scan showed slight dilatation of the right renal pelvis and subtle thickening of the right ureter without evidence of metastasis or lymphadenopathy.

A 48-year-old woman with a 1½-year history of abdominal wall dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans that had transformed into fibrosarcoma underwent routine staging. She was asymptomatic; vital signs were stable, and chest auscultation was clear. Initial CT of the chest showed multiple small bilateral pulmonary nodules characterized as benign of uncertain nature; CT of the abdomen and pelvis was normal. No PET scan was obtained. Over the next 18 months, she remained well, but serial chest CT showed interval enlargement of two nodules: one in the right middle lobe increasing from 0.9 cm to 1.2 cm and another in the right lower lobe increasing from 1.0 cm to 1.5 cm. Because of the growth in the setting of known fibrosarcoma, she underwent right thoracotomy with wedge resections of both nodules for presumed metastases.

A 17-year-old girl from central India presented with a one-year history of whitish, foul-smelling vaginal discharge containing fragmented bits. She denied vaginal bleeding. Despite alternative treatments, her symptoms persisted. One month before admission, she developed acute urinary retention and was catheterized.

On examination, her general condition was fair; a Foley catheter was in situ, and pelvic examination revealed an enlarged uterus with pyometra.

Laboratory studies showed:
- Hemoglobin 9 g/dL, RBC count 3.32 ×10^12/L, hematocrit 26.8%, MCV 80 fL  
- C-reactive protein 8.54 mg/dL (normal <1 mg/dL)  
- Lactate dehydrogenase 242 U/L and elevated alkaline phosphatase  

Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis demonstrated a soft-tissue mass involving the anterior and posterior vaginal walls and anterior sacrum, displacing the bladder anteriorly; the mass was hyperintense on T2 and hypointense on T1 sequences; no pelvic lymphadenopathy was noted.

Computed tomography of the thorax revealed a subcentimeter mediastinal lymph node and multiple subpleural nodules in both lungs. Abdominal CT showed bilateral kidney pressure changes with dilated ureters; other abdominal organs were unremarkable. Pelvic CT identified a heterogeneously enhancing 10 × 9.8 × 9 cm mass in the vagina narrowing the cervix, extending to the introitus, and displacing the bladder; no ascites or lymphadenopathy was present. Pelvic ultrasound confirmed hematometra and minimal septated pelvic fluid.

Biopsy of the vaginal mass revealed sheets of undifferentiated small round cells with scant cytoplasm, uniform chromatin, and focal rosette formation on hematoxylin–eosin staining. Immunohistochemical staining showed:
- Diffuse positivity for vimentin  
- Membranous positivity for MIC2 (CD99)  
- Positivity for BCL-2 and FLI-1  
- Negative stains for cytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, desmin, MyoD-1, myogenin, and smooth muscle actin

An 18-year-old woman with a history of asthma presented with an 18-month history of progressively worsening shortness of breath and dysphagia. Initially, she had intermittent mild dyspnea, and a chest radiograph demonstrated a small mediastinal mass that reportedly resolved on follow-up imaging one year later. Cardiology evaluation, including electrocardiography and echocardiography, was normal. She was diagnosed with moderate-persistent asthma and treated with inhaled corticosteroids and albuterol, but her symptoms continued to worsen. She then developed chest pain, dyspnea with exertion, dysphagia to solids and liquids, and intermittent left arm numbness. A repeat chest radiograph showed interval enlargement of an anterior mediastinal mass, and she was referred to the emergency department.  
In the emergency department, chest radiographs demonstrated a large superior mediastinal soft-tissue mass with significant rightward deviation and focal stenosis of the trachea. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a 7.5 × 7.4 × 7.6 cm heterogeneous mass with internal calcifications extending from the left lower neck into the upper anterior mediastinum, causing mass effect on and compression of the trachea, esophagus, and great vessels; there was abutment of the ventral surfaces of the lower cervical and upper thoracic vertebral bodies without definitive CT evidence of bone invasion. MRI of the thoracic spine showed a heterogeneous T2-hyperintense, enhancing lesion in the upper mediastinum abutting the ventral surface of the cervical spine without signal abnormalities of the vertebral bodies.

A 64-year-old woman from central Nepal presented with a slowly growing, skin-covered, gray-brown mass in her right inguinal region of 1 year’s duration and bleeding from the mass for the past 4 days. She reported a dull, aching pain at the site but denied fever, weight loss, or other similar lumps. Her medical history was unremarkable, and she was not on any medications. On examination, there was a single, non-tender, globular, smooth, mobile mass measuring 7.5 cm by 6.0 cm in the right inguinal region, with bleeding from its tip. The mass was nonpulsatile, and there was no impulse on coughing. Ultrasonography showed a heterogeneous echogenicity mass with irregular margins and slightly increased vascularity.

A 51-year-old woman who works outdoors in a high-altitude region presented with a 5-year history of a gradually enlarging mass at the lateral aspect of her right lower eyelid, which had accelerated in growth over the past 3 months. She reported intermittent itching and occasional bleeding from the lesion. Thirty years earlier, she had noted a similar pea-sized lesion at the same location in her left lower eyelid; it was excised at age 25 for cosmetic reasons but recurred, and histologic examination of the recurrent left-eyelid lesion revealed a pigmented nodular basal cell carcinoma. She has hypertension and diabetes mellitus, treated intermittently. 

On examination, the right lower eyelid bore a 25 × 30 mm pigmented, ulcerated nodular mass that was firm, adherent to underlying tissues, and caused slight lid eversion; there was no regional lymphadenopathy. The left lower eyelid showed postsurgical scarring with mild conjunctival redness. The remainder of her systemic examination was unremarkable.

Routine blood tests revealed elevated fasting and postprandial blood sugars; hemogram, liver and kidney function tests were normal. Chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasonography showed no abnormalities.

A 60-year-old man presented with a painless growth on the left buccal mucosa. He had smoked for 10 years. On examination, there was a yellowish-white, cauliflower-shaped exophytic lesion measuring 11 × 7 mm, which was soft and asymptomatic. No regional lymphadenopathy was noted, and he had no other systemic illnesses. A provisional diagnosis of papilloma was made, and an excisional biopsy was performed to rule out malignancy.

A 52-year-old right-handed woman presented with a 2-year history of intermittent, nonradiating, achy pain in her left wrist without numbness or tingling. She denied trauma or prior surgery. On examination, there was no edema or skin changes; however, a firm, mobile, tender soft-tissue mass was palpable over the volar aspect of the left wrist. Transillumination was inconclusive, and an ultrasound was obtained.

Ultrasound examination demonstrated a 0.6 × 0.6 × 0.4 cm, well-defined, solid, oval hypoechoic soft-tissue mass in the volar lateral wrist abutting the radial artery. There was no internal calcification or necrosis, and color Doppler showed little to no intrinsic vascularity; the radial artery and veins were patent. 

Differential diagnosis included complex ganglion cyst, angioleiomyoma, schwannoma, neurofibroma, thrombosed pseudoaneurysm, nodular fasciitis, and leiomyosarcoma.

A 17-year-old female presented with a 4-year history of a gradually enlarging, painless swelling in the left upper neck. There was no history of dysphagia, dyspnea, dysphonia, trauma, or similar swellings elsewhere. On examination, there was a 4×3 cm soft, non-tender, nonpulsatile mass in the left anterolateral upper neck. It did not expand with Valsalva maneuver and had no palpable thrill. The overlying skin was normal, and oral cavity examination was unremarkable. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. A provisional diagnosis of branchial cyst was made.  
Ultrasonography revealed a well-defined hyperechoic mass suggestive of a highly vascular lesion. Fine-needle aspiration cytology yielded findings consistent with a vascular lesion. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed an inhomogeneous hypodense lesion closely abutting the left thyroid cartilage with no clear separation from the strap muscles. The CT report raised a differential of vascular malformation versus hemangioma.

A 14-year-old right-hand–dominant girl presented with a 1-year history of pain and swelling at the base of her right thumb. The swelling was initially pea-sized, gradually enlarging over a year, and became painful (dull, nonradiating, aggravated by thumb movement) 2 months after onset. There was no trauma, fever, weight loss, or other medical history.

On examination, there was a single hard, tender, smooth, well-defined 2.5×2.5 cm swelling fixed to the head of the first metacarpal. The overlying skin was normal and pinchable. First metacarpophalangeal joint movement was terminally restricted and painful.

Routine blood tests were normal. Radiographs showed a solitary, expansile, lytic lesion of the first metacarpal head, involving epiphyseal and metaphyseal regions up to the articular surface, with a narrow zone of transition and a sclerotic rim; there was no periosteal reaction, cortical breach, or soft-tissue extension. A comparison radiograph 4 months earlier showed a smaller lesion.

MRI of the hand revealed that the lesion was hypointense on T1 and T2 sequences, hyperintense on STIR sequences, and exhibited endosteal scalloping. Based on these benign-appearing findings and the lesion’s location, the radiologist suggested a diagnosis of enchondroma of the first metacarpal head.

An 11-year-old boy presented to the emergency department with a 1-month history of nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, and snoring. He also reported a 2-week history of progressive left visual field loss, initially as a small black dot that evolved to complete blackness. On examination, he had a high-arching, floppy posterior soft palate and inflamed nasal turbinates. Vital signs were within normal limits.

He was referred for an immediate dilated ophthalmologic examination and an MRI of the brain and orbits, and he was also referred to otolaryngology for evaluation of persistent allergic rhinitis versus bacterial sinusitis. He was discharged with cetirizine and oxymetazoline and instructed to return if symptoms worsened.

Four days later, an MRI of the orbits and sinuses showed a 7 × 7 × 7 cm, multi-spatial mass centered in the nasopharynx and nasal cavity. The mass involved the left sphenopalatine foramen, extended anteriorly along the turbinates into the nasal passage, invaded and replaced the bony sella posteriorly, tracked laterally through the pterygomaxillary fissure, and extended caudally anterior to the adenoids, causing complete nasopharyngeal airway obstruction. A CT scan of the facial bones confirmed the large, destructive, expansile bony changes associated with the mass.

He was admitted and underwent bilateral nasal endoscopy with biopsy of the left nasal mass, which revealed extensive involvement under the inferior turbinate. Histopathology showed a highly vascular, benign-appearing mesenchymal proliferation most suggestive of capillary hemangioma. The differential diagnosis included solitary fibrous tumor and juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

A 40-year-old Caucasian man with a 5-year history of occasional abdominal discomfort presented with acute, stinging pain in the right upper abdomen. He smokes and has no prior abdominal surgeries. Laboratory studies showed mildly elevated transaminases and a C-reactive protein level of 22 mg/L. Outpatient abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 9 cm polycystic lesion in the right flank. On physical examination, the abdomen was soft, non-tender, and without palpable masses. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated an 83 × 43 × 61 mm polylobate, hypodense formation with multiple thin internal septa that enhanced after contrast administration. The radiologist’s differential diagnosis included peritoneal lymphangiomatosis, enteric duplication cyst, and—even in a man without prior abdominal surgery—benign multicystic peritoneal mesothelioma. A multidisciplinary team recommended exploratory laparoscopy for definitive diagnosis.

An 87-year-old man was referred after a punch biopsy of a penile lesion was reported as showing Bowen’s disease. He had a 6-month history of an enlarging lesion on the shaft of his penis that had been treated with topical agents and antibiotics without improvement. Ten years earlier, he had a similar lesion excised by his general practitioner, but no histology report was available. He had no other masses, no inguinal adenopathy, and no family history of similar disease. His comorbidities included ischaemic heart disease, Alzheimer’s disease, and venous ulcers. On examination, there was a 2.5 cm erythematous, fleshy, exophytic plaque at the base of the penile shaft with a proximal satellite lesion; inguinal lymph nodes were not palpable. Given a clinical suspicion of an invasive malignancy, the patient underwent wide local excision of the primary and satellite lesions.

A 32-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 12-month history of recurrent headaches and paroxysmal visual impairment. He had no prior medical conditions. On examination, his neurologic status was normal: Glasgow Coma Scale score 15, pupils equal and reactive, full extraocular movements, no nystagmus, no paresis or sensory deficits, intact coordination and gait, and negative meningeal signs. Ophthalmologic evaluation showed symmetrical palpebral fissures, normal fundi apart from slight temporal pallor and peripheral atrophy, and tortuous vessels. Optical coherence tomography diagnosed astigmatism myopicus OU. Brain MRI revealed a 4.6 × 4.0 × 2.5 cm lobulated mass in the anterior cranial fossa with mass effect on the optic chiasm. On T1‐weighted images the lesion was markedly hyperintense, on T2‐weighted images it was variably hyper- to hypointense, and on susceptibility‐weighted imaging it showed hypointense foci with a blooming artifact. Diffusion‐weighted imaging demonstrated high signal with slight diffusion restriction and reduced ADC values. The radiologist’s preliminary differential diagnosis was a dermoid versus an epidermoid cyst.

A 42-year-old man presented with a 15-day history of intermittent, dull abdominal pain and a palpable mass in the epigastrium and left hypochondrium, accompanied by weight loss. On examination, a roughly 15 × 10 cm firm mass was palpable in the epigastrium and left upper quadrant. Routine blood tests, including liver function tests, were normal. Chest radiography showed elevation of the left hemidiaphragm. Ultrasonography revealed a large, heterogeneous mass measuring approximately 18 × 15 cm arising from the liver and extending to the splenic hilum. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a well-defined, lobulated mass of 18 × 14 × 13 cm arising from the left hepatic lobe, with multiple cystic and necrotic areas and mass effect on the stomach and spleen. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed external compression of the anterior gastric wall. The initial differential diagnosis included a primary hepatic adenoma and hepatocellular carcinoma. The patient had no known risk factors for hepatic malignancy, and serum α-fetoprotein levels were within normal limits. A metastatic workup, including CT of the chest and pelvis, showed no evidence of metastatic disease.

A 22-year-old man presented with a one-year history of a right-sided parotid mass and ipsilateral neck swelling. The mass was initially painless, then slowly enlarged, prompting evaluation. He had no history of radiation exposure, and his family and social history were unremarkable. On examination, there was a visible, palpable, non-tender, non-fixed swelling at the angle of the right mandible; no other lymphadenopathy was noted. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed a 2.9 × 3.1 cm superficial hypo-enhancing mass in the tail of the right parotid gland with ipsilateral cervical lymphadenopathy in levels Ib and IIa, consistent with a primary parotid neoplasm and nodal metastases. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy was suspicious for malignancy. The patient underwent a superficial parotidectomy with modified radical neck dissection.

Gross examination revealed a single, well-circumscribed, soft to friable 2.8 cm mass within the parotid gland. Microscopic examination showed a non-encapsulated lesion with solid, microcystic, and papillary-cystic architecture. Tumor cells had clear to eosinophilic cytoplasm with foamy to bubbly intracytoplasmic secretions, and colloid-type secretions were noted within cystic spaces and glandular lumina.

A 62-year-old woman was referred to otolaryngology with a 3-month history of right-sided ptosis and headache. On examination, she had complete immobilization and decreased visual acuity of the right eye. She denied weight loss, nasal discharge, infectious symptoms, or bone pain. She appeared well, with no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Neurologic examination revealed paralysis of the right oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV), and abducens (VI) nerves, along with hypesthesia in the distribution of the right trigeminal nerve (V1 and V2). Fundoscopy showed an atrophic optic disc on the right; the remainder of the neurologic examination was normal.

Noncontrast CT and MRI of the head demonstrated an expansile mass in the right sphenoid sinus with erosion of its lateral wall and roof. The lesion extended into the right orbital apex and superior orbital fissure and encased the right internal carotid artery. CT angiography confirmed an intact internal carotid artery.

An 8-year-old girl presented with a 6-month history of a painless swelling in the right posterior mandible. On extraoral examination, a firm, non-tender swelling (approximately 4 × 3 cm) caused buccal and lingual cortical expansion of the body and angle of the mandible. Aspiration yielded no fluid. A panoramic radiograph revealed a well-defined radiolucent lesion extending from the region of tooth 54 to the mandibular ramus, containing scattered bony spicules. Teeth 46, 47, and 48 were in the process of eruption, and there was root resorption of teeth 84 and 85.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of diffuse headaches that had intensified over the past week and only responded transiently to over-the-counter analgesics. She also noted a 2-week history of unsteadiness. She denied loss of consciousness, nausea, vomiting, visual or hearing changes, swallowing difficulty, focal weakness, or sensory loss. There was no personal or family history of tumors; she had undergone a prior tumor resection one year earlier for similar complaints. On examination, her pain was rated 8/10 on a visual analog scale. Neurological examination was notable for a positive Romberg test on the left; other findings were normal. Brain MRI showed an extra-axial cystic lesion in the left cerebellopontine angle that was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with posterior compression of the left cerebellar hemisphere, rightward displacement of the pons, and rightward shift and narrowing of the fourth ventricle, resulting in noncommunicating hydrocephalus.

A 60-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes presented with acute low back pain radiating bilaterally to the legs, progressing over several days to difficulty ambulating. He was initially treated for a presumed urinary tract infection without relief and later received a spinal steroid injection. Two weeks after onset, he developed urinary incontinence and bilateral leg paralysis. During a 2-week hospitalization, CT pulmonary angiography diagnosed a pulmonary embolism. MRI of the brain and spine revealed abnormal foci of enhancement in the lumbar spine and at T12. A skeletal survey was negative, and a CT-guided bone marrow biopsy showed no malignancy. Lumbar puncture demonstrated 13 white blood cells/mm3 (82% lymphocytes), protein 132 mg/dL, and negative PCR testing for herpes simplex virus and West Nile virus. One day of intravenous steroids improved pain but not weakness; steroids were stopped. He then developed bowel incontinence and was treated with IV immunoglobulin and transferred for further evaluation. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and scrotal ultrasound showed no solid tumor. Repeat spinal MRI showed cauda equina nerve root enhancement. Electromyography revealed an axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Laboratory studies were notable for an ACE level of 83 U/L, ANA 1:160 speckled, and LDH 2722 IU/L. A second lumbar puncture showed normalized cell counts; CSF cytology and flow cytometry were negative for malignancy. He underwent plasma exchange for presumed acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy without improvement, and a repeat MRI showed a new 3-cm T2 hyperintense focus in the lower lumbar cord with worsening cauda equina enhancement, raising concern for neurosarcoidosis. He received high-dose methylprednisolone and plasmapheresis, with temporary improvement, then was discharged on prednisone. Outpatient PET revealed patchy thoracolumbar marrow uptake with focal increased uptake at the left lateral aspect of L2. Despite increased prednisone and gabapentin, his lower extremity strength declined, requiring a wheelchair, and bowel and bladder dysfunction persisted. A third spinal MRI showed new hyperintense lesions in the thoracic cord, diffuse paraspinal myositis, and leptomeningeal enhancement. After another course of methylprednisolone with mild relief, a muscle biopsy of the left vastus lateralis showed type 2 myofiber atrophy without overt myopathic features or granulomatous inflammation.

A 46-year-old Sri Lankan man with paraplegia secondary to thoracic laminectomy presented with gradually worsening difficulty in evacuating his bowels; he previously relied on manual evacuation. On examination, the rectum was empty but a mass was palpable in the posterior rectal wall. Routine blood tests were normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed a dilated sigmoid colon. Lower gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed external compression at 20 cm in the sigmoid colon with a mass located posterior to the bladder. Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis demonstrated a presacral mass lesion of apparent neurogenic origin. MRI of the pelvis confirmed a well-circumscribed presacral mass causing anterior displacement of the rectum.

A 76-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of intermittent colicky lower abdominal pain associated with bilious vomiting and mild abdominal distension. She had a history of left breast cancer diagnosed 18 years earlier, treated with wide local excision, radiotherapy, and 5 years of tamoxifen, and a regional recurrence with bone metastases treated palliatively 17 years after the initial diagnosis. On examination, vital signs were stable. The abdomen was mildly distended with peri-umbilical tenderness and guarding. Laboratory studies, including hematological, biochemical, inflammatory, and coagulation profiles, were within normal limits. A plain abdominal radiograph was unrevealing. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated dilated small bowel loops consistent with obstruction, with two intraluminal filling defects: one in the proximal ileum suspicious for a non-calcified gallstone and a second area of narrowing in the terminal ileum. The patient was resuscitated and taken for laparotomy, which revealed a proximal impacted gallstone and a separate distal ileal stricture. The surgical team performed resection of both segments with primary end-to-end anastomoses. The intraoperative clinical impression was dual pathology, including gallstone ileus and Crohn’s disease.

A 30-year-old Chinese woman with a remote history of childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia in remission presented with a 3-week history of worsening headaches, giddiness, and vomiting. Neurological examination revealed cerebellar signs consistent with an infratentorial mass. Noncontrast and contrast-enhanced CT of the head showed a large (4.0 × 4.1 × 4.8 cm) posterior fossa cystic mass with an eccentrically located enhancing nodule measuring 1.5 × 1.9 cm. The lesion compressed the midbrain and fourth ventricle, resulting in dilation of the third and lateral ventricles and tonsillar herniation. 

Subsequent MRI confirmed the cystic posterior fossa mass with an eccentrically located nodule adjacent to the vein of Galen. The nodule was hyperintense on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences, hypointense on T1-weighted images, and showed avid gadolinium enhancement. No dural-tail enhancement was seen. Periventricular FLAIR hyperintensities were consistent with acute hydrocephalus. MR spectroscopy of the nodule demonstrated a reversal of the choline-to-creatine ratio with slight reduction in the N-acetylaspartate peak. Diffusion-weighted imaging and ADC mapping showed restricted diffusion within the mural nodule. After review, a radiological diagnosis of hemangioblastoma was made, and the patient was scheduled for surgical resection.

A 60-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of epigastric abdominal pain, unintentional 33 lb weight loss, and intermittent melena. Her medical history was notable for irritable bowel syndrome and diet-controlled gluten intolerance; she denied tobacco and alcohol use. On examination, her abdomen was soft and nontender without organomegaly. Laboratory testing showed normocytic anemia with a hemoglobin level of 11.6 g/dL. An abdominal CT scan was unremarkable. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a 1.5 cm semipedunculated polyp (Paris Isp) in the gastric body, the same color as the surrounding mucosa, with a smooth surface lacking overlying mucus or prominent vessels. There was a heterogeneous surface pattern with uniform pitting near the base; no ulcerations or depressions were noted. The polyp was completely resected by snare polypectomy, and several other small sessile polyps were biopsied.

A 75-year-old man was referred after an incidental intra-abdominal mass was detected on surveillance CT. His history was notable for left upper lobectomy for lung adenocarcinoma and multiple lines of chemotherapy, followed by a six-year complete response. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed two tumorous lesions: one in the region of the cecum and appendix (40 mm) and one near the sigmoid colon (24 mm), both showing enhancement. PET-CT demonstrated fluorodeoxyglucose uptake with maximum standardized uptake values of 10.7 and 9.5, respectively. MRI showed isointensity on T1-weighted images, mildly high intensity on T2-weighted images, and high intensity with low ADC values on diffusion-weighted sequences. Lower gastrointestinal endoscopy, including biopsy and fine-needle cytology, revealed no mucosal lesions or submucosal tumors. Tumor markers showed a mildly elevated CA19-9 (68 U/mL) and a normal soluble interleukin-2 receptor. Based on these findings, gastrointestinal stromal tumor of the colon and mesentery, recurrence of lung cancer, and malignant lymphoma were considered. A definitive diagnosis could not be established preoperatively, and exploratory laparoscopy with tumor excision was planned.

A 68-year-old Japanese man with no significant past medical, surgical, drug, family, or psychosocial history was referred for evaluation of an anterior mediastinal mass incidentally discovered on computed tomography (CT) performed to exclude pneumonia in the setting of a cough and low-grade fever. He was 165 cm tall, weighed 76 kg, and his physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including tumor markers, were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated:  
• A 38 × 24 mm anterior mediastinal mass with enhancement in the equilibrium phase, abutting the ascending aorta.  
• Concomitant wall thickening of the rectosigmoid colon measuring approximately 5 cm with peritoneal lymphadenopathy.

Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a 38 × 30 mm anterior mediastinal lesion in broad contact with the ascending aorta and right atrial appendage without definitive invasion. Colonoscopy and barium enema further revealed a Borrmann type II lesion in the rectosigmoid colon, 5 cm in diameter and 18 cm from the anal verge. Biopsy specimens from the rectal lesion were nondiagnostic, but imaging strongly suggested a primary rectal malignancy.

What is the most likely diagnosis of the anterior mediastinal mass?

A 39-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a right proximal thigh mass that had been growing slowly over 4 years. He also reported numbness over the medial aspect of the thigh in the distribution of the obturator nerve and a 20-kg weight loss over 6 months. He denied trauma, constitutional symptoms, respiratory or gastrointestinal issues, and had no family history of malignancy.

On examination, vital signs were stable. There was a 7 × 10 cm soft‐firm, rubbery mass in the anteromedial thigh with intact overlying skin; the mass was nonmobile, nontender, and not warm. Sensation was decreased over the medial thigh; no lymphadenopathy was present.

Plain radiographs of the right femur and hip showed a faint soft tissue swelling without calcification or bone involvement. CT of the pelvis revealed an 8.7 × 8.6 × 11 cm fatty‐density mass in the right groin extending into the upper medial thigh, displacing adjacent muscles. MRI with contrast demonstrated a large intramuscular anteromedial thigh mass arising near the psoas and invading the pectineus, encasing the posterior division of the obturator nerve; it was isointense on T1, hypointense on T2, and showed heterogeneous enhancement. Chest radiography was unremarkable.

CT-guided biopsy was performed.

A 7-year-old girl was referred for asymptomatic skin-colored papules and nodules on the left labium majus and perineal area that had rapidly increased in size over one month. At birth, she had five café au lait macules (>5 mm) overlying the perineal lesions. On examination, the left buttock was larger than the right, with the perineal nodules felt as a “bag of worms.” There was no axillary freckling, no other medical history, and no family history of neurocutaneous disease.

Pelvic MRI showed extensive, multifocal, conglomerated enhancing nodular lesions involving both labia majora, vestibular fossa, obturator internus, ischiocavernosus, urethral orifice, ischioanal fossa, and extending into the left gluteal muscle and external anal sphincter, with atrophy of the left gluteus maximus.

A skin biopsy from a nodule demonstrated an intraneural tumor confined by thickened perineurium, with tortuous plexiform bundles. Schwann cell fascicles followed the nerve’s long axis, and the endoneurial space was widened and mucinous, containing loosely spaced rounded endoneurial cells. Tumor cells were S-100 positive on immunohistochemistry.

A 74-year-old man presented with biliary colic, nausea, and vomiting. Laboratory tests showed an aspartate aminotransferase level of 55 IU/L and an alkaline phosphatase level of 204 IU/L. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 12.7-cm liver without focal lesions and a gallbladder containing multiple stones and sludge, with pericholecystic fluid and mild wall thickening; the common bile duct measured 0.6 cm. His history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and renal failure; he denied alcohol use and had no family history of cancer. During laparoscopic cholecystectomy, empyema and dense fibrous adhesions in Calot’s triangle were encountered, limiting visualization of the liver bed. The resected gallbladder measured 7.0 × 4.5 × 2.0 cm, and an adjacent 2.0 × 1.3 × 1.0 cm piece of necrotic tissue was identified. Microscopic examination confirmed acute cholecystitis, but the necrotic tissue contained nests and trabeculae of polygonal cells with clear cytoplasm and macronuclei; clear cells comprised more than 95% of the tumor, with nuclear pleomorphism, mitotic activity, and multifocal tumor necrosis indicating a high-grade malignancy.

A 10-year-old girl presented with a 1-year history of a rapidly enlarging left breast mass. There was no history of pain, trauma, fever, anorexia, or weight loss. She was premenarcheal, and there was no significant family history. On examination, the left breast had a 20 cm × 20 cm well-circumscribed, firm, non-tender, mobile lump; the right breast was normal. The mass was not fixed to skin or underlying muscle. The overlying skin was tense and shiny with prominent superficial veins. There was no nipple discharge and no axillary lymphadenopathy. Routine hematological and biochemical tests, including ESR, were within normal limits. A chest radiograph was normal. Ultrasonography of the left breast revealed a heterogeneous parenchymal pattern suggestive of fibroadenoma. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the lump showed pathology suggesting fibroadenoma.

A 44-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a 10-day history of an intermittent cough and hemoptysis, sometimes accompanied by sudden shortness of breath. He had no history of tuberculosis, asthma, diabetes, or hypertension. He smoked one to two cigarettes per day, did not drink alcohol, and had an unremarkable family history. On examination, breath sounds were bilaterally symmetrical without adventitious findings. Routine laboratory tests, including a white-cell count of 7900/mm3, hemoglobin, differential leukocyte count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, liver and kidney function tests, and CBNAAT for tuberculosis, were within normal limits. A chest radiograph was essentially normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax revealed a smoothly marginated, well-defined 15 × 14 mm solitary nodule within the right main bronchus. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy demonstrated a 3 × 2 cm pedunculated polypoid mass in the right main bronchus.

A 76-year-old woman with no smoking history presented with painless vision loss in the left eye for 3 days and a right-sided neck mass noted over 3 months. On awakening, she described a central and nasal visual darkening in the left eye with relatively preserved temporal fields. She denied other systemic or ocular symptoms and took no medications. 

On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and light perception in the left eye. The left pupil had a 3+ relative afferent pupillary defect. Intraocular pressures were 13 mmHg OD and 14 mmHg OS. Ocular motility demonstrated a left abduction deficit, esotropia, and hypertropia of the left eye; there was mild left enophthalmos. Right cervical lymphadenopathy was palpable. Optical coherence tomography of the macula was normal.

CT and MRI of the head, neck, and orbits showed necrotic right cervical lymph nodes suspicious for squamous cell carcinoma and a 27×10×20 mm left extraconal orbital mass along the medial wall extending toward the orbital apex, displacing the medial rectus and optic nerve sheath. Sinonasal opacification of the sphenoid and ethmoid sinuses suggested a sinonasal primary.

Ultrasound-guided biopsy of a right level IIb lymph node revealed “metastatic keratinizing moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma, invading the soft tissue.” Immunohistochemistry on the nodal specimen was p16 negative and PD-L1 5–10%; perineural invasion was present.

The patient then underwent left anterior orbitotomy with debulking of the orbital mass. Histologic examination of the orbital specimen showed lobules and cords of moderately to poorly differentiated cells with distinct squamous and glandular differentiation. Individual cell keratinization and occasional signet ring–like cells were noted. PAS–Alcian blue staining demonstrated focal stromal and intracytoplasmic mucin. Mucicarmine staining was positive both stromally and within tumor cells.

Immunohistochemical stains on the orbital tumor were positive in the squamous component for p40, p63, CK5/6, and BER-EP4, and in the glandular component for CEA and CK7; they were negative for CK20, p53, TTF-1, and p16. Ki-67 labeling was 20–30%. Fluorescence in situ hybridization for MAML2/CRTC1 translocation was negative, with the MAML2 gene intact.

A 77-year-old Caucasian man presented to the emergency department in December 2023 with a two-week history of worsening asthenia, cachexia, paradoxical dysphagia, and a 20-kg weight loss over the past year. His medical history included hypertension and left vocal cord palsy with dysphonia diagnosed in 2020. On neurologic examination, he had fluent speech, preserved ocular motility, left facial muscle hyposthenia with a Bell phenomenon, ipsilateral hearing loss, and tongue protrusion. Laboratory studies showed mild anemia (hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL). Brain and brainstem MRI demonstrated T2-FLAIR hyperintensity and contrast enhancement of the intracisternal segments of cranial nerves V, VII, VIII, IX, X, and XI, linear enhancement of cranial nerves III and VI, and leptomeningeal enhancement over the C1–C2 spinal surface. The differential diagnosis included inflammatory, neoplastic, neurolymphomatosis, and granulomatous diseases. Serologic tests for extractable nuclear antigens, ANCA, ANA, paraneoplastic antibodies, and IgG subclasses were negative. Spine MRI showed pseudonodular enhancement of the medullary cone and cauda equina nerve roots. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed xanthochromia, a lymphocytic pleocytosis (49 cells/mm3, 70% lymphocytes with some atypical forms), hypoglycorrhachia (34 mg/dL), and hyperproteinorrachia (350 mg/dL); cultures and viral PCRs were negative. CSF cytology showed erythrocytes, rare neutrophils, and occasional histiocytes without definitive malignant cells. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a 9 mm pre-pyloric gastric wall thickening without lymphadenopathy.

A 48-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of persistent right-sided neck pain, reduced neck and jaw range of motion, and mild proximal bilateral upper-limb weakness. She had a recent diagnosis of cervical cancer. To exclude metastases, a PET/CT scan was performed, showing moderate to intense FDG uptake in the upper cervical spine between the clivus and the anterior arch of C1. Diagnostic CT revealed a 15 × 12 mm nodular soft-tissue thickening between the superior margin of the anterior arch of C1 and the clivus, extending posteriorly around the right lateral aspect of the odontoid peg, with minor bony spurring but no bony destruction. Repeated MRI demonstrated a stable 16 × 10 mm uniformly enhancing mass on the superior surface of the anterior arch of C1 abutting the tip of the odontoid peg, with no bony erosion, no invasion of prevertebral muscles, and no spinal-cord compression; the lesion was isointense on T1, hypointense on T2, and did not show diffusion restriction. The differential diagnosis at this point included joint-based pathology such as crystal deposition disease, metastatic cervical cancer, and a primary soft tissue tumour. Given the lesion’s location, a stereotactic endoscopic endonasal biopsy was performed; intraoperatively the lesion was hard, fibrous, and ill-defined. Histology of the biopsy demonstrated a low grade fibrohistiocytic tumour with proliferation of mononuclear epithelioid to spindled cells in a fibrotic stroma, mild nuclear pleomorphism, giant cells, and CD68 positivity.

A 60-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a 3-month history of pelvic heaviness and dyspareunia. On examination, a firm mass was palpated in the cul-de-sac of Douglas. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a 14-cm retro-uterine solid mass with cystic areas; the uterus was normal in size and appearance. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a well-defined, ovoid, left-sided tumor posterior to the uterus measuring 13.8×8.7×9.7 cm, with posterior compression by the sacral promontory. The lesion showed heterogeneous enhancement on contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images and restriction on diffusion-weighted imaging with corresponding low ADC signal. The right ovary appeared normal, and there was no ascites. Staging CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no distant metastases or other intra-abdominal abnormalities. Serum CA-125, CA19-9, and CEA levels were all within normal limits.

A 44-year-old surgeon underwent uneventful bilateral phacoemulsification with intraocular lens implantation for high myopia. Three months later, she developed progressive blurred vision in both eyes. Ultrasonography showed severe vitreitis with intense flare cells and dense membranes, and visual acuity declined to 20/200 OU. Slit-lamp examination revealed mild anterior-segment inflammation, well-positioned lenses, and dense vitreitis; intraocular pressure was 18 mmHg in both eyes. A comprehensive workup for uveitis was unremarkable. Despite repeated topical, subconjunctival, and sub-Tenon steroid injections, oral prednisone (1 g/kg/day), and later cyclosporine A, her vision worsened to light perception, and intraocular pressures rose to 35 mmHg OD and 50 mmHg OS. Antiglaucomatous therapy and cessation of systemic steroids produced no improvement. She then underwent pars plana vitrectomy and trabeculectomy OS without visual gain, as dense anterior-chamber inflammation recurred and IOP relapsed. Subsequent immunosuppression with prednisone and methotrexate also failed to help. By 12 months after symptom onset, her vision was light perception OU, IOP remained elevated despite therapy, and she exhibited personality changes. One day she fainted and was taken to the emergency department.

A 30-year-old woman presented with a three-month history of progressively worsening low back pain and neuropathic pain in both legs, more pronounced on the right and refractory to medical therapy. She described paresthesia of both lower limbs extending to the inguinal regions, worse at night. She denied weakness, bowel or bladder dysfunction, and had no upper limb symptoms. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable.

On examination, general physical findings were normal. Neurologic examination revealed mild clasp-knife spasticity in both lower limbs (right > left), bilateral extensor plantar responses, brisk knee and ankle reflexes, and a sensory level at L1 including a saddle distribution to pin-prick. 

Contrast-enhanced lumbosacral MRI showed an intradural extramedullary lesion at the conus medullaris (L1 level) that was isointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and demonstrated strong homogeneous enhancement post-contrast.

A 71-year-old woman with a history of total thyroidectomy and radioactive iodine ablation 43 years earlier for papillary thyroid carcinoma presented with a 2-month history of a palpable, non-tender left lateral neck mass. Physical examination demonstrated a firm mass in the left level III region; the thyroid bed was free of palpable abnormalities. Neck ultrasonography showed no residual thyroid tissue and revealed a 2.8 × 1.7 cm solid, inhomogeneous, vascular mass in the left level III region that did not have the sonographic appearance of a normal lymph node. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck confirmed a 2.8 × 1.7 cm enlarged lymph node in the left level III, with no other neck or thyroid-bed lesions. Two ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsies yielded cellular specimens with groups of epithelial cells in flat sheets and papillary-like clusters; the cells demonstrated enlarged nuclei with grooves and occasional intranuclear inclusions. Immunohistochemistry on the cell block was positive for thyroid transcription factor 1. A whole-body FDG PET study showed uptake only in the known left neck mass and no other FDG-avid lesions.

A 94-year-old South Asian woman with a history of atrial fibrillation, a stroke two months earlier, stage 3b chronic kidney disease, and moderate dementia presented in March 2019 with severe dyspnea and progressive pedal edema over one week. On examination, her blood pressure was in the 160s mmHg systolic, heart rate 143 beats per minute and irregular, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. She was in atrial fibrillation with an elevated jugular venous pressure of 12 cm H₂O, an S₃ gallop, occasional bibasilar crackles, and moderate pitting edema. Electrocardiography confirmed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response and nonspecific ST–T–wave changes. A portable chest radiograph showed florid pulmonary edema with diffuse Kerley B lines and prominent hilar congestion. Laboratory studies revealed a D-dimer of 323 ng/mL (normal ≤500), pro–BNP 3468 pg/mL (normal ≤300), CK-MB 7 U/L (normal <20), troponin I 0.03 ng/mL (normal ≤0.15), hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL (normal 12–15), a normal white-cell count, and serum creatinine 1.6 mg/dL (normal 0.6–1.2). Bedside transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a 59 × 43 mm mass arising from the left atrial free wall, preserved left ventricular systolic function (ejection fraction 65%) without regional wall motion abnormalities, moderate left atrial enlargement (38 mL/m²), severe diastolic dysfunction with restrictive physiology (estimated left atrial pressure 22 mmHg), and moderate pulmonary hypertension (52 mmHg). There was no prolapse of the mass through the mitral valve orifice.

A 59-year-old Caucasian man was referred for a routine dental evaluation. He was asymptomatic.  
– Panoramic, occlusal, and periapical radiographs showed a unilocular radiolucent area with a well‐circumscribed sclerotic border in the anterior right maxilla.  
– All maxillary teeth except the left cuspid had been removed uneventfully over the years; the most recent extractions were 7 years earlier.  
– He had no history of trauma or surgery to the maxilla, was a non‐smoker, and reported no other illnesses.  
– On examination, the alveolus was of normal consistency with no expansion or swelling; there was no pain, tenderness, or change in the color of the overlying mucosa, and no lymphadenopathy.

A 42-year-old woman with iron deficiency anemia presented with melena and generalized weakness. Vital signs were within normal limits. Examination revealed orthostatic hypotension and mucosal pallor. Laboratory testing showed a hemoglobin level of 4.9 g/dL, for which she received 3 units of packed red blood cells. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 3.1 × 2.9 × 2.4 cm intraluminal lobulated mass along the greater curve of the gastric body. Upper endoscopy revealed a 7 × 10 cm ulcerative, necrotic, fungating mass at the fundus extending into the body. Biopsy showed hyperplastic gastric mucosa with ulceration, fibrinopurulent exudate, granulation tissue, severe chronic active gastritis, positivity for Helicobacter pylori, and no evidence of malignancy. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated only glandular epithelium. Diagnostic laparoscopy identified enlarged perigastric lymph nodes; surgical biopsy of a node revealed no malignant cells. The patient completed H. pylori eradication therapy but returned one month later with recurrent melena. Repeat CT showed that the gastric mass had increased to 5.2 × 5.2 × 5.4 cm. Upper endoscopy findings were unchanged. Endoscopic ultrasound revealed a homogeneous, hypoechoic, 4.5 × 3.5 cm mass originating from the muscularis propria. Multiple deep biopsies again showed findings consistent with inflammatory gastritis, and core fine-needle biopsy demonstrated myofibroblastic tissue with a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate. Immunohistochemistry was negative for CD117, S-100, and ALK-1 and positive for smooth muscle actin, desmin, and vimentin.

An 8-year-old girl with a history of recurrent upper respiratory infections, pneumonias with pleural effusions, and hypogammaglobulinemia was diagnosed with common variable immunodeficiency (IgG 268–497 mg/dL [NR 952–1538], IgA < 6 mg/dL [111–335], IgM 55–122 mg/dL [59–151], absent specific antibody responses). She received prophylactic antibiotics and monthly IVIG with a reduced infection rate but recurrent hospitalizations for septic shock, pneumonia, otomastoiditis, CMV infection, and UTIs.  

At age 12, she developed pancytopenia (Hb 10.2 g/dL, WBC 3790/mm³, platelets 108 000/mm³), hepatosplenomegaly, reticulocyte count 1.2%, and LDH 164 mg/dL. Two bone marrow aspirations showed erythroid hyperplasia and granulocyte hypoplasia. Autoantibodies including ANA, RF, anti-dsDNA, and antiphospholipid antibodies were negative.  

At age 17, she presented with fever, oral ulcers, alopecia, arthritis of wrists and elbows, headache, and cough. She developed pleural and large pericardial effusions requiring ICU admission. Labs showed Hb 7.9 g/dL, WBC 1000/mm³, platelets 17 000/mm³, reticulocyte count 0.32%, proteinuria 3.0 g/day, C3 72 mg/dL (79–152), C4 4 mg/dL (16–38). PCRs for EBV and blood/urine cultures were negative. Autoantibodies now included ANA 1:320 (dense fine speckled), anticardiolipin IgM 100 MPL, RF, and lupus anticoagulant. She met the ACR criteria for SLE.  

Additional findings: hepatosplenomegaly; AST 58 IU/L (0–20), ALT 111 IU/L (6–20), triglycerides 456 mg/dL (< 130), ferritin 6034 ng/mL (36–92), LDH 791 mg/dL. She fulfilled preliminary pediatric MAS criteria and was treated with IV methylprednisolone, IVIG, chloroquine, azathioprine, and prednisone. Bone marrow aspiration at that time showed pan-hypoplasia without hemophagocytosis or neoplastic cells. Renal biopsy revealed chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis and focal acute tubular necrosis without glomerular injury and negative immunofluorescence. Liver biopsy showed drug-induced hepatitis without neoplastic cells.

A 49-year-old woman was referred to the dermatology clinic for evaluation of a small mass on the dorsal aspect of the right fourth finger. She reported that the lesion had been present for approximately 15 years, with a slight increase in size, but it caused no pain or functional limitation. Her medical history was significant only for a mitral valvuloplasty 20 years earlier. There was no history of trauma to the area, no family history of similar lesions, and she denied systemic symptoms.

On examination, there was a firm, round, immobile, and nontender subcutaneous mass measuring about 1 cm in diameter over the proximal interphalangeal joint of the right fourth finger. The overlying skin appeared normal, and the range of motion of the finger was intact. No other abnormalities were noted on physical examination.

Given the persistence and growth of the lesion, an excisional biopsy was performed and the specimen was sent for pathologic evaluation.

A 79-year-old man with no prior medical history and an ECOG performance status of 0 was referred to the rapid-access prostate clinic for an elevated prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level of 29.9 ng/mL. He had undergone asymptomatic testing because of a family history of prostate and breast cancer. He reported mild storage lower urinary tract symptoms but denied visible haematuria or other red-flag symptoms. On digital rectal examination, his prostate was enlarged and the left lobe felt firm and irregular.

A bone SPECT scan showed a focus of uptake suspicious for a left pubic tubercle metastasis and an additional focus in the left posterolateral bladder wall. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated prostatic enlargement; a mixed sclerotic lesion on the left pubis consistent with metastatic disease; a polypoid mass on the left side of the bladder highly suspicious for a primary bladder tumour; and left external iliac lymphadenopathy (largest node 16 mm).

Flexible cystoscopy revealed an enlarged, occlusive prostate and a calcified lesion at the bladder neck of uncertain prostatic or urothelial origin. No urine cytology was obtained. The patient was scheduled for simultaneous transurethral resection of the bladder lesion (TURBT) and transperineal prostate biopsy. Intraoperatively, a 2–3 cm calcified mixed solid and papillary growth was resected from the left bladder wall; it was not in continuity with the prostate lobes. A limited TURP was performed to resect the base of the growth. A second nodule on the left inter-ureteric bar was also resected, and a ureteric stent was placed given proximity to the left orifice. Transperineal prostate biopsies were obtained in the same setting.
