A 70-year-old man, a retired surgeon and smoker with Lynch syndrome diagnosed 35 years earlier after colon adenocarcinoma, presented with a one-month history of swelling and severe inflammation of his right index finger, associated with restricted interphalangeal joint motion. His history included multiple colectomies, a liver segmentectomy for metastases, chemotherapy, and, 12 years earlier, multiple cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas of the arm, scalp, nose, mandible, thorax, and nasal wall. Five months before this presentation, chest CT had shown a 22-mm mass in the right upper lobe with ipsilateral and contralateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy; biopsy confirmed squamous cell carcinoma with 80% PDL1 expression, and staging with PET–CT and brain MRI established stage IIIC non–small-cell lung cancer. He had received four cycles of gemcitabine and carboplatin, after which acral and skin metastases appeared. On examination, the right index finger was markedly swollen and tender, with focal soft-tissue necrosis and melanosis; interphalangeal motion was limited, and sensory and motor function in the remaining digits was intact. Radiographs of the right hand revealed an aggressive, lytic lesion in the distal phalanx of the index finger with surrounding soft-tissue swelling.

A 58-year-old man with a nine-year history of celiac disease, in histologic and clinical remission on a strict gluten-free diet, presented with subacute gait ataxia, undirected dizziness, double vision, and cognitive impairment progressing over four days. His history included refractory celiac disease type II diagnosed six months earlier on the basis of ulcerative jejunitis and abnormal intraepithelial lymphocytes, for which he was on methylprednisolone and azathioprine with slight improvement in gastrointestinal symptoms.

On examination, he had a cerebellar syndrome with gait ataxia and dysdiadochokinesia; the remainder of the neurologic and systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, renal and liver function, inflammatory markers, and serologic tTG-IgA antibodies, were within normal limits. Fecal calprotectin was elevated. 

Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain showed multifocal T2-hyperintense, partially ring-enhancing lesions in cortical, subcortical, periventricular regions, basal ganglia, mesencephalon, and cerebellum. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a normal cell count, no malignant cells, no pathogens, and no oligoclonal bands. Polymerase chain reaction assays for neurotropic pathogens were negative. Electroencephalography demonstrated moderate diffuse cerebral dysfunction without epileptiform discharges. Onconeural antibodies and antibodies to neuronal surface antigens in serum and CSF were negative. 

Given rapid neurologic worsening, intravenous high-dose methylprednisolone was administered, with prompt clinical improvement, although follow-up MRI showed stable intracranial lesions in size and distribution.

An 86-year-old Caucasian woman presented to the emergency department after a syncopal episode. She reported multiple prior syncopal events, including one three months earlier that resulted in a right femur fracture and for which cardiac and neurologic evaluations at that time were unrevealing. Her medical history was notable for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and breast cancer treated with bilateral mastectomy. Emergency medical services found her unresponsive with a blood glucose level of 38 mg/dL; she was given 50 mL of 50% dextrose in water and subsequently became responsive, with a repeat glucose measurement of 260 mg/dL. She attributed the initial hypoglycemia to skipping lunch and reported multiple falls over the past year. 

On admission, blood pressure was 151/70 mmHg; other vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination, including a complete neurologic assessment, was unremarkable. Postural blood pressure readings did not show any orthostatic hypotension. Initial laboratory studies revealed: serum glucose, 125 mg/dL; hemoglobin A1C, 4.7%; and C-peptide, 2.16 ng/mL. Thyroid-stimulating hormone, electrocardiogram, troponin levels, and computed tomography of the head were all within normal limits. 

During hospitalization, she experienced recurrent hypoglycemic episodes, with fasting blood sugars as low as 56 mg/dL on hospital day 3, requiring frequent intravenous dextrose boluses and eventually a continuous dextrose infusion. A morning cortisol level was normal. Screening for exogenous hypoglycemic agents, including sulfonylureas, was negative. A 72-hour fast was performed; at 48 hours she developed symptomatic hypoglycemia with a glucose of 32 mg/dL, an insulin level of 22.05 μIU/mL, and a C-peptide level of 3.61 ng/mL.

A 20-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of left hip pain and 6 months of progressive difficulty walking. He denied trauma, fever, weight loss, and had no known chronic illnesses. He was treated empirically with 9 months of anti-tubercular therapy after an outside diagnosis of left hip tuberculosis, but his pain and stiffness persisted. On examination, there was mild tenderness over the left hip, wasting of the thigh and leg, and no true limb shortening. Hip movements were restricted: flexion deformity 30°, adduction 10°, and external rotation 15°. 

Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the pelvis showed decreased left hip joint space and calcified nodular masses over the superior and inferior femoral head and anterior femoral neck. Computed tomography of the pelvis confirmed multiple intra-articular loose bodies (largest 3.0 × 2.2 cm) and early secondary osteoarthritic changes, without joint effusion or bony erosions. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed early arthritic changes, intra-articular loose bodies, and less than 10% articular erosion of the posterosuperior acetabulum.

A 35-year-old woman presented with an 8-month history of radicular pain radiating from her lower back down the left leg, with occasional tingling. The pain progressively worsened and was particularly severe by August. She denied any weakness, autonomic symptoms, history of trauma, or injury. On examination, she had mild hypesthesia in the left L5–S1 dermatome but normal muscle strength, normal abduction and adduction, and negative Lasègue, Kernig, Bragard, and Sicard signs. Electromyography showed neuropathic irritation of the left L4, L5, S1, and S2 roots, most severe at L5, with no denervation. Lumbosacral gadolinium-enhanced MRI revealed a solitary, completely cystic mass in the left L5–S1 foraminal zone extending along the course of the sciatic nerve into the left ischial groove, measuring approximately 13.9 cm in length and 1.9 cm in maximal diameter. The lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and demonstrated peripheral rim enhancement, causing severe foraminal stenosis without attachment to pelvic organs. MR neurography confirmed that the mass arose from the sciatic nerve at the left ischial groove.

A 48-year-old man underwent abdominal CT for evaluation of a gallbladder polyp detected on ultrasonography. The study revealed well-defined, heterogeneous soft-tissue density lesions in the bilateral retroperitoneum at the sites of the adrenal glands, with densities indicating adipose tissue. The left mass measured 8.0 cm in maximum diameter and the right 1.8 cm. The right adrenal gland was discernible but the left was not. 

His medical history was notable for 4 years of hypertension, treated with antihypertensive medication. He had no specific symptoms, and the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed elevated plasma epinephrine (67.8 pg/ml; reference 1–20 pg/ml), norepinephrine (340.8 pg/ml; reference 15–80 pg/ml), and ACTH (158 pg/ml; reference 10–90 pg/ml). Twenty-four-hour urinary 17-ketosteroids (48.5 mg/day; reference 8–22 mg/day) and 17-hydroxycorticoids (55 mg/day; reference 5–23 mg/day) were elevated. Plasma cortisol, renin, aldosterone, and 24-hour urinary cortisol, free cortisol, metanephrine, vanillylmandelic acid, and homovanillic acid were all within normal limits.

On abdominal MRI, the left and right tumors measured 8.2 cm and 2.0 cm, respectively, showed high signal intensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images, and low signal intensity on T1 fat-suppressed and chemical-shift images. An I-123 metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scan showed no significant uptake in either lesion.

A 65-year-old Turkish man presented with dyspnea. He had undergone orthotopic heart transplantation 10 months earlier and was maintained on cyclosporine–based immunosuppression. His medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (40 pack–year smoking history), hypercholesterolemia, hypothyroidism, gout, normocytic anemia, steroid-induced myopathy, obesity, and a recent PCR-confirmed cytomegalovirus infection. 

Initial chest CT revealed a small nodule in the left lower lobe. Bronchial lavage was non-contributive for viral, bacterial (including mycobacteria), fungal pathogens, or malignancy. Follow-up CT scans at three and four months showed three progressively enlarging nodules (up to 1.6 cm) in the left upper and lower lobes and one in the right lower lobe. There were no palpable lymph nodes and no cutaneous or mucosal lesions.

Because the lesions were not accessible bronchoscopically or thoracoscopically, an open thoracotomy was performed, and wedge resections of the left upper and lower lobe nodules were obtained for diagnosis.

A 58-year-old man, previously healthy and active, noted a 4-month history of gradual weight gain despite daily aerobic exercise and no change in diet. Three months before presentation, he observed progressive abdominal distension, describing it as feeling “like a large ball in my belly.” He subsequently developed intermittent abdominal discomfort that increased in intensity and frequency, constipation, and severe gastroesophageal reflux, for which he began taking laxatives and a proton-pump inhibitor. 

He underwent contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen, which revealed a large unilocular retroperitoneal cystic mass measuring 32 cm by 25 cm. The mass did not communicate with the pleural space or any other abdominal viscera, displaced the entire bowel to the left, spanned from the pelvis inferiorly to the liver hilum superiorly, and compressed the liver and stomach. 

He had no history of asbestos exposure or other occupational risks (silica, cadmium), no family history of malignancy, no significant alcohol or tobacco use, and no history of trauma.

A 67-year-old man with no significant comorbidities presented with one week of progressive confusion on a background of three weeks of tension-type headaches. Three days before admission, a contrast-enhanced CT of the brain was normal. His history was notable only for stage IB superficial spreading melanoma and in-situ melanoma excised from the back and shoulder five years earlier, with no evidence of recurrence. On examination he was disoriented to time and place; vital signs were normal, and there were no meningeal signs, focal neurologic deficits, or new skin lesions. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 13.9×10^9/L with neutrophilia (12.1×10^9/L), C-reactive protein 8.5 mg/L, and otherwise normal chemistry, thyroid, and liver function tests. On Day 1, lumbar puncture revealed clear, straw-colored cerebrospinal fluid with a markedly low glucose of 0.4 mmol/L (reference 2.2–3.9), elevated protein of 4.0 g/L (reference <0.45), and a monocytic pleocytosis (20 leukocytes/mm^3, 19 monocytes, 1 neutrophil); Gram stain was negative. Non-contrast brain MRI showed possible communicating hydrocephalus. Empiric treatment for meningoencephalitis with intravenous benzylpenicillin, ceftriaxone, and acyclovir was initiated. All microbiology tests returned negative by Day 3, but as the patient’s condition worsened, empiric antituberculous therapy was started on Day 5. A repeat lumbar puncture demonstrated an opening pressure >30 cm H2O, bloodstained fluid, glucose 0.3 mmol/L, protein 2.3 g/L, leukocyte count 130/mm^3 (122 monocytes, 8 neutrophils) and 60 unidentified cells. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the brain revealed leptomeningeal enhancement within the interpeduncular cistern and communicating hydrocephalus.

A 55-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of globus pharyngeus and dysphagia. She denied fever, odynophagia, dysphonia, dyspnea, cough, or choking. Her medical history was otherwise unremarkable, and she reported no weight loss or family history of similar symptoms.

On rigid laryngoscopy, there was a smooth, submucosal bulge on the medial wall of the right pyriform fossa. The right false vocal cord was elevated by the mass, preventing visualization of the right true vocal cord. Both true vocal cords moved normally. Examination of the neck revealed no visible abnormalities or palpable cervical masses.

Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 15 × 21 mm, round-to-oval, hypodense mass in the right paraglottic space near the pyriform fossa. The lesion was well encapsulated, showed no calcification, and exhibited patchy, gradual enhancement with nonenhancing low-density areas. There was no evidence of infiltration, cartilage destruction, or lymphadenopathy.

MRI revealed that the mass was isointense on T1-weighted images, inhomogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and lacked diffusion restriction. Post-contrast images showed regional, inhomogeneous enhancement. The lesion caused mild medial displacement of the false and true vocal cords and aryepiglottic fold, slight widening of the cricothyroid space, and narrowing of the glottic fissure. The subglottic airway and cervical esophagus remained patent, and there were no signs of necrosis or liquefaction.

A 42-year-old man presented with a brown plaque on his right posterior thigh that had been present for 1 year and had thickened over the last several months without symptoms. On examination, there was a 16 × 16 cm dusky red, thick plaque with scale on the right posterior thigh. Additional findings included a 1 × 1 cm scaly erythematous patch on the abdomen and scattered hypopigmented patches and thin pink plaques on the buttocks, back, and lower extremities; the hypopigmented patches had been present for many years. Total body‐surface‐area involvement was estimated at 2 % patches and 0.5 % plaques, consistent with stage IA mycosis fungoides.

A biopsy of a hypopigmented patch confirmed a paucicellular CD8+ epidermotropic infiltrate characteristic of hypopigmented MF. A biopsy of the posterior thigh plaque revealed two components: superficially, an epidermotropic, band‐like infiltrate of small‐ to intermediate‐sized cerebriform lymphocytes; and in the deeper dermis, a diffuse and nodular lymphocytic infiltrate. The deeper cells had round nuclei, small basophilic nucleoli, and an eosinophilic rim of cytoplasm with eccentric nuclei, imparting a monocytoid appearance.

Immunohistochemical studies showed that both the superficial and deeper infiltrates were CD8 positive with loss of CD5 and CD7. The superficial component expressed granzyme and TIA-1. The deeper component demonstrated a perinuclear dot-like staining pattern for CD68.

A 60-year-old Asian man presented with 20 days of painless gross hematuria. His only past medical history was well-controlled hypertension on enalapril. He denied any family history of genetic disorders.

Laboratory studies were unremarkable. Ultrasonography revealed an extremely hypoechoic mass at the lower pole of the left kidney, enlargement of the right kidney, and multiple hypoechoic areas in the right kidney, suggestive of cysts or space-occupying lesions. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated an enlarged right kidney with a patchy low-density, infiltrative lesion of lower attenuation than the renal cortex, along with enlarged perirenal and retroperitoneal lymph nodes. Bilateral renal cysts, calcification of a left renal cyst wall, and bilateral nephrolithiasis were also noted. Eight years earlier, a complex cyst had been seen in the right kidney, which had not been treated.

The patient underwent a laparoscopic radical nephrectomy of the right kidney. Gross examination showed a 65 × 35 × 20 mm mass in the mid–upper pole that breached the capsule and invaded perirenal fat. The cut surface was gray-red with cystic and solid regions and focal yellow areas.

Microscopic examination revealed that the cystic regions were lined by a monolayer of cuboidal tumor cells. In the solid areas, tumor cells formed papillary structures, glandular tubules, nests, and sheets. The cells had unclear borders, eosinophilic to lightly clear cytoplasm, and enlarged, atypical nuclei with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli and a peripheral halo. Abnormal mitoses were present, and there was a mild lymphocytic stromal infiltrate without definite necrosis or hemorrhage.

A 5-month-old girl was brought for evaluation of a 2-month history of gradually increasing upper abdominal distension without pain or gastrointestinal or genitourinary symptoms. Her birth history was uneventful, and there was no maternal illness, radiation exposure, or drug intake during pregnancy. On examination, a firm focal bulge was palpable in the left hypochondrium and epigastrium. Abdominal radiography demonstrated a faint curvilinear bony structure traversing the midline, resembling an axial skeleton. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a large heterogeneous solid-cystic mass in the upper abdomen with predominantly echogenic (fatty) content, linear echogenic structures casting posterior acoustic shadowing suggestive of calcification, and an encapsulated eccentric cystic component. A suspicion of infantile teratoma was given with differential diagnosis of fetus in fetu.

A 71-year-old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and ischemic heart disease presented with a 2-month history of intermittent painless hematuria with passage of clots. She denied dysuria, frequency, or other lower urinary tract symptoms, and there was no family history of malignancy. On examination, vital signs and abdominal and pelvic exams were unremarkable. Laboratory evaluation showed a hemoglobin level of 8.6 g/dL requiring blood transfusion; serum creatinine and other biochemical parameters were within normal limits. Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a 2.9 × 2.5 × 2.4 cm polypoidal mass arising from the posterolateral wall of the bladder dome; both kidneys and the upper tracts appeared normal. Pre- and postvoid bladder volumes were 180 mL and 44 mL, respectively. Cystoscopy demonstrated an exophytic solid tumor measuring 1.5 × 2.0 cm on the anterior fundal wall, covered with slough. A deep transurethral resection of the bladder tumor was performed. Histopathological analysis revealed an adenocarcinoma composed of mucinous and signet-ring cell components. Thus, a secondary adenocarcinoma or a rare variant of primary adenocarcinoma of the bladder was suspected.

A 30-year-old man presented with a one-year history of a slowly growing mass in the left upper‐medial arm. He reported no pain or neurovascular symptoms. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-circumscribed mass with intermediate signal intensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images. A metastatic work-up, including CT of the chest and abdominal ultrasound, was negative.

A 73-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of right nasal obstruction and frequent blood-tinged crusting.  Endoscopic examination revealed a soft, fungating mass resembling a nasal polyp in the right middle meatus, partially adherent to the nasal septum and measuring more than 1 cm at its greatest dimension. The surrounding mucosa was hyperemic, with scattered blood clots but no active bleeding.  

Paranasal sinus CT showed a 2.2 cm polypoid lesion in the right middle meatus with well-defined margins and heterogeneous iso-intensity; there was slight expansion and erosion of the anterior cortex of the maxilla. The mass appeared to originate from the nasal septum and occupied the middle meatus without evidence of sinusitis.  

The lesion was completely excised via endoscopic sinus surgery, removing the septal mucosa while preserving the septal bone and cartilage. Grossly, the specimen was a relatively circumscribed, pinkish soft tissue mass measuring 2.2 × 1.5 × 0.7 cm.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of a progressively enlarging right submandibular swelling and a 2-year history of anterior basicervical enlargement without dysphagia, dysphonia, or dyspnea. On examination, there was a multinodular goiter predominantly of the right thyroid lobe and a firm, well-circumscribed, painless submandibular mass measuring 3 cm in diameter. Neck ultrasonography confirmed a heterogeneous multinodular goiter and identified a suspicious right submandibular lymph node enlargement. Thyroid function tests, including TSH and free T4, were within normal limits. The patient underwent total thyroidectomy and excision of the submandibular mass.

A 42-year-old man presented with bleeding from the extraction site of the right lower second premolar for the past 4 days. He had noted mobility of that tooth for 1 month before extraction. The day after extraction, bleeding recurred.

His medical history was noncontributory. On examination, a diffuse soft, nontender swelling was present on the right lower face, 2 cm from the corner of the mouth to 1 cm anterior to the angle of the jaw, without lymphadenopathy. Intraorally, a well-defined, firm, nontender, reddish-black nodular growth measuring 2×1 cm was attached to the gingiva at the extraction site; its surface was lobulated. An orthopantomogram showed no abnormalities.

Based on the appearance of a reddish-black exophytic gingival mass after recent extraction, the initial differential diagnoses included epulis granulomatosa, traumatic neuroma, malignant melanoma, angiosarcoma, and Kaposi’s sarcoma.

A 35-year-old nulligravida woman presented with a 2-year history of a progressively enlarging, painless lump in her right perineum. On examination, there was a mobile, soft, non-fluctuant, non-tender mass in the right perineal region. Pelvic ultrasonography showed a heterogeneous mass with complex internal vascularity, highly suggestive of malignancy. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 36×28×23 mm lesion at the posterior aspect of the right vulva that abutted the skin surface but was separate from the anus, vagina, and urethra, and was deemed suspicious for soft-tissue sarcoma.

A 37-year-old gravida 4 para 3 woman at 24 weeks 5 days’ gestation presented with respiratory distress and 4 days of absent fetal movements. She had 10 days of fever, cough, and diarrhea and tested positive for COVID-19 six days earlier. On examination, she was tachypneic, with an oxygen saturation of 87% on room air; the abdomen was nondistended with no palpable mass. Ultrasound revealed intrauterine fetal demise with biometry consistent with 23 weeks and no cardiac activity. A cesarean delivery was performed, and a macerated fetus was extracted; the amniotic fluid was stained. The placenta weighed 256 g and measured 19 × 10 × 4.5 cm. The trivascular umbilical cord was eccentrically inserted, 19 cm in length, and exhibited a fusiform dilation near the placental end. Within this dilation were three cohesive, solid nodules measuring 6.5, 7.7, and 10 cm, each with a smooth surface. On sectioning, the nodules were solid, reddish, and contained multiple vascular channels. Placental thrombi were identified.

A 53-year-old Thai woman presented with a mass on the right forearm that had rapidly grown over 5 months. She had no pain, preserved forearm and hand function, and no sensory complaints. On examination, there was a firm, approximately 8-cm mass over the volar aspect of the right forearm, not fixed to bone, with unremarkable overlying skin and no motor or sensory deficits. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a hypervascular soft-tissue mass with multiple feeding vessels adjacent to the flexor tendons. Ultrasound-guided core biopsy revealed a malignant, poorly differentiated epithelioid neoplasm with clear cell features and focal necrosis. A staging workup, including chest radiography and abdominal imaging, showed no visceral metastases. A technetium bone scan demonstrated increased radiotracer uptake in the right seventh rib posteriorly, L2 vertebra, right sacroiliac region, left proximal humerus, and right proximal femur, raising concern for osseous metastases.

A 77-year-old woman presented with a 24-month history of a progressively enlarging thyroid gland. On examination, the thyroid was diffusely enlarged without tenderness or cervical lymphadenopathy. Ultrasonography showed diffuse bilobate enlargement with poorly defined boundaries and heterogeneous nodularity. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) of a 4.3 × 2.2 cm nodule in the right lobe was performed. Cytologic smears revealed a prominent population of monotonous non-cohesive large cells with coarse chromatin, one or more prominent eosinophilic nucleoli, and moderate abundant cytoplasm. Scattered germinal and transformed “blast” cells were seen; there were no granulomas, thyroid follicular cells, Hürthle cells, or oncocytic changes. A cell block was prepared and immunohistochemical studies showed that the atypical cells were positive for CD45 and CD20. Imaging studies and bone marrow examination did not reveal involvement elsewhere. Hematologic parameters and thyroid function tests were normal; anti–thyroid peroxidase antibodies were undetectable. Based on these findings, a cytologic diagnosis of high-grade non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma with a differential of lymphocytic thyroiditis was made, and a bilateral total thyroidectomy was performed.

A 57-year-old Urhobo man presented in January 2009 with an 8-month history of persistent left calf swelling and a 1-week history of generalized body swelling. Five months earlier, he had undergone excision of the calf swelling at another hospital; no histologic report or margin assessment was available. The mass recurred three weeks after excision. The patient described tenderness of the swelling and difficulty moving his left leg. He had no history of diabetes or hypertension and no other swellings.

On examination, he was in painful distress. There was a solitary left inguinal lymph node and non-pitting edema of the left lower limb. A fungating mass measuring 6×8 cm was present on the left calf, with a bleeding wound with everted edges. The initial clinical impression was recurrent soft-tissue sarcoma.

An abdominal ultrasound revealed multiple hepatic metastases, each about 3 cm in diameter. Laboratory studies showed a random blood sugar of 16.1 mmol/L, fasting blood sugar of 10.6 mmol/L, and a packed cell volume of 27%. Chest and left leg radiographs were normal. A CT scan was not performed due to financial constraints.

A 3-month-old girl was brought with a 3-week history of blood in both anterior chambers, first in the right eye, then the left. There was no history of trauma, fever, or family history of sickle cell disease, bleeding disorders, or glaucoma. On general examination, she was active and afebrile. Multiple hyperpigmented macules were noted on the inner thighs and right upper arm, and a single pinkish 1 mm nodule was present on the occiput. Ophthalmic examination revealed intraocular pressures of 32 mm Hg (right) and 36 mm Hg (left). Both eyes showed mild conjunctival injection, cloudy corneas, deep anterior chambers, a yellowish membrane over each pupil, and a small yellow-colored iris growth inferonasally mixed with blood. The fundus could not be visualized. The remainder of the systemic examination was unremarkable. The infant was started on topical timolol, dorzolamide, latanoprost, apraclonidine, and prednisolone acetate drops. On examination under anesthesia on hospital day 2, intraocular pressures had decreased to 23 mm Hg bilaterally. Ultrasound biomicroscopy revealed narrow angles except superiorly, an anteriorly rotated ciliary body, and persistent hyphema. B-scan ultrasonography was normal. MRI of the brain and orbits was obtained to exclude intraocular or intracranial masses. A shave biopsy of the occipital skin nodule was then performed.

A 32-year-old woman, with a 3-pack-year history of light smoking in her youth and otherwise unremarkable past medical history, underwent a routine chest radiograph for an international visa application. The radiograph revealed a 30×30 mm rounded opacity in the mediastinum, surrounded by normal lung parenchyma and without associated adenopathy, atelectasis, or pleural effusion. Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated a 38×29×28 mm heterogeneous solid mass with well-defined borders, attached to the pericardium and abutting the main pulmonary artery trunk; no other masses or lymph nodes were identified. On examination, vital signs were normal, and there was no palpable lymphadenopathy in the cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, or inguinal regions. Lung fields were clear, and cardiac and pleural examinations were unremarkable. The patient denied fever, night sweats, weight loss, cough, dyspnea, chest pain, or other systemic symptoms. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, metabolic panel, and tumor markers (β-hCG, α-fetoprotein, CEA, CA19-9, and thyroglobulin), were within normal limits. Initial differential diagnoses included pericardial cyst, congenital cyst, lymphoma, mesothelioma, metastatic tumor, sarcoma, teratoma, and thymoma.

A 65-year-old man was diagnosed in 2010 with right lacrimal gland adenoid cystic carcinoma, staged T2N0M0, and was treated in 2011 with surgical resection followed by adjuvant radiotherapy. He underwent annual surveillance with liver MRI and chest radiography. In October 2021, a routine liver MRI demonstrated an incidental right lower lobe pulmonary nodule. He was asymptomatic with no respiratory or systemic complaints and had a WHO performance status of 0. His past history included a 25-pack-year smoking history, quit 10 years earlier. Physical examination was unremarkable. A CT scan of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a solitary 1.6 cm ovoid subpleural lesion in the right lower lobe with background emphysema. A contrast-enhanced CT of the head showed no peri-ocular recurrence. PET imaging demonstrated that the nodule was not FDG avid. Lung function tests were within normal limits.

A 7-year-old girl with no prior medical history presented with a 2-week history of asymptomatic skin lesions on her right hand and wrist, which had rapidly increased in number and size. She denied fever, trauma, animal contact, or systemic symptoms. On examination, multiple hyperkeratotic erythematous and dark blue nodules measuring 2 × 2 mm to 1 × 1 cm were noted on the palmar and dorsal aspects of the right hand extending to the wrist. Initial differential diagnoses included acquired angiokeratoma or other vascular tumors, acral pseudolymphomatous angiokeratoma of children, bacillary angiomatosis, Kaposi sarcoma, or giant molluscum contagiosum. A skin biopsy of a representative lesion showed vascular ectasia of the papillary dermis extending into the epidermis with hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and elongation of the rete ridges, with the epidermis encircling the dilated vascular spaces. Periodic acid–Schiff and Grocott-Gomori’s methenamine silver stains were negative for microorganisms. A complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, coagulation profile, and HIV screening were all within normal limits.

A 66-year-old right-handed Caucasian woman presented with a first episode of generalized tonic–clonic seizure, treated with levetiracetam. Five years earlier, she had been diagnosed with unresectable adenocarcinoma of the pancreatic tail (T4N1M1) when CT showed a 30 mm mass encircling the celiac trunk and abutting the splenic artery with precaval and retrocaval lymphadenopathy. Biopsy confirmed pancreatic adenocarcinoma; initial tumor markers were CEA 21.3 μg/L and CA19-9 900 kU/L. She received two cycles of FOLFIRINOX and 5-fluorouracil, then ten cycles of Abraxane with gemcitabine, achieving normalization of CEA and CA19-9 and no evidence of disease on CT at four-year follow-up. Six months later she developed headaches and seizure; neurologic and physical examinations were unremarkable. MRI of the brain revealed a 5 cm cortical and white-matter mass in the left middle frontal gyrus with a small extraaxial dural component, central necrosis, peripheral gadolinium enhancement, marked vasogenic edema, midline shift, and subfalcine herniation. Laboratory studies including liver and pancreatic function tests and complete blood count were normal.

A 21-year-old woman presented with a 6- to 7-year history of a right upper abdominal lump that had gradually increased in size. The discomfort was a dull ache, intermittent in nature. She denied fever, weight loss, altered bowel habits, or urinary symptoms. Menstrual history was unremarkable, and there was no family history of twins or teratomas.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination revealed an ill-defined, soft-to-firm, irregular mass in the right upper quadrant that did not move with respiration; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies, including β-human chorionic gonadotropin and alpha-fetoprotein, were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a large, ill-defined heterogeneous mass adjacent to the liver on the right, containing multiple hypoechoic areas and echogenic foci with no internal vascularity.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 22.5×14.1×12.5 cm heterogeneous retroperitoneal mass on the right, containing cystic regions, fat-attenuating areas, calcifications, and malformed skeletal parts resembling long bones, ribs, and vertebrae, along with heterogeneous soft-tissue components showing minimal peripheral enhancement. The mass displaced the right liver lobe anteriorly and to the left, elevated the right hemidiaphragm, displaced the right kidney inferiorly and medially, and shifted bowel loops inferiorly and to the left; fat planes with adjacent organs were preserved. The uterus and adnexa were normal.

A 15-year-old girl presented with a 2–3-month history of a painless swelling in the upper front tooth region. On examination, there was a well-defined, sessile exophytic growth measuring approximately 1.0 cm × 0.5 cm with a pinkish-red color, a smooth surface, and no secondary changes. The lesion extended from the distal aspect of the left maxillary permanent lateral incisor to the mesial aspect of the first deciduous molar. On palpation, it was soft to firm and showed no tendency to bleed. The patient’s medical and dental histories were unremarkable. Panoramic and periapical radiographs showed no remarkable changes. Based on these findings, a provisional diagnosis of a benign lesion or cyst was made. All hematological investigations and parathyroid hormone levels were within normal limits. An excisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia, and the specimen was sent for histopathological examination.

A 12-year-old boy presented with a 1-year history of progressively worsening intermittent dysphagia and vomiting. One year earlier, barium esophagography at another clinic led to a diagnosis of gastro-esophageal reflux disease, and he received antireflux medication without improvement. On presentation, he had no remarkable findings on physical examination, and routine blood tests were normal. An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed narrowing of the middle esophagus with a small area of mucosal erosion; insufflation of air did not relieve the narrowing, and the endoscope could not be advanced. Contrast esophagography demonstrated a 1.6-cm segment of esophageal narrowing at the level of the carina with mild passage disturbance. To evaluate for a possible vascular ring and other structural abnormalities, computed tomography angiography of the thoracic aorta was performed, revealing a 25-mm mass involving the esophageal or periesophageal region posterior to the paratracheal segment of the esophagus.

A 45-year-old man presented with progressively enlarging masses initially in the anterior cervical region over 2 years, with later appearance of similar lesions in the occipital and dorsal areas. He reported only esthetic embarrassment, without pain, dysphagia, hoarseness, or dyspnea. His medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, asymptomatic chronic pancreatitis, and alcohol abuse (1 L/day for 10 years); he denied other comorbidities. On examination, there were soft, non-tender, bulging masses symmetrically involving the anterior and posterior cervical regions, the pre- and post-auricular areas, and the upper back. Vital signs were normal. Cervical CT revealed a prominent, unencapsulated excess of subcutaneous adipose tissue in the submandibular and posterior cervical regions bilaterally, with no mediastinal involvement or vascular engorgement.

An 18-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of pain and swelling in the right foot. The pain developed insidiously without trauma, gradually worsened, and markedly increased over the preceding two months, causing difficulty in walking. She denied fevers or chills. Her medical history included a liver abscess at age 4 and open-heart surgery for tetralogy of Fallot at age 7. 

On examination, there was tenderness and swelling over the calcaneocuboid region of the right foot; the overlying skin was warm but without soft-tissue involvement or lymphadenopathy. She could not bear weight on the foot and exhibited severe pain with ankle dorsiflexion.

Plain radiographs of the right foot showed a lytic lucent lesion in the cuboid bone with internal septations and intact cortex, without fracture or dislocation. MRI demonstrated mild expansion of the cuboid, cystic areas with fluid–fluid levels, intact cortex, and no involvement of adjacent tarsal bones. The lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and enhanced with contrast.

A 59-year-old woman presented with a chronic productive cough, night sweats, fatigue, and occasional shortness of breath. Her medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, gastroesophageal reflux disease, deep vein thrombosis, depression, and anxiety. She was a lifelong nonsmoker with no history of malignancy. Physical examination and initial laboratory test results were unremarkable. Spirometry revealed normal pulmonary function. An extensive laboratory workup was negative for autoimmune and infectious etiologies. Non-contrast chest CT showed numerous bilateral pulmonary nodules, each measuring up to 5 mm and randomly distributed throughout both lungs.

A 26-year-old woman presented with a 1.5-year history of swelling in the right posterior mandible, associated with intermittent, dull aching pain for the past 6 months and loosening of adjacent teeth. On extraoral examination, there was a firm 3 × 2 cm swelling at the right mandibular angle causing mild facial asymmetry; right submandibular lymph nodes were palpable but non-tender. Intraorally, a firm 5 × 5 cm swelling occupied the right retromolar trigone, obliterating the buccal vestibule and involving the right mandibular second molar, which was grade III mobile; the overlying mucosa was intact. 

Panoramic radiography showed a mixed radiolucent and radiopaque lesion extending from the distal root of the first molar to the mandibular ramus, bounded by a sclerotic margin anteriorly and posteriorly with loss of continuity of the lower mandibular border inferiorly. Within the lesion was an impacted third molar with tooth-shaped radiopacity adjacent to the inferior margin. The roots of the second molar were resorbed, the first molar’s distal root was resorbed, and the third molar was displaced occlusally.

A 25-year-old woman presented with a painless lump in the left cheek, first noted nine months earlier. She reported no toothache, numbness, or systemic symptoms and had no significant medical history. On examination, there was left facial asymmetry without skin changes. Palpation revealed a firm, mobile, non-tender mass approximately 4 cm in diameter, located deep in the left buccal space and extending below the zygomatic arch; no cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. Intraorally, there was a bulge of the left buccal mucosa; palpation confirmed a well-defined, firm, non-tender mass.

An orthopantomogram showed no bony destruction of the mandible or maxilla, with only a healed post-extraction socket in the region of tooth 36. Ultrasonography of the left cheek demonstrated a discrete, well-demarcated, hypoechoic solid mass measuring 2.6 × 2.0 cm, overlying the parotid gland, with no increase in internal vascular flow or calcification. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck revealed a well-bordered, slightly enhancing soft-tissue tumor measuring 2.7 × 3.7 × 4.0 cm in the left buccal space, indenting but not destroying adjacent bones (including the posterior maxillary sinus wall, medial pterygoid, masseter, and temporal muscle), and extending into the temporal space; the mass was supplied by branches of the left buccal artery.

Fine-needle aspiration biopsy yielded a hypocellular sample with erythrocytes, histiocytes, and neutrophils but showed “no signs of malignancy.” An intraoral incisional biopsy demonstrated “wide fibroblast proliferation, extremely similar to a fibroma.”

A 58-year-old Iranian woman with a history only of lumbar vertebral pain presented to the surgical emergency ward with acute epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. She reported no smoking history and had no prior surgeries or significant family history. On examination, her vital signs were stable, and abdominal palpation revealed tenderness in the left upper quadrant along with a notably large palpable mass.

Initial laboratory studies showed:
• Amylase 98 U/L (30–110 U/L)  
• Lipase 27 U/L (0–160 U/L)  
• White blood cell count 11.8 × 10^3/µL (4.0–10.5 × 10^3/µL)  
• Hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL (12.0–15.5 g/dL)  
• Platelets 212 000/µL (150 000–450 000/µL)  
• BUN 7 mg/dL (7–20 mg/dL)  
• Creatinine 0.76 mg/dL (0.6–1.2 mg/dL)  
• Sodium 135 mEq/L (135–145 mEq/L)  
• Potassium 3.8 mEq/L (3.5–5.0 mEq/L)  
• AST 20 U/L (10–40 U/L)  
• ALT 9 U/L (7–56 U/L)  
• Alkaline phosphatase 182 U/L (44–147 U/L)  
• Calcium 9.4 mg/dL (8.5–10.2 mg/dL)  
• Phosphorus 2.8 mg/dL (2.5–4.5 mg/dL)  
• Total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL (0.1–1.2 mg/dL)  
• Direct bilirubin 0.3 mg/dL (<0.3 mg/dL)  
• Quantitative troponin <1.5 ng/mL (<0.04 ng/mL)  
• Qualitative troponin negative  

These results indicated no acute pancreatitis or myocardial infarction, aside from mild leukocytosis. 

Abdominal ultrasound revealed a large lobulated anechoic structure. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 105 × 112 × 74 mm cystic, lobulated mass in the left upper quadrant, anterior to the kidney and medial to bowel loops, containing thin septations and no significant enhancement, suggesting a differential diagnosis of lymphangioma versus a mesenteric cyst.

A 34-year-old man was referred after a liver mass was discovered incidentally on screening ultrasonography. He reported no symptoms, medication use, alcohol intake, or relevant family history. His body mass index was 26.8 kg/m2, and the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests revealed: WBC 5,400/µL, Hb 14.2 g/dL, platelets 289,000/µL, normal liver enzymes, negative viral hepatitis markers, AFP 2.4 ng/mL, and PIVKA-II 76.0 mAU/mL.  
Abdominal ultrasonography showed a well-defined, heterogeneous echogenic lesion in the liver’s posterior segment with abundant peripheral and intratumoral Doppler flow. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 70×100 mm lesion with heterogeneous arterial-phase enhancement and washout in the delayed phase. On MRI, the lesion was isointense to liver on T1- and T2-weighted images, without fat suppression, and contained a linear scar-like area (T1 hypointense, T2 hyperintense). After Gd-EOB-DTPA administration, there was heterogeneous arterial-phase enhancement, rapid washout in the transitional phase, and near isointensity to the liver in the hepatobiliary phase.

An 18-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a painful swelling of the left breast involving the nipple and areolar region, with associated serous nipple discharge. On examination, the lesion was firm to hard, mobile, and was initially diagnosed clinically as gynecomastia. Fine-needle aspiration cytology yielded cellular smears composed predominantly of cohesive clusters and occasional papillae, with polygonal cells showing moderate cytoplasm ranging from clear to eosinophilic and granular, oval nuclei with smooth membranes and distinct nucleoli; many cells demonstrated clear cytoplasm, and the background contained hemorrhage. A cytologic diagnosis of a benign adnexal tumor was rendered. 

The excised specimen was a skin-covered, well-encapsulated, globular mass measuring 4×3×2 cm, yellow-brown and firm. On sectioning, there were gray-white solid areas and cystic spaces. Microscopic examination revealed a well-demarcated, lobulated dermal tumor with solid and cystic regions. The solid portions showed two cell types: round to polyhedral cells with finely granular, eosinophilic cytoplasm and round to oval nuclei, and cells with clear cytoplasm and small eccentric nuclei. The cystic spaces were lined by dark cuboidal epithelium with lumina filled with eosinophilic material. Occasional squamous morules and eosinophilic hyalinizing stroma were present. No nuclear atypia, necrosis, or abnormal mitoses were identified. Periodic acid–Schiff staining demonstrated diastase-resistant material within the clear cells and lumina.

A 17-year-old male with xeroderma pigmentosum and a history of multiple nonmelanoma skin cancers presented with a 3-month history of a new, enlarging lesion on the parietal scalp. He denied fever, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. Examination revealed a hyperkeratotic, firm 1.3 × 1.5-cm nodule with hemorrhagic crust on the left posterior parietal scalp. A frozen biopsy showed a bland vascular neoplasm in the papillary dermis with a monomorphic infiltrate. Given an inconclusive frozen section and a differential that included pyogenic granuloma versus malignancy, a deeper shave biopsy was obtained for permanent sections. The deeper biopsy demonstrated atypical epithelioid cells forming vascular channels. Immunostaining was positive for erythroblast transformation-specific related gene (ERG) and negative for p40 and human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8).

A 3-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of a slowly progressive, asymptomatic swelling of the right mandible. The exact onset was unclear. She reported intermittent mild pain. Her medical history was unremarkable, with no trauma, paresthesia, or systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a 3×2-cm firm, non-tender, smooth-surfaced mass fixed to the right mandibular body, causing slight facial asymmetry. Oral mucosa was intact, teeth erupted normally, with no mobility, inflammation, or malocclusion; regional lymph nodes were not enlarged. Panoramic radiography revealed a large, well-demarcated radiolucent lesion in the right mandibular body surrounded by a narrow radiopaque border and no internal calcifications. In the absence of systemic disease, central osteoma, ameloblastic fibroma, ameloblastoma, odontogenic cyst, vascular lesion, and giant cell lesion were included in the differential diagnosis. Routine blood tests were normal, and an excisional biopsy was planned.

A 19-year-old man presented with a 6-week history of intermittent swelling and pain in his left knee that worsened with activity but was absent at rest. On examination, flexion of the left knee revealed a 2 × 3 cm soft-tissue swelling over the lateral infrapatellar region. Stability tests—including the Lachman, anterior and posterior drawer, varus and valgus stress, McMurray, and Apley tests—were all negative. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and inflammatory markers, were within normal limits. Standard radiographs of the knee showed no abnormalities. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-circumscribed, heterogeneous 3 × 2 cm lesion within the infrapatellar (Hoffa) fat pad, hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images.

A 57-year-old woman (BMI 23) with a history of daily alcohol use and 15 cigarettes per day was under surveillance for an asymptomatic periapical infection on tooth 46. In February 2016, a routine dental panoramic radiograph showed a new supracentimeter radiolucency at the apices of teeth 46 and 47. Oral examination revealed buccal and lingual swelling of the right mandibular body and mild spontaneous pain. Cone-beam CT demonstrated a 30 mm unilocular radiolucent lesion in the right mandibular body with thinning of the buccal cortex and partial interruption of the lingual cortex. MRI with gadolinium showed a well-vascularized homogeneous lesion in the right mandibular body extending into the sublingual space. Multiple biopsies revealed a proliferation of mononuclear cells without atypia, admixed with numerous osteoclast-like giant cells. P63 immunostaining was positive in over 50 % of mononuclear cells. High-resolution melting analysis detected no H3F3A or H3F3B mutation. Expert opinion was sought from the French Bone Pathology network (RESOS).

A 49-year-old man with bipolar disorder, depression, and migraines presented with a 4-week history of progressive ataxia, dysarthria, and vertigo. An MRI of the brain and spinal cord was unremarkable. Lumbar puncture revealed a CSF pleocytosis (WBC 159 cells/µL; 78% lymphocytes), elevated protein, and positive oligoclonal bands; extensive infectious testing in blood and CSF was negative. He received intravenous steroids for presumed autoimmune cerebellar syndrome with minimal improvement. Repeat CSF analysis still showed pleocytosis (WBC 40 cells/µL); cytology and lymphoma markers were negative. An autoimmune movement-disorder panel was positive for anti-Tr antibodies in the CSF (titer 1:128) and glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies in the serum. Malignancy screening with bone marrow biopsy and flow cytometry, CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, and testicular ultrasound revealed no abnormalities. A whole-body PET scan showed four small periaortic and aortocaval lymph nodes (largest 6×6 mm) with an SUV of 5.45, deemed too small for biopsy. While awaiting repeat imaging, he received plasmapheresis, IVIG, and rituximab with modest clinical improvement. A CT scan 3 months later demonstrated resolution of the lymph nodes. A second serum movement-disorder panel again detected both anti-Tr and GAD antibodies. He continued to have severe dysarthria, ataxia, and swallowing difficulties requiring gastrostomy. Six months after the initial PET scan, a repeat PET scan again demonstrated two nonenlarged periaortic lymph nodes measuring 7 mm with an SUV of 5.5.

A middle-aged woman presented with a 5-year history of radiating pain in her left lower leg, ankle, and sole and a 6-month history of a painful swelling on the medial aspect of the left ankle. She had previously been treated for lumbosacral radiculopathy, tarsal tunnel syndrome, and complex regional pain syndrome without relief. On examination, there was a 6 × 4 × 4 cm firm, tender mass just posterior to the medial malleolus that was nonfluctuant, noncompressible, nonpulsatile, and mobile side to side but not longitudinally; overlying skin and local temperature were normal. Ankle motion was full, distal pulses and sensation were intact, and Tinel’s sign was positive over the swelling. Routine blood tests and ankle radiographs were normal. A prior MRI of the lumbar spine was normal. Neurophysiological studies showed normal nerve conduction without axonopathy. MRI of the left ankle revealed a well-circumscribed 5 × 4.5 × 2 cm mass arising from the tibial nerve adjacent to the medial malleolus.

A 71-year-old man with a 12-year history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and prior chemo-refractory disease treated with fludarabine-cyclophosphamide-rituximab, bendamustine-rituximab, and ibrutinib, presented with a transient epileptic seizure. On admission, he had grade 1 anemia, grade 2 thrombocytopenia, and no lymphocytosis. Examination revealed an enlarged spleen and palpable axillary and cervical lymph nodes, consistent with progression of CLL under ibrutinib. Neurologic exam showed decreased strength in the left upper limb with pyramidal signs, left hemianopsia, and visual hallucinations. Bone marrow aspiration revealed 12% lymphocytes (25% with CLL phenotype; TP53 mutation variant allele frequency = 1.5%). Lumbar puncture detected no evidence of CLL or infection. Brain MRI demonstrated increased signal in the right parietotemporal leptomeninx on FLAIR and diffusion sequences. EEG showed generalized periodic epileptiform discharges, more prominent on the right. A broad CSF infectious work-up—including bacterial, mycobacterial, fungal cultures; HSV, BKV, JCV PCR; TPHA; Borrelia serology; QuantiFERON; nucleic acid amplification tests for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Toxoplasma gondii; galactomannan and cryptococcal antigen tests; and oligoclonal Ig synthesis—was performed. All tests were normal or negative.

A 78-year-old woman with cirrhosis due to hepatitis C, atrial fibrillation, and right-sided heart failure was admitted with two weeks of abdominal pain, generalized weakness, and a sudden 6 kg weight gain. On examination she had bilateral lower-extremity edema, a distended abdomen with fluid wave, mild abdominal tenderness, and a few spider telangiectasias on her upper chest. Three firm, mobile inguinal lymph nodes measured 3 to 7.5 cm. There was no hepatosplenomegaly. Pulmonary, cardiovascular, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed iron-deficiency anemia (hemoglobin 8 g/dL), leukocytosis (45 × 10^3/µL) with neutrophil predominance, and mild thrombocytopenia (100 × 10^3/µL). Liver function tests were consistent with cirrhosis (hypoalbuminemia, elevated transaminases). Urea, sodium, and potassium levels were normal. HIV serology was negative.

Abdominal CT showed a nodular, heterogeneous liver with moderate ascites, and no splenomegaly or deep lymphadenopathy. Diuretics, antibiotics, paracentesis, and nutritional support were initiated, and an excisional biopsy of the largest inguinal node (7.5 × 4 × 1.5 cm; whitish, focally nodular cut surface) was performed.

Histologic examination showed partial effacement of nodal architecture by vaguely nodular proliferations. Nodules were centered by aggregates of plasmablastic cells with eccentric, often multilobulated nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant acidophilic cytoplasm; these cells extended into mantle zones. Adjacent parenchyma exhibited concentric “onion-skin” layering of small lymphocytes around germinal centers.

Immunohistochemical stains revealed that tumor cells were positive for EMA, LMP1, CD38, CD138, HHV8 latency-associated nuclear antigen, and kappa light chains, and negative for AE1/AE3, CD20, CD3, cyclin D1, CD56, CD15, CD30, CD10, and bcl2. Follicular dendritic cell meshworks (CD21+) contained HHV8-positive cells. In situ hybridization for EBER was positive, confirming EBV infection and monotypic kappa light-chain expression. PCR analysis of Ig gene rearrangements showed a polyclonal pattern.

An 18-month-old girl was referred after an incidental discovery of a left renal mass. She had a history of microcrania (cranial perimeter 41 cm, >3 SD below mean), congenital cataracts repaired uneventfully, strabismus, and a single idiopathic seizure treated with valproic acid. There was no family history of malformations or cancer. On examination, vital signs were normal. Neurologic exam was unremarkable apart from microcrania; the abdomen was soft, nontender, without palpable masses. Laboratory tests showed normal hematology, electrolytes, renal and hepatic function, except for polycythemia. The APTT was prolonged at 63 s; PT and Rosner index were normal, and lupus anticoagulant was ruled out. Urinalysis was normal without hematuria. 

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 26 × 28 mm, well-defined, hyperechoic, weakly vascularized solid mass in the mid-portion of the left kidney without calcifications. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a 28 × 27 × 27 mm subcapsular, well-circumscribed tumor in the medial left kidney, with areas of necrosis, homogeneous enhancement, and no evidence of metastasis. Wilms’ tumor was considered, but radiologic features were inconclusive. After interdisciplinary discussion, a CT-guided percutaneous biopsy was planned.

A 63-year-old Kashmiri man presented with a 16-day history of intermittent, colicky right upper abdominal pain that occasionally radiated to the back. Physical examination was unremarkable, and routine hematological parameters were within normal limits.  
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a hyperechoic mass with ill-defined margins in the right suprarenal region measuring 5.9 × 4.5 cm. A contrast-enhanced multidetector-row CT scan of the abdomen showed a well-circumscribed, round lesion in the right suprarenal area measuring 6.1 × 4.0 cm, with central soft-tissue attenuation of 38–42 Hounsfield units and peripheral fat attenuation of –52 to –65 Hounsfield units.

A 58-year-old Caucasian woman presented with two weeks of continuous remittent fever up to 38 °C, polyarthralgias, cervical pain, headache, and erythematous painful edema of the lower limbs. She had not improved with paracetamol or cephalosporin. On examination, her temperature was 38 °C and there was erythematous painful swelling of both lower legs.

Laboratory tests showed:
- ESR 120 mm/h, CRP 225 mg/L, ferritin 2076 mg/L, fibrinogen 223 mg/dL  
- AST 83 U/L, ALT 114 U/L, LDH 746 U/L  
- Albumin 2.7 g/dL, total plasma protein 5.5 g/dL  

Extensive infectious workup was negative, including serologic tests for hepatitis A, B, C, and E viruses; HIV; CMV; parvovirus B19; EBV; echoviruses; poliovirus; coxsackieviruses; Treponema pallidum; Coxiella burnetii; Toxoplasma; Salmonella typhi; Legionella pneumophila; Mycoplasma pneumoniae; Leishmania donovani; Chlamydia; Brucella; Leptospira; Rickettsia; and Borrelia species IgM. IgG positivity for EBV, VZV, HSV, and CMV indicated past exposures. Borrelia IgG by IIF was not confirmed by Western blot. ASO titers were negative. Nasopharyngeal and rectal swabs were negative for bacteria and fungi; Candida albicans and Candida glabrata grew from oral and vaginal swabs. Peripheral smear excluded malaria. Mantoux test was negative. Blood, stool, and urine cultures were sterile. CSF examination and galactomannan test were negative.

Additional studies:
- Immunoglobulins and autoantibodies were normal.  
- Transesophageal echocardiography showed no vegetations.  
- Abdominal ultrasound revealed mild hepatomegaly, normal spleen.  
- Whole-body CT, leukocyte scintigraphy, bone and lung scans, and FDG-PET were unremarkable.  
- Brain MRI showed nonspecific subacute inflammatory changes.  
- Esophagogastroduodenoscopy with duodenal biopsy was inconclusive for Whipple disease.  
- Liver biopsy revealed mild piecemeal necrosis, spotty lobular necrosis, and cholestatic changes.  
- Initial bone marrow trephine biopsy was hypocellular with mild granulopoietic and erythropoietic hyperplasia, reactive plasmacytosis, and no evidence of leishmanial infection.

Despite ciprofloxacin, imipenem, prednisone, and NSAIDs, fever persisted and lower limb lesions remained unchanged. She developed progressive normocytic anemia, hypoalbuminemia, rising acute-phase reactants (CRP 38.6 mg/dL, fibrinogen 920 mg/dL), and worsening liver tests (LDH 1131 U/L, ALP 617 U/L, bilirubin 11.87 mg/dL, ALT 129 U/L, AST 64 U/L). Empirical doxycycline and liposomal amphotericin B were administered for suspected chlamydial or leishmanial infection, without improvement.

Subsequently she developed intermittent delirium, dyspnea with hypoxia, and thrombotic microangiopathy with severe thrombocytopenia (3 × 10^9/L). A second bone marrow trephine biopsy showed mild hypocellularity, pronounced plasmacytosis, and hemophagocytosis. Prednisone was increased to 80 mg/day and plasma exchange was initiated.

An 83-year-old man presented with a mass on the dorsal aspect of the right index finger at the proximal phalanx, first noted 40 years earlier. The lesion was initially asymptomatic but became painful following trivial trauma. He reported no other symptoms. On examination, the firm, noncompressible mass was not fixed to skin, tendon, or bone; active and passive range of motion of the finger was normal, and radial and ulnar pulses were intact. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein, were within normal limits. Plain radiographs showed a soft-tissue shadow without bony involvement or calcifications. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-circumscribed lesion abutting the tendon sheath that was homogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images and isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images, with avid, homogeneous enhancement after gadolinium. The imaging characteristics were felt to be most consistent with a giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath, and surgical excision was planned.

A 21-year-old man presented with progressive right shoulder pain of several weeks’ duration. He had no history of trauma or heavy lifting and no family history of malignancy. On examination, his right shoulder was asymmetrically deformed compared with the left, and palpation of the distal third of the right clavicle elicited tenderness.  

Plain radiographs showed a well-defined osteolytic lesion with cortical thinning in the distal third of the right clavicle. MRI with contrast demonstrated an enhancing mass in the lateral third of the clavicle. Multislice CT of the chest and abdomen, plus a complete bone survey, revealed no other lesions. Based on the clinical and radiological findings, a primary benign bone lesion was suspected (Bone RADS score 1). Three days later, an open biopsy with curettage, bone grafting, and internal fixation via an anterior clavicular approach was performed.  

Microscopic examination of the curetted tissue revealed diffuse sheets of moderately sized tumor cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm. Some cells had oval or eccentric nuclei with nuclear grooves. The background contained numerous eosinophils, lymphocytes, and multinucleated osteoclastic giant cells.

A 27-year-old man was referred for preoperative evaluation before bilateral tonsillectomy. He had no history of tuberous sclerosis. His BMI was 47.4 kg/m². Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests: WBC 8800/µL; RBC 4.33×10⁶/µL; hemoglobin 12.7 g/dL; platelets 174×10³/µL; HbA1c 6.3%; CRP 0.32 mg/dL.

Abdominal ultrasonography showed a solid 14 cm tumor in the upper left abdomen, continuous with the spleen, with smooth borders and mixed high- and low-echoic areas; it abutted but did not invade the pancreatic tail, left kidney, or stomach.

Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a 14 cm mass on the ventral spleen with clear margins, containing low-density (fat) regions around blood vessels and a solid component with strong enhancement. The splenic artery fed the mass, and a dilated draining vein joined the splenic vein. No other lesions were identified in the liver, pancreas, or kidneys. MRI was not performed due to claustrophobia.

A 17-year-old unmarried girl presented with one month of progressive psychotic symptoms and poor self-care. Three months earlier, she developed a persistent, mild-to-moderate, constricting headache that worsened with reading. Two weeks after headache onset, she awoke one night screaming that “something was pressing” on her body; she remained fully conscious yet became restless, fearful, and wandered aimlessly. Over subsequent days, she exhibited impulsivity, touching and pulling at others without cause, decreased sleep, purposeless nodding and hand gestures, smiling to herself, drooling, and incontinence of urine and stool without apparent distress. She lost shame, disrobed publicly, and gradually became mute. Without treatment, she had partial spontaneous improvement after two to three weeks: speaking irrelevantly returned but dishevelment, self-smiling, muttering, incontinence, and prolonged fixed postures persisted.

There was no history of seizures, delirium, substance use, bipolar mood shifts, dissociation, or other medical or surgical disorders. On examination, she was conscious; attention was easily aroused but ill-sustained; orientation was mildly impaired. She followed simple commands but had impaired judgment. Hygiene was poor, speech was hesitant, mostly irrelevant with loosening of associations, and affect was inappropriate and labile. Neurologic exam showed mildly brisk deep-tendon reflexes bilaterally and equivocal plantar responses. The on-call psychiatrist diagnosed acute and transient psychotic disorder according to ICD-10. Routine blood tests were normal. A noncontrast brain MRI was ordered.

A 66-year-old Caucasian woman with no comorbidities presented with epigastric pain. Physical examination of the abdomen was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed an elevated C-reactive protein level; all other hematological parameters were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a regular hypoechoic nodular formation at the lower pole of the spleen measuring 8 cm in maximum diameter, with an internal calcification spot. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a 77 mm hypodense splenic lesion with intralesional calcifications and identified a 1 cm accessory spleen adjacent to the lower pole. MRI characterized the mass as a 6.3 cm × 8.2 cm lesion with heterogeneous signal intensity: iso- to hypointense on T1-weighted images and predominantly hypointense on T2-weighted images, with centrally scattered hyperintense areas on fat-saturated precontrast sequences. On dynamic contrast imaging, there was peripheral enhancement in the arterial phase with progressive centripetal filling in a radiating pattern on delayed images.

A 74-year-old man with atrial fibrillation, diabetes mellitus, and hypertension underwent Mohs micrographic surgery for a 2.0 cm, well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma on the left forearm. During the first Mohs stage, frozen hematoxylin and eosin sections showed a dense, monomorphic lymphocytic aggregate in the dermis and subcutaneous fat. The tumor was cleared after two stages. To evaluate for possible single-cell squamous cell–carcinoma infiltration, cytokeratin 5 immunohistochemistry was performed on frozen en face sections, which confirmed no residual carcinoma cells. Because of the dense lymphocytic infiltrate, a complete blood count was ordered, revealing a lymphocyte-predominant leukocytosis of 27.7 × 10^3/mcL, raising concern for a lymphoproliferative disorder such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia or the leukemic phase of a marginal zone lymphoma.

A 55-year-old right-handed woman presented with a history of medication-refractory seizures beginning at age 47. Her typical events consisted of staring, lip smacking, unresponsiveness, asymmetric posturing without head or eye deviation, and occasional secondary generalization lasting 3–5 minutes, followed by prolonged postictal confusion. Seizures clustered every 2–3 months, mostly during sleep, despite trials of levetiracetam, lacosamide, and lamotrigine. Neurologic examination was unremarkable.

Brain MRI revealed a 6.5×3.6 cm lobulated, nonenhancing mass in the left quadrigeminal plate cistern extending into the cerebellar vermis and tail of the left hippocampus. On MRI, the lesion was hypointense on T1 and ADC, hyperintense on T2, diffusion-weighted, and FLAIR images, indicating restricted diffusion. The left hippocampus was small with T2 hyperintensity consistent with mesial temporal sclerosis.

Neuropsychological testing showed average cognition with mildly impaired memory lateralizing to the left. Wada testing demonstrated left-hemisphere language dominance and bilateral memory capacity. Long-term video-EEG captured multiple stereotyped seizures with oral automatisms arising from the left anterior-midtemporal region and rhythmic theta activity at onset; interictal EEG showed frequent left anterior-midtemporal slowing and occasional sharp waves, consistent with a hippocampal seizure pattern.

A 59-year-old man and ex-smoker presented with a 4-month history of nonproductive cough, stridor, and exertional dyspnea. He denied weight loss, fevers, or night sweats. On spirometry, the flow-volume loop was flattened in both inspiratory and expiratory phases, indicating a fixed central airway obstruction. Routine laboratory studies were unremarkable. A chest radiograph showed no abnormalities. Thin-section multislice CT of the chest revealed a sharply bordered, intraluminal polypoid mass measuring 15 mm in diameter arising from the membranous part of the middle third of the trachea and occluding approximately 80% of the lumen; there was no evidence of cartilage invasion or mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Coronal and sagittal reformations showed the upper margin of the lesion to be 3.5 cm below the vocal cords. Virtual bronchoscopy confirmed severe airway narrowing. Flexible bronchoscopy demonstrated a sessile tumor on the posterior tracheal wall, starting at the level of the third tracheal ring.

A 77-year-old woman with diabetes and hypertension presented with two months of generalized intermittent moderate abdominal pain and intermittent fresh per rectum bleeding. She denied fatigue, anorexia, diarrhea, jaundice, weight loss, smoking, or alcohol use. On examination she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable, without pallor or jaundice; her abdomen was soft and non-tender, and anoscopy showed an empty rectum. Laboratory tests, including leukocyte count, CEA, CA19-9, and α-fetoprotein, were all within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed focal polypoidal thickening of the proximal sigmoid colon (3 cm in length, 2 cm wall thickness) and several hypodense liver nodules (largest in segment IV, 3.4 × 2.7 cm) “highly suspicious for liver metastasis.” MRI of the abdomen showed two left hepatic lesions (segments IV and II/III; largest 2.7 × 2.4 × 2.8 cm) with intermediate-high T2 and low T1 signal intensity, faint peripheral rim enhancement in all phases, and no central filling in delayed phase, described as “highly suspicious of colorectal liver metastasis.” Colonoscopy identified a nonobstructing polypoidal lesion in the proximal sigmoid colon, and biopsy revealed moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma.

A 78-year-old Japanese man presented with sudden, asymptomatic gross hematuria accompanied by pyuria and clot retention that began 6 days earlier. He was afebrile and denied chills, flank pain, or weight loss. His medical history was significant for transurethral resection of the prostate and bladder lithotripsy 11 years earlier, and for nonfunctional pancreatic neuroendocrine carcinoma with liver and nodal metastases treated surgically followed by chemotherapy; treatment was discontinued 17 months before presentation due to adverse effects. Physical examination revealed no palpable abdominal masses or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies confirmed hematuria and pyuria. Cystoscopic examination showed a solitary, non-papillary, pedunculated mass approximately 1.2 cm in diameter on the lateral wall near the left ureteral orifice. The lesion’s surface was reddish and highly vascular, and prominent feeding vessels were seen in its stalk. A transurethral resection of the mass was performed, and the specimen was submitted for histopathologic evaluation.

A 46-year-old man was brought to the emergency department unconscious after a suspected cardiac arrest. He worked in building demolition with no known asbestos exposure. On examination, he was tachycardic, hypotensive, and had jugular venous distension, cyanosis, and a pulsus paradoxus. An electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia with electrical alternans. Chest radiography demonstrated cardiomegaly. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a large pericardial effusion with signs of cardiac tamponade. Pericardiocentesis drained 800 mL of hemorrhagic fluid, but the patient died suddenly despite resuscitative efforts.

A 37-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of left knee pain and swelling, with worsening pain intensity and tumor growth over the past 3 months. On examination, there was a 3 × 4 cm firm, non-tender, well-defined swelling on the anterolateral proximal tibia. Knee range of motion was full but painful at terminal flexion; distal neurovascular function was intact.  
Plain radiography and CT demonstrated an eccentric lytic epiphyseo-metaphyseal lesion with well-defined margins confined to the proximal tibia. MRI revealed a locally aggressive lesion extending into the tibialis anterior, lateral soft tissues, and fibular head, hypointense on T1 and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, suggestive of a locally aggressive giant cell tumor.

A 76-year-old woman with coronary artery disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and type 2 diabetes presented with a 4-day history of cough productive of green–yellow sputum. She denied fever, chills, or night sweats but reported upper back pain and a 10– to 15–pound weight loss over 3 months. She was a former smoker (40 pack-year history) who had switched to electronic cigarettes 8 months earlier. On examination, her vital signs were stable. Lung auscultation and percussion were normal bilaterally, and cardiac, abdominal, neurologic, and other systemic examinations were unremarkable. A chest radiograph showed a cavitary lesion in the left upper lung field. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a 6.0 × 6.0 × 8.0 cm bilobed, thick-walled cavitary mass in the left upper lobe invading the posterior mediastinum with destruction of the T2 and T3 vertebral bodies and extension into the spinal canal. MRI of the thoracic spine confirmed an infiltrative mass filling the left T2–T3 neural foramen with spinal cord compression. A bone scan demonstrated tracer uptake in the left fourth rib and T2–T3 vertebrae, correlating with tumor involvement. Brain MRI with and without contrast showed no evidence of metastasis.

A 31-year-old man initially presented with daily vertigo triggered by head movements, accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and difficulty maintaining balance in confined spaces. His examination was notable only for right-sided high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss; half a year later, an MRI of the cerebellum and cerebellopontine angle was normal. He was diagnosed with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo and given home exercises.  

Three years later, he re-presented with a persistent, non-positional balance disturbance and reported difficulty detecting fast-moving objects in his lateral visual fields. Neurologic evaluation showed bilateral horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze, a tandem gait below age expectation, unsteadiness with eyes closed, and a right-predominant positive Dix–Hallpike test. Audiometry again confirmed right high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, and repeat contrast-enhanced MRI with thin slices remained unremarkable.  

Six months after that, he developed progressive balance difficulty, slowed information processing with typing errors, dysarthria, decreased vision with diplopia, and photophobia. Neurologic examination revealed a broad-based ataxic gait; right-eye hypometria; spontaneous torsional nystagmus with left-eye extorsion that increased on downward right gaze; horizontal saccades; and dysdiadochokinesis on the right. There was no hypotonia, dysmetria, headache, or vomiting. Caloric testing showed bilateral hyperreactivity. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis and serum studies, including Borrelia testing, were normal.  

Repeat MRI demonstrated a diffuse T2-hyperintense signal on the dorsolateral aspect of the fourth ventricle extending into the cerebellar vermis bilaterally, subtle diffusion restriction, and nodular contrast enhancement. Compared with earlier scans, the lesion had progressed but exerted no clear mass effect.

A 70-year-old man with a recent diagnosis of leukemia cutis of the eyelid presented with one week of epigastric abdominal pain and jaundice. On examination, he had scleral icterus and a slightly distended, nontender abdomen. Laboratory studies showed a total bilirubin of 12.1 mg/dL (0.1–1.2), direct bilirubin of 7.8 mg/dL (0.1–0.2), aspartate aminotransferase 261 U/L (5–40), alanine aminotransferase 435 U/L (5–50), alkaline phosphatase 670 U/L (25–125), white blood cell count 7,600/μL (4,400–11,000), carcinoembryonic antigen 0.8 ng/mL (0–5), and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 461.7 U/mL (0–35). Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen revealed an ill-defined mass in the inferior pancreatic head and uncinate process with predominantly hypovascular components, small hypervascular areas, and upstream biliary ductal dilation. Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated a 20 mm hypoechoic lesion near the distal common bile duct. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography showed a high-grade distal biliary stricture, for which a sphincterotomy was performed and a plastic stent placed. A core sample was obtained from the pancreatic mass for histologic evaluation.

A 6-year-old girl was admitted with 5 days of progressive generalized abdominal distention, acute lower abdominal pain, nausea, and mild fever. She had no history of constipation or vomiting. On examination, the abdomen was distended and tender to light and deep palpation, with no palpable masses. Fresh and old bloodstains were noted in her undergarments. Her hemodynamic status was stable. Physical examination revealed breast enlargement (thelarche) without pubic hair or other signs of puberty.

Transabdominal ultrasound showed a multilocular–solid right-sided abdominal mass measuring approximately 63 × 40 mm with heterogeneous echogenicity. A contrast-enhanced pelvic CT scan demonstrated a 122 × 106 mm mixed solid-cystic mass in the pelvic cavity with a clear boundary, partly abutting the uterus.

Laboratory studies revealed:
• FSH <0.55 IU/L (normal 1.2–12.5)  
• LH <0.10 IU/L (normal 0.3–2.5)  
• Estradiol 115 pg/mL (normal <9)  
• Androstenedione 5.8 nmol/L (normal 0.0–3.0)  
• DHEAS 0.57 μmol/L (normal 0.090–3.350)  
• Testosterone 1.01 nmol/L (normal 0.0–2.2)  
• AMH 1322 pmol/L (normal 0.1–38.6)  
• AFP 12 kIU/L (normal 1–33)  
• β-hCG 0.11 IU/L (normal 0.0–5.0)  
• Inhibin A 291 pg/mL (normal <4.7)  
• Inhibin B 956 pg/mL (normal <111)

A 63-year-old woman with chronic renal disease and hypertension presented with a one-year history of a painless swelling in her left labia majora. She first noticed a peanut-sized lesion that gradually enlarged. She denied pain, erythema, or systemic symptoms. On examination, the swelling at the left Bartholin’s gland region was non-tender, non-fluctuant, and hard, measuring 3 × 4 cm. There were no palpable inguinal lymph nodes. The clinical diagnosis was a chronic left Bartholin’s gland cyst. Although conservative management was offered due to her asymptomatic status, the patient requested removal for cosmetic reasons. Complete excision of the presumed Bartholin’s gland was performed, and the mass was enucleated in toto.

A healthy male infant was noted at birth to have a congenital mass of the left lower eyelid.
