On examination at 37 weeks’ gestation (cesarean delivery), there was a 5 mm subcutaneous pedunculated lesion immediately inferior to the punctum of the left lower eyelid, with occasional mild epiphora and discharge. The lesion extended 3 mm above the lid margin, raising concern for amblyopia. A partially mucosalized demarcation line was seen on its superior surface. The remainder of the eyelid structures—including the punctum and medial canthus—were intact. Pupils were equal, round, and reactive; there was no afferent pupillary defect. The cornea was clear, the sclera and conjunctiva were normal, and extraocular movements were full with symmetric orbits. The fundus and the contralateral eye were unremarkable. Intraoral and general physical examinations were normal. Six weeks later, the mass remained unchanged, and the parents reported episodic tearing and discharge. To address lacrimal obstruction, prevent amblyopia, and improve cosmesis, the decision was made to excise the lesion and explore the nasolacrimal system.

A 30-year-old woman presented with a two-week history of right floor-of-mouth swelling that had progressively increased in size. She noted that her tongue was displaced toward the left side but denied pain, numbness, or other symptoms. Her medical and dental histories were unremarkable. On intraoral examination, there was a well-demarcated, elliptical nodular mass covered by normal mucosa in the right floor of the mouth, measuring approximately 40×20 mm. The mass was slightly movable and was not palpable extraorally. There was no evidence of lingual or hypoglossal nerve dysfunction. 

Contrast-enhanced CT showed a heterogeneously enhancing lesion filling the right posterior sublingual and submandibular spaces, with delayed enhancement and localized fluid, displacing the genioglossus, mylohyoid, hyoglossus, and digastric muscles and the submandibular gland; no lymphadenopathy was seen. Malignancy or vascular malformation was suspected. 

MR imaging demonstrated a heterogeneously enhancing lesion in the right sublingual space that pushed the mylohyoid muscle inferiorly and the extrinsic tongue muscles medially; there was no invasion of surrounding muscles. The clinical diagnosis was a sublingual gland tumor, not ruling out malignancy. The possibility of a neurogenic tumor was also considered.

A 14-year-old boy presented with a 3-year history of progressively increasing hirsutism, skin darkening, and disfiguring “bulges” over the right occipital, temporal, facial, cervical, and supraclavicular regions. He also reported an abnormal bony protrusion over the sternal region. On examination, there were extensive café-au-lait spots over the involved areas, and palpation of the soft-tissue masses elicited a “bag of worms” sensation.  
Ultrasonography of the right head and neck revealed a mixed-echogenicity mass in the cutaneous and subcutaneous planes extending from the occiput to the shoulder. The lesion comprised multiple hypoechoic tubular, serpiginous, and spherical foci on a hyperechoic background, with some foci demonstrating a hypoechoic nodule surrounded by a hyperechoic rim (“target sign”). Color Doppler showed central and peripheral vascularity with normally tapering vessels and high-resistance flow; the hypoechoic foci themselves were avascular.  
Noncontrast CT of the skull base, neck, and thoracic inlet demonstrated a lobulated hypoattenuating mass in the subcutaneous and cutaneous planes of the right preauricular, parotid, submandibular, cervical, supraclavicular, retrosternal, and shoulder regions. There was remodeling of the right clavicle and manubrium.  
MRI (T2-weighted and STIR sequences) showed a heterogeneously hyperintense, infiltrating mass in the subcutaneous and cutaneous tissues of the right infratemporal fossa, face, neck, supraclavicular area, and shoulder, displacing the rotator cuff muscles. The mass contained multiple scattered spherical and tubular foci, several of which displayed a “target sign” (central hypointensity with a hyperintense rim). Coronal images indicated involvement of branches and fascicles of the right C2 to C6 nerves. On T1-weighted images, the lesion had a mixed hyperintense background with internal foci hypointense to adjacent muscle.

A 71-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a short-term history of gross hematuria and mild low back pain. He was neurologically intact, with no motor weakness, sensory loss, or bowel/bladder dysfunction. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated an expansile lesion involving the S2-S4 segments of the sacrum with indolent widening of the spinal canal and left S2-S4 neural foramina. A large, well-circumscribed exophytic soft-tissue mass extended anteriorly into the presacral space and lacked an internal matrix.

Pelvic MRI (1.5 Tesla) showed the combined osseous and extraosseous mass measuring approximately 11 × 10 × 10.8 cm. On MRI, the lesion was predominantly low to intermediate signal on T1-weighted images, with scattered linear and nodular areas of T1 hyperintensity that corresponded to fat on fat-suppressed T2 images. The mass was largely T2 hyperintense with patchy intermediate and low T2 areas, and it exhibited minimal internal enhancement with a few hazy enhancing foci. 

FDG PET-CT revealed minimal metabolic activity within the mass (SUVmax 3.0).

A 15-year-old girl presented after a fall with pain and swelling of her left hand and occasional aching in the distal inner aspect of her forearm. On examination, there was a mild diffuse swelling over the distal third of the left forearm; the overlying skin was normal, without signs of inflammation. The swelling was soft, tender on palpation, and exhibited an “eggshell” crackling sensation. Wrist and elbow range of motion were full and painless, and there was no neurovascular deficit.

Plain radiographs of the hand, wrist, and forearm demonstrated a fracture of the fifth metacarpal and an expansile lytic lesion with multiple septations in the diaphyseal region of the ulna.

A 6-year-old girl was referred for gradual decreased vision in the right eye. Her neonatal history was unremarkable, developmental milestones were normal, and there was no history of ocular surgery, trauma, or systemic illness. On initial examination, uncorrected visual acuity was no light perception in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye showed a retrolental floppy membrane, retinal detachment, and pre-retinal infiltration; the left eye was normal. A clinical diagnosis of endophthalmitis was made and a vitreous tap with intravitreal cefazolin and vancomycin was performed.

Two weeks later, there was no improvement. Intraocular pressure in the right eye was 18 mm Hg. Slit-lamp examination revealed a clear cornea, deep anterior chamber, ectropion uvea, neovascularization of the iris, a dilated fixed pupil, and a complicated cataract. One week later, she developed progressive leukocoria. At our hospital, vision was light perception in the right eye and normal in the left. Intraocular pressure measured 30 mm Hg in the right eye and 15 mm Hg in the left. Motility was full bilaterally, and external adnexa appeared normal. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye showed inferonasal conjunctival injection, a clear cornea, deep anterior chamber with 4+ cells, a dilated nonreactive pupil, ectropion uvea, and a retrolental whitish hemorrhagic membrane. There was no fundus view. The left eye examination, including the fundus, was normal.

Ultrasound biomicroscopy of the right eye revealed a posterior cavity mass, a ruptured lens, dense vitreous opacities with an area of calcification, an open funnel-shaped retinal detachment, a subretinal cyst nasally, and mild subretinal opacities. MRI of the brain and orbits demonstrated a heterogeneously enhancing soft-tissue mass in the posterior chamber of the right globe with multiple calcific flecks, a funnel-shaped total retinal detachment with low T2 signal, increased vitreous signal on FLAIR, heterogeneous contrast enhancement, vitreous seeding, and hemorrhage behind a thinned, deformed lens. There was no optic nerve or intracranial invasion.

A 25‐year‐old Turkish woman presented with a 3‐year history of a palpable abdominal mass and recent abdominal pain, weakness, anorexia, and a 7–8‐kg weight loss. She had first noted the mass during her second pregnancy but declined further evaluation until now. On physical examination, a 15 × 20‐cm, well‐circumscribed mass was palpable in the periumbilical region. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 13 g/dL, white blood cell count 10 500/mm³, platelets 302 000/mm³, sodium 135 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 28 mg/dL, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, glucose 110 mg/dL, AST 36 IU/L, and ALT 41 IU/L. Abdominal radiography demonstrated rightward displacement of all intestinal loops. An intravenous pyelogram revealed a mass arising from the left kidney. Contrast‐enhanced CT and MRI showed an 18 × 11 × 12‐cm, capsulated, heterogeneously enhancing mass in the mid to lower pole of the left kidney, with moderate hydronephrosis and lateral displacement of the ureter. The right kidney appeared normal. On CT, the mass was interpreted as consistent with renal cell carcinoma.

A 35-year-old woman presented with an eight-month history of right heel pain that had gradually increased over the past two months. The pain commonly occurred at night, was unrelated to activity, and was felt at rest. There was no history of trauma. She smoked 20 cigarettes per day for 10 years and had no other medical conditions or family history of hereditary disease. Physical examination showed no abnormal findings. Blood tests, including inflammatory markers, were normal. A plain radiograph showed a 21 mm cystic lesion along the long axis of the calcaneus. MRI revealed a 22 × 20 mm intraosseous lesion in the posterior calcaneus that was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images.

A 32-year-old Caucasian man with no personal or family history of disease presented with a two-year history of pain and serous exudation of the left great toenail. One year earlier, the nail had been avulsed without improvement. He denied any trauma and took no regular medications. Dermatologic examination revealed distal onycholysis with subungual hyperkeratosis and a round reddish area in the center of the nail plate of the left first toe; the other nails were normal. Radiographs and magnetic resonance imaging of the toe showed no lesions. On nail plate avulsion, an 8 mm reddish papule was seen in the middle of the nail bed. Histologic examination of the papule demonstrated an acantholytic phenomenon in the epidermis, dyskeratotic keratinocytes, and hyperkeratosis overlying the bone of the distal phalanx.

A 74‐year‐old Caucasian man with a history of papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) diagnosed in 1999—treated with total thyroidectomy and radioactive iodine—and subsequent pulmonary metastases identified in 2018, presented in early 2022 with a 3‐month history of a painful mass along the medial aspect of his right arm. The mass produced radiating pain to his fingers on palpation, prompting imaging. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right humerus demonstrated a 3.5 × 2.3 × 1.8 cm solid lesion within the neurovascular bundle of the medial arm that was hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2, and showed postcontrast enhancement. An ultrasound‐guided core biopsy was performed, and the findings were nonspecific but suggested a benign lesion.

A 55-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a one-year history of a persistent right axillary mass. She denied fever, night sweats, weight loss, anorexia, tuberculosis exposure, unpasteurized dairy consumption, or animal contact. She had no family history of hematologic malignancy. 

On examination, vital signs were normal. A 5 cm, firm, mobile lymph node was palpated in the right axilla; there were no other palpable lymph nodes, and the breast examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and C-reactive protein level. A tuberculin skin test was negative. Chest radiography was normal. Bilateral mammography and breast ultrasound were unremarkable. Axillary ultrasound confirmed a 5 cm lymph node with an indeterminate appearance, prompting excisional biopsy.

Histopathological examination of the lymph node revealed marked distension of interfollicular spaces by a mixed inflammatory infiltrate of macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and occasional neutrophils. The macrophages were large, with abundant clear to foamy cytoplasm, and contained intact lymphocytes (emperipolesis). Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated diffuse expression of S100 protein in the macrophages and absence of CD1a staining.

A 16-year-old male presented with a 2-year history of slowly progressive right proptosis and inferior displacement of the right globe. He denied headache, numbness, orbital pain, or visual changes. There was no significant medical history or family history of orbital tumors. On examination, Hertel exophthalmometry confirmed 7 mm of proptosis and hypoglobus measured 1 cm. There was no blepharoptosis, periorbital sensory deficit, or epiphora. Uncorrected visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally, with normal intraocular pressure, and anterior, pupillary, and funduscopic examinations were unremarkable. Extraocular movements were full and painless without diplopia.

Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI of the orbits revealed a 2 × 2 cm homogenous, contrast-enhancing soft tissue mass in the superolateral extraconal space of the right orbit, with extension into the intraconal space and anterior-inferior displacement of the globe. The lesion encroached upon the superior rectus muscle but spared the optic nerve, and there was no significant bony erosion. The patient deferred intervention until after school, and repeat imaging at 3 months showed enlargement of the lesion to 3.2 × 2.2 × 1.8 cm.

A 26-year-old white man with a history of asthma presented with chest pain. Two months earlier, he had similar pain that was attributed to musculoskeletal injury versus costochondritis after acute coronary syndrome was ruled out, and he was discharged on NSAIDs. On re-presentation he reported dyspnea on exertion, fever, night sweats, and weight loss. 
Chest CT demonstrated a 10.5 cm anterior mediastinal mass compressing the main pulmonary artery and a large pericardial effusion with evidence of invasion into the pericardium. Transthoracic echocardiography confirmed a large pericardial effusion without tamponade physiology. He underwent pericardiocentesis with drain placement and biopsy of the pericardium and intrapericardial mass. 
On hospital day 5, he developed acute dyspnea and hypoxia. CT angiography ruled out pulmonary embolism but showed 95% stenosis of the main pulmonary artery from external compression. He received one fraction of emergent radiation therapy with symptomatic improvement. 
Laboratory studies revealed an elevated alpha-fetoprotein level of 341 ng/mL, elevated lactate dehydrogenase of 742 U/L, and normal beta–human chorionic gonadotropin, CEA, and beta-2 microglobulin levels. Cytology of the pericardial fluid was consistent with a malignant pericardial effusion.

A 38-year-old Caucasian woman was referred for evaluation of a lesion on her lower lip.  
- History of present illness: The lesion had been present for approximately eight years, with very slow growth. The patient noted intermittent changes in size and occasional bleeding during the winter months.  
- Past medical history: Unremarkable. No known allergies.  
- Social history: Non-smoker; minimal alcohol consumption.  
- Physical examination: A soft, pedunculated, submucosal nodule measuring 6 × 6 mm was observed at the midline of the lower lip, adjacent to the vermilion border.  
- Management plan: After discussion, the patient elected to have the lesion excised for cosmetic reasons. An encapsulated soft tissue mass was removed under local anesthesia, with a cuff of adipose tissue.  
- Preliminary differential diagnosis at clinical examination included mucocele, liposarcoma, and myxoma.

A 39-year-old woman presented for a routine annual exam with a request for permanent sterilization. She had no significant past medical or surgical history, had three full-term vaginal deliveries, and no family history of note. Routine preoperative blood tests were unremarkable, and no imaging was performed. Fifteen days later, she underwent laparoscopic bilateral tubal ligation. Intraoperatively, countless firm, white-tan nodules, ranging from under 1 mm to 10 mm, coated the peritoneal surfaces—most prominently on the right pelvic side wall and along both broad ligaments. Several nodules were excised for histopathologic evaluation. Grossly, two tissue fragments contained multiple firm tan nodules measuring up to 4 mm. Microscopic examination showed well-circumscribed, unencapsulated nodules composed of interlacing fascicles of plump spindle cells with tapered ends and rare perinuclear vacuoles; there was no necrosis, mitoses, or cellular atypia. Immunohistochemical studies revealed strong desmin positivity, negative staining for S100 and pankeratin, and a low Ki-67 proliferation index.

A 13-year-old boy presented with a painless, progressively enlarging mass in his left inguinal region, first noted 2 months earlier. His past history included spinal surgery 6 years previously, resulting in paraplegia and chronic decubitus ulcers on his left foot. On examination, the inguinal mass measured approximately 3.5 × 2.4 cm, was mobile over deeper structures and the overlying skin, nontender, and without erythema or warmth. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies revealed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 119 mm/hr; results of a complete blood count, liver-function tests, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, and lactate dehydrogenase were all within age-appropriate reference ranges. A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated enlarged lymph nodes inferior to the inguinal ligament (largest, 3.5 × 2.4 cm) with no other lymphadenopathy or organomegaly.

A 36-year-old Asian man presented with progressive fatigue and decreased vision over 1 month. Two months earlier, he had been treated for anemia with transfusions without lasting improvement. On admission, physical examination revealed hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. Laboratory studies showed:
– RBC count 1.81 × 10^12/L, hemoglobin 54 g/L  
– Platelet count 214 × 10^9/L  
– WBC count 38.2 × 10^9/L with 51.5% blasts  

Bone marrow aspirate demonstrated 80.6% blasts with negative myeloperoxidase staining. Cytogenetic analysis revealed a Philadelphia chromosome (t[9;22]); flow cytometry was positive for CD10, CD19, and TdT. CSF cytology was negative for malignant cells. He was diagnosed with Philadelphia-positive lymphoid blast crisis of chronic myeloid leukemia.

One day after initiation of oral corticosteroids for leukemia, ophthalmic evaluation showed:
– Best-corrected visual acuity: 1.2 OD, 0.8 OS  
– Intraocular pressures normal OU  
– Slit-lamp exam: no anterior chamber or vitreous cells  
– Fundus examination: bilateral SRD involving the fovea, peripheral retinal hemorrhages, and Roth spots OU  
– OCT: subretinal fluid accumulation, thickened choroids OU without visible choroid–scleral interface; no subretinal septa  
– Fluorescein angiography: multiple pinpoint hyperfluorescent spots in the early phase, pooling in the subretinal space, and late optic disc leakage  

Differential diagnosis included Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada disease and central serous chorioretinopathy.

A 24-year-old woman with polycystic ovarian syndrome was referred for evaluation of a right shoulder lesion thought to be a keloid. She noted that the lesion had been present for 2 years, was slowly enlarging, and pruritic, with no history of trauma, pain, bleeding, or topical treatments. She denied any history of keloids, weight loss, fevers, chills, or night sweats. Her only medication was an oral contraceptive. On examination, there was a 2-cm soft, shiny, pink nodule on the right lateral shoulder. Because the lesion lacked the firm, indurated quality of a keloid, a punch biopsy was performed. 

Histopathology revealed a diffuse dermal lymphoid infiltrate with no epidermal involvement and lacking germinal center formation. The infiltrate consisted of mostly small, irregular lymphocytes with scattered larger cells showing multiple nucleoli. Immunohistochemical stains showed sheets of CD20-positive B cells that coexpressed BCL-2, with variable BCL-6 expression in the majority of B cells. In situ hybridization for kappa and lambda light chains demonstrated a polytypic plasma cell population. MUM-1 and CD10 were negative. Next-generation sequencing for B-cell clonality was positive for Ig Kappa rearrangement. 

Staging workup with positron emission tomography showed no evidence of avid lymphoma. Laboratory studies revealed mild leukocytosis without lymphocytosis, and peripheral blood flow cytometry was unremarkable. Colonoscopy was also unremarkable.

A 48-year-old man was found to have a left paraspinal mass on a preoperative chest radiograph obtained for knee arthroscopy. He reported an 8-month history of relatively constant sharp left axillary pain radiating to the anterior chest wall. Vital signs were within normal limits, and the physical examination was unremarkable. A scout film from a chest CT scan demonstrated a lesion obscuring the left supralateral contour of the aortic arch. Noncontrast CT of the chest revealed a well-circumscribed left paraspinal mass measuring 3.3 × 5.6 × 9.2 cm, abutting the descending thoracic aorta and the posterior aspects of the left fifth through seventh ribs. The lesion was of heterogeneous attenuation, with a central region consistent with fat density and punctate calcifications in the peripheral soft-tissue component. MRI of the thoracic spine showed a mass in the left paravertebral groove extending from T4 to T7 without expansion of or extension into the neural foramina. The central portion exhibited intrinsic T1 hyperintensity that was suppressed on fat-suppressed sequences, confirming fatty composition. The peripheral soft-tissue components demonstrated intermediate-to-low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, intermediate signal intensity on T2-weighted images, and heterogeneous enhancement after administration of gadolinium. There was no evidence of bony erosion, reactive edema, or remodeling.

A 58-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of whole-body edema, “moon-like” facies, and weakness of the lower limb muscles. Laboratory studies showed lactate dehydrogenase 652 U/L (normal 119–229), potassium 1.6 mmol/L (normal 3.5–5.0), chloride 92 mmol/L (normal 98–108), adrenocorticotropic hormone 384.9 pg/mL (normal 7.2–63.3), and cortisol 44.3 μg/dL (normal 4.5–21.2). Multiparametric MRI of the abdomen demonstrated soft tissue shadows protruding from the left renal pelvis to the dorsal cortex with surrounding hematoma. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a large hypovascular left renal mass and normal-sized adrenal glands. Brain MRI performed after surgery showed no pituitary lesion, and the pituitary gland was normal in size.

A 21-year-old man with no past medical history presented with two weeks of left eye pain and blurry vision. He denied flashes or floaters but reported acute loss of vision in the left eye four days before presentation. He also endorsed a one-month history of cough.

Visual acuity was 20/30 in the right eye and 20/70 in the left eye; intraocular pressure measured 12 mm Hg right and 9 mm Hg left. The left pupil was ovoid and nonreactive. Slit-lamp examination of the left eye revealed conjunctival injection, 3+ pigmented cells, 2+ flare, and a large pigmented ciliary body mass extending from 6 o’clock to 10:30 with internal vascularization. Dilated fundus examination showed extensive subretinal fluid, hemorrhage, and exudates; the right eye was normal. Gonioscopy demonstrated erosion of the iris root with invasion of the angle. B-scan ultrasonography of the left eye showed a dome-shaped tumor arising from the ciliary body measuring 11.2 × 12.8 mm with low internal reflectivity and an inferior retinal detachment.

Because of the pigmented nature of the lesion and ultrasound characteristics, initial concern was for uveal melanoma, and imaging for staging was planned.

A 64-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of a painless, slowly enlarging mass on the right cheek. On examination, the lesion was elastic, hard, movable, and measured approximately 40 mm in the right buccal submucosa and subcutaneous tissue. MRI revealed a well-defined, regular 40 × 36 × 31 mm mass in the right buccal space that was pale hyperintense on axial T1-weighted images and heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted and STIR images. Fine-needle aspiration cytology showed multilayered clusters of oval to spindle-shaped nuclei. A minor salivary-gland myoepithelial tumor (e.g., pleomorphic adenoma) was suspected on cytology, but distinguishing it from a nonepithelial neoplasm was difficult.

A 57-year-old healthy woman presented with progressive right eye proptosis. Visual acuity was 20/25 bilaterally. Pupils were equal and reactive, and confrontation visual fields were full. Ocular motility testing revealed a mild (−1) restriction on downgaze in the right eye. Hertel exophthalmometry demonstrated 3 mm of right proptosis with resistance to retropulsion. Optical coherence tomography of the optic nerve and automated perimetry showed no evidence of optic nerve compression.

Cross-sectional imaging with contrast-enhanced CT and MRI demonstrated a lobulated, contrast-enhancing intraconal mass adjacent to the optic nerve in the right orbital apex. The lesion extended through the inferior orbital fissure into the pterygopalatine fossa and further into the middle cranial fossa, lying near the cavernous sinus and internal carotid artery.

A 27-year-old electrician presented with a 1-year history of a slowly expanding swelling in the left cheek, without pain or discharge. On examination, there was a single, dome-shaped, 3×3 cm firm, non-tender, freely movable mass in the left buccal region. The overlying skin was non-erythematous but showed an indurated, non-draining sinus centrally. No submandibular or submental lymph nodes were palpable. Intraoral examination revealed intact dentition and no swelling. An orthopantomogram showed no bone involvement. Initially, a buccal space infection was suspected; the differential diagnosis included periodontal abscess, lymphadenitis, infected epidermoid or sebaceous cyst, hemangioma, and antibioma. Aspiration with a wide-bore needle yielded no material owing to the thick consistency of the lesion. Surgical excision was performed under local anesthesia: a horizontal stab incision extruded cheesy, keratinous material through a well-defined cyst wall, and the entire cyst lining was removed. A tissue sample was sent for histopathological evaluation.

A 12-year-old boy was referred with a 1-year history of a left knee swelling and pain aggravated by running, with a preceding history of trauma. There were no constitutional symptoms, bleeding diathesis, or other joint involvement. Over the past year, three aspirations of the swelling by a practitioner each yielded blood, yet the mass continued to enlarge.

On examination, there was a 4×3 cm asymmetric, boggy, noncompressible, nonpulsatile swelling in the anteromedial suprapatellar region of the left knee. The overlying skin was normal without discoloration or warmth. The fossae on either side of the patellar tendon were normal, the patellar tap was negative, and there were no distal neurovascular deficits or bruits. Limb lengths were equal, and knee motion was full.

An X-ray obtained five months earlier showed minimal soft tissue swelling. Ultrasound revealed a hypoechoic, irregular mass within the muscle plane with increased vascularity and multiple calcific areas, features favoring haemangioma. A repeat knee radiograph demonstrated multiple phleboliths in the suprapatellar soft tissues along with minimal soft tissue swelling.

A 59-year-old African-American man with hypertension and no alcohol or drug use presented with several weeks of pruritus, jaundice, nausea, and weight loss. On examination he was icteric, without hepatosplenomegaly or ascites; the abdomen was benign. Laboratory tests showed an obstructive pattern of liver‐function–test abnormalities. Extensive infectious studies (hepatitis A, B, C, E; leptospirosis; VDRL; malaria smear) were negative. Further evaluation (ANA, smooth muscle antibody, antimitochondrial antibody, IgG levels, α₁-antitrypsin, and CA 19-9) was also negative. Abdominal ultrasonography showed hepatic steatosis. CT of the abdomen showed an enlarged celiac-axis lymph node (>1 cm) and portal lymphadenopathy, but no biliary‐duct dilatation on endoscopic ultrasound; cytology from the celiac node showed only small lymphocytes. An ultrasound-guided liver biopsy demonstrated noncaseating granulomas and bile-duct damage. Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme levels were elevated, and chest CT showed mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy. He was started on budesonide and 6-mercaptopurine, with marked symptomatic and laboratory improvement.

Approximately 8 months later, he returned with 6 months of worsening jaundice, itching, pale stools, and weight loss. Laboratory tests showed severe direct hyperbilirubinemia despite methylprednisolone therapy. Abdominal ultrasonography now revealed a dilated common bile duct (1.6 cm) with biliary sludge. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography demonstrated persistently enlarged periportal lymph nodes and a mass in the ampulla of the pancreas.

A 17-year-old male presented with an 8-month history of a hard, diffuse swelling of the right lower one-third of his face. On extraoral examination, there was a 3 cm × 2 cm swelling of the right mandibular region. Intraorally, there was diffuse swelling extending from the lower right second premolar into the retromolar area, obliterating the buccal vestibule. Panoramic radiography demonstrated a well-defined multilocular radiolucency in the right mandibular body and ramus, with displacement of the unerupted third molar toward the mandibular notch. Periapical films showed root resorption of adjacent teeth, and occlusal views revealed expansion of buccal and lingual cortical plates with internal radiopaque septations. An incisional biopsy was performed, and on the basis of those results, a hemimandibulectomy was undertaken.

A man in his early 60s presented with a painless, non-tender, non-pruritic, mobile nodule on the right lower eyelid below the inferior orbital rim. The lesion had grown to 15 × 9 mm over eleven months. There was no antecedent trauma, infection, or neoplasm at this site and no history of atopic dermatitis. Physical examination revealed no other cutaneous lesions and no evidence of systemic disease. Laboratory tests showed a normal serum tryptase level (5.3 ng/mL; normal < 11.5 ng/mL) and a complete blood count notable only for mild anemia. An excisional biopsy of the eyelid nodule was performed.

A 13-year-old girl first presented in 2009 with a 5-month history of a painless, pedunculated gingival mass in the maxillary anterior region that bled on brushing. Excision and histopathology confirmed a pyogenic granuloma. Twelve days later, a 2 × 3 cm palatal growth recurred and was again confirmed as a pyogenic granuloma. 

Five years later, she returned with swelling and mobility of the maxillary anterior teeth. On examination, there was an ulcerated, fiery-red mass extending from the labial to palatal gingiva of teeth 12 through 23, with ill-defined margins; the lesion was soft and non-tender. Tooth 11 had Grade II mobility, and tooth 21 had Grade III mobility. Panoramic radiography revealed bone loss in the anterior maxilla. Excessive bleeding occurred during extraction of tooth 21, necessitating transfusion of five units of blood. Hematologic studies showed a transient prolongation of bleeding time, clotting time, and prothrombin time, which normalized with vitamin K. 

The lesion was excised under general anesthesia, and teeth 11, 22, and 23 were removed. Histopathologic examination revealed an ulcerated epithelium overlying a cellular stroma with numerous capillaries of varying sizes lined by proliferating endothelial cells and a diffuse chronic inflammatory infiltrate. Decalcified sections of the alveolar bone showed numerous dilated blood vessels, indicating extension of the lesion.

A 17-year-old male presented with a one-month history of progressive, bilateral painless visual loss. Three weeks later he developed sudden, progressive bilateral hearing loss with vertigo but no ear discharge, fullness, or tinnitus. He also reported intermittent low-grade fever, night sweats, lethargy, and undocumented weight loss over the past year, along with headaches and irritability. He had a history of pulmonary tuberculosis exposure.

On examination, he was pale and lethargic, with a temperature of 100 °F and nontender bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. Neurologic examination revealed intact motor function; sensory and higher functions could not be assessed due to severe hearing and vision loss. Cranial-nerve testing showed bilateral optic and vestibulocochlear impairment. Ophthalmologic findings included dilated pupils with sluggish light reflexes, impaired color vision, visual acuity limited to hand movements, and fundoscopy showing deep retinal hemorrhages with blurred disc margins and obscured vessels (Grade V papilledema). The anterior segments were normal. Pure-tone audiometry demonstrated profound bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable, with no meningeal signs, petechiae, bruises, or bone tenderness.

Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 407 × 10^3/μL, a platelet count of 109 × 10^3/μL, and a red-cell count of 1.88 × 10^6/μL. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 45 mm/hour. A peripheral-blood smear revealed marked leukocytosis with immature granulocytes, eosinophilia, and basophilia.

A 48-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a known right middle ear mass. A routine chest radiograph revealed enlargement of the left pulmonary hilum. He was asymptomatic, with blood pressure 117/75 mmHg, pulse 93/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and temperature 36.3 °C. Examination showed no lymphadenopathy, normal sinus and oropharyngeal findings, a midline trachea, a barrel chest, and clear bilateral breath sounds. Bronchoscopy was unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies including serum calcium, urine Bence-Jones protein, and plasma electrophoresis for M protein were negative. A bone marrow biopsy demonstrated a normal pattern of cell distribution. There was no history of tuberculosis; he had a 10-year smoking history. Past medical history was notable for surgical removal of a right tympanic cavity tumor, diagnosed postoperatively as extramedullary plasmacytoma. No family history of similar disease existed.

A chest CT scan showed a well-circumscribed 2.7 × 1.5 × 2.5 cm mass in the left lower lobe dorsal segment. On the lung window, it was homogeneous with lobulated, spiculated margins and adjacent pleural retraction causing bronchiolar obstruction. On contrast-enhanced images, the nodule exhibited moderate uniform enhancement with tiny internal vessels. No mediastinal lymphadenopathy was present. A skeletal survey (skull, spine, pelvis) revealed no osteolytic lesions. CT interpretation favored peripheral lung cancer.

A 13-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of progressive abdominal distension over several months. He had no fever, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or appetite changes. On examination, his liver edge was palpable 6 cm below the right costal margin without tenderness or guarding. Laboratory studies showed a mildly elevated lactate dehydrogenase level of 263 U/L (normal, 74–250 U/L); complete blood count, liver function tests, other liver enzymes, and serum alpha-fetoprotein were all within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a partially defined mass in the right lobe of the liver with multiple internal cystic foci and increased intralesional vascularity. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 17 × 18 × 20 cm heterogeneous mass in the right hepatic lobe that was predominantly cystic with thick internal septations, residual solid components, and peripheral neovascular formation.

An 82-year-old man presented with painless right testicular swelling of several weeks’ duration without systemic symptoms. His history included glaucoma, prostatic adenomectomy, and hernioplasty; medications were dorzolamide, lansoprazole, and dutasteride. Testicular ultrasound showed enlargement and inhomogeneity of the right testis and epididymis with ipsilateral hydrocele. After 10 days of amoxicillin–clavulanate for presumed orchiepididymitis, swelling persisted. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT confirmed testicular pathology and revealed new bilateral macronodular adrenal enlargement measuring 15×12 mm on the right and 27×18 mm on the left, with homogeneous attenuation; these nodules were absent on a CT scan 3 years earlier. An 18 FDG PET/CT showed intense uptake (SUVmax 25.5) in the right testis but no uptake in the adrenal glands. Laboratory evaluation revealed normal electrolytes, blood count, iron studies, protein electrophoresis, glucose, renal and liver function, thyroid profile, LDH, and β2-microglobulin. Serologies were negative for active HCV and EBV (positive for past EBV). Clinically, he had no asthenia, headaches, abdominal pain, striae, or “buffalo hump,” and his blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg without hypertensive peaks on 24-hour monitoring.

A 41-year-old woman with presumed spinocerebellar ataxia presented with progressive dyspnea on exertion and bilateral lower extremity edema over several months. Vital signs were notable for mild tachycardia and normal blood pressure. Physical examination revealed elevated jugular venous pressure, a right ventricular heave, and pitting edema of both lower extremities. 

Chest radiograph demonstrated moderate cardiomegaly and right heart enlargement. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed an amorphous, invasive superior left mediastinal mass encasing and nearly occluding the main and left pulmonary arteries, with complete occlusion of the left pulmonary arterial tree, severe narrowing of the right pulmonary artery, and several scattered small nonspecific pulmonary nodules. PET imaging revealed marked FDG avidity of the mediastinal mass. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a severely dilated right atrium and right ventricle with leftward septal bowing, consistent with right heart failure.

During her initial hospitalization, an intravascular biopsy yielded only thrombus material and a minute fragment of unremarkable intima. A second biopsy via bronchoscopy was nondiagnostic, showing fragments of fibrous tissue with a mixed inflammatory infiltrate. A third intravascular biopsy also failed to establish a diagnosis, revealing vessel wall fragments with myxoid degeneration and few small crushed cells, suggestive of inflammation. Empiric therapy was deferred pending a definitive diagnosis. To relieve obstruction, she underwent stenting of the right pulmonary artery, resulting in immediate hemodynamic improvement without complications.

A 25-year-old man presented with a several-week history of urinary retention and voiding dysfunction.  
On digital rectal examination, the prostate was smooth, enlarged, and without discrete nodules.  
Transabdominal ultrasound revealed a homogeneous prostate measuring approximately 50–60 cm³.  
The serum PSA level was 0.91 ng/mL (normal range).  
He was treated with tamsulosin for 4 weeks, after which urinary function subjectively improved.  
Repeat ultrasound showed a postvoid residual volume of 150–200 mL and further enlargement of the prostate to 150 cm³.  
Pelvic MRI demonstrated a 9 × 8.5 × 7.5 cm inhomogeneous mass arising from the prostate with polypoid extension into the bladder.  
Prostate biopsies were obtained 6 weeks after initial presentation.  
Staging chest CT revealed bilateral pulmonary nodules consistent with metastatic disease; FDG-PET–CT and bone-marrow examination showed no additional sites of metastasis.

A 38-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of a slowly enlarging swelling on the right side of her palate and a 1-month history of intermittent dull pain in the area. Her past medical and dental histories were unremarkable. Family history was notable for similar palatal swellings and multiple cutaneous nodules in her father and newly developing nodules in her 17-year-old daughter. 

On general examination, diffuse brownish-black pigmented nodular masses of varying sizes were noted over the body; these nodules were noninflammatory and ranged from soft to firm on palpation. Ophthalmologic examination revealed Lisch nodules and early-onset cataract without glaucoma. A 1 × 1 cm right submandibular lymph node was palpable, mobile, nontender, and firm. 

Intraoral examination showed a solitary, oval, well-defined pedunculated swelling on the upper right palate, extending from the attached gingiva of teeth 11 and 12 to the distal region of tooth 16, approximately 1 cm from the midpalatal suture. The lesion measured about 2 × 3 cm, was irregular in shape, pink, non-tender, nonfluctuant, and of variable consistency. Differential diagnoses included lipoma, fibroma, schwannoma, and hemangioma. 

Panoramic and posterior–anterior skull radiographs showed no bone involvement. Based on the diffuse pigmented skin nodules, Lisch nodules, intraoral tumor, and a positive family history, a provisional diagnosis of neurofibroma associated with neurofibromatosis type I was made.

A 33-year-old woman presented with a 4-year history of a painless, slowly enlarging mass in her right abdominal flank and mild dyspeptic symptoms. She was a 15-pack-year smoker, in otherwise good health, with a BMI of 20.5. Four years earlier, an ultrasound had shown a 1.5-cm slightly hyperechoic mass in the right para-umbilical region, thought to be a lipoma. On current examination, her vital signs were normal. Physical examination revealed a palpable, mobile, non-tender mass in the right abdominal quadrant; no other lymphadenopathy was noted. Laboratory studies were unremarkable except for an elevated CA-125 level of 81.4 U/mL (normal < 35 U/mL). Repeat abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a well-defined, heterogeneous solid lesion measuring 8.2 × 6.1 × 6.8 cm beneath the inferior hepatic edge, adjacent to the inferior vena cava and the lower pole of the right kidney. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 9 × 7 × 6 cm hypervascular, heterogeneous mass with internal calcifications that was well circumscribed from the pancreatic head, liver, and the right kidney; there was no bowel obstruction, no additional masses, and no lymphadenopathy.

A 65-year-old woman presented with 6 months of diffuse abdominal pain, weakness, and occasional vomiting of ingested material. She had undergone abdominal surgery at an outside hospital 6 months earlier, and the biopsy performed then was reported as suggestive of gastrointestinal stromal tumor. She denied abnormal uterine bleeding, oral contraceptive use, or gynecologic surgery. On examination, she appeared chronically ill, was emaciated and slightly pale, and had a long midline abdominal scar; there was mild generalized abdominal tenderness on deep palpation. Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin level of 9.3 g/dL, a white-cell count of 6900/μL, normal liver and renal function studies, and a normal chest radiograph. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed innumerable hypoechoic masses of varying sizes throughout the peritoneal cavity and a large hypoechoic lesion measuring 7.5×4.7 cm in the right lobe of the liver. At laparotomy, there were innumerable globular masses arising from the mesentery and the walls of the small bowel (some pedunculated, most sessile), a large mass in the right hepatic lobe approximately 8×10 cm, and a grossly normal pelvis. Multiple biopsies were obtained from the mesenteric and superficial small intestinal lesions; the liver mass was left untouched to avoid bleeding.

An 83-year-old Middle Eastern man living in a sunny climate presented with a 10-year history of a slow-growing skin tumor on his right lower eyelid and lateral canthus. He has hypertension and a remote history of stroke. Visual acuity was counting fingers at 1 m in the right eye due to cataract; extraocular movements were full and intraocular pressures were normal bilaterally. On examination, the lower lid mass measured 2 × 1.5 × 0.5 cm, was skin-colored and multilobulated, showed telangiectatic vessels without surface ulceration, and encroached on the lateral half of the lid margin. Multiple small satellite lesions were confined to the anterior lamella without involvement of the tarsus, meibomian glands, or palpebral conjunctiva, and without lash loss. Given the lesion’s size, location, and appearance raising concern for malignancy, an excisional biopsy with a 2 mm safety margin was performed, and the defect was closed primarily.

An 80-year-old man presented with a swelling on the dorsal surface of the tongue that had recurred several months after superficial removal by a dentist. He reported intermittent bleeding from the lesion over the preceding five months. His medical history was notable only for hypertension, and he denied any other similar lesions elsewhere. 

On intraoral examination, there was a 1×1 cm oval, reddish, sessile, slightly indurated, and painless swelling in the midline of the dorsal tongue. A biopsy was performed. 

Grossly, the specimen was an oval, creamy-to-brownish, elastic soft tissue mass covered by epithelium, measuring 10×7×5 mm. 

Microscopic examination showed a relatively well-circumscribed nodular proliferation of mostly clear cells beneath the parakeratinized stratified squamous epithelium. The cells were arranged in nests separated by fibrous septa and featured pleomorphic vesicular to hyperchromatic eccentrically located nuclei, clear to eosinophilic cytoplasm, sharp cell membranes, and a rich capillary network. 

Special stains showed negative mucicarmine staining and PAS staining that was highly focal. Immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratin 7 was negative.

A 24-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of progressive left hip pain radiating to the anterior thigh. The pain began as a dull aching groin discomfort, worsened over weeks, was severe at night, and was associated with weight loss and anorexia. There was no history of trauma. 

On examination, he had an antalgic gait, reduced range of motion of the left hip in all planes with spasms, and tenderness deep in the left groin. Straight-leg raising was negative, and neurologic examination was normal.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein, were within normal limits. A pelvic radiograph was unremarkable. Initial MRI of the left hip showed synovitis and marrow edema without fracture. He received 6 months of empirical anti-tubercular therapy without clinical improvement.

An open synovial biopsy was performed; all cultures were negative, and histology showed mild to moderate chronic synovitis with lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates. Rheumatologic evaluation, including serologic studies, was unremarkable. A repeat MRI of the hips demonstrated a well-defined T1-hypointense, STIR-hyperintense lesion with a thick sclerotic rim in the anterolateral cortex of the left femoral head, associated marrow edema, moderate joint effusion, and synovitis.

A 24-year-old man was referred for two years of left heel pain that progressed gradually, was partially relieved by analgesics, and led to functional limitation without systemic symptoms. He had no significant medical history and did not smoke. On examination he was afebrile and stable, with antalgic gait despite crutches, tenderness over the calcaneus, and hindfoot swelling without overlying skin changes; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 8200/mm3, platelet count of 378 000/mm3, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 8 mm/h, and C-reactive protein level of 6 mg/L. A plain radiograph of the ankle demonstrated a lytic lesion at the inferior border of the calcaneus without trabeculation or periosteal reaction. MRI revealed a 68 × 55 × 47 mm, well-circumscribed lesion centered on the calcaneal tuberosity with multiple loculations and several fluid–fluid levels, expanding but not breaching the cortex, and without any extraosseous soft-tissue component.

A 25-year-old man presented with one week of right upper quadrant swelling pain without other symptoms. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. Physical examination was normal. Laboratory tests, including complete blood counts, liver function tests, and serum tumor markers (α-fetoprotein 4.14 ng/mL, carcinoembryonic antigen 1.30 ng/mL, CA19-9 6.06 U/mL), were within normal limits. Hepatitis B surface antibody was positive; other hepatitis markers were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed an 18×15×11 cm heteroechoic mass with a clear boundary in the right hepatic trisegment and no remarkable blood flow signal. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound demonstrated peripheral hyperenhancement in the arterial phase, peripheral hypoenhancement in the portal phase, and no enhancement centrally. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a well-capsulated, cystlike lesion in the right hepatic lobe containing stripe-like hyperdense and patchy hypodense areas that were hyperenhanced in the arterial phase and hypoenhanced in the portal phase, with a nonenhancing central region. Based on these findings, liver echinococcosis was suspected, and right hepatic trisegmentectomy was planned.

A 28-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of bilateral knee pain and a 1-month history of locking in the right knee. There was no history of trauma; her medical history was notable only for childhood thrombocytopenia. Examination of the right knee revealed tenderness from the patellar tendon to the anterolateral joint line and a positive Watson-Jones test; there was no effusion, ligament instability, or McMurray sign. Range of motion was 0° to 145°, with pain at the extremes. The Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) was 49.4. Examination of the left knee showed tenderness in the popliteal fossa and a painful McMurray sign; there was no effusion or instability. Range of motion was 0° to 145°, with pain at the extremes. The KOOS score was 84.5. Plain radiographs of the lower limbs and both knees were normal. MRI of the right knee showed a 24 × 9 mm mass in the anterior compartment with homogeneous low signal on T1-weighted images and heterogeneous low signal with clear borders on T2-weighted images. MRI of the left knee showed a 26 × 10 mm mass in the posterior compartment with similar signal characteristics.

A 68-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a three-month history of a mass in the right upper gum adjacent to the hard palate, which developed after extraction of a right upper molar. The lesion progressively enlarged. On examination, there was a firm, 6 × 6 × 5 cm flattened mass covering the entire palate except the anterior and left lateral dental arch, extending into the right cheek. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed an 80 × 64 × 58 mm heterogenous expansile lesion destroying the right maxilla but sparing the floor of the orbit. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography demonstrated cortical disruption and erosion of the right maxillary alveolar septa and zygomatic process by an 84 × 76 mm unilocular soft-tissue mass extending into the oral cavity and cheek soft tissues; the lesion measured 45–111 Hounsfield units and contained both hypodense and vascularized areas. Three-dimensional vascular reconstruction showed moderate perfusion of the lesion via the right facial and internal maxillary arteries. Preoperative endovascular angiography confirmed these findings, and the feeding vessels were embolized.

A 38-year-old man presented with a painless, progressively enlarging swelling over the right upper back and shoulder. He first noticed the mass incidentally; it was painless at rest, with only mild discomfort during shoulder flexion and extension. He denied numbness, paresthesia, trauma, or systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a firm, mobile, non-tender subcutaneous swelling without overlying skin changes, superficial to the trapezius muscle.

Noncontrast MRI of the right shoulder demonstrated a lobulated subcutaneous lesion with fatty components. The soft-tissue portion was predominantly hyperintense on T2-weighted images and hypointense on T1-weighted images, with no aggressive features. The lesion was thought to represent a slow-flow vascular malformation, such as a hemangioma, and a vascular surgery consultation with contrast-enhanced MRI was recommended. 

Three months later, a postgadolinium MRI showed an avidly enhancing soft-tissue mass with non-enhancing fatty and septal components and no invasion of surrounding structures. The radiologic interpretation remained that of a slow-flow vascular malformation (hemangioma).

A 17-year-old boy presented with new-onset seizures characterized by focal motor activity of the right upper and lower extremities with secondary generalization. He was otherwise healthy, with no family history of seizures or tuberous sclerosis, and reported no other symptoms. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, thyroid-stimulating hormone level, and comprehensive metabolic panel, were within normal limits. Neurologic examination revealed no focal deficits. Electroencephalography in awake and drowsy states, as well as during photic stimulation and hyperventilation, was normal.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated a 1.8 × 2.4 × 2.2 cm mass in the subcortical and deep white matter and adjacent cortex of the left occipital lobe. On T2-weighted images, the lesion was predominantly hypointense with internal linear hyperintensities. On T1-weighted images, it showed peripheral mild hyperintensity with a central hypointense core. Susceptibility-weighted imaging revealed marked hypointensity. Postcontrast T1-weighted images disclosed a few small areas of central enhancement, whereas the remainder of the lesion enhanced minimally. No enlarged feeding arteries or draining veins were identified to suggest an arteriovenous malformation. The leading considerations on MRI were cavernous malformation, calcified low-grade tumor, and dystrophic cerebral calcification.

A 4-year-old child presented with a 1-week history of oliguria, weakness, anorexia, vomiting, and abdominal pain. There was no significant past medical history. On examination, the child had mild edema and hypertension (blood pressure 125/80 mm Hg). Laboratory studies showed: normal complete blood count; serum creatinine 130 µmol/L (normal 27–60); blood urea nitrogen 11 mmol/L (normal 2.5–6.4); uric acid 6.5 mg/dL (normal 1.7–5.9); sodium 140 mmol/L; potassium 4.5 mmol/L; lactate dehydrogenase 540 IU/L (normal 150–500); and normal liver enzymes. Urinalysis revealed no leukocytes, blood cells, or proteins. Renal ultrasound demonstrated diffuse enlargement of both kidneys, hypoechoic with loss of corticomedullary differentiation. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed bilateral nephromegaly with multiple hypoenhancing areas of poorly defined margins relative to normal parenchyma and no hydronephrosis. No lesions were seen in other organs, and there were no enlarged abdominal lymph nodes. Differential diagnoses included acute tubular necrosis, pyelonephritis, acute papillary necrosis, and renal lymphoma.

A 46-year-old man with a 90 pack-year smoking history and no prior malignancy was found to have an anterior mediastinal mass on routine imaging. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 7.0 × 5.5 cm lesion in the prevascular region, with suspected invasion into the left upper lobe and left innominate vein. Brain MRI and whole-body PET-CT revealed no other lesions. CT-guided biopsy of the mediastinal mass demonstrated adenocarcinoma. Given the appearance, the on-site team considered stage III non-small cell lung cancer and initiated induction chemoradiotherapy (cisplatin plus vinorelbine with 40 Gy). Post-treatment CT showed tumor shrinkage to 3.8 × 2.0 cm. The patient then underwent surgery via trap-door thoracotomy, including thymectomy, wedge resection of the left lung, and partial resection of the left innominate vein, achieving macroscopically complete resection.  

Gross examination revealed a firm mass adherent to the lung and vein but discontinuous from lung parenchyma. Histologic sections showed glandular formations of atypical cells amid lymphoid tissue, with no residual thymic tissue. Immunohistochemical staining of both the biopsy and resected specimens yielded:  
- CK7: positive  
- Synaptophysin: positive  
- Chromogranin A: positive  
- Thyroid transcription factor-1: negative  
- Napsin A: negative  
- CD5: negative  
- CK20, CK14, p63, Pax8, NCAM: all negative

A 50-year-old Asian woman presented with sudden anterior chest pain. Her medical history was notable for a total abdominal hysterectomy performed at age 37 for uterine leiomyoma. She denied smoking and drank alcohol only socially. Physical examination was unremarkable. Hematology, serum biochemistry, and arterial blood gas analyses were within normal limits. Chest computed tomography revealed two lesions: a 1.3-cm ground-glass opacity in the left S10 segment and a 5-mm solitary nodule in the left S4 segment. Primary lung carcinoma was initially suspected, but the patient declined bronchoscopic evaluation or surgical biopsy. On follow-up CT several weeks later, the ground-glass opacity had increased slightly in size, whereas the small nodule remained unchanged.

A 14-year-old boy with no prior medical or family history of neoplasia had 4 months of intermittent back pain that improved spontaneously. One month before admission, he noted progressive lower‐limb weakness; an initial workup with spinal radiographs and blood tests was unremarkable. Over the next weeks, he developed difficulty standing and eventually urinary retention and constipation.  

On admission, manual muscle testing of the lower limbs was 3/5 in the iliopsoas and quadriceps and 4/5 in other muscle groups; upper limbs were normal. He had numbness below the nipple line and loss of pain sensation; there was no anal sphincter contraction and he required catheterization.  

Spinal radiographs were normal. MRI of the thoracic spine showed a posterior epidural mass extending from T3 to T7 with low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, homogeneous high signal on T2-weighted images, and partial enhancement after gadolinium; the lesion compressed the spinal cord and extended into bilateral T4 foramina. There were no vertebral signal changes. CT revealed no calcifications or bone erosion.  

Given the rarity of thoracic epidural lesions in adolescents, a preoperative differential included neoplastic (especially malignant) and cystic diseases based on the clinical course and imaging findings.

A 45-year-old African American woman presented to the emergency department with new-onset dizziness, difficulty walking, and hypotension. Her medical history included hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and a recent urinary tract infection. She smoked tobacco and had no history of asbestos exposure, viral illness, or illicit drug use. On exam, vital signs were notable only for low blood pressure, and physical findings were otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits, and she was discharged home.

The next day, she returned to the ED with worsening symptoms. Shortly thereafter, she developed multiorgan failure and cardiac arrest with pulseless electrical activity. Resuscitation was unsuccessful, and she was pronounced dead. At autopsy, approximately 1 L of blood was found in the pericardial cavity. The pericardial sac was focally adherent to the heart, and the epicardial surface appeared markedly granular and thickened. Over the anterior left ventricle, a focal disruption of the pericardium without overt tearing was noted, with ongoing oozing of blood. No gross malignancy was seen in the pleura, lungs, lymphoreticular system, abdomen, or pelvis.

A 27-year-old man presented with an 8-month history of intermittent posterior occipital distension and a sensation of heaviness. Over time, his headache worsened. He had no other neurologic symptoms, and physical and neurologic examinations were unremarkable.  
Noncontrast brain CT suggested a mass in the fourth ventricle. Subsequent MRI showed a 26×19×33 mm solid–cystic lesion centered in the fourth ventricle, extending downward and compressing the brainstem, with resultant supratentorial ventricular enlargement. On T1-weighted imaging, the lesion was mixed iso- to hypointense; on T2-weighted imaging, it was hyperintense. Diffusion-weighted imaging demonstrated no obvious diffusion restriction. After gadolinium administration, the lesion showed heterogeneous, obvious enhancement.  
Based on imaging, a diagnosis of ventricular meningioma was made.

A 39-year-old man with a history of treated tuberculosis presented with two weeks of fever, generalized weakness, vague abdominal pain, vomiting, headache, body aches, and moderate nasal bleeding. On examination, he had a 2×1 cm submandibular lymph node and hepatomegaly (7 cm below the costal margin), without gastrointestinal symptoms or skin lesions. Laboratory studies showed urea 18.8 mmol/L, creatinine 141 µmol/L, lipase 182 U/L, myoglobin 108 ng/mL, ferritin >40 000 µg/L, vitamin B12 <111 pmol/L, normal fibrinogen, and triglycerides. Viral serologies were negative. Complete blood count revealed pancytopenia: hemoglobin 6.4 g/dL, WBC 1.7×10^3/µL, ANC 0.9×10^3/µL, platelets 2×10^3/µL. Head CT showed bilateral subdural hemorrhages without midline shift. Whole-body CT demonstrated bilateral pleural effusion, extensive pulmonary consolidation, thrombosis of the celiac artery with splenic infarction, mild hepatomegaly, and massive splenomegaly with infarction. 

Initial peripheral smear showed very few atypical cells; a repeat smear revealed marked leukopenia and 13% abnormal blastoid cells of medium size with fine nuclear chromatin, unevenly distributed coarse basophilic granules, and occasional bilobed nuclei. Bone marrow aspirate was hypercellular with 26% immature metachromatic blasts—cells with eccentric nuclei, abundant cytoplasm, and coarse giant granules—as well as some agranular high N/C blasts and spindle-shaped cells. There was trilineage dysplasia with megaloblastic changes in granulocytes and erythroid precursors, dysplastic megakaryocytes, and frequent mitoses. Both histiocytes and the atypical cells demonstrated erythrophagocytosis.

A 64-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of pain localized to the posterior aspect of his right lower limb. Over the past 6 months, he noted progressive numbness in the same dermatome without identifiable precipitating factors or alleviating measures. On admission, neurologic examination was unremarkable, and physical examination of the abdomen revealed no palpable mass.

Noncontrast CT of the spine demonstrated a 44 mm × 55 mm inhomogeneous soft-tissue mass arising from the right L5–S1 neural foramen, with a colliquative anterior portion. The mass extended along the lumbar spine to the ipsilateral sacroiliac joint and eroded the right posterolateral aspect of the L5 vertebral body. It also expanded into the retroperitoneal space posterior to the iliac vein and displaced the ipsilateral psoas muscle.

MRI showed a neoplastic lesion with homogeneous low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, heterogeneous signal intensity on T2-weighted images, and strong enhancement after gadolinium administration. The lesion affected the right side of the L5–S1 intervertebral foramen, eroded the L5 vertebral body without compromising spinal stability, and displaced the right psoas muscle.

Electroneurography and electromyography of the lower extremities revealed neurogenic damage with denervation signs in the right L5 nerve.

A 64-year-old Caucasian man with lower urinary tract symptoms and a nonfunctioning right kidney from chronic ureteropelvic junction obstruction was undergoing routine urologic follow-up. In July 2016, an abdominal CT scan showed an oval, posteromedial perirenal mass with fat attenuation on the left, measuring approximately 3 × 2 cm, without lymphadenopathy. He underwent transurethral resection of the prostate for benign prostatic hyperplasia in 2017 and remained asymptomatic. At outpatient follow-up in 2019, a repeat CT scan demonstrated that the left perirenal mass had enlarged to 7.1 × 5.0 × 7.0 cm, still without suspicious lymph nodes. The decision was made to perform a laparoscopic transperitoneal resection of the retroperitoneal mass. In the immediate postoperative period, he was observed in the ICU for 24 hours and then transferred to the ward, where he remained stable and was discharged in satisfactory condition. The surgical specimen was sent for histopathologic examination.

A 42-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of progressive pain and swelling of the left thumb. He denied fevers, weight loss, or other constitutional symptoms. On examination, there was a firm, globular swelling measuring approximately 6×4×5 cm over the proximal phalanx and interphalangeal joint of the thumb. The overlying skin was tense but freely mobile over the mass. The thumb was tender throughout, with severely limited motion at both the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints. 

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, white blood cell count 6,800/mm3, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 27 mm/h, and C-reactive protein 9 mg/L; all other routine blood tests were within normal limits. 

Plain radiographs of the left hand demonstrated an expansile, lytic lesion of the entire proximal phalanx of the thumb with a “soap-bubble” appearance, cortical thinning, soft-tissue extension, and destruction of the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints.

A 43-year-old woman, gravida 4, para 2, was referred for evaluation of a breast lesion detected on contrast-enhanced MRI performed because of a family history of breast cancer in her mother at age 50. She had no personal history of breast disease, trauma, or hormone use. Physical examination revealed no palpable masses, skin changes, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Diagnostic full-field digital mammography and bilateral breast ultrasound were unremarkable. On 1.5-T contrast-enhanced MRI, a 6-mm lesion with irregular margins was identified in the right lower inner quadrant. After gadolinium administration, the lesion demonstrated a type 3 enhancement curve, with rapid initial rise followed by washout in the delayed phase, raising suspicion for malignancy. A second-look targeted ultrasound and repeat mammography failed to visualize the lesion. Given the discordance and persistent concern, the patient consented to MRI-guided wire localization and wide local excision of the lesion.

A 46-year-old man was referred to our clinic for evaluation of right-sided hearing loss and chronic tympanic effusion. His medical history was notable for central diabetes insipidus of unknown etiology diagnosed 7 years earlier. An 18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated multiple FDG-avid lytic lesions involving the skull base, right temporal bone, mandible, and maxilla, with no lesions seen outside the head and neck. MRI of the skull base and infratemporal region showed an infiltrative mass in the right medial infratemporal fossa, erosive defects of the skull base, and erosion of the alveolar ridges. On intraoral examination, there was exposed alveolar bone and ulcerative granulation tissue in the right posterior mandible and left maxilla; prior tooth extractions had shown prolonged or incomplete healing. Cone beam CT confirmed extensive bone loss of the right mandible extending to the inferior alveolar canal and complete resorption of the left maxillary alveolar ridge.  
What is your differential diagnosis?

A 45-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with severe left lateral abdominal pain and fever. She had no significant past medical or drug history. On arrival, her blood pressure was 148/83 mmHg, heart rate 120 beats per minute, and temperature 38.2°C. Physical examination revealed tenderness on compression in the left lateral abdomen. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 10,340/μL, hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, platelet count 222 ×10^3/μL, albumin 4.6 g/dL, and C-reactive protein 2.34 mg/dL.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 60-mm intraperitoneal mass between the stomach and spleen with no arterial-phase enhancement, and there was fluid around the spleen and on the liver surface without active extravasation. Plain CT suggested that the greater omentum lay ventral to the mass and that the perisplenic fluid had a density consistent with blood. The patient had no signs of peritoneal irritation and her symptoms improved with conservative measures.

On hospital day 2, abdominal ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic heterogeneous lesion between the stomach and spleen, and contrast-enhanced ultrasound revealed no lesion enhancement or extravasation. Paracentesis yielded bloody ascites with negative cytology. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI showed a low-intensity mass with a high-intensity rim on T1-weighted images, a heterogeneous high-intensity mass on T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted images, and an area of decreased gadolinium enhancement on the posterior surface of the tumor suggestive of a ruptured capsule.

A 20-month-old Korean boy was referred for evaluation of a painless, soft, slowly growing mandibular mass that had been present for 6 months. He was born at term via cesarean section after an uneventful pregnancy. He required brief neonatal intensive care for respiratory difficulty but had no other abnormalities at birth and no family history of consanguinity. 

By 3 months of age, he had hip dislocation, stiffness, and multiple joint contractures treated with orthosis and rehabilitation. Gingival hypertrophy developed at 10 months, causing feeding difficulties. A single perianal skin lesion had been noted earlier and treated conservatively.

On examination at 20 months, there was a 3-cm, soft mandibular mass extending from the lower lip to the chin. Pinkish maculopapular nodules were present in the submandibular region, anterior neck, and at both nasolabial folds. Intraoral exam showed severe gingival hypertrophy with labial nodules. There were flexion contractures of the fourth and fifth fingers, both knees, and pelvic joints.

Skull radiographs demonstrated multiple osteolytic lesions. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the neck revealed an enhancing submental nodular lesion. An excisional biopsy of the submandibular mass and a gingival lesion was planned under general anesthesia.

A 70-year-old woman with a history of asbestos exposure and prior epithelioid mesothelioma presented with progressive exertional dyspnoea. Initial CT had shown a right hydropneumothorax requiring chest-tube drainage, and thoracoscopic biopsy confirmed epithelioid mesothelioma. Six weeks later, surveillance CT revealed mild enlargement of pleural nodules and new ground-glass opacities in the right middle and lower lobes. She reported a cough but had no fever, other infective symptoms, or peripheral leukocytosis. A course of antibiotics yielded no improvement. Four months after biopsy, repeat CT demonstrated significant progression of the right-sided pulmonary infiltrates and pleural disease, as well as intrathoracic lymphadenopathy. PET scan showed these infiltrates were FDG-avid. Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 6.4 × 10^9/L and a CRP of 11 IU/L. Atypical infection, lymphangitis carcinomatosis, and tumour infiltration were considered.

A 73-year-old man, who underwent right nephrectomy 7 years earlier for stage I clear cell renal cell carcinoma, was asymptomatic when a follow-up CT scan at 6 years after surgery detected a 6.4-mm polypoid lesion in the body of the gallbladder. One year later, repeat CT showed that the lesion had more than doubled in size. Laboratory tests, including serum CA19-9, were within normal limits. Ultrasonography revealed a 13.9 × 10 mm smooth-surfaced lesion in the gallbladder body. Color Doppler US demonstrated hypervascularity within the lesion. Contrast-enhanced CT in the arterial phase showed a polypoid mass with very high and homogeneous contrast enhancement. Based on these clinical backgrounds and imaging findings, the possibility of gallbladder malignancy, including metastatic cancer from RCC, was considered, and laparoscopic cholecystectomy was performed.

A 38-year-old previously healthy Hispanic man was referred for evaluation of progressive lower extremity weakness and sensory changes. Four months earlier, he noted paresthesia in his toes that progressed over three weeks to symmetrical ascending lower extremity weakness and unsteady gait. He also reported impotence, polyuria, polydipsia, hyperpigmentation, and hypertrichosis. 

Initial evaluation revealed albuminocytologic dissociation on cerebrospinal fluid analysis, and he was treated with a five‐day course of intravenous immunoglobulin for presumed Guillain‐Barré syndrome with minimal improvement. He was discharged to rehabilitation but relapsed four weeks later with new paresthesia in his hands. Nerve‐conduction studies showed a demyelinating pattern, and repeat lumbar puncture demonstrated oligoclonal bands. Antibodies against Hu and myelin basic protein were negative. He was treated for presumed chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy with plasmapheresis, intravenous immunoglobulin, and a short course of intravenous steroids, again with only partial improvement.

On referral, he had profound proximal lower extremity weakness (left greater than right), dysesthesias, paresthesias, and hyporeflexia in the lower limbs; sphincter tone was preserved, and there were no cranial nerve deficits or fasciculations. He complained of persistent abdominal and left inguinal pain with exquisite point tenderness over the left hip. Repeat serum protein electrophoresis revealed a monoclonal spike, and he was admitted for further evaluation.

A 9-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a right lower-thigh mass. Over the past 6 months, he had noticed a slow-growing, painless swelling on the anteromedial aspect of his right thigh. He had no history of trauma, pain, functional limitation, prior interventions, or significant family or medication history.

On examination, there was an approximately 10 cm × 6 cm oval, elastic, immobile, non-tender mass on the anteromedial lower thigh; the overlying skin was normal and sensation was intact. Vital signs were within normal limits.

Plain radiographs of the right lower thigh showed a poorly defined area of soft-tissue prominence along the anteromedial cortex of the distal femur without mineralization. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the right thigh revealed a 10 cm × 6 cm × 8 cm well-defined, lobulated lesion abutting the distal femoral cortex on the anteromedial side. The mass was heterointense but predominantly had the signal characteristics of fat on all pulse sequences, and it did not enhance after contrast administration. The lesion was sharply demarcated from the surrounding musculature.

A 75-year-old Caucasian woman presented with several months of progressive dysphonia and headache. She had undergone an unspecified vocal-cord surgery months earlier. She denied smoking, alcohol use, environmental exposures, dysphagia, or dyspnea.

On examination, the oral cavity was unremarkable and there were no palpable neck masses. Flexible laryngoscopy revealed a 2.0-cm left-sided cystic swelling of the supraglottic space with intact overlying mucosa, impinging on the left vocal cord and narrowing the airway.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck demonstrated a 1.9 × 1.7 cm bilobed cystic lesion arising from the left Morgagni ventricle, extending into supraglottic parapharyngeal fat and reducing the glottic airway.

A 53-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of a sensation of a foreign body in the back of her throat, which had worsened over the past 2 weeks. She denied hoarseness, dysphagia, odynophagia, or systemic symptoms. Examination revealed no thyroid enlargement or palpable cervical lymphadenopathy; systemic examination was unremarkable. Indirect laryngoscopy showed a soft tissue lesion in the posterior pharynx with medialization of the right vocal cord. Routine blood tests and thyroid function were normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a right supraglottic enhancing mass within the pyriform fossa measuring 2.0 × 1.8 × 2.2 cm and two small thyroid nodules (0.2 × 1.0 cm on the right and 1.3 × 1.3 cm on the left). Neck ultrasonography reported a right ACR-TIRADS 1 nodule (0.5 × 0.8 × 1.0 cm), a left ACR-TIRADS 2 nodule (0.4 × 0.5 × 0.6 cm), and normal-appearing subcentimeter cervical lymph nodes. An initial biopsy of the posterior pharyngeal mass showed benign mucosal tissue.

A 35-year-old Afro-Trinidadian man presented with a 2-month history of right-sided, mildly tender neck swellings and progressive bilateral nasal obstruction. He had received a 2-week course of broad-spectrum antibiotics without improvement. He denied comorbidities, recent travel, or animal exposures, and reported a 15–pack-year smoking history.

On examination, there was right-sided level 2–4 lymphadenopathy, the largest node measuring 2 cm, mildly tender to palpation. Oral, ear, and cranial-nerve examinations were unremarkable. Flexible nasopharyngoscopy revealed an enlarged, polypoidal mass arising from the nasopharyngeal wall.

Laboratory studies were notable for negative serologic tests for HIV, hepatitis B, monospot, Mantoux, and HTLV. Serum electrolytes, renal function, and glucose were within normal limits. The white-cell count was 7.0 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL, and lactate dehydrogenase was elevated at 465 U/L. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck confirmed right-sided cervical lymphadenopathy and a nasopharyngeal mass. Fine-needle aspiration of a cervical lymph node was inconclusive. Excisional biopsy of a lymph node and biopsy of the nasopharyngeal mass demonstrated reactive hyperplasia on hematoxylin and eosin staining.

An eight-month-old girl was referred for cardiac evaluation after an electrocardiographic abnormality was noted during workup for seizures. She had no cardiac symptoms and was on Vigabatrin, Valproic Acid, and Clobazan for epilepsy. Family, prenatal, and neonatal histories were unremarkable. On examination, hypochromic macules were noted on her back and left leg. Respiratory and cardiovascular exams were normal. Laboratory tests—including hemoglobin, creatinine, electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, ammonia, glucose, TSH, free T4, CK-MB, and troponin—were all within age-appropriate reference ranges. Chest radiography was normal.
