Her first ECG showed sinus rhythm at 125 b.p.m., PR interval 90 ms, QRS duration 70 ms, axis +50°, QTc 375 ms, and a pronounced dome-shaped ST-segment elevation in leads V2 and V3. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a single hyper-echogenic, regular nodule measuring 0.4 cm² in the mid part and right face of the interventricular septum. Cardiac chambers and Doppler flows were normal without inflow or outflow tract obstruction. Twenty-four-hour Holter monitoring showed sinus rhythm with a mean heart rate of 111 b.p.m., normal PR interval and QRS duration, and no arrhythmias.

A 34-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a suspected pancreatic mass detected on CT performed during hospitalization for mild acute pancreatitis. He had no palpable abdominal mass, was a social drinker, and had no family history of cancer. Laboratory studies revealed normal serum amylase, lipase, carcinoembryonic antigen, and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels. Multiphase dynamic CT demonstrated a mildly enhancing nodule within the main pancreatic duct (MPD) in the head of the pancreas. MR cholangiopancreatography showed poor delineation of the MPD head with upstream ductal dilatation. T2-weighted MRI revealed a low-signal, indistinct lesion occupying the dilated duct, and diffusion-weighted imaging showed high signal intensity in the same area. Endoscopic ultrasonography identified a 12 mm isoechoic mass in the MPD head; contrast-enhanced harmonic EUS showed early and persistent enhancement, and Doppler imaging revealed abundant blood flow. No mucin was observed at the major duodenal papilla. Endoscopic retrograde pancreatography demonstrated a smooth filling defect in the MPD head, and intraductal ultrasound depicted a friable isoechoic mass predominantly within the duct with partial parenchymal infiltration. Pancreatic juice cytology revealed adenocarcinoma with a superimposed “islet-like” conglomerate of small cells atypical for ductal carcinoma. Intraductal tubulopapillary neoplasm was the primary preoperative diagnosis.

A 36-year-old Egyptian man presented with a 14-month history of a painless swelling of the left thigh that had gradually increased in size over 10 months and then remained static. He had no relevant medical history, did not smoke, and had an unremarkable systemic review. On examination he was well-nourished and vitally stable. There was a firm, non-tender, 3 cm diameter mass in the mid-lateral aspect of the left thigh with normal overlying skin and no regional lymphadenopathy. A prior soft-tissue ultrasound scan showed a well-defined subcutaneous mass abutting the tensor fascia lata, measuring 2.4 × 1.9 cm, with minimal vascularity and was “suggestive of epidermal inclusion cyst.” The patient was taken for surgical excision under local anesthesia. On dissection, the lesion was a hard, calcified mass measuring approximately 4 × 3 × 1.5 cm, adherent to the surrounding fascia. It was excised en bloc and sent for histopathological assessment.

A 58-year-old right-handed male amateur cyclist presented with a 1-month history of tingling, numbness and burning pain extending from his right hand up to the supraclavicular region. He rated his pain as 6/10 at the clavicle and shoulder and 3/10 at the arm and fourth/fifth digits. The symptoms began in the shoulder and clavicular fossa (8/10) while training on a bicycle roller during pandemic lockdown and then radiated distally. He reported brief episodes of sharp pain at the clavicular fossa and anterior deltoid followed by transient numbness and weakness of the arm and hand after prolonged roller sessions, which resolved with self-stretching. He denied systemic symptoms, weight loss, malignancy history or constitutional complaints.

On musculoskeletal examination, criteria for specific and non-specific shoulder pain and for cervical radiculopathy were not fully met: there were no antalgic postures, no dermatomal sensory loss, and nerve-tension and compression tests were negative. Given the pattern of symptoms, the physical therapist evaluated for thoracic outlet syndrome. QuickDASH score was 83/95 and CBSQ was 100/120, indicating mild random sensory disturbance and motor weakness in the lower brachial plexus. Tenderness was noted at the anterior scalene, upper trapezius, anterior deltoid and pectoralis minor. The Elevated Arm Stress Test was positive, and grip strength of the fourth and fifth digits was mildly reduced on the right. Halstead, Wright’s, and Cyriax Release maneuvers were performed to exclude vascular TOS and were only slightly positive. The therapist and the patient’s general practitioner agreed on a diagnosis of neurogenic TOS and initiated a conservative program of manual therapy and strengthening exercises, and obtained MRI of the cervical spine and brachial plexus.

Cervical MRI showed straightening of the cervical lordosis, widespread spondyloarthrosis, wide bulging disks at C5–C6 and C6–C7, and signal hyperintensity of the right brachial plexus trunks. Electromyography of the brachial plexus was normal. The patient then underwent three soft-tissue mobilization sessions and six exercise sessions over three weeks to address neurogenic TOS.

A 33-year-old woman with an otherwise unremarkable medical history except for a complicated twin pregnancy conceived by in vitro fertilization four years earlier presented with chest pain and dyspnea. A computed tomographic angiogram of the chest was negative for pulmonary embolism but showed incidental pulmonary nodules, sclerosis of the T7 vertebral body, and multiple enhancing lesions in the liver and spleen. Her respiratory symptoms resolved, and she underwent outpatient evaluation. A triphasic CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated scattered sclerotic foci throughout the spine, a 9 mm nodule in the left lower lobe of the lung, multiple hypodense hepatic lesions (largest, 5.5 × 3.3 cm), and an enlarged spleen containing hypodense lesions (11.4 × 6.4 cm). No lymphadenopathy was identified. MRI of the abdomen confirmed multiple large hepatic lesions (largest, 9 cm) and splenic lesions (largest, 13 cm) that did not exhibit the typical MR characteristics of hemangiomas. Hemogram and chemistry profiles were within normal limits, and levels of CEA, CA 125, CA 19-9, and α-fetoprotein were all normal. On re-evaluation, she denied constitutional symptoms, her dyspnea had resolved, and physical examination was notable only for a palpable spleen without hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy, or spinal tenderness.

A 31-year-old man presented with dysuria, occasional macroscopic hematuria, and urinary retention. He had no relevant medical history and was a nonsmoker. Pelvic ultrasonography revealed an ill-defined prostatic mass measuring approximately 8 × 5 cm, protruding into the bladder. Six days later, cystoscopy with transurethral resection was performed. Histologic examination disclosed a malignant tumor composed of haphazardly arranged spindle and epithelioid cells infiltrating the bladder wall, with alternating hypercellular and hypocellular areas set in loose myxoid stroma, foci of necrosis, marked cellular pleomorphism, and variable mitotic activity. At the periphery, the tumor infiltrated between residual prostatic glands. Immunohistochemical studies showed tumor-cell positivity for CD34 and progesterone receptors and absence of smooth muscle actin, CK8/18, CD117, S100, EMA, desmin, myogenin, and CK7.

A 47-year-old Caucasian man presented with a painless gingival mass first noted 1 year earlier. He had undergone allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation 15 years before for acute lymphoblastic leukemia, and 2 years post-transplant had developed chronic graft-versus-host disease involving the mouth, liver, and lungs, treated intermittently with dexamethasone mouthrinse.

On intraoral examination, there was a well-circumscribed, sessile, yellowish, verrucous nodule on the right canine gingiva, multiple similar yellowish verrucous nodules on the hard palate, and additional verrucous nodules on the left buccal mucosa. Examination of the tongue revealed white reticular striae with areas of erythema and ulceration consistent with known oral cGVHD, and an adjacent erythematous patch suspicious for erythroplakia.

An incisional biopsy – 6 mm punch specimens from the hard palate nodule and the erythematous tongue patch – was performed and sent for routine histopathological processing.

A 54-year-old African American man with a 2-year history of hypertension, heart failure, and diabetes mellitus presented with progressive dyspnea and edema. He had episodes of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia. An echocardiogram showed dilated left-sided chambers with moderate global hypokinesis and an ejection fraction of 35–40%. He was treated, stabilized, and transferred for consideration of an implantable defibrillator. Further history revealed a 20-lb weight loss, decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, and breast development over 1–2 years. 

On examination, vital signs were stable (blood pressure 122/66 mm Hg, pulse 100 beats/min, regular) and BMI was 23. There were no rales, S3 gallop, or peripheral edema. He had gynecomastia, a hyperdynamic precordium, and a firm mass in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen. Testes were soft, 20 mL bilaterally. 

Chest radiograph showed an elevated left hemidiaphragm. CT of the abdomen revealed a 12 × 11 × 17 cm mass in the left upper quadrant displacing the left kidney, likely arising from the left adrenal gland. 

Laboratory studies showed a serum estradiol level of 3853 pg/mL (normal < 52 pg/mL in males), confirmed on repeat assay. Low-dose dexamethasone testing failed to suppress cortisol, 24-hour urine free cortisol was mildly elevated, DHEA-S and androstenedione were elevated, and plasma ACTH was suppressed. 

A 12-lead ECG demonstrated normal sinus rhythm with a prolonged corrected QT interval of 477 msec and nonspecific anterior T-wave abnormalities. Chest CT, abdominal MRI, and bone scan showed no evidence of metastatic disease.

A 56-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a 20-day history of a rapidly growing, painful expansion of the left mandible. She reported traumatic luxation of her lower left central and lateral incisors in a fall, followed by extractions; the site failed to heal and began enlarging, interfering with eating. Her medical history included hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and bowel disease. 

On intraoral examination, there was a diffuse 3×3-cm swelling of the left anterior mandible, extending from the right central incisor to the left canine. The overlying mucosa was erythematous, ulcerated, and necrotic, and the lesion was soft to firm on palpation. No cervical lymphadenopathy was present.

A panoramic radiograph showed a unilocular radiolucency with ill-defined borders from the right lateral incisor to the left second premolar. Cone-beam CT revealed a large destructive lesion with irregular borders, extensive perforation of the buccal cortical plate, thinning and erosion of the lingual cortical plate, and root resorption of teeth #22, #21, and #20. 

An incisional biopsy was performed. Microscopic sections showed a malignant epithelial neoplasm composed of nests, tubules, and cystic and papillary structures with fibrovascular cores lined by cuboidal and columnar cells. The nuclei had a ground-glass appearance. Eosinophilic colloid-like material, hemorrhage, and inflammatory cell infiltration were also observed, and the tumor was covered by ulcerated epithelium.

A 32-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of a painless swelling in the upper left posterior region of the mouth. She noted a small buccal swelling that gradually extended palatally and enlarged; it bled if traumatized during chewing. She reported a 10-year history of twice-daily mishri use. Her medical history was unremarkable. Extraoral examination was normal, without lymphadenopathy or facial asymmetry. 

Intraorally, there was an exophytic, sessile, bluish-red, firm nodular growth on the maxillary buccal interdental gingiva between the second premolar and first molar, measuring 1 × 1 cm, extending palatally as a pedunculated, irregular, multilobulated mass measuring 2.5 × 2.5 cm. Oral hygiene was poor, and an over-retained root fragment of a deciduous second molar was noted adjacent to the lesion.

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, were within normal limits. A periapical radiograph showed superficial erosion of the alveolar crest between the second premolar and first molar “as is usually observed in cases of PGCG.” An occlusal radiograph revealed no significant bone loss. An orthopantomogram demonstrated interdental bone loss in the same region. Cone-beam CT confirmed a soft-tissue–density mass originating from the left maxilla, measuring approximately 23.3 × 16.6 mm.

After initial periodontal therapy, incisional biopsies of both buccal and palatal components were obtained for histopathologic evaluation.

A 92-year-old Caucasian woman was evaluated for a slowly enlarging pedunculated soft-tissue mass on the plantar surface of her right forefoot. Four years earlier, after swimming in the Atlantic Ocean on Fuerteventura Island, she had noticed a small flap of tissue on her foot sole without bleeding. The lesion had increased gradually in size without pain or functional disturbance until, within the past week, she experienced local discomfort when walking. She had no diagnosed comorbidities and reported no vascular or neurological symptoms in the foot. On examination, the mass measured approximately 8.5 cm in length, 5 cm in width, and 2–3 cm in thickness, and the surface was ulcerated. Sensation and distal pulses in the foot were intact. A plain radiograph of the foot showed no bony erosion adjacent to the lesion.

A 29-year-old man presented with tingling and swelling of the lateral aspect of his left lower leg due to a mass that had been slowly enlarging over 2 years. He had no medical history or apparent history of trauma. On examination, there was a hard, spindle-shaped, 15-cm mass with poor mobility near the fibula; there was no tenderness, motor paralysis, or sensory disturbance. Laboratory tests were unremarkable. Plain radiographs of the left leg showed a slightly lobulated soft-tissue lesion with clear margins, smooth borders, and marked heterogeneous calcification with a calcified rim, without cortical destruction or periosteal reaction. MRI revealed a well-defined lesion within the peroneus longus muscle, isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images, mildly hyperintense on T2-weighted images with signal voids in calcified areas, and strong, uniform enhancement after gadolinium except in calcified regions. The tentative differential diagnosis based on the imaging studies included ectopic calcification, tumoral calcinosis, and soft tissue sarcoma with calcification. A core needle biopsy revealed spindle cells resembling normal smooth muscle cells densely proliferating in bundle-like arrangements with oval or cigar-shaped nuclei and no nuclear atypia, along with degenerative hyalinization and calcification. Immunohistochemically, the tumor was diffusely positive for smooth muscle markers (desmin, α-smooth muscle actin, HHF35, h-caldesmon) and negative for estrogen receptor.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a three-month history of nasal obstruction, yellow nasal discharge, and forehead pain refractory to treatment for allergic rhinitis. She had a history of B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia diagnosed six years earlier, treated with Hyper-CVAD and an allogeneic stem-cell transplant; she had been off immunosuppression for 20 months. Examination revealed a mass involving the nasal septum and lower nasal cavity extending into the nasopharynx. Laboratory tests showed a normal lactate dehydrogenase level. Histologic examination of a nasal-septal biopsy demonstrated a monomorphic infiltrate of immature cells positive for CD19, PAX-5, HLA-DR, CD34, TdT, and CD56, consistent with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head showed a soft-tissue mass centered on the posterior nasal septum extending into the nasopharynx without bony erosion. CT of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no lymphadenopathy or organ involvement. Bone marrow biopsy and cerebrospinal fluid analysis by cytospin and flow cytometry were normal.

A 27-year-old woman, gravida 3 with one prior infant death and one living child, presented at 32 weeks of gestation with one month of progressive abdominal distension and vague lower abdominal discomfort. She had no history of diabetes or anemia. On examination, her blood pressure was 130/80 mm Hg. The abdomen was markedly overdistended to the xiphisternum; fetal parts were not palpable, and fetal heart sounds could not be localized. 

Obstetrical ultrasound showed a single live fetus appropriate for 32 weeks, polyhydramnios with an amniotic fluid index of 28 cm (normal range, 8–20 cm), and no gross fetal anomalies. The placenta was located on the anterior upper uterine segment, grade II. A well-defined, echogenic mass measuring 11.5 cm by 12 cm, distinct from the rest of the placenta, was seen bulging into the amniotic cavity on the fetal side.

The patient subsequently went into spontaneous preterm labor and delivered a female infant weighing 1.6 kg with Apgar scores of 9 and 10 at 1 and 5 minutes. The placenta weighed 2 kg, and a 12 cm by 12 cm lobular mass was noted attached by a pedicle to the fetal surface.

A healthy 14-year-old girl presented with a right upper eyelid mass that had been stable in size for 6 months. She described one episode of pain, redness, and sticky discharge, which resolved after topical and oral antibiotics, but the swelling persisted. There was no relevant personal or family history. On examination, a 2 × 2 mm round, firm, red nodule was noted just below the lateral eyebrow. The lesion was adherent to the skin but not fixed to underlying tissue, had defined margins, and the overlying skin was otherwise normal with no visible punctum. The remainder of the ophthalmic examination was unremarkable. Based on the site, the lesion’s nodular nature, and the history of inflammation and discharge, a provisional diagnosis of a ruptured epidermal cyst was made, and the patient was scheduled for excisional biopsy under local anesthesia.

A woman in her 70s presented with two weeks of moderate pain on the dorsum of her right wrist and tenderness over the third and fourth carpometacarpal joints, without known trauma. Her history included hypertension, COPD, GERD, asthma, prior MRSA of the right knee, bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, and remote smoking cessation (22 years).  
Initial hand radiography showed no fracture but demonstrated bony demineralization and joint‐space narrowing of the interphalangeal and first carpometacarpal joints. Two weeks later, an orthopedic hand surgeon noted inflammation over the extensor digitorum communis and diagnosed extensor tenosynovitis; a wrist brace and corticosteroid injection provided only short‐term relief. Six weeks after presentation, the patient returned with recurrent pain and new edema.  
The surgeon obtained MRI, three‐phase bone scan (TPBS), white blood cell (WBC) scan, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), complete blood count (CBC), and C‐reactive protein (CRP). MRI was interpreted as a differential diagnosis of osteomyelitis, soft tissue cellulitis, and tenosynovitis. TPBS after technetium-99m methylene diphosphonate showed increased uptake in all three phases at the right wrist and the proximal and midshaft third metacarpal; the radiology report stated these findings were compatible with CRPS. Delayed WBC images demonstrated asymmetric uptake in the right hand at the metacarpal level, and the reading noted that these findings can be seen in CRPS. Laboratory studies revealed elevated CRP (2.01 mg/dL) and ESR (49 mm/hr) with a normal WBC count.  
Based on the TPBS and WBC scan readings, the patient was referred to a pain medicine specialist for evaluation of complex regional pain syndrome.

A 23-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of a palpable mass in her left breast. She had no personal or family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Breast ultrasonography showed a 4.0 × 1.6 cm hypoechoic mass with poorly demarcated margins in the left breast, and granulomatous mastitis was considered; the right breast was normal. An ultrasound-guided core-needle biopsy revealed stromal fibrosis of breast tissue. Subsequent breast MRI demonstrated two lesions in the lower-inner quadrant of the left breast (lesion 1, 2.0 × 4.3 × 4.0 cm; lesion 2, 2.4 × 3.7 × 2.6 cm) that were isointense on T1-weighted imaging, mildly hyperintense on T2-weighted imaging, and showed slightly restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging and ADC maps. On dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI, lesion 1 exhibited an initial increase in signal intensity followed by a plateau, while lesion 2 showed rapid enhancement with a washout pattern; both lesions had irregular shapes, poorly defined margins, and surrounding dominant draining veins on maximum intensity projection images. No axillary lymphadenopathy was present. The findings were categorized as ACR BI-RADS 4b.

A 58-year-old man was referred in January 2023 for bilateral corneal ulcers. He had a history of late‐stage Sézary syndrome diagnosed in January 2022 and was receiving extracorporeal photopheresis. He had no prior ocular disease or surgery. Initial treatment with ciprofloxacin drops and Prokera lenses had failed.

On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/150 in the left eye; intraocular pressures were normal. Slit-lamp examination revealed in the right eye a 1.5 × 1.0 mm epithelial defect in the inferior midperipheral cornea with 50% stromal thinning and in the left eye a 2.1 × 1.2 mm epithelial defect with 90% stromal thinning. No stromal infiltrates were present. Eyelids and adnexa were normal; palpebral fissures were normal, lid closure was excellent, and there was no ectropion or entropion.

The patient was diagnosed with peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK) and started on oral prednisone 80 mg daily, topical tobramycin, aggressive lubrication, and bilateral bandage contact lenses. A broad infectious and autoimmune laboratory evaluation—including anti-dsDNA, ANCA titers, CRP, anti-CCP antibodies, ESR, uric acid, rheumatoid factor, QuantiFERON TB, lysozyme, ACE, Lyme, ANA, syphilis, and hepatitis A, B, and C panels—was unremarkable.

Over several days, the epithelial defects healed; visual acuity remained 20/20 on the right and improved to 20/40 on the left. Prednisone was tapered to 10 mg daily by May 2023, at which time the patient remained stable.

A 69-year-old woman noted a painless, slowly enlarging mass in her right eye over 18 months. Her history included treated uterine cancer with no recurrence. Visual acuity was 20/25 OU, and intraocular pressures were normal. Slit-lamp examination revealed a dark-red, lobulated subconjunctival lesion (7 × 5 mm) on the temporal side of the right eye. The lesion was noncompressible, nonpulsatile, not reducible, and did not enlarge with Valsalva. The overlying conjunctiva was freely mobile, whereas the mass itself moved minimally along the horizontal meridian. There was no proptosis; ocular alignment and motility were normal. The rest of the anterior and posterior segments were unremarkable. Provisional diagnosis was a benign vascular tumor. Anterior-segment OCT showed multiple intralesional hyporeflective spaces filled with moderate to high reflectivity causing back-shadowing, consistent with blood‐filled vascular lumens.

A 69‐year‐old woman presented with episodes of hemoptysis. Over the previous five months, she noted increasing drooling of saliva and progressive difficulty swallowing. On examination, there was a large, smooth‐surfaced, nodular mass in the midline of the tongue base, which was richly vascularized. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the neck showed a 30 mm solid lesion in the right tongue base occupying most of the oropharynx without enlarged regional lymph nodes. Thyroid scintigraphy and ultrasound demonstrated a normally located thyroid gland and no thyroid tissue at the tongue base. Selective external carotid arteriography revealed a rich vascular supply to the mass from bilateral lingual artery branches and the left maxillary artery. Prophylactic embolization of the feeding vessels was performed to minimize bleeding risk prior to biopsy.

A 47-year-old premenopausal woman presented with acute lower abdominal pain. Four months earlier, she had reported lower abdominal discomfort and was being followed for a presumed uterine leiomyoma. Two months later, she developed atypical genital bleeding and was treated with progestin. One month before this admission, pelvic MRI revealed a 15 cm subserosal mass in the uterine body with heterogeneous mild hyperintensity and multiple cystic changes on T2-weighted imaging. Within the mass, a small area of hyperintensity on fat-suppressed T1-weighted images suggested intratumoural hemorrhage. On diffusion-weighted imaging the solid portions were hyperintense with corresponding low signal on the ADC map; the mean ADC value in this region was 0.88 × 10−3 mm2/s.

On admission, laboratory tests showed lactate dehydrogenase 590 U/L, C-reactive protein 9.3 mg/dL, white blood cells 10.3 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, hematocrit 26.9%, and platelets 434 × 10^3/µL. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated that the uterine-origin tumour had enlarged to 20 cm, with disruption of the left uterine margin, hemorrhagic ascites, and a small omental lesion. No lymphadenopathy was seen.

A 50-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a progressively enlarging swelling in the left axilla. Initially small, the lesion grew to 7 cm × 5 cm. He reported intermittent fevers over the same period. His medical history was unremarkable. On examination, there was no regional lymphadenopathy and no other abnormal findings. Local inspection revealed a 7 cm × 5 cm firm, non-tender, pedunculated mass in the left axilla; the overlying skin was inflamed and ulcerated. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. With a clinical and radiological impression of soft tissue sarcoma, the patient underwent fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC). Cytological smears were highly cellular and showed cohesive clusters of malignant cells composed of two distinct cell populations: polyhedral cells with dense basophilic cytoplasm and pale/clear cells containing glycogen. The nuclei were pleomorphic, hyperchromatic, round to oval with coarse chromatin and prominent nucleoli, and were eccentrically located within a moderate amount of basophilic cytoplasm, giving a plasmacytoid appearance. Numerous bi- and multinucleated cells were present, along with occasional squamous differentiation. In places, acinar and tubular patterns were noted, with numerous mitotic figures.

A 60-year-old woman with stage IIIC papillary serous ovarian adenocarcinoma treated surgically in November 2006 and with adjuvant intraperitoneal and intravenous chemotherapy presented approximately one year later with new right breast symptoms. Her ovarian cancer had persisted around the vaginal cuff and her CA-125 had risen to 123 U/ml despite eight cycles of carboplatin and Abraxane, and she was enrolled in a trial of Avastin and Tarceva. Baseline imaging for the trial showed new right axillary lymphadenopathy—the largest node measuring 1.1 × 1.8 cm—and “suspicion of a new primary breast cancer was raised.” A breast MRI with gadolinium showed no suspicious lesions or masses, and she continued on trial therapy with dose reduction for rash. 

In October 2007, she noted right breast edema with increased erythema, thickness, and warmth. She was treated with a 10-day course of antibiotics, with no change in symptoms. A breast ultrasound revealed an ill-defined hypoechoic area in the right upper outer quadrant with multiple enlarged lymph nodes. Mammography showed scattered fibroglandular densities and an area of architectural distortion with punctate calcifications. Fine-needle aspiration of the breast demonstrated cells consistent with adenocarcinoma. A second bilateral breast MRI confirmed an 8 × 4 cm area of heterogeneous enhancement with areas suspicious for chest wall extension. A punch biopsy of the right breast was then performed; pathologic analysis showed multiple foci of high-grade adenocarcinoma with dermal lymphatic invasion and morphology similar to that of the previous ovarian cancer.

A 16-year-old boy presented with a 4-month history of a painless right scrotal mass that had gradually increased in size. He had no prior medical, surgical, or trauma history and no family history of cancer. On physical examination, there was a firm, renitent mass in the right testis; the left testis was normal. Scrotal ultrasonography showed a heterogeneous intratesticular mass measuring 93 × 81 mm. Serum α-fetoprotein, β-human chorionic gonadotropin, and lactate dehydrogenase concentrations were within normal limits. A thoraco-abdominopelvic CT scan demonstrated a 94 × 81 × 70 mm mass confined to the right testis, with no evidence of pulmonary, abdominal, or lymph-node lesions.

A 59-year-old woman presented with a 6-year history of neck pain. Approximately 10 months before evaluation she noted back pain radiating into both lower limbs and toward the little toes, with intermittent claudication and a fear of falling. On neurologic examination, triceps strength was reduced (left more than right), and hip flexor and quadriceps strength were decreased; all deep-tendon reflexes were brisk. MRI of the spine showed multiple lobulated, discrete intradural extramedullary masses from T4 to L3 that were hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and uniformly enhanced with contrast. Similar lesions were identified at C6–C7 and C1–C2, with smaller foci elsewhere; brain MRI was normal. Based on these findings, lymphoma was suspected, and an excisional biopsy of a cervical lesion was planned.

A 45-year-old woman with no significant past medical history and no family history of cancer presented with a 2-week history of a painful, palpable mass in her right axilla and intermittent fever. She noted recent contact with a stray cat and multiple scratches on her arms. On physical examination, there was tender right axillary lymphadenopathy; breast examination was otherwise unremarkable. 

Diagnostic workup included diagnostic mammography, which revealed fibro-glandular breast tissue (ACR-B) and an area of fine linear microcalcifications in the retro-areolar region of the right breast, with no distortion or suspicious findings elsewhere. Radiopaque oval images suggestive of enlarged lymph nodes were seen in the right axilla on the mediolateral-oblique view but not in the contralateral breast.

Magnified mammographic views confirmed finely linear microcalcifications spanning approximately 2 cm in the retro-areolar area of the right breast. Breast ultrasound showed no suspicious lesions. Ultrasound of the right axilla demonstrated at least three markedly hypoechoic oval lymph nodes (largest 2.9 cm) with thickened cortex and loss of the fatty hilum; color Doppler did not show increased vascularity.

To further evaluate, a contrast-enhanced MRI of the breasts and axillae was performed. The MRI showed no suspicious breast lesions after contrast administration but confirmed multiple enlarged axillary lymph nodes with marked contrast enhancement.

A 55-year-old woman with infrequent medical follow-up presented with confusion and generalized lethargy. She noted increased urinary frequency and believed she was dehydrated. She also reported a left breast lump first noticed six months earlier that had been progressively enlarging.

She had no history of fever, weight loss, night sweats, or bone pain except intermittent back discomfort. She denied headaches, focal neurologic deficits, gastrointestinal, or respiratory symptoms. She was a 30–pack-year smoker; family history was negative for malignancy.

On examination, vital signs were normal. There was a firm, nontender 15-cm mass in the left breast extending into the axilla without overlying skin changes or nipple discharge. No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly was present.

Laboratory studies showed:  
- Serum creatinine 2.1 mg/dL  
- Adjusted calcium 20.3 mg/dL  
- Uric acid 11.1 mg/dL  

Noncontrast CT of the head revealed multiple lucent calvarial defects consistent with lytic lesions. Mammography demonstrated a 19 × 14 × 17 cm hyperdense, lobular mass with smooth margins in the left breast and a 6 cm abnormal lymph node in the left axilla.

A 53-year-old man presented with a 12-year history of hoarseness. He denied dyspnea or dysphagia but reported symptoms of gastric acid reflux. He was a former smoker (quit 6 months earlier) and a politician with chronic voice overuse. Flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy demonstrated a 0.5 cm pedunculated, cystic-appearing mass on the medial free edge of the middle third of the right true vocal fold; vocal-fold mobility was normal. The rest of the ENT examination was unremarkable. Given the long-standing hoarseness, history of voice abuse, and appearance of a solitary polypoidal lesion, a preoperative diagnosis of a laryngeal polyp was made. No imaging was performed. The patient underwent microlaryngeal surgery with lesion excision using cold instruments. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient reported near-normal voice at the one-week follow-up.  
On histologic examination, the lesion was a polypoidal tumor lined by hyperplastic stratified squamous epithelium. Beneath the epithelium was an unencapsulated, paucicellular lesion composed of small, bland spindle to stellate cells with indistinct cytoplasmic margins and hyperchromatic nuclei, set in an abundant myxoid matrix. There was no significant atypia, mitotic activity, or necrosis. Immunohistochemical stains were negative for CD34, smooth muscle actin, and S100.

A 15-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of swelling and pain in the upper neck for two months. On examination, there was a tender, palpable mass in the left submandibular region at the base of the mouth. Routine blood tests were within normal limits. Sonography of the neck revealed an oval, thick-walled cystic lesion measuring 58 × 34 mm at the base of the mouth extending into the left submandibular space; the lumen contained dispersed solid nodules each under 15 mm in diameter, and color Doppler sonography showed no internal blood flow, revealing a “sack of marbles” sign. The thyroid gland had a heterogeneous echo pattern with fibrous septa and hypoechoic regions, and laboratory studies showed: TSH 0.017 μU/ml (0.27–4.2), free T4 2.81 ng/dl (0.93–1.97), and anti-TPO 651 IU/ml (0–40). Contrast-enhanced MRI of the neck demonstrated a smooth-margined, thick-walled mass on the left side of the mouth floor that was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, composed of multiple small nodules producing a “sack of marbles” appearance; the rims of the nodules had intermediate signal on T1, low signal on T2, showed no suppression on fat-saturated sequences, and there was no enhancement after contrast administration.

A 27-year-old previously healthy woman presented with sudden onset of right upper abdominal pain radiating to her back. She was afebrile, and vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed tenderness in the right upper quadrant without other abnormalities. 

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen showed a multilocular cystic mass with enhancing septa, measuring 82 × 66 mm in segment 8 of the liver; no other lesions were detected. Ultrasound-guided aspiration yielded bloody, mucinous fluid; bacterial cultures were sterile, and cytology revealed clusters of small round atypical cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasm ratio but was inconclusive. 

Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis (13.0 × 10^3/µL), normal transaminase levels, and negative hepatitis B surface antigen and antibody, hepatitis C antibody, HIV antibody, and Entamoeba histolytica antibody. Carcinoembryonic antigen and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels were within normal limits. 

Color Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated thickened, irregular septa and nodular walls with internal blood flow. Contrast-enhanced ultrasonography showed enhancement of the septa and nodular walls to the same degree as the surrounding liver parenchyma. Magnetic resonance imaging provided no additional information. 

We made a presumed diagnosis of mucinous cystadenoma of the liver based on the imaging studies.

A 79-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of nausea. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. On examination, her temperature was 36.6 °C, blood pressure 120/84 mmHg, heart rate 72 bpm, respiratory rate 15 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. A soft mass was palpable in the left upper quadrant. Laboratory studies showed slight anemia (hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL); carcinoembryonic antigen, cancer antigen 19-9, and cancer antigen 125 were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed a large multilocular mass with cystic and solid components occupying the left upper quadrant and compressing the stomach; only a small rim of normal splenic parenchyma remained, and the pancreatic tail was in close contact but showed no discrete mass. MRI showed the solid component to be heterogeneously hyperintense on T1-weighted images and hypointense on T2-weighted images, suggesting internal hemorrhage. PET–CT demonstrated intense FDG uptake in the solid portion of the tumor (SUV 35.9) without distant metastases. Although a definitive preoperative diagnosis could not be made, primary splenic angiosarcoma was suspected, and laparotomy was planned.

A 34-year-old woman with neurofibromatosis type 1 presented with a 4-day history of motor weakness of the right arm and sensory disturbances of the lower limbs. She had no fever, systemic symptoms, cancer history, or trauma. On examination, she had paraparesis, upper-extremity hypoesthesia, and generalized lower-limb hyperreflexia. Cervical spine MRI showed an extensive intraspinal intradural infiltrative expansile lesion involving nearly the entire cervical spinal cord and extending cranially to the lower medulla oblongata, including the area postrema. The lesion exhibited homogeneous peripheral and eccentric enhancement of both intramedullary and exophytic components. Brain MRI revealed only bilateral subcutaneous epicranial lesions in the occipital regions consistent with neurofibromas and a left parotid lesion suggestive of a plexiform neurofibroma. Oligoclonal bands in CSF and serum antibodies to aquaporin-4 were negative.

An 84-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of obstipation (absence of flatus and stool) and vomiting, without fever or other symptoms. He had no significant past medical or surgical history, no family history of neurofibromatosis, and took no medications. On examination, temperature was 37 °C, heart rate 75/min, respiratory rate 18/min, and blood pressure 129/72 mmHg. The abdomen was nondistended with diffuse tenderness; rectal examination revealed an empty vault. There were no café-au-lait spots, axillary freckling, peripheral neurofibromas, or iris hamartomas. Routine blood tests and tumor markers were normal. Upright abdominal radiography showed multiple air-fluid levels. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated dilation of the jejunum and ileum with a “target sign” in the ileum consistent with ileo-ileal intussusception around an ileal mass. At laparotomy, an ileo-ileal intussusception was found approximately 100 cm from the ileocecal valve, with a solitary bowel tumor; no lymphadenopathy, ascites, liver lesions, or metastases were observed. A segmental small-bowel resection with end-to-end hand-sewn anastomosis was performed, and the specimen was sent for histologic analysis.

An 85-year-old woman presented for a full-body skin examination. On the left thigh, there was an isolated, black-colored nodule measuring 1.0 cm in greatest dimension, with an asymmetric and irregular border. The lesion was asymptomatic, without any history of trauma or prior treatment. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included dermatofibroma, melanoma, or other melanocytic lesions. The lesion was completely excised and submitted for pathology.

A 39-year-old Caucasian man was referred for panoramic and CBCT imaging to plan oral rehabilitation. He was asymptomatic, with no intraoral or extraoral clinical findings and an unremarkable medical history. On panoramic radiograph, there was absence of 11 teeth (4 in the mandible), alveolar bone loss, thickened trabecular bone, cortical erosion of the mandible, and an elongated styloid process. Bilaterally, the mandibular canals and mental foramina were enlarged in an inferior–superior direction. Lateral teleradiography confirmed enlargement of the mandibular canal from the retromolar trigone through the ramus on both sides. CBCT multiplanar reconstructions demonstrated marked, bilateral enlargement of the mandibular canals and mental foramina. The cortices of the canal walls were intact but markedly thinned; on the right side, there was focal discontinuity of the medial cortical wall. The lesions appeared as unilocular fusiform radiolucencies that were separate from teeth and root apices. Initial diagnostic hypotheses included bilateral hemangioma, malignant lymphangioma, syndromes affecting Schwann cells (eg, neurofibromatosis), multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2b, arteriovenous malformation, vascular leiomyoma, and extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

A 27-year-old woman presented with a painless swelling in the left infra-auricular region noted for cosmetic concern. She had no fever or constitutional symptoms. On examination, there was a firm, nonmobile, 3 × 3 cm spherical swelling over the left infra-auricular region. Ultrasonography showed a well-defined, 3 × 2.5 cm hypoechoic cystic lesion in the superficial lobe of the left parotid, with necrotic areas suggestive of an abscess. A contrast CT scan demonstrated a 3.2 × 2.5 cm well-defined fluid-density lesion in the superficial lobe of the left parotid gland. For further evaluation, ultrasound‐guided fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) was performed, yielding inconclusive results and was presumptively reported as a lymphoepithelial cyst. Differential considerations at that time included sebaceous cyst, lipoma, pleomorphic adenoma, and adenocarcinoma.

A 58-year-old man, former heavy smoker (2 packs/day until 3 months earlier), was referred for progressive shortness of breath over 6 months. The dyspnea worsened with exertion and when supine and was partly relieved by rest. He also reported a productive cough with whitish sputum but denied hemoptysis, weight loss, chest pain, hoarseness, or systemic symptoms. He had no prior medical history and no known family history of cancer.

On arrival, he was in respiratory distress with an SpO2 of 85% on room air, improving to 96% on 3 L/min of oxygen. Temperature was 36.5°C, blood pressure 132/64 mm Hg, pulse 67 bpm. Examination showed decreased air entry on the right, normal vesicular breath sounds on the left, and no adventitious sounds. The remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Laboratory evaluation revealed a white blood cell count of 11 290/µL; electrolytes, liver and kidney function tests were normal. The serum free light chain ratio remained well below 100. Chest radiography was normal. Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated a well-defined, smoothly marginated, enhancing mass in the right main bronchus at the level of the carina, causing complete intraluminal obstruction and partial extension into the trachea.

Urgent bronchoscopy showed a large, rounded, hypervascular mass completely occluding the right main bronchus and bleeding easily on manipulation. After irrigation and topical measures, multiple biopsy fragments were obtained.

Given the presence of an endobronchial mass, a differential diagnosis of lipoma, leiomyoma, carcinoma, and secondary malignant metastasis was suspected.

A 61-year-old postmenopausal woman, gravida 0, was referred for evaluation of elevated serum tumor markers: CA125 389 U/mL (normal <35) and CA19-9 785 U/mL (normal <37). She was asymptomatic. Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 7.3 cm heterogeneous mass in the left posterolateral uterine wall composed of an enhanced solid area and a fluid-filled component, raising suspicion for a degenerated leiomyoma or leiomyosarcoma. Endometrial and cervical cytology were negative for malignancy. Positron-emission tomography showed significant FDG uptake in the lesion. The patient underwent total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. 

Gross examination showed an 8 × 6.5 cm polypoid yellow–white tumor entirely confined within an intramural cyst in the myometrium of the left posterolateral corpus. Microscopic examination demonstrated two components: (1) an intracystic component with tubular, papillary, acinar, and solid areas. The predominant tubular pattern comprised back-to-back small round tubules lined by cuboidal cells with densely eosinophilic PAS-positive luminal secretions; tumor cells were relatively bland with occasional mitoses. (2) An invasive myometrial component exhibiting a ductal pattern, moderate cytologic atypia, and frequent mitotic figures. 

Immunohistochemical studies showed diffuse positivity for CK7 and PAX8 and negativity for CK20, inhibin, PgR, and WT1. Focal luminal CD10, focal calretinin, and focal GATA3 staining were present. Tumor cells in the tubular and acinar areas were positive for vimentin and TTF-1; the solid areas lacked TTF-1. CA125 and CA19-9 were expressed in all patterns. Ki-67 labeling was low in the tubular/acinar patterns and high in the solid and ductal components. p53 expression was not significant.

A 21-year-old virgin woman presented with mild lower abdominal pain, hirsutism of the thighs, and oligomenorrhea. Her menarche was at age 13. One year before presentation she developed hirsutism and menstrual cycles more than 60 days apart and was treated empirically with oral contraceptives, with mild symptom improvement. Family history was notable only for her mother’s hysterectomy for leiomyomas. On examination her BMI was 19.1 kg/m²; she had mild hirsutism and a palpable tender pelvic mass. Pelvic ultrasonography revealed a 154×104 mm solid left ovarian mass compressing the uterus without lymphadenopathy or free fluid. CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed no other lesions. Because of the size and mass effect, she underwent unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. Grossly, the specimen was a well-circumscribed, lobulated, solid yellow-brown mass measuring approximately 15×9 cm; cut surfaces showed orange-yellow nodules with areas of necrosis and hemorrhage.

A 32-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with right knee pain, effusion, and intermittent locking that began after a soccer game. He denied instability or previous trauma. On examination, there was a 15° extensor lag, mild effusion, and tenderness along the lateral joint line. Lachman-Noulis, Pivot-Shift, McMurray, and Apley tests were all negative. Routine laboratory tests were normal. Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the knee were unremarkable. Sagittal and coronal T1-weighted MRI of the right knee revealed a round lesion with a hypointense signal obscuring the anterior cruciate ligament.

A 75-year-old Caucasian man presented with a long-standing, asymptomatic abdominal wall mass in the mesogastrium that he had first noticed approximately 3 years earlier; it had increased in size over recent years. His history was notable for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy in 2008 for cholelithiasis. The operative specimen showed chronic cholecystitis and an incidental adenocarcinoma in situ arising in a 12 mm adenomatous gallbladder polyp; the gallbladder was accidentally opened during removal, and no adjuvant therapy or follow-up was undertaken. On examination, a 12 × 6 cm, stony-hard, non-tender mass was palpable in the mesogastrium without evidence of peritonitis. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed a heterogeneous, predominantly cystic mass with internal septations involving the rectus abdominis muscle. MRI confirmed a multilocular lesion in the anterior abdominal wall and showed no abnormalities of the liver, biliary tree, or pancreas. Gastroscopy was unremarkable. Colonoscopy revealed tumours in the descending colon and sigmoid colon, and biopsies from both sites confirmed adenocarcinoma.

A 50-year-old woman presented with several months of prolonged menstrual bleeding and right iliac fossa discomfort. She had a history of endometriosis, a partially septate uterus, and two prior cesarean deliveries. She was not on tamoxifen or hormone therapy. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a normal uterus and ovaries, but revealed a 28×20×25 mm cystic lesion in the left posterior vaginal fornix containing low-level internal echoes and a 13 mm hypervascular soft-tissue nodule on Doppler. A non-contrast pelvic MRI confirmed a well-defined, predominantly cystic 24×31×24 mm lesion in the left vaginal fornix that was mildly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, intermediate to high signal on T1-weighted images with mild fat suppression signal, and contained an internal solid component of intermediate T2 signal with a hyperintense rim and low T1 signal; there was no fat suppression on STIR. As she was asymptomatic, no intervention was performed. Two years later, she returned with persistent vaginal bleeding; repeat imaging showed the cystic component had grown to 38×44×38 mm, while the solid nodule remained unchanged.

An 85-year-old Black woman with a 7-year history of type II diabetes mellitus presented with a chief complaint of a longstanding, recurrent ulcer of the left great toe. She reported that previous episodes healed after 6–10 weeks of antibiotics and wound care, only to reopen, but the current ulcer has persisted for 2 years despite aggressive care including surgical debridement and a skin graft. Her daughter noted similar “on and off” ulcerations for 20 years.

Her medical history was significant for chronic venous insufficiency, bilateral knee arthritis, hypertension (15 years), and hypercholesterolemia. She denied smoking, alcohol, or drug use. She had an ACE inhibitor–induced cough, and her medications were unavailable.

On examination, there was a 3-cm ulcer on the medial and dorsal left hallux with a 50/50 mixture of fibrous and granulation tissue, no undermining, erythema, exudate, edema, foul odor, or pain out of proportion. Bilateral lower extremities showed varicosities, lipodermatosclerosis, and hemosiderin deposition without edema. Skin was warm; pedal pulses were present but diminished; Doppler waveforms were biphasic and left ankle–brachial index was 0.994. Neurologic testing revealed absent vibration and pinprick sensation and absent protective monofilament sensation bilaterally; reflexes, range of motion, and strength were normal.

Plain films showed normal bone density without cortical erosion or osteomyelitis. Given the ulcer’s chronicity and recalcitrant nature, a neoplastic process was considered. The differential diagnosis included amelanotic melanoma, carcinoma cuniculatum, basal cell carcinoma, and Marjolin’s squamous cell carcinoma, all of which can present as long-standing ulcers and warrant early biopsy.

A 67-year-old man undergoing evaluation for sigmoid colon cancer had, on contrast-enhanced CT, a 20-mm homogeneous, well-defined nodule in the right paratracheal region. FDG-PET showed increased uptake in this lesion (maximum SUV, 5.3). He was asymptomatic, with an unremarkable medical and family history, and normal blood tests except for a mild leukocytosis. After laparoscopic sigmoidectomy (pathologic stage I), a repeat CT 3 months later showed no change in the nodule’s size. Given the high FDG uptake, a preliminary diagnosis of malignant lymphoma or metastatic lymph node was made, and surgical resection of the nodule was recommended without preoperative biopsy.

A 55-year-old postmenopausal, nulligravida woman presented with a 2-month history of a protruding umbilical mass. She had no personal or family history of gynecologic or breast cancer. On examination, she was afebrile, pale, and asthenic. The umbilical lesion measured 5 × 4 cm, appeared necrotic, and bled on contact. Laboratory studies revealed severe hypochromic microcytic anemia with a hemoglobin level of 5 g/dL. Pelvic ultrasonography showed an enlarged uterus (12 × 7 cm) with an indistinct endometrial outline and nonvisualized adnexa. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a pelvic soft-tissue mass measuring 93 × 80 × 90 mm, peritoneal carcinomatosis nodules, secondary involvement of the cutaneous umbilical region, and a large umbilical hernia. MRI depicted a large pedunculated mass on the anterior cervical wall (95 × 80 mm). A skin-punch biopsy of the umbilical lesion revealed a proliferation of atypical tumor cells exhibiting both epithelial and mesenchymal characteristics, suggesting a biphasic neoplasm.

A female term neonate was noted at birth to have a deformity of her left lower limb, with an anterolateral tibial bow associated with marked varus angulation and procurvatum. Delivery was by cesarean section at 40 + 4 weeks for failure to progress, with an otherwise uncomplicated perinatal course. Antenatal ultrasound screening was normal. Clinical examination was otherwise unremarkable, with no neurocutaneous stigmata.  
Plain radiographs of the left ankle on day 0 showed anterolateral bowing of the tibia and fibula (the fibula being hypoplastic compared to the contralateral side), with focal osteolytic lesions in the distal tibial and fibular metadiaphyses and extensive surrounding and internal patchy sclerosis. A skeletal survey demonstrated no other osseous lesions.  
What is the most likely diagnosis?

A previously healthy 4-year-old girl presented to the pediatric emergency department with a few hours’ history of constant pressure–type lower-quadrant abdominal pain and an urge to urinate, following a low-energy blunt abdominal trauma while playing. On examination, she had localized tenderness of the lower abdomen without other remarkable findings. Laboratory studies showed a neutrophilic leukocytosis (white blood cells 14 810/mm3, 71% neutrophils) and a C-reactive protein level of 122 mg/L. An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a hyperechoic, inhomogeneous solid mass measuring 10×4×8 cm cranial to the bladder, with no vascular signal on color Doppler, and the left ovary was not visualized. Serum tumor markers revealed an elevated cancer antigen 125 level of 220.9 IU/mL, with beta human chorionic gonadotropin, alpha-fetoprotein, and carcinoembryonic antigen within normal limits. Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy was initiated, and, suspecting an ovarian mass and/or adnexal torsion, the patient was taken for abdominal exploration through a Pfannenstiel incision.

A 28-year-old woman, a professional Muay Thai athlete since age 16, presented with 6 months of persistent pain in the metaphyseal lateral aspect of the right tibia. She had no history of other medical conditions or familial tumors. On examination, there was mild swelling, slight bruising, and tenderness on palpation of the distal two-thirds of the posterolateral tibial border. The pain was constant, with intermittent sharp exacerbations not always related to athletic activity.

Initial standing radiographs of the distal right tibia showed a periosteal reaction and cortical thickening, findings that were initially interpreted by the radiologist as consistent with an osteoid osteoma. Ultrasonography demonstrated soft-tissue edema in the region, while a CT scan revealed a 28 × 9 mm area of increased density within the central cortex alongside the lateral tibial border but “without an evident nidus.” To further characterize the lesion, and to distinguish among fibrous dysplasia, adamantinoma, and fibroma, an MRI of the tibia was obtained. MRI with and without contrast demonstrated an oval cortical lesion in the distal tibial shaft with intermediate signal on T1, high signal on long TR sequences, a sclerotic border, and no contrast enhancement.

A 38-year-old white woman, G0, with no prior medical history presented with one month of left-sided vulvar pain, most pronounced during and for hours after sexual intercourse. She reported feeling a firm structure at the vaginal introitus. On gynecologic examination, at the 6 o’clock position of the hymen was a 1 × 2 cm nodular, well-demarcated, tender, solid lesion; the remainder of the examination was normal. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a 10 mm regular endometrial stripe, a 42 × 36 mm type 6 fibroid in the posterior uterine corpus, and normal ovaries. She had never undergone cervical cytologic screening; HPV testing was positive for types 16 and 31, and Pap smear revealed high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HGSIL). The patient underwent cervical conization, and the hymenal lesion was completely excised and sent for pathological examination.

A 65-year-old man presented with a 9-month history of weight loss, anorexia, and generalized fatigue without localizing symptoms. He appeared dehydrated and cachectic. Vital signs on arrival: heart rate 109 bpm, blood pressure 78/54 mm Hg, respiratory rate 17/min, oxygen saturation 97% on room air; after 3 L of crystalloid, blood pressure rose to 93/69 mm Hg. Examination showed scattered ecchymoses on the extremities, occasional coarse crackles in bilateral lower lung zones, nontender splenomegaly, and a firm, nonpulsatile periumbilical mass; there was no peripheral lymphadenopathy or edema. Initial laboratory tests revealed hemoglobin 62 g/L, platelet count 48 × 10^9/L, blood glucose 2.9 mmol/L, arterial blood gas with pH 7.22, pCO2 26 mm Hg, HCO3– 10 mmol/L, anion gap 26, and serum lactate 18.8 mmol/L. He was admitted for fluid resuscitation, blood transfusion, and empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics; blood and urine cultures were negative. D-lactate level was normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen showed diffuse cervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, nodular consolidation in the left upper lobe, and a 3.9 × 1.8 cm mesenteric mass concerning for a lymphoproliferative process. He continued to have asymptomatic hypoglycemia (2.5–3.9 mmol/L) requiring continuous dextrose infusion despite oral intake. Bronchoscopy, gastrointestinal endoscopies, and bronchoalveolar lavage were non-diagnostic.

A 45-year-old woman presented with intermenstrual bleeding. Examination revealed a polypoid cervical mass, and an excisional biopsy was interpreted as a benign cervical polyp. Three months later she returned with recurrent bleeding and a persistently enlarged cervical polyp. A second biopsy was sent for expert pathological review. Pelvic MRI showed a 4 cm fibroid in the uterine corpus and multiple Naboth cysts, with no identifiable cervical mass or abnormal contrast enhancement. Whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated no abnormal uptake in the cervix or elsewhere. The patient underwent a C1-type hysterectomy; intraoperatively there was no peritoneal disease. Grossly, the cervical lesion measured 30×7 mm, had a polypoid “bunch-of-grapes” appearance, and prolapsed through the cervical os. Multiple leiomyomas were present in the myometrium. Microscopically, the polypoid lesion consisted of spindle-shaped cells with oval nuclei set in a myxoid, edematous stroma. The surface was covered by benign squamous epithelium overlying a dense band of stromal cells immediately beneath the epithelium (“cambium layer”). In deeper areas the tumor cells were more compact and basophilic. No heterologous elements were seen.

A 38-year-old woman presented with a painless midline neck mass that had been present for 3 years. She reported no dysphagia, dyspnea, or hoarseness, and had no history of neck irradiation. She was clinically euthyroid. On examination, there was a 2 × 2 cm soft, cystic mass in the thyrohyoid region that moved with swallowing and tongue protrusion. The thyroid gland was not enlarged and there was no cervical lymphadenopathy.  
Ultrasonography of the neck showed a 1.8 × 2.4 cm midline cystic lesion with internal septations and a solid mural component containing microcalcifications. The thyroid gland contained a separate 4 mm right lobe nodule. No abnormal lymph nodes were visualized.  
A fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the midline mass was performed without imaging guidance and was nondiagnostic.

An 18-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of a slowly enlarging, firm, nontender mass over her lower back. On examination, the lesion measured approximately 25 × 12 cm, was superficial to the lumbar spine, fixed to deeper tissues, and had no overlying skin changes or regional lymphadenopathy. MRI of the lumbar spine showed a large lesion in the superficial subcutaneous tissue abutting the deep fascia, with intermediate signal intensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images. CT-guided core biopsy of the mass revealed spindled and histiocyte-like cells that were strongly S100+ and CD163+; these cells were negative for smooth muscle actin, nuclear β-catenin, CD34, and keratin AE1/3. Additional studies showed p16 negativity, a wild-type p53 pattern, focal weak cyclin D1 expression, absence of MDM2 amplification by FISH, and a low Ki-67 index (<1%). A chronic perivascular infiltrate of CD3+ T cells and CD20+ B cells was also noted. Given the benign cytologic features and immunoprofile, a benign process was favored, and the differential diagnosis included a regressing Rosai–Dorfman lesion versus localized massive lymphedema. The patient elected to undergo surgical excision of the mass.

A 31-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of recurrent perirectal ulceration. Over 3 weeks, he developed generalized sluggishness, diarrhea, and then acute altered mental status for 24 hours, leading to ICU admission for shock and encephalopathy. On admission, a new diagnosis of HIV infection was made: CD4+ count, 45 cells/mm3; viral load, >2 million copies/mL. He developed oral thrush but no other opportunistic infections. ART was started (TAF/FTC + DTG). Laboratory studies showed an absolute lymphocyte count below 1000/mm3. CT imaging demonstrated hepatomegaly and multiple mediastinal and axillary lymph nodes of varied sizes. Infectious work-ups were negative, and supportive care stabilized his condition. Brain imaging showed bilateral hippocampal changes; he was treated with five sessions of plasmapheresis for presumed limbic encephalitis, with partial improvement.

On skin examination, persistent ulcers on the left medial buttock revealed beefy-red granulation tissue with well-defined edges and minimal exudate; they were non-tender and non-indurated. Tests for CMV, HSV PCR, and fungal serologies were negative. A punch biopsy of the ulcer showed sporadic groups of large atypical pleomorphic cells amid lymphocytes and histiocytes, with subtle “horseshoe”-shaped nuclei. Immunohistochemical staining showed these cells to be CD30+, CD2+, CD4+, CD5+, CD43+, and MUM-1+, and negative for ALK-1, CD3, CD8, EMA, CD20, and PAX-5; CD45 was inconclusive. A bone marrow biopsy for pancytopenia showed no lymphoma.

A PET scan one month after admission demonstrated hypermetabolic axillary and mediastinal nodes thought to be reactive to the buttock lesion. Despite localized radiation therapy, new buttock ulcerations appeared. Five months after initial presentation, CT imaging detected multiple pulmonary nodules and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. At eight months, CT showed enlarging pulmonary nodules and a 5.6-cm soft-tissue mass near the liver.

A 70-year-old man with hypertension, asthma, a history of heavy alcohol use, and a 60-year, two-to-three–pack-per-day smoking history presented with a painless left submandibular mass. He first noticed the mass one year earlier; it had grown slowly. On examination, the mass measured approximately 8–9 cm and was non-tender. Cervical ultrasound showed an oval, hypoechoic mass that did not infiltrate the thyroid or the submandibular gland. A contrast CT scan of the neck was obtained. Fine-needle aspiration of the lesion yielded a low-cellularity smear dominated by large polygonal to round cells with abundant acidophilic granular cytoplasm. A chest radiograph showed no acute pulmonary process.

A 36-year-old man was referred for an asymptomatic, slowly enlarging nodular lesion on the right buccal mucosa of approximately one year’s duration. His medical history was noncontributory. On examination, there was a well-circumscribed, moderately mobile, non-tender fibroelastic mass measuring about 3 cm in diameter on the right buccal mucosa. The overlying mucosa was smooth with mild inflammation.

The patient underwent intraoral excision of the lesion. Gross examination revealed a smooth, encapsulated, round mass measuring 2.4 cm in greatest dimension with a white-grey cut surface. Microscopic examination showed fibroblast-like spindle cells arranged in fascicular and focally storiform patterns, with interspersed plump polygonal histiocytic cells. The stroma was collagenized with abundant vascularity and a scattered lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate. There were no mitotic figures, cellular pleomorphism, multinucleated giant cells, nuclear atypia, or necrosis.

Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated strong positivity for vimentin, focal weak positivity for CD34, and positivity for CD68 in histiocytic cells. Tumor cells were negative for desmin, α-smooth muscle actin, S-100 protein, Leu7, and CD117.

An 18-year-old man was referred for painful bilateral testicular masses. Scrotal ultrasonography confirmed tumors in both testes. Magnetic resonance imaging of the scrotum revealed a 2.5 cm lesion in the right rete testis and a 3.0 cm lesion in the left rete testis. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, luteinizing hormone of 4.9 mIU/mL (normal 1.5–9.3), follicle-stimulating hormone of 5.1 mIU/mL (normal 1.6–8.0), and total testosterone of 398 ng/dL (normal 249–836). Serum beta-human chorionic gonadotropin, α-fetoprotein, and lactate dehydrogenase were all within normal limits. Both masses increased in size before surgery. Bilateral partial orchiectomies were attempted; the right side was converted to a radical orchiectomy with a prosthesis due to concerns about testicular viability, and a partial orchiectomy was completed on the left. Intraoperative frozen sections were inconclusive for germ cell tumors, Leydig cell tumors, or other histology. Formal pathology showed proliferation of tumor cells throughout the testicular parenchyma and rete testis in nodules ranging from <1 to 10 mm, a low proliferation index (Ki-67 positive in 1% of cells), negative p53 staining, and no necrosis, mitotic figures, or pleomorphism. A presumptive diagnosis of Leydig cell tumors versus testicular adrenal rest tumors was suggested.

A 51-year-old man noted a slowly enlarging lesion posterior to his left nipple over 3 years. He described mild pain on palpation but denied fevers, chills, fatigue, weight loss, nipple discharge, trauma, infection, insect bites, skin disease, new medications, or prior surgery. His medical history was notable for diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease (eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2), with no family history of breast or ovarian cancer.

On examination, a mobile, approximately 3 cm mass was palpated behind the left nipple without skin changes or nipple retraction; the axilla was unremarkable. The patient declined mammography. Ultrasonography showed a superficial, well-circumscribed, ovoid, hypoechoic lesion measuring 34 mm parallel to the skin, with posterior acoustic enhancement and no internal vascularity on Doppler; there was no axillary lymphadenopathy.

Magnetic resonance imaging revealed the lesion to be mildly hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images. Diffusion-weighted imaging demonstrated marked diffusion restriction with an ADC value of 0.7×10^−3 s/mm^2.

A 3-year-old boy presented with a 3-day history of watery diarrhea and postprandial vomiting. On the day of admission, he passed a “cherry-jelly” discharge per rectum. There was no history of severe pain episodes, crying spells, or family history of deformities or tumors.  

On examination, he appeared in good general condition. The abdomen was soft, non-distended, and without palpable masses. Digital rectal examination revealed a spontaneously tightened sphincter and, on insertion, the examiner’s finger ran parallel to a palpable intraluminal structure with a trace of blood on the glove.

Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin of 12.8 g/dL, white-cell count 8000/mm3, and platelets 432 000/mm3.  

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated an ileocolic intussusception in the left iliac fossa measuring approximately 3×3 cm, with no peristalsis in the involved bowel loops and no features of obstruction. A repeat ultrasound raised suspicion of a mass at the cecum within the intussusception.

A 93-year-old woman with chronic hypertension and no smoking or relevant family history was referred for evaluation of a perianal lesion present for three months that had not improved with antibiotics and topical antiseptics. She reported intermittent scant bleeding but no weight loss, gastrointestinal symptoms, or other skin lesions.

On examination, there was a 4.5 × 3.2 cm ulcer located in the perianal area between the 9- and 3-o’clock positions. The ulcer had an elevated, pearly-white border that was indurated on palpation, with isolated pigmented globules at the margins. The ulcer’s center was friable and bled easily on contact. There were no palpable inguinal lymph nodes, satellite skin lesions, or abdominal masses.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and creatinine of 1.46 mg/dL. HIV serology was negative, and VDRL was nonreactive. Rigid proctoscopy demonstrated that the lesion involved the anal margin without impairing sphincter continence; no deeper masses were seen within 8 cm of the anal canal. Pelvic MRI revealed a 26 × 27 × 10 mm mass infiltrating the intergluteal skin immediately posterior to the anus, in contact with but not invading the anal sphincter, with perilesional edema; the sphincter complex and levator ani were intact.

A 47-year-old woman presented with bilateral lower extremity edema, left lower limb pain, abdominal purplish striae, and abdominal distension of 9 months’ duration. Two years earlier, she had undergone hysterectomy for uterine fibroids; she had no history of radiotherapy or other relevant medical conditions. On examination, her weight was 90 kg, height 165 cm (BMI 33), and blood pressure 146/115 mm Hg. She had centripetal obesity, moon facies, buffalo hump, thin dry skin with acne and hirsutism, and pedal edema. Laboratory studies confirmed diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and hypokalemia. Endocrine evaluation revealed a serum ACTH level of 169 pg/mL (reference 5–50), cortisol 933 nmol/L at 8 am (reference 138–690) and 778 nmol/L at 4 pm (reference 69–345), loss of circadian rhythm, <50% suppression of cortisol on a low-dose dexamethasone suppression test, and >50% suppression on a high-dose test. Serum prolactin, FSH, LH, testosterone, FT3, FT4, and TSH were within normal limits. Adrenal CT showed no abnormalities. Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI of the head demonstrated a 3.0 × 3.0 cm spherical enhancing mass in the right frontal convexity with a dural tail sign, and in the sellar region a 7.8 × 6.4 mm lesion with lower enhancement than the surrounding pituitary tissue and displacement of the pituitary stalk to the right.

A 35-year-old man with a history of asthma presented with a 4-year history of noisy breathing that had worsened over the past few weeks, accompanied by increasing dyspnea, bilateral aural fullness, dysphagia, and a muffled voice. He also reported recurrent nasal discharge and postnasal drip. On examination, both tympanic membranes were dull, and there was no nasal airflow bilaterally. Inspection of the oropharynx revealed a mass protruding from the nasopharyngeal isthmus that extended into the oropharynx and tented the soft palate. No cervical lymphadenopathy was palpable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck showed a globular, nonenhancing soft-tissue mass occupying the nasopharynx and bilateral posterior nasal cavities, obliterating the pharyngeal recesses, extending inferiorly to the oropharynx, displacing the soft palate anteriorly, and causing severe narrowing of the pharyngeal airway. The lesion measured 73.8 × 26.3 × 28.6 mm. No pathologically enlarged cervical lymph nodes were identified.

A 72-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of intermittent dysphonia. Her medical history was notable for hypothyroidism and hypertension managed with medications. She denied weight loss, dyspnea, dysphagia, or fever.

On two successive external laryngoscopies, a vegetating lesion measuring 3.5 × 2.5 cm was noted on the left lateral wall of the oropharynx, merging with the left palatine tonsil. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head and neck showed a mixed cystic and solid lesion with a thick content measuring 23 × 22 × 24 mm.

The lesion was resected via suspension laryngoscopy with a CO₂ laser. A solid, fibroelastic mass measuring 3 × 2 cm was removed intact. One month later, laryngoscopy showed good healing without residual lesion.

Histopathological analysis revealed a benign, well-delimited neoplasm. Microscopic examination showed:  
• An epithelioid area  
• A triple epithelial cell phenotype with plasmacytoid, myoepithelial, and ductal cells  
• A highly cellular, monomorphic lesion with a scarce stromal component  
• Very limited tumor extension to the surgical margin

A 21-year-old woman presented with facial asymmetry first noticed 4 years earlier. She had no history of facial trauma or ear infection. On examination, crepitus was noted in the left temporomandibular joint and clicking in the right, without pain. Her maximum mouth opening was 40 mm, and the mandibular midline deviated 5.5 mm to the left, with secondary malocclusion. A panoramic radiograph showed an irregular bony outgrowth on the anterior aspect of the right mandibular condyle. Cone-beam CT revealed a well-defined exophytic bony mass arising from the anteromedial surface of the right condylar neck, producing a bifid condylar head and a focal depression of the adjacent skull base. A three-phase bone scan after injection of 20 mCi 99mTc-HDP demonstrated increased tracer uptake in the right condylar region.

A 68-year-old Asian man presented with an 8-year history of a slowly enlarging mass in the distal left forearm. He reported focal tenderness at the site but denied cold hypersensitivity. On examination, percussion over the lesion elicited a positive Tinel’s sign and numbness; there was no motor weakness, radiating pain, or sensory loss distal to the mass. The lesion was round, soft, approximately 0.8 cm in diameter, and mobile within a narrow range. The patient had no pain unless the lesion was pressed. Laboratory studies and plain radiographs of the forearm were unremarkable. High-resolution ultrasonography revealed a 0.9 cm, well-defined, hypoechoic nodule in the subcutaneous fat layer with slight posterior acoustic enhancement. A feeding vessel was noted within the lesion, and Doppler imaging demonstrated hypervascularity. Based on the location, clinical presentation, and ultrasound findings, a hemangioma or a glomus tumor was suspected.

A 54-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of a black mass on his right forearm. On examination, there was a solitary, well-defined, sessile black tumor measuring 3 × 4 cm with a central granulating protrusion. The patient’s vital signs were normal, and the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory tests, including complete blood count, serum chemistries, urinalysis, and a chest radiograph, were within normal limits. A punch biopsy of the lesion showed an ulcerated tumor nodule with neoplastic proliferation of polygonal cells exhibiting eccentric nuclei, a single prominent nucleolus, large hyaline cytoplasmic inclusions, and scattered melanin pigment. Immunohistochemical studies revealed that the neoplastic cells were positive for HMB-45, S100 protein, Fontana-Masson silver, and vimentin, while negative for smooth muscle actin, CD68, CD34, CD99, synaptophysin, desmin, and periodic acid–Schiff (PAS); vimentin staining showed diffuse and globular perinuclear accentuation.

A 55-year-old man with a 17-year history of HIV infection, well controlled on antiretroviral therapy (current CD4 count 2200 cells/mm3, nadir 1300 cells/mm3; undetectable viral load), was referred for routine anal cancer screening. He denied gastrointestinal or anorectal symptoms. On external inspection, a single, smooth, flesh-colored papule measuring 3 mm was noted at the anal margin, approximately 1 cm from the anal verge. Anal cytology obtained at the visit was benign. Digital anorectal examination and high-resolution anoscopy were otherwise normal. To establish a definitive diagnosis, the lesion was excised under local anesthesia in the office.

A 48-year-old white Irish man presented with progressive central vision loss in his right eye over 2 weeks, associated with photosensitivity, facial pain, and headache. His history included bilateral dacryocystorhinostomy, asthma, eczema, a 10–pack-year smoking history, and intermittent unilateral upper-limb sensory disturbances but no other systemic symptoms. On initial examination, visual acuity was 6/18 in the right eye and 6/9 in the left eye; there was a right relative afferent pupillary defect and reduced color vision (Ishihara 9/13 right, 13/13 left). Slit-lamp and dilated funduscopic examinations were unremarkable, intraocular pressures were 17 mm Hg bilaterally, and extraocular movements were full without ptosis or lid abnormalities. The initial working diagnosis was retrobulbar optic neuritis, and MRI of the brain was requested. Four weeks later, vision in the right eye had declined to 6/60 with color vision 1/13; examination now showed 3 mm of right proptosis. Visual field testing revealed a monocular paracentral scotoma with sparing of the superior nasal quadrant.

A 14-year-old girl presented with a 2-year history of right cheek swelling that had gradually increased in size, causing discomfort with chewing and swallowing. She had been treated empirically for a presumed dental infection with analgesics and antibiotics, without resolution. She denied trauma, mechanical irritation, or systemic symptoms. There was no family history of similar lesions, and she did not use tobacco or alcohol.

On examination, the overlying skin and mucosa were normal. There was a large, smooth, lobulated swelling of the right cheek extending to the submandibular region. The mass was painless, non-tender, without skin changes or dilated veins, and facial sensation was intact. Fine-needle aspiration yielded negative results.

Laboratory studies showed a slightly low mean corpuscular volume, mean corpuscular hemoglobin, and mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration, with mildly elevated platelets; lipid profile and blood glucose were normal.

Ultrasonography of the right cheek demonstrated a 30 × 12 mm irregular cystic lesion with internal echogenic foci.
