Contrast-enhanced CT of the face revealed a 44 × 42 mm fat-containing cystic lesion in the right cheek and a periapical radiolucency at the lower right second molar. Doppler ultrasound showed a well-encapsulated right cheek mass with no internal blood flow.

A 35-year-old man presented with a six-year history of a painless, slowly enlarging swelling of the left middle one-third of the face. The mass caused facial asymmetry and restricted mouth opening but no paresthesia or discharge. There was no history of trauma or systemic illness. On examination, a 2 cm × 2 cm diffuse, sessile, bony‐hard swelling was palpated just anterior and 1 cm below the left tragus; the overlying skin was normal. Intraoral examination was unremarkable. A provisional diagnosis included peripheral osteoma, periosteal reaction, exostosis, peripheral osteoblastoma, and osteochondroma. Panoramic and paranasal sinus radiographs showed a well-defined radiopacity at the left posterior mandibular ramus. Axial CT demonstrated a 3.4 × 2.9 × 3.6 cm osseous outgrowth arising from the posterior edge of the ramus, with central medullary continuity and sclerotic cortical periphery, assuming a mushroom shape. MRI revealed continuity of the mandibular medullary cavity with the lesion; the center was isointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with a peripheral hypointense rim, suggesting a cartilage cap. Mass effect with lateral displacement of the facial nerve was noted.

A 58-year-old man with hypertension and chronic kidney disease on hemodialysis was referred after a routine transthoracic echocardiogram showed a mobile mass on the mitral valve. He was asymptomatic, afebrile, and had a regular heart rate with no murmurs. Initial 2D TTE demonstrated a 12 × 17 mm mobile mass on the atrial side of the anterior mitral leaflet moving in synchrony with the valve. Laboratory studies, including inflammatory markers, were within normal limits, and multiple blood cultures were negative. Repeat TTE confirmed a 1.5 cm round, homogeneously speckled, mobile mass attached to the anterior mitral leaflet without significant mitral regurgitation or obstruction. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the heart was inconclusive.

A 77-year-old Asian man with no significant past medical history presented with a 2-month history of mild, intermittent left trepopnea (shortness of breath when lying on the left side) and palpitations. He denied syncope, fever, arthralgias, weight loss, or fatigue. His only risk factors were tobacco use, age, and a sedentary lifestyle; he was not on chronic medications.

On examination, heart sounds were regular without murmurs; there was no abdominal distension or lower-extremity edema. An electrocardiogram showed atrial tachycardia with an average ventricular rate of 60 beats per minute. Chest radiography demonstrated normal lung fields and an enlarged right lower cardiac contour suggestive of right atrial enlargement. Laboratory studies, including C-reactive protein, complete blood count (hemoglobin 13 g/dL), and serum interleukin-6 (7 pg/mL), were within normal limits.

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a large, smooth-edged, spheroid mass in the right atrium measuring 86 × 63 mm, causing mild functional tricuspid flow obstruction and slightly reduced left ventricular systolic function; no stalk was visualized. The inferior vena cava was normal in size, and assessment of pulmonary artery pressure was limited by patient dyspnea and poor acoustic windows. The patient declined transesophageal echocardiography.

Cardiac computed tomography confirmed a 9.3 cm diameter, round mass in the right atrium with smooth margins, microcalcifications, and no invasion of surrounding tissues. Coronary angiography showed normal coronary arteries.

An 80-year-old woman noted a gradually enlarging lump in her left breast over the past 6 months. She had no personal or family history of breast or ovarian cancer and was otherwise in good health. On examination, there was a 16 × 10 cm soft, well-circumscribed mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast without palpable axillary lymphadenopathy. 

Mammography demonstrated a well-circumscribed, lobulated mass. Breast ultrasound showed a hypoechoic lesion with posterior acoustic enhancement in the same area; the radiologist assigned a BI-RADS category 4A (suspicious). 

Ultrasound-guided core-needle biopsy revealed a microlobulated proliferation of well-differentiated carcinoma (Scarf–Bloom–Richardson grade 1). Low-power views showed nests of tumor cells floating in large lakes of extracellular mucin separated by delicate fibrous septa. The tumor contained more than 90% mucin. At higher magnification, cells exhibited mild to moderate nuclear atypia, and mitoses were rare (4 per 10 high-power fields). No lymphovascular invasion or perineural spread was seen, and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes were absent. Immunohistochemical studies showed strong positivity for estrogen receptor and progesterone receptor, absence of HER-2/neu overexpression, and a low Ki-67 proliferation index.

A 58-year-old multiparous woman presented with a one-year history of colicky epigastric and hypogastric pain, dyspepsia, nausea, and constipation every 2–3 days, accompanied by progressive abdominal distension. She also reported a sense of perineal heaviness, vaginal mucosal discharge, urinary frequency, urgency, and occasional incontinence. Her medical history was notable for hypertension, ischemic heart disease, and recurrent urinary tract infections. On examination, she was obese and had a large, hard, mobile, well-circumscribed lower abdominal mass measuring >15 cm in diameter, with an irregular surface and mild tenderness. Laboratory studies were within normal limits, stool occult blood was negative, and tumor markers (CA125, CEA, CA19-9) were all normal. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasound showed ascites and a large irregular heterogeneous pelvic mass measuring approximately 15 × 19 cm. CT and MRI demonstrated the mass abutting the superior bladder wall without intraluminal extension, with no lymphadenopathy or metastases identified. Multiple paracenteses showed no malignant cells. At surgical exploration via a lower midline incision, there was serous ascites and a lobulated, hypervascular mass (~15 × 15 cm) arising from the greater omentum, not attached to any abdominal organs or intestines, and no peri-aortic lymphadenopathy. A complete gross resection of the tumor was performed.

A 66-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes managed with insulin, hypertension, and alcohol-related chronic liver disease presented with severe epigastric pain on a background of months of fatigue, anorexia, and a 10-kg weight loss. On examination he had a low-grade fever, profound symptomatic hypotension, generalized skin hyperpigmentation, and epigastric tenderness. Laboratory evaluation revealed hypo-osmolar hyponatremia (serum sodium 123 mEq/L) with urinary sodium wasting. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated bilateral hypoechoic suprarenal masses. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed bilateral adrenal masses measuring approximately 98 × 42 × 56 mm on the left and 96 × 52 × 61 mm on the right, compressing the inferior vena cava. Primary adrenal insufficiency was confirmed by a low morning cortisol (3.7 µg/dL) and elevated ACTH level (444.5 pg/mL). Plasma and urine metanephrine levels were elevated but normalized after initiation of hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone replacement. An 18F-FDG PET scan showed intensely avid uptake in both adrenal masses and numerous surrounding abdominal lymph nodes, with no other sites of abnormal FDG activity.

A 24-year-old man presented with 10 days of sudden-onset left flank pain that worsened over 5 days, associated with nausea and three episodes of nonprojectile, greenish vomiting. He denied fever, prior medical or surgical history was unremarkable, and he was afebrile. On abdominal examination, there was significant tenderness in the left flank without masses, bruits, or signs of ascites. Baseline blood tests were normal.  
An abdominal ultrasonogram was unremarkable except for a kidney, ureter, and bladder study showing moderate left hydronephrosis and proximal ureteral dilation; there was a suspicion of an upper left ureteric calculus measuring 5.6 mm. A noncontrast CT of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder was obtained to evaluate for a stone and revealed an incidental 42.4 × 40.1 × 35.2 mm well-circumscribed, homogeneous mass in the left retroperitoneum, abutting the infrarenal aorta, pushing the left renal vessels superiorly, and in close proximity to the left ureter.  
A CT-guided tru-cut biopsy yielded spindle-cell proliferation with fibrillary stroma and a few admixed skeletal muscle fibers; there was no pleomorphism, mitotic activity, or necrosis. Immunohistochemical staining showed S100 protein positivity and negative staining for smooth muscle antibody, desmin, and DOG1. A provisional diagnosis of a nerve sheath tumor without atypia or necrosis was made.

A 72-year-old man was evaluated for a left-sided nasal mass that he had noticed 35 years earlier. He reported progressive left nasal obstruction, reduced sense of smell, recurrent episodes of epistaxis, and intermittent headaches. On nasal endoscopy, a reddish, polypoid mass filled and occluded almost the entire left nasal canal and bled easily on contact. CT angiography and MR angiography of the facial sinuses revealed a hypervascular tissue mass occupying the left nasal cavity and left maxillary sinus, with extension posteriorly into the nasopharynx and laterally across the midline into the right nasal cavity. The imaging appearance was suggestive of nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

An 80‐year‐old man presented with a 3‐week history of swelling on the palate. His medical history was notable for constipation and hypertension managed with daily antihypertensive medication. He denied tobacco, alcohol, or other substance use. Intraoral examination revealed a 2 cm, reddish, painless, pedunculated nodule with ulcerated areas on the palate between the left upper first and second molars. A radiograph of the region showed intact underlying bone. The initial clinical diagnostic considerations were squamous cell carcinoma, a malignant salivary gland neoplasm, and pyogenic granuloma. An incisional biopsy demonstrated columnar epithelium forming papilliferous areas, mucous cells, and cystic‐like spaces, along with neoplastic cells showing prominent nucleoli, hyperchromatic nuclei, and atypical mitotic figures. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for cytokeratin 20.

A 37-year-old man presented with three months of right-sided, ventilatory-dependent chest pain and a progressively enlarging mass on the anterior right hemithorax. He also described facial edema and neck vein distension. He had a 10-year history of smoking (20 cigarettes per day), quitting 8 years earlier; his mother died at age 35 of metastatic breast cancer. On examination, there was a painless, erythematous, infiltrative tumor over the right anterior chest wall, facial edema, and jugular venous distension. Laboratory studies showed hypergammaglobulinemia with elevated IgM, IgA, and IgG, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 85 mm/h. Contrast-enhanced chest MRI revealed an infiltrative retrosternal lesion extending into soft tissues and intercostal muscles between the first and fourth right costal cartilages. Surgical biopsy via thoracotomy demonstrated fusiform cell proliferation in curved bundles with foamy histiocytes, plasma cells, and multinucleated cells without atypical lymphocytes, consistent with an inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT). Because the lesion was unresectable, prednisone (1 mg/kg) was started. After one month, the chest wall mass regressed, but facial edema and superior vena cava syndrome worsened. A PET/CT scan showed the retrosternal lesion with heterogeneous uptake (SUV 3.8) and new mediastinal lymphadenopathy with intense uptake (SUV 19.9).

A 30-year-old African-American woman, 28 weeks pregnant, with multidrug-resistant HIV infection presented with a 10-year history of asymptomatic hyperpigmentation of the gingiva and vermillion lip. Over the past 3 months—during her current pregnancy—she noticed the areas had darkened and coalesced. She denied pain, bleeding, or ulceration. Her medications included antiretroviral therapy. On examination, there was an asymmetric, ill-defined, 3-cm dark brown to black plaque involving the vermillion and mucosal lip, maxillary gingiva, and adjacent hard palate. No cervical lymphadenopathy was palpable. Laboratory evaluation showed a CD4 count of 177 cells per cubic millimeter and an HIV viral load of 624 copies per milliliter.

A 70-year-old man with a history of prostate cancer presented with a two-year history of progressive dysphagia. Initially, he described epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Over the past three months, he progressed from difficulty swallowing solids to an inability to tolerate any oral intake. An upper endoscopy and contrast-enhanced chest CT performed three months after symptom onset revealed a giant pedunculated polyp in the upper esophagus, 28 cm from the dental arcade, obstructing but not invading the lumen. Surgical resection was recommended, but the patient declined. 

One month later, he experienced severe weight loss and underwent an attempted endoscopic resection at another center. During the procedure, he suffered a sudden cardiorespiratory arrest, was resuscitated, and was diagnosed with hypoxic–ischemic encephalopathy. He remained unresponsive, required a tracheostomy and open gastrostomy, and recovered partially from neurological deficits but became fully care dependent. His dysphagia continued and progressively worsened: he was unable to swallow liquids or saliva. 

One year after the initial endoscopic diagnosis, repeat endoscopy showed the polyp completely obstructing the esophageal lumen, and CT imaging demonstrated further growth without invasion of surrounding structures. On admission, he was alert and followed simple commands, with a tracheostomy and gastrostomy in place. He was severely malnourished (BMI 17 kg/m^2, prealbumin < 8 mg/dL) and was admitted for nutritional supplementation. Once his nutritional status improved, surgical management was planned.

A 30-year-old multiparous woman presented with a 2-year history of a palpable, centrally situated, firm to hard mass in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast. Multiple firm satellite nodules were palpable along the medial and inferior aspects of the lump. Fine-needle aspiration cytology showed a highly cellular smear composed of pleomorphic tumor cells with scant cytoplasm and bizarre nuclei in singles and small clusters. Numerous uni-, bi-, and multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells and atypical mitotic figures were seen against a background of monolayered sheets of benign ductal epithelial cells. A cytological diagnosis of malignant breast neoplasm was made.

A 1-day-old full-term female neonate, born vaginally at 38 weeks’ gestation to a healthy mother, was referred for evaluation of a left upper quadrant abdominal mass identified prenatally. The infant weighed 3035 g, had Apgar scores of 8 and 9, and was in no acute distress. Preoperative vital signs were temperature 37 °C, heart rate 146 beats/min, respiratory rate 60 breaths/min, blood pressure 73/38 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Examination revealed a palpable, non-tender mass in the left upper quadrant; the remainder of the airway, cardiac, and respiratory examinations was unremarkable. The neonate experienced emesis after birth, raising concern for gastric outlet obstruction.

A routine prenatal ultrasound at 33 weeks’ gestation showed a well-circumscribed cystic mass measuring 58.5 × 36 × 46.8 mm in the left upper quadrant, displacing the stomach anteriorly and the left kidney inferiorly. The lesion contained fetoid solid internal components, was acardiac and acephalic, and demonstrated rudimentary incomplete extremities with long bones and a very rudimentary spine with distinct vertebrae. Color Doppler imaging revealed a vestigial cord vessel with forward arterial flow; the feeding vessel was not definitively identified but was thought to arise from the mesenteric circulation. At 35 weeks’ gestation, magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a 6-cm mass in the left upper quadrant with mass effect on surrounding structures, consistent with a highly organized cystic and solid lesion.

A 70-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of constant, throbbing abdominal pain in the left upper quadrant. The pain was often spontaneous, worse at night and in the early morning, and markedly aggravated by bathing in cold water. He denied any prior trauma, surgery, or significant medical or family history.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Abdominal inspection was unremarkable. Palpation revealed a 3.0 × 2.5 × 2.0 cm soft swelling in the left hypochondrium of the abdominal wall without overlying skin changes. There was focal tenderness aggravated by deep palpation; the mass was nonpulsatile, with normal overlying skin temperature, no bruit, and a negative transillumination test. Carnett’s test was positive.

Laboratory studies, including routine blood tests, were within normal limits. No gastrointestinal cause for the pain was identified. Abdominal and parietal-wall ultrasonography demonstrated a 27 × 22 × 21 mm hypoechoic lesion within the muscular layer of the abdominal wall, showing increased local blood flow.

A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus on metformin and a heavy tobacco history presented with a 3-month history of a painful mass on the left hard palate. He reported rapid growth of the lesion over this period; the pain had lessened over time. He denied fever, night sweats, or weight loss. He had no known drug allergies and no significant alcohol use. His father had lung cancer; his mother had diabetes mellitus.

On intraoral examination, there was an ulcerative, exophytic, pigmented lesion with irregular margins, measuring approximately 4 × 2 × 2 cm on the left hard palate. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy, and cranial nerve examination was normal.

Maxillofacial CT (axial and coronal) demonstrated a focal bony defect in the left maxillary canine–premolar region with preservation of the inferior cortical bone and no involvement of the maxillary sinus floor. Contrast-enhanced paranasal sinus CT revealed a destructive 12 mm lesion in the left maxilla extending into the alveolar process, with an adjacent 27 mm infiltrative soft-tissue mass.

Differential diagnoses at this stage included peripheral giant cell granuloma, peripheral fibroma, and soft-tissue malignancies such as squamous cell carcinoma, adenoid cystic carcinoma, and mucoepidermoid carcinoma. An incisional biopsy was performed under general anesthesia for definitive diagnosis.

A 53-year-old man with hypertension and small-cell lung cancer (anaplastic microcellular carcinoma) diagnosed two months earlier and treated with etoposide and cisplatin was admitted after a right-sided clonic seizure one day earlier. On examination, he had slight right facial asymmetry, mild right upper-extremity weakness, and mild dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing. Contrast-enhanced head CT performed on admission showed hyperdense foci in the left frontal and parietal cortex without enhancement, interpreted as possible calcifications or hemorrhagic strokes. Two days later, brain MRI demonstrated multiple small T2 and FLAIR hyperintensities in the bilateral parieto-frontal regions, left temporal cortex, bilateral occipital lobes, left thalamus, and lenticular nucleus. These lesions did not enhance after contrast administration and lacked surrounding edema. On diffusion-weighted imaging, most lesions were hyperintense with corresponding hypointensity on apparent diffusion coefficient maps.

A 38-year-old man with no chronic illness presented with 30 minutes of acute left-sided chest pain, shortness of breath, vomiting, and intermittent epigastric pain. He reported a 7 kg weight loss over the past month. On arrival, he was afebrile, heart rate 122 bpm, respiratory rate 30 breaths/min, blood pressure 110/90 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 91% on room air. Chest examination revealed decreased breath sounds at the left lower zone and a 2 cm painless, fixed, round mass with regular borders at the left anterior chest wall (3rd intercostal space). The remainder of the examination was normal. Laboratory studies showed elevated lactate dehydrogenase (957 U/L), D-dimer (1.59 mg/L), and pro-BNP (3215 pg/mL). Electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus tachycardia with nonspecific T-wave inversions. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a severely dilated right ventricle with severely reduced function, compression of the main pulmonary artery, and indeterminate pulmonary artery pressure due to absence of a tricuspid regurgitation jet. A CT pulmonary angiogram showed no filling defects in the pulmonary arteries but demonstrated a large (9 × 8 cm) mediastinal soft-tissue mass encasing the main pulmonary artery and its branches, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, scattered pulmonary nodules, and bilateral pleural effusions.

A 9-year-old boy was referred to a pediatric dentistry clinic for evaluation of a “ball of gingiva” noted by his mother, with three months of progressive growth. His medical history was unremarkable, and he was not taking any medications. Both he and his mother reported a habit of picking his teeth and “poking” the gingiva. On intraoral examination, there was an asymptomatic, rounded, pink, smooth-surfaced soft-tissue lesion with fibrous consistency, approximately 1.5 cm in diameter, located on the attached gingiva between the upper left permanent lateral incisor and the primary canine. The patient was in mixed dentition, had active carious lesions, and demonstrated poor oral hygiene. A radiograph showed no bone involvement or other abnormalities. Based on the clinical and radiographic findings, the presumptive diagnosis was pyogenic granuloma.

A 66-year-old postmenopausal woman with no family history of breast cancer and a remote history of right breast invasive ductal carcinoma (ER/PR positive, HER2-negative) treated two years ago by wide local excision and radiation was undergoing routine surveillance. She reported no breast symptoms. On exam, her right breast scar was intact; there were no palpable masses or axillary lymphadenopathy on either side.

Bilateral breast ultrasound revealed in the left breast at 12 o’clock a 1.0 × 0.7 × 0.7 cm irregular, spiculated, hypoechoic lesion with posterior acoustic shadowing and mild cortical thickening of a left axillary lymph node. Mammography confirmed an irregular, necrotic-appearing 1.1 × 1.0 cm lesion at 12 o’clock in the left breast. Breast MRI showed a heterogeneously enhancing mass in the corresponding location with no other suspicious findings. Staging CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and a bone scan showed no evidence of metastatic disease.

Ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the left breast lesion demonstrated sheets of neoplastic cells with abundant granular, vacuolated cytoplasm and small, relatively inconspicuous nuclei. Immunohistochemical stains showed positivity for GCDFP-15 and androgen receptor and negativity for E-cadherin.

A 68-year-old woman presented with progressive numbness and tingling in both feet, sensory loss to mid-calf, and worsening balance. She also noted new red papules on her shoulders, lower abdomen, and back, and had unintentionally lost 15 lb over 6 months. She had been diagnosed with vitamin B₁₂ deficiency and received weekly B₁₂ injections without neurologic improvement.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Skin showed scattered red papules on the shoulders, abdomen, and back. Neurologic examination revealed decreased sensation to light touch and vibration in both lower extremities to the mid-calves, with mild ataxia.

Laboratory studies:
• Serum M protein: 0.1 g/dL with immunoglobulin G monoclonal protein and lambda light‐chain specificity on immunofixation  
• Serum lambda light chain: 85 mg/L  
• 24-hour urine total protein: 135.7 mg (normal)  
• Urine protein electrophoresis: normal  
• Bone marrow biopsy: hypercellular marrow (50% cellularity) with 10% plasma cells  
• HIV and HHV-8 serologies: negative  

Imaging:
• Skeletal survey: expansile lytic lesion at L3  
• PET–CT: L3 lesion (SUV 14.8) and enlarged left periaortic lymph node (SUV 9.4)  
• MRI spine: large lobulated lytic expansile mass at L3  
• Abdominal ultrasound: no hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, or free fluid  

Neurophysiology and CSF:
• EMG: demyelinating sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy  
• CSF: glucose 58 mg/dL, protein 81 mg/dL, RBCs 131/μL, nucleated cells 12/μL (18% neutrophils, 74% lymphocytes, 8% macrophages)  

Additional biopsies:
• Fat‐pad biopsy (two occasions): negative for Congo red staining and amyloid  
• Excisional biopsy of a shoulder papule: cherry angioma

A 70-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, fibromyalgia, rheumatoid arthritis, and depression presented with a 1-month history of progressive dysphagia to solids, 2–3 episodes of daily vomiting, and a 30-lb weight loss. She underwent upper endoscopy, which revealed luminal narrowing in the lower third of the esophagus without an esophageal web or ring. Gastric intubation was difficult but showed nonbleeding erosive antral gastropathy. Six days later, her dysphagia had progressed to include liquids, and she was admitted for inability to tolerate oral intake. A barium swallow demonstrated abrupt tapering of the gastroesophageal junction with a bird-beak configuration. She underwent palliative botulinum toxin injection of the lower esophageal sphincter, but her symptoms did not improve. Given the lack of clinical improvement, a computed tomography scan of the chest and abdomen was obtained to evaluate for possible extrinsic compression of the esophagus.

A 54-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 3-month history of lethargy, a 4-stone weight loss, and diminished appetite. Physical examination revealed a non-tender left pelvic mass. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a solid 4-cm mass in the left adnexa and, incidentally, an enlarged left kidney with a solid mass in the middle and upper poles. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 10×8-cm intensely enhancing heterogeneous mass arising from the upper pole of the left kidney and a 1.5-cm para-aortic lymph node at the level of the renal hilum. The CT also revealed a 4-cm heterogeneous mass with fairly intense enhancement adjacent to the left lateral margin of the uterus, which was initially interpreted as a pedunculated fibroid.

A 66-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of neck and shoulder pain and intermittent fevers up to 38.9 °C. His pain was dull, nonradiating, and relieved by NSAIDs. He had no neck stiffness or neurologic deficits. Empirical moxifloxacin for presumed infection provided no lasting improvement, and fevers recurred.

His medical history was notable for diabetes mellitus and cervical spondylosis. On examination, he was febrile but had no palpable lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, or skin lesions.

Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (14.39 × 10^9/L with 84.4% neutrophils), elevated C-reactive protein (126.3 mg/L), mildly elevated transaminases (ALT 71 U/L; AST 51 U/L), elevated alkaline phosphatase (208 U/L), elevated LDH (313 U/L), and hypoalbuminemia (32.5 g/L). Testing for EBV VCA IgG was positive. Tuberculosis antibody tests and tubercle-specific immune responses were negative. Blood and urine cultures were negative. Serum protein electrophoresis and tumor markers were normal. Bone marrow biopsy showed hypocellularity and granulocyte hyperplasia but no cellular atypia; flow cytometry detected no atypical lymphocytes.

Chest CT revealed local bronchiectasis and an osteolytic lesion in the T10 vertebral body. MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrated destructive lesions of the T2 and T10 vertebrae concerning for malignancy. PET-CT showed multiple hypermetabolic osteolytic lesions (SUV max 18.64) in the left sphenoid wing; C4–C5, T2, T10, L5, S1, and S5 vertebrae; right humeral head; bilateral humeri; and right proximal femur. No lymph node enlargement or extranodal organ involvement was identified.

What is your differential diagnosis?

A 13-year-old Syrian girl presented with a 2-month history of right flank pain. She denied hematuria, dysuria, weight loss, or a history of thyroid or renal disease. On examination, her abdomen was soft and non-tender, with no palpable masses; blood pressure was slightly elevated. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL, creatinine 0.61 mg/dL, and normal thyroid function; the remainder of her blood work was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a heterogeneous mass measuring 13 × 14 cm in the right kidney. Contrast-enhanced MSCT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed a large centrally necrotic right renal tumor with homogeneous contrast enhancement, no evidence of thoracic metastases or lymphadenopathy, no ovarian masses, and multiple stones in the left kidney.

An 18-year-old Chinese woman noted a grey dot in the central vision of her left eye 4 days before presentation. She had a known plexiform neurofibroma of the arm confirmed by biopsy 1 year earlier; otherwise, she denied medical history, trauma, family history, smoking, coffee, tea, illicit drugs, or oral contraceptive use. Blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg. Visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye, with no relative afferent pupillary defect. Slit-lamp examination showed mild subcapsular cataracts bilaterally. Automated perimetry revealed a small central scotoma in the left eye. Fundus examination demonstrated a swollen optic disc in the right eye and, in the left eye, a parafoveal grey-white deep retinal lesion and a cotton-wool spot in the posterior pole. Fluorescein angiography showed a focal retinal filling defect corresponding to the cotton-wool spot and hypofluorescence without leakage at the right optic disc. Swept-source optical coherence tomography of the left macula revealed hyperreflective bands in the inner nuclear layer consistent with paracentral acute middle maculopathy. Carotid Doppler ultrasound and transthoracic echocardiography were normal. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count with differential, liver enzymes, renal function, lipid profile, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, blood glucose, hemoglobin A1C, antinuclear antibody, anti–double-stranded DNA antibody, anti–neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, syphilis serology, HIV, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, angiotensin-converting enzyme, and tests for protein C, protein S, antithrombin III, and homocystinuria, were unremarkable. Magnetic resonance angiography of the brain was normal. Brain MRI with and without contrast showed bilateral vestibular schwannomas, a parasellar mass consistent with a meningioma, and a cervical extramedullary lesion. Orbital CT showed normal optic nerve contours and calcified lesions in the right temporal lobe.

A 70-year-old man was evaluated for a 3-month history of fever, malaise, and chills. His past history included primary aldosteronism with a right adrenal mass treated medically for two years. Initial laboratory tests showed anemia (hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (28×10^3/µL), leukopenia (3.19×10^3/µL), elevated lactate dehydrogenase (586 U/L), and an elevated soluble interleukin-2 receptor level; aldosterone was below the lower limit of normal. Computed tomography revealed bilaterally enlarged adrenal glands (right 4.3×1.6 cm, left 4.0×2.5 cm) and hepatosplenomegaly (spleen 12.5×3.6 cm) without lymphadenopathy or ascites. On examination, he was febrile (39.0℃), tachycardic (122 beats/min), and hypotensive (91/56 mmHg off antihypertensives); there was abdominal distention and pretibial edema but no palpable lymphadenopathy.

A random skin biopsy was negative for lymphomatous infiltration. Bone marrow biopsy showed diffuse proliferation of large atypical lymphoid cells that were CD20-positive, bcl-6–positive, MUM-1–positive, CD5-negative, CD10-negative, and had no intravascular infiltration on CD34 staining; EBV in situ hybridization was negative. A transjugular liver biopsy demonstrated similar lymphoid infiltrates. Extranodal diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (non–germinal-center type) was diagnosed, and bilateral adrenal dominance supported a diagnosis of primary adrenal lymphoma. He received immunochemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisolone, and rituximab, complicated by tumor lysis syndrome, disseminated intravascular coagulation with splenic hemorrhage, and congestive heart failure, all of which resolved. Two weeks after rituximab, laboratory abnormalities normalized.

On day 42 after admission (two weeks after completing chemotherapy), he developed bilateral neuralgia of the upper and lower extremities that was symmetrical, more proximal than typical vincristine toxicity, and rapidly progressive, followed by limb weakness.

A 78-year-old man presented with progressively enlarging bilateral eyelid masses over 12 months. He denied vision changes, itching, photophobia, floaters, or diplopia. On examination, he had bilateral, rubbery, mobile, tender masses at the superior temporal aspects of the anterior orbits. The masses were excised; grossly they comprised yellow, lobulated tissue up to 1.0 cm. A touch imprint demonstrated a monotonous small-cell lymphoid population. Flow cytometry of the lesion showed that lymphocytes comprised 29% of events, with T cells (CD3+) making up 62% and B cells (CD19+) approximately 15%. Most B cells coexpressed CD5, were 14% FMC-7 positive, and demonstrated lambda light-chain restriction (kappa:lambda ratio, 1:13). Permanent histologic sections showed a monotonous population of small, mature lymphocytes with angulated, hyperchromatic nuclei and scant cytoplasm, within a background of hyalinized vessels.

A 76-year-old woman with a history of heart failure and non–insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus presented with a two-week history of gross hematuria and dysuria. Physical examination was unremarkable. An abdominal ultrasound showed a mass on the right lateral wall of the urinary bladder. Rigid cystoscopy revealed a 4–5 cm hemorrhagic, exophytic, and invasive lesion involving the right lateral bladder wall and ureteral orifice. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a soft-tissue mass with multiple calcified foci in the right bladder wall, extending posteriorly, with dilation of the ipsilateral ureter. CT of the chest and a bone scan showed no evidence of metastasis. The clinical stage was determined to be cT3N0M0. The patient underwent transurethral resection of the tumor.

A 26-year-old African American man with AIDS presented with pleuritic chest pain, exertional dyspnea, and hemoptysis for 3 weeks. He reported a 10-pound weight loss over 6 months, drenching night sweats, and fever. He denied tobacco use, neurological, gastrointestinal, or dermatological symptoms, and had no recent travel. He was poorly compliant with dapsone and elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir. Three months earlier, he was admitted for similar complaints and diagnosed with atypical pneumonia; a CT scan then showed diffuse fine noncalcified nodular densities in both lungs and small to moderate bilateral axillary, mediastinal, and hilar adenopathy. Bronchoscopy was unrevealing, and bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii, acid-fast bacilli, and fungal infection.

On examination, he had bilateral axillary and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy and signs of right lower lung zone consolidation. There were no skin or mucosal lesions. Laboratory studies showed normocytic anemia, a normal metabolic panel, and a CD4 count of 102 cells/μL (17%). A repeat CT scan of the chest showed significant worsening of fibronodular infiltrates with consolidation in the right middle and lower lobes and left upper and lower lobes, along with bilateral axillary, supraclavicular, mediastinal, and hilar lymphadenopathy.

A 39‐year‐old woman presented with a 4-year history of a progressively enlarging mass in the left temporal scalp region. She reported left‐sided facial pain and weakness, difficulty opening her mouth and chewing, and hearing loss in the left ear. Previous symptomatic treatments provided no relief. On examination, she appeared ill and cachectic, with trismus grade 2 and left facial nerve palsy grade 3. A non‐tender, soft, warm scalp mass measuring 15 cm by 20 cm occupied the left temporal and parotid regions; the inferolateral skin was tense and shiny, and the left external auditory canal was obliterated. She was otherwise healthy, with no personal or family history of cancer; she neither smoked nor drank alcohol. Contrast CT and MRI of the head and neck demonstrated a destructive mass eroding the temporal bone with intracranial extension. CT scans of the chest and abdomen–pelvis showed no evidence of distant metastases. A working impression of a malignant scalp tumor was made, and an incisional biopsy was performed, yielding a diagnosis “suggestive of basal cell carcinoma.”

A 67-year-old man from a rural region of Nepal presented with a 2-month history of vague abdominal pain, discomfort, and a sudden reduction in appetite. He was a non-smoker, non-alcoholic farmer with no significant family or exposure history. On examination, a large, firm mass was palpable, filling both flanks; cardiopulmonary and other systemic examinations were unremarkable, and bowel and bladder habits were normal. Routine hematological, serological, urine, and coagulation studies were within normal limits. A chest radiograph showed no pleural masses or bony lesions. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a large mass occupying the abdominal and pelvic cavities with bilateral mild hydronephrosis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a well-defined, heterogeneously enhancing abdomino-pelvic mass with central areas of degeneration and necrosis, displacing adjacent viscera. “CT differentials of gastrointestinal stromal tumor or soft tissue sarcoma were given.” Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology yielded highly cellular smears composed of spindle-shaped tumor cells with moderate cytoplasm and elongated nuclei; necrosis and atypical mitoses were absent. The cytology impression was “spindle cell lesion,” and a biopsy was advised.

A 61-year-old man with hypertension and a remote smoking history presented with nonspecific abdominal pain and 30 lb of unintentional weight loss. Laboratory evaluation revealed hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL (MCV 94.1 fL), alkaline phosphatase 226 U/L, ALT 76 U/L, AST 71 U/L, total bilirubin 2.2 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL.

Upper endoscopy showed an edematous pylorus that was traversed with difficulty. In the duodenal bulb, there was a medium-sized fungating, polypoid, ulcerated mass with stigmata of recent bleeding. Multiple biopsies were obtained. Colonoscopy was normal.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 7.8 × 7.0 × 7.1 cm irregular heterogeneous mass contiguous with the duodenum, gastric antrum, and pancreas, with pancreatic duct dilatation, two hepatic lesions, mild intrahepatic biliary ductal dilatation, encasement of the celiac axis and branches, and occlusion of the portal and splenic veins.

Biopsy specimens showed a spindle cell neoplasm with surface ulceration. Immunohistochemical stains for CK117, S-100, CD34, SMA, and AE1/AE3 were performed, and the specimen was sent for tertiary review.

A 66‐year‐old Japanese woman was referred for evaluation of a left posterior mediastinal mass. The lesion had been noted incidentally on chest radiography decades earlier and was unchanged over 5 years. She was asymptomatic, with only mild hypertension on examination and normal routine laboratory tests, including tumor markers. 

Contrast‐enhanced CT showed a well‐demarcated mass adjacent to the left thoracic spine, with a central soft‐tissue density (27 HU) and slight heterogeneous enhancement (35 HU). MRI demonstrated intermediate to high T2 signal and low T1 signal in the central portion, with mild heterogeneous enhancement; fat‐suppressed T1 images confirmed abundant peripheral fat. FDG‐PET/CT revealed uptake in the central region (SUVmax, 2.26), suggesting low‐grade malignancy. 

CT‐guided needle biopsy from the central area revealed mature adipocytes, spindle cells in a fibrotic background, scant ganglion cells, and S100‐positive spindle cells. A peripheral nerve sheath tumor, spindle cell lipoma, and well‐differentiated liposarcoma were all considered, but no definitive diagnosis could be made.

A 48-year-old woman with hypothyroidism, peptic ulcer disease, and a history of malignant melanoma of the left heel (stage IIB excised in early 2019; progressed to stage IV in late 2019) was treated with nivolumab and ipilimumab. In January 2021, she presented with colicky abdominal pain and vomiting 4 days after immunotherapy. Abdominal CT scan showed intussusception of the mid–to–distal ileal loops without signs of bowel compromise or perforation. She was stable and managed conservatively, with symptom resolution; a second similar episode occurred four days later and was again managed conservatively. In May 2021, she returned with two days of colicky abdominal pain, one day of obstipation, and bilious vomiting. CT scan revealed ileo–ileal intussusception without perforation or bowel compromise.

A 33-year-old right-handed woman with a 15-year history of slowly progressive proximal muscle weakness, previously diagnosed as spinal muscular atrophy type IV based on EMG and SMN gene studies, presented with new neurologic symptoms. Over 2 months she developed intermittent neck pain radiating to both arms, worse on the right, with numbness along the medial forearm and the little and middle fingers. She noted worsening leg weakness with frequent falls and difficulty walking, significantly affecting daily activities. She denied sphincter dysfunction at that time.

On examination, vital signs were stable. Mental status and cranial nerves were normal. In the upper limbs she had proximal muscle wasting with fasciculations, hypotonia, hyporeflexia, and strength 4/5. In the lower limbs she had spasticity, hyperreflexia with sustained clonus, an extensor plantar response, and strength 3/5. A sensory level was present at T4. Gait was waddling but coordination was intact.

MRI of the spinal cord revealed an intramedullary mixed solid and cystic lesion extending from C3 to T4, causing cord expansion; the solid component was low signal on T1, high signal on T2, and demonstrated gadolinium enhancement. MRI of the brain was normal.

A 50-year-old man presented with a more than one-year history of recurrent left lumbar pain. He had no significant medical, surgical, or family history. The pain was initially relieved by self-administration of paracetamol but later became more intense and prolonged, with diminishing relief from analgesics. On examination in primary care, vital signs were normal, and abdominal and flank examinations were unremarkable; a urine dipstick test was negative. Laboratory studies showed preserved renal function. Renal ultrasonography suggested a cystic lesion at the superior pole of the left kidney with exophytic extension. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a well-defined, lobulated, unilocular cystic mass measuring 110×50×30 mm in the left perirenal space, with bumpy contours and no enhancement after iodinated contrast, abutting the posterior-superior aspect of the left kidney but preserving the renal capsule. No additional lesions were identified in the contralateral kidney or intraperitoneal cavity.

A 17-year-old nulliparous female presented with a two-year history of gradually progressive abdominal distension. She initially sought evaluation for bloating but was advised to diet for presumed weight gain. She denied pain, vaginal bleeding, or systemic symptoms. There was no personal or family history of cancer. On examination, her BMI was 20.5 kg/m2, blood pressure 125/85 mmHg, pulse 89/min, and SpO2 95% on room air. The abdomen was markedly distended with a palpable mass rising approximately 3 cm above the umbilicus. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated an 18 cm diameter ovarian tumor. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL with a microcytic profile (MCV 73.2 fL); APTT, INR, electrolytes, urea, and creatinine were normal. Tumor markers included HE4 69.1 pmol/L (N ≤ 60.5), LDH 202 U/L (N ≤ 48.5), with alpha-fetoprotein 4.54 ng/mL (N ≤ 5.8), CA-125 23.1 U/mL (N ≤ 35), and β-hCG <0.2 mIU/mL all within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a large, fluid-filled lesion measuring 19.3 × 6.2 × 21 cm, located in the pelvis and mid-abdomen, displacing the uterus and compressing the aorta and inferior vena cava. The lesion appeared unilocular with a 1.5 mm wall and no septations or solid components, and was suggestive of an ovarian origin.

A 52-year-old Han man presented with a several-month history of a gradually enlarging mass on the left side of his tracheal stoma and progressive dyspnea. His history was notable for squamous cell carcinoma of the glottis treated with partial laryngectomy in September 2011, followed by recurrence in 2016 managed with total laryngectomy, cervical lymph node dissection, and 60 Gy of radiotherapy over 1½ months. He had healed uneventfully until April 2018, when the parastomal mass was first noted.

On examination in October 2018, there was an immobile, well-defined, partially compressible, non-pulsatile 4 cm × 4 cm mass at the left lateral margin of the tracheal stoma, causing tracheostomal stenosis. No other cervical lymphadenopathy was present. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed a 5 cm × 4 cm, well-circumscribed, non-enhancing, cystic–solid mass adjacent to the left side of the stoma. Fine-needle aspiration yielded about 10 mL of yellowish-white fluid with a triglyceride level of 26.5 mmol/L, protein 58.0 g/L, glucose 8.5 mmol/L, and a white-cell count of 1.0 × 10^9/L (96% lymphocytes), consistent with chyle. The mass shrank after aspiration but refilled by the next day, and a second aspiration yielded similar fluid. Neck ultrasonography revealed a 43 mm × 36 mm mixed-echoic mass between the left thyroid lobe and the great vessels. Other preoperative studies were unremarkable.

A previously healthy 10-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of partial seizures occurring during sleep. She responded well to carbamazepine. On examination, her vital signs were normal, and routine hematology and serum chemistry showed no abnormalities. Noncontrast CT of the head revealed a well-circumscribed, superficial, hyperdense solid nodule in the left frontoparietal lobe with remodeling of the inner table of the skull. MRI demonstrated a lesion that was isointense on T1-weighted images with perilesional contrast enhancement and hypointense on T2-weighted images. There was no significant mass effect or ventricular involvement. The patient underwent gross total resection of the mass. On gross examination, the specimen was a white, firm nodule measuring 1.8 cm × 1.6 cm.

A 73-year-old man presented with dyspnoea on exertion and lower limb swelling for more than 1 month. His New York Heart Association functional class was II. He had been noted to have a 5 × 4 cm pericardial cyst on routine CT 3.5 years earlier, which had not been treated. His medical history included a lacunar infarction 4 years earlier without sequelae. On examination, neck veins were slightly dilated with a mildly positive Kussmaul’s sign. High-sensitivity troponin-T was 48.52 pg/mL (normal 0–14) and N-terminal pro–b-type natriuretic peptide was 1184 pg/mL (normal 0–125); all other blood tests were normal. ECG showed atrial flutter and right bundle branch block. Enhanced ECG-gated cardiac CT revealed that the cyst had grown to 7 × 4.5 cm and compressed the superior vena cava and right atrium. Transthoracic echocardiography confirmed a large elliptical cystic mass compressing these structures with preserved left ventricular function and no regional wall motion abnormalities. Coronary angiography demonstrated diffuse 30% stenosis and calcification of the left anterior descending artery, 30% ostial stenosis of the left circumflex artery, and no stenosis or compression of the right coronary artery. The working diagnosis was a pericardial or epicardial cyst causing his symptoms. A median sternotomy with cardiopulmonary bypass on standby was planned.

A 47-year-old Japanese woman presented with a painless, palpable tumor on the left side of her anus. On examination, the lesion was elastic, firm, smooth-surfaced, and non-tender. She reported no other symptoms. 

Computed tomography of the pelvis demonstrated a well-circumscribed mass in the sacrococcygeal space without invasion of the rectum. T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging revealed heterogeneous high signal in the periphery of the mass and extremely high signal intensity centrally, suggesting abundant internal blood flow. Rectoscopic evaluation showed an intact mucosal surface, and endoscopic ultrasonography confirmed that the lesion did not originate from the rectal wall. Fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography yielded a maximum standardized uptake value of 2.64 (benign soft-tissue masses: 1.42–1.80; malignant soft-tissue masses: 3.16–4.20). 

Because of its vascularity, the preoperative differential diagnosis included solitary fibrous tumor, fibrous histiocytoma, synovial sarcoma, mesenchymal chondrosarcoma, and hemangiosarcoma. A biopsy was deferred to avoid the risk of needle‐track seeding.

A 34-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 2 with two prior cesarean deliveries (last childbirth 6 years earlier), presented with worsening lower abdominal pain of one day’s duration. Her menstrual cycles were regular without dysmenorrhea; last menstrual period was 21 days earlier. There was no history of trauma, bowel or bladder changes. On admission, vital signs showed tachypnea, tachycardia, and blood pressure 90/60 mmHg. Hemoglobin was 8.0 g/dL. Abdominal examination revealed a firm lower-segment mass and mild tenderness. 

Transabdominal ultrasound demonstrated echogenic free fluid consistent with intraperitoneal hemorrhage, a 15 × 10 cm and a 5.9 × 4.7 cm uterine myoma, endometrial thickness of 8 mm, and bilaterally polycystic-appearing ovaries. A urine β-hCG level was 1.2 mIU/L. Computed tomography was planned but deferred due to hemodynamic instability. The working diagnosis was intra-abdominal hemorrhage of unknown origin with an incidental uterine fibroid. The patient received packed-cell transfusion, and an interdisciplinary team arranged for diagnostic laparoscopy.

A 30-year-old woman initially presented with an ovarian mass and underwent left oophorectomy; histopathology showed an atypical carcinoid tumor of the ovary. Two years later, during a caesarean section, an atypical carcinoid was found in the right ovary. She remained disease-free for two years, then developed chest discomfort. Chest CT demonstrated massive pericardial fluid accumulation, pleural effusion, and an osteolytic lesion in the left second rib. Contrast-enhanced CT of the upper abdomen revealed heterogeneous, hyperenhancing masses in the ribs, anterior mediastinum, pancreas, and liver. Bone scintigraphy showed increased uptake in the skull, multiple vertebrae, ribs, humerus, and pelvis. PET-CT demonstrated hypermetabolic lesions in the parathyroid glands, thymus, lung, pancreas, adrenal glands, and metastatic foci in bones, liver, and lymph nodes. A needle biopsy of the left second rib lesion showed cellular nests of small, round epithelial cells with neuroendocrine architecture; the cells were synaptophysin positive and had a Ki-67 index <1%. Review of the initial left ovarian tumor confirmed trabecular and insular patterns, areas of increased mitoses and necrosis, synaptophysin positivity, and a Ki-67 index ≈15%; tumor cells were negative for TTF-1, PAX-8, CDX-2, CD99, inhibin-α, and calretinin. Laboratory evaluation revealed a serum calcium of 2.17 mmol/L (normal 2.11–2.52) and an intact PTH of 33.9 pg/mL (normal 12–88); thyroid hormones were normal.

A 52-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with a 12-month history of progressive right-eye proptosis. On examination, the right visual acuity was decreased, the globe was displaced inferiorly, there was severe conjunctival chemosis, and corneal sensitivity was reduced; the left eye was normal. An incisional biopsy at an outside institution reported a fusocellular neoplasm with a hemangiopericytoma pattern “compatible with monophasic synovial sarcoma.” Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI of the orbit showed a well-defined right intrasonic mass measuring 5.3 × 4.6 × 3.6 cm, causing globe displacement but without extension into the temporal fossa. On admission, his Karnofsky score was 90% and his ECOG performance status was grade 0.

A 72-year-old woman, lifelong non-smoker, with hypertension, dyslipidemia, GERD, allergic rhinitis, and asthma treated with inhaled budesonide–formoterol and montelukast, presented with a 6-week history of wheezing, mild productive cough with mucous sputum, and hemoptysis. She denied fever, chest pain, dyspnea, night sweats, or weight loss.  
On examination: afebrile (36.5 °C), blood pressure 128/60 mmHg, pulse 80 bpm, oxygen saturation 97% on room air; pulmonary auscultation revealed bilateral wheezing and rhonchi.  
Laboratory tests: leukocytes 15 000/μL (neutrophils 60.5%), eosinophils 1.1%, lymphocytes 28.7%, monocytes 9.4%; hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL; platelets 227 000/μL; C-reactive protein 0.0 mg/dL; total IgE 17 UI/mL; HIV serology negative.  
Chest imaging: elongated 3.4 cm mass in the left upper lobe, suggestive of mucocele with a “finger in glove” pattern.  
Bronchoscopy: gelatinous, digitiform mass emerging from the apico-posterior subsegmental bronchus of the left upper lobe, which was nearly removed on biopsy; cultures negative. Histopathology of the biopsy specimen showed fungal structures compatible with Aspergillus and no malignant cells.  
Serologic tests for Aspergillus (galactomannan, precipitins) and skin prick testing were negative. The patient received itraconazole 200 mg twice daily. One month later, she had clinical improvement but no change on imaging.  
Given persistent radiographic abnormality, endobronchial aspergilloma coexisting with a malignancy was suspected. The patient declined repeat bronchoscopy; an ^18F-FDG PET-CT was performed, revealing a left upper lobe mass with contiguous bronchial involvement and an SUV of 19. No other abnormal uptake was identified; head CT was unremarkable.

A 76-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of a gradually enlarging, painful lump over the right clavicle. There was no history of trauma, weight loss, night sweats, fever, or prior malignancy. On examination, a hard, nonmobile mass measuring approximately 5 cm was palpable in the right supraclavicular region. Laboratory studies, including inflammatory markers and biochemical bone profile, were within normal limits. 

Plain radiographs of the right clavicle demonstrated a permeative lesion in the diaphysis. MRI of the right clavicle revealed high signal intensity on STIR sequences and low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, replacing the normal fatty marrow, with an associated soft-tissue mass. Postcontrast MRI showed generalized enhancement of the lesion. Both MRI and ultrasound demonstrated preservation of the bony cortex, and Doppler ultrasound showed no neovascularization within the mass.

A 6-month-old female infant was referred for evaluation of a right upper-quadrant abdominal mass. She had a one-month history of fever unresponsive to antibiotics, right hypochondrial pain, and progressive abdominal enlargement without jaundice. Perinatal and developmental history were unremarkable. On examination, her liver was palpable with a span of 8 cm (normal 5–5.5 cm) with tenderness in the right hypochondrium. Laboratory tests revealed microcytic hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin 8.4 g/dl), leukocytosis (13.1×10^3/mm^3), thrombocytosis (620×10^3/mm^3), a slightly elevated alpha-fetoprotein level (26.6 ng/ml), and normal liver function tests. Abdominal ultrasound showed a well-defined heterogeneous mass in the right lobe of the liver with cystic degeneration and calcific foci, measuring 7.4×8.4 cm. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a large nonenhancing hypodense cystic lesion occupying segments V–VII of the right liver (8×8×8.3 cm), with an exophytic component encroaching on the right suprarenal region and inferior displacement of the right kidney; no enlarged abdominal lymph nodes were seen. Based on imaging, the mass was highly suggestive of a mesenchymal hamartoma of the liver, with hepatoblastoma as an alternative consideration. The patient was scheduled for surgical resection and histopathological confirmation.

A 31-year-old woman, G2P2, with no significant medical history, presented with a painless swelling of the right labia majora that she had noticed for several months. She reported no discomfort, skin changes, bleeding, discharge, dyspareunia, urinary symptoms, or defecatory dysfunction. On examination, there was a 100 × 40 mm non-tender, soft-tissue mass with a smooth surface on the right labia majora, extending to the right lateral vaginal wall and the anal canal. Inguinal lymph nodes were not enlarged. 

Transvaginal ultrasound revealed echogenic fluid in the right ischiorectal fossa extending to the perineum, suspected to be an abscess, but this finding was not correlated with the patient’s symptoms. Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging showed a mass measuring 137 × 60 mm in the axial plane and 190 mm in the coronal plane, possibly related to a neurogenic tumor, without invasion of surrounding organs but adjacent to the lower rectum. The lesion was homogeneously hypointense on T1-weighted images and exhibited a mixed, mostly hypointense signal with streaks of hyperintensity on T2-weighted images.

A 53-year-old man presented with progressive dyspnea and chest pain following a COVID-19 infection. He had no significant past medical history, but a family history notable for head and neck cancer, colorectal cancer, and lymphoma. He was a current smoker without occupational exposures or recent travel. Laboratory studies, including blood count and chemistry panels, were within normal limits. 

Transthoracic echocardiography showed acute right heart strain with interventricular septal flattening and reduced right ventricular ejection fraction. Computed tomography angiography of the chest revealed a large central filling defect in the pulmonary trunk, extending into the right pulmonary artery, causing subtotal occlusion and consistent with pulmonary embolism. Coronary artery disease was excluded by cardiac catheterization. Thrombolytic therapy produced no significant reduction in the filling defect, and the patient underwent surgical thrombectomy of the right ventricular outflow tract, pulmonary trunk, and right pulmonary artery.

Gross examination of the specimen showed mixed older thrombotic material and a firm tumor mass. Microscopic examination revealed a malignant embolus with areas of clear-cell morphology and areas of spindle-cell morphology. Portions contained a poorly differentiated mesenchymal neoplasm with high cellularity and pleomorphism. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated strong nuclear expression of MDM2 and weak nuclear expression of CDK4, with negative staining for pan-cytokeratin, CD31, CD34, desmin, smooth muscle actin, and S100. Fluorescence in situ hybridization showed MDM2 amplification.

A 58-year-old Ukrainian woman presented with a 10-month history of progressive hoarseness, dry cough, and dyspnea. Her past medical history was notable for autoimmune thyroiditis with a left thyroid nodule treated with levothyroxine since 2019 and for endometrial clear cell carcinoma managed 16 years earlier by total hysterectomy, lymph node dissection, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy; she had not attended follow-up for over 10 years. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. Neck ultrasound demonstrated a 32 × 14 mm hypoechoic nodule in the posterior aspect of the left thyroid lobe adjacent to the trachea and the expected course of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the nodule was benign (Bethesda category II). Flexible fibrolaryngoscopy showed bowing and immobility of the left vocal fold in the median position without intrinsic laryngeal lesions. A provisional diagnosis of idiopathic left vocal cord palsy was made, and a contrast-enhanced chest CT scan was recommended.

A 73-year-old man presented with two friable, fungating, bleeding lesions over the right pre-auricular region and the angle of the mandible. One year earlier, he noted a painless swelling over the right pre-auricular area without facial weakness; two months before presentation the overlying skin broke down into a fungating mass, followed shortly by a second lesion at the mandibular angle. He had no fever, weight loss, other skin lesions, or relevant medical history; he quit smoking 12 years ago.

On examination there were two ulcerating nodules measuring approximately 2×3 cm (pre-auricular) and 3×2 cm (mandibular angle), with enlargement of the right parotid gland. Facial nerve function was intact, and there was no cervical lymphadenopathy. Naso-endoscopy and oropharyngeal exam were unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck showed exophytic, homogeneously enhancing masses with ulceration involving the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland (mass measuring 1.9×3.0×2.6 cm) and diffuse enlargement of that lobe (4.8×2.5×5.4 cm) with loss of the fat plane. CT of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a hypodense, enhancing lesion in segment IVa of the liver measuring 2.5×2.9 cm, confirmed as metastatic on ultrasound.

While awaiting further evaluation, a wedge biopsy of all skin lesions was performed. Histopathological examination showed diffuse intradermal infiltration of large pleomorphic malignant lymphoid cells with irregular (reniform) nuclei, prominent nucleoli, moderate to abundant cytoplasm, and a heavy neutrophilic background. There was no evidence of epidermotropism.

A 10-year-old boy presented with a 3-week history of gradually progressive jaundice and tea-colored urine but no acholic stools or pruritus. He denied abdominal pain, bleeding, weight loss, anorexia, bowel changes, fever, or vomiting. There was no history of worm passage, medication use, tuberculosis exposure, or family liver disease. On examination, he was well nourished with generalized jaundice. The abdomen was flat with normoactive bowel sounds, non-tender on deep palpation, and no ascites. The liver edge was firm and palpable 3 cm below the right costal margin; the spleen was not palpable.

Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 86 g/L, WBC 15.2 ×10^9/L, platelets 623 ×10^9/L without eosinophilia. AST was 127 IU/L, ALT 65 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 745 IU/L, GGT 496 U/L; total bilirubin 11.58 mg/dL with direct bilirubin 10.15 mg/dL. INR was 2.34; albumin was 44 g/L. Serologies for hepatitis A and B were non-reactive.

An initial abdominal ultrasound showed tubular hyperechoic structures in a dilated common bile duct (7 cm). The patient received mebendazole but symptoms and jaundice worsened. A repeat ultrasound revealed an 8.3 × 2.1 cm heterogeneous focus spanning from the gallbladder neck to the dilated common bile duct (1.3 cm) with intrahepatic ductal dilatation; the tubular structures were no longer seen.

A 10-month-old male infant was brought by his parents for an asymptomatic swelling of the palate.  The mother first noticed the lesion several weeks earlier; no swelling was noted at birth, and the patient’s age limited reporting of pain or tenderness.  On examination, there was a firm, nonmobile mass in the right posterior hard palate extending from the maxillary tuberosity medially almost to the midline.  Multi-detector CT of the maxilla demonstrated a well-defined, expansile lesion of the maxillary crest with mixed radiolucent and radiopaque internal structure, causing thinning and perforation of the maxillary sinus walls and lateral displacement of the nasal cavity wall.  Based on these radiographic findings, a cemento-ossifying fibroma was considered the most likely diagnosis.

A 54-year-old man with a history of EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma metastatic to pleura, contralateral lung, and bone—treated initially with osimertinib but later with bevacizumab and pemetrexed—was referred for rapid cognitive decline. One week after his most recent chemotherapy, he developed asthenia and dizziness. On examination, he could not recognize family members and scored 13 on the Mini-Mental State Examination. He had an unsteady gait, dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing, and a positive Romberg sign; cranial nerves, strength, sensation, reflexes, and meningeal signs were otherwise normal. Enhanced cranial MRI revealed interstitial brain edema without focal lesions. Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 220 mm H₂O; CSF protein was 196 mg/dL, glucose 2.70 mmol/L, lactate dehydrogenase 4 U/L. CSF culture, smears for Cryptococcus neoformans and acid-fast bacilli, and IgM for common viruses and syphilis were all negative. CSF cytology revealed only a few lymphocytes.

A 51-year-old man presented with a 15-year history of a slow-growing midline dorsal tongue lesion. He denied dysphagia or airway impairment but noted recent changes in speech articulation. The lesion was asymptomatic except during upper respiratory infections, when it would swell and occasionally bleed after trauma. His medical history was notable only for diverticulitis, prior hernia repair, and chronic knee pain. He took ibuprofen and celecoxib and had no known allergies.

On examination, there was a firm, nodular, 2.5 cm by 1.5 cm lesion on the anterior dorsal midline tongue, covered by intact mucosa with normal papillae; small healing tip ulcers were attributed to trauma. The lesion was non-tender. The remainder of the oral cavity and oropharynx was unremarkable. Palpation of the tongue base was normal, laryngeal appearance was normal, and nasopharyngoscopy showed no abnormalities.

To establish a definitive diagnosis and relieve potential functional impairment, the patient underwent excision under local anesthesia with 5 mm margins via a midline glossectomy. The procedure was well tolerated, and on follow-up the tongue had healed without evidence of recurrence.

A 39-year-old woman with AML in morphologic remission underwent sibling-matched allogeneic stem cell transplantation 57 days prior and presented with 1 week of painless left eye redness and swelling. On examination, visual acuity was 6/9 in the left eye, with periorbital oedema, marked conjunctival chemosis, limited extraocular motility, intraocular pressure of 38 mmHg, and anisocoria with a dilated unreactive pupil. The anterior chamber had 1+ white cells, and the posterior segment showed serous retinal detachments without optic disc swelling, retinitis, or vasculitis. She was admitted and treated empirically with systemic antibiotics, antifungals, topical steroid drops, and glaucoma therapy for suspected orbital cellulitis or infectious scleritis. CT of the orbits revealed subtle left lacrimal gland thickening. Because of progression to enlarging serous retinal detachments, she received three pulsed doses of 1 g intravenous methylprednisolone with resolution of chemosis, revealing a subconjunctival mass. One week later, she returned with left eye pain, headache, nausea, and vomiting. Her visual acuity worsened to counting fingers; intraocular pressure was 55 mmHg, a hypopyon was present, and gonioscopy showed 270° angle closure with anterior ciliary-body rotation. OCT demonstrated retinal folds and dependent subretinal fluid from an exudative detachment. Fluorescein angiography showed diffuse pooling within the detachment without vascular leak or ischaemia. FDG-PET showed metabolically active soft tissue thickening in the left globe, and MRI confirmed exudative retinal detachments with thickening of the globe wall. She was diagnosed with secondary acute angle-closure glaucoma due to rapidly enlarging serous retinal detachments.

A 66-year-old Middle Eastern man with a 10-year history of controlled hypertension presented with a 6-month history of insidious, dull left hypochondriac pain radiating to the back and rated 6/10, partially relieved by over-the-counter analgesics. He denied gastrointestinal symptoms, B symptoms, toxin exposures, trauma, or prior similar complaints. He smoked 100 pack-years and took an angiotensin receptor blocker and a calcium channel blocker. On examination, vital signs were normal. The abdomen was distended; there was tenderness, guarding, and dullness to percussion in the left hypochondrium, and deep palpation was limited by pain. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including a comprehensive panel, were within normal limits. Transabdominal ultrasound revealed two well-demarcated heterogeneous masses with necrotic components in the left upper quadrant, measuring approximately 13×12.5 cm and 15×10×13 cm, with no free fluid. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis confirmed two large heterogeneous isointense masses with peripheral contrast uptake in the left hypochondrium—one measuring 16×11×14 cm adjacent to the stomach and extending into the retroperitoneum, the other 13×8×9 cm beneath the left hemidiaphragm near the spleen—and showed no lymphadenopathy, metastases, or free fluid.

A three-year-old boy, born full term with normal development, presented with an eight-month history of a gradually enlarging, painless abdominal lump and distention. He also had a one-month history of low-grade fever and a diffuse rash. There was no history of vomiting, jaundice, or significant past medical or family history.

On examination, a large, non-tender abdominal mass was palpable in the right hypochondrium, epigastrium, and periumbilical region, crossing the midline. There was no splenomegaly or other stigmata of chronic liver disease.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, normal liver and renal function tests, and a normal serum alpha-fetoprotein level. Viral markers for hepatitis B and C and an echinococcal antigen test were negative.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated an avascular, hypoechoic liver mass with internal septations. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 10.0 × 5.9 cm, well-defined, multiloculated, variably sized, peripherally enhancing cystic lesion in segments IV A and IV B of the left hepatic lobe. No other intra-abdominal abnormalities were noted.

A preoperative diagnosis of a complex hepatic cyst was made, and the patient underwent a left partial hepatectomy. The resected specimen measured 8 × 7 × 3 cm and contained multiple cysts (largest 6 cm) separated by gray-white septa, filled with pale yellow serous fluid. No necrosis, hemorrhage, or solid nodules were identified.

Microscopically, the lesion comprised multiple thin-walled cysts lined by cuboidal biliary epithelium, separated by fibromyxoid stroma containing spindled to stellate mesenchymal cells. At the periphery, clusters and nodules of cytologically bland hepatocytes retained normal plate architecture.

A 65-year-old Japanese man with a 17-year history of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) maintained on prednisolone and cyclophosphamide was evaluated after a new right lower lobe nodule was detected on chest imaging at age 64. His GPA had been diagnosed at age 47 on the basis of positive PR3-ANCA serology and biopsies showing necrotizing granulomatous inflammation in the nasal mucosa, lung, and kidney. At age 64, a chest radiograph confirmed a nodular shadow in the right lower field. He had a smoking history of 56 pack-years. Laboratory studies showed renal dysfunction, an elevated C-reactive protein level, and positive C-ANCA without an increase from prior levels. Prednisolone was increased because of suspected relapse, but the nodule did not change in size. Serum tumor markers rose: squamous cell carcinoma antigen from 3.2 to 6.2 ng/mL. On examination, breath sounds were decreased in the right middle and lower lung fields. Repeat chest radiography revealed an irregular opacity with lobar collapse in the right lower field. PET/CT showed FDG uptake in the right lower lung nodule, mediastinal lymph nodes, thoracic wall, right iliac bone, and right retroperitoneum. He was admitted for diagnostic bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration.

A 64-year-old man, former smoker (20 cigarettes/day from ages 20 to 25), with a history of asthma treated with inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting β₂-agonists and an ECOG performance status of 0, was referred after an abnormal chest X-ray on routine screening. He was asymptomatic, and routine laboratory tests were normal.

Contrast-enhanced chest CT showed a 6-cm mass abutting the anterior mediastinum and the right upper lobe, multiple nodular shadows along the right pleura, and a moderate right pleural effusion. The origin of the mass (mediastinal vs. pulmonary) was unclear. Bronchoscopic sampling with endobronchial ultrasound guidance of a right upper lobe lesion was non-diagnostic. CT-guided needle biopsy of the mass revealed a solid tumor composed of malignant, non-keratinized squamous cells with surrounding fibrosis; immunohistochemical staining was positive for p40 and CK5/6.

18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated intense uptake in the primary mass (SUVmax 10.95) and multiple pleural nodules (SUVmax 7.08), consistent with pleural dissemination. Molecular testing showed no EGFR mutations, ALK fusions, or ROS1 rearrangements. PD-L1 expression (22C3) was low at 5–10%. The lesion was deemed unresectable. A multidisciplinary team convened to determine whether this represented primary lung cancer or a thymic carcinoma.

A 28-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of abdominal discomfort and blood-tinged urine. Vital signs were normal, and laboratory testing confirmed hematuria. CT intravenous urography showed:
• A 13.4 × 11.7 × 7.3 mm well-defined hypodense lesion in the body of the right adrenal gland with homogeneous avid postcontrast enhancement.  
• An irregular heterogeneous exophytic lesion measuring 4.2 × 3.3 × 3.6 cm in the upper pole of the right kidney, with enhancing septations.  
• A 2.4 × 1.4 × 1.4 cm well-defined hypodense lesion (< 50% exophytic) in the upper pole of the left kidney, with enhancing septations.  
• Multiple simple cortical cysts in both kidneys.  
• A 10.5 × 8.4 mm well-defined hypodense lesion in the body of the pancreas without postcontrast enhancement.  

Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain revealed a 3.3 × 3.3 cm cystic lesion with an avidly enhancing eccentric mural nodule in the right brachium pontis, consistent with a hemangioblastoma; no spinal lesions were seen. Twenty-four-hour urinary metanephrine, normetanephrine, and vanillylmandelic acid levels were all within normal limits.

A 29-year-old woman with hypothyroidism and a history of nasopharyngeal carcinoma treated with radiotherapy and chemotherapy 10 years earlier presented with a 6-month history of gradually worsening right upper-limb weakness, neck pain, and intermittent needle-like pain in a C5–C6 distribution, rated 3–4/10 on the VAS and worse at night, now 6–7/10 and interfering with sleep. On examination, the right deltoid was 0/5, biceps 3/5, wrist extension 3/5, triceps and intrinsic hand muscles 4/5, with hypoesthesia in the C5 and C6 dermatomes; the right biceps and radial reflexes were absent. Nerve conduction studies showed axonal injury of the right brachial plexus, and needle electromyography indicated damage to the brachial plexus. Two months before presentation, PET-CT revealed a new area of increased FDG uptake (SUVmax 7.05) correlating with soft-tissue thickening around the right C5 vertebra. Cervical MRI showed thickening and enhancement of the right C4–5 nerve roots. Brachial plexus MRI demonstrated uniform thickening, hyperintense signal on fluid-sensitive images, and diffuse postcontrast enhancement of the C5 (and to a lesser extent C6) nerve roots extending to the upper trunks, divisions, and cords of the right plexus; the radiology report stated that “these observations may be indicative of neuritis associated with radiation treatment, emphasizing the need for clinical correlation and subsequent follow-up scans.” The multidisciplinary tumor board favored late‐onset radiation-induced brachial plexopathy, and a trial of steroids was initiated without symptomatic improvement. Three months later, repeat MRI showed progression of the thickening with lobulated appearances involving the right C4–5 and C5–6 nerve roots, extension into the lateral plexus and medial intraspinal space at the C4–5 foramen causing cord displacement, described as a “strong indication for the presence of a metastatic process involving the nerves.” PET-CT at that time confirmed advancement of a hypermetabolic lesion along the right neural foramina into the plexus. Urgent decompressive laminectomy at C5–6 was performed, and the resected intradural mass was sent for pathological examination.

A 54-year-old gravida 4, para 4 woman presented with two months of persistent abnormal vaginal bleeding. Her last pregnancy was 12 years earlier, and she had no personal or family history of gestational trophoblastic disease. Vital signs were stable. Cardiac, pulmonary, and extremity examinations were normal. Gynecological examination showed minimal vaginal bleeding and an enlarged, soft uterus approximately the size of an 8-week pregnancy, with mild adnexal tenderness. Laboratory testing revealed a β-hCG level of 199,217 mIU/mL. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated an intracavitary mass measuring 8 × 4 cm with chaotic vascularization on color Doppler. Pelvic MRI confirmed a poorly defined, heterogeneous intrauterine mass measuring 96 mm along its longest axis, with invasion of the cervical stroma and myometrium.

An 8-year-old boy was brought to his pediatrician for right-sided neck swelling of 4 days’ duration. He had no pain, fever, itching, sore throat, fatigue, cough, otalgia, or sick contacts. His medical history was notable only for obesity, and there was no family history of anatomic defects or lymphatic conditions. On examination, there was a soft, nonerythematous, nontender right-sided neck mass measuring 4 × 5 cm; the remainder of the examination was normal.

An oropharyngeal swab was positive for streptococcal infection, and he was prescribed oral amoxicillin. Tests for SARS-CoV-2, influenza, and RSV were negative. Three days later, the mass had become firmer, and by day 5 it measured 5 × 6 cm despite adherence to antibiotics. He was referred to the emergency department.

Laboratory studies showed a normal white-cell count, hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL, serum protein 7.9 g/dL, alanine transaminase 77 U/L, and C-reactive protein 1.62 mg/dL. He was started on intravenous clindamycin.
