Ultrasonography of the right neck soft tissues demonstrated a large, multilocular, multicystic lesion containing mainly anechoic fluid and some internal debris, with moderate blood flow within septations and no solid, nodular, or mass-like areas with internal blood flow. Adjacent soft tissues showed no definite inflammatory changes.

Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a lobulated, multilocular cystic structure in the posterior lateral right neck measuring 6.2 × 4.3 × 7.7 cm, causing mass effect on the sternocleidomastoid muscle and narrowing of the right internal jugular vein; there was mild tonsillar tissue enlargement.

MRI showed a 5.3 × 5.1 × 7.2 cm multilocular lesion that was T2 hyperintense, with T1 hyperintense contents compatible with proteinaceous or hemorrhagic debris, enhancement of septations, and no focal nodular enhancement.

A 42-year-old Haitian man with mixed connective tissue disease, pulmonary hypertension on home oxygen, and chronic diastolic heart failure (preserved ejection fraction) presented with 14 days of progressive shortness of breath, weight loss, fatigue, and pedal edema. He was transferred after rapidly progressive acute kidney injury. 

On admission to the tertiary center:
• Serum creatinine 3.07 mg/dL  
• Urinalysis: 2+ protein, 2+ blood; dysmorphic red cells on microscopy  
• Hemoglobin 6.0 g/dL; MCV 87.5 fL; hematocrit 20.3%  
• White blood cells 5300/mm3 with 90% neutrophils  
• Platelets 130,000/mm3  
• Viral serologies for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV negative  
• Quantiferon TB negative  
• Serologic autoimmune panel (ANA, ANCA, HLA-B27, anti-Smith, anti–SS-A, anti–SS-B, anti–centromere B, anti-Jo, MPO antibody, and CCP) negative except for anti-RNP; ESR elevated  
• Serum albumin 2.1 g/dL; globulin 4.7 g/dL  

Renal biopsy showed:
• Light microscopy: ischemic glomeruli with wrinkled capillary walls; mild interstitial fibrosis/tubular atrophy; fibrin thrombi in some arterioles; mild to moderate arteriosclerosis  
• Immunofluorescence: no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q, fibrinogen, albumin, or light chains; nonspecific tubular cast staining for IgA and light chains  
• Electron microscopy: no immune-type electron-dense deposits; mild podocyte foot-process effacement  

The biopsy was interpreted as renal thrombotic microangiopathy with mild tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis.  

Over the next 4 weeks, the patient remained anemic (hemoglobin ~8 g/dL) requiring transfusions. Additional labs showed LDH 359 U/L, haptoglobin <8 mg/dL, and schistocytes on peripheral smear. Platelets dropped to 74,000/mm3 with normal marrow megakaryocytes. A diagnosis of TMA was made, and plasma exchange (1.5 plasma volumes daily for 5 days) was initiated. Despite therapy, renal function worsened and hemodialysis was required; after 25 days urine output improved and creatinine stabilized at 2.0 mg/dL.

A 10-year-old girl was brought with recurrent swelling of the left labium majus associated with pruritus lasting about one day. The swelling had recurred four times and then spontaneously regressed. She had no fever, rash, or systemic symptoms. There was no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy on examination. An excision biopsy of the lesion was performed. Grossly, the specimen was a single skin-covered soft tissue mass measuring 2.3 × 1.3 × 0.4 cm; on cut section, it was gray-white.

A 42-year-old woman presented with 3 months of abnormal vaginal bleeding. She had one prior vaginal delivery and one induced abortion, and was not on any medications, including hormonal therapy. On pelvic examination, there was a tender, smooth-surfaced mass on the anterior vaginal wall. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a well-circumscribed vaginal mass. MRI revealed a round, well-circumscribed 22×22×32 mm tumor in the vagina with heterogeneous high signal on T2-weighted images, intermediate signal on T1-weighted and fat-suppressed T1-weighted images, and a cord-like structure of markedly low signal on both T1 and T2 sequences extending from the anterior vaginal wall to the mass. The lesion showed high signal on diffusion-weighted imaging (b=1000) and on ADC maps (ADC 1.8–1.9×10^−3 mm^2/s), consistent with T2 shine-through. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated heterogeneous strong enhancement of the tumor, with the low-signal region on T2WI showing more intense enhancement than the high-signal area. No malignant lesions were identified in the pelvis or elsewhere.

A 54-year-old woman with a history of stage IA, HER2-overexpressing invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast underwent lumpectomy, sentinel-node biopsy (no nodal metastasis), six cycles of docetaxel/carboplatin plus trastuzumab, and adjuvant breast radiotherapy completed in May 2023. During radiation she noted minor vaginal bleeding without pain; she initially did not seek care. Two months later the bleeding increased. 

On gynecologic ultrasound, the endometrial thickness was 11 mm with heterogeneous echogenicity and no focal masses; the myometrium and adnexa appeared unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis indicated the possibility of a hysteromyoma. Serum CA-125 was 14.2 U/ml (normal), and CA19-9 was 21.1 U/ml (normal).

A 71-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a forehead skin lesion that appeared immediately after a traumatic injury. He had no prior medical history. On examination, there was a 2.5-cm crusted, erythematous, ulcerated plaque with slightly elevated borders on the forehead; no other skin lesions were noted and there was no hepatosplenomegaly. Further evaluation with CT of the chest and abdomen showed periportal and perihepatic lymphadenopathy and small bilateral pleural effusions. A complete blood count was notable only for mild lymphocytosis (absolute lymphocyte count, 4500/μl). Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy performed elsewhere showed a normal population of hematopoietic cells without evidence of involvement. Brain CT revealed no central nervous system involvement. An incisional biopsy of the skin lesion was performed.

A 34-year-old man presented with 6 days of lower abdominal pain and rectal bleeding, passing dark maroon stools three to four times daily, and reported dizziness and fatigue. He denied fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, chest pain, or dyspnea. His medical history included a single episode of diverticulitis 7 years earlier; he had no prior endoscopies or abdominal surgeries. On examination, he was afebrile, normotensive, and mildly tachycardic. Abdominal palpation revealed tenderness in the left lower quadrant with normoactive bowel sounds. Rectal examination showed dark blood. Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 14 800 per µL, hemoglobin 8.0 g/dL, and hematocrit 23.9%; renal function, electrolytes, and urinalysis were normal.  
A noncontrast CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 7.0 × 7.6 cm mass with an attenuation of 37.3 Hounsfield units in the anterior left midpelvis, appearing inseparable from a loop of bowel and “possibly an unusual diverticulum.” The patient received IV fluids and transfusion, and empirical ciprofloxacin and metronidazole. Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy were performed and showed no acute pathology.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 7.2 × 6.8 × 6.1 cm lesion arising from a mid-to-distal small-bowel loop with no significant enhancement, appearing mobile in the mesentery compared with prior images.

A 63-year-old man presented initially with two months of nasal obstruction and recurrent epistaxis. He had 20 years of anosmia, several months of right ptosis, and a 40-year history of flooring installation with varnish and glue exposure. Examination revealed a polyp in the olfactory cleft and mucopurulent secretions. CT imaging showed a tissue mass invading the posterior ethmoid, olfactory cleft, and nasal septum, with maxillary sinus opacification but no skull base or intracranial extension. Biopsy under local anesthesia demonstrated a well-differentiated intestinal-type adenocarcinoma. He underwent endoscopic resection followed by conformational fractionated radiotherapy (56 Gy in 28 fractions).

Eighteen months later, the patient developed progressive trismus four weeks after minor facial trauma, accompanied by right infraorbital pain and hypoesthesia. CT imaging revealed a right zygomatic fracture and partial lysis of the posterolateral and lateral walls of the maxillary sinus. Endoscopic evaluation showed no visible recurrence, and osteoradionecrosis was initially diagnosed.

A 42-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of itching and discomfort of the maxillary gingivae. He had been treated unsuccessfully for oral candidiasis. He was provisionally diagnosed with erosive lichen planus and referred for specialist assessment. On examination, there was florid erythroleukoplakia of the hard palate and buccal gingivae, and all maxillary teeth were mobile. There were no cutaneous lesions. He had a 25–pack-year smoking history and drank up to eight cans of cider daily.

A 35-year-old man with no prior health issues presented with a 1-month history of numbness and heaviness in his lower limbs. The symptoms progressed gradually until he became unable to walk and developed difficulty passing urine and fecal incontinence. On examination, he had paraplegia with muscle strength of 2/5 in both lower limbs; deep tendon reflexes were absent, and plantar responses were extensor bilaterally. There was no sensory level or upper-limb involvement. Magnetic resonance imaging of the thoracic spine revealed an 8.0 cm × 1.2 cm dorsal extradural lesion extending from T7 to T10. The mass was hyperintense on T1- and T2-weighted images, heterogeneous on STIR sequences, and showed homogeneous enhancement after intravenous contrast, with marked compression of the spinal cord. Initial considerations included meningioma, metastasis, and chronic extradural hematoma.

A 72-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a six-month history of severe epigastric discomfort, recurrent vomiting, and epigastric pain that did not improve with proton-pump inhibitor therapy. His medical history included mild hypertension, hepatitis C infection, and prior laparoscopic appendectomy and cholecystectomy; he was not taking any medications and had no known allergies. His BMI was 25. On examination, his abdomen was soft with diffuse tenderness but no palpable mass. Laboratory tests revealed a hemoglobin level of 14.3 g/dL, normal coagulation studies, normal amylase, lipase, liver function tests, and normal CA 19-9 and CEA levels.

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed a broad-based lesion on the posterior-inferior wall of the second portion of the duodenum, close to the pylorus, deforming the pylorus and duodenal bulb; the lesion was bypassable by the endoscope, and there were no signs of ulceration or active bleeding. Biopsy attempts were unsuccessful.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 40 × 16 mm whorled, vegetant lesion in the first part of the duodenum with inhomogeneous arterial enhancement, abutting the pyloric area and lacking a clear plane of resection; there was no biliary or pancreatic ductal dilation.

Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated a approximately 4 cm submucosal lesion of mixed echogenicity arising from the second–third portions of the duodenum, with heterogeneous parenchymal enhancement on contrast injection; no clear interface with the head of the pancreas and no lymphadenopathy were seen.

A 21-year-old man presented with 3 months of moderate low back pain radiating down his right lower limb. The pain was worse with activity, standing, or sitting and relieved partially by lying down and analgesics. He reported low-grade fever, malaise, and anorexia. There was no history of trauma, infection, or known tuberculosis exposure. He denied involvement of other joints and had no urinary or rectal symptoms.

On examination, there was localized tenderness over the right sacroiliac joint, and sacroiliac provocation tests were positive. The lumbar spine, hips, left sacroiliac joint, peripheral joints, and neurologic examination were normal.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 45 mm/h, hemoglobin of 10.8 g/dL, and leukocyte count of 12,500/mm3. Serum chemistry and urinalysis were normal. Chest radiograph was unremarkable, and a tuberculin skin test was 8 mm at 72 hours. Pelvic radiographs showed blurring of the right sacroiliac joint margin with juxta-articular sclerosis. MRI of the pelvis demonstrated T1 hypointense and STIR hyperintense marrow signal in the right sacroiliac region with an intraosseous collection, findings suggestive of infective sacroiliitis, most likely tubercular in etiology.

The patient was started on standard antitubercular therapy. At 1-month follow-up, his symptoms improved and the ESR decreased to 9 mm/h. Therapy was continued. After 3 months, he complained of recurrent, more intense right sacroiliac pain and intermittent low-grade fever. A repeat contrast-enhanced MRI of the pelvis was obtained.

A 64-year-old Caucasian man with a history of coronary artery disease status post coronary artery bypass grafting presented with an 8-week history of a palpable right breast mass. He reported that approximately 3 months earlier he had been stuck by a 4-inch thorn in the right breast, after which he experienced localized pruritus and irritation. His primary care physician obtained a diagnostic mammogram, which showed a well-circumscribed round mass in the right breast without calcifications or architectural distortion. A targeted ultrasound examination revealed a well-circumscribed hypoechoic mass with internal septations and echoes and minimal Doppler flow. Ultrasound-guided core-needle biopsies of the mass were performed. Histologic examination demonstrated a hemangioma with predominant features of a cavernous hemangioma, characterized by variably sized dilated thin-walled vessels and focal feeder muscular veins; there was no atypia or increased mitotic activity, and a few thrombosed vascular spaces were noted, possibly related to the prior injury.

A 36-year-old man presented with several months of dull abdominal pain and a sensation of fullness. He had no other significant symptoms, and his past medical history was unremarkable. On examination, his abdomen was soft without a palpable mass. Complete blood counts and serum biochemistry were normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed a well-demarcated, mildly hyperechoic mass measuring 6 × 25 × 24 cm, apparently in the left hepatic lobe. Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI demonstrated a well-circumscribed, lipomatous mass within the greater omentum measuring 9 × 24 × 27 cm, without discrete enhancing soft-tissue components or signs of local invasion. CT showed several foci of coarse internal calcification, and MRI revealed corresponding areas of low T1 and T2 signal with a thin peripheral rim enhancement, suggestive of focal fat necrosis. Intra-abdominal mass effect was noted but no acute complications. FDG-PET showed no metabolically active disease. Given the rarity of omental lesions and the possibility of malignancy, the case was discussed at a multidisciplinary meeting, and a consensus was reached to proceed with curative surgical resection without prior biopsy.

A 54-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes presented with 3 days of diffuse abdominal pain, distension, and obstipation after an alcoholic binge. He also had severe anorexia, nausea, irritability, incomprehensible speech, and abnormal behavior over 2 days, and an 8-kg weight loss over 2 months. Six years earlier, he underwent a patellectomy and received 6 units of whole blood. There was no family history of malignancy.

On examination, he was dehydrated, tachypneic, and cyanosed, with a blood pressure of 200/110 mm Hg, heart rate of 116 bpm, and erythematous face and trunk. He had generalized lymphadenopathy. Abdominal examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly, generalized tympanitic resonance, and absent bowel sounds. Chest auscultation disclosed diffuse crepitations. Neurologic and cardiac examinations were otherwise unremarkable. The findings suggested paralytic ileus. Initial differential diagnoses included acute pancreatitis, diabetic ketoacidosis, porphyria, and hypercalcemia.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL; leukocyte count 174 × 10^9 cells/L with 70% lymphocytes; platelet count 156 × 10^9/L; ESR 63 mm/h; urea 112 mg/dL; creatinine 3.9 mg/dL; potassium 6.0 mmol/L; uric acid 10.6 mg/dL; LDH >5× upper limit of normal; normal pancreatic enzymes; negative urine ketones and porphyrinogen; serum calcium 15.8 mg/dL; phosphate 5.8 mg/dL; normal magnesium; parathyroid hormone 8.8 pg/mL (low); alkaline phosphatase >3× upper limit of normal. These results were suggestive of malignancy-associated hypercalcemia. Duodenal aspirate and biopsy were negative for Strongyloides larvae.

A 57-year-old woman was admitted for a 1-month history of daily episodes of dizziness, fatigue, cold sweats, tremors, changes in behavior, anxiety, and occasional seizures or altered consciousness. During a recent psychiatric hospitalization, a random capillary glucose measurement was 19 mg/dL. She denied alcohol use and any use of insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents. Her medical history was unremarkable, with no diabetes, endocrine syndromes, or significant illnesses. Her body-mass index was 25.6 kg/m2, with abdominal obesity; the rest of the physical examination was unremarkable.

On admission, she had repeated hypoglycemic episodes (plasma glucose < 55 mg/dL) not related to food intake, accompanied by confusion, dizziness, cold sweats, and tremor. Episodes were refractory to oral carbohydrates and required intravenous boluses of 33% glucose and continuous infusion of 10% glucose. Two incidental plasma glucose readings off infusion were ≥ 200 mg/dL (fasting 209 mg/dL, postprandial 227 mg/dL). During a hypoglycemic episode, laboratory values were: plasma glucose 44 mg/dL, serum insulin 16.3 µU/mL (2.2–24.9), C-peptide 3.72 ng/mL (1.1–4.4), HbA1c 4.99%, negative urinary ketones, and anti-insulin antibodies < 0.03 U/mL (< 0.4). Seven-month prior HbA1c was 5.1%. 

Further evaluation excluded adrenal insufficiency (normal 8 a.m. ACTH and cortisol), thyroid dysfunction (normal TSH, FT4, FT3), organ failure (normal renal and hepatic function), and sepsis (normal blood counts and inflammatory markers). Ophthalmoscopy, abdominal ultrasound, cranial CT, and chest CT were normal. Given the biochemical evidence of endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia, cross-sectional abdominal imaging was performed.

Abdominal CT showed in the anterior part of the pancreatic body–tail a 15.3 × 15 mm isodense rounded lesion with intense enhancement in the arterial phase that persisted in the venous phase. Complementary MRI demonstrated a hypervascular pancreatic lesion, hypointense to isointense on T1, slightly hyperintense on T2, homogeneous post-contrast enhancement, and diffusion restriction.

A 6-week-old boy, born at 37 weeks’ gestation, was evaluated for persistent jaundice. At 1 week of age, he had indirect hyperbilirubinemia treated with phototherapy. At 6 weeks, laboratory tests showed: total bilirubin 13.3 mg/dL, conjugated bilirubin 0.3 mg/dL, AST 60 U/L, ALT 38 U/L, INR 1.0, with a normal CBC and reticulocyte count. Both infant and mother are O-positive; the newborn screen suggested sickle cell trait, and the mother has alpha-thalassemia trait and sickle cell trait. The infant is exclusively breastfed, thriving, and has no symptoms except for jaundice on examination. An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a normal‐appearing liver and “echogenic foci within the wall of the gallbladder with a comet-tail artifact.”

A 63-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 3-year history of a tender mass in the right side of his neck. He denied other symptoms. His medical history was unremarkable. He denied tobacco use and reported an average of 15 alcoholic drinks per week. On examination, there was a 1.5 cm, firm, nonmobile nodule in the right submandibular region above the level of the hyoid bone. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a well-defined, homogeneously enhancing 1.6 × 1.3 cm mass in the inferior pole of the right submandibular gland. A fine-needle aspiration biopsy yielded clusters of monotonous, polygonal epithelial cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and a low nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio; the cells had round nuclei and prominent nucleoli. No significant lymphoid population, mitotic figures, or necrosis were seen. Cytologic features were suggestive of a submandibular oncocytic neoplasm.

A 43-year-old woman (BMI 23.6 kg/m2) presented with 3 weeks of gross hematuria. Kidney–ureter–bladder radiography revealed no stone-like lesions. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed severe left hydronephrosis, a small distal left periureteral mass, bilateral adnexal cystic lesions, and adenomyosis with small myomas; no lymphadenopathy was noted. The radiology impression was left obstructive uropathy, suspected to be caused by a left distal ureteral tumor, and endometriosis-related adhesion was also considered. Pelvic examination disclosed tightness of the left adnexa with mild tenderness. Carcinoembryonic antigen and CA-125 levels were within normal limits, and a Pap smear was normal. Under the presumption of hydronephrosis caused by ureteric endometriosis and uterine adenomyosis, the patient underwent robotic resection of the left distal ureteral mass, supracervical hysterectomy, and placement of a ureteric stent. Intraoperatively, no endometriosis-like cystic lesion or pelvic adhesions were observed; instead, a 1.5-cm retroperitoneal lobulated solid mass was identified at the lower third of the ureter, causing luminal narrowing.

A 51-year-old man presented with a 10-year history of pain in the plantar aspect of his right foot and a 4-year history of progressive swelling between the first and second metatarsal shafts. He had no prior surgery or trauma, denied constitutional symptoms, and was otherwise healthy. He had taken NSAIDs for pain relief, but over the past year the pain began to limit daily activities despite analgesia.

On examination, there was a 6 × 3 cm irregular, erythematous, firm, nonmobile, tender, and warm swelling between the first and second metatarsal shafts, extending plantarly and medially over the first metatarsal. Ankle plantarflexion and dorsiflexion were normal and pain-free, and subtalar inversion and eversion were normal. Range of motion at the first and second metatarsophalangeal joints was limited by pain. Neurovascular examination was intact, and gait was antalgic.

Plain radiographs of the right foot showed soft-tissue swelling with a 4 × 3 cm area of calcification between the first and third metatarsal shafts without bone involvement. MRI demonstrated a large, nonhomogeneous mass between the first and third metatarsal shafts extending plantarly, with mixed fibrous tissue and bony structures.

A 2-year-old girl was evaluated for a 1-month history of swelling of the left upper eyelid. There was no redness, pain, or other ocular symptoms. Her birth and developmental history were unremarkable, and there was no family history of cancer. She had normal growth parameters and no abdominal complaints. Thoracic and abdominal CT scans showed no masses. On ophthalmic examination, there was a firm mass at the lateral superior orbital rim of the left eye, associated with congestion and edema of the superotemporal conjunctiva and swelling of the lower eyelid. Orbital CT revealed a soft-tissue mass at the lateral superior orbital rim with destruction of the lateral orbital wall. The patient underwent surgical resection under general anesthesia. Intraoperatively, the lesion was cord-like, dark red, irregular, and adherent to surrounding tissues, with extensive bone destruction. Two gross specimens measured 2.5 × 2.0 × 1.5 cm and 2.5 × 1.5 × 1.0 cm.

An 8-year-old boy with homozygous sickle cell anemia was evaluated during a routine ultrasonographic check. He had a history of multiple vaso-occlusive crises, including acute splenic sequestration, parvovirus B19 infection, and pulmonary toxoplasmosis. Despite a baseline hemoglobin level of 7–8 g/dL, his growth and psychomotor development were normal.

Physical examination was unremarkable, with no splenomegaly or hepatomegaly. Laboratory studies showed a red blood cell count of 2.03 × 10^12/L, a white blood cell count of 17.70 × 10^9/L, and a platelet count of 294 × 10^9/L. Hemostasis tests, liver enzymes, total bilirubin, serum creatinine, and carcinoembryonic antigen levels were all within normal limits.

Abdominal ultrasonography followed by contrast-enhanced CT scan revealed splenomegaly with three hyperechoic splenic masses measuring 3.0 cm, 2.5 cm, and 2.0 cm. The masses had irregular shapes, poorly defined borders, and a rough capsule. Possible differential diagnoses included angiosarcoma, primary splenic lymphoma, and multiple splenic metastases.

A 53-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of hoarseness. Initial laryngoscopy showed polypoid degeneration of the right true vocal cord, which was observed clinically. On follow-up examination, a submucosal swelling of the right false vocal cord was noted. The patient’s renal function was normal. 

Unenhanced CT revealed an expansile, heterogeneously iso-to-low attenuating mass (40 × 45 × 46 mm) centered in the right thyroid cartilage, with cortical thinning and erosion; contrast enhancement was heterogeneous. The lesion displaced the laryngeal mucosa medially at the level of the false vocal cord but appeared submucosal.

On 3-T MRI, the mass exhibited marked hypointensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images. Diffusion-weighted imaging showed no restricted diffusion, and the apparent diffusion coefficient map was hypointense, likely reflecting susceptibility effects. Post-contrast T1-weighted imaging demonstrated heterogeneous enhancement.

FDG-PET showed intense uptake in the lesion (maximum SUV, 12.3) without evidence of lymph node involvement.

A 49-year-old woman presented with a 16-month history of a left breast lump that exhibited rapid growth over the past 2 months. Her history included bilateral lumpectomy in 2014 (frozen section: fibroadenoma; postoperative pathology of left lesion: benign phyllodes tumor) and excision of a 10.4×5.5 cm left breast mass in 2018 (frozen section: fibroepithelial tumor; postoperative pathology: benign phyllodes tumor). She reported no systemic symptoms. On exam, the left breast was enlarged with attenuated, discolored skin and prominent subcutaneous veins. A 15 cm, hard-elastic, multilobulated, mobile mass occupied the outer lower quadrant without axillary lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests were normal. Chest CT and abdominal ultrasound showed no metastases. Breast ultrasound revealed a large, oval, circumscribed, hypoechoic mass with peripheral vascular flow and posterior acoustic enhancement (BI-RADS 5), measuring >10.5×7.0 cm. MRI demonstrated a 12.8×9.1×11.6 cm lobulated, heterogeneously enhancing mass with several enlarged axillary lymph nodes. Core needle biopsy showed a fibroepithelial tumor with cell proliferation.

A 15-year-old male presented with a 1-week history of right-sided neck pain and sore throat but no fever. He was initially treated with antibiotics and analgesics; subsequently he noted a painless mass on the right side of his neck. On examination, there was a 4.5-cm hard, non-tender, well-circumscribed, mobile nodule in the right cervical region. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.  
  
Ultrasonography showed two enlarged right cervical lymph nodes (up to 3.0 cm) and one left cervical node (1.0 cm). Routine laboratory studies were normal. Serologic tests for toxoplasmosis, cytomegalovirus, hepatitis A, B, and C viruses, HIV, and syphilis were all negative.  
  
An excisional biopsy of the right cervical node was performed, yielding five irregular fragments of lymphoid tissue; the largest measured 4.5 × 3.2 × 1.9 cm, was brownish on cut section, and had a fibro-elastic consistency. Specimens were cultured for mycobacteria, but no growth occurred.

A 46-year-old man presented with a 3-week history of left-sided hearing loss and a sensation of fullness in the ear. He denied ear pain, otorrhea, or any other otologic symptoms. On otomicroscopy, a polypoid mass was seen occluding the left external auditory canal; the tympanic membrane was not visible. Pure-tone audiometry revealed a conductive hearing loss on the left and normal hearing on the right. A non-contrast CT scan of the temporal bones demonstrated a pedunculated polypoid lesion confined to the lateral portion of the external auditory canal, with normal aeration of the middle ear and mastoid air cells and intact bone without erosion.

A 14-year-old boy with a history of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), including two relapses and a cord blood transplant 18 months earlier, presented with a 2-month history of intermittent right flank pain that acutely worsened over 24 hours. Three months before presentation, he had vague right flank discomfort attributed to posture; an abdominal radiograph was negative. He denied hematuria and had no history of nephrolithiasis.  

On examination, he was afebrile, with normal vital signs. He had mild right paraspinal tenderness but was otherwise unremarkable.  

Laboratory studies showed microhematuria without pyuria on urinalysis, negative urine culture, and normal blood urea nitrogen and creatinine levels.  

A renal ultrasound one year earlier demonstrated mild right hydronephrosis. In the emergency department, repeat renal ultrasound revealed marked right hydronephrosis with a long segment of the distal right ureter replaced by a mass-like lesion that exhibited internal blood flow on Doppler imaging. Differential considerations at that time included relapse of ALL, an infiltrating tumor, and an atypical presentation of BK virus; the appearance did not suggest edema from recent passage of a ureteral stone.  

Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed right-sided hydronephrosis and proximal hydroureter with an abrupt transition in the mid-right ureter and demonstrated segmental wall thickening and contrast enhancement of the mid- and distal ureter.

A 69-year-old woman with coronary artery disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and polymyalgia rheumatica presented with one month of worsening abdominal pain, weakness, fatigue, weight loss, and anorexia. She had no prior malignancy or asbestos exposure. On examination, she appeared pale but hemodynamically stable. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 25.8×10^9/L (reference 3.5–12.0) with neutrophils 23.05×10^6/L and monocytes 1.67×10^6/L, hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL (reference 12.0–16.0) with MCV 78 fL, RDW 20.7%, platelets 729×10^9/L, and a globulin level of 5.3 g/dL (reference 1.5–3.9) with a globulin/albumin ratio of 0.4 (reference 1.0–1.8). 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 9.5×8.5×7.0 cm soft-tissue mass in the right paracolic gutter abutting the inferior margin of the liver, the lateral abdominal wall, and effacing the descending colon, with areas of low attenuation suggestive of necrosis. A concurrent 8.5×6.7 cm cystic mass was noted in the left adnexa without calcifications or solid nodules. Serum CA-125 was within normal limits. Colonoscopy showed no intrinsic colonic lesions. A preoperative PET scan demonstrated uptake only in the right abdominal mass.

An ultrasound-guided core-needle biopsy of the mass was performed.

A 40-year-old man presented with a 10-day history of pain and swelling over the right elbow. He had sustained trauma to the elbow 15 days earlier. Ten years ago, he had tuberculosis of the right elbow that was treated with antituberculosis therapy and surgical synovectomy; he recovered well. On examination, there was tenderness over the lateral aspect of the elbow, restricted range of motion, and wasting of the forearm muscles. The overlying skin was normal without signs of inflammation.

Plain radiographs of the elbow showed a pathological fracture of the radial head with an eccentric, ballooned, expansile radiolucent lesion surrounded by a well-circumscribed margin. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a mildly expansile lesion involving the proximal radial epiphysis and metaphysis, extending to the subarticular region and abutting the articular cartilage.

A 79-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of progressive nasal obstruction and intermittent epistaxis. At an outside hospital, she underwent resection of a right middle turbinate mass, with additional biopsies from the right nasal septum and ethmoid sinus. Pathologic examination showed a spindle‐cell proliferation with abundant foamy macrophages and inflammatory cells, including plasma cells and neutrophils. Special stains for acid-fast bacilli, fungi, and bacteria were negative, and an immunohistochemical stain for cytokeratin showed no immunoreactivity in the spindle‐cell component. Flow cytometric analysis of the tissue showed no evidence of B-cell or T-cell lymphoma. A diagnosis of “inflammatory pseudotumor (inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor)” was suggested.

Despite surgery, her nasal obstruction and bilateral epistaxis persisted, and she sought a second opinion. On examination, she had bilaterally enlarged (3–5 cm), soft, smooth, mobile, non‐tender submandibular lymph nodes. A fine‐needle aspiration (FNA) of a left submandibular lymph node was performed. Diff‐Quik–stained smears revealed numerous multinucleated giant cells up to 100 μm in size within a background of mixed inflammatory cells (lymphocytes, neutrophils, plasma cells). Many of the giant cells contained intact lymphocytes, neutrophils, and occasional plasma cells within their cytoplasm (emperipolesis). No mitoses or necrosis were observed.

A 23-year-old man with a 10-year history of generalized anxiety disorder presented with a 2-month history of a recurrent swelling in the right mandibular body. He recalled a similar self-resolving episode one year earlier. He had no drug allergies.

On extraoral examination, there was a firm, nonerythematous swelling in the mid–right mandibular body without lymphadenopathy or trismus. Intraorally, the crown of tooth 35 was distally tipped, and there was a 0.7×0.5-cm mass in the lower vestibule between teeth 35 and 36, extending to the buccal mucosa. The mass was nontender at rest, firm, mildly painful to palpation, and covered by normal mucosa. Cold testing elicited normal responses in teeth 35 and 36; axial percussion was negative for tooth 35 and equivocal for tooth 36.

A panoramic radiograph obtained three years earlier showed a well-circumscribed, unilocular radiolucency with a sclerotic border interposed between the roots of the second premolar (35) and first molar (36), causing slight mesial curvature of the root of tooth 35. The lesion appeared continuous with the lamina dura of tooth 35, extending from the amelocemental junction to the apical third of the roots.

Contemporary intraoral radiography confirmed a similar lesion now extending approximately 0.2 cm beyond the root of tooth 35 and 0.6 cm beyond the distal root of tooth 36; the periodontal ligament space was obliterated at sites of contact.

A CT Dentascan demonstrated a well-defined cystic lesion within the mandibular body. The buccal cortical plate was partially destroyed in its midportion and thinned superiorly, and the lingual cortex was bowed, but the mandibular canal cortex was intact. There was no root resorption, though features of local bone aggression were present.

Based on the lesion’s interradicular location, small size, tooth vitality, radiographic continuity with the lamina dura, and slow evolution, a lateral periodontal cyst was strongly suspected. Giant cell granuloma and ameloblastoma were also considered because of the cortical bone changes seen on CT.

A 63-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 10-day history of left-sided burning chest pain radiating to the right side. He denied fever, weight loss, or abdominal symptoms. On examination, his abdomen was soft without peritoneal signs. Three firm, palpable masses were noted in the soft tissues of the left breast, right gluteal region, and left leg. Routine blood tests, HIV serology, and EBV testing were all normal or negative.

A chest radiograph revealed a rounded subpleural mass in the upper left hemithorax without rib invasion. Doppler ultrasound of the right gluteal mass showed a hypoechoic solid intramuscular lesion with internal arterial flow. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax confirmed a solitary, well-circumscribed, homogeneous subpleural mass forming an obtuse angle with the chest wall and sparing adjacent ribs. Abdominopelvic CT demonstrated multiple retroperitoneal masses involving both adrenal glands, the left kidney, retrocrural space, intraperitoneal and retroperitoneal fat, as well as multiple intramuscular masses.

A 63-year-old man, a lifelong nonsmoker with a history of hypertension and coronary heart disease, presented with a 2-month history of a dry cough without dyspnea, wheezing, hemoptysis, night sweats, or weight loss. Seven years earlier, he had undergone resection of the right middle and lower lobes for a biopsy-proven atypical endobronchial carcinoid; nodal and margin status had been negative, and postoperative CT and PET scans showed no residual disease. On examination, breath sounds were decreased in the right lower chest, with no wheezing or rhonchi. Chest radiography showed right hilar fullness. Contrast CT of the chest revealed an 8.1 × 7.4 cm right hilar mass without endobronchial lesion seen on imaging. PET scan demonstrated that the right hilar mass was not FDG-avid. Flexible bronchoscopy disclosed numerous polypoid lesions on the vocal cords, trachea, and main bronchi. Biopsy of a lesion in the right mainstem bronchus revealed a well-differentiated tumor of neuroendocrine-appearing cells forming small tubular and glandular-like structures, without significant atypia or mitotic activity. Immunostaining was positive for chromogranin and synaptophysin, and Ki-67 labeling was low.

An 83-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus, hypertension, spinal canal stenosis, and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis presented with pruritus. Laboratory studies showed total bilirubin 4.6 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 3.7 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 1333 U/L, and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 350 U/L. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed intrahepatic bile duct dilatation. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 13-cm mass in the right hepatic lobe causing compression of the hilar bile ducts. ERCP confirmed extrinsic compression at the hepatic hilum; nasobiliary drainage improved jaundice. Biliary cytology showed disturbed architecture with variation in internuclear distances and dyskaryosis, raising suspicion for malignancy. On transfer, cholestatic enzymes had improved (total bilirubin 1.1 mg/dL; direct bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL; alkaline phosphatase 600 U/L; γ-GTP 57 U/L) but revealed coagulopathy (platelet count 9.6×10^3/mm^3; fibrinogen 122.5 mg/dL; fibrin-fibrinogen degradation products 200 µg/mL; D-dimer 88.8 µg/mL). Repeat CT showed a well-demarcated, nonenhancing 13-cm lesion in segments IV–V with intrahepatic ductal dilation. Review of CT from 5 years earlier revealed a 28-mm low-density lesion at the same site. MRI demonstrated a 13-cm mass with low T1 and slightly high T2 signal intensity, heterogeneous appearance, and fluid–fluid levels at the margins. ERCP again showed a 2-cm common bile duct stricture from extrinsic compression, with segmental intrahepatic ductal dilation.

A 45-year-old man with a 20-year history of a left shoulder lesion noted rapid growth over 12 months and recent blood spotting. He had known osteochondromatosis but was otherwise healthy.
On examination: normal vital signs, no anemia; a 20 cm pedunculated mass in the left cervicoscapular region arising from subcutaneous tissue, with early cutaneous pressure ulcers and signs of skin infection; shoulder abduction limited, other movements preserved.
Laboratory tests were within normal limits.
Radiography showed a giant soft-tissue mass on the left shoulder and bone deformities compatible with osteochondromatosis.
CT scan demonstrated a large adipose-density tumour in the left scapular region without metastases.
MRI revealed a 19 × 18 × 14.4 cm polylobulated subcutaneous lesion with multiple septa and contrast enhancement of nonadipose components, plus a 0.9 cm axillary lymph node; findings were highly suggestive of liposarcoma with nodal metastasis.
Core-needle biopsy immunohistochemistry showed diffuse CD34 positivity in the spindle/pleomorphic component and S100 positivity in the adipose component; negative for CK AE1/AE3, EMA, AML, Desmin, SOX100, HMB45, CD31, STAT6, MDM2, and CDK4.
FISH demonstrated no amplification of MDM2.

A 32-year-old white man with type 1 diabetes and acne rosacea presented with a 7-mm reddish-brown papule on the left temple along the hairline that appeared suddenly and grew over several weeks. The lesion was asymptomatic, without pain, pruritus, ulceration, or bleeding. Three weeks before lesion onset, he had undergone intense pulsed light (IPL) therapy (500–670 nm for vascular lesions) for rosacea, during which he sustained several second-degree burns in the area where the papule eventually appeared. Initial clinical differential diagnoses included a follicular cyst, hemangioma, dermatofibroma, seborrheic keratosis, basal cell carcinoma, and amelanotic melanoma. The lesion was treated empirically with intralesional triamcinolone acetonide (0.5 mL of Kenalog-10) and oral doxycycline (120 mg daily) for one month, resulting in approximately 80% reduction in size but incomplete resolution; the papule recurred within a month. An incision and drainage with an 11 blade yielded no keratinaceous material. A 4-mm punch biopsy was performed to rule out a neoplastic process.

A 24‐year‐old Asian man presented with a painless, slowly growing mass on the right side of his hard palate that he first noticed a few weeks earlier. He reported no medical problems, medications, or family history of similar lesions. On intraoral examination, there was a large exophytic lesion about 5 × 4 cm extending from the hard palate toward the soft palate. The mass was oval, yellowish in color, and soft to palpation. It was compressible, had a smooth surface with numerous small blood vessels, but did not blanch or feel pulsatile on palpation. The lesion was fixed with well‐defined margins. The working clinical diagnosis was lipoma. The differential diagnosis included lipoma, a cystic lesion or other soft tissue tumor, and pleomorphic adenoma. A 5 mm incisional punch biopsy was performed from the center of the mass.

A 43-year-old African American woman presented with bilateral leg pain of recent onset without trauma. She had a history of hysterectomy for fibroids and was on hormone replacement therapy; she denied tobacco and alcohol use. On examination, she had mild point tenderness over the medial aspect of her left knee without effusion or limitation of motion. 

Plain radiographs showed well-defined lytic lesions in the left distal femur and medial tibial plateau, and multiple ill-defined radiolucent lesions in the distal radius and scaphoid of the left wrist; right wrist and knee films were normal. 

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver, renal, and thyroid function tests, serum lipid panel, serum protein electrophoresis, B and T lymphocyte flow cytometry, and bone marrow biopsy, were all within normal limits. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the left knee and wrist revealed areas with high signal intensity on T1-weighted images and corresponding low signal on fat-suppressed T2-weighted images, matching the radiographic lesions. There was no periosteal reaction, cortical breach, or soft-tissue abnormality; an eccentric lesion was noted in the distal radius.

A 65-year-old woman was referred after an incidental finding on routine follow-up imaging. In July 2020, she was diagnosed with a 2 × 3.3 cm palpable mass in the left breast; core needle biopsy revealed ductal carcinoma in situ, and she underwent lumpectomy followed by 40 sessions of radiotherapy through 2021. In August 2022, she developed progressive dysphagia; endoscopy showed a submucosal polypoid lesion in the middle third of the esophagus, and biopsy confirmed squamous cell carcinoma (stage T2-N0). She received concurrent chemoradiation. One month later, an abdominopelvic CT scan demonstrated a solid enhancing lesion measuring 26 × 18 mm in the posteromedial aspect of the midportion of the right kidney, adjacent to a simple renal cyst. In October 2022, she was asymptomatic, with a heart rate of 86 /min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, oxygen saturation 96%, and normal physical examination. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, hematocrit 36.4%, WBC count 6400/mm^3, BUN 9.6 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.78 mg/dL.

An 18-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with a 5-day history of vomiting, generalized abdominal pain, and fever. She reported a 3-month history of vague, intermittent abdominal discomfort that did not respond to medical treatment and had been labeled as irritable bowel syndrome. On examination, she was febrile and had moderate abdominal distention with generalized tenderness. Bowel sounds were decreased. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 15,000 per mm3 and a C-reactive protein level of 11.5 mg/dL. An abdominal ultrasound revealed a large cystic lesion. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated an oval, fluid-filled structure with regular but thickened walls and post-contrast enhancement, located adjacent to the small bowel.  
What is your differential diagnosis?

A 68-year-old man presented with a 10-week history of an asymptomatic mass on his right chin that had grown rapidly. On examination, the lesion measured 2 × 5 cm, was soft, mobile, and appeared subcutaneous; the overlying skin was normal, and there was no palpable connection to intraoral structures. Ultrasound imaging revealed a well-defined, moderately dense mass above the mandibular margin without invasion of or compression on deeper structures; color Doppler study showed mostly peripheral vascularity. 

An incisional biopsy exposed a gelatinous gray mass within the subcutaneous tissue without a gross capsule. Histopathologic examination of frozen and permanent hematoxylin-eosin sections showed numerous small, elongated blood vessels and scattered spindle cells embedded in an abundant myxoid stroma; the spindle cells lacked cytologic atypia and mitotic activity. The myxoid stroma stained metachromatically with toluidine blue on frozen sections. Permanent-section immunohistochemical staining for retinoblastoma (Rb) nuclear antigen demonstrated positivity in approximately 25% to 50% of the spindle cells.

A 59-year-old woman with a history of grade III invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast treated with lumpectomy and radiotherapy in July 2007 underwent staged bilateral cemented total hip replacements, with the left hip performed in August 2008. She made an uneventful recovery and was asymptomatic until 8 months after the left procedure, when she presented with progressive left hip pain and a limp. She was afebrile with normal vital signs. Pelvic radiography showed extensive destruction of periacetabular bone around the left acetabular component. Baseline blood tests were essentially normal apart from a C-reactive protein level of 22 and an alkaline phosphatase level of 432.

A 59-year-old man with no known past medical history presented with four months of diffuse, intermittent pain and subjective fevers. The pain involved proximal muscle groups, especially the hips, shoulders, neck, and lower back, and was associated with daily sweats, worsening weakness, fatigue, and dyspnea. He had made three prior ED visits, each revealing elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP); he was treated with analgesics and referred for outpatient rheumatology. On the day of presentation, he looked ill and was sent to the ED again.

On review of systems, he denied headache, temporal pain, vision changes, or urinary symptoms. Vital signs: temperature 98.5°F, blood pressure 135/77 mmHg, heart rate 102 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 99% on room air. He was morbidly obese and uncomfortable. Examination showed global muscle tenderness (especially limb girdles), generalized weakness (strength 4/5), and reduced range of motion in all extremities; sensation and reflexes were intact. HEENT examination was unremarkable without temporal tenderness; the remainder of the exam was normal.

Initial investigations included a normal chest radiograph and negative cardiac workup; blood cultures were obtained. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL, ESR >140 mm/hr, CRP >380 mg/L, ALT 48 U/L, AST 56 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 2285 U/L, and creatine kinase 175 U/L. He was diagnosed with polymyalgia rheumatica, started on stress-dose steroids in the ED, and admitted for further evaluation.

A 6-year-old girl presented with a 1-week history of dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain that was worse when supine, associated with orthopnea, mild agitation, and fever. Her parents also reported intermittent fever over the preceding 3 months. There was no significant past medical history and no known contact with COVID-19 patients. On examination, she was febrile, alert, and in mild respiratory distress. Lung auscultation was clear except for decreased breath sounds at the right lower zone. Cardiac examination revealed muffled heart sounds; peripheral pulses were normal. Vital signs: blood pressure 100/65 mm Hg, heart rate 120 beats/min, respiratory rate 30 breaths/min. Abdominal examination showed hepatomegaly.

Initial investigations included:
- Chest radiograph: mediastinal widening  
- ECG: sinus tachycardia with low-voltage QRS and electrical alternans  
- Laboratory studies: WBC 11.4×10^9/L, hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, platelets 565×10^9/L, LDH 1061 U/L, CRP 66 mg/L, ESR 57 mm/h; electrolytes, renal and liver function tests, troponin I, and COVID-19 PCR were unremarkable.

Further evaluation with transthoracic echocardiography showed a large pericardial effusion without signs of tamponade. Contrast-enhanced thoracic CT revealed an anterior mediastinal mass accompanied by moderate pleural and pericardial effusions.

A 9-year-old boy presented with 4 days of lower abdominal pain, recurrent vomiting, inability to eat or drink, and no bowel movement. He had an old right inguinal hernia repair scar. Vital signs were normal; he had lost 2.7 kg and had sunken eyes. Abdominal examination showed slight tenderness over the bladder region. Oral rehydration was ineffective. Urinalysis showed pH 5.5, blood +1, ketones +3, protein trace; no leukocytes, glucose, or nitrite. Arterial blood gas revealed metabolic alkalosis (bicarbonate 31.6 mmol/L); other blood tests were normal. 
Ultrasound demonstrated a large anechoic fluid collection extending from the epigastrium to the pelvis (approximately 5 × 8 cm) with a few thin, mobile septa and no signs of bowel obstruction or abscess. The findings were interpreted as free intraperitoneal fluid with fibrin debris, prompting a tentative diagnosis of perforated hollow-organ with reactive peritonitis. 
An abdominal MRI (T2-weighted) showed a 9 × 11 cm fluid-filled lesion with internal septa, without diffusion restriction, extending from the epigastrium to the lower abdomen. There was gastric and proximal duodenal dilatation and a possible whirl sign. Radiologists raised the possibility of internal herniation or a benign cystic tumor. The patient was taken for acute surgical exploration.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 7-year history of occasional pain on the volar-radial aspect of her right mid-forearm. The pain had gradually worsened and was significantly increased on palpation. She recalled no traumatic event and had no relevant family history. On physical examination, touching a well-localized area elicited “spark-like” pain, but there were no sensory alterations or temperature hypersensitivity. No contour deformities or visible skin lesions were identified. Laboratory examinations, plain radiographs, and CT scans were normal. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the forearm demonstrated a 5×3×2 mm oval subcutaneous mass leading to a small vessel. The mass had intermediate intensity on T1-weighted images, inhomogeneous high signal on T2-weighted images, and homogeneous strong enhancement with contrast.

A 20-year-old unmarried girl, deaf and mute since birth, presented with a 6-month history of a slowly enlarging left vulvar swelling that had become extremely painful during the past week. She had no fever or vaginal discharge. On examination, her vital signs were stable and she was afebrile, with no inguinal lymphadenopathy. Local examination showed a left labial swelling with signs of inflammation, and a clinical diagnosis of Bartholin’s abscess was made; she was started on parenteral antibiotics. Within 24 hours, her pain decreased and the inflammation subsided. Because the patient and her parents insisted that she was sexually naïve, the lesion was reexamined. Now noted was a 5 × 5 cm swelling of the left labia majora without signs of inflammation; the mass was firm (not cystic), the labia minora were not everted, and the hymen was intact.

An 84-year-old Chinese man with hypertension, prior stroke, and atrial fibrillation on dabigatran presented with acute urinary retention. After Foley-catheter placement, he had light hematuria. His serum creatinine was 130–150 μmol/L. Renal ultrasonography showed a 5.7 cm left renal mass with cystic spaces. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a 5.2 × 5 × 6 cm enhancing mass at the upper to mid pole of the left kidney with internal cystic components, tiny calcifications, and hyperdense soft-tissue areas. These features were considered suggestive of cystic renal cell carcinoma. A 2.5 cm heterogeneously enhancing soft-tissue nodule was also identified in the left adrenal gland, with differential diagnoses of adenoma versus metastatic disease. The patient underwent laparoscopic left radical nephrectomy and adrenalectomy without intraoperative complications.

A 34-year-old nulliparous woman at 37 weeks’ gestation, with a history of uterine fibroids treated by two previous myomectomies, presented for routine fetal assessment. Pregnancy had been uneventful until cardiotocography revealed a sinusoidal tracing. She was admitted and underwent cesarean delivery. Intraoperative findings included an irregular uterine contour with two bulky fibroids. A live male infant was delivered breech into meconium-stained amniotic fluid; Apgar scores were 6 and 7 at 1 and 5 minutes, and neonatal resuscitation was required. Cord blood gas analysis showed a hemoglobin concentration of 4.3 g/dL, pH 7.32, and base excess −2.9 mmol/L. A neonatal blood sample confirmed severe anemia (RBC count 1.06 × 10^6/μL, hemoglobin 4.0 g/dL, hematocrit 12.7%), and the infant developed hypovolemic shock and pulmonary hypertension requiring transfusion and intubation. The placenta weighed 600 g, measured 16 cm in diameter, and had marginal umbilical cord insertion.

An 8-month-old boy, born at term to a consanguineous marriage with normal development and vaccinations, presented with 15 days of abdominal pain, constipation, and decline in general condition. On examination, he was well-appearing, weighed 8 kg, and had a palpable left lumbar mass. Abdominal ultrasound showed a left renal mass with two components: predominantly echogenic tissue with central and peripheral anechoic cystic zones, and a “shoulder sign” with adjacent healthy renal parenchyma. Catecholamine levels were normal. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a poly-lobed upper and mid-pole left renal mass that was solidocystic, predominantly isodense solid tissue with heterogeneous enhancement, nonenhancing hypodense areas, and peripheral and central cystic components; progressive enhancement was noted in the late phases.

A 13-year-old, spayed female inland bearded dragon presented with gradual onset of lethargy, right‐sided head tilt, exophthalmos, and ventrotemporal strabismus of the right eye. The owner also noted occasional dyspnea. On examination, the lizard was dehydrated, with left‐sided enophthalmos and increased skin wrinkling; body condition score was 2/5, with marked muscle atrophy of the tail and pelvic muscles and generalized muscle tremors. Coelomic palpation revealed a single, irregular, round mass about 3.5 cm in diameter in the mid‐coelomic cavity. Hematology showed a leukocytosis of 44 × 10^3/µL with marked heterophilia and toxic granulation; plasma biochemistry was significant only for hyperglycemia (570 mg/dL). Ultrasound revealed a 4 × 3.3 cm multilobulated oval mass with multiple septa and cysts at the site of previous ovarian surgery. Computed tomography demonstrated lytic lesions of the right frontal bone with retrobulbar soft tissue expansion, osteolysis of thoracic vertebrae T11 and T13/T14, and multiple soft tissue nodules in the lungs, liver, and fat bodies.

A woman in her early 50s presented with several months of right-sided nasal obstruction. She had a history of gastroesophageal reflux disease and obstructive sleep apnea managed with CPAP. She denied nasal trauma, discharge, or epistaxis, and had no relevant family history; she was a non-smoker.  

On nasal endoscopy, there was a 2 cm vascular-appearing mass on the right anterior nasal septum; the middle meati and nasopharynx were clear. Contrast-enhanced CT of the sinonasal region demonstrated a 1.4 × 1.2 cm soft-tissue lesion on the right anterior septum with mild post-contrast enhancement, causing obliteration of the right nostril. There was no bony erosion of the septum, no extension into adjacent spaces, and no lymphadenopathy or abnormalities of the thyroid or salivary glands. Routine blood tests were normal. A vascular lesion such as a hemangioma was suspected.

A 40-year-old woman presented with a four-year history of right-sided aural fullness accompanied by recurrent otalgia, itching, headache, and postural instability. She had cluster headaches in 2015 and 2018; during the latter, she experienced mucopurulent otorrhea in the right ear and was treated with antibiotics. Two prior brain CT scans revealed inflammation of the right hypotympanum and mesotympanum. She had no history of neoplastic disease, smoking, or alcohol use. Examination showed an intact right tympanic membrane with whitish material visible retrotympanically. Audiometry demonstrated bilateral normal hearing thresholds. MRI of the ears showed no hyperintensity on diffusion-weighted imaging to suggest cholesteatoma of the right middle ear. An excisional biopsy was planned for definitive diagnosis.

A 40-year-old primigravida at 39 weeks and 3 days of gestation underwent routine ultrasound, which revealed polyhydramnios and a left cervical mass not previously noted in earlier trimesters. Fetal MRI showed two contiguous solid nodules (41 × 44 mm and 53 × 47 mm) extending from the base of the tongue to the left buccal region, adjacent to the airway. Concerns for postnatal airway obstruction led to transfer for planned ex utero intrapartum treatment (EXIT).

At 39 weeks and 5 days, the infant was delivered by cesarean section with EXIT, and a tracheostomy was performed before clamping the umbilical cord. Apgar scores were 2, 3, and 4 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes. In the NICU, the sedated infant was mechanically ventilated. Birth weight was 2870 g (–0.3 SD), head circumference 33.5 cm (+0.1 SD), and length 51 cm (+1.0 SD). Physical examination confirmed a left cervical mass and a mass at the base of the tongue; several subcutaneous nodules were present on the limbs and trunk.

Laboratory tests showed an elevated lactate dehydrogenase level (2470 IU/L), alpha-fetoprotein 42 580 ng/mL, human chorionic gonadotropin 19.3 mIU/L, and normal urinary vanillylmandelic acid and homovanillic acid. Postnatal day 0 ultrasound demonstrated a heterogeneous solid cervical mass (40 × 32 × 49 mm) with abundant blood flow and areas of calcification; the subcutaneous nodules varied in vascularity and echotexture. Contrast-enhanced CT on day 5 revealed central necrosis of the cervical mass and additional lesions in the right lower lung lobe and thymus, suggestive of metastases, with no intracranial invasion.

A 21-year-old man presented with a painless right hemiscrotal swelling of several months’ duration and no systemic symptoms. He had a history of a single episode of right orchitis two years earlier, which resolved with antibiotics. On examination, the right scrotum contained a firm, non-tender mass; the right testis appeared atrophic. The left testis was normal. Serum tumour markers were within normal limits: alpha-fetoprotein 0.86 μg/L, β-human chorionic gonadotropin <0.5 mIU/mL, and lactate dehydrogenase 241 U/L. Scrotal ultrasound demonstrated a well-defined, slightly heterogeneous, hyperechoic 21 × 14 mm mass in the right epididymal region, separate from a small right testis, with smooth contours. The left scrotum was unremarkable.

A term female neonate presented on day 1 with pallor, a single episode of rectal bleeding, and severe anemia (hemoglobin, 10.6 g/dL; mean corpuscular volume, 110 fL). Physical examination was notable only for pallor. After an erythrocyte transfusion, the hemoglobin rose to 14.7 g/dL but then fell to 11.0 g/dL over 6 days. Intravenous antibiotics were administered for 7 days for presumed perinatal infection, but hematologic laboratory studies were otherwise unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a solid 6.2 × 5.2 × 2.5 cm mass initially on the right side, then on repeat imaging on the left side of the abdomen, suggesting mobility. A solid ovarian neoplasm was suspected. Other considerations included an intestinal duplication cyst, an immature teratoma, a germ cell tumor, and neuroblastoma stage 4S. Magnetic resonance imaging was attempted but nondiagnostic because of patient movement.

A 71-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 2-week history of right-sided abdominal pain unresponsive to acetaminophen. On evaluation her blood pressure was 144/78 mmHg, temperature 37.7 °C, and she had mild right abdominal tenderness. Laboratory studies showed WBC 5800/µL and CRP 20.16 mg/dL; HIV test was negative. Tumor markers revealed an elevated neuron-specific enolase of 44.6 ng/mL. All hormonal studies—including plasma cortisol, ACTH, DHEAS, aldosterone, renin activity, catecholamines, and 24-hour urine cortisol, aldosterone, metanephrines, normetanephrines, and 17-ketosteroids—were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a poorly enhancing, heterogeneous 10 × 6 × 11 cm right adrenal mass with a normal adrenal gland visible dorsally, an infiltration shadow at the base of the right lung, mediastinal and inguinal lymphadenopathy, and obstruction of the inferior vena cava. MRI showed the 11 cm heterogeneous adrenal lesion without signal drop on out-of-phase imaging and T1-weighted hyperintensity in the IVC extending into the iliac veins, consistent with venous thrombosis. An ^131I-MIBG scan was negative.

A 1-year-9-month-old girl with no significant past medical or surgical history was referred for evaluation of an intra-abdominal mass versus abscess. She had a 10-day history of severe epigastric pain radiating to the left upper quadrant, fever up to 39 °C responsive to paracetamol, nausea, vomiting, and anorexia. On examination, she had epigastric tenderness with left upper quadrant guarding; her abdomen was otherwise soft and lax, and no mass could be palpated.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 21.8×10^3/mm^3, hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, platelets 832×10^3/mm^3, C-reactive protein 203 mg/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 83 mm/h, lipase 10 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase 633 U/L, carcinoembryonic antigen 2.78 ng/mL, and a negative Quantiferon test. Blood cultures were negative.

Abdominal ultrasound revealed a well-defined, multiloculated cystic lesion in the epigastrium extending to the left upper quadrant, the largest locule measuring 4.8×4.0×5.6 cm with swirling debris and foci of calcification, and no hyperemia. CT with contrast confirmed a multiloculated, thick, enhancing-walled fluid collection in the mesentery extending to the left flank, the largest locule measuring 6.7×6.2 cm with tiny calcifications displacing adjacent bowel loops. Mild pelvic fluid and subcentimetric enhancing mesenteric lymph nodes were noted.

Findings were interpreted as an organized abscess secondary to an infected mesenteric cyst or a lymphangioma. A true-cut biopsy yielded only fibrinoid material without viable cells, precluding a definitive diagnosis.

A 16-year-old boy presented with multiple sharply demarcated, waxy, brown-black, oval-shaped papules and plaques with a stuck-on appearance on the cheeks, chin, and posterior to his left ear. The lesions measured up to 1 cm in diameter and had been present since he was about 7 years old, without any change in size or appearance over the past 2–3 years. He had no other medical conditions, was not taking any medications, and had no family history of similar lesions. A dermatologist performed a biopsy, and histologic examination revealed basaloid keratinocyte proliferation without dysplasia and hyperkeratosis with horn pseudocyst formation.

A 69-year-old man with a history of rectal cancer treated with preoperative chemoradiotherapy and low anterior resection (pathologic stage ypT2N0M0), followed by adjuvant 5-fluorouracil–based chemotherapy, presented for his fifth annual follow-up. Colonoscopy showed no recurrence, and carcinoembryonic antigen was 1.5 ng/mL. Pelvic MRI revealed multiple small nodules in the pelvic bones suggestive of bony metastases. 18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated multiple hypermetabolic foci in the bilateral humeri, femurs, scapulae, ribs, spine, and pelvic bones. A Tc-99m MDP bone scan showed increased uptake in the right anterior sixth rib, the T9 spinous process, and bilateral sacroiliac joints. Under a presumptive diagnosis of bone metastases from rectal cancer, palliative XELOX chemotherapy was planned but was delayed for five weeks because of anemia, leukocytopenia, and a mildly elevated serum creatinine level. After the first dose, the patient developed worsening pancytopenia, rising creatinine, poor oral intake, and nausea, which were attributed to chemotherapy adverse effects. Chemotherapy was withheld for two months, yet the pancytopenia and renal dysfunction persisted, prompting referral to nephrology for evaluation of renal impairment.

A 20-year-old man with a history of Sturge-Weber syndrome presented with 2 days of right-sided weakness, slurred speech, altered consciousness, and an episode of oral dyskinesia while playing basketball. He denied trauma and reports two recent episodes of vomiting and feeling cold but no fevers, headaches, visual changes, or chest pain. He had childhood seizures, the last at age 12, and has not taken antiepileptic medications since.

On examination, he was alert and oriented with slowed responses and slurred speech, but no facial droop and intact extraocular movements. Motor strength was 3/5 in the right upper extremity, 5/5 in the left upper extremity, 4/5 in the right lower extremity, and 5/5 in the left lower extremity. Decreased tactile sensation was noted in both lower extremities up to the knees. Herpetic vesicles were present on the lower lip, and finger-to-nose coordination was preserved on the left but impaired on the right.

Laboratory studies showed a prolactin level > 200 ng/mL; CBC, CMP, and urinalysis were normal; urine drug screen was positive for marijuana. EEG demonstrated moderate generalized background slowing suggestive of diffuse cerebral dysfunction and possible sharp wave activity in the occipital region.

Noncontrast head CT demonstrated a heterogeneously hyperdense lesion in the suprasellar cistern with central hypodensity, measuring approximately 3.0 cm, extending from the sella turcica and causing mass effect on the optic chiasm. Subsequent MRI with and without contrast confirmed a 3 cm sellar and suprasellar mass with heterogeneous enhancement and cystic areas.

A 49-year-old African-American perimenopausal woman with a history of metastatic estrogen receptor–positive, progesterone receptor–negative, HER2-negative invasive ductal breast carcinoma on maintenance tamoxifen therapy presented with abnormal uterine bleeding. She had been diagnosed 8 months earlier with biopsy-proven liver metastases and completed anthracycline-based chemotherapy 3 months before starting tamoxifen. She denied abdominal pain, distension, changes in bowel or bladder function. 

On examination, blood was noted at the cervical os and the uterus felt bulky and firm. Routine blood tests showed hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL and hematocrit 35.5%. Serum CA 15-3 and CA 27.29 were within normal limits; carcinoembryonic antigen was mildly elevated at 5.5 ng/mL. Pelvic ultrasound revealed an enlarged uterus without fibroids and a thickened endometrial lining measuring 9.0 mm. 

Endocervical curettage demonstrated rare atypical cells with marked nuclear enlargement and numerous mitoses. Endometrial biopsy showed invasive carcinoma in sheets of cells with round to ovoid nuclei and abundant finely granular cytoplasm. Immunohistochemical staining of the tumor revealed positivity for cytokeratin 7, gross cystic disease fluid protein-15, HER2, and Ki-67 with mild CEA staining, and negativity for estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, cytokeratin 20, p40, and p16.

An 89-year-old Japanese woman presented with a several months’ history of an asymptomatic, gradually enlarging pigmented skin lesion on the dorsum of her left foot, initially 1 mm and now 5 mm in diameter. On examination, there was a single hyperpigmented oval macule measuring 5 mm with a rough surface; the color ranged from dark brown to light brown, and the lesion was slightly elevated. Dermoscopic examination demonstrated an atypical pigment network with small dotted vessels, and irregular flossy streaks were noted at the periphery. Because of the clinical and dermoscopic features, very early superficial spreading melanoma was suspected, and the lesion was excised with a 3 mm margin.

A 30-year-old woman presented with a 1–1.5-month history of right-sided abdominal pain and significant weight loss. She noted a progressively enlarging right abdominal mass for the past 2 weeks and had one episode of hematuria 4–5 months earlier. On examination, there was a smooth, well-defined, firm to hard mass in the right hypochondrium and lumbar region that moved with respiration. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a large heterogeneously enhancing isodense to hypodense mass arising from the right kidney and replacing most of the renal parenchyma; the renal capsule and perirenal fat planes were preserved. CT angiography demonstrated contiguous extension of the mass as a hypodense thrombus through the infra- and supra-hepatic inferior vena cava into the right atrium. 

Given these findings, the patient was taken for a right radical nephrectomy with removal of the inferior vena cava and atrial thrombus.

A 3-month-old infant presented with marked abdominal distention. Medical history was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed mildly elevated serum transaminases (AST 54 IU/L; ALT 45 IU/L) and an increased neuron-specific enolase level of 21.9 ng/mL. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 10 × 10 × 12 cm heterogeneous cystic mass in the right suprarenal area displacing the right kidney downward and a 2 × 2 × 2 cm anechoic cystic lesion in the left adrenal gland. The border between the right adrenal lesion and the right hepatic lobe was indistinct. Multiple anechoic cystic lesions up to 10 mm in diameter were present in both hepatic lobes. Contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated that both adrenal and all hepatic lesions were cystic, with thickened walls showing contrast enhancement, no solid components, and calcifications in the posteroinferior portion of the right adrenal mass; the hepatic lesions showed no enhancement.

A 33-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of worsening right knee pain and a progressively enlarging mass on the anterior aspect of the knee. He denied fevers, weight loss, or night sweats and had no involvement of other joints. His past medical history was notable only for chronic right knee pain for 10 years with intermittent locking and giving way; he had undergone arthroscopies 10 and 2 years previously, the latter showing advanced cartilage degeneration.

On examination, there was a 4×5 cm firm, non-tender mass on the anterolateral aspect of the right knee adjacent to the patellar tendon. The knee had full range of motion; deep flexion worsened the pain. Examination was otherwise unremarkable. Inflammatory markers were within normal limits.

Plain radiographs and CT of the right knee showed advanced degenerative changes with intraarticular loose bodies and a large nonhomogeneous lesion adjacent to the patellar tendon, with a second smaller lesion near the proximal tibiofibular joint. MRI demonstrated a well-circumscribed 4.2×2.6 cm lesion filling the inferior Hoffa’s fat pad with tenting of the patellar tendon, and a second similar lesion adjacent to the proximal tibiofibular joint. A lateral meniscal tear and advanced degenerative changes were also noted.

A 32-year-old man presented with chronic left knee pain of 1½ years’ duration. The pain persisted at rest, worsened at night, and was temporarily relieved by NSAIDs. He had no history of trauma. On examination, there was swelling and tenderness on the anteromedial aspect of the left knee; meniscal tests were negative, quadriceps muscle showed moderate atrophy, and range of motion was intact. Plain radiographs of the knee showed no abnormalities. Initial MRI performed at the onset of symptoms demonstrated bone marrow edema in the medial tibial plateau. A repeat MRI, obtained recently, showed a focal nidus-like lesion with surrounding bone marrow edema in the same region.

A 78-year-old woman presented with a 12-month history of a gradually enlarging, painless mass over her right eye. She denied visual loss, diplopia, epiphora, or xerophthalmia. Her medical history included hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with an implantable defibrillator; otherwise, she was in good health. On examination, there was a firm mass palpable in the palpebral lobe of the right lacrimal gland beneath the supraorbital rim. Visual fields and ophthalmoscopy were normal, and visual acuity was 20/70 bilaterally, appropriate for her age. Cranial nerve, ear, nose, and throat examinations showed no abnormalities. Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits demonstrated a soft-tissue tumor arising from the palpebral lobe of the right lacrimal gland without invasion or compression of adjacent structures. The patient was scheduled for removal of the right lacrimal gland via orbitotomy with a working diagnosis of pleomorphic adenoma.

A 27-year-old man with a history of a 5 mm‐thick melanoma on his posterior neck treated six years earlier by wide local excision (no sentinel lymph node biopsy, no adjuvant therapy) presented with hemoptysis and dyspnea. Vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination was notable only for scattered breath sounds without stridor. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a 3.1 × 2.7 × 3.6 cm mass in the right lower lobe. Endobronchial ultrasound–guided fine-needle aspiration of the lung lesion demonstrated a malignant small round blue cell tumor. Molecular studies were negative for an EWSR1 translocation but otherwise were interpreted as consistent with Ewing sarcoma/primitive neuroectodermal tumor (PNET). 

Positron emission tomography (PET)/CT showed an FDG-avid right lower lobe mass and an intensely FDG-avid, partially calcified 4.1 × 2.3 × 2.8 cm expansile lesion within the right hyoid bone. Ultrasound–guided core needle biopsy of the hyoid lesion was nondiagnostic, yielding only rare atypical epithelial cells amidst lymphocytes.

A multidisciplinary sarcoma tumor board concluded that the hyoid lesion most likely represented a synchronous primary bone tumor (e.g., plasmacytoma, chondrosarcoma, or osteosarcoma). Given his pulmonary symptoms and the potential for chemotherapy to treat both lesions, he received 14 cycles of vincristine, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, and etoposide (VCD/IE). 

Mid-treatment PET/CT demonstrated a substantial decrease in size and complete metabolic response of the lung mass but development of right neck adenopathy and interval growth of the hyoid bone lesion, suggesting a distinct pathology.

A 48-year-old man presented with a dry cough and occasional hemoptysis. Chest imaging revealed two discrete lung lesions: a 2.5 cm mass in the right lower lobe and a 0.7 cm nodule in the right upper lobe. PET/CT showed mild uptake in the larger lesion and no other abnormalities. Surgical specimens included the right lower lobe lobectomy containing the dominant lesion, a wedge biopsy of the smaller nodule, and multiple mediastinal lymph nodes, which were negative for tumor.

Microscopic examination showed unencapsulated but well-circumscribed nodules with a prominent capillary network and intervening stromal cells displaying eosinophilic to clear cytoplasm with fine lipid vacuoles. Occasional solid lobules lacking vasculature demonstrated increased cytological atypia. On frozen section, the tumor appeared highly vascular with microcystic changes and epithelioid cells mimicking renal cell carcinoma.

Initial immunohistochemistry revealed nonreactivity for pancytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, synaptophysin, chromogranin, Melan-A, and CD10, findings that did not support carcinoma, melanoma, or neuroendocrine tumor. The lipid-containing cells were negative for Melan-A, inconsistent with adrenal cortical neoplasm. Further stains were negative for the histiocytic markers CD68, CD1a, CD45, and lysozyme.

Communication with the referring hospitals disclosed two prior posterior fossa surgeries for brain tumors 20 and 7 years earlier. Additional immunohistochemical studies demonstrated that the stromal cells were positive for inhibin-A, neuron specific enolase (NSE), S-100, and vimentin. CD34 highlighted only the capillary vasculature; fewer than 5% of cells reacted for Ki-67, and GFAP was negative.

A 57-year-old woman presented with several months of chest discomfort and mild dyspnea on exertion (mMRC grade 1). She denied cough, sputum production, fever, weight loss, or night sweats. Her medical history was notable only for dyslipidemia; she was a never smoker with no occupational or environmental exposures. On examination, vital signs were normal, and oxygen saturation was 99% on room air; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, C-reactive protein, and electrolytes. Serologic testing for antinuclear antibody, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and rheumatoid factor was negative. A purified protein derivative skin test was negative.
