Pulmonary function tests revealed normal spirometry (FVC 2.8 L [88% predicted], FEV₁ 2.28 L [93% predicted]) and a diffusion capacity of 18.1 ml/min/mmHg (101% predicted). High-resolution CT of the chest demonstrated ill-defined, multifocal centrilobular nodules with ground-glass opacity in both lungs, predominantly in dependent and peripheral regions, measuring 1–7 mm in diameter. No mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy was present. Abdominal and pelvic CT scans showed no evidence of malignancy or other abnormalities.

A 20-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of intermittent abdominal pain, recurrent vomiting, and melena. She had no significant past medical history and no family history of cancer. On examination, she had mild abdominal tenderness; gynecological examination was normal. Laboratory studies revealed iron-deficiency anemia; white blood cell and platelet counts were normal. Upper and lower endoscopies were unremarkable. Magnetic resonance enterography demonstrated a focal segment of small-bowel wall thickening measuring 15 mm by 2 mm. An exploratory laparotomy revealed an exophytic ileal mass with mesenteric lymphadenopathy but no peritoneal or hepatic metastases. A wide segmental resection was performed without complication.

Gross examination showed a 30 mm by 25 mm polypoid, tan-white, lobulated mass arising from the small-intestinal wall. Microscopically, the lesion was a transmural, infiltrative proliferation of uniform epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in nested and fascicular patterns, with variable eosinophilic or clear cytoplasm, round to oval vesicular nuclei, inconspicuous nucleoli, and up to 10 mitoses per 10 high-power fields; there was mucosal ulceration but no melanin pigment, lymphovascular invasion, or perineural invasion, and three mesenteric lymph nodes were negative for tumor.

Immunohistochemical analysis showed diffuse, strong positivity for S100 protein and SOX10; HMB45 and Melan A were negative. There was patchy synaptophysin expression. CD117, DOG1, cytokeratin, CD34, smooth muscle actin, desmin, chromogranin, and CD56 were all negative.

A woman in her 50s with hypercholesterolemia, osteoporosis, mild aortic-root dilation, and recurrent atypical chest pain presented with recurrent bilateral flank pain. She had a history of occasional alcohol use and was a former smoker (20 pack-years, quit 4 years earlier). Medications included atorvastatin, ezetimibe, calcium/vitamin D, and sublingual glyceryl trinitrate as needed.

Family history was notable for her daughter’s recurrent spontaneous pneumothoraces and bilateral renal cysts, and her brother’s bilateral renal cysts with mild aortic-root dilation. Her mother had emphysema; her father had lung cancer.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen showed bilateral renal cysts and an enlarged right adrenal gland. She underwent multiple percutaneous aspirations of symptomatic renal cysts. Skin lesions suggestive of fibrofolliculomas were biopsied and reported as milia. CT of the chest showed no pulmonary cysts.

Targeted next-generation sequencing of FLCN, FH, MAX, RET, SDHA, SDHAF2, SDHB, SDHC, TMEM127, and VHL genes did not identify a pathogenic variant.

Over the ensuing months she experienced episodic hypertension, anxiety, diaphoresis, and headaches. Laboratory studies revealed an elevated 24-hour urine norepinephrine level. Metaiodobenzylguanidine scintigraphy demonstrated a 2.4-cm right adrenal lesion that was avid.

A Palestinian woman in her late 50s presented with a 10-year history of progressive difficulty swallowing solid foods, worsening over the past 2 years. She also reported mood disturbances and increased urination. Her medical history included osteoporosis, subclinical hypothyroidism, and a 5-year history of hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcemia. There was no family history of hypercalcemia, kidney stones, or fragility fractures.

On examination, her vital signs were stable and the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a parathyroid hormone level of 99.6 pg/mL, a serum calcium level of 11.5 mg/dL, and a serum phosphorus level of 2.25 mg/dL; thyroid function tests were normal.

Neck ultrasonography revealed a well-defined, homogenous, hypoechoic nodule below the lower pole of the left thyroid lobe measuring approximately 0.43 × 0.42 × 0.78 cm. Fine-needle aspiration of the nodule showed follicular cells in a colloid background. A 99mTc-sestamibi scan demonstrated homogeneous tracer uptake in the thyroid gland with a distinct focal activity inferior to the lower pole of the left thyroid lobe. Subsequent single-photon emission computed tomography confirmed a 6.6 × 3.8 mm lesion consistent with a left inferior parathyroid adenoma.

A 33-year-old man presented with gradual-onset complete paralysis and sensory loss of both lower limbs over one month, associated with upper and lower back pain. He denied trauma, fever, weight loss, night sweats, headache, visual changes, incontinence, or constitutional symptoms. He had no significant medical or family history and took no medications. On examination, vital signs were normal. There was tenderness over the thoracic and lumbar spine. Upper-limb neurologic examination was normal; lower limbs had flaccid paralysis and loss of sensation bilaterally. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 120 mm/h and a total serum protein concentration of 9.9 g/dL; a complete blood count, coagulation profile, C-reactive protein, electrolytes, liver and kidney function tests, thyroid function tests, urinalysis, and blood cultures were unremarkable. Serum protein electrophoresis revealed mild hypoalbuminemia and marked monoclonal hypergammaglobulinemia; immunofixation identified an IgA λ monoclonal protein. A chest radiograph showed a left paraspinal posterior mediastinal opacity above the aortic arch. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a left paraspinal mass extending through the left T2–T3 neural foramen into the posterior epidural space, and bone-window images revealed multiple well-defined “punched-out” lytic lesions with endosteal scalloping in vertebral bodies. CT of the lumbar and cervical spine confirmed multiple lytic lesions in vertebral bodies, sacrum, and iliac bones, with a micronodular pattern and osteopenia in the cervical spine. MRI of the entire spine showed multiple infiltrative high-signal bone marrow lesions on T2/STIR sequences involving C4, upper dorsal vertebrae, and D4 spinous process, with a large lobulated left paraspinal and epidural mass compressing the spinal cord. A delayed whole-body bone scan was unremarkable.

A 12-year-old boy presented with a 3-year history of pain and swelling in his left knee, without prior trauma or treatment. Physical examination revealed a soft, non-tender, palpable 3×4 cm mass on the medial aspect of the knee that became more pronounced in full flexion. There was no knee effusion, no instability, a full range of motion, normal lower-extremity strength, and negative McMurray and Apley tests. Leg lengths were equal, and there were no cutaneous lesions. Medical, developmental, and family histories were unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including a complete coagulation profile, were within normal limits. Plain radiographs of the knee were normal. MRI showed a well-defined, lobulated mass with internal septations within the suprapatellar pouch infiltrating the vastus medialis muscle. The lesion was low to intermediate signal on T1-weighted images and markedly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with thin fibrofatty septae creating a characteristic lace-like pattern. The differential diagnosis mainly included pigmented villonodular synovitis (PVNS) and synovial sarcoma, with consideration of other arthropathies such as rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile chronic arthritis, hemophilic arthropathy, synovial osteochondromatosis, and lipoma arborescens.

A 58-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 50-day history of right hemimandibular pain. Her only past medical history was hypothyroidism managed with replacement therapy. Initially evaluated by a dentist for presumed odontogenic pain, she underwent extraction of the lower right third molar without relief; her pain then worsened, extending to the right ear with muffling, hyposensitivity of the right tongue and hemipalate, and a mild right facial nerve deficit. She denied odynophagia. Empirical amoxicillin/clavulanic acid prescribed by her general practitioner yielded no benefit.

On arrival, she was prostrated by pain but afebrile. Examination revealed right hemifacial swelling and palpable right lateral cervical lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests showed WBC 11.3×10^9/L, hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL, platelets 382×10^9/L, creatinine 0.58 mg/dL, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, calcium 9.3 mg/dL, AST 32 U/L, ALT 21 U/L, C-reactive protein 0.34 mg/dL, procalcitonin <0.1 ng/mL, TSH 1.95 μU/mL, CEA 1.3 ng/mL, and CA 19-9 31.7 U/mL. Otoscopic examination showed right catarrhal otitis. Oropharyngoscopy demonstrated medialization of the right tonsil with ipsilateral hemipalate swelling but no clear abscess; laryngeal examination was normal.

Neck ultrasound revealed a 30-mm hypoechoic, nonhomogeneous mass adjacent to the right pharynx and multiple pathological submandibular and laterocervical lymph nodes; the thyroid and salivary glands were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound showed ring-shaped hyperenhancement of the lesion with a nonperfused central area. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a 35×38-mm mass in the right tonsillar region with central hypodensity, thick irregular walls, uneven enhancement, and calcifications, displacing the trachea and inseparable from adjacent muscles and the parotid gland, along with multiple right-sided lymphadenopathies. Noncontrast brain CT identified two rounded hypodense lesions in the right frontal and right cerebellar regions with peripheral enhancement and moderate perilesional edema. Brain MRI further characterized these intracranial lesions, favoring a neoplastic over an abscess etiology.

A 19-year-old man presented with firm, painless swellings on the fingers of both hands and on the medial aspect of the left foot, along with several bluish soft nodules over the left heel. The lesions first appeared at age 5 and had gradually enlarged.  

On plain radiographs of the hands and feet, there were multiple well-defined expansile osteolytic lesions in the phalanges and metacarpals of both hands and in the first metatarsal of the left foot, with cortical thinning, endosteal scalloping, and a few areas of cortical absence. In the soft tissues of the feet, there were multiple round calcifications suggestive of phleboliths.  

Ultrasound of the medial soft-tissue swellings on the left foot revealed multiple well-defined hyperechoic areas with mild marginal blood flow on color Doppler.  

Fine-needle aspiration biopsy of a bony lesion from a finger showed lobules of chondroid tissue containing chondrocytes. Biopsy of a soft-tissue nodule from the foot demonstrated anastomosing vascular channels lined by plump endothelial cells.

A 10-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a 3-week history of an enlarging right orbital mass. He reported mild pain on palpation of the lesion but denied vision changes or history of trauma. His past medical history was notable only for longstanding exotropia. On examination, visual acuity was 20/25 in each eye, and intraocular pressures were 19 mmHg OD and 20 mmHg OS. Extraocular movements were full, with a 15-prism-diopter exotropia on alternate cover testing. Hertel exophthalmometry measurements were symmetric without proptosis; there was 2–3 mm of hypoglobus on the right. Cranial nerves V1, V2, V3, and VII were intact. A firm, tender mass fixed to the superolateral orbital rim was palpated. The remainder of the anterior and posterior segment examinations was unremarkable.

The patient underwent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with and without contrast and computed tomography (CT) without contrast. MRI demonstrated a 2.7 cm mass centered in the bone of the superolateral right orbit with adjacent bone destruction, extension into the extraconal space, and abnormal signal in the right frontal bone and sphenotemporal buttress. CT showed bone erosion with only a thin shell remaining between the lesion and the intracranial compartment.

A 69-year-old man with a history of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma diagnosed in January 2021, treated with docetaxel, vincristine, Adriamycin, dexamethasone, and both intravenous and intrathecal methotrexate, presented in October 2021 with swelling in the left popliteal fossa, neuropathic pain, and weakness. On examination, there was a palpable mass in the left popliteal fossa. Ultrasonography demonstrated a heterogeneous echogenic mass with internal vascularity in the popliteal fossa, with the sciatic and tibial nerves appearing as a cable-like edematous structure within the mass. MRI of the left knee revealed a fusiform, infiltrating mass lesion measuring 83×44×35 mm with intermediate signal intensity on T1-weighted images, high signal intensity on T2-weighted and STIR images, and heterogeneous predominantly peripheral enhancement; perilesional edema and partial encasement of the popliteal artery were noted. The distal sciatic and proximal tibial nerves were enlarged, infiltrated, and coursed through the mass.

A 50-year-old man presented with 6 months of slowly progressive, painless bilateral scrotal swelling (left > right) and 1 month of abdominal discomfort and difficulty walking due to the swelling. He had no significant past or family history. On examination, both testes were enlarged and firm without tenderness or skin changes; there was mild abdominal distension. 

Scrotal ultrasonography showed diffuse bilateral testicular enlargement with a heterogeneously hypoechoic echotexture and raised vascularity on Doppler, bulky heterogeneous epididymides, and hypoechoic thickening of the left spermatic cord with increased flow; a small bilateral hydrocele was noted. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated bilaterally enlarged hypoechoic kidneys with mild left hydronephrosis and a left retroperitoneal mass encasing the aorta.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed:
- Bilaterally enlarged, heterogeneously enhancing testes and epididymes with bilateral hydrocele.
- An enhancing soft-tissue mass extending contiguously from the left scrotum along the left spermatic cord and gonadal vein into a large retroperitoneal nodal mass encasing major vessels and left ureter.
- Bilateral heterogeneous kidneys with striated nephrogram pattern, perinephric stranding, and left hydroureteronephrosis.
- Diffuse enlargement of both adrenal glands.
- Homogeneously enhancing mediastinal and left axillary lymph nodes.
- Multiple lytic bone lesions with enhancing soft tissue and at least one pathological fracture.

Laboratory studies showed elevated lactate dehydrogenase (725 U/L; normal 140–280 U/L) with normal alpha-fetoprotein (4.02 ng/mL) and beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (<1.2 mIU/mL).

A 63-year-old man presented with right-sided chest pain. He had a history of hypertension. On admission, his serum calcium was 13.6 mg/dL (normal 8.6–10.1), inorganic phosphorus 2.3 mg/dL (2.2–4.1), whole PTH 7 pg/mL (9–39), and intact PTHrP 49.2 pmol/L (<1.1). Tumor markers were notable for CEA 31.3 ng/mL (<5.0), CA19-9 2139.4 U/mL (<37.0), and AFP 55.5 ng/mL (<10). Abdominal CT revealed multiple liver masses up to 8 cm with peripheral enhancement and multiple lymphadenopathy. Neck CT demonstrated metastatic lymph nodes. Chest CT showed osteolytic lesions in the thoracic vertebrae, but whole-body bone scintigraphy was negative. No parathyroid enlargement or other primary tumors were seen on CT or ultrasound, and upper and lower endoscopy were unremarkable. A biopsy of a left neck lymph node revealed moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma.

A 30-year-old previously healthy woman presented with a 2-week history of worsening fatigue, easy bruising, low back pain, and low-grade fever. On examination, vital signs were normal; there was mild oozing of blood from the gums and a 3-cm ecchymosis on the right flank. Initial laboratories revealed severe thrombocytopenia, anemia, and coagulopathy. Magnetic resonance imaging of the thoracolumbar spine demonstrated a pathologic process involving the marrow of all visualized osseous structures. A bone marrow aspirate and core biopsy were obtained. The aspirate showed no immunophenotypic evidence of acute leukemia, lymphoma, or plasma cell neoplasm, and the core was hypercellular (80–90%) with a normal blast percentage. Hematoxylin and eosin staining of the core revealed 60% involvement by a poorly differentiated, high-grade neoplasm with large pleomorphic nuclei, mitotic figures, prominent nucleoli, abundant vacuolated cytoplasm, and occasional multinucleated dark brown pigmented cells.

A 40-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of pain and swelling on the right side of her face. She reported that an ameloblastoma had been excised from the same region 6 months earlier. On extraoral examination, there was a firm, nonmobile swelling extending from the right corner of the mouth anteriorly to the pinna posteriorly, and from the zygomatic arch superiorly to the upper neck inferiorly. Intraorally, a pedunculated, irregular-surfaced gingival mass was noted on the lower-right side, extending from tooth 44 to 48, with spontaneous bleeding. A panoramic radiograph showed a unilocular radiolucency in the lower-right posterior mandible (44–48) with alveolar bone resorption and displacement of adjacent tooth roots. A CT scan revealed cortical perforation on the coronal and lingual aspects of the lesion. An incisional biopsy was performed, and a provisional diagnosis of malignant ameloblastoma and non–Hodgkin’s lymphoma was made.

A 55-year-old postmenopausal Syrian woman presented with 10 days of massive vaginal bleeding accompanied by constant abdominal pain, diarrhea, and vomiting. She entered natural menopause 15 months earlier and had 14 prior term deliveries, with the last delivery 13 years ago. She denied any history of spontaneous abortion, contraceptive use, or molar pregnancy. On examination, a pelvic mass was palpable up to 3 cm above the umbilicus. Serum β-human chorionic gonadotropin was 542 250 mU/mL. Pelvic ultrasonography revealed an enlarged uterus, equivalent to a 24-week gestation, containing a heterogeneous, vesicular-appearing mass obliterating the endometrial cavity; the ovaries appeared normal. Abdominopelvic CT confirmed a well-demarcated uterine mass measuring 25 × 20 × 13 cm with very high-density central cystic content. The primary differential diagnosis included a metastatic endometrial leiomyosarcoma, a choriocarcinoma, and an invasive mole. Chest and cranial CT scans showed mild bilateral pleural effusion and multiple nodular lesions in the basal lung segments, with no other metastatic lesions detected.

A 54-year-old right-handed woman presented with a 10-year history of progressively intense pain, cold sensitivity, and severe tenderness localized to the pulp of her left little finger. She reported no trauma, systemic disease, or notable social history. The pain worsened upon exposure to cold and at night. Prior evaluation by a primary care physician yielded no diagnosis.

On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs. Inspection of the left little finger revealed a firm, 1.5-cm subcutaneous nodule on the pulp of the distal phalanx, pinkish-red in color and streaked with telangiectasias. Polarized contact dermoscopy showed peripheral clearing of the reddish coloration, revealing a yellow-to-white background with multiple surface telangiectasias. Neurologic examination of the hand was normal, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Initial differential diagnoses included glomus tumor, schwannoma, mucous cyst, and neurofibroma. Radiographs of the left hand demonstrated a soft-tissue mass at the distal pulp with no bony erosion. Ultrasonography and MRI were not performed because a glomus tumor was considered highly probable.

A 54-year-old Chinese man presented with 1 month of progressive left upper-limb weakness and numbness. His medical history was notable only for diabetes mellitus. On examination, motor strength in the left upper extremity was 3/5, with hypoesthesia in the left C8 and T1 dermatomes and normal deep-tendon reflexes. MRI of the cervicothoracic spine and left brachial plexus showed a 1.3 × 0.7 × 0.8 cm infiltrative intraspinal mass at T1 on the left, with poorly defined margins, iso- to hypointense signal on T2-weighted images, heterogeneous contrast enhancement, intramedullary expansion and edema, and thickening and enhancement of the left T1 nerve root with foraminal widening and an extramedullary nodule. The initial working diagnosis included an infective or inflammatory process, secondary metastatic deposits, or an underlying primary central nervous malignancy. MRI of the brain and CT of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis showed no other lesions. Lumbar puncture revealed cerebrospinal fluid without organisms, viral DNA, or malignant cells.

A 12-year-old girl presented with a 6-month history of dull, aching pain in her left pelvis and hip, accompanied by a slight limp. There was no radiation of pain and no sensory changes. On examination, there was no visible swelling of the left hemipelvis, but mild tenderness on pressure. The range of motion of the hip joint was full and pain free.  
An anteroposterior radiograph of the pelvis demonstrated expansile osteolytic lesions throughout the left iliac bone extending to the roof of the acetabulum. Computed tomography confirmed a globally ballooned, expansile lesion of the iliac bone with thinning of the cortex. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a well-defined, multilobulated cystic mass (12 × 10 × 5 cm) in the left ilium containing multiple fluid–fluid levels. A three-phase bone scan revealed solitary heterogeneous uptake in the left ilium on delayed images. SPECT-CT demonstrated a multilocular expansile cystic lesion with internal septations and a thin cortical rim without periosteal reaction.

A 28-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of abdominal pain, postprandial vomiting, mucoid, tar-colored stools, and an 18.6-kg weight loss. Symptoms began as intense five-minute lower abdominal cramps after eating, with bloating; over six months, she deteriorated to tolerating only small liquid meals and required parenteral nutrition. In January 2022, she underwent myomectomy for a uterine myoma without relief of GI symptoms. In March 2022, sigmoidoscopy was nondiagnostic due to poor preparation. She was treated for irritable bowel syndrome with antidepressants and for peptic ulcer disease, but symptoms persisted. Laboratory tests revealed a hemoglobin level of 9 mg/dl. Endoscopy ruled out peptic ulcer. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a well-defined, round, concentric mass measuring 5.4×4.9 cm in the left hemiabdomen with fat within the lesion and a “bowel within bowel” appearance, consistent with colo-colic intussusception.

A 35-year-old Thai woman presented with a 6-month history of a single asymptomatic, acne-like lesion on her left cheek. After dental treatment for caries, the lesion rapidly enlarged, and a few new erythematous papules appeared on the face. She denied fever, weight loss, night sweats, or other systemic symptoms, and had no significant past medical history. Family members were unaffected.

On examination, there was a reddish-yellow, tumor-like lesion measuring 5 cm in diameter on the left cheek and several 1–1.5 cm erythematous papules on the right face. No lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or other abnormalities were noted. 

Computed tomography of the brain, neck, chest, and abdomen showed only a non-significant 0.8 cm cervical lymph node. Bone marrow studies and basic laboratory tests were within normal limits.

A 64-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of right upper abdominal pain without nausea, vomiting, chills, or fever. She had no history of hepatitis, surgery, or hereditary disease, and no underlying medical conditions. On examination, she was afebrile and oriented; there was right upper abdominal tenderness without rebound or palpable masses, no hepatosplenomegaly, and negative Murphy’s sign and shifting dullness.

Laboratory studies showed:  
• AFP 2.4 µg/l (normal 0.0–7.0)  
• CEA 11.6 µg/l (normal 0.0–5.0)  
• CA-125 32.3 KIU/l (normal 0.0–35.0)  
• CA19-9 228.0 KIU/l (normal 0.0–30.0)  
• Other liver enzymes and blood counts largely within reference ranges, except WBC 11.9×10^9/l (normal 3.5–9.5×10^9/l).

Ultrasonography revealed a heterogeneous echoic mass near the gallbladder fossa in the right liver lobe, calcifications in the right liver, multiple gallstones with gallbladder wall thickening, and enhanced pancreatic echogenicity. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a lesion in the right hepatic lobe adjacent to the gallbladder fossa, multiple enlarged hepatic hilar lymph nodes, and findings of gallstones with cholecystitis. Liver MRI demonstrated an occupying lesion in the right lobe with mild intrahepatic bile duct dilatation, raising the possibility of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, along with gallstones and cholecystitis. No extrahepatic primary tumor was identified.

A 55-year-old man with hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (20 pack-year smoking history), untreated hepatitis C, and active cocaine use was admitted with progressive dyspnea of one-month duration and a productive cough with yellow sputum.
On presentation, he was afebrile, and his oxygen saturation was 96% on 2 L per minute of supplemental oxygen by nasal cannula. Physical examination revealed bilateral rhonchi and crackles, predominantly in the left lower lobe.
Laboratory studies showed a normal white-cell count and a troponin I level of 0.2 ng/mL with no ischemic changes on electrocardiogram. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no evidence of heart failure or wall-motion abnormalities.
A chest radiograph showed diffuse bilateral upper and lower lobe patchy air-space opacities with nodular appearance, suggestive of multilobar pneumonia. The patient was started on broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy but subsequently required intubation for hypoxemic respiratory failure.
Chest computed tomography demonstrated extensive bilateral parenchymal infiltrates with mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) revealed fluid positive for aspergillus antigen and herpes simplex virus 1 DNA by PCR; serum aspergillus antigen was negative. The remainder of the infectious work-up — including acid-fast bacilli smear, mycobacterial cultures, BAL fluid bacterial cultures and Gram stain, serum cryptococcal antigen, and HIV antigen/antibody testing — was negative. An autoimmune panel, including antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and myositis autoantibodies, was negative. Empirical intravenous methylprednisolone was administered for possible associated pneumonitis.

A 20‐year‐old woman presented with acute onset of epigastric and chest pain, shortness of breath, and vomiting that began after eating a tuna sandwich earlier that day. Her medical history included hypothyroidism, depression treated with sertraline, and dysmenorrhea. She had been taking oral contraceptive pills for seven years. Her body‐mass index was 34. Vital signs were notable for blood pressure 164/81 mmHg and pulse 99 bpm. Physical examination revealed palpable hepatomegaly.

Initial laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (16,000/mm3), aspartate aminotransferase 267 U/L, and alanine aminotransferase 333 U/L. A SARS‐CoV‐2 PCR test was negative. Viral hepatitis panels and tumor markers (carcinoembryonic antigen, CA 19-9, CA 125) were within normal limits.

Because of concern for pulmonary embolism, a CT angiogram of the chest was obtained; it was negative for embolism but demonstrated multiple large hyperenhancing masses in both hepatic lobes. To further characterize these liver lesions, MRI of the liver was performed, which showed hepatic steatosis and multiple masses: one 9.0 × 8.5 cm hemorrhagic lesion in the hepatic dome causing mass effect on the intrahepatic inferior vena cava; a second 5.9 × 5.1 cm nonhemorrhagic lesion inseparable from the dominant mass; and several additional nonhemorrhagic lesions smaller than 4.5 cm.

A previously healthy four-year-old boy presented with fever and a gradually enlarging lump in the right parotid region. On examination, the mass measured approximately 6 × 5 cm, was nontender, firm to hard, and irregular, with associated proptosis of the right eye. The swelling extended superiorly to the zygomatic region, inferiorly to the mandible, anteriorly toward the maxilla, and posteriorly toward the retromandibular space.

Contrast-enhanced radiological studies demonstrated a large, solid, ill-defined lesion along the right mandibular ramus, extending into the masseteric space and toward the skull base, with involvement of the nasopharynx, posterior ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses and associated sinus‐wall remodeling—findings suggestive of a neoplastic process. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included rhabdomyosarcoma, lymphoma, and primitive neuroectodermal tumor. Routine laboratory investigations were within normal limits except for mild anemia.

Microscopic examination of a parotid biopsy revealed sheets of round to oval tumor cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, hyperchromatic and irregular nuclear membranes, and occasional angulated nuclei. Scattered eosinophilic precursors, neutrophils, and lymphoid cells were noted. There was no acinar differentiation or lymphoglandular bodies. On histopathologic grounds, a diagnosis of Langerhans cell histiocytosis versus granulocytic sarcoma was considered. To clarify the diagnosis, immunohistochemical studies were performed.

A 15-year-old previously healthy African boy presented with sudden onset dyspnea without chest pain. Two weeks earlier he had developed progressive exertional dyspnea, malaise, and a >6 kg weight loss, but no fever or other constitutional symptoms. On examination he was tachycardic (116 beats/min), tachypneic (36 breaths/min), and pale, with scattered crackles in both lung fields and clinical evidence of a left-sided pneumothorax. Chest radiography confirmed a left pneumothorax and showed extensive bilateral nodules suggestive of metastases. A left intercostal drain was placed, improving his respiratory status.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin of 4.7 g/dL with iron-deficiency and anemia of chronic disease indices; white cell and platelet counts were normal, and no atypical cells were seen on blood smear. Tumor markers (alpha-fetoprotein, beta-hCG, CA 19-9) were not elevated, and an HIV test was negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen revealed diffuse well-defined pulmonary nodules and a filling defect within the right atrium; other solid organs appeared normal. Thyroid and testicular ultrasound and a skeletal survey were unremarkable.

Transthoracic echocardiography showed a large, inhomogeneous, broad-based mass at the junction of the inferior vena cava and right atrium with frond-like projections prolapsing through the tricuspid valve and a small circumferential pericardial effusion.

A 19-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of persistent left hind-foot pain and swelling. He was a recreational tennis player with no history of trauma or systemic illness. Initial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at a community clinic showed bone-marrow edema of the calcaneus, and he was treated empirically for a stress fracture with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and physiotherapy, with no relief. Four months after symptom onset, T2-weighted MRI demonstrated persistent bone-marrow edema of the calcaneus and development of arthritis in the posterior region of the subtalar joint; no discrete bony lesion was seen, and he was diagnosed with subtalar arthritis and treated with a splint, NSAIDs, and ice, with only partial improvement. Six months after symptom onset, on referral, physical examination revealed tenderness at the tarsal sinus and pain with supination and pronation of the ankle; the patient also reported refractory night pain. Laboratory tests, including C-reactive protein and other biochemical markers, were normal, and plain radiographs of the foot and ankle were unremarkable.

A 43-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 2-week history of frontal headache and blurred vision. His medical history included surgically excised malignant melanoma of the right cheek and a recent right-sided Bell’s palsy treated with acyclovir and steroids. On examination, temperature was 36.9 °C, blood pressure 129/79 mmHg, heart rate 68 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. Neurologic examination showed left-sided third-nerve palsy (weakness of adduction and ptosis), ipsilateral conjunctival injection and a dilated pupil, and left seventh-nerve palsy with facial droop and drooling. Deep tendon reflexes were 1+ in all extremities, with generalized decreased sensation to pinprick and light touch; motor strength was normal. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 5.6×10^3/μL, hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL, and platelet count 268×10^3/μL. Serum chemistry and chest radiograph were normal. A noncontrast CT scan of the head showed multiple broad-based bilateral retro-orbital masses along the medial aspect of the lateral rectus muscles, the largest measuring 10 mm. CT and MR angiography of the head were unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis demonstrated clear fluid with glucose 108 mg/dL, total protein 95 mg/dL, 1 WBC/mm^3, and 1 RBC/mm^3; no malignant cells were seen. Infectious and autoimmune studies, including HIV, Lyme disease, cryptococcosis, coccidioidomycosis, West Nile virus, California encephalitis, St. Louis encephalitis, eastern equine encephalitis, ANA, and ANCA, were all negative.

He was started on vancomycin, ceftriaxone, acyclovir, and intravenous methylprednisolone, which temporarily improved his headache. On hospital day 8, repeat CT head showed stable orbital masses, and a needle biopsy of the left orbital lesion yielded only adipose tissue without evidence of malignancy.

A 41-year-old man with a history of alveolar soft part sarcoma (ASPS) of the anal region resected 10 years earlier presented for routine follow-up. In 2009, CT had shown a pulmonary metastasis that was resected; in 2011, a head-skin metastasis was excised. In 2012, surveillance CT detected a mass in the pancreatic head. Abdominal ultrasound revealed isodense masses measuring 34 mm in the pancreatic head and 60 mm in the spleen, both showing enhancement on contrast study. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed solitary enhancing lesions in the pancreatic head, spleen, and a small lesion in the liver. MR cholangiopancreatography showed no pancreatic-duct stenosis. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 12.3 g/dl, hematocrit 24.3%, total protein 6.6 g/dl, and normal CEA and CA19-9 levels. Based on these findings, the working diagnosis was a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor versus pancreatic metastasis of ASPS.

A 60-year-old woman presented with abnormal vaginal bleeding. She had no prior history of postmenopausal bleeding, significant medical issues, medications, or supplements. On pelvic examination, there was a 1–2 cm firm, nonulcerated mass on the left vaginal wall. Routine laboratory tests, cervical cytology, and endometrial cytology were all normal. A transvaginal ultrasound did not clearly identify the mass because of indistinct margins. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis was then performed. On T2-weighted images, a well-defined 1 cm lesion was inhomogeneously hyperintense relative to surrounding vaginal wall and myometrium. The lesion was isointense on T1-weighted images. Diffusion-weighted imaging (b = 800 s/mm2) showed high signal intensity within most of the mass, but the mean apparent diffusion coefficient value was 2.1 × 10–3 mm2/s, suggesting a T2 shine-through effect.

A 39-year-old woman presented with an 11‐month history of mobility and pain of the upper right teeth. She reported no systemic symptoms. Intraoral examination revealed normal gingival appearance but marked mobility of most upper right teeth. Panoramic and periapical radiographs showed a diffuse osteolytic lesion of the right maxilla with extensive alveolar bone destruction and floating teeth; the cortical bone was destroyed without expansion of the buccal or palatal plates. CT of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated bilateral maxillary sinus mucosal thickening and polypoid lesions, as well as extensive resorption of the right maxillary alveolar bone.

A 28-year-old man presented with a central forehead swelling that had been gradually enlarging over several months. He reported no pain, headaches, epistaxis, nasal discharge, obstruction, or smell disturbances. He denied systemic symptoms such as fever or weight loss. His medical history was unremarkable, with no history of facial trauma or sinonasal disease. He was a nonsmoker and had no occupational exposures.

On examination, there was a firm, smooth, oval, 5-cm mass just superior to the medial eyebrows. The overlying skin appeared normal. The mass was mildly tender to palpation but showed no pulsations or bruits. No other head or neck abnormalities were found, and an intranasal examination was unremarkable.

A computed tomography scan of the head and paranasal sinuses demonstrated an isolated soft-tissue mass occupying the left frontal sinus. The lesion produced a locally expansile effect with partial erosion of the anteroinferior frontal sinus wall. There was no extension into the nasal cavity or ethmoid sinuses.

A 32-year-old man was referred for evaluation of an asymptomatic, 7 cm right lateral neck mass noted on routine examination. He had no family history of paragangliomas or multiple endocrine tumors. On ultrasound, the mass was hypoechoic and hypervascular, located at the carotid artery bifurcation on the right. A computed tomography angiogram demonstrated a well-circumscribed tumor encasing the internal and external carotid arteries at the bifurcation, consistent with a Shamblin III lesion. Biochemical testing with 24-hour urine catecholamines was negative.

A 47-year-old woman presented for an annual health checkup. She denied fever, chills, allergies, or changes in bowel habits. Her medical history was notable for anemia of unknown etiology for 20 years and remote cesarean sections. She had no significant family history or substance use. On examination, her abdomen was soft, nontender, without organomegaly; a 10-cm transverse lower abdominal scar was present.

Laboratory evaluation showed hemoglobin 85 g/L (normal 115–150 g/L), with normal white-cell and platelet counts. Tumor markers (CEA, CA-125, AFP, CA19-9), coagulation profile, and liver function tests were within normal limits. Bone marrow biopsy confirmed iron deficiency anemia.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 5.9 cm × 5.1 cm hypoechoic lesion at the upper pole of the spleen. Noncontrast CT confirmed a 5.9 cm × 5.1 cm hypodense solid splenic lesion, and contrast-enhanced CT showed mild progressive enhancement of the lesion.

A 2-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of a painless swelling and deformity over his left scapular region. The parents noted an insidious, gradually enlarging mass over the past 3 months. There was no history of trauma, fever, weight loss, or similar lesions elsewhere. Developmental milestones were age-appropriate, and there was no relevant family history.

On examination, the left scapula appeared asymmetric compared with the right, with prominence and elevation of the medial border at rest. A firm, immobile, non-tender swelling measuring approximately 5×4×4 cm was palpable, arising from the underlying bone and not adherent to skin. The overlying skin was intact. Shoulder and cervical spine range of motion were normal and unrestricted. Neurologic examination of both upper limbs—including sensory, motor, and reflex testing—was within normal limits, with no evidence of nerve or vascular compromise.

Plain radiographs of the shoulder showed a bony lesion arising from the scapula. A computed tomography scan demonstrated a well-corticated bony excrescence originating from the ventral surface of the left scapular body, approximately 3 cm proximal to its inferior angle, with continuity of the lesion’s cortex and medullary cavity with that of the scapula. There was no fracture of the bony stalk.

A 21-year-old African American woman with a nine-month history of ulcerative colitis treated with mesalamine and a brief course of prednisolone presented with a one-month history of an enlarging mass over her left lower abdomen. She denied pain, fever, gastrointestinal symptoms, or systemic complaints. On examination, vital signs were normal. Abdominal inspection revealed a 3.0×2.0×2.0 cm slightly erythematous, firm, non-mobile nodular mass in the left lower quadrant with superficial ulceration and minimal serous discharge. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 3.2×2.4×2.3 cm superficial cystic lesion of the anterior abdominal wall. A retrospective review noted the lesion on an earlier CT study that had been overlooked. The patient was provisionally diagnosed with a questionable sebaceous cyst and underwent incision and drainage, yielding moderate serosanguinous fluid; the wound was left open and antibiotics prescribed. At one-week follow-up the wound had not healed and continued to discharge. She then underwent surgical excision of the lesion with primary wound closure.

An 84-year-old woman with hypertension presented with a 3-month history of lower abdominal pain. On examination, there was tenderness in the hypogastric region with a palpable, firm area of induration. Laboratory studies revealed a hemoglobin concentration of 8 mg/dL and a C-reactive protein level of 35 mg/L.  
An abdominal ultrasound showed an abdominopelvic hypoechoic mass that appeared to arise from the anterior uterine wall, with poorly defined margins. To better evaluate its origin and extent, a pelvic MRI was obtained and demonstrated a well-circumscribed abdominopelvic mass with intermediate signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images, restricted diffusion (ADC, 0.7 × 10^-3 mm^2/s), and moderate enhancement after gadolinium administration. Intralesional cystic changes were noted. The mass was in contact with the anterior uterus, the bladder dome, and the abdominal wall, but a well-demarcated cleavage plane separated it from the uterus. The lesion also lay in close relation to adjacent loops of bowel.

A 64-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a long-standing history of left nasal obstruction. He denied epistaxis, facial pain, or prior facial trauma. On anterior rhinoscopy, there was a deviation of the nasal septum to the right and a polyp-like mass occupying the left nasal cavity. An endoscopic biopsy of the mass demonstrated polypoid tissue with fibrinoid necrosis. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the paranasal sinuses showed total opacification of all sinuses and a lobulated soft-tissue mass within the left nasal cavity containing peripheral foci of calcification. The lesion exhibited intense peripheral enhancement and caused lateral displacement of the medial wall of the maxillary sinus. These findings were interpreted as consistent with chronic rhinosinusitis combined with either nasal polyps or a benign sinonasal tumor.

A 78-year-old man was admitted with a 4-month history of progressive asthenia, anorexia, an unintended 6-kg weight loss, and two weeks of high spiking fevers. His medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypercholesterolemia, a prior transient ischemic attack, and coronary stent placement two months earlier.  

On examination, his temperature was 38.2°C and blood pressure was 100/60 mmHg. No peripheral lymphadenopathy or organomegaly was detected, and the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.  

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 23 mm/hour, serum potassium 8.1 mEq/L, sodium 128 mEq/L, creatinine 2.3 mg/dL, C-reactive protein 11.2 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 1383 IU/L, and ferritin 7275 mg/dL. Suspecting adrenal insufficiency, hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone were initiated, resulting in correction of electrolyte abnormalities and improved renal function. Despite glucocorticoid replacement, daily fevers up to 39°C persisted, resolving transiently with naproxen.  

Endocrine evaluation revealed a baseline serum cortisol of 13 μg/dL with no response to ACTH stimulation, plasma ACTH of 217 pg/mL (normal <50 pg/mL), and a 24-hour urinary free cortisol of 13 μg (normal 20–90 μg).  

Contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography demonstrated heterogeneous masses measuring approximately 6 cm in diameter in each adrenal gland, with no additional structural abnormalities or lymphadenopathy. A subsequent ^18F-FDG PET/CT scan showed intense uptake in both adrenal lesions, highly suggestive of malignancy.

A 17-year-old white male student presented with a 3-day history of difficulty swallowing that was painless and worse for solids than for liquids. Over the preceding weeks, he had felt a foreign-body sensation in his throat with a nonproductive cough that disturbed his sleep. On the day of presentation, he began to have difficulty swallowing saliva, prompting evaluation in the emergency department. He had no prior medical history or allergies. Vital signs were normal. Examination of the oral cavity with tongue depression revealed a large, oval, pale, pedicled mass originating from the upper pole of the right tonsil, partially obstructing the airway. The remainder of the oral cavity, nasopharynx, and laryngopharynx appeared normal, and there was no lymphadenopathy. A right tonsillectomy was performed under general anesthesia, and the specimen was sent for histological examination.

A 6-year-old boy presented with 10 days of rapidly progressive, painless swelling of both orbits. Over the preceding 2 months, he had lost 3 kg without anorexia or fever. His medical history was notable for L2 acute lymphoblastic leukemia treated with the FRALLE B2 regimen. On examination, visual acuity was normal bilaterally, and there was no diplopia. Complete blood count was within normal limits. Facial MRI revealed bilateral enlargement of the lacrimal glands with well-defined borders. On T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences, the glands had intermediate signal intensity; on T1-weighted imaging they were isointense to white matter and showed homogeneous enhancement after contrast administration.

A 53-year-old man presented with right lower quadrant abdominal pain for 2 weeks, accompanied by acid reflux, belching, and nonbloody, nonnegatively digested emesis. He denied fevers, night sweats, weight loss, or blood in the stool. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. On examination, the abdomen was soft with right-sided tenderness but no rebound or guarding; bowel sounds were normal. A mobile mass with unclear borders measuring approximately 4 × 6 cm was palpated in the right lower abdomen. Laboratory studies showed mild monocytosis (0.987 × 10^9/L), decreased eosinophils (0.1%), anemia (hemoglobin 119 g/L), low prealbumin (14.9 mg/dL), and thrombocytosis (418 × 10^9/L); serum tumor markers were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed an 8.1 × 4.0 cm heterogenous mass in the right iliac fossa communicating with the small intestinal lumen, with areas of low attenuation and calcification. Multiple metastatic lesions were seen in both adrenal glands, liver, pancreas, and lung, and enlarged retroperitoneal and mediastinal lymph nodes (largest 2.3 cm) were present.

A 53‐year‐old right‐hand–dominant Sri Lankan policeman presented with a 2‐year history of a slowly enlarging lump on the palmar aspect of his right hand. Over the preceding months, he developed numbness and paresthesia in the radial three and a half digits and difficulty making a fist and performing precision grip, which interfered with his work as a fingerprint analyst. He had undergone carpal tunnel decompression on the same side 7 years earlier. He had no other medical history of note.

On examination, there was a 5 × 5 cm soft‐to‐firm, nontender, lobulated mass with poorly defined margins in the thenar and mid‐palmar region extending into the second web space. Sensation was diminished over the thumb, index, and middle fingers. Thenar muscle strength and finger abduction/adduction were preserved, and Froment’s sign was negative. The lump mechanically impeded fist formation. Plain radiographs showed no bony abnormality.

Ultrasonography demonstrated two 13 × 8 mm masses extending into deep tissues and was interpreted as suggestive of chronic inflammatory pathology. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-demarcated, dumbbell-shaped lesion in the palmar space measuring 57 × 56 × 80 mm that passed between flexor tendons into the mid-palmar compartment, showed T1 and T2 hyperintensity with signal suppression on fat-suppressed sequences, and abutted the flexor pollicis brevis. Nerve-conduction studies were consistent with median nerve compression.

A 38-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of swelling in the left preauricular region and a 6-month history of progressively limited mouth opening. The swelling was initially small but gradually enlarged. She also noted clicking sounds from the left temporomandibular joint (TMJ) followed by sudden reduction in mouth opening, pain with chewing, and recent hearing difficulty on the left.

On examination, there was a diffuse, non-tender, bony-hard protuberance in the left preauricular area measuring approximately 4 × 3 cm, extending from the zygoma to the tragus with a smooth surface. Maximum interincisal opening was 4–5 mm, and an intraoral crossbite was present on the right posterior teeth.

Panoramic radiograph showed a diffuse radio-opaque mass engulfing the left condyle, interarticular space, and temporal bone, involving the left TMJ. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck revealed a large, expansile bony proliferation of the left mandibular condylar process with solid periosteal reaction measuring about 3 × 1.5 cm. The lesion extended to the arch of the left zygomatic bone and the petrous part of the temporal bone, and there was partial bony ankylosis between the condyle and mastoid portion of the temporal bone.

A 7-year-old girl presented with a 1-year history of progressive swelling in the right parotid region. The mass was firm, approximately 5 cm in diameter, mobile but attached to deeper planes, and tender to palpation. She denied systemic symptoms. Physical examination confirmed a hard, mobile mass in the right parotid area, fixed to deep structures, eliciting pain on palpation. Because of concern for malignancy, she underwent a total right parotidectomy with level I–III cervical lymph node dissection.

A 23-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of progressive shortness of breath and a 1-month history of right-sided chest pain, dry cough, and abdominal cramps. He denied fever and night sweats. One month earlier, he had been hospitalized for chest pain. On examination, he appeared moderately ill. Blood pressure was 130/70 mmHg, heart rate 108 beats/min, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, temperature 36.8 °C, and oxygen saturation 94 % on room air (98 % on 3 L nasal cannula). The anterior chest showed symmetrical movement and diminished breath sounds in the right lower lung. On posterior chest examination, there was a palpable lump in the right postero-inferior chest wall. Laboratory testing revealed thrombocytosis and an elevated D-dimer level. Chest radiography showed a mass in the right lower posterior lung field with moderate right pleural effusion. Thoracic ultrasonography demonstrated a right-sided lung mass partially adherent to the inner chest wall and moderate pleural effusion. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax revealed a lobulated soft-tissue mass measuring approximately 7.7 × 7 cm along the right posterolateral thoracic wall or pleura, with an expansile component involving the right 11th rib. MRI of the thorax showed a 14 × 11 × 10 cm necrotic mass in the posterior right lower thoracic wall, infiltrating soft tissue, eroding posterior ribs 8 and destroying ribs 9 and 10, and extending into the thoracic cavity; there were also lesions in the left lateral ribs 3–5 and atelectasis of the right lower lobe. The working imaging differential was a soft-tissue sarcoma versus a malignant bone tumor. The patient subsequently underwent transthoracic needle aspiration and core biopsy.

An 80-year-old obese woman with a history of mastectomy for breast cancer presented with acute dyspnea and intermittent fever for 1 month. Initial chest radiography suggested bilateral pleural effusions. Laboratory testing on admission showed thrombocytopenia and renal dysfunction (plasma creatinine, 2.31 mg/dL). There were no abnormal findings on the initial physical examination.

She was treated for presumed infection with penicillin–sulbactam and levofloxacin. Ten days later, she developed an erythematous rash on the face and abdomen resembling a malar rash. The antibiotics were discontinued, but the rash persisted.

Blood and urine cultures were negative. Screening tests for EBV, CMV, HIV, HCV, echovirus, coxsackievirus, and adenovirus were negative. Transthoracic echocardiography was normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed moderate splenomegaly.

Given the malar rash and fever, an autoimmune workup was performed. Urinalysis showed proteinuria, but ANA, anti-ENA, and ANCA were negative. Serum LDH, β2-microglobulin, and uric acid levels were elevated. Angiotensin-converting enzyme activity was at the upper limit of normal.

A total-body FDG-PET scan revealed systemic lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly.

An 85-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of epigastric and right upper-quadrant abdominal pain. Her medical history was notable only for mild hypertension and a squamous cell carcinoma of the right hand excised 4 years earlier. She reported a 5-kg weight loss over 2 months but denied hematemesis, hematochezia, or melena. On examination, her sclerae appeared mildly pale. Laboratory studies showed a hematocrit of 34%, hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 113 fL, and red-cell distribution width 13.5%. The alpha‐fetoprotein level was markedly elevated at 155 000 IU/mL; other serum tumor markers were within normal limits, and tests for hepatitis B and C were negative. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a mass in the gastric antrum. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT confirmed a 7-cm antral mass and multiple liver lesions consistent with metastases.

A 27-year-old right-hand-dominant woman presented with a 4-week history of insidious onset, excruciating pain and swelling of the right elbow without any antecedent trauma. Examination showed supination limited to 50°, elbow flexion–extension from 20° to 130° due to pain, and full pronation. Plain radiographs revealed a well-circumscribed radiolucent lesion in the proximal radius with metaphyseal cortical thinning and a rim of epiphyseal bone. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-defined centric lytic lesion in the meta-diaphyseal region involving the radial tuberosity and proximal third of the radius, measuring 2.7 × 1.5 × 5 cm and located 7 mm from the articular surface. Endocrine and laboratory studies were normal.

A 69-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with a mildly elevated cutaneous lesion on the right lower lip. The lesion had central ulceration covered by brownish-black necrotic tissue and had grown slowly to 1 cm in diameter over 2 months. It was excised under local anesthesia, and histopathology showed ulceration with necrotic tissue and chronic inflammation around skin appendages.

Three months later, he returned with two new nodules: one on the right buttock— a diffusely bulging nodule with a central brownish-black necrotic area — and another on the left auriculotemporal region with similar central necrosis. Both nodules were excised. Histologic examination revealed extensive hemorrhagic necrosis with ulceration and dermal/subcutaneous infiltration of medium-to-large pleomorphic anaplastic cells intermixed with small lymphocytes. T-cell receptor gene rearrangement demonstrated clonality. Immunohistochemistry showed CD3(+), CD5(+), CD20(–), CD56(–), CD30(+) in >75% of large atypical lymphoid cells, CD4(–), CD8(–), Ki-67 labeling index >80%, and both epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) translocation were negative. Epstein-Barr virus in situ hybridization was negative. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography revealed no lymph node involvement or distant metastasis.

A 60-year-old Bulgarian man presented to the emergency department for the seventh time within 20 days with a 2-month history of worsening, spasmodic abdominal pain. He had a history of coeliac disease, previously attributed to non-compliance with a gluten-free diet, and had one prior inpatient admission in 2019 for abdominal pain. He was non-smoking, non-drinking, and worked in a meat processing plant. He spoke no English; earlier visits used Google Translate, leading to a discharge diagnosis of non-specific abdominal pain after normal blood tests and a normal CT scan on his fourth visit. 

On this visit, an accredited telephone interpreter was used. The patient reported strict adherence to a gluten-free diet, new severe spasmodic abdominal pain, weight loss, diarrhea, nausea, and fatigue over 2 months. He had no dietary or lifestyle changes. He complained of inability to manage pain at home and difficulty returning to the hospital. He vomited undigested food in the ED. 

Vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination revealed a tender epigastrium and mild distension. Complete blood count, C-reactive protein, and liver-function tests were unremarkable. Abdominal radiography showed distended bowel loops in the left upper abdomen and was “suspicious for small bowel obstruction.” Given the updated history and after senior advice, he was admitted for observation. 

Within 24 hours, repeat CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a proximal jejunal lesion with adjacent adenopathy, indicative of primary small bowel neoplasm.

A 70-year-old man presented with a one-year history of a gradually enlarging swelling in the lower left posterior tooth region. He was otherwise healthy, with no significant medical or family history. On examination, there was a 3 × 3 cm mass in the left retromolar area. The mucosa overlying the mass was of normal color, the surface was smooth, the lesion was soft, tender on palpation, and relatively mobile; the remainder of the oral cavity was unremarkable. Vital signs were normal and complete blood count results were within normal limits. Cone beam computed tomography showed a heterogeneous lesion in the left buccomasseteric region extending into the retromolar area. Clinically, the lesion appeared to be a benign soft tissue neoplasm, and a provisional diagnosis of intraoral lipoma was made. Excision of the mass was performed with adequate surgical margins, and the specimen was sent for histopathological examination.

A 22-year-old Caucasian man presented with bilateral neck lymphadenopathy, fatigue, and sore throat that did not improve after antibiotics and a short course of steroids. Over the preceding month, he developed persistent cough, exertional dyspnea, intermittent right-sided chest pain, hoarseness, difficulty swallowing solid foods, and facial and neck swelling. He had no significant medical or family history and denied cigarette smoking, though he reported smoking one marijuana joint three times a week for three years.

On examination, his heart rate was 130 beats per minute, and he had facial plethora, enlarged non-tender cervical lymph nodes, and decreased breath sounds in the right upper lung field, suggestive of superior vena cava obstruction. A chest radiograph showed a large right hilar mass with a right paratracheal soft-tissue mass. Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed a 13 cm × 6 cm anterior mediastinal mass compressing the superior vena cava, a right pleural effusion, and subcarinal and pericardiac lymphadenopathy. A PET scan demonstrated a hypermetabolic mediastinal mass extending to the subcarinal region and along the right cardiac border (maximum SUV, 6.5).

Laboratory studies were negative for HIV, hepatitis B and C, and β-human chorionic gonadotropin; α-fetoprotein and lactate dehydrogenase levels were normal. Testicular ultrasound was normal. CT-guided core biopsy of the mediastinal mass showed extensive necrosis with little viable tissue. Immunohistochemical stains on the limited sample were negative for lymphoid markers (CD3, TdT, CD20, PAX-5, CD10) and for germ cell markers (AFP, PLAP, CD30, OCT-4).

A three-week-old African American female was referred for evaluation of “cysts in her gums.” She was born at term via vaginal delivery with an unremarkable prenatal history and had no other medical problems. Her mother noted the lesion in the mouth at birth and reported that it appeared to be decreasing in size over the past three weeks.  
On intra-oral examination, there was a bilobed, sessile nodular lesion approximately 1.5 cm in greatest dimension on the right maxillary alveolar ridge in the region of the unerupted canine. The surface was smooth, healthy pink, and non-hemorrhagic. There was no pain, discomfort, or cervical lymphadenopathy.  
A maxillary periapical radiograph showed no bony or dental abnormalities. Urine vanillylmandelic acid was measured to exclude a neuroectodermal tumor of infancy and was negative. A complete blood count with differential was within normal limits.  
The patient’s mother preferred non-surgical management, and in consultation with pathology, the decision was made to observe the lesion with weekly visits for one month followed by monthly follow-up.

A 24-year-old man, previously healthy, presented with a 6-month history of bilateral knee pain and a palpable mass over the left proximal fibula. He described pain with activity but denied numbness, tingling, or weakness in the peroneal nerve distribution. On examination, there was a firm, non–tender swelling at the head and neck of the left fibula; the right fibular region was not palpable. Distal motor and sensory function of the lower extremities was intact.

Plain radiographs of the left knee demonstrated an expansile, lytic lesion involving the epimetaphyseal region of the proximal fibula without periosteal reaction. Radiographs of the right knee revealed a smaller, similar-appearing lesion at the proximal fibular neck. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left knee showed a well-defined, expansile intramedullary lesion extending to the subchondral bone without soft-tissue invasion.

A 4-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of progressive enlargement of the right thumb and index finger noted since infancy. She reported intermittent pain—worse at night—and tingling in the affected digits, with occasional bluish discoloration. There was no history of trauma. 

On examination, the right thumb measured 6.0 × 2.0 cm and the right index finger 6.0 × 1.9 cm, both markedly larger than the contralateral digits and her mother’s hand (mother’s thumb 4.0 cm × 1.5 cm; index 5.0 cm × 1.5 cm). The second finger angulated 20° toward the ulnar side at the distal and middle phalanges. There was no tenderness; sensation and range of motion were normal, and grasp was intact. 

Plain radiographs of the right hand showed diffuse soft-tissue swelling and increased density around the first and second digits, with enlargement of the corresponding phalanges. Further evaluation with magnetic resonance imaging was planned but delayed due to limited availability.

An 11-year-old girl presented with a 1-year history of a progressively enlarging, painful mass on her left forearm. She had a remote fall onto her right arm but denied prior similar complaints or family history of bone disorders. Laboratory studies, including hemoglobin 14.3 g/dL, hematocrit 42.6%, leukocyte count 8.69 × 10³/µL, erythrocyte count 4.95 × 10⁶/µL, and platelet count 440 × 10³/µL, were within normal limits. On examination, there was a tender, solid mass measuring 2.5 × 2.5 × 6 cm on the distal ulna with regular borders and well-defined margins. Radiographs revealed a lytic, expansile lesion with septations in the diaphysis of the left ulna. MRI showed a 2.6 × 2.7 × 5.8 cm mass that was isointense with hypointense foci on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2 fat-saturated sequences without diffusion restriction, and demonstrated peripheral enhancement with an internal cystic region on postcontrast sequences.

A 6-year-old boy was referred with a 2-week history of a painless swelling of the left mandible that was gradually increasing in size. He had no difficulty chewing, no paresthesia, and no discharge. He was systemically well; full blood count was normal; there was no relevant medical or family history. On examination, there was no facial asymmetry or lymphadenopathy. Intraorally, there was a localized, hard, non-tender swelling expanding the buccal cortex from the left canine to the first permanent molar; the overlying mucosa was normal. The lower left first and second deciduous molars were splayed by the lesion and were carious; all other deciduous molars were carious. A panoramic radiograph showed a multilocular radiolucent lesion with scalloped margins in the left hemimandible, extending from the distal aspect of the unerupted canine to the mesial aspect of the first permanent molar, approaching the inferior border; the roots of the lower left deciduous molars were resorbed and the first and second premolar tooth germs were absent. CT imaging demonstrated marked cortical thinning with focal breaches and some internal calcification but no internal septations. An incisional biopsy was then performed under general anaesthesia, and the specimen was submitted for histopathological examination.

A 15-year-old girl presented with a bump on the back of her head that she had noticed one month earlier. She had no history of occipital trauma (only a remote fall at age 3, with a forehead scar). Her physical and neurologic examinations were normal, and she had no other complaints. Plain skull radiographs were interpreted as normal. Cranial CT revealed a 3 × 3 cm bony defect in the right occipital bone. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI showed the defect with pronounced enhancement of the adjacent tissue; the lesion abutted the transverse sinus, was attached to the dura, and was isointense on T1-weighted images.

A 45-year-old woman with no prior cardiac disease was admitted for rapidly worsening dyspnea, orthopnea, and fatigue. On arrival, her systolic blood pressure was 80 mmHg and she was oliguric. Electrocardiography showed rapid atrial fibrillation (150 bpm) with nonspecific repolarization abnormalities. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a normal left ventricular dimension and severely depressed ejection fraction (≈20%) with diffuse hypokinesis. Laboratory studies demonstrated a slight increase in myocardial necrosis markers without a significant time–activity slope, leukocytosis, acute renal and hepatic failure, and metabolic acidosis with elevated lactate. Coronary angiography showed no obstructive lesions. She was managed with an intra-aortic balloon pump and dopamine infusion, and acute renal failure was treated with renal replacement therapy. On hospital day 1, she developed coagulopathy consistent with disseminated intravascular coagulation and experienced multiple episodes of melena requiring red-cell transfusions; plasma and platelet transfusions over 10 days led to gradual normalization. Empiric piperacillin–tazobactam was initiated. The balloon pump was removed on day 3, and by day 10 her ejection fraction improved to 50%; atrial fibrillation was controlled with digoxin and heparin anticoagulation. Physical examination revealed café-au-lait spots, cutaneous fibromas, and axillary and inguinal freckling, leading to a clinical diagnosis of type 1 neurofibromatosis. Despite normalization of coagulation, renal function, and ventricular function, direct bilirubin remained elevated. Abdominal ultrasonography showed dilated bile ducts without hepatic lesions, normal kidneys, and a right adrenal mass.

A 69-year-old man with hypertension, coronary artery disease, ischemic cardiomyopathy, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and alcohol dependence was admitted after cardiac arrest and underwent emergent cardiac catheterization. During the admission, he was noted to have a hemoglobin concentration of 4.6 g/dL (baseline 14.2 g/dL four years earlier) with a mean corpuscular volume of 65 fL. Iron studies showed an iron level < 10 µg/dL and ferritin of 3.3 ng/mL, confirming iron deficiency anemia. 

To evaluate for occult malignancy, a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was obtained. The chest CT was unremarkable. The abdominal and pelvic CT demonstrated a 2.4 × 3.2 cm soft-tissue mass at the tip of the appendix and a 5.3 × 2.5 cm lobular perirectal mass, with borderline enlargement of perirectal and pelvic lymph nodes. Pelvic MRI again showed an infiltrative rectal soft-tissue lesion described as nonspecific.

A colonoscopy revealed a normal-appearing appendiceal orifice and normal rectal mucosa without visible masses. Flexible sigmoidoscopy with endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) of the rectum showed no discrete rectal mass and only small, benign-appearing perirectal lymph nodes, so biopsies were not taken. Carcinoid tumor was considered; however, gastrin was 39 pg/mL, chromogranin A was 2 nmol/L, and serotonin was 86 ng/mL. Because of the presence of concurrent appendiceal and rectal masses, tissue sampling was pursued. 

Three 18-gauge core needle biopsies of the appendiceal mass were obtained and submitted for pathological evaluation.

A 60-year-old Iranian woman presented with pain and swelling in her right arm after a minor fall. She was in good general condition, normotensive, with a pulse of 92 beats per minute and a temperature of 37°C. Laboratory values were: hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, leukocytes 22 × 10^3/mm^3, platelets 200 × 10^3/μL, sodium 141 mEq/L, potassium 4 mEq/L, glucose 11.6 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 15.1 mmol/L, and creatinine 250 μmol/L.

A plain radiograph of the right humerus showed a pathologic mid-shaft fracture with a large, ill-defined soft-tissue mass. MRI demonstrated a huge lobulated mass destroying the humeral shaft, bright on T2-weighted images, dark on T1-weighted images, and showing marked enhancement after gadolinium administration.

Her history was significant for a sacrococcygeal chordoma treated by surgical resection and postoperative radiotherapy 4 years earlier, with local recurrence requiring further surgery after 1 year. A biopsy of the humeral lesion revealed a lobulated mass composed of cuboidal to polygonal cells with eccentric nuclei, clear to eosinophilic cytoplasm, pools of extracellular mucin, and occasional physaliferous (bubble-bearing) cells.

Immunohistochemical studies showed strong positivity for AE1/3, EMA, S100 protein, and vimentin. Additional staining for CD10 was negative. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography and CT scans of the chest and abdomen showed no abnormalities.

A 63-year-old man presented with a lesion on his right upper eyelid present for 7 years. He reported no prior treatment.  
On examination, the lesion measured 5.0 cm × 7.0 cm, was nodular, ulcerated, indurated, and erythematous, and extended to involve the lower eyelid. Visual acuity was no light perception in the right eye and 20/20 in the left; intraocular pressure could not be measured on the right and was 18 mmHg on the left. The left orbit and regional lymph nodes were unremarkable. The patient was otherwise well, with no relevant family history, no history of trauma, and worked as a farmer.  
A CT scan of the orbits showed right anterior orbital invasion without bony or lacrimal gland involvement.  
An incisional biopsy of the eyelid lesion revealed squamous cell invaginations extending from the epidermis into the dermis. The invaginations and papillary projections were lined by a bilayer epithelium: a luminal layer of columnar cells with decapitation secretion and an outer layer of small cuboidal cells, showing significant nuclear pleomorphism and increased mitotic activity.  
Immunohistochemical staining was positive for epithelial membrane antigen, cytokeratin 8/18, and a broad-spectrum cytokeratin cocktail, and negative for GCDFP-15 and carcinoembryonic antigen.

A 28-year-old Chinese woman, gravida 1, para 0, conceived naturally after ovulation induction with clomiphene citrate. At 7 weeks of gestation she noted slight vaginal discharge and was treated with oral dydrogesterone; thereafter, there was no vaginal bleeding. A pelvic color Doppler scan confirmed a dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy. Routine blood tests, liver and kidney function, thyroid function, and urinalysis were within normal limits.

At 23+0 weeks she presented with generalized pruritus. Total bile acid (TBA) was elevated at 30.1 μmol/L (normal 0–10), and she was diagnosed with intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP). Treatment with bile acid–lowering agents, liver protection, and dexamethasone for fetal lung maturation was initiated. Her blood pressure ranged from 138–170/80–103 mmHg, and she was transferred for specialist care. On admission, TBA was 14.6 μmol/L, ALT 81 U/L (normal 7–40), AST 45 U/L (13–35), and 24-hour urinary protein was 0.41 g/24h (normal <0.15), consistent with preeclampsia and ICP. An oral glucose tolerance test showed borderline gestational diabetes, managed with diet and exercise.

Repeat pelvic Doppler ultrasound showed two live fetuses; fetus A measured consistent with 23+3 weeks, and fetus B measured 22+6 weeks. The placenta of fetus B exhibited partial honeycomb-like changes, raising concerns about possible placental mesenchymal dysplasia (PMD) or partial molar pregnancy. Amniocentesis was recommended for diagnosis and karyotyping but was declined by the patient and her family.

At 27+5 weeks, ultrasound demonstrated fetal growth discrepancy (14% weight discordance), an elevated cardiothoracic ratio in fetus B, and persistent placental honeycomb changes. The patient was counseled regarding risks of molar pregnancy, including hemorrhage, metastasis, chemotherapy, and abnormal fetal karyotype; she again declined amniocentesis.

At 29 weeks, pruritus worsened; ALT rose to 238 U/L, AST to 117 U/L, TBA to 51.4 μmol/L, and 24-h urinary protein to 3.39 g/24h. Blood pressure ranged 121–180/69–81 mmHg. Ultrasound showed intermittent absent end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery of the smaller fetus and decreased middle cerebral artery pulsatility index, suggesting fetal distress. A cesarean section was performed at 30+5 weeks, with estimated blood loss of 420 mL. Two female infants were delivered, weighing 720 g (Apgar 9-9-10) and 1270 g (Apgar 10-10-10). Both required neonatal intensive care for respiratory distress and were later discharged in good condition.

An 18-month-old boy was referred for evaluation of a “corrosive” lesion over a known vascular lesion on the anterior surface of his scrotum. He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy; no antenatal anomalies were detected. Fifteen days after birth, a reddish mass was noted on the anterior scrotum and followed by the family doctor, with rapid growth but no prior complications. Forty days before presentation, parents observed an ulcer forming on the surface of the lesion, leading to increased discomfort during urination and defecation.

On examination, there was a soft, compressible, bluish-red mass measuring 2.5 × 2.3 cm over the anterior scrotal skin. An overlying ulcer measured approximately 2.1 × 1.9 cm with irregular edges but no purulent discharge. Palpation revealed smooth intrascrotal extension to the mesoscrotal diaphragm; bilateral testicles and epididymes were normal on exam. 

Color Doppler ultrasonography of the scrotum, perineum, inguinal regions, and pelvis demonstrated increased vascular flow within the mass, no evidence of extension into the lesser pelvis or adjacent organs, and preserved echotexture of both testes and spermatic cords.

A 47-year-old man with well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension and a history of bilateral nephrolithiasis treated with percutaneous nephrolithotomy and ureterorenoscopy presented with gross hematuria. Cystoscopic examination revealed a papillary-appearing lesion within the mid penile urethra extending distally. The urethral meatus, prostatic urethra, and bladder neck were normal, and examination of the external genitalia revealed no lesions. A cystoscopic biopsy of the urethral lesion was obtained.

Grossly, the specimen was a small papillary tan tissue fragment. On microscopic examination, there was a papillary proliferation of hyperplastic non-keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium. In focal areas there were changes of nuclear wrinkling with perinuclear halos and binucleated cells.

A 52-year-old man presented with a right scrotal and inguinal mass that had gradually enlarged over 2 years. He had no other medical conditions and was not immunosuppressed (HIV negative). On examination, there was a 10 cm × 15 cm warty, friable mass involving the scrotum, and bilaterally fixed, voluminous inguinal lymph nodes.  
 
An abdominal and pelvic CT scan, pelvic MRI, and PET scan showed marked uptake in the inguino-scrotal mass and metastatic inguinal and pelvic lymph nodes (largest measuring 7 cm on the left). No other primary lesions or distant metastases were identified.  

Multiple skin biopsies of the inguinal mass demonstrated a dense proliferation of atypical epithelial cells in the dermis with ulceration of the overlying epidermis. Numerous mitotic figures and apoptotic cells were noted, along with focal squamous and glandular differentiation. Immunohistochemical studies showed diffuse positivity for CK5/6 and CK AE1/AE3, p63 positivity except in cells bordering glandular lumina, and GATA3 positivity in a subset of tumor cells.  

Based on the histologic and immunophenotypic findings, the initial differential diagnosis included malignant adnexal carcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, and a urothelial carcinoma metastasis.

A 40-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 4-hour history of sudden, sharp right-sided abdominal pain. On examination, she was tachycardic (heart rate 120 bpm) but afebrile and hemodynamically stable, with tenderness in the right flank. She had no history of trauma, chronic illness, or known kidney disease. Point-of-care ultrasonography demonstrated a mass in the right kidney. Initial laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin concentration of 11.2 g/dL, which subsequently fell to 8.2 g/dL, and normal coagulation parameters.
