After fluid resuscitation and transfusion, contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen was obtained and revealed a heterogeneously enhancing mass arising from the hilum of the right kidney, compressing the inferior vena cava and displacing the pancreatic head and duodenum, along with a large perirenal, retroperitoneal, and pelvic hematoma measuring 24 × 60 × 81 mm.

A 52-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of a painless perineal mass that had progressively increased in size and was causing difficulty with sitting and walking. He denied lower urinary tract symptoms, fevers, defecation difficulties, prior perineal surgery or trauma, cigarette smoking, and human papilloma virus infection. On examination, the external genitalia were normal, pubic and perineal hair had been shaved, and both testes were normal in size and consistency. There was a well-circumscribed, smooth-surfaced, freely mobile, firm, non-tender, roundish midline mass on the perineum measuring approximately 7 cm × 9 cm; the overlying skin was normal and there was no induration. Laboratory studies—including a full blood count, urinalysis, serum creatinine, and random blood sugar—were within normal limits. Ultrasonography of the mass revealed a well-emarginated ovoid lesion with echogenic contents.

A 75-year-old woman presented for evaluation of pelvic organ prolapse and stress urinary incontinence. She denied any defecatory symptoms, including tenesmus, bleeding, pain, constipation, or fecal incontinence. On pelvic examination, she had a cystocele and a grade III uterine prolapse. 

Pelvic floor ultrasound with an endovaginal probe revealed a well-defined, hypoechoic mass measuring 3 × 4 cm in the right ischioanal fossa. Although the lesion appeared adjacent to the external anal sphincter at the midlateral third of the right anal canal, a beak sign indicated that the mass and sphincter were separate structures. Power-Doppler imaging demonstrated a peripheral vascular pattern, suggesting origin from the internal sphincter.

Subsequent pelvic MRI showed the following characteristics:
- On T1-weighted images, the mass had homogeneous low signal intensity, similar to pelvic musculature.  
- On T2-weighted images, it exhibited subtle heterogeneous high signal intensity relative to muscle, surrounded by a thin low-signal rim.  
- On contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images with fat suppression, the lesion demonstrated strong, homogeneous enhancement without necrosis or cystic change.  
- There was clear demarcation between the mass and the external anal sphincter, although a beak sign of the sphincter fibers persisted.

A 47-year-old woman presented for routine dental evaluation and reported occasional episodes of diffuse pain and discomfort in the left posterior mandibular region. Her medical history was unremarkable. On extra-oral examination, there was slight facial asymmetry. Panoramic and intra-oral radiographs revealed an intraosseous, circular formation with radiopaque external limits and a radiolucent interior in the left mandibular third-molar region. A computed tomography scan demonstrated preservation of the surrounding bone integrity and clear separation from adjacent neurovascular structures.

A 22-year-old man with a 12-year history of chronic epigastric pain refractory to endoscopic and medical therapy underwent abdominal CT, which revealed a 6.2 × 5.9 × 4.8 cm, well-circumscribed retroperitoneal mass thought to arise from the lateral limb of the left adrenal gland and abutting the posterior pancreatic tail and anterosuperior left kidney. On examination, there was no abdominal tenderness or palpable mass. Adrenal biochemical studies, including ACTH, cortisol, dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate, free testosterone, aldosterone, renin, and plasma fractionated metanephrines, were within normal ranges, and an 8 AM cortisol was appropriately suppressed after 1 mg dexamethasone. Serum tumor markers (CA 19-9, CEA, chromogranin A) and glucose homeostasis studies (insulin, proinsulin, C-peptide, glucose) were normal. The patient underwent a left adrenalectomy with en bloc resection of the mass. Grossly, the lesion was firm, white-tan, and well circumscribed. Histologically, it showed a hypocellular proliferation of bland spindle cells within densely hyalinized collagen, a chronic lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, and scattered dystrophic calcifications; mitotic activity was 0–1 per 10 high-powered fields, without atypia or multinucleation. Immunohistochemical studies revealed that the spindle cells were negative for smooth muscle actin, desmin, ALK, S100, CD34, and CD117; plasma cells were polytypic, with an IgG4:IgG cell ratio of approximately 11:183 in hotspot fields.

A 44-year-old man presented with gradually progressive nocturnal snoring and daytime fatigue over 8 years, and new-onset obstructive sleep apnea for 6 months. He had no chronic illnesses, neurologic deficits, or relevant family history. On examination, he was in good general condition. A soft, painless swelling anterior to the parotid lodge elevated the earlobe. Intraorally, there was a firm mass displacing the soft palate and uvula to the right. Nasofibroscopy showed a smooth mass in the nasopharynx reaching the choanae, with posterior displacement of the epiglottis and mobile vocal cords. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a retropharyngeal mass causing mass effect on the soft palate and extending into the nasopharynx. MRI demonstrated a well-defined retropharyngeal lesion measuring 92 × 40 mm sagittally and 60 × 27 mm axially, hyperintense on T1- and T2-weighted images and uniformly suppressed on fat-saturation sequences, without involvement of adjacent pterygoid muscles or parotid glands.

A 14-year-old boy with known ataxia telangiectasia presented with one month of redness and swelling of the left lower eyelid and medial canthus that failed to improve despite topical ciprofloxacin and erythromycin, intravenous ampicillin plus vancomycin, and oral linezolid and co-amoxiclav. He had no systemic symptoms (no fever, weight loss, night sweats, fatigue, abdominal cramps, or cough). He was wheelchair dependent due to his neurologic condition. 

On ophthalmic examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 8/20 in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was 14 mm Hg in the right eye; measurement in the left eye was not possible. There was swelling and erythema of the left inferior eyelid and medial canthus with an ulcerative lesion in the medial canthus. Ocular motility of the left eye showed a –2 limitation in downgaze and adduction. Funduscopic and slit-lamp examinations of both eyes were otherwise normal. No regional lymphadenopathy was palpable. 

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, were within normal limits. Because of his history of ataxia telangiectasia, CT was avoided and an MRI was obtained. Coronal T1- and T2-weighted images showed an infiltrative mass involving the inferior surface of the left orbit, the left ethmoidal sinus, and the left maxillary sinus, with extension toward the contralateral ethmoidal sinus. Gadolinium-enhanced sequences revealed marked enhancement of the lesion.

A 52-year-old man with no prior medical history initially presented with an eight-month history of diffuse abdominal pain, obstipation, and an 8-kg weight loss. Three weeks before admission he had a chronic cough; chest radiograph and spirometry were normal, and inhaler therapy relieved his symptoms. On admission, his C-reactive protein was elevated at 96.1 mg/L, white blood cell count was 13.85 × 10^3/µL, and hemoglobin was 13.7 g/dL. He received empiric cefuroxime and metronidazole. Colonoscopy was unremarkable, and abdominal CT showed pathologically enlarged retroperitoneal lymph nodes and ascites.

While under evaluation for suspected lymphoma, he developed sudden‐onset dyspnoea. Arterial blood gases showed pH 7.48, pO2 56 mmHg, pCO2 25 mmHg. ECG revealed new T-wave inversions in leads V1–V3. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a markedly dilated right ventricle, reduced RV function (TAPSE 1.5 cm), and estimated systolic pulmonary artery pressure of 70 mmHg. 

A CT pulmonary angiogram showed no evidence of pulmonary arterial embolism or deep vein thrombosis but did show small bilateral ground-glass opacities and pleural effusions. Laboratory studies revealed an NT-pro-BNP of 17 126 pg/mL (baseline 558 pg/mL), D-dimer 11.6 mg/L, and a stable, modest elevation of high‐sensitivity troponin I at 123.2 pg/mL. His oxygen requirement increased to 8 L/min, and a ventilation/perfusion scan demonstrated diffuse, subtle perfusion defects “compatible with mild bronchial obstruction rather than PAE.”

A 7-month-old previously healthy male was referred for evaluation of a congenital right mid–upper thoracic spinal prominence noted since birth. He was born at term via cesarean delivery for breech presentation. Developmental milestones were appropriate, and he had no pain or neurologic complaints. On examination, motor and sensory function in all extremities was normal, cranial nerves were intact, and muscle tone and deep-tendon reflexes were preserved. Visual inspection revealed slight thoracic levoscoliosis without cutaneous stigmata of spinal dysraphism. Plain radiographs of the thoracic spine demonstrated levoscoliosis and an osseous projection from the right posterior aspect of a mid-thoracic rib. Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine revealed a multilobulated, partially cystic, calcified, heterogeneous mass centered at the right T5–T6 paravertebral space that extended into the dorsal intrathoracic cavity, the right paraspinal musculature, and the spinal canal, causing severe spinal cord displacement, spinal stenosis, and bilateral foraminal stenosis. No intracranial abnormalities were seen.

A 40-year-old man presented with 2 years of progressive weakness, tingling, and numbness in his lower limbs. One year prior, he noted lower-limb swelling and skin changes over the face, hands, and feet. For the past 6 months, he experienced erectile dysfunction and loss of libido. He had no history of bone pain, drug abuse, tuberculosis, diabetes, or hypertension.

On examination, there was bilateral pitting pedal edema. The skin was thickened and hyperpigmented over the face, fingers, and shins. Bilateral gynecomastia and testicular atrophy were present. Abdominal examination revealed hepatomegaly and ascites. Funduscopic examination showed bilateral papilledema. Muscle strength was normal in the upper limbs; in the lower limbs there was distal weakness (Medical Research Council grade 4/5 at the hips and 4−/5 at the ankles). Deep-tendon reflexes were diminished (+1) in the upper limbs and absent at the knees and ankles. All sensory modalities were impaired below the knees, and Romberg’s sign was positive.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, creatine phosphokinase, serum ferritin, and vitamin B12. Serum total protein was 7.1 g/dL, albumin 3.0 g/dL, globulin 4.1 g/dL (A:G ratio 1:1.3). Fasting and postprandial glucose levels were normal. Thyroid-stimulating hormone was elevated at 16.62 mIU/L (normal 0.4–4.0). Luteinizing hormone was 15 IU/L (normal 1.8–8.6) and testosterone 111 ng/dL (normal 300–1000). Antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, HIV, and hepatitis B and C serologies were negative.

Abdominal ultrasonography confirmed hepatomegaly (16 cm), moderate ascites, and enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes. Fine-needle aspiration of a mesenteric node was inconclusive. Ascitic fluid was an exudate (SAAG <1.1), with normal adenosine deaminase and no malignant cells. Nerve-conduction studies demonstrated sensorimotor demyelinating and axonal polyneuropathy in both upper and lower limbs. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal. Pelvic radiography revealed multiple osteosclerotic lesions in the left femoral head and right iliac crest, whereas skull and spine films were normal. Serum protein electrophoresis showed gamma globulinemia without a monoclonal (“M”) spike.

A 70-year-old man with a long-standing history of complicated Crohn’s disease presented with 3 days of nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and constipation—symptoms similar to prior obstructions that had resolved with conservative management. His surgical history included bilateral iliac artery angioplasty with stent placement. Medications were loperamide, simethicone, and aspirin. Laboratory studies showed mild anemia and slight hypokalemia. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated focal mucosal thickening in the mid-descending colon and upstream colonic dilation with mild mucosal thickening. A colonic stricture and bowel obstruction were suspected, and he underwent exploratory laparotomy with lysis of adhesions, partial colectomy, and diverting loop ileostomy. At surgery, a stricture at the mid-descending colon was excised. Gross examination revealed an unusual mass-like lesion. Histologic examination of the specimen showed a fissuring ulcer typical for Crohn’s disease and a proliferation of spindle-to-stellate cells intermixed with mast cells, without appreciable mitotic figures. The cell proliferation extended from the subserosa into the muscularis propria and focally into the submucosa, protruding into the bowel lumen.

A 39-year-old man presented with a several-month history of back pain. His medical history was significant for seminoma treated 12 years earlier with orchiectomy and four cycles of cisplatin and etoposide. Follow-up at our hospital showed no recurrence over 12 years. On examination, vital signs were normal, and there were no palpable abdominal masses. Laboratory tests, including serum alpha-fetoprotein and β-human chorionic gonadotropin, were within normal limits. An abdominal and pelvic computed tomography scan revealed a 6.9 × 4.4-cm homogeneous, unilocular cystic mass with smooth borders in the left pararenal space and no mural nodules, ascites, lymphadenopathy, or peritoneal implants. The neoplastic nature of the mass was uncertain.

A 77-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of right hip pain and progressive difficulty bearing weight after a cemented Exeter total hip replacement performed three years earlier. Over the preceding four weeks she had become housebound; her pain occurred at rest and sometimes woke her from sleep. Six months earlier she had received high-dose oral steroids for presumed polymyalgia rheumatica. She had no trauma history. Medical history included osteoarthritis and iron deficiency anemia. On examination, she was frail and afebrile, with no erythema or swelling around the hip. There was severe tenderness over the greater trochanter, active flexion limited to 20°, and severely restricted range of motion otherwise. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 86 g/L, white-cell count 32.5×10^9/L, C-reactive protein 246 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 100 mm/hr. Plain radiographs were unremarkable. CT imaging demonstrated a cystic mass adjacent to the prosthesis. A technetium-99m bone scan with SPECT showed intense hypervascularity at the medial proximal femur. MRI revealed a large periarticular lesion with solid components and areas of liquefaction necrosis. Given the clinical signs and imaging suggestive of infection, a provisional diagnosis of periprosthetic joint infection was made. Hip aspiration yielded slightly turbid fluid; Gram stain, culture, and sensitivity were negative. Intravenous antibiotics were started, but the patient remained unwell with rising white-cell count and CRP. An open biopsy of the soft-tissue collection was planned.

A previously healthy 9-year-old girl presented with swelling under the right jaw that had slowly increased in size over the past two years. She reported no fever, pain, voice changes, breathing difficulty, dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, or tuberculosis exposure. She had a history of exposure to cats. On examination, there were two firm, nodular, nonmobile swellings: one in the right submandibular area measuring approximately 2 × 2 inches, and one in the submental area measuring approximately 1.5 × 1.5 inches. The remainder of the ear, nose, and throat examination was normal. Laboratory tests, including cat scratch serology and toxoplasma IgG, were negative. Ultrasonography of the neck showed two calcified masses with heterogeneous echotexture. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the head and neck revealed a nonenhancing, multilobulated mass with peripheral rim calcification in the right submandibular region crossing the midline, measuring 4.88 × 3.55 cm; the right submandibular gland was distinct from the lesion, and the other salivary glands and cervical vessels appeared normal. The CT characterization suggested a benign mesenchymal lesion, and the imaging differential included a calcified lymph node, a calcified plunging ranula without any intraoral component, and liposarcoma.

A 33-year-old man was evaluated for 3 months of severe low back, sacroiliac, and sternal pain that worsened with movement and woke him at night. He reported a 12-kg weight loss but denied fever, night sweats, nausea, visual changes, or trauma. He consumed unpasteurized dairy products but had no significant family history. Multiple NSAIDs provided no relief.

On examination, there was tenderness over the sternum, right lower ribs, lumbar spine, and right sacroiliac joint. Lumbar flexion and lateral bending were reduced. Motor strength and deep tendon reflexes were normal; plantar responses were downgoing bilaterally.

Initial laboratory studies showed WBC 2500/mm3, neutrophils 1375/mm3, hemoglobin 8.0 g/dL, platelets 41 000/mm3, ESR 130 mm/h, calcium 11.5 mg/dL, albumin 3.6 g/dL, and negative Wright, 2-ME, RF, and HLA-B27 tests. Abdominal ultrasound noted mild splenomegaly.

Cranial radiographs revealed multiple lytic skull lesions. Thoracolumbar MRI demonstrated numerous abnormal vertebral body lesions and diffuse marrow signal changes. Serum protein electrophoresis showed a beta-1 spike. Urine protein electrophoresis revealed elevated free light chains and Bence Jones proteinuria.

An 82-year-old woman presented with symptomatic hypoglycemia (blood glucose 2.4 mmol/L), corrected to 6.8 mmol/L with IV dextrose. She had a three-year history of fasting episodes marked by dizziness, hunger, confusion, and visual changes, all relieved by glucose intake. She had no history of diabetes, other endocrinopathies, or gastric surgery. Medications: simvastatin and esomeprazole.  
On examination: blood pressure 130/60 mmHg, heart rate 90 bpm, O₂ saturation 98% on room air. Abdominal exam: tenderness in the right upper quadrant but soft elsewhere without masses; cardiac, respiratory, and neurologic exams were unremarkable.  
A 72-hour fast produced a hypoglycemic episode (1.7 mmol/L) with elevated insulin (12 mU/L [<3 mU/L]) and C-peptide (1.31 pmol/mL [≤0.20 pmol/mL]). Sulfonylurea screen and insulin antibodies were negative. Cortisol peak during a short Synacthen test was 749 nmol/L (normal), and TSH and growth hormone were normal.  
Triple-phase CT of the pancreas showed a bulky body but no discrete mass. 68Ga-DOTA-octreotate PET/CT was negative. 68Ga-DOTA-exendin-4 (GLP-1R) PET/CT showed diffuse pancreatic uptake (SUVmax 6.3), “suggestive of nesidioblastosis in this clinical context.” Persistent hypoglycemia required dexamethasone, frequent meals, and dextrose infusions.  
Given ongoing fasting hypoglycemia, a selective arterial calcium stimulation test with hepatic venous sampling was performed. It demonstrated a >2-fold rise in insulin in the proximal and distal splenic arteries and gastroduodenal artery, “suggesting the presence of a hyperfunctional lesion in the body and/or tail region of the pancreas.”

A 54-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of a non-healing scaly rash and itching of both nipples and areolae. She had no personal or family history of breast or ovarian cancer. The rash had been treated empirically with topical anti-allergy agents by general practitioners and a dermatologist with no improvement. On examination, there were eczematous scaly lesions with excoriation and central ulceration affecting both nipple-areola complexes, right nipple retraction, and no discharge. Palpation revealed an irregular, firm 2 × 2 cm retro-papillary mass in the right breast and a 1 × 2 cm mass in the left breast; axillary lymph nodes were not palpable.  
Breast ultrasonography showed on the right a spiculated hypoechoic lesion with calcification measuring 1.61 × 2.06 × 1.78 cm in the retro-papillary region and on the left an amorphic, irregular lesion measuring 0.82 × 0.67 × 1.73 cm, with both lesions classified as BIRADS IV. Mammography demonstrated in the right breast an amorphic hyperdense lesion 1.26 × 2.12 cm, 1.75 cm from the nipple, and in the left breast multiple retro-papillary microcalcifications, with associated skin thickening.

A 56-year-old man with a 30-pack-year smoking history presented with a 3-month history of malaise, early satiety, weight loss, and progressive jaundice, and a 2-day history of epigastric pain. On examination, he was jaundiced and cachectic, with a palpable right upper quadrant mass. Laboratory studies showed a serum lipase of 1105 U/L and a total bilirubin level of 93 μmol/L. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 12.5 × 11.3 cm heterogeneous mass arising from the right kidney, an ipsilateral non-contiguous adrenal lesion, and retrocaval lymphadenopathy adjacent to the pancreatic head, with dilation of the biliary and pancreatic ducts. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated mediastinal lymphadenopathy. MRCP revealed a double-duct sign secondary to malignant invasion of a retroperitoneal mass, with reactive changes and luminal distortion of the second and third portions of the duodenum, indicating gastric outlet obstruction.

A 42-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of dull abdominal pain. He denied fever, jaundice, or vomiting and had no history of alcohol use. On examination, there was a tender, palpable mass in the epigastric region.

Laboratory studies showed elevated alkaline phosphatase, SGPT, and SGOT, with normal alpha-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), and Cancer Antigen 19.9. Viral hepatitis serologies (HBsAg, HCV Ag) were negative, and other blood tests were within normal limits.

Abdominal ultrasound revealed hepatomegaly with multiple heterogeneously hypoechoic and mildly hyperechoic lesions of varying sizes in both liver lobes. Color Doppler demonstrated flow signals predominantly at the periphery of the lesions. Shear wave elastography of the lesions showed stiffness values ranging from 140.8 to 159.0 kPa, suggesting a malignant process.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed multiple well-defined, heterogeneously hypodense lesions scattered throughout the liver, some coalescing into a large exophytic mass (15 × 19 × 13 cm) in the left lobe, with central areas of low attenuation. There was mass effect on adjacent organs but no vascular invasion, tumor thrombus, or lymphadenopathy.

Given the imaging appearance of multiple liver masses, clinical suspicion was raised for a metastatic tumor or multifocal hepatocellular carcinoma. A whole-body PET-CT demonstrated heterogeneous FDG uptake in the hepatic lesions (SUVmax 10.9) with a characteristic peripheral “ring of fire” appearance in larger lesions, and no pathologic uptake elsewhere. 

An image-guided liver biopsy was performed for definitive diagnosis.

A 28-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented for evaluation of chronic headache. She denied a history of recurrent throat infections or odynophagia. On examination, her palatine tonsils were symmetrically enlarged without erythema, exudate, or tenderness; the throat isthmus was unremarkable. There were no palpable cervical lymph nodes or other head-and-neck abnormalities. To evaluate her headache, an intravenous contrast–enhanced computed tomography scan of the head and neck was obtained, which demonstrated a cystic formation in the right palatine tonsil that exhibited peripheral enhancement with a central fluid-density component.

A 54-year-old woman presented with a two-year history of a palpable mass in the posterior aspect of her left ankle. She reported intermittent localized pain when walking and a catching sensation during plantar dorsiflexion. She had no history of trauma, infection, or lipid-metabolism disorders. On examination, an elastic, soft, smooth lesion was palpable on the lateral aspect of the Achilles tendon; it moved with dorsiflexion and plantar flexion, suggesting a relationship with the tendon. A plain radiograph showed a soft-tissue opacity without calcification dorsal to the Achilles tendon. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-circumscribed, oval lesion lateral to the tendon that was isointense to subcutaneous fat on T1- and T2-weighted images and was suppressed on fat-suppressed T2-weighted images. The lesion was surrounded by a low-signal rim on T1 and a high-signal rim on T2, distinguishing it from adjacent adipose tissue. The continuity of the Achilles tendon was intact. Based on these findings, a benign, fat-containing soft tissue tumor such as a lipoma was suspected.

A 7-year-old child was referred for evaluation of a right parotid‐region mass that had been slowly enlarging over 2 years. There was no pain, trismus, facial weakness, prior trauma, or family history of neurofibromatosis. On examination, a soft, 4 cm mass in the right pretragial area moved with both superficial and deep tissue planes. An MRI of the parotid gland demonstrated a well‐defined, multilobulated lesion involving the superficial and deep lobes of the right parotid gland, measuring 26 × 25 × 46 mm, with regular borders and late, homogeneous enhancement after contrast. On T2-weighted images, the mass had a fluid-like signal and extended cranially toward the skull base in the expected course of the facial nerve. The decision was made to proceed with a parotidectomy.

A 22-year-old woman presented with an 8-day history of dull right upper quadrant abdominal pain associated with abdominal distention, anorexia, weight loss, and bilateral lower leg edema. She also reported recurrent severe headaches with occasional visual disturbances and, over the prior two weeks, new-onset eyelid ptosis and diplopia. Her medical history was notable for surgical removal of an ovarian teratoma six months earlier. She reported irregular menstruation but no known endocrine disorders. On examination, she appeared distressed and pale, with a distended abdomen, epigastric tenderness, shifting dullness, hepatomegaly, and bilateral pitting edema. An abdominal ultrasound revealed massive ascites, surface irregularity and heterogeneous echogenicity of the liver, abdominal lymphadenopathy, and suspicious hepatic nodules suggestive of metastatic disease. A head CT scan showed a 3.7 × 2.1 × 1.6 cm, lobulated, well-circumscribed suprasellar mass isodense to gray matter, with stippled internal calcifications, avid post-contrast enhancement, and small non-enhancing, fluid-attenuating areas. The optic chiasm and infundibulum were slightly displaced anterosuperiorly; the internal carotid arteries were bilaterally encased by approximately 180 degrees; the lesion abutted but did not encase the basilar artery; and there was no extension into the pituitary fossa. The brain parenchyma and ventricular system were otherwise normal. Bilateral maxillary and ethmoid sinuses were partially opacified without air-fluid levels. The right globe was internally rotated.

A 42-year-old man presented with right-sided chest pain that was not related to exertion and progressive shortness of breath on exertion. He denied cough, fever, or weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable, and routine hematological studies were within normal limits. A chest radiograph (posteroanterior view) showed a well-defined, radiopaque mass without calcification or cavitation, with its medial border merging with the right cardiac silhouette; a lateral radiograph confirmed an anterior mediastinal location. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a heterogeneously enhancing mass in the right anterior mediastinum, with areas of necrosis and adherence to the pericardium. Bronchoscopic examination demonstrated extrinsic compression of the trachea and the right main bronchus.

A 46-year-old woman with a history of depression, asthma, and uterine leiomyomas presented with 5 days of progressive abdominal pain, bloating, nausea, and subjective fevers. She reported several months of weight gain and intermittent crampy right lower quadrant pain that had become constant and severe over the past 5 days. Her surgical history included a myomectomy 5 years earlier and a laparoscopic hysterectomy 2 years later. She consumed four to five alcoholic drinks nightly but had abstained since symptom onset. Family history was notable for breast cancer in a maternal grandmother, skin cancer in her mother, and colon cancer in an uncle.

On arrival, she was tachycardic, mildly hypotensive, and febrile to 39.4 °C. The abdomen was soft, distended, and diffusely tender without peritoneal signs. Laboratory studies revealed a leukocytosis of 15 × 10^3 cells/µL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed moderate-volume ascites containing complex fluid with extensive gas and peripheral rim enhancement, a thickened fluid-filled appendix, and a soft-tissue–density cystic lesion in the anterior abdominal wall; markedly enlarged, septated cystic lesions were noted in the pelvis. The radiologist’s impression was that the origin was unclear and that a ruptured adnexal cyst should be considered given the pelvic findings.

The patient was resuscitated with 2 L of intravenous fluid, after which her hemodynamics normalized. Given stability, a nonoperative approach with broad-spectrum antibiotics and interventional radiology–guided fluid drainage and biopsy was undertaken. Core needle biopsy of the abdominal wall lesion revealed a uterine leiomyoma implant, and cytologic analysis of the peritoneal fluid aspirate demonstrated pools of acellular mucoid material.

A 72-year-old Japanese woman was referred for evaluation of a whitish lesion on the left lateral tongue. She first noticed discomfort at the site 5 months earlier. Her medical history included appendicitis and clear cell renal cell carcinoma; there was no documented history of Epstein–Barr virus infection. Oral examination revealed a unilateral, non-detachable white patch on the left lingual edge. A local biopsy yielded a diagnosis of “atypical epithelium that does not rule out neoplastic change.” The patient declined surgical treatment, and the lesion was observed. Eleven months later, an indurated, exophytic mass measuring approximately 12 × 6 mm with a pale whitish anterior margin was present at the same site. A second biopsy confirmed squamous cell carcinoma. Contrast-enhanced CT and FDG-PET revealed no cervical lymphadenopathy. The tumor was staged as cT2N0M0. A partial glossectomy with 10-mm margins was performed.

A 48-year-old man with chronic alcohol abuse and hypertension presented with an 8-month history of progressive right-sided neck swelling associated with dyspnea and dysphagia. Physical examination confirmed an increase in volume on the right side of the neck. Nasofibrolaryngoscopy demonstrated decreased upper airway caliber due to extrinsic compression of the pharynx and hypopharynx, causing airway obstruction. Neck ultrasonography revealed a poorly defined echogenic area along the course of the right sternocleidomastoid muscle and small (<1 cm) lymph nodes. Fine-needle aspiration cytology showed scarce fragments of adipose and fibrous connective tissue on a hemorrhagic background. Computed tomography of the neck demonstrated a hypodense lesion with an attenuation coefficient of –112 HU in the right parapharyngeal region extending to the hypopharynx, superior mediastinum, and bilateral supraclavicular areas, with anterior displacement of the submandibular gland and extrathoracic airway.

A 56‐year‐old man presented with a 5‐year history of left anterior thigh pain, left sciatica, and intermittent claudication that had worsened over the past year. He had no history of corticosteroid use or endocrinopathy. On examination, he was obese (BMI 30.9 kg/m2), had limited lumbar extension, a positive left Kemp sign, and severe limitation of the left straight‐leg–raise test, but no motor weakness or sensory deficits. Plain radiographs of the lumbar spine were unremarkable. Computed tomography showed posterior vertebral scalloping of L3, L4, and L5 without cortical or medullary bone erosion and Schmorl’s nodes at the endplates of L3–L5. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed an epidural mass posterior to the vertebral bodies of L3–L5 with signal intensity identical to subcutaneous fat. On axial T1‐ and T2‐weighted images with gadolinium administration, a hyperintense mass at L4 asymmetrically compressed the left side of the dural sac and the left L4 nerve root. Thus, a spinal epidural lipoma was suspected, with differential diagnoses of epidural tumor and neurinoma.

A 62-year-old man presented with a 45-day history of generalized pruritus. Initial treatment with antihistamines and emollients provided incomplete relief. He had no history of tobacco or alcohol use and a medical history significant only for hypertension. On examination, vital signs were normal, and the only finding was mild scratch marks on the skin. 
Laboratory studies showed:
- Normal complete blood count, urinalysis, chest radiograph, liver chemistry, and renal and thyroid function tests
- Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 35 mm/h
Imaging studies revealed:
- Color duplex sonography: a large hypervascular, low-level echo, heterogeneous mass in the right kidney
- Intravenous pyelogram: irregularity of the margins of the right renal calices
- Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis: a heterogeneous mass arising from the upper pole of the right kidney infiltrating the calices
- CT angiography: a tumor thrombus in the right renal vein without extension into the inferior vena cava
- Bone scan: no evidence of metastatic disease

A 67-year-old Caucasian woman was brought to the hospital for acute changes in mental status characterized by confusion, transient aphasia, and a brief period of unresponsiveness. Over several days she had experienced generalized malaise, body aches, and fatigue. Her past medical history was notable for treated hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage III (baseline SCr 1.1 mg/dL), anemia of chronic disease, chronic back pain, and polymyalgia rheumatica treated with low-dose prednisone. Ten days earlier she had been hospitalized for viral gastroenteritis and had received intravenous contrast for an abdominal CT. She took ibuprofen intermittently for pain.

On examination she was lethargic but arousable, oriented only to person, with dry mucous membranes and diffuse abdominal and extremity tenderness. She was afebrile, blood pressure 84/53 mm Hg, pulse 104 bpm, respirations 16/min, and pulse oximetry 96% on room air.

Initial laboratory studies showed: WBC 18,900/µL without bands, hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, platelets 211,000/µL; sodium 132 mEq/L, potassium 6.7 mEq/L, chloride 100 mEq/L, bicarbonate 15 mEq/L, BUN 62 mg/dL, SCr 5.6 mg/dL, calcium 11.2 mg/dL (corrected 11.8 mg/dL), phosphorus 4.5 mg/dL; lactate 1.0 mg/dL; albumin 3.2 g/dL. Urinalysis showed 1+ protein and blood; microscopy revealed no casts. Urine sodium 100 mEq/L, urine creatinine 29 mg/dL, specific gravity 1.007; urine protein 321 mg/dL, urine albumin 58.4 mg/dL; fractional excretion of sodium 14.6%. Estimated GFR was 7 mL/min.

Chest radiograph was unremarkable. Noncontrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed no hydronephrosis, masses, or lymphadenopathy. CT of the brain excluded acute stroke. An EKG showed sinus tachycardia without peaked T waves. Rapid influenza B test was positive.

She was diagnosed with severe sepsis from influenza, hyperkalemia, hypercalcemia, and acute renal failure. Treatment included oseltamivir, intravenous fluids, bicarbonate, insulin with dextrose, and sodium polystyrene for hyperkalemia. Over the next two days, her hemodynamics, mental status, leukocytosis, and electrolyte abnormalities normalized, and urine output remained adequate. However, her renal function continued to worsen despite fluid resuscitation, correction of hypercalcemia, and avoidance of nephrotoxins, and she had no indications for dialysis.

A 12-year-old boy presented in December with a half-day history of acute left upper abdominal pain. He denied abdominal distention, nausea, vomiting, fever, urinary symptoms, or hematuria. An abdominal ultrasound at a local hospital showed an approximately 81×79 mm mass with low and weak echo, clear edges, nonuniform internal echo, and an unclear boundary with the left kidney. On transfer, examination revealed a left subcostal mass approximately 7.0×7.9 cm; there was no flank tenderness or vascular bruit. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Abdominal CT demonstrated a round left renal tumor measuring 7.0×8.5×8.7 cm that showed contrast uptake; enhancement in venous and delayed phases was more extensive but of reduced intensity, with areas of irregular, flaky enhancement and an ill-defined border with renal parenchyma. Preoperative blood tests, ECG, and chest radiography were normal. Laboratory results included a leukocyte count of 6.82×10^9/L, hemoglobin 127 g/L, platelets 378×10^9/L, prealbumin 18.9 mg/dL, creatinine 80.9 µmol/L, and urinalysis positive for occult blood.

A 77-year-old woman with diabetes and hypertension presented with 1 month of worsening dyspnoea on exertion and 1 week of chest discomfort with nocturnal cough. Body‐mass index was 24.5 kg/m2. Heart rate was 70 bpm, blood pressure 112/78 mm Hg, respiratory rate 14/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Cardiac examination was unremarkable, and ECG and transthoracic echocardiography showed no signs of right ventricular overload (tricuspid regurgitation velocity 2.3 m/s). Contrast‐enhanced CT revealed a massive, homogeneous filling defect extending from the left main pulmonary artery into the lower lobe branches. Serum D–dimer was undetectable, and there was no evidence of peripheral venous thrombosis. Measured tumour markers, including CEA, CA19‐9, CA125, and soluble interleukin‐2 receptor, were all negative. Intravenous unfractionated heparin was started. On day 4, contrast‐enhanced MRI showed no enhancement of the lesion. On day 5, ^67Ga scintigraphy showed no pathological uptake. On day 14, PET‐CT demonstrated no abnormal accumulation of ^18F‐FDG in the mass (max SUV 0.90). After 3 weeks of anticoagulation (heparin followed by apixaban), repeat CT showed no reduction in the size of the filling defect.

A 75-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of a painless right axillary lump. He had no systemic symptoms, a history of diabetes mellitus, and no prior skin cancers. On examination, there was a discrete 3-cm soft mass in the mid-axillary skin with mild red discoloration but no punctum, ulceration, or signs of acute inflammation; the axillary lymph nodes were not palpable. The initial clinical differential diagnosis was between a sebaceous (epidermoid) cyst and a lipoma, and an ultrasound was obtained. The ultrasound showed a well-defined, heterogeneous, 10 × 13 mm lesion confined to the skin with both peripheral and internal vascularity on Doppler imaging. Because the degree of vascularity was atypical for a benign epidermoid cyst, a repeat ultrasound was arranged after a 12-week delay. The second study demonstrated interval growth to 21 × 15 mm, lobulated margins, marked internal vascularity, and extension into the subcutaneous tissue, with no lymphadenopathy. Given these concerning features, an ultrasound-guided core biopsy was performed.

A 12-year-old female presented with a swelling in the left lower posterior jaw. On intraoral examination, there was a diffuse, smooth, firm, and nontender expansion of both the buccal and lingual cortices in the left mandibular angle region, associated with an impacted second molar. Mouth opening was normal.  
A panoramic radiograph showed a 4 cm × 3 cm radiopaque mass with well-defined borders and a surrounding radiolucent halo in the left mandibular angle, associated with the impacted second molar tooth.  
Computerized tomography demonstrated a well-defined, rounded, amorphous, densely ossified mass arising from the left lower impacted second molar, with an intact but thinned mandibular cortex and lower border.  
The lesion was provisionally diagnosed as a complex odontome. The differential diagnosis would include osteoma and cemento-ossifying fibroma.

A 67-year-old Japanese woman presented with a 4-year history of idiopathic thrombocytopenia unresponsive to steroid therapy and, over the past 6 months, progressive pancytopenia. She denied any immunosuppressive disorders, immunosuppressive medications, or atypical infections. Physical examination revealed mild weakness but was otherwise unremarkable.  
Serial abdominal CT scans demonstrated progressive, heterogeneously enhanced splenomegaly measuring 48 × 39 mm three years prior, 95 × 34 mm two years prior, and 130 × 80 mm at the time of surgery, without discrete masses or nodular lesions.  
On admission, laboratory studies showed:  
• WBC 1,300/mm3, hemoglobin 5.7 g/dL, platelets 8,000/mm3  
• Total protein 4.9 g/dL, albumin 1.6 g/dL, γ-globulin 0.6 g/dL  
• C-reactive protein 4.07 mg/dL, serum interleukin-2 receptor 1,306 U/mL  
Given the clinical picture of hypersplenism and progressive cytopenias, a splenectomy was performed. The patient died 6 months later from bone marrow involvement of the underlying disease.

A 59-year-old Pakistani woman with hypertension and a family history of breast, ovarian, and pancreatic cancer underwent a preoperative chest radiograph for total left knee replacement, which revealed an incidental nodular density in the right lower lung zone measuring approximately 2.5 cm × 2 cm. She reported only occasional blood-tinged sputum in the morning and denied cough, dyspnea, weight loss, or systemic symptoms. She was afebrile, with normal vital signs and oxygen saturation on room air. Physical examination of the chest and other systems was unremarkable.

A high-resolution [18F]FDG PET/CT scan showed a lobulated soft-tissue lesion measuring 23 mm × 23 mm with internal cavitation in the anterior segment of the right lower lobe; the lesion’s maximum standardized uptake value was 2.7. No hypermetabolic lymphadenopathy or distant lesions were identified.

CT-guided core biopsy demonstrated a spindle‐cell lesion without significant cytologic atypia or increased mitotic activity. Immunohistochemical stains showed focal positivity for S-100 and patchy positivity for CD34, and were negative for SOX-10, ASMA, Melan A, HMB-45, and STAT6. A benign spindle‐cell lesion of probable neural origin was diagnosed, and surgical resection was planned.

A 42-year-old man presented with a 13-year history of intractable tonic seizures. Noncontrast CT of the head showed a 40-mm mass in the right parietal lobe with calcification and cystic components. MRI revealed marked signal hypointensity around the solid component on T2- and T2*-weighted images, consistent with calcification or hemosiderin, and heterogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. The mass was adjacent to the lateral ventricle, with mild enlargement of the posterior part of the ventricle; the normal choroid plexus remained in its usual location, and no continuity between it and the lesion was seen. Cerebral angiography showed no tumor staining or vascular abnormality. The provisional diagnosis was cerebral cavernous angioma with a hemorrhagic episode.

A 30-year-old man presented after a forced inversion injury of his left foot. He had no relevant medical or family history and was taking no medications. On examination, there was edema over the left lateral malleolus, tenderness with movement and weight bearing, no deformity, and palpable distal pulses of normal intensity and frequency.  

Plain radiographs of the left foot showed soft-tissue edema and a discrete lesion in the first metatarsal. MRI of the left foot with gadolinium demonstrated, in both sagittal and coronal planes, a heterogeneous intramedullary lesion in the base and proximal diaphysis of the first metatarsal that was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with evidence of cortical injury related to the lesion.

A 60-year-old man with a 5-year history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and a 32–pack-year smoking history (quit at age 51) was referred for evaluation of gradually enlarging mediastinal lymphadenopathy and ground-glass opacity in the lower lung fields on CT. He reported dry cough and mild dyspnea (mMRC grade I). Physical examination revealed fine crackles at both lung bases; no superficial lymphadenopathy was palpable. 

Laboratory studies showed WBC 7400/μL, hemoglobin 14.5 g/dL, platelets 250 × 10^3/μL, total protein 6.4 g/dL, albumin 3.7 g/dL, creatinine 1.09 mg/dL, LDH 247 IU/L, β2-microglobulin 2.4 mg/L, soluble IL-2 receptor 469 U/mL, KL-6 805 U/mL, ACE 37.4 U/L, IgM 791 mg/dL (reference 33–183), IgG 531 mg/dL (861–1747), and IgA 52 mg/dL (93–393). Urinalysis detected kappa-type Bence-Jones proteins. 

Pulmonary function testing showed obstructive impairment (FEV1/FVC 61%). ECG and echocardiography were normal. Enhanced chest CT demonstrated upper-zone emphysema, lower-zone ground-glass opacities with septal thickening, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and a paravertebral soft tissue shadow. FDG-PET revealed SUVmax 2.5 in mediastinal soft tissue and 2.4 in retroperitoneal soft tissue. 

Bronchoalveolar lavage was unremarkable. Transbronchial lung biopsy showed lymphocytes and plasma cells in alveolar walls. Given elevated IgM, urinary Bence-Jones protein, and lymphadenopathy, the initial differential included lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, MALT lymphoma with plasma cell differentiation, and multiple myeloma. 

Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy revealed normocellular marrow with kappa-predominant lymphocytes and plasma cells; the smear showed 24.2% lymphocytes, 3.0% plasma cells, and some atypical cells. Flow cytometry demonstrated kappa-predominant B cells. These findings supported the diagnosis of lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma but were not definitive.

A 71-year-old woman with hypertension and diabetes was evaluated for a massive goiter. Thyroid function tests showed TSH 5.51 μIU/L (0.27–4.2), free T3 3.67 pmol/L (2.8–7), free T4 9.98 pmol/L (12–22), thyroid peroxidase antibody 319 IU/mL (0–34), and thyroglobulin antibody 683 IU/mL (0–115). Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated bilaterally enlarged, heterogeneous lobes (right lobe 6.9×3.0×2.7 cm; left lobe 7.4×3.1×3.8 cm) with prominent vasculature and microcalcifications but no discrete nodules. A radioisotope scan showed homogeneous uptake of 1.7% Tc99m. Findings were consistent with autoimmune (Hashimoto’s) thyroiditis. 

One year later, she underwent elective thyroidectomy. At surgery, her TSH had risen to 11.0 μIU/L, and free T4 was 9.84 pmol/L. The procedure was uneventful; she was discharged with asymptomatic hypocalcemia (calcium 1.95 mmol/L [2.12–2.52]) and hypoalbuminemia (albumin 25 g/L [40.2–47.6]). Intraoperative frozen section demonstrated chronic thyroiditis with a prominent plasma cell component.

Gross examination of the thyroid revealed lobes measuring 9×6×3.5 cm (left) and 10×6×3.5 cm (right), with prominent capsular vessels, gray-yellow cut surfaces, and firm consistency. Microscopy showed diffuse sheets of mature plasma cells separated by fibrous septa, occasional binucleation and mitoses, focal lymphoid follicles with germinal centers, and residual oncocytic thyroid follicles. Immunohistochemical studies revealed tumor cells positive for kappa light chain, CD38, and CD45, and negative for lambda light chain, CD138, thyroglobulin, CD20, synaptophysin, chromogranin, NSE, CD30, calcitonin, and Bcl-2.

A 42-year-old previously healthy man presented with a 15-day history of diffuse lower back pain that acutely worsened over 2 days. The pain was a constant dull ache, radiating to both lower limbs, without fever or constitutional symptoms. On exam, he was well nourished, with mild tenderness over the L3–L5 spinous processes and paraspinal muscle spasm; neurologic examination was normal. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 84 mm/h; other blood tests were normal. Plain radiographs of the lumbosacral spine showed mild loss of height of the L4 vertebral body with sclerosis. MRI of the lumbosacral spine demonstrated a heterogenous signal and a fracture of L4, with extradural and paravertebral collections compressing the cauda equina; contrast-enhanced MRI showed homogeneous enhancement of the L4 lesion and adjacent collections. The patient underwent L3–L5 posterior instrumentation and decompression, with transpedicular biopsy of the L4 vertebral body and intracanalicular tissue. Intraoperative cultures and tissue staining were negative; PCR for tuberculosis was negative. Histopathological examination showed bony spicules, fibrocollagenous tissue, marrow elements, focal congestion, and mild chronic inflammation, with no evidence of malignancy; immunohistochemistry was negative. On the basis of endemic prevalence and imaging, a presumptive diagnosis of tuberculous spondylitis was made and antitubercular therapy was started. One month later, he developed progressive lower-extremity weakness (motor power grade 1 in L4–S1 distribution) with preserved sensation and sphincter function. Repeat MRI showed increased soft-tissue extension from L3 to L5, causing complete canal stenosis, with greater prevertebral, paravertebral, and intraspinal involvement. PET–CT revealed increased fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the L4 vertebral body and prevertebral, paravertebral, and epidural regions.

A 29-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of intermittent dull aching right flank pain and associated vomiting. She denied hematuria, dysuria, fever, weight loss, or appetite change. On examination, vital signs were normal. Abdominal palpation revealed a firm, ballotable mass measuring approximately 10 × 8 cm in the right hypochondrium extending into the right lumbar and umbilical regions; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Renal ultrasonography showed a 17 × 9 cm heterogeneous mass lesion with internal vascularity involving the lower half of the right kidney. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated a 12.6 × 13.2 × 15.4 cm heterogeneously enhancing soft-tissue density mass arising from the right kidney, compressing the renal cortex, extending into the right retroperitoneal space, and displacing bowel loops. There were also suspicious soft-tissue deposits along the left thoracic paravertebral space and in the pericardium adjacent to the right atrium.

An FDG PET scan corroborated these findings, with a maximum SUV of 2.0 in the primary renal lesion and 1.9 in the suspected metastatic sites. An additional 5 × 5 mm heterogeneously FDG-avid subcutaneous soft-tissue thickening was noted on the medial aspect of the right thigh.

A 36-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of fevers, chills, productive cough, chest pain, dyspnea on exertion, loss of appetite, and generalized weakness. His chest pain was mid-back, pressure-like, constant, non-radiating, non-pleuritic, and rated 5/10. His medical history included resection of a “mediastinal PEComa” (initially misdiagnosed as rhabdomyoma), essential hypertension, and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation status post appendage ligation (off anticoagulation). 

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. He had an irregularly irregular heart rhythm and a sternotomy scar. Laboratory data, including inflammatory markers, were unremarkable. Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm, first-degree atrioventricular block, and left atrial enlargement. Chest radiograph was unremarkable.

Given concern for tumour recurrence, transthoracic echocardiography was performed and showed a globular mass involving the posterior left atrium and pulmonary veins measuring approximately 20 mm circumferentially. Subsequent transesophageal echocardiography revealed a large bilobed mass arising from the posterior left atrium near the roof, abutting the interatrial septum, extending into the right atrium, and involving the right upper pulmonary vein; one lobe measured 36 mm × 36 mm.

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 40 mm × 53 mm bilobed posterior mediastinal mass abutting the roofs of the left and right atria, compressing the right inferior pulmonary vein, extending superiorly to the main pulmonary artery and inferiorly to the inferior vena cava. On T1-weighted images, the mass was isointense to myocardium; on T2-weighted images, it was hyperintense to skeletal muscle. First-pass perfusion images showed hypervascularity, and delayed enhancement signified a rich stroma and neovascularization. No myocardial scar was detected.

What is your differential diagnosis?

A 64-year-old woman with hypertension and chronic headaches presented with a 2-year history of gradually worsening left-sided pulsatile tinnitus and ear fullness that did not respond to medical therapy. She recently developed left otalgia but denied otorrhea, sudden hearing changes, or prior otologic surgery. On examination, the left tympanic membrane was intact, and a red mass was visible deep to the posteroinferior quadrant; the external auditory canal was otherwise normal. Audiometry showed mild to moderate mixed hearing loss on the left with a type A tympanogram. A noncontrast CT scan of the temporal bones demonstrated an enhancing soft-tissue mass in the hypotympanum adjacent to the inferior tympanic canaliculus. Urinary metanephrines were within normal limits. A CT angiogram revealed a vascular blush in the left tympanic region supplied by the ascending pharyngeal artery.

A 13-year-old boy presented with a 3-month history of recurrent low-grade fever, throat discomfort, intercostal and back pain, initially treated as a viral infection. Ten days before admission, he developed progressive bilateral lower-limb weakness, numbness, hypoesthesia below the xiphoid level, constipation, and difficulty squatting. Neurologic examination revealed normal cognition, grade 4/5 strength in both lower limbs, hypesthesia below T6, a positive Babinski sign, a positive Romberg sign, and a negative Hoffman sign. He had no relevant past surgical or family history. On admission, he was febrile; routine blood tests were normal, but herpes-simplex virus IgM was positive. Antiviral therapy normalized his temperature. Thoracic spine MRI showed a 1.2×0.8 cm intradural extramedullary mass on the right dorsal aspect of the spinal canal at T5, causing canal stenosis and spinal-cord compression. The lesion was intermediate on T1-weighted images, slightly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and homogeneously enhanced with gadolinium, exhibiting clear borders and a dural tail sign. No other lesions were identified on radiological evaluation. Based on imaging, the lesion was initially considered to be a thoracic meningioma.

A 64-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of progressive hoarseness. He was a former smoker (10 pack-years, quit 5 years earlier) and denied excessive alcohol use. Flexible laryngoscopy revealed thickening and fixation of the left true vocal fold. A roughly 3-cm mass arising from the left true vocal fold invaded the left arytenoid and occupied the ventricle. Under general anesthesia, a suspension microlaryngoscopy with biopsy was performed. Histopathological examination of the biopsy specimen showed fused cells of variable dimensions with eosinophilic cytoplasm, irregular hyperchromatic features, and large or multiple nuclei. Contrast-enhanced CT scans of the neck, chest, and abdomen showed no evidence of lymphadenopathy or distant metastases. The tumor was clinically staged as T3N0M0 glottic cancer.

A 53-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of dull, aching pain and progressive swelling of the right upper arm after lifting a heavy object. The pain was sudden in onset, radiated to the scapular region, and was not relieved by rest. Over the same period, he noted a lemon-sized swelling that gradually enlarged, associated with paresthesia, numbness, restricted shoulder motion, and unintentional weight loss with anorexia. There was no history of trauma or prior irradiation.

On examination, there was a diffuse, ill-defined swelling over the right shoulder and scapular area measuring 15×10×7 cm, with variegated consistency, stretched shiny skin, and engorged cutaneous veins; no bruit was palpable. Laboratory studies showed a tenfold elevation in serum alkaline phosphatase and a marked increase in lactate dehydrogenase.

Plain radiographs of the right shoulder revealed a large expansile lytic soft-tissue mass in the proximal humerus involving cortex and medulla, with a wide zone of transition and no sclerotic margins. Non-contrast CT confirmed a 10.8×7.8×9.2 cm heterogeneously low-attenuation expansile lesion in the upper third of the humerus, abutting adjacent muscles. MRI demonstrated a well-defined expansile lesion that was hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2/PD FS, containing multiloculated cysts and multiple blood–fluid levels, with soft-tissue infiltration of the subscapularis and supraspinatus muscles. A Tc-99m MDP bone scan showed increased uptake in the proximal humerus and scapula; an 18F-FDG PET scan showed no evidence of metastatic disease.

Given these findings, a malignant osseous tumor, particularly of vascular origin, was suspected.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a lesion on her chin that began as pinkish plaques 7 years earlier. Over time, the lesion slowly enlarged, became tender to touch, and changed from pink to purple with overlying telangiectasia and increased perspiration. The patient noted that the enlarging lesion began to interfere with her speech. 

On examination, there was a poorly circumscribed, pinkish, infiltrated plaque measuring approximately 4 × 4 cm on the chin, with overlying telangiectasia and extension into the intraoral gingival mucosa. The remainder of the general and systemic examination was unremarkable. An iodine–starch test over the lesion demonstrated profuse hyperhidrosis.

A 5-mm punch biopsy was obtained. Histopathologic examination revealed nodular clusters of dilated vessels intimately associated with an increased number of mature eccrine glands, with an unremarkable epidermis. A closer view showed ectatic blood vessels admixed with dilated sweat glands and mature fat cells.

A 39-year-old man presented with 1 month of nasal obstruction and foul-smelling discharge, accompanied by headache, poor appetite, and bilateral neck masses. On examination, firm, nontender lymph nodes were palpated over bilateral level II regions. Fiberoptic endoscopy of the left nasal cavity showed mucosal erosions with whitish exudates. Laboratory studies revealed mild anemia and an elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase level; HIV testing was negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck demonstrated iso-enhancing masses in the left nasal cavity, nasopharynx, and paranasal sinuses with adjacent bony destruction and multiple enlarged lymph nodes at bilateral levels IB through V. 

Ultrasound-guided FNA of a left cervical lymph node yielded hypercellular smears with a mixed population of small, intermediate, and large lymphoid cells; there were no follicular center cells, histiocytes, tingible body macrophages, or lymphohistiocytic aggregates, and plasma cells and eosinophils were scant. Liu’s-stained smears showed lymphogranular bodies in the background. Medium-to-large atypical cells exhibited irregular nuclei with one to several nucleoli, pale blue cytoplasm, cytoplasmic projections with tongue-like protrusions, and fine or coarse azurophilic granules; mitotic figures were readily found, and necrosis was inconspicuous. In liquid-based cytology, atypical lymphoid cells were oval or elongated with cytoplasmic processes. A cell block showed scattered medium-to-large lymphoid cells with pleomorphic nuclei and small nucleoli among a mixed background population. 

Punch biopsy of the left nasal mucosa revealed diffuse mucosal necrosis with granulation tissue and a dense infiltrate of atypical lymphoid cells of varying sizes, prominent nuclear irregularity, pale cytoplasm, apoptosis, mitotic figures, an angiocentric growth pattern, and angiodestruction with mural fibrinoid necrosis and hemorrhage; pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia of the overlying epithelium was also noted.

A 41-year-old African-American woman presented with an enlarging, painful mass in the right knee area. Four years earlier, she had been treated for osteosarcoma of the same leg with neoadjuvant docetaxel and gemcitabine, radical resection, and hinge-knee replacement. Six months after an initial biopsy of the new mass (reported elsewhere as a high-grade soft-tissue sarcoma), she returned with marked growth of the right-knee mass and increased pain, with decreased range of motion. On examination, there was a 150×200 mm hard, fixed, tender mass around the right knee and a 15×20 mm hard, mildly tender right inguinal lymph node. No rash, edema, or sensory deficits were present; distal pulses were intact. Initial laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 126.7×10^9/L with neutrophils 57.02×10^9/L and eosinophils 60.82×10^9/L, peaking on hospital day 5 with eosinophils 77.79×10^9/L. A bone-marrow biopsy revealed marked eosinophilia and neutrophilia without increased blast cells. Testing for JAK2 mutation was negative as was flow cytometry. Additional investigations included IgE 3 IU/mL, C3 174 mg/dL, C4 35 mg/dL, haemolytic complement 276 units, and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody negative.

A 64-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of urinary difficulty and tightness across the upper back. Two months after onset she developed progressive right lower-extremity weakness, culminating in inability to walk over 2 weeks. On examination, she had monoplegia of the right lower extremity and an asymmetric decrease in light-touch and pain sensation below the nipples, worse on the left, with hyperreflexia and bilateral Babinski signs. Routine blood tests were unremarkable, and there was no personal or family history of cancer. Given the clinical findings suggestive of a Brown-Séquard syndrome at the thoracic level, an MRI of the spine was obtained, showing a 1.5-cm intradural extramedullary mass at T3. The lesion demonstrated intermediate T1 signal, mildly increased T2 signal, and avid enhancement after gadolinium administration. There was no evidence of bony involvement or other lesions on radiologic evaluation.

A 68-year-old man, former smoker, presented with a one-month history of rapidly progressive swelling in the left mandibular region without other local or systemic complaints. On examination, there was a 5 × 5 cm firm, fixed, mildly tender mass over the left mandibular ramus and a separate 1 × 2 cm lobular, tender swelling in the left retromolar trigone. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the swelling was reported as myoepithelioma. A panoramic radiograph showed an osteolytic lesion involving the left ramus of the mandible. Contrast-enhanced CT of the parotid region revealed an osteolytic lesion of the inferior middle third of the left ramus and posterior body with erosion and effacement of adjacent cortices, involvement of the left alveolar canal, and large soft-tissue components displacing the masseter and medial pterygoid muscles. Doppler ultrasonography of the neck demonstrated a well-defined soft-tissue mass in the submandibular region with extensive central and peripheral vascularity arising predominantly from branches of the external carotid artery.

A 49-year-old woman presented with one month of persistent epigastric pain radiating to the back, worsening over time and unrelated to meals. She reported poor appetite, early satiety, and postprandial nausea without changes in bowel habits or systemic symptoms. Her medical history was significant only for uterine fibroids; second-degree relatives had pancreatic and gastric adenocarcinomas. On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs and had mild to moderate epigastric tenderness without peritoneal signs. Laboratory tests showed a microcytic, hypochromic iron-deficiency anemia (Hb 11.2 g/dL) and otherwise normal ESR, renal and liver function, pancreatic enzymes, coagulation tests, bilirubin, and tumor markers (CA19-9, AFP, CEA). 

Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 48 × 40 mm heterogeneous hypo- and hyperechoic lesion at the pancreatic head adjacent to the liver hilum. Contrast CT of the abdomen showed a well-defined 45 × 46 mm hypodense mass near the celiac trunk abutting the left gastric artery, with engorged mesenteric vessels, mild gastric wall thickening, and subcentimeter porta hepatis lymph nodes. Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated a 43 × 45 mm hypoechoic lesion posterior to the stomach, encasing the left gastric artery and a short segment of the celiac trunk without ductal dilation; elastography strain ratio was 22. EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration was performed but yielded indeterminate results.

A 61-year-old man with peptic ulcer disease and hemorrhoids presented with a 3-week history of a rash on the back of his neck and muscle pain. The rash had spread to his face and abdomen, and he reported bilateral proximal muscle weakness and abdominal discomfort. There was no family history of autoimmune disease or malignancy.

On examination, he had a heliotrope rash of the periorbital skin, Gottron papules over the metacarpophalangeal joints, and poikiloderma on the posterior neck and abdomen. Muscle testing revealed symmetric proximal muscle weakness.

Laboratory studies showed AST 311 U/L, ALT 142 U/L, creatine kinase 7400 U/L, and aldolase 39.5 IU/L. Autoantibody testing was negative for anti–Jo-1 antibody and antinuclear antibodies (1:40). Serologic tests for hepatitis B and C viruses were negative. Serum PIVKA-II was 176,000 mAU/mL and α-fetoprotein was >1000 ng/mL.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a large hypoechoic mass in the left hepatic lobe abutting the diaphragm, multiple smaller right-lobe lesions, and para-aortic lymphadenopathy. Electromyography of the biceps brachii and extensor digitorum muscles showed fibrillation potentials and low-amplitude motor units, consistent with dermatomyositis.

A 56-year-old woman presented with fatigue, chest pain, shortness of breath, and dyspnea on exertion. She also reported diffuse left upper quadrant tenderness and a 15-lb unintentional weight loss. Her history was notable for longstanding symptomatic normocytic anemia and hypothyroidism; she had received multiple red-cell transfusions and had undergone several nondiagnostic endoscopies and colonoscopies. She smoked one pack per day for 40 years. On examination, she appeared pale and had tenderness in the left upper quadrant without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies showed:  
• WBC 15.3 × 10^9/L  
• Hemoglobin 7.1 g/dL, hematocrit 23.4%  
• Platelet count 153 × 10^9/L  
• MCV 83.4 fL, RDW 19.7%  

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed marked splenomegaly with heterogeneous enlargement and multiple low-attenuation masses. A PET scan demonstrated hypermetabolism throughout the spleen without evidence of other FDG-avid lesions.

A 49-year-old Asian woman was referred for evaluation of acute urinary retention after a total hysterectomy performed elsewhere for uterine myoma. She reported a years-long history of lower urinary tract symptoms—frequent, incomplete, and irregular voiding—that had never been investigated. Postoperatively, she developed acute retention after multiple unsuccessful urethral catheterizations and required a suprapubic catheter for relief.

On examination, a firm, protruding lump was noted at the vaginal introitus. Laboratory studies showed mild anemia and leukocytosis. Abdominal ultrasonography suggested bladder cystitis and adnexal fluid collection. Cystography demonstrated posterior and inferior bladder prolapse consistent with a cystocele and a diverticulum on the left lateral bladder wall. Pelvic MRI revealed a well-circumscribed mass extending from the proximal to distal thirds of the urethra, posterolateral bladder diverticula, and a mid-urethral stricture.

A 27-year-old woman at 17 weeks’ gestation presented for a routine prenatal visit. She was asymptomatic, with an unremarkable medical and obstetric history. Abdominal examination revealed a smooth, non-tender mass arising from the right hemi-pelvis, extending approximately 10 cm above the umbilicus. Transabdominal ultrasound confirmed a live 17-week fetus and an incidental unilocular cystic mass measuring 210 × 180 × 120 mm in the right pelvis. Serum tumor markers were within normal limits (CA-125, 8.6 U/mL; α-fetoprotein, 25.4 ng/mL). Pelvic MRI demonstrated a 203 × 210 mm homogeneous cystic mass, with all other pelvic structures appearing normal.

A 41-year-old G3P3 woman presented with constant, burning left lower quadrant abdominal pain and vomiting. She had five episodes of emesis and required morphine in the ED. She had no significant medical history and had not seen a gynecologist for over 13 years. On examination, there was left adnexal fullness and tenderness without rebound or guarding; the cervix appeared normal with no cervical motion tenderness. 

Laboratory tests showed an elevated CA 19-9; CA-125 and CEA were normal. Transvaginal ultrasound revealed an enlarged right ovary with multiple cysts and a 13.9-cm left ovarian cyst with septations and an anterior daughter cyst. CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated bilateral adnexal masses without ascites or peritoneal disease. A Pap smear was negative for intraepithelial malignancy, and HPV testing was negative.

She underwent laparoscopic bilateral ovarian cystectomy for presumed ovarian torsion. Intraoperative findings included a 13-cm left ovarian cyst twisted three times on the infundibulopelvic ligament with venous congestion, and a 5-cm right ovarian cyst with intraoperative rupture of clear mucinous fluid and several small white nodules on the right pelvic side wall. Bilateral ovarian cysts, peritoneal washings, and a pelvic side wall nodule were sent for pathology.

Initial pathology showed bilateral mucinous adenocarcinoma, most consistent with ovarian primary.

A 26-year-old woman presented with a 6-year history of pain in the right great toe. She described the pain as worsening at midnight and partially relieved by NSAIDs taken intermittently. She had been evaluated elsewhere for hyperuricemia and inflammatory arthritis, both of which were negative. Despite over-the-counter analgesics, she never experienced complete relief, and her daily activities were affected. 

On examination, there was localized tenderness over the proximal phalanx of the right great toe without erythema, swelling, or nail abnormalities. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein level were within normal limits. 

A plain radiograph of the right foot showed a purely lytic lesion in the proximal phalanx of the great toe without periosteal reaction or joint involvement. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a circumscribed lesion in the same location that was iso- to hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, showed discrete enhancement, and had subtle surrounding edema, with only minimal adjacent joint effusion.

A 46-year-old man presented with a two-month history of painless swelling of his right buttock, progressively causing difficulty in movement. He denied fever, night sweats, or weight loss. On examination, he was well-nourished with no cervical, axillary, or inguinal lymphadenopathy. Systemic examination was unremarkable except for a large, firm, fixed, deep right gluteal mass, associated with ipsilateral lower-extremity weakness. Chest radiograph was normal. Laboratory studies, including fasting blood sugar, complete blood count, serum electrolytes, liver function tests, and coagulation profile, were within normal limits.

Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging revealed an extensive mass involving the right gluteal, iliopsoas, obturator, and piriform muscles, with abnormal signals in the right iliac bone and sacral ala; pelvic organs were intact. An incisional biopsy under local anesthesia showed only lipomatous tissue. Because of concern for soft-tissue malignancy—particularly sarcoma—excisional surgery was performed. Intraoperatively, a giant firm mass was found infiltrating adjacent muscle, extending into the sciatic groove with involvement of the sciatic nerve and bone; extensive resection was performed.

One month postoperatively, the patient developed pitting edema of the right lower limb and genitalia. Serum lactate dehydrogenase was 1281 IU/L. Abdominopelvic CT demonstrated an abnormal infiltrative mass in the right pelvic cavity extending toward the ischioanal fossa and a recurrent infiltrative lesion at the surgical site.

A 56-year-old man presented with a right axillary mass that had been present for over 1 year. Initially diagnosed elsewhere as hidradenitis suppurativa and treated with antibiotics without improvement, he re-presented one year later with an enlarged 5 × 4 cm mass, attached to and erythematous overlying skin. There were no palpable lymph nodes. A clinical diagnosis of an inflamed sebaceous cyst was made, and the mass was excised along with overlying skin. 

Seven weeks after this excision, he was referred for further evaluation. His past medical history included hypertension, dyslipidemia, and benign prostatic hypertrophy; he was a nonsmoker with no alcohol use. Family history was notable for lung cancer in his father and breast cancer in his sister. On examination, the excision site was healing well with some firmness but no discrete mass or inflammation. There was no generalized lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, goiter, breast lumps, or skin lesions. 

ENT evaluation with panendoscopy showed no malignancy. A PET–CT scan was normal except for mild uptake at the surgical site, attributed to postsurgical changes. Breast ultrasound, mammography, and MRI showed no lesions. 

Microscopic examination of the original specimen revealed a dermal neoplasm with papillary–cystic architecture. Papillary fronds were lined by large cells with ample eosinophilic cytoplasm and mildly atypical nuclei; occasional mitoses were seen. Benign apocrine glands were noted adjacent to the tumor. The lesion was well-circumscribed but involved the inked margin focally; areas of hemorrhage and necrosis were present. 

Immunohistochemical studies showed tumor cells positive for CK7, E-cadherin, GCDFP-15, and focal CEA, and negative for S100, p63, ER, PR, TTF-1, CK20, and PSA.

A 35-year-old woman presented with 3 months of progressive dysphagia and a sensation of a foreign body in her throat. She also reported sore throat and an irritating cough when eating. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. A TV-monitored rhinolaryngofiberscopic evaluation revealed a large, smooth-mucosa bulge arising from the left pharyngeal wall, extending down to the glottis in the supraglottic oropharynx; the boundary of the mass was obscure, but the overlying mucosa was intact. The patient declined CT and MRI evaluation because she had recent fertility considerations.

A 40-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an incidentally discovered left pararenal mass. She denied abdominal discomfort, flank or back pain, weight loss, sweating, fatigue, or fever. Her medical history was unremarkable. On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs; there was no peripheral lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, serum biochemistry, and tumor markers (CA 19-9, CA-125, CEA, AFP, and NSE), were all within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax and abdomen revealed a 7.6×5.3×12 cm heterogeneous lesion adjacent to the left kidney that was hypervascular with regular margins and showed no invasion of surrounding structures; imaging of the remainder of the thorax, mediastinum, and abdomen was otherwise unremarkable. MRI of the abdomen demonstrated heterogeneous T1- and T2-weighted hyperintensity of the mass. Based on these findings, the differential diagnosis included malignancy and a lymph nodal mass. Given the diagnostic uncertainty, the decision was made to proceed with surgical exploration.

A 65-year-old Chinese man with chronic hepatitis B (on entecavir) and longstanding hypertension (on metoprolol) was admitted for elective hemorrhoidectomy. Preoperative CT of the abdomen revealed multiple abnormal signals in the liver. Liver MRI showed numerous low-density circular lesions of varying sizes, the largest measuring 2.1 × 2.0 cm in the right posterior lobe. A PET/CT scan demonstrated intensely increased metabolic activity in regions of the intestinal wall, mesentery, omentum, and peritoneum (SUVmax 16.3), raising concern for a malignant process. Exploratory laparoscopy revealed a 5 × 4 cm polypoid mass in the omentum, which invaded through the muscularis propria into the subserosal soft tissue and exhibited lymphovascular invasion. A biopsy specimen was obtained for further analysis.

An 85-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of progressive asthenia, loss of appetite, lower urinary tract symptoms, and a painful pelvic swelling. He had no prior chronic illnesses or surgeries. On examination, his abdomen was distended by an ill-defined, fixed pelvic mass measuring approximately 15 cm in greatest dimension. Digital rectal examination revealed an enlarged, lumpy prostate. Laboratory studies showed a hypochromic microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL) and a markedly elevated serum PSA of 300 μg/mL. Ultrasonography demonstrated a 15-cm, heterogeneous, lobulated mass with areas of necrosis in the left lower abdominal quadrant; the liver, spleen, and kidneys were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a large lobulated necrotic extraperitoneal pelvic mass displacing the bladder and causing mild bilateral hydroureteronephrosis; the mass was adjacent to a calcified, enlarged prostate and was associated with multiple lomboaortic and iliac lymph nodes measuring 26–39 mm. Bone scintigraphy revealed suspicious lytic lesions in the right ischium and the posterior sacral vertebrae.

A term male infant was born after an uneventful pregnancy and vaginal delivery. On examination at birth, he had a large hairy pigmented nevus (>20 cm) on his back and buttocks, with multiple smaller satellite nevi. Neurologic examination was normal. Family history was notable for large congenital nevi in a paternal great aunt and the paternal grandfather.  

On the day of birth, transfontanellar ultrasound revealed several small echogenic foci in the left thalamus and left choroidal fissure without associated mass effect. Brain MRI confirmed those foci as T1-hyperintense lesions and showed additional T1-hyperintense foci in the right thalamus, bilateral basal ganglia, and right cerebellum. The lesions were T2-hypointense and demonstrated corresponding susceptibility effects; there was no leptomeningeal enhancement.
