A 67-year-old woman was referred after a routine health examination detected a mass in her gallbladder; she had vague abdominal complaints but no tenderness or jaundice. Her medical history included renal insufficiency and atrial fibrillation; she had no prior abdominal surgery. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 10.9 × 10^9/L, estimated glomerular filtration rate of 32 mL/min/1.73 m^2, hemoglobin 8.6 mmol/L, total bilirubin 5 μmol/L, alanine aminotransferase 20 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 17 U/L, γ-glutamyltranspeptidase 59.1 U/L, carcinoembryonic antigen within normal limits, and Ca 19-9 of 173 U/L. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a well-defined isoechoic polypoid mural mass in the body of the gallbladder with intact overlying mucosa and no intralesional blood flow; cholecystolithiasis was noted in the neck. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated a homogeneous, high-density, ovoid mural mass measuring 30 × 35 × 18 mm with clear boundaries and no central necrosis or calcifications; the remainder of the gallbladder appeared normal. Differential diagnosis included adenomyomatosis of the gallbladder, gallbladder polyp, gastrointestinal stromal tumor, and gallbladder cancer.

A 77-year-old Caucasian woman with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and degenerative joint disease presented with a 4- to 5-month history of a left cheek nodule that had grown rapidly over the preceding weeks. Two months earlier, shave biopsy of the 14 mm firm nodule had shown Merkel cell carcinoma extending to peripheral and deep margins with perinuclear dot-like CK20 positivity, synaptophysin positivity, weak AE1/AE3 reactivity, and negative TTF-1. PET/CT revealed intense FDG uptake in the primary left cheek mass and multiple intraparotid nodes without distant metastases. Core biopsy of a left submandibular lymph node confirmed lymphatic invasion. She was staged as IIIB (T2pN1bM0) and started on pembrolizumab (200 mg IV every 3 weeks) plus radiotherapy to the left cheek and neck.

One week after the first pembrolizumab dose, she developed acute abdominal pain and nausea; labs including CMP, CBC, troponin, and lipase were normal. Gastroenterology judged her symptoms likely pembrolizumab-related; she received IV fluids and antiemetics and improved. She completed radiotherapy and, after three pembrolizumab doses, developed oropharyngeal discomfort treated empirically for thrush. A few days later, she presented with nausea, vomiting, fatigue, somnolence, slurred speech, and dyspnea. Laboratory studies showed ALT 213 U/L (0–40), AST 252 U/L (0–37), total bilirubin 4.5 mg/dL (0.0–1.2), direct bilirubin 4.0 mg/dL (0.0–0.3), ALP 535 U/L (39–117), INR 1.3 (0.9–1.1), troponin T 67 ng/L (0–9), creatinine 2.70 mg/dL (0.5–1.5), leukocytosis, and lactatemia. She was treated empirically with broad-spectrum antibiotics and IV fluids for presumed sepsis; immune‐related toxicity was also high on the differential.

Electrocardiogram demonstrated normal sinus rhythm with anterior Q waves. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed an ejection fraction of 61% without wall motion abnormalities. Right upper quadrant ultrasound revealed hepatomegaly with heterogeneous increased echotexture suggestive of fatty infiltration and cholelithiasis but no focal lesions or biliary obstruction. Renal function and lactate normalized with fluids, but liver tests worsened. On hospital day 3, she received IV methylprednisolone 80 mg daily for presumed autoimmune hepatitis and possible autoimmune myocarditis and was transferred to our center. Viral and autoimmune hepatitis panels were unremarkable. On hospital day 4, she developed a nonpruritic eruption on the chest, back, and arms. Punch biopsy showed interface dermatitis with dyskeratosis and a superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate. By hospital day 5, steroids were escalated to pulse dose (1 g/day).

A 44-year-old man presented with several months of hip pain, inability to bear weight on his lower limbs, and right shoulder pain. He had no history of trauma or systemic symptoms but had been treated for presumed multiple sclerosis for more than 5 years. The pain did not respond to NSAIDs or other analgesics. On examination, there was muscle weakness and lower limb claudication. A transrectal prostate examination revealed an asymmetrically enlarged prostate. The PSA level was 258.3 ng/mL (normal, 0–4 ng/mL). Given his age, he was initially diagnosed with acute prostatitis and given antibiotics for 2 weeks. Three weeks later, his symptoms persisted and PSA had risen to 435.1 ng/mL. A whole-body bone scan showed multiple focal areas of increased uptake in the right clavicle and shoulder, right scapula, sternum, several ribs, pelvic bones, femur, many vertebral bodies, and skull. The differential diagnoses included metastatic cancer and multiple myeloma. Prostate ultrasonography showed an enlarged gland of 45 mL. Laboratory tests revealed an elevated alkaline phosphatase level (146 U/L; normal, 30–120 U/L) with normal calcium, phosphorus, 25(OH) vitamin D₃, and parathyroid hormone levels, effectively excluding primary bone disease.

A 68-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of progressive left nasal obstruction without hyposmia, dysgeusia, or epistaxis. He had no history of smoking, allergies, atopy, or prior sinonasal disease. On examination, left nasal airflow was severely reduced. Anterior rhinoscopy revealed a large, fleshy, non-papillomatous, non-vascular tumour in the left nasal cavity. Nasendoscopy showed a solid, polypoidal mass filling the inferior aspect of the left nasal passage and occluding the posterior choana; it prolapsed into the postnasal space without bleeding on contact. The right nasal cavity and the remainder of the upper airway appeared normal. There was no otitis media, lymphadenopathy, or other head and neck findings. 
Non-contrast CT of the sinuses with a bone algorithm demonstrated a large polypoid mass in the left nasopharyngeal space obstructing the posterior choanae, with evidence of intralesional calcification.

A 27-year-old woman presented with atypical chest pain that had worsened over recent weeks. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. An electrocardiogram and serial troponin assays were not suggestive of acute coronary syndrome. Contrast-enhanced chest CT angiography excluded pulmonary embolism and aortic dissection. Transthoracic echocardiography showed marked interventricular septal hypertrophy (24 mm) without left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. A 24-hour Holter monitor demonstrated sinus rhythm with normal atrioventricular conduction and a normal corrected QT interval.

Cardiac MRI revealed a well-circumscribed mass in the interventricular septum measuring 42 × 32 × 50 mm, bulging into the right ventricle within an overall thickened septum. On MRI, the lesion was isointense on T1 with a hypointense central core; on T2-STIR it was inhomogeneous and slightly hypointense; early gadolinium enhancement was inhomogeneous, with intralesional late enhancement. To distinguish tumoural phenocopies from hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, an ^18F-FDG PET scan was performed, showing focal uptake in the septum (SUV 7.9). A percutaneous biopsy of the mass was non-diagnostic. Coronary angiography performed preoperatively showed myocardial bridging with a marked “milking” effect in the mid-left anterior descending artery and its first septal branch.

A 52-year-old North African woman presented with recent-onset left flank pain and a palpable, tender mass in the left flank and iliac fossa with posterior dorsal extension. She had no fever, vomiting, urinary symptoms, or gynecologic complaints. Her medical history was unremarkable except for two cesarean deliveries and chronic constipation for 6 months. On examination, the mass had regular margins and was tender on deep palpation; there was no jaundice and no neurologic deficits.

Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 7000/mm3, hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL, normal platelets, C-reactive protein 11 mg/L, normal liver and kidney function, and normal levels of CA-125 and carcinoembryonic antigen. 

Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a large left-sided heterogeneous abdominopelvic mass with mass effect on the left kidney; Doppler imaging suggested it was nonvascularized. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a well-circumscribed, heterogeneous, hypervascular mass measuring 16 × 17 × 22 cm with vascular supply appearing to arise exclusively from the left renal artery, causing mass effect on adjacent organs but with patent renal vein and inferior vena cava. 

Selective renal angiography confirmed that all tumor vessels originated from the left renal artery.

A 13-year-old boy with no past medical history presented with a 2-day history of left-sided epistaxis. The bleeding episodes occurred intermittently and resolved spontaneously after 5–10 minutes without pressure. He also reported on-and-off left nasal obstruction but denied dizziness, loss of consciousness, or choking. On examination he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable, with no cyanosis or cervical lymphadenopathy. Nasal speculum examination revealed a left intranasal mass obstructing the cavity. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 141 g/L, white blood cell count 7.30 K/μL, INR 1.02, prothrombin time 11.4 s, and partial thromboplastin time 28.3 s. A computed tomography scan of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated an enhancing lesion in the left nasal cavity. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed an oval mass filling the anterior nasal cavity, measuring approximately 3 × 1.1 × 2.5 cm (anteroposterior × transverse × craniocaudal) with high signal intensity on T2-weighted images.

A 1-year-old girl was admitted for progressive abdominal distension and irritability. She had no other symptoms, and her developmental milestones were appropriate for age. On examination, she was active and playful, with a height of 70 cm and weight of 6.5 kg. Abdominal palpation revealed hepatomegaly, with the liver edge 6 cm below the right costal margin.

Laboratory studies showed:
- Hemoglobin 8 g/dL (11.5–15.5 g/dL)
- White blood cell count 12 400/μL (4500–11 000/μL)
- Platelet count 720 × 10^3/μL (150–450 × 10^3/μL)
- AST 73 U/L (10–34 U/L), ALT 20 U/L (7–56 U/L), ALP 394 U/L (53–128 U/L), GGT 260 U/L (0–51 U/L)
- Total bilirubin, albumin, PT, and INR were within normal limits.
- Serum alpha-fetoprotein was 160 000 ng/dL (normal < 10 ng/dL).

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a well-defined hypodense lesion spanning segments I, IV, V, and VII of the liver, containing punctate calcifications and without vascular invasion. Small nodular lesions were noted in the apical segment of the left lower lobe and the posterior segment of the right lower lobe.

An ultrasound-guided biopsy of the liver lesion showed scattered islands of abnormal hepatocytes and haphazardly arranged bile duct structures in a myxoid stroma, suggesting a mesenchymal hamartoma.

A 33-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 3-month history of progressively enlarging neck swelling, fever, and dyspnea. He was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Examination revealed multiple skin lesions and bilateral cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy; the largest left cervical node measured 4 × 6 cm. Systemic examination was otherwise unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed a large infiltrative, heterogeneously enhancing mass in the superior, anterior, and middle mediastinum encasing the trachea, superior vena cava, brachiocephalic veins, pulmonary trunk, and veins. A punch biopsy of a skin lesion showed only inflammatory changes. Excisional biopsy of the left cervical lymph node revealed effaced architecture with sheets of atypical lymphoid cells with pleomorphic nuclei and prominent nucleoli. Immunohistochemical staining showed leukocyte common antigen positivity, CD20 negativity, and positivity for CD79a and PAX5.

A 28-year-old woman, 9 weeks pregnant, presented with a 3-month history of a painful swelling in the left mandibular angle region. Extraction of the left second and third molars one month earlier provided no relief. She reported progressive enlargement of the mass and difficulty eating. On examination, there was a bony hard, tender swelling over the left mandibular angle and tender, mobile left submandibular lymph nodes. Intraorally, the extraction socket had a thin fibrinous pseudomembrane and the buccal vestibule was obliterated; the mucosa appeared normal. An orthopantomogram demonstrated a poorly defined radiolucency in the ramus and angle of the mandible with radially oriented radiopaque streaks giving a “sunburst” appearance. With obstetrician approval, an incisional biopsy through the unhealed socket and fine-needle aspiration were performed. Cytologic smears showed small round cells singly and in clusters, with moderate anisonucleosis, scant cytoplasm, and finely granular chromatin without nucleoli. A provisional diagnosis of a small round cell tumor of bone was made.

A 39-year-old man presented with a 15-day history of hematuria and a sensation of heaviness in the right flank. On physical examination, a soft, palpable mass was noted in the right hypochondrium. Ultrasonography of the abdomen revealed an irregular cystic lesion measuring approximately 25 × 30 mm in the lower pole of the right kidney, with internal echoes. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen demonstrated a significantly enhancing mass in the lower pole of the right kidney, with central areas of necrosis and a thrombus in the right renal vein. Based on these clinical and radiologic findings, a diagnosis of right-sided renal cell carcinoma was made, and the patient underwent right radical nephrectomy with thrombectomy.

An 11-month-old girl was referred for a one-month history of watery diarrhea (7–8 episodes per day) without blood or mucus, associated with malnutrition and marked abdominal distension. There was no vomiting or fever. She was born at 38 weeks’ gestation, with normal early growth and development. At 10 months of age, diarrhea began and persisted despite empirical outpatient trials, including a protein-hydrolysate, lactose-free formula (for presumed cow’s milk allergy) and antiparasitic therapy for unproven giardiasis. On admission, her weight was 8 kg (25th percentile), length 70 cm (5th percentile), heart rate 85/min, and blood pressure 80/55 mmHg. Examination revealed facial flushing and a distended abdomen without palpable masses. Laboratory tests showed mild metabolic acidosis and hypokalemia; blood counts and biochemistry were otherwise normal. Infectious enterocolitis, intestinal parasitosis, celiac disease, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency/mucoviscidosis, and cow’s milk protein allergy were excluded. Abdominal radiography showed dilated bowel loops with air-fluid levels. Sonography and CT scan identified a 6×4 cm calcified mass anterior to the L1–L4 spine and aorta, separate from the pancreas. Endocrine evaluation revealed VIP 180 pmol/L (normal ≤30), 24-hour urinary homovanillic acid and vanillylmandelic acid within normal limits, and elevated neuron-specific enolase.

A 65-year-old man with hypothyroidism and restless-leg syndrome and a 2-year history of stage 4 prostate adenocarcinoma (Gleason score 9) metastatic to bone and liver, treated with leuprolide, abiraterone, cabazitaxel, radium-223, and enzalutamide, presented with 2 weeks of progressive generalized weakness and 1 week of nonbilious, nonbloody vomiting. He denied fever, cough, abdominal pain, dysuria, or focal neurologic symptoms. On admission, vital signs were normal. Physical examination, including a complete neurologic assessment, was unremarkable with intact cranial nerves and no deficits; he was not cachectic. Laboratory studies showed white blood cell count 2.5 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL, corrected calcium 6.6 mg/dL, potassium 3.1 mmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 221 U/L, prostate-specific antigen 182 ng/mL, and ferritin 1336 ng/mL. Brain MRI with gadolinium demonstrated bilateral temporal lobe edema, dural thickening and enhancement of the middle cranial fossae extending to both orbital apices and the right cavernous sinus, and leptomeningeal enhancement in the posterior fossa. Contrast CT of the head showed irregular nodular dural thickening and enhancement in the right temporal region with adjacent temporal and frontal lobe edema. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed multiple sclerotic lesions in the pelvis, spinal vertebrae, and ribs, and several 1–2 cm hepatic masses consistent with metastatic disease.

A 23-year-old immunocompetent Syrian man presented with rapidly enlarging swellings on his nose and left lower jaw that appeared immediately after suture removal from facial lacerations sustained in a road-traffic accident. On examination, there were two firm, painless, erythematous, ulcerated, lobular lesions measuring 2 cm × 2 cm on the nasal dorsum and 10 cm × 2 cm along the left mandibular region. He had no history of diabetes, HIV infection, relevant familial disorders, or use of systemic medications.

A 68-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of abdominal fullness and discomfort and a 2-week history of reduced appetite. He had hypertension managed with amlodipine and no history of liver disease. On examination, he had minimal right upper quadrant tenderness without rebound or guarding. Laboratory testing showed a GGT of 264 U/L (normal 11–49 U/L), elevated ALP, SGOT, and SGPT, and a borderline AFP of 17.5 ng/mL (normal 0–15 ng/mL). Abdominal ultrasound revealed mildly altered hepatic echotexture and a non-obstructive right renal calculus. A triphasic contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated an irregular exophytic lesion with solid and cystic components in segment III of the left hepatic lobe measuring 76 × 64 × 93 mm; the lesion showed minimal heterogeneous arterial enhancement with progressive enhancement in the portal and venous phases and exerted mass effect on the stomach. To exclude an extrahepatic primary malignancy, upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy, a Technetium-99 m bone scan, and a chest CT scan were performed and revealed no evidence of primary tumor or metastases. Given the concern for a neoplastic lesion, a left lateral hepatectomy was performed without preoperative biopsy to avoid seeding.

A 45‐year‐old woman presented with a 6‐month history of a progressively enlarging ulcerated mass in her right breast. She reported no prior breast trauma, radiation exposure, or family history of breast cancer. On examination, there was a large, lobulated, ulcerated mass replacing the right breast. Her hemoglobin level was 7.5 g/dL. Chest radiography and abdominal imaging showed no abnormalities. Fine‐needle aspiration cytology of the mass was reported as suggestive of carcinoma of the breast. The patient underwent a modified radical mastectomy. The surgical specimen measured 24 × 15 × 13 cm, with a 14 × 9 × 6 cm skin flap. On the skin surface, there was a large gray‐white lobulated ulcerated growth. On serial sectioning, an ill‐defined gray‐white mass measuring 18 × 15 × 12 cm was seen, extending to within 0.8 cm of the resection margin; the cut surface was solid with areas of necrosis and cystic change. Ten axillary lymph nodes were isolated and appeared grossly uninvolved.

A 71-year-old woman with obesity, insulin-dependent diabetes, long-standing hypertension, and chronic kidney disease on peritoneal dialysis was brought to the emergency department for intense epigastric abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. On examination she was drowsy, hypertensive, tachycardic, and noted to have scleral jaundice and signs of peritoneal irritation. She denied any history of gastrointestinal bleeding. 

Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 17,000/μL, total bilirubin 3.8 mg/dL (direct 2.63 mg/dL), alkaline phosphatase 639 U/L, ALT 185 U/L, AST 311 U/L, and GGT 425 U/L. 

Right upper-quadrant ultrasound showed an enlarged gallbladder (113 × 35 × 39 mm) containing a 13-mm stone in the neck and echogenic material suggestive of acute cholecystitis. 

Because of clinical instability and signs of biliary obstruction, an emergency open cholecystectomy was performed. During surgery, the gallbladder contained abundant clots and a single stone in the neck.

A 70-year-old man of Indian origin presented with a 3-month history of pain, limited mobility, and swelling over the anterior aspect of the right leg above the ankle. He reported a history of a recurrent ulcer at the same site. He denied any trauma, fever, sensory loss, comorbid illness, or gastrointestinal or respiratory symptoms. 

On examination, there was a well-demarcated erythematous firm lesion over the anterior lower leg with peripheral nodular areas and accompanying lymphedema of the distal foot. No other cutaneous or oral lesions were found on full‐body examination. He had no history of similar lesions, and tests confirmed he was not immunocompromised and had no sexually transmitted infections.

Plain radiographs of the right leg showed a lobulated soft-tissue swelling in the anterior lower one-third of the leg with a few calcific areas and periosteal reaction of adjacent bone. CT imaging demonstrated soft-tissue edema, heterogeneous linear densities, faint calcifications within the lesion, and a short segment of thick unicortical periosteal reaction of the tibia. MRI confirmed these findings and revealed an intramuscular lesion that was iso- to hypo-intense on T1‐weighted images, hyperintense on T2‐weighted images, with surrounding perilesional edema and no bone marrow involvement.

A 16-year-old girl with a known history of multiple cartilaginous exostoses presented with a 1-year history of progressively worsening pain on the inferior aspect of her right heel. Over the past few months she noted a palpable mass at the site. There was no antecedent trauma. She experienced significant discomfort with walking and could not participate in sports. She had taken non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs without relief. She denied fever or systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a firm, immobile, tender mass measuring approximately 2 × 1.5 cm on the posterolateral heel. Ankle range of motion was normal. Plain radiographs of the foot (AP, lateral, and oblique views) revealed a 2 × 1.5 × 1 cm pedunculated bone lesion arising from the posterolateral aspect of the calcaneus, with no evidence of fracture.

A 74-year-old woman was referred to the emergency unit for acute dyspnoea on a background of a 1-month history of progressive globus sensation. On admission, arterial blood gas analysis showed pH 7.35, PaCO₂ 82.9 mmHg, and PaO₂ 52 mmHg. Chest radiography was unremarkable. Her medical history included excision of a cutaneous melanoma (no evidence of disease), carotid thromboendoarterectomy, resection of a CNS meningioma with ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement, and a traumatic vocal-cord lesion causing mild dysphonia after prior intubation. Flexible laryngoscopy revealed a smooth, pedunculated mass on the left aryepiglottic fold extending into the glottic space with near-complete airway obstruction. No cervical lymphadenopathy was palpable. She underwent an emergency tracheostomy and incisional biopsy, which demonstrated nonspecific fibrous submucosal tissue. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed a 3.5 × 3 × 2.8 cm round, heterogeneously enhancing mass extending from the left aryepiglottic fold to the false vocal cord.

A 22-month-old boy was brought for evaluation of a painless swelling in his left hand that had been noticed by his parents 4 months earlier and gradually increased in size. The lesion caused difficulty in grasping objects and appeared as a 40 × 30 mm mass predominantly in the palmar aspect, widening the second and third web space and extending dorsally to the proximal phalanx of the second digit. The overlying skin was normal. On palpation, the mass was firm, nonmobile, and nonpulsatile. 

Plain radiographs of the hand showed a lobulated, homogeneous, smoothly outlined soft-tissue mass widening the space between the second and third metacarpals and phalanges, with normal underlying bone. High-resolution ultrasound of the palmar subcutaneous tissues demonstrated a well-defined, heterogenous, predominantly echogenic, lobulated mass measuring approximately 40 × 25 mm, with intervening linear hypoechoic areas. The deeper aspect abutted but did not invade the flexor tendons or muscles. Color Doppler imaging revealed minimal internal vascularity, with splaying of the adjacent digital arteries. 

Based on the child’s age, the insidious, slow-growing, painless nature of the lesion, and the fat-containing appearance with minor mesenchymal components, a benign adipocytic tumor was suspected. Differential diagnoses included lipoma, lipoblastoma, and fibrous hamartoma of infancy. A biopsy was planned to establish a definitive diagnosis.

A 62-year-old woman with a 20-year history of non-toxic multinodular goiter presented for surgical management of a slowly enlarging thyroid mass. She denied dysphagia, dyspnea, or dysphonia. Six years earlier, she had undergone a left nephrectomy for clear cell renal carcinoma. On examination, there was a non-tender subhyoid swelling with multiple palpable rounded nodules. Preoperative neck ultrasound showed an enlarged thyroid gland with a retrosternal left lobe. The entire left lobe was occupied by an isoechoic, vascularized macronodule measuring 53 mm. No suspicious central or lateral cervical lymph nodes were identified. Given the size, vascularity, and retrosternal extension of the lesion, fine-needle aspiration cytology was deferred, and a total thyroidectomy was performed. The patient had an uneventful postoperative course and was discharged on postoperative day two.

A 37-year-old woman with no significant medical history, taking desogestrel/ethinylestradiol oral contraception, was referred for fatigue on moderate exertion and anemia noted on routine laboratory testing. Vital signs were normal. On examination she appeared pale but was hemodynamically stable; there was no lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or stigmata of chronic liver disease. Laboratory evaluation showed hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL, MCV 67.7 fl, serum iron 17.6 µg/dL, ferritin 17 ng/mL, normal transaminases, alkaline phosphatase 250 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 91 U/L, normal bilirubin, CRP 4.78 mg/dL, and ESR 81 mm/h. Menstrual blood loss was normal, diet was unrestricted, and investigations for GI blood loss (upper endoscopy and colonoscopy) were unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound and CT scan revealed hepatomegaly with multiple focal solid lesions: a 12.5×12.3×6 cm mass abutting the gastric wall, a 6 cm lesion in segment VI, and a 2 cm lesion in segment VIII. Additional tests showed negative CEA, α-fetoprotein, and CA 19-9; β2-microglobulin 2.48 mg/L; and negative viral hepatitis serologies.

An 18-year-old woman presented with a one-week history of a palpable left breast lump. Her past medical history was significant for biphenotypic acute lymphoblastic leukemia at age 7, treated to complete remission, and an anal mass diagnosed one year earlier as rhabdomyosarcoma treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy. On examination, the left breast contained a firm, round, nontender 3×3 cm mass without overlying skin changes; the right breast and both axillae were normal.  
Breast ultrasonography revealed a 2.3 cm circumscribed oval hyperechoic mass with a central hypoechoic portion. Core-needle biopsy of the breast lesion was consistent with rhabdomyosarcoma.  
Staging studies including chest, abdominal, and pelvic CT scans and 18F-FDG PET/CT showed intense FDG uptake in the left breast mass and in the retrocrural space at the level of the L1 vertebra, with no other sites of disease.

A 41-year-old man presented with a one-month history of right nasal obstruction. He had no B symptoms and an excellent performance status. Physical examination was unremarkable except for a firm mass in the right nasal fossa. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, metabolic panel, liver function tests, and LDH level, were within normal limits. Serum protein electrophoresis did not show a monoclonal spike. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head, neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed an isolated mass in the right nasal fossa and no other lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. An incisional biopsy of the nasal lesion showed sheets of large neoplastic cells with plasmablastic morphology—round nuclei, dispersed chromatin, a single central nucleolus, and moderate amphophilic cytoplasm—effacing normal architecture. Bone marrow biopsy was negative for involvement. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated that the tumor cells were positive for CD45, MUM1, EMA, and ALK (granular cytoplasmic pattern), and negative for CD4, CD20, and CD30. Tests for Epstein-Barr virus (LMP-1) and human herpesvirus 8 were negative.

A 78-year-old right-handed man presented with a 7-year history of soft-tissue swelling on his right wrist, recently increasing in size and accompanied by new tingling and numbness in the median-nerve distribution and progressive functional impairment. He had longstanding bilateral wrist arthritis managed with oral analgesics and intermittent steroid injections. Serial wrist radiographs over the years demonstrated bilateral radiocarpal, distal radioulnar, scapho-trapezium-trapezoid, carpo-metacarpal, and metacarpophalangeal joint degeneration with joint-space narrowing, large subarticular cysts, and chondrocalcinosis at the triangular fibrocartilage complex; these were interpreted as features of crystal arthropathy, but ultrasound-guided aspiration was negative for crystals. On examination, there was loss of wrist motion, firm nodular lumps over the radial aspect of the right wrist and triangular fibrocartilage complex, negative squeeze test, and mild tenderness at the right second metacarpophalangeal joint without warmth or erythema. Recent radiographs showed enlarging periarticular soft-tissue swelling with internal mineralization and progressive bone erosions. MRI demonstrated profuse synovial proliferation forming large periarticular soft-tissue masses. Given the neurological symptoms and functional compromise, the patient was referred for median-nerve decompression, debulking of the presumed tophaceous material, and biopsy.

A 59-year-old man was referred with right upper chest pain, chronic cough, and weight loss. He had no history of tuberculosis, diabetes, hypertension, malignancy, or dyspnea, and no family history of similar disease. Vital signs were normal except for a respiratory rate of 26 breaths per minute. 

Initial chest radiography showed fibrosis in the right upper lobe. GeneXpert MTB/RIF testing was negative. Six months later, contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed fibro-consolidation and bronchiectasis in the apical segment of the right upper lobe and right infraclavicular lymphadenopathy; HIV testing was negative. 

Because of local TB endemicity and his symptoms, a 6-month anti-TB regimen was initiated despite the negative GeneXpert. After 2 months, a sputum AFB smear was negative; at 5 months, repeat GeneXpert remained negative. 

At the end of therapy, chest X-ray and CT showed increased opacity in the right upper lobe, thickening of the right upper pleura, osteolytic lesions of the second and third right ribs, and an enlarging heterogeneously enhancing mass in the right upper lobe. His cough and dyspnea persisted, and he developed severe right shoulder pain radiating into the arm, unrelieved by analgesics.

A 77-year-old man presented with a right scrotal swelling that he had first noticed several months earlier. He denied pain, discomfort, trauma, prior scrotal surgery, or exposure to asbestos. On examination, the right hemiscrotum was tense but non-tender, and the clinical findings were consistent with a hydrocele. Scrotal ultrasonography revealed a 7–8 cm multiloculated fluid collection in the right tunica vaginalis. After review, the patient underwent surgical exploration and complete excision of the scrotal mass; the specimen consisted of a tense, multicystic lesion, which was submitted for histopathological evaluation.

A 54-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of progressive right-sided nasal obstruction and mild epistaxis. She denied smoking, toxic exposures, and had no family history of neoplasms. On nasofibroscopy, there was an irregular vascular lesion occupying most of the right nasal cavity. A computed tomography scan showed a heterogeneous, contrast-enhancing mass displacing the nasal septum toward the left side. Under endoscopic guidance, the lesion arising from the nasal septum was completely resected; the ipsilateral septal mucosa and cartilage were removed as surgical margins, and the contralateral mucosa was preserved. The resected specimen consisted of multiple brown tissue fragments measuring 6.0 × 3.0 × 1.0 cm in aggregate, which were submitted for pathological examination.

A 41-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of right iliac fossa abdominal pain. He was subpyretic on admission. On examination, there was slight tenderness and a palpable mass in the right iliac fossa and flank without peritoneal signs; bowel sounds were present. Laboratory studies showed mildly elevated C-reactive protein (2.10 mg/dL) and fibrinogen (471 mg/dL) without leukocytosis or other abnormalities.  
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed an oval 72 mm mass with hyperechoic septa and hypoechoic–anechoic areas, with two adjacent smaller similar areas; this was initially interpreted as saccate peritonitis complicating acute appendicitis.  
Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a 61×42 mm fluid-over-fluid–containing oval mass contiguous with the cecal fundus, with fluid effusion in the pouch of Douglas and along the right parietocolic recess to the hepatic flexure; small perilesional lymph nodes were noted.  
Ultrasound-guided aspiration yielded cloudy dark fluid; cytologic, chemical, and culture studies showed an exudative inflammatory effusion without significant cytological alteration.

A 45-year-old Japanese man presented with sudden, severe headache and marked hypertension. Two days earlier, he had received an intra-articular injection of betamethasone (2 mg) into his right elbow for pain. On the morning of admission, he noted general fatigue; two hours later, he developed the headache and was brought by ambulance. 

His history was notable only for hypertension diagnosed at age 44 years, controlled with lisinopril 10 mg daily. He had no episodic headaches. He smoked 20 cigarettes per day and drank 50–100 g of alcohol daily. There was no family history of diabetes or endocrine tumors.

On examination, blood pressure was 240/126 mmHg, pulse 120 beats/minute, temperature 37.6 °C, and respiratory rate 25 breaths/minute. He was diaphoretic and tachycardic; otherwise, the physical and neurologic exams were unremarkable. 

Because of the headache and severe hypertension, subarachnoid hemorrhage was suspected. Head CT and MRI were normal, and lumbar puncture revealed clear cerebrospinal fluid. 

Laboratory tests showed:  
•  WBC 19,600/μL, Hgb 16.1 g/dL, platelets 129,000/μL  
•  Arterial blood gas (on 6 L/min O₂): pH 7.21, PaCO₂ 30.2 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 11.8 mmol/L, lactate 11.75 mmol/L, anion gap 26.2 mEq/L  
•  Plasma glucose 523 mg/dL, HbA1c 5.7%  
•  Total ketone bodies 289 μmol/L (acetoacetic acid 54, 3-hydroxybutyric acid 235)  
•  Insulin 7.8 μU/mL, C-peptide 2.64 ng/mL, GAD antibody < 0.5 U/mL  

Based on the severe hyperglycemia, high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, and normal HbA1c level, diabetic ketoacidosis caused by fulminant type 1 diabetes mellitus was initially suspected.

A 17-year-old male high-school wrestler presented with a six-month history of right knee pain. He reported that the pain began after landing directly on his knee during a match. The pain was located on the anterior medial aspect of the knee, occurred only with kneeling during wrestling activities, and was described as severe and burning, sometimes accompanied by a shocking, shooting sensation over the affected area without radiation. He denied locking, catching, giving way, and had no pain with walking, running, or at rest. 

On initial evaluation by an outside surgeon, a small extra-articular mass at the medial border of the patella was palpated and presumed to be a fibroma within the prepatellar bursa. Plain radiographs were unremarkable. The patient underwent prepatellar bursa resection and excision of the fibroma; pathology showed dense fibrosis and fibroadipose tissue with mild inflammation. After three months with no improvement, a second surgeon obtained an MRI, which demonstrated mild subcutaneous edema anterior to the knee (thought to be postsurgical) and a tibial tubercle non-united ossicle consistent with prior Osgood-Schlatter disease; no other abnormalities were noted. A diagnostic arthroscopy revealed an 8 mm × 9 mm chondral lesion on the medial femoral condyle, and a chondroplasty was performed; again, there was no relief after 10 weeks.

At presentation to our clinic, a landmark-guided intra-articular injection of lidocaine and ropivacaine provided no relief. He then tried topical diclofenac gel and lidocaine patches for one month without change. Physical examination without kneeling was benign. When asked to kneel, he immediately noted burning pain; palpation with the knee flexed beyond 90° localized the pain to a small, subtle, fibrous-like band medial to the patella. A landmark-guided injection of lidocaine and triamcinolone into that band produced no significant relief.

A 72-year-old man was referred for progressive neurological symptoms, visual disturbances, and necrosis of distal body parts over 6 months. Two weeks after lithotripsy for a ureteral stone, he developed paresthesia and sensory loss in his lower limbs, predominantly the right leg. Within 3 months, he exhibited necrosis of fingers, toes, areas of the face (lips, nose, ears), and glans penis, accompanied by pain and weakness that left him bedridden, intermittent blurred vision, low-grade fevers without chills, and a 15-kg weight loss. Physical examination showed ecchymoses, purpura, pale conjunctivae, cotton-wool spots on retinal exam, hepatosplenomegaly, and coalescing patchy necrotic skin lesions.  
Laboratory studies revealed low albumin with elevated α1, α2, and γ fractions on serum protein electrophoresis; serum immunofixation demonstrated a dense IgM band; the serum IgM concentration was 3.0 g/dL; and blood viscosity was 10 centipoise (normal <1.8). Peripheral‐blood flow cytometry showed approximately 30% lymphoid cells (predominantly mature T cells with an inverted CD4/CD8 ratio), the remainder B cells, and 3% NK cells. A bone marrow aspirate yielded a diluted smear with numerous plasma cells.

A 38-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with one week of subjective fever, myalgias, profuse sweating, generalized body pain, decreased appetite, weight loss, inguinal lymphadenopathy, and blurred vision in both eyes. He denied cough, hemoptysis, diarrhea, urinary symptoms, or rash.  
On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/800 in the right eye and 20/200 in the left. Pupils were round and reactive without an afferent pupillary defect. Intraocular pressures and the anterior segment examination were normal. Fundus examination revealed bilateral serous detachments of the macula. Optical coherence tomography confirmed subretinal fluid in both eyes. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated multiple punctate hyperfluorescent leaks at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium in both eyes.  
CT of the abdomen showed inguinal lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, peritoneal thickening, and ascites. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis with lymphocytosis, thrombocytopenia, elevated uric acid, and high lactate dehydrogenase levels. Serologic testing returned positive for Epstein–Barr virus, herpes simplex virus, hepatitis B core antibody, and interferon-γ release assay; CT of the chest showed no evidence of active tuberculosis. Further testing was negative for HIV RNA, monospot test, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C, syphilis, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, Lyme serology, and angiotensin-converting enzyme. Blood cultures were sterile, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed no malignant cells.

A 40-year-old man presented with intermittent lower left back pain for two years, accompanied by numbness and tingling from the left lowest rib to the upper left thigh. The pain was worse with standing or walking and relieved by rest, and had progressed over the past year to impair daily activities. He previously underwent a lumbar laminectomy, which partially relieved his symptoms, but he continued to have pain around the left lowest rib. He was referred for evaluation of a suspected pathological fracture of a thoracic vertebra.

On examination, there was no visible spinal deformity or mass. Mild tenderness was present over the thoracic spine, and spinal range of motion was limited by pain. Motor and sensory examinations were intact. His medical history was notable for HIV infection, managed with antiretroviral therapy.

Spinal radiography showed thoracic kyphosis (Cobb angle 18.8°), mild lateral deviation, and decreased height of the T9 vertebral body. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the thoracic spine revealed a solid lesion centered in the T9 vertebral body, extending into the left pedicle, costovertebral junction, and posterior left ribs, with obliteration of the T9–T10 neural foramen. Additional lesions were noted at T7 and in the soft tissues at T4.

A 4½-year-old boy was referred for bilateral undescended testes and short stature. He was born at term with a birth weight of 2.5 kg and had delayed motor and mental milestones. His parents noted that he remained shorter than peers (his 2-year-younger sister is taller). There was no history of systemic disease, neonatal seizures, prolonged jaundice, or signs of raised intracranial pressure. On examination, his height was 84 cm (<3rd percentile; standard deviation score –4), upper-to-lower segment ratio 0.9, weight 13 kg, and head circumference 51 cm. He had frontal bossing, doll-like facies, central obesity, and a micropenis (stretched penile length 2 cm). Both gonads were palpable in the suprascrotal region with a poorly developed empty scrotal sac. Vitals and the remainder of the systemic examination were normal. Laboratory studies showed: hemoglobin 13.6 g/dl (11–15), total lymphocyte count 5600/mm^3 (4–11 000), ESR 15 mm/h (5–20), random blood glucose 94 mg/dl (90–130), creatinine 0.8 mg/dl (0.6–1.5), free T4 0.9 ng/ml (0.93–1.7), TSH 7.27 mIU/ml (0.3–5.5), bone age 1 year, basal cortisol 13.76 μg/dl (8–20), FSH 0.63 mIU/ml (1.5–10.2), LH 0.1 mIU/ml (1.9–12), basal testosterone 0.025 ng/ml (3–6.5), stimulated testosterone after hCG 0.68 ng/ml (suggestive of normally functioning testes), and undetectable IGF-1. Scrotal ultrasound confirmed bilateral suprascrotal testes. Brain MRI demonstrated a 3.8 × 3.6 cm suprasellar cystic lesion compressing the pituitary gland; the lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images.

A 62-year-old man, lifelong non-smoker with type II diabetes mellitus and a remote history of sarcoidosis, presented with a 5-month history of an enlarging right neck mass associated with neck pain, dysphagia, and dysphonia. Physical examination and contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a large base-of-tongue mass crossing the midline into the suprahyoid epiglottis and a 4.6 × 3.4 cm necrotic confluence of lymph nodes in right level IIA and IIB. Biopsy confirmed non-keratinizing, p16-positive squamous cell carcinoma of the oropharynx. PET/CT demonstrated bilateral level III lymphadenopathy without evidence of distant metastases. The patient was staged as cT4aN2c HPV-OSCC and received definitive chemoradiation comprising 70 Gy in 35 fractions to the primary and involved nodes (56 Gy to uninvolved nodes) with concurrent weekly cetuximab.  

Five weeks post-treatment, contrast-enhanced CT showed resolution of all disease except a residual 2 cm lymph node in right level II. Two months after finishing therapy, he developed binocular vertical diplopia. Examination revealed a new pupil-sparing left cranial nerve III palsy that progressed over 1.5 weeks to include a right cranial nerve VI palsy. Electromyography showed no evidence of myasthenia gravis or myopathy. MRI of the sella disclosed two separate enhancing lesions in the cavernous sinuses—one on the left encasing the internal carotid artery with extension into the sella, and one on the right involving the cavernous sinus and clivus. PET/CT confirmed resolution of the primary and cervical nodes but demonstrated intense focal FDG uptake in both cavernous sinus lesions and a new 1 cm hypodense lesion in segment 4A of the liver.

A 15-year-old girl presented with a pigmented lesion on the lateral aspect of her left arm for 1 year, which had been slowly enlarging and itchy for the past 2 months. On examination, there was an 8 mm brown-blue, irregular but well-defined macule with black-brown dots at the periphery. Dermoscopic evaluation showed a homogenous black-brown lesion composed of structureless areas, peripheral streaks, and satellite gray-blue lesions.

A 30-year-old African American woman presented with three weeks of progressive dyspnea, dysphagia, difficulty managing oral secretions, and decreased oral intake. Her family noted a left mandibular swelling for one month that had been treated presumptively as an odontogenic infection with amoxicillin-clavulanate for seven days without improvement. On examination, she required 4 L of oxygen by nasal cannula and could not lie flat. Intraorally, there was a large expansile ulcerative mass arising from the left posterior mandible that completely obliterated the oropharynx. An awake tracheostomy, direct laryngoscopy, and incisional biopsy were performed. Contrast-enhanced CT of the maxillofacial region and neck revealed a massive expansile lesion originating from the left posterior mandibular body invading the posterior pharyngeal wall with complete oropharyngeal obliteration and a suspicious enlarged level 1B lymph node. 

Histologic examination of multiple soft-tissue fragments showed a hypercellular proliferation of stellate spindle cells in a myxoid background, with surface ulceration, extensive necrosis, and mitotic activity of 10 per 10 high-power fields. No epithelial component was identified.

A 47-year-old woman presented with a 1-day history of vague, generalized abdominal pain that later localized to the right lower quadrant. Ten years earlier she had undergone total abdominal hysterectomy for menorrhagia and had been on estrogen patch hormone-replacement therapy since. On examination, she was afebrile but had localized peritonism in the right and upper central abdomen. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 12.1×10^9/L and a C-reactive protein level of 16 mg/L. Abdominal sonography demonstrated a hypoechoic, ovoid, irregular lesion with a blind end in the region of the hepatic flexure; probe-induced tenderness was noted over the lesion. Given the acute presentation and suspicion of an inflammatory or perforated colonic lesion, she underwent exploratory laparoscopy. At surgery, a firm, irregular omental mass (approximately 2 cm) was identified adjacent to the proximal transverse colon, appearing to extend from the colon; the appendix was normal, the right adnexa appeared normal, and the left adnexa could not be fully visualized owing to adhesions. A necrotic omental nodule (18×15×12 mm) was biopsied. Histologically, the lesion showed extensive hemorrhagic necrosis and residual monomorphic ovoid to spindle-shaped cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. Immunohistochemical staining showed strong positivity for CD10, estrogen receptor, and progesterone receptor, raising the possibility of endometrial stromal sarcoma.

A 49-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of an acute, painless central scotoma in his left eye, associated with a left-sided headache but no metamorphopsia, floaters, flashes, nausea, or vomiting. His medical history was notable only for functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) for left nasal polyps 4 years earlier; there was no recent trauma or ocular surgery. On examination, visual acuity was hand movements in the left eye and 6/9 in the right eye. There was a left relative afferent pupillary defect. Extraocular movements were full; there was no proptosis or globe displacement. Anterior segments were normal. Funduscopy showed a pink left optic disc with a sharp margin and normal cup–disc ratio; the retina and macula were unremarkable. The right eye exam was normal. Automated perimetry revealed a normal right field and generalized depression of the left field with a mean defect of –32.63 dB. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits disclosed a 14.8×12.6 mm discrete nodule at the left orbital apex compressing the superior rectus muscle and the optic nerve; the lesion was hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2, and did not enhance with contrast. There was an incidental right ethmoidal cystic lesion suggestive of a mucocele. There was no intracranial or extraorbital extension or bony erosion. Computed tomography of the paranasal sinuses showed a small bony defect between the lesion and the left sphenoid sinus without clear extension into the sinus. 

Based on the clinical assessment and imaging, a working diagnosis of left compressive optic neuropathy secondary to a discrete orbital apex nodule was made.

A 51-year-old postmenopausal woman, lifelong nonsmoker with no respiratory complaints or known exposures, was referred for evaluation of multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules and cysts noted incidentally on an abdominal CT performed for nephrolithiasis. Physical examination was unremarkable. A dedicated chest CT showed multiple bilateral noncalcified pulmonary nodules and cysts, the largest measuring 1.1 cm in the superior segment of the left lower lobe. Pulmonary-function testing revealed a mild obstructive defect not responsive to bronchodilators, normal lung volumes, and a mildly decreased diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide. Rheumatologic and alpha-1-antitrypsin evaluations were negative. Genetic testing for Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome was negative. Positron-emission tomography showed no avidity in the nodules. Lymphangioleiomyomatosis and malignancy remained on the differential. The patient underwent video-assisted thoracoscopic wedge resection of the left lower lobe. Pathological examination demonstrated a pulmonary hamartoma. Cystic lesions were lined by normal respiratory epithelium, and no malignant component was identified. Immunostains for HMB-45, Melan-A, MITF, HHF-35, and beta-catenin were negative.

A 14-year-old right-handed male presented with a painless swelling on the lateral aspect of his left hand that he and his family first noticed about 4 years earlier when it was pea-sized. The mass had gradually enlarged without preceding trauma, numbness, or limitation of motion. On examination, the swelling over the second metacarpal was firm to hard, minimally tender, not adherent to the skin but fixed to the underlying bone, and measured approximately 4.6 × 2.8 × 1.5 cm.

Plain radiographs of the left hand showed a well-corticated, expansile, lytic lesion originating from the diaphysis of the second metacarpal, involving the medullary cavity, with lateral exophytic growth into the soft tissue, sclerotic margins, and dense calcifications. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a hypointense T1 and hyperintense T2 expansile lesion with an exophytic component, narrow zone of transition, sclerotic margins, internal areas of calcification, and septations consistent with a chondroid matrix.

Given these findings, the lesion was considered of chondroid etiology, and an incisional biopsy was performed, which suggested a diagnosis of osteochondroma.

A 78-year-old man (173 cm; 100 kg) with coronary artery disease and a recent non–ST-elevation myocardial infarction was scheduled for coronary artery bypass grafting. His medical history included hypertension, atrial fibrillation, congestive heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, gastroesophageal reflux disease, dyslipidemia, prostate carcinoma, and polycythemia vera treated with periodic phlebotomy. Preoperative laboratory values were: hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, white-cell count 15.36 × 10^3/µL, platelet count 769 × 10^3/µL, normal PT/INR, and activated partial thromboplastin time 123 s. He had received a heparin infusion for 7 days, which was stopped before line placement; the baseline activated clotting time was 159 s. Epsilon-aminocaproic acid was given as a 50 mg/kg bolus followed by 25 mg/kg/hr. During conduit harvest, arterial pressure fell from 84/55 mmHg to 37/30 mmHg, pulmonary-artery pressure rose from 48/34 mmHg to 57/44 mmHg, central venous pressure rose from 24 mmHg to 27 mmHg, end-tidal CO2 fell from 28 mmHg to 17 mmHg, and the bispectral index fell to zero. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed thrombus in all four cardiac chambers.

A 55-year-old man presented with a 5-year history of localized aching pain and swelling on the dorsum of his right foot. Over time, the pain intensified at night, was exacerbated by cold temperatures and the lightest touch, and eventually made walking impossible. There was no history of trauma, and his past medical and surgical history was unremarkable. On examination, a soft, nodular mass measuring approximately 2×2 cm was palpated over the fourth metatarsal on the dorsum of the foot; it was exquisitely tender to palpation. An ultrasound study demonstrated a 23×5 mm subdermal hypoechoic lesion over the fourth tarsometatarsal joint with both internal and peripheral vascularity, encasing the adjacent tendon, and without signs of liquefaction or calcification. Baseline laboratory investigations, including complete blood count, coagulation profile, viral serologies, and blood glucose, were all within normal limits. Based on these findings, a provisional diagnosis was made and surgical excision was planned.

A three-year-old girl with no prior medical history was brought with a two-week history of a progressively enlarging, mildly painful mass on the volar aspect of her left wrist. There was no history of trauma or known congenital anomalies. On examination, a 1 × 1 cm soft, mildly tender mass was palpable over the center of the volar wrist. Wrist and finger range of motion were full, but passive wrist movement elicited distress. Inspection revealed no polydactyly or café-au-lait spots, and formal Tinel’s and Phalen’s tests could not be reliably performed.  
Ultrasonography demonstrated a severely edematous and hypertrophied median nerve from the wrist into the palm with low-echogenic intraneural multiple fascicles. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the left wrist showed fusiform enlargement of the median nerve extending from the distal third of the forearm to the metacarpal area, with longitudinally oriented, cable-like structures and invasion of the flexor retinaculum.

A 48-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 2-week history of a palpable left breast mass, noted on self-examination. Diagnostic mammography revealed a 1.1-cm oval focal asymmetry with an indistinct margin at the 6-o’clock position in the left breast. Targeted ultrasound identified four lesions, including a 1.6-cm mass at 7-o’clock classified as BI-RADS 4A. An ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy of the 1.6-cm lesion was performed using a 14-gauge needle. Histologic examination showed intersecting fascicles of bland spindle cells with oval nuclei and no significant pleomorphism, necrosis, or mitotic activity. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated that the spindle cells were diffusely and strongly positive for S100 protein but negative for cytokeratin AE1/AE3, P63, desmin, actin, CD10, and CD117.

A 58-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 2-week history of progressive asthenia, anorexia, and unintentional weight loss. On examination, she appeared pale; her skin and mucous membranes were pallid. Abdominal examination revealed a soft but tender mass in the left hypochondrium. Laboratory studies showed hematocrit 24%, hemoglobin 8 g/dL, red cell count 2,500,000/mm3, and blood glucose 152 mg/dL; all other values were within normal limits.  
An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a mass approximately 10 cm in diameter situated between the tail of the pancreas, the left adrenal gland, and the upper pole of the left kidney. Contrast-enhanced CT imaging confirmed a large 10 cm × 15 cm retroperitoneal tumor that appeared to surround and originate from the left adrenal gland, although “the possibility of another type of primary retroperitoneal tumor could not be excluded.” An intravenous pyelogram showed only slight displacement of the left kidney, and a chest radiograph was unremarkable.  
Given these findings, the decision was made to proceed with surgical exploration.

A 63-year-old man, 40 pack-year smoker, presented with a 2-month history of cough, hemoptysis, fever, and weight loss. On initial evaluation, chest CT showed a 2.8×3.5 cm soft-tissue opacity in the right upper lobe with surrounding patchy shadows. PET-CT revealed a 2.5×3.5 cm right hilar mass (mean SUV 4.9, peak 9.6) and a 4.9×3.3 cm patchy shadow in the right upper lobe (mean SUV 4.7, peak 6.0). Two CT-guided percutaneous lung biopsies demonstrated chronic pneumonia and organizing pneumonia with local necrosis, and transbronchial biopsy showed chronic bronchial inflammation. He was treated for community-acquired pneumonia with cefotiam and clindamycin: fever resolved but cough and hemoptysis persisted. Repeat CT on hospital day 21 showed shrinkage of the puncture-site lesions but enlargement of other opacities and persistent right hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. 

On transfer two weeks later, he was afebrile, with clear lung sounds and no peripheral lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests: WBC 10.81×10^9/L (65.6% neutrophils), hemoglobin 119 g/L, platelets 246×10^9/L, ESR 73 mm/h, CRP 52.2 mg/L, negative T-spot, normal blood gases except PaO2 69 mmHg. Tumor markers: CA 125 68.3 U/mL, CYFRA 21-1 3.7 ng/mL; ANA (cytoplasmic) 1:100; other autoantibodies negative. Pathology review confirmed organizing pneumonia with eosinophil infiltration and focal hemosiderin deposition. Intravenous corticosteroids were administered for two weeks, after which most symptoms resolved except for occasional hemoptysis. Follow-up CT showed marked reduction of the puncture-site lesions but progression of other lesions and persistent lymphadenopathy.

A 79-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of a painless swelling of the hard palate, which had enlarged progressively over the last 2 months. An incisional biopsy performed at an outside hospital was reported as a poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma, and review at our institution likewise noted a poorly differentiated carcinoma. Oral examination revealed a firm, painless, submucosal mass measuring 3×4 cm in the hard palate; the overlying mucosa was ulcerated. There was no regional lymphadenopathy. The remainder of the physical examination and routine laboratory studies were unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head and neck region demonstrated a solid mass confined to the hard palate. The lesion was resected transorally with a 1-cm margin, including periosteum; there was no invasion of periosteum or bone. The postoperative course was uncomplicated. 

Grossly, the specimen was an unencapsulated, tan-white, solid tumor measuring 3×4 cm; the overlying mucosa was ulcerated, and there were punctate yellowish foci on cut section. 

Microscopic examination showed two distinct neoplastic cell populations. The predominant component consisted of large polyhedral (plasmacytoid) cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm, eccentric round nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and marked pleomorphism; these cells were arranged in sheets or loose aggregates within a myxoid stroma and exhibited 18 mitoses per 10 high-power fields, including atypical forms. A second, less pleomorphic population of spindle-shaped, fibroblast-like cells formed interlacing bundles. Small foci of necrosis were present, and noncohesive single tumor cells infiltrated at the tumor periphery. There was no perineural or vascular invasion, and surgical margins were free of tumor.

A 65-year-old man presented with progressive upper abdominal swelling and pain of several weeks’ duration. He reported no fever, vomiting, melena, or history of abdominal trauma. His vital signs were within normal limits, and he had not experienced any weight loss. On examination, there was a large, tense, slightly mobile mass in the left upper quadrant; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Routine blood tests, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a large unilocular cyst. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen revealed a 17 × 16 × 15 cm unilocular cystic lesion abutting the anterior gastric wall and forming a claw-like indentation. The cyst wall measured up to 1.4 cm in thickness and contained no internal solid or papillary components; it compressed the pancreatic body but did not cause gastric outlet obstruction. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed intact, normal gastric mucosa.

A 62-year-old man was referred for evaluation of an enlarging right cervical mass of two months’ duration associated with dyspnea when supine. He had undergone left nephrectomy for T1N0M0 renal cell carcinoma 12 years earlier and had been disease–free since; he also had a history of bladder carcinoma treated in 2010. Medications included paroxetine, mexazolam, and clomipramine. On examination, he was afebrile and normotensive. A firm, mobile, 4-cm nodule was palpated in the right thyroid lobe without cervical lymphadenopathy. Thyroid function tests were within normal limits. Neck ultrasonography revealed an asymmetrically enlarged thyroid gland with a 49 × 30 mm solid, well-circumscribed nodule with peripheral vascularity in the right lobe. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the nodule was classified as Thy2.

A 46-year-old man was evaluated for gradually decreasing libido, worsening hypertension, sleep interruptions, higher nocturnal glucose readings on continuous glucose monitoring, and a 10-lb weight gain over 6 years. He denied easy bruising, striae, or other cushingoid features and reported normal bone density (T score +0.4). He had no history of exogenous steroid, hormone, or supplement use. His medical history included hypertension diagnosed at age 25 (treated with losartan and recently amlodipine), mild anxiety and depression (on citalopram), and five episodes of central serous chorioretinopathy over the previous 4 years. Family history was notable for hypertension in his brother and father. He did not smoke and consumed 3–5 alcoholic drinks weekly.

On examination, BMI was 25.7, blood pressure 130/82 mm Hg. He appeared muscular with slight facial rounding compared to older photographs but no dorsocervical fat pad, skin thinning, striae, or ecchymoses.

Laboratory studies showed elevated cortisol and ACTH measured at multiple time points, several elevated late-night salivary cortisol levels, and a 3.5- to 6-fold increase in 24-hour urinary free cortisol. Morning testosterone was low-normal; fasting glucose, insulin, hemoglobin A1c, and lipid profile were within normal limits. Sequencing of the NR3C1 (glucocorticoid receptor) gene and whole-exome sequencing revealed no pathogenic variants. Pituitary MRI demonstrated a 3-mm microadenoma.

Urinary steroid profiling by liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry revealed a reduced (THF + allo-THF)/THE ratio of 0.75 (normal male mean, 1.3). Inferior petrosal sinus sampling demonstrated a central source of ACTH.

A 35-year-old Indian man presented with 6 months of gait imbalance, bilateral tinnitus, and left-sided hearing loss that worsened over the past 5 days. He also reported bilateral upper- and lower-limb tingling and numbness and a “cotton wool” sensation when walking, along with right-sided spastic weakness. He denied headache, nausea, or vomiting. His history was notable for ear discharge 2 years earlier, which resolved with medication, and positional dizziness for 2 years. He was conscious and oriented, with stable vital signs. On skin inspection there were no café au lait spots. Neurologic examination showed increased tone in all four limbs, 4/5 strength bilaterally, right grip 80%, left grip 90%, and hyperreflexia (3+) throughout. Romberg’s sign, Babinski sign (extensor), and Hoffman’s sign were positive; cerebellar signs were absent, and the abdominal reflex was absent. Cranial-nerve testing revealed bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, worse on the left. Otoscopic examination showed an intact right tympanic membrane with grade 1 retraction and a healed central perforation on the left. Tympanometry demonstrated a type A curve, with minimal to moderate sensorineural hearing loss on the right and moderate sensorineural hearing loss on the left; ipsilateral and contralateral reflexes were absent until 4 kHz. MRI of the spine revealed a well-defined T2-hyperintense extramedullary lesion on the posterior aspect of the craniovertebral junction causing cervical cord compression, suggestive of meningioma, and a dumbbell-shaped intra- and extramedullary lesion at C2 suggestive of neurofibroma. MRI of the brain showed bilateral cerebellopontine-angle lesions (larger on the left) suggestive of vestibular schwannomas, meeting criteria for neurofibromatosis type 2. Additional findings included intramedullary lesions at C1–C2 (suggestive of ependymomas) and hyperintense signal changes at C3 (suggestive of a syrinx). A CT scan of the spine demonstrated a broad-based lesion in the foramen magnum region with focal hyperdensities, likely calcifications, causing spinal canal stenosis and consistent with meningioma.

A 54-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of severe headache, vomiting, and progressive confusion. On examination, he was alert but disoriented, with no focal motor deficits. An urgent CT scan demonstrated triventricular hydrocephalus and a solitary hemorrhagic lesion centered in the septum pellucidum. An external ventricular drain was placed, relieving his symptoms. MRI of the brain revealed an inhomogeneous intraventricular mass, hyperintense on T1- and T2-weighted images, with strong gadolinium enhancement and extension into the third ventricle causing stenosis of the foramina of Monro. The patient underwent right frontal craniotomy and transcallosal gross total excision of the bleeding tumor, followed by a septostomy. A postoperative total-body CT scan showed no extracranial lesions. Two months later, the patient’s neurologic status declined, and he died. No autopsy was performed.  
Histologic examination of the surgical specimen revealed an extensively necrotic and hemorrhagic neoplasm composed of large, pleomorphic, round to polygonal epithelioid cells with vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. The cells were arranged in sheets and nests, with occasional tubular structures and irregular thick-walled vessels lined by atypical epithelioid cells. Mitotic figures were numerous, including atypical forms, and the Ki-67 labeling index was very high.

A two-month-old girl was hospitalized because of an abdominal mass present since birth. On physical examination, there was a smooth, firm, non-tender mass in the right flank. Conventional abdominal radiography showed a large right abdominal soft-tissue mass containing several calcifications. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a large, hyperechoic, heterogeneous intra-abdominal mass with areas of calcification. A CT scan demonstrated a large retroperitoneal soft-tissue mass with long hyperdense opacities that resembled fetal bones. Based on these findings, surgical exploration was recommended.

A 14‐year‐old boy presented with a right chest‐wall mass first noted 5 years earlier, which had recently enlarged rapidly. He reported nocturnal, referred pain from the lesion but no constitutional symptoms or weight loss. On examination, there was a 4 cm, soft, slightly mobile, non‐tender, rounded mass in the right scapular region. 

Contrast‐enhanced chest CT demonstrated a poorly marginated, 6.06 × 5.69 cm soft‐tissue lesion in the right paraspinal area at T8–T9, with marked heterogeneous enhancement (mean CT value, 71 HU) and striated/flocculent internal enhancement. The lesion abutted and appeared to invade the right erector spinae muscle, which was swollen. 

MRI revealed a 5.98 × 5.62 cm paravertebral mass at T8–T9 with mixed signal: isointense on T1-weighted images with small areas of high signal; predominantly high-signal on T2-weighted images with scattered higher-signal foci on T2 fat suppression; and partial extension into the spinal canal causing cord compression. There was localized bone destruction of the right 8th and 9th posterior ribs and the right T8 transverse process, with expansion of the 9th rib. 

Whole-body emission CT showed normal skeletal structure, while bone scintigraphy revealed increased radionuclide uptake in the right 8th and 9th posterior ribs only.

A 60‐year‐old woman presented with a 20‐year history of a slowly enlarging anal mass and recent rectal bleeding and pain during defecation. She had hypertension but no prior surgeries and underwent regular mammography without abnormalities. On examination in the left lateral decubitus position, a 25 mm polypoid lesion with a 20 mm base was noted at the 5 o’clock position on the left posterolateral distal anal canal. The lesion was covered by normal skin, was firm and fibrotic in consistency, non‐tender, and without spontaneous or inducible bleeding or discharge. A posterior anal fissure was also seen. Under sedation, colonoscopy revealed no other lesions. After local anesthesia, the encapsulated polyp was removed en bloc by diathermy without sphincter involvement or need for suturing. Grossly, the mass was well‐circumscribed, oval, covered by regular skin, firm, gray‐white, and measured 25 × 15 × 20 mm.

A 67-year-old Mediterranean man presented with new-onset seizures and episodes of altered consciousness and was started on levetiracetam. MRI of the brain with and without gadolinium showed a 4.8×4.0×4.8 cm well-defined left frontal cystic mass that was isointense to CSF on T1-weighted and FLAIR images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and contained sausage-shaped debris of high FLAIR signal in its dependent portion with an internal septation. There was no enhancement of the lesion or surrounding capsule after contrast administration. Diffusion-weighted and diffusion tensor imaging demonstrated a high T2 signal wall surrounded by a low-signal capsule. Functional MRI localized the primary motor cortex to the posterior and lateral margins of the cyst and the supplementary motor area to its medial margin. Tractography revealed that adjacent white-matter tracts were cleaved and displaced but not infiltrated. CT of the thorax and abdomen, performed as part of a workup for suspected hydatid disease, revealed a mesenteric cystic lesion. Albendazole therapy was initiated for a presumed hydatid cyst.

A 71-year-old woman presented with a 6-week history of intermittent lower abdominal pain, subjective fevers, and altered bowel habits without obstruction or bleeding. Her medical history included well-controlled hypertension, chronic kidney disease, and a smoking history. On examination, there was tenderness in the lower abdomen without palpable masses. Laboratory studies showed a carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) level of 4.0 ng/mL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated findings consistent with uncomplicated diverticulitis and incidentally revealed a lobulated, exophytic 54 × 54 mm mass arising from the transverse colon with adjacent enlarged lymph nodes. Colonoscopy was limited by diverticulosis, showed no intraluminal mass, and revealed desmoplastic mucosal changes at the splenic flexure; biopsies were nondiagnostic. CT of the chest showed no evidence of metastatic disease. The patient underwent a laparoscopic-assisted left hemicolectomy with en bloc resection of the lesion. The tumour capsule integrity was maintained, and an end-to-end hand-sewn anastomosis was created.

A 35-year-old Saudi man presented with a two-week history of a right conjunctival lesion that was increasing in size and darkening in color, accompanied by redness, foreign-body sensation, tearing, and pain. His medical history was notable for irritable bowel syndrome (not on regular medications), a treated episode of pancreatitis four years earlier, and an indeterminate pancreatic lesion undergoing evaluation. On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. In the right eye, there was a vascularized, cystic mass on the temporal bulbar conjunctiva with a limbal component covering the corneal margin between 7 and 9 o’clock and severe conjunctival injection; the remainder of the ophthalmic examination was unremarkable. Verruca vulgaris papules were noted on his knees and knuckles, but he denied any history of genital warts. Laboratory studies were negative for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C, and showed leukopenia (3.5 × 10^9/L). Orbital CT, ultrasound biomicroscopy, and anterior-segment OCT demonstrated a cystic conjunctival lesion measuring 1.46 mm in depth and 10.46 mm in diameter, abutting the cornea inferotemporally without scleral invasion. Given the atypical appearance and his pancreatic history, the differential diagnosis included conjunctival squamous cell carcinoma and metastatic disease. The patient subsequently underwent excisional biopsy of the lesion with safe conjunctival margins, and an amniotic membrane transplant was used to cover the bare sclera.

A 16-year-old female presented with a 3-month history of pain in the distal right thigh. She had no history of trauma, prior surgeries, or systemic disease, and no family history of bone lesions. Initial supportive care and a course of physiotherapy for presumed muscle cramps provided no relief, and she subsequently noted a palpable lump in the same region. 

A radiograph of the right thigh revealed an oval, soft-tissue lesion measuring approximately 4.0 cm × 6.0 cm × 4.3 cm with well-defined, calcified margins and internal cystic spaces; there was no apparent connection with the adjacent femur. MRI demonstrated a well-circumscribed soft-tissue mass within the quadriceps femoris muscle, bounded by hyposignal margins, containing multiple cystic areas with fluid–fluid levels, surrounding muscle edema, and internal T1 hypersignal consistent with hemorrhage. A bone scan showed increased tracer uptake in the region on perfusion, blood-pool, and delayed images. 

On the basis of these clinical and imaging findings, a benign soft-tissue lesion was suspected, and the patient was referred for complete surgical resection.

A 58-year-old woman presented with intermittent lower abdominal pain for one week. She had no other symptoms. She was taking fluvoxamine maleate, sulpiride, and brotizolam for depression and insomnia. On admission, her blood pressure was 147/101 mm Hg, heart rate 63 beats/min, and temperature 36.5 °C; height 151 cm, weight 48 kg. The abdomen was soft and flat, with a palpable fist-sized elastic hard mass in the left lumbar/middle region without tenderness or skin changes. Laboratory studies showed an elevated gamma-glutamyl transferase of 60.4 IU/L (normal 9–32); other serum chemistries, complete blood count, and tumor markers (CA 19-9, CEA) were normal. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy, colonoscopy, and enteroscopy were normal. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a 36 × 38 × 44 mm elliptical, heterogeneously enhancing mass with a smooth surface and a poorly enhanced region suggestive of necrosis or cystic change; the small and large bowels were displaced away, and the origin (retroperitoneum vs small-bowel mesentery) was uncertain; no dissemination or ascites were seen. MRI showed the mass to be isointense to psoas muscle on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with no fat signal on out-of-phase sequences, and high signal on diffusion-weighted images. FDG-PET showed uptake in the lesion (SUVmax 6.03) without metastatic lesions. The differential diagnoses included desmoid tumor, leiomyoma/leiomyosarcoma, gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST), and malignant lymphoma.

A 52-year-old African-American man with no prior abdominal surgeries and a history of multiple myeloma and venous thromboembolism presented with a 6-day history of nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. He had not passed flatus for 24 hours and denied fever, chills, or malaise. He was diagnosed with multiple myeloma 4 months earlier after a pathologic left humerus fracture and was undergoing chemotherapy (bortezomib, lenalidomide, dexamethasone) and localized radiation therapy; he completed his second cycle 10 days before presentation. His bone marrow biopsy had shown 25% clonal plasma cells with kappa restriction; FISH revealed a 17p13 deletion in 30% of cells and a t(14;16) rearrangement in 5.7% of cells. He also had stage II disease by the International Staging System. Other conditions included hypertension, obesity, sleep apnea, vitamin D deficiency, and a pulmonary embolism treated with enoxaparin. On examination, vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the right lower quadrant with mild guarding. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen showed a 5.4-cm soft-tissue mass involving a loop of distal ileum with dilation of the proximal small bowel and a right-sided fluid collection containing air suggestive of perforation.

A 74-year-old woman presented with dyspnea on exertion and nocturnal cough. Chest computed tomography revealed bilateral heterogeneous ground-glass shadows throughout both lung fields. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) showed increased lymphocytes, while atypical cells, mycobacteria, and bacteria were not detected. Transbronchial lung biopsy was deferred because of severe hypoxemia during the procedure. She received empirical corticosteroid therapy for presumed inflammatory lung disease but remained unresponsive, and follow-up CT showed progression with predominantly subpleural, nonsegmental ground-glass opacities, new subpleural consolidations in both upper lobes, and a subpleural nodule in the right lower lobe. On readmission, laboratory studies demonstrated leukocytopenia, thrombocytopenia, renal dysfunction, an elevated lactate dehydrogenase level (861 IU/L), and an increased soluble interleukin-2 receptor level (3220 U/mL; normal 145–519 U/mL). Abdominal imaging and examination revealed splenomegaly and hepatomegaly. From the laboratory data and the presence of splenomegaly and hepatomegaly, intravascular lymphoma was suspected.

A 40-year-old Mexican woman presented with a progressively enlarging mass in her right breast. She first noticed a small lump 3 years earlier; 1 year later, blisters appeared on the nipple.
