Over the most recent year, the lesion developed erythema, a prominent venous network, a foul odor, skin ulceration with bleeding, and rapid enlargement, prompting evaluation.

She had no relevant personal or family history. On examination, the right breast measured about 25 × 22 cm, with irregular margins, erythematous and hyperemic skin, ulceration of the nipple with hemorrhagic discharge, and tenderness on palpation. The axilla was without palpable lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (12 700/μL) with neutrophilia (9 700/μL); other values were within normal limits. Breast ultrasonography showed a large mass with mixed cystic degeneration and solid areas, poorly defined margins, irregular vascularity, and thick hyperechogenic septa. An ultrasound-guided core biopsy demonstrated a fibroepithelial neoplasm with hyalinized, myxoid, and hypercellular stromal areas, compatible with fibroadenoma; the Ki-67 proliferation index was 2%.

18F-FDG PET/CT revealed a right breast mass measuring 24.6 × 17.3 cm in the axial plane and 22.5 cm in the cephalocaudal plane, with loss of the interface with the pectoralis major muscle, internal hyperdense linear and nodular areas, and two ipsilateral axillary lymph nodes each measuring 9 mm.

A 22-year-old Caucasian man with no significant past medical history was brought to the emergency department after a motor vehicle collision. He complained of sudden, severe left upper quadrant abdominal pain. On arrival he was pale and diaphoretic, with a blood pressure of 80/40 mm Hg, pulse 125 bpm, and respiratory rate 26 per minute. There was no fever. His medication and social histories were unremarkable, and there was no family history of bleeding or clotting disorders.

On examination, the abdomen was mildly distended; there was marked tenderness with both superficial and deep palpation in the left upper quadrant, with guarding and rebound tenderness. Initial laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin concentration of 7.5 g/dL. After a bolus of crystalloid fluids, his blood pressure improved transiently but tachycardia persisted. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest and abdomen revealed splenic rupture with massive hemoperitoneum. 

The patient was taken emergently to the operating room for exploratory laparotomy. During surgery, the spleen was found to have multiple large capsular tears. A total splenectomy was performed, and the resected spleen was sent for histopathologic examination.

A 53-year-old man presented with a slow-growing, non-tender, hard mass in the right parotid gland area. He had no other symptoms or history of autoimmune disease or malignancy. Laboratory tests showed no abnormalities. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed a 3.3×2.0-cm homogenous mass with multiple enhanced nodules adjacent to the lesion. The CT findings suggested a Warthin tumor, with a low possibility of a mixed tumor or low-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma. Superficial parotidectomy was planned for both diagnosis and treatment.

A 33-year-old woman presented with a two-year history of a progressively enlarging, mildly painful mass in the lower right jaw. On examination, a firm swelling was palpable in the body and angle of the right mandible without overlying skin changes or intraoral ulceration. 

Noncontrast CT of the nasal sinuses demonstrated a multiloculated lytic lesion in the body and angle of the right mandible, with cortical expansion and thinning. The lesion was in intimate contact with the roots of the right inferior canine, first and second premolars, and second molar. Sagittal reconstructions revealed fine septa oriented perpendicular to the lesion borders, partitioning the mass into small rectangular spaces.

A 64-year-old man presented with a 2.5-month history of fatigue, fever, chills, night sweats, and a 65-lb weight loss. CT imaging demonstrated hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly. An outside hospital evaluation included lymph node and skin biopsies and cytologic examination of a pleural effusion; all sites showed a polymorphic population of T and B lymphocytes with occasional rare atypical CD20-positive B cells, but clonality studies were negative and no definitive diagnosis was made. On transfer, a second excisional lymph node biopsy showed a polymorphous infiltrate of medium-to-large lymphocytes with clumped chromatin, multiple nucleoli, scant to moderate cytoplasm, frequent mitoses, and intermixed T lymphocytes, immunoblasts, histiocytes, eosinophils, and plasma cells, extending into surrounding fibroadipose tissue. Immunohistochemical stains revealed that the atypical large cells were strongly CD20 positive, Bcl-2 negative, CD10 negative, and Bcl-6 negative, with a high Ki-67 proliferation index.

A 62-year-old man of Chinese origin presented with a 2-month history of cough, expectoration, dyspnea, bilateral lower-extremity edema, and a 5-kg weight loss over the past month. He had a history of coronary artery disease and carotid artery stenosis. On examination, he was tachycardic with jugular venous distension, no Kussmaul’s sign, and symmetric concave lower-extremity edema. Laboratory tests showed an elevated NT-proBNP (4051 pg/mL; normal <125 pg/mL) and C-reactive protein (7.89 mg/dL; normal <0.8 mg/dL), with normal blood counts, liver, and renal function. Electrocardiography revealed sinus tachycardia, low‐voltage limb leads, and T-wave changes. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated pericardial thickening up to 9.4 mm without effusion, ventricular septal bounce, biatrial enlargement, reduced LVEF (42%), diastolic dysfunction, and plethoric IVC with reduced inspiratory collapse. Contrast-enhanced cardiac CT showed pericardial thickening without calcification, a dilated aorta with wall thickening and soft-tissue infiltration encasing the coronary arteries, and bilateral pleural effusions. Cardiac MRI confirmed diffuse pericardial and aortic‐wall thickening with late gadolinium enhancement, atrial enlargement, septal bounce, reduced LVEF (40%), and IVC plethora. Chest CT noted interlobular septal thickening in both lower lobes and bilateral pleural effusions. Abdominal CT revealed bilateral perirenal soft-tissue halos causing mild hydronephrosis, thickening of the abdominal aortic wall, adrenal glands, and peritoneum. Pituitary MRI showed pituitary enlargement with loss of neurohypophysis T1 hyperintensity and tentorial thickening. Orbital MRI revealed bilateral enhancing orbital soft-tissue masses.

A 53-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of right lower quadrant abdominal pain, for which he had taken oral antibiotics without relief. He denied nausea, vomiting, anorexia, or changes in bowel function. He had no fevers until presentation, when his temperature was 38.3 °C. On examination, there was tenderness at McBurney’s point with rebound tenderness. His medical history was notable for gastric adenocarcinoma treated with subtotal gastrectomy and chemotherapy 3 years earlier; surveillance imaging had shown no recurrence. He had no other chronic illnesses and took no regular medications. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 12 750/µL (73.5% neutrophils) and a C-reactive protein level of 5.82 mg/dL. Chest and abdominal radiographs were unremarkable. He underwent an open appendectomy through a McBurney incision. Intraoperatively, the appendix was gangrenous without perforation and there was a small amount of peritoneal fluid. The postoperative course was uneventful, and he was discharged on postoperative day 5. Pathologic examination of the excised appendix revealed extensive infiltration of the entire appendix by highly differentiated adenocarcinoma with mucosal ulceration; surgical margins were free of disease.

A 34-year-old man presented with a one-year history of progressive, painless proptosis of the left eye without preceding trauma or systemic illness. He also reported frontal headaches and occasional left eye pain over the same period. On examination, there was left eccentric proptosis with inferotemporal displacement of the globe, fullness in the superonasal orbit, and left-sided forehead prominence. Visual acuity was 6/6 in both eyes, with a normal anterior segment and unremarkable fundus. Extraocular movements were full. Contrast-enhanced multidetector CT of the orbits showed a large multilobulated ossified mass (73 × 60 mm) centered in the frontal sinuses and extending into the ethmoid sinuses. The lesion involved the orbital roofs bilaterally with focal thinning and erosions. On the left, it extended superomedially into the extraconal space, compressing the globe and superior rectus muscle, correlating with the proptosis. Post-contrast images showed no enhancement of the mass lesion.

A 58-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a growth in the right cheek region associated with pain. He first noted a slowly enlarging swelling without antecedent trauma, pus discharge, or burning sensation. His medical history was noncontributory. He had a 10-year history of alcohol use, cigarette smoking, and tobacco chewing. 

On extraoral examination, there was no facial asymmetry or palpable lymphadenopathy. Intraoral examination revealed a well-defined, smooth, pink, pedunculated nodule measuring approximately 3 × 3 cm on the right buccal mucosa adjacent to tooth 44. The lesion was soft to firm, fluctuant, tender on palpation, and showed no bruit or pulsations. Panoramic radiography was unremarkable.

A provisional diagnosis of irritational fibroma was made, and an excisional biopsy was performed.

A 77-year-old man was referred for evaluation of suspected unilateral iris rubeosis in his right eye found on routine examination before cataract surgery. He was asymptomatic. Medical history included hypertension with renal involvement, metabolic syndrome, atrial fibrillation, prostatic syndrome, moderate COPD, and longstanding childhood divergent strabismus with left‐eye amblyopia.

On examination, visual acuity was 0.5 in the right eye and 0.15 in the left eye, with divergent strabismus. Slit‐lamp biomicroscopy of the right eye revealed radial vascular engorgement of the iris at the 5–7 o’clock position, with vessels originating in the iris stroma and extending circumferentially. Gonioscopy showed a grade IV open angle and a 360° vascular racemose network in the iridocorneal angle. No sentinel episcleral vessels or iris masses were seen. Intraocular pressures were 10 mmHg in the right eye and 12 mmHg in the left eye; the left eye exam was otherwise normal.

Fundus examination of the right eye showed an oblique optic disc, myopic chorioretinitis, and no exudates, hemorrhages, or neovascularization. There were no clinical signs of diabetic retinopathy, central or branch retinal vein or artery obstruction. Indentation fundus exam with maximal mydriasis revealed no peripheral tumors (eg, choroidal melanoma, retinoblastoma, metastasis, or ciliary body lesions). Supra‐aortic Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated no hemodynamically significant carotid stenosis.

An anterior‐segment OCT demonstrated poorly defined intrastromal hyporeflective spaces corresponding to the vascular lumina. Fluorescein angiography showed normal contrast uptake without extravasation in the iris, iridocorneal angle, or retinal vessels, with early filling of the iris vessels and no diffusion of dye.

A 61-year-old woman presented with a 50-year history of intermittent cough, sputum production, and chest tightness that had worsened over the past 10 days. She denied chest pain, dyspnea, fever, weight loss, or night sweats. Her history was notable for overlap syndrome (Sjögren’s syndrome and rheumatoid arthritis) diagnosed 3 years earlier, treated with glucocorticoids and immunosuppressants, as well as pulmonary fibrosis, emphysema, bronchiectasis, and autoimmune hepatic cirrhosis. She had no history of smoking or tuberculosis. On examination, her temperature was 36.7°C, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, pulse 79 bpm, and blood pressure 17.5/10.1 kPa. Lung auscultation revealed coarse breath sounds without rales. Laboratory studies showed WBC 2.90×10^9/L, hemoglobin 78 g/L, ESR 114 mm/h, CRP 9.6 mg/L, ALT 300 U/L, GGT 110 U/L, total protein 87.1 g/L, albumin 32.9 g/L, with normal calcium and phosphorus. Chest CT demonstrated an irregular, lobulated mass in the right middle and lower lobes with spotted calcifications, moderate heterogeneous enhancement, adjacent pleural retraction, bronchial obstruction, enlargement of the pulmonary artery trunk, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. A bone survey was normal. Echocardiography showed mildly reduced left ventricular function. Sputum cultures and tumor markers (CA-125, CEA, NSE, SCC) were negative; CA 19-9 was 61.4 U/mL (normal ≤ 33). Serum immunofixation revealed elevated IgG (2520 mg/dL), κ-light chain (2270 mg/dL), λ-light chain (1260 mg/dL) without monoclonal gammopathy; β2-microglobulin was 6.07 µg/mL. Urine was negative for Bence-Jones protein. Autoimmune serologies were positive (ANA, anti-SSA/Ro60KD, anti-SSA/Ro52KD, anti-SSB, ANCA; RF 4077 IU/mL). 99mTc-MDP bone scan showed focal uptake in bilateral eighth ribs, right acetabular edge, and pubic ramus. Bronchoscopy revealed only inflammatory changes without malignancy. Bone marrow examination showed <5% plasma cells without dyscrasia.

A 40-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of a gradually enlarging swelling in the left upper front jaw. He noted mild intermittent pain, occasional bleeding, excessive salivation, and loosening of a tooth. There was no numbness or paresthesia. His medical, dental, and social histories were unremarkable.  

On intraoral examination, there was a solitary, well-defined, dome-shaped, lobulated swelling measuring approximately 2×1 cm on the labial aspect of the maxillary left lateral incisor and canine (teeth 22 and 23). The lesion was the same color as adjacent mucosa, was firm to hard, sessile, tender on palpation, non-fluctuant, and bled on provocation. Tooth 22 exhibited grade III mobility.  

An intraoral periapical radiograph demonstrated an ill-defined homogeneous radiolucency around the root of tooth 22. A maxillary cross-sectional occlusal radiograph showed a well-defined radiopaque nidus surrounded by a thin radiolucent border in the region of teeth 22 and 23.  

Based on the clinical and radiographic features, a differential diagnosis included ossifying fibroma, peripheral osteoma, and osteoblastoma.

A 32-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks’ gestation with poor antenatal care presented with premature rupture of membranes. Her vital signs were normal. Abdominopelvic ultrasound showed polyhydramnios, absence of fetal cardiac activity, and a suspected placental cyst. Laboratory results were hemoglobin 10 g/dL, total leukocyte count 33 000/mm^3, platelet count 230 000/mm^3, and a positive C-reactive protein. An emergency cesarean delivery was performed, yielding a stillborn male infant. The placenta was sent for histopathological examination. On gross inspection, the cut surface of the placenta revealed a well-circumscribed marginal mass measuring 4 cm.

A 52-year-old woman with hypertension presented with sudden episodes of falling to the ground without loss of consciousness over the past 5 months. Each episode lasted approximately 1 minute and was followed by full neurological recovery. She experienced 1–2 such events per day, often associated with giddiness. On examination, she had mild hyperreflexia in all four limbs but no other focal deficits.

Diagnostic studies included:
• Twenty-four-hour electroencephalography, which was normal.  
• Electromyography and nerve conduction studies of all four limbs, which were normal.  
• Cardiovascular evaluation, including electrocardiography and Holter monitoring, which were normal.

A 22-year-old man was admitted with 10 days of vomiting and abdominal distention; he had experienced similar, intermittent symptoms over the past year. On examination, the abdomen was distended with a vague umbilical swelling. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and metabolic panel; the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated at 70 mm at 30 minutes and 118 mm at 1 hour. A Mantoux test was negative. Abdominal radiographs demonstrated multiple air-fluid levels. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed focal ileal wall thickening and enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes. At laparotomy, a 34 × 6 cm segment of ileum with omental adhesions was resected. On gross inspection, an intraluminal polyp (1.5 cm diameter) lay 18 cm from the proximal margin; two shallow ulcers with undermined edges and fibrotic bases lay 14 cm and 20 cm from the proximal margin; a stricture was noted 9 cm from the distal margin with proximal dilation; and several serosal lymph nodes (up to 4 × 5 cm) appeared whitish and firm. Histologic sections showed:  
• The polyp had a smooth-muscle core.  
• Ulcerated mucosa with edematous lamina propria rich in eosinophils and lymphocytes, and congested vessels in the submucosa.  
• Dense lymphocytic infiltration of the muscularis propria and serosa.  
• A lymph node with partial architectural effacement, necrosis, fibrosis, and epithelioid cell aggregates without well-formed granulomas.  
• Thickened bowel wall areas with sheets of lymphocytes transmurally extending to periserosal fat.  
• Remaining mucosa with focal erosions, increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, and focal villous shortening.  

In view of a high suspicion for both intestinal tuberculosis and lymphoma, additional studies were ordered, including acid-fast staining, polymerase chain reaction for mycobacteria, and immunohistochemical analysis.

A man in his mid-50s presented with over one year of unsteady gait and mild short-term memory impairment, initially concerning for normal-pressure hydrocephalus. He also reported mild, nonspecific visual changes. His medical history was significant for hyperlipidemia and a solitary kidney from birth. Neurologic examination revealed a shuffling gait but normal vision; he denied other focal symptoms. Outpatient MRI of the brain showed a complex hemorrhagic and calcified lesion in the right atrium of the lateral ventricle, mild triventricular enlargement without transependymal flow, and a separate enhancing lesion at the outflow of the cerebral aqueduct. Surrounding the atrial mass were multiple large intraparenchymal cysts with cerebrospinal fluid signal on all sequences. Systemic workup was negative for metastatic disease.

A 46-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 5-year history of chronic dysphonia and progressively worsening dysphagia. She denied dyspnea or oral bleeding. Examination revealed a hard, painless 4 cm mass at the base of the tongue and no cervical lymphadenopathy. Nasofibroscopy showed a large pedunculated red–blue oropharyngeal mass of uncertain origin; the vocal cords appeared normal. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated an oropharyngeal lesion occupying approximately 70% of the oropharyngeal space with intrinsic microcalcifications. MRI of the face and neck revealed a bulky tongue‐base mass measuring 44 × 42 mm, isointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and heterogeneously enhancing after gadolinium administration, displacing the epiglottis and filling the valleculas. Thyroid scintigraphy showed a normally situated, functioning thyroid gland and abnormal uptake in the tongue base, findings deemed compatible with an ectopic thyroid. The serum TSH level was within the normal range.

A 51-year-old Caucasian man underwent routine screening colonoscopy. He was asymptomatic and denied bleeding, pain, weight loss, fevers, or chills. He had no significant medical or surgical history and took no medications. Family history was unremarkable for cancer. On examination, vital signs were normal and the abdomen was soft, non-tender, with no palpable masses. Skin examination revealed no pigmented lesions. Laboratory tests including CBC, metabolic panel, liver function, coagulation studies, and hepatic serologies were all within normal limits.  
Colonoscopy showed a 3 cm submucosal pedunculated polyp 15 cm from the anal verge. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a 2.3 cm × 1.4 cm submucosal lesion without adenopathy. Endoscopic ultrasound revealed a 2.8 cm × 1.52 cm avascular, mixed-echogenicity lesion confined to the submucosa with no involvement of the muscularis mucosa or propria.  
Fine-needle biopsy of the lesion showed a bland spindle cell proliferation in a uniform fascicular pattern with edematous stroma. The cells were elongated with oval, wavy nuclei; no mitotic figures, necrosis, or hemorrhage were seen. Immunohistochemical stains demonstrated strong, diffuse S100 positivity with rare penetrating axons, negative staining for c-kit and desmin, and a low Ki-67 index.

A 58-year-old man with hypertension and a prior left inguinal hernioplasty presented with a several-month history of increased urinary frequency. He denied back pain, incontinence, or systemic symptoms. Physical examination revealed a firm, palpable mass extending from just above the pubic bone to below the umbilicus. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were unremarkable. Serum tumor markers (CEA, CA 19-9, and PSA) were within normal limits.  
Pelvic ultrasound demonstrated a large mass in the extraprostatic space. Subsequent MRI of the pelvis showed a well-circumscribed 12 × 13 × 10 cm pelvic mass without evidence of invasive growth, extending through and dilating the S1–S2 intervertebral foramen, displacing the rectosigmoid colon to the right and elevating the urinary bladder.

A 70-year-old man presented with a 4-year history of a painless swelling involving the submental region and right angle of the mandible. The mass first appeared intraorally and gradually increased in size, occasionally discharging a thick creamy fluid. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. He had a long history of tobacco and cigarette use but no history of dental trauma. 

On examination, there was a solitary, hard, non-tender, 4 × 4 cm swelling extending from the submental area to the right mandibular angle above an anterior edentulous alveolar ridge. Intraorally, the buccal vestibule was elevated. The mass was fixed to underlying structures and there was numbness of the right lower lip. Oral hygiene was poor. There was no lymphadenopathy or increased local temperature.

Laboratory studies were unremarkable. Orthopantomogram showed a multilocular radiolucent lesion in the right mandible with a mixed honeycomb and soap-bubble appearance. Contrast-enhanced CT of the mandible revealed a well-defined expansile mixed-density cystic lesion measuring 3.6 × 3.9 cm; enhancing areas corresponded to solid components, and non-enhancing areas corresponded to cystic components. The right mental foramen was not visualized.

A 44-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a hepatic mass that had been discovered incidentally five years earlier. Initial ultrasound had shown a 4.24 × 2.63 cm hypoechoic nodule in the right liver lobe. Non-contrast CT revealed a well-circumscribed, low–density oval mass in segment 6; contrast-enhanced CT at that time suggested peripheral enhancement and a hemangioma. During four years of surveillance, the mass grew slowly. In January 2020, contrast-enhanced CT showed a 7.8 cm mass located between segment 6 of the liver and the right adrenal gland, with marked peripheral enhancement in the arterial phase and hypointensity in the portal and delayed phases compared with adjacent liver. The patient remained asymptomatic. Laboratory studies were notable for negative hepatitis B surface antigen, negative anti–hepatitis C virus, positive hepatitis B surface antibody, and normal levels of α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and carbohydrate antigen 19-9. He had no history of smoking, alcohol use, liver disease, or relevant family history. Physical examination was unremarkable.

A 60-year-old woman with no significant medical history noted progressive “shimmery lights in the top part of my vision” in her right eye over 2 months. Thirty-six years earlier, she had repair of a macula-on rhegmatogenous retinal detachment in that eye with cryopexy and an encircling scleral buckle; she had been followed annually or biannually since and was last seen within one year.

On examination, visual acuity was 20/60 in the right eye and 20/30 in the left eye (no improvement with pinhole). Pupils, extraocular motility, and intraocular pressures were normal. Slit-lamp examination revealed 2+ nuclear sclerotic cataracts in both eyes. Dilated fundus examination of the right eye showed an intact scleral buckle and an elevated, darkly colored lesion along the inferior buckle contour.

The initial differential diagnosis included choroidal detachment, intraocular buckle intrusion with hemorrhage, and choroidal melanoma. On referral to an ophthalmic oncology center, multimodal imaging was performed:
• Fundus examination demonstrated a pigmented, inferior choroidal lesion overlying and adjacent to the buckle contour.  
• Fundus autofluorescence showed hypo-autofluorescence over the lesion.  
• Fluorescein angiography revealed double circulation with increased hyper-fluorescence in late frames.  
• Ultrasonography showed a highly elevated, dome-shaped inferior choroidal mass with medium internal reflectivity, heterogeneous appearance, and an adjacent exudative retinal detachment; the scleral buckle indented the globe anterior to the mass. The lesion measured 14.9 mm × 14.1 mm with a thickness of 7.1 mm.

A 44-year-old G5P4 Hispanic woman with a history of essential hypertension and chronic iron-deficiency anemia was evaluated for persistent abnormal uterine bleeding, pelvic pressure, and stress urinary incontinence. Menorrhagia and dysmenorrhea had worsened over the past 5½ years, and she noted a sensation of pelvic “bulging” for approximately 1½ years. Despite daily ferrous sulfate supplementation, her hemoglobin level declined to 9.9 g/dL.

Physical examination revealed uterine prolapse on Valsalva maneuver. A transvaginal pelvic ultrasound showed an enlarged uterus measuring 10.7 × 5.8 × 7.7 cm^3 and three well-circumscribed uterine masses; the largest was 3.9 × 2.2 × 3.2 cm in the posterior uterine wall. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis confirmed an intermediate-sized posterior left uterine myometrial lesion with conspicuous enhancement, whereas the other myometrial masses did not enhance.

Based on these data, a preoperative diagnosis of abnormal uterine bleeding secondary to leiomyomata and pelvic organ prolapse was made. A Pap smear revealed atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance, and colposcopic biopsy was benign.

An 81‐year‐old woman with asthma presented for routine pulmonary evaluation. She had undergone resection of a “benign” ovarian mass 40 years earlier. She was a non‐smoker and asymptomatic on review of systems. Vital signs and physical examination were normal. A surveillance CT scan of the chest performed to follow an ascending aortic aneurysm revealed a right paratracheal mediastinal lesion measuring 2.6 × 2.0 × 4.0 cm, which had increased in size since prior imaging and demonstrated regions of hypoattenuation and peripheral calcification. A PET‐CT scan showed a right paratracheal nodal conglomerate without hypermetabolic activity and otherwise normal physiological 18‐FDG uptake. Given the interval enlargement, the patient underwent endobronchial ultrasound with transbronchial needle aspiration. The EBUS revealed a well‐circumscribed mass in the 4R lymph node region, and the TBNA samples demonstrated an epithelioid neoplasm without evidence of lymphoid tissue.

A 63-year-old woman was admitted with insidious upper abdominal pain unrelated to food ingestion and nausea, and after an episode of intense acute abdominal pain. She denied hematemesis or melena. Her medical history included untreated dyslipidemia and well-controlled hypertension on methyldopa. She was a smoker of ten cigarettes per day and had no family history of cancer. Physical examination was normal except for a palpable, movable mass in the upper abdomen. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood count, were normal without anemia. Abdominal ultrasound showed a large echogenic mass in the gastric antrum compatible with an expansive lesion. Conventional endoscopy revealed a large submucosal bulging mass in the posterior gastric wall with three Forrest III–type ulcerated areas; biopsy attempts failed to sample the submucosal mass, and ulcer biopsies showed only necrotic mucosa. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a well-defined, homogeneous, oval mass arising from the posterior gastric wall, measuring approximately 10×6×11 cm, compressing the second portion of the duodenum; the lesion had fat-tissue attenuation with central contrast enhancement and trabecular architecture but did not invade the peripheral layers.

A 57-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of sudden-onset headache accompanied by nausea and vomiting. She denied loss of consciousness, focal weakness, speech disturbance, seizures, or memory changes. Her medical history was notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus and remote obstetric hemorrhage requiring transfusion. On admission, vital signs were stable. Laboratory studies showed an elevated lactate dehydrogenase level of 277.6 U/L. Brain MRI demonstrated a 6.3 × 5.5 cm irregular, well‐demarcated lesion at the junction of the left parietal, occipital, and temporal lobes, hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with ring-like enhancement after contrast and surrounding edema. After glycemic control with insulin, she underwent neurosurgical resection. Intraoperatively, the mass in the mesial temporal lobe was solid, whereas the adjacent paraventricular component was cystic and contained yellow purulent fluid. Both lesions were separately excised and sent for histopathologic examination. Postoperatively, she remained hemodynamically stable with intact cognition and motor strength, but with persistent speech clarity difficulties.

A 49-year-old African American woman (G2P2002) with a history of hypertension on an angiotensin receptor blocker, long-term cigarette smoking, pancreatitis, and a mature cystic teratoma of the left ovary (status post left oophorectomy 1 month earlier) presented with persistent abdominal and back pain and an 85-pound weight loss over 1 year. CT imaging revealed masses in the body and tail of the pancreas and in the uterus/right adnexa. Serum tumor markers were within normal limits except for a minimally elevated human chorionic gonadotropin level of 20 pg/mL. 

Because of concern for a uterine or right adnexal primary malignancy, the patient underwent total abdominal hysterectomy with right salpingo-oophorectomy and intraoperative exploration of the pancreatic mass. At surgery, the pancreatic mass was sclerotic, involved the superior mesenteric artery, and was considered unresectable; multiple biopsies were taken. On gross examination of the hysterectomy specimen, the uterus showed leiomyomas and the right adnexa contained a mature teratoma. 

Histologic examination of the pancreatic biopsies revealed two distinct components: a high-grade spindle cell sarcoma and an adjacent moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma. The background stroma was prominently fibrotic, containing myofibroblasts positive for desmin and smooth muscle actin. A hepatic lymph node showed a 0.85-mm focus of metastatic adenocarcinoma. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated that the adenocarcinoma component stained positively for AE1/AE3, cytokeratin 7, CDX2, and villin, whereas the sarcomatous component was negative for cytokeratin AE1/AE3, focally positive for desmin and smooth muscle actin, and strongly positive for CD10. Ki-67 labeling was approximately 50% in the adenocarcinoma and 90% in the sarcoma.

A 24-year-old man presented with a gradual, painless swelling of the right upper eyelid involving the medial aspect for over 10 years. He reported no redness, diplopia, or visual changes. His medical history was unremarkable, and there was no history of trauma. On examination, vital signs were normal. Visual acuity was 20/20 in each eye, and extraocular movements were full without restriction. There was marked fullness of the right upper eyelid with downward and lateral displacement of the globe. Pupils were equal and reactive with no afferent pupillary defect. Intraocular pressures were within normal limits. Anterior and posterior segment examinations were unremarkable bilaterally. Magnetic resonance imaging of the orbits revealed a 1.95 × 3.16 × 2.62 cm, partially lobulated, well-defined lesion in the right medial orbital extraconal space. The lesion was isointense to extraocular muscles on T1-weighted images and hyperintense with homogeneous enhancement after contrast administration, causing inferior and lateral globe displacement.

A 69-year-old Caucasian woman was admitted for excision of giant dorsal haemangiomas. She had a 30-year history of immune thrombocytopenic purpura under long-term corticosteroids, cyclosporine, and azathioprine, and a multinodular goiter with hyperthyroidism. She denied smoking and constitutional or respiratory symptoms aside from the skin lesions.

Preoperative platelet count was 75 000/μL (reference 150 000–400 000); after surgery it fell to 19 000/μL with active bleeding from the incisions. Pulse methylprednisolone and continuation of immunosuppression raised the platelet count to 47 000/μL and bleeding resolved.

Over the next weeks she developed ascites and bilateral pleural effusions. Paracentesis and thoracentesis yielded exudative fluid without pathogens or malignant cells. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.6 g/dL, white cells 14.9×10^9/L, platelets 3 000/μL, D-dimer 35 923 μg/L, fibrinogen 1.2 g/dL, C-reactive protein 5.97 mg/dL, free T4 3.02 ng/mL, and TSH 0.006 mIU/L. Blood and urine cultures grew Enterococcus faecium. She was diagnosed with disseminated intravascular coagulation in the setting of Kasabach-Merritt syndrome and sepsis, and received immunoglobulin, methylprednisolone, plasma, cryoprecipitate, and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Platelets stabilized at ~30 000/μL but she continued to lose weight and deteriorate.

A full-body CT scan showed no tumors, lymphadenopathy, or bone lesions. After weeks, Löwenstein–Jensen culture of bronchoalveolar lavage grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis; standard antitubercular therapy was begun but modified for hepatotoxicity. Four months after admission she was discharged on maintenance therapy.

Two months later she was readmitted with massive left pleural effusion, dyspnea, and respiratory insufficiency. Laboratory tests: hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL, platelets 3 000/μL, alkaline phosphatase 196 IU/L, GGT 308 IU/L, C-reactive protein 11.1 mg/dL. Bone marrow aspirate showed a reactive marrow without pathogens or malignant cells. She then developed acute gastrointestinal bleeding with hemoglobin falling to 4 g/dL; rescue therapy with rituximab briefly improved platelets and lowered the D-dimer. Despite all interventions, she died.

A 69-year-old woman presented with a 26-week history of a gradually enlarging right preauricular swelling. She reported no pain or facial weakness. On examination, there was a firm, immobile 3-cm mass near the lateral border of the right orbit in the region of the superior masseter; there was no cervical lymphadenopathy and examination of the oral cavity, larynx, and pharynx was normal. Ultrasound confirmed a homogeneous 3-cm lesion. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology showed sheets of undifferentiated small blue cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. Given the patient’s age and anatomical site, the provisional diagnosis was lymphoma.

A 64‐year‐old woman with hyperlipidemia and osteoporosis noted new constipation, thin‐caliber stools, and bloating but denied bleeding or urinary symptoms. Her last colonoscopy 12 years ago was normal. She had no smoking or alcohol history. Surgical history included tubal ligation and appendectomy. BMI was 20.49 kg/m2; family history was negative for breast, ovarian, or colon cancer. On examination, there was a mildly tender, midline suprapubic mass extending above the umbilicus without ascites. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood count, were normal.

Contrast‐free CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a large, heterogeneous pelvic mass without fat or calcification; the right adnexa was identified separately but the origin remained undetermined. MRI demonstrated a partially necrotic mass with heterogeneous enhancement abutting the anterior uterine wall without definitive invasion and closely related to the bladder wall, with enlarged vessels between the mass and bladder. Diffusion‐weighted imaging revealed areas of low ADC consistent with hypercellularity.

A 39-year-old man was referred for evaluation of an incidental cervical mass found on screening ultrasonography. He reported no compressive or systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a 3-cm soft, non-tender anterior neck mass that moved with swallowing. Serum calcium and PTH levels were within normal limits. Neck ultrasonography revealed a 50-mm cystic lesion situated behind the left thyroid lobe. Cervical MRI confirmed a well-circumscribed, non‐enhancing cystic lesion measuring 45×41×35 mm, exerting mass effect on the trachea and esophagus. Fine-needle aspiration yielded clear, watery fluid; cytologic examination showed a paucicellular specimen without cytologic signs of malignancy.

A 30-day-old girl, born at term via uncomplicated vaginal delivery, presented with a 5-day history of increasing dyspnea, hoarseness, feeding-associated cyanosis, and lethargy. She had been treated elsewhere for RSV pneumonia, requiring supplemental oxygen and parenteral feeding; however, feeding-induced cyanosis persisted, and she was referred for a second opinion. On arrival, her oxygen saturation was 89% on room air and improved to 100% with supplemental oxygen. She was alert, had no audible stridor at rest, and had only mild subcostal retractions. Heart and lung examinations were normal. Bedside nasoendoscopy by otolaryngology demonstrated left vocal fold paralysis with a 3 mm glottic gap; the right fold was mobile and no other abnormalities were noted. There were no palpable neck masses, and the ear and oral examinations were unremarkable. A chest radiograph showed mild air-space consolidation in the right perihilar and left retrocardiac regions, consistent with pneumonia. She was treated for presumed aspiration pneumonia and was weaned off supplemental oxygen after several days. To evaluate the unilateral vocal fold paralysis, a magnetic resonance imaging scan was performed.

A 46-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 2, with morbid obesity and hypertension but no thyroid disease, was referred for preoperative evaluation before bariatric surgery. Pelvic ultrasound revealed a right ovarian enlargement (57 × 38 mm) containing a peripherally located cystic lesion measuring approximately 44 × 43 mm; the left ovary appeared normal. Six months after gastric sleeve, repeat abdominopelvic ultrasound showed interval growth of the right ovarian cyst. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a right adnexal mass (79 × 66 × 72 mm) with a multiloculated, predominantly cystic architecture, reduced solid components, and two small nodules posterior to the external iliac vessels; there was apparent abutment of visceral peritoneum without clear separation. The patient was asymptomatic, with no abdominal pain or palpable mass. Serum CA-125 was 80 UI/mL (reference < 35 UI/mL). Thyroid function tests were normal (TSH 1.21 µUI/mL, fT4 0.94 ng/dL). Exploratory laparotomy revealed a well-defined right adnexal mass (~120 mm) without obvious invasion, and a right adnexectomy was performed.

A 35-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of a slow-growing, painless mass in the left lower one-third of the face. On examination, the mass measured approximately 3.0 × 2.0 cm at the left inferior border of the mandible; it was hard, immobile, fixed to underlying tissue, non-tender, deep, and without overlying skin changes. No regional lymphadenopathy was present, and systemic examination was unremarkable.

Routine blood tests and a chest radiograph were normal. Aspiration biopsy suggested granulomatous inflammation. High-resolution ultrasonography showed an ill-defined, hyperechoic mass abutting the left mandibular body. Computed tomography revealed a well-defined, encapsulated, fusiform soft-tissue–density lesion (HU 20–30) measuring 3.0 × 1.7 × 2.8 cm adjacent to the left mandible, with minimal enhancement and scalloping of the adjacent cortex.

A percutaneous core (Trucut) biopsy suggested a possible benign nerve sheath tumor. Clinical and radiologic impressions included intramuscular myxoma, myxoid liposarcoma, and benign nerve sheath tumor. An excisional biopsy was planned to establish a definitive diagnosis.

A 6-year-old boy was brought with a 1-month history of a slow-growing, nontender swelling on the right side of his face. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. Vital signs were stable. Extraoral examination showed mild facial asymmetry due to a hard, ill-defined swelling over the right mandibular body; the skin was normal. Temporomandibular joint movements were somewhat restricted, and small lymph nodes were palpable. Intraorally, there was obliteration of the right buccal sulcus in the molar region with buccal and lingual cortical expansion; the swelling was fluctuant, nontender, and fixed to bone. A panoramic radiograph revealed a large radiopaque mass surrounded by a radiolucent rim, extending from the region of the lower right first molar posteriorly along the mandibular body. Routine blood tests were within normal limits.

A 10-year-old boy presented with a four-month history of progressive left-sided nasal obstruction and intermittent epistaxis. He had an episode of fever 5 days earlier but was otherwise healthy, and coagulation studies were normal.

On anterior rhinoscopy, a fragile, lobular, red-grayish, smooth, polypoidal mass was seen arising anteroinferior to the left inferior turbinate and filling the nasal vestibule. Posterior rhinoscopy was normal. 

A CT scan of the nose and paranasal sinuses showed a soft-tissue opacity filling the vestibule of the left nasal cavity without sinus invasion or bony destruction. On postcontrast images, the lesion demonstrated intense enhancement.

A 30-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 2, at 39 weeks 4 days of gestation presented with severe acute upper abdominal pain. Her only prior pregnancy was a spontaneous term delivery of a healthy infant four years earlier. She had no significant medical or family history.  

At 18 weeks, she was hospitalized for similar pain; ultrasound showed a small amount of free intraperitoneal fluid, mild leukocytosis, normal CRP, and no signs of infection or surgical pathology; she was observed and discharged.  

At 27 weeks, she again had upper abdominal pain. She was hemodynamically stable (T 36.1 °C, pulse 97 bpm), hemoglobin 100 g/L, ultrasound demonstrated ascites up to 4.2 cm, dilatation of the right renal collecting system, and normal liver and biliary structures; cancer markers (CA-125, CA 27.29, CA 19-9, CEA) were normal; she was monitored and discharged.  

At 32 weeks, a third episode of severe generalized abdominal pain occurred; she was stable, abdominal exam was soft without peritoneal signs, ultrasound again showed free fluid, labs were unremarkable, and transvaginal ultrasound excluded placental abruption; she received NSAIDs and was discharged after symptom resolution.  

Now at 39 + 4 weeks, she presents with significantly more severe pain. Vital signs: pulse 97 bpm, blood pressure 154/119 mm Hg. Fetal heart tracing showed baseline 142 bpm with moderate decelerations < 80 bpm; no vaginal bleeding or contractions; Bishop score was 3; membranes intact.  

An emergency cesarean section was performed for fetal compromise. A live male infant was delivered (Apgar scores 5 and 8). Intraoperatively, 1000 mL of blood clots were evacuated. A heterogeneous 6 cm mass adherent to the right ovary and fallopian tube, with adhesions to the abdominal wall and cecum, was identified. The intestines showed deserosation and the ovaries appeared hyperstimulated. A right salpingectomy with excision of the mass and peritoneal biopsies was performed and specimens were sent for histologic examination.  

Postoperative chest, abdominal, and pelvic CT scans showed no metastases. Serum β-hCG on postoperative day 1 was 139,482 IU/L.

A 25-year-old nulliparous woman with no significant medical history presented in June 2009 with acute onset of severe abdominal pain. On examination, she had a large, fixed pelvic mass measuring approximately 20 × 18 cm. Laboratory evaluation showed an inflammatory syndrome with an elevated C-reactive protein and accelerated erythrocyte sedimentation rate; serum calcium was 2.29 mmol/L (normal 2.25–2.60 mmol/L), and CA 125 was 186.8 IU/mL (approximately 5 × normal). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 24 × 18 × 15 cm heterogeneous cystic and solid mass arising from the left ovary, moderate peritoneal fluid with peritoneal thickening, and mild bilateral hydronephrosis. The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy, which revealed an irregular, highly vascular solid-cystic tumor of the left ovary measuring approximately 40 × 35 cm; the right ovary appeared normal. A total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and multiple peritoneal biopsies were performed.

A man in his 70s was referred for evaluation of worsening right‐sided facial edema of 4 months’ duration. At onset, he experienced fever and generalized malaise, which subsequently resolved. The edema progressively involved his right eyelid, cheek, postauricular skin, scalp, and anterior neck, and serous drainage soaked through his pillow at night. He denied pruritus, dysphagia, or dyspnea but reported a 14‐lb weight loss and decreased appetite. He had completed two courses of clindamycin and was taking cephalexin, 500 mg twice daily, for a suspected infectious etiology, with only mild improvement. On examination, there was erythematous, nonpitting, indurated edema of the right face and neck with serous drainage over the malar area and a superficial erosion on the postauricular skin; the area was warm and tender. Flexible laryngoscopy was unremarkable. A neck ultrasound did not show thrombosis of the neck veins. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head showed patent vascular structures and diffuse right‐sided skin and soft tissue thickening with several small enlarged right‐sided lymph nodes.

A 53-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of indurated, erythematous, draining nodules on her right and left calves that were moderately painful and pruritic. Two months before the skin eruption, she had an isolated episode of vomiting and intermittent right upper quadrant abdominal pain. She reported chronic gastroesophageal reflux managed with a proton pump inhibitor for 3 months. She denied weight loss or fevers and had a history of spontaneous pneumothorax 1 year earlier. On initial evaluation, laboratory studies showed a lipase level of 8,880 U/L, an amylase level within normal limits, and normal aspartate and alanine aminotransferase levels. A punch biopsy of a nodule demonstrated lobular panniculitis with mixed infiltrate and basophilic deposits and enzymatic fat necrosis with characteristic ghost cells. Given the severity of her presentation, she was started on a prednisone taper and referred for imaging. Computed tomography of the abdomen revealed three liver masses (two up to 10 cm and one 2 cm) without evidence of cirrhosis. There was some atrophy of the tail of the pancreas but no obvious pancreatic mass.

A 76-year-old woman noted a slowly enlarging mass adjacent to her right lateral malleolus over 3 months, causing discomfort with shoes and walking. She denied trauma or infection. On examination, there was a firm, 4 cm retromalleolar mass without overlying skin changes or regional lymphadenopathy and no sensorimotor deficits.  
Standard ankle radiographs showed only soft-tissue swelling, with no osteolysis. Ultrasound revealed a solid, heterogeneous, multilobulated mass measuring 40 × 29 mm within Kager’s fat pad, between the Achilles and peroneal tendons, with moderate superficial vascularity on Doppler.  
CT of the ankle demonstrated bone edema of the posterior talar process, a focal lateral talocrural arthropathy, moderate joint effusion, and mechanical synovitis.  
MRI confirmed a well-delineated fibrous tissue lesion in the posterolateral soft tissues of the ankle measuring 40 × 33 × 42 mm, abutting the Achilles tendon and peroneal retinaculum. There was no intralesional hemosiderin. The lesion showed heterogeneous progressive enhancement without washout.

A 61-year-old woman with no personal or family history of breast cancer noted a palpable lump in the right retroareolar area. On examination, there was a well-defined, round, indeterminate but probably benign mass.  
Digital mammography showed a 37 mm round mass with indistinct margins in the right retroareolar region (BI-RADS 3).  
Breast ultrasound revealed a 30 mm oval, hypoechoic, partially circumscribed and partially microlobulated mass without posterior acoustic features; the axilla was normal.  
Ultrasound-guided core biopsy (14 G) identified a cellular fibroepithelial lesion, possible benign phyllodes.  
Surgical excision demonstrated disorganized mammary glandular elements, adipose tissue, and stromal smooth muscle differentiation without atypia, consistent with benign myoid hamartoma; margins were clear, and the patient was discharged.  
Two years later, screening mammography was normal. Three years after that (five years from the initial diagnosis), she presented with a new palpable irregular mass in the same region.  
Mammography showed a 40 mm spiculated mass in the right retroareolar area (BI-RADS 4). Ultrasound demonstrated a 34 mm irregular, spiculated hypoechoic mass without posterior acoustic features; the axilla remained normal.  
Repeat core biopsy identified a fibroepithelial lesion “consistent with the previous diagnosis of myoid hamartoma with no evidence of malignancy.”

An 8-year-old girl was evaluated for a left ocular mass that had been present since birth but had recently enlarged, causing discomfort and a foreign-body sensation. Her systemic history was unremarkable, and there was no history of trauma. Visual acuity was 6/6 in both eyes, refraction was normal, and intraocular pressures were 14 mmHg in the right eye and 12 mmHg in the left eye. Examination of the left eye revealed a superotemporal subconjunctival mass, approximately 6 × 6 mm in diameter, whitish, hard in consistency, located 10 mm from the limbus. The overlying conjunctiva was intact, and dilated blood vessels surrounded the lesion. The provisional diagnoses were lipodermoid and a subconjunctival foreign body.

A 33-year-old man with no known comorbidities presented with sudden onset of headache and severe central chest pain radiating to the back. He arrived 3½ hours after symptom onset and remained in severe pain. Blood pressure was 180/125 mmHg, heart rate 105 bpm, temperature 36.1 °C, oxygen saturation 98%, and respiratory rate 28/min. Arterial blood gas showed pH 7.14, pO₂ 15.4 kPa, pCO₂ 4.5 kPa, bicarbonate 12 mEq/L, base excess –16 mmol/L, and lactate 12 mmol/L. A 12-lead ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm with slight ST-segment depressions in leads V4–V6. Bedside echocardiography revealed regional hypokinesia of the lateral left ventricle and an estimated LVEF of 20–30%. Laboratory studies showed a troponin T concentration of 300 ng/L, a white blood cell count of 39×10⁹/L, and a normal C-reactive protein level. An immediate thoracic and abdominal CT scan was negative for aortic dissection or large pulmonary embolism but showed a 6 cm mass in the left adrenal gland. During the first hours of observation, the patient’s symptoms spontaneously resolved, his vital signs normalized, and repeat blood gas analysis showed pH 7.33 and lactate 5.6 mmol/L. The evening before admission he had consumed multiple energy drinks. He reported two similar episodes 9 and 4 years earlier, each with headache, back pain, hypertension, and elevated lactate that resolved within hours, and no diagnosis was established at those times.

A 21-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of left hip pain that began after a trivial fall. He reported an inability to perform strenuous activities such as running or jumping. On examination, terminal ranges of hip motion were painful, the FABER test was positive on the left, and he was able to perform an active straight-leg raise. Plain radiographs of the left hip showed an oval, well-defined, eccentric osteolytic lesion along the inferomedial subcapital region of the femoral neck; there was no periosteal reaction or calcification. MRI of the left hip demonstrated a cystic-appearing lesion involving the synovial lining near the head-and-neck junction of the femur.

A 67-year-old man was admitted with a 1-month history of recurrent gross hematuria, dysuria, left testicular pain and enlargement, lumbar and sacral back pain, night sweats, and a 3 kg unintentional weight loss. He had occupational asbestos exposure and a body mass index of 37.8 kg/m2.  

On examination, he had bilateral lower‐extremity edema and a uniformly enlarged, tender left testis without discrete nodules. Scrotal ultrasonography showed diffuse enlargement of the left testis without focal lesions.  

Laboratory studies revealed a serum β-subunit human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) concentration of 644.4 mIU/mL; lactate dehydrogenase, α-fetoprotein, and prostate-specific antigen were within normal limits.  

Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 62 mm mass in the posterior prostate gland infiltrating the seminal vesicles and anterior rectal wall, with bilateral iliac lymph node enlargement. Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis confirmed pelvic lymph node metastases.

A 45-year-old man with a history of multiple myeloma presented with bilateral, painful proptosis and photophobia. He was initially diagnosed with multiple myeloma several years earlier and treated with thalidomide, dexamethasone, and bortezomib. Two years after diagnosis he relapsed with testicular and clavicular plasmacytomas treated with orchiopexy, radiation, and additional chemotherapy regimens, including VDT-PACE. Four years after his initial diagnosis, he developed fever and malaise; labs showed elevated monoclonal lambda light chains and IgG, and he was admitted for aggressive chemotherapy. During that admission he noted worsening eye redness and was treated with topical naphazoline/pheniramine drops. One week later, ophthalmology evaluation showed visual acuity of 20/80 in both eyes, severely limited extraocular movements on the right and mild limitation on the left, intraocular pressures of 22 mm Hg bilaterally, marked bilateral proptosis with greater chemosis on the right, mechanical ectropion, and exposure keratoconjunctivitis of the right cornea.  
A CT scan of the brain and orbits revealed multiple large intraorbital masses suggestive of metastases and a hyperattenuating extra-axial mass in the right temporal lobe with vasogenic edema. The patient was started on IV vancomycin, piperacillin–tazobactam, and acyclovir. MRI of the orbits, performed one week after the CT, demonstrated bilateral enhancing intraorbital masses causing proptosis and mass effect on the globes and optic nerves without bone destruction. Repeat examination revealed visual acuity of 20/400 in both eyes, a 2–3+ afferent pupillary defect in the right eye, and intraocular pressures of 28 mm Hg OD and 30 mm Hg OS. Concern arose for orbital compartment syndrome.

A 45-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of an isolated swelling of the left arm that had progressively increased in size and pain without fever, weight loss, or history of trauma. He had no significant medical or surgical history. On examination, there was a 5 cm firm, well-defined, painful, mobile mass on the lateral aspect of the left upper arm without overlying skin changes. Ultrasound revealed a fatty tissue tumor with clear margins relative to the surrounding muscle. MRI showed a 5 cm highly vascularized mass in the left arm with T1- and T2-weighted hyperintensity and contrast enhancement after gadolinium injection, features suggestive of a well-differentiated liposarcoma.

An 84-year-old right-hand–dominant man with a history of total thyroidectomy in 2007 for thyroid carcinoma presented with a 2-month history of increasing pain and swelling at the distal part of the right thumb. He denied any history of trauma to the hand and had no prior joint pain. Physical examination revealed swelling of the distal thumb without erythema or warmth. Laboratory studies showed normal complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein values. Plain radiographs demonstrated soft-tissue swelling and lysis of the distal phalanx of the thumb, findings described as “compatible with infection priority or metastatic disease.” A technetium bone scan revealed no other pathologic lesions.

A 60-year-old woman with a history of orbital extranodal MALT-type marginal zone B-cell lymphoma treated with rituximab presented with a 3–4 cm tender, indurated, slightly erythematous mass on the left side of her neck. She denied fever, weight loss, or night sweats. CT of the neck showed a soft tissue mass in the left lateral mid-neck extending into the overlying subcutaneous tissue and skin that was not seen on prior scans. Excisional biopsy revealed large pleomorphic malignant cells admixed with inflammatory cells, centered in the deep dermis with satellite nodules in the superficial dermis, and no identifiable lymph nodes in the specimen. Immunohistochemical staining showed malignant cells strongly positive for CD30, CD15, PAX5, and CD79a, and negative for CD45; CD20 and EBER were negative, and there was no overlying skin ulceration. Staging PET-CT and bone marrow biopsy were negative for nodal or systemic involvement.

A 35-year-old woman was evaluated for what was thought to be an intramural pregnancy. Her obstetric history included an elective cesarean delivery in 2016, an abortion for a blighted ovum (histology unremarkable) in October 2020, and a repeated evacuation 7 days later without histologic sampling. Two months after the abortion, a urine pregnancy test was positive. Transvaginal ultrasound revealed a 30 mm hypoechoic lesion in the posterior uterine wall with a peripheral structure resembling a yolk sac. Color Doppler imaging demonstrated well-defined peripheral and central blood flow. Her serum β-hCG was 1092 mIU/ml, and an intramural pregnancy was diagnosed. She underwent open resection of the uterine lesion and excision of a right ovarian cyst, with an uneventful postoperative course. One week after surgery, her β-hCG had fallen to 245.7 mIU/ml and returned to normal by 2 months.

An 11-year-old boy presented with a swelling on the left lower border of the mandible of 3 cm × 3.5 cm, extending from 5 cm posterior to the corner of the mouth toward the ramus, superiorly to an imaginary line from the tragus to the mouth corner, and involving the inferior border of the mandible. Orthopantomogram showed an irregular, well-defined radiolucent area with a mixed radiopaque mass measuring 2 cm × 2.5 cm in the region of the lower border of the mandible. A CT scan of the region showed no perforation of the lingual cortex.

A 66-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and morbid obesity noted an 18-kg intentional weight loss over recent months. He discovered a mass in his right pre-auricular region measuring approximately 3 × 3 cm. On examination, the mass was firm, fixed, and non-tender; facial nerve function was intact and there was no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy.  
An ultrasound of the area reported a necrotic lymph node. Subsequent MRI of the head and neck revealed a 27 × 28 mm ovoid heterogeneous lesion in the right parotid gland that was hypointense on T1, isointense on T2, with well-defined borders and an internal area of hemorrhage. The radiologic interpretation was a probable pleomorphic adenoma with hemorrhagic transformation.  
The patient underwent a right superficial parotidectomy with preservation of the facial nerve, and the gland was excised with a 4 × 4 cm mass. A surgical drain was placed.

A 35-year-old woman presented with visual field abnormality in her left eye. Best-corrected visual acuity was 1.0 in both eyes. Slit-lamp examination of the left anterior segment was normal. Fundus examination of the left eye revealed a yellowish, dome-shaped choroidal mass approximately four disc diameters in size temporal to the macula, associated with exudative retinal detachment. The right eye was unremarkable. Fluorescein and indocyanine green angiography demonstrated pooling of dye within the lesion. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left orbit showed a 5.3×5.7×6.0 mm mass with high signal on T1-weighted and gadolinium-enhanced sequences and low signal on STIR. Computed tomography revealed a hyperdense lesion, and B-scan ultrasonography showed high internal reflectivity with acoustic shadowing. Single-photon emission computed tomography with 123I-IMP at 24 hours showed no uptake. Serum 5-S-cysteinyldopa was elevated at 9.5 nmol/L (normal range 1.5–8.0 nmol/L). These findings were interpreted as compatible with amelanotic malignant melanoma, but calcification was also suspected.

A 25-year-old African woman presented with a 2-year history of a slowly enlarging gingival mass in the anterior mandible. She was in good general health with unremarkable extra-oral findings. Intraorally, there was a solitary, well-defined, roughly oval swelling arising from the attached and free labial gingiva overlying teeth 33 and 34. The lesion measured 2 × 2 cm, was firm, non-tender, had a smooth surface, intact mucosa of normal color, and there were no symptoms of pain, bleeding, discharge, or numbness. Oral hygiene was inadequate. A periapical radiograph demonstrated minor arc-shaped bone loss adjacent to teeth 33 and 34. Based on these clinical and radiographic findings, a diagnosis of pyogenic granuloma was made, with a differential that included peripheral ossifying fibroma, peripheral giant cell granuloma, and fibrous epulis; rare considerations were benign connective tissue tumors and peripheral odontogenic neoplasms. The lesion was excised under local anesthesia and submitted for histopathological examination.

A 37-year-old man presented with a 4-year history of an asymptomatic lump in the right lower neck. He had no significant past medical history, trauma, skin malignancies, or family history of cancer. On examination, there was a hard mass in the inferior third of the right sternocleidomastoid muscle. Fine-needle aspiration showed atypical spindle cells suspicious for malignancy. A core biopsy revealed a low-grade spindle cell neoplasm with a fascicular growth pattern and moderate atypia. Computed tomography of the head and neck demonstrated a 44×27×24 mm well-defined, homogeneously enhancing mass in the right supraclavicular region at the level of the thyroid gland. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a lobulated lesion that was mildly hyperintense on T1, markedly hyperintense on T2, with diffuse enhancement and moderate restricted diffusion; the mass was confined to the sternocleidomastoid muscle without locoregional spread. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. The lesion was widely excised with a cuff of muscle. Macroscopic examination revealed a sharply circumscribed, encapsulated white-to-yellow intramuscular tumor with a whorled cut surface. Histologically, it was a well-circumscribed spindle cell neoplasm with a thick fibrous capsule, composed of short fascicles of moderately pleomorphic cells with nuclear hyperchromasia and conspicuous nucleoli, admixed with lymphocytes and xanthoma cells. Immunohistochemical studies showed diffuse desmin and smooth muscle actin expression, focal myogenin expression, and negative staining for S100, cytokeratin AE1/AE3, and ALK1; in situ hybridization for Epstein–Barr virus–encoded RNA was also negative.

A 50-year-old male farmer and former heavy smoker (10 pack-years) presented with a 1-year history of a gradually enlarging, non-tender left lateral neck mass, initially about 2×2 cm. He also reported chronic constipation but denied abdominal pain, changes in stool caliber, melena, or hematochezia. He had no lower urinary tract symptoms, no thyroid symptoms, and no family history of malignancy.

At a local hospital, neck ultrasound showed multiple coalescing complex foci in the left lateral neck (largest 2.8 cm) with perilesional Doppler uptake. The thyroid gland was normal in size and echotexture; thyroid function tests were normal. Fine-needle aspiration of the neck mass revealed atypical epithelial cells. Digital rectal examination was unremarkable.

When he presented to our center, he had unintentional weight loss, occasional hypogastric discomfort, persistent constipation, and the neck mass had grown to approximately 7×7.5 cm. Abdominopelvic CT with contrast demonstrated markedly enlarged retroperitoneal lymph nodes encasing the aorta and iliac vessels, bilateral hydronephrosis, and a mass inseparable from both the prostate and rectum. A small benign-appearing liver cyst was noted, and mixed lytic and blastic bone lesions were seen throughout the spine, pelvis, left femur, and ribs. Carcinoembryonic antigen was 5.94 ng/mL. Chest radiography showed a left neck soft-tissue density extending into the thorax, displacing the trachea to the right.

Colonoscopy revealed a circumferential, partially obstructing mass 10–20 cm from the anal verge with nodular, friable, edematous mucosa. A pediatric colonoscope passed beyond the narrowing to normal-appearing mucosa; small rectal polyps were seen beyond the mass. Multiple biopsies of the circumferential mass were taken. Histopathology showed medium to large atypical cells with a high nuclear‐to‐cytoplasmic ratio, poorly formed glands, pleomorphic hyperchromatic nuclei, and prominent nucleoli, consistent with a poorly differentiated carcinoma.

A 3-year-old girl presented with a one-month history of non-productive cough and recurrent bronchial infections despite symptomatic treatment and antibiotics. There was no significant family history or underlying medical illness. On examination, she appeared unwell; oxygen saturation was 87% on room air, and breath sounds were absent at the left lung base. She was afebrile with no focal neurological deficits. A chest radiograph showed an opaque mass occupying the left hemithorax with contralateral mediastinal deviation. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a large, well-defined mass filling nearly the entire left hemithorax, with heterogeneous enhancement, associated pleural effusion, and no evidence of costal erosion or diaphragmatic invasion. A scan-guided needle biopsy was performed, and histological analysis suggested rhabdomyosarcoma. Staging studies ruled out other tumor localizations.

A 64-year-old man with stage IA1 lung adenocarcinoma in remission (radiation 5 months earlier), prior pulmonary coccidioidomycosis treated 5 years ago, chronic sarcoidosis on prednisone 10 mg daily, and COVID-19 infection 2 months earlier presented with 4 months of generalized weakness, nonproductive cough, headache, and self-reported fevers up to 106 °F on the day of admission. He also had two episodes of sore throat over the preceding 2 months treated unsuccessfully with antibiotics. He was diagnosed with sarcoidosis 2 years earlier after inguinal lymphadenopathy, night sweats, and a lymph node biopsy showing noncaseating granulomas with a negative infectious workup. He was a former firefighter with significant smoke exposure and a 30-year history of 3–4 cigars per day.

On examination, he was pale and dry, with conjunctival pallor, dry mucous membranes, non-tender submandibular and inguinal lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. There were no focal neurologic deficits. Laboratory studies revealed pancytopenia with an absolute neutrophil count of 670 cells/µL and an elevated C-reactive protein of 80.5 mg/L. A fluorine-18–fluorodeoxyglucose PET-CT scan demonstrated new FDG-avid lymphadenopathy in the cervical, mediastinal, and inguinal regions.

A 33-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of a thyroid nodule that had recently increased in size. She had a family history of thyroid disease but no history of radiation exposure or prior malignancy. Thyroid-stimulating hormone levels were normal. Thyroid ultrasound revealed a 3.9 cm solid, isoechoic nodule nearly replacing the right lobe. An ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration was performed. Diff-Quik smears showed abundant thin colloid and a moderate number of follicular cells arranged in honeycombed and syncytial patterns. Some follicular cells exhibited nuclear overlapping of enlarged round to ovoid nuclei, small prominent nucleoli, and a few nuclear grooves; rare intranuclear inclusions and occasional multinucleated giant cells were also identified. Papanicolaou-stained smears revealed cells with fine powdery chromatin and small nucleoli. The FNA was reported as suspicious for papillary thyroid carcinoma.

A 41-year-old woman noted a painless lump in her right breast. On examination, there was a firm, irregular, fixed mass measuring approximately 2.5 cm in the upper outer quadrant extending toward the axilla. Ultrasonography revealed a 2.8 × 1.7 cm hypoechoic, polylobulated lesion with irregular hyperechoic margins and intralesional vascularity; bilateral axillary lymphadenopathy was also present. MRI demonstrated an enhancing mass in the axillary prolongation with rapid contrast wash-in and plateau kinetics. A vacuum-assisted core biopsy was performed. Histologic sections showed large areas of necrosis and numerous atypical round to spindled cells, sometimes in small clusters, within an amorphous basophilic, myxoid to vaguely chondroid stroma. Immunohistochemical studies revealed strong, diffuse positivity for vimentin; focal positivity for pankeratin; and negative staining for CK7, CK5/6, S100, estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, EMA, and HER2.

A 77-year-old woman was admitted with a 1-month history of recurrent, painless gross hematuria. Two weeks prior, she underwent ultrasonography at a local hospital, which revealed bilateral renal calculi; urinalysis was positive for leukocytes. Treatment with cephalosporin was ineffective. She had a 15-year history of renal calculi. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 10.0 g/dL, leukocyte count 12.2 × 10^9 cells/L, and numerous red blood cells in the urine; three urine cytopathologic analyses were negative for malignant cells. Abdominal ultrasound confirmed bilateral stones but did not show a mass. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a 4.1 cm × 3.2 cm slightly heterogeneously enhancing mass in the middle pole of the left kidney and ipsilateral adrenal enlargement, suspected to represent metastatic disease.  
Preoperative diagnosis: A malignancy, particularly renal cancer, was highly suspected.

A 2-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of a 4-month history of fixed convergent strabismus in her left eye and an abnormal red reflex noted 2 months after the strabismus began. Visual acuity was normal in the right eye and only light perception in the left eye. The Hirschberg test showed 10° esotropia in the left eye. The anterior chamber was formed, the lens was clear, and there was iris neovascularization in the lower periphery. Biomicroscopy revealed a yellow retrocrystalline lesion with whitish dots suggestive of calcification and hemorrhage, obstructing the fundoscopic view of the left eye. The right eye examination was normal.

The patient was born full term by vaginal delivery, with a normal red reflex at birth and no family history of eye disease. She occasionally visited a rural property with animals but had no exposure to puppies. Laboratory tests, including serology for Toxocara canis, were normal.

Ocular ultrasound of the left eye showed a reduced axial length of 19 mm; a hyperechogenic septal lesion connecting the papillary to the retrocrystalline region; hyperechogenic punctate lesions with posterior acoustic attenuation indicating calcification in the retrocrystalline area; a posteriorly tented retinal detachment with peripapillary retina adhered to the septal structure causing traction; and subretinal punctate echoes suggestive of cellular material. Doppler examination demonstrated internal flow within the intraocular septal structure. MRI of the orbits showed a retrolental septal structure with intermediate T1 signal intensity, low T2 signal intensity, contrast enhancement, and subretinal cellular material consistent with hemorrhage. Both optic nerves appeared intact in diameter and signal.

A 20-year-old man presented with a 5-year history of progressively worsening generalized sweating. He denied fever, tremor, flushing, palpitations, headache, diarrhea, chest pain, or abdominal pain. His body mass index was 28.9 kg/m2. Vital signs were notable for blood pressure 138/82 mm Hg and heart rate 60 beats per minute. Laboratory evaluation showed a white blood cell count of 11 000 cells/µL with a normal differential and a fasting glucose of 111 mg/dL. Thyroid function tests were normal (free thyroxine, 1.0 ng/dL [0.78–1.33 ng/dL]), and a purified protein derivative skin test for tuberculosis was negative. A 24-hour urine collection revealed norepinephrine 1002 µg/24 h (reference, 0–135 µg/24 h), epinephrine 10 µg/24 h (0–20 µg/24 h), and dopamine 301 µg/24 h (0–510 µg/24 h). Plasma studies showed normetanephrine 2873 pg/mL (0–145 pg/mL), norepinephrine 2869 pg/mL (0–874 pg/mL), with normal plasma metanephrine, epinephrine, and dopamine levels.

A 36-year-old man presented with 2 months of painless jaundice, new-onset hyperglycemia, and a 10-kg weight loss without diarrhea or vomiting. He had been diagnosed previously with autoimmune pancreatitis elsewhere and had no response to steroids. He smoked 10 pack-years and had no other significant personal or family history. On examination he appeared cachexic and mildly jaundiced; a nontender 5-cm epigastric mass was palpable, and the abdomen was soft with normal bowel sounds. Laboratory studies showed a normal white blood cell count, mild anemia (118 g/L), thrombocytosis (476 ×10^9/L), elevated ALT (97 U/L), AST (46 U/L), alkaline phosphatase (377 U/L), γ-GT (337 U/L), total bilirubin (107.6 μmol/L), direct bilirubin (77.6 μmol/L), indirect bilirubin (30.2 μmol/L), and low albumin (31.8 g/L). ANA and rheumatoid factor were negative; IgG4, amylase, and lipase were normal. Tumor markers showed elevated AFP (475.6 ng/mL) and CA-125 (77.1 U/mL) with normal CEA (2.2 μg/L) and CA 19-9 (15.94 U/mL). Hepatitis B and C and HIV serologies were negative. MRI of the abdomen revealed a diffusely enlarged, “sausage-shaped” pancreas with loss of lobular structure; the lesion was isointense to hypointense on T1, isointense to hyperintense on T2, and had a mixed DWI signal with central necrosis. A distinct hyperintense rim demonstrated delayed enhancement, giving a capsule appearance. MRCP showed upstream dilation of the proximal common bile duct and intrahepatic ducts from strictures of the main pancreatic duct and distal common bile duct. A percutaneous ultrasound-guided pancreatic biopsy was then obtained.

A 24-year-old unmarried man presents with acute left testicular pain. He has no prior medical history. On examination, there is a firm mass at the upper pole of the left testis. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, creatinine, prothrombin time, alpha-fetoprotein, beta-human chorionic gonadotropin, and lactate dehydrogenase, are all within normal limits. Scrotal Doppler ultrasound reveals a 29×13×21 mm heterogeneous, hypoechoic mass with blurred margins and small calcification foci in the upper anterior aspect of the left testis, with no evidence of hypervascularity or epididymal or scrotal wall inflammation.

A 48-year-old woman was found to have a hepatic cystic lesion during a routine exam in October 2022. Imaging suggested a simple cyst and she underwent laparoscopic fenestration with drainage; pathology at that time showed a benign cyst. Follow-up CT in June 2023 demonstrated an enlarged cyst in the left lobe and intrahepatic bile duct dilation, but she was asymptomatic and remained under observation.

In September 2023, she developed progressive abdominal distension, generalized jaundice, and dark urine without pruritus, pale stools, chills, or fever. Laboratory studies showed alanine aminotransferase 109 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 78 U/L, total bilirubin 136.7 μmol/L, direct bilirubin 99.6 μmol/L, and CA 19-9 96.9 U/mL. 

Abdominal ultrasound revealed a large anechoic cystic lesion (11.2 × 9.6 cm) in segments 4/5 with poor acoustic transmission, no internal Doppler flow, and marked dilation of intrahepatic bile ducts. Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI confirmed a well-defined 10.8 × 9.5 cm intrahepatic cystic mass without enhancement, mildly lobulated, compressing the confluence of the left and right hepatic ducts and causing bile duct dilation.

On 26 September 2023, ultrasound-guided cyst aspiration yielded clear, colorless fluid and temporarily relieved her abdominal distension. She was discharged with a drainage catheter.

On 12 October 2023, she noted yellow-brown drainage fluid at ≈500 mL/day and was readmitted with suspected biliary leakage. Repeat labs showed ALT 36 U/L, AST 44 U/L, GGT 52 U/L, ALP 122 U/L, total bilirubin 213.4 μmol/L, and direct bilirubin 160.8 μmol/L, confirming worsening obstructive jaundice.

A 70-year-old Asian man presented with a 2-year history of intermittent dysuria characterized by a thin urine stream, decreased urinary volume, prolonged urination, and a sense of incomplete emptying, accompanied by urinary urgency and frequency. His symptoms had gradually worsened over the past few months. He had no significant past medical or family history. On physical examination, vital signs were stable, and the only abnormal finding was a diffusely enlarged prostate on digital rectal examination. Laboratory tests revealed a serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level of 0.404 ng/mL (reference range 0–4 ng/mL). Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging showed a mass occupying the peripheral zone of the prostate, with apparent invasion of both seminal vesicles, the posterior bladder wall, and the anterior rectal wall, as well as enlarged pelvic lymph nodes.

A 4½-year-old girl presented with a 6-week history of weight loss, decreased appetite, and subsequent development of fever and abdominal pain. On examination she appeared pale, undernourished, and had a low-grade fever; other vital signs and the remainder of the physical exam were unremarkable. Laboratory testing revealed elevated LDH (670 U/l), ferritin (146 ng/ml), NSE (260.2 µg/l), C-reactive protein (65 mg/l), and D-dimer (422 µg/l), with hemoglobin 10.4 g/dl and MCV 71 fl. Urine homovanillic acid and vanillylmandelic acid levels were not elevated.
