Abdominal MRI showed an 8.8×7.9×9.4 cm retroperitoneal mass arising from the upper pole of the left kidney with noninfiltrative growth but extension into the left renal vein and inferior vena cava; no calcifications or vessel encasement were seen. Ipsilateral lymph nodes were mildly enlarged. Chest X-ray and echocardiogram were normal, but chest CT revealed multiple small bilateral pulmonary lesions suggestive of metastases and occlusion of both inferior lobe arteries by thrombus or tumor. Meta-iodobenzylguanidine scan, bone scan, and cranial MRI were all negative.

A 39-year-old woman presented after an accidental fall causing an occipital laceration. She reported months of fatigue, polyuria, polydipsia, intermittent abdominal pain, and severe weight loss. On examination, blood pressure was 110/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and cardiac auscultation revealed no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Surface ECG showed sinus rhythm at 85 bpm with diffuse low QRS-wave amplitude and QT prolongation (600 ms by Bazett’s formula). Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 18,590/mm3 (70% neutrophils), C-reactive protein of 154 mg/L, procalcitonin of 2.64 ng/mL, and creatinine of 1.75 mg/dL. 

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a large pericardial effusion without tamponade and marked thickening of the right atrial free wall (1.65 cm) and interatrial septum; left ventricular systolic function was preserved. Abdominal CT revealed bilateral hydronephrosis, thickening of the perirenal soft tissue, and adrenal gland enlargement.

During her first hospital night, she had a self-limited episode of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with Torsade-de-Pointes morphology. Continuous monitoring then showed junctional rhythm at 50 bpm. Over subsequent days she developed persistent QT prolongation, paroxysms of atrial fibrillation with slow ventricular response, extreme sinus bradycardia, bouts of junctional rhythm, and recurrent Torsade-de-Pointes. A temporary pacemaker was placed, stabilizing the rhythm, but she later experienced ventricular fibrillation requiring external DC shock.

Brain MRI revealed T2 and FLAIR hyperintensity of the neurohypophysis, cerebellum, and brain stem. Her marked polyuria and polydipsia promptly responded to desmopressin, confirming central diabetes insipidus.

A 29-year-old man with a history of neurofibromatosis type 1, diagnosed at age 28 due to multiple café-au-lait spots, cutaneous neurofibromas, and a positive family history, underwent routine surveillance CT. He was asymptomatic with no abdominal pain or gastrointestinal complaints. Physical examination confirmed multiple neurofibromas and café-au-lait macules on the trunk and extremities. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 8540/µL and a C-reactive protein level of 0.00 mg/dL. Routine blood counts, biochemistry, and coagulation studies were unremarkable. Tumor markers were within normal limits: CEA 1.1 U/mL, CA19-9 5.1 U/mL, AFP 3.0 ng/mL, NSE 9.0 ng/mL, and pro-GRP 44.3 pg/mL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed an enlarged appendix with a diffusely thickened wall that was well enhanced in the delayed phase; there were no enlarged lymph nodes or other intra-abdominal masses. No central or peripheral nervous system tumors were detected. Colonoscopy demonstrated hyperplastic lymphoid tissue in the terminal ileum but no lesion at the appendiceal orifice. A barium enema study showed no dilation or filling defects of the appendix. Given the suspicion of an appendiceal neoplasm, a laparoscopic appendectomy was planned for diagnostic treatment.

An 11-year-old boy was evaluated for progressive midline facial ulceration. Six months earlier, he had sustained a nasal fracture with septal hematoma treated surgically, with complete recovery after one month. Three months after the injury, an ulcer resembling an insect bite appeared on his nose; over two weeks it enlarged and was accompanied by nasal obstruction and purulent discharge. He was initially treated for chronic sinusitis without improvement.

On admission, he had fever, headache, appetite loss, disfiguring erosion of the nose, bilateral periorbital swelling, conjunctivitis, and purulent nasal discharge. There were no intraoral lesions or regional lymphadenopathy. Chest examination and radiographs were normal.

CT imaging showed an irregular, enhancing lesion involving both nasal cavities and the ethmoid sinus with erosion and perforation of the nasal septum; the brain parenchyma appeared normal.

Laboratory evaluation revealed leukocytosis and lymphocytosis. HIV serology and syphilis testing were negative. A culture of the purulent discharge grew fungal hyphae, and Amphotericin-B was initiated. 

A first biopsy during debridement showed mucoid material with a fibrinopurulent exudate and no evidence of malignancy. A second biopsy revealed only nonspecific inflammation.

A 91-year-old woman was admitted with a 2-month history of progressive leg, abdominal, and breast edema, along with asthenia and declining ability to perform daily activities. Her medical history included Parkinson disease, mild cognitive impairment, polymyalgia rheumatica, and diverticulitis. Home medications were omeprazole, levodopa/carbidopa, furosemide, quetiapine, rivastigmine, and allopurinol. She was partly dependent (Barthel index 60/100) and required assistance to walk.

On examination, there was severe pitting edema of the legs, abdomen, and breasts, and telangiectatic vascular lesions on the chest, back, and abdomen. Heart rate and rhythm were regular; lung auscultation was normal; there were no signs of ascites.

Laboratory studies showed a normocytic anemia (RBC count 3.00×10^12/L, hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, MCV 92 fL), elevated lactate dehydrogenase (969 U/L), elevated ferritin (892 ng/mL), and NT-proBNP of 1800 pg/mL. Total serum protein was 6.2 g/dL with normal albumin. Tumor markers were negative. Serology for Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, Rickettsia, and Leishmania was negative.

Chest radiography was normal. A body CT scan demonstrated subcutaneous edema of the lateral abdominal wall, pelvis, and lower extremities; the deep venous system was permeable; there were no solid lesions and no pleural, pericardial, or peritoneal effusions. Transthoracic echocardiography and breast ultrasound were unremarkable. Other possible causes such as cardiopathy, liver disease, renal impairment, malnutrition, rheumatologic conditions, and pharmacologic toxicity were excluded. Diuretic therapy led to mild improvement of edema and a 10-kg weight loss, but the asthenia, functional impairment, and telangiectasias persisted.

A 58-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of occasional epigastric pain, decreased food intake, and nausea. Her medical history was notable for hypertension (11 years), type 2 diabetes mellitus (11 years), hypothyroidism (38 years), a prior cholecystectomy, and hysterectomy. She had no history of alcohol or drug use, and her only allergy was to dipyrone. There was a family history of malignancy: her father died of peritoneal carcinomatosis; no familial genetic mutations were identified.  

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits and the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a serum CA 19-9 level of 25 U/mL (reference range 0–37 U/mL) and a carcinoembryonic antigen level of 2 ng/mL (reference range 0–2.5 ng/mL).  

An abdominal ultrasound revealed a retroperitoneal mass. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated an 8 cm tumor in the distal pancreas, closely abutting the splenic vessels and the renal hilum.

An 89-year-old Mexican woman presented with a 7-month history of an erythematous, non-tender lesion of the left lower eyelid. Seven months earlier, a chalazion had been diagnosed and treated with oral and topical antibiotics without improvement. Her ocular history included cataract surgery in the right eye 5 years before and a conjunctival squamous neoplasia in the left eye treated successfully with topical interferon alfa-2b 5 years earlier.  

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/30 in the right eye and 20/100 in the left eye. Ocular motility was full bilaterally, pupils were normal, and intraocular pressures were 13 mmHg (right) and 14 mmHg (left). Anterior-segment examination revealed a senile cataract in the left eye; funduscopic exam showed small drusen in both eyes.  

Slit-lamp examination of the left eye revealed a palpable, pinkish, smooth-surfaced, dome-shaped tumor measuring approximately 25 × 15 mm, poorly mobile, causing mild lid eversion at the external third of the lower palpebral conjunctiva. There was no loss of eyelashes and no palpable preauricular or cervical lymphadenopathy. Systemic examination was unremarkable.

A 51-year-old Caucasian woman presented with painless right visual loss (visual acuity 2/10 with corrective lenses) and a central scotoma on perimetry. Visual evoked potentials confirmed delayed conduction in the right optic nerve. She had no other neurologic symptoms or signs. An initial brain and orbital MRI demonstrated a tortuous, enlarged right optic nerve with a peripherally increased signal on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery and on coronal T2-weighted fat-suppressed sequences. Uniform contrast enhancement involved the posterior third of the optic nerve. Three months later, a follow-up MRI showed persistent signal abnormalities and contrast enhancement in the same segment of the optic nerve. A comprehensive biologic workup, including cerebrospinal fluid analysis after lumbar puncture, was entirely normal.

A 54-year-old man with hypertension, coronary artery disease status post percutaneous coronary intervention, dyslipidemia, and a history of smoking presented with a left scrotal wall lesion that he had noticed for several months and that was progressively increasing in size. He denied testicular pain or urinary symptoms. On examination, a firm, 3-cm lesion with a narrow neck was palpated on the left scrotal wall; the testes and epididymides appeared normal. Scrotal ultrasound revealed a well-circumscribed, mixed-echotexture lesion measuring 4×2 cm in the scrotal wall, with an echogenic wall and internal necrotic or turbid components; vascularity was noted within the solid-appearing elements. Both testes and epididymides had normal size, echotexture, and vascularity, and no hydrocele was seen. An inflammatory pathology such as a cold abscess or an infected cyst was considered among the differentials, although the possibility of a soft tissue neoplasm could not be ruled out, and histopathological correlation was suggested.

A 52-year-old woman was referred after a routine ophthalmological screening identified blurred margins of the left optic nerve head (ONH). She was otherwise healthy, with a family history of age-related macular degeneration, and denied any visual changes or associated symptoms. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 (−0.75 D) in the right eye and 20/25 (−1.50 D) in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was 16 mmHg bilaterally. The anterior segment and vitreous examination were unremarkable. Axial length measured 26.0 mm in the right eye and 26.5 mm in the left eye. Fundus examination of the right eye was normal. In the left eye, there was a tessellated and irregular fundus, a tilted disc with blurred margins in the superior quadrants, and gliosis-associated changes in the inferior quadrants.

Infrared reflectance imaging of the ONH and posterior pole was unremarkable. Structural spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed elevation of the superior quadrant of the ONH with a posterior hyporeflective round space. Swept-source OCT angiography with custom segmentation demonstrated a void of flow and tissue compatible with a cyst. B-scan ultrasonography revealed slight elevation of the ONH and a hypoechogenic round structure beneath the optic disc. Visual field testing showed a slight enlargement of the blind spot in the left eye, consistent with prior visual field testing. Orbital and brain magnetic resonance imaging were unremarkable.

A 52-year-old African American man with a known diagnosis of tuberous sclerosis complex presented for evaluation of longstanding facial lesions. His extracutaneous manifestations included bilateral subependymal nodules, cortical tubers, a renal angiomyolipoma, and multiple renal cysts. On examination, there were multiple firm brown dome-shaped papules on the cheeks, nose, and chin; several skin-colored papules and plaques on the forehead and right cheek; and numerous hypopigmented macules on the thighs. The largest skin-colored nodule on the right cheek was removed by shave biopsy. Histopathologic examination of this nodule revealed multiple foci of thin epithelial strands radiating from the upper part of the isthmus, surrounded by compact thin collagen fibers containing fibroblasts that stained for CD34, consistent with multiple fibrofolliculomas. An elastic stain revealed an absence of elastic fibers in the stroma surrounding the epithelial strands within the fibrofolliculomas; between the fibrofolliculomas, elastic fibers were irregularly distributed with decreased amounts in some areas.

A 20-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of gradually worsening lower abdominal pain. Initially mild and localized to the left lower quadrant, the discomfort became more intense and diffuse over several days. She denied urinary symptoms, fever, nausea, or vomiting. Her menstrual cycles were regular (28 ± 2 days), with normal flow; she was on day 3 of her cycle at presentation. Her medical, surgical, and family histories were unremarkable.

On examination, she appeared well, with no pallor or lymphadenopathy. The abdomen was soft and scaphoid, with a palpable, ill-defined, non-tender mass (~6 × 6 cm) in the left iliac fossa, not fixed to skin. Bowel sounds were present; other systems were normal.

Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a complex heterogeneous solid-cystic lesion in the left adnexa, measuring approximately 9.9 × 6.0 × 6.4 cm. Subsequent MRI of the abdomen and pelvis showed an 11.7 × 8.2 × 4.8 cm heterogeneous retroperitoneal mass, located medial to the left psoas muscle and lateral to the iliac vessels. The lesion contained multiple irregular cystic areas, variable-thickness septa, solid components, and numerous flow voids suggestive of marked vascularity. It displaced the psoas muscle laterally and the iliac vessels medially. With these imaging characteristics, the provisional radiologic differential included retroperitoneal soft tissue sarcoma and neurogenic tumor.

A 38-year-old Persian woman, virgin, presented with sudden onset of right-sided abdominal pain that began in the right upper quadrant 2 hours earlier and was accompanied by one fainting episode. Her last menstrual period was 7 days ago. She reported no trauma or prior surgery. On examination, her pulse rate was 110 beats/min, blood pressure was 80/– mm Hg, and temperature was 37.5 °C. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the right upper and lower quadrants and a tender mass extending to the umbilicus. She had a known history of uterine leiomyoma. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL, hematocrit 35%, white blood cell count 13.9 × 10^3/µL, and platelet count 333 × 10^9/L. Echocardiogram, electrocardiogram, lower-limb arterial Doppler, troponin, and CK-MB were normal. Transabdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 9.5 × 6.5 cm intramural subserosal leiomyoma with cystic degeneration at the uterine fundus, normal-appearing ovaries, free fluid up to Morison’s pouch, and a large pelvic fluid collection with internal echoes suggestive of clot. A serum pregnancy test was negative.

A 38-year-old man presented with a 5-year history of persistent productive cough and occasional hemoptysis. He denied fever, dyspnea, heartburn, dysphagia, weight loss, or aspiration. He is a barber with no significant medical or surgical history, but has a 38-pack-year smoking history. Over four years, he was treated for presumed asthma with inhalers and antihistamines without improvement.

On examination, he was comfortable, with an oxygen saturation of 97% on room air. Chest auscultation revealed reduced air entry and expiratory wheezes in the right lung; the left lung was normal. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory studies including CBC, coagulation, and blood chemistry were all within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated a soft-tissue endobronchial lesion partially obstructing the bronchus intermedius, resulting in partial collapse of the right middle and lower lobes.

An 18-year-old male was referred for evaluation of an asymptomatic gingival enlargement of one month’s duration. On examination, there was a 5×5 mm exophytic lesion with an erythematous, irregular surface on the buccal gingiva between the lower premolar and first molar. Oral hygiene was adequate, there was no pain or history of trauma, and clinical and radiologic assessment showed no bone involvement. His medical history was significant for acute lymphoblastic leukemia treated with chemotherapy one year earlier. Because of the lesion’s benign appearance and small size, an excisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia. Histologic sections stained with hematoxylin and eosin showed a proliferation of fusiform cells arranged in bundles and randomly, with intense deposition of amorphous eosinophilic material among them. Odontogenic epithelial strings and islets were scattered throughout the lesion. The specimen was positive to Congo red under polarized light, confirming the amyloid origin of the eosinophilic material.

A 35-year-old man was referred to the Oral and Maxillofacial Medicine Department with a 6-month history of a mobile mandibular molar. He had a history of central diabetes insipidus treated with desmopressin nasal spray and reported polyuria. He also complained of pruritic, erythematous crusted macules on his legs. On intraoral examination, several molars in the posterior mandible were mobile.

Cone-beam CT and orthopantomography demonstrated a well-defined radiolucent lesion extending from the mesial aspect of the right mandibular canine to the distal aspect of the right first molar, with a “scooped-out” periphery, buccal and lingual cortical destruction, loss of the alveolar crest, displacement of the inferior alveolar canal, loss of the lamina dura, and multiple teeth appearing to “float in air.” Similar osteolytic changes with severe alveolar destruction were noted in both maxillary molar regions, with loss of the posterior maxillary sinus floors and marked mucosal thickening of the maxillary sinuses. MRI confirmed severe mucosal thickening of both maxillary sinuses.

Laboratory studies showed elevated triglycerides, low hematocrit and mean corpuscular hemoglobin, and elevated AST and ALT levels, suggesting anemia and liver dysfunction. Urinalysis was normal with no glucosuria despite ongoing polyuria. Given the combination of diabetes insipidus, cutaneous rash, and destructive jaw lesions, a multisystem disorder was suspected. On the basis of imaging, squamous cell carcinoma and Langerhans cell histiocytosis were initially considered, and aggressive periodontal disease was ruled out.

A 15-year-old Indian girl was referred for evaluation of a left maxillary swelling. She was asymptomatic, with an unremarkable medical history and good general health. Intraoral examination revealed a nontender buccal expansion of the left maxilla and absence of the left maxillary canine; the overlying mucosa was intact and normal. There was no neural deficit or lymphadenopathy.  
Panoramic radiography showed a well-defined unilocular radiolucency of the left maxilla, causing expansion and thinning of all bony walls, associated with an unerupted upper left canine; adjacent first and second premolars showed displacement and root resorption. A 64-slice CT scan confirmed a well-circumscribed mass occupying the left maxilla around the impacted canine.  
Under local anesthesia, the lesion was enucleated completely along with the impacted canine. Grossly, the specimen measured 4.5 cm × 2.5 cm × 4 cm, had a smooth external surface, was associated with the canine, and contained no visible calcifications within the lumen.

A 30-year-old woman presented with anterior chest pain and cough of 6 months’ duration. A CT scan obtained by her primary care physician showed a giant anterior mediastinal polycystic mass measuring 11.2 × 7.7 × 7.2 cm that compressed the trachea and right main bronchus. A thymoma or germ-cell tumor was suspected. Before her scheduled outpatient evaluation, she developed sudden dyspnea and arrived at the emergency department.

On examination, her blood pressure was 154/84 mmHg, heart rate 135 bpm (sinus tachycardia), respiratory rate 16/min, and SpO2 94% on room air. Arterial blood gas on room air showed a PaO2 of 72 mmHg and a PaCO2 of 33 mmHg. Wheezing was heard bilaterally, and she could not tolerate the supine position due to respiratory distress. Laboratory studies revealed a WBC count of 7950/µL, C-reactive protein of 0.03 mg/dL, and normal levels of alpha-fetoprotein, human chorionic gonadotropin, and soluble interleukin-2 receptor. Repeat CT imaging confirmed progressive airway stenosis.

The patient was intubated, but manual ventilation remained poor with an end-tidal CO2 of 28 mmHg. Bronchoscopy demonstrated correct tube placement, external compression of the trachea, and inability to visualize the right main bronchial inlet. The endotracheal tube was exchanged for a 35-Fr double-lumen tube to ventilate the left lung, but oxygenation remained marginal (SpO2 95% on FiO2 0.80).

A 71-year-old man presented with increasing pain and swelling in the scrotum over several days and weeks. He denied trauma, dysuria, or fever. Two years earlier, he had a shave biopsy of a melanoma on his upper back (at least 2.3 mm thick) followed by wide local excision and negative sentinel lymph node biopsy. He subsequently developed subcutaneous, pulmonary, axillary, and small bowel metastases and received temozolomide with sorafenib for six months, followed by excision of metastases and enrollment in a bioimmunotherapy trial. One month ago, during a palliative small bowel resection, he first noted left scrotal pain that briefly subsided but then recurred and intensified. His past surgical history included a remote right orchiectomy of unclear indication. 

On examination, the scrotum was inflamed, and the left testis contained a tender, firm, non-fluctuant 5–6 cm mass. 

Scrotal ultrasound revealed an enlarged left testicle with a 5 cm lobulated, heterogeneous, solid mass replacing the testicle and showing some peripheral vascularity on color Doppler; a complex loculated hydrocele with echogenic debris was also present. 

A retrospective review of PET-CT images from eight months earlier demonstrated focal FDG uptake in the scrotum corresponding to the left testicle, with a maximum standardized uptake value of 12.

A 60-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of progressively worsening pain and swelling in the proximal left arm, accompanied by limited flexion, extension, and abduction of the left shoulder. On inspection, there was loss of the normal shoulder contour due to a diffuse swelling of the pectoral girdle, with normal overlying skin and mild venous prominence. Palpation revealed a tender, bony-hard mass approximately 6 cm by 4 cm, fixed to underlying structures. 

Plain radiographs of the left shoulder demonstrated an ill-defined, expansile osteolytic lesion of the humeral neck and proximal shaft, with a wide zone of transition, endosteal scalloping, cortical breakthrough, several specks of calcification within the lesion, and an adjacent soft-tissue component. An additional calcified nodular opacity was noted in the peripheral left lung mid zone.

A 5 mm–slice CT scan from the superior shoulder to mid-arm confirmed an osteolytic expansile lesion with endosteal scalloping, cortical thinning and multiple cortical breaches, matrix calcifications, and anterolateral soft-tissue extension displacing the deltoid muscle.

MRI of the left arm showed a well-defined lobulated lesion that was predominantly hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with low-signal septations. The glenohumeral joint space was preserved and the neurovascular bundle was uninvolved.

A 52-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of a persistent, nontender erection associated with mild penile discomfort, perineal pain, dysuria, and polaquiuria. He reported a 14-kg weight loss over the preceding 2 months and denied fever. On examination, there was a partial erection with rigid but nontender corpora cavernosa and small, soft, pink nodules at the coronal sulcus. Digital rectal examination revealed an enlarged, tender prostate with a 15-mm central soft nodule.  

Laboratory studies showed normochromic, normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL), leukocytosis (13.08×10^9/L; 75.5% neutrophils), and an elevated C-reactive protein level (15.2 mg/dL). Urinalysis revealed leukocyturia (125 cells/µL) and hematuria (80 cells/µL).  

A diagnosis of acute prostatitis with presumed high-flow priapism was made, and the patient was treated with intravenous ceftriaxone and diclofenac. After 5 days, his priapism and nodules persisted, and repeat tests showed hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL and C-reactive protein 19 mg/dL.  

Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen demonstrated bilateral pulmonary infarcts, multiple pulmonary nodules of unknown etiology, and multiple prostatic abscesses. Penile and transrectal ultrasound revealed a lateral and distal hypoechoic nodule in the left corpus cavernosum (most likely an arterio-sinusoidal fistula), a hyperechoic lesion in the right corpus cavernosum, stable arterial flow, and a prostatic abscess. Pus was aspirated for culture, and histopathological examination of the aspirate was noncontributory; cultures were negative for aerobes and anaerobes. The patient was discharged against medical advice.

A 50-year-old woman presented with an 8-month history of nonproductive cough and progressive dyspnea. She also reported fatigue and unquantified weight loss. She had no history of chemical exposures, bleeding diatheses, or immunodeficiency, and she was HIV negative.

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. Lung auscultation revealed decreased breath sounds over the left hemithorax without wheezing or crackles. No lymphadenopathy or skin lesions were noted.

A chest radiograph showed nonspecific volume loss of the left lung with lateral displacement of the left hilum and no pleural effusion or consolidation. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a 13.9 × 7.7 cm heterogeneously enhancing mass in the left paracardiac pleural region causing compression of the pericardium and encasement of the pulmonary trunk and superior vena cava. There was subsegmental collapse of the right middle lobe and of the left middle and lower lobes.

A 77-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an incidental mediastinal mass that had been noted on chest radiographs over a 2-year period. She was asymptomatic, with no peripheral lymphadenopathy or significant family history. Physical examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. Tumor markers—including cytokeratin 19 fragment, pro-gastrin-releasing peptide, soluble interleukin-2 receptor, alpha-fetoprotein, and carcinoembryonic antigen—were all normal; human chorionic gonadotropin was mildly elevated at 1.8 mIU/mL (reference range, 0.0–0.7 mIU/mL). Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed a well-circumscribed, smoothly marginated mass measuring approximately 6.0 × 1.5 × 1.5 cm in the superior mediastinum. The lesion demonstrated relatively strong enhancement and was closely adjacent to the aortic arch, brachiocephalic artery, left carotid artery, and trachea but showed no evidence of invasion. Hilar lymph nodes were not enlarged.  
Preoperative differential diagnoses included thymoma, malignant lymphoma, teratoma, and benign lymph node enlargement such as that associated with Castleman disease.

A 77-year-old woman was referred after an abnormal opacification was noted on routine chest radiography. She was asymptomatic and had no history of cutaneous lesions or occupational exposure to silica, beryllium, or asbestos. 
On chest computed tomography, there was a solitary, well-demarcated, solid nodule measuring 2.3 cm in the right lower lobe. Systemic CT revealed no other tumors. 
The patient underwent video-assisted thoracoscopic wedge resection of the right lower lobe. Intraoperatively, the nodule was firm and solid; on sectioning, it appeared yellow-white. A frozen section showed proliferation of fibromuscular tissue with a few mitotic figures, suggesting a mesenchymal tumor, prompting completion of a right lower lobectomy. 
Permanent histopathology demonstrated a well-circumscribed nodular lesion in the pulmonary parenchyma, composed of bland spindle or oval cells arranged in storiform and loose fascicular patterns. Numerous branching or anastomosing blood vessels with hemangiopericytomatous features were present, and occasional mitoses were seen.

A 25-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of a painless, palpable mass in her left upper eyelid and mild proptosis. On examination, the mass was mobile, hard, smooth, non-tender, well delineated, and measured approximately 15 mm in diameter. Computed tomography of the orbits showed a homogeneous, isodense, ovoid mass with distinct margins and no bone invasion in the lacrimal gland fossa. On magnetic resonance imaging, the lesion was encapsulated by a 1-mm low-intensity rim and exhibited high signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images, with scattered low-intensity areas within. The preoperative diagnosis was lacrimal gland tumor or deep dermoid cyst.

A 33-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a painless, well-demarcated, pink to yellowish mass with a delicate papillary surface on the right ventral tongue. The lesion measured 2.2 × 1.2 cm and had been present for at least 4 years. On palpation, the mass was soft. There were no extraoral lesions or cervical lymphadenopathy, and routine laboratory results were normal. With a provisional diagnosis of benign papillary lesions (including large squamous papilloma, verruciform xanthoma, and condyloma acuminatum), an excisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia. Microscopic examination revealed a papillary hyperparakeratotic acanthotic epithelium with parakeratin plugging between the papillary projections. The rete ridges were elongated to a uniform depth, and the connective tissue papillae were filled with numerous large macrophages with foamy cytoplasm (xanthoma cells).

A 70-year-old man with a history of left hip replacement and depression presented with arthralgias of the neck, hips, and knees. Two months earlier his blood counts had been normal. On presentation, his white-cell count was 16.7×10^9/L with an absolute neutrophil count of 13.2×10^9/L and a platelet count of 1346×10^9/L. The differential showed 78% segmented neutrophils and 6% basophils. Hemoglobin was 13.8 g/dL, and the RDW was 15.9%. A peripheral blood smear showed neutrophilia with some hypersegmented neutrophils, moderate anisopoikilocytosis of red cells, and giant platelets. Physical examination revealed no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. 

Bone marrow biopsy was mildly hypercellular (50%) with trilineage hematopoiesis and a normal myeloid-to-erythroid ratio. There was megakaryocytic hyperplasia (9.5 megakaryocytes per high-power field) with dysmegakaryopoiesis. Iron stores were normal, and no ring sideroblasts were seen. A reticulin stain demonstrated mildly increased reticulin fibers (grade 2+ of 4). Cytogenetic analysis revealed a normal male karyotype (46,XY). Lactate dehydrogenase was 251 IU/L (normal 50–175 IU/L).

A 66-year-old man with a history of papillary thyroid carcinoma (status post thyroidectomy and radioiodine ablation), type II diabetes mellitus, and hypertension presented with a 7-month history of a slowly enlarging right anterior neck tumor. He also reported a 3- to 4-year history of symmetric, pruritic, ovoid patches in the bilateral axillae, waist, and flanks unresponsive to topical clotrimazole and betamethasone (pruritus relieved by topical triamcinolone).

On examination, the right anterolateral neck mass measured approximately 5×7 cm and protruded 3 cm from the skin surface, with a serosanguinous crust over a background erythematous plaque. Two months after lesion onset, a biopsy of the neck mass showed a folliculotropic and epidermotropic atypical lymphoid infiltrate that stained positive for CD3 and CD20. 

At presentation to our clinic, punch biopsies of the neck tumor and a left chest wall patch both demonstrated an atypical lymphocytic infiltrate featuring folliculotropism and epidermotropism with Pautrier microabscesses. Immunohistochemical studies revealed the atypical lymphocytes to be CD3+ and CD4+, with very few CD8+ or CD79a+ cells; CD20 colocalized with approximately 80% of the CD3+ cells. A monoclonal T-cell population was confirmed in the neck tumor by T-cell receptor γ–chain gene rearrangement analysis. 

Flow cytometry of peripheral blood and bone marrow was negative for lymphoma. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography showed an intensely hypermetabolic right anterolateral neck mass and mildly to moderately hypermetabolic lymph nodes in the right cervical level IIB, right intraparotid, pancreaticoduodenal, and left inguinal regions. Laboratory studies, including lactate dehydrogenase, serum electrolytes, and complete blood count with differential, were within normal limits.

A 56-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of chest pain. He had no significant past medical history but was a heavy smoker (60 cigarettes per day for 38 years). On examination, breath sounds were diminished over the right hemithorax. A chest radiograph demonstrated a large mass in the right lung. Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed a 9.3 × 7.5 cm lesion in the right lower lobe with low attenuation (19 Hounsfield units) and thin, mildly enhancing septa. There was no mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and CT of the brain and abdomen showed no evidence of metastatic disease. Bronchoscopy revealed no endobronchial lesion, and CT-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology was nondiagnostic.

An 86-year-old man with no significant personal or family history presented with a several-month history of diarrhea and occasional rectal bleeding, but no lower urinary tract symptoms. Physical examination was unremarkable. Digital rectal examination revealed a vegetant, friable, hemi-circumferential mass approximately 4 cm from the anal verge. 

Laboratory studies showed a carcinoembryonic antigen level of 4.3 μg/L (normal <5.1 μg/L), hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, normal platelet count, prothrombin time 70%, and hypoalbuminemia (31 g/L). While undergoing bowel preparation for colonoscopy, he developed large-bowel obstruction. CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated circumferential rectal wall thickening narrowing the lumen and invading the prostate and mesorectum, with upstream bowel dilation but no lymphadenopathy or distant metastases. A diverting colostomy was performed without incident.

Colonoscopy through the colostomy revealed a large, circumferential, infiltrative, friable, stenosing submucosal mass with erythematous overlying mucosa resembling grape clusters. Three successive mucosal biopsies showed: (1) invasive poorly differentiated carcinoma interpreted initially as a neuroendocrine tumor; (2) inflammatory changes without malignancy; and (3) poorly differentiated carcinoma. Pelvic MRI performed without contrast (due to claustrophobia) confirmed circumferential rectal wall thickening invading the posterior prostate, bladder base, left seminal vesicle, and mesorectum; the radiologist favored either rectal cancer invading the urogenital tract or prostate cancer invading the rectum. Serum prostate-specific antigen was 25.59 μg/L (normal <4 μg/L).

A 61-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 5-year history of a slowly growing, painless, spherical nodule over the right temporal scalp. The 1.5 × 1 cm mass was subcutaneous, tethered to the skin but mobile over the skull, firm, noncompressible, nonpulsatile, without central punctum. There was no pain, secretion, redness, or regional lymphadenopathy. She had undergone regular screening for breast and colorectal malignancies, with no abnormalities detected. An excisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia without complications, and the wound was closed primarily.

Histopathological examination showed hair-bearing skin with underlying lakes of mucin separated by delicate fibrous septae. Floating within these mucinous lakes were nests, clusters, and cords of predominantly uniform round to cuboidal epithelial cells with mild to moderate nuclear variability, focal duct formation, and occasional cribriform proliferation. There was no connection to the overlying epidermis or adnexal structures. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated strong positivity for cytokeratin 7, estrogen receptors, and progesterone receptors, with negativity for cytokeratin 20 and Her-2-neu. The morphologic and immunohistochemical features were consistent with mucinous adenocarcinoma. Because histopathological distinction between a primary eccrine mucinous adenocarcinoma and metastatic mucinous adenocarcinoma is almost impossible, a complete extracutaneous work-up—especially to exclude a breast primary—was recommended.

A 16-year-old Asian Bangladeshi girl presented with a one-year history of multiple recurrent, painless left breast lumps. She had menarche at age 13, no use of oral contraceptives, no family history of breast cancer, no clinical features of neurofibromatosis, and no prior chest irradiation. Over that year, she underwent four surgeries:

First excision: five small nodules (largest 11×11×6 cm). Histology showed a benign phylloides tumor in the larger nodule and fibroadenoma in the smaller.

Four months later: multiple painless nodules recurred in the upper inner quadrant. Ultrasound identified six hypoechoic lesions (largest 3.2×2.6 cm) and a 2.8 cm left axillary lymph node. Excision of four nodules (largest 4×3×3 cm) showed a spindle-cell stromal tumor with mild pleomorphism and 0–1 mitoses per high-power field; diagnosed as phylloides tumor.

Fifteen days later: multiple painful nodules and fever. Fine-needle aspiration suggested malignant phylloides. Modified radical mastectomy revealed a 10 cm growth with deep margin involvement; histology showed an anaplastic spindle-cell tumor in a herringbone pattern with >10 mitoses per 10 HPF; interpreted as low-grade fibrosarcoma.

Two weeks post-mastectomy: multiple nodules along the scar, with normal chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasound. Two months later, wide local excision yielded a skin-covered specimen (11×9×4 cm) with a 5×3 cm gray-white fleshy growth. Microscopy revealed predominantly atypical spindle cells with alternating hypercellular and hypocellular myxoid areas, palisading nuclei, and 2–3 mitoses per 10 HPF; no ductal component was seen. 
A provisional diagnosis of high grade stromal sarcoma with a differential diagnosis of malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor was made.

A 55-year-old man presented with atony of both lower extremities and malaise for over 6 months. He reported progressive fatigue and thirst for 2 months, night sweats, a 5-kg weight loss, and intermittent fever. Physical examination revealed splenomegaly. Laboratory testing showed a white-cell count of 38.22×10^9/L, a platelet count of 390×10^9/L, and an LDH level of 1122 U/L. A bone marrow aspirate demonstrated hypercellularity with prominent dysgranulopoiesis: 0.5% myeloblasts, 3.5% promyelocytes, 9% myelocytes, 3% metamyelocytes, 10% eosinophils, 4.5% lymphocytes, 2% nucleated red cells, and 9.5% monocytes. A manual peripheral-blood differential confirmed granulocytosis with circulating myelocytes and metamyelocytes. Bone marrow biopsy showed marked neutrophilic leukocytosis (84%) with left shift, 6–8 megakaryocytes per high-power field without karyolobism, and grade 1 fibrosis. Immunohistochemistry was MPO+, CD71+, CD61+, CD117–, and CD34+/–. Testing for the BCR-ABL fusion gene was negative, and JAK2 V617F was detected. Cytogenetic analysis revealed a normal karyotype (46, XY). A preliminary diagnosis of prefibrotic primary myelofibrosis was considered, with other myeloid neoplasms to be excluded.

A 29-year-old primigravid woman at 20 weeks’ gestation noted a new, painless right labial swelling. She had no significant past medical or surgical history and an otherwise uncomplicated pregnancy.  
Physical examination revealed a 2 × 2 cm polypoidal, mobile, non-tender, edematous mass on the right labium majus; the left labium majus was normal. Condyloma acuminatum was suspected, and observation was advised.

Over the ensuing weeks, the right labial mass continued to enlarge, causing discomfort. By 37 weeks’ gestation, the lesion measured 7 cm in length, obstructing the vaginal canal, and a new discrete, painless, <1 cm mass was noted on the left labium majus. A biopsy of the right lesion was recommended but deferred at the patient’s request.

At 39 weeks, the patient underwent an elective cesarean delivery under spinal anesthesia to reduce the risk of birth trauma. Concurrently, excision of the right labial mass was performed; the mass measured 4.5 cm at surgery. The smaller left labial lesion was left in situ to minimize invasive procedures.

Gross pathology of the excised right labial lesion showed a polypoid fragment of edematous, lobulated, wrinkled tan skin with an edematous stalk-like base. On sectioning, the lesion had a markedly edematous, “botryoid” cut surface.

An 18-year-old man presented with a two-week history of fever, fatigue, and pain in both elbows, hips, and knees. He had been treated for acute pharyngitis without improvement. He also reported night sweats but denied gastrointestinal or respiratory symptoms or weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory testing showed a normal complete blood count, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 65 mm/h, and a C-reactive protein level of 64.4 mg/L. Electrolyte levels, liver and renal function tests, complement titer, thyroid function, autoantibodies, and cytomegalovirus and Epstein–Barr virus antibody levels were within normal limits. One week later, he noted numbness of the left lower lip and jaw (hypaesthesia). A dental examination was normal. Whole-body non-contrast CT, brain MRI, and abdominal ultrasonography revealed no primary lesion.

A 64-year-old woman presented with 2 days of high fever, dyspnea, and nonproductive cough. Her history was notable for type II diabetes mellitus. On examination, she was febrile (38.9°C), tachycardic (116 bpm), hypotensive (100/60 mm Hg), and hypoxemic (SpO₂ 88% on room air). Cardiac auscultation revealed an early diastolic murmur best heard at the fifth intercostal space; pulmonary exam showed decreased breath sounds at both lung bases. Nasopharyngeal swab was positive for SARS-CoV-2 by rRT-PCR. Chest CT demonstrated moderate bilateral pleural effusions and multilobar lung consolidations with ground-glass opacities. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a highly mobile 70×50 mm mass in the left atrium that protruded into the left ventricle through the mitral valve during diastole, mimicking severe mitral stenosis; left ventricular ejection fraction was 55%. Coronary angiography showed no significant disease. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed an 8×5 cm mass in the left atrium.

A 21-year-old Caucasian man with no prior medical history presented with an asymptomatic mass on the anterolateral aspect of his left calf. Physical examination revealed a 28 × 14 × 20 mm subcutaneous lesion that was well circumscribed, depressible, elastic, and encapsulated. Laboratory studies were within normal limits, and there was no regional lymphadenopathy. Doppler ultrasound demonstrated a well-defined, hypervascular subcutaneous tumor with surrounding tissue edema. The conclusion was a subcutaneous hypervascular tumor, and an angioma was suspected. After clinical examination, the initial differential diagnosis included an angioma or a sebaceous cyst with fibrosis.

A 29-day-old neonate weighing 4.2 kg was referred with respiratory distress since day four of life. The child was born at 37 weeks (birth weight, 3.5 kg) after an unremarkable pregnancy and delivery. At admission, the infant was poorly active, with a respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute and a pulse rate of 140 beats per minute. Heart sounds were normal, but there was decreased air entry on the right side. Biochemical and hematological investigations were within normal limits. 

Chest radiography showed a homogeneous opacity in the right middle and lower lung fields with leftward mediastinal shift; no vertebral defects were seen. A chest tube was placed for presumed pneumothorax. Ultrasound revealed a well-defined cystic lesion in the right lower lung field. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography confirmed a well-defined multilocular cystic collection in the posterior aspect of the middle and lower zones of the right hemithorax. 

Based on the clinical and radiological findings, a differential diagnosis of a foregut duplication cyst versus congenital cystic adenomatoid malformation was suggested.

A 14-year-old girl with a 1-year history of Crohn’s disease involving the esophagus, ascending colon, ileocecal valve, and terminal ileum, in clinical remission on azathioprine and adalimumab, underwent a routine surveillance colonoscopy. On examination of the cecum, a well-defined, submucosal, yellowish mass was noted. The lesion was smooth, dome-shaped, and covered by normal mucosa; there were no ulcerations, luminal obstruction, or signs of intussusception. When gently compressed with the colonoscope tip, the mass flattened and promptly regained its shape (the “pillow sign”). Given the lesion’s size, the patient’s young age, and the absence of symptoms, biopsies were obtained rather than proceeding directly to endoscopic resection.

A 77-year-old woman presented with a 19-year history of a progressively enlarging mass on the medial aspect of her left ankle. The lesion recurred 15 years after a prior excision. She denied pain but reported restricted ankle motion. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender, non-compressible, immobile mass without erythema, warmth, or transillumination; a healed surgical scar overlaid the swelling. Plain radiographs of the ankle demonstrated a soft-tissue opacity over the anteromedial tibiotalar joint. MRI revealed a well-defined, multilobulated, encapsulated lesion involving the medial tibiotalar joint with both intra- and extra-articular components and signal intensity identical to fat on all sequences.

A 5‐year‐old spayed female Chinchilla cat was referred for evaluation of a 4-week history of weight loss and inappetence. On examination, the cat was bright and alert with a body‐condition score of 2/9. Palpation revealed a 1.5 cm intestinal mass in the mid‐abdomen; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Hematology and serum biochemistry were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a 14 mm eccentric intramural mass in a small intestinal loop; the mass was hypoechoic, heterogeneous, and appeared to arise from the muscularis layer, causing focal distortion of wall layering but no obstructive pattern. The remainder of the abdomen was unremarkable, aside from globally altered small intestinal wall layering. Fine‐needle aspiration of the mass on two occasions yielded poorly cellular, nondiagnostic samples. An exploratory coeliotomy was performed; intraoperatively, diffuse ileal thickening and a 1.5 cm mass on the antimesenteric border of the distal jejunum were identified and resected with margins. Enlarged mesenteric and ileocecocolic lymph nodes were also biopsied. All specimens were submitted for histopathological examination.

A 32-year-old woman presented with intermittent per-vaginal bleeding for 1 month and progressive abdominal distension for 5 months, accompanied by decreased appetite, significant weight loss, and an evening fever over the past week. She denied nausea, vomiting, gastrointestinal bleeding, respiratory symptoms, or palpable lymphadenopathy. Her obstetric history was G2P2 with two living children.

On examination, she was pale and mildly dehydrated, with a temperature of 100.4°F and stable other vital signs. No cervical, axillary, or inguinal lymph nodes were palpable. Abdominal palpation revealed a firm, slightly mobile 12×12 cm mass in the lower abdomen. Rectal examination confirmed a palpable anterior mass; the remainder of her systemic examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 5.1 g/dL and PCV 18%; CA-125, CA19-9, and CEA were within normal limits. The tuberculin test was negative. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography demonstrated bowel wall thickening in the right adnexal region extending to the left iliac fossa, with several enlarged periumbilical and left iliac fossa lymph nodes (up to 16×13 cm). Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a lobulated exophytic mid-ileal mass measuring 10 cm in length and 4 cm in thickness, adherent to adjacent small bowel loops and the dome of the urinary bladder, described as a “possible small bowel gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST).” Heterogeneously enhancing nodular lesions were noted in the parauterine region (largest 3×2 cm) and small para-aortic lymph nodes; there was no mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

A 22-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of recurrent left-sided epistaxis and progressive nasal obstruction. She had no personal or family history of tuberous sclerosis complex, hamartomas, or epilepsy, and her past medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Physical examination revealed a polypoid mass occupying the anterior part of the left nasal cavity, with deviation of the nasal septum to the right. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. 
 
A noncontrast CT scan of the sinuses showed a 1.5-cm polypoid lesion in the left nasal fossae filling the inferior meatus, with homogeneous density, preservation of the bony framework, and no evidence of bone erosion. Coronal and sagittal T1-weighted MRI after gadolinium administration demonstrated a homogeneously enhancing mass confined to the left nasal cavity, without signs of infiltration of adjacent structures.

A 36-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of a painless swelling of the left body of the mandible. He denied systemic illness or history of trauma. On extraoral examination, there was facial asymmetry and a firm, diffuse swelling over the left mandible; the overlying skin was normal. Intraoral examination revealed a buccal vestibular swelling in the same region; lower left teeth showed pathologic mobility (incisors and canine Miller grade I; premolars and first molar grade II). There were no palpable cervical lymph nodes. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated a multilocular radiolucency with fine trabeculation extending from the left canine to the first molar, without root resorption. A subsequent CT scan showed destruction of the buccal cortex of the left mandibular body.

A 27-year-old man presented with irritation and a yellowish mass in his left eye. He had worn soft contact lenses monthly for more than 10 years, frequently sleeping in them and rubbing his left eye because of itching. Two months before presentation, he felt a tiny mass at the superior limbus, which gradually enlarged. He was treated with topical fluorometholone acetate for 3 months at another hospital without change in the lesion’s appearance. 

On examination at our hospital, uncorrected visual acuity was 20/200 in both eyes; best-corrected visual acuity improved to 20/32 in the right eye and 20/80 in the left eye with –2.50 D contact lenses. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy of the left eye showed a well-circumscribed, yellowish mass measuring 6.5 × 10.0 × 2.0 mm, extending 2 mm onto the cornea with vascularization at the superior limbus. Anterior-segment optical coherence tomography revealed a hyporeflective lesion at the 12 o’clock limbal area. Iris examination and posterior-segment evaluation were unremarkable. Complete blood cell counts, serum lipid levels, creatinine clearance, plasma viscosity, liver function tests, and chest radiography were all within normal limits.

A 56-year-old Trinidadian woman presented with intermittent left-sided chest pain for 3 days, worsened by exertion, and associated with shortness of breath. Over the preceding year, she had experienced headache, fatigue, a 15–20-lb weight loss, and bilateral lower extremity pain. Physical examination revealed numerous facial xanthelasmas. 

A chest radiograph showed an enlarged cardiac silhouette, possible pulmonary vascular congestion, and subcentimeter calcifications attributed to old granulomatous disease. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated small pericardial and left pleural effusions and a large left upper-lobe paramediastinal mass with extensive mediastinal and supraclavicular adenopathy. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed soft-tissue infiltration surrounding both kidneys. Noncontrast and contrast CT of the head identified enhancing lesions in the right frontal cortex and right posterior cerebellum with mild mass effect; these were confirmed on brain MRI. A whole-body bone scan showed abnormal uptake in the seventh thoracic vertebral body and intense uptake in the distal femurs and tibias bilaterally.

CT-guided biopsy of a superior mediastinal lymph node revealed poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma positive for cytokeratins AE1/AE3 and TTF1, compatible with a lung primary. The patient was referred for dermatologic biopsy of a right cheek xanthelasma.

A 61-year-old woman was evaluated in the colorectal clinic for a 3-month history of decreased ileostomy output, weight loss, and general malaise. She had undergone panproctocolectomy with end ileostomy for ulcerative colitis at age 13. Four months earlier she had been admitted with small-bowel obstruction, which resolved with conservative management; follow-up small-bowel barium studies were normal. Her medical history included atrial fibrillation on warfarin, hypertension, and prior hysterectomy. On abdominal examination, the mucocutaneous junction of the ileostomy showed an ulceroproliferative growth extending from the 9 o’clock to the 6 o’clock position, and the stoma appeared thickened and stenosed. She was scheduled for biopsy of the lesion.

A 21-year-old gravida 2, para 1 woman at 25 weeks 5 days of gestation presented with a 4-day history of severe epigastric pain, vomiting, and decreased fetal movement. She had no history of trauma and an unremarkable past medical history. On examination, she appeared pale and dehydrated. Vital signs were: pulse 140 beats/min, respiratory rate 35 breaths/min, blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg, temperature 101 °F, and Glasgow Coma Scale score 15/15. Abdominal examination revealed a firm, tender epigastric mass measuring approximately 10 cm by 8 cm; the uterus was palpable at 22 weeks’ size. Two uterine contractions were noted in 10 minutes, and fetal heart sounds were not audible. On a cervical examination, the cervix was midline, medium in consistency, 1 cm dilated, 20–30% effaced, with a show present. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 4.4 g/dL, platelet count 33 000 cells/mm³, prothrombin time 60 seconds, INR 5.0, and potassium 2.4 mEq/L; serum amylase and lipase were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated intrauterine fetal death at 26–27 weeks, a complex retroperitoneal mass in the epigastric region, and gross hemoperitoneum. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen revealed an 18 cm by 12.5 cm heterogeneously enhancing mass arising from the body of the pancreas and a large high-density peritoneal fluid collection consistent with hemoperitoneum.

A 34-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 0, at 9 weeks’ gestation was evaluated for recurrent episodes of hypertension. Over the previous 8 months, she had experienced 2–3 paroxysmal spikes per month lasting 1–2 minutes, with systolic pressures of 220–240 mm Hg and diastolic pressures of 140 mm Hg. Each episode was accompanied by palpitations, headache, sweating, nonspecific gastrointestinal discomfort, and a persistent heavy sensation in the right renal area. Physical examination of the abdomen was unremarkable. Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a 9.0 × 7.5 cm mixed-echogenic mass with low vascularity between the right kidney and liver. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a well-defined, 9 cm round mass lateral to the aorta and between the right kidney and liver, displacing the kidney. On T1-weighted images, the lesion was heterogeneously hypointense relative to muscle with isointense areas suggesting hemorrhage. On T2-weighted images, peripheral regions were markedly hyperintense (“light-bulb bright”). Contrast enhancement was rapid, heterogeneous, and intense. No extra-adrenal lesions or lymphadenopathy were identified.

A 22-year-old woman presented for evaluation of malaligned teeth. On examination, all permanent teeth had erupted except the third molars in both arches and the lower left lateral incisor. There was mild spacing between the lower left central incisor and the canine. She had Class II, Division 1 malocclusion with crowding in the maxillary anterior region. There was no history of prior dental extractions.

A panoramic radiograph and a mandibular occlusal film showed an unerupted lower left lateral incisor with an associated well-defined radiopaque lesion in the left mandibular anterior region, surrounded by a thin radiolucent halo, which appeared to obstruct the eruption path of the tooth.

A 51-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of intermittent abdominal pain, 5% unintentional weight loss, low-grade fevers, and night sweats. On examination, she was orthostatic with conjunctival pallor and tenderness in the right upper quadrant. Laboratory evaluation showed normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL) and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (87 mm/h). Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 3.7 × 4.9 cm cyst-like mass without septation in segment IV of the liver. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 4 × 5 cm hypodense, nonenhancing lesion with smooth margins in the left lobe of the liver. There was no history of chronic liver disease or viral hepatitis. Serologic tests for hepatitis B and C were negative. Alpha-fetoprotein and CA19-9 levels were within normal limits. Colon cancer screening six months earlier had been unremarkable.

A 25-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an incidental, painless radiolucency in the right mandibular ramus. She had no swelling, no cortical expansion, no mucosal lesions, no limitation of mouth opening, no deviation of mandibular movement, and no history of trauma or familial cancer. Sensation in the distribution of the inferior alveolar nerve was intact.  
Panoramic radiograph demonstrated a well-defined radiolucent area in the right posterior mandible.  
Computed tomography showed a unilocular, well-circumscribed radiolucent lesion with a sclerotic margin in the mandibular ramus.  
Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a hyperintense lesion on both T1- and T2-weighted sequences, with signal loss on fat-suppression sequences.  
As the CT scan and MRI strongly indicated a benign lesion, no exploratory biopsy was performed.

A 38-year-old man presented with a 5-month history of left testicular enlargement, progressive left inguinal lymphadenopathy, weight loss and abdominal distention. An inguinal lymph-node biopsy performed at an outside clinic showed infiltration by undifferentiated malignant cells “compatible with infiltration by myeloblasts, seen through immunohistochemical analysis.” The patient initially declined treatment, but over the subsequent months experienced further enlargement of the testicle and lymph nodes, and worsening symptoms, prompting referral to our institution.

On admission, he had acute postrenal kidney failure due to extrinsic urinary-tract compression, requiring emergency hemodialysis and percutaneous nephrostomy. The complete blood count showed a leukocyte count of 14.8 × 10^9/L with circulating blastic cells, without anemia or thrombocytopenia. A bone marrow aspirate revealed that 26% of the nucleated cells were blasts, with a flow-cytometric immunophenotype defined as CD45+, CD13+, CD33+, HLA-DR+ and CD11c+, consistent with a myeloid lineage.

Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated extensive infiltration of the mesentery, parietal peritoneum and right colon; bilateral hydronephrosis from ureteral compression; and an enlarged left testicle (volume, 76 mL) with an infiltrative process involving the epididymis, spermatic cord, and overlying skin and subcutaneous tissue. Computed tomography of the abdomen showed involvement of the left diaphragm, ileocecal junction and a periaortic–pericaval lymph-node cluster, along with severe ascites and moderate bilateral pleural effusions.

A 73-year-old man was referred for evaluation of elevated PSA (8.0 ng/ml). He underwent transrectal ultrasound-guided prostate biopsy, which revealed a Gleason score 4+3=7 mixed ductal and acinar carcinoma in all 3 cores from the left base. Staging multiparametric MRI of the prostate showed a 17×7×15 mm PI-RADS 5 lesion in the left peripheral zone. Additionally, there was a multiloculated cystic mass arising from the prostatic base and extending into the bladder, measuring 72×41×53 mm. On the right side of the lesion, locules had intermediate T2 signal intensity with areas of restricted diffusion, likely blood products; on the left side, locules had higher T2 signal, no restricted diffusion, and variable T1 signal intensities, likely simple fluid or proteinaceous material. No imaging features of local invasion were observed. Flexible cystoscopy confirmed that the mass did not invade the bladder, and diagnostic cytology showed no malignant cells.

A 53-year-old woman presented with 1.5 months of progressively worsening painless obstructive jaundice and a 7 kg weight loss. She palpated an abdominal mass but denied pain. Five years earlier, she had left breast invasive lobular carcinoma (pT2N0M0, ER/PR positive, HER2-negative) treated with wide local excision, radiotherapy, and 5 years of hormonal therapy. Family history included breast cancer in her mother and maternal aunt. An 8-month-old mammogram was unremarkable, and she had no current breast or nipple symptoms.

On examination, she was jaundiced, had hepatomegaly 2 cm below the costal margin, and a 2 cm right breast mass at the 11 o’clock position; there were no skin changes, axillary lymphadenopathy, pleural effusion, or bony tenderness. Laboratory tests showed normal leukocyte count and hemoglobin, total bilirubin 87 μmol/L (conjugated 41 μmol/L), markedly elevated liver enzymes, and CA 19-9 95.6 U/mL.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed gross intra- and extrahepatic biliary dilatation (common bile duct 18 mm, pancreatic duct 5 mm) without an obvious obstructing lesion, enhancement over the right breast lower outer quadrant, a 4 mm left axillary node, and widespread sclerotic bone lesions. Endoscopic ultrasound identified a 14 mm hypoechoic subepithelial ampullary mass, but fine-needle aspiration was nondiagnostic. Dedicated pancreatic CT showed the mass was hyperenhancing in both the arterial and portal venous phases. Four endoscopic and radiologic attempts at cytology or histology of the pancreatic lesion were nondiagnostic.

Breast ultrasonography identified three right breast nodules (up to 12 mm at 2, 7, and 12 o’clock) and a 5 mm left axillary node; ultrasound-guided biopsy yielded Grade 2 invasive lobular carcinoma (ER > 90%, PR < 1%, HER2 negative).

At this point, it was yet to be ascertained whether the pancreatic mass represented a synchronous primary tumor or a manifestation of metastatic breast cancer.

A 35-year-old woman presented with severely restricted mouth opening for 1 year, causing difficulty with food intake and requiring her to eat through a small gap between posterior teeth. She reported progressive right-sided facial swelling since childhood and underwent soft-tissue debulking in adolescence; operative records were unavailable. Her primary concern was her inability to open her mouth. 

On examination, there was a soft right hemifacial swelling extending from the preauricular region to the midline and from below the lower eyelid to the right submandibular area, with a linear postoperative scar in the lower part of the mass. The preauricular component was firm. The right corner of the mouth was deviated downward, and the right lips were hypertrophied, with overall deviation of the mouth toward the left side. 

All blood tests, a chest radiograph, and an abdominal ultrasound were within normal limits. Neurologic examination was unremarkable, and no cutaneous lesions were noted. 

An orthopantomogram showed marked expansion and remodeling of the bones of the right temporomandibular joint with ankylosis. A CT scan of the face revealed enlargement of the right foramen ovale, greater palatine foramen, sphenopalatine foramen, inferior orbital foramen, and nasolacrimal duct; diffuse fatty infiltration of the right cheek, masticator space, parotid gland, masseter, medial and lateral pterygoid, and temporalis muscles; involvement of the upper and lower lips and right half of the tongue; and a hypertrophied bony mass ankylosing the right temporomandibular joint.

A 64-year-old woman presented with 6 months of progressive generalized weakness and dyspnea. She had no risk factors for thromboembolism. Her history was notable for headache, weight loss, nonproductive cough, and one presyncope episode the previous year.

Vital signs on admission: temperature 38.0°C; blood pressure 120/70 mmHg; pulse rate 90/min; respiratory rate 24/min; oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Arterial blood gas showed PaO₂ 26 mmHg and PaCO₂ 40 mmHg. On examination, there was no evidence of deep-vein thrombosis. Cardiac auscultation revealed a grade III/VI systolic murmur at the lower left sternal border.

Laboratory studies showed normal serum CA-125, CA-99, and CEA levels. Electrocardiography was unremarkable.

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated severe pulmonary hypertension (estimated pulmonary artery pressure 120 mmHg), severe right ventricular hypertrophy and dysfunction, moderate to severe tricuspid regurgitation, and a large nonhomogeneous mass occupying the main pulmonary artery with minimal flow on the left side and a peak gradient of 55 mmHg.

Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed a lobulated heterogeneous left hilar mass in the precarinal and subcarinal regions invading the pulmonary trunk and left main pulmonary artery, right ventricular and atrial enlargement, mild pericardial effusion, and right-sided pleural effusion. The CT report suggested a malignant tumoral lesion such as lymphoma, angiosarcoma, or bronchogenic carcinoma.

Thoracic MRI showed bilateral pleural effusions and a polypoid lesion in the pulmonary trunk extending into the left main and first-order branches, without obvious extraluminal extension or significant enhancement, along with mild right ventricular and atrial dilatation. MRI findings were interpreted as suggesting pulmonary thromboembolism, with a tumoral lesion such as angiosarcoma to be ruled out.

A 6-year-old girl presented with swelling and tenderness of her left shoulder after a trivial fall. There was restricted shoulder movement. She had no fever, weight loss, or appetite change. Initial treatment by a traditional bone setter included splinting for 6 weeks.  
On radiography of the left shoulder, there was an expansile osteolytic lesion in the proximal humerus with a pathologic fracture and a relatively narrow zone of transition.  
MRI (STIR, GRE, axial and coronal) showed a 5.4×4.8×10.6 cm heterogeneous, expansile mass involving the epiphysis, metaphysis, and diaphysis of the proximal humerus. The lesion demonstrated fluid–fluid levels, diffusion restriction, and moderate heterogeneous enhancement on post-contrast images.

A 42-year-old Hispanic man presented with a 1-year history of progressive pain, numbness, tingling, and swelling in the thumb, index, and long fingers of his right hand and distal forearm. He reported frequent nighttime awakenings, difficulty eating, and functional limitation at work. A painless mass between the palm and wrist had been present since childhood but began to increase in size with the onset of symptoms. He had no history of trauma or relevant family history. He underwent an uncomplicated open carpal tunnel release at age 16, with complete resolution of symptoms until recurrence 1 year ago.

On examination, there was macrodactyly with ulnar deviation of the second and third digits of the right hand and a palmar wrist scar. A localized, tender, 4 × 2 cm subcutaneous mass was palpable over the volar wrist and distal forearm. Muscle weakness was noted in the thenar intrinsic muscles (abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, and flexor pollicis brevis), without hypoesthesia. Radial pulse and capillary refill were normal. Tinel’s sign and Phalen’s test were both positive; there was no thenar muscle atrophy.

A high-frequency ultrasound demonstrated a 5.4 × 1.3 × 2.8 cm ventral hypoechoic fusiform mass in continuity with the median nerve, extending from the flexor tendons and muscles into the distal carpal tunnel. Electromyography showed decreased conduction velocity and prolonged motor latency of the right median nerve, consistent with entrapment neuropathy at the wrist. Radiographs revealed soft-tissue swelling of the middle finger with a calcified phlebolith but no bony erosions.

A 29‐year‐old woman with treated hypothyroidism presented with a five‐year history of a right nasal mass that had gradually increased in size. The mass was painless, nonpulsatile, and primarily caused cosmetic concern. She denied nasal obstruction, bleeding, rhinorrhea, or changes in skin pigmentation. There was no family history of similar lesions. General and neurologic examinations were normal. On nasal inspection, there was a spherical, cystic, movable, nontender enlargement of the right nasal ala extending from the lower to upper lateral cartilage, without overlying skin changes or lymphadenopathy. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the nose showed an isolated, poorly defined soft‐tissue swelling in the right anterior lateral nasal wall with mild heterogeneous enhancement and no expansion into adjacent structures. MRI demonstrated an oval, 0.5 × 0.7 cm lesion that was isointense on all sequences, with homogeneous postcontrast enhancement, distinct surrounding fat planes, and no invasion of the septum or nearby tissues; comparison with an MRI from 2018 showed only modest growth. The patient opted for surgical excision after discussion of risks and benefits.

A 35-year-old man presented with a painless, progressively enlarging mass on the palmar surface of his long finger for 5 years. He initially noted minimal discomfort but over time experienced decreased finger flexion and reduced grip strength. On examination, there was a firm, nonmobile mass approximately 10 cm in length along the course of the flexor tendon of the long finger. The overlying skin was intact without erythema or tenderness, and neurovascular examination was normal.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the hand demonstrated:
• T1-weighted images: intermediate signal intensity of the lesion.  
• T2-weighted images: heterogeneous signal with areas of low signal intensity.  
• Gradient-echo sequences: pronounced blooming artifact corresponding to low-signal foci.  
• Postcontrast T1-weighted fat-saturated images: heterogeneous contrast enhancement of the mass, with nonenhancing regions correlating with low-signal areas.

A 52‐year‐old Vietnamese woman with hypothyroidism and a 19‐year history of essential thrombocythemia (JAK2‐negative, calreticulin‐positive) presented with chronic anemia, leukocytosis, pancreatitis, hepatomegaly, portal/splenic/mesenteric vein thromboses, recurrent pleural and pericardial effusions, constrictive cardiomyopathy, restrictive lung disease, and multi‐organ fibrosis on multiple biopsies. Workup was negative for infectious, rheumatologic, or malignant etiologies. She required supplemental oxygen for chronic dyspnea and had multiple hospitalizations.

At age 51 she noted left‐eye proptosis. Visual acuity was 20/30 OD and 20/40 OS; intraocular pressures were normal; pupils were reactive without afferent defect; extraocular movements were full; left upper eyelid retraction and resistance to retropulsion were present, with 3.5 mm of proptosis. Fundus examination showed normal optic nerves and bilateral inferior placoid orange subretinal lesions with subretinal fluid. Visual fields in the left eye revealed an enlarged blind spot and a superior arcuate defect. Spectral‐domain OCT showed sub‐RPE hypolucent masses with foveal subretinal fluid in the right eye and choroidal elevation without fluid in the left eye. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated hyperfluorescence of the placoid lesions with late staining consistent with non‐exudative, multifocal choroidal infiltrates in both eyes.

MRI of the brain and orbits revealed a T1/T2‐hypointense, heterogeneously enhancing mass in the left superomedial orbit measuring 2.9 × 1.6 × 2.5 cm displacing the optic nerve, and a 4 mm superolateral lesion in the right orbit; brain imaging also showed symmetric enhancing lesions along the tentorial leaflets.

A 58-year-old African-American woman presented with abdominal pain and diarrhea. Physical examination, including abdominal, vaginal, cervical, and rectal examinations, was unremarkable.  
CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed a 3.2 cm heterogeneous mass anterior to the coccyx with central hypodensity and peripheral rim enhancement; the mass appeared separate from the posterior rectal wall, and no other pelvic abnormalities were identified.  
A CT-guided biopsy of the mass was consistent with a neuroendocrine tumor.  
Colonoscopy revealed no primary tumor in the rectum.  
Transanal endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated a heterogeneous, hypoechoic mass at 13 cm from the anal verge, clearly separate from the muscularis propria of the rectum, with no lymphadenopathy; the posterior vaginal wall was unremarkable.  
Somatostatin receptor scintigraphy showed uptake only in the presacral mass and no other sites of disease.  
Her history was notable for an imperforate anus repaired during childhood with coloanal pull-through procedures and creation of a neoanus at age 10. Prior to evaluation, her bowel function included fecal continence with occasional loose stools.  
She had no flushing, wheezing, pellagra, or other symptoms of carcinoid syndrome. Her abdominal pain resolved before any treatment for the presacral mass and was felt to be unrelated; the neuroendocrine tumor was considered an incidental finding.

A 57-year-old woman presented with a 6–7-month history of a painless swelling in the lower left jaw that began after tooth extractions and had gradually increased in size, with intermittent discharge over the past 1–2 months. Her medical, surgical, dental, family, and personal histories were unremarkable.

On extraoral examination, there was facial asymmetry from the left corner of the mouth to 2 cm anterior to the left ear and from the oral commissure to the inferior border of the mandible. The overlying skin was normal, with a localized increase in temperature. The swelling was firm to hard and nontender. Submandibular, sublingual, and cervical lymph nodes were palpable.

Intraorally, a bony hard swelling measuring approximately 4 cm × 4 cm extended from the left mandibular second premolar region to the ramus, with buccal and lingual cortical expansion and perforation. The swelling was tender on palpation.

A panoramic radiograph showed a multilocular radiolucency extending from the left mandibular second premolar to the ramus, with expansion of the buccal and lingual cortical plates and infero-border involvement.

An incisional biopsy revealed islands and nests of odontogenic epithelium with areas of cystic degeneration. The epithelium was lined by tall columnar ameloblast-like cells with hyperchromatism, reverse polarity, and central stellate reticulum-like cells. Scattered within the epithelium were aggregates of enlarged, eosinophilic ghost cells, some showing basophilic calcifications. Adjacent to the epithelial component were amorphous eosinophilic deposits consistent with dysplastic dentin.

A 49-year-old woman presented with a left lower neck mass of one year’s duration, noting rapid enlargement over the preceding two weeks. She denied symptoms of thyroid dysfunction. She reported new-onset pain radiating to the back of her left ear and dysphagia. She had no history of tobacco or alcohol use. On examination, the left thyroid lobe was enlarged (3 cm × 3 cm), and a level IV cervical lymph node was palpable. Fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid mass reportedly showed papillary carcinoma. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a soft-tissue–density mass arising from the inferior aspect of the left thyroid lobe, extending to the thoracic inlet and across midline to the right, with compression of the esophagus. Fiberoptic laryngoscopy was normal. The patient was scheduled for total thyroidectomy and left radical neck dissection.

A 63-year-old Caucasian man with a previously diagnosed well-differentiated grade 2 small-bowel neuroendocrine tumor (Ki-67 17%) and multiple liver metastases underwent ileocecal resection to control increasing local symptoms. Shortly after surgery, he developed significant watery diarrhea with up to five bowel motions per day characterized by explosive large-volume stools, fecal urgency, and persistence during fasting. His symptoms deteriorated rapidly after surgery, prompting consideration of short gut syndrome or bile acid diarrhea.  
Laboratory evaluation revealed:  
• Serum chromogranin A < 85 ng/mL; vasoactive intestinal peptide 0.0–50.0 pmol/L within range; glucagon 50–150 pg/mL within range.  
• Urine 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) 1727 µmol/24 hours (normal 0–40 µmol/24 hours).  
Full blood count, liver function tests, B12, thyroid function, folate, vitamin D, celiac serology, and calcium were unremarkable. Fecal analysis (culture, calprotectin, chymotrypsin, osmolality, pancreatic elastase) showed no significant findings. Flexible sigmoidoscopy, gastroscopy, and colonoscopy with biopsies revealed no anatomical defects or inflammation.

A 19-month-old girl presented with a 1-month history of an oral mass arising from the left underside of the tongue. Initially small and asymptomatic, the lesion was treated empirically with antibiotics for 2 weeks with minimal change; over the subsequent 2 weeks it rapidly enlarged, covering more than two-thirds of her mouth, pushing the tongue to the right, preventing mouth closure, impairing speech, and causing continuous drooling.
