There was no stridor or dyspnea, but she had difficulty feeding and was limited to pureed diet without choking. The mass emitted a foul odor, had a whitish surface coating, and bled on contact. There was no fever, trauma, other swellings, or bleeding diathesis. On examination, she was afebrile and irritable. A firm, nonfluctuant, oval mass (5×4×3 cm) with whitish debris and pink-purple undersurface occupied three-quarters of the oral cavity, arising from the left floor of the mouth; the mobile tongue was displaced to the right. Other systems were normal. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin of 7 g/dL, normal leukocyte and platelet counts, and normal electrolytes. A COVID-19 PCR test was negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck demonstrated a well-circumscribed, contrast-enhancing mass in the left oral cavity with intact fat planes in the floor of mouth and tongue.

A 47-year-old G1P1 African American woman presented with a four-month history of an intermittently painful right groin mass that had recently increased in size. She denied gastrointestinal or urinary symptoms, weight loss, fever, or chills. Her medical history was unremarkable, with no known uterine fibroids or long-term estrogen use. Surgical history included cesarean section, abdominoplasty, and laparoscopic appendectomy. On examination in the standing position, there was a visible bulge in the right inguinal area; palpation revealed a round, firm, ~4 cm mass that was tender only with deep pressure. The mass was partially reducible when the patient was supine. Vital signs were normal, and routine blood work was within normal limits. No imaging studies were obtained. A working diagnosis of incarcerated right inguinal hernia was made, and elective surgical repair was planned.

A 14-year-old boy presented with sudden onset of right‐sided chest pain and dyspnea. He had no prior medical history or asbestos exposure. On initial evaluation at another hospital, a chest CT revealed a massive right pleural effusion; 700 mL of blood-stained fluid was aspirated. Five days later, he was transferred after an additional 1 000 mL of blood-stained pleural fluid was drained. Routine blood tests were within normal limits except for a low eosinophil count. Blood and sputum cultures were negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed a heterogeneously enhancing solid mass occupying the upper two-thirds of the right hemithorax, compressing the right lung. The mass wall demonstrated enhancement, particularly at a mural nodule and thickened areas. There was also a large pleural effusion with underlying pulmonary atelectasis in the lower hemithorax. No hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy was noted. Preoperative serum tumor markers, including HCG, CEA, AFP, CA 72-4, CA 125, CA 19-9, and CA 15-3, were all negative.

A 61-year-old Hispanic man with a history of gastroesophageal reflux disease, treated hepatitis C, and alcohol and tobacco abuse presented with 2 months of progressive dysphagia (solids then liquids), 15 lb weight loss, occasional nausea, and intermittent blood-tinged vomiting after retching. He reported food “sticking” in the mid-esophagus. Examination revealed cachexia, a painless, firm 2 cm nodule along the left zygomatic crest, and a firm, fixed ~1 cm nodule at the right base of the tongue. Initial laboratory studies, including complete blood count, metabolic panel, liver function tests, and coagulation studies, were normal. Fluoroscopy showed a 3 cm distal esophageal mass. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a 1.8 cm left anterior facial soft-tissue mass, a 1.2 × 1.7 × 1.3 cm right floor-of-tongue nodule, and multiple small nodules in neck muscles. CT of the thorax showed a 4.6 cm eccentric distal esophageal wall thickening (1.8 cm thickness) with an adjacent 8 mm lymph node. CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed an enlarged, enhancing left adrenal gland, scattered right iliopsoas hyperenhancing nodules (largest 1.8 cm), paraspinal musculature nodules (~1 cm), and several subcutaneous nodules up to 0.6 cm in the left flank.  
Per initial radiologist review, the esophageal mass was highly concerning for malignancy. The face and neck soft-tissue findings were unusual for esophageal spread, raising the possibility of a second primary such as melanoma, and the abdominal/pelvic nodules were likewise suspicious for metastases versus metastatic melanoma.  
What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 40-year-old woman in good health presented with more than 50 flat, verrucous, lightly tanned papules clustered on normally pigmented skin of the left thigh. Each lesion measured 0.2 to 1.1 cm. The papules had been present since her teenage years and had remained stable in number and size for several years. A few similar papules were also noted on the posterior thigh and proximal calf of the same leg; the remainder of her skin was unremarkable except for 10 to 15 evenly distributed typical nevi on the trunk and other limbs. She reported no symptoms and had observed no recent changes in the lesions. Her medical history was unremarkable, and there was no family history of melanoma or atypical nevi. On the basis of the clinical appearance, the initial differential diagnosis included seborrheic keratosis, common warts, and agminated Spitz nevi.

A 65-year-old woman was admitted with a 2-week history of rapidly progressive visual reduction, drowsiness, polyuria, and polydipsia. Her medical history included a temporal arachnoid cyst with seizures and a vestibular schwannoma treated by gamma-knife radiosurgery 2 years earlier. On examination, she had bitemporal hemianopsia; no other neurological deficits or flushing or diarrhea were noted.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed a 2-cm sellar/suprasellar mass compressing the optic chiasm and extending toward the left cavernous sinus. The lesion was predominantly isointense to gray matter on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with diffuse homogeneous enhancement after contrast administration. An MRI performed 2 years earlier demonstrated a normal pituitary gland.

Endocrinological evaluation revealed a thyroid-stimulating hormone level of 1.31 mU/ml, free thyroxine 3.9 pg/ml, free triiodothyronine 2.4 pg/ml, and prolactin 77 ng/ml.

A 3-year-old girl with no significant medical history was noted by her parents to have a growth in the floor of her mouth for two months. The lesion was asymptomatic, without dysphagia or dyspnea, and there was no fever or palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. On examination, a well-circumscribed, fluctuant mass was seen in the anterior midline of the floor of the mouth; the overlying mucosa was normal, and the lesion was not fixed to deeper tissues. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a 2.0 × 1.5 cm, well-encapsulated cystic mass confined to the sublingual space without infiltration of adjacent structures.

A 54-year-old man presented with right-sided chest pain of 4 weeks’ duration. His medical history was notable only for surgery for perforated appendicitis in 1976 and pneumonia in 1984. On initial examination, thoracic and lumbar spine radiographs showed prominent degenerative changes and mild scoliosis but no acute pathology. Neurologic examination, including muscle strength testing and deep-tendon reflexes of the lower extremities, was normal. He was treated with a trigger-point injection for presumed myofascial pain syndrome, nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs, muscle relaxants, and physical therapy. 

One week later, he reported improvement in chest pain but new numbness and weakness in both legs. Repeat neurologic examination remained without focal deficits. Two weeks after initial treatment, he had persistent lower-extremity weakness. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the thoracic spine revealed a lesion involving the fifth vertebral body and posterior elements, displacing the spinal cord to the left; the lesion had low signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images and did not breach the cortical bone. 

Laboratory studies, including serum and urine free light chains (κ, λ), urine Bence-Jones protein, serum β2-microglobulin, and tumor markers, were within normal limits. A skull radiograph was unremarkable. Somatosensory evoked potentials showed right-sided sensory conduction defect; motor evoked potentials were normal. Bone scintigraphy demonstrated only slight uptake at the fifth thoracic vertebra, with no other abnormalities.

A previously healthy 13-year-old boy presented in December 2019 with a three-month history of neck pain, swelling, stiffness, and restricted neck movement but no neurologic deficits. He was in good general condition (ECOG 0), and the neurologic examination was normal. Cervical CT showed a 66 × 55 × 46 mm mass at C2 with calcification and lytic changes. Cervical MRI revealed a large lesion in the C2 spinous process extending to the pedicles, containing a characteristic fluid–fluid level and hemorrhage, and bulging into the right spinal canal with thecal sac compression. MR findings raised the following differential diagnoses: aneurysmal bone cyst, giant cell tumor of bone, and telangiectatic osteosarcoma.

A 30-year-old Asian man presented with a 6-month history of recurrent pain localized to the lateral side of his left knee. On examination, there was slight tenderness and swelling over the lateral joint line without other abnormalities. Plain radiographs were unremarkable, and routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. MRI demonstrated a 1.5 cm intra-articular space-occupying lesion invading the tibial plateau. On T1-weighted images, the lesion was homogeneous and isointense to muscle; on T2-weighted images, it appeared heterogeneous with internal specks and was unremarkable on fat-saturated T2 sequences. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI showed enhancement confined to the peripheral rim of the mass, with no satellite lesions identified.

A 36-year-old man with chronic myeloid leukemia on nilotinib presented with a 1-week history of progressive upper back pain and an unsteady gait, limiting him to only a few steps of ambulation. On neurologic examination, lower-limb strength was markedly reduced with hip and knee flexion graded 1/5 and ankle and toe movements graded 4/5 (MRC scale). Hyperactive knee and ankle reflexes were noted bilaterally. MRI of the thoracic spine showed extradural soft-tissue lesions from D5 to D9 on the right side, displacing the cord to the left; T1-weighted images were hypointense and STIR sequences showed hyperintense lesions in the dorsal and lumbar vertebrae, pelvis, and proximal femora. To exclude an epidural infection such as tuberculosis, a needle biopsy was performed and showed no evidence of infection.

A 26-year-old man was referred with a 10-month history of a swelling on the lingual aspect of the lower anterior teeth. He had no systemic disease or medication use. One month earlier, the mandibular central incisors had been extracted for mobility and the socket curetted, but the lesion recurred within days. 

On extraoral examination there was no lymphadenopathy or facial asymmetry. Intraorally, there was a 2.5 cm pinkish nodular lesion on the lingual surface of the anterior mandible in the area of the missing central incisors. The lesion was rubbery, with surface telangiectasia, and bled occasionally after trauma.

A review of prior panoramic radiographs showed a well-defined radiolucency in the mandibular anterior region. Cone-beam CT of the mandible showed no pathological changes in the underlying bone. 

Aspiration yielded passive blood. Ultrasound revealed a heterogeneous, ill-defined mass in the lingual gingiva containing three calcified foci (24, 13, and 16 mm) and marked blood flow on Doppler imaging.

A 14-year-old girl presented with a 3-year history of a slowly enlarging mass in her left breast. On examination, there was a 10 × 7 cm soft, smooth, and mobile mass occupying the lower two-thirds of the left breast without axillary lymphadenopathy. Mammography showed a high-density 10-cm mass with well-defined borders. Ultrasound revealed a well-circumscribed 10-cm hypoechoic lesion. MRI demonstrated a uniformly enhancing tumor occupying two-thirds of the left breast. Core needle biopsy revealed tissue composed of epithelial and stromal components with maintained biphasic epithelium, a MIB-1 labeling index of less than 1%, and was interpreted as a fibroadenoma.

A 17-year-old male was referred to a periodontist for evaluation of a gingival enlargement on the buccal aspect of the right mandibular central and lateral incisors. He reported that the lesion had appeared gradually over the past year and that biting solid foods caused easy bleeding. Medical history was unremarkable. On examination, vesicular, asymptomatic lesions with an intact surface were present on the attached and marginal buccal gingiva of the involved teeth; the lingual gingiva was unaffected. Complete blood count, bleeding time, clotting time, prothrombin time, and partial thromboplastin time were all normal. Periapical and panoramic radiographs showed no bony or dental abnormalities. Initial management included oral hygiene instruction and scaling and root planing of all teeth except the two involved incisors, achieving a plaque control record ≥ 90%. Two weeks after scaling and root planing, a biopsy of the lesion was performed, and the specimen was sent for histopathological examination with a differential diagnosis of pyogenic granuloma and hemangioma.

A 63-year-old Caucasian man with a history of smoking and cardiovascular disease presented with a 1-month history of right cheek swelling. He was afebrile. Examination revealed a painless, non-erythematous, mobile, round mass (~2 cm) in the right parotid region.  
Ultrasonography showed a single lobulated, well-circumscribed, hypoechogenic cystic lesion with irregular edges and acoustic enhancement in the superficial parenchyma of the right parotid gland; a few echogenic foci suggested debris.  
Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration yielded a cystic background with “dirty” necrosis and pseudopapillary clusters of moderately atypical cells with cyanophilic cytoplasm. The specimen was classified as category V (suspicious for malignancy) by the Milan System, and salivary duct carcinoma was initially considered.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the face and thorax demonstrated a homogeneously enhancing nodular lesion in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland, surrounded by a thin fibrous capsule, with no suspicious cervical lymph nodes or thoracic lesions.

A 57-year-old man with a history of renal transplantation 18 years earlier for chronic kidney disease and hypertensive nephropathy presented with fever, fatigue, decreased appetite, and a 40-pound weight loss over three months. His medical history included gout and hypertension, and his medications included antihypertensives, xanthine oxidase inhibitors, prednisone, cyclosporine, and mycophenolate. On admission, laboratory evaluation showed a neutrophil-predominant leukocytosis of 89% (reference 44–65%) and lymphopenia of 3% (reference 25–46%). Microbiologic testing was negative for EBV, BK virus, CMV, histoplasmosis, legionella, influenza A and B, aspergillus, and MRSA; blood and urine cultures were also negative. Imaging revealed an 18-cm heterogeneous hepatic mass and multiple bilateral native renal masses; a 6-cm mass with a calcified, thickened wall in the lower pole of the right kidney was suspected to be the primary lesion. A diagnosis of septic shock and probable posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorder was considered.  
CT-guided needle core biopsy of the right renal mass showed highly cellular cores almost entirely replaced by sheets of noncohesive large cells infiltrating and replacing renal tubules. The tumor cells were pleomorphic, three to four times larger than tubular epithelial cells, with abundant eosinophilic to vacuolated cytoplasm, coarse chromatin, and prominent nucleoli; large multinucleated forms, hemophagocytosis, intermixed neutrophils, atypical mitoses, and necrosis were noted. Immunohistochemical staining showed tumor-cell positivity for CD68, lysozyme, HAM56, and CD4, and negativity for CD45, myeloperoxidase, CD21, CD23, CD1a, CD3, CD20, CD56, CD99, pancytokeratins, EBV/LMP-1, and S-100. Gomori methenamine silver stain was negative for fungal organisms.

An 18-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a right adrenal mass detected on imaging. Her medical and surgical history was unremarkable. She had no symptoms, and on examination there was no palpable abdominal or flank mass. Routine laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, renal, hepatic, bone, and coagulation profiles, as well as tumor markers (CEA, AFP, and CA 12-5), were all within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 4.2 × 3.2 cm heterogeneous, noncalcified mass in the region of the right adrenal gland. The right renal vein and inferior vena cava were intact. No pleural effusion, ascites, lymphadenopathy, or pelvic masses were identified. The patient was scheduled for surgical resection of the presumed adrenal lesion.

A 52-year-old woman was evaluated for intermittent right upper-quadrant pain without jaundice, nausea, vomiting, or bowel-habit changes. Liver-function tests showed a cholestatic pattern (alkaline phosphatase 139 U/L, γ-glutamyltransferase 67 U/L; total bilirubin 6 μmol/L). Complete blood count was normal. Abdominal ultrasound revealed cholelithiasis, a normal biliary tree, fatty liver infiltration, and incidentally a 3 cm, well-circumscribed, hyperechoic lesion at the inferior splenic pole without significant Doppler flow. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a hypodense, well-defined splenic lesion with some internal arterial and venous enhancement, becoming isodense on delayed images. On MRI, the lesion was hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2, showed internal linear enhancement in the portal venous phase after gadolinium, and became isointense on delayed sequences. A Tc-99m–labeled red-blood-cell scan demonstrated a “cold” splenic defect. Ultrasound-guided core biopsy was nondiagnostic, showing only skeletal muscle. Given the benign radiologic appearance, the lesion was initially observed. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy was then performed with resolution of her biliary colic. Six months later, follow-up CT demonstrated interval enlargement of the splenic lesion and development of an adjacent satellite nodule with similar imaging characteristics. A decision was made to perform a splenectomy.

A previously healthy 10-year-old girl was evaluated for a 4-year history of dyspnea on exertion and progressive spinal deformity. She had no fever or other respiratory symptoms. On examination, she was not in respiratory distress; breath sounds were diminished in the left lung field, especially at the base, with dullness to percussion. 

Chest radiography showed a large opacity occupying the left hemithorax, containing amorphous calcifications and causing a rightward shift of the cardiomediastinal silhouette. Contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography revealed a giant, well-defined, encapsulated mass in the anterior mediastinum measuring 135 × 150 × 197 mm. The lesion had areas of soft-tissue density, cystic change, and calcification, with heterogeneous enhancement, extended beyond the midline into the retrocardiac space, displaced and compressed the left lung (rendering it hypoplastic), and shifted the thymus to the right. 

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and biochemical profile, and negative levels of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (B-HCG).

A 38‐year‐old woman presented with a painless right‐sided neck mass. She had no significant past medical history. On examination there was a palpable, firm, semi‐mobile, pulsatile 1 cm mass at level II/III on the right. Neck ultrasound showed a 2 × 1.3 × 2 cm hypoechoic, vascular solid nodule just anterior to the carotid bifurcation. MRI of the neck demonstrated a well‐circumscribed, homogeneous, T1 hypointense, T2 hyperintense, gadolinium‐enhancing mass anterior to the right carotid bifurcation, appearing to contact and possibly encase the external carotid artery without significant luminal narrowing. A preliminary diagnosis of paraganglioma was made, and the patient underwent digital subtraction angiography. Angiography revealed a moderately vascular, rounded mass anterior‐medial to the right common carotid bifurcation supplied by multiple branches of the superior thyroid artery, mildly displacing the external carotid artery. The carotid bifurcation was not splayed.

A 45-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a rapidly growing mass on the temporal conjunctiva of his left eye, associated with redness and irritation. He had undergone excision of a similar lesion at the same site one year earlier. On examination, there was a vascularized, whitish, elevated lesion at the temporal limbus with an infiltrative appearance. The lesion extended onto the cornea, producing folds in the perilesional stroma, involved the temporal bulbar conjunctiva, and caused retraction of the tarsal conjunctiva.

A 37-year-old G5P3 woman presented with a one-year history of intermittent postcoital bleeding. Her menstrual cycles were regular, and a Pap test three months earlier was normal. She had no history of cervical dysplasia. She smoked five to six cigarettes per day for two years. On pelvic examination, a friable lesion was noted on the cervix. A punch biopsy reportedly favored a benign reactive process. On review, pathology raised the possibility of “an atypical epithelioid mesenchymal proliferation extending to the biopsy margin.” The differential at that time included a perivascular epithelioid cell tumor or an epithelioid smooth muscle neoplasm. Colposcopic re-biopsy was indeterminate for dysplasia, “favoring reactive atypia versus a low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion,” and endocervical curettage showed benign endocervical fragments. The colposcopic impression was “an atypical cervical fibroid,” and an excisional biopsy was recommended. Ten weeks later, the patient underwent excisional biopsy of the cervix, which “returned as perivascular epithelioid cell tumour (PEComa) with maximum contiguous diameter 9 mm and positive peripheral and deep resection margins.”

An 18-year-old Turkish man with no comorbidities presented with right lower-quadrant abdominal pain. Physical examination findings were normal, and routine laboratory tests were within reference ranges. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a heterogeneous, well-defined mass measuring 5.0×7.0 cm in the left adrenal region. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a relatively homogeneous left adrenal mass measuring 5.2×4.3×7.1 cm with faint calcifications and well-defined margins. MRI demonstrated a solid 5.0×4.0×7.0 cm adrenal lesion that was slightly hypointense on T1-weighted images and slightly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with progressive, heterogeneous, delayed enhancement after gadolinium administration. An endocrine evaluation—including 24-hour urinary catecholamines, serum cortisol measurements, and a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test—was unremarkable. To further assess for malignancy, an 18F-FDG PET scan was performed, revealing an SUV of 4.1 in the left adrenal mass, but imaging could not definitively categorize the lesion as benign or malignant.

A 37-year-old woman presented with 3 months of heavy menstrual bleeding and dysmenorrhea. Her medical history included asthma, depression, and anxiety; she had previously undergone a cesarean section. Family history was noncontributory. On examination, the uterus was enlarged, mobile, and otherwise unremarkable.  
Pelvic ultrasound and CT scan showed a thickened endometrium and peritoneal thickening, with no ascites, lymphadenopathy, or distant metastases. Serum CA125 was 23 kU/L (normal range).  
Hysteroscopy revealed a diffusely thickened endometrium without distinct masses, and dilation and curettage yielded predominantly benign endometrium with two small fragments of poorly preserved epithelioid tumor. These cells were arranged in trabeculae within fibrous stroma and stained positively for AE1/3, calretinin, and CD10. Based on these findings, the lesion was interpreted as a uterine tumor similar to an ovarian sex cord tumor, and the patient was scheduled for exploratory laparotomy with possible ovarian preservation.  
At laparotomy, there were opaque ascites, omental caking, and multiple small nodules studding the pelvic peritoneum; the uterus and adnexa appeared macroscopically normal. A total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingectomy, and omentectomy were performed with optimal cytoreduction.  
Histologic examination of the uterus and cervix showed patchy infiltration by an epithelioid malignancy eroding through the myometrium and endometrium, with extensive lymphovascular and perineural invasion and involvement of the fallopian tube serosa. The omental tumor measured up to 70 mm and displayed mixed tubulopapillary, trabecular, and solid architecture.  
Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated positivity for calretinin, CK5/6, D2-40, and CK7 (focally CK20), and negativity for PAX-8 and Claudin-4. There was loss of nuclear staining for BAP1.

A 36-year-old Asian woman presented with a rapidly progressive, diffuse lump in her left breast. She first noted bluish-purple skin discoloration in July 2021, initially attributed to trauma. From January to March 2022 her left breast enlarged significantly. She had no history of breast surgery, breast irradiation, chronic or genetic diseases, smoking, or drug use. Menarche was at age 13; she has had two live births and no oral contraceptive use.

On examination, the upper outer quadrant of the left breast contained a firm, slightly tender 8 cm × 5 cm mass with poor mobility, overlying bluish-purple discoloration, and a local rise in temperature. There was no nipple retraction, skin dimpling, dilated veins, or palpable axillary lymph nodes.

On March 26, 2022, routine blood tests and tumor markers (CA125, CA15-3, CEA) were within normal limits. Mammography showed an ill-defined, non-calcified area, suspected to be an inflammatory lesion. Ultrasonography (USG) revealed a large area of uneven echogenicity, highly suspicious for granulomatous mastitis. A subsequent USG demonstrated several possibly abnormal lymph nodes in the left axilla, the largest measuring 1 cm × 0.7 cm; an ultrasound-guided axillary lymph node biopsy showed no tumor cells. PET-CT revealed a hypermetabolic thickened tissue in the left upper breast with an SUV max of 3.5 and small axillary lymph nodes with an SUV max of 1.3, suspected to be inflammatory; no distant organ metastasis was seen.

A 23-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of left great-toe pain that prevented him from wearing shoes. Two years earlier, he had undergone nail‐bed excision for an ingrown toenail by a general surgeon; since then he had nightly throbbing pain relieved by nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. He had also taken an unidentified antibiotic and etodolac 500 mg twice daily. On examination, the left great toe was noticeably enlarged compared with the right, and was warm and tender to palpation. His medical and family history were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein level, and leukocyte count. Plain radiographs demonstrated a lytic bone lesion with a sclerotic rim in the medial part of the distal phalanx. Magnetic resonance imaging showed bone marrow and soft tissue edema in the distal phalanx, compatible with osteomyelitis. A 99mTc bone scan revealed increased uptake in the left great toe.

A 37-year-old man presented in October 2018 with a rapid increase in size of a right lower abdominal wall mass. He first noticed a right inguinal swelling in 2010 but sought no treatment until January 2018, when he underwent en-bloc resection via a right flank incision; intraoperatively the tumor involved the internal oblique and transversus abdominis without distant disease. Histopathology showed a neoplastic lesion in a lobular configuration composed of spindle-shaped cells arranged in cords and nests. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated p63 positivity, focal AE1/AE3 positivity, and patchy S-100 and EMA positivity. From January to October 2018 he was stable, then noted a rapid enlargement of the site over a few months. On examination, he was afebrile with normal vital signs. There was a firm, non-tender, fixed mass approximately 10×10 cm in the right lower lumbar to inguinal region without overlying skin changes or lymphadenopathy; the rest of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed a hypermetabolic soft-tissue mass with a necrotic component in the right lateral abdominal wall measuring 134.4×71.5 mm, with no evidence of distant metastases.

A 48-year-old man with a one-year history of hypertension on therapy presented with one day of right-sided weakness, facial palsy, and generalized tonic–clonic seizures lasting two minutes each. On examination, he was alert and oriented, with right upper and lower limb strength 4/5 and equivocal plantar responses.  
 
Noncontrast head CT showed a partially well-defined heterogeneous lesion in the posterior corpus callosum and septum pellucidum, a low-density ill-defined area in the left parietal lobe containing multiple high-density calcifications, and effacement of left cerebral sulci. Ischemic stroke was initially suspected, but the calcifications raised concern for tuberculous infection. The patient was treated with anticonvulsants, antibiotics, neurotrophic support, and was discharged after five days on ongoing antihypertensives and supportive medications.  
 
Two weeks later, he returned with loss of consciousness. Brain MRI on T1-weighted images demonstrated an irregular lesion involving the splenium of the corpus callosum extending into the left periventricular parietal lobe with cystic foci in the septum pellucidum, showing low signal intensity. T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences showed high signal intensity in the same regions. Post-gadolinium T1-weighted images revealed an irregularly outlined, heterogeneously enhancing “butterfly” lesion involving the body and splenium of the corpus callosum and extending into bilateral periventricular parietal lobes.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 2-day history of worsening left upper quadrant abdominal pain radiating to the flank. Since April 2020, following intrauterine device placement, she had experienced left lower quadrant pain, progressive vaginal bleeding, mild dysuria, fever, generalized malaise, and left-sided flank pain. 

On evaluation at an outside hospital, a contrast-enhanced CT scan showed a 4.7 × 12 × 11 cm multilobulated heterogeneous retroperitoneal mass of fat and soft-tissue attenuation in the left posterior pararenal space, as well as a 2.0 × 2.3 × 2.2 cm left adnexal mass consistent with a tubo-ovarian abscess. She was admitted for treatment of the abscess and had persistent fever and leukocytosis; nephrology was consulted for elevated creatinine. After resolution of her initial symptoms, repeat CT and MRI redemonstrated a 12.7 cm heterogeneous fat and soft-tissue–containing retroperitoneal mass, which was “suspicious for dedifferentiated liposarcoma.” MRI images were significantly degraded by susceptibility artifacts from spinal fixation hardware. Differential considerations included retroperitoneal teratoma and extramedullary hematopoiesis. The mass abutted her native left kidney; she had previously undergone kidney transplantation for membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.

A 56-year-old man was referred with acute dysarthria and left hemiparesis. His history included arterial hypertension and permanent atrial fibrillation, for which he was not anticoagulated due to a previous intracerebral hemorrhage. On examination, he was alert and oriented, with slurred speech but no aphasia, residual spastic hemiparesis of the left limbs, left-sided ataxia, and cardiac arrhythmia on auscultation. 

Laboratory studies were notable only for a marginally elevated creatinine (1.44 mg/dL) and troponin (18 ng/L). Cranial CT showed no acute infarction or hemorrhage. MRI demonstrated diffusion restriction in the left corona radiata extending into the precentral gyrus, consistent with acute ischemia, plus hemosiderin in the right thalamus from prior hemorrhage. Neurosonography showed no significant stenosis.

The stroke was initially attributed to cardioembolism from atrial fibrillation. Given his contraindication to oral anticoagulation, he was referred for left atrial appendage closure. Transesophageal echocardiography performed to assess the appendage revealed a mass adjacent to the left atrial appendage, which was interpreted as thrombus. Anticoagulation with apixaban was initiated, and further imaging was planned.

A 55-year-old healthy White man was found on routine optometry screening to have an intraocular pressure (IOP) of 25 mmHg in the left eye and 13 mmHg in the right eye, with normal visual acuity of 20/20 bilaterally. Optic disc cupping and retinal nerve-fiber-layer thinning were noted in the left eye, without rubeosis iridis or inflammation; Humphrey visual fields were normal. He was diagnosed with primary open-angle glaucoma and treated with timolol and later tafluprost, with IOP in the left eye ranging from 13 to 19 mmHg over two years. In October 2022, he noted reduced vision in the left eye (BCVA 20/32) and was found to have a cortical cataract. In November 2022, prior to planned cataract surgery, dilated slit-lamp examination revealed a pale tan tumor with dilated surface vessels between 11 and 1 o’clock, causing a sectorial cortical cataract and mild lens subluxation. Gonioscopy showed an open, lightly pigmented angle. Ultrasound biomicroscopy demonstrated a partially cystic lesion with heterogeneous internal reflectivity, 5.7 mm in thickness and 6.0 mm in basal diameter. The patient was referred for evaluation of a suspected ciliary body malignancy.

An 18-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with left leg and knee pain on walking of 2 months’ duration. He denied trauma; examination showed no signs of infection.  
Magnetic resonance imaging of the left knee revealed focal areas of bone signal alteration in the distal femur and subcutaneous tissue, initially considered nonspecific. A repeat MRI performed two months later showed marked enlargement of these bone lesions in the left femur, tibia, and fibula, along with new soft tissue masses in multiple tissue planes.  
Positron-emission tomography–CT demonstrated fluorodeoxyglucose–avid small osteolytic cortical lesions with periosteal and endosteal erosion in the distal femur, patella, tibia, fibula, talus, and calcaneus of the left lower limb, associated with muscular and subcutaneous masses.  
Excisional biopsies were obtained from subcutaneous nodules in the left thigh and leg and from lesions in the distal fibula and calcaneus. Histopathology showed epithelioid-to-spindle cells with dense eosinophilic cytoplasm, few intracytoplasmic lumens, no apparent vascular channels, mild-to-moderate cytologic atypia, low mitotic activity, and admixed neutrophils. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed:  
• CAMTA-1 Polyclonal: Negative  
• INI-1 MRQ-27: Preserved expression  
• Pan-cytokeratin AE1/AE3: Positive  
• CD31 JC70A: Positive  
• ERG EP111: Positive  
• CD34 QBEnd10: Negative  
• S100 Polyclonal: Negative  
• Desmin D33: Negative  
• Myogenin F5D: Negative  
• Smooth muscle actin 1A4: Negative

A 46-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an abdominal mass that had been growing progressively over the past 2 years. Six years earlier, she had been diagnosed with recurrent myoepithelial carcinoma of the parotid gland, treated with multiple surgical resections (including an extended radical parotidectomy 4 years before), combination chemotherapy (doxorubicin, paclitaxel, carboplatin, leucovorin, and 5-fluorouracil), and radiotherapy, achieving only a partial response. Over the course of her cancer therapy, she lost 12 kg and noted an egg-shaped mass in the upper left abdomen. She was asymptomatic and initially deferred evaluation of the mass, which continued to enlarge in parallel with her weight loss.

On examination, a palpable, firm mass occupied the left upper quadrant. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed a 12.7 × 13.2 × 14 cm heterogeneous intraabdominal mass in the left upper quadrant, with central necrosis. The mass appeared to originate from the posterior aspect of the stomach or the mesentery adjacent to the body of the pancreas, extended anteriorly to involve the parietal peritoneum, and compressed the pancreas, abdominal aorta, and inferior vena cava medially without obvious vascular invasion. The radiologic appearance suggested a mesenchymal or sarcoma-like tumor. Given her history, the differential diagnosis included metastatic disease to the pancreas versus a primary gastrointestinal stromal tumor of gastric or pancreatic origin.

A 50-year-old man presented with 2 months of progressive dysphagia to solids. His family history was unremarkable. On physical examination, there were no pigmented skin lesions or lymphadenopathy. Routine blood and urine studies were within normal limits. Upper endoscopy revealed a large bluish intraluminal lesion compromising the lumen of the entire esophagus. Endoscopic ultrasound showed a heteroechoic, solid mass without calcifications; the layer of origin was difficult to define. Fine-needle aspiration cytology suggested a poorly differentiated carcinoma. Immunohistochemical analysis of a biopsy specimen was positive for human melanoma black (HMB)-45, S-100, and vimentin, and negative for cytokeratin and p53. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated an esophageal mass and a 7 mm nodule in the left upper lobe of the lung, with no evidence of lymphadenopathy in the mediastinum, abdomen, or liver lesions.

A 28-year-old nulliparous woman with no prior medical problems presented with a two-week history of postprandial abdominal pain. She took oral contraceptives and had no family history of cancer. On examination, a firm abdominal mass was palpable. Laboratory studies showed a CA 125 level of 71 U/mL and a negative alpha-fetoprotein level. Transabdominal ultrasound demonstrated ascites and multiple solid masses throughout the peritoneum. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed moderate ascites and multiple well-circumscribed peritoneal nodules, the largest measuring 6.5 × 8 cm in the right upper quadrant.

A 12-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a palatal swelling first noted about 5 years earlier. He had no pain, speech or swallowing difficulties, or systemic symptoms. His only medication was methylphenidate for ADHD. On examination, there was a 2 cm firm, nonfluctuant, nontender, immobile nodular mass with intact mucosa on the left hard palate in the bicuspid-molar region. No cervical lymphadenopathy was present. Dental radiographs were unremarkable. MRI revealed a well-demarcated mass on the left hard palate without bone invasion.

A 45-year-old man with HIV infection for 9 years on highly active antiretroviral therapy (undetectable viral load, CD4 count 800 cells/mm3), type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypertension presented with a 4-month history of right lower extremity pain. Four days before admission, he noted new ulcerations on the right lower extremity associated with swelling and subjective fevers. He was diagnosed with cellulitis, underwent surgical debridement, and received doxycycline. He was discharged in stable condition but returned 12 days later with worsening pain and ulcerations. On examination, there was a chronic wound with overlying scaling and raised erythematous indurated lesions on the right lower extremity and similar new lesions on the left lower extremity. Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy failed to improve the skin lesions. A second debridement was performed, and a tissue sample was obtained for biopsy. Culture of the tissue grew Staphylococcus aureus and Enterococcus faecalis.

A 9-year-old spayed female Pointer (15 kg) was evaluated for a 9-month history of intermittent vomiting and progressive weight loss. The dog was originally from Greece, spent one year in Germany, and had lived in Finland for 6 years.  

On examination, body condition was 3/9 with mild periodontitis. CBC was unremarkable. Serum biochemistry showed mild hypoproteinaemia (53 g/l; RI 58–77), hypoalbuminaemia (25.7 g/l; RI 30–41), and hypocobalaminaemia (163 pg/ml; RI 200–850). C-reactive protein was mildly elevated (26.2 mg/l; RI <10). Leishmania infantum antibody titre was markedly elevated (1:512; RI <1:32). Serum gastrin was within normal limits (26 ng/l; RI 10–40). Tests for Dirofilaria immitis antigen and antibodies to Borrelia, Anaplasma, and Ehrlichia were negative. Faecal parasite exam and bacterial cultures were negative. Abdominal ultrasound revealed mild focal gastric wall thickening with slight loss of layering, mild colonic mucosal thickening, enlarged mesenteric and medial iliac lymph nodes, and hyperechoic renal cortical spots.

An elimination hydrolysed diet was initiated along with famotidine, ondansetron, maropitant citrate, and oral cobalamin supplementation, but clinical signs persisted.

One month later, gastroduodenoscopy showed grossly irregular, giant cerebriform folds in the corpus, fundus, and proximal antrum; the distal antrum and duodenum appeared normal. Duodenal biopsies revealed mild chronic lymphoplasmacytic enteritis. Gastric mucosal biopsies demonstrated moderate multifocal chronic granulomatous gastritis with macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells; occasional 3–6 µm PAS- and silver-positive single-cell organisms within macrophages; severe Helicobacter-like organism colonization; and multifocal mild cystic dilation of mid-mucosal glands.

A 5-month-old dark-skinned boy was seen for evaluation of a congenital skin lesion on the left supraclavicular area. At birth, the lesion measured 11 cm × 3.5 cm; at 5 months it measured 10 cm × 2.5 cm. On examination, it was a single, nonpulsatile, well-demarcated, dark brown atrophic plaque with a linear midline depression and an elevated, compressible, soft border that was paler than the central portion. Birth and neonatal history were unremarkable; the patient was healthy and not on medications. The initial differential diagnosis included smooth muscle hamartoma, semiannular lipoatrophy, and, less likely, a rapidly involuting congenital hemangioma (RICH). A small vein (~0.3 mm) was visible to the naked eye within the plaque. To avoid puncturing larger vessels during a planned biopsy, an AccuVein AV400 infrared vein finder was used; it revealed one large vein with an extensive network of small superficial branching vessels localized to the area of the atrophic plaque. A working diagnosis of probable RICH was made.

A 63-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of progressively painful swelling in the right preauricular region. She had no history of trauma. One year earlier, she had undergone excision of a cutaneous malignant melanoma (pT1a, cN0, cM0) from the left knee. Her medical history was otherwise notable only for hypertension and allergic rhinoconjunctivitis.

On extraoral examination, there was marked facial asymmetry with deviation of the chin to the left and a firm, bony swelling over the right condylar region. Mouth opening was possible without pronounced clicking or crepitus. Intraorally, she wore partial dentures; five teeth remained in the maxilla and nine in the mandible. Occlusion was Angle Class I.

An orthopantomogram showed similar size and form of both condyles. Ultrasonography of the right preauricular area revealed unsharp, circumscribed, possibly calcified lesions cranial to the mandibular condyle, without increased vascularization; both TMJs showed symmetric degenerative changes. A computed tomography scan demonstrated multiple loose calcified bodies within and outside the right joint capsule, forming a medial sacculation. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a well-circumscribed, cystic, high-intensity lesion on T2-weighted images surrounding the right TMJ and enhanced contrast uptake on T1-weighted images.

The radiologic differential diagnosis included an ectopic parotid adenoma or a sacculation of the joint capsule with calcifications. No imaging evidence of malignancy was identified. Therefore, no further imaging was performed.

A 43-year-old man presented with progressively worsening visual disturbances when reading, which evolved into bilateral hemianopsia. One year earlier, he had undergone bariatric surgery for obesity; otherwise his general examination was unremarkable.

Noncontrast CT of the brain demonstrated a well-circumscribed, oval, slightly hyperdense mass centered in the midline within the third ventricle, with its greatest dimension oriented craniocaudally. Subsequent MRI showed that the lesion was isointense to gray matter on T1-weighted images, slightly heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and exhibited vivid, homogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. A small cystic component was present. The mass compressed the optic chiasm, producing edematous swelling of the chiasm and optic tracts, and exerted mass effect on the hypothalamus, extending into the interpeduncular cistern.

Biochemical screening revealed normal levels of testosterone, prolactin, and thyroglobulin.

A 20-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of progressively increasing right knee pain, described as a constant, dull ache aggravated by walking and climbing stairs, and a 2-month history of knee swelling. He denied trauma, fever, weight loss, or appetite change. On examination, there was a 2 × 2 cm swelling over the anterior knee, more prominent in full flexion; the joint line was non-tender, there was no warmth, range of motion was full, and there was no instability or limb-length discrepancy. Laboratory studies, including blood counts, coagulation profile, and inflammatory markers, were normal. Knee radiographs were unremarkable. Ultrasonography showed a thick-walled hypoechogenic lesion (14.4 × 5 mm) inferomedial to the patella with tortuous vascular channels, and a second small lesion in the suprapatellar recess. MRI demonstrated two intra-articular lesions (one in Hoffa’s fat pad, one in the suprapatellar pouch adherent to the lateral femoral condyle) that were hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted and fat-suppressed sequences, and showed contrast enhancement; multiple dilated vascular channels were noted adjacent to the lesions, and there was no invasion of muscle or bone. Fine-needle aspiration yielded blood cells and synovial cells without granuloma or malignancy.

A 74-year-old man was evaluated for dyspnea on exertion of 4 days’ duration and a 5-kg weight gain over 1 week. His medical history included chronic heart failure from cardiac amyloidosis, hypertension, deep venous thrombosis, chronic kidney disease, and dyslipidemia. Medications included tolvaptan, edoxaban, bezafibrate, and bisoprolol. 

On initial admission, dyspnea progressed to resting dyspnea. Chest radiography showed a large left pleural effusion with rightward mediastinal shift. Chest CT confirmed a left pleural effusion without lymphadenopathy. Echocardiography showed normal cardiac function and no pericardial effusion. Thoracentesis over 4 days yielded 3300 mL of hemorrhagic fluid, with symptomatic relief; the patient was discharged after 1 week. Cytologic examination noted atypical lymphocytes, and the effusion gradually recurred.

One month later, he presented with recurrent dyspnea, weight gain, low-grade fever, night sweats, anorexia, malaise, and chest pain. Temperature was 36.5 °C, blood pressure 134/80 mm Hg, pulse 87 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. He had no conjunctival pallor or jugular venous distension. Breath sounds were diminished on the left; cardiac auscultation was normal. He had bilateral lower-extremity edema.

Laboratory studies showed a white cell count of 3.5 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 109 g/L, platelets 128 × 10^9/L, AST 32 IU/L, ALT 13 IU/L, LDH 209 IU/L, serum protein 6.2 g/dL, albumin 3.6 g/dL, CRP 0.11 mg/dL, creatinine 1.19 mg/dL, BUN 12.6 mg/dL, and sodium 141 mEq/L. An interferon-γ release assay for tuberculosis and serologic tests for hepatitis B and C, HIV, and HTLV-1 were negative.

Pleural fluid analysis revealed pH 7.6; total nucleated cell count 26 932/µL (atypical lymphocytes 90.5%); protein 4.1 g/dL; albumin 2.5 g/dL; glucose 13 mg/dL; LDH 683 IU/L; and ADA 140.7 IU/L. Pleural fluid cultures and PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis were negative. Cytology confirmed atypical lymphocytes. Molecular studies showed immunoglobulin gene rearrangement. Flow cytometry demonstrated CD19+, CD20+, CD79a+ and CD3–, CD10–, CD23–. Pleural fluid was negative for HHV-8 DNA. Whole-body CT revealed no lymphadenopathy, ascites, or mass lesions.

A 35-year-old Afghan man presented with a 1-year history of swelling and stiffness in the floor of the mouth, which had increased in size over the past 6 months and was first noticed when eating. He reported no ulceration, pain, systemic disease, medications, or family history of cancer.  
On extraoral examination, findings were unremarkable. Intraoral examination revealed a lobular, sessile, pink mass with superficial telangiectasia on the lingual aspect of the mandible, extending from the left canine region to the right first molar region; the overlying mucosa was intact and the lesion felt bony hard.  
A panoramic radiograph and mandibular occlusal film showed only a small opacity that did not account for the size of the lesion.  
Cone-beam CT imaging demonstrated a 28-mm peripheral erosive lesion from the midline to the mesial aspect of the right first molar, with a well-defined ragged border and saucerization resorption of the mandible, without involvement of the inferior alveolar canal or the teeth.

A previously healthy 2½-year-old boy was referred for acute fever, abdominal pain, and decreased oral intake. He had also had linear splinter hemorrhages of the nails for several weeks. His past history was unremarkable except for a recent tonsillectomy.

On examination he was febrile, tachypneic (respiratory rate 36/min), tachycardic (heart rate 165/min), and hypoxemic with room-air saturations of 89–93% (improving to 97–98% on 1 L/min of oxygen by nasal cannula). Blood pressure was 121/76 mmHg. Auscultation revealed decreased air entry over the left hemithorax and a pleural friction rub; hepatomegaly was present.

Laboratory studies showed: C-reactive protein 333 mg/L (normal <10), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 37 mm/h (3–13), platelet count 573 × 10^9/L (150–450), and white blood cell count 24.6 × 10^9/L (4.0–10.0) with 86.6% neutrophils and 6% immature neutrophils. 

A chest radiograph demonstrated a basal consolidation in the left lower lobe with opacification along the lateral chest wall and rightward mediastinal shift, findings consistent with pneumonia and pleural effusion; a reticulonodular pattern was also noted in the right lung and left upper lobe. Ultrasound confirmed a left pleural effusion. He was started on amoxicillin–clavulanic acid and gentamicin, and blood cultures remained negative.

After four days he redeveloped dyspnea and increased oxygen requirements. Ultrasound showed increased, organizing pleural effusion. Bacterial endocarditis was excluded by negative blood cultures and a normal cardiac ultrasound. He underwent mini-thoracotomy and decortication; pleural fluid analysis revealed an exudate (pH 6.92, glucose <0.6 mmol/L, protein 35.7 g/L, LDH 2677 U/L) with cultures negative, although 16S-PCR identified Streptococcus pneumoniae. He recovered fully over 10 days and was discharged on oral antibiotics.

Eight weeks after recovery, chest radiography continued to show a reticulonodular pattern with features of honeycombing. High-resolution CT of the thorax revealed numerous bilateral cysts of different sizes and varying wall thickness, without emphysema or bronchiectasis.

A 54-year-old man presented with four months of gradually increasing abdominal distension. He denied abdominal pain, bowel or bladder symptoms, and had no history of hypertension, diabetes, or other systemic illness. On examination, large firm to hard masses were palpable in both lumbar regions; there was no lower-limb edema. Ultrasonography showed large, well-defined hypoechoic masses in the bilateral perirenal spaces with distortion of the renal outlines, no hydronephrosis, and displacement of adjacent organs. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed large, homogeneous, hypodense, minimally enhancing masses in both perirenal spaces completely encasing the kidneys and causing scalloping of the renal cortex. The residual renal parenchyma had normal enhancement and excretion, and a few tiny renal calculi were noted on the noncontrast images. No enlarged intra-abdominal lymph nodes or ascites were present. Laboratory tests showed normal renal function.

A 72-year-old woman was evaluated for a two-year history of a light brown macule on the lateral segment of her right inferior eyelid. She had no history of nevi, rashes, or scaling at that site. Her medical history included basal cell carcinoma, melasma, and numerous solar lentigines on sun-exposed skin; she denied a family history of skin cancer. She reported extensive sun exposure and past tanning. Three months earlier, she had undergone fractional resurfacing laser therapy (1,550 nm) to the face and neck, with only mild erythema and swelling. 

On examination, the lesion measured 3 mm × 2 mm, was flat and well-circumscribed, and varied from tan to dark brown. It resembled other facial lentigines and was clinically diagnosed as a solar lentigo. Given the low clinical suspicion for malignancy and the sensitive eyelid area, no biopsy was performed. The patient elected for cosmetic removal, and the lesion was treated with a Q-switched 1,064 nm Nd:YAG laser. 

Three months after laser therapy, she returned with perceived recurrence: the lesion now measured 4 mm × 2 mm, appeared asymmetric, and ranged in color from tan and dark brown to black.

A 25-year-old man presented with a 4-year history of progressive weakness, numbness, and loss of movement, initially in the right upper limb and later involving the left upper limb and both lower limbs. Over time, he developed bowel and bladder dysfunction. One year before presentation, he had a fall during sleep with loss of consciousness but no fever or seizures. He had received Ayurvedic treatment without improvement.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Grade II pressure ulcers were noted over sacral areas. Neurologic findings included bilateral extensor plantar responses and hyperreflexia (3+ reflexes) at the knees and ankles.

Laboratory and imaging studies:
- Abdominal ultrasound showed thickened, irregular bladder walls with internal echoes and debris, consistent with cystitis.
- A plain cervical spine radiograph obtained at an outside facility revealed a bony lesion in the posterior column at C1.
- Noncontrast CT of the cervical spine demonstrated a well-defined, sclerotic, expansile lesion arising from the right posterior arch of C1 and extending across midline, measuring 2.4 × 2.9 × 2.5 cm. Bony trabeculae were continuous with the medullary cavity of adjacent bone. There was no periosteal reaction, soft-tissue mass, or bone destruction.
- MRI of the cervical spine showed the lesion to be isointense to bone on all sequences. A small T2/STIR hyperintense anteroinferior component, measuring 5.2 mm in thickness, was consistent with a cartilaginous cap. The lesion caused marked posterior dural compression and displacement of the spinal cord to the left at C1–C2, with anteroposterior canal diameter reduced to approximately 2.5 mm. Intramedullary T2/STIR hyperintensity spanned 2.5 cm at the level of maximum stenosis, indicating myelomalacia. Post-contrast MRI showed no enhancement of the lesion.

A 29-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with a 1-month history of progressively worsening severe back pain unrelieved by analgesics and associated with unintended weight loss. On examination, there was a large, palpable mass in the left abdomen. Routine blood and urine tests were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a large heterogeneous soft‐tissue lesion occupying the left abdomen with marked vascularity on Doppler imaging. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 190 × 133 × 227 mm left retroperitoneal mass of heterogeneous density and enhancement, containing central necrotic fluid collections, multiple calcifications, and no fatty component. The mass extended from L2 to S4, eroded the left transverse processes of L4 and L5, infiltrated adjacent paravertebral and iliacus muscles, displaced the small bowel and colon medially, abutted the anterior abdominal wall without breach, and reached the lower pole of the left kidney. MRI demonstrated heterogeneous signal on T2-weighted images—high signal (fluid), intermediate signal (soft tissue), and low signal (hemorrhage) (“triple sign”)—areas of diffusion restriction on DWI with low ADC values, and heterogeneous post-​gadolinium enhancement distinguishing solid from nonenhancing regions.

A 2-year-old girl presented with a 1-month history of a painful mass in the right mandible. She was initially treated for gingivitis with oral hygiene instruction and antibiotics without improvement. One week later, the mass increased in size, with pain and fever, and she was admitted for further evaluation.

On examination, vital signs included fever. A 1 × 1 cm tender mass was noted over the right body of the mandible, extending from the lip commissure to the angle; the overlying skin was normal, and there was no lip paresthesia. Submandibular lymph nodes were palpable, tender, and movable. Mouth opening was normal. Intraorally, there was a soft, painful swelling from teeth #83 to #85, obliterating the right buccal sulcus; teeth #84 and #85 were mobile and displaced. The overlying mucosa was red, ulcerated, and overgrew the crown of tooth #85.

Orthopantomogram showed a multilocular, mixed radiolucent and radiopaque lesion with a poorly defined border in the region of teeth #84 and #85, with resorption of the lamina dura, roots of #84 and #85, and the furcation of #84. Axial and coronal CT revealed a poorly defined lesion in the right mandibular body with buccal cortical destruction, soft-tissue infiltration, reactive lymph nodes, and partial lingual cortex damage. Chest CT showed no metastatic deposits.

A 78-year-old Japanese woman presented with blurred vision in her right eye. She was referred for suspected rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD). Examination showed visual acuity 4/20 OD and 10/20 OS, and intraocular pressure 12 mmHg OD and 16 mmHg OS. Slit-lamp examination revealed clear anterior chambers, senile cortical cataracts OU, and mild pigmented anterior vitreous cells OD. Fundus examination of the right eye showed inferior and nasal retinal detachment with a round retinal hole and a yellowish, flat choroidal elevation nasal to the hole. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated mild subretinal fluid in the macula. Fluorescein angiography showed hyperfluorescence corresponding to the detached retina without areas of nonperfusion. Indocyanine green angiography revealed hypofluorescence in the nasal quadrant corresponding to the elevation. B-mode ultrasonography measured a mild choroidal elevation less than 2 mm in height.

A 65-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a long smoking history noted slowly enlarging, non-tender, non-pruritic lesions on his left cheek, posterior left shoulder, and left upper arm over several months. He denied respiratory symptoms. On examination, there was a 10 × 10 cm indurated lesion on the left cheek, a 5 × 5 cm lesion on the posterior left shoulder, and a 2 × 3 cm lesion on the right upper arm. No lymphadenopathy or organomegaly was present. 

Biopsy of the left cheek lesion showed sheets of foamy macrophages surrounded by a dense plasma cell and lymphocytic infiltrate, with scattered neutrophils and focal granuloma formation. Special stains for organisms were negative. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated histiocytes strongly positive for S100 protein and CD68, and negative for CD1a. The plasma cells were polyclonal on kappa and lambda in situ hybridization.

A chest CT scan revealed bilateral thin- and mildly thick-walled pulmonary cysts, some rounded and others multiloculated with internal septations, along with numerous ground-glass nodules measuring from 1–2 mm up to several centimeters. The findings showed upper-lung-zone predominance with sparing of the lung bases and the anteromedial portions of the middle lobe and lingula. No intrathoracic lymphadenopathy or pleural effusion was seen.

A 45-year-old woman presented with a cutaneous mass on the scalp that had been present for 6 years. She noted only mild pain when the lesion was touched or her hair was combed and denied any systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a firm, mildly tender, nonpulsatile, oval nodule measuring 3 × 2 cm on the scalp without a central punctum. The lesion was excised under local anesthesia. On gross inspection in the histology laboratory, the cut surface revealed solid yellow-white lobulated material, leading to consideration of a sebaceous cyst, epidermoid cyst, lipoma, or pilomatrixoma.

A 59-year-old man underwent colonoscopic evaluation for a positive fecal occult blood test. He reported chronic constipation managed with laxatives but denied abdominal pain, hematemesis, hematochezia, or melena. He had no prior colonoscopy and no family history of colorectal cancer. Physical examination was unremarkable, and routine blood tests were within normal limits. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed no abnormalities. During colonoscopy, a 10 mm short-pedicle polyp with a smooth contour was found at the recto-sigmoid junction. The lesion was lifted with methylene blue and removed by hot snare polypectomy; three hemoclips were applied to the resection site. The specimen was retrieved and sent for histopathologic analysis.

A 74-year-old woman underwent screening esophagogastroduodenoscopy, which revealed discoloration of the ampulla of Vater and a polypoid mass directly above it. Biopsy of the ampullary lesion showed a tubular adenoma with low-grade dysplasia; biopsy of the polypoid mass showed chronic inflammation. She denied gastrointestinal symptoms, and physical examination and laboratory tests—including complete blood count, electrolytes, liver and renal function tests, and CA19-9—were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated no ampullary mass, no bile or pancreatic duct dilatation, and no enlarged lymph nodes or distant metastases. The ampullary adenoma was removed by en bloc endoscopic papillectomy with prophylactic pancreatic stenting. Subsequent side-viewing endoscopy showed a 2.0-cm yellowish, firm, subepithelial tumor at the minor papilla with a normal overlying mucosa. Pushing the lesion with biopsy forceps did not elicit a rolling sign. Given its size, firmness, and absence of lymphadenopathy or metastasis on CT, the lesion was completely removed by endoscopic mucosal resection with hemoclip closure.

A 62-year-old man presented with sudden right upper limb weakness and loss of consciousness. Brain MRI revealed a well-defined lesion in the left parietal lobe, which was excised. Histopathology of the brain lesion showed glandular and papillary architecture with high-grade nuclei and frequent mitoses, and the tumor was diffusely positive for CK7 and thyroid transcription factor 1, consistent with metastatic adenocarcinoma. He underwent whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT for staging. PET/CT demonstrated focal FDG uptake in a prevascular mediastinal node and low-grade uptake in a left lung consolidation. Additionally, there was a large, well-defined enhancing soft-tissue mass arising from the prostate and seminal vesicle that showed no FDG uptake. Serum prostate-specific antigen level was 0.3 ng/mL.

A 16-year-old boy presented with a 1-month history of fever, anorexia, and abdominal pain, followed by 1 week of progressive abdominal distension. Ultrasonography at an outside center revealed ascites, omental thickening, and bilateral pleural effusions. Diagnostic paracentesis yielded purulent fluid; a percutaneous catheter was placed. Ascitic fluid analysis showed 17,000 cells/mm3 with lymphocyte predominance, degenerated cells, and a normal adenosine deaminase level. Acid-fast bacilli staining and nucleic acid amplification testing for Mycobacterium tuberculosis were negative, and the Mantoux test was nonreactive. He was started on antitubercular therapy and antibiotics without improvement and was referred to our hospital.

On transfer, he had tachycardia and tachypnea without pallor or peripheral lymphadenopathy. The abdomen was distended and firm, with shifting dullness; no organomegaly or discrete mass was palpable. Initial laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 14.9 × 10^9/L, normal hemoglobin and platelet counts, and normal liver-function tests. Repeat ultrasonography showed a large peritoneal collection, omental thickening, and multiple hypoechoic lesions in the liver. Chest radiography showed bilateral pleural effusions; echocardiography revealed a small pericardial effusion. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated ascites, thickened and nodular omentum, enhancing soft-tissue thickening in the retroperitoneum extending into the mesentery and encasing the superior and inferior mesenteric vessels, and 2–3 hypodense bilateral renal nodules (largest, 2 cm) and hypodense hepatic lesions encasing portal-vein branches; no lymphadenopathy was noted.

A new peritoneal catheter drained white-colored fluid. The fluid had a total cell count of 2.56 × 10^12 cells/L with 90% atypical lymphocytes, a lactate dehydrogenase level of 2864 U/L, a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 0.9, total protein 3.7 g/dL, albumin 2.7 g/dL, and glucose 24 mg/dL. Pleural fluid cytology similarly showed atypical lymphocytes.

An 8-year-old girl weighing 44.5 kg with no significant medical history presented with a 1-week history of progressive abdominal pain, distension, nausea, and vomiting. Physical examination revealed notable abdominal distension without guarding or rebound. Initial abdominal ultrasonography showed a 17 × 9 cm mixed solid and cystic mass occupying the right hepatic lobe with compression of the inferior vena cava (IVC). By hospital day 7, worsening abdominal distension and concern for abdominal compartment syndrome prompted percutaneous biopsy of the mass and placement of a drain. Over the next several days, persistent sanguineous output from the drain led to anemia and concern for hemorrhage. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated an infrarenal IVC thrombus and a near-occlusive embolus in the left pulmonary artery. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed compression of the distal IVC at its junction with the right atrium, with otherwise normal biventricular function and no evidence of elevated right heart pressures.

A 48-year-old woman presented with a 1-week history of a right breast mass. She has two children (ages 19 and 15), irregular menses, no hormonal medications, and no personal history of breast cancer. Family history was notable for pancreatic cancer in her father, uterine cancer in her paternal grandmother, and lung cancer in her mother. She had no prior breast trauma. 

On examination, there was a 10 cm mobile mass in the right upper outer quadrant (9–11 o’clock), 3 cm from the areola; the nipples and skin were unremarkable, and no axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy was present.  

Full-field digital mammography showed a circumscribed, rounded, high-density heterogeneous mass surrounded by a thin capsule in the right upper outer quadrant, with no microcalcifications, skin thickening, or edema. Ultrasound revealed an ill-defined, rounded, heterogeneous predominantly solid lesion with variable-sized cystic areas measuring 6.0 × 4.0 × 3.5 cm and scant internal vascularity, with no suspicious lymph nodes (BI-RADS 4).  

Breast MRI demonstrated a 7.0 × 6.5 × 5.5 cm circumscribed mass at the deep retroareolar region extending to 9–10 o’clock, with predominantly low T1-weighted signal intensity and scant anterior high T1 signal; heterogeneous low and high signal on T2-weighted, STIR, diffusion-weighted, and ADC images without diffusion restriction; and intense heterogeneous postcontrast enhancement.  

A core biopsy and wide local excision were advised.

A 40-year-old Hispanic woman was referred for evaluation of persistent thrombocytopenia and multiple splenic lesions. She had experienced drenching sweats and left upper-quadrant abdominal pain associated with progressive thrombocytopenia over four months but denied weight loss, fever, or chills. She had no significant past medical or surgical history, and her family history was noncontributory. 

On examination, she was afebrile with no hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, or lymphadenopathy. Initial laboratory studies showed a platelet count of 37 000/mm^3, a white-cell count of 10 300/μL, hemoglobin of 14.0 g/dL, and an otherwise unremarkable biochemical profile. Further evaluation including serum protein electrophoresis, peripheral-blood flow cytometry, and fine-needle aspiration of a right cervical lymph node were unremarkable. Two bone-marrow biopsies did not show evidence of a lymphoproliferative disorder.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the spleen revealed a normal-sized organ (10 cm in greatest dimension) with multiple T1 hypointense, T2 hyperintense lesions. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography demonstrated mild uptake (SUV 3.5) in one splenic-hilum lesion, with all other splenic nodules nonavid; a small cervical node (SUV 3.3), a left breast nodule (SUV 2.1), and increased activity in several bone sites (brightest at T3, SUV 4.3) were also noted.

A male infant was delivered at 31 weeks’ gestation via cesarean section to a 33-year-old G4P2 mother with hypothyroidism after an unremarkable prenatal course. Prenatal ultrasound performed for decreased fetal movements revealed hydrops fetalis, reduced fetal movement, and decelerations. At birth, APGAR scores were 3, 6, and 7 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes; the infant weighed 2494 g, had a crown-heel length of 43.9 cm, and was noted to have generalized edema, hypotension, and respiratory distress. Imaging showed bilateral pleural effusions, atelectasis, pneumothorax, and abundant ascites. A chest radiograph demonstrated persistent pneumothorax despite chest‐tube insertion and an expanded cardiothymic silhouette. A 2D echocardiogram revealed a pericardial effusion, a patent ductus arteriosus, mild tricuspid regurgitation, and trivial mitral regurgitation. Pericardiocentesis was performed, and the infant received dopamine, furosemide, albumin, high-flow oxygen, surfactant, and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Infectious causes were investigated but cultures and serology were negative. Laboratory tests showed anemia, leukopenia, and marked acidosis. Despite aggressive support, the infant died on day 7 of life.

A 77-year-old Caucasian man presented with a one-month history of progressive dysphagia and hoarseness. He also reported dyspnea on exertion in the setting of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease managed with salmeterol (50 µg twice daily), a long-term history of smoking, hyperlipidemia, and an allergy to aspirin.

Physical examination was notable for no cervical lymphadenopathy. Flexible endoscopy revealed a mass at the base of the tongue. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the neck confirmed a well-defined lesion involving the tongue base without evidence of regional lymphadenopathy or distant metastases. 

An incisional biopsy of the lesion demonstrated an ulcerated and infiltrative malignant epithelial neoplasm with spindle-cell morphology involving the base of the tongue and the free edge of the epiglottis. Further immunohistochemical studies were requested to clarify the diagnosis.

A 25-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a darkly pigmented tumor in the left optic disc area found on routine examination. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. Visual acuity was 1.0 in both eyes, and intraocular pressures were 17 mmHg OD and 18 mmHg OS. Pupillary reactions and slit-lamp biomicroscopy of the anterior segments were normal bilaterally. 

Color fundus photography of the left eye showed a black to dark brown, slightly elevated mass in the inferior quadrant of the optic disc with feathery margins and an obscured superonasal disc margin. B-scan ultrasonography demonstrated a hyperechoic, dome-shaped lesion measuring 2.83 mm in basal diameter and 1.11 mm in thickness. 

Fluorescein angiography revealed hyperfluorescent staining of peripapillary hyperreflective ovoid structures at the superonasal disc rim and diffuse blocked hypofluorescence throughout the pigmented lesion, without evidence of late-phase hyperfluorescence. Fundus autofluorescence showed a completely hypofluorescent mass with sharply demarcated, feathery edges.

A 5-year-old boy with known tuberous sclerosis presented with a 1-week history of runny nose, cough, and fever. On examination, his tonsils were congested and air entry was decreased in the right lung. There were no chest compressive symptoms or abdominal complaints. A chest radiograph showed a large mass in the right lower hemithorax with a broad-based attachment to the mediastinum and multiple small nodular and tubular infiltrates in the right lower lobe. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 6 × 7 cm exophytic mass arising from the lower pole of the left kidney, multiple small hyperechoic lesions in both renal cortices, and several hyperechoic liver lesions. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated an 11 × 9 × 8 cm well-demarcated anterior mediastinal mass inseparable from the right cardiac border, and a lobulated 9.5 × 7 × 3.5 cm exophytic mass in the lower pole of the left kidney without capsular extension. Both masses measured ≈60 HU on precontrast images, enhanced to ≈97 HU in the arterial phase, and decreased by 20 HU on delayed images; neither mass contained visible fat, calcification, or cystic change. There were multiple enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes but no abdominal or pelvic lymphadenopathy. Brain MRI showed numerous cortical and subcortical tubers, multiple subependymal hamartomas, and a 1.2 × 1 cm enhancing lesion at the left foramen of Monro.

A 48-year-old Egyptian woman presented with an 8-month history of sharp right upper chest pain, initially intermittent but persistent over the past 3 months, predominantly at night. Over the preceding few weeks, she noted exertional dyspnea. She denied fever, chills, night sweats, cough, tobacco use, or illicit drug use, and reported a 13-lb weight loss over 3 months. Vital signs and physical examination were within normal limits. Laboratory studies, including cardiac enzymes (troponin-T <0.01 ng/mL) and pro–B-type natriuretic peptide (157.1 pg/mL), were unremarkable. Thyroid–stimulating hormone was 5.3 mIU/L with a normal free thyroxine level.  
A chest radiograph showed an enlarged cardiac silhouette and a left basilar airspace opacity. Electrocardiogram demonstrated normal sinus rhythm, left atrial enlargement, low-voltage QRS complexes, and a prolonged QT interval (525 msec). Chest CT with contrast revealed numerous bilateral pulmonary nodules up to 4.5 mm (upper and mid-lung zone predominance) and a large pericardial effusion without mediastinal lymphadenopathy or masses. Echocardiography confirmed a pericardial effusion with diastolic right atrial collapse; left ventricular function was normal.  
A pericardial window was performed with biopsy and fluid sent for bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial studies; all were negative. Abdominal CT identified a 6.0 × 5.3-cm hypoattenuating lesion in the right hepatic lobe with mild peripheral enhancement and gradual centripetal filling on delayed images.  
One month later, the patient had recurrent tamponade. Pericardial fluid cytology revealed clusters of carcinoma cells positive for epithelial membrane antigen. Triple-phase CT of the liver showed a 5.8 × 6.4 × 6.8-cm mass in segments IV A and IV B with a continuously enhancing rim in the arterial phase, increasing enhancement in the portal venous phase, and patchy central enhancement on delayed images.

A 71-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of intermittent headaches and episodes of blurred vision. Her medical history was notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, osteoarthritis, and Raynaud syndrome. Medications included aspirin, diltiazem, losartan, gabapentin, baclofen, tramadol-acetaminophen, calcium, fish oil, and others. She had no focal neurologic deficits on examination, with pupils equal and reactive, intact extraocular movements, and no lymphadenopathy. 

Visual evaluation by a retinal specialist showed visual acuity of 20/80 bilaterally, intraocular pressures of 17 mmHg (right) and 14 mmHg (left), thinning of the macula on fundus exam, and bitemporal visual field loss. 

An MRI of the brain with and without contrast revealed an inhomogeneously enhancing mass in the pituitary fossa measuring approximately 1.8 × 1.8 × 1.5 cm, extending into the suprasellar region with cavernous sinus involvement, partially displacing the optic chiasm and hypothalamus superiorly. No acute infarct or hemorrhage was seen. A separate focus of gadolinium enhancement (<6 mm) was noted in the left caudate head adjacent to the internal capsule. 

A comprehensive pituitary hormone panel—including ACTH, cortisol, FSH, LH, prolactin, TSH, free T4, and IGF-1—was within normal limits.

A 35-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of lower abdominal pain. On pelvic examination, a firm, non-tender mass measuring approximately 15 to 18 cm was palpated. Transabdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a large right ovarian mass. The patient underwent ovarian cystectomy. 

Gross examination revealed an 18 × 11 cm unilocular ovarian cyst with a smooth, whitish external surface and a 2 cm nodular elevation. On sectioning, the cyst contained mucinous fluid and a 2 cm gray-brown mural nodule.

Microscopic sections of the cyst wall showed papillary projections lined by tall columnar mucinous epithelium, consistent with mucinous cystadenoma. Sections of the mural nodule demonstrated a cellular stroma composed of monomorphic spindle and polygonal cells interspersed with numerous osteoclast-like giant cells. There was no nuclear atypia, and mitotic figures numbered 1–5 per 10 high-power fields. Immunohistochemical stains revealed diffuse vimentin positivity in the stromal cells and only focal pancytokeratin positivity.

A 43-year-old Thai man presented with a 2-month history of sensitivity over the left ala of his nose.
