Two months earlier, he had undergone extraction of an upper left deciduous canine; one month after the extraction, he noted persistent swelling of the left cheek. Periapical radiography at a private clinic showed an impacted upper left permanent canine and small radiopaque foci inferior to it.

On examination, there was mild extraoral swelling of the left cheek with effacement of the nasolabial fold. Intraorally, there was mild buccal vestibular swelling from the left maxillary central incisor to the first premolar; the left maxillary canine was clinically absent, and palpation revealed a soft tissue mass on its palatal aspect. Electric pulp testing indicated non-vital teeth at the left maxillary central and lateral incisors.

Panoramic radiography demonstrated a unilocular radiolucent lesion surrounding the embedded canine, containing a few non-homogeneous radiopaque components, with indistinct margins and involvement of the roots of the left lateral incisor and first premolar. Periapical radiographs showed irregular widening of the periodontal ligament space around the lateral incisor root without root resorption, diffuse radiolucent trabeculations near the central and lateral incisor apices, and small radiopaque structures surrounded by thin radiolucent rims, resembling tooth-like fragments.

Axial cone-beam computed tomographic images revealed extension of the lesion into the incisive foramen and bilateral anterior nasal cavities, involvement of the nasal septum and left lateral nasal wall (medial wall of the left maxillary sinus), perforation of the labial cortical plate across the midline, and perforation of the palatal cortex from the left lateral incisor to the first molar region. Coronal views showed obliteration of the left ostiomeatal complex and presence of tooth-like structures between the roots of the lateral incisor and second premolar, with the impacted canine located superior-posteriorly. Sagittal sections demonstrated extension into the anterior half of the left maxillary sinus with mucosal thickening.

A 68-year-old man with a 43-year history of smoking (15 cigarettes per day), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and prior mitral valve annuloplasty was found to have an asymptomatic pulmonary lesion on routine chest imaging. Chest radiography and computed tomography showed a 22-mm mass in the left upper lobe. FDG PET–CT demonstrated uptake in the lung lesion (maximum standardized uptake value, 6.1) without hilar or mediastinal lymph-node involvement, and a separate focus of uptake in the sigmoid colon. Colonoscopy confirmed sigmoid colon cancer, and the patient underwent laparoscopic sigmoidectomy (clinical stage T4aN3M1a). Two months later, CT showed growth of the left-upper-lobe lesion to 28 mm. The patient underwent a video-assisted thoracoscopic segmentectomy (S1+2).

Gross examination of the lung specimen revealed a yellow-white, well-circumscribed mass measuring 28 × 21 × 35 mm with surrounding obstructive pneumonia. Microscopically, the tumor was composed of intermixed carcinomatous and sarcomatous elements. The carcinomatous component included well-differentiated squamous epithelium with central keratinization and glandular epithelium; immunohistochemistry showed two-phase p40 positivity in epithelial areas and negativity for TTF-1. The sarcomatous component comprised spindle cells, areas of chondrosarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma. Immunohistochemical staining revealed diffuse AE1/AE3 positivity in epithelial regions and focal positivity in chondroid areas; S100 positivity in cartilage; myogenin positivity in striated-muscle areas; vimentin positivity in sarcomatous regions; negativity for germ-cell markers SALL4 and CD30; no neural elements identified by HE and S100 staining; retained nuclear SMARCA4 (BRG1) expression; absence of p53 staining in both components; tumor proportion score for PD-L1 < 1%; negative margins; and no adenocarcinoma resembling the patient’s colon cancer.

A 66-year-old Japanese woman was admitted for evaluation of melena ongoing for 3 days. Her medical history included diabetes, hypertension, cerebral infarction, and angina. On admission, her temperature was 36.2 °C, blood pressure 118/70 mm Hg, pulse 84 beats/min, respiratory rate 19 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. She was alert. Physical examination revealed pale conjunctiva; the abdomen was soft, nondistended, and nontender, with no palpable masses. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 4.3 g/dL and blood urea nitrogen 33.6 mg/dL. Emergent upper GI endoscopy revealed no vascular abnormalities, mass lesions, or ulcerations. Colonoscopy showed no lesions but altered blood throughout the colon and terminal ileum, suggesting a small-bowel source. She received transfusions with initial stabilization, but on hospital day 5 she developed hypotension (BP 68/40 mm Hg) with renewed melena. Abdominal CT showed an ill-defined mass lesion in the small bowel, but its precise location and nature were unclear. The differential diagnosis included small intestinal tumor (such as GIST), inflammatory disease, and vascular abnormalities. On hospital day 7, capsule endoscopy was performed; by day 9, active bleeding was visualized in the upper small bowel. An emergency SMA angiogram localized a vascular tumor in a jejunal arterial branch, and coil embolization achieved hemostasis.

A 46-year-old right-handed Asian woman presented with a 4-year history of a painless mass on the palm of her left hand. The lesion began as a marble-sized nodule and gradually enlarged to the size of a small ball over 2 years. She denied other lumps, systemic symptoms (including weight loss or anorexia), or a personal history of malignancy; family history of cancer was unclear. She is a housewife and recalled forearm trauma 1 year earlier, treated with internal fixation. She had no allergies, congenital or chronic illnesses. On examination, there was a solid, non-tender, mobile mass measuring 2.0 × 1.5 × 1.0 cm with well-defined margins on the palmar aspect; distal sensation and range of motion were normal. Plain radiographs (anteroposterior and lateral views) demonstrated a soft tissue mass containing areas of fat attenuation and internal calcifications.

A 19-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 15-day history of intermittent fever to 102 °F, rigors, and lower-back pain radiating bilaterally to the legs. Eight days before admission, she noted progressive bilateral lower-limb weakness accompanied by urinary retention, fecal incontinence, and numbness. She also reported undocumented weight loss and decreased appetite. Her grandfather has active tuberculosis.

On examination, the right lower leg was warm, tender, shiny, and swollen to the shin. Motor testing revealed 0/5 strength in both lower limbs and 4/5 in both upper limbs; tone was increased on the left, and reflexes were absent in the lower limbs with mute plantar responses. A sensory level was noted at T10. Cerebellar assessment of the lower limbs was limited by swelling.

An MRI of the lumbar spine was unremarkable. Screening MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine demonstrated signal abnormalities on STIR and T2 sequences within multiple vertebral bodies (C2, C5–C7, T1, and T3) and the posterior elements. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the dorsal spine revealed multilevel enhancing abnormal bone-marrow signals in the vertebral bodies and posterior elements, with gadolinium enhancement indicating tissue infiltration. At the D9–D10 level, there was a high-signal component and a large posterior and left epidural soft-tissue mass extending through the left neural foramen, causing anterior displacement of the thecal sac and spinal cord. These findings were concerning for neoplastic lesions with metastatic involvement.

A previously healthy one-year-old boy presented with a two-week history of rapidly progressive proptosis of the left eye. There was no fever, night sweats, weight loss, or prior illness. Developmental milestones were appropriate, and vaccinations were up to date. On examination, vital signs were stable, and the child was alert and active. Ophthalmic examination of the left eye showed upper and lower lid edema, proptosis with mild downward and outward displacement, and mildly restricted extraocular movement; there was no chemosis or sign of inflammation. Visual behavior was central, steady, and maintained; intraocular pressure was normal. The anterior segment, pupil reaction, lens, and fundus were unremarkable. Examination of the right eye and general physical examination, including lymph node palpation, were normal. Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 84.01 × 10^9/L with atypical and blast cells on the peripheral blood smear; chemistry results were normal. Noncontrast and contrast-enhanced CT of the head and orbits showed a 2.5 × 1 × 0.6 cm ill-defined extra-conal mass in the superomedial left orbit, causing inferolateral displacement of the globe, periosteal reaction, and opacification of ethmoid and maxillary sinuses. MRI demonstrated an isointense extra-conal superomedial left orbital mass with homogeneous enhancement, bone erosion of the medial orbital wall, and preserved surrounding fat planes. The initial differential diagnosis included leukemia, lymphoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, eosinophilic granuloma, and idiopathic orbital inflammation.

A 54-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of a nontender, relatively fast-growing lesion beneath her clitoral hood that bled easily. She denied any genital trauma or prior surgery. Her medical history was unremarkable, and she took no medications. On examination, there was a 2.5-cm by 0.5-cm pedunculated, erythematous, granulation-tissue–like lesion under the clitoral hood. The remainder of the vulvar and vaginal examination was normal. Routine laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits.

A 59-year-old woman with diabetes and hypertension was referred for evaluation of a pelvic mass, discovered incidentally. She reported only slight generalized abdominal pain and peri-anal discomfort, with no prior similar symptoms. Physical examination, including abdominal and rectal, was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis showed a 96×66×48 mm infiltrative mass in the left peri-anal region with central necrosis, displacing the left levator ani and supplied by the left pudendal artery; there was no invasion of muscle, bone, or adjacent organs. Pelvic MRI revealed a large, intensely enhancing T2 hyperintense lesion in the left peri-anal soft tissue with tortuous dilation of the left pudendal artery, prompting consideration of soft tissue sarcoma or malignant nerve sheath tumor. Peri-anal ultrasound demonstrated a hypoechogenic ischiorectal mass without distinctive features. A sonographically guided needle biopsy reported a spindle-cell tumor with eosinophilic cytoplasm and rare mitoses but no nuclear atypia or necrosis, and was interpreted as compatible with low-risk GIST. Digital angiography confirmed a hypervascular mass arising from the left internal iliac artery.

A 59-year-old African American woman presented to the emergency department with tachycardia, palpitations, chest tightness, shortness of breath, and a 60-lb weight loss over the past year. She was admitted with an acute exacerbation of chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and was discharged after three days when her condition stabilized. Three months later, she reported persistent hypertension, diaphoresis, and ongoing weight loss. 

Plasma studies revealed norepinephrine 31 792 pg/mL (normal 80–520 pg/mL) and dopamine 544 pg/mL (normal 0–20 pg/mL). Urinary studies showed normetanephrine 6451 μg/d (normal 95–650 μg/d) and norepinephrine 12 649 μg/g creatinine (normal 0–400 μg/g creatinine). 

A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with and without intravenous contrast demonstrated a 6.7 × 6.6 cm heterogeneously enhancing mass arising from the right inferolateral wall of the urinary bladder and a 2.5 × 3.0 cm right pelvic lymph node. The adrenal glands appeared normal.

A 16-year-old Malay boy presented with a one-month history of nonproductive cough and persistent fever unresponsive to antipyretics. He had no weight loss or anorexia and no significant family history. Three months after symptom onset, a CT scan of the thorax revealed a solitary left lower-lobe nodule (12×11 mm), for which he received empiric antituberculous therapy without clinical improvement. One month into treatment he developed pancytopenia and declined a bone marrow biopsy. Four months after initial admission, repeat CT showed enlargement of the original lung nodule to 32×31 mm, multiple new pulmonary lesions (5–11 mm), and an anterior mediastinal mass (26×46×40 mm). A hematologic malignancy or fungal infection was suspected, but the patient left against medical advice. Two months later he was readmitted with persistent fever, diarrhea, dehydration and cachexia. On examination he had reduced basal breath sounds with crepitations, hepatosplenomegaly and no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 5.1 g/dL, white blood cell count 0.6×10^9/L (neutrophils 0.1×10^9/L; lymphocytes 0.5×10^9/L), platelets 57×10^9/L, and an elevated LDH of 550 U/mg. Blood cultures, rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, leptospirosis serology, malarial film and Monospot tests were negative. CT imaging again confirmed pulmonary and mediastinal lesions, hepatosplenomegaly and right iliac lymphadenopathy. Bone marrow biopsy showed hypocellularity, hemophagocytosis and scattered medium- to large-sized lymphoid cells with kidney-shaped nuclei and prominent nucleoli. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated CD2+, CD3+, CD4+ with scattered CD8+, and negativity for CD20, CD56 and ALK1. Ki-67 staining showed a high proliferative index, and in situ hybridization for EBV-encoded RNA revealed EBV-positive atypical lymphoid cells.

A 44-year-old man with no significant past medical history underwent a left radical inguinal orchiectomy 18 months ago. The orchiectomy specimen showed classic seminoma with necrosis and vascular invasion, confined to the testis. He elected surveillance without adjuvant therapy.

He now presents with a gradually enlarging, non-tender fullness in the left flank. Laboratory tests show an alpha-fetoprotein level of 2.1 ng/mL (normal) and a beta-human chorionic gonadotropin level of 4.6 mIU/mL (normal). Abdominal ultrasonography reveals a 12.3 × 11.3 cm lobulated retroperitoneal mass with left hydronephrosis. Contrast-enhanced CT confirms a 14 × 12 × 11 cm para-aortic soft tissue mass without evidence of distant metastases.

A percutaneous tru-cut biopsy is performed to characterize the mass. The patient then receives four cycles of bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin (BEP) followed by four cycles of vinblastine, ifosfamide, and cisplatin (VIP), with no radiologic improvement. He is referred to radiation oncology, receives 20 Gy to the bulk of the mass and para-aortic nodes, then 16 Gy to the residual lesion. Two months after radiotherapy, CT shows a residual mass measuring 11 × 7 × 4 cm with no new lesions.

A 45-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of a painless right submandibular mass that had rapidly enlarged over the past 2 months. She denied facial weakness, cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, recent dental work, or trauma. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. On examination, there was a firm, mobile, 2.5-cm mass in the right parotid region; it was non-tender, and facial nerve function was intact. No cervical lymphadenopathy or other masses were palpated. Nasopharyngoscopy revealed no lesions in the nasopharynx or Waldeyer’s ring. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a 2.5 × 1.5 × 1.0 cm well-circumscribed mass in the deep lobe of the right parotid gland. The patient underwent a total right parotidectomy with removal of a satellite lymph node.

A 49-year-old man presented with a two-hour history of severe, dull left upper-quadrant abdominal pain. He reported an identical episode one week earlier, along with four months of fatigue, insomnia, severe weight loss, nocturnal sweating, impotence, and two episodes of macroscopic hematuria. Two days prior to presentation, he had a syncopal episode.

On prior evaluation three months earlier, abdominal CT had shown a moderately enlarged spleen (16 × 10 × 7 cm) without nodules and left ureteral stenosis for which a stent was placed; autoimmunity and viral serologies were negative. A month later, he was hospitalized for right facial nerve paralysis; brain imaging, electromyography, and CSF studies were unremarkable, and paralysis resolved spontaneously.

On current admission, vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed splenomegaly without lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 8 g/dL; tumor markers CEA and CA19-9 were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated hemoperitoneum and a splenic intraparenchymal hematoma. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a 7-cm splenic hematoma with variable enhancement and free intra-abdominal blood; the left kidney and ureteral stent appeared normal.

Over the next 24 hours, his hemoglobin fell acutely by 5 g/dL despite hemodynamic stability. A decision was made to perform a laparotomic splenectomy and nodal sampling.

A 39-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented to the emergency department with one month of progressive dyspnea on exertion and two syncopal episodes over the previous ten days. She also described intermittent chest pain radiating to her upper extremities and the right side of her back, and she noted bilateral lower-extremity swelling for one month. On examination, her blood pressure was 235/148 mm Hg, and an electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia without other abnormalities. A point-of-care echocardiogram revealed an abnormal soft tissue density in the right atrium, right ventricle, and inferior vena cava. A subsequent CT pulmonary angiogram showed a small subsegmental pulmonary embolism in the left lower lobe and a 4.2 cm hypoattenuating area in the right atrium suggestive of an atrial thrombus, along with relative enlargement of the inferior vena cava. A 2D Doppler echocardiogram measured a 2.4 × 2.0 cm echogenic mass, and cardiac MRI confirmed a large mass originating in the inferior vena cava that was prolapsing across the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.

A 74-year-old man was referred for repair of a presumed left inguinal hernia after he noticed a gradually enlarging mass over 10 years. On examination, there was an elastic, hard, slightly mobile mass in the left inguinal region that could not be reduced, even after analgesia. No skin changes were observed. Ultrasonography revealed a 9 cm × 4 cm, rigid, inhomogeneous structure originating in the left inguinal space beneath the skin without extension into the hemiscrotum. Doppler sonography demonstrated prominent, rich vascularity. Noncontrast CT of the scrotum showed a 13 cm, round, inhomogeneous lesion within the anterior abdominal wall fat at the level of the left spermatic cord, displacing the left testis.

A 70-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 3-month history of progressive dysphagia and an unintentional 10-kg weight loss. On examination, he appeared dehydrated and undernourished but had no other abnormalities. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed an impassable submucosal tumor filling the Killian triangle, preventing endoscopic biopsy. Contrast-enhanced thoracic CT showed a 60-mm, homogeneous, well-defined mass centered on the upper esophagus, causing luminal narrowing without invasion of adjacent structures. A CT-guided fine-needle biopsy of the lesion was performed.

A 10-year-old girl presented in February 2020 with left-eye proptosis.  
Initial CT and MRI demonstrated a 50×32×65 mm expansile lesion at the left cranio-orbital junction.  
She underwent craniotomy; margins were positive. Histopathology showed irregular bone trabeculae within mature cortical bone and a loose stroma rich in dilated, thin-walled blood vessels.  
Postoperatively, she received propranolol, cyclophosphamide, vincristine (6 cycles), and sirolimus, but MRI in May 2022 revealed tumor progression.  
In July 2022, a second craniotomy again had positive margins; microscopic analysis confirmed new bone trabeculae with osteoblasts and irregular vascular proliferation between trabeculae, leading to a diagnosis of intraosseous hemangioma.  
Osteoid osteoma was excluded given the lack of a central nidus and presence of a vascularized stroma. Immunohistochemistry showed CD31(+), CD34(+), D2-40(–), Factor VIII(+), Ki67 3%, and EMA(–).  
In August 2023, she developed firm, non-tender swellings on the left scalp and preauricular region. MRI revealed a 96×71×112 mm blood-rich lesion involving the left middle cranial fossa, supraorbital wall, pterygoid area, and adjacent skull bones: heterogeneous hypointensity on T1, heterogeneous hyperintensity with linear low-intensity areas on T2, marked contrast enhancement, and diffusion restriction with reduced ADC. There was mass effect on the brain. Neurologic examination was normal, with no meningeal signs.  
Because of two recurrences, she was referred for proton beam therapy.

A 19-year-old nulliparous woman (G1P0) was referred at 8 weeks of gestation after a pelvic mass was detected on routine pregnancy ultrasound. She had no significant prior history and no symptoms attributable to the mass. Transabdominal ultrasonography showed a well-circumscribed hyperechoic mass measuring 130 mm displacing the uterine body superiorly. Tumor markers (CA125, CA19-9, CEA, SCC, NSE, LDH) were within normal limits. 

At 12 weeks, MRI demonstrated a bulky, well-circumscribed retroperitoneal mass measuring 115×150×160 mm. The lesion exhibited low-signal bands on T1-weighted images, high-signal whorl-like formations on T2-weighted images, significant hyperintensity on diffusion-weighted imaging, and contained a fat component. 

Based on these imaging features, aggressive angiomyxoma was suspected, with cellular angiofibroma and angiomyofibroblastoma in the differential.

An 83-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of malaise and a rapidly enlarging left testicular swelling. He reported a 14-kg weight loss and had a body-mass index of 19.3 kg/m2; his WHO performance status was 2. On examination, there was no cutaneous lesion, but bilateral superficial inguinal lymphadenopathy was noted. Scrotal ultrasonography showed a well-defined, heterogeneous hypoechoic nodule in the left testis measuring 14 × 20 mm with central and peripheral hypervascularity on Doppler imaging; multiple small nodules were also seen in the subcutaneous tissue of the scrotum. Laboratory studies, including testicular tumor markers, were within normal limits. A left inguinal orchiectomy with testicular prosthesis placement was performed for diagnostic purposes.

A 72-year-old man presented with progressive shortness of breath over the past year and hemoptysis for 1 week. He had a history of untreated dermatophytosis for 4 years, a 20 pack-year smoking history (quit 6 months earlier), and a 10-year history of alcohol use. On examination, he had cyanosis of the zygomatic regions and lips, a positive hepatojugular reflux, and a grade 2/6 systolic murmur at the pulmonary valve area; his oxygen saturation was 97% on room air. Two-dimensional transthoracic echocardiography revealed a 57 × 36 mm solid mass attached to the pulmonary valve orifice, with a clear outline, uniform moderate-to-strong internal echo, and no mobility, causing marked stenosis. The right atrium and right ventricle were enlarged, and the interventricular septum bowed into the left ventricle, producing a “D” sign. Color Doppler flow imaging showed moderate tricuspid regurgitation with an 8.8 cm2 regurgitant area, a peak velocity of 420 cm/s, and a pressure gradient of 70 mmHg. Computed tomography angiography demonstrated low-density filling defects in the right ventricle and the root of the pulmonary artery, findings interpreted as likely thrombosis, although neoplastic lesions were not excluded.

An 84-year-old woman presented with a 2- to 3-day history of progressive umbilical pain and nausea without vomiting. Her medical history included hypertension and a hysterectomy with right oophorectomy 45 years earlier for fibroids. On examination, there was a painful 6 cm periumbilical mass; the abdomen was non-distended, with mild tenderness but no guarding.  
Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated an umbilical hernia with a 15 mm orifice containing omental tissue and no bowel. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis and elevated C-reactive protein; serum lactate was normal.  
The patient underwent emergency surgery, during which a 10 × 6 cm segment of omentum and hernia sac was resected for ischemia without necrosis. The defect was closed.  
Histopathology revealed a moderately well-differentiated invasive adenocarcinoma with a papillary growth pattern and psammoma bodies. Immunohistochemical staining was strongly positive for CK19, CA 125, and CK7, and negative for TTF-1 and CK20, findings deemed consistent with either primary peritoneal carcinoma or primary ovarian carcinoma.  
A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen showed a slight enlargement of the left ovary but no other intra-abdominal lesions. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy revealed no suspicious lesions. Serum CA 125 level was 22.08 U/mL (within normal limits).

A 61-year-old Bahraini man with diabetes and hypertension presented with several months of left flank pain. He had no other significant complaints.  
Physical examination and vital signs were unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies showed mild normochromic normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL). Urea and electrolytes, prostate-specific antigen, thyroid function tests, and autoimmune serologies were normal. Midstream urine revealed 3–5 RBCs/hpf and 2–4 WBCs/hpf; no protein, casts, crystals, or bacteria were seen. No tumor markers were measured.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 16 × 10.7 × 11.7 cm heterogeneously enhancing mass at the upper pole of the left kidney, displacing the lower pole and with mild perinephric fat stranding, interpreted as a renal neoplasm.  
Subsequent MRI demonstrated an 11 × 12 × 13 cm oval mass with heterogeneous enhancement and a nonenhancing cystic degeneration area in the anteromedial aspect of the left kidney, displacing it posteroinferiorly. The mass abutted the splenic vein and abdominal aorta and stretched the left renal vein and artery, suggesting an adrenal origin. The right kidney, liver, right adrenal gland, gallbladder, and abdominal lymph nodes were normal.  
Radiological differential diagnoses included pheochromocytoma, adrenocortical carcinoma, and leiomyosarcoma.

A 77-year-old woman (BMI 19.6 kg/m2) presented with 1 week of postmenopausal bleeding, preceded by intermittent vaginal spotting for 1 year and genital itching for 2 weeks. Transvaginal ultrasound initially showed an endometrial thickness of 1.47 cm; she declined biopsy. Two weeks later, ultrasound revealed an increased thickness of 2.36 cm and a 7 cm mixed-echogenic lesion within the endometrial cavity. Endometrial curettage demonstrated poorly differentiated carcinoma. Pelvic MRI revealed an 8.6 × 3.7 cm heterogeneously enhancing mass filling the endometrial cavity with evidence of cervical stromal invasion.

A 23-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of very intense nocturnal right chest pain rated 8/10 on the visual analog scale. He had no history of trauma. On examination, he was in good general condition with normal vital signs and no palpable chest wall mass. A CT scan showed an osteocondensing lesion at the junction of the middle and posterior arches of the right sixth rib, suggesting Ewing’s sarcoma. A PET CT was obtained and showed a regular, non-hypermetabolic, inhomogeneous condensation at the same location.

A 28-year-old Japanese man presented with a 6-week history of cough and left-sided chest pain. His past medical and family histories were unremarkable. He smoked 20 cigarettes per day for 6 years. On examination, his lungs were clear, and vital signs were normal.

Chest radiography showed an enlarged mediastinum. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a bulky mediastinal mass causing right bronchial stenosis, enlarged lymph nodes in the right hilum and supraclavicular area, and a 4.4 × 3.0 cm mass in the right middle lobe. ^18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated hypermetabolic involvement of multiple bones (spine, scapula, ribs, sternum, pelvis, and femur).

Laboratory studies showed elevated lactate dehydrogenase (667 IU/L; normal 119–229), C-reactive protein (0.82 mg/dL; normal 0.01–0.4), soluble IL-2 receptor (770 U/mL; normal 112–496), and alpha-fetoprotein (163.8 ng/mL; normal 0–20). Levels of β-hCG, CEA, pro-GRP, and CYFRA were within normal limits.

Endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration of a mediastinal lymph node revealed loosely cohesive ovoid and spindle-shaped cells with prominent necrosis, scant cytoplasm, and irregular hyperchromatic nuclei. Immunohistochemical staining showed that <5% of cells were positive for AE1/AE3, squamous markers (p40 and p63) were weakly positive in 10–20% of cells, and markers for neuroendocrine tumors (chromogranin, synaptophysin), lymphoid cells (LCA), muscle (MyoD1, myogenin), germ cell tumors (placental alkaline phosphatase, hCG), c-kit, TTF-1, CA19-9, and CD30 were all negative. Flow cytometry of surface markers was not compatible with lymphoma.

At this point, the clinical presentation suggested lung cancer, lymphoma, and a mediastinal germ cell tumor, but the histologic and immunophenotypic findings remained inconclusive.

A 14-year-old boy was evaluated for a painless swelling of the tongue that he had first noticed three months earlier. He denied bleeding, pain, or trauma. His medical history was unremarkable, with no diabetes, hypertension, or allergies. He led a healthy lifestyle. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and basic metabolic panel, were within normal limits.

On examination, there was a well-demarcated, firm mass measuring approximately 1.7 × 1.5 cm on the right side of the tongue involving the apex and body. The overlying mucosa was intact except for a small area of peripheral ulceration noted on gross inspection. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy.

Given the size and location of the lesion, the patient underwent a wide surgical excision of the mass. The specimen measured 17 × 15 × 4 mm and on sectioning revealed a vaguely nodular, gray-to-red lesion with ill-defined borders and a 10-mm ulcerated area at the periphery.

A 72-year-old man with a 65–pack-year smoking history presented with a 1-year history of progressive enlargement of a painful mass on the left retromolar pad that occasionally bled. He had no history of surgery or chronic infection. On examination, there was an irregular, exophytic lesion measuring approximately 3×3 cm on the left retromolar pad with a papillomatous hemorrhagic surface. Further otolaryngological and systemic examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, serum biochemistry, and coagulation studies, were within normal limits. An incisional biopsy showed dilated duct-like structures with overlying squamous epithelium; the ducts were lined by two to three layers of epithelium with prominent papillary proliferations and thin fibrovascular cores. Computed tomography of the head showed a 19-mm lytic lesion in the left mandibular corpus. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed reactive lymphadenopathy in the region.

A 23-year-old man presented with atraumatic right elbow pain for 6 months and progressive restriction of motion for 3 months, particularly flexion over the past month. He used nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs as needed with only transient relief. There was no diurnal variation of pain and no relation to activity. On examination, there was mild swelling and tenderness over the anterior elbow. Active extension was full; active flexion was severely limited, and passive flexion reached only 90°. There was no warmth, the distal neurovascular examination was intact, and no other joints were involved. Initial elbow radiographs showed no significant abnormality except a faint cortical irregularity and a small fleck of radio-opacity anterior to the distal humerus. MRI of the elbow demonstrated joint effusion, bone marrow edema around the distal humerus, and synovial hypertrophy; these findings were interpreted as suggesting elbow arthropathy, and, given the monoarticular involvement, a provisional diagnosis of elbow tuberculosis was made.

A 57-year-old Caucasian man with a 10-year history of T-cell leukemia presented with 4–5 weeks of worsening abdominal distension, decreased appetite, a 30-lb weight loss, nausea, vomiting, dry cough, and night sweats. He denied intravenous drug use, blood transfusions, or travel outside the United States. On examination, he had diffuse axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy; diffusely decreased breath sounds with mild bibasilar crackles; moderate ascites; hepatosplenomegaly; and a scaly macular skin lesion over the sacrum measuring 9 × 4 cm.  
Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 281,900 /mm3, elevated lactate dehydrogenase of 330 mg/dL, albumin of 1 g/dL, blood urea nitrogen of 31 mg/dL, and calcium of 13.9 mg/dL. Serologies for hepatitis A, B, and C and HIV-1 and ‑2 were negative. CT imaging of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated generalized lymphadenopathy with hepatosplenomegaly; skeletal survey showed no lytic lesions.  
Peripheral blood smear showed medium-to-large lymphoid cells with convoluted nuclei, coarsely clumped chromatin, scant basophilic cytoplasm, floret forms, blast cells, and CLL-like cells. Flow cytometry revealed an abnormal T-cell population expressing CD2 (96%), CD4 (94%), CD5 (95%), and CD25 (81%), with negative TdT and negative CD7. EIA detected serum antibodies to HTLV-1, which were confirmed by Western blot.

A 31-year-old woman with no past medical or family history of thyroid disease, radiation exposure, colonic polyps, or familial adenomatous polyposis was found to have a thyroid nodule on routine examination. She reported no symptoms. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed normal thyroid-stimulating hormone and free T4 levels; anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody was elevated at 548 IU/mL (reference <34 IU/mL). Thyroid ultrasonography demonstrated a solid, hypoechoic, wider-than-tall 12 mm nodule with smooth margins, heterogeneous echotexture of the gland, and no calcifications (TI-RADS 4). Fine-needle aspiration cytology revealed papillary growth of tall, spindle-shaped cells with elongated nuclei and an increased nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio, consistent with Bethesda category VI, favoring papillary thyroid carcinoma. Preoperative molecular testing (ThyroSCAN panel) on the aspirate was negative for BRAF V600E, NRAS Q61R/K, HRAS Q61R/K mutations, and for RET, PPARG, NTRK, and other fusions.
In our differential diagnosis, we considered cribriform morular thyroid cancer and the tall cell variant of PTC.

A 32‐year‐old Asian woman with hypothyroidism and primary infertility presented in 2016 with left‐sided hemiparesis and systemic hypertension. Brain MRI showed an acute ischemic infarct in the right posterior cerebral artery territory. Examination revealed a grade 2/6 short systolic murmur at the mitral area; ECG showed normal sinus rhythm with nonspecific T‐wave inversions in leads V5 and V6. Inflammatory markers were unremarkable. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a 13×0.5 mm vegetation‐like mass attached to the P2 segment of the mitral valve leaflet. Blood cultures were negative, but she was treated empirically with intravenous ceftriaxone and gentamicin. The neurologic deficit resolved but the mitral‐valve mass persisted. She declined surgery and was discharged on antiplatelet therapy.

Three years later, she had a second ischemic stroke, with MRI showing acute infarcts in the left posterior cerebral artery territory, left parietal cortex, and left superior frontal gyrus. Workup for young stroke, including autoimmune and connective‐tissue panels, was negative, and there was no family history of premature vascular disease. Repeat TTE and TEE showed masses on both the anterior and posterior mitral leaflets. Again treated empirically with IV antibiotics despite negative cultures, she recovered neurologically but the lesions persisted. In February 2020, she underwent intracardiac excision of the mitral‐valve mass with ring annuloplasty; postoperative recovery was uneventful. On follow‐up in November 2021, TTE revealed a 14×11 mm mass on the P2 leaflet and severe mitral regurgitation, and TEE confirmed recurrent masses on the mitral leaflets.

A 44-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with lower back pain radiating to both groins for 2 months. Vital signs were normal. Physical examination was unremarkable, and routine laboratory studies were within normal limits. A CT scan of the spine showed a mixed sclerotic and lytic lesion in the T12 vertebral body. A CT scan of the chest revealed multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules and mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy concerning for metastatic disease. CT-guided biopsy of a pulmonary nodule demonstrated a malignant neoplasm composed of spindle cells. Immunohistochemical staining of the tumor cells was positive for Bcl-2, vimentin, EMA, CD56, CD99, and TLE-1, and negative for CD34, CD10, p63, cytokeratin, S100, desmin, and synaptophysin.

A previously healthy 20-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of abdominal pain that began in the epigastrium and migrated to the right iliac fossa, intensifying despite analgesics, and was accompanied by nausea and decreased appetite. On examination, he was febrile (38.5 °C) and had an asymmetric abdomen with a palpable mass extending from the right iliac fossa to the hypogastrium and mesogastrium; the mass was tender with positive McBurney’s and Blumberg’s signs. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 15 g/dL, leukocyte count 16,000/µL with 1% bands, platelets 198,000/µL; liver tests showed AST 420 IU/L, ALT 1521 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 1304 IU/L, prothrombin time 12.9 s, and INR 1.1. His Alvarado score was 9. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated a heterogeneous 12 × 12 × 11 cm mass with peripheral inflammatory changes in the right iliac fossa, described as “compatible with appendicular plastron or tumor mass.”

A 44-year-old woman presented with a sensation of swallowing difficulty in the neck. Initial evaluation for an esophageal diverticulum by upper endoscopy revealed only chronic Helicobacter pylori gastritis. Neck ultrasonography demonstrated a 44 × 25 × 23 mm hypoechoic mass adjacent to the left thyroid lobe without a clear cleavage plane. Serum studies showed a calcium level of 10.6 mg/dL (normal 8.5–10.1 mg/dL) and a parathyroid hormone (PTH) level of 238.6 pg/mL (normal 10–65 pg/mL); thyroid antibodies were also elevated. A 99mTc-sestamibi scan was negative. Fine-needle aspiration of the cystic lesion yielded fluid with an intracystic PTH concentration exceeding 5000 pg/mL.

A 54-year-old obese Caucasian woman and current smoker presented with one week of intermittent vaginal bleeding and a sensation of a mass in the vaginal area. Her history was notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and an abdominal hysterectomy 30 years earlier for benign heavy menstrual bleeding. On pelvic examination, a pedunculated mass measuring 2.0 × 1.5 × 1.3 cm was noted on the vaginal wall at approximately the 7 o’clock position and was excised. Histologic examination of the lesion revealed clear cell carcinoma. Immunohistochemical stains showed positivity for CD10, PAX-8, and carbonic anhydrase 9/IX (CA-IX) and negativity for cytokeratin 7 (CK7).

A 16-year-old healthy girl underwent a routine school health examination and was found to have an abnormal heart sound. She was asymptomatic with stable vital signs. Cardiovascular examination revealed a wide, fixed splitting of the second heart sound. An electrocardiogram showed right bundle branch block. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a large, homogeneously hyperechoic lesion within the interventricular septum. Noncontrast cardiac computed tomography confirmed a solid infiltrative lesion in the interventricular septum with fat density (–90 HU). Noncontrast cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed an inhomogeneous mass with poorly delineated borders and an infiltrative pattern in the interventricular septum; the lesion was hyperintense on T1- and T2-weighted sequences and exhibited complete signal suppression on a fat-suppression (STIR) sequence. The mass did not compress the ventricles or obstruct the left ventricular outflow tract.

A 52-year-old woman, 6 months after total thyroidectomy for an 8 mm papillary microcarcinoma, presented with anorexia, fatigue, and right upper-quadrant abdominal pain. An abdominal ultrasound showed multiple hypoechoic hepatic lesions suspicious for metastases. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a large hypodense enhancing lesion in the right liver lobe. FDG-PET-CT showed the lesion to be hypermetabolic, suggesting metastatic disease. Fine-needle aspiration of a liver lesion was reported as metastatic carcinoma. Serum thyroglobulin was <2 ng/mL. After four weeks off thyroxine, she received 100 mCi of empirical I-131; the posttherapy whole-body scan showed no abnormal radioiodine uptake in the liver.

A 43-year-old man presented with a 4-year history of lower back pain, a 40-lb unintentional weight loss over 17 months, and one month of urinary urgency. His medical history included Bell’s palsy, hyperlipidemia, cervical osteoarthritis, and vertigo. On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. Abdominal examination revealed a firm, non-tender, mobile mass in the right side of the abdomen without distention. Laboratory studies showed normal hematologic, biochemical, and coagulation parameters. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 10-cm retroperitoneal mass in the mesenteric region. Ultrasound-guided core biopsy revealed a spindle cell neoplasm in a myxoid stroma with a delicate vascular network. The neoplastic cells had small oval nuclei with mild atypia; no mitoses or necrosis were seen. Immunohistochemical staining showed the tumor cells to be negative for SMA, desmin, β-catenin, S100, SOX10, AE1/3, EMA, CD117, and CD34. DOG1 staining showed only rare nonspecific positivity, and Ki-67 highlighted less than 5% of cells.

A 26-year-old woman presented with an 11-month history of a painless swelling in the anterior mandible. On examination, there was a firm swelling in the mandibular central incisor region, with grade 1 mobility of the central incisors. Vitality testing confirmed that the central and lateral incisors were vital. Panoramic radiography revealed a well-defined, unilocular radiolucent defect with severe alveolar bone loss localized between the diverging roots of the mandibular central incisors. Based on these clinical and radiographic findings, an initial diagnosis of periodontosis was made. The lesion was completely excised under local anesthesia, and thorough curettage was performed. Tissue specimens were submitted for histologic examination.

A 32-year-old Japanese man was referred for evaluation of a left adrenal mass discovered incidentally on CT after an abnormal chest radiograph. He denied headache, palpitations, sweating, anxiety, or weight loss. His blood pressure was 131/79 mm Hg supine and 127/72 mm Hg standing, with 24-hour ambulatory monitoring showing mean pressures of 128/80 mm Hg daytime and 104/68 mm Hg nighttime without paroxysms. Physical examination was unremarkable. Routine labs, including complete blood count and electrolytes, were normal except for mildly elevated triglycerides. Baseline serum cortisol, aldosterone, and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate were normal, and a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test showed no autonomous cortisol secretion. Noncontrast CT showed a 6 cm left adrenal tumor (30 Hounsfield units) with heterogeneous contrast enhancement. Three consecutive 24-hour urine collections revealed noradrenaline 199 μg/d (reference 31–160) and normetanephrine 0.33 mg/d (reference 0.10–0.28). A glucagon stimulation test produced no abnormal rise in plasma catecholamines, and a clonidine suppression test demonstrated an appropriate decrease in plasma catecholamine levels.

A 66-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of left shoulder pain without trauma. Initially diagnosed with periarthritis at another clinic, she noted a small axillary lump 2 months after pain onset that progressively enlarged. On examination, there was a hard, tender, poorly mobile 6×5 cm mass under the left axilla and restricted left shoulder external rotation.

Plain radiographs of the left shoulder showed a well-circumscribed, oval osteolytic lesion with sclerotic margins in the lesser tubercle of the humerus. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a soft-tissue mass invading the adjacent humerus. MRI revealed a 70×35×30 mm lesion within the subscapularis muscle, with clear margins, low signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted and STIR images, and mild internal enhancement on gadolinium-enhanced, fat-suppressed T1-weighted images.

Because the tumor was a deep-seated lesion larger than 5 cm, a soft-tissue sarcoma was suspected, and a core needle biopsy was performed. Histological examination revealed a uniformly paucicellular tumor composed of widely spaced, bland spindle- to stellate-shaped cells embedded in a myxocollagenous stroma. Immunohistochemical analysis showed that the tumor cells were diffusely positive for FOSL1 and negative for α-smooth muscle actin, desmin, CD34, β-catenin, and S-100.

A 28-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of pain and swelling over the dorsum of her left hand, worsening over the past 6 months. The swelling was insidious in onset, gradually increased to 1.5 × 1.5 cm, and was occasionally associated with dull, diffuse, nonradiating pain. She had two prior episodes of similar symptoms 4 and 6 years earlier, each diagnosed clinically and radiologically as a ganglion cyst and surgically excised with histopathological confirmation.

On examination, there was a 4-cm longitudinal scar over the dorsal third web space. A firm, non-tender, 1.5 × 1.5 cm diffuse swelling was palpable just radial to the scar at the level of the midcarpal joint, more prominent on palmar flexion. Wrist and finger range of motion were full.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 10,000 per mm3, an ESR of 20 mm/h, and a CRP of 1.1 mg/L. Radiographs of the left wrist showed slight radiolucency over the hamate and capitate bones. MRI demonstrated: (1) a focal small cyst beneath the extensor digitorum tendon at the base of the third metacarpal (suggestive of an occult ganglion cyst); (2) a similar cyst on the ventral aspect between the capitate and hamate bones; and (3) subchondral cysts in the hamate and capitate.

With the clinical suspicion of a recurrent ganglion cyst with associated osteomyelitis, excision of the lesion in toto was planned.

A 48-year-old man presented with a 5-year history of a swelling on the dorsum of his left hand. The lesion was insidious in onset, gradually progressive, and asymptomatic—with no history of trauma, constitutional symptoms, or weight loss. On examination, there was a lobulated 5 × 4 cm mass over the third to fifth metacarpal region of the left hand. It had well‐defined margins, a smooth surface, and soft to cystic consistency. The overlying skin was pinchable. The lesion was mobile horizontally but fixed vertically and became more prominent when the fingers were extended. Radiographs of the left hand showed a soft‐tissue opacity on the dorsum with scalloping and cortical erosion of the distal third metacarpal; the remainder of the skeleton appeared normal. With clinical differentials of a ganglion cyst versus a chondroid lesion, fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) was performed. FNAC showed abundant cellular material comprising giant cells admixed with myxoid stromal elements and multivacuolated cells, leading to a report of “Giant cell rich soft tissue neoplasm.”

A 58-year-old woman presented with a three-week history of a painless mass in her left leg accompanied by lower-extremity edema. On examination, a firm mass was palpable deep to the skin along the course of the short saphenous vein. There were no other skin lesions or systemic symptoms. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. Venous ultrasonography revealed a luminal mass in the short saphenous vein. Magnetic resonance imaging of the leg showed a 15 × 10 × 7 mm heterogeneous intravascular mass extending toward the Achilles tendon, findings that were thought to represent thrombosis of the short saphenous vein.

A 70-year-old woman presents with several weeks of general fatigue and is noted to have intrahepatic bile-duct dilatation on ultrasound. Her serum tumour markers are: AFP 5 ng/mL (normal), PIVKA-II 25 mAU/mL (normal), CEA 3 ng/mL (normal), and CA19-9 843.6 U/mL (elevated). Liver biochemistry shows alkaline phosphatase 601 IU/L, γ-GT 318 IU/L, albumin 3.3 g/dL, and normal bilirubin. The indocyanine green retention rate at 15 minutes is 4.6%, and the Child-Pugh score is 6 (Grade A). Cross-sectional imaging with CT and MRCP reveals a right umbilical portion anomaly and a 25-mm mass adjacent to the RUP, with nearly complete occlusion of the RUP and dilation of the intrahepatic bile ducts. The tumour appears to involve the confluence of the left lateral, left medial, and right anterior hepatic ducts, while the right posterior duct remains intact.

A 35-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive gait imbalance and daily, dull, global headaches. Over the past month, she experienced two generalized tonic–clonic seizures and developed progressively worsening blurred vision for 2 weeks, accompanied by projectile vomiting. She denied fevers, cough, tuberculosis exposure, weight loss, or night sweats. Her medical history was unremarkable; she had no history of immunosuppression.

On examination, vital signs were stable and the Glasgow Coma Scale score was 15. Pupils were midsize and sluggish; visual acuity was no light perception bilaterally. Motor strength was 4/5 in both lower extremities with brisk reflexes. Cranial nerves and sensory examination were otherwise normal.

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, and an HIV test, were within normal limits. A urine β-hCG test was negative. CT scans of the chest and abdomen were unrevealing. Brain MRI showed multiple bilateral cortical and subcortical masses deep in the periventricular regions that were T1-hypointense, T2-heterogeneously hyperintense, demonstrated diffusion restriction, and had surrounding vasogenic edema with heterogeneous postcontrast enhancement.

An 11-day-old male neonate was brought for evaluation of a swelling in the upper lip present since birth, associated with difficulty in suckling. The infant was irritable and cried continuously. Examination revealed a 5×3 cm tender, firm ovoid mass involving the upper lip and adjacent upper face, causing anterior nares stenosis. The overlying skin was normal without sinus, punctum, or ulceration; the alveolus was spared. Patchy skin induration and engorged veins were noted over the buccal aspect of the lesion. 

Noncontrast CT and MRI of the head and neck demonstrated soft‐tissue–intensity lesions in the upper lip, ipsilateral orbit, and the submandibular (parapharyngeal) space. 

Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the lip mass revealed clusters and dispersed populations of small round cells with scant to moderate cytoplasm, round to oval nuclei, fine chromatin, and inconspicuous nucleoli; no cytoplasmic vacuoles or rosettes were identified. 

Immunocytochemistry was performed using a panel of leucocyte common antigen (LCA), CD99, Desmin, and Myogenin to clarify the diagnosis.

A 7-year-old girl presented with one week of abdominal pain localized to the left iliac fossa and right lumbar region. She had no fever, anorexia, vomiting, hematochezia, or diarrhea, and had slight relief with analgesics. There was no relevant family history. On examination, she was well appearing; vital signs were normal. Her abdomen was soft without guarding, but a palpable mass was noted in the right iliac fossa extending into the corresponding lumbar region, which was tender on palpation, without signs of peritoneal irritation. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, white blood cell count 13,000/mm3, and platelet count 487,000/mm3. All tumor markers, including CEA, CA 125, CA 19-9, AFP, and β-hCG, were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a large cyst filling the cecum and ascending colon without connection to the liver or right kidney. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a large cystic mass lateral and superior to the cecum and ascending colon, also without evidence of connection to adjacent organs.

A 54-year-old woman (gravida 3, para 2) presented with three months of intermittent, irregular vaginal bleeding and mild abdominal pain. Her last delivery was a term cesarean 20 years earlier; she had a complete molar pregnancy at age 36 managed by suction and curettage. Over the past year her menstrual periods became irregular, with three months of amenorrhea. She had no significant medical history, including hypertension, diabetes, or thyroid disease. Physical examination revealed normal vital signs, an enlarged uterus equivalent to a 17-week gestation, and slight uterine bleeding on speculum examination; the cervix appeared healthy. Transabdominal ultrasound showed the uterine cavity filled with a central heterogeneous mass containing multiple anechoic spaces of varying size and shape; a 2 × 3 cm subserosal fibroid was noted at the fundus. Maternal serum β-human chorionic gonadotropin was 97,000 IU/L.

An 11-year-old boy was evaluated for a mass in his oral cavity and difficulty chewing and swallowing solid foods for the past 3 years. He denied dyspnea, pain, prior surgery, or trauma to the oral cavity or neck. On examination, there was a 40×35 mm sublingual mass with normal overlying mucosa that displaced the tongue superiorly and posteriorly. Palpation of the neck revealed a firm midline swelling in the submental area extending to the level of the thyroid notch. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a 40×35 mm well-circumscribed, non-enhancing cystic mass extending from the sublingual region to the thyroid notch; the contents were homogeneous. To exclude thyroid pathology, a thyroid scintigraphy was performed and was normal.

A 6-year-old boy presented with a painless, progressive enlargement of the right scrotum over several weeks. On examination, there was a non-tender, soft, compressible mass in the right hemiscrotum that did not transilluminate. The right testis was palpable separately from the mass; the left hemiscrotum was normal. Scrotal ultrasonography showed multiple cystic lesions with internal septations in the right hemiscrotum extending to the proximal inguinal canal; both testes appeared normal. These findings were considered consistent with either a cystic hygroma or a complex or infected spermatocele.

A 17-year-old female presented with a 1-week history of sudden onset limping of the left leg. She initially had difficulty moving the left lower limb and was found to have a small swelling over her spine, which an ultrasound reported as a lipoma. She was reassured but had temporary improvement. Two months later, the limp recurred and progressed over another month to complete inability to walk, requiring a wheelchair. She also developed urinary retention followed by incontinence. 

On examination, she was alert and oriented. Vital signs were normal. Neurologic examination revealed intact cortical sensation, impaired temperature and vibration senses, left lower-limb weakness (1/5) and right lower-limb weakness (3/5), depressed patellar and Achilles reflexes (+1), and a back hump from T8 to T12. There was no bowel incontinence. Routine blood tests, including complete blood count, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and renal function, were all normal.

MRI of the thoracic spine showed a large dumbbell-shaped soft-tissue mass in the left paraspinal area at T10–T12, with an anterior component measuring 5.4 × 4.9 cm and a posterior component measuring 7.5 × 3.7 cm. The lesion extended through the left T11–T12 neural exit foramina, with severe compression and rightward displacement of the spinal cord. The mass was iso-intense on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously intense on T2-weighted images, hyper-intense on T2-STIR, and heterogeneously intense with a well-enhancing rim on post-gadolinium T1 sequences. There was scalloping of T11 and widening of the spinal canal at that level. Vertebral bodies appeared normal in signal, size, shape, and height.

The radiologic differential diagnosis of the mass was a nerve sheath tumor of the spinal cord, most probably neurofibroma or schwannoma.

A 61-year-old man with a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus was referred for evaluation of an elevated serum carcinoembryonic antigen level of 6.9 ng/mL (normal < 5.0). Upper endoscopy revealed a slightly elevated, reddish lesion with small depressed areas located 28 cm from the incisors. Narrow-band imaging showed brownish changes in the central depressed areas, and these areas failed to stain with Lugol’s iodine. Biopsy specimens demonstrated dispersed, atypical glands with a bilayered structure. Endoscopic ultrasonography suggested infiltration into the submucosal layer. A definitive diagnosis could not be made on the biopsy specimens, and the lesion was removed endoscopically for thorough evaluation.

A 69-year-old man with a history of Merkel cell carcinoma of the left eyebrow, treated by wide local excision in 2010 with no residual disease, has been under regular surveillance. His medical history is notable for non–insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and atrial fibrillation. In 2012, a routine FDG–PET/CT scan revealed a 1.3 cm left intraparotid lymph node of uncertain significance. There were no new skin lesions, and the patient was asymptomatic.

A 30-year-old woman with no significant medical history was found to have a mediastinal mass on a screening chest radiograph. She was asymptomatic, and retrospective review showed the mass unchanged over seven years. Physical examination was unremarkable, and routine blood tests were normal. MRI demonstrated a subcarinal azygoesophageal recess mass that was hyperintense relative to skeletal muscle on both T1-weighted and T2-weighted images; flow voids suggestive of enlarged intralesional vessels were seen. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a homogeneously and intensely enhancing mass with enlarged feeding vessels just cephalad to the lesion; there was no invasion of the chest wall. The differential diagnosis of this very slow-growing, hypervascular middle mediastinal tumor included paraganglioma and Castleman's disease.

A 63-year-old woman presented with a 5-week history of progressive, severe headaches accompanied by tinnitus, a sensation of pressure in her right ear, and dizziness. The headaches worsened during prolonged periods of walking. Physical examination, including auditory and vestibular function tests, was unremarkable. Initial management included analgesics for headache and antiemetics and antihistamines for dizziness. A noncontrast CT scan of the head was negative for intracranial hemorrhage. Brain MRI showed a 5 mm round lesion in the right cerebellopontine angle, posterior and superior to the internal auditory canal; the lesion was hyperintense on both T1- and T2-weighted images and was surrounded by a hypointense halo, findings thought to represent either a partially thrombosed aneurysm of the right anterior inferior cerebellar artery or a lipoma. Cerebral angiography demonstrated no aneurysms. Three-dimensional cone beam CT performed in the angiography suite revealed a well-defined 5 mm lesion abutting the internal auditory canal, with a hypodense center and hyperdense rim.

A 33-year-old man with no significant medical or family history presented with several months of vague, diffuse abdominal pain initially attributed to constipation. He underwent a contrast-enhanced CT scan, which revealed a large soft-tissue mass in the mid abdomen extending into the upper pelvis, measuring 15.7×28.6×24.2 cm; the mass contained hypodense regions and multiple vessels and displaced but did not obstruct bowel loops. 

An ultrasound-guided core-needle biopsy showed neoplastic spindle cells. Immunohistochemical staining was moderately positive for muscle-specific actin, S-100, and CD117, and negative for cytokeratin AE1/AE3, desmin, and CD34. Cytology revealed no clonal proliferation of lymphocytes. Given the clinical presentation and histopathology, there was high suspicion that the lesion represented a large gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST). The patient began neoadjuvant imatinib.

After four months of therapy, his pain, anorexia, and weight loss persisted. A repeat CT scan showed that the mass had increased to greater than 20×37×32 cm and was now compressing the small bowel, ureters, and kidneys. Because of progression on medical therapy, surgical resection was planned.

A 58-year-old woman who underwent wide local excision and axillary dissection for a T2 N0 M0 grade 1 invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast five years ago now presents with a 15-cm, painless, mobile mass in the upper outer quadrant of her left breast. She reports no nipple retraction or discharge. Mammography shows a BI-RADS 5 lesion. Core-needle biopsy reveals breast tissue containing areas of bone formation with partially calcified osteoid material, surrounded by stellate and spindle-shaped stromal cells, along with osteoclast-like giant cells. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen demonstrates a large lobulated left breast mass with cystic and calcific foci measuring 7.1 × 10.7 × 11.6 cm, without invasion of the chest wall or skin and no evidence of pulmonary, hepatic, or bony lesions.

A 20-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of a right-sided, painless facial swelling. He was otherwise healthy. On examination, there was a diffuse extraoral swelling extending from the right ala of the nose to the right outer canthus and from the infra-orbital region to the oral commissure, without lymphadenopathy. Intraorally, a 5×3 cm soft, fluctuant swelling was noted along the right maxillary alveolus from the canine to the second molar, with obliteration of the buccal vestibule; teeth were non-tender and without mobility. Laboratory studies were within normal limits.

Panoramic radiography demonstrated a single unilocular radiolucency with smooth corticated margins from the apex of the right maxillary canine to the tuberosity, enclosing an impacted right third molar displaced superiorly into the opacified right maxillary sinus. The posterior sinus wall was destroyed, and slight root resorption was seen in the right first and second premolars and first molar. 

CT of the facial bones revealed a well-defined, nonenhancing hypodense osteolytic lesion measuring 5.2×5.0×4.7 cm, occupying the right maxillary bone and sinus, with complete opacification of the antrum, thinning and erosion of the sinus walls, and displacement of the impacted third molar to the anteromedial sinus wall. 

A provisional diagnosis of a dentigerous cyst associated with the right maxillary third molar was made.

A 71-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a nodule in the high parietal region of the scalp. His history was notable for trigeminal neuralgia and multiple sclerosis; there was no personal or family history of malignancy or allergies. Clinical examination showed a red-brown, ulcerated nodule approximately 1 cm in diameter. A prior biopsy and computed tomography scan performed elsewhere had led to a diagnosis of stage I malignant melanoma (pT2, sN0, Mx). 

Under general anesthesia, the lesion was excised with a 1 cm margin down to subcutaneous tissue, and a sentinel lymph node biopsy was performed. The specimen was submitted for histologic and immunohistochemical analysis. 

Histologic examination showed an erosive lesion with a monomorphic population of small cells with prominent nucleoli. Immunohistochemical stains were negative for cytokeratins (MN116) with only scattered MNF116 reactivity, and negative for melanoma markers (SOX-10, S-100) and INI-1. Stains were positive for CD10, Vimentin, and Desmin, with focal positivity for MyoD1 and a high proliferative index (Ki-67 up to 90%).

A 34-year-old woman with a history of bilateral submuscular silicone breast augmentation 3 years earlier presented with a 6-month history of a gradually enlarging mass in her left breast. She reported a motor vehicle accident 3 months before symptom onset with chest impact on the steering wheel. On examination, the inferior pole of the left breast projected higher than the right, and a firm 7 × 4 cm mass was palpable at the 11 o’clock position, 9 cm from the nipple, distinct from the implant; the right breast was unremarkable.

Targeted ultrasound of the left breast showed a well-defined, heterogeneously hypoechoic mass abutting the superior medial aspect of the intact implant, with internal vascularity. The lateral margin displayed a beak-like “fascial-tail” sign, and the lesion extended into the intercostal space. No suspicious axillary lymphadenopathy was seen.

Breast MRI without contrast revealed a slightly lobulated 8.1 × 4.7 × 7.1 cm mass in contact with the unruptured implant, extending into the anterior intercostal space between the second and third ribs without clear chest wall invasion. On T1-weighted images, the mass was heterogeneous and low signal; on T2-weighted sequences it was hyperintense. The pectoralis major muscle lay over the mass without definite involvement.

A core-needle biopsy demonstrated a spindle cell lesion with diffuse nuclear β-catenin positivity and absence of CD34 expression. No cytologic atypia or mitotic figures were observed.

A 70-year-old man with a history of childhood pleural effusion, a prior stroke, nasopalpebral basal cell carcinoma excised 5 years earlier, and severe heart disease (New York Heart Association class III) presented with chest pain and progressive dyspnea unresponsive to medical therapy. Chest radiography revealed a large right hemithoracic mass. Computed tomography of the chest demonstrated a well-delineated mass in the right hemithorax with areas of fat attenuation and evidence of compression of adjacent structures. Bronchoscopy showed extrinsic compression of the trachea and right main bronchus without mucosal invasion, and upper endoscopy revealed external compression of the esophagus without direct invasion. Because of persistent symptoms, he was referred for surgical removal of the mass.

A 32-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1 with regular menses and no history of reproductive tract tumors, noted a 2 × 1.5 cm lump in her left breast on self-examination in July 2010. In August, breast ultrasound confirmed a 1.8 × 1.2 cm hypoechoic mass. In January 2011, PET-CT revealed hypermetabolic lesions in the left breast, left kidney, and two pulmonary nodules; contrast CT confirmed lesions in the lung and kidney. A core-needle biopsy of the breast mass showed no malignant cells. Serum human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG) was 22 931 U/L (normal < 5 U/L). In February 2011, an excisional biopsy of the breast mass was performed, and histopathology was reported as invasive ductal carcinoma.

A 73-year-old Japanese man with HER2-negative advanced tubular gastric adenocarcinoma (cardia invading lower esophagus) and peritoneal dissemination had received first-line S-1 plus oxaliplatin (partial response, then S-1 maintenance), second-line ramucirumab plus paclitaxel (stable disease), and third-line nivolumab for ~1 year (initial tumor marker decrease and tumor shrinkage, followed by gradual primary tumor enlargement).

He developed a 5-day history of occipital headache unrelieved by NSAIDs, and noted tongue deviation with dysarthria. On neurologic examination, there were glossopharyngeal (IX) and hypoglossal (XII) nerve palsies. Plain CT of the head and noncontrast brain MRI showed no evidence of stroke, hemorrhage, or parenchymal metastasis. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI disclosed a heterogeneously enhancing mass in the clivus involving the right jugular process and right hypoglossal canal. Retrospective review of CT revealed irregularity of the bone cortex near the right hypoglossal canal.

A 74-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with fever and right upper-quadrant abdominal pain of acute onset. She had no significant medical or surgical history. On examination, her temperature was 38.2 °C, and she had tenderness and guarding in the right hypochondrium. Her body-mass index was 32. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis and an elevated C-reactive protein level; other routine tests were unremarkable. An abdominal ultrasound showed a gallbladder with multiple gallstones and a thickened wall. A laparoscopic cholecystectomy was performed, and intraoperative inspection revealed multiple nodular implants on the omentum, parietal peritoneum, and intestinal serosa in the right iliac fossa; biopsies of the nodules were obtained.

Grossly, the resected fat tissue contained multiple nodules of variable size. Histologic examination showed that more than 75% of the lesion consisted of psammoma bodies, with occasional papillary structures and isolated nests of epithelial cells. The epithelial cells exhibited low-to-moderate nuclear atypia, with small nuclei, inconspicuous nucleoli, and rare mitoses. There were no solid areas of epithelial proliferation, and neither vascular emboli nor perineural invasion was identified.

A 25-year-old Dravidian Indian female presented with a 1-month history of swelling in the right lower back tooth region. There were no extra-oral abnormalities. Intra-oral examination revealed a 4 × 4 cm fluctuant, translucent, mildly tender, smooth-surfaced swelling centered on the right retromolar area, more lingual in position, obliterating the right posterior lingual sulcus, with visible telangiectatic surface vessels. The lesion was soft and mildly tender on palpation. Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI of the neck showed multilobulated cystic spaces exerting a mild mass effect on the right pre-styloid parapharyngeal space. Fine-needle aspiration cytology yielded dirty brown fluid; microscopy demonstrated mucous cells, a few squamous cells, and a papillaroid arrangement of hyperchromatic cells in a mucinous background. A salivary gland neoplasm was suspected. Incisional biopsy suggested low-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma, cystadenoma, and sclerosing polycystic adenosis, and complete excision with frozen-section margin evaluation was planned.

A 32-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of slow but progressive swelling near her gluteal cleft. She denied fevers, chills, pain, drainage, bleeding, or rectal bleeding. On examination, there was a 4 × 4 cm area of swelling just left of the natal cleft at the level of the tip of the coccyx, with mild blanching erythema of the overlying skin but no fluctuance, purulence, or visible pilonidal pits. Given a high suspicion for abscess, percutaneous aspiration was performed in clinic but no fluid was obtained. The differential diagnosis at this time included inclusion cyst and soft-tissue tumor. The patient was scheduled for surgical excision. In the operating room, a 6-cm vertical incision was made over the lesion in the prone jack-knife position. A complex and septated 6 × 4 × 4 cm mass was excised from the subcutaneous tissue near the coccyx, with a rim of healthy tissue; the mass was adherent to subcutaneous fat but did not involve the coccyx or anal sphincter. The specimen was oriented with sutures and sent for permanent pathology, and the wound was closed primarily.

A 49-year-old premenopausal woman (G2P2) presented with a 1-day history of dull, gradual-onset right lower-quadrant abdominal pain and mild nausea. She also described a 1-year history of abdominal distension, anorexia, and early satiety, and noted irregular menstrual bleeding for 6 months. She denied vaginal bleeding or discharge. Her medical history included hypertension and peptic ulcer disease treated with medication, and she used combined oral contraceptive pills. There was no personal or family history of ovarian, uterine, bowel, or breast cancer.

On examination, her blood pressure was 160/83 mmHg; other vital signs and blood glucose were normal. The abdomen was distended, rigid, and tender in the right lower quadrant; a smooth, firm pelvic mass was palpable. Bowel sounds were not clearly audible. Vaginal examination revealed full fornices and a normal-appearing cervix. Other systems were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed markedly elevated CA-125 and CEA levels; β-hCG and α-fetoprotein were normal. Complete blood count, liver and renal function tests were within normal limits. ECG and echocardiography were normal.

Pelvic MRI demonstrated a well-defined septated cystic lesion measuring 15 × 26 × 27 cm arising from the right adnexa, without enhancing solid components. The uterus was bulky with multiple intramural and subserosal leiomyomas.

An exploratory midline laparotomy revealed a 20 × 20 × 19 cm smooth cystic mass of the right ovary, without obvious solid areas and with minimal ascitic fluid. The uterus was bulky with fibroids. A total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy was performed, and the mass was sent for histopathological evaluation.

A 69-year-old man presented with a right infra-auricular neck mass that he first noticed more than 10 years ago, which had grown more rapidly over the past 4 months. He denied pain, facial asymmetry, trismus, or overlying skin changes. On examination, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. There was a well-defined, mobile, multilobulated, non-tender mass measuring approximately 10 × 10 cm, extending from the tail of the parotid gland superiorly to the level of the cricoid inferiorly. A T2-weighted fast spin-echo MRI of the neck (noncontrast) showed a large, discrete, rounded heterogeneous lesion with soft-tissue signal in the right parotid region, measuring 11.5 × 10.5 × 11.5 cm, causing mass effect on adjacent structures; the mandible appeared preserved and no lymphadenopathy was noted.

A 55-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with a 1-month history of night sweats, palpitations, asthenia, and a 7-kg weight loss. On examination, he was alert but tachycardic (113 bpm) and hypotensive (98/77 mmHg); he appeared pale without peripheral lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or hemorrhagic signs. Laboratory studies showed a normochromic, normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL) and thrombocytopenia (72,000/mm3); other cell lines were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography suggested bilateral adrenal masses. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated large, bilaterally homogenous, polylobed adrenal masses (right: 130 × 103 × 91 mm; left: 114 × 91 × 78 mm) with mild enhancement and multiple retroperitoneal, para-aortic, and celiac-mesenteric lymphadenopathies. FDG-PET showed intensely hypermetabolic bilateral adrenal lesions (SUVmax 47 right, 50.2 left) along with hypermetabolic supra-clavicular, mediastinal, and external iliac lymph nodes.

A 56-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of a painless mass in the upper external left gluteal region. Two years earlier, she had undergone an abdominal hysterectomy for an enlarging pelvic mass between the uterus and rectosigmoid colon. Preoperative CA 125 was 61.9 U/mL. The resected mass was bilobular (9×7×6.5 cm and 5.2×5×5 cm) with hard and soft elements, alongside multiple intramural uterine leiomyomas. Histology showed interlacing bundles of spindle cells with medium-grade atypia, giant cells, and up to 50 mitoses per 10 high-power fields. Immunohistochemistry was positive for vimentin, smooth muscle actin, and desmin. She received postoperative radiotherapy and gemcitabine–docetaxel chemotherapy. One year later, she underwent left upper lobectomy for a solitary lung lesion; histology matched the pelvic tumor. 

Two years after the hysterectomy, MRI of the pelvis revealed an ovoid subcutaneous mass lateral to the left gluteus maximus and a smaller lesion in the right gluteus maximus muscle, both with central necrosis and peripheral enhancement. A diagnosis of soft-tissue metastatic disease was suggested, and both masses were surgically resected. Histologic examination confirmed a spindle-cell sarcoma with central necrosis and morphologic features similar to the previous tumor. A subsequent abdominal CT scan showed only postsurgical changes, edematous sigmoid-colon wall, and presacral fat edema attributed to prior radiotherapy.

A 49-year-old woman with an unremarkable medical history presented with a 12-month history of lower abdominal pain and an enlarging “mass sensation” along her prior cesarean section scar. She reported increased urinary frequency and nocturia but denied urgency, incontinence, dysuria, or hematuria.

On examination, a firm, nontender anterior pelvic mass was palpated in the midline suprapubic region, slightly to the left. 

An abdominal ultrasound revealed a 15-cm mass localized to the dome of the urinary bladder. Pelvic MRI confirmed a 14.0 × 8.5 × 7.3-cm mass arising from the left lower rectus abdominis muscle, extending anteriorly into subcutaneous tissue and posteriorly impinging on the bladder dome. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated an enhancing lesion involving the bladder wall.

Based on these imaging findings, the differential diagnosis included soft tissue sarcoma, dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, and desmoid tumor.

A 67-year-old Caucasian woman with a strong family history of ovarian cancer and a newly identified BRCA1 mutation underwent a prophylactic laparoscopic bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. Her menopause had occurred at age 52. Preoperative laboratory studies, bimanual pelvic examination, and transvaginal ultrasound were unremarkable, aside from an atrophic uterine corpus and thin postmenopausal endometrium; no adnexal masses were seen. At laparoscopy, the uterus appeared atrophied, and both ovaries and fallopian tubes appeared normal. Both adnexa were removed without complication. On gross pathologic examination, a 0.5 cm cream-colored, poorly circumscribed solid lesion was identified in the distal right fallopian tube. Microscopic examination of hematoxylin and eosin–stained sections revealed predominantly pseudoglandular structures. Immunohistochemical staining showed strong positivity for calretinin, WT-1, and cytokeratin 7, with negative staining for PAX8 and CD34.

A 47-year-old man presented three months earlier with unexplained nausea and vomiting and underwent cholecystectomy for gallstones.
