Two months postoperatively, a left retroperitoneal mass was incidentally discovered. On admission, he reported intermittent nausea and vomiting but denied chest tightness, chest pain, low back pain, or intestinal or urinary symptoms. His medical history included eight years of hypertension and twenty years of hepatitis B infection; his mother had liver cirrhosis and hypertension. Laboratory tests showed elevated alkaline phosphatase (144.5 U/L; normal 30–120 U/L), low total protein (64.2 g/L; normal 65–85 g/L), low albumin (36.8 g/L; normal 40–55 g/L), mildly reduced LDL cholesterol (2.01 mmol/L; normal 2.07–3.10 mmol/L), and platelet distribution width of 17.3% (normal 9.0–17.0%); all other parameters, including cortisol, ACTH, platelets, coagulation studies, and D-dimer, were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed an irregular 3.2×2.0 cm soft-tissue density mass below the left renal pole and anterior to the psoas major muscle, with marked arterial-phase enhancement, persistent venous-phase enhancement, and waning enhancement in the delayed phase. MRI showed an oval lesion at the same location that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted and fat-suppressed T2-weighted images, hyperintense on diffusion-weighted imaging, with no change in the apparent diffusion coefficient. No other abnormal signals or enlarged lymph nodes were identified. Given the imaging features and his history of hypertension, a paraganglioma was suspected, and laparoscopic resection of the mass was planned.

A 35-year-old woman presented with two months of diarrhea, right lower quadrant abdominal pain, and cramps. She had studied in Nepal for one year; her medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 105 g/L, hematocrit 0.34 L/L, erythrocytes 3.70×10^12/L), vitamin B12 deficiency (130 ng/L), elevated serum iron (35.3 μmol/L), increased ferritin (1042 μg/L), normal transferrin, and neutrophilic leukocytosis (leukocytes 11.52×10^9/L, neutrophils 9.30×10^9/L). Magnetic resonance imaging revealed mural thickening of the ileocecum and appendix, interpreted as inflammatory, and a 7.9-cm nonhomogeneous cystic mass of the left ovary. Gastroscopy and proctoscopy were unremarkable. Colonoscopy showed multiple well-circumscribed, ulcerated, tumor-like masses in the ascending colon, measuring 8–33 mm, with livid-colored peripheries and necrotic centers. A larger, more solid lesion (4.5 cm) was present at the ileocecal valve extending into the adjacent cecum and appendix. These endoscopic findings were inconclusive; while atypical for Crohn’s disease, the differential diagnoses included tuberculosis, lymphoma, and carcinoma.

A 71-year-old man with a history of atrial fibrillation underwent transoesophageal echocardiography (TEE) during preprocedural workup for pulmonary vein ablation, which revealed an ostium secundum atrial septal defect (osASD). He underwent successful transcatheter osASD closure with a 27-mm Figulla Flex II device and was discharged on apixaban. Thirty-two months later, he was readmitted for atrial fibrillation recurrence; he was asymptomatic and physical examination was unremarkable. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a left atrial mass attached to the left disc of the closure device and moderate mitral regurgitation. Anticoagulation was switched from apixaban to acenocoumarol. Four months later, TEE showed that the mass remained unchanged in size; it was attached to the infero-posterior margin of the left disc, had an isoechoic aspect with irregular margins, and exhibited extreme mobility. Severe mitral regurgitation persisted. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging revealed that the mass was isointense on T1 and T1 fat-saturated sequences, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2 sequences, showed no first-pass perfusion enhancement, and late gadolinium enhancement sequences were inconclusive. Coronary angiography demonstrated neovascularization of the mass arising from the left circumflex artery.

A 14-year-old female presents with a 2-month history of severe right ear pain, persistent otorrhea, mild hearing loss, and a sensation of a foreign body in the right ear. She has no history of ear trauma, surgery, or medication use. On otoscopic examination, there is a solitary, red, soft, well-circumscribed nodule in the right external auditory canal measuring approximately 10 × 12 mm. No other abnormalities are noted on head and neck examination. Basic laboratory studies are within normal limits.

A 64‐year‐old man presented with several months of lower abdominal discomfort. An initial CT scan revealed a 2 cm retroperitoneal pelvic mass with fat attenuation, radiologically considered to be a lipoma. The patient elected to observe the lesion; annual CT scans showed no significant change for 6 years. In the seventh year, CT demonstrated that the mass had grown to approximately 6 cm × 5 cm. A colonoscopy was performed and was unremarkable. Because of the increase in size and concern for sarcoma, the patient underwent surgical excision of the mass. Preoperative laboratory evaluation revealed a hemoglobin of 13.8 g/dL, hematocrit 40.1%, MCV 84.6 fL, platelet count 251,000/μL, and white blood cell count 9,500/μL with a differential of 74% neutrophils, 16% lymphocytes, 7% monocytes, 2% eosinophils, and 1% basophils. A peripheral blood smear confirmed these findings without absolute lymphocytosis.

A 71-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 1-week history of abrupt-onset blurry vision, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and ataxia. He denied vertigo or headache and had no prior stroke history; he was taking aspirin for a patent foramen ovale. In the emergency department, a noncontrast head CT showed no masses or hemorrhage. MRI was contraindicated because of ocular shrapnel. Carotid Doppler ultrasound showed no stenosis, and CT angiography demonstrated no vascular compromise. The working diagnosis was cerebellar stroke, and he was transferred to inpatient stroke rehabilitation. Despite therapy, his symptoms worsened. A repeat noncontrast head CT 9 days after admission revealed indistinct, masslike lesions in the cerebellum—one lesion with hemorrhage, surrounding vasogenic edema, and mild hydrocephalus. Contrast-enhanced CT later that day showed three intensely enhancing masses in the right cerebellar hemisphere. He was started empirically on steroids for vasogenic edema, resulting in rapid improvement of his symptoms.

A 1-year-old child was referred for a congenital lesion of the left thigh that had gradually increased in size. The lesion was soft, papillomatous, noninfiltrated, and asymptomatic. No other abnormalities were found on examination, including a normal neurologic assessment and no deafness. Microcystic lymphatic malformation was initially suspected, and an ultrasound examination was performed, consistent with this diagnosis. Over time, the lesion increased in size and became complicated by local infection. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a lesion strictly localized to the skin, and surgical management was decided.

A 57-year-old man presented with a 5-year history of a progressively enlarging, painful, fungating mass with draining sinuses over the anterior aspect of his left leg. On examination, there was a 15×10×10 cm expansile, gray-white, ulceroproliferative lesion involving the lower half of the tibia and fibula, with areas of hemorrhage and necrosis. Distal pulses were markedly diminished on the affected side, and the fibula could not be palpated separately.

Plain radiographs of the left leg revealed an expansile, mixed lytic and sclerotic lesion with a honeycomb appearance involving the entire tibia and fibula, with anteromedial bowing of the shafts and innumerable radiolucencies surrounded by ring-shaped densities.

MRI showed a heterogeneous, lobulated mass occupying the full length of the tibia and fibula, with T1 isointensity, T2 heterogeneous hyperintensity, diffusion restriction, and heterogeneous postcontrast enhancement with nonenhancing necrotic areas. The lesion involved all compartments of the leg, extended to the subarticular margins proximally and distally without intra-articular extension, and encased the posterior tibial vessels.

A metastatic workup, including contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen and a Tc-99m MDP bone scan, was negative for distant disease, although the bone scan confirmed heterogeneous radiotracer uptake in the left tibia and fibula without involvement of the knee or ankle joints.

Based on radiologic and nuclear medicine findings, the differential diagnosis included primary carcinoma with sarcomatous transformation, adamantinoma, the active phase of Paget’s disease with possible superimposed infection, and, less likely, metastasis.

A man in his 50s presented with a 6-month history of pruritus and widespread scaly, pink-brown indurated plaques covering about 60% of his body surface. Three months earlier, a skin biopsy had shown spongiosis with a mixed superficial dermal infiltrate without epidermotropism, and he was treated with dupilumab for presumed adult-onset atopic dermatitis. His rash worsened after two injections, and a repeat biopsy demonstrated an atypical lymphocytic infiltrate consistent with cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. 

Laboratory evaluation revealed a white blood cell count of 25,000/µL. Peripheral blood flow cytometry showed 40% involvement by phenotypically abnormal CD3+ CD4(dim) CD7– CD26– T cells, with a CD4/CD8 ratio of 17.6, consistent with leukemic CTCL (ISCL Stage IVA, B2). He began extracorporeal photopheresis (2 consecutive days every 4 weeks) and oral bexarotene 225 mg daily. 

Shortly thereafter, he developed oral erosions with odynophagia. Viral PCR studies were negative, and he was started empirically on valacyclovir. 

One week later, he returned with fever (to 101.1°F), dozens of 1–2 cm tense bullae that rapidly progressed to widespread blistering with a positive Nikolsky sign, and denuded patches confined to his CTCL plaques. He also had worsening intranasal and oral erosions. Lesional PCR for HSV, VZV, and CMV were negative. 

A skin biopsy of a blistered plaque showed lichenoid inflammation with subepidermal clefting and an atypical lymphocytic infiltrate with focal epidermotropism.

A 10-year-old girl with no prior medical history presented with progressive left facial asymmetry over several months. On examination, there was a firm mass over the left temporomandibular area, marked lateral deviation of the mandible, and reduced mouth opening. Intraorally, the mucosa was intact but both the internal and external cortices of the left mandibular ramus were palpably bulging. There were no neurological deficits.

An orthopantomograph demonstrated a poorly defined, multilobulated radiolucent lesion involving the left mandibular ascending ramus and condyle. Subsequent CT imaging confirmed an expansile, multiseptated, osteolytic intraosseous lesion in the left condyle and ramus with cortical thinning and bulging but no soft-tissue invasion. Multiple vascular-appearing “lagoons” were noted within the lesion, prompting a provisional diagnosis of a suspected aneurysmal bone cyst.

A 68-year-old immunocompetent man with diabetes, morbid obesity, coronary artery disease, hypertension, and atrial fibrillation presented with several months of new-onset headache and tremor. On examination, he had a left homonymous hemianopsia. 

Noncontrast head CT showed a mass-like lesion in the right parietal–occipital region with extensive surrounding edema in the parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes, causing mass effect on the right occipital horn without midline shift. 

MRI of the brain with and without IV contrast revealed a 4.2 × 3.2 × 3.2 cm ring-enhancing mass in the right occipital lobe, with surrounding edema extending into the right parietal and temporal lobes and mass effect on the occipital horn, but no midline shift. The ADC map demonstrated a hypointense signal centrally, indicating low diffusivity. There were scattered findings of chronic small-vessel ischemic disease and a chronic cortical infarct in the right frontal lobe. 

Staging CT scans of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis and a bone marrow aspirate failed to identify a primary lesion or metastatic disease elsewhere. 

The imaging-based differential diagnosis included glioblastoma IDH-wild type, metastasis, abscess, and lymphoma. Ring enhancement in lymphoma is typically seen in immunocompromised patients. Neurosurgery was consulted for potential biopsy or resection.

A 47-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a soft-tissue growth on the palate. The lesion appeared suddenly and expanded rapidly over 2 months without initial pain; mild pain developed in the past week. On examination, there was a diffuse, proliferative soft-tissue mass on the hard palate, extending from the marginal gingiva of the anterior teeth to the hard–soft palate junction, with overlying erythema of attached gingiva on both palatal and buccal aspects. All anterior and posterior maxillary teeth exhibited Grade III mobility. Cervical lymph nodes were not palpable.

A panoramic radiograph demonstrated severe bone loss around all maxillary teeth consistent with generalized periodontitis, without other definitive findings. Cone-beam CT of the maxilla revealed a bilateral moth-eaten appearance of the palate, invasion of the nasopalatine canal, external resorption of all maxillary tooth roots, and extension into the anterior and middle ethmoidal sinus, right eustachian tube, and nasopharynx. Based on these findings, an intraosseous malignancy of the palate was suspected.

A 57-year-old woman was referred to the hematology clinic with anemia, fatigue, malaise, weight loss, night sweating, and abdominal fullness. She had no family history of cancer or known carcinogen exposure. Laboratory studies showed a white-blood-cell count above 90,000/μL, a platelet count above 550,000/μL, absolute neutrophilia, and normocytic anemia. Peripheral-blood flow cytometry demonstrated left-shifted neutrophils without blasts. Bone marrow biopsy was hypercellular for age with myeloid hyperplasia, rare erythroid dyspoiesis, and small hyperlobulated megakaryocytes; no increase in blasts was seen. Cytogenetic testing revealed der(22)t(9;22)(q34;q11.2) in all 20 metaphases, and FISH showed BCR::ABL1 fusion in 99.5% of interphase nuclei, establishing a diagnosis of chronic myelogenous leukemia.

Review of the record revealed that eight years earlier she had presented with anemia and mild cytopenia. Non-neoplastic causes of anemia and cytopenia were excluded. Bone marrow examination at that time was normocellular with no evidence of myeloid neoplasm or infiltration; differential counts showed no granulocytic increase and blasts and basophils were each <1%. Karyotype analysis and FISH then identified only an isolated del(20q) in all 20 metaphases. No treatment was given.

A 35-year-old man presented with a 6–7-month history of gradually enlarging swelling and mild intermittent pain over the right lower face. His medical history was unremarkable. On examination, there was a single, smooth, slightly tender, hard, fixed 7 × 5 cm swelling involving the right mandible. Intraorally, a firm-to-hard oval swelling (8 × 6 cm) extended from the right canine to the second molar, causing bucco-lingual cortical expansion; the overlying mucosa was intact but erythematous, and teeth remained stable. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated a well-demarcated mixed radiolucent-radiopaque lesion with a sclerotic border, cortical expansion and thinning, scattered calcifications, posterior displacement of the second molar, inferior displacement of an impacted third molar, root resorption of premolars and molars, and loss of the inferior alveolar canal. CT imaging showed a large expansile, well-circumscribed mass with both isodense and hypodense areas in the right mandibular body and ramus, bucco-lingual expansion, lingual cortical erosion, and patchy contrast enhancement.

A 52-year-old man presented with a large mass in the upper back. He reported that the lesion began as an “itchy bump” 9 years earlier and had approximately doubled in size each year. He sought care when the mass began bleeding and developing purulent discharge.  
On evaluation, vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies showed normocytic anemia with an RBC count of 3.29 M/μL (reference 4.7–6.1) and an MCV of 82.1 fL (80.0–94.0), consistent with anemia of chronic disease. The white-cell count was 14.5 × 10^3/μL (4.5–11.0) but normalized after a brief course of antibiotics.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a large, heterogeneously enhancing, partially calcified, centrally necrotic soft-tissue mass in the subcutaneous tissues of the thoracolumbar back region, located immediately deep to the skin without involvement of deeper musculature. A chest radiograph showed a double-density opacity overlying the cardiac silhouette on the PA view that was extrinsic to the bony thorax on the lateral view.

A 63-year-old Japanese woman presented with a 2-week history of fever. Initial chest CT showed multiple bilateral lung nodules. Blood cultures were negative, and echocardiography revealed no vegetations. Her soluble interleukin-2 receptor level was elevated at 673 U/mL, but bone marrow aspiration showed no abnormalities. Bronchoscopy with transbronchial lung biopsy was nondiagnostic; bronchoalveolar lavage fluid demonstrated lymphocytosis without malignant cells, and cultures were negative. She was treated with steroid pulse therapy and antibiotics for presumed organizing or bacterial pneumonia, but radiologic findings did not improve. Twenty-four days after symptom onset, she was referred for further evaluation. On admission, her temperature was 36.0 °C; respiratory rate, 18/min; and oxygen saturation, 94 % on 3 L/min nasal oxygen. Physical examination revealed mild conjunctival pallor and diminished breath sounds. Laboratory studies showed WBC 3560/μL, LDH 439 U/L, sIL-2R 1467 U/mL, and EBV DNA 7.0×10^4 copies/mL. Chest CT revealed multiple mass lesions with irregular margins, surrounding ground-glass opacities, small bilateral pleural effusions, and hepatosplenomegaly, without lymphadenopathy.

A 42-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of right hypochondrial pain associated with fever and vomiting. Vital signs were stable, and there was no jaundice. On examination, he had right upper-quadrant tenderness; the remainder of the abdominal and systemic examination was normal. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein; malaria smear, dengue IgM, and leptospirosis tests were negative. Liver function tests, including bilirubin, transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, and gamma-glutamyl transferase, were within normal limits. Serologic tests for hepatitis B and C were negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a distended gallbladder with hypodense calculi in the neck (largest 13 × 8 mm), gallbladder wall thickening of 7 mm, pericholecystic fluid, and adjacent fat stranding, consistent with acute calculous cholecystitis; the liver showed hepatomegaly with fatty changes. The patient was taken for laparoscopic cholecystectomy, during which the gallbladder contained frank pus. The liver surface was noted to be studded with multiple subcentimetric greyish-white lesions involving both lobes, and biopsy specimens of these lesions were obtained.

A 57-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of upper abdominal discomfort, nausea, fatigue, intermittent low-grade fever, and weight loss. Four months earlier, gastroscopy had revealed Helicobacter pylori infection, for which she received treatment. She had no other significant medical history. 

On examination, there was a large, tender epigastric mass with significant hepatomegaly; no splenomegaly or peripheral lymphadenopathy was noted. 

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, white-cell count 13.9×10^3/µL, aspartate aminotransferase 47 IU (normal <31), alanine aminotransferase 22 IU (normal <34), alkaline phosphatase 134 IU (normal <120), γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 147 IU (normal <38), and lactate dehydrogenase 555 IU (normal <247). Serologic tests for hepatitis B and C and for HIV were negative. Tumor markers revealed CA 19-9 58.1 IU/mL (normal <27), CA 15-3 31.5 IU/mL (normal <5), and CA 125 88.9 IU/mL (normal <35); α-fetoprotein and carcinoembryonic antigen were within normal limits. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 15×10×9 cm solid, heterogeneously enhancing mass occupying the left hepatic lobe and extending into the right lobe. MRI demonstrated a mass with low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, with heterogeneous internal characteristics. 

Our differential diagnosis included primary hepatocellular carcinoma, focal nodular hyperplasia, and metastasis from gastrointestinal cancer; gastrointestinal metastases were excluded by gastroscopy and colonoscopy.

A 13-year-old boy presented for routine dental examination. He was asymptomatic. Oral examination revealed retention of the maxillary right primary canine and failure of the permanent successor to erupt. A panoramic radiograph showed a unilocular radiolucent lesion surrounding the crown of the impacted permanent maxillary right canine, with a corticated border. The radiolucent space measured 5 mm on the distal aspect and 10 mm on the mesial aspect of the crown.

Because of the radiographic appearance, an excisional biopsy was performed under the presumption of a dentigerous cyst. Microscopic examination showed a fairly cellular fibrous connective tissue with collagen fibers arranged in interwoven bundles in some areas. Odontogenic epithelium appeared as strands and nests throughout the lesion. Calcifications of basophilic cementum-like material and dentinoid were present in some foci.

Since these microscopic findings overlapped among several pericoronal lesions, the diagnosis remained uncertain.

A three-year-old boy presented with a one-month history of left submandibular swelling and a one-day history of lower back and left leg pain. His mother reported fever, decreased urine output, and constipation, and he had received antibiotics from his pediatrician without improvement of the neck swelling. On examination, he was afebrile, with a firm 3 cm × 3 cm left submandibular mass. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 120 mm/h (normal 0–19 mm/h), C-reactive protein 0.665 mg/dL (normal 0–0.500 mg/dL), and hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL (normal 11.0–16.0 g/dL). Abdominal ultrasound revealed grade I left hydronephrosis. Ultrasound of the submandibular mass showed an intermediate echogenic lesion with prominent color Doppler flow. On hospital day 2, an excisional biopsy of the mass was performed. Histologic examination demonstrated small round blue cells with scant pink cytoplasm and focal neuropil structures. Immunohistochemical staining was diffusely positive for synaptophysin and ALK-1, negative for S-100, and Ki-67 exhibited a high proliferation index of 95%. Fluorescence in situ hybridization for N-MYC showed no amplification, and ALK mutation analysis was negative.

A 65-year-old man was evaluated for a recurrent nodule on his left ear. Three years earlier, a 6-mm papule on the superior helix was excised; biopsy had shown a spindle cell tumor with negative immunostaining for S-100, CD34, and MNF-116. One year later, a new 5-mm nodule at the same site was biopsied; again, the spindle cells were cytologically atypical, and immunostains for S-100, CD34, and MNF-116 were negative, leading to a diagnosis of recurrent atypical fibroxanthoma and a radical resection with 1-cm margins. The patient denied prior radiation, trauma to the head and neck, and exposure to arsenic, thorium dioxide, or vinyl chloride. 

On examination, there was a 2.0-×2.0-cm violaceous nodule on the superior helical rim of the left ear. A punch biopsy showed a poorly circumscribed dermal neoplasm of atypical, pleomorphic spindle cells dissecting collagen bundles. Immunostaining revealed strong positivity for erythroblast transformation-specific–related gene (ERG) and CD31, with negative staining for S-100, Melan-A, MNF-116, and CD34.

A 10-year-old Dusun girl with no prior medical or surgical history presented with a one-week history of dull, aching pain in the left hypochondrium and recent loss of appetite without significant weight loss. There was no history of trauma, haematuria, or relevant family history. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. Abdominal palpation revealed a non-tender, smooth, ballotable mass in the left hypochondrium extending into the left lumbar region. Initial blood tests showed a mildly elevated lactate dehydrogenase level and normal renal function; serum amylase and tumour markers (alpha fetoprotein and beta human chorionic gonadotropin) were unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a large heterogeneous solid-cystic mass in the left retroperitoneum and a solitary segment VI hypoechoic liver lesion; both kidneys appeared normal in size and echotexture.

A 54-year-old woman with spina bifida and congenital proximal femoral focal deficiency has been wheelchair-bound for 40 years. She had a chronic right buttock pressure ulcer, previously treated surgically with initial healing followed by recurrence. She self-managed the wound for the past 29 years without specialist care. Several months before presentation, she noted severe pain and progressive enlargement of the ulcer and sought help from community nurses.

On examination, the buttock and sacral wound measured 17 cm × 8 cm × 9 cm. The ulcer bed was 100% granulation tissue with rolled edges and surrounding chronic blanching purple skin changes. The wound edges showed excessive granulation, were nodular, fragile, and easily bled. There was no foul odor, sinus drainage, or other clinical signs of infection.

Magnetic resonance imaging was attempted but not tolerated, so computed tomography was performed. CT showed a large circumferential pressure ulcer on the right buttock with markedly hypertrophied, lobulated margins and extension to the posterior cortex of the proximal femur. Chronic periosteitis and cortical sclerosis were present, with new cortical erosions compared to prior imaging. A few enlarged regional lymph nodes were noted.

MRI findings of the ulcer margins demonstrated a 4-cm-thick mass-like appearance with low signal on T1-weighted images and high signal on T2-weighted and STIR images. The posterior femoral cortex showed mild subcortical edema at STIR but no marrow replacement on T1WI.

The imaging findings were not conclusive for osteomyelitis, but the unusual ulcer margins prompted referral for specialist opinion and incisional biopsy of the ulcer edge.

A 66-year-old G1P1 woman presented with intermittent postmenopausal spotting over the prior year and a sensation of anal pressure without other bowel symptoms. She had no personal or family history of malignancy. On examination she was overweight, with normal external genitalia and no signs of androgen excess; the uterus felt approximately 10-week size, there were no palpable adnexal masses, and she had focal right levator ani tenderness. 

Transvaginal ultrasonography showed a 10.8×6.9×6.2 cm uterus with two small fibroids and a 4.6×2.3×4.3 cm well-circumscribed heterogeneous intracavitary lesion. The left ovary was not visualized; the right ovary measured 1.7×1.2×1.7 cm. In-office endometrial biopsy revealed a benign polyp.

Two weeks later at hysteroscopy, new clitoromegaly (6×2 cm) was noted. No intracavitary mass was seen, and curettage again yielded benign polyp fragments. At the postoperative visit two weeks after that, the patient reported worsening discomfort from clitoromegaly. 

Laboratory evaluation showed a serum testosterone level of 945.2 ng/dL (normal 10.0–75.0), DHEA-S 61 mcg/dL (normal 9–118), hemoglobin 16.5 g/dL (11.3–15.0), and hematocrit 47.6% (33.6–44.6%). A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was unremarkable. Repeat transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a similar intracavitary lesion, a right ovary of 2.2×1.2×1.5 cm, and a left ovary of 3.8×1.6×2.2 cm containing a 1.8×1.7×1.4 cm hypoechoic cystic lesion.

A 63-year-old man presented with a 6-year history of left‐sided otalgia, progressive hearing loss, lower cranial nerve palsies, and recurrent bleeding from the left ear. On otoscopic examination, a reddish-blue mass was seen bulging behind the left tympanic membrane. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a large heterogeneous mass involving the left petrous temporal bone with bone destruction, extending medially into the left cerebellopontine angle cistern and inferiorly below the skull base. The lesion demonstrated heterogeneous signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images and strong homogeneous contrast enhancement. Computed tomography revealed extensive destruction of the posterior petrous bone and middle ear structures with involvement of the internal auditory canal. The preoperative diagnosis was a glomus jugulare tumor.

An 86-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of severe pain in the anterior aspect of her right thigh and an inability to walk. She had been febrile for 5 days before presentation. She denied trauma, radiculopathy, paresthesias, weakness, weight loss, abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting, nausea, urinary symptoms, alcohol use, or drug use.

On examination, the right lower limb was held in flexion and external rotation. There was a tender swelling measuring approximately 10 cm × 8 cm in the right flank, and a psoas sign was positive. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8 g/dL, white-cell count 28 000/µL with 85% neutrophils, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 140 mm/h. Plain radiographs of the pelvis, hip joints, right thigh, and lumbosacral spine were normal. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen revealed a right-sided iliopsoas abscess measuring 16 cm × 9 cm × 9 cm, extending from the L3 vertebral level to the proximal thigh.

A 79-year-old woman presented with a two-week history of left jaw pain and swelling accompanied by left facial weakness and droop. On examination, there was weakness of the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve and a diminished gag reflex. MRI of the head with intravenous contrast showed a 1.5 × 1.5 × 1.8 cm heterogeneous, low-intensity, peripherally enhancing lesion in the deep lobe of the left parotid gland abutting the posterior aspect of the left lateral pterygoid muscle and involving the facial nerve at the stylomastoid foramen. 

Given high suspicion for malignancy, the patient underwent a left total parotidectomy with facial nerve resection and reconstruction. Intraoperatively, the tumor was very firm, located deep within the gland, and extended into deep neck muscles without adherence to surrounding structures; margins were noted to be distorted. Five regional lymph nodes appeared benign.

Grossly, two nodules were submitted: one measured 2.5 cm with extensive calcification and hyalinization; the other measured 1.9 cm, surrounded nerve bundles, and showed focal necrosis. 

Microscopic examination revealed identifiable foci of pleomorphic adenoma, including benign glandular and tubular structures within a predominantly acellular hyalinized and focally calcified nodular area. There was also a spindle-cell proliferation with fascicular to storiform architecture, elongated cigar-shaped nuclei, increased mitotic activity including atypical mitoses, focal necrosis, and evidence of perineural and perivascular invasion extending into periparotid soft tissues and parotid parenchyma.

Immunohistochemical stains were variably positive for smooth muscle actin, smooth muscle myosin heavy chain, desmin, and calponin, and negative for pan-cytokeratin, S100 protein, CD34, and ALK1.

A 48-year-old man with a history of heavy smoking, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and polysubstance use presented with two weeks of worsening dyspnea and productive cough. On examination, he was in respiratory distress (respiratory rate 28/min), with diminished breath sounds bilaterally, crackles over the right middle zone, bilateral wheezes, and anterior central dullness on percussion; there were no signs of cor pulmonale or peripheral lymphadenopathy. He was treated as an acute COPD exacerbation.  

A chest radiograph showed a new large, multilobulated anterior mediastinal mass compared with imaging seven months earlier. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest confirmed a non-enhancing, smooth, lobulated mass centered in the anterior mediastinum, extending to the middle and posterior compartments, displacing and encasing the pulmonary arteries, aorta, and heart, with small pleural and pericardial effusions; no calcifications were noted.  

Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, anemia of chronic disease, elevated C-reactive protein, markedly elevated lactate dehydrogenase, and normal α-fetoprotein and β-human chorionic gonadotropin levels.  

An ultrasound-guided transthoracic core-needle biopsy was performed. Histologic examination (H&E) demonstrated sheets of relatively uniform epithelioid cells with irregular nuclei containing fine chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, and pale eosinophilic to clear cytoplasm. Tumor necrosis was prominent; rhabdoid features were absent.  

Immunohistochemistry showed:  
- Pan-cytokeratin (MNF116): negative  
- CAM5.2: focal staining in <5% of cells  
- EMA: positive  
- CD45: negative  
- SALL4: positive  
- CD117, PLAP, CD30, α-fetoprotein: negative  
- CD34: positive in majority of cells  
- HepPar1: patchy cytoplasmic staining in approximately 10% of cells  
- Claudin-4: negative  
- NUT: negative  
- SMARCB1 (INI1): retained expression

A 66-year-old African American woman with no known chronic illnesses presented with acute-onset altered mental status. The night before admission, after a two-mile walk, she was asymptomatic; the following morning she was found drowsy, confused (attempting to drink her hair), complaining of generalized weakness and right groin pain, then became progressively somnolent and unresponsive to verbal commands. In the emergency department, temperature reached 106°F, heart rate 145 bpm, respiratory rate 25/min, blood pressure was normal; she was responsive only to painful stimuli and had no meningeal signs. Examination revealed no organomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed:

• CBC: Hb 6.6 g/dL (MCV 91 fL), platelets 77,000/mm3, WBC 13,400/mm3 (ANC 11,800/mm3).  
• LDH 1248 U/L, reticulocyte count 3.5%, total bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL (indirect predominant), creatinine 1.2 mg/dL.  
• Normal vitamin B12, folate, PT, PTT, INR, and fibrinogen 402 mg/dL.  
• Iron studies: serum iron 6 µg/dL, TIBC 257 µg/dL, ferritin 378 ng/mL.  
• Urinalysis: microscopic hematuria and proteinuria (30 mg/dL).  
• HIV screen negative.  
• Peripheral smear: marked schistocytosis and dysplastic neutrophils.  
• Chest radiograph and head CT: unremarkable.

Given microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, altered mental status, fever, and renal involvement, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) was strongly considered; ADAMTS-13 activity was sent, and daily plasmapheresis with corticosteroids was initiated. Over the next 3 days, platelet count fell to 9,000/mm3, schistocytosis persisted, and ESR was 5 mm/hr. ADAMTS-13 activity returned at 52% (normal 68–163%) with a haptoglobin of 120 mg/dL (normal 14–250 mg/dL), and plasmapheresis was discontinued. Urine and blood cultures were negative; CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast and CT angiography of the lower extremities were unremarkable. Flow cytometry revealed no evidence of B-cell lymphoma, T-cell lymphoma, acute leukemia, or increased blasts.

A 17-year-old male presented with a slowly enlarging swelling over the volar aspect of his left hand. The lesion began as a peanut-sized nodule and progressively involved the palm—from the distal forearm at the wrist to the thenar eminence and the bases of the second, third, and fourth digits—over an unspecified period. He reported periodic episodes of tingling and paresthesia in those same fingers. There was no history of trauma. On examination, there was an irregular fusiform swelling extending from the ulnar aspect of the left wrist to the thenar eminence and base of the second through fourth digits. The consistency was softer over the ulnar side and firmer over the third and fourth metacarpals. The overlying skin was pinchable and nonadherent. Neurologic examination revealed no motor weakness or sensory loss. Wrist motion demonstrated terminal restriction of palmar and dorsiflexion. No other lesions were present.

Noncontrast MRI of the left hand showed gross thickening of the median nerve. There was diffuse lipomatous tissue—hyperintense on T1- and T2-weighted sequences and hypointense on SPAIR—interdigitating between prominent thickened nerve fascicles (hypointense on T1 and T2) in a coaxial cable–like pattern. This involvement extended from the distal forearm through the distal metacarpal regions of the second to fourth digits, with compression and displacement of flexor tendons and convex deformation of the carpal tunnel retinacular sheath. Lipomatous tissue tracked into the second and third intermetacarpal spaces. There were no focal osseous lesions, and the tendons appeared normal in signal intensity.

A 32-year-old woman presented with gradual onset of a painful swelling in the lower third of the left side of her face. Extraoral examination showed a dome-shaped tender swelling with normal overlying skin; the patient reported spontaneous pain and hypoesthesia of the left lower lip and chin. Her medical history included a renal infection and urethral prolapse; she took folic acid and had a family history of similar jaw lesions. Intraoral examination revealed a firm lesion in the left mandibular buccal and lingual vestibules, extending from the first premolar to the third molar; the mucosa was normal, aspiration was negative, and there was severe mobility of the second premolar and the first and second molars. Panoramic radiography demonstrated a well-defined, unilocular radiolucency in the left mandibular body, extending from the apex of the first premolar to the upper third of the ramus and from the alveolar crest to the inferior border, with marked expansion, knife-edge root resorption of the first and second molars, and thinning of the alveolar crest and inferior border. Cone-beam computed tomography confirmed severe buccal and moderate lingual cortical expansion, with lesion dimensions of 37.2 mm (labiolingual), 42.9 mm (superoinferior), and 63.8 mm (anteroposterior); small calcification foci were noted within the radiolucency. According to the radiographic findings, the list of differential diagnoses included ossifying fibroma, central giant cell granuloma, and aneurysmal bone cyst.

A 64-year-old woman was admitted with several months of abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, weight loss, and intermittent nausea and vomiting treated empirically as gastritis. Seven years earlier, she had a 32 mm grade 1 infiltrating lobular breast carcinoma (T2 N0 M0, ER positive, PR negative) treated with lumpectomy, axillary node clearance, radiotherapy, and five years of tamoxifen, with no evidence of recurrence on follow-up. She takes no medications, does not smoke, and has no family history of breast or gastrointestinal malignancy. On examination, she had pale sclera and mild lower abdominal tenderness without rebound; bowel sounds were present. Rectal examination was normal, but fecal occult blood testing was positive. Laboratory studies showed a normocytic, normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, MCV 88 fL, MCH 29 pg) and a white-cell count of 11,000 × 10^9/L. Upper endoscopy revealed nodular thickening of the gastric antrum and proximal duodenum. Colonoscopy showed nodular thickening at the hepatic flexure. Biopsy specimens demonstrated infiltrating adenocarcinoma with signet ring cell morphology suspicious for a primary gastric tumor.

A 45-year-old man presented with more than 10 years of chronic, recurrent diarrhea and a 4-year history of an anal fistula. Six years earlier, he had been diagnosed with inflammatory bowel disease and specifically Crohn’s disease after multiple relapses and had received 5-aminosalicylic acid, corticosteroids, azathioprine, and twice-administered infliximab, with poor response and development of systemic edema. He was admitted for worsening diarrhea.

He denied smoking, alcohol use, and a family history of gastrointestinal disease. On examination, he had mild bilateral lower-extremity edema; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory testing showed hemoglobin 78 g/L (normal 130–175), normal leukocyte and platelet counts, C-reactive protein 25.4 mg/L (normal 0–8), total protein 57.4 g/L (normal 65–85), albumin 17.5 g/L (normal 40–55), fecal calprotectin >1662 µg/g (normal 0–200), and serum EBV viral load 5.81 × 10^4 copies/mL (normal 0–5 × 10^3). Tests for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, stool cultures, and tumor markers were negative.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the small intestine demonstrated segmental thickening of loops, abnormal enhancement, and enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes. Ultrasound confirmed multiple enlarged mesenteric nodes (largest 3.2 × 1.3 cm). A biopsy of an enlarged lymph node showed loss of normal architecture with diffuse proliferation of atypical cells. Immunohistochemistry was positive for CD3, CD5, CD20, CD23, CD35, CD43, CD138, CD163, Bcl-2, and Ki-67 (15%), and negative for CD10, Bcl-6, CyclinD1, and CMV.

Colonoscopy revealed congested, edematous mucosa with multiple ulcers throughout the ileum and colon, including two large ulcers in the distal ileum and sigmoid colon. Gastroscopy showed chronic atrophic gastritis.

A 30-year-old man presented with an 18-month history of right elbow pain, swelling, and stiffness. He noted partial relief with nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs and had been treated with disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs. There was no fever, nocturnal pain, history of trauma, or involvement of other joints. On examination, moderate joint effusion was present, flexion–extension ranged from 20° to 110°, pronation–supination was normal, and the elbow was stable. Plain radiographs of the elbow were unremarkable. Inflammatory markers were within normal limits. Synovial fluid analysis revealed nonspecific inflammation and sterile cultures. Computed tomography of the elbow demonstrated a 5 mm well-defined lucent nidus with a central sclerotic focus breaching the articular margins of the trochlear notch, with minimal surrounding sclerosis, periosteal reaction, and adjacent soft-tissue edema. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a hypointense central nidus on both T1- and T2-weighted sequences with minimal peripheral T2 hyperintensity and surrounding sclerosis, as well as bone marrow edema of the proximal ulna, small joint effusion, and synovial proliferation.

A 34-year-old woman with a history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hypothyroidism, arthritis, chronic renal impairment, and hepatitis C presented with intermittent, sharp left upper quadrant abdominal pain of one month’s duration that radiated to her back and affected her daily activities. She also reported weight loss without bleeding, constipation, loss of appetite, or night sweats. On examination, her vital signs were stable, and deep palpation elicited tenderness in the left upper quadrant. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10 g/dL, normal white-cell and platelet counts, creatinine 4.05 mg/L, and urea 21.5 mmol/L. Esophagogastroscopy was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT scans of the abdomen and chest, performed after nephrology clearance, showed a normal-sized spleen containing multiple, well-defined, hypodense cystic lesions, the largest measuring 2.5 × 2.5 cm, with no contrast enhancement or solid components. The liver had fatty changes, and the lungs showed interstitial pneumonitis. No lymphadenopathy was identified. A follow-up ultrasound and repeat CT scan one month later showed stable lesions in the spleen.

An 18-year-old female presented with a 4-month history of headache and dizziness and a 3-day history of lethargy and vomiting. On neurologic examination, she had papilledema, impaired tandem gait, and right-sided dysmetria. Noncontrast head CT demonstrated a posterior fossa mass with coarse calcifications, a cystic component, and hydrocephalus. Brain MRI showed a fourth-ventricular mass with both solid and cystic components that were heterogenous and hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and exhibited heterogenous enhancement after gadolinium administration. Diffusion-weighted imaging revealed no significant restricted diffusion, and susceptibility-weighted imaging demonstrated areas of susceptibility effects corresponding to calcification and some hemorrhage. Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery images showed heterogeneous signal intensity in the lesion with adjacent small edema in the cerebellum.

A 41-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of a painful, enlarging papule beneath the nail of the right fourth finger. On examination, there was a 6 mm skin-colored, smooth, tender subungual papule elevating the central nail plate. A shave biopsy of the exophytic portion encountered a firm structure. Histopathology revealed deposits of bony elements within the dermis, but the specimen was transected at its base, precluding a definitive diagnosis. A radiograph of the distal phalanx showed a 2 mm peripherally calcified low-density lesion overlying the dorsal tuft, with an intact distal phalanx cortex. These imaging findings were interpreted as inconsistent with subungual exostosis and raised the possibility of a calcified epidermal inclusion cyst. Subsequent high-frequency ultrasound of the nail unit demonstrated a hypoechoic nail bed containing multiple small round hyperechoic foci, an intact phalangeal cortex, and no hypervascularity on Doppler assessment.

A 25-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of right shoulder discomfort related to a dorsal scapular mass. He described pain when lying on his back, which sometimes disturbed his sleep, and mild weakness when using his right arm below shoulder level. His history was notable for a solitary kidney and nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma treated with chemotherapy and mantle-field radiotherapy 12 years earlier, with no recurrence.

On examination, there was a nonmobile, hard, tender mass measuring approximately 3 cm transversely by 3 cm anteroposteriorly by 2 cm craniocaudally at the posterior superomedial angle of the right scapula. Muscle bulk was symmetrical. The right shoulder had a full range of motion, but there was pain and weakness with active elevation and abduction. 

A shoulder radiograph (AP, lateral, and Neer views) was reported as normal. A thoracic CT scan demonstrated a 2.6 cm × 2.6 cm × 2.2 cm solid, well‐defined bony mass on the posterior aspect of the superomedial angle of the scapula, without cortical destruction or adjacent soft-tissue mass. 

MRI of the right shoulder showed that the lesion’s medullary cavity was continuous with that of the scapula, the cartilage cap was thin, and there were no features suggestive of malignancy; the spinal accessory nerve was compressed between the lesion and the deep layer of the trapezius, but there was no muscle atrophy.

A 64-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of constant left flank pain, dysuria, testicular discomfort on the left side, and generalized fatigue. He also noted obstructive lower urinary tract symptoms. His medical history included hypertension, diabetes mellitus, sinus tachycardia, and hemorrhoids; he was taking tamsulosin. On examination, a palpable mass was noted in the left flank. 

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count except for monocytes of 11.6% (reference range 3–8%), hemoglobin A1c of 6.9%, estimated average glucose of 151 mg/dL, fasting glucose 113 mg/dL, and a quantitative C-reactive protein of 10 mg/L (normal <6 mg/L). Urinalysis was unremarkable except for mucus; serum creatinine and urea were within normal limits. 

Renal ultrasound demonstrated an echogenic structure with thick, reactive walls and a murky fluid core near the lower pole of the left kidney. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 9 × 12 cm heterogeneous mass with blurred borders in the left kidney, multiple retroperitoneal lymph nodes measuring 10–25 mm, and possible invasion of Gerota’s fascia. CT scans of the chest and neck were normal, and bone marrow biopsy showed no abnormalities. The imaging was highly suggestive of renal cell carcinoma.

A 42-year-old woman was admitted with a 4-month history of weakness, pain, and numbness in all extremities and a 10-year history of persistent neck pain. The neck pain began after a fall that resulted in head trauma and was located suboccipitally, radiating to the right retroauricular region; it had been present without diagnosis despite various treatments and worsened gradually. On examination, she had spastic quadriparesis (3/5 strength), hypoesthesia below the C2 level, hyperactive deep tendon reflexes, ankle and knee clonus, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Her Japan Orthopedic Association (JOA) myelopathy score was 10 of 18. A lateral cervical radiograph showed a hypertrophic lesion in the posterior arch of C1. CT demonstrated a bony outgrowth from the right anterior aspect of the C1 posterior arch. MRI confirmed a homogeneous, irregularly contoured bony mass compressing the spinal cord with increased intramedullary signal consistent with myelopathy; adjacent structures appeared normal. A skeletal survey revealed no other lesions.

A 69-year-old Japanese man presented with pain and a 10-mm polypoid mass on the left lower gingiva. He had undergone chemoradiotherapy 15 years earlier for squamous cell carcinoma of the left buccal mucosa, with no recurrence until now. He denied tobacco or alcohol use. On examination, vital signs were normal; trismus was present. Intraoral inspection revealed a rough-surfaced polypoid lesion in the left lower molar gingiva covered by a whitish pseudomembrane. Panoramic radiography showed a moth-eaten pattern of mandibular bone resorption. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated an enhancing soft-tissue mass with irregular mandibular bone destruction. A biopsy specimen showed loose granulation tissue with scattered atypical spindle and pleomorphic cells in a fibrin-rich edematous stroma alongside inflammatory cells. The overlying squamous epithelium exhibited only slight nuclear enlargement without dysplasia. The spindle cells had basophilic cytoplasm, bizarre nuclei, and atypical mitoses; many contained neutrophils within cytoplasmic vacuoles. Immunohistochemical staining revealed that the spindle cells were positive for vimentin, α-smooth muscle actin, p63, p53, and CD68, but negative for pan-cytokeratin and other epithelial markers; Ki-67 labeling index was approximately 50%. These findings prompted consideration of a malignant spindle cell process.

A man in his early 70s with a 63 pack-year smoking history presented with a two-week history of persistent bloody sputum progressing to haemoptysis. Initial evaluation by an otolaryngologist nine days after onset was unremarkable. He was treated for presumed pneumonia by an outside physician but continued to worsen and was referred to our hospital 14 days after symptom onset. On presentation, temperature was 36.4°C, blood pressure 123/71 mmHg, pulse 71 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Physical examination was notable only for decreased breath sounds over the right lung. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL and C-reactive protein 10.75 mg/dL; tumor markers were within normal limits. Chest CT demonstrated widespread ground-glass opacity with interlobular septal thickening in the right lower lobe, two marginal irregular masses in right S9 (15 mm) and S10 (33 mm), a cavity-like lesion containing material in the right basal area, patchy ground-glass opacities in the left lung, and mildly enlarged hilar and subtracheal lymph nodes. He was diagnosed with pneumonia and airway hemorrhage and received haemostatic therapy and antibiotics. Bronchoscopy showed blood throughout the tracheobronchial tree, especially in right B10, but no endobronchial tumors or vascular lesions; bronchial washings were negative on cytological and bacterial studies. Despite broad antibacterial and antifungal therapy and supportive transfusions, his condition did not improve. Eighteen days after admission, repeat CT showed regression of ground-glass opacities but enlargement of the right S9 and S10 masses with denser consolidation, volume loss, a new pleural effusion, suspected pleural seeding nodules, and further mediastinal lymph node enlargement. A systemic CT survey revealed no distant metastases.

A 6-month-old female infant was brought by her family after her grandmother noted a palpable, left-sided solid abdominal wall mass. There was no history of trauma, fever, or family history of similar conditions. The patient was born at 39 weeks’ gestation with a birth weight of 3.2 kg after an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery; prenatal ultrasounds were normal and she was otherwise healthy.

An outpatient ultrasound showed a well-defined, heterogeneous, hypoechoic mass measuring approximately 3.7 × 3.5 cm; it was unclear whether the lesion arose from the abdominal wall or intra-abdominally, but it was separate from the left kidney and spleen. Color Doppler imaging demonstrated detectable peripheral arterial vascularity; venous flow within the mass was not well assessed. The patient was referred for further evaluation.

On presentation, vital signs were normal, and physical examination was notable only for the firm mass in the left lateral abdominal wall. Laboratory studies revealed an elevated activated partial thromboplastin time of 58.5 s (normal, 30–40 s), a low mean corpuscular volume of 72.2 fL (normal, 80–95 fL), and a reversed neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (neutrophils 23.4% [normal, 55–70%]; lymphocytes 63.6% [normal, 20–40%]); all other values were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 4.3 × 4 × 4 cm round, heterogeneous mass in the left lateral abdominal wall with internal calcifications; there was significant peripheral enhancement in the arterial phase with centripetal filling in the delayed phase. Multiple feeding vessels arose from the left inferior epigastric artery, internal and external iliac arteries, and a descending vessel from the left lateral chest wall. The differential diagnosis at this stage included rhabdomyosarcoma, fibromatosis, hemangioma, and lymphatic malformation.

Subsequent coronal T2-weighted MRI confirmed a heterointense mass in the left lateral abdominal wall with peripheral enhancement consistent with a vascular malformation. The liver, spleen, and both kidneys appeared normal on imaging.

A 35-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of a gradually enlarging, painless swelling on the anterior hard palate with associated displacement of the maxillary central incisors. He denied trauma. On examination, there was a well-defined, firm, nontender swelling on the left side of the anterior hard palate that crossed the midline. The crown of the left central incisor was displaced labially and mesially, overlapping the right central incisor. Vitality tests of both central incisors were negative.  
Panoramic occlusal radiography revealed a well-defined, round radiolucency approximately 2.5 cm in diameter with corticated margins in the midline between the central incisors; the lesion displaced the incisor roots and extended superiorly to the floor of the nasal fossa, with deviation of the nasal septum to the right.  
CT imaging demonstrated a 2.6 × 2.8 cm well-defined radiolucency in the region of the incisive canal, displacing the central incisor roots without lateral extension beyond the roots, reaching inferiorly to the crest of interdental bone, with loss of corticulation buccally and palatally, mild elevation of the nasal fossa floor anteriorly, and rightward deviation of the nasal septum. A mucosal polyp was noted on the floor of the left maxillary sinus.  
Initial differential diagnoses included periapical (radicular) cyst, nasopalatine duct cyst, enlarged nasopalatine duct, central giant cell granuloma, root cyst of the upper centrals, supernumerary tooth follicular cyst, primordial cyst, and nasoalveolar cyst.

A 65‐year‐old woman presented with right lower abdominal pain of mild to moderate intensity for 1 hour following blunt trauma. Her vital signs were stable, and abdominal examination revealed mild tenderness on deep palpation. Extended Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma (EFAST) showed minimal free fluid in the pelvis and cholelithiasis. 

Because of persistent aching pain, contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen was obtained. No solid‐organ or bowel injuries were seen. However, a 10 × 7 mm hypodense lesion (−41 HU) was identified at the junction of the pancreatic head and uncinate process. Additionally, there was a 5.4 × 1.8 cm hypodense lesion (−44 HU) within the left proximal sartorius muscle. 

MRI of the upper abdomen with MRCP was performed due to obscured visualization of the common bile duct on ultrasound. It demonstrated a T2‐hyperintense focus in the proximal pancreatic head that showed signal loss on fat-saturated sequences; the common bile duct was of normal caliber without stones.

A 2-year-old boy, previously healthy with no birth defects or family history of tumors, was brought for evaluation of a left shoulder swelling first noted by his mother 2 weeks earlier. He met developmental milestones and had normal immunizations. On examination he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. There was a firm, approximately 2 cm mass in the left shoulder region, which had been increasing in size; it was non-tender, without warmth, erythema, or skin discoloration. Laboratory studies, including inflammatory markers, were within normal limits. Ultrasound showed a 2.3 cm heterogeneous intramuscular lesion with central vascularity. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the left shoulder revealed an intramuscular, lobulated mass arising from the posteroinferior deltoid fibers, containing thin internal septations and areas of fat signal intensity. Two small axillary lymph nodes (6×3 mm and 8×4 mm) were noted. The lesion was separable from the axillary nerve and circumflex arteries.

A 10-year-old boy presented with a painless swelling below the tongue of 5 months’ duration. He reported no significant change in the size of the lesion. On examination, there was a single firm, nontender, pedunculated nodule measuring approximately 9 mm on the lingual aspect of the mandibular gingiva adjacent to teeth 41, 42, 83, and 84. Radiographs showed no evidence of bony involvement. Based on the clinical presentation, the initial differential diagnosis included fibrous hyperplasia and fibroma. An excisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia, and the specimen was submitted for histopathological analysis.

A 25-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of an asymptomatic left-sided neck mass. On physical examination, two painless masses measuring 2.5 × 1.0 mm and 1.0 × 1.0 mm were palpable in the left lower neck. Ultrasound revealed a 28 × 19 × 8 mm cystic structure contiguous with the left thyroid lobe and a separate thyroid nodule. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the cyst revealed squamous epithelial cells suggestive of a branchial cyst, and biopsy of the thyroid nodule was suggestive of hyperplasia or adenoma. Thyroid function tests, including triiodothyronine, thyroxine, and thyroid-stimulating hormone, were within normal limits. One year later, ultrasonography showed growth of the cystic lesion to 35 × 26 × 16 mm. Laboratory evaluation at that time revealed a serum ionic calcium concentration of 1.25 mg/dl (reference range, 1.16–1.32 mmol/l), a parathyroid hormone level of 35 pg/ml (11–67 pg/ml), a thyroid-stimulating hormone level of 1.21 mIU/ml (0.4–4.0 mIU/ml), and a free T4 level of 0.95 ng/dl (0.8–1.9 ng/ml).

A 48-year-old woman with no significant past medical history noted a mass on the anterior proximal aspect of her right thigh that had grown over the previous five months. On examination, the lesion was mobile, firm, and measured approximately 10 × 4 cm. Examination of the hip joint was unremarkable and there were no systemic symptoms.

Plain radiographs of the right hip region showed thickening of the soft tissues with scattered calcifications. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-circumscribed, 11 × 4 cm mass in the upper anterior compartment of the thigh that was not attached to adjacent bone structures. The mass was hyperintense on T1-weighted images, hypointense on T2-weighted images, and demonstrated no enhancement after gadolinium administration. Based on these imaging features, a diagnosis of lipoma was rendered, and surgical excision was planned.

A 55-year-old North African woman with no comorbidities underwent treatment eight months previously for FIGO stage IIb squamous cell carcinoma of the uterine cervix (pelvic radiotherapy 46 Gy with cisplatin and high-dose-rate intracavitary brachytherapy), achieving clinical and radiographic remission. She now reports a painful 2 cm hard nodule in the left breast and left upper-quadrant abdominal pain.  
On examination, vital signs were normal. The left breast showed a firm 2 cm mass in the upper-inner quadrant without skin changes or axillary lymphadenopathy.  
Mammography revealed two suspicious lesions in the same quadrant (BI-RADS IV). Excisional biopsy demonstrated a poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma with estrogen receptor negative, progesterone receptor 1% status.  
Pelvic examination under anesthesia revealed no recurrence. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, pelvis, and brain showed a solitary 100 mm hypodense lesion in the spleen and no lymphadenopathy or other visceral lesions.

A 56-year-old Saudi man presented during a routine follow-up with a 3-month history of neck swelling and hoarseness that had rapidly increased in size over the past week, causing dyspnea and dysphagia to solids. Five years earlier, he had undergone a left radical nephrectomy for papillary renal cell carcinoma (pathologic stage pT2N0 M0, Fuhrman grade II). He had no other medical conditions, did not smoke, and had stable weight. On examination, there was a hard, fixed mass in the thyroid region; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Computed tomography of the neck showed an 8.0 × 7.5 cm vascularly enhancing mass in the right thyroid lobe, with no cervical lymphadenopathy and a clear postoperative renal bed. A bone scan and CT of the chest revealed no other metastatic lesions.

A woman in her late 20s noted a pea-sized right vulval mass at the end of her second trimester. On examination 8 weeks postpartum, there was a soft 3 cm mass at the 7–8 o’clock position in the right posterior labia majora near the site of the Bartholin’s gland; an attempted drainage at delivery was unsuccessful. Her history was notable for genital warts and a prior low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion on Pap smear; there was no other significant medical or family history. Under anaesthesia, the lesion was excised. 

Gross examination revealed a soft, solid cream-coloured mass in the dermis with a normal overlying epidermis. On microscopy, there was a well-demarcated spindle cell tumour beneath a grenz zone. The tumour showed a rim of lymphocytes and eosinophils, with the same inflammatory cells around intratumoural blood vessels. The neoplasm was composed of bland spindle cells with short, wavy nuclei set in a hyalinised to oedematous stroma; small blood vessels were scattered throughout. No infiltration of the adjacent dermis, cytologic atypia, or mitotic figures were observed.

A 23-year-old healthy primigravida underwent routine transabdominal ultrasound at 30 weeks of gestation, which demonstrated a left orbital cystic mass measuring 36 × 33 × 18 mm. A follow-up ultrasound at 34 weeks showed a stable lesion. She underwent an uncomplicated cesarean delivery at 38 weeks. On day 1 after birth, magnetic resonance imaging of the orbits revealed a 3.4 × 2.7 × 2.1 cm lesion with intraconal and extraconal components and a possible decreased caliber of the left optic nerve, most suspicious for a lymphatic lesion. At 1 week of age, examination under anesthesia disclosed severe left-sided exophthalmos with inability to close the eye. Slit-lamp examination showed significant conjunctival injection and diffuse punctate epithelial erosions of the left cornea. The anterior chamber was slightly shallow, the lens appeared clear, and dilated fundus examination revealed a small optic-nerve cup-to-disc ratio without edema or pallor.

A 45-year-old woman presented with a 9-month history of left upper-quadrant abdominal pain, unintended weight loss, and intermittent fevers. On examination she was afebrile with stable vital signs. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 10,000/mL with 70% segmented neutrophils, a C-reactive protein level of 109 mg/L, fibrinogen of 5.11 g/L, a normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and a hemoglobin level of 9 g/dL. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a well-circumscribed, hypoechoic splenic mass without detectable vascular flow on Doppler imaging. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen identified a 6.5 cm × 7 cm mass at the superior pole of the spleen with heterogeneous enhancement in the portal venous phase; the mass abutted the posterior wall of the stomach and the upper pole of the left kidney without radiologic evidence of invasion. On the basis of this appearance, a sarcomatous origin was evoked.

An 82-year-old man with chronic lymphocytic leukemia and a history of multiple squamous cell and basal cell carcinomas on sun-exposed skin presented with 2 months of a tender, erythematous, hyperkeratotic nodule on the left central frontal scalp, measuring 1.7 cm in diameter. A shave biopsy showed a dermis-based proliferation of spindle and epithelioid cells arranged in sheets and fascicles, with scattered multinucleated giant cells, cytoplasmic vacuolization, marked nuclear pleomorphism, prominent nucleoli, and scattered mitoses. There was no focal necrosis, lymphovascular invasion, or perineural invasion. Immunohistochemical staining of the neoplastic cells was negative for keratin, S100 protein, Melan-A, and desmin, and showed prominent CD68 positivity. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of atypical fibroxanthoma extending to the deep margin was made. The patient underwent Mohs micrographic surgery, achieving clear margins after two stages, without subcutaneous involvement of tumor.

A 17-year-old male presented with a 1-week history of acute onset abdominal pain. He had undergone a previous laparotomy for acute abdomen, though no records were available. Family history was notable for his mother and sister having pigmented macules on the lips, but no abdominal complaints. On examination, multiple hyperpigmented macules were present on the lips, palms, and soles. Abdominal examination revealed diffuse tenderness without palpable masses or organomegaly. An emergency ultrasound demonstrated a large mass in the periumbilical region. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a heterogeneous, peripherally enhancing mass in the mesentery just above the renal hilum that was inseparable from jejunal loops and abutting the superior mesenteric artery with preserved fat plane; the lesion was presumed malignant based on heterogeneous enhancement and infiltration of adjacent jejunum and mesentery. The study also revealed two sites of colonic telescoping: the descending colon into the sigmoid colon and the cecum into the ascending colon, each with a large enhancing polypoid mass at its lead point. Additional intraluminal enhancing polyps were seen in the stomach, jejunum, and colon. 

Subsequent upper endoscopy confirmed multiple polyps in the stomach and duodenum.

A 30-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of a right parietal region mass that began enlarging after her pregnancy in 2010. She denied trauma, pain, seizures, visual symptoms, or motor or coordination deficits, but reported altered sensation over the lesion. Her past history included surgically repaired pulmonary artery stenosis and medically managed irritable bowel syndrome. She did not use tobacco, alcohol, illicit drugs, or hormonal contraception.

On examination, she was well-nourished and in no distress. Cranial nerves were intact without visual field deficits or papilledema. Strength, reflexes, coordination, and gait were all normal. Sensation was intact except for mild hypesthesia over the right parietal region.

Noncontrast CT of the head showed a 6.4 × 6.4 × 4.0 cm right parietal calvarial mass expanding the diploic space with mass effect on the underlying parietal lobe but no evidence of cortical destruction. MRI revealed a lesion centered in the right parietal bone, extending into the extra-axial space over the right posterior-frontal and parietal lobes, causing cerebral compression. The mass was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2, did not enhance with gadolinium, and there was no parenchymal edema or other lesions identified.

A 45-year-old previously healthy Middle Eastern woman presented with a 4-month history of intermittent, ill-defined abdominal pain rated 6/10, unrelated to meals or specific aggravating factors and mildly relieved by analgesics. She also experienced intermittent nonbilious vomiting without blood, pus, or mucus. She denied fever, weight change, genitourinary symptoms, trauma, infections, or prior radiotherapy or chemotherapy. Her only surgical history was five cesarean deliveries. Family, drug, allergic, and psychosocial histories were unremarkable. Her BMI was 26 kg/m2.

On examination, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Abdominal palpation was nontender, and no masses or lymphadenopathy were noted. Laboratory studies were within normal limits.

Abdominal ultrasonography revealed an anechoic cystic formation with well-defined borders measuring 8.5 × 5.2 cm between the right kidney and the liver; the remainder of the study was normal. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a well-demarcated, isointense cystic lesion approximately 4 × 3.5 cm that appeared to be attached to the right adrenal gland, with no lymphadenopathy and otherwise normal abdominal organs.

Fine-needle biopsy or aspiration was deemed unfeasible owing to the highly cystic nature of the lesion. Preoperative differential diagnoses included a renal cyst, adrenal mass, pancreatic pseudocyst, abscess, ovarian cyst, and cystic teratoma.

A 50-year-old man was admitted with sudden onset of severe, ongoing haematochezia. He denied haematemesis, had no history of anaemia or previous surgery, and no family history of haematologic disorders. On examination, temperature was 36.4 °C, pulse 92 bpm, blood pressure 108/67 mmHg, and respiratory rate 19/min. He appeared pale; his abdomen was soft, non-tender, with active bowel sounds. Laboratory studies revealed haemoglobin 52 g/L (normal 120–175 g/L) and albumin 28 g/L (normal 40–55 g/L).  
Noncontrast abdominal CT showed thickening of the fourth portion of the duodenal wall with luminal narrowing. Upper GI endoscopy revealed a dark-red, submucosal mass filling the fourth duodenal segment, with oedematous raised margins, a central variceal-like area, and active spontaneous bleeding; biopsies were deferred due to bleeding risk. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a hypervascular duodenal lesion with peripheral, progressive, discontinuous arterial-phase enhancement, homogeneous portal-phase uptake, and central low-density areas on delayed imaging. No extramural extension or enlarged lymph nodes were seen, and CT angiography showed no large feeding vessels.

A 65-year-old man presented with a 9-month history of gradually progressive intermittent dysphagia and significant weight loss but no hematemesis or melena. His medical history was unremarkable, and physical examination was normal.

A barium oesophagogram showed dilation of the entire oesophagus, multiple air bubbles with a mottled appearance, and contrast-filling defects extending from the cervical oesophagus to the upper body of the stomach. 

Computed tomography of the chest revealed a relatively smooth, sausage-shaped intraluminal mass with a bulbous distal tip, extending from the cervical oesophagus to the upper body of the stomach, and containing soft-tissue densities with a central area of fat attenuation.

Endoscopy demonstrated a smooth submucosal mass occluding the oesophageal lumen. Endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration yielded benign fibro-fatty elements on cytological examination.

A 78-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of progressive hoarseness. Her medical history was notable only for hypertension managed with medication. Flexible laryngoscopy revealed a 1.0 × 0.8 cm round, polypoid mass on the posterior wall of the subglottic region, obstructing approximately 80 percent of the tracheal lumen. Neck computed tomography showed a well-circumscribed 1.0 × 0.8 cm polypoid lesion at the posterior subglottic wall without involvement of the vocal cords.

A 65-year-old man presented with one week of hematemesis and intermittent melena, associated with decreased appetite, dizziness, and exertional dyspnea. He had an episode of syncope the day before admission. One week prior, he was diagnosed with diverticulitis and was on cephalexin and metronidazole; he also had been taking ibuprofen up to 800 mg daily. He denied weight loss, fevers, chills, or other bleeding sites. His medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, cholelithiasis, and an abdominal aortic aneurysm. He was a former heavy smoker, drank alcohol socially, and took simvastatin. 

On arrival, hemodynamics were stable. Nasogastric lavage yielded coffee-ground material. Physical examination was unremarkable except for mildly hyperactive bowel sounds and positive fecal occult blood. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL and normal metabolic panel. He was kept NPO, given IV fluids and a proton-pump inhibitor, and ibuprofen was discontinued. Overnight, melena recurred, and his hemoglobin dropped, requiring transfusion.

A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis, performed earlier at another hospital, revealed a polypoid mass arising from the gastric antrum without other intra-abdominal lesions. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy demonstrated a partially obstructing, ulcerated, polypoid mass in the gastric body. Mild antral gastritis was noted without active bleeding. Biopsies were obtained. 

Initial differential diagnosis: gastric lipoma, gastric carcinoma, gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST).

A 73-year-old African-American woman, gravida 4 para 4, presented with a three-week history of postmenopausal vaginal bleeding, associated suprapubic pain, and urinary retention for the past two days. On pelvic examination, there was a 5-cm fungating mass on the left vaginal wall extending to the bladder trigone; the cervix was closed, there was no cervical motion tenderness, and no palpable adnexal masses. Abdominal examination revealed suprapubic tenderness without palpable mass. 

Pelvic and transvaginal sonography showed a thickened complex endometrial echo of 2.4 cm; the uterus measured 9.7 × 6.2 × 5.4 cm, and both ovaries were normal in size. Contrast-enhanced CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated a heterogeneous vaginal lesion and two hepatic masses measuring 7.7 cm and 3.4 cm. CT of the brain with contrast and a bone scan showed no metastatic disease. 

Two biopsies were obtained from the endometrial and vaginal wall masses for histopathological evaluation.

A 73-year-old woman presented with recent shortness of breath and fatigue and was found to have an infiltrative middle mediastinal lesion on chest CT. One year earlier, she had an episode of sudden-onset upper abdominal pain, anorexia, nausea, and vomiting. Examination at that time revealed mild upper abdominal tenderness; laboratory studies were notable only for an elevated alkaline phosphatase level of 160 U/L (normal, 6–45 U/L). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a 1.9×1.6 cm ill-defined hypoattenuating lesion in the tail of the pancreas with adjacent fat stranding. MRI of the pancreas revealed an ill-defined solid lesion with high T2 signal, intermediate T1 signal, restricted diffusion on DWI, and heterogeneous peripheral enhancement after gadolinium. An ^18F-FDG PET scan demonstrated intense uptake in the pancreatic-tail lesion (SUVmax, 8.9) and in sclerotic lesions of both trochanteric regions.
Five months later, follow-up CT revealed a new 3.2×2.6 cm hypoattenuating mass at the pancreatic head–uncinate junction. In the retroperitoneum, there was symmetric perinephric soft-tissue thickening (“hairy kidney”), mild hydronephrosis, and circumferential soft-tissue infiltration around the abdominal aorta (“coated aorta”). A ^68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT scan showed no uptake in the pancreatic lesions, suggesting absence of a neuroendocrine tumor, but revealed intense uptake in diffusely sclerotic diaphyseal areas of the long bones.
The patient also reported headache, fatigue, polydipsia, polyuria, and blurred vision. MRI of the brain with gadolinium demonstrated diffuse pachymeningeal thickening, enlargement and enhancement of the pituitary stalk, and bilateral well-defined intraconal orbital masses associated with mild exophthalmos.

A 24-year-old woman, at 12 weeks’ gestation, was referred with a cystic liver-hilum mass. Six weeks earlier she had presented with jaundice (total bilirubin 12 mg/dL) and left upper-quadrant pain radiating to the left shoulder; bilirubin improved to 3 mg/dL over one week. On transfer she was mildly jaundiced and had a soft, tender mass in her left upper abdomen.

Laboratory studies showed total bilirubin 2.3 mg/dL (normal 0.2–1.2), alkaline phosphatase 194 U/L (normal 38–126), γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 117 U/L (normal 7–50); aminotransferases and pancreatic enzymes were normal. Serum CA 19-9 and CEA were normal; AFP was 16 ng/mL (normal <7). Hydatid serologies were negative.

An MRI in October showed a 37×40 mm multilocular cystic lesion between segments 3 and 4, with dilatation of the left hepatic duct (12 mm) and common hepatic duct (15 mm); the right hepatic duct and common bile duct were normal. On admission, MRI demonstrated a 19×17×10 cm fluid collection anterior and inferior to the left lobe, with apparent communication between the cystic lesion and intrahepatic ducts of segments 2 and 3. Percutaneous drainage yielded bile-stained fluid (fluid bilirubin 18 mg/dL vs serum 2 mg/dL) and CA 19-9 of 52 652 IU/mL (serum <34). Daily external bile output was 1000–1500 mL for nine days, then ceased.

At 14 weeks’ gestation, contrast MRI showed enhancing internal septations within the cystic liver mass.

A 35-year-old African man presented with an eight-year history of left upper limb pain and paresthesia so severe that he was unable to sleep.
