He described near-constant burning pain and paresthesias radiating from the left side of his neck down the entire limb. Notably, he reported that the pain had initially begun at the tip of his left middle fingertip and over years spread proximally.

He denied any antecedent trauma and had no stigmata of neurofibromatosis. The pain was exacerbated by cold weather, lifting heavy objects with his left hand, and direct pressure on his left middle finger. He found temporary relief by self-applied rubber-band tourniquets and by rubbing the finger against a rough surface.

Over the course of eight years, he had been treated for multiple diagnoses—including neurogenic pain, neuroma, gout, and thoracic outlet syndrome—and had undergone computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine and brachial plexus. He also received twelve stellate ganglion blocks, all without lasting improvement.

On examination, there was tenderness over the brachial plexus roots in the neck and along the entire left upper limb. The left middle finger appeared mildly thickened and dry; any palpation of the fingertip elicited exquisite pain, preventing further detailed examination.

Given the spontaneous, disproportionate upper limb pain, hyperalgesia, trophic changes in the fingertips—most pronounced in the middle finger—and a preceding focal onset in the fingertip, a diagnosis of chronic regional pain syndrome (CRPS), most likely secondary to an occult lesion, was made. Previous MRI studies of the fingertip had been inconclusive. With a consideration for a focal glomus lesion, we proposed surgical exploration of the left middle fingertip.

A 34-year-old woman (G3P3) presented with a 4-month history of heavy menstrual bleeding associated with dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and low back pain. She denied weight loss or systemic symptoms and took no medications. On examination the abdomen was soft, non-tender, and non-distended. Pelvic examination revealed a normal uterus; the left ovary was enlarged and non-tender, while the right ovary was normal. Transabdominal pelvic ultrasonography showed a heterogeneous left ovarian mass measuring 7.0 × 5.0 × 5.0 cm. Transvaginal ultrasonography characterized it as a large, complex adnexal mass with neovascularization; it appeared vegetative rather than fluid-filled. Serum CA 125 and CEA levels were within normal limits. T1- and T2-weighted pelvic MRI revealed a multicystic tumor with a solid component and a multilobulated surface on the left ovary, displaying low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and very low signal intensity on T2-weighted images, findings suggestive of viscid, gelatinous material.

An 80-year-old man with chronic renal failure noted a right facial swelling 2 months earlier and was referred for evaluation. On extraoral examination, there was enlargement of the right parotid and submandibular regions, with extensive ipsilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. Intraoral inspection revealed two masses: one on the left side of the hard palate and another on the floor of the mouth. Tongue mobility was normal, and there was no lingual nerve paresthesia.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the neck showed the following findings:
- Right parotid gland: a solid, expansive mass in the superficial lobe with low signal on T1-weighted images and high signal on T2-weighted images, plus two nodular lesions in its inferior pole.
- Left parotid gland: three small nodular lesions in the superficial lobe with signal characteristics similar to the right.
- Left hard palate: an expansive mass causing ipsilateral narrowing of the pharyngeal airway.
- Posterior two-thirds of the left tongue and both lingual tonsils: expansive lesions displacing the epiglottis posteriorly and obliterating the vallecula.
- Floor of the mouth and sublingual/submandibular areas: multiple masses not infiltrating the major salivary glands.
- Bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy.

On the basis of these clinical and imaging findings, a working diagnosis of a malignant disease was made.

A 33-year-old man with a history of laparoscopic adrenalectomy for primary aldosteronism underwent routine abdominal imaging one year after surgery. He was asymptomatic, with a normal abdominal examination. Laboratory studies, including serum CA19-9 and CEA, were within normal limits. Plain CT revealed a 20 mm, low-density, well-circumscribed, circular lesion in the spleen without cystic change, necrosis, or calcification. Contrast-enhanced CT showed centripetal, delayed enhancement with a wheel-like appearance. MRI demonstrated that the splenic nodule was hypointense on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images. The main radiologic differential diagnoses were hamartoma, sclerosed hemangioma, and inflammatory pseudotumor. As no sign of malignancy was present, the lesion was observed. Two years later, CT showed the mass had increased to 50 mm, and one year after that it measured 70 mm. Because malignant neoplasm could not be completely excluded given such progressive growth, splenectomy was performed.

A six-year-old girl presented with a three-day history of fever, persistent cough, and dyspnea. She had no history of recurrent respiratory infections. Laboratory testing showed a C-reactive protein level of 9.67 mg/dL (reference range, 0–0.5). A chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral pulmonary opacities consistent with pneumonia. Initial differential diagnoses included inhalation of a foreign body, tuberculous pneumonia, and interstitial pneumonia. She received oxygen, bronchodilators, inhaled and then intravenous steroids, and ceftriaxone, but her respiratory status worsened, requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. A computed tomography scan confirmed multiple bilateral pulmonary consolidations and revealed a 12 × 8 mm solid-appearing protrusion arising from the tracheal wall. SARS-CoV-2 testing was negative, and all microbiological studies were unrevealing. Bronchoscopic examination with bronchoalveolar lavage and biopsy of the tracheal lesion was then performed.

A 25-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of exertional dyspnea and palpitations. On examination, she had a systolic murmur. Bedside transthoracic ultrasound demonstrated moderate tricuspid regurgitation and possible pulmonary hypertension. A contrast-enhanced chest CT scan showed dilation of the main pulmonary artery, which was filled with a hypodense mass containing areas of calcification adjacent to both right and left pulmonary arteries. The mass appeared to nearly obliterate the lumens of the main and hilar pulmonary arteries without attachment to the pulmonary valve or extension into the peripheral branches. Lung perfusion scintigraphy revealed markedly decreased blood flow throughout both lungs except the left upper lobe. The plasma D-dimer level was 1.9 μg/mL (normal ≤ 1.0 μg/mL).

A 24-year-old Asian man presented with a one-month history of intractable vomiting, hematemesis, melena, epigastric pain, generalized weakness, and weight loss. He had no history of HIV infection or immunosuppression. On exam, he appeared underweight and pale, with profound jaundice; abdominal palpation revealed a palpable epigastric mass and hepatosplenomegaly. Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 6.0 g/dL, hematocrit 18.5%, total bilirubin 9.35 mg/dL, γ-glutamyl transferase 764 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase 2310 IU/L; other blood counts and renal function were normal. Serologic tests for HIV, hepatitis B and C, and Helicobacter pylori IgG were negative. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy demonstrated an irregular, circumferential ulcerated mass in the first portion of the duodenum extending into the second portion, with a large clean-based ulcer and overlying clot. Triphasic CT of the abdomen revealed a 16 cm long, 2.6 cm thick lesion in the second part of the duodenum infiltrating the pancreatic head, causing biliary and pancreatic duct dilation, along with necrotic pelvic and right renal soft-tissue nodules and enlarged para-aortic nodes. Biopsy showed sheets of medium-to-large atypical cells with plasmacytoid morphology, high mitotic rate, and elevated Ki-67. By immunohistochemistry, the tumor cells were positive for LCA, CD79a, Pax-5, Mum-1, and CD138, and negative for CD20, CD3, and CD30.

A 41-year-old woman presented with long-standing right wrist pain and palpable soft tissue nodules over the volar and dorsal aspects of the wrist. She reported progressively worsening flexion contractures of the middle and ring finger metacarpophalangeal joints of the right hand. On examination, there were soft tissue nodules and flexion contractures with markedly reduced movement of the affected MCPJs.

A plain radiograph of the right hand showed flexion deformities of the middle and ring fingers, erosions at the proximal interphalangeal joint of the ring finger, and early cortical irregularity at the base of the index metacarpal and ring finger proximal phalanx. 

Ultrasound demonstrated hypoechoic nodules along the flexor and extensor tendon sheaths of the wrist, marked tenosynovitis, and tendinosis of the flexor tendons, with particular thickening at the A1 pulley level and compression of the median nerve. Power Doppler imaging revealed moderate vascularity. No evidence of synovitis or tenosynovitis was seen in the left wrist.

MRI of the wrist and hand revealed extensive tenosynovitis of both extensor and flexor compartments, with intermediate to low signal intensity on STIR and T1-weighted sequences, areas of blooming artifact on gradient echo images, and mild fluid distension. There was lobulated synovial proliferation of low signal intensity surrounding the carpus and tracking distally along the flexor tendons to involve the index, middle, and ring finger MCPJs, as well as the thumb interphalangeal joint.

A 50-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of a slowly enlarging mass over the left lacrimal sac area, associated with intermittent tearing and pain but no blood discharge or visual changes. Six months after initial onset she underwent dacryocystectomy elsewhere, and pathology was reported as malignant melanoma. Three months post-operatively, she noted gradual enlargement of a mass at the left medial canthus and was referred for further evaluation.

On examination, there was a 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm firm, well-circumscribed mass at the left medial canthus and a healed surgical scar; there was no cervical lymphadenopathy. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits showed a partly well-defined soft-tissue mass in the left lacrimal sac fossa extending into the nasolacrimal duct and anterior ethmoid sinus, with attenuation of 49 HU on noncontrast images and marked enhancement to 103 HU in the arterial phase and 95 HU in the venous phase. Bone windows demonstrated enlargement of the nasolacrimal duct and focal bone erosion. No intraocular involvement or regional metastases were seen.

MRI revealed a 1.2 cm × 1.3 cm × 2.3 cm mass in the left lacrimal sac with intermediate signal intensity on T1-weighted images and iso- to hyperintense signal on T2-weighted images, slight hyperintensity on diffusion-weighted images, and intense, but heterogeneous, enhancement after gadolinium administration. The lesion infiltrated adjacent orbital septa and subcutaneous tissue.

A 16-year-old male presented with a 10-month history of persistent pain and stiffness of the interphalangeal joint of the left hallux, resulting in difficulty walking. He denied any preceding trauma. Examination revealed localized tenderness over the proximal phalanx of the hallux and a reduced range of motion at the interphalangeal joint. Plain radiographs of the left forefoot demonstrated an oval-shaped radiolucent lesion in the condyle of the proximal phalanx of the hallux. Noncontrast CT of the area showed a 7 × 8 mm, well-circumscribed osteolytic lesion at the distal aspect of the proximal phalanx, containing a central region of higher density surrounded by a mild sclerotic rim, with subchondral involvement of the distal articular surface.

A 4-year-old girl presented with fever, right upper-quadrant abdominal pain, weight loss, night sweats, and decreased appetite. Two weeks earlier, she had bacterial sinusitis. On examination, she had pale mucous membranes, multiple enlarged lymph nodes, and hepatomegaly. Laboratory studies showed elevated lactate dehydrogenase (1374 U/L), alanine aminotransferase (114 U/L), aspartate aminotransferase (68 U/L), a normal alpha-fetoprotein level (1.19 ng/mL), and a mild normocytic, normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 11 g/dL, hematocrit 34.5%). Chest radiography revealed well-defined radiopaque nodules in both hemithoraces. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated hepatomegaly due to a 14×7×9.5 cm heterogeneous intrahepatic mass with calcification, cystic and necrotic components, irregular lobulated borders extending into the hepatic hilum, compression of the right kidney and inferior vena cava, flow on Doppler, and locoregional lymphadenopathy. Non-contrast chest CT confirmed multiple subpleural nodules up to 10 mm in both lung fields. Contrast-enhanced abdominal MRI showed a large, heterogeneous hepatic mass with necrotic areas involving multiple segments and the hilum, smaller satellite lesions, an adjacent paravertebral mass extending through the vertebral foramen with psoas muscle edema, absence of intralesional fat, peripheral diffusion restriction, and heterogeneous contrast enhancement.

A 64-year-old woman with no significant past medical history was referred for evaluation of a new polyurodypsic syndrome. Laboratory testing confirmed diabetes mellitus that required insulin. Over the preceding weeks she noted a progressive deterioration in her general condition. Because of insulin dependence and worsening symptoms, an abdominal ultrasound was performed, revealing a left renal mass. 

On admission her Karnofsky Performance Status was estimated at 50%. She denied hematuria and flank pain. Physical examination revealed a small, deep-seated nodule in an anterior intercostal space. 

A contrast-enhanced thoraco-abdomino-pelvic CT scan showed:
• A large left renal tissue mass with a necrotic center and intralesional calcifications  
• Multiple pulmonary nodules consistent with metastases and a parietal pleural nodule  
• Multiple lesions in the pancreas  
• A small secondary lesion in the right kidney

A 22-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with a painless, enlarging vulvar mass for two months. Examination showed a well-defined, firm, crusted 3-cm cyst on the right labia majora; there was no inguinal lymphadenopathy and a pelvic examination was otherwise normal. Laboratory evaluation, including a complete blood count, was unremarkable. The lesion was excised under local anesthesia.  

Histopathology demonstrated a dermal spindle-cell proliferation with lobulated cellular myxoid nodules and collagenous hypocellular areas exhibiting abrupt transitions. Tumor cells were arranged in short fascicles with plump spindled to ovoid nuclei, mild hyperchromasia, and rare atypical mitoses (<2 per 10 high-power fields). Foci of small, curved vascular arcades with perivascular sclerosis were noted. There was no tumor necrosis or lymphovascular invasion. Immunohistochemical studies showed no staining for AE1/AE3, EMA, hormone receptors, SMA, h-Caldesmone, Desmin, CD34, S-100 protein, or CD10. The Ki-67 index was approximately 10%. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no evidence of metastatic disease.

A 71-year-old Caucasian man presented with sudden swelling of the left side of his neck immediately after sneezing while lying supine with his hands overhead. He recalled a slight, painless neck swelling for several months but denied dyspnea, pain, or other systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a semi-firm, non-tender mass on the left side of the neck extending from the clavicle to the submandibular region, without erythema, warmth, or ecchymosis. Indirect laryngoscopy demonstrated rightward displacement of the larynx with intact vocal-cord mobility. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 4900 cells/μL, hemoglobin of 14.1 g/dL, and serum calcium of 9.6 mg/dL; inflammatory markers were within normal limits. Ultrasonography revealed a well-defined heterogeneous mass medial to the left sternocleidomastoid muscle, displacing the carotid artery and internal jugular vein. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the neck demonstrated a 6 × 7 × 12 cm mass originating from the left thyroid lobe, displacing the trachea and larynx to the right, extending from the subclavicular to the submandibular regions, with enhancement of the capsule and the caudal portion of the lesion.

A 36-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of a left breast mass without systemic symptoms. On examination, the left breast was replaced by a 20 × 20 cm ulcerative lesion in the outer quadrants, and ipsilateral axillary nodes appeared inflammatory and measured 1 cm in diameter. The right breast and axilla were normal. Chest CT showed a necrotic mass occupying the entire left breast with infiltration of the skin and pectoral muscle and ipsilateral pectoral and axillary lymphadenopathy. Abdominal and pelvic CT scans showed no distant metastases. Core-needle biopsy of the lesion demonstrated a high-grade malignant spindle cell neoplasm with an osteochondral component, extensive necrosis, and negative cytokeratin staining, raising consideration of a phyllodes tumor versus a primary breast sarcoma.

A 42-year-old man with no prior medical, surgical, or social risk factors presented with a 3-year history of persistent, progressive dysphonia. He denied dyspnea and dysphagia. Physical examination, including flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy, revealed a 1.0 × 0.8 cm rounded, whitish lesion on the anterior and middle third of the left vocal cord. The lesion appeared covered by intact epithelium, and left vocal-cord mobility was preserved. No other abnormalities were noted.

A 62-year-old man was admitted with a two-month history of weakness, periodic vomiting, and involuntary weight loss of more than 20 kg due to severe dysphagia that progressed to complete inability to swallow liquids or solids over the two days before admission. He had undergone hip arthroplasty four months earlier, without perioperative hypercalcemia noted. An otorhinolaryngologic examination and flexible endoscopy showed normal vocal cord function and no salivary retention. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed only a small hiatal hernia without any obstructive lesion, and a nasogastric tube was placed. Contrast-enhanced neck CT demonstrated massive ventral spondylophytes at the postcricoid segment of the hypopharynx, impinging on prevertebral structures, and a 3.6 × 2.6 × 2.5 cm mass located posterior to the left thyroid lobe. Neck ultrasound confirmed the mass to be hypoechoic. Laboratory studies showed a parathyroid hormone level of 102 pmol/L (reference, 1.8–7.9), a serum calcium level of 4.12 mmol/L (2.14–2.53), an ionized calcium level of 2.13 mmol/L (1.18–1.32), and a normal serum albumin level. Technetium-99m sestamibi scintigraphy demonstrated intense uptake at the site of the neck mass.

A 72-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and hypothyroidism receiving levothyroxine presented with abdominal pain and bilateral lower-limb swelling. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 5.5 cm × 4.4 cm well-encapsulated mass in the upper pole of the right kidney showing inhomogeneous contrast enhancement with central necrosis. The patient underwent a laparoscopic right radical nephrectomy. Gross examination showed a well-circumscribed gray-tan tumor measuring 4.5 cm × 4.5 cm × 3 cm in the upper pole. Microscopic examination raised a differential diagnosis of metastatic thyroid malignancy versus primary thyroid-like follicular carcinoma of the kidney. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated strong positivity for pan-cytokeratin, thyroid transcription factor-1, and thyroglobulin.

A 59-year-old woman presented with a lump in the lower outer quadrant of her left breast. Six years earlier, she had undergone breast-conserving surgery with endocrine therapy and radiation (50 Gy in 25 fractions) to the left breast for an upper inner quadrant carcinoma. On examination, there was a 20 mm firm mass fixed to the pectoralis major muscle; the overlying skin was uninvolved and there were no palpable axillary lymph nodes.

Mammography showed a focal asymmetrical density in the retromammary space. Ultrasonography revealed a lobulated, well-defined mass measuring 17.5 × 16.4 × 10.6 mm with relatively hypoechoic, heterogeneous internal echoes. A core-needle biopsy of the lesion suggested only atrophic mammary glands. On three-month follow-up, the lesion had increased in size.

A 54-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of an enlarging, slightly painful left flank nodule without preceding trauma or insect bite. She denied fever, chills, rash, cough, shortness of breath, hemoptysis, arthralgias, dysuria, or weight loss. Her medical history included chronic anemia, treated latent tuberculosis, cervical dysplasia, and hysterectomy. She had no tobacco, second-hand smoke, or occupational exposures. Family history was notable for various cancers (father with bone cancer; brother with an unknown facial cancer; uncle with liver cancer; aunt with a brain tumor).

On examination, there was a single 2×2 cm firm, slightly tender, freely mobile, nonfluctuant left flank mass without overlying skin changes. No other masses or lymphadenopathy were present. Laboratory tests showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 35 mm/hr and a lactate dehydrogenase level of 220 IU/L. Autoimmune, HIV, and hepatitis studies were negative, and thyroid function was normal. A chest radiograph and whole-body CT performed 3 years earlier for anemia were unremarkable.

With a presumptive diagnosis of neurolipoma, she underwent excision with wide margins. Operative findings revealed a reddish-brown 2 cm firm subcutaneous mass superficial to the fascia, surrounded by fat.

A 7-month-old boy presented with a 2-week history of fever and persistent crying. Parents noted a swelling over the left upper tibia. On examination, there was a diffuse, tender swelling measuring approximately 8×3×3 cm at the anteromedial junction of the upper and middle third of the left leg, with shiny overlying skin, no visible veins or pulsations, and no deformity or other bone involvement. Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the left tibia demonstrated an expansile, osteolytic, poorly demarcated lesion in the metaphyseal–diaphyseal region without periosteal reaction. MRI of the left tibia revealed a well-defined expansile intramedullary metadiaphyseal lesion (4.3×1.9×1.7 cm) in the proximal and mid tibia, with marked lateral cortical thinning and possible breach, associated periosteal thickening, and adjacent marrow edema. Ultrasonography of the abdomen and CT of the chest and abdomen were normal.

A 9-year-old Caucasian boy presented with a 3-year history of a persistent swelling in the natal cleft that had been treated as a pilonidal abscess with multiple courses of antibiotics without improvement. On examination, there was a soft‐tissue swelling measuring 50×30 mm in the natal cleft; there were no sinus tracts, midline pits, or overlying skin changes. The lesion was excised en bloc down to the periosteum without capsular breach. 

Grossly, the specimen was a firm, cream‐coloured, solid mass measuring 50×35×30 mm. Microscopic examination revealed a lobulated, subcutaneous tumour composed of pleomorphic epithelioid cells. Immunohistochemical stains showed diffuse, strong positivity for S100, CD56, vimentin, glial fibrillary acidic protein, and TFE3; stains for epithelial and neuroendocrine markers were negative. Sections suggested possible involvement of one lateral circumferential margin. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the neuraxis confirmed that the lesion was extraspinal in origin, with no involvement of the sacral canal or adjacent bone.

A 4-month-old male infant was admitted for recurrent respiratory infections since birth, occasionally requiring hospitalization. On examination, there was no dyspnea or cyanosis, but left chest wall excursion was limited and breath sounds were diminished on the left. A chest radiograph showed a round, homogeneous opacity occupying the upper two-thirds of the left hemithorax without mediastinal shift. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a heterogeneous, well-delineated mass measuring 3.8 × 6 cm in the posterior mediastinum, compressing the left lung. Echocardiography was normal, and routine blood tests were unremarkable.

A 61-year-old man presented in August 2020 with dyspepsia, left‐lower‐neck swelling, and mild dysphagia. He was a hepatitis B carrier and a chronic drinker and smoker. Initial blood tests showed α-fetoprotein >500 ng/mL and carcinoembryonic antigen 19.8 ng/mL. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed liver and left adrenal masses and enlarged mediastinal, abdominal, and left supraclavicular lymph nodes. A PET/CT scan demonstrated a 3.4-cm mass at the anterior gastric wall; multiple upper abdominal lymph node metastases; more than 10 liver metastases (up to 3.5 cm); a left adrenal metastasis; and multiple left neck lymph node metastases. Biopsies of a neck lymph node and the esophagogastric junction showed tumor cells positive for AFP, SALL4, and CDX2. HER2 immunohistochemistry was scored 2+, and fluorescence in situ hybridization revealed HER2–CEP17 clusters with a HER2/CEP17 ratio >2.0 and a HER2/nuclei ratio >4.0. PD-L1 expression by immunohistochemistry yielded a combined positive score of 5.

A 75-year-old woman presented with several days of fatigue, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and jaundice. She denied fever, sick contacts, recent infections, travel, or new medications. Her past history included Parkinson’s disease managed with aspirin, calcium–vitamin D3, and rasagiline. On examination she was afebrile and icteric. Laboratory values at initial presentation showed hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL; white blood cell count 6.35 k/µL (63% neutrophils, 21% lymphocytes, 13% monocytes); platelets 30 k/µL; alkaline phosphatase 92 U/L; AST 62 U/L; ALT 104 U/L; total bilirubin 4.5 mg/dL (direct 2.4 mg/dL). Serologic tests for Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, hepatitis viruses, and HIV were negative. Autoimmune markers including antinuclear, antimitochondrial, anti–Smith, and liver–kidney microsomal antibodies were negative. Magnetic resonance cholangiogram revealed marked hepatomegaly, moderate splenomegaly, and nodular areas of decreased T2 signal in the liver and spleen. Over the next few days, she became confused with tense, tender abdominal distension and palpable splenomegaly. On transfer, labs showed hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL; white blood cell count 6.29 k/µL (75% neutrophils); platelets 9 k/µL; alkaline phosphatase 92 U/L; AST 34 U/L; ALT 79 U/L; total bilirubin 16.4 mg/dL (direct > 10 mg/dL); LDH 123 U/L; prothrombin time 21.2 s (INR 1.8); D-dimer 3.41; fibrinogen 159 mg/dL. Rapidly she developed fulminant encephalopathy, rising AST to 1,669 U/L, ALT to 518 U/L, total bilirubin to 19.8 mg/dL, acute renal failure, worsening coagulopathy, and metabolic acidosis. A hematology consultant noted rare large blast cells on the peripheral smear; peripheral blood flow cytometry did not detect these.

A 43-year-old man presented with a one-month history of dysuria and difficulty initiating urination. His medical history was unremarkable. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits, and no abnormalities were noted on physical examination. Laboratory studies, including a prostate-specific antigen level and urine analysis, were normal. To relieve symptoms and obtain tissue for diagnosis, transurethral resection of the prostate was performed; the pathology report described a low-grade stromal sarcoma of the prostate. Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 5.2 × 4.9 × 5.6 cm, well-demarcated, heterogeneous mass in the right prostate lobe with both cystic and solid components. There was no evidence of capsular invasion or involvement of the bladder or seminal vesicles.

A 66-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of longstanding hypercalcemia and recurrent episodes of acute pancreatitis. She had two prior admissions for pancreatitis, 6 months and 3 years earlier. There was no history of gallstone disease or significant alcohol abuse. Her usual intake was 350 mL of beer four times per week. On review of prior abdominal computed tomography, there were multiple renal stones but neither gallstones nor pancreatic calcifications. Physical examination revealed no palpable neck mass. Laboratory testing showed: serum calcium 12.4 mg/dL (reference, 8.3–10.3), albumin 4.0 g/dL, phosphorus 2.4 mg/dL (2.4–4.7), and intact PTH 253 pg/mL (8.7–79.5). Renal function was normal. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the neck demonstrated a well-defined, heterogeneous 28 mm soft-tissue mass within the left thyroid lobe. Technetium-99m-MIBI scintigraphy showed focal uptake in the left thyroid lobe on both early and delayed images.

A 28-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of a slowly enlarging swelling on the lower left side of her face and intermittent dull aching pain for the past 3 months. The swelling began small and gradually attained its present size. On intraoral examination, there was a diffuse, oval swelling measuring approximately 3 × 4 cm, extending from the left mandibular canine (tooth 33) to the second molar (tooth 37); the overlying mucosa appeared normal. Panoramic and posteroanterior radiographs showed a homogeneous radiopaque lesion with a thin, uniform radiolucent border in the left mandible from teeth 33 to 37, involving the mandibular canal but without root resorption.

A 13-year-old boy presented with a left mandibular mass first noted 4 years earlier, slowly enlarging over time. He had no history of trauma or toothache. Over the past year, he experienced pain on mouth closure due to contact between his upper teeth and the lesion. Physical examination revealed a 16 × 12 cm hard, non‐tender mass involving the left mandible, extending from the zygomatic arch to 5 cm below the mandibular border. The overlying skin and oral mucosa were intact and of normal appearance. Intraorally, the lesion displaced adjacent teeth peripherally and pushed the tongue to the contralateral side, causing difficulty chewing and speaking. No cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. Vital signs and routine laboratory studies were normal.

Contrast‐enhanced CT of the head and neck showed a large, well‐defined expansile mass arising from the left mandible with cortical erosion, loosening of adjacent teeth, a unilocular radiolucent area, and multiple internal calcifications. The surrounding soft tissues, airway structures, and intracranial contents were unremarkable. CT scans of the chest and abdomen were normal.

Based on the clinical findings, history of presenting illness, and radiological features, differential diagnoses of ossifying fibroma, ameloblastoma, and fibrous dysplasia were entertained.

A 6-year-old Caucasian girl with a history of juvenile diabetes mellitus was referred for evaluation of a slowly progressive lesion of the right upper eyelid, noted over the past two years. She reported no pain, itching, discharge, or preceding trauma. On examination, vital signs were normal. The right upper eyelid showed a non-tender, flesh-colored papule measuring 1.5 × 1.0 mm along the lash margin. A single white eyelash, approximately three times the length of the surrounding lashes, emerged from the lesion. There was no madarosis, surrounding inflammation, or distortion of the eyelid margin.

A 65-year-old previously healthy Caucasian man presented with a 3-week history of recurrent rigors, fevers, and night sweats. Initial evaluation at a district hospital revealed acute kidney injury and thrombocytopenia. On transfer, laboratory studies showed a platelet count of 55×10^9/L (reference 150–400), a white-cell count of 3.2×10^9/L (reference 4.0–10.0) with lymphocytopenia (0.47×10^9/L; reference 0.8–4.0), elevated liver enzymes (ALT 1.16 μkat/L [<0.73]; AST 3.56 μkat/L [<0.67]), and hypoalbuminemia (21.9 g/L; reference 35.0–53.0). A whole-body CT scan showed a 13×8×8 cm infiltrative lesion in the retroperitoneal space involving the ascending mesocolon and mesenteric root. Exploratory laparotomy confirmed a tumor in the mesocolon ascendens invading the radix mesenterii, and a surgical biopsy was obtained. Subsequently, he developed progressive pancytopenia, coagulopathy with a fibrinogen level of 0.7 g/L, and a C-reactive protein concentration of 140 mg/L. Despite intensive supportive measures, he progressed to multiorgan failure and died 22 days after initial presentation; the underlying disease remained undetermined at death.

A 51-year-old man presented with a gradually enlarging mass in his left thigh, first noted 10 years previously and painful for the past 6 months. On examination, there was a 20 × 10 cm swelling over the anterior and anterolateral aspects of the thigh. Plain radiographs showed no bone involvement. MRI demonstrated a heterogeneous intramuscular mass, likely malignant, with preservation of the plane between the lesion and the neurovascular bundle. Fine-needle aspiration cytology (22-gauge needle) yielded cellular smears showing sheets and clusters of monotomous cells in a prominent myxoid stroma. Individual cells had vesicular nuclei, well-delineated borders, and occasional nuclear grooves. At places, cells formed small anastomosing cords and exhibited a single-file arrangement without significant pleomorphism. Based on the clinical, radiological, and cytological findings, a diagnosis of a myxoid sarcoma was favored.  
What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 59-year-old Malay man with no prior medical history presented with 3 weeks of fever, lethargy, headache, skin bruising, anorexia, and weight loss. He was a nonsmoker and teetotaler, with no family history of hematologic disease. On examination, he was pale, ECOG performance status 0, blood pressure 110/60 mm Hg, pulse 96 bpm, and had bruises on the lower limbs. There was no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 6.5 g/dL, white blood cell count 1.5×10^9/L, platelet count 21×10^9/L, and lactate dehydrogenase 550 U/L. Viral hepatitis and HIV serologies were negative. Peripheral blood smear revealed anisopoikilocytosis, nucleated red blood cells, numerous mononuclear cells, and giant platelets. Chest radiograph showed no mediastinal widening.

Bone marrow aspiration demonstrated hypercellularity with trilineage dysplasia and 52% medium-to-large blasts with scant basophilic cytoplasm and cytoplasmic blebs. Trephine biopsy showed clusters of blasts with increased reticulin fibrosis (Grade 2). Flow cytometry of the marrow revealed 55% blasts expressing CD13, CD33, CD34, CD36, CD41, and CD61, and negative for cytoplasmic myeloperoxidase and HLA-DR. Cytogenetic analysis showed −7q and trisomy 8.

A 78-year-old man presented with a 10-year history of a slowly enlarging, painful nodule on his back. The lesion caused worsening pain with pressure but no cold intolerance or hypersensitivity. On examination, there was a well-defined, smooth, dome-shaped, whitish-purple nodule measuring 15 mm in diameter on the left scapular region. Polarized, noncontact dermoscopy showed irregular structureless purpuric macules throughout the lesion, overlaid by white reticular macules and white lines, set against a dark red background. The margins were surrounded by a well-demarcated white-to-yellow ring, and some reticular white spots appeared yellowish. Under polarized contact dermoscopy, thick fibrous white linear structures were noted in the compressed margin, and the skin surface of the lesion displayed a ring-like yellowish hue.

A 47-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 1-year history of progressive left temporal headache, described as constant and dull with intermittent nausea and vomiting. There were no photophobia, phonophobia, visual changes, aura, or identifiable triggers. Over-the-counter analgesics provided no relief. He denied trauma, substance use, or family history of neurologic disease or malignancy.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Neurologic assessment revealed intact cranial nerves, normal strength and sensation bilaterally, no focal deficits, and a normal fundoscopic examination. There was no neck stiffness or meningeal irritation; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed a well-defined, lobulated intra-axial mass in the left temporoparietal lobe measuring 72×72×57 mm, with solid and cystic components. On T1-weighted images, portions were hypointense and isointense; on T2-weighted images, portions were hyperintense and isointense. Postcontrast T1 sequences demonstrated marked heterogeneous enhancement. The lesion compressed the atrium of the left lateral ventricle, abutted the superior tentorial surface, and partially invaded the left transverse sinus. Diffusion tensor imaging suggested displacement and compression of white matter tracts in the region.

A 12-year-old girl presented with a 6-month history of a slowly enlarging swelling on the left side of her face. On extraoral examination there was a diffuse, non-tender swelling over the left cheek, involving the lateral nose and infraorbital region, with intact overlying skin. Intraorally, there was firm to hard expansion of the buccal cortical plate in the left upper canine–premolar region; the palatal mucosa was normal and there were no draining sinuses. The upper left central incisor and canine were tilted, and the lateral incisor was missing. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated an ill-defined, mixed radiolucent lesion in the left maxilla with displacement of adjacent teeth. CT imaging showed that the lesion completely obliterated the left maxillary sinus while the palatal bone and posterior wall of the sinus remained intact.

A 30-year-old woman presented 4 weeks after sustaining third-degree burns over 60% of her body surface area from hot oil. She received daily silver sulfadiazine dressings, intravenous antibiotics, and full-thickness skin grafting of her thigh wound using donor skin from the left forearm. Twenty-four days after the injury, she noted the appearance of multiple papillary and nodular lesions at the periphery of the burn site and around the forearm donor site. The lesions enlarged over days and bled easily with minor contact. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver-function, and renal-function tests, were within normal limits. Serologic testing for HIV and human T-lymphotropic virus was negative. Blood and fresh tissue cultures for Bartonella species were negative. Histopathologic examination of a representative lesion showed hyperkeratosis, dermal edema, intense lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, and proliferation of blood vessels with variable luminal diameters in an edematous stroma.

A 58-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and distension. He had a similar self-limited episode one year earlier but declined further evaluation. On examination, he had increased metallic bowel sounds in the right lower quadrant, diffuse abdominal distension, tenderness, and rigidity. Laboratory tests showed a leukocyte count of 12.4×10^9/L and a C-reactive protein level of 1.9 mg/L. Abdominal ultrasonography was nondiagnostic because of posterior acoustic shadowing. Because of worsening symptoms, an abdominopelvic CT scan with oral, rectal, and intravenous contrast was obtained. The scan revealed an approximately 8-cm intussusception at the ileocecal valve, with proximal small-bowel dilation up to 4.5 cm and air–fluid levels consistent with acute mechanical intestinal obstruction. Within the intussusception, there was a 2.5-cm homogeneous lipoid mass.

A 71-year-old man with a 3-month history of suprapubic catheter drainage following acute urinary retention and failed urethral catheterizations presented for evaluation. He reported a long-standing history of lower urinary tract symptoms—frequency, weak stream, and a sense of incomplete bladder emptying—along with two episodes of painless gross haematuria. He denied tobacco use, chemical exposures, or pelvic irradiation. On examination, he was afebrile with normal vital signs. Abdominal examination revealed a 22-Fr suprapubic catheter draining clear urine and no palpable masses. Digital rectal examination showed prostatomegaly with benign features. Laboratory tests showed a prostate-specific antigen level of 6.1 ng/mL (normal <4), serum creatinine 75 μmol/L, random blood sugar 5.24 mmol/L, hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL, leukocytes 5.22 × 10^9/L, platelets 386 × 10^9/L, and urine culture grew Klebsiella oxytoca sensitive only to meropenem.  
Antegrade and retrograde urethrography revealed a normal anterior urethra with normal tapering at the bulbomembranous junction, contrast extravasation at the bulbous urethra, a closed bladder neck, and a large filling defect in the bladder.  
Transabdominal ultrasound demonstrated a well-defined heterogeneous mass in the urinary bladder measuring 8.6 cm × 11.1 cm with normal upper tracts. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a heterogeneous enhancing soft tissue mass arising from the posterolateral bladder wall, measuring approximately 8.89 cm × 8.4 cm × 6.93 cm; the prostate measured 5.75 cm × 6.73 cm × 5.05 cm. No lymphadenopathy, bone lesions, or free peritoneal fluid were identified.

A 39-year-old woman with a history of hypertension, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and a prior cesarean section initially presented in November 2010 with dysfunctional uterine bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasonography was normal; she underwent dilation and curettage and was started on oral contraceptives without improvement. Two months later, she developed a protracted upper respiratory infection and was treated with antibiotics. A follow-up CT scan of the chest was obtained; the thoracic images were unremarkable, but the lower cuts demonstrated a large left retroperitoneal mass abutting the superior pole of the left kidney. 

A contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed an encapsulated mass measuring 19.3 cm × 13.5 cm × 10.7 cm with prominent vascularity arising from the left renal vasculature. In addition, a 2 cm homogeneous fatty lesion was noted in the inferior midpole of the left kidney. Subsequent MRI of the abdomen characterized the lesion as a fully encapsulated fatty tumor measuring 19 cm × 14.4 cm × 13.8 cm, displacing the left colon laterally and tightly abutting the superior pole of the left kidney; the small 2 cm intrarenal lesion was again seen. 

Given the location and appearance of the lesion, the differential diagnosis included a retroperitoneal liposarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, lipoma, angiomyolipoma, adrenal adenocarcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, or leiomyoma with fatty change.

A 12-year-old girl presented with a 3-month history of a “blister on the upper lip.” The lesion had bled easily after application of a solvent (“thinner”). It was asymptomatic, grew slowly, and continued to bleed, causing the patient distress due to teasing at school. She had no relevant medical history and denied systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a 1 cm, reddish-yellow, ulcerated, superficial nodule involving the left mucocutaneous junction of the upper lip; it bled on touch and was resilient. No cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and VDRL test, were within normal limits or nonreactive. A chest radiograph showed normal pulmonary fields, and the patient was in good general health.

A 70-year-old woman with a one-year history of mild, nonproductive cough presented for evaluation. She denied rhinorrhea, postnasal drip, reflux symptoms, wheezing, or dyspnea. Her medical history was notable for hypertension, anxiety disorder, and dyslipidemia managed with amlodipine/valsartan, hydrochlorothiazide, alprazolam, bupropion, and atorvastatin. She was a lifelong non-smoker. Family history included lung and breast cancer in her mother and laryngeal cancer in her father.

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits and the physical exam was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits.

A chest radiograph revealed a rounded opacity in the left lower lobe. Contrast-enhanced chest CT showed a 3.3 × 3.2 cm well-defined, solid mass in the apical segment of the left lower lobe with heterogeneous enhancement, and a separate 7.3 mm nodule in the lateral basal segment of the same lobe. There were no enlarged lymph nodes or other parenchymal abnormalities. Abdominal and pelvic imaging were normal.

Given the solitary vascularized pulmonary lesion and absence of a clear diagnosis, the patient was referred for video-assisted thoracoscopic surgical resection with intraoperative pathology assessment.

A 16-year-old female presented with a swelling on the left side of her face. Her medical history was noncontributory; there was no history of trauma or congenital bone disorder. On examination, there was a diffuse 3 × 3 cm swelling over the left zygomatic region in the closed-mouth position, which became more prominent on mouth opening and returned to baseline on closing. The swelling was non-tender, there was no deviation on opening or closing, and the maximum interincisal distance was 43 mm. An audible click was noted over the left temporomandibular joint, and increased pressure was felt over the left zygoma during mandibular opening. Intraoral examination revealed good oral hygiene with no remarkable findings.

A panoramic radiograph demonstrated increased radiopacity and altered morphology of the left mandibular coronoid process compared with the right. To clarify the extent and shape of the lesion, cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) was obtained. On axial CBCT images, an enlarged left coronoid process approximated the medial aspect of the left zygomatic arch, which appeared remodeled outward. Coronal images showed the coronoid enlargement extending toward, but not impinging upon, the inner surface of the zygomatic arch. Sagittal images revealed an anteriorly projecting exophytic growth of the coronoid process. Three-dimensional CBCT reconstruction confirmed a distinct bone-like mass arising from the left coronoid process.

A 46-year-old Japanese woman, with a 12-pack-year smoking history and no asbestos exposure, presented with a chronic dry cough. Chest radiography showed decreased radiolucency in the right lung fields and dullness at the right costophrenic angle. Chest computed tomography revealed diffuse thickening of the right pleura with pleural effusion. Cytologic examination of right pleural fluid was positive for malignant cells. A percutaneous pleural biopsy demonstrated non-squamous non-small cell carcinoma without cytological cornification. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for Ber-EP4 and slightly positive for carcinoembryonic antigen, and negative for calretinin and D2-40. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of stage IV non-squamous non-small cell lung cancer was made. Gefitinib was initiated empirically but discontinued after four weeks when no EGFR mutation was identified and no tumor response was observed.

A 63-year-old man with a history of orthotopic liver transplantation in 2010 for hepatitis C–related cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma presented with an 8-month history of nonbloody diarrhea, occurring more than six times per day, accompanied by bloating, cramping, and a 15-pound weight loss. He denied fevers or night sweats. Three months earlier, MRI performed for mild elevations in liver enzymes showed stable prominent mesenteric lymph nodes, the largest measuring 11 mm. His medications included mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg twice daily, cyclosporine 100 mg twice daily, and ursodiol; he reported taking only half the prescribed immunosuppressive doses. On examination, the abdomen was soft without tenderness or organomegaly. Laboratory studies revealed an AST of 37 IU/L and ALT of 75 IU/L. No stool studies were obtained because the diarrhea was attributed to noninfectious causes, and bulking agents led to symptomatic improvement. Upper endoscopy showed duodenal inflammation; colonoscopy revealed continuous mild erythema in the rectosigmoid colon up to 30 cm from the anal verge. Biopsies from the duodenum and colon demonstrated a prominent infiltrate of small atypical lymphocytes with round to irregular nuclei, mature chromatin, and scant clear cytoplasm. There was no evidence of intraepithelial lymphocytes or villous atrophy to suggest celiac disease. Immunostaining of the biopsies was negative for cytomegalovirus.

A 34-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 2, presented for a routine annual gynecologic examination. She had no significant medical history except for treated hyperthyroidism, and her previous Pap smear was normal. On speculum examination, a dark, fully pigmented, smooth-bordered growth was observed, completely covering the external cervical os; the parametrium appeared uninvolved. An incisional biopsy yielded three darkly pigmented tissue fragments (0.4–1.0 cm in diameter). Microscopic examination showed epithelioid tumor cells containing melanin pigment, and a Masson-Fontana stain was positive. Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated diffuse positivity for HMB-45, S-100, and Melan-A antigens and negativity for MNF116 antigen. Pelvic MRI, PET/CT scanning, and abdominal ultrasound showed no evidence of lymph node involvement or distant metastases. A comprehensive evaluation, including ophthalmoscopy and inspection of the skin and other mucosal sites, revealed no additional melanotic lesions.

A 10-year-old girl presented with right forearm pain after being caught between the floor and a friend who fell upon her. She had no prior symptoms at the site and no significant medical history. On examination, the right forearm was deformed but without neurovascular compromise. 

Plain radiographs of the forearm showed a transverse fracture through osteolytic lesions with well-defined sclerotic rims in the diaphysis of the right radius. 

Computed tomography of the right forearm revealed polycystic, lucent lesions measuring 33.5 mm in maximal length, with cortical thinning in the diaphysis of the radius, and a transverse fracture through the center of these lesions.

A 29-year-old woman presented with a long history of left-sided abdominal pain. She denied hematuria, urinary tract infections, or lower urinary tract symptoms. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. Physical examination of the thyroid and abdomen was normal. Laboratory studies, including thyroid-function tests, were within normal limits. Renal ultrasound revealed a complex, multiseptated, partly cystic mass arising from the lower pole of the left kidney. A contrast-enhanced CT scan showed a 5.7 × 4.9 × 5.8 cm lobulated, low-attenuation lesion in the lower pole with no measurable enhancement; there was no renal vein involvement, lymphadenopathy, or metastases. MRI confirmed lack of hemorrhagic component and no enhancement after gadolinium. A percutaneous renal biopsy demonstrated epithelial tissue with follicular architecture and follicles containing eosinophilic material.

A 15-year-old boy was referred for left knee pain and progressive restriction of motion present for one year after a fall onto his knee at school. He had no prior medical or surgical history and took no medications. On examination, there was no swelling or signs of inflammation. Range of motion was limited to 60° of extension and 80° of flexion. Lachman and pivot-shift tests were negative, and there was no joint-line tenderness. Plain anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the knee were normal. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 33 mm, well-circumscribed lesion arising from the anterior cruciate ligament at its intercondylar notch attachment. The lesion had low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high signal intensity on fat-saturated proton-density images. The MRI appearance was interpreted as compatible with an intra-articular mucoid cyst of the anterior cruciate ligament, and arthroscopic excision with biopsy was planned.

A 73-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of painless jaundice and cholestatic liver-function abnormalities. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed intrahepatic bile-duct dilation and hypodense lesions in segments IVa and IVb of the liver causing mass effect on the common hepatic duct, raising suspicion for cholangiocarcinoma. He reported a sensation of heaviness in his eyes, but the initial neurologic examination was normal. He underwent ERCP with stent insertion, which relieved the biliary obstruction; cytologic brushings were nondiagnostic.

During the admission, he developed partial left eyelid ptosis, complete right eyelid ptosis, binocular diplopia, and retro-orbital pain. Examination confirmed a partial left and complete right oculomotor (CN III) palsy. Noncontrast CT of the head was unremarkable. MRI of the brain and orbits revealed subtle bilateral nodular lesions within the cavernous sinuses. 18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated diffuse intense metabolic activity in nodal and extranodal sites throughout the abdomen, bone, and soft tissues, as well as bilateral intense uptake in the cavernous sinuses.

A 39-year-old African American woman with a 20-year history of HIV infection on antiretroviral therapy (bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide) and hypertension presented with 2 weeks of abdominal pain and decreased urinary output. Two weeks earlier she suffered a mechanical fall and had taken ibuprofen for pain. On presentation, her serum creatinine was 5.5 mg/dL (baseline 0.91 mg/dL 3 months earlier). Urinalysis showed 3+ proteinuria and microscopic hematuria without casts; the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio was >10 g/g. CD4 count was 267/µL and HIV viral load 1,220 copies/mL. Tenofovir was discontinued, and ART was adjusted. Noncontrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed mild bilateral hydronephrosis, marked diffuse irregular bladder wall thickening, and ascites. Cystoscopy revealed diffuse nodules throughout the bladder wall without ureteral obstruction. Serologic workup—including complements, ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM antibody, and hepatitis B and C serologies—was negative. Serum protein electrophoresis showed no monoclonal protein, but serum free κ light chains were 1,988 mg/L with a κ/λ ratio of 36.4; urine immunofixation revealed monoclonal free κ light chains. A bone marrow biopsy was unsuccessful, and diagnostic paracentesis was negative for malignancy. Hemodialysis was initiated on hospital day 6 for progressive renal failure.

A 3-week-old girl was referred for evaluation of a left-sided neck swelling. She was born at 38 weeks’ gestation via forceps delivery (birth weight 2,950 g). There was no family history of fibrous tissue tumors or congenital torticollis. On examination, growth parameters and vital signs were normal. A soft, nontender swelling was palpated over the lower and middle third of the left sternocleidomastoid muscle. Passive rotation of the head to the left was limited to approximately 70° (normal 90–110°), whereas right rotation was 100°. No cervical lymphadenopathy or overlying skin changes were present. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable, and routine laboratory tests were normal.  
Ultrasonography showed a fusiform, homogeneous thickening of the ventral aspect of the left sternocleidomastoid muscle that was isoechoic to muscle, moved synchronously with muscle contraction, and maintained normal fibrillar architecture. There was no increase in internal vascularity, no lymphadenopathy, and no evidence of vascular invasion or bony involvement. The right sternocleidomastoid muscle was normal.

A 42-year-old Japanese man was admitted with a 4-day history of headache, nausea, and progressive gait instability. Neurologic examination revealed mild ataxia but no focal deficits. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated a 58-mm mass in the frontal lobe with prominent cystic components; T1-weighted post-gadolinium images showed ring enhancement, and T2-weighted images revealed only slight surrounding edema. Proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy of the solid nodule showed an increased choline-to-creatine ratio and an apparent lactate peak, whereas the N-acetylaspartate peak was within background noise. On the basis of these neuroimaging findings, a primary malignant brain tumor such as glioblastoma multiforme or a metastatic brain tumor was suspected.

An 82-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer 5 years earlier presented with upper abdominal pain. Laboratory studies showed an elevated carbohydrate antigen 19-9 level of 185 U/mL (reference <37 U/mL); serum amylase, carcinoembryonic antigen, DUPAN-2, and SPAN-1 were within normal limits. Noncontrast CT revealed a lobulated hypoattenuating mass without calcification in the pancreatic tail. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated an ill-defined, multilocular cystic mass measuring 52 × 37 mm; the main pancreatic duct was not dilated or visible within the lesion. The splenic vein was obstructed by the mass with collateral gastroepiploic venous dilation, and the splenic artery was stenotic at the site of involvement. The cyst walls showed gradual enhancement on arterial, portal venous, and equilibrium phases, with a honeycomb appearance most evident on equilibrium-phase images. No peripancreatic lymphadenopathy was identified. MRI showed the mass to be hypointense on T1-weighted images and inhomogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, containing multiple 2–15 mm cysts with irregular, thick, hypointense walls. There was no diffusion restriction on DWI or ADC mapping. MR cholangiopancreatography confirmed a multilocular honeycomb cystic mass; the main pancreatic duct remained undilated. These findings were suspicious for a serous cystic neoplasm or, less likely, a branch-duct intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm. Though a definitive diagnosis could not be made preoperatively, a distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy was performed because of the elevated CA19-9 level and vascular involvement by the mass.

A 53-year-old woman presented with a three-month history of headache and diplopia. She denied fever, weight loss, or night sweats. Her medical history was unremarkable, with no diabetes, hypertension, or prior neurologic disease. On examination, she had complete left oculomotor nerve palsy, manifest as ptosis, mydriasis, and an ‘down-and-out’ position of the left eye; the rest of the neurologic and general physical examinations were normal. Routine serum laboratory and endocrine studies were within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head demonstrated a homogeneous soft-tissue lesion occupying the left sphenoid sinus with invasion into the left cavernous sinus; the mass enhanced uniformly after gadolinium administration, and there was no intradural extension. A space-occupying lesion in the sphenoid sinus, such as a carcinoma, mucocele, or ectopic pituitary adenoma, was suspected as a preliminary diagnosis.

A 68-year-old woman presented with refractory neuroglycopenic symptoms. Over three weeks, she experienced episodes of confusion, diaphoresis, and severe weakness that improved with food intake; in the preceding 4–5 months, she lost 30 pounds despite a normal appetite. She had no history of diabetes or use of antidiabetic medications. Her medical history was notable only for hypertension and gastroesophageal reflux disease; she denied tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drug use.  

On examination, she was found to have a palpable, mildly tender right upper quadrant mass and hepatomegaly. Initial blood glucose measurements in the emergency department repeatedly fell below 50 mg/dL despite IV dextrose and oral intake.  

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed an 18.6 cm lobulated mass in the region of the right adrenal gland, composed of three confluent lesions, with compression of the inferior vena cava.  

To characterize her hypoglycemia, a dextrose infusion was stopped; her venous glucose fell to 47 mg/dL, she became symptomatic, and samples were drawn. C-peptide, insulin, pro-insulin, and beta-hydroxybutyrate levels were all low. IGF-2 measured during hypoglycemia was within the normal range. A 1 mg glucagon challenge raised her glucose to 82 mg/dL with resolution of symptoms.  

Screening for oral hypoglycemic agents was negative, and insulin antibodies were undetectable. Serum renin, aldosterone, 11-deoxycorticosterone, and 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels were normal. Urinary 5-HIAA and metanephrine levels were also normal.  

Given the negative biochemical workup apart from the large retroperitoneal mass, a decision was made to proceed with surgical resection.

A 59-year-old woman was referred after an incidental calvarial lesion was discovered on CT of the head performed for unrelated reasons. She reported occasional headaches and recent memory disturbances but denied prior head trauma or other pathology. Physical examination revealed normal vital signs and an intact neurological examination. CT of the head demonstrated a 24-mm area of osteolysis within the right frontal bone. MRI showed irregular areas of increased signal intensity on T2-weighted images and mixed signal intensity with contrast enhancement on T1-weighted images, confined to the bony calvarium without intracranial soft-tissue mass. Routine laboratory tests, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits.

A 30-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented for evaluation of worsening thoraco-abdominal venous collaterals that had developed during her pregnancy five years earlier. She had no other complaints. Vital signs were normal. Abdominal and cardiovascular examinations revealed no signs of portal hypertension or superior vena cava syndrome. Duplex ultrasound showed dilated collateral veins; the inferior vena cava was patent. Contrast-enhanced chest CT angiography demonstrated an intraluminal heterogeneous mass in the superior vena cava, extending from the left brachiocephalic venous trunk to the distal third of the vessel, with no other masses or adenopathy. Thoracic MRI confirmed an 80 × 33 mm intraluminal tumour in the superior vena cava, with a cystic component showing heterogeneous T1- and T2-weighted signals; the azygos vein was not invaded. FDG-PET imaging showed moderate uptake (SUV max, 4.8). Transthoracic echocardiography revealed no extension into the right atrium. The oncology multidisciplinary team suspected either a primary superior vena cava tumour or superior vena cava thrombosis. A percutaneous or endovascular biopsy was deemed either unsafe or insufficient for diagnosis. It was decided to proceed with surgical resection without preoperative radiotherapy or chemotherapy.

A 70-year-old previously healthy man presented with acute onset of memory disturbance, attention deficit, and gait instability. Neurological examination revealed depressed mood, cognitive impairment, and an unsteady gait; skin inspection was unremarkable. Brain diffusion-weighted MRI showed multiple scattered high‐intensity areas predominantly in the left frontal subcortex and the right posterior cingulate gyrus; FLAIR images demonstrated corresponding hyperintense lesions.

An initial diagnosis of acute embolic stroke was considered, but no embolic source was identified. Over the next weeks, his symptoms worsened and MRI lesions increased in number. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed 5 lymphocytes/mm^3, protein 118 mg/dL (normal <40), glucose 66 mg/dL (normal 40–70), and no malignant cells. Whole‐body CT scans showed no evidence of metastases.

Serum lactate dehydrogenase levels rose from 337 to 522 U/L (normal 115–245), interleukin-2 receptor was 1090 U/mL (normal 145–519), and β2-microglobulin was 4.1 mg/L (normal 1.0–1.9). A random skin biopsy was negative for malignancy.

Gadolinium-enhanced brain MRI showed no abnormal enhancement. FDG-PET demonstrated decreased uptake in the areas corresponding to the FLAIR lesions, without extracranial foci. In contrast, MET-PET revealed increased methionine uptake in the left frontal cortex, with a standardized uptake value of 2.30 and a lesion-to-normal ratio of 1.35.

A 30-year-old woman presented with a 15-year history of painful papules and nodules confined to the right half of her body. The lesions first appeared on the right upper limb and shoulder and over years extended to the right trunk, gluteal region, and thigh. Each lesion began as a small papule and slowly enlarged into a nodule. She reported that the lesions were painful, especially on exposure to cold or with touch. Her menstrual history was unremarkable, and there was no family history of similar skin lesions or uterine fibroids. 

On examination, her vital signs and general physical examination were normal. Dermatologic examination revealed multiple tender, erythematous papules and nodules, each measuring 0.5–2 cm, distributed in a sharply demarcated, segmental pattern over the right upper limb, trunk (C5 and T6 dermatomes), and the right thigh/gluteal region (S1 dermatome). Routine hematologic tests, blood urea, serum creatinine, and abdominal ultrasonography were within normal limits. HIV serology was negative.

A 39-year-old female presented with a 3-year history of a left parotid region swelling. On examination, the mass was mobile and nontender, measuring 2.5 × 2.0 cm, with no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. Fine-needle aspiration cytology showed a few atypical-appearing cells in a mucoid background, resulting in a category of “suspicious of uncertain malignant potential” (Milan IVb). Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a heterogeneously enhancing lesion in the superficial lobe of the left parotid gland, with radiologic considerations of Warthin’s tumor or pleomorphic adenoma. The patient underwent a superficial parotidectomy. Grossly, the specimen contained a 3.0 × 2.5 × 2.0 cm encapsulated tumor without hemorrhage or necrosis. Microscopic examination demonstrated a well-demarcated, focally infiltrative lesion with a lobular growth pattern. The tumor displayed predominantly microcystic areas, macrofollicular (colloid-like) cysts, papillary and solid sheet arrangements. The microcystic spaces contained gray-blue mucoid material that was periodic acid–Schiff–positive, diastase-resistant, and alcian blue–PAS positive. The cells were round to polygonal with moderate eosinophilic, vacuolated cytoplasm, bland vesicular nuclei, inconspicuous nucleoli, and a mitotic rate of 1 per 10 high-power fields. Based on these histomorphologic features, the differential diagnosis included acinic cell carcinoma (zymogen-poor), low-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma, and mammary analog secretory carcinoma.

A 68-year-old man presented with an induration and swelling in the left submandibular region. He first noted a small irregular mass in this area at age 25, which was asymptomatic and left untreated, but slowly enlarged over decades. On examination, there was firm induration and swelling confined to the left submandibular region; findings in the ears, nose, throat, head, and neck were otherwise normal. Contrast-enhanced CT showed nodular shadows with marked calcifications in the left submandibular region and a separate calcified nodule in the upper mediastinum. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. Ultrasonography-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the submandibular lesion was performed three times, but no evidence of malignancy was obtained.

A 68-year-old woman with osteoarthritis and a history of chronic hypertension and hypothyroidism presented for bilateral knee arthroplasties under spinal anesthesia. Home medications were amlodipine, losartan, and levothyroxine. Preoperative labs, including metabolic panel, complete blood count, and thyroid function, were within normal limits. On arrival in the operating room, her blood pressure was 142/70 mmHg and heart rate was 85 beats per minute. 

Spinal anesthesia was administered with 1.7 mL of 0.75% hyperbaric bupivacaine and 20 μg of fentanyl at the L4–L5 interspace. Bilateral sensory blockade to the T4 level was confirmed. Blood pressure fell to 97/62 mmHg after the block and responded to 10 mg of ephedrine. A propofol infusion was initiated. Approximately 15 minutes later, a right lower extremity tourniquet was inflated and the surgical incision was made. After 97 minutes, the tourniquet was deflated, and the patient acutely became hypertensive (235/105 mmHg) and bradycardic (52 BPM). Hydralazine lowered the blood pressure to 190/80 mmHg, but the patient then developed supraventricular tachycardia at 140 BPM with persistent hypertension. She remained hypertensive and tachycardic despite 20 mg of esmolol, 2.5 mg of metoprolol, and 25 μg of fentanyl. 

General anesthesia was induced, and an arterial blood gas showed metabolic acidosis (pH 7.20, HCO3– 17.1 mmol/L) and hyperglycemia (glucose 350 mg/dL). Anesthesia was maintained with sevoflurane, and hemodynamics gradually stabilized. The surgery lasted 3 hours and 3 minutes. She was extubated and in the postanesthesia care unit her blood pressure was 105/54 mmHg and heart rate was 109 BPM.

A 44-year-old woman with known breast cancer on chemotherapy underwent a routine Tc-99m MDP bone scan, which showed patchy increased uptake over the right frontal and right fronto-parietal skull on SPECT imaging. She denied headache, seizures, loss of consciousness, nausea, vomiting, fever, or weakness. Neurological examination was unremarkable. MRI of the brain demonstrated a well-defined extra-axial mass overlying the right frontal lobe that was iso-intense to gray matter on T1 and T2 sequences, showed no diffusion restriction in DWI and ADC sequences, and enhanced avidly after intravenous gadolinium administration, with surrounding edema.

A 59‐year‐old woman presented with visual disturbance of the left eye and hyperemia of both eyes. She reported painless facial swelling over the past year and right‐sided neck stiffness for 3 months. Previous imaging (ultrasound and CT) had shown bilateral enlargement of the lacrimal glands, bilateral extraocular muscles, and right parotid gland; two parotid biopsies were nondiagnostic.

On examination, she had a “moon face” appearance without tenderness. Visual acuity was 20/25 in both eyes; exophthalmometry measured 15 mm bilaterally. The left eye showed blepharoptosis and hypertropia. Motility testing revealed limited upward gaze in the right eye and limited downward and rightward gaze in the left eye; she denied diplopia or pain. Slit‐lamp examination showed bilateral chemosis and conjunctival hyperemia; fundi were normal.

Contrast‐enhanced orbital MRI demonstrated discrete, spindle‐shaped enlargement of the bellies of all extraocular muscles in both orbits, with well‐defined borders and no extension into the orbital fat. There was also enlargement of the lacrimal and parotid glands and thickening of the facial subcutaneous tissue.

Laboratory studies revealed normal white‐cell count, C‐reactive protein, serum IL‐2, IgG4, and thyroid‐related hormones; lactate dehydrogenase and ferritin were mildly elevated. Serologic tests for HIV and HTLV-1 were negative; EBV antibodies were positive. Systemic imaging and bone marrow studies showed no evidence of malignancy.

A 67-year-old man with no history of immunosuppression or HIV infection presented with a 4-week history of worsening pain in his left arm. On examination, there was a palpable mass in the right abdomen and bilateral inguinal lymph-node enlargement.  
  
An X-ray of the left humerus showed lytic bone lesions with a proximal humeral fracture surrounded by a soft-tissue mass. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed left axillary, mesenteric, and inguinal lymphadenopathy (largest node 3.5 cm) and a mass at the ileocecal valve.  

Laboratory studies showed normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL, MCV 81.1 fL), a white-cell count of 16.3×10^9/L with 44% lymphocytes, serum calcium 10.8 mg/dL, and albumin 2.8 g/dL. Serum protein electrophoresis was normal, and urine testing detected no Bence-Jones protein.  

Biopsy specimens from the ileocecal mass and the humeral lesion demonstrated diffuse sheets of large neoplastic cells with plasmablastic morphology. Immunohistochemical staining showed positivity for CD38, CD138, MUM-1/IRF4, CD79a, and CD30, with kappa light-chain restriction and a Ki-67 index of 75–85%. Markers negative on tumor cells included CD45, CD20, PAX5, CD56, CD5, CD23, ALK, LMP, EMA, cyclin D1, bcl6, and bcl2. In situ hybridization for EBV-encoded RNA was positive.  

Because of peripheral lymphocytosis, flow cytometry of peripheral blood was performed and revealed a monoclonal B-cell population consistent with CLL (Matutes score 4). Bone marrow biopsy showed 10–15% interstitial infiltration by CD20+, CD23+, CD5+ B cells, and cytogenetic analysis was normal (46,XY).

A 70-year-old African-American woman presented with one month of progressive dyspnea that had worsened to the point of resting dyspnea, accompanied by a minimally productive cough, bilateral pleuritic chest pain, anorexia, and 10 lb of unintentional weight loss. She denied orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, lower extremity swelling, tuberculosis exposure, asbestos exposure, radiotherapy, or prior thoracic surgery. Her medical history was notable only for COPD and a 70 pack-year smoking history.

On examination, she was tachypneic (RR 28 breaths/min), saturating 90% on room air, blood pressure 100/70 mm Hg, heart rate 90 bpm. The left hemithorax had diminished expansion, dullness to percussion, and decreased breath sounds; the trachea was shifted rightward. Cardiac and other system examinations were unremarkable.

Point-of-care ultrasound and chest radiography showed a large left pleural effusion with mediastinal shift. Thoracentesis yielded hemorrhagic fluid. Pleural fluid analysis demonstrated a pH of 7.27, red-cell count 440,000/mcL, white-cell count 14,000/mcL, fluid-to-serum protein ratio >0.5, fluid-to-serum LDH ratio >0.6, and hematocrit of 31%, consistent with an exudative, hemorrhagic effusion.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed a left upper lobe mass with multiple pleuroparenchymal nodules in both lungs and pleurae.

A 38-year-old woman with a known history of Ebstein’s anomaly presented with several weeks of progressive dyspnea. She had been undergoing routine follow-up for her congenital tricuspid valve abnormality. On examination, transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated severe tricuspid regurgitation with marked displacement of the tricuspid leaflets. A mobile, pedunculated mass was visualized in the left atrium, attached to the interatrial septum, which prolapsed through the mitral valve with each cardiac cycle.

A 57-year-old man presented with a two-month history of vague, intermittent abdominal discomfort. He denied weight loss, hematuria, change in bowel habits, or flank pain. His medical, surgical, and family histories were noncontributory, and he was a lifelong nonsmoker. Examination revealed a soft, non-tender abdomen; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, serum chemistry, urea, and urinalysis, were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a well-defined, heterogeneous enhancing lesion measuring 2 × 1.5 cm at the posterolateral upper pole of the left kidney, abutting but not invading the renal capsule, with patency of the renal vein and no hydronephrosis or nephrolithiasis. These radiologic features were interpreted as consistent with a small renal cell carcinoma, and the patient was scheduled for partial nephrectomy.

An 18-year-old man with a history of traumatic right eye enucleation five years earlier presented with headache, vomiting, and a decreased level of consciousness. Noncontrast CT of the head showed hydrocephalus and a hyperdense lesion in the right thalamus with surrounding edema, mass effect, and midline shift; a ventriculoperitoneal shunt was placed. On transfer, he was alert (Glasgow coma scale 15), with stable vital signs and an otherwise normal neurologic examination. MRI revealed a large right thalamic mass compressing the lateral ventricles. A stereotactic biopsy yielded insufficient tissue for immunohistochemical staining but demonstrated discohesive pleomorphic cells, reactive lymphocytes, necrosis, and vascular proliferation, leading to a provisional differential of high-grade glioma versus lymphoma. CSF cytologic examination showed benign mature lymphocytes without malignant cells, and a bone marrow biopsy revealed no evidence of lymphoma.

A 39-year-old white woman presented with a two-week history of a painless swelling in the anterior right maxilla. Examination revealed a hard, asymptomatic intraoral swelling of the palatal and buccal mucosa extending from the right central incisor to the first premolar. The overlying mucosa was intact and of normal color. She had no history of trauma, infection, tumors, or radiation, and all teeth in the quadrant were vital. Cone-beam CT showed a well-defined, corticated unilocular radiolucent lesion measuring 21.3×20.4 mm, causing buccal and palatal cortical expansion and divergence of the central and lateral incisor roots. Aspiration of the lesion was negative. Based on the clinical, radiographic, and aspiration findings, ameloblastoma and odontogenic myxoma were included in the differential diagnosis. An incisional biopsy was then performed.

A 42-year-old Caucasian man presented with recent onset of dysphonia. He had no significant medical history. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory testing showed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (38 mm/h; normal range, 0–17 mm/h) but a normal complete blood count, normal urea and electrolytes, normal liver function tests, normal lactate dehydrogenase level, and negative HIV serology. Serum tumor markers—including chorionic gonadotropin, neuron-specific enolase, prostate-specific antigen, carcinoembryonic antigen, CA-125, and CA-19.9—were all negative.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the mediastinum revealed a 6 × 4 × 5 cm solid lesion in the left paratracheal area, extending into the aortopulmonary window and displacing the distal trachea and branches of the left bronchus. On T2-weighted images, the lesion was homogeneously hyperintense; on T1-weighted images and on the apparent diffusion coefficient map, it was hypointense. Postcontrast T1-weighted images showed poor enhancement. No lymphadenopathy was seen elsewhere in the chest.

The MRI was extended to the abdomen, where three solid lesions (in segments II, III, and VIII) demonstrated signal characteristics identical to those of the mediastinal mass on T1- and T2-weighted images before and after contrast. There was no evidence of vascular or biliary invasion, and no abdominal lymphadenopathy was present.

A 62-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of dyspepsia and mild pain in the left hypochondrium, accompanied by a 10-kg weight loss over 3 months.
