He had a history of mild hypertension; family history was unremarkable. On examination, he had slight tenderness in the left hypochondrium without visceromegaly. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, electrolyte panel, renal, hepatic, and pancreatic function tests, and lactic acid dehydrogenase, were within normal limits. Tumor markers were also normal (CEA 2.4 U/mL; CA 19-9 22.8 U/mL; CA 125 37 U/mL). Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a hypoechogenic, solid, well-demarcated lesion measuring 57 × 38 × 27 mm in the neck and body of the pancreas. MRI showed a well-circumscribed, oval lesion that was hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2, and exhibited slight post-contrast enhancement; there was no involvement of major vessels or regional lymphadenopathy. A CT scan of the chest and further abdominal imaging excluded lymph nodes or lesions outside the pancreas. A percutaneous fine-needle aspiration biopsy was performed but yielded inadequate tissue for diagnosis.

A 34-year-old primigravida was referred at 31 2/7 weeks’ gestation for evaluation of a fetal left lung lesion. Ultrasound showed a solid mass in the left lung measuring 4.6 × 4.0 × 3.9 cm, with a CPAM volume ratio of 0.41 and mixed hyperechoic and hypoechoic areas. Color Doppler and SlowflowHD modes demonstrated internal microvascular flow within the lesion. The fetus was appropriate for gestational age with no other structural anomalies, but polyhydramnios was present (maximum vertical pocket, 9.2 cm). On fetal MRI, the lesion in the left lung was predominantly hypointense on T2-weighted images. Based on these prenatal imaging findings, the possibilities of an atypical CPAM versus a congenital peribronchial myofibroblastic tumor were considered.

A 20-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of secondary amenorrhea and virilization. She had menarche at age 11, irregular menses subsequently, and was diagnosed with polycystic ovarian syndrome at age 13; combined oral contraceptives regularized her cycles. Four months after stopping therapy, amenorrhea recurred and virilization signs—acne, low-pitched voice, temporal hair thinning, hypotrophic breasts, clitoromegaly (clitoral index 120 mm2), Tanner V pubic hair, Tanner III breasts, and a Ferriman–Gallwey score of 12—worsened. Her BMI was 27.5 kg/m2; blood pressure was 120/70 mmHg.

Laboratory studies revealed: negative pregnancy test; total testosterone 7.0 ng/mL (0.02–0.45); free testosterone 47 pg/mL (0.1–6.4); androstenedione 24 ng/mL (0.3–3.5); 17-hydroxy-progesterone 4.6 ng/mL (0.6–1.2); DHEA 9.5 ng/mL (1.3–9.8); DHEA-S 184 µg/dL (35–430); LH and FSH in the low-normal follicular range; normal cortisol and TSH. After an overnight dexamethasone suppression test, 17-hydroxy-progesterone fell to 2.3 ng/mL and free testosterone to 13.8 pg/mL but remained elevated.

Pelvic and transvaginal ultrasound showed an enlarged right ovary containing a heterogeneous, solid 5×4×2-cm mass with increased Doppler flow. Abdominopelvic CT confirmed a hypodense solid lesion in the right adnexa.

A 41-year-old woman presented with a left occipital scalp mass that had slowly increased in size over six years. She denied any history of trauma, surgery, medical conditions, medications, or allergies. On examination, the lesion measured approximately 9.0 × 8.0 cm, was soft and elastic, and was neither tender nor erythematous, with no overlying warmth. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the head revealed a well-defined subscalp mass in the left occipital region. The lesion’s internal structure was heterogeneous, with low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and isointense signal on T2-weighted images.

A 27-year-old woman with no significant medical history noted a slowly enlarging mass in the right parotid region over several months. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender swelling behind the right mandibular angle with overlying rose-colored skin; facial nerve function was intact. Ultrasonography showed a 5-cm solid mass within the right parotid gland with marked intraparenchymal hypervascularity and low peripheral vascular resistance. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration yielded blood fibrin material with lymphomonocyte elements but was non-diagnostic. Three months later, MRI of the neck demonstrated an oval, hypervascular mass in the posterior right parotid gland displacing the internal and external carotid arteries medially. Given the atypical localization, hypervascular imaging features, and inconclusive cytology, the working diagnosis was an atypical vagal paraganglioma, and preoperative embolization was planned prior to excision.

A 37-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of nonresolving left axillary lymphadenopathy. He had undergone a small-bowel transplant in childhood for necrotizing enterocolitis and intestinal atresia, followed by two living-donor kidney transplants for end-stage renal disease secondary to calcineurin-inhibitor toxicity. He was Epstein–Barr–virus positive and had recurrent posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) on three occasions, each treated with rituximab, and was maintained on tacrolimus and low-dose prednisone.

Four years after his last PTLD remission, he noted a new palpable lymph node in his left axilla but reported no weight loss, fevers, night sweats, or gastrointestinal symptoms. An ultrasound showed an enlarged left axillary lymph node measuring 10 × 26 mm with prominent fat and a thin hypoechoic cortex, thought to be benign. Given that he had received a COVID-19 booster vaccine a few weeks earlier, vaccine-related lymphadenopathy was suspected. Six weeks later, repeat ultrasound demonstrated interval growth to 29 × 19 × 13 mm.

A PET–CT scan revealed multiple fluorodeoxyglucose-avid lymph nodes in the left cervical region, left axilla, mediastinum, and left inguinal region, findings interpreted as suspicious for PTLD. There was no abnormal tracer uptake in solid organs, including the bowel. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed circumferential mural thickening of proximal jejunal loops without discrete masses or obstruction.

A 48-year-old woman, gravida 4, para 4, with a recent diagnosis of uterine fibroids and no menstrual periods for 2 years, presented to the emergency department with vaginal bleeding and passage of a foul-smelling, amorphous mass per vagina. She was pale but hemodynamically stable (BP 140/90 mmHg) and had a distended, tender lower abdomen with a uterine size reaching the umbilicus. On vaginal examination, a 30 cm pinkish-gray mass protruded through the cervix. Speculum and bimanual examinations were limited by the expelled tissue. Laboratory evaluation showed hemoglobin 10 g/dL, a normal white-cell count, platelets 627×10^3/mm^3, normal coagulation studies, electrolytes, and renal and liver function. Transabdominal pelvic ultrasonography demonstrated an enlarged, heterogeneous uterus (705 cm^3) with multiple nodules and a submucosal fibroid in continuity with the cervix; there was no free fluid in the cul-de-sac. Under general anesthesia, uterine curettage was performed, removing 2000 g of fetid, purulent, bloody tissue. During the procedure, brisk bleeding required transfusion of 600 mL of packed red cells, and broad-spectrum antibiotics were started.

A previously healthy 12-year-old boy presented with two months of paresthesia, pain, and limited movement in his lower right extremity. Initial treatment with nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs provided only mild relief. On examination two months after symptom onset, a firm mass was palpable in the right groin, and no other abnormalities were noted. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 4.4 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 76.9 fL, ferritin 4.2 µg/L, transferrin saturation 8.2%, normal liver and renal function tests, and lactate dehydrogenase 225 IU/L. Contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT showed a 7-cm mass in the right iliopsoas muscle with no lymphadenopathy. The patient received a blood transfusion, and an ultrasound-guided Tru-Cut biopsy of the pelvic mass demonstrated a small round blue cell tumor. On that basis, rhabdomyosarcoma was the initial presumptive diagnosis, and immunohistochemical studies were pending.

A 71-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation on rivaroxaban, and prior prostate radiation presented with intermittent hemoptysis over several years. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies showed a hematocrit of 41% (reference 41–50%), MCV 80 fl (80–100 fl), and bicarbonate 19 mEq/L (23–30 mEq/L); other values were unremarkable. On examination, there was a large, erythematous, soft, nontender lesion involving the right floor of the mouth with intact overlying mucosa and a blue-purple discoloration; minor manipulation produced oozing of blood. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a large, heterogeneously enhancing soft-tissue mass in the right sublingual space extending into the submandibular space, displacing the genioglossus muscle to the left. MRI of the neck demonstrated that the lesion was isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed heterogeneous enhancement on postcontrast T1-weighted images. Time-resolved contrast-enhanced MRA showed progressive, heterogeneous late arterial enhancement with neovascularity and without early dilated draining veins.

A 38-year-old healthy woman presented with a 3-month history of a painless, slowly enlarging lump on the left side of her face. She had no history of facial trauma or infection. On examination, there was a 2 cm × 3 cm, soft, mobile, nontender, well-demarcated swelling over the left parotid region; the facial nerve was intact, and there was no cervical lymphadenopathy. The clinical impression was a left parotid mass, most likely a pleomorphic adenoma or Warthin’s tumor.  
Ultrasonography showed a 2.0 cm × 1.7 cm, hypoechoic, well-defined lesion in the lateral aspect of the left parotid gland with minimal vascularity, suggestive of pleomorphic adenoma. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a 2.8 cm × 2.2 cm × 1.9 cm, well-demarcated, macrolobulated, hypodense lesion in the superficial lobe of the left parotid gland without significant contrast enhancement. The preoperative diagnosis was a lipoma of the superficial lobe of the left parotid gland, and a left superficial parotidectomy with facial nerve preservation was planned.

A 67-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of progressive abdominal pain and blood-tinged stool. His medical history was notable for well-controlled hypertension and a 20-pack-year smoking history. On examination, he had a distended, protuberant abdomen and a large, tender intra-abdominal mass. Laboratory tests, including blood counts, electrolytes, liver and renal function, and serum alkaline phosphatase, were all within normal limits. Colonoscopy revealed a 5-cm solid mass protruding from the colonic wall with overlying blood clots and necrotic debris. Biopsy of this lesion showed a sarcoma of undetermined type. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen demonstrated a 15 × 9.7 cm heterogeneously enhancing mass in the left upper quadrant with mottled calcifications and a cystic component.

A 77-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a 2-month history of right inguinal swelling. She had no personal or family history of malignancy. Physical examination revealed a hard, movable 12-cm right inguinal subcutaneous mass. Plain MRI of the mass showed a multilocular cystic structure with internal septa and a solid component; the solid areas had high signal on diffusion-weighted images and low signal on the apparent diffusion coefficient map. Serum tumor markers showed CA125 36 U/mL (reference ≤ 35 U/mL), with squamous cell carcinoma antigen and CA19-9 within normal limits. 

The mass was surgically excised. Histopathological analysis demonstrated a poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma with papillary architecture, hemorrhage, and necrosis. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for PAX-8, focally positive for WT-1, showed p53 overexpression, and was positive for cytokeratin 7, but negative for cytokeratin 20, CDX-2, and GATA3. Based on these findings, a gynecologic origin was suspected.

Transvaginal ultrasonography, contrast-enhanced pelvic MRI, and thoracoabdominal-pelvic CT revealed only hydrometra with no abnormal findings in the uterus or ovaries. Uterine cervical cytology was negative for intraepithelial lesions.

A 4-year-old girl, born to consanguineous parents, was referred for evaluation of pain and palpable lumps in the right labia majora, present since age 2. She had undergone two prior fine-needle aspirations and core biopsies, both interpreted as enchondroma without malignant features. The patient now returned with recurrent pain and firm masses in the genital region. On examination, an ill-defined, firm mass was noted within the right labia majora skin fold. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis revealed a lobulated lesion measuring 35 × 20 × 19 mm, exhibiting high signal intensity on T2-weighted images in the right prepubic space with extension into the suprapubic and retropubic (Retzius) spaces, without any evidence of bone involvement. On T1-weighted imaging after contrast, the mass showed patchy peripheral enhancement. A whole-body bone scan demonstrated no areas of increased uptake.

A 54-year-old woman presented with several months of pelvic pain and recurrent urinary tract infections. Ten years earlier, she had stage IIB cervical adenocarcinoma treated with concurrent chemotherapy, pelvic radiotherapy, and brachytherapy, completed nine years before presentation. On initial evaluation, the physical examination and pelvic ultrasound were unremarkable. A PET scan and pelvic MRI showed no evidence of recurrent disease. Urine cultures, cystoscopy, and random bladder biopsies revealed no lesions, and she was diagnosed with chronic cystitis and treated with antibiotics.

One month later, she returned with persistent vaginal pain and purulent discharge. Examination revealed a vaginal mass with green secretions. Vaginal cultures were obtained and empirical antibiotics were started. CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated dilation of the right collecting system and ureter, suggesting an obstruction that could be due to progression of cervical cancer or post-therapeutic fibrosis. New nodules in the right lower quadrant raised concern for peritoneal deposits. The clinical impression was recurrent cervical tumor in the vagina causing ureteral compression and secondary hydronephrosis with pyelonephritis. A biopsy of the vaginal mass was then performed.

A 70-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with pain in the right wisdom-tooth region persisting for 2 months; a wisdom tooth was extracted, but 6 months later he reported recurrent right mandibular pain at rest and with chewing, associated with numbness along the distribution of the inferior alveolar nerve and a visible swelling on the right mandible. On intraoral examination, there was a well-defined nodular mass at the junction of the mandibular angle and body; the overlying mucosa was intact. Palpation revealed multiple firm submandibular lymph nodes. A panoramic radiograph showed a mixed radiolucent–opaque lesion involving the right mandibular angle with displacement of tooth 18. Contrast-enhanced CT of the mandible demonstrated a 47-mm multilobulated, osteolytic, hypodense lesion containing areas of calcification, extending into the masseter and anterior digastric muscles. An incisional biopsy yielded five firm, whitish fragments (largest 1.7 cm). Microscopically, the lesion consisted of sheets and irregular lobules of atypical cells with cartilaginous differentiation; cells exhibited partial loss of lacunar arrangement, nuclear enlargement, hyperchromasia, focal binucleation, and a mitotic rate of three per ten high-power fields. Lobules were separated by thick fibrous bands, and peripheral zones contained oval to spindle dedifferentiated cells. The stroma was composed of hyaline chondroid matrix with myxoid areas; there was focal necrosis but no overt osteoid formation. The findings suggested a malignant bone tumor with predominant cartilage production, raising the possibilities of chondroblastic osteosarcoma and chondrosarcoma.

A 31-year-old man was hospitalized with fever, fatigue, and abdominal discomfort. He had no history of travel, allergies, or alcoholism. On admission his temperature was 38.3℃, pulse 92/min, blood pressure 125/75 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 18/min. Examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, and pitting edema of both legs.  
Initial laboratory studies showed:  
• Hemoglobin 8.3 g/dL, WBC 12,300/µL (eosinophils 35%, 4,310/µL), platelets 77,000/µL; eight months earlier his eosinophil count had been 2,233/µL.  
• Lactate dehydrogenase 496 IU/L; total protein 12.7 g/dL; albumin 2.2 g/dL.  
• IgE > 3,000 IU/mL; IgG > 5,000 mg/dL; IgA 152.7 mg/dL; IgM 162.8 mg/dL; Bence-Jones protein positive; β2-microglobulin 4.70 mg/L.  
• ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-mitochondrial antibody, hepatitis B surface antigen, and anti–hepatitis C antibody were negative.  
Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy showed a hypercellular marrow with 19.1% eosinophils and 22.9% plasma cells, without increased myeloid precursors. Cytogenetic analysis was 46,XY, and FISH for PDGFR and BCR/ABL was negative.  
Stool examination for parasites and a multiple antigen simultaneous test (MAST) were negative.  
Chest CT showed right pleural effusion. Abdominal CT demonstrated hepatosplenomegaly, perihepatic fluid, ascites, and enlarged abdominal lymph nodes. Echocardiography revealed minimal pericardial effusion, septal hypertrophy, and mild global hypokinesia of the left ventricle.  
Liver biopsy showed parenchymal infiltration by numerous eosinophils and plasma cells. Cytology of ascitic and pleural fluid revealed plasma cells and eosinophils.  
Serum protein electrophoresis demonstrated a monoclonal peak in the gammaglobulin region, and immunofixation electrophoresis revealed IgG with both kappa and lambda light chains.

A 7-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of a six-month history of progressive swelling and pain in the left lower face. Her medical history was noncontributory. On examination, she had facial asymmetry with a firm, partly resilient, and slightly crackling mass in the left submandibular and parotid-masseteric region extending to the ipsilateral neck; the overlying skin was intact. Intraorally, there was obliteration of the left lower gingival sulcus, with otherwise healthy mucosa and a mixed dentition; the relevant posterior teeth were intact. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, coagulation profile, and metabolic panel, were normal. Panoramic radiography demonstrated a mixed radiolucent–radiopaque lesion in the left mandible. CT of the face confirmed an expansile lesion of the left mandibular body with cortical bulging. Cervical ultrasonography revealed a vascularized mass without distinct lymphadenopathy. The preoperative surgical risk was Class 1, Grade I. Differential diagnoses considered included lymphoma, ameloblastoma, keratocystic odontogenic tumor, and aneurysmal bone cyst. An incisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia with intravenous sedation.

A 62-year-old man presented to the emergency department with sudden onset of severe abdominal pain. He denied any preceding trauma and had no known comorbidities. On arrival, he appeared pale and was hypotensive. His abdomen was distended, with localized guarding in the right upper quadrant. Laboratory studies revealed a hemoglobin concentration of 6.5 g/dL, a serum urea level of 88 mg/dL, and a serum creatinine level of 2.8 mg/dL; liver function tests were within normal limits. Ultrasonography and a noncontrast computed tomographic scan of the abdomen demonstrated moderate hemoperitoneum and an ill-defined mass with signs of recent hemorrhage abutting the liver, gallbladder, and hepatic flexure.

A 16-year-old previously healthy Caucasian male presented with a 3-week history of progressively increasing abdominal girth. He denied fever, night sweats, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, or changes in bowel habits. On examination, his temperature was 37.0°C, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, heart rate 82/min, and respiratory rate 16/min. He had marked abdominal distension with shifting dullness; there were no palpable masses or peripheral lymphadenopathy.

Initial laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, white-cell count 10.05×10^3/μL, total bilirubin 7 μmol/L, alanine aminotransferase 38 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 58 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 151 U/L, creatinine 47 μmol/L, urea 3.8 mmol/L, and lactate dehydrogenase 2596 U/L. Tumor markers including CEA, CA 19-9, and AFP were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed large-volume ascites, nodular thickening of the peritoneum, and a hypodense, heterogeneous appearance of the mesentery and omentum. Diagnostic paracentesis yielded chylous, exudative ascites (protein 45 g/L; triglycerides 0.45 g/L). 

An exploratory laparoscopy was performed and demonstrated voluminous chylous fluid, a micronodular omentum, and multiple small-bowel adhesions. Peritoneal and omental biopsies were obtained.

A 63-year-old man presented with two days of sudden bilateral chest pain, sharp and pleuritic in nature, associated with shortness of breath and a mild cough. He reported progressive dyspnea over the past month. He also noted a lesion on his scalp that had enlarged over 6 weeks; a dermatologist had performed a biopsy one week earlier, and the histopathology was pending. He had no hemoptysis, no history of cancer, diabetes, or tuberculosis, and no known family history of these conditions.

On examination, he appeared acutely ill. Blood pressure was 100/70 mmHg, pulse 130 beats per minute, temperature 37.6 °C, respiratory rate 35 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 80% on room air. A nonpainful, violet-colored lesion measuring 8 × 10 cm with dome-shaped elevation and irregular borders was present in the right occipito-parietal scalp region. Breath sounds were diminished bilaterally with scattered crackles at the lung bases. Other findings were unremarkable.

Initial laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 14,500/mm³ (80% neutrophils, 25% lymphocytes), hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL, and platelet count 278,000/mm³; serum biochemistry was within normal limits. Differential diagnoses included tuberculosis, Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia, Nocardia, fungal infection, malignancy, and Langerhans cell histiocytosis.

Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral pneumothorax. High-resolution CT of the chest revealed multiple cystic lesions in both lungs, patchy ground-glass opacities, and nodules, in the setting of bilateral pneumothorax. Bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for infectious pathogens.

A 64-year-old Hispanic woman was referred for evaluation of acute-onset right calf claudication of 1 month’s duration, now accompanied by anteromedial thigh pain and numbness and tingling on the dorsum of the right foot. She denied fevers, chills, night sweats, weight loss, trauma, infection, or intravenous drug use. Her medical history was notable for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, active tobacco use, and invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast (pT1a, cN0, cM0, ER+, PR+, HER2−) treated 1 year earlier with partial mastectomy, radiation, and exemestane. On examination, there was no palpable mass or skin change, but there was significant tenderness of the proximal medial right thigh. Peripheral pulses were 3+ bilaterally, and motor and sensory function were intact.  

A computed tomography angiogram of the right thigh showed a 16-mm lesion abutting the proximal superficial femoral artery and femoral vein. The initial differential diagnosis included thrombosed pseudoaneurysm, neoplasm, and metastatic disease. Magnetic resonance angiography favored a superficial femoral or profunda femoral branch artery pseudoaneurysm with luminal thrombus, old blood products, and perilesional enhancement. Ultrasound examination revealed a hypoechoic area with both arterial and venous flow, prompting consideration of a pseudoaneurysm or an arteriovenous fistula. A multidisciplinary team recommended surgical excision given the symptomatic vascular involvement.

A 60-year-old man presented with left knee pain of 5 years’ duration, accompanied by numbness, nighttime pain unresponsive to analgesics, and intermittent pins and needles in the left foot. He had undergone left knee arthroscopic surgery 2 years earlier at another hospital, with no relief of symptoms. There was no history of trauma or comorbid disease. 

On examination, gait was normal but with reduced stride, toe-off, and heel-strike. The knee joint had no tenderness, no palpable masses, full range of motion, and symmetric pulses. Examination of the back was unremarkable. Neurologic examination of the left lower extremity revealed decreased sensation (1/2) over the dorsal foot and mild weakness of dorsiflexion (4/5). 

Laboratory studies were within normal limits. Plain radiographs of the knee showed early tricompartmental degenerative changes with maintained joint spaces. Ultrasound of the popliteal region demonstrated a homogeneous prominent mass measuring approximately 17.4 × 85.4 mm, continuous with the tibial nerve proximally and distally; Doppler flow was patent, and the mass was noncompressible. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the popliteal fossa showed a fusiform-shaped mass with tapered ends of the sciatic nerve just above the popliteal crease, with multiple small ring-like hypodense structures on T2-weighted and contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images; the popliteal vessels and intra-articular knee structures were normal. Nerve conduction studies showed normal amplitudes, latencies, and sensory responses; electromyography revealed active denervation in the tibial-innervated muscles with neurogenic recruitment; the peroneal nerve was normal.

A 23-year-old man presented with a 4-week history of painless, diffuse swelling involving the left side of his neck and upper chest and a 1-week history of progressive shortness of breath. He also noted early satiety and unquantified weight loss. He was a farmer, did not smoke or drink alcohol, and had no prior surgeries or trauma. 

On examination, he was afebrile, normotensive, with a respiratory rate of 26 breaths per minute and pulse rate of 98 beats per minute. There was nonerythematous, non-tender lymphedema of the left neck extending to the mammary area; the jugular venous pressure was not elevated. Respiratory examination revealed signs of a left pleural effusion; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 13.7 g/dL, leukocytes 8000 cells/µL with 78% neutrophils, platelets 210 × 10^3/µL; total protein 5.5 g/dL, albumin 2.7 g/dL, normal transaminases, alkaline phosphatase 1848 U/L; creatinine 0.8 mg/dL; LDH 203 U/L. 

Chest radiography demonstrated a large left-sided pleural effusion. Diagnostic thoracentesis yielded milky white fluid with 708 cells/µL (98% lymphocytes), protein 3.4 g/dL, LDH 172 U/L, glucose 90 mg/dL, ADA 5.8 U/L, amylase 18 U/L, triglycerides 274 mg/dL, cholesterol 104 mg/dL. Cytology was negative for malignant cells and gram stain showed no organisms. These findings were consistent with a chylous exudative effusion. 

He was started on a low-fat, medium-chain triglyceride diet, octreotide, and had an intercostal drain placed, with 300–400 mL of fluid drained daily. He denied any history of recent trauma, surgery, or febrile illness. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed moderate lymphangitis in the left lung, a left-sided pleural effusion, minimal right-sided effusion, and minimal ascites. CT of the neck revealed multiple enlarged left submandibular, posterior triangle, and supraclavicular lymph nodes (largest 2.2 × 1.3 cm) and an 80% narrowing of the left internal jugular vein compared with the right.

A 47-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of increasing abdominal distension. She also reported menorrhagia, dyspepsia, and weight loss.  
On examination, she had massive ascites and a palpable lower central abdominal mass; the uterus could not be felt separately from this mass.  
Her serum CA-125 level was 477.1 IU/mL (normal < 30 IU/mL). Clinically, an ovarian tumor or uterine sarcoma was suspected.  
Transvaginal ultrasound showed a large mass posterior to the uterus and massive ascites.  
Abdominal CT demonstrated a large, predominantly solid pelvic mass with loss of the fat plane between the lesion and the uterine myometrium; the ovaries were not visualized. There was massive ascites and a small left-sided pleural effusion.  
Cytological examination of the ascitic fluid revealed no malignant cells.  
The patient was scheduled for exploratory laparotomy and definitive surgical management.

A 64-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, coronary artery disease, and hyperlipidemia experienced a transient loss of consciousness lasting a few seconds while traveling abroad. Noncontrast CT of the head revealed a lobular hyperdensity in the right posterior periventricular region tracking into adjacent parietal subcortical white matter. MRI showed an infiltrating lesion extending from the right peritrigonal area across the corona radiata into subcortical white matter. The lesion was hyperintense on T2-weighted, hypointense on T1-weighted imaging, and demonstrated gadolinium enhancement. Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery imaging noted subcortical plaques. Our differential diagnosis included primary neoplasm, demyelinating or other inflammatory processes. MR spectroscopy revealed delayed perfusion without hyperperfusion in the enhanced area, suggestive of a small vessel process. Owing to the solitary space-occupying nature of the lesion, a surgical biopsy and excision were recommended.

A 45-year-old woman presented with a several–year history of cyclical pain localized to her umbilicus, worsening during menses. She had no prior abdominal surgeries or caesarean sections and two vaginal deliveries. On examination, the umbilicus showed a normal overlying skin surface but a firm, well-circumscribed subcutaneous nodule measuring approximately 1 × 1 cm, tender to palpation and more prominent during her menstrual period. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies, including tumor markers, were not performed. Ultrasonography of the periumbilical region revealed a round, well-defined subcutaneous nodule with nonhomogeneous echotexture abutting but not attached to the underlying muscle fascia, and no connection to intraperitoneal structures or organs. Because of the characteristic clinical and ultrasound findings, no additional imaging was obtained.

A 40-year-old man was referred with a suboccipital lump present for several years. He noted gradual enlargement without pain or other symptoms and had no significant past or family history. On examination, the lesion measured 4–5 cm in diameter, had an unusual punctum, was adherent to the overlying skin, and felt cystic. Differential diagnoses tended toward a sebaceous cyst rather than a lipoma, and clinical suspicion for malignancy was low. No imaging was obtained, and the patient was scheduled for excision under general anaesthesia.

A 61-year-old man underwent a routine health maintenance examination. His medical history was notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and IgM monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance. He reported no cardiovascular or systemic symptoms and exercised regularly. Vital signs were blood pressure 139/81 mm Hg and heart rate 70 beats per minute with a regular rhythm. Cardiac auscultation revealed no murmurs, gallops, or rubs. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. A baseline electrocardiogram showed minor nonspecific abnormalities. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated normal left ventricular size and function but incidentally identified a subaortic membrane with a highly mobile mass arising from it. Transesophageal echocardiography confirmed a 9 mm by 3 mm mobile mass on the subaortic membrane within the left ventricular outflow tract without significant obstruction. A preoperative cardiac computed tomography angiogram showed only an insignificant coronary plaque and confirmed the presence of the mass on a nonobstructive subaortic membrane 11 mm below the aortic valve.

A 60-year-old man was admitted after a syncopal episode following two melena episodes the previous night. He reported a 7-kg weight loss over 3 months, and during the past week experienced asthenia and low-grade fever. His medical history included a sigmoidectomy for colonic adenocarcinoma 4 years earlier, with no evidence of recurrence.

On examination he was pale, hypotensive (blood pressure not specified), tachycardic, and well hydrated. Lung and heart examinations were unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed splenomegaly and mild lymphadenopathy in the groin and bilateral axillary regions. During the evaluation, he had vomiting with hematemesis. After hemodynamic stabilization with crystalloids and blood transfusion, upper endoscopy demonstrated a bleeding arteriolar stump in normal gastric mucosa, classified as a Forrest Ib Dieulafoy lesion, which was successfully clipped.

A pretransfusion peripheral blood count showed hemoglobin 3.9 g/dL, hematocrit 12.5%, leukocyte count 31,470/mm³ (19% medium-sized cells with basophilic cytoplasm, medium nucleus/cytoplasm ratio, loose chromatin, and an evident nucleolus), and platelets 52,000/mm³. Lactate dehydrogenase was 2612 U/L; renal function, electrolytes, hepatic enzymes, and coagulation studies were normal. Bone marrow aspiration revealed erythroid hyperplasia and 23.6% lymphocytes of varied morphology, including 2.8% large cells with basophilic cytoplasm and loose chromatin.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen showed heterogeneous, enlarged confluent lymph nodes up to 4.1 × 1.6 cm in the retroperitoneum (periaortic, interaortocaval, portocaval) and in the perigastric, peri-esophageal, and pericardial regions; the spleen was enlarged with heterogeneous attenuation consistent with infarction. Axillary lymph nodes measured up to 1.5 × 1.3 cm.

A 38-year-old man with clear-cell renal cell carcinoma diagnosed 9 months earlier, with known brain, lung, and adrenal metastases, was hospitalized for worsening respiratory distress. His initial treatment included radical nephrectomy, resection of a left frontal brain lesion, whole-brain radiation, and 5 months of sunitinib, after which he was switched to nivolumab for disease progression. During his admission, he reported multiple painful penile growths that had been increasing in number over the past 6 months. He denied dysuria, hematuria, urethral discharge, or trauma to the genitalia.

On examination, several tender, pedunculated, flesh-colored to bright red vascular-appearing nodules were noted on the corona of the penis, without regional lymphadenopathy. Laboratory evaluations for herpes simplex type 2, syphilis, HIV, gonorrhea, and chlamydia were all negative. Clinical morphology strongly suggested pyogenic granuloma.

A 54-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of sudden-onset left eye pain that had recently worsened and was associated with bulging of the eye. Family members noted intermittent squinting of the left eye. She denied nasal obstruction, epistaxis, fever, or other sinonasal symptoms. Her medical history was notable only for hypertension; there was no personal or family history of malignancy or chronic sinusitis.

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. General, neurologic, cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Ophthalmologic assessment revealed mild limitation of left extraocular movements and mild exophthalmos (21 mm by exophthalmometry) without conjunctival injection or chemosis.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the brain and paranasal sinuses showed a 2.5 × 2.0 × 1.7 cm heterogeneously enhancing mass in the left fronto-ethmoidal region, causing bone expansion and remodeling of the lamina papyracea with mild compression of the left optic nerve. MRI confirmed a left ethmoidal soft-tissue lesion with low T1 signal, high T2 signal, and contrast enhancement, without evidence of intracranial parenchymal extension.

A 34-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of gradually developing weakness in the distal lower limbs, dysesthesias, and paresthesias, beginning two months postpartum. She had increasing difficulty climbing stairs and required assistance walking; she also reported blurred vision and throbbing morning headaches. 

Past history included episodes of diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, fatigue, and intermittent night fevers; infectious workup was negative. On examination, she had facial and neck hyperpigmentation, acrocyanosis of the upper limbs, mild distal-predominant lower-limb weakness, reduced vibratory and position sense, and absent tendon reflexes. 

Nerve conduction studies and electromyography showed severe mixed axonal and demyelinating polyneuropathy in all four extremities with active denervation in the distal lower limbs. During hospitalization, her lower-limb weakness progressed to inability to move her feet. 

Laboratory tests demonstrated thrombocytosis, serum and urine IgA-lambda monoclonal gammopathy, elevated free light chains, increased plasma β₂-microglobulin, and subclinical hypothyroidism. 

Brain MRI showed signs of intracranial hypertension—including optic nerve tortuosity with sheath enlargement, flattening of the posterior sclera, and optic disc enhancement—and angio-MRI revealed constriction of the dural venous sinuses at the transverse–sigmoid junction, with secondary causes excluded. Fundoscopy confirmed bilateral papilledema. 

Abdominal MRI revealed hepatosplenomegaly and pelvic free fluid.

A 41-year-old man with a 10-year history of systemic lupus erythematosus (meeting ACR criteria) and secondary antiphospholipid syndrome (two prior DVTs, positive anticardiolipin antibodies, lupus anticoagulant) presented with 2 months of fatigue, fever, arthralgias, oral lesions, and elevated ESR. His regular medications included prednisolone 7.5 mg/day, azathioprine 100 mg/day, hydroxychloroquine 400 mg/day, and warfarin.

After increasing prednisolone to 15 mg/day and azathioprine to 150 mg/day, he developed dyspnea, persistent symptoms, and new pancytopenia. Rituximab was added and azathioprine discontinued. Two weeks later, on admission he was febrile (38 °C), tachypneic (RR 30/min), mildly tachycardic (HR 100/min), with O2 saturation 89% on room air. Exam showed splenomegaly and 1–2 cm cervical lymphadenopathy. He had painless oral ulcers and bilateral wrist swelling without motion limitation.

Laboratory studies showed pancytopenia (WBC 1.9 ×10^3/μL, Hb 8.7 g/dL, platelets 26 ×10^3/μL), ESR 102 mm/h, CRP 187 mg/L, anti-dsDNA 23.5 IU/mL, low C3 and C4, hypercalcemia (12 mg/dL), elevated pro-BNP (786 pg/mL), and negative blood cultures, HIV, EBV, CMV, and Coombs tests. Urinalysis showed trace protein.

Transthoracic echo revealed mild pericardial effusion. Chest CT was unremarkable; abdominal CT showed splenomegaly. He received IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3 days, broad-spectrum antibiotics for presumed infection, and IV pamidronate for hypercalcemia. Fever and oral lesions improved, and pancytopenia converted to bicytopenia, but anemia, thrombocytopenia, and hypercalcemia persisted despite treatment.

A 53-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of progressive stiff neck and a subjective right shoulder-blade fullness not noted on examination. He initially had right upper-extremity pain that later involved the left arm, radiating posteriorly to the proximal left wrist. He took ibuprofen with minimal relief. The next morning he awoke with sudden non–antigravity left arm weakness, and the pain resolved. A cervical spine MRI obtained by his primary provider revealed a bony lesion, and he was referred to orthopedics. One month later, his left arm pain recurred; he and his wife noted progressive atrophy of the left biceps and deltoid muscles and an unintentional 10-lb weight loss over 3 months. On examination, he appeared emaciated and fatigable. Strength in the left upper extremity was 2/5 overall, with 3/5 in the biceps and 4−/5 in handgrip; the right deltoid was 3/5 and other right arm muscles were 4/5; bilateral lower extremity strength was 5/5. There were no myelopathic signs. Repeat MRI at our institution showed an ill-defined, predominantly extradural enhancing lesion along the left side of the cervical spinal canal, most pronounced at C6–C7 and extending from C2 to C7. A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no evidence of other primary disease. Shortly after admission, he developed increased gait difficulty and an episode of urinary incontinence.

A 26-year-old man was admitted with two months of recurrent hemoptysis and progressive dyspnea. He had no fever or weight loss. Three weeks earlier he had been treated empirically for disseminated tuberculosis (pulmonary and pericardial) with anti-tubercular therapy and oral steroids after presenting elsewhere with hypotension, diffuse bilateral opacities on chest radiograph, and pericardial effusion. 

On examination he was afebrile; blood pressure 120/80 mm Hg; pulse 80 /min; respiratory rate 18 /min. He had grade II digital clubbing and scattered crackles over both infrascapular areas; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 13 g/dL; leukocyte count 7600/mm3 (64% neutrophils); platelets 210 000/mm3. Blood glucose, renal and liver function tests, electrolytes, urinalysis, coagulation studies (bleeding time, clotting time, prothrombin time) were normal. HIV serology was negative. Peripheral smear revealed a microcytic hypochromic picture. 

Chest radiograph showed diffuse bilateral alveolar opacities. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated multiple patchy ground-glass opacities in both lungs with small subpleural nodular opacities. Bronchoscopy revealed blood oozing from all segmental bronchi. Bronchoalveolar lavage contained numerous hemosiderin-laden macrophages. Transbronchial lung biopsy showed only chronic inflammation without vasculitis or malignancy. Echocardiography confirmed a small loculated pericardial effusion without ventricular dysfunction. 

Serologic testing for ANA, anti–double-stranded DNA, cytoplasmic and perinuclear ANCA, rheumatoid factor; immunoglobulin levels and complement; and 24-hour urinary protein were all normal, excluding collagen-vascular and renal causes of DAH.

A female newborn was delivered vaginally at 39 weeks’ gestation to a 32-year-old mother after an uneventful pregnancy. A routine prenatal ultrasound at 22 weeks demonstrated a 6-cm cystic mass in the left upper abdominal quadrant, associated with mild fetal pyelectasis. Follow-up ultrasounds showed persistence of this cyst. At birth, the infant was asymptomatic. Birth weight was 4000 g, length 51 cm, and head circumference 35 cm. She passed meconium on the first day and tolerated full enteral feeding without incident. 

Postnatal abdominal ultrasound revealed a 60 × 33 × 22 mm anechoic, fluid-filled, para-aortic mass in the left retroperitoneum. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a unilocular retroperitoneal cyst in the upper left abdomen, displacing the left kidney inferiorly. No other congenital anomalies were identified.

A 57-year-old woman was admitted with persistent fever and pancytopenia following debridement of a right buttock abscess. Three years earlier, she had developed thrombocytopenia and anemia after treatment for H. pylori–associated gastric ulcers; a bone marrow examination then showed hypercellular marrow with a myeloid left shift, and CT revealed splenomegaly without lymphadenopathy. She was treated for presumed Evans syndrome with prednisone and azathioprine, with only partial improvement in cytopenias. 

On current presentation, her temperature was 37.7°C, blood pressure 126/68 mm Hg, respiratory rate 28/min, pulse 122/min, and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. Findings included pallor, mild jaundice, a 2/6 systolic murmur, splenomegaly, a 3×3 cm right buttock eschar, ecchymoses on the arms and flank, and 3+ lower-extremity edema. She was disoriented to time and place.

Laboratory studies showed: WBC 2.7×10^9/L, hemoglobin 73 g/L, platelets 15×10^9/L; sodium 126 mmol/L; bicarbonate 21 mmol/L; total bilirubin 46 μmol/L; AST 78 U/L; ALT 53 U/L; albumin 29 g/L; LDH 1068 U/L; triglycerides 4.2 mmol/L; ferritin 20 392 μg/L; fibrinogen <0.6 g/L; PT 22.5 s; INR 1.93; D-dimer 3.43 mg/L. Direct antiglobulin test was negative; peripheral smear showed no schistocytes. ANA was negative.

Chest CT showed bibasilar patchy consolidation, small pleural effusions, and calcified mediastinal nodes. Abdominal CT demonstrated splenomegaly with multiple low-density lesions, similar liver lesions, bilateral renal infarcts, and a left psoas hemorrhage.

A 5-year-old girl presented with a 2-month history of an enlarging scalp mass at the site of minor blunt trauma from a ground-level fall. One week after the fall, the mother noted a flesh-colored bump that enlarged to approximately 3.0 × 3.0 cm. The patient denied fever, pain, itching, drainage, vision changes, or hearing changes.

On examination, she was well appearing. On the left frontotemporal scalp was a 3.0 × 3.0 cm oval, circumscribed mass that was firm, nonmobile, painless, and erythematous.

Unenhanced CT of the head showed a circumscribed superficial soft-tissue mass with a small internal calcification, confined to the subcutaneous fat and skin, without underlying bony involvement, osseous destruction, fat stranding, or surrounding inflammatory changes.

Ultrasound demonstrated a heterogeneous solid mass with a peripheral hypoechoic rim, internal hyperechoic foci with posterior shadowing suggestive of calcification, and prominent internal flow on Doppler imaging.

MRI revealed a heterogeneous mass with patchy and reticulated areas of increased T2 signal, peripheral rim enhancement with irregular internal reticular enhancement, a few internal foci of susceptibility artifact, and no diffusion restriction.

A 34-year-old woman with no personal or family history of breast cancer presented after an incidental finding of a right breast mass. On examination, a hard 1-cm lump was palpated in the superomedial quadrant of the right breast. An echomammogram revealed a 14-mm hypoechogenic mass with irregular contours in the internal areolar region, classified as ACR 4a. A core-needle biopsy reported an atypical papillary proliferation without definitive diagnosis. The patient underwent lumpectomy. Histological examination showed circumscribed nests of epithelial cells with delicate fibrovascular cores occasionally containing foamy histiocytes, lined by columnar cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and apical nuclei with grooves. On immunohistochemistry, tumor cells were diffusely positive for cytokeratin 5/6 and calretinin, negative for estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, HER-2, and thyroid transcription factor 1. Staining for p63 was negative, and the Ki-67 proliferation index was 5%.

A 63‐year‐old man with hypertension and a history of metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma (T3 N2 M1) treated with sunitinib followed by cryo‐reductive nephrectomy presents one year later with a new lesion on his tongue. On flexible nasendoscopy, there is a 0.5-cm by 0.5-cm pedunculated nodule on the midline dorsum of the tongue. The patient reports occasional bleeding from the lesion but has no dysphagia or odynophagia. Examination is otherwise unremarkable. Vitals are stable, and routine laboratory studies are within his baseline. A biopsy under local anesthesia is planned.

A 54-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of intermittent, pressure-like epigastric and right upper quadrant abdominal pain that was relieved by eating. She denied nausea, vomiting, jaundice, melena, hematochezia, or changes in bowel habits. She had no known medical or surgical history, no regular medications or supplements, and no alcohol, tobacco, or drug use. She emigrated from Mexico at age 16, had no primary care, and reported no environmental or animal exposures. Her family history was negative for cancer and inflammatory bowel disease.

On examination, her body mass index was 36 kg/m2 and vital signs were within normal limits. Abdominal examination revealed hepatomegaly and moderate tenderness in the epigastric and right upper quadrant regions without rebound tenderness or guarding. An electrocardiogram was normal.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, renal chemistry, coagulation studies, thyroid function, troponin, lipase, urinalysis, and urine drug screen. Liver tests revealed aspartate aminotransferase 85 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 113 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 303 U/L, γ-glutamyl transferase 344 U/L, total bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin <0.2 mg/dL. Lipid studies showed total cholesterol 284 mg/dL, HDL cholesterol 28 mg/dL, LDL cholesterol 202 mg/dL, and triglycerides 267 mg/dL. Hemoglobin A1C was 9.1%. Tumor markers included α-fetoprotein 5.2 ng/mL, carcinoembryonic antigen 50.3 ng/mL, and CA 19-9 38,892 U/mL.

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated gallbladder wall thickening, hepatomegaly (23 cm), hepatic steatosis, multiple hypodense hepatic lesions, and mild common bile duct dilation (7.3 mm) without stones, findings interpreted as acute cholecystitis and multifocal liver abscesses.

An extensive diagnostic workup for infectious (viral: Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, HIV; parasitic: ova and parasites, Echinococcus, Entamoeba; bacterial/mycobacterial: QuantiFERON tuberculosis), metabolic (ceruloplasmin, ferritin, iron profile), autoimmune (antinuclear antibodies, smooth muscle antibody, anti-LKM1, soluble liver antigen, antimitochondrial antibody, anti–tissue transglutaminase antibody, deamidated gliadin antibody, immunoglobulin levels), and hereditary/genetic (α-1 antitrypsin) etiologies revealed no significant abnormalities.

A 65‐year‐old man was evaluated for a 3‐month history of an acute onset of painful erythematous plaques around the umbilicus. A general practitioner initially prescribed a topical steroid, and when the pain intensified a few days later, herpes zoster was suspected. Over subsequent weeks, the lesions spread across the abdomen to both flanks, and the pain required opiate analgesia. Two months before presentation, he developed exertional dyspnea (New York Heart Association functional class II); a pleural effusion was detected and treated as heart failure with diuretics.

His medical history was notable for a poorly differentiated (grade II–III) transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder diagnosed 3 years earlier, with submucosal invasion but no muscular involvement, treated by transurethral resection and intravesical BCG; surveillance cystoscopy 10 months before admission showed no recurrence.

On examination, there were extensive, highly tender, erythematous, and firm plaques on the abdominal skin, centered around the umbilicus and radiating bilaterally to the flanks, with papulonodular components. Breath sounds were diminished at the right lung base. Abdominal examination was limited by pain on superficial palpation.

A biopsy of a plaque on the right upper abdomen showed skin tissue infiltrated by neoplastic cells with atypical large hyperchromatic nuclei and prominent nucleoli in a diffuse pattern with small clusters, and foci of perineural invasion. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated strong positivity for CK7 and thrombomodulin, focal positivity for P63, and negativity for CK20.

A 45-year-old woman (G3P3L3) presents with 1 year of progressive abdominal distension associated with abdominal pain, bloating, scanty foul-smelling whitish vaginal discharge, heartburn, palpitations, dizziness, generalized weakness, and bilateral lower limb swelling. She also reports anorexia, nausea, vomiting, weight loss, early satiety, incomplete rectal emptying, urinary frequency, and urgency; bowel movements and urine output are otherwise normal. Her history is notable for hypertension on medication for 5 years and a subtotal hysterectomy in 2017; she has no personal or family history of gynecologic or gastrointestinal malignancy.

On examination, she is afebrile, pale, BP 153/101 mmHg, HR 86/min, RR 20/min, SpO2 99% on room air, random blood glucose 6 mmol/L, weight 80 kg, height 160 cm, abdominal circumference 78 cm. She has bilateral pitting edema of the lower limbs and a distended abdomen with a mobile, smooth, firm mass corresponding to a 30-week gravid uterus; an extended midline scar is present. Vaginal exam shows a normal cervix, full fornices, and an anterior mass compressing the bladder with minimal foul-smelling discharge. Chest auscultation reveals bilaterally decreased air entry. On digital rectal exam, the mass compresses the rectum with free mucosa.

Laboratory studies: hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL; creatinine 274 µmol/L; GFR 17 mL/min; serum albumin 24 g/L; other electrolytes, liver enzymes, and renal function tests are unremarkable. Tumor markers β-hCG and alpha-fetoprotein are within normal limits; CA-125 is 19 U/mL and CEA is 2.358 ng/mL (both within reference ranges).

Pelvic ultrasound demonstrates a large vascular heterogeneous lobulated mass measuring 17×13 cm; the uterus and ovaries are not visualized; there is bilateral hydronephrosis with cortical thinning and dilated ureters. Pelvic MRI shows a well-circumscribed bilobular mass measuring 18×18×14 cm, inseparable from the posterior bladder wall, displacing the bladder and ureters with severe bilateral hydronephrosis; the findings are reported as consistent with uterine leiomyoma.

A 64-year-old Caucasian man presented with a ten-year history of mild diffuse abdominal pain and anorexia. He denied weight loss and had no significant family or surgical history. On examination, a mobile mass was palpable in the left upper quadrant. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a homogeneous, non-enhancing 70×100 mm mass in the mesenteric region adjacent to the small bowel, with a consistency suggesting thick mucinous or proteinaceous material, raising suspicion for an intestinal wall tumor. No other abnormalities were noted.

At laparotomy, an 80×100×120 mm solid mass was found at the root of the jejunal mesentery, infiltrating adjacent adipose tissue and the bowel wall, and abutting the superior mesenteric and middle colic vessels. Several large mesenteric lymph nodes and a small amount of free peritoneal fluid were present. The mass was excised en bloc with a loop of jejunum. Postoperatively, venous obstruction led to bowel ischemia, necessitating resection of an additional 600 mm of small intestine and primary anastomosis.

Gross examination of the resected tumor (120×80×100 mm) revealed a tan, whorled, firm cut surface without necrosis, cystic change, or hemorrhage. Histologic sections showed loosely arranged spindle cells with bland, oval nuclei and minimal cytoplasm, interspersed with plump spindle cells having eosinophilic cytoplasm. Numerous thin-walled vessels of varying caliber were present; there were no epithelioid cells, inflammatory cells, calcification, osseous metaplasia, necrosis, or mitotic figures. The tumor infiltrated the muscularis propria but had non-infiltrating margins.

Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated that the tumor cells were negative for CD117, S100, CD34, and smooth muscle actin, and positive for desmin. Peritoneal fluid was negative for malignant cells.

A 30-month-old boy was evaluated for a progressively enlarging abdominal distension over the past year. Two months before presentation, he began experiencing intermittent vomiting but maintained normal stooling. Over the week prior, he developed mild respiratory distress. He was born full term via vaginal delivery (3100 g) with no antenatal abnormalities and no family history of twinning. On examination, his temperature was normal, and he had a well-defined, firm, round, non-tender mass palpated in the left upper abdomen. Complete blood count and liver and kidney function tests were within normal limits. Serum β-human chorionic gonadotropin and α-fetoprotein levels were normal; carcinoembryonic antigen was elevated at 52.86 ng/mL (normal < 4.6 ng/mL). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a large, complex retroperitoneal mass with solid, cystic, and calcified components. The calcifications appeared to form a vertebral body and long bones resembling fetal lower extremities, and the mass displaced the left kidney anteriorly.

A 70-year-old man presented with a two-month history of painless, gradual reduction of vision in both eyes. He was systemically well. On examination, visual acuity was 6/15 in both eyes, with a left relative afferent pupillary defect. Fundoscopy showed bilateral optic disc swelling and choroidal folds. An initial CT scan of the orbits showed no space-occupying lesion. Laboratory tests revealed an elevated ESR of 60 mm/hr and CRP of 73 mg/L. Idiopathic inflammatory syndrome was initially considered, and oral prednisolone 60 mg once daily was started. 

One month later, his vision in the left eye had declined to 6/38 and xanthelasma was noted on both eyelids. Further blood tests—including ANCA, tuberculosis screen, serology for Treponema pallidum, serum ACE, vitamin B12/folate levels, and immunoglobulins—were unremarkable. Orbital MRI demonstrated bilateral, diffuse, homogenous intraconal masses with contrast enhancement. A full-body CT scan revealed periaortic inflammation, pleural involvement, bilateral perinephric fat stranding with mild hydronephrosis, and sclerotic changes in the pelvic bones and tibiae. 

An urgent orbital biopsy was performed; histology showed adipose tissue infiltrated by foamy CD68-positive histiocytes, including Touton-type multinucleated giant cells, with scattered lymphocytes. There was no IgG4 or CD1a staining.

A 24-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of a large, painless swelling in the left lower third of the face. He also noted progressive limitation of mouth opening, with maximal incisal opening of less than 1 cm. On panoramic radiography, there was cortical bone destruction and irregularity along the left sigmoid notch and ascending ramus. Contrast-enhanced CT of the mandible demonstrated an ill-defined, destructive lesion centered at the left sigmoid notch with peripheral periosteal new bone formation; the spicules radiated perpendicular to the cortex, producing a “sun-ray” appearance. Ultrasonography of the region revealed a hypo-echogenic soft-tissue mass with a well-defined border adjacent to a hyper-echogenic hard-tissue component with an ill-defined border. There was expansion and erosion of the buccal cortex, and the periosteal new bone spicules were seen radiating at 90° to the cortical surface, corroborating the CT findings.

A 68-year-old man presented with dysphagia that had progressed gradually over two months, accompanied by a weight loss of 2 kg per month. Physical and laboratory examinations were unremarkable. Upper endoscopy revealed an elevated, irregular mass with ulcerative lesions in the middle intrathoracic esophagus. Chest computed tomography demonstrated a large anterior mediastinal mass and swelling of the subcarinal lymph node; coronal views showed that the subcarinal node extended directly into the esophageal lumen. CT-guided percutaneous biopsy of the anterior mediastinal mass and endoscopic biopsy of the esophageal mass were performed. Histopathological examination of both specimens revealed squamous cell carcinoma.

A 28-year-old woman presented with a 14-day history of epigastric pain partially relieved by mild analgesics. She also reported diffuse pruritus, jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools. Examination showed a well-appearing but jaundiced patient with a firm, palpable mass in the epigastric and right hypochondrial regions. Laboratory studies revealed a cholestatic pattern of liver‐function tests; CEA and CA19-9 levels were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a large (approximately 13 × 9 × 13 cm), heterogeneous, hypoechoic mass with internal cystic areas located between the left hepatic lobe and pancreas, with dilation of the intrahepatic bile ducts and proximal common bile duct. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a well-defined, 12.8 × 12.1 × 10.9 cm lesion centered in the pancreatic head and body, with mixed solid and cystic components, intense enhancement, displacement but no invasion of adjacent structures, and marked dilation of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts.

A 41-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 10–12-week history of a painless swelling in the molar region of the hard palate that had grown slowly and symmetrically. He denied dysphagia, odynophagia, or systemic symptoms. Family history was unremarkable. On examination, there was a 1.5 × 3.0 cm firm, elastic, non-ulcerated swelling on both sides of the hard palate in the molar–premolar area. No cervical lymphadenopathy was detected. Routine serum chemistry, including lactate dehydrogenase (3.95 μmol/l) and albumin (61%), was within normal limits. Serologies for hepatitis A, B, and C were negative. During excision, the palatal bone appeared uninvolved, and the wound healed slowly over 4–5 weeks.

A 17-year-old female with no prior medical history presented with a 5-day history of recurrent central abdominal pain and multiple episodes of vomiting. On examination her abdomen was non-distended with minimal tenderness in the central quadrant. An abdominal ultrasound revealed a well-circumscribed hypoechoic lesion measuring 6.5 cm in diameter near the left hepatic lobe. Subsequent MRI of the abdomen demonstrated a pancreatic mass with both cystic and solid components. A thoraco-abdominal CT scan was performed, and serum pancreatic tumour markers (chromogranin A, CA19.9, CA125) were within normal limits.

A 75-year-old postmenopausal woman with no family history of breast cancer presented with a palpable mass in the right breast. Physical examination revealed no axillary lymphadenopathy. Mammography showed two lesions in the right breast: an irregular mass measuring 1.5 × 1.4 cm in the upper-outer quadrant (BI-RADS 5) and a second retromammary lesion measuring 1.9 × 1.0 cm (BI-RADS 1). A core-needle biopsy of the BI-RADS 5 lesion demonstrated small, uniform tumor cells floating in lakes of extracellular mucin, some with signet-ring cell morphology, alongside areas of single-cell infiltration characteristic of lobular carcinoma. No ductal or lobular in situ components were identified. Immunohistochemical studies revealed complete loss of membranous E-cadherin in tumor cells with positive internal control, negative staining for chromogranin A and synaptophysin, positive estrogen receptor, and negative progesterone receptor and HER2.

A 45-year-old man, non-smoker with no comorbidities, presented with a one-month history of change in voice and difficulty swallowing without pain, fever, breathlessness, or stridor. Indirect laryngoscopy revealed a large submucosal swelling in the supraglottic region involving the right pyriform sinus and false vocal cord with medialization of the right false cord; the true vocal cords were not seen. The provisional clinical diagnosis was a supraglottic laryngeal malignancy. CT of the neck showed a multilobulated, well-encapsulated lesion of fat attenuation (–83 HU), measuring 1.7 × 3.1 × 1.9 cm, in the right aryepiglottic fold with multiple thin septations, nonenhancing septae, and obliteration of the right pyriform sinus; the ventricles and true vocal cords appeared normal. Video laryngoscopy demonstrated a pedunculated, smoothly marginated, soft tissue mass arising from the right aryepiglottic fold, moving with respiration and obscuring the endolarynx.

A 50-year-old man presented with a three-month history of hoarseness, persistent dry cough, and intermittent dyspnea, which had worsened over the preceding two weeks. He denied fever, neck swelling, weight loss, night sweats, hemoptysis, tuberculosis exposure, or symptoms of laryngopharyngeal reflux. He worked as a mechanic, had a 30-year, 90–pack-year smoking history, and frequently strained his voice. 

On examination, he had a severely hoarse voice. On the GRBAS scale, his overall grade was 3 (severe hoarseness) with grade 3 roughness; his maximum phonation time was seven seconds. Flexible laryngoscopy revealed an irregular, pinkish mass involving the middle third of both true vocal folds, with whitish lesions at the edges. Vocal fold mobility was preserved on phonation and inspiration. A chest radiograph was normal.

Given his age, smoking history, symptoms, and the irregular appearance of the bilateral lesions, a provisional diagnosis of glottic carcinoma was made.

A 17-year-old girl presented with somewhat severe upper abdominal pain radiating to her shoulder. She reported a 2-month history of pain awakening her from sleep, partially responsive to analgesics, worse when supine, and unrelated to eating. She had a long history of intermittent, nonspecific abdominal and back pain over several years that responded to analgesics and antispasmodics. She also noted nausea and anorexia that responded to Cypro-Vita™, but denied weight loss, persistent diarrhea, or flushing. There was no surgical or allergy history, and family history was noncontributory.

On examination, she had tenderness in the upper abdomen; the remainder was unremarkable. Laboratory studies—including complete blood count, liver and kidney function tests, prolactin, thyroid-releasing hormone, growth hormone, and parathyroid hormone—were all within normal limits. 

Abdominal ultrasonography revealed multiple hyperechoic lesions with a hypoechoic rim in both liver hemilobes without biliary dilation. Upper and lower endoscopies and breast ultrasonography were normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed numerous well-defined hypodense liver masses (10–40 mm) with peripheral contrast enhancement involving about half of the liver, and a blurred hypodense lesion measuring ~25 mm between the pancreatic body and tail. Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated a streaked-appearing pancreas with reactive peripancreatic lymph nodes but no discrete mass.

A 10-year-old previously healthy boy presented with gradually worsening visual acuity over 1 year, associated with fatigue, severe polyuria–polydipsia (168 cc/kg/day), and gait instability, without fever or systemic symptoms. On examination he was afebrile and normotensive, with diuresis of 7 cc/kg/h. Neurologic findings included ataxic gait, cutaneous hyperesthesia, impaired deep sensation, hyperreflexia, and vertical gaze palsy (Parinaud’s syndrome). Ophthalmologic evaluation revealed visual acuity of 3/10 (right) and 2/10 (left), decreased pupillary light reflexes, semi-mydriasis, and bilateral grade-2 papilledema. Tanner staging was I. Laboratory tests showed normal serum potassium, HbA1c, and renal function; urinary osmolality was 64 073 mosm/L. Hormonal studies demonstrated an 8-am cortisol of 1.7 µg/dL and TSH of 2320 µU/mL. CSF β-hCG was elevated at 15.54 mIU/mL; plasma β-hCG and α-fetoprotein were negative. CSF immunohistochemistry for placental alkaline phosphatase and GFAP was negative. Brain CT (noncontrast and contrast) showed a well-circumscribed 10×12 mm suprasellar lesion abutting the optic chiasm and an 8×10 mm lobulated pineal lesion with a macrocalcification; both enhanced homogeneously. MRI additionally revealed multiple small T2/FLAIR hyperintense, contrast-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia, internal capsules, cortex, nodular ependymal enhancement, and pial involvement consistent with cerebro-medullary dissemination.

A 56-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of intermittent headaches that had increased in severity over the past 2 months. The headache was located mainly in the right parietal region, throbbing in nature, without diurnal variation, and rated 7–8 of 10 on a numerical pain scale. Analgesics (acetaminophen and ibuprofen) provided only partial relief. She also reported mild right nasal congestion and intermittent mild otalgia. On physical examination, vital signs were normal and the only notable finding was a deviated nasal septum. 

Noncontrast CT of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated expansion of the sphenoid bone with a diffuse ground-glass matrix and sclerosis obliterating the sphenoid sinus cavity. Subsequent MRI showed an expanded mass in the sphenoid bone with hypointense signal on T1-weighted images, low (dark) signal on T2-weighted images, and heterogeneous enhancement on post-contrast sequences.

A 69‐year‐old man presented with left‐sided pleural effusion that had progressively increased over two years despite repeated drainage. He had no significant respiratory symptoms beyond mild dyspnea. Laboratory tests showed a white‐cell count of 9170/μL and a C‐reactive protein level of 0.99 mg/dL. Serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) was mildly elevated at 10.2 ng/mL but decreased spontaneously on follow‐up; brain natriuretic peptide was <5.8 pg/mL. PET–CT showed no abnormal fluorodeoxyglucose uptake. Diagnostic thoracentesis yielded an exudative, lymphocyte‐dominant effusion (99% lymphocytes). Pleural fluid cytology was class II, and fluid CEA was 3.3 ng/mL. Adenosine deaminase in the fluid was 20.2 U/L; acid‐fast staining and cultures of sputum and fluid were negative. Because the effusion recurred over more than two years without an identified cause, medical thoracoscopy was performed. Pleural biopsy specimens showed no specific findings, but an unexpected mass was visualized on the parietal pleura and was completely resected.

A 3-year-old boy had a 2-year history of intermittent abdominal pain, worsened over the past 7 days—more at night and after feeding—associated with nonprojectile vomiting. He passed hard stool every 4–5 days and had been anuric for 2 days, with some weight loss. No relevant medical, surgical, or family history. Exam: malnourished, pale; a 3×3 cm mass palpable below the umbilicus; no distension; normal bowel sounds; other systems unremarkable. Labs: CBC, PT-INR, electrolytes normal; BUN 53.03 mmol/L, creatinine 176.84 μmol/L (normalized during admission); HIV, HBV, HCV negative; total protein 45 g/L; urine 2–3 WBCs/HPF. USG abdomen: echogenic 5.5×5.1 cm lesion in lower abdomen/pelvis with twisting of vessels and mesentery; “differential diagnosis of mesenteric mass and thickened mesentry.” CT abdomen/pelvis: a 15.7×6.4×11.5 cm well-defined, lobulated, homogeneous nonenhancing cystic mass with thin internal septations; “swirling appearance of the mesentery and superior mesenteric vein around the superior mesenteric artery in an anticlockwise direction representing midgut malrotation with middilatation of bowel loops suggesting volvulus.”

A 43-year-old man presented with a painless mass in the right preauricular region that had been slowly enlarging over one year. He denied any history of facial trauma. On examination, there was a firm, 2 cm diameter mass in the right preauricular area. Otoscopic examination revealed swelling of the anterior wall of the right external acoustic meatus covered by normal skin. There was no tenderness over the temporomandibular joint, no trismus, and no hearing loss. The remainder of the physical and general examinations was unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a solid, lobulated lesion adjacent to the capsule of the right temporomandibular joint. The lesion was isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and demonstrated partial enhancement after gadolinium administration. Clinically, a benign tumor of the right temporomandibular joint was suspected.

A 31-year-old woman presented with 2 months of progressive abdominal distention. She had no significant past medical or surgical history. On examination, there was moderate ascites but no abdominal pain or palpable mass. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a well-defined hyperechoic mass in the left lumbar region with intratumoral cysts and dilation of surrounding blood vessels, large volumes of free intraperitoneal fluid, and a left pleural effusion. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 34 × 76 mm, well-defined mass in the left upper abdomen that demonstrated vivid, homogeneous enhancement in both the arterial and venous phases. The lesion was supplied by a markedly dilated right gastro-omental artery with serpiginous peripheral vessels. No invasive features were noted.

A 63-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a tongue nodule. His history included Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome and atrial fibrillation, both well controlled. Physical examination revealed slight swelling at the right lateral edge of the tongue, and the patient reported spontaneous pain. The lesion was initially diagnosed as inflammation of the foliate papilla and managed with local care. 

Two years later, an elastic, soft mass measuring 4 mm in diameter was observed at the same site. The mass was clinically considered a benign tumour and was excised under local anaesthesia. 

Microscopic examination showed a well-delineated lesion without a distinct capsule, composed of multiple cysts of various sizes and shapes, many containing eosinophilic fluid. The stroma consisted of fibrous connective tissue without lymphocytic infiltration. The cystic cavities were lined by a bilayered epithelium of luminal columnar cells and basal cuboidal cells; both cell types exhibited eosinophilic cytoplasm, and scattered clear cells were present. There were no mitotic figures or cellular atypia.

A 35-year-old nonsmoking man presented with a 15-day history of rapidly progressive dyspnea, facial puffiness, and hoarseness of voice. He denied hemoptysis, headache, or prior tuberculosis. His medical and surgical history was unremarkable. On examination, he was tachypneic with stable vital signs. He had marked facial plethora, periorbital and upper-body edema, and dilated veins on the chest and neck wall. There was no pallor, clubbing, lymphadenopathy, ptosis, or Horner’s syndrome. Chest auscultation revealed decreased breath sounds in the right parasternal third and fourth intercostal spaces. The remainder of the examination was normal.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, leukocyte count 8500/mm3, and platelets 320,000/mm3. Serum electrolytes, renal and liver function tests were within normal limits. Levels of LDH, AFP, and β-HCG were normal. Bone marrow examination showed no malignant infiltration. Serology for HIV and hepatitis B and C was negative.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax revealed a well-defined, enhancing soft-tissue mass measuring 10.3 × 9.3 cm in the superior mediastinum, with compression of the superior vena cava, trachea, and right upper-lobe bronchus, and encasement of the right innominate and subclavian vessels.

A 40-year-old woman in good health was referred for planned liposuction-assisted excision of a left upper arm lipoma. One year earlier, an outside ultrasound had shown a 5.5 × 2.9 cm hypoechoic mass “consistent with a superficial lipoma.” She now reported continued growth and new discomfort in the upper arm but denied numbness or paresthesia. On examination, there was a firm, mobile subfascial mass in the left upper arm. Surgical excision was scheduled. On the day of surgery, it was noted that the mass became more prominent with elbow flexion and less prominent with extension, suggesting a possible intermuscular or intramuscular lesion.

A 35-year-old man presented for follow-up with a complaint of a sensation of something moving in the anterior aspect of his right knee. He had no pain or swelling. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender, mobile mass palpable medial to the patellar ligament on the anterior knee. Standard radiographs of the knee showed two radio-opaque loose bodies: one immediately anterior to the patellar ligament and another within the suprapatellar pouch. Four years earlier, he had undergone extended curettage and polymethylmethacrylate cementing for a Campanacci grade 1 giant cell tumor of the right distal femur. He had an uneventful recovery, returned to full activity, and had no clinical or radiological evidence of tumor recurrence at the distal femur.

A Japanese woman in her late twenties, a non‐smoker with no significant medical or family history, was referred after routine chest radiography detected a right hilar mass. She was asymptomatic. Vital signs were normal (blood pressure 101/69 mmHg; pulse 103 beats/min; respiratory rate 16 breaths/min; O2 saturation 98% on room air). Examination revealed clear lung fields and a normal heart without murmurs. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within reference ranges.

Chest computed tomography showed a uniform, uncalcified mass approximately 40 mm in length adjacent to the vertebral body of the seventh thoracic vertebra, contacting the pleura and vertebra without extension into the intervertebral foramen. T1‐weighted MRI demonstrated a mass with signal intensity similar to muscle, abutting the pleura. T2‐weighted MRI showed high signal intensity, especially at the margins. Diffusion‐weighted imaging revealed diffusion restriction around the lesion’s rim. Contrast‐enhanced T1‐weighted MRI showed strong, homogeneous enhancement. Based on CT, the mass was thought to be a schwannoma; however, the T1WI and T2WI findings were atypical for that diagnosis.

A 31-year-old African-American man presented with a 1-year history of multiple bumps on the right chest and right arm. The lesions were nontender, occasionally pruritic, and bled with mild trauma. On examination, there were multiple closely distributed pink-to-violaceous papules and nodules on the right lateral chest, interspersed with hyperpigmented macules; the larger lesions had overlying hyperkeratotic scale. Similar hyperpigmented macules and rare papules were noted on the right arm. The patient denied high-risk behaviors for HIV, was in a monogamous heterosexual relationship, and had no history of immunosuppression. He was otherwise healthy, with an unremarkable review of systems; an HIV test within the past year was negative.

A punch biopsy from a chest lesion was performed. Hematoxylin and eosin staining showed epidermal hyperplasia overlying a well-circumscribed proliferation of epithelioid cells in the papillary dermis. The epithelioid cells had pale-staining cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, and intracytoplasmic vacuoles; there was no nuclear atypia or abnormal mitoses. A mixed inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes, neutrophils, and eosinophils was present. Scattered within the lesion were small vascular channels lined by a single layer of plump endothelial cells and areas of extravasated red blood cells.

Immunohistochemical studies revealed CD31 positivity in the vessel lining and in rare cells within the nodule, and factor VIII–related antigen highlighted numerous epithelioid cells. Stains for human herpes virus 8 and Warthin-Starry were negative.
