A 30-year-old man, recently treated with total thyroidectomy and lymph node dissection for papillary thyroid carcinoma with cervical nodal metastases, presented with progressive left shoulder and arm pain and paresthesia. He had no motor or sensory deficits on neurologic examination. Physical examination revealed a few enlarged cervical lymph nodes. Laboratory studies were unremarkable, and serum thyroglobulin level was low.

CT and MRI of the spine showed a left paraspinal mass centered in the left side of the C6 vertebral body with extension from C4 through C7 and a large extra-osseous soft-tissue component. Additional findings included multiple enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes, pulmonary nodules, and other lytic bone lesions. The initial clinical impression was widespread metastasis from thyroid carcinoma versus a primary malignant nerve sheath tumor of the cervical paraspinal area.

Endoscopic ultrasound–guided fine-needle aspiration of paratracheal and subcarinal lymph nodes revealed scattered non-necrotizing granulomas without malignancy. Excisional biopsy of a lung nodule showed sheets of epithelioid to spindle cells with pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, irregular vesicular nuclei, prominent tumor necrosis, scattered well-formed non-necrotizing granulomas, and focal clear-cell change. Immunohistochemical stains demonstrated strong, diffuse positivity for pankeratin, cytokeratin 19, and epithelial membrane antigen, and negativity for thyroid transcription factor-1, PAX8, and thyroglobulin.

An 18-year-old woman fell from a horse, sustaining forced traction of her left middle finger. Over 4 months, she reported insidious burning pain and numbness over the dorsal proximal interphalangeal joint of that finger, worsening with direct pressure. She denied fever or weight loss.

On examination, there was a 1 × 1 cm diffuse, mobile mass on the ulnar-dorsal aspect of the left middle proximal phalanx. There was pain on palpation and a positive Tinel’s sign at that site. Range of motion of the finger joints was limited to mild flexion; no skin changes, lymphadenopathy, or paresthesias were noted. Sensation was intact.

Plain radiographs of the middle finger revealed a 6.5 × 5 mm circular radiolucent area with thinning of the posterior cortex of the proximal phalanx. Ultrasound showed vascular trajectories with ectasic venous flow communicating with an arterial branch. MRI without gadolinium demonstrated a 36 × 5 × 11 mm lesion on the dorsal proximal phalanx displacing the extensor tendons; after gadolinium, the lesion enhanced and there was a 1 mm focal cortical discontinuity with an ectasic vascular channel.

A 55-year-old man presented with a slowly growing, asymptomatic tumoral lesion in the frontal region of the scalp, first noted 3 years earlier. He reported no pain, discharge, or overlying skin changes. His medical history was notable for significant head trauma 24 years earlier, resulting in a frontal bone fracture, right brachial plexus injury with resultant right arm palsy, encephalomalacia, and epilepsy managed with levetiracetam, oxazepam, and folic acid. He also had a remote subdural hematoma from a second head injury and a history of alcohol abuse.

On examination, there was a 2 × 3 cm firm, ovoid subcutaneous mass in the frontal area. The lesion was adherent to the underlying tissues but covered by normal-appearing skin. No cervical lymphadenopathy was palpable. 

A cranial computed tomography scan demonstrated a 2- to 3-cm soft-tissue mass in the frontal scalp, with an underlying bony defect in the frontal bone. There was evidence of encephalomalacia and ventricular asymmetry consistent with prior imaging, but no intracranial mass lesion was identified.

A 47-year-old man was referred with a 6-month history of a gradually enlarging, painful mass in the right posterior mandible. Four years earlier, he had undergone extraction of an impacted third molar at the same site and was diagnosed with an odontogenic keratocyst. He now reports slight paresthesia but no drainage or tooth displacement. 

On examination, intraoral inspection revealed a 3×4 cm tumefaction in the right mandibular molar region with lingual cortical expansion; the overlying mucosa was intact. Extraorally, there was right facial swelling and buccal vestibule expansion. No skin lesions or other features suggestive of naevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome were noted. Laboratory studies, including blood counts and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. A chest radiograph showed no abnormalities.

Panoramic radiography demonstrated a multilocular, “soap-bubble” radiolucency with periosteal reaction along the lower border of the right mandible. Cone-beam CT revealed a well-defined, expansile radiolucent lesion with corticated borders in the right mandibular angle extending into the ramus and body, associated with the distal root of the second molar and showing root resorption. There was focal perforation of the buccal and lingual cortical plates with outward expansion of the lingual cortex.

A 50-year-old man presented with a 7-month history of a growth on the lower anterior gingiva. His medical history was notable for epilepsy managed with medication and hypertension; he had a 32-pack-year smoking history and occasional alcohol use. On intraoral examination, a 3.0 × 2.5 × 1.0 cm sessile, firm, nontender lesion was noted on the labial gingiva extending from the left mandibular canine to the first premolar, with slightly erythematous but intact mucosa and no bleeding. Associated teeth were unremarkable, and regional lymph nodes were not palpable. A periapical radiograph demonstrated mild alveolar bone rarefaction in the region of the left mandibular lateral incisor to first premolar. A provisional diagnosis of pyogenic granuloma was made, and an incisional biopsy was performed.

Microscopic examination showed sheets of large ovoid to polygonal tumor cells with pale eosinophilic granular cytoplasm and eccentrically placed nuclei; there was nuclear pleomorphism, a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli, frequent mitoses, and focal spindle-cell morphology. Hematoxylin–eosin and Masson-Fontana stains did not demonstrate melanin pigment.

A 55-year-old man with no smoking history and no prior medical conditions was diagnosed one month earlier with a moderately differentiated pulmonary adenocarcinoma of the right lower lobe after presenting with hemoptysis. He was referred to urology for evaluation of macroscopic hematuria. Further history revealed urinary frequency, urgency, and intermittent episodes of visible hematuria over the past three months. On examination, he appeared in reduced general condition but had no other abnormalities; urine appeared normal in color. A dipstick test showed hematuria (2+). Routine laboratory studies were within normal limits, and the prostate-specific antigen level was 2 ng/mL. As part of staging for his lung cancer, a thoracoabdominal-pelvic CT scan showed the known right lower lobe lung mass with mediastinal lymphadenopathy and demonstrated focal thickening of the right lateral bladder wall with arterial enhancement; the upper urinary tracts were unremarkable and no other metastatic sites were identified. Cystoscopy under locoregional anesthesia revealed a normal urethra and prostate, but inflammatory, bullous lesions on the trigone and right lateral bladder wall; these areas were biopsied with a resectoscope.

A 30-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with a several-month history of loss of axillary and facial hair. He denied headaches, visual changes, or other neurologic symptoms. Physical examination confirmed loss of secondary body hair; the remainder of the general and neurologic examinations was normal.  
Laboratory studies revealed:  
• Testosterone 0.18 ng/mL (reference, 3–12 ng/mL)  
• FSH 0.63 mIU/mL (1.3–11 mIU/mL)  
• LH 0.59 mIU/mL (1.1–10 mIU/mL)  
• Prolactin 20.3 ng/mL (2–10 ng/mL)  
• TSH, free T4, and cortisol response to a 1 μg synacthen test were within normal limits.  
Ophthalmologic examination showed preserved visual acuity and a normal fundus.  
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and sella demonstrated a large suprasellar mass with diffuse cerebral and spinal leptomeningeal enhancement.  
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was unremarkable; PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis was negative, and cytology and tumor markers in CSF and blood were negative. Angiotensin-converting enzyme levels were normal. A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no other lesions.

A 42-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a pararectal mass incidentally found on routine examination. He denied urinary or gastrointestinal symptoms and had no significant medical history. Physical examination revealed a smooth-margined, firm, elastic mass in the left ischiorectal fossa; the rectal mucosa appeared normal on digital rectal examination. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 5-cm, well-defined solid mass abutting the left anal wall and extending into the inferior perineum, with intense heterogeneous arterial enhancement, persistent delayed-phase enhancement, and a feeding vessel. MRI showed homogenous intermediate signal intensity on T1-weighted images; T2-weighted images revealed heterogeneous low and intermediate signal intensity with linear low-signal bands and focal high-signal areas; delayed fat-suppressed, gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted images exhibited homogenous enhancement. These findings suggested a hypervascular lesion with a fibrous component. The differential diagnosis included solitary fibrous tumor, gastrointestinal stromal tumor, aggressive angiomyxoma, leiomyoma, neurogenic tumor, and soft tissue sarcoma.

A 58-year-old woman presented with a 6-week history of left upper eyelid swelling, aching around the left eye, and intermittent vertical binocular diplopia. She denied changes in visual acuity, fever, weight loss, or night sweats. On examination, there was proptosis with downward displacement of the globe and a non-tender palpable mass in the region of the left lacrimal gland. A CT scan showed a well-circumscribed 2.9 × 1.9 × 2.9 cm mass in the left extraconal soft tissue involving the lacrimal gland. Her medical history was significant for follicular lymphoma diagnosed 9 years earlier on cervical lymph node biopsy, treated with eight cycles of CHOP, with subsequent remission. Given this history, the orbital mass was clinically thought to be possible relapsed follicular lymphoma. Other considerations included epithelial neoplasm, idiopathic orbital inflammatory disease, and other specific inflammatory diseases.

A 7-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of a dark brown papule with an ecchymotic halo on his left upper back. His mother reported that the lesion had appeared as a black macule at birth and had recently increased in size. The patient denied symptoms and any history of trauma. On examination, the lesion was a well-demarcated, 4 mm, dark brown, irregularly shaped papule surrounded by a thin pale zone and a peripheral ecchymotic ring. A punch biopsy was performed. Histologic examination revealed dilated vascular channels in the upper dermis lined by endothelial cells protruding into the lumen (“hobnail” appearance) with occasional intraluminal papillary projections. In the deeper dermis, narrower vascular channels dissected collagen bundles, and there were numerous extravasated erythrocytes. Immunohistochemical staining showed a strong positive reaction with CD31 and focal positive reactions with CD34 and D2-40. The lesion resolved completely after the biopsy.

A 67-year-old man was referred for further evaluation of icterus and upper abdominal pain. His medical history was notable for hypertension and urolithiasis; he was a 10–pack‐year smoker and drank little alcohol. On examination, he was jaundiced and had tenderness in the epigastrium. Laboratory studies showed a total bilirubin of 9.6 mg/dL, elevated hepatobiliary enzymes, an HbA1c of 7.2%, a carcinoembryonic antigen level of 28.8 ng/mL, a CA19‐9 level of 76.6 U/mL, and normal serum IgG4 and amylase levels. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a diffusely enlarged, sausage-shaped pancreas with delayed enhancement and a capsule-like rim, together with intrahepatic bile-duct dilation. MRI confirmed diffuse pancreatic enlargement with low T1 signal, slightly high T2 signal, and high diffusion-weighted imaging signal. FDG-PET showed diffuse uptake in the pancreas (SUVmax 8.6) and multiple hypermetabolic lymph nodes (SUVmax 10.0). ERCP demonstrated a stenosis of the lower bile duct and diffuse narrowing of the main pancreatic duct.

A 50-year-old woman with a history of thalassemia minor presented with several weeks of vaginal bleeding.  
Pelvic MRI showed a 3.2 × 1.9 × 4.0 cm expansile cervical mass with heterogeneous T1/T2 signal, homogeneous gadolinium enhancement, diffusion restriction, and no enlarged lymph nodes.  
FDG PET/CT demonstrated a 4.0 cm hypermetabolic cervical lesion (SUVmax 12.0) with possible left parametrial involvement and no distant metastases.  
Biopsy of the cervix revealed solid sheets of small-to-medium pleomorphic neoplastic cells, extensive necrosis and hemorrhage, brisk mitoses, and plasmacytoid/rhabdoid cytologic features with focal pseudoacinar arrangements.  
Immunohistochemical staining was diffusely positive for vimentin, WT1, CD99, and p16, with preserved INI1; scattered cells were positive for cytokeratins AE1/AE3, CD138, and FLI1; all other markers (including desmin, myogenin, CD34, CD31, MelanA, HMB45, chromogranin, synaptophysin, TLE1, p63, and PAX8) were negative.

A 34-year-old woman, asymptomatic, was referred after a right lung nodule was noted on chest radiography and followed for 10 years at another clinic. Serial CT imaging showed growth of the tumor from 3.0 to 5.0 cm over that time; the lesion was well enhanced and closely abutted the right pulmonary artery. FDG-PET demonstrated increased uptake in the lesion (maximum SUV 5.50) with no other sites of abnormal accumulation. Based on the clinical history and radiographic appearance, malignancy was suspected, including slow-growing lung carcinoma or a mediastinal neoplasm such as lymphoma or teratoma. The patient underwent endobronchial ultrasound–guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) under local anesthesia. EBUS revealed a hypervascular mass adjacent to the trachea, and three passes were made with a 22-gauge needle, yielding sufficient core tissue. No complications occurred.

A 70-year-old woman with a 45-pack-year smoking history and a history of well-differentiated tubular adenocarcinoma of the colon (pT3N0M0, stage II) underwent surveillance chest CT 2 years after hemicolectomy. A 0.2-cm nodule in the right lower lobe was first noted at the time of colectomy, grew to 0.3 cm at 12 months, and to 0.5 cm at 14 months postoperatively. The lesion had developed a central cavity with slightly irregular wall thickness. Serum tumor markers were within normal limits (CEA 2.9 ng/mL; CA19-9 6.8 U/mL; CA125 4.0 U/mL). Because of concern for colorectal cancer metastasis, a thoracoscopic wedge resection was planned.

A 73-year-old woman presented with a 15-pound weight loss over 4 months and intermittent abdominal pain. Her medical history included cardiovascular disease on aspirin, hypertension, an appendicectomy, and three C-sections. On examination, she had abdominal tenderness without signs of peritonism. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a heterogeneous 4 cm mass spanning the D3–D4 segments of the duodenum. Upper-endoscopy–guided biopsy at an outside center suggested an epithelioid stromal gastrointestinal tumor (GIST). 

She underwent D3–D4 duodenectomy with cholecystectomy and duodenojejunal anastomosis. Gross examination of the resected intestinal segment (15 × 2.5 × 3.5 cm) showed a 4.5 × 3.5 × 3.5 cm exophytic mass on the mesenteric side with an overlying mucosal ulceration. 

Histologic evaluation demonstrated nested epithelioid cells with large round basophilic nuclei, vesicular chromatin, prominent nucleoli, eosinophilic fibrillary cytoplasms, and occasional neuroblastic rosettes. Immunohistochemical staining revealed diffuse strong positivity for S100, SOX10, synaptophysin, and CD56, and negativity for CD117 (c-kit), DOG-1, MelanA, HMB45, PanCK, and chromogranin. The Ki-67 proliferation index was 30%. Nerve involvement was present; one lymph node and the gallbladder were free of tumor.

A 66-year-old woman of Vietnamese background presented over 1 year with diarrhoea, back pain, suprapubic pain, dehydration, and intermittent rectal bleeding. Physical examination was normal. Laboratory studies showed hyponatraemia (sodium 122 mmol/L), a normal potassium level, a haemoglobin concentration of 99 g/L, an elevated carcinoembryonic antigen level of 5.7 mg/mL, negative other tumour markers, and non-significantly elevated inflammatory markers. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 150 mm segment of circumferential mid-sigmoid colon wall thickening with homogeneous density (42 HU precontrast, 76 HU postcontrast), no proximal obstruction, no perisigmoid fat stranding, no lymphadenopathy, no ascites, and no liver lesions. Colonoscopy revealed a 50 mm, large, frond-like, circumferential, partially obstructing sigmoid mass without active haemorrhage. Biopsies showed fragments of a tubulo-villous adenoma with low-grade dysplasia and no evidence of malignancy.

A 50-year-old Caucasian man with congenital dyserythropoiesis, secondary hemosiderosis, and systemic hypertension was asymptomatic but underwent routine thoracic and abdominal CT scanning. The scan revealed a 3.5 cm right posterior mediastinal, paravertebral nodule of soft-tissue density that enhanced after intravenous contrast. He was a former smoker and had undergone splenectomy and liver biopsy 5 years earlier; histologic review then showed splenic congestion and hemosiderin deposits in both spleen and liver but no evidence of myeloid metaplasia. Given his chronic anemia and the imaging findings, a video-assisted thoracoscopic resection was performed with the presurgical differential diagnosis of paraganglioma, schwannoma, and nodal hematopoietic tumor infiltration.

A 55-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of increasing left upper abdominal pain. She denied fever, weight loss, hematemesis, or melena. Her temperature was 37°C, pulse 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and blood pressure 150/80 mmHg. Examination revealed mild tenderness in the upper abdomen. Hematological, biochemical, and coagulation tests were within normal limits. She had no history of abdominal surgery, trauma, or comorbidities, and her family history was unremarkable.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated an anechoic cystic structure measuring 3.4 × 3.4 cm within a normal-sized spleen with a normal border and a non-dilated splenic vein. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed a normal-sized spleen containing three hypodense lesions; the largest lesion, in the lower pole, measured 3.4 × 2.4 × 2.6 cm. These lesions exhibited peripheral nodular enhancement in the arterial phase and progressive peripheral enhancement in later phases. No other abdominal abnormalities were noted.

The initial differential diagnosis included hamartoma, hemangioma, lymphangioma, and lymphoma.

A 62-year-old Asian man presented with five months of mild dysphagia to solid foods without chest pain, nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain. His history was notable for Billroth II gastrectomy six years earlier for gastric cancer, exploratory laparotomy with adhesiolysis and inguinal hernia repair two years earlier, and eight cycles of XELOX chemotherapy. He had hypertension treated with nifedipine. He did not smoke or drink and had no relevant family history.

On examination, temperature was 36.1 °C, heart rate 61 bpm, respiratory rate 17 breaths/min, blood pressure 153/84 mmHg; lung and abdominal examinations were normal, and there was no peripheral edema.

Laboratory tests showed elevated anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies, glycosylated hemoglobin 7.1%, total bilirubin 21.2 μmol/L, indirect bilirubin 14.2 μmol/L, and CYFRA21-1 40 ng/mL; all other laboratory values were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated a 55 × 35 × 29 mm round lesion in the middle and upper esophagus with homogeneous enhancement and luminal stenosis. Upper endoscopy revealed a smooth, elevated lesion 25–30 cm from the incisors with intact mucosa. Endoscopic ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic, homogeneous mass approximately 41 mm in diameter arising from the muscularis propria, and it was provisionally diagnosed as a stromal tumor.

A 29-year-old woman presented with an eight-month history of dull, paroxysmal epigastric pain that was unrelated to meals and did not radiate. Two days before admission, she experienced a single episode of hematemesis. Physical examination was notable only for mild epigastric tenderness without palpable mass. Complete blood count revealed hypochromic microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 6 g/dL, MCV 66.7 fL, MCHC 27 g/dL); liver and renal function tests were normal. Serum carcinoembryonic antigen and CA 19-9 levels were within normal limits. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed a 7-cm polypoid submucosal lesion near the gastric cardia on the posterior wall, approximately 30 cm from the incisors, but endoscopic biopsy was nondiagnostic. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated a 7-cm solid-cystic tumor arising from the posterior wall of the stomach near the cardia with heterogeneous enhancement.

A 29-year-old woman in otherwise good health presented with several nodules on the left external auditory canal. The lesions were:  
• Reddish to pink, approximately 1 × 2 cm in size  
• Slowly enlarged over several months  
• Severely pruritic but non-tender  
• Fixed, firm, and smooth-surfaced, without ulceration, crusting, or discoloration  
No regional lymphadenopathy was noted. Routine complete blood counts were within normal limits.

A 29-year-old woman was referred after an incidental finding of abnormal echoes in her left kidney on routine ultrasonography. She was asymptomatic, with no urinary symptoms, hematuria, flank pain, fever, or weight loss. Her medical history was unremarkable, with no hypertension, diabetes, or family history of hereditary disorders; she neither smoked nor drank alcohol. On examination, vital signs were normal, and there were no palpable masses, costovertebral angle tenderness, or skin stigmata of tuberous sclerosis. Laboratory studies, including renal function and urinalysis, were within normal limits. An abdominopelvic CT scan revealed an irregular soft-tissue mass in the upper pole of the left kidney with heterogeneous density and stranding of the perirenal fat; multiple small cortical cysts were noted bilaterally. After multidisciplinary discussion, the patient underwent a da Vinci–assisted laparoscopic partial nephrectomy. Intraoperatively, a 3 × 4 cm mass was found in the superior pole, with two satellite nodules measuring up to 0.8 cm. All lesions were excised without complication. Rapid intraoperative pathology described an eosinophilic cell tumor, and margins appeared clear. The procedure was completed, and the patient recovered uneventfully.

An 8-month-old male infant, born full term to non-consanguineous parents, was brought for evaluation of progressive right-eye proptosis and blackish discoloration of the temporal sclera, present since birth. Multiple well-circumscribed, smooth, non-compressible cutaneous nevi (1–3 mm) were noted on the back and limbs; there was no periocular skin pigmentation. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable, with no lymphadenopathy and no family history of pigmentary disorders. Examination under anesthesia of the right eye confirmed three-quadrant scleral pigmentation sparing the nasal side, an anterior nodulo-ulcerative swelling adjoining the cornea, a hazy cornea, and an unrecordably high intraocular pressure; the left eye was normal. MRI of the brain and orbits showed no intraocular mass lesion, a T1-weighted hyperintense signal corresponding to the anterior nodule, thinning of the sclera, and a stretched optic nerve, findings suggestive of a right-eye staphyloma.

A 55-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 10-month history of spontaneous, progressively painful umbilical discomfort. A few days after the onset of pain, he noted a firm nodule at the umbilicus that gradually increased in size and became ulcerated and tender. On examination, he was in good general condition. The umbilical lesion measured 6 cm by 6 cm, was ulcerated over its entire surface, and bled on contact. Deep palpation of the abdomen revealed a poorly defined, firm mass approximately 8 cm in diameter in the right hypochondrium. Biopsy of the umbilical lesion demonstrated a well-differentiated, infiltrating adenocarcinoma. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed homogeneously enhancing umbilical tissue growth and irregular, circumferential thickening of the right third of the transverse colon measuring approximately 8.3 cm. Total colonoscopy revealed no endoluminal lesion.

A 66-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, and psoriasis presented with three days of fever, cough, and shortness of breath. On admission, temperature was elevated; blood pressure 115/52 mm Hg; heart rate 75 b/min; respiratory rate 20 b/min; oxygen saturation 93% on room air; BMI 29 kg/m2. Physical examination showed bilateral chest crackles; cardiovascular examination was normal. ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm with right bundle branch block and left axis deviation. Chest radiography revealed patchy peripheral ground-glass opacities in both lungs and soft consolidations in the right middle lobe. SARS-CoV-2 PCR was positive. Laboratory studies showed WBC 5.9 × 10^3/μL, hemoglobin 10 g/dL, CRP 146 mg/L, ferritin 2619 μg/L, creatinine 190 μmol/L, and D-dimer 2.3 mg/L FEU. He became severely hypoxic shortly after admission and was managed with nasal-cannula oxygen, then CPAP in the ICU to maintain SpO2 95%.  
Transthoracic echocardiography revealed normal biventricular size and function, mild pulmonary hypertension (estimated RVSP 48 mm Hg), and two right atrial masses: an echodense mass on the right atrial roof in the four-chamber view and an echolucent mass protruding into the tricuspid annulus on the RV inflow view. A TTE one month earlier had shown no intracardiac mass.  
Because of the patient’s severe COVID-19 and elevated D-dimer, the right atrial masses were presumed to be thrombi, and he was anticoagulated with heparin followed by warfarin (INR target 2–3). Repeat TTE after two weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation showed no change in the masses. A transesophageal echocardiogram was deferred due to respiratory instability, and a cardiac MRI was planned for further evaluation.

A 23-year-old nulliparous woman at 7 weeks of gestation presented with right iliac fossa pain. She had a history of appendicectomy and obesity, but no other comorbidities. Her inflammatory blood markers were normal. Transabdominal ultrasound confirmed a viable intrauterine pregnancy, a normal left ovary, and a 6.4 cm × 4 cm multiloculated cystic mass in the pelvis; the right ovary was not visualized separately. The differential diagnoses of a cystic right ovarian mass or multicystic benign mesothelioma were considered. As her acute symptoms settled with analgesia, expectant management was chosen for the first trimester.

Six weeks later, she returned with increasing pain. Examination revealed localized peritonitis with tenderness and guarding in the right iliac fossa. Repeat ultrasound showed that the multicystic mass had grown to 13 cm × 7 cm. Given the increasing pain, peritoneal signs, and uncertain nature of the mass, a decision was made to perform an exploratory laparotomy at 14 weeks of gestation.

A 49-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of a slowly enlarging mass on the volar distal aspect of the right middle finger. He denied trauma. He reported pain with minor trauma and movement. His history included gastroesophageal reflux disease, hyperlipidemia, and gout; medical therapy for gout did not affect the finger lesion. On examination, the lesion measured 1.0 cm by 1.7 cm, was tender to palpation, and had a central area of ulceration with an overlying scab. The finger had full range of motion and intact neurovascular status. Initial clinical differential diagnoses included glomus tumor, pyogenic granuloma, ganglion cyst, or other neoplasm. A shave biopsy was performed. Initial histopathology showed a well-circumscribed multinodular tumor within the dermis and subcutis, with ulceration of the epidermis. There were focal papillary structures and evidence of lymphovascular invasion. Histologic findings were concerning for digital papillary adenocarcinoma, and slides were sent for expert consultation.

A 50-year-old Indian woman with diabetes and hypertension presented with right upper abdominal discomfort, loss of appetite, and low-grade fever. She denied jaundice.  
On examination, she had hepatomegaly and tenderness in the right hypochondrium.  
Laboratory studies showed normal liver-function tests. Serological tests for amoebiasis and hydatid disease were negative. A chest radiograph was normal.  
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed an 11 × 7.5 × 11.2 cm predominantly anechoic, thick-walled lesion arising from the inferior surface of the liver, with low-level internal echoes and a homogeneous echogenic area in its superolateral portion. The gallbladder was not visualized separately; other abdominal viscera were normal.  
Aspiration of the lesion yielded turbid fluid, but the lesion persisted despite repeated aspirations and antibiotic therapy.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a well-defined, lobulated cystic lesion with a solid component in its superior part, abutting the colon and duodenum. The lesion was interpreted as an infected non-parasitic cyst.

An 82-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of progressive left scrotal enlargement and a sensation of heaviness. He had no history of genital infection. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender, painless mass in the left scrotum that was adherent to the overlying skin and the underlying testis. The right testis was normal in size and consistency, and no inguinal lymphadenopathy was palpable. Routine blood and urine tests were within normal limits.

Scrotal ultrasonography showed a 7 × 4 cm intratesticular extra-testicular, well-circumscribed mass with mixed heterogeneous echogenicity, minimal color Doppler flow, and adherence to the left testis and scrotal wall. The left testis demonstrated a striated echotexture with alternating hyper- and hypoechoic lines and reduced volume compared to the right. A small ipsilateral hydrocele with fine internal echoes was present; the right scrotum was unremarkable.

Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a left paratesticular mass with intermediate signal intensity on T1-weighted sequences, low heterogeneous signal on T2-weighted images, and minimal enhancement on post-contrast T1-weighted images. The lesion abutted the left testis and scrotal wall. The right testis appeared hypoplastic but showed homogeneous enhancement. The hydrocele corresponded to a spermatic cord collection.

The lesion’s slow growth and imaging characteristics suggested a benign process; however, because of its size, adherence to the scrotal wall, and involvement of the ipsilateral testis, malignancy could not be excluded based solely on imaging.

A 30-year-old woman with a history of pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect and major aortopulmonary collateral arteries presented with worsening dyspnea and progressive exercise intolerance. In infancy, she underwent unifocalization of right- and left-sided collateral arteries with Gore-Tex grafts, and at age 7 she had VSD patch closure and placement of a 20 mm RV-to-pulmonary-artery homograft connected to a 20 mm Gore-Tex conduit. 

On examination, she was normotensive, heart rate 110 bpm, with elevated neck veins (estimated CVP 15 cm H₂O). Cardiac auscultation revealed a normal first heart sound and a 4/6 high-pitched ejection systolic murmur at the left parasternal border; the second heart sound was normal. Laboratory tests showed monocytosis of 12.2% (reference 2–10%) and NT-proBNP 4843 pg/mL (reference 30–125 pg/mL).

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a severely dilated and hypertrophied right ventricle with moderately reduced systolic function; the left ventricle had normal systolic function (EF 55–60%). The estimated RV systolic pressure was near systemic (∼90–100 mmHg) based on the tricuspid regurgitation Doppler signal. The RV-PA conduit was severely calcified with peak outflow velocity 4.2 m/s and peak gradient 70–80 mmHg.

Cardiac CT revealed a stenotic RV-PA conduit due to a calcified mural mass, with evidence of subsegmental pulmonary emboli.

A 67-year-old postmenopausal woman was referred to gynecologic oncology after a right salpingo-oophorectomy performed by her general gynecologist for an incidentally discovered complex ovarian mass. She had presented complaining of pelvic “heaviness” and increased urinary frequency. Her obstetric history included three vaginal deliveries and two spontaneous abortions; she underwent menopause at age 54. She had a remote history of left salpingo-oophorectomy at age 29 for ovarian torsion, with a benign pathology.

Laboratory evaluation showed a CA-125 level of 31 U/mL. A preoperative colonoscopy was normal. Pelvic ultrasound and subsequent MRI demonstrated an 11-cm complex right adnexal mass; there was no ascites, lymphadenopathy, or carcinomatosis, and the endometrial thickness was 3.9 mm.

Histologic examination of the ovarian specimen revealed an infiltrative neoplasm with a mixture of tubular, glandular, papillary, corded, and solid growth patterns. The tumor cells had scant cytoplasm, moderately atypical vesicular nuclei with overlap, variably prominent nucleoli, increased mitotic activity, and focal intraluminal eosinophilic secretions.

Immunohistochemical stains showed that the tumor cells were strongly positive for CK7 and PAX8, and focally positive for HNF1B, GATA3, TTF1, CD10, and p16. They were negative for estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, WT1, and calretinin. Staining for p53 was wild-type, and DNA mismatch repair proteins (MLH1, PMS2, MSH6, MSH2), PTEN, and ARID1A were retained.

An 83-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of abdominal pain that worsened with breathing and movement. Her medical history was notable only for hypertension. On examination, she had tenderness and rebound tenderness in the right lower quadrant. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 14.93 × 10^3/µL (reference range, 4–10 × 10^3/µL) with 88.0% segmented neutrophils (reference range, 50.0%–75.0%) and a C-reactive protein level of 11.4 mg/dL (reference range, 0–0.3 mg/dL). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated an ovoid, well-demarcated, homogeneously enhancing mass, 1.3 cm in diameter, at the cecal tip (appendix orifice), associated with distal appendiceal dilatation, appendiceal wall thickening, and surrounding fat infiltration. On coronal and sagittal reconstructions, the mass appeared to be located in the submucosal layer with normal overlying mucosa. Therefore, a subepithelial tumor, similar to a neuroendocrine neoplasm, was presumed, accompanied by acute appendicitis.

An 84-year-old woman was found incidentally to have a clival mass on CT after a head injury. She was followed with imaging, and 2 years later the lesion extended into the intranasal space through the sphenoid sinuses, prompting a biopsy at an outside hospital that yielded a diagnosis of olfactory neuroblastoma. She was referred for further evaluation.  
MRI showed a lesion centered on the clivus extending laterally into the cavernous sinuses, superiorly to the sella turcica, and anteriorly into the sphenoid sinuses and posterior nasal aperture; it was isointense on T1-weighted images, iso- to hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and homogeneously enhanced with gadolinium. CT demonstrated extension from the clivus to the ethmoidal sinuses and posterior nasal aperture with erosion of the sphenoid bone. Whole-body 18F-FDG PET detected no extracranial lesions.  
Serum levels of anterior pituitary hormones were within or near normal limits.  
A repeat biopsy of the intranasal component revealed sheets and lobules of oval atypical cells with uniform nuclei and scant cytoplasm. Immunohistochemical studies showed positivity for cytokeratins AE1/AE3, synaptophysin, chromogranin A, and CD56; weak, patchy expression of ACTH; and negativity for GFAP, S-100, Pit-1, SF-1, GH, TSH, PRL, FSH, and LH. The mitotic count was approximately three per 10 high-power fields, and the Ki-67 index was 1%–5%. Electron microscopy demonstrated scattered cytoplasmic neuroendocrine granules.

A 16-year-old girl presented with a 2-year history of a painless, gradually enlarging swelling of the right perimandibular region. She delayed presentation due to COVID-19 restrictions. On facial examination there was hard, non-tender, diffuse swelling of the right mandible with normal overlying skin. Intraorally, there was a buccal vestibular swelling extending from the second premolar to the retromolar area with superficial mucosal ulceration distal to the second molar. There was no paresthesia of the lower lip. Laboratory tests showed normal blood counts, biochemistry, and coagulation; ESR was 24 mm/h (normal 0–10), and procalcitonin was 0.41 ng/mL (normal 0.17–0.35), suggesting mild superinfection. Chest radiograph and cardiac evaluation were unremarkable. Cone-beam CT of the mandible revealed a well-defined expansile radiolucent lesion measuring 64×25×26 mm in the right mandibular body, angle, ramus, and sigmoid notch. There was bucco-lingual cortical thinning with areas of perforation, inferior displacement of the impacted right third molar into the mandibular angle, resorption of the roots of the first and second molars, and inferior displacement of the mandibular canal.

A 62-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of worsening right lower-quadrant abdominal pain and constitutional symptoms. He had coeliac disease, gastro-oesophageal reflux, and iron deficiency. Three weeks before presentation, a CT scan in the community showed a 6 cm × 8.5 cm × 7 cm soft-tissue mass in the right lower quadrant arising from distal ileal loops with associated lymphadenopathy. A recent colonoscopy showed a 5 mm tubular adenoma in the descending colon and noted mass effect at the terminal ileum, but no intraluminal lesions. On arrival at the emergency department, he was hemodynamically stable, temperature was 37.8°C, and he had tenderness and a palpable, tender fullness with focal guarding in the right iliac fossa without generalized peritonitis. Laboratory tests showed a leukocyte count of 21.1 × 10^9/L, thrombocytosis of 600 × 10^9/L, neutrophilia of 14.97 × 10^9/L, lymphocytosis of 4.20 × 10^9/L, monocytosis of 1.88 × 10^9/L, normal hemoglobin, normal electrolytes, normal liver function tests, normal CEA, and a C-reactive protein of 151 mg/L. A repeat contrast CT scan demonstrated an interval increase in the mass to 10.9 cm × 8.2 cm × 10.6 cm communicating with small-bowel loops, right-sided omental caking, and mild ascites. He was started on broad-spectrum IV antibiotics. The next day, a CT angiogram of the abdomen and pelvis showed findings most consistent with a contained perforation secondary to a neoplastic process; the mass was adjacent to the ileocolic branches of the superior mesenteric artery without vascular aberrancy.

A 46-year-old West Indian man presented with a two-day history of intermittent rectal bleeding, coffee-ground vomitus, and symptoms of anemia. He had a history of peptic ulcer disease but denied nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory–drug use. Three weeks earlier, he noted jaundice with pruritus, dark urine, constitutional symptoms, and back pain.

On examination, he was anemic and deeply jaundiced but hemodynamically stable. There was minimal epigastric tenderness and a palpable, non-tender distended gallbladder (Courvoisier’s sign). Digital rectal examination revealed altered blood, and nasogastric aspirate was coffee-ground in appearance. Clinicians considered an upper gastrointestinal bleed secondary to peptic ulcer disease, periampullary pancreatic carcinoma, and locally advanced gastric carcinoma.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, normal coagulation studies and electrolytes, and liver-function tests consistent with obstructive jaundice. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a normal liver, a distended gallbladder (109 mL), a dilated biliary tree, and a bulky, heterogeneous pancreas.

Over the next two days, persistent rectal bleeding led to a further drop in hemoglobin to 4.4 g/dL. Limited blood availability and unavailability of endoscopy prompted laparotomy. At surgery, an actively bleeding duodenal ulcer in the first part of the duodenum was oversewn. A bosselated mass was noted in the head and neck of the pancreas without evidence of local invasion. A biopsy of the pancreatic mass was taken.

A 68-year-old woman with a history of hysterectomy and a maternal history of Crohn’s disease was transferred for recurrent severe lower abdominal pain. Four weeks earlier, she had presented with constant lower abdominal pain without diarrhea, intermittent constipation, and a 4-pound weight loss. She denied smoking, alcohol, or drug use. 

Initial abdominal CT showed abnormal wall thickening and fat stranding within the terminal ileum consistent with an infectious or inflammatory process; mesenteric lymph nodes in the right lower quadrant were mildly prominent, and neoplastic disease could not be ruled out. Colonoscopy revealed normal mucosa except for superficial linear erosions in the distal rectum, sigmoid diverticulosis, and an 8 mm ascending colon polyp. The terminal ileum appeared diffusely congested without ulcerations; biopsy specimens from the ileocecal valve showed no pathology. 

Laboratory studies demonstrated a hemoglobin of 12 g/L, hematocrit 37.5%, WBC 10.2 cells/mcL, platelets 338 cells/mcL, normal serum chemistries, C-reactive protein 45 mg/L, and calprotectin 408 µg/mL. Tuberculosis T-spot and hepatitis panels were negative.

She was diagnosed with Crohn’s disease and treated with intravenous methylprednisolone, transitioned to oral prednisone, and discharged. Ten days later, she returned with recurrent pain; a repeat CT was similar, and she was treated with ciprofloxacin, metronidazole, and a prednisone taper with planned outpatient infliximab. Two days after discharge, she again developed worsening abdominal pain. A third CT showed terminal ileal wall thickening, fat stranding, free fluid, ileus, and a possible abscess or phlegmon. 

On transfer, she was hemodynamically stable and afebrile, with ongoing abdominal pain but no nausea, diarrhea, bleeding, fever, or chills. Labs again showed slight anemia with otherwise normal counts and chemistries. Gastroenterology performed a repeat colonoscopy with biopsy of the terminal ileum; histology revealed only mild inflammatory changes and congestion.

A 39-year-old man presented with a one-week history of epigastric pain and hematemesis. He had no significant medical or surgical history, took no medications, and had no allergies. He was a smoker and did not drink alcohol. On examination, vital signs were stable, the abdomen was soft without tenderness, and a rectal examination revealed no melena. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 6.3 g/dL; after transfusion, it rose to 10 g/dL. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a submucosal lesion in the gastric antrum with ulceration of the overlying mucosa. Biopsy showed no malignant features. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed a well-defined, heterogeneous, pre-pyloric mass measuring 6×5 cm with fat attenuation in the antropyloric region.

A 35-year-old Caucasian woman was referred to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon for evaluation of a firm, painless lump in her left cheek that had progressively enlarged over 12 months. She reported no constitutional symptoms, had no significant past medical history, and was a non-smoker who drank alcohol only rarely.

On examination, there was a 3 × 3 cm firm, well-circumscribed mass adjacent to the left mandibular body, anterior to the parotid gland and masseter, with no overlying cutaneous or mucosal changes and no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. Systemic examination was unremarkable. A dental examination and an orthopantomogram excluded an odontogenic origin.

The lesion was excised intraorally under general anesthesia. The gross specimen measured 30 × 23 × 20 mm and appeared as a tan, fibrofatty mass. Microscopically, skeletal muscle fibers were infiltrated by epithelioid tumor cells with abundant pale eosinophilic cytoplasm and mildly pleomorphic, hyperchromatic nuclei with inconspicuous nucleoli. Patchy pseudoacini and rosette formation were present, along with increased apoptosis and geographic necrosis. No lymphovascular or perineural invasion was identified.

A 28-year-old man presented with severe pain in the right posterior mandible for 3 months. He had no extraoral swelling or obvious deformity. Intraoral mucosa appeared normal, but palpation revealed obliteration of the right ascending ramus. A panoramic radiograph showed a well-defined multilocular radiolucent lesion extending from the mesial aspect of tooth #47 into the ascending ramus. Pulp vitality testing of the adjacent tooth was positive. Based on the clinical history and radiographic appearance, a provisional diagnosis was made.

A 48-year-old woman presented with a painless right parotid swelling of 12 years’ duration, which had slowly increased in size over the past several months. She denied weight loss, fevers, or night sweats. Her medical and surgical histories were unremarkable. On examination, there was a firm, smooth-margined, non-tender, immobile mass in the right parotid region; the overlying skin was normal, there was no facial nerve weakness or paresthesia, and no cervical lymphadenopathy was evident.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the head and neck revealed a mildly lobulated lesion centered in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland measuring approximately 4.3 × 3.2 × 5.2 cm, extending anterior to the mandibular ramus into the masticator space. The lesion was T2 hyperintense, T1 intermediate, demonstrated avid contrast enhancement, and was well-marginated with preserved adjacent parotid parenchyma.

Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration of the mass yielded mostly blood and no diagnostic cellular material.

A 54-year-old man with hypertension and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis presented with two months of generalized weakness and a 20-kg weight loss. He had undergone a PAN-CT scan that revealed extensive innumerable lesions in the liver, lungs, bones, spleen, and thyroid. A liver biopsy showed infiltration by a high-grade undifferentiated malignant neoplasm. He was treated for hypercalcemia with hydration and denosumab and received a reduced first cycle of CVP chemotherapy without immediate complications.

On admission he was cachectic but hemodynamically stable. Initial blood pressure was 101/65 mmHg, heart rate 65 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Laboratory studies showed hypercalcemia managed as above; creatinine and BUN were at baseline for his ESRD. Two weeks into his hospital stay, he experienced a hypoglycemic episode during a PET scan and was treated with intravenous dextrose. Review of serial capillary glucose measurements revealed values ranging from 1.7 to 5.1 mmol/L. At the time of a documented hypoglycemic episode (glucose <2.8 mmol/L), the following studies were obtained:

• Serum insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, and β-hydroxybutyrate  
• Thyroid-stimulating hormone 21.57 mIU/L (0.35–4.94) and free T4 6.15 pmol/L (9.00–19.00)  
• Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) 25 ng/mL (61–200)  
• Random glucose 1.7 mmol/L  
• Estimated GFR 11 mL/min/1.73 m2  
• Electrolytes unchanged from baseline  

He was labeled as having hypoglycemia, and the initial differential diagnosis included lymphoma infiltration of the adrenal glands, end-stage renal disease causing hypoglycemia, and nutritional inadequacy.

A 10-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a mass in the distal left forearm that limited pronation and supination. Two years earlier, he had sustained a distal radius fracture; follow-up radiographs after healing then had shown no abnormalities. On current evaluation, radiographs demonstrated a 6.5-cm lesion in the distal syndesmosis arising from the radius, with pressure erosions on the distal radius and ulna and slight splaying of the bones. A triple-phase bone scan revealed moderately increased radiotracer uptake in the distal shafts of the left radius and ulna and in the distal radial physis. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a large mass at the distal radial and ulnar metadiaphyses measuring approximately 6 cm craniocaudad, 3.7 cm anteroposterior, and 3 cm transverse; it was isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images and had overall increased signal intensity on T2-weighted images with a central area of decreased signal.

A 60-year-old man with a history of heavy cigarette smoking, emphysema, hypertension, and prostate cancer in remission presented with a 4-hour history of acute right lower-quadrant abdominal pain. On admission, he was febrile (38.5°C), hypotensive (systolic blood pressure 90 mmHg), and tachycardic (heart rate 110/min); examination revealed peritonism in the right lower quadrant. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a perforated appendix with a 51×31×26 mm collection and surrounding fat stranding, innumerable hepatic nodules, mural thickening of the cecum and sigmoid colon, and marked mesenteric, para-aortic, and portocaval lymphadenopathy; there was also pulmonary consolidation and collapse in the right lower lobe. The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy, which revealed a perforated appendix with four-quadrant purulent contamination and a thickened, woody sigmoid colon; a subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy was performed. Postoperatively, he remained ventilated. On day 2, CT of the chest for staging demonstrated bulky multi-station mediastinal lymphadenopathy contiguous with soft tissue thickening enveloping the right lower and middle lobe bronchi. An extubation attempt on day 3 failed, and the patient died on day 6 after withdrawal of care.

A 59-year-old man presented with acute onset of chest pain. Two years earlier, he had undergone complete resection and postoperative radiotherapy for tongue cancer, with no recurrence over the past three years. He had no history of diabetes, hypertension, or cardiovascular disease. On arrival, he was in no distress. Vital signs were: blood pressure 130/75 mmHg, pulse 75 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, temperature 36.7 °C, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. Cardiac and pulmonary examinations were unremarkable. A 12-lead ECG showed sinus rhythm with ST-segment elevation in leads V1 through V6, findings compatible with acute anterior wall myocardial infarction. He underwent immediate coronary angiography, which revealed only noncritical stenoses in the coronary arteries. A chest radiograph showed clear lung fields and a mildly dilated cardiac silhouette.

A 7-month-old girl was referred for rapidly worsening dyspnea and failure to thrive.  
History of present illness: Beginning at 2–3 months of age, she had intermittent respiratory symptoms with upper respiratory infections; over the next several months these episodes became more frequent, lasted longer, and were accompanied by anorexia and poor weight gain.  
Vital signs on admission: temperature 36.5°C; blood pressure 90/50 mm Hg; heart rate 135 bpm; required FiO₂ 5 L/min to maintain SpO₂ of 95%.  
Physical examination: marked dyspnea; breath sounds absent over the right hemithorax.  
Laboratory studies: WBC 19.2 × 10³/mm³ (62.6% neutrophils); hematocrit 34.5%; platelets 695 × 10³/mm³; total protein 5.3 g/dL; albumin 2.8 g/dL; iron 17 µg/dL; IgA 30 mg/dL; IgG 625 mg/dL; ESR 44 mm/hr; CRP 5.05 mg/dL.  
Imaging: Chest radiograph showed complete opacification of the right hemithorax with mediastinal shift to the left. CT scan revealed a large heterogeneous mass occupying the entire right hemithorax, causing total right lung collapse, contralateral tracheal displacement, deformation of the right sixth rib, and enlarged mediastinal and right axillary lymph nodes.

A 36-year-old Afghan woman presented with a 6-month history of progressively increasing right axillary swelling and pain. In December 2021, she underwent excision of a right axillary lump in Afghanistan without prior biopsy; histopathology then reported a fragmented, poorly differentiated spindle cell tumor (6 × 5 × 1.5 cm). Post-excision CT of the axilla showed no residual disease, and she received four cycles of ifosfamide and doxorubicin through May 2022. Despite chemotherapy, she noted a new right axillary mass that continued to enlarge.

She had no comorbidities, no family history of malignancy, and no breast symptoms. On examination, there was a curvilinear right axillary scar overlying a 5 × 6 cm firm, nonfixable mass; the breasts were normal.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen showed a 5.1 × 3.7 × 5.5 cm right axillary mass with cystic cavities abutting the axillary artery (no encasement) and complete thrombosis of the axillary vein with collateral formation; no metastases were identified. Bilateral mammography was unremarkable.

Core-needle biopsy of the axillary mass revealed spindle cell proliferation. Immunostains for CK A1/A3, CAM5.2, EMA, and CK7 were negative. A differential diagnosis of metaplastic carcinoma (fibromatosis type) versus soft tissue sarcoma was raised. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the right shoulder demonstrated a 4.8 × 4.3 × 6.1 cm solid-cum-cystic, hemorrhagic lesion bordering intercostal muscles and ribs, in contact with the axillary artery and compressing the axillary vein. Genetic testing was advised but not performed due to financial constraints.

A 38-year-old man presented with an 8-month history of chronic constipation, intermittent abdominal pain, and flatulence. He had no significant family history and had undergone an appendectomy one month earlier. Physical examination was unremarkable. Routine blood tests, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. A colonoscopy showed intact mucosa without lesions or ulcers. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a dolichocolon with a markedly elongated sigmoid loop rising above the iliac crests; all other abdominal viscera appeared normal. Given refractory symptoms and the radiologic finding of a redundant sigmoid colon, a decision was made to proceed with sigmoid colectomy and end-to-end colorectal anastomosis.

A 49-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of a painful mass in her left calf. She first noticed a 3 cm lesion that had been progressively enlarging and became tender only on palpation. There was no history of trauma. On examination, there was a 3 cm soft tissue mass on the medial aspect between the proximal and middle thirds of the left calf; it was located deep in the subdermal plane, mobile, and not fixed to the fascia. Ultrasound showed a heterogeneous, predominantly hypoechoic mass with increased through transmission and marked hypervascularity. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a well-defined 3 cm soft tissue tumor in the subcutaneous fat of the left calf without involvement of the underlying muscles or bones.

A 57-year-old woman presented with epigastric and right upper-quadrant pain and jaundice. Laboratory studies showed alanine aminotransferase 922 IU/L, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 1705 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase 177 IU/L. Hydatid serology was negative.  
Magnetic resonance imaging with cholangiography demonstrated a cystic lesion in segment IV of the liver with a thick, contrast-enhancing wall; a 1 cm tissue nodule adjacent to the cyst’s caudal aspect; and a mural nodule protruding into the left bile duct.  
Aspiration of the cyst fluid revealed carbohydrate antigen 19-9 >70 000 U/mL and carcinoembryonic antigen 5.8 ng/mL, with no scolex or other pathogenic agents.

A 55-year-old woman presented with progressive blurred vision in her left eye over several months, worsening in recent weeks. Her medical and ocular history was unremarkable except for a 2-year history of taking Gui Lu Er Xian Jiao, a Chinese compound medicine. At presentation, best-corrected visual acuity was 1.0 in the right eye and 0.5 in the left eye. Pupils were equal, round, and reactive to light. Anterior segment examination revealed only mild bilateral lens opacity. Fundus examination of the left eye showed an orange-red elevated mass with overlying pigmentary changes and subretinal fluid superior to the vascular arcade, with associated macular detachment.  
B-scan ultrasonography demonstrated a solid choroidal mass with high internal reflectivity. Optical coherence tomography confirmed subretinal fluid at the macula. Fluorescein angiography revealed a large hyperfluorescent mass with intense staining and late dye pooling. Systemic tumor markers (CEA, CA125, CA153, CA199) were within normal limits. Brain MRI showed focal thickening with enhancement at the posterior aspect of the left globe without other abnormal findings.

A 24-year-old woman presented with intermittent right iliac fossa pain for 1 year and a sensation of heaviness in the lower abdomen for 4 months. She denied vomiting, abdominal distension, rectal bleeding, fever, or a history of tuberculosis. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender mass palpable in the right iliac fossa. Ultrasonography of the abdomen demonstrated ileocolic intussusception with a hypoechoic mass. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed ileocolic intussusception with a thickened ileal wall and identified two well-defined, heterogeneously enhancing masses (68×74 mm and 68×99 mm) adherent to the cecum and in the right lower paravertebral region, respectively, with central areas of necrosis; smaller similar nodules were noted prevertebrally. There was no ascites, and major vessels were normal. USG-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology suggested a poorly differentiated carcinoma. Serum carcinoembryonic antigen was 0.5 ng/mL; lactate dehydrogenase was 579.2 U/L; other laboratory tests and chest radiography were normal. The patient underwent right hemicolectomy with excision of the retroperitoneal mass. Grossly, a 6.5-cm polypoid tumor at the ileocecal region and five fleshy nodular masses up to 11 cm were identified in the peri-intestinal fat. Histopathological examination revealed interlacing fascicles of spindle-shaped cells with elongated, plump nuclei admixed with small lymphocytes, occasional storiform areas, nuclear pleomorphism, and 7–8 mitoses per 10 high-power fields; the overlying mucosa was ulcerated. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the tumor cells expressed CD35, CD23, and CD21 and were negative for CD34, CD45, CD19, c-kit, DOG-1, EMA, cytokeratin, EBV, Desmin, SMA, and S-100 protein.

A 48-year-old mixed-ethnicity woman presented with a mass extruding from her vaginal orifice, associated with bleeding and pain for several hours. She brought the mass in a container. She denied any history of menstrual delay or medication use. A recent ultrasound had shown an endometrial nodule with a vascular pedicle measuring 20 × 12 cm², suggestive of a polyp or submucous myoma. On admission, she appeared calm, with only abdominal tenderness on palpation. Speculum examination revealed a closed cervix and a moderate amount of bleeding. On bimanual examination, the uterus was fibroelastic in consistency and tender. The team then dissected the extruded structure, initially thinking it was a clot; however, it was found to be very hard—a long mass that was difficult to diagnose.

A 38-year-old woman was referred for persistent pain and teeth mobility in the anterior mandible 1 year after treatment at another clinic. Initial orthopantomography showed a 15×10 mm unilocular radiolucent lesion surrounding the roots of the left mandibular lateral incisor and canine; it was presumed to be a radicular cyst and both teeth were root-canaled without vitality testing. Pain persisted, the central incisor was also root-canaled, and symptoms remained, prompting referral.

Medical history was unremarkable. Extraoral examination showed normal overlying skin. Intraorally, there was a mild, diffuse, non-tender enlargement from the left first premolar to the right canine; the lingual cortex was bony hard, the buccal plate was doughy, and five mandibular anterior teeth were moderately mobile; mucosa was intact.

Repeat imaging with orthopantomography and cone beam CT revealed a well-defined multiloculated expansile osteolytic lesion with small internal septa, buccal cortex expansion with areas of cortical destruction, and root resorption of the left central and both central and lateral right incisors. The lesion measured 31.2×21.0 mm, extended from the left first premolar to the right canine, and crossed the midline.

A 50-year-old Japanese man presented with a 3-month history of a rapidly enlarging, painless swelling of the right scrotum. Three months earlier, a puncture attempt yielded red fluid. He denied trauma or infections. His medical history was notable only for hypertension, treated with an angiotensin receptor blocker. He had no known allergies and was a non-smoker.

Scrotal ultrasonography revealed a multilocular cyst with septations attached to the right testis; the testis itself appeared normal. Preoperative MRI showed a 7.0 cm fluid-filled sac and multiple adjacent cysts without any solid component or contrast-enhanced rim. The cyst contents were hyperintense on T1-weighted imaging and were interpreted as consistent with hematoma.

The patient underwent a right radical orchiectomy. Gross examination disclosed two cysts measuring 7.0 cm and 3.0 cm attached to the right testis. The larger cyst was characterized as a hydrocele with an inflamed wall. The smaller cyst was located at the head of the epididymis.

Microscopic examination of the smaller cyst revealed a lining of a single layer of bland columnar to cuboidal cells, some ciliated. Immunohistochemical staining showed EpCAM(+), BerEP4(+), calretinin(−), D2-40(−), WT-1(+), estrogen receptor (ER)(+) in nearly 100% of cells, and progesterone receptor (PR)(+) in approximately 20% of cells. No intracellular mucin, papillary growth, or stromal invasion was observed.

A 37-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 7-month history of a right inguinal bulge that had slowly increased in size. He reported no pain or systemic symptoms. On examination, vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination revealed a reducible right inguinal hernia.  

He underwent open hernia repair. Intraoperatively, a direct right inguinal hernia sac and a 4 × 5 cm spermatic cord mass that appeared lipomatous were noted. The hernia was repaired with a lightweight mesh, and the cord mass was excised and sent for histopathologic evaluation.  

Microscopic examination of the specimen showed on low-power view a lobulated lesion in which mature fat cells separated collagen bundles and blood vessels. On intermediate-power view, there was a mixture of vascular channels, myxoid stroma, and adipose elements without overt cytologic atypia.

A 53-year-old woman, 3 years postmenopausal, presented for a routine gynecologic examination. She denied any vaginal bleeding, pelvic pain, or fullness. Her obstetric history was notable for two prior vaginal deliveries, and she had no history of hormonal contraception or hormone replacement. Her medical history was significant only for well-controlled hypertension. She reported no family history of gynecologic cancer. On examination, the cervix appeared normal, and cervical cytology was negative for malignancy. Laboratory studies revealed hematocrit 40.1%, hemoglobin 13.3 g/dL, platelets 233×10^3/mL, blood urea nitrogen 35 mg/dL, creatinine 0.7 mg/dL, electrolytes within normal limits, and inflammatory markers and urinalysis unremarkable. Tumor markers (CA 125, CA 15-3, CA 19-9) were negative. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a 39×25 mm round, solid, well-defined mass within the endometrial cavity. Doppler assessment showed increased vascularity within the mass. The uterus was of normal size and the adnexa were unremarkable.

An 81-year-old Asian man with chronic hepatitis B on tenofovir (undetectable viral load, no cirrhosis) presented with several months of early satiety, anorexia, weight loss of >4.5 kg, and right-sided chest pain. Examination revealed normal cardiovascular and respiratory findings, no lymphadenopathy, and a benign abdominal examination without ascites or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies showed a normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 98 g/L; previously 140 g/L) and an elevated alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) level of 45 µg/L (normal <4.4 µg/L); other tests were unremarkable. Given his hepatitis B history, computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the liver were performed and failed to reveal any hepatic lesion. Over the next 2 months, his AFP increased to 540 µg/L. He then developed a 1-week history of melena without hematemesis; hemoglobin was 80 g/L and blood urea nitrogen was 9.1 mmol/L. Upper endoscopy revealed a 3-cm ulcerated, friable mass along the lesser curvature of the gastric antrum, confined to the antrum without pyloric extension. Biopsies were obtained for histopathology.

A 55-year-old premenopausal woman underwent routine gynecologic examination, which revealed bilateral adnexal cysts. She had three prior vaginal births and three miscarriages, with no pelvic pain or menstrual irregularity. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a 7.9 × 5.9 × 4.8 cm unilocular hypoechoic cyst with thin walls and minimal peripheral blood flow adjacent to the left ovary, classified as IOTA B1; the right adnexa contained a 3.4 × 2.7 × 2.1 cm hydrosalpinx. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a 7.5 × 4.4 × 4.9 cm cystic lesion posterior to the left side of the uterus with wall enhancement; the left ovary appeared normal. Serum CA-125 and HE4 levels were within normal limits. No other abnormalities were noted on examination.

A 33-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of diffuse dull abdominal pain aggravated at night and relieved when prone, accompanied by difficulty in passing stools and passage of mucus. Over the past 6 months, he noted loss of appetite, early satiety, and occasional nausea without fever, vomiting, melena, or weight loss. He had previously been treated for irritable bowel syndrome. On examination, there was a well-defined, firm, tender 10 × 10 cm mass in the left lumbar and umbilical regions, freely mobile perpendicular to the mesentery, with a nodular surface, no respiratory excursion, and impaired resonance on percussion. Rectal examination was normal.  
Ultrasonography of the abdomen demonstrated a lobulated hypoechoic intra-abdominal mass lesion with areas of vascularity. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed an 8.6 × 9.7 × 9.0 cm neoplasm arising from the small-bowel mesentery, displacing adjacent intestine without invasion, and no evidence of liver metastases or lymphadenopathy.

A 10-year-old girl presented with a 4-month history of dull, aching neck pain extending from the mid-cervical region to the occiput. The pain was constant, without radiculopathy, worsened at extremes of flexion and rotation, and was relieved by a cervical collar. There was no history of trauma, fever, or neurological deficits. On examination, local tenderness was elicited over the C5 spinous process with rotation; motor strength and sensation in the upper extremities were normal.

Laboratory studies showed a total leukocyte count of 7000 cells/mm3, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 10 mm/h, and C-reactive protein of 0.6 mg/dL. A plain radiograph of the cervical spine revealed a radiolucent lesion with surrounding sclerosis in the C5 vertebral body. MRI of the cervical spine demonstrated a T1-weighted hypointense, T2-weighted heterogeneous lesion confined to the C5 body, with mild peripheral enhancement on contrast-enhanced, fat-suppressed images and no associated soft-tissue mass.

A complete skeletal survey and an abdominal ultrasound showed no evidence of additional lesions. Given the solitary anterior vertebral lesion, a mini-open core biopsy of C5 was performed under fluoroscopic guidance for histopathological and microbiological evaluation.

A 50-year-old woman with hepatitis B–related cirrhosis (Child–Pugh C, MELD 22) underwent orthotopic liver transplantation in January 2022. Induction immunosuppression was methylprednisolone for 3 days, followed by maintenance tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisolone. Posttransplant, she received hepatitis B immunoglobulin and tenofovir. Routine follow-up demonstrated normal graft function, normal complete blood counts, and unremarkable liver imaging.

Five months after transplantation, she was found to have leukocytosis (WBC 99.4 × 10^3/μl) on surveillance labs but was asymptomatic. Physical examination revealed only bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. Epstein–Barr virus serology was negative. Neck ultrasonography showed multiple oval lymph nodes in all neck zones, the largest in the jugulodigastric region (short axis, 13 mm). A guided biopsy of a cervical lymph node demonstrated hypercellular neoplastic tissue composed of diffuse infiltration of blastic cells with hyperchromic nuclei, suggestive of a myeloid tumor.

A 55-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and atrial fibrillation presented with paroxysmal right upper-quadrant pain but no fever or jaundice. Her abdominal examination was unremarkable, and liver function tests were normal. Transabdominal ultrasound demonstrated an 8.6 × 6.0 cm anechoic lesion in segments II, III, and IV with a thin, regular wall, internal septa, and no vascularity on Doppler imaging. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a partially septated, fluid-density lesion without an enhancing wall. MRI revealed a T2-hyperintense, T1-hypointense, fluid-filled mass with fine septa, no diffusion restriction, and no enhancement after gadolinium administration. A percutaneous biopsy was not performed because of the risk of rupture.

A 23-year-old woman presented with dull periumbilical pain of two months’ duration. She denied weight loss, fever, diarrhea, or vomiting and had no history of abdominal surgery, trauma, drug use, or hereditary disease. On physical examination, the periumbilical area was tender without guarding or rebound, and a firm, fixed mass was palpable. Laboratory tests were within normal limits.  

Pelvic CT revealed a 7.0 × 5.0 × 9.0 cm heterogeneously enhancing soft-tissue mass with a necrotic portion anterior to the aortic bifurcation; no calcification was present. The mass abutted the abdominal aorta and surrounded and compressed the inferior vena cava and right common iliac artery. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a presacral, slightly heterogeneous hypoechoic solid mass abutting the sacrum, without increased intralesional vascularity. MRI demonstrated that the mass was isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images, relatively low in signal intensity on T2-weighted images, and showed relatively homogeneous, strong enhancement on fat-saturated contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images.  

The preoperative radiologic impression was a neurogenic tumor or a smooth-muscle–origin mass.

A 33-year-old white woman presented with pain and a tumor on the posterior aspect of the left knee. Three years earlier, she had twisted this knee, and since that time had experienced pain and progressive swelling. On examination, there was a large, soft mass with overlying varicose veins on the posterolateral left knee; the veins were painful without inflammation. Flexion of the knee was limited, with tenderness on palpation and pain on walking. The patient was HIV-positive without signs of AIDS.  
Ultrasound showed an 8-cm heterogeneous mass lateral to the left popliteal fossa. CT revealed a heterogeneous lesion with lacy enhancement affecting muscle and subcutaneous tissues in the distal third of the left thigh. MRI characterized it as lipoma.  
The patient underwent surgical excision, yielding soft, friable brownish-yellow fragments measuring 10 × 8 × 6 cm and weighing 80 g. Microscopic examination revealed a proliferation of fusiform cells without atypia admixed with mature adipocytes, abundant hemosiderin pigment, and small vessels with hyalinized walls; at the center there was evidence of old hemorrhage. Immunohistochemistry was positive for vimentin and CD34, and negative for cytokeratin, desmin, smooth-muscle actin, HHF-35, protein S-100, and CD99.

A 4-year-old boy presented with constipation, loss of appetite, mild abdominal distension, and intermittent fever for one year. On examination, he was pale but afebrile, with mild abdominal distension. The liver was palpable to the right lumbar region; it was firm, non-tender, and had a smooth surface. The spleen was not palpable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL; other hematological and biochemical tests, including liver function tests, were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed hepatomegaly with a multiloculated round cystic lesion measuring 4.3 × 4.5 × 4 cm in the caudate lobe; the lesion had internal septations but no calcifications or hyperechoic foci. Contrast-enhanced CT scan confirmed a well-defined, multiloculated cystic lesion in the caudate lobe, measuring 43.8 × 43 × 41 mm with multiple septations and calcification. Hydatid serology (IgG by ELISA) was negative.

A 15-year-old girl presented with a 1½-year history of dull, intermittent pain in the anterolateral aspect of her mid-left leg, aggravated by walking and relieved by analgesics. She reported a fall one year prior, after which the pain increased in intensity, especially at night, and a gradually enlarging swelling appeared in the same region. She now ambulated with a crutch. There were no fevers, weight loss, or other constitutional symptoms.

On examination, her vital signs were normal. Local inspection of the left tibia revealed a 6 × 7 cm firm, tender, ill-defined swelling on the anterolateral mid-diaphysis, warm to touch, fixed to underlying structures but mobile overlying skin, with intact distal neurovascular status and no lymphadenopathy. Knee and ankle range of motion were full.

Laboratory studies showed Hb 12.6 g/dL, WBC 13 630/mm³, CRP 2.16 mg/L, PTH 120 pg/mL, calcium 9.6 mg/dL, phosphate 2.5 mg/dL, TSH 1.22 μIU/mL, LDH 198 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 86 U/L; Mantoux test was negative. Chest radiograph was normal.

Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the left tibia demonstrated an osteolytic, expansile, eccentric lesion with a sclerotic margin in the diaphysis, suggesting osteofibrous dysplasia. Bone scintigraphy showed an osteoblastic mid-shaft lesion. MRI of the left tibia revealed a mixed-signal, expansile lobulated cortical lesion of the lower diaphysis, hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2/STIR with internal fluid levels, and heterogeneous contrast enhancement; surrounding soft tissues were normal. These MRI findings were thought to be suggestive of an adamantinoma of the tibial diaphysis.

A core-needle biopsy of the lesion was performed and sent for histopathological examination.

A 26-year-old woman presented with a three-month history of a left-sided neck “fullness” that became painful and was associated with hoarseness. She denied snoring, dysphagia, odynophagia, fever, weight loss, neurological, or otological symptoms. Her past history was notable only for sleeve gastrectomy, abdominoplasty, and cholecystectomy. She smoked 10 pack-years. Examination: afebrile; normal vital signs; cranial nerves intact; no nystagmus; oropharynx and tympanic membranes normal. A tender, firm 2×2 cm mass lay anterior to the left sternocleidomastoid with no overlying skin changes or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies, including CBC, electrolytes, fasting glucose, cholesterol, and triglycerides, were normal. Neck ultrasonography showed a well-defined, oval, deeply hypoechoic lesion posterior to the left external carotid artery measuring 29×10 mm with no significant internal or peripheral vascularity. Contrast CT of the neck confirmed a left carotid-space mass. MRI of the neck revealed a left parapharyngeal carotid‐space solid lesion, described as most likely a carotid body tumor or a schwannoma. Fine-needle aspiration was not performed due to concern for a vascular tumor. A 24-hour urinary metanephrine level was normal.

A 66-year-old woman presented with an irregular, pigmented nodular lesion of the left breast measuring 2 cm, associated with nipple retraction, skin thickening, and hyperpigmentation, without ulceration or palpable lymphadenopathy. Mammography showed architectural distortion with irregular margins. Ultrasound revealed a 25 mm dishomogeneous hypoechoic area. MRI confirmed a 24 × 14 × 16 mm nodule with retraction of the nipple–areola complex. Bone scintigraphy was negative, and CT of the chest and abdomen showed a 20 mm left retroareolar contrast-enhancing nodule without distant lesions. Core biopsy demonstrated two neoplastic foci: the first was a 2.1 cm high-grade (G3) invasive ductal carcinoma with solid, glandular, and papillary patterns; the second comprised epithelial cells with nevoid features infiltrating the epidermis in a pagetoid fashion. The overlying epidermis was thinned, and tumoral necrosis, acantholysis, and vascular tumor emboli were present. Elongated dendritic melanocytes containing abundant melanin pigment were interspersed among the carcinoma cells. Immunohistochemistry showed that the epithelial neoplastic cells were positive for pancytokeratin, GATA3, estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and HER2 (score 2), with a Ki-67 index of 10%, and negative for Melan-A, S100, and HMB-45, whereas the dendritic melanocytes were positive for Melan-A and S100.

A 46-year-old man with hypertension and obesity was referred for excision and curettage of a lesion in the right proximal tibia, presumed to be chronic osteomyelitis. Two and a half years earlier, he noted acute localized pain, warmth, and swelling in his right knee after moving furniture. He received an intra-articular corticosteroid injection with transient relief, but no synovial fluid analysis was performed. One year later, symptoms recurred; radiographs showed a lytic lesion of the right proximal tibia, and a bone biopsy demonstrated necrosis with acute inflammation. The patient was afebrile. Laboratory studies revealed a CRP of 13.9 mg/L (normal <10 mg/L), an ESR of 30 mm/h (normal 0–22 mm/h), and a WBC count of 7.2 × 10^9/L. He underwent excision and curettage with placement of vancomycin- and tobramycin-impregnated beads. Intraoperatively, the bone appeared grossly abnormal and malodorous, but cultures were negative. He completed an 8-week course of empirical vancomycin, ciprofloxacin, and metronidazole, with normalization of inflammatory markers.
