One month later, radiographs showed only postsurgical sclerosis without lesion progression. Four months after surgery, he again developed right knee pain, swelling, and impaired ambulation. He denied trauma, unusual exposures, or IV drug use. MRI revealed a rim-enhancing fluid collection in the proximal tibia with cortical breakthrough and adjacent soft-tissue extension. His CRP was 24.6 mg/L, ESR 31 mm/h, and WBC count 4.0 × 10^9/L. A second excision and curettage was performed; operative findings again included friable, abnormal tissue. Empirical intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam were started postoperatively, but intraoperative bone and blood cultures remained negative. The patient faced the prospect of another prolonged course of antibiotics and possible above-the-knee amputation if symptoms recurred.

A 59-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of upper abdominal discomfort, weight loss, and intermittent vomiting. She also reported hot flushes over the preceding 3 months. Her past medical and family histories were unremarkable, and the physical examination was without focal findings. Laboratory tests showed mild to moderate anemia (hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, hematocrit 35.4%, MCV 81.5 fL, MCH 24.9 pg) and an elevated lactate dehydrogenase level (378 IU/L; normal <280 IU/L). Abdominal ultrasonography was unremarkable. Magnetic resonance enterography revealed circumferential thickening of the proximal jejunal wall with proximal bowel distention, shouldering of the lumen margins, mucosal disruption, and an enlarged lymph node along the posterior aspect of the greater curvature of the stomach. Given the evidence of partial small-bowel obstruction and concern for an underlying malignancy, the patient underwent a segmental jejunal resection with primary anastomosis, with grossly intact anastomotic integrity noted intraoperatively. A feeding jejunostomy was placed postoperatively. On gross examination, the resected jejunal segment (20 cm in length) showed a 4 × 3 × 2 cm exophytic mass invading from the mucosa through the serosa into the peri-intestinal fat; regional lymph nodes appeared free of tumor.

A 69-year-old Caucasian man was referred for evaluation of a newly noted pigmented iris mass in the left eye, initially presumed to be an iris–ciliary body melanoma. His history was notable for well-controlled diabetes with annual eye exams; the lesion had not been previously observed and the patient reported progressive growth over several months. Three months earlier, he had herpes zoster ophthalmicus in the distribution of the ophthalmic division of cranial nerve V, treated with oral valacyclovir and topical prednisolone acetate tapered to one drop daily; he still experienced intermittent left frontal headaches.

On examination, visual acuity was 20/30 in each eye, pupils were equally reactive without an afferent defect, and intraocular pressures were 13 mm Hg (right) and 16 mm Hg (left). Slit-lamp examination of the right eye showed only a nuclear sclerotic cataract. In the left eye, there was pigment on the endothelium and, overlying the iris, a sharply demarcated, darkly bilobed pigmented mass arising from the nasal angle and displacing the pupillary margin, with associated stromal atrophy and no seeding of the remaining iris surface. The lesion transilluminated under retroillumination, and no sectoral cataract was seen.

Gonioscopy revealed the mass obscuring the nasal angle without circumferential extension or excessive pigmentation elsewhere. Dilated fundus examination showed a flat pigmented macular nevus and peripheral chorioretinal scars inferonasally. Ultrasound biomicroscopy of the left eye demonstrated a bilobed, echolucent, cyst-like structure measuring approximately 1.4 × 4.0 × 4.1 mm arising from the hyperreflective layers of the iris pigment epithelium. B-scan ultrasound revealed no discrete mass adjacent to the iris lesion.

An 8-year-old boy presented with a swelling in the anterolateral aspect of the right lower thigh of 1 year’s duration. The mass had gradually increased in size and had become painful over the past 2 months. There was no history of trauma, no constitutional symptoms, and no bleeding tendencies. Physical examination revealed an asymmetric, boggy, non-compressible, non-pulsatile swelling in the anteromedial right lower thigh measuring approximately 10 cm × 7 cm. The overlying skin was normal without discoloration, venous engorgement, or inflammatory signs. There was fullness of the medial para-patellar fossa without joint effusion, tenderness over the quadriceps (more anteromedial), no distal neurovascular deficit or bruit, equal limb lengths, and full knee range of motion. Initial differential diagnoses included lipoma, cold abscess, suprapatellar bursitis, synovitis, sarcoma, fibroma, or other extra-articular soft tissue tumors. Magnetic resonance imaging of the thigh showed a soft tissue mass measuring about 14 cm × 5 cm within the vastus medialis and intermedius that was of high-signal intensity on T1-, T2-, and proton-density FAT-SAT–weighted images.

A 71-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of intermittent right lower abdominal pain and an unintended 6-kg weight loss. She had a history of well-controlled hypertension and Parkinson’s disease and no prior abdominal surgery. On examination, she was pale; temperature and other vital signs were normal. Abdominal palpation revealed a 5–6-cm, soft, immobile, tender mass in the right lower quadrant. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 7.61×10^3/µL (67.8% neutrophils, 24.0% lymphocytes) and C-reactive protein of 0.89 mg/dL; liver and renal function tests, carcinoembryonic antigen, and CA 19-9 were within normal limits. Abdominal radiography was unremarkable. Colonoscopy identified an irregular, ball-like obstructing mass in the proximal colon; biopsies revealed ulceration, necrotic debris, and nonspecific active cellular infiltration. A chest radiograph showed no pulmonary lesions. An abdominal CT scan demonstrated a 2.8×3.4-cm heterogeneously enhancing lesion in the proximal ascending colon and multiple small nodules in the cecal mesentery.

A 46-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of left flank pain, an abdominal lump, and intermittent hematuria. She had been diagnosed elsewhere with renal cell carcinoma and was referred for further evaluation. At our hospital, her hematological and biochemical parameters were normal. Urine microscopy showed deformed red blood cells. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a large (approximately 16.0 × 13.6 × 12.1 cm) irregular, well-defined heterogeneous lesion in the left hypochondrium, lumbar, and supra-umbilical regions, predominantly cystic and nonenhancing, with no calcifications. The mass appeared to involve the upper half of the left kidney. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the lesion was suggestive of sarcomatoid renal cell carcinoma. A metastatic work-up, including a bone scan and CT of the thorax, was negative. With a provisional diagnosis of renal cell carcinoma, she underwent surgery. Intraoperatively, a large retroperitoneal mass arising from the left kidney could not be separated from the renal parenchyma, so a left nephrectomy and adrenalectomy with complete excision of the tumor were performed.

A 77-year-old woman presented with right elbow pain and inability to move the arm after a fall from standing height. She was hemodynamically stable. On examination, the right elbow was moderately swollen and tender, without erythema, warmth, or palpable mass; distal pulses and sensation were intact. Plain radiographs showed an olecranon fracture and, incidentally, a well-defined, lobulated radiolucent lesion with a thin sclerotic rim in the proximal ulnar metaphysis; there was no calcification or periosteal reaction. MRI revealed a 7.8×4.4×3.6 cm expansile intraosseous mass extending into adjacent muscle and subcutaneous tissue. The working diagnosis was a right ulnar olecranon pathological fracture, and the initial differential diagnosis of the lesion included mesenchymal soft tissue neoplasm (e.g. low-grade sarcoma), giant cell tumour at an atypical age, or low-grade intraosseous lymphoma.

An 8-year-old girl was evaluated for a slowly enlarging plaque-like lesion on the left chest wall that had been present for 2 years. Initially palpable only beneath the skin, the lesion became visible over the last several months and measured approximately 0.5 cm in diameter with a light violet color. On ultrasound examination, there was a 0.5-cm ovoid, well-demarcated lesion in the subcutaneous region with dermal involvement and without clear separation from the underlying pectoralis major muscle. The internal echotexture was heterogeneously hypoechoic with small echogenic foci and no posterior acoustic enhancement or shadowing.

Given the persistence of the lesion, a complete surgical excision was performed. Grossly, the specimen had a polypoid appearance with raised epidermis; on sectioning, a firm white-gray nodule was seen, centered in the dermis and extending focally into the subcutaneous tissue. Histologic examination showed hyperplastic epidermis with hyperkeratosis and elongated rete ridges. Within the dermis, there was a spindle‐cell proliferation in a storiform to whorled pattern; the cells had eosinophilic cytoplasm, monomorphic nuclei, and sparse mitotic activity. Tumor cells infiltrated fat lobules in a honeycomb fashion, and the stroma was collagenous. 

The differential diagnosis based on hematoxylin and eosin staining included dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans and dermatofibroma.

A man in his early 60s presented with a 2-week history of progressive constipation, multiple episodes of non-bilious vomiting, and inability to tolerate oral intake. He had no personal or family history of cancer. On examination, he was tachycardic with a distended but non-tender, non-rigid abdomen; no lymphadenopathy was noted. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 44,000/µL (previous counts had been normal) and a lactate level of 3.7 mmol/L. A chest radiograph showed an elevated right hemidiaphragm. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated signs consistent with an internal hernia and small-bowel obstruction. He underwent an exploratory laparotomy, which revealed a hemorrhagic, infarcted omentum, diffuse small-bowel inflammation, and ascites. A subtotal omentectomy was performed, the small bowel was released, and a negative-pressure device was placed. Samples of ascitic fluid and omental tissue were sent for pathology. Over the next two days, he required two additional abdominal revisions for edematous, woody-textured bowel with dense adhesions; a liver biopsy was also obtained. Cytologic examination of ascitic fluid showed a neoplastic population with diffuse CD45 positivity; immunostains were negative for MOC-31, CEA, calretinin, D2-40, TTF-1, BER-EP4, CK7, CK20, CDX2, and SOX10. Cultures of the ascitic fluid grew Massilia timonae. Broad-spectrum antibiotics and antifungal agents were started for intraabdominal infection in the context of malignancy.

A full-term male neonate was noted to have mild tachypnea and right-sided heart sounds on routine examination at birth; he otherwise appeared well. A chest radiograph suggested dextrocardia, prompting further evaluation. A computed tomography scan on day 1 of life revealed a 6.5×6×2.5 cm well-circumscribed, hypodense intraparenchymal mass in the left lung with predominantly solid density and focal cystic areas, causing compression of the lower left lobe and a mediastinal shift. A radiologic diagnosis of congenital pulmonary airway malformation was suggested. Because of the mediastinal shift, the mass was surgically excised on day 21 of life.

A 52-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes presented with a 1-month history of a penile ulcer associated with unmeasured fever, asthenia, and a 5-kg weight loss over 4 months. On examination, there was a 4-cm circular ulcer at the base of the penis with a clean but bleeding base and verrucous papules at the margins. Palpable inguinal and axillary lymphadenopathy was noted. Laboratory studies revealed a normocytic normochromic anemia, thrombocytopenia, total protein of 15.99 g/dL, a monoclonal peak on serum protein electrophoresis, and an IgM level of 12 900. Abdominal ultrasonography showed hepatosplenomegaly.

A 63-year-old man noted a right-sided neck mass gradually enlarging over 2 years. On examination, a firm 8-cm thyroid mass displaced the trachea medially. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed a 76-mm, lobulated, heterogeneous solid mass in the right thyroid lobe with internal macrocalcifications and necrotic areas, displacing the trachea, common carotid artery, and sternocleidomastoid muscle. Multiple enlarged cervical lymph nodes (levels II–V and supraclavicular), mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and lung nodules suggestive of metastases were present.

Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) yielded a hypercellular sample with single cells and insular/trabecular arrangements. Colloid was scarce. Necrosis and polymorphonuclear leukocytes were present in the background. The tumor cells were uniform, with large granular (oncocytic) cytoplasm, a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, round slightly hyperchromatic nuclei, and prominent macronucleoli. Nuclear membrane irregularity (“rasinoid”) was noted, but nuclear features of papillary thyroid carcinoma and medullary thyroid carcinoma were absent.

Immunohistochemistry on the cell block revealed diffuse nuclear positivity for TTF-1 and PAX-8; p53 positivity in 9.2% of nuclei; extensive pan-cytokeratin staining; weak focal thyroglobulin staining; and a Ki-67 proliferation index of 10%. Carcinoembryonic antigen, calcitonin, and Bcl-2 were negative.

A 57-year-old man presented with refractory ascites of 2 years’ duration. He denied alcohol use, metabolic syndrome, fever, chest pain, rash, oral ulcers, arthralgias, visual changes, recent travel, or sick contacts. His medical history included hypertension, hypothyroidism, and chronic nephritis, treated with nifedipine and thyroxine. Prior evaluations—including blood tests, ascites analysis, gastroscopy, colonoscopy, and abdominal CT—failed to yield a diagnosis, and diuretics plus paracentesis provided only transient relief.

On examination, he appeared chronically ill. Palpable cervical and inguinal lymph nodes measured up to 1 cm. His abdomen was distended without tenderness, with positive shifting dullness. He had mild bilateral lower-limb edema and a spleen palpable 3 fingerbreadths below the left costal margin.

Laboratory studies showed: WBC 4.44×10^9/L, hemoglobin 111 g/L, platelets 93×10^9/L; urine protein weakly positive; urine microalbumin 82.4 mg/L (0–30), urine IgG 33.4 mg/L (0–8.5), transferrin 3.29 mg/L (0–2.2), α1-microglobulin 54.2 mg/L (0–12), β2-microglobulin 0.19 mg/L (0–0.22); uric acid 520 μmol/L; albumin 36.6 g/L; ESR 26 mm/h; TSH 5.54 mIU/L; FT4 14.81 pmol/L; FT3 1.74 pmol/L. CRP, liver and renal function, stool studies, vitamin B12, folate, IgG4, hepatitis A–E serologies, CA125, CA199, CEA, AFP, PSA, BNP, PPD, T-spot, ANA, ANCA, RF, HIV, EBV, CMV, and Toxoplasma tests were all unremarkable.

Echocardiogram showed a small pericardial effusion. Chest and abdominal CT revealed bilateral pleural effusions, ascites, and patchy pneumonia.

Ascitic fluid was yellow and clear with 40×10^6 nucleated cells/L (80.6% mononuclear), a negative Rivalta test, ADA 2.6 U/L (0–25), LDH 74 IU/L (120–250), albumin 15.7 g/L, CA125 542 ng/mL (0–7), normal ascitic CEA, AFP, and CA199, and no malignant cells or mycobacteria. The serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) was 20.9 g/L.

A 34-year-old G3P1011 woman was referred at 24 weeks’ gestation for evaluation of a fetal brain abnormality. Her medical history was unremarkable, with a prior cesarean delivery only. Carrier screening and cell-free DNA testing were low risk.  
Routine ultrasound at 21 weeks showed dilation of the right lateral ventricle and a “dangling” choroid plexus. At 24 weeks, a fetal anatomy scan revealed a 6.4 × 4.1 cm midline intracranial mass; 2D color Doppler demonstrated a relative lack of blood flow in the lesion. Maternal and paternal testing for human platelet antigen incompatibility was negative.  
Fetal MRI at 25 weeks and 5 days showed a heterogeneous midline supratentorial mass measuring approximately 9.5 × 8.2 × 7.5 cm, with solid and cystic components, severe ventriculomegaly with head enlargement, peripheral compression of brain parenchyma, and downward displacement of the cerebellum. The sagittal sinus appeared engorged, and areas of dark gradient signal suggested calcifications and/or hemosiderin deposition.

A 22-year-old healthy man presented with a 4-day history of pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. He had no history of smoking or asbestos exposure and had received his second BNT162b2 COVID-19 vaccine 1 month earlier. On examination, he was tachycardic (heart rate 121 bpm), blood pressure was 144/95 mmHg, and he was afebrile. Electrocardiography showed diffuse ST-segment elevations. Laboratory tests revealed a white-cell count of 11 930/μL. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a moderate pericardial effusion with normal biventricular function. Acute pericarditis was diagnosed, and he was treated with ibuprofen and colchicine. Two days later, pericardiocentesis drained 900 mL of serosanguineous exudative fluid, with clinical improvement.  

One month later, he developed recurrent chest pain and dyspnea. Repeat pericardiocentesis yielded 1 L of fluid; pericardial cytology was negative for malignant cells, and bacterial culture and acid-fast staining were negative. Despite prednisone therapy, his symptoms persisted. Cardiac computed tomography showed pericardial thickening with moderate effusion. A pericardial window biopsy revealed benign acute and chronic inflammation with benign mesothelial proliferation.  

Four months after the initial presentation, he was readmitted with recurrent pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. He was tachycardic (110 bpm) with elevated jugular venous pressure but no fever. Troponin and creatine kinase levels were normal; C-reactive protein was elevated at 5 mg/dL. Blood cultures and COVID-19 PCR tests were negative, as were serologic tests for HIV, Rickettsia, Q fever, and cytomegalovirus. Chest radiography showed cardiomegaly; electrocardiography demonstrated sinus tachycardia with lateral T-wave inversion. A new CT scan revealed a heterogeneous pericardial layer measuring 4 cm in thickness. Transthoracic echocardiography showed right ventricular dysfunction and a large pericardial effusion with constrictive physiology. He underwent exploratory thoracotomy and pericardiectomy.

A 34-year-old multiparous woman presented with a 4-month history of a palpable nodule in the posterior aspect of the left labia majora. The lesion was discovered incidentally and was not associated with pain or ulceration. She had no personal or family history of malignancy. On examination, there was a 2-cm, nonulcerated, subcutaneous nodule with a smooth surface and firm consistency; the lesion was nontender. No inguinal lymphadenopathy or other abnormalities were noted. Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 2.4 × 2.0 × 1.4-cm soft-tissue mass confined to the left labia majora without pelvic or inguinal lymphadenopathy. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest and abdomen showed no evidence of distant metastases.

A 36-year-old nonalcoholic woman with a 15-year smoking history presented with epigastric pain radiating to her back that was not relieved by NSAIDs. She also reported multiple episodes of nonbilious vomiting, nausea, and intermittent nonbloody diarrhea. On examination, a palpable mass was noted in the epigastric region. Laboratory studies were normal except for mild anemia (hemoglobin 11 g/dL). Abdominal ultrasound and noncontrast CT scan showed a unilocular cystic lesion measuring 8 cm in the tail of the pancreas, adherent to the spleen. She underwent distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy; three regional lymph nodes were removed. Grossly, there was an 8 cm cystic mass in the distal pancreas adherent to the spleen, with no other solid component. Microscopic examination of the cyst wall revealed nests of neoplastic histiocyte-like cells embedded in a fibrovascular stroma; the cells had clear to granular cytoplasm and uniform round to oval nuclei without mitoses or vascular invasion. Margins, lymph nodes, and spleen were free of tumor. Initial immunohistochemical stains showed tumor-cell positivity for CD56 and cyclin D1, weak positivity for neuron-specific enolase, and negativity for CK7, CK20, panCK, chromogranin A, synaptophysin, CD68, S100, vimentin, EMA, and SMA.

A 15-year-old boy presented with a one-year history of persistent pain and swelling in his left middle finger. He was otherwise healthy and reported no history of trauma or infection. On examination, there was localized swelling and tenderness over the distal phalanx, and interphalangeal motion was full. He described nocturnal exacerbations of pain that were promptly relieved by NSAIDs. 

Plain radiographs of the finger showed a small, ovoid lucent lesion with surrounding sclerosis in the tuft of the distal phalanx. CT confirmed a subcentimeter expansile lucent lesion with sclerotic margins centered in the dorsal cortex, just beneath the nail bed. 

Differential diagnosis based on imaging included subperiosteal hematoma, osteomyelitis, enchondroma, and osteoid osteoma. Lack of a soft-tissue lesion made a glomus tumor unlikely.

A 56-year-old woman with hyperthyroidism and a remote cesarean delivery was referred for evaluation of postmenopausal uterine bleeding. Initial pelvic examination, endometrial biopsy, transvaginal ultrasound, cervical cytology, colposcopy, and hysteroscopy were unremarkable. One year later, a follow-up transvaginal ultrasound again showed an atrophic uterus and ovaries but revealed an incidental, well-defined, hypoechoic nodular lesion measuring 26 × 23 mm in a retrovesical location more than 18 cm from the anal verge. The lesion was surrounded by a thin hyperechoic rim (consistent with intraluminal gas) and demonstrated strong vascularity (vascular score 4/4). After referral to gastroenterology, colonoscopy identified an inflammatory-appearing submucosal lesion 30 cm from the anal verge. Biopsies showed mesenchymal subepithelial tissue with a neural immunophenotype and a low proliferation index, suggesting schwannoma or neurofibroma as diagnostic possibilities.

An 11-year-old Asian boy was referred for evaluation of a progressively enlarging mass of the right lower eyelid. He had homozygous hemoglobin E disease but no anemic symptoms, no prior ocular history, and no family history of malignancy. Four months before presentation, he noted a painless, 1-cm mass. Two months later, contrast-enhanced orbital MRI showed a well-circumscribed, lobulated 3.2×2.1×3.7-cm mass along the right lower eyelid abutting the inferior rectus and displacing the globe superiorly. On exam, best-corrected visual acuity was 2/60 OD and 6/12 OS, pupils were reactive, and there was a firm, painless 5-cm lower eyelid mass causing superior globe displacement, complete ptosis, marked conjunctival chemosis, and limitation of downward gaze. The left eye was normal. Initial clinical differential diagnoses included an orbital tumor not otherwise specified and vascular malformations (venous lymphatic and cavernous venous malformations). One month later, MRI showed growth to 4.9×3.9×3.2 cm with posterior extension into the extraconal space. Incisional biopsy revealed a pleomorphic spindle-cell neoplasm with hyperchromatic nuclei, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, coarse chromatin, and some cells with lipoblast-like features; mitotic figures were rare (0–9 per 10 high-power fields). Immunohistochemistry was negative for AE1/AE3, EMA, S100, and HMB45. Systemic imaging showed no evidence of metastasis.

A 30-year-old man was referred for evaluation of an asymptomatic, calcified mass on the right anterior maxilla that had been present for 18 months. On intraoral examination, there was a mucosal fenestration through which a hard, mineralized structure approximately 1 cm in diameter was visible. A periapical radiograph of the upper right premolar area demonstrated a discrete radiopaque lesion. The initial diagnostic hypothesis was maxillary exostosis. An incisional biopsy was performed to remove a fragment of the lesion, which was submitted for histopathological analysis.

A 32-year-old woman with no comorbidities presented with 12 hours of dull, aching epigastric pain radiating to the back. She had undergone laparoscopic cholecystectomy 3 months earlier for chronic cholecystitis. On examination, she was febrile (101 °F), tachycardic (110 bpm), and icteric. Abdominal examination revealed a 3 × 3 cm firm, tender, ill-defined lump in the epigastrium beneath a right upper quadrant scar. Laboratory studies showed elevated serum bilirubin, ALT, AST, ALP, and GGT; disproportionate elevation of ALP with direct hyperbilirubinemia indicated cholestatic jaundice. Serum CA 19-9 (13.79 U/mL) and IgG4 (41.74 mg/dL) were within normal limits. Empiric intravenous piperacillin/tazobactam was started for presumed cholangitis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated an ill-defined, isodense solid mass in the pancreatic head with gradual delayed enhancement, causing obstruction of the main pancreatic and bile ducts and associated obstructive pancreatopathy and biliopathy; there was thrombosis of the portal vein extending into its right and left branches and the superior mesenteric vein, while dissection planes around the celiac trunk, hepatic artery, and superior mesenteric artery appeared preserved. Endoscopic ultrasound confirmed an irregular hypoechoic lesion measuring 25 × 24 mm in the pancreatic head with abrupt termination of the common bile duct and dilation and tortuosity of the main pancreatic duct at the neck.

A 48-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of left-sided nasal obstruction and frequent episodes of bleeding from the same side. He had no other nasal symptoms and an unremarkable medical and surgical history. Nasal endoscopy revealed a pinkish, smooth, polypoidal mass between the left nasal septum and the inferior turbinate. Routine blood tests were within normal limits; his hemoglobin level was 11 g/dL. Non-contrast computed tomography of the nose and paranasal sinuses showed a homogeneously hypoattenuating soft-tissue density lesion occupying the right mid-posterior nasal cavity and extending into the nasopharynx, with widening of the right posterior nasal cavity suggestive of bone remodeling. On contrast-enhanced CT, the lesion demonstrated mild enhancement and displaced the medial wall of the right maxillary sinus and the nasal septum.

A 77-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of frontal and parietal alopecia and progressive abdominal swelling. She denied hirsutism, deepening of the voice, increased muscle mass, or abnormal uterine bleeding. Her menarche was at age 17 with regular cycles; she had two children and entered menopause at age 52. She had never had a gynecologic examination.

On examination, blood pressure was 125/80 mmHg, pulse 88 bpm, height 1.74 m, weight 53 kg (BMI 24.5 kg/m^2), and waist circumference 99 cm. She exhibited male-pattern baldness (Ludwig II-2/III), no significant hirsutism (modified Ferriman–Gallwey score 3), and marked abdominal distension with a large palpable mass in the right hemiabdomen. Pelvic examination revealed clitoromegaly; no other abnormalities were noted.

Laboratory evaluation showed a total testosterone of 659 ng/dl (normal 10–70), dehydroepiandrosterone-sulfate 1950 ng/ml (170–900), FSH 75 IU/l, LH 28 IU/l, and estradiol 25 pg/ml. Serum β-hCG, α-fetoprotein, CEA, CA-125, CA19-9, and LDH were within normal limits. Transvaginal ultrasonography revealed a 22 × 16 cm right adnexal cystic mass. Abdomino-pelvic MRI confirmed a 20 × 14 × 22 cm cystic lesion arising from pelvic structures. Both radiologic and laboratory data were consistent with an ovarian neoplasm.

A 50-year-old multiparous, postmenopausal woman presented with a one-month history of burning micturition. Her blood pressure was 140/96 mmHg and pulse 76 beats/minute. Vaginal examination revealed an 8 cm × 8 cm cystic mass in the anterior fornix. Urinalysis showed pus cells; other laboratory studies were unremarkable. Pelvic ultrasonography demonstrated a well-defined, thick-walled cystic mass measuring 7.6 cm × 6.8 cm in the left adnexa with a few incomplete septa; the left ovary was not seen separately, and no free fluid was present. The findings were interpreted as suggesting an ovarian neoplastic mass. At exploratory laparotomy, the uterus and both ovaries were atrophic; an 8 cm × 6 cm cystic mass was identified in the left broad ligament and excised. Frozen section revealed a cyst wall lined by sheets of tumor cells with eccentric vesicular nuclei and moderate eosinophilic granular cytoplasm, and a diagnosis of sex cord–stromal tumor was rendered. Complete excision of the lesion was performed, and omental biopsy and peritoneal fluid were obtained.

A 29-year-old woman presented with menoxenia of 5 years’ duration and, over the past year, polyuria, polydipsia, hyperglycemia, and lethargy. Menoxenia was diagnosed in 2013 and treated with hormone replacement. In 2017, she developed diabetes insipidus and lethargy; brain MRI showed a sellar mass. Incomplete resection of this mass demonstrated histiocytic aggregates that were CD1a–negative, Langerin–negative, and S100–positive. Next-generation sequencing of 183 genes, including BRAF V600E and MAPK-pathway genes, showed no pathogenic mutations.

Two years later, with progression of the intracranial lesions, examination showed no remarkable abnormalities on physical exam. Laboratory studies demonstrated normal tumor markers, mild elevation of alkaline phosphatase (178 U/L) and γ-glutamyltransferase (72 IU/L), and slight increases in C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and tumor necrosis factor α. Enhanced brain MRI revealed multiple lesions involving the sella, suprasellar region, pons, and hypothalamus. A 99mTc-MDP bone scan showed symmetrical uptake in the frontal bones and the metaphyses of the distal femora and proximal tibiae; HR-pQCT confirmed osteosclerosis of the tibia. FDG PET/CT demonstrated hypermetabolic foci in the bilateral frontal lobes, nasal septum, sella, gallbladder, and the body and tail of the pancreas. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed slightly enlarged pancreas with hypointense nodules in the body and tail, showing reduced enhancement in arterial and portal phases, without ductal dilation. Endoscopic ultrasound revealed multiple 2-cm hypoechoic lesions, and EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration of the pancreas showed no malignant cells, only normal pancreatic ductal cells.

A 38-year-old man presented with a painful nodule on the lateral inferior aspect of his right upper arm. He reported that the lesion recurred approximately one year after a prior excision. He denied cold sensitivity, trauma, allergies, or other medical conditions. On examination, the nodule was purplish, 1 cm × 1 cm, tender, rough, immobile, and had regular, rounded borders. There were no neurological or vascular deficits in the limb. Under local anesthesia, an excisional biopsy was performed. Hematoxylin-eosin staining of the subcutaneous, well-circumscribed specimen revealed sheets of uniform cells with scant eosinophilic cytoplasm, indistinct borders, and round-to-ovoid central nuclei with inconspicuous nucleoli; branching vessels lined by endothelial cells were surrounded by these uniform cells. No cellular atypia was identified, and the Ki-67 proliferation index was very low.

A 23-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with a 3-month history of progressive abdominal pain, bloating, nausea, and intermittent vomiting that intensified over the past several days. On physical examination, a firm, centrally located abdominal mass was palpated, eliciting mild tenderness. Routine laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a large (11.9 × 18 × 16.4 cm) heterogeneous, predominantly hypodense mass centered within the mid to right abdominal mesentery. The lesion contained complex cystic and solid components, featured a large fluid-filled center with an enhancing peripheral wall, and extended from the L2 vertebral level to S1. It displaced adjacent bowel loops without causing obstruction. No intralesional calcifications were identified. Mesenteric vessels around the mass were patent, with no evidence of vascular encasement or invasion. Minimal omental thickening and adjacent fat stranding were noted at the lesion’s inferolateral border.

A 41-year-old man with a history of hypertension treated with amlodipine and perindopril presented with a 3-day history of right upper quadrant abdominal pain. The pain began mildly and rapidly progressed to severe intensity, providing only partial relief with paracetamol. He also reported nausea and one episode of vomiting but denied fever, heartburn, or diarrhea. 

On examination, his blood pressure was 190/120 mm Hg and heart rate 89 beats/min. The abdomen was soft and non-distended, with mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant without palpable masses, organomegaly, or flank tenderness. He required fentanyl for pain control.

Laboratory studies revealed normal renal function and serum electrolytes. Liver enzymes were elevated (alanine aminotransferase 161 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 80 U/L), while serum amylase and lipase were within normal limits. A viral hepatitis panel was negative. 

Abdominal ultrasonography showed a focal hypoechoic lesion in the right hepatic lobe.

A 55-year-old woman with a history of sleep apnea and chronic tobacco use was referred for increasing dyspnea on exertion. Nasofibroscopy revealed leukoplakia of the right vocal cord and bilateral Reinke’s edema. On examination, an elastic, non-tender mass was palpated along the anterior border of the left sternocleidomastoid muscle, 2 cm below the left mandibular angle, and it was partly fixed to deeper structures. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a 23×17×25 mm solid nodule with coarse calcifications in the left thyroid gland and, in the ipsilateral level IIA lymph node group, a 24×25×35 mm well-delineated hypodense mass that did not have typical features of metastatic lymph nodes. Neck ultrasonography showed the thyroid lesion to be slightly hyperechoic to muscle, hypervascular, with coarse peripheral calcifications, while the level IIA mass was well defined, homogeneously hypoechoic, hypovascular, and separated from the submandibular gland by a visible fatty cleavage plane.

A 4-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of bilateral breast enlargement noted over the past months. There was no history of chronic illness, medication use, or familial disorders. His height was 114 cm (+1.2 SDS) and weight was 20 kg (+0.7 SDS). On examination, he had palpable bilateral gynecomastia consistent with Tanner stage 2 breast development. There was no axillary or pubic hair. Stretched penile length was 6 × 1.5 cm. Testicular volumes were 2 mL on the right and 5 mL on the left. Laboratory evaluation showed hormone levels within normal ranges and negative tumor markers. Scrotal ultrasonography revealed an 8 × 12 mm solid lesion with a cystic component in the left testis.

A 62-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of irritation of the left lower eyelid, with worsening swelling, redness, itching, pain, and a foreign-body sensation. She was initially treated by her primary provider for chalazion and meibomianitis with hot compresses, lid wipes, and topical and oral antibiotics, but her symptoms persisted. She was then referred to an ophthalmologist, and an excisional biopsy of the left upper eyelid revealed invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Three additional biopsies of the left lower eyelid demonstrated severe dysplasia and squamous cell carcinoma in situ. She was referred for Mohs micrographic surgery. On arrival at Mohs surgery, examination disclosed diffuse erythema and swelling of the upper and lower eyelids and a diffusely verrucous appearance of the conjunctiva. Histologic examination of the first Mohs stage showed islands of atypical epithelioid cells with a high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio located in the subconjunctival dermis, full-thickness epidermis, and full-thickness conjunctiva. Notably, involvement of the epidermis was minimal, and the majority of carcinoma was present on the conjunctival surface. After the second Mohs stage, invasive carcinoma was observed tracking onto the bulbar conjunctiva beneath the eye shield and could not be excised safely; carcinoma in situ remained within the conjunctiva despite additional stages.

A 50‐year‐old man presented with a painless, progressively enlarging swelling over his lower back for 3 years. On examination, there was a firm, non‐tender soft‐tissue mass measuring 12 × 8 × 5 cm with two surface nodules (6 × 5 × 4 cm and 1.5 × 1 × 1 cm). Fine‐needle aspiration yielded thick, mucoid, gelatinous material. Cytologic smears showed cells in loose cohesive clusters and discrete cells embedded in chondromyxoid material; the cells were round to oval with centrally located nuclei, fine chromatin, moderate to abundant cytoplasm, and occasional prominent nucleoli.

A 78-year-old man and chronic smoker presented with a 6-week history of difficulty swallowing solids and pharyngeal pain. On examination, there was a 3 × 2 cm solitary pedunculated lesion on the right side of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue crossing the midline; tongue mobility was normal, and there was no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. Systemic examination of the chest, abdomen, and heart was unremarkable. A biopsy of the lesion was initially reported as a primary squamous cell carcinoma with some clear cell changes. Blood tests, including renal function, were normal. While awaiting staging MRI, he developed severe oral pain and worsening dysphagia; the tongue lesion doubled in size over two weeks and began to protrude outside the mouth. Because this behavior was unusual for a primary tongue carcinoma, the pathology was reviewed and described as infiltration by carcinoma nests with extensive clear cell changes. The differential diagnosis included squamous cell carcinoma with clear cell changes, metastatic salivary gland neoplasm, and metastases from renal cell carcinoma. An urgent CT scan was arranged, and surgical debulking of the tongue lesion was planned to improve symptoms.

A 45-year-old man reported one year of gradually worsening numbness and weakness in both lower extremities, with marked decline over the past four months leading to dependence on a walker. He also had intermittent urinary incontinence and chronic constipation.  

On examination, sensation to light touch, pinprick, and proprioception was diminished from the T2 level downward, more on the right than the left. Motor testing revealed 0/5 strength in the right leg and 4/5 in the left leg. Bilateral clonus and muscle spasms were noted in the lower extremities.  

Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine showed an intramedullary lesion in the upper thoracic cord with diffuse contrast enhancement and cord expansion. Imaging of the remainder of the neuraxis was unremarkable. Testicular ultrasound and CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis were normal. Serum and cerebrospinal fluid levels of α-fetoprotein and β-HCG were within normal limits.  

Differential diagnoses included primary spinal cord neoplasms (astrocytoma, ependymoma), hemangioblastoma, intradural metastasis, lymphoma, ischemia, and lupus myelitis. The patient was scheduled for an open spinal cord biopsy.

A 17-year-old female student presented in March 2021 with 3 months of gradually progressive left-sided chest pain associated with cough, dyspnea, and chest tightness. The pain worsened when she lay on her left side. She denied hemoptysis, fever, night sweats, weight loss, exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, or prior tuberculosis exposure. Her medical history was unremarkable, and she did not smoke or drink alcohol.
On examination, she was comfortable, with a temperature of 36.4 °C, pulse rate 100 beats/min, blood pressure 116/79 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. The trachea was deviated to the right, and air entry was reduced over the left hemithorax. Cardiovascular and other systems were normal.
Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, serum creatinine 72 μmol/L, prothrombin time 11.3 s, INR 0.89, and normal electrolytes. A chest radiograph confirmed tracheal deviation to the right and a mass occupying the left hemithorax.
Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a large, well-circumscribed mass in the left posterior hemithorax measuring 12.3 cm (AP) × 14.4 cm (transverse) × 22.8 cm (craniocaudal), causing partial collapse of the left lung and mediastinal shift to the right; the mass abutted the descending aorta without bone destruction. These findings were read as “suggestive of pleuropulmonary blastoma vs. neurogenic tumor (ganglioneuroma).”
A CT-guided core-needle biopsy was performed.

An 80-year-old man was referred for evaluation of progressive weakness and sensory symptoms of 8 months’ duration and new-onset lower-extremity edema. He had become wheelchair-bound with marked decline in activities of daily living. Two months earlier, pleural effusions and leg edema had been noted elsewhere without a definitive diagnosis.

On admission, temperature was 37.6°C, blood pressure 135/76 mm Hg, and heart rate 90/min. Physical examination showed scattered hemangiomatous lesions on the chest and pitting edema of both lower legs.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL, platelets 102 × 10^3/μL, serum creatinine 1.07 mg/dL (eGFR 51 mL/min/1.73 m^2), and C-reactive protein 0.75 mg/dL. Urinalysis demonstrated 0.5 g protein per gram of creatinine without hematuria or Bence-Jones proteins. Serum IgA was elevated at 480 mg/dL; IgG and IgM were within normal limits. Complement levels were normal. Anti-nuclear, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic, and anti-GBM antibodies were negative. Immunofixation electrophoresis revealed biclonal bands of IgG-κ and IgA-λ. Free light-chain levels were 250 mg/L (κ) and 140 mg/L (λ) with a κ/λ ratio of 1.78. Serum IL-6 was 40.0 pg/mL; serum and plasma VEGF levels were markedly elevated at 1030 pg/mL and 170 pg/mL, respectively. Prolactin was 26.1 ng/mL (normal 4.3–13.7).

Nerve conduction studies showed diffuse sensorimotor polyneuropathy with demyelinating and secondary axonal features. Bone marrow biopsy revealed 5–10% plasma cells with a normal immunophenotype. Biopsies of the skin and stomach showed no evidence of amyloidosis.

On hospital day 10, a renal biopsy was performed. Of 23 glomeruli, 5 were globally sclerotic; the remainder showed diffuse mesangiolysis, segmental double contours of capillary loops, moderate enlargement, and prominent endothelial cell hypertrophy without hypercellularity or thrombus formation. Immunofluorescence demonstrated only sparse staining for IgG, IgA, κ, and λ light chains. The findings were summarized as glomerular microangiopathy without significant immunoglobulin deposition.

A 14-year-old boy presented with a swelling in the left side of his neck for two years. The swelling was insidious in onset and gradually increasing in size. He had no significant past medical or surgical history, was not on medications, and had no family history of genetic disease or malignancy. On examination, there was a single, firm, non-tender, mobile swelling measuring approximately 5 cm × 4 cm in the left posterior triangle of the neck; the remainder of the head and neck examination was normal. Neurologic examination revealed normal muscle strength, no sensory deficits, no pathologic reflexes, and no long-tract signs. Vital signs were stable. Laboratory studies, including total leukocyte count, peripheral blood smear, and urinary catecholamine level, were within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging of the neck showed a well-defined, ovoid mass in the left posterior cervical space measuring 6 × 4.5 × 2.5 cm; the lesion was T1 isointense, T2 hyperintense, had an enhancing solid component, extended into the left C5–C6 neural foramen causing its widening, displaced the carotid space anteromedially, abutted and displaced the sternocleidomastoid muscle anteriorly, and extended inferiorly into the left supraclavicular region. No clinical or radiologic stigmata of neurofibromatosis were present.

A 45-year-old blond man presented with a 6-month history of a rapidly enlarging nodular lesion on the anterior thigh. He denied pain but reported bleeding after minor trauma. Fourteen years earlier, he received a kidney transplant and had been maintained on tacrolimus, prednisolone, and mycophenolate mofetil; he had developed chronic graft rejection. He had no personal or family history of melanoma or nonmelanoma skin cancer. On examination, there was a firm, well-circumscribed nodule about 3 cm in diameter with a red hue obscured by a blood-crusted surface. No regional lymphadenopathy or organomegaly was noted. Laboratory studies were notable only for elevated creatinine (3.3 mg/dL) and urea (78 mmol/L). Viral serologies, including HIV, were negative.  
Given the bleeding, rapid growth, and nonpigmented appearance, the initial differential diagnoses included pyogenic granuloma, amelanotic melanoma, and squamous cell carcinoma. A plan was made for complete surgical excision and histopathological evaluation.

A 21-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 1-week history of breast pain, abdominal distension, and weakness. Her personal, gynecologic, and family histories were unremarkable. On examination, she was tachypneic (22 breaths/min), tachycardic (110 beats/min), hypotensive (mean arterial pressure 55 mmHg), febrile (37.5 °C), and lethargic. Her breasts were swollen and tender. The abdomen was distended, diffusely tender, and dull to percussion.

Bedside ultrasound showed markedly enlarged ovaries and a large volume of free ascitic fluid. Laboratory testing revealed a leukocyte count of 30,000/μL (95% neutrophils), platelet count of 90,000/μL, evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation, elevated urea and creatinine levels, elevated bilirubin, elevated transaminases, and severe lactic metabolic acidosis. HIV testing was negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen confirmed bilateral ovarian enlargement, pleural effusions, and large-volume ascites.

Given her hemodynamic instability and deterioration, a diagnostic laparotomy was planned.

A 38-year-old woman with a history of well-controlled asthma and no smoking history presented with persistent high fever and pneumonia despite appropriate antibiotic therapy. Chest CT revealed left lower lobe atelectasis and a water-density mass within the left main bronchus. Bronchoscopic examination showed a polypoid tumor occluding approximately 90% of the left main bronchial lumen. Partial bronchoscopic snaring of the lesion led to radiographic resolution of atelectasis. 

Grossly, the snared specimen was a well-circumscribed, firm, tan nodule measuring 1.5 cm in diameter. Microscopically, the lesion was submucosal and composed of sheets of oval to cuboidal cells with centrally located round nuclei and amphophilic cytoplasm. Abundant small- to medium-sized thin-walled vascular channels—some surrounded by tumor cells—were present. There was no necrosis, vascular invasion, cellular atypia, or mitotic activity.

A 14-year-old girl presented with a 5-year history of a gradually enlarging, painless swelling over the buttock region extending to the lower back. The lesion began as a small lump with no history of trauma, pain, skin changes, discharge, fever, weight loss, or neurological symptoms. She reported functional difficulty with sitting and wearing clothes.

On examination, she was well appearing, with stable vital signs and no peripheral lymphadenopathy. Local inspection revealed a large, lobulated mass covering the entire buttock and lower back, measuring approximately 28 cm × 34 cm. The overlying skin was intact and of normal color. Palpation showed a firm, partially mobile, non-tender mass with multiple roots at different positions; it was not fixed to underlying muscle and did not obstruct the anal opening. Rectal and other systemic examinations were normal.

Laboratory studies were unremarkable: WBC 6.07 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, platelets 340 × 10^9/L, creatinine 30 μmol/L, BUN 3.22 mmol/L, K 3.9 mmol/L, Na 138.3 mmol/L, HIV and syphilis tests negative.

MRI of the pelvis demonstrated a large, well-circumscribed mass in the gluteal region with no connection to the spine and unclear tissue origin.

A 50-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 6-month history of intermittent, worsening left lower back pain that limited his activity. He denied unexplained weight loss. Vital signs were within normal limits. Abdominal examination was unremarkable. An initial abdominal ultrasound identified a left kidney stone. A noncontrast CT scan of the abdomen subsequently revealed a mass in the left lower abdomen. CT urography with contrast demonstrated a prominently calcified solid mass infiltrating adjacent structures in the left retroperitoneum. Based on imaging, the leading considerations were adrenal carcinoma or a retroperitoneal sarcoma. On January 13, 2022, the patient underwent laparotomy with resection of a left retroperitoneal tumor that was found to infiltrate the pancreas, spleen, gastric region, and left kidney.

A 27-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a right-sided abdominal mass. She was asymptomatic, with good performance status, no weight loss, and no comorbidities. On examination, there was a firm, nontender liver mass extending 6 cm below the right costal margin with rounded borders. Laboratory investigations, including liver function tests, viral hepatitis markers, and tumor markers, were normal (alpha-fetoprotein 0.4 ng/mL). Duplex ultrasound showed a 10 × 8 cm heteroechoic mass in the right liver lobe with invasion of the right portal vein. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy findings were normal. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated a 10 × 10 × 13 cm heterogeneously enhancing lesion in segments V through VIII, with early arterial enhancement that persisted in later phases, a prominent feeding right hepatic artery, and right portal vein thrombosis; no extrahepatic lesions were seen. A chest CT scan was unremarkable. Fine-needle aspiration cytology had suggested hepatocellular carcinoma. On the basis of these findings, a right hepatectomy was planned.

An 86-year-old man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus has been on continuous cycling peritoneal dialysis since February 2017. He presented to the home dialysis unit with two nights of cycler drain alarms and “whitish” dialysate. He denied abdominal pain, fever, or other constitutional symptoms, noting only weight loss as his peripheral edema resolved. He had no prior episodes of peritonitis or history of tuberculosis exposure. Physical examination was unremarkable, with normal vital signs and no abdominal tenderness.

Per unit protocol, 1 L of 2.5% dextrose dialysate was instilled and allowed to dwell for 2 hours. The effluent appeared milky and was sent for cell count with differential, bacterial and mycobacterial cultures, and triglyceride measurement. Empiric intraperitoneal ceftazidime and vancomycin were administered. The total nucleated cell count was 354 × 10^6/L (87% lymphocytes, 8% monocytes, 3% neutrophils), and all cultures were negative. The triglyceride concentration in the dialysate was 6.3 mmol/L (557 mg/dL).

A 31-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 2-month history of unintentional weight loss (approximately 5% of body weight) and right upper-quadrant abdominal pain. His father had undergone liver resection for an unspecified hepatic neoplasm 12 years earlier. The patient had arterial hypertension treated with ramipril and nebivolol, denied alcohol use, and had no history of viral hepatitis. 

On examination, vital signs were normal. The abdomen was distended, and a firm, palpable mass was noted in the right upper quadrant without ascites or splenomegaly. Laboratory studies showed a gamma-glutamyl transferase level of 349 U/L and a leukocyte count of 13.8×10^3/mm^3. Serologies for hepatitis B and C, autoimmune hepatitis, and HIV were negative. Serum α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 22×13×25-cm, lobulated, multinodular mass replacing the right hemi-liver, extending into segment 4 and the caudate lobe, with central calcifications. The lesion demonstrated heterogeneous early arterial enhancement with washout on portal and delayed phases. The right portal vein branch and the right and middle hepatic veins were not visualized due to tumor infiltration, and the left hepatic lobe was hypertrophied.

A 68-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of nausea, vomiting, upper abdominal pain localized to the left hypochondrium and lumbar region, and unintentional weight loss. She has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus on insulin, hypertension, and thoracolumbar discopathy. She does not smoke, drinks alcohol occasionally, and has no family history of malignancy. On examination, she had epigastric tenderness without palpable masses. 

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed two sessile, crater-like ulcerated lesions in the gastric fundus measuring 2.5–3.0 cm in diameter; biopsies were obtained. 

Abdominal and pelvic MRI showed two irregular, enhancing masses in the gastric fundus measuring 1.45×1.9 cm and 2.8×2.4 cm, both with restricted diffusion. Additional findings included pelvic girdle bone lesions suggestive of metastases, bilateral adrenal adenomas, and uterine fibromatous nodules. 

Subsequent thoracoabdominal CT confirmed the gastric masses and demonstrated multiple bone and pulmonary metastatic lesions.

A 30-year-old woman, G2P1, presented 14 months after delivery with 2 weeks of nausea, vomiting, and severe abdominal pain. She reported occasional bright red blood per rectum for 4 months and a 5-kg weight loss over 2 weeks.  
On CT of the abdomen, there was an ill-defined 6-cm collection in the mid-abdomen with adjacent thickened loops of small bowel and sigmoid colon, along with hypodense lesions in the liver. Colonoscopy demonstrated mucosal congestion and a narrowing in the sigmoid colon that could not be traversed; biopsy yielded only colonic mucosa.  
One month later, serum β-hCG was 5.9 IU/l (normal, 0.02–0.8 IU/l). Abdominal MRI showed multiple hepatic lesions. A liver biopsy revealed moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma with abundant necrosis. Serum carcinoembryonic antigen was 5.4 ng/ml (normal ≤ 5.0 ng/ml) and CA19-9 was 1,168 U/ml (normal ≤ 35 U/ml). Immunohistochemical analysis of the liver biopsy was consistent with a colorectal primary.  
Repeat colonoscopy confirmed severe stenosis of the sigmoid colon; biopsy showed poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma with immunohistochemical markers consistent with colonic origin.  
Prior to planned mFOLFOX6 chemotherapy, serum β-hCG measured 260.1 IU/l. Transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasonography showed no intrauterine or ectopic pregnancy. A suction dilation and curettage was performed; repeat transvaginal ultrasound again showed no evidence of intrauterine or ectopic gestation.

A 36-year-old multiparous woman (G3P2) was referred for evaluation of acute pelvic pain and a 2-year history of a protruding bulge from her vagina, associated with discomfort and dyspareunia. She had been diagnosed elsewhere with a vaginal prolapse and occasionally reduced the bulge digitally. Her medical history included migraines with aura and exercise-induced asthma; she had never had a Pap smear. On bimanual examination, there was a well-delineated, solid mass on the midline anterior vaginal wall, measuring 5 cm by 5 cm; the uterus and vaginal walls above the mass were well supported, and the cervix was visible without tenderness. A Pap smear was attempted with difficulty. CA-125 was 29 U/mL. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a 2.9 cm left ovarian cyst suggestive of endometrioma and a solid mass inferior to the uterus and anterior to the vagina, displacing the bladder. Pelvic MRI revealed a 45 mm × 50 mm solid mass in the vesicovaginal septum with a well-defined margin, displacing the bladder anteriorly and the urethra to the left. On T2-weighted images, the lesion was predominantly hypointense and heterogeneous, with areas of hyperintensity; there was mild gadolinium enhancement. Endometriosis deposits were noted elsewhere in the pelvis.

A 72-year-old woman presented after a bicycle accident with an effusion and pain primarily over the lateral joint space of her right knee. She had no palpable masses and an otherwise unremarkable medical history. Radiographs of the knee were initially read as normal, though in retrospect they show a subtle low-density structure adjacent to the lateral joint space suggestive of a fat-containing lesion. MRI demonstrated a tear of the medial meniscus posterior horn and body, and also revealed a well-circumscribed soft-tissue lesion with fatty consistency located beneath the lateral collateral ligament and the popliteus tendon. On MRI, the mass was slightly inhomogeneous, showing subtle intralesional foci of intermediate signal on T1-weighted images and high signal on fat-suppressed T2-weighted images.

A 56-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of progressive bilateral vision loss and visual field defects, worse in the right eye. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/40 in the right eye and 20/50 in the left eye. Intraocular pressure and anterior segment examinations were normal in both eyes. Fundus examination showed multiple serous retinal detachments in both eyes without vitreous cells, local flake depigmentation nasal to each optic disc, and retinal folds at the posterior pole. B-scan ultrasonography revealed neuroepithelial detachment, retinal elevation, and marked choroidal thickening without scleral involvement. Ultrasound biomicroscopy demonstrated focal suprachoroidal effusion and diffuse ciliary-body thickening. Optical coherence tomography showed a wavy contour of the neuroepithelial and retinal pigment epithelial layers, subretinal hyporeflective spaces, and choroidal thickening (921 µm in the right eye, 882 µm in the left eye). Fluorescein angiography revealed early focal hyperfluorescence and late staining without obvious leakage. Indocyanine green angiography demonstrated persistent hypofluorescent spots of varying sizes in both eyes. An anterior chamber tap showed an interleukin-10/interleukin-6 ratio of 0. The patient declined chorioretinal biopsy and agreed to systemic evaluation.

A 29-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of progressive imbalance on walking and diplopia. Nine years earlier, he had undergone subtotal resection of a pineal-region tumor followed by cerebrospinal fluid diversion and, 2 years later, radiation therapy, with no residual lesion on imaging thereafter. 

On current presentation, magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed a lobulated 5 cm × 3 cm × 2 cm pineal mass that was solid–cystic and showed heterogeneous enhancement; spinal MRI showed no evidence of metastasis. He underwent subtotal resection via a supracerebellar-infratentorial approach.

Histopathological examination showed a tumor composed of cuboidal cells forming perivascular rosettes and lacked pineocytomatous rosettes, mitosis, necrosis, or microvascular proliferation. Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated negative glial fibrillary acidic protein staining; focal positivity for synaptophysin and epithelial membrane antigen; positive S100 protein and pancytokeratin (AE1/AE3); and a Ki-67 proliferation index of less than 1 percent.

A 27-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 5-year history of mixed right knee pain and an indolent, noninflamed swelling on the anteromedial aspect of the knee. There was no limitation of motion, no sensory or motor deficits, and no systemic symptoms. Initial knee radiographs showed a 4-cm, well-corticated, homogeneous bony outgrowth arising from the metaphyseal-epiphyseal region of the proximal tibia without cortical breach or periosteal reaction. The lesion was initially interpreted as a benign bone tumor (osteochondroma), and the patient did not follow up. She returned 5 years later; the mass had enlarged to 7 cm in its long axis, still without functional impairment or systemic signs. Repeat radiographs confirmed the size increase. CT demonstrated a cortical lesion without medullary extension. MRI showed involvement of the anterior tibial tuberosity and patellar tendon, with no extension into posterior or lateral soft tissues. Regional staging revealed no distant metastases.

A 35-year-old man with hypertension and a family history of inflammatory bowel disease and colon cancer in a maternal grandmother presented with three months of chest pain, shortness of breath, and unintentional 30 lb weight loss. Vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination was unremarkable.  
Chest CT revealed a 7.6 × 2.6 cm anterior mediastinal mass with associated lymphadenopathy and no other lesions. Initial differential diagnosis included thymoma, thymic cyst, lymphoma, germ cell tumor, and metastatic disease.  
The patient underwent robotically assisted thymectomy via a left thoracoscopic approach. Intraoperatively, the mass was noted to involve the thymus and was partially resected due to extension into the right thorax.  
Histopathological examination showed a poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma with enteric histomorphology, involvement of more than five lymph nodes with extranodal extension, and prominent lymphovascular invasion; no residual normal thymic tissue was identified.  
Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated that the tumor was diffusely positive for CDX2, CK20, β-catenin, and CK7, and negative for TTF-1, PAX8, cKIT, and SALL4.  
We were unable to definitively determine whether this lesion represented a primary thymic adenocarcinoma or a metastatic adenocarcinoma.

A 60-year-old woman noted a mass in her left lower neck for 5 months. A prior open biopsy was reported as spindle cell sarcoma. On examination, there was an extremely soft, palpable mass in the left lower anterior neck. 

Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 60×26×42 mm well-marginated soft-tissue mass displacing the sternocleidomastoid muscle anteriorly, with heterogeneous enhancement and low-density areas suggestive of intralesional fat. MRI showed the lesion to be isointense to soft tissue with scattered areas of high signal on T1- and T2-weighted images consistent with fat, and on fat-suppressed gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted images, the mass enhanced markedly with suppression of the high-intensity areas. FDG-PET/CT revealed a maximum SUV of 2.1 in the tumor.

Histopathology of the initial open biopsy showed spindle cells with epithelioid differentiation. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated both spindle and epithelial cells positive for cytokeratin AE1/3; the spindle cells were α-smooth muscle actin positive, S100 negative, desmin negative, Bcl-2 positive, and TdT negative. Based on these findings, synovial sarcoma and spindle cell carcinoma were suspected.

An 8-year-old boy was referred with a “boil” in the upper right posterior maxillary gingiva that had been enlarging over 6 months. Six months earlier, a similar lesion in the same location had been excised by a general dentist. Medical history was noncontributory. On examination, there was a sessile, reddish nodular lesion measuring 1.5 × 0.5 × 1.0 cm on the maxillary right gingiva. The lesion was fluctuant and bled easily on slight pressure but showed no blanching or purulent exudate. An intraoral periapical radiograph demonstrated a radiolucency surrounding the developing maxillary right premolar, with focal loss of the alveolar crest. Grossly carious mandibular right molars were noted to be traumatizing the area. Extraction of the lower molars to remove the irritant was considered.

A 45-year-old woman was diagnosed in 2007 with a sacral tumor after a 2-year history of lower back pain radiating to the coccygeal and perianal regions, accompanied by left perianal hypoesthesia. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging revealed a large, lobulated mass extending from S2 to S5 with invasion of the left gluteal muscle. In January 2008, she underwent a partial sacrectomy. Histologic examination showed nests of neoplastic cells with physaliferous cytoplasm and a chondroid stroma; immunohistochemical staining was diffusely positive for pancytokeratin, vimentin, and S-100 protein and focally positive for epithelial membrane antigen, with negative margins.

Eleven months later, an asymptomatic locoregional recurrence was detected on MRI and excised, followed by adjuvant radiotherapy. One year after that, a new locoregional recurrence and a soft-tissue lesion at L4 were deemed unresectable, and imatinib (800 mg daily) was started. Six months later, progression with a subcutaneous mass at L4 prompted a switch to sunitinib (37.5 mg daily), but within 3 months liver, bone, and lung metastases appeared. Third-line therapy with weekly cisplatin and daily imatinib achieved stable disease for 7 months.

By September 2013, with extensive metastatic disease, she was noted to have a firm, nontender, erythematous nodule measuring 2 × 2 cm on her left cheek.

A 39-year-old man with a 20–pack-year smoking history presented with a several-day history of painful oral ulcers that did not respond to fluconazole or valacyclovir. He denied fever, chills, night sweats, anorexia, or weight loss. Ten days later, he developed diffuse bullous and erosive skin lesions on the chest, abdomen, and arms. Initial blood tests showed isolated neutropenia. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed an 18 × 8.9 cm necrotic, irregular mesenteric mass without lymphadenopathy. A percutaneous core biopsy was nondiagnostic. On transfer, he had febrile neutropenia (WBC 900/mm3), persistent oral ulcers, and widespread cutaneous lesions. Viral serologies (HBV, HCV, HIV) and EBV PCR were negative. Bone marrow biopsy showed 80% cellularity with left-shifted granulopoiesis, mild dysmegakaryopoiesis, and reactive plasmacytosis, but “no evidence of an epithelial or mesenchymal tumor, lymphoproliferative disorder, or acute leukemia.” A repeat core biopsy of the abdominal mass showed a cellular proliferation of mildly to moderately atypical oval-to-spindle-shaped cells in fascicular to vaguely storiform arrangements with a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated tumor cells positive for vimentin, CD21, and CD68, weakly positive for CD45, focally positive for S100 protein, CD34, and SMA, and negative for ALK, CD117, DOG-1, CD3, CD20, CD23, and EBER.

A 23-year-old woman presented with a right lateral thigh mass first noted 1 year earlier that had enlarged over the past 2–3 months. She had no history of trauma. On examination, the mass was palpable, non-tender, mildly warm, initially firm but softer as it grew, with no discharge or sinus.  
Ultrasonography revealed a well-circumscribed large subcutaneous cystic mass composed of a main cyst containing hypoechoic fluid and debris in its dependent portion with a hyperechoic nodular lesion inside, and an adjacent daughter cyst with debris-like material; Doppler imaging showed no vascular signal.  
Magnetic resonance imaging two months later showed a 5.5×4.8×2.4 cm cystic lesion with high signal intensity and a low-signal wall on both T1- and T2-weighted images; the daughter cyst had slightly lower T2 signal; a low-signal nodular lesion within the main cyst; a solid component contiguous with the cyst walls; and, with gadolinium, both the cyst wall and solid portion demonstrated diffuse enhancement.  
The preoperative differential diagnoses based on imaging were a complicated epidermoid cyst, cystic change of a neurogenic tumor, and a parasitic cyst such as a hydatid cyst.

An 11-year-old boy was referred with a 10-month history of swelling and constant pain localized to the distal end of his fourth toe, with no history of trauma or systemic symptoms. Laboratory studies showed an elevated antinuclear-antibody titer but normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein levels. A fine-needle aspiration yielded no organisms and insufficient tissue for histology. Technetium-99m bone scintigraphy demonstrated intense focal uptake in the affected toe. Plain radiography revealed a partially sclerotic, slightly lobulated mass replacing the distal two-thirds of the distal phalanx, demarcated by a radiolucent rim, with an intact growth plate. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a central hyposignal lesion at the distal phalanx with surrounding inflammatory changes and edema on T2-weighted images; postgadolinium T1-weighted images demonstrated rim enhancement around a relatively avascular center.

A 34-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of dyspnea on exertion (stage II) and intermittent chest pain without cough or hemoptysis. He had no significant past medical history. On examination, he was afebrile, conscious, with a respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute, heart rate 85 beats per minute, and blood pressure 135/80 mm Hg. Pulmonary examination revealed dullness to percussion over the left basal hemithorax. A chest radiograph showed an opacity occupying the lower half of the left hemithorax, silhouettes the left heart border and diaphragm, suggesting an anterior mediastinal mass without pleural effusion. Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated a large, well-defined heterogeneous mass with predominant fat attenuation mingled with focal areas of soft-tissue density, extending from the anterior mediastinum to the left diaphragm and displacing the adjacent lung superiorly, with no signs of pulmonary or adjacent-tissue infiltration.

A 69-year-old man presented with a one-year history of right scrotal swelling and discomfort. He underwent hydrocelectomy, during which non-homogeneous tissue was noted intraoperatively. No preoperative ultrasound or CT imaging had been performed. On referral, physical examination revealed an edematous right scrotum with a hard, tender mass and no palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy. The patient denied any history of scrotal trauma or asbestos exposure. His medical history was notable for prostate adenocarcinoma (Gleason score 3 + 3 = 6, cT1cN0M0) treated 8 years earlier with external-beam radiotherapy and a subsequent course of androgen-deprivation therapy; his PSA level at the time of the current evaluation was 0.1 ng/mL. He had no other comorbidities. Serum alpha-fetoprotein and beta human chorionic gonadotropin levels were within normal limits.

A 70-year-old woman presented with a one-week history of headache, generalized weakness, fatigue, right eyelid drooping, and double vision. On neurologic examination, she had right palpebral ptosis and impaired function of cranial nerves II, III, IV, V, and VI on the right side. Magnetic resonance imaging of the sellar region showed a mass involving the pituitary gland and infundibular stalk, extending into the right cavernous sinus and the sphenoid sinus. Vital signs were notable for a blood pressure of 120/70 mmHg and a pulse rate of 80 beats per minute. There was no lymphadenopathy or goiter.  
Laboratory studies revealed a serum sodium of 141 mEq/L, serum osmolarity of 295 mOsm/kg H₂O, and a urine osmolality of 173 mOsm/kg H₂O. Thyroid function tests showed a free T4 of 20.4 pmol/L and a TSH of 0.705 mIU/L. Morning cortisol was 16.7 µg/dL with an ACTH of 41 ng/L. Gonadotropins were low (LH 0.1 mIU/mL, FSH 1.8 mIU/mL) with an estradiol of 8.1 pg/mL. Prolactin was elevated at 102.4 ng/dL. A complete blood count showed hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, WBC 11,760/mm³, lymphocytes 1,400/mm³, neutrophils 9,660/mm³, and platelets 123,000/mm³.

A 47-year-old man presented with a cough. Chest CT performed by his pulmonologist revealed an incidental left adrenal mass measuring 8 × 6 × 3 cm. Evaluation for hormonal activity—including pheochromocytoma, Cushing syndrome, and hyperaldosteronism—was negative. Dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI of the left adrenal gland showed diffuse heterogeneous enhancement of the lesion. FDG PET/CT revealed increased uptake in the left adrenal gland (SUVmax 19.60) without other sites of abnormal uptake. On the basis of these findings, the patient underwent a left laparoscopic adrenalectomy for presumed adrenal carcinoma.

A 45-year-old Chinese woman presented with anterior chest pain of 10 days’ duration. Review of systems was otherwise unremarkable. On examination, vital signs, physical findings, and routine laboratory tests were normal. Enhanced computed tomography of the chest revealed a 2.4×1.4×2.8 cm nodule beneath the left thyroid lobe, mild bilateral pulmonary inflammation, and a 4.0×2.5 cm mass in the anterior mediastinum; both lesions demonstrated increased density on enhanced images similar to thyroid tissue. Serum thyrotropin and free thyroid hormone levels were within normal limits, and antithyroglobulin and antithyroid peroxidase antibodies were negative. Neck ultrasonography showed multiple hypoechoic nodules in the left upper lobe (largest, 0.6×0.4 cm) and right lower lobe (largest, 1.2×1.0 cm) with normal color Doppler flow; a separate 2.4×1.4×2.8 cm nodule under the left lobe had low-level Doppler flow and no cervical lymphadenopathy. Abdominal ultrasonography was unremarkable. Technetium-99m pertechnetate scintigraphy demonstrated no increased uptake in either the left-lobe nodule or the anterior mediastinal mass.

A 66-year-old woman with a history of laparoscopic cholecystectomy was referred after an abnormal upper gastrointestinal X-ray at a routine medical checkup revealed a gastric lesion. She was asymptomatic. Upper endoscopy showed an elevated submucosal mass on the greater curvature of the stomach with intact mucosa and no ulceration. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography demonstrated a well-defined 52 mm mass at the greater curvature, with both intraluminal and extramural components. Laboratory tests, including serum carcinoembryonic antigen, were within normal limits.

An 82-year-old Caucasian woman presented to the emergency department with a 1-month history of a tender umbilical nodule. Over the past 3 days, the lesion had ulcerated, bled intermittently, and produced a serous-purulent discharge. She denied fever, weight loss, or changes in her long-standing constipation, but noted mild fatigue. Vital signs were stable, and routine blood tests were within normal limits.

On examination, the umbilical lesion measured approximately 18 × 16 mm, was firm and fibrous in consistency, and was painful to palpation; there was no surrounding erythema or warmth. To exclude a strangulated hernia or an abscess, a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen was obtained.

CT demonstrated a soft-tissue density nodule arising from the umbilical scar with intense enhancement after contrast administration and no adjacent fat-stranding. Incidentally, there was a 25-mm segment of enhanced caecal wall thickening (maximum thickness 6 mm) with three enlarged pericaecal lymph nodes (up to 7 mm). No hepatic, peritoneal, chest, or brain lesions were identified.

A 30-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of swelling in the left lower posterior tooth region. She had undergone extraction of mobile teeth in that area 18 months earlier; 5–6 months after extraction, she noted a gradually enlarging swelling associated with mild intermittent left ear pain but no discharge. Medical and family histories were unremarkable. 

On examination, mild facial asymmetry was seen over the left angle and ramus of the mandible. Palpation revealed a hard, nontender 2 cm × 2 cm swelling on the lower third of the left face extending from the mandibular body to just anterior to the angle. Intraorally, the left lower molars were missing; the mucosa appeared normal. A 3 cm × 2 cm hard, nontender expansion of both buccal and lingual cortices obliterated the buccal sulcus from distal to the left second premolar to the anterior border of the ramus.

A panoramic radiograph showed a well-defined multilocular radiolucency in the left mandible. Computed tomography demonstrated a well-defined expansile lytic lesion of the left mandibular angle and ramus with cortical thinning and a breach of the lingual cortex. Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed a lesion that was heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, isointense on T1-weighted images, with heterogeneous enhancement and minimal soft-tissue extension along the floor of the mouth; the left inferior alveolar nerve canal was displaced.

A 36-year-old man was referred with suspicion of a right incarcerated inguinal hernia. He reported right-sided scrotal swelling and severe pain for 1 day. He noted a right inguinal and scrotal mass that had been present for 2 years, gradually increasing in size and occasionally disappearing. There was no fever or trauma. On examination, a firm 15×10 cm mass occupied the right hemiscrotum and extended into the inguinal region; the left testis was normal. Serum levels of human chorionic gonadotropin, lactate dehydrogenase, and alpha-fetoprotein were within normal limits. A chest radiograph showed cardiomegaly. A kidney-ureter-bladder radiograph revealed no urinary tract stones. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a mass in the McBurney area previously thought to be intestine, and scrotal ultrasound indicated an extratesticular mass within the scrotum.

A 17-year-old female presented with a 3-week history of generalized papulonecrotic eruptions on the trunk and extremities. She was afebrile and had no systemic symptoms. There was no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. She denied any underlying disease or family history of malignancy. Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 12,300 per cubic millimeter; liver-function tests and lactate dehydrogenase levels were normal. A skin biopsy of a papulonecrotic lesion on the right arm was performed. Histologic examination showed marked epidermal necrosis with dense superficial and deep perivascular and perifollicular infiltrates. The infiltrate consisted predominantly of small-to-medium–sized atypical lymphocytes with mitotic activity, admixed neutrophils, and extravasated erythrocytes. Angioinvasion, characterized by atypical cells within vascular lumina, and angiodestruction, evidenced by fibrinoid necrosis and intraluminal thrombi, were also present.

A 38-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of progressive left upper-quadrant fullness and dull abdominal discomfort. She denied weight loss, fevers, jaundice, or prior liver disease. Physical examination revealed a firm, non-tender mass palpable in the left upper quadrant. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and liver‐function tests, were within normal limits.
