Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a solitary, well-circumscribed, large hypodense lesion in the left hepatic lobe without evidence of necrosis or cirrhosis of the remaining liver.

A 36-year-old Asian man presented with a 4-month history of worsening headaches and complete right homonymous hemianopia. Two years earlier, he had a left occipital intracerebral hematoma of unknown cause. On examination, vital signs were normal, and neurologic testing confirmed the visual field defect without other focal deficits.

Noncontrast head CT showed a left occipital intraparenchymal hemorrhage. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI revealed a left tentorial extra-axial enhancing mass with adjacent parenchymal hemorrhage, suggesting a cavernous angioma. The patient underwent a left occipital craniotomy; intraoperatively, the mass was found to invade the falx cerebri and adjacent cortex, limiting resection to subtotal removal. Postoperative CT showed no complications.

Histopathological examination demonstrated spindle cells forming masses with branching ectatic vasculature, focal collagenous regions, and up to 20 mitoses per ten high-power fields. Immunohistochemical studies showed strong immunoreactivity for CD31, CD99, and Fli-1, with scattered S100-positive cells, and negative staining for CD34, EMA, desmin, muscle-specific actin, and Bcl-2.

A 16-year-old neutered female domestic shorthair cat was evaluated for acute inappetence, ataxia, disorientation, and vacant staring. On examination, the bladder was markedly distended and resistant to manual expression; the cat was lethargic and ataxic, with an absent left menace response and reduced left nasal sensation. Between episodes, it stared vacantly. The cat experienced multiple brief focal seizures each day—rightward head turn and circling with facial twitching, lip-smacking, salivation, mydriasis, and occasional vocalization—lasting ~30 seconds. CBC showed a mild non-regenerative anemia; serum biochemistry was normal except for a low total T4 (9.4 nmol/L). Blood pressure was normal. FeLV antigen and FIV antibody tests were negative. Thoracic and abdominal radiographs were unremarkable. Brain MRI demonstrated an ill-defined intra-axial mass in the right piriform lobe extending into the internal capsule; it was hypointense on T1-weighted images, mildly heterogeneous hyperintense on T2-weighted, T2-FLAIR, and diffusion-weighted images, homogeneously hyperintense on T2*-weighted images, and showed marked homogeneous contrast enhancement with extensive perilesional edema and a leftward midline shift. There was bilateral hippocampal swelling with heterogeneous T2 and T2-FLAIR hyperintensity and marked contrast enhancement. Cisternal CSF analysis revealed elevated protein (75 mg/dL) without pleocytosis. Toxoplasma gondii serology was negative. While a preliminary diagnosis of glioma associated with moderate post-ictal hippocampal changes was established, the possibility of concurrent limbic encephalitis could not be entirely ruled out.

A 24-year-old Afro-Caribbean man with no significant medical history presented with a 1-year history of multiple relapsing pruritic macules. He denied fever, chills, night sweats, and weight loss. Treatment with topical low- and mid-potency steroids had been ineffective. On examination, there were numerous 3–5 mm hyperpigmented and erythematous macules on the upper arms, trunk, and bilateral hips. No lymphadenopathy or other systemic signs were found. A 4-mm punch biopsy showed irregular epidermal hyperplasia, spongiosis, and a moderately intense inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes, eosinophils, and scattered atypical enlarged lymphocytes. Immunohistochemical staining revealed predominantly CD3+ T cells with some loss of CD7 expression in atypical cells, a CD4:CD8 ratio of 4:1, and increased CD30 positivity with some clustering in the atypical cells. Routine laboratory tests were normal, except for an initial antinuclear antibody that proved falsely positive on repeat testing.

A 22-year-old woman presented with intermittent epigastric pain and back pain of 2–3 hours’ duration, typically at night. At age 15, a screening CT scan for suspected peritonitis or ovarian torsion had incidentally detected a 3.3-cm multilocular cystic mass in the tail of the pancreas. Routine surveillance over the next 6 years showed gradual growth to 5.1 cm (approximately 0.3 cm/year), followed by rapid expansion to 6.3 cm over 3 months, coinciding with onset of her pain.

She had no significant medical, surgical, familial, or allergic history. On examination, there was no abdominal tenderness or palpable mass. Laboratory studies, including pancreatic tumor markers, were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a solitary, irregularly formed, multilocular cystic lesion with thin septa and focal calcification in the pancreatic tail; the septa and capsule were not enhanced, and the splenic artery and vein were uninvolved. MRI showed low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted images. Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated a multilocular cystic lesion with calcification but no mural nodules. Endoscopic retrograde pancreatography revealed no communication between the cysts and the main pancreatic duct, no mucin discharge, displacement of the distal duct, and preservation of small branch ducts around the mass.

A 64-year-old Iranian man presented with a 6-week history of progressive paresthesia and asymmetric weakness of the lower extremities. The paresthesia began in the left foot, then involved the right, followed within 1 week by weakness in the distal lower limbs that progressed proximally over 4 weeks. He also reported anorexia and a 10 kg weight loss over 6 weeks. He had no history of diabetes, autoimmune or neoplastic disease, toxin exposure, or drug use. On examination, he was afebrile with normal vital signs. General examination, including skin and lymph nodes, was unremarkable. Neurologic examination showed decreased muscle strength in the lower limbs (left < right), absent deep-tendon reflexes in the lower limbs, asymmetric distal hypoesthesia in all limbs, and bilateral atrophy of the first dorsal interosseous muscles. Electrophysiologic studies revealed distal axonal sensory-motor polyneuropathy with ongoing axonal loss and a pattern consistent with mononeuritis multiplex. Initial laboratory studies showed microcytic anemia (Hb 9.9 g/dL; MCV 69.4 fL; RDW 21%) and elevated ESR (45 mm/h). Serum iron was 10 µg/dL (normal 65–175), ferritin 600 ng/mL (30–300), transferrin 170 mg/dL (200–360). Glycated hemoglobin was normal. Serum and urine electrophoresis showed no monoclonal protein. Rheumatologic and vasculitis panels (ANA, Anti-Ro, Anti-La, RF, C3, C4, p-ANCA, c-ANCA) were within normal limits. Viral and infectious screens (HCV Ab, HIV Ab, viral markers, VDRL, PPD) were negative. Paraneoplastic markers (CA19-9, CA15-3, CEA, PSA, AFP, βHCG) were negative. CT of the chest and abdomen demonstrated splenomegaly without lymphadenopathy. A superficial peroneal nerve biopsy was performed.

A 25-year-old man presented with 2 months of progressive swelling at the left medial canthus, located below the medial canthal tendon, accompanied by tearing. He had been treated elsewhere for presumed preseptal cellulitis with medial canthal swelling but had no improvement on antibiotics. His visual acuity was 6/9 in both eyes. Examination revealed a 2 × 3 cm non-tender, firm, immobile mass with a smooth surface and overlying skin inflammation at the left medial canthus. The anterior segments and fundi were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits showed a 3 cm enhancing lesion in the lacrimal drainage region, extending into the middle nasal meatus and with destruction of the adjacent maxillary bone. The patient underwent an incisional biopsy and debulking; intraoperatively, a whitish, firm mass with bony destruction of the left maxillary bone was noted.

A 42-year-old healthy woman was referred to gynecology for a livid-colored umbilical nodule that had gradually increased in size over the past three years. She reported severe dysmenorrhea (NRS 10), dyspareunia (NRS 10), dyschezia (NRS 7), tenesmus, and cyclical umbilical bleeding synchronized with menstruation during withdrawal bleeding. She had irregular menses and was taking an ethinylestradiol–gestodene oral contraceptive. Her obstetric history included a cesarean delivery nine years earlier; five years ago she underwent laparoscopic appendectomy via an umbilical port, and the appendix showed histologic endometriosis. There was no family history of endometriosis.

On examination, the umbilicus contained a 1.2 cm soft, irreducible nodule with two bluish-purple dots and normal overlying skin; the lesion was painless. The rest of the abdominal exam was normal with no signs of hernia. Hormonal therapy was changed to continuous dienogest 2 mg, resulting in amenorrhea and cessation of umbilical bleeding.

Ultrasonography of the umbilical nodule revealed an image suggestive of a dermoid cyst. Pelvic CT scan demonstrated two contiguous left adnexal cystic lesions with peripheral contrast enhancement, for which the differential diagnosis included endometrioma, tubo-ovarian abscess, and serous cystadenoma. A second ultrasound of the nodule showed two superficial 2 mm cysts and a deeper 4 mm cyst with a nonspecific appearance compatible with sebaceous or dermal inclusion cysts. Pelvic MRI showed a 92 × 40 × 58 mm uterus with multiple small T2-hypointense intramural nodules consistent with leiomyomas, 6 mm endometrial thickness with findings suggestive of adenomyosis, and two left ovarian cysts (40 × 33 mm and 28 × 18 × 24 mm) with T1 hyperintensity and slight T2 hyperintensity, suggesting hemorrhagic cysts or endometriomas.

A 7-year-old girl presented with a 6-month history of continuous, non-positional headache, followed by blurred vision for 4 months, postural imbalance for 3 months, and complete loss of vision for the past month. She had no seizures, vomiting, or weight loss. On examination, she was alert but had no light perception in either eye; funduscopic examination revealed bilateral optic atrophy. She had bilateral cranial-nerve III, IV, and VI palsies. Her weight was 19 kg and height 108 cm (normal BMI-for-age; height-for-age indicates stunting). Laboratory studies showed mild leukocytosis (10 230 cells/mm^3). CSF analysis demonstrated elevated glucose (91 mmol/L) and protein (55 mmol/L) levels. Head CT with contrast showed a well-circumscribed isodense mass measuring 3.6 × 4.6 × 4.4 cm arising from the right cerebellum, with an inner hypodense component and regular rim enhancement, causing compression of the fourth ventricle and right cerebellar hemisphere, obstructive hydrocephalus, and transependymal edema.

A 30-year-old man with acute myeloid leukemia diagnosed 7 years earlier and treated with fludarabine, idarubicin, and cytarabine, in clinical remission for the past year but lost to follow-up, presented with 2 months of rapidly progressive bilateral vision loss and diplopia. He also reported headaches, nausea, vomiting, and a 26-lb weight loss over 2 months. He had been evaluated by an optometrist who prescribed new glasses without improvement.

On examination, the right eye had restricted extraocular movements in all directions, ptosis, a relative afferent pupillary defect, and minimal light perception. The left eye had normal extraocular movements and pupillary responses but severely restricted visual fields and decreased foveal acuity. Visual findings fluctuated rapidly. Dilated fundoscopic examination revealed bilateral Grade IV papilledema.

Magnetic resonance imaging showed a lobulated extra-axial mass centered in the sella turcica, extending anteriorly along the floor of the anterior cranial fossa, crossing both cavernous sinuses into the middle cranial fossae, and posteriorly into the suprasellar and prepontine cisterns. The mass also extended into bilateral orbital apices and the sphenoid and ethmoid sinuses, encasing both internal carotid arteries, cavernous sinus contents, and optic nerves. It was hypointense on T1, isointense on T2, with homogeneous enhancement on postcontrast T1.

Computed tomography of the head demonstrated a hyperdense sellar mass with erosion of the ethmoidal portion of the anterior skull base. CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis were unremarkable. Laboratory evaluation revealed decreased ACTH, FSH, and LH. The patient was started on dexamethasone for optic nerve compression and adrenal insufficiency.

A 71-year-old woman presented with a one-week history of periumbilical abdominal pain accompanied by fever, diarrhea, and passage of blood per rectum. She had no history of trauma. Her medical history was notable only for a recent urinary tract infection; she had no known chronic gastrointestinal or systemic illnesses. On examination, she was febrile and had periumbilical tenderness without rebound tenderness or guarding. During episodes of pain, a palpable, fluctuant mass approximately 10 cm in diameter was noted in the mid-abdomen; the mass was not palpable when her pain subsided. Laboratory tests revealed a leukocytosis and a positive fecal occult blood test; stool bacterial cultures were negative. An abdominal ultrasound failed to detect a discrete cystic lesion. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a lumpy, low-density mass surrounding the upper mid-small bowel, measuring 86 mm by 42 mm, with no enhancement. Subsequent MRI demonstrated a well-circumscribed cystic lesion in the anterior wall of the mid-abdomen, measuring 110 mm by 40 mm, with long T1 and long T2 signals and no abnormal enhancement.

A 61‐year‐old man presented with a 2-month history of slight pain and progressive swelling of the right upper jaw. His medical, family, and social history was unremarkable, with no known systemic disease or history of smoking or alcohol use.

On examination, there was a diffuse, tender swelling of the right maxilla that interfered with mouth closure and eyelid closure on that side. Intraorally, a soft tissue mass with an ulcerated surface perforated the alveolar ridge of the right maxilla.

Panoramic radiography revealed a destructive radiolucent lesion in the right maxilla, with loss of the sinus floor and alveolar bone. CT and MRI demonstrated an ill‐defined lesion filling the right maxillary sinus and destroying the maxillary tuberosity and the lateral nasal wall.

An incisional biopsy was performed, and the lesion was diagnosed as a peripheral giant cell granuloma. Within days, the mass enlarged further, prompting referral for re-evaluation. On re-examination, extraoral findings included facial pallor without erythema or new swelling; intraorally, the ulcerated mass persisted.

A repeat biopsy showed hypercellular proliferation of atypical spindle‐shaped fibroblastic cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, intermixed with pleomorphic histiocytic‐like cells arranged in a storiform pattern. The stroma was fibrovascular with hemorrhage and extravasated erythrocytes. Numerous abnormal mitotic figures and multinucleated giant cells were present. In limited superficial areas under the epithelium, lace-like pseudo-osteoid deposits were identified.

A 60-year-old man presented with progressive dyspnea and dizziness. Two months earlier, he underwent upper endoscopy, colonoscopy, and cardiac imaging for anemia and exertional dyspnea, all of which were normal. A chest wall mass biopsy and cervical lymph node aspiration performed at that time were nondiagnostic. During the month before admission, he developed worsening dyspnea, a 7-kg weight loss over two months, and melena five days before presentation. He had no history of immunosuppression.

On examination, he had a 2.5-cm ovoid submandibular mass and similar smaller lesions on the forehead, chest wall, and right oral vestibule. There were right supraclavicular and bilateral axillary lymphadenopathies. The white-cell count was 6800/µL, hemoglobin 6.2 g/dL, and platelets 397,000/µL. Iron studies were consistent with iron-deficiency anemia; liver and renal function tests, lactate dehydrogenase, and urinalysis were normal. HIV tests were negative on admission and at three-month follow-up. Tumor markers (CEA, CA 19-9) were normal.

Conventional esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed a friable ulcerofungating mass over a 10-cm segment in the proximal jejunum. Multiple endoscopic biopsies revealed diffuse infiltration of neoplastic lymphoid cells with plasmablastic differentiation. CT of the abdomen showed a 9.4×9.0-cm lobulated, enhancing mass in the proximal jejunum and multiple enhancing nodules in the greater omentum, transverse mesocolon, and left retroperitoneum. CT of the face and chest identified a 2.3-cm right submandibular mass, multiple musculoskeletal soft-tissue nodules, and lymphadenopathies in the chest.

A 29-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of progressive altered mental status, lower-extremity weakness, nausea, and vomiting; he also reported headaches, dizziness, multiple falls, and right facial numbness and tingling during that period. His symptoms dated back more than 6 years, and he had a history of seizures that were well controlled with medication. A presumptive diagnosis of hydrocephalus had led to placement of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt prior to neurosurgical referral. On examination, he had mild dysarthria, a nonreactive left pupil, nystagmus on primary gaze of the left eye, bilateral horizontal nystagmus, and mild action tremors in both hands. 

Noncontrast and contrast-enhanced CT of the head showed diffuse enhancement of the basimeninges and heterogeneously enhancing cystic and solid lesions in the right temporal lobe and left cerebellum. Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI of the brain revealed extensive nodular basimeningeal enhancement, a 5 × 4 cm solid and cystic mass in the right temporal lobe, a 2.3 × 1.1 cm enhancing mass in the prepontine cistern with an associated cystic component, and a solid enhancing mass crossing the midline in the left cerebellum. On T2-weighted images, the cystic components were extremely hyperintense and suppressed on FLAIR, while on T1-weighted images they were hypointense.

Initial laboratory studies were notable only for elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. CT of the chest showed no evidence of pulmonary sarcoidosis. Biopsies of the right temporal lobe and dura were negative for neoplasm or other abnormalities, and analysis of aspirated cyst contents was negative for inflammation or malignancy. A presumptive diagnosis of neurosarcoidosis was made, and the patient was treated with prednisone, resulting in symptomatic improvement. 

Eleven months later, follow-up MRI demonstrated increased size of the intracranial lesions, and imaging of the spinal axis showed diffuse nodular meningeal enhancement.

A 77-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a tumor near the gastric fornix that had been detected incidentally on esophagogastroduodenoscopy 2 years 7 months earlier as a 10-mm submucosal-appearing lesion. Contrast-enhanced CT at that time showed a 20-mm low-density, round mass between the upper stomach and the left lateral segment of the liver. T2-weighted MRI revealed a high-signal lesion distinct from the stomach. Five months later, MRI showed slight growth. Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS) then demonstrated a cystic structure continuous with the gastric wall, raising concern for a gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST). Due to conflicting imaging findings, she was referred for detailed evaluation. On admission, she was asymptomatic, with normal vital signs and laboratory studies. She had Sjögren syndrome and no other systemic disease. Repeat EUS concluded that the cystic tumor with solid components did not originate from either liver or stomach, and, because of the risk of tumor dissemination, fine-needle aspiration was not performed. The differential diagnoses included bronchogenic cyst, epidermoid cyst, lymph node with cystic degeneration, and neurogenic tumor. Serial imaging over 1½ years demonstrated gradual growth to 25 mm, and CT showed an uncertain boundary with the gastric wall. Although GIST could not be excluded, the patient elected to proceed with laparoscopic surgical resection.

A 62-year-old Chinese woman presented with an 8-year history of intermittent headache, which had worsened over the past week. Her family history was unremarkable. General and detailed neurological examinations were normal. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the head showed an oval mass, measuring 3.1 × 1.6 cm, in the right cerebellum with heterogeneous enhancement. Computed tomographic angiography revealed a highly vascular tumor without obvious changes in the basilar, vertebral, or posterior cerebral arteries. Radiographically, the lesion was interpreted as a hemangioblastoma. She underwent a right suboccipital craniotomy for resection of the mass, which was well demarcated from surrounding cerebellar tissue, with focal slight adhesion. A 3.2 × 2 × 1.7 cm tumor was completely excised. The patient remains alive with no evidence of tumor recurrence or metastasis at 9 months of follow-up.

A 32-year-old gravida 2 para 2002 presented seven days after a repeat cesarean section with severe abdominal pain. She had two prior uncomplicated full-term cesarean deliveries. On arrival she was tachycardic; hemoglobin was 6.3 mg/dL and quantitative hCG was 5 038 mIU/mL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed multiple hemorrhagic pulmonary nodules, hepatic masses with a subcapsular hematoma, and a seven-centimeter uterine mass. Interventional radiology performed emergent embolization of the hepatic hematoma. Brain MRI demonstrated hemorrhagic lesions in the left middle frontal gyrus and the left parieto-occipital junction. Core needle biopsy of a liver lesion was reported as metastatic gestational choriocarcinoma. Given the large disease burden and risk of hemorrhage, low-dose induction etoposide-cisplatin chemotherapy was initiated.

A 60-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of a painless swelling in the right upper neck. Her medical history was notable for treatment of right breast carcinoma (T3N1M0) 7 years earlier, consisting of mastectomy, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and 5 years of letrozole. On examination, there was a well-circumscribed, firm 6 cm × 5 cm mass in the right upper neck. There was no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy and examination of the upper aerodigestive tract, remaining breast tissue, chest wall, axillae, and supraclavicular fossae was normal. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the mass showed poorly differentiated carcinoma. A staging 18F-FDG PET/CT scan revealed a 6 cm × 5 cm × 4 cm irregular, lobulated, FDG-avid (SUVmax 9.1) soft-tissue mass in the right parapharyngeal space abutting the deep lobe of the parotid gland, extending from C1 to C5, with mass effect on the major neck vessels and infiltration of the internal jugular vein. No other sites of abnormal uptake were seen. The provisional diagnosis was a malignant salivary gland tumor of the parapharyngeal space, with metastasis from breast carcinoma as a rare alternative.

A 51-year-old man presented with recurrent chest tightness for 4 months, worsened over the past 2 weeks. On initial evaluation, ECG showed ST-segment elevation in lead aVL and T-wave changes in leads V2–V6. Cardiac enzymes were elevated (troponin T 254.9 pg/mL, CK 440 U/L, CK-MB 30.3 U/L, myoglobin 103.1 ng/mL). Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a left ventricular ejection fraction of 70%, left ventricular wall thickening, regional wall motion abnormality, moderate mitral regurgitation, and a small pericardial effusion. Selective coronary angiography revealed no significant stenosis and TIMI grade 3 flow, and coronary spasm was considered.

One month later, he returned with chest tightness and dyspnea. Physical examination revealed wet rales. ECG showed sinus rhythm with ST-T changes. Echocardiography revealed local pericardial thickening and adhesion of the inferior and lateral left ventricular walls. Cardiac enzymes were normal, but NT-proBNP was elevated at 5407 pg/mL. He was treated for left ventricular hypertrophy with chronic heart failure.

Two months later, he was re-hospitalized for recurrent chest tightness. Echocardiography showed extensive involvement of the aorta, pulmonary arteries, left ventricle, and left atrium with decreased systolic and diastolic function. Rheumatic immune diseases could not be ruled out, and IgG4-related disease was suspected. Tumor markers CA125 and neuron-specific enolase were elevated.

A 30‐year‐old woman with a history of an eating disorder presented with a persistent, left facial mass that had been slowly enlarging over several years. She first noted a firm, painless “hard zit” near her left oral commissure about 7 years earlier. A skin punch biopsy performed before the COVID‐19 pandemic showed a benign chondroid syringoma extending to the margins. Despite this, the lesion continued to grow, leading to left‐sided facial discomfort, difficulty with facial movements and expression, and significant cosmetic concern. She reported slight pain on palpation but denied drainage or numbness. Five surgeons declined to excise the mass due to concern for facial nerve injury. On intraoral examination, a firm, movable, ovoid submucosal mass measuring approximately 40 × 20 mm was palpable lateral to the left buccinator muscle, extending toward the oral commissure. There was no apparent involvement of the overlying skin, subcutaneous tissue, parotid fascia, or facial nerve branches.

A 20-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a three-week history of nausea, multiple episodes of vomiting, and moderate headache partially relieved by analgesics. There were no focal neurologic deficits. On noncontrast computed tomography of the brain, there was a partially calcified, soft-tissue density mass in the left lateral ventricle, broad-based on the septum pellucidum and occupying the foramen of Monro, with marked ventricular dilatation, effacement of sulci, and transependymal edema. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a voluminous intraventricular lesion that was isointense to gray matter on T1-weighted images and slightly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with subtle peripheral cystic components and septations bridging to the ventricular wall, giving a scalloped contour. Susceptibility-weighted images revealed signal voids within the lesion corresponding to vascular structures and calcifications. Diffusion-weighted imaging and apparent diffusion coefficient mapping demonstrated restricted diffusion. After intravenous contrast, the lesion enhanced heterogeneously, with prominent intralesional vessels. Digital subtraction angiography indicated multiple small arterial feeders from anterior and middle cerebral branches and venous drainage to the left internal cerebral vein. A dynamic susceptibility contrast perfusion study showed a relative cerebral blood volume of 3.4 compared with contralateral white matter.

A 72-year-old man with JAK2 V617F–positive polycythemia vera and possible early post-polycythemia myelofibrosis reported 3 months of left upper quadrant abdominal pain, a 30 lb weight loss, early satiety, poor appetite, and fatigue. Three months earlier, CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a predominantly cystic/solid splenic mass measuring 10.7 × 9.7 × 13.6 cm; hematoma, malignancy, or an abscess was considered, with abscess thought less likely. Repeat CT demonstrated interval growth to 14 × 11.5 × 15.4 cm and perisplenic stranding. PET-CT 1 week later revealed a hypermetabolic, necrotic splenic lesion, extensive upper abdominal lymphadenopathy, and a sternal lesion concerning for malignancy; possible gastrosplenic fistula was uncertain. He denied fever, chills, night sweats, bleeding, or trauma. Vital signs were normal. Examination showed fatigue, significant splenomegaly, and left upper quadrant tenderness. Laboratory studies revealed microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL), thrombocytosis (422 × 10^3/µL), leukocytosis (18.1 × 10^3/µL; neutrophils 15.36, lymphocytes 0.84), elevated ALT (127 U/L), AST (95 U/L), and alkaline phosphatase (351 U/L) with normal bilirubin. CT angiogram of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 14 × 11.5 × 15.4 cm centrally necrotic splenic mass containing gas and fluid, with communication between the spleen and the greater curvature of the stomach consistent with a gastrosplenic fistula; there was also malignant-appearing abdominal and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy and a 0.9 cm splenic artery aneurysm.

A 75-year-old Japanese man presented with a sudden onset of asymptomatic gross hematuria. Initial ultrasonography and abdominal radiography suggested a bladder calculus. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a 1.8 cm intramural right ureteral calculus and a well-circumscribed, 2.1 cm hypervascular mass at the right trigone of the bladder; there was no hydronephrosis. Cystoscopic examination showed a nonpapillary, nodular submucosal mass covered by normal-appearing urothelium at the right trigone, and the right ureteral orifice could not be identified. T2-weighted MRI demonstrated no invasive growth of the lesion. Urine cytology was negative for malignant cells. The patient underwent transurethral resection of the bladder mass, which revealed the right ureteral orifice and allowed removal of the calculus without perioperative complications. Follow-up imaging at 5 months showed no recurrence.

A 27-year-old man with congenital hypoplastic kidney–related renal failure underwent renal transplantation in 1992. He presented to the dermatology transplant clinic with a 2-year history of pruritic plaques in the axillae and inguinal folds that did not respond to topical corticosteroids, tacrolimus 0.1% ointment, or topical antifungals. His medical history included bilateral optic neuritis, hypertension, and epilepsy. His long-standing immunosuppressive regimen comprised tacrolimus 2 mg orally twice daily, mycophenolate mofetil 750 mg orally twice daily, and prednisone 5 mg orally daily. On examination, there were symmetric erythematous, fissured, macerated plaques in the axillae, intergluteal, and inguinal folds; no lymphadenopathy was palpated. The differential diagnosis included allergic or irritant contact dermatitis, dermatophytosis, cutaneous candidiasis, recalcitrant frictional intertrigo, inverse psoriasis, granular parakeratosis, Hailey-Hailey disease, and pemphigus vegetans.

A 45-year-old African woman with no significant medical history presented with intermittent decreases in visual acuity and headache. Cranial MRI revealed a 2.0 × 1.5 × 1.0-cm solid sellar mass arising from the adenohypophysis, with suprasellar extension but no evidence of invasive growth, and marked contrast enhancement on T1-weighted images. Laboratory evaluation of pituitary function showed normal levels of follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone, prolactin, corticotropin, and thyrotropin. A nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma was suspected, and the mass was completely resected via transsphenoidal surgery with no adjuvant therapy. Postoperatively, the patient developed panhypopituitarism that was managed with hormone replacement.

A 48-year-old African-American man with no significant tobacco history presented with a slow-growing left neck mass and an 11-kg weight loss over 9 months. He also reported left arm pain and weakness, intermittent fever with chills, and denied dyspnea or cough. His medical history included diabetes mellitus, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and prior left shoulder nerve impingement.

On examination, a 3 × 3 × 1 cm mass was palpable on the left side of the neck just above the sternoclavicular joint. He had left-sided ptosis and miosis, hoarseness of speech, and decreased, coarse breath sounds at the left apex. Strength was 3/5 in the left arm with visible muscle atrophy; other muscle groups were normal. The remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Ultrasound of the neck mass showed an ill-defined heterogeneous mass lateral to the left thyroid lobe with mild mass effect. A chest radiograph revealed a mass extending from the hilum of the left lung, gross tracheal deviation, and elevation of the left hemidiaphragm. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a large multiloculated pleural-based mass in the left lung that surrounded the left common carotid and subclavian arteries, interfaced broadly with the aortic arch, and extended into the left neuroforamina from C4/C5 through T1/T2.

A percutaneous core-needle biopsy of the neck mass showed fibrohistiocytic tissue with mild chronic inflammation but was negative for malignancy.

A 60-year-old man presented for a routine urologic examination. His history was notable for hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, myocardial infarction three years earlier, and ischemic stroke thirteen years earlier. On digital rectal examination, the prostate was nontender, asymmetrically enlarged, and firm. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and serum chemistries, were within normal limits. The serum prostate-specific antigen concentration was 1.0 ng/mL. Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a solid, large mass abutting the urinary bladder; the calculated prostate volume was 31 mL, with a postvoid residual urine volume of 62 mL. Contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT showed a lobulated, well-circumscribed solid mass arising from the left peripheral zone of the prostate with possible left seminal vesicle involvement; the bladder wall was normal. Transrectal ultrasound–guided biopsy of the prostate demonstrated a smooth muscle tumor with uncertain malignant potential (STUMP). Pelvic MRI showed a 6.5 × 6.5 × 6.0 cm fusiform, lobulated, well-circumscribed mass in the left peripheral zone, with T2 hyperintensity, T1 hypointensity, thin internal septa, regular borders, compression of adjacent rectum, bladder, and seminal vesicle, intact surrounding fat planes, and heterogeneous postcontrast enhancement. Chest CT and bone scintigraphy were negative for metastases. An ^18F-FDG PET–CT scan revealed increased uptake in the prostatic mass.

A 27-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of a gradually enlarging, asymptomatic swelling of the lower left jaw and intermittent pus discharge from the lower left posterior teeth region. Ten to twelve years earlier, he had undergone extraction of a lower left molar, leaving an unhealed socket that had been unsuccessfully treated by multiple practitioners. The patient was otherwise healthy and alert. 

On extraoral examination, there was a 7 × 5 cm ill-defined, noncompressible, nonfluctuant swelling over the left angle of the mandible, fixed to underlying structures; a soft, fluctuant notch was noted in the body of the mandible 3 cm anterior to the angle, and the jaw deviated toward the right on opening. Intraorally, there was buccal cortical expansion from tooth 35 to the angle, egg-shell crackling near tooth 37, lingual plate expansion at teeth 37–38, and yellow discharge from the socket of tooth 38 and the root stump of tooth 36. Tooth 37 was nonvital on pulp testing. 

A provisional clinical diagnosis was ameloblastoma of the left mandible, with a differential that included residual cyst, dentigerous cyst, keratocystic odontogenic tumour, central giant cell granuloma, and radicular cyst. Intraoral periapical radiography showed a radiolucency extending beyond the film margins. A panoramic radiograph revealed a multilocular radiolucency with scalloped, hyperostotic borders, extending from the posterior body of the mandible through the angle, ramus, coronoid process, and condyle, with downward expansion of the inferior mandibular border, a 3 × 2.5 cm radiolucent “window” below tooth 37, and resorption of the mesial and distal roots of tooth 37. 

CT imaging confirmed involvement of the coronoid process, condyle, ramus, and body of the left mandible, and demonstrated medial deflection of the left lateral pterygoid plate and of the left maxillary posterior alveolar arch.

A 41-year-old premenopausal woman with no family history of breast cancer was referred after routine screening detected an abnormality. On examination, there was a firm palpable mass in the right breast and palpable masses in the right axilla.

Mammography showed heterogeneously dense breast parenchyma with no suspicious findings in either breast, but a 1.5-cm hyperdense, mass-like lesion in the right axilla.  
Breast ultrasonography revealed:  
• A 1.1-cm hypoechoic mass with indistinct margins in the right inner breast at the 3 o’clock position.  
• In the right axilla, within accessory breast tissue, two small (≤0.6 cm), irregular low-echoic masses with nonparallel orientation and increased vascularity.  

MRI demonstrated an irregular >1 cm enhancing mass in the right inner breast and two small irregular enhancing masses in the right axillary breast tissue corresponding to ultrasound findings. The lymph nodes in the axillary fossa were normal in size and shape.

A 58-year-old woman with autoimmune hepatitis and primary biliary cirrhosis was referred for evaluation of an incidentally detected left renal mass. She denied hematuria and reported only occasional right flank discomfort. There was no history of hypertension, headaches, palpitations, or sweating. Physical examination was unremarkable, and her blood pressure was normal.

An abdominal ultrasound identified a left renal lesion. Contrast-enhanced CT scan revealed a 3.5 × 3.0 cm exophytic mass arising from the posterior lower pole of the left renal cortex, abutting the collecting system without hydronephrosis. No retroperitoneal or mesenteric lymphadenopathy was noted. The left renal vein and inferior vena cava were patent, and the adrenal glands appeared normal. MRI demonstrated a heterogeneous, T2-hyperintense lesion with enhancement.

On the basis of these findings, a provisional diagnosis of renal cell carcinoma was made, and the patient underwent a robotic-assisted laparoscopic retroperitoneal left partial nephrectomy. The tumor was completely enucleated.

A 25-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of generalized headache. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable, and neurologic examination findings were normal. Plain skull radiography demonstrated a calcified lesion in the right frontoparietal region. Brain MRI with and without contrast revealed a lobulated intra-axial mass in the right frontoparietal lobe with heterogeneous enhancement, mild surrounding edema, and a shift of the falx cerebri to the left. The radiologic diagnosis was low-grade glioma or meningioma.

A 60-year-old man presented with 3 months of postprandial projectile vomiting, nausea, and a 12-kg weight loss, accompanied by intermittent fevers and nocturnal diaphoresis. His medical history included chronic back pain (on intermittent meloxicam) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; surgical history was unremarkable. On examination, he appeared malnourished but was haemodynamically stable; his abdomen was mildly distended with a succession splash and no palpable lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies revealed normal hemoglobin, unremarkable carcinoembryonic antigen, CA 19-9, alpha-fetoprotein, and liver function tests with no biliary obstruction on imaging. Abdominal CT showed a large soft-tissue mass in the second part of the duodenum with loss of the fat plane between the duodenum and the uncinate process. MRI demonstrated mural thickening of the duodenal bulb and possibly the D2 segment, without a focal pancreatic head lesion. Gastroscopy revealed large mucosally denuded regions in proximal D2 suggestive of an infiltrative lesion rather than ulceration. Biopsies were obtained.

A 26-year-old woman, G3P3, presented with persistent abdominal and pelvic pain 3 months postpartum. She had no significant past medical history except for a recent cesarean delivery. She reported increasing abdominal discomfort over the preceding 2 weeks. On examination, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable, with diffuse abdominal tenderness but no palpable mass. Laboratory evaluation was unremarkable.

An initial abdominal ultrasound revealed a 93 × 74 mm uterine fibroma. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 7 cm well-circumscribed solid mass with homogeneous density. MRI demonstrated a 7 cm mass in the right hypochondrium within the small-bowel mesentery, extending toward the right colon, appendix, and cecum. Based on these imaging findings, the leading considerations were an intra-mesenteric desmoid tumour versus a gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST); however, no definitive diagnosis could be made without tissue sampling.

A 56-year-old woman with no personal or family history of tumors presented with a 7-month history of a right-sided, painless cervical swelling that had progressively enlarged. She denied trauma, upper respiratory infection, and compressive symptoms. 

On examination:
- Location: right submandibular region  
- Size: lobular mass with ill-defined margins  
- Consistency: soft, non-tender, freely movable  
- Overlying skin: normal  
- Cervical lymphadenopathy: none detected  
- Cranial nerves: facial and lingual nerve function intact  

Imaging:
- Ultrasonography: anechoic, multilobulated cystic lesion in the submandibular space  
- Magnetic resonance imaging: 4.0 × 4.0 × 3.5 cm cystic mass beneath the right mandible, adherent to the submandibular gland; the lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images  

A branchial cleft cyst was initially suspected, and surgical excision was planned.

A 67-year-old man was evaluated for progressive dysphagia and a painless skin nodule on his left shoulder, first noted one month earlier. His medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperuricemia, and a remote myocardial infarction. He had a 50-pack-year smoking history. On examination, there was a 30 × 25 mm hard, stone-like, red mass on the left shoulder without other skin lesions or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies were unremarkable except for a mildly elevated carcinoembryonic antigen level of 5.4 ng/mL (normal <5.0 ng/mL). Fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose PET-CT demonstrated hypermetabolic foci in the middle thoracic esophagus (SUVmax 11.0), the right recurrent laryngeal nerve lymph node (SUVmax 4.4), and the left shoulder skin lesion (SUVmax 5.0). Esophagogastroscopy revealed an ulcerative, infiltrative lesion in the middle thoracic esophagus. Endoscopic biopsy of the esophageal lesion showed nests of atypical cells with round to oval or short spindle-shaped hyperchromatic nuclei and scant keratinization. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for cytokeratin 19 and Bcl-2, supporting a diagnosis of basaloid rather than conventional squamous cell carcinoma.

A 27-year-old white man was referred with a two-month history of a lump in his right buttock that caused sharp pain radiating down his leg whenever he sat, especially on hard surfaces. He had no other symptoms and no relevant personal or family history. On exam, there was a well-localized, soft, approximately 2 cm mass in the deep dermis or subcutaneous fat of the right buttock, without attachment to muscle or overlying skin changes. Neurologic and lymph node examinations were normal. Clinically, the mass was thought to be a lipoma or neurofibroma, and a cyst was also included in the differential. The lesion was excised under local anesthesia without prior imaging because it was small, well circumscribed, and not adherent to deeper structures. Intraoperatively, the specimen appeared well localized and resembled a sebaceous cyst or pilomatrixoma.

A 40-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of malaise, dyspnea, multiple episodes of syncope, and recurrent chest pain. She had type 2 diabetes mellitus and no other significant medical or family history. On examination, there was a grade II/VI systolic murmur at the left fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line and mild dyspnea (NYHA class II). Electrocardiography showed normal sinus rhythm, left axis deviation, poor R-wave progression, and an rS pattern in leads III and aVF. Chest radiography demonstrated mild bilateral hilar congestion with a normal cardiac index. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography revealed a heterogeneous, lobulated, pedunculated mass in the left atrium measuring 3.43 × 3.47 cm, with a broad-based attachment to the atrial septum. The mass moved toward the mitral valve during diastole without prolapsing or causing obstruction. Central mitral regurgitation (1.5/4), a dilated left atrium (44 mm in systole), normal ventricular volumes (EDV 126.6 mL, EF 67%), systolic pulmonary artery pressure of 35 mmHg, and mild tricuspid regurgitation (<1/4) were noted. No intracardiac thrombi or pericardial effusion were seen. The diagnosis was presumed to be a myxoma, and emergent surgical removal was planned to prevent secondary complications.

A 6-year-old boy presented with a four-week history of right neck swelling. On examination, there was a single 3 × 2 cm right cervical lymph node; no other lymphadenopathy, fever, or weight loss was noted. A skeletal survey showed no osseous lesions, and a PET scan was normal. Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) of the lymph node was performed. Cytology smears revealed numerous mono- and multinucleated histiocytes with abundant vacuolated cytoplasm and grooved, folded, indented nuclei. The background contained abundant eosinophils, a mixed lymphoid population, and lymphohistiocytic aggregates; mitotic activity was not significant.

A 3½-year-old boy presented with a painful lump in his right abdomen of one week’s duration. On examination, there was a large, hard, irregular mass in the right flank measuring 12 cm × 10 cm and crossing the midline. Initial ultrasonography performed elsewhere was interpreted as a liver abscess. Repeat ultrasonography and contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 10 cm × 8.5 cm × 7.6 cm heterogeneous mass arising from and almost replacing the right kidney, abutting the inferior surface of the liver, containing necrotic areas, and attenuating the inferior vena cava at that level. A chest radiograph showed no lung metastases. A core-needle biopsy was obtained, and while awaiting histopathology, the patient received two weeks of vincristine and actinomycin D, yet the mass showed no response.

A 42-year-old man presented after a motor vehicle accident with chest and extremity pain. A noncontrast CT scan revealed a 3.2 × 5.5 cm soft-tissue mass centered between the posterior tracheal wall and anterior esophagus, without adjacent lymphadenopathy and causing mild airway narrowing; the patient denied dyspnea, dysphagia, voice changes, or sleep disturbances. He was a former smoker with a 20 pack-year history and otherwise had no significant medical history. MRI demonstrated a 3.1 × 5.5 × 4.7 cm smoothly enhancing mass in the superior mediastinum/inlet, separate from the thyroid and esophagus.

A 35-year-old Sudanese man with oculocutaneous albinism and a family history of the condition (affected sibling and son) presented in late December 2023 with a 2-month history of a rapidly enlarging right axillary mass. He had no history of extensive sun exposure. His medical history was notable for a squamous cell carcinoma of the chest that was excised with clear margins in early 2021. 

On examination, the right axilla harbored a 15 × 20 cm firm, rounded mass with a 10 × 8 cm ulceration on its surface; it was not adherent to overlying skin or underlying structures. A second mass in the left axilla measured 10 × 8 cm, was firm and fixed to the skin but mobile over deeper tissue, non-tender, and without overlying skin changes. Distal pulses, motor function, and sensation in the upper limbs were intact. Chest and abdominal examinations were unremarkable.

Preoperative blood tests and imaging studies were within normal limits. In early January 2024, the right axillary tumor was excised and the defect reconstructed with a latissimus dorsi myocutaneous flap. The postoperative course was uneventful and the patient was discharged on day 5. Three weeks later, the left axillary mass was excised and the wound closed primarily; he was discharged on postoperative day 1 in good condition.

A 36-year-old man presented with a two-month history of dull, nonradiating back pain. He denied urinary symptoms, limb weakness, or sensory changes. His medical history, physical examination, and laboratory studies were unremarkable. Lumbar MRI revealed a well-circumscribed 5 cm lesion in the left retroperitoneal space, adjacent to the iliopsoas muscle, with low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted images. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed a 52×47 mm mass anterior to L4, abutting the left ureter and left common iliac artery, with heterogeneous enhancement. Brain and chest CT scans were normal. On PET-CT, the mass demonstrated fluorodeoxyglucose avidity with an SUVmax of 5.2. A CT-guided core-needle biopsy was then performed.

A 60-year-old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, obesity (grade II) and dyslipidaemia presented with intermittent epigastric pain and postprandial vomiting over 6 months, with worsening symptoms over the past 3 months and a single episode of hematemesis without hemodynamic instability. She denied weight loss, melena or changes in bowel habits. Physical examination was unremarkable, and routine blood tests were within normal limits. 

Upper GI endoscopy revealed a large subepithelial mass arising from the posterior wall of the gastric antrum, occupying more than 50% of the lumen and demonstrating softness when pressed with biopsy forceps; multiple mucosal biopsies were non-diagnostic. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a well-circumscribed 8 × 3 cm lesion in the gastric antrum that did not enhance with contrast and exhibited uniform adipose density. 

Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated a homogeneous, hyperechoic lesion confined to the submucosal layer of the gastric wall.

A 20-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of progressive abdominal pain and distension. On examination, a palpable mass was noted in the right abdomen. Pelvic ultrasonography showed a solid, heterogeneous, hypoechoic mass measuring 280 × 100 mm extending from the pelvis to the upper abdomen. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a solid mass up to 223 mm in the pelvic cavity and rectouterine pouch, extending into the right abdominal cavity and encasing mesenteric vessels. MRI revealed a large T2-hyperintense mass measuring 216 × 134 mm in the pelvis, with extension into the right upper quadrant and adhesions to the uterine fundus. Serum CA-125 was 134 IU/mL, HE4 was 34.6 pmol/L, and the Risk of Malignancy Algorithm score was 3.55%. With suspicion of an ovarian germ cell tumor, probably dysgerminoma, she underwent a staging laparotomy.

A 59-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of a painless mass behind her left lower posterior teeth that had noticeably enlarged over the past 2 weeks, with slight tenderness on palpation and occasional left-sided neck pain. She had no systemic illnesses or drug allergies. On examination, her facial contours were symmetric, temporomandibular joints were normal, and maximal mouth opening was 37 mm. Intraoral examination revealed a well-defined 1 × 1 cm round, slightly firm, moderately mobile mass in the left retromolar pad; the overlying mucosa was intact and normal in color without erythema or erosion. The tongue moved freely, and there was no cervical or submandibular lymphadenopathy. Cone beam computed tomography showed continuity of the left mandibular cortical bone without obvious abnormality, with a low-density shadow around the distal root of tooth 38 suggestive of periodontal inflammation and dental restorations on adjacent teeth. Based on the clinical and imaging findings, a benign mucocele was suspected, but the possibility of a tumor such as mucoepidermoid carcinoma could not be ruled out. A decision was made to excise the lesion with a 5 mm margin under local anesthesia for definitive diagnosis.

A 48-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of right-sided abdominal pain without hematuria or other urinary symptoms. She has a 5-year history of hypertension and no family history of tumors. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits, and there was mild right-sided tenderness. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a well-demarcated 10×7 cm mass in the right kidney with cystic components. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed an 8×7 cm right renal mass with distinct margins, cystic contents, and no invasion of adjacent structures. The patient underwent a right radical nephrectomy via a retroperitoneal approach. Grossly, the specimen demonstrated a sharply circumscribed tumor with mixed cystic and solid areas. Histologic examination showed thin septa lined by large cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and a hobnail appearance.

A 38-year-old man presented with an 18-month history of progressive swelling and pain of the left thigh. Two months earlier, elsewhere, fluid aspiration and an excision biopsy were performed without symptomatic improvement. On examination, there was a large, soft, ill-defined swelling over the distal left thigh with a healed lateral surgical scar. Knee range of motion was restricted at the terminal arc, and there was no neurovascular deficit.

Plain radiographs of the left femur and knee showed an enlarged soft-tissue shadow over the distal femur extending up to the patella, without evidence of bony erosion or periosteal reaction. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left thigh and knee demonstrated diffuse, frond-like synovial thickening of markedly low signal on both T1- and T2-weighted sequences, a large, thick-walled hemorrhagic collection within the vastus medialis and intermedius muscles, and a focal area suggestive of a sequestrated synovial fragment.

A 34-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of a painless mass in the posterior wall of his right external auditory canal associated with decreased hearing. He noted that the lesion had appeared and grown rapidly over that period. On otoscopic examination, a smooth, nontender, skin-covered nodule nearly occluded the external auditory meatus. Threshold tonal audiometry demonstrated a conductive hearing loss in the right ear. An MRI of the temporal bone showed a 1.5 × 0.8 cm, well-circumscribed lesion in the superior and posterior canal wall that was hyperintense on T2-weighted images, without evidence of bony erosion.

A 39-year-old woman presented with a two-month history of progressive foreign-body sensation in her throat and discomfort with swallowing. She first noticed a painless mass on the right side of her soft palate, which had gradually increased in size. She was otherwise healthy, with no history of smoking, alcohol use, or familial tumor syndromes. On examination, there was a solitary, cystic, non-tender soft tissue mass protruding from the right side of the soft palate; no cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck demonstrated a well-defined, non-enhancing, homogeneous, pedunculated soft tissue lesion measuring 2.1 × 1.6 × 1.5 cm arising from the posterior edge of the right soft palate, with smooth margins and no signs of invasion.

A 60-year-old woman with hypothyroidism presented with a right breast mass noted several weeks earlier. She has no family history of cancer and breast-fed nine children. Examination revealed a firm, slightly nodular, oval mass measuring 2.0 × 1.5 cm at the 10 o’clock position of the right breast; no axillary lymphadenopathy was palpable.  
Mammography showed a fatty breast with an asymmetric density in the right upper outer quadrant without definite calcifications; spot compression views demonstrated an ill-defined, elongated mass with faint calcifications.  
Ultrasound revealed a 1.3 × 0.8 cm hypoechoic, lobulated, horizontally oriented lesion with mildly increased peripheral vascularity.  
Breast MRI demonstrated an irregularly enhancing lesion with architectural distortion and benign-appearing axillary lymph nodes.  
An ultrasound-guided core-needle biopsy was obtained for histologic evaluation.

A 9-year-old boy presented with a 1-month history of progressive lower back pain that was aggravated by bending and associated with an inability to stand upright. He denied any history of trauma or febrile illness. He also reported a focal, pin-point left chest pain. On examination, he appeared unwell and had lower limb paresthesia with reduced muscle power and bulk.

Laboratory studies showed:  
• White‐cell count 4.0×10^9/L (normal 4.0–10.0×10^9/L)  
• LDH 25 U/L (normal <40 U/L)  
• Urea 6.0 mmol/L (normal 2.5–8 mmol/L); creatinine 70 μmol/L (63–115 μmol/L)  
• Potassium 4.0 meq/L (3.5–5.5 meq/L); sodium 136 meq/L (135–155 meq/L)  
• Calcium 6.0 mg/dL (8.5–10.5 mg/dL)

Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine showed a destructive lesion at L3. CT of the chest revealed an osteolytic lesion in the left third rib, and CT of the head demonstrated an osteolytic lesion in the left calvarium. Histologic examination of the L3 lesion demonstrated cells with eccentric nuclei and prominent Golgi apparatus. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for CD138 and CD56, and in situ hybridization revealed a small serum monoclonal IgA spike of kappa light chain. Bone marrow evaluation was normal.

A 66-year-old man was referred for recurrent perianal abscesses over 12 months. His history included perianal trauma from sitting on broken glass in childhood; comorbidities were vascular dementia, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, atrial fibrillation, and gout. He reported no perianal warts, sexually transmitted diseases, immune deficiency, inflammatory dermatoses, arsenic exposure, or family history of malignancy. Examination revealed a fluctuant left lateral perianal mass without external fistulas. Ultrasound‐guided aspiration yielded 15 cc of purulent fluid; Gram stain and cultures were negative, but cytology showed atypical squamous cells. Postdrainage differential diagnosis included squamous cell carcinoma, cyst, condyloma, or large abscess. Two months later, the mass had enlarged, prompting concern for a fistula. Surgical drainage again yielded purulent fluid without microbial growth. On examination under anesthesia less than one month later, an external sinus tract into the mass was noted but no fistula to the anal canal. It was then decided to excise the mass completely and close the defect primarily.

A 40-year-old woman with a history of curative resection of a malignant spindle cell tumour from the right thigh 5 years earlier (clear margins, no adjuvant therapy, no recurrence) presented with sudden onset of severe generalized abdominal pain and collapse. She had no external bleeding, no trauma history, and was otherwise well. On arrival, she was in class III hemorrhagic shock (pulse 125 beats/min, blood pressure 90/60 mmHg), with a distended, diffusely tender abdomen. She was resuscitated with crystalloids and blood. Serum β-Human Chorionic Gonadotropin was negative. Hemoglobin was 5 g/dL; other blood counts and clotting studies were normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed a moderate amount of free fluid and a mass near the proximal pancreas; there was no abdominal aortic aneurysm and other solid organs appeared normal. A CT scan was not obtained due to hemodynamic instability. An emergency midline laparotomy revealed 4.5 L of hemoperitoneum, a linear tear in the gastrocolic omentum with a hematoma in the lesser sac, and active bleeding from a nidus posterior to the pancreatic body. The pancreas and other organs were otherwise normal. Hemostasis was achieved by ligation and local hemostatic agents, and a biopsy of the bleeding lesion was obtained.

An 11-year-old boy presented with a 3-year history of a left breast mass that was painful, bled easily, and occasionally discharged pus, accompanied by intermittent low-grade fevers. He had undergone resection of a similar mass at age 6, which recurred after 2 years; no histopathology had been performed at that time.

On examination, he was alert, mildly pale, and afebrile with stable vital signs. The left breast mass extended into the axilla and measured 10 × 10 × 6 cm; the overlying skin was necrotic with pus discharge, and the lesion was firm with a softer tip and mild tenderness.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL, leukocyte count 9.48 × 10^9/L, platelet count 647 × 10^9/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 80 mm/h. Chest radiography revealed a large left chest wall soft-tissue mass extending into the axilla and involving the inferior angle of the scapula. Chest CT demonstrated a 9.6 × 8.5 × 10.9 cm soft-tissue mass infiltrating the pectoralis major and minor muscles, with multiple enlarged left axillary lymph nodes (largest 1.1 × 1.05 cm). Abdominal and pelvic ultrasound were normal.

He underwent wide local excision; intraoperatively the tumor infiltrated pectoralis muscles, and an R1 resection was performed. Initial histopathology showed diffuse proliferation of mononuclear spindle cells admixed with occasional multinucleated giant cells in a variably myxoid to chondroid stroma. Immunohistochemical testing was non-specific. A diagnosis of chondromyxoid fibroma was rendered, with inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor as an initial differential.

Seven months later, the mass recurred at the same site. A second wide excision including pectoralis major was performed.  
Histologically, the specimen demonstrated zonal architecture with lobules of myxoid to chondroid tissue and intervening spindle or stellate cells with myxoid stromal degeneration. Areas of infiltrative growth, necrosis, and cellular pleomorphism were noted.

A 28-year-old Saudi woman with no significant medical history presented with 2 weeks of sudden, severe, right-sided tension-type headaches associated with nausea, infrequent vomiting, and blurred vision. She denied trauma, loss of consciousness, seizures, or thyroid/hormonal symptoms. She reported lifelong irregular menses but no prior evaluation. There was no family history of brain tumors or endocrine disease, and she took no regular medications.

On examination, vital signs were normal. She was alert and oriented. Visual field testing revealed bitemporal hemianopia; cranial nerves II–XII, motor, sensory, and cerebellar functions were otherwise intact. Routine hormonal and laboratory studies were within normal limits.

Brain MRI showed a 2.5-cm intrasellar and suprasellar mass compressing the optic chiasm and displacing the anterior communicating artery. The lesion was predominantly cystic with an internal area of mixed signal intensity and enhancement along the anterolateral cyst wall.  

Based on the radiological features, the preoperative diagnosis was cystic craniopharyngioma.

A 10-month-old girl was brought for evaluation of a left supraclavicular mass. The mass had been present for 6 months and had enlarged more rapidly over the preceding 2 months. There was no history of trauma, infection, or systemic symptoms.

On examination, there was a 6-cm, painless, firm mass in the left supraclavicular region. The mass was non-pulsatile, fixed to underlying structures, and mobile relative to the overlying skin. There were no overlying inflammatory changes, no cervical adenopathy, and no cranial nerve deficits. Vital signs were normal.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed a well-defined, lobulated left supraclavicular mass measuring 62 × 43 × 41 mm. The lesion had a homogeneous fatty (greasy) density similar to subcutaneous fat and was crossed by internal septa. It abutted the subclavian vessels, which remained patent.

A 63-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with exertional dyspnea. Her white blood cell count was 7270/µL, with 72.5% of cells classified as “other,” indicating abnormal circulating cells. Contrast-enhanced chest CT showed a poorly defined, irregular soft-tissue mass measuring 16 cm from the anterior to the middle mediastinum, with homogeneous enhancement, compression of the left brachiocephalic vein (which remained patent), and associated left pleural effusion and atelectasis. FDG PET–CT revealed intense uptake in the mediastinal mass (SUVmax 9–12), nodular and linear uptake along the left chest wall, and multiple nodular uptakes in the para-aortic region and above the left clavicle (SUVmax 4–6). Based on these findings, the differential diagnosis included lymphoma, thymic epithelial tumor, and lung cancer.

A full-term newborn boy presented at birth with noisy breathing and mild subcostal retractions but without stridor or desaturation on room air. Examination showed no external nasal deformity. Bedside nasoendoscopy revealed a soft, fleshy mass occupying the left nasal cavity, yet a 6-French catheter could be passed beyond the mass into the nasopharynx, suggesting no choanal atresia. The right nasal cavity was normal except for septal deviation caused by the mass effect. The oral cavity and oropharynx were clear, with no cleft palate.  
Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI of the nose demonstrated a left intranasal mass arising from the roof of the nasal cavity and extending into the posterior choana. There were no underlying bony skull-base defects or intracranial herniation.  
The differential diagnosis at presentation included congenital midline nasal mass (e.g., nasal glioma) and intranasal tumor (e.g., nasal chondromesenchymal hamartoma or nasal teratoma).

A 72-year-old man presented with an ulcerated swelling of the right thumb. One month earlier, he had noted a small nodule on the distal phalanx of the thumb that progressively enlarged and ulcerated over the skin one week before presentation. He reported bleeding from the wound margins, tenderness, and pain on movement. His medical history was notable for stage IV non–small cell lung cancer with spinal metastasis, managed palliatively. He also reported weight loss, anorexia, and weakness. 

On examination, there was an ulcerated lesion involving the nail bed of the right thumb with necrotic slough at the ulcer floor. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis (26.4 × 10^3/mm^3), hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, serum urea 170 mg/dL, creatinine 1.44 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 400 IU/L, and serum albumin 2.5 g/dL. The patient tested positive for COVID-19. 

A chest radiograph demonstrated a left pulmonary mass. Right thumb radiographs revealed complete destruction of the distal phalanx cortex with sparing of the interphalangeal joint. Contrast-enhanced CT of the right hand showed a 3 × 2 × 2 cm soft-tissue mass destroying and expanding the distal phalanx, with cortical breakdown, extension into dorsal and palmar soft tissues, increased vascularity, and invasion of tendons and muscles; the interphalangeal joint was spared. 

A biopsy of the lesion was performed. Histopathological examination of H&E-stained sections revealed partly skin-covered, partly ulcerated tissue composed of trabecular sheets of atypical basaloid cells and many multivacuolated cells; nuclei showed marked atypia and numerous (including atypical) mitoses, with areas of necrosis and involved margins. The biopsy was suggestive of a malignant adnexal tumour of the skin with sebaceous differentiation.

A 40-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of gastric wall thickening detected on a screening upper gastrointestinal series. She was asymptomatic. Her medical history was notable for asymptomatic Sjögren’s syndrome diagnosed at age 35. She had no medication or smoking history. Family history included breast cancer in a maternal relative and rheumatoid arthritis in her father. Laboratory studies revealed hypergammaglobulinemia (IgG 2750 mg/dL; IgA 625 mg/dL; IgM 241 mg/dL) with a normal serum soluble interleukin-2 receptor level (362 U/mL). A chest radiograph was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed localized wall thickening of 22 mm with enhancement in the middle gastric body along the greater curvature. Chest CT demonstrated a well-circumscribed heterogeneous mass measuring 49 × 22 mm in the anterior mediastinum and multiple thin-walled cysts in both lungs. MRI of the mediastinum confirmed a multilocular mass without invasion of adjacent structures. Endoscopic incisional biopsy of the gastric lesion revealed lymphocytic infiltration without atypical cells or light chain restriction, findings consistent with inflammatory changes. The patient underwent video-assisted thoracoscopic total thymectomy for presumed thymoma and wedge resection of a right upper-lobe lung cyst to rule out lymphangioleiomyomatosis.

A 64-year-old Japanese man with no stigmata of tuberous sclerosis underwent routine follow-up after ileocecal cancer resection, with no evidence of metastasis and normal tumor markers (α-fetoprotein, PIVKA-II, CEA, CA 19-9). He reported no symptoms. Physical examination was unremarkable, with no hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. Tests for hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C virus antibodies were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 25-mm low-density tumor with a high-density area in segment 2 of the liver. Gadolinium ethoxybenzyl diethylenetriamine pentaacetic acid–enhanced MRI showed a 22×12-mm lesion in segment 2 that was slightly hyperintense on T2-weighted images and hypointense on T1-weighted images. On dynamic imaging, the lesion demonstrated marked heterogeneous high signal intensity in the arterial phase with visible central filiform vessels and capsular enhancement, relative reduction of signal in the portal venous phase (still slightly higher than surrounding liver), and lower signal than liver parenchyma in the equilibrium phase. There was no uptake in the hepatobiliary phase at 20 minutes.

A 46-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of a cyclically painful suprapubic lump beneath the scar of a prior laparoscopic port. Her medical history was notable for a laparoscopic supracervical hysterectomy for leiomyomas performed 1 year earlier; no endometriosis was noted at the time, and the morcellated uterine corpus was removed in a sealed bag through the right iliac port. On examination, there was a hard, fixed mass adherent to the underlying layers of the abdominal wall under the suprapubic trocar scar.

An ultrasound scan revealed a 4-cm inhomogeneous mass with mild vascularization, extending from the rectus muscle to the subcutaneous fat. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a 36×32×26 mm solid, irregularly shaped mass with heterogeneous high contrast enhancement, infiltrating from the subcutaneous tissue to the transversalis fascia.

To rule out malignancy, a through-cut needle biopsy was performed, yielding a diagnosis of endometriosis. The patient was started on dienogest (2 mg daily). Over the next two months, her pain resolved, but the mass remained stable in size.

A woman in her 20s was referred for vision loss in her right eye. Her medical history was notable for stage IV T-cell lymphoma in infancy treated with chemotherapy and bone marrow transplantation; subsequent cerebral cavernous haemangioma; primary ovarian insufficiency; type 1 diabetes with growth hormone deficiency; gout; hypertension; fatty liver disease; diabetic retinopathy; and an autonomously functioning thyroid nodule. She had no significant family history.

On examination, corrected visual acuity was 20/600 in the right eye and 20/22 in the left eye. Funduscopic examination of the right eye revealed vitreous hemorrhage from proliferative diabetic retinopathy, and the left eye showed severe diabetic retinopathy with a yellowish-white, elevated lesion measuring approximately two optic disc diameters in the temporal periphery. The right eye underwent vitrectomy with cataract extraction, and panretinal photocoagulation was performed in both eyes.

One year later, visual acuity in the left eye declined to 20/600 due to macular hemorrhage, and the temporal lesion had enlarged. Ultrasound biomicroscopy demonstrated a 3.5–4.0 mm ciliary body mass. Given concern for malignancy, total excision of the ciliary tumour combined with vitrectomy, silicone oil tamponade, and cataract extraction was planned in the left eye.

A 39-year-old woman presents with a several-week history of intermittent vaginal bleeding. On colposcopic examination, a friable, solid mass measuring approximately 5 × 5 cm is noted on the posterior lip of the uterine cervix and bleeds easily when touched. A cervicovaginal specimen is obtained using a liquid-based cytology (SurePath™) technique, and a punch biopsy of the lesion is performed.

Cytologic findings:
• Hypercellular sample composed of isolated cells and tightly cohesive, multilayered clusters of endocervical cells in a clean background  
• Presence of papillary frond-like structures with smooth contours  
• Nuclear overlapping within cell clusters  
• Individual cells with high nuclear:cytoplasmic ratios; nuclei round to oval with irregular membranes  
• Nuclei hyperchromatic with evenly distributed granular chromatin and distinct nucleoli  
• Occasional mitotic figures and apoptotic debris

A 48-year-old man presented with sudden-onset seizures affecting his left lower limb. He had no prior seizures or history of neurofibromatosis. On admission, vital signs were stable, and both physical and neurologic examinations were unremarkable, with no cutaneous stigmata of neurofibromatosis. Brain MRI revealed a well-defined mass in the right parieto-frontal convexity that was isointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted and FLAIR images, and demonstrated homogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. Curvilinear enhancement was observed beneath the parietal bone but was considered unlikely to represent a “dural tail sign.” T2-weighted images also showed perilesional edema. Digital subtraction angiography demonstrated feeding arteries from branches of the right middle cerebral artery, right anterior cerebral artery, and right middle meningeal artery. Preoperative embolization of the middle meningeal artery branch was performed. A whole-body evaluation revealed no evidence of malignancy. Based on these findings, an extra-axial tumor such as convexity meningioma was suspected.

A 73-year-old man with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and former smoking presented with a several-week history of dry cough. He had an ECOG performance status of 1. Physical examination revealed diminished breath sounds over the middle and lower left hemithorax. A chest radiograph showed a large, homogeneous opacity in the middle-to-lower left lung field. Contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography demonstrated an 11 × 14 cm bronchopulmonary mass extending from the costal pleura to the hilum without mediastinal lymphadenopathy. FDG-PET CT showed low metabolic uptake in the mass. Bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy revealed a mesenchymal neoplasm of moderate cellularity composed of oval and fusiform nucleated cells without necrosis or significant pleomorphism. The tumor cells stained diffusely for vimentin, bcl-2, CD99, and STAT-6 and were negative for cytokeratin 19 and TTF1. The Ki-67 proliferation index was less than 1%.

A 45-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of headache, memory deficits, visual disturbances, and a 20-kg weight gain. On examination, she had right temporal hemianopia and a left diffuse visual defect. Endocrine testing revealed normal levels of luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone, prolactin, estradiol, and progesterone. Brain MRI with contrast demonstrated a well-defined, multilobulated, solid mass in the anterior aspect of the third ventricle. The lesion was isointense on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted and FLAIR images compared with gray matter, and showed restricted diffusion. The mass exhibited vivid and homogeneous enhancement. It extended into the supraoptic recess, compressed the optic chiasm downward and forward, bowed the floor of the third ventricle and infundibulum backward and downward, and compressed the bilateral hypothalamus. The lesion contacted the terminal segment of the right internal carotid artery, the A1 segment of the right anterior cerebral artery, and the tip of the basilar artery. Adjacent brain parenchyma and optic tracts were hyperintense on FLAIR. The pituitary gland and suprasellar cistern appeared intact.

A 57-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of pain and a 3-year history of progressive swelling of her left thumb. She denied trauma or other relevant medical history. On examination, there was a tender, palpable mass measuring approximately 2.5 cm × 2.5 cm × 1.5 cm over the dorsal aspect of the carpometacarpal joint of the left thumb, without overlying skin changes. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. Plain radiographs of the hand demonstrated mild soft-tissue swelling and multiple radiopaque bodies around the carpometacarpal joint of the left thumb without erosion of the base of the first metacarpal bone or trapezium. Computed tomography showed a 2.1 cm × 1.9 cm × 1.4 cm nodule adjacent to the joint capsule. Magnetic resonance imaging was not obtained.

A 35-year-old man presented with a one-week history of pus discharge from the lower left jaw. Two months earlier, he had noted swelling in the same area and took oral medications for two weeks without relief. Three days before presentation, he underwent extraction of the left lower first molar elsewhere, again with no improvement.

On extraoral examination, there was a diffuse, firm-to-hard, tender swelling over the left body of the mandible. Intraorally, the extraction socket of the lower left first molar was noted. There was expansion of the buccal and lingual cortical plates and loss of vestibular depth from the left lateral incisor through the first molar region. The left second premolar exhibited grade II mobility, and teeth from the right lateral incisor to the left second premolar were tender to percussion. On the lingual aspect of the lower right first and second premolars, two supernumerary teeth were visible.

Radiographic evaluation included an intraoral periapical radiograph of the lower left first molar region, a mandibular occlusal view, and a panoramic radiograph. These demonstrated a well-corticated, unilocular radiolucency extending from the distal aspect of the right canine to the distal aspect of the left second molar, containing two supernumerary premolars. Superiorly it reached the alveolar ridge, and inferiorly it caused thinning of the mandibular border. Buccal and lingual cortical expansion was evident.

A 47-year-old man with a history of muscular dystrophy and schizophrenia presented with an 11-year history of a slowly enlarging, protuberant mass arising from his left chin. He used a wheelchair after multiple fractures from falls and was taking risperidone. On examination, an extraoral, well-defined, non-tender, bony hard growth extended from the left anteroinferior border of the mandible downward; the lesion was not freely mobile, and the overlying skin was slightly distended.
