Cone-beam CT showed a midline soft-tissue radiopacity inferior to the chin, consisting of an outer cortical layer and inner trabecular bone, with no visible attachment to the mandible or to adjacent muscles. Based on the clinical and radiographic features, the consensus was to proceed with excisional surgery under general anesthesia.

A 55-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive asthenia and a rapidly enlarging neck lump causing dyspnea, dysphagia, cough, and vomiting. Seven weeks earlier, a 3.4-cm benign right thyroid nodule was diagnosed without lymphadenopathy. She denied prior neck irradiation or thyroid cancer in her family. On examination, a hard, painless, immobile 10 × 10 cm mass occupied the anterior neck. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed a right thyroid lobe mass measuring 8.8 × 6.8 × 6.4 cm with endoluminal tracheal invasion and deviation. Flexible bronchoscopy and laryngoscopy demonstrated mobile vocal folds, diffuse mucosal inflammation, and a hypervascular exophytic lesion causing 70% obstruction between the first and second tracheal rings. Given the rapidly progressing obstructive symptoms, a malignant thyroid neoplasm was suspected, and surgical planning was undertaken.

A 16-year-old spayed female domestic shorthair cat was referred for a 9-day history of progressive right pelvic limb lameness. She was receiving methimazole for well-controlled hyperthyroidism. CBC, serum biochemistry and total thyroxine concentration were within reference intervals, and retroviral screening for FeLV and FIV was negative. On physical examination, she had a grade 2/6 left parasternal systolic murmur and a thin body condition. Neurologic examination revealed normal cranial nerves and limb reflexes except in the right pelvic limb, where postural reactions and sciatic reflexes (cranial tibial, gastrocnemius and withdrawal) were diminished; the patellar reflex was intact. The limb was only advanced by hip flexion, and when weight bearing the hock rested in hyperflexion, producing a plantigrade stance. Mild lumbar spinal pain was noted. Findings localized to the right sciatic nerve root or sciatic nerve proper.

Initial diagnostics included Doppler analysis of femoral and pedal arteries and electrocardiography, all within normal limits. Thoracic radiographs showed no pulmonary nodules, and echocardiography revealed mild left ventricular free-wall hypertrophy. Non-contrast and contrast-enhanced 3 T MRI of the caudal lumbar spine and pelvis demonstrated a 6.4–9 mm wide mass invading the right sciatic nerve (left sciatic nerve 2.9–3.7 mm wide). The lesion was isointense to spinal cord on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on STIR, and homogeneously, avidly enhanced after gadolinium. It arose from the right lateral conus medullaris at L6–7, exited via the L7–S1 and S1–2 foramina, and tracked distally along the sciatic nerve path to the femur.

Abdominal ultrasound revealed a hyperechoic mesentery, markedly hypoechoic enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes, and diffuse jejunal and ileal muscularis thickening, with one loop showing loss of wall layering and severe thickening. Fine-needle aspiration of the bowel loop yielded cytology suggestive of lymphoma. Ultrasonography-guided aspiration of the sciatic mass was unsuccessful.

A 40-year-old woman was referred with six months of intense lower facial pain and progressive left mandibular swelling. She had undergone root canal therapy on the left second premolar and first molar without relief. An incisional biopsy at another center was reported as “malignant Pindborg tumor.” On examination, there was diffuse swelling of the left mandible with tenderness and lower-lip paresthesia, and an approximately 4 cm rubbery mass with intact overlying skin and ulcerated oral mucosa. No cervical lymphadenopathy was noted, and there was no dysphagia, trismus, or dysphonia. Panoramic radiograph and cone-beam CT showed a well-defined lesion extending from the left canine to the second molar, from the alveolar crest to the mandibular inferior border, containing multiple small internal radiopaque foci, with buccal and lingual cortical perforations and involvement of the inferior alveolar canal.

A 26-year-old man presented with nasal obstruction and congestion for 3 years. He denied headache, epistaxis, visual changes, or cranial nerve symptoms. On examination, a firm mass was visible in the naso-oropharynx, displacing the uvula anteriorly. Contrast-enhanced MSCT of the head revealed a well-defined, lobulated mass measuring approximately 5 × 6 cm in the midline naso-oropharyngeal region without involvement of the clivus. A chest radiograph was unremarkable, and routine hematological and biochemical tests were within normal limits. Multiple superficial biopsies showed nonspecific chronic inflammation. The patient received antibiotic and anti-inflammatory therapy without clinical improvement.

A 45-year-old woman presented with 9 months of progressive virilization including centripetal obesity, hirsutism, facial acne, hypertension, and oligomenorrhea. She noted a gradually enlarging, palpable mass in her right upper quadrant. Laboratory studies showed markedly elevated dehydroepiandrosterone, dehydroepiandrosterone-sulfate, cortisol, and testosterone levels consistent with a functional suprarenal tumor. Abdominal ultrasonography and noncontrast CT revealed a 16.2 × 13.2 × 12.7 cm solid mass occupying most of the right liver lobe, displacing the right kidney downward. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated heterogeneous enhancement of the lesion, stenosis of the inferior vena cava from the left renal vein to the hepatic veins, and no thrombus in the portal vein.

A 10-year-old boy presented with a progressively enlarging, painless swelling of the left mandible over 6 months. Extraoral examination showed facial asymmetry caused by a firm hard swelling of the left lower jaw without paresthesia. Intraorally, the swelling extended from the distal aspect of the lower left first permanent molar to the retromolar area. Orthopantomogram revealed a large, well-defined unilocular radiolucent lesion with a sclerotic border, extending anteriorly from the developing second premolar to mid-ramus posteriorly, superiorly abutting the coronoid process, and inferiorly approaching the mandibular border; the developing second molar was displaced to the lower edge of the radiolucency. The initial differential diagnosis included dentigerous cyst, odontogenic keratocyst, and ameloblastoma.

A 48-year-old man with no prior medical history underwent routine abdominal ultrasonography, which revealed three well-defined hypoechoic hepatic masses in segments 1 (67×53 mm), 6 (13 mm), and 2 (9 mm). He was asymptomatic. Laboratory studies showed normal total bilirubin (0.6 mg/dL) and albumin (4.2 g/dL), with mildly elevated AST (37 IU/L), ALT (70 IU/L), ALP (176 U/L), and GGT (170 IU/L). Tumor markers, including alpha-fetoprotein (2.9 ng/mL), PIVKA-II (11 mAU/mL), and CA19-9 (4.0 IU/L), were within normal limits. 

Dynamic contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 65 mm low-density mass with an irregular margin in the caudate lobe, showing peripheral early ring enhancement in the arterial phase and heterogeneous internal enhancement in the delayed phase. EOB-MRI revealed a hypointense mass on T1-weighted images containing several hyperintense areas on T2-weighted images, and the lesion remained hypointense in the hepatobiliary phase. On diffusion-weighted imaging (b = 1000), the lesion was hyperintense relative to liver, with ADC values of 2.11×10^−3 mm^2/s peripherally and 2.45×10^−3 mm^2/s centrally (mean 2.33×10^−3 mm^2/s). FDG-PET showed no radiotracer accumulation in any of the hepatic lesions. Hepatic arteriography demonstrated hypervascular masses in segments 1, 6, and 2 without pooling. Gastroscopy and colonoscopy were unremarkable.

A 23-year-old woman with no significant medical or family history presented with a sensation of discomfort and slight pain in the left retromolar region. Extraoral examination revealed no facial asymmetry. Intraoral examination showed poor oral hygiene, no swelling, and deep caries of the left first mandibular molar. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated a well-defined, corticated radiolucent lesion spanning the entire left mandibular ramus, in relation to an impacted lower third molar. CT imaging revealed a unilocular osteolytic lesion with a tissue matrix, sparse millimetric calcifications, slight contrast enhancement, thinning of the internal cortical surface without rupture, and involvement of the mandibular canal; dimensions were 34 mm in the coronal plane and 10 × 25 mm in the axial plane. Based on these clinical and radiological features, the initial working diagnoses were calcifying epithelial odontogenic tumour (Pindborg tumour) or ameloblastoma.

A previously healthy 2-year-old girl presented to the emergency department with abdominal pain. Physical examination was unremarkable, and routine laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver function tests, serum α-fetoprotein, and β-human chorionic gonadotropin, were within normal limits.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 12 × 11 × 10 cm, well-circumscribed hypoechoic lesion in the right hepatic lobe containing cystic areas. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 12 × 11 × 11 cm hypodense mass occupying the entire right lobe, with peripheral serpiginous vessels and septa showing enhancement in the portal phase.

Given the size and complexity of the lesion, MRI was performed for further characterization. On T1-weighted images, the lesion was predominantly hypointense with hyperintense areas and fluid–fluid levels. On T2-weighted images, it appeared predominantly hyperintense with hypointense septations. Diffusion-weighted imaging showed heterogeneous restriction. On postcontrast sequences, there was progressive enhancement of the septa but not of the entire lesion. The mass abutted and compressed the inferior vena cava, hepatic veins, and portal vein branches.

A 36‐year‐old Greek woman presented with a 6‐month history of progressive left abdominal and pelvic pain and a 2‐year history of constipation intermittently relieved by laxatives. Recto‐sigmoidoscopy showed extrinsic compression of the rectum. A plain abdominal radiograph revealed a pelvic mass without extension to the sacrum. Pelvic ultrasonography demonstrated a hypoechoic tumor in the lower sacrococcygeal region. CT of the pelvis showed a mixed‐type mass with soft‐tissue elements, inhomogeneous fatty tissue, and calcifications, displacing the rectum and bladder anteriorly, without evidence of bone destruction. MRI revealed a 6×5×4.5 cm heterogeneous mass anterior to the distal sacrum and coccyx that was not attached to the sacrum or rectum, with normal lower spinal cord, normal sacrum, no infiltrative disease in bone or adjacent tissues, and no lymphadenopathy. Routine laboratory tests were normal, and hCG and serum tumor markers (αFP, CEA, CA 19‐9, CA 125, CA 15‐3) were not elevated.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of low-grade fever (up to 38.5°C), weight loss, anorexia, fatigue, and night sweats. She had no history of travel, dental procedures, tick or animal exposures. On examination, temperature was 38.2°C, blood pressure 100/55 mmHg, pulse 73/min, respiratory rate 13/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. The abdomen was soft and non-tender, with no palpable masses; there was no lymphadenopathy, skin rash, or neurologic deficit.

Laboratory results showed hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, hematocrit 28%, normocytic indices, white-cell count 6430/mm3 (67% neutrophils, 22% lymphocytes), platelets 256,000/mm3, and reticulocytes 56,000/mm3. C-reactive protein was 137 mg/L (normal <5), haptoglobin 4.65 g/L (normal 0.3–2), lactate dehydrogenase 533 U/L (normal 5–248), and β2-microglobulin 4.56 mg/L (normal 1.2–2.5). Liver enzymes were elevated (AST 73 U/L, ALT 132 U/L). Serum creatinine was 72 µmol/L (eGFR 77 mL/min/1.73 m2), and there was no proteinuria. Serum protein electrophoresis showed a polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. Reticulocyte count, iron studies, vitamin B12, and folate were normal. Thyroid-stimulating hormone was 0.37 µIU/mL.

Blood, sputum, and urine cultures were negative; serologies for Brucella, Rickettsia, Chlamydophila, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Borrelia, and syphilis were negative. Antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. A whole-body CT scan was unremarkable except for marked bilateral kidney hypertrophy. Microscopic examination of the urine sediment was normal.

A 49-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with right upper‐quadrant abdominal pain. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed normal liver function tests. Serum tumor markers, including carcinoembryonic antigen, CA19-9, and alpha-fetoprotein, were within normal limits. Viral hepatitis markers were negative. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a nodular formation in the right hepatic lobe. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated an 18 × 12 × 20 cm lobulated cystic mass with thin enhancing septa occupying the right liver lobe. MRI confirmed a heterogeneous mass with fluid levels and thin septa, findings described as suggestive of an atypical hemangioma; the right hepatic vein was inseparable from the lesion. Given the size of the lesion and risk of complications, a right hepatectomy was performed without intraoperative rupture, and the resected tumor measured approximately 20 cm in greatest dimension.

A 77-year-old man with a history of diabetes presented with a 1-month history of a persistent lump on the left vertex of his scalp after mild blunt head trauma. He reported intermittent mild headache but no focal neurologic symptoms, and neurologic examination was unremarkable. On examination, the lesion was soft, erythematous, mildly tender, and showed slight necrosis of the overlying skin. Routine laboratory studies were within normal limits. Noncontrast CT of the head demonstrated no skull fracture or intracranial hemorrhage but revealed an irregular exophytic soft‐tissue lesion over the left frontoparietal scalp and underlying focal osseous destruction with innumerable stippled and serpentine osteolytic foci in the adjacent bone. The lesion was initially presumed to be a nonresolving infected subgaleal hematoma.

A 46-year-old nulligravid German woman presented with a 15-year history of slowly increasing abdominal girth and two episodes of polymenorrhea and menorrhagia. She denied bowel or bladder complaints. Her past avoidance of medical care led to sporadic consultations during which no imaging was performed, and her abdominal enlargement was attributed to weight gain.

On examination, her BMI was 32.1 kg/m2. She appeared well, with no pallor or edema. Her abdomen was massively distended and pendulous, with flank fullness, and an irregular mass extending from the pelvis to the xiphisternum. A vaginal examination was not possible because of patient anxiety.

Transabdominal ultrasound revealed a huge intraabdominal mass, impaired appearance of the right kidney, compensatory enlargement of the left kidney, and a small amount of ascites. An urgent CT scan showed a 32 × 27 × 34 cm heterogeneous mass occupying the abdominopelvic cavity that could not be visibly separated from the uterine cavity, bladder, or liver. The mass contained cystic and necrotic areas and solid components, compressed the intestines, right kidney, and ureters, and was associated with mild splenomegaly and minimal ascites. No lymphadenopathy was identified. Due to the slow growth of the tumor, few ascites, and negative lymph nodes, malignancy was considered highly unlikely.

A 25-year-old man with a history of a mediastinal mixed germ cell tumor treated by resection and combination chemotherapy presented 6 months after completing therapy with easy fatigability and generalized weakness. On examination, he was pale without lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 6.0 g/dL, leukocyte count 3,000/µL, and platelets 20,000/µL; the peripheral smear showed no blasts. Bone marrow aspiration was a dry tap. Trephine biopsy revealed blast infiltration; blasts were negative for myeloperoxidase and leukocyte common antigen but positive for CD61, consistent with acute megakaryoblastic leukemia. He received daunorubicin and cytarabine. Six months later, he developed a single 4×4 cm right cervical lymph node. Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) of the node and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination were performed.  

Microscopic examination of the FNA smears revealed numerous blasts 2–3 times the size of mature lymphocytes, with scant to moderate granular cytoplasm, fine chromatin, and single or multiple prominent nucleoli. Some blasts had nuclear notches, indentations, and folds. Cells were mostly single but formed small clumps reminiscent of marrow particles. A few larger cells exhibited moderate to abundant cytoplasm with lobated, indented, or horseshoe-shaped nuclei. Bi- to multinucleated cells reminiscent of megakaryocytes were present, along with numerous anucleate pale-blue cytoplasmic fragments.  

Cytocentrifuge preparations of the CSF showed blasts with scant to moderate granular cytoplasm, irregular nuclear margins, fine granular chromatin, and prominent nucleoli, as well as binucleate and multinucleate forms.

A 45-year-old woman with no significant past medical or surgical history presented with a three-month history of L5 sciatica without sensory or motor deficits. She was not taking any medications, and her family history was unremarkable. On examination, there was a firm, ill-defined 11 × 7 cm mass in the right gluteal region. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis revealed a solid mass with a necrotic center in the right gluteal region extending to the greater sciatic notch, sparing the sciatic nerve and the initial portion of the right gluteal artery. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated a solitary pulmonary nodule in the right lower lobe.

A 55-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a painless, progressively enlarging mass on the left palate, accompanied by left-sided nasal blockage, facial pain, and intermittent epistaxis. He smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 18 years and denied alcohol use. On examination, he had left-sided facial swelling and palpable left cervical lymphadenopathy. Nasal endoscopy revealed a frail, vascular mass nearly filling the left nasal cavity, with extension into the left palate. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a heterogeneous mass of the left maxillary sinus and nasal cavity with destructive extension through the hard palate into the retromaxillary and premaxillary spaces; there was no intracranial or intraorbital spread. Multiple necrotic lymph nodes were noted in the left upper deep cervical, submental, and submandibular regions. Biopsies of the nasal mass and a cervical lymph node were reported as undifferentiated carcinoma.

A 71-year-old man with ischaemic heart disease, insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and stage 4 chronic kidney disease presented with four weeks of progressive dyspnoea, cough, weight loss, and new haemoptysis. He had a left brachiocephalic arteriovenous fistula created 34 months earlier that had never been used for haemodialysis. Three months before presentation, he developed swelling and warmth at the fistula site; duplex ultrasound confirmed partial fistula thrombosis, and over the next month he reported pain and tenderness consistent with mild thrombophlebitis.

In respiratory clinic, he had a 60 pack-year smoking history, possible asbestos exposure, and a prominent swelling over the AVF. He was admitted with bilateral pleural effusions and severe anaemia (hemoglobin 64 g/L; baseline 110 g/L). CT of the thorax revealed bilateral pulmonary and pleural nodular and mass-like opacities with bilateral pleural and pericardial effusions. A chest drain yielded strongly blood-stained fluid; cytology showed non-specific inflammatory cells and no malignant cells.

On admission he was febrile with erythema at the AVF site, diagnosed as cellulitis and treated with intravenous flucloxacillin. He received 2 units of packed red blood cells. Coagulation studies were normal and platelet counts remained within the reference range despite aspirin use; he was not on anticoagulants. Renal surgeons assessed the arm lesion and suggested a distal fistula aneurysm with proximal haematoma. Given the lesion’s unusual appearance, a decision was made to proceed to surgery. On Day 5, the necrotic soft tissue mass and associated haematoma were excised, the thrombosed fistula ligated, and loose closure performed; tissue was sent for histological analysis.

A 24-year-old healthy woman with no significant family history presented with a 24-month history of a lump in the lower inner quadrant of her left breast. Two years earlier, an incisional biopsy had been interpreted as a benign lesion. She subsequently became pregnant, and approximately 1 year after delivery the breast mass enlarged markedly. On clinical examination, there was diffuse enlargement of the left breast without overlying skin ulceration. Mammography demonstrated an asymmetric area of increased density in the left breast. Multiple-site core needle biopsy was nondiagnostic. The patient was taken to the operating room for an open biopsy under general anesthesia. A 2×2 cm specimen was excised, revealing a blood-filled cavity; upon removal of clots, diffuse uncontrollable bleeding ensued, with an estimated blood loss of 1500 mL despite packing. The following day, repacking was required after severe hemorrhage recurred when the initial pack was removed. Contrast-enhanced chest CT showed a large, well-enhanced mass in the left breast without invasion of the skin or pectoralis muscles, enlarged left axillary lymph nodes, and no pulmonary metastases.

A 69-year-old man was admitted with severe left back pain, acute kidney injury, and an inflammatory syndrome. Two years earlier, he had been diagnosed with bilateral xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis after abdominal CT showed diffuse bilateral irregular perinephric soft-tissue thickening with ureteral dilatation, and a percutaneous renal biopsy demonstrated foamy xanthomatous histiocytes, chronic inflammatory cells, and surrounding fibrosis without evidence of malignancy or immunoglobulin G4–related disease. His renal function then remained stable (creatinine 95.9 µmol/L, MDRD 72 ml/min/1.73 m²). On current presentation, his blood pressure was 180/90 mmHg, temperature 38 °C, and the rest of the examination was normal. Abdominal CT showed progression of perinephric soft tissue with bilateral ureteral stenosis causing hydronephrosis and acute kidney injury (creatinine 337 µmol/L, MDRD 17 ml/min/1.73 m²); bilateral ureteral stents were placed. Complete autoimmune and bacteriological studies were negative. MRI of the abdomen revealed perinephric infiltration that was iso-intense on T1-weighted images, slightly hypo-intense on T2-weighted images, with slow contrast enhancement—findings felt to be inconsistent with simple xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis and suggestive of a systemic process.

A 60-year-old man, asymptomatic, was referred after an incidental left sphenoid sinus mass was identified on screening magnetic resonance imaging.  
  
Neurologic and general physical examinations were unremarkable.  
  
MRI and CT demonstrated a mass filling the left sphenoid sinus, causing adjacent bone destruction and encasing the cavernous segment of the internal carotid artery; there was no regional lymphadenopathy or distant metastasis.  
  
Under general anesthesia, a transnasal biopsy was performed. Immunohistochemical studies revealed strong positivity for CD56, synaptophysin, and chromogranin A, and negativity for cytokeratin AE1/AE3. A small number of S-100 protein–positive cells were noted. To exclude other small round-cell tumors, additional staining for NKX2.2 and CD99 was performed and found to be negative.  
  
Based on these findings, a diagnosis of ectopic olfactory neuroblastoma (Hymas grade I, Kadish stage C) was made. A multidisciplinary team planned complete tumor resection via a combined transcranial and transnasal approach, employing a high-flow radial-artery bypass from the M2 segment of the left middle cerebral artery to the cervical external carotid artery, supplemented by a superficial temporal artery–MCA bypass, so that the internal carotid artery could be trapped and resected en bloc with the tumor.

A 49-year-old man was admitted for evaluation of an abdominal mass. Eight years earlier, he had been diagnosed with Budd–Chiari syndrome after presenting with abdominal wall varices, lower extremity edema, and abdominal distention. Inferior vena cavography showed hepatic vein occlusion and long-segment inferior vena cava obstruction, and he underwent a meso-cavo-atrial shunt, which relieved his symptoms. He had surveillance ultrasonography every six months.

On current examination, the liver was palpable 10 cm below the right costal margin, and the spleen was enlarged. Ultrasonography demonstrated patent artificial vessels and ascites. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed multiple, small, hypervascular hepatic lesions with marked homogeneous enhancement in the arterial phase without washout in the portal or delayed phases.

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 99 g/L, platelets 71 000/mm3, white blood cells 2400/mm3; ALT 14 IU/L; AST 26 IU/L; total bilirubin 36.2 μmol/L; total protein 48.9 g/L; albumin 29.6 g/L; aPTT 48.4 seconds; fibrinogen 2.17 g/L; hepatitis B and C serologies negative; α-fetoprotein 2.2 ng/mL (normal); and indocyanine green retention at 15 minutes 42.3%.

A 59-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of hoarseness and shortness of breath. He had smoked 20–60 cigarettes daily for 40 years and had a family history of lung cancer. His only comorbidity was well-controlled hypertension. On examination, findings were unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL (normal 13–17.5 g/dL) and a positive fecal occult blood test. Tumor markers were elevated: CEA 212.5 ng/mL (≤ 5), CA19-9 1111.5 U/mL (≤ 43), and CA125 681.2 U/mL (≤ 24).  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed an irregular 3.8 × 3.1 cm mass in the left upper lobe with spiculation, lobulation, pleural retraction, and mild heterogeneous enhancement, along with enlarged mediastinal and left hilar lymph nodes. Abdominal CT showed uneven thickening of the sigmoid colon wall and a 2.5 cm lymph node anterior to the left psoas major muscle.  
A CT-guided biopsy of the lung mass confirmed non–small cell lung cancer with loss of SMARCA4 expression; tumor cells were CK⁺, CK7⁺, and had a Ki-67 index > 40%. Colonoscopy demonstrated an annular neoplasm causing luminal obstruction 30 cm from the anal verge.  
At multidisciplinary discussion, it remained unclear whether the sigmoid lesion represented a primary colon cancer or metastatic disease.

A 45-year-old woman was referred for implant consultation. Her medical history was unremarkable, and she had no history of mandibular trauma. Extra-oral examination was normal. Intra-oral examination revealed normal mucosa, no soft-tissue expansion, and teeth of normal color. Periodontal tissues were healthy. All mandibular incisor teeth were asymptomatic, with no pain on percussion or palpation, and were vital on electric pulp testing.

For implant planning, a cone-beam CT scan was obtained. On axial, sagittal, and coronal images, a multifocal lesion was noted at the apices of the lower incisors, extending from the mesial aspect of the right lateral incisor to the distal aspect of the left lateral incisor. The lesion measured approximately 16.6 mm mesiodistally and 6.9 mm superoinferiorly. On panoramic reconstruction, the lesion at the left lateral incisor apex was radiolucent, at the left central incisor apex was mixed radiolucent–radiopaque, and at the right central incisor apex was radiopaque with a surrounding radiolucent rim. Axial images showed two areas of buccal cortical thinning (mesial to the right canine and between the left central and lateral incisors) and multiple consecutive sections demonstrated discontinuity of the lingual cortex between the two central incisors. A periapical radiograph confirmed loss of the lamina dura around the involved apices and widening of the periodontal ligament space, particularly around the left lateral incisor, without root resorption or tooth displacement.

A 26-year-old nulliparous woman presented with a 1-month history of a left vulvar mass, irregular vaginal bleeding, and night sweats. She had no significant past medical or family history. On pelvic examination, the left vulva, vagina, and cervix were swollen, and bimanual examination revealed a mass fixed to the pelvic wall. Serum α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, CA-125, CA19-9, and β-hCG were within normal limits. Initial complete blood count showed a white-cell count of 3.7×10^9/L with blasts on peripheral smear; hemoglobin and platelet counts were normal. A biopsy of the vulvovaginal mass demonstrated a malignant small round cell tumour. Two weeks later, the white-cell count rose to 18.9×10^9/L, hemoglobin was 102 g/L, platelets were 24×10^9/L, and peripheral smear revealed 79% blasts. Contrast-enhanced pelvic MRI showed an ill-defined, irregular 10.5×9.0-cm diffuse mass involving the vagina, paravaginal tissue, urethra, posterior bladder wall, left ischiorectal fossa, pelvic diaphragm, and pelvic floor; the lesion was homogeneously isointense on T1-weighted images, slightly hyperintense on T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted images with restricted diffusion, and showed homogeneous enhancement greater than muscle. Bilateral obturator lymph nodes were enlarged. PET/CT demonstrated high FDG uptake in the pelvic mass and enlarged obturator nodes; thoracic CT was unremarkable.

A 59-year-old African American woman with a remote history of intermediate-grade ductal carcinoma in situ of the left breast treated 13 years earlier with partial mastectomy, whole-breast radiation, and tamoxifen presented after routine screening mammography detected a focal asymmetry in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast. She reported no palpable mass, pain, skin changes, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Targeted ultrasonography revealed a cluster of multiple hypoechoic lesions, the largest measuring 1.0 cm (BIRADS 4). Given her history, the differential diagnosis included multifocal breast carcinoma and intraparenchymal lymph node metastasis. An ultrasound-guided core-needle biopsy was performed.

An 81-year-old man, former smoker with known ischaemic heart disease treated by mid-left anterior descending artery stenting and an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placed 2 months earlier for sustained ventricular tachycardia, was admitted with recent-onset dyspnoea and signs of decompensated heart failure.  
On arrival: blood pressure 130/70 mmHg, heart rate 72 b.p.m., oxygen saturation 95% on 3 L/min O₂. Physical examination revealed no murmurs.  
An ECG showed sinus rhythm with abnormal R-wave progression and ST-segment elevation in leads V2–V5 and II, III, aVF. A prior ECG 2 months earlier had shown only negative T-waves in leads V2–V3 with normal R-wave progression.  
Laboratory tests revealed troponin I 83 ng/L (normal <26 ng/L), brain natriuretic peptide 1400 pg/L (normal <100 pg/L), C-reactive protein 93 mg/L (normal <4 mg/L), and white blood cell count 14 G/L (normal <10 G/L). Given a coronary angiogram 2 months earlier showing no new stenoses, emergent angiography was deferred.  
Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a left ventricular ejection fraction of 40% (inferior and posterior wall akinesia) and a 5 cm × 3 cm thickening of the mid and apical interventricular septum with moderate pericardial effusion. Contrast-enhanced echocardiography at low mechanical index revealed a myocardial mass involving the apices of both ventricles; very-low–mechanical-index perfusion imaging showed peripheral contrast enhancement with a central hypoenhanced zone.  
An ECG-gated cardiac CT confirmed a 6 cm × 4 cm × 8 cm intra-septal apical mass with a hypodense centre and peripheral enhancement. The same CT also demonstrated a 9 cm × 6 cm mass in the left lower pulmonary lobe with mediastinal lymphadenopathy and possible left adrenal involvement.

A 55-year-old man with a history of recurrent nodular malignant melanoma of the right pinna presented three years after his last excision with a two-month history of a firm, immobile right‐sided neck mass. He denied pain, dysphagia, voice changes, weight loss, or limitation of head movement. On examination, there was also a pink, lobular lesion superior to the right eyebrow measuring 2.5 × 1.7 × 0.7 cm, first noticed six months earlier and asymptomatic.

Neck ultrasound showed a 3.0 × 2.8 × 3.3 cm hypoechoic mass with poorly defined margins and peripheral vascularity. CT of the neck demonstrated a similarly sized mass suggestive of a necrotic lymph node. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration of the neck mass revealed loosely cohesive tumor cells in a lymphocyte-predominant background. Immunohistochemical stains showed tumor cells negative for melanoma markers (S-100, melan-A, SOX-10, and HMB-45), moderately positive for CKAE1/AE3 and BerEP4, and positive for CD56 and synaptophysin but negative for cytokeratin 20. At this point, the differential diagnosis included a metastatic neuroendocrine neoplasm of the skin such as Merkel cell carcinoma versus neuroendocrine neoplasms of other origins, such as lung or gastrointestinal tract.

A 63-year-old woman was referred after an incidental right thyroid nodule was found on MRI performed for cervical spondylitis. She denied compressive symptoms and had no palpable thyroid enlargement. Thyroid‐stimulating hormone and free T4 levels were normal.  
She was a 35 pack‐year smoker, had no prior head or neck irradiation, and a history of bilateral breast cancer treated with mastectomy and chemotherapy. Family history was notable for lung cancer and a benign brain tumor.  
Neck ultrasound showed a 2.2 × 2.2 × 2.3 cm circumscribed, hypoechoic nodule with internal echoes and significant calcification in the lower pole of the right lobe; the left lobe was normal. Fine‐needle aspiration was nondiagnostic because of calcification.  
She underwent right thyroid lobectomy. The lobe weighed 14.5 g and measured 6.0 × 3.0 × 2.0 cm. The lower‐pole nodule measured 2.8 × 2.5 × 1.6 cm and was encapsulated by a thick, fibrotic, calcified capsule.  
Microscopic examination revealed a follicular adenoma. One area contained osseous metaplasia with mature ectopic bone formation, without vascular invasion or other marrow elements. The surrounding thyroid tissue was unremarkable, and no malignant features were identified.

A 35-year-old man presented with a 7-month history of a lesion on the left nasal soft triangle. He noted that it began as a small, soft, oval mass and enlarged gradually by approximately 3 mm per month. He denied pain, fever, bleeding, breathing difficulty, trauma, or prior nasal surgery. His family history was negative for similar lesions. On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. There was a 2.0 × 1.5 cm pedunculated, skin-colored, oval nodule on the left soft triangle of the nose, which was mobile and non-tender. No cervical lymphadenopathy or other skin lesions were observed. The remainder of the ENT examination was unremarkable. A biopsy of the lesion was performed.

A 22-year-old woman presented with a several-week history of progressive weakness and numbness in both lower limbs. On examination, she had diminished pain and temperature sensation below the T1 dermatome, loss of vibration and proprioception in all extremities, motor strength of 2/5 in the lower extremities, mild weakness of right finger flexion, global hyperreflexia, bilateral ankle clonus, and positive Babinski signs. Cervical MRI showed a lesion extending from C5 to C8 that was hypointense relative to the spinal cord on T1-weighted images and slightly hyperintense on T2-weighted images. After gadolinium administration, the mass enhanced homogeneously and comprised two portions: an infiltrative intradural component with ill-defined borders and an extradural component. On coronal contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images, the lesion formed a dumbbell-shaped expansion through the left C6–C7 and C7–T1 neural foramina. A CT scan of the cervical spine demonstrated macroscopic calcification within the lesion.

A 36‐year‐old African man presented with a large right‐sided facial mass causing massive disfigurement. On examination, his right ear was displaced superiorly and his mouth deviated to the left. The mass appeared necrotic and foul‐smelling, with purulent and bloody excretions. He reported that it had been growing over the past eight years, despite multiple resections in Africa, including a right parotidectomy. He also had fevers up to 38.5 °C without other systemic symptoms.

Contrast‐enhanced CT of the head and neck showed a 28.0 × 9.5 × 23.5 cm exophytic, lobulated mass in the right preauricular region that was moderately hypoattenuated with moderate contrast enhancement and no calcifications. There was bone scalloping of the right posterior mandibular ramus, external auditory canal, and mastoid, suggesting a slow‐growing process. CT angiography demonstrated multiple branches of the external carotid artery circumferentially encased by the tumor. Chest imaging revealed findings in the right upper lobe compatible with active tuberculosis. 

On MRI, the lesion was hypointense on T1‐weighted images, moderately hyperintense on T2‐weighted images, and showed marked homogeneous contrast enhancement with peripheral zones of necrosis. The adjacent right masseter, medial and lateral pterygoid, and perioral muscles were not separately visible, indicating deep muscular invasion; there was anteroinferior displacement of the submandibular gland and parapharyngeal spaces without clear signs of invasion. PET‐CT revealed F‐18 fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in both the right facial mass and the right upper lobe but no distant metastases.

Based on these findings, the differential diagnosis included chronic tuberculous lymphadenitis, plexiform neurofibroma, liposarcoma, dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, and giant pleomorphic adenoma.

A 55-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of new-onset dyspepsia and gastroesophageal reflux symptoms. She had a history of Helicobacter pylori gastritis successfully treated 1 year earlier.  
On examination, vital signs were normal, and the physical examination was unremarkable. Routine biochemical and hematological tests were within normal limits.  
Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a 1-cm nodule in the gastric antrum along the greater curvature with normal overlying mucosa. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen showed no gastric lesions, lymphadenopathy, or other abnormalities.  
Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated a 7.1 × 6.7 mm, isoechoic, subepithelial lesion with hyperechoic foci arising from the gastric wall.  
An endoscopic mucosal resection of the nodule was performed without complications, and the patient was discharged the same day on a proton pump inhibitor.

A 65-year-old woman with a history of Steven–Johnson syndrome, major depressive disorder, and hypothyroidism presented with epigastric pain most pronounced in the right upper quadrant. She reported no rebound tenderness or guarding. On admission, vital signs were stable. Physical examination revealed tenderness in the epigastric region and right upper quadrant. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 25.7 × 10^3/μL, aspartate aminotransferase 77 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 80 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 525 U/L, and C-reactive protein 95.5 ng/L. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated findings consistent with emphysematous cholecystitis: gallbladder wall thickening with echogenic foci but no positive Murphy sign. Incidentally, two hyperechoic lesions were noted adjacent to the left kidney: one measuring 96 × 88 mm near the upper pole and another 45 × 37 mm near the lower pole, neither contiguous with renal parenchyma. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed emphysematous cholecystitis and revealed (1) a round left adrenal mass composed predominantly of fat with interspersed soft-tissue elements and (2) a para-aortic mass with fat density and soft-tissue components extending toward the pelvis near the left iliac vessels.

A 15-year-old boy presented with two months of left posterior mandibular pain. He was initially treated for acute pulpitis of tooth #37 with pulp extirpation, without relief. Over the subsequent weeks he developed progressive left facial swelling and received unspecified herbal therapy without improvement. He then noted an intraoral mass, tongue displacement, and left lower lip numbness. One month before referral, MRI of the face showed a 64×68 mm soft-tissue mass around the left mandible with local bone destruction; the lesion was isointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted and fat-suppressed sequences, and showed high signal on diffusion-weighted imaging. The tongue and left submandibular gland were displaced, and multiple small cervical lymph nodes were noted. A core biopsy revealed a spindle cell lesion of the left mandible. On examination, he had facial asymmetry with a firm, immobile 7×7 cm mass over the left mandible without overlying skin changes. Intraorally, a firm 3×5 cm nonpedunculated mass extended from tooth #35 to #38 on the lingual side, covered by a white pseudomembrane and bleeding easily on palpation. No lymphadenopathy was palpable. Past history was unremarkable, and there was no family history of similar conditions. Institutional pathological consultation suggested a benign fibrous proliferative lesion.

A 2-year-7-month-old previously healthy boy was evaluated for several weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss. He also had a pruritic scalp rash. Laboratory studies demonstrated hypernatremia, hypotonic urine, and a water-deprivation test consistent with central diabetes insipidus. A bone survey showed multiple calvarial lytic lesions with “punched-out” margins and beveled edges. Brain MRI demonstrated absence of the normal T1 hyperintense posterior pituitary signal without infundibular thickening or abnormal enhancement, as well as enhancing soft-tissue lesions in the sphenoid wings and an isolated enhancing dural thickening at the level of the torcula. Whole-body FDG-PET–CT revealed intense uptake (SUV-max 11.4) in the calvarial and skull base lesions, the dural lesion at the torcula, multiple skeletal sites, a solitary pulmonary nodule, and scattered subcutaneous nodules.

A 19-year-old Japanese woman presented with a 3-month history of painless swelling and local warmth over the lateral aspect of her left ankle. She denied trauma, and the overlying skin showed no color change. Ankle range of motion was full and painless.  
Plain radiographs revealed only a 5 mm osteolytic lesion in the navicular bone. Laboratory tests, including C-reactive protein (0.2 mg/dL) and white blood cell count (4600/µL), were within normal limits.  
CT and MRI showed an ill-defined, heterogeneous subcutaneous mass (maximum diameter, 17 cm) anterior and lateral to the ankle, with low T1 signal, high T2 signal, and heterogeneous gadolinium enhancement. Bone and gallium scintigraphy demonstrated increased uptake in the left ankle. The lesion had enlarged slightly at follow-up.  
An incisional biopsy of a 5 mm tissue fragment demonstrated an inflammatory and edematous thickened tendon sheath with lymphocytes and plasma cells. The patient was treated with antibiotics for 4 weeks for presumed tenosynovitis, but the mass did not regress.

An 80-year-old man presented with a painless mass in the upper inner quadrant of his left breast, first noticed by the patient. He had hypertension but no history of breast injury or systemic disease. On examination, there was a nontender, hard, mobile mass with regular contours; no axillary lymphadenopathy or skin changes were present. Mammography showed a 3.0 × 2.0 cm well-defined, round, medium-density mass without calcifications, architectural distortion, or gynecomastia. Ultrasound demonstrated a well-defined homogeneous hypoechoic solid mass with no acoustic shadowing or increased through-transmission. On 1.5 Tesla dynamic contrast–enhanced MRI, the lesion was oval with circumscribed margins, hypointense on precontrast T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed early strong enhancement with nonenhancing internal septations. The lesion’s apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) value was 2.280 × 10⁻³ mm²/s. FDG-PET revealed a 12 mm nodular lesion with a hypodense center and low FDG uptake (SUV max, 1.2). An ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy was performed, but the results were inadequate to differentiate between invasive carcinoma and a benign lesion.

An 11-year-old premenarcheal girl presented with bilateral, rapidly increasing breast lumps over two months associated with a dull ache. There was no history of trauma, nipple discharge, fever, anorexia, weight loss, or significant family history. On examination, each breast harbored a solitary, mobile, slightly tender, lobulated mass; the right measured 22 × 20 cm with overlying skin ulceration, and the left 18 × 16 cm. No axillary lymphadenopathy was noted. Routine hematological and biochemical tests were within normal limits, and a chest radiograph was normal. Ultrasonography of both breasts showed a heterogeneous parenchymal pattern. Fine-needle aspiration cytology demonstrated aggregates of cohesive epithelial cells with a few bipolar and bare nuclei and no evidence of malignancy.

A 5-year-old boy presented with a one-year history of gradually progressive abdominal swelling, beginning in the epigastrium and eventually filling the entire abdomen. He reported loss of appetite and unquantified weight loss but denied vomiting, jaundice, abdominal pain, diarrhea, or bleeding. There was no significant past medical or family history. On examination, he had gross abdominal distension and low weight for age; other findings were normal. Complete blood count and liver function tests were within normal limits; serum sodium was 127.2 mmol/L. Tests for HBsAg and HCV antibodies were negative. Tumor markers (CEA, AFP, CA 19-9) were not available. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a large multiloculated anechoic mass lesion in the peritoneal cavity. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 26 cm × 23 cm × 18 cm multiloculated cystic mass with enhancing thick walls and septations, attached to the inferior surface of the left hepatic lobe, displacing bowel loops. Preoperatively, a mesenteric cyst was considered given the uncertain origin, and after CT review, hepatic mesenchymal hamartoma was entertained as the working diagnosis because of the patient’s age and imaging findings.

A 41-year-old man presented with a long-standing history of left plantar heel pain. Over two and a half years, he underwent extensive physiotherapy for presumed plantar fasciitis and tight gastrocnemius muscles, treatment with anti-inflammatory and analgesic medications, and two separate surgical releases (endoscopic plantar fascia release and minimally invasive gastrocnemius release) with only temporary relief. On re-presentation, he reported recurrent heel pain upon return to work.

On examination, he walked with an antalgic gait. The gastrocnemius remained tight with a positive Silfverskiöld test, and there was non-specific tenderness over the plantar aspect of the calcaneus at the insertion of the plantar fascia. 

Weight-bearing dorsoplantar and lateral radiographs of the foot demonstrated normal bony relationships with no fractures, lesions, or signs of arthritis. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left foot showed no thickening of the plantar fascia and no signal alteration in adjacent soft tissues or bone marrow. However, MRI revealed a pedunculated bony protrusion arising from the posterolateral plantar aspect of the calcaneus, measuring approximately 1.1 cm × 0.9 cm.

A 19-year-old man presented with mild left upper quadrant pain. He had no significant medical history, was a nonsmoker, and did not consume alcohol. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests were within normal limits except for an elevated alkaline phosphatase level of 210 U/L (normal range, 44–147 U/L). 

Abdominal ultrasound showed a 45 × 55 mm hypoechoic round mass anterior to the pancreatic tail and medial to the splenic hilum, with significant vascularity on color Doppler. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a retroperitoneal mass adjacent to the pancreatic tail that showed a similar enhancement pattern to the spleen in the arterial and portal phases. 

To assess the origin of the lesion, Tc99m–denatured red blood cell scan and octreotide scintigraphy were performed; neither study showed uptake in the mass. MRI with intravenous contrast revealed that the lesion had heterogeneous early arterial and portal enhancement comparable to the spleen, was hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and exhibited high diffusion signal on DWI and ADC sequences.

A 61-year-old Thai woman presented with a nontender mass in the left posterior thigh that had rapidly grown over 6 months. She reported pain when walking and slight limitation of left leg function. She had no significant medical history or prior surgeries. On examination, there was a firm, nonpulsatile mass over the left medial thigh measuring approximately 10 × 6 cm. The overlying skin was unremarkable, the mass was not fixed to bone, there was no sensory deficit, and no inguinal lymphadenopathy was palpable. A contrast-enhanced CT scan showed an 11 × 8 × 7 cm intramuscular, well-defined fatty lesion in the posteromedial thigh with thin streaks of fibrous tissue. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration suggested lipoma “but liposarcoma cannot be excluded.”

A 73-year-old woman with hypertension, peripheral arterial disease, asthma, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and diabetes mellitus presented with a five-year history of a slowly enlarging, nonpainful “nodule” behind her left ear. She denied discharge, dysphagia, or weight loss but reported decreased hearing, dry mouth, and hoarseness. She had a 20-pack-year smoking history. On examination, there was a fixed, nontender 2 cm mass in the left posterior auricular region; cranial nerves including the facial nerve were intact, and no cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. Flexible nasopharyngeal laryngoscopy showed arytenoid edema but normal vocal fold mobility. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a multilobulated, cystic-appearing mass within the left parotid gland with an infiltrative appearance and no pathologic lymphadenopathy. The initial differential diagnosis included benign mixed tumor (pleomorphic adenoma), Warthin’s tumor, epidermoid tumor, and adenoid cystic carcinoma. A fine-needle aspiration was nondiagnostic. The decision was made to perform a left superficial parotidectomy.

A 45-year-old man presented with one month of chest distress and palpitations. Physical examination was unremarkable. Enhanced computed tomography of the chest revealed a 4.2 × 3.4 cm heterogeneously enhancing mass in the anterior mediastinum attached to adjacent vessels. Serum tumor markers (CEA, CA19-9, β-hCG, and AFP) were within normal limits. Tracheoscopy showed no abnormalities. The patient underwent thoracoscopic resection of the mediastinal mass with part of the adjacent left lung.

Gross examination showed a firm nodular mass measuring 3.5 × 3.0 × 2.0 cm; the cut surface was grayish-white and yellow. Microscopic sections demonstrated an invasive, lobulated tumor separated by dense fibrous stroma with areas of hyalinization and multifocal necrosis. Tumor cells were polygonal to focally spindle-shaped with predominantly clear cytoplasm and small round to oval nuclei.

Immunohistochemical studies revealed diffuse positivity for AE1/AE3, CK18, and EMA; focal expression of CD10, PAX8, and vimentin; and a Ki-67 index of 30%. The tumor cells were negative for TTF-1, Napsin A, synaptophysin, CK19, PTH, TdT, HMB-45, Melan-A, PLAP, OCT3/4, SALL4, CD30, RCC marker, P63, P40, CD117, and CD5. Fluorescence in situ hybridization for EWSR1 translocation was negative.

A 26-year-old African American man with a history of depression and tuberculosis presented to the gastroenterology clinic with several months of rectal pain and occasional dark-red bleeding. He described the pain as right-sided, occurring about twice weekly during bowel movements and resolving afterward. He reported one bowel movement daily with variable consistency; hard or bulky stool exacerbated his pain. He also noted a slight increase in bowel movement frequency coinciding with the onset of pain and the appearance of dark-red blood in his stool. He denied abdominal pain, changes in appetite, weight loss, dysphagia, odynophagia, skin rashes, fever, or rigors. There was no family history of colon cancer or inflammatory bowel disease.

On examination, bowel sounds were normal; the abdomen was soft, nontender, and nondistended, with no hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. A rectal examination revealed a small external hemorrhoid but no fissures or masses. Fecal occult blood testing was negative with a positive control. The patient was scheduled for colonoscopy and started on zinc sulfate suppositories and fiber supplements for presumed hemorrhoids and constipation.

Colonoscopy with retroflexion revealed a solitary hyperpigmented lesion in the distal rectum and internal hemorrhoids.

A 12-year-old Caucasian boy presented with a four-week history of jaw pain that made eating difficult. He developed gingivitis and bleeding gums. One week before admission, he noted tailbone pain and had difficulty initiating urination, with retention symptoms and intermittent dysuria. His family reported a 15-lb weight loss over the prior month. He denied fever but had mild night sweats and low energy, missing a week of school. His past medical and family histories were noncontributory; immunizations were up to date.

On examination, there was symmetric swelling around the lower incisors with upward displacement of the teeth by almost 1.0 cm, and both teeth were loose; there was no purulent discharge. Facial and lower jaw swelling was present without palpable lymphadenopathy. Hepatosplenomegaly was noted, and bruises were seen on the knees, shins, forearms, and elbows, which were felt to be from baseball. The remainder of the examination was normal.

Laboratory studies showed platelets 33×10^9/L, WBC 15.9×10^9/L, hemoglobin 141 g/L, a left shift with a few circulating blasts on smear, slight elevations in liver enzymes and creatinine (87 μmol/L), lactate dehydrogenase >2500 U/L, and uric acid 1025 μmol/L.

A plain radiograph of the jaw demonstrated loss of alveolar bone adjacent to the roots of the lower first molars bilaterally with erosion of the distal roots, consistent with “floating teeth.” MRI of the brain, face/palate, and pelvis revealed multiple mandibular and maxillary lesions that were T2 hyperintense, T1 isointense to muscle, and homogeneously enhancing, with cortical erosion. Pelvic imaging showed a well-circumscribed 3×4×4 cm periurethral mass in the left prostate lobe (slightly T2 hyperintense with irregular central hypointense regions and faint postcontrast enhancement) and a 2 cm mass at the superior/posterior bladder with similar signal characteristics. Hepatosplenomegaly was again noted. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed multiple bilateral subcentimeter hypodense renal lesions, asymmetric prostatic enlargement with rightward urethral deviation, and an enlarged left internal mammary lymph node. A bone scan was normal.

An 11-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a suspicious lesion in the left distal ulna noted on routine radiographs. He reported hyperesthesia and increased sensitivity to pain in that region. Five years earlier, he had undergone incisional biopsy, curettage, autogenous bone grafting, and plate fixation for an aneurysmal bone cyst of the same site at another center.

On examination, there was hyperesthesia and tenderness along the ulnar aspect of the left forearm in the ulnar-nerve distribution. The distal ulna was deformed, with restricted pronation and supination. Plain radiographs demonstrated an eccentric, lytic lesion in the distal ulnar diaphysis. Given his surgical history, the differential included bone-graft lucency, recurrence of aneurysmal bone cyst, or delayed graft consolidation. Close radiographic monitoring was recommended.

One year later, follow-up radiographs revealed interval progression of the lytic lesion. Magnetic resonance imaging showed an expansile lesion involving the distal third of the ulna with a ground-glass matrix, areas of necrotic bone, and a fluid–fluid level. Although the imaging features suggested a benign process, malignancy could not be excluded, and biopsy was planned for definitive diagnosis.

A 79-year-old man was found to have an 80% asymptomatic stenosis of the right internal carotid artery on ultrasound and underwent a standard right carotid endarterectomy under general anesthesia. His history included well-controlled hypertension, hyperlipidemia, prior coronary and lower limb revascularization, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. Preoperative platelet count was 382×10^9/L, serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, fibrinogen 3.68 g/L, and D-dimer 3.66 mg/L FEU. Aspirin was held only on the day of surgery and resumed on postoperative day 1. The surgery and initial recovery were uneventful, with minimal wound drainage and systolic blood pressure maintained below 130 mmHg. 

On postoperative day 2, he developed low back pain, malaise, mild gingival bleeding, and a small neck hematoma with bloody drainage, followed by oral and nasal bleeding. Over the next 2 hours his oxygen saturation fell to 90% on room air, and the hematoma enlarged without tracheal deviation. He became agitated, and despite supplemental oxygen his saturation fell to 74%, with blood pressure 188/97 mmHg and heart rate 100 bpm, at which point he lost consciousness. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.7 mg/dL, platelets 163×10^9/L, prothrombin time 22.0 s, activated partial thromboplastin time 62.5 s, fibrinogen <0.4 g/L, and D-dimer 378.55 mg/L FEU, consistent with disseminated intravascular coagulation. He was intubated, given 1 g of human fibrinogen, and taken to the operating room for hematoma evacuation. Intraoperatively, a large volume of non-clotting blood was found without an obvious bleeding vessel, and he received packed red cells, platelets, fresh frozen plasma, fibrinogen, and prothrombin complex concentrate. His coagulation parameters normalized by the end of surgery, and he was transferred to the ICU.

A 50-year-old previously healthy woman presented with several months of daily headaches, blurry vision, progressive daytime somnolence, and memory difficulties. She reported sleeping 12 to 14 hours daily despite fatigue, a 40-pound weight gain, polydipsia with intake of 10 L of fluid per day, polyuria, nocturia, and a constant feeling of thirst. She had been amenorrheic for 5 years with no vaginal bleeding. She denied nausea, vomiting, heat or cold intolerance, and galactorrhea. Her medical history included hypertension treated with medication; there was no family history of endocrine disorders. On examination, she had bilateral peripheral visual field loss; the remainder of her neurological and general examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed panhypopituitarism: free thyroxine 0.52 ng/dL (normal 0.90–1.80), prolactin 42 ng/mL (2.8–29.0), luteinizing hormone <1 IU/L (postmenopausal 15.9–54.0), follicle-stimulating hormone 2.1 IU/L (23.0–116.3), insulin-like growth factor 38 ng/mL (100–250), and 4:00 p.m. cortisol <1.5 µg/dL (4.3–22.4). A contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain revealed a 25 × 22 × 20 mm intensely enhancing suprasellar mass involving the hypothalamus and optic chiasm, appearing separate from the pituitary gland. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast showed no evidence of neoplastic disease. Cerebral angiography demonstrated mild displacement of thalamic perforating arteries by the mass and minimal tumor vascularity. A preliminary differential diagnosis included metastatic lesion, central nervous system lymphoma, chordoma of the pituitary stalk, glioma, germinoma, sarcoidosis, and Langerhans cell histiocytosis.

A 29-year-old morbidly obese woman presented with a 6-month history of left anterior knee pain localized to the patellar region. She reported no systemic symptoms. Her past medical history was unremarkable. Physical examination of the knee revealed mild tenderness over the patella without swelling or joint effusion. Vital signs were within normal limits. A complete blood count and knee ultrasound were normal. Conventional radiographs of the knee showed no abnormalities. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left knee identified an 8 mm well-defined round lesion in the superior aspect of the patella with an edematous-type signal: hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on fat-saturated sequences. At that time, the differential diagnoses were chondroblastoma and osteoblastoma, which may overlap in their radiological appearance.

A 49-year-old woman was transferred to our emergency department for evaluation of a suspected malignant brain tumor. One week earlier, she had experienced a generalized tonic–clonic seizure. Her primary complaint was visual-field disturbance. On examination, she had a right homonymous hemianopsia and papilledema.  
Brain CT showed a 4.0-cm, iso-dense intra-axial ovoid mass in the left temporo-occipital region.  
On T2-weighted MRI, the mass contained an internal cystic component, abutted the choroid plexus, and appeared to invade the trigone of the lateral ventricle. Gadolinium enhancement demonstrated homogeneous enhancement of the solid portion, suggesting a high-grade glioma or metastatic tumor.  
The radiologist recommended MR spectroscopy and a metastasis work-up.

A 58-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of abdominal pain, vomiting, and 70-pound weight loss. A nasogastric tube was placed for presumed obstruction. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy with endoscopic ultrasonography revealed a 2-cm duodenal mass. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed multiple masses in the small bowel, bilateral adrenal glands, cervical lymph nodes, lungs, liver, and retroperitoneum, consistent with metastatic disease. Biopsy of the duodenal mass demonstrated tumor cells that were positive for vimentin and caldesmon and negative for chromogranin, synaptophysin, S100, Melan A, Sox10, inhibin, desmin, CD45, c-kit, and DOG1.

A 25-year-old woman presented with a 4-year history of a gradually enlarging right gluteal swelling associated with deep lower abdominal and pelvic pain, constipation, and increased urinary frequency. She reported difficulty ambulating and sitting. On examination, there was a 15 cm × 15 cm firm, non-tender mass in the right gluteal area displacing the perineal body contralaterally. Abdominal examination revealed a poorly defined abdomino-pelvic mass extending to the level of the umbilicus. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin of 9.8 mg/dl; liver and renal function tests were normal. Serum alpha-fetoprotein, human chorionic gonadotropin, and carcinoembryonic antigen levels were within normal limits. Pelvic MRI revealed a 35 cm × 25 cm × 20 cm multiseptated cystic and solid sacrococcygeal mass involving the perineal area and remodeling the coccyx, with superior displacement of the vagina, uterus, and bladder. Based on these findings, the differential diagnoses of teratoma, fibrosarcoma, and neurofibroma were considered.

A 63-year-old man presented with urinary retention. Ultrasonography revealed a cystic mass surrounding the prostate and bladder. His serum prostate-specific antigen level was 11.71 ng/mL, and a transrectal ultrasound–guided biopsy showed prostate adenocarcinoma (Gleason score 3 + 3). Pelvic MRI demonstrated:  
• A 30 × 40 × 33 mm multilocular cyst projecting into the bladder from the inner prostate gland, with high signal intensity on fat-suppressed T1-weighted images consistent with hemorrhage, and high signal intensity with shading on T2-weighted imaging.  
• A 22 × 22 × 20 mm multilocular cyst between the prostate and right seminal vesicle showing similar hemorrhagic T1-hyperintensity and T2-hyperintensity.  
• The inner prostate gland with high T2 signal and tiny hyperintense spots on fat-suppressed T1-weighted images.  
• At the margin of the hemorrhagic multilocular cysts, a solid portion with mildly low T1 signal and markedly restricted diffusion (low signal on ADC and high signal on diffusion-weighted imaging) was observed, suggesting a focal prostate malignancy.

A 59-year-old woman presented with a 10-year history of a progressively enlarging forehead mass. The lesion was painless, hard, immobile, nonpulsatile, and non-tender; the overlying skin was normal. She denied any history of head trauma and had no neurological symptoms. On examination, vital signs were normal.  

A skull radiograph revealed a radiolucent osteolytic lesion involving the left frontal bone. Noncontrast cranial CT showed a 3.1 × 1.7 × 3.6-cm lesion situated between the outer and inner tables of the left frontal bone, exhibiting a “sunburst” trabecular pattern and causing expansion of the outer table with preservation of the inner table; the lesion lay superior and lateral to the left frontal sinus.

An 18-year-old Dravidian woman presented with a 3–4-month history of right submandibular swelling. Examination revealed a firm, non-tender 3 cm × 3 cm mass in the right submandibular region. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed a minimally enhancing hypodense lesion measuring 4.5 cm × 3.7 cm × 2.6 cm within the right submandibular gland, surrounded by an enhancing rim of normal gland tissue, with no other lesions in the head and neck. Fine-needle aspiration cytology yielded moderately cellular smears of polygonal to spindle-shaped cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, arranged in loose clusters and sheets with occasional whorling; nuclei were round to ovoid with finely granular chromatin, and a few cells showed intranuclear cytoplasmic inclusions. Based on these findings, the lesion was interpreted as a neoplastic submandibular gland tumor suggestive of oncocytoma, although primary ectopic meningioma was also considered.

A 48-year-old man with no significant medical or family history presented with a 4-month history of a painless lump on the right anterior chest wall. He reported no fever or weight loss. On examination, there was a soft, tender mass over the right first rib without overlying skin changes or regional lymphadenopathy. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed a tissue mass centered on the right first rib with a large area of osteolysis, without invasion of the chest wall, intrinsic calcification, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, or intrapulmonary lesions. There were no features of cartilaginous calcification.

A 76-year-old man was referred to otolaryngology with right-sided nasal obstruction and rhinorrhea. His medical history included hypertension, angina, and benign prostatic hypertrophy. Examination revealed a polypoidal mass on the right inferior turbinate and deviation of the nasal septum to the right. A nonenhanced CT scan of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated a 15-mm rounded soft-tissue lesion arising from the right inferior turbinate, thinning the medial wall of the right maxillary antrum and slightly bulging into the sinus. Clinically, a benign nasal tumor—most likely an inverted papilloma—was diagnosed. Because the lesion did not appear suspicious for malignancy, no preoperative MRI was obtained.

A 62-year-old man with type-2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuritis, and Cushing’s disease secondary to pituitary adenoma resection presented after two episodes of left‐leg deep vein thrombosis. At the time of the second event, a soft‐tissue mass was noted in his left thigh. On examination, there was an approximately 6 cm mobile, irregular, firm mass in the medial left thigh without inguinal adenopathy or organomegaly. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a lobular 6.3 × 5.4 × 3.4 cm mass in the medial subcutaneous fat of the proximal to mid left thigh that was slightly hyperintense to muscle, showed homogeneous enhancement with a small hypoenhancing area suggestive of necrosis, displaced the underlying musculature posterolaterally, and appeared to extend to the skin. The imaging differential diagnosis included synovial sarcoma, malignant fibrous histiocytoma, dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, and nerve sheath tumor with malignant degeneration. 

An ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy and concurrent core needle biopsy of the mass were performed. The FNA smears demonstrated numerous discohesive atypical round to polygonal to spindled cells with pleomorphic nuclei; scattered cells showed abundant cytoplasm, multinucleation, and prominent nucleoli; a few cells had wreath-like nuclei; and mitotic figures were present. Inflammatory cells and lymphoglandular bodies were absent. On the FNA, a high-grade sarcoma with a differential diagnosis of rhabdomyosarcoma and malignant fibrous histiocytoma was favored, and other considerations included metastatic poorly differentiated carcinoma, melanoma, and high-grade non-Hodgkin lymphoma including anaplastic lymphoma. 

The core needle biopsy revealed dense connective tissue infiltrated by large cells with amphophilic cytoplasm and single, bi-, and multinucleation; several horseshoe-shaped nuclei were noted, and numerous mitotic figures were present, similar to the FNA cell block.

A 49-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of a rapidly enlarging, painful mass in the right breast. She had no history of trauma, and her medical and family histories were unremarkable aside from an ovarian cystectomy 15 years earlier. On examination, there was a firm, painful mass in the medial half of the right breast, with additional tender nodular formations near the areola and in the right axilla. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies showed an elevated C-reactive protein, with all other values normal.  
Breast ultrasonography revealed a 14-cm hypoechoic, lobulated mass with heterogeneous content in the medial right breast, an adjacent nodular lesion near the areola, and two enlarged right axillary lymph nodes. Pleural ultrasonography showed mild bilateral pleural effusions. Abdominal ultrasonography was normal.  
Chest computed tomography demonstrated a high-density right breast mass infiltrating the chest wall and a separate metastatic lesion in the right lung. Abdominal and pelvic CT scans were unremarkable.  
What is your differential diagnosis?

A 64-year-old man was referred for evaluation of early transverse colon cancer. His medical history included hypertension, gout, prostate enlargement, and untreated hepatitis B virus infection; there was no relevant family history. Initial laboratory tests showed mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL), a leukocyte count of 6100/mL, a platelet count of 35 × 10^9/L, and a C-reactive protein level of 4.4 mg/dL; carcinoembryonic antigen and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels were normal, and peripheral blood smear findings were unremarkable. Rapid plasma reagin, Treponema pallidum hemagglutination, and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption tests were positive. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed multiple nodules in the lungs, bone, mediastinum, and subcutaneous tissue, along with thickening of the aortic arch wall and occlusion of the left subclavian artery; multiple metastases from colon cancer were considered unlikely given the early stage. Further serologic testing showed a positive proteinase 3 anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody test; antinuclear, anti–double-stranded DNA, and anticardiolipin antibodies and rheumatoid factor were negative, and soluble interleukin-2 receptor and immunoglobulin G4 levels were within normal limits. Systemic vasculitis due to syphilis was suspected, and the patient received a three-week course of ceftriaxone. A subsequent lung biopsy showed no evidence of vasculitis, and renal biopsy revealed focal and segmental lesions without evidence of anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody–associated glomerulonephritis. One week after completing antibiotic therapy, PET–CT demonstrated multiple areas of increased uptake throughout the lungs, mediastinum, bone, soft tissues, and intestinal tract.

A 50-year-old man presented with a 5-month history of a painful, progressively enlarging mass over the ulnar border of his left wrist. He denied any antecedent trauma. On examination, there was painful restriction of wrist motion and an ill-defined, immobile, tender, hard mass measuring 5 × 3 cm.  

A plain radiograph of the forearm and wrist showed an ill-defined permeative lytic lesion with cortical thinning involving the distal ulna.  

Magnetic resonance imaging of the wrist and forearm demonstrated an ill-defined, lobulated soft-tissue lesion at the dorsoulnar aspect of the distal forearm adjacent to the carpus, with extension through the medial and lateral cortices of the distal ulna and abutment of the ulnar neurovascular bundle.  

Positron emission tomography–computed tomography revealed an FDG-avid lesion confined to the distal forearm and ulna, with no other sites of uptake.  

Core needle biopsy and fine-needle aspiration cytology showed a spindle cell tumor with an intersecting fascicular pattern, focal prominent nuclear pleomorphism, and necrosis, suggestive of a spindle cell sarcoma.

A 71-year-old man with a history of stomach disease presented with dull epigastric pain for 1 month that sometimes spread to his left chest and back. He denied cough, cyanosis, or syncope. He self-medicated with proton-pump inhibitors and antispasmodics without relief. On admission, vital signs were normal and the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies—including hematology, biochemistry, immunology, coagulation, and urinalysis—were within normal limits. Electrocardiography and chest radiography showed no abnormalities. Abdominal ultrasonography was normal. 

Incidentally, transthoracic echocardiography revealed a 1.3×1.7×1.4 cm isoechoic mass attached by a narrow base to the right ventricular free wall, changing shape with cardiac contraction; cardiac function was preserved and there was no pericardial effusion. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest and abdomen in arterial and portal venous phases did not demonstrate the mass. 

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium showed a 17×14×13 mm mass on the right ventricular wall with regular margins. The lesion was isointense or slightly hypointense relative to myocardium on T1- and T2-weighted images, hyperintense on STIR images, and demonstrated early perfusion enhancement followed by more intense late (equilibrium) enhancement compared with normal myocardium. These images suggested a benign tumor (myxoma, papillary fibroelastoma, hemangioma) that should be followed up.

A 60-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of progressive headache and an enlarging scalp mass over the left temporal region. Five years earlier, he had undergone surgical resection of a left adrenal pheochromocytoma that had manifested with paroxysmal hypertension. His medical history also included gout. There was no family history of von Hippel–Lindau syndrome, multiple endocrine neoplasia, or neurofibromatosis.

On examination, blood pressure was 138/86 mmHg and heart rate 83 beats/min. A hard, fixed mass measuring 6.0 × 4.0 × 2.0 cm was palpable in the left temporal scalp; the remainder of the neurologic and physical examinations was unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies revealed normal 24-hour urinary vanillylmandelic acid and metanephrine levels. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the head showed a well-defined biconvex epidural mass (6.0 × 4.0 × 3.4 cm) compressing the left temporal lobe, extending both extracranially and intracranially. The lesion was mixed hypo- and hyperintense on T1- and T2-weighted images and demonstrated homogeneous enhancement with a dural tail after gadolinium administration. Cranial CT demonstrated multiple lytic lesions in the left temporal bone. Abdominal CT was unremarkable.

Based on these findings, the preliminary differential diagnosis included malignant meningioma, skull neoplasm, and even rare malignant pheochromocytoma.

A 51-year-old man presented with progressive abdominal pain. Physical examination was notable for a palpable pelvic fullness without peritoneal signs. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed an 18×17×12 cm lobulated mass in the mesogastric and hypogastric regions extending into the pelvis anterior to the rectum, arising near the level of the renal hilum. The lesion had a mixed appearance, with a solid component showing strong contrast enhancement and multiple pseudocystic areas. The radiologist’s impression was leiomyosarcoma. The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy, which confirmed a large retroperitoneal tumor extending to the pelvic and rectal tissues. The ureters were dissected free, vascular structures were preserved, and the mass was completely excised. A Hartmann procedure was performed due to concern about rectal vascularization. Metal clips were placed at the presumed stalk for potential postoperative radiotherapy, and a drain was left in the pouch of Douglas. The immediate postoperative course was uneventful.

A 28-year-old woman presented with a three-month history of a swelling in the left upper abdomen associated with local, non-radiating pain. Her performance status was ECOG 1. On examination, there was a 4×4 cm ill-defined, globular, smooth-surfaced swelling with cystic consistency and mild tenderness in the left hypochondrium. 

Ultrasonography revealed a hypoechoic lesion of approximately 1.5 cm in the abdominal wall at the left periumbilical location, with no intra-abdominal extension. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 19×15 mm ill-defined enhancing mass in the ventral abdominal wall deep to the muscle planes, with possible invasion of the peritoneal layer and no organ involvement. MRI demonstrated a 19×18 mm hyperintense nodular lesion in the left anterior abdominal wall posterior to the muscle layer and anterior to the parietal layer, with surrounding inflammatory edema.

Fine-needle aspiration cytology from the lesion showed loose clusters of spindled to stellate cells, numerous multinucleated giant cells, and histiocytic cells in a hemorrhagic background. A cytological diagnosis was rendered as a low-grade spindle cell neoplasm suggestive of fibrous histiocytoma.

A 72-year-old gravida 10, para 10 woman with hypertension was referred for evaluation of a pelvic mass of 2 months’ duration and progressive dyspnea. On examination, she had a palpable lower abdominal mass; the uterus was of normal size, and there was no lymphadenopathy. Chest radiography and CT scan showed a massive right pleural effusion. Pleural fluid cytology revealed inflammatory cells without malignant changes; cultures and tuberculosis smears were negative.
