Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a 53-mm multilocular cystic-solid mass of the right ovary with 6.8-mm septa and a 19-mm mural nodule; the right ovarian artery had a low-resistance flow pattern (RI = 0.61). Free intraperitoneal fluid was noted. Abdominopelvic CT with contrast revealed a 95 × 120 mm multicystic pelvic mass with irregular calcified mural nodules. Serum tumor markers were: CA125 607.4 U/ml, CA19-9 62.72 U/ml, CEA 1.92 ng/ml, and inhibin A < 0.1.

A 12-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of pain in the maxillary left central incisor and the mandibular left lateral incisor. She had a two-year history of untreated Ellis class II trauma and grade II mobility of these teeth. On examination, there was an 8-mm enlargement of the soft tissue on the left posterior hard palate. The mass was firm, painless, and non-tender, located near teeth 24 and 27, with normal overlying mucosa; the median palatal raphe was intact. She denied any symptoms related to this palatal lesion. Adjacent teeth exhibited no mobility or displacement, and they responded normally to electrical pulp testing. Panoramic and periapical radiographs showed no alveolar bone resorption and an intact maxillary sinus floor. Axial CT imaging revealed a moderately enhancing soft-tissue density lesion extending posteriorly and inferiorly, with destruction of the hard palate and alveolar process. No submandibular or cervical lymphadenopathy was palpable. Fine-needle aspiration of the lesion yielded no fluid.

A 7-year-old boy with Ebstein’s anomaly and negative pretransplant EBV serology underwent orthotopic heart transplantation and received mycophenolate mofetil induction, then tacrolimus and sirolimus maintenance. Four months posttransplant, he was admitted with fever and odynophagia; streptococcal pharyngitis and EBV viremia (7270 IU/mL) were documented. Neck CT with contrast showed enlargement and striated enhancement of the palatine tonsils and enlarged cervical lymph nodes with central hypoenhancement. He received IV antibiotics, defervesced, and was discharged without change in immunosuppression. Two weeks later, he returned with fever, stertorous breathing, and an increased EBV load (9810 IU/mL). Nasolaryngoscopy revealed adenotonsillar hypertrophy; CT showed interval decrease in adenotonsillar and nodal enlargement, so immunosuppression was reduced to tacrolimus monotherapy. Four days later, he was readmitted with lethargy, odynophagia, and markedly elevated EBV load (284 000 IU/mL). Neck CT showed increased adenotonsillar enlargement and diffuse cervical adenopathy. He underwent adenotonsillectomy and cervical lymph node excision; biopsy showed polymorphic posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorder. He received four weeks of rituximab infusions while continuing tacrolimus monotherapy. Two weeks into rituximab, he developed fevers, odynophagia, and emesis. CT demonstrated new heterogeneous hypopharyngeal enhancement; direct laryngoscopy showed sloughing debris and plaques in the interarytenoid region. Biopsy revealed necrosis and scattered EBV-positive B cells of uncertain significance, and he was treated for presumed infectious laryngitis. Two months later, he was readmitted with fever, diarrhea, weight loss, and CT showed a heterogeneous supraglottic mass narrowing the airway, pulmonary nodules, and intestinal wall thickening. Endoscopic biopsies of the hypopharynx, supraglottis, stomach, and small bowel revealed monomorphic EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. One month later, in the setting of altered mental status, brain MRI showed paranasal sinus lesions extending intracranially into the inferior frontal lobes. Coronal CT sinus imaging showed diffuse opacification of the maxillary and ethmoid sinuses with erosion of the ethmoid septations and cribriform plates.

A 77-year-old woman with hypertension, acquired hypothyroidism (post-radioiodine for Graves’ disease), and prior hysterectomy was referred for evaluation of an incidental right pelvic mass discovered during workup for recurrent urinary tract infections. Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis showed a 9.2 × 9.6 × 10.8 cm heterogeneous mass in the right hemipelvis, likely ovarian in origin; there was no lymphadenopathy and only small, non-metastatic pulmonary nodules. Serum tumor markers were within normal limits (CA 125, 14 U/mL; CEA, 2.4 ng/mL). Eleven days after consultation, the patient underwent surgical exploration. A friable, fleshy, >10 cm right ovarian mass densely adhered to the pelvic sidewall was noted, with no gross evidence of metastatic disease. A frozen-section diagnosis was rendered as either a sex cord–stromal tumor or an epithelial ovarian neoplasm, and bilateral pelvic and para-aortic lymph node dissections were performed.

A 19-year-old man presented with extensive bilateral cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy. He had no prior medical history, skin lesions, or other physical findings. A CT scan showed multiple matted lymph nodes in the cervical, supraclavicular, mediastinal, axillary, abdominal, pelvic, and inguinal regions; nasopharyngeal fullness with enlarged palatine and lingual tonsils; thyroid enlargement; and hepatomegaly (liver span 18 cm). The spleen was at the upper limit of normal size. A PET scan confirmed extensive hypermetabolic lymphomatous masses in these areas.

Laboratory tests revealed a hemoglobin of 13.7 g/dL, a leukocyte count of 2.2 × 10^9/L, and a platelet count of 286 × 10^9/L. The peripheral smear showed a leukoerythroblastic reaction with approximately 3% blasts; cerebrospinal fluid was free of blasts.

A cervical lymph-node biopsy demonstrated medium-to-large malignant cells positive for CD3 (partial), CD7, TdT, CD2, CD43, and bcl-2, and negative for CD4, CD8, CD5, CD20, Pax5, CD79a, bcl-6, MPO, and other B-cell and myeloid markers.

Staging bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy showed 47% intermediate-to-large mononuclear blasts with nuclear indentations and granulocytic dysplasia. Flow cytometry on bone marrow revealed a blast population expressing dim CD45, HLA-DR, CD16/56, CD2, CD7, CD34, and CD38; a subpopulation expressed cytoplasmic CD3 (20%) and CD117 (10%); and blasts were negative for B-cell and myeloid markers and CD4, CD5, and CD8. PCR analysis showed germline configuration of IgH and TCR genes.

A 50‐year‐old woman presented with a 20-month history of right‐sided neck swelling. The mass was gradual in onset, progressively enlarging, painless, and produced mild discomfort on swallowing. There were no ear, nose, respiratory, or neurologic complaints. 

Vital signs were normal. General physical and neurologic examinations were unremarkable. On local examination, there was a pinkish, shiny, ovoid, firm‐to‐hard, nonpulsatile mass measuring approximately 5 × 4 cm in the right parapharyngeal region with posterolateral attachment, crossing the midline medially.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a well-defined hypodense mass (7.5 × 5.6 × 2.6 cm) in the right parapharyngeal space, showing mild heterogeneous enhancement. The mass displaced the right internal and external carotid arteries anteriorly, reached superiorly to the skull base, distorted the oropharynx medially, and abutted adjacent muscular and bony structures. 

CT angiography demonstrated a heterogeneously enhancing soft-tissue mass (4.5 × 5.1 × 6.7 cm) in the right parapharyngeal space, displacing the internal carotid artery anteriorly and the internal jugular vein posterolaterally.

MRI of the neck showed a well-defined soft-tissue mass in the right carotid space (3.5 × 5.6 × 5.7 cm) lying posterior to the carotid bifurcation with anterior displacement of the carotid vessels and mild compression of the internal jugular vein. The mass effaced the parapharyngeal space and indented the oropharynx. It was hypointense on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted/STIR images, with some internal hypointense components resembling the target sign. Postcontrast sequences demonstrated strong heterogeneous enhancement. No extension into neural foramina was observed.

A 55-year-old woman with no prior major illnesses presented with a 2-year history of a painless, elastic soft-tissue mass in the right arm that had gradually increased in size to 5.0 × 4.5 × 2.5 cm. She had no systemic symptoms. On examination, there was no axillary lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Routine laboratory investigations were unremarkable. Radiographs of the arm showed a mild periosteal reaction of the underlying bone. Ultrasonography suggested a primary hypervascular soft-tissue tumor. Fine-needle aspiration cytology yielded highly cellular smears showing a polymorphous population of predominantly small lymphocytes and a few tingible-body macrophages. Scattered large oval cells with pale cytoplasm, fine chromatin, and inconspicuous nucleoli were seen. There was prominent vascularity with capillaries; no epithelioid cells, giant cells, or necrosis were identified. Few immunoblasts and few plasma cells were present. The cytological interpretation was reactive lymphoid hyperplasia with additional findings of capillaries among germinal center cells, raising the possibility of Castleman’s disease.

A 34-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 3-month history of a gradually enlarging right inguinal swelling that was not associated with pain. She denied fever, weight loss, or other swellings. Her medical history was unremarkable. On examination, vital signs were normal. Laboratory tests and an abdominal radiograph were within normal limits. Abdominal examination revealed a 6 cm × 6 cm non-tender, non-reducible mass in the right inguinal region. An attempt at reduction was unsuccessful, and a provisional diagnosis of incarcerated inguinal hernia was made. The patient was taken to the operating room for surgical management.

A 35-year-old man presented for routine follow‐up 11 years after a left total hip arthroplasty with a ceramic‐on‐ceramic articulation. Over the preceding 3 months, he had left buttock and greater trochanteric pain, initially attributed to overuse. He denied fevers or systemic symptoms. On examination, range of motion of the left hip was full and painless; there was focal tenderness over the posterior buttock and greater trochanter but no palpable mass. Anteroposterior radiographs of the pelvis and left hip were unchanged compared with images obtained 1 year earlier. A diagnosis of greater trochanteric bursitis was made, and an intra‐bursal corticosteroid injection was administered, resulting in partial symptom relief.

Six weeks later, he returned with persistent buttock pain and intermittent electric shock–like sensations radiating down the left leg. Physical examination now revealed decreased and painful range of motion of the left hip with continued tenderness over the greater trochanter. A lumbar spine radiograph was normal. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 22 mm/h (reference range, 2–28), a C‐reactive protein level of 14.4 mg/L (reference, <10.0), and an alkaline phosphatase level of 318 IU/L (reference, 40–125). Hip aspiration yielded 10,750 white cells/μL; all cultures were negative. Serum cobalt and chromium levels were within normal limits. A metal artifact reduction sequence MRI revealed a left periprosthetic soft‐tissue mass measuring 9 × 8 × 10 cm, without bony involvement or bone‐marrow edema.

A 62-year-old woman presented with a two-month history of a right temporal fossa swelling. The lesion was initially painless but rapidly increased in size, eventually causing temporal pain radiating to the ipsilateral eye. On examination, there was a firm, non-mobile, erythematous 4-cm mass in the right temporal region; no cervical lymphadenopathy was noted and the rest of the head and neck examination was unremarkable. Non-contrast CT of the facial bones demonstrated a 3.2×2×1-cm subcutaneous mass of intermediate density in the right lateral orbital region with moderate adjacent fat-plane swelling. Subsequent brain MRI with gadolinium revealed a subcutaneous encapsulated right temporal lesion that was isointense on T1, hypointense on T2, hyperintense on diffusion imaging, and showed peripheral (rim) enhancement with internal septations.

A 44-year-old man noted swelling of the left parotid region, with associated left cervical lymphadenopathy. Nine years after initial onset, MRI revealed a 40 × 42 × 70 mm irregular mass in the left parotid gland, with low intensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images. Clinical staging was cT4aN2bM0, and a total parotidectomy was performed. On gross examination, the specimen contained an ill-defined gray-white mass with a discrete whitish, elastic-hard nodule in its center. 

Microscopic examination showed that the central nodule consisted of hyalinized stroma with spindle-shaped myoepithelial cells embedded in myxoid stroma, consistent with residual pleomorphic adenoma. At the periphery of this nodule, atypical ductal epithelial cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm formed irregular glands within a retained myoepithelial layer. Surrounding the nodule and in the invasive front, there was a diffuse proliferation of noncohesive ovoid cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm, eccentric nuclei, marked nuclear atypia, and prominent nucleoli. Similar rhabdoid-appearing cells were also present in multiple metastatic lymph nodes.

A 49-year-old woman presented with a 7-year history of multiple masses in her right palm and wrist and 6 months of progressive numbness in the thumb, index, and middle fingers. She recalled an injection over the wrist crease 7 years ago but did not know its contents. On examination, there was a 2 × 3 cm mass in the thenar area and a 3 × 4 cm mass proximal to the radiocarpal joint. Sensation was decreased in the median nerve distribution, and Tinel’s sign over the carpal tunnel was positive; thenar muscle bulk was preserved. Plain radiographs showed no bony abnormalities or calcifications. Nerve conduction studies were consistent with moderate carpal tunnel syndrome. MRI of the forearm and hand revealed fusiform enlargement of the median nerve extending from the distal forearm into the palm. On axial T1-weighted images, low-intensity nerve fascicles were surrounded by high-intensity fat, producing a “coaxial cable-like” appearance; on coronal and sagittal sequences, the nerve bundles appeared “spaghetti-like” within adipose tissue.

A 64-year-old man presented with an 18-month history of a scar-like lesion on the volar pulp of the left fifth digit. Over the past three months, the lesion enlarged rapidly, became occasionally painful, and darkened in color. He denied weight loss, anorexia, or fatigue. Physical examination revealed a healthy-appearing man with a 1 cm, mobile, nontender, darkish, round, firm mass on the distal volar surface of the left fifth digit. Vital signs were: temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 162/98 mmHg, pulse 78 beats/min. Laboratory studies showed a random blood sugar of 9 g/dL, hemoglobin 10 g/dL, a normal white-cell count with differential, body-mass index 28.6 kg/m2, and creatinine 24.1 mmol/L. An incisional biopsy of the lesion revealed infiltrating, hyperchromatic glandular structures with micropapillary formations within the dermis; the overlying skin was intact. These histomorphological features were highly suggestive of metastatic papillary adenocarcinoma, possibly originating from the breast, colon, or thyroid. A search for a primary tumor included thyroid-function tests and serum markers (CEA, CA-19-9, CA-125), all within normal limits; esophagogastroduodenoscopy, colonoscopy, and ultrasound of the neck were unremarkable; and thoracoabdominal CT scan did not reveal a primary lesion.

A 47-year-old previously healthy woman presented with a 4-month history of fever, anorexia, and 10% weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies revealed normocytic anemia, thrombocytopenia (35 000/μL), elevated C-reactive protein (23.6 mg/dL), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (110 mm/h), hypertriglyceridemia (546 mg/dL), and marked hyperferritinemia. A CT scan showed only mild homogeneous splenomegaly. Extensive infectious, serologic, and autoantibody testing, cardiac ultrasound, upper and lower endoscopy, and bronchoscopy were normal. Bone marrow biopsy demonstrated normocellular marrow without morphologic abnormalities. Liver and transbronchial lung biopsies showed reactive inflammation. A spleen biopsy revealed extensive histiocytosis with erythrophagocytosis. Soluble CD25 level was 7460 U/mL, fulfilling seven of eight HLH diagnostic criteria; neuron-specific enolase was elevated at 92.7 µg/L. Four weeks after admission, she had a complex partial seizure with rightward conjugate eye deviation and left hemiparesis. Brain MRI showed a right temporal subcortical hyperintense lesion on T2-FLAIR without diffusion restriction or enhancement, plus small bilateral supratentorial T2 lesions. Cerebrospinal fluid contained six lymphocytes; bacterial, viral, and anti-neuronal studies were negative. She received levetiracetam, a 5-day course of IV methylprednisolone, and IV immunoglobulin, with marked radiographic improvement. Persistent cytopenias and HLH markers prompted initiation of the HLH-94 protocol (dexamethasone and etoposide), resulting in normalization of ferritin levels and complete symptomatic remission. She was discharged after 6 weeks.

A six-month-old girl was brought for evaluation of one month of progressive abdominal distension and pain. Her weight was 5.5 kg. On examination, her abdomen was markedly distended; palpation revealed a firm, tender, irregular mass occupying the entire left lumbar and pelvic regions that moved with respiration. Liver and renal function tests and complete blood counts were all within normal limits. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a left pelvic kidney measuring 18 cm in diameter with marked dilation of the collecting system and mixed internal cystic and solid components. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen confirmed a mass arising from the left kidney containing low-density areas; the right kidney was normal, and no other masses were identified. Given that congenital mesoblastic nephroma is the most frequent neonatal renal tumor and that ectopic kidneys have a heightened risk for Wilms’ tumor, the leading preoperative considerations were congenital mesoblastic nephroma versus Wilms’ tumor arising in an ectopic kidney. The patient was taken for exploratory laparotomy and left renal mass excision. After an uneventful postoperative course, the specimen was sent for histopathological examination.

A 61-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of intermittent left lower back pain that progressed to involve the left lower abdomen. He noted abdominal distension but denied diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, or fever. There was no history of abdominal trauma, prior surgery, or significant weight change. His medical history was unremarkable, and he was taking no medications. Family history was notable only for a mother who died of stomach cancer, not felt to be hereditary.

On physical examination, vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination revealed mild tenderness in the left lower quadrant without rigidity or rebound. A soft, mobile, well-defined mass approximately 10 cm in diameter was palpable in the left lower abdomen. Routine blood counts, biochemical tests, and tumor markers were all within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen demonstrated a large, well-circumscribed, cystic mass occupying the left peritoneal cavity. The lesion could not be definitively characterized on imaging and was thought to represent one of several space-occupying lesions, requiring surgical excision and pathological examination for a definitive diagnosis. The clinical differential diagnosis included mesenteric cyst, lymphangioma, enteric duplication cyst, omental cyst, and stromal cell tumor.

A 12-year-old girl presented with progressive hirsutism, deepening of the voice, increased muscle strength, and absence of breast development. Pubic hair first appeared at age 6 years. On examination, she was normotensive with marked hirsutism, mild facial acne, Tanner stage 2 breast development, Tanner stage 4 pubic hair, and clitoromegaly. Bone age was 15 years. Initial laboratory testing by chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry showed 17-hydroxyprogesterone 976 ng/dL (reference <80–285), testosterone 172 ng/dL (<7–75), and androstenedione 670 ng/dL (80–190); values for ACTH, 11-deoxycortisol, and DHEA-S were within normal limits. Pelvic ultrasound demonstrated normal-appearing ovaries (right 3.2×1.0×1.0 cm; left 3.0×1.4×1.1 cm) and uterus with numerous peripheral follicles. Hydrocortisone was started at 16 mg/m2/day for presumed nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia and increased to 26 mg/m2/day, yet symptoms persisted and 17-OHP paradoxically rose. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen and pelvis were unremarkable. CYP21A2 gene analysis revealed no disease-causing mutations.

A 50-year-old woman presented with a 4-year history of right knee swelling that had gradually increased over the past year. The swelling fluctuated in size, and was associated with mild pain not limiting daily activities. She denied fever, night pain, weight loss, bleeding tendencies, or trauma. Previous treatments included medications, physiotherapy, knee aspiration, and intra-articular kenacort injections.
On examination, there was massive joint swelling of the right knee with painful, restricted terminal range of motion. There were no signs of inflammation. Meniscal, collateral ligament, and cruciate ligament tests were negative.
Plain radiographs of the knee showed early osteoarthritic changes and a dense soft-tissue opacity in the suprapatellar region. Laboratory studies revealed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 66 mm/hr and a C-reactive protein level of 23 mg/dl; anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, serum uric acid, and coagulation studies were within normal limits.
Magnetic resonance imaging of the knee demonstrated a large effusion distending the suprapatellar and infrapatellar regions, frond-like fatty areas in the peri-condylar recess and joint cavity, synovial thickening and hypertrophy, and associated medial compartment degeneration.

A 35-year-old Thai woman presented with a 5-year history of pain and swelling over the dorsum of her left foot, worsening over the past month despite medication. The pain was aggravated by walking or standing, particularly over long distances. On musculoskeletal examination, there was mild swelling and a tender, firm mass over the 2nd and 3rd metatarsal bones. Vascular, neurologic, and dermatologic examinations of the lower extremity were normal.  
Plain radiographs of the foot showed bone destruction at the bases of the 2nd and 3rd metatarsals and cuneiforms, surrounded by soft-tissue calcifications and phleboliths.  
Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 4×3×3 cm lobulated mass in the midfoot involving the middle and lateral cuneiforms and bases of the 2nd and 3rd metatarsal bones, with tortuous blood vessels and dark foci characteristic of phleboliths. The lesion was bright on T2-weighted images and enhanced in parallel with blood vessels on postcontrast imaging, with insinuation into surrounding muscle.  
Routine laboratory tests were normal.

A 33-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 23 weeks of gestation was admitted emergently with acute abdominal pain and signs of hemodynamic shock. Her blood pressure was 80/05 mm Hg, pulse 115 bpm, and respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute. She reported progressive abdominal distension over 10 days. Her obstetric history included one prior cesarean delivery for a placental anomaly; there was no other significant medical history. Fetal cardiac activity was present at 132 bpm. Physical examination revealed diffuse abdominal tenderness and a positive Flot’s sign indicating free fluid in the abdomen.  

One week earlier, a transabdominal ultrasound at a primary care facility confirmed a 23-week intrauterine mono-fetal pregnancy with normal fetal heart activity. The ovaries were not visualized, and no ascites or adnexal mass was reported.  

On admission, laboratory evaluation showed a hemoglobin level of 8.9 g/dL, urea 0.18 g/L, creatinine 8 mg/L, blood glucose 0.85 g/L, and prothrombin level 97%. Renal and coagulation studies were otherwise normal. The patient was resuscitated with two large-bore intravenous lines, macromolecule infusions, and supplemental oxygen.  

Given the patient’s hemodynamic instability and persistent abdominal fluid, an exploratory laparotomy was planned for definitive diagnosis and management.

A 48‐year‐old man presented with two months of persistent pain and swelling in the periapical region of the left upper molars. He had been diagnosed with apical periodontitis of teeth #26 and #27 at another clinic and undergone endodontic treatment, but his symptoms persisted. He denied fever, weight loss, or systemic illness. 

On extraoral examination, there was a hard, tender bony swelling (3.0 × 4.0 × 2.0 cm) over the left maxilla with obliteration of the buccal sulcus; there was no infraorbital numbness or lymphadenopathy. Intraorally, a firm swelling involved the buccal alveolar mucosa of teeth #25–27. Teeth #26 and #27 had temporary fillings, were nonresponsive to cold and electric pulp tests, and were slightly tender to percussion but not mobile. Teeth #25 and #28 responded normally.

A periapical radiograph showed incomplete endodontic treatment of teeth #26 and #27 and a well-defined radiolucent area at their apices. Cone-beam computed tomography revealed a poorly defined osteolytic lesion (29.5 × 28.5 × 20.5 mm) at the apices of teeth #25–27 with thin, straight internal septa; destruction of the buccal and palatal cortices; a soft‐tissue mass invading the left maxillary sinus; and no root resorption. Blood and urine biochemistry were within normal limits.

A 33-year-old man presented with persistent fever and worsening abdominal pain despite prior outpatient treatment. He had no significant medical or surgical history. On examination, he was febrile to 39°C and had severe tenderness of the left flank with muscle guarding. Laboratory tests revealed a neutrophil count of 7553/mm3 and a C-reactive protein level of 13.9 mg/dL. An enhanced abdominal CT scan showed multiple low-density, round lesions (up to 30 mm in diameter) with peripherally enhancing rims and surrounding edema in the region of the descending mesocolon. These were suspected to represent multiple cysts in the descending mesocolon or retroperitoneum, and peritonitis secondary to these cystic lesions was diagnosed. Emergency exploratory laparotomy was planned.

A 19-year-old woman with atopic dermatitis presented with a 3-month history of right dorsal pain, worsening to incapacitating (7/10) over the prior week without alleviating or aggravating factors. She had no history of trauma or surgery. On presentation, she was tachycardic and diaphoretic, with a normal mean arterial pressure. Physical examination showed dehydration, pallor, and a palpable mass in the right hypochondrium with tenderness and a positive Giordano’s sign. Laboratory tests revealed hemoglobin 6.5 g/dL, and she received two units of packed red blood cells, after which vital signs stabilized. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed an 11.4×10.2×10.3 cm ovoid lesion replacing the right adrenal gland, with active bleeding into the peritoneum and mass effect on the liver, inferior vena cava, and right kidney. A retroperitoneal hematoma and probable adrenal angiomyolipoma were suspected. Interventional radiology performed angiography and selective embolization of the right inferior adrenal artery, controlling the hemorrhage. One week later, she was discharged for follow-up. On follow-up, she was asymptomatic. Biochemical evaluation showed cortisol 15.2 μg/dL (normal 5–25), 24-hour urine metanephrines 338 μg (normal <400), and vanillylmandelic acid 7.6 mg (normal <8), indicating a nonfunctional tumor. Four months after embolization, repeat CT showed a reduced adrenal mass measuring 6.3×6.1×5.5 cm without active bleeding, still displacing the liver and right kidney. After multidisciplinary review, elective open right supra-adrenalectomy was planned.

A 40-year-old gravida 4 para 4 woman was referred with a slowly enlarging abdominal and perineal mass over 3 years. She reported progressive abdominal distension, constipation (1–2 stools per week), difficulty voiding, and an 8-kg weight loss. She denied pain. On examination, there was a large, firm, nontender abdominal mass protruding through an incisional hernia, and a second 40-cm mass occupied the internal gluteal region, with a pedicle extending through the right ischiorectal fossa. Perineal examination revealed a grade IV hysterocele. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a huge, well-demarcated, solid, homogeneous mass with moderate enhancement occupying the abdomen and pelvis and herniating through the perineum. A core-needle biopsy was performed.

A 32-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with two months of intermittent, mild discomfort below the left costal margin without nausea, vomiting, or weight loss. She was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Abdominal examination revealed no tenderness, guarding, or palpable mass. Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin level of 13.7 g/dL and a normal white-cell count of 5.4×10^9/L; other serum chemistries, including pancreatic enzymes, were within normal limits. An abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable. Subsequent magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen revealed an 18 mm focal lesion at the junction of the body and tail of the pancreas, without invasion of surrounding vascular structures or communication with the main pancreatic duct. Serum tumor markers were within reference ranges. On multidisciplinary review, the differential diagnosis included a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor, a pseudotumor, and an intrapancreatic splenunculum.

A 28-year-old previously healthy white man of Eastern European descent presented with a 2-week history of vomiting, anorexia, and abdominal pain.  
On examination, he had mild tenderness in the epigastrium and left upper abdomen.  
Laboratory investigations showed aspartate aminotransferase 150 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 387 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 234 U/L, total bilirubin 2.5 mg/dL, lipase 1132 U/L, and lactate dehydrogenase 391 U/L.  
Abdominal ultrasound revealed lymphadenopathy posterior to the pancreatic head and dilation of the proximal extrahepatic bile duct to 11 mm.  
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography demonstrated bulky retroperitoneal, periportal, mesenteric, retrocrural, and lower thoracic lymphadenopathy; extrahepatic and intrahepatic biliary ductal dilatation; and ill-defined thickening of the gastric antrum.  
Subsequent studies showed a β-human chorionic gonadotropin level of 872 mIU/mL and an α-fetoprotein level of 244 IU/L; testing for antinuclear antibody, HIV, and anti–immunoglobulin G antibodies was negative.  
Thoracic, abdominal, and pelvic computed tomography confirmed acute interstitial edematous pancreatitis, mural thickening of the distal gastric body and duodenum, and diffuse lymphadenopathy suggestive of lymphoma.

A 55-year-old man presented with a 10-year history of a large polypoidal growth on the penis, scrotum, and right upper thigh. He initially noted progressive itching at the penile tip, followed by small skin-colored lesions that oozed clear fluid when scratched. Over months, these lesions enlarged circumferentially over the prepuce, and similar polypoidal growths appeared on the scrotum and right upper thigh. The lesions became hard and mildly pruritic but were not painful. There was no history of similar lesions elsewhere. Sexual activity was normal for the first 2 years but compromised over the past 8 years. 

On examination, there was a circumferential polypoidal lesion involving the preputial skin, a 3×2-cm polypoidal growth at the scrotal tip, and a 3×2-cm polypoidal lesion on the right upper thigh. The perianal and gluteal regions and the rest of the skin were free of lesions. Urination was normal. His wife’s genital examination and Pap smear were normal. Complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, and immune status were all within normal limits. 

A provisional diagnosis of giant condyloma acuminata, verrucous carcinoma of the genitalia, and giant acrochordons was made, and the patient underwent shave excision of all lesions under general anesthesia.

A 58-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of bilateral lower abdominal pain radiating to the back, a 5-pound weight loss, and irregular watery bowel movements. He denied nausea, vomiting, melena, hematochezia, fevers, or urinary symptoms. His medical history was unremarkable, and he had no family history of colorectal cancer or inflammatory bowel disease. He did not smoke or use recreational drugs and drank one alcoholic beverage daily.  
On examination, vital signs were normal, and the abdomen was soft, nondistended, and nontender without palpable masses. Stool testing was hemoccult negative. Laboratory evaluation revealed a carcinoembryonic antigen level of 5.9 ng/mL; CA-125 and CA 19-9 were not obtained.  
Colonoscopy showed a long rectosigmoid stricture requiring a gastroscope for traversal; the cecum and the appendiceal orifice appeared normal. Biopsies of the rectosigmoid stenosis were nondiagnostic.  
CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated an irregular rim-enhancing heterogeneous mass measuring 6.7 × 2.8 cm, originating from the base of the cecum and extending across the midline, tethered to the rectosigmoid junction without evidence of fistula.  
What is your differential diagnosis?

A 72-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a painful enlargement of the left parotid gland. Seven years earlier, she had been treated for mantle cell lymphoma of the left submandibular gland with surgery, radiotherapy, and CHOP chemotherapy. She had no other symptoms.  
On examination, there was a tender left parotid enlargement without cervical lymphadenopathy. Vital signs were normal.  
Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 5100/μL with a normal differential, hemoglobin 12.7 g/dL, hematocrit 38.4%, and platelets 219,000/μL. Bone marrow biopsy showed no lymphoma.  
Ultrasound of the left parotid gland revealed multiple cystic lesions within the parenchyma. MRI demonstrated enlargement of the left parotid gland with total replacement of the normal parenchyma by mixed solid and cystic lesions; the solid components showed mild enhancement after intravenous contrast. Whole-body CT showed no pathologic lymphadenopathy, and the chest and abdominal organs were normal.

An 85‐year‐old Caucasian woman with diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia was evaluated for a right dorsal foot lesion first noticed about 12 years earlier. She had not sought care because it was slow‐growing and asymptomatic until, over the past 3 weeks, it enlarged more rapidly and developed a foul odor. She denied pain, paresthesias, weight loss, trauma, smoking history, and significant sun exposure. On examination, there was an 8.0 × 8.0 × 0.6 cm exophytic, fungating, malodorous mass on the dorsum of the right foot that was insensate to light touch without surrounding erythema. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses were palpable, and she had full range of motion. The remainder of her skin exam was unremarkable. Subsequent magnetic resonance imaging showed a large soft‐tissue irregularity surrounding the second to fifth extensor tendons.

A 34‐year‐old woman presented with central chest pain followed by a large left‐sided pleural effusion causing pleurisy and dyspnea. Her history included autoimmune hepatitis, premature ovarian failure, and possible myelodysplastic disease with trisomy 8. She denied trauma or family lymphatic disorders and was a lifelong non‐smoker. Therapeutic drainage via an intercostal catheter yielded milky fluid. Pleural fluid analysis showed chylomicrons, reactive mesothelial cells, and negative microbiology. Initial chest CT showed normal pulmonary parenchyma with no pleural thickening, mass, or nodules. 

Over the ensuing year, she underwent three additional drainages of left‐sided chylous effusions. A lower‐limb lymphoscintogram demonstrated delayed tracer movement on the right and accumulation in abnormal soft tissue of the left superior mediastinum. PET/CT revealed multiple enlarged superior mediastinal lymph nodes (up to 15 mm) with abnormal uptake in mediastinal nodes and lower neck soft tissue masses. Mediastinal MRI showed a complex multilobulated high T2–weighted structure extending from the anterior neck down to the superior mediastinum and surrounding the great vessels. A fine‐needle aspiration biopsy of a left cervical lymph node demonstrated benign mesothelial cells.

Mediastinal inflow obstruction led to thrombosis of the proximal left subclavian and left internal jugular veins, requiring anticoagulation and resulting in facial edema and dilated chest‐wall veins. Excisional biopsy of a left supraclavicular lymph node revealed atypical reactive mesothelial cells. Progressive MRI scans characterized the lesion as a large thoracic and neck complex lymphangioma associated with left‐sided chylothorax.

Eighteen months after initial presentation, she was admitted with a persistent left‐sided pleural effusion despite compliance with a very‐low‐fat diet and subcutaneous octreotide. The pleural fluid no longer appeared chylous and contained no chylomicrons. After drainage, a plain chest X‐ray demonstrated a pleural‐based soft tissue mass at the apex of the left thoracic cavity.

A 22-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 2-week history of headaches and several episodes of vomiting, accompanied by gait disturbances and ataxia for 3 weeks. On examination, he was alert, with notable ataxic gait but no focal cranial-nerve deficits. Routine blood tests were unremarkable. 

Noncontrast cranial CT revealed a solid, spontaneously hyperdense mass in the left posterior fossa, causing effacement of the fourth ventricle, resulting in tri-ventricular obstructive hydrocephalus and periventricular trans-ependymal edema.

Brain MRI demonstrated a well-defined, extra-axial mass in the left cerebellopontine angle measuring 37 × 48 × 30 mm. The lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images, isointense on FLAIR, and slightly hyperintense on T2, with a thin rim of CSF between the mass and cerebellar parenchyma. Diffusion-weighted imaging showed hyperintensity with corresponding low ADC values, and after gadolinium administration the lesion exhibited homogeneous enhancement. There was pronounced vasogenic edema adjacent to the tumor and in the periventricular regions. The mass effect included inferior herniation of the right cerebellar tonsil and compression of the fourth ventricle, contributing to hydrocephalus.

Spinal MRI revealed multiple contrast-enhancing extramedullary nodular lesions at cervical, thoracic, and lumbar levels.

A 32-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of persistent lower back pain radiating to his left lower limb. The pain was constant, dull in character, worsened with movement, and was unresponsive to over-the-counter analgesics. He denied any history of trauma, prior back problems, urinary incontinence, or saddle anesthesia. On examination, strength in the left lower limb was 4/5, while sensation and deep-tendon reflexes were preserved bilaterally. Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 11,000/µL (reference range, 4000–11,000/µL) and a random blood glucose level of 169 mg/dL (reference range, 70–140 mg/dL). Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis demonstrated a well-defined presacral soft-tissue mass on noncontrast axial T2-weighted and sagittal T1-weighted images.

A 17-year-old female high-school middle-distance runner with no prior medical history presented with a 1-year history of progressive swelling of her distal right leg. There was no history of trauma or systemic symptoms. Over the past few months she developed pain, initially at the end of training sessions and later at rest, forcing cessation of sports.

On examination, she ambulated without an obvious limp but had slight instability on the right single‐leg stance. There was an ill‐defined, firm, fixed swelling over the supramalleolar region of the right tibia, tender to palpation; overlying skin was normal. The knee and ankle joints were stable with full range of motion. No café-au-lait spots or other abnormalities were noted on skin inspection.

Plain radiographs of the right leg showed a well-circumscribed metaphyso-diaphyseal multiloculated radiolucent lesion in the distal tibia, extending approximately 7 cm proximally, filling the medullary canal and expanding but not disrupting the cortices; no periosteal reaction was present. A similar 2 cm lucent lesion was identified in the adjacent distal fibular diaphysis.

MRI demonstrated a 36 × 42 × 77 mm metaphyseal/diaphyseal lesion of the distal tibia with a predominantly fibrous component: T1 hypointense, heterogeneous T2 hyperintense signal, heterogeneous gadolinium enhancement, and circumferential cortical thinning without soft-tissue invasion. A second smaller lesion of identical appearance measured 7 × 12 × 22 mm in the distal fibula.

Core biopsy yielded friable light brown material. Histologic examination revealed a benign giant‐cell–rich tumor composed of multinucleated giant cells mixed with spindle cells, without atypia or mitoses, morphologically suggestive of either a non-ossifying fibroma or a solid variant of an aneurysmal bone cyst. Giant cell tumor was considered unlikely.

A 20-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a left breast cyst that recurred despite multiple fine-needle aspirations performed by her primary care physician. She reported a visible bulge and intermittent mastodynia at the site but denied systemic symptoms such as fever, chills, or weight loss. Fluid obtained on aspiration was sent for cytologic evaluation and showed no atypia or neoplastic features.

On examination, there was a palpable, fluctuant mass measuring more than 6 cm in greatest dimension in the upper, inner quadrant of the left breast at the 10 o’clock position near the sternal border. The overlying skin was unremarkable, with no erythema, cellulitis, nipple retraction, or focal tenderness.

Breast ultrasound demonstrated a 6.1-cm, lobulated, anechoic lesion with internal debris and several thin, partial septations. Color Doppler imaging revealed no flow within the lesion or its septations, and posterior acoustic enhancement was present.

A 28-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of a painless swelling on the right side of her neck. She denied any difficulty swallowing or breathing and had no history of recent trauma or upper respiratory infection. On examination, there was a single, ill-defined, lobular, soft, freely movable mass measuring approximately 6.5 × 3 cm in the right posterior triangle of the neck. The mass did not move with deglutition, and the overlying skin was normal. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy.

Ultrasonography showed an 8 × 7 × 3 cm elliptical, multiloculated cystic lesion posteromedial to the right sternocleidomastoid muscle, extending medially to the right submandibular gland, with thin peripheral septae. The lesion was avascular, and its deep wall abutted the carotid artery and internal jugular vein.

Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 66 × 54 × 27 mm thin-walled, multilobular cystic mass in the intermuscular plane on the right side of the neck. The lesion was hyperintense on T2-weighted images and hypointense on T1-weighted images. It abutted the sternocleidomastoid muscle laterally, the parotid gland superiorly, and the carotid sheath medially, and showed no communication with the pharynx or surrounding inflammatory changes.

Fine-needle aspiration yielded yellow, viscous fluid containing numerous lymphocytes.

A 3-year-6-month-old boy with a history of tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) type 1 was undergoing routine surveillance. His past medical history included epilepsy beginning at 3 months of age and multiple hypomelanotic skin lesions. Early brain MRI showed subependymal nodules and cortical tubers; genetic testing confirmed a de novo pathogenic TSC1 mutation (c.989dupT). He also had nonobstructive cardiac rhabdomyomas and bilateral renal angiomyolipomas on ultrasound. At 3 years and 6 months of age, after endoscopic resection of a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, an abdominal MRI revealed a 0.4-cm lesion in the posterior body of the pancreas. Three months later, the lesion measured 0.45 cm; at 3 years and 10 months, it measured 1.0 cm. On MRI, the pancreatic mass was hypointense on T1-weighted images, mildly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and exhibited minimal central enhancement. Endocrine laboratory studies were as follows: glucose 81 mg/dL; insulin 4 µIU/mL (2.6–24.9); gastrin 83 pg/mL (2–168); neuron-specific enolase 8.9 ng/mL (0.0–12.5); chromogranin A 2 nmol/L (0–5); IGF-1 59 ng/mL (20–141); IGF binding protein-3 1960 ng/mL (972–4123). What is your differential diagnosis?

A 19-year-old woman presented with swelling of the left upper jaw for one year. Two months after exfoliation of a deciduous tooth in that region at age 12, she noticed a white nodule in the canine–premolar area. One year ago the nodule reddened and suddenly enlarged. Five months earlier, an incisional biopsy was performed and reportedly showed chronic inflammatory enlargement.

On examination, there was no facial asymmetry. Intraorally, there was a diffuse erythematous, firm, tender swelling between the left maxillary canine and first premolar, measuring 2.6 cm anteroposteriorly and 4.2 cm buccopalatally, extending to the occlusal level. The overlying mucosa was immobile.

Intraoral periapical, panoramic, and occlusal radiographs demonstrated a multilocular lesion with mixed radiolucent and radiopaque areas. A computed tomographic scan revealed a multilocular radiolucency with slight cortical expansion and cortical perforation in the left maxillary alveolus.

A 3-month-old boy was referred after routine urine analysis, performed for unrelated reasons, revealed microhematuria. He was well appearing, with no other symptoms or signs of urinary tract infection. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a single, regular, grossly hypoechogenic 1.2 × 1.5 cm mass arising from the bladder trigone and protruding into the lumen; the remainder of the urinary tract and other viscera were unremarkable. Cystoscopic examination revealed normal bladder mucosa and an easily biopsied exophytic lesion at the trigone. Histologic examination of the biopsies demonstrated uniform cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and a low mitotic index, with no atypia or necrosis. Immunohistochemical staining showed positivity for CD34 and negativity for S100.

A 38-year-old man presented with a 10-year history of a slowly enlarging growth on the right side of the tip of his tongue. The lesion was initially small and painless, but over time increased to approximately 1×1 cm. The patient reported occasional bleeding associated with trauma during mastication; bleeding stopped spontaneously. He denied pain at rest. His medical and personal histories were unremarkable, although he reported a 10–15-year history of tobacco chewing. On examination, there was a well-circumscribed, sessile, ovoid, brownish, granular-surfaced lesion measuring about 1×1 cm on the dorsal surface of the tongue tip. The lesion was non-tender and rough to palpation. No other intraoral or extraoral lesions were noted. Routine hematological investigations were unremarkable. Under local anesthesia, the lesion was completely excised and submitted for histopathological examination.

A 50-year-old Palestinian woman with a history of breast cancer treated in 2005 (mastectomy, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and 10 years of hormonal therapy) presented with her first episode of repetitive, rhythmic, uncontrolled movements of the right side and loss of consciousness lasting about 5 minutes. She had no preceding headache, dizziness, visual symptoms, or tinnitus. Her family history was negative for malignancy; she had no known allergies and no tobacco, alcohol, or drug use.

On examination she was alert and in no distress. Vital signs were normal. Neurological examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits.

Noncontrast head CT revealed a left frontal lobe space-occupying lesion. Brain MRI showed a well-defined intra-axial lesion in the left frontal lobe that was mainly hypointense on T1- and T2-weighted images, exhibited slight heterogeneity, demonstrated blooming artifact on susceptibility-weighted imaging, and was surrounded by vasogenic edema with peripheral and central punctate enhancement after contrast administration. The radiologic differential diagnosis included hemorrhagic metastasis, cavernoma, or hemorrhagic glioma.

Whole-body CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no evidence of breast cancer recurrence or other lesions. Serum tumor markers (CA 15-3 and CEA) were negative. The patient was referred for neurosurgical evaluation of a presumed primary brain tumor.

A 75-year-old man was referred by his family dentist for evaluation of a mass on the left mandibular gingiva that had been present for 1 month and had not resolved. His medical history was notable for hypertension treated with amlodipine. He had smoked 13 cigarettes daily since age 20 and consumed approximately 350 mL of beer daily. 

Oral examination revealed a relatively firm, well-circumscribed, 10 mm nodular lesion with normal mucosal coloration on the lingual gingiva adjacent to the left mandibular premolar. The lesion was located away from the floor of the mouth. No other intraoral abnormalities or regional lymphadenopathy were noted.

A periapical radiograph of the left lower first premolar region showed no bony changes. With a working clinical diagnosis of gingival fibroma, the mass was excised under local anesthesia.

A 38-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of right-ear hearing loss and recurrent episodes of otorrhea. She denied otalgia and pulsatile tinnitus. Her medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Otoendoscopic examination revealed a dark purple, nonpulsatile mass partially obstructing the right external auditory canal and preventing visualization of the tympanic membrane. Pure-tone audiometry demonstrated moderate conductive hearing loss in the affected ear. High-resolution computed tomography of the temporal bone showed a 6 × 10 mm soft-tissue lesion in the bony external auditory canal in continuity with the tympanic membrane, with no evidence of bone erosion, middle-ear invasion, or exostoses.

A 50-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 1, 1 year postmenopausal, presented with a 2-month history of progressive abdominal distension, anorexia, and exertional dyspnea. Physical examination revealed a markedly distended abdomen. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed marked ascites and a left ovarian mass measuring 8 cm with both cystic and solid components. Chest radiography demonstrated a large right-sided pleural effusion without pulmonary lesions. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis confirmed massive ascites extending under the diaphragm and a heterogeneous 8 cm left adnexal mass; parts of the solid component had higher attenuation and there were calcifications along the cyst wall, with no lymphadenopathy or peritoneal implants. Pelvic MRI showed the left mass to be uniformly low intensity on T1-weighted images and heterogeneous on T2-weighted images, with cystic areas of varying signal separated by thick septa; the solid septa enhanced uniformly, and no fatty elements were identified. Laboratory tests revealed a serum CA 125 level of 1237 U/mL (normal <35 U/mL), with normal CEA, CA 19-9, and SCC antigen levels. The clinical picture suggested advanced ovarian cancer. A whole-body ¹⁸F-FDG PET/CT scan showed no abnormal FDG uptake in the pelvic mass or elsewhere. Multiple cytological examinations of ascitic fluid revealed only benign mesothelial cells, with no malignant cells detected.

A 7-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of a persistent, firm, painless swelling of the right upper jaw. She was otherwise healthy, and examination revealed facial asymmetry with a hard, non-tender intraoral mass obliterating the right maxillary vestibule from deciduous tooth #53 distally to permanent tooth #16. The overlying mucosa was normal; there was no lymphadenopathy. A panoramic radiograph showed a well-defined radiolucent lesion in the right maxilla and absence of tooth #54, which had been extracted previously in an unsuccessful attempt at treatment. Cone-beam computed tomography demonstrated a well-circumscribed mixed radiolucent–radiopaque lesion extending from the distal of tooth #53 to the mesial of tooth #55, from the alveolar crest to the canine germ. The lesion had fine internal trabeculae, caused buccal, palatal, and crestal expansion, and disrupted the buccal cortical plate; the right maxillary sinus was unremarkable. An incisional biopsy was performed. Microscopic examination showed a proliferation of spindle-shaped cells with regular nuclei arranged in bundles in a storiform pattern, associated with multinucleated giant cells. Embedded within these irregular strands were mineralized pieces in the form of trabeculae of woven bone. The overlying stratified squamous epithelium exhibited moderate acanthosis and hyperkeratosis.

A 69-year-old woman was referred for investigation of elevated serum liver enzyme levels and obstructive jaundice. She complained of tenderness in the right hypochondriac region. Laboratory tests showed aspartate transaminase 91 U/l, alanine transaminase 249 U/l, alkaline phosphatase 990 U/l, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 761 U/l, and total bilirubin 1.7 mg/dl. Serum carcinoembryonic antigen, carbohydrate antigen 19-9, alpha fetoprotein, and protein induced by vitamin K absence or antagonist-II were within normal limits. Child–Pugh grade was A. 

Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 49×29 mm cystic lesion with a septum in segment 4 of the liver. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 4-cm multilocular cystic lesion with multiple septations showing a “cyst-in-cyst” appearance in segment 4, and a polypoid nodule extending from the left hepatic duct into the common bile duct, suspected to arise from the cystic wall. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiography showed a smooth contrast defect from the left hepatic duct to the common bile duct consistent with a nodular intraductal lesion. Bile cytology and biopsy of the nodular lesion showed no malignant findings. Based on these findings, intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm of the bile duct (IPNB) and mucinous cystic neoplasm of the liver (MCN-L) with possible malignancy were considered.

A term female neonate was delivered via Cesarean section to a 36-year-old mother with gestational diabetes and a history of two previous healthy pregnancies. Prenatal ultrasound at 31 weeks of gestation revealed a 30 × 19 mm lesion in the anterior fetal mouth that kept the mouth open and led to polyhydramnios. At birth, Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. Immediately after delivery, examination revealed two smooth, pedunculated masses, each approximately 2.0 × 2.0 cm, attached to the maxillary and mandibular alveolar ridges; the masses had the same color as surrounding mucosa, were firm, noncompressible, nonreducible, and non-tender. The neonate was unable to close her mouth and could not breastfeed, so a nasogastric tube was placed for feeding. There were no signs of airway obstruction or respiratory distress, and no other structural anomalies were noted.

A 28-year-old woman in the third trimester of her first pregnancy noted progressive visual deterioration over several weeks. Her visual acuity declined to 20/40 in the left eye and 20/400 in the right eye, initially intermittently with flickering, then persistently with only vague light perception during worst episodes. She reported concurrent reappearance of a dermatomyositis, previously diagnosed by skin biopsy and in remission on immunosuppressive therapy. Initial ophthalmologic and neurologic evaluations were unremarkable, and her visual loss was treated as a dermatomyositis flare with steroids without improvement.

On repeat ophthalmologic examination, both eyes showed amelanotic choroidal masses: one at the posterior pole involving the peripapillary area and another superior to the optic disc in the right eye; a single lesion nasal superior to the optic disc in the left eye; each was associated with inferior exudative retinal detachment. 

On examination, she appeared well but had reddish, thickened, flaking skin. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal exams were normal. Visual acuity remained reduced bilaterally, and she described paresthesias in both feet. Laboratory tests showed a mildly elevated creatine kinase of 193 U/L (normal ≤170 U/L), C-reactive protein 2.77 mg/dL (normal ≤0.5 mg/dL), hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, uric acid 6.5 mg/dL (normal 2.4–5.7 mg/dL), lactate dehydrogenase 959 U/L (normal ≤250 U/L), and platelets 789 G/μL (normal ≤450 G/μL). 

Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a large anterior mediastinal mass with pleural thickening, pulmonary nodules, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Computed tomography was deferred due to her pregnancy.

A 42-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of mild chest tightness. Her medical history was unremarkable. On examination, the muscles of her left arm were thicker than those on the right, and breath sounds were diminished over the upper left lung field. A chest radiograph showed a mass in the superior mediastinum. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a 10.0 cm × 5.5 cm mass in the middle superior mediastinum with areas of fat density; on postcontrast images the lesion was slightly heterogeneously enhanced, and an adjacent blood vessel was surrounded by the mass with an obscure boundary. Laboratory tests, including β-hCG and α-fetoprotein, were negative. Given the size, location, and imaging characteristics, the mass was considered possibly to be a liposarcoma, and surgical biopsy was planned.

A 2-year 11-month-old male neutered Jack Russell Terrier was evaluated for a 7-day history of focal seizures and neck pain. On neurologic examination, the dog was obtunded, had bilaterally absent menace responses, and demonstrated cervical hyperesthesia, localizing to both the forebrain and cervical spinal cord. Routine hematologic and biochemical tests were within normal limits. Under general anesthesia, magnetic resonance imaging of the head revealed a large (20 × 21 × 18 mm), well-demarcated, irregularly margined, left-sided, extra-axial mass arising with a broad base from the left occipital bone and compressing the occipital lobe and cerebellum. The lesion was hypointense on T1-, T2-, FLAIR-, and T2*-weighted sequences and showed peripheral contrast enhancement; a midline shift and foramen magnum herniation suggested increased intracranial pressure. MRI of the cervical spinal cord demonstrated syringomyelia. Thoracic and abdominal CT was unremarkable. CT of the head showed the mass had attenuation similar to bone, contained stippled mineralized densities, and distorted the occipital and parietal bones. Multilobular tumor of bone, osteosarcoma, and chondroma were considered the most likely differential diagnoses.

A 14-year-old adolescent male presented with a 2-week history of persistent headache, 5 days of projectile vomiting and neck stiffness, and a single episode of generalized tonic–clonic seizure lasting 10 minutes. On neurologic examination, papilledema was noted, and there was right-sided hemiparesis (power 2/5) with hyperactive deep tendon reflexes and a positive Babinski sign. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed a 6.2×5.2×4 cm heterogeneously enhancing mass centered in the left lateral ventricle, with extension into the ipsilateral parietooccipital white matter, surrounding vasogenic edema, and a 6 mm midline shift. MR spectroscopy demonstrated reduced N-acetyl-aspartate, elevated choline, and a lactate peak. There was no evidence of spinal cord involvement.

A 16-year-old male presented with a 12-month history of progressively enlarging bilateral painless scrotal lumps, with no size variation during the day and no history of trauma. On examination, both testes were normal in size and location; adjacent to each testis was a nonreducible, nontender, oval, soft scrotal mass. Scrotal ultrasound demonstrated two large cystic masses arising from the tails of both epididymides, measuring 46×21 mm on the left and 46×24 mm on the right; both testes were normal in size, shape, echogenicity, and Doppler flow. Serum lactate dehydrogenase, human chorionic gonadotropin, and alpha-fetoprotein levels were within normal limits.

A 40-year-old woman, gravida 5 para 4 at 32 weeks of gestation, presented with repeated episodes of vaginal bleeding. On abdominal examination, the uterine fundal height was disproportionately large for her gestational age. Transabdominal ultrasound revealed a single viable intrauterine fetus consistent with 32 weeks’ gestation. Screening of the adnexal regions showed bilateral complex masses with high vascularity measuring 8 × 6 cm on the right and 12 × 8 cm on the left. Transvaginal ultrasound identified a highly vascular polypoidal mass projecting into the upper vagina, indistinct from a bulky cervix, and solid peritoneal deposits in the pouch of Douglas. A non-contrast pelvic MRI performed one week later showed bilateral complex cystic adnexal masses and an upper vaginal mass on T2-weighted images. On diffusion-weighted imaging, these masses exhibited persistent bright signal intensity and low apparent diffusion coefficient values. Laboratory tests were within normal limits except for an elevated CA-125 level.

A 38-year-old woman without relevant medical history presented with recurrent left hypochondrial pain of 6 months’ duration. On examination she had a tense mass in the lower abdomen. Ultrasonography revealed left hydronephrosis and a large retroperitoneal cyst. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a retroperitoneal mass extending from the level of the common iliac vessels to the renal vasculature, with associated left hydronephrosis. MRI demonstrated a monolocular cyst measuring 18 cm in diameter without a solid component; the wall was thin and smooth. Tumor markers (CEA, CA19-9, CA125, α-fetoprotein) and routine laboratory studies were unremarkable. A radiological diagnosis of retroperitoneal lymphangioma was established.

A 26-year-old woman at 14.1 weeks of gestation presented with a 5-day history of lower-limb and facial edema, headache, severe nausea with multiple episodes of vomiting, epigastric pain, phosphenes, and photophobia. She denied any vaginal bleeding or discharge. Her blood pressure was 175/108 mm Hg, heart rate 131 bpm, respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, temperature 36.3 °C, and oxygen saturation 94 % on room air. On examination, she was alert, had generalized hyperreflexia, anasarca, tachycardia, and diminished basal breath sounds. Her fundal height was 22 cm, approximately double the expected size for gestational age, and no fetal heart tones were audible. Pelvic examination revealed mild labial edema and a closed, soft, posterior cervix without bleeding. Lower-extremity pitting edema extended to the knees. Transabdominal ultrasound showed a uterus measuring 24 × 18 cm filled with a “snowflake” pattern and multiple hypoechoic areas, no identifiable fetus, and bilaterally enlarged adnexa with cystic structures suggestive of theca-lutein cysts; a right ovarian cyst measured >3 cm. The patient underwent manual intrauterine aspiration, yielding abundant trophoblastic tissue described as grape-like clusters.

A 79-year-old woman with a history of vertigo was found 5 years ago to have a right frontal bone intradiploic lesion, initially diagnosed as an intradiploic epidermoid cyst and followed without intervention. She noted swelling of the right frontal region that developed 5 years after the initial finding and enlarged over 2 months. 

On examination, neurological findings were normal. Palpation revealed an elastic, soft mass approximately 6 cm in diameter in the right frontal area. Blood tests showed no inflammatory reaction. 

Computed tomography demonstrated a cystic lesion measuring 60 × 50 × 47 mm in the right frontal bone with loss of normal bone structure and dissociation between the inner and outer tables. Magnetic resonance imaging showed homogeneous low signal intensity on T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted sequences; contrast enhancement was limited to the cyst wall and adjacent diploe. The boundary with the periosteum was clear and smooth, whereas the margin against the dura mater was ill-defined. 

Percutaneous aspiration yielded dark red, serous fluid that did not clot and contained no platelets. Fluid analysis revealed slightly lower hemoglobin, total protein, albumin, and glucose levels, and higher total bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase levels compared with venous blood; other chemistries and blood cell counts were unremarkable.

An 11-year-old girl presented with sudden-onset horizontal diplopia when gazing at distant objects for 2 weeks. She had no history of head trauma, systemic illness, or psychogenic stress. Her daily near-work time was approximately 3 hours. Uncorrected visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. Refraction was −0.50 + 0.50 × 170° in the right eye and +0.00 + 0.25 × 175° in the left eye. Intraocular pressures were 19 mm Hg OD and 17 mm Hg OS. Pupils were equal and reactive, and no nystagmus was observed. Anterior segment and funduscopic examinations were unremarkable. Cover testing revealed basic esotropia of 30 prism diopters at near and 35 prism diopters at distance. Ocular ductions were full without nystagmus. Hess red-green testing showed inward displacement of both eyes, and under 45Δ base-out prism neutralization, equal field sizes confirmed comitant esotropia. As acute acquired comitant esotropia was suspected, brain MRI was performed to detect intracranial disease.

A 51-year-old woman presented with five months of right lower-limb pain and one month of lower abdominal pain accompanied by hematuria. On gynecologic examination, the uterus was enlarged and a hard, palpable mass was noted in the right adnexal area. Serum CA-125 was elevated at 71.5 kU/L; other tumor markers were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a 12.8 × 11.6 × 7.8 cm solid mass in the right adnexal region, with invasion of the right lower ureter causing upstream dilation and extension into adjacent small intestine and cecum. 

At surgery, the right ovary was greatly enlarged and nodular; the cut surface was cystic and solid with red-white areas. Microscopically, the lesion was composed of spindle-shaped cells forming intercellular slit-like spaces, with atypical pleomorphic nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and a mitotic rate of 12 per 10 high-power fields, along with extensive hemorrhage and necrosis. Immunohistochemical studies showed tumor cells positive for caldesmon, CD31, and CD34, with a Ki-67 proliferation index of approximately 50%. The cells were negative for cytokeratin (CK), epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), CK5/6, desmin, CD10, p16, estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, programmed death ligand 1, and placental prolactin protein. Fluorescence in situ hybridization demonstrated c-MYC gene amplification.

A 75-year-old woman with a 60-year history of tobacco use was found to have a right hilar mass on a routine chest radiograph. She reported a mild cough productive of yellow sputum but denied dyspnea or hemoptysis. CT and MRI scans demonstrated a 4.5 cm well-defined, slightly lobulated mass between the upper and lower lobes posterior to the right hilum. The lesion’s attenuation was approximately 24 HU compared with 35 HU in the aorta and 46 HU in skeletal muscle, suggesting a cystic rather than solid mass. There was no lymphadenopathy or airway compression. PET scanning revealed increased uptake in the thyroid; ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration diagnosed multinodular colloid goiter and thyroiditis. Further evaluation showed no evidence of metastatic disease. The patient underwent right upper lobectomy with superior segmentectomy of the right lower lobe. Grossly, there was a 5.5 cm nodular cystic mass with abundant mucoid material. Microscopic examination revealed a well-demarcated multicystic tumor without solid areas; the cysts were filled with pale basophilic mucin. In some regions, the lining was simple columnar mucinous epithelium without atypia or mitoses, while in others there was epithelial tufting, stratification, nuclear hyperchromasia, pleomorphism, and mitotic activity. At the periphery, mucinous tumor cells lined alveoli in a lepidic/bronchioloalveolar pattern. Immunohistochemical studies showed strong CK7 positivity, focal CK20 positivity, negative TTF-1 and p53 staining, and a low proliferation index (MIB-1 < 10%).

A 63-year-old woman presented with a mass in the left breast for 3 months that had gradually enlarged during the last month. On examination, there was a 5 × 4-cm immovable mass in the lower inner quadrant of the left breast, without nipple discharge or axillary lymphadenopathy. She had undergone right breast fibroadenoma resection 10 years earlier and had no family history of breast cancer. Sonography demonstrated two well-demarcated heterogeneous hypoechoic adjacent solid masses measuring 4.2 × 1.5 cm and 2.0 × 1.2 cm, with prominent color signals on Doppler imaging. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound after injection of SonVue showed enhancement from the periphery to the center of both lesions. On MRI, the lesions were hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and the dynamic contrast-enhanced time–signal intensity curve showed a plateau (type II) pattern. After gadolinium administration, the larger lesion exhibited peripheral enhancement with central non-enhancement, while the smaller lesion demonstrated homogeneous intense enhancement. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology revealed oval-to-spindle-shaped cells with focal myxoid degeneration and no cytologic atypia or mitoses.

A 2-day-old female neonate was noted to have a smooth-surfaced, non–fixated, pink soft-tissue mass arising from the left anterior mandibular alveolar mucosa. Prenatal ultrasonography had been unremarkable, and there was no relevant family or medical history. On examination, the lesion measured 1.0 × 1.0 × 1.8 cm, was pedunculated, and the adjacent gingiva appeared normal. Between the first and second visits the mass increased in size and developed superficial ulceration. On the seventh postpartum day, the lesion was surgically excised under general anesthesia.

A 58-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with a 2-month history of mild lower back pain that responded to celecoxib. Over that time, he developed bilateral numbness along the back of his legs, worse on the left, consistent with S1 radiculopathy. A lumbosacral CT scan was unremarkable, and symptoms persisted.

Two weeks before admission, his back pain and radiculopathy dramatically worsened, with non-dermatomal numbness and distal lower-limb weakness more pronounced on the left, impacting his daily activities. He also reported constipation and urinary incontinence. On examination, bilateral straight-leg-raise tests were positive; sensory examination revealed hypoesthesia in the S1 dermatomes. Patellar reflexes were present; Achilles reflexes were decreased. Muscle strength (manual muscle test) was 3/5 for left foot dorsiflexion and plantarflexion and 4/5 on the right; proximal muscles were intact. Pre- and post-void ultrasound suggested neurogenic bladder.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine showed a 7-cm oval intradural extramedullary mass extending from L3/L4 to L5/S1 with intermediate T1, low T2 signal intensity, and homogeneous enhancement after contrast administration. During hospitalization, he had acute worsening of lower-limb power, with dorsiflexion, extensor hallucis longus, and plantarflexion dropping to 1/5 on the left. Repeat MRI demonstrated heterogeneous contrast enhancement and increased cephalocaudal dimension of the lesion, consistent with acute intratumoral hemorrhage.

A 67-year-old man presented with one month of inappetence and generalized weakness. He reported intermittent fever up to 38.6 °C but had no known precipitating factors. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including AFP, CA 125, CA 19-9, and other tumor markers, were within normal limits, and there were no obvious signs of infection; he had no history of hepatitis B. 

Right upper-quadrant ultrasound showed thickening of the lateral gallbladder wall with hypoechoic areas, inadequate blood flow, and a segmental protrusion of the inner wall into the lumen. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated uneven gallbladder wall thickening with marked delayed-phase enhancement and preserved fat planes between the gallbladder and liver. 

MRI revealed cirrhosis of the liver. On T2-weighted images, the right posterior wall and fundus of the gallbladder exhibited “comb-tooth”–like protrusions into the lumen with clear edges; the outer wall was smooth. The lesion was isointense on T1 and T2, hyperintense on DWI, and hypointense on ADC (ADC values 1.1 × 10^–3 to 1.7 × 10^–3 mm^2/s). Dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI showed strong arterial-phase enhancement with slight washout in the delayed phase.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 10-month history of a painless swelling in the right inguinal region. She reported no change in size or discomfort with activity or straining. On examination, a 4 × 2 cm soft, non-tender mass was palpable in the right inguinal area without a cough impulse or enlargement during the Valsalva manoeuvre. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis revealed an oval lesion measuring 3.9 × 2.6 × 2.4 cm adjacent to the round ligament in the right inguinal canal, showing hypointense signal on T1-weighted images and hyperintense signal on T2-weighted images. Pelvic ultrasound demonstrated an anechoic cyst in the same location. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were unremarkable.

A 48-year-old man presented with a 7-month history of a painful, slow-growing mass on the anterior surface of his right thigh. On examination, the lesion was round, erythematous, and 5 cm in diameter. An excisional biopsy revealed a yellowish-brown mass with an irregular surface. Histologically, the tumor involved the deep dermis and superficial subcutis, showing infiltrative growth toward the dermis and a well-defined boundary toward the subcutis. There was a mixture of xanthomatous cells and spindle-shaped or ovoid cells with variably sized, bizarre, hyperchromatic nuclei. The mitotic rate was 0–1 per 50 high-power fields, and no necrosis was seen. Additional findings included multinucleated giant cells, hemosiderin deposits, mixed inflammatory cells (lymphocytes, eosinophils, plasma cells), and intranuclear pseudoinclusions. Immunohistochemical staining showed diffuse CD34 positivity; tumor cells were negative for S100 protein, desmin, smooth muscle actin, and cytokeratin (AE1/AE3). The Ki-67 proliferation index was 1–2%.

A 64‐year‐old man was referred with a 3-week history of an asymptomatic growth on his lower right lip that had failed to respond to antibiotics and antifungal therapy. He initially attributed the lesion to shaving trauma. On examination, the lesion measured approximately 4 cm in diameter, was soft, erythematous, and had overlying crusting. The patient was otherwise well. His medications included omeprazole and amlodipine. Six months earlier, he had undergone a laparoscopic nephrectomy for a renal tumor that was histologically Fuhrman grade IV clear-cell renal cell carcinoma. He was an ex-smoker and consumed alcohol within safe limits. On the basis of the history and appearance, the provisional diagnosis was a rapidly growing squamous cell carcinoma or keratoacanthoma.

A 64-year-old African-American woman presented with a two-year history of asymptomatic enlargement in the right anterior region of her edentulous mandible. On clinical examination, there was a firm, multi-lobulated expansion measuring approximately 2 cm in diameter in the area of the right lower canine, covered by intact mucosa. An occlusal radiograph revealed a well-demarcated multilocular radiolucent lesion in the same region. Based on these findings, a cyst of odontogenic origin was suspected.

A 55-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of gradual, painless swelling of the floor of the mouth and submental region, accompanied by difficulty in speech and swallowing. She had no history of trauma, surgery, fever, diabetes, hypertension, tuberculosis, or chronic illness. Vital signs were normal. Examination of the central nervous, cardiovascular, chest, and abdominal systems was unremarkable. Local examination revealed cystic, nonpulsatile, noncompressible, nontender, nontranslucent swellings in both the sublingual and submental areas. The submental swelling did not move with tongue protrusion, and there were no signs of inflammation. Compression of one swelling did not transmit pulsation to the other. The initial clinical diagnosis was plunging ranula versus dermoid/epidermoid cyst. 
Ultrasonography showed, in the sublingual lesion, a cystic mass with uniform low-level echogenicity and internal particulate content without vascularity on color Doppler; in the submental lesion, a cystic mass containing multiple floating echogenic lobules (“stack of marbles”) without posterior acoustic shadow or internal vascularity. Noncontrast CT of the face demonstrated hypodense cystic lesions in both the sublingual and submental regions. MRI revealed two separate cystic lesions that were T1-weighted hyperintense, T2-weighted and STIR hyperintense, and showed diffusion restriction on DWI and ADC sequences; the submental lesion additionally contained discrete T1-/T2-weighted/STIR hypointense nodules within the fluid. No fat signal was seen within either lesion.

A 79-year-old woman was admitted for progressive asthenia and severe hyponatremia (serum sodium 114.8 mEq/L). Over the previous months, she had developed attention deficits and slight memory loss. Her only medication was a calcium-channel blocker for mild hypertension. She and her relatives denied excessive water intake. She had a 10-year history of HCV-related liver disease. On examination, she was euvolemic, BMI was 20.5 kg/m2, blood pressure 145/90 mmHg, heart rate regular, and there was no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed a low plasma osmolality (253 mOsm/L), urinary sodium 151 mEq/L, and normal blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, thyroid and adrenal function, urinary catecholamines, and chromogranin A. Chest radiography demonstrated mediastinal enlargement.
