Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a 10 × 8 × 7 cm inhomogeneous solid mass in the anterior mediastinum abutting the left pleural space, and a nodular lesion in the liver (segment 3). Brain imaging was normal. An 18F-FDG PET/CT scan showed intense uptake in the mediastinal mass (SUVmax = 10). Despite 6 days of continuous 3% hypertonic saline infusion, her serum sodium increased only to 128.5 mEq/L.

A 46-year-old man presented with an asymptomatic growth on the lingual gingiva of the left mandibular second premolar and first molar, first noted 4 years earlier and enlarging over the past 4 months, now interfering with chewing. He was otherwise healthy, with noncontributory medical and family histories. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender, well-circumscribed, sessile mass about 10 mm in diameter on the lingual gingiva of the left second premolar and first molar; the overlying mucosa was intact. Bilateral mandibular tori were also present near the second premolars. A 12 mm clinical attachment loss was recorded between the left second premolar and first molar. Occlusal and panoramic radiographs revealed a well-circumscribed, radiopaque, spherical mass on the lingual aspect of the left premolar-molar region.

A 16-year-old male presented with a 6-month history of right knee pain and intermittent clicking. He denied trauma, fever, or prior knee surgery. On examination there was no effusion or ligamentous laxity. A palpable click occurred at terminal flexion. Range of motion was 0° to 130°, with painful limitation at full flexion.

Anteroposterior radiographs of the knee were normal. On the lateral view, there was a well-defined radio-opaque shadow at the posterior aspect of the distal femur. Sagittal and axial T2-weighted MRI of the knee demonstrated a lobulated, heterogeneously hyperintense lesion arising from the medial aspect of the lateral femoral condyle, with continuity of its medullary cavity with that of the lateral femoral condyle.

A 40-year-old man presented in January 2017 with a 6-month history of dozens of painful, erythematous nodules on his chest, arms, and shoulders, accompanied by progressive severe abdominal and joint pain. His past medical history included lymphocytic vasculitis and rotator cuff injury. Medications were azathioprine, prednisone, and intravenous immunoglobulin. On examination, multiple erythematous and painful papules and nodules, up to 1.5 cm in diameter, were bilaterally distributed on his forearms, upper arms, and shoulders. 

In 2017, a punch biopsy showed a moderate superficial and deep lymphocytic perivascular infiltrate with small lymphoid cells and minimal cytologic atypia, interpreted as a vasculopathic reaction.

Ten months later, he returned with approximately 12 persistent painful erythematous nodules measuring 2–3 cm in diameter on his arms and chest; the lesions lacked necrosis, purpura, or petechiae. A second punch biopsy again revealed a moderate superficial and deep perivascular lymphoid infiltrate with minimal cytologic atypia. Given the clinical persistence and cellularity of the infiltrate, the dermatopathologist elected to perform immunohistochemical staining to further characterize the lesional cells.

A 74-year-old man presented with a one-month history of progressive dysphagia, moderate dyspnea, hoarseness, and neck pain. He had a known multinodular goiter for 10 years. On examination, there was painless diffuse neck stiffness. Laboratory tests showed TSH 1.63 μIU/mL, free T3 3.26 pg/mL, free T4 1.13 ng/dL, anti-thyroperoxidase antibody 5.04 IU/mL, calcitonin 1.05 pg/mL (all within normal limits), and an elevated thyroglobulin antibody of 619.4 IU/mL.  
Neck ultrasound revealed a conglomerated isoechoic nodule filling the right lobe with microcalcifications and poorly delineated borders, and similar nodules in the left lobe; right cervical levels 2 and 3 lymph nodes (largest 14 × 17 × 24 mm) had the same appearance. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of both thyroid lobes and the cervical lymph nodes was reported as “compatible with thyroid anaplastic carcinoma,” after which a right-sided neck hematoma developed. Coagulation studies and platelet function were normal, and the hematoma resolved.  
Contrast-enhanced neck CT showed bilaterally heterogeneous thyroid enlargement with calcifications, enlargement of the right sternocleidomastoid muscle, multiple enlarged bilateral neck lymph nodes (up to 3 cm), edema of the right supraclavicular fat and skin, right paralaryngeal soft-tissue thickening causing airway narrowing, and leftward deviation of the larynx. Endoscopy confirmed laryngeal edema and right vocal cord paralysis.  
Thoracic CT demonstrated multiple pulmonary nodules suggestive of metastases. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy revealed active hemorrhage from the right upper bronchus, but brush and lavage samples were negative for malignant cells.

A 26-year-old man presented with a one-year history of constant pain in his left hindfoot after an ankle injury. Initially managed with oral analgesics, he experienced only transient relief. Over the past year, he noted progressive pain and swelling localized to the left calcaneal region. MRI of the left ankle showed high STIR signal within the calcaneus consistent with marrow edema, minimal surrounding soft-tissue edema, and no associated mass, periosteal reaction, or fluid collection; the findings were interpreted as inflammatory change. He was diagnosed with atypical rheumatoid arthritis and treated with steroids and analgesics, but his symptoms remained unremitting, and he continued to limp with pain. On examination, there was local swelling with mild to moderate tenderness over the calcaneus, without overlying skin discoloration, and full ankle joint motion.

A 65-year-old woman presented with a self-palpated small lump in the left breast. Her history included three prior lumpectomies for benign lesions; she took no medications and had no family history of breast cancer. On examination, a 19 × 14 × 19 mm nodule was palpable medially at 9 o’clock in the left breast. Mammography and ultrasound showed a spherical, homogeneous, non-cystic, well-defined mass situated close to the pectoralis major muscle, with imaging features suspicious for muscle invasion. Doppler ultrasonography revealed prominent perilesional and peripheral vascularization. Several enlarged ipsilateral axillary lymph nodes were noted. Core needle biopsies (CNBs) were obtained from the breast lesion and one enlarged axillary lymph node. The breast CNB showed a sharply defined spindle cell lesion separated from surrounding fat: variable cellularity with bland spindle cells in dense collagenous stroma or loose myxoid areas, no infiltrative permeation, and absent mitotic figures. The axillary lymph node biopsy showed no malignancy. Due to discordance between the radiological suspicion of malignancy and the bland CNB findings, a complete local excision was performed. Grossly, the 19 mm nodule was sharply delineated, white, and firm, with regular borders and an 8 mm surgical margin. Histologically, the resection specimen showed small clusters of epithelioid cells with vesicular nuclei and occasional mitoses, focal invasion into adipose tissue with entrapped ducts and lymphocytes, and a central scar-like sclerotic zone. Immunohistochemical studies of the spindle cells revealed diffuse positivity for α-SMA, p63, and cytokeratin AE1/AE3; focal positivity for S100, desmin, and caldesmon; negativity for ER, PR, HER2, CD34, Bcl-2, CD10, and ALK; β-catenin showed cytoplasmic but no nuclear staining; and the Ki-67 labeling index was approximately 2%.

A 65-year-old man with a history of obesity, hypertension, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, type II diabetes mellitus, congestive heart failure, and coronary artery disease (recent stent placement and dual antiplatelet therapy started 3 weeks earlier) presented with two weeks of progressive anterograde amnesia, intermittent confusion, one episode of urinary incontinence, and worsening ataxic gait. On examination, he was alert and oriented except for impaired word recall; there were no focal neurologic deficits.

Noncontrast head CT revealed a heterogeneously hyperdense, lobulated mass measuring 2.8 cm in diameter in the region of the posterior septum pellucidum without ventriculomegaly. MRI of the brain showed a hemorrhagic mass within the cavum vergae, posterior to the columns of the fornix and foramen of Monro, displacing the internal cerebral veins laterally. The lesion had an irregular contour with asymmetric posterior and inferior extension, producing bilateral thalamic mass effect.

A 56-year-old man presented with intermittent dysphagia to solids for several weeks, describing food sticking in the substernal area. He had no weight loss, maintained a good appetite, and had no past medical history or risk factors for esophageal cancer. On examination, he was well-nourished; there were no palpable masses, lymphadenopathy, abdominal tenderness, or organomegaly. 

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed Los Angeles grade A distal esophagitis and a solitary 6 mm nodule at the gastroesophageal junction. Biopsy of the GEJ nodule showed squamous mucosa with ulceration, acute and chronic inflammatory infiltrates, and nests of atypical cohesive cells with clear cytoplasm and mild nuclear pleomorphism in the submucosa. 

Immunohistochemical stains demonstrated vimentin (+), PAX-8 (+), CD10 (focally and weakly positive), and EMA (focally and weakly positive). The atypical cells were negative for TTF-1, S100 protein, CD68, cytokeratin 5/6, pancytokeratin, p63, cytokeratin 7 and 20, p40, and pan-melanoma marker. Histological features and staining patterns were consistent with metastatic clear cell carcinoma.

A 49-year-old Asian woman with a 2-week history of progressive exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, bilateral lower‐limb edema, and palpitations was admitted. She had mild hypertension previously but no other systemic disease. On examination, her blood pressure was 195/138 mmHg, pulse 163 beats per minute and irregular, jugular venous distention was 18 cm, bilateral basal crackles were present, and there was grade II edema of the lower limbs. Cardiac auscultation revealed an irregularly rapid rhythm without murmurs. An electrocardiogram showed atrial flutter. Chest radiography demonstrated a patch over the lower left lung field and bilateral lung infiltrates. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis, an elevated D-dimer (14.14 mg/L), elevated creatinine (3.11 mg/dL), high lactate dehydrogenase (1367 U/L), elevated uric acid (20.9 mg/dL), mildly elevated troponin-I (0.067 ng/mL), CK-MB (11.9 ng/mL), and B-type natriuretic peptide (704 pg/mL). 

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed three intracardiac masses: a fixed, round hyperechoic mass with central necrosis at the left ventricular apex; an oscillating hyperechoic nodule on the anterior mitral annulus; and an irregular heterogeneous mass arising from the lateral wall of the right atrium. Tumor markers were elevated (CA-125, 298.10 U/mL; CA-199, 52.00 U/mL; CA-153, 33.80 U/mL). Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed a lobulated 6.0 × 2.3 cm mass bulging from the right atrial lateral wall and two smaller nodules in the left ventricle, all near isointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, without evident invasion of the myocardium. Enhanced chest CT demonstrated a consolidated patch with central necrosis in the lower left lung and enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes, but no discrete pulmonary nodules or emboli. Despite these findings and the high tumor markers, we could not differentiate between diagnoses of multiple myxomas or multiple metastatic lung tumors.

A 51-year-old man presented with an 8-month history of a sensation of heaviness in the right upper abdomen and a 5-month history of dull, intermittent right flank pain. He denied weight loss, hematuria, fever, or urinary complaints. He was a nonsmoker with no history of hypertension. On examination, he had mild pallor and tenderness in the right flank; no lymphadenopathy was noted. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 10.2 g/dL with normocytic, normochromic red cells, an ESR of 40 mm/h, and normal serum urea and creatinine. Urinalysis revealed mild pyuria that was sterile on culture, negative dip-stick for blood, a normal red-cell count, and mild proteinuria. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a solitary, heterogeneously enhancing, well-delineated mass in the lower pole of the right kidney without hydronephrosis, calculi, or invasion of adjacent organs; no retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy was seen. Chest CT and a bone scan showed no evidence of metastases.  
What is your differential diagnosis?

A 51-year-old man presented with a nine-year history of a painless mass in his left scrotum that had progressively enlarged. Over the past five years, its size caused discomfort and interfered with urination and sexual activity. He denied trauma, weight loss, or any family history of similar masses. On examination, there was a 30 × 30 cm soft, smooth, non–transilluminating mass in the left scrotum that obscured palpation of the left testis and spermatic cord. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies including a complete blood count, serum alpha-fetoprotein, beta–human chorionic gonadotropin, lactate dehydrogenase, and a chest radiograph were all normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 31.1 × 15.1 × 30.5 cm mass of fat density (–3 to –55 HU) extending to the left spermatic cord, without lymphadenopathy.

A 6-year-6-month-old girl was evaluated for severe iron-deficiency anemia. Over the preceding 6 months she had three admissions for hemoglobin as low as 2.8 g/dL, requiring repeated red-cell transfusions and intravenous iron; her hemoglobin fell again to 5–6 g/dL shortly after therapy. There was no history of overt bleeding, but fecal occult blood testing was persistently positive. Compliance with oral iron was poor. She lived with her grandmother in low socioeconomic conditions. On examination she was pale, had failure to thrive (weight 12.5 kg; height 105 cm; BMI 12 kg/m2, z-score −4.98), and a systolic cardiac murmur; her abdomen was soft; stools were black but of normal consistency without fresh blood. Laboratory studies showed severe regenerative iron-deficiency anemia (low serum iron, anisocytosis, poikilocytosis), with normal leukocyte and platelet counts, no inflammatory markers, and normal fecal calprotectin. Abdominal ultrasound and abdominopelvic CT scan were normal. Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy with biopsies showed no bleeding source or pathology. A Tc-99 scan was negative for Meckel’s diverticulum. Celiac disease and inflammatory bowel disease were ruled out by normal anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies, lack of endoscopic findings, and normal fecal calprotectin.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of recurrent diarrhea associated with weight loss, fever, night sweats, and abdominal pain. Colonoscopy revealed a large ulcer in the ileocecal region, and biopsy showed a monomorphic epithelial intestinal T-cell lymphoma. Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated: CD3+, CD5–, CD4–, CD8+, CD56+, TIA+, Bcl-2+, Ki-67 approximately 40%, CD20–, PAX5–, CD10–, Bcl-6–, CD21–, CD23–, CyclinD1–, PD-1–, CD79α–, CD30–, C-Myc–, and EBER–. Targeted gene testing identified a JAK3 deletion mutation with a variant allele frequency of 24.6%. 

Her past medical history was notable for diabetes mellitus and cervical spondylosis. She had no known personal or family history of gastrointestinal disorders. On examination, there was no palpable lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, or skin lesions. Routine hematologic and biochemical tests, including liver and renal function and lactate dehydrogenase level, were within normal limits. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy showed no evidence of lymphoma involvement.

18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated a slightly thickened ileocecal wall measuring up to 2.6 cm with increased FDG uptake (maximum SUV 6.3), multiple pericolic lymph nodes up to 1.5 cm in short axis with elevated uptake (maximum SUV 6.1), and increased uptake in the rectal and colorectal walls (maximum SUV ~7.0).

A 29-year-old G2P2 woman with an uncomplicated pregnancy underwent routine prenatal ultrasonography, which at 30 weeks’ gestation revealed a solid mass in the left fetal lung. She delivered a female infant by cesarean section at 34 weeks; birth weight was 2.4 kg, length 48 cm, and Apgar scores 10 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes. The neonate had no respiratory distress and was discharged home. At 20 days of age, the infant developed sudden cyanosis and was admitted for evaluation. Chest computed tomography showed a solid, irregularly marginated mass in the left lower lobe, closely related to the bronchial airway, with slight mediastinal shift to the right.

A 36-year-old Caucasian man noted a volar wrist mass 4 years ago that gradually increased in size. He now reports paraesthesia in the median nerve distribution, worsened by repetitive flexion of the long fingers. On examination, there is a firm, non-tender, poorly demarcated mass on the volar wrist, attached to the flexor digitorum profundus tendon of the index finger. There is mild thenar weakness without clear muscle wasting.

An MRI performed at presentation showed a 50 × 14 mm T2-hyperintense lesion arising from the index-finger profundus tendon and displacing the median nerve. Thallium-201 scintigraphy demonstrated focal tracer uptake at 30 minutes with complete washout at 4 hours, suggesting a benign process. A CT-guided core biopsy yielded gelatinous material; histology revealed a chondroid matrix with bland cells, reported as suggestive of synovial chondromatosis.

Twelve months later, a repeat MRI showed no change in size. The lesion remained fluid-rich with irregular T2-hypointense septations that enhanced with contrast. The mass displaced the flexor digitorum superficialis tendons of the ring and little fingers volo-ulnarly and those of the index and middle fingers volo-radially. The median nerve was compressed anteriorly with associated T2 hyperintensity over its passage through the carpal tunnel.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 49-year-old man presented in December 2015 with a 3-month history of a painless swelling of the gums on the inner (lingual) surface of the lower anterior teeth. He had smoked 4–5 cigarettes per day for 20 years and used alcohol frequently. His medical history included hypertension treated with nifedipine for 5 years and interstitial nephritis under nephrology care for 5 years. He underwent regular dental prophylaxis. A local dentist had prescribed topical metronidazole gel without improvement.

On periodontal evaluation, he had chronic generalized periodontitis. The lingual gingiva of the mandibular incisors exhibited a firm, sessile, exophytic growth measuring 4 cm × 3 cm, with an irregular surface and areas of ulceration. Probing revealed 6–8 mm deep lingual pockets and mobility of the incisors, with bleeding on probing. Extraorally, firm, mobile, nodular left submandibular lymph nodes were palpable.

An intraoral periapical radiograph showed extensive bone loss around teeth 31, 32, 33, and 41. Based on the history, clinical examination, and radiograph, a provisional diagnosis of pyogenic granuloma was made, with squamous cell carcinoma included in the differential. Nonsurgical periodontal therapy and chlorhexidine mouthwash were prescribed. At 1-week recall, there was no change in the gingival enlargement.

A 53-year-old previously healthy man presented in April 2020 with several weeks of progressive epigastric pain and fatigue.  
Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed a 4.3 × 4.2 × 4.0 cm mass in the pancreatic tail, peripancreatic lymphadenopathy, and multiple liver lesions. His pretreatment CA 19-9 level was markedly elevated at 1.1 × 10^6 U/mL.  
Biopsy of the pancreatic mass confirmed ductal adenocarcinoma with intact mismatch repair proteins and a KRAS G12V mutation. With excellent performance status, he began modified FOLFIRINOX.  
A pretreatment baseline CT demonstrated progression of hepatic metastases, enlarging lymph nodes, new bone lesions, and small pulmonary nodules, as well as bilateral pulmonary emboli; anticoagulation was started.  
After four cycles of FOLFIRINOX, CA 19-9 levels declined exponentially, reaching a nadir of 28,612 U/mL. Follow-up CT in mid-July showed decreased size of hepatic lesions (for example, segment 6 lesion from 3.2 × 3.1 cm to 2.1 × 1.7 cm) and reduced lymphadenopathy, but new bone lesions, increasing ascites, and “redemonstration of multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules with associated nodular interlobular septal thickening, overall subtle but increased from prior exam.”  
Given the discordant biomarker and imaging findings, he was referred to pulmonology to evaluate the lung abnormalities, including progression of pulmonary metastatic disease, failure of anticoagulant therapy, drug toxicity, or infection.

A 10-year-old boy presented with two months of progressively worsening low back pain and bilateral lower extremity pain, worse at night and on waking. He reported difficulty bending at the waist but denied sensory or motor deficits and had no bladder or bowel dysfunction.  
On lumbar spine CT, there was a well-defined hyperdense lesion at the L3 level. On MRI, the lesion was intradural and extramedullary, displaced the cauda equina ventrally, appeared faintly hyperintense on T1-weighted images, hypointense on T2-weighted images, and showed uniform contrast enhancement without a dural tail sign. There was no clear continuity with the dura mater on imaging. MRI of the cervical, thoracic, and intracranial compartments revealed no additional lesions.  
The preoperative diagnosis was thought to be a meningioma, including the possibility of a clear cell subtype.

An 11-year-old girl presented with a 2-year history of a slowly enlarging swelling on the right lateral border of her tongue. The mass was painless, had no associated bleeding, dysphagia, or voice changes, and she reported occasional tongue biting while eating. She had no relevant medical, dental, or family history. On examination, there was a 4×2 cm hard, non-mobile, non-tender mass on the middle third of the tongue’s lateral border, extending from the dorsal to the ventral surface, with intact mucosa and preserved tongue mobility. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the tongue showed a 9×8 mm well-defined, rounded, enhancing mass on the right lateral middle third of the tongue, confined to intrinsic muscles and not crossing the midline.

A 41-year-old woman presented with an asymptomatic lesion on the nape of her neck that had enlarged slowly over 5 years. She denied prior trauma. Her medical, surgical, and medication histories were unremarkable. On examination, there was an ill-defined, linear, reddish-brown, indurated plaque measuring approximately 7 × 3 cm over the posterior neck. Based on the clinical presentation, the differential diagnosis included dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, dermatofibroma, morphea, and hypertrophic scar. A 3 mm punch biopsy was obtained under local anesthesia and sent for histopathological examination.

A 46-year-old man presented in February 2001 with a complaint of a “brown spot” on his left eye that had been enlarging in size. On slit-lamp examination, there was a darkly pigmented, subconjunctival mass in the inferonasal quadrant of the left eye. Gonioscopy demonstrated tumor infiltration of the anterior chamber angle. Ultrasound biomicroscopy revealed an echolucent channel communicating between the pars plana internally and the subconjunctival mass externally. The patient underwent en bloc removal of the tumor via iridocyclectomy with placement of a corneoscleral patch graft. The resected tissue measured approximately 9.5 × 7.5 mm and included portions of sclera, ciliary body, and iris.

A 49-year-old man presented with spontaneous epistaxis and left periorbital pain of one month’s duration. He had a 20-pack-year smoking history and no significant past medical or family history. On referral, CT and MRI demonstrated a mass with bone destruction involving the left maxillary, ethmoid, and frontal sinuses, and a focal contrast-enhanced lesion in the left ilium. PET/CT showed intense FDG uptake in the nasal mass (SUVmax 22.7) and in the left ilium (SUVmax 7.8). Vital signs were normal. Examination revealed left facial erythema, blepharoptosis, and proptosis; the left pupil was fixed with impaired adduction and V1 sensory loss. Routine laboratory studies including SCC antigen and soluble IL-2 receptor were within normal limits. Nasal biopsy showed sheets of undifferentiated round cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. Immunohistochemistry was diffusely positive for CD99 and cytokeratin CAM5.2, focally positive for S-100 protein, and negative for cytokeratin AE1/AE3, CD3, CD20, CD56, synaptophysin, desmin, and myoglobin. On the basis of these findings, the tumor was diagnosed as a metastatic Ewing’s sarcoma family tumor, and treatment with vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and doxorubicin (VDC) was initiated.

A 60-year-old man with a 30-pack-year smoking history and multiple sexual partners presented with a 5-year history of a slowly enlarging lesion on the lateral aspect of the penile shaft. He reported recurrent episodes of urethritis in the past. He first noted a small maculopapular spot that gradually increased in size and became erythematous. He did not seek medical attention initially due to embarrassment. On examination, there was a solitary, well-demarcated erythematous plaque on the lateral shaft; no inguinal lymphadenopathy was palpable. Serologic testing was positive for human papillomavirus, type 16. A punch biopsy of the lesion revealed an in situ squamous cell carcinoma of the penis.

A 69-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of cough that worsened over the previous month. Her family physician noted a right pleural effusion on chest radiography and referred her for further evaluation. Her medical history included fibromyalgia, lumbar spinal canal stenosis, and chronic eczema. She had smoked a few cigarettes daily at age 20, had office and then homemaker occupations, and reported no known asbestos or dust exposure.

On presentation, contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax and abdomen showed a mass in the posterior mediastinum without obvious invasion of the esophagus or trachea, and bilateral pleural effusions with right-side predominance. Esophagogastroscopy performed to evaluate a possible esophageal submucosal tumor revealed no abnormal findings. Three weeks later, after right thoracic drainage for increased effusion, PET-CT demonstrated a large posterior mediastinal mass with patchy 18F-FDG uptake extending into the dorsal right lobe of the thyroid gland.

Laboratory studies showed mild elevation of soluble interleukin-2 receptors; other values were within normal limits. Analysis of the right pleural fluid revealed a pale yellow, viscous exudate with a hyaluronic acid level of 271 000 ng/mL. Cytologic examination was suggestive of malignant mesothelioma but was not definitive.

A 32-year-old man presented with massive swelling of his left lower limb since childhood, first noted at age 4. Over 28 years, the swelling gradually increased. Six months before presentation, he developed multiple bullae on the lateral upper aspect of the leg, some measuring up to 3 × 3 cm; several ruptured, causing painful superficial ulcers exuding serosanguinous fluid. One ulcer developed a vegetative growth. On examination, the skin was indurated with red-to-brown macules and papules; a focus of healing ulceration was noted. Inguinal lymph nodes were not palpable. He had no family history of lymphedema and no response to prior antifilarial treatment; buffy coats were repeatedly negative for filarial organisms.

Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the thickened skin around the ulcers yielded a moderately cellular smear with clusters and singly scattered plump pleomorphic cells exhibiting a vasoformative pattern and occasional vacuolated cytoplasm. The cells were large, with dark hyperchromatic nuclei and moderate eosinophilic cytoplasm, leading to a preliminary diagnosis of a vasoproliferative lesion, probably angiosarcoma.

A skin biopsy from the same site showed focal epidermal ulceration. The upper dermis contained large vascular spaces lined by flattened to mildly plump endothelial-type cells. The lower dermis demonstrated collections of neoplastic squamoid cells in islands with wide areas of necrosis infiltrating into the subcutis; a focal nest contained a squamous pearl, yielding a provisional diagnosis of poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma versus angiosarcoma. Immunohistochemical studies were performed for further confirmation.

A 94-year-old African-American woman was admitted with cellulitis of the right lower extremity and a 3-month history of rapidly developing, painful, and bleeding cutaneous lesions in the same area. She had chronic bilateral lower extremity lymphedema since age 34 but denied prior trauma, malignancy, pelvic surgery, infection, thrombosis, or family history of lymphedema. Her medical history included diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, and chronic venous stasis with ulcerations. 

On examination, there was an ulcerated plaque with jagged borders and multiple firm black nodules above the right medial malleolus. Smaller skin-colored to black nodules and a few bullae extended proximally on the right lower leg. Diffuse nonpitting edema and hyperpigmented macules and patches were present bilaterally. No popliteal or inguinal lymphadenopathy was noted.

Differential diagnoses included acroangiodermatitis, Kaposi’s sarcoma, squamous cell carcinoma, melanoma, and angiosarcoma. Two punch biopsies were taken from the edge of the tumor. Histologic examination showed an inflamed scale/crust with underlying epidermal hyperplasia and prominent ectasia of the superficial vasculature. In the mid to deep reticular dermis, there were poorly formed vessels lined by pleomorphic and hyperchromatic endothelial cells; occasional mitotic figures were noted, and the vessels dissected between the dermal collagen bundles.

A 47-year-old man with a 29 pack-year smoking history was transferred for progressive paraparesis, chronic infected left buttock pyoderma, and persistent fever. Seventy-one days earlier, CT had shown an L2 vertebral fracture and a 20×25 mm left adrenal mass; debridement of the buttock pyoderma then grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus anginosus. He developed complete paraplegia and MRI revealed spinal canal stenosis from mass-like vertebral lesions. He reported a 10 kg weight loss over one year. On admission, he was febrile (38.4 °C), hypotensive (99/61 mmHg), and tachycardic (121 bpm). Examination showed diminished breath sounds, abdominal distension, bilateral flank edema, chronic left buttock pyoderma, and a painless 20 mm subcutaneous nodule in the right buttock. Neurologic exam demonstrated flaccid paralysis of both lower limbs with sensory loss below the nipples. Laboratory tests revealed leukocytosis, normocytic anemia, hypoalbuminemia, elevated LDH (433 U/L) and CRP (15.81 mg/dL), hyponatremia, coagulation abnormalities, and elevated carcinoembryonic antigen (6.6 ng/mL) and neuron-specific enolase (33.8 ng/mL). Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 10 mm right upper lobe lung nodule, bilateral pleural effusions, osteolytic changes in the thoracolumbar vertebrae, a 70×40 mm mass around the right seventh rib, bilateral adrenal enlargement (right 84×100 mm, left 79×60 mm) with liver invasion, and multiple subcutaneous buttock nodules. Pleural fluid was exudative with reactive mesothelial cells. On hospital day 2, a biopsy of the right buttock nodule was performed.

A 28-year-old man with no smoking history presented with 8 weeks of recurrent mild haemoptysis. His medical history was otherwise unremarkable. A chest radiograph showed a 1.5 × 2.0 cm coin lesion in the posterior segment of the right upper lobe. Computed tomography of the chest confirmed a solid mass in that location with an area of central lucency and no hilar lymphadenopathy. Sputum microscopy, culture, and cytological examination were noncontributory. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 14 mm/hr, haemoglobin 14.6 g/dL, and leukocyte count 8.8 × 10^9/L; other hematological and biochemical tests were normal. Despite a course of antibiotics, the patient’s haemoptysis persisted.

A 33-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of pain and swelling of the right vulva. Five years earlier, she had undergone resection of a mass in the right labia majora, which was diagnosed histopathologically as an aggressive angiomyxoma; she received no adjuvant therapy. Two years later, the lesion recurred and was again excised. She now presents with a second recurrence.

She has no other medical conditions or medications. On examination, there is a well-circumscribed, non-tender, soft, 8 × 8 cm mass on the right side of the perineum, extending from the labia majora into the ischiorectal fossa. There is no lymphadenopathy, no anemia or weight loss, and no bowel or bladder dysfunction. Gynecological exam is otherwise normal.

Pelvic ultrasonography is unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a tubular mass in the right perineal region extending into the intergluteal cleft. On T1-weighted sequences the lesion is hypointense; on T2-weighted sequences it is heterogeneously hyperintense with a laminated appearance. After contrast administration, the mass shows weak, patchy enhancement.

A 19-year-old woman presented after a sudden “drop attack” accompanied by headache. She had no prior medical history or similar episodes. On examination there were no focal neurologic deficits and vital signs were within normal limits. Brain MRI demonstrated a 3.0 × 2.6 cm lesion in the posterior body/atrium of the right lateral ventricle, extending 3.6 cm craniocaudally. The mass was isointense to gray matter on T1, hypointense on T2, and showed avid heterogeneous post-contrast enhancement with a central nonenhancing necrotic area. It extended into the right pericallosal and periventricular white matter and produced moderate vasogenic edema in the right parietal and posterior frontal lobes. At this stage, the leading radiologic considerations were two malignant intraventricular tumors: choroid plexus carcinoma and glioblastoma.

A 52-year-old woman with a history of left total mastectomy and adjuvant hormone therapy for breast cancer at age 32, disease-free for 20 years, presented with a 2-month history of oral dryness and nocturia. Her urine output was 4355 mL/day, with urine osmolality of 210 mOsm/kg. During a 5% hypertonic saline infusion, serum sodium rose from 145 to 159 mEq/L without an increase in plasma vasopressin (0.4 pg/mL). After administration of vasopressin, urine output decreased and urine osmolality increased to 563 mOsm/kg, confirming central diabetes insipidus.  
Contrast-enhanced MRI performed one month after the initial study revealed a 10 × 5 × 10 mm mass in the posterior pituitary. On T1-weighted imaging, the mass was hypointense with loss of the normal posterior pituitary bright spot; on T2-weighted imaging, it demonstrated moderate signal intensity. The lesion enhanced uniformly after contrast and extended into the suprasellar cistern with contiguous thickening of the pituitary stalk. Compared with the prior MRI, the mass had increased in size by 1 mm over one month.

An 82-year-old man presented with an 18-month history of a right preauricular mass that was nontender but had grown rapidly over the past 6 months. His medical history included untreated chronic lymphocytic leukemia (diagnosed in 2004), right-sided renal cell carcinoma treated with partial nephrectomy in 1990, and a left adrenal mass resected in 2007 whose pathology was consistent with renal cell carcinoma. On examination, a firm, mobile mass was palpated in the right parotid region without facial nerve weakness. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a 4.0 × 3.5 cm enhancing lesion involving both the superficial and deep lobes of the right parotid gland. Fine-needle aspiration yielded a sanguineous specimen containing a high proportion of small, monotonous lymphocytes. Flow cytometry of the aspirate was reported as consistent with chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

A 34-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of dysuria and feelings of incomplete bladder emptying. Physical examination findings were unremarkable, and routine laboratory studies were within normal limits. Bladder ultrasound revealed a 15 mm × 11 mm hyperechogenic cystic fluid–filled mass over the area of the left vesicoureteric junction, suggestive of a left ureterocele; pre-void volume was 257 ml, post-void volume was 22 ml, and prostate size was 17.7 ml. There was no hydroureteronephrosis. Cystoscopic evaluation showed a lesion protruding into the bladder lumen from the left lateral and anterior bladder wall with normal overlying urothelium. The patient underwent an uneventful transurethral resection of the bladder tumor. Both ureteric orifices appeared intact, and the resected lesion was firm and solid in consistency with no fluid content. The catheter was removed on postoperative day 5, and the patient was discharged in good condition.

A 71-year-old man was admitted for right upper quadrant discomfort. Seven months earlier, a 20-cm liver mass suggestive of hepatocellular carcinoma had been identified but was deemed unresectable, and he declined further evaluation. For the past three weeks, he experienced reduced appetite, fatigue, and abdominal fullness. On examination, temperature was normal, and the liver was palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin without tenderness. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.0 g/dL; WBC count 68,800/mm3 with 95% neutrophils; CRP 21.63 mg/dL; bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL; AST 60 U/L; ALT 10 U/L; alkaline phosphatase 2,820 U/L; albumin 2.4 g/dL; INR 1.49; AFP 1.3 ng/mL (normal < 8.1); PIVKA II > 2,000 mAu/mL (normal < 40). Viral hepatitis markers were negative. Peripheral smear showed a leukemoid reaction. Blood, urine, and sputum cultures were negative. Chest radiograph and urinalysis were normal. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the liver showed an increase in the known mass from 20 cm to 24 cm, with central necrosis, multiple new small hepatic lesions, and enhancing peritoneal nodules.

A 23-year-old man presented with an 8-year history of a slowly enlarging, painless swelling below his right ear. Nine years earlier, he had a similar swelling excised; histopathology at that time was reported as a dermoid cyst. Examination revealed a 3 × 2 cm mobile, smooth, soft swelling near the angle of the mandible with a previous surgical scar; there was no lymphadenopathy or neurologic deficit. Ultrasonography showed a homogeneous right parotid gland with a well-defined cystic lesion measuring 31 × 22 × 25 mm with internal echoes in the superficial lobe. Fine-needle aspiration cytology demonstrated a proteinaceous background with sparse histiocytes, lymphocytes, and adipocyte clusters, suggestive of a cystic lesion. Contrast-enhanced CT of the parotid revealed a well-defined cystic lesion measuring 21 × 23 mm in the right superficial parotid gland, containing areas of fat attenuation.

A 71-year-old Caucasian man presented with two weeks of nontender erythema of his right ear. He denied trauma, fever, chills, diaphoresis, hearing changes, weight loss, or otorrhea. His medical history included aortic and mitral valve replacements, atrial fibrillation on warfarin, and chronic splenomegaly.

He was started on a prednisone taper (20 mg daily) by his primary care provider, but after two weeks the rash persisted and became bilateral with new nasal tip involvement and onset of tenderness. He was prescribed topical triamcinolone and evaluations were ordered: erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 101 mm/h (normal 0–15 mm/h), antinuclear antibody (ANA) was negative at a 1 : 80 dilution, and rheumatoid factor was negative at < 15 IU/mL.

On referral to otolaryngology, examination revealed erythematous, edematous, tender auricles bilaterally (the left auricle demonstrating lobule-sparing inflammation) and a tender nasal tip; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. A punch biopsy of the auricular skin was performed due to clinical suspicion for relapsing polychondritis.

A 45-year-old woman with a 2-year history of relapsed, refractory immunoglobulin A kappa multiple myeloma presented with a one-month history of progressive blurred vision in her left eye after an initial outside diagnosis of optic neuritis. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and hand motion in the left eye, with a left relative afferent pupillary defect; she denied diplopia or pain with eye movement. She reported bilateral frontal headaches and had a chronic 2-mm ptosis of the left eyelid. Extraocular movements were full. Confrontation visual fields were intact in the right eye but could not be assessed in the left eye. Red desaturation testing showed 100% in the right eye and 30% in the left eye. Dilated fundus examination revealed a normal right optic disc and, in the left eye, disc edema with hyperemia, superior splinter hemorrhages, and a small, lobulated elevation on the nasal aspect of the optic nerve head with blurring of the disc margin and obscuration of small vessels.

A 36-year-old man presented with intermittent left testicular pain refractory to antibiotic and NSAID therapy. Scrotal ultrasound revealed a suspicious left testicular mass, and a left radical orchiectomy was performed. Pathological examination showed a 2.2-cm teratoma associated with malignant intratubular germinal cells and syncytiotrophoblastic cells (stage pT1 pNx pMx). At diagnosis, lactate dehydrogenase was 579 IU/L (normal, 313–618), β-HCG was elevated at 126.6 mIU/mL (normal, <5.0), and α-fetoprotein was 5.5 ng/mL (normal). Liver and renal function tests, electrolytes, and complete blood count were normal.

Thoracic and abdominal CT revealed left paratracheal lymph nodes measuring 11 mm and left lomboaortic lymph nodes measuring 19 mm. The patient received two cycles of bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin. Postchemotherapy β-HCG normalized, but residual retroperitoneal nodes persisted, so a retroperitoneal lymphadenectomy was performed. Histological examination of the resected 4.5-cm polycystic mass showed only teratomatous tissue without any residual nodal invasion.

Three months later, surveillance CT revealed new mediastinal lymphadenopathy. The patient remained asymptomatic, and serum tumor markers, including β-HCG and α-fetoprotein, were within normal limits.

A 49‐year‐old man presented with a 2‐year history of odynophagia, progressive dysphagia to liquids, and regurgitation that had worsened over the past month. He denied weight loss, appetite changes, or aspiration. Physical examination revealed no lymphadenopathy. Routine laboratory studies were within normal limits.

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed a partially obstructing submucosal mass in the upper esophagus with ulceration of the overlying mucosa; the postcricoid region appeared free of lesion on direct laryngoscopy. Biopsy of the mass suggested sarcoma versus sarcomatoid carcinoma.

Contrast‐enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated circumferential thickening of the cervical esophageal wall and a large heterogeneous intraluminal mass compressing the posterior wall of the trachea without invasion. MRI of the neck confirmed a 57×47×43 mm heterogeneous solid esophageal mass with low T1 signal, high T2 signal, marked postcontrast enhancement, and loss of the fat plane with the prevertebral fascia.

A 51-year-old woman presented in March 2022 with a 1-month history of insidious, progressive right knee pain, aggravated by movement and relieved by rest and analgesics. She noted local warmth but no erythema. Initial examination revealed joint tenderness and limited range of motion. She was diagnosed as having synovitis and treated empirically with antibiotics and painkillers, but her pain persisted.

One week later she returned with the same knee pain plus fever. An MRI of the right knee showed a suspected meniscus tear, anterior cruciate ligament degeneration, synovitis, and joint-capsule fluid; no bone lesions or lymphadenopathy were described. She underwent arthroscopic drainage under antibiotic coverage; no tissue was sent for histology.

Over the next 3 weeks, she developed severe knee pain, marked swelling, high-grade fevers to 103°F, profound malaise, unintentional 5-kg weight loss, and near-complete loss of knee mobility. A second arthroscopy was performed 6 weeks after the first; synovial tissue was sent for histopathology, which was negative for malignancy and for Koch’s disease. She was treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics and steroids without improvement.

A repeat MRI showed polypoidal soft-tissue thickening throughout the knee joint, mildly enhancing post-contrast, and multiple linear T2-hyperintense fracture-like signals in the fibular head with marrow edema. Two weeks later, an ^18F-FDG PET-CT demonstrated a large, FDG-avid, peripheral enhancing soft-tissue mass around the right knee (SUV 52.4), mild cortical erosion of the medial femoral condyle, and juxta-articular osteopenia. A mildly FDG-avid right popliteal lymph node and metabolically active right external iliac and inguinal nodes were noted, though no lymphadenopathy was palpable. One week later, she underwent open debulking of the knee lesion and excisional biopsy of the popliteal node; specimens were sent for histopathology and immunophenotyping.

A 78-year-old woman with hypertension and hyperlipidemia, who had never undergone colorectal cancer screening, presented for colonoscopy. On review of systems, she reported mild dysphagia. Physical examination revealed a soft, non-tender anterior cervical lymph node and enlargement of the left supraclavicular lymph node (Virchow’s node). Upper endoscopy showed a partially occluding submucosal lesion in the oropharynx without ulceration or mucosal involvement; a few small polyps were noted in the esophagus, and the stomach and duodenum appeared normal. Colonoscopy demonstrated innumerable uniform polyps, increasing in number from the transverse colon to the cecum, resembling a polyposis syndrome. Multiple biopsies were obtained from the cecum, ascending colon, and transverse colon. Initial pathology returned as an atypical lymphocytic infiltrate.

A 28-year-old primigravida at 29 weeks’ gestation experienced a 3-minute generalized tonic–clonic seizure in the community and was brought to the emergency department. On arrival, her consciousness had returned to baseline. She denied headache or visual symptoms. Her blood pressure and other vital signs were within normal limits. Physical and neurologic examinations were unremarkable. Her pregnancy history had been uncomplicated, with no prior medical or family history of seizures or neurologic disease. Laboratory investigations, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were normal. Obstetric ultrasound confirmed a single live fetus in cephalic presentation without placental or amniotic fluid abnormalities. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed a 5.3 by 3.2 cm extra-axial dural-based mass overlying the left frontal and temporal lobes, with moderate mass effect. She was started on dexamethasone and levetiracetam and admitted for observation.

A 45-year-old Saudi woman presented with an 8-month history of a right buttock swelling that had rapidly increased in size over the past 2 months and caused pain on sitting. She also reported lethargy but no weight loss or history of trauma. Her medical history included type 1 diabetes mellitus for 11 years and hypothyroidism for 4 years, treated with insulin and thyroxine 50 µg daily. She was a non-smoker.

On examination, vital signs were stable. In the right gluteal region there was a fixed, hard, noninflammatory mass measuring approximately 13 × 10 cm, moderately tender, with no inguinal lymphadenopathy. The remainder of the musculoskeletal and neurologic examinations was unremarkable. Neck examination revealed an enlarged, non-tender right thyroid lobe without cervical lymphadenopathy. Chest, cardiovascular, and abdominal examinations were normal.

Routine hematology, serum electrolytes, and liver and renal function tests were within normal limits. MRI of the pelvis demonstrated a 13 × 11.7 × 6.8 cm lobulated heterogeneous mass centered within the right gluteus medius muscle, also involving the gluteus maximus and piriformis muscles, and extending to the right iliac bone and sacroiliac joint. The anteroposterior center of the lesion lay within muscle, suggesting a primary muscular origin rather than a bone lesion.

A 17-year-old male presented with a 1-week history of intermittent generalized colicky abdominal pain and bloody stools. Initially his stools were well formed with bright red blood; over the week he noted increased frequency, urgency, and melena. He denied fevers, nausea, vomiting, rash, joint pain, recent travel, medications, or sick contacts, and had no prior gastrointestinal bleeding. His medical history included mild persistent asthma on inhaled corticosteroids and candida esophagitis several years earlier. Family history was notable for rheumatoid arthritis, ulcerative colitis, and celiac disease on the maternal side.

One day before admission, a complete blood count showed a hemoglobin level of 14.0 g/dL, an abdominal CT scan with oral contrast was normal, and stool cultures were negative. On presentation, repeat testing revealed hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, normal white-cell count, and C-reactive protein 25 mg/L (normal < 7). Intravenous H₂-receptor antagonist improved his pain, but his hemoglobin fell to 10.7 g/dL the next day. A Meckel’s scan was negative. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed no source of bleeding. Colonoscopy revealed a single large bleeding pedunculated polyp in the sigmoid colon measuring approximately 2.0 × 1.5 × 1.5 cm. The lesion was completely removed endoscopically; the remainder of the colon and terminal ileum appeared normal.

Gross examination of the polypoid mass with a 0.5 cm stalk measured 2.0 × 1.5 × 1.3 cm. Microscopic sections showed lesional cells in a nested pattern within the mucosa and submucosa; the cells had clear to eosinophilic granular cytoplasm, well-defined borders, and round nuclei with prominent nucleoli. Resection margins were free of tumor. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated positive reactivity for HMB-45 and TFE3, and negative reactivity for pan-cytokeratin (AE1/AE3), PAX8, synaptophysin, chromogranin, smooth muscle actin, desmin, CD117, CD68, CD34, and Melan-A.

A 24-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of polydipsia, polyuria, headache, blurry vision, and an 11.3-kg weight loss over 6 months. Her medical history included generalized anxiety disorder, depression, and chronic interstitial cystitis; medications were cyclobenzaprine and lorazepam as needed. Initial laboratory evaluation showed a serum sodium of 145 mEq/L and a glycated hemoglobin A1c of 5.1%. A 24-hour urine collection revealed a volume of 8400 mL, urine sodium of 202 mEq/24 h, and urine osmolality of 88 mOsm/kg. A water deprivation test was recommended but not pursued.

Two months later, she returned with progressive, atraumatic thoracic back pain inadequately relieved by acetaminophen, NSAIDs, muscle relaxants, and ice and heat. Lumbar spine radiography showed mild rightward curvature and spondylosis without acute findings. MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrated prominent stenosis from T2 to T4 with a low-signal–intensity mass anterior to the cord. While awaiting neurosurgical evaluation, she developed worsening lower extremity weakness and numbness and sustained a fall. CT of the thoracic spine confirmed an unchanged stenotic lesion. She underwent emergent surgical decompression.

During the 10 hours of preoperative fasting, her serum sodium rose from 143 to 160 mEq/L, and urine osmolality was 109 mOsm/kg. After administration of 5% dextrose in water and 0.01 μg IV desmopressin, her urine osmolality increased to 689 mOsm/kg. MRI of the pituitary gland revealed mild enlargement and loss of the normal posterior pituitary bright-spot signal.

A 52-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a painless bulge in his calf that had been present for 1 year. On examination, a well-defined soft tissue mass was palpated superficial to the Achilles tendon. MRI of the calf revealed a homogeneous oblong mass superficial to the Achilles tendon that was isointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2*-weighted images, and showed homogeneous moderate enhancement after intravenous gadolinium administration.

A 77-year-old man presented with progressively worsening low back pain for 5 months and mild weakness in both legs for 4 months. On neurological examination, he had paraparesis of both lower extremities, with muscle strength graded as 2/5 in the left leg and 3/5 in the right leg. Magnetic resonance imaging of the thoracic and lumbar spine demonstrated an intradural-extramedullary mass extending from T10 to T12 on the ventral side of the spinal cord. The lesion was isointense relative to the spinal cord on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed homogeneous enhancement after contrast administration. On axial postcontrast images at the T11–T12 level, the mass extended laterally into the right intervertebral foramen.

A 46-year-old woman presented with 1–2 months of persistent lower abdominal pain. On examination, a right lower abdominal mass approximating a 16-week gestation size was palpated. Serum levels of β-hCG, LDH, α-fetoprotein, CA-125, and CEA were all within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the abdomen and pelvis showed a well-defined, multilobulated 5.8×6.3×5.7 cm lesion in the pelvic cavity, separate from the uterus and ovaries. The mass was heterogeneously hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2/STIR sequences, with multiple T2-hypointense septae and cystic spaces. Mild diffusion restriction was noted in the solid component (ADC, 1.3×10⁻³ mm²/s). On dynamic contrast-enhanced study, the lesion demonstrated avid progressive enhancement with delayed washout. There was no abnormal enhancement or thickening of the adjacent peritoneum.

A 1-month-old girl was found to have a firm, palpable mass anterior-inferior to the right external auditory canal over the right parotid gland. There was no overlying skin lesion; the mass did not appear adherent to bone or muscle. The patient was otherwise healthy; she was born at term by cesarean delivery as one of a dichorionic twin pair.

Ultrasound of the parotid gland showed a well-defined, encapsulated heterogeneous mass in the superficial lobe measuring 39.4 × 23.6 × 33 mm with posterior attenuation and multiple peripheral echogenic round spots. Color-Doppler imaging revealed peripheral vascularization in an incomplete spoke-wheel pattern; arterial vessels did not reach the lesion’s center and the resistance index was 0.62. No abnormal lymph nodes were seen.

Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an intraparotid lesion that was isointense to muscle on T1-weighted and STIR images, with a peripheral rim of enhancement after intravenous contrast.

Fine-needle aspiration revealed immature atypical cells with no cytoplasm. Immunohistochemical staining was negative for CD1a, S-100, CD99, desmin, and myeloperoxidase, and positive for smooth muscle antibody, vimentin, and leukocyte common antigen. Based on these findings, myofibroblastic sarcoma was proposed as a potential diagnosis.

A 22-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of progressive left leg weakness and sensory loss below the T2 dermatome. On examination, she had decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick below T2 on the left and mild weakness of the left lower extremity. Magnetic resonance imaging of the thoracic spine showed a 2.2×1.3 cm intradural extramedullary mass at the T1–T2 level with well-defined margins and widening of the adjacent neural foramen. The lesion was isointense to the spinal cord on T1- and T2-weighted images, demonstrated homogeneous enhancement on postcontrast T1-weighted images, and contained numerous small low-signal speckled dots on the contrast-enhanced sequences.

A 36-year-old Caucasian woman at 21 weeks’ gestation (normal fetal ultrasound; no comorbidities or medications) presented with a 6-month history of left nasal obstruction and rhinorrhea, which worsened during the first trimester. She also reported episodes of sleep apnea and hyposmia. Nasal endoscopy revealed a grayish polypoid mass with a multinodular surface occupying the entire left nasal fossa. CT and MRI of the paranasal sinuses showed a 24×28×26 mm lesion that was hyperintense on T1-weighted images and hypointense on T2-weighted images, displaying a convoluted cerebriform pattern. The mass completely obliterated the left maxillary sinus, obstructed the anterior osteomeatal unit, and was associated with ethmoidal sinusitis. Vital signs were within normal limits.

A 39-year-old woman with well-controlled HIV infection (CD4 560 cells/mm3; undetectable viral load) presented with a 5-month history of an asymptomatic rash on her bilateral lower legs. On examination, there were indurated, hyperpigmented papules and nodules coalescing into plaques on both thighs. Initial clinical differential diagnoses included morphea, deep fungal infection, and atypical mycobacterial infection. Tissue cultures for bacteria, fungi, and acid-fast bacilli were negative. 

Punch biopsy showed an alternating light and dark appearance at low magnification from histiocytic and lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates spanning the dermis and lobules of the subcutis, with fibrosis, lobular panniculitis with fat necrosis, and edema. There was no obliterative phlebitis. Numerous dense lymphoplasmacytic aggregates with Russell bodies were present. Lipidized mononuclear cells comprised most of the histiocytic infiltrate. Fite-Faraco, Ziehl-Neelsen, Grocott methenamine silver, periodic acid–Schiff, Von Kossa, human herpesvirus 8, and Gram stains were negative. Kappa and lambda in situ hybridization showed a polytypic plasmacytoid population. Immunostaining revealed an IgG4/IgG ratio of 50 percent with 80 IgG4-positive cells per high-power field, and the histiocytic infiltrate was diffusely CD68-positive and CD1a-negative.

A 78-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 4-year history of progressive gait disturbance characterized by imbalance, slow walking, and repeated falls, accompanied initially by a head tremor. One year after onset, she developed recent memory impairment and occasional psychotic episodes. Over the subsequent years, her walking disability worsened to a rigid-akinetic syndrome requiring support for ambulation, and she eventually became wheelchair-bound. Nonmotor symptoms included reduced speech output, impaired comprehension, emotional lability, and dependency in daily activities.  

On brain MRI performed in 2022, there was diffuse, generalized hyperintensity of the supratentorial white matter on T2/FLAIR sequences involving all cerebral lobes. No contrast enhancement was seen on T1 postgadolinium images, and diffusion-weighted imaging showed no areas of restricted diffusion.  

Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a mildly elevated protein concentration of 56.6 mg/dL (reference range, 15–45 mg/dL), with a normal cell count (0 cells/mm3) and glucose level (59 mg/dL). Tests for KOH, bacterioscopy, culture, cytology, and JC virus in the CSF were negative.

A 40-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 2-hour history of left flank pain radiating to the groin. Her medical history was notable for aortic regurgitation, nephrolithiasis, surgically treated stress urinary incontinence, and obesity (BMI 40.8). On examination she was afebrile; vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination revealed left costovertebral angle tenderness (positive Giordano’s sign) without palpable mass. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 12.7 g/dL, normal coagulation studies, and normal renal function. Initial treatment with anti-inflammatory agents alleviated symptoms. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 7.0 × 6.7 cm heterogeneous solid mass without calcifications in the left kidney and an associated perinephric hematoma; there was no evidence of distant lesions.

A 50-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a painless mass on the right side of the frontal bone. On examination, the mass measured approximately 4.0 × 3.5 cm, was well circumscribed, soft, nonmobile, and non-tender. Laboratory studies and neurologic examination were unremarkable.

Plain radiography of the skull showed a large, circumscribed radiolucent lesion in the right frontal bone without adjacent soft-tissue swelling. CT of the head demonstrated a lytic lesion of the frontal bone with a soap-bubble appearance, cortical destruction of the inner and outer tables, and an associated soft-tissue component. Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed a lobulated frontal-bone mass measuring 3.7 × 3.3 × 2.8 cm that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed avid enhancement on postcontrast sequences.

A 21-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of a gradually enlarging, nonpainful swelling of the upper front tooth region, causing mild discomfort. On extraoral examination, there was a 3 × 3 cm, hard, nontender, diffuse swelling of the left midface. Intraorally, a retained deciduous tooth (#63) and a missing permanent tooth (#23) were noted; there was vestibular obliteration from teeth #22 to #25 with an eggshell crackling on palpation. Fine-needle aspiration yielded 3.8 mL of straw-colored fluid. Periapical and occlusal radiographs showed a well-defined radiolucent lesion from teeth #22 to #26 with root resorption of #63, #24, and #25. Orthopantomogram confirmed a unilocular radiolucency in the left anterior maxilla associated with an impacted #23 and adjacent root resorption. A provisional diagnosis of a dentigerous cyst was made, and the differential diagnoses included adenomatoid odontogenic tumor, unicystic ameloblastoma, and calcifying epithelial odontogenic cyst.

A 64-year-old woman with a 30-pack-year smoking history and a history of stage IVa follicular non-Hodgkin lymphoma diagnosed in 2003 presented in September 2008 with progressive dyspnea and loss of appetite. Her lymphoma had previously involved iliac lymph nodes and bone marrow, and she received palliative radiotherapy to iliac and supraclavicular sites in 2003 and 2007. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax, neck, and abdomen showed massive left hilar lymphadenopathy compressing adjacent bronchus and veins, mediastinal (subcarinal) and parasternal lymphadenopathy, and a small left pleural effusion. PET scanning revealed multifocal FDG uptake in these regions and low-level uptake in the para-aortal lymph nodes.

Bronchoscopy demonstrated mild edema of the left lower lobe bronchial mucosa; bronchial brushing, lavage, and endobronchial biopsies were performed along with transbronchial needle aspiration of the subcarinal node and pleural fluid sampling. In addition, transthoracic fine-needle aspiration of a left sternal mass was obtained. All these tests failed to establish a diagnosis.

A 34-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of recurrent episodes of breathlessness, fever, and cough with haemoptysis. Two months earlier, diagnostic and therapeutic rigid bronchoscopy had been performed after a CT scan showed a bronchial mass; during that procedure he had bronchospasm and desaturation that responded to oxygen, bronchodilators, and steroids. 

On current evaluation, routine laboratory tests were normal except for a haemoglobin concentration of 10 g/dL. Electrocardiogram and pulmonary-function tests (forced vital capacity 4.43 L [98% predicted], FEV1 3.16 L [82% predicted]) were normal. CT of the chest showed a 15 × 19 × 20 mm mass in the left main bronchus projecting into the carina and trachea. Flexible bronchoscopy revealed a polypoid, vascularized tumour occluding the left main bronchus and arising from its posterior wall.

A 61-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of headache and left eyeball pain. She had no significant medical history. On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally and intraocular pressure was 12 mm Hg in the right eye and 15 mm Hg in the left eye. The left eye showed 2 mm of proptosis, complete ptosis, and marked limitation of extraocular movements in all directions, along with conjunctival injection. There was no lymphadenopathy. A CT scan of the orbits revealed subtle enlargement of the left extraocular muscles. Under the impression of nonspecific orbital inflammation, she was treated with oral prednisone, with initial improvement of pain and motility. Two months later, she returned with worsened left-eye pain and headache. Examination now showed no light perception, 4 mm of left proptosis, a pale fundus consistent with central retinal artery occlusion, and decreased sensation in the V1 and V2 distributions on the left. Repeat CT of the left orbit demonstrated diffuse, homogeneous enlargement of the extraocular muscles and haziness of the intraorbital fat.

An 88-year-old Asian woman presented with a cutaneous mass on her right thigh that had been present for 30 months. The lesion began as a slightly elevated papule and gradually enlarged into a brown-colored, verrucous lump. Her medical history included hypertension for over 10 years and surgery for squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue 21 years earlier. She denied any family history of autoimmune disease, malignancy, or genetic conditions. 

On examination, her temperature was 36.8 °C, heart rate 82 beats/min, blood pressure 130/80 mmHg, and respiratory rate 19 breaths/min. A well-demarcated, 3.0 cm × 2.8 cm tumour with areas of exulceration was noted on the right thigh, and no palpable lymphadenopathy was present.

Laboratory tests showed a glomerular filtration rate of 59 mL/min, uric acid 456 µmol/L, triglycerides 2.74 mmol/L, and total cholesterol 6.30 mmol/L. Routine stool, blood, and urine examinations were unremarkable.

Dermoscopy of the lesion revealed hyperkeratosis with fine scales, dotted vessels, linear telangiectasia in the papillae, a white-to-red structureless area, and exulceration.

A 71-year-old man was transferred for assessment of a recurrent large left pleural effusion. He had a nine-month history of progressive dyspnea on exertion and a dry cough, and over the past month he noted worsening shortness of breath. He also reported an 11-kg unintentional weight loss, nausea, and taste changes but denied chest pain or hemoptysis. His past medical history included hypertension, diverticular disease, hyperlipidemia, and gout. He was an ex-smoker (12 pack-year history) and had 27 years of occupational asbestos exposure.

On examination, he was afebrile, heart rate 80 bpm, blood pressure normal, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He appeared cachectic. Chest auscultation revealed diminished breath sounds at the left lower zone. Laboratory studies showed an acute kidney injury (creatinine 116 μmol/L; eGFR 54 mL/min/1.73 m²); the complete blood count was otherwise unremarkable.

A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a nodular thickening of the left pleura extending along the hemithorax and hemidiaphragm, associated with a complex pleural effusion; a 5-mm right upper lobe nodule was also noted. MRI of the brain showed no intracranial lesions. An 18F-FDG PET scan demonstrated extensive FDG uptake throughout multiple pleural masses in the left hemithorax—more prominent inferiorly and extending to the apex—with invasion of the mediastinum and extension into the inferior costophrenic recesses. No FDG-avid lymphadenopathy was identified.

An 11-year-old boy presented with a painless mass in his left iliac region that had been present since birth and had gradually increased in size. He had no significant past medical or family history. On examination, the lesion measured 6 × 5 cm, was soft, mobile, and covered by pigmented skin. Ultrasound imaging revealed a subcutaneous mass with echogenicity similar to adipose tissue and mild perfusion on Doppler assessment.

A 64-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of swelling in the left clavicular region that had progressively increased in size and become painful. She reported long-term polyarthralgia and myalgia but had no motor or sensory deficits in the left upper limb. Routine laboratory tests were unremarkable. A chest radiograph showed increased opacification in the left medial clavicular area, and a focused clavicle radiograph demonstrated concentric thickening of the medial and middle thirds of the left clavicle without cortical disruption. Non-contrast CT revealed a 49 × 28 × 21 mm soft-tissue lesion under the left pectoral muscles—between the first rib, its chondrocostal joint, and the clavicle—containing chondroid calcifications, associated with new bone formation and erosions of the inferior clavicular margin. MRI confirmed a heterogeneous soft-tissue mass adjacent to the distal clavicle, isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images with a hypointense peripheral rim corresponding to calcifications, significant contrast enhancement, and a poor cleavage plane with the subclavian neurovascular bundle. Because of these findings, the initial diagnostic consideration was synovial osteochondromatosis, although it was not possible to completely rule out a primary cartilaginous tumor of the soft tissue, such as chondroma, periosteal chondroma, or chondrosarcoma.

A 12-year-old girl presented with a 3-month history of intermittent discomfort and swelling on the left side of her lower jaw, with rapid growth over the past 3 weeks. Her medical history was unremarkable. On extraoral examination, there was a diffuse, fixed, hard swelling (5 × 6 cm) over the left mandible that was mildly tender but without neurosensory deficits. Intraorally, a firm, immobile, nontender swelling involved the left retromolar region, with marked buccolingual cortical expansion and absence of the left second molar. The overlying mucosa and skin appeared normal.

An orthopantomograph showed a well‐demarcated, spherical osteolytic radiolucent lesion with smooth, circumscribed margins extending from the left second molar region posteriorly into the ramus up to the coronoid process, displacing the inferior alveolar canal. A CT scan confirmed significant buccal cortical expansion and lingual perforation. Aspiration of the lesion yielded no fluid. A differential diagnosis of ameloblastoma, odontogenic myxoma, and adenomatoid odontogenic tumor was formulated based on clinical and radiologic findings.

A 55-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease status post–bypass surgery and emphysema presented with chest pain, dyspnea, cough, night sweats, and a 20-pound unintentional weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic profile, were within normal limits. A noncontrast chest CT revealed a retrocardiac necrotic mediastinal mass measuring 1.2 × 8.6 × 10.7 cm, causing mass effect on the esophagus, left atrium, and pulmonary veins. Transbronchial needle aspiration of a right hilar mass showed benign bronchial cells. EUS-guided FNA of an oval, hypoechoic posterior mediastinal lesion (68 × 70 mm) obtained a core biopsy that demonstrated a spindle cell neoplasm with large nuclei and prominent nucleoli. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for CD117, DOG1, Cam5.2, and AE1/AE3. Somatic genetic analysis of cKIT and PDGFRA revealed no mutations, and germline testing was positive for NF1, suggesting wild-type GIST. Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy identified no other lesions. PET imaging showed FDG uptake in multiple pulmonary nodules, hilar lymph nodes, and a pleural-based lesion on the seventh rib. The patient was started on imatinib.

A 59-year-old Caucasian man with a history of hypothyroidism and fatty liver was diagnosed in 2018 with myelodysplastic syndrome with multilineage dysplasia and very low risk. Initial blood counts showed leukocytes 3.9×10^9/L (neutrophils 1.5, monocytes 1.49), platelets 113×10^9/L, hemoglobin 115 g/L. Bone marrow blasts were 1.4%, normal cytogenetics, and NGS detected SETBP1 mutation (VAF 21%). He was observed without specific therapy.

In December 2019 he developed a 13 kg weight loss, night sweats, fatigue, and anorexia. Vitals: T 36.7 °C, HR 95 bpm, BP 103/64 mmHg, SpO2 100% RA. Exam was unremarkable. Labs: leukocytes 29.7×10^9/L (neutrophils 23.46, monocytes 1.78), platelets 83×10^9/L, hemoglobin 78 g/L. Bone marrow aspiration showed major dysplasia without excess blasts, consistent with CMML-0, and hydroxyurea was started.

In January 2020 he was admitted for psychomotor slowing. He then acutely worsened with decreased consciousness (Glasgow 11), bilateral nonreactive myosis, and right central facial paralysis; no definite limb deficits could be assessed. Labs: hemoglobin 77 g/L, platelets 36×10^9/L, leukocytes 37×10^9/L (neutrophils 31, monocytes 3). Infectious studies, including cultures and serologies (Cryptococcus, Toxoplasma, HIV, HBV, HCV, CMV, EBV, syphilis) and β-D-glucan, were negative. Autoimmune markers including ANA were negative.

Noncontrast CT of the head showed multiple hyperdense nodular hemorrhagic lesions. MRI demonstrated multiple supra- and infratentorial heterogeneous hemorrhagic lesions of varying ages without gadolinium enhancement, with surrounding edema and early left temporal herniation.

A 17-year-old African American male presented with a 2-week history of fatigue, abdominal pain, jaundice, and worsening pallor. On examination, he was pale and icteric, and his spleen was tender and palpable 5–6 cm below the costal margin. Initial laboratory studies showed a hematocrit of 17%, a total bilirubin of 3 mg/dL, a platelet count of 39 000/mm3, and both direct and indirect Coombs tests were negative. A peripheral-blood smear showed anisopoikilocytosis, abundant spherocytes, teardrop cells, and polychromasia, with normal granulocytes and decreased platelets. Bone marrow aspiration revealed a hypercellular marrow without blasts, dysplasia, or hemophagocytosis.

Based on a presumptive diagnosis of Coombs-negative Evans syndrome, the patient received oral prednisone (2 mg/kg/day), weekly rituximab for four doses, and two doses of intravenous immunoglobulin; however, the hemolytic anemia persisted, and he required 2–4 units of packed red cells weekly to maintain a hematocrit above 25%. His spleen enlarged further (palpable below the umbilicus) with increasing pain and distension, and he was referred for further evaluation.

Further work-up included a negative autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome panel, negative cold-agglutinin screen, a reticulocyte count of 10%, a total bilirubin of 5 mg/dL (predominantly indirect), and an undetectable haptoglobin level. Flow cytometry of peripheral blood showed no abnormal blast population and normal RBC expression of CD55 and CD59. Urinalysis was negative for blood or hemosiderin. Infectious studies for Bartonella, brucellosis, tuberculosis, and malaria were negative. An abdominal PET-CT demonstrated marked splenomegaly with multiple heterogeneous, hypermetabolic foci throughout the spleen and in the retroperitoneum, findings suggestive of a lymphoproliferative and neoplastic process.

A 4-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of a swelling between the left scapula and spine. The mother had first noted a painless lump in this area 1 year earlier. Initial assessment by the general practitioner led to a wait-and-see approach for presumed lipoma. Two months later, ultrasound was ordered but delayed by the family; the lesion remained asymptomatic and unchanged in size. 

On referral, there were no systemic symptoms—no fever, weight loss, or night sweats—and no limitations of shoulder movement. Physical examination revealed a firm, nonmobile, nonpainful 5 cm subcutaneous mass just medial to the left scapula; the overlying skin was normal. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

An ultrasound of the shoulder demonstrated a highly vascular, inhomogeneous mass measuring 50 × 21 × 26 mm that appeared fused to the underlying scapula. MRI of the thoracic spine showed a multilobulated mass originating from the left T6–T7 neuroforamen, extending into the lung apex, mediastinum, and left paravertebral muscles without bone destruction; the spine was displaced to the right. ¹²³I-MIBG scintigraphy showed no tracer uptake. Abdominal ultrasound was normal. Comprehensive blood tests, including complete blood count, inflammatory markers, liver and kidney function, lactate dehydrogenase, uric acid, and creatine kinase, were all within normal limits. A 24-hour urine collection showed no elevated catecholamines.

An 8-year-old girl with a history of acute myeloid leukemia (monocytic subtype) in remission for four years presented with a 4-day history of nontraumatic left knee swelling. She denied pain, fever, or ambulatory difficulties. She had experienced similar, trauma-preceded episodes two years earlier that resolved spontaneously. On examination, she was afebrile with stable vital signs, ambulated without a limp, and had diffuse left knee swelling without erythema or ecchymosis; there was full extension and minimal limitation of flexion. Plain radiographs were unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, renal function, peripheral smear, and inflammatory markers, were within normal limits. Ultrasound and MRI of the knee demonstrated marked joint effusion with internal septations and debris but no hemarthrosis, and a focal area of bone marrow edema in the proximal medial tibial metaphysis. Ultrasound-guided aspiration yielded 30 mL of fluid; cytology showed a mixed population of lymphocytes and macrophages with scant neutrophils and eosinophils and no blast forms. A diagnosis of juvenile rheumatoid arthritis was made and treated, but the swelling persisted. One year later, repeat MRI showed persistent synovitis, effusion, and an enlarging, well-defined focal lesion in the proximal tibial metaphysis. During hospital admission, all laboratory studies remained normal; peripheral smear showed no blasts, and bone marrow aspirations from both iliac crests revealed no increase in blast cells.

A 47-year-old multiparous woman was referred for evaluation of a mass in her inferior vena cava discovered on abdominal ultrasound. Over the preceding 2 months, she had experienced nausea, anorexia, and progressive bilateral lower-limb swelling. Her history was notable for partial hysterectomy and right adnexectomy 3 years earlier for menometrorrhagia and uterine leiomyomas; she had no other comorbidities and was not taking medications.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Prominent jugular venous distention and bilateral lower extremity edema were present. Laboratory tests and coagulation studies were unremarkable, and the D-dimer level was within normal limits.
