Transthoracic echocardiography showed a large, highly mobile mass extending from the inferior vena cava into the right atrium and through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, causing severe functional tricuspid stenosis. The mass was stalk-free and nonadherent to the chamber walls. There was severe right ventricular dilation with impaired contractility and a small to moderate pericardial effusion.

A thoracoabdominal CT scan demonstrated a mass traversing from the right ovarian veins through the inferior vena cava into the right atrium, right ventricle, and right ventricular outflow tract, with no evidence of pulmonary embolism. Additionally, a heterogeneous mass was noted in the uterine bed. A dedicated cardiac CT confirmed a homogeneous mass extending from the inferior vena cava through the right heart chambers into the outflow tract, without adhesion to the cardiac walls.

A 15-year-old male presented with an 8-month history of a slowly enlarging mass in the posterior soft palate, associated with a foreign‐body sensation and difficulty chewing, swallowing, and speaking; there was no pain. He was otherwise healthy, with no history of smoking, alcohol use, genetic syndromes, or relevant medical conditions. 

On intraoral examination, there was a solitary, grayish-pink, non-ulcerated, oval soft‐tissue mass on the right side of the soft palate measuring approximately 2 cm × 2 cm × 2 cm. The lesion was firm, non-tender, non-pulsatile, non-bleeding, non-compressible, and non-reducible. Extraoral examination was unremarkable, and no cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. 

A provisional diagnosis of a benign salivary gland tumor was made, and a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the face demonstrated a well-defined, hypodense soft-tissue mass arising from the right soft palate, measuring 2.5 cm × 2.3 cm × 1.5 cm, extending medially to the midline, laterally to 1 cm medial to the alveolar process, anteriorly to the posterior margin of the hard palate, and posteriorly to 1 cm anterior to the posterior margin of the soft palate. Routine blood tests were within normal limits. 

An excisional biopsy under general anesthesia was planned to establish a definitive diagnosis.

A 70‐year‐old man was referred for evaluation of sideropenic anemia discovered on routine blood testing. His medical history included diabetes mellitus, ischemic heart disease with prior coronary stent, bipolar disorder, dyslipidemia, hepatic steatosis, and COPD. He had no evidence of JAK2 mutation, and bone marrow biopsy showed a well‐cellular hematopoietic marrow without clear myeloproliferative changes. Peripheral blood flow cytometry was unremarkable.

An esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed nodular gastric mucosa and, in the pre‐pyloric antrum, a 3.0-cm pedunculated polyp surrounded by hyperemic mucosa. Biopsies of the gastric body were negative for neoplasia and for Helicobacter pylori. Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated a homogeneous, hypoechoic mass arising within the second and third sonographic layers of the gastric wall. The lesion was removed en bloc by endoscopic mucosal resection without complication.

Grossly, the polyp measured 3.3 × 3.0 × 2.0 cm and had a mushroom‐shaped, multilobulated appearance. Microscopic examination showed a submucosal, partially ulcerated lesion composed of spindle- to epithelioid stromal cells with small nucleoli and rare mitotic figures. These cells were arranged in a concentric, “onion‐skin” pattern around small vessels, in a background of myxoid stroma, edema, and a mixed inflammatory infiltrate rich in lymphocytes and eosinophils.

A 22-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of a painless growth in the left posterior maxillary gingiva. It began as a small nodule and gradually enlarged. He denied pain, discharge, or sensory changes but reported mild discomfort while chewing. He has a 4-year history of tobacco chewing. Medical and family histories were unremarkable.

On extraoral examination there was mild facial asymmetry over the left middle third of the face. On palpation the swelling was bony hard and non-tender. A single left submandibular lymph node was palpable, mobile, and non-tender.

Intraorally, there was a well-defined, lobulated, non-tender 3 × 5 cm mass extending from teeth 23 to 27, crossing the midline of the palate, and obliterating the buccal vestibule. Teeth 24 and 26 were vital with grade 2 mobility; tooth 25 was clinically missing. Fine-needle aspiration cytology yielded no fluid. Based on the clinical examination, a provisional diagnosis of ameloblastoma was made, with differentials of ossifying fibroma, central giant cell granuloma, dentigerous cyst, pleomorphic adenoma of the palate, and intraosseous mucoepidermoid carcinoma.

A panoramic radiograph showed a well-defined unilocular radiolucent lesion between teeth 22 and 27, with a sclerotic border and scattered radiopaque flecks. The impacted tooth 25 was displaced apically, and there was root resorption of teeth 24, 26, and 27. Radiographic differentials included dentigerous cyst, adenomatoid odontogenic tumor, calcifying epithelial odontogenic tumor, calcifying odontogenic cyst, ameloblastic fibro-odontoma, and odontogenic fibromyxoma.

A woman in her late 40s (parity 1) with a history of grade 1 endometrioid ovarian carcinoma (FIGO stage IC2), treated 4 years earlier with total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, omentectomy, peritoneal washings, and five cycles of carboplatin/paclitaxel (sixth omitted for toxicity), was referred for suspected recurrence. Her medical history also included asthma and obesity (BMI 37). Routine follow-up included appointments every four months for two years, then every six months. 

Three years after surgery she reported mild abdominal discomfort and intermittent lower back pain. CA 125 was 42 kU/L. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed a complex pelvic mass measuring approximately 7 cm. Diagnostic laparoscopy with biopsy showed tissue “in keeping with an atypical endometrioma,” and she received 6 months of GnRH analogue therapy with serial imaging.

On reevaluation, a CT abdomen and pelvis now demonstrated a 12 cm pelvic mass with wall thickening “in keeping with malignant change.” MRI of the pelvis revealed a part-cystic, part-solid mass with restricted diffusion. PET-CT showed high FDG avidity in the mass. Imaging also described adhesions between the pelvic mass and bowel, without lymph node involvement or distant metastases. The right ureter was obstructed by the mass, producing hydronephrosis and marked right renal atrophy. A DMSA scan confirmed minimal right kidney function. 

An MDT recommended a two-stage surgical approach: exploratory laparoscopy to assess resectability with intent to achieve R0 resection, followed by radical exenterative surgery if feasible.

A 53-year-old heterosexual man and smoker presented with a 7-year history of a progressively enlarging cauliflower-like tumor in the perianal region. He reported constipation, occasional fecal incontinence, decreased appetite, and unintentional weight loss. He had no prior surgeries, immunosuppressive medications, or known hereditary disorders. On examination, there was a circular verrucous mass measuring 13 × 9 cm completely encircling the anal verge; there was no palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy. ECG and chest radiograph were unremarkable. Colonoscopy and anoscopy showed no anal-canal or sphincter invasion. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. Serologic testing was negative for HIV. Viral serology was negative for HPV-16 and HPV-18.

A 5-year-old girl presented with a 3-day history of high-grade fever, lethargy, headache, and vomiting. One month earlier, she had been treated elsewhere for presumed bacterial meningitis with vancomycin and ceftriaxone for 14 days. She had no history of head trauma. On admission, temperature was 38.6 °C, heart rate 144 beats/min, respiratory rate 22/min, blood pressure 110/69 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Physical examination revealed severe neck stiffness and a patchy red discoloration with a small skin dimple at the midline of the occiput. Laboratory tests showed a C-reactive protein of 140 mg/L (normal <5), leukocytosis (21 × 10^3 cells/mm^3) with 90% neutrophils. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed 1920 white blood cells/mm^3 (88% neutrophils), 60 red blood cells/mm^3, glucose 11 mg/dL (normal 40–80), and protein 9.9 mg/dL (normal 10–60); CSF cultures and PCR assays for common bacteria and viruses were negative. Empirical therapy with cefepime and vancomycin was started. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head showed a 21 × 13 mm oval hypodense collection with peripheral rim enhancement between the cerebellar hemispheres. Three-dimensional volume rendering demonstrated smooth, well-corticated funneling of the inner table of the occipital bone and a 1 mm midline defect in the outer table. Brain MRI with contrast revealed that the inter-cerebellar collection had restricted diffusion, heterogeneous T2 signal, and peripheral enhancement, and it communicated through the bone defect with a subcutaneous nodular lesion of low T2 signal intensity and homogeneous enhancement. There were additional signs of ventriculitis and early cerebellitis. Based on MR images, the differential diagnosis included an epidural abscess or an infected dermoid cyst.

A 58-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of a slowly growing mass in his right popliteal region, noting more rapid enlargement over the past 6 months. He reported mild pain and intermittent paresthesia of the right leg and foot. On examination, there was a 4 × 2 cm mobile, solid mass posterior to the knee without erythema, warmth, or ulceration. Tinel’s sign was positive over the mass. Sensory and motor function of the lower extremity were normal. Ultrasound imaging showed a solid mass separate from the adjacent muscles and tendons. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-defined, solid, heterogeneous, dense mass originating from the tibial nerve.

An 84-year-old man with a history of pararectal gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST) diagnosed 22 months earlier—initially metastatic to mesorectal and iliac lymph nodes and iliac bone—presented with rapidly progressive stridor, aphagia, and dysphonia. His prior therapy included 6 months of imatinib halted for Stevens-Johnson syndrome, surgical resection (ypT4 N0 MX L0 V0 Pn0 RX with 10 mitoses/50 HPF), and stereotactic radiotherapy to bone metastases. On examination he had a “hot potato” voice and position-dependent stridor. Endobuccal inspection revealed a 3-cm, round, elastic, non-pulsatile mass on the posterior wall of the lower oropharynx with normal overlying mucosa, obstructing the laryngeal inlet; the larynx was otherwise unremarkable and functional. Cervical palpation was normal. Videoendoscopy bypassed the mass and confirmed vocal cord mobility. Cervicofacial CT showed an infiltrative prevertebral lesion at C3 with partial destruction of the C2 and C3 vertebral bodies causing a mass effect on the oropharynx and hypopharynx. Cervicofacial MRI revealed a 7.2×5.2×4.8 cm mass compatible with a vertebral lesion.

A 71-year-old Caucasian woman was referred after an incidental retroperitoneal mass was discovered on magnetic resonance imaging performed during a routine gynecological examination. The MRI showed an exophytic presacral lesion measuring 2.6 × 6 × 1.9 cm at the level of S2, clearly demarcated, inhomogeneous, isodense to muscle, with moderate contrast enhancement and extension into both S2 intervertebral foramina. The patient reported a 6-kg weight loss over 6 months without fever or diarrhea. On physical examination, there were no neurological deficits. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 11,900/mm3 with a normal differential and no immature or abnormal cells.

A 44-year-old Venezuelan woman presented with a 2-week history of asthenia, fatigue, fever, productive cough, and dyspnea. Her medical and surgical history was unremarkable. On examination, she had grade II hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 5 g/dL; leukocyte count 23.1×10^9/L with 23% neutrophils, 20% lymphocytes, 9% monocytes, 2% eosinophils, 2% myelomonocytes, 4% metamyelocytes, and 40% basophils; platelet count 120×10^9/L. Bone marrow aspirate contained 80% cells with basophilic granules and 20% immature nuclei. A few blasts were myeloperoxidase-positive; blasts and mature basophils were metachromatic on toluidine blue stain, negative for chloroacetate esterase and acid phosphatase; Auer rods were absent. Immunophenotyping showed blasts positive for CD34, CD33, and CD9 and negative for HLA-DR and CD14. Ultrastructural examination revealed azurophilic granules. Conventional cytogenetics on 20 metaphases demonstrated trisomy 19 and t(9;22); fluorescence in situ hybridization detected the BCR-ABL fusion in 95% of nuclei.

A 49-year-old woman with no significant past medical or family history presented with a 6-month history of non-specific upper respiratory symptoms that were COVID-19 and mycobacterial smear negative. Over subsequent weeks, she developed progressive upper abdominal pain (VAS score 8/10) and increasing dyspnea without supplemental oxygen requirement. On examination, her ECOG performance status was 2 with tachypnea, and palpation revealed a large abdominal mass occupying the entire abdominal cavity; there was no peripheral lymphadenopathy or stigmata of tuberous sclerosis. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed a 22 × 13 × 14 cm mass spanning the intraperitoneal and retroperitoneal spaces, with a predominantly fatty component and areas of soft-tissue density. Multiple well-defined nodules up to 2 cm were present in both lung fields. Routine blood counts, biochemistry, renal and liver function tests, LDH, and tumor markers were within normal limits.

A percutaneous core biopsy of the retroperitoneal mass was performed.

A 77-year-old multiparous woman presented with a 2-week history of generalized abdominal pain and distention. She had undergone menopause at age 50 and had a history of dysmenorrhea without prior gynecologic follow-up. On examination, mild to moderate ascites was noted. Pelvic ultrasound showed severe abdominopelvic ascites, omental thickening, and a 155 × 87 mm solid-cystic mass with internal vascularity in the right adnexal region; the left ovary appeared atrophic. MRI of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a mainly cystic mass with a large enhancing mural nodule, ascites, omental thickening, a thickened irregular right fallopian tube, and adhesion of ileal loops to the mass. Laboratory studies included WBC 9300/mm3, hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, platelets 499,000/mm3, negative β-hCG, normal LDH, CA-125 740 U/mL (normal 0–35), CA19-9 78 U/mL (0–37), and HE4 262 pmol/L (<140). Laparoscopy at another center yielded only inflammation and necrosis on biopsy. At laparotomy, severe inflammation, ascites, extensive adhesions, and endometrial implants were noted. A total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, supracolic omentectomy, and partial small-bowel resection were performed. Peritoneal cytology was negative for malignancy. Grossly, the right adnexal mass infiltrated adipose tissue with extensive necrosis; no lymphovascular invasion was identified. Immunohistochemical studies of the right adnexal tumor were positive for vimentin, CD10, WT1, ER, and PR.

A 49-year-old man presented with left testicular bloating and dull pain for 20 years, acutely worsening over the past 10 days. He denied other medical history. On examination, the left testis was enlarged, firm, smooth, without discrete nodules or tenderness, and transillumination was negative; the right testis, epididymides, and vas deferens were normal. Scrotal Doppler ultrasound showed both testes of normal size and contour, bilateral epididymal cysts (largest 0.67 × 0.46 cm), a 1.09 × 0.79 cm well-circumscribed hypoechoic lesion in the left testis with internal blood flow, and a small left hydrocele. Laboratory studies revealed a serum CA19-9 level of 57.5 U/mL (normal <27 U/mL); alpha-fetoprotein, human chorionic gonadotropin, and other tumor markers were within normal limits.

A 35-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of heart palpitations and a palpable mass in the left side of her neck. She had been diagnosed with idiopathic arrhythmia on electrocardiography, and her cardiac ultrasound was normal. She denied diabetes, hypertension, or prior cerebrovascular events.
On examination, a soft, smooth 3 cm × 2 cm mass was noted in the left mid-cervical region; palpation of the mass exacerbated her palpitations. Computed tomography angiography of the common carotid arteries revealed a solid mass at the left carotid bifurcation without abundant vascularity. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a nonhomogeneous lesion at the same site. Preoperative electrocardiography showed a sinus rhythm with frequent premature ventricular beats and a heart rate of 70 bpm.

A 20-year-old woman presented with amenorrhea, left flank pain, and a sense of heaviness for 1 year. She denied weight loss. On examination, her vital signs were stable, and a homogeneous mass was palpable in the left flank. Laboratory studies were within normal limits except for a hemoglobin concentration at the lower limit of normal. Renal ultrasonography revealed a homogeneous mass occupying most of the left kidney. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 180-mm mass involving the entire left kidney with infiltrative borders but without invasion of the renal capsule, renal vessels, ureter, or ipsilateral adrenal gland. An atypical renal cell carcinoma was suspected, and the patient was scheduled for radical nephrectomy.

A 58-year-old woman with a history of childhood acute rheumatic fever and resultant mitral stenosis presented with palpitations, dyspnea, and chest pain. On examination, she had hepatomegaly and a 3/6 systolic murmur at the mitral focus. Electrocardiography showed atrial fibrillation in all leads. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed severe mitral stenosis, tricuspid insufficiency, and a 5-cm mass with areas of calcification on the superior wall of the left atrium; the left atrium measured 17 × 13 cm. Laboratory tests were within normal limits. The patient underwent mitral valve replacement, tricuspid De Vega annuloplasty and plication, and resection of the giant left atrium. A 5 × 1.5 × 1 cm gelatinous, soft, brown, hemorrhagic lesion was removed from the atrial wall and sent for histopathological examination.

A 72-year-old man presented with a 5-month history of sharp, continuous pain and burning in the lower right posterior jaw. He first noted a small ulcer in the right posterior tonsillar region that gradually enlarged. The pain was nonradiating and worsened when eating hot food. He had a 40-pack-year history of bidi smoking. 

On examination, right submandibular lymph nodes were palpable. Intraoral inspection revealed an irregular ulcer measuring approximately 1.5 × 2.5 cm on the right tonsillar region, extending from the retromolar area to the posterior faucial pillar and from the side of the uvula to the pterygomandibular raphe. The ulcer surface was covered with a yellowish-white slough and was soft and tender on palpation. 

Routine blood tests were within normal limits except for a reduced hemoglobin value and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. A panoramic radiograph showed no abnormalities. A posteroanterior chest radiograph was unremarkable.

An incisional biopsy was performed. Hematoxylin and eosin–stained sections revealed superficial dysplastic stratified squamous epithelium invading the underlying connective tissue stroma. The stroma contained islands, strands, and cords of neoplastic epithelial cells characterized by peripheral palisading basaloid cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and scant cytoplasm. In the center of these basaloid islands and strands, there was a component of squamous differentiation.

A 24-year-old man presented with one month of right flank pain. He had no significant family history. On examination, he was afebrile, his vital signs were within normal limits, and the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed an elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase level of 278 U/L (normal, 114–240 U/L) and a plasma D-dimer level of 3.34 mg/L (normal, <0.55 mg/L). Color duplex sonography revealed a round, well-circumscribed, heterogeneous mass in the middle and lower poles of the right kidney. Dynamic contrast-enhanced ultrasonography demonstrated early heterogeneous enhancement with slight delayed enhancement; the decay time was 60 seconds. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a large heterogeneous mass in the same location infiltrating the renal calices, with no evidence of metastatic disease.

A 72-year-old African American man presented with progressive erythroderma and keratoderma of the palms and soles of unknown etiology for more than three years. He was treated by his primary care physician with topical antifungal cream for a presumed tinea infection without improvement. In dermatology clinic, multiple skin biopsies over time were nondiagnostic, revealing nonspecific pathologic diagnoses such as spongiotic dermatitis and psoriasiform dermatitis. He failed to improve after many months of high-dose topical steroids and a short course of oral methotrexate. One month after methotrexate was discontinued, he developed violaceous and erythematous nodules on the cheeks, trunk, and all four extremities.

A 5-month-old girl presented with a 2-month history of slowly growing, asymptomatic yellowish papules and nodules on her face, shoulders, upper back, and flanks. The lesions began as a 0.4-cm reddish papule on the left shoulder, which became yellowish, enlarged, and ulcerated; similar lesions then appeared on the face and torso. There were no fevers, systemic symptoms, or relevant family history.

On examination, there were 12 discrete, non-tender red-to-yellow papules and nodules measuring 0.5 to 1.7 cm, some with telangiectasias and central crusting. Mucous membranes were normal, and there was no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly.

A punch biopsy of two lesions showed a dense dermal proliferation of epithelioid histiocytes with foamy cytoplasm, interspersed spindle cells in a storiform pattern, and a few Touton giant cells. Immunohistochemical stains were diffusely positive for CD4, CD68, and fascin, and negative for c-KIT, myeloperoxidase, CD1a, langerin, S100, melan-A, factor XIIIa, CD3, CD10, CD34, CD21, CD23, CD30, and pan-keratin. Acid-fast and periodic acid–Schiff stains were negative. Phosphohistone H3 staining revealed 40 mitoses per 10 high-power fields, and the Ki-67 proliferative index was 60%.

A 17-year-old male presented with a 3-week history of polydipsia and polyuria. Outpatient tests showed serum sodium of 150.4 mmol/L (normal 135–145) and low urine osmolality. He denied headache, visual changes, fever, or history of head trauma or surgery. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. Physical examination was normal. Twenty-four-hour urine output was 13 L and fluid intake was 10.5 L. Endocrine studies revealed a slightly elevated growth hormone (17.90 ng/mL; reference 0–8) but suppression on a glucose-inhibition test; normal circadian cortisol rhythm; and otherwise normal pituitary hormones. Chest CT, brain/skull CT, and thyroid and abdominal ultrasound were normal. A fluid-deprivation–vasopressin test confirmed central diabetes insipidus. Gadolinium-enhanced pituitary MRI showed diffuse thickening of the pituitary stalk involving the funnel and uniform enhancement of the posterior pituitary.

A 78-year-old man presented with diffuse abdominal pain. He had undergone total excision of a dorsal cutaneous malignant melanoma 4 years earlier, with no evidence of metastatic disease at that time. On examination, he appeared well; his abdomen was soft, without palpable masses. There was no melena, and laboratory studies were within normal limits. Hepatobiliary ultrasound showed multiple hyperechoic nodules measuring at least 1 cm in the fundus, body, and neck of the gallbladder, with minimal to absent acoustic shadowing. The remainder of the abdomen was poorly visualized because of adiposity. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed these gallbladder lesions, which exhibited early intense enhancement followed by progressive washout, and revealed multiple solid masses up to 5 cm in the stomach, duodenum, and ileum with similar enhancement patterns, as well as diffuse peritoneal nodules, mesenteric lymphadenopathy, and pelvic ascites. Chest CT demonstrated bilateral solid pulmonary nodules without pleural effusion. The possibility of metastatic disease was considered.

A male infant was born at 39 weeks and 4 days’ gestation to a primigravida after in vitro fertilization. Apgar scores were 9 and 10. The mother had prelabor rupture of membranes and was group B streptococcus positive. Within the first hour after birth, the infant developed multiple 1–4 mm purple, nonblanching papules and purpura scattered over the body. New lesions continued to appear over the next several hours. The newborn appeared pale but was hemodynamically stable and had no hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies, including a full blood count, infection markers, liver-function tests, and coagulation studies, were all within normal limits. Intravenous antibiotics were initiated because of concern for perinatal infection but were discontinued after 48 hours in the setting of a negative blood culture and clinical stability. Given the ongoing cutaneous lesions and lack of infectious findings, the differential diagnosis included vasculitis or another dermatologic condition, and a biopsy of one of the papules was performed.

A 38-year-old bisexual man with a history of splenomegaly secondary to viral hepatitis presented with fever and non-itchy maculopapular skin lesions. He reported no neurologic symptoms, was a non-smoker, and drank alcohol occasionally. On examination, there were maculopapular lesions on the upper and lower limbs, trunk, back, and soles of the feet; purpuric lesions were noted on the distal third of both legs. A rapid HIV test was positive. Laboratory studies showed WBC 5500/µL, lymphocytes 1200/µL, hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, and platelets 133 000/µL. Serologic tests were positive for syphilis (VDRL and ECLIA) and CMV (IgM and IgG) and negative for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and toxoplasmosis; hepatitis A IgM and IgG were positive. HIV infection was confirmed by a viral load of 251 000 copies/mL and a CD4 count of 182/mm3. Secondary syphilis was confirmed. Pulmonary tuberculosis was excluded by a negative tuberculin skin test, negative sputum smears, and non-specific chest X-ray findings. Chest CT revealed multiple bilateral solid nodules and micronodules at the lung bases. Oral examination identified maculopapular lesions on the hard and soft palate mucosa.

A 70-year-old woman presented in April 2017 with acute cough and dyspnea. Chest radiography and CT showed a left-sided pneumothorax and multiple well-defined nodules in both lungs. She had been aware of bilateral lung nodules since 2002 and was followed without treatment until she discontinued follow-up 7 years ago. Her past surgical history was notable for bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with hysterectomy in 1994 for uterine leiomyoma. She was not on hormonal therapy. Body mass index was 20.9 kg/m2. Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery was performed to treat the pneumothorax and to obtain lung tissue. Histologic examination of the lung biopsy revealed well-differentiated smooth muscle cells without atypia. To assess disease extent, abdominal CT was performed and identified asymptomatic pelvic masses; biopsy of a pelvic lesion showed similar histology. Immunohistochemical staining of both lung and pelvic specimens was positive for estrogen receptor and progesterone receptor. Symptoms improved after resolution of the pneumothorax, and the patient was managed with regular follow-up without additional therapy.

A 66-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and benign thyroid nodules presented with a 5-month history of a gradually enlarging left parietal scalp lesion. She had no personal history of cancer and was up to date with screening mammography. A scoop excision of the lesion revealed a malignant dermal neoplasm extending to the margins. Initial immunohistochemical stains showed strong positivity for estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and E-cadherin; focal weak positivity for cytokeratin 20; and negativity for cytokeratin 7. 

On second-opinion review, additional stains demonstrated strong positivity for GATA-3 and confirmed negativity for cytokeratin 7, cytokeratin 20, p63, and TTF-1. There was no evidence of Her2/neu amplification. Clinical breast examination was unremarkable. A 3D mammogram performed 4 weeks after the biopsy showed no abnormalities. A PET/CT scan 6 days later revealed only a mild left scalp defect consistent with recent surgery and no adenopathy or distant metastases. Four months after the biopsy, bilateral breast MRI showed no identifiable breast lesion.

A 4-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a swelling of the left anterior maxillary gingiva. The parents first noticed bilateral small gingival enlargements 5 months earlier; the right lesion resolved spontaneously, but the left continued to enlarge despite manipulation. Three months before presentation, the primary central and lateral incisors had been extracted by a general dentist for a presumed periapical abscess, but the gingival mass persisted and grew. The patient denied pain and spontaneous bleeding, reporting only occasional interference with mastication. His medical history was unremarkable. Examination revealed slight facial swelling over the left anterior maxilla without lymphadenopathy. Intraorally, there was a 20 × 15 × 12 mm pedunculated, lobular soft‐tissue mass on the left maxillary gingiva at the incisor region. The lesion was firm, with tan, red, and bluish mucosal areas and a focal ulceration. A periapical radiograph showed superficial erosion of the underlying alveolar bone without deeper bony involvement. Based on these findings, a benign gingival lesion was suspected, and the differential diagnosis included parulis, pyogenic granuloma, peripheral ossifying fibroma, peripheral giant cell granuloma, and peripheral odontogenic fibroma. Malignancy was considered unlikely. The lesion was scheduled for excisional biopsy under local anesthesia.

A 30-year-old man with no significant medical history first presented in July 2012 with progressive dysphagia, a sensation of a neck mass, and dysphonia following an upper respiratory tract infection. On examination, a polylobed, mucoid-appearing mass was seen in the right vallecula displacing and deforming the suprahyoid epiglottis and narrowing the airway to a triangular slit approximately 5 cm in length. Hypopharyngoscopy and direct laryngoscopy identified a vallecular cyst, which was removed endoscopically under general anesthesia, with an initially favorable outcome.

In January 2013, he returned with inspiratory dyspnea, worsening dysphagia, stomatolalia, and fever. Examination revealed pronounced inspiratory stridor and a multiform tumor in the right vallecula again displacing the epiglottis, with no pathologic findings on chest radiography. Computed tomography of the neck showed a 105 × 65 × 85 mm, multiloculated, polycystic–appearing mass with internal septa and multiple 3–4 mm calcifications arising in the right vallecula, an appearance that suggested a possible chondroma. 

Under local anesthesia, a tracheotomy was performed, followed by transvalecular excision of the mass including hyoid resection. Epiglotopexy, laryngopharyngography, nasogastric feeding tube placement, and tracheal cannulation were also performed. The postoperative course was notable for a tongue-base hematoma that was surgically evacuated; by postoperative day 4, the tracheal cannula was removed and the patient was breathing normally.

Gross examination of the specimen revealed a polylobate, polycyclic, firm, encapsulated mass with red-violet and light brindle areas. Histologic sections showed nodular myxochondroid proliferation delineated by collagenous fibrosis, chondrocytes with irregular hyperchromatic nuclei (rarely binucleate), low mitotic activity, areas of bone metaplasia, and adjacent striated muscle tissue. The histopathologic appearance suggested a hamartoma tumor (choristoma) but required further evaluation to distinguish it from a low-grade chondrosarcoma.

A 43-year-old woman presented with constipation, a sensation of pelvic fullness, recurrent low back pain, stress incontinence, urinary retention, and nocturia. She had no prior surgeries, comorbidities, or family history of neoplasia. On examination, her abdominal wall was distended, and digital rectal examination revealed an extraparietal soft, elastic mass covered by normal mucosa. Pelvic ultrasonography detected a large mass, which was further characterized by CT and MRI. Imaging showed an 8 × 5.5 cm well-circumscribed, homogeneous fatty mass in the mesorectal and ischiorectal regions, displacing the vagina, rectum, and distal sigmoid colon. There was no evidence of pathological lymph nodes, no ureteral dilation, and only scant free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Renal function was normal.

A 49-year-old woman noted a slowly enlarging, painless mass in her right supraclavicular region for one year. On examination, there was a firm, mobile swelling without weakness, numbness, or functional loss in the right upper limb; skin color and pulses were normal. The remainder of her neck and her ENT examination were unremarkable. Her medical and family histories were noncontributory.

Ultrasound suggested a solid neck mass, and fine-needle aspiration cytology was performed. During the procedure, she experienced painful sensations on the dorsum of the right thumb and forefinger. Cytologic analysis suggested a mesenchymal tumor.

Magnetic resonance imaging showed a sharply delineated, spindle-shaped lesion measuring 61 × 28 × 34 mm closely abutting the C7 nerve roots at the C5–C6 level and the middle trunk of the brachial plexus, with moderate heterogeneous contrast enhancement. On palpation of the mass, the patient again reported unpleasant sensory sensations in the C6 dermatome. Preoperative nerve conduction studies revealed normal motor and sensory responses.

A 24-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 6-month history of swelling of her left eyelid and a sensation of pressure behind the eye. There was no family history of ocular tumors. On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally, intraocular pressures were 20 mmHg in each eye, and there was no afferent pupillary defect. The left eye was slightly proptotic and displaced inferiorly, with exophthalmometer readings of 15 mm on the left and 13 mm on the right. Extraocular movements and visual fields were intact, and the anterior segment examination was normal. Dilated fundus examination showed clear vitreous, normal optic nerves with cup-to-disc ratios of 0.3 on the right and 0.2 on the left, a flat macula on the right, and slightly congested retinal vessels on the left. Optical coherence tomography revealed a horizontal fold in the left macula. Magnetic resonance imaging of the orbits demonstrated an enhancing, well-defined, solid extraconal mass in the left orbit. The patient underwent a left lateral orbitotomy and excisional biopsy of the mass.

A 30-year-old man presented with a 4-year history of a slow-growing, non-tender skin lesion over his left gluteal region. Over the preceding month, he noted focal ulceration of the lesion. He denied any history of trauma, bleeding, or systemic symptoms. His medical and family histories were unremarkable.

On examination, there was a single, pedunculated polypoid mass measuring approximately 3.0 × 2.0 × 2.0 cm with a focally ulcerated surface but otherwise intact skin. The remainder of the skin examination was normal. No regional lymphadenopathy was noted.

Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies including a complete blood count, serum biochemistry, coagulation profile, and urinalysis were all within normal limits; lipid profile was not obtained.

Provisional clinical diagnoses included acrochordon and papilloma.

A 44-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with a several-month history of headache and intermittent visual disturbances described as “flashlights.” On examination, she had early papilledema but was otherwise neurologically intact.

Noncontrast CT of the head showed a left frontal parasagittal, extra-axial mass measuring approximately 4.0 × 4.0 × 2.0 cm. The lesion was mostly isodense, featured a large central calcification, and was associated with overlying hyperostosis. MRI demonstrated a well-demarcated, dural-based mass that was hypointense on T1-weighted images and of mixed intensity on T2-weighted sequences. There was no perilesional edema, and the lesion appeared to compress and narrow the lumen of the adjacent superior sagittal sinus.

Based on these imaging characteristics—an extra-axial, calcified, dural-attached mass without edema—the working diagnosis was a meningioma. Malignant lesions, such as chondrosarcoma, were considered less likely given the lack of perilesional edema and infiltrative features. Surgical resection was therefore planned.

A 67-year-old woman, lifelong nonsmoker, presented with a 2-month history of a mild productive cough and hematic sputum for 24 hours, along with progressive left-sided dorsal pain for 1 month. She had a history of deep vein thrombosis but no occupational exposures or family history of lung disease. Physical examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory studies were within normal limits. Spirometry showed a forced vital capacity of 1.59 L (69.1% predicted), FEV1 of 1.16 L (60.7% predicted), FEV1/FVC of 76%, and a DLCO/VA of 103.3%. A chest radiograph demonstrated a poorly defined opacity in the left lower lung field and blunting of the left costophrenic angle. Bronchoscopy with lavage and transbronchial biopsy was negative for infection or rheumatologic disease but showed an atypical cellular infiltrate with immunohistochemical features suggestive of a proliferative vascular lesion. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a mass in the left lower lobe with a necrotic component abutting the pleura, associated partial atelectasis, and multiple small nodules scattered throughout both lungs; there was a single ipsilateral hilar lymph node without mediastinal adenopathy or significant pleural effusion. CT-guided lung biopsy demonstrated “intense fibrosis and focal changes suggestive of a proliferative vascular lesion,” and a subsequent biopsy revealed the “presence of atypical epithelioid-like tumor cells.”

A 46-year-old HIV-positive woman on antiretroviral therapy presented with a 4-year history of a gradually enlarging swelling on the lateral aspect of her left thigh. The mass was painless, with no discharge, ulceration, sensory changes, or tingling, but it limited limb use by mass effect. Vital signs were within normal limits. Local examination showed a firm, smooth, non-tender, non-mobile mass measuring approximately 40 cm × 30 cm on the lateral left thigh; the overlying skin was normal and there was no inguinal lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 4.73 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 14.1 g/L, platelets 254 × 10^9/L; electrolytes, liver enzymes, and renal function were all within normal limits. A trucut biopsy of the lesion showed mature adipocytes, features suggestive of a lipoma. Magnetic resonance imaging was not performed due to financial constraints. The patient was scheduled for elective surgical excision of the mass.

A 33-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of left-sided temporomandibular joint (TMJ) morning stiffness. She had no prior TMJ treatments or procedures and an unremarkable medical history. On examination, there was a small preauricular swelling on the left with tenderness localized to the joint. Mouth opening was limited to 35 mm by pain, but excursive movements were normal with no malocclusion or lateral deviation.  
Computed tomography of the TMJs showed superior joint-space effusion with multiple small low-density foci within the fluid and extensive erosions of the glenoid fossa, articular eminence, and root of the zygoma. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated marked distension of the superior joint compartment with multiple small low-signal-intensity foci on T2-weighted images and scalloped, lobulated erosion of the left temporal bone.  
These imaging findings were reported to be highly suggestive of left-sided TMJ synovial chondromatosis.

A 20-year-old man presented with a 5-month history of progressive left knee stiffness and intermittent pain, initially mild but increasingly limiting his walking ability. Physical examination revealed pain localized to the left distal femur and a reduced range of motion of the left knee. Initial noncontrast radiographs of the left knee showed a subtle, irregular lucency within the medial femoral condyle. MRI of the left distal femur demonstrated a 2.9 × 4.0 × 3.9 cm intraosseous lesion centered in the medial femoral condyle that was hypointense relative to muscle on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously intermediate to high on STIR sequences, extending along the medial cortex without an associated soft-tissue mass; postcontrast images showed moderate enhancement. At this stage, the differential diagnosis included chondroblastoma, giant cell tumor, osteomyelitis, or a vascular lesion. Laboratory studies showed an ESR of 9 mm/hr (normal 0–15), CRP of 0.6 mg/L (normal 0–5), WBC count of 5.4 × 10^3/µL (normal 4.5–11), and LDH of 163 U/L (normal 100–220).

A 36-year-old African American man with stage IVA Epstein–Barr virus–positive squamous cell carcinoma of the nasopharynx, diagnosed 8 months earlier, presented with worsening dyspnea, dysphagia, and difficulty managing secretions. He was actively receiving chemotherapy with cisplatin and gemcitabine; his symptoms intensified following his most recent cycle, completed the day before presentation. On arrival, his respiratory rate was 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation was 98% on room air. Physical examination revealed a muffled voice, drooling, use of accessory muscles of respiration, and inspiratory and expiratory stridor. A computed tomography scan of the head and neck showed a large, necrotic mass causing near-total obstruction of the posterior pharynx. Laboratory analysis demonstrated neutrophil-predominant leukocytosis with respiratory acidosis.

A 47-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of nausea, repeated vomiting, epigastric pain, and intermittent constipation. He also reported acid regurgitation, heartburn, anorexia, and significant weight loss over 6 months. His medical history was notable only for appendectomy and remote severe left thoracoabdominal trauma. On examination, there was a firm, palpable mass in the left hypochondrium and flank. Laboratory studies revealed iron deficiency (serum iron 46 μg/dL) and leukocytosis. Upper endoscopy showed a deformed stomach with extrinsic compression of the antrum causing difficulty traversing the pylorus but no mucosal abnormalities. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a heterogeneous mass with solid and cystic components extending from the left hepatic lobe to the splenic hilum. Contrast-enhanced ultrasonography revealed arterial‐phase enhancement and late washout of the solid component, with nonenhancing cystic/necrotic areas. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a 17×15×14 cm heterogeneous mass containing numerous necrotic and cystic regions, originating from the fundus and greater curvature of the stomach, with extraluminal growth and mass effect on adjacent organs.

A 49-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of a slowly growing, painless mass in the left parotid region. A contrast-enhanced CT scan showed a 1-cm partially cystic lesion confined to the superficial lobe of the left parotid gland, without involvement of adjacent nerves, vessels, or lymph nodes. Fine-needle aspiration cytology demonstrated sheets of epithelial cells with scant stroma in a cystic background, suggestive of a salivary gland neoplasm of uncertain malignant potential.

The patient underwent complete excision of the left parotid gland lesion. Grossly, the specimen contained a 1-cm well-circumscribed, homogeneous tan nodule with partially cystic areas; the remainder of the gland appeared unremarkable. Histologic examination (H&E) revealed a predominantly intracystic epithelial neoplasm with focal invasion, composed of macrocystic and microcystic architecture as well as solid and papillary areas. The lesional cells were cuboidal, with abundant eosinophilic vacuolated cytoplasm, round to oval nuclei with homogeneous chromatin, and subtle nucleoli. Surgical margins were clear.

Immunohistochemical studies showed that the tumor cells were strongly and diffusely positive for mammaglobin and S100, as well as vimentin, CK7, CK19, BRST2, Cam5.2, and 34βE12. P63 demonstrated only focal nuclear staining in lesional cells, and SMA highlighted scattered blood vessels without outlining a continuous myoepithelial layer. The tumor cells were negative for DOG1, CK5/6, EMA, CD117, and ER. Mucin was confirmed by colloidal iron, Alcian blue, and PAS with and without diastase.

Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) for ETV6 gene rearrangement was negative after examination of 200 tumor nuclei.

Electron microscopy showed epithelial cells forming nests with lumina lined by small microvilli, abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum, and a few small intracytoplasmic electron-dense granules; diagnostic zymogen granules were not identified.

A previously healthy 10-month-old boy was admitted with one week of fever, rash, and malaise. He appeared lethargic and was febrile to 102°F with a heart rate of 180 beats per minute. Examination revealed a purpuric petechial rash over the trunk and extremities, an erythematous bulging right tympanic membrane, and hepatomegaly with the liver palpable 4 cm below the costal margin; the spleen was not palpable.
Initial laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 3.9×10^9/L with 68% lymphocytes and 13% atypical lymphocytes, hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, and platelets 36×10^9/L. Serum aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, and lactate dehydrogenase were elevated at 152 U/L, 146 U/L, and 2041 U/L, respectively. Epstein–Barr virus serologies indicated acute infection, and quantitative viral load demonstrated persistent viremia. Serum immunoglobulin levels were within normal limits.
He was treated for otitis media with ceftriaxone. Over the next several days, his lethargy improved, but his pancytopenia worsened, requiring red-cell and platelet transfusions. His total bilirubin rose to 8 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase to 1890 U/L, and aspartate aminotransferase to 7300 U/L. Triglycerides were elevated at 319 mg/dL, and fibrinogen was low at 107 mg/dL. A bone marrow biopsy revealed hypocellular marrow with no evidence of hemophagocytosis.

A 77-year-old woman presented with one month of abdominal pain and anorexia. On examination, she had right upper-quadrant tenderness and rebound tenderness in the lower abdomen. Laboratory tests showed an aspartate aminotransferase level of 75 IU/L (normal 7–38 IU/L), a lipase level of 63 U/L (normal 7–60 U/L), and an elevated carbohydrate antigen 125 level of 279.5 U/mL; carcinoembryonic antigen, carbohydrate antigen 19-9, and alpha-fetoprotein levels were normal. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT and MRI revealed a 10 × 5 cm mass arising from the tail of the pancreas, invading the spleen and adjacent bowel loop; the tumor wall showed slight enhancement, and no regional lymphadenopathy, ascites, or distant metastases were seen. The patient underwent a distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy, along with left hemicolectomy and partial gastrectomy for direct invasion.

A 36-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of bilateral lower limb weakness. She denied respiratory or swallowing difficulties. Four years earlier, she had sudden lower-limb weakness requiring potassium supplementation; two years later, she had a similar episode involving the right upper limb. The cause remained uncertain. Her medical history included polycystic ovary disease, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and diabetes mellitus diagnosed 4 years ago, all refractory to maximal oral therapy. Medications were metformin, voglibose, glimepiride, and oral contraceptive pills. She denied vomiting, diarrhea, use of β-adrenergic agonists, diuretics, corticosteroids, or excessive licorice. There was no personal or family history of autoimmune disorders.

On examination, BMI was 29.0, blood pressure 150/100 mm Hg. She had androgenic alopecia, acanthosis nigricans around the neck, and mild knuckle pigmentation. There were no striae, dorsocervical fat pad, or moon face initially.

Initial laboratory results showed:
– Serum potassium 2.0 mmol/L (normal 3.5–5.5)  
– Serum bicarbonate 26.2 mmol/L (19–31)  
– Serum magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.85–1.1)  
– pH 7.49 (7.35–7.45)  
– Triglycerides 3.45 mmol/L (0.45–1.58)  
– HDL cholesterol 0.77 mmol/L (1.1–2.27)  
– HbA1c 12.3%  
– Plasma renin concentration 5.09 ng/dL (2.52–39.2 upright)  
– Plasma aldosterone 0.63 µIU/mL (4.4–46.1 upright)  
– Aldosterone/renin ratio 8.08 (2–17, mean 5.5)  
– Serum ACTH 196 pg/mL (10–46)  
– 24-hour urinary potassium 21 mEq/day (<15)  
– 24-hour urinary cortisol 3543.84 nmol/day (9.66–124.2)  
– Urinary K/Cr ratio 2.9 (<1.5)

An 8 AM cortisol was 19.62 µg/dL (5–23). A 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test showed a cortisol of 17.6 µg/dL (normal <1.8), consistent with Cushing syndrome. At this point, CS was considered a possibility.

A 60-year-old Saudi man with diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and chronic renal impairment, and no family history of malignancy, was referred to the breast oncology surgery clinic for evaluation of an axillary lesion of unknown origin. One year earlier, he noted a self-palpated, right axillary mass of three months’ duration. At a secondary hospital, this 1 × 1 cm, painless, mobile, subdermal mass was clinically diagnosed as a sebaceous cyst, excised under local anesthesia, and sent for histopathology, which revealed malignant cells. 

At our clinic, physical examination showed grade I gynecomastia bilaterally; the left breast and axilla were unremarkable, and the right breast and axilla were unremarkable except for a healed scar in the right axilla. No cutaneous lesions were noted on the ipsilateral limb. Mammography and ultrasound of the breasts and axillae were normal (BI-RADS 1), and a whole-body PET–CT scan showed no FDG-avid malignancy. 

Review of the histopathology slides confirmed an adenocarcinoma “favors primary breast origin” with grade 1 lymphovascular invasion. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for GATA-3, mammaglobin, GCDFP-15, estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and androgen receptor; HER2/NEU was negative (score 1+), and Ki-67 was 10 %.

A 35-year-old man was airlifted from Bhojpur, Nepal, after 24 hours of severe headache, multiple episodes of vomiting, abnormal body movements, and loss of consciousness. He reported one month of dizziness following treated typhoid fever. He had a two-year history of hypertension managed with medication. On arrival, his vital signs were stable and his Glasgow Coma Scale score was 7; he was immediately intubated. Brain MRI showed a well-defined cystic lesion approximately 1.8 × 1.8 cm in the anterosuperior third ventricle that was hyperintense on both T1- and T2-weighted images, with persistent high signal on FLAIR. There was active noncommunicating hydrocephalus with mild periventricular ooze. Diffusion-weighted and ADC imaging demonstrated infarcts in the bilateral occipital lobes, midbrain, pons, left thalamus, and left superior cerebellum; the cyst did not show diffusion restriction.

A 44-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of facial swelling, neck distension, and dyspnea on exertion (mMRC grade 1). His past medical history was unremarkable, and he had a 24-pack-year smoking history. Chest radiography revealed a mass in the right upper anterior mediastinum. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 10-cm mass extending from the superior to the anterior mediastinum, with narrowing yet maintained patency of the brachiocephalic vein and superior vena cava and small areas of necrosis. Diffusion-weighted MRI demonstrated high signal intensity within the mass, and FDG-PET revealed hypermetabolism (SUV max 10.4; delayed phase 12.0). There was no lymphadenopathy on imaging or examination. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 0.38 mg/dL and a soluble interleukin-2 receptor level of 575 U/mL (normal <496 U/mL); tumor markers, IgG, and IgG4 were normal, and Histoplasma antibody was negative.

A CT-guided percutaneous needle biopsy (21-G) demonstrated infiltration of lymphocytes and plasma cells in dense fibrous tissue without malignancy, leading to a diagnosis of fibrosing mediastinitis. Video-assisted thoracoscopic biopsy confirmed the same findings. Over the next 2 months, the mass enlarged and dyspnea worsened. Histoplasmic infection, tuberculosis, IgG4-related disease, sarcoidosis, and collagen diseases were excluded, and systemic prednisolone (60 mg/day) was started, producing a reduction in mass size. When the dose was tapered to 20 mg/day, the mass regrew; increasing to 30 mg/day failed to control progression. After 6 months of glucocorticoid therapy, a second percutaneous needle biopsy (17-G) again showed fibrosing mediastinitis. Prednisolone 30 mg/day was maintained, but the mass continued to enlarge, and superior vena cava syndrome worsened. Four months later, the soluble interleukin-2 receptor level rose to 1623 U/mL. Based on these clinical and laboratory findings, we strongly considered the mass to be a malignant lymphoma.

A 41-year-old woman with French-American-British M5 acute myeloid leukemia with an FLT3 mutation underwent matched sibling peripheral blood stem cell transplantation after cyclophosphamide and total body irradiation; GVHD prophylaxis included tacrolimus and short-term methotrexate. Complete remission was confirmed 1 month post-transplant, and immunosuppression was discontinued at 5 months. Two weeks after withdrawal, she noted bilateral upper extremity pain, lichen planus–like oral lesions, a corneal ulcer from dry eyes, and elevated liver enzymes. She was admitted with suspected chronic GVHD. Over the next 2 weeks, her pain localized to the left forearm and hand, with paresthesia of the first through third fingers. Examination showed normal strength, sensation, and deep tendon reflexes in all extremities; there was no palpable neck mass. A nerve conduction study of the left upper extremity was unremarkable. Differential diagnoses included myofascitis, cervical spondylotic myelopathy, idiopathic brachial plexopathy, GVHD-associated brachial plexopathy, and extramedullary relapse of AML. Contrast-enhanced MRI performed 38 days after pain onset revealed a perineural enhancing swelling of the left brachial plexus. Bone marrow examination showed no relapse. She was treated with prednisone and tacrolimus, resulting in resolution of systemic cGVHD signs but persistent left upper extremity paresthesia. Three months after pain onset, follow-up MRI showed an enlarged brachial plexus lesion, and a mass was now visible and palpable in the left supraclavicular region.

A 47-year-old woman with no past medical history previously underwent resection in 2007 of a 57×33 mm left atrial mass attached to the fossa ovalis; histopathology at that time was reported as an organized thrombus after a negative thrombophilia workup.  

In May 2021, routine transthoracic echocardiography revealed a new left atrial mass that had not been present 4 years earlier. The patient was asymptomatic. Vital signs were stable: afebrile, blood pressure 115/70 mm Hg, heart rate 72 bpm; physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, renal and hepatic function, and inflammatory markers, were within normal limits. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm without conduction or repolarization abnormalities.  

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a mobile mass in the left atrium attached to the interatrial septum, with normal biventricular function and no significant valvular disease. Transoesophageal echocardiography revealed a 13×11 mm mobile, pedunculated, filamentous mass attached to the interatrial septum, with no spontaneous echo contrast or left atrial appendage thrombus. Given the prior diagnosis of atrial thrombus, rivaroxaban 20 mg daily was initiated. After 6 weeks of effective anticoagulation, repeat transoesophageal echocardiography showed no significant reduction in the size of the mass. Considering the discrepancy between clinical findings and the previous histological diagnosis, a review of the 2007 histopathological preparations was requested.

A 71-year-old Asian woman presented with a 6-month history of a solitary skin lesion on the tip of her right nipple. She denied pain, discharge, or other nipple symptoms. Her medical history was unremarkable. On examination, there was a 0.2 × 0.2 cm, well-demarcated, fairly dome-shaped, firm papule that was centrally erythematous with a violaceous periphery. No other skin or breast abnormalities were noted. Given its appearance, a benign skin lesion was initially suspected, and a local excisional biopsy was performed.

A 54-year-old man with a 34-year history of smoking (20 cigarettes per day) was referred after incidental detection of multiple lung nodules on CT performed during evaluation of abdominal pain. He was asymptomatic. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including tumor markers (CEA, CA19-9, CYFRA, NSE, proGRP, PSA), were within normal limits. Chest CT showed multiple well-defined, round nodules up to 14 mm in diameter, some with cystic change, in both lung fields. FDG-PET/CT demonstrated no significant FDG uptake in any pulmonary nodule and no other abnormal uptake suggestive of a primary malignancy. A CT-guided biopsy of a nodule was non-diagnostic. Follow-up CT scans every 2 months over 6 months showed cystic change in some nodules without significant size change. To establish a diagnosis, thoracoscopic surgical biopsy was planned.

A 57-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of a right mandibular margin mass that had recently increased in size. Her medical history was notable for bilateral metachronous breast cancer, treated surgically between 10 and 17 years earlier. On examination, there was a 15-mm, painless, nonpitting, indurated mass at the right mandibular margin. Oral mucosa was unremarkable, and the lesion was difficult to palpate intraorally because of the buccal frenulum. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-circumscribed 15-mm nodule at the right mandibular margin with low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted images. Computed tomography showed a 15-mm low-density nodule without calcification, bone invasion, or lymphadenopathy. The lesion was radiologically diagnosed as an epidermoid cyst. The differential diagnoses included schwannoma, neurofibromatosis, pleomorphic adenoma, and a powdery mass.

A 17-year-old man with a history of Hb H disease requiring splenectomy at age 5 for transfusion dependency was referred for evaluation of elevated platelet counts. He was asymptomatic. Physical examination revealed no anemia or jaundice, hepatomegaly 2 cm below the right costal margin, and a splenectomy scar. Laboratory studies showed:  
• Hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL; hematocrit 36.5%  
• WBC 29,200/µL (neutrophils 66%, lymphocytes 16%, monocytes 8%, eosinophils 9%, basophils 1%) with 9 nucleated red cells per 100 WBC  
• Platelets 2,206,000/µL (previously 976,000/µL two months earlier)  
Peripheral blood smear demonstrated marked thrombocytosis with variation in platelet size and staining, hypochromic microcytic red blood cells, nucleated red cells, and leukocytosis.  
Bone marrow biopsy revealed hypercellularity with increased megakaryocytes, erythroid cells, and myeloid precursors with normal maturation, myeloid-to-erythroid ratio of 1:2. Cytogenetics showed 46,XY. JAK2 V617F mutation testing was positive.  
Hemoglobin analysis by high-performance liquid chromatography demonstrated HbA2 1.7% and combined Hb Bart’s and Hb H 12.3%, confirming Hb H-Constant Spring disease. Alpha-globin gene analysis identified the Constant Spring mutation without common deletions; red cell inclusion bodies were present after methylene blue staining. During follow-up, his hemoglobin rose to 12–12.9 g/dL, exceeding the 99th percentile for non-deletional Hb H disease in Thailand.  
Low-dose aspirin was initiated for thrombosis prevention; cytoreductive therapy was deferred.

A 53‐year‐old man presented with mild, persistent right flank pain of several weeks’ duration. He denied any colicky pain or gross hematuria. On examination, there was no tenderness or palpable mass at the right costovertebral angle. Routine laboratory tests, including renal function and urinalysis, were within normal limits.  
Renal ultrasonography demonstrated a multicystic mass with multiple thick septa located near the right renal pelvis; Doppler evaluation showed no internal vascular flow. An intravenous urogram revealed dilatation of the right renal pelvis and lower calyces. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen identified a 7-cm multilocular cystic lesion in the lower pole of the right kidney, with a sharp interface between the lesion and the adjacent renal parenchyma, and no wall thickening, calcification, or contrast enhancement. There was no regional lymphadenopathy or evidence of metastatic disease.

A 6-month-old male infant was brought to dermatology with a solitary lesion on his left arm. The lesion first appeared at age 4 months as a dark flat spot that slowly enlarged and changed color. There was no pain, bleeding, or other symptoms. The infant was born at term by cesarean section without complications and otherwise is healthy.

On examination, there was a firm, painless hyperkeratotic projection on the left arm measuring approximately 1 cm in width and 2.5 cm in height. The apex of the projection was black, the middle segment brown, and the base yellow. No other skin lesions were noted, and ophthalmologic examination was normal.

The lesion was excised, and a punch biopsy was taken from the base. Histopathologic analysis of the biopsy specimen revealed a dense, monomorphic foamy histiocytic infiltrate with scattered eosinophils, and notably, no Touton giant cells were identified.

A 34-year-old Arab woman was referred for evaluation of upper gastrointestinal bleeding after endoscopy at an outside hospital revealed a gastric antral submucosal mass. Three months earlier, contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 2.5×3.5×3 cm soft-tissue mass in the gastric antrum with heterogeneous arterial-phase enhancement and intense venous-phase enhancement with a small central necrotic area; there was no lymphadenopathy or metastasis.

Over the preceding four months, she had epigastric pain radiating to the back, constipation, and multiple episodes of melena, along with headaches, fatigue, and dizziness. She denied weight loss. Her only medical history was hypothalamic hypogonadism; she took no medications and had no family history of cancer.

On examination she appeared pale; vital signs were stable, and the abdominal examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed microcytic hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL, hematocrit 23.2%); other laboratory tests were within normal limits.

On hospital day 4, esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed an ulcerated antral submucosal mass with an actively bleeding vessel, which was clipped. Endoscopic ultrasound showed a 34×32 mm well-defined isoechoic mass arising from the muscularis propria of the gastric antrum. Fine-needle biopsy of the lesion demonstrated a cluster of monomorphic cells with plasmacytoid features and bland nuclei with salt-and-pepper chromatin, findings described as mostly consistent with a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor.

A 59-year-old man noted a slowly enlarging growth on his right Achilles tendon region for 3 years. He believed it was a benign callus and had no history of trauma or systemic symptoms.  
On examination, there was a well-circumscribed, firm, yellow-pink tumor measuring 2.5 × 2.0 cm over the right posterior calf at the level of the Achilles tendon. No palpable lymphadenopathy was present in the popliteal or inguinal regions.  
An incisional skin biopsy revealed cords and nests of basaloid and atypical cells with ductal structures infiltrating a sclerotic dermis. Perineural invasion was identified. Immunohistochemical staining showed positivity for AE1/AE3, p63, and epithelial membrane antigen, and negativity for carcinoembryonic antigen.

A 44-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with acute-onset vertigo and vomiting. Neurologic examination revealed no cranial nerve deficits and no motor or sensory abnormalities. Routine laboratory studies, chest radiography, and electrocardiography were all normal. Because of concern for a posterior fossa lesion, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was obtained. MRI demonstrated an extra-axial, cystic-appearing lesion in the prepontine cistern measuring 19 × 32 × 34 mm, with no evidence of lytic bone destruction. On MRI the lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed intermediate signal on FLAIR. There was pronounced restricted diffusion with high signal on diffusion-weighted imaging and low signal on the apparent diffusion coefficient map. No enhancement was seen after intravenous gadolinium administration. The mass exerted a mass effect on the pons, medulla, and left middle cerebellar peduncle, encased the basilar artery, and abutted the cisternal segments of the left facial and both trigeminal nerves. Based on these imaging features, a presumptive diagnosis of epidermoid cyst was made.

A 53-year-old man with known neurofibromatosis type 1 and essential hypertension was referred preoperatively after detection of an ejection systolic murmur. He had residual cervical myelomalacia and resultant neuromuscular atrophy from prior cervical laminectomy but no symptoms of ischemia, syncope, or heart failure. On examination, a loud ejection systolic murmur was heard best at the right upper sternal border with radiation to the neck; peripheral pulses were normal. Electrocardiography showed normal sinus rhythm without conduction abnormalities. Transthoracic echocardiography suggested a bicuspid aortic valve with mixed valve disease: peak velocity 3.2 m/s, maximal and mean gradients 41 and 24 mmHg, and an aortic regurgitation pressure-half-time of 488 ms; ventricular dimensions and wall thickness were within normal limits. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging confirmed fusion of the left and right aortic valve leaflets with mild aortic stenosis (peak velocity 2.6 m/s) and moderate aortic regurgitation (regurgitant volume 28 mL, fraction 31%), and revealed normal left ventricular volumes and function. Avid late gadolinium enhancement was noted exclusively in the posteromedial papillary muscle. There was no other myocardial enhancement and no evidence of aortopathy on MR angiography.

A 59-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of intermittent chest pain and exertional dyspnea. He had no past medical history, no risk factors for cardiac disease, and no family history of cardiac disease or malignancy. Vital signs were normal: blood pressure 121/79 mmHg, pulse 76/min, respiratory rate 18/min, temperature 36.4°C. Cardiac examination showed a slightly accelerated regular rhythm and a fixed splitting of S2 without murmur. Lung and abdominal examinations were unremarkable; there was no lymphadenopathy or peripheral edema. Laboratory studies revealed WBC 8,500/µL, hemoglobin 14.4 g/dL, platelets 352,000/µL, negative viral serologies (HBsAg/Ab, HCV, HIV), and an elevated LDH of 248 IU/L. Chest radiograph showed mild cardiomegaly. Electrocardiography demonstrated first-degree atrioventricular block, right axis deviation, and possible right ventricular hypertrophy. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a 6×4 cm nonmobile ovoid mass with a broad base along the atrial and membranous septum of the right atrium, nearly obstructing right ventricular inflow, with preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (69%) and moderate pericardial effusion. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed a poorly enhanced mass compressing both atria and part of the left ventricle with associated pericardial effusion; abdominal CT was normal. Cardiac MRI demonstrated that the mass invaded the left atrium, extended into the pericardial space and intra-atrial cavity, and encased the aortic root, proximal right coronary artery, and left main coronary artery. It was iso-intense on T2-weighted images, showed diffuse enhancement on contrast imaging, and was iso- to slightly hyperintense compared with myocardium on T1-weighted images, with no evidence of myocardial infarction.

A 21-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of neck pain, stiffness, and tingling with paresthesias in his right arm in the C6–C8 dermatomal distribution. He also reported loss of dexterity, decreased grip strength, and gait instability. On examination, he had a right Babinski sign and mild visual impairment. Routine brain MRI was normal. Contrast-enhanced cervical spine MRI revealed an intradural extramedullary, T1-isointense, T2-hypointense, enhancing mass at C2–C3, causing severe canal stenosis, posterior cord displacement, compression, and cord edema. Neurosurgery performed bilateral C2–C3 laminectomies and attempted resection; however, full excision was aborted due to loss of motor signals, and only posterior decompression was achieved. The postoperative course was uneventful. Pathologic evaluation of tissue fragments showed tightly packed small blue cells with markedly increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios and focal areas of cartilage. The specimen was sent for further analysis.

A 50-year-old man with known neurofibromatosis type 1 and multiple cutaneous neurofibromas, and no history of smoking, was admitted for recurrent urinary retention and sepsis. A transurethral resection of the prostate revealed fibroleiomyomatous hyperplasia, but urinary function did not improve. Laboratory studies and a CT scan showed diffuse irregular polypoid thickening of the entire bladder wall without a discrete mass. Because of compromised bladder function, the patient underwent cystoprostatectomy. 

On gross examination, the bladder wall was diffusely thickened, firm, and gray–white, with near–complete loss of the detrusor muscle. Histologic evaluation revealed in the superficial wall a diffuse bland spindle cell proliferation with comma-shaped nuclei and a collagenous matrix. In the deeper wall, there was a dense, perivascular spindle cell proliferation with prominent cytological atypia, frequent mitoses, and an infiltrative growth pattern. The tumor was in close contact with peripheral nerves. 

Immunohistochemical studies showed that the tumor cells were positive for S100, p16, neurofilaments, and CD56, and negative for pan-cytokeratin, EMA, MDM2, p63, ALK, CD117, DOG1, myogenin, desmin, and smooth muscle actin.

A 39-year-old woman with well-controlled HIV infection on antiretroviral therapy for 6 years, hypertension, ESRD secondary to HIV-associated nephropathy, and secondary hyperparathyroidism presented with several weeks of progressive abdominal distension, weight loss, leg swelling, and muscle weakness. She had been on peritoneal dialysis for 5 years with no prior abnormalities and was recently converted to intermittent hemodialysis. A few weeks after the change, she developed ascites requiring paracentesis of 5–7 L every other week. There were no respiratory or cardiac symptoms. She was anuric.  
On examination, blood pressure was 160/80 mmHg, heart rate 74/min, respiratory rate 16/min, temperature 36.9 °C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Physical findings were notable only for moderate ascites and bilateral lower-extremity edema; there were no signs of chronic liver disease, organomegaly, or heart failure.  
Laboratory data showed a normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 10 g/dL), serum calcium 8.6 mg/dL, CD4 count 600/mm3, HIV viral load 986 copies/mL, creatinine 10.3 mg/dL, AST 13 U/L, ALT 17 U/L, bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL, INR 1.01, albumin 2.3 g/dL, amylase 105 IU/L, lipase 40 IU/L. Tumor markers CA 15-3 and CA 19-9 were normal; CA-125 was repeatedly elevated (197–416 U/mL; normal < 34.9 U/mL).  
Ascitic fluid analysis showed albumin 1.5 g/dL, protein 3.5 g/dL, and a serum-to-ascites albumin gradient < 1.1. Cultures were negative for acid-fast bacilli; calcofluor white stain revealed no fungi; Histoplasma and Aspergillus antigens were negative. Computed tomography showed a normal pancreas.  
Serum β2-microglobulin was elevated at 47.30 mg/L (normal 0.80–2.3). Serum protein electrophoresis revealed hypoalbuminemia, decreased total protein, and a minimal monoclonal M-component (IgG-κ 0.30 g/dL in the γ zone). Immunofixation electrophoresis showed polyclonal immunoglobulins with polyclonal light chains. κ and λ free light chains were increased to 66.86 mg/dL and 18.55 mg/dL, respectively, yielding a ratio of 3.6 (normal 0.26–1.65).

A 27-year-old man with a 9-month history of advanced HIV infection on antiretroviral therapy presented with 2 weeks of intermittent palpitations, chest pain, reduced exercise tolerance, one near-syncope with exertion, fever up to 38.9°C, dry cough, and loose stools. On admission, he was tachycardic (114 bpm), blood pressure 103/63 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Physical examination was unremarkable: regular heart sounds without murmurs, clear lungs, no peripheral oedema or infective stigmata, and normal abdominal and lymph node examinations. 

The initial ECG showed sinus tachycardia, first-degree AV block, and frequent atrial ectopics. Continuous monitoring revealed intermittent complete AV block with a broad complex escape rhythm at 54 bpm, episodes of junctional tachycardia, and supraventricular tachycardia correlating with palpitations. Chest radiography demonstrated cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio 60%). Blood cultures were negative. Laboratory studies showed haemoglobin 9.7 g/dL, white cell count 6.1×10^9/L, platelets 247×10^9/L, creatinine 64 µmol/L, troponin I 98 ng/L, LDH 895 U/L, normal tumour markers, and elevated LDH.

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a large mass in the right atrioventricular groove, abnormal basal septal thickening, normal left ventricular ejection fraction (60%), and a large pericardial effusion without tamponade. CT of the neck, thorax, abdomen, and pelvis showed intracardiac masses along the right atrial wall and interventricular septum encasing the proximal right coronary artery, with pericardial effusion and no other lesions. ECG-gated coronary CT angiography confirmed complete encasement of the right coronary artery without luminal compromise. 

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a mass isointense to myocardium on T1- and T2-weighted sequences, minimal first-pass contrast uptake, and patchy heterogeneous delayed enhancement.

A 25-year-old woman presented with a 4-year history of a gradually enlarging swelling over the dorsum of her right foot, associated with progressive pain during exertion for the past 6 months. There was no history of trauma, fever, chills, weight loss, or loss of appetite. On examination, there was a firm swelling over the fourth metatarsal region with a healed scar and minimal tenderness; no sinuses or discharge were present. Weight-bearing exacerbated the pain, and distal neurovascular status was intact. 

She had undergone a biopsy elsewhere, which showed atypical osteoid proliferation, and a working diagnosis of low-grade osteosarcoma versus osteoid osteoma versus osteoblastoma was made. Baseline blood investigations were within normal limits. 

Plain radiographs of the right foot showed a well-defined eccentric lesion with a homogeneous matrix involving the distal two-thirds of the fourth metatarsal, with mild expansion into the intermetatarsal space. CT of the foot demonstrated a 4.6 × 3.2 × 3.6 cm, well-defined, exophytic, lobulated, dense sclerotic lesion with an osteoid matrix arising from the medial aspect of the distal fourth metatarsal shaft, causing mild thinning of the adjacent third metatarsal shaft. MRI revealed an expansile lesion of the fourth metatarsal with homogeneous hypointense signal on both T1- and T2-weighted images and low-signal internal areas, without any soft-tissue component.

A 44-year-old man with a 29-month history of moderately differentiated esophageal adenocarcinoma (treated with neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy and surgical resection, ypT3N0) presented with a 3-day history of floaters in the left eye. Visual acuity was 6/6 in both eyes. The right eye was unremarkable. Examination of the left eye revealed a normal anterior segment, grade-1 vitritis, and a focal area of localized periphlebitis superonasally around the equator. Serologic testing for toxoplasmosis, cytomegalovirus, and herpes simplex virus was negative. Brain and orbital MRI scans were normal. Rheumatologic evaluation for systemic diseases, including sarcoidosis and Behçet disease, was unremarkable. Idiopathic inflammatory retinal vasculitis was suspected, and the patient was treated with oral steroids. On follow-up, the intraocular inflammation regressed and remained stable for 3 months while he received palliative chemotherapy for progressive lung metastases. The patient then discontinued chemotherapy. Three weeks later, he returned with a significant decrease in left-eye visual acuity to 6/60. Dilated fundus examination showed new severe vitritis with vitreous clouds, dense white-to-yellow vitreous clumps in the inferior retina, and increased perivascular infiltrates at the previous periphlebitis site.

A 76-year-old man with hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia presented with 10 months of persistent pruritus and erythema in the perianal area. He was initially treated by a dermatologist with topical corticosteroids for presumed eczema without improvement. A colonoscopy performed to evaluate colorectal malignancy did not reveal any lesion in the anal canal. Two months later, surveillance ultrasonography for his prostate revealed multiple liver lesions. CT of the abdomen confirmed numerous liver lesions and right inguinal lymphadenopathy.  
Biopsy of the perianal erythematous skin demonstrated intraepidermal pagetoid cells and poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma. Immunohistochemical staining showed that the malignant cells were positive for cytokeratin-7 and cytokeratin-20 and negative for gross cystic disease fluid protein-15. A biopsy of the inguinal lymph node also confirmed metastatic carcinoma. He was referred for further evaluation and management.
