An 80-year-old Caucasian woman was referred for evaluation of a 12-month history of a painless exophytic lesion in the interdental papilla between the first and second upper left molars noted during routine dental examination. She had no history of trauma or infection, was a nonsmoker, and took atenolol 50 mg daily for hypertension. Periodontal therapy combined with antiseptic chlorhexidine 0.2% rinse was attempted without improvement.

On intraoral examination, there were two sessile, fibroelastic, exophytic growths at the level of the interdental papilla: a 9 mm×7 mm lesion on the buccal aspect and a 5 mm×5 mm lesion on the palatal aspect. The lesions matched the color of adjacent mucosa. No bleeding occurred on probing, and the involved teeth were vital.

Panoramic radiography showed horizontal bone loss attributed to periodontal disease, with no significant radiographic changes over the preceding three years. A clinical diagnosis of pyogenic granuloma was made. An excisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia with antiseptic measures.

An 83-year-old woman presented with a one-week history of vaginal bleeding. She had a similar bleeding episode six years earlier, when an endometrial polyp was diagnosed on biopsy. Her medical history included pulmonary emboli, hypertension, osteoarthritis, gout, and a cardiac pacemaker. On examination, there was active bleeding from the cervix. Transvaginal ultrasound showed an endometrial thickness of 13 mm with multiple cystic foci and polypoid formations; both ovaries were atrophic without masses. Diagnostic hysteroscopy with polypectomy and endometrial curettage was performed. Histologic examination revealed adenocarcinoma infiltrating the surface of an endometrial polyp, characterized by papillary and micropapillary formations and eosinophilic cytoplasm; there was no necrosis. On initial morphologic assessment, high-grade serous carcinoma and clear cell carcinoma were considered.

A 47-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of progressive dysphagia and sore throat. He smoked 40 cigarettes daily, consumed alcohol heavily, and had a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus. On examination, there was a right lateral cervical swelling, and intraoral inspection revealed an ulcerated mass on the right palatine tonsil. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed a solid lesion in the right tonsillar region with lobulated, ill-defined margins. An incisional biopsy was performed.  
Light microscopy (H&E) demonstrated a neoplasm of glandular epithelial origin in the lamina propria beneath nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium; tumor cells were arranged in sheets, exhibiting uniform morphology with rare mitotic figures, and focal clear cells were present. Immunohistochemistry revealed positivity in neoplastic cells for CK-7, CK-13, and CK-14, and negativity for vimentin, smooth muscle actin, and p16. Periodic acid–Schiff with diastase digestion (PAS + DD) and mucicarmine stains highlighted mucous‐containing areas within the tumor.

A 63-year-old Greek woman was referred for persistent numbness and weakness of the left hand. Over the past three years she had undergone two carpal tunnel releases elsewhere without relief, and her symptoms had progressively worsened. She now reported tingling in both the median and ulnar nerve distributions and noted a slowly enlarging mass in the left palm and thenar eminence.

On examination, there was a soft tissue mass in the palm that was slightly tender to palpation. Wrist extension was limited to 40° and flexion to 60°. She was unable to flex the distal phalanx of the thumb. Thenar muscle strength was decreased, and sensation was diminished in the median and ulnar territories.

Plain radiographs of the hand showed a soft tissue opacity overlying the palm. MRI demonstrated an 8.0 × 4.0 × 3.75 cm well-defined lesion in the deep palmar space, extending between the tendons and metacarpals with preservation of the periosteum. The lesion was hyperintense on T1-weighted images and showed low signal on fat-suppressed sequences, suggesting a lipomatous tumor.

A nerve conduction study revealed prolonged latencies and reduced amplitudes of both the median and ulnar nerves consistent with compressive neuropathy.

A 61-year-old woman with type II diabetes noted a progressively enlarging, painful abdominal mass over 1 year, with more rapid growth recently. She denied features of tuberous sclerosis. On examination, vital signs were stable. Abdominal palpation revealed right iliac fossa tenderness and a firm, mobile abdominopelvic mass.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed large (25 × 18 × 13 cm), necrotic, highly vascularized abdomino-pelvic masses compressing adjacent structures; the uterus and ovaries were not visualized. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a partially solid and cystic mass with moderate contrast uptake thought to arise from the left ovary, and a second 18-cm intraperitoneal heterogeneous enhancing mass. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy was normal. Serum CA19-9 was 98 000 U/L (normal < 35 000) and CA-125 was 140 600 U/L (normal < 35 000); carcinoembryonic antigen was normal. The working diagnosis was an ovarian tumor.  
The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy, which revealed a smooth-surfaced mass arising from the omentum, adherent to the distal small bowel and rectum without a clear cleavage plane, and two cystic masses in the pouch of Douglas. An omental mass excision and radical pelvic cytoreduction were performed with no visible residual disease.

A 75-year-old man with a history of coronary artery bypass grafting 11 years earlier, congestive heart failure (ejection fraction 25%), atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia presented with progressive dyspnea and left-sided chest pain. He denied tobacco use and had no known asbestos or other occupational exposures. On examination, breath sounds were diminished over the left hemithorax. A chest radiograph showed a large left pleural effusion. He recalled a similar effusion 4 months earlier that was drained without available fluid analysis. 

On this admission, diagnostic and therapeutic thoracentesis yielded 700 mL of milky fluid. Pleural fluid analysis revealed a lymphocyte-predominant exudate with a triglyceride level of 1406 mg/dL consistent with chylothorax; microbiologic studies were negative. Cytologic examination demonstrated reactive-appearing mesothelial cells that were positive for calretinin and WT-1 and negative for BerEP4 and MOC-31. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest performed after drainage showed a left lower lobe airspace infiltrate, pleural calcifications, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

A 15-year-old male presented with a 6-month history of headache and vomiting, accompanied by a single seizure. He was initially treated empirically with antituberculous therapy after a fourth-ventricular lesion was seen on imaging, without symptomatic relief. On referral, his neurologic examination was unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated a well-defined solid–cystic lesion in the region of the fourth ventricle that was hyperintense on T2‐weighted sequences and showed minimal, irregular peripheral enhancement after gadolinium administration. The imaging interpretation was pilocytic astrocytoma. The patient subsequently underwent a midline suboccipital craniectomy with C1‐arch excision and subtotal tumor decompression.

A 95-year-old woman noticed a mass in her left breast and was referred for suspected breast cancer. On examination, the 2-cm mass was well defined, mobile, with normal overlying skin and nipple–areola; axillary lymph nodes were not palpable. She had no café-au-lait spots, no family history of breast cancer, and no comorbidities. Mammography showed a round, well-defined, hyperdense mass without calcification in the mid-lateral left breast. Ultrasonography revealed a 16 × 16 × 15 mm round lesion with circumscribed margins, posterior acoustic enhancement, mixed hypoechoic and heterogeneous hyperechoic areas, no internal blood flow on Doppler, and a Tsukuba elasticity score of 4. Tumor markers (CEA, CA 15-3) were within normal limits. Core needle biopsy showed a spindle cell lesion with no malignant features. Two months later, ultrasound showed the mass had increased to 27 × 26 × 19 mm, but repeat biopsy was similarly non-diagnostic. Because of its growth and persistent uncertainty regarding malignancy, the decision was made to resect the tumor.

A 51-year-old Caucasian woman with refractory hypertension underwent abdominal ultrasonography to exclude renal artery stenosis. She was asymptomatic with no abdominal pain, fever, weight loss, or other complaints. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including liver enzymes and blood counts, were within normal limits.

Gray-scale sonography demonstrated a 2 cm well-defined, solid, hypoechoic lesion in segment V of an otherwise homogeneous liver. Color Doppler ultrasound showed peripheral flow signals in the lesion. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound with SonoVue revealed marked homogeneous hyperenhancement in the arterial phase (28 seconds after injection), persistent isoenhancement during the portal venous phase, and mild central washout with a rim of enhancement in the late parenchymal phase.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a 2 cm lesion with a strongly accentuated rim in the early arterial phase and isoenhancement in the portal venous phase; no other liver lesions were seen. Chest CT revealed a 6 mm right lung nodule, reported as most consistent with a small granuloma. Upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopies were normal.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 74-year-old man was referred for excision of a mass in the left renal pelvis. The lesion was detected incidentally on pelvic ultrasonography performed for urinary retention secondary to prostatic hypertrophy. The patient had no significant medical history; physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, biochemistry, and renal function tests, were all within normal limits. Renal ultrasonography revealed a well-defined, solid-cystic mass in the renal pelvis measuring approximately 4 cm in greatest diameter. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a heterogeneous mass in the left renal pelvis, measuring 4.0 × 3.7 × 2.6 cm, with peripheral irregular enhancement. Given the location and imaging characteristics, the leading preoperative diagnosis was urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis, and the patient underwent radical nephrectomy.

A 10-month-old male was brought with one month of jaundice, decreased appetite, and dark urine. He initially had no fever or pale stools. Two weeks prior, laboratory tests showed liver dysfunction with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Initial abdominal ultrasonography revealed an enlarged left hepatic lobe, intrahepatic biliary dilation, low-echogenic perihepatic tissue, and expansion of the Glisson’s sheath. After ten days of medical treatment including glutathione and ademetionine, the patient developed fever and was referred to our center.

Physical examination disclosed mild scleral and skin jaundice and a liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin. There was no splenomegaly or ascites. Laboratory evaluation showed lymphocytosis, hemoglobin 102 g/L, normal platelets, normal inflammatory markers, alanine aminotransferase 159 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 164 U/L, total bilirubin 87.5 μmol/L (direct 75.5 μmol/L), triglycerides 4.34 mmol/L, and ammonia 176 μmol/L. Alkaline phosphatase, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase, albumin, globulin, total bile acid, and coagulation parameters were within expected ranges. Alpha-fetoprotein and CA19-9 were negative. Viral serologies demonstrated EBV VCA-IgM and IgG positivity; hepatitis B and C serologies were negative. Metabolic workup, including urine organic acids and tandem mass spectrometry, was normal.

Repeat hepatosplenic ultrasound showed inhomogeneous hepatic parenchyma, cavernous transformation of the portal vein, and splenomegaly. After poor response to cholestatic hepatitis treatment (glutathione, diammonium glycyrrhizinate, ursodeoxycholic acid), a follow-up ultrasound detected a new anechoic cystic mass between the liver and right kidney. Diffusion-weighted MRI of the abdomen confirmed dilated intrahepatic bile ducts, increased vascularity at the porta hepatis, absence of a clear gallbladder, and a hyperintense lesion on DWI between the liver and right kidney.

A 4-year-old previously healthy girl presented with a 3-month history of progressive abdominal distention and rapid weight gain. She was noted to have hoarseness, marked hirsutism, cliteromegaly, and a rounded “moon face” with facial flushing. Over the same interval, her weight had increased by 3.8 kg, whereas her height increased by only 2.0 cm, and bone age was approximately 3 years greater than her chronological age.  
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed an 80 × 50 × 50 mm right ovarian mass. CT and MRI demonstrated a fat-containing, bimodal pelvic mass, and PET-CT showed no metastatic lesions.  
Laboratory studies showed a serum testosterone level of 242.3 ng/dL, a daytime cortisol concentration of 21.5 μg/dL, an adrenocorticotropic hormone level suppressed to 1.4 pg/mL, and normal aldosterone, luteinizing hormone, and follicle-stimulating hormone levels. Tumor-marker evaluation revealed a lactate dehydrogenase level of 364 U/L and a neuron-specific enolase level of 36.6 ng/mL; other tumor markers were within normal limits.

A 64-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of nausea and vomiting. His medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension treated with metformin and irbesartan; he had no prior renal disease. On examination, blood pressure was 110/70 mm Hg, pulse 96 beats/minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths/minute, and temperature 37°C. He had splenomegaly without hepatomegaly or lymphadenopathy; the fundus was normal.

Initial laboratory studies showed leukocytes 18.6×10^9/L (65% lymphocytes), hemoglobin 78 g/L, platelets 265×10^9/L, BUN 48 mg/dL, creatinine 2.2 mg/dL (eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73 m^2), sodium 137 mEq/L, potassium 3.2 mEq/L, LDH 378 U/L, uric acid 4.5 mg/dL, albumin 3.7 g/dL, gamma globulin 2.5 g/dL, and ESR 51 mm/h. Serologic tests were negative for ANA, ANCA, anti–GBM antibody, HBsAg, and anti-HCV; C3 and C4 levels were normal, and cryoglobulin was negative. Serum and urine immunoglobulins and free light chains were normal. Urinalysis revealed mild proteinuria (100 mg/24 h) without dysmorphic cells or casts. Peripheral smear showed mild mature lymphocytosis; ECG was normal. Renal ultrasonography demonstrated normal kidney size. Bone marrow biopsy was consistent with chronic lymphocytic leukemia; immunophenotyping showed monoclonal B lymphocytes positive for CD5, CD20, CD23, and CD79.

A 63-year-old woman with a history of left breast cancer treated by modified radical mastectomy and axillary dissection two years earlier underwent routine follow-up. She was asymptomatic. Physical examination and laboratory studies, including serum tumor markers, were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a complex cystic mass in the pancreatic head measuring 5.5 × 4.5 cm with internal calcifications and mural nodularity. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed a 65 × 63 × 55 mm cystic lesion in the uncinate process with a smooth-walled capsule containing calcifications, enhancing septa, millimetric nodules, and soft-tissue components, without distant metastases or intraabdominal lymphadenopathy. Her anesthetic evaluation classified her as ASA-2, and an exploratory laparotomy was scheduled.

A 49-year-old man presented with several weeks of difficulty urinating, dysuria, pelvic pain, occasional hematuria, and subjective fevers. He had been treated as an outpatient with tamsulosin and finasteride without meaningful relief. On examination, vital signs were stable; there was mild suprapubic tenderness but no costovertebral angle tenderness or urethral discharge. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, prostate-specific antigen 0.4 ng/mL, lactate dehydrogenase 347 U/L, and otherwise normal routine tests. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 7 × 4 cm lobulated mass below the bladder base arising from the superior prostate and invading the seminal vesicles, along with right pelvic and inguinal lymphadenopathy (largest node 2 cm) but no distant metastases.

A 60-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of chest pain and dyspnea. He was a current smoker (2 packs per day for 45 years) with hypertension. He reported progressive chest pain and mMRC grade-I dyspnea but denied wheezing, cough, anorexia, or weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable; oxygen saturation was 98% on room air, chest wall expansion was symmetric, and breath sounds were vesicular without adventitious sounds. Laboratory studies, including inflammatory markers, were within normal limits. A chest radiograph showed an opacity in the right upper lobe. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a 6 × 3 cm soft-tissue mass with irregular, spiculated enhancement located between the right upper and middle lobes; the right upper lobe bronchus appeared embedded in the mass, which also abutted the right pulmonary artery and pericardium. Flexible bronchoscopy demonstrated occlusion of the anterior bronchus of the right upper lobe by an enlarged spur. Histopathologic examination of endobronchial biopsy specimens showed no malignant cells.

A 28-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of low back pain that occasionally radiated to his left thigh. He denied numbness, bowel or bladder disturbances, and erectile dysfunction. Vital signs were within normal limits. On neurological examination, his Glasgow Coma Scale score was 4–5–6; motor strength and sensation were intact throughout; and deep tendon reflexes were normal (2+ bilaterally). Routine laboratory tests, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were unremarkable. 

Contrast-enhanced MRI of the lumbosacral spine revealed a well-defined, complex cystic lesion within the spinal canal extending from the inferior endplate of L4 to the midbody of S1. On T1-weighted images, the lesion’s walls and septae were isohypointense, and on T2-weighted and T2 FLAIR sequences, the cystic areas were hyperintense. After gadolinium administration, there was enhancement of the lesion’s walls and internal septations. The mass compressed the cauda equina nerve roots bilaterally, and there was mild bladder distension suggestive of neurogenic bladder.

A 66-year-old white man with no prior medical history received three doses of the BNT162b2 COVID-19 vaccine, the most recent (booster) administered in his right arm in October 2021. Approximately 10 days after the booster, he noted a painful, mobile right axillary lymph node. He had no other systemic symptoms. Three months later, he presented with further enlargement of the right axillary node and a new ipsilateral supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. On examination, both nodes were palpable, tender, and mobile. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest confirmed a right axillary lymph node measuring 6.99 cm and a right supraclavicular lymph node measuring 2.36 cm.

A 42-year-old woman with bilateral silicone breast implants noted a palpable lump in her left breast for 5 months, with more rapid growth over the past month. She denied skin changes, nipple retraction, or discharge. On examination, the left breast was asymmetrically enlarged, with a firm, minimally tender mass in the upper inner quadrant adjacent to the sternal border; the overlying skin and nipple were unremarkable. Mammography at an outside institution showed extremely dense breast tissue without a definite mass. Ultrasound revealed a 6.6-cm hypoechoic, heterogeneous, solid, vascular mass anterior to the implant capsule at the 11-o’clock position, with posterior acoustic shadowing. An ultrasound-guided 14-gauge core biopsy demonstrated a proliferation of spindle cells. Immunohistochemical stains showed the spindle cells to be positive for vimentin, beta-catenin, and smooth muscle actin, and negative for CD34, CD54, S100, estrogen receptor, CK903, and pan-cytokeratin.

A 29-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a slowly enlarging, palpable mass deep to the left breast near the thoracic wall. She reported no trauma but over 12 months noted progressive aching pain, nocturnal awakenings from neuropathic pain, and limited left arm function. On examination, there was a firm, nonmobile 8-cm mass in the retromammary region without overlying skin changes. Vital signs were normal.

Laboratory evaluation was unremarkable. Mammography did not reveal any lesion. MRI of the left chest wall showed an irregularly shaped soft-tissue mass measuring approximately 8 × 7 × 3 cm with moderate contrast enhancement, infiltrating the pectoralis major and minor muscles, serratus anterior, latissimus dorsi, intercostal muscles, and subcutaneous tissue. PET-CT demonstrated only minor fluorodeoxyglucose uptake (maximum SUV 3.2).

Ultrasound confirmed a nonsymmetric, diffusely demarcated lesion. Ultrasound-guided core biopsy revealed a fibrous lesion of spindle-shaped cells in a fascicular pattern with uniform nuclei and no epithelial components. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated strong positivity for vimentin, β-catenin, and actin 1A4; slight positivity for desmin; focal positivity for actin HHF35; weak estrogen receptor positivity only in endothelial cells; and a Ki-67 index <5%. Additional molecular diagnostics detected a mutation in exon 3 of CTNNB1 (codon S45F).

A 45-year-old man was evaluated after presenting with sinusitis, when multiple palpable thyroid nodules were noted on examination. He reported no symptoms of hypo- or hyperthyroidism and had no history of neck irradiation. Family history was negative for thyroid disease. Thyroid function tests were within normal limits, and levothyroxine suppression therapy was initiated. Baseline ultrasound of the thyroid gland demonstrated three nodules: in the right lobe, a 0.58 cm ovoid solid mass and a 3.08 × 2.82 × 2.11 cm purely cystic mass; and in the left lobe, a 0.21 cm ovoid cyst. On serial ultrasound examinations, the large cystic nodule initially decreased in size but, at 19 months, had increased by approximately 2% and appeared as a well-defined cyst without internal vascularity or calcifications. Fine-needle aspiration of this lesion yielded blood and colloid.

Chief complaint: progressive upper thoracic back pain and lower limb weakness.  
History of present illness: A 39-year-old man with no history of trauma or constitutional symptoms reported dull upper thoracic back pain for 8 months. The pain was gradually progressive, not posture related, and initially responsive to NSAIDs. Over the 4 days before presentation, the pain intensity increased markedly, and he developed inability to walk and urinary incontinence.  
Vital signs: afebrile; stable hemodynamics.  
Physical examination: motor strength 3/5 in all lower-limb muscle groups; sensory level at the nipples (T4); tenderness over T1–T2 spinous processes; remainder of examination unremarkable.  
Investigations: CT and MRI of the thoracic spine revealed an osteolytic, expansile lesion eroding the T1 and T2 vertebral bodies, extending into the spinal canal, with heterogeneous gadolinium enhancement.

A 53-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of multiple subcutaneous nodules and ulcerations over the right lower extremity associated with unilateral lymphedema. He had a 6-year history of a nonhealing right fifth toe injury that required surgical repair and ultimately toe amputation 1 year ago for osteomyelitis; the ulceration persisted despite long-term antibiotic therapy. In recent months, he developed progressive right lower-extremity edema, nodules on the leg, and ulcerations on the dorsum of the right foot.

On examination, he had an amputated fifth toe, three irregular deep ulcerations on the dorsum of the right foot (about 5 cm in diameter), and multiple erythematous subcutaneous nodules throughout the right lower extremity. The limb was edematous from the foot to the groin, precluding lymph node palpation. Magnetic resonance imaging of the leg showed a few subcentimeter lymphadenopathies.

An incisional biopsy of a nodule and the margins of an ulceration was performed to evaluate for sporotrichosis, actinomycosis, and atypical mycobacterial infection. Simultaneous tissue cultures grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus and Acinetobacter species, and he was treated with intravenous ampicillin/sulbactam and oral ciprofloxacin. Despite wound care with wet and antiseptic dressings and the antibiotics, the ulcerations gradually enlarged, became necrotic, and by day 15 of hospitalization had developed myiasis, which was managed with irrigation and removal of larvae.

A 52-year-old woman with neurofibromatosis type 1 and a long-standing ventriculoperitoneal shunt for hydrocephalus presented with altered mental status. Three weeks earlier, she had undergone her most recent shunt revision after two weeks of right upper quadrant abdominal pain. At that time she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Examination revealed right upper quadrant tenderness and diffuse cutaneous neurofibromas. Laboratory studies showed an alkaline phosphatase level of 137 U/L and alanine transaminase of 146 U/L. CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a perihepatic fluid collection surrounding the shunt tip, appendiceal and peritoneal thickening, stranding along the right hemiabdomen, and diffuse peritoneal nodularity with partial calcification. Laparoscopic exploration revealed inflammatory adhesions in the right hemiabdomen, and cerebrospinal fluid cultures grew Staphylococcus epidermidis; she received intravenous antibiotics. 

Two weeks later, she returned with confusion, decreased appetite, several days of abdominal pain, and one episode of emesis. She was afebrile, blood pressure 140/92 mm Hg, heart rate 125 bpm, and oriented only to place. Abdominal examination showed tenderness in the right upper quadrant, right lower quadrant, and suprapubic region. Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 12.1×10^3/mm^3 with neutrophil predominance, alkaline phosphatase 149 U/L, INR 1.6, and persistent Staphylococcus epidermidis in cerebrospinal fluid. Repeat CT revealed a right lower quadrant fluid collection with a tract to the shunt tip, scattered calcified nodules within the omentum, peritoneum, and sigmoid colon, and appendiceal thickening. She was treated with another course of intravenous antibiotics, her shunt was removed, and an external ventricular drain was placed. Follow-up CT scans five days apart showed resolution of the fluid collection but no change in the right lower quadrant anatomy, raising suspicion for an appendiceal versus gynecologic neoplasm. A diagnostic laparoscopy was planned.

A 22-year-old man was referred with a 2-year history of left facial swelling following trauma. He had mild infraorbital swelling without skin changes. Intraorally, there was a firm, mildly expanded area of the left maxilla with purple gingival discoloration and purulent discharge causing halitosis. Cone-beam CT showed a well-defined, expansile multilocular lesion (40 × 57 × 60 mm) in the left maxilla with wispy septations, expansion of the anterolateral, posterolateral, and medial walls of the maxillary sinus, and displacement of molar teeth. A panoramic radiograph confirmed a well-defined expansile lesion in the periapical and interradicular regions of the left upper molars with some calcifications. The initial radiographic differential diagnosis included calcifying odontogenic cyst, central giant cell granuloma, calcified odontogenic fibroma, and ameloblastoma. An incisional biopsy was performed, and microscopic diagnosis was reported as “infiltrative odontogenic tumor arising in odontogenic keratocyst,” with solid odontogenic keratocyst and keratoameloblastoma suggested as possibilities pending excisional histology.

A 68-year-old woman with a history of medically refractory Crohn disease and recurrent small-bowel obstruction presented with a 3-day history of abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed a diffusely tender abdomen without peritoneal signs. Laboratory studies showed a mild leukocytosis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated diffuse wall thickening of the mid-small bowel through the terminal ileum, with marked dilation of a 23-cm segment of distal ileum and mesenteric stranding 8–10 cm proximal to the ileocecal junction. A 7-mm fluid collection with surrounding phlegmon suggested a developing abscess or early fistula. The patient underwent ileocolic resection. Intraoperatively, the proximal small bowel was dilated, and an unexpected intussusception in the mid jejunum was identified, with a palpable intraluminal mass as the lead point. The terminal 20 cm of ileum showed active Crohn disease with stricture formation. Gross examination of the jejunal segment revealed a 4.2-cm, well-circumscribed, gray-white, lobulated submucosal mass with a fleshy cut surface.

A 51-year-old Caucasian man with hypertension (diagnosed 2 years ago, treated with lisinopril 10 mg daily) and a history of nephrolithiasis presented with 3 days of intermittent, sharp right testicular pain radiating to the right flank. He rated the pain 5/10, noted worsened discomfort with movement and relief at rest. He denied headaches, sweating, flushing, palpitations, or episodes of severe hypertension.  
On examination, his temperature was 98.6 °F, heart rate 81 bpm, blood pressure 137/96 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Laboratory testing showed a white blood cell count of 12 900 cells/mL. A thorough scrotal examination and ultrasound ruled out torsion, epididymitis, varicocele, hydrocele, and other intrinsic testicular causes.  
Because of persistent flank radiation and his history of nephrolithiasis, a noncontrast CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was obtained and revealed a large right suprarenal mass. A dedicated CT adrenal protocol confirmed a 5.1 cm enhancing right adrenal lesion. Subsequent MRI of the abdomen with contrast demonstrated slightly increased signal intensity on T2-weighted images and heterogeneous enhancement of the lesion.

A 48-year-old previously healthy, nonsmoking man underwent routine screening colonoscopy, which revealed two sessile, smooth, firm, yellowish polyps in the sigmoid colon measuring 0.2 cm and 0.3 cm. Fifteen months later, a second colonoscopy demonstrated two histologically confirmed hyperplastic polyps in the sigmoid colon. Twenty-eight months after the initial examination, a third colonoscopy identified a 0.5 cm submucosal, infiltrated, and ulcerated polyp in the cecum adjacent to the appendiceal orifice; the sigmoid colon appeared normal. The patient remained asymptomatic throughout. Cross-sectional imaging showed no evidence of extracolonic involvement.

Histologic examination of all lesions revealed submucosal nodules composed of sheets of large cells with indistinct borders and abundant lightly eosinophilic cytoplasm. The nuclei were reniform to oval, with fine vesicular chromatin, nuclear grooves, and single inconspicuous nucleoli. Central necrosis was present, and the cecal lesion demonstrated focal mucosal infiltration and ulceration. No giant cells, mitotic figures, or enlarged nucleoli were identified. Immunohistochemical staining showed strong, diffuse positivity for CD1a and CD207, with weak, multifocal staining for S100 and CD68.

A 32-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of intermittent abdominal pain without changes in bowel habits or bleeding. An abdominal ultrasound was normal. Colonoscopy revealed a submucosal polyp in the cecum near the appendicular orifice, involving less than one third of the circumference; biopsy specimens showed only unremarkable mucosa and submucosa with no evidence of tumor. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 2.8×2.0×1.8 cm, well-defined, smoothly marginated, homogeneously enhancing mass predominantly involving the cecal wall without adjacent wall thickening, findings favored a benign neoplasm. The patient underwent laparoscopic resection with primary anastomosis. On gross examination, the lateral wall of the cecum showed a bulge; on sectioning, there was a well-circumscribed, solid, yellowish tumor measuring 2.8×2.0×1.8 cm confined to the bowel wall without hemorrhage or necrosis, and the overlying mucosa was intact. Microscopic examination revealed a well-circumscribed intramuscular neoplasm composed of sheets of polygonal to spindle cells with abundant coarse granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and uniform bland nuclear chromatin. The cytoplasmic granules were positive on periodic acid–Schiff and luxol fast blue stains. Mitotic figures were infrequent (<1 per 10 high-power fields), and there was no atypia or necrosis. A thin layer of stretched muscularis propria surrounded the tumor on all sides.

A 57-year-old woman with Child–Pugh B cirrhosis from prior alcohol excess underwent routine surveillance. Her α-fetoprotein level was 5330 mcg/L (normal <9 mcg/L), but liver ultrasound showed no focal lesion. A multiphase contrast-enhanced CT scan revealed a 4 cm lesion in segment 2 of the liver that lacked arterial-phase enhancement and showed only peripheral enhancement in the portal-venous phase. A follow-up liver MRI confirmed a similar 4 cm lesion in segment 2 without arterial enhancement and with peripheral portal-venous enhancement. No other lesions were identified.

A previously healthy 23-year-old Caucasian woman presented with left-sided hemiplegia and a fever of 39°C. On arrival, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 7/15, and she was intubated and admitted to the ICU. A brain CT scan showed a massive right sylvian infarction with severe cerebral edema, and she underwent decompressive craniectomy. Physical examination was notable for multiple palpable left inguinal lymph nodes. Laboratory tests revealed leukocytosis (WBC 17,900 cells/mm³, 91% neutrophils), hemoglobin 10 g/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 356 IU/L, and C-reactive protein at 197 and 8 mg/L. An abdominal CT scan demonstrated multiple enlarged lymph nodes and a retroperitoneal mass adjacent to the left psoas muscle. Transesophageal echocardiography was normal. Blood cultures were negative for bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial pathogens. Serologic tests for cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, Epstein–Barr virus, HIV, tularaemia, Yersinia pestis, brucellosis, leptospirosis, Lyme disease, syphilis, and Toxoplasma gondii were inconclusive. Cerebrospinal fluid examination was negative. Peripheral blood smear and bone marrow aspiration were nondiagnostic. Further laboratory tests for autoimmune disorders were also inconclusive. A diagnostic workup for inherited causes of thrombophilia (protein C and S deficiency, antithrombin III deficiency, factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation, hyperhomocysteinemia, elevated lipoprotein(a), polycythemia vera) revealed no pathology. Furthermore, acquired prothrombotic states such as paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, nephrotic syndrome, hyperviscosity disorders (Waldenström’s macroglobulinemia, multiple myeloma), and sickle cell anemia were excluded. A CT-guided biopsy of the retroperitoneal mass showed no specific infection or malignancy.

A 60-year-old man with a history of vitiligo and anemia presented with several weeks of diffuse, intensely pruritic skin lesions over his entire body. Three weeks earlier, his primary care physician performed a punch biopsy and diagnosed dermatitis; he was treated with topical nystatin. He worked in a metal refinery and at a shipping dock, smoked one pack per day for 35 years, drank alcohol daily, and denied illicit drugs. He was sexually active with multiple female partners and had no travel history or family history of skin disease.

On examination, there were dry, circular rashes and palpable inguinal, axillary, and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies including CBC, CMP, lactate dehydrogenase, and angiotensin-converting enzyme were within normal limits; HIV testing was negative. He was diagnosed with nummular eczema and prescribed topical hydrocortisone, oral cetirizine, naproxen, and a prednisone taper.

One month later, examination revealed edematous nasal mucosa, posterior oropharyngeal erythema, and a maculopapular rash; he was treated with topical triamcinolone and oral hydroxyzine. In January, he was referred to dermatology for persistent pruritus. He felt well otherwise and denied constitutional symptoms. Lesions were noted on the face, chest, and abdomen. A documented differential diagnosis included sarcoidosis, lichen planus, disseminated lupus erythematosus, lymphoma, and syphilis.

Punch biopsies were obtained from the left upper chest and abdomen. Results showed morphologic, immunophenotypic, and molecular findings consistent with cutaneous T-cell lymphoma; immunophenotype was CD3+, CD4+, CD8+, with a CD4:CD8 ratio >2:1, significant loss of CD7 staining, rare scattered CD20+ B lymphocytes, and CD30+ in <5% of cells. Treponema pallidum stain was negative. T-cell gene rearrangement studies were positive for a monoclonal T-cell population. Histology demonstrated an atypical lymphoid epidermal infiltrate with highly irregular nuclear contours, epidermal-dermal splitting, and a dermal inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes, histiocytes, and eosinophils.

A 59-year-old woman presented with several weeks of worsening fatigue, shortness of breath on exertion, and palpitations. Her hemoglobin was 6.9 g/dL. Because of suspected gastrointestinal bleeding, an upper endoscopy was performed, revealing a submucosal mass with mucosal ulceration on the posterior wall of the duodenal bulb. A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed a 5.2 × 4.9 × 4.8 cm heterogeneous mass in the duodenal bulb without evidence of metastatic disease. Endoscopic biopsy demonstrated a spindle cell neoplasm without features of lymphoma, neuroendocrine tumor, or adenocarcinoma. Immunohistochemical staining was negative for CD34, CD117, DOG1, S100, desmin, BCL2, neuron-specific enolase, synaptophysin, chromogranin A, and pancytokeratin AE1/AE3; staining was diffusely positive for vimentin and patchily positive for smooth muscle actin.

A 26-year-old man underwent a chest radiograph as part of an annual check-up, which showed a protrusion of the aortopulmonary window. Seven months later, he remained asymptomatic but was referred for further evaluation. His medical history was notable only for epilepsy managed with medication; he was a never smoker and worked as a carbon-fiber researcher with organic solvent exposure. Chest CT revealed a thin-walled multilocular cystic tumor, 9.0 cm in diameter, in the anterior mediastinum; the septa of the tumor enhanced with contrast, and the mass compressed the left brachiocephalic vein without clear invasion of surrounding structures. MRI confirmed a multilocular cystic lesion with focal mural nodules in the same region. Laboratory studies showed a mildly elevated carcinoembryonic antigen level of 5.4 ng/ml (normal <5.0 ng/ml); alpha-fetoprotein, beta-human chorionic gonadotropin, anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody, and soluble interleukin-2 receptor levels were normal. The preoperative working diagnosis was a cystic thymoma or malignant lymphoma, and no needle biopsy was performed because of the thin cyst wall.

A 42-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of intermittent dry cough and exertional dyspnea. Approximately one year earlier, a chest radiograph had shown a small left pneumothorax that did not require treatment. Two months before admission, her symptoms worsened, and chest CT demonstrated bilateral pneumothorax and diffuse thin-walled cysts; her symptoms improved after closed thoracic drainage. Two weeks before presentation, she had another episode of bilateral pneumothorax.

She denied fever, chest pain, hemoptysis, or weight loss. Her past medical history was unremarkable. She was a housewife, had never smoked, and had no family history of cancer. On examination, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. There was no clubbing, cyanosis, or palpable lymphadenopathy. Breath sounds were decreased bilaterally.

High-resolution CT of the chest showed bilateral pneumothoraces and numerous round or oval thin-walled lung cysts, 3–10 mm in diameter, predominantly in the upper and middle lung zones and more extensive on the right. Small ground-glass nodules were seen along vascular branches and in subpleural regions, and a cavitary nodule measuring 1.5 cm was present in the left lower lobe.

Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, urinalysis, liver and renal function, and arterial blood gas analysis, were within normal limits. Carcinoembryonic antigen was elevated at 52.43 ng/mL (normal < 5 ng/mL). Antinuclear antibody tests were negative. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and brush cytology showed no tumor cells, and transbronchial lung biopsy revealed only non-specific inflammation.

A 17-year-old female presented with a slight, asymptomatic swelling in the posterior left mandible. She denied pain and was unsure of the duration of the lesion. Cone beam computed tomography revealed a well-defined, unilocular radiolucent lesion adjacent to the pericoronal follicle of the impacted mandibular left third molar (#38), with expansion and perforation of the lingual cortical plate. An incisional biopsy was performed, during which the lesion appeared cystic with both liquid and semisolid contents.

A 30-year-old woman with no past medical history presented with a one-year history of mild, intermittent left upper-quadrant abdominal pain that had progressively worsened and was now accompanied by nausea. On examination, she was afebrile, and abdominal palpation revealed tenderness and a palpable, firm mass in the left upper quadrant without rebound. There was no vomiting, hematemesis, hematochezia, or systemic “B” symptoms. Laboratory studies showed a leukocytosis with neutrophilia and an elevated C-reactive protein level. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated an enlarged spleen (15 × 10 × 5.5 cm) containing two well-demarcated, low-density masses measuring 5.4 × 5.1 cm and 5.3 × 2.3 cm, respectively. Given the concern for splenic neoplasm and acute abdominal pain, a laparoscopic splenectomy was planned.

A 38-year-old woman presented with a painless swelling in the left inner cheek that had been present for 28 years. It began as a small nodule and gradually enlarged to approximately 2×2×3 cm. On intraoral examination, a solitary, non-tender, fluctuant swelling was noted in the left retro-commissural buccal mucosa, exhibiting a small white surface discoloration. Palpation revealed a soft consistency with several hard, globular structures within the lesion. A clinical differential diagnosis of long-standing lipoma, mucocele, and benign minor salivary gland tumor was considered. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated multiple dense homogeneous radio-opaque structures of varying sizes and shapes in the left mandibular posterior soft-tissue region, corresponding to the site of the lesion and to the palpated hard nodules.

A 17-year-old healthy woman presented with a 9-month history of right groin pain. The pain initially occurred with long-distance walking, without any history of trauma, and gradually progressed to occur at night; it was associated with a palpable swelling in the same region. She denied fever, weight loss, or other constitutional symptoms. On examination, there was a mildly tender, firm, localized swelling over the right pubic area without overlying skin changes or pulsations. The range of motion of the right hip was full and painless. A pelvic radiograph showed an expansile lytic lesion of the right superior pubic ramus. Pelvic MRI demonstrated an expansile multicystic bony lesion measuring 6.8 × 3.3 × 4.5 cm with multiple fluid–fluid levels in the right pubic ramus. Routine blood tests, including complete blood count, kidney function, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and alkaline phosphatase, were all within normal limits.

A 60-year-old man underwent a routine abdominal ultrasound, which demonstrated a bulging of the bladder floor with mild left ureteral dilation. He was asymptomatic; his medical history was unremarkable. On examination, the prostate was estimated at 40 cm3. Laboratory studies, including PSA (2.1 ng/mL), were within normal limits. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a well-delineated, homogeneous retrovesical solid mass measuring 5 × 3 cm. MRI confirmed a noninfiltrative lesion between the rectum and bladder, surrounded by a thin low-signal T2 capsule. A transrectal ultrasound–guided core-needle biopsy was performed. Hematoxylin and eosin sections revealed a spindle-cell proliferation; immunostaining showed expression of CD34 antigen and vimentin.

A 47-year-old woman with Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome presented for routine gynaecological follow-up. She had primary amenorrhea diagnosed at age 16, with laparoscopy showing bilateral normal ovaries and fallopian tubes connected to a fibrous band. At age 17, a neovagina was created via Davidov’s technique, and she commenced coital activity within 2 months. At age 21, an abnormal Pap smear (Papanicolaou class III) led to colposcopy and biopsy showing high-grade intraepithelial neoplasia (VAIN 2) in the neovagina; HPV type 16 was detected and treated with laser vaporization. Her Pap smears remained normal until age 47, when high-risk HPV (non-16/18) was positive; biopsies revealed HPV infection in the neovagina and a low-grade vulvar intraepithelial lesion, managed conservatively. At that visit, a mobile pelvic mass was palpated. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a right-sided solid tumour measuring 55 mm with moderately variable echogenicity and acoustic shadows; a small homogeneous area suggestive of uterine rudiments lay lateral to the mass, but the right ovary was not visualized. Ovarian tumour markers (CA125, HE4, CEA) were within normal limits. Four weeks later, repeat ultrasound measured the mass at 60 × 52 mm, Doppler showed sparse blood flow, and both uterine rudiments and ovaries with small antral follicles were identified bilaterally.

A 65-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an asymptomatic anterior neck mass. She had no dysphagia, odynophagia, dyspnea, or thyroid dysfunction symptoms. Her history was notable only for breast papillary carcinoma; there was no personal or family history of endocrine disorders. On exam, there was fullness in the anterior neck extending to the sternal notch without signs of infection or malignancy. CT of the neck showed an enlarged multinodular thyroid with mediastinal extension, rightward tracheal deviation, and a mixed cystic–solid lesion in the left thyroid lobe extending below the aortic arch. She underwent ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration of the dominant cystic lesion, yielding 15 mL of clear fluid that was cytologically benign and “most consistent with a benign colloid nodule.” She elected observation. One year later she reported mild dysphagia, and repeat CT revealed further inferior extension of the lesion. She again chose observation. Two years after initial presentation, she remained minimally symptomatic but CT showed a 1 cm increase in inferior extension of the cyst to the level of the aortic arch. Given progressive growth, she opted for definitive surgical resection.

A 24-year-old Egyptian woman presents after a syncopal fall and head trauma. Over the preceding month, she has had multiple falls accompanied by left-sided weakness, diplopia, ataxia, and dysphagia. On examination, she has a left abducens nerve palsy, bilateral upper and lower extremity weakness (2/5), and is unable to stand due to pain; a 1 cm soft-tissue mass is palpable in the left pelvis. Laboratory studies show an elevated lactate dehydrogenase level of 375 U/L, with otherwise normal complete blood count and metabolic panel. A prior mandibular fracture with bilateral plate placement is noted. 
CT of the brain and maxillofacial region reveals soft-tissue masses eroding the skull base, mandible, sphenoid, and extending into the left orbit. CT of the spine shows paraspinal and epidural soft-tissue masses with vertebral erosion. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrates multiple soft-tissue lesions infiltrating the chest wall and left hemipelvis, along with diffuse lytic vertebral lesions and mild compression fractures. MRI of the brain and entire spine confirms multiple lytic and expansile lesions of the calvarium, skull base, facial bones, orbit, and neuraxis, with epidural and leptomeningeal involvement but no acute ischemic changes. 
The initial differential diagnosis includes metastatic solid tumors, atypical neuroblastoma, and lymphoma. Empiric dexamethasone is administered, and a CT-guided biopsy of a sternal soft-tissue mass is planned.

A 64-year-old male smoker presented with a 10-year history of a slowly enlarging, painless swelling of the left cheek. He had no dysphagia, dysphonia, otalgia, or facial weakness. Examination showed a 4×4 cm firm, well-defined, non-tender mass in the left preauricular region, without cervical lymphadenopathy; facial-nerve function was intact. Hematological, liver, and renal tests were normal; HIV and hepatitis B serologies were negative. Fine‐needle aspiration yielded 8 mL of brown fluid; smears were hypocellular, with scant macrophages in serous fluid, and were reported as non‐diagnostic but benign. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the neck revealed a 43×41×39 mm well‐defined cystic lesion in the left parotid gland with peripheral enhancement and deep‐lobe extension. A benign lymphoepithelial cyst or Warthin’s tumor was suspected.

A 3-year-old girl was referred for management of recurrent exotropia 1½ years after primary strabismus surgery. At 15 months of age, she had a 30-prism-diopter divergent strabismus; dilated fundus exam then was normal. After 3 months without improvement, bilateral lateral rectus recessions were performed at 18 months, with an uneventful postoperative course. At 3 years of age, the exotropia recurred.  
Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/50 in the left eye. Cycloplegic refraction was +0.5 D in the right eye and +1.00 D in the left eye. Cover–uncover testing revealed variable-angle left exotropia. Slit-lamp examination was normal in both eyes.  
Dilated fundus examination showed normal findings in the right eye. In the left eye, there was a subtle elevated greyish lesion in the papillomacular region with loss of the foveal reflex and associated epiretinal gliosis; no foveal dragging or vascular tortuosity was noted.  
Optical coherence tomography of the right eye was normal. In the left eye, OCT revealed marked thickening of the inner retinal layers (retinal nerve fiber, ganglion cell, and inner plexiform layers) with an epilesional gliotic reaction, loss of the foveal depression, and no epiretinal membrane. Foveal retinal thickness measured 500 μm in the left eye versus 218 μm in the right eye. Subfoveal choroidal thickness was 224 μm in the left eye and 283 μm in the right eye. A “shark-teeth” sign and marked outer nuclear layer thickening were present on OCT sections near the fovea.  
Near-infrared imaging was normal in the right eye. In the left eye, there was generalized hyporeflectivity of the macular region with oblique linear hyperreflectivity corresponding to the epiretinal gliosis.

A 37-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with a 1-day history of severe dysuria, urgency, frequency, fever, and chills. He denied hematuria or flank pain and had never experienced similar symptoms. He was a heavy smoker. On examination, he appeared ill, was febrile to 39.3 °C, and had normal blood pressure. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis with a left shift. Urinalysis showed numerous white blood cells, 1–2 red blood cells per high-power field, and bacteria.  
A renal and bladder ultrasound demonstrated a well-defined lobulated heterogeneous isoechoic mass with possible mural calcification and internal blood flow at the right anterolateral bladder wall; the kidneys were normal without hydronephrosis. A contrast-enhanced CT scan confirmed a 5.5 × 4.3 cm oval mass on the right bladder wall with mild dilation of the right distal ureter.  
He was admitted with a diagnosis of febrile urinary tract infection and started on intravenous imipenem–cilastatin and supportive care. Four days later, he improved clinically. Urine culture grew Escherichia coli resistant to most antibiotics except imipenem and ertapenem. Urine cytology was negative for malignancy.  
Under general anesthesia, cystoscopy revealed a large bulging mass arising from the right lateral bladder wall with intact, smooth overlying mucosa. Examination under anesthesia confirmed a mobile lower abdominal mass. A transurethral resection of the bladder tumor was performed, and tissue was sent for histopathologic analysis.

A 70-year-old Chinese man presented with a 3-month history of fever and progressive swelling and pain in the left lower extremity, without antecedent trauma or infection. Initial evaluation at a local hospital with color Doppler US showed dilated deep and intramuscular veins with slow flow, and decreased echogenicity with increased vascularity in left thigh and calf muscles; intramuscular venous thrombosis and cellulitis were suspected. He received anticoagulation (dabigatran) and IV antibiotics (penicillin G), but the swelling, pain, and fever worsened (peak temperature 42 °C), and he was transferred for further evaluation.

On examination, temperature was elevated, and there was a hard, non-tender, ill-defined mass in the left inguinal region. The left lower extremity was markedly swollen, tender, dark red, and warm. Neurologic exam was normal. No hepatosplenomegaly. Initial labs showed CRP 292 mg/L, ESR 58 mm/h, ferritin 993.7 ng/mL, CA125 66 U/mL, β2-microglobulin 9.42 mg/L, normal LDH, and decreased IgG and IgA levels. 

US of the left lower extremity revealed large, ill-defined, hypoechoic regions diffusely involving muscles of the medial and posterior thigh and calf, with preservation of muscle architecture and hypervascularity on color and power Doppler. An enlarged left inguinal lymph node had a thick hypoechoic cortex, hyperechoic medulla, and increased vascularity. MRI of the calves showed diffuse muscle swelling with minimally heterogeneous hypointense signal on T1-weighted images and hyperintense signal on T2-weighted fat-suppressed sequences, with indistinct margins. Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis and thighs demonstrated enlarged muscles of the medial and posterior thigh compartments containing patchy hypodense regions with indistinct margins, mild patchy enhancement, and preserved adjacent fat planes; no thrombosis was seen.

A 78-year-old man presented with a dark red, round mass on the right upper quadrant of his abdomen that had been present for several months. The lesion measured approximately 50 × 60 mm, had a smooth surface, and was non-tender and non-pruritic. There were no other skin lesions or palpable lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 6.78 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 14.0 g/dL, and platelet count 243 × 10^9/L. Liver enzymes, uric acid, lactate dehydrogenase, and alkaline phosphatase were all within normal limits. Computed tomography of the chest was unremarkable. Abdominal and pelvic CT demonstrated a 4-cm discoid, hyperattenuating mass in the abdominal wall skin without enlarged lymph nodes. Upper and lower endoscopy yielded normal findings. ^18F-FDG PET/CT revealed a single hypermetabolic lesion in the abdominal wall (SUV = 12.8). A biopsy specimen of the skin lesion suggested lymphoma.

A 20-year-old man presented with a five-month history of dull, aching pain in the right hip, worsened when rising from sitting. There was no trauma, fever, or night pain. He had no systemic symptoms. On examination, the right hip had painful range of motion without swelling, erythema, or neurovascular deficit. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and parathyroid hormone levels, were all within normal limits.  
Anteroposterior radiographs of the pelvis and hips showed a well-defined, geographic, predominantly lytic lesion, approximately 2.0×2.5 cm, located anteroinferiorly in the right femoral head. There were punctate calcifications within the lesion, a narrow zone of transition, and no periosteal reaction, cortical destruction, or soft-tissue mass.  
Computed tomography of the lesion confirmed a 2×2.5 cm lytic, mildly expansile lesion in the femoral head without cortical breach or pathological fracture. The CT impression was that of a benign bone lesion.

A 74-year-old woman with a 55 pack-year smoking history underwent right upper lobectomy five years earlier for stage IIA lung adenocarcinoma (pT2bN0M0) and received no adjuvant therapy. She remained asymptomatic and continued smoking. During routine surveillance, chest computed tomography revealed multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules up to 10 mm in diameter, some containing thin-walled cavities predominantly in the lower lobes. Positron emission tomography–CT demonstrated a mix of 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose–avid lesions (maximum SUV, 8.6) and nonavid lesions in the lungs, with additional uptake in the liver. Blood tests showed no evidence of inflammation and normal levels of lung cancer tumor markers.

A 3-year-old Caucasian boy presented with a 2-week history of left periorbital swelling. The swelling began gradually after blunt trauma in a traffic accident. On initial evaluation at another hospital, he had left periorbital ecchymosis, subconjunctival hemorrhage, and proptosis without visual loss. Two weeks later, persistent proptosis led to referral. Examination at our center revealed slight left proptosis and a tender mass in the inferior orbit displacing the globe upward. Extraocular movements and pupillary responses were normal, and slit-lamp and fundoscopic examinations were unremarkable. Intraocular pressures were within normal limits. Neurologic examination was nonfocal, and there was no hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, bone pain, or systemic symptoms.

Craniofacial CT showed a 29×19 mm spontaneously hyperdense, oval extraconal mass in the inferior orbit, displacing the inferior and lateral rectus muscles, with no bone erosion or significant contrast enhancement.

Given the history of trauma and imaging, an inferolateral subperiosteal hematoma was suspected. An inferior mediopalpebral incision was performed, but instead of a hematoma, a pale yellowish mass was encountered and excised.

Microscopic examination showed sheets of small round cells infiltrating fibrocollagenous tissue.

A 58-year-old man was referred in May 2014 for evaluation of suspected duodenal lymphoma. He had a long history of chronic dyspepsia and esophagitis following laparoscopic fundoplication in 2004 and recurrent need for proton-pump inhibitors. Over the preceding 6 months he noted increasing postprandial abdominal discomfort despite regular pantoprazole. His medical history also included resolved hepatitis B (PCR negative) and moderate COPD (GOLD II). He denied recent antibiotic use.

On presentation he was asymptomatic apart from intermittent abdominal discomfort and had an ECOG performance status of 0. Vital signs were normal. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed normal blood counts and normal renal and liver function tests. Serologic and histologic screening for Helicobacter pylori was negative. Autoimmune serologies (ANA, ANCA, thyroid antibodies, rheumatoid factors, SS-A/SS-B) were negative.

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed multiple small nodules with superficial erosions in the post-bulbar duodenum and otherwise normal gastric and esophageal mucosa; gastric and esophageal biopsies showed only mild chronic gastritis and esophagitis without lymphoma. Multiple biopsies of a duodenal nodule showed a follicular lymphoid infiltrate composed of small centrocytes with fewer than 5 centroblasts per high-power field. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated CD20+, CD79a+, bcl2+, CD10+, bcl6+, and CD3–/CD5–. 

An 18F-FDG PET/CT scan showed no abnormal tracer uptake in the duodenum or elsewhere in lymph nodes or other organs.

A 54-year-old man with childhood-onset psoriasis well controlled on low-potency topical steroids presented with a 4-month history of a worsening rash. One year earlier, he had developed dystrophic nail changes. Three months after noticing these changes, he began risankizumab injections (150 mg) for nail psoriasis. Within 4 months, his nail symptoms improved, but he developed multiple new, faintly erythematous patches on his trunk, back, and thighs that appeared different from his previous psoriasis lesions. 

Toenail clippings showed morphologic features of psoriasis without onychomycosis. A skin biopsy revealed an atypical CD4-dominant epitheliotropic lymphocytic infiltrate suspicious for evolving T-cell dyscrasia. He was referred for further evaluation.

On examination, he had well-demarcated, erythematous, scaly plaques on the face, neck, back, buttocks, arms, and legs, and numerous faintly erythematous patches of variable shape, 1–5 cm in diameter, scattered across his thighs, abdomen, flank, and back, some with follicular prominence. He also had onychodystrophy of all fingernails and toenails. There was no lymphadenopathy.

A 40-year-old woman presented with a 6‐month history of dyspeptic symptoms. She denied nausea, vomiting, changes in bowel habits, hematemesis, melena, or weight loss. On examination, her vital signs were normal. She was obese and had mild pallor but no icterus, thyromegaly, lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 11.0 g/dL, white‐cell count 11 000/µL, platelet count 226 × 10^3/µL, and normal renal function and electrolytes. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed chronic active Helicobacter pylori gastritis and a 2.0-cm submucosal mass in the gastric antrum. Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated a submucosal lesion arising from the third echo layer without lymphadenopathy. Biomarkers for neuroendocrine tumors, including serotonin, chromogranin A, and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid, were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed thickening of the gastric antrum at the site of the lesion without evidence of extragastric extension or metastases.

A 10-year-old intact female Yorkshire terrier was presented for chronic pain of unknown origin and progressive weight loss; body weight was 0.86 kg. Physical examination findings included poor body condition, muscle atrophy, and pale mucous membranes. A firm, well-demarcated subcutaneous mass (~2 cm diameter) was palpated on the right mid-thorax. Laboratory tests showed mild monocytosis, mild neutrophilia, and mild to moderate anisocytosis on blood smear. Faecal analysis revealed Strongyloid-type ova. Due to her deteriorating condition and owner financial constraints, humane euthanasia was performed, followed by necropsy.

External post-mortem evaluation confirmed poor body condition and revealed an ingested lamb bone lodged over the left carnassial tooth. In the thoracic cavity, the left caudal lung lobe contained an 8 cm × 8 cm mass; multiple smaller nodules were scattered throughout other lung lobes. Sectioning of the large mass revealed a necrotic center with thick yellow-green fluid. A single, well-circumscribed skin mass was noted on the right thoracic wall. Tissue impression smears from the lung and skin masses revealed neoplastic epithelial cells with moderate pleomorphism, prominent nucleoli, and occasional mitoses.

Histopathological examination of lung tissue showed non-encapsulated, expansile epithelial proliferations with papillary, micropapillary, and solid growth patterns, moderate cellular pleomorphism, indistinct cytoplasmic margins, and lymphovascular invasion. Histology of the skin mass demonstrated similar neoplastic epithelial cells, microvilli-like cytoplasmic projections, and lymphovascular invasion.

A 36-year-old man with no medical history was referred after routine imaging revealed an asymptomatic radiolucent lesion in the right posterior mandible. Cone-beam computed tomography showed a well-defined unilocular radiolucency measuring 17 × 12.5 mm associated with the crown of an unerupted right mandibular third molar and extending to the distal root of the second molar. Intraoral examination revealed healthy gingiva, absence of teeth 16, 36, 37, and 46, no cortical expansion, and clinical attachment loss on the distal root of tooth 47 with normal pulp vitality. Aspiration yielded no fluid, and a working diagnosis of dentigerous cyst was made.

A 71-year-old woman, gravida 6 para 4, presented with a two-week history of general malaise. She had no history of gynecological surgery. A routine cardiac ultrasound revealed an echogenic mass in the right atrium, and she was referred to cardiology. Her medical history included hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and atrial fibrillation, for which she was receiving anticoagulant therapy.

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory tests showed normal tumor markers, liver and kidney function, and D-dimer levels, except for expected coagulation abnormalities related to anticoagulation.

Dynamic contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen demonstrated a hypodense mass within the uterus and dilation of the right uterine artery. Multiplanar reconstructions revealed several small arteries arising from the right uterine artery that coursed through the right ovarian vein, progressively enlarged, and continued into the inferior vena cava, right atrium, and right ventricle. A plexus of small arteries from the right ovarian, subcostal, and uterine arteries surrounded and interconnected along this pathway.

Pelvic MRI showed a 13×7×6 cm uterine lesion diffusely involving the myometrium. On T1-weighted images, the lesion had low signal similar to myometrium with multiple tiny hyperintense foci that suppressed on fat-saturated sequences. T2-weighted images revealed inhomogeneous high signal with scattered hypointense nodules. On contrast-enhanced fat-suppressed T1-weighted images, the lesion enhanced strongly but contained poorly demarcated hypointense areas. Diffusion-weighted imaging and ADC mapping showed slightly increased signal within the lesion.

A 29-year-old woman previously underwent left-sided adnexectomy for a yolk sac tumor and enucleation of a right ovarian mature cystic teratoma. Preoperative contrast-enhanced CT at that time showed a 10 mm lesion in segment 3 of the liver, which was thought to be benign. She received four cycles of bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin. Two years later, surveillance imaging revealed that the liver lesion had increased to 20 mm in diameter. She was asymptomatic, and her examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, coagulation profile, renal function, and liver function tests, were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 20 mm tumor in segment 3 with heterogeneous components, including areas consistent with adipose tissue and regions of early arterial-phase enhancement. Fat-suppressed MRI confirmed the presence of intralesional adipose tissue.

An 85-year-old man with a history of cerebral infarction and mild residual right hemiparesis presented with a 6-month history of progressive gait disturbance, lower-limb hypesthesia, and bladder and bowel dysfunction. Neurologic examination revealed muscle strength of 3/5 in the right lower limb and 1/5 in the left, with diminished pinprick, temperature, and light-touch sensation at and below the T10 dermatome. Deep tendon reflexes in both lower limbs were decreased. Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine showed an oval, well-defined intradural extramedullary mass at the T10 level that was isointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and demonstrated intense peripheral ring enhancement with homogeneous central enhancement after gadolinium administration. A T2-weighted sequence also revealed an intramedullary hyperintense area extending from T4 to the conus medullaris, with partial enhancement at T10. Whole-body computed tomography showed no evidence of metastatic disease.

A 14-year-old boy with no prior medical history presented with 5 days of progressive left hip pain and inability to bear weight. He was afebrile. On examination, there was severe pain with hip movement and limited range of motion. Initial pelvic radiographs were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 4.5 mg/dl (normal 0.0–0.5 mg/dl), a normal white blood-cell count (5.91×10^3/µL), and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 18 mm/h (normal 0–15 mm/h). Given concern for septic arthritis, fluoroscopy-guided aspiration of the hip joint was performed 2 hours after admission. The aspirate was serohemorrhagic and contained 12,000 red blood cells/mL, 37,170 leukocytes/mL with 85% neutrophils, and a negative Gram stain. Twenty-four hours after admission, contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging of the hip revealed a 3×4 cm well-circumscribed, lobulated synovial nodule with mild heterogeneous contrast enhancement, confined within the joint and without evidence of bony invasion.

A 52-year-old woman presented with 9 months of neck pain and 4 months of progressive weakness in all four limbs, beginning with right triceps then involving right and left thigh muscles and left biceps, accompanied by urinary urgency and frequency. On examination, she was quadriparetic (MRC grade 4 on the right, 3 on the left), with hyperesthesia in the C2 dermatome, hyperreflexia, bilateral extensor plantar responses, difficulty swallowing, and respiratory compromise. No stigmata of neurofibromatosis were noted, and routine blood tests were normal. Sagittal and axial MRI of the craniocervical junction showed a well-defined, purely posterior, dural-based mass at the foramen magnum measuring 2.0 × 2.5 cm that was hypo-intense on T1-weighted images, iso- to hypo-intense on T2, and demonstrated inhomogeneous enhancement after contrast administration.

A 47-year-old woman with no history of smoking presented with a 1-month history of headache, progressive weakness in both lower extremities, and urinary retention. Two months earlier, she had been diagnosed with miliary tuberculosis–associated meningitis and type 2 diabetes and treated empirically for tuberculosis based on chest radiographic and CT findings without bacteriologic confirmation. One week before transfer, she developed headache, low fever, and worsening lower-limb weakness; urinary retention followed after five days. 

On examination at our hospital, she was in average condition. Respiratory, cardiovascular, and abdominal exams were unremarkable. Lower-limb muscle strength was 2/5; sensation was intact. Testing for meningoencephalitis was negative. Sputum studies for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (acid-fast bacilli smear, culture, Xpert MTB) were negative. Complete blood count, serum biochemistry, and urinalysis were within normal limits. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed 10 cells/mm3, protein 0.69 g/L, positive Pandy test, chloride 109 mmol/L, glucose 3.8 mmol/L, and negative Xpert MTB. 

A chest radiograph demonstrated numerous small nodules predominantly in the upper lung zones. Chest CT (lung window) showed uniform, evenly distributed central lobular nodules of similar size and density in both upper lobes; the lower lobes and costophrenic angles were normal. Brain MRI after gadolinium revealed multiple nodules of varying size with hollow cores and strong enhancement scattered throughout the brain and brainstem without surrounding edema. Thoracic spine MRI with contrast showed an oval, 15×24 mm mass at the T12 level with a clear border, hollow core, and homogeneous enhancement, causing cord compression.

In response to these clinical, laboratory, and imaging findings, the differential diagnoses included tuberculosis in the lungs and brain; metastases to the lungs, brain, and spinal cord; and toxoplasmosis affecting the brain and spinal cord.

A 65-year-old man presented with a six-year history of swelling below the left earlobe. The lesion was insidious in onset and had gradually increased to about 5 cm in greatest dimension. His medical and family histories were noncontributory; he had smoked for 25 years but did not drink alcohol. Examination revealed a smooth, firm, well-defined mass extending from the left earlobe to the lower border of the mandibular ramus and posterior to the ear. The swelling was mildly tender without overlying skin changes or increased temperature. Intraoral examination was unremarkable; parotid stimulation yielded normal saliva. Aspiration produced a light brown, viscous fluid. Routine blood tests and an orthopantomogram were within normal limits. Ultrasonography showed a well-defined hypoechoic mass measuring 4.34 × 2.49 × 3.39 cm in the lower pole of the left parotid gland without ductal dilatation. Computed tomography demonstrated a rounded, well-defined cystic lesion in the superficial lobe of the left parotid gland. Clinical differential diagnoses included pleomorphic adenoma, low-grade parotid malignancy, lipoma, and neurofibroma.

A 65-year-old Asian man presented with a 2-year history of progressive difficulty voiding, worsening over the past 6 months despite α-blocker therapy. He denied hematuria, fever, or weight loss but noted dry ejaculation for more than one year. Initial transrectal ultrasound revealed a prostate volume of 230 cm³ with an irregular shape, heterogeneous echotexture, and multiple cysts. A systemic core-needle biopsy showed nodular hyperplasia with inflammation and some atypical glands but no evidence of malignancy. He underwent two transurethral resections of the prostate four months apart; both specimens demonstrated nodular hyperplasia and chronic prostatitis without malignancy. Symptoms recurred, and repeat ultrasound showed a residual prostate volume of 131.3 cm³, with uroflowmetry revealing a low peak flow rate and a large postvoid residual. He then underwent green-light laser prostatectomy. One year later, he again experienced progressive voiding difficulty. On examination, digital rectal examination revealed a large, elastic prostate without induration. Laboratory studies showed a PSA level of 4–6 ng/mL and normal urinalysis. CT of the pelvis demonstrated an 8.2 × 8.1 × 7.8 cm multiloculated cystic mass arising from the prostate, abutting but not invading adjacent organs. MRI confirmed an 8.0 × 7.3 × 6.4 cm retrovesical multiseptate lesion with solid components and heterogeneous enhancement; no pelvic lymphadenopathy was present.

A 51-year-old woman (G3P3) was referred for evaluation of an abnormal lesion on the vulva. She first noticed a small wart-like lesion 10 months earlier that continued to grow and eventually resembled a small cauliflower. She denied pain but reported discomfort and occasional bleeding. Her medical history was notable for hypertension and hyperthyroidism, both controlled with medication. 

On gynecologic examination, there was a 2 cm lobulated, reddish mass on the upper part of the right labia majora, parallel to the clitoris, with ulceration at its distal end. Vaginal and cervical examinations were normal. 

During the office visit, a decision was made to perform a wide local excision under local anesthesia, and the entire lesion was removed and sent for histopathological examination.

An 82-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a progressive rash. She had been admitted two months earlier for acute pancreatitis; during treatment, erythema appeared over her trunk and extremities. Although her pancreatitis resolved, the rash worsened. On examination, there were multiple erythematous blisters and erosions on the extremities and trunk. Laboratory studies showed no inflammatory response; tumor markers and collagen‐disease markers, including antinuclear antibodies, were within normal limits. Trace elements (zinc) and essential fatty acids were normal, and glucagon levels were normal. Two skin biopsies were performed; autoimmune bullous diseases, such as pemphigus, were negative, and the subcutaneous adipose tissue showed no abnormalities. No source of infection was found, and infectious, drug‐related, and collagen‐disease causes were ruled out. Upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated dilatation of the main pancreatic duct and a multifocal cystic mass in the pancreatic body. MRI confirmed main duct dilatation and a septated cystic lesion in the head–body region. Endoscopic ultrasonography revealed a 6-mm mural nodule in the main pancreatic duct with contrast enhancement, suggestive of a mixed-type intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm with high-risk stigmata. Despite topical therapies, systemic steroids, immunosuppressants, nutritional supplementation, and immunoglobulin therapy, the rash continued to worsen, and oral involvement impaired intake, causing fatigue and weight loss.

A 10-year-old Caucasian girl presented with a 3-month history of diffuse abdominal pain that worsened after eating. She had postprandial vomiting of food contents and daily episodes of noninflammatory diarrhea. Abdominal distension developed over the past 2 months, and she lost 6 kg during this period. On examination, she appeared pale, and a cystic, fluctuant mass occupied the entire abdomen.

Abdominal ultrasonography revealed an extensive heterogeneous mass with interposed cystic areas, measuring 25.0 cm × 17.6 cm × 8.0 cm, filling the abdominal cavity. Contrast-enhanced CT scan showed a large heterogeneous lesion, predominantly cystic with thick enhancing septa, measuring 22 cm × 20 cm × 13 cm, with a small amount of adjacent free fluid. MRI of the abdomen demonstrated a 22 cm × 18 cm × 10.4 cm mass with T2 hyperintensity arising from the mesentery, compressing but not infiltrating adjacent structures.

The initial differential diagnosis included neuroblastoma and lymphoma.

A 79-year-old man presented with sudden loss of vision in both eyes. His ocular history was unremarkable, and he denied any recent trauma. He also reported nausea and upper abdominal pain of recent onset. His medical history included irritable bowel syndrome and chronic gastritis managed with ranitidine and omeprazole. Family history was notable for a father who had pancreatic cancer.

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/40 in the right eye and 20/50 in the left eye. Anterior segments, intraocular pressures, and pupillary reactions were normal. Funduscopic examination revealed multiple large yellow-white spots and superficial retinal hemorrhages surrounding the optic discs in both eyes. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated early hypofluorescence corresponding to the yellow-white patches and late hyperfluorescence in the same regions.
