Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, alanine aminotransferase 100 U/L (normal 0–48), alkaline phosphatase 240 U/L (20–125), lactate dehydrogenase 840 U/L (50–240), and gamma-glutamyl transferase 160 U/L (10–50). Serum amylase and lipase were within normal limits.

A 48-year-old man with well-controlled epilepsy presented with swelling of the volar aspect of his left wrist, discomfort in the radial three fingers, and paresthesia in the thenar region. He noted a soft, 2 × 1 cm lump on the volar wrist extending into the palm. On examination, distal pulses and capillary refill were normal, and sensory and motor functions of the radial, ulnar, and median nerves were intact. Tinel’s and Phalen’s tests were negative, and there was no thenar atrophy.  
Ultrasonography revealed a hyperechogenic lesion measuring approximately 2 × 0.64 cm adjacent to the wrist, without vascular activity. A separate thickened area at the base of the left thumb measured 0.51 × 0.84 cm.  
Magnetic resonance imaging of the left wrist demonstrated an abnormally enlarged median nerve with a characteristic “coaxial cable” or “spaghetti-like” appearance, reflecting enlarged cylindrical fascicles with a central intermediate signal on T1-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, surrounded by fatty tissue.

A 36-year-old man presented with a 3-week history of severe, retrosternal chest pain that worsened when lying flat, associated with progressive dyspnea, high-grade fevers, and episodes of delirium. His medical and family histories were unremarkable; he had a 40–pack-year smoking history. On examination, he was febrile to 39.2 °C, tachypneic, and had facial and upper-limb edema. Laboratory testing revealed mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL), a slightly elevated monocyte percentage (13.7%), and a normocytic red‐cell distribution width of 18.4%. Chest radiography showed widening of the mediastinum. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest demonstrated a 12-cm anterior mediastinal mass compressing and infiltrating both right and left brachiocephalic veins and the superior vena cava, with an intraluminal filling defect consistent with thrombus, and a separate nodule on the right diaphragm suggestive of metastasis.

A 16-year-old male presented with a soft, nontender, well-defined mass on the posterior scalp. He had noted the lesion for an unspecified duration and denied pain or other symptoms except for sparse hair growth over the area. 

On examination, the lesion measured approximately 4 cm in diameter, was mobile over the underlying structures, and the overlying skin was unremarkable aside from localized alopecia. Vital signs were within normal limits.

Noncontrast computed tomography of the head showed a 4.7 × 3.6 cm homogeneous fatty mass in the right parietal scalp without evidence of intracranial extension or bone involvement; the brain parenchyma was normal, and there was no high- or low-density lesion in the intracranial compartment.

Given the clinical impression of a lipoma, the patient was scheduled for surgical excision of the scalp mass.

A 13-year-old girl presented with one month of dull right knee pain on motion without rest pain, swelling, or tenderness. Range of motion in the right hip, knee, and ankle was normal. There was no history of endocrine dysfunction, including precocious puberty, and no cutaneous abnormalities. Radiographs of the right lower limb showed multiple radiolucent lesions with sclerotic contours in the diaphyses of the right femur, right tibia, patella, pelvis, and tarsal bones. Similar lesions were also present in the distal epiphysis of the femur and in the proximal and distal epiphyses of the tibia; the growth plates were open. The diaphyseal lesions in the femur and tibia caused cortical thinning. Technetium bone scintigraphy revealed increased uptake in the right femur diaphysis, right tibia diaphysis, right pelvis, and around both knees and ankles. On MRI, the epiphyseal lesions of the distal femur and proximal tibia were low on T1, high on fat-suppressed T2, and showed marked gadolinium enhancement. On the basis of these radiological findings, benign bone tumors such as polyostotic fibrous dysplasia or nonossifying fibroma were suspected.

A 2-year-old girl was brought with a diffuse right midfacial swelling of 1 year’s duration that, after 6 months, had extended to the left midface; nasal blockage was noted. On examination, there were diffuse, non-tender swellings extending to the zygomatic arches. Intraorally, a non-tender, lobulated, firm-to–bony-hard swelling caused labial and buccal cortical expansion bilaterally, extended to the pterygoid plates, and produced palatal bone thickening; the mucosa was intact. Family history was notable: her 5-year-old sister had a similar maxillary swelling 3 years earlier, treated surgically with a histopathologic diagnosis of ameloblastic fibroma and no recurrence to date. Computed tomography with three-dimensional reconstruction showed a hyperdense mass involving the labial and buccal cortices, extending to the pterygoid plates, and irregular palatal bone thickening. A presumptive preoperative diagnosis of an odontogenic tumor was made.

A 65-year-old man with a history of ischemic heart disease and IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD) presented in June 2022 with progressive dyspnea on exertion. He had been diagnosed with IgG4-RD in November 2020—based on multi‐site lymphadenopathy, retroperitoneal fibrosis, renal enlargement, elevated serum IgG4, and lymph node biopsy—and had achieved remission on prednisolone tapered to 7.5 mg daily by February 2022. Whole-body imaging in May 2022 showed stable lymph nodes and pancreas, and laboratory studies then showed normal serum IgG4 and soluble interleukin-2 receptor (sIL-2R) levels. 

On current presentation, chest CT revealed moderate pericardial and bilateral pleural effusions. Laboratory tests showed lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) of 770 IU/L, sIL-2R of 642 U/mL, and a normal serum IgG4 level of 53 mg/dL. Prednisolone was increased to 30 mg daily, considering possible IgG4-RD relapse. Five days later, his dyspnea acutely worsened, and he arrived at the emergency department with hypotension, tachycardia, and signs of shock.

A 41-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of a lump on the back of her head that had gradually enlarged from 1 cm to over 10 cm in diameter. Over the past 5 months, the lesion became intermittently painful and developed a wound with purulent discharge. She delayed seeking care until the mass began to interfere with daily activities.  
On examination, vital signs were normal. In the mid-occipital scalp, there was a solitary, fixed, lobulated mass measuring 19 × 12 × 10 cm, with irregular skin coloration, discharge, and foul odor.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the head revealed a mixed-density extracalvarial mass in the mid-occipital region without intracranial involvement. Three-dimensional angiography showed that the mass was highly vascular, receiving blood supply from bilateral superficial temporal arteries and occipital arteries.  
The initial differential diagnosis included scalp hemangioma and basal cell carcinoma.

A 15-year-old male presented with a 20-day history of a painless swelling in the anterior mandible. He was otherwise healthy with no history of trauma or systemic disease. On extraoral examination, there was a firm, nontender swelling in the parasymphyseal region of the mandible, extending superiorly to obliterate the mentolabial sulcus and inferiorly to the lower border of the mandible; the overlying skin was normal. Intraorally, a firm, nontender, nonadherent swelling measuring 7 cm × 5 cm extended from the right second premolar to the left first premolar, with expansion of buccal and lingual cortical plates. The overlying mucosa was intact. There was severe mesial tilting of the four incisors, mild mesial displacement of adjacent canines and premolars, and retention of the right deciduous canine. All anterior teeth were non-tender to percussion with Grade I mobility.

A mandibular occlusal radiograph showed a well-circumscribed unilocular radiolucency with a radiopaque border, measuring 7 cm × 5 cm, extending from the right second molar to the left first premolar, causing tooth displacement without root resorption and with cortical plate expansion but no perforation. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated a well-defined unilocular radiolucency in the anterior mandible containing an impacted right mandibular canine. The differential diagnosis based on clinical and radiographic findings included a dentigerous cyst, unicystic ameloblastoma, and adenomatoid odontogenic tumor.

A 12-year-old girl noted a painless swelling over the distal right humerus for 1 month. She denied trauma. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender mass deep to the triceps just proximal to the elbow. Elbow and shoulder function were full, with no neurovascular deficit or lymphadenopathy. 

Plain radiographs of the right humerus demonstrated a dense, sclerotic bony protuberance arising from the posterior cortex of the distal humerus. MRI showed a 6-cm exophytic bony lesion terminating just proximal to the olecranon, with extension into the underlying medullary canal. Staging studies, including chest CT and whole-body bone scan, revealed no metastatic disease. 

A core needle biopsy was performed, which showed features consistent with a parosteal osteosarcoma.

A 49-year-old man with severe bilateral knee osteoarthritis presented with one week of progressive right hip pain and difficulty ambulating. He uses oxycodone and paracetamol for pain and ambulates with a walker. Examination revealed pain with log roll of the right hip, intact bilateral sensation, and unpalpable distal pulses.

CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed a right femoral transcervical neck fracture with a large surrounding soft tissue mass and multiple lytic lesions in the axial and appendicular skeleton. Hip radiographs confirmed an osteolytic lesion with a soft tissue component around the right femoral head and neck and additional osteolytic lesions of the innominate bones, sacrum, lower lumbar spine, and bilateral femora.

Laboratory studies revealed an alkaline phosphatase level of 259 U/L, normal hemoglobin, normal renal function, and normal calcium levels. Workup for multiple myeloma, including serum and urine protein electrophoresis and quantitative immunoglobulins, was within normal limits except for a mildly elevated serum kappa free light-chain level of 24.1 mg/L. Tumor markers (CA 19-9, PSA, CEA) and endocrine studies (TSH, PTH) were unremarkable. Infectious studies, including tests for Coccidioides, syphilis, tuberculosis, Brucella, Histoplasma, and Bartonella henselae, were negative.

An open biopsy of the right proximal femur with hemiarthroplasty was performed. Histological examination showed a small blue cell tumor encasing trabecular bone with oval to spindled cells and abundant multinucleated giant cells. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for ERG and SATB2, with no evidence of grungy calcification. Differential diagnoses included osteosarcoma, high-grade chondrosarcoma, and phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor.

A 32-year-old Hispanic woman presented with sharp upper to mid abdominal pain. She reported a 15-lb unintentional weight loss over 6 months, despite abdominal distension during that time. She had no significant medical history. On admission, her abdomen was distended, and a 3/6 systolic murmur was auscultated at the left upper sternal border. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis to 17.5×10^3/µL (normal 4.0–10.5×10^3/µL), AST 273 U/L (normal 13–39 U/L), ALT 149 U/L (normal 7–52 U/L), and cancer antigen-125 of 4663 U/mL (normal <35 U/mL). Urinalysis was positive for protein, ketones, and red blood cells. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 13-cm complex cystic mass in the left adnexa with moderate hyperdense ascites and omental nodularity, findings suspicious for ovarian neoplasm with carcinomatosis. Pelvic ultrasound confirmed a large left adnexal complex cystic structure with low-level internal echoes. Chest CT showed no intrathoracic neoplasm or infection. Diagnostic and therapeutic paracentesis yielded 700 mL of brownish opaque fluid; cytologic examination revealed benign histiocytes and mesothelial cells.

A 54-year-old multiparous woman presented with a vulvar mass of three years’ duration. She was seven years postmenopausal and had been sexually inactive for over eight years. The mass had progressively enlarged, causing itching and an offensive discharge, but she denied vaginal bleeding, weight loss, or abdominal distension. Her medical and surgical history was unremarkable, and she took no medications. On examination, her cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal findings were normal. Vulvar inspection revealed a pedunculated, cauliflower-like mass arising from the right labium majus, measuring approximately 20 cm × 15 cm on a 5 cm × 1 cm stalk. No inguinal lymphadenopathy was noted. Speculum examination showed a normal vagina and cervix. An abdominopelvic ultrasound revealed a bulky, anteverted uterus with multiple calcified fibroid nodules but no adnexal masses or free fluid. A Pap smear showed normal cytology. The initial differential diagnosis included a benign vulval mass; however, given the cauliflower-like appearance, vulvar carcinoma was also considered.

A 51-year-old woman presented with a rapidly enlarging, ulcerated swelling on her right upper arm. She reported that the lesion had been pea-sized and unchanged for three decades but had grown progressively over the past six months. The lesion recently became painful, pruritic, and bled slightly. On examination, there was a 12 cm × 6 cm nodulo-ulcerative plaque over the right upper arm. MRI showed a mass measuring 12 cm × 6 cm × 1.5 cm invading the deltoid and triceps brachii muscles. A needle biopsy demonstrated proliferation of spindle cells in a storiform pattern within the dermis, and immunostaining was negative for CD34 and factor VIII, suggesting a benign tumor. However, given the large size, ulceration, muscle invasion, and recent rapid growth, wide surgical resection with a myocutaneous flap was planned to exclude malignancy.

A 56-year-old woman underwent elective outpatient surveillance colonoscopy because her sister had colon cancer at age 36. Her history was notable for menorrhagia, hypertension, depression, and two cesarean deliveries. Her medications included nebivolol, venlafaxine, and amlodipine–valsartan. 

On colonoscopy, the appendiceal orifice appeared prominent with edematous changes, and multiple biopsies were obtained. Histologic examination of the biopsies showed mild neutrophilic inflammation and a dense lymphocytic infiltrate of the lamina propria. 

Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 2.4 × 2.6 cm mass in the cecal tip involving the proximal appendix. Magnetic resonance imaging failed to further characterize the lesion.

A 55-year-old man (ASA I) presented with a two-week history of a single episode of biliary colic. He had no symptoms of cholangitis, no significant past medical or surgical history, and a normal physical examination. Routine laboratory tests, including liver function tests and complete blood count, were within normal limits. A screening abdominal ultrasound demonstrated multiple gallbladder stones but no liver lesions. He underwent an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Intraoperatively, the gallbladder contained multiple calculi without signs of acute cholecystitis. Unexpectedly, multiple firm to hard, whitish nodules were noted on liver segments II, IVB, VI, and VIII; the remainder of the peritoneal cavity appeared normal. A standard cholecystectomy was completed, and laparoscopic wedge biopsies of the liver nodules in segments IVB and VI were obtained. The patient’s immediate postoperative recovery was uneventful.

A 72-year-old man presented with a 4-week history of anorexia, fatigue, progressive shortness of breath, and a nonproductive cough. His medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and remote coronary artery bypass grafting. On examination, breath sounds were absent over the left hemithorax. Chest radiography and computed tomography revealed a massive left pleural effusion without detectable lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Positron emission tomography–CT showed no abnormal uptake elsewhere. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated an ejection fraction of 40% and no pericardial effusion. Therapeutic thoracentesis yielded hemorrhagic pleural fluid; biochemical analysis indicated an exudate (LDH, 2386 U/L; albumin, 2.6 g/dL). Cytomorphologic analysis of the pleural fluid revealed a high-grade malignant lymphoma.

A 12-year-old girl presented with a 6-month history of dull, constant right‐sided head pain rated 7/10, exacerbated by combing her hair. She denied trauma. Examination showed moderate tenderness over the right parietal bone without palpable mass or neurologic deficits. One month earlier she had undergone appendectomy complicated by a single postoperative seizure; EEG abnormalities led to 9 months of carbamazepine therapy, and no further seizures occurred. There was no family history of headache or epilepsy. 
Non-contrast CT of the head (bone window) demonstrated a 7-mm, well-defined lytic lesion in the right parietal diploic space, surrounded by sclerosis and mild diploic expansion. MRI revealed an isointense lesion on T1-weighted images, ring enhancement with adjacent pachymeningeal enhancement on postcontrast T1, and a central low–signal-intensity nidus with peripheral high signal on T2-weighted images.

A 76‐year‐old man presented with a 2‐year history of a slowly enlarging, 2‐cm variably dark‐brown and erythematous scaly plaque on his left lower leg. He denied trauma, prior treatments, pruritus, or burning. His medical history was notable for diabetes mellitus. On examination, there were no other cutaneous lesions in the axilla, groin, genitalia, perianal area, or umbilicus, and no palpable cervical, axillary, or inguinal lymphadenopathy. A punch biopsy of the lesion revealed acanthosis with epidermal tumor cells showing abundant pale cytoplasm and large pleomorphic nuclei. Immunohistochemical staining of the biopsy specimen was focally positive for cytokeratin 7 (CK7).

A 57-year-old woman was transferred for workup of a suspected stroke. The previous afternoon, her friend noted that she suddenly began to lean to the left and developed left-sided weakness. At the outside emergency department, noncontrast CT of the head revealed no acute abnormality. Her NIH Stroke Scale score was 12, with partial lateral gaze paresis, flaccid left upper and lower extremities, limb ataxia on the left, right partial facial paralysis, and dysarthria. She received intravenous tissue plasminogen activator, and CT angiography of the head and neck showed no large-vessel occlusion. 

On arrival in the neurological ICU, she was alert and oriented with mild dysarthria. Cranial-nerve examination showed a mild right gaze preference but no sustained facial droop. Motor strength was 4/5 in the left upper and lower extremities and 5/5 on the right; sensation and coordination were intact. Her repeat NIH Stroke Scale score was 4. The remainder of the examination was within normal limits. 

Electrocardiography showed normal sinus rhythm with right atrial enlargement, right ventricular hypertrophy, and right-axis deviation. Diffusion-weighted MRI of the head demonstrated hyperintense lesions in the right thalamus, bilateral cerebellar hemispheres, left parietal lobe, right frontal and parietal lobes, and bilateral temporal lobes, consistent with acute thromboembolic infarcts. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a severely enlarged left atrium containing a large, heterogeneous, dense, mobile 4.0 × 9.0-cm mass with a wide-base attachment to the interatrial septum that occupied most of the left atrium and prolapsed into the left ventricle.

A 51-year-old man presented with 1 month of fatigue, exertional dyspnea, dry cough, night sweats, and a 5-month, 11-lb weight loss. He noted dyspnea when lying on his right side and associated palpitations. One week prior, he discovered a painless lump on the left side of his neck. His past history was notable for chronic lymphocytic leukemia in remission for 16 years (treated with FCR) and Crohn’s disease in remission. 

On examination, blood pressure was 167/105 mmHg, heart rate 100 beats/min, temperature 36°C, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. A 5–6 cm, non-tender left supraclavicular lymph node was palpable; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed leukocytes 2.6 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 17.4 g/dL, platelets 51 × 10^3/µL, normal kidney and liver function tests, lactate dehydrogenase 243 U/L, ferritin 221 ng/mL, negative viral hepatitis panel, HIV, and monospot tests. Total globulin level was 2.1 g/dL; immunoglobulin quantification showed IgG 535 mg/dL, IgA 79 mg/dL, IgM 161 mg/dL. Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation revealed a 0.2 g/dL IgG kappa monoclonal gammopathy; serum free light chains were unremarkable.

An electrocardiogram demonstrated left atrial enlargement and left axis deviation. A CT scan of the chest revealed an 8.8 cm soft-tissue mass occupying most of the right atrium and extending into the right ventricle with probable pericardial involvement, along with enlarged left supraclavicular and mediastinal lymph nodes. A transesophageal echocardiogram and cardiac MRI confirmed a 10 × 7.4 cm infiltrating mass in the right atrium and ventricle, extending into the inferior vena cava and coronary sinus, with slight gadolinium uptake on first-pass perfusion indicating tumor vascularity.

A 45-year-old previously healthy Asian man presented with a 2-month history of intermittent fever with chills and rigors, night sweats, anorexia, and weight loss. He noted a transient macular rash at the onset of fever that resolved spontaneously. Over the previous month he developed generalized lymphadenopathy—cervical, axillary, and inguinal—that became extremely painful a few days before admission. Following admission he developed synovitis of the small joints of the lower limbs, which progressed over 3 days to involve lower-limb large joints and, subsequently, both small and large joints of the upper limbs in a symmetric pattern.

He had no personal or family history of arthritis, no known toxic exposures, and denied alcohol or tobacco use. On examination he was emaciated, febrile, and pale. There were bilateral, firm, matted, tender lymph nodes (2–3 cm) in the cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions, and tender hepatosplenomegaly. A few days later he had marked synovitis of the distal and proximal interphalangeal joints of the lower limbs, with symmetric involvement of other joints.

Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis, normocytic anemia, normal platelet count, and elevated inflammatory markers that rose further after arthritis onset. Liver and renal function tests were normal. Rheumatoid factor, anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, and antinuclear antibodies were negative. HIV 1 and 2 antibodies, Epstein–Barr virus IgG and IgM, cytomegalovirus IgG and IgM, and Toxoplasma antibodies were negative or within normal limits. Serum uric acid was marginally elevated. Radiographs of the hands and feet showed soft-tissue swelling without erosions or osteopenia. A cervical lymph node biopsy showed a reactive lymph node.

A 77-year-old man was evaluated for recurrent falls and episodes of dizziness over several weeks. He sustained a proximal humerus fracture after a fall and was discharged for rehabilitation. During a follow-up outpatient visit 3 weeks later, severe nocturnal hypoglycemia was noted, requiring him to awaken nightly to consume a snack. His weight was stable, with no other symptoms reported. His medical history included hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, a transient ischemic attack, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He was not taking insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents but was receiving amlodipine, lisinopril, simvastatin, tamsulosin, and clopidogrel. On examination, he had benign-appearing skin verrucae; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed mild normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 8.3 mmol/L), normal renal function and electrolytes except for mild hyperchloremia, normal liver markers except for mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase and lactate dehydrogenase, and normal TSH and morning cortisol levels. Potential causes such as alcohol withdrawal, starvation, organ failure, sepsis, and hypocortisolism were considered unlikely. A test for secretagogue medications and insulin was negative. During a supervised fast, after 2 hours his plasma glucose was 2.3 mmol/L with suppressed C-peptide (0.05 nmol/L) and insulin levels (<2.0 µIU/mL). A PET–CT scan demonstrated a 14 × 14 × 11 cm solid mass in the right pleura with limited FDG avidity, especially at the periphery.

An 11-month-old boy was referred for evaluation of poor weight gain (<3rd percentile) despite increased caloric intake over the previous 5 months. He was a full-term infant born to first-degree consanguineous parents; family history was unremarkable. Psychomotor development was appropriate. On examination he appeared pale and emaciated, with dry skin, sunken anterior fontanel, and prominent muscle wasting. His weight was 5 kg (<3rd percentile), with normal length and head circumference. He had left-eye nystagmus but no focal neurologic deficits; deep tendon reflexes and cranial nerves were normal. He was afebrile, with stable vital signs. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, and electrolytes. Hormonal assays were within reference ranges (FSH 0.32 mUI/ml [1.5–14], LH 0.16 mUI/ml [1.2–10], testosterone 0.078 ng/ml, 8 AM cortisol 18.5 µg/dl [3.7–19.4], ultrasensitive TSH 2.59 mUI/l [0.27–4.2], FT4 21.8 pmol/l [12–22]). Serum tumor markers were normal (AFP 1.2 mUI/l [0–7]; HCG 6.82 ng/ml [0–7]). Brain MRI demonstrated a suprasellar mass measuring 59 × 41 × 40 mm that was isointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed homogeneous enhancement. The mass had a solid, noncalcified configuration without peritumoral edema or parenchymal infiltration, extended into the optic chiasm, retrosellar region, and right hypothalamus, and displaced the anterior and middle cerebral arteries while compressing the temporal lobes, cerebral peduncles, and anterior pons.

A 12-year-old female with no prior ocular history presented with a three-month history of a right conjunctival mass and progressive foreign-body sensation in the superotemporal eyelid.  
Visual acuity was 20/20 OU, intraocular pressures 19 mmHg OU, pupils equal and reactive, full extraocular movements, and orthotropic alignment.  
Slit-lamp examination revealed a 5×5 mm firm nodule in the superotemporal bulbar conjunctiva of the right eye with feeder vessels. The lesion was firmly adherent to the sclera on gentle manipulation. There was no ulceration, necrosis, neovascularization, or abnormal pigmentation.

A 50-year-old man noted a slowly enlarging, diffuse swelling of his left scalp over 4 months. He had no fever, weight loss, or neurologic symptoms. On local examination, the mass involved the left parietal and occipital regions, measured over 10 × 10 cm, had an irregular surface, intact overlying skin, patchy alopecia, and was non-tender, non-translucent, and non-pulsatile. There was no palpable lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits; hepatitis B surface antigen was positive. Bone marrow aspiration was normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head showed a soft-tissue density over the left parietal bone with underlying bony erosions, cortical thickening, periosteal reaction, and a moth-eaten pattern of destruction, as well as an associated subdural collection; there was no intracranial (extradural or meningeal) or orbital invasion and no regional lymphadenopathy. CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no other sites of disease.

A 19-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1 at 36 weeks’ gestation, presented with a 1-month history of rapidly enlarging bilateral breast swelling. She noted that her breasts had doubled in volume over the past month, were painful but afebrile, and did not improve after a 3-day course of unspecified antibiotics. On examination, both breasts were markedly enlarged, tender, erythematous, and visibly engorged with superficial vessels. 

Breast ultrasonography showed multiple, variably sized masses in both breasts, each with an irregular shape, parallel orientation, indistinct margins, complex cystic and solid echotexture, posterior enhancement, internal vascularity, hypervascular adjacent tissue, overlying skin thickening, and edema; no axillary lymphadenopathy was seen. 

Laboratory studies demonstrated a white blood cell count of 10.3 K/μL, neutrophils 72.8%, lymphocytes 14.8%, C-reactive protein 9.6 mg/L, and procalcitonin 0.15 ng/mL. HIV testing was negative. 

Given the rapid progression and atypical features, an ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy of one of the breast masses was performed, with results pending.

A 72-year-old man presented with a two-month history of a slowly enlarging, painful mass in the left cervical region. He had no significant past medical history. On examination, a 4 cm hard, fixed lymph node with overlying inflammation was noted on the left side of the neck. One month earlier, he had also developed a 1.5 cm ulcerated skin nodule on his forehead. No other lesions were found on systemic examination. Cervical ultrasonography and CT scan confirmed enlarged cervical lymph nodes. Random biopsies of the nasopharyngeal mucosa were normal. The patient underwent an excision of the forehead lesion and a cervical lymph node biopsy.  
The excised skin lesion showed a dermal carcinoma with a prominent nonneoplastic lymphocytic infiltrate intermingled with a poorly differentiated epithelial proliferation displaying a syncytial appearance, suggestive of a lymphoepithelioma-like carcinoma. The lymph node specimen revealed a dense infiltrate of monomorphic small basophilic cells with very fine chromatin, scant cytoplasm, and frequent mitotic figures, raising concern for neuroendocrine carcinoma.

A 38-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of diffuse, intermittent, periumbilical abdominal pain and postprandial vomiting. She denied abdominal distension, fever, hematemesis, jaundice, or urinary symptoms, and she continued to pass flatus. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits; she appeared mildly pale and dehydrated. Abdominal examination revealed diffuse tenderness most pronounced in the epigastrium without guarding or rebound; bowel sounds were present. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10 g/dl, white cells 7×10^3/µl, platelets 350×10^3/µl; AST 57 U/l, ALT 43 U/l, and amylase 191 U/l; urinalysis was unremarkable. Initial plain abdominal films were normal; the most recent film demonstrated distended small bowel loops with multiple air–fluid levels. Abdominal ultrasound revealed fluid collections without localized mass. Gastroscopy showed a mild duodenal ulcer with bile reflux. CT scan and MRI were unavailable.  
Despite conservative management, the differential diagnoses included chronic peptic ulcer disease, cholecystitis, acute pancreatitis, and partial intestinal obstruction.

A 38-year-old nulliparous woman presented with a 10-year history of progressive right-sided abdominal distention and the onset of pain 5 months before admission. She had regular menstrual cycles and no history of amenorrhea. There was no significant medical or surgical history. On abdominal examination, a mobile, non-tender, round, firm mass was palpable in the right pelvic area.  
Laboratory studies were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a 17 × 15 cm right pelvic cystic mass with heterogeneous echotexture ranging from anechoic to hyperechoic areas, a demonstrable fat–fluid level, multiple linear hyperechoic interfaces floating within the cyst, and numerous echogenic foci with distinct acoustic shadowing. The preoperative impression was of a mature cystic teratoma.

A 49-year-old man with a 5-year history of gastroesophageal reflux presented with a 6-month history of progressive dyspepsia, reflux symptoms, dysphagia to solids and some liquids, and a 50-lb unintentional weight loss. Vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed a firm, non-tender mass overlying his right shoulder. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. 

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed a large, nearly obstructing mass in the distal esophagus at 35–40 cm; the stomach and duodenum were unremarkable. Biopsy of the esophageal lesion demonstrated invasive, moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma arising in Barrett esophagus. An esophageal stent was placed for palliation of dysphagia.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the right shoulder revealed a 4.7-cm heterogeneous soft-tissue mass within the deltoid muscle, separate from the humerus. The radiologic differential diagnosis included sarcoma, vascular-origin tumor, and, less likely, metastasis. The patient underwent surgical resection of the soft-tissue mass, which was grossly described as a superficially calcified nodular lesion within subcutaneous and muscle tissue.

A 46-year-old woman presented with a 1-week history of difficulty swallowing. Her medical history was unremarkable. On examination, vital signs were stable, and neck, chest, abdominal, skin, and extremity examinations were all normal. Laboratory studies showed a thyroid-stimulating hormone level of 2.46 mIU/mL (reference range 0.4–4.0 mIU/mL), a serum calcium level of 9.54 mg/dL (8.5–10.5 mg/dL), and a parathyroid hormone level of 112.8 pg/mL (15–65 pg/mL). Neck ultrasonography revealed a well-defined cystic nodule measuring 46 × 30 × 25 mm at the posterior base of the neck. Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated a well-defined, thin-walled, fluid-filled cystic lesion measuring 47 × 43 × 31 mm in the superior mediastinum adjacent to the right lateral esophageal wall, causing mild mass effect, with no enhancement or obvious communication to the esophagus, trachea, or thyroid gland; an esophageal duplication cyst was suspected. The patient underwent esophagogastroduodenoscopy, which was normal.

A 63-year-old man presented with an acute episode of blurry vision, along with a two-month history of headache and intermittent nausea. He denied pain or infectious symptoms. Examination revealed bilateral proptosis with lid retraction, ophthalmoplegia in all directions, and reduced visual acuity without visual field defects; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. A nonenhanced CT of the head showed symmetric enlargement of all extraocular muscles with sparing of the musculotendinous junctions. Thyroid function tests were within normal limits, and anti-thyroid peroxidase and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies were negative. On further history, he reported 22 kg of unintentional weight loss over 3 months and a 40 pack-year smoking history. A screening chest radiograph revealed a large right middle lobe mass. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the head and orbits demonstrated symmetric extraocular muscle enlargement with intra- and extraconal edema, sparing of the musculotendinous junctions, and no evidence of an infiltrative process. Serum vasculitic studies, angiotensin-converting enzyme level, parathyroid hormone studies, and urinary paraprotein studies were unremarkable. Serum potassium and corrected calcium were borderline elevated at 5.5 mmol/L and 2.63 mmol/L, respectively; all other electrolytes, including ionized calcium, were normal. Paraneoplastic autoantibodies, including anti-Hu, anti-Ri, anti-Yo, anti-PCA-2, anti-VGCC, and anti-VGKC, were negative.

A 40-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of left scrotal swelling that had progressively increased in size and was associated with intermittent pain. He had no history of undescended testis, prior scrotal surgery, chronic illness, or a family history of testicular cancer. He was initially diagnosed with hydrocele at a primary care center and underwent attempted scrotal surgery, but intraoperatively a solid mass was found and the procedure was aborted. On referral, he was conscious, afebrile, and had no palpable lymphadenopathy. Abdominal examination was unremarkable. Examination of the external genitalia revealed a median raphe incision and a mildly tender, firm, irreducible left hemiscrotal mass measuring approximately 7 × 10 cm; the left testis could not be palpated separately from the mass, and the mass was nonreducible. Laboratory investigations, including α-fetoprotein (5.92 IU/mL), β-HCG (0.05 IU/mL), and lactate dehydrogenase (304 U/L), were within normal limits. Scrotal ultrasound showed normal testes with normal intratesticular blood flow and a large heterogeneous, vascularized lesion in the left tunica vaginalis measuring 10 × 6 cm. Abdominal ultrasound findings were normal.

A 34-year-old woman presented with several months of progressive shortness of breath on exertion, reduced exercise capacity, and signs of fluid overload, including peripheral edema and ascites. Her heart rate was 103 beats/min, blood pressure 119/77 mm Hg, respiratory rate 20 breaths/minute, temperature 36.3 °C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Physical examination revealed a jugular venous pressure of 6 cm above the sternal angle, muffled heart sounds, and bilateral peripheral edema.  

Ten years earlier, at age 25, she had developed polyuria and polydipsia from diabetes insipidus, tenosynovitis with joint effusions, and skin lesions. Lymph node and skin biopsies at that time were interpreted as histiocytosis with S100 positive and CD1a positive cells, and she was diagnosed with Langerhans histiocytosis. She received methotrexate and intermittent prednisone.  

Current investigations included biopsy of a skin lesion, which showed foamy histiocytic cells in loose clusters throughout the dermis, with immunohistochemical staining positive for CD68K and CD68P and mostly negative for S100. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated moderate bilateral pleural effusions, a loculated pericardial effusion, a pericardial thickness up to 18 mm, preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (69%), and a septal shift with inspiration. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed hepatic vein flow reversal, septal bounce, and increased pericardial echogenicity consistent with constrictive pericarditis. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography confirmed a thickened pericardium with moderate pericardial and bilateral pleural effusions. Fluorodeoxyglucose PET–CT showed moderate pericardial effusion and diffuse FDG uptake in the pericardial, pleural, peritoneal spaces, and tibiae. An endomyocardial biopsy displayed mild myocardial hypertrophy without infiltration.

A 72-year-old man presented with a one-week history of severe, intermittent spontaneous nocturnal pain in the left maxillary posterior region. Three days earlier he had undergone pulpectomy of the maxillary left first premolar (#12) for presumed apical periodontitis at a local clinic, after which he took analgesics and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs but continued to have severe pain and hypnalgia.

On extraoral examination there was no lymphadenopathy or facial swelling. Intraorally, the dentition was poorly maintained. The maxillary left second molar (#15) showed extensive coronal structural loss and a fracture surface 2–3 mm below the gingival margin, with a 5–6 mm buccal periodontal pocket and gingival inflammation. The first molar (#14) had an exposed pulp chamber, mild mobility, and a 5 mm periodontal pocket. The first and second premolars (#12–#13) were percussion-sensitive. Electric pulp testing indicated necrotic pulps in teeth #12–#14.

A cone-beam CT scan revealed multiple well-defined hypoattenuating lesions apical to teeth #12–#13 and #15, one within the root canal of the residual root of #15, and an extensive soft-tissue mass filling the left maxillary sinus, extending from the medial sinus wall to the palate in the premolar and molar region. 

On the basis of the clinical and CBCT findings, root canal therapy was performed on teeth #12–#14 and the residual root of #15 was extracted. A subsequent CT scan showed a large soft-tissue density lesion occupying most of the left maxillary sinus, with destruction of multiple sinus walls, extension into the nasal cavity and turbinates, and inferior destruction of the hard palate and alveolar process.

The patient was diagnosed with left maxillary sinusitis and treated with ornidazole and ceftriaxone sodium, after which he reported slight pain relief. Fourteen days after his initial visit, he returned with recurrent nocturnal pain in the upper left molar region and facial paresthesia of three days’ duration. Intraorally, the extraction socket of #15 was poorly healed with surrounding nontender edema, and a soft, well-defined, crater-like erythematous ulceration was noted on the buccal gingiva adjacent to teeth #13 and #14.

An 80-year-old man presented with a 12- to 18-month history of a slowly enlarging swelling over the radial aspect of the right thumb at the proximal interphalangeal joint crease. The lesion was initially painless but began causing discomfort when the hand was rested against a hard surface. On examination, there was a firm, nodular mass palpable at the described location. The thumb had a full range of motion, and the mass did not move with flexion or extension.  

Ultrasound of the thumb showed a 20 mm × 9 mm × 13 mm noncompressible lesion with mixed echogenicity and moderate internal vascularity. The adjacent interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints and tendons appeared normal.  

MRI demonstrated a well-defined lesion with a low-signal capsule and heterogeneous contents that were isointense with muscle on T1-weighted images and slightly hyperintense on T2-weighted images. The lesion’s long axis ran parallel to the digital connective tissue, and it was separate from the underlying bone and tendons.

A 62-year-old Caucasian woman was evaluated for a few days of abdominal pain associated with nausea and vomiting, as well as dysphagia, cachexia, and progressive dyspnea when supine. She reported painless, progressive abdominal distension and a weight gain of over 15 kg during the past year (body-mass index, 30.5). She denied hirsutism, skin changes, or other signs of hormonal excess. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable for gynecological disease.

On examination, her abdomen was markedly distended. Office transabdominal ultrasound revealed massive ascites. Laboratory studies showed a CA 125 level of 1744.3 mUI/ml; carcinoembryonic antigen, α-fetoprotein, and CA 19-9 were within normal limits. A second-level ultrasound (transvaginal and transabdominal) identified a 20-cm mobile solid mass in the right adnexa with a smooth surface, color score 2, and acoustic shadows; there was no evidence of pelvic-structure infiltration or carcinomatosis. The uterus was of normal size, and a small uterine fibroid was noted.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed abundant peritoneal fluid and demonstrated a 17-cm abdominal mass of uncertain origin, as well as a 4.3-cm uterine fibroleiomyoma. CT of the chest showed a moderate left pleural effusion.

A 64-year-old man with a heavy smoking history was referred with a 2-week history of dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, weight loss, and a painful nodule on his left cheek that appeared concurrently with his respiratory symptoms. His past medical history included coronary artery disease and type II diabetes mellitus. On examination, he appeared comfortable, vital signs were within normal limits, and there were no palpable lymph nodes. Cutaneous examination revealed a 1.5 cm tender nodule on the left cheek with surrounding erythema, and the rest of the skin and systemic examination was unremarkable.

A chest radiograph showed a mass in the left upper lobe with mediastinal lymphadenopathy and no pleural effusion. Bronchoscopy with bronchial biopsy and washings showed no malignant cells. For staging, computed tomography scans of the brain and abdomen, as well as a bone scan, were all normal. Given the suspicious facial lesion, the patient underwent excisional biopsy of the nodule.

An 8-year-old boy presented with a 1-month history of a painless left-sided neck mass. He denied weight loss, dysphagia, numbness, or difficulty with mastication. His medical, family, and social histories were noncontributory. Physical examination revealed a diffuse, soft, nontender, partially mobile mass measuring approximately 7.5×5 cm in the left upper neck without cervical lymphadenopathy; the overlying skin was normal. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the lesion yielded an impression of pleomorphic adenoma. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the neck demonstrated an enhancing mass measuring 5.0×3.6×2.5 cm in the left posterior parapharyngeal (carotid) space and posterior cervical space, displacing the carotid arteries and jugular vein anterolaterally, with multiple small neck lymph nodes. The mass was separated from the deep lobe of the parotid gland, lay adjacent to the left submandibular gland inferiorly, and abutted the anterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Axial short-tau inversion recovery magnetic resonance imaging confirmed these findings. Imaging suggested a benign neoplasm, and the differential diagnosis included pleomorphic adenoma of a salivary gland in the parapharyngeal space versus a benign nerve-sheath tumor.

An 8-year-old Moroccan girl presented with painful swelling of both forearms. The swelling first appeared on her left forearm and, six months later, on her right forearm. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. She reported progressive pain despite daily use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and narcotic analgesics.

On examination, she was afebrile and in good general condition. There was swelling over the upper one-third of the right forearm and the upper two-thirds of the left forearm, with inflammatory signs.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10 g/dL, white blood cell count 11,210/μL with 80% neutrophils, and C-reactive protein 60 mg/L.

Plain radiographs demonstrated osteolytic lesions of the upper one-third of the right ulna and the upper two-thirds of the left radius, without mineralized matrix but with cortical breakthrough and internal trabeculations.

Magnetic resonance imaging revealed osteolytic masses in those locations that invaded the elbow joints, were hyposignal on T1-weighted images, hypersignal on T2-weighted and STIR images, contained septa, showed annular enhancement after gadolinium administration, crossed the physis from the diaphysis, and were associated with a soft-tissue mass and edema.

A 49-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of progressive swelling on the left side of her face. The swelling involved the entire cheek, obliterated the nasolabial fold, and extended intraorally over the left maxillary alveolar ridge. On examination it was soft to firm (“rubbery”), non-tender, and without pitting edema; there were no systemic symptoms. Over the preceding month she had visited four dental clinics: the first three clinicians prescribed oral and IV antibiotics, and the fourth performed incision and drainage with only partial relief. A panoramic radiograph obtained before referral showed a soft-tissue shadow over the left maxilla with diffuse alveolar bone destruction that was not associated with any carious tooth or periodontal pocket.

A 14-year-old boy presented with a 3-month history of left knee pain. The pain began suddenly, was worse in the evening, and was relieved by 200 mg of ibuprofen. There was no history of trauma or previous surgery.  
On examination, his temperature was normal. Laboratory studies showed normal white blood cell count, hemoglobin, platelets, and hematocrit. Physical examination revealed mild tenderness over the medial distal femur and proximal tibia, with minimal limitation of knee range of motion.  
Plain radiographs of the left knee were unremarkable. MRI proton-density fat-suppressed images demonstrated extensive bone marrow edema in the medial tibial epiphysis with a small round hypointense area abutting the growth plate.  
Nonenhanced CT of the left knee showed a small focal 5 mm lucent nidus with a central area of sclerosis and subtle surrounding sclerosis…

A 21-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 6-month history of pain and swelling in her right knee, especially aggravated by physical activity. Examination showed mild quadriceps atrophy, pain at terminal flexion, and mild swelling beneath the patellar tendon. Plain radiographs of the knee were unremarkable. T2-weighted fat-suppressed MRI revealed a 3 cm×2 cm mass with high signal intensity posterior to the patellar tendon. Laboratory studies, including coagulation parameters, were all within normal limits. The radiologists included synovial sarcoma in the differential diagnosis, and an open excisional biopsy was planned to characterize the lesion.

A 43-year-old woman with no past medical history presented with a one-month history of a painless, firm right axillary mass. She denied systemic symptoms and had no other lymphadenopathy. Her family history was notable for a second-degree relative with breast cancer. Physical examination was unremarkable except for the right axillary lymph node. Routine laboratory studies were normal. Axillary ultrasound revealed a 20.3 × 30.7 mm conglomerate of right lymph nodes with suspicious features. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy showed invasive ductal carcinoma. Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated 100% estrogen and progesterone receptor positivity, c-erbB2 3+, and a Ki-67 index of 80% (Luminal B-like). Breast ultrasound, mammography, and magnetic resonance imaging revealed no pathological findings. PET-CT showed hypermetabolic uptake only in the right axillary lesion, with no abnormal FDG uptake in the breast parenchyma or elsewhere.

A 67‐year‐old Caucasian man presented with a 1‐year history of left preauricular and facial pain and headaches, and a 4‐month history of progressively worsening trismus. He denied trauma. The pain was a persistent, dull ache worsened by talking and mastication, with minimal relief from ibuprofen. He noted occasional, non‐tender bilateral TMJ clicking but no prior jaw locking. Over the past month, he lost 6 pounds due to difficulty opening his mouth and was using a liquid protein supplement diet. He also reported 3 months of sinus problems and recurrent left ear infections, with intermittent bloodstained nasal discharge. Two prior interventions—extraction of the left maxillary third molar and a course of antibiotics for presumed otitis—provided only transient relief. His medical history was notable for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder treated with risperidone, and a 40‐pack‐year smoking history. He denied HIV infection. Vital signs were normal. On examination, he appeared anxious and cachectic. Extraoral inspection revealed no facial swelling or lymphadenopathy; cranial nerves II–XII were intact. Intraoral examination was limited by a maximum interincisal opening of 20 mm (Mallampati class 4); mild left TMJ pain with a soft reciprocal click was noted, and the mandible deviated to the right on opening. The masticatory muscles were tender, worse on the left. At this point, internal derangement of the left TMJ, headache, and myofascial pain were considered in the differential diagnosis, and an MRI of the bilateral TMJs (open and closed; T1‐ and T2‐weighted sagittal and coronal images) was ordered to evaluate the cause of his trismus.

A 61-year-old man presented with a 3-week history of right eyelid ptosis that fluctuated throughout the day and worsened in the afternoon. He denied dysphagia, limb weakness, or other neurologic symptoms. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. On admission, vital signs were stable. Neurologic and ophthalmologic examinations were otherwise normal. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. The serum acetylcholine receptor antibody level was elevated at >16 nmol/L (normal <0.40 nmol/L). A diagnosis of myasthenia gravis was made, and ptosis improved with prednisolone, pyridostigmine, and azathioprine. Spiral computed tomography of the chest revealed a well-circumscribed, hypodense lesion measuring 6 × 3 cm in the anterior mediastinum without invasion of adjacent structures. On the basis of its anatomical location and fat density, the mass was radiologically diagnosed as thymoma, and the patient was scheduled for plasmapheresis followed by surgical resection.

A 55-year-old Indian woman presented with a 2-year history of a swelling on the right side of her neck. Two years earlier, she underwent a wide local excision of a similar lesion, with histopathology revealing a granular cell tumor that extended to the excision margin. She was lost to follow-up. Her medical history is notable for moderately controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus on metformin and glimepiride and a remote thyroidectomy for colloid goiter. She is normotensive, does not smoke or drink, and has no family history of cancer.

On examination, there was a 3 × 3 cm nodular, mobile, firm swelling on the right side of the neck. It did not move with tongue protrusion or swallowing. No other swellings were found, and systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, WBC 8000/mm³ (70% neutrophils), fasting blood sugar 166 mg/dL, and post-prandial blood sugar 179 mg/dL. Given her history and clinical findings, there was a high suspicion for recurrence of a granular cell tumor.

An 83-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of a painless, slowly enlarging, hardened, red lump with erosion in her left axilla. The lesion measured approximately 1.0 cm, and no axillary lymphadenopathy was palpable. Her medical history was significant only for hypertension, and there was no personal or family history of breast cancer. 

An incisional biopsy of the lesion showed an adenocarcinoma with apocrine differentiation. The tumor cells had abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and large round nuclei with clear nucleoli, and Alcian blue–positive mucus was seen on the luminal surface. On immunohistochemistry, the neoplastic cells were positive for cytokeratin 7, gross cystic disease fluid protein 15 (GCDFP15), and GATA-binding protein 3, and negative for estrogen receptor.

Digital mammography and breast ultrasonography showed no abnormalities. Axillary ultrasonography revealed a hypervascular, homogeneous, hypoechoic, round mass measuring approximately 8.8 × 7.4 × 8.6 mm projecting from the skin; no accessory breast tissue was identified in either axilla. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography demonstrated no significant fluorodeoxyglucose uptake.

A 90-year-old man was referred for diagnosis and treatment of an oral lesion that he first noticed approximately 1 year earlier. The lesion had grown gradually and then enlarged rapidly over the past 6 months. His medical history included atrial fibrillation treated with warfarin, hyperlipidemia, resected rectal cancer, and internal carotid artery stenosis treated by carotid endarterectomy. He had smoked from age 23 to 48 years (Brinkman index 3000). 

Oral examination revealed a hard mass measuring 35 × 27 mm on the floor of the oral cavity, attached to bone, with partial mucosal ulceration. The mass displaced the tongue posteriorly, resulting in a Mallampati score of IV, and caused difficulty with speech and swallowing. There was no cranial nerve paralysis or cervical lymphadenopathy. 

Cone-beam CT showed an inhomogeneous mass connected to the cortical bone of the left mandibular body. MRI demonstrated low signal intensity of the mass relative to muscle on both T1- and T2-weighted axial images. PET/CT revealed abnormal accumulation of fluorodeoxyglucose in the mandibular lesion (maximum standardized uptake value, 7.2) with no other areas of abnormal uptake. 

Biopsy of the mass was suspicious for chondrosarcoma.

A 30-year-old man presented with an 18-month history of progressive swelling in the right mandibular region. He had no significant past medical or family history and a three-year history of cigarette smoking. After extraction of his right lower third molar by an oral surgeon, the extraction site failed to heal, and he reported mild facial swelling near the right mandibular angle. 

On examination, intraoral inspection revealed a nonhealing socket at the right lower third molar site with otherwise normal dentition and mucosa; there was no inferior alveolar nerve paresthesia. Extraoral examination showed adequate mouth opening, an intact mandibular border, and no cervical lymphadenopathy.

An orthopantomogram demonstrated a large, radiolucent lesion extending from the right lower second molar to the mandibular ramus without fracture. Contrast CT of the mandible revealed a 4.7 × 3.4 × 8 cm expansile, destructive lesion centered at the right mandibular angle, with extension into the ramus, coronoid, and condylar processes and areas of cortical perforation, suggesting a locally aggressive tumor.

An incisional biopsy performed at an outside facility was reported as pleomorphic adenoma.

A 43-year-old man presented with non-coagulated hematuria and intermittent lower-abdominal pain. He had experienced episodes of hematuria on several prior occasions. Physical examination was unremarkable. Ultrasonography revealed a 14 mm × 10 mm polypoid lesion on the left lateral wall of the urinary bladder. The lesion was resected transurethrally, and hematoxylin-and-eosin–stained sections demonstrated villous structures lined by columnar intestinal‐type epithelium with mild dysplastic changes in some nuclei and abundant mucinous material. Immunohistochemical staining showed diffuse positivity for carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), focal positivity for cytokeratin 20 (CK-20) and cytokeratin 7 (CK-7), and negativity for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA).

A 29-year-old man with a body mass index of 48 presented with 3 weeks of back pain, dyspnea on exertion, bilateral leg swelling, and orthopnea. He denied weight loss, night sweats, fevers, or chills and had no significant past medical or family history. His blood pressure was 118/90 mm Hg, heart rate 88 bpm, respiratory rate 23 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Examination revealed mild bilateral lower-extremity edema; cardiopulmonary and other systems were unremarkable.

Transthoracic echocardiography showed a large pericardial effusion with early tamponade physiology. He underwent pericardiocentesis yielding serosanguinous fluid. On transfer, repeat pericardiocentesis demonstrated a lymphocytic predominance, negative flow cytometry, and cytology showing atypical cells favored to represent reactive mesothelial cells. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no lymphadenopathy or detectable mass, with only poor visualization of the left atrial appendage. Complete blood count, chemistries, and rheumatologic testing—including antinuclear antibody and anti–double-stranded DNA—were normal. Pericardial fluid cultures grew Staphylococcus lugdunensis, which was presumed to be a contaminant. After no reaccumulation of fluid, he was discharged on penicillin G for 2 weeks for presumed idiopathic/post-viral pericardial effusion.

Two months later, he reported improved symptoms despite echocardiographic recurrence of a large pericardial effusion, and an outpatient rheumatologic workup was recommended. Five months after initial presentation, he returned with worsening dyspnea and orthopnea. Vital signs were within normal limits; examination again showed lower-extremity edema and distant heart sounds. His B-type natriuretic peptide was 155 pg/mL; other labs were unremarkable. He was admitted, and CT of the chest showed a high-density pericardial effusion markedly increased from the study 5 months earlier.

A 70-year-old woman presented with a painless, gradually enlarging lesion on her forehead that had been present for 30 years but had recently grown more rapidly. She reported no pruritus, ulceration, bleeding, or history of trauma at the site. Her medical, surgical, family, and medication histories were unremarkable; she did not smoke or drink alcohol. On examination, there was a pedunculated dark black warty lesion measuring 9 cm in its longest dimension, with papillomatosis and a verrucous surface attached to the underlying skin by a thin stalk. The adjacent skin was unremarkable, and no similar lesions were seen elsewhere on the body. Given the pigmentation and morphology, clinical suspicion included verrucous melanoma and pigmented basal cell carcinoma, and an excisional biopsy was performed.

A 53-year-old woman with a congenital upper-limb developmental defect was admitted in May 2009 for evaluation of normocytic anemia and a left adnexal mass noted on transvaginal ultrasound. At laparotomy, a tumor arising from the sigmoid colon was resected; histologic analysis revealed a well-differentiated tubular adenocarcinoma (pT3N0M0), and adjuvant chemotherapy was initiated. As part of staging to exclude distant metastases, an abdominal ultrasound demonstrated multiple ill-defined lesions in the spleen. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed these splenic lesions, raising suspicion for metastatic involvement. A bone marrow biopsy showed no evidence of hematologic malignancy. Contrast-enhanced ultrasonography of the spleen suggested multiple hemangiomas. MRI of the abdomen revealed splenic lesions that were not typical of metastatic disease, and clinical monitoring was recommended. In February 2011, PET/CT without contrast demonstrated no abnormal FDG uptake in the spleen. Over the subsequent years, the patient had persistent normocytic anemia and developed fluctuating thrombocytopenia despite normal gynecologic and hematologic evaluations. A PET/CT scan in September 2016 demonstrated progressive splenomegaly. Splenectomy was then scheduled.

A 31-year-old man presented with a several-day history of worsening epigastric pain, peaking over the previous 12 hours. He had a remote history of alcoholic hepatitis but continued to drink, and no other significant personal or family history. On examination, he was afebrile, heart rate was 58 bpm, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 12/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air; he had mild upper abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs. Laboratory tests showed a slight increase in alkaline phosphatase but no elevation of inflammatory markers or pancreatic enzymes; tumor markers (CEA, CA19-9, DUPAN-2, SPan-1) were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a 40 mm hypovascular mass in the head of the pancreas with uneven internal density and a cyst-like low-density area in parts; the mass enhanced heterogeneously over arterial, portal, and delayed phases, and the main pancreatic duct upstream measured 7 mm in diameter. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a well-defined, circular, hypoechoic mass in the pancreatic head. MRI demonstrated low signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images with focal high T2 signal, and marked upstream ductal dilatation on MR cholangiopancreatography. FDG-PET showed intense uptake in the mass (SUVmax 5.56).

A 74-year-old woman was followed for a nodule in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast that had grown slowly over five years. She first noted the lesion by self-palpation. At initial evaluation, imaging suggested a mammary hamartoma; fine-needle aspiration cytology was negative, and she was observed as an outpatient. On repeat evaluation, mammography showed a dense, round to oval solid nodule with a clearly defined border in the upper lateral quadrant of the left breast. Ultrasound depicted a 27 × 24 × 11 mm oval lesion composed of mixed hyperechoic and hypoechoic regions.  

Her medical history was notable only for diverticulitis of the rectum with perforation. She had no history of smoking, alcohol use, or relevant family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Physical examination was unremarkable beyond the palpable breast mass; her height was 137 cm, weight 39 kg (BMI 20.8 kg/m2).  

A core-needle biopsy of the lesion revealed multiple nests of epithelioid cells within an adipo-fibrous stroma without stromal reaction. Nuclear atypia was subtle, mitotic figures were sparse, and Ki-67 labelling was less than 1% per high-power field. No mammary ducts or lobules were seen within the lesion. Immunohistochemical studies showed negativity for cytokeratin AE1/AE3, CK7, α-smooth muscle actin, p63, CD10, CD117, and synaptophysin; positivity for vimentin and S-100 protein; and oestrogen receptor positivity with progesterone receptor and HER-2 negativity. The lesion was presumed benign, but its exact histologic nature remained uncertain.

A 31-year-old man with a history of asthma and obesity was referred for evaluation of a left breast mass. He first noticed the lesion approximately three years earlier; since then it had progressively enlarged and become painful. He had initially been evaluated in 2021 but was lost to follow-up. 

On presentation he was hemodynamically stable. Compared with the right breast, the left breast contained a large, soft, uniformly palpable mass. The overlying skin showed prominent veins, and the nipple was deviated inferiorly without discharge. There was no skin discoloration, dimpling, or thickening. He denied endocrine abnormalities, breast trauma, and a family history of breast disease. 

All laboratory tests, including routine blood work and tumor markers, were within normal limits. A diagnostic bilateral mammogram demonstrated a 20 cm encapsulated fatty mass occupying most of the left breast (BI-RADS category 4); the right breast was unremarkable. A focused ultrasound of the left breast showed a well-defined hypoechoic mass at the 12 o’clock position.

A 43-year-old man presented with a painless swelling in the left mandibular premolar region noted for over one year. He had no systemic disease. On examination, there was a well-circumscribed, fluctuant 9–12 mm gingival swelling between the left mandibular canine (tooth 33) and first premolar (tooth 34). The swelling was nontender, the adjacent teeth were vital on cold and electric testing, and there was no lymphadenopathy. Aspiration yielded clear fluid. A panoramic radiograph showed a well-circumscribed unilocular radiolucency with a sclerotic margin measuring approximately 1.5 cm × 1.2 cm between the roots of teeth 33 and 34, with slight root displacement but intact lamina dura. Cone-beam CT confirmed a cystic lesion between these roots with resorption of both buccal and lingual cortical plates.

A 1.5-year-old girl, born at term (birth weight 3200 g, normal APGAR scores) to non-consanguineous parents, was brought for evaluation of progressive limb weakness. She weighed 7 kg at presentation. Six months earlier, her parents noted decreased movement of her lower extremities, which gradually involved her arms, and episodes of agitation. On initial examination she was alert with normal cognitive function; gait and stance were abnormal, and she had spasticity with hyperreflexia in all four limbs but intact cranial nerves and sensation.

She underwent metabolic screening with high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) and tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS), which yielded normal results. Brain MRI showed only a small cyst in the left internal capsule, deemed unrelated to her symptoms. An eye examination and eye-movement study, performed to evaluate for Niemann-Pick disease, were normal. Empiric therapy with piracetam and topiramate produced no improvement.

Given her quadriparesis and hyperreflexia without cognitive impairment, a spinal cord lesion was suspected. Sagittal T2-weighted MRI revealed an epidural mass extending from C2 to T6, with invasion into paraspinal soft tissues, the retropharyngeal space, and both anterior and posterior elements of the involved vertebrae, resulting in severe spinal cord compression.

A 33-year-old woman presented with progressive neck pain, radicular pain at C3, and signs of high cervical myelopathy. On examination she had upgoing plantar responses, spasticity in the lower limbs, and sensory loss in the C4 and C5 dermatomes. Imaging demonstrated collapse and instability of the C3 vertebra with cord signal changes, a heterogeneous enhancing lesion in the C3 vertebra, and a collection interpreted as pus occupying the anterior one-third of the spinal canal, compressing the cord from the clivus to C4. She underwent C3 corpectomy with drainage of the collection, anterior decompression, and fusion with a cage and plate. Postoperatively her neurological status improved. Histopathological examination of vertebral fragments and the collection showed no evidence of infection, especially tuberculosis, and revealed only a mononuclear infiltrate without malignant cells or chronic inflammation. She was referred for oncology evaluation but was lost to follow-up and did not undergo immunohistochemical or cytogenetic studies. Two years later she returned with spastic quadriparesis and bowel and bladder dysfunction. Imaging showed a recurrent anterior collection compressing the cord, and she underwent repeat anterior decompression; histopathology was again inconclusive. Empiric antituberculous therapy was initiated based on endemic prevalence and radiologic appearance, but after two years she had no improvement and then rapidly deteriorated to quadriplegia with complete sensory loss below the neck. An emergency posterior laminectomy from C3 to C7 was performed, but there was no postoperative neurological improvement, and she was transferred to a neurorehabilitation center.

A 58-year-old healthy Caucasian man with a history only of a right shoulder lipoma presented with a 4-year history of an asymptomatic, enlarging, palpable right gluteal mass. Two years earlier, a core-needle biopsy had shown a low-grade spindle cell tumor of myxoid variety, but he declined surgical excision. Over the subsequent two years, the mass continued to grow and he returned to clinic. On examination, there was a 7-cm, mobile, subcutaneous mass in the intergluteal cleft without overlying skin changes; inguinal lymph nodes were nonpalpable. A CT scan showed an irregular, lobulated subcutaneous soft-tissue mass measuring 7.2 × 4.3 cm (previously 5.1 × 1.7 cm). The patient underwent surgical excision. Grossly, there was a well-circumscribed 5.5 × 5.0 × 4.0 cm mass without a definitive capsule, and margins were negative. Histologic evaluation revealed a bland spindle-to-epithelioid cellular proliferation with rare “lipoblast-like” cells set in collagenous to myxoid stroma with a prominent network of thin, arborizing vessels.

A 37-year-old woman, gravida 4 para 4, presented seven weeks postpartum with a 5/10 low back and right gluteal pain radiating into the posterolateral thigh, calf, and heel, with foot tingling. Her labor at 36.6 weeks was 24 hours long; despite epidural analgesia, she experienced severe back, hip, gluteal, and sciatic pain during labor. She had occasional mild similar pain in prior years but noted severe pain when sitting, driving, or standing. Her sleep was limited by pain. 

Medical history includes polycystic ovary syndrome, vulvar keloid, anxiety (on sertraline), and hypertension (on amlodipine). She denied trauma, bowel or bladder symptoms, fever, or weight loss. 

On examination, active lumbar motion was normal except that right rotation worsened her right low back and gluteal pain. Palpation revealed hypertonicity and tenderness of right gluteus medius/maximus, piriformis, and tensor fascia lata. Right hip extension and flexion strength were 4/5 with pain; other motor, sensory, and reflex exams were normal. Right seated straight-leg raise, FABER, and Kemp’s tests reproduced her pain. 

Initial differential diagnoses included lumbosacral radiculopathy from disc herniation, gluteal or piriformis tendinopathy, and sciatic neuropraxia related to lithotomy positioning or vaginal delivery. She underwent chiropractic manual therapies and piriformis stretching with transient low back improvement but persistent sciatic pain. 

Three weeks later, radiographs of the lumbar spine were normal. She then developed right popliteal fossa pain; Doppler ruled out DVT, and she was provisionally diagnosed with a Baker’s cyst. Physical therapy aggravated her symptoms. By 18 weeks postpartum she had recurrent falls due to right leg giving way and hip weakness. A spine surgeon reproduced her symptoms, and lumbar MRI at 26 weeks was normal. At 29 weeks, given persistent falls, hip weakness, and normal lumbar studies, the chiropractor discarded radiculopathy and ordered right hip radiographs.

A 31-year-old woman presented with a 1-week history of right upper quadrant pain. She had no significant medical history. On examination, her temperature was 36.4 °C, blood pressure 110/60 mmHg, and pulse 80 beats/min; her abdomen was tender in the right upper quadrant without guarding or rebound. Laboratory tests, including liver function and serum tumor markers (CEA, CA125, and CA19-9), were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography showed multiple tiny gallstones with segmental thickening of the gallbladder wall and a 6.5 cm multiloculated cystic mass in the left retroperitoneal space just below the spleen. The preoperative differential diagnoses included cystic mesothelioma, mucinous cystic neoplasm, cystic lymphangioma, and chronic cholecystitis. The patient underwent laparoscopic exploration. In the right semi-lateral decubitus position, laparoscopy revealed a large, well-demarcated cystic mass behind the inferior pole of the spleen with no apparent attachment to adjacent organs. The mass was completely excised without spillage, and a cholecystectomy was performed.

A 49-year-old woman presented during a routine annual gynecologic examination with a painful abdominal wall mass. Her history included appendectomy, two births, a cesarean section 15 years earlier, and excision of an endometriotic mass from the cesarean scar at that time. She reported that the mass had increased in size over several months and that the pain was cyclical, correlating with her menstrual periods, similar to her previous lesion. Prior gynecologic examinations were normal, and no abdominal nodule had been noted.

On physical examination, there was a 6 cm × 6 cm tender mass in the midline of the abdominal wall, 3 cm above the Pfannenstiel scar; the mass was painful on movement and Fothergill sign positive. The rest of the gynecologic examination was unremarkable. Mammography and pelvic ultrasound were normal. Soft-tissue ultrasound of the abdominal wall showed a 70 × 60 mm lesion in the mesogastrium caudal to the umbilicus, described as “compatible with fibrous soft tissue tumor (desmoid tumor).” Given her history, endometriotic implants could not be ruled out. Fine-needle aspiration cytology revealed a benign process compatible with endometriosis. Serum tumor markers were: CA-125, 243 U/mL (elevated); CEA, < 0.5 ng/mL. A provisional diagnosis of abdominal wall endometriosis was made, and surgery was scheduled for removal of the mass with exploration of the abdominal cavity.

A 75-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a painless, slowly enlarging mass on the dorsum of her right wrist. She first noticed the swelling 1 year earlier, and her local physician initially presumed it to be a ganglion. Her medical history included hypertension, osteoarthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, and a malunited right distal-radius fracture sustained 5 months prior, for which she declined surgical intervention. 

On examination, the wrist was radially deviated with a classic “dinner fork” deformity. A 6 × 9 cm, round, painless mass on the dorsum of the distal radius was firmly adherent to underlying structures and overlying skin, did not transilluminate, and had an area of overlying skin necrosis. There was no lymphadenopathy, no breast masses, no organomegaly, and clear lung fields. Pulses and capillary refill in the right hand were normal, and sensory and motor function were intact. 

Laboratory studies revealed a normal blood count, normal renal and liver function, an elevated ESR of 74 mm/hr, and a hemoglobin concentration of 11 g/dL. A Mantoux test was negative. 

Ultrasonography showed a large vascularized soft-tissue mass infiltrating the extensor tendons on the dorsal aspect of the wrist. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a large mass causing extensive osteolysis of the distal radius, replacement of the distal one third of the marrow, involvement of the entire extensor-tendon group, and infiltration through the subcutaneous tissues into the dermis. Computed tomography of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis, along with a whole-body bone scan, confirmed an isolated lesion with no evidence of dissemination.

A 43-year-old man presented for evaluation of a painless lesion on the hard palate that was discovered during a routine dental examination two months earlier. He was a current smoker. On oral examination, there was a ~5 mm lesion with a verrucous surface and scattered erythematous spots adjacent to the first upper right molar. The presumptive clinical diagnosis was squamous cell carcinoma or traumatic ulcer, and an excisional biopsy was performed.

Histopathologic examination of the surgical specimen showed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and elongated rete pegs of the oral epithelium. In the underlying connective tissue, there were numerous foam cells with clear cytoplasm and pyknotic nuclei, and periodic acid–Schiff staining of these cells was negative. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed that the foam cells were positive for CD68, and Ki-67 staining was restricted to the basal layer of the epithelium and was negative in the foam cells.

A 53-year-old Caucasian man was referred after detection of a retroperitoneal mass. He reported a months-long history of unexplained weight gain, progressive abdominal distension, and occasional constipation. He denied dietary changes, appetite loss, pain, or a personal or family history of neoplasia. On examination, he was 180 cm tall with a BMI of 27.5 kg/m2, appeared in good condition except for abdominal enlargement with left-sided distension. Palpation revealed a slightly mobile, fibroelastic mass approximately 30 × 15 cm, extending from the left flank to the umbilicus. Routine blood tests showed mildly elevated triglycerides; other values, including cardiovascular assessment, were unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a large retroperitoneal mass of heterogeneous echotexture, of uncertain origin. Contrast CT and MRI confirmed a well-defined fatty retroperitoneal tumor measuring approximately 365 × 210 × 165 mm, extending from the left splenic flexure down to the left ischiorectal fossa, displacing the left colon medially, and traversed by the left ureter. MRI also revealed three small fatty nodules with irregular margins and contrast enhancement. The imaging could not exclude malignancy.

A 36-year-old woman presented with epigastric pain and anemia.
