Upper endoscopy revealed an elevated mucosal lesion with linear ulceration on the anterior wall of the gastric antrum, immediately adjacent to the pylorus. An incisional biopsy was non-diagnostic. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed anemia; tumor markers were within normal limits. Endoscopic ultrasonography demonstrated a 20 mm heterogeneous, echoic tumor confined to the submucosal layer without involvement of the muscularis propria. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a nodular soft-tissue mass in the gastric antrum without regional or distant metastases. On PET/CT, there was no significant uptake of ^18F-FDG in the lesion. The results were inconclusive for excluding malignant potential of the tumor.

A 49-year-old woman with no smoking history was referred for evaluation of an abnormality on a routine chest X-ray. She was asymptomatic.  
On examination, vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies, including carcinoembryonic antigen (1.4 ng/mL), cytokeratin fragment (1.5 ng/mL), and progastrin-releasing peptide (58.0 pg/mL), were unremarkable.  
Chest CT showed:  
• A pure ground-glass nodule in the right upper lobe (segment 3)  
• A 13-mm solid nodule in the right lower lobe (segment 9)  
• A 47-mm mass in the left upper lobe (segments 1+2) invading the interlobar pleura adjacent to segment 6, without enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes  
PET-CT demonstrated maximum standardized uptake values of 2.3 in the right lower lobe lesion and 6.8 in the left upper lobe lesion. Brain MRI and PET-CT showed no metastatic lesions, and no extrathoracic tumour was identified.  
Transbronchial biopsies under fluoroscopic and endobronchial ultrasound guidance yielded adequate tissue from the left upper lobe mass and the right lower lobe nodule. Both specimens showed papillary adenocarcinoma with positive thyroid transcription factor 1 and napsin A staining, making it challenging to distinguish advanced-stage metastatic disease from potentially resectable multiple primaries.

An 87-year-old woman presented with a lesion involving her left cheek, nasal ala, medial canthal area, and eyelids. She had no known precipitating factors and an unremarkable medical history.

On examination, there was an irregular cutaneous lesion extending across the left cheek, nasal skin, medial canthus, and eyelids. Two small, non-orientable grayish skin biopsies (0.8 cm and 0.6 cm) were obtained.

Histologic examination of 16 levels revealed a malignant, infiltrative proliferation composed predominantly of basaloid cells with focal squamous differentiation and an inflammatory infiltrate rich in plasma cells, lymphocytes, and melanophages. Neither specimen showed clear margins.

A contrast-enhanced CT scan demonstrated a 22 × 6 mm mass with ragged edges on the left cheek skin extending to the nasal skin. There was no invasion of adjacent bone or deeper adipose tissue and no skull metastases. No lymphadenopathy was seen in the neck or abdomen; a single mediastinal lymph node measured 1.5 cm. Fluid was noted in both maxillary sinuses; no free fluid was present in the abdomen or pelvis.

A 24-year-old Caucasian woman presented with an area of multiple itchy nodules in her left infra-axillary region. Three months before presentation, she had noted a single reddish, pearly nodule (4–5 mm in diameter) in the left axilla. Over the next three months, she developed multiple similar nodules clustered over a 20 × 5 cm area, all of which were pruritic. On examination, the nodules were smooth, well defined, and 4–5 mm in size, and no regional lymphadenopathy was palpable. Laboratory studies showed an absolute eosinophil count within the normal range and a normal serum immunoglobulin E level.

A 38-year-old woman presented with a 10-day history of dizziness, palpitations, and fatigue accompanied by inappetence, black stools, and tenesmus. She denied recent weight loss or abdominal pain. Three days earlier, gastroduodenoscopy at an outside hospital revealed gastric mucosal ischemia and spherical lesions in the duodenum. She had no prior surgeries. On arrival, her temperature was 36.8°C, pulse 88/min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, respiration 18/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Physical examination was notable only for pallor; the abdomen was soft and nontender, and digital rectal examination confirmed black stool but no masses. Laboratory studies demonstrated hypoalbuminemia, hypocalcemia, a positive fecal occult blood test, and microcytic hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin 58 g/L). Abdominal CT showed a heterogeneous, nonobstructing mass in the stomach extending into the second and third parts of the duodenum. Repeat gastroscopy revealed a large polypoid mass originating from the anterior wall of the gastric antrum and protruding through the pylorus into the second part of the duodenum; the surface was red but lacked mucosal ulcerations or stigmata of recent bleeding. Random biopsies showed mild acute and chronic inflammation with significant proliferation of blood vessels and fibroblasts.

A healthy 7-year-old girl presented with a 2-month history of a firm, tender swelling in the right posterior mandibular region that was gradually increasing in size. She had primary dentition, adequate oral hygiene, and both primary right mandibular molars were vital and structurally intact on testing. A panoramic radiograph revealed a well-circumscribed calcified mass measuring approximately 2.8 × 2.1 cm, surrounded by a uniform radiolucent halo. The internal structure showed a mixed radiolucent–radiopaque pattern with a “wheel-spoke” appearance, and the lesion was intimately associated with the roots of the right mandibular second primary molar.

A 14-year-old girl presented with a 1-year history of an asymptomatic, slowly enlarging mass on the right side of her neck. There was no history of hoarseness, nasal regurgitation, pain, fever, or trauma. She had received three courses of oral antibiotics without change in the size of the mass. 

On examination, there was a 6×4-cm immobile, solitary right-sided neck mass deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle, with smooth regular borders and no overlying skin changes. No cervical lymphadenopathy was palpable, and the oropharynx appeared normal without displacement of the peritonsillar structures. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. 

Routine blood tests, including lactate dehydrogenase, were within normal limits. Ultrasound of the neck showed a solid, well-circumscribed homogeneous mass within the fascial planes, with low-level Doppler venous flow, displacing the great vessels to the right. An MRI of the neck was subsequently obtained.

A 59-year-old African American woman presented with a 3-month history of worsening urinary symptoms, including voiding difficulties and one episode of gross hematuria. Her medical history was notable for hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, cerebrovascular disease with residual right hemiparesis, and end-stage renal disease on thrice-weekly hemodialysis. She had a remote history of left adrenal adenoma excision and surgical plus radiotherapy treatment for invasive breast carcinoma; she had declined chemotherapy. She smoked 30 pack-years but quit 20 years earlier; there was no family history of cancer. Her medications included metoprolol, calcium acetate, simvastatin, omeprazole, polyethylene glycol, paroxetine, and latanoprost eye drops. 

On examination, vital signs were stable. She was well-nourished, oriented, and wheelchair-bound. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal examinations were unremarkable; there was right hemiparesis and slurred speech. Urinalysis showed microscopic hematuria with a large amount of blood. Complete blood count, liver function tests, and basic metabolic panel (supported by dialysis) were unremarkable. A urine culture grew Escherichia coli (>10,000 CFU/mL), which was treated. 

A CT urogram revealed a 3-cm polypoid mass on the posterior inferior bladder wall near the neck. The patient underwent transurethral resection of the bladder tumor. Histologic examination of hematoxylin and eosin–stained sections showed flat, cuboidal to columnar cells with clear to eosinophilic cytoplasm and a hobnail appearance, arranged in tubulocystic and papillary patterns. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated that the neoplastic cells were diffusely positive for cytokeratin 7, cancer antigen 125, and α-methylacyl-coenzyme A racemase; focally positive for cytokeratin 20, protein 53, and carcinoembryonic antigen; and negative for thyroid transcription factor 1.

A 48-year-old man with a history of left-sided renal cell carcinoma treated with radical nephrectomy and radiotherapy in 2004, who later developed adrenal, pulmonary, and mediastinal metastases treated with interferon until 2007, presented in December 2009 with a 2-month history of progressive dysphagia, alteration in his voice, and a 2–3 kg weight loss. On examination, he had a 5 × 5 cm exophytic mass in the oropharynx centered at the right base of the tongue, extending into the right tonsillar fossa and adjacent soft palate and crossing the midline. Tongue mobility was normal, and there was no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. Contrast-enhanced CT of the face, neck, thorax, abdomen, and pelvis revealed widespread visceral and osseous metastatic deposits, including the base-of-tongue lesion, with no cervical adenopathy.

A 71-year-old woman presented with persistent low back pain. She had no prior history of abdominal complaints. An initial lumbar spine CT performed by an orthopedist revealed incidental abdominal cystic formations. On examination, she had a palpable lower abdominal mass with mild tenderness but no ascites. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were unremarkable. Pelvic ultrasound confirmed a large multicystic mass, and an abdominal MRI showed the following:
• A multilocular cystic lesion, measuring 11 × 12 × 12.5 cm, with thin septations and no papillary projections, primarily in the pelvis behind the uterus.  
• Multiple small cysts in the perirectal fat, pericolonic regions, and greater omentum.  
• A second cystic lesion in the intraperitoneal subhepatic space measuring 9.5 × 11.5 × 15 cm.  
No solid components or significant nodularity were identified.

A 21‐year‐old otherwise healthy woman presented with a 4‐month history of a pulsatile mass over the dorsal aspect of the right hallux. She reported that the lesion appeared after a moderate trauma and then rapidly increased in size, with intermittent pain. On examination, there was a mildly tender, firm, 3×3 cm pulsatile, angiomatous mass on the right hallux, with areas of hemorrhagic crusting and superficial venous dilatation. No lymphadenopathy was palpable. Routine laboratory tests were normal.  
Doppler ultrasonography showed a high‐flow vascular lesion with arteriovenous shunting. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well‐circumscribed, 3 cm vascular mass over the distal phalanx characterized by a tangled mesh of dilated arteries and veins connected by focal shunts and no discrete soft‐tissue mass signal. T2‐weighted gradient‐echo sequences demonstrated hyperintense fast‐flow vessel networks.

A 45-year-old man noted a painless, slowly enlarging subcutaneous nodule of the left upper eyelid over the past 2 years. He had no similar nodules elsewhere on the face and no prior interventions. On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes, extraocular movements were full, and the remainder of the ophthalmic examination was unremarkable. Inspection and palpation of the left upper eyelid revealed a firm, solid subcutaneous mass measuring 8 × 7 mm, with no attachment to the overlying skin. Eversion of the upper eyelid revealed an overlying pyogenic granuloma. Given the chronic presentation and location of the lesion, the presumed diagnosis was an upper eyelid chalazion. The patient consented to complete excision through a transconjunctival approach. Intraoperatively, the mass was noted to be attached to the upper tarsus without infiltration of surrounding tissues.

A 66-year-old man presented with sudden sharp right thigh pain and an audible “crack” while lifting a box one day earlier. He was unable to bear weight and noted his thigh appeared crooked. He denied trauma elsewhere, fevers, or prior ambulation difficulties. He reported a 5-kg weight loss over 3 months. His medical history was notable only for well-controlled hypertension; there was no history of malignancy, radiotherapy, or family history of cancer. On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. The right thigh showed marked swelling over the distal femur (10 × 12 × 4 cm), slight external rotation of the hip, and marked tenderness with limited range of motion. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, platelets 123,000/μL, LDH 288 U/L, calcium 2.02 mmol/L, BUN 31 mg/dL, and creatinine 3.43 mg/dL. Plain radiography of the right femur demonstrated a complete, comminuted fracture of the distal third with surrounding osteolytic lesions and cortical destruction.

A 31-year-old woman reported a one-year history of a vaginal lump that protruded during activity and had increased in size over the past two weeks. She denied pain, discharge, trauma, itching, or urinary symptoms. She was unmarried, had no history of sexual intercourse, no prior treatments, and no family history of similar conditions. Physical examination revealed a 5 × 2 × 4 cm smooth, fluctuant, freely mobile, nontender cystic mass arising from the left paraurethral region. Urethral sondage showed no communication with the mass. Rectal examination was unremarkable; the uterus and adnexa were normal. Routine blood tests were within normal limits. Translabial ultrasound demonstrated a 5.4 × 2.33 × 2.53 cm monolocular cystic lesion with homogeneous hypoechoic internal echoes, clear borders, and no connection to the urethra.

A 47-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of a slowly enlarging, asymptomatic swelling in the right maxillary anterior alveolar and upper lip region, noted for facial asymmetry. He had undergone surgery for a similar lesion 15 years earlier without complication; his medical history was otherwise noncontributory.

On examination, there was a single, sessile, well-defined reddish ulcerated mass measuring approximately 4 × 3 cm, extending from the vermilion border of the upper lip to the maxillary anterior alveolus and overlapping the incisal surfaces of the anterior teeth. The lesion was firm, mildly tender, and bled slightly on palpation.

Panoramic and periapical radiographs showed an irregular pattern of alveolar bone loss and displacement of the maxillary anterior teeth. Contrast-enhanced CT of the maxilla demonstrated an expansile, unilocular hypodense lesion extending into the right maxillary sinus, with altered marrow signal in the underlying alveolus suggestive of intraosseous invasion.

An incisional biopsy revealed hyperplastic stratified squamous epithelium overlying a poorly circumscribed proliferation of spindle- and stellate-shaped cells arranged in short fascicles within a copious myxoid stroma containing numerous blood vessels.

A 20-year-old woman presented with an 8-year history of a solitary small red swelling below her right lower eyelid that had been gradually increasing in size. She reported occasional throbbing pain and sweating over the lesion, both of which were aggravated by physical exertion and emotional stress. She denied any history of trauma, systemic symptoms, or similar family illnesses. 

On examination, there was a solitary, irregular, erythematous, soft, slightly elevated plaque measuring approximately 3 × 2 cm just below the right lower eyelid. The surface was smooth and moist. The lesion was mildly tender on palpation. Beaded drops of sweat were observed on the surface with mild stroking and after physical exertion. No pulsation or bruit was noted. 

Color Doppler ultrasonography of the lesion showed mild to moderate vascularization in the deep dermis.

A 45‐year‐old man presented with a 1‐week history of hematochezia and a 4‐kg weight loss over 3 months. He had no significant past medical history. Vital signs were stable, and initial laboratory studies, including tumor markers, were within normal limits.  
Colonoscopy demonstrated a 2.5×2.0 cm pedunculated lesion with surface ulceration located 10 cm from the anal verge; biopsy of the lesion revealed a villous adenoma.  
Abdominopelvic CT showed a polypoid lesion of approximately 3 cm in the upper rectum. PET–CT demonstrated multiple hypermetabolic lymph‐node metastases along the inferior mesenteric artery, in the mesorectum, and along the superior rectal artery.  
Under the presumptive diagnosis of advanced upper rectal adenocarcinoma, the patient underwent low anterior resection with lymph‐node dissection.

A 41-year-old Hispanic man with a history of recurrent nephrolithiasis presented with acute, right-sided abdominal pain. He had no prior routine medical evaluations.  

His family history was notable for multiple paternal first-degree relatives with skin nodules; tumors of the brain, thoracic cavity, abdomen, and thyroid gland; and hypercalcemia.  

On examination, he was lean without cushingoid features. Multiple brown, subcentimeter cutaneous nodules were noted on his torso, and a 1-cm pedunculated nodule was present on his right arm.  

Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast showed a 7.9-cm heterogeneous, hypoattenuating right adrenal mass, an 11-cm right posterior hepatic mass, and a hepatic subcapsular hematoma.  

Laboratory studies on admission included:  
• Total calcium 11.7 mg/dL (8.4–10.4)  
• Albumin 3.6 g/dL (3.4–4.7)  
• Corrected calcium 12.0 mg/dL (8.4–10.4)  
• Parathyroid hormone 181 pg/mL (18–84)  
• 25-Hydroxyvitamin D 19 ng/mL (>29)  
• Creatinine 0.97 mg/dL (0.62–1.66) and eGFR 97 mL/min/1.73 m2 (>60)  
• Magnesium 2.0 mg/dL (1.4–2.6)  
• Phosphorus 1.0 mg/dL (2.3–5.6)  
• 24-hour urine calcium 482 mg (42–353)  

These findings were diagnostic of primary hyperparathyroidism.  

Preoperative biochemical evaluation demonstrated:  
• 24-hour urine metanephrine 261 μg/day (55–320)  
• 24-hour urine normetanephrine 1098 μg/day (114–865)  
• Plasma metanephrine 0.17 nmol/L (0.00–0.49)  
• Plasma normetanephrine 0.94 nmol/L (0.00–0.89)  
• 24-hour urine free cortisol 364.6 μg/day (≤60)  
• 1-mg dexamethasone suppression test cortisol 10.1 μg/dL (<1.8)  
• ACTH 9 pg/mL (0–46)  
• Dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate 41 μg/dL (80–560)  
• Androstenedione 0.816 ng/mL (0.230–0.890)  
• 17-Hydroxyprogesterone 95.97 ng/dL (≤138)  
• Renin 8.7 ng/mL/h (0.2–1.6)  
• Aldosterone 13.9 ng/dL (≤16.0)  

Based on these evaluations, suspicion for pheochromocytoma and adrenocortical carcinoma was low.

A 48-year-old woman with a 7-year history of a submucosal tumour below the esophagogastric junction, monitored periodically since 2004, presented in November 2011 with melena and progressive anemia; her hemoglobin level was 7.5 g/dL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 70 × 50 × 55 mm hypoechogenic, subcardial mass on the posterior gastric wall. In December 2011, the lesion was resected endoscopically by a piecemeal technique under general anesthesia, and histopathology reportedly confirmed a lipoma. Six weeks later, endoscopic evaluation demonstrated a recurrent bleeding tumour at the same site.

A 52-year-old Caucasian man with a 3-year history of moderate, pharmacologically treated hypertension, and no other symptoms, underwent abdominal ultrasonography during routine evaluation. US revealed a large hyperechoic mass (~20 cm in diameter) interposed between the spleen and left kidney, displacing the left kidney inferiorly. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a 20–25 cm expansive lesion arising from the left adrenal gland, with mean attenuation of –130 HU, sharp regular margins, and starlike central calcifications. The mass displaced the spleen cranially, stretched the left renal artery and vein, and produced an ipsilateral spermatic varicocele. Routine blood tests including complete blood count and liver and kidney function were normal. Serum cortisol levels were elevated at 10 a.m. (743 nmol/L; normal 171–536 nmol/L), 2 p.m. (637 nmol/L; normal 64–327 nmol/L), and 6 p.m. (649 nmol/L). Fasting glucose was 122 mg/dL (normal 60–110 mg/dL). Urinary catecholamines were normal.

A 61-year-old woman with hypertension and diabetes presented with a one-month history of progressive headaches, episodes of vomiting, and dizziness. On examination, she was fully conscious but had a static and left kinetic cerebellar syndrome; there was no cranial-nerve deficit and no palpable masses elsewhere. Brain MRI revealed two intra-axial lesions, each approximately 3 cm in diameter, in the left cerebellar hemisphere, extending toward the left latero-mesencephalic cistern and involving the superior cerebellar peduncle. On MRI these lesions were hypointense on T1-weighted images, heterogeneous on T2, and showed slight enhancement after gadolinium, with cystic intratumoral areas. They were hyperintense on diffusion-weighted imaging with corresponding ADC restriction. Perfusion imaging did not show neoangiogenesis, and MR spectroscopy demonstrated a tumoral profile with elevated choline and lipids, decreased N-acetylaspartate, and an increased choline/creatine ratio. A mild perilesional T2–FLAIR edema was present. There was no mass effect on the fourth ventricle or hydrocephalus. A body CT scan showed no evidence of extracranial tumors.

A 17-year-old female presented with a 5-year history of persistent bilateral knee swelling. There was no history of trauma. At age 14, she was diagnosed with juvenile idiopathic arthritis based on bilateral knee swelling and fifth metacarpal joint pain and was treated with sulfasalazine without improvement. On examination, she had large bilateral knee effusions and limited range of motion without redness or warmth; bilateral sacroiliac joints were tender. Autoantibodies and rheumatoid factor were negative. Routine blood studies, including leukocyte count and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, were within normal limits. Ultrasonography revealed bilateral frond-like villous projections of the synovium and massive effusion in the suprapatellar pouches. MRI of both knees demonstrated frond-like synovial masses with synovial hypertrophy and large joint effusions; the lesions followed the signal intensity of fat on all sequences.

A 65-year-old man presented with a progressive, painless growth of the left upper eyelid over 5 years. On examination, there was a 12 × 10 mm blackish lesion of the left upper eyelid with irregular borders, central ulceration, and telangiectatic vessels on the surface. The remainder of the eye examination was unremarkable. A provisional clinical diagnosis of basal cell carcinoma versus malignant melanoma was made, and an excisional biopsy was performed.

A 33-year-old Caucasian man with biopsy-proven tattoo-associated sarcoidosis and concomitant pulmonary involvement (on systemic corticosteroids) was referred after routine ophthalmic examination revealed an amelanotic choroidal mass in his amblyopic right eye. He reported no ocular symptoms. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/70+ OD (no pinhole improvement) and 20/40 OS; intraocular pressures were 11 mmHg OD and 13 mmHg OS. Anterior segments were normal bilaterally, and there was no vitritis. Fundus examination OD showed a subretinal, amelanotic mass 1 mm from the foveola with overlying fluid and an inferotemporal serous retinal detachment involving the fovea; the OS was unremarkable. Optical coherence tomography confirmed subretinal fluid with a foveal thickness of 234 μm. Fundus autofluorescence revealed increased orange pigment peripheral to the lesion, and fluorescein angiography demonstrated early intrinsic leakage. B-scan ultrasonography showed an acoustically hollow choroidal lesion measuring 9.1 × 8.2 mm at the base and 2.6 mm in thickness, with an associated exudative detachment. Based on his history of sarcoidosis, he was treated with 80 mg of oral prednisone daily. Over the next month, visual acuity and fundus appearance remained unchanged, with worsening ocular discomfort and increased subretinal fluid.

A 48-year-old man with hypertension and a 20-pack-year smoking history presented with a 2-week history of intermittent fevers up to 39°C, severe back pain, a 20-kg weight loss over 6 months, and cough productive of purulent, blood-tinged sputum.  

On chest radiography there was a well-defined cavitary mass in the right lower lung field, multiple scattered pulmonary nodules, and osteolytic lesions in the right clavicle. Contrast CT of the chest confirmed a thick-walled cavitary mass with irregular inner borders in the right lower lobe, additional pulmonary nodules, and multiple osteolytic bone lesions.  

On examination, he was disoriented and febrile (39.4°C), with blood pressure 136/97 mmHg, heart rate 133 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on 3 L/min nasal cannula. Bilateral rales were present.  

Laboratory studies showed WBC count 28,100/mm3 (92% neutrophils), hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL, platelets 274,000/mm3, CRP 17.6 mg/dL, creatinine 1.62 mg/dL, corrected calcium 13.5 mg/dL, and LDH 346 IU/L. Sputum studies were negative for Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgM and Aspergillus galactomannan.  

Empiric ceftaroline and voriconazole were started, and hydration with zoledronic acid was administered for hypercalcemia.

A 38-year-old woman presented with a two-year history of progressive swelling and dull pain in her left thigh and hip. She had no preceding trauma and no significant personal or family history. On examination, there was a 20×10-cm soft-tissue mass over the anterolateral left thigh extending to the hip, with mild tenderness and pain-limited hip motion; the remainder of the systemic examination was unremarkable. Routine hematologic and biochemical tests, including alkaline phosphatase, were within normal limits. CT and MRI of the left femur demonstrated ill-defined, heterogeneous marrow signal in the upper metaphysis extending into the epiphysis and diaphysis, with cortical disruption and extension into adjacent soft tissues; the lesion was hyperintense on T2/STIR sequences and hypointense on T1 images. A bone scan confirmed a solitary lesion. Radiologic features were suggestive of a malignant neoplasm. A core biopsy of the soft-tissue component revealed a spindle cell tumor with focal nuclear pleomorphism, intercellular collagenous stroma, and occasional mitotic figures. With an initial diagnosis of malignant mesenchymal tumor, the patient underwent proximal femoral resection and prosthetic reconstruction.

A 13-year-old boy presented with a 6-month history of swelling in the right lower jaw without any history of trauma. On extraoral examination, there was a 4 × 3 cm tender, hard, noncompressible, nonreducible swelling over the right lateral body of the mandible extending to the ramus. Intraorally, the right mandibular second molar was absent, with slight mucosal discontinuity distal to the first molar; palpation revealed vestibular tenderness and a sharp point distal to the first molar. A panoramic radiograph showed a radioopaque mass surrounded by a thin radiolucent line, with its superior aspect protruding toward the mandibular border, and an unerupted second molar with one-quarter root formation. CT imaging demonstrated perforations of both the lingual and buccal cortical plates and delineated the anteroposterior extent of the lesion. Based on these findings, a provisional diagnosis of complex odontoma was made, and ameloblastic fibroodontoma and ameloblastic odontoma were included in the differential diagnosis.

A 3-year-old girl presented with a painless, progressively enlarging left-sided neck mass noted since birth. On examination, the mass was nontender, mobile, and multinodular, measuring 8 cm by 6 cm; no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy was present. Thyroid function tests were normal. Neck ultrasonography showed a solid lesion predominantly in the upper pole of the left thyroid lobe. Fine-needle aspiration cytology was suspicious for malignancy. A plain radiograph of the neck demonstrated deviation of the trachea to the right.

A 76-year-old Japanese man with a history of insulin-treated diabetes mellitus and prior ischemic stroke on long-term antiplatelet therapy presented with cognitive changes and new-onset seizures. One year earlier, he had been diagnosed with systemic B-cell non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (flow cytometry: CD19+, CD20+, kappa+, CD5–, CD10–) involving spleen and bone marrow and had achieved complete remission after eight courses of reduced-dose R-CHOP without CNS prophylaxis.

Three days before admission, he became unable to recognize playing cards and exhibited confusing behavior. On the day of admission, he developed prolonged generalized tonic-clonic seizures and was transferred to the emergency department.

On exam, he was febrile (40.5 °C), tachycardic (157 bpm), hypertensive (187/79 mm Hg), and in a postictal state (GCS E1V1M4) with right conjugate gaze deviation and no neck stiffness. There was no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. 

Laboratory studies showed WBC 15.1 × 10^9/L, Hb 9.9 g/dL, platelets 188 × 10^9/L, LDH 313 U/L, CRP 0.75 mg/dL, normal coagulation, renal, and liver panels, and normal glucose and electrolytes. 

Noncontrast brain CT revealed a high-density mass with surrounding edema and intratumoral hemorrhage in the left temporal lobe. MRI showed the lesion to be iso- to hypointense on T1-weighted images, hypointense on T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted images, and to enhance heterogeneously after gadolinium. Diazepam and levetiracetam were started, and a stereotactic brain biopsy was scheduled for definitive diagnosis.

A 3-month-old boy presented with respiratory distress and bilateral chest wall masses noted since birth, the right measuring approximately 6 cm. Breath sounds were markedly decreased on the right. Initially on face-mask oxygen, he deteriorated over 48 hours and required intubation and mechanical ventilation. 

Chest X-ray showed bilateral expansile lytic lesions with bony and soft-tissue components deforming the thoracic cage and shifting the trachea to the left. Contrast CT of the chest revealed multiple bilateral anterior chest wall masses, the largest (5.7 cm × 4.1 cm) on the right, involving upper ribs, extending into intercostal spaces, with multiloculated soft-tissue lesions, areas of calcification, mediastinal shift, and rib destruction. 

An incisional biopsy yielded multiple tan-brown hemorrhagic fragments (3 cm × 2 cm × 1 cm). Microscopic examination showed islands of multilobulated hypercellular hyaline cartilage within a bland spindle–cell stroma, occasional mitotic figures, mild atypia, focal endochondral ossification with trabeculae mimicking osteoid, and areas of aneurysmal bone cyst–type hemorrhagic cystic spaces. On frozen section, the possibility of osteosarcoma was raised; permanent sections demonstrated benign hypercellular cartilage and no malignant osteoid.

A 46-year-old Chinese woman and lifetime non-smoker, with a history of small cell lung cancer diagnosed in August 2018 by transbronchial lung biopsy showing synaptophysin positivity, CD56 positivity, focal AE1/AE3 positivity, TTF-1 positivity, chromogranin A negativity, and a Ki-67 index of 60%, received radiochemotherapy. Four months later, she presented with progressive abdominal distension. Serum CA125 was elevated at 400.3 U/mL (normal 0–35); CA19-9 and neuron-specific enolase were within normal limits. Pelvic ultrasound demonstrated bilateral heterogeneous ovarian masses measuring 118×85 mm on the left and 97×79 mm on the right with internal Doppler flow. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed two round, uneven-density masses adjacent to the uterus (83×88×111 mm and 95×94×128 mm) with slight arterial phase enhancement of solid components, and a soft-tissue density lesion anterior to the sacral promontory. Radionuclide bone scintigraphy showed focal uptake in the first sacral segment.

A 29-year-old healthy man noted persistent swelling of his left breast for four years. Initially, ultrasonography had shown gynecomastia (BIRADS II) attributed to anabolic-steroid use, which he discontinued. He now reports a new, mildly tender, firm 1-cm subareolar mass under the left nipple. Repeat ultrasonography demonstrates a 1.5-cm long, solid structure with lobular architecture. Mammography reveals a lobulated retroareolar mass approximately 1.5 cm in diameter without microcalcifications (BIRADS III).

A 61‐year‐old man presented with a 4‐year history of right cheek swelling. He was otherwise healthy. On extraoral examination, there was a diffuse, firm, non‐tender, slightly compressible nodular swelling approximately 2.5 × 2.5 cm over the right buccal region, extending from below the zygoma to the lower border of the lip. Intraorally, a firm, non‐tender nodular mass of similar size was noted in the right buccal mucosa; the overlying mucosa appeared normal.

Ultrasonography showed a well‐defined, homogeneously hyperechoic focal lesion measuring 4.3 × 3.7 × 3.4 cm in the right cheek, with normal parotid sonomorphology and no duct obstruction. Based on these findings, a cystic lesion—most likely a mucocele—was suspected.

Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well‐defined lobular T2‐ and T1‐hyperintense lesion measuring 5.6 × 2.2 × 3.0 cm, extending deep to the right masseter muscle, suggestive of a benign cystic lesion with high‐protein content. A lymphangioma or lymphatic cyst was then considered.

Fine‐needle aspiration yielded brownish fluid containing numerous squamous cells, neutrophils, and lymphocytes.

A 32-year-old woman, 7 months postpartum, presented with left-sided lower back pain that began in the second trimester and persisted after delivery. She described the pain as worse when supine, with occasional radiation to the left gluteal area. She denied systemic symptoms and had no neurological deficits. Physical examination showed no spinal tenderness, normal symmetric strength and sensation, intact reflexes, and a normal gait.

A plain radiograph of the hip revealed bony irregularity along the left border of the T12 vertebral body and to a lesser extent at T11, with mild thoracolumbar curvature convex to the left. CT of the lumbar spine demonstrated a 10 cm irregular, destructive expansile soft-tissue mass centered on the T11–T12 vertebral bodies and left pedicle, with destruction of left posterior elements. The mass contained cystic and soft-tissue densities, thin irregular bony septations, and prominent heterogeneous enhancement. It invaded the central canal, causing severe stenosis at T12 and involvement of the T11–T12 and T12–L1 neural foramina.

MRI showed a well-circumscribed lesion measuring 8.1 × 7.4 × 9.8 cm with multiple fluid–fluid levels and scalloping of adjacent bone, indicating a chronic locally aggressive process. The mass eroded into the central canal, displacing the cord and completely effacing cerebrospinal fluid, yet without cord edema. Extension into the proximal left psoas muscle produced soft-tissue edema and inflammatory changes.

A 27-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of headache, vomiting, and blurring of vision, and a 1-month history of imbalance and swaying to the right. On examination, he had a dilated pupil and ptosis on the right side, a visual acuity of 6/24 in that eye, and a relative afferent pupillary defect. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head showed a well-defined suprasellar mass measuring approximately 3.0×2.5×3.5 cm that was T1 isointense, T2 heterointense, and homogeneously contrast-enhancing with a lobulated appearance. The lesion compressed the midbrain, displaced the third ventricle upward with proximal ventriculomegaly and periventricular lucencies, was predominantly in the interpeduncular cistern extending across the midline, effacing the aqueduct and compressing the cerebral peduncle, and extended anteriorly along the cavernous sinus toward the superior orbital fissure with compression of the adjacent optic nerve.  
Differential diagnosis at that time included meningioma, schwannoma of cranial nerve, vascular pathology (thrombosed giant aneurysm), and lymphoma.

A 27-year-old woman presented with an 8-year history of gradual dystrophy of the right index-finger nail. She had been treated empirically with oral and topical antifungal agents for 4 years without improvement. She denied trauma to the nail and had no personal or family history of skin cancer or other dermatologic disorders.

On examination, the nail plate of the right index finger was markedly thickened, dark yellow, and exhibited scattered splinter hemorrhages and longitudinal overcurvature. A fungal culture of nail clippings was negative. Radiographs of the finger showed no bony abnormalities. High-resolution ultrasonography of the nail unit demonstrated a hypoechoic lesion in the nail matrix and a hyperechoic area with multiple thin projections extending into the overlying nail plate; Doppler imaging showed low blood flow.

A 31‐year‐old non‐smoking man presented with progressive asthenia and exertional dyspnoea of 4 months’ duration. His medical history and physical examination were unremarkable. Prior testing included normal spirometry; a high‐resolution CT scan showing a non‐specific inflammatory parenchymal pattern and an enlarged pulmonary‐artery trunk; and transthoracic echocardiography demonstrating a mass in the pulmonary arterial trunk with an increased trans‐pulmonary peak flow velocity.

On admission, vital signs were stable and oxygen saturation was normal. Laboratory studies showed D‐dimer 528 μg/L, fibrinogen 609 mg/dL, hs‐CRP 23 mg/L, low ferritin, and normal white‐cell count, haemoglobin, renal, hepatic, and cardiac enzymes. A thrombophilia screen was negative. Repeat echocardiography confirmed an irregular‐bordered mass almost occluding the pulmonary trunk, with peak velocity 3.8 m/s and gradient 60 mmHg; all other right‐heart findings were normal.

Compression ultrasonography excluded deep‐vein thrombosis. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the chest revealed a dilated pulmonary trunk containing an irregular intraluminal filling defect with minimal contrast enhancement and scattered ground‐glass opacities in the lung fields; broad‐spectrum antibiotics were started. Colonoscopy and esophagogastroduodenoscopy were negative for malignancy. After 10 days of low‐molecular‐weight heparin, follow‐up echocardiography showed right‐ventricular dilation and increased systolic pressure, and the patient remained symptomatic.

An 8-year-old female spayed Russian Blue cat was presented for acute-onset progressive dyspnea. The cat was strictly indoor with no history of trauma. On presentation, the respiratory rate was 68 breaths per minute with marked increased effort. Point-of-care ultrasound revealed bilateral pleural effusion. Under sedation (butorphanol and midazolam) and oxygen supplementation, bilateral thoracocentesis evacuated 310 ml of milky white fluid, after which respiratory effort improved markedly. A complete physical examination was otherwise unremarkable.

Thoracic radiographs confirmed large-volume pleural effusion with secondary atelectasis. Laboratory evaluation showed eosinopenia (0.1 × 10^9/l; RI 0.17–1.57), hyperglycemia (12.56 mmol/l; RI 3.95–8.84), low alanine aminotransferase (10 U/l; RI 12–130) and alkaline phosphatase (13 U/l; RI 14–111), and a mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis (pH 7.18; RI 7.35–7.46; pCO2 58.1 mmHg; RI 32–43; base excess –6.7 mmol/l; RI –2 to 2). Tests for feline leukemia virus antigen and feline immunodeficiency virus antibody were negative. Pleural fluid analysis showed a total nucleated cell count of 3920/µl with 54% neutrophils and 39% lymphocytes; most macrophages contained fine cytoplasmic vesicles. Based on cytology and gross appearance, the effusion was classified as chylous.

The next morning, a transthoracic echocardiogram performed by a cardiologist showed a structurally normal heart, excluding a cardiogenic cause of chylothorax. A multiphase contrast-enhanced CT scan of the thorax and abdomen demonstrated large-volume bilateral pleural effusion, a small right-sided pneumothorax, thickened pleura with pulmonary hypoinflation, widening of the caudodorsal mediastinum and cranial retroperitoneal space by fluid, and a large (12.6 × 5.3 × 3.2 cm), lobulated, encapsulated, fluid-attenuating, cystic mass in the mid-abdomen. Indirect contrast lymphography (450 mg iohexol injected into the metatarsal pads) revealed multifocal contrast pooling in the caudal dorsal mediastinum and cranial retroperitoneal area, as well as pooling within the peritoneal mass, which was confluent with a distended cisterna chyli.

A 16-year-old male with high-risk TCF3-HLF–positive B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, in morphologic remission after induction and consolidation chemotherapy, was admitted for allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation. Conditioning included total-body irradiation, etoposide, and anti-thymocyte globulin. At the start of conditioning, his white-cell and neutrophil counts were normal; prophylaxis included levofloxacin, acyclovir, and posaconazole. Shortly before irradiation, he became febrile and received piperacillin–tazobactam. During irradiation, he developed a marked surge in C-reactive protein and procalcitonin, accompanied by pain and swelling of the right forearm. Radiographs of the right ulna showed cortical thinning, destruction, and a periosteal reaction. He underwent surgical irrigation and debridement of the right ulna, which appeared purulent and necrotic; gentamicin beads were placed. Intraoperative cultures grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus and Acinetobacter pittii, and histopathological analysis showed no evidence of malignancy. He completed conditioning, received his graft, and had recurring fevers during the pre-engraftment period despite negative blood cultures. New pain developed in the left forearm, and ultrasound revealed a similar lesion in the left ulna; intravenous antibiotics were continued without immediate surgery.

A 32-year-old man presented with a six-year history of a painless swelling in the left supraclavicular region that had gradually enlarged from the size of an almond to that of a lime. He reported no history of trauma, fever, or systemic illness, and no weakness, numbness, or loss of function in the upper limb. On examination, there was a 4.0-cm diameter, round, firm, non-tender mass in the left supraclavicular area that was mobile in the medio-lateral direction. An ultrasound showed a superficial heterogeneous round cystic mass measuring 47 × 33 mm lateral to the sternocleidomastoid muscle, with well-defined smooth margins and multiple intralesional septa; its lower border lay adjacent to the subclavian artery and its medial border abutted the carotid artery and external jugular vein. The ultrasound was interpreted as a branchial cleft cyst with an atypical location. Fine needle aspiration was performed, and the cystogram findings corroborated this diagnosis. The patient was scheduled for surgical excision of the suspected branchial cleft cyst.

A 50-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of a progressively enlarging growth on her vulva. It began as a small pigmented patch on the right side and gradually grew into a large, polypoidal mass involving both labia majora, labia minora, the fourchette, and the mons pubis. The lesion was initially asymptomatic but had recently developed a foul odor. There was no pain or discharge. She and her spouse reported no history of sexual promiscuity. On examination, the mass measured approximately 15 × 10 cm, was pigmented, and had areas of reddish and whitish verrucous surface change. The vaginal mucosa appeared normal. We considered a differential diagnosis of condyloma acuminata and giant seborrheic keratosis.

A 50-year-old man was referred after an incidental finding on chest radiography performed before repair of a tibial fracture. He was asymptomatic, a nonsmoker, and had an unremarkable medical history. Physical examination was normal. Routine blood counts and biochemical tests were within normal limits.

Chest radiograph showed a 5 cm left-sided pleural or mediastinal mass. Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed a well-circumscribed, lobulated pleural mass in a posterior paraspinal location adjacent to the descending thoracic aorta, with homogeneous enhancement and no invasion of adjacent tissues or widening of neural foramina. On MRI, the lesion was slightly hyperintense to muscle on T1-weighted sequences, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted sequences, and demonstrated avid homogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed no abnormalities.

A 54-year-old man presented with a painless red lesion on the right forearm of 4 years’ duration, which had been slowly increasing in size over the past 2 years. He reported occasional bleeding from the lesion after trivial trauma. His other medical history was unremarkable. On cutaneous examination, there was a single, pedunculated, nontender, firm pink nodule measuring 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm on the extensor aspect of the right forearm. The lesion had a nodular surface with visible telangiectasias. No regional lymphadenopathy was noted. On clinical examination, the differential diagnosis of pyogenic granuloma, giant acrocordon, and dermatofibroma was considered. The nodule was surgically excised and sent for histopathological examination.

A 4-year-old Japanese girl with no significant birth, family, or medical history presented when her parents noticed she had stopped using her left hand. On examination, she had left-dominant upper flaccid paralysis and left lower spastic paralysis. MRI of the spine revealed a mass lesion in the gray matter from C3 to T4 with enlargement of the spinal canal. On T1-weighted images the mass was hypointense and on T2-weighted images it was hyperintense; it was left-sided in dominance but extended through the central canal to the right side. A cystic lesion showing high intensity on fat-suppressed T2WI was present at one end of the mass. There was no hemosiderin cap on T2* images, no significant diffusion restriction on DWI or ADC maps, and only slight enhancement on gadolinium-enhanced T1WI. CT showed a homogeneous hypodense lesion without calcification. No lesions were seen elsewhere in the CNS. Preoperative imaging suggested a low-grade glioma, such as pilocytic astrocytoma.

A 46-year-old man presented with 15 days of intermittent left flank pain accompanied by fever and chills and 1 week of generalized weakness. He had undergone open pyelolithotomy 8 years earlier. On examination, he was tachycardic (100/min), pale, and had left flank tenderness with guarding; no palpable mass was noted. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 24 500/mm3 and a serum creatinine level of 1.1 mg/dL; blood and urine cultures were obtained. Third-generation cephalosporin therapy was initiated.  
Renal ultrasonography revealed gross left hydronephrosis with internal echoes. CT urography confirmed left hydronephrosis without an obvious obstructing calculus. A left percutaneous nephrostomy (PCN) was placed, yielding 200 mL of frank pus, and the patient’s symptoms initially improved. Two days later, PCN output had decreased markedly, but the leukocyte count had risen to 28 500/mm3. Repeat ultrasonography showed persistent hydronephrosis with septations and internal echoes around the in‐situ PCN. A second PCN was placed in the midpole, draining 50 mL of pus, after which output again ceased. Despite antibiotics and two drains, the patient continued to have fever spikes and marked leukocytosis.  
What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 67-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a 5-month history of increased hair growth on her upper lip and armpits (Ferriman–Gallwey score 8) and clitoromegaly. She denied acne, voice changes, or exogenous hormone use. Menarche was at 18 years, menopause at 56 years, with two healthy children and no miscarriages. Physical examination showed BMI 22.6 kg/m2, hirsutism, clitoromegaly, and no signs of Cushing syndrome.  
Laboratory studies revealed total testosterone 714.8 ng/dL (reference 14–56), while DHEAS (145.8 ng/mL), androstenedione (2.4 ng/mL), and 17-hydroxyprogesterone (1.7 nmol/L) were within normal limits. FSH, LH, prolactin, AMH, hCG, TSH, renin, aldosterone, ACTH, serum cortisol, 24-h urinary free cortisol, and a 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test were all normal. Ovarian tumor markers (CA 125, CEA, CA 19-9) were normal. A mid-dose dexamethasone test (0.75 mg four times daily for 5 days) showed no suppression of testosterone.  
Pelvic ultrasound showed no ovarian mass, while adrenal ultrasound identified a hypoechoic nodule in the left adrenal gland. Pelvic MRI confirmed normal ovaries and a submucous uterine myoma. Adrenal CT demonstrated a 1.5 cm mass in the left adrenal gland. PET-CT confirmed a round nodule in the external branch of the left adrenal gland with slight FDG uptake (SUV max 2.56), suggesting a benign adenoma; no ovarian or other ectopic tumors were detected.

A man in his mid-30s was referred for further management of a forehead mass initially thought to be a lipoma. The lesion had appeared 1 year earlier after minor forehead trauma and had slowly enlarged over the past 4 months without pain or other symptoms. His history was notable for extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma of the left foot treated 9 years earlier with below‐knee amputation and adjuvant ifosfamide–doxorubicin chemotherapy.

On examination, there was a 10 cm × 8 cm soft, compressible mass on the right forehead extending from the hairline to the mid‐forehead. In the operating suite, a full‐thickness skin and frontalis incision exposed a gray, well‐circumscribed mass. A palpable bony step‐off at the base prompted aborting resection and closing the incision.

Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a mass arising from the right frontal diploic space with intracranial extension and possible involvement of the superior sagittal sinus. Noncontrast head CT revealed a lytic lesion of the right frontal bone with hypodense soft‐tissue extension into the scalp.

An 18-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of constant lower abdominal fullness, which had intensified over the past 3–4 months. She denied nausea, vomiting, or pain. Her medical history and physical examination were unremarkable. She had recently traveled to Australia and Sardinia, regions endemic for cystic echinococcosis. Laboratory studies revealed a mild elevation in CA 19-9. Transvaginal ultrasonography demonstrated a large cystic mass spanning the abdominal and pelvic regions. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a markedly enlarged, wandering spleen (24.5 × 16.0 × 12.0 cm) located in the left lower abdomen and extending into the anterior mid-pelvis without evidence of venous or arterial obstruction. Within the inferior pole of the spleen was a 16.0 × 15.7 × 1.4 cm lesion composed of a central cystic space and multiple peripheral cystic structures, with minimal calcification along septations. A 1.7 × 1.5 × 1.6 cm solid-appearing area in the mid-anterior spleen was thought to represent part of the vascular pedicle. To prevent torsion of the splenic pedicle, an open splenectomy was planned.

A 3-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of progressive abdominal distension over the past year. The distension was associated with loss of appetite and intermittent nausea but no vomiting. There were no changes in bowel habits, jaundice, melena, fevers, or night sweats. The parents also noted unintentional weight loss.  
On examination, her pulse was 138 beats per minute, oxygen saturation 99% on room air, and temperature 36.7°C. The abdomen was asymmetrically distended with a 17 cm × 15 cm soft, mobile mass in the right lower quadrant that was tender on deep palpation. There was no palpable hepatosplenomegaly, and bowel sounds were normal.  
Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 12.3 g/dL, a leukocyte count of 5.03 × 10^9/L, a platelet count of 341 × 10^9/L, serum creatinine 22 μmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 2.56 mmol/L, and normal liver enzymes.  
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a large intra-abdominal hyperechoic mass of indeterminate origin. A contrast-enhanced CT scan demonstrated an 8.8 cm × 16.5 cm circumscribed low-fat–density mass occupying the peritoneal cavity, with features suggestive of a peritoneal teratoma versus peritoneal lipoma. Elective surgical resection was planned.

A 62-year-old man was referred for management of an abnormal chest CT obtained during evaluation of atypical chest pain.  
His medical history included chronic hepatitis C–related cirrhosis and poorly differentiated hepatocellular carcinoma treated with chemoembolization, radiofrequency ablation, and ultimately orthotopic liver transplantation. The explanted liver demonstrated extensive necrosis, two 4.5 cm lesions, and intravascular tumor thrombus involving the inferior vena cava.  
Posttransplant, he was maintained on tacrolimus and prednisone, later switched to sirolimus after prostatectomy for prostate cancer.  
On examination, breath and heart sounds were normal, and the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Cardiac enzymes and electrocardiography excluded myocardial injury.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed an enlarged right paratracheal lymph node and an enlarged right hilar lymph node.  
To obtain tissue for diagnosis, endobronchial ultrasound–guided transbronchial needle aspiration of the right paratracheal lymph node (station 4R) was performed.

A 47-year-old man presented with a more than three-year history of a slowly enlarging, painless swelling on the left floor of the mouth. He noted only slight interference with speech, mastication, and tongue movement. There was no history of trauma or of pain on eating. His medical and family histories were unremarkable.

Oral examination revealed a well-circumscribed, soft mass beside the left side of the tongue. The overlying mucosa was intact and normal in appearance. On bimanual palpation, the mass extended into the submental region, caused slight elevation of the tongue, but did not restrict its movement. Salivary flow from the submandibular (Wharton) duct was normal, and there was no sensory deficit. Occasional globus pharyngeus was reported, but there were no symptoms of nausea, dysphagia, snoring, or noisy breathing. Examination of the neck revealed no lymphadenopathy.

Imaging with CT and MRI demonstrated an irregular mass in the region of the genioglossus muscle extending from the base of the tongue to the skin overlying the mylohyoid muscle with a density similar to adjacent subcutaneous fat. On a fat‐suppression MRI sequence at the level of the first molar, the lesion was hypointense, suggesting an infiltrating intramuscular lipoma.

A tentative clinical diagnosis of lipoma was made. The differential diagnosis included ranula, salivary gland neoplasm, dermoid cyst, and epidermoid cyst.

An 11-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of a bleeding gingival swelling that had developed gradually over 3 months. She was in orthodontic treatment, took no medications, and had no relevant medical history. There was no history of trauma, smoking, or dental infection, and her oral hygiene was excellent.

On examination, the lesion on the gingival papilla between teeth 44 and 45 measured 15 × 10 × 13 mm. It was sessile, violaceous, lobulated, and depressible, with telangiectasias and fibrinous ulcerations, and it bled easily on palpation. Over the preceding five years she had undergone six complete surgical excisions of similar lesions, with each recurrence appearing within months of excision.

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, were normal. Periapical radiography and cone-beam CT of the area showed no anomalies of the adjacent teeth or alveolar bone. Under local anesthesia, the lesion was excised with healthy margins, and the specimen was sent for histopathological analysis.

A 64-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis presented with a 10-day history of intermittent fever (maximum, 102°F), chills, rigors, decreased appetite, generalized weakness, and new bluish skin patches. She had no sick contacts. She was afebrile at presentation (100.5°F), tachycardic (heart rate, 104 beats/min), and hypotensive (blood pressure, 90/60 mmHg); examination was notable for pallor. Initial laboratory tests showed leukocytosis (51,400 cells/mm3), anemia (hemoglobin 8.2 g/dl), and thrombocytopenia (≈10,800 cells/mm3). Urinalysis revealed numerous pus cells. Dengue NS1 antigen was positive; dengue IgM and IgG were negative. IgM ELISA for leptospirosis and brucellosis were both negative. A peripheral blood smear demonstrated anisopoikilocytosis with microcytic hypochromic red cells, pencil cells, and polychromasia; leukocytosis with 70% blast cells (2–3 times the size of lymphocytes, scant to moderate agranular cytoplasm, oval to cleaved nuclei, fine chromatin); and large to giant platelets in reduced number.

A 56-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of dry cough and a 10-kg weight loss. He had no known systemic disease but had a 40 pack-year smoking history. On examination, vital signs were normal and the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed normal tumor markers. In an autoimmune panel, the only abnormality was an elevated rheumatoid factor (IgM 14.5 IU/mL). HIV and HHV-8 serologies were pending at that time.

A chest radiograph showed increased interstitial markings on the right side and patchy consolidations in the right lung. Chest CT revealed multiple enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes, unilateral small centrilobular nodules, and smooth peribronchovascular interstitial thickening most pronounced in the right lung. Bronchoscopy showed no endobronchial lesions.

Based on these findings, the differential diagnosis included lung cancer with nodal metastasis and sarcoidosis, and adequate tissue sampling was planned to establish a diagnosis.

A 61-year-old woman presented with epigastric pain. She had mild epigastric tenderness on examination and a 32–pack-year smoking history but no history of tuberous sclerosis, malignancy, alcohol use, or diabetes. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, hematocrit 23.2 %, white cells 4600/mm3, platelets 232 000/mm3; normal CEA, CA 19-9, AFP, elastase 1, SPAN-1, and DUPAN-2; gastrin 370 pg/mL (normal < 200), somatostatin 23 pg/mL (normal 1–12), and normal glucagon, VIP, serotonin, and insulin levels. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 56 mm hypo- to iso-echoic, gourd-shaped mass in the pancreatic head and body with slight upstream duct dilation. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a well-circumscribed, low-density 7 cm mass in the pancreatic body with mild upstream duct dilation but no invasion or lymphadenopathy. MRI demonstrated a heterogeneously enhancing round mass on T1- and T2-weighted images. Endoscopic retrograde pancreatography showed downward deviation of the main pancreatic duct from extrinsic compression without evidence of invasion. Neuroendocrine neoplasm, acinar cell carcinoma, ductal adenocarcinoma variants such as clear cell carcinoma, and solid-pseudopapillary neoplasm were suggested before operation.

A 41-year-old man presented with metamorphopsia and decreased vision in his right eye. Four years earlier, he had noted these symptoms and, at that time, best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/20. Fundus examination showed a whitish lesion in the macula, and optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealed serous retinal detachment (SRD) accompanied by a fibrin-like deposit. He was diagnosed with central serous chorioretinopathy (CSC). Five months later, BCVA declined to 16/20, and OCT demonstrated recurrent SRD and macular edema. Laboratory studies did not suggest infectious or noninfectious inflammation. Solitary idiopathic choroiditis (SIC) was suspected, and oral prednisolone was given for over 2 months without change. 

On referral, slit-lamp examination and intraocular pressure were normal. Funduscopy showed a subretinal yellowish-white lesion, approximately 1.0-mm disc diameter, located between the fovea and optic disc. OCT disclosed SRD and intraretinal fluid extending to the foveal center, a dome-like elevation of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) corresponding to the lesion, and shallow RPE detachment. Beneath the RPE, a horizontal lamellar-like structure was seen within the choroid. Bruch’s membrane and the sclera–choroidal junction were intact around the lesion, and the choriocapillaris and part of the choroidal vessels were not visible within it. 

Fluorescein angiography showed late-phase staining of the plaque, and indocyanine green angiography revealed early hypofluorescence and late hyperfluorescence. B-scan ultrasonography through the eyelid suggested a thin hypoechoic shadow but was not diagnostic.

A 57‐year‐old man presented with a 10‐year history of episodic dizziness and left aural fullness. He denied tinnitus or otorrhea. Otoscopic examination revealed an intact left tympanic membrane. Audiometry disclosed a conductive hearing loss on the left. A HINTS (head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew) examination was negative. Videonystagmography, auditory brainstem responses, and brain MRI showed no abnormalities. A high‐resolution CT scan of the temporal bone demonstrated a soft‐tissue opacity filling the left hypotympanum and protympanum without evidence of bone erosion.

A 25-year-old man was referred for surgical removal of a painless lesion in the left posterior mandible, discovered incidentally on a routine radiographic examination. His medical history was unremarkable. On intraoral examination there was no expansion of the buccal or lingual cortical bone and no suspicious features. Teeth 36, 37, and 38 were vital. Panoramic radiography revealed a well-defined, unilocular radiolucent lesion attached to the roots of the vital, erupted left third mandibular molar. Under local anesthesia, an excisional biopsy was performed. The lesion appeared solid; the surgical specimen measured 6.0 × 2.8 × 2.0 mm and was loose without nodules. On microscopic examination (H&E staining), the normal mandibular structure was completely replaced by mature adipose tissue, and many capillaries were easily detected. No malignancy was observed.

A 15-year-old male presented with a 4-month history of intense oral pain, burning, difficulty chewing, gingival swelling, and bleeding. Medical and family histories were noncontributory except for vague abdominal pain; abdominal ultrasonography was normal. On examination, oral hygiene was poor with halitosis. The gingiva was hyperplastic, erythematous, sessile, diffuse, and fragile, with punched-out interdental papillae in the lower anterior region. Multiple necrotic ulcerations with pseudomembranous slough were present on buccal and palatal mucosa, and the tongue was coated. Spontaneous and profuse gingival bleeding occurred. Periodontal probing revealed generalized deep pockets (4–12 mm) and severe tooth mobility (grade I–III). Panoramic radiograph showed generalized alveolar bone loss. Laboratory studies were normal except for an elevated alkaline phosphatase; liver, coagulation, thyroid profiles, and urinalysis were normal. A skull PA view and skeletal survey showed no other lytic lesions. A provisional diagnosis of acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis or pubertal periodontitis was made. The patient underwent full-mouth prophylaxis, hydrogen peroxide mouthwash, and a 2-week course of doxycycline. Initial improvement occurred, but after 1 week there was further deterioration and persistent inflammation despite reinforced oral hygiene measures.

A 19-year-old woman presented with dysuria and a progressively enlarging right flank mass that became palpable on examination. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen showed a large, lobulated, heterogeneously enhancing mass arising from the right kidney, with internal calcifications, hypodense necrotic areas, and extension into the right renal vein and inferior vena cava. Chest CT for metastatic workup revealed several subcentimeter, noncalcified pulmonary and pleural-based nodules, with no pleural effusion or mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

The patient underwent right radical nephrectomy. Gross examination of the bivalved specimen revealed a 20.3 × 14.4 × 11.7 cm ill-defined, irregularly shaped, firm to friable, lobulated, yellow–tan mass with extensive hemorrhage and necrosis, almost completely replacing the renal parenchyma, and a large tumor thrombus in the renal vein.

Microscopic sections showed a tumor with predominantly lobulated, nested, and papillary-fused architecture, central necrosis bordered by thin hyalinized and vascularized septa, and neoplastic cells with moderate to marked pleomorphism, vesicular nuclei (occasional multinucleated forms), prominent nucleoli, abundant pale eosinophilic to clear cytoplasm, and distinct cell borders. Several psammoma bodies and scattered foci of melanin pigment were identified. There was microscopic involvement of the capsule and renal sinus; all other hilar structures were free of tumor.

A 5-year-old girl was evaluated for a right-sided facial swelling that had been progressively enlarging over the past 2 years. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender mass measuring approximately 7 × 6 cm arising from the right mandible with smooth, regular margins; mouth opening was normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the face showed a 6.5 × 6 × 4.5 cm expansile lytic lesion involving the right ramus and body of the mandible with thinning of the cortex and no overt soft-tissue mass.

A 63-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with 2 months of lower abdominal pain. Her past medical and family histories were unremarkable. On physical examination, her abdomen was soft and non-tender. Ultrasonography revealed a solid left ovarian mass measuring 38 × 40 × 46 mm with significant enhancement; the right ovary measured 14 × 16 mm. Non-contrast and contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a solid, enhancing left ovarian mass and noted small lymph nodes in the mesentery and bilateral external and internal iliac regions. Serum CA-125 was elevated at 327 IU/mL and CEA at 0.85 ng/mL. A staging laparotomy was performed, and frozen-section analysis of the left ovarian mass showed atypical cells with moderate pleomorphism and anisonucleosis without mitoses or necrosis, suggesting a stromal tumor.

A 59-year-old woman presented with a small, slowly enlarging, painless tumor on the tip of her nose. She reported no other symptoms. On examination, there was an 8 mm hemispherical, immobile, sharply demarcated nodule at the upper border of the right nostril, with slight subcutaneous extension toward the tip and columella. The lesion had a smooth surface without ulceration or signs of irritation. Further head and neck evaluation, including laryngopharyngoscopy and cervical sonography, was unremarkable. Because the lack of irritation was inconsistent with acute infection, and the sharp demarcation, smooth surface, and absence of ulceration made a primary malignancy unlikely, an excision biopsy was performed under local anesthesia. The lesion and surrounding capsule were completely resected without macroscopic infiltration of adjacent structures, and postoperative healing was uncomplicated. Histopathologic examination revealed fibrous connective tissue partly covered by intact, nondysplastic squamous epithelium. The corial connective tissue was infiltrated by nonkeratinizing squamous cells with pleomorphism of size and nuclei. These findings corresponded to a moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.

A 68-year-old woman underwent routine screening mammography, which revealed a nonpalpable mass in the left breast. Her medical history was notable only for controlled hypertension and mild osteoarthritic changes. She had three pregnancies, two deliveries, and breastfed for a total of 30 months. She denied any breast pain, nipple discharge, skin changes, or prior breast surgery or biopsy. A mammogram two years earlier was normal.

On physical examination, there was no palpable mass, skin erythema or dimpling, nipple retraction, or axillary lymphadenopathy.

Diagnostic imaging:  
• Mammography demonstrated an isodense, circumscribed, oval mass, 1.8 × 1.0 cm, at the junction of the upper quadrants of the left breast.  
• Ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic, homogeneous, oval lesion measuring 1.4 × 0.7 cm, parallel to the skin, with two lobulations, circumscribed margins, and no posterior acoustic shadowing or hyperechoic halo.  

The lesion was classified as BI-RADS category 4.

A 33-year-old soldier presented with intermittent headaches over the past year that recently worsened after an acute, thunderclap-type episode. He had no focal neurologic deficits on examination. MRI of the brain showed a sellar and suprasellar cystic lesion compressing the optic chiasm; the cyst wall enhanced with gadolinium, and a small intralesional parenchymal component was isointense to slightly hyperintense. Endocrine studies revealed normal anterior pituitary hormones except for low thyroid-stimulating hormone and low testosterone; there was no diabetes insipidus. An endoscopic transsphenoidal approach was undertaken. Upon opening the sellar floor, a yellow capsule released clear, straw-colored fluid. A pulsating cyst capsule was tightly adherent to the surrounding pituitary tissue and was only partially removed.

A 25-year-old man presented with a 20-year history of pain and swelling in his right knee. He had never seen an orthopedician and managed symptoms with simple analgesics. He denied trauma but reported recurrent knee effusions.  
On examination, there was a soft, non-tender, compressible 3 cm × 3 cm mass on the lateral aspect of the knee that became more prominent in full flexion and refilled when pressure was released. Range of motion was near normal; there were no signs of instability. McMurray’s and Apley’s tests were negative. There was no leg-length discrepancy or cutaneous lesions.  
Laboratory tests, including a complete coagulation profile, were within normal limits.  
Plain radiographs of the knee were unremarkable.  
Magnetic resonance imaging showed a synovial-based lesion beneath the patella that was hyperintense on T2-weighted sequences and hyperintense compared with muscle on T1-weighted images, suggestive of a vascular synovial tumor.  
Initial differential diagnosis: synovial hemangioma versus synovial sarcoma.

A 39-year-old African man presented with 4 months of left-sided posterior chest‐wall pain and numbness. The pain increased with breathing and exertion and was unresponsive to analgesics. He also reported a 7-kg weight loss and anorexia over this period. He denied cough, fever, night sweats, trauma, or risk factors for pulmonary disease. He was a lifelong nonsmoker with no significant personal or family medical history.

On examination, he was afebrile with normal vital signs. There was asymmetric chest‐wall expansion and a palpable swelling over the left supero-dorsal chest. Breath sounds were decreased on the left side. The abdomen was soft and nontender, without organomegaly.

A posteroanterior chest radiograph showed near-complete opacification of the left hemithorax, obscuration of the left 3rd–6th posterior ribs, and mediastinal shift to the right. The right lung was clear.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a large, heterogeneous, pleural-based mass with a rim of linear calcification, causing near-total collapse of the left lung. The lesion was predominantly cystic with an enhancing solid component in the supero-dorsal aspect. There was destruction of the left 3rd–6th posterior ribs and infiltration of adjacent paraspinal musculature. No significant hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy was seen.

Gadolinium-enhanced MRI demonstrated a complex, partially solid and cystic lesion measuring approximately 12.5 × 17.5 × 13.5 cm occupying most of the left hemithorax. The mass contained areas of necrosis, hemorrhage, and scattered calcifications, and it invaded the left 3rd–6th posterior ribs with extra-thoracic extension into the paraspinal muscles and subcutaneous tissues. The solid component showed restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging.

A 43-year-old woman with a one-year history of restrictive lung disease and remote idiopathic bilateral chylothorax status post talc pleurodesis presented with shortness of breath, myalgias, and generalized fatigue. She was found to be severely thrombocytopenic and in disseminated intravascular coagulation requiring transfusions. Initial CT demonstrated enhancing nodularity along the pleural and peritoneal cavities with infiltrative processes around the pericardium and mediastinum. Over the next six months, extensive laboratory testing for infectious, malignant, and autoimmune causes—including HIV, β-hCG, CEA, CA-19-9, lactate dehydrogenase, and ANA—was unrevealing. A bone marrow biopsy showed mild hypercellularity and pleomorphic megakaryocytes, leading to a presumptive diagnosis of myelodysplastic syndrome, which was ultimately ruled out by flow cytometry and fluorescence in situ hybridization. The patient’s DIC recurred, prompting multiple ED visits. On admission, chest radiograph revealed bilateral pleural thickening and interlobular septal thickening initially thought to represent loculated effusions and pulmonary edema. Contrast-enhanced CT showed unchanged low-density infiltrative soft tissue with thin enhancing septations diffusely involving the pleura, pericardium, gallbladder wall, and right flank. T2-weighted MRI demonstrated fluid signal with thin septations in the same regions, and fat-saturated T1-weighted images showed delayed enhancement of both the septations and fluid components, consistent with extensive lymphangiomatosis.

A 43-year-old Caucasian man with no significant past medical history presented with progressively worsening lower back pain over several months. He had no fevers, weight loss, or gastrointestinal symptoms. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including routine blood counts, chemistries, and tumor markers, were within normal limits. An abdominal CT scan revealed a 9.6 cm × 9.3 cm solid, well-defined, non-enhancing mass in the retroperitoneum anterior to the aorta. The mass displaced the inferior vena cava, pancreas, superior mesenteric artery, and renal vessels but did not invade them.

A 29-year-old primigravida presented at 12 weeks of gestation with lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. She denied urinary frequency, dysuria, or hematuria, and had no history of prior pelvic surgery. Transvaginal ultrasonography revealed a solid 2 cm lesion on the right bladder wall. Flexible cystoscopy confirmed a firm, well‐circumscribed 2 cm lesion near the right ureteric orifice with intact urothelium. At 15 weeks’ gestation, she underwent complete transurethral resection of the lesion; histopathology was initially reported as a mesonephric remnant. She delivered a healthy infant at 37 weeks. 

During her second pregnancy, obstetric ultrasonography at 13 weeks again demonstrated a solid lesion on the right bladder wall in the same location. Given the presumed benign nature, resection was deferred. At 28 weeks, she experienced an intrauterine fetal demise and subsequently delivered vaginally. Four weeks postpartum, she underwent repeat transurethral resection. Histopathological analysis showed glands lined by simple columnar mucinous epithelium resembling endocervical epithelium; immunohistochemical staining was positive for estrogen receptor and progesterone receptor. 

Four months later, pelvic magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 2.6 cm low‐intensity mass on the right posterolateral bladder wall near the ureteric orifice, concerning for recurrence.

A 13-year-old boy presented with a 1-year history of right ankle pain and swelling. The pain was insidious in onset, dull, nonradiating, worse at night, and partially relieved by NSAIDs. The swelling was diffuse over the anteromedial aspect of the ankle and had progressively increased over 6 months. He denied trauma, fever, weight loss, or other joint involvement. On examination, there was a soft, ill-defined swelling anterior and inferior to the medial malleolus, with tenderness but no warmth or skin changes. Ankle dorsiflexion was limited to 20° and plantar flexion to 40°, both movements eliciting pain; subtalar inversion and eversion were full and painless. Anteroposterior radiographs were normal, but the lateral view showed a solitary, osteolytic, circular lesion in the neck of the talus with a homogeneous matrix, sclerotic rim, and narrow zone of transition, without periosteal reaction or soft-tissue abnormality. MRI T2-weighted images demonstrated a small hyperintense lesion in the dorsal talar neck surrounded by diffuse bone marrow edema.

A 52‐year‐old man presented with a 1‐year history of decreased libido. He was referred for evaluation of a possible pituitary tumor. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory testing showed a low free testosterone level; all other pituitary and routine labs were within normal limits. A neuro‐ophthalmologic examination revealed an upper right quadrant visual field defect.  
Magnetic resonance imaging showed a 20 mm sellar mass that was isointense on T1‐weighted images, hyperintense on T2‐weighted images, and demonstrated homogeneous enhancement with gadolinium. Computed tomography demonstrated strong contrast enhancement of the lesion.

A 34-year-old woman presented with four months of gingival swelling and loosening of the lower right canine. She had no systemic disease and no relevant habits. Four months earlier she had pain in the lower right posterior mandible, underwent pulpotomy of the lower right first premolar, and 20 days later noted brief loosening of that tooth and an exophytic vestibular lesion. Two weeks of cephalexin and metronidazole produced no improvement, and the lesion nearly tripled in size.

Extraoral examination revealed mild facial asymmetry from firm swelling in the left lower mandibular border. No cervical lymphadenopathy was detected. Intraorally, a dome-shaped exophytic lesion measuring approximately 2.5 × 3 cm occupied the buccal vestibule from the distal of the lower right second premolar to the distal of the lower right second molar. The overlying mucosa was intact with telangiectasia. The lesion was uniformly firm, with areas of palpable bone thinning. The lower right canine was grade 2 mobile; the adjacent premolar and molar were grade 1 mobile. The patient reported tenderness to touch and on occlusion. On the lingual aspect, a hard extension from the distal of the lower right second premolar to the mesial of the lower right second molar was evident.

A panoramic radiograph showed an ill-defined radiolucent area in the region of the lower right canine through second molar, with faint trabeculae within, band-like widening of the periodontal ligament space at the distal canine and mesial first premolar, displacement of the canine through second molar, root erosion, and preservation of the superior border of the mandibular canal.
