Cone-beam CT demonstrated a radiolucent lesion with distinct borders and a multilocular “wispy” pattern, perforation of the buccal and lingual cortices, root resorption, and tooth displacement.

Aggressive central giant cell granuloma, juvenile central ossifying fibroma (radiolucent phase), and osteosarcoma were considered in the differential diagnosis.

A 15-year-old Kenyan girl presented with a diffuse, painful swelling of the right cheek that consistently increased in size just before and during meals. Her past medical and dental histories were unremarkable except for treatment for otitis media 3 months earlier. On examination, she appeared well but had tenderness over the right parotid area without skin changes. Intraoral inspection revealed inflammation of the right Stensen’s duct papilla; slight pressure on the papilla yielded a small amount of pus. A diagnosis of acute suppurative sialadenitis was made, and she was treated with increased fluid intake, oral amoxicillin–clavulanate and paracetamol for 5 days, and povidone-iodine gargle for 7 days, with complete resolution of symptoms.

Approximately 1 year later, she had a similar episode of painful premeal cheek swelling. The same treatment regimen was administered. After the infection resolved, cannulation of the right Stensen’s duct showed no obstruction. About 2 years after her initial presentation, she again returned with recurrence of the same signs and symptoms. It was immediately decided to perform a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan.

A 66-year-old edentulous man presented with a 3-month history of a gradually enlarging palatal swelling that had recently ulcerated and interfered with his upper denture. The lesion was tender, without spontaneous bleeding or paresthesia. Over the past two months, he reported weight loss, fatigue, nausea, and lethargy. His medical history was significant for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (on theophylline, loratadine, and furosemide) and a smoking history; there was no history of trauma or known infections such as hepatitis C or HIV.

On extraoral examination, the right nasolabial fold was mildly blunted and no cervical lymphadenopathy was palpable. Intraoral examination showed a sessile, exophytic, bosselated mass on the posterior right palate measuring approximately 3 × 4 × 5 cm, firm peripherally and rubbery centrally, with two crater-like, fibrin-covered ulcers.

Panoramic radiography revealed an irregular radiolucent lesion filling the right maxillary sinus with erosion of the sinus walls and adjacent pharyngeal wall. Cone-beam CT confirmed invasion of the lesion into the maxillary sinus and nasal concha.

An incisional biopsy demonstrated diffuse sheets of medium-to-large pleomorphic lymphoid cells with frequent mitoses and apoptotic bodies and “no evidence of specific differentiation.” Immunohistochemical studies showed that the tumor cells were positive for CD3, CD7, CD8, and CD56; negative for CD4, CD5, CD6, CD10, CD20, Cyclin-D1, and BCL-6; the proliferation index (Ki-67) was > 60 %. In situ hybridization was positive for Epstein–Barr virus–encoded small RNAs.

A 44-year-old man was evaluated by his general practitioner for symptoms of gastroenteritis. An abdominal ultrasound revealed a 9 cm mass at the upper pole of the right kidney. His medical and family history were unremarkable except for a 7–pack-year smoking history. He reported no weight loss (height 183 cm, weight 79 kg, BMI 23.9 kg/m2), and his blood pressure was normal. He had no abdominal or pressure-related symptoms. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen showed an encapsulated, sharply delineated, rounded inhomogeneous mass measuring 87 × 76 × 87 mm displacing the right adrenal gland. The lesion was isodense to fat, exhibited no contrast enhancement, and had an average attenuation of –30 Hounsfield units. No pathological lymphadenopathy was identified.

A 45-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of dyspnea, palpitations, chest pain, peripheral numbness, weight loss, and hypotension. Six months earlier, a mediastinal mass had been detected on CT; a CT-guided biopsy was non-diagnostic and complicated by cardiac tamponade. He declined further intervention and received dexamethasone for symptom relief. He had no other medical history.

On examination, he had bilateral lower-leg edema, a loud systolic heart murmur, heart rate 66 b.p.m., respiratory rate 23 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 93% on room air, and blood pressure 100/60 mmHg. Laboratory tests were unremarkable except for C-reactive protein 15.9 mg/L (normal <3 mg/L) and troponin I 0.16 µg/L (normal <0.04 µg/L). ECG showed sinus rhythm, ST-segment depression in leads II, III, and aVF, and T-wave inversion in leads I, aVL, and V4–V6. Chest radiography revealed a left pleural effusion, left lower lobe consolidation, and an enlarged cardiac silhouette.

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a 5 × 4 × 2 cm heterogeneous, hyperechoic mass projecting into the left atrium and pericardial cavity, compressing the left atrium and causing mild mitral regurgitation; left ventricular ejection fraction was 45%, with hypokinesia of the inferior and lateral walls but no constrictive features.

ECG-gated CT showed a 14 × 8 × 12 cm heterogeneous, contrast-enhancing, markedly calcified pericardial lesion along the left heart, extending into the left atrial walls, occluding the left pulmonary veins, with small bilateral pleural effusions.

Cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a 14 × 7 × 14 cm solid pericardial mass along the anterior and lateral left ventricular walls, invading the left atrium with adjacent intra-atrial thrombus. The mass was heterogeneous on T1-weighted imaging with fat saturation, enhanced after gadolinium administration, and exhibited low apparent diffusion coefficient values. Invasion of the left pulmonary veins was noted, along with satellite pericardial nodules along the right atrial wall and coronary sinus, and a separate nodule in the left cardiophrenic angle.

A 40-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of low back pain and 1 month of progressive lower-limb weakness, with bladder incontinence beginning 7 days before admission. She appeared pale and depressed without lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. There was tenderness over the lower thoracic spine. Neurologic examination revealed reduced tone in both legs, grade 1 paraplegia (Medical Research Council scale), absent knee and ankle reflexes, unelicitable plantar responses, and sensory loss below the mid-thigh level. Serum biochemistry was normal except for an alkaline phosphatase level of 15 KAU/L (normal, 2–13). The total white-cell count and differential were within normal limits, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 24 mm in the first hour. A lumbosacral spine radiograph showed flattening of the T10 vertebral body (vertebra plana) with sclerosis and preserved disc spaces. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed no organomegaly or enlarged lymph nodes. A bone marrow biopsy showed normal bony trabeculae. MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrated flattening of T10 with complete marrow replacement of the vertebral body and posterior elements, along with a homogeneously enhancing soft-tissue mass in the adjacent prevertebral, paravertebral, and epidural spaces causing severe canal stenosis and cord compression. Although the radiological findings were not suggestive of tuberculosis, antitubercular therapy was initiated; the patient did not improve.

A 62-year-old woman reported five months of increasing abdominal distention, weight loss, and a palpable abdominal mass without gastrointestinal symptoms or vaginal bleeding. On examination, she had gross abdominal distention with shifting dullness, no tenderness, normal bowel sounds, and on pelvic examination a firm nodular mass with minimal mobility. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a 15 cm complex predominantly solid mass with cystic changes in the left adnexa; the right ovary was not seen and the endometrium was not visualized. There was moderate ascites around the liver, spleen, and lower quadrants. CT of the abdomen and pelvis confirmed a large mainly solid complex mass in the lower abdomen and pelvis displacing the uterus to the right with extensive ascites and possible omental nodularity; chest CT showed no pleural effusion. Laboratory tests showed normal blood counts, electrolytes, and liver function; serum CA-125 was elevated at 1291 U/mL. Endometrial biopsy revealed endometrial hyperplasia with atypia. A provisional diagnosis of metastatic epithelial ovarian cancer was made, and neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by interval debulking was planned. Four paracenteses each drained approximately 4 L of ascites; cytology was negative for malignant cells on all occasions. A CT-guided core biopsy of the mass showed a spindle cell tumor negative for desmin, CD10, pankeratin, low- and high-molecular-weight keratin, CK7, CK20, S-100, and CD34, undetermined for CD117, with Ki-67 immunoreactivity in 5% of cells. Ongoing symptomatic ascites and inconclusive pathology led to the decision to proceed with laparotomy and primary debulking for presumed ovarian cancer.

A 29-year-old woman was referred for management of an incidentally diagnosed uterine “fibroid” found on screening ultrasonography. She was asymptomatic and had no significant medical or family history. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies were notable only for microhematuria (5–9 red blood cells per high‐power field). Ultrasonography demonstrated a 6.0 × 4.6 cm solid mass between the uterine wall and bladder. To clarify its origin, pelvic MRI was obtained. Sagittal T2-weighted images showed a 6.0 × 4.6 cm mass situated between the cervical region and the urinary bladder, protruding into the bladder lumen, with relatively increased signal intensity suggesting high cellularity.

A 60-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of a slowly enlarging mass on the dorsal aspect of his right index finger. The patient had no history of trauma, no underlying medical conditions, and took no medications. He first noticed the mass approximately 2 years earlier, but it was asymptomatic until the past 2 months, when he developed difficulty fully extending the finger. He denied pain, numbness, or paresthesias. On examination, there was a 6.5 × 2.2 × 1.5 cm soft, mobile, elastic mass over the proximal phalanx of the right index finger. There were no signs of inflammation, and neurovascular examination was normal. A plain anteroposterior radiograph showed no bony involvement. Subsequent MRI accurately delineated the lesion and demonstrated internal characteristics most consistent with a lipomatous tumor. Based on these findings, surgical excision was recommended.

A 3-year-old boy with no significant medical history was referred for evaluation of a 6-month history of progressive gait difficulty and lower-body pain. The pain, described in the hips and legs, disrupted sleep, was often accompanied by fever, and responded to acetaminophen.

On examination, there was no tenderness, erythema, or swelling of the lower limbs. Neurologic assessment showed a markedly wide-based gait, inability to perform tandem walking, and inability to walk on the toes. Deep tendon reflexes were normal, and muscle tone, strength, and bulk were preserved. Speech, eye movements, and upper-limb coordination were normal.

Radiographs of the hips, lumbar spine, and right femur were unremarkable. Brain and cervical-spine magnetic resonance imaging showed no abnormalities. Laboratory studies, including tests for sickle cell disease, human T-cell lymphotropic virus, rheumatoid arthritis serologies, and alpha-fetoprotein, were within normal limits.

A 48-year-old man presented with nasal congestion and evaluation of a right-sided sinonasal mass. His medical history included right-sided conductive hearing loss, hypertension, and 5 years of eustachian tube dysfunction treated with multiple pressure equalization tubes. On nasal endoscopy, there was a large polypoid mass with prominent vessels obstructing the right nasal cavity, encompassing the posterior septum and extending into the left nasal cavity. MRI showed a well-circumscribed 4.5 × 2.4 × 4 cm mass centered in the right fossa of Rosenmuller with anterior extension to the basal lamellae and contralateral spread; the torus tubarius was obliterated, and there was a right-sided mastoid effusion. Physical examination revealed a patent pressure equalization tube with clear thick fluid. A biopsy of the mass was taken and was suggestive of mucoepidermoid carcinoma of intermediate grade.

A 45-year-old premenopausal Korean woman, gravida 4, para 2, presented with one month of persistent vaginal bleeding. Cervical liquid-based cytology showed atypical endometrial cells, and hysteroscopy revealed an endocervical mass. A biopsy of the mass revealed poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. On referral, colposcopy was unsatisfactory due to an invisible transformation zone; bimanual examination showed a soft parametrium without palpable masses. Her medical history was unremarkable. Laboratory evaluation revealed hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL with normal leukocyte and platelet counts; squamous cell carcinoma antigen was 0.9 ng/mL. An HPV DNA chip test on cervical cytobrushing was negative for high-risk types. MRI and PET-CT demonstrated a 3.1-cm mass at the anterior endocervix without lymphadenopathy or distant metastases. The patient was clinically staged as FIGO IB1 cervical cancer and scheduled for radical hysterectomy with bilateral pelvic lymph node dissection and ovarian transposition.

A 28-year-old man presented with an incidentally detected left renal mass, noted 10 months earlier on ultrasonography performed for abdominal pain and dyspepsia. He denied haematuria or dysuria, and physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, and urinalysis, were all within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT renal angiography showed a heterogeneously enhancing solid mass, measuring 4.1 × 3.3 × 3 cm, occupying the upper and mid pole of the left kidney; the lesion was entirely endophytic, invaded the central sinus fat, and abutted the upper pelvicalyceal system, leading to concern for a neoplastic process (T1bN0Mx). Given its apparently low aggressive potential, imaging surveillance was initially pursued. However, interval growth and further sinus fat invasion prompted laparoscopic enucleation of the tumour. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the specimen was submitted for histopathological evaluation.

A 61-year-old woman presented with right buttock and hip pain. She had fallen onto the area 6 years earlier, developing an acute hematoma that resolved. One year before presentation, the pain recurred, and 6 months before evaluation it became severe, limiting her activities. 

On examination, there was a firm, ill-defined mass in the right gluteal region. A CT scan of the right hip and proximal femur showed a well-marginated 11.4 cm soft-tissue mass within the gluteus maximus muscle adjacent to the sciatic nerve, with heavy calcification. 

Over the past year the mass had grown and the pain increased, especially when seated, standing for prolonged periods, or lying on that side. She denied fever, chills, or night sweats but reported possible weight loss. Her only medical history was hypertension. 

Physical examination revealed a large, firm, tender mass about 15 cm across in the right gluteus, with no skin changes, no neurovascular deficits, and full range of motion. Review of the CT images showed no nerve impingement. 

One month later, with no symptom relief, a complete metabolic workup was normal. Plain radiographs demonstrated an unchanged, heavily calcified fusiform mass. At that time, the radiographic images were felt to be most consistent with calcific myonecrosis.

A 56-year-old woman with a 2-year history of allergic asthma treated with immunotherapy and subclinical hypothyroidism on levothyroxine initially presented with fluctuating cough, dyspnea, sore throat, and mild haemoptysis. Clinical examination revealed scattered wheezes, and spirometry showed an obstructive pattern attributed to asthma. She was lost to follow-up and returned 3 years later with progressive dyspnea, neck discomfort, deepening of her voice, and wheezing. Examination now showed prolonged expiration with wheezing. Despite oral corticosteroids, her symptoms worsened, and she developed inspiratory stridor and severe dyspnea with spirometric evidence of severe upper airway obstruction. She was admitted to the intensive care unit. Computed tomography of the neck and mediastinum revealed a 3.5×2.8×3.7-cm lesion originating from the right thyroid lobe invading the tracheal lumen and causing severe obstruction; no lymphadenopathy was noted.

A 56-year-old man with a history of appendectomy presented with acute right upper-quadrant and epigastric abdominal pain and oral intolerance. On examination, he had no signs of peritoneal irritation or systemic inflammatory response. Initial laboratory tests, including inflammatory markers, were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed images suggestive of retroperitoneal lymph node involvement. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed a round, homogeneous, solid mass measuring approximately 5 cm in diameter in the mesogastrium, causing compression of the inferior vena cava and displacement of the second portion of the duodenum.

An 83-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 12-month history of a painless scalp lesion that had gradually increased in size. Physical examination showed a 40 mm, irregularly shaped, firm, exophytic nodule on the scalp with overlying ulceration and hemorrhagic crust. No other skin lesions or palpable lymphadenopathy were noted. Given a high clinical suspicion for malignancy, the lesion was excised with 5-mm surgical margins, and the defect was repaired with a rotational flap under local tumescent anesthesia. 

Histopathologic examination revealed an irregular infiltrating tumor in the dermis extending into the subcutaneous tissue, composed of spindle and pleomorphic polyhedral to cuboid cells with moderate to abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. The cells showed marked nuclear pleomorphism, prominent nucleoli, numerous mitotic figures including atypical forms, epidermal ulceration, and perineural invasion. 

Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated diffuse CD10 positivity in the tumor cells, while staining was negative for pancytokeratin, p63, keratin 5/6, MelanA, HMB45, and S-100.

A 50-year-old premenopausal woman (gravida 0) presented with labial swelling and occasional pruritus. On gynecologic examination, the right labia majora and part of the labia minora were markedly enlarged (approximately five times normal size) with a grayish-white hue but no ulceration or discrete lesions. Her recent Pap smear showed ASCUS; otherwise her gynecological history was unremarkable. There were no palpable inguinal lymph nodes. CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no abnormalities. Bilateral bone marrow biopsy revealed mild-to-moderate hypocellularity without metastatic carcinoma, adequate megakaryocytes, and no granulomas or peritrabecular lymphoid infiltrates. Peripheral blood studies were unremarkable, and a B-cell leukemia/lymphoma panel was negative. A thorough skin examination revealed no other lesions.

A 2-year-old girl was hospitalized for fever. Chest radiography revealed a space-occupying lesion in the right thorax, and needle biopsy was performed. Postoperative pathology showed a primitive neuroectodermal tumor. She received five courses of alternating vincristine–cyclophosphamide–topotecan and vincristine–cyclophosphamide–cisplatin–etoposide chemotherapy. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a smaller irregular right mediastinal mass, and resection was undertaken. Histopathology of the mediastinal lesion indicated type II pleuropulmonary blastoma. She then completed 15 courses of alternating vincristine–cyclophosphamide–topotecan–cisplatin and vincristine–cyclophosphamide–topotecan–actinomycin D, with no evidence of recurrence on follow-up. Seven years later, after a head injury, she developed severe headache. Brain MRI showed a large patchy lesion with high density in the right frontal and temporal lobes, measuring 6.4 cm × 5.9 cm × 6.2 cm, causing compression of surrounding brain tissue.

A 60-year-old woman (G4 L4) with menopause 12 years earlier presented with a 2-month history of vaginal bleeding. Her medical history was notable for right mastectomy for breast cancer 8 years earlier followed by chemotherapy and ongoing tamoxifen 10 mg twice daily since that time; she also had hypertension managed with telmisartan. She denied postmenopausal estrogen therapy and had no family history of cancer. 

On examination, she appeared anemic. The abdomen was soft, with mild lower-quadrant tenderness and no organomegaly or ascites. Pelvic and speculum examinations were unremarkable; bimanual exam showed an anteverted, irregular, soft, and enlarged uterus with free adnexal areas. Other systemic findings were normal.

Laboratory studies revealed microcytic, hypochromic anemia; normal renal and liver function; and negative infectious serologies. Chest radiograph was normal. Transvaginal ultrasound showed an irregular, heterogeneous endometrium measuring 22.2 mm in thickness. A Pap smear was negative for dysplasia or malignancy.

Fractional curettage yielded multiple soft gray-brown fragments measuring 2 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm. Microscopic examination demonstrated a well-differentiated adenocarcinoma with predominant papillary and glandular patterns. Tumor cells were tall, columnar, mildly to moderately pleomorphic, with small vesicular uniform nuclei and fine chromatin. The cytoplasm was clear with marked supranuclear and subnuclear vacuolization. The mitotic rate was 2–3 per high-power field with atypical forms, and there was stromal invasion.

A diastase-sensitive Periodic Acid–Schiff stain revealed eosinophilic fine granular material in the vacuolated cells, while mucin stains were negative. Immunohistochemical studies showed strong nuclear positivity for estrogen receptor and progesterone receptor, high p53 expression, and a Ki-67 proliferation index of 60%.

A 49-year-old woman presented with persistent fever, myalgia, and bilateral lower-limb pain. Initial evaluation showed anemia, leukocytosis, and thrombocytopenia; she did not respond to empirical treatment for presumed hematologic malignancy and was referred for further management.

On arrival, she reported severe back pain and exhibited paraparesis. Clinical features were consistent with acute kidney injury. Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine showed a posterior C5–C6 disc bulge effacing the anterior thecal sac with spinal cord compression and diffuse altered marrow signal in the cervical, dorsal, lumbar, and sacral vertebrae, suspicious for leukemic infiltration; multiple lytic lesions were noted throughout the axial and appendicular skeleton. A CT scan of the abdomen demonstrated bulky, edematous kidneys.

Laboratory studies revealed a hemoglobin level of 5.8 g/dL and a platelet count of 34,000/cumm. Peripheral-blood smear showed marked rouleaux formation and 54% atypical cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and numerous coarse azurophilic cytoplasmic granules. Additional tests showed a serum total protein of 11.5 g/dL with an albumin-to-globulin ratio of 3.3:8.2, a creatinine level of 3.86 mg/dL, and a calcium level of 13.2 mg/dL.

A 43-year-old woman with an unremarkable medical history presented with a slowly enlarging, painless swelling of the left maxilla, first noted 3 years earlier. On extraoral examination there was mild asymmetry of the left paranasal area. Intraorally, a well-defined, firm, mucosa-covered nodule measuring approximately 32 × 30 mm involved the left anterior maxilla in the region of teeth 21, 22, and 25; teeth 23 and 24 were congenitally absent. CBCT of the maxilla revealed a well-defined, mixed hyperdense and hypodense lesion causing buccal cortical expansion, resorption of the roots of teeth 21 and 22, and extension into the lateral wall of the nasal cavity. Based on the clinical and radiographic appearance, the initial differential diagnosis included ossifying fibroma, calcifying epithelial odontogenic tumor, calcifying cystic odontogenic tumor, complex odontoma, dentinogenic ghost cell tumor, and adenomatoid odontogenic tumor.

A 49-year-old G2P2 woman with a history of endometriosis presented with dull pelvic pain, worse on the left, and low-grade fever for several days. Vital signs were within normal limits. Urinalysis was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed no leukocytosis, but a neutrophil percentage of 73.5% (reference range, 40–70%) and an elevated C-reactive protein level of 64.7 mg/L (reference range, 0–5 mg/L). She was admitted with a presumed diagnosis of pelvic inflammatory disease.

Transvaginal ultrasonography revealed a right adnexal lesion consistent with an endometrioma and a complex cystic lesion with thick walls and septations on the left. Pelvic MRI with intravenous contrast was performed to evaluate for a possible tubo-ovarian abscess. Compared with imaging six months earlier, the left adnexal endometrioma (previously T1 hyperintense) had enlarged and become T1 hypointense and T2 hyperintense, with peripheral and septal contrast enhancement but no discrete solid mural nodule. In the medial portion of the right-sided endometrioma, a new focal area of T1 hypointensity corresponded to T2 hyperintensity; this area showed no contrast enhancement.

The patient was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics (sulbactam/ampicillin, clindamycin, and gentamicin) and underwent testing for tumor markers, which revealed a mildly elevated CA-125 of 87.1 U/mL (reference range, 0–35 U/mL); other tumor markers were within normal limits. Blood cultures were sterile.

On hospital day 3, she developed fever, worsening pelvic pain, signs of peritonitis, a rise in C-reactive protein to 299.5 mg/L, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 95 mm/h, leukocytosis (12 × 10^3/mm^3), and neutrophils 91.4%. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed extensive pelvic fat-stranding, peritoneal thickening, diffuse intra-abdominal fluid, and bilateral adnexal cystic lesions with thick, enhancing walls. Antibiotics were changed to meropenem and vancomycin.

By hospital day 10, her clinical status improved: leukocyte count normalized, neutrophils were 72%, and C-reactive protein decreased to 46.75 mg/L. Follow-up ultrasonography demonstrated regression of the left tubo-ovarian abscess and resolution of free fluid, while the right adnexal cyst remained, with low-level internal echoes and mildly thickened walls.

On hospital day 11, she acutely developed high fever and marked suprapubic tenderness despite continuing broad-spectrum antibiotics. Repeat pelvic MRI showed that the left lesion had largely regressed, but the right adnexal lesion had increased in volume by 50%, with a progressive increase in the T1 hypointense, T2 hyperintense nonenhancing component and extensive T2 hyperintensities in the pelvic fat consistent with inflammation.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of paroxysmal, dull epigastric pain that intensified and sometimes radiated to her back. She denied loss of appetite, postprandial vomiting, or gastrointestinal bleeding. Proton-pump inhibitors failed to relieve her symptoms. Physical examination and routine laboratory tests were unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 5.8 × 3.9 cm heterogeneous, cystic and solid submucosal mass arising from the thickened posterior wall of the gastric antrum proximal to the pylorus. The lesion had irregular mixed cystic and solid components with thick walls and intracystic fluid; the solid portion enhanced unevenly in the arterial phase, and the cystic wall showed persistent enhancement into the venous phase.

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a submucosal elevation from the posterior antral wall to the gastric angle with normal overlying mucosa. Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated a smooth 5.5 × 3.8 cm mixed cystic and solid, anechoic lesion in the submucosal layer, partially extending into the muscularis propria and serosa; the cyst wall became notably thicker toward the pylorus, features suggestive of a lymphangioma.

A 66-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of dizziness, progressive weakness, and gait ataxia. On examination, he had dysarthria and bilateral lower-limb weakness (muscle strength grade 2); he was unable to complete heel–knee–tibia and left finger–nose–finger tests. His Karnofsky performance status was 30. T2-weighted MRI of the brain showed a hyperintense signal in the right side of the pons. Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted imaging revealed marked enhancement within the lesion. Three-dimensional arterial spin-labeling showed increased cerebral blood flow in the right pons. Based on these findings, a brainstem glioma was diagnosed radiologically, with a differential that included ependymoma, hemangioma, and metastasis.

A 74-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of bilateral lower-extremity swelling and progressive dyspnea on exertion. She also noted occasional mild cough with scant hemoptysis but denied chest pain, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, weight loss, or fevers. Her medical history was notable for non–insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and hypertension; she had never smoked and drank alcohol only occasionally. Two weeks before transfer, an outside hospital evaluation including echocardiography and cardiac catheterization was normal, but she returned with persistent symptoms. A contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed a filling defect in the right ventricle extending into the right ventricular outflow tract, occlusions of bilateral segmental pulmonary arteries, a small to moderate pericardial effusion, and small bilateral pleural effusions. Transthoracic echocardiography confirmed a right ventricular mass.  

On transfer, she was afebrile; blood pressure was 103/56 mmHg, pulse 86 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on 2 L nasal oxygen. She was dyspneic on minimal exertion. Jugular venous pressure was 12 cm of water; heart sounds were normal without gallops but there was a 3/6 holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border increasing with inspiration. She had 1+ pitting edema in the lower extremities. Pulmonary, abdominal, and neurologic examinations were otherwise unremarkable. A Foley catheter yielded dark yellow urine without hematuria.  

Laboratory studies showed sodium 132 mEq/L, albumin 3.0 g/dL, hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, hematocrit 32%, MCV 83.5 fL, white blood cell count 14,600/µL (77% granulocytes), and platelet count 54,000/µL, which fell to 16,000/µL the next morning. Urinalysis revealed large numbers of squamous cells and elevated urobilinogen; heparin-induced thrombocytopenia antibodies were negative. ECG demonstrated a right bundle branch block.  

A repeat echocardiogram confirmed a mobile mass in the right ventricle attached to the septum and extending into the outflow tract. Cardiac MRI demonstrated an avascular right ventricular mass originating from the interventricular septum with multiple nodular irregularities of the visceral pericardium and a moderate pericardial effusion. Lower-extremity Doppler ultrasound showed no deep-vein thrombosis, and CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed no masses or lymphadenopathy. The working diagnosis was a malignant mass with possible overlying thrombus. She received catheter-directed alteplase without change in mass size, and a transvenous ultrasound-guided biopsy was performed.

A 27-year-old man presented with a 10-year history of a recurrent soft-tissue mass on the plantar surface of his right foot, previously excised five times but never completely removed. He now reported progressive painful swelling that interfered with walking. He was in otherwise good health. On examination, there was a poorly defined, firm, tender oval mass measuring 10 cm by 7 cm on the sole, fixed to deeper structures but not to the skin. No overlying inflammation, vascular compromise, or neurologic deficits were noted. 

A plain radiograph showed increased soft-tissue density with a lytic lesion in the cuboid bone. CT of the right foot demonstrated a heterogeneous soft-tissue mass with small areas of necrosis on the plantar aspect. MRI revealed a plantar mass that was hypointense on both T1- and T2-weighted images and enhanced diffusely after gadolinium administration. 

A surgical biopsy was performed for histologic evaluation.

A 68-year-old woman with well-controlled hypertension presented with 2 weeks of progressively decreasing vision in her right eye. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/66 OD and 20/28 OS. Anterior-segment examination showed 1+ nuclear sclerosis bilaterally. Funduscopic examination of the right eye revealed a 2.3-mm yellowish-red intraretinal mass at the superior temporal arcade, surrounded by hard exudates and retinal hemorrhages. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated a prominent intraretinal mass with an overlying epiretinal membrane and subretinal fluid extending to the subfoveal area. Fluorescein angiography revealed early hyperfluorescence with tortuous, telangiectatic vessels within the lesion and slight late leakage, with no dilated or tortuous feeder vessels.

A 44-year-old woman was found to have iron deficiency anemia (hemoglobin, 7.6 g/dL) on routine blood tests. Five years earlier, endoscopy had shown no gastrointestinal abnormalities. On abdominal ultrasonography at screening, uterine fibroids were suspected, and subsequent MRI revealed a 74 × 98 × 122 mm homogeneous, well-demarcated pelvic mass near the cranial end of the uterus, with low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and mostly low but partially high signal intensity on T2-weighted images. On physical examination, the abdomen was flat and soft, and a poorly mobile elastic mass the size of an infant’s head was palpated from below the umbilicus to above the pubis. Blood tests showed no abnormalities in CEA, CA19-9, SCC antigen, or interleukin-2 receptor levels. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a well-demarcated, contrast-enhancing oval pelvic mass with a smooth margin supplied by the superior mesenteric artery; surrounding lymph nodes appeared enlarged. Upper endoscopy revealed an easily bleeding tumor with an ulcer covering half the circumference of the third part of the duodenum. Biopsy from the lesion showed only inflammatory exudates and granulation tissue without malignant cells. FDG-PET/CT demonstrated heterogeneous uptake within the tumor (maximal SUV, 6.3) and mild uptake in the enlarged lymph nodes (maximal SUV, 2.6).

An 8-year-old girl presented with a 4-month history of swelling over the right parietal region of the skull associated with an offensive odor. There was no discharge, vomiting, trauma, or medication use. She reported a mild headache but denied fever, symptoms of increased intracranial pressure, or neurologic deficits. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. A noncontrast CT scan of the head demonstrated a lytic lesion of the right parietal bone. Subsequent MRI revealed a 2.5 × 1.5 cm bone defect of the parietal calvarium with adjacent soft-tissue swelling.

A 46-year-old man presented with 2 months of progressive paraparesis and sensory loss in both lower limbs, accompanied by urinary and fecal incontinence. Neurologic examination showed flaccid paraplegia and a sensory level at T11. One month earlier, an attempt to resect a conus medullaris mass had been unsuccessful. MRI of the dorsolumbar spine revealed a well-circumscribed, homogeneously enhancing intramedullary lesion at the D12–L1 level; prior D11–L1 laminectomy defects were also noted. The patient underwent re-exploration: via a posterior midline myelotomy on the conus, a firm grey mass was grossly totally excised. Histopathological analysis demonstrated a poorly differentiated carcinoma characterized by cellular and nuclear atypia, brisk mitotic activity, pleomorphism, scattered bizarre cells, and vascular emboli.

A 43-year-old woman presented with a several-month history of a progressively noticeable mass in her left flank, associated with dysuria and worsening abdominal pain. She recalled intermittent, dull left abdominal discomfort for the past six years (visual analog scale, 1–2) that had gone untreated. She denied weight loss. On examination, there was a marked bulge of the left flank; palpation revealed a hard, mobile, non­tender mass. Laboratory studies showed mild anemia and hypoalbuminemia. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a large, well-circumscribed mass occupying the left side of the abdomen. By imaging appearance and location, the lesion was initially presumed to be a liposarcoma, and surgical exploration was planned.

A 23-year-old Indian man presented with a 3-month history of nasal stuffiness, epistaxis, nasal twang of voice, anosmia, and worsening headache. Examination revealed fullness of the left cheek and nasal cavity without palpable lymphadenopathy. Serum α-fetoprotein and β-hCG levels were normal. CT and MRI showed a large, bone-destroying, heterogeneously enhancing lobulated mass involving the left nasal cavity, maxillary, ethmoid, and frontal sinuses, extending into the right nasal cavity with intracranial and retrobulbar extension. Complete blood count and biochemical tests were within normal limits. Four cycles of neoadjuvant cisplatin and adriamycin were administered, after which post-chemotherapy MRI demonstrated a partial response in the extracranial component and no change in the intracranial portion. The first endoscopic biopsy showed crushing artifacts, extensive necrosis, and a few degenerating atypical round cells; immunohistochemical evaluation was not possible, and lymphoma, olfactory neuroblastoma, and alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma were considered. A second biopsy revealed only a malignant basaloid squamous epithelial component with fibrous stroma and no round cells, leading to a diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma. Review of these findings raised suspicion for a sinonasal teratocarcinosarcoma, and a more generous biopsy was requested.

A woman in her 60s, multiparous and with no personal or family history of cancer, presented with a 20 mm nodule on the left labium minus. On examination, her performance status was ECOG-PS 0. An excisional biopsy revealed a 32 mm nodular neoplasm with cribriform and papillary architecture, occasional solid areas, moderate cytologic atypia, and a mitotic index of 31 mitoses per 10 high-power fields. There was no evidence of lymphovascular or perineural invasion. Surgical margins were 0.3 mm deep and 0.9 mm lateral.

Immunohistochemical studies showed tumour cells positive for estrogen receptors (90–100%), CK7, CAM5.2, and GATA3, and negative for progesterone receptors, GCDFP-15, SOX10, p63, and CK20. HER-2 staining was equivocal (2+), and FISH analysis showed no HER-2 gene amplification. The histological type was reported as invasive ductal carcinoma of no special type.

Clinical examination, breast ultrasound, and mammography revealed no primary breast tumour. Chest CT was unremarkable, and gastrointestinal evaluation was normal. Whole-body PET with 18F-FDG showed no hypermetabolic lesions other than the vulvar lesion.

A 49-year-old woman presented to the spine clinic with a 2-year history of progressive low back pain radiating to the left L5 and S1 distribution, accompanied by intermittent numbness and tingling. She also reported a limp. A frontal pelvic radiograph demonstrated a lucent lesion of the left acetabulum with internal mineralization. MRI of the pelvis revealed a 6 × 3 × 5 cm expansile lesion in the left acetabulum. Noncontrast CT of the pelvis confirmed a mixed lytic and sclerotic expansile lesion in the left acetabulum with internal amorphous mineralization. Based on these imaging findings, the differential diagnosis included fibrous dysplasia, chondrosarcoma, and metastasis.

A 4-year-old boy presented with a 1-week history of painful swelling of the left cheek. He had trismus, with a maximum interincisal opening of 20 mm. On examination, the left mandibular region was diffusely swollen and tender; palpable submandibular lymph nodes were mobile and tender.

Laboratory studies were unremarkable. CT of the face showed osteolysis with indistinct borders in the left mandibular ramus, rupture of the buccolingual cortical bone, and a periosteal reaction. Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI demonstrated a contrast-enhancing mass extending outside the buccolingual cortex with surrounding soft-tissue edema and an internal unstained area. Bone scintigraphy and FDG PET-CT both showed uptake (SUV max 4.90) confined to the left mandible.

These imaging findings were atypical for ameloblastoma. The clinical differential diagnosis included Langerhans cell histiocytosis, myeloma, lymphoma, and plasmacytoma, but all were atypical and histopathological examination was required.

An older woman presented with a submental mass that had been enlarging gradually over the previous 2 years and was associated with dysphagia. She denied odynophagia, hoarseness, or shortness of breath. Her medical history was notable for hypertension and a penicillin allergy; there was no family history of carcinoma. On examination, there was a 4.5 × 4 × 3.5 cm hard, smooth submental mass that did not move with deglutition; there was no extension into the oral cavity and no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. The thyroid gland was enlarged (right lobe, 5 × 3 × 1.5 cm; left lobe, 4.5 × 2 × 1.2 cm). Neck ultrasonography revealed a 13.7 mL soft-tissue mass at the submandibular level with multiple small calcifications, thick septations, and arterial vascularity; bilaterally enlarged thyroid lobes; and enlarged cervical lymph nodes in level III on the right and level IV on the left. Fine-needle aspiration of the mass suggested metastatic thyroid carcinoma.

A 90-year-old white man presented with a painless skin tumor on the right ear, first noticed 2 months earlier and progressively enlarging. He had a history of basal cell carcinoma on the leg 1 year prior, with no recurrence. On examination, there was a firm, ulcerated, nodular lesion approximately 1.5 cm in diameter. An excisional specimen measured 3.2 × 2.5 cm and included skin and underlying cartilage. Macroscopically, the epidermis overlying the lesion was nodular, ulcerated, and hyperchromic, measuring 1.3 × 0.2 cm. 

Histologic examination showed a poorly circumscribed ulcerated dermal nodule composed of a mesenchymal proliferation of pleomorphic spindle cells in a disorderly, fascicular, and storiform arrangement. The lesion infiltrated the deep dermis and subcutis and exhibited malignant features, including bizarre nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and atypical mitotic figures. Multinucleated giant cells, dilated capillaries, and a mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate were present. There was no vascular or perineural invasion, no cartilage invasion, and adnexal structures were surrounded but not destroyed.

Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated positive staining for alpha-1-antitrypsin, CD68, vimentin, and Ki-67, and negative staining for cytokeratin (clones AE1 and AE3), CD34 (clone QBEnd 10), S-100 protein, and epithelial membrane antigen (clone E29).

A 4-year-old Caucasian boy was referred for evaluation of an extensive oral lesion. He had been born 8 weeks premature with a birth weight of 2.2 kg, was never breast-fed, and remained at the lower limit of growth charts; at 4 years, he weighed 18 kg and measured 107 cm. His mother had been treated with growth hormone during childhood, but he had normal growth-hormone levels and no other medication.

On extraoral examination, his cheeks appeared slightly swollen and he could not fully close his mouth due to intraoral swelling. Intraorally, there was a painless, firm, sessile, exophytic gingival mass with pink-to-red ulcerated areas that covered nearly all maxillary and mandibular teeth and interfered with mastication. There was no family history of gingival overgrowth.

Laboratory tests—including complete blood count, immunoglobulins, growth hormone, parathyroid hormone, glycosaminoglycan levels, and plasminogen activity—were all within normal limits. Occlusal, panoramic, and periapical radiographs showed an extensive, radiopaque lesion with an explosive pattern of mineralization confined to the gingiva, without destruction of underlying bone.

A 50-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B and D coinfection was found on ultrasound and transient elastography to have cirrhosis. Screening esophagogastroduodenoscopy disclosed small esophageal varices and an unbiopsied submucosal gastric nodule. One year later, he presented with a 3-month history of intermittent dysphagia to solids. His weight was stable, and vital signs and physical examination were normal. Repeat upper endoscopy revealed a submucosal polyp with central erosion in the distal body/proximal antrum measuring 1.2 × 0.7 × 0.5 cm. Endoscopic ultrasound showed a submucosal nodule of mixed echogenicity with prominent mucosal irregularity extending into the submucosa.

A 63‐year‐old African American woman with a history of invasive ductal breast carcinoma treated by lumpectomy in 2005 and 2008 presented in 2009 with right wrist and hand pain. Initial radiographs showed mild osteoarthritis of the interphalangeal joints, and conservative treatment yielded no improvement. Electrophysiologic evaluation suggested cubital tunnel syndrome, and surgical release was performed without symptomatic relief. She subsequently developed progressive neck pain, right upper extremity pain, and weakness. Cervical spine MRI showed degenerative spondylosis without neural compression. Dedicated MRI of the right shoulder and brachial plexus revealed a 2.4 × 3.9 × 5.5 cm soft tissue mass in the axilla and along the brachial plexus. The lesion was heterogeneously enhancing, hypointense on T1‐weighted images, and hyperintense on T2‐weighted images, displacing adjacent neurovascular structures.

A 12-year-old female presented with sudden-onset right shoulder pain following a traction injury to her right arm. The pain was diffuse, relieved by rest, and exacerbated by movement. Over the next two months, the pain intensified and persisted despite rest. Radiographs of the shoulder revealed a lesion in the proximal humerus without evidence of recent fracture. On outpatient examination one month later, there was increased volume of the proximal right humerus with a palpable, indurated mass. Shoulder abduction was limited to 60°, while internal and external rotation were preserved. Comparative radiographs and computed tomography of the shoulder showed a cystic lesion in the proximal humerus with sclerotic margins, cortical thinning, and internal septations; the expansile, multilobulated tumor measured approximately 5 × 3 cm. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a heterogeneous cystic lesion confined to the humeral head, measuring 4.5 × 4.1 × 5.1 cm, with thin septations, fluid-fluid levels, cortical thinning, intra-articular fluid, and surrounding soft-tissue edema. A clinical suspicion of a bone tumor was raised, and an incisional biopsy and metastatic bone survey were scheduled.

A 27-year-old man underwent an annual health checkup during which an abdominal ultrasound identified a hyperechoic lesion in the pancreatic tail. He had no family history of pancreatic disease. Complete blood count, biochemistry, and coagulation tests were normal. Tumor markers (CEA 4.4 ng/ml; CA 19-9 23.1 U/ml) were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT showed a well-defined 13-mm mass in the pancreatic tail with slight hypoattenuation on noncontrast images, arterial-phase enhancement, and isoattenuation in the portal and equilibrium phases. The mass abutted but did not encase the splenic vessels; no lymphadenopathy or metastases were seen.

MRI demonstrated a homogeneous lesion with low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, high intensity on T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted images, and slightly high intensity on the ADC map. MRCP revealed a high-intensity irregular lesion in the tail without main pancreatic duct dilation or stenosis.

Endoscopic ultrasound revealed a slightly hyperechoic, homogeneous mass with distinct borders and abundant internal blood flow on Doppler imaging. EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration yielded epithelial cells with minimal atypia forming glandular duct structures, but no definitive diagnosis was made.

A 47-year-old woman with a history of asthma presented with 3 months of upper thoracic spine pain and intermittent lower limb weakness. Physical examination was unremarkable. A chest radiograph showed a right pleural effusion. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a well-circumscribed tissue mass in the right paravertebral gutter measuring 86 × 67 × 54 mm, extending through the T10–T11 and T11–T12 neural foramina, with an associated large pleural effusion. MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrated a 105 mm mass in the right costo-vertebral gutter, hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2, and exhibiting homogeneous enhancement, with right foraminal extension but no intraspinal canal involvement or metastases. Percutaneous biopsy showed a neurogenic tumor with positive PS100 and CD56 staining.

A 76-year-old Caucasian woman underwent right superficial parotidectomy and neck dissection two years ago for a slow‐growing right parotid mass. Histopathology at that time showed a low‐grade carcinoma with tubular and cribriform architecture and eosinophilic colloid‐like material; the tumor was positive for mammaglobin and S100 protein. Margins were negative, and there was no lymphovascular invasion or nodal metastasis.

She presented two years later with new onset of back and left flank pain. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed multiple hepatic lesions, the largest measuring 5.4 cm in the left lobe. A core‐needle biopsy of the largest lesion was performed.

Microscopic examination of the liver biopsy showed a carcinoma with a cribriform pattern and eosinophilic proteinaceous secretions in the centers of cystic spaces. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated strong positivity for mammaglobin and S100 protein.

A 30-year-old woman presented with a 15-year history of a painful mass on her right thumb. Fifteen years ago, she had sustained a crush injury to the right thumb, with subsequent subungual bleeding and bruising. Over the following year, a round, solid mass slowly developed at the injury site, associated with progressive paroxysmal pain and tenderness. Multiple previous providers treated her medically with short courses of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, without relief. She denied changes in temperature sensation around the mass and had no relevant family history, did not smoke or use recreational drugs, and rarely drank alcohol.

On examination, a 3 mm × 4 mm bead-like lump without discoloration was noted on the distal phalanx of the right first digit, with slight nail deformity. The mass was firm, slightly mobile, and exquisitely tender to palpation. There was no overlying skin change.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the right hand, including T1-weighted and proton density–weighted sequences, showed a zone of hyperintensity at the peri-ungual distal pulp of the right first digit. The imaging demonstrated a soft tissue mass continuous with the subcutaneous tissue of the pulp of the digit and not an extension of the distal phalanx bone.

A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a one-year history of irregular vaginal bleeding and a two-month history of a mass protruding at the vaginal opening. The bleeding began as scant dark red spotting without pain, increased in frequency and volume over time, and was self-managed with traditional Chinese medicine. Two months before admission, she noted a reducible, egg-sized mass at the vaginal introitus, which became irreducible two days before presentation, accompanied by bright red bleeding with large clots.

Her gynecologic history included menarche at 13 years, menopause at 56 years, regular 30-day cycles without dysmenorrhea, and no sexual activity for seven years. Her obstetric history was G5P1 with two ectopic pregnancies and two early miscarriages. She underwent a right salpingectomy in 2000 and conservative treatment for an ectopic pregnancy in 2005. Five years prior, cervical screening reportedly showed no abnormalities, but results were unavailable.

On examination, the abdomen was slightly distended with a firm tender mass palpable below the umbilicus. A 10×8 cm purplish-black mass with purulent discharge filled the vagina; the mass was necrotic, foul-smelling, and nonreducible. Dark red blood was flowing from the vagina. Anorectal examination confirmed a large mildly tender vaginal mass, with a smooth anterior rectal wall.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 41 g/L, white blood cell count 7.14×10^9/L (85.1% neutrophils), ESR 0.15 L/L, CRP 28.37 mg/L, prothrombin time 15.1 s, D-dimer 1.69 mg/L, and fibrinogen degradation products 5.11 mg/L. CA-125 and CA-199 were normal; squamous cell carcinoma antigen was 2.97 ng/mL; HE4 was 246.8 pmol/L.

Pelvic ultrasound revealed a 17.8×9.7×8.9 cm heterogeneous mass in the uterine bed with irregular internal echogenicity. A central hyperechoic area with abundant blood flow extended downward toward the perineum, while the lower portion showed sparse flow and scattered fluid areas. The mass had a smooth capsule and relatively regular shape. Structures below the symphysis pubis were indistinct. Conclusion: a heterogeneous echogenic pelvic mass suggesting uterine prolapse complicated by infarction; associated mass not ruled out.

A 40-year-old woman presented with severe back pain of several months’ duration that progressed to bilateral lower limb weakness. Her medical history was unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine revealed multiple, variable-sized, well-defined, round lesions with associated soft-tissue masses compressing the spinal cord. She underwent spinal fixation. The initial working diagnosis was metastasis of unknown origin. On clinical examination, a palpable lump was noted in the left breast. Mammography showed dense breasts without a discrete mass. Ultrasonography of both breasts demonstrated a well-defined hypoechoic solid lesion at the 4 o’clock position in the left breast measuring 18 mm × 13 mm and a second similar lesion at the 1 o’clock position measuring 16 mm × 7 mm; both lesions were classified as U3. Ultrasonography-guided core biopsies of both lesions were then performed.

A 9-year-old boy presented with a painless right facial swelling noted since birth and progressively enlarging. On examination, there was facial asymmetry with a soft, non-tender, mobile right hemifacial mass measuring about 10 × 15 cm from the lower border of the right mandible to the inferior margin of the right lower eyelid. The right ear was enlarged, and there was a bulge on the right parietal scalp with postauricular hyperpigmentation. Deviation of the lip and nose to the left and obliteration of the right nasolabial sulcus indicated right facial nerve palsy. Oral examination revealed enlargement of the right lip and tongue, a right palatal bulge, right-sided dental malalignment with an anterior open bite, and calculus deposition. CT of the head showed a large lipomatous mass involving the subcutaneous tissues of the right face, the right parotid gland, the masticator space, and the tragus, measuring approximately 13.8 × 8.5 cm. There was marked hyperplasia of the right mandible (width, 1.9 cm vs. 0.9 cm contralaterally), lateral pterygoid plate (0.9 vs. 0.2 cm), and maxilla (2 vs. 1 cm), with associated facial asymmetry and disorganized right-sided dentition. No other body areas were involved.

A 40-year-old woman in her usual state of health was incidentally found, on routine medical examination, to have a 1.2-cm nodule in the right lower lobe of the lung. She had no symptoms, her family history was noncontributory, and physical and laboratory examinations were unremarkable. A CT scan of the chest confirmed a well-circumscribed pulmonary nodule. Concurrent lumbar MRI showed a lytic lesion in the left transverse process of the fifth lumbar vertebra, confined to bone and separate from the spinal canal. Initial biopsy specimens of both lesions showed a bland spindle cell neoplasm, but were too small for definitive diagnosis. 

Over the next 5 years, both lesions increased slightly in size. The patient underwent video-assisted thoracic surgery for the pulmonary lesion and curettage of the vertebral lesion. The lung specimen was a 13-mm well-circumscribed solid lesion composed of fascicles of bland spindle or polygonal cells without necrosis or mitoses. The tumor cells contained intranuclear cytoplasmic inclusions. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the cells were positive for epithelial membrane antigen, D2-40, progesterone receptor, vimentin, and S100 antigen, and negative for alpha-smooth muscle actin; the Ki-67 labeling index was approximately 1.5%. The vertebral lesion demonstrated identical morphology and immunoprofile.

A 12-year-old girl presented with a one-month history of eczematous changes of the left areola and bloody nipple discharge. Topical treatment had not improved her symptoms. She had no prior breast trauma, no significant medical history, and no family history of breast cancer. On examination, the left areola showed eczematous changes with adherent blood clots. A firm, movable, non-tender mass was palpated beneath the left nipple, and gentle compression revealed bloody discharge from a single duct orifice. There was no axillary lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. 

Breast ultrasound with a 15-MHz linear transducer showed a 3.6 cm, oval, circumscribed mass in the left subareolar region that was mostly solid, with heterogeneous internal echoes (hyperechoic and hypoechoic areas) and small anechoic foci at the periphery. Color Doppler imaging demonstrated mildly increased internal vascularity. Shear wave elastography revealed intermediate elasticity. No dilated ductal structures were identified around the lesion. The right breast had normal fibro-glandular tissue without focal lesions. Based on these findings, the lesion was assigned BI-RADS category 4a.

A 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes managed on oral agents presented with a 2-month history of peri-umbilical pain, constipation, and melaena, which worsened over 3 days with nausea, vomiting, and obstructive symptoms; he remained afebrile but reported overall health deterioration. Blood pressure was 180/90 mm Hg, respiratory rate 19/min, pulse 86 beats/min. Abdominal examination revealed distension and tympany without a palpable mass or hernias; rectal and remaining examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.7 g/dL, white cells 8950/mm³, platelets 193 000/mm³, sodium 129 mg/L, potassium 4.9 mmol/L, urea 1.32 g/L, creatinine 20.8 mg/L, AST 20 U/L, ALT 22 U/L, C-reactive protein 37.8 mg/L, prothrombin rate 102%, APTT 26 s, and albumin 39 g/L. Abdomino-pelvic CT demonstrated small-bowel dilation (33 mm in diameter) with air-fluid levels upstream of a transition point at the umbilicus, no wall enhancement defect or pneumatosis, and a moderate left iliac fossa effusion. A 124 × 86 × 126 mm oval, fat-density mass with regular borders was noted in the left hypochondrium and flank, compressing the colon, contiguous with the abdominal wall without signs of invasion; several coeliomesenteric, lumbar, and aortic lymph nodes were also present.

A 53-year-old man presented with a 5-month history of progressive right-sided nasal obstruction without epistaxis. He had no history of nasal trauma, infection, or surgery. On nasal endoscopy, there was a soft, mobile, non-pulsatile mass arising from the right side of the septum partially occluding the nasal airway. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the paranasal sinuses showed a well-outlined mass originating from the right nasal septal mucosa without evidence of bone erosion.

A 74-year-old Japanese woman presented with a 2-month history of slowly increasing nodules on her left hand and forearm. On examination, there was a 2-cm ulcerated nodule on the dorsum of the left hand and multiple smaller satellite lesions on the hand and forearm. The initial differential diagnoses included subcutaneous mycosis and malignant melanoma. A skin biopsy of a nodule showed ulceration and granulomatous lesions with multinucleated giant cells in the deep dermis. A periodic acid–Schiff stain revealed no fungi, but tissue culture grew Alternaria species. A diagnosis of dermal cutaneous alternariosis was made, and itraconazole therapy was initiated. Two months later, her nodules had increased in size and number. Rebiopsy of a nodule on the palm showed a proliferation of atypical polygonal or oval epithelioid cells in the dermis with lymphocytic infiltration.

A 60-year-old man presented in November 2008 with a 2-month history of progressive dysphonia and lethargy. He had a 40 pack-year smoking history, consumed 20 units of alcohol per week, and had mild COPD. Examination revealed firm, well-circumscribed bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy (levels II–III) and flexible nasendoscopy demonstrated a fixed left hemilarynx. Under anaesthesia, a large transglottic tumour of the left vocal cord crossing the anterior commissure with slight subglottic extension was noted. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck confirmed a locally invasive transglottic mass with bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy and no distant metastases. He underwent total laryngectomy with bilateral modified radical neck dissections; histology showed a 3.5 cm moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma (T4) with microvascular, perineural, and thyroid cartilage invasion, and metastatic cervical lymph nodes with extracapsular spread (N2c). Two months later, a small parastomal lesion was excised and shown to be recurrent SCC, and chemoradiotherapy was initiated. Six months after initial presentation, he developed a 5-week history of mild swelling in the extensor compartment of his right forearm. The swelling was mildly tender, non-erythematous, and enlarged despite a short course of amoxicillin. At orthopaedic review, there was no history of injury or loss of range of motion, and the swelling measured approximately 10 × 7 cm.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 1-week history of a left submandibular mass and sore throat. On examination, the mass was fixed, soft, and non-tender; she had a stiff neck but no dyspnea, dysphagia, or neurologic deficits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a 3.5 cm dumbbell-shaped mass at C2–3, extending into the spinal canal, left neural foramen, and left retropharyngeal space, with widening of the left C2–3 neural foramen. T2-weighted MRI showed a 3.5 × 3.1 × 4.1 cm hyperintense lesion abutting the left C3 nerve root, with minimal invasion of the left lateral C2 vertebral body; gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted images demonstrated heterogeneous enhancement. Transfemoral angiography revealed a feeding artery originating from the left proximal external carotid artery.

A 48-year-old woman presented with multiple subcutaneous masses over her arms, hands, shoulders, back, and thighs. She first noticed a single 1×1 cm mass at age 24; over decades these lesions enlarged to approximately 4×4 cm. She experienced mild pain only during the initial formation and with rapid enlargement. She also noted numerous small red moles distributed similarly to the masses. Two years earlier she had been diagnosed with Dercum’s disease and managed conservatively. Her medical history included asthma, allergic rhinitis, and dermatitis; several family members had similar subcutaneous masses.

On examination, there were about 30 palpable masses on the right upper limb and 24 on the left, ranging from 2×2 cm to 4×3.5 cm. None were warm; a few were tender. A positive slip sign was elicited. In addition, 18 cherry hemangiomas and 20 small moles (0.05×0.05 to 0.2×0.2 cm) were interspersed among the masses, with more than 80 moles noted elsewhere; one nevus had irregular borders. There were no café au lait spots, intertriginous freckling, or neurofibromas.

Ultrasonography of the right forearm demonstrated multiple well‐defined subcutaneous masses consistent with lipomas, most numerous along the arm and the lateral forearm.

A 61-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of progressive nasal obstruction associated with conductive hearing loss, hyposmia, nasal discharge, and nasality of speech. Nasal endoscopy revealed a tumor in the posterior part of the left nasal cavity extending into both sides of the nasopharyngeal space. CT and MRI demonstrated a destructive 4 × 5 cm mass in the left posterior nasal cavity, left ethmoid and maxillary sinuses, with spread into the nasopharynx, upper parapharyngeal space, petroclival region, and extensive skull base erosion. The patient underwent an endoscopic endonasal resection augmented by a Caldwell-Luc procedure. Histopathological examination revealed nests of tumor cells with clear cytoplasm set in a hyalinizing stroma. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for CK7, AE1/AE3, vimentin, and focally for EMA, and negative for HMB45, SMA, CD10, and S100.

A 60-year-old woman presented with intermittent upper abdominal pain of several years’ duration. Physical examination was unremarkable. She denied anorexia or weight loss but reported mild dyspepsia. Serum tumor markers, including CEA, CA19-9, NSE, and chromogranin A, were within normal limits. 
Abdominal MRI revealed an 8-cm, egg-shaped, heterogeneous mass arising from the lower head of the pancreas; the main pancreatic duct appeared normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed the mass without evidence of invasion of the gastroduodenal wall, retroperitoneal connective tissue, or common bile duct, and no liver or lymph node involvement. 
On 18F-FDG PET-CT, the lesion demonstrated only moderate tracer uptake. Endoscopic ultrasound showed a well-defined, hypoechoic, heterogeneous mass appearing to arise from the duodenal wall.

A 17-year-old Caucasian female presented with 5 days of right eye redness, pain, blurred vision, and intermittent photopsia. She reported vague systemic symptoms including nausea, headaches, left shoulder pain, and long-standing night sweats. Her ophthalmic history included recurrent right eye conjunctivitis and papillary edema since 2017, responsive to topical corticosteroids, with preserved visual acuity. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 1.0 in both eyes. Slit lamp exam of the right eye showed non-necrotizing scleritis, endothelial haze, and 1+ anterior chamber cells. Fundus examination revealed vitreous turbidity, inferior condensations, vitreous snowballs, papillary edema, and peripheral white-yellow chorioretinal lesions. Fluorescein and indocyanine green angiography demonstrated peripheral vasculitis, hyperfluorescent chorioretinal lesions, a “hot disc,” and peripheral hypofluorescent spots. Spectral-domain OCT was normal. The left eye was unremarkable. Initial treatment included hourly topical prednisolone, twice-daily tropicamide, and oral ibuprofen. Over one week, right eye pain worsened, visual acuity dropped to 0.8, scleritis and vitreous condensations persisted, papillary edema progressed, and new peripheral lesions appeared. A multidisciplinary workup showed normal lymph nodes on exam and normal systemic imaging apart from ocular findings. A broad infectious and systemic inflammatory panel was negative for toxoplasmosis, Whipple’s disease, syphilis, Lyme disease, cat-scratch disease, HSV, VZV, CMV, sarcoidosis, Behçet’s disease, and SLE. Interferon-gamma release assay was positive, but Quantiferon testing was negative. Oral corticosteroids were started with gradual symptomatic and anatomic improvement. A whole-body PET-CT revealed hypermetabolic left supraclavicular and bilateral mediastinal lymph nodes, leading to a differential diagnosis of lymph node tuberculosis, lymphoma, sarcoidosis, IgG4–related disease, or Castleman’s disease.

A woman in her early 60s presented with a 6-month history of a gradually enlarging mass in her right breast. She denied pain, nipple discharge, skin changes, or axillary symptoms. Two years earlier, her screening mammogram had been normal, and she had no family history of breast cancer. On examination, there was a 20×18 cm firm, non-tender, mobile mass in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast without skin dimpling, nipple retraction, or palpable axillary lymphadenopathy; the left breast was unremarkable. 

A diagnostic mammogram showed a well-defined oval mass with circumscribed margins and no microcalcifications or architectural distortion. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a large, well-defined enhancing mass in the right breast. Fine-needle aspiration revealed sheets of mature and immature plasma cells, including binucleate and multinucleate forms. A core needle biopsy was performed, and simultaneous work-up for multiple myeloma included complete blood counts with peripheral smear, serum calcium, serum protein electrophoresis, renal function tests, urine analysis, bone scan, bone marrow biopsy, and whole-body PET-CT; all were unremarkable. The peripheral smear showed no rouleaux formation, and the bone marrow biopsy contained only 1–2% plasma cells. Immunohistochemistry on the biopsy specimen showed cells positive for CD38 and CD138 with lambda light-chain restriction, a Ki-67 index <5%, and negativity for leukocyte common antigen, CD56, and pan-cytokeratin.

A 78-year-old man with a 10-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus (on oral hypoglycemics) and mild renal impairment for 3 years presented with a 2-week history of headache and drooping of the left upper eyelid. On examination, there was an isolated left pupil-involving third cranial nerve palsy. Best-corrected visual acuity was 6/9 in both eyes; intraocular pressures and fundoscopy were normal. The remainder of the cranial nerve and neurologic examination was unremarkable. Routine hematology showed thrombocytosis, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 77 mm/hour, and a C-reactive protein level of 4.7 mg/dL. There were no signs of temporal artery thickening, scalp tenderness, or jaw claudication. Magnetic resonance imaging and angiography of the brain and orbits were normal. A lumbar puncture was unremarkable, and chest radiography showed no abnormalities. The patient was started on oral steroids for pain management. A temporal artery biopsy—performed to evaluate for atypical giant cell arteritis—showed only hypertensive changes and was negative for vasculitis. On follow-up, his periorbital pain was unchanged with steroids, and involvement of the left ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve became apparent.

A 12-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a painless swelling on the left side of his neck, first noticed 4 months earlier. He reported dyspnea on exertion. On examination, the mass extended from the left carotid sheath into the mediastinum behind the sternum. It was soft, nontender, poorly demarcated, and brilliantly translucent on transillumination. Fine-needle aspiration yielded clear yellow fluid without tumor cells. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a well-defined, multiloculated cystic lesion in the left upper anterior triangle of the neck, deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle, involving the carotid sheath and extending into the left mediastinum behind the sternum.

A 71-year-old man underwent abdominal CT during follow-up of an intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm of the pancreas, which revealed an incidental presacral mass. He was asymptomatic. His medical history was notable for alcoholic liver disease. On examination, his abdomen was soft without palpable masses, and there were no signs of sacral nerve involvement such as urinary or defecation disturbances. Laboratory studies were unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 43 mm heterogeneous mass in the presacral space containing low-density areas suggestive of fat and small enhancing areas suggesting soft-tissue islands. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a 43 mm mass anterior to the sacrum with heterogeneous high signal on T1- and T2-weighted images. Chemical shift out-of-phase imaging revealed signal loss within the lesion. There was no restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging, and no invasion of the sacral cortex, nerve roots, or pelvic lymph nodes was observed.

A 44-year-old woman presented for a routine visit; postvisit laboratory testing revealed a hemoglobin level of 5 g/dL. She reported 2 months of progressive fatigue and an unintentional 60-lb weight loss. Initial laboratory studies showed evidence of autoimmune hemolytic anemia (C3 positivity, elevated lactate dehydrogenase, low haptoglobin, elevated reticulocyte count, elevated RDW-CV, positive direct Coombs test), thrombocytopenia, and proteinuria. She was diagnosed with Evans syndrome and was treated with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (500 mg daily for 2 days), followed by an oral prednisone taper. During her hospital stay, she developed a new band-like pain wrapping around her chest. Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast revealed a compression fracture of the L1 vertebral body.

A 56-year-old woman presented with a two-week history of headache, nausea, and appetite loss. She had no history of malignancy. On admission, vital signs were stable and the neurologic and general examinations were normal. Laboratory studies showed an elevated lactate dehydrogenase level of 435 U/L and a soluble interleukin-2 receptor level of 1850 U/mL; coagulation parameters were within normal limits. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a protein concentration of 220 mg/dL and a cell count of 18 mature lymphocytes, with normal cytology. A noncontrast CT scan of the head demonstrated a low-density lesion in the left cerebellum with minimal mass effect. T2-weighted and FLAIR MRI sequences showed multiple hyperintense lesions in the left cerebellum and right frontal lobe that were iso-intense on diffusion-weighted imaging. Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images revealed slight enhancement of these lesions, particularly in the vermis and along the left cerebellar sulci. Some dilated vessels were noted on the cerebellar and right frontal surface.

A 42-year-old woman with one prior pregnancy and a history of cesarean section seven years earlier and resection of Pfannenstiel-scar endometriosis two years ago was evaluated for an eight-month history of progressive enlargement at the previous scar site. She reported a bulging mass in the right anterior abdominal wall with cyclical local pain coinciding with her menstrual cycle. She denied genitourinary or gastrointestinal symptoms and had no systemic complaints.

On examination, there was a solid, nonfluctuant mass measuring approximately 10 cm by 6 cm in the anterior abdominal wall bordering the pubis, extending superiorly to the umbilical scar and laterally to the upper border of the iliac crest. No inguinal lymphadenopathy was palpable.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, inflammatory markers, and tumor markers (CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA, and α-fetoprotein), were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a heterogeneous, predominantly hypoattenuating mass with internal septations, measuring 10.6 cm × 4.7 cm × 8.3 cm in the anterior pelvic wall and involving the rectus abdominis muscle, along with enlarged lymph nodes in the external and inguinal iliac chains.

A 70-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of a persistent anal abscess unresponsive to amoxicillin–clavulanate. Laboratory studies performed to evaluate his infection revealed:  
• Thrombocytopenia (platelets, 30×10^3/µL), macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin, 8.9 g/dL; MCV, 103 fL), and a leukoerythroblastic blood smear with erythroblasts (190/µL) but a normal leukocyte count.  
• Mildly elevated LDH (386 U/L) and CRP (15.7 mg/L); calcium and renal function were normal; β2-microglobulin was markedly elevated (8.12 mg/L).  

On further review, he reported a 20-kg weight loss over several months, increasing fatigue, decreased exercise tolerance, right hypochondrial discomfort, and no night sweats. Examination showed hepatomegaly without lymphadenopathy. His history included hypercholesterolemia, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, and a negative HIV test 3 months earlier.  

A bone marrow aspirate demonstrated 75% blasts with pleomorphic morphology: half resembled monoblasts and a quarter exhibited a perinuclear halo suggestive of plasmablasts. Flow cytometry showed 2% plasma cells, excluding plasma cell leukemia, and a dominant CD45–, CD19^dim, CD34–, MPO–, cytoplasmic CD3–, cytoplasmic CD79a–, CD7– population. A plasma‐cell panel revealed CD38^bright, CD138^+, CD19^dim, CD45–, CD28–, CD56– neoplastic cells with no cytoplasmic or surface light-chain expression.  

Bone marrow biopsy showed diffuse infiltration by neoplastic cells positive for CD38 and CD138, as well as MUM1 and cyclin D1; pan–B-cell markers (PAX5, CD79a, CD20) were absent. Kappa and lambda were not detected by immunohistochemistry, and staining for HHV-8, LMP1, and MYC was negative.

A 14-year-old boy with no personal or family history presented with a lesion on his middle back that had been present for several months and became painful and swollen during the week before his visit. On examination, there was a large subcutaneous tumor measuring 6 × 4 cm with two overlying protruding, crusted, erythematous nodules, each with umbilicus-like openings and noted discharge. An inflamed follicular cyst was diagnosed initially. Multiple incisions and drainages were performed; bacterial culture grew Staphylococcus aureus. Over the following months, he received oral antibiotics (cephalexin, doxycycline, clindamycin) and topical antibiotics (gentamicin cream, spersin ointment), with gradual improvement in swelling and pain. Total excision of the tumor was arranged six months after the first visit.

A 9-year-old girl presented with a one-year history of a painless increase in size of the left mandible, resulting in mild facial asymmetry. On intraoral examination, the vestibular bone over the left mandibular body was expanded; the overlying mucosa was intact and non-tender. A panoramic radiograph revealed a well-defined radiolucent lesion occupying the left mandibular body, containing thin bony septa and causing displacement of adjacent teeth, giving a “honeycomb” appearance. Computed tomography of the mandible confirmed a hypodense, well-circumscribed lesion in the left mandibular body with marked buccal and lingual cortical expansion but no cortical perforation.

A 59-year-old man presented with jaundice. His history included hyperuricemia and dyslipidemia. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed total bilirubin 1.8 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 624 IU/L, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 263 IU/L, carcinoembryonic antigen 5.8 ng/mL, and CA 19-9 351 U/mL.
