Multiphase contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 3.7 cm solid mass in the pancreatic head that was isodense on precontrast and arterial phases, hypo-iso dense on the pancreatic phase, hypodense on the portal-venous phase, and isodense on delayed images. MRI showed a well-defined mass with inhomogeneous iso-high signal on T2-weighted images, homogeneous low signal on T1-weighted images, and homogeneous hyperintensity on diffusion-weighted imaging compared to normal pancreas. MRCP revealed mild dilation of the bile duct and main pancreatic duct without evidence of mucin overproduction, and a signal defect in the pancreatic head surrounded by high-intensity fluid within dilated branch ducts. FDG-PET/CT showed focal uptake in the pancreatic mass (SUVmax 6.9) and identified a 4.4 cm right renal lesion suspicious for renal cell carcinoma. Based on the enhancement patterns and smooth margins on CT and MRI, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma was considered unlikely, but neuroendocrine tumor and metastasis from the presumed renal cell carcinoma remained in the differential diagnosis.

A 46-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of a painful lump in her left upper arm. She described the pain as sharp and intermittent, worsened by physical activity, with no relationship to cold exposure. There was no history of trauma to the area. On examination, a firm, tender 3 cm mass was palpable in the left upper arm, with overlying erythema and adjacent axillary lymphadenopathy.  
Ultrasound of the region showed a well-circumscribed, heterogeneous, hypoechoic, pedunculated soft-tissue mass measuring 4 × 3 cm with internal vascularity.  
Shoulder MRI demonstrated a lobulated margin soft-tissue mass lesion within the posterior mid-arm subcutaneous tissue, involving the skin with a polypoid exophytic projection, associated with conglomerated axillary lymphadenopathy and diffuse skin thickening over the dorsal mid-arm and axillary region.

An 8-year-old boy presented with a 3-week history of neck pain and stiffness, temporarily relieved by analgesics and massage, followed by 1 week of progressive weakness of all four limbs, impairing his ability to sit or stand, and subsequent bladder and bowel incontinence. He had no cough, weight loss, fever, or night sweats. He was HIV and EBV seronegative and had been previously healthy.

On examination, he lay supine, unable to sit or stand. There was no cervical or thoracic spinal deformity. Dermatomal sensation was intact. Muscle strength was Medical Research Council grade 3/5 in right C5, 2/5 in left C5, 1/5 in C6–T12 bilaterally, and 1/5 in L2–S1 bilaterally. Tone was reduced in all limbs, bulk and reflexes were normal, and the bulbocavernosus reflex was present. No lymphadenopathy was noted.

Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 15.2 g/dL, a white-cell count of 7300 per μL, and a platelet count of 153,000 per μL. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate and liver-function tests were normal. Abdominopelvic ultrasonography showed no lymphadenopathy. Plain radiographs of the cervical spine were unremarkable.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical and upper thoracic spine revealed an infiltrating intradural extramedullary lesion from C2 to C4 that was isointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and mildly enhancing after contrast, with extension into the extradural space from C3 to T2 and further extension into the right semispinalis cervicis, semispinalis capitis, trapezius, levator scapulae, and anterior scalene muscles. Severe spinal stenosis was noted from C3 to T2; there were no vertebral-body marrow changes. CT and MR myelography demonstrated complete absence of contrast in the leptomeningeal space from C2 to T1, with normal opacification below T1.

Hence, based on the imaging findings, the provisional diagnosis of an intradural extramedullary spinal tumor with extraspinal extension and a differential diagnosis of lymphoma was made.

A 61-year-old woman with a history of ulcerative colitis diagnosed at age 14 underwent total proctocolectomy with Brooke ileostomy. At age 34, she developed recurrent abdominal pain; ileoscopy showed Crohn’s enteritis with small-bowel strictures, and she was maintained in remission on azathioprine and mesalamine. Forty-seven years after her initial diagnosis, she noted stoma retraction associated with pain and an expanding peristomal ulcer that did not improve with topical silver nitrate or a course of oral steroids. On examination, she had a right-sided ileostomy with a retracted, stenosed stoma and an adjacent 3-cm ulceration with a friable raised border. She was started on empiric intravenous corticosteroids for presumed pyoderma gangrenosum. Magnetic resonance enterography revealed multiple areas of ileal wall thickening and enhancement concerning for active inflammation and multiple hypoenhancing liver lesions concerning for metastatic disease.

A 47-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with a 1-year history of right-sided hearing loss, tinnitus, a sensation of ear blockage, and jaw claudication on the right. He denied nasal symptoms or focal neurologic deficits. On examination, there was a 2 × 2 cm deep, rubbery, nonmobile, non tender swelling in the right peri-auricular region. Otoscopic examination revealed a dull right tympanic membrane and a normal left tympanic membrane. No cervical lymphadenopathy was palpable, and the remainder of the head and neck examination was unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated a heterogeneous soft-tissue mass in the right infratemporal fossa inseparable from the undersurface of the temporal and sphenoid bones, with thin peripheral calcifications, cortical sclerosis, and erosion of the outer cortex, displacing the mandibular condyle posteriorly. MRI showed a well-defined 20 × 3.5 × 4.4 cm mass in the right infratemporal fossa adherent to the skull base floor, uniformly hypointense on T1 and T2 with scattered hyperintense foci, no enhancement post-contrast, and no intracranial or dural involvement.

A postmenopausal woman in her 60s presented with two episodes of vaginal bleeding over the past year. Cervical cytology demonstrated changes consistent with high-grade dyskaryosis and invasive squamous carcinoma. On cervical biopsy, histomorphology showed features suggestive of poorly differentiated invasive keratinizing squamous (basaloid) cell carcinoma. Immunohistochemical staining of the tumor tissue revealed positive expression of chromogranin, synaptophysin, pancytokeratin, TTP1, and CEA and negative expression of p40 and estrogen receptor. A mixed poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma with a neuroendocrine tumor component was suggested. The tumor was staged as pT1b1pN0 (FIGO stage IB1). Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging showed a 2.7 × 1.8 × 3.2 cm mass in the lower uterine body and cervix, with an ulceroproliferative growth measuring 1.8 × 1.5 × 1.2 cm on the posterior lip of the cervix. The parametrium and pelvic walls were normal. The depth of invasion was 1.8 cm with evidence of lymphovascular emboli.

A 65-year-old woman presented with paroxysmal dyspnea occurring commonly at bedtime without warning, characterized by sudden difficulty breathing that resolved within seconds to a minute. She was an ever-smoker (20 pack–year history) and had been treated for bronchial asthma and psychosomatic symptoms without improvement. On admission, her blood pressure was 140/65 mmHg, pulse 64 beats/min, temperature 36.2 °C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Cardiovascular examination was normal and breath sounds were clear. Chest computed tomography revealed an internal septal cavity on the right side of the trachea, suggestive of a tracheal diverticulum. Fiberoptic nasopharyngoscopy identified a small wart-like tumor at the left base of the tongue. Although papilloma was suspected, the lesion was deemed too small to cause airway obstruction, so the patient was initially managed conservatively. A tracheal diverticulum was assumed to be the cause of her dyspnea, and therefore bronchoscopy was performed. She was placed supine with her neck extended for observation of the vocal cords.

A 52-year-old G4P3 woman presented with several years of heavy irregular menstrual bleeding and new right elbow pain and swelling. She denied weight loss, lightheadedness, palpitations, dyspnea, urinary symptoms, or difficulty with bowel movements. On pelvic examination, the external genitalia were normal, but there was a large firm mass involving the lower uterus and cervix. Physical examination also revealed an enlarged, firm right supraclavicular lymph node and a swollen right elbow with severely limited range of motion due to pain.

Transvaginal ultrasound showed a heterogeneous uterine echotexture with possible masses, a thickened endometrial stripe, and a vascular soft-tissue lesion in the posterior bladder wall. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated a large heterogeneous mass centered in the uterus and cervix, invading more than 50% of the myometrium, with local invasion of the bladder, bilateral pelvic and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, and findings suggestive of a rectovaginal fistula. A right supraclavicular lymph node was noted. A radiograph of the right elbow revealed an aggressive lytic lesion in the proximal ulna. MRI of the right elbow confirmed an enhancing mass in the proximal ulna with adjacent soft-tissue invasion.

A 63-year-old Chinese man presented with an 8-month history of progressively worsening back pain, which acutely intensified over the 5 days before admission, accompanied by bilateral lower-limb numbness and weakness. He denied trauma, urinary or bowel dysfunction, and had resorted to a walking stick for ambulation. On examination, he had an unsteady gait, pain on spinal movement, paravertebral tenderness from T5 to T10, decreased sensation in both lower limbs, and bilateral lower-limb paraparesis (grade 2/5). There was no saddle anesthesia, and anal tone was intact; upper-limb neurologic examination was normal.
Laboratory studies showed a normal white-cell count, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and electrolytes. Thoracolumbar spine radiographs demonstrated slight loss of the T6 anterior vertebral height, sclerosis of the T5–T6 endplates, and mild disc-space narrowing at T5–T6 without fracture or spondylolisthesis. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the spine revealed a 1.6 × 1.0 × 1.2 cm enhancing lesion at the T9 level, predominantly intradural and extramedullary, causing compression of the thoracic cord with extensive cord edema from T1 to the conus, and suggestion of intramedullary invasion.

A 65-year-old Caucasian woman with a history of stage IIIC papillary serous ovarian adenocarcinoma treated two years earlier with total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, omentectomy, and combination chemotherapy (carboplatin, paclitaxel, cisplatin) and with a normal CA-125 level and no evidence of recurrence at her last oncology visit, presented with progressive neurological symptoms. The symptoms began with dysesthesias and numbness of the limbs and advanced over several weeks to quadriparesis and urinary retention. 

On examination, she had weakness in all four extremities and sensory deficits consistent with a cervical spinal cord process. Serum CA-125 remained within normal limits. A computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no new lesions. Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine demonstrated a 1.3 × 4.4 cm heterogeneous, contrast-enhancing intramedullary lesion from C2 to C5 with cord expansion and associated edema extending rostrally into the medulla and caudally toward the thoracic cord. An investigation for possible sources of infection was negative.

A 44-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus, anemia, and hemorrhoids presented with a 4-month history of worsening nausea, asthenia, oppressive right hypochondrial pain, and marked weight loss over the past month. On examination, she had hepatomegaly with a liver span of 17 cm. Laboratory studies revealed severe anemia (hemoglobin 7.9 mg/dL), thrombocytosis (platelet count 1 006 000/mm3), gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase 1114 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 898 U/L. Contrast CT of the abdomen demonstrated hepatomegaly with heterogeneous parenchyma and multiple lobulated hypoattenuating liver lesions. The gastric fundus and body showed irregular wall thickening, and mesenteric, paraaortic, and iliac lymph nodes were enlarged. Upper endoscopy revealed an infiltrative, exophytic lesion with defined borders narrowing the esophagogastric junction and involving the fundus, body, and lesser curvature; it appeared nodular with necrotic zones and was suggestive of Borrmann III gastric carcinoma. Tumor markers showed mildly elevated CEA and CA-125 and markedly elevated AFP at 49 800 ng/mL. A triphasic CT angiographic study of the liver was performed to assess for hepatocellular carcinoma but did not demonstrate wash-out in the lesions.

A 12-year-old schoolboy presented with insidious-onset right ankle pain of 3 months’ duration. The pain progressively worsened, caused him to limp, and was not relieved by conservative measures. He reported stiffness of the ankle and localized tenderness over the posterior aspect. His AOFAS Ankle-Hindfoot Score was 44.

Plain radiographs of the right ankle demonstrated a large cystic lesion involving the body of the talus with preserved ankle and subtalar joint spaces and maintained bone contour.

Computed tomography of the ankle revealed a unilocular bone cyst in the talar body measuring 25 mm × 22 mm, extending through the superior and inferior subchondral bone, with a pathological fracture of the superior subchondral bone and posterior talar process.

Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed intact articular cartilage surrounding the cyst, absence of bone marrow edema, and no extension of the lesion beyond the margins of the talus.

In summary, there was a large cystic lesion within the body of the talus with an associated pathological fracture.

A 12-year-old girl presented with an 8-month history of recurrent pain and swelling in her right knee. During this period, she underwent multiple joint aspirations for a presumed right knee effusion, with only transient relief and progressive worsening of symptoms. She had no family history of rheumatological conditions. 

On examination, the right knee was swollen with a limited range of motion. Laboratory investigations, including inflammatory markers, were within normal limits. 

Ultrasound of the right knee demonstrated a joint effusion measuring approximately 20 mm in thickness and a hypoechoic, irregularly thickened synovium. 

Computed tomography of the knee confirmed joint effusion, diffuse irregular synovial thickening, and subchondral bone cysts of the medial tibial plateau. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the right knee revealed diffuse irregular synovial thickening that was slightly hypointense on T1-weighted images and hypointense on T2-weighted images (attributed to hemosiderin deposition), with strong enhancement of the synovium after contrast administration and persistent joint effusion.

A 54-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive dyspnea and 10 days of orthopnea. She also reported hemoptysis and significant weight loss over this period. She was a lifelong nonsmoker with no prior medical history. On examination, she was tachypneic and hypoxic (oxygen saturation 88% on room air), with stable blood pressure and sinus tachycardia. Complete blood count, renal function, and liver function tests were within normal limits. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a large (8.8 cm × 4.5 cm), heterogeneous mass occupying most of the left ventricular cavity; all other cardiac chambers and valves appeared normal. There was large pleural and pericardial effusion, both of which were drained. Fluid analysis was exudative, and cytology was negative for malignant cells. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed a thick-walled cavitary lesion in the right upper lobe, a hypodense filling defect in the left ventricular cavity, pericardial effusion, and bilateral moderate pleural effusions.

An 18-year-old man presented with gradually progressive abdominal distention over 1 year, associated with intermittent dull abdominal pain. He reported 2 days of painless, blood-stained urine, intermittent low-grade fevers, and significant unintentional weight loss. He denied vomiting and had normal bowel habits. On examination, his BMI was 17 kg/m2, and multiple bilateral inguinal lymph nodes were palpable. Vital signs were within normal limits. The abdomen was grossly distended and moved with respiration; there was an inverted umbilicus, no visible superficial veins, and a huge nontender mass extending from the left hypochondrium across the midline to the right iliac fossa. Percussion over the mass was dull; shifting dullness and fluid thrill were negative. Bowel sounds were present and normal. Laboratory tests showed a leukocyte count of 7.5×109/L, hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, platelets 299×109/L, serum urea 3.67 mmol/L, creatinine 67 µmol/L, normal liver enzymes, mild proteinuria, and severe hematuria on urinalysis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 24×28.4×31 cm heterogeneous solid mass with central calcifications arising from the posterior cortex of the left kidney, crossing the midline, displacing the left kidney to the right lower quadrant, shifting the aorta and pancreas contralaterally, and pushing small bowel loops inferiorly into the pelvis. There was no evidence of renal vessel thrombosis or lymphadenopathy.

A 32-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of a left-sided neck swelling that had been slow-growing until rapidly enlarging over the past 2 weeks. The enlargement was associated with jaw pain radiating to the auricle and a left-sided throbbing headache. She denied fever, chills, weight loss, night sweats, dyspnea, dysphonia, or syncope.

On examination, her vital signs were stable. There was a single, oval, non-tender mass measuring approximately 4 × 2 cm located anterior to the left sternocleidomastoid muscle in the upper neck. The lesion had well-defined margins, normal overlying skin, no visible pulsations, and was partially mobile, decreasing in size with contraction of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. No cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy was detected.

Soft-tissue ultrasound of the neck showed a well-demarcated, oval, homogeneously hypoechoic mass with internal debris and posterior acoustic enhancement, measuring 3.8 × 4.7 cm. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a 4.2 × 3.1 cm cystic lesion of fluid density with thin walls, situated anterior to the carotid arteries and partially compressing the internal jugular vein.

A 33-year-old man was referred after a mediastinal mass was noted on lung computed tomography (CT). One year earlier, CT had demonstrated a well-circumscribed, round soft-tissue density in the anterior superior mediastinum measuring 2.1 × 2.7 cm, with a CT attenuation of approximately 41 HU and minimal pericardial thickening. On presentation, repeat CT showed that the lesion had enlarged to 5.3 × 2.2 cm and remained attached to the pericardium. The patient reported generalized weakness but denied fever, night sweats, or weight loss. His past medical history was notable only for excision of a right retroperitoneal mass (reported as paraganglioma) one year before. On the basis of the location and imaging characteristics, an initial diagnosis of thymoma was made. The patient underwent surgical resection of the mass along with the thymus and a portion of the pericardium.

A 6-year-old boy presented with a 2-week history of abdominal pain, vomiting, fever, and diarrhea. On examination, he had abdominal tenderness but was hemodynamically stable. Laboratory tests were unremarkable except for a positive fecal occult-blood test. Abdominal ultrasound showed marked thickening of the descending and sigmoid colon wall. Colonoscopy revealed extremely edematous, reddish mucosa with ulcerations covered by exudates in the sigmoid and ascending colon. Endoscopic biopsies showed chronic inflammation with granulation tissue. He was treated with antibiotics, prednisolone, and mesalazine. Over the following months, his symptoms persisted, and he developed progressive abdominal distention and left iliac-fossa pain. During a repeat colonoscopy, the friable colon perforated, necessitating surgical resection of the sigmoid colon.

A 55-year-old Asian Indian woman presented with a several-month history of menorrhagia, abdominal discomfort, and pain. On examination, a non-tender, fixed mass was palpable in the lower abdomen. Ultrasound revealed an abdominopelvic mass and ascites. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a lobulated, calcified mass measuring 17 × 15 × 16 cm in the abdominopelvic cavity. Cytologic examination of ascitic fluid was positive for malignant cells. At exploratory laparotomy, both ovaries were enlarged with intact capsules. A total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy was performed; no pelvic or retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy or peritoneal nodules were identified. Grossly, the left ovary measured 24 × 20 × 20 cm with a smooth, lobulated surface; on sectioning it was solid, gray-white, gritty, and granular without necrosis. The right ovary measured 7 × 6 × 2 cm and showed small cysts filled with clear fluid.

A 43-year-old woman presented with a 7-month history of a painless, bruise-like lump in the natal cleft region. The lesion had increased gradually in size but was not tender and there was no history of trauma. She had no significant medical, surgical, family, or psychosocial history and took no regular medications. On examination, there was a well-circumscribed, firm, subcutaneous lump measuring approximately 3 cm in greatest dimension in the mid-line natal cleft without overlying skin changes. An ultrasound scan showed a 35 mm well-defined vascular nodule within the subcutaneous tissue of the natal cleft. The patient was referred for elective surgical excision.

A 46-year-old Hispanic man from Bogotá presented with 15 days of disorientation, altered thought content, stereotyped upper‐limb movements, and episodes of heteroaggressive behavior. His history included obstructive sleep apnea treated with CPAP, a 5 pack-year smoking history, and a recently identified right lung mass on outpatient chest CT. He had no other significant personal or family history. 

On admission, he was afebrile with normal vital signs. Examination revealed digital clubbing of both hands, skin thickening between the eyes (pachydermoperiostosis), absent breath sounds over the right hemithorax, and a normal neurologic examination. 

Laboratory studies showed normal blood counts and electrolytes. Endocrine tests revealed C-peptide 0.06 ng/ml (reference 0.78–5.19), insulin <1.6 µU/ml (2.9–19.0), and IGF-1 146 ng/ml (94–252). A 72-hour fasting test demonstrated non-hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia. Cranial CT and contrast-enhanced MRI were normal, and a 12-hour EEG showed no ictal activity. 

Chest radiography revealed a radiopaque mass occupying the right hemithorax. Chest CT confirmed a large pleura-based mass compressing the right lung parenchyma. During an incisional biopsy, he developed stupor, upward gaze deviation, profuse diaphoresis, and a glucose level of 35 mg/dL, which reversed with intravenous dextrose. Despite a continuous infusion of 10% dextrose at 20 ml/h, he continued to experience hypoglycemic episodes.

A 32-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of right buttock pain. She had no significant past medical history. On examination, there was localized swelling and erythema over the right buttock. Vital signs were normal, and routine blood tests were within reference ranges.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis demonstrated a 6.8 × 5.3 × 8.0 cm irregularly enhancing mass centered in the right gluteus maximus muscle, with central hypoenhancement suggestive of necrosis, hypertrophied intralesional and peritumoral vessels, and several satellite nodules (~1 cm) medially. The mass abutted the piriformis medially and the gluteus medius anteriorly, with probable involvement of the right sciatic nerve. Marked neovascularity was noted in the gluteal musculature and overlying subcutaneous tissue, findings suggestive of a highly vascular soft tissue tumor.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and lung bases revealed a 1.6 cm arterial-enhancing nodule in segment VII of the liver, suggestive of a vascular metastasis, and numerous small nodules throughout both lungs, consistent with metastatic disease. No pleural effusion was present.

Ultrasound of the right gluteal region identified a 7.5 × 3.4 × 7.3 cm lobulated, hypoechoic intramuscular mass with pronounced internal and perilesional vascularity. Ultrasound-guided biopsy was performed.

A 4-year-old female neutered Scottish Fold cat was evaluated for a 1-week history of progressive lethargy and acute onset of rightward circling. On examination she was reduced but alert; general physical examination was unremarkable. Neurologic examination showed intermittent, non-compulsive circling to the right, mild ataxia and abducted forelimbs when sitting; proprioception and cranial nerve function were normal. No pathologic nystagmus was observed.

Complete blood count was within reference intervals. Serum biochemistry showed mild hyperproteinaemia (85 g/l; RI 64–80) and mild hypercholesterolaemia (8.7 mmol/l; RI 2.6–6.8). The cat lived exclusively indoors in Switzerland, was regularly vaccinated and dewormed, and had a history of breed-related osteochondrodysplasia.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed a right-sided, diffuse swelling of the cerebral grey matter forming an ill-defined intra-axial mass in the right piriform lobe. The lesion was iso- to mildly hyperintense on fluid-sensitive sequences and iso- to mildly hypointense on T1-weighted images. It was partially surrounded by irregular, thick extra-axial T2W and FLAIR hyperintensity affecting the pachy- and leptomeninges, with a dural tail sign and leptomeningeal enhancement after contrast administration. There was mild perilesional and moderate distant vasogenic edema, marked mass effect with subfalcine and transtentorial herniation, and secondary syringomyelia from C2 to C5.

At the right frontotemporal region, there was severe osteolysis of the calvarium with extension into an enhancing right temporal muscle lesion. Regional lymphadenopathy was present: the right parotid, right lateral retropharyngeal and both medial retropharyngeal lymph nodes were enlarged and strongly contrast-enhancing.

Imaging summary: an intra-axial right piriform lobe mass with diffuse meningeal infiltration, vasogenic edema, aggressive calvarial osteolysis with muscle invasion, and contrast-enhancing regional lymph nodes.  
Primary imaging differentials included:  
• Neoplasia such as histiocytic sarcoma or T-cell lymphoma  
• Aggressive meningioma or glioma  
• Primary bone tumour (e.g., osteochondrosarcoma or other sarcoma)  
Less likely: granular cell tumour, meningeal carcinomatosis, fungal disease, granuloma or bacterial abscess with reactive lymphadenopathy

A 23-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of progressive left gluteal and left lower extremity pain, worse at night, accompanied by perianal paresthesia and claudication. He had been treated elsewhere for presumed lumbar disc disease. On examination, the straight-leg–raising test was negative; there was no motor deficit, decreased sensation in the S2–S3 dermatomes, and tenderness over the left sacroiliac joint. Plain radiographs were unremarkable. MRI showed a well-defined, 14 × 11 mm hyperintense lesion on T2 at the left S3 level without sacroiliac joint involvement. Given the concern for a neoplastic lesion, CT was obtained, revealing a 10 × 7 mm mixed-density mass in the left sacral canal with punctate calcification, suggestive of osteoid osteoma or osteoblastoma.

A 65-year-old man presented with a 5–6-month history of fever, occasional epistaxis, and easy fatigability. On examination, he was pale but otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.0 g/dL, leukocyte count 2100/µL, and platelet count 11,000/µL. The peripheral blood smear demonstrated rouleaux formation, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 200 mm in the first hour. Chest radiography revealed infiltrative shadows, and abdominal ultrasonography was normal. A bone marrow aspirate revealed 22% blasts and 25% mature plasma cells; the remaining marrow cells included promonocytes (8%), myelocytes (6%), metamyelocytes (3%), polymorphonuclear leukocytes (2%), lymphocytes (8%), monocytes (10%), eosinophils (6%), and nucleated red blood cells (10%).

A 65-year-old woman with Fitzpatrick type V skin presented with an asymptomatic keratotic papule in her right knee. She had had a single focal vitiligo patch at that site for 10 years, for which she had received no treatment. She reported no history of excessive sun exposure, x-irradiation, or chronic arsenic exposure. The papule was first noticed 6 months earlier and grew insidiously to its current size. On examination, there was a round, firm-to-hard, non-tender keratotic papule measuring 1.5 cm in diameter with an irregular surface and no ulceration, fixation, or regional lymphadenopathy. Routine blood investigations and X-rays of the chest and right knee were normal. A provisional diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma was made, with seborrheic keratosis and keratoacanthoma as differential diagnoses.

A 70-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a painless mass in the left submandibular region that had been present for 1 year. She had a history only of dyslipidemia, with no prior surgeries, smoking, or alcohol use. On examination, the mass measured approximately 20 mm, had slightly limited mobility, and was nontender; the remainder of the head and neck examination was unremarkable.  

Neck ultrasonography showed a heterogeneous, well-circumscribed mass measuring 21 × 20 × 16 mm posterior to the left submandibular gland, with low internal echogenicity and mixed papillary hyperechogenic foci at its margins. The submandibular gland itself appeared normal. The thyroid gland was in its usual location and contained multiple 10–20 mm cystic and hypoechoic nodules, consistent with an adenomatous goiter.  

Contrast-enhanced cervical CT revealed a well-defined mass behind the left submandibular gland. On noncontrast images, the mass was mostly hyperdense with areas of lower density; it showed minimal enhancement after contrast administration. The thyroid gland was confirmed to lie in its normal cervical position.  

Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology of the mass yielded a bloody specimen with foamy cells but no epithelial cells, and was nondiagnostic.

A 13-year-old girl presented with a 1-month history of right upper quadrant pain and abdominal distension, associated with fever, dark stools, weight loss, and scleral jaundice. She had no prior jaundice or history of transfusion. Immunization history was reportedly complete, but records were unavailable.

On examination, she was febrile (39.0 °C), tachycardic (134 bpm), mildly pale, wasted, and had scleral icterus. Abdominal examination revealed a tender, firm, nodular liver 23 cm below the right costal margin. There were no peripheral stigmata of chronic liver disease.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 20.9 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 14.2 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL, platelets 644 × 10^9/L, and ESR 136 mm/hr. Blood and urine cultures yielded no growth. AST was 55 U/L, ALP 448 U/L, GGT 170 U/L; ALT and albumin were normal. INR was 1.89 and aPTT 67.7 s. Serum alpha-fetoprotein was 1677.1 IU/mL; β-hCG was normal. Renal function and electrolytes were unremarkable. Viral screening was positive for HBsAg and negative for HCV and HIV. Viral profiling confirmed chronic HBV infection with high infectivity (HBsAg, core antibody, and HBeAg positive; HBcIgM and HBsAb negative) and a viral load of 2053 copies/mL.

Abdominal ultrasound showed an enlarged liver (20–23 cm) with multiple solid echogenic nodules of varying sizes in both lobes; the spleen was normal. Chest radiograph was normal.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a markedly enlarged, nodular liver with multiple ill-defined hypo- and hyperdense lesions predominantly in the right lobe; the largest measured 11.1 × 9.6 cm in segment 5. The lesions demonstrated arterial phase enhancement with minimal portovenous washout and areas of nonenhancement suggestive of necrosis or hemorrhage. Enlarged lymph nodes were present along the superior mesenteric artery and celiac trunk. There was mild ascites. The portal vein was dilated with a filling defect consistent with tumor thrombosis, and the lesions compressed the intra- and infrahepatic inferior vena cava. Other abdominal organs were normal.

A 28-year-old man presented with a 3- to 4-month history of progressive shortness of breath, nonproductive cough, chest pain aggravated by coughing, and an unintentional weight loss of 4 kg. He had no personal or family history of cancer. On examination, he had elevated jugular venous pressure, prominent collateral veins over the chest wall and abdomen, asymmetry of the chest, limited movement of the left hemithorax, decreased tactile fremitus, dullness to percussion, and diminished breath sounds on the right side.

A chest radiograph showed a homogeneous opacity occupying the right hemithorax. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a 12.1 × 16 × 20.7 cm solid mass with irregular margins and central necrosis in the anterosuperior mediastinum, encasing the right pulmonary vessels, with nonvisualization of the superior vena cava, tumor thrombus extending toward the right atrium, and extensive mediastinal collateral veins. There was also a subcentimeter left upper paratracheal lymph node and a calcified nodule in the anterior segment of the left upper lobe. No bone marrow involvement was evident on initial survey.

Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the mediastinal mass was performed.

An early-80s man with a history of colonic and prostatic adenocarcinomas presented with a gradual increase in the size of a hard mass in the right parotid region and new-onset facial paralysis. Laboratory studies, including blood cell count, blood chemistry, and tumor markers, were within normal limits except for a mildly decreased total protein level (6.2 g/dL) and white blood cell count (4100/μL). Neck CT revealed a well-demarcated, enhanced nodule measuring 22 × 18 mm with a central low-density area arising from the right parotid gland. Full-body CT showed no evidence of metastatic disease. Coregistered ^18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated a focal hypermetabolic lesion corresponding to the parotid nodule.  
Fine-needle aspiration cytology yielded numerous small clusters, single cells, and sheet-like groups composed of a mixture of plasmacytoid, oval to spindled, and large epithelioid cells. The cells exhibited hyperchromatic pleomorphic nuclei, abundant cytoplasm with occasional inclusion-like material, and prominent nucleoli in a relatively clean background. There was no necrotic or hemorrhagic background, and Giemsa staining showed no metachromatic stroma. We first interpreted these findings as indicating carcinoma, suggestive of myoepithelial differentiation.

A 36-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 3-day history of sudden-onset right upper quadrant pain, intermittent fever, and anorexia. On examination, her temperature was 38.2 °C, and the right upper abdomen was tender and guarded. Complete blood count and liver function tests were within normal limits. Plain abdominal radiographs were unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a double-walled solid mass in the right upper quadrant adjacent to the liver and bilateral ovarian cysts. CT scan and colonoscopy were not available. With a working differential that included ruptured hydatid cyst, duodenal ulcer perforation, acute acalculous cholecystitis, and an ulcerated gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST), an emergency diagnostic laparoscopy was performed. Laparoscopy revealed a purulent and fibrinous reaction in the subhepatic region, prompting conversion to an open midline laparotomy. At laparotomy, an 8 × 7 × 5 cm mass arising from the hepatic flexure of the colon was identified, and a right hemicolectomy with ileotransverse anastomosis was carried out.

A 73-year-old woman was transferred for evaluation of a cardiac mass detected on transthoracic echocardiography after an episode of transient binocular diplopia diagnosed as a transient ischaemic attack. Her only vascular risk factors were hypertension and dyslipidaemia, and she had no prior embolic events. On transfer, her neurological and cardiovascular examinations were normal, and laboratory tests showed no abnormalities.

Repeat two-dimensional and three-dimensional transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a 10 × 9 mm pedunculated mass with irregular morphology and wide, independent movement, anchored to the anterolateral papillary muscle in the left ventricle. Myocardial contractility was normal. After infusion of Sonovue®, there was no visualization of the mass, ruling out thrombus. With the differential diagnoses of papillary fibroelastoma versus myxoma of atypical location, further imaging was pursued for tissue characterization.

A 49-year-old woman with hypertension, depression, polycystic ovarian syndrome, prior primary hyperparathyroidism (status post 3.5-gland parathyroidectomy), facial angiofibroma resection, obesity treated with sleeve gastrectomy in 2018, and type 2 diabetes diagnosed in 2003 presented with frequent episodes of fasting hypoglycemia. Her diabetes had been managed with metformin and exenatide; all hypoglycemic agents were withdrawn at the time of her sleeve gastrectomy. Six months after surgery her hemoglobin A1c was 5.1%, and she initially lost 36 kg. One year post-operatively, she developed recurrent fasting glucose readings of 40–50 mg/dL on continuous glucose monitoring, with symptoms of perioral numbness, diaphoresis, and confusion relieved by glucose tablets. She regained 7 kg by eating every 2 hours to prevent episodes, but hypoglycemia worsened, leading to several emergency visits with glucose levels as low as 30 mg/dL. Family history included hypertension, diabetes, coronary artery disease, and a sister who died suddenly at age 47 of unknown cause. Physical examination revealed a fleshy papule on the left cheek.

Previous laboratory evaluation showed a normal cosyntropin stimulation (peak cortisol 24.9 mcg/dL), mild prolactin elevation (36.2 ng/mL), intermittent hyperparathyroidism (parathyroid hormone 61–89 pg/mL with calcium 9.9–10.8 mg/dL), IGF-1 140 ng/mL, TSH 1.0 uIU/mL, free T4 1.4 ng/dL, and hemoglobin A1c 4.8%. At that time, the differential diagnosis included late dumping syndrome, noninsulinoma pancreatogenous hypoglycemia syndrome (NIPHS), and insulinoma. 

She was admitted for a 72-hour fast, which confirmed symptomatic hypoglycemia with a serum glucose of 37 mg/dL approximately 2 hours into the fast. Concurrent measurements showed β-hydroxybutyrate 0.6 mmol/L, insulin 2 mU/L, proinsulin 7.7 pmol/L, and c-peptide 0.8 ng/mL. The oral hypoglycemic panel was negative. VIP, gastrin, and glucagon levels were negative. Chromogranin A was elevated at 145 ng/mL (reference 0–103). 

A pancreatic protocol CT scan revealed a 1.2 cm heterogeneous arterial enhancing lesion in the pancreatic body, a 0.6 cm focus in the tail, a 1.6 cm enhancing lesion in the liver, and a 1.4 cm abdominal wall mass.

A 54-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a 5-year history of progressive generalized bone pain and muscle weakness that culminated in a femoral neck fracture 3 months earlier. She used a walker for ambulation. Her medical history was notable only for one year of intermittent nasal bleeding and increasing nasal fullness; there was no family history of bone or mineral disorders.

Laboratory studies since 2018 consistently demonstrated:
• Serum phosphate 1.3–2.1 mg/dL (normal 2.6–4.5)  
• 24-hour urine phosphate 1439 mg (normal 400–1300)  
• Alkaline phosphatase 164–643 U/L (normal 30–104)  
• Serum calcium and 25-hydroxyvitamin D within normal limits  
• Parathyroid hormone elevated to 102.8 pg/mL (normal 15–68)

Neck ultrasonography and technetium-99m sestamibi scan did not reveal a parathyroid lesion, making primary hyperparathyroidism unlikely. Bone densitometry showed osteoporosis (hip T score –5.9; spine T score –2.7).

Computed tomography of the sinonasal region revealed an expansile, heterogeneous soft-tissue mass occupying the right nasal meatus with deviation of the septum. An outpatient biopsy of the mass demonstrated compact collections of multinucleated giant cells in a vessel-rich spindle-cell stroma, suggestive of a peripheral giant cell granuloma.

Because her bone pain and laboratory abnormalities persisted despite phosphate and vitamin D supplementation, complete surgical excision of the sinonasal mass was performed. The 5 × 4 × 2 cm tumor had a smooth surface and variegated cut appearance. Histologically, the lesion comprised bland spindle-cell proliferation in a background of hemangiopericytoma-like vessels, hemorrhage, hemosiderin deposition, focal adipose tissue with thick-walled vessels, and scattered osteoclast-like giant cells with areas of osteoid formation. Mitotic figures were 1–2 per 10 high-power fields; there was no pleomorphism or necrosis.

Immunohistochemical staining showed variable smooth muscle actin positivity in tumor cells and negativity for CD34, S100, HMB-45, Melan-A, CD99, p63, desmin, and SALL4. CD68 labeled only histiocytic cells, and Ki-67 highlighted approximately 2% of tumor nuclei.

A 77-year-old woman with no prior medical or familial history presented with progressive bilateral visual loss of more than eight weeks’ duration. The left eye became affected first, two months before presentation, followed by involvement of the right eye four weeks later. She had been evaluated at three outpatient clinics without diagnostic imaging. Two weeks before referral, she attended an emergency department because of worsening visual field disturbances.

Noncontrast CT of the head revealed a suspected lesion at the left optic chiasma. Subsequent brain MRI showed a space-occupying lesion in the left chiasma: it was isointense on T1 without contrast, relatively hyperintense on T2, and demonstrated contrast enhancement on T1 sequences.

Based on these findings, the lesion was initially presumed inflammatory and treated with dexamethasone. Despite corticosteroid therapy, her visual acuity continued to deteriorate. On ophthalmologic examination at our center, visual acuity was 12/20 in the right eye and only light perception in the left eye. Formal perimetry demonstrated a right quadrantanopia and severely restricted responses in the left eye. Laboratory tests for systemic inflammatory diseases, including sarcoidosis and toxoplasmosis, were negative. Given the rapid progression, lack of steroid response, and imaging consistent with a mass lesion, an open surgical biopsy was proposed.

A 48-year-old white man, a lifelong non-smoker with a remote bronchoscopic resection of a tracheal carcinoid 17 years earlier, presented with a three-month history of mild hemoptysis and cough without dyspnea. He also noted a non-tender, 2 × 2 cm subcutaneous mass on his left forearm without overlying skin changes. On examination, his vital signs were normal with an oxygen saturation of 94% on room air. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, and coagulation profile, were all within normal limits. A chest CT scan showed a polypoid lesion in the precarinal tracheal region adjacent to the anterior wall. Flexible bronchoscopy revealed a mass arising from the anterior tracheal wall just above the main carina, causing an 80% obstruction of the right main bronchus and 70% obstruction of the left main bronchus. The lesion was resected bronchoscopically with electrocautery, restoring full airway patency without complication. On hematoxylin–eosin staining, the tumor consisted of large nests of eosinophilic cells within a collagenous and myxoid matrix, and a carcinoid tumor was initially suspected.

A 69-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of vague postprandial abdominal discomfort of 1 year’s duration. She denied weight loss, vomiting, or other gastrointestinal symptoms. Her medical history included hypertension, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, and irritable bowel syndrome. On examination, she was overweight with a small epigastric hernia; she was not anemic and had no jaundice. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin concentration of 12 g/dL and normal liver function tests. Endoscopic ultrasound revealed a hypoechoic cystic lesion with heterogeneous internal echotexture and regular margins. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a 75-mm cystic mass arising from the greater curvature of the stomach and abutting the pancreas, without liver lesions. The differential diagnoses included either a gastric duplication cyst or a gastrointestinal stromal tumor with significant cystic degeneration. An ultrasound of the liver was normal.

A 29-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of cough and blood-tinged sputum. He was a nonsmoker with no significant past medical history. On examination, vital signs were stable; general physical examination was unremarkable. Chest examination revealed dullness to percussion over the right lower chest. Routine laboratory studies, including hematology, serum chemistry, ECG, and abdominal ultrasound, were normal. A chest radiograph showed an opacity in the right lower lobe. Pulmonary function testing demonstrated an obstructive pattern. Sputum examinations for acid-fast bacilli and malignant cells were negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a well-defined, homogeneous, nonenhancing soft-tissue lesion measuring 6 cm × 5 cm in the superior basal segments of the right lower lobe; there was no pleural effusion or lymphadenopathy, and the trachea remained midline. Flexible bronchoscopy showed no endobronchial lesions. The patient underwent a right posterolateral thoracotomy, which revealed a solid, firm, well-circumscribed yellowish-white mass in the right lower lobe. Intraoperative imprint and squash smears of the mass showed high cellularity with spindle to epithelioid cells in clusters and singly; the cells had moderate uni- or bipolar cytoplasm, spindle to oval nuclei with granular chromatin and prominent nucleoli, frequent mitotic figures, and small foci of calcification. A preliminary diagnosis of spindle-cell sarcoma was made.

A 61-year-old Caucasian woman with primary biliary cirrhosis and a history of T3N1M0, HER-2–positive left breast invasive ductal carcinoma treated with neoadjuvant docetaxel-carboplatin-trastuzumab, mastectomy, axillary dissection, radiation, and adjuvant trastuzumab and anastrozole presented in February 2013. Three months after completing trastuzumab maintenance, she noted two 0.5-cm erythematous nodules on the left upper chest wall. Restaging PET-CT demonstrated increased activity in the anterior mediastinum and subcutaneous tissue along the medial left breast reconstruction area concerning for recurrence. There was no evidence of distant metastatic disease aside from underlying cirrhosis, portal hypertension, and splenomegaly.

A 48-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of urinary frequency and nocturia. On examination, a palpable mass was noted in the right upper abdominal quadrant. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a right adrenal mass measuring 86 × 83 mm. MRI of the abdomen showed a 90 × 65 mm hypervascular solid mass originating from the right adrenal gland and extending toward the right hepatic lobe, with intense contrast enhancement. Routine laboratory studies and chest radiograph were unremarkable. Serum PSA and digital rectal examination were normal. Twenty-four–hour urinary vanillylmandelic acid, metanephrine, normetanephrine, and free cortisol levels were all within normal limits; aldosterone and renin were not measured due to normotension, and sex steroid levels were not obtained given the absence of related findings.

The patient underwent laparoscopic exploration converted to open adrenalectomy due to bleeding. The mass did not invade adjacent structures and was excised completely. The resected adrenal gland measured 110 × 80 × 65 mm and weighed 370 g. On sectioning, there was a yellow-cream white solid mass with central necrosis beneath a thick fibrous capsule. Histologic examination showed spindle-cell proliferation with occasional bizarre giant cells, widespread apoptosis, patchy mitoses, and diffuse plasma cell infiltration in necrotic areas. Immunohistochemical staining of the tumor cells was negative for pancytokeratin, inhibin, synaptophysin, chromogranin, CD30, CD31, CD34, CD117, S100, ALK, myogenin, and both lambda and kappa light chains. The cells were diffusely positive for vimentin, moderately positive for smooth-muscle actin, and had a Ki-67 index of 4%.

A 63-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of progressive gluteal swelling and chronic lower back pain of several months’ duration. She had a remote history of a congenital cyst excised in infancy and, more than 17 years earlier, had undergone hysterectomy and right oophorectomy for benign disease. Her medical history included diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and gastroesophageal reflux.

On examination, there was a palpable cystic mass in the gluteal region. Needle aspiration was attempted, but the fluid reaccumulated and she developed multiple abscesses and fistulas. A posterior surgical approach was used to resect the cystic mass; postoperative recovery was uneventful and her back pain resolved. At initial evaluation at our center, only scar thickening was noted in the gluteal area.

Laboratory studies showed normal blood counts, liver and renal function. Tumor markers (CEA and CA 19-9) were not obtained initially. Fluid aspirate cytology was negative for malignancy.

Pelvic MRI demonstrated a large, multiloculated cyst in the ischiorectal fossa with a clear fat plane separating it from the rectum; no other abnormalities were seen. A staging CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no thoracic metastases but revealed an ill-defined solid mass in the right adnexa and a 1.6-cm left inguinal lymph node. Pelvic ultrasonography confirmed a solid right adnexal mass. A repeat pelvic MRI showed postoperative fluid collection in the presacral region (likely hematoma), diffuse soft-tissue and muscular edema at the surgical bed, circumferential rectal wall thickening, an unremarkable right ovary, and a 1.4-cm left inguinal lymph node.

Because a gynecologic or gastrointestinal primary malignancy was considered, colonoscopy was performed and showed no masses in the anal canal, rectum, or colon. A gynecologic examination and imaging review revealed no ovarian or cervical abnormalities.

A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman noted a left breast mass and was referred for evaluation. On examination, there was a 2.0-cm, well-defined, mobile, elastic-hard mass in the lower outer quadrant of the left breast; no axillary lymphadenopathy was palpable. 

Mammography demonstrated a 2.0-cm micro-lobulated, high-density mass with internal polymorphic calcifications. Breast ultrasonography showed a 1.3×1.0×1.1-cm irregular hypoechoic mass with angular margins and calcifications. MRI revealed a 1.9×1.8×1.7-cm irregular tumor with early contrast enhancement and washout in the late phase, with heterogeneous internal enhancement.

A 16-gauge core needle biopsy showed fibrosis in all specimens, with duct components and squamous-epithelium–like cells in some samples; spindle cells had low mitotic activity and low nuclear grade, and AE1/AE3 was negative. A subsequent 10-gauge vacuum-assisted biopsy again demonstrated fibrosis and inflammatory cell infiltration without malignant features. 

Three months later, ultrasound showed growth of the mass to 1.8×1.7×1.5 cm. A repeat 16-gauge core needle biopsy revealed proliferation of fibroblast-like spindle cells and clusters of squamous-like cells with low-grade atypia in all specimens. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated positivity for CK5/6 and AE1/AE3 in both spindle cells and squamous cells; CK14, p63, and p40 were also positive, and CAM5.2 was partially positive in squamous cells but negative in spindle cells.

A 55-year-old man underwent right hemicolectomy for moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon, staged as IIIB (T4N1M0). He had no thrombophilic disorders. Preoperative carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) and CA19-9 levels were normal. He completed six months of adjuvant chemotherapy. Thirteen months after surgery, follow-up CT revealed a 25 mm lesion in segment 8 of the liver.  
On readmission, hepatitis B and C serologies were negative. Tumor markers including CEA, CA19-9, α-fetoprotein, and PIVKA-II were all within normal limits.  
CTA demonstrated a liver tumor with two components: a solid portion that enhanced in the early phase and washed out in the delayed phase, and a cystic component. CTAP showed absence of the right portal vein and a perfusion defect throughout the right lobe, suggestive of portal vein tumor thrombus.  
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiography showed no communication with the biliary tree, and bile cytology was negative for malignancy.  
For preoperative diagnosis, an echo-guided biopsy was performed.

A 17-year-old previously healthy male was transferred for management of acute hydrocephalus and intraventricular hemorrhage. He had a 3-day history of headache responsive to paracetamol, followed on the day of transfer by severe headache, persistent vomiting, and a decreased level of consciousness. On arrival, his Glasgow Coma Scale score was 9 of 15; pupils were equal and reactive bilaterally, and there was spontaneous movement of all limbs.

Noncontrast head CT showed a well-defined, lobulated mass measuring 6.0 × 5.0 × 3.0 cm filling the frontal horn and body of the right lateral ventricle. The mass was predominantly hyperdense with heterogeneous attenuation and areas of calcification; there was no gross contrast enhancement. The lesion displaced the septum pellucidum and extended across midline by about 3 cm, causing obstructive hydrocephalus. Hyperdense blood was noted in the dependent portions of both lateral ventricles and in the third and fourth ventricles.

An external ventricular drain was placed emergently, yielding bloody cerebrospinal fluid under high pressure. Preoperative MRI of the brain revealed a heterogeneous mass approximately 40 mm in maximal diameter within the right lateral ventricle. The lesion was hypointense on both T1- and T2-weighted images and showed no contrast enhancement. Findings were consistent with an intraventricular tumor associated with hemorrhage, most pronounced in the right lateral ventricle.

A 54-year-old postmenopausal woman was referred for evaluation of a left adrenal mass discovered incidentally during workup for a spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage. She had no smoking history and a family history significant for hypertension and ischemic heart disease. In November 2016, she underwent craniotomy for evacuation of a right parietal hematoma; concurrent abdominal ultrasound showed a 15-mm left adrenal lesion. Initial urinary catecholamine testing revealed elevated adrenaline (64 μg/day; normal 1.7–22.4 μg/day) with normal noradrenaline and dopamine. Random aldosterone was 9.4 ng/dL (normal 3.7–31.0 ng/dL). She was discharged on ramipril, amlodipine, doxazosin, metoprolol, and lamotrigine.

At endocrinology clinic: BMI 21.2 kg/m2, blood pressure 130/85 mmHg, heart rate 60 bpm, no signs of hypercortisolism. Serum cortisol after 1-mg dexamethasone suppression was 0.9 μg/dL (normal), adrenal androgens were normal, and tumor markers (CEA, CA19-9, CA125, CA15-3, neuron-specific enolase, cytokeratin 19 fragments, α-fetoprotein, chromogranin A) were within normal ranges. Serum IgG4 was 17.4 mg/dL (normal 39.2–86.4 mg/dL).

Contrast-enhanced CT (adrenal protocol) showed a 14×13 mm left adrenal mass with noncontrast density 32 HU, venous-phase density 157 HU, delayed-phase density 93 HU, absolute washout 51%, and relative washout 40%. The right adrenal gland was normal. An 18F-DOPA PET scan was negative. Six months later, CT showed stable lesion size; 18F-FDG PET scan demonstrated bilateral adrenal hypermetabolism, more circumscribed on the left (SUVmax adrenal/liver 4.0/2.4).

A 64-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of chronic abdominal pain. She described spasmodic epigastric pain radiating to the back, intermittent over 1 year, without relationship to food intake. The pain was severe enough to prompt occasional emergency visits for intravenous analgesia. She also reported dyspepsia and early postprandial satiety but denied acid reflux or dysphagia. Her medical history included asthma, dermatomycosis, and endometriosis. 

On examination, the abdomen was soft and nondistended, with no palpable masses or hernias and no signs of acute abdomen. Laboratory tests were unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound confirmed cholelithiasis without evidence of cholecystitis or choledocholithiasis and incidentally revealed a lesion in the posterior wall of the stomach. 

A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen demonstrated multiple radiolucent gallstones and an isolated well-circumscribed submucosal lesion in the posterior gastric wall, with no lymphadenopathy. The differential diagnosis for the gastric lesion included leiomyoma and gastrointestinal stromal tumour. Percutaneous biopsy was deemed infeasible, and an MRI was scheduled for further characterization.

A 61-year-old man presented with a 4–5-year history of a gradually enlarging swelling on the left chin region without pain, paresthesia, or mastication difficulty. He reported no trauma or dental procedures in the area. He chewed tobacco 3–4 times daily for 10–15 years. Physical examination revealed a 5 cm × 3 cm smooth, soft, nonfluctuant, non-tender swelling near the left oral commissure without lymphadenopathy. Intraorally, there was a 3 cm × 2 cm round, yellowish, sessile mass with smooth surface in the lower left labial vestibule, extending from the canine to the first molar. An incidental 1 cm × 0.5 cm sessile, erythematous, lobulated lesion with irregular borders was noted on the ventral tongue. Neither lesion blanched on pressure. Panoramic radiograph was unremarkable. Ultrasonography of the vestibular mass showed a well-defined echogenic intramuscular lesion measuring 2.2 × 0.8 cm, with no calcification or vascularity; surrounding bone and muscle appeared normal. Fine-needle aspiration twice yielded no material. A provisional diagnosis of lipoma was made, and the patient was referred for excisional biopsy under general anesthesia.

A 28-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of a painless, firm swelling of the right cheek and intermittent dull pain. Vital signs were normal. Facial inspection showed a well-defined swelling from the lateral nasal wall to 2 cm anterior to the ear and from the infraorbital margin to the mouth corner. Intraorally, a firm, non-tender swelling extended from the upper right central incisor to the first molar, obliterating the buccal vestibule; the overlying mucosa appeared normal. The right maxillary canine was absent. A right submandibular lymph node was palpable. All teeth responded normally to pulp testing.

Panoramic radiography revealed an impacted right maxillary canine and a radiolucent lesion with an irregular corticated border around the crown. CT scan showed a 4.9 × 3.1 cm lesion in the right maxilla causing expansion and thinning of the sinus walls and displacing the inferior sinus floor; the unerupted canine was adjacent to the medial sinus wall. Aspiration yielded straw-colored fluid. On the basis of these findings, a diagnosis of dentigerous cyst was made. The differential diagnosis included adenomatoid odontogenic tumor and odontogenic keratocyst.

A 15-year-old male was evaluated for bleeding from nodules on his left palm and fingers for 1 day. He had a 9-year history of multiple nodules on both upper limbs without pain or pruritus and had previously received oral traditional Chinese medicine without a definitive diagnosis. He was born full-term to healthy non-consanguineous parents, with no deformities at birth, and had no family history of similar lesions.

On examination, he was of short stature and exhibited valgus deformity of the left knee, varus deformity of the right knee, and a 15 cm shortening of the left lower limb compared with the right. Numerous light-blue, soft, subcutaneous nodules with clear borders were present over the left hand. Dark-red nodular lesions measuring approximately 4 × 3 cm were noted on the left upper arm and 1 × 1 cm on the left elbow. Additional subcutaneous nodules were palpable in the thenar eminence of the right palm, scrotum, and perineum.

Plain radiographs of the upper and lower limbs and scapulae showed multiple expansile, radiolucent lesions with punctate calcifications consistent with enchondromas, developmental malformations of the left humerus, radius, femur, tibia, and fibula, and solitary soft-tissue masses suggestive of hemangioma. CT of the left upper and lower limbs confirmed multiple endophytic chondroid lesions, bony deformities, and a phlebolith within the soft-tissue hemangioma of the hand.

A 69-year-old woman noted a hard mass in her left neck six months ago. She had no pain, systemic symptoms, or relevant medical history. On examination, there was a quail-egg–sized, firm, non-tender mass with poorly defined borders over the left levator scapulae region.  
MRI of the neck revealed a well-demarcated 2.5 × 3.5 cm soft-tissue lesion within the left levator scapulae muscle, isointense on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted and STIR sequences, and showing marked gadolinium enhancement.  
A core-needle biopsy showed spindle cells with minimal atypia arranged in fascicular and storiform patterns within fibrous stroma. Immunohistochemical staining of the biopsy specimen was focally positive for α-smooth muscle actin and negative for S-100 protein, suggesting a low-grade spindle-cell sarcoma.

A 64-year-old Japanese man was referred after a routine medical checkup revealed a mass in the right upper abdomen on ultrasonography, accompanied by an acoustic shadow. He had hypertension and a history of appendectomy at age 13. On examination, his blood pressure was 146/76 mmHg, pulse 66 beats/min, oxygen saturation 97 %, and temperature 36.2 °C. His abdomen was flat and soft without palpable masses. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, inflammatory markers, liver and renal function tests, electrolytes, and coagulation panels, were all within normal limits.

Plain computed tomography of the abdomen showed a 6.5-cm mass with extremely high densities, located between the undersurface of the right hepatic lobe and the right kidney. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen revealed no other lesions. On magnetic resonance imaging, the mass demonstrated low signal intensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images.

Because of the dense calcification, the lesion was initially thought to represent a large peritoneal pearl body or sponge-induced granuloma related to his remote appendectomy. Malignant fibrous histiocytoma, dedifferentiated liposarcoma, and extraskeletal osteosarcoma were also considered, although each was regarded as atypical or rare given the imaging characteristics. The patient was informed of the low likelihood of malignancy and elected to undergo observation. Two years later, imaging remained stable, and he requested surgical excision.

A 53-year-old man presented with a swelling behind his right ear of one month’s duration, which had progressively enlarged. Examination revealed a painful, firm mass measuring 3 × 2 × 2 cm in the right postauricular region. The lesion exhibited prominent capillary markings and was fixed to adjacent tissues. The clinical impression was a dermoid cyst, and the lesion was completely excised. His medical history was notable for a right nephrectomy performed three years earlier for renal cell carcinoma.

A 3-day-old female infant was referred for evaluation of a swelling of the right lower leg. She was born at term by spontaneous vaginal delivery without perinatal complications. Family history was unremarkable. On examination, there was fusiform swelling over the right tibial diaphysis without warmth or redness; the remainder of the physical examination was normal. Laboratory tests, including serum biochemistry, urine analysis, and C‐reactive protein, were within normal limits.

Plain radiographs of the tibia and fibula demonstrated an expansile osteolytic lesion with inner ground‐glass areas occupying nearly the entire metaphysis and proximal half of the diaphysis of the right tibia, which was enlarged and flared. The lesion had irregular but relatively well‐defined contours with a narrow zone of transition. The cortex was thinned and disrupted at some points, with evidence of a pathologic fracture. There was no periosteal reaction, no soft‐tissue mass, and the epiphysis was spared.

CT scans confirmed the expansile osteolytic lesion with ground‐glass matrix and cortical thinning, and 3-D reconstructions well‐delineated its extent. MRI showed a cortical mass with heterogeneous hyperintense signal on T2-weighted and STIR images, intermediate–low signal on T1-weighted images, and heterogeneous enhancement on postcontrast T1-weighted images. There was no clear medullary canal involvement and no restricted diffusion; mild edema of the surrounding soft tissues was noted.

A 36-year-old man presented with a 7-year history of a progressively enlarging, painless swelling behind his right ear. He denied pain, hearing loss, dizziness, cranial nerve symptoms, or prior scalp infection. His only concern was cosmetic deformity.  
On examination, there was a 2.5 cm × 2.5 cm bony hard, sessile, non-tender swelling over the right mastoid; the overlying skin was normal. Facial nerve function was intact; both external auditory canals were unremarkable. The remainder of the ear, nose, throat, ophthalmologic, and systemic examinations were normal.  
Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits.  
CT of the right temporal region showed a well-demarcated, radiodense, broad-based swelling arising from the mastoid and squamous temporal bone. The middle and inner ear structures were normal, and no other lesions were noted in the temporal bone.

A 37-year-old woman presented with 3 to 4 days of right upper quadrant abdominal pain and tenderness, with referred right shoulder pain on deep inspiration. Approximately 5 years earlier, two right-lobe liver masses, most suggestive of hemangiomas, were identified on CT and remained stable on follow-up. A current CT scan showed multiple new ring-enhancing low-density lesions in both hepatic lobes, the largest measuring 2.1 cm in the right lobe.

Her history was notable for Philadelphia chromosome–negative acute B-cell lymphoblastic leukemia diagnosed 6 years earlier (treated) and myelodysplastic syndrome with excess blasts-2 (MDS-EB-2) diagnosed 6 months earlier. Three days before this presentation, bone marrow aspiration and biopsy showed extensive reticulin fibrosis (MF-3), trilineage dysplasia, increased blasts (10%–19%), and near–100% cellularity, consistent with MDS-EB-2. Cytogenetic analysis revealed a complex karyotype including −5, −7, and del(17)(p12). JAK2 V617F and CALR exon 9 mutations were not detected.

Complete blood count: WBC 0.5 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL, hematocrit 20.0%, MCV 86.1 fL, RDW 12.4%, platelets 4 × 10^9/L. Differential: granulocytes 12%, lymphocytes 85.5%, monocytes 4%.

A CT-guided core biopsy of a liver lesion revealed on hematoxylin-eosin staining megakaryocytes and sinusoidal capillarization adjacent to areas of fibroblastic proliferation, with numerous atypical megakaryocytes intermingled with fibrosclerosis and prominent cholestasis outside the fibrous areas. Immunohistochemical studies showed Pax-5 and myeloperoxidase negative; keratin positive only in hepatocytes; myosin highlighting smooth muscle and a few scattered cells; CD31 and CD34 staining vessels and scattered cells; CD61 staining megakaryocytes; CD163 staining numerous histiocytes. No significant blasts or leukemic infiltrate were identified.

A 10-year-old neutered male domestic shorthair cat presented with a 2–3-month history of weight loss, coughing, lethargy and progressive dyspnea. The cat had been anorexic for 2–3 days with one episode of regurgitation the night before presentation. Previous empirical treatment with cefovecin, prednisone and chloramphenicol had yielded no improvement. FeLV and FIV tests were negative.

On examination, the cat was in poor body condition, tachypneic with increased respiratory effort and both inspiratory and expiratory stridor. A grade II/VI left parasternal systolic murmur was present. Mucous membranes were pale pink and tacky; mild dental calculus and a flea infestation were noted. 

CBC revealed lymphopenia (775 × 10^3/µl; RI 1500–7000) and eosinophilia (1550 × 10^3/µl; RI 0–750). Serum biochemistry showed elevated ALT (184 U/l; RI 26–77), AST (288 U/l; RI 12–45), CK (13 207 U/l; RI 100–250), hypocalcemia (9.0 mg/dl; RI 9.5–11.6), hypophosphatemia (3.1 mg/dl; RI 4.3–5.9) and hypochloremia (107 mEq/l; RI 114–120). Urinalysis showed low specific gravity (1.023) and hematuria attributed to cystocentesis.

Thoracic radiographs demonstrated an irregularly narrowed tracheal lumen from C7 through T4 with dorsal and ventral soft-tissue opacities overlying the trachea. Echocardiography showed mild mitral regurgitation but normal chamber dimensions and function. 

CT of the cervical and thoracic trachea confirmed tracheal narrowing at C6 through T1 due to a dorsal soft-tissue mass and ventral flattening of the canal. Esophagoscopy was unremarkable. Bronchoscopy revealed an irregular, multilobulated intraluminal tracheal mass partially circumferential distal to the thoracic inlet. Biopsies and impression cytology samples were obtained, and dexamethasone was administered post-procedure to reduce inflammation.

A 73‐year‐old woman presented with a 4-month history of an asymptomatic mass on the lateral edge of her tongue. Her medical history was unremarkable. On examination, there was a 0.5-cm, well-circumscribed, sessile nodule with slight peripheral pedunculation, a yellow-whitish verrucous surface, and firm consistency. The lesion was fixed to the lateral tongue. These findings were suggestive of condyloma acuminatum, verruca vulgaris, or giant cell fibroma. An excisional biopsy was performed.

A 4-day-old Asian Chinese female newborn was referred for evaluation of multiple masses protruding from her gums that interfered with feeding. The infant was born at 38 weeks of gestation via cesarean section with a birth weight of 2650 g and had no family history of hereditary disease. Physical examination revealed six round, soft, pedunculated swellings: two on the maxillary anterior alveolar ridge and four on the mandibular anterior alveolar ridge, the largest measuring 3.5 × 3.0 cm. The lesions were well defined, firm, smooth, and pink on gross inspection, and the infant was unable to close her mouth completely; respiration was normal. Because of progressive enlargement of the masses and feeding difficulties, surgical excision under general anesthesia was planned on day 6 after birth. Hemostasis was achieved by placement of a transfixion suture on the alveolar ridge before excision, and all lesions were removed without intraoperative complications. The specimens were fixed in 10% neutral buffered formalin and submitted for histopathological evaluation.

A 42-year-old previously healthy Thai man presented with a 2-month history of slowly progressive ataxia, motor aphasia, and frontal-release signs. Noncontrast CT of the brain revealed multiple hypodense lesions in bilateral occipito-parieto-frontal and cerebellar regions consistent with cerebral infarctions. He was started on aspirin (300 mg daily); transthoracic echocardiography was unremarkable. Initial laboratory tests showed mild anemia (Hb 10.1 g/dL), white blood cell count 6270 cells/mm3, platelet count 192 000 cells/mm3, ESR 89 mm/hr, CRP 64 mg/L, and LDH 873 U/L (normal 225–450 U/L). Tests for lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies, anti-β2-glycoprotein 1 antibodies, ANA, and VDRL were negative.

Two weeks later, his neurologic status worsened with left hemiplegia and decreased consciousness. He developed low-grade fever without an identifiable infectious source, hypoxemia (PaO2 59.5 mmHg, O2 saturation 92%), and further elevation of LDH (1203 U/L). Repeat CBC again showed only anemia. Doppler ultrasound of the lower extremities was normal. MRI of the brain demonstrated diffuse, multistage intraparenchymal infarctions and hemorrhages in both cerebral and cerebellar hemispheres, while MRA revealed normal patency of all major intracranial arteries. Vasculitis was considered, and he received pulse methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 5 days), with partial clinical improvement. Given the constellation of findings, a random skin biopsy from both thighs was planned.

A 65-year-old woman presented following a fall onto her left chest wall 2 months earlier, with persistent pain in the left hemithorax. Outpatient chest radiography revealed a pathological fracture and an expansile osteolytic lesion of the left eighth rib. On referral to a sarcoma center, she reported no current pain, shortness of breath, B symptoms, or history of malignancy. Physical examination of the left chest wall was unremarkable, without tenderness or palpable mass.

Chest X-ray confirmed a pathological fracture of the left eighth lateral rib with an ill-defined osteolytic area. CT of the chest demonstrated an expansive, osteolytic intraosseous lesion measuring 3 × 2 cm with a sclerotic rim and associated fracture of the eighth rib. MRI of the thorax showed a contrast-enhancing lesion without significant surrounding soft-tissue reaction. Staging CT of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a stable, arterial hypervascularized hepatic lesion but no other abnormalities. Laboratory studies were within normal limits.

A 49-year-old woman of African origin presented with a 10-year history of a right‐sided scalp mass that had been stable and nontender until it was excised at a peripheral clinic 5 months ago (no histopathology was done). Over the next 5 months, the lesion recurred, gradually enlarged, ulcerated, and bled easily. She denied headaches, convulsions, or neurologic deficits. On examination, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. There was no pallor, jaundice, or palpable peripheral lymphadenopathy. Local scalp examination revealed two lesions on the right side: a fungating, tender, 9 × 7 cm mass prone to bleeding and mild mobility, and a second non‐fungating, 3 × 3 cm lesion. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and basic metabolic panel. Chest radiography and abdominal/pelvic ultrasound were unremarkable. A head and neck CT scan demonstrated a multilobulated, hyperdense, ulcerative right frontal scalp lesion measuring 9 × 7.8 × 6 cm without skull bone erosion or intracranial extension, along with enlarged cervical lymph nodes at levels I and II. MRI of the spine revealed a pathological compression fracture of T10 and a hyperintense lesion in T8, raising suspicion for vertebral metastases. Clinical staging was considered stage IVc.

A 68-year-old man was transferred for further management after an inferior wall ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction. His medical history was notable for malignant fibrous histiocytoma of the right preauricular and left jugular regions, with regional relapse and a focal lung metastasis treated surgically, as well as essential hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, type II diabetes mellitus, and tobacco use. He also had a family history of coronary artery disease. On examination, his blood pressure was 135/85 mm Hg, and cardiac auscultation was normal without murmurs.

Electrocardiography showed normal sinus rhythm and inverted T waves in leads II, III, aVF, and V3–V6. A coronary angiogram revealed no critical stenoses of the coronary arteries. On the following day, he had multiple episodes of witnessed cardiac arrest due to polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, which required defibrillation. Routine laboratory tests, including electrolyte levels, were within normal limits. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a 6.2 × 4.0 cm mass in the left ventricle, fixed to the interventricular septum.

A 13-month-old girl was referred for evaluation of vaginal bleeding that had persisted for more than 20 days. She was born at term without complications and had unremarkable family history. On examination, her abdomen was soft, without hepatosplenomegaly. The external genitalia appeared normal; a small amount of blood and a friable mass protruding through the vaginal orifice were noted. Routine blood counts, coagulation tests, and biochemistry were within normal limits. Serum tumor markers showed a markedly elevated α-fetoprotein level of 2695 IU/ml (normal 0–6.7 IU/ml), with normal carcinoembryonic antigen and CA-125 levels. Pelvic ultrasonography revealed a ~3 cm solid, highly vascular mass within the vagina. MRI demonstrated a 28.8×16.5 mm heterogeneously enhancing tumor confined to the vaginal canal, with no invasion of adjacent structures or evidence of distant metastasis.

A 39-year-old woman presented with an 8-month history of a right submandibular lump that failed to respond to anti-inflammatory and steroid treatments. She was a former light smoker with well-controlled Hashimoto thyroiditis. Physical examination was unremarkable except for a firm right submandibular mass. She underwent a right scialoadenectomy. Initial histopathology showed a high-grade epithelial carcinoma with solid architecture, cystic areas, squamous differentiation, diffuse necrosis, and isolated intracytoplasmic mucus-containing elements. Immunohistochemical studies revealed tumor cells positive for cytokeratins AE1/AE3 and P40, and negative for LCA, S-100, CD-117, GFAP, AML, chromogranin A, and synaptophysin. Staging one month later included head and neck MRI, which demonstrated a 22-cm solid lesion in the right submandibular region, and FDG PET, which showed focal uptake (SUVmax 14.2) at that site. A right radical neck dissection (levels I–V) identified five lymph nodes with extracapsular metastatic spread. For diagnostic clarification, a pathology review was performed at a referral center. Morphologically, the tumor was a poorly differentiated carcinoma with focal abrupt keratinization. Repeat immunohistochemistry showed tumor cells positive for p63, p40, and CK8/18, and negative for synaptophysin, actin 1A4, S100, CD99, NKX2.2, and androgen receptors.

A 61-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of left nasal obstruction, occasional epistaxis, and facial pain. He denied visual changes, atopy, or prior nasal trauma.
