His weight was stable and his general health was satisfactory. On rigid nasal endoscopy, there was marked deviation of the septum to the right and a large polypoid mass filling the left nasal cavity; there was no evidence of rhinosinusitis, and the postnasal space and cervical lymph nodes were normal. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses showed well‐pneumatised sinuses and a 2.0 × 2.2 × 1.4 cm soft‐tissue mass in the anterior left nasal cavity, arising from the septum. The lesion had a smooth surface, preserved overlying mucosal lining, and was well-localised. An incisional biopsy of the septal mass was obtained for histologic evaluation.

A 16-year-old girl presented with left-sided abdominal pain radiating to her back. Her medical history was unremarkable. CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a 70 × 70 × 60 mm mass in the upper pole of the left kidney, multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules (largest 16 mm), and widespread bone metastases in the vertebrae, sacrum, and left femoral head. A laparotomy-guided biopsy established malignancy, and she underwent a left radical nephrectomy.

On gross examination, the tumor occupied the entire upper half of the kidney, appeared as a solid, white, unencapsulated lesion with sharp borders, and measured 7.5 × 7 × 7 cm. Microscopically, the lesion diffusely infiltrated renal parenchyma, separating normal elements. The neoplastic cells were small, monotonous, epithelioid with clear to pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, and were arranged in single files, cords, nests, or irregular aggregates within a collagenous matrix. Nuclei were round to oval with indistinct nucleoli. Hypercellular areas alternated with hypocellular zones of dense hyalinization or myxoid stroma. A lobular architecture was noted, with entrapped renal tubules at the centers surrounded by concentric inner hypocellular and outer hypercellular zones. Enmeshed tubules were lined by a single layer of cuboidal epithelium without atypia, showing occasional shallow papillary hyperplasia. The mitotic rate was 1 per 10 high-power fields, and focal necrosis was present.

A 75-year-old man with Usher syndrome and retinitis pigmentosa presented with a sensation of left-sided nasal blockage on deep inspiration but no pain, swelling, or epistaxis. He was legally blind in both eyes. He denied hepatitis, HIV, or other chronic viral illnesses; he was a former 60 pack-year smoker without IV drug or alcohol use and no family history of cancer. 

On nasal examination, a pink polypoid mass was seen at the left nasal orifice, with indeterminate deeper extension. 

CT of the sinuses showed a 3.1 × 4.4 × 3.2 cm mass arising from the left nasopharynx, causing rightward deviation of the nasal septum. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, as well as PET, revealed no other sites of disease. 

Biopsy of the mass demonstrated a diffuse infiltrate of large atypical cells with variably eccentric nuclei, abundant amphophilic cytoplasm, prominent nucleoli, occasional binucleated forms, and a few Dutcher bodies. Mitoses were markedly increased with atypical forms, apoptosis was prominent, and focal necrosis was present. Immunohistochemical studies showed the neoplastic cells to be positive for CD38 (strong), CD138, CD79a, MUM-1, kappa, IgA, BCL-2, and CD43, and negative for CD20, PAX-5, CD45, CD30, EMA, EBER by ISH, ALK-1, HHV8, lambda, IgG, IgM, IgD, CD56, CD5, CD10, BCL-6, BCL-1, CAM5.2/AE1, and CD117. Ki-67 labeling was variable (30–80%, overall 60%).

Laboratory studies: WBC 6.22 × 10^3/μL; hemoglobin 15.9 g/dL; platelets 244 × 10^3/μL; ANC 3.42 × 10^3/μL. Electrolytes and liver enzymes were within normal limits; calcium 10.2 mg/dL; BUN 17 mg/dL; creatinine 0.86 mg/dL. Myeloma workup showed no M protein; total protein 7.2 g/dL; albumin 4.0 g/dL; globulin 2.9 g/dL; IgG 852 mg/dL; IgA 241 mg/dL; IgM 98 mg/dL; kappa light chains 18.1 mg/L; lambda light chains 13.7 mg/L; kappa/lambda ratio 1.34. 

Bone marrow biopsy revealed normal cellularity for age (20–30%) with trilineage hematopoiesis and no increase in plasma cells.

A 37-year-old Caucasian man with no significant medical history presented with a 6-month history of lower chest and left upper quadrant discomfort. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen revealed a 7.8 × 7.3 cm irregular, partially cystic mass in the body and tail of the pancreas and two hepatic lesions consistent with metastases. Endoscopic ultrasound showed a 4.9 × 3.7 cm irregular, hypoechoic, heterogeneous, lobulated, multicystic, septated mass in the pancreatic body and tail, as well as two masses in the left hepatic lobe (1.9 × 1.5 cm) and the perihilar region (2.2 × 2.2 cm). EUS-guided FNA of the left-lobe hepatic lesion was performed via a transgastric approach with three passes of a 22-gauge needle under on-site cytopathologist assessment.

Diff-Quik and Papanicolaou-stained smears were hypercellular, showing abundant malignant epithelial cells arranged singly, in sheets, and in loosely cohesive clusters with vaguely acinar and trabecular formations. The cells had pleomorphic nuclei (round, oval, or carrot-shaped), fine granular chromatin, occasional small to prominent nucleoli, and scant to moderate cytoplasm; scattered large tumor cells with giant nuclei were also present. Cell-block sections showed tumor cells in solid sheets, thick trabeculae, and poorly formed glandular or acinar patterns, with eosinophilic granular cytoplasm, centrally located nuclei, small to conspicuous nucleoli, brisk abnormal mitoses, and necrosis. A metastatic pancreatic endocrine tumor was initially suspected.

A 51-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of progressive muscle weakness in the right lower extremity and dysesthesia in both lower extremities. Neurologic examination revealed severe loss of all sensory modalities below the L1 dermatomes. Motor examination showed monoparesis of the right lower limb with muscle strength graded 1/5 in the tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, gastrocnemius, and flexor hallucis longus muscles. Deep tendon reflexes in both lower limbs were hyperactive. He also reported slight bladder and rectal disturbances, including constipation and urinary retention.

Sagittal T2-weighted MRI of the thoracic spine showed cord expansion and a hyperintense signal extending from the Th7 to Th12 levels, surrounding both the anterior and posterior aspects of the cord. Sagittal T1-weighted images demonstrated an isointense mass lesion without a clear interface between the spinal cord and tumor. Gadolinium-enhanced images revealed a small enhancing portion. Axial T2-weighted images confirmed extension of the lesion along the bilateral surfaces of the spinal cord with severe cord compression and steep expansion at the tumor margins, suggesting an intramedullary tumor.

A 91-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 4-week history of progressive right periorbital edema associated with a gritty sensation and clear eye discharge. He denied itch, pain, visual change, fever, trauma, or sinus symptoms. He had no known allergies. On examination, the swollen eyelids showed no warmth or tenderness; the cornea and conjunctiva were normal. Visual acuity was 6/7.5 in the right eye and 6/6 in the left. He was initially diagnosed with periorbital cellulitis and given cephalexin. Six weeks later, despite two courses of cephalexin and amoxicillin/clavulanate, topical corticosteroids, and warm compresses, his right eyelid edema worsened to the point that he could not open the eye. A CT scan of the head, orbits, and sinuses showed mild to moderate inflammatory changes in the paranasal sinuses and soft-tissue swelling over the right orbit and nasal bone.

A 59-year-old man with no prior medical comorbidity presented with a 3-year history of recurrent cholangitis. Three years earlier, he was admitted with jaundice, mild upper abdominal pain, fever, and chills; ERCP showed a 14 mm dilated bile duct with sludge, and MRCP was “suggestive of a type IV choledochal cyst.” He underwent biliary stenting, with symptom resolution, but had two further admissions over the next seven months for similar symptoms; ERCP again showed a dilated extrahepatic biliary tree and left ductal system, with pus seen from the papilla, and he was treated as recurrent pyogenic cholangitis. He was referred for definitive therapy but delayed presentation until two years later with severe acute cholangitis. On examination, he was febrile (103 °F) and icteric, with hepatomegaly. Labs: total bilirubin 15 mg/dL, ALP 1098 U/L, AST 78 U/L, ALT 106 U/L, INR 1.4, WBC 16,500/mm3; hepatitis B and C serologies were negative. After antibiotic therapy, repeat ERCP attempt again yielded pus from the papilla. Cross-sectional imaging was then obtained:  
– MRCP revealed dilatation of the left hepatic duct and extrahepatic bile duct, a 23 × 58 × 36 mm cystic lesion overlapping the left hepatic duct, crowding of peripheral ducts, left lobar atrophy, and a few solid mural nodules arising from the wall of the cystic lesion.  
– Triphasic CT scan demonstrated dilation of both the extrahepatic biliary tree and left ductal system, with the left hepatic duct forming a large cistern and containing a few enhanced mural nodules in the late arterial phase.  
He was scheduled for left hepatectomy with or without extrahepatic bile duct excision and reconstruction.

An 8-year-10-month-old boy was referred by his family dentist for evaluation of an unerupted mandibular left first permanent molar. He was in good general health, with no history of orthodontic treatment or dental trauma. Clinical examination revealed a symmetrical face with a convex profile and early mixed dentition, with all incisors and first permanent molars erupted except the lower left first molar. Oral hygiene was poor, and several deciduous molars had large restorations. Extraoral examination showed a non-tender, enlarged lymph node in the retromolar region without any bone swelling. Intraoral findings included active caries, pathological abrasion, and no soft-tissue inflammation; the alveolar process dimensions were normal. Dental relations were Class II with increased overjet and overbite and mild maxillary anterior crowding. A small portion of the clinical crown of the lower left first molar was visible through the gingiva.

A panoramic radiograph revealed a well-defined calcified lesion approximately 3 cm in diameter with a radiolucent rim and adjacent cortical bone layer at the distal aspect of the unerupted tooth. Cone-beam computed tomography demonstrated a focal mass with radiodensity similar to dental hard tissues surrounded by a narrow radiolucent zone, measuring 25 × 20 × 17 mm, extending to the lower border of the mandible. The lesion displaced the developing first permanent molar downward and mesially; its roots were approximately two-thirds formed. The superior aspect of the lesion lacked overlying alveolar bone over a 20 × 6 mm area.

A 19-year-old nonsmoking man was referred for evaluation of an abnormal shadow on a routine chest radiograph. He was asymptomatic, with unremarkable physical examination findings and normal hematologic and biochemical studies. The chest radiograph showed a mass in the right infrahilar region. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) revealed a well-defined, lobulated soft-tissue density mass with small calcifications measuring 5.0 × 4.8 cm in the right lower lobe around the intermediate and basal bronchi, compressing adjacent vascular and bronchial structures; no other lymphadenopathy was observed. Dynamic CT demonstrated contrast enhancement beginning peripherally and becoming diffuse. Three-dimensional CT angiography showed a rich vascular supply from two right bronchial arteries. On magnetic resonance imaging, the lesion was isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed heterogeneous enhancement on dynamic sequences. Endobronchial ultrasound confirmed increased vascularity at the tumor surface, and bronchoscopy revealed no endobronchial abnormality. The patient's history and these imaging features supported a presumptive diagnosis of unicentric Castleman's disease.

A 56-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of abnormal bloody vaginal discharge. She had two prior vaginal deliveries, no family history of cancer or neurofibromatosis, and no café-au-lait spots. An initial biopsy of a cervical and vaginal mass yielded a diagnosis of large cell nonkeratinizing squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix and chronic inflammation with edema in the vaginal biopsy. High-risk HPV testing was negative. 

On speculum examination, a 3 cm rubbery, yellow-reddish mass was noted on the lower left vaginal wall. A repeat biopsy of the vaginal lesion and endocervical and endometrial curettage were performed. 

Pelvic MRI showed a 16 × 23 × 32 mm lesion in the proximal left vaginal wall, with low T1 and high T2 signal intensity and homogeneous post-contrast enhancement; the cervix was normal. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no lymphadenopathy or distant metastases. 

The vaginal mass was excised vaginally with a 2 cm margin of overlying mucosa, and a cold-knife cervical cone biopsy was performed. Gross examination of the vaginal specimen revealed a 3 × 4 × 2 cm yellow-reddish, rubbery mass with an irregular surface and no necrosis.

A 65-year-old man, a nonsmoker, presented with a painless mass on the right lateral border of his tongue, first noted 4–5 months earlier and gradually enlarging; speech was slightly impaired. On examination, the mucosa overlying the lesion appeared normal; the mass was doughy in consistency, non-tender, and without pulsations. His personal and family history were unremarkable. The preliminary differential diagnosis included angioedema, neurofibroma, lipoma, fibrolipoma, glandular cell tumor, schwannoma, and dermoid cyst of the tongue. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a 2 cm × 4 cm well-demarcated lesion within the intrinsic muscles of the tongue, findings reported as consistent with a lipoma. First, an incisional biopsy was performed, and it was diagnosed as lipoma.

A 16-year-old boy presented with a 2-month history of progressive weight gain, abdominal distention, acne, and hypertension. He had a moon face, hirsutism, and hyperpigmentation. Blood pressure was 142/88 mmHg. Physical examination revealed a painless mass in the right upper abdominal quadrant. 

Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 17.9 × 10^9/L, platelet count of 431 × 10^9/L, normal electrolytes, creatinine, and glucose, and a mildly elevated γ-glutamyltransferase concentration (145 U/L). Endocrine evaluation demonstrated a plasma ACTH concentration of 285 ng/L and a cortisol concentration of 785 nmol/L. MRI of the brain was negative for a pituitary tumor. MRI of the abdomen revealed a large mass in liver segments 4 through 8 without evidence of distant metastases. 

A core needle biopsy of the liver lesion was performed, and the mass was deemed surgically resectable.

A previously healthy 3-month-old male presented with a 4-day history of cough, nasal congestion, increased work of breathing during sleep, and intermittent wheezing with feeds. He was afebrile, without emesis or skin lesions, and was initially diagnosed with a viral respiratory infection and sent home with supportive care. He re-presented with worsening respiratory distress and was referred to the emergency department, where he had grunting, nasal flaring, and significant intercostal and subcostal retractions. He was started on high-flow nasal cannula at 6 L/min with clinical improvement and admitted to the pediatric ward. On the ward, his work of breathing worsened despite escalation of high-flow nasal cannula to 15 L/min with 30% FiO₂. A chest radiograph demonstrated right lung hyperinflation suggestive of air-trapping, and he was transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit. Repeat imaging again showed hyperaeration of the right lung with leftward mediastinal shift. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest revealed a 2.0 × 1.5 × 1.9 cm right hilar vascular mass causing complete occlusion of the right mainstem bronchus, associated with hyperexpansion of the right lung, decreased left lung volume, and leftward mediastinal shift.

A 25-year-old Moroccan man with no significant medical history first noted a pigmented mass on his right second toe two years ago. The lesion varied in color from dark brown to black, had irregular borders, asymmetry, a raised nodular surface, and overlying ulceration. An initial biopsy was interpreted as malignant melanoma, but the patient did not return for follow-up. 

Eighteen months later, he presented with recurrence of the lesion. On examination, there was a painless, ulcerated tumor measuring 3 cm in diameter on the right second toe, with fibrin and pigmented areas on its surface. Surrounding the primary lesion were several firm, fixed, erythematous nodules. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the foot demonstrated a lesion centered on the tendon sheaths, with loss of tissue in the first and second phalanges and filling of the first and second interphalangeal joints. The imaging appearance raised considerations of giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath, tenosynovial giant cell tumor, pigmented villonodular synovitis, synovial sarcoma, or metastatic disease.

A 72-year-old man presented with a painless gingival growth in the right mandibular premolar region, noted over the past year. He had a similar lesion excised 6 years earlier, diagnosed as an ameloblastoma, but records were unavailable. His medical history was notable for well-controlled diabetes mellitus. Examination revealed a 1×1 cm oval exophytic mass on the lingual gingiva of the right first and second premolars, with a pebbly surface, sessile base, and firm consistency; no cervical lymphadenopathy was present. Panoramic radiography showed no bone involvement. The initial working diagnosis was pyogenic granuloma, although recurrence of ameloblastoma could not be excluded. An incisional biopsy was performed, and microscopic examination showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia.

A 77-year-old man presented with a 3-week history of right iliac fossa pain radiating to the inguinal region and right testicle. He denied weight loss, hemoptysis, changes in bowel habits, bleeding, or urinary symptoms. His surgical history included total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid carcinoma in 2021, and he smoked 20 cigarettes daily. Family history was notable for lung, cervical, and breast cancers, and a brother with multiple myeloma.

On examination, the abdomen was tender to mid and deep palpation in the right iliac fossa without peritoneal signs, palpable masses, or inguinal lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests were within normal limits. An abdominal CT scan with contrast showed a stromal-dependent tumor on the lateral wall of the cecum with surrounding fat infiltration. Colonoscopy revealed no intraluminal lesion.

A 24-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 4-month history of dry cough and a 12-kg weight loss, accompanied over the preceding month by fever, progressive dyspnea, and bilateral knee pain. She initially avoided in-person evaluation during the COVID-19 pandemic and self-managed symptomatically. On presentation, she was febrile and tachypneic (respiratory rate 24/min), with a room-air oxygen saturation of 94%. Breath sounds were absent over the entire left hemithorax, with stony-dull percussion. Examination also revealed bilateral firm supraclavicular lymphadenopathy and eczematous lesions on the lower limbs; there was no organomegaly.

Laboratory studies showed microcytic hypochromic anemia, neutrophilic leukocytosis, mild lymphocytopenia, and an elevated lactate dehydrogenase level; renal, liver, and thyroid function tests were normal. A chest radiograph demonstrated near-total homogeneous opacification of the left hemithorax with contralateral mediastinal shift. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax revealed a large heterogeneously enhancing soft-tissue mass occupying the entire left hemithorax with only a small aerated patch in the left lower lobe. Enlarged perivascular, subcarinal, supraclavicular, and left axillary lymph nodes were present. The mass extended extrathoracically into the anterior chest wall and left breast, with a small left pleural effusion, minimal pericardial effusion with nodular deposits, and focal erosion of the left third anterior rib.

Based on the history and imaging findings, a malignant etiology was highly probable and the differentials entertained were bronchogenic carcinoma (with mediastinal lymph node spread and chest wall invasion), lymphoma with parenchymal and pleural involvement, Askin tumor, pulmonary sarcoma, primitive neuroectodermal tumor, germ cell tumor like teratoma, and other rare entities.

A 31-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a left nasal conjunctival lesion present for two years without growth or change. He denied ocular irritation, vision changes, fevers, night sweats, or weight loss. His ocular history included refractive error; medical history was notable for seasonal allergies and a remote jaw fracture repair. He took no medications. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 OD and 20/20 OS. Extraocular motility, confrontation visual fields, and intraocular pressures were within normal limits. On external examination, small, non-tender submandibular lymph nodes were palpable. Slit-lamp examination showed an elevated, glistening, well-circumscribed salmon-colored patch measuring 9.5 × 7.5 mm on the nasal bulbar conjunctiva with overlying superficial vessels and apparent tortuous feeder vessels. Dilated fundus examination was unremarkable in both eyes. Given the lesion’s appearance and possible lymphadenopathy, an excisional biopsy was performed using a “no-touch technique,” with placement of an amniotic membrane graft.

A 69-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of discomfort and pain in his left testis. Two years earlier, he had undergone a laparoscopic left radical nephrectomy for renal cell carcinoma (grade II, pT1b N0M0) with negative preoperative CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. On examination, there was no groin lymphadenopathy or hernia. The prostate was soft and unremarkable on digital rectal examination. Both testes were normal in size without palpable masses, but palpation of the upper pole of the left testis elicited pain, and the overlying scrotal skin was normal.  
Scrotal ultrasonography revealed a 15×12 mm hypoechoic mass at the upper pole of the left testis, highly suspicious for malignancy. Laboratory studies—including white blood cell count, C-reactive protein, complete blood count, coagulation studies, and urinalysis—were normal. Serum levels of alpha-fetoprotein, human chorionic gonadotropin, and lactate dehydrogenase were within normal limits.

A 27-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a left adrenal tumor. At age 24 she was found to have hypertension and dyslipidemia and experienced weight gain; she was treated with azilsartan and esaxerenone. An abdominal CT at another hospital revealed a left adrenal mass, and Cushing syndrome was suspected.

On admission, her BMI was 25.1 kg/m2, and blood pressure was 144/90 mmHg despite antihypertensive therapy. She had a moon face. Laboratory studies showed eosinopenia and an elevated total cholesterol level; serum electrolytes and glucose tolerance were normal. Plasma ACTH was low at 2.5 pg/mL, serum cortisol was 15.2 μg/dL, and DHEA-S was slightly decreased. A 24-hour urinary free cortisol was elevated at 302 μg/day; nighttime serum cortisol was 16.9 μg/dL, and a 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test showed incomplete suppression (14.4 μg/dL), confirming ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome. Plasma renin activity and aldosterone concentration were within reference ranges.

Imaging studies showed a 2-cm left adrenal mass with a mean unenhanced CT attenuation of 44 Hounsfield units and heterogeneous enhancement. 131I-adosterol scintigraphy showed no uptake in the tumor, whereas 18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated intense uptake (SUVmax 14.9). These radiological findings were atypical for a cortisol-producing adenoma, and the possibility of adrenal carcinoma could not be excluded. Adrenal venous sampling confirmed unilateral cortisol secretion from the left adrenal mass.

A 40-year-old Japanese woman (gravida 2, para 2) presented with prolonged menorrhagia and severe anemia. Her history was notable for cervical carcinoma in situ treated with conization 10 years earlier, without recurrence. Six years before admission, transvaginal ultrasound identified a 3.5-cm uterine leiomyoma, which grew to 5 cm two years later. Over the last year, clinicians noted a 5-cm extrauterine mass protruding from the posterior uterine wall. On admission, MRI revealed a 10 × 9 × 7 cm pelvic mass in the left posterolateral myometrial wall with extrauterine extension and hemorrhagic cysts. Total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingectomy was performed for suspicion of uterine sarcoma or degenerated leiomyoma.

An 82-year-old Caucasian woman with no significant medical history was referred after biopsies of a longstanding pubic skin lesion. She was asymptomatic and in her usual state of health. On examination, there was a 2-cm ulcerated lesion on the pubis without palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy. Genital examination was normal. A biopsy performed at an outside center was reported as poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma, and excision margins were positive. At multidisciplinary review, a wide local excision was performed. Histologic examination of the reexcision specimen revealed a 4-mm–deep dermal lesion extending to the hypodermis, with nuclear atypia, high mitotic activity, an ulcerative surface with fibrinous leukocytic exudate, and vascular emboli; margins were clear by 1 cm.

A 35-year-old woman presented with mild right upper-quadrant abdominal pain without fever, jaundice, or weight loss. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. Physical examination of the abdomen was normal. Laboratory tests showed an alpha-fetoprotein concentration of 14 922.6 ng/mL (normal < 20 ng/mL); concentrations of CA 19-9, CEA, and HCG were within normal limits. Liver enzymes (ALT, AST) and bilirubin were normal. Serologic tests for hepatitis B and C viruses were negative.  
Abdominal ultrasound revealed a well-defined 13 cm lesion in the right hepatic lobe with mixed echogenicity (solid and cystic), scattered calcifications, and a small adjacent mixed-echogenicity satellite nodule; color Doppler imaging showed poor internal perfusion. Noncontrast CT confirmed a heterogeneous right-lobe mass measuring 13 × 8.6 × 9 cm containing fat and calcifications. MRI demonstrated a mixed cystic–solid lesion with multiple septa, internal fat signal, poor enhancement of the solid components, invasion of the liver capsule and right hemidiaphragm, and a 1.4 cm satellite nodule immediately inferior to the main mass. No lesions were identified in other organs.

A 75-year-old woman presented with a 1-week history of binocular horizontal diplopia. She had been treated for atypical pneumonia on the medical ward and reported several months of anorexia and weight loss. Sputum tests for tuberculosis were negative. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 98 mm/hour and a C-reactive protein level greater than 139 mg/dl; a temporal artery biopsy was performed and reported as normal. On ophthalmic examination, her best-corrected visual acuity was 6/6 in both eyes. There was subtle localized episcleral injection near the insertion of the right lateral rectus muscle. The optic discs and maculae were normal bilaterally. Ocular motility testing revealed an isolated abduction deficit of the right eye.

A 13-month-old girl was referred for evaluation of a sublingual mass. She had a 7-month history of progressive swelling in the right submandibular region and floor of the mouth, associated with swallowing difficulties. On examination, the mass was soft, movable, non-tender, and the overlying mucosa appeared normal. Ultrasonography showed a well-defined ovoid lesion adjacent to the right submandibular gland, with heterogeneous internal echoes and multiple small foci; Doppler imaging revealed internal vascular flow. Fine-needle aspiration yielded abundant cheese-type material.

A 55-year-old man was referred for evaluation after new-onset anemia, borborygmi, and difficulty passing stool for more than 2 years. He also reported an unexplained 7 kg weight loss. His medical history was notable for type 2 diabetes managed with metformin; he had no prior cancers and no tobacco use. Physical examination revealed normal vital signs and a digital rectal examination demonstrated a large, firm, solid mass compressing the rectum posteriorly. Laboratory tests showed mild iron deficiency anemia; other values were within normal limits.

An attempted colonoscopy was aborted due to inadequate bowel preparation. Pelvic MRI and contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax and abdomen were performed. MRI demonstrated a well-demarcated retrorectal lesion measuring 14 × 9.5 × 17.5 cm with heterogeneous signal: a central cystic component without diffusion restriction and a solid periphery showing marginally increased diffusion signal and marginally decreased ADC values. Post-gadolinium images showed enhancement of the peripheral areas but not the center. The lesion caused severe mass effect with anterior and lateral displacement of the rectum and superior displacement of the bladder; there was no bone destruction. CT showed a homogenous hypodense center without enhancement and a heterogeneously enhancing peripheral rim. No ascites, lymphadenopathy, or distant metastases were identified.

A 29-year-old woman was referred after incidental discovery of a middle mediastinal cystic lesion. In April 2017, she was asymptomatic. CT and MRI showed a 5.1 × 4.8 cm cystic mass posterior to the superior vena cava and lateral to the trachea and esophagus, findings that were interpreted as suggestive of a bronchogenic cyst. She was lost to follow-up and returned in March 2020 with a few days’ history of chest and neck pain, dysphagia, and dyspnea at rest. On examination, she was tachypneic and tender to palpation over the right side of her neck, chest, and back. A CT angiogram revealed an 8 cm × 10 cm × 7.4 cm non-enhancing, low-attenuation mass in the right middle mediastinum extending to the right superior mediastinum, abutting the right lung apex and causing significant extrinsic compression of the distal trachea.

A 35-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of pain and progressive swelling in the right inguinal region. He had no significant medical history. On examination, a hard, tender mass measuring 6 cm was palpable in the right inguinal area without overlying erythema; it was fixed in relation to the deep plane, and there was no sensory or motor deficit in the right lower limb. An inguinal ultrasound revealed a solid-cystic mass measuring 60 mm. Pelvic MRI showed a mass behind the inguinal ligament and fascia, measuring 40 mm in anteroposterior diameter, 60 mm in height, and 62 mm in transverse diameter. The mass was adherent to the iliac muscle with a compromised safety margin and abutted the common femoral artery without evidence of invasion. No distant metastases were identified.

A 50-year-old woman with a 6-month history of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma in remission after six cycles of chemotherapy (negative PET-CT and bone marrow biopsy) presented with a 20-day history of pain and redness in her left eye. She was initially diagnosed with primary angle-closure glaucoma and acute iridocyclitis and treated with timolol, brimonidine, and brinzolamide eye drops plus Nd:YAG laser iridectomy, but her intraocular pressure remained elevated and pain worsened. A local ophthalmologist then performed phacoemulsification with intraocular lens implantation and trabeculectomy with adjunctive 5-fluorouracil, but the effects were temporary and pain persisted. On examination at our hospital, visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and light perception in the left; intraocular pressure was 11 mm Hg in the right eye and 50 mm Hg in the left. The left eye had conjunctival hyperemia, corneal edema, and hyphema. High-frequency ultrasound biomicroscopy showed intumescence of the ciliary body roots in both eyes, complete closure of the anterior chamber angles, and destruction of the anatomical structure of the left eye. Given her history of lymphoma and these ocular findings, rare systemic involvement was suspected. Differential diagnosis included secondary lymphomatous involvement of the iris and amelanotic melanoma.

A 28-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 2, presented with a 4-year history of a gradually enlarging mass on the left vulva. She first noted an itchy swelling the size of a thumb shortly after the delivery of her second child. Over the next four years, the lesion grew steadily, and she also reported an increase in leucorrhoea but denied bleeding, trauma, or sexually transmitted disease symptoms. Her menstrual history was unremarkable. She had used hormonal contraception (three-monthly progesterone injections followed by combined oral contraceptive pills) for three years. She had no other medical or surgical history, did not smoke, and denied alcohol or drug use.

On examination, she was obese (BMI 36.3 kg/m²). Gynecologic inspection revealed a large, firm, nontender, nonulcerating, skin-colored pedunculated mass measuring approximately 15 × 10 × 8 cm arising from the left labium majora. The right labium and clitoral hood were also enlarged and firm, measuring 9 × 4 × 2 cm. An internal pelvic examination was within normal limits. Routine laboratory test results were within normal limits. Given the size and firmness of the lesion, a biopsy was planned for definitive diagnosis.

A 3-week-old male Sprague-Dawley rat was housed under standard conditions and assigned to a control group in a pharmacological study. At 7 weeks of age, the rat appeared clinically normal and was euthanized under anesthesia. At necropsy, the liver and other organs appeared grossly unremarkable, and serum AST and ALT levels were within normal limits.

A sample from the left lateral liver lobe was fixed in formalin, embedded, and stained with hematoxylin and eosin, Azan, and Watanabe’s silver stain. Histologically, there were multifocal basophilic foci located predominantly in the perilobular region. Within these foci, polygonal to short spindle-shaped cells formed small nests and sheets within dilated sinusoids without encapsulation. The tumor cells exhibited clear cell borders, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, hyperchromatic nuclei, frequent mitotic figures, and sparse hepatocellular necrosis. Narrow spaces containing erythrocytes were noted between tumor cells, and local invasion into adjacent blood vessels was seen. Azan and silver stains demonstrated reticular fibers forming a loosely connected, irregular network within tumor cell aggregates.

A 14-year-old boy presented to the emergency department with right knee pain and difficulty flexing the knee after falling down a flight of stairs at school. He had no significant past medical or surgical history. On examination, there was tenderness of the right knee, which worsened with stress maneuvers. Vital signs were normal.

Plain radiographs of the right knee showed no fracture but revealed a poorly defined radiolucent zone on the distal medial femoral metaphysis with a thickened cortical lining of the medial femoral condyle and no adjacent soft-tissue mass or aggressive periosteal response.

A CT scan demonstrated an irregular sclerotic cortical layer on the posteromedial aspect of the distal femur at the insertion sites of the medial gastrocnemius and adductor magnus tendons, with no soft-tissue mass or aggressive periosteal reaction.

MRI of the right knee showed slight edema in the cortical irregularity area and at the tendon attachment sites, minimal contrast enhancement in these regions, and no underlying bone marrow edema or adjacent soft-tissue mass.

A 23-year-old man with known congenital adrenal hyperplasia presented with right-sided testicular pain and a large right testicular lump. He reported adherence to prednisolone and fludrocortisone. On examination, both testes were diffusely swollen, enlarged, and nodular; there were no signs of hyperandrogenism or Cushing syndrome. Laboratory studies showed elevated ACTH and 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels, with normal urea, electrolytes, and morning testosterone. Scrotal ultrasound demonstrated that normal testicular parenchyma was entirely replaced by ill-defined hypoechoic hypervascular masses, with gross bilateral enlargement. A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no distant metastases, and the partially imaged testes were hyperattenuating and avidly enhanced relative to skeletal muscle. MRI revealed both testes enlarged to 7 cm with lobulated margins, homogeneous iso- to hypointense replacement of parenchyma that was hyperintense to skeletal muscle on T1 and T2, intense homogeneous postcontrast enhancement, and generalized diffusion restriction; paratesticular structures and pelvic lymph nodes appeared normal. This appearance was thought to be most in keeping with an unusual presentation of testicular adrenal rest tumour, however, a primary testicular germ cell tumour could not be definitively excluded on imaging and a biopsy was performed for confirmation.

A 15-day-old female infant was referred for intraoral masses causing feeding problems. She was born at 39 weeks’ gestation (birth weight 3200 g; Apgar scores 9 and 10) by normal vaginal delivery. The lesions were first noted at birth and originated from the anterior mandibular alveolus, occupying the oral entrance and partially protruding outside the mouth. On examination, there was a 5×4 cm reddish, pedunculated, smooth, erythematous mass with surface scales attached to the anterior mandibular gingiva; two smaller, similar tumors were adjacent. Palpation revealed firm, non-compressible, non-tender lesions that prevented mouth closure but did not cause airway compromise. A nasogastric tube was placed for feeding. General physical examination and laboratory studies were otherwise normal.

A 30‐year‐old man with no significant medical history was referred for recurrent tonsillitis. While awaiting tonsillectomy, he developed new‐onset snoring, a sense of airway obstruction relieved by neck extension, and a lump‐in‐throat sensation. He denied smoking or alcohol use.

On examination, flexible nasendoscopy showed a firm, smooth swelling arising from the left lateral pharyngeal wall, extending from the soft palate superiorly to the level of the epiglottis inferiorly. The oral cavity, oropharynx, larynx, and piriform fossae appeared normal.

Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well‐defined 2.9×1.9 cm low‐signal mass on T1-weighted precontrast images, inseparable from the left longus capitis muscle, displacing well‐preserved prevertebral fat anteriorly, with no locally aggressive features. There was uniform enhancement with contrast and no diffusion restriction. Overall, the appearances were in keeping with a benign soft tissue tumor.

Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed absence of calcification or enhancement, supporting a benign process with no aggressive features. Fine‐needle aspiration of the neck and biopsy of the pharyngeal mass showed only inflammatory cells and numerous benign squamous epithelial cells with occasional macrophages.

The case was discussed at a head and neck multidisciplinary meeting, and local excision of the lesion was recommended to relieve symptoms.

A man in his early 40s was referred for evaluation of a 2-week history of a lump in his throat. His medical history was notable for type 1 diabetes mellitus complicated by focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, leading to end-stage renal disease and a live-donor kidney transplant 2 years earlier. He was maintained on a calcineurin inhibitor and a corticosteroid for immunosuppression and also had hypertension. He denied fevers, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. Fiberoptic laryngoscopy showed a 30×20 mm reddish-purple, irregularly hypertrophic, ulcerated lesion at the base of the tongue. Examination of the neck revealed enlarged cervical lymph nodes. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and biochemistry, were within normal limits, and HIV testing was negative. Cervical ultrasound demonstrated lymph nodes measuring up to 25 mm in diameter.

A 54-year-old Nigerian man was brought to the emergency department in an acute confusional state. He reported a three-week history of colicky abdominal pain associated with intermittent vomiting, hiccupping, and polydipsia; he denied weight loss, hematemesis, or rectal bleeding. The day before presentation, he underwent oesophago-gastro-duodenoscopy, which showed gastritis and a gastric ulcer in the antrum and pre-pyloric region, with a large volume of retained gastric contents despite a 10-hour fast; biopsies were taken. His medical history was notable only for hypertension; he had no prior abdominal surgery or family history of fibromatoses or polyposis syndromes.

On examination, he was febrile, dehydrated, and disoriented, with no focal neurologic deficits. Chest and cardiovascular examinations were unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed mild distention and tenderness without peritoneal signs or palpable masses; bowel sounds were scanty. Rectal examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed mild normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL), leukocytosis (WBC 29.5 × 10^9/L), elevated C-reactive protein (238 mg/L), impaired renal function (urea 23.4 mmol/L, creatinine 233 µmol/L), severe hyponatremia (Na 104 mmol/L), low serum osmolality (244 mosmol/kg), low urinary sodium (27 mmol/L), low urinary osmolality (206 mosmol/kg), and elevated lactate (3.4 mmol/L). A chest radiograph and head CT were normal.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed two soft-tissue masses: one measuring 6.8 cm in the mid abdomen, causing proximal small-bowel obstruction, and a second 5 cm lesion adjacent to the ileocecal region, with a small amount of free fluid.

A 65-year-old man presented with several months of progressive, bilateral pitting leg edema and episodes of paroxysmal dyspnea. The swelling initially involved the feet and ankles and then extended above the knees; there was no erythema, tenderness, or palpable mass. He had a history of hypercholesterolemia managed with atorvastatin, mild exercise-induced asthma on montelukast, and a remote nephrolithiasis episode; he did not smoke or use alcohol regularly. He denied chest pain, orthopnea, hemoptysis, or symptoms of liver or kidney disease. Vital signs were normal. Physical examination was notable only for bilateral lower-extremity pitting edema.

Evaluations of the cardiorespiratory system—including electrocardiography, chest radiography, stress echocardiography, spirometry, and diffusing capacity—were normal, as were hepatic and renal function tests. Serum albumin concentration and routine blood and urine studies were within normal limits. The edema transiently improved with compression stockings and diuretic therapy.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen revealed a large mass superior to the right kidney with compression of the intrahepatic inferior vena cava and upstream venous distension. Laboratory studies showed an elevated serum cortisol level of 18.0 µg/dL (normal < 11.3 µg/dL), 24-hour urinary cortisol of 73 µg (normal 3.5–45 µg), and serum dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate of 734 µg/dL (normal 35–212 µg/dL). Serum adrenocorticotropic hormone was suppressed at < 5.0 pg/mL (normal 7.2–63 pg/mL), and free testosterone was low at 28 pg/mL (normal 30–140 pg/mL). Measurements of plasma and urine metanephrines, estradiol, renin, and aldosterone were normal.

A man in his 70s with known mantle cell lymphoma on zanubrutinib was admitted for hypoxic respiratory failure due to bacterial pneumonia and treated with cefepime and azithromycin. Because of immunosuppression, trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole was added with prednisone (initially 80 mg/day, tapered to 20 mg/day) for presumed Pneumocystis jiroveci prophylaxis. One week later, he developed a diffuse morbilliform rash beginning on his trunk. On examination, there were edematous pink macules and papules on the trunk and extremities, most prominent over the lower chest and back. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 216 000 cells/µL with eosinophilia (8800 cells/µL); a metabolic panel was unremarkable. Suspecting a drug hypersensitivity reaction, cefepime, azithromycin, and trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole were discontinued, and topical triamcinolone was initiated. After one week, the rash showed minimal improvement.

A 64-year-old man, a current smoker (20 cigarettes daily) and moderate drinker (20 g alcohol daily), presented with a several-month history of progressively worsening pain in his right lower limb. He reported no weight loss, fevers or known liver disease. On examination, he was afebrile, and there was marked functional impotence of the right lower limb without overlying skin changes. Laboratory studies showed: AFP 3.4 ng/mL (normal ≤ 8), AST 133 U/L, ALT 35 U/L, ALP 161 U/L, GGT 95 U/L, bilirubin 1 mg/dL. A contrast-enhanced multidetector CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a large, solid, contrast-enhanced mass involving the right psoas, iliac, and gluteus minor muscles with infiltration of the right iliac bone and thinning of the acetabular roof. Pelvic MRI confirmed a destructive, heterogeneous, highly vascularized lesion of the right iliac blade.

A 56-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of intermittent vertigo. She had no hearing loss, tinnitus, headache, or other neurologic symptoms. Both neurologic and otorhinolaryngologic examinations were unremarkable. Audiometric testing, including auditory brainstem responses, was normal bilaterally. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed a 5.5 × 3.8 mm well-demarcated lesion in the left cerebellopontine angle cistern, immediately above the internal auditory canal. On MRI, the lesion was homogeneously hyperintense on T1-weighted sequences and became hypointense on fat-saturated sequences.

A 51-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of progressive pelvic heaviness and chronic constipation without urinary or gynecological symptoms. Her medical history was notable for a total hysterectomy for uterine fibroids performed 8 years earlier. On physical examination, a firm, regular-bordered mass was palpable in the left flank with posterior and iliac extension. Laboratory studies, including complete blood counts, serum electrolytes, renal and liver function tests, CA-125, and carcinoembryonic antigen, were all within normal limits. Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 32 × 29 × 12 cm retroperitoneal soft-tissue mass that was isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images and showed homogeneous enhancement after contrast administration.

A 37-year-old woman was evaluated for deformity of the left pupil. She had no ocular pain or vision loss. On slit-lamp examination, there was a neoformation in the inferotemporal quadrant of the iris causing dyscoria, corectopia, and uveal ectropion. The lesion was light pink in color and richly vascularized.  
Ultrasound biomicroscopy demonstrated a mass localized to the iris stroma, poorly demarcated from adjacent tissue, protruding into the iridocorneal angle but without evident invasion of the ciliary body.  
Fluorescein angiography of the iris showed numerous newly formed vessels with abundant leakage within the lesion.  
After a complete workup, suspicion of an uveal amelanotic melanoma was raised, and surgical excision of the lesion was planned.

An 11-year-old girl presented with an 8-month history of a painless swelling in the left frontoparietal region of her scalp that had gradually increased in size. She had no headache, vomiting, fever, seizures, or focal neurologic deficits. On local examination, there was a hard, non-tender mass measuring approximately 50 × 48 mm with normal overlying skin. Sensory and motor examinations were normal, and her general and systemic examinations revealed no abnormalities. Routine blood tests were within normal limits.  
A CT scan of the head showed a well-defined lytic lesion in the left frontoparietal bone. Subsequent MRI revealed a 60 × 53 mm lytic calvarial lesion in the same region with a characteristic sun-ray periosteal reaction, and both subgaleal and epidural soft-tissue components causing mild bulging of the underlying brain parenchyma.

A 48-year-old perimenopausal woman (gravida 2, para 2) presented with 4 months of lower abdominal pain and intermenstrual bleeding. Vital signs were unremarkable. On pelvic examination, an 8 × 8 cm solid, ulcerated, necrotic mass protruded through the cervix into the vagina, obscuring the cervical body. Hemoglobin was 10.0 g/dL; other blood counts and biochemistry were normal. Transvaginal ultrasound could not be performed because of the unreducible, tender mass. Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis showed a well-circumscribed, low-density, pedunculated mass (9 × 8 cm) in the cervical canal and vagina, attached to the posterior uterine corpus by a 5 cm stalk with slight contrast enhancement. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a 9 × 8 cm lobulated mass distending the cervix and vagina, connected to the myometrium by a 4.5 cm stalk containing thin linear low-signal structures (“Broccoli sign”). The mass had heterogeneous T2 signal with peripheral hemorrhagic foci hyperintense on T1 and DWI, but no true diffusion restriction. On dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging, it showed progressive heterogeneous enhancement paralleling the uterine myometrium.

A 67-year-old previously healthy woman with a 55–pack-year smoking history was referred for evaluation of a mediastinal mass incidentally noted on chest radiograph several months after an episode of pneumonia. She denied weight loss, fever, chills, night sweats, chest pain, or shortness of breath. Physical examination was unremarkable. Vital signs were stable except for blood pressure of 150/90 mm Hg. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and basic metabolic panel, were within normal limits except for a serum potassium of 3.2 mmol/L.

Low-dose CT of the thorax showed a 19 × 21 mm nodule in the left upper lobe, left hilar lymphadenopathy, and intralobular septal thickening suspicious for pulmonary venous obstruction. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest confirmed a 3.3 × 2.4 cm mass in the aortopulmonary window that extended proximally into the left superior pulmonary veins and into the left atrium. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a 3.0 cm × 1.6 cm mobile, hypoechoic mass with a variegated surface attached to the roof of the left atrium, projecting from the pulmonary vein and occupying over half of the atrial cavity. MRI of the brain, CT abdomen and pelvis, and nuclear bone scan showed no evidence of metastatic disease, and an incidental adrenal lesion was characterized as a benign adenoma on follow-up MRI. A multidisciplinary team including neurology, thoracic/cardiac surgery, pulmonary, and interventional radiology was convened to plan further diagnostic evaluation and management.

A 25-year-old nulliparous woman presented with 2 months of right lower abdominal pain without fever. She had no significant medical history and regular menstrual cycles. On examination, there was a mobile mass in the right lower abdomen. Pelvic ultrasonography showed a right paraovarian cyst with a smooth outline, areas of vaguely nodular wall thickening, and uniformly hypoechoic content without a solid component. Serum β-hCG was <3 IU/L, and other laboratory studies were normal. Initial management was observation, but after 2 months her abdominal pain worsened, and she underwent laparotomy. An 8-cm smooth-walled ovarian cyst was identified; yellowish fluid was drained, and the cyst was removed intact. On gross examination, the cyst was thin-walled (0.2–0.5 cm), with a smooth external surface and multiple small (0.2–0.3 cm), whitish, firm, sometimes coalescent vegetations on the internal surface. Microscopic examination showed slightly atypical serous or endometrioid epithelial linings with an atypical stromal component. The mesenchymal stroma resembled endometrial stromal sarcoma, with slight-to-moderate atypia, fibrous foci, prominent subepithelial cuffs of cellular stroma, intracystic protrusions, and scattered hyaline globules. Up to two mitotic figures per 10 high-power fields were seen in both stromal and epithelial elements. There was no vascular or perineural invasion, the ovarian capsule was intact, and no sarcomatous overgrowth was identified.

A 19‐year‐old South Sudanese woman presented with right upper‐quadrant abdominal pain and nonbloody vomiting for several days. She denied fever, night sweats, weight loss, jaundice, or bleeding. She had no significant medical or family history and did not smoke or drink. On examination she was pale, afebrile, and hemodynamically stable. There was tender hepatomegaly but no palpable lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9 g/dL, normal white‐cell and platelet counts, normal electrolytes, renal function, liver enzymes, bilirubin, albumin, and coagulation studies. Serologic testing was positive for hepatitis B virus (confirmed by PCR) and negative for hepatitis C and HIV. Alpha‐fetoprotein and carcinoembryonic antigen levels were within normal limits. An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 10 × 13 cm hypoechoic mass in the left hepatic lobe and mild ascites; cytologic analysis of ascitic fluid was negative for malignant cells. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen revealed a 14 × 14 cm well-defined left‐lobe mass that was hypodense in the arterial phase, retained contrast in the venous phase, and showed mixed enhancement on delayed images. The spleen was normal, and there was no enlargement of intra-abdominal lymph nodes.

To exclude extrahepatic malignancy, upper endoscopy was normal, CT scans of the chest and neck showed no lesions or lymphadenopathy, and a bone marrow biopsy demonstrated normal cellularity.

A 75-year-old Caucasian man presented with progressive dysphagia. He had no significant past medical or family history. Physical examination was unremarkable. Complete blood count, chemistry, and tumor markers were within normal limits. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a polypoid mass in the mid-to-distal esophagus (31–39 cm from the incisors) measuring 8.0 cm with distal mucosal erosion. Brushing cytology suggested a poorly differentiated small cell neoplasm; immunohistochemical analysis of the cell block showed tumor cells negative for cytokeratins (MNF116) and chromogranin. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen confirmed a bulky esophageal lesion extending from the carina to the cardia, multiple hypodense lesions in all eight liver segments, and enlarged pericardial, lesser curve, and celiac lymph nodes; PET-CT findings were concordant. Exploratory laparotomy revealed widespread nodules on the diaphragmatic peritoneum, omentum, and paracardial region; biopsies were obtained. The patient received no further therapy and died three months later.  
Histologic examination of the paracardial nodules showed a diffuse proliferation of polygonal and spindle cells with round to oval nuclei, clear to granular cytoplasm, and radial perivascular arrangement; necrosis was absent and mitotic count was three per 50 high-power fields. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated strong positivity in tumor cells for HMB45, S100, vimentin, microphthalmia transcription factor (Mitf), and HHF35; staining was negative for desmin, CD45 (LCA), CD99, chromogranin, and cytokeratins.

A 32-year-old woman presented 4 months postpartum with intermittent fevers up to 38.5 °C, malaise, unclear blood loss, and right upper-quadrant flank pain. She had no significant past medical or family history. On exam, her temperature was 38.5 °C; she had right upper-quadrant tenderness without jaundice or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory tests showed a normal white blood cell count, C-reactive protein 181 mg/L, AST 31 U/L, ALT 49 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 466 U/L, γ-glutamyl transferase 424 U/L, and normal bilirubin (6 μmol/L). Serum CA 19-9, α-fetoprotein, hepatitis serologies, and echinococcosis markers were all negative. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a round, encapsulated 8 cm lesion in liver segment IVa/b. A noncontrast CT confirmed the 8 cm liver mass and excluded urolithiasis. Contrast CT and MRI of the upper abdomen demonstrated an 8 cm × 8 cm lesion in segment IVa/b “suspected to be a liver adenoma.” The case was discussed at a multidisciplinary tumor board, and a PET-CT was performed, which “showed the known lesion as a metabolically active tumor resembling an inflammatory pseudotumor of the liver or a malignant tumor of unclear origin.” No other lesions were identified.

A 65-year-old man with hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and chronic angina presented with sudden onset of left visual-field deficit and left upper-extremity weakness while working at his computer. On arrival, his visual symptoms had resolved but examination showed partial left-sided hemianopia, 4/5 strength in the left arm with pronator drift, a body-mass index of 40.5 kg/m2, blood pressure of 147/82 mm Hg, and normal heart sounds. A chest radiograph showed mild cardiomegaly. Noncontrast head CT was unremarkable. His NIH Stroke Scale score was 3, and he received intravenous tPA without clinical improvement. Brain MRI revealed multiple small, scattered, bilateral cortical infarcts in the right frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes and in the left occipital lobe, all with diffusion restriction and corresponding ADC map abnormalities. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a small, rounded echodensity on the right coronary cusp of the aortic valve. Transesophageal echocardiography confirmed a structurally normal aortic valve with a round, pedunculated, mobile mass measuring approximately 11×15 mm attached to the right coronary cusp, partially prolapsing into the left ventricular outflow tract.

A 9-year-old boy, otherwise healthy, presented with 3 months of daily bright-red hematuria accompanied by intermittent dysuria and lower abdominal pain. An initial renal and bladder ultrasound was unremarkable. Cystoscopy revealed a sessile mass in the left posterolateral bladder wall with prominent dilated submucosal vessels. To further characterize the lesion, a CT urogram was obtained, demonstrating a lobulated mass along the left bladder wall without evidence of extravesical extension. Repeat cystoscopy confirmed a 1.5-cm lesion with a wide-based stalk, marked submucosal hypervascularity, and areas of active bleeding; the mass was biopsied and fulgurated. Histopathology showed acute inflammation with eosinophils, leading to a diagnosis of eosinophilic cystitis. Allergy evaluation yielded no identifiable triggers, and the patient was started on antihistamines and bladder hygiene measures. 

Three years later, he returned with recurrent gross hematuria, passage of clots, and mild dysuria. A repeat bladder ultrasound revealed a focal nodular area of thickening along the left lateral wall without internal Doppler flow. Cystoscopy showed an increased number and size of vascular lesions, which were biopsied and fulgurated again. To assess for an underlying vascular malformation, pelvic MRI was performed; it demonstrated an enhancing sessile lesion arising from the left bladder wall without extravesical extension.

A 19-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of severe holocephalic headaches associated with nausea, occasional vomiting, and generalized weakness, which worsened over the 5 days before admission. She had no prior medical history and took no regular medications. A noncontrast head CT revealed a right parietal extra-axial mass measuring approximately 6.2 × 5.5 × 5.8 cm, with surrounding vasogenic edema, mass effect, and a midline shift. Subsequent brain MRI demonstrated a large right parietal extra-axial lesion and two additional right temporal lobe lesions. All lesions exhibited diffusely increased T1 signal intensity without significant contrast enhancement.

A 51-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 10-month history of intensely pruritic papules on sun-exposed areas of his extremities, causing sleep disturbance. He had no prior dermatologic evaluation and no personal or family history of cancer. His medical history was significant for arterial hypertension, hyperuricemia, coronary heart disease, idiopathic end-stage kidney disease (with two kidney transplants in 1990 and 2001 complicated by rejections), peritoneal dialysis (2007–2017), and ongoing hemodialysis since 2017. He also carried a factor V Leiden mutation. His medications included felodipine, bisoprolol, clonidine, ramipril, urapidil, cholecalciferol, aspirin, allopurinol, phenprocoumon, thyroxine, iodine, fluvastatin, calcium acetate, omeprazole, and sevelamer carbonate. 

On examination, there were approximately 100 scaly, ulcerated papules and nodules measuring 3–20 mm scattered over the sun-exposed upper and lower extremities. There were no signs of chronic actinic damage, mucosal involvement, or lymphadenopathy.

Tangential biopsies and fusiform excisions of the 18 largest nodules on the upper extremities were performed because cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma was suspected. Histopathology of 15 lesions showed "prominent keratinization, slightly enlarged, hyperchromatic nuclei with abundant amounts of cytoplasm, and moderate atypia," findings described as conclusive for "well-differentiated SCC or keratoacanthoma." The remaining three excised lesions were diagnosed as inverted verrucae vulgaris (viral papilloma).

An axillary ultrasound showed diagonally oval, presumptively reactive lymph nodes less than 1 cm in diameter and “no evidence of metastases.” Abdominal ultrasound revealed no ascites, hepatosplenomegaly, or advanced fibrosis. Thoracic and abdominal CT scans suggested hepatopathy of unknown origin, a dilated main pulmonary artery, a 43 mm thoracic aortic aneurysm, generalized vasosclerosis, bilaterally polycystic and atrophic kidneys, pancreatic calcifications, and diffusely increased bone density. Differential blood count and FACS analysis "did not detect any abnormalities and ruled out hematologic disease." There was "no evidence of hereditary alpha-1 anti-trypsin deficiency," and rheumatologic workup (ANA, AMA, ASMA) was negative. PCR-based array testing for multiple HPV types was "negative within a sample from a representative lesion."

A 29-year-old man underwent a routine health examination. He was asymptomatic, with unremarkable vital signs and physical examination. Medical history included surgical repair of an inguinal hernia at age 3, foam sclerotherapy for superficial varicose veins at 19, and left varicocele repair at 20. Family history was notable for premature aortic dissection in his mother and hematologic malignancies in other relatives. Laboratory studies showed mild elevations of total cholesterol, total bilirubin, urate, and iron; all other values, including markers for lymphoma, were within normal limits.

Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 12 × 7 cm inhomogeneous, minimally vascularized mass in the lower left abdominal quadrant and fatty liver changes. A multiphasic CT scan of the abdomen, pelvis, and upper thighs demonstrated a sharply marginated, slightly lobulated mass in the left retroperitoneum, extending from the lower pole of the left kidney to the distal third of the left thigh. The lesion measured 90 mm in maximum transverse diameter, had fluid attenuation (17–24 HU), few thin septa, and no significant contrast enhancement or evidence of tissue infiltration. There was marked hypotrophy of the left sartorius and vastus medialis muscles, while all vascular structures remained patent and lymph nodes were normal.

Whole-body PET/CT showed mildly increased FDG uptake in the mass (SUV max 3.5) without other areas of abnormal uptake. MRI of the pelvis and left thigh confirmed a well-circumscribed, multiloculated lesion with fluid or slightly cellular matrix. A few nodular septal thickenings showed mild vascular enhancement and diffusion restriction. No biopsy was performed. According to the imaging characteristics and anatomical spread, the initial differential diagnoses included retroperitoneal lymphatic malformation, lymphoma, and myo-/liposarcoma.

A 10-year-old girl with insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus diagnosed 4 years earlier presented with a 4-month history of weight loss (≈10% of her body weight). She denied gastrointestinal symptoms but noted nontender left groin lymphadenopathy that varied in size and transiently improved with antibiotics. Her history was notable for a recent infected insect bite on her arm, cat exposure, and household contact with a person with suspected tuberculosis. On examination, only left inguinal lymph nodes were palpable; there was no additional lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies obtained under general anesthesia showed a normal hemoglobin and white-cell count, a platelet count of 600 × 10^9/L, a C-reactive protein of 29 mg/L, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 36 mm/h; a peripheral blood film was unremarkable. An antitissue transglutaminase antibody assay was 16 U/mL initially and 0.7 U/mL on repeat (normal range, 0–7 U/mL). Duodenal biopsy demonstrated villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes (Marsh 3a-b), confirming coeliac disease. Ultrasonography of the groin and abdomen confirmed enlarged inguinal and para-aortic lymph nodes. A subsequent CT scan revealed additional cervical and abdominal lymphadenopathy.

A 61-year-old woman with a known BRCA1 mutation and no personal history of cancer underwent prophylactic total laparoscopic hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. Intraoperatively, a firm, white nodule measuring 0.5 × 0.1 × 0.3 cm was identified on the fimbriated end of the right fallopian tube. Frozen sections showed small, tightly packed tubules and nests of epithelioid cells in a fibrous stroma with numerous psammoma bodies. On permanent sections, the epithelioid cells were small with regular, round nuclei, even chromatin, and inconspicuous mitoses; larger cells contained intracytoplasmic vacuoles resembling signet-ring cells; psammoma bodies were abundant; and thread-like bridging was noted in several areas. A mucicarmine stain for mucin was negative. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated positivity for WT1, calretinin, PAX8, and D2-40, and negativity for p53, estrogen-progesterone receptors, and epithelial markers (BerEP4/EpCAM, MOC-31, B72.3).

A 4-year-old boy was referred with a 2-year history of a painless swelling on the left side of his back that had grown slowly. He was otherwise well. On examination there was a firm, nonfluctuant, nonpulsatile mass in the left paraspinal region without skin changes or tethering; the remainder of the examination was normal. Ultrasound showed a tense cystic paraspinal mass. MRI demonstrated a well-defined intramuscular mass overlying the lower thoracic spine that had fat signal intensity with multiple large areas of low signal consistent with calcification; there was no involvement of the posterior spinal elements or intraspinal extension. CT confirmed a lesion composed of fat and other soft tissue with peripheral mineralisation. All imaging investigations pointed towards a provisional diagnosis of a tumour with very high fat content which, in this age group, could be lipofibromatosis, fibrolipoma, or lipoblastoma.

A 65-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a 2-month history of vaginal bleeding that was initially intermittent and minimal but became continuous and heavy. She also reported foul-smelling vaginal discharge, pelvic pain, dysuria, fatigue, and loss of appetite. She denied any history of diabetes, hypertension, immunosuppression, trauma, or bleeding from other sites. 

On examination, she appeared chronically ill and emaciated. Vital signs were within normal limits. Genitourinary examination revealed a hard mass arising from the cervix and involving the upper one-third of the vagina; there was no palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy. 

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count (WBC 8.8 × 10^9/L, Hgb 13.3 g/dL, platelets 276 × 10^9/L), urinalysis with 3+ blood and 10–15 RBCs per high-power field, and normal liver and renal function tests. 

Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a heterogeneously hypoechoic cervical mass measuring 8.6 × 6.7 cm extending into the lower uterine segment and upper vagina with a clear fat plane to the rectum and bladder and a mild hydrometra. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed an ill-defined cervical soft-tissue mass measuring 6.6 × 6.2 × 7.2 cm with internal calcifications, extension into the upper vaginal canal, and an associated endometrial collection, but without parametrial or pelvic sidewall invasion. 

A Pap smear showed atypical glandular cells, favor neoplastic, not otherwise specified (NOS). A cervical biopsy for histopathologic correlation was performed.

A 16-year-old girl presented with a 2-year history of chronic anterior left ankle pain. She had no prior injuries or medical history. Initial ultrasonography at an outside clinic showed synovial hyperplasia in the anterior ankle, and she was diagnosed with anterior ankle impingement syndrome. On examination, there was tenderness and swelling over the anterior left ankle without warmth or erythema. Active ankle range of motion was full, but forced dorsiflexion elicited marked pain. She described worsening pain with sports and noted pain at rest that was particularly severe upon awakening. Laboratory studies showed a normal white blood cell count, normal C-reactive protein, normal matrix metalloproteinase-3 levels, and negative rheumatoid factor and anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies. 
Plain radiographs revealed a small exostotic bony bulge and a recess on the talar neck. Computed tomography demonstrated an 8 mm radiolucent lesion in the talar neck with marginal sclerosis and central calcification. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a bone lesion at the talar neck surrounded by bone marrow edema, synovial thickening anteriorly, and joint effusion.

A 20-year-old woman presented with one month of progressively worsening neck pain rated 8/10, with minimal relief from analgesics. She also reported four months of dysphagia. There were no constitutional symptoms or history of trauma. On examination, there were no surgical scars, skin defects, or muscle atrophy. Palpation elicited tenderness over the lower cervical spine. Muscle strength was 5/5 in both upper extremities, but she had bilateral upper-limb radiculopathy with pain in the left shoulder and elbow and decreased sensation in the palms. The patient was mobilizing without difficulty.

Plain radiography of the cervical spine showed bone destruction of the anterior aspect of the C7 vertebral body. MRI of the cervical spine demonstrated vertebra plana at C7 with an associated enhancing prevertebral and left paravertebral soft-tissue mass and an epidural component causing mild spinal-cord compression. A subsequent bone scan and CT angiography confirmed a lytic lesion at C7 with a prevertebral soft-tissue component. All biochemical investigations, including complete blood count, inflammatory markers, calcium and alkaline phosphatase levels, were within normal limits.

A 24-year-old woman, at 15 weeks of her second pregnancy, presented with a 4–5-month history of right upper-quadrant pain and nausea. She had no significant medical or surgical history and had used norethisterone two years earlier. An abdominal ultrasound at 11 weeks’ gestation revealed an 8×6 cm heterogeneous lesion in segment III of the liver with internal vascularity. Laboratory studies—including complete blood count, liver-function tests, and hepatitis B and C serologies—were within normal limits. MRI deferred during pregnancy was obtained three months postpartum because of recurrent pain. MRI showed a well-defined, 9.1×7.5 cm exophytic lesion in segment III that was hyperintense on T2-weighted imaging, demonstrated homogeneous arterial-phase enhancement post-contrast, and remained isointense to slightly hyperintense in portal-venous and delayed phases without washout. A 12 mm gallstone was also noted. Serum alpha-fetoprotein and other preoperative tests were within reference ranges. Given the lesion’s size, imaging characteristics, and symptoms, the clinical team recommended surgical excision of the liver mass and cholecystectomy.

A 60-year-old man with hypertension and Parkinson’s disease presented with 3 months of progressive lower extremity edema and acute onset of altered mental status. On admission, he was somnolent and disoriented; examination showed symmetric lower extremity edema, hepatomegaly, and ascites without stigmata of chronic liver disease. Laboratory tests revealed AST 3877 U/L, ALT 2939 U/L, total bilirubin 4.5 mg/dL, INR 3.8, white blood cell count 19.4×10^3/μL, platelets 63×10^3/μL, lactic acid 13.9 mmol/L, BUN 67 mg/dL, creatinine 3.3 mg/dL, with a negative acetaminophen level and toxicology screen. Viral hepatitis panels, Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and HIV testing were negative. A diagnostic paracentesis was negative for infection or malignancy. Tests for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, hemochromatosis, and Wilson’s disease were unremarkable. The patient developed hepatorenal syndrome requiring continuous venovenous hemofiltration.  
Lower-extremity Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated extensive bilateral femoral–popliteal and iliac vein thrombosis. IVC filter placement was aborted due to clot burden. Hepatic ultrasonography with Doppler showed hepatic vein thrombosis and reversal of portal venous flow. Contrast CT of the abdomen, thorax, and pelvis revealed thrombus extending into the right atrium. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a large echodense mass in the right atrium with preserved left ventricular function. Cardiac MRI demonstrated a 10.6×5.0×5.6-cm heterogeneous pericardial mass invading the right atrium.

A 28-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 1-month history of a small, asymptomatic lesion on her tongue. She had no relevant medical history and denied trauma. On intraoral examination, there was a 0.4 cm yellowish nodule with a regular contour located on the posterior left lateral border of the tongue. No other intraoral or extraoral abnormalities were noted. Based on the appearance and location of the lesion, the clinical differential diagnosis included a lymphoepithelial cyst or a hyperplastic lingual tonsil. An excisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia for definitive diagnosis.

A 49-year-old man presented with a 9-year history of a right chest wall swelling. He first noted the mass as a small, painless bulge that gradually increased in size. There were no constitutional symptoms such as weight loss, fevers, or night sweats. He denied prior trauma, surgery, or family history of similar conditions.

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. The right lower anterior chest wall contained a 5-cm, firm, nonmobile, non-tender mass without overlying skin changes. 

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, renal function, liver function, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, were all within normal limits.

A chest radiograph at a local center showed a densely calcified lesion centered on the right ninth rib. Subsequent noncontrast chest CT revealed a large expansile, lytic lesion of the right ninth rib with radiating (“sunburst”) internal calcification and cortical destruction. He was referred with a working diagnosis of chondrosarcoma for confirmation and management.

A 9-year-old boy presented with a tender nodule on the radiopalmar aspect of the interphalangeal joint of the left thumb. He first noticed a painless small swelling at this site 3 months earlier; over time it became tender. There was no history of trauma, deformity, or pain elsewhere in the thumb. On Doppler ultrasonography, a 12×9-mm heterogeneous hypoechoic lesion with poor vascularity was seen, and a narrow continuity with the interphalangeal joint space was noted. Computed tomography of the thumb revealed a subcutaneous tumor with heterogeneous internal intensity but no morphological abnormalities in the adjacent phalanges. Based on these imaging findings, the lesion was diagnosed preoperatively as a ganglion cyst.

A 39-year-old woman, gravida 10 para 2, presented in November 2018 with sudden severe left abdominal pain, nausea, transient syncope, and three months of irregular vaginal spotting. She had a history of an invasive molar pregnancy in 2014 treated with two cycles of methotrexate, after which she was lost to follow-up. She was not using contraception. On examination, her heart rate was 108 beats per minute; she was pale and had generalized abdominal tenderness with guarding, preventing clear palpation of the uterus and adnexa. Laboratory studies showed anemia and a β-HCG level above 15,000 mIU/mL (upper limit of the assay). Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a large volume of free intraperitoneal fluid, a 6.75 × 7.27 cm heterogeneous mass on the splenic surface suggestive of rupture, several smaller solid lesions in the liver, and a normal-appearing uterus and adnexa. An emergent abdominal CT scan confirmed these findings. Culdocentesis yielded nonclotted blood.

A 52-year-old previously healthy man presented with a 2-week history of progressively worsening abnormal behavior and gait disturbance. On admission, nonenhanced brain MRI showed an oval lesion in the splenium of the corpus callosum that was hyperintense on T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted images with decreased apparent diffusion coefficient. A small hyperintense lesion was also noted in the left frontal subcortical region on diffusion-weighted imaging. Laboratory testing revealed a lactate dehydrogenase level of 650 U/L and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 45 mm/h. Cerebrospinal fluid examination showed 9 cells/µL and a protein level of 125 mg/dL; encephalitis was suspected, and antiviral, antibacterial, and antiepileptic therapy was initiated. The patient’s symptoms initially improved, but he subsequently developed fever, impaired consciousness, hypercalcemia, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. No tumor was identified on imaging studies or endoscopy. Follow-up MRIs at 2 weeks and 1 month showed reduction in size and signal of the splenial lesion. Two months after onset, MRI revealed mottled multiple hyperintense areas in the bilateral cerebral white matter on T2-weighted, FLAIR, and diffusion-weighted images—predominantly in watershed areas—while the splenial lesion continued to regress. T1-weighted images demonstrated diffuse low signal in the bone marrow, and gadolinium-enhanced images showed dural thickening and enhancement. Laboratory studies now showed hemoglobin 7.1 g/dL, platelet count 192 × 10^3/µL, white-cell count 16.3 × 10^3/µL, lactate dehydrogenase 506 U/L, albumin 2.2 g/dL, C-reactive protein 10.05 mg/dL, and serum soluble interleukin-2 receptor 2956 U/mL.
