A 63-year-old woman with a history of hypertension presented with persistent chest and back pain. Two months earlier, she noted chest discomfort and dyspnea on exertion that gradually worsened. On arrival, her electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with diffuse ST-segment depression and ST elevation in lead aVR, along with occasional premature ventricular complexes. Laboratory studies revealed an elevated cardiac troponin I level of 620 pg/mL. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated diffuse hypokinesis of the left ventricle. A contrast-enhanced CT scan was obtained to investigate the cause, which showed a 6.3 cm×4.5 cm×5.5 cm cystic mass above the left atrium; on noncontrast images the mass had heterogeneous attenuation (15–56 Hounsfield units) and it exhibited slight contrast enhancement. Shortly after the CT, the patient developed transient cardiogenic shock that responded to noradrenaline support.

A 40-year-old woman with no past medical history presented with sudden onset of severe lower abdominal and pelvic pain. Ultrasonography revealed a right-sided 7 cm mass with both cystic and solid components. Diagnostic laparoscopy with peritoneal biopsies showed a spindle cell proliferation with a dense vascular network, scant nuclear atypia, and occasional mitotic figures. On immunohistochemical staining, tumor cells were focally positive for SMA, EMA, Cytokeratin AE1/AE3, and DOG1, and negative for C-KIT, CD34, S100, Melan A, PAX8, p53, WT1, calretinin, mesothelin, and D2-40. A presumptive diagnosis of gastrointestinal stromal tumor was made, and the patient underwent a contrast-enhanced CT scan, which demonstrated a large (20 × 15 × 10 cm), heterodense, multilobulated lesion occupying the pelvis and extending to the supra-umbilical region. There was no clear invasion of adjacent viscera or vascular structures, and the mass was deemed resectable.

A 42-year-old Caucasian woman presented with an 8-month history of right-sided exophthalmos and epiphora. She had no history of trauma or inflammatory orbital disease. Her medical history was notable only for allergic rhinitis treated intermittently; her family history was noncontributory for endocrine or orbital disorders.  

On examination, her BMI was 24.8 kg/m2 and vital signs were normal. Ophthalmologic evaluation revealed right exophthalmos (22 mm) with intact visual acuity, visual fields, and extraocular movements; there was no optic atrophy or papilledema. Neurologic examination was normal.  

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, glucose, renal and liver function tests, and thyroid hormone levels (with negative thyroid autoantibodies), were within normal limits. Neck ultrasonography showed a normal thyroid gland.  

Orbital MRI demonstrated a well-defined 4.0 × 2.2 × 2.7 cm mass in the right lacrimal gland region with a septate, pseudocystic appearance, small hemorrhagic areas, heterogeneous signal intensity, and a mass effect on adjacent structures but no bone remodeling.

A 72-year-old man was referred with a 2-week history of lumbago and severe fatigue. He denied weight loss, melena, night sweats, chills, or fever. On examination, he had conjunctival pallor and no palpable lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.6 g/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 22 003 U/L, ferritin 17 040 ng/mL, and C-reactive protein 30.95 mg/dL. A peripheral smear showed decreased red cells with normal morphology and no blasts. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a low-density area around the T12 vertebral body and osteolytic changes in the sacrum and ilium without lymphadenopathy. Brain MRI revealed several acute microinfarctions in the left hemisphere. A random skin biopsy for suspected intravascular lymphoma was negative. Initial bone marrow aspiration was a dry tap, prompting a core biopsy; a second aspiration yielded a small volume showing slight hypocellularity with 64% myeloperoxidase-negative abnormal cells. These cells were medium to large, with condensed chromatin, distinct nucleoli, and basophilic cytoplasm with blebs and vacuoles. Upper and lower endoscopies showed no primary malignancy. FDG-PET revealed intense uptake in the femur, sacrum, and ilium; moderate uptake throughout other bones and the spleen; and slight uptake in the left lung field. Flow cytometry of marrow aspirate (132 cells) showed abnormal cells partially positive for CD4, CD13, CD33, CD71, glycophorin A, and HLA-DR, with other lineage markers negative. A CT-guided biopsy of the sacrum was then performed.

A 45-year-old woman was referred after a positive fecal occult blood test. She had no symptoms, and physical examination and routine laboratory tests, including a complete blood count and blood chemistry, were normal. Colonoscopy revealed two red, polypoid lesions: a 20-mm Paris 0-IIa+Isp lesion in the transverse colon with a granular surface resembling a gastric hyperplastic polyp, and a 10-mm Paris 0-Isp lesion in the sigmoid colon without granularity. Both lesions were resected endoscopically.

On histologic examination, the surface epithelium showed congestive and hyperplastic changes without cytological atypia. In the lamina propria, there was a dense proliferation of spindle cells with ovoid nuclei. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated that the spindle cells were diffusely positive for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) and focally positive for glucose transporter-1 (GLUT1).

A 72-year-old man presented to his primary care physician with three days of neck pain radiating to his upper back and shoulders after lifting heavy wood and using a snow blower. His medical history was notable for hypertension, atherosclerotic disease with prior myocardial infarction and coronary bypass surgery, hypercholesterolemia, hypothyroidism, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. On examination, he had neck stiffness with right posterior paraspinal tenderness aggravated by passive and active motion of the left shoulder; there were no neurologic deficits or cervical lymphadenopathy. A cervical spine radiograph showed mild degenerative changes without erosions or unusual calcifications. He was treated for acute torticollis with muscle relaxants and heat, with resolution of pain but occasional recurrences.

Two and a half months later, he noted a painless left upper arm lump of 6–8 weeks’ duration at the site of his prior bypass‐graft donor arm. Examination revealed a 5–8 cm nonmobile mass in the left posterior arm with mild tenderness, preserved range of motion, and no overlying erythema or regional lymphadenopathy. Plain radiographs showed subchondral sclerosis in the femoral head and a suspected permeative lesion in the proximal humerus. An ultrasound demonstrated a 7 cm heterogeneous intramuscular soft‐tissue and fluid mass. MRI of the left arm revealed a poorly defined 12.5 × 4.5 × 2.5 cm soft-tissue mass infiltrating the lateral head of the triceps muscle, with possible marrow-replacing lesions in the proximal humerus. Staging PET showed multiple FDG-avid intramuscular foci in the left posterior upper arm corresponding to the MRI mass and an additional 1.6 cm FDG-avid nodule in the right suboccipital region posterior to C1. Foci of mixed lytic and sclerotic lesions in the left proximal humeral diaphysis also demonstrated increased FDG uptake. A concern for metastatic disease or lymphoma was raised, and CT-guided biopsy and fine-needle aspiration of the muscle and bony lesions were performed.

A 70-year-old Caucasian woman was evaluated for one month of progressively worsening low back pain and weakness. She denied gastrointestinal symptoms. Her history was notable for multiple basal and squamous cell skin cancers and Merkel cell carcinoma of an inguinal lymph node 5 years earlier, treated with resection, radiotherapy, and carboplatin, with no recurrence on surveillance CT 3 years later.

On examination, she had a 5 mm mobile lymph node in the left supraclavicular area and no focal neurologic deficits. Stool guaiac testing was negative. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.1 g/dL, hematocrit 21.1%, iron 15 µg/dL, total iron-binding capacity 330 mg/dL, and transferrin saturation 5%, consistent with severe iron-deficiency anemia.

A contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan revealed bulky retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy encasing the aorta, inferior vena cava, and renal arteries, along with circumferential thickening of a loop of small bowel in the left hemiabdomen. A small-bowel series was unremarkable. Colonoscopy was performed and demonstrated a semi-sessile, smooth, pale polyp measuring approximately 1 cm in the ascending colon; it was removed en bloc with a hot snare.

A 34-year-old man presented with a 17-month history of progressive, severe pain localized to the tip of the right great toe. The pain was most severe at night and was dramatically relieved by nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; it was severe enough to prevent him from wearing shoes. He had no history of trauma. On examination, the distal phalanx of the right hallux was swollen and tender but showed no erythema or increased warmth. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. Plain radiographs of the toe revealed a small, oval radiolucent lesion at the tip of the distal phalanx with surrounding cortical sclerosis. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a well-defined nidus and a cortical defect at the distal phalangeal tip.

A 54-year-old gravida 2 para 2 Japanese woman presented with a 2-month history of fever and left vulvar pain. Her past medical history included appendicitis, erythema nodosum, and hypertension; menopause occurred at age 53. Initial examination revealed a 10×6 mm firm, ulcerative mass on the inner side of the left labium minorum. A presumptive vulvar abscess was treated with antibiotics without improvement. A needle biopsy strongly suggested squamous cell carcinoma, and she was referred for further care.

On admission, the ulcerative mass had grown to 31×24 mm. Pelvic MRI showed a 31×24 mm mass of moderate-to-high intensity in the left vulvar region without involvement of the urethra or anus. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no inguinal lymphadenopathy or distant metastases. With a preoperative diagnosis of vulvar squamous cell carcinoma, she underwent radical local excision and bilateral inguinal lymphadenectomy.

A 45-year-old woman was referred after an intramural rectal mass was detected on screening colonoscopy. She had a history of diabetes mellitus and was taking tamoxifen for left breast cancer treated with lumpectomy and radiation. She was asymptomatic, and physical examination was unremarkable. Colonoscopy demonstrated a well-defined, 2 cm submucosal mass bulging into the rectal lumen 6 cm from the anal verge. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a well-circumscribed, homogeneous rectal wall mass. Pelvic MRI confirmed a well-demarcated, homogeneous lesion in the left lateral wall of the rectum. Serum carcinoembryonic antigen and CA19-9 levels were within normal limits. Based on these findings, the patient underwent robot-assisted low anterior resection by the colorectal surgery team for a suspected gastrointestinal stromal tumor of the rectum.

A 64-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 4-year history of an asymptomatic nodular mass in the right buccal mucosa. On examination, there was a pedunculated, well-circumscribed nodule approximately 1 cm in diameter, with a fibrous consistency, smooth surface, and intact overlying mucosa. The clinical impression was a traumatic fibroma, and an excisional biopsy was performed. 

Microscopic examination showed connective tissue fragments composed of spindle cells in a background of thick, ropey collagen fiber bundles and a diffuse infiltrate of mast cells. In some sections, a central area of mature adipose tissue was noted. The lesion was well vascularized and covered by stratified squamous epithelium exhibiting areas of acanthosis, hyperplasia, basal layer duplication, and hydropic degeneration.

A 70-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a four-month history of left-sided lumbar radiculopathy. She rated her pain as 7 of 10 on the visual analogue scale and ambulated with crutches. On examination, there was left hip flexor paresis, paresthesia and numbness in the left L3 distribution, and absence of the left patellar reflex. Her medical history was notable for pulmonary adenocarcinoma (T2 N1 G2 R0 M0) treated by left partial pulmonary resection 13 years earlier, and invasive ductal breast cancer (T1b N0 G2 R0) treated by right mastectomy and sentinel lymph node dissection 5 years earlier, with no evidence of recurrence or metastasis on follow-up. Lumbar magnetic resonance imaging without gadolinium (contraindicated owing to renal insufficiency) revealed a space-occupying lesion in the left L3–L4 neuroforamen compressing the L3 nerve root, without a clear connection to the intervertebral disc. Radiological differential diagnosis included a herniated lumbar disc or a neurinoma. Conservative management of her pain failed and neurologic deficits progressed, prompting admission for surgical decompression.

A 48-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of odynophagia and voice change. He reported intermittent blood-stained sputum every few days and unintentional weight loss of 5 kg. He denied dyspnea or fever.

He had a 20–pack-year smoking history and no other medical conditions. There was no family history of malignancy.

On examination, he was afebrile; blood pressure was 111/79 mmHg, heart rate 91 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation was normal on room air. A laryngeal mass was noted on oropharyngeal examination, with palpable bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 10.8 g/dL; platelet count and coagulation profile were within normal limits.

Neck CT demonstrated a 4.6 cm × 3.6 cm × 2.8 cm mass involving the supraglottic larynx with focal erosion of the left side of the hyoid bone and multiple enlarged bilateral cervical lymph nodes. Biopsy confirmed supraglottic squamous cell carcinoma.

Staging CT of the chest and abdomen revealed a 3.8 cm × 2.2 cm hypodense lesion in the left atrium, which exhibited faint 18F-FDG uptake on PET/CT.

Transthoracic echocardiography showed a 4.1 cm × 2.8 cm heterogeneous mobile echogenic mass occupying most of the left atrium, attached by a broad base to the interatrial septum and prolapsing through the mitral valve orifice, causing mitral inflow obstruction with a peak gradient of 17 mmHg and a mean gradient of 6 mmHg.

A 75-year-old man with a presumed history of high-grade urothelial carcinoma of the bladder treated by transurethral resection and intravesical BCG in 2004 was followed with surveillance cystoscopy without evidence of recurrence. Six years later, he presented with partial small-bowel obstruction and diffuse abdominal pain. Abdominal CT showed suspicious lesions in the stomach and duodenum. Upper endoscopy revealed an extensive, thickened lesion in the body and antrum of the stomach; biopsy was reported as poorly differentiated gastric carcinoma. After six cycles of epirubicin, oxaliplatin, and capecitabine, the lesions regressed and the patient underwent total gastrectomy with jejunoesophageal anastomosis; no peritoneal or hepatic metastases were palpated, and the gastric specimen showed no evidence of malignancy. He remained disease free for approximately one year, then developed right flank pain, urinary frequency, fatigue, weight loss, and diarrhea. Repeat PET-CT demonstrated liver lesions, peritoneal carcinomatosis, right hydronephrosis extending to a diffusely thickened bladder wall. Cystoscopic examination at our center revealed a diffusely thickened, erythematous bladder wall with bullous lesions and mucosal oozing but no discrete tumor; the right ureteral orifice was markedly stenotic. Random bladder biopsies were obtained and a right ureteral stent placed.  
   
Histologic examination of the bladder biopsies showed high-grade plasmacytoid malignant cells arranged in discohesive clusters with prominent pericellular retraction artifacts and an edematous stroma. Immunohistochemical studies revealed that the tumor cells were immunoreactive for CK7, CK20, MUC1, and CD138, focally positive for intracytoplasmic mucin, and demonstrated markedly diminished E-cadherin staining.

A 10-month-old full-term female was referred after a 4–6-month history of delayed motor milestones and progressive increase in head circumference. An external ventricular drain had been placed at an outside hospital for hydrocephalus before transfer. On neurologic examination, she had mild limitation of upgaze and moderate axial hypotonia without dysmetria. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed a large posterior fossa mass. Diffusion-weighted imaging and apparent diffusion coefficient sequences showed decreased diffusivity. On T2-weighted and post-gadolinium T1-weighted sequences, the lesion displayed an extensive, nodular, grape-like appearance. Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine showed no evidence of leptomeningeal spread.

A 34-year-old man presented with a one-month history of a progressively enlarging, painful swelling in the lower anterior mandible associated with pus-like discharge. He reported a similar episode three months earlier that resolved after spontaneous discharge. His history included facial trauma 18 years prior, root canal therapy on teeth 31, 41, and 42, and a crown on tooth 11. On examination, there was a 3 × 2.5 cm firm, tender, oval swelling from teeth 33 to 43 on the labial aspect, with a lingual bulge at tooth 41. Vertical percussion elicited tenderness in teeth 31, 32, 41, and 42. Electric pulp testing revealed a response level of “3” in teeth 32, 33, 34, 43, and 44. Aspiration produced straw-colored fluid tinged with blood. A panoramic radiograph showed a mixed radiolucent–radiopaque lesion extending from the distal aspect of tooth 32 to the distal aspect of tooth 43, containing an irregular radiopaque mass suggestive of extruded root canal filling material. Clinically, a radicular cyst was diagnosed, with a calcifying odontogenic cyst in the differential. An incisional biopsy was performed, and the specimen was sent for histopathological examination.

A 61-year-old woman with type II diabetes presented with several days of urinary retention and inability to ambulate in the setting of a 1-year history of progressive lower-extremity weakness and a 100-lb unintentional weight loss. Her weakness began in the proximal left leg, gradually involved the right leg and both hands, and was accompanied by worsening numbness and tingling in her feet; she became wheelchair-dependent within 6 months. She denied pain, flank pain, hematuria, fevers, visual changes, speech or swallowing difficulty. On examination, she was alert and oriented. Cranial nerves II–XII were intact. She had bilateral weakness of hip flexors, knee flexors, knee extensors, and intrinsic hand muscles, with atrophy of the hands and thighs. Sensation to light touch was reduced in the feet, with slight impairment of vibration and proprioception. Reflexes were 2+ in the upper extremities and absent at the knees and ankles; plantar responses were flexor. Bladder catheterization yielded 1.8 L of retained urine. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count; sodium 117 mmol/L; chloride 87 mmol/L; blood urea nitrogen 0.89 mg/dL; creatinine 25 mg/dL. Urine was negative for protein or bacteria. CSF analysis revealed protein 175 mg/dL, glucose 105 mg/dL, 1 WBC, 0 RBC; CSF cytology was negative for malignancy. Lyme serology, autoimmune panel, and a comprehensive paraneoplastic antibody panel were negative. Hemoglobin A1c was 6.5 g/dL. On hospital day 4, electromyography and nerve conduction studies demonstrated decreased amplitudes in motor and sensory nerves, slowed conduction velocities, prolonged distal latencies, and absent sensory responses, suggesting a chronic length-dependent sensorimotor demyelinating polyneuropathy with superimposed chronic lumbosacral plexopathy. MRI of the pelvis showed bilateral femoral nerve enlargement without enhancement.

A 65-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of progressively worsening low back pain. He had no prior medical conditions or medications associated with osteoporosis. On examination, his vital signs were normal. 

Laboratory studies showed:  
• Hemoglobin, platelet count, and lactate dehydrogenase within normal limits  
• No hypercalcemia  
• Serum IgM κ M-component, 6 g/L  
• β2-Microglobulin, 6.4 mg/L  
• Serum albumin, 24 g/L  

MRI of the spine revealed multiple thoracic and lumbar vertebral fractures with underlying osteopenia. CT imaging demonstrated enlarged lymph nodes in both the thoracic and abdominal regions. 

An excisional biopsy of a right inguinal lymph node showed diffuse infiltration by small, uniform B-lymphocytes and plasmacytoid cells that were strongly positive for CD20, PAX5, and BCL2 and negative for cyclin D1, CD5, CD10, and BCL6. PCR analysis of the node detected a MYD88 L265P mutation. 

A whole-body 18F-FDG PET scan showed a few mildly hypermetabolic lymph nodes (Deauville score 3–4) but no abnormal FDG uptake in osseous structures.

A 35-year-old Asian woman presented with a 2-year history of a gradually enlarging swelling in her left groin. She had no pain, gastrointestinal symptoms, or systemic signs. On examination, her vital signs were normal. There was a 7 × 5 cm, soft, fluctuant, partially reducible mass lateral to the left pubic tubercle, extending into the labia majora; there was no cough impulse or evidence of bowel obstruction.  
An ultrasonographic examination revealed an 11.6 × 2.6 cm oval, isoechoic to hypoechoic soft-tissue mass in the superficial fat plane of the left inguinal region with smooth margins and no internal vascularity, findings thought to be suggestive of a lipoma. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a well-encapsulated cystic lesion in the left inguinal region, hyperintense on T1-weighted images and markedly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with thin septations, interpreted as likely representing an inguinal hernia.  
Fine-needle aspiration cytology yielded scant cellular material composed of occasional spindle cells in a greasy background, interpreted as possibly representing a benign lipomatous growth.  
The patient was scheduled for surgical exploration.

A 41-year-old woman with a history of WHO B2, stage IVA thymoma diagnosed in February 2016 underwent six cycles of cisplatin, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide with stable disease. In November 2016 she developed headaches, fatigue, and dizziness. Laboratory evaluation showed:  
• Normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 6.1 g/dL) with reticulocyte count < 0.1% indicating erythroid underproduction, but normal white blood cell and platelet counts  
• Evidence of hemolysis with haptoglobin < 6 mg/dL, positive direct antiglobulin test, and warm autoantibody  
Bone marrow biopsy at that time was hypocellular (approximately 20% cellularity). She was diagnosed with pure red cell aplasia and warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia and was treated with methylprednisolone and octreotide, achieving transfusion independence.

Four months later she presented with neutropenic fever (absolute neutrophil count 0 × 10^3/µL), painful lymphadenopathy, and oropharyngeal candidiasis. Parvovirus B19 testing and blood cultures were negative. Bone marrow biopsy showed cellularity 10–20% with absent granulopoiesis, markedly decreased erythropoiesis, adequate megakaryocytes, and increased lymphocytes; cytogenetic analysis was normal. She received granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, tacrolimus, and equine anti-thymocyte globulin, with recovery of granulocytes but a progressive decline in platelet counts over subsequent months.

In February 2018, 11 months after ATG therapy and while on maintenance tacrolimus and methylprednisolone, laboratory studies showed a WBC count of 10.1 × 10^3/µL with 67.1% lymphocytes (absolute lymphocyte count 6.77 × 10^3/µL) and worsening thrombocytopenia despite a trial of intravenous immunoglobulin (discontinued for side effects).

A 59-year-old woman was referred for an open‐access upper endoscopy because of a history of dyspepsia. She had long-standing gastroesophageal reflux disease and noted new left lower back pain for the past 2 months. She denied urinary or bowel symptoms. Her medications included co-codamol and celecoxib; the celecoxib exacerbated her dyspepsia. She was a nonsmoker, drank minimal alcohol, and remained active caring for her husband. Her father had lung cancer at age 50, and her mother had breast cancer at age 80.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL (11.5–16.0), MCV 79 fL (78–100), neutrophils 3.99 × 10^9/L (1.5–7.0), and platelets 357 × 10^9/L (150–400). Serum sodium was 141 mmol/L (137–144), potassium 4.5 mmol/L (3.5–4.9), creatinine 80 µmol/L (60–110), and urea 6.9 mmol/L (2.5–7.0).

Endoscopy revealed a solitary 5 mm sessile nodule in the fundus of the stomach. Multiple biopsies were obtained for histopathological analysis.

A 27-year-old woman presented with spiking fevers of unknown origin occurring every 8 weeks for 12 years, often accompanied by sore throat, myalgias, or abdominal pain. She had hypothyroidism treated medically and a prior inguinal hernia repair; family history was unremarkable. On presentation, she was afebrile and in good condition. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, erythrocytes 3.6 × 10^6/μL, lymphocytes 47.3%, neutrophils 1.8 × 10^3/μL, creatinine 0.5 mg/dL, and GFR > 90 mL/min/1.73 m^2; rheumatologic workup was non-contributory. Abdominal CT (90 s after contrast) revealed a 12 × 11 × 11 mm, well-circumscribed, homogeneous, hypodense cortical mass in the midportion of the left kidney (approximate density 90 HU). Contrast-enhanced ultrasound showed a 12 mm lesion with well-defined borders, slight inhomogeneity, low echogenicity, no significant vascularity on Doppler, and slight contrast enhancement in the late phase. MRI demonstrated a well-demarcated cortical mass that was hypointense on T2-weighted images, slightly hypointense on non-contrast T1-weighted images, showed slight diffusion restriction, and exhibited slight heterogeneous contrast enhancement (portal venous and venous phases) with wash-out kinetics compared with renal cortex. Despite benign-appearing features (well-defined border, bulging outline), malignancy could not be excluded.

A 78-year-old man with well-controlled type 2 diabetes underwent an annual abdominal ultrasound. He was asymptomatic, denying weight loss, nausea, jaundice, or fever. He had no history of alcohol or tobacco use. Physical examination revealed a soft, non-tender, non-distended abdomen without masses and normal bowel sounds.

Contrast-enhanced ultrasound identified an 8 × 6 cm hypervascular mass in segment I of the liver with apparent extension into the pancreatic head. MRI demonstrated an 8 cm hypointense mass, thought to originate from the liver and extending retroperitoneally to the pancreatic head; large vessels appeared compressed but not invaded. Laboratory studies revealed a monoclonal IgA gammopathy (MGUS) with urine protein excretion of 69 mg/g creatinine. Serum alpha-fetoprotein, CA 19-9, and CEA levels were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and thorax confirmed an 8 cm hypodense mass between the pancreatic head and liver and identified an additional hemangioma in liver segment 8; no metastatic disease was evident.

A 50-year-old woman underwent preemptive living-donor kidney transplantation for diabetic end-stage kidney disease. She received induction with basiliximab and maintenance immunosuppression with tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisolone. Before transplantation, EBV viral capsid antigen IgG titers were >750 U/mL in both donor and recipient. Because of stable graft function, tacrolimus dose was halved, mycophenolate was discontinued, and sirolimus 1 mg daily was initiated. Four months after transplantation, the EBV viral load rose to 652,111 copies/mL, and she received preemptive rituximab (375 mg/m2) for six months. At eight months, the EBV load decreased to 375,412 copies/mL, but abdominopelvic CT showed new multifocal wedge-shaped low-enhancement lesions in the spleen, suggestive of infarction, with evaluation for thromboembolic causes (peripheral smear, echocardiography, coagulation studies) unrevealing. Nine months after transplantation, she was admitted with fever (40.0 °C), flank pain, abnormal liver function (ALT 161 IU/L), and an EBV load of 1,921,952 copies/mL. Abdominopelvic CT revealed para-aortic lymphadenopathy and progression of splenic lesion margins. PET/CT demonstrated increased metabolic activity in the spleen and iliac-chain lymph nodes.

A 56-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 1-month history of severe headache associated with vertigo, nausea, and vomiting. His temperature was 37.4°C, blood pressure 130/80 mmHg, heart rate 90/min, and respiratory rate 18/min. Physical examination was limited by poor cooperation but revealed no focal neurologic deficits. Laboratory tests showed mild leukocytosis (WBC 14.5 × 10^9/L), normocytic normochromic anemia (Hb 8.4 g/dL; MCV 93 fL), thrombocytopenia (platelets 89 × 10^9/L), elevated creatinine (1.9 mg/dL) and BUN (85 mg/dL), and elevated liver enzymes (AST 89 IU/L; ALT 122 IU/L). Electrolytes were normal. Noncontrast brain CT demonstrated an intra-axial mass in the right fronto-temporal lobes with extensive vasogenic edema and a midline shift.

A 63-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive dyspnea, decreased exercise tolerance, and a heavy sensation in her chest. She denied fever, weight loss, hemoptysis, or constitutional symptoms. There was no history of recent surgery or trauma. She took no medications and had no substance use.  

On examination, her vital signs were normal. Breath sounds were decreased over the right hemithorax with dullness to percussion; there was no peripheral edema, ascites, lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly.  

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 5.9×10^9/L, hematocrit 44%, platelets 192×10^9/L, creatinine and liver-function tests within normal limits, albumin 42 g/L, and total protein 76 g/L.  

A chest radiograph demonstrated a large right pleural effusion. Thoracentesis revealed turbid, milky fluid. Pleural‐fluid analysis showed a triglyceride level of 79 mmol/L with chylomicrons, cholesterol 4.6 mmol/L, and lymphocyte predominance; cytology demonstrated lymphocytosis but no malignant cells, and flow cytometry of the fluid was negative for B‐cell or T‐cell lymphoma.  

A PET-CT scan revealed a PET-avid, bulky intraperitoneal mass encasing vessels around the abdominal aorta and pancreas, extending into the pelvic inlet. There were no mediastinal lymphadenopathy or suspicious pelvic lesions.

A 53-year-old man was referred after routine EGD detected a 15 mm submucosal‐appearing elevated lesion on the greater curvature of the proximal gastric antrum. He was asymptomatic. His history included duodenal ulcer perforation surgery, diabetes mellitus on oral agents, 30 pack-year smoking, and social alcohol use; family history was noncontributory. Physical examination and routine labs, including CEA and CA 19-9, were unremarkable. 

Initial EGD showed a 15 mm SMT-like lesion covered by normal mucosa without erosion or erythema; background antral mucosa had mild atrophic gastritis. EUS revealed a homogeneous, well-circumscribed, hypoechoic lesion (15 × 7 mm) originating from the second sonographic layer with subtle obliteration of the third layer. Initial biopsy specimens were negative for neoplasm. Abdominal CT showed a 15 mm intraluminal mass without lymphadenopathy or distant metastasis. The patient declined invasive evaluation and was lost to follow-up.

Three years later, screening EGD again showed a 15 mm lesion with new marked erythema of the overlying mucosa; biopsy remained negative for neoplasm. One year afterward (4 years after initial detection), he presented with mild indigestion. Repeat EGD showed lesion enlargement to 18 mm, a 5 mm central ulcer, and overlying reddish granularity. EUS demonstrated an 18 × 9 mm homogeneous, well-circumscribed, hypoechoic mass from the second layer with slight heterogeneity. CT again showed no lymphadenopathy or metastasis, and biopsy revealed tubular adenoma with high-grade dysplasia.

A 43-year-old man first presented in 2014 with a 6-month history of multiple erythematous, dome-shaped papules on his right auricle. A skin biopsy showed nodular proliferation of spindled endothelial cells arranged in intersecting fascicles with intervening slit- and sieve-like vascular channels, blood-filled vascular spaces with red blood cell extravasation, a patchy lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltrate, and occasional mitotic figures and apoptotic bodies. The lesions were completely excised.

In 2018, he returned with recurrence of a solitary papule on the right ear; it was excised, and histopathology was similar. 

In April 2020, he presented with recurrent papules on the right ear and a new erythematous plaque on his right foot of one year’s duration. Biopsies of both sites were performed. Routine laboratory evaluations, including complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, were normal, and HIV testing was negative. The patient was otherwise healthy and took no medications.

A 6-month-old girl was referred for evaluation of gingival swelling and intraoral fibrinous coating along the alveolar ridges of both the maxilla and mandible, associated with feeding difficulties (total intake 700 mL/day, maximum 140 mL per feed). On examination, white layers were noted on the dorsum of the tongue, and scaly light-brown macules were present on the torso. Apart from feeding issues, her general condition was preserved. Two months earlier, she had been treated for suspected oral thrush without improvement. Osteomyelitis or aseptic necrosis of the jaw had also been suspected, leading to removal of several prematurely erupted primary teeth. 

Under general anesthesia, a contrast-enhanced head and neck MRI demonstrated up to 1 cm–broad T2-weighted hyperintense, inhomogeneously contrast-enhancing lesions in bilateral maxillary bones extending toward the poorly pneumatized sinuses, and an additional lesion in the anterior right mandible. During the same procedure, biopsies were obtained from the jaw lesions, and additional loose primary teeth were extracted to prevent aspiration. These samples were sent for histologic analysis.

A 58-year-old woman presented with 4 months of deep lower pelvic pain and progressive difficulty with flatulence. She had been referred for evaluation of a suspected rectal leiomyosarcoma or pedunculated uterine myoma after colonoscopy and abdominopelvic CT at an outside hospital. Two days before her planned admission, she developed severe left lower-quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, and dizziness, and was found to have a perforated colonic mass with abscess. After stabilization on antibiotics, she was prepared for surgery.

On examination, digital rectal evaluation revealed a fixed, circumferential fungating mass with central ulceration approximately 8 cm from the anal verge. At presentation in the emergency center, temperature was 38.9 °C, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, pulse 78/min, and respiratory rate 20/min. Laboratory tests showed WBC 23,900/µL (93.9% neutrophils), hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, platelets 416,000/µL, CRP 16.14 mg/dL, albumin 3.2 g/dL, alkaline phosphatase 265 IU/L, sodium 132 mEq/L, chloride 93 mEq/L, and prothrombin time 73.2%.

Chest radiography demonstrated a solitary nodule in the right upper lung field without other lesions. Colonoscopy revealed a large submucosal mass with focal ulceration spanning 8–15 cm from the anal verge. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a poorly marginated 7.4×6.3×5.5 cm mass between rectum and uterus, separated from the uterus by fat, with necrotic areas but no enlarged lymph nodes. Pelvic MRI confirmed a 7.2 cm exophytic right lateral rectal wall mass with cystic and hemorrhagic components and multiple enlarged iliac and presacral nodes; a 2.2 cm multiseptated cystic uterine fundal lesion was also noted. PET-CT revealed intense FDG uptake (SUVmax 15.1) in the rectal mass with suspected uterine invasion, and additional uptake (SUVmax 4.0) in pelvic lymph nodes.

A 71-year-old African-American man with a history of nephrolithiasis and prostate adenocarcinoma treated 20 years earlier (external-beam radiation and bilateral orchiectomy) presented with acute renal failure and bilateral hydronephrosis. He had undergone transurethral bladder resection and bilateral ureteral stent placement at an outside hospital, where biopsy showed bladder adenocarcinoma invading the muscularis propria. 

On referral for possible cystoprostatectomy, preoperative colonoscopy revealed only a tubular adenoma. Serum PSA was <0.01 ng/mL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated: 
• Multiple pulmonary nodules up to 0.6 cm in both upper lobes and the lingula  
• Retroperitoneal adenopathy (para-aortic and aortocaval lymph nodes up to 1.9 cm)  
• Bilateral hydronephrosis and hydroureter  
• Diffuse bladder wall thickening with perivesical stranding  
• Multiple filling defects within the bladder lumen consistent with invasive tumor  

FDG-PET showed no uptake in the pulmonary or retroperitoneal lesions but revealed FDG avidity in a left cervical lymph node and a 1 cm nodule within the left flank abdominal wall musculature. An attempted fine-needle aspiration of the cervical node was nondiagnostic. CT-guided core biopsy of the abdominal wall mass yielded: 

Cytology: Crowded clusters of tumor cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios and prominent small nucleoli.  
Histology: Malignant glands lined by intestinal-type columnar cells with occasional goblet cells, necrotic debris in the lumina, infiltrating skeletal muscle, and a desmoplastic stroma.  
Immunohistochemistry: Tumor cells were positive for CK7, membranous/cytoplasmic β-catenin, CDX2, and AMACR, and negative for CK20, p63, PSA, and PSAP.

A 56-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of progressive lower extremity weakness and cognitive decline. Initial studies at an outside hospital showed:  
• Hemoglobin 90 g/L (mild anemia); erythrocyte sedimentation rate 44 mm/h; C-reactive protein 50.71 mg/L; lactic dehydrogenase 867 U/L.  
• Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF): protein 0.97 g/L; no pleocytosis.  
• Brain MRI: multiple bilateral periventricular, centrum semiovale, and frontal lobe lesions hypointense on T1 and hyperintense on T2 and FLAIR.  

On transfer, examination revealed:  
• Mini-Mental State Exam score 8/30, orientation and memory deficits.  
• Bilateral lower extremity strength 4/5; left Babinski sign positive.  
• Serum treponemal tests (TPPA, FTA-ABS IgG) positive; CSF treponemal tests nonreactive; no clinical evidence of neurosyphilis.  
• CSF studies for chemistry, cytology (neoplastic/atypical cells), bacteria, fungi, and viruses were negative; HIV testing negative.  

Repeat brain MRI showed:  
• T1-weighted imaging: a hypointense area with focal hyperintensity in the left temporal lobe, suggesting patchy hemorrhage.  
• T2 and FLAIR: unchanged multifocal hyperintense lesions.  
• Contrast-enhanced MRI: irregular spotty enhancement of some lesions and adjacent leptomeningeal enhancement.  
• T2*-weighted MRI: multiple hypointense foci in the right parietal lobe, bilateral basal ganglia, and cerebellum, indicating hemosiderin deposition in locations not corresponding to the T1 hemorrhagic focus.  

Given the discrepancy between T1-visible hemorrhage and widespread T2*-hypointensities, a silent hemorrhagic process due to malignancy was suspected.

A 45-year-old woman with a history of total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingectomy for cervical carcinoma in situ and multiple leiomyomas presented in early 2014 with a 50 mm mass in the upper left lobe of the lung on CT scan. She underwent lobectomy; the initial pathology report diagnosed carcinosarcoma of the lung. A second review noted a spindle-cell sarcoma. Postoperative CT scans were negative for other lesions. Five months later, CT showed an 18 mm left pulmonary nodule; the patient received three cycles of carboplatin and paclitaxel, after which the lesion grew to 27 mm. A segmentectomy of the lower left lobe was performed. Three months later, a new right lung lesion was treated with radiofrequency ablation complicated by a small pneumothorax that resolved. One month thereafter, a 4–5 mm pulmonary nodule was noted and medroxyprogesterone acetate was started. No progression was seen until December 2015, when bilateral lung lesions reappeared. In January 2016, she developed a rapidly enlarging soft tissue mass in the left periscapular region; biopsy showed a spindle cell neoplasm similar to the lung tumor.  
Histologic examination of the original lung mass revealed a diffuse proliferation of uniform spindle cells with mild atypia, foci of necrosis, and a fibromyxoid stroma. Oval to plump spindle nuclei had inconspicuous nucleoli, and small thick-walled vessels were scattered throughout. Despite thorough assessment, no endometriotic foci were identified in the lesion or adjacent tissue.

A 92-year-old patient presented with a 15-day history of swelling in the upper right posterior region at a recent extraction site and mild discomfort on eating. The patient reported little pain. On extraoral examination, there was mild swelling of the middle third of the face on the right side. Intraorally, there was a single large, round swelling measuring approximately 3 cm × 2 cm × 2 cm on the right maxillary ridge extending from tooth 13 to 17, buccally into the vestibule and palatally about 1 cm (not crossing the midline). The swelling had a sessile base, well-defined borders, a firm consistency, and overlying mucosa that was reddish-pink with a bluish tinge. No cervical lymphadenopathy was palpable. Routine hemogram, urine analysis, and chest radiography were normal. Serologic tests for HIV and hepatitis B virus were negative. 
  
Plain axial and coronal CT of the paranasal sinuses showed a 2.8 cm × 1.7 cm × 2.4 cm soft-tissue mass involving the superior alveolar process of the right maxilla, with local bone destruction of the canine, premolar, and first molar. The lesion extended superiorly into the right maxillary sinus, inferomedially into the oral cavity, and laterally into the right cheek.  

A bone scan demonstrated preserved skeletal tracer uptake appropriate for age. Single-photon emission CT of the cervical and lumbar spine revealed increased radiotracer uptake in the left 5th and 6th ribs and trochanteric region of the left femur (noted as “could represent metastasis? stress factor?”) and in multiple cervical and lumbar vertebrae (noted as “could represent degenerative etiology”), with additional degenerative changes in both shoulders (right > left) and knees (right > left).

A 34-year-old woman with no family history presented with one month of epigastric pain, dyspepsia, and postprandial abdominal distension. She had known uterine leiomyomatosis and denied estrogen–progestin use or abdominal trauma. On palpation, a mass was felt in the left upper quadrant. Abdominal ultrasound showed a bulky, solid mass with irregular margins that was homogeneously hypoechoic with anechoic areas of necrosis, located lateral to the tail of the pancreas and medial to the upper pole of the left kidney and the lower splenic pole. Laboratory tests revealed normal cancer markers (AFP 1.3 ng/mL, CEA <0.50 ng/mL, TPS 38.8 ng/mL, CA 19-9 <2 U/mL, CA 125 4.5 U/mL, CA 15-3 15.8 U/mL), a modest elevation of ALP (141 U/L), ALT (70 U/L), and LDH (614 U/L), and neutrophilic leukocytosis (12.36×10^3/mL) with a normal platelet count. A percutaneous ultrasound-guided core-needle biopsy of the mass was interpreted as adenocarcinoma (stage II). The patient was admitted for surgical resection.

A 12-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of a painless growth on the left side of her maxilla. The patient and her mother had noticed the mass approximately 4 months earlier. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable.

On examination, there was facial asymmetry caused by a mass in the left buccal area without palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. Intraoral inspection revealed a lobular growth of the left maxilla measuring about 4.0 × 3.0 cm, extending from the second premolar to the maxillary tuberosity along the buccopalatal aspect. The adjacent teeth were displaced and mobile. On palpation, the mass was firm, slightly tender, and associated with expansion of both buccal and palatal cortical plates; egg-shell crackling was noted over portions of the buccal cortex.

A panoramic radiograph showed a radiolucent lesion displacing the molars with root resorption. A Water’s view demonstrated destruction of the floor of the left maxillary sinus with complete haziness of the sinus, ill-defined borders, and superior displacement of an impacted third molar. Computed tomography of the maxilla revealed an irregular soft-tissue mass causing osteolytic destruction of the upper left maxillary alveolus and the floor, medial wall, and lateral wall of the left maxillary sinus.

What is your differential diagnosis?

A 2-month-old female infant was referred for evaluation of a painless, slowly progressive left proptosis noted for 15 days. She was born at 37 weeks’ gestation by cesarean section, and her personal and family histories were unremarkable. Laboratory investigations, including a complete blood count and routine blood chemistry, were normal. On clinical examination, there was mild axial proptosis of the left eye with fullness of the eyelids, but no pupillary abnormalities or other neurologic deficits. No cutaneous hemangiomas were present on the head or neck. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits at 66 days of age revealed a large, multilobulated lesion in the left extra- and intraconal spaces, measuring 37 × 19 × 27 mm. The lesion was slightly T1-weighted hypointense, T2-weighted isointense with multiple serpiginous flow voids, and demonstrated homogeneous contrast enhancement with marked enhancement of intratumoral vessels.

A 46-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with acute lower chest pain and a 3-month history of skin nodules. He reported a 5-kg weight loss over the past month. On examination, there was a 2 × 1 cm dome-shaped, indurated, erythematous-purplish nodule on the nose surrounded by atrophic, telangiectatic skin. Similar firm, homogeneously erythematous nodules were present on the forehead and left forearm. All lesions were asymptomatic. The remainder of the skin, oral cavity, and lymph nodes were unremarkable. Laboratory studies revealed:  
- Leukocyte count 17,700/mm3 (3,600 lymphocytes without blasts; 12,900 neutrophils)  
- Hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL  
- Platelets 35,000/mm3  
- Lactate dehydrogenase 1,569 IU/L  

The initial diagnostic impression was cutaneous lymphoma, and a skin biopsy specimen was obtained for histopathologic examination.

A 42-year-old G0 woman presented with several months of pelvic pain and vaginal discharge. Vaginal ultrasound revealed bilateral adnexal masses and her serum CA125 was 429 U/mL. She underwent total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, omentectomy, and pelvic and periaortic lymphadenectomy. Pathology revealed bilateral ovarian serous borderline tumor with noninvasive implants in the omentum and peritoneum, involvement of 2 of 6 pelvic lymph nodes, no micropapillary pattern or microinvasion, and stage IIIC disease. Six months later, her serum CA125 was 106 U/mL. PET-CT showed left cervical lymphadenopathy, and thyroid ultrasound revealed a 5-mm left mid pole nodule with possible microcalcifications. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration and core biopsy of a left level IV cervical lymph node were performed. Pap-stained smears showed numerous papillary groups of epithelioid cells in a background of lymphoid cells, psammomatous calcifications, and intermediate-to-large cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, oval nuclei with fine chromatin, prominent nuclear grooves, and irregular nuclear membranes; definite cytoplasmic intranuclear pseudoinclusions were not seen. Because of the papillary groups, psammoma bodies, and nuclear grooves, the diagnosis of metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma was entertained.

A healthy 6-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of a liver lesion incidentally discovered on routine ultrasound during assessment for recurrent urinary tract infections. She had no abdominal pain, fever, or weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed no cholestasis and a normal serum AFP level (3410 UI/mL). 

Right hepatic lobe ultrasound confirmed an 8.2 × 7.3 × 7.3 cm complex mass that was predominantly hypoechoic with isoechoic solid components and thick, irregular septations; color Doppler showed no significant vascularity. 

Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a large, well-circumscribed hypodense, partially exophytic lesion with peripheral high-attenuation areas suggesting hemorrhage and necrosis, predominantly hypoenhancing with minimal patchy delayed enhancement; perihepatic fat planes were intact. 

MRI revealed a heterogeneous mass with predominantly low T1 and high T2 signal intensity, focal T1 hyperintense areas, a hypointense rim on both sequences, linear hypointense septations, and no significant postgadolinium enhancement.

A 73-year-old woman was referred for surgical management of sigmoid colon carcinoma. On preoperative evaluation, physical examination revealed an asymptomatic, palpable mass on the left chest wall. She had no history of chest trauma or rib fractures and no other remarkable findings on examination.

Preoperative chest CT demonstrated a 2.9 × 2.5 × 1.9 cm expansile, osteolytic lesion involving the left sixth rib, extending into adjacent soft tissues, with contrast enhancement. MRI showed low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, and early-phase enhancement after contrast administration; surrounding chest wall muscles appeared edematous. ^18F-FDG PET revealed a maximum standardized uptake value of 2.66 in the lesion. 

An aspiration needle biopsy of the mass yielded predominantly blood cells and benign mesenchymal cells, with no malignant cells identified.

A 46-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with 3 months of postmenopausal bleeding and progressive abdominal distension associated with weight loss and anorexia. She had no bladder or bowel symptoms.  
An abdominal ultrasound showed multiple ill-defined hypodense lesions in the anterior and posterior myometrium. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 7.2×9.5×7.6 cm solid–cystic mass with significant contrast enhancement in the posterior uterine wall, suggestive of sarcomatoid change in a leiomyoma; the rest of the uterus and adnexa appeared normal. Multiple heterogeneous enhancing lesions were noted in bilateral common and internal iliac and mesenteric lymph nodes.  
On examination, there was a large, nontender, solid, mobile abdominopelvic mass corresponding to a 22-week gravid uterus. Speculum examination showed a normal-appearing cervix without discharge. Vaginal examination confirmed a nontender pelvic mass. Routine blood tests were unremarkable.  
At laparotomy, the mass was found to arise from the uterus; the bilateral fallopian tubes and ovaries were grossly normal and separate from the lesion. A biopsy specimen was obtained and sent for histopathological examination.

A 19-year-old previously healthy man had a one-year history of mild to moderate low back pain managed by a chiropractor. He then developed progressive left hip pain; radiographs showed osteopenia of the left femoral head and neck, and he was treated for presumed Perthes’ disease with non–weight-bearing precautions. Three months later, he sustained a pathological fracture of the left femoral neck after a fall. 

A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a large, heterogeneously enhancing exophytic left renal mass measuring 11.6 × 10.7 cm, infiltrating the renal pelvis and lower pole calyceal system with small calcifications and extension to the lateral and posterior abdominal wall; no significant lymphadenopathy. MRI confirmed these findings. CT of the head, chest, and mediastinum was normal. Imaging also showed osteolytic lesions in the L4 vertebral body, left proximal femur, and left acetabulum. A bone scan demonstrated increased radionuclide uptake in the left femur diaphysis, lower lumbar spine, and left hemipelvis, consistent with metastatic disease.

Percutaneous biopsy of the renal mass showed a mixture of spindle cells (predominant) and epithelioid cells with abundant amphophilic, clear, and focally granular eosinophilic cytoplasm; epithelioid cells often lined spaces and spindle cells formed fascicles; no necrosis. Immunoperoxidase stains on the biopsy specimen were as follows:  
• Positive: MS Actin (focally 0–1+), Myo-D1, EMA (rare), CD10 (rare)  
• Negative: Vimentin (in tumor cells), pancytokeratin (CKAE1/AE3), Desmin, Inhibin, RCC marker, Melan-A (MART1)  

A variety of tumors were in the differential diagnosis, including alveolar soft part sarcoma, alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma, chromophobe carcinoma, translocation renal cell carcinoma, and atypical angiomyolipoma, but the mixed pattern of histology required further immunohistochemistry for final diagnosis.

A 50-year-old Indian woman presented with a 1½-year history of intermittent low-grade fever, weakness, and slowly enlarging, painless nodules on the right side of her neck and right groin. She denied night sweats, weight loss, or anorexia. Her medical and drug histories were unremarkable. On examination, she was of average build with mild pallor. There was generalized, nontender, firm lymphadenopathy: multiple matted right cervical nodes (up to 2.0×1.5 cm), a right axillary node (1.0×1.0 cm), and a right inguinal node (2.0×2.5 cm). A firm, ill-defined, nontender lump (1.0×1.0 cm) was palpable on the left chest wall in the midaxillary line at the level of the 4th–6th ribs. Abdominal examination revealed no hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL, leukocyte count 11,500/mm3 with 81% neutrophils, 16% lymphocytes, 2% eosinophils, ESR 65 mm/h, and platelets 258,000/mm3. Peripheral smear showed normocytic to microcytic red cells with mild hypochromia and no immature forms. Chest radiography demonstrated clear lung fields and enlarged hilar shadows. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed normal liver and spleen without free fluid or retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of a lymph node and the chest wall lump showed inflammatory infiltrates of lymphocytes, plasma cells, sparse neutrophils, and numerous large histiocytes with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei (some binucleate), and frequent emperipolesis; no malignant cells or granulomas were identified.

A 31-year-old man with end-stage renal disease secondary to membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis underwent a living nonrelated kidney transplant at age 16. He received cyclosporine A, prednisone, and azathioprine but was poorly compliant, suffered multiple acute rejection episodes, and developed severe chronic allograft damage. Eleven years posttransplant, he resumed hemodialysis; four weeks later he presented with a 3-day history of watery diarrhea, vomiting, fever with rigor, mild diffuse abdominal pain, and one episode of gross hematuria. His temperature was 37.9°C, pulse 101/min, respiratory rate 20/min, blood pressure 138/93 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Examination revealed mild generalized abdominal and graft tenderness. Urinalysis showed WBCs 7/HPF, RBCs 1/HPF, and protein 600 mg/dL. Laboratory tests revealed hemoglobin 143 g/L, WBC count 3.9×10^9/L, platelets 150×10^9/L, normal electrolytes, BUN 6.2 mmol/L, and creatinine 801 µmol/L. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 14.3 cm allograft with a well-defined, round, midzonal lesion measuring 1.8 cm, suspicious for malignancy; both native kidneys were atrophic without cysts or focal lesions. CT of the abdomen confirmed a 1.8 cm enhancing lesion in the middle third of the renal allograft. He was treated for presumed acute gastroenteritis with cefazolin and gentamicin, which resolved his gastrointestinal symptoms. Electively, he underwent embolization of the renal artery supplying the graft followed by graft nephrectomy.

A 48-year-old otherwise healthy woman presented with a 5-day history of headache, nausea, and vomiting. Physical examination and laboratory tests were within normal limits. She was diagnosed with tension headache and sinusitis and discharged on trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole. Three days later, her headache had resolved but vomiting persisted twice daily; she was treated with an over-the-counter proton pump inhibitor for suspected gastroesophageal reflux. Over the following week, she developed ataxia, diplopia, and recurrence of her headache. 

She presented to the emergency department, and a T2-weighted MRI of the head showed increased signaling of the left temporal lobe, bilateral pontine regions, left peridentate nucleus, and cervical spinal cord. These findings were thought to represent an acute demyelinating process. Clinical suspicion for myasthenia gravis was high, and she was administered a trial of pyridostigmine without improvement. During hospitalization, her blood pressure rose to 190/90 mmHg, serum sodium was 123 mEq/L, glucose 176 mg/dL, and white-cell count 12,800 cells/mL. Neurologically, she had decreased sensorium, hallucinations, diminished attention span, and gait disturbance. A lumbar puncture showed an elevated opening pressure. 

Based on radiographic, laboratory, and clinical findings, a diagnosis of acute demyelinating encephalopathy was made, and suspicions of infectious encephalitis, collagen vascular disease, and toxic encephalitis were high. She received plasmapheresis without improvement. A follow-up T2-weighted MRI showed progressive enlargement of the bilateral pontine regions with hydrocephalus and mass effect on the fourth ventricle. Because of the absence of pathological enhancement of the pons, this was felt to represent either an aggressive demyelinating process or a low-grade glioma. The patient continued to deteriorate, became comatose, and died approximately four weeks after admission.

A 51-year-old woman with a history of systemic hypertension treated with atenolol presented with a 4–5 day history of progressively worsening headache, neck pain, severe anxiety, chest discomfort, nausea, vomiting, abdominal distension, tachypnea, dry cough, and lightheadedness. She denied fever or urinary symptoms. Laboratory evaluation demonstrated leukocytosis (22,500 leukocytes/mm3) with neutrophilia. She was started on ceftriaxone for suspected meningitis.

On arrival, she was alert and oriented, with preserved motor function. Extremities were cold and poorly perfused. Vital signs were: BP 110/70 mmHg, HR 140 bpm, RR 42 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 85% on room air (96% with 5 L/min supplemental O2). Cardiac examination was normal. Pulmonary auscultation revealed diffuse inspiratory rales bilaterally. The abdomen was distended. There was no neck stiffness or focal neurologic deficit. Pupils were equal and reactive; plantar responses were flexor; deep tendon reflexes were normal.

Noncontrast cranial CT was unremarkable, and a lumbar puncture was performed. Working diagnoses included meningitis, endocarditis, and severe sepsis secondary to pneumonia. Blood and urine cultures were obtained. Chest radiography showed bilateral infiltrates consistent with acute respiratory distress syndrome. She received intravenous fluids, clarithromycin, and amoxicillin–clavulanate.

Shortly thereafter, she developed severe hypoxemia and hypotension (BP 90/60 mmHg), requiring escalating norepinephrine. She became agitated, confused, then suffered respiratory arrest followed by pulseless electrical activity; return of spontaneous circulation occurred after 15 minutes of resuscitation. She was intubated and sedated. Later, her blood pressure became undetectable despite maximum vasopressor support, and she experienced a second cardiopulmonary arrest from which she did not recover. She died approximately six hours after presentation.

Postmortem laboratory results showed persistent leukocytosis (26,680 leukocytes/mm3; neutrophils 82%), troponin I 0.9 ng/mL, and D-dimer 6,907.9 ng/mL. Blood and urine cultures and cerebrospinal fluid studies were negative.

A 25-year-old man who worked as a camel keeper presented with a 7-year history of a gradually enlarging swelling of the lateral aspect of his left leg following trauma. He denied pain, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. On examination, he appeared well; vital signs were normal. A firm, non-tender swelling measuring 24×10 cm involved the lateral left leg; the overlying skin was intact, joint range of motion was preserved, and neurovascular findings were normal. There was no regional lymphadenopathy. A frontal radiograph showed a large expansile lytic lesion with internal trabeculations in the proximal two thirds of the left fibula. Coronal and axial T2-weighted fat-saturated MRI images demonstrated an expansile lesion of the proximal fibula with multiple cystic areas, some containing fluid–fluid levels. Imaging features were primarily thought to be those of a telangiectatic osteosarcoma; giant cell tumor or aneurysmal bone cyst was also considered.

A 74-year-old woman presented with a 10-day history of subacute visual decline in her right eye. She denied eye pain, flashes, or floaters. Associated symptoms included dizziness, metallic taste, reduced appetite, shortness of breath, and night sweats; she denied fevers, chills, cough, fatigue, abdominal pain, chest pain, mucosal bleeding, infections, or nausea. Her medical history was notable for well-controlled hypertension on amlodipine, prediabetes, hyperlipidemia on atorvastatin, and minimally symptomatic rheumatoid arthritis not on therapy. She reported recent stress due to her vision loss affecting her work.

Ocular examination revealed visual acuity of 20/50 in the right eye and 20/30 in the left eye (no improvement with pinhole). Intraocular pressures were 13 mmHg OD and 14 mmHg OS. Slit-lamp examination was normal except for visually significant bilateral cataracts.

Fundus examination of the right eye showed a posterior vitreous detachment, a blunted foveal reflex, retinal hemorrhages in the superior macula and superonasal periphery, and cotton wool spots along the inferior arcade, peripapillary region, and superior periphery. The left eye had a posterior vitreous detachment and cotton wool spots along the inferior arcade, superior arcade, and peripapillary region.

Autofluorescence imaging demonstrated hypoautofluorescent patches corresponding to hemorrhages and cotton wool spots in both eyes and a stippled hyperautofluorescent area in the superior macula of the right eye. Optical coherence tomography of the macula showed a shallow neurosensory retinal detachment with focal retinal pigment epithelium changes in the superior macula of the right eye and peripapillary nerve-fiber-layer thickening corresponding to a cotton wool spot in the left eye. Fluorescein angiography revealed early multifocal hyperfluorescent spots in the macula, blockage from hemorrhages, late diffuse small-vessel peripheral leakage in both eyes, and no evidence of late-phase fluorescein pooling.

B-scan ultrasound of the right eye showed a mildly thickened choroid without masses, sub-Tenon fluid, or a “T-sign.”

Due to concern for a systemic process, laboratory studies were obtained the same day.

A 71-year-old man was referred for evaluation of slight fever and dull right upper-quadrant abdominal pain. His history was notable for drug-eluting coronary stent placement 4 years earlier and rheumatoid arthritis treated with weekly oral methotrexate for over 6 years. Routine abdominal ultrasonography had been normal through annual checkups until 2 years ago. On examination, he was afebrile with mild icterus. Abdominal ultrasound on admission revealed multiple oval lesions, up to 35 mm in diameter, with mixed high and low internal echoes in both lobes of the liver. Review of contrast-enhanced CT performed 2 years previously after his coronary intervention showed no liver abnormalities, but contrast CT on this admission demonstrated multiple low-attenuation lesions throughout the liver. Laboratory studies showed elevated inflammatory markers, a total bilirubin level of 6.4 mg/dL, normal α-fetoprotein and CEA, and a slightly elevated PIVKA-II at 45 mAU/mL; tests for hepatitis B and C were negative. Taken together with the imaging and laboratory findings, metastatic liver tumors or cholangiocarcinomas were highly suspected. Upper and lower endoscopic examinations revealed no abnormalities in the esophagus, stomach, duodenum, colon, or rectum. As his liver function worsened, methotrexate was discontinued and an endoscopic biliary drainage tube was placed. A percutaneous biopsy of the largest liver lesion was then performed.

A 45-year-old man with HIV-1 infection (diagnosed 2010) on tenofovir/lamivudine/dolutegravir presented after 1 week of fever, productive cough, and dyspnea. He was 3 months into treatment for extrapulmonary tuberculosis. On examination, temperature 38.1°C, pulse 114/min, blood pressure 88/56 mmHg. He had bilateral posterior cervical lymph nodes (3×2 cm and 1×1 cm), which were mobile, non-tender, and rubbery; splenomegaly 8 cm below the costal margin; and mild epigastric tenderness. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 5.5 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 69.5 fL, WBC 3.8×10^9/L, creatinine 712 µmol/L, urea 43 mmol/L, eGFR 8.8 mL/min/1.73m^2, direct bilirubin 19.1 µmol/L, total protein 10.7 g/dL, AST 11.2 U/L, ALT 4.2 U/L, LDH 243.4 U/L. Viral load was undetectable; CD4 count 219 cells/µL. Chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and obscured right cardiac border. Ultrasound revealed hepatomegaly, mild splenomegaly, small pericardial and left pleural effusions, and increased renal echogenicity. Sputum smear and GeneXpert for Mycobacterium tuberculosis were negative.  
Differential diagnoses included lymphoma and tuberculous lymphadenitis, and an excisional lymph node biopsy was performed.

A 54-year-old woman with a history of FIGO stage Ib nonkeratinizing squamous cell carcinoma of the uterine cervix underwent radical hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, pelvic lymphadenectomy, and adjuvant radiotherapy in 1996. She remained disease-free on annual follow-up for 16 years until 2012, when L2–L3 vertebral metastases were treated with conformal radiotherapy and stereotactic body radiotherapy. In October 2013 and January 2014, successive spinal metastases at Th12 and L1 were similarly irradiated. 

In January 2014, she noted acute onset of right upper leg weakness accompanied by new-onset left eyelid drooping, nausea, and vomiting. On examination, strength in the right upper leg was Grade 2. Cranial nerve examination demonstrated left mydriasis, a decreased left pupillary light reflex, and impaired adduction, supraduction, and infraduction of the left eye, consistent with left oculomotor nerve palsy. Physical examination and laboratory tests revealed no evidence of infection or diabetes. Noncontrast brain CT was unremarkable. Brain MRI with gadolinium demonstrated abnormal enhancement and swelling of the left oculomotor nerve without midbrain abnormalities or diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement. MR angiography showed no intracranial aneurysm.

A 46-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a tongue lesion that had grown progressively over 3 months. Examination showed an exophytic, pedicled, elastofibrotic mass, 1 cm in diameter, located at the midline on the dorsum of the tongue. The lesion was painless, nonfriable, and did not bleed; tongue mobility was normal, and there was no cervical lymphadenopathy. Other physical findings were unremarkable. 

An excisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia. Grossly, the specimen included ulcerated mucosa overlying granulation tissue. Microscopic examination revealed a highly cellular mesenchymal proliferation in both superficial and deep layers, composed of small-to-medium undifferentiated cells with atypical, hyperchromatic, frequently nucleolated nuclei and scant cytoplasm. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated positivity for desmin, smooth muscle antigen HHF35, and myogenin, with a Ki-67 proliferation index of 65%.

A 57-year-old man with a recent diagnosis of nasopharyngeal carcinoma (clinical stage cT1N2M0) presented for evaluation of a new left parotid-region mass. He had previously undergone endoscopic biopsy confirming undifferentiated carcinoma of the nasopharynx and was found on examination to have bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. On palpation, a 1.5-cm firm mass was noted overlying the left parotid gland. Ultrasound of the parotid region demonstrated a hypoechoic lesion measuring 1.5 cm in the left parotid gland. Fine-needle aspiration of the lesion yielded malignant cells consistent with carcinoma in a lymph node. 18F-FDG PET/CT revealed focal uptake in the left parotid gland lesion (SUV max 17) without other distant foci of disease.

A 57-year-old woman presented with a 36-week history of moderate lower–limb pain, cramps, and gait disturbances without sphincter dysfunction. Neurologic examination revealed a dissociated sensory disturbance below the T11 level, decreased deep-tendon reflexes in both lower limbs, and muscle strength graded 4/5 in the left iliopsoas and quadriceps muscles, with flexor plantar responses. Gait was ataxic, with instability on tandem walking and a positive Romberg sign. MRI of the thoracolumbar spine showed an intramedullary lesion extending from the superior border of T11 to the inferior border of T12. On T1-weighted images, the lesion was isointense and demonstrated moderate homogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. T2-weighted images revealed a hyperintense, well-defined “foamy-like” lesion occupying most of the cord diameter, associated with vasogenic edema of the cord and filum terminale. A syrinx extended from T11 to T4, with an intramedullary cystic cavity adjacent to the lesion.

A 44‐year‐old woman was referred with a 15‐day history of pain and swelling in the right posterior mandible, beginning soon after the extraction of a mobile wisdom tooth. She also noted numbness of the lower lip on that side. Her medical history was unremarkable. On intraoral examination there was a 4 cm × 3 cm soft‐to‐firm ulceroproliferative mass in the posterior right mandibular region. A lateral oblique radiograph of the mandible demonstrated osteolytic areas with ill-defined, irregular borders involving the right mandibular angle and ramus. An incisional biopsy revealed fascicles of spindle-shaped cells with interspersed collagen fibers; the cells had hyperchromatic nuclei and an increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio.

A 76-year-old man was admitted with abnormal liver function tests and septic shock. During his hospitalization, multifocal lymphadenopathy was noted in the cervical and inguinal regions, and an ultrasound-guided biopsy of an inguinal lymph node was performed. Histologic examination showed diffuse infiltration by large lymphoid cells with necrosis, moderate cytoplasm, round nuclei, and prominent nucleoli. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated that the tumor cells were positive for CD20, cyclin D1, BCL6, and MUM1, and negative for CD5, CD10, and SOX11. Epstein–Barr virus in situ hybridization (EBER) was negative, and the proliferation index (Ki-67) was approximately 80%. Interphase fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) revealed CCND1/IgH fusion signals in 23% of nuclei, an atypical BCL6 signal pattern in 39–52% of nuclei, and no evidence of MYC or IGH/BCL2 rearrangement.

A 46-year-old Asian man with obesity, gallstones, and hypertension presented with a 4-day history of frontal headache, dizziness, anorexia, gait instability, and short-term memory loss. Neurologic examination was otherwise normal.  

Noncontrast CT of the brain showed diffuse nodular hyperdense lesions along the lateral ventricles with nonobstructive hydrocephalus. MRI demonstrated homogeneously enhancing, T2-weighted hypointense periventricular and ependymal/subependymal lesions with moderate restricted diffusion, scattered punctate foci of susceptibility, and a trace of intraventricular hemorrhage. No parenchymal enhancing lesions or leptomeningeal enhancement were seen.  

Laboratory studies revealed normal blood cell counts and lactate dehydrogenase. Lumbar puncture yielded elevated opening and closing pressures and a CSF white cell count with 61% lymphocytes; CSF cultures and PCR were negative. A CT scan of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis, an autoimmune panel, and an HIV screen were unrevealing.  

Over the next 5 days, the patient became progressively confused and drowsy. Repeat MRI showed increased extent of the periventricular lesions, greater susceptibility suggesting more hemorrhage, and increased mass effect and cerebral edema.

A 40-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of a slowly enlarging swelling on the left side of his face. By the time of evaluation, the mass measured approximately 5 cm × 5 cm. On examination, there was a firm, non-fluctuant, asymptomatic mass at the left angle of the mandible; the overlying skin was normal. The swelling became more prominent on clenching the teeth and on contraction of the masseter muscle, extending from the posterior border of the mandibular ramus toward its anterior border, with no intraoral component.  
Ultrasonography was suggestive of a lipoma. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a well-defined, oval lesion in the left masticator space, adjacent to the masseter muscle and superficial lobe of the parotid gland, with hyperintense signal on both T1- and T2-weighted images.

A 92-year-old man with hypertension, gout, chronic kidney disease, sciatica, and a history of prostate cancer under surveillance since 2019 was referred to hematology after treatment for an unprovoked extensive left-leg proximal deep-vein thrombosis. During a telephone hematology consultation, he reported severe back pain and marked swelling of the right leg and scrotum. Laboratory studies showed a mildly elevated PSA level of 24 µg/L (reference range 0–15 µg/L), normal complete blood count, normal bone profile, and normal serum protein electrophoresis; Bence Jones protein was not detected. A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a para-aortic soft tissue mass around the infrarenal abdominal aorta, lytic lesions in the pelvis, and multiple lytic lesions in the L4 and L5 vertebral bodies causing spinal cord compression. The patient was admitted for pain control, and a blind bone marrow trephine biopsy from the pelvis showed a normocellular marrow with only a 1% CD5-positive clonal cell population and no increase in plasma cells.

A 53-year-old woman presented with several months of recurrent fever, cough, night sweats, and generalized weakness. Initial laboratory tests showed:  
• WBC 37.85×10^3/µL (normal 4.1–10.8×10^3/µL) with 85.1% neutrophils and 8.5% lymphocytes  
• Platelets 127×10^3/µL (normal 150–350×10^3/µL)  
• Blood film: neutrophilia with left shift, normal RBCs and platelets  
• ANA negative; abdominal ultrasound unremarkable  

On referral, a hematology blood film again showed leukocytosis with band forms and myelocytes. Multiple myeloma was excluded by bone marrow biopsy showing no increase in CD138-positive plasma cells. Real-time PCR for BCR-ABL major and minor transcripts was repeatedly negative. Flow cytometry of peripheral blood revealed 2% blasts, 89% granulocytes, 2% lymphocytes, and 3.6% monocytes.  

Further molecular tests in February included CALR exon 9 mutation analysis and MPL W515L/K testing by PCR and Sanger sequencing, both negative. Quantitative PCR for the BCR-ABL p210 fusion transcript was not detected. Serum protein electrophoresis showed low albumin and mild increases in alpha-1 and gamma fractions.  

On repeat evaluation in late February, WBC was 90.1×10^3/µL, platelets 90×10^3/µL, neutrophilia, mild basophilia (0.15×10^3/µL), and persistent thrombocytopenia. A third BCR-ABL RT-PCR remained negative. She was started on hydroxyurea.  

Bone marrow aspirate was hemodiluted. A core biopsy revealed hypercellular marrow (95% cellularity) with marked granulocytic hyperplasia, decreased megakaryocytes, normal lymphocytes and plasma cells, and reticulin grade 1 fibrosis. Immunohistochemistry for MPO, CD34, and CD99 was negative. A follow-up marrow sample again showed no evidence of BCR-ABL fusion.

A 68-year-old Caucasian man presented with three weeks of macroscopic hematuria. He had no history of smoking, carcinogen exposure, or prior urologic disease. Physical examination was unremarkable. Ultrasonography of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 28×13 mm hyperechoic, sessile lesion on the right lateral wall of the bladder; no other masses or hydronephrosis were noted. Laboratory studies, including routine blood counts and serum chemistries, were within normal limits. 

He underwent transurethral resection of bladder tumor. Histologic examination of the resected tissue demonstrated a predominant inflammatory infiltrate with conspicuous lymphoid aggregates. Within this background, there were nests and sheets of undifferentiated cells showing highly pleomorphic nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and frequent mitotic figures.

A 49-year-old man presented with non-specific abdominal pain. His medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, glaucoma, and post-mumps deafness. He had no prior abdominal surgeries. On examination his body mass index was 22 kg/m2, and findings were unremarkable. Liver function tests were normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 10.7 × 7.6 × 8.9 cm mass in liver segments V–VI with heterogeneous enhancement and calcifications. MRI confirmed a peripheral hepatic lesion of similar size. An ultrasound-guided liver biopsy showed a spindle cell neoplasm with smooth-muscle differentiation. After multidisciplinary discussion, the team agreed to proceed with surgical resection of what was presumed to be a resectable peripheral liver tumor.

A 19-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of a progressively enlarging swelling of the tongue that accelerated over the past 3 months. She reported difficulty speaking, chewing, and episodes of nasal regurgitation. She had no significant past medical history.  
On examination, performance status was 1. Intra-oral exam revealed a lobulated swelling involving the entire tongue, with an ulcerated area and marked restriction of tongue mobility. Multiple bilateral level I A and I B cervical lymph nodes, up to 3 cm on the left, were firm and fixed. Examination of skin, abdomen, chest, cardiovascular system, and neurologic status was normal.
