MRI of the tongue demonstrated an enhancing mass measuring >5 × 4 cm, involving intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles, with loss of lingual septum definition, extension into the right sublingual space, encasement of the neurovascular bundle, and anterior spread to the tip. There was no bony erosion or invasion of carotid or bucco-masticator spaces. MRI of the neck confirmed metastatic lymphadenopathy at levels I–IV on the left and level II on the right.  
The clinical impression was an infiltrative epithelial malignancy or minor salivary gland tumor. A punch biopsy from the ulcerated lesion showed solid sheets of moderately pleomorphic tumor cells with round to oval, central to eccentric nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm, suggestive of an undifferentiated malignant neoplasm with rhabdoid differentiation. Immunohistochemistry showed strong vimentin positivity and was negative for desmin, pan-cytokeratin, and S-100 protein.

A 48-year-old man with Down syndrome presented with a one-month history of painless left scrotal swelling. He had known hyperthyroidism and hyperuricemia. Ultrasonography demonstrated a left testicular mass and hydrocele. Computed tomography revealed a 5.6 × 6.0 × 6.2 cm left testicular tumor within the hydrocele and eight enlarged pelvic and pararenal aortic lymph nodes, the largest measuring 6.1 cm. Serum lactate dehydrogenase, α‐fetoprotein, total human chorionic gonadotropin, and carcinoembryonic antigen levels were all within normal limits. The patient underwent a radical left orchiectomy. Grossly, the specimen measured 45 × 50 × 60 mm; the tumor was centered in the testis and para-testis without surface involvement of the tunica vaginalis. Histologic examination showed high-grade tumor cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasm ratio and prominent nucleoli growing in solid, nested, and sheet-like patterns with extensive necrosis. Small foci of spindle-shaped cells with finely granular chromatin and absent nucleoli were present. Carcinoma in situ was identified in the rete testis, and no germ cell tumor in situ was seen in the testis. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for AE1/AE3, calretinin (focal), PAX8 (focal), and CAIX, and negative for WT1, AFP, OCT3/4, PLAP, myogenin, S100A, STAT6, EMA, CK7, CK20, GATA3, CD34, CD56, CD99, SALL4, HMB45, chromogranin A, and synaptophysin.

A 72-year-old Hispanic man with hypertension, atrial fibrillation, congestive heart failure, and diabetes was referred for follow-up of a right popliteal mass previously biopsied one year earlier. The initial biopsy demonstrated benign synovial hyperplasia, chronic inflammation, and hemosiderin deposition, findings confirmed at a national referral center. Given minimal symptoms, conservative management was elected.

At one-year follow-up, the patient reported increased discomfort and fullness behind his right knee without systemic symptoms. Examination revealed a non-tender popliteal enlargement limiting flexion, with intact neurovascular function. Plain radiographs were unremarkable. MRI of the knee showed a large, lobulated, heterogeneous mass posterior to the distal femur and anterior to the neurovascular bundle, containing multiple nodules measuring 0.7–3.9 cm. Bone scintigraphy and chest CT with contrast revealed no evidence of distant disease.

A second incisional biopsy was performed, exposing a 7.0 cm multilobulated mass abutting the common peroneal nerve and popliteal vessels. Intraoperative frozen sections were inconclusive, and tissue was submitted for expert consultation.

A 61-year-old man presented with a single episode of gross hematuria without fever, flank pain, dysuria, weight loss, or neurologic symptoms. He had a history of coronary artery disease and well-controlled hypertension. A CT urogram revealed a 3.5 × 2.1 × 1.3 cm arterially enhancing mass in the lateral mid to lower pole of the left kidney and a branching calculus in the left lower-pole calyces; renal function was normal. There was no family history of von Hippel–Lindau disease. Cystoscopy showed no tumor in the urethra, bladder, or ureter. One month later, the patient underwent a laparoscopic left partial nephrectomy. Gross examination showed a well-circumscribed, nonencapsulated, round, tan-white mass measuring 3.0 × 2.1 × 1.3 cm, with partial fibrosis and mild hemorrhage. Histologically, the lesion was lobulated and traversed by a prominent arborizing network of thin-walled vessels in a hyalinized stroma. Tumor cells were oval to polygonal with abundant clear to eosinophilic cytoplasm, occasional fine vacuoles, and eosinophilic hyaline globules; nuclei were bland, and there was no necrosis or mitotic activity. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated diffuse positivity for S100, alpha-inhibin, neuron-specific enolase, vimentin, and PAX8; AE1/AE3 staining was weak and focal. The tumor cells were negative for EMA, CA9, CD10, KRT7, CD117, p504s, synaptophysin, chromogranin, melanin A, HMB45, and SF-1. Ki-67 showed a proliferative index of <1%.

An 85‐year‐old woman was found to have a left renal mass on screening abdominal ultrasonography. She reported intermittent lower abdominal pain for several months. Initial ultrasonography showed dilation of the left renal pelvis. Because of her age, she chose observation. Four days before planned surgery, she developed severe left‐sided abdominal pain and presented for evaluation.

Her medical history included chronic heart failure, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia, and osteoporosis. Physical examination revealed tenderness in the left abdomen without other abnormalities. Laboratory studies showed normal blood cell counts, liver enzymes, coagulation, and tumor markers (CA 19-9 and CEA). BUN was 11.0 mg/dL, creatinine 0.74 mg/dL, eGFR 55.7 mL/min/1.73 m2, and CRP 1.64 mg/L. Urinalysis revealed proteinuria and occult blood; urinary cytology was negative for high-grade urothelial carcinoma.

Renal ultrasonography demonstrated a homogenous low‐echogenic lesion with layered echoes and septations, suggestive of a cystic mass. Contrast‐enhanced CT showed a 120 mm left renal mass with low attenuation (~20 HU), irregular soft tissue density at the margins, wall and septal enhancement, and gradual enhancement of the solid components. There was thinning of the renal parenchyma and a duplicated ureter, one of which was contiguous with and dilated by the mass. MRI revealed the majority of the lesion to be low on T1 and high on T2, consistent with a cystic lesion, and the solid portion to be low on T2 with gradual enhancement and diffusion restriction (ADC 0.9–1.1 × 10−3 mm2/s). Retrograde pyelography confirmed continuity between the dilated pelvis and one ureter. Cystoscopy showed discharge of mucinous urine from the ureteral orifice.

A 58-year-old woman with hypertension and dyslipidemia presented with eight months of rectal pressure and mild constipation, without bleeding, diarrhea, or weight loss. Pelvic MRI showed only sigmoid diverticulosis. Endoscopic ultrasound revealed a single 0.8 × 0.7 cm hypoechoic nodule at the anorectal junction. The lesion was removed en bloc by band-assisted endoscopic mucosal resection without complication. 

Grossly, the specimen measured 1.3 × 1.3 × 0.6 cm of soft red mucosal tissue. Microscopic examination demonstrated a submucosal nodule of poorly differentiated cells with large vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and indistinct cell borders forming a syncytial growth pattern, accompanied by a dense lymphocytic infiltrate with germinal centers; the overlying squamous and colonic mucosa was unremarkable.  

Immunohistochemical studies showed diffuse strong tumor cell expression of p16, p40, and p63, with variable CK7 and EMA positivity. Tumor cells were negative for CDX-2, CK20, CEA, chromogranin, synaptophysin, p53, SOX-10, and S100. The Ki-67 proliferation index was approximately 50%, and nuclear expression of the mismatch-repair proteins MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2 was intact.

A 9-year-old girl presented with a red, raised lesion on her left shoulder that had been gradually enlarging over 5 years. She reported pain on palpation but denied any preceding trauma, bleeding from the lesion, systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, night sweats), or regional lymphadenopathy. On examination, there was a single dark red, tender, firm nodule measuring 4 × 3 cm with a smooth, telangiectatic surface. No other skin findings or lymph node enlargement were noted. Given the appearance and history, the initial clinical differential diagnosis included an appendageal tumor, pyogenic granuloma, dermatofibroma, and dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans. An excision biopsy was performed.

A 40-year-old man with no prior medical or surgical history presented with vague, nonradiating abdominal pain localized to the right lumbar and iliac fossa. He denied fever, vomiting, or prior similar episodes. On examination, there was a diffuse, non-tender mass in the right abdomen extending from the hypochondrium to the iliac fossa. 

Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 14.5 × 7.5 × 15.9 cm multiseptated intraperitoneal lesion anterior to the cecum and terminal ileum, with no solid component and septal venous vascularity. The liver surface showed no scalloping. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis confirmed an irregular, multiseptated multicystic lesion engulfing the ascending colon and cecum without bowel wall thickening or luminal growth. Serum CEA and CA 19-9 levels were within normal limits.

A multidisciplinary discussion generated a differential diagnosis of appendicular abscess versus mucinous cyst adenoma or adenocarcinoma of the appendix. Colonoscopic biopsy was deemed unnecessary due to absence of bowel wall involvement on imaging, and CT-guided aspiration was deferred because of concerns regarding diagnostic yield and potential tumor seeding. The team elected to proceed with diagnostic laparoscopy.

A 45-year-old woman was referred for surgical evaluation of progressive dyspnea. One year earlier, she was hospitalized with acute dyspnea following influenza infection and underwent CT after an abnormal chest radiograph. She is an ex-cleaner, with a 1.5-pack-year smoking history, no asbestos exposure, and no known genetic conditions such as tuberous sclerosis or alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. She was followed in a nodule clinic with a provisional diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and experienced progressive dyspnea with occasional antibiotic-treated lower respiratory tract infections. Her comorbidities included prior alcohol dependence and depression.  
Pulmonary function tests showed FEV1 1.53 L (53% predicted), FVC 2.52 L (79% predicted), DLCO 5.25 mmol/min/kPa (62% predicted), and a 6-minute walk distance of 414 m.  
CT of the chest demonstrated severe, heterogeneous right-sided bullous emphysematous changes with a basal predominance and multiple large bullae in the right lower lobe, a 7 mm benign-appearing nodule in the right upper zone, hyperinflation with mediastinal shift to the left, complete right middle lobe collapse, and compression of the right upper and middle lobes.  
Echocardiography showed normal right ventricular size and function without pulmonary hypertension. She was counseled regarding risks and scheduled for right thoracotomy and lower lobectomy.

A 55-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of moderate pain in the left side of her abdomen. On examination, there was a large, palpable mass occupying the left abdomen. Laboratory studies, including carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), carbohydrate antigens CA 19-9, CA 125, and CA 15-3, were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 17 cm hypoechoic mass with internal septations. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 10 × 25 cm fluid-filled mass extending from the diaphragm to the left iliac region and adherent to the pancreatic tail and splenic vessels. ^18F-FDG PET/CT showed peripheral low tracer uptake with no metabolic activity within the mass. A preoperative working diagnosis of mucinous cystic neoplasm of the pancreas was made, and surgery was planned.

An 8-year-old boy presented with a one-month history of a rapidly growing, painless swelling of the left side of his face. There was no history of trauma or tooth pain. On general examination, he had mild pallor and weight loss. Facial asymmetry was noted due to an expansile, non-tender, bony hard lesion measuring approximately 4×5 cm on the left cheek; the overlying skin was intact and there was no lymphadenopathy or sensory deficit. Intraorally, a smooth swelling obliterated the left maxillary vestibule from the lateral incisor to the deciduous second molar; the adjacent teeth were neither mobile nor carious, and the mucosa appeared normal. Routine blood studies, including a complete blood count and serum alkaline phosphatase, were within normal limits. Computed tomography revealed a well-defined, expansile, destructive lesion of the left maxilla with preservation of the cortical boundary and no involvement of the maxillary sinus. A panoramic radiograph confirmed the lesion without evidence of tooth displacement or root resorption.

A 48-year-old woman presented with airway obstruction and dysphagia. On examination, there was a conspicuous bulge on the right soft palate occupying the entire oropharyngeal isthmus. Endoscopic evaluation revealed a pulsating swelling in the right lateral wall of the nasopharynx extending into the oropharyngeal area. Palpation of the right neck identified a soft, elastic, painless, pulsating, immobile mass. Contrast-enhanced CT showed an intensely vascularized structure measuring 47 × 40 × 47 mm, exhibiting characteristics indicative of a carotid body or vagal paraganglioma. MRI depicted a vascularized formation originating from the jugular fossa, destroying the apex of the petrous bone and the corresponding portion of the occipital bone.

A 20-year-old woman with mental retardation and epilepsy presented with lower abdominal pain. On examination, her lower abdomen was soft with slight swelling and no tenderness. Ultrasonography revealed a multicystic tumor in the pelvic cavity. MRI showed a multicystic mass occupying the abdominal cavity without solid components or gadolinium enhancement. Serum CA-125, CA19-9, and CEA levels were normal. Laparotomy revealed enlarged bilateral ovaries: a right ovarian tumor approximately the size of an adult head and a left ovarian tumor the size of a fist. A right oophorectomy and left ovarian cystectomy were performed. Histopathology showed a mucinous cystadenoma of the right ovary and an intestinal-type mucinous borderline tumor of the left ovary. No adjuvant therapy was given.

Two years and nine months later, follow-up ultrasonography detected a 10-cm multilocular tumor in the pelvic cavity. Contrast CT showed a multicystic lesion without contrast enhancement. MRI demonstrated round cystic lesions with low to intermediate intensity on T1-weighted images and high intensity on T2-weighted images; a small portion of the cyst wall exhibited slight enhancement after gadolinium administration. The preserved left ovary could not be separately identified. Therefore, a recurrent ovarian borderline tumor was suspected.

A 19-year-old woman was admitted with acute, severe left upper-quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and nonbloody vomiting unresponsive to oral medications. Three months earlier, she had experienced milder abdominal pain radiating to the right shoulder and scapula, relieved by nonopioid analgesics. She reported a 5 kg weight loss over eight weeks. Her only medication was an oral contraceptive; she denied fever, substance use, prior surgery, and relevant travel. Examination revealed a tender, palpable mass from the epigastrium to the left hypochondrium. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, mild elevations in AST (50 U/L), ALT (40 U/L), GGT (321 U/L), ALP (390 U/L), INR 1.5, and albumin 2.9 g/dL. AFP was 1.3 ng/mL, CA19-9 11 U/mL, and CEA 0.5 ng/mL. Contrast CT and MRI demonstrated an 18 × 12.1 × 12.5 cm lobulated, multilocular, cystic-solid, heterogeneous liver mass with a fibrous pseudocapsule, sparing only segment 6. There was no portal or arterial thrombosis. The three major hepatic veins were not visualized, but an inferior right hepatic vein (9.3 mm in diameter) drained segment 6. After multidisciplinary discussion, early resection was planned, with consideration of ruptured hepatocellular adenoma, atypical hemangioma, and mucinous cystadenocarcinoma.

A 34-year-old woman presented with an 8-month history of white nipple discharge from her left breast. On examination, there was a 3-cm palpable mass in the lower outer quadrant of the left breast, approximately 4 cm from the nipple. Bilateral breast ultrasonography and contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated a 16.5×7.5 mm lobulated fluid collection in the left breast at 5 o’clock, 2 cm from the nipple, and a 23.5×10 mm heterogeneous, inflamed parenchymal area without clear borders at 4 cm from the nipple. An atypical left axillary lymph node measuring 28.5×14.5 mm, with cortical thickening of 7.5 mm and a preserved fatty hilum, was also identified. The radiological evaluation was considered compatible with an abscess. Cytological evaluation of the nipple discharge and abscess drainage was performed, and tetracycline was administered; the patient’s symptoms regressed, and cytology was consistent with an abscess. During follow-up, the discharge became bloody, the breast mass enlarged, and overlying skin changes suggested invasion. A core-needle biopsy of the lesion was then planned.

A 75-year-old man presented with a one-year history of a progressively enlarging mass on his left upper arm. On examination, there were two oval masses: one measuring 16 × 13 cm extending from the elbow to mid-forearm and a second measuring 6.4 × 4.5 cm over the lower third of the humerus. Both were well-vascularized, nonadherent to bone or muscle, and without palpable regional lymphadenopathy.

Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI of the forearm demonstrated two large, well-vascularized soft-tissue masses without bone or muscle invasion or distant metastases; the radiographic appearance was felt to suggest a sarcomatous origin.

An incisional biopsy of the larger lesion showed a malignant tumor composed of markedly pleomorphic cells with hyperchromatic nuclei, poorly defined cytoplasm, and numerous mitoses. Immunohistochemical studies revealed tumor cells that stained positively for SOX10, PS100, Melan-A, HMB-45, and diffusely for PRAME, and negatively for pancytokeratin, desmine, myogenin, CD45, CD34, CD31, and ERG. The Ki-67 proliferation index was approximately 20%.

A 50-year-old Filipino woman presented with 2 months of abdominal pain, weight loss, and irregular vaginal bleeding. She also reported fatigue and intermittent diarrhea for 1 month. She had regular menses until 2 months ago and no history of gynecologic disease. She denied chronic illnesses or recent surgeries. On examination, she was alert with mild conjunctival pallor and no lymphadenopathy. Respiratory rate was 22 breaths per minute; chest examination suggested free fluid in the right pleural cavity. Abdominal examination showed a distended, soft abdomen with a large, non-tender, cystic pelvic mass. Speculum examination revealed cervicitis; bimanual exam found a bulky uterus, restricted mobility, and a left adnexal mass. Chest radiography demonstrated a large right pleural effusion with near-total lung collapse. CT of the chest showed a 5.6 × 5 mm pulmonary nodule in the right upper lobe, fibroatelectatic changes, and minimal right pleural effusion. CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 19 × 22 × 9 cm complex cystic and solid mass arising from the left adnexa, displacing bowel loops, mild left hydronephrosis, hydroureter, and ascites; the right ovary was enlarged to 4.6 × 4 cm. A thoracocentesis yielded serous fluid negative for malignant cells.

A previously healthy 10-year-old girl presented with a 2-month history of intermittent abdominal pain. Vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination revealed mild right-sided tenderness without a palpable mass. An abdominal CT scan to rule out appendicitis demonstrated a 4 × 3 cm cystic lesion in the region of the pancreatic head, with uncertain involvement of the pancreas. Laboratory studies, including liver function tests, were unremarkable. The patient underwent an exploratory laparotomy for diagnosis. Intraoperative frozen-section analysis of the cyst wall biopsy showed a true pancreatic cyst without malignancy. The cyst was drained and unroofed. Cyst fluid analysis revealed an amylase level of 60 U/L. Her symptoms resolved, and she was placed on ultrasound surveillance at 3-, 5-, and 8-month intervals, then annually. Over the next 15 years, she remained asymptomatic and had an uncomplicated pregnancy, but the lesion grew from 4.2 cm to 6.2 cm in diameter. In the past 5 months, she developed occasional right mid-abdominal pain and discomfort. A pylorus-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy was planned due to recurrent pain and enlargement of the lesion.

A 64-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of bilateral adnexal masses and pelvic lesions identified on magnetic resonance imaging. She reported no metrorrhagia or other gynecologic symptoms and had not used hormone replacement therapy. Five months earlier, she had undergone resection of an 18-cm abdominopelvic mass at another hospital; initial histopathologic interpretations included extra-uterine low-grade endometrioid stromal sarcoma, sex-cord stromal tumor, and smooth muscle tumor. An endometrial biopsy at that time showed only atrophic endometrium without evidence of neoplasm. She has a history of hypertension. On MRI, two solid-cystic latero-uterine masses measuring 60×53 mm on the left and 47×40 mm on the right were present, along with two pelvic masses in the rectovaginal fascia and adjacent to the cervix; the uterus appeared normal radiologically.

A 74-year-old farmer presented in January 2011 with a 6-year history of a progressively enlarging plantar lesion on the right heel. He first noted a 1 cm superficial wound in May 2003 and underwent multiple local treatments elsewhere, including excisions, superficial biopsies, and parenteral antibiotics. A culture grew Proteus mirabilis, and earlier histological examinations demonstrated only epithelial hyperplasia without malignancy. Despite topical agents for verruca vulgaris and antibiotic courses, the lesion slowly enlarged and became ulcerated.

His medical history was notable for spinal trauma 30 years earlier, treated with vertebral fixation, resulting in permanent urinary catheterization but otherwise healed fractures. On examination, there was a large ulcerated, verrucous plaque over the calcaneus of the right foot; no other lesions were present. Laboratory studies remained nondiagnostic. The patient underwent aggressive debridement with marginal excision and multiple deep biopsies.

High-quality radiographs and CT scan of the right foot showed extension of the lesion into the soft periosteal tissues and expansion beneath the calcaneus, suggesting bone invasion.

A 15-year-old undernourished boy presented with a 4-month history of intermittent low-grade fevers, dry cough, anorexia, and weight loss, and a 1-month history of progressively worsening exertional dyspnea that now limited his activities. He had received only symptomatic treatment, and his symptoms persisted.

On examination, he appeared thin and in mild respiratory distress. Vital signs showed tachypnea but no hypotension or hypoxia at rest. Chest auscultation revealed diminished breath sounds over the entire left hemithorax.

A chest radiograph showed complete opacification of the left lung with ipsilateral mediastinal shift. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax demonstrated an intraluminal mass occluding the left main bronchus with total collapse–consolidation of the left lung, as well as a second endobronchial lesion in the right lower lobe bronchus.

Fibreoptic bronchoscopy confirmed a large obstructing tumor in the left main bronchus and a second growth in the right lower lobar bronchus. Guided biopsies were obtained from both lesions. The left-sided specimen consisted of necrotic tissue, and the right-sided specimen was reported as a neuroendocrine tumor (carcinoid tumor).

Within days, his respiratory distress worsened, requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. A repeat bronchoscopy with endobronchial biopsies was performed under sedation; those specimens were sent for histopathologic evaluation.

An infant boy was referred for evaluation of a congenital left neck mass. At 1 month of age, magnetic resonance imaging revealed a multicystic lesion adjacent to the pharynx and parotid gland. His history, physical examination, and MRI findings suggested a lymphatic malformation. He underwent OK-432 sclerotherapy at 2, 3, and 6 months of age, with each session resulting in the expected reduction in volume. At 3 years of age, a persistent bulge prompted a fourth sclerotherapy attempt, but aspiration could not reach the cystic component. MRI at 5 years showed that most of the lesion had become thick, wall-like tissue with only a small residual cystic component. A further attempt at sclerotherapy was abandoned because the cyst wall was judged too thick. Ultrasound at 5 years demonstrated virtually no cystic component and no fluid flow, findings interpreted as consistent with lymphatic malformation, postsclerotherapy scar, or blood clots. At 6 years of age, surgical resection was planned.

A 16-year-old male presented with a 1-year history of left knee pain associated with stiffness that interfered with daily activities. He reported no fever, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. On examination, there was diffuse tenderness of the left knee and a moderate joint effusion; the remainder of the musculoskeletal and systemic examination was unremarkable.  
Plain radiographs of the knee showed a lucent, rounded lesion with a sharp sclerotic margin involving the distal anterior femoral epiphysis and metaphysis. MRI with intravenous contrast demonstrated a lesion centered in the distal femoral epiphysis extending through the physis into the metaphysis. The lesion was T2 hyperintense and T1 hypointense, with extensive surrounding bone marrow edema, slight adjacent periosteal reaction, and hyperintense signal on both pre- and postcontrast T1 fat-suppressed sequences.

A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a right breast mass noted for more than 1 year, recently associated with skin ulceration. The mass had gradually enlarged, was hard in texture, non-tender, and mobile. One month before presentation, she observed a 3-cm area of skin breakdown with mild exudation and bleeding over the lesion.

On examination, a 4.5 × 5.5 cm irregular, poorly defined, hard mass was palpable at the 1 o’clock position in the right breast, 2.5 cm from the nipple, with overlying ulceration and slight serosanguinous discharge. The lesion was fairly mobile without palpable axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. The left breast was normal.

Breast ultrasound and MRI both classified the lesion as BI-RADS category V. Chest CT demonstrated a right breast mass suggestive of malignancy. Serum breast tumor markers were within normal limits.

A 68-year-old Japanese man with an 11-year history of rheumatoid arthritis presented with a four-month history of dry cough, two-week anorexia, a 4-kg weight loss, and progressive dyspnea. His arthritis had been treated with prednisolone, methotrexate, and golimumab, then switched to infliximab, with resultant minimal disease activity. He had no history of allergy, asthma, drug use, recent travel, or inhalational exposures. On examination, his temperature was 37.0°C, respiratory rate 27 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91% at rest, decreasing to 80% on mild exertion; the only abnormal finding was bilateral ulnar drift deformity of the hands. Laboratory studies were notable for lactate dehydrogenase 473 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 550 IU/L, C-reactive protein 3.57 mg/dL, and carcinoembryonic antigen 7.2 U/mL; other values were within normal limits. A chest radiograph showed bilateral infiltrative shadows. High-resolution computed tomography of the chest revealed extensive ground-glass opacities, emphysematous changes, partially irregular thickening of the interlobular septa and bronchovascular interstitium, slight pleural effusion, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Electrocardiography and echocardiography were normal.

A 45-year-old woman reported two months of blurring in the left visual field. Over the two weeks before presentation, she noted progressive visual blurring in her left eye accompanied by intermittent headaches and photophobia. On neurologic examination, no visual field defect was detected, and visual evoked potentials were normal. Endocrine evaluation showed normal pituitary hormones except for a mildly elevated serum prolactin level of 61.29 ng/mL. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed a solid sellar mass that was isointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed marked homogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration; the mass compressed the optic chiasm.

A 68-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of persistent, nonproductive cough. She had no history of hemoptysis, smoking, or significant medical conditions. Physical examination was unremarkable.  
A chest radiograph showed a well-defined mass in the right upper lung zone. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a 5.6 × 5.4 × 5.0 cm soft-tissue mass in the right upper lobe, with an endobronchial component filling the right upper lobe bronchus and extending approximately 1 cm distal to the carina. The lesion measured 42–50 Hounsfield units and contained internal specks of coarse calcification, with secondary atelectasis of the anterior segment of the right upper lobe. No enlarged thoracic lymph nodes, other lesions, or skeletal abnormalities were identified.  
PET–CT demonstrated low fluorodeoxyglucose activity in the lesion (maximum standardized uptake value, 3.8) and no other areas of abnormal uptake.  
The initial clinical and radiologic impressions were pulmonary carcinoid tumor.

A 42-year-old Caucasian woman presented with 6 months of pain and regional deformity in the distal third of her right calf. The pain was episodic, worsened with physical activity, sometimes pulsating, and accompanied by calf swelling.  
Initial radiographs and contrast-enhanced CT of the right leg showed a 37×22×16 mm osteolytic lesion in the distal tibial shaft with cortical thinning, minimal cortical interruptions, and periosteal reaction. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed only a benign left breast cyst. Three-phase bone scintigraphy demonstrated increased vascularization and heterogeneous hypercaptation in the distal right tibia, with no other abnormal uptake.  
An excisional biopsy with trepanation of the tibial cortex yielded a “chronic intraosseous inflammatory process with areas of regenerative appearance at the periphery.”  
On referral, examination revealed a firm, elastic, well-defined subcutaneous mass on the anteromedial right leg at the biopsy site, adherent to bone but not to skin and tender on palpation. Laboratory studies showed ESR 29 mm/h (normal 0–20), fibrinogen 485 mg/dL (normal 180–450), CRP 6.44 mg/L (normal <5), and normal alkaline phosphatase.  
Repeat radiography, CT, and MRI demonstrated enlargement of the lesion to 5.5×1.95×2.2 cm, persistent osteolysis with cortical thinning and disruption, periosteal reaction, and extraosseous extension through the biopsy defect into encapsulated subcutaneous tissue.  
A percutaneous needle biopsy again showed a chronic inflammatory lesion, this time with xanthogranulomatous cells; bacteriological cultures were negative.

A 25-year-old woman (G2P2) presented with two weeks of progressive, asymmetric right-sided abdominal distention and intermittent discomfort radiating from the right iliac fossa to the right hypochondrium and thigh. She reported irregular menses with menorrhagia managed with oral contraceptives, as well as fatigue, nausea, anorexia, urinary urgency, and constipation unrelieved by laxatives. Her obstetric, surgical, and medical histories were otherwise unremarkable; she denied tobacco or alcohol use and had a family history of breast and endometrial cancer. On examination she appeared well, was hemodynamically stable, and had mild pallor. Abdominal examination revealed right-sided distention and a tender mass; other systems were normal. Laboratory studies showed a platelet count of 425 × 10^9/L, hematocrit 35%, hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, normal leukocytes, negative echinococcus antibody, and elevated CA 19-9 and CA 125 levels (69.59 U/mL and 64.08 U/mL, respectively). Pelvic ultrasound demonstrated a 25 × 15 cm multicystic mass with thick septations extending to the umbilicus; the uterus, liver, and spleen appeared normal, and there was minimal free fluid in the cul-de-sac. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis confirmed an irregular, multiloculated cystic mass measuring 25 × 10 cm with no lymphadenopathy.

A 34-year-old woman was evaluated for a 2-month history of intermittent diffuse abdominal pain. Her medical history was unremarkable. On examination, the abdomen was mildly distended, with rebound percussion tenderness in the right iliac fossa. Routine blood tests were within normal limits. A double-contrast barium enema demonstrated an ovoid filling defect in the cecum and ascending colon. Colonoscopy was attempted but could not be advanced beyond the hepatic flexure. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed an ovoid endoluminal mass extending from the cecum into the ascending colon with homogeneous fatty density and no evidence of extramural extension.

A 6-year-old boy with no significant medical history presented with 1 month of progressive hoarseness and 2 weeks of breathing difficulty. There was no fever, weight loss, or appetite change, and no history of trauma or prior head and neck surgery aside from a childhood tongue ‑tie release. Vital signs were stable, and the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Flexible laryngoscopy revealed a polypoidal mass measuring approximately 1 × 1 cm on the free border and undersurface of the right vocal cord, extending into the subglottis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck confirmed a 1 × 1 cm polypoid nodule arising from the right vocal cord, projecting into the airway lumen without invasion of the anterior commissure or deep cartilage.

A 2-month-old boy was referred for evaluation of an anechoic formation in the right lower abdomen detected on prenatal ultrasound. There was no history of acute illness or trauma. On admission, vital signs were normal and the patient was afebrile. Laboratory studies, including liver function tests, were within reference ranges. 

Postnatal abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a 34×23 mm cystic formation in the right lower quadrant with parietal stratification of three alternating hyper- and hypoechoic layers (“gut sign”) and an internal septum separating a round from a tubular component.

To further characterize the lesion and aid in surgical planning, an abdominal MRI was obtained under sedation. MRI showed a 50×34×30 mm cystic lesion in the right lower abdomen with simple fluid signal (hyperintense on T2, hypointense on T1), an internal septum between tubular and round portions, and no obvious communication with the gastrointestinal tract. There were no vertebral or other anomalies.

A 53-year-old right-handed woman presented with a 5-year history of insidious, progressive left shoulder pain and a 2-year history of similar left elbow pain. There was no history of trauma, surgery, or systemic disease. The pain increased with shoulder extension, internal rotation, and abduction, and with elbow extension, and was relieved by rest. 

On examination, the left shoulder showed no swelling or erythema; active forward flexion was 80°, abduction 50°, external rotation 35°, and internal rotation reached the lumbosacral level. Neer’s, Hawkins’s, and Jobe’s tests were positive. The left elbow had flexion to 100° and extension to 10° with full pronation and supination, and no varus or valgus laxity. The right shoulder and elbow were normal.

Plain radiographs of the left shoulder demonstrated numerous oval calcifications in the subacromial space, severe degenerative changes of the glenohumeral joint, cartilage erosion, and narrowing of the subacromial space. Radiographs of the left elbow showed multiple calcified bodies in the humeroradial joint with mild degenerative changes. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the shoulder revealed granular material in the subacromial area with signal intensity similar to bone and a massive rotator cuff tear. MRI of the elbow showed proliferative synovium in the humeroulnar joint.

A 9‐year‐old girl was referred for a mass on the left hard palate that had been growing over several weeks and was associated with discomfort during mastication and tooth brushing and minor bleeding. On examination, there was an ulcerated, firm mass of the left hard palate; the ulcer did not oppose the lower teeth. CT of the maxillofacial region showed a 2.2 × 1.3 × 2.6 cm heterogeneously enhancing expansile mass of the left lateral hard palate with bone destruction, extending into the ipsilateral alveolar recess and maxillary antrum without orbital extension. An initial biopsy at an outside institution revealed a small fragment of ulcerated squamous mucosa with a submucosal bland spindle cell proliferation. The specimen was too limited to permit immunohistochemical studies, and a definitive diagnosis could not be established.  
What is your differential diagnosis and next diagnostic step?

A 57-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of progressive difficulty swallowing. She had no other neurological complaints. On examination, she was found to have right hypoglossal nerve palsy; no other deficits were noted. Her medical history was notable for breast cancer, treated successfully several years earlier.

A noncontrast CT scan of the head showed bone erosion extending from the right hypoglossal canal to the anterior aspect of the foramen magnum. MRI of the brain demonstrated a lesion within the right hypoglossal canal that was hyperintense on T2-weighted and FLAIR images and iso- to hypointense on T1-weighted and diffusion-weighted images. After administration of gadolinium, the lesion exhibited irregular peripheral enhancement. A cerebral angiogram showed no tumor stain. PET-CT revealed no abnormal uptake in the lesion or elsewhere.

Based on these findings, the preoperative differential diagnosis included schwannoma of the hypoglossal nerve, chordoma, breast cancer metastasis, and chondroma.

A 59-year-old man presented with a 12-hour history of right-sided limb weakness, stiffness of the right hand and leg, slurred speech, and right facial paresis. He also reported a six-month history of intermittent headaches and decreased hearing but denied ear or tooth infections and weight loss. His medical history was notable for Parkinson’s disease treated with levodopa and mecobalamin since 2016. On examination, there was paresis of the right seventh, eighth, and twelfth cranial nerves and right-sided motor lateralization. A chest radiograph was normal. Noncontrast head CT revealed a 6.15×5.47×5.7 cm, well-defined hypodense lesion containing irregular calcifications in the right cerebellar region, with surrounding hypodense shadowing, erosion of the right occipital bone, distortion of the fourth ventricle, third-ventricle ballooning, and signs of noncommunicating hydrocephalus. MRI of the head showed an intra-axial cystic lesion with an irregular margin in the right cerebellar hemisphere that was isointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, exhibited restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging, and demonstrated subtle contrast enhancement. MR angiography showed a patent circle of Willis without aneurysm or vascular malformation. MR spectroscopy showed no increase in the choline/creatinine or choline/N-acetylaspartate ratios, and MR perfusion showed no increase in relative cerebral blood volume.

A 78-year-old man presented with a 30-day history of redness, itching, sensation of tightness, and swelling of the lower legs that had spread to the trunk. He reported no fevers or weight loss. His medical history was notable for Rai stage 0 chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), diagnosed 7 years earlier with CD5+ and CD23+ lymphocytes on bone marrow biopsy; he had never required treatment. 

On dermatological examination, there were multiple livid papules on the feet and medial lower legs converging into grayish-black plaques. Similar single papules were seen on the upper trunk and proximal upper extremities. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 118 g/L, platelet count 212 × 10^9/L, leukocyte count 38.6 × 10^9/L (lymphocytes 32.4 × 10^9/L, with Gumprecht shadows). Abdominal ultrasound revealed no splenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Serologic tests were negative for HIV and hepatitis B and C. 

He received systemic antihistamines and corticosteroids with marked improvement in itching and swelling, although the papules persisted. Initial differential diagnosis included angioma, pigmented purpuric dermatosis, hemangioendothelioma, and Kaposi sarcoma. Two papules from the lower leg and trunk were excised for biopsy.

A 51-year-old woman noted a new left axillary mass. Physical examination revealed a 3.1×1.5 cm left axillary lymph node; no masses or nipple discharge were present in either breast, and the right axilla was normal.  
Breast ultrasound and mammography were unremarkable. Axillary ultrasound showed three homogeneous hypoechoic left axillary masses with irregular margins; the largest measured 3.11×1.61 cm.  
PET/CT demonstrated increased glucose uptake in left axillary lymph nodes (SUVmax = 9.56) with no abnormal uptake in the breasts.  
Fine-needle aspiration cytology of a left axillary node showed invasive ductal carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry of the node revealed Ki-67 70%, ER + (90%), PR + (80%), HER-2 (score 2+), E-cadherin +, AR + (90%), CK5/6 –, p63 –, calponin –, SOX10 –, GATA-3 + and GCDFP-15 +.  
Serum tumor markers (AFP, CEA, PSA, CA 19-9, CA 15-3) were all within normal limits. The patient had no personal or family history of malignancy.

A 13-year-old girl presented with a 7‐month history of right‐sided nasal obstruction, anosmia, intermittent epistaxis, snoring, and hearing loss. She denied trauma, anorexia, or weight loss. On examination, a mass occupied the right nasal cavity, displaced the septum toward the left, and extended into the nasopharynx, pushing the soft palate downward. Otoscopic examination revealed bilateral tympanic‐membrane retraction and dullness. Cranial nerves were intact, and there was no cervical lymphadenopathy. Hematologic and biochemical laboratory tests were within normal limits. Computed tomography of the paranasal sinuses showed complete opacification of the right nasal cavity, maxillary, ethmoidal, sphenoid, and frontal sinuses, with remodeling of the nasal septum toward the left side.

A 29-year-old woman was admitted for evaluation of a ruptured liver mass. Four months earlier she had undergone a cesarean section followed by L-carnitine therapy. She had no history of hepatitis or cirrhosis. On examination, the right upper abdomen was slightly distended. A 10-cm hypogastric surgical scar was present. A firm, smooth, non-tender 5×6 cm mass was palpable in the right upper quadrant. Laboratory studies showed normal liver and renal function, electrolytes, and a normal α-fetoprotein level.  
Ultrasound revealed a heterogeneous hyperechoic mass measuring 15.5×9.6×14.2 cm in the right hepatic lobe, with an irregular anechoic area, a clear margin, and no detectable blood flow on Doppler imaging. Plain CT showed a large right anterior hepatic lobe mass with mixed high and low internal densities. Dynamic contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated uneven arterial enhancement, more homogeneous enhancement in the venous and equilibrium phases, a large non-enhancing area within the mass, multiple enlarged peritumoral vessels, and a low-density rim. MRI confirmed a large right anterior hepatic lobe lesion with heterogeneous signal intensity, uneven contrast enhancement, and an internal liquefactive necrotic region. A hepatic adenoma was diagnosed based on imaging.  
During surgery, the lesion was found in segment V of the liver, measured approximately 10 cm, had cystic and solid components, and invaded the gallbladder and part of segment VI. The patient underwent segment V resection, partial segment VI resection, and cholecystectomy. Postoperative recovery was uneventful.

A 19-year-old woman presented with a two-month history of headache, nausea, and vomiting. Neurologic examination revealed cerebellar ataxia, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and bilateral papilledema. Noncontrast CT of the head showed two hypodense lesions in the right cerebellar hemisphere and the vermis, each demonstrating peripheral heterogeneous enhancement after contrast administration and causing mass effect on the fourth ventricle. Cranial MRI demonstrated irregularly contoured mass lesions in contact with the fourth ventricle, heterogeneous signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images suggestive of subacute intratumoral hemorrhage with discrete surrounding edema, and lesions measuring 3×4 cm with heterogeneous ring enhancement and central necrosis.

A 56-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of a painless right breast lump that rapidly increased in size and developed a bluish discoloration of the overlying skin. She had no personal or family history of cancer, breast surgery, or irradiation. On examination, there was a firm, fixed, ill-defined 5 cm mass involving the upper quadrants of the right breast; the overlying skin was bluish but not ulcerated. There was no nipple retraction, axillary lymphadenopathy, or lymphedema. Mammography showed a large, homogeneous mass without spiculation or suspicious calcifications. A core needle biopsy revealed anastomosing round-to-oval vascular spaces containing erythrocytes; the lining cells had thin, elongated, hyperchromatic nuclei that protruded into lumina, and vascular channels invaded adipose tissue. Immunohistochemical stains showed membranous reactivity for CD31 and CD34. These findings were initially interpreted as a benign vascular tumor.

An 8-day-old full-term neonate presented with increased respiratory rate and bluish discoloration of the nails and lips. Antenatal scans had revealed a right atrial mass. There was no family history of congenital heart disease or atrial myxoma, and no maternal drug exposures other than routine supplementation.

On day 2 of life, transthoracic echocardiography showed a heterogeneous, pedunculated right atrial mass (10 × 8 mm) attached to the interatrial septum, mild tricuspid regurgitation, and a peak right ventricular systolic pressure of 61 mmHg (suggestive of severe pulmonary hypertension). Echocardiographic screening of family members was normal.

On day 8, the neonate was tachypneic and mildly cyanotic (SpO₂ 84% on room air). Cardiovascular examination revealed an ejection systolic murmur and a loud P₂. Chest radiography showed pulmonary plethora and mild cardiomegaly. Repeat transthoracic echocardiography identified a 10 × 9 mm right atrial mass attached at the atrioventricular junction of the interatrial septum, a restrictive atrial septal defect with right-to-left shunt, dilated pulmonary arteries, and severe pulmonary hypertension. Two right-sided pulmonary veins formed a common chamber draining into the superior vena cava, and one right pulmonary vein drained directly into the superior vena cava. 

Computed tomography confirmed that the right superior and right inferior pulmonary veins formed a common chamber draining to the superior vena cava, and that the left pulmonary veins joined to form a common vein that coursed infradiaphragmatically to the portal vein. A diagnosis of right atrial mass with mixed total anomalous pulmonary venous connection and severe pulmonary hypertension was made, and surgical intervention was planned.

A 74-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 2-year history of left knee pain, chiefly when kneeling or descending stairs. On examination, there was a tender, mildly diffuse swelling over the left patella with overlying mild erythema. He had full range of motion, an intact straight-leg raise, and normal ligamentous, meniscal, and ipsilateral hip examinations. 

His medical history was notable for treated prostate cancer (now discharged), excision of a basal cell carcinoma, and a permanent pacemaker for bradyarrhythmia; he took only a statin and reported no systemic symptoms.

Radiographs obtained 19 months earlier had shown joint-space narrowing in the patellofemoral compartment with early medial narrowing and a subchondral lucency in the patella, which was described as a subarticular cyst secondary to patellofemoral degeneration. Repeat radiographs, performed 19 months after the initial films, revealed a large lucency in the patella and a discontinuity in the anterior cortex of the inferior pole, suggesting a pathologic fracture. 

A bone scan demonstrated isolated increased tracer uptake around the left patella. CT of the knee confirmed a large lucent area occupying most of the patella with multiple foci of cortical disruption along the anterior border. Ultrasound of the lesion revealed extensive neovascularization and increased flow.

A 56-year-old woman was referred to the retina service after being told she had a nevus in the back of her right eye. She was asymptomatic. Visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. Biomicroscopic examination and intraocular pressures were normal. 

Dilated fundus examination of the right eye revealed a small, heavily pigmented, well-circumscribed, slightly elevated lesion located superonasal to the fovea and temporal to the optic disc, without retinal traction, hemorrhage, or subretinal fluid. The left fundus was normal.

Fluorescein angiography of the right eye showed blockage of fluorescence at the lesion and no leakage. Optical coherence tomography through the lesion demonstrated elevation of the retina, increased optical reflectivity on its inner surface, optical shadowing of deeper structures, and sharply demarcated margins; the surrounding retina and choroid appeared normal. Fundus autofluorescence revealed blockage of background autofluorescence at the lesion. Ocular ultrasonography did not reveal any mass or abnormality.

A 36-year-old woman, gravida 5 para 4, was found to have a right ovarian cyst during a routine fetal anomaly ultrasound scan at 20 weeks’ gestation. On transabdominal sonography, the cyst measured 11.5 × 9.8 × 8.8 cm, had a ground-glass appearance, and contained two papillary projections with grade 1 flow on Doppler (largest projection 4.1 × 3.3 × 3.1 cm). The mass was non-tender, and there was no free fluid in the pelvis. Serum tumor markers were within normal limits (CA 125 31 U/mL [0–35], CA 19-9 11 U/mL [0–35], CEA 2 ng/mL [0–4.7]). The differential diagnosis included mucinous borderline tumour, ovarian malignancy, and decidualised endometrioma. An MRI at 20 weeks, and a repeat MRI at 23 weeks, showed no significant change in the size or appearance of the cyst. After multidisciplinary discussion, the patient was offered ultrasonographic monitoring of the cyst every 4 weeks, with delivery by elective Caesarean section at 34 weeks and planned oophorectomy at the same time.

A 26-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with 14 months of axial neck pain radiating to both shoulders and progressive left shoulder weakness. He had no skin lesions or stigmata of neurocutaneous syndromes.  
Spinal MRI revealed an anterior intradural-extramedullary mass at C2–C3 that was hyperintense on non-contrast T1-weighted images, isointense on T2-weighted images, and showed contrast enhancement, along with a second T1-hyperintense, contrast-enhancing intradural lesion at T7–T8. Brain MRI identified extra-axial lesions in the left cerebellopontine angle and in the suprasellar region, both T1 hyperintense, T2 hypointense, and heterogeneously enhancing post-contrast.  
CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no systemic abnormalities. Based on the patient’s age and multiple enhancing intradural lesions, a presumptive diagnosis of NF2-related schwannomatosis was made.

A 32-year-old woman presented with a subacute onset of weakness in all four limbs and gait disturbance. Neurologic examination showed symmetrical grade IV tetraparesis, hyperactive deep tendon reflexes, a positive Hoffmann sign, and posterior cord syndrome with loss of proprioception and vibration sense in the lower extremities. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory tests were unremarkable. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine revealed an intradural extramedullary, nodular lesion located dorsally at the midline of the C6–C7 level. The lesion was isointense on T1-weighted images, hypointense on T2-weighted and STIR images, and exhibited avid enhancement after gadolinium administration. There was severe compression of the spinal cord, with pial engorgement and surrounding myelomalacia extending into the upper thoracic segments.

A 44-year-old man with no significant medical or family history underwent curative proximal sigmoidectomy for tubular adenocarcinoma (stage T3N0M0, Stage IIA). Postoperative CEA normalized from 11.0 to 3.3 ng/mL, and no adjuvant chemotherapy was given.  
Twelve months after surgery, CEA rose to 9.0 ng/mL; CT and colonoscopy showed no recurrence. Three months later, CEA further increased to 17.2 ng/mL. PET-CT revealed abnormal fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the rectum.  
Repeat colonoscopy showed a submucosal tumor–like lesion 10–15 cm from the anal verge; biopsy revealed tubular adenocarcinoma. CT and PET-CT identified no lymph node or distant metastases.  
Under the differential diagnosis of an atypical primary rectal cancer versus a rare intramural recurrence, the patient underwent curative low anterior resection with tumor-specific mesorectal excision and a 3 cm distal margin.

A 3-month-old female, with an unremarkable birth history, was referred for evaluation of an enlarging right chest-wall mass that had not improved with antibiotic therapy. On examination, there was a 5-cm subcutaneous mass over the right 8th rib with overlying skin redness and tenderness. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 11,000/µl and a C-reactive protein level of 4.8 mg/dl; serum tumor markers were within reference ranges. A chest radiograph revealed an increased radiolucent lesion at the right 8th rib. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a 28 × 27 mm multicystic mass with homogeneous enhancement, and three-dimensional reconstruction confirmed an osteolytic defect of the 8th rib. MRI showed a mass with a thickened septum that enhanced after gadolinium administration. These imaging features suggested mesenchymal hamartoma. However, malignant neoplasms such as Ewing sarcoma, neuroblastoma, fibrosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, and chondroblastoma were also considered. During the hospital course, the mass self-destructed with serous fluid discharge and decreased markedly in size; the overlying erythema and tenderness resolved gradually. Despite this spontaneous regression suggesting a benign process, surgical resection of the mass with surrounding tissue was performed to obtain a definitive diagnosis.

A 65-year-old right-hand–dominant woman noted a mass on the ulnar side of her right elbow approximately 5 months before presentation. Initial MRI at an outside facility showed a 15×10×10 mm homogenous lesion with low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, located along the ulnar nerve and not attached to bone. Because a benign soft-tissue tumor such as schwannoma was suspected, an excisional biopsy was performed. Intraoperatively, a subcutaneous mass was found attached to the ulnar nerve and “it did not resemble a schwannoma or neuroma.” A marginal excision was undertaken to preserve the nerve. 

One week after the procedure, she was referred for further evaluation. On examination, there was a well-healed scar without erythema, warmth, or sensory deficits. Repeat MRI of the elbow demonstrated a 12×5×5 mm contrast-enhancing lesion adjacent to the ulnar nerve, suspicious for local recurrence.

A 15-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of painless swelling in the anterior maxilla and failure of his upper left central incisor to erupt. He had no history of trauma or infection in the orofacial region. On examination, there was an asymptomatic, expansile swelling over the left anterior maxillary ridge, covered by normal mucosa, and the left central incisor was not in the dental arch. A provisional diagnosis of an odontoma or a dentigerous cyst was considered.

A panoramic radiograph demonstrated a large radiopaque mass in the midline of the maxilla composed of numerous tooth-like structures, each surrounded by a thin radiolucent rim; the left central incisor was horizontally impacted, and the adjacent central and lateral incisors were displaced distally. A cone-beam CT scan confirmed a dense, calcified mass in the anterior maxilla causing expansion and thinning of the facial cortical bone.

A 63-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of a waxing and waning, tender rash in the intergluteal cleft. He had applied topical terbinafine 1%, tolnaftate 1%, clotrimazole 1%, triple antibiotic cream, and hydrocortisone 1% without improvement. His medical history was notable for primary sclerosing cholangitis status post liver transplantation 5 years earlier (on mycophenolate mofetil and tacrolimus) and melanoma in situ on the left heel 3 years earlier. On examination, there were pink plaques with numerous coalescing “punched out” erosions symmetrically affecting the superior intergluteal cleft and bilateral buttocks in a “kissing” distribution; no satellite lesions were seen. The differential diagnosis included herpetic infection, extramammary Paget disease, intertrigo, and allergic or irritant contact dermatitis. Initial work-up included a viral swab, which was negative for herpes simplex virus and varicella zoster virus.

A 47-year-old man presented with retrosternal chest pain not related to exertion and progressive shortness of breath on exertion. He denied cough, hemoptysis, fever, or weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL, leukocytes 8500/mm3, platelets 360 000/mm3, normal electrolytes, renal function, and liver function. Serum LDH, AFP, and β-HCG were within normal limits. Chest radiography revealed a large mass in the left thoracic cavity adjacent to the mediastinum. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed a 14 cm heterogeneously enhancing anterior mediastinal mass. CT-guided core-needle biopsy was performed and reported as sarcoma.

An 18-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a growth on the left half of his lower lip. He first noticed a small lesion that gradually enlarged over 1 month. He reported mild, occasional pain but denied paraesthesia, numbness, or similar lesions elsewhere. His medical, dental, family, and social histories were unremarkable.

On intraoral examination, there was a solitary, well-defined, oval, nodular, exophytic lesion on the left lower labial mucosa measuring approximately 9 × 7 mm. Anteroposteriorly, it extended from 0.5 cm below the vermilion border to 1 cm above the vestibular sulcus; mediolaterally, from 1.5 cm lateral to midline to 1.5 cm anterior to the left commissure. The surface was whitish centrally and erythematous peripherally. On palpation, the lesion was sessile, slightly tender, firm, and arose from underlying soft tissue. 

Complete blood count and biochemistry were within normal limits. Based on the history and clinical features, a provisional diagnosis of irritational fibroma was made. Differential diagnoses included fibrosed mucocele, peripheral giant cell granuloma, and extragingival pyogenic granuloma. The lesion was excised under local anesthesia, and the specimen was sent for histopathological evaluation.

A 28-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of daily morning headaches that were unresponsive to medical therapy. She was neurologically intact on examination, with no peripheral lymphadenopathy or pigmented skin lesions, and had a right prosthetic eye. Ten years earlier, she underwent enucleation of the right eye for a histologically confirmed choroidal melanoma. Routine laboratory tests were normal. On hospital day 2, noncontrast head CT revealed a hyperdense lesion in the left frontal lobe. MRI showed the lesion to be hyperintense on T1-weighted images, isointense on T2-weighted images, and isointense on gradient-echo sequences.

A previously healthy 5-year-old girl was admitted with a 4-week history of nausea, vomiting, intermittent abdominal pain, and diarrhea. On physical examination she was moderately dehydrated. Dermatologic examination revealed asymptomatic, firm, well-demarcated plaques of confluent reddish-brown papules over both groins, the pubic area, and gluteal folds, each measuring approximately 2 × 7 cm. There was no hepatosplenomegaly or palpable lymphadenopathy. Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, white-cell differential 70% neutrophils and 25% lymphocytes, normal phosphorus and parathyroid hormone levels, and a markedly elevated serum calcium of 17.9 mg/dL. A 4-mm punch biopsy of a skin lesion revealed amorphous basophilic deposits in the reticular dermis; von Kossa staining was positive, confirming calcinosis cutis. Chest radiography was unremarkable. Renal ultrasonography demonstrated nephrocalcinosis, but renal function tests were normal and there was no evidence of visceral calcifications elsewhere.

A 28-year-old Caucasian man presented to the emergency department with acute urinary retention and lower abdominal pain. He reported consuming approximately 1 L of wine and several beers in the hours before presentation. He had no prior urinary symptoms, no significant medical history, and no family history of genitourinary disease. He was a regular smoker and alcohol consumer, with no medication use. On examination, he was afebrile with normal vital signs. The lower abdomen was distended; digital rectal and neurologic examinations were unremarkable.  
   
Point‐of‐care ultrasound showed normal kidneys and a distended bladder without wall irregularities; the prostate appeared unremarkable (size not documented). A Foley catheter drained 1 L of clear urine. Urinalysis was normal. He was given diclofenac and, two days later, passed a trial without catheter.  
   
One month later, he returned with acute urinary retention without recent alcohol intake. Examination and ultrasound revealed an enlarged prostate (approx. 50 mL). Laboratory tests, including prostate-specific antigen and lactate dehydrogenase, were within normal limits. He was started on tamsulosin, but trial without catheter failed, requiring re-catheterization. He developed intermittent tenesmus treated with trospium chloride. Cystoscopy showed diffusely erythematous and villous prostatic urethral mucosa extending to the bladder neck, with large obstructive lobes. A transurethral resection was scheduled in one month.  
   
Before surgery, he developed persistent right-sided flank pain. Urinalysis showed leukocyturia, and right pyelonephritis was treated with ciprofloxacin. Two days later, he presented with hematuria and right-sided hydronephrosis; renal colic and hemorrhagic cystitis were suspected, and analgesics and antibiotics were continued. A low-dose CT scan showed no stones but identified a mass in the prostate. Repeat cystoscopy again revealed obstructive prostatic lobes and erythematous mucosa. The working diagnosis was passing ureteral calculus with cystitis superimposed on benign prostatic hyperplasia. A trial without catheter relieved symptoms temporarily.  
   
Over the next days, he developed left-sided flank pain and bilateral second-degree hydronephrosis with a slight rise in creatinine; lactate dehydrogenase remained normal. Cystoscopy now showed a partly villous and solid tumor in the prostatic urethra infiltrating the bladder trigone and ureteric orifices. Biopsies were taken endoscopically, and bilateral ureteral stents were placed.

A 22-year-old woman with no prior pregnancies presented with progressive abdominal distension. On examination, she had a large, palpable abdominal mass. Pelvic MRI confirmed a sizable pelvic cavity lesion, and contrast‐enhanced CT showed a complex, heterogeneously enhancing mass invading the abdominal cavity and displacing adjacent bowel and ovary. Laboratory studies revealed an elevated serum CA-125 level of 285.3 U/mL (normal <35 U/mL); CA 19-9, CEA, and AFP were normal. A probe laparotomy with tumor biopsy was performed; intraoperatively the mass was soft, immobile, nontender, and very vascular. Postoperatively the patient developed ascites and abdominal tenderness, and a frozen section was interpreted as suspicious for a mesenchymal tumor, prompting initiation of doxorubicin and ifosfamide. Permanent sections showed diffuse infiltration by short spindle cells and small round cells with irregular nuclei, a large necrotic area, and a mitotic rate of 60 per 10 HPF. Immunohistochemical staining revealed positivity for epithelial membrane antigen, vimentin, desmin, and synaptophysin, and negativity for S-100 protein, cytokeratin 7, cytokeratin 20, CAM5.2, and AE1/AE3.

A 36-year-old primiparous woman presented with a 2-month history of a persistent, painful umbilical swelling and spontaneous catamenial bleeding from the umbilicus during her menstrual periods. Her menstrual cycles were regular. She had no history of abdominal or uterine surgery, no umbilical trauma, and no known endometriosis; she had never used oral contraception. On examination, there was a 1.5-cm solid black umbilical swelling that was tender, irreducible on palpation, and discharged a bloody fluid; there was no sign of infection. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a non-vascularized, tissue-like subcutaneous mass at the umbilicus measuring 24 mm × 19 mm. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a small umbilical tissue nodule measuring 23 mm × 19 mm that did not extend beyond the muscle plane. Given the cyclical nature of the pain and bleeding coinciding with her menstrual cycle, umbilical endometriosis was suspected. The initial differential diagnosis included a simple inclusion cyst, benign or malignant neoplasms of the umbilicus, and umbilical granuloma.

An 18-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with a third episode in three months of painful, prolonged erections unrelated to sexual stimulation. Previous episodes resolved with cold showers; at the first ED visit he received pseudoephedrine and ice, and at the second he received terbutaline without success. During the second visit, a corporal blood gas showed pH 7.12, PCO2 30 mmHg, and PO2 43 mmHg, suggestive of ischemic priapism; the hemoglobin level on that blood gas was reported as “results incalculable.” On his third presentation he had symptoms for at least six hours. He was not taking any medications and had no other symptoms. Urology performed penile aspiration and irrigation, and emergency physicians obtained laboratory studies. A complete blood count revealed a white blood cell count of 588 × 10^3/µL with differential showing marked neutrophilia (264.6 × 10^3/µL), lymphocytosis (17.64 × 10^3/µL), monocytosis (11.76 × 10^3/µL), eosinophilia (11.76 × 10^3/µL), basophilia (5.88 × 10^3/µL), myelocytes (164.64 × 10^3/µL), metamyelocytes (35.28 × 10^3/µL), promyelocytes (64.68 × 10^3/µL), and peripheral blasts (11.76 × 10^3/µL). Hemoglobin was 7.3 g/dL and platelet count was 109 × 10^3/µL. He was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit and started on hydroxyurea pending further evaluation.

A 48-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of left ankle pain without trauma. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. On examination, there was mild swelling and edema over the lateral lower leg and ankle with tenderness localized to the distal fibula. Ankle motion was full but painful at end range; there was no neurovascular deficit or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, calcium, phosphorus, and alkaline phosphatase, were normal. 
Plain radiographs of the left ankle showed a coarse, perpendicular periosteal reaction with a “hair on end” pattern and cortical thickening of the distal fibular shaft, without cortical scalloping or medullary erosion. Computed tomography confirmed a periosteal lesion involving about one-half of the fibular circumference, with foci of mineralization, and no evidence of medullary involvement. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated periosteal elevation along a 7-cm segment of the distal fibula, with a 2.1 × 1.7 cm lytic focus within the periosteal reaction that was T2 hyperintense, T1 hypointense, and showed mild diffusion restriction; minimal adjacent marrow edema was noted. 
After imaging, the leading considerations were metastatic disease versus a primary bone tumor. Ultrasonography of the abdomen and thyroid, plus mammography, showed no primary lesion, favoring a primary bone lesion.

A 55-year-old woman underwent total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy one year earlier for a mucinous adenocarcinoma infiltrating the ovary and peritoneum. She now presents with progressive abdominal distension, mild dyspnea, and a 12-kg weight loss. On examination, she appeared debilitated (WHO performance status 3), with diffuse dullness to percussion of the abdomen and no palpable masses or collateral venous circulation. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated large-volume ascites. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed unilateral right pleural thickening with lobulated subpleural and fissural masses of water density and curvilinear calcifications, without pulmonary parenchymal lesions or mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed abundant ascites containing arciform calcifications and scalloping of the liver and spleen surfaces, with no appendiceal lesions, hepatic nodules, or lymphadenopathy.

A 59-year-old woman was noted to have an anterior mediastinal mass on chest CT performed for cough 9 years ago. At that time, the 31-mm lesion (CT value ~44.5 HU) lay anterior to the trachea, slightly compressing and shifting it to the left. A contrast-enhanced CT scan showed enlargement of the mass and “the presence of a single enlarged lymph node (lymphoma, Metastasis, or Inflammation).” 18F-FDG PET-CT demonstrated an upper paratracheal lesion with a maximal diameter of 50 mm and SUVmax 6.27. Four different hospitals rendered a diagnosis of Castleman disease, and no biopsy or treatment was undertaken. Annual CT scans documented slow growth; over the past six months she developed progressive neck tightness and dyspnea. A recent CT showed a single 46 × 51 × 72 mm mass with uniform density (CT value ~40 HU), a distinct border, and compression of the trachea and great vessels. On examination, temperature was 36.1 °C, pulse 71 bpm, respiratory rate 17 bpm, blood pressure 133/73 mmHg; superficial lymph nodes were not palpable. Contrast-enhanced CT with three-dimensional reconstruction revealed a soft-tissue mass in the superior anterior mediastinum (57 × 51 mm) with non-uniform enhancement and patchy low-density areas; the margins with the superior vena cava and brachiocephalic veins were unclear, and tortuous vessels surrounded the tumor. MRI showed a mixed long T1 and T2 signal, vascular flow voids, diffusion-weighted imaging high signal, apparent diffusion coefficient slightly low (53.3 × 48 × 64 mm), and uneven enhancement similar to adjacent large vessels. Laboratory studies—including blood count, electrolytes, adrenal and hepatic function—and ultrasound of superficial lymph nodes, heart, liver, biliary system, and spleen were normal.

A 22-year-old woman noted a bulging neck mass. At a primary clinic, fine-needle aspiration was interpreted as “papillary carcinoma.” On transfer for surgery, ultrasonography showed a well-defined hypoechoic mass measuring 3.9 × 3.4 cm in the left thyroid lobe; cervical lymph nodes were unremarkable. During thyroidectomy, frozen-section examination with touch preparation cytology was performed. The frozen sections demonstrated predominantly papillary epithelial configurations with a focal spindle-cell component. Touch preparation smears were highly cellular, showing tight clusters of spindle or ovoid tumor cells forming papillary configurations. The spindle cells had scant cytoplasm, indistinct borders, and elongated, cigar-shaped nuclei. No intranuclear cytoplasmic inclusions or nuclear grooves were seen.

A 2-year-old boy was brought to the oral mucosa clinic because of whitening of his buccal mucosa that had been present for 1 year. The child was asymptomatic.  
Family history revealed similar oral lesions in his father and in his 6-month-old monozygotic twin sisters. The family pedigree was consistent with an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, and none of the affected family members reported lesions at other mucosal sites.  

On examination, the boy’s buccal mucosa on both sides showed large, creamy-white, corrugated folds of uneven thickness. Gentle swabbing removed the flaking mucosa without bleeding or erosion of the underlying tissue. The tongue and floor of the mouth were normal. Vital signs were within normal limits.  

Given the clinical presentation and positive family history, the provisional diagnosis was white sponge nevus. A biopsy of an intraoral lesion and expectant management with possible pharmacologic therapy were planned.

A 59-year-old woman with a history of right breast invasive lobular carcinoma (luminal A subtype, ER-positive, PgR-positive, HER2-negative, Ki-67 5%) treated 4 years earlier with neoadjuvant epirubicin/cyclophosphamide, left oophorectomy for presumed primary ovarian tumor (histopathology revealed breast cancer metastasis), followed by docetaxel and anastrozole with complete response, presented with upper abdominal discomfort and distention.

On first evaluation, vital signs were stable. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed an ulcer at the gastric angle without evidence of pyloric stenosis or tumor, and her symptoms improved with nasogastric decompression.

Two months later, she redeveloped symptoms. Repeat endoscopy demonstrated diffuse thickening of the gastric antrum with stenosis at the pyloric ring but no visible mass. Histopathological examination of biopsy specimens showed no malignant cells. Endoscopic balloon dilatation of the pylorus provided no lasting relief. Given persistent obstructive symptoms and inconclusive biopsies, a gastro-jejunal bypass surgery was planned.

A 9-year-old girl was evaluated for pain and a localized swelling on the left side of the mandible adjacent to the lower left first molar. The pediatric service initially diagnosed a periapical abscess and obtained an orthopantomogram, which showed a well-defined radiolucency measuring 3.5 cm anteroposteriorly and 2 cm superior-inferiorly in the region of the mandibular left first molar. The patient’s history was notable for treated large-intestine malignancy managed with chemotherapy; dental history was otherwise unremarkable. On examination, there was mild left facial swelling, and intraoral inspection revealed a badly broken-down lower left first molar with pulpal exposure. An aspiration biopsy under local anesthesia was negative. Contrast-enhanced multi-slice CT of the facial bones demonstrated wide buccolingual expansion with perforation of both buccal and lingual cortical plates. Under local anesthesia, an incisional biopsy was performed; histologic analysis showed multinucleated giant cells of probable fibroblast origin along with extravasated erythrocytes, consistent with a giant-cell lesion. Laboratory tests including parathyroid hormone, serum calcium, serum phosphorus, and renal function studies were all within normal limits, effectively excluding primary or secondary hyperparathyroidism. According to size and cortical perforation criteria, the lesion was classified as an aggressive variant of a giant-cell lesion.

A 50-year-old left-handed woman with lifelong, drug-resistant epilepsy was referred for neurosurgical evaluation. Seizures began in early childhood and, despite multiple antiepileptic regimens, never fully remitted. Over the past two years, she experienced 3–4 daily episodes of mental confusion, reduced consciousness, right upper-limb dyskinesia, and rightward gaze deviation, with occasional secondary generalization. Her medical history was notable for hypothyroidism. On examination, she was moderately mentally impaired, with slowed speech and gait; no focal motor or sensory deficits were observed. Preoperative brain CT revealed a densely calcified lesion in the left temporal lobe extending into the insula. Brain MRI showed a hypointense, nonenhancing mass on both T1- and T2-weighted images, surrounded by a hyperintense rim on long-TR sequences. The patient was scheduled for surgical resection.

An 18-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of insidious, progressive pain and swelling in the left wrist. The swelling was bony hard, nonadherent to the skin, and ulnar deviation of the wrist elicited pain. Routine vital signs were normal. On examination, there was localized tenderness over the ulnar aspect of the wrist without overlying skin changes; wrist range of motion was limited by pain on ulnar deviation.

Plain radiographs of the left wrist (anteroposterior and lateral views) showed a well-demarcated, lytic lesion involving the pisiform bone and adjacent distal ulna. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated expansion of the pisiform with an irregular cortical outline. The lesion was isointense on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with a lobulated internal matrix. No fluid-fluid levels were described. The imaging appearance raised the possibility of a giant cell tumor or an aneurysmal bone cyst.

A 31-year-old woman noted a slowly enlarging swelling and mild pain in the right maxilla for several months. Her medical history was notable for chronic bronchitis and penicillin intolerance; she smoked ten cigarettes daily. On examination, there was a hard, non-fluctuant, painless swelling in the vestibule of the right maxilla (FDI regions 15–17), with intact facial sensation and no palpable lymphadenopathy. All right maxillary teeth responded normally to cold testing and had physiologic mobility.  

A periapical radiograph showed a well-demarcated radiolucent lesion between the roots of the upper second premolar and first and second molar. Cone-beam CT demonstrated a 30 × 20 × 12 mm ovoid osteolytic lesion in the right maxilla, expansile into the maxillary sinus and buccal vestibule, bounded by a thin radiopaque margin with small interruptions, and in direct contact with adjacent tooth roots without resorption or displacement.
