Clinically and radiologically, an odontogenic keratocyst was most strongly suspected. Although a lateral periodontal cyst, a central giant cell granuloma, and odontogenic tumors were among the differential diagnoses considered, they were deemed less likely in this case.

A 64-year-old woman with a 20-year history of hypertension presented with dizziness and head discomfort of 3 days’ duration. Her blood pressure at presentation was 190/100 mmHg. She had no gastrointestinal symptoms (no abdominal pain, melena, hematemesis, or dysphagia).

An abdominal ultrasound was performed to evaluate her hypertension and incidentally revealed a 4.7 cm × 4.4 cm hypoechoic lesion with a clear, regular boundary located between the upper pole of the spleen and the abdominal aorta, without detectable blood flow. The radiologist noted that the lesion appeared to originate from the stomach and suggested a gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST).

After blood-pressure control, she was admitted for further evaluation. Vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination was unremarkable, and routine blood tests, blood biochemistry, fecal occult blood, and tumor markers were all normal.

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed a 5.5 cm × 4.3 cm smoothly marginated soft-tissue mass in the gastric wall protruding beyond the serosal contour, with marked enhancement and surrounding lymph-node enlargement (nodes up to 1.0 cm). Malignancy, including GIST with nodal metastases, could not be excluded.

Upper endoscopy revealed a smooth, hemispherical submucosal elevation on the gastric fundus. Endoscopic ultrasonography demonstrated a 3.7 cm × 4.4 cm hypoechoic, heterogeneous mass arising from the muscularis propria, with no internal vascularity.

EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration obtained scant gastric mucosal tissue and few spindle cells with areas of calcification, raising the possibility of a spindle cell tumor but without definitive typing. A second EUS-FNA was performed, yielding similar findings.

A 60-year-old Saudi man presented with an 18-month history of erythroderma affecting his entire body and face. Five years earlier, he had developed slightly pruritic, slowly progressive erythematous lesions on his trunk and retroauricular area that were misdiagnosed as severe eczema and treated with multiple courses of oral prednisolone and cyclosporine without improvement. On examination, there were confluent lichenified erythromelanotic plaques with overlying thick greasy scales on the face, neck, trunk, genitalia, upper and lower extremities, palms, and soles, with sparing of the nails and scalp. Bilateral lower‐lid ectropion was present; there was no palpable lymphadenopathy. Three skin punch biopsies (lower back, left buttock, right upper extremity) demonstrated epidermotropism of a large number of atypical lymphocytes—single and in clusters—and a superficial dermal band‐like lymphocytic infiltrate with dermal fibrosis. Direct immunofluorescence was negative for fibrinogen, C3, IgA, IgM, and IgG. Immunohistochemical staining showed tumor cells positive for CD3 and CD45RO but negative for CD4, CD8, and CD7; CD30 was positive in fewer than 25% of lymphocytes.

A 74-year-old white British woman attended a routine outpatient review complaining of a few weeks’ history of frontal headache and progressive drooping of her left eyelid. She had a 9-year history of metastatic well-differentiated grade 2 nonfunctional small intestinal neuroendocrine tumor with known liver metastases, initially managed by palliative distal ileal resection followed by multiple lines of systemic and locoregional therapies. She was 1 month into seventh-line treatment with capecitabine and temozolomide (CAPTEM). 

She denied visual loss, falls, trauma, or other sensory or motor symptoms. Her medical history included diet-controlled hypertension and a prior partial thyroidectomy; she took no regular medications besides her chemotherapy and had no allergies. On examination, she had a complete left ptosis and left ocular palsy consistent with oculomotor nerve involvement; her forehead was spared, visual fields were intact, and all other cranial nerves, speech, and limb examinations were normal. Vital signs were within normal limits, and routine blood tests, including renal and liver function, were satisfactory.

In view of isolated left third cranial nerve palsy, a posterior communicating artery stroke, demyelinating disease, myasthenia gravis, and metastatic involvement were all considered. An urgent contrast-enhanced MRI of the head was performed on the same day.

A 79-year-old Chinese woman with a 5-year history of hypertension presented for evaluation of persistent erythrocytosis. She reported years of palmar erythema, facial flushing, and pruritus and had undergone multiple phlebotomies for presumed erythrocytosis. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (169,000/μL [normal <10,000]), erythrocytosis (7.00 million red cells/μL; hemoglobin 18.3 g/dL; hematocrit 57.7%), and thrombocytosis (915,000/μL). Measurements of red cell volume by chromium-51 labeling were elevated at 2698.2 mL (51.6 mL/kg; normal 20–30 mL/kg), and plasma volume was elevated at 2497.6 mL (47.8 mL/kg; normal 30–45 mL/kg). On the basis of a plasma volume ≥32 mL/kg and a leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score of 167, a diagnosis of absolute erythrocytosis was made, and hydroxyurea was started. Urine vanillylmandelic acid was 7.5 mg/day (normal). Renal ultrasonography demonstrated a 3.9 × 2.0 cm oval hyperechogenic lesion without acoustic shadow in the left adrenal area. Computed tomography of the abdomen showed a left renal tumor without lymphadenopathy.

A 56-year-old woman presented with diffuse abdominal pain of 3 weeks’ duration. She denied nausea or vomiting and reported normal passage of stool and gas. On examination, she was hemodynamically stable. Abdominal palpation elicited diffuse pain with tenderness, most pronounced in the upper quadrants; peristalsis was reduced, tympanism was normal, and Blumberg sign was positive. Laboratory studies showed elevated C-reactive protein, fibrinogen, and γ-glutamyltransferase, and a significant drop in hemoglobin over 24–36 hours. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed wall thickening of the right colon and proximal transverse colon, stretching of the mesentery and adjacent vessels, surrounding lymphadenopathy, and a characteristic “target” appearance. Within the lumen was a round 44×43 mm mass of mixed density, predominantly adipose in attenuation.

A 70-year-old man presented with multiple erythematous to violaceous papules and excoriations on both lower extremities for two weeks. The lesions began as pea-sized papules on the ankles and spread over the entire lower extremities; excoriations occasionally bled and were macerated. Empiric oral steroids and antibiotics produced no improvement. He had no prior medical conditions, family history of skin cancer, or systemic symptoms. 

On examination, vital signs were stable, and numerous non-tender 1–2 cm papules overlying erythema with pitting edema were noted on both legs. 

Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (63,500/mm^3), elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (41 mm/h), elevated C-reactive protein (24.3 mg/L), alkaline phosphatase (458 U/L), and lactate dehydrogenase (1,067 U/L). Abdominal CT revealed splenomegaly and hepatomegaly. 

Peripheral blood smear demonstrated >90% segmented neutrophils and 4.6% neutrophilic precursors including promyelocytes, myelocytes, and metamyelocytes. Bone marrow biopsy was hypercellular with abundant neutrophils and scant erythroid cells and megakaryocytes. 

Skin biopsy of a new lesion showed diffuse dermal infiltration by inhomogeneous neutrophils with pustules; higher magnification revealed mature and immature neutrophils with nuclear atypia, mitotic figures, and bizarre segmented bands. Myeloperoxidase staining of the infiltrate was strongly positive.

A 61-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease presented with a 2-year history of a white, verrucous lesion covering the right buccal mucosa. She was a lifelong non-smoker and non-drinker. An initial biopsy of the right buccal mucosa revealed an oral squamous papilloma. One year later, a second biopsy again showed an oral squamous papilloma. Six months after the second biopsy, she noted progressive enlargement of the lesion with a change in consistency, causing discomfort and some dysfunction. 

On examination, the exophytic lesion involved the right buccal mucosa, extended inferiorly to the floor of the mouth, and breached the extraoral skin of the right cheek. Bilateral submandibular lymph nodes were palpable and suspicious. 

MRI and contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a well-defined soft-tissue mass measuring 6.2 × 2.5 × 3.5 cm adjacent to the right mandibular body with no bone erosion. The lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on STIR images, and showed faint homogeneous post-contrast enhancement. Multiple submental and bilateral submandibular lymph nodes measured up to 17 × 10 mm without calcification or central necrosis.

A 40-year-old African American woman with morbid obesity was referred for evaluation of a slowly enlarging left buttock mass. She noted minor discomfort and was unable to tolerate prolonged sitting. The mass had been growing over six months. She denied urinary, rectal, or gynecological symptoms and had no prior surgeries. 

On examination, there was a 25 × 14 cm soft mass in the left perineal area. Pelvic examination revealed a bulging mass on the left lateral vaginal wall without invasion; the rectal tone was normal but the left lateral rectal wall was displaced toward midline. 

Endoscopic ultrasound showed a demarcated fat plane between the rectum and the mass; in contrast, CT imaging showed no clear fat plane. Cross-sectional imaging demonstrated a subcutaneous mass in the left perirectal region displacing the anal canal to the right and elevating the levator ani muscle. Uterine leiomyomas and colonic diverticulosis were noted incidentally. 

MRI measured the lesion at 23 × 8 × 11 cm, with well-defined walls, no muscular or osseous invasion, and marked enhancement. The radiologist’s preliminary impression was a pedunculated leiomyoma, although a soft-tissue sarcoma could not be excluded. On the basis of imaging, a large leiomyoma was suspected, but a low-grade soft-tissue sarcoma remained in the differential.

A 60-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of progressive hoarseness and a 3- to 4-month history of exertional dyspnea. He smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years; his other medical history was unremarkable. Videolaryngoscopy revealed a 1.5 cm vascularized, pedunculated, polypoid lesion with a smooth surface, originating from the posterior half of the right vocal cord and the vocal process of the arytenoid, subtotally obstructing the endolarynx. To secure the airway, a tracheotomy was performed under general anesthesia, and the mass was excised via endolaryngeal microsurgery. At 4-month follow-up, videolaryngoscopy showed a well-healed incision with no residual or recurrent lesion.

A 51-year-old woman with hypothyroidism and a history of treated pulmonary tuberculosis presented with a 3-year history of intermittent upper abdominal pain associated with dark, tarry stools. Over the past year, these episodes increased in frequency. Initial evaluation revealed anemia (hemoglobin 11.0 g/dL) and a positive fecal occult blood test. 

Upper endoscopy showed a 103 × 46.6 mm submucosal mass on the lesser curvature of the stomach, 5 cm from the cardia, with normal overlying mucosa. Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated a low-echo lesion with regular, clear margins confined to the submucosal layer; color Doppler imaging revealed a vascular signal extending from the periphery into the center of the lesion. Fine-needle aspiration under EUS guidance was performed without complication. 

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT confirmed a 102 × 56.3 × 46.6 mm gastric mass without evidence of additional masses or lymphadenopathy.

A 78-year-old previously healthy white man presented with a 2-month history of watery diarrhea and an unintended 20-kg weight loss. He denied fevers or night sweats. One month before admission, he noted progressive lower-limb edema extending to his thighs and a red, tender eruption on the anterior surfaces of both legs. On the day of admission, he developed intense, diffuse abdominal pain radiating to the back. 

On examination, he appeared pale, dehydrated, and ill-looking. Temperature was normal, pulse 120/min, BP 90/50 mmHg. The lower limbs were edematous with bullous lesions overlying erythematous skin on both shins. Heart and lung examinations were unremarkable. The abdomen was distended and diffusely tender, a firm mass was palpable in the hypogastrium, bowel sounds were absent, and rebound tenderness was present.

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, leukocytes 9.1×10³/mm³ with left shift (promyelocytes 1%, myelocytes 3%, metamyelocytes 5%, bands 25%), platelets 509×10³/mm³, sodium 138 mEq/L, potassium 5.3 mEq/L, urea 57 mg/dL, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, total protein 3.7 g/dL, albumin 1.0 g/dL. Serologies for HIV, hepatitis B and C, and HTLV-1 were negative.

A chest radiograph showed free air under the diaphragm. Exploratory laparotomy revealed copious enteric fluid and two perforations of the jejunum, at 15 cm and 220 cm from the ligament of Treitz; both segments were resected. On gross inspection, each 42-cm jejunal segment contained a 5.5-cm ulcerated, infiltrative, whitish, soft tumor; one segment had a perforation with suppurative serositis. Multiple enlarged whitish lymph nodes (up to 3.0 cm) were adherent to the bowel segments, and the surrounding mucosa and bowel wall appeared thickened and rubbery.

A 14-year-old girl presented with a 2-month history of left abdominal and flank pain, a palpable left hypochondrial mass, generalized fatigue, anorexia, and weight loss. On examination, there was a tender mass in the left hypochondrium. MRI of the abdomen showed a large lobulated retroperitoneal left-sided tumor (20×16×14 cm) that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, heterogenous with central necrosis on T2-weighted images, and showed contrast enhancement after gadolinium; the mass invaded the left kidney, causing ipsilateral pelvicalyceal dilatation. Staging CT demonstrated retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, peritoneal nodules, pulmonary nodules, and osteolytic bone lesions. An ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the mass revealed sheets and nests of medium-sized cells separated by fine fibrovascular septa; the cells had round to oval nuclei with finely granular chromatin and pale-to-clear scant cytoplasm.

A full-term newborn girl (birth weight 3880 g) was delivered by Caesarean section after an uneventful pregnancy. Prenatal ultrasound reports were normal, and there was no family history of congenital diseases. Immediately after birth, examination revealed a pedunculated, pink mass measuring approximately 2 × 1 × 0.6 cm, attached to the anterior ventral surface of the tongue and protruding from the oral cavity. The lesion prevented normal closure of the mouth but did not impair respiration. Because of partial interference with breastfeeding, a nasogastric tube was used for feeding. Aside from the oral mass, general physical examination and laboratory tests were unremarkable.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of severe inflammatory arthralgia affecting both hands, wrists, knees, and ankles. The symptoms began one week after receipt of the BNT162b2 Covid-19 mRNA vaccine and were initially attributed to the vaccine. She received a subsequent ChAdOx1-S Covid-19 vaccine three months later; low-dose prednisolone provided minimal relief. Initial investigations showed a C-reactive protein of 101 mg/L (normal < 5) and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 64 mm/hr (normal < 14); rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP antibody, antinuclear antibodies, and extractable nuclear antigens were negative.

Two weeks later, with persistent symptoms, she was evaluated in person. She reported mild dyspnea but denied chest pain or syncope. Her temperature was 38°C, pulse 100 beats/min, and blood pressure 120/70 mm Hg. Examination revealed bilateral wrist swelling, non-tender bilateral knee effusions, bilateral ankle swelling, marked bilateral fingernail clubbing, a loud apical systolic murmur, right ventricular heave, and bibasal crackles. There were no peripheral stigmata of infective endocarditis.

On hospital admission, the C-reactive protein had risen to 207 mg/L, the erythrocyte sedimentation rate to 104 mm/hr, hemoglobin was 80 g/L with a microcytic index, and albumin was 24 g/L. Repeat autoimmune serologies remained negative. Urine and blood cultures and extensive infectious serologies were negative. Arthrocentesis of the left knee yielded non-inflammatory fluid. Chest radiography showed bibasal pleural effusions. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was normal.

A transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a large villous mass attached to the posterior left atrial wall, prolapsing across the mitral valve into the left ventricle and causing significant inflow obstruction. A chest CT demonstrated extension of the mass into the pulmonary veins. A brain MRI showed multiple small right-sided infarcts of differing ages.

A 35-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of bilateral knee pain and swelling, spontaneous in onset without any antecedent injury, and progressive despite physiotherapy. He was otherwise well. On examination, both knees had suprapatellar effusions with palpable thickened synovium, mild quadriceps wasting, extension limited by 5°, flexion to 120°, no joint-line tenderness, and stable ligaments. Plain radiographs of the knees were unremarkable. MRI of both knees demonstrated multiple villous synovial proliferations and a frond-like synovial mass with fat‐signal intensity on T2-weighted and fat-suppressed sequences. A 99-technetium bone scan showed increased uptake in both knees.

A 78-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of gradually worsening memory disturbance without headache. On examination, he had dementia (MMSE 21/30), left lower-limb hemiparesis (manual muscle test 4/5), and gait disturbance. There were no signs of urinary incontinence, retention, or sexual dysfunction. Head CT showed ventricular dilatation (Evans index 0.40). Lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 150 mmH₂O, a normal cell count (4.0 cells/μL), and an elevated protein level (3842 mg/dL). Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the lumbar spine demonstrated a homogeneously enhancing intradural, extramedullary mass compressing the cauda equina at the L3–4 level.

A 35-year-old Ethiopian woman presented with an 11-year history of left lateral neck swelling that had gradually increased in size and was associated with dull aching pain. She reported no dyspnea, dysphagia, weight loss, or prior radiation exposure, and her medical history was unremarkable. There was no family history of similar conditions. On examination, vital signs were normal. The sclerae were non-icteric and the conjunctivae pink. In the left cervical region, there was a 5×4-cm non-tender, hard, irregularly bordered mass fixed to underlying structures but not to the overlying skin; the skin was intact without discoloration or discharge. There were no café au lait spots, axillary freckling, skin nodules, or lymphadenopathy, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a hematocrit of 39.5%, a white-cell count of 6400/mm3, and a platelet count of 241,000/mm3; renal and liver-function tests were normal. Neck ultrasonography revealed a 6.2×2.3-cm isoechoic mass in the left carotid space displacing the carotid vessels anteromedially and the internal jugular vein anterolaterally, with cystic areas, peripheral flow, no calcification, and no invasion; the differential diagnosis included schwannoma and neurofibroma. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed an 8.0×3.5×3.4-cm ovoid, mildly enhancing mass in the left carotid space lateral to the common carotid artery, compressing the artery and the left thyroid lobe without invasion of adjacent structures. Fine-needle aspiration cytology yielded spindle cells organized in fascicles and stromal fragments, and the cells exhibited minimal nuclear atypia but no mitosis or necrosis.

A 27-year-old woman, pregnant at 9 weeks’ gestation, was referred for evaluation of Cushing’s syndrome. Over the preceding 2 months, she noted progressive proximal muscle weakness. Examination revealed a Cushingoid appearance, wide purplish striae on the abdomen, easy bruising, and proximal muscle weakness. Her blood pressure was 160/100 mm Hg, and her body-mass index was 32.2 kg/m2. She had a history of hypertension, dyslipidemia, and impaired fasting glucose diagnosed 1 year earlier, none of which had been treated, and she had gained 20 kg in the past 2 years.

Laboratory testing at 9 weeks’ gestation showed an 8 am serum cortisol level of 32.4 μg/dL (reference, 5.0–18.0), a late-night salivary cortisol level of 0.7 μg/dL (reference, < 0.4), a mean 24-hour urinary free cortisol level of 237.6 μg (reference, 21.0–143.0), and plasma ACTH levels of 48.4 and 39.6 pg/mL (reference, 0–46.0). At 12 weeks’ gestation, noncontrast MRI of the pituitary gland showed a mildly bulging contour on the right side of the lateral pituitary without a discrete adenoma. At 14 weeks’ gestation, a desmopressin stimulation test was performed, with serial ACTH measurements rising from 34.7 pg/mL at baseline to 58.9 pg/mL at 15 minutes (a 70% increase), and serum cortisol remaining approximately 30 μg/dL.

A 35‐year‐old Caucasian woman presented with a 1‐day history of intermittent, nonpositional epigastric and left upper quadrant abdominal pain and progressive jaundice. She denied nausea, vomiting, changes in bowel habits, or urine‐color changes. Two weeks earlier, she had been hospitalized for acute pancreatitis on the basis of a lipase level of 386 U/L (normal, 0–70) and sonographic findings; she was discharged one week later with a lipase level of 200 U/L, amylase 88 U/L (normal, 0–90), and a normal MRCP. Her medical history was notable only for G6PD deficiency; she had no relevant habits or family history. On examination, vital signs were stable. Abdominal palpation revealed tenderness in the epigastrium and left upper quadrant, a soft abdomen, and a positive Murphy’s sign. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, blood‐urea nitrogen, creatinine, albumin, amylase, INR, and PTT. HIV and HTLV‐1 serologic tests were negative. AST and ALT were elevated at 375 and 318 U/L (normal <40), respectively; alkaline phosphatase was 604 U/L (normal <105); and lipase was 274 U/L (normal <160). Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated dilated intrahepatic bile ducts; an elongated gallbladder with sludge; a prominent pancreas with heterogeneous hypoechoic areas and faint peripheral flow in the head; absent vascular flow in the neck and tail; and oval lymph nodes (maximum short‐axis diameter, 10 mm) in the porta hepatis and peripancreatic region. Supportive therapy for pancreatitis was initiated, but her condition did not improve after 2 days. Other possible diagnoses, including autoimmune diseases, granulomatous disorders, and malignancies, were considered, and a contrast‐enhanced multidetector CT scan was ordered.

A 19-year-old man with no chronic illnesses presented with a 2-month history of vague, colicky abdominal pain, reduced appetite, weight loss, and intermittent diarrhea with occasional blood mixed in the stools. There was no family history of inflammatory bowel disease or malignancy, and no significant past surgical history. He smoked only briefly in the past.  
On examination, he was afebrile with mild right upper quadrant tenderness. There was no lymphadenopathy, and both digital rectal and scrotal examinations were unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, white blood cells 12.2×10^3/μL, platelets 375×10^3/μL, ALT 61 U/L, AST 44 U/L, ALP 120 U/L, bilirubin 12 μmol/L, INR 1.4, alpha-fetoprotein 2492 IU/mL (reference 0–6), beta-hCG 4 mIU/mL, and negative viral serologies including HIV, HBsAg, and anti-HCV.  
Abdominal ultrasound revealed an enlarged liver (19.7 cm) with multiple heterogeneous hyperechoic lesions (largest 9.9×9.7 cm in the right lobe and 10×8.3 cm in the left lobe), portal vein thrombosis, periportal lymphadenopathy, and mild ascites.  
MRI of the abdomen confirmed an enlarged liver with numerous focal lesions (up to 11 cm) in all segments, tumor thrombus in the portal branches, dilated intrahepatic bile ducts, and enlarged retrocaval, porta hepatis, paraaortic, and mesenteric lymph nodes. Radiologic impression favored a multicentric primary liver malignancy, most consistent with hepatocellular carcinoma rather than metastases.  
The case was discussed in a tumor board, and plans were made for an ultrasound-guided liver biopsy, colonoscopy, and pan-CT scan to evaluate for other primary lesions.

A 49-year-old man presented with a two-month history of progressively worsening dyspnea and an unintentional 10-kg weight loss. His medical history included childhood asthma, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, and coronary artery bypass grafting two years earlier. He had been empirically started on first-line antituberculous therapy 15 days before presentation by a general practitioner. He was a lifelong non-smoker with no known tuberculosis exposure.  

On examination, he had bilateral pitting pedal edema and numerous hyperpigmented nevi distributed over his body, none of which had changed in size, shape, or color. Auscultation revealed decreased breath sounds at the left lung base.  

Chest radiography showed a moderate left pleural effusion. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated left-sided pleural fluid with irregular, nodular pleural thickening. Thoracic ultrasound confirmed septated and loculated fluid. Ultrasound-guided thoracentesis yielded black pleural fluid. Analysis of the fluid revealed an exudate with protein 3.9 g/dL, total nucleated cell count 700 cells/µL (30% neutrophils, 70% lymphocytes), and glucose 231 mg/dL. Gram stain, bacterial culture, acid-fast bacilli smear and culture, Xpert MTB/RIF assay, and fungal culture were all negative. Pleural fluid cytology showed atypical cells.

A 48-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of slurred speech, unsteadiness, and fatigue. She had a history of iron deficiency anemia and a melanoma excised 13 years earlier. One year before presentation, she experienced lethargy, intermittent headaches, nausea, diarrhea, and 16 kg of unintentional weight loss over 6 months, and was diagnosed with depression.  
On examination, she was ataxic, unable to walk heel-to-toe, and had subtle dysarthria; there was no other focal neurologic deficit. Cardiorespiratory and other examinations were unremarkable.  
Noncontrast CT of the brain revealed multifocal haemorrhagic foci in both cerebral hemispheres and the right cerebellar hemisphere, the largest measuring 3 cm. The initial differential included haemorrhagic metastases—possibly recurrent melanoma—and an atypical presentation of amyloid angiopathy.  
She was started on dexamethasone and referred for neurosurgical evaluation. A staging CT of the chest and abdomen and a stealth brain MRI were arranged. MRI confirmed multiple supra- and infratentorial lesions, haemosiderin staining in the sulci consistent with low-volume subarachnoid blood, and a 4 mm aneurysm of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery.  
Staging CT of the chest demonstrated a mass in the left atrium concerning for an atrial myxoma.

A 62‐year‐old man with no prior medical history presented with a 1‐day history of progressive abdominal pain, distention, and vomiting. On examination, his abdomen was slightly distended with tenderness in the left hypochondrium; no mass was palpable. Digital rectal examination revealed an empty, collapsed rectum. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen showed obstruction of the left colon caused by an intraluminal mass with fatty density measuring 5.0 × 3.5 × 6.5 cm, with resultant fecal stasis in the transverse and right colon.

A 42-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with menorrhagia. Transvaginal ultrasonography revealed submucosal uterine fibroids. Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 27 mm left adnexal mass that was low signal on T2-weighted images and high signal on T1-weighted images, with signal loss on fat-suppressed T1-weighted images. The low T2 signal was interpreted as consistent with an ovarian fibroma or Brenner tumor, whereas the fatty signal characteristics raised the possibility of a mature teratoma. Mesenteric lipoma was not included in the differential diagnosis due to its rarity. Following two preoperative doses of a gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist, laparoscopic total hysterectomy with removal of the left ovarian mass and right oophorectomy was planned.

A 44-year-old man, a former heavy smoker originally from Ecuador, was referred for evaluation of an abnormal chest radiograph and persistent cough. He reported a three-week history of productive cough, daily fevers, and night sweats, along with an unintentional 40-lb weight loss over four months. He denied known tuberculosis contacts or wheezing and had never previously had a tuberculin skin test. Two years earlier, he had right lower lobe pneumonia treated as an outpatient. On admission, his tuberculin skin test was 20 mm. Physical examination revealed decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion at the right lung base. Laboratory testing showed a mild leukocytosis of 13 300 cells/µL without bandemia; basic metabolic and liver function panels were normal. Posteroanterior and lateral chest radiographs and contrast-enhanced chest CT scans were obtained. Pulmonary function tests were within normal limits. Flexible bronchoscopy demonstrated a smooth, round, white polypoid lesion with a broad base at the distal end of the bronchus intermedius, nearly occluding the lumen; thick white mucoid material was noted exuding from the right middle lobe bronchus.

A 40-year-old woman presented with a 6-year history of intermittent serous nasal discharge from both nostrils, a 2-month history of weight gain, polydipsia, polyuria, and generalized weakness, and a 2-week history of blurred vision. On examination, she was hypertensive, had generalized facial and trunk hyperpigmentation, bilateral proptosis, and decreased vision in the left eye. Bone CT scans demonstrated erosion of the bilateral sphenoid and ethmoid sinus bones. T2-weighted MRI of the head showed a slight hyperintense lesion in the anterior cranial fossa with flow-voids along its superior margin. Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed an enhancing mass in the anterior cranial fossa infiltrating the sphenoid sinus, ethmoid sinus, left maxillary sinus, and nasal cavity. Abdominal CT scans showed bilateral adrenal gland hyperplasia. Laboratory studies demonstrated a serum potassium level between 1.92 and 2.82 mmol/L, a fasting blood glucose level between 14.9 and 20.0 mmol/L, a basal ACTH level of 33.72 pmol/L (reference <2.20 pmol/L), a 6 a.m. serum cortisol level of 1779.78 nmol/L (reference 83–359 nmol/L), and a testosterone level of 8.43 nmol/L (reference 0.17–2.53 nmol/L).

A 45-year-old woman presented with intermittent left-sided headache of >1 year’s duration. The pain lasted minutes to an hour, was sometimes accompanied by nausea and vomiting, and improved with rest. There was no history of dizziness, visual disturbance, seizures, sensory changes, or focal neurologic deficits, and the physical examination was unremarkable. 

Brain MRI revealed a dural-based soft-tissue mass in the right frontal lobe. The lesion was surgically excised. On gross examination, the formalin-fixed specimen measured 2.0 × 2.0 × 0.8 cm, was gray-white, smooth, and attached to the dura mater.

Microscopic examination showed a network of dense small vessels and thick-walled larger vessels, most with marked hyalinization, interwoven throughout the lesion. In focal areas, a faint “whirlpool-like” arrangement of tumor cells was noted. Scattered cells exhibited bizarre, large, hyperchromatic, and irregularly distributed nuclei. No mitotic figures were identified.

Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated that the tumor cells were strongly positive for Vimentin and SSTR2A, with focal positivity for EMA and partial positivity for progesterone receptor. CD34 and ERG highlighted only the vascular endothelium, with no staining in tumor cells. GFAP, Olig-2, and HMB45 were negative. The MIB-1 (Ki-67) labeling index was less than 3%.

An 18-year-old unmarried woman presented with a 6-month history of a right breast lump. The lesion began as a small, marble-sized, mobile mass and gradually enlarged without pain, skin changes, or nipple discharge. There was no history of trauma, fever, respiratory symptoms, chest irradiation, oral contraceptive use, or family history of breast disease. Menarche was at age 13 with regular cycles. Vital signs and routine laboratory studies were within normal limits. On examination, the right breast contained a well-circumscribed, firm, non-tender, freely mobile mass measuring approximately 10 × 9 cm in the central and upper and lower quadrants; the overlying skin was tense with distended superficial veins, and the nipple appeared slightly fissured. No axillary lymphadenopathy was noted. The left breast was unremarkable. Ultrasonography of the right breast demonstrated an inhomogeneous, solid mass measuring 85.9 × 74.6 mm with posterior acoustic enhancement, suggestive of fibroadenoma. Patient declined fine-needle aspiration cytology. Bilateral mammography showed dense fibroglandular parenchyma and a well-defined, large, oval, equal-to-low-density lesion with lobulated margins in the peri-areolar region of the right breast (BI-RADS 3).

A 15-year-old girl presented in April 2013 with a two-month history of occipital headache, three weeks of intermittent diplopia, and one week of daily vomiting. MRI of the brain with intravenous contrast showed a 5.8×4.7×4 cm heterogeneous mixed solid and cystic enhancing mass in the right frontal lobe, with surrounding vasogenic edema and local mass effect but no diffusion restriction. The on-call radiologist felt that the lesion most likely represented a high-grade glioma, with ependymoma and primitive neuroectodermal tumour (PNET) as additional differentials.

The next day, a right frontal–pterional craniotomy was performed. Postoperative imaging revealed significant residual disease. Histologic analysis demonstrated lymphocytic infiltration and a high-grade tumour that stained positive for INI1, vimentin, and histiocytic markers. A diagnosis of histiocytic sarcoma was proposed, and cross-sectional imaging of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no evidence of metastatic disease. The patient underwent focal radiotherapy with concurrent temozolomide, followed by seven cycles of adjuvant temozolomide, completing treatment in March 2014 with no radiologic evidence of residual or recurrent disease.

In May 2015, now 17 years old, she reported one month of increasing shortness of breath, lethargy, and was found to have iron-deficiency anemia attributed to heavy menstruation. A brain MRI in June 2015 remained unchanged. In August 2015, she had a further drop in hemoglobin without iron deficiency and developed evening fevers. A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a 4.6×3.5×3 cm filling defect in the left atrium, which was noted to have measured 2×2×1.6 cm on a CT from 2013. The mass was centered on the mitral valve, and the radiologist suggested it could represent either a chronic vegetation with a diseased mitral valve or a mass lesion.

Five days later, a dedicated cardiac MRI demonstrated a tumour-like mass attached to the posterior wall of the left atrium, closely abutting the posterior mitral leaflet, causing obstruction of mitral inflow. Left ventricular ejection fraction was 55% and right ventricular ejection fraction was 28%. Urgent surgical resection was planned.

A 35-year-old schoolteacher presented with 10 days of fever and 5 days of epigastric discomfort worsened by inspiration. She had taken doxycycline without relief and noted a 6-kg weight gain. Her only past medical history was polycystic ovaries; she was otherwise well. On exam, temperature was 38.4 °C, pulse 104/min, blood pressure 110/80 mmHg, oxygen saturation 99% on room air, and weight 68 kg. She was pale, had an atypical systolic murmur at the left sternal border, and right-upper-quadrant tenderness with a positive Murphy’s sign. Laboratory tests revealed hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL, albumin 3.1 g/dL, INR 1.36, CRP 7.63 mg/dL, ESR 98 mm/h, with normal bilirubin and liver enzymes. Chest radiograph showed a normal cardiac silhouette and clear costo-phrenic angles. Abdominal ultrasound on admission showed gallbladder wall thickening (11 mm) with a layered appearance; no ascites was reported. An abdominal CT obtained five hours later demonstrated marginal gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, and a moderate pelvic ascites. A repeat ultrasound on hospital day 5 showed normalization of gallbladder wall thickness (3.5 mm) and no ascites. Analysis of right-sided pleural fluid on day 8 revealed a transudate. Given persistent fever, elevated inflammatory markers despite antibiotics, absence of risk factors for acalculous cholecystitis, and the new murmur with pleural effusion and hepatic synthetic dysfunction, she was transferred for internal medicine evaluation. After stopping antibiotics, blood cultures were drawn and cardiac ultrasound was requested.

A 37-year-old previously healthy woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive enlargement of her left globe and associated pain. On examination, there was proptosis of the left eye and partial limitation of abduction; visual acuity was normal, and she had no diplopia or other neurologic deficits. There were no cutaneous stigmata of neurofibromatosis. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left orbit demonstrated a well-defined 2.27 cm × 2.07 cm × 2.69 cm solid-cystic mass situated between the optic nerve and the lateral rectus muscle. The mass caused stretching of the lateral rectus muscle with loss of the fat plane between mass and muscle, medial displacement of the optic nerve, and anterior displacement of the globe. The lesion was heterogeneously isointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with a brightly enhancing solid component and a nonenhancing cystic component.

An 81-year-old Swedish woman presented with redness and a foreign-body sensation in her left eye. Visual acuity was 1.0 in the right eye and 0.6 in the left eye with her habitual correction. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy showed the left upper eyelid to be thicker and redder than the right, and she was diagnosed with blepharitis. She was treated with a combination corticosteroid–antibiotic ointment and asked to return in 2–3 weeks. At follow-up, she reported some improvement but still had persistent redness and a foreign-body sensation. On referral to oculoplastic surgery, eversion of the upper eyelid revealed a tumor-like growth on the palpebral conjunctiva. Magnetic resonance imaging of the orbits suggested possible extension into the lateral rectus muscle, whereas computed tomography of the neck, abdomen, and thorax showed no evidence of metastatic disease.

A 54-year-old woman with a history of stage III invasive ductal breast carcinoma treated with mastectomy and chemoradiation 4 years earlier presented with urinary frequency, worsening right-sided pelvic pain, and weight loss. MRI of the pelvis showed multiple fibroids and a heterogeneous 9.4 cm lesion involving the right uterine fundus/cornua. Intraoperatively, the mass was found in the right retroperitoneal space, tracking along the broad ligament and encasing the right external iliac artery; it was transected from the right uterine cornua. Grossly, the specimen was a detached, fragmented, ill-defined mass (14 × 12 × 4 cm) with fleshy solid and cystic components, central hemorrhage, and necrosis. Microscopically, the tumor invaded from the serosal surface into the myometrium and comprised sheets of small, round hyperchromatic cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, frequent mitoses (32 per 10 high-power fields), pseudo-rosette formation, foci of cytoplasmic clearing, and necrosis. Immunohistochemical stains showed diffuse positivity for CD99, KIT, and cyclin D1 and negativity for keratin, DOG1, synaptophysin, desmin, myogenin, WT-1, CD45, inhibin, GATA-3, and SOX-10.

A 61-year-old woman with a history of autoimmune hepatitis underwent orthotopic liver transplantation in 1990. At her annual visit, she reported a 1-year history of recurrent episodic tremors that had worsened over the past few months, and a new onset of severe episodic headaches without aura. She was started on sumatriptan with only partial relief. She denied shortness of breath, palpitations, fever, or hypertension symptoms and had no family history of pheochromocytoma or multiple endocrine neoplasia. Her immunosuppressive regimen included cyclosporine 100 mg daily, azathioprine 50 mg daily, and prednisone 1 mg daily. 

As part of routine screening, an abdominal ultrasound revealed a new 3.1 × 2.2 × 2.6 cm heterogeneous mass in the right adrenal gland. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a 2.9 × 2.8 cm right adrenal nodule of intermediate density (42 HU). A 24-hour urine collection showed total metanephrines of 2,973 mcg/24 hr (reference < 616 mcg/24 hr) and normetanephrine of 2,304 mcg/24 hr (reference < 521 mcg/24 hr). An iodine-123 MIBG scan demonstrated avid uptake in the right adrenal gland with no other abnormal tracer accumulation.

A 39-year-old woman presented for evaluation of subfertility. She was asymptomatic with respect to abdominal pain or systemic features. Her medical history included obesity (BMI 40 kg/m2), hypothyroidism on levothyroxine, and iron deficiency anemia; she was allergic to penicillin and a current smoker (3 cigarettes/day). Her performance status was WHO grade 0.

Pelvic MRI performed for fertility investigations revealed a 120 × 50 × 75 mm lipomatous mass overlying the right iliopsoas, displacing the right iliac vessels, uterus, and bladder without invasion of adjacent structures, and compressing the common iliac vein at the L5/S1 level. There was no lymphadenopathy or marrow signal abnormality. MRI raised concern for deep-venous thrombosis in the right external iliac vein, but CT venography excluded thrombosis. PET CT demonstrated mildly avid soft tissue elements within the mass and no nodal or distant metastases.

Radiologists had a high index of suspicion for liposarcoma based on CT and PET CT features. Because of the risk of tumor spillage, percutaneous biopsy was not recommended. The sarcoma multidisciplinary team therefore recommended marginal surgical excision of the mass.

A 70-year-old Asian man with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis for 20 years presented with chest discomfort during exercise. He had hypertension, hyperuricemia, and reflux esophagitis. He was afebrile, blood pressure 114/50 mmHg, pulse 61/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on ambient air. Examination revealed no rales, murmurs, or focal neurologic deficits. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 14.0 mg/dL, WBC 4700/mm³, platelets 134 000/mm³, total bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL, AST 24 IU/L, ALT 34 IU/L, BUN 54.2 mg/dL, creatinine 11.1 mg/dL, CRP 0.16 mg/dL, normal serum calcium and phosphorus, and BNP 605.1 pg/mL. Blood cultures were negative. Chest radiograph demonstrated mild cardiomegaly without pulmonary congestion. ECG showed left ventricular hypertrophy with nonspecific ST–T changes. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed severe mitral annular calcification and a highly mobile, 8×6 mm echogenic mass attached to the ventricular side of the posterior mitral leaflet, with similar echogenicity to the annulus and mild mitral stenosis; left ventricular systolic function was normal. Cardiac CT confirmed a calcified mass at the mitral annulus with heavy annular calcification. Given the high mobility and embolic risk, the patient underwent surgical resection of the mass.

A 55-year-old woman was admitted with progressive weakness, shortness of breath, and swelling of the right forearm, hand, and both lower extremities. Eighteen years earlier, she had mixed cellularity Hodgkin lymphoma IVA involving mediastinal and pericardial nodes; she underwent thoracotomy with partial lung and pericardial resection, combination chemotherapy, and radiotherapy, achieving stable remission. 

In April 2015, she developed dry cough, dyspnea, low-grade fever, and pleural effusion; tuberculosis was excluded and antibacterial therapy improved her symptoms. In late 2016, symptoms recurred, and chest CT showed changes attributed to post-radiation fibrosis. In spring 2017, she was hospitalized for severe dry cough and dyspnea; CT demonstrated extensive fibrous degeneration, pleural effusion, and right lower-lobe infiltration. Echocardiography revealed pericardial adhesions and fibrous changes of the aortic and mitral valves. She was diagnosed with postradiation pulmonary fibrosis, cardiomyopathy, pneumonia, and heart failure, and treated with antibiotics and diuretics.

In July 2017, she noted recurrent dyspnea, weakness, weight loss, and limb swelling. Doppler ultrasound revealed occlusive thrombosis of the right subclavian and jugular veins, and she was started on dabigatran. On physical examination, she had significant bilateral lower-extremity and right upper-extremity edema, distant heart sounds with a heart rate of 110 bpm, enlarged liver by 5 cm, and pulmonary dullness with diminished breath sounds at both lung bases. Laboratory studies showed an elevated γ-glutamyl transferase (124 U/L). Electrocardiography demonstrated right-axis deviation and low QRS voltage. 

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a moderate pericardial effusion and multiple echogenic masses in the left atrium, precluding assessment of valvular and myocardial function. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis confirmed bilateral hydrothorax, post-radiation lung changes, thrombosis of the right subclavian and brachiocephalic veins, and pericardial masses suggestive of neoplastic involvement; the pleural effusion was a transudate. 

Cardiac MRI showed soft-tissue nodules lining the pericardium, partially coalescing to deform both atria and ventricles, and one lesion was contiguous with the aorta, raising concern for myocardial invasion.

A 60-year-old woman with a 35 pack-year smoking history and known HIV infection was referred after an incidental chest radiograph revealed a right upper lobe nodule. She was asymptomatic. 

On chest CT, there was an irregular, spiculated 15-mm lesion in the lateral segment of the middle lobe. PET/CT demonstrated intense uptake in the lesion (SUV 7). Pulmonary function testing showed an FEV1 of 2.69 L (103% predicted) and a predicted postoperative FEV1 of 2.41 L; the Thoraco-score predicted a 1.02% operative mortality risk. 

Because of the lesion’s proximity to the right atrium, the patient underwent a video-assisted thoracoscopic wedge resection. Intraoperative frozen section revealed nonsmall cell lung carcinoma, prompting completion lobectomy with mediastinal lymphadenectomy. 

Gross examination showed a 1.1-cm, white-gray, subpleural nodule with pleural retraction in the middle lobe. Microscopically, there was a solid proliferation of neoplastic signet-ring cells with focal, nontransmural visceral pleural infiltration.

A 15-year-old female presented with a swelling over the distal one-third of her right forearm that had been present for 5 years. The swelling was insidious in onset, slowly increasing in size, and associated with mild, localized dorsal forearm pain without radiation. There was no history of trauma, infection, sinus, or other swellings. On examination, there was a solitary, diffuse, oval 3.5×2.5 cm mass over the dorsal radial aspect of the distal forearm with a smooth surface, indistinct margins, and firm consistency. The mass was non-pulsatile, non-fluctuant, non-transilluminant, non-compressible, non-reducible, and non-adherent to skin or underlying structures. No muscle wasting, bruits, or venous hum were present. Distal neurovascular examination was normal, Finkelstein’s test was negative, and wrist motion was full and painless. There was no regional lymphadenopathy. The initial differential diagnoses included intramuscular lipoma, muscular fibroadenoma, hemangioma, angiofibroma, lymphangioma, neurofibroma, nodular fasciitis, and peripheral nerve sheath tumors. A plain radiograph of the right wrist revealed a calcified spot in the distal radius. Ultrasound showed numerous irregular hypoechoic areas suggestive of a low-flow vascular tumor. MRI demonstrated a lobulated intramuscular lesion in the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis measuring 1.8×1.2×4.2 cm, with T2 and PD/SPAIR hyperintense signals.

A 23-year-old Arab woman with no significant past medical or family history presented with 26 days of progressive left flank pain and abdominal distension. She had lost 1 kg over 1 month and took NSAIDs with moderate relief. She denied alcohol or tobacco use, had regular menstrual cycles, and reported no hypertension, flushing, or other signs of hormone excess. On examination, her temperature was 37.3 °C, blood pressure 125/80 mmHg, heart rate 87 beats/min, and neurologic examination was normal. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11 g/dL, with normal hepatic and renal function. Endocrine evaluation revealed normetanephrine and metanephrine levels within normal limits, a urinary free cortisol of 370 μg/L, and two negative dexamethasone suppression tests. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 14 × 11 cm invasive left suprarenal mass with moderate enhancement, regional lymphadenopathy, and no venous thrombosis or distant lesions.

A 78-year-old Chinese woman was found to have an isolated 2.0×2.0 cm firm, non-tender nodule in the upper outer quadrant of her right breast during a health checkup. She reported a two-month history of cough and expectoration without fever, chest pain, dyspnea, or other symptoms. On physical examination, the breast nodule was firm, mobile, and non-tender; there was no palpable lymphadenopathy. Routine blood tests and tumor markers were unremarkable. Autoantibody testing revealed positive anti-SS-A and anti-SS-B antibodies. Serum immunoglobulins were elevated: IgA 485 mg/dL (70–400), IgG 2030 mg/dL (700–1600), κ light chain 432 mg/dL (170–370), and λ light chain 249 mg/dL (90–210). 

For staging of a presumed malignant breast lesion, whole-body 18 F-FDG PET/CT was performed 60 minutes after injection of 6.5 mCi of tracer. Maximum-intensity-projection images showed intense uptake in the right breast nodule (SUVmax 7.30) and mild uptake in bilateral posterior cervical lymph nodes (SUVmax 4.48) and hilar regions. Axial PET/CT showed a 2.3×1.9 cm well-circumscribed, homogenous isodense breast lesion with intense FDG uptake. Multiple irregular pulmonary nodules were noted, the largest in the right lower lobe measuring 2.7×2.5 cm with ring-like FDG uptake (SUVmax 2.96). Given these findings, a primary breast malignancy with pulmonary metastases was suspected.

A 76-year-old woman with a history of dementia presented with a 1-month history of pruritus localized to her right nipple. Topical corticosteroids produced minimal improvement. On examination, there was no palpable breast mass or axillary lymphadenopathy. The right nipple was swollen, erythematous, and bled occasionally; the areola appeared normal. Mammography showed no abnormalities. Ultrasonography demonstrated swelling of the right nipple, an internal punctiform hyperechoic area, and increased blood flow. Based on these clinical findings, inflammatory changes in the right nipple and Paget’s disease of the breast were considered as differential diagnoses, and a punch biopsy of the right nipple skin was performed. Histopathological examination revealed proliferating, highly atypical squamous cells accompanied by occasional mitotic figures, with no evidence of Paget cells or invasion of atypical cells beyond the basement membrane.

A 63-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 2-week history of a painful mass in her left latissimus dorsi that had gradually increased in size. There was no history of trauma. Physical examination revealed a solid 4–6 cm mass on the posterior aspect of the left shoulder; the overlying skin was normal. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits.  
Ultrasound of the mass showed a heterogeneously echogenic intramuscular lesion in the latissimus dorsi with preservation of the normal fibrillary pattern and traversing continuous muscle fibers.  
MRI demonstrated a well-defined mass in the posterior shoulder within the latissimus dorsi that was isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images and homogeneously hyperintense on T2- and proton-density–weighted images. Linear hypointense strands corresponding to preserved muscle fibers were seen within the lesion. There was no hemorrhage or adjacent bone abnormality. After intravenous gadolinium, the lesion showed homogeneous but ill-defined enhancement, suggesting marked edema and an inflammatory process, although a neoplasm could not be excluded.

A 41-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of a slowly enlarging lump on the anterior aspect of her left upper arm. Her medical history was notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus of 10 years’ duration; otherwise it was unremarkable. On examination, there was a 2-cm, firm, non-tender mass in the distal left biceps brachii muscle. There were no motor or sensory deficits in the distal arm, and range of motion was normal. Routine blood tests were within normal limits. An ultrasound scan of the left biceps brachii revealed a 2.0 × 2.0 cm, well-defined, heteroechogenic lesion with a cystic component.

A 77-year-old man was found collapsed with coffee-ground vomit. Over the prior 6 weeks he had malaise, anorexia, rapid weight loss, and postprandial epigastric pain with vomiting treated empirically with ranitidine. His history included treated hypertension only. On admission, temperature 36.7°C, heart rate 110/min, blood pressure 152/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 23/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air; GCS 14. Physical examination was unremarkable, with no melena. Head CT showed a chronic subdural haematoma with midline shift. Initial arterial blood gas: pH 7.27, lactate 18 mmol/L, bicarbonate 11 mmol/L, base excess −19, delta ratio 1.9:1, indicating pure lactic acidosis. White cell count 25.48×10^9/L (neutrophils 9.98, lymphocytes 2.4, monocytes 7.58), thrombocytopenia; blood film showed dysplasia and occasional blasts. Blood cultures were negative, and chest radiograph was normal. Continuous veno-venous haemofiltration was started 6 hours after ICU admission. Initial renal and hepatic function tests were within normal limits.

A 28-year-old previously healthy man presented with a two-week history of right-side scrotal swelling and a three-month history of left-side scrotal enlargement. He reported a single episode of dull right scrotal pain that resolved within a day. He had no history of scrotal surgery, cryptorchidism, or infections. On examination, the right hemiscrotum was mildly swollen, and the left hemiscrotum was markedly enlarged with a palpable hard mass. Scrotal ultrasound revealed bilateral heterogeneous testicular masses: the right mass was hypoechoic with a diffuse hypovascular area on Doppler imaging, and the left was hyperechoic with iso- to hypervascular flow. Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis showed the right testis to be normal in size with decreased enhancement, whereas the left testis was enlarged with heterogeneous enhancement. These findings raised a differential of bilateral testicular germ cell tumors, but the right testis did not have typical features of a germ cell tumor; therefore, further imaging was pursued.

A 63-year-old man noted in 2006 a mass on the palmar side of the left index finger at the middle phalanx, which gradually enlarged. In May 2010, MRI at another hospital suggested a soft-tissue tumor, and he was referred in June 2010. 

On examination, an approximately 4-cm elastic, hard, immobile mass with slight redness and no tenderness or warmth was present over the palmar aspect of the middle phalanx of the left index finger. Flexion at the distal interphalangeal joint was 0 degrees. Hematologic and urinalysis results were normal.

Plain radiographs showed a soft-tissue shadow with faint internal calcification on the palmar side of the middle phalanx; lateral views revealed no bone destruction and only slight indentation of the palmar cortex. MRI demonstrated a well-demarcated 40×38-mm mass along the flexor tendon sheath with heterogeneous isointensity and low signal on T1-weighted images and mixed high and low signal on T2-weighted images, with low-signal areas corresponding to calcification. No imaging findings of bone invasion or destruction were seen, and the lesion was felt to be a benign cartilaginous tumor.

A 67-year-old man presented with a 4-year history of pain, bleeding, and discoloration of the left thumbnail. Bleeding was profuse after trivial trauma, and intermittent throbbing pain had intensified over the past 1.5 months, requiring oral analgesics for relief. He had no history of major thumb trauma or bleeding diathesis but had taken aspirin, 75 mg daily, for 5 years. He had previously been treated elsewhere for a presumed verruca vulgaris of the nail bed with three intralesional MMR vaccine injections, without improvement. 

On examination, the nail plate showed yellowish discoloration and distal onycholysis. After nail-plate avulsion, there was an erythematous, elevated, tender plaque measuring 1.5 × 1.0 cm on the medial half of the nail bed. There was no regional lymphadenopathy. Dermoscopy revealed a fuzzy lesion edge, structureless white areas, and multiple reddish areas with white rail lines. 

The differential diagnosis included pyogenic granuloma, glomus tumor, and squamous cell carcinoma of the nail bed. A nail-bed punch biopsy was performed.

A 64-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an elevated serum α-fetoprotein (AFP) level. She was followed for a pituitary adenoma treated microscopically 2 years earlier but was otherwise asymptomatic. Laboratory tests showed an AFP of 226.3 µg/mL (normal, 0–7.4 µg/mL). Serologic markers for hepatitis B and C viruses were negative. There was no history of chronic hepatitis, alcohol abuse, or known cirrhosis, and no family history of liver cancer. On physical examination, she appeared well, with normal vital signs and no hepatomegaly or weight loss.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen revealed an oval, solid mass in the epigastrium, closely adjacent to the fundus of the stomach. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy demonstrated an external imprint on the gastric fundus mucosa, findings interpreted as compatible with a gastrointestinal stromal tumor. Endoscopic ultrasound showed a 40 mm by 20 mm oval mass appearing to arise from the gastric wall and deemed consistent with a gastric leiomyoma.

A 41-year-old premenopausal Indian woman with diabetes (BMI 28.6) noted a 2×2 cm mobile lump in the right upper outer breast for 2 weeks. The overlying skin was uninvolved, and a single mobile right axillary lymph node was palpable. There was no family history of breast cancer. FNAC of the lump suggested ductal carcinoma. Mammography showed a BIRADS IV hypoechoic lesion with slightly irregular margins in the right upper outer quadrant and right axillary lymphadenopathy. PET-CT revealed a 2.3×1.3 cm enhancing nodule (SUV 10.8) in the same site and metabolically active right axillary lymph nodes (SUV 11) without distant metastases. She underwent breast-conserving surgery with axillary clearance. The specimen contained a 2.2×2.8 cm grey-white infiltrating tumor with clear margins. Microscopically, the tumor comprised solid sheets of >90% large cells with distinct borders and clear cytoplasm; there was an extensive intraductal component of comedo and solid type. No cytoplasmic vacuoles were seen. The cytoplasmic material was PAS-positive and diastase-sensitive. Thirteen of 26 lymph nodes showed metastases with extracapsular extension. Immunohistochemistry showed HER2 positivity, ER and PR negativity, and a Ki-67 index of 50%. Pathologic stage was pT2N3a.

A 33-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of cough and sputum production. She had no fever but reported progressive dyspnea. Initial peripheral blood counts showed leukocytosis; chest radiographs were unremarkable, and she was treated empirically for allergic bronchitis without lasting benefit. On return, laboratory studies again demonstrated leukocytosis (white cell count elevated) with a normal absolute eosinophil count, an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, negative autoantibodies, carcinoembryonic antigen below reference range, and a weakly positive tuberculin skin test. Chest radiography and computed tomography revealed a 5.0×4.8 cm mass in the right upper lobe with associated atelectasis and no mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy. Bronchial mucosal biopsy and CT-guided percutaneous needle aspiration showed extensive eosinophil infiltration but no definitive malignant cells. A positron-emission tomography scan and bone marrow biopsy were normal. Repeated sputum cultures, parasite antigen testing, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid smears for acid-fast bacilli, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA assays were all negative. The lesion was provisionally diagnosed as eosinophilic granuloma, and a trial of systemic glucocorticoids led to symptomatic relief. However, follow-up CT showed enlargement of the mass, and a repeat lung biopsy was undertaken; bone marrow biopsy remained normal and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate stayed elevated.

A 32-year-old Albanian man presented with fatigue, cough, shortness of breath, progressive dyspnea, liver distention, and lower-extremity edema. He was initially treated for tracheobronchitis without improvement.  
His vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination showed jugular venous distention, hepatomegaly, and bilateral pitting edema.  
Laboratory testing revealed mild hyperbilirubinemia attributed to biliary stasis; parathyroid hormone, phosphate, and calcium levels were normal. Antithrombin III activity was mildly reduced at 60 U/ml (normal, 80 U/ml). There was no evidence of deep-vein thrombosis in the legs.  
Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated a 4 × 10 cm calcified mass in the right ventricle attached to the pulmonary valve, a dilated pulmonary trunk (4 cm diameter), and thrombosis at the origin of the right pulmonary artery; the pulmonary trunk and left pulmonary branch enhanced uniformly.  
Transthoracic echocardiography showed a 4 × 7 cm hyperechogenic, calcified right ventricular mass broad based on the papillary muscles and trabeculae, extending into the infundibulum and pulmonary valve, with slight tricuspid annular calcification. The mass moved with ventricular contraction and did not prolapse into the right atrium. The right atrium and ventricle were dilated with volume and pressure overload; estimated pulmonary arterial pressure was 70 mmHg. Transesophageal echocardiography confirmed these findings.

A 32-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with 2 days of epigastric pain, which worsened over the last 12 hours. He was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. On examination, the abdomen was distended with diffuse tenderness. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 15.9 g/dL, a white-cell count of 13,900/mm3, and a C-reactive protein level of 33 mg/L. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed diffuse wall thickening of the jejunum and proximal ileum with mesenteric fat infiltration, a 51 × 33 mm mesenteric fluid collection, and a moderate volume of ascites tracking into the pelvis.

A 66-year-old woman presented with long-standing dull abdominal pain radiating to the back that had become progressively worse over several months. Her past medical history was significant for hypertension treated with medication and a remote left hip replacement; there was no recent surgery or trauma. On examination, a palpable mass was noted in the left abdomen. Transabdominal ultrasound confirmed a large left para-aortic retroperitoneal mass. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a well-defined lobulated mass along the left lateral wall of the distal abdominal aorta and left common iliac artery, anteromedial to the left psoas muscle. The lesion exhibited heterogeneous intense peripheral enhancement in the porto-venous phase, with preserved fat planes and no evidence of local invasion.

A 5-year-old boy with no prior medical history presented with one month of a progressively enlarging, painless, firm right facial mass, initially measuring 3 cm. There was no history of trauma.  
CT of the orbits showed a lytic, osseous-based mass arising within the right zygoma, with a nonossified component extending into the orbit and mass effect on the globe without scleral invasion.  
Systemic workup—including CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and a technetium bone scan—demonstrated no other lesions or primary malignancy.  
A fine-needle biopsy was inconclusive, revealing only compact and woven bone. Two months after symptom onset, the lesion had grown to 5 cm, and an incisional biopsy of the soft-tissue component again showed no malignant cells.  
Ophthalmic examination revealed best corrected visual acuity of 20/25 OD and 20/20 OS, 2 mm of right proptosis, normal pupils, and full extraocular motility. The remainder of the ophthalmic and general physical examination was unremarkable.  
MRI of the orbits demonstrated a 5.3 cm zygomatic mass with suggestion of intralesional vascular channels on T2-weighted and postcontrast sequences.

A 78-year-old man with diabetes mellitus, hypertension, a history of moderately differentiated prostatic adenocarcinoma without evidence of metastasis, and nodular basal cell carcinoma presented with a lesion on the glans penis. On examination, there was a 2 × 2 cm irregular, friable mass on the glans. A deep shave biopsy showed nearly complete epidermal ulceration with replacement by an in-situ and diffusely infiltrative atypical clear cell tumor. Within the epidermis, the cells displayed diffuse pagetoid spread. The tumor consisted of large irregular nests and lobules of clear cells with abundant multivacuolated cytoplasm, nuclear indentations, and vesicular to hyperchromatic nuclei. Lymphovascular invasion was present. The initial differential diagnosis included a high-grade clear-cell squamous cell carcinoma and a metastatic clear-cell carcinoma.

A 33-year-old man presented with a 20-day history of insidious onset and progressively worsening weakness of both lower limbs and weak hand grips. He also had urinary retention for 7 days and mild upper dorsal back pain, worse at night and relieved by analgesics. He denied fever, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms.

On examination, he was of average build. Neurologic findings included:
- Lower limbs: muscle wasting, hypertonia, motor power 1/5, exaggerated deep tendon reflexes, sustained bilateral ankle clonus, and extensor plantar responses.
- Sensation: diminished to all modalities below the T10 level.
- Upper limbs: muscle strength 5/5 except grip strength 1/5; triceps reflexes absent; Hoffmann’s sign negative.
- A urinary catheter was in place for retention.

Laboratory studies showed normal complete blood count, C-reactive protein, blood glucose, and creatinine levels; serologic tests for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV were negative; blood and sputum cultures were negative.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine demonstrated a large, elongated posterior epidural mass extending from C4 to T6 levels, causing flattening and anterior displacement of the cord. The lesion was isointense to spinal cord on T1-weighted images with homogeneous contrast enhancement, and iso- to minimally hyperintense on T2-weighted images.

A 30-year-old woman was referred with a 3-year history of a painless, hard swelling in the submental region of the lower jaw. The lesion was initially pea-sized and gradually enlarged over 2½ years to its current size, which remained stable for the past 6 months. Her medical history included treated tuberculosis 2 years earlier; there was no history of trauma or discharge. 

On extraoral examination, there was a single, firm, nodular, immobile, nonfluctuant, noncompressible, nontender swelling in the submental region, measuring approximately 2–4 cm lateral to the midline of the mandible. The overlying skin was normal, with no warmth, suppuration, sinus tracts, or lymphadenopathy; the temporomandibular joints were normal.

Intraorally, there was no associated swelling, sinus tract, or occlusal disturbance, and all teeth were present except the third molars. 

Panoramic radiography demonstrated a well-defined, oval-to-round, homogeneous radiopaque mass approximately 2.0 × 1.5 cm in size, extending from the lower left canine to the first premolar region. A mandibular occlusal film confirmed a diffuse radiopaque area of about 1.8 × 1.2 cm in the same submental soft-tissue region.

A 54-year-old Hispanic woman, postmenopausal and asymptomatic, was referred after a screening mammogram showed a lesion at the junction of the upper quadrants of her left breast. She had a family history notable for a great-grandmother and maternal aunt with breast cancer diagnosed before age 40.  
On ultrasound, there was a solid 0.8 × 0.7 cm nodule with irregular borders at the 12 o’clock position, 5 cm from the nipple; no axillary abnormalities were detected. The lesion was assigned BI-RADS category 5, and an ultrasound-guided core-needle biopsy was performed.  
Histologic examination revealed an infiltrating carcinoma with tubular and cribriform patterns and both mucinous and eosinophilic luminal secretions. Immunohistochemical staining showed positivity in epithelial cells for cytokeratin 7, epithelial membrane antigen, and CD117, and positivity in myoepithelial cells for p63 and calponin. Tumor cells were negative for estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and HER2; the Ki-67 index was 10%, and the PD-L1 combined positive score was 15.  
Contrast-enhanced breast MRI demonstrated multicentric areas of enhancement with probable ductal extension, but no suspicious lymphadenopathy was seen.

A 13-year-old male with a 2-year history of swelling of the left hemimandible associated with mild pain, edema, induration, and delayed eruption of the ipsilateral posterior molar. Extraoral examination revealed facial asymmetry from enlargement of the left mandibular body and angle, with paresthesia since onset, and bilateral, mobile submandibular nodes <1 cm. Intraorally, cortical expansion of the left retromolar area was noted with slight tenderness on palpation of the lingual plate, a stony consistency, and intact mucosa. Panoramic radiograph showed a large multilocular radiolucent lesion divided by thick radiopaque septa extending from the left parasymphysis to the condylar neck and coronoid process, with displacement of tooth 38 into the coronoid area. CT with 3D reconstruction confirmed a lesion centered in the left hemimandible involving the condylar neck, ramus, angle, and body, with cortical thinning. Fine-needle aspiration yielded 3 cc of citrine fluid followed by hemorrhagic fluid. An incisional biopsy via the level of tooth 37 yielded bone samples, and a drain was placed.

A 40-year-old man was admitted 7 days after onset of fever (37.0–38.0°C) and 3 days of taste and smell disturbance. He had a 260–Brinkman‐index smoking history, quit 8 years earlier, and no other medical history. On admission, temperature was 37.8°C, blood pressure 114/83 mmHg, heart rate 99/min regular, SpO₂ 99% on room air; examination was unremarkable. Nasopharyngeal PCR for SARS‐CoV‐2 was positive. Chest radiograph showed bilateral ground‐glass opacities and infiltrative shadows. Thin‐section CT revealed multiple round to elliptical ground‐glass opacities and consolidations bilaterally, some with central consolidation; one lesion in the right lower lobe measured 21.4 mm (ground‐glass) and 9.3 mm (consolidation) (CTR 0.435). Laboratory tests showed WBC 4300/μL, neutrophils 70.8%, ALT 50 U/L, LDH 234 U/L, CRP 6.16 mg/dL; KL‐6 was 218 U/mL. He received inhaled ciclesonide and oral levofloxacin. His temperature normalized by day 4, SpO₂ remained >95%, and PCR on days 18 and 19 was negative; he was discharged on day 20. A CT at 1 month showed marked improvement of most opacities, but the right lower lobe lesion remained unchanged in form and size. At 6 months, CT showed the same lesion had increased slightly to 23.1 mm (ground‐glass) and 10.3 mm (consolidation) (CTR 0.446); it demonstrated vessel convergence, pleural indentation, and notch formation. No metastatic lesions were seen in liver, adrenals, or bone; there was no pleural or pericardial effusion, ascites, or lymphadenopathy. FDG‐PET/CT showed a maximal SUV of 2.0. Brain MRI was negative for metastases, and serum CEA was 1.73 ng/mL.

A 45-year-old North African woman with no significant medical history presented in March 2021 with a 7-month history of purulent rhinorrhea, intermittent epistaxis, and progressive swelling of the left nasal cavity.  
On examination, a firm, tender, whitish mass measuring approximately 6 cm filled the left nasal cavity, displacing the nasal dorsum and tip toward the right.  
Facial magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-defined tissue process occupying the left nasal cavity.  
An initial endonasal biopsy was interpreted as suggestive of synovial sarcoma.  
She subsequently received two cycles of neoadjuvant chemotherapy, achieved some tumor shrinkage, and then underwent surgical resection.

A 28-year-old woman presented with profuse nocturnal sweating but no other symptoms. She had no history of abdominal surgery. Physical examination of the abdomen was normal without palpable masses. Laboratory studies showed an elevated lactate dehydrogenase level.  
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a well-delimited, subhepatic retroperitoneal cystic mass measuring 8 cm in diameter. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 9.4 cm retroperitoneal cystic lesion that did not enhance after venous contrast administration, contained a short internal septum, and had no features suggestive of malignancy.  
MRI of the upper abdomen confirmed an 11 × 9 × 5 cm retrohepatic septated cystic lesion with homogeneous fluid signal, low intensity on T1-weighted images, high intensity on T2-weighted images, and no nodular enhancement or solid intralesional components.

A 73-year-old woman noted blurred vision and swelling of her right eyelid that persisted despite 1 month of topical steroids for presumed anterior uveitis. On examination, visual acuity was 20/100 in the right eye and 20/15 in the left; intraocular pressure was 30 mmHg in the right eye and 14 mmHg in the left. The right conjunctiva showed injection and chemosis. The right cornea had 50–100 pigmented keratic precipitates and 2+ cells in the anterior chamber, with no inflammation of the vitreous, retina, or choroid; the left eye was unremarkable. She had no systemic symptoms. MRI of the orbits showed a poorly marginated large mass surrounding the right eyeball, with no extraorbital lesions, and was suspected to represent an inflammatory pseudotumor. Aqueous humor multiplex PCR was positive for Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) DNA (8.5 × 10^4 copies/ml), leading to a tentative diagnosis of EBV-associated anterior uveitis with inflammatory pseudotumor. The patient received oral prednisolone (30 mg/day), followed by high-dose methylprednisolone pulse therapy and intravenous acyclovir, but her eyelid swelling worsened markedly.

A female infant was delivered at 26 weeks and 6 days of gestation to a healthy 26-year-old primigravida mother after an uneventful pregnancy until 19 weeks, when routine ultrasound identified a 34×28 mm sacrococcygeal mass with internal and external components. Amniocentesis showed a normal array comparative genomic hybridization, and a fetal echocardiogram was normal. At 22 weeks, MRI demonstrated a 60×70×57 mm sacrococcygeal mass with mixed features—predominantly solid with a 40 mm cyst—and no invasion or compression of pelvic structures or the coccyx (Altman type II). Subsequent ultrasounds showed rapid growth to 80×60 mm with profuse vascularization.

Spontaneous vaginal delivery occurred after antenatal steroids. The infant’s birth weight was 1300 g, and Apgar scores were 0, 0, and 5 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes. She required positive-pressure ventilation with FiO₂ up to 1.0 and intravenous adrenaline, with return of heart rate after 6 minutes. A single dose of surfactant was administered.

On admission to the NICU, vital signs were: heart rate 103/min, respiratory rate 70/min, blood pressure 19/15 mm Hg (mean 17), and axillary temperature 34.1 °C. She was ventilated on SIMV with volume guarantee (PIP 25 cm H₂O, PEEP 5 cm H₂O, rate 70/min, FiO₂ 1.0, VG 6 mL/kg). Physical examination revealed pallor, prolonged capillary refill, and a 14×7×4 cm, approximately 750 g, reddish sacrococcygeal mass with visible active bleeding. Initial management included repeated saline and glucose boluses, transfusion of red blood cells (30 mL/kg), fresh-frozen plasma (10 mL/kg), and platelets (10 mL/kg). Post-transfusion hemoglobin remained 5.8 g/dL. Severe metabolic acidosis was noted (pH 6.80, HCO₃⁻ 8.6 mmol/L, base excess −25).

A 59-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of itching and redness of the vulva and a 6-month history of diffuse vulvar swelling. Examination revealed an asymmetrical, well-defined, indurated erythematous plaque (5×4 cm) over the right labia majora extending onto the mons pubis. Within this plaque were multiple papules and nodules and a central superficial ulcer (1.5×1 cm), and there was diffuse pitting edema of the entire vulvar region with bilateral firm, non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. Per speculum examination could not be performed due to pain and induration. Initial clinical considerations included cutaneous tuberculosis, cutaneous Crohn’s disease, invasive squamous cell carcinoma, and amelanotic melanoma. 

Biopsy specimens were obtained from both the plaque and one of the nodules. CT of the chest demonstrated multiple metastatic nodules in the liver but showed no evidence of breast, lung, bladder, or gastrointestinal neoplasm. PET–CT revealed tracer uptake in the liver, bilateral inguinal lymph nodes, and maximal uptake in the vagina. 

Histologic examination of the plaque biopsy showed singly scattered and nested tumor cells within the epidermis; these cells had moderate to abundant clear cytoplasm, round to oval nuclei, and conspicuous nucleoli. The nodule biopsy revealed dermal nests and islands of tumor with foci of signet-ring cell differentiation without glandular or cribriform architecture.
