Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated tumor-cell positivity for cytokeratin 7, carcinoembryonic antigen, HER2/neu, gross cystic disease fluid protein 15, and androgen receptor; and negativity for cytokeratin 20, p40, CDX2, and estrogen receptor. Periodic acid–Schiff with Alcian blue staining highlighted intracytoplasmic mucin vacuoles in the signet-ring cells. 

Colonoscopy revealed no mass lesions; a solitary polyp was removed and found to be a hyperplastic polyp on microscopy.

A 48-year-old woman presented with a painless left anterior abdominal mass that had been gradually increasing in size over the past year. She had no history of trauma, abdominal surgery, or intestinal polyposis. She was a non-smoker, did not consume alcohol, and had no significant medical or family history. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender, immobile mass in the left lower quadrant measuring approximately 18 cm, with normal overlying skin. Routine blood tests, including tumor markers, were within normal limits. An abdominal CT scan showed a well-circumscribed 18 × 14 × 11 cm mass with attenuation similar to muscle, localized to the left rectus abdominis muscle extending toward the iliac crest, and no evidence of invasion into intra-abdominal organs or distant structures.

A 48-year-old man underwent routine cardiovascular risk assessment. His medical history was notable for an intermediate cardiovascular risk profile; physical examination, laboratory studies, and electrocardiography were unremarkable.  
Coronary artery calcium scanning revealed a calcium score of zero and incidentally detected a 5.3 × 3.8 cm anterior mediastinal mass. Cardiovascular computed tomographic angiography (CCTA) further characterized the lesion, demonstrating well-defined borders, independent vascular supply, and its proximity to the left anterior descending coronary artery and both cardiac ventricles.  
To assess for local invasion, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was performed; it demonstrated a well-circumscribed pericardiac mass without evidence of invasion.

A 37-year-old woman presented with a painless, palpable vulvar mass first noted 3 years earlier, which had gradually increased in size and caused only mild discomfort. She had no personal or family history of cancer or genetic disorders, and her general health was good without weight loss. On examination, vital signs were normal. There was a 3×2 cm firm, immobile, non-tender subcutaneous mass immediately superior to the clitoris in the midline of the vulva. The overlying skin and adjacent vulvar and vaginal mucosa were normal, with no ulceration, bleeding, or inguinal lymphadenopathy; pubic hair distribution was normal. Laboratory tests, including tumor markers, were within normal limits. Pelvic MRI showed a well-defined, round, 4.6 cm mass confined to the vulva, with low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, slight hypersignal intensity on T2-weighted images, and heterogeneous enhancement after contrast administration.

A 65-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a 2-week history of vaginal bleeding. Her Pap smear demonstrated high-grade cytologic atypia. Transvaginal ultrasonography revealed an endometrial stripe measuring 12 mm and a diffusely inhomogeneous myometrium. Colposcopy with directed biopsies showed atypical squamous cells suspicious for carcinoma. On bimanual examination, the uterus was enlarged. 

Her past medical history was noncontributory; surgical history included four cesarean deliveries and bilateral tubal ligation. She was a former smoker with a four pack-year history. Menarche occurred at age 12 and menopause at age 50, with no prior postmenopausal bleeding.

Hysteroscopy with dilation and curettage and cervical conization were performed. Curettage specimens showed a highly atypical squamous epithelial proliferation replacing the endometrium, while the cervical cone biopsy was benign. Pathology raised three main considerations: primary squamous cell carcinoma of the endometrium, squamous metaplastic change in an endometrioid adenocarcinoma with pauci-glandular proliferation, and metastatic squamous cell carcinoma to the endometrium from a distant site or cervical extension. P16 immunohistochemical staining was negative, effectively excluding a cervical primary. Endocervical curettage also showed p16-negative atypical squamous cells.

The case was reviewed at a multidisciplinary tumor board, and surgical staging was recommended.

A 42-year-old man with a history of smoking and methamphetamine use presented with a 3-month history of occipital headache that radiated to the frontal region. The headache was pulsatile, worsened by Valsalva maneuvers, and became daily during the week before admission. On the day of admission, he experienced vomiting and an intensification of the headache. On examination, he had papilledema and an indifferent gaze deviation but no focal motor or sensory deficits. A CT scan of the head revealed an extra-axial lesion in the right posterior fossa.

A 24-year-old man presented with progressive protrusion of his right eye over the past year without other ocular or neurologic symptoms.  
On examination, there were no obvious abnormalities in the right orbit.  
Plain radiographs of the skull showed destruction of the left frontal bone.  
Orbital computed tomography revealed a 3 cm × 3 cm × 3 cm well-circumscribed lesion in the upward wall of the right orbit, destroying the surrounding bone and penetrating into the internal skull while sparing the external table.  
Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated two similar circumscribed masses—one in the right orbital roof and one in the left frontotemporal bone—both of which were T1-isointense, T2-hyperintense, showed strong homogeneous enhancement, exhibited an enhancing dural tail, and extended intracranially without surrounding edema.

A 23-year-old healthy man presented with a draining lesion on the left side of his face for 3 months. Five months earlier he had experienced mild, dull aching pain in the left lower cheek, followed two days later by a mild swelling. A general physician prescribed antibiotics and analgesics, which temporarily relieved his symptoms, but after 7 weeks the pain and swelling recurred, and he noted an opening on the left cheek with foul-smelling, yellowish discharge. Dermatologic treatment with topical and systemic antibiotics over 2 months failed to heal the lesion. He denied prior tooth pain or dental consultation but reported difficulty chewing on the left side.

On extraoral examination, there was a 0.5×1.0-cm erythematous area in the left lower third of the face with a central opening discharging scant purulent material; culture was sterile. A 28-gauge wire inserted into the opening passed through a sinus tract but did not communicate with the oral cavity. Intraoral examination showed mild erythema around the intact left lower second molar and an unerupted left lower third molar; palpation revealed mild tenderness and thinning of the buccal cortex in that region, with no intraoral discharge and no carious teeth.

A panoramic radiograph with gutta-percha tracing demonstrated a well-defined radiolucency around the bucco-lingually positioned impacted left lower third molar. Cone-beam CT revealed a 3.0×4.0×2.5-cm unilocular radiolucent lesion with a sclerotic border surrounding the linguoverted impacted third molar, closely approximating the superior border of the inferior alveolar nerve canal, with focal cortical thinning and perforation of the buccal plate. Hence, an oro-cutaneous fistula due to an infected dentigerous cyst was formulated as a provisional diagnosis.

A 70-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of a slowly enlarging mass in the posterior aspect of her left thigh. She was afebrile, with preserved general health. On examination, the lesion measured approximately 7×12 cm, was firm, mobile relative to the skin but fixed to deeper tissues, non-tender, exhibited prominent collateral venous circulation, and there was no regional lymphadenopathy or distal neurovascular deficit. A standard radiograph of the thigh was unremarkable. Soft-tissue ultrasound demonstrated a heterogeneous, well-vascularized mass with fatty characteristics, raising suspicion for liposarcoma. MRI confirmed a 9×19 cm mass displacing the femoral vessels medially; it was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2 and fat-saturation sequences, contained areas of necrosis and hemorrhage, and showed marked gadolinium enhancement, especially on fat-saturation sequences.

A 53-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive abdominal distention and worsening early satiety, accompanied by an increase in abdominal circumference and limb thinning. She denied pain, fever, nausea, or vomiting. She had been postmenopausal for 5 years with no vaginal bleeding. Her medical history was notable only for well-controlled hypertension on loxone; she had no history of diabetes, coronary disease, or malignancy and had not had a physical examination in over 10 years. On examination, her BMI was 23.3. A giant rubbery abdominal mass extended to the xiphisternum; it was non-tender, with no rebound tenderness and normal bowel sounds. Laboratory studies, including liver and renal function tests, fecal occult blood, coagulation profile, electrolytes, and tumor markers, were all within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 30 cm × 17 cm well-defined hyperechoic mass with internal septations and minimal blood flow. Non-contrast CT showed a 16.6 cm × 28.6 cm homogeneous fat-containing mass with thin septa displacing the bowel loops and uterus to the right.

A 53-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of a palpable mass in her right axilla. She had a history of hypertension treated with daily medication. On examination, the right axillary mass measured 10 cm and was non-tender. Laboratory studies revealed a mildly elevated carcinoembryonic antigen level (5.2 ng/mL; normal < 5.0 ng/mL); all other laboratory tests were unremarkable. Mammography demonstrated a high-density mass in the right axilla. Ultrasonography showed an irregularly shaped mass with indistinct margins, internal hypoechogenicity, and increased peripheral vascularity. An ultrasound-guided core-needle biopsy revealed invasive carcinoma. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest confirmed a 12 cm lobulated, heterogeneously enhancing mass in the right axilla. 18F-FDG-PET revealed intense uptake in the right axillary mass (SUV max 12.7) and a focal uptake in the right adrenal gland (SUV max 4.7). Follow-up CT of the abdomen and pelvis identified a 1.5 cm lobulated mass in the right adrenal gland with mild enhancement and invasion into the liver.

A 23-year-old woman presented with palpable left breast masses and left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. She had no underlying disease and no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. One year earlier she was diagnosed with stage IIB cervical cancer (treated as squamous cell carcinoma) and underwent laparoscopic ovarian transposition with bilateral salpingectomy followed by definitive concurrent chemoradiation. Surveillance had shown no recurrence.

On current examination, there were two left breast masses measuring approximately 2 cm and 3 cm, and a 4 cm left supraclavicular lymph node; no axillary lymphadenopathy was noted. Breast ultrasonography revealed two microlobulated hypoechoic masses with vascularity in the left upper outer quadrant (2.0 cm and 3.5 cm). Contrast-enhanced CT showed two left breast masses, an enlarged left supraclavicular lymph node, multiple lung and mediastinal lymph node lesions, peritoneal and right back subcutaneous metastases, and normal-appearing uterus and ovaries.

Core needle biopsies of both breast masses and the supraclavicular node demonstrated small cell tumors with papillary features. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for pan-cytokeratin (AE1/AE3), synaptophysin, chromogranin, paired-box gene 8 (PAX8), and p16, and negative for cytokeratin 5/6, gross cystic disease fluid protein-15, estrogen receptor, and progesterone receptor.

A 19-year-old Japanese woman presented with left temporal headache. Brain MRI revealed a well-defined, heterogeneously contrast-enhancing 10 mm lesion in the left temporal lobe with high T2 signal. She underwent left frontotemporal craniotomy and gross total resection. Histology showed an astrocytic tumor with fewer than 1 mitosis per 10 high-power fields, and the initial diagnosis was low-grade glioma. She was followed without adjuvant therapy and had no evidence of recurrence for 3 years, then declined further examinations.

Twelve years after the initial surgery, she returned with left temporal headache, diplopia, and tinnitus. MRI demonstrated a local recurrence around the surgical cavity measuring approximately 42 × 45 × 47 mm with prominent perifocal edema. At second surgery the tumor was highly vascular with dural feeders and was weakly positive on 5-aminolevulinic acid photodynamic diagnosis. H&E staining showed an astrocytic neoplasm with necrosis, microvascular proliferation, infiltration, and five mitoses per 10 high-power fields; eosinophilic granular bodies were absent. Immunohistochemical studies were positive for Olig2, retained INI1 and ATRX, approximately 21% of cells were Ki-67 positive, and IDH1-R132H was negative. Retrospective review of the first specimen revealed spindle-shaped cells with nuclear pleomorphism and eosinophilic granular bodies. Both specimens lacked reticulin fibers and CD34 expression.

Multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification and pyrosequencing on both resections detected a BRAF V600E mutation (mutant allele frequencies 16% initially and 49% at recurrence). The initial tumor had intact 1p/19q and CDKN2A, whereas the recurrent tumor showed 19q deletion and CDKN2A homozygous deletion. No mutations were found in IDH1/2, H3F3A, HIST1H3B, TERT promoter, or FGFR1.

A 40‐year‐old Caucasian man presented with a 3‐month history of a rapidly enlarging, vegetating lesion in the right external auditory canal. On examination, there was a 2.5-cm bleeding, ulcerated mass occluding the canal, with associated complete ipsilateral hearing loss and peripheral facial nerve paralysis. An incisional biopsy showed large pale cells with pleomorphic nuclei and prompted a suggestion of extramammary Paget’s disease, with a possible differential diagnosis of amelanotic melanoma or pagetoid Bowen’s disease. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated positivity for human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (Her2/Neu), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), cytokeratin-7 (CK7), and gross cystic disease fluid protein of 15 kDa (GCDFP-15); markers for p63, HMB-45, Melan-A, and 34BE12 were negative. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the head revealed an infiltrative lesion in the right external ear with paravertebral and middle ear extension, involving the anterior wall of the internal carotid artery and the facial nerve. Magnetic resonance imaging showed an expansile tumor with ill-defined margins, no clear plane with the carotid artery, extension into the parapharyngeal space, invasion of the middle cranial fossa, and associated meningeal enhancement.

A 62-year-old Caucasian woman was referred by her general physician for evaluation of asymptomatic cutaneous lesions that appeared eight months earlier on the left arm and right forearm. Her medical history was unremarkable, and routine blood tests, including HIV serology, were normal. She denied any history of solid-organ transplantation or immunosuppressive therapy. Over the past two months, similar lesions appeared on the abdomen, right thigh, and back. Dermatological examination revealed asymmetric, painless erythematoviolaceous papules measuring 3–10 mm in diameter. Punch biopsies of the lesions were performed.

A 39-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of blurred vision in her right eye. Neurologic examination was unremarkable, and there was no history of neurofibromatosis. Brain MRI demonstrated a well-defined, round solid mass measuring 3.6 × 2.9 × 3.7 cm in the right occipital–cerebellar tentorial region. The lesion was isointense on T1-weighted images, slightly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and relatively homogeneous on FLAIR sequences. On contrast-enhanced T1-weighted imaging, the mass exhibited homogeneous enhancement with a dural tail sign. CTA and MRV revealed the occipital transtentorial lesion compressing and narrowing the adjacent straight sinus, confluence of sinuses, right transverse sinus, and sigmoid sinus. To sum up, the diagnosis based on preoperative imaging tended to be meningioma.

A 63-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an incidentally discovered large mediastinal and left pulmonary mass. She had initially presented with dysphonia due to recurrent left vocal cord paralysis. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the head and neck revealed an 18 cm × 11 cm mass arising in the mediastinum, infiltrating the hilum and left upper lobe. Aside from vocal cord paralysis, she was asymptomatic. 

Her medical history included mixed anxiety-depressive disorder, left cataract surgery 2 years earlier, and a radical hysterectomy with salpingo-oophorectomy for a uterine smooth muscle tumour of uncertain malignant potential (STUMP) 14 years before. She had a 45 pack-year smoking history and continued to smoke until surgery. Family history was unremarkable.

A total-body contrast CT scan confirmed an extensive vascularized solid mass originating in the mediastinum, extending into the left hemithorax and occupying the entire left upper lobe. PET-CT showed FDG uptake with an SUVmax of 6.4. Pulmonary function tests were at the limits of operability (FVC 0.89 L [30%], FEV1 0.69 L [28%], DLCO 12 L [50%], DLCO/VA 2.19 L [41%]). Lung perfusion scintigraphy revealed 98% perfusion to the right lung and 2% to the left. A CT-guided transthoracic needle biopsy was inconclusive. During workup, she developed acute respiratory distress requiring supplemental oxygen, and the team planned a salvage left pneumonectomy.

A 30‐year‐old woman presented with an 8‐year history of a slowly enlarging swelling on the inner side of the lower left posterior mandible. Eight years ago, the lesion measured approximately 5 mm; it gradually increased to 1 cm. The swelling was asymptomatic until recently, when she experienced discomfort while chewing. She denied trauma, and her medical and family histories were unremarkable, with no other swellings noted elsewhere.

On intraoral examination, there was a solitary, oval, pedunculated swelling on the lingual aspect of teeth 36 and 37, covered by normal mucosa. The lesion was lobulated, non‐tender, and uniformly bony hard.

A mandibular occlusal cross‐sectional radiograph showed a well‐defined, irregularly shaped, radiopaque mass attached to the lingual cortex of tooth 37 by a narrow stalk, with radiodensity equivalent to adjacent mandibular bone.

A 35-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of a slowly enlarging swelling in the right axilla associated with intermittent purulent discharge. He denied weight loss, decreased appetite, night sweats, tuberculosis, diabetes, or hypertension. He had no history of smoking, alcohol use, or family history of malignancy.

On examination, he was afebrile. There was a firm-to-hard 3 × 2 cm swelling in the right axilla with a sinus tract discharging pus-like fluid and pale granulation tissue; it was tender and warm. The contralateral axilla and both breasts were unremarkable, and no lymphadenopathy was palpable.

Given the chronic sinus, tuberculosis was suspected. A Mantoux test, sputum for acid-fast bacilli, and chest radiograph were all negative. Routine hematological and biochemical tests were within normal limits. Culture of the discharge grew Enterobacter species.

Ultrasound of the axilla showed a heterogeneous mass lesion without clear involvement of lymph nodes. Fine-needle aspiration yielded pus-like fluid. May-Grünwald-Giemsa–stained smears revealed cellular smears with atypical epithelial cells in papillary clusters, sheets, and acini; these cells had moderate cytoplasm, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, mild nuclear pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, and prominent nucleoli. Focal apocrine cytoplasmic changes were noted. Background elements included foamy macrophages and hemorrhage. An impression of a malignant epithelial lesion favoring adenocarcinoma with apocrine and cystic change was made.

A 15-year-old man with cystic fibrosis, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, and CF-associated liver disease presented with a 5-week history of intermittent spasmodic abdominal pain, increased frequency of nonbloody stools, and symptoms worsened by stress. Physical examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies—including CBC, ESR, CRP, electrolytes, amylase, lipase, and fecal occult blood—were within normal limits; a liver panel showed mild transaminase elevations consistent with his known liver disease. He was initially treated for functional abdominal pain with antispasmodics. 

Because of refractory symptoms, he underwent esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) and colonoscopy. EGD was visually normal; colonoscopy showed mild scattered colonic exudates and a normal terminal ileum. Biopsies demonstrated chronic active eosinophilic ileitis and colitis, leading to initiation of sulfasalazine and oral budesonide. 

Despite adherence, symptoms persisted. He was admitted for presumed distal intestinal obstruction syndrome (DIOS) based on radiologic evidence of organized contents in the distal small bowel and treated with polyethylene glycol and N-acetylcysteine. On follow-up, he reported continued pain. Repeat EGD and colonoscopy showed resolution of colitis but revealed a protruding intraluminal mass with a smooth surface and normal overlying mucosa in the terminal ileum; biopsies, including from the mass, were normal. 

Small-bowel capsule endoscopy was normal. Magnetic resonance enterography showed thickening of the ileocecal valve but no discrete mass, polyp, or external compression. Repeat CBC remained normal. He was readmitted for recurrent bowel obstruction; repeat colonoscopy confirmed a nonocclusive mass in the terminal ileum but was otherwise visually unremarkable. Biopsies again showed small-bowel and colonic mucosal eosinophilia. Given normal biopsy histology, laboratory and imaging results, the mass was presumed benign, and recurrent obstruction was thought secondary to DIOS.

A 55-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of progressive fatigue, anorexia, and an unintentional 20-kg weight loss. He also reported intermittent left upper abdominal discomfort, early satiety, and increasing abdominal girth. He denied fevers, night sweats, bleeding, recent travel, illicit-drug use, or alcohol use. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. He appeared pale. No lymphadenopathy was noted. Abdominal examination revealed a firm, non-tender spleen palpated 22 cm below the left costal margin; the liver was not enlarged. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 81.6 fL, platelet count 108 × 10^3/μL, white-cell count 6.8 × 10^3/μL with 4.2 × 10^3/μL lymphocytes, and normal renal and liver biochemistry. Lactate dehydrogenase was 250 U/L. Peripheral blood smear showed anisocytosis and poikilocytosis without circulating blast or smear cells. Tests for hepatitis B and C, HIV, EBV, and CMV were negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated massive splenomegaly measuring 18 × 11 × 26 cm without focal lesions, with normal liver size and attenuation and no portal-system abnormalities.

A 64-year-old woman noted a painless palpable lump in her left breast on self-examination. She had no family history of breast cancer, entered menopause at age 50, and took a mild beta-blocker for hypertension. Mammography showed a small (≈1 cm) irregular high-density mass with indistinct margins, few fine pleomorphic grouped calcifications, and focal architectural distortion in the left upper outer quadrant. Ultrasound revealed an approximately 1 cm oval, heterogeneous hypoechoic lesion with indistinct margins and anomalous vascularity; axillary lymph nodes appeared normal. Core needle biopsy demonstrated high-grade malignant neoplasia, non-lobulocentric, composed of epithelioid cells with anisocariotic and pleomorphic nuclei; receptor profile was estrogen- and progesterone-receptor negative, HER2 score 0, and Ki-67 index 70%, consistent with malignant mesenchymal histogenesis. Immunohistochemistry was positive for vimentin, cytokeratin AE1/AE3, p63, CK5/6, CD10, and weakly positive for HHF35 and E-cadherin. Serum tumor markers (CEA, CA 15-3, CA 125, CA 19-9) were within normal limits. Dynamic contrast-enhanced breast MRI confirmed an irregular 12 mm mass with type III kinetics in the left upper outer quadrant and incidentally detected a 14 mm homogeneously enhancing oval lesion in the left anterior superior mediastinum. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and brain showed no other metastatic lesions and confirmed the anterior mediastinal nodule.

A 47-year-old man was transferred with an ulcerating left testicular mass that he had noted growing over 3 years. In the days before admission, he developed scrotal ulcerations, fever, and 3 weeks of left leg swelling, redness, and pain. He had no prior medical history or medications. 

Initial CT showed an approximately 22 × 18 cm ulcerating left testicular mass with bilateral para-aortic, iliac, and inguinal lymphadenopathy, and extensive deep venous thrombosis of the left leg with subcutaneous and perifascial edema; there were no parenchymal distant metastases. He received antibiotics and tinzaparin. During hospitalization, he developed hemorrhagic shock from tumor bleeding and bilateral acute pulmonary embolism with right heart strain; anticoagulation was managed despite bleeding. MRI of the head and SPECT bone scan excluded brain and bone metastases.

Serum tumor markers were markedly elevated: lactate dehydrogenase, beta-human chorionic gonadotropin, and alpha-fetoprotein. Hormonal studies revealed low luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, and testosterone, consistent with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. 

An inguinal lymph node biopsy showed predominantly scar-like fibrosclerosis and subtotally necrotic infiltrates of a small-cell neoplasia. Immunohistochemical staining of viable cells was positive for SALL4, podoplanin, and OCT4, negative for PLAP, CD45, and CD30, with focal CAL1 expression.

A healthy 40-year-old woman presented with right periauricular pain and a several-month history of vertigo with nausea. Neurologic and ENT examinations were normal except for apparent enlargement of the right mandibular condyle.  

CT of the facial skeleton revealed a 34 × 30 × 28 mm bone lesion of the right condyle with cystic deformation but no involvement of the inferior alveolar nerve or adjacent structures. MRI showed an expansile lesion of the condyle with heterogeneous signal intensity on T1, T2, and postcontrast images, causing compression of the parotid gland without invasive growth.  

Initial differential diagnoses included giant cell tumour, aneurysmal bone cyst, ameloblastoma, fibrous dysplasia, and myxoma. A biopsy performed under general anesthesia demonstrated predominantly pre-existing bone with high turnover and new bone formation; fibrous dysplasia was considered most likely, but a definitive diagnosis could not be made, and there were no signs of malignancy.  

Four months later, physical examination showed a narrowed right external auditory canal, hypertrophic and tender masseteric and pterygoid muscles, and a maximum mouth opening of 13 mm with deviation to the right. Repeat CT was stable. Bone scintigraphy revealed a monostotic active fibrous distension in the right mandible.  

She was treated with daily olpadronate and physiotherapy, resulting in mild pain relief and an increase in mouth opening to 17 mm, but she still experienced significant morbidity. She had two episodes of otitis externa due to canal compression, requiring hospitalization and intravenous antibiotics. Because of the repeated functional deficits and considerable morbidity, surgical therapy was therefore indicated.

A 58-year-old woman with no comorbidities presented with a one-year history of a fast-growing mass in her right lower abdominal wall. She had no systemic symptoms or family history of malignancy. On examination, there was a tender, nonreducible, nonmobile mass in the right lower quadrant. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, platelet count 230,000/µL, prothrombin time 97%, and normal renal and hepatic function. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a well-circumscribed, heterogeneous soft-tissue mass in the abdominal wall measuring 13 × 10 × 8 cm.

A 15-year-old, spayed, mixed-breed female dog (14 kg) presented with a 1-month history of progressive coughing and exercise intolerance. Lung auscultation was unremarkable; echocardiography showed moderate mitral insufficiency. Thoracic radiographs revealed a large (8.0 × 7.5 × 3.0 cm) round, air-filled cystic lesion with thick, irregular walls in the left caudal lung lobe, compressing adjacent bronchi and accompanied by bronchial wall thickening. Contrast-free thoracic CT demonstrated a 6.6 × 4.5 × 5.9 cm oval air-filled structure in the perihilar left caudal lobe with hyperattenuating, irregular walls ~0.4 cm thick, in contact with bronchial branches and showing air bronchograms; there was no lymphadenopathy or pleural abnormality.

A 70-year-old man noted a right subareolar mass about 1 year earlier. The lesion had gradually enlarged, prompting evaluation. Physical examination revealed a 5-cm, elastic yet firm, subareolar mass of the right breast without overlying skin or nipple changes, nipple discharge, or palpable axillary lymphadenopathy.

Ultrasonography demonstrated a well-defined, 50-mm intracystic tumor immediately beneath the nipple. A broad-based, papillary solid component arose from the cyst wall, and Doppler imaging showed abundant internal vascularity. The cyst contained a fluid level, suggesting blood.

Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a multifocal intracystic mass with a rapid-plateau enhancement pattern after contrast administration. Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen showed no invasion of underlying muscle, no lymphadenopathy, and no distant metastases. Routine blood tests, including breast tumor markers, were within normal limits.

Fine-needle aspiration of the cystic fluid yielded blood-tinged fluid with small clusters of atypical cells, raising suspicion for malignancy. A subsequent vacuum-assisted core biopsy demonstrated ductal epithelial tissue with mild nuclear atypia but was insufficient for a definitive diagnosis.

A 50-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of progressively worsening vision in his right eye. He denied fever, headache, vomiting, seizures, photophobia, or focal weakness. On examination, he was alert, oriented, and afebrile. There was no peripheral lymphadenopathy. Visual testing revealed only light perception in the right eye; the remainder of the neurologic examination was normal. Routine endocrinological studies, including pituitary function tests, were within normal limits. A contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain demonstrated an intensely enhancing solid mass in an extradural location within the suprasellar cistern adjacent to the pituitary stalk, with anterior extension into the right orbital apex.

A 30-year-old woman presented with a painless lump in her left breast of 10 months’ duration. She reported no trauma, fever, nipple discharge, or retraction, and there was no family history of breast malignancy. On examination, there was a single, well-circumscribed 3.0×2.5 cm mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast. The overlying skin, nipple, and areola were unremarkable, and there was no axillary lymphadenopathy. 

Fine-needle aspiration (23-gauge needle) yielded 3 mL of straw-colored fluid, after which the swelling decreased in size. May-Grünwald-Giemsa–stained smears showed scant cellularity in a hemorrhagic background, with a few histiocytes. The epithelial cells present were round to oval, arranged in cohesive clusters, and demonstrated nuclear crowding, mild pleomorphism, and absence of bare nuclei. Occasional loosely cohesive clusters contained cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm.

A 39-year-old Asian woman presented with a 2-month history of headache, dizziness, and progressive right-sided hearing impairment. She had no focal neurologic deficits on examination; vital signs and routine laboratory results were within normal limits. Nonenhanced CT of the head showed a 50 × 40 × 28 mm slightly hyperdense mass in the right cerebellopontine angle with solid and cystic-like components, causing mass effect on the fourth ventricle and upstream ventricular dilation. MRI revealed a lobulated right tentorial mass with mixed T2 and FLAIR signal intensity, restricted diffusion with an apparent diffusion coefficient of 0.404 × 10^−3 mm^2/s, and poor post-contrast enhancement with small intralesional vessels. A 3D-constructive interference in steady-state sequence demonstrated preservation of the right internal acoustic meatus and anterior displacement of the VII/VIII cranial nerve complex.

A 60‐year‐old maintenance worker presents with several years of nontraumatic, posterior throbbing pain in his right shoulder. A few months ago, he sustained a traction injury to the same shoulder while pulling a lawn‐mower starter cord; since then he has noted new, sharp anterolateral shoulder pain that limits his work.

Six months after the injury he was diagnosed clinically with rotator cuff tendinopathy and underwent three months of physiotherapy. At follow‐up, his anterolateral pain had mildly improved, but his longstanding posterior pain persisted.

On examination, there was mild tenderness over the acromioclavicular joint and pain at 90° of active abduction despite a full range of motion in all planes. Neer and Hawkins impingement tests were positive. The Jobe test elicited pain without weakness; other rotator cuff muscles were normal. A “Popeye sign” suggested rupture of the long head of the biceps tendon. Neurovascular examination of the right upper extremity was unremarkable.

Plain shoulder radiographs showed no bony abnormalities apart from indirect signs of rotator cuff tendinopathy. MRI of the shoulder demonstrated moderate‐to‐severe acromioclavicular joint osteoarthritis without significant inferior osteophytes, subscapularis tendinopathy, a partial‐thickness supraspinatus tear, and a long head of biceps tendon rupture. Importantly, there was a well‐circumscribed 6 cm × 2 cm × 5 cm homogeneous mass with signal characteristics of fat, located deep to the posterior deltoid, adjacent to the infraspinatus and teres minor, extending under the acromion, and without invasion into the rotator cuff or surrounding tissues.

History of Present Illness: A 33-year-old man presents with a 2-year history of a progressively enlarging, tender mass on the ulnar aspect of the right wrist. The lesion first appeared shortly after local injury with glass foreign-body debris. Tenderness has been present since onset and worsened over the past 3–4 months, prompting emergency department evaluation.

Emergency Department Evaluation: On initial ED presentation the mass was lanced, yielding mild bloody drainage without abscess. Radiographs of the right wrist showed a 2.1 × 1.7 cm rounded area of soft-tissue density along the ulnar aspect of the distal ulna, with no osseous abnormality or radiopaque foreign body.

Orthopedic Examination: The mass was soft, somewhat mobile, and very tender, with no overlying warmth or erythema. Neurovascular function was intact. A small skin incision was noted from the ED drainage attempt.

MRI of the Wrist (with contrast): A well-circumscribed, lobulated, septated subcutaneous soft-tissue mass measuring 2.1 × 1.3 × 1.6 cm was centered in the subcutaneous fat along the ulnar wrist. The lesion was isointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and demonstrated avid, relatively homogeneous postcontrast enhancement. Central areas of internal T2 hypointensity and nonenhancement likely represent blood products or internal hemorrhage. No involvement of adjacent bone, muscle, tendon, nerve, or vascular structures was seen.

Given this presentation and imaging, what is your differential diagnosis?

A 47-year-old African American woman presented with a 1-year history of progressive left nasal obstruction and intermittent epistaxis. Her medical history included well-controlled hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and coronary artery disease; she had no history of immunosuppression, neurofibromatosis, or prior malignancy. On examination, a left nasal cavity mass was suspected. 

A CT scan of the sinuses demonstrated a left nasal mass measuring 3.4 × 3.1 × 2.4 cm with thinning of the medial orbital wall, nasal septum, and medial wall of the maxillary sinus. A subsequent MRI of the brain revealed a 2.1 × 1.7 × 3.5 cm avidly enhancing lesion in the superior left nasal cavity without perineural, intracranial, or cavernous sinus extension. A CT scan of the chest showed no evidence of metastatic disease.

An 18-year-old Iranian woman was referred for evaluation of progressively worsening oral lesions over 15 weeks. Fifteen weeks earlier, she noted gingival attachment loss with migration of the maxillary right first molar gingiva toward the buccal surface, and alveolar bone no longer supported that tooth. Eight weeks before presentation, an oral biopsy showed only mixed inflammatory-cell infiltration without evidence of malignancy on immunohistochemistry.

Her medical history was significant for an 18-month history of chronic cough and dyspnea initially diagnosed as asthma and treated without improvement. She subsequently underwent evaluation that revealed a mediastinal mass, pulmonary cavitation, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, but cytologic and immunohistochemical analyses were non-diagnostic. She also reported unexplained weight loss and nausea. There was no history of malignancy in her family.

On intraoral examination, there was a painless exposed area of maxillary bone on the posterior right hard palate, surrounded by pink, non-necrotic mucosa with an irregular border. Bone loss was noted on the buccal surface of the maxillary right first molar, and a small ulceration was observed on the left maxillary tuberosity. The involved teeth were vital without mobility. Extraoral examination was unremarkable; she was afebrile with no cervical lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin concentration of 10 g/dL, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (65 mm/h), and C-reactive protein level of 24 mg/L. White-cell and platelet counts and lactate dehydrogenase were within normal limits. Serologic tests for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were negative. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (C-ANCA and P-ANCA) were negative.

Cone-beam computed tomography of the maxilla demonstrated destruction of the buccal and palatal cortices bilaterally from the upper molar alveolar bone to the tuberosity, floating appearance of the molar teeth, an abnormal trabecular pattern, and mucosal thickening of both maxillary sinuses.

A 10-year-old girl presented with a 6-month history of severe right knee pain that worsened at night and disturbed her sleep. She was otherwise healthy and active until the onset of pain. Laboratory studies including hemoglobin, hematocrit, white-cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and alkaline phosphatase were all within normal limits.

Two radiographs of the right knee showed a small subperiosteal lucency of the lateral femoral condyle. MRI of the right knee revealed minimal edema, a possible small nidus, and no bone sclerosis; a consultative pediatric radiologist suggested a subchondral osteoid osteoma. The patient was treated with paracetamol and ibuprofen without relief.

On examination, she held her knee in pain but had a normal gait without limp and could hop bilaterally without discomfort. The range of motion in the right knee was full, with no effusion; examination of both hips was normal. The spine was straight with full flexion and extension, and neurologic examination including tendon reflexes and sensation in both legs and feet was normal.

Due to uncertainty about the diagnosis, CT of the right knee with 5-mm slices was performed, without evidence of a nidus or sclerosis. A technetium bone scan showed no increased uptake in the right knee or elsewhere. Pelvic, hip, and lumbar-spine radiographs (AP and lateral) were normal.

On the following day, MRI of the right femur, pelvis, and lumbar spine was obtained to search for possible pathology.

A 51-year-old woman with a history of a uterine polyp status-post curettage and gastritis treated empirically with omeprazole presented with 15 days of mild epigastric pain, nausea, loose stools, and fever. Two days before admission, her pain became diffuse and intensified, prompting evaluation. On examination, she was tachycardic and had decreased breath sounds at the left lung base. Abdominal examination showed slight distension, severe tenderness to palpation, positive McBurney’s sign, and rebound tenderness. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis with a left shift, mild anemia, and hypoalbuminemia. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a thickened cecal appendix, enlarged ileocolic lymph nodes, free perisplenic fluid, and an exophytic mass at the splenic flexure. Diagnostic laparoscopy revealed 1000 mL of purulent fluid throughout the peritoneal cavity, a thickened appendix without signs of inflammation, and an inflammatory-appearing tumor at the splenic flexure with abundant fibrin and multiple paracolic lymph nodes, prompting conversion to an open procedure. Intraoperatively, the colon and rectal stump mucosa were studded with numerous polypoid lesions. A total colectomy with end ileostomy was performed for presumed familial adenomatous polyposis. The patient recovered well and was discharged for oncology follow-up.

A 19-year-old man presented with a one-month history of mild pain and swelling in the right posterior mandible. The pain was intermittent, occurring during mastication, and the swelling had gradually increased in size. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender swelling expanding both buccal and lingual cortices from the right first premolar to the third molar region, obliterating the buccal vestibule; the overlying skin was normal and there was no paresthesia. A panoramic radiograph revealed a large, well-defined, sclerotic-margined, multilocular radiolucent lesion with a “soap-bubble” appearance extending from the lower right canine to 1 cm distal to the third molar, with mesial root resorption of the first molar. A mandibular occlusal radiograph confirmed multilocular radiolucency with expansion of the buccal and lingual cortices. Fine-needle aspiration, performed to exclude odontogenic cysts, yielded negative results.

A 35-year-old woman presented with multiple nontender palpable lumps in both breasts and diplopia of the left eye. Thirteen months earlier, she had been diagnosed with primary extramedullary plasmacytoma of the epidural soft tissue at the C6–T1 level and of the stomach; at that time, bone marrow biopsy showed normocellular marrow with 6.2% plasma cells, no bone lesions, no end-organ damage, and no monoclonal protein. She received 12 cycles of melphalan and prednisolone and localized radiotherapy, with no recurrence on surveillance MRI and CT for one year. 

Breast ultrasonography revealed multiple well-defined, oval, markedly hypoechoic masses in both breasts. Mammography showed multiple circumscribed or obscured, oval or round, hyperdense masses bilaterally. Breast MRI demonstrated multiple well-defined, oval or round, strongly enhancing masses with iso- to high signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images; diffusion-weighted imaging showed high signal intensity with low apparent diffusion coefficient values, indicating restricted diffusion. Dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI revealed massive (780%) initial enhancement with a delayed washout kinetic curve, suggestive of malignancy.

A 3-year-old girl presented with a four-month history of intermittent abdominal pain exacerbated when sitting and during urination. On examination, she appeared well; head, neck, chest, and cardiovascular exams were normal. The abdomen was soft and non-tender without palpable masses, lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly. Perineal examination revealed a firm presacral mass palpable into the right buttock.  
Baseline laboratory studies, including complete blood count, bone marrow aspiration, urinary vanillylmandelic acid clearance, blood β-HCG, alpha-fetoprotein, electrolytes, alkaline phosphatase, and liver and kidney function tests, were all within normal limits.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed a 74×76×155 mm noncalcified presacral soft-tissue mass and a 50×43×47 mm hypodense hepatic nodule. MIBG scintigraphy demonstrated uptake in the left paramedian pelvis without skeletal or hepatic foci.  
A CT-guided biopsy of the presacral mass revealed a small round cell proliferation expressing cytokeratin and CD56 but negative for CD45, suggesting neuroblastoma, though a desmoplastic small round cell tumor could not be excluded as desmin was not tested. A second biopsy again showed small round cells positive for CKAE1/AE3, CD56, and CD99; the main differential diagnoses included a tumor of the Ewing family or an Ewing-like sarcoma.  
On the basis of the tumor’s abdominal location, CD56 positivity, and MIBG uptake, a diagnosis of neuroblastoma was made, and the patient received four cycles of chemotherapy per the COG A3961 protocol (alternating carboplatin/etoposide with carboplatin/cyclophosphamide/doxorubicin). Post-treatment CT of the pelvis and abdomen revealed no change in the size of either the presacral mass or the hepatic lesion.

A 58-year-old man with well-managed glaucoma (on a topical agent twice daily) and psoriasis presented with mild left eye pain and conjunctival hyperemia but no change in vision or photophobia. Vital signs were normal. On examination, visual acuity was 20/40 OD and 20/25 OS. In the left eye, there was a salmon-colored lesion on the superior bulbar conjunctiva. Directly beneath this lesion, there was an area of peripheral corneal thinning with an epithelial thickness of 40 μm and a partial fluorescein staining defect consistent with a peripheral ulcerative keratitis lesion. There was mild conjunctival hyperemia without evidence of episcleritis, scleritis, corneal infiltrate, or anterior chamber inflammation. There were no findings of blepharitis, tear-film abnormalities, or dry eye. Fundus examination of the left eye revealed faint cream-colored lesions along the superior vascular arcade. The remainder of the ocular and systemic examination was unremarkable.

A 41-year-old woman with no prior medical or surgical history presented with 3 days of diffuse lower abdominal pain and severe watery diarrhea. She had no fever. On arrival, her blood pressure and heart rate were normal. Examination showed mild lower abdominal tenderness; the abdomen was soft, nondistended, and nontympanic. Laboratory studies were within normal limits except for a segmented neutrophil proportion of 89.4%. Abdominal CT performed at an outside hospital revealed a right‐sided colonic intussusception with a 6.2 cm septated cystic mass serving as the lead point. Based on these imaging findings, the radiologist’s differential diagnosis included duplication cyst, mucocele, endometriosis, lymphangioma, or myxoma.

A 64-year-old woman with a history of treated left breast carcinoma presented with a new palpable mass in the inferior-internal quadrant of her right breast. Mammography demonstrated a medium-density, oval, circumscribed mass with partially indistinct margins and no calcifications. Ultrasound revealed an 8 × 5 mm solid lesion with regular contours and heterogeneous echogenicity; there were no palpable axillary lymph nodes. Ultrasound-guided core biopsy showed a well-circumscribed tumor composed of glandular structures lined by two cell layers: inner epithelial cells with basally located nuclei without atypia, and outer myoepithelial cells with large nuclei, fine chromatin, and a low nucleocytoplasmic ratio, all embedded in a dense fibro-hyaline stroma.

A 35-year-old Bengali man presented with a two-year history of intermittent epigastric pain with occasional vomiting. Over the past year, he experienced repeated episodes of heartburn followed by vomiting lasting several days, recurring every two to three months. He denied weight loss, gastrointestinal bleeding, or other systemic symptoms. Previous courses of anti-ulcer medication provided only transient relief.

On physical examination, vital signs were normal and the abdominal examination was unremarkable, with no tenderness, masses, or organomegaly.

An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was performed and revealed duodenal ulcer disease in remission and a deformed first portion of the duodenum. Review of prior endoscopies showed, 14 months earlier, erosions and a submucosal swelling in the gastric antrum with a duodenal bulb ulcer; and, eight months earlier, a healed duodenal ulcer with partial narrowing of the duodenal channel.

Because of recurrent intermittent pain, a barium meal follow-through was obtained, demonstrating deformation of the duodenal bulb and a smooth filling defect with an eccentric linear passage of contrast, suggesting a mass lesion in the proximal duodenum. Abdominal ultrasonography identified a well-circumscribed complex mass with solid and cystic components in the epigastric region, superimposed on the first part of the duodenum. A contrast-enhanced CT scan confirmed a well-defined, oval, mixed-density, soft-tissue mass measuring 9.1 × 5.0 × 5.1 cm in the upper abdomen, compressing the duodenum but separate from the pancreas, right kidney, gallbladder, and liver.

Ultrasonography-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology of the mass revealed blood products and a small number of mononuclear cells without anaplastic cells.

A 1-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of an incidentally noted abdominal mass during assessment for distention and chronic diarrhea. On examination, he was asymptomatic with normal vital signs and a good appetite. There was a painless, mobile, nontender mass extending from the left upper quadrant to the umbilicus. There was no vomiting, constipation, or abdominal pain. Laboratory tests were normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed a hyperechoic soft-tissue lesion approximately 10 cm in diameter, displacing the intestine to the right without luminal obstruction. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a homogeneous, well-vascularized, encapsulated mass measuring 9.4 × 10.6 cm, with thin septation medially, fat density, and defined margins, filling the left abdomen and shifting the small bowel to the right.

A 9-year-old boy was evaluated for a slowly progressive, painless swelling of the left mandible over the past year. Extraoral examination revealed mild facial asymmetry with a well-defined 3–4 cm swelling of the left mandible; no cutaneous pigmentations, mouth-opening limitations, or submandibular lymphadenopathy were present. Intraorally, there was buccal cortical expansion from the left mandibular incisor to the first molar, with absence of the first deciduous molar; the lesion was hard, fixed, and noninflamed, without paresthesia. Panoramic radiography showed loss of trabecular structure and a radiopaque “ground-glass” appearance englobing the permanent second premolar germ. Cone-beam CT revealed a well-defined radiopaque lesion with buccal cortical thinning and expansion, displacement of the dental germ centrally within the lesion, and buccal and inferior displacement of the mandibular canal. Based on these findings, a provisional diagnosis of fibrous dysplasia was made, and McCune–Albright syndrome, Mazabraud’s syndrome, and hyperparathyroidism were considered.

A 50-year-old woman with no personal or family history of alopecia or autoimmune disease noted an asymptomatic, erythematous papule on the posterior mid-scalp. Five months later, she developed an area of alopecia surrounding this papule and was referred for excision.

Excisional pathology showed a circumscribed neoplasm with focal, irregular infiltration into deep adipose tissue. The tumor was contiguous with the epidermis and exhibited deep trichoblastic and superficial squamous components merging together within a distinct cellular fibrous stroma. Fibromyxoid stroma with separation artifact was absent. Both components demonstrated low-grade cytologic atypia with occasional mitotic figures and apoptotic bodies, and there was a patchy, mild inflammatory reaction. The deep margin was focally involved.

Adjacent nonneoplastic skin revealed prominent features of alopecia areata, including a brisk peribulbar lymphocytic infiltrate around the majority of follicles, follicular miniaturization, an increased proportion of catagen and telogen follicles, trichomalacia, abnormally thin hair shafts, lack of follicular scarring, and retained sebaceous glands.

A 17-year-old male presented with a gradually enlarging mass adjacent to his left posteromedial ankle. He first noticed the lesion three years earlier; it became symptomatic two months before presentation when he experienced discomfort from ski and inline-skating boots. He had no history of trauma and was otherwise healthy.

On examination, there was a firm, 4×4-cm mass at the posteromedial aspect of the ankle. Plantar flexion and dorsiflexion were both limited to 10°. The overlying skin showed only slight redness. Ligamentous stability was intact, and neurovascular status was normal.

Plain radiographs (anteroposterior and lateral views) revealed a polycyclic, slightly condensed bony structure dorsal to the tibiotalar joint. A CT scan of the ankle demonstrated a 4.0×3.0×2.8-cm mass posterior to the talus with slight sclerotic reactions. Discrete irregularities of the margins with focal osteolytic changes were noted at the posteromedial talar contour. A second, smaller soft-tissue–density structure measured 2.8×1.7×1.2 cm. Otherwise, the ankle joint appeared intact.

A 67-year-old man was found to have an esophageal tumor during routine follow-up after surgery for oral carcinoma. His medical history included hypertension, angina pectoris, diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia. On examination, enlarged lymph nodes were palpable in the right cervical region. Routine laboratory findings were unremarkable except for a slightly elevated serum squamous cell carcinoma–related antigen (2.4 ng/mL; normal range, 0–1.5 ng/mL). Esophagoscopy revealed a type 1 tumor in the cervical esophagus, and biopsy specimens confirmed squamous cell carcinoma. An upper gastrointestinal barium study showed a 15-mm filling defect at the cervical esophagus. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated weakly enhanced, swollen lymph nodes in the right cervical region without evidence of distant metastasis. On the basis of these findings, the patient was clinically staged as having esophageal carcinoma T2N2M0, Stage IIIA.

A 55-year-old Japanese woman with no personal history of malignancy or immunosuppression noted a right breast nodule one month ago. Family history was notable for an aunt with breast cancer and a father with colorectal cancer. On examination, a reddish, firm, >3-cm mass was palpable in the right upper medial breast. Laboratory studies, including blood counts, chemistries, and tumor markers, were within normal limits except for a slight elevation of CA 15-3 at 35.1 U/mL.  
Breast ultrasound revealed an intracystic lesion measuring approximately 3.5 cm comprising heterogeneous solid and cystic components. CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no evidence of lymph node or distant metastases. MRI demonstrated a heterogeneous hyperintense cystic mass on T2-weighted images with an irregularly enhancing wall.  
Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the lesion yielded predominantly individual mono- or multinucleated bizarre giant cells in a hemorrhagic and inflammatory background, along with small clusters of cohesive sheet-like malignant cells. The tumor cells were large (up to ~100 μm), with hyperchromatic pleomorphic nuclei, abundant cytoplasm, prominent nucleoli, and numerous mitotic figures, including atypical forms.

A 62-year-old woman presented with a 4-year history of progressive swelling at the left angle of her mouth, associated with pain on pressure and numbness of the left lower lip and chin. She had longstanding hypertension and diabetes. On examination, there was a hard, ill-defined, tender distension at the left mouth angle with overlying skin pigmentation; sensation in the left lower lip and chin was decreased. Intraorally, there was a poorly defined, firm, tender, sessile nodule measuring 1.5 cm in diameter on the buccal mucosa adjacent to the first and second left mandibular premolars; the teeth were intact and not mobile. No cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. Cone-beam CT imaging demonstrated an enlarged left mandibular canal and markedly distended mental foramen. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a localized widening of the left mandibular canal with a slightly enhancing soft-tissue density mass occupying the canal.

A 38-year-old North-Indian man, nonsmoker, presented with a 1-year history of exertional dyspnea (NYHA class I) and cough, initially dry but productive of mucoid sputum for 1 month. He reported 5–6 daily episodes of hemoptysis (5–10 mL/day), an 8-kg weight loss over 2 months, anorexia, and lower back pain for 2 months. He had no history of tuberculosis or tuberculous contact. Vital signs were normal; he appeared cachectic. Lung examination revealed decreased air entry on the left. Chest radiograph showed heterogeneous opacification of the left hemithorax, ipsilateral mediastinal shift, elevation of the left hemidiaphragm, rib crowding on the left, and right lung hyperinflation, consistent with left lung volume loss and a left bronchial cutoff sign. High-resolution CT of the chest demonstrated cutoff of the left main bronchus by a soft-tissue lesion in the left upper lobe. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 9×8×7 cm lobulated, heterogeneously enhancing mass centered on and occluding the left main bronchus, with complete collapse of the left upper lobe, mediastinal shift, compensatory hyperinflation of the right lung, minimal left pleural effusion, and no lymphadenopathy. The mass completely encased the aortic arch, involved >150° of the right pulmonary artery with narrowing, and encased >180° of the descending aorta. Abdominal CT revealed two hypoenhancing lesions in liver segments VI and VIII (largest 3.8×4 cm), and sagittal bone images showed a focal lytic lesion in the left pedicle of the L5 vertebra.

An 85-year-old man was referred for evaluation of an ulcerated lesion on his chest. He reported that a nodule had appeared in the midline of his previous sternotomy scar five years after an uncomplicated coronary artery bypass grafting and had enlarged rapidly over two months. He had no pain, bleeding, trauma, or signs of infection at the site, and his medical history was otherwise unremarkable. On examination, there was a 3-cm diameter ulcerated nodule situated at the midpoint of the healed sternotomy scar; the surrounding skin was indurated, and the center of the lesion contained a keratin-filled crater. No cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy was detected. A chest CT scan showed cardiomegaly and ground-glass opacities in the lower lungs suggestive of chronic heart failure. A skin biopsy of the lesion was performed.

A 78-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a one-year history of a painless, hard mass on the right labia majora and occasional burning micturition but no vaginal bleeding or discharge. She had a history of hypothyroidism. She denied weight loss and fever. On examination, the abdomen was normal. External inspection showed a 5 × 6 cm solid, ulcerative periurethral mass arising from the labia majora. Pelvic examination confirmed the mass originated from the periurethral area; the cervix appeared healthy with no discharge.

Transvaginal sonography revealed a well-defined, homogeneous 6.0 × 4.0 cm mass in the anterior vaginal wall filling the lumen with increased intrinsic vascularity. An initial biopsy was interpreted as chronic nonspecific inflammation. Pelvic MRI showed a well-defined, encapsulated 7.0 × 5.1 × 4.8 cm lesion inferior to the pubic symphysis, between the urethra and vagina, extending to the bladder neck superiorly, the introitus inferiorly, abutting the anal canal posteriorly, and displacing the vestibular structures. Cystoscopy confirmed external compression of the distal urethra. Laboratory tests revealed an elevated lactate dehydrogenase level of 219 U/L; the peripheral blood smear was unremarkable. CT of the neck and chest showed small cervical lymph nodes and prominent mediastinal lymph nodes (largest 1.6 × 1.7 cm). Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy revealed no atypical lymphoid cells. A punch biopsy of the vulvar mass was obtained for definitive diagnosis.

A 73-year-old man with a history of diabetes mellitus and atrial fibrillation on acenocoumarol presented with an 18-month history of mild inflammatory pain in the right knee. There was no history of trauma, weight loss, or fever. On examination, he was in good general condition. There was mild tenderness to fingertip palpation around the proximal tibia, but no swelling or erythema, and the range of motion of the right knee was normal. 

Plain radiographs of the right knee revealed a well-defined, round osteolytic lesion centered in the epiphysis and metaphysis of the proximal tibia, with surrounding osteocondensation, consistent with a Lodwick type IA lesion. A CT scan of the knee demonstrated a 50 mm × 30 mm intrabony lesion of soft-tissue attenuation confined to bone, without cortical breach or soft-tissue extension.

A 43-year-old woman presented after a routine examination revealed a hepatic lesion. She had a >20-year history of hepatitis B but no symptoms. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed: AFP 1.22 ng/mL (normal <7), positive HBsAg, HBeAb, and HBcAb; negative HBeAg; HBV DNA 5.29×10^4 IU/mL; normal liver-function tests.  
Abdominal ultrasound showed a 19.9×14.2 mm heterogeneous hypoechoic nodule with clear margins in the right hepatic lobe.  
Contrast-enhanced ultrasound demonstrated slight hyperenhancement of the lesion at 11 seconds, peak at 14 seconds with a wedge-shaped hyperenhanced rim, followed by rapid central washout at 22 seconds; the portal and delayed phases showed low enhancement.  
MRI revealed an 18×14 mm mass in segment 6 that was T2 hyperintense, T1 hypointense, and diffusion-weighted hyperintense. On Gd-BOPTA–enhanced sequences, there was heterogeneous arterial-phase enhancement with vague margins, rapid washout in portal and delayed phases, low signal in the hepatobiliary phase, and pseudocapsule enhancement.  
After multidisciplinary discussion, malignancy could not be excluded and surgical resection was planned.

A 62-year-old Asian man presented with asymptomatic gross hematuria.  
Enhanced CT, MRI, and bone scintigraphy demonstrated an advanced bladder tumor.  
A transurethral biopsy revealed invasive urothelial carcinoma, and he underwent radical cystectomy with ileal conduit.  
Pathological examination showed invasive urothelial carcinoma with glandular differentiation (periodic acid–Schiff positive), staged as pT2N0M0.  
He was monitored as an outpatient.  
Six years later, surveillance CT revealed a solitary, 2 cm nodule in segment 5 of the liver.  
Gd-EOB-DTPA–enhanced MRI showed a defect in the hepatobiliary phase, and diffusion-weighted images displayed mildly increased signal intensity.  
Ultrasound-guided fine-needle biopsy of the lesion revealed high-grade adenocarcinoma.  
Immunohistochemical staining showed positivity for cytokeratin 7 and negativity for cytokeratin 20 and uroplakin, matching the prior cystectomy specimen.

A 71-year-old man with a history of poorly differentiated gastroesophageal-junction carcinoma, initially thought to be small-cell carcinoma, was treated with carboplatin, etoposide, and radiotherapy, achieving mixed response. Eighteen months later, he developed an enlarging abdominal-wall mass, which was resected. Histopathology revealed a poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma. Immunohistochemical staining of the resected tumor showed:  
- CK7 negative  
- CK20 positive  
- CD56 negative  
- Chromogranin negative  
- Synaptophysin weakly positive  
- TTF-1 negative  

No cutaneous primary lesion was identified. A core needle biopsy of a residual pelvic mass demonstrated the same morphology and immunophenotype, with additional findings: CK99 positive, FLI-1 positive, and AE1/AE3 strongly positive.

A 42-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of painless bloody urethral discharge and lower back pain. Physical examination was unremarkable, and she reported no urinary dysfunction. Routine laboratory studies were within normal limits. Cytologic examination of urine sediment was highly suggestive of adenocarcinoma.

Contrast-enhanced CT and pelvic MRI revealed a 47-mm mass involving the region surrounding the urethra, with no abnormalities of the gynecologic organs and no intra-abdominal or intrapelvic lymphadenopathy. Cystourethroscopy demonstrated two urethral diverticula, each with a whitish papillary and villous lesion protruding into the urethral lumen.

Biopsy and transurethral resection (TUR) specimens showed papillo-tubular structures lined by a single layer of cuboidal epithelial cells, some exhibiting a hobnail configuration. A few cells contained clear cytoplasm. The epithelial cells displayed mild cytologic atypia, a mitotic rate of 10 per 10 high-power fields, and frequent intraluminal necrotic debris. No stromal invasion was identified.

Immunohistochemical studies on the TUR specimens revealed tumor-cell positivity for cytokeratin 7, epithelial membrane antigen, CA125, and focal CD15, and negativity for CK5/6, CK20, carcinoembryonic antigen, thrombomodulin, uroplakin III, prostate-specific antigen, calretinin, estrogen receptor, and progesterone receptor. The histologic features suggested clear cell adenocarcinoma, but the absence of stromal invasion precluded a definitive diagnosis of malignancy in these limited samples.

A 19-year-old man presented with a 5-year history of a slowly enlarging, painless mass in the right ischioanal fossa. He denied bleeding per rectum or changes in bowel habits. Prior perianal Doppler ultrasound identified a solid lesion with abundant blood flow, leading to a diagnosis of haemangioma. On examination, there was a 5 cm × 3 cm multilobulated, cystic-solid mass that was ductile, elastic, non-tender, movable, and smooth; no fistula, lymphadenopathy, or skin lesions were noted. Rectal examination was normal. Routine laboratory tests and CT scans of the chest and abdomen were unremarkable. Pelvic MRI revealed a well-circumscribed, lobulated subcutaneous mass surrounded by a thin complete capsule; the lesion was isointense on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and demonstrated homogeneous intense enhancement of multiple nodules separated by intratumoral nonenhancing fibrous capsules. A neurogenic tumor was suggested by the radiologist.

A 35-year-old woman with no systemic illness presented with pain in her left eye. Her ocular history included retinal surgery and secondary intraocular-lens implantation after blunt trauma at age 5, followed by trabeculectomy at age 20 for glaucoma. She was on brimonidine 0.15%, dorzolamide 2%, and timolol 0.5% twice daily. On presentation, visual acuity in the left eye was hand motion, and intraocular pressure was 38 mmHg, which fell to 10 mmHg after stat topical therapy. Slit-lamp examination showed a flat bleb, decompensated cornea with edema, a mid-dilated pupil, a mildly dislocated IOL, and advanced optic-nerve cupping. Two weeks later, with intraocular pressure of 40 mmHg despite maximal medical therapy, she underwent micro-pulse cyclophotocoagulation under local anesthesia. The postoperative course was unremarkable, and intraocular pressure remained controlled. One year after the procedure, she reported pain and could not fully close her left eyelids because of a protruding white mass on the cornea that had been enlarging. Visual acuity was light perception only; intraocular pressure was estimated at 30–40 mmHg. Examination revealed a large, pedunculated, whitish corneal mass. Ultrasound biomicroscopy showed a cystic mass overlying the cornea, localized to the anterior space without invasion. Anterior-segment OCT revealed a hyperreflective lesion within the subepithelial space with cystic components.

A 30-year-old woman presented with epigastric pain. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a 15-mm submucosal tumor in the greater curvature of the gastric body. Endoscopic ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic lesion with an acoustic shadow, consistent with calcification. Laboratory values were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a calcified submucosal gastric mass without mucosal ulceration or irregularity. The lesion was observed with periodic endoscopy; one year later, the tumor had enlarged. A gastrointestinal stromal tumor was suspected, and, based on clinical guidelines, gastric wedge resection via laparoscopy and endoscopy cooperative surgery was planned.

A previously healthy 3-year-old girl was referred for serosanguineous, purulent discharge from her right ear of 3 weeks’ duration, partially responsive to antibiotics. On examination, a polypoid, reddish, fragile mass filled the right external auditory canal; the facial nerve function was intact, and fetid discharge was present. Routine biochemistry tests were normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the temporal bone showed soft-tissue density in the mastoid and middle ear extending into the external auditory canal, with ragged erosion of the mastoid air cells and the external surface of the mastoid bone. Neoplastic change was suspected, and rhabdomyosarcoma was considered most likely because of the patient’s age; metastatic neuroblastoma, lymphoma, and leukemia were also in the differential diagnosis. An incisional biopsy of the mass was performed, and the pathologist reported keratinizing squamous epithelium, granulation tissue, and abscess formation.

A 46-year-old Hispanic woman was admitted with a 3-day history of bluish-black discoloration and pain of the left second toe. She reported 2 months of intermittent claudication in the same limb, arthralgias involving proximal interphalangeal joints, shoulders, elbows, and knees with morning stiffness, and foamy urine. She denied trauma.  
Her medical history included hypertension, hypertriglyceridemia, and aortoiliac atherosclerosis; she took amlodipine, captopril, hydrochlorothiazide, and gemfibrozil.  
On examination, the left second toe was necrotic, tender, and had delayed capillary refill, but pedal pulses were palpable bilaterally. Skin examination revealed livedo reticularis and scattered brown macules on the thighs; no ulcers were seen.  
Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12 g/dL, hematocrit 37%, leukocytes 10 200/mm³ (76% neutrophils), platelets 564 000/mm³, creatinine 1.64 mg/dL, BUN 25 mg/dL, glucose 121 mg/dL, PT 14.7 s (INR 1.03), PTT 29/28.5 s, ESR 2 mm/h, and CRP 1.2 mg/dL. Urinalysis revealed 300 mg/dL proteinuria, 6 RBCs/hpf, 4 WBCs/hpf, and RBC casts.  
Arterial and venous Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated patent vessels. Given the digital ischemia with renal findings, small-vessel vasculitis was suspected, and methylprednisolone pulses were initiated. Renal and skin biopsies were ordered, and serum protein electrophoresis was obtained.  
Serum protein electrophoresis did not show monoclonal spikes or any other abnormality, and despite immunosuppressive therapy, her condition worsened with progressive kidney injury requiring hemodialysis.

A 32-year-old man was found on a routine examination to have a neck mass. He had no symptoms, a normal medical history, and no neurologic deficits. On ultrasound, there was an 18×21×31 mm oval, heterogeneous, hypoechoic lesion with well-defined borders and internal vascularity along the posterior surface of the left thyroid lobe. MRI of the neck demonstrated a 33×24×25 mm volumetric lesion on the lateral posterior surface of the left thyroid lobe that was heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images with well-defined margins and no diffusion restriction. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 21×24×25 mm mass of 18 HU that enhanced with contrast and lay between the thyroid gland and the vertebral column. Laboratory studies revealed a parathyroid hormone level of 4.06 pmol/L, ionized calcium of 1.22 mmol/L, TSH 2.7 mIU/L, T3 1.7 nmol/L, and T4 89 nmol/L; all were within normal limits. Fine‐needle aspiration of the lesion was performed twice and each time was non-diagnostic (Bethesda category I). To plan definitive management, he was referred for surgical evaluation.

A 78-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of constipation and thinning of stool caliber. His medical history included benign prostatic hyperplasia and hypertension. Laboratory studies were notable for an elevated prostate-specific antigen level of 409 ng/mL; other results were unremarkable. On digital rectal examination, the rectal lumen was narrowed and rigid. Sigmoidoscopy revealed luminal narrowing of the mid to lower rectum with grossly indurated, non-ulcerated mucosa. Contrast-enhanced CT showed circumferential rectal wall thickening (mean thickness, 1.3 cm) with marked homogeneous enhancement and mild perirectal fat stranding. Pelvic MRI demonstrated concentric thickening of the mid to lower rectum (length, 6–7 cm) with stratification on coronal and sagittal T2-weighted images. On axial T2-weighted images, the rectal wall showed three layers: an isointense middle layer and hypointense inner and outer layers. Diffusion-weighted imaging revealed a corresponding concentric ring pattern with restricted diffusion in the middle layer. The prostate gland was enlarged, showing a diffuse infiltrative lesion with low signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images and a low apparent diffusion coefficient value. The left seminal vesicle also had low signal intensity, and bilateral external iliac lymph nodes were enlarged. PET/CT demonstrated diffuse mid to lower rectal wall thickening without significant FDG uptake and no abnormal FDG uptake elsewhere.

A 4-month-old boy was referred for right leukocoria noted by his parents for 1 week. Examination under anesthesia showed intraocular pressures of 13 mm Hg in the right eye and 16 mm Hg in the left eye, with normal anterior segments bilaterally. Fundus examination of the right eye revealed a white vascularized retinal tumor in the temporal macula measuring 10 × 9 × 3.6 mm. Germline testing for RB1 was negative, and a baseline MRI of the brain and orbits was normal. The patient was diagnosed with unilateral Group B retinoblastoma of the right eye. He was treated with one session of intra-arterial chemotherapy (melphalan 4.8 mg), followed by three sessions of diode laser transpupillary thermotherapy at four- to six-week intervals, after which complete clinical regression of the primary tumor was achieved.

At 45 weeks after initial treatment, a new cyst-like retinal lesion was identified at the superior margin of the regressed tumor scar. Fundus photography showed a dome-shaped, translucent lesion at the edge of the scar. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated abnormal vascularity and leakage within the lesion. Optical coherence tomography revealed an irregularly thickened floor and dome-shaped roof with effacement of the normal retinal layers. Optical coherence tomography angiography showed abnormal blood vessels located primarily within the roof of the lesion in the superficial vascular complex.

A 29-year-old woman presented with a two-year history of a nontender, slowly growing itchy skin lesion overlying the right breast, associated with an underlying lump. A prior ultrasound at another institution had been interpreted as benign, so she had not sought care until she noted recent enlargement. On examination, there was a nodular pigmented lesion with irregular margins at the 12 o’clock position of the right breast, measuring approximately 4 × 4 cm, overlying a firm, non-tender subcutaneous mass. 

Breast ultrasound demonstrated a large cutaneous and subcutaneous soft-tissue lesion in the upper inner quadrant, para-areolar region, with heterogeneous echogenicity, central necrosis, a surrounding echogenic halo, posterior acoustic enhancement, and increased internal vascularity. The largest component measured 5.0 × 2.0 × 4.7 cm and appeared well-defined from the underlying breast parenchyma.

Breast MRI showed that the solid portion of the lesion was hyperintense relative to breast tissue on both T1- and T2-weighted images, with high signal on STIR sequences and diffusion restriction. After contrast administration, the lesion exhibited avid enhancement with an early washout kinetic pattern.

A 60-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a painful swelling in the left upper posterior gingiva that bled during tooth brushing. His medical history was notable for hypertension, managed with medication, and a history of smoking. Extraoral examination was unremarkable. Intraoral examination revealed a solitary, sessile, tender, purplish overgrowth measuring approximately 3 cm × 5 cm in the left maxillary buccal vestibule, with an irregular periphery extending to the marginal gingiva adjacent to tooth 26. Deep proximal caries was noted in tooth 26, and multiple pigmented macules were observed on the hard palate. A complete blood count and biochemical tests were within normal limits. Panoramic radiography showed a radiolucent area at the root apices of teeth 26, 27, and 28. An incisional biopsy yielded only a small fragment insufficient for diagnosis. An excisional specimen, brownish-black and firm, measured 3 cm × 3 cm × 1.5 cm. Histologic sections showed spindle and plump cells arranged in intersecting fascicles, bundles, clusters, and chains; the cells had round, ovoid, or elongated nuclei with moderate atypia, increased mitotic activity, and only a few cells containing intracytoplasmic melanin pigment.

A 29-year-old African American man presented with right upper quadrant abdominal pain and early satiety. He reported five years of daily alcohol consumption and occasional marijuana use. On examination, he had tenderness in the right upper quadrant without stigmata of chronic liver disease. 

Initial laboratory tests showed mild transaminase elevations (AST 74 U/L, ALT 51 U/L) and alkaline phosphatase 93 U/L. A contrast-enhanced CT scan revealed hepatomegaly with a 14 cm mass in the left hepatic lobe. He was discharged for outpatient follow-up.

One month later, he returned with similar symptoms. MRI demonstrated a 19 cm enhancing left hepatic lobe mass.
