Laboratory tests again showed mild transaminase elevations, a negative hepatitis viral panel, and normal tumor markers, including AFP, CEA, and CA 19-9. He was discharged with plans for biopsy.

Two months after the initial visit, he presented to a different emergency department with worsening abdominal pain, vomiting, early satiety, and 10 lb weight loss. CT angiography showed a 21 cm hepatic mass centered in the left lobe. Laboratory results were AST 93 U/L, ALT 45 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 451 U/L; tumor markers remained within normal limits (AFP 1.97 ng/mL; CEA 5.28 ng/mL; CA 19-9 <14 U/mL). Chest CT revealed innumerable bilateral pulmonary nodules up to 8 mm in diameter, suggestive of metastases. The patient was admitted for biopsy and staging imaging.

A one-day-old female newborn was referred for evaluation of a mass in her right axilla. She was delivered at term by spontaneous vaginal delivery, with Apgar scores of 9 and 10 at one and five minutes and a birth weight of 3 kg. The pregnancy was uncomplicated, with normal obstetric ultrasound findings. 

On examination, the infant was active, afebrile, and feeding well. In the right axilla, there was a 12 cm diameter swelling with hyperpigmented overlying skin and visible superficial veins. The mass was soft, cystic, nontender, not warm, nonpulsatile, and without audible bruits. 

A chest radiograph showed a normal thoracic cage and cardiac silhouette, with a homogeneous dense region in the right axilla and no bony abnormalities. 

Ultrasonography of the lesion revealed both cystic and solid components, internal vascularity, and no clear tissue of origin. The mass was adjacent to the parietal pleura without pleural effusion, and the axillary vessels appeared normal. 

Preoperative laboratory studies and vital signs were within normal limits.

A 55-year-old woman presented with respiratory symptoms. Her history was notable for an endometrial cyst in the left ovary 24 years earlier. PET/CT imaging revealed an FDG-avid mass in the right lung and uptake in a cystic lesion in the liver; no abdominal or pelvic lesions were detected. Laboratory studies showed elevated cancer antigen 15-3 at 131.9 U/mL and cytokeratin fragment at 3.1 ng/mL; neuron-specific enolase, carcinoembryonic antigen, protein induced by vitamin K absence-II, and α-fetoprotein were within normal limits. A transbronchial lung biopsy demonstrated atypical cells with large nuclei and amphophilic cytoplasm proliferating in a hobnail pattern. Immunohistochemical staining showed cytoplasmic positivity for CK7 and napsin A and negativity for CK20 and thyroid transcription factor 1. On the basis of these findings, the tumor was diagnosed as primary adenocarcinoma of the lung. The patient received three courses of carboplatin plus pemetrexed and had a partial response; she declined further chemotherapy. Two months after her last treatment, she was admitted with abdominal fullness due to ascites; her condition deteriorated over the following month, and she died.

A 72-year-old Caucasian woman presented with two days of diffuse abdominal pain and discomfort, nausea, and vomiting. Her medical history was notable for diabetes mellitus and hypertension, managed with medication. She had no relevant family history and denied tobacco or alcohol use.

On examination, she appeared tachycardic and demonstrated signs of an acute abdomen, with a palpable, tender mass in the left abdomen. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 13,000 cells/mm3. Chest and abdominal radiographs were unremarkable.

Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a complex cystic mass with internal septa and no increased vascularity; the organ of origin could not be identified. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed an 18.7 × 13.2 × 22 cm, well-defined, hypodense intra-peritoneal mass in the upper left abdomen—between the greater curvature of the stomach, spleen, and tail of the pancreas—and extending to the upper pelvis, compressing adjacent organs. The lesion had no internal septa on CT, no enhancement after intravenous contrast, and there was no abnormal lymphadenopathy.

A 21-year-old right-handed woman presented with a 7-month history of painful swelling over the dorsal mid–right wrist. The pain did not respond to aspirin or nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs. She denied any trauma, and there was no decrease in wrist range of motion. On examination, a firm, immobile, tender swelling was noted over the dorsal aspect of the wrist. Routine laboratory tests were normal. Anteroposterior radiographs of the right wrist showed no obvious abnormality. Computed tomography of the wrist revealed a well-defined lesion located in the dorsal portion of the capitate bone. Differential diagnoses included osteoblastoma, giant cell tumor, osteoid osteoma, chondrosarcoma, aneurysmal bone cyst, and osteosarcoma.

A 50-year-old perimenopausal woman with a history of cervical cancer treated by radical hysterectomy 10 years ago and no family history of breast or ovarian cancer presented with pain and a long-standing enlarged lump in her right axilla. Her vital signs were normal. Examination of both breasts was unremarkable; in the right axilla there was a hard, fixed, irregular 3-cm mass attached to the skin, with a palpable 1-cm lymph node. A routine bilateral breast and axillary ultrasound showed a 2.3 × 1.3 cm right axillary mass infiltrating surrounding subcutaneous tissues, surrounded by fatty lobules, and containing micro-calcifications. Fine-needle aspiration of the mass and enlarged lymph node revealed breast carcinoma and atypical lymph node hyperplasia. An ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the mass demonstrated invasive ductal carcinoma, grade II; immunohistochemical studies showed ER +++, PR –, HER2/Neu 1+, and a Ki-67 index of 10%.

A 27-year-old woman, G3P2, with no prior pregnancy surveillance presented at 26 weeks’ gestation for an obstetric ultrasound that revealed a complex, predominantly solid 3 cm hepatic lesion in the fetus without other anatomic abnormalities.  
At 30 weeks, ultrasound showed a heterogeneous, predominantly hypoechoic 3 cm hepatic lesion with marked peripheral Doppler flow. Fetal echocardiography demonstrated normal cardiac anatomy with vena cava displacement by the mass. Serial ultrasounds at 33 and 35 weeks showed stable lesion size and features; umbilical artery Doppler was normal.  
At 36 weeks, a 3300 g boy was delivered (Apgar 9/10). On examination, there was visible thoracoabdominal circulation, abdominal distension, and a palpable liver; no cutaneous hemangiomas or petechiae were present. Laboratory studies on day 5 demonstrated an elevated γ-glutamyltransferase; other values were unremarkable. Chest and abdominal radiographs were normal.  
Postnatal abdominal ultrasound revealed a 5 cm heterogeneous mass in the caudate lobe with marked hepatopetal flow. Unenhanced MRI showed a 7.3×5.1 cm nodular mass involving both lobes, low signal on T1-weighted images, high signal on T2-weighted images, and, after contrast, peripheral enhancement with centripetal filling and slow wash-out. The lesion’s vascularity caused a distal aortic caliber decrease, and follow-up labs showed worsening cholestatic and hepatic enzyme elevations.

A 40-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of intermittent pain in his left hand, worst at night, without preceding injury. On examination, there was stiffness and tenderness over the dorsum of the second metacarpal bone. Routine blood and urine tests, as well as blood biochemistry, were all within normal limits. Plain radiographs of the left hand revealed cortical expansion and a well-demarcated lucency in the shaft of the second metacarpal bone. CT imaging demonstrated a 4 mm intracortical lucent lesion with surrounding sclerosis and a central punctate calcification on the ulnar side of the second metacarpal shaft; no fracture was seen. MRI showed a well-defined lesion with low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, high signal intensity on T2-weighted and STIR images, and on contrast-enhanced axial images only the lesion’s periphery enhanced. There was no abnormal signal in the adjacent bone marrow or soft tissues.

A 73-year-old woman with a history of Helicobacter pylori gastritis (eradicated), coronary artery disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and tobacco use presented with several months of postprandial epigastric pain. The abdomen was soft and nontender on examination without palpable masses. Laboratory studies, including liver function tests, serum lipase, and the tumor marker carbohydrate antigen 19-9, were within normal limits (CA 19-9 <3 U/mL; normal range, 0–37 U/mL). An abdominal CT scan with intravenous and oral contrast showed an ill-defined, 3.5 × 3.4 × 3.0 cm hypodense lesion in the head of the pancreas without dilation of the pancreatic duct or evidence of pancreatic atrophy. Endoscopic ultrasound identified a 40 × 46 mm lesion in the pancreatic head and neck.

A 60-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a hepatic mass that was incidentally found on a CT scan performed for right lower quadrant abdominal pain. She had no history of liver disease or other malignancies. Laboratory studies showed normal levels of α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and carbohydrate antigens 19-9 and 15-3. 

Precontrast CT demonstrated a 35 mm irregular, low-attenuation mass in segment 8 with internal spotty calcifications. On contrast-enhanced dynamic CT, the lesion showed a small nodular peripheral enhancement in the arterial phase that extended centripetally during the portal phase and persisted into the delayed phase, with extensive internal nonenhancing areas. Hepatic capsular retraction was noted adjacent to the lesion. 

Given these findings, hepatic sclerosing haemangioma and cholangiocellular carcinoma were included in the differential diagnosis, and MRI was performed. On MRI, the mass was homogeneously hypointense on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images. In the equilibrium phase of contrast-enhanced fat-suppressed T1-weighted imaging, there was a small area of enhancement at the ventral margin. Diffusion-weighted imaging (b value 800) showed hyperintensity of the lesion, and the ADC map showed corresponding hypointensity, suggesting diffusion restriction. The mean ADC of the lesion was 1.51 × 10⁻³ mm²/s (background liver 1.76 × 10⁻³ mm²/s). 

Cholangiocellular carcinoma was suspected based on the restricted diffusion, and partial hepatectomy was performed.

A 65-year-old man underwent laparoscopic abdominoperineal resection for stage T3N1M0 rectal adenocarcinoma in October 2013, followed by adjuvant FOLFOX chemotherapy. He had annual abdominal CT scans, colonoscopies, and serum CEA measurements without evidence of recurrence or metastasis for six years.

In October 2019, he developed right-sided back pain. Chest CT showed osteolytic destruction of the right seventh posterior rib. A technetium bone scan demonstrated increased uptake in the same rib. Abdominal CT and colonoscopy showed no local recurrence or peritoneal disease, and CEA was within normal limits. He was presumed to have bone metastasis from rectal cancer.

Spinal MRI revealed multiple lesions in the thoracic, lumbar, and sacral vertebrae, as well as involvement of appendages and bilateral iliac bones. PET/CT demonstrated osteolytic lesions with mildly increased FDG uptake in the sternum, multiple vertebrae, and right sixth and seventh ribs; no visceral metastases were identified. He received six additional cycles of FOLFOX and was treated sequentially with zoledronic acid and denosumab, but his bone pain persisted, and follow-up bone scans showed new lesions in the left tenth rib, upper sternum, and first lumbar vertebra.

In November 2020, he noted a 10×10-cm lump around his colostomy stoma and intermittent abdominal discomfort. Abdominal CT confirmed a parastomal hernia. Preoperative blood counts, coagulation studies, and liver and kidney function tests were normal. He underwent parastomal hernia repair with subcutaneous drainage placement and was discharged on postoperative day 3 with the drain in situ.

Five days later, he returned with swelling, pain, and bleeding at the surgical site. Abdominal CT showed a new hematoma. Despite hemostatic drugs and compression, fresh blood continued to drain. Coagulation studies revealed a progressive prolongation of aPTT to 60 seconds. He remained anemic (hemoglobin 45–68 g/L) despite multiple transfusions. A bone marrow biopsy was performed to investigate the persistent bleeding.

A 15-year-old girl presented with a two-week history of intermittent fever, cough, dyspnea, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Her medical history was notable for bronchiolitis in infancy and four episodes of pneumonia since age 13, all requiring hospitalization. She lived near a stone-crushing plant and reported chronic exposure to stone dust. 

On examination, she appeared pale with facial fullness, tachycardia, and tachypnea. Pulmonary auscultation revealed decreased tactile fremitus and dullness at the right lung base. The abdomen was tense and tender with a questionable fluid wave; the remaining examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed hypochromic microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 8.0 g/dL). 

Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated bilateral pleural effusions (the right loculated), pleural thickening, basal segmental atelectasis, and an abrupt cutoff of the intermediate bronchus suggestive of extrinsic compression versus an endobronchial lesion. 

Bronchoscopy revealed a lobulated, pearly lesion completely obstructing the bronchus intermedius; it bled easily on contact and discharged a small amount of purulent material. Biopsy specimens showed compact round and polygonal cells with uniform nuclei, no pleomorphism or mitoses, delicate fibrovascular septa, and dilated vascular spaces without necrosis. Immunohistochemical staining was strongly positive for smooth muscle actin and negative for cytokeratin (AE1/AE3), chromogranin, synaptophysin, TTF-1, and CD34. The Ki-67 proliferation index was 2%.

A 66-year-old woman presented with a slowly enlarging left neck mass noted for approximately one year. She had previously undergone a facelift and initially presumed the bulge to represent postoperative changes. On examination, there was a nontender, soft mass palpable along the left floor of the mouth and submandibular region. The remainder of the neck examination was unremarkable, and flexible laryngoscopy showed no abnormalities. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a well-circumscribed, homogeneously enhancing mass involving the left sublingual gland, conforming to glandular morphology, and extending across the posterior mylohyoid sling into the submandibular space. Similar density lesions were identified in the right thyroid bed with infrasternal extension along the median raphe of the tongue and in the left parapharyngeal fat space; the thyroid region mass extended into the superior mediastinum. All lesions demonstrated identical morphology and enhancement patterns. 

Given the multifocality and homogeneous enhancement, the primary imaging differential diagnoses were lymphoproliferative conditions and inflammatory conditions such as IgG4-related disease.

A 24-year-old Caucasian woman was admitted with pharmacoresistant epilepsy. Her seizures began at age 11 as complex partial atonic events; within months she developed cognitive and behavioral decline. Multiple antiepileptic drugs failed to control her seizures, which occurred daily.

Initial CT of the head showed a left temporoparietal diffuse hypodense area that was inhomogeneous and lacked mass effect. Four years later MRI demonstrated a 32.3 × 43.1 × 28.3 mm multicystic cortico–subcortical parietal lesion divided by septations, with no edema, no mass effect, and no contrast enhancement. On admission 13 years after seizure onset, neurologic examination was normal except for neuropsychological deficits; laboratory tests, chest radiograph, and cardiac evaluation were unremarkable. Tc99m-MIBI single-photon emission CT of the brain showed no tumor metabolic activity. Electroencephalography revealed interictal spikes and polyspikes, and one minute of hyperventilation provoked a generalized tonic–clonic seizure recorded on EEG.

A 30-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy presented in April 2014 with a  gradual-onset, moderate, continuous pain on the right side of the maxilla and preauricular region that radiated to the ipsilateral temporal and auricular areas. Her pain intensity was 8 on a visual analogue scale. Examination revealed tenderness of the right temporomandibular joint and muscles of mastication, and bilateral attrition of the maxillary and mandibular first molars. A diagnosis of temporomandibular joint disorder secondary to bruxism was made, and she was instructed on night-guard use, restricted mouth opening, a soft diet, and physiotherapy. After 20 days of treatment, her pain decreased to a visual analogue scale score of 4.

In December 2015, she returned with aggravated, shock-like facial pain that worsened with brushing and washing her face, accompanied by tinnitus, hearing impairment in the right ear, and intermittent loss of balance. Radiographic examination showed no abnormalities of the temporomandibular joint or surrounding structures. She was referred to an otolaryngologist; audiometry revealed a 48 dB hearing loss in the right ear. Because her pain had a neuropathic quality and presentation, carbamazepine was prescribed, resulting in decreased pain intensity. Further evaluation with advanced imaging was then requested.

A 12-year-old boy presented with a 4-month history of progressive spinal deformity without pain or neurological symptoms. Two years earlier, he underwent resection of an aneurysmal bone cyst at the T11 vertebra with bone-graft augmentation and posterior instrumentation from T10 to T12; histopathology at that time confirmed an aneurysmal bone cyst. He had no family history of scoliosis or malignancy.

On examination, he had a mild left thoracic scoliosis by Adam’s forward bend test, full spinal range of motion, and no neurological deficits. Hips and feet were normal. Standing full-spine radiographs demonstrated a left thoracic curve with a Cobb angle of 24° and intact posterior spinal instrumentation from T10 to T12. 

A full-spine MRI revealed an expansile bone lesion at T11 with fluid–fluid levels, a moderate compression fracture, extension into the posterior elements, severe right foraminal stenosis, and mild cord compression.

A 52-year-old man with end-stage renal disease due to autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease underwent a living-donor renal transplant and received induction alemtuzumab followed by maintenance tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisolone. Three years after transplantation, he developed chronic antibody-mediated rejection and his tacrolimus and mycophenolate doses were increased, with prednisolone resumed. One month later, he reported a one-week history of abdominal pain, faecal urgency, and passage of frank blood. Mycophenolate was switched to mycophenolic acid, but diarrhoea persisted, and he experienced a 14-kg weight loss over the next year despite normal stool cultures, CMV and EBV PCR, faecal elastase, and negative gastric parietal-cell and enterocyte antibodies. Colonoscopy and flexisigmoidoscopy were normal, as were bile acid studies and cross-sectional imaging (CT enterography, MRI small bowel) and PET. EBV DNA in serum fluctuated intermittently. Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy with duodenal biopsies showed subtotal villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, and he was started on a gluten-free diet.

A 61-year-old white man presented with rapidly enlarging, tender, dome-shaped nodules with central ulceration and necrosis measuring 7 to 8 cm on the left posterior calf and the left forearm. He also reported fatigue and night sweats for the prior week. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable, with no other skin findings or palpable lymphadenopathy.

Initial skin biopsy of the left forearm revealed a diffuse and nodular lymphohistiocytic and granulomatous infiltrate in the superficial and reticular dermis, centered around skin appendages and blood vessels (angiocentric), extending into subcutaneous adipose tissue. One month later, repeat biopsy demonstrated a thinned epidermis with impending ulceration, extensive necrosis, lymphocyte exocytosis, basal vacuolization, and Civatte bodies. The dermis now showed diffuse sheets of monotonous medium-sized cells with hyperchromatic nuclei infiltrating the epidermis, including approximately 25% large atypical lymphocytes.

Immunophenotypic studies showed a predominantly T-cell infiltrate with scattered CD20+ B cells. Epstein–Barr virus–encoded small RNAs (EBER) were positive in about 75% of infiltrating cells. Atypical lymphocytes stained positively for CD2 and CD3 with loss of CD7 expression; approximately 75% of cells were CD4+, 25% were CD8+. BF-1 was positive in about 75% of cells; LCA, TIA-1, and granzyme B stained 50% of cells; CD30 stained 30%; FOXP3 and CD123 stained 10%; CD56 and CD34 were negative; CD57 stained rare cells. Ki-67 labeled about 50% of the infiltrate. Southern blot showed no T-cell receptor (TCR)-β chain rearrangement; TCR-γ chain rearrangement was indeterminate due to an inhibitor preventing amplification.

An man in his 80s presented with a 2-month history of right-sided sciatica, gross hematuria, and progressive edema of the right lower extremity. Two months earlier he had been treated for sciatica, but his pain and leg swelling worsened. On emergency CT, there was a 28-mm right internal iliac artery aneurysm (IIAA) with surrounding fluid and right hydronephrosis. His medical history included a pacemaker for sick sinus syndrome, percutaneous coronary intervention for angina, and aortic arch replacement.

On transfer, his temperature was 35.4 °C, blood pressure 86/58 mmHg, and heart rate 61 beats/min. Examination confirmed gross hematuria and marked right leg edema. Laboratory tests showed WBC count 12,340/µL, C-reactive protein 21.0 mg/dL, hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, albumin 1.8 g/dL, blood urea nitrogen 41.8 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.97 mg/dL. Urinalysis revealed turbidity, occult blood, and pyuria. Blood cultures grew Staphylococcus hominis in one of four sets; urine cultures yielded methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and Enterococcus faecalis. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a 15-mm mobile mass on the pacemaker lead in the right atrium.

A diagnosis of suspected secondary infected right IIAA was made, attributed to either urinary tract infection or pacemaker lead infection. Intravenous meropenem and vancomycin were started, and the pacemaker was removed on hospital day 2. By day 3, his WBC count had fallen to 7030/µL and CRP to 9.97 mg/dL. Antibiotic therapy was planned for approximately 3 weeks before aneurysm management.

On day 18, hypotension recurred and CT showed increased retroperitoneal fluid around the right IIAA; anemia worsened and hematuria intensified. Emergency coil embolization of the right IIA and endovascular aneurysm repair from the right common to external iliac artery were performed to control bleeding. On day 21, FDG PET–CT demonstrated uptake corresponding to the perianeurysmal fluid.

A two-staged surgical plan was made: EVAR followed by abscess drainage and aneurysmectomy. At the first laparotomy, no perianeurysmal abscess was seen, but a mass in the iliopsoas muscle was incised, yielding a cottage cheese-like white discharge. Cultures of the material were negative, and only irrigation drainage was performed. Postoperatively, a strong inflammatory response persisted and his overall condition remained poor.

A 65-year-old overweight man with a 20–year history of heavy smoking and known right pulmonary tumor with adrenal metastases presented in December 2019 with dyspnea (SpO2 77%), fatigue, and productive cough. Chest CT showed minimal right pleural effusion, a right pulmonary mass, mediastinal and retrocrural lymphadenopathy, and bilateral adrenal masses. Laboratory studies revealed neutrophilic leukocytosis, an inflammatory syndrome, severe azotic retention, low creatinine clearance, and an eGFR consistent with chronic renal failure. He was treated with antibiotics, diuretics, systemic corticosteroids, and expectorants, with transient improvement, but then rapidly deteriorated and died. 

At autopsy, there was a 4 × 3 cm poorly defined lesion in the middle lobe of the right lung and multiple bilateral necrotic pulmonary nodules (0.5–1.5 cm). The stomach harbored a 1 cm ulcerative-infiltrative lesion. Both kidneys and adrenal glands had multiple poorly defined lesions. 

Histopathology (H&E) showed:
• Lung lesions: malignant polygonal epithelial proliferation with pleomorphic nuclei, frequent atypical mitoses, clear nucleoli, moderately eosinophilic cytoplasm, solid growth pattern with focal papillary features, lymphovascular invasion, and necrosis.
• Renal and adrenal lesions: malignant epithelial proliferation with cytological and architectural features identical to the lung (alveolar growth, necrosis, lymphovascular tumor emboli).
• Gastric lesion: malignant epithelial proliferation of the mucosa with glandular differentiation extending into the muscular layer, with lymphovascular invasion, consistent with moderately differentiated gastric adenocarcinoma.

What is the most likely explanation for the multiple tumors in this patient?

A 50-year-old woman underwent routine gastroscopy during a health checkup, which revealed a 3.0 cm mass on the greater curvature of the stomach. She denied abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, hematemesis, melena, weight loss, or systemic symptoms. Physical examination was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed a lobulated mass measuring 2.5 × 2.0 cm protruding from the greater curvature, with clear borders, suggestive of a gastric stromal tumor. 

Without preoperative biopsy, a laparoscopic partial gastrectomy was performed; intraoperatively, the lesion was excised without invasion of surrounding organs and no lymphadenopathy. Fifteen days later, based on an initial pathologic interpretation of well-differentiated adenocarcinoma, a radical gastrectomy with removal of a 2 cm margin and dissection of 26 regional lymph nodes was performed; all nodes were negative.

Gross examination of the partial gastrectomy specimen revealed a submucosal mass measuring 4.1 × 2.5 × 2.0 cm; cut surfaces were yellow-gray to pink-tan. Histologically, the tumor was well circumscribed, centered in the muscularis propria, extending from the mucosa to the serosa, and demonstrated a biphasic architecture. The epithelial component formed glands and luminal structures containing inspissated eosinophilic material, with occasional necrosis. The mesenchymal component comprised spindle cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and ovoid nuclei surrounding the glands. There was no vascular or perineural invasion; mitotic figures were rare. Ki-67 proliferation indices were approximately 40% in epithelial cells and 3% in mesenchymal cells.

Immunohistochemical studies showed that the epithelial cells were positive for pancytokeratin (AE1/AE3), CEA, MUC5ac, and synaptophysin. The spindle cells were positive for TLE1 and focally positive for desmin, synaptophysin, CD10, CD68, and CD163. Both components were negative for S100, DOG-1, HER-2, PDGFRA, and SMA. DNA- and RNA-based next-generation sequencing revealed low tumor mutation burden, microsatellite stability, and no KIT mutations or fusion genes. Fluorescence in situ hybridization with an SS18 break-apart probe showed no gene rearrangement.

A man in his late 30s with a 5-year history of well-controlled HIV (on dolutegravir–lamivudine, undetectable viral load, CD4 >500) presented with a 1-year history of pink plaques on the left side of the scrotum and at the left base of the penis, associated with mild pruritus and a burning sensation. On examination, there was a well-demarcated pink plaque on the left scrotum with peripheral hyperpigmentation and a similar patch at the penile base. Because of the chronicity and indeterminate appearance, two punch biopsies were obtained from the scrotal plaque for histopathologic evaluation.

A 40-year-old Arabic woman was referred for evaluation of progressive abdominal distension over 6 months, recent dyspnea, and asthenia. She had no significant medical history. On examination, she was pale and had a grossly distended abdomen with a firm splenomegaly extending beyond the umbilicus; there was no hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy, or skin lesions. Laboratory studies showed microcytic hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin 7.1 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (98,000 platelets/mm3), and a white blood cell count of 6110/mm3; other tests were normal. Contrast-enhanced thoracoabdominal CT revealed a 25 cm splenic mass composed of multiple hypodense nodules of variable size with regular contours and no enhancement, displacing the stomach without invasion. No other lesions were identified. Based on imaging, a splenic lymphoma was suspected. A bone marrow biopsy showed normal histopathology.

A 63-year-old white man, a farmworker with no significant past medical or family history, presented with a 2-month history of progressively worsening headache accompanied by imbalance and difficulty walking. On examination, he was alert and oriented, with mild left peripheral facial paresis (House–Brackmann grade I), left upper-limb dysmetria, and gait ataxia, but normal strength elsewhere. Noncontrast brain CT showed a small, isodense lesion in the left cerebellopontine angle without calcification or bony remodeling of the internal auditory canal. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI revealed a 2.6 × 2.7 × 2.4 cm lesion in the left CPA that was isointense on T1-weighted images, heterogeneous hypointense on T2-weighted images, and demonstrated intense, homogeneous enhancement; it extended superiorly to the tentorial notch and displaced the superior cerebellar peduncle and dorsal midbrain. Given the lesion’s location and imaging characteristics, the leading preoperative considerations were a meningothelial (meningioma) lesion or a vestibular schwannoma, with lack of internal acoustic remodeling making schwannoma less likely. Surgical resection was planned.

A 19-year-old woman was referred with a 1-month history of intermittent chest pain radiating to her back. Over the past 2 months, she noted progressive dyspnea and an unintentional 9-kg weight loss. Her father had been treated for tuberculous lymphadenitis 4 months earlier. 

On examination, her temperature was 38.2°C. There was delayed expansion and dull percussion over the right hemithorax. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. 

A chest radiograph demonstrated a mediastinal mass extending into the right hemithorax. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax confirmed an anterior mediastinal soft-tissue mass occupying the right hemithorax. Bronchoscopic evaluation showed bronchial stenosis from mass effect; cytology was negative for malignant cells, and no Mycobacterium tuberculosis was detected. 

In view of the high local incidence of tuberculosis and CT attenuation suggesting fluid, a diagnosis of tuberculous mediastinal abscess was made, and a standard anti-tuberculosis regimen was initiated. After 2 months without clinical or radiographic improvement, a re-review of the CT scan suggested a pericardial cyst. The patient was referred for advanced evaluation while continuing the tuberculosis regimen.

A 9-year-old girl was referred by her dentist to an Interdisciplinary Airway Clinic for evaluation of sleep-disordered breathing and dental malocclusion. On extraoral examination, there was no facial asymmetry, palpation of the neck revealed no lymphadenopathy, and the temporomandibular joints were unremarkable. Intraoral examination showed early mixed dentition without caries, normal gingiva and mucosa, tonsillar hypertrophy, and an initially unremarkable soft and hard palate. Cone beam CT of the maxillofacial region revealed two incidental findings: a foreign body in the right external ear canal and a well-defined concavity in the right palatal process of the maxilla in the premolar region, measuring approximately 10 mm × 10 mm × 5.7 mm. The concavity extended medially to the midpalatine suture and displaced the nasal floor superiorly. The soft tissue within and around the concavity appeared unremarkable. The radiographic features were consistent with a benign cystic tumor. Subsequent intraoral photographs showed mild hard palate asymmetry corresponding to a small submucosal swelling.

A 46-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of severe left-sided headache. His medical history was unremarkable, and the neurologic examination was normal. Contrast-enhanced head CT showed a destructive, lucent soft-tissue lesion of the left frontal bone. Brain MRI with and without intravenous contrast demonstrated a 24×20×30 mm osseous lesion with heterogeneous enhancement, destruction of both the inner and outer tables, and thickening of the underlying dura mater concerning for invasion. Whole-body SPECT-CT confirmed a solitary osteoblastically active lesion. Laboratory tests, including creatinine, calcium, alkaline phosphatase, and hemoglobin, were within normal limits.  
What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 25-year-old Hispanic woman of African descent, previously healthy and a non-smoker, presented with a 1-month history of dyspnea on exertion, intermittent dry cough, hyporexia, and unquantified intermittent fever. She delayed care until an acute worsening of dyspnea led to emergency department evaluation, where she developed acute respiratory failure and pulseless electrical activity arrest. After orotracheal intubation and stabilization, she was transferred to our institution.

On arrival, she was sedated on mechanical ventilation. Vital signs were notable for blood pressure 200/140 mmHg, heart rate 100 bpm, respiratory rate 16 bpm, temperature 36 °C, and oxygen saturation 78% on ventilatory support. Physical examination revealed anisocoria (right pupil 5 mm, left 3 mm), jugular venous distension, sinus tachycardia, and bilateral coarse rales; no skin lesions or peripheral edema were present.

Chest radiography showed a homogeneous right paratracheal mediastinal mass compressing and displacing the trachea to the left, with adjacent right upper-lobe infiltrates. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest and neck demonstrated an 11 × 8.6 × 9.5 cm lobulated solid mass arising from the right thoracic operculum/pleura, with a nodular pleural component, mass effect on the right hilum, supra-aortic vessels, and superior vena cava, pneumomediastinum, left pneumothorax, and lytic destruction with cortical fracture of the T1 and T2 vertebrae. Centrilobular opacities in the left upper lobe suggested aspiration pneumonitis.

Laboratory tests showed WBC 13.47 × 10^3/µL (85% neutrophils), hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, platelets 303 × 10^3/µL, INR 1.39, lactic acid 2.83 mmol/L, C-reactive protein 4.20 mg/dL, LDH 592 U/L, calcium 6.58 mg/dL, phosphorus 3.73 mg/dL; arterial blood gas revealed pH 7.30, PCO2 44.5 mmHg, PO2 122 mmHg, HCO3 22.3 mmol/L, BE –3.7 mmol/L, and SO2 98%. She received dexamethasone and piperacillin/tazobactam. Given the atypical imaging features and concern for possible hematologic malignancy, video-assisted thoracoscopic biopsy was planned to obtain adequate tissue.

A 58-year-old Hispanic woman presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of wheezing and dry cough without fever, sore throat, chest pain, hemoptysis, night sweats, odynophagia, or hoarseness. Her medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. Over the past 6 months, she had four emergency visits and two primary care visits for similar symptoms. She had used an albuterol inhaler as needed without sustained improvement. She had a 15–pack-year smoking history and no known occupational exposures. 

On examination, her temperature was 97.6°F, pulse 102/min, respiratory rate 18/min, blood pressure 112/69 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and BMI 15 kg/m^2. She appeared emaciated but well hydrated. Lung auscultation revealed equal air entry with inspiratory wheezes bilaterally; cardiac examination showed sinus tachycardia without murmurs. Abdominal and neurologic examinations were unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, serum chemistries, liver function tests, and calcium, were within normal limits. Chest radiography showed no pulmonary infiltrates. Spirometry performed in the pulmonary clinic demonstrated flattening of the inspiratory flow–volume loop.

A 62-year-old man with Fitzpatrick skin type II presented with a slowly enlarging, mildly pruritic, erythematous, scaling 1.4 cm patch on his left cheek. Physical examination revealed a well-demarcated, mildly scaly erythematous plaque without ulceration or nodularity. A shave biopsy at 20× magnification showed an atypical lentiginous proliferation of cells arranged singly and in nests with prominent pagetoid scatter.

A 52-year-old Malay woman presented with a 3-week history of intermittent fever and an unintentional 10-kg weight loss over 3 months. Her medical history included asthma, hypertension, and hyperlipidaemia. She denied cough, sputum, haemoptysis, dysuria, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, or recent travel. On examination, her temperature was 40 °C, heart rate 113 beats/min, and blood pressure was normal. Cardiac and pulmonary examinations were unremarkable. The abdomen was soft and non-tender, with no masses. There was no lymphadenopathy or stigmata of chronic liver disease. Initial laboratory tests showed microcytic hypochromic anaemia (haemoglobin 9.8 g/dL; MCV 75.2 fL) and lactate dehydrogenase 2140 U/L; renal function was normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis revealed bilateral homogeneous adrenal masses (left, 3.7 × 5.4 × 6.4 cm; right, 5.5 × 2.7 × 5.9 cm), a 0.8-cm left supraclavicular lymph node, and subcentimetre mediastinal nodes. Early-morning cortisol was low at 242 nmol/L, and a 250-µg short Synacthen test failed to show adequate cortisol response. Acid-fast bacilli stain and culture, as well as PCR for tuberculosis, were negative.

A 54‐year‐old Caucasian woman presented with a 10‐year history of mild postprandial abdominal pain and a sensation of fullness. Her medical history was notable for hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and hypercholesterolemia. She was obese (body‐mass index, 31 kg/m2). On examination, abdominal inspection and palpation were unremarkable; there was mildly increased tympany on periumbilical percussion, and bowel sounds were normal. The remainder of the physical examination and routine laboratory tests were normal.

An abdominal CT scan with oral contrast revealed a well‐circumscribed, retroperitoneal mass measuring 16 × 14 × 7 cm arising from the left adrenal gland and surrounded by a thin capsule. The lesion exhibited both adipose‐tissue density and soft‐tissue elements, with Hounsfield units consistent with fat. It abutted but did not invade adjacent structures, including small intestine, pancreas, spleen, and left kidney. No lymphadenopathy or vascular invasion was noted.

A 31-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of asymptomatic, progressive, multiple erythematous papules and nodules on his face, trunk, and extremities. He was otherwise healthy, with no family history of similar lesions. A punch biopsy of a forehead nodule showed foamy histiocytes and Touton giant cells. Laboratory studies revealed a normal lipid profile (cholesterol 159 mg/dL; triglycerides 74 mg/dL; HDL 50 mg/dL; LDL 106 mg/dL) but elevated liver enzymes (AST 60 U/L; ALT 114 U/L; ALP 399 U/L). Two months later, skin lesions had increased in size and number, and new gingival and laryngeal lesions were noted; liver enzymes remained elevated (AST 85 U/L; ALT 119 U/L; ALP 443 U/L). Serum protein electrophoresis was unremarkable. A biopsy of an abdominal lesion showed foamy histiocytes and fibrosis without Touton giant cells; immunohistochemistry showed weak S-100 positivity, CD163 positivity, factor XIIIa positivity, and CD1a negativity. 

Computed tomography of the abdomen revealed heterogeneous enhancement in the left hepatic lobe, multiple low-attenuation lesions in both kidneys, and two pulmonary nodules in the left lung. Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen demonstrated infiltrative or nodular lesions in the abdominal wall and musculoskeletal system. A liver biopsy showed histiocytic proliferation with focal S-100 expression. Neck CT identified multiple skin nodules, osteolytic bone lesions, and intraglandular nodules in both submandibular glands. Positron emission tomography–CT confirmed widespread uptake in skin and subcutaneous tissues, liver, pancreas, intra-abdominal sites, bones, mediastinum, muscles, and lungs.

A 69-year-old woman with a history of treated breast cancer underwent routine surveillance for sigmoid diverticulitis.  
A contrast-enhanced CT scan revealed an incidental 43 × 40 × 39 mm solid mass at the splenopancreatic border that was absent on imaging 12 months earlier. The lesion was heterogeneous with a necrotic center, showed no calcification or enhancement, and was not hypermetabolic on PET–CT. MRI demonstrated a well-defined splenic lesion with high signal intensity on T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted images.  
A percutaneous biopsy showed extensive necrosis and a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate of plasma cells and lymphocytes without epithelial elements. The patient was asymptomatic and in good general health; vital signs were normal. Infection-related blood tests were negative, and the C-reactive protein level was 8 mg/L.  
On the basis of these findings, the decision was made to perform a splenectomy with caudal pancreatectomy.

A 52-year-old woman (gravida 7, para 3) presented with a 2-day history of heavy postmenopausal bleeding and passage of vesicular tissue per vaginum. She had been menopausal for 5 years, and her last pregnancy occurred 12 years earlier; she denied any history of molar pregnancy or abortion. On examination, she was severely pale with a pulse of 110 beats/min and blood pressure of 90/60 mm Hg. Abdominal examination revealed a uterus palpable to the level of a 16-week gestation. On pelvic examination, the cervix was long and soft, the os was open, and fleshy vesicles were noted in the cervical canal. She received crystalloid resuscitation and three units of blood. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin concentration of 6.4 g/dL and a serum β-hCG level of 96 484 mIU/mL. Chest radiography, thyroid function tests, liver and renal function tests, and coagulation profile were within normal limits. Transvaginal ultrasonography demonstrated a large, moderately echogenic mass with numerous cystic spaces filling the central uterine cavity; both ovaries appeared normal. A diagnosis of gestational trophoblastic disease was made, and suction evacuation was planned.

An 85-year-old Japanese man with a history of stroke and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease presented with acute chest discomfort. An electrocardiogram was consistent with acute coronary syndrome. Emergent percutaneous coronary intervention was attempted, but catheterization of the left main trunk led to cardiopulmonary arrest; return of spontaneous circulation was achieved with resuscitation, and a covered stent was placed in the narrowed segment of the left coronary artery.  
Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 93,900/μL with 83.5% myeloblasts that were positive for myeloperoxidase activity, a hemoglobin concentration of 5.1 g/dL, and a platelet count of 510,000/μL. Given his poor performance status, no chemotherapy was administered. He initially stabilized sufficiently to eat but died of respiratory failure 25 days after admission; by then, the white-cell count had risen to 291,700/μL.

A 70-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of tongue swelling and altered mental status. Six months earlier, she had undergone left upper lobectomy for pulmonary pleomorphic carcinoma (stage T4N1M0) harboring MET exon 14 skipping and PIK3CA mutations, with 75% PD-L1 positivity, and was started on capmatinib. One month before admission, she had a left vocal cord injection for vocal cord paralysis.

Two weeks before presentation, she developed progressive tongue swelling, dysphagia, and odynophagia. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the neck was grossly unremarkable, though visualization was limited by dental streak and motion artifacts. Her oncologist held capmatinib and initiated a methylprednisolone dose pack, suspecting an allergic reaction to the drug, but the swelling worsened, and she became unable to tolerate oral intake. Increasing lethargy prompted presentation to the emergency department.

Her medical history was notable for atrial fibrillation, deep venous thrombosis, and osteoarthritis. She was a former 25 pack-year smoker, quitting 25 years ago. On examination, SpO2 was 84% on room air. The tongue and floor of mouth were severely edematous; the deep oral tongue was firm; the mucosa was intact and normal in color; the submental space was mildly full; and no cervical lymphadenopathy was palpable. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 20.85 × 10^3/µL. A repeat contrast CT of the neck identified a 2.7 × 3.2 × 1.9 cm lesion within the tongue with peripheral enhancement and central hypoattenuation.

A 44-year-old woman presented with 4 months of pulsatile left upper quadrant abdominal pain and pressure radiating to her back, accompanied by nausea. She has a history of hepatitis C virus infection, treated successfully with Harvoni. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen in the portal venous phase revealed a new 2.5 cm splenic lesion with a hypoenhancing thick rind of soft tissue and central fluid density suggestive of necrosis. On delayed-phase imaging, the peripheral component enhanced similarly to splenic parenchyma, while a central low-density region persisted. This lesion was absent on a CT scan obtained one year earlier.

Subsequent contrast-enhanced MRI of the abdomen showed the lesion to be intermediate to hyperintense peripherally on T2-weighted images, with a central region mirroring fluid signal intensity. Diffusion-weighted imaging (b = 800 s/mm2) demonstrated restricted diffusion, confirmed on the ADC map. On T1-weighted images, the lesion was mostly isointense precontrast and exhibited gradual homogeneous peripheral enhancement on delayed sequences, with a nonenhancing central cystic or necrotic area. 

A differential diagnosis of splenic hemangioma and hamartoma was considered. To further evaluate the lesion, a PET-CT scan was performed, which demonstrated that the splenic mass was intensely hypermetabolic, raising concern for malignancy.

A 59-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a crusty lesion in the right fronto-orbital region present for several months. He had no significant past medical history. On examination, there was an irregularly shaped 5 × 3 cm plaque with multiple superficial crusts. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. 

An excisional biopsy of the lesion showed lobules and detached aggregates of eosinophilic keratinocytes with pleomorphic nuclei and prominent nucleoli infiltrating the reticular dermis; there was no clear evidence of basaloid nests, and the diagnosis rendered was invasive cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. 

On April 24, he began treatment with cemiplimab 350 mg every 3 weeks. Before therapy, ^18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated a focal area of uptake in the supraorbital lesion (SUVmax 6.9; metabolic tumor volume, 2 cc). After five cycles, the plaque had regressed markedly, but several discrete papular lesions remained. Dermoscopic evaluation of these papules revealed features typical of basal cell carcinoma. A follow-up PET/CT at 12 weeks showed decreased uptake in the original lesion (SUVmax 4.8; metabolic tumor volume, 0.5 cc), consistent with partial metabolic response.

A 41-year-old woman presented with a 6-year history of right calf pain. Initial conservative therapy with aspirin and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs failed to provide relief. Over the past three months, her pain progressed and began to limit daily activities. Although she did not report classic night pain, minimal pressure over the affected area caused severe pain that awakened her from sleep. There was no history of trauma or infection, and her medical history was otherwise unremarkable. 

On examination, palpation of the mid-calf elicited significant pain; there was no palpable mass, warmth, bruit, or overlying skin changes. Knee and ankle range of motion were full. Laboratory studies were normal.

Plain radiographs of the right leg showed an irregular sclerotic periosteal reaction along the posterior mid-diaphyseal cortex of the tibia. The lesion was not well visualized on the anteroposterior view but was apparent on the lateral projection. There was no osseous destruction, fracture, or adjacent calcification, and soft tissues and joints appeared normal.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the tibia revealed a cortically based sclerotic lesion arising from the posterior diaphysis (2.01 cm × 4.79 cm × 0.67 cm) without cortical breakthrough. 

Although osteoid osteoma was a concern despite an atypical presentation, other pathological osteoskeletal processes such as periostitis, eosinophilic granuloma, hemangioma of bone, non-ossifying fibroma, Paget’s disease, and avascular necrosis of the bone were also considered.

An 80-year-old man with a history of a known right inguinal hernia presented with 48 hours of intermittent right-groin pain and multiple episodes of vomiting. On examination, there was a painful right inguinal mass and a tender abdomen with decreased bowel sounds. Abdominal radiographs revealed multiple air–fluid levels and distended small-bowel loops. Based on his history and clinical examination, a diagnosis of strangulated inguinal hernia was made, and he was taken emergently to the operating room for open hernia repair.

A 48-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of nausea, colicky nonradiating epigastric pain not associated with food, and intermittent constipation. His medical history was significant only for bipolar disorder controlled on lithium. On examination, he was anicteric, with no lymphadenopathy. The abdomen was mildly distended with moderate epigastric tenderness but no rebound, guarding, organomegaly, or masses; bowel sounds were normal. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver enzymes, renal function, and electrolytes, were all within normal limits. Abdominal CT showed concentric wall thickening of the third and fourth portions of the duodenum, adjacent soft-tissue encasement of the superior mesenteric artery, and prominent mesenteric lymph nodes; the mass measured 6.1 × 5.9 × 8.0 cm. At that time, the differential diagnosis included lymphoma, carcinoma, or neuroendocrine tumor of the duodenum. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed diffuse edematous and erythematous mucosa in the third portion extending to the fourth portion, causing luminal narrowing, and a 5 mm ulceration in the fourth portion was biopsied. Histologic examination showed diffuse infiltration of uniformly blastoid-appearing cells occupying the mucosal space. Immunohistochemical staining of the biopsy was positive for CD45 (weakly +), CD34 (+), CD117 (+), CD33 (+), MPO (+), CD43 (bright +), and Bcl-2 (+); Ki-67 highlighted 70–80% of cells. A peripheral blood smear revealed no circulating blasts. Bone marrow aspirate showed normal cell morphology and normal percentages of blasts, promyelocytes, and granulocytes, and flow cytometry indicated no immunophenotypic evidence of hematolymphoid malignancy.

A 3-year-old boy presented with a history of trauma to his right tibia followed by pain and swelling. Over several weeks, a bead-sized lump developed on the anteromedial aspect of the proximal tibial shaft and gradually increased in size. On examination, the mass at the mid-shaft was hard, immobile, ill-defined, and tender (pain score 3–4). The circumferential diameter was 24 cm on the affected side versus 23 cm contralaterally. Hip and knee range of motion and distal neurovascular findings were normal.  
Plain radiography of the right tibia showed a geographic lytic lesion with septations in the mid‐shaft, narrow transitional zone, well‐defined margins, no periosteal reaction, no cortical breach, and no soft-tissue involvement.  
MRI of the lesion demonstrated an anterior tibial cortical lesion that was isointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed homogeneous contrast enhancement without intramedullary or soft-tissue extension. The MRI report concluded that this was a primary benign bone tumor, suggestive of osteofibrous dysplasia.

A 25-year-old Afrodescendant man presented with a large, fluctuant, painless swelling of resilient consistency involving the submental and left submandibular regions. Intraorally, there was a small, smooth-surfaced, normochromic, movable mass in the floor of the mouth adjacent to the lingual frenulum. Ultrasonography of the left submandibular gland showed a well-defined, homogeneous, round, hyperechoic mass measuring 6.8×4.7 cm between the geniohyoid and mylohyoid muscles without ductal dilatation or lithiasis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a well-defined unilocular cystic lesion in the submental and submandibular space without peripheral enhancement. Fine-needle aspiration yielded friable white material.

A 19-year-old man with no prior health issues presented with two months of progressively worsening bilateral leg weakness. He reported dull, persistent mid-thoracic back pain and gradual paralysis of both lower extremities. He described numbness from just above the umbilicus extending into both legs and noted new urinary retention and constipation. He denied fevers, night sweats, weight loss, or any swollen lymph nodes.

On examination, he was alert and fully oriented. Motor strength in both legs was grade I. Patellar and ankle reflexes were hyperactive, and sensation in both lower extremities was reduced. There was no cranial nerve palsy, lymphadenopathy, or signs of sinusitis. The remainder of the physical examination was normal.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine revealed an extradural mass extending from T6 to T9 that was heterogeneous and hyperintense on T2-weighted and STIR images, isointense on T1-weighted images, and showed vivid contrast enhancement. The spinal cord at these levels was markedly compressed and edematous. Thyroid and abdominal ultrasonography and a chest radiograph were unremarkable. Complete blood count, coagulation studies, and standard chemistry panels were within normal limits.

A woman in her late 20s presented with a 1-week history of fever and intermittent right upper–quadrant abdominal pain. She reported noticing a palpable mass in her abdomen. Her medical history was notable for extensive resection and adjuvant chemotherapy for osteosarcoma of the left femur 15 years earlier. On examination, she was febrile; other vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory tests revealed a C-reactive protein level of 8.56 mg/dL; liver enzymes were normal. Serum tumor markers, including carcinoembryonic antigen, CA19-9, alpha-fetoprotein, and des-gamma-carboxy prothrombin, were within normal limits. Serologic tests for hepatitis B and C were negative.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a well-defined, 9-cm mass in the right posterior segment of the liver that was mildly enhancing but largely hypovascular. MRI demonstrated mixed high and low signal intensity within the lesion: cystic areas were hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, while focal regions showed T1 hyperintensity and T2 hypointensity, compatible with intratumoral hemorrhage. PET–CT showed uptake of ^18F-FDG in parts of the solid component (SUV-max 11.11).

A percutaneous needle biopsy of the lesion showed a proliferation of malignant pleomorphic atypical cells with areas of necrosis. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated positivity for cytokeratin markers AE1/AE3 and CAM5.2.

An 80-year-old woman presented with a painless left mandibular swelling that had gradually increased in size over 18 months following extraction of a lower-left first molar. She had no other symptoms, no significant medical history, and no family history of malignancy. Examination revealed an 8 × 6 cm hard, smooth, tender, immobile swelling over the left mandible with normal overlying skin. Intraorally, multiple left mandibular teeth were absent, and the swelling extended into both buccal and lingual vestibules. A panoramic radiograph showed destruction of the left mandibular body and multiple missing teeth. The preliminary differential diagnosis included ameloblastoma, odontogenic keratocyst, and a malignant lesion. Incisional biopsy via an intraoral approach yielded tissue consistent with ectopic thyroid. Ultrasonography of the lesion demonstrated a heterogeneous 5.3 × 4 cm swelling with multiple nodules, cystic changes, central vascularity, and smooth margins. Neck ultrasonography revealed an enlarged right thyroid lobe containing a 2.3 × 2 cm cystic nodule and a normal left lobe, with no significant cervical lymphadenopathy. Contrast-enhanced CT of the mandible showed an expansile lytic lesion of the left mandibular body associated with a large inhomogeneously enhancing soft tissue mass, radiologically suggesting osteosarcoma.

An 82-year-old man presented with progressive phimosis over several weeks and complained of frequent, painful urination. He had a history of chronic hepatitis C.  
On examination, there was a large, well-demarcated penile ulcer with a necrotic base. The penile shaft and prostate were firm on palpation. Multiple enlarged inguinal lymph nodes were palpable, and there was mild lower abdominal tenderness; there was no urethral discharge, scrotal abnormality, or hepatosplenomegaly.  
Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, serum biochemistry, and electrolytes, were within normal limits. Serum prostate-specific antigen was 0.52 ng/mL.  
Abdominal ultrasound showed normal kidneys, irregular thickening of the bladder wall, and an enlarged prostate (80 mL) that was hypoechoic with indistinct borders. Transrectal ultrasound revealed a solid, ill-defined, hypoechoic mass infiltrating the penile shaft and right prostatic lobe, with multiple irregular masses protruding into the bladder lumen.  
Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis confirmed pelvic lymphadenopathy and marked prostate enlargement; CT of the chest showed no pulmonary metastases or thoracic lymphadenopathy.  
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis demonstrated a nodular, inhomogeneous tumor in the region of the seminal vesicles and prostate with minimal contrast enhancement, focal bladder wall thickening, and a filling defect between 5 and 9 o’clock; no other abdominal organ or lymph node abnormalities were identified.

A 19-year-old Irish Caucasian woman presented with a 3-day history of gradually worsening lower abdominal pain and fever, associated with nausea and one episode of vomiting. She reported no urinary symptoms, and her last menstrual period had ended the previous day. Her medical history was notable only for viral meningitis two years earlier; she had no history of sexually transmitted disease, recent urinary tract infection, prior surgery, or regular medications, and no allergies. On examination, her temperature was 37.4 °C and other vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination revealed a tender mass in the right iliac fossa. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 10,500/mm3, hemoglobin 13.3 g/dL, platelets 212,000/mm3, normal electrolytes and renal function, a urine test negative for leukocytes, and a negative urinary β-hCG. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 10.4 × 4.5 × 3.8 cm loculated cystic mass in the right pelvis that appeared to contain the tip of the appendix. The patient remained febrile, leading to a working diagnosis of an appendix mass with a tubo-ovarian abscess considered as a differential. She received intravenous antibiotics, and an ultrasound-guided drain was placed into the largest locule, yielding 30 mL of serous fluid without pus. Cultures of the aspirate and blood remained sterile, and the drain was removed after three days. After five days of antibiotics, she was clinically well and discharged. Two weeks later, she was readmitted for a diagnostic laparoscopy because of suspicion for a noninfective pathology based on the nature of the drain output; she consented to an appendectomy if no other lesion was identified.

A 25-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of cough with minimal sputum production and a 4-week history of low-grade continuous fever, 10 kg weight loss, and anorexia. He also noted noncolicky right hypochondrial pain without jaundice or bowel changes. He had been empirically treated elsewhere with four drugs for presumed tuberculosis for one month due to right pleural effusion; there was no prior personal or family history of tuberculosis.

On examination, he was thin and afebrile with normal vital signs. Findings included pallor, decreased air entry in the right infrascapular and infra-axillary areas, and tender hepatomegaly 4–5 cm below the right costal margin; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL, leukocytosis (24 000/µL) with neutrophilia, ESR 60 mm/h, and LDH 798 U/L; other chemistries were normal. HIV test was negative. Chest radiograph revealed right pleural effusion. Pleural fluid was exudative (500 cells, 80% lymphocytes; fluid protein 3.2 g/dL, serum protein 6.0 g/dL), with sugar 50 mg/dL and ADA 48 U/L. Fluid was negative for malignant cells and organisms. Sputum AFB smear was negative.

Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly with multiple variable hypoechoic lesions in both lobes and minimal ascites. An initial impression of multiple liver abscesses with right‐sided exudative pleural effusion was made; antitubercular therapy was continued and intravenous antibiotics were started. Ultrasound-guided aspiration of a liver lesion was sent for cytology, AFB stain, Gram stain, and culture.

Over the next days, he developed progressive breathlessness and abdominal distention corresponding to further enlargement of the liver. Repeat labs: hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, leukocytosis (22 800/µL), LDH 1098 U/L. Repeat chest radiograph showed mediastinal widening with a new left upper-zone opacity in addition to the persistent right pleural effusion. Repeat pleural fluid was again negative for malignant cells. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy were performed.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen revealed nodular lesions in the mediastinum and left upper lung and multiple hypodense hepatic lesions. Cytology of the liver aspirate yielded cells suspicious for a round cell tumor. A CT-guided biopsy of the left lung mass was planned.

An 8-month-old boy with Down syndrome and congenital hypothyroidism presented with a 1-month history of hematemesis and progressive pallor. On examination, he was pale and had a palpable, firm mass in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 2.4 g/dL, hematocrit 9.8%, white-cell count 14 220 cells/mm3, and negative HIV serology. A plain abdominal radiograph revealed a soft-tissue density in the left upper quadrant. Gastroduodenoscopy demonstrated a large ulcerated intragastric soft-tissue mass. An incisional punch biopsy of the mass showed infiltration by immature myeloid cells. A bone marrow biopsy revealed active trilineage hematopoiesis without evidence of malignancy. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 7.4 × 6.9 × 4.9 cm heterogeneous hyperattenuating mass arising from the lesser curvature of the stomach, containing punctate calcifications and a focal area of macroscopic fat.

A 20-year-old man presented with a 10-day history of left-sided nasal obstruction and epistaxis. He noted a reddish-black swelling on the left anterior nasal septum that gradually increased in size over 10 days and was associated with two to three daily episodes of fresh bleeding, initially profuse and later dripping. He denied pain, anosmia, ear symptoms, or a history of bleeding disorders. His history was notable for nasal trauma from a frontal blow 3 years earlier. 

On anterior rhinoscopy, there was a reddish mass filling the left nasal cavity and a left-sided septal deviation. External examination showed a grade 2 external nasal deformity with a left alar bulge. Cottle’s test was positive on the left. Posterior rhinoscopy, ear, and throat examinations were unremarkable. The lesion was initially diagnosed as a bleeding nasal polyp. 

Laboratory studies, including coagulation tests and renal function, were within normal limits; alkaline phosphatase was slightly elevated at 119.2 U/L. Contrast-enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses revealed a left-ward deviated septum, compensatory hypertrophy of the right inferior turbinate, mild bilateral ethmoid sinusitis, and a 2.1 × 1.3 × 2.1 cm soft tissue lesion originating from the left anterior nasal septum.

A 28-year-old woman presented with a 15-year history of a progressively enlarging swelling over her right parietal region. She denied pain, neurologic symptoms, or systemic complaints. On examination, there was a firm to hard, non-tender, immobile mass measuring approximately 6 cm in diameter over the right high parietal area. Routine hematologic tests were normal. A skull radiograph showed a completely radio-opaque bony mass in the right parietal region. Noncontrast CT of the head (bone window) demonstrated a uniform hyperdense mass measuring 6.3 × 5.3 × 5.6 cm in the right high parietal bone, with complete erosion of both the inner and outer tables. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed enhancement of an extradural soft-tissue component and buckling of the underlying gray matter.

An 18-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of low back pain and progressive weakness of both lower extremities, with new onset of bowel and bladder dysfunction over the past week. On examination, there was tenderness over the lower back, flaccid paraplegia (0/5 strength) of both lower limbs, and approximately 90% sensory loss to all modalities without sacral sparing. MRI of the spine showed an intramedullary lesion extending from T11 to L2 that was predominantly isointense on T1-weighted images, demonstrated homogeneous contrast enhancement, and contained interspersed cystic or necrotic areas. A differential diagnosis of intramedullary ependymoma (myxopapillary variant), paraganglioma, other glial neoplasms, metastases, or inflammatory pathology was considered. The patient underwent laminectomy and tumor decompression.

A 28-year-old Asian woman underwent evaluation in October 2023 after the incidental detection of a right thyroid nodule on routine ultrasound earlier in May. She had no symptoms, no significant medical or exposure history, and normal laboratory studies.  
On thyroid ultrasound, there was a slightly hypoechoic, irregular mass in the middle-upper right thyroid lobe measuring approximately 1.17×0.95 cm, with an aspect ratio >1, ill-defined margins, and strong punctate echoes. The left lobe and isthmus were unremarkable.  
Neck ultrasound revealed multiple small low-echo foci in the right level IV and VI lymph node regions (largest 0.8×0.6 cm) and a 4.6×1.9 cm hypoechoic mass in the left supraclavicular fossa with a regular shape, clear borders, and poorly defined corticomedullary differentiation.  
Physical examination showed an asymptomatic, painless, fixed mass in the left supraclavicular fossa.  
Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration of the right thyroid nodule yielded Bethesda category VI cytology, consistent with papillary thyroid carcinoma. FNA of the left supraclavicular mass showed numerous lymphocytes without malignant epithelial cells.  
Chest CT demonstrated only a tracheal diverticulum; no other abnormalities were noted. Laryngoscopy showed chronic pharyngitis and vocal nodules.  
The working diagnosis was papillary thyroid carcinoma with presumed left supraclavicular lymph node metastasis, and surgical planning included right lobectomy, isthmusectomy, central lymph node dissection, and bilateral cervical lymph node exploration.

An 11-year-old girl presented with a 3-month history of a midline frontal, non-tender scalp swelling that had recently grown rapidly. She also had recurrent headaches, giddiness, mild behavioral changes, epiphora, diplopia, and blurring of vision. Fundoscopic examination revealed bilateral papilledema; no focal neurologic deficits were detected.

Non-contrast CT of the head showed a 7.0 × 5.0 × 5.0 cm, densely calcified, mushroom-shaped, parasagittal hyperdense mass arising from the anterior falx. The non-calcified portion of the lesion enhanced markedly with intravenous contrast. There was destruction of both the inner and outer tables of the overlying calvarium with transcalvarial–subgaleal extension and extensive perilesional vasogenic white-matter edema.

On MRI, the mass was predominantly hypointense on T1-weighted images with internal hyperintense foci corresponding to calcifications and was heterogeneously isohyperintense on T2-weighted images. Diffusion-weighted imaging and ADC mapping showed no areas of restricted diffusion. Post-gadolinium T1-weighted images demonstrated heterogeneous enhancement. MR angiography revealed extensive neovascularity with splaying and posterolateral displacement of both anterior cerebral arteries. MR venography showed nonvisualization of the anterior one-third of the superior sagittal sinus, consistent with thrombosis or invasion. MR spectroscopy was noninformative due to the calcification and high vascularity. MRI of the spine and thoracoabdominal CT scans were negative for additional lesions.

A 76-year-old man presented with a small, elastic nodule on the left side of his penis that had been growing over the past year and had begun to cause discomfort. On examination, a non-tender 7 mm mass was palpable in the corpus cavernosum. Scrotal ultrasound showed a hypervascular, hyperechoic, well-circumscribed, solid mass. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a smoothly marginated lesion with peripheral low signal intensity on T2-weighted images. Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis revealed no evidence of distant metastases. The patient had no significant medical history. Considering the patient’s discomfort and the possibility of malignancy, surgical removal was planned to obtain tissue for a definitive diagnosis.

A 60-year-old rural Syrian woman was referred after a routine oncology check-up revealed a painless, palpable mass in her right breast. Her medical history was unremarkable. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender mass in the upper medial quadrant of the right breast, associated with nipple retraction and overlying skin erythema. 

Laboratory studies showed anemia (hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL) and thrombocytosis (platelet count 537 × 10^9/L). Breast ultrasonography demonstrated a 55 × 48 mm hypoechoic, heterogeneous mass with irregular borders in the right breast and ipsilateral axillary lymphadenopathy; the left breast ultrasound was normal. Chest CT confirmed the right breast mass with axillary node enlargement; CT of the brain, abdomen, and pelvis was unremarkable.

A partial core biopsy yielded firm white tissue. Histologic examination revealed nests of large round cells with mild pleomorphism, hyperchromatic nuclei, mitotic figures, and focal necrosis. Immunohistochemical staining of the tumor cells was positive for chromogranin-A, cytokeratin, estrogen receptor, GATA-3, and focally for mammaglobin; the Ki-67 index was approximately 60%. Stains were negative for progesterone receptor, HER2/neu, and leukocyte common antigen (LCA-CD45).

A 12-year-old girl presented with a 5-month history of a painless swelling in the right suboccipital region. She had no other symptoms or neurologic signs on examination. Skull radiographs showed focal thinning of the occipital bone beneath the mass. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head revealed a soft-tissue lesion adherent to the outer table of the diploic bone, with bone thinning but no frank bone destruction, no intracranial extension, no calcifications, and mild inhomogeneous contrast enhancement. MRI demonstrated an encapsulated spindle-shaped mass in the subcutaneous soft tissues of the right suboccipital area, broadly attached to the outer table of the diploe; the lesion was of intermediate signal intensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images, with focal areas of high T2 and low T1 signal, and showed inhomogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. Laboratory studies were unremarkable except for a mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase level. After radiologic and oncologic consultation, she was scheduled for surgical excision of the mass.

An 81-year-old woman was admitted with a chief complaint of chest discomfort. Her medical history included appendectomy, hypertension, colon polyps, and osteoporosis. On examination, there was no abdominal tenderness or palpable mass. Laboratory studies were unremarkable, with normal hemoglobin and normal tumor markers, including carcinoembryonic antigen and CA19-9.

Barium esophagography demonstrated a sliding esophageal hiatal hernia and defects in the lower esophagus and gastric wall caused by a large mass. Esophagogastroscopy confirmed a severe hiatal hernia and revealed a large, hard, elastic submucosal tumor extending from the lower esophagus to the gastric fundus.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest and abdomen showed a 12.7-cm solid mass with areas of low attenuation in the mediastinum. The mass was continuous with the gastric wall, and its border with the esophagus was clearly demarcated. On the basis of these findings, a diagnosis of a submucosal gastric tumor complicated by an esophageal hiatal hernia was made, and the patient was scheduled for surgical resection.

A 60-year-old postmenopausal Iranian woman presented with an 8-month history of heavy vaginal bleeding. She had three prior vaginal deliveries, menopause at age 50, and a medical history of diabetes mellitus, depression, and osteopetrosis; her medications included metformin, sertraline, vitamin D, and calcium. She denied sexually transmitted infections or hormonal therapy. She had sustained two osteopetrosis-related lower extremity fractures over the past decade. There was no family history of malignancy. On admission, her hemoglobin was 6.0 g/dL; other laboratory studies were unremarkable. Under anesthesia, pelvic examination revealed a markedly enlarged uterus and a 10-cm soft, hemorrhagic mass arising from the posterior cervix and protruding into the vagina. Excisional biopsy of the cervical mass was performed. Abdominopelvic CT showed a large uterus with a 15-cm mass in the posterior uterine wall and enlarged pelvic lymph nodes. Chest CT and whole-body bone scan were normal.

A 33-year-old G4P3013 woman with a recent pregnancy of unknown location initially managed with two doses of methotrexate in April 2018 had a slow decline of β-hCG to normal levels. In June 2018 she was found to have a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation and underwent coil embolization. She was followed with weekly β-hCG levels until they were undetectable in July 2018, then was lost to follow-up.

In October 2018 she presented with right shoulder pain, abdominal pain, and shortness of breath. On examination she had abdominal tenderness with rebound. Her quantitative β-hCG level was 1011 mIU/mL. Transvaginal ultrasound showed free pelvic fluid, and liver enzymes were elevated (AST 193 U/L, ALT 270 U/L). Because of concern for a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, she underwent emergent laparotomy. At surgery there was 650 cc of hemoperitoneum, but both fallopian tubes appeared normal; the bleeding source was a ruptured subcapsular hepatic hematoma without active bleeding at that time.

Postoperatively, CT of the abdomen revealed multiple foci of active contrast extravasation in both hepatic lobes, concerning for hepatic arteriovenous malformations. A head CT angiogram showed a left parietal subarachnoid hemorrhage, and cerebral angiography identified a left parietal micro–arteriovenous malformation. Daily β-hCG levels over the next several days were 1011 → 748 → 861 → 1185 mIU/mL.

A 29-year-old man noted a large, nonpainful left lateral–cervical mass that had gradually increased in size over several months and was initially neglected. Fifteen days before admission, he developed dyspnea. He was otherwise healthy and afebrile. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender mass in the left lower neck extending toward the clavicle.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and chest showed a large (10.4 × 6.6 × 18.9 cm), well-circumscribed, nonenhancing soft-tissue density lesion in the upper and middle mediastinum with cervical extension, containing peripheral microcalcifications. The mass displaced the trachea, esophagus, and azygous vein to the right and surrounded the left subclavian and vertebral arteries without evidence of invasion; it contacted the vertebral bodies from C7 to T6 without bone erosion.

MRI demonstrated a mediastinal mass with uniformly low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, and no marked enhancement after gadolinium.

The patient underwent a cervical biopsy. Histologic evaluation showed a non‐atypical myxoid spindle cell proliferation. Immunohistochemical staining suggested a low-grade myxoid spindle cell tumor, favoring either low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma or low-grade myxoid liposarcoma.

A 55-year-old Dominican man presented with a 2-year history of progressively enlarging skin lesions on both lower extremities. He had lived in the United States for 2 years. His medical history was notable for diabetes mellitus and hypertension. He had previously received oral antibiotics for a presumed skin infection and intralesional steroids for presumed dermatitis without improvement.

On examination, temperature was 98.4 °F, blood pressure 120/70 mmHg, pulse 88 beats/min, and respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. Dermatologic examination revealed a cluster of dark nodular lesions on the medial right thigh and multiple purple plaques of varying sizes below both knees. There was left lower-limb edema. A violaceous lesion was also noted on the soft palate. There was no lymphadenopathy; lungs were clear; heart sounds were normal; and the abdomen was without hepatosplenomegaly.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 13.7 g/dL, hematocrit 42%, white blood cell count 4.9 × 10^9/L, platelet count 224 × 10^9/L, and normal renal and hepatic chemistries. Serologic tests for HIV were negative, and the CD4 count was 350 cells/mm^3 with a CD4/CD8 ratio of 1.10.

A 32-year-old G1P0 woman at 16 weeks 4 days of gestation presented with a 2-week history of progressive abdominal fullness and intermittent chest tightness. Pelvic sonography at 12 weeks had shown no adnexal masses. She had no relevant medical or family history. On examination, her abdomen was distended with shifting dullness.
