Signs of virilization included acne, hirsutism, and a deepened voice. Laboratory tests showed: CA-125 9.10 U/mL (normal <30.2), CA 19-9 5.53 U/mL (normal <37), HE4 27.32 pmol/L (normal <140), CEA <0.50 ng/mL (normal <5), SCC antigen 1.43 ng/mL (normal <2.5), NSE 0.73 ng/mL (normal <16.3), and AFP 36.20 IU/mL (normal <6.7); other serum markers, including estradiol and testosterone levels, were within reference ranges. Transabdominal ultrasound revealed a viable 16-week intrauterine pregnancy, large-volume ascites, and a 10.3×9.2×7.1 cm solid right adnexal mass containing a central cystic area with low-velocity, low-resistance peripheral blood flow; the left ovary and uterus were otherwise unremarkable. She received supportive hypervolemic therapy for presumed ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, but symptoms persisted. Percutaneous peritoneal drainage yielded a total of approximately 5000 mL of fluid; cytologic analysis showed no malignant cells, and immunohistochemical studies of the fluid were nondiagnostic. Subsequent clinical follow-up revealed no increase in tumor size or reaccumulation of ascites, and CA-125 transiently rose to 35.66 U/mL in weeks 27–29.

A 67-year-old Saudi woman presented for routine follow-up with a 2-month history of intermittent epigastric pain and indigestion that had become more frequent over the past 2 weeks. She had been taking antispasmodics and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs with minimal relief. Her medical history included hypertension and diabetes mellitus for 20 years, both well controlled, and a total thyroidectomy with neck dissection for follicular-variant papillary thyroid carcinoma (pathologic stage pT2N1cM0) in 2002, followed by two radioactive iodine ablations for rising serum thyroglobulin levels.

On examination, her vital signs were stable. Abdominal palpation revealed deep tenderness in the epigastrium without masses or organomegaly. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable. The clinical differential diagnosis included chronic pancreatitis, primary pancreatic adenocarcinoma, or metastatic disease.

Laboratory tests showed normal hematological, renal, and liver function tests, normal serum electrolytes, normal thyroid-stimulating hormone and thyroxine levels, and a negative tuberculin test. Serum tumor markers carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) and cancer antigen 19-9 (CA19-9) were within normal limits, but the thyroglobulin level was elevated at 672.8 ng/mL (reference range 5–25 ng/mL).

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen demonstrated decreased enhancement of the neck, body, and tail of the pancreas, with a normal-appearing pancreatic head, and also revealed bilateral multiple pulmonary nodules. Whole-body iodine scintigraphy was nondiagnostic due to lack of iodine avidity. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography revealed a 1.8 × 1.5 cm hypovascular lesion in the neck of the pancreas, with low signal intensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images, no arterial enhancement, and faint delayed enhancement; the lesion abutted and narrowed the superior mesenteric vein below its confluence with the splenic vein, whereas the superior mesenteric artery was unremarkable.

A 33-year-old man presented with a two-year history of a painless right scrotal mass that had grown from the size of a marble to that of a tennis ball. He had no personal or family history of tumors or systemic illness; he smoked one pack of cigarettes daily. Physical examination revealed an oval, smooth, non-tender mass in the right scrotum that was clearly separate from the right testis. There was no inguinal lymphadenopathy. Scrotal ultrasonography showed a 6.9-cm solid right intrascrotal mass displacing the epididymis. Serum tumor markers (AFP, β-HCG, and LDH) were within normal limits. The patient underwent inguinal exploration under spinal anesthesia. Intraoperatively, the mass was found to arise from the parietal layer of the tunica vaginalis and was easily separated from the testis, epididymis, and spermatic cord, with no evidence of infiltration or adhesion. A testis-sparing complete excision of the mass was performed.

A 49-year-old Chinese woman presented for extraction of impacted teeth. Panoramic tomography revealed a well-defined radiolucent lesion at the apex of tooth #32. The lesion was asymptomatic. Extraoral examination was unremarkable. Intraoral examination showed no mucosal lesions, no caries, and no periodontal disease; two enamel defects (“melon seed teeth”) were noted on teeth #21 and #31. Percussion elicited mild discomfort in the left mandibular anterior region. Pulp vitality testing showed all mandibular anterior teeth were vital except tooth #31. An intraoral periapical radiograph demonstrated a radiolucent lesion surrounding the apex of tooth #31, a widened periodontal ligament space, and loss of the lamina dura. Sagittal CBCT images showed intact labial cortical plates at teeth #32 and #33 but erosion of the labial cortex at tooth #31. Coronal CBCT sections revealed mixed radiolucent–radiopaque masses with radiolucent halos around teeth #32, #33, and #41, and a purely radiolucent lesion at the apex of tooth #31.

A 74-year-old man presented with a  left knee pain and lameness. He denied any history of trauma, fever, weight loss, or malaise. On examination, there was no swelling, redness, or warmth over the patella, and the range of motion of the left knee was 0° to 110°. A prior plain radiograph showed radiolucent, osteolytic shadows on the anterior and medial aspects of the patella. MRI demonstrated a 1.5 × 2 × 1 cm mass on the anterior and medial surfaces of the patella with low signal intensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images and marked enhancement after gadolinium administration. CT confirmed osteolytic changes on the anterior and medial patellar surfaces.

An 82-year-old man with atrial fibrillation (status post ablation), atrial flutter, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes, and coronary artery disease status post coronary artery bypass grafting presented with progressive shortness of breath. He denied cough, chest pain, or fever. Physical examination revealed mild lower extremity swelling. Vital signs were: blood pressure 156/78 mmHg, pulse 70/min, respiratory rate 16/min, temperature 36.3 °C, and SpO₂ 97% on room air. His BMI was 29.5 kg/m².

Laboratory studies showed microcytic anemia and chronic thrombocytopenia; electrolytes and urinalysis were normal. Hepatitis C serology was negative. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated normal left ventricular systolic function (LVEF 60–65%) with only trace valvular regurgitations. A 12-lead ECG showed atrial flutter with 4:1 AV conduction. Chest radiography revealed a large right pleural effusion with associated atelectasis. CT of the chest confirmed a moderate right pleural effusion without discrete pulmonary masses.

The patient underwent right video-assisted thoracoscopic pleural biopsy, talc pleurodesis, and placement of an indwelling pleural catheter, draining 2300 mL of serosanguinous fluid. Pleural biopsy histology showed dense fibrous tissue, chronic inflammation, lymphoid aggregates, and granulation tissue. Immunohistochemical stains demonstrated a mixed T-cell (CD3, CD5, CD43) and B-cell (CD20) population; CD10 and BCL1 were negative, BCL6 was focally positive, BCL2 highlighted T cells, CD21 highlighted follicular dendritic networks, HHV-8 was negative, and Ki-67 was low (<10%). Flow cytometry on the biopsy specimen showed no monoclonal B-cell or aberrant T-cell populations. Cultures of pleural fluid were sterile.

Cytologic examination of the pleural fluid revealed large atypical lymphoid cells with irregular nuclei, prominent nucleoli, coarse chromatin, and moderate cytoplasm; some cells had plasmacytoid features. Immunohistochemistry on the fluid cells showed positivity for CD45, CD20, PAX-5, MUM-1, BCL6, BCL2, and MYC with a high proliferation index (Ki-67 >80%), and negativity for CD3, CD10, CD138, and HHV-8.

A 65-year-old Japanese woman was referred after an incidental finding on surveillance imaging. Two years earlier, she had undergone left adrenalectomy and nephrectomy for adrenocortical carcinoma. She was asymptomatic. Medical and family histories were negative for liver disease.

On examination, she appeared well; vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory tests were unremarkable. Serologic tests for hepatitis B and C were negative. Alpha-fetoprotein and des-γ-carboxy prothrombin levels were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed a heterogeneous, ring-enhancing 11-mm mass in the right hepatic lobe. Dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI of the abdomen showed a 16-mm lesion with cystic and solid components containing fat. The solid portions exhibited arterial enhancement with rapid washout on T1-weighted images. Opposed-phase imaging demonstrated signal drop consistent with lipid. There were no signs of cirrhosis, and no other intraabdominal or retroperitoneal masses were identified.

Given the imaging characteristics but absence of cirrhosis and viral hepatitis, hepatocellular carcinoma was considered unlikely. In light of her history, metastasis of adrenocortical carcinoma was suspected. A laparoscopic partial hepatectomy was planned for definitive diagnosis and treatment.

A 54-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a left thyroid mass discovered incidentally during a routine health examination. One year earlier, she had undergone rectectomy and lymph node dissection for moderately differentiated rectal tubular adenocarcinoma, staged as T3N1M0; she declined adjuvant chemotherapy. She had no history of neck irradiation. On examination, there were no palpable cervical lymph nodes. A firm, 1.3 cm × 1.0 cm nodule was noted in the left thyroid lobe; the right side was unremarkable. Thyroid function tests, calcitonin, carbohydrate antigen 19-9, and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels were all within normal limits. Neck ultrasonography showed a 1.17 cm × 1.25 cm × 1.03 cm irregular hypoechoic nodule with rich peripheral blood flow in the lower pole of the left thyroid; there was no lymphadenopathy. Under ultrasound guidance, fine-needle aspiration (FNA) was performed with three passes using a 23-gauge needle. Cytology was reported as “suspicious for malignancy.”

A 4-month-old girl was referred for a 2-week history of cloudiness and redness in the left eye. Her medical history, including pregnancy and birth, was unremarkable, and the parents denied any history of trauma or signs of allergy. On examination, the left intraocular pressure was 40 mm Hg (right eye 16 mm Hg), with mild corneal edema and a primary hyphema up to the pupillary edge, which later formed a pseudohypopyon; slight anisocoria and heterochromia (left green, right blue) were noted. Treatment with topical acetazolamide, timolol, and steroids lowered the left IOP to 16 mm Hg and regressed the hyphema. Ten days later, a suspicious yellow-brown, irregularly vascularized mass appeared on the inferior iris. Under general anesthesia, ultrasound biomicroscopy (35 MHz) showed multiple nodular irregular hyperreflective lesions in the peripheral iris between 2 and 7 o’clock, extending into the anterior chamber angle and toward the corneal endothelium; the iris pigment epithelium was intact and the ciliary body uninvolved. Fluorescein angiography revealed slight late-phase staining. Posterior-segment examination and B-scan echography showed no vitreous, retinal, choroidal, or optic nerve lesions, thus ruling out retinoblastoma. A yellowish-brown papule on the abdomen was excised and submitted for histology. Histologic examination revealed a dense dermal infiltrate of histiocytes, lymphocytes, and plasma cells without Touton giant cells; immunohistochemistry was positive for CD68 and negative for CD1a and S100, and a malignant lymphoma was excluded.

A 40-year-old woman from southern Nepal presented with a 5-year history of progressive, painless enlargement of her left breast. She denied nipple discharge, skin changes, fever, weight loss, trauma, hormonal medication, and had no family history of breast cancer. Menstrual cycles were regular. On examination, the left breast contained a well-defined, soft mass measuring 34×26×6 cm with dilated surface veins; the overlying skin, nipple, and areola were normal, and there was no axillary lymphadenopathy. The right breast was unremarkable. Ultrasonography showed a homogeneously hyperechoic mass deep to the breast and pectoralis major muscle without cystic areas, calcifications, or internal vascularity, and no axillary lymph node enlargement. Mammography revealed a heterogeneous lucent mass in the left retromammary region involving the pectoralis muscle, with benign calcifications in both breasts. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-defined, homogeneous T1- and T2-hyperintense mass measuring approximately 15×13×10.2 cm that suppressed on fat-suppressed sequences, was encapsulated with multiple thin septa, and showed no thoracic extension or bony erosion. A core biopsy was not performed because the clinical and imaging findings were consistent with a benign lesion.

A 73-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of sudden onset left-sided weakness of the lower facial nerve. She had slightly weak movement of the mouth on maximal effort (House–Brackmann grade III) but normal eyelid closure and forehead motion. She denied systemic symptoms. Her medical history included hypertension and a remote right-thalamic ischemic event with no residual deficits. She took metoprolol, ramipril, hydrochlorothiazide, and aspirin. She was a lifelong non smoker and nondrinker. 

On examination, only the left marginal mandibular branch was affected; all other cranial-nerve and neurologic findings were normal. Vital signs were within normal limits. A noncontrast head CT, performed to exclude a central lesion, showed multiple masses in the left parotid gland. Laboratory studies, including inflammatory markers, electrolytes, blood counts, liver and renal function tests, and borreliosis serology, were unremarkable. 

High-resolution ultrasound demonstrated multiple round, well-defined, hypoechoic lesions along the course of the left mandible without a hilar structure, hypervascularization, or intranodal reticulation. MRI of the head without contrast confirmed multiple masses in the left parotid gland tracking along the facial nerve.

An 80-year-old man presented with progressive fatigue of one month’s duration. He had a five-year history of interstitial pneumonia but no smoking, drinking, or significant comorbidities. On examination, temperature was 36.5 °C, pulse 76/min, respirations 19/min, blood pressure 130/80 mmHg. Lung auscultation revealed coarse breath sounds with scattered wet and dry rales. There was mild anemia, a large ecchymosis on the left thigh, and sternal tenderness. Abdominal examination showed no hepatosplenomegaly.

Laboratory studies showed:  
• White-cell count 324.06×10^9/L with neutrophils 285.38×10^9/L; hemoglobin 100 g/L; platelets 102×10^9/L.  
• Fibrinogen 0.6 g/L (normal 2–4 g/L); prothrombin activity 46.1% (normal 80–120%).  
• Urea 9.7 mmol/L; creatinine 169.3 μmol/L; uric acid 844 μmol/L.  
• Procalcitonin 0.701 ng/mL; respiratory pathogen antibodies negative.  
• Urinalysis: occult blood 1+; protein 1+; ferritin >1650 ng/mL.  
• Autoantibodies including anti-neutrophil antibodies, G/GM, and stool studies were unremarkable.

Peripheral blood smear revealed >80% mature neutrophils with rod-shaped and lobulated nuclei; immature granulocytes <10%; no blasts or dysplastic forms. Bone marrow aspiration showed marked granulocytic hyperplasia, rare erythroids, no increase in eosinophils or megakaryocytes. Reticulin stain was positive (MF-1 fibrosis). Karyotype analysis was normal.

An 81-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, coronary artery disease (status post CABG), atrial fibrillation on warfarin, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and diabetes mellitus presented with two weeks of worsening dyspnea. One week prior to admission, he developed orthopnea and persistent shortness of breath. He also reported spontaneous epistaxis over the past week and a single episode of sharp left-sided abdominal pain two weeks earlier that resolved without intervention.

On arrival, he was afebrile, tachycardic, tachypneic, and hypoxic to 83% on room air. Physical examination showed no focal neurologic deficits; further exam details were not reported.

Initial laboratory studies revealed WBC 21,500/mm3 with 5% atypical lymphocytes and 22% bands, hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, platelets 42,000/μL, INR 4.4, PT 40.9 s, APTT 46.3 s, creatinine 3.4 mg/dL (baseline 1.5 mg/dL), total protein 6.5 g/dL, albumin 3.2 g/dL, AST 310 U/L, ALT 22 U/L, uric acid > 30 mg/dL, and LDH 12,851 U/L. Calcium was normal. Serum free light chains showed kappa 13,889 mg/L with a kappa/lambda ratio of 491.5. No M-spike was detected. HIV testing was negative, and EBV serology was consistent with prior exposure (IgM negative, IgG positive).

He rapidly required intubation for hypoxemic respiratory failure. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis without contrast showed extensive mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy up to 2 cm in size, increased since imaging six months prior, and no lytic bone lesions.

A 45-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of a gingival growth on the right anterior mandible and intermittent pain for the past 6–7 months. The lesion began small and gradually enlarged, displacing adjacent teeth. His general health was unremarkable.

Extraoral examination revealed a tender, diffuse 1.5 × 1.5 cm swelling on the right lower face with normal overlying skin. Intraorally, there was a roughly circular, firm, 3.5 × 3.5 cm exophytic mass on the interdental gingiva between the right canine and first premolar, extending from the attached gingiva to the lingual sulcus. The surface was pebbled with indentations matching the opposing teeth; the mucosal color was normal. Adjacent teeth were vital but tender, with grade I mobility. No cortical expansion was evident.

A periapical radiograph showed a multilocular “soap bubble” radiolucency at the canine and first premolar, with knife-edge root resorption of the premolar. A panoramic radiograph revealed a 4 × 4 cm radiolucency extending from the distal lateral incisor to the mesial second premolar. An occlusal film confirmed no cortical expansion. Routine blood tests and serum chemistries were within normal limits.

A 56-year-old Caucasian man with a 60–pack-year smoking history and obstructive sleep apnea presented with two months of progressive abdominal distention and painless right testicular swelling. On examination, he had tense ascites and a firm, enlarged right testis. Laboratory tests revealed a normal complete blood count and biochemistry but an elevated serum CA 125 level of 319 μ/mL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen showed minimal left pleural effusion, diffuse peritoneal fluid, and peritoneal implants. Upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopic examinations revealed no abnormalities. Scrotal ultrasound demonstrated an enlarged right epididymis and a small hydrocele. Diagnostic paracentesis yielded exudative fluid containing neoplastic signet-ring cells.  
 
The patient underwent surgical exploration of the right scrotum. Grossly, multiple poorly defined, whitish, firm foci were noted throughout the testicular parenchyma, epididymis, and spermatic cord, with thickening of the tunicae. Microscopically, the lesion was a poorly differentiated carcinoma composed of signet-ring cells with abundant intracytoplasmic mucin (PAS and Alcian Blue positive), as well as perineural and vascular invasion. Immunohistochemical staining showed tumor cells diffusely positive for cytokeratin 20 and EMA, focally positive for cytokeratin 7, CEA, and c-kit (CD117), and negative for PLAP, α-fetoprotein, CD30, inhibin, calretinin, PSA, p504S (AMACR), TTF-1, and Melan A. Tissue HER2 staining was negative.

A 54-year-old Japanese man, with no significant past medical or surgical history, was found on a routine abdominal ultrasound to have an incidental solid mass in the abdominal cavity. He was asymptomatic and had no abdominal pain, ascites, or other lesions on whole-body evaluation. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a solitary 3 cm mass in the greater omentum adjacent to the posterior gastric and transverse colonic walls. The patient underwent an open laparotomy because malignancy could not be excluded clinically and biopsy risked tumor dissemination. Intraoperatively, a solitary omental tumor was identified without adhesion to adjacent organs. The resected lesion measured 27 × 25 × 20 mm, and on cut section was grayish-white, heterogeneous, and firm, with no calcification or necrosis. Histologically, the tumor was composed of spindle cells arranged in whorls and fascicles; individual cells had short spindle-shaped nuclei with mild chromatin increase and eosinophilic cytoplasm. There was no necrosis, no hyalinization, no abundant blood vessels, and the mitotic count was less than 1 per 50 high-power fields.

A 54-year-old Cuban man with emphysema and a 105–pack-year smoking history presented in April 2012 with recurrence of a mass on his right upper back. The lesion had first appeared in October 2011 and been excised in Cuba. On examination, there were multiple satellite nodules in the right axilla and palpable right axillary lymphadenopathy. In October 2012, a biopsy of the recurrent back mass was reported as a grade 2/3 malignant granular cell tumor, composed of aggregates and sheets of intermediate-size spindle and polyhedral cells with granular eosinophilic cytoplasm; vesicular nuclei with nucleoli; five mitoses per high-power field; and foci of necrosis. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for S100 and CD68 and negative for keratin, EMA, CD34, MART1, and synaptophysin; the Ki-67 proliferation index was 25%. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest demonstrated recurrence of the primary lesion involving skin and muscle, a large right axillary mass with lymphadenopathy, and multiple pulmonary nodules concerning for metastases. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed an ill-defined hypodense intramuscular lesion in the right upper thigh, and a CT-guided biopsy confirmed metastatic malignant granular cell tumor.

A 57-year-old man noted a painless right testicular mass one month earlier during self-examination. He had no history of tuberous sclerosis complex or prior tumors. On examination, the mass was firm without overlying skin changes. Vital signs were normal. 

Pelvic MRI demonstrated a well-circumscribed, 10-mm mass confined to the right testis with no evidence of lymphadenopathy or distant metastases. Laboratory studies, including tumor markers (AFP, β-hCG, LDH), were within normal limits.

The patient underwent a right radical orchiectomy. Grossly, the lesion was a 1.0-cm, well-demarcated, solid, yellow-tan fleshy nodule.

Microscopically, the tumor infiltrated minimally into adjacent testicular parenchyma and was composed of epithelioid cells arranged in nests and sheets separated by delicate fibrovascular septa. Many cells showed marked nuclear atypia, pleomorphism, and abundant granular eosinophilic to clear cytoplasm. Multinucleated giant cells and “spider-like” cells were present. No necrosis was identified, and the mitotic count was up to 2 per 10 high-power fields.

Immunohistochemical staining revealed the tumor cells were strongly positive for cathepsin K, HMB-45, and TFE3, and negative for PAX8, AE1/AE3, EMA, CD10, CK7, CK20, calretinin, inhibin, Melan A, S100, SMA, desmin, and others. The Ki-67 proliferation index was approximately 5%.

A 41-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of postprandial upper-quadrant abdominal pain. He had no other symptoms. Routine blood tests were normal. Endocrinological assays, including plasma catecholamines and 24-hour urinary catecholamines, showed no significant alterations. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 17×12-cm mass in the right adrenal region with an attenuation of –20 Hounsfield units and a 2.3×2.5-cm lesion in the left adrenal gland with –5 Hounsfield units. MRI confirmed bilateral adrenal masses containing predominantly fat with multiple septa.

A 63-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 3-month history of progressive dyspnea, hacking cough, and distended neck veins. Seven years earlier, he had been diagnosed with early polycythemia vera (JAK2 V617F–positive) and treated with hydroxyurea. He denied fever, weight loss, or night sweats. 

On examination, he had a facial rash with periorbital and facial edema, bilateral obliteration of the supraclavicular fossae, prominent jugular venous distension, and mild right-sided ptosis. Neurologic examination was otherwise normal, and there were no signs of Horner syndrome or phrenic nerve involvement. A firm 3-cm mass was palpable over the right sixth rib.

Laboratory studies showed relative lymphocytosis (17.5%), absolute lymphocyte count 1.57×10^3/μL, lactate dehydrogenase 423 U/L, C-reactive protein 1.8 mg/dL, fibrinogen 414 mg/dL, immunoglobulin A 549 mg/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 27 mm/h, and β2-microglobulin 2.6 mg/dL. Serologic tests were negative for hepatitis C virus, HHV8, and HIV, and positive for hepatitis B core IgG and for EBV.

Chest radiography revealed upper mediastinal widening with rightward tracheal deviation. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a 9.7×8.0×5.7 cm polylobulated anterior–middle mediastinal mass compressing the right internal jugular vein and superior vena cava, along with a chest wall lesion of similar appearance. One month later, the mediastinal mass had enlarged to 12×14×7.5 cm. Ultrasound of the neck showed nonocclusive thrombosis of the right internal jugular vein despite anticoagulation, with a patent left vein.

A percutaneous ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the mediastinal mass and resection of the chest wall lesion were performed under local anesthesia, and samples were sent for histopathology and immunophenotyping.

A 53-year-old Hispanic man presented with painful left lower-extremity swelling and erythema. Six months earlier, incidentally noted bilateral adrenal and periaortic retroperitoneal masses were not further evaluated. He reported intermittent fevers, episodic night sweats, decreased appetite, and palpitations. He denied trauma or injury to the leg. On examination, the left calf had ill-defined, warm, confluent erythema, edema, and tender induration. Laboratory studies showed mild lymphocytopenia, moderate anemia, elevated creatine kinase, elevated aldolase, and elevated lactate dehydrogenase; peripheral-blood flow cytometry was unremarkable. CT and MRI of the leg revealed gastrocnemius myositis, extensive subcutaneous and superficial myofascial edema, and popliteal lymphadenopathy without evident lymphatic obstruction. He was started on intravenous ceftriaxone for presumed cellulitis and pyomyositis but did not improve. A punch biopsy of skin from the lower leg showed a sparse perivascular and interstitial infiltrate of enlarged atypical mononuclear cells in the reticular dermis and subcutis, not consistent with cellulitis.

A 5‐year‐9‐month‐old, 170‐kg domestic llama mare was referred for a 1‐week history of dyspnea and inspiratory noise. The owner reported that an esophageal obstruction had been suspected by the referring veterinarian, but spasmolytics and passage of a gastric tube did not improve the signs. On presentation, the llama was bright, alert, in good condition (body‐condition score 3.5/5) with normal vital signs. In the middle third of the ventral cervical region, there was a 10 × 8 × 3‐cm subcutaneous mass that was partially firm and fluctuant, slightly painful, and mildly warm; the overlying skin appeared normal. No dysphagia, other masses, or lymphadenopathy were detected. A CBC showed mild leukocytosis (23,690/µL; reference 8,700–17,500/µL) with neutrophilia (92.4%; reference 42.4–76.4%) and lymphopenia (3.0%; reference 7.0–32.5%); eosinophils were decreased; hematocrit was 39.8% (reference 27.0–39.0%), MCV was mildly increased, and MCHC was mildly decreased. Flexible endoscopy of the esophagus and trachea under sedation revealed no abnormalities. Cervical ultrasonography showed a well‐demarcated, heterogeneously echogenic, encapsulated mass with no communication with the trachea or esophagus and no intrinsic vascular flow. Thoracic and cervical radiographs demonstrated a ventral soft‐tissue‐density mass in the mid‐to‐caudal cervical region causing a mild mass effect on the trachea; no pulmonary lesions or further abnormalities were noted.

A 54-year-old man presented with 4 days of diffuse abdominal pain and distention. The pain began in the epigastrium, became generalized, and was associated with nausea but no vomiting or jaundice. He reported a 4-kg weight loss over 3 months. He drank alcohol only rarely, did not smoke, and had no pertinent family history.

On examination, his blood pressure was 120/60 mmHg, pulse 75/min, respiratory rate 21/min, and temperature 37.7°C. There were no stigmata of biliary obstruction; palpation elicited diffuse abdominal tenderness.

Laboratory studies showed normal serum amylase, lipase, and IgG4 levels. Tumor markers were elevated: CA19-9 at 69.6 U/mL (normal ≤37 U/mL) and CA242 at 82.1 U/mL (normal ≤20 U/mL). Bilirubin, alpha-fetoprotein, and HBsAg were within normal limits.

Abdominal ultrasound revealed a diffusely enlarged, heterogeneous, hypoechoic pancreas with slight peripancreatic fat infiltration and no fluid collection. The liver contained multiple solid hypo- or hyperechoic masses.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed diffuse enlargement of the pancreas with relatively homogeneous enhancement in the arterial phase and washout on delayed images. Multiple liver lesions demonstrated early arterial enhancement with delayed washout, suggestive of hypervascular metastases. The pancreatic duct and biliary tract were not dilated, and there were no pathological lymph nodes.

MRI confirmed a diffusely enlarged pancreas with low signal on T1-weighted images, heterogeneous high signal on T2-weighted images, restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging, and relatively homogeneous enhancement on postcontrast T1-weighted images. Multiple hepatic lesions had imaging characteristics similar to those seen on CT.

A 58-year-old woman presented with a long history of intermittent paresthesias and dysesthesias of the left heel and dorsolateral foot, each episode lasting minutes to an hour and precipitated by walking, sitting, or running. Over time, she noted similar symptoms in the left distal lower extremity, thigh, pelvis, and ulnar distribution of the left hand. On initial neurologic examination, there was patchy reduction of sensation in the left lower limb with preserved vibration sense, no motor weakness or atrophy, and a negative Lhermitte sign. A thoracic and lumbar spine radiograph demonstrated minor spondyloarthritic changes at L4–L5 and L5–S1, and lumbar CT showed no disc herniation or protrusion. Multiple sclerosis was considered unlikely given the long‐standing fluctuating course in the absence of central nervous system lesions. Given the abrupt onset and patchy distribution, Wartenberg’s migratory sensory neuropathy was initially suspected, and other considerations included hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies, insertional tendinopathy, radiculopathy, and restless‐leg syndrome. When small involuntary jerks appeared in the right periorbital region, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis was excluded, and electrophysiologic studies failed to reveal peripheral neuropathy. A psychiatric evaluation attributed her symptoms to panic attacks and hyperventilation, and she was started on paroxetine. At a subsequent outpatient visit, examination revealed a mild central left facial palsy, slight hyperreflexia on the left, hypesthesia and hypoalgesia in the left S1 dermatome, and left orbital myokymia. Based on these findings, a cranial and cervical MRI was obtained.

A 5-year-old girl underwent a routine physical examination, which revealed a hard, non-tender, palpable mass in the right abdomen. She had no urinary symptoms, flank pain, hematuria, or systemic complaints. Ultrasonography identified a mass in the right kidney. Laboratory studies were notable only for an elevated carbohydrate antigen 19-9 level of 128.4 U/mL (reference <25); other tumor markers and blood counts were normal. Noncontrast CT showed a well-circumscribed right renal mass with multiple internal high-density calcifications. On contrast-enhanced CT, the lesion demonstrated marked enhancement in the cortical phase and decreased enhancement in the medullary phase. MRI confirmed significant cortical enhancement with washout in the delayed phase.

A 56-year-old woman noted a slightly painful, noninflammatory mass in her right breast one month ago. She denied trauma and reported no growth of the mass. On examination, there was a firm, mobile, tender mass with a clear boundary.  
Ultrasound revealed a 35×36×34 mm hypoechoic, irregular mass with poorly defined borders and a hyperechoic halo; color Doppler showed peripheral blood‐flow signals.  
Mammography (craniocaudal and mediolateral oblique views) demonstrated a 38×42 mm dense, lobulated, spiculated mass without obvious internal calcification; surrounding vessels were compressed, and a few enlarged axillary lymph nodes were noted bilaterally.  
Digital breast tomosynthesis showed a clear sclerotic border around the mass.

A 49-year-old woman presented with progressive lower abdominal pain. Four months earlier, ovarian enlargement had been noted on routine ultrasonography that revealed a 12×12 cm solid polycystic mass in the lower abdomen. Her medical history was significant only for depression; her father had prostate cancer. Laboratory testing showed a CA-125 level of 42 U/mL (normal, 0–35). Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 13 cm mass with both solid and cystic components, ill-defined dorsal margin, internal septations, and a mesenteric vein at its periphery. MRI showed heterogeneous signal in the solid portion on T1- and T2-weighted images with restricted diffusion (ADC, 1.04×10^−3 mm^2/s). The uterus appeared normal except for typical leiomyomas, and both ovaries were normal. FDG-PET/CT showed uptake in the solid component (SUVmax, 4.5 at 1 h and 5.9 at 2 h) without evidence of metastasis. A mesenteric malignancy was suspected and laparotomy was performed. Intraoperatively, the uterus and ovaries were intact and the mass was confirmed to arise from the mesentery; it was completely resected without evidence of metastasis or dissemination.

A 62-year-old woman with no comorbid conditions presented with a 1-year history of recurrent vomiting, bloatedness, and weight loss. She denied fever or changes in bowel habits and had no family history of malignancy. Prior evaluations, including a complete blood count, bleeding parameters, and serum electrolytes, were normal. An abdominal CT scan without contrast showed a long segment of wall thickening from the third part of the duodenum to the proximal jejunum, and was interpreted as partial small-bowel obstruction secondary to enteritis of unknown etiology. She was referred for single-balloon enteroscopy, which revealed a normal upper GI tract to D2, poorly distensible mucosa in D3, and purplish discoloration of the mucosa from D4 through the proximal jejunum over 15–20 cm. Biopsies showed focal mild cryptitis and mildly dilated mucosal capillaries without dysplasia. Based on these findings, an endoscopic diagnosis of ischemic enteritis was made and mesenteric CT angiography was obtained. Angiography demonstrated circumferential wall thickening of the duodenum to jejunum and fullness in the pancreatic head and uncinate process that encased the superior mesenteric artery. A serum CA19-9 level was elevated at 1209 U/mL (normal 0.55–1.47).

A 57-year-old Caucasian man presented for evaluation of a 5-year history of recurrent paronychia and a persistent subcutaneous mass with nail deformity at the ulnar side of the distal phalanx of the right fourth digit. His medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease on long-term steroids, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, and impaired fasting glucose. On examination, there was a hemipincer nail on the ulnar side of the right fourth digit with tenderness, swelling, and erythema at the skin–nail junction; the adjacent subcutaneous mass was painless. Slight asymptomatic proximal interphalangeal joint hyperextension was noted, with full active extension at the distal interphalangeal joint. Range of motion, sensation, and vascular examination of the digit were unremarkable, and there was no lymphadenopathy in the elbow or axilla. A three-view radiograph of the digit showed no evidence of osteomyelitis but revealed a subtle bony erosion at the ulnar distal phalanx adjacent to a soft tissue shadow; the soft tissue density was similar to the contralateral digit without calcifications. MRI of the hand demonstrated a deep subcutaneous mass adjacent to the distal phalanx. Given persistent symptoms and concern for underlying pathology, a marginal excisional biopsy of the mass with culture and partial nail bed ablation was performed.

Seventeen patients (7 men and 10 women; mean age, 35 years) presented between 2015 and 2023 with up to 1 year of chronic pain, deformity, and discoloration beneath the nails of their fingers. All reported a history of local trauma to the affected digit. Systemic diseases (eg, diabetes, hypertension) were absent. On examination, each patient had a tender subungual lesion, with 29.5% exhibiting nail-bed discoloration, 23.5% showing nail deformity, and 41.2% demonstrating underlying distal phalanx bone involvement on physical assessment. Imaging studies—including plain radiography (anteroposterior and lateral views) and T1-weighted CT scans of the affected digits—were obtained to characterize the size, location, and extent of the lesions.

A 74-year-old Caucasian man, a former heavy smoker (75 pack-years), presented with a 3-month history of significant weight loss. He had undergone radical prostatectomy with bilateral iliac lymphadenectomy and vesiculectomy five years earlier for Gleason 9 (4+5) prostate adenocarcinoma (pT3b) and received adjuvant pelvic radiotherapy. His last oncologic follow-up two years post-treatment showed no relapse. He denied respiratory symptoms, and physical examination was unremarkable with no lymphadenopathy or masses. Laboratory studies, including markers of inflammation, were within normal limits. Chest CT revealed multiple bilateral pulmonary lesions, some with excavated appearances: an 18×16 mm nodule in the right upper lobe and a 19×12 mm nodule in the posterobasal segment of the right lower lobe. A PET–CT with fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) showed no increased uptake in these lesions. Initial diagnostic hypotheses included a mycobacterial infection or systemic autoimmune lung disease. A tuberculin skin test was negative, and video-bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and bronchoaspirate was performed to exclude infection. Autoimmune serologies (ANCA, ANA, ENA, and rheumatoid factor) were negative.

A 44-year-old man presented with a 10-year history of a slowly enlarging intraoral swelling on the soft palate. Over time, he developed progressive difficulty swallowing, snoring, and speech disturbance but denied pain, bleeding, fevers, night sweats, or prior trauma. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender, well-circumscribed, faintly lobulated mass measuring 9.4 × 7.9 × 8.3 cm on the soft palate, extending to the uvula and anterior tonsillar pillars; the overlying mucosa was smooth and intact, and there was no cervical lymphadenopathy. Vital signs and routine laboratory studies were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck showed a well-circumscribed, encapsulated solid soft-palate mass with prominent internal vessels and no bony invasion. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the lesion was suggestive of pleomorphic adenoma. The working diagnosis was pleomorphic adenoma, with carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma, polymorphous adenocarcinoma, and epithelial myoepithelial carcinoma in the differential diagnosis.

A 64-year-old white man was admitted in March 2016 with acute-onset abdominal pain and anemia. He had been on therapeutic anticoagulation for paroxysmal “pre-shimmering.” His history included two hypervascular liver lesions in segment IV, first noted in August 2015; biopsies at that time showed histologically proven adenoma without malignancy. On presentation, he was hemodynamically stable but had a hemoglobin level of 4.4 mmol/L. He reported no weight loss, fever, or constitutional symptoms. Laboratory studies showed α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels within normal ranges; serum human chorionic gonadotropin was not measured. Abdominal ultrasound revealed subcapsular hepatic bleeding. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed active bleeding from one of the two hypervascular lesions in segment IV. After angiographic embolization and conservative management, bleeding resolved. In April 2016, follow-up CT showed persistent hypervascular lesions without typical features of hepatocellular carcinoma. Additional MRI demonstrated hypervascular lesions with central necrosis. Because of suspicion for an atypical hepatocellular carcinoma, an elective surgical resection was planned.

A 13-year-old boy presented with a 3-month history of a right flank mass and occasional dull, localized pain. He also had intermittent episodes of painless hematuria but no fever, urinary tract infection, anorexia, or weight loss. On examination, there was an 8 × 6 cm firm, mobile mass in the right lumbar and hypochondrial regions that crossed the midline. Laboratory investigations were within normal limits. Renal ultrasonography showed a 10.2 × 9.4 × 10.3 cm heteroechoic nodular mass in the right kidney with calcifications and vascular invasion. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 9.6 × 7.8 cm heterogeneously enhancing soft-tissue mass in the mid and lower pole of the right kidney with patchy calcifications encasing the inferior mesenteric artery and vein. The left kidney had multiple hypodense lesions in the lower pole and a large left para-aortic lymph node; bilateral cortical cysts were also noted. There was no inferior vena cava thrombus. Chest CT was normal. An ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy demonstrated tumor cells arranged in tubules within a mucoid matrix. Immunohistochemistry revealed positivity for vimentin and epithelial membrane antigen and negativity for CD10, CK-7, and CK-19. No high-grade mitotic activity, malignant features, or sarcomatoid histology were seen.

A 69-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an intracardiac mass. In 2008, an abnormal chest radiograph led to transthoracic echocardiography, which revealed a calcified, immobile mass on the posterior mitral valve leaflet. Her history was notable for pulmonary tuberculosis in childhood and systemic hypertension; there was no history of infective endocarditis, chest trauma, or hypercoagulable states. She underwent echocardiographic follow-up every 6 months. In March 2011, she reported chest discomfort and was admitted in October 2011. On transthoracic echocardiography, a calcified mass measuring 19×8 mm was located between the P2 and P3 segments of the posterior mitral leaflet; there was no mitral regurgitation, the ejection fraction was 67%, and there were no findings suggestive of infective endocarditis. Coronary angiography showed intact coronary arteries without thrombo-occlusive lesions. Non–contrast and contrast-enhanced cardiac CT confirmed a severely calcified mass on the posterior mitral leaflet with a hypodense central area. Laboratory test results were unremarkable.

A 25-year-old woman presented with a 6-year history of lower back and right lower quadrant abdominal pain and progressive numbness of the anterior right leg after walking short distances. She had no fever, trauma, weight loss, or significant medical or family history. On examination, there was a large palpable mass over the right iliac wing protruding inward toward the psoas muscle; the abdomen was non-tender and the rest of the exam was normal. Abdominal CT and MRI showed a well-marginated exophytic mass arising from the superior-medial aspect of the right iliac crest, approximately 7 cm in diameter, with no obvious cortical destruction, a narrow short continuity of the ilium’s medullary canal at the lesion base, intramedullary and soft-tissue edema, and contrast enhancement. The lesion exerted a mass effect on the right psoas muscle.

A 26-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a several-week history of progressive left-sided headache and, more recently, visual impairment of the left eye. She was alert and oriented, with no other complaints. On examination, confrontation testing revealed a right homonymous quadrantanopia; fundoscopic examination was normal. Noncontrast CT of the head showed a 5.6 × 3.8 cm hypodense mass in the left occipital lobe without enhancement on postcontrast CT. MRI demonstrated a heterogeneous intra-axial lesion in the left occipital lobe that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences, with mild heterogeneous central enhancement and no peripheral enhancement on gadolinium T1-weighted imaging. Diffusion-weighted imaging showed no restriction, and the lesion had increased ADC relative to normal parenchyma. Susceptibility-weighted imaging revealed punctate hypointense foci consistent with small hemorrhages. There was no peritumoral edema. Careful review noted that the lesion was adjacent to the occipital and atrial portions of the left lateral ventricle.

A 64-year-old man with hypertension and hyperlipidemia presented with one week of progressive shortness of breath and a near-syncopal episode, accompanied by blurry vision. He also reported several weeks of melena, two months of fatigue, and mild unintentional weight loss. He took daily aspirin, had a normal colonoscopy one year ago, and denied smoking or significant alcohol or drug use.  
Vital signs: T 98.2 °F, HR 91 bpm, RR 20/min, BP 124/55 mmHg, SpO₂ 98% on room air. Physical exam showed a soft, non-tender abdomen with normoactive bowel sounds; remainder unremarkable.  
Laboratory tests revealed hemoglobin 5.4 g/dL, MCV 78.6 fL, RDW 17.5%, BUN 33 mg/dL (BUN/Cr ratio 24), glucose 141 mg/dL, and D-dimer 2070 ng/mL. Chest radiograph was normal. CT pulmonary angiography excluded pulmonary embolism. Abdominopelvic CT showed non-obstructing, moderately prominent jejunal wall thickening without significant inflammation or adenopathy.  
He was transfused 3 units of packed red cells, started on IV pantoprazole, and underwent esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD), which found linear erosions in the gastric fundus and a small hiatal hernia; biopsies were taken. Given ongoing anemia and unrevealing upper endoscopy, outpatient video capsule endoscopy (VCE) was performed, revealing two small-bowel masses: a proximal hemorrhagic lesion causing capsule retention, and a second distal mass with abnormal mucosa.  
He was readmitted, transfused further, and IV pantoprazole resumed. Push enteroscopy localized a mid-distal duodenal hemorrhagic mass (marked with clip and tattoo) and a non-bleeding jejunal lesion with abnormal mucosa. Surgical consultation was obtained for possible segmental small-bowel resection.

An 81-year-old Japanese woman presented with a 2-week history of abdominal distension. Her medical history was notable only for a cesarean section; there was no prior malignancy. Laboratory studies, including carcinoembryonic antigen, squamous cell carcinoma antigen, and cytokeratin-19 fragment levels, were within normal limits.

Upper endoscopy revealed:  
• A mildly granular elevated lesion with slightly depressed, irregular mucosa extending along the distal esophagus.  
• A separate 10-mm superficial elevated tumor in the lower body of the stomach.

Biopsy results:  
• Gastric lesion: well-differentiated tubular adenocarcinoma.  
• Esophageal lesion: intraepithelial clusters of large clear cells with atypical nuclei and prominent nucleoli; no glandular structures or intracellular mucin. Differential diagnoses included malignant melanoma, pagetoid spread of adenocarcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma, and Paget’s disease.

Immunohistochemistry of the esophageal cells showed:  
• Diffuse positivity for CK7 and partial positivity for CK20.  
• Negative staining for S100 protein and HMB-47 (excluding melanoma).  
• Negative for mucin core proteins MUC2, MUC5AC, and HIK1083.  
• Overexpression of p53 in tumor cells.

Staging imaging with enhanced CT and ^18F-FDG PET/CT revealed no lymph node or distant metastases; FDG uptake was noted only in the gastric region correlating with prior endoscopic submucosal dissection.

How do you integrate these findings into a unifying diagnosis?

A 69-year-old Chinese woman presented with a recently self-detected mass on the left side of her neck. She denied pain, fever, hoarseness, dysphagia, a personal history of thyroid disease, or relevant family history. On examination, there was a firm, well-defined, non-tender mass in the left thyroid lobe that moved with swallowing; no axillary, supraclavicular, or subclavian lymphadenopathy was noted.

Neck ultrasonography revealed a 19 mm × 12 mm × 5 mm nodule with heterogeneous echotexture and a clear boundary within an enlarged left thyroid lobe. Laboratory evaluation showed a normal thyroid-stimulating hormone level (2.66 mIU/L), normal total triiodothyronine (1.73 nmol/L) and thyroxine (104.8 nmol/L) levels, and normal free T3 and T4 levels. Thyroid antibodies were elevated (antithyroid peroxidase antibodies 106.1 IU/mL; antimicrosomal antibodies 382.9 IU/mL; antithyroglobulin antibodies 990 IU/mL). Routine blood counts, serum amylase, glucose, and liver and kidney function tests were within normal limits. Abdominal CT and chest radiography showed no abnormalities.

A 34-year-old man with no significant medical history was referred for evaluation after a routine chest radiograph revealed pulmonary nodules. He was asymptomatic. Vital signs were normal. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed a normal leukocyte count and C-reactive protein level. Tumor markers (CEA, CA19-9, and SCC), β-D glucan, cryptococcal antigen, Aspergillus antibody, and Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) antibody were all within normal limits. Chest radiographs demonstrated multiple nodular opacities in both lung fields, predominantly on the right. Chest CT confirmed multiple nonspecific nodules in both lungs. Abdominal CT revealed multiple nodules scattered throughout the liver. Contrast-enhanced CT of the entire body showed no additional lesions. Upper and lower endoscopies were unremarkable. A percutaneous liver biopsy was non-diagnostic.

A 30-year-old Japanese woman presented with chronic cough and was found incidentally to have a cystic lesion near the pancreas. She had hyperlipidemia but no history of pancreatitis. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies showed no inflammation or anemia; serum amylase, lipase, aminotransferase, and bilirubin were within normal limits. Tumor markers (CEA, CA19-9, AFP) were not elevated. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 5 cm thin-walled, nonenhancing cystic mass abutting the body of the pancreas, left gastric artery, stomach, and abdominal esophagus. MRI showed a multilocular lesion without internal nodules or septations and no communication with the main pancreatic duct. Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated iso- and hypoechoic cyst contents with a thin wall and no mural nodules. No fine-needle aspiration was performed. Differential diagnosis included a mucinous cystic neoplasm, a pancreatic cyst, or a retroperitoneal cystic lymphangioma. The patient was referred for diagnostic laparoscopy.

A 72-year-old man with a history of hypertension and diabetes presented to the emergency department with dysarthria, headache, and a seizure. On admission, his Glasgow Coma Scale score was 9 of 15, and laboratory analyses were unremarkable.

Noncontrast CT of the head revealed an extra-axial, round, hypodense lesion with marginal calcifications in the right frontal bone. There was condensation of the inner table and erosion of the outer table; the lesion measured 19 × 16 mm.

Brain MRI showed a well-demarcated, extra-axial lytic lesion (20 × 15 mm) in the right frontal bone with erosion of the inner table. The lesion was hyperintense on T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and FLAIR sequences, with no enhancement after gadolinium administration. On diffusion-weighted imaging, the lesion was hyperintense with corresponding apparent diffusion coefficient restriction. An adjacent subcutaneous lesion demonstrated similar signal characteristics on all sequences and measured 19 × 9 mm.

A 21-year-old woman, G2P1 at 27 weeks’ gestation, presented with one week of progressive intermittent lower abdominal pain. She denied vaginal bleeding or discharge and reported normal fetal movements. On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs. The abdomen was gravid with a Pfannenstiel scar and was diffusely tender without rebound or guarding; fundal height measured 34 cm. Her obstetric history was notable only for a prior cesarean delivery in 2019. Prenatal care began at 19 weeks’ gestation, with three visits; a first-trimester ultrasound was reportedly normal. Laboratory studies including blood glucose, liver enzymes, renal function tests, and electrolytes were within normal limits. Infectious workup, including urine culture, syphilis test, toxoplasmosis, brucella, and rubella IgM, was negative. Transabdominal ultrasound demonstrated a single live intrauterine fetus with estimated weight 734 g and a normal biophysical profile. A large 5.2 × 7.1 cm mass was noted in the anterior aspect of the fetal neck, containing both solid and cystic components with prominent vascularity, causing hyperextension of the neck. No cardiac, skeletal, or other structural anomalies were identified.

A 51-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of progressive abdominal distension and fatigue. She had no personal or family history of tumors. On examination, a firm mass was palpable from the right subcostal area to the epigastric region. Laboratory studies revealed impaired renal function attributed to inferior vena cava (IVC) compression by the mass; tumor markers were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the trunk showed a hemorrhagic retroperitoneal tumor measuring 22×9×15 cm, compressing the IVC and displacing the portal vein, with enlargement of para-aortic lymph nodes. Whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated intense uptake in the retroperitoneal lesion (SUVmax 8.8) without distant metastases. Endocrinological assays, including blood and 24-hour urine catecholamines and metanephrines, were normal. ¹²³I-MIBG scintigraphy showed no abnormal uptake, effectively excluding catecholamine-secreting tumors.

A 49-year-old Japanese man, with no regular medical care, presented with a 2-month history of progressive fatigue and constipation. Sixteen days before admission, he experienced left abdominal discomfort while sleeping; a noncontrast CT at an outside hospital showed adipose‐tissue turbidity around the left adrenal gland, and the pain resolved spontaneously over several days. On the day of admission, he developed excruciating right back pain (9–10/10) after lunch; analgesics were ineffective.

He reported that his systolic blood pressure had persistently ranged from 80 to 90 mmHg over the preceding 2 weeks. He smokes (Brinkman index 580) and drinks >50 g of alcohol daily. His father had colorectal cancer.

On examination, T 38.5 °C, pulse 101 beats/min, blood pressure 148/84 mmHg, respirations 18/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. He was alert. Conjunctival pallor was noted. The abdomen was soft and flat, with diffuse tenderness most pronounced in the epigastrium; there were no peritoneal signs. The back was non‐tender to palpation.

Laboratory studies on admission showed: WBC 3.5 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 79.1%, lymphocytes 14.6%, hemoglobin 100 g/L, hematocrit 0.293, platelets 900 × 10^9/L, PT-INR 1.14, APTT 27.4 s, D-dimer 1.12 mg/L, CRP 60 nmol/L. Sodium 141 mmol/L, potassium 3.3 mmol/L, chloride 105 mmol/L, glucose 13.2 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.8%. Liver enzymes and LDH were elevated; renal function was normal. TSH, free thyroxine, GH, LH, FSH, somatomedin C, prolactin, and soluble IL-2 receptor were within reference ranges. The antinuclear antibody titer was <40, and the anticardiolipin antibody level was 2 U/mL.

Contrast-enhanced thoracoabdominal CT revealed bilaterally enlarged adrenal glands with low-attenuation internal areas and surrounding adipose tissue stranding; there were no high-attenuation regions to suggest hemorrhage and no other intra-abdominal abnormalities. On hospital day 3, contrast-enhanced abdominal MRI showed persistently enlarged adrenal glands with a focal area of low density on post-contrast T1-weighted images, with otherwise preserved enhancement.

A 43-year-old woman presented with a 7-month history of dysphagia and dyspnea and a 5-month history of a progressively enlarging neck mass without hoarseness or weight loss. She had hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine and a family history of goiter. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender, macronodular, fixed midline neck mass measuring 10×7 cm without cervical lymphadenopathy. Routine laboratory studies, including thyroid‐function tests, were within normal limits. Cervical ultrasonography revealed a heterogeneous, hypervascular, mixed solid and cystic thyroid mass with a 93×46×15 mm hypoechoic nodule in the lower left lobe and multiple hypoechoic nodules in the right lobe (largest, 34×28 mm). Contrast‐enhanced CT of the neck confirmed a 90×45×65 mm heterogeneous thyroid mass with central necrosis and no invasion of adjacent structures. Fine‐needle aspiration cytology was reported as consistent with undifferentiated carcinoma of the thyroid. CT of the thorax and abdomen showed no distant metastases. The patient was referred for total thyroidectomy.

A 13-year-old girl with a history of intermittent asthma presented with six days of generalized weakness and fatigue and several months of unquantified weight loss. She noted early satiety and a progressive increase in abdominal girth but denied fever, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or jaundice. There was no history of sexual activity, blood transfusions, or significant exposures. Menstrual history was unremarkable. On examination, her body mass index was 17.6. The abdomen was soft with mild epigastric prominence; there was tender hepatomegaly (liver span 24 cm) and right upper quadrant tenderness without splenomegaly, shifting dullness, or fluid thrill. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, electrolytes, and coagulation profile; liver function tests were normal except for elevated alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a coarse, enlarged liver (24.2 cm) with multiple ill-defined isoechoic masses and small-volume perihepatic free fluid; heterogeneous hypovascular masses were also noted in the adnexal and pelvic regions. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a large heterogeneous pelvic mass with central low-attenuation areas causing mass effect on adjacent structures, innumerable low-attenuation hepatic lesions, extensive peritoneal deposits, lymphadenopathy, and ascites.

A 12-year-old girl presented with sudden onset of severe upper abdominal pain and no history of trauma. On examination she was tachycardic with a blood pressure of 100/60 mm Hg and had a vague, tender epigastric mass. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography suggested internal bleeding within a pancreatic pseudocyst occupying the lesser sac. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a well-demarcated, 10 cm × 13 cm mass arising from the body of the pancreas, composed of solid and cystic components with enhancement of the solid portions. The mass filled the lesser sac, abutted the splenic vessels posteriorly, and showed a breach in its anterolateral capsule with minimal hemoperitoneum.

A 60-year-old woman with a history of permanent pacemaker implantation 8 years earlier (switched off 2 years ago) and active smoking underwent a routine occupational checkup. Electrocardiography showed atrial fibrillation with intermittent dizziness and episodes of ventricular tachycardia. She denied chest pain, dyspnea, or other cardiac symptoms. 

On examination, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable (BP 116/86 mmHg; HR 77 bpm; RR 20/min; SpO₂ 96% on room air). Cardiovascular and pulmonary exams were unremarkable. 

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a large, oval, pedunculated, nonmobile mass with smooth margins attached to the apex and occupying most of the left ventricular cavity, causing obstruction of the left ventricular outflow tract and interfering with mitral valve function. Left ventricular systolic dysfunction was present (LVEF 20%). The atria and all other valves were normal; no pericardial effusion was seen. 

Coronary angiography showed normal coronary arteries. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a lobulated, well-defined hypodense mass measuring 5.0 × 4.3 × 4.0 cm within the left ventricle. Cardiac MRI confirmed the presence of a well-circumscribed left ventricular mass without extracardiac lesions. The patient was referred for surgical excision of the left ventricular mass.

A 52-year-old man with a 20-month history of EGFR-mutant (exon 21 L858R) stage IV non–small cell lung cancer presented with several months of fluctuating general weakness. His prior cancer therapies included six cycles of paclitaxel and carboplatin, three cycles of gemcitabine and vinorelbine, stereotactic radiosurgery (23 Gy) and whole-brain radiotherapy (30 Gy) for brain metastases, followed by 11 months of erlotinib 150 mg daily. He had been receiving levetiracetam and low-dose prednisolone to prevent seizures. He was a former smoker (26 pack-years) who had quit one year earlier. On examination he appeared chronically ill but vital signs were normal. Complete blood count showed white blood cells 7600/μL (absolute neutrophils, 500/μL), hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, and platelets 83 000/μL. The peripheral smear demonstrated 44% blasts. Lactate dehydrogenase was 293 U/L (normal 106–211 U/L). Bone marrow aspiration revealed 77.3% myeloblasts.

A 32-year-old woman with no prior pulmonary symptoms was transferred for management of a second tension pneumothorax occurring two weeks after initial chest-tube drainage. Chest radiography demonstrated a right-sided tension pneumothorax and bilateral homogeneous emphysematous changes composed of cysts and fibrous strands. After chest-tube placement, a CT scan of the chest showed multiple bilateral thin-walled cysts, up to 10 cm in diameter, distributed throughout both lungs, with normal intervening lung parenchyma and no nodules or fluid collections. She is a never-smoker, and serum α₁-antitrypsin levels were within normal limits. A thoracoscopic wedge resection of the right upper lobe was performed. Histologic examination revealed large cystic spaces with smooth muscle structures in the walls and interlobular septa. Some cyst walls were lined by CD31- and D2-40–positive endothelial cells; CD34 was negative. Rare HMB-45–positive perivascular epithelioid cells were identified. Parts of the cystic walls showed fibrosis, and some cysts appeared to have a lymphatic origin.

A 65-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a rapidly enlarging nodule on the left preauricular cheek. Her history was notable for type II diabetes, hypertension, and immunosuppression following renal transplantation 8 years earlier. Two years prior, she had a cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma in situ on her left third finger treated with Mohs micrographic surgery. On examination, there was a 1.5 cm eroded, erythematous nodule on the left preauricular cheek. A shave biopsy revealed an ulcerated neoplasm throughout the dermis comprised of irregular islands of atypical cells that stained uniformly with antibodies to pan keratin and uniformly negative with antibodies to S100 protein, leading to a diagnosis of poorly differentiated carcinoma. The lesion was excised by Mohs surgery in one stage with negative frozen-section margins, resulting in a 3.5 × 2.3 cm defect. Permanent sections showed a deeply infiltrating undifferentiated carcinoma extending into subcutaneous fat without keratinization but with foci of duct formation; the neoplasm was connected to and continuous with the epidermis, suggesting undifferentiated squamous cell carcinoma, while the presence of ducts raised consideration of eccrine carcinoma.

A 76-year-old woman underwent mastectomy for a low-grade ductal adenocarcinoma of the breast (stage T1 N0). Three months after surgery she noted visual deterioration in her right eye. Fundoscopy by her oncologist revealed a choroidal lesion that was presumed to be metastatic disease, and she received palliative external beam radiotherapy (20 Gy in five fractions) to the right orbit. Eighteen months later she was referred to ophthalmology for further evaluation. Corrected visual acuity in the right eye was 6/18. Dilated fundus examination showed an 11 × 10 mm elevated choroidal mass in the peripheral fundus, mainly yellow in color with some intrinsic pigmentation and no associated sub-retinal fluid. B-scan ultrasonography demonstrated a mushroom-shaped lesion with choroidal excavation through Bruch’s membrane and low internal reflectivity. Fluorescein angiography revealed a “double circulation,” with intrinsic tumor vasculature and overlying retinal vessels. Examination of the left eye was unremarkable.

A 38-year-old woman presented with an 11-month history of secondary amenorrhea and galactorrhea. Examination revealed bilateral, multiduct galactorrhea; the remainder of the general and gynecological examinations was unremarkable. Pelvic and breast ultrasonography were normal. Laboratory studies showed a serum prolactin level of 320 ng/mL; routine blood tests and the remainder of the hormonal panel were within normal limits.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the head demonstrated a well-defined mass occupying the sphenoid sinus. On T1-weighted sequences the lesion was isointense to white matter, and on T2-weighted sequences it was mildly hyperintense. There was no evidence of bony invasion of the sinus walls or of the sella turcica floor; however, the mass obstructed the sphenoid sinus ostium and was associated with mucoid retention. The pituitary stalk appeared intact, traversing a cerebrospinal fluid–filled sella turcica (infundibulum sign), and no normal pituitary tissue was visualized within the sella. On dynamic contrast-enhanced sequences, the stalk enhanced normally without intrasellar pituitary parenchyma, and the sphenoid sinus lesion showed mild, persistent enhancement without surrounding pituitary tissue.

A 7-year-old boy with no prior medical history presented with a left laterocervical swelling of one year’s duration, without episodes of infection. On examination, there was a 3 cm soft, subdigastric mass on the left side, with bilateral small cervical lymph nodes. Cervical ultrasound showed an oval multiloculated cystic mass in the left carotid space, measuring 47 × 30 mm, with retrolaryngeal extension and intimate contact with the left common carotid artery and its internal and external branches; these findings evoked a cystic lymphangioma, a third branchial cleft cyst, or a laryngocele. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a multiloculated paracervical fluid collection measuring 50 × 27 × 24 mm, with extension into the retropharyngeal space causing a mass effect on the oropharynx and suspected fistulous communication with the ipsilateral piriform sinus, favoring a cystic lymphangioma or fourth branchial cleft cyst. Cervical MRI demonstrated a multiloculated, T2-hyperintense left laterocervical lesion with retropharyngeal extension and pharyngolaryngeal mass effect but no evidence of a fistulous tract, which favors a cystic lymphangioma.

A 53-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of an asymptomatic, slow-growing, soft mass in her right breast. On examination, there was a palpable, non-tender, solitary, soft mass measuring approximately 10 cm × 10 cm × 8 cm in the upper-outer quadrant of the right breast; the contralateral breast and both axillae were unremarkable. Routine laboratory tests—including blood counts, electrolytes, coagulation parameters, and liver, renal, and cardiopulmonary function tests—were all within normal limits. There was no family history of breast cancer. Breast ultrasonography showed a well-circumscribed, hyperechoic nodule of dense fat in the upper-outer quadrant of the right breast. Mammography demonstrated a round, sharply demarcated, non-calcified mass occupying most of the upper outer and inner quadrants of the right breast. Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed a heterogeneous low-density lesion with a maximum cross-sectional diameter of approximately 70 mm by 40 mm and attenuation values ranging from –38 to 12 Hounsfield units.

A 25-year-old man presented with a 5-month history of an insidious periumbilical mass that had grown gradually, with a more rapid increase over the past 2 months and mild dragging pain for the last month. He reported a 4-kg weight loss during the last month and had no significant past medical or family history. He did not smoke or consume alcohol. On examination, there was a firm, smooth-surfaced, mobile intraperitoneal mass measuring approximately 18 × 15 cm, occupying the umbilical, hypogastric, right lumbar, and iliac regions; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen revealed a 21 × 17 × 11.4 cm heterogeneously enhancing intraperitoneal soft-tissue mass with scattered calcifications, multiple nonenhancing cystic and necrotic areas, posterior displacement of mesenteric vessels, peripheral displacement of small-bowel loops, and a small amount of pelvic free fluid.

A 50-year-old woman was referred to endocrinology for suspected pituitary apoplexy. She had an unremarkable past medical history and reported secondary amenorrhea since age 40 (etiology unknown). Over several months, she developed headache, visual disturbances, generalized weakness, nausea, vomiting, and episodes of hypoglycemia; she denied polyuria. Four months before referral, laboratory studies showed an 8-h cortisol level of 502 nmol/L, free thyroxine (FT4) of 10.6 pmol/L, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) of 0.66 mIU/L, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) of 25 IU/L, luteinizing hormone (LH) of 2.5 IU/L, and prolactin of 71 μg/L. 

Initial pituitary MRI revealed a large sellar mass involving the sphenoid sinus and nasopharynx, interpreted as an invasive pituitary macroadenoma. On examination, her body mass index was 21.7 kg/m2, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, and pulse 80 beats/min. Thyroid, abdominal, and detailed neurologic examinations were normal. Repeat biochemical testing demonstrated corticotropin, thyrotropin, and gonadotropin deficiencies with a low TSH index of 0.71 and hyperprolactinemia. Ophthalmologic evaluation revealed left visual acuity of 5/10 with an upper temporal quadrantanopia.

A second MRI showed nodular nasopharyngeal thickening contiguous with an enlarged sella turcica forming a heterogeneous intra- and suprasellar mass (20 × 17 mm) with a fluid-filled component, compression and T2 hyperintensity of the optic chiasm extending into the optic tracts, and an enhancing nodular thickening of the pituitary stalk. The findings raised suspicion for an invasive nasopharyngeal process extending into the sella.

A 19-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of intermittent tingling on the right side of her face without pain. There was no history of trauma, headache, fever, or other neurologic symptoms. Her past medical and family histories were unremarkable. On examination, vital signs were normal, and there were no motor deficits, cranial-nerve abnormalities, or signs of increased intracranial pressure. Given the focal sensory complaint and lack of systemic findings, intracranial pathology was suspected.  
Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-defined extra-axial cystic lesion in the right cerebellopontine angle extending into the ambient cistern. On T1-weighted images, the lesion was hypointense; on T2-weighted images, it was hyperintense. Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences showed a “dirty” hyperintense signal within the lesion. Diffusion-weighted imaging demonstrated marked diffusion restriction, and susceptibility-weighted imaging showed no evidence of blooming. The lesion caused mass effect on the right side of the pons and displaced the right trigeminal nerve.

A 45-year-old man with hypertension presented with a tender nodule on the dorsal aspect of the left fifth finger. He had a history of a soft-tissue tumor at the same site excised one year earlier; pathology at that time revealed adenocarcinoma. On examination, there was a solitary, firm, 2 × 1 cm nodule with overlying skin scarring; motor and sensory function were intact. The patient underwent resection of the lesion. 

Grossly, multiple fragments of pink-tan soft tissue were received. Microscopic examination showed an infiltrative growth pattern, cytologic atypia, and an absence of myoepithelial cells; the tumor infiltrated into the reticular dermis without lymphovascular invasion.

A 63-year-old woman was referred for numbness in the distribution of the right median nerve. Six months earlier, she had undergone a mini-open palmar release for presumed idiopathic carpal tunnel syndrome, with complete early relief of symptoms. She now reports recurrence of numbness in the same distribution.

Her medical history is notable for hypothyroidism, hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia, treated with levothyroxine, bisoprolol, and atorvastatin. On examination, there is a 5 cm soft, non-tender, well-circumscribed mass in the thenar eminence of the right hand, and pain on flexion and abduction of the thumb. Neurologic examination shows symmetric motor function and sensation compared with the left hand.

Standard radiographs of the right hand are unremarkable. Ultrasound reveals a well-defined, homogeneous, hyperechoic lesion in the thenar space. MRI of the hand demonstrates a 46 × 31 × 17 mm, capsulated, homogeneous adipose-density lesion that molds the flexor tendons and median nerve but remains separate from the nerve, with no evidence of surrounding tissue invasion.

A 46-year-old man with a history of testicular seminoma treated with surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy presented with a painless, tan-colored papule on his right upper eyelid. The lesion measured 4 mm in diameter, had been present for 10 months, and was initially thought to be a papilloma. An excisional biopsy was performed.

On histologic examination, the lesion was a well-circumscribed, sharply demarcated epithelial tumor in the upper dermis. Findings included keratin-filled cysts, superficial basaloid cells arranged in a sheet-like or plate-like proliferation with broad attachments to the overlying epidermis, and aggregates of mature sebaceous cells forming clusters and lobules in the lower portion of the tumor. Foci of ductal differentiation were present, and no mitotic figures were observed.

A 58-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of intermittent left temporal headaches accompanied by hearing disturbance and a sensation of fullness in her left ear. Her only medical history was hyperlipidemia; there was no relevant family history. On neurologic examination, mental status, cranial nerves, and motor function were normal. Noncontrast brain CT demonstrated a roughly 1.5-cm mass at the left temporal base that was isoattenuating to gray matter with surrounding low-attenuation perilesional edema. Bone-window images showed mild hyperostosis of the adjacent left greater wing of the sphenoid. Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed a lobulated, dural-based mass with avid heterogeneous enhancement, intratumoral cystic or necrotic areas, and dural tails. T2-weighted imaging showed extensive high-signal edema extending into the adjacent white matter and basal ganglia with thinning of the cortex. Susceptibility-weighted imaging showed no hemorrhage or prominent vessels.

A 68-year-old woman underwent routine barium follow-through examination of the upper gastrointestinal tract, which revealed a duodenal polyp. Her only medication was for hyperlipidemia; she had no history of gastrointestinal disease. Physical examination was unremarkable, with no peripheral lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests showed a total cholesterol level of 254 mg/dL; carcinoembryonic antigen, carbohydrate antigen 19-9, and blood cell counts were within normal limits. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy identified a pedunculated polyp approximately 20 mm in diameter in the second portion of the duodenum; the lesion was covered by smooth, intact mucosa and had a long stalk that allowed it to migrate into the stomach. Magnified narrowband imaging confirmed an intact duodenal mucosal surface over the lesion. Endoscopic ultrasonography demonstrated at least three cystic structures within the head of the polyp.

A 27-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 2-week history of gross hematuria, right lower-quadrant pain, and low-grade fever. She had been treated empirically for presumed urinary tract infection with nitrofurantoin without relief; her hematuria recurred and flank pain worsened, prompting emergency evaluation.

On examination, her temperature was 38.8 °C. There was tenderness to palpation in the right upper and suprapubic regions. Urinalysis showed 2+ blood but no evidence of infection; urine β-hCG was negative. Laboratory studies revealed a normal white-cell count and mild anemia (hemoglobin, 11.2 g/dL; hematocrit, 33.2 %). Renal and hepatic function tests were normal.

A noncontrast abdominopelvic CT scan showed a large, heterogeneously attenuating right renal mass (approximately 10 cm) with foci of hyperattenuation suggesting hemorrhage and ipsilateral retroperitoneal edema; no nephrolithiasis or hydronephrosis was seen, and the left kidney was normal. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a heterogeneously enhancing expansile mass in the upper pole of the right kidney with invasion of the collecting system, right renal vein, and inferior vena cava. Subsequent contrast-enhanced MRI confirmed a large right upper-pole renal mass with intralesional cystic change and hemorrhage, marked diffusion restriction, and tumoral extension into the right renal vein and inferior vena cava. A staging chest CT showed multiple small bilateral pulmonary nodules.

A 70-year-old man was referred from outpatient gastroenterology to the emergency department for evaluation of weakness and dehydration.
