He reported a several-month history of constipation with dark “coffee-ground” stools, occasional blood per rectum, and a change in stool caliber, as well as an unintentional 29-pound weight loss over 3 months. He also noted new-onset polyuria and polydipsia. In the emergency department, his random blood glucose level was 722 mg/dL, and serum creatinine was 2.0 mg/dL. His most recent colonoscopy 6 years earlier had shown tubular adenoma and a hyperplastic polyp.

Given the concern for an underlying gastrointestinal malignancy, a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was obtained. It demonstrated four heterogeneous hypodense lesions in the right hepatic lobe with peripheral heterogeneous enhancement in the portal venous phase. There was also circumferential prominence of the distal rectal wall, thought to reflect either rectal collapse or an underlying mass. There were no lesions identified in the pancreas, kidneys, bladder, prostate, or small bowel.

Based on the clinical history and imaging findings, an initial diagnosis of a rectal mass with multiple hepatic metastases was offered.

A 42-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 14-day history of sudden, painless swelling of the right mandible. She reported numbness and tingling of the lower lip but denied malocclusion or marked tooth mobility. Her medical, family, and social histories were unremarkable. On examination, there was severe loosening of the mandibular teeth on the affected side. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated a large, well-defined radiolucent expansile lesion extending from the distal aspect of tooth 35 to the distal aspect of tooth 45. Cone-beam CT confirmed a multilocular cystic lesion with cortical bone perforation of the right mandibular body; there was no root resorption. An incisional biopsy of a 5-mm fragment was performed, but the histologic sample was insufficient to reach a definitive diagnosis. The primary differential diagnosis at that time included a dentigerous cyst and other cysts lined by squamous epithelium.

A 37-year-old previously healthy Thai man was evaluated in October 2008 for a 3-cm left supraclavicular lymph node enlargement. A lymph-node biopsy showed metastatic well-differentiated adenocarcinoma. Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen revealed:
• Mildly reticular densities at the right lung apex.  
• A lobulated heterogeneous soft-tissue mass in the left neck extending down to the level of the aortic arch, with invasion of the left common carotid and subclavian arteries, involvement of the left thyroid lobe, and abutment of the esophageal wall.  
• Left paraaortic multilobulated lymph nodes at the renal level (maximum diameter, 7.4 cm), displacing the left renal vein, with mild dilation of the left renal pelvis and partial abutment of the aorta and pancreatic body.

Serum levels of α-fetoprotein, lactate dehydrogenase, and carcinoembryonic antigen were within normal limits. On the basis of these findings, a preliminary diagnosis of metastatic adenocarcinoma of presumed pulmonary origin was made, and the patient received two cycles of carboplatin and paclitaxel, followed by two cycles of cisplatin and etoposide after disease progression. After a 1-year absence from follow-up, the lymph-node pathology was reviewed and reported as metastatic papillary adenocarcinoma.

A 74-year-old man with a history of metastatic prostate cancer and a known left upper lobe lung mass presented with four weeks of progressive vertigo, described as the sensation that “the floor was wobbling” and “the room was swaying,” leading to difficulty ambulating. A few days before admission, he developed severe bifrontal throbbing headaches with nausea and vomiting. Two days prior, he was evaluated at an outside emergency department, tested positive for adenovirus, and was discharged after supportive treatment without symptom relief.

His oncology history included stage III prostate adenocarcinoma treated with prostatectomy and radiation in 2013, followed by detection of bilateral lung nodules and sclerotic bone lesions in 2016, and a 2020 biopsy of a left upper lobe lesion confirming mismatch repair deficient, androgen receptor–positive metastatic prostate cancer treated with enzalutamide, then abiraterone acetate and prednisone, and palliative radiation.

On presentation, vital signs were: temperature 37°C, heart rate 90 beats/min, blood pressure 164/81 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. Neurologic examination revealed no focal motor or sensory deficits; intact coordination on dysdiadochokinesia, finger-to-nose, and heel-to-shin testing; an intact gait despite dizziness; and a positive right-sided Dix–Hallpike maneuver with horizontal nystagmus.

Noncontrast head CT showed a 3 cm left cerebellar hemispheric mass with surrounding vasogenic edema causing mild partial effacement of the fourth ventricle and left quadrigeminal cistern. The patient received dexamethasone. MRI of the brain demonstrated a cystic enhancing lesion in the left cerebellar hemisphere with mass effect; no other intra-axial lesions were identified. Cerebral angiography revealed no abnormal hyperemia at the site of the lesion.

A hemangioblastoma was considered the leading diagnosis; other considerations included metastases and infarction.

A 51-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of shortness of breath on exertion. He had smoked 10 pack-years but had no other significant medical history. On arrival, his physical examination was unremarkable. Electrocardiography showed normal sinus rhythm. Routine laboratory studies, including complete blood count and inflammatory markers, were within normal limits. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a mass on the aortic valve, and the patient was admitted for further evaluation. Transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a normal left ventricular ejection fraction and no abnormalities of the mitral or tricuspid valves, but identified a 6.9 × 9.5 mm echogenic, highly mobile mass attached to the right coronary cusp of the aortic valve. Cardiac computed tomography confirmed a normal coronary artery anatomy and showed a 10 × 8 mm mixed-density mass on the right coronary cusp of the aortic valve, raising suspicion for a papillary fibroelastoma. The patient’s Society of Thoracic Surgeons risk score was 0.91 %.

A 61-year-old woman was referred with a 3-month history of palpitations and breathlessness. One week before presentation, she noted mild neck swelling. Her history included hypertension and a partial right nephrectomy for a benign lesion. Examination showed mild, generalized neck swelling. Three months earlier, thyroid function tests were normal. Current tests showed a free T4 of 22.3 pmol/L and a TSH of 0.05 mU/L. Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a multinodular goitre with retrosternal extension and possible cystic cervical lymphadenopathy. CT of the neck confirmed diffuse thyroid enlargement with bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy causing tracheal deviation, findings concerning for malignancy. One week later, she presented acutely with progressive neck swelling and palpitations; free T4 was 23.2 pmol/L and TSH <0.01 mU/L. Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies were negative. She was started on carbimazole and propranolol to treat thyrotoxicosis.

A 24-year-old man presented with gradually progressive, diffuse swelling of his right lower limb since childhood without paresthesia or motor impairment. He also had multiple, asymptomatic facial papules since early childhood; his sister had similar facial lesions and seizures. On examination, the right lower limb was diffusely swollen from the groin to mid–leg with multiple dilated, tortuous veins but no visible capillary or venous malformations. On the face, there were multiple firm, discrete reddish-brown telangiectatic papules over the nasolabial folds and cheeks. On the trunk, there were multiple ash leaf–shaped hypopigmented patches and soft, skin-colored papules coalescing into a plaque on the left lateral aspect. Oral examination revealed dental pits and gingival fibromas. Fine-needle aspiration from the thigh swelling showed lobules of mature adipose tissue. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right lower limb demonstrated T1- and T2-hyperintense signals throughout the musculature of all compartments, consistent with fatty infiltration, along with multiple prominent tortuous vessels and cortical thickening of the right femur and tibia with anterior bowing of the femur. Doppler ultrasonography revealed multiple incompetent perforators in the great saphenous vein territory.

A 63-year-old woman presented with a three-month history of pelvic pain, urinary and fecal incontinence, and palpitations. She had no significant past medical or surgical history. On examination, she appeared ill and was found to be in atrial flutter. A nontender, mobile, elastic-hard mass measuring 2 × 1 cm with a smooth surface was palpated in the lower inner quadrant of the left breast; there was no axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy and no nipple discharge or skin changes.

Thoracic CT revealed a mediastinal mass compressing the heart and identified the breast lesion as a 1 cm hypodense nodule. Abdominal and pelvic MRI showed multiple lymphadenopathies, and a Tru-Cut needle biopsy of a pelvic node established a diagnosis of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. The patient was started on R-CHOP chemotherapy.

After two cycles, PET-CT showed no FDG uptake in lymph node regions but demonstrated FDG accumulation in the breast mass with an SUVmax of 3, with no change in size from the initial CT. Mammography revealed a circumscribed round-shaped nodule, and ultrasonography showed a well-demarcated hypoechoic ovoid mass with low-amplitude internal echoes and shadowing at the edges. The differential diagnosis included fibroadenoma, breast cancer, and lymphoma involving the breast.

A 20-year-old woman was referred for deformity and bulging of the anterior chest wall over the sternum, associated with mild pain. On chest radiography, an abnormal opacity was noted in the sternal region. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a large expansile lesion centered in the sternum, with thinning of the cortical bone and extension toward the mediastinum; the differential diagnosis included a primary sternal tumor or an anterior mediastinal mass invading the sternum. A core-needle biopsy of the lesion was performed, and the pathology report was compatible with a giant cell tumor.

A 65-year-old woman noticed a right cervical mass in mid-January 2020 and was referred to a local hospital in mid-February. She had no systemic symptoms.  
On examination, an elastic hard, slightly tender, 42-mm mass was palpable in the right level II region with good mobility. Oropharyngeal inspection revealed an irregular mucosal lesion at the lower pole of the right palatine tonsil extending to the tongue base.  
Contrast-enhanced CT showed mild mucosal thickening (major axis, 16 mm) on the right oropharyngeal wall and a 54-mm lymph node in the right level IIA region with irregular enhancement, which had grown since imaging four months earlier.  
FDG-PET revealed abnormal uptake in a 26 × 12 × 33-mm oropharyngeal tumor (SUVmax 24.6) and multiple right level IIA lymph nodes (SUVmax up to 24.7). A colonic uptake (SUVmax 6.4) was seen but colonoscopy was negative for malignancy.  
Tonsillar biopsy showed nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium with lymphocytic inflammation but no malignant cells. Fine-needle aspiration of the cervical node revealed atypical cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and prominent nucleoli in a necrotic and inflammatory background; carcinoma was suspected.  
Given a working diagnosis of oropharyngeal carcinoma (cT1N2bM0) of uncertain primary origin, transoral resection of the oropharyngeal lesion and ipsilateral neck dissection were performed to achieve both definitive diagnosis and treatment.

A 73-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a painful mass in her left breast. She reported being bitten on the breast by a toddler several weeks earlier and denied any prior palpable or painful breast abnormalities. On examination, there was a well-circumscribed, tender 2 cm nodule at the 1:00 position, 2 cm from the nipple. Diagnostic mammography and ultrasonography confirmed a 19 × 13 × 12 mm solid and cystic mass with internal vascularity. The lesion was classified as BI-RADS 4 (suspicious abnormality). Surgical consultation was obtained, and the patient underwent excisional biopsy.

A 52-year-old man was referred to the otolaryngology clinic for evaluation of a painless swelling on the right side of his neck that had been present for 10 months. He denied pain, dysphagia, hoarseness, dyspnea, cough, systemic symptoms, or weight loss. On examination, there was a single, mobile, non-tender mass in the right cervical level III region, measuring approximately 2.5 × 2 cm; the overlying skin was normal. 

Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the mass suggested a probable schwannoma. Flexible fiber-optic laryngoscopy showed normal vocal‐cord motion bilaterally and no mucosal lesions. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the neck, with and without gadolinium, demonstrated a well-circumscribed, heterogeneous mass on the right side, measuring 16 × 16 × 23 mm. On T1-weighted images, the lesion was isointense to muscle; on T2-weighted images, it was hyperintense. The mass enhanced heterogeneously after contrast administration.

An 81-year-old Japanese man was referred for a 1-month history of productive cough and wheeze. He had smoked 56 pack-years and had a history of pulmonary tuberculosis in adolescence and chronic pyothorax treated with intravenous antibiotics one year earlier. His temperature was 37.2°C. Pulmonary examination revealed wheezes and reduced air entry in the right mid-lung; no lymphadenopathy was noted. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis (12,500/µL), normal lactate dehydrogenase (223 IU/L), mildly elevated carcinoembryonic antigen (5.8 ng/mL), and soluble interleukin-2 receptor (575 U/mL). Chest radiography demonstrated hypolucency of the right middle lung field. CT of the chest revealed chronic pyothorax with calcified foci in the right lung and a mass within the bronchus intermedius, without mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Flexible bronchoscopy identified a smooth, pedunculated endobronchial tumor obstructing the bronchus intermedius. Biopsy showed predominantly small atypical lymphocytes. Immunohistochemical staining of the biopsy specimen revealed positivity for CD3, CD4, CD5, and CD7; negativity for CD8, CD20, and CD30; and a low Ki-67 labeling index. PET-CT demonstrated intense uptake (maximum standardized uptake value, 20.6) confined to the endobronchial lesion, with no abnormal uptake at the site of pyothorax, mediastinal nodes, or elsewhere.

A 70-year-old woman with a history of lobular carcinoma of the breast treated with mastectomy and adjuvant radiochemotherapy 4 years earlier, with no evidence of recurrence, was referred for hypotension. She reported 1 week of right upper quadrant pain, jaundice, and asthenia without dizziness, weakness, or altered mentation. On admission, her mean arterial pressure was 63 mmHg. Examination showed scleral icterus and moderate ascites; there was no fever, pruritus, hepatomegaly, or encephalopathy. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 8.8 g/dl, mean corpuscular volume 90.5 fl, ferritin 5485 ng/ml, transferrin saturation 74%, and transferrin 126 mg/dl; aspartate aminotransferase 240 IU/l, alanine aminotransferase 431 IU/l, gamma-glutamyl transferase 550 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 431 IU/l, total bilirubin 11.6 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 6.7 mg/dl, and INR 1.8. Noncontrast CT of the abdomen showed ascites and heterogeneous hepatic attenuation suggestive of cirrhosis but no focal lesions. She was managed conservatively with fluids, and an extensive workup was initiated, including MR imaging of the abdomen, viral serologies (HAV, HBV, HCV, CMV), paracentesis, and autoimmune panels. MR imaging again demonstrated a cirrhotic liver without overt focal lesions and excluded pancreatic or biliary mass. Four days later, she developed bleeding from intravenous sites, her bilirubin rose to 16 mg/dl (direct 9 mg/dl), and INR increased to 2.1. A working diagnosis of rapidly progressive liver failure due to hemochromatosis or autoimmune hepatitis was assumed.

A 46-year-old man presented with pleuritic chest pain, a swollen painful right knee impairing weight bearing, and hip and back pain after a fall. He reported a 40-kg weight loss over 2 years, poor appetite, fever, night sweats, and increased infections. He has a 16-year history of untreated hepatitis C (genotype 3) and a history of intravenous heroin use. He had prior pulmonary embolism, disc prolapse, mild depression, osteomyelitis with digit amputation, and multiple fracture repairs.

On examination he was cachectic with rib and mediastinal tenderness, hepatomegaly (6 cm below costal margin), non-tender lymphadenopathy in the left jugular chain and bilateral groins, and a warm right knee effusion. Vital signs were normal. 

Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 102 g/L, elevated C-reactive protein, calcium 2.57 mmol/L, albumin 23 g/L, and a transient mild elevation of free T4. Liver function, renal function, coagulation, α-fetoprotein, vasculitic screen, iron studies, B12, urate, and globulins were normal. HIV tests were negative on two assays; hepatitis C serology was positive; CMV and EBV were reactive; HHV-8 was not detected.

CT of the chest and abdomen revealed enlarged para-aortic lymph nodes and lytic lesions in T8 and T9. CT pulmonary angiogram, chest X-ray, and troponin I were normal. Knee aspiration grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus and was treated as septic arthritis. Transesophageal echocardiography excluded infective endocarditis.

Further workup for suspected hematologic malignancy showed normal β2-microglobulin and LDH, no monoclonal band on serum or urine electrophoresis, and normal B- and T-cell subsets by flow cytometry. A bone scan demonstrated destructive thoracic lesions, and MRI confirmed T8–T11 osteomyelitis with epidural involvement. A bone marrow biopsy excluded lymphoma and multiple myeloma.

A 30‐year‐old woman presented with a 2-month history of a swelling in her right cheek associated with severe pain. On examination, there was a diffuse extraoral swelling over the right cheek. Intraorally, a solitary, mobile, 2 cm × 2 cm submucosal mass with ill-defined borders and a smooth mucosal surface was noted on the right buccal mucosa without colour change. Ultrasonography showed a well-defined, hypoechoic lesion in the right cheek region. Based on the clinical and radiographic findings, a provisional diagnosis of an ectopic lymph node versus a lipoma was made.

A 34-year-old man with a known history of unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease—including pulmonary atresia, non-restrictive ventricular septal defect, non-confluent pulmonary arteries, and four major aortopulmonary collateral arteries—presented with a painless, slowly enlarging mass on the left side of his neck for 1½ years. He had central cyanosis, finger clubbing, and polycythemia but no family history of similar conditions. On examination, there was a pulsatile, level II mass on the left (approximately 40 × 40 × 30 mm) with restricted vertical mobility; there was no dysphagia, dyspnea, dysphonia, or cranial nerve deficits.  
Neck ultrasonography revealed a solid, hypervascular spherical mass (36 × 36 × 38 mm) at the left carotid bifurcation with hypoechoic islands, and a smaller similar lesion (20 × 13 × 25 mm) on the right. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the neck confirmed bilateral enhancing masses at the carotid bifurcations. Plasma metanephrine, normetanephrine, and chromogranin A levels were all within normal limits.  
Chest CT angiography and echocardiography confirmed the known congenital cardiac anatomy, including pulmonary atresia, major aortopulmonary collateral arteries, right ventricular hypertrophy, and markedly dilated aorta.

A 15-year-old boy presented with a 4-year history of recurrent mild epistaxis, managed intermittently with silver nitrate cautery. He denied smoking, anticoagulant use, anemia, heart disease, or antihypertensive medications. His only medical history was seasonal allergies treated with antihistamines. During the last month he had daily 1-hour bilateral nosebleeds, worse on the right. Physical examination initially showed a midline septum and prominent intranasal vessels on the right. Cautery provided temporary relief. Thirteen months later, he experienced multiple 1-hour bleeds over 2 days, this time worse on the left; exam showed left septal deviation and cautery was repeated. Four months later, he reported persistent symptoms, and exam revealed left septal spurring, mucosal edema, congestion, rhinorrhea, and bilateral nasal clots. Nasal endoscopy demonstrated left septal spurring, inferior turbinate hypertrophy, polypoid swelling in the middle meatus, purulence in the right nasal floor, and soft tissue swelling obstructing the right nasopharynx. Adenoiditis was suspected, and he received doxycycline, prednisone, and saline spray. On follow-up he had continued epistaxis, intranasal clots, and right-sided nasal obstruction impacting breathing and daily activities. A noncontrast CT of the sinuses showed a right-sided soft tissue density mass causing widening of the right pterygopalatine fossa, globulation of its margins, and bowing of the posterior wall of the right maxillary sinus without aggressive bony destruction. Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma, nasopharyngeal polyp, and rhabdomyosarcoma were considered, and contrast-enhanced MRI was recommended.

A 62-year-old male farmer presented with a large mass on the volar surface of his dominant right forearm. He reported that the mass appeared immediately after a venipuncture in the antecubital fossa 12 months ago and gradually increased in size, with more rapid growth over the last 6 months. He noted slight discomfort during elbow flexion but denied pain at rest. His past medical history was notable for hypertension; he was a social drinker and nonsmoker. On examination, there was a large, palpable, painless soft mass in the upper half of the right forearm without overlying skin changes. The range of motion at the elbow, forearm, and wrist was normal, and there were no sensory or motor deficits or vascular compromise. Plain radiographs excluded bone pathology, and routine blood tests were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI demonstrated a well-encapsulated, multilobular lesion measuring approximately 4.8 × 4.7 × 7.0 cm, with predominantly lipoid content, internal septa, and septal enhancement indicating rich vascularity but no evidence of surrounding tissue infiltration. The imaging findings suggested a lipoma, but could not exclude sarcomatous transformation due to the septa and heterogeneous signal density.

A 44-year-old Caucasian man presented with an 8-month history of reflux and heartburn that was partially relieved by esomeprazole. He underwent upper endoscopy, which revealed a single, polypoid mass measuring 1.0 cm at the gastroesophageal junction. Endoscopic ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic lesion confined to the deep mucosa and submucosa, without invasion into deeper layers. The lesion was removed en bloc using endoscopic mucosal resection. Gross examination disclosed a 1.0-cm tan-pink soft-tissue nodule that was completely submitted for histologic evaluation.

A 33-year-old woman with a 3-year history of asymmetric cardiac hypertrophy and sustained ventricular tachycardia (VT) had multiple antiarrhythmic drugs and an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) placed. She experienced recurrent VT despite metoprolol, amiodarone, sotalol, and dofetilide, requiring several ICD shocks. Endocardial radiofrequency ablation and subcutaneous ICD array placement were unsuccessful. Six months earlier, she underwent cardiac sympathetic denervation and renal artery denervation because her VT was stress-precipitated. 

On the current admission, she had symptomatic recurrent VT and received 22 ineffective ICD shocks before a 200 J external shock restored sinus rhythm. At our center, her heart rate and blood pressure were normal. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed a troponin level of 11.1 ng/ml and normal electrolytes. A 12-lead ECG demonstrated normal sinus rhythm with T-wave inversions in the inferior and septal leads, extreme left axis deviation, left ventricular hypertrophy, and incomplete right bundle branch block.

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed asymmetric inferolateral left ventricular wall hypertrophy with myocardial enhancement measuring 19 × 45 mm and a preserved ejection fraction (55%–60%). Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging confirmed an asymmetric inferolateral wall thickening with delayed gadolinium enhancement and a hypokinetic center. Coronary angiography showed normal coronary arteries. A fluorodeoxyglucose PET scan revealed no evidence of active sarcoidosis or high-grade neoplasm. An incisional myocardial biopsy demonstrated fibrosis and nonspecific myocardial hypertrophy. At electrophysiology study, multiple VT morphologies were induced, and ablation was unsuccessful due to extensive transmural scar and lack of good endocardial targets.

A 31-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of a swelling in the left floor of her mouth that had gradually increased in size. On extraoral examination, there was a diffuse left submandibular swelling. Intraorally, there was a well-defined, encapsulated, tender, firm, nonfluctuant mass extending from the midline of the floor of the mouth to the left second molar region. The patient reported altered sensation of the left lateral tongue border and lingual mucoperiosteum. Fine-needle aspiration cytology was negative. Axial CT imaging of the head and neck revealed a dense 33 × 23 mm mass in the left floor of the mouth with a dilated lingual nerve traversing the lesion.

A 49-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of right-sided pulsatile tinnitus. He denied hearing loss, vertigo, otorrhea, or facial weakness, and had no relevant medical or surgical history. Otoscopic examination of the right ear revealed a red-colored, soft, nonpulsatile mass partially obscuring the tympanic membrane; mobility of the membrane could not be clearly assessed. The left ear was normal. A pure-tone audiogram showed mild high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear at 3000–8000 Hz. Temporal-bone CT demonstrated an isolated 0.8 × 0.5 cm soft-tissue mass just lateral to the right tympanic membrane with no bony erosion or middle-ear invasion.

A 22-year-old male football player presented with a two-week history of right knee pain localized to the medial joint line after a mild on-field injury. He experienced immediate swelling and pain that persisted despite rest, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and physiotherapy. He had no prior knee trauma or significant medical history. On examination, there was mild knee swelling without increased warmth, tenderness on palpation of the anteromedial aspect, discomfort with McMurray’s test, and limitation of flexion to 115° (contralateral full flexion), with no ligamentous laxity. Neurovascular examination was normal. Plain radiographs showed increased density in the infrapatellar region on the lateral view but were otherwise unremarkable. MRI demonstrated a homogeneous, well-defined mass (approximately 5 cm) posterior and medial to the patellar tendon, exhibiting low signal intensity on both T1- and T2-weighted sequences and diffuse enhancement after intravenous gadolinium.

A 50-year-old nulliparous woman with hypertension presented 11 months after completion of treatment for ovarian cancer with several weeks of redness and swelling of her right breast. Her history included a clear cell carcinoma of the ovary confined to the left adnexa, treated by surgery (with intraoperative cyst rupture) and six cycles of paclitaxel–carboplatin, after which serum CA-125 normalized and imaging showed no residual disease. On examination, the right breast was markedly erythematous, warm, and edematous, with a peau d’orange appearance; there was no discrete mass or ulceration, and the left breast was normal. Mammography demonstrated diffuse skin thickening and multiple small hypoechoic nodules and cysts in both breasts (BI-RADS 3). Serum CA-125 was 117.2 U/mL. A skin punch biopsy of the affected area revealed clusters of adenocarcinoma cells within dermal lymphatic spaces.

A 77-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of persistent dry cough. Physical examination was unremarkable. Routine blood tests, including tumor markers, showed no abnormalities. Chest radiography revealed a giant mass occupying the left side of the mediastinum that was not present on a radiograph obtained 1 year earlier. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a well-circumscribed 11-cm mass in the left anterior mediastinum with a mean attenuation of 40 Hounsfield units (range, 20–70) and no areas of fatty density. FDG-PET–CT showed uptake in the lesion with a maximum standardized uptake value of 3.3. Based on these radiologic findings, the preoperative differential diagnosis included thymoma, solitary fibrous tumor, neurogenic tumor, and thymic carcinoma.

A 71-year-old woman presented with a slowly enlarging lesion of the right lower eyelid that had been present for at least 5 years. She was otherwise healthy and had no personal or family history of neurofibromatosis. On ophthalmic examination, visual acuity was normal, intraocular pressures were within normal limits, and the remainder of the ocular examination was unremarkable. Inspection of the right lower eyelid revealed an 11 × 4 mm pink-to–skin-colored papule on the eyelid margin. The lesion demonstrated loss of eyelashes (madarosis) centrally, a small area of ulceration, and a raised telangiectatic border. There was no associated pain or tenderness. The patient was referred to oculoplastic surgery for further evaluation and biopsy.

A 71-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of loss of appetite, 9-kg weight loss over 2 months, and pale (white) stools. He had no personal or family history of malignancy and reported daily alcohol use and a 15-pack-year smoking history. On evaluation, routine blood tests were unremarkable: carcinoembryonic antigen 2.4 ng/mL, IgG4 51.1 mg/dL, and a mildly elevated carbohydrate antigen 19-9 at 49.7 U/mL. Enhanced abdominal CT showed focal stenosis of the third portion of the duodenum, main pancreatic duct dilatation, and atrophy of the pancreatic head. Endoscopic ultrasonography revealed a 20-mm hypoechoic area in the deep pancreatic head near the ductal narrowing, but artifact and duodenal stenosis prevented safe EUS-guided FNA. Upper GI endoscopy demonstrated a one-third circumferential, easily bleeding mucosal irregularity extending from the anal side of the major papilla to the inferior duodenal angulus; multiple biopsies showed only inflamed mucosa without malignant cells. Severe stenosis from the inferior angulus to the third portion prevented passage of the scope and led to contrast reflux into the stomach.

A 13-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of left cheek swelling. The lesion first appeared 6 years earlier; he deferred treatment until it recently increased in size and caused intermittent pain. On examination, there was mild swelling of the left buccal cheek and lower lip, not conspicuous externally. A firm, mobile mass was palpated over the anterior portion of the mandibular angle without bruits, pulsations, or lymphadenopathy. Intraorally, the lesion bulged under the buccal mucosa, which appeared reddish-blue with several aciniform nodules. Dentition and surrounding mandible were normal. A plain radiograph showed no evident calcifications. MRI demonstrated a well-circumscribed mass on the left buccal cheek beneath the buccinator and depressor anguli oris muscles, isointense on T1-weighted images and brightly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, containing several internal vacant spaces suggestive of calcified bodies.

A 17-year-old boy presented with a one-year history of progressive right-sided nasal blockage, two episodes of epistaxis, and deterioration of vision. On examination, there was a mass in the right nasal cavity extending across the postnasal space bilaterally. Fundoscopic examination showed signs of left-eye compression and optic neuropathy. 

Laboratory tests were unremarkable. A CT scan of the head revealed a hypodense mass in the nasopharynx extending into the sellar and parasellar regions, with erosion of the pituitary fossa, clivus, and middle cranial fossa. MRI of the brain demonstrated a large clival-based tumor involving the dura along the entire clivus and compressing the brain stem anteriorly. Cerebral angiography showed a nonvascular mass supplied by branches of both maxillary arteries. 

Initial differential diagnoses included chordoma, angiofibroma, pyogenic granuloma, and nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

A 43-year-old man with a long-standing masticatory and speech disorder presented with a 15-year history of progressive right cheek swelling. The mass was nonpainful but caused discomfort with eating and talking. On intraoral examination, there was a smooth, elastic, soft, circular, pedunculated lesion approximately 40 mm in diameter on the right buccal mucosa, with associated right cheek swelling and no facial nerve palsy. A panoramic radiograph showed few teeth, collapsed occlusion, a faint shadow under a residual right maxillary root, and no jaw bone resorption. MRI revealed an oval neoplastic lesion (40 × 20 mm) between the epithelium and buccal muscle: it was hyperintense on both T1- and T2-weighted images, showed low signal on fat-suppression and diffusion-weighted sequences, and demonstrated a well-defined border that displaced but did not invade adjacent muscle and fascia.

A 56-year-old woman presented with periodic lower abdominal pain for more than a year and worsening right inguinal pain over the past few months. Her history was notable for endometriosis treated by laparoscopy and a supravaginal hysterectomy for fibroids and heavy bleeding. She had a body mass index of 23 and had been on estradiol replacement therapy for three years. A gynecologic examination including transvaginal ultrasound was unremarkable. 

Four months later, she was admitted to the emergency ward with severe right inguinal pain, and an abdominal CT scan was obtained. CT revealed:
• a 55 × 40 mm multicystic, calcified tumor in the right ovary  
• a herniated, partially calcified soft-tissue mass in the right groin  
• small calcified nodules in the pouch of Douglas and the greater omentum  

At first, tuberculosis or some form of teratoma was suspected. However, a chest x-ray was normal and a Mantoux test was negative. An 18F-FDG PET/CT showed slight uptake in the groin mass but no uptake in the ovarian lesion or peritoneal nodules. A Tc-99m-HDP bone scan showed no extraosseous uptake. Tumor markers CA125, HE4, and CEA were within normal limits.

A 42-year-old man was referred to the emergency department for anemia and vision changes. Over two weeks, blurred vision in the left eye progressed to a central black spot with peripheral sparing; over the preceding five days he noted blurred vision in the right eye. He also reported occasional floaters and flashes bilaterally and a 60-pound unintentional weight loss over four months. He denied eye pain, headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, fevers, or chills.

His medical history included hypertension (on nifedipine), hyperlipidemia (on simvastatin), and longstanding left-eye strabismus. He had recently been hospitalized for symptomatic anemia, found to have low vitamin B12 and borderline iron levels; he received a transfusion and was started on ferrous gluconate and cyanocobalamin before discharge. He used non-injection heroin.

On examination, he was afebrile, blood pressure 160/87 mm Hg, heart rate 75 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and SpO₂ 98% on room air. He appeared comfortable. Neurologic and cardiac examinations were normal. Head and neck examination revealed mild left-eye strabismus and decreased central vision in the left eye. Fundoscopic exam showed significant retinal hemorrhage in the left eye. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies demonstrated a red blood cell count of 2.31 M/µL, hemoglobin 7.0 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 104 fL, platelets 94 × 10³/µL, creatinine 1.37 mg/dL, glucose 156 mg/dL, prothrombin time 17.2 s, partial thromboplastin time 28.7 s, and calcium 8.9 mg/dL. The differential count showed 0.1 K/µL absolute plasma cells (3%), and red cell morphology exhibited rouleaux formation.

Ophthalmology evaluation revealed visual acuity 20/60 uncorrected and 20/40 with pinhole in the right eye, and counting‐fingers vision in the left eye. Visual fields were full on the right and revealed a central scotoma on the left. Intraocular pressures were 9 mm Hg in the right eye and 7 mm Hg in the left eye. Slit lamp exam showed clear corneas, no conjunctival injection, and clear lenses bilaterally. Dilated fundus exam demonstrated sharp optic discs without edema, macular edema (possible right, definite left), diffuse retinal hemorrhages, vascular tortuosity, and flame hemorrhages inferior to the discs in both eyes.

He was diagnosed with bilateral central retinal vein occlusions, acute kidney injury, and symptomatic anemia.

A 78-year-old woman with hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and a 3-year history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia was hospitalized for poor appetite, a 10-lb weight loss over 2 months, and drenching night sweats. She was afebrile; blood pressure, 138/78 mm Hg; pulse, 82 beats/min; respirations, 16 breaths/min; and oxygen saturation, 98% on room air. Examination revealed no palpable lymphadenopathy; the abdomen was soft, nondistended, and nontender, with no palpable organomegaly. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 13.3 g/dL, white-cell count 68.4×10^3/μL (92% lymphocytes), platelet count 180×10^3/μL, total bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL, AST 14 U/L, and ALT 15 U/L. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed mild splenomegaly (13 cm) and two hypodense pancreatic lesions (1.4×1.4 cm in the body and 1.2 cm in the head). Endoscopic ultrasound–guided fine-needle aspiration of one lesion yielded a sample without blood contamination. Flow cytometry showed coexpression of CD5 and CD23.

A 37-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of a swelling on the right buccal mucosa. On examination, there was a well-circumscribed red-to-purple firm nodule measuring 2 × 2 cm. The lesion was nontender, with intact overlying mucosa and no ulceration. The patient denied chronic cheek biting or extraoral swelling. A provisional diagnosis of mucocele was made, and aspiration with a 25-gauge needle yielded frank blood. Cytological examination ruled out mucocele. Ultrasound showed no feeder vessel within the lesion. After correlation of the clinical, cytological, and ultrasound findings, surgical excision under local anesthesia was planned.

A 44-year-old Japanese woman underwent a routine ultrasound that identified a 5.9-cm uterine myoma–like lesion. Twelve months later, the lesion had nearly doubled in size, and she was referred for further evaluation. On internal examination, the uterus was enlarged to approximately the size of a newborn head; cervical and vaginal examinations were unremarkable, and no adnexal masses were palpable. Routine blood tests were within normal limits. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed an isoechoic solid mass with an ill-defined boundary between the lesion and the uterus. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 110 × 90 × 80 mm lesion in the right pelvis with smooth margins, mild lobulation, T1 signal intensity similar to myometrium, low T2 signal intensity, and flow-void areas forming a bridging vascular sign. These findings suggested a subserous uterine myoma, but the continuity with the uterus was unclear and the right ovary was not visualized, prompting consideration of an ovarian fibroma or thecoma. The left ovary appeared normal. A preliminary diagnosis of subserous myoma was made, and laparoscopic myomectomy was planned. Intraoperatively, a 10-cm right ovarian mass was identified without adhesion or rupture; the uterus and left adnexa were normal. A right adnexectomy was performed, and serous ascitic fluid was collected—cytology was negative.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of fullness and dull pain in her left knee. She noted a progressively enlarging mass and reported difficulty flexing the knee, sitting cross-legged, or squatting. There was no history of trauma or constitutional symptoms. On examination, there was fullness on the medial aspect of the left knee and a palpable nodular mass measuring approximately 6 × 4 cm over the infrapatellar region medial to the patellar tendon. The mass was non-tender, bony hard, immobile, and more prominent on flexion than on extension. Active knee flexion was limited to 100°. Neurovascular examination of the limb was normal. 

Plain radiographs of the knee showed a mineralized mass situated between the anterior tibial tubercle and the patella, occupying the infrapatellar fat pad; the femoral condyles and tibial plateau appeared normal. MRI revealed a large mineralized mass lying within Hoffa’s fat pad with no attachment to the skeletal tissue.

A 7-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of progressive nasal obstruction and snoring. He had experienced two days of intermittent epistaxis. His surgical history included adenotonsillectomy at age 2½ years and adenoidectomy at age 5 without pathological examination; his nasal congestion had improved after each procedure but recurred over time. On examination, otoscopy was normal without effusion, and multiple small (<2 cm) palpable cervical lymph nodes were noted. Flexible nasal endoscopy revealed a soft tissue mass in the nasopharynx thought to represent adenoid hypertrophy. A lateral radiograph of the nasopharynx confirmed a nasopharyngeal obstruction consistent with adenoid enlargement, and an adenoidectomy was planned. During surgery, the lateral pharyngeal bands appeared fibrotic and tight, and the nasopharyngeal tissue was unexpectedly hard and dense compared to typical adenoid tissue. The specimen was sent for postoperative pathological evaluation.

A 31-year-old man presented with an asymptomatic, slowly enlarging, exophytic, brownish nodule on the abdominal wall that showed surface telangiectasia. Four years earlier, a lesion at the same site had been resected and was misdiagnosed as dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans. His general health was otherwise excellent, and systemic examination was unremarkable. The recurrent nodule, measuring 22 mm in diameter, was completely excised; on gross examination it was a firm, well-demarcated dermal nodule with dark-brown and yellow areas on cut surface.

Microscopically, the lesion was an unencapsulated dermal nodule with overlying epidermal hyperplasia and a grenz zone, extending superficially into subcutaneous tissue. At the periphery, there were hyaline, large, round collagen bundles. The tumor consisted of dense interlacing fascicles and storiform arrays of histiocyte-like and fibroblast-like spindle cells, intermingled with mononuclear and giant cells exhibiting foamy cytoplasm and large, hyperchromatic, irregular nuclei. Mitotic activity was 4 figures per 10 high-power fields; atypical mitoses and necrosis were absent. Prominent blood-filled spaces, siderophages, and hemosiderin deposits were noted.

Immunohistochemical studies showed focal positivity for CD68 and complete negativity for S100 protein, HMB45, CD34, and alpha smooth muscle actin.

A 33-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 2, presented with acute pelvic pain and vaginal bleeding. Her history was notable for a medical abortion three months earlier. On admission she was afebrile, tachycardic, and hypotensive. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin concentration of 9.0 g/dL and a serum human chorionic gonadotropin level of 9.98 mIU/mL. Transvaginal and transabdominal ultrasound revealed a 45×35 mm inhomogeneous intrauterine lesion with high vascularity that appeared to infiltrate the posterior uterine wall, as well as free intraperitoneal fluid consistent with haemoperitoneum. An emergency laparoscopy evacuated 800 mL of blood but identified no obvious bleeding source. Subsequent pelvic angiography demonstrated bilaterally enlarged uterine feeding vessels. Bilateral selective uterine artery embolization was then performed.

A 59-year-old woman presented with a crusted plaque on her right breast of 1-month duration, unresponsive to a topical dexamethasone acetate preparation. On examination, the breast was otherwise normal, with no axillary lymphadenopathy, edema, peau d’orange change, or varicose veins. There was an irregular, asymptomatic, 5×5-cm plaque on the right breast, with an unsmooth, scaly, and scarred surface and a small area of ulceration. Breast ultrasonography showed no masses and no abnormal lymph nodes in the axillae or supraclavicular fossae. A skin biopsy revealed hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, and epidermal pustules; irregular acanthosis with full-thickness epidermal atypia; and a dermal lymphocytic infiltrate. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated negativity for cytokeratin 7 and cytokeratin 20, with a Ki-67 proliferation index of 60%.

A 37-year-old man presented with a two-year history of painless, nonprogressive blurring of vision in his right eye. He had no systemic illnesses, medications, or relevant family history. Best corrected visual acuity was 6/18 in the right eye and 6/6 in the left. Intraocular pressure was 12 mmHg in the right eye; there was a right relative afferent pupillary defect. The anterior segment was unremarkable. Dilated funduscopic examination of the right eye revealed a dark brownish pigmented mass covering the entire optic disk and extending into the vitreous, with pigmentation into the surrounding retina including the papillomacular bundle and superotemporal area. The lesion measured 4.8 mm vertically and 4.6 mm horizontally. Neovascularization was noted on the superior aspect of the lesion. The superotemporal retinal vessels appeared white, and dot hemorrhages were present in the temporal macula.  
B-scan ultrasonography of the right eye showed an elevated echogenic mass projecting into the vitreous from the optic disk. Fundus fluorescein angiography revealed extensive nonperfusion in the superotemporal retina with absence of dye transit in the corresponding artery and vein; there was late leakage from neovascularization on the optic disk. Fundus autofluorescence demonstrated hypoautofluorescence of the disk and a peripapillary ring of hypoautofluorescence sparing the fovea. Optical coherence tomography through the lesion showed thinning and stretching of the adjacent retina at the base of the mass and a flattened top.

A 16-year-old boy with no prior medical history presented with a 2-month history of persistent right leg pain that gradually extended to both thighs and knees, accompanied by swelling of the right lower leg. On examination, there was tenderness of the right lower leg radiating to the thighs and knees, and right foot muscle strength was approximately 2/5. MRI of the lower extremities revealed an ill-defined, lobulated soft-tissue mass in the right anterior tibial muscle, showing intermediate T2 signal with necrotic areas, low heterogeneous T1 signal, and marked heterogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. Multiple bilateral intramedullary lesions were also seen in the tibias and femurs, each with ill-defined margins, heterogeneous T2 hyperintensity, T1 hypointensity, and heterogeneous post-gadolinium enhancement. An excisional biopsy of the mass was performed. Histopathology showed sheets of uniform small round cells with oval nuclei, scant pale cytoplasm, and areas of necrosis, with occasional pseudorosette formation. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated diffuse membranous positivity for CD99 and for vimentin, and negativity for cytokeratin, actin, neuron-specific enolase, and leukocyte common antigen.

A male neonate (birth weight 3.3 kg) was delivered at term by spontaneous vaginal delivery. He had abdominal distention noted at birth and developed jaundice on day 2 of life, associated with clay-colored stools. On day 7, he was referred for further evaluation. 

Examination revealed icterus, a distended abdomen with an everted umbilicus, dilated abdominal veins, and a firm, irregular mass (approximately 15 × 10 cm) occupying the entire abdomen. 

Laboratory studies showed total bilirubin 9.7 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 7.2 mg/dL, AST 78 U/L, ALT 69 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 423.6 U/L; other routine blood tests and serum alpha-fetoprotein and β-hCG levels were normal. 

Abdominal radiography demonstrated three separate areas of multiple radiodensities. Ultrasound revealed an encapsulated sac containing three malformed fetiform structures. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a well-encapsulated anterior pararenal sac containing three malformed fetuses located in the right hypochondrium, right lower pelvis, and left hypochondrium; the mass displaced the duodenum anteriorly, compressed the common bile duct (resulting in intrahepatic biliary dilation) and right kidney (causing hydronephrosis), and shifted bowel loops to the left.

A 45-year-old man with no prior illness presented with a 5-day history of flu-like symptoms (rhinorrhea, dry cough, headache, and myalgia), which resolved except for persistent dry cough and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. He denied dyspnea, fever, or weight loss. He was a lifelong nonsmoker and reported a brother who died of metastatic renal cancer. On examination, vesicular breath sounds were abolished at the right lung base. Vital signs were normal. 

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, electrolytes, and liver and renal function tests, were unremarkable. Chest radiography showed a moderate right pleural effusion. Diagnostic thoracentesis yielded yellow, turbid fluid with the following results: pH 8.5; protein 5.3 g/dL (pleural/serum protein ratio 0.74); LDH 221 IU/L (pleural/serum LDH ratio 1.09); glucose 125 mg/dL; 10 nucleated cells/mm3 (100% lymphocytes); 60 red cells/mm3; no bacteria on smear; negative BK and Xpert MTB/RIF; and cytology negative for atypical cells.

Contrast-enhanced chest CT confirmed right pleural effusion and revealed well-circumscribed osteolytic lesions in the sternum and a thoracic vertebra. Prostate-specific antigen was normal; serum protein immunofixation showed no monoclonal band; viral serologies (HBV, HCV, HIV) were negative; alkaline phosphatase, parathyroid hormone, and vitamin D levels were normal. Bone scintigraphy showed tracer uptake in the shoulders consistent with degenerative change, and FDG PET–CT demonstrated multiple lytic bone lesions without sclerotic rims or cortical destruction and only mild glycolytic activity (maximum standardized uptake value, 2.9).

In view of the unexplained lytic lesions and lack of a primary tumor, a bone biopsy was planned.

A 64‐year‐old woman presented with a two‐month history of an asymptomatic, progressive pigmented lesion under the nail of her left fifth finger. She denied pain, bleeding, or tenderness. One year earlier, she had struck this finger against a door. Her medical history was notable only for surgically managed lumbar disc herniation 25 years ago and treated brucellosis 7 months ago; she had no personal or family history of skin cancer. On examination, the nail plate was ruptured and onycholysis was present with a brown‐to‐black lesion spanning the entire nail bed. Hutchinson’s sign was positive. The remaining fingers and clinical examination were unremarkable.  
Given the clinical appearance and differential diagnoses—including squamous cell carcinoma, pyogenic granuloma, and melanoma—an elliptical incisional biopsy (2 × 1.5 × 0.5 cm) was performed under local anesthesia, and the specimen was sent for pathological examination.

A 28-year-old healthy right-handed male cook presented with an 18-month history of right wrist swelling and pain, worse with extension. Examination revealed right wrist flexion 5°, extension 10°; pronation and supination 80° each; grip strength 6 kg (13% of left); VAS pain 4/10; Q-DASH 38.64/100; Mayo wrist score 60/100.  
Plain radiography (frontal) showed a radiolucent zone in the lunate with osteosclerosis; lateral view revealed radiocarpal osteoarthritic changes. MRI STIR demonstrated low signal in the lunate and high signal in the scaphoid, pisiform, and distal radius, resembling wrist arthritis and not typical for Kienböck’s disease. Differential diagnoses included Kienböck’s disease; rheumatoid arthritis; tuberculosis; atypical mycobacterial disease; and bacterial arthritis.  
Laboratory tests were notable for negative white blood cell count, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, procalcitonin, interferon-γ assay for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, anti-mycobacterium antibodies, and autoantibodies.  
CT of the wrist revealed a low-density area in the lunate abutting the radiocarpal surface with surrounding osteosclerosis.

A 29-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of a sensation of pelvic heaviness. She had no relevant medical or family history, and her menstrual cycles were regular. On physical examination, no abnormalities were noted.

Pelvic ultrasonography demonstrated an oval, lobulated, well-demarcated mass of mixed echogenicity. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography confirmed a moderately enhancing pelvic mass.

At laparotomy, the mass was pseudo-encapsulated, regular in shape, and showed no invasion into surrounding tissues. A complete local resection was performed. On gross examination, the tumor measured 15 cm in its longest axis, was well demarcated without a true capsule, and had a yellowish-white, homogeneous cut surface without hemorrhage or necrosis.

Microscopic examination revealed a well-circumscribed lesion with alternating hypercellular and hypocellular edematous areas containing abundant thin-walled blood vessels. The tumor cells were spindle-shaped with fine chromatin, and no mitotic figures were identified.

A 52-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of a painless growth on the upper anterior gums. He reported chewing paan-zarda 10 times per week and drinking alcohol three times per week; his medical and family histories were otherwise noncontributory. On examination, there was a solitary, sessile, yellow-white lesion with a pebbled surface on the attached gingiva at the sites of teeth 13 and 14, measuring 0.8 cm × 2.0 cm. Adjacent oral mucosa showed blanching, and palpation revealed bilateral vertical fibrous bands from teeth 26 to 36; interincisal opening was 35 mm. An intraoral periapical radiograph demonstrated intact crowns, roots, and interdental bone, consistent with a soft-tissue lesion. Based on these findings, a provisional diagnosis of verrucous hyperplasia with oral submucous fibrosis was made, and a differential diagnosis of verruciform xanthoma, papilloma, and verrucous carcinoma in the setting of OSF was given. An excisional biopsy, including a margin of adjacent gingiva, was performed and sent for histopathologic evaluation.

A 49-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with 5 months of progressive back pain and 5 days of rapid onset numbness and paralysis in both lower limbs. Neurologic examination revealed marked paresthesia and weakness of proximal and distal muscle groups in both lower extremities (MMT grade 3/5). Plain radiographs of the spine showed a compressive deformity and heterogeneous sclerosis of the T10 vertebra. MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrated a T10 vertebral lesion with low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, moderately high signal on T2-weighted images, and gadolinium-enhanced axial images revealing extraosseous extensions compressing the spinal cord. Contrast-enhanced CT of the spine confirmed heterogeneous sclerosis and remarkable irregular extraosseous bone proliferation at T10. Whole-body CT (neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis) showed no primary tumor, and blood tests revealed no positive tumor markers. Two days after admission, her lower-limb strength worsened to MMT grade 2/5, and urgent surgical intervention was planned.

A 42-year-old woman with known MEN1 syndrome was under surveillance. Two years earlier, she had undergone right mastectomy and axillary dissection for a 7-cm infiltrating lobular carcinoma (solid-alveolar variant, G2, ER 95%, PgR 80%, Ki-67 20%, Her2 negative; pT3 N9/18 M0). She completed adjuvant chemotherapy and hormonal therapy without evidence of recurrent disease. BRCA1/2 testing was negative.

Because she had a breast expander in place, she did not undergo MRI. Instead, a fluorodeoxyglucose PET–CT scan showed intense uptake (SUVmax 14.6) in a 25 × 12 × 50 mm elongated, thickened area along the left mid-axillary line adjacent to the 4th–6th ribs. There was also mild hypermetabolism in bilaterally enlarged adrenals.

Bilateral ultrasound and mammography of the left breast and axilla showed no focal lesions. A contrast-enhanced chest CT confirmed a 30-mm hyperdense mass contacting the pectoralis major muscle but without lymphadenopathy or imaging features typical of local recurrence. The patient was asymptomatic and total-body CT was otherwise negative for metastases.

A 57-year-old woman was evaluated for mild direct hyperbilirubinemia and recurrent cholangitis. Her history was notable for hypertension and a prior laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Initial abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated small stones in the common bile duct. She underwent elective ERCP, during which biliary stones were removed and a plastic stent was placed. Cholangiography also revealed a distal bile duct stenosis, thought to be caused by extrinsic compression from a cystic lesion in the head of the pancreas. Serum CA 19-9 was 343 U/mL (normal < 40). Subsequent MRI with cholangiographic sequences showed a 3-cm cystic cluster in the pancreatic head responsible for biliary compression. Endoscopic ultrasound confirmed an IPMN-like cystic lesion but did not demonstrate communication with the pancreatic ducts; there were no worrisome features or solid components. After multidisciplinary review, the patient was referred for surgical resection.

A 26-year-old man presented with a two-month history of cough, dyspnea, and a progressively enlarging left-side neck mass. Physical examination revealed a multilobulated, firm, mobile, non-tender mass in the left cervical region; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. A chest radiograph demonstrated masses in the anterior and right middle mediastinum. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a 20 cm × 18 cm × 8 cm heterogeneous mass in the right upper quadrant extending to the subhepatic region. Serum α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and β-human chorionic gonadotropin concentrations were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck, chest, and abdomen revealed heterogeneous, lobulated masses with predominant fat density: one in the left neck, a 12 cm × 8 cm × 6 cm encapsulated mass in the left anterior mediastinum, another in the right middle mediastinum at the subcarinal region, and a mass in the right abdomen; there was no evidence of chest wall or pericardial invasion or focal calcification. Testicular, pelvic, and inguinal ultrasound examinations were normal.

A 33‐year‐old man with no significant medical history presented with 3 months of progressive right leg pain, calf swelling, and difficulty walking. He denied trauma, fever, chills, chest pain, abdominal symptoms, or urinary changes. Physical examination revealed tenderness and edema of the right lower leg. A venous ultrasound showed a large cystic mass in the medial thigh compressing the distal femoral vein and associated deep venous thrombosis of the distal femoral and popliteal veins. He was started on apixaban. 

At surgical follow‐up, examination disclosed a 5 × 5 cm firm, non‐tender mass in the right upper medial thigh without inguinal lymphadenopathy. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the right thigh demonstrated a 4.6 × 4.0 × 3.2 cm mass in the Hunter’s canal. MRI of the thigh revealed a 4.8 × 4.2 × 5.1 cm lesion along the superficial femoral vessels that was heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, hypointense on T1-weighted images, exhibited large areas of solid enhancement, contained a central cystic component, and showed partial encasement of the superficial femoral vessels.

An 80-year-old Caucasian woman presented with acute chest pain and one week of progressive dyspnea on exertion on a six-month background of fatigue. Her medical history included hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and depression; medications were a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, a statin, an antimuscarinic agent, a proton-pump inhibitor, and calcium supplementation. She had no history of autoimmune disease, malignancy, tuberculosis, or HIV.

On examination, she had bilateral peripheral edema, bibasal crackles, and mild epigastric tenderness. Blood pressure was normal and heart sounds were unremarkable without added sounds; there was no jugular venous distension.

Electrocardiography revealed complete heart block with small QRS complexes. CT pulmonary angiography was negative for pulmonary embolism but showed a large pericardial effusion (>3 cm depth), small to moderate bilateral pleural effusions, and two enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated normal left ventricular systolic function (ejection fraction, 60%) and a circumferential pericardial effusion measuring 27 mm with right ventricular and right atrial diastolic collapse.

Laboratory evaluation revealed a normal complete blood count, a creatinine level of 96 µmol/L, a high-sensitivity troponin level of 108 ng/L, and a brain-type natriuretic peptide level of 464.8 ng/L. Early in her admission she became hemodynamically unstable from cardiac tamponade (blood pressure, 88/46 mm Hg; bradycardia to 48 bpm). Emergency pericardiocentesis drained 700 mL of blood-tinged fluid, and a dual-chamber permanent pacemaker was implanted. Cytologic analysis of the pericardial fluid was negative for malignant cells, and lactate dehydrogenase was elevated at 1955 IU/L.

A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis performed after drainage revealed a lobulated soft-tissue mass surrounding the right coronary artery, extending transmurally to the atrioventricular junction and encroaching into the right atrium, measuring 52 mm at maximum diameter. Findings were suggestive of a cardiac neoplasm, and the differential diagnosis included lymphoma and sarcoma.

A 49-year-old homosexual man with a history of AIDS on chronic antiretroviral therapy presented with worsening neck pain and progressive weakness of the left distal arm and hand. On examination, he had decreased strength (3/5) in left wrist and finger extension; sensation was intact. Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine revealed an erosive mass within the C4 vertebral body extending through the left pedicle, with severe spinal canal stenosis; adjacent cervical vertebral bodies also showed involvement, most markedly at C4. To search for a primary source, the patient underwent a positron emission tomography scan and computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis; both were unrevealing. He also had a recent screening colonoscopy and upper endoscopy, which showed no lesions. No other osseous or visceral lesions were identified.

A 57‐year‐old man presented with 2 months of left chest pain and an 8‐kg weight loss. He had a 40–pack‐year smoking history and a family history of lung cancer in his father. Physical examination was unremarkable. Initial CT showed multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules and lytic lesions in the left eighth rib, ninth thoracic vertebra, and right iliac bone. A biopsy of the rib lesion revealed malignancy, suspected adenocarcinoma of the lung, but the sample was inadequate for full typing. 

PET-CT showed FDG uptake in the left eighth rib (SUVmax 2.8), ninth vertebra (SUVmax 6.0), right iliac bone (SUVmax 4.1), and left neck lymph node (SUVmax 3.5), but no uptake in the pulmonary nodules. Brain MRI revealed multiple asymptomatic metastases. Sputum cytology was negative. Upper endoscopy found a duodenal elevated lesion, but biopsy showed Brunner’s gland hyperplasia without malignancy. Renal and bladder ultrasound showed no tumors, and urine cytology was negative.

Laboratory studies revealed elevated CA15-3 (286 U/ml; normal 0–28) and KL-6 (2330 U/ml; normal 105–435), with other tumor markers within normal limits. Despite exhaustive evaluation, no primary tumor was identified, and the patient was initially treated as a cancer of unknown primary.

A 26-year-old male student presented with mid back pain for one year and sudden onset of bilateral lower limb weakness and inability to walk over one week. On examination, he had ataxia with a broad-based gait, bilateral lower limb hypertonia, muscle strength of MRC grade 2–3, hypoesthesia below the T7 dermatome, hyperreflexic knee and ankle jerks with ankle clonus, and a positive Babinski sign. Perianal sensation and bowel–bladder function were normal. Laboratory tests revealed a hemoglobin level of 17.5 g/dL; all other routine blood tests were normal. Spine radiographs showed straightening of the dorsolumbar spine without other abnormalities. MRI demonstrated a well-defined, homogeneously enhancing mass in the posterior epidural space from T6 to T8 with right T7 foraminal extension; the lesion was hyperintense on T2-weighted images and iso- to hypointense on T1-weighted images with contrast enhancement. A PET scan showed a low-grade intraspinal lesion at T6–T8 with low FDG uptake and no evidence of metastasis or other primary foci.

A 24-day-old term male infant presented with a 48-hour history of non-bilious projectile vomiting. He was born at 39 weeks’ gestation via uncomplicated vaginal delivery, with birth weight 3050 g, length 47 cm, and head circumference 35.5 cm. Prenatal sonograms were normal. On examination, the infant appeared well, with no skin lesions and no palpable organomegaly. 

An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated pyloric muscle thickness of 4 mm and pyloric canal length of 25 mm, consistent with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Incidentally, the liver was enlarged and had a heterogeneous appearance with multiple hypoechoic nodules in both lobes. 

Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, electrolytes, liver function tests, thyroid function tests, alpha-fetoprotein, vanillylmandelic acid, and neuron specific enolase, were all within normal limits. 

Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging showed diffuse hepatomegaly with innumerable nodules throughout both lobes; the lesions were hyperintense on T2-weighted images with prominent flow voids and hypointense on T1-weighted images. 

A transthoracic echocardiogram showed normal cardiac anatomy and function, with no evidence of high-output heart failure.

A 42-year-old woman presented with a right retroauricular mass that had been slowly enlarging over 20 years, causing a marked cosmetic deformity. She had no pain, trauma, hearing loss, or history of infection or surgery in the area. On examination, both tympanic membranes were intact, and there was a huge, firm, painless, bony mass in the right mastoid region. A temporal bone CT scan showed a 2.3 × 2.3 × 4.3 cm well-demarcated, high-density bony outgrowth arising from the cortex of the right mastoid bone and squama, with a broad base and no involvement of middle or inner ear structures.

A 9-month-old female infant was brought for evaluation of a right posterior chest wall swelling noted by her parents 3 months earlier that had progressively increased in size. The infant was otherwise healthy; her perinatal history was unremarkable. On examination, she appeared well, with stable vital signs and no respiratory distress. There was a large, firm, fixed, non-tender mass over the right posterior chest wall. A complete blood count was within age-appropriate normal limits. A frontal chest radiograph showed a large nonspecific opacity over the right hemithorax, with normally expanded lungs. Sonography demonstrated a homogeneously echogenic lesion. Non-contrast chest CT revealed a 9.7 × 6 × 3.3 cm well-encapsulated posterolateral chest wall mass at levels T1–T10 that was predominantly fat in density with thick internal soft-tissue strands and a small intrathoracic extension between the second and third ribs. There were no calcifications, rib changes, or disturbance of subcutaneous fat.

A 54-year-old man with a 20-year history of poorly controlled small-bowel Crohn’s disease was referred for evaluation of a 2-month history of worsening abdominal pain, bloating, emesis, and a 50-lb weight loss. He had no history of intra-abdominal surgery apart from drainage of a perirectal abscess and seton placement for a fistula. Medications included omeprazole, budesonide, mesalamine, and recently started adalimumab. A capsule endoscopy performed during Crohn’s induction showed distal small-bowel ulceration, erythema, and edema.

On examination, he appeared uncomfortable and mildly pale, with dry mucous membranes. Vital signs were normal. The abdomen was soft, distended, and tympanitic without tenderness, peritoneal signs, scars, or hernias. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, hematocrit 36.6%, normal white-cell count, electrolytes, and renal function. Upright and supine abdominal radiographs demonstrated centrally located, dilated small-bowel loops with air-fluid levels up to 6.7 cm. A contrast CT scan confirmed markedly dilated proximal small-bowel loops consistent with a high-grade small-bowel obstruction, but no transition point or mass was identified.

A 15-year-old girl was evaluated for episodic altered behavior over 5 months. Parents noted 30-minute episodes each morning of fatigue, confusion, poor concentration, irritability, and “staring off,” which resolved after breakfast; the patient had no recall. Initial laboratory studies, including basic metabolic profile, thyroid function tests, and urine drug screen, were normal. An outpatient electroencephalogram (EEG) was scheduled; during the study she became unresponsive. Point-of-care testing at that time showed a glucose level of 36 mg/dL (reference 65–110), an insulin level of 36.8 μIU/mL (2.6–24.9), a C-peptide level of 4.6 ng/mL (1.1–4.4), and a β-hydroxybutyrate level of 0.6 mg/dL (0.2–2.8). Her mental status promptly improved after intravenous dextrose. To localize a possible insulin-producing lesion, an abdominal CT scan with contrast was performed and reported as negative. Because her EEG was interpreted as abnormal, valproic acid was started for presumed seizure activity. She was discharged with a home glucometer and neurology follow-up. An outpatient endoscopic ultrasound was also unremarkable. Subsequently, she was admitted to a tertiary pediatric center because of near-daily morning episodes. During a supervised fast, her blood glucose fell to 40 mg/dL within 6 hours. A critical laboratory sample obtained during hypoglycemia showed a glucose concentration of 43 mg/dL, insulin 38.1 μIU/mL, C-peptide 4.1 ng/mL, and β-hydroxybutyrate <100 μmol/L. Testing for sulfonylurea ingestion was negative.

An 18-month-old girl presented with right eye pain and outward deviation, initially treated as conjunctivitis. Two months later she developed gait imbalance, frequent falls, left-sided weakness, and drooling of saliva on the left. On examination she was afebrile, normotensive, conscious, and alert, with normal tone and reflexes and no signs of raised intracranial pressure. Neurologic findings included an ataxic gait, left-sided drooling, and decreased motor strength on the left. Noncontrast head CT showed an isodense to hyperdense, well-circumscribed mass in the right lateral pons, middle cerebellar peduncle, and cerebellopontine angle, causing partial effacement of the fourth ventricle and leftward pontine deviation without hydrocephalus or herniation. Brain MRI revealed the lesion to be hypointense on T1-weighted images, mildly hyperintense on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences, with minimal postcontrast enhancement, mild diffusion restriction on DWI/ADC, and mildly elevated relative cerebral blood volume on perfusion. Whole-spine MRI and CSF cytology showed no evidence of metastasis. The patient underwent a right suboccipital craniotomy for tumor debulking. Histology demonstrated multilayered rosettes composed of pseudostratified neuroepithelium with central lumina amid sheets of small, poorly differentiated cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios. Immunohistochemistry showed tumor cells positive for CD56 and synaptophysin and negative for SMA, EMA, chromogranin, and NeuN; GFAP highlighted only reactive astrocytes; P53 was focally positive; and INI-1 nuclear staining was intact. Genetic testing for C19MC amplification was not performed.

A 41-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of progressively decreased visual acuity and right peripheral facial paralysis. She had no significant past medical history and no family history of neoplasm or neurological disorders. Brain MRI demonstrated an expansile, well-defined oval lesion measuring 19 × 17 × 16 mm, located above the sella turcica. The lesion was isointense on both T1- and T2-weighted images and showed homogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. It abutted the optic chiasm and the mammillary bodies, laterally displacing the optic tracts, without signal abnormality or contrast enhancement of the optic nerves. There was no calcification, and the anterior pituitary gland appeared normal. These radiological findings raised the differential diagnosis of pituicytoma versus craniopharyngioma.

A 57-year-old woman with a history of primary mediastinal non-Hodgkin lymphoma in 1992 and multiple relapses of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma treated with chemotherapy, autologous and allogeneic stem-cell transplantation, CAR T-cell therapy, and cranial and ocular radiation presented with new painless vision loss in her left eye.

On initial examination, left eye visual acuity was 20/150 with a central scotoma, color plates 1/10, and an afferent pupillary defect. The anterior chamber was quiet. Fundus examination revealed optic disc swelling with splinter hemorrhages, possible early retinitis-like lesions inferior to the fovea, and perivascular infiltrates. MRI of the orbits with and without contrast demonstrated focal enhancement of the left optic nerve head without other lesions.

Six weeks later, her visual acuity had deteriorated to counting fingers at 2 feet. Examination showed 1+ anterior chamber cell, 1+ vitreous cell, diffuse pallid disc swelling and infiltration, and translucent perivascular sheathing consistent with frosted branch angiitis in the left eye.

A 32-year-old woman presented with a 1½-year history of swelling in the left neck. She was a nonsmoker and nondrinker; her medical history was unremarkable except that her mother had undergone surgery for a carotid body paraganglioma. On examination, a 1.5 cm soft, mobile mass was palpated anterior to the left sternocleidomastoid muscle; there were no cranial nerve deficits and no lymphadenopathy. Laryngoscopic examination was normal. Blood and urine catecholamine levels were within normal limits.

Ultrasonography showed a well-defined, oval, hypoechoic, solid 25 × 32 mm hypervascular mass at the left carotid bifurcation, with splaying of the internal and external carotid arteries. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a hypervascular mass in the same location and revealed an additional well-defined, ovoid, 10 × 12 mm hypervascular mass in the right preepiglottic space. MRI demonstrated that both lesions were isointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed homogeneous intense enhancement.

A 29-year-old Indian woman presented with a 2-week history of a non-tender mass on her left upper eyelid. She had noted a small erythematous lesion that increased in size despite warm compresses. She denied visual changes, trauma, or constitutional symptoms. Her medical history was notable only for iron deficiency anemia. On examination, visual acuity was 6/9.5 bilaterally, intraocular pressures were normal, and extraocular movements were full without a relative afferent pupillary defect. Eversion of the left upper eyelid revealed a smooth, homogeneous, firm, rubbery mass measuring approximately 1 cm × 1 cm. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable, and vital signs were within normal limits.

The lesion was treated as a presumed pyogenic granuloma with intralesional triamcinolone. One month later, after slight initial improvement, swelling recurred with intermittent pain and blurred vision; visual acuity was 6/12 bilaterally. Because the lesion persisted, an incisional biopsy was performed with repeat intralesional triamcinolone.

Histopathologic examination showed a mass composed predominantly of histiocytic cells, including epithelioid histiocytes and Touton-type multinucleated giant cells, with admixed lymphocytes, plasma cells, and polymorphonuclear cells. Immunohistochemical stains demonstrated lesional cells positive for CD163 and CD68 and negative for S100, CD1A, and Langerin. The lesion extended to the peripheral and deep margins of the specimen.

A 62-year-old woman with a 30-year history of classical migraine presented because, over the preceding six months, her headaches changed from intermittent, migrainous attacks with nausea and vomiting to a continuous, right-sided pain of increasing intensity without associated nausea or vomiting. She also noticed a gradually enlarging lump over the right parietal area of her skull. On examination, she was alert and oriented. She complained of moderate headache. Palpation of the right parietal bone revealed a hard, slightly tender, ill-defined, elliptical prominence measuring approximately 7 × 8 cm.  
Laboratory studies were unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head showed an osteoblastic lesion centered in the diploic space of the right parietal bone, involving both inner and outer tables, without evidence of dural extension.

A 54-year-old Saudi woman presented with a 3-month history of left neck swelling and hoarseness, which had enlarged rapidly over 1 week, causing dyspnea and dysphagia to solids. Her medical history included type II diabetes mellitus and hypothyroidism treated with metformin and levothyroxine. She was a non-smoker with stable weight. On examination, vital signs were normal. A fixed, hard 8×8 cm mass with an inflammatory surface occupied the left thyroid lobe; there was no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. Chest, cardiac, neurologic, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Ultrasonography showed a largely solid and partially cystic 8.5×9 cm mass in the left thyroid lobe. CT of the neck revealed a 10×10 cm partially necrotic mass in the left thyroid lobe, invading adjacent skin and the trachea, with no cervical lymphadenopathy.
