Serum T4, TSH, thyroglobulin, and calcium levels were within normal limits. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the mass was performed, which revealed squamous cell carcinoma.

A 71-year-old woman with a history of sarcoidosis and gastrointestinal non-Hodgkin lymphoma presented with crushing right eye pain, headaches, and diplopia. One year earlier, a right orbital tumour had been partially excised; histopathology then showed fibrous tissue with vascular proliferation without atypia or mitotic activity, and no further treatment was given. Symptoms recurred and progressively worsened. On admission, right exophthalmos was evident, with paresis of cranial nerves III and IV. Visual acuity was unchanged at 0.8. Diplopia was exacerbated on gaze in directions of the affected extraocular muscles; no other cranial nerve deficits were noted. MRI revealed a 2 cm mass in the right orbit; CT demonstrated a defect in the orbital roof from prior surgery. Surgical resection via a right pterional approach and complete orbitotomy was performed. Intraoperatively, a fibrous tumour embedded in scar tissue was found in periorbital fat, adherent to extraocular muscles, and was completely resected. Histopathologic examination of the lesion revealed numerous blood vessels and fibrous tissue accompanied by a dense mixed inflammatory infiltrate including eosinophils, lymphocytes, and plasma cells; focal lymphoid aggregates were present, but no granulomas. The vascular walls were thick and lined by mildly polymorphic, plump endothelial cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and vesicular nuclei. Necrosis and mitotic figures were absent.

A 9-year-old girl was evaluated for a right-sided facial swelling present since birth that had progressively increased in size. There was no pain. On examination, the right cheek and lip were enlarged, creating facial asymmetry. A painless, nontender, firm, fixed soft-tissue mass with ill-defined borders involved the entire right cheek, the lower half of the parotid and masseteric regions, and part of the submandibular area. The overlying skin was normal without discoloration or visible vascular changes. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy. Routine blood tests were within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging of the face and upper neck on the right side revealed a nonenhancing, ill-defined infiltrative lesion with inhomogeneous signal on T1-weighted images and moderately decreased signal on T2-weighted images. On T1-weighted fat-suppression images, the lesion showed partial suppression consistent with fat. The mass had fuzzy margins and no clear cleavage plane from adjacent hypertrophied temporalis and masseter muscles.

A 65-year-old woman presented with right dorsal pain. Laboratory studies showed total bilirubin 1.3 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 452 IU/L, and γ-glutamyl transferase 167 IU/L. The indocyanine green plasma disappearance rate was 0.103, and the 15-minute retention rate was 23.9%, indicating depressed liver function. Tests for hepatitis B and C viral markers were negative. Serum levels of α-fetoprotein, PIVKA-II, CEA, and CA19-9 were within normal limits; DUPAN-2 was 200 U/mL, CA125 was 321.8 U/mL, and neuron-specific enolase was 29.2 ng/mL.  
Abdominal CT revealed a well-defined, low-density, heterogeneous, multilocular cystic tumor with septa replacing the right hepatic lobe and medial segment of the left lobe, measuring 16 cm in diameter, with an enhancing solid compartment and a nonenhancing cystic compartment, compressing the umbilical portion of the portal vein, the right portal vein, and the left hepatic vein. MRI showed mixed high and low signal intensity: cysts were low on T1-weighted images and high on T2-weighted images, and areas of high T1 and low T2 signal suggested intratumoral hemorrhage. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a honeycomb-like tumor with solid components. PET–CT showed FDG uptake in the solid components of the cyst. From these imaging findings, the preoperative diagnosis of mucinous cystadenocarcinoma or sarcoma of the liver was made.

A 52-year-old G4P2 woman, menopause at age 49, was referred for evaluation of an ovarian cyst. Transvaginal ultrasound revealed multiple uterine fibroids, the largest measuring 40 mm. Pelvic MRI showed a 39 × 32 × 41 mm mass protruding from the anterior uterine wall. On T1- and T2-weighted images the lesion had mixed low-intensity areas and faint high-intensity areas; the hyperintense regions were suppressed on fat-suppression sequences, suggesting fat. The mass was interpreted as a subserous lipoleiomyoma. Given her postmenopausal status, she underwent annual pelvic exam, cervical cytology, and ultrasound, all without significant change until age 58, when her previous physician noted enlargement of the lesion. Repeat MRI demonstrated uterine retroflexion and a 49 × 40 × 49 mm anterior wall mass. The lesion remained heterogeneous on T1 and T2, largely hyperintense with fat suppression, and showed no abnormal signal on diffusion-weighted imaging. Compared with her MRI at 52, the maximal diameter had increased by 23% (volume by 85%). Although postmenopausal, the tumor had grown, and malignancy was discussed. The patient consented to total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.

A 69-year-old woman was referred with a 2-month history of cough productive of white sputum and progressive dyspnea on exertion, accompanied by a 1-week history of fever (37.3–39.8°C). Physical examination revealed cyanosis of the lips, lower-limb edema, clear consciousness, and no skin rashes, nodules, hemorrhagic spots, or hepatosplenomegaly. Chest CT demonstrated bilateral ground-glass opacities with areas of consolidation, prominent interlobular septal and bronchovascular bundle thickening producing tram-track like changes, and no mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy. Empirical treatment with imipenem–cilastatin and antipyretic acetaminophen produced no clinical or radiographic improvement.

A 19-year-old man presented with a one-week history of epigastric and back pain, as well as a one-year history of intermittent hematuria and blood-tinged sputum. He reported a three-month history of decreased appetite and weight loss but denied fever, dyspnea, or cough. On examination, his blood pressure was 120/70 mm Hg, pulse 78 beats/min, chest auscultation was clear, and the cardiovascular examination was normal. Abdominal examination revealed a firm, non-tender mass palpable in the epigastric and left hypochondriac regions. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 11.4 g/dL, normal complete blood count, coagulation profile, serum electrolytes, and liver function tests, and an elevated lactate dehydrogenase of 1070 U/L (normal range, 100–190 U/L). HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C antibody tests were nonreactive. A chest radiograph demonstrated a widened mediastinum and bilateral hilar enlargement. Ultrasonography of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a large heteroechoic mass replacing the entire left renal parenchyma with multiple enlarged left para-aortic lymph nodes. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed multiple conglomerate mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes, deposits in the left lower lung lobe, bilateral prominent axillary lymph nodes, and a large heterogeneously enhancing mass lesion replacing the left kidney with renal vein infiltration. Multiple conglomerate celiac and retroperitoneal lymph nodes were seen, and lytic destruction of the D4 and D5 vertebral bodies, the left superior pubic ramus, and the right ischium was noted. A working diagnosis of metastatic renal cell carcinoma versus lymphoma was made.

A 65‐year‐old man presented with a 3-year history of right-sided throbbing headache, progressive vision loss in the right eye, tinnitus, right ear hearing loss, and right-sided gait ataxia. He was afebrile with normal vital signs. Neurologic examination showed diminished sensation on the right half of the face, blindness in the right eye, and conductive hearing loss in the right ear; other findings were normal. Noncontrast CT of the brain demonstrated a lobulated heterogeneous, predominantly hypodense mass in the right Meckel’s cave, middle cranial fossa, and pterygomaxillary fossa, with extension into the right sphenoid sinus and suprasellar cistern and erosion of the clivus, sella turcica, and sphenoid and petrous temporal bones. MRI revealed an ill-defined lobulated mass in the middle cranial fossa and skull base extending anteriorly into the anterior cranial fossa and ethmoid sinuses, medially into the sphenoid sinus and suprasellar cistern, and inferiorly into the pterygomaxillary region. The lesion was heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, hypointense on T1-weighted images, and showed heterogeneous avid contrast enhancement. Susceptibility-weighted imaging demonstrated multiple microhemorrhages. Balanced fast-field echo images showed a small tail of the lesion extending into the cerebellopontine angle along the trigeminal nerve. Magnetic resonance angiography revealed encasement and medial displacement of the right internal carotid artery. Diffusion-weighted imaging showed a few hyperintense areas with corresponding decreased ADC values. Based on clinical and imaging findings, a differential diagnosis was formulated.

A 34-year-old woman with no relevant medical history discovered during self-examination a painless, mobile nodule in the inner lower quadrant of her left breast. On examination, the 2-cm mass was well-circumscribed without skin changes or palpable axillary lymphadenopathy. Breast ultrasonography revealed a solitary, hypoechoic, lobulated lesion measuring 2.0 × 2.0 × 1.5 cm without calcifications, classified as ACR 3–4. A core-needle biopsy demonstrated a biphasic proliferation of epithelial cells surrounded by myoepithelial cells; there were no cytologic abnormalities or infiltration, and the mitotic index was low. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for smooth muscle actin, p63, cytokeratin 14, and cytokeratin 5 (myoepithelial markers) and AE1/3 (epithelial marker); estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and HER2 were negative.

A 76-year-old Brazilian man presented with a two-week history of epigastric abdominal pain, sporadic fever, weight loss, nausea, and vomiting. His medical history included insulin-dependent type II diabetes mellitus, chronic hypertension, and non-dialytic chronic renal failure. He denied alcohol or tobacco use. Two months earlier, he had been hospitalized for hepatic and splenic abscesses with positive blood cultures for Staphylococcus aureus.

On examination he was afebrile; pulse 92 beats per minute; blood pressure 150/80 mmHg; and slightly edematous in the lower limbs. Pulmonary auscultation revealed bilateral basal rales. The abdomen was diffusely tender, most pronounced in the epigastrium and left upper quadrant; the liver edge was palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin. Laboratory studies showed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL; leukocytes 3.7 × 10^9/L; platelets 102 × 10^9/L), elevated lactate dehydrogenase (704 U/L), and mild elevations of amylase (149 U/L) and lipase (136 U/L).

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated gallbladder wall thickening with microcalculi, diffuse pancreatic enlargement with heterogeneous echotexture, and hyperechogenic peripancreatic tissue extending through the retroperitoneum. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed diffuse pancreatic enlargement surrounded by infiltrative tissue extending to the splenic and hepatic hila and the retroperitoneum, with moderate peritoneal fluid. Acute pancreatitis was diagnosed, and treatment was initiated, but there was no clinical improvement after four days. Paracentesis of the peritoneal fluid revealed atypical cells suspicious for malignancy along with numerous necrotic or degenerated lymphoid cells.

A 4-year-old boy was brought by his parents after they incidentally noted a non-tender swelling near the right lower molars. The patient denied pain or other symptoms.  
Laboratory studies, including serum calcium, phosphorus, and parathormone levels, were within normal limits.  
On examination, a smooth, non-tender mass was palpated in the right mandibular molar region; the rest of the oral cavity appeared normal.  
Maxillofacial computed tomography revealed a well-defined, 25 mm × 16 mm osteolytic lesion of the right mandibular ramus with cortical erosion.

A 20-year-old woman was referred with a three-year history of a swelling on the left hard palate that fluctuated in size and was occasionally painful. Her medical history was notable for hypothyroidism, fatty liver, prediabetes, and neuroblastoma treated surgically with cyclophosphamide and etoposide chemotherapy at 18 months of age. 

On examination, there was a 2.5–3 cm bluish-purple, smooth, sessile mass on the left posterior hard palate, with a focal area of telangiectasia. All teeth in the region were vital, and aspiration yielded no mucinous fluid. 

Periapical and panoramic radiographs showed no bony defects. Cone-beam CT demonstrated a shallow depression of the alveolar bone surface beneath the lesion without evidence of cortical destruction or nasal floor invasion. 

An incisional biopsy under local anesthesia was planned to establish a definitive diagnosis.

A 40-year-old woman was referred for management of an incidentally discovered radiolucent lesion associated with an impacted right mandibular third molar. Her medical and family history were unremarkable, and she had no symptoms. Extraoral examination was normal. Intraorally, there was a well-circumscribed, firm, sessile nodule approximately 1 cm in diameter on the gingiva distal to the right second molar; the overlying mucosa appeared normal, and the third molar was clinically absent. 

Panoramic radiography revealed a unilocular, expansile, homogeneous radiolucency at the right mandibular angle associated with the impacted third molar. Cone-beam computed tomography showed a well-defined 2 cm × 1.5 cm × 1 cm hypodense lesion with cortical expansion of the posterior mandible and displacement of the inferior alveolar canal.

Differential diagnoses included odontogenic cysts, odontogenic keratocyst, dentigerous cyst, ameloblastoma, and osteolytic lesions such as a brown tumor. Serum parathyroid hormone, vitamin D, phosphate, and calcium levels were obtained; all were within normal limits except for a decreased vitamin D level.

A 2-year-old girl was evaluated for a skin lesion on her abdomen that had been present since birth. The lesion consisted of a hyperpigmented patch with blurred edges and, within it, a fixed, firm, brownish nodule measuring approximately 25 × 20 mm. The patch and nodule were asymptomatic but had shown progressive growth over time. On examination, the edges of the patch were not well demarcated, and the underlying nodule was indurated and nonmobile. Given the lesion’s persistence and slow enlargement since birth, an incisional skin biopsy was performed to exclude malignancy.

A 16-year-old girl was referred because her upper right baby tooth had not fallen out. She had no relevant medical history. Intraoral examination showed that the right maxillary deciduous central incisor was retained and that the corresponding right permanent central incisor had not erupted, although the left permanent central incisor was fully erupted. A periapical radiograph of the area revealed a well-defined radio-opaque, tooth-like structure apical to the retained deciduous incisor, with the path of eruption of the impacted right permanent central incisor blocked by this mass.

A 17-year-old male competitive athlete presented with a 1-month history of progressive right knee pain. He first noted lateral knee discomfort during sports training, which worsened with activity and became present at rest and at night over the preceding 2 weeks. Nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs provided minimal relief. 

Initial imaging studies at an outside hospital included:  
• Plain radiographs of the knee showing a sclerotic mass in the lateral femoral epiphysis.  
• CT revealing a 32-mm lesion adjacent to the epiphyseal scar with intact trabecular structures at the metaphysis.  
• T2-weighted MRI demonstrating inhomogeneous signal changes within the epiphysis.

Three weeks later, on referral, repeat imaging demonstrated progressive changes:  
• Radiographs showing a nearly circular radiolucent lesion with ill-defined margins, extensive articular contact on the lateral femoral condyle, and internal sclerosis.  
• CT showing enlargement of the mass across the epiphyseal scar and partial destruction of the adjacent metaphyseal trabeculae.  
• T2-weighted MRI revealing altered signal intensity in the cartilage and new joint effusion.

Laboratory tests showed normal white-cell count, neutrophil count, and C-reactive protein.

A 30-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of a gradually enlarging, painless swelling over the anterolateral aspect of his right distal leg. He had no difficulty bearing weight. On examination, there was a 7×6×4 cm dome-shaped, hard mass adherent to the underlying bone, with distinct borders, no tenderness or overlying skin changes, full ankle range of motion, and intact neurovascular status. 

Plain radiographs of the right leg revealed an expansile, lobulated sclerotic lesion with multiple small lytic areas, a narrow zone of transition in the metadiaphyseal region of the distal tibia, and soft-tissue bulging. Routine blood and biochemical tests were normal. 

Non-contrast CT showed a cauliflower-like meta-diaphyseal sclerotic lesion with lytic areas arising from the posterior cortex of the distal tibia and invading the posterior cortex and possibly the medullary cavity of the distal fibula. The findings were reported as “an aggressive bone lesion likely Parosteal osteosarcoma or a malignant osteochondroma.” 

MRI demonstrated a pedunculated, mixed osseous and chondroid mass (7.3×5.7×4.4 cm) arising from the lateral cortex of the distal tibia, with a thick cartilage component, mild diffusion restriction, and chronic pressure changes in the adjacent fibula, suspicious for “malignant degeneration of the osteochondroma.” 

A tru-cut biopsy and fine-needle aspiration yielded a benign cartilaginous lesion described as “possibly bizarre parosteal osteochondromatous proliferation (BPOP lesion),” with osteochondroma as a secondary consideration.

A 9-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of blurry vision and headaches OS. She had a history of an irregular left pupil noted at age 7 and a new pigmented iris lesion seen at age 9. On examination:  
• Visual acuity: 20/20 OD, 20/200 OS (pinhole to 20/70 OS)  
• Relative afferent pupillary defect OS  
• Intraocular pressure: 15 mmHg OD, 50 mmHg OS (Goldmann applanation)  
• Right eye normal. Left eye: white, quiet conjunctiva; clear cornea; quiet anterior chamber; irregular pupillary margin with uveal ectropion, corectopia, and multiple thin, tapioca-like patches over the iris with prominent underlying vessels  
• Gonioscopy OS: fine membrane with light pigmentation and scattered tan nodules over the trabecular meshwork in all quadrants  
• Fundus OS: marked optic-nerve cupping; normal periphery  
After acetazolamide and topical brimonidine/timolol, IOP was 12 mmHg OD and 24 mmHg OS. The patient was started on latanoprost QHS, timolol-dorzolamide BID, brimonidine TID, and acetazolamide QID OS.  
Investigations:  
• Humphrey 24-2: full field OD; small central island OS  
• Anterior-segment OCT and ultrasound biomicroscopy: areas of iris thickening nasally and temporally with iridotrabecular contact  
• Anterior-segment fluorescein angiogram: hyperfluorescence corresponding to the iris lesion, with regional staining/leakage  
• Endothelial cell count: 4255 cells/mm2 OD, 5025 cells/mm2 OS, inconsistent with an iridocorneal endothelial (ICE) syndrome  
What is the diagnosis?

A 44-year-old woman presented with a right breast mass. Mammography showed a heterogeneous spiculated 18×16 mm opacity with microcalcifications in a ductal distribution (BI-RADS 5). On examination, there was cutaneous retraction of the right nipple, an 8×6 cm firm, painless mass in the upper-inner quadrant, and a 2×1 cm right axillary node. Chest CT confirmed the breast and axillary lesions; brain CT identified an unrelated frontal arteriovenous malformation and maxillary sinusitis. 

She underwent right modified radical mastectomy with axillary lymphadenectomy. Grossly, the specimen contained a poorly defined translucent nodule measuring 1.4×1.6×1.7 cm and erosions of the nipple–areola complex. 

Histologic examination showed invasive ductal carcinoma (not otherwise specified), Nottingham grade 2 (score 7), with perineural and lymphovascular invasion, and associated ductal carcinoma in situ of solid, flat, and comedo type. Two of 14 axillary lymph nodes contained metastases. 

In addition, the nipple epithelium contained medium-large polygonal cells with pale eosinophilic cytoplasm and conspicuous nucleoli, arranged in nests, occasional tubules, and singly, with minimal (<1 mm) dermal invasion. These features suggested Paget’s disease of the breast, and immunohistochemical studies were recommended.

A 6-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of a small growth at the left angle of her upper lip that had slowly enlarged over 6 months to approximately 6 mm in diameter. The patient reported a history of trauma at the site during dental work. On examination, the lesion was firm, dome-shaped, and smooth, with focal brown speckling; its color resembled normal mucosa. No regional lymphadenopathy was noted. A provisional clinical diagnosis of a traumatic fibroma was made, with additional consideration of melanocytic naevus, haemangioma, pyogenic granuloma, viral wart, molluscum contagiosum, and dermatofibroma. An excisional biopsy was performed.

Microscopic examination (H&E) revealed hyperkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium with variable thickness, acanthosis, and areas of pseudo-epitheliomatous hyperplasia. In the underlying connective tissue there appeared to be cords, nests, and islands of dysplastic-appearing epithelial cells with intraepithelial keratin pearl-like formations, focal spindle cell change, and scattered pigment deposition, accompanied by chronic inflammatory infiltrates and extravasated red blood cells. At first glance, these features resembled a moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.

A 64-year-old healthy man presented with a 2-year history of ocular discomfort and a painless, slow-growing, pinkish nodular lesion at the inferotemporal peri-limbal bulbar conjunctiva of the right eye. There was no history of ocular trauma or surgery, and his family, medical, and medication histories were unremarkable. Uncorrected visual acuity was 20/30 in both eyes. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye revealed a non-tender, mobile, raised lesion measuring 9 mm × 7 mm with fine intrinsic vascularity; the left eye was normal. Gonioscopic and dilated fundus examinations were normal, and there was no lymphadenopathy. The clinical impression was conjunctival lymphoma, and an excisional biopsy under local anesthesia was planned.

A 33-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of gradual, nonpainful swelling in the left mandible. Recently, she noted mild numbness of the left lower lip. She denied fever, trismus, or relevant medical history. On examination, there was a hard, non‐tender swelling of the left mandible without cervical lymphadenopathy. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated a well‐defined, multilocular radiolucent lesion extending from the left lateral incisor to the medial aspect of the lower left second molar. On the basis of the clinical and radiographic characteristics, the initial differential diagnosis included odontogenic keratocyst, central giant cell granuloma, and multicystic ameloblastoma.

A 43-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of left flank pain, intermittent gross hematuria, generalized weakness, and unintended weight loss. She has a history of hypertension; family history and physical examination were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11 g/dL and microscopic hematuria. Urine cytology and blood chemistry, including alkaline phosphatase and liver function tests, were within normal limits. Cystoscopy revealed no abnormalities. An abdominal CT scan demonstrated a 15-cm hypodense mass arising from the left kidney, with irregular internal calcifications. Chest radiography was normal.

A 64-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of dyspnea on exertion, severe fatigue, anorexia, and a 5-kg weight loss. One week prior, endoscopic evaluation revealed advanced rectal adenocarcinoma. He denied fevers, night sweats, or chills. He smoked 44 pack-years and drank minimally. On arrival, he was distressed: temperature 35.8°C, blood pressure 80/57 mm Hg, heart rate 96 beats/min, respiratory rate 30/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on 2 L/min nasal oxygen. Examination showed conjunctival pallor, jaundice, and 4+ pitting edema of the lower extremities; there was no jugular venous distension, murmur, or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies revealed white blood cell count 21 000/mm3, hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL, platelets 65 000/mm3, INR 1.90, fibrinogen 343 mg/dL, sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 6.5 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 101 mg/dL, creatinine 2.05 mg/dL, uric acid 13.8 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 478 U/L, total bilirubin 3.0 mg/dL, albumin 1.6 g/dL, lactate 19.6 mmol/L, C-reactive protein 12 mg/dL, procalcitonin 3.6 ng/mL, ferritin 900 ng/mL, and soluble interleukin-2 receptor 13 677 U/mL. Arterial blood gas showed pH 7.13 with bicarbonate 3.3 mmol/L. Blood cultures were sterile; urinalysis was unremarkable. Chest radiograph and ECG were normal. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated splenomegaly without lymphadenopathy or other masses. Despite aggressive fluid resuscitation, he remained hypotensive and was transferred to the ICU, where vasopressors and broad-spectrum antibiotics were initiated for presumed septic shock.

A 58-year-old man with a 36-pack-year smoking history and possible asbestos exposure was referred for evaluation of an abnormal chest radiograph. He was asymptomatic, with no significant family history. Chest CT revealed a solid 15 mm nodule directly beneath the pleura in the lingual segment of the left lung, which had clearly enlarged compared with imaging performed 10 years earlier. Video-assisted wedge resection was undertaken; no pleural plaques were observed intraoperatively. Grossly, the lesion was a well-circumscribed, 1.3 cm tumor protruding from the peripheral lung parenchyma without invasion, surrounded by a fibrous capsule. Histologically, the lesion was multinodular and lobulated, composed of star- to spindle-shaped cells growing in a reticular pattern within a myxoid stroma. Immunohistochemistry showed negativity for calretinin and D2-40, partial positivity for AE1/AE3 and CD68, focal positivity for smooth muscle actin, negativity for S100 and calponin, weak positivity for epithelial membrane antigen, and positivity for CD99. FISH analysis with an EWSR1 break-apart probe demonstrated split red and green signals, indicating EWSR1 gene rearrangement.

A 15-year-old girl presented with intermittent chest pain for more than 2 months and a 10-day history of cough and wheezing. She had no personal or family history of malignancy. On examination, percussion over the left thorax was dull, and breath sounds were decreased on that side. Laboratory studies showed a procalcitonin level of 26.59 ng/ml, an interleukin-6 level of 15.2 pg/ml, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 28 mm/h. Thoracic drainage yielded bloody, turbid pleural fluid; routine cytology showed no tumor cells, but carcinoembryonic antigen and lactate dehydrogenase levels were each more than three times the upper limit of normal. Acid-fast staining and tuberculosis gene sequencing of the fluid were negative. Chest CT revealed a 15.7 × 11.7 × 10.5 cm soft-tissue mass adjacent to the left mediastinum, multiple pleural nodules, and left pleural effusion; contrast enhancement showed moderate heterogeneous uptake with small intralesional vessels. Abdominal and brain imaging were unremarkable.

A 78-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of continuous dizziness and gait disturbance. His medical history was notable for gastrectomy for gastric cancer 15 years earlier. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the head revealed a large, densely enhancing solid mass with a peripheral cystic component in the left posterior fossa, attached to the left tentorium and surrounded by vasogenic edema. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI showed a 5.6×4.8×3.2-cm heterogeneously enhancing mass in the left posterior cranial fossa. On diffusion-weighted imaging, the solid portions exhibited high signal intensity, and the cystic areas were low in signal. A dural tail sign was present, and the lesion had a suspicious infiltrative appearance into the left cerebellum. Intratumoral hemorrhage was also noted. Based on these findings, a high-grade meningioma or dural metastasis was suspected, and surgery was planned.

A 5-year-old girl presented with a 2-month history of swelling in the left lower jaw. She had no difficulty swallowing or breathing, facial pain, neural changes, or history of trauma; medical and family histories were unremarkable. Laboratory studies were normal except for a low mean corpuscular volume attributed to iron deficiency. Examination revealed a solitary, fixed, firm, non-tender 4×5 cm mass in the left submandibular region, normal overlying skin, no cervical lymphadenopathy, and normal mouth opening. Intraoral mucosa was intact; bilateral primary first molar caries were present. The initial clinical impression was an inflammatory lesion of the left primary molar despite lack of inflammatory signs; given the rapid growth, malignant mesenchymal tumors were also considered. Panoramic radiograph showed a poorly defined radiolucency in the left mandibular body with spicules of bone from the inferior border and absence of the left second premolar crypt. Cone-beam CT revealed destruction of lingual alveolar bone, diffuse periosteal bone spicules on buccal and lingual cortices, and an overlying soft-tissue mass.

A 15-year-old girl with a history of obesity (BMI 34.4 kg/m2) and irritable bowel syndrome was referred for evaluation of recurrent non-bilious, non-bloody vomiting. An esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) performed for this symptom revealed an incidental submucosal lesion in the middle third of the esophagus. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, C-reactive protein, thyroid function tests, celiac serologies, stool studies (including calprotectin and occult blood), were all within normal limits. Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) demonstrated an oval intramural lesion at 29–30 cm from the incisors, measuring 8.2 × 4.3 mm, hypoechoic, arising from the submucosal layer (layer 3), with well-defined borders.

A 58-year-old woman with a history of FIGO stage IIIC high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma had undergone primary debulking surgery and six cycles of paclitaxel-carboplatin, with complete radiographic response and normal CA 125. One year later, she presented with new axillary lymphadenopathy. On examination, there was a hard, relatively fixed 1.0 × 1.5 cm left axillary lymph node and a 1.0 × 1.0 cm right axillary lymph node. Breast and pelvic examinations were unremarkable. Breast MRI showed a 10 mm left breast lesion (BIRADS 4a). CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no other abnormalities aside from the axillary nodes. Serum CA 125 was mildly elevated at 41.2 U/L. Core-needle biopsies were obtained from the left breast lesion and both axillary nodes. Histology showed a fibroadenoma in the breast lesion and metastatic carcinoma in the axillary node.

A 60-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of gradually progressive pain and swelling over the dorsum of his right foot. He denied trauma, fever, weight loss, or appetite changes. On examination, there was a firm, tender, well-defined 5 cm × 3 cm oval swelling over the dorsum of the foot at the level of the second to fourth metatarsals; the overlying skin was normal, with no warmth or erythema. Radiographs of the right foot showed an expansile, osteolytic lesion of the third metatarsal with cortical thinning, sparing the proximal one-third of the bone, and no periosteal reaction; the tarsometatarsal joints were preserved. MRI demonstrated a well-defined, expansile, mixed solid-cystic lesion measuring 4.4 × 3.1 × 3.1 cm arising from the medullary cavity of the distal shaft and head of the third metatarsal, with surrounding soft-tissue edema but no soft-tissue extension or intra-articular invasion.

A 73-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 48-hour history of diffuse abdominal pain and nausea and a one-month history of fatigue with several episodes of melena. He denied fever, hematochezia, or changes in bowel habits. His past medical and surgical history was unremarkable.  
On examination, he appeared pale. Vital signs were: temperature normal, heart rate 101 bpm, blood pressure 140/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min. The abdomen was distended with rebound tenderness and guarding. Rectal examination revealed black tarry stool.  
Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 4.0 g/dL, hematocrit 11.1%, MCV 124.7 fL (83–97), MCH 44.9 pg (27–33), MCHC 36.0 g/dL (32–36), serum iron 12 µg/dL (65–157), ferritin 3.59 ng/mL (16.4–323); electrolytes, urinalysis, and coagulation studies were within normal limits.  
Abdominal CT showed a 42 mm low-density, non-enhancing cystic mass in the ascending colon, moderate free peritoneal fluid, and moderate pericardial and bilateral pleural effusions. There were no air-fluid levels, and the liver, spleen, pancreas, kidneys, and adrenals appeared normal.

A 66-year-old woman presented with several months of progressive bilateral proptosis, decreased visual acuity, retrobulbar pressure, orbital pain, temporal-region swelling, and headaches. On evaluation in the emergency department, she was hemodynamically stable and neurologically intact. Ophthalmologic examination confirmed reduced visual acuity and more pronounced right-sided exophthalmos. Brain MRI demonstrated:
• Bilateral hyperostotic changes of the greater wings of the sphenoid bone, hypointense on both T1- and T2-weighted sequences.  
• Bilateral dural thickening and enhancement in the anterior temporal regions, invading the cavernous sinuses, prechiasmatic optic nerves, and lateral rectus muscles via the superior orbital fissures, with more marked involvement on the right.  
• Postcontrast sagittal images showed thickening and enhancement of the free border of the tentorium cerebelli and the retroclival dura.

A 40-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of bleeding from the left nasal cavity and mild left eye proptosis. On examination, he had marked deviation of the nasal septum and a pinkish mass occupying the left nasal cavity.  
  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses and orbits showed a soft-tissue mass filling the left ethmoid and sphenoid sinuses, extending into the left nasal cavity, eroding the nasal septum, invading the left orbit, and extending intracranially into the basifrontal region.  
  
Endoscopic biopsy revealed a poorly differentiated malignant neoplasm composed of small to intermediate cells with scant cytoplasm and frequent mitoses. The mitotic count was 30–40 per 10 high-power fields.  
   
Immunohistochemical staining showed that the tumor cells were positive for cytokeratin, synaptophysin, and chromogranin, and negative for S-100.

A 3-week-old female neonate was referred for evaluation of lower-extremity weakness. She was born at term (3.145 kg) via cesarean delivery for breech presentation; maternal history was notable only for enoxaparin use for antiphospholipid syndrome. On examination, she had a prolapsed anus, a midline lumbar dimple, absent deep-tendon reflexes, preserved primitive reflexes, flaccid distal paresis of the right leg, proximal and distal paresis of the left leg, and lax anal sphincter tone.

MRI of the brain and spine revealed a large infiltrative, avidly enhancing lesion occupying the spinal canal from T10 to S1 (8.3 cm craniocaudal), with bilateral dumbbell‐shaped extraspinal components through expanded neural foramina, abutting the psoas muscles and involving adjacent paraspinal musculature. The mass was hyperintense on T2-weighted images, hypointense on T1-weighted images, and exhibited extensive flow voids; there was no fat signal, and T2 hyperintensity in both psoas muscles suggested possible denervation edema. The spinal cord was obliterated at the level of the lesion; the remainder of the cord was normal.

Contrast-enhanced CT showed a high-attenuation mass expanding the spinal canal and neural foramina, without calcifications. Non-fusion of the posterior elements from L4 caudally was noted, consistent with spina bifida.

An ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the lesion demonstrated hypoechoic protruding masses with high vascularity on Doppler imaging. Histologic examination showed lobular proliferation of capillary-sized vascular spaces lined by bland endothelial cells, with areas of focal intravascular thrombosis.

A 30-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of swelling and tenderness in the left scrotum, accompanied by dysuria and urinary frequency but without fever or weight loss. On examination, there was a hard, tender nodule at the head of the left epididymis. Scrotal ultrasonography showed a 1.6 cm hyperechoic lesion over the left epididymis. He was treated empirically for epididymitis with doxycycline and acetaminophen for 1 week without improvement. A partial epididymectomy was then performed through a transverse scrotal incision under spinal anesthesia; intraoperatively, an 8 mm hard mass was found on the head of the epididymis, and a separate 7 mm papillary-appearing nodule protruded between the epididymis and testis, with associated epididymal swelling.

A 57‐year‐old man was referred for evaluation of a 12-month history of progressive left-sided hearing loss and intermittent tinnitus; he also reported occasional headaches over several years. Neurologic examination was notable for decreased hearing on the left, with no facial weakness or ataxia. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head revealed a 3.0 × 3.5 cm homogeneously contrast-enhancing mass in the left cerebellopontine angle extending into the internal auditory canal, with mass effect on the cerebellum, pons, and medulla; ventricular size was normal without hydrocephalus. The lesion was presumed to be a vestibular schwannoma, and the patient underwent a suboccipital transmeatal approach with partial left C1 laminectomy. During surgery, the tumor was debulked, the intracanilicular portion was removed after drilling the petrous ridge, and the vestibulocochlear nerve was sacrificed for complete resection. A specimen sent for intraoperative pathology consultation was interpreted as a vestibular schwannoma. Postoperatively, the patient developed left sigmoid sinus thrombosis, dysphagia, and urinary retention, all of which resolved by one month.

A 26-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of increasing tooth mobility, intense oral pain, and difficulty chewing. His medical history was unremarkable. On intraoral examination, there was generalized gingival enlargement, most pronounced on the hard palate. The enlarged gingiva were sessile, soft, red, ulcerated, and covered with a necrotic slough. There was widespread gingival recession, deep periodontal pockets, spontaneous bleeding, and halitosis. A panoramic radiograph showed severe, diffuse alveolar bone loss corresponding to the mobile teeth. Maxillofacial CT revealed multiple alveolar lesions with poorly defined, invasive margins. The most mobile teeth were extracted, and periodontal therapy targeting aggressive periodontitis was initiated, but there was no clinical improvement. Consequently, an incisional biopsy of a palatal lesion was performed for histopathological examination.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of a slow-growing, painless mass in her right shoulder. She had no other medical conditions. On examination, there was a 5×5 cm palpable, mobile, partially fluctuating mass located in the right deltoid muscle extending to the proximal lateral arm; it was non-tender. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right shoulder demonstrated a lobular-contoured, cystic-appearing mass measuring 34×23×37 mm, situated caudal to the lateral compartment of the deltoid muscle, with interstitial edema in the adjacent deltoid. Complete blood count, biochemical tests, and other laboratory studies were within normal limits.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 7-day history of severe right iliac fossa pain accompanied by loose motions, nausea, vomiting, and giddiness. She reported a 6-month history of chronic dull, nonradiating lower abdominal pain unrelieved by symptomatic medications, and intermenstrual spotting over the past 2 months. Her menstrual cycles were otherwise regular, with moderate, painless bleeding lasting 4–5 days; her last menstrual period was 10 days before presentation. Four years earlier she had undergone a laparoscopic myomectomy, with no evidence of pelvic endometriosis at that time.

On examination she was afebrile, pulse 78/min, and blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg. Abdominal palpation revealed lower-abdominal tenderness. Pelvic examination showed an anteverted, mobile, normal-sized uterus, tenderness in the right lateral and posterior vaginal fornices, and a firm, well-defined mass palpable through the right lateral fornix.

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, leukocyte count 15 400/mm³, platelet count 249 000/mm³, negative β-hCG, and CA-125 of 75 U/mL. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a mildly bulky uterus with tiny fibroids, endometrial thickness 6.9 mm, normal ovaries, and a large, thick-walled, dumbbell-shaped right adnexal collection measuring 7.6 × 3.8 cm with internal echoes and septations. MRI of the pelvis confirmed multiple small subserosal and myometrial fibroids, and a well-defined dumbbell-shaped lesion in the right adnexa (7.1 × 3.5 cm) with up to 7 mm thick walls and high proteinaceous content, appearing adherent to a small bowel loop; there was mild pelvic free fluid and normal ovaries.

The differential diagnosis based on imaging was pelvic endometriosis versus hematosalpinx.

An 18-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of gradually enlarging pain and swelling on the medial plantar aspect of her left foot. The dull pain was rated 7 out of 10 and was associated with a slowly enlarging mass, initially excised 3 years earlier but subsequently recurred. There was no history of recent trauma or similar familial conditions, and she had not taken any regular medications. On examination, she walked with a non-antalgic gait and had a slightly high-arched foot. The plantar surface over the origin of the plantar fascia was mildly swollen without erythema or warmth, and capillary refill was normal. There was tenderness at the distal plantar fascia but full symmetric passive range of motion of the ankle and midtarsal joints without pain. Motor strength, sensation, reflexes in both lower extremities, and Tinel’s test at the tarsal tunnel were all normal. Plain radiographs of the left foot were unremarkable. MRI of the left foot revealed a heterogeneous, multilobulated mass arising near the medial plantar structures, with increased signal intensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images, findings that were initially considered suggestive of malignancy.

A 35-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and no history of hypertension presented with a three-month history of a gradually enlarging epigastric lump. Three months earlier, she had a sudden onset of severe, cramping upper abdominal pain radiating to the back, accompanied by nausea and vomiting; the pain subsided with injectable analgesics. Since then she has had mild persistent epigastric discomfort and early satiety. She denied anorexia, weight loss, fever, jaundice, gastrointestinal bleeding, or trauma. She is a non-smoker, non-drinker, and mother of three.  

Her surgical history was notable for a laparotomy two years ago for drainage of a large hemorrhagic pancreatic pseudocyst; only intracystic fluid was evacuated, and no biopsy or resection was performed. She was asymptomatic for the following two years.  

On examination she was afebrile with normal vital signs and no pallor or jaundice. The abdomen showed an upper midline scar. Palpation revealed a firm, immobile, nontender mass measuring approximately 10 × 8 cm in the epigastrium extending into both hypochondria, with an ill-defined border and irregular surface. There was no hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, or lymphadenopathy; other systems were unremarkable.  

Laboratory studies showed mild anemia and leukocytosis. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 12.9 × 8.8 cm hypoechoic mass with internal anechoic areas in the epigastrium/left hypochondrium; the lesion’s origin was unclear. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed an 11.2 × 8.5 × 7.0 cm well-defined, lobulated, mildly thick-walled cystic lesion arising from the pancreatic body, with thin internal septations, anterior wall calcifications, and moderate heterogeneous enhancement; there was no lymphadenopathy or ascites, and the remaining pancreas was unremarkable (impression: large chronic pancreatic pseudocyst). MRCP showed an atrophied pancreas and failed to delineate the main pancreatic duct because of the lesion’s size, supporting the impression of a pseudocyst.

A 53-year-old African American woman presented with a 6-month history of asymptomatic growths on the scalp. She denied fever, night sweats, weight loss, or other constitutional symptoms. Her medical, family, and social histories were unremarkable. On examination, there was a cluster of five erythematous to yellow nodules, each measuring 0.5 to 1.5 cm, on the midline vertex of the scalp. No lymphadenopathy was noted.

An outside deep shave biopsy was reported as granulation tissue with inflammation and was negative for malignancy; bacterial and fungal stains were negative. A subsequent excisional biopsy revealed a dense dermal infiltrate of histiocytes with abundant light eosinophilic cytoplasm and distinct nucleoli extending from the papillary to the reticular dermis. Foam cells, lymphoid aggregates, focally prominent plasma cells, and sparse granulocytes were present. Immunohistochemical stains showed strong, uniform S100 positivity in the histiocytic cells and highlighted numerous cells demonstrating emperipolesis; CD1a was negative.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated a small focus of full-thickness calvarial erosion underlying the scalp lesions, without intracranial extension. A CT scan of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis was unrevealing. Laboratory studies showed elevated lactate dehydrogenase and erythrocyte sedimentation rate; urine and serum protein electrophoreses were normal.

A 49-year-old woman presented with a firm, painless subcutaneous mass in her lower abdominal wall that had enlarged over the preceding 3–4 months adjacent to a previous surgical scar. Approximately 5 years earlier, she had undergone a radical hysterectomy and 135 Gy of concurrent chemoradiotherapy for cervical cancer. She had no personal or family history of neurofibromatosis type 1, and there were no café-au-lait spots or cutaneous neurofibromas on examination. Vital signs were normal. On palpation, the mass measured approximately 1 cm in diameter with no inguinal lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. 
Abdominal CT demonstrated a 1.3 cm midline nodular lesion infiltrating the rectus abdominis muscle. Whole-body CT (chest, abdomen, pelvis), PET/CT, and colonoscopy revealed no evidence of metastatic disease (T1N0M0).

A 55-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and opioid use disorder presented with worsening abdominal distention and a 60-lb unintentional weight loss over 1 year, along with increasing difficulty with bowel movements. He denied melena, nausea, vomiting, fevers, flank pain, dysphagia, or odynophagia, and had no history of abdominal surgery.

Three weeks before admission, abdominal CT with contrast showed a small-bowel obstruction with a transition point in the right-mid abdomen and focal small-bowel wall thickening, plus mesenteric adenopathy. His symptoms improved without intervention, and he was discharged.

He returned 3 weeks later with diffuse abdominal pain. Repeat CT showed multiple dilated loops of small bowel with air-fluid levels. Colonoscopy revealed two polyps; cold-forceps biopsies showed non-specific chronic inflammation without features of inflammatory bowel disease. Video capsule endoscopy demonstrated erythematous gastritis, multiple small-bowel ulcers, and an atrophic duodenum. Two weeks later, double-balloon enteroscopy identified multiple jejunal strictures and areas suggestive of inflammatory bowel disease, and outpatient IBD management was planned.

Two months later, he presented with severe abdominal pain, new nausea, and vomiting. Abdominal radiographs suggested pneumoperitoneum. Exploratory laparotomy revealed a perforated ulcer in the terminal ileum, which was repaired, and a proximal Brooke ileostomy was created. Biopsies around the perforation showed ulcerated mucosa with non-specific chronic inflammation. He was discharged after a 21-day hospital stay.

One month later, he was re-hospitalized for non-specific abdominal symptoms and increased ostomy output. Ileoscopy showed scalloped mucosa with blunted villi throughout the ileum, and biopsies were taken. Histologic examination revealed extensive lymphocytic infiltrates with epitheliotropism but no definitive atypical morphological features, raising suspicion for a lymphoid neoplasm. A hematopathology consultation was obtained.

A 47-year-old gravida 3 para 3 premenopausal woman with no significant medical history presented with a four-month history of a mass protruding through the vagina, accompanied by intermittent vaginal bleeding and pelvic pain. On examination, she had diffuse abdominal distension and pelvic tenderness. Gynecologic evaluation revealed a 30 cm mass protruding from the vaginal introitus with areas of necrosis; the cervix was not visualized. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, hematocrit 28.4 %, and white-cell count 12 100/mm3. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a large, heterogeneous anterior mass arising from the cervix measuring 30 cm, prolapsed into the vagina; the urinary bladder was displaced superiorly and there was right-sided hydronephrosis due to mass effect.

A 41-year-old man with no significant past medical history underwent a routine health examination in which a pulmonary nodule was incidentally discovered. He reported no respiratory symptoms, and the physical examination was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest showed a solitary, approximately 1 cm nodule in the mediobasal segment of the left lower lobe; the lesion had relatively well-defined but focally irregular margins, raising suspicion for malignancy. Because the nodule was deep in the lung parenchyma, a wedge resection was performed to establish a diagnosis.  

Intraoperative frozen-section analysis suggested a high likelihood of pleomorphic adenoma, but a definitive diagnosis was deferred. On permanent histopathological examination, the lesion exhibited an abundant myxoid matrix with embedded spindle-shaped, stellate, and rounded or epithelioid cells arranged in a reticular pattern. The cells showed mild atypia and rare mitotic figures, and there were no giant or bizarre tumor cells.

A 50-year-old man underwent evaluation after a positive fecal occult blood test. He had no relevant past medical or surgical history. On digital rectal examination, a firm mass was palpated on the posterior wall of the rectum 5 cm from the anal verge, and there was no evidence of anal fistula or abscess. Colonoscopy revealed a rectal tumor below the peritoneal reflection occupying three-quarters of the circumference. Biopsy showed a well-to-moderately differentiated tubular adenocarcinoma. CT and MRI demonstrated no regional lymphadenopathy or distant metastases. The lesion was staged as cT3N0M0 (stage IIa).

The patient received neoadjuvant chemoradiation therapy (45 Gy in 25 fractions with concurrent tegafur/gimeracil/oteracil). Four weeks after completion, CT and MRI showed a partial response of the primary tumor and an incidental small liver lesion subsequently characterized as a hemangioma. He then underwent six cycles of consolidation chemotherapy (three cycles of XELOX followed by three cycles of capecitabine alone). Follow-up colonoscopy showed complete clinical response of the rectal tumor, and CT revealed residual rectal wall thickening.

Two weeks after the last chemotherapy session, he presented with persistent anal pain. Anorectal examination revealed tenderness and induration on the posterior aspect of the anus, separate from the original tumor site. MRI demonstrated a high-signal intensity tract extending from the anal crypt to the perianal skin, consistent with an anal fistula. To distinguish between a benign fistula and possible metastasis, a coring-out fistulectomy was performed. Histopathological examination of the fistula tract revealed tubular adenocarcinoma with morphology similar to the primary rectal cancer, and tumor cells were present at the cauterized margin.

A 47-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of neck pain, 2 days of shoulder pain, right-sided chest numbness, and weakness of the upper limbs. He denied weight loss, hypertension, diabetes, smoking, or alcohol use. Neurological examination showed mild left facial weakness, hypoaesthesia below T4 on the right, normal muscle tone, upper-limb strength 4–/5, lower-limb strength 5/5, normal tendon reflexes, negative Kernig’s and Brudzinski’s signs, positive bilateral Babinski signs, and a left Hoffmann sign. Tests for viral antibodies, syphilis serology, and HIV antibodies were negative. Lumbar puncture revealed normal opening pressure; CSF had 10 red cells/µL, 220 nuclear cells/µL, protein 91 mg/dL, normal chloride and glucose, no oligoclonal bands, and no tumor cells. Flow cytometry of CSF showed no abnormal cell differentiation. Serum antinuclear antibodies, extractable nuclear antigen, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were all negative. Serum cytokines showed slightly elevated IL-6 and TNF-α; IL-2, IL-10, IL-17, and IFN-γ were normal. Serum anti-AQP4 antibodies were positive at a titer of 1:10. MRI of the cervical spinal cord revealed multiple T2-hyperintense, enhancing lesions from C2 to T1 with cord enlargement and brain-stem involvement. Brain MRI showed FLAIR hyperintensities in the bilateral thalami, periventricular regions, basal ganglia, and cerebral peduncles. The working diagnosis was neuromyelitis optica, and the patient received high-dose methylprednisolone and immunoglobulin, with progressive symptomatic improvement.

A 77-year-old woman was evaluated for a two-month history of swelling and pain in the left floor of the mouth. She is edentulous and noted that the lesion began after trauma from her complete dentures. On intraoral examination, there was a single, soft, tender, sessile nodule measuring approximately 1.1 × 0.9 × 0.7 cm with clinically normal overlying mucosa in the anterior left sublingual region. No cervical lymphadenopathy was palpable. Her medical history was noncontributory. The clinical differential diagnosis included inflammatory fibrous hyperplasia and a mucous retention cyst, and an excisional biopsy was performed.

A 54-year-old post-menopausal woman (G0P0) with a BMI of 41.5 and poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 6.8%) presented with a 2-year history of intermittent menometrorrhagia progressing to severe abnormal vaginal bleeding and iron-deficiency anemia (Hb 9.3 g/dL). Two years earlier, pelvic MRI had shown a 31 mm intramural fibroid. In the preceding 12 months, she underwent three dilatation and curettage procedures, all negative for malignancy. Because of ongoing suspicion, a fourth D&C revealed leiomyosarcoma. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a 14.5 × 10.2 × 9 cm uterine mass with blurred margins and a small fluid collection in the pouch of Douglas. Chest CT showed multiple bilateral lung nodules (up to 16 mm) suggesting metastases, with normal mediastinal and axillary nodes. Serum studies revealed an elevated β-hCG level of 383.3 IU/L (normal <5 IU/L) and normal CEA, CA-125, CA 15-3, CA 19-9, and AFP. Despite her post-menopausal status, no sexual activity in the past year, and negative D&C histology, an ultrasound was performed to exclude pregnancy, which it definitively did.

A 58-year-old man presented with a painless left infraorbital mass that had gradually increased in size over 6 months. He had no history of trauma or significant medical or family history. On examination, there was a firm, mobile, non-tender, 2 cm round subcutaneous mass in the left infraorbital region; the overlying skin was normal. Visual acuity, visual fields, and color vision were intact. Extraocular movements were full without pain or restriction, and all cranial nerve functions and facial sensations were normal. Slit-lamp and funduscopic examinations were unremarkable. Hertel exophthalmometry showed 5 mm of axial proptosis and approximately 4 mm of superior displacement (dystopia) of the left globe.  

Noncontrast CT of the orbits revealed a homogeneous, non-calcified mass enlarging the left infraorbital canal, with posterior bowing into the maxillary sinus and anterior rotation toward the globe. MRI demonstrated a well-defined, non-invasive infraorbital mass that was homogeneously hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed no significant enhancement after gadolinium administration, consistent with cystic changes.

A 55-year-old Asian man presented in August 2021 with a 1-month history of fever, fatigue, anorexia, and an abnormal dragging sensation in the abdomen. On arrival, he was febrile to 38.5°C, tachycardic, tachypneic, and appeared ill. On examination, there were multiple cherry-red cutaneous hemangiomas over the trunk, pallor, and generalized lymphadenopathy; lung and cardiac examinations were otherwise unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 6.9 g/dL, total leukocyte count 700 cells/mm3 with 85% neutrophils, platelets 155,000/mm3, serum albumin 3.0 g/dL, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, sodium 128 mmol/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 57 mm/h, C-reactive protein 192 mg/L, and a positive antinuclear antibody test (48.93 AU/mL). Urine culture grew Proteus mirabilis. Echocardiography showed moderate aortic and tricuspid regurgitation. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated multilevel lymphadenopathy—including submandibular, cervical, mediastinal, abdominal, and pelvic nodes, some conglomerated (largest 34 × 20 mm)—splenomegaly (15.3 cm), and a few ground-glass pulmonary nodules.

A 31-year-old man noted a palpable 1.5 cm nodule in the lower pole of the right thyroid lobe. Thyroid function tests were normal. An initial fine-needle aspiration (FNA) without ultrasound guidance showed intrathyroidal lymphoid hyperplasia. Over the next 5 years, the nodule slowly enlarged without compressive symptoms. Repeat FNA yielded a Hürthle cell lesion. The surgeon planned a right thyroid lobectomy.  
Preoperative studies revealed:  
• Serum calcium 13.5 mg/dL (8.5–10.1) and phosphorus 1.9 mg/dL (2.5–4.5).  
• Parathyroid hormone level 1,859 pg/mL (15–65).  
• Renal function normal.  
On dedicated neck ultrasound, a 2.8 cm heterogeneous, hypervascular mass was seen posterior to the right inferior pole of the thyroid. A Tc-99m sestamibi SPECT scan showed increased uptake corresponding to this mass.  
History elicited 7 years of chronic knee pain. Bone radiographs demonstrated generalized demineralization, multiple osteolytic lesions in the distal femur, proximal tibia, fibula, and patella, subperiosteal bone resorption of the middle phalanges, and acroosteolysis of the digital tufts—findings compatible with osteitis fibrosa cystica.  
Bone mineral density Z-scores were −3.8 at the lumbar spine, −3.7 at the femoral neck, and −7.5 at the distal radius.  
At this point, parathyroid carcinoma was suspected.

A 62-year-old man with no smoking history was admitted with several weeks of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, arthralgia, and weakness. On examination, he was hemodynamically stable, with a pulmonary ejection murmur and an accentuated pulmonic second heart sound; heart rate was sinus tachycardia. There was no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed mild elevations in IgG (1398 mg/dL; normal 543–1360) and IgA (280 mg/dL; normal 58–259), with normal 24 h urine protein (115 mg), ESR (13 mm/h), and CRP (0.6 mg/dL). Chest radiography revealed a mildly enlarged cardiac silhouette, signs of pulmonary hypertension, congestion, and small bilateral pleural effusions. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a large right atrial mass and minimal pericardial effusion, with normal biventricular function. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest confirmed a 3.2 cm × 2.8 cm right atrial myocardial mass involving the auricle and atrial septum, without lymphadenopathy or osteolytic lesions. Transesophageal echocardiography–guided fine-needle aspiration yielded a hypercellular malignant neoplasm with atypical polyhedral cells suspicious for a plasma cell tumour. Immunohistochemical staining of the aspirate was positive for CD138, kappa light chain clonality, and epithelial membrane antigen, consistent with plasmacytoma.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of fatigue. Examination revealed conjunctival pallor and tarry stools. Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin level of 4.0 g/dL; other values were near normal. She received a blood transfusion. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy failed to identify a bleeding source. Enhanced CT of the abdomen was unremarkable. Video capsule endoscopy revealed a submucosal lesion with active bleeding in the jejunum. Antegrade double-balloon enteroscopy showed a 20 mm submucosal lesion in the distal jejunum with dense white spots on the mucosal surface and continuous bleeding.

A 45-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of painless swelling of both sides of his neck, followed by swellings in both axillae. He reported intermittent fevers and night sweats. Multiple courses of antibiotics produced no improvement. On examination, vital signs were stable (temperature 37°C, blood pressure 150/70 mmHg). He had generalized, non-tender lymphadenopathy involving preauricular, occipital, axillary, and inguinal regions, with nodes up to 8 × 5 × 4 cm in size, and mild splenomegaly. Initial laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 3.3 × 10^9/L with 1.5% monocytes, hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, platelets 158 × 10^9/L, lactate dehydrogenase 684 U/L, and C-reactive protein 186 mg/L; liver and renal function tests were normal. Viral studies for EBV, HIV, HBV, and HCV were negative. Contrast CT of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed bilaterally enlarged cervical, axillary, mediastinal, hilar, intraparotid, para-aortic, retrocaval, portahepatis, mesenteric, iliac, and inguinal lymph nodes, the largest measuring 8 × 5 cm in the right axilla; the spleen was mildly enlarged (14 cm) without focal lesions. During admission his temperature peaked at 38°C, and he was started empirically on Augmentin and Tazocin.

A 76-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of a rapidly enlarging mass on her abdominal wall. Five years earlier, she had undergone a partial resection for endometrial cancer, after which keloid scars formed at the incision site without any recurrence of malignancy or wound infection. Four months before presentation, a nodular growth arose within one of these keloid scars and began to protrude through the skin, enlarging quickly. On examination, there was a pedunculated lesion continuous with the keloid scar, measuring approximately 3 × 3 × 2 cm. A core-needle biopsy revealed high cellularity, marked nuclear pleomorphism, abundant mitotic activity, and spindle-cell morphology, suggesting a pleomorphic spindle-cell sarcoma. One week later, MRI showed a 5 × 4 × 3 cm subcutaneous mass protruding from the abdominal wall without extension into the peritoneal cavity. Over the next two weeks, the lesion further increased in size to 6 × 6 × 2 cm and projected even more prominently.

A 40‐year‐old woman with no comorbidities presented with a 3‐month history of a swelling on the inner aspect of her right thigh. She noted gradual enlargement from pea‐sized to lemon‐sized. She denied pain, discharge, functional limitation, or systemic symptoms. There was no personal or family history of similar lumps. 

On examination, there was a 5 × 5 cm firm, non‐tender mass over the medial proximal thigh. The lesion was fixed to underlying tissues but mobile relative to the skin. There were no overlying skin changes, lymphadenopathy, or neurovascular deficits. Routine blood and urine tests were normal.

Ultrasonography showed a well‐defined, hypoechoic solid lesion measuring 2.2 × 2.9 cm in the lower thigh, suggestive of a benign process. MRI of the right thigh demonstrated a well‐defined focal cystic lesion within the substance of the vastus medialis muscle, approximately 3.2 × 3.5 cm, with high signal intensity on T2‐weighted images and no bony erosion.

A 37-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, was found on routine blood screening at 10 weeks’ gestation to have pancytopenia: platelet count 85×10^9/L, white-cell count 2.3×10^9/L (neutrophils 1.3×10^9/L, monocytes 0.2×10^9/L), and hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL. She reported occasional easy bruising over the prior two months but no bleeding, lymphadenopathy, or splenomegaly. Her only prior pregnancy, 13 months earlier, was uncomplicated with normal platelet counts. She had equivocal hypothyroidism, a family history of thyroid disease and systemic lupus erythematosus, and no new medications. Thyroid function, immunoglobulins, folate, and vitamin B12 were normal; antinuclear antibody was negative. Ferritin was low, and iron supplements were started.

She was given a presumptive diagnosis of immune thrombocytopenia in pregnancy. Her fatigue persisted but she had no bleeding complications. At 38 weeks’ gestation, with a platelet count of 61×10^9/L, prednisolone 20 mg daily was initiated without response (platelets 65×10^9/L), followed by intravenous immunoglobulin at 1 g/kg (platelets 52×10^9/L). She underwent spontaneous vaginal delivery at 38 weeks with minor bleeding; her platelet count was 52×10^9/L, and the neonate’s platelet count was normal.

Five weeks postpartum, she developed a pustular rash on the left upper arm, abdomen, and back. Skin biopsy showed dermal neutrophils with upper dermal edema and a subepidermal blister, consistent with bullous Sweet’s syndrome. Her blood counts remained low: hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL, white-cell count 1.7×10^9/L (neutrophils 0.5×10^9/L, monocytes 0.1×10^9/L), and platelets 49×10^9/L.

An 18-year-old man presented with epigastric and left upper quadrant pain. On examination, his abdomen was distended, and a palpable mass was noted. He recalled that at age 7 he had similar abdominal distension, pain, nausea, and vomiting. At that time, ultrasound demonstrated a hypoechoic mass with smooth margins between the liver and splenic hila. Laparotomy revealed multiple cysts measuring 30 × 20 cm within the bursa omentalis; 2.5 L of yellow transudative fluid were drained, and the cyst walls and vessels were excised. Histologic examination showed dilated lymphatic channels lined by flattened endothelium in loose connective tissue.

On current ultrasound, there was a 14 × 15 × 20 cm anechoic multiloculated mass with thick septations and internal echogenic foci suggestive of calcifications. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a nonenhancing, low-attenuation (+12 HU) mass with hyperdense calcific foci, encasing the body and tail of the pancreas, extending posteriorly into the left renal space, displacing the pancreas anteriorly, and reaching the left abdominal wall. MRI revealed the lesion to be hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, extending inferiorly toward the gallbladder.

A 32-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of a progressively enlarging, swollen left foot with a bleeding, fungating interdigital ulcer. He had undergone two prior excisions at other facilities, with recurrence each time; an earlier biopsy was reportedly benign. He had applied local herbs without benefit. One day before referral, he experienced sudden generalized weakness after profuse bleeding from the wound. He denied fevers, cough, dyspnea, or trauma. 

On examination, he was alert, moderately pale, and mildly jaundiced, with a blood pressure of 96/43 mmHg, temperature 36.5 °C, and random glucose 5.9 mmol/L. The left foot was markedly swollen with a green-stained dressing over a dorsal ulcer; it was nontender, and ankle motion was limited. 

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 6.5 g/dL. Chest radiograph was normal. Radiographs of the left foot showed a large soft-tissue mass with underlying bone destruction, and of the left tibia showed focal cortical thickening. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography were unremarkable. 

An incisional biopsy demonstrated monotonous epithelioid cells with clear cytoplasm embedded in a dense collagenous stroma, raising suspicion for a sclerosing epithelioid neoplasm. The differential diagnoses of low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma, solitary fibrous tumor, as well as other entities, were considered.

A 15-year-old male presented with a 6-month history of deep left groin pain that began after a fall playing noncontact football. The pain was constant, worsened with deep squatting, sitting, and twisting, and he noted a mild ache around the hip at night. NSAIDs provided minimal relief.

Physical examination and plain radiographs were consistent with cam-type femoroacetabular impingement. An MR arthrogram showed an anterosuperior labral tear; no other osseous abnormalities were noted. He underwent left hip arthroscopy with femoral osteochondroplasty, labral repair, and routine capsular closure. Intraoperatively, there was a labral tear from 1 to 3 o'clock, softened acetabular cartilage from 12 to 3 o'clock, and pitting at the femoral head–neck junction. Osteochondroplasty achieved appropriate clearance on dynamic examination.

Three weeks postoperatively, he felt well, and radiographs confirmed an adequate osteochondroplasty. He completed eight sessions of physical therapy by two months. Over the next five months, he noted a gradual return of deep, achy left hip pain. At seven months postoperatively, he reported continuous hip pain, worst at night, partially responsive to NSAIDs. Physical examination showed no signs of residual impingement or instability, and radiographs remained unchanged. An ultrasound-guided intra-articular corticosteroid and local anesthetic injection provided no pain relief.

A 67-year-old woman presented with a solitary tender nodule on her left heel. She first noticed the lesion 12 months earlier, and it had slowly enlarged over the past 3 months. Her medical history was notable only for hypertension; she denied any trauma to the area and had no relevant family or social history. On examination, there was a 1.5 cm bluish, indurated nodule on the plantar surface of the left heel.

A 56-year-old woman with a history of HIV (on HAART), treated hepatitis C, and cholelithiasis presented with abdominal pain and nonspecific dyspeptic symptoms. Vital signs were normal. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, WBC 4.6×10^3/µL, platelet count 136×10^3/µL, an undetectable HIV viral load, CD4 count 742 cells/µL, and an ESR of 25 mm/hr. Upper endoscopy revealed a 1 cm yellowish, sessile nodule in the esophagus just distal to the gastroesophageal junction; the gastric mucosa showed mild erythema. Biopsies were taken from the nodule and surrounding gastric mucosa. Gastric biopsies were positive for Helicobacter pylori. Histologic examination of the esophageal nodule showed cells with granular cytoplasm that were positive for S100 and negative for pancytokeratin, and PAS staining highlighted cytoplasmic granules.

An 86-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of a nodular lesion on his left eye. The lesion had not changed in size, but he noted increased discharge and intermittent blurring of vision. He had no pain, no limitation of eye movement, and no other ocular symptoms. His medical and family histories were unremarkable; he had no allergies, did not smoke, and did not drink alcohol.

On examination, visual acuity was 0.8 in the right eye and 1.2 in the left eye. Intraocular pressures were 14 mmHg bilaterally. Laboratory tests were within normal limits except for a slightly elevated C-reactive protein level of 0.15 mg/dL (normal 0.00–0.14). On inspection, the lesion was located on the medial aspect of the left lower palpebral conjunctiva; it was smooth and slightly erythematous but without surrounding edema or obvious inflammation.

Based on the nodularity of the lesion, hyperplasia rather than inflammation was thought to be more probable. An excisional biopsy of the lesion was performed to obtain a pathological diagnosis.

A 62-year-old woman presented with what appeared to be a left-sided gluteal abscess. On examination, a firm nodule was palpated in the gluteal region. Her white-cell count was 9500 per μL, and a random serum glucose level was 140 mg/dL. The lesion was surgically drained and excised, and culture of the drained fluid yielded Escherichia coli susceptible to amikacin and cefepime; therapy with cefepime was initiated. Gross examination of the specimen revealed a 6.5×2.5×1.2 cm piece of fibro-fatty tissue covered by skin and containing a relatively circumscribed, soft-to-firm yellowish nodule measuring 3.5×2 cm, with a least surgical margin of 0.2 cm. Microscopic examination showed a downward proliferation attached to the epidermis and extending into the deep dermis, composed of cords and nests of small uniform keratinocytes sharply delimited from the adjacent epidermis; duct-like structures and occasional islands of squamous epithelium were present, along with dermal reactive vessels and mixed inflammatory cells with neutrophil collections. The reporting pathologist suggested a diagnosis of poroma versus a low-grade malignant tumor; subsequent blinded consultation by three additional pathologists confirmed the diagnosis of eccrine poroma with clear margins.

A 57-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of progressively enlarging recurrent swellings in the upper cervical and occipital regions. She had undergone prior excision of an occipital mass diagnosed as a “malignant chondroid syringoma.” The new lesions were firm to hard, fixed to underlying structures, each measuring approximately 3 × 3 cm, with surrounding satellite nodules of 2–3 mm.

Fine‐needle aspiration cytology of both swellings, stained with May–Grünwald–Giemsa and Papanicolaou stains, yielded highly cellular smears with a striking mucoid and chondromyxoid/fibromyxoid background. Within this matrix were clusters and tissue fragments of round to polygonal cells with malignant features, as well as a few discrete plasmacytoid cells.

Subsequent histologic examination of a dermal neoplasm showed nests and cords of tumor cells, large areas of comedonecrosis, and prominent lymphovascular emboli in the papillary dermis. An occasional focus of epithelial cells suggested sebaceous differentiation. The histologic differential diagnosis included metastatic adenocarcinoma and a malignant cutaneous adnexal tumor. In this inconclusive situation, additional cytologic material was submitted for ancillary studies.

A 34-year-old woman presented with several months of progressive difficulty swallowing and an enlarging mass on the left side of her neck, associated with pain radiating to her left shoulder and mild shortness of breath. Her history was notable only for cervical spinal surgery with instrumentation at C5–C6 three years earlier; there was no family history of cancer or history of smoking or alcohol use. 

On examination, she was hemodynamically stable. The chest was clear, abdomen soft, and neurological examination normal. There was an immobile, non-tender, non-pulsatile swelling on the left side of the neck.

Laboratory studies revealed a normal blood cell count, electrolytes, renal, liver, and thyroid function tests; the C-reactive protein level was elevated at 21.9 mg/L (normal <5 mg/L), and alpha-fetoprotein was within normal limits.

Cervical spine radiographs showed a well-aligned spine with a radio-opaque metallic disc spacer at C5–C6 and slight rightward tracheal displacement. 

Neck ultrasound demonstrated a normal thyroid gland without cervical lymphadenopathy and a hypoechoic, tubular, lobulated paraspinal soft-tissue mass in the left carotid region measuring approximately 30 × 34 × 80 mm, displacing the left common carotid artery anteriorly and the trachea laterally, with minimal vascularity on Doppler imaging. 

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the neck revealed a well-defined, iso-to-hypodense mass (85 × 32 × 26 mm) in the left carotid space from the carotid bifurcation to the thoracic inlet, lying between the common carotid artery and internal jugular vein, with homogeneous faint delayed enhancement, displacement of adjacent structures, and no calcifications or local invasion.

Magnetic resonance imaging showed a well-defined T2-hyperintense lesion of similar dimensions in the left carotid space, displacing the common carotid artery anteromedially and the trachea and esophagus to the right, with homogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration.

A 39-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 6-month history of a slowly enlarging reddish mass in the left eye. He denied ocular pain, photophobia, or changes in vision but reported a 12-kg weight loss over the previous 9 months. He had no history of trauma, chronic medication use, or blood transfusion, and he denied sexual activity or illegal drug use. 

On examination, he had no oral lesions, mucocutaneous changes, or lymphadenopathy. Visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. Intraocular pressures were 14 mm Hg OD and 19 mm Hg OS. Slit-lamp examination of the left eye revealed a large, diffuse, elevated, dark-reddish, fleshy mass over the bulbar conjunctiva with areas of subconjunctival hemorrhage sparing the superior bulbar and palpebral conjunctiva. The lesion was loosely attached to the underlying tissue. The right eye and fundoscopic examination of both eyes were normal. 

Given the size and appearance of the lesion, an incisional biopsy and local debulking were planned. An amniotic membrane graft was used to close the excision site to minimize scarring.

An 18-year-old African woman presented with a 6-month history of progressive, painless right-sided abdominal swelling that later became intermittently painful.
