She also reported loss of appetite and early satiety but denied nausea, vomiting, gastrointestinal bleeding, or jaundice. Three months before admission, she developed gradual-onset throbbing frontal headaches unassociated with exertion. The headaches were relieved by opioids and accompanied by nonexertional palpitations and generalized diaphoresis. There was no syncope, seizures, vision changes, or sleep disturbance. She had no significant medical or family history and did not use tobacco or alcohol.

On examination, her blood pressure was 159/95 mmHg, pulse was  normal, and she had diaphoresis and tachycardia without edema. Abdominal examination revealed a firm, irregular, tender mass in the right hypochondrium extending into the right lumbar and umbilical regions, about 10 × 10 cm below the costal margin, with limited upward mobility. Mild tender hepatomegaly was noted; there was no lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, or abdominal bruits.

Laboratory studies showed moderate anemia (hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL) with normal electrolytes, liver and renal function, thyroid and coagulation profiles. Morning cortisol was slightly elevated (39.6 µg/dL). A neuroendocrine workup demonstrated elevated 24-h urinary vanillylmandelic acid at 28.48 mg/L, epinephrine 358 nmol/24h, dopamine 549 nmol/24h, and metanephrine 283 nmol/24h (VMA-to-creatinine ratio 32.57 mg/g). Cardiac evaluation including ECG and echocardiogram was normal.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 6.3 × 12.1 cm heterogeneous right retroperitoneal mass arising from the adrenal gland, with central necrosis and calcific foci, displacing the right kidney, inferior vena cava, aorta, and liver medially and inferiorly. Chest CT showed no metastases. Based on her symptoms and elevated catecholamine levels, pheochromocytoma was initially suspected.

A 37-year-old primigravida presented at 25+4 weeks of gestation with increasing abdominal distension and discomfort. She denied significant past medical or family history. On examination, she was obese with a grossly distended, soft, non-tender abdomen. Initial obstetric ultrasound confirmed a singleton intrauterine pregnancy at 25+4 weeks, a long closed cervix, and identified a complex pelvic lesion with internal septations and vascularity. 

Magnetic resonance imaging revealed:
- A 28×28×29 cm lobulated, complex cystic mass in the upper abdomen with nodularity and papillary wall projections.
- A second 7.0×4.6×9.8 cm cystic lesion abutting the left kidney with internal septation.
- Moderate-volume ascites.

Laboratory studies showed normal antenatal biochemistry. Tumor markers: CEA <1.0 μg/L, CA19-9 120 kU/L, CA125 11 kU/L, AFP 150 μg/L, Inhibin B <10 ng/L. ESR was elevated at 85 mm/hr and CRP 5.8 mg/L.

At 26+1 weeks, 1.5 L of cloudy brown ascitic fluid was drained; cytology and cultures were negative. Fetal ultrasound remained reassuring. An infectious‐disease evaluation for Echinococcus granulosus returned negative serology. A staging chest CT at 27 weeks showed only small anterior paracardiac lymph nodes.

At a multidisciplinary meeting, the mass was initially presumed to be metastatic ovarian malignancy. Other considered diagnoses included benign ovarian cysts, other abdominal malignancies (gastric, hepatic, colonic), lymphangioma, inflammation or infection of unknown etiology, pancreatic abscess or pseudocyst, and splenic enlargement. The patient underwent a second ascitic drainage of 4 L at 27+4 weeks; fluid again showed no malignant cells. Follow-up MRI demonstrated a stable 32×27 cm lobulated cyst. Serial fetal ultrasounds showed appropriate growth and normal Dopplers.

With steroids for fetal lung maturity, at 33+6 weeks she underwent an elective classical cesarean section with exploratory laparotomy. The neonate was delivered in good health. Intraoperatively, the mass did not appear to originate from the ovaries, prompting involvement of colorectal and hepatobiliary surgeons and recommendation for further imaging.

A 2-year-old girl presented with swellings over her right frontal and occipital skull regions for 1 year. On examination, these were fluctuant, ill-defined soft tissue masses measuring 2×2 cm and 3×3 cm, respectively. A left cervical lymph node (1×1 cm), firm, tender, and slightly mobile, was also palpable. There was no fever, weight loss, or hepatosplenomegaly.

Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 10 g/dL with microcytic hypochromic anemia. The white-cell differential count demonstrated 38.3% neutrophils, 38.9% lymphocytes, 19% monocytes, 2.5% eosinophils, and 1.3% basophils; platelet count was normal.

Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) of the lymph node yielded a whitish aspirate; FNA of the skull masses yielded hemorrhagic fluid that was processed into smears and a cell block. Smears were highly cellular, revealing numerous large atypical histiocytes singly and in loosely cohesive clusters, admixed with eosinophils, neutrophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells, foamy macrophages, and reactive histiocytic giant cells. The atypical histiocytes had moderate to abundant pale blue cytoplasm and round to oval vesicular nuclei with prominent nuclear grooves and indentations; occasional intranuclear pseudoinclusions were noted. The cells were pleomorphic, with occasional mitoses, cytoplasmic processes, and both mono- and multinucleated forms. Numerous rhomboid and needle-shaped Charcot-Leyden crystals were present extracellularly and within giant cells. On the cell block, these atypical histiocytes showed cytoplasmic and nuclear S-100 protein positivity.

A plain skull radiograph demonstrated lytic lesions corresponding to the frontal and occipital swellings. Computed tomography with three-dimensional reconstruction confirmed sharply demarcated “punched-out” lytic lesions of the frontal and occipital bones with homogeneous scalp soft-tissue swelling, without dural breach or other systemic involvement.

A 48-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 15-day history of worsening headaches, drowsiness, weakness, fatigue, visual hallucinations, polydipsia, and intermittent hypoglycemic episodes. She had no prior chronic illness and no tobacco or alcohol use. Family history was notable for diabetes mellitus in both parents. On examination, her BMI was 32.7 kg/m2; pulse 117 beats/min; blood pressure 90/60 mmHg; temperature 35.9 °C. Neurologic examination showed confusion and somnolence with preserved person and place orientation but impaired time orientation; there were no focal motor deficits or cranial-nerve findings. Initial laboratory studies revealed hypernatremia (Na 149 mmol/L), elevated serum osmolality (301 mOsm/kg), low urine osmolality (112 mOsm/kg), and low urine specific gravity (1.003), consistent with diabetes insipidus. Endocrine evaluation demonstrated low morning cortisol (0.68 μg/dL; ref 6.7–22.6), low ACTH (8.7 pg/mL; 0–45), low FSH (1.55 mIU/mL; 4.5–22.5), low LH (0.2 IU/L; 19–103), low free thyroxine (0.47 ng/dL; 0.61–1.2), normal IGF-1 (117 μg/L; 61–201), and elevated prolactin (45 ng/mL; 3.3–26.7). Early findings were suggestive of pituitary apoplexy. Brain MRI showed a 22×15×27 mm homogeneously enhancing mass in the hypothalamic region with diffusion restriction and marked surrounding edema; the pituitary gland appeared shrunken, with a partial empty sella. The angiotensin-converting enzyme level was normal. CT scans of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no lymphadenopathy or evidence of systemic malignancy, and there were no B symptoms. On this basis, the differential diagnoses considered were lymphoma, sarcoidosis, and germinoma.

A 33-year-old woman, 2 weeks postpartum, presented with a large painful mass in her left breast. The mass had been noted during the first trimester and measured 4.5 cm in the third trimester; just before delivery it rapidly enlarged to 15 cm, causing debilitating pain, erythema, and skin ulceration but without adherence to the chest wall or lymphadenopathy. On inspection, the medial half of the left breast was virtually replaced by a protruding mass, and the patient was unable to lie supine. Ultrasound performed in a semierect position showed a circumscribed, predominantly solid mass of mixed echogenicity extending from the nipple to the medial breast edge, without associated internal vascularity. Clinically, an occluded milk duct abscess or infected galactocele was suspected, and ultrasound-guided aspiration was attempted; no fluid or blood was obtained. Surgical exploration of the unhealed biopsy tract yielded multiple fragments of tan rubbery tissue with no evidence of an abscess, raising the possibility of an angiosarcoma. The patient was admitted for pain management and planned surgical excision of the mass for definitive diagnosis.

A 10-year-old boy was referred to a dental clinic because of premature loss of his two primary mandibular canines and the primary right maxillary canine. On intraoral examination, slight malpositioning of the anterior teeth was noted. His medical history was unremarkable. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated four impacted canines, each surrounded by a pericoronal radiolucent zone approximately 4 mm wide; additionally, the maxillary central incisors had shortened roots, and the lateral incisors showed root resorption. The initial radiographic interpretation was that of “multiple dentigerous cysts.” Under local anesthesia, the pericoronal lesions were enucleated via an osteotomy through the alveolar crest, and orthodontic buttons were bonded to the exposed crowns for subsequent traction.

A 39-week-gestation male infant was born to a healthy primiparous woman admitted for preeclampsia and a suspicious fetal brain mass. A 36-week fetal US was normal; at 39 weeks, US for fetal weight estimation revealed a  hyperechoic mass in the fetal right frontal lobe without detectable vascular flow. The infant was delivered vaginally, birth weight 3156 g, Apgar scores 9/10. Physical examination was unremarkable; no skin lesions were noted. On day 1, noncontrast cranial CT showed three well-circumscribed, round hyperdense intra-axial lesions of varying size in the right frontal lobe with extensive surrounding edema and a smaller hyperdense lesion in the left frontal lobe. On day 6, skin discoloration of the right scrotal sac prompted scrotal and abdominal US, which revealed a right hydrocele and a 4-cm predominantly hyperechoic liver mass with central hypoechoic area in the left hepatic lobe. On day 13, contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated an avid peripheral nodular arterial enhancing mass with central hemorrhage in the left liver lobe and multiple small hypervascular lesions in the right lobe; arterial-phase imaging also showed several strongly enhancing lesions in the paraspinal muscles. On day 17, abdominal MRI confirmed these findings. Oral propranolol at 3 mg/kg/day was initiated for multiple hepatic hemangiomas and probable intracranial hemangiomas.

A five-year-old girl presented with an eight-month history of a swelling in her left lumbar region that had gradually increased in size and caused pain. There was no history of trauma, fever, or bladder or bowel dysfunction. Her past medical and family histories were noncontributory. On examination, a 10 cm × 10 cm lobulated, firm swelling was noted over the lower back; the overlying skin was unremarkable, and there were no sensory or motor deficits. Systemic examination was normal. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a multinodular, plexiform subcutaneous tumor in the lumbosacral region extending from the L1 to S1 vertebral levels, isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with no intraspinal extension. The radiologic impression was of a subcutaneous multinodular tumor, possibly plexiform neurofibroma or schwannoma.

A 22-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of left iliac fossa pain radiating to the suprapubic region and hypomenorrhea. She reported a 2-year history of bone aches diagnosed previously as osteoporosis. Family history was notable for lung cancer. On examination, there was a tender, palpable lower abdominal mass measuring approximately 20 cm without palpable lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed mild elevations in CA-125 (60.9 U/ml) and CA-19-9 (61.44 U/ml); CEA, AFP, β-hCG, and LDH were within normal limits. Pelviabdominal ultrasound demonstrated a large multicystic lesion (>14 × 10 cm) extending to the epigastrium. Contrast-enhanced pelvic MRI revealed a midline multilocular cystic left ovarian mass measuring 14.6 × 16.8 × 23.3 cm, displacing the uterus and bladder, with thick septal and wall enhancement but no ascites or lymphadenopathy. Chest CT was unremarkable. 

A fertility-sparing approach was undertaken with left salpingo-oophorectomy and omental and peritoneal biopsies. Grossly, the ovarian mass measured 17 × 13 × 4 cm and was multilocular, filled with clear fluid and gelatinous brown-green material. Microscopic examination of the ovarian lesion revealed multiple nodules of thyroid tissue composed of variable macro- and microfollicles lined by cuboidal to columnar epithelial cells with colloid, and secondary changes of fibrosis, infarction, hemorrhage, and calcification; no vascular invasion was seen. Peritoneal and omental biopsies, appearing grossly normal, contained microscopic deposits of small thyroid follicles with colloid. Immunohistochemistry showed tumor cells positive for nuclear TTF1 and cytoplasmic thyroglobulin.

A 20-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a progressively enlarging liver mass. He had a history of Klinefelter syndrome and pulmonary valve stenosis. The lesion was discovered incidentally after routine laboratory tests showed mild liver dysfunction. The patient was asymptomatic. Vital signs were normal. Physical examination revealed a palpable, non-tender mass in the right upper quadrant. There were no cushingoid features.

Laboratory tests:
- Hepatitis B surface antigen: negative
- Hepatitis C antibody: negative
- Liver function tests: mild dysfunction
- Alpha-fetoprotein and carcinoembryonic antigen: within normal limits
- Neuron-specific enolase: elevated

Ultrasonography showed a solid, low-echoic tumor >80 mm in diameter with partial calcification in the anterior right lobe. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed an 81 × 76 × 72 mm heterogeneously enhancing mass in the right hepatic lobe with dense focal calcification. PET/CT demonstrated a hepatic mass with an SUV of 22.4 and no evidence of extrahepatic metastasis. On MRI, the lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and demonstrated early arterial enhancement with washout in parts of the tumor. These findings raised concern for hepatocellular carcinoma, particularly fibrolamellar subtype.

A 69-year-old man presented with exertional dyspnea and shortness of breath. He denied cough, hemoptysis, night sweats, fever, or weight loss and had never smoked. Routine laboratory results were normal. Examination revealed slightly diminished breath sounds in the right lower lung field. A noncontrast ECG-gated multidetector CT scan of the heart, performed to assess coronary calcium, showed no coronary calcification but incidentally revealed a 1.9 cm round mass in the right intermediate bronchus with fat-equivalent density values; there was no contrast enhancement or popcorn calcification, and lymph nodes were not enlarged. One month later, dyspnea on exertion recurred and atrial fibrillation was ruled out. A contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated early middle-lobe pneumonia. Flexible bronchoscopy identified a smooth, round lesion subtotally occluding the intermediate bronchus; the lesion could not be traversed by the bronchoscope. Bronchoalveolar lavage grew Escherichia coli, and amoxicillin–clavulanate was started. Histopathological examination of bronchoscopic biopsy specimens showed benign bronchial mucosa with edema, fibrosis, and chronic inflammation and, in deeper layers, marginal areas of mature fatty tissue suggesting a lipoma or lipomatous hamartoma.

A 67-year-old man presented with a slowly enlarging mass in the intergluteal cleft that he first noticed 1 year earlier. He reported no pain, systemic symptoms, or changes in bowel habits. His medical history was notable only for well-controlled hypertension. On examination, there was a 2.5×2.5 cm soft, non-tender, freely mobile subcutaneous mass with normal overlying skin, and bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy (1 cm on the right and a 4.5×7 cm conglomerate on the left). Mohs surgery was performed, and biopsy of the tumor and right inguinal lymph node revealed a high-grade malignancy of cutaneous appendage origin with basaloid differentiation, glandular and alveolar tubular structures, focal myxoid degeneration, microcalcifications, and lymphatic and vascular permeation; tumor was within 1 mm of the margins. Abdominal CT with contrast confirmed a 2.3 cm mass in the intergluteal cleft and a 4.5 cm left inguinal lymph node conglomerate. Chest CT demonstrated bilateral pulmonary nodules (6.4 mm on the right, 11 mm on the left) and axillary and cervical adenopathy.

A 4-year-old girl presented to the emergency department with painful left hip and fever. She had no prior medical history. On examination, she walked with a limp; movements of the left hip, especially external rotation, were painful but not restricted. A single cervical lymph node was palpable. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, a normal white‐cell count, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 123 mm/h, and a C‐reactive protein level of 149.7 mg/L. A pelvic radiograph was normal. Ultrasound of the left hip revealed a small effusion and synovitis. Ultrasound-guided aspiration of the hip joint yielded fluid that was macroscopically compatible with reactive arthritis, and samples were sent for general and bacteriological analysis.

A 23-year-old man presented with insidious onset of abdominal distension over the past year that had progressed rapidly, along with intermittent episodes of intestinal obstruction for 6 months. He was cachectic, febrile, and tachycardic. There were no features suggestive of von Recklinghausen’s disease. On examination, his abdomen was distended by an enormous, rounded, immobile, nontender mass of variegated consistency, extending from below the costal margins to the pelvis with indistinct borders. Routine blood tests were normal except for a hemoglobin level of 6.0 g/dL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a large lobulated, relatively well-defined, heterogeneously enhancing solid-cystic mass occupying the abdominopelvic cavity, extending superiorly to the pancreas, arising from the rectovesical pouch with anterior displacement of the bladder and posterolateral displacement of the rectum, anterolaterally abutting the abdominal wall with lateral displacement of bowel loops, and posteriorly compressing the inferior vena cava, aorta, and common iliac vessels. There was right moderate hydronephrosis with delayed contrast excretion. Image-guided fine-needle aspiration yielded approximately 1 L of frank pus and was suggestive of an abscess; culture for acid-fast bacilli was negative.

A 67-year-old man presented to the emergency department with syncope. Seven months earlier, he had been diagnosed with pT3 NX M0 stage III high-grade urothelial carcinoma of the right renal pelvis with perineural and perivascular invasion and underwent laparoscopic right nephroureterectomy with bladder cuff. 

Four days after surgery, he developed acute severe shortness of breath and hypotension that responded to fluids. CT angiography of the chest revealed extensive filling defects in the distal main pulmonary arteries extending into bilateral upper and lower segmental arteries, with a low likelihood of right heart strain. Bilateral lower-extremity Doppler ultrasonography showed no evidence of deep-vein thrombosis. He was started on systemic anticoagulation with a warfarin bridge.

Two months later, while on warfarin, he had another episode of acute severe dyspnea and was found to have new pulmonary emboli; an inferior vena cava filter was placed, and anticoagulation was changed to rivaroxaban.

One month after that, he again developed acute dyspnea; CT angiography showed a new pulmonary embolus in the right main pulmonary artery with right heart strain, and anticoagulation was switched to fondaparinux with aspirin 325 mg.

One month later, he presented with worsening dyspnea, palpitations, tachycardia, and hypotension responsive to fluids. CT angiography demonstrated extensive occlusive pulmonary emboli in the left main pulmonary artery and branches of the right lower-lobe pulmonary artery. Echocardiography showed significant right heart strain, biventricular failure (LVEF 40%), moderate-to-severe pulmonary hypertension, and moderate tricuspid regurgitation. He was anticoagulated with enoxaparin; thrombolytic therapy was deferred, and he was started on diuretics and a beta-blocker.

Four days after discharge, he had another syncopal episode while defecating and presented with hypoxia requiring 2 L of oxygen, tachypnea, and tachycardia with normotension. CT angiography again showed a large clot burden in the pulmonary arteries, and he was taken for bilateral pulmonary endarterectomy with thrombo-embolectomy.

A 71-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease presented with one month of painless intermittent gross hematuria and urinary frequency. He had no history of radiotherapy or neurofibromatosis. Physical examination was unremarkable, with no skin lesions; the prostate was mildly enlarged without nodularity. Laboratory tests showed PSA 2.46 ng/mL, BUN 69 mg/dL, creatinine 1.30 mg/dL, and microscopic hematuria (33 erythrocytes/hpf). Ultrasound revealed a 45 × 35 mm bladder diverticulum containing a 30 × 20 mm papillary projection. Cystoscopy confirmed a 30 mm papillary lesion on the diverticulum and a 10 mm lesion on the right posterolateral bladder wall. Initial TURBT of both lesions showed non-invasive low-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma. Three months later, surveillance cystoscopy identified papillary projections at both resection sites; repeat resection again yielded non-invasive low-grade urothelial carcinoma, but a specimen near the right ureteric orifice also contained atypical mesenchymal cell infiltration in the lamina propria. These cells were positive for S100, SOX10, and vimentin; NF1 mutation analysis was negative.  

Four months later, after patient delay, re-TURBT revealed a 5 × 5 cm area of irregular bladder wall with diffuse solid lesions. Incomplete resection material showed a highly cellular tumor composed of epithelioid cells with round vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant eosinophilic to amphophilic cytoplasm arranged in lobules, nests, and cords, along with a smaller spindle cell component in fascicles. Mitotic rate was 42/10 HPF with atypical figures, and necrosis was present. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated strong, diffuse staining for S100, SOX10, vimentin, and p16, focal staining for cytokeratin 7 and epithelial membrane antigen, and negative staining for Myo-D1, desmin, CD34, smooth muscle actin, myogenin, CD117, GATA3, and ALK. INI1 expression was retained, and the Ki-67 index was 10%.

A 34-year-old man presented with a left popliteal mass that had been present for 1 year and was gradually enlarging and painful. He had no distal neurologic or vascular compromise. One month before presentation he noted new left inguinal pain. The remainder of the review of systems was negative.  
On MRI of the left knee, there was a large, lobulated, T2-weighted hyperintense soft-tissue mass in the popliteal fossa with local mass effect and surrounding edema, suspicious for a soft-tissue sarcoma. Staging contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed necrotic left external iliac lymphadenopathy and both a right lung mass and a pulmonary nodule, concerning for metastatic disease.  
CT-guided core biopsy of the popliteal mass and an inguinal lymph node revealed a proliferation of rounded epithelioid to spindle-shaped cells with hyperchromatic nuclei arranged in a trabecular architecture within hyalinized stroma.  
Immunohistochemical staining showed positivity for vimentin, CAM5.2, and focal CKAE1/3, EMA, and synaptophysin, and negativity for S-100, desmin, chromogranin, and CD45. Additional staining demonstrated pankeratin positivity and focal EMA positivity, with negative results for GFAP, calponin, p63, CD99, FLI-1, CD34, MUC-4, ERG, and TLE-1.  
FISH analysis was negative for rearrangements of the EWSR1 (22q12) locus, the SS18 (SYT; 18q11.2) locus, and NR4A3.

A two-month-old female infant was brought for evaluation of a mass on the anteromedial side of the proximal left tibia. On examination, the lesion was oval, soft, compressible, and painless. Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs showed soft-tissue swelling without bony erosion. Doppler ultrasound demonstrated a 12 mm × 4 mm cystic lesion with blood flow and confirmed an intact bone cortex.

A 35-year-old woman with no significant past medical history except for an appendectomy 20 years earlier presented with a 1-day history of worsening abdominal pain, vomiting, and fevers. She reported a slowly enlarging abdomen over several years but no previous symptoms. On examination, she had a distended, diffusely tender abdomen without peritoneal signs. Pregnancy was excluded. 

Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated large volumes of ascites containing dot‐like calcifications and subtle septations encasing small‐bowel loops, ovaries, and the uterus, with some extensions into the retroperitoneum. The ovaries appeared prominent. Laboratory studies showed an elevated CA-125 level of 78.9 U/mL (normal 0–35 U/mL), with normal CEA and CA 19-9 levels. 

At a multidisciplinary team meeting, the findings were considered highly suspicious for ovarian cancer, with pseudomyxoma peritonei as a differential. A gynecological evaluation revealed no pelvic pathology. Endoscopic evaluation with OGD and colonoscopy was unremarkable. 

Ten days later, repeat CT showed a marked increase in ascites and new scalloping of the liver surface. Inflammatory markers remained elevated (CRP 207 mg/L; WBC 11.7×10^3/μL) with persistent fevers up to 39 °C. Empiric piperacillin/tazobactam was initiated for suspected spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. After re-discussion, the MDT concluded that pseudomyxoma peritonei was the most likely diagnosis and recommended cytoreductive surgery with HIPEC.

A 52-year-old woman with well-controlled HIV (viral load <40 copies/mL, CD4 count 290 cells/mm3) was found to have a 20% weight loss (12 kg) over one year, initially intentional but accelerating in recent months. She reported no fevers, night sweats, gastrointestinal symptoms, or gynecological complaints. On examination, there was a palpable mass in the right iliac fossa. Laboratory studies showed a drop in hemoglobin from 13 g/dL to 10 g/dL, a lactate dehydrogenase level of 643 U/L, a C-reactive protein level of 80 mg/L, and a normal white-cell count. Her past history included a hysterectomy for micro-invasive cervical carcinoma in 2002; no operative records were available. An urgent CT scan of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a 15 cm mass possibly arising from the vaginal wall with a potential fistulous connection to the cecum, and mesenteric lymph nodes measuring up to 27 mm but no distant metastases. Serum tumor markers (CA19-9, CEA, CA125) were all negative.

A 30-year-old nulligravid woman with polycystic ovary syndrome presented with one month of mild, left-sided lower abdominal pain without fever, chills, weight loss, or changes in bowel habits. She had a body-mass index of 40 kg/m2. Her menstrual cycles were regular, and she denied any personal or family history of gynecologic or breast cancer. Physical examination was unremarkable except for mild tenderness in the left lower quadrant. Laboratory studies showed a normal thyroid-stimulating hormone level and hemoglobin A1c. Serum CA-125 was 12 U/mL and HE4 was 31 pmol/L, both within normal limits. Transvaginal ultrasound revealed an enlarged left ovary without follicles and a 4-cm hypoechoic solid mass; Doppler imaging showed no significant flow. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a hyperintense T2 signal and minimally hypointense T1 signal in the left ovarian mass. Postcontrast T1-weighted images at 30, 60, 90, and 120 seconds showed avid enhancement with progressive centripetal “filling-in” of the lesion. The decision was made to proceed with diagnostic laparoscopy.

A 60-year-old woman presented with sudden onset of severe, incapacitating lower abdominal pain accompanied by nausea and vomiting. She reported a 2-year history of mild intermittent pelvic pain and a sensation of a pelvic “foreign body,” but no dyspareunia, fever, vaginal bleeding, or abnormal smear tests. Her only surgeries were a hysterectomy and oophorectomy performed years earlier without complications. On examination, she was hemodynamically stable, but palpation elicited tenderness in the lower abdomen. Bimanual genital exam revealed a firm, retrocervical mass approximately 3 × 3 cm that was mildly tender on mobilization. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a 10 × 4 cm mass appearing to arise from the vaginal cuff. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a 10 × 5 × 4.7 cm heterogeneous mass attached to the vaginal cuff and abutting bladder and bowel loops without clear invasion, with mixed fatty and soft-tissue densities. MRI T2-weighted images revealed a multilocular heterogeneous mass with hyperintense walls, septations, and small cystic areas, located near the vaginal cuff and originating from the small-bowel mesentery. All laboratory studies, including inflammatory markers, were within normal limits.

A 29-year-old man with grade I obesity presented with new-onset sclero-tegumentary jaundice, pruritus, and epigastric pain. A prior CT scan revealed cholelithiasis and choledocholithiasis. Laboratory evaluation showed cholestatic liver test abnormalities and mild hepatocellular injury without leukocytosis or anemia. Endoscopic ultrasonography followed by ERCP with papillosphincterotomy was performed; two biliary stones were extracted and a 10 Fr/7 cm biliary stent placed. During ERCP, a subtle, slightly elevated lesion adjacent to the major papilla with normal overlying mucosa was noted. Repeat EUS demonstrated a well-delineated 14 × 7 mm homogeneous hypoechoic submucosal mass in the periampullary region of the second portion of the duodenum, with Doppler flow and a mixed elastographic pattern. EUS-guided fine-needle biopsy (22G Franseen needle, three passes) yielded tissue showing monomorphic ovoid cells with mild nuclear atypia, low mitotic activity, and no necrosis. Immunohistochemical stains were positive for synaptophysin, chromogranin A, and CD56; focally positive for pan-cytokeratin AE1/AE3; and negative for S100, CD34, and muscle-specific actin; Ki67 index was 1%. The lesion was classified as a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor (NET grade 1). Cross-sectional CT and MRI demonstrated no local invasion or distant metastases and confirmed that the lesion was amenable to resection.

A 65-year-old Japanese man underwent distal pancreatectomy with portal vein resection for a T3N1M0 pancreatic ductal carcinoma one month ago. He is asymptomatic at follow-up.  
Vital signs are within normal limits; he is afebrile. Physical examination is unremarkable. Laboratory studies show no leukocytosis and normal inflammatory markers; liver enzymes are mildly elevated, consistent with recent surgery.  
Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the liver reveals multiple new tumors with perilesional ring enhancement in the arterial phase. Diffusion-weighted images show high signal in the periphery of these lesions. On T2-weighted HASTE images, the lesions are hyperintense with a fluid–fluid level suggesting intratumoral hemorrhage.

A 79-year-old Saudi man presented with a solitary, asymptomatic skin lesion on his scalp that had appeared suddenly 1 month earlier and remained stable in size. His history was notable for adenocarcinoma of the sigmoid colon with metastases to the liver and lung; the primary tumor was resected 6 months earlier, and he had undergone subsequent resections for recurrent liver and lung lesions and was receiving palliative chemotherapy. On examination, there was a firm, pink, 8 × 7 mm nodule on the scalp. Dermoscopic examination showed polymorphic vessels (dotted, linear, and serpentine) and a white structureless area on a pink-to-red background. The differential diagnoses included cutaneous metastasis, basal cell carcinoma, sebaceous tumors, and amelanotic melanoma.

A man in his late 30s was referred for orthopedic evaluation after 4 months of nontraumatic, insidious low back pain rated 7/10, worsened by sitting and walking and relieved by lying flat. He reported numbness in both lower limbs without weakness or sphincter dysfunction and denied abdominal pain or gastrointestinal bleeding. MRI of the spine at the referring facility was interpreted as consistent with tuberculous spondylitis, and empirical antituberculosis therapy was initiated.

After 2 months of therapy, he developed shortness of breath, low-grade fever, drenching night sweats, and unintentional weight loss. Chest radiography showed a left-sided pleural effusion. Analysis of the exudative pleural fluid revealed a pleural fluid/serum protein ratio of 0.8, an adenosine deaminase level of 47 IU/L, and no malignant cells, and treatment for pleural tuberculosis was begun.

Two weeks later, he experienced intractable vomiting, abdominal pain, and anorexia without overt bleeding. On examination, he was cachectic and pale, with tachypnea and an oxygen saturation of 90% on room air. Respiratory examination showed reduced left-sided chest expansion, diminished breath sounds, and stony dullness. Neurologic assessment revealed a sensory level at T6, loss of anterolateral lower-limb sensation, brisk reflexes, and upgoing plantar responses. Laboratory results demonstrated normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL), elevated lactate dehydrogenase (1182 U/L), C-reactive protein 11.9 mg/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 75 mm/h, and an AST five times the upper limit of normal. Alpha-fetoprotein and CA-125 were normal; carcinoembryonic antigen was 2.7 ng/mL. HIV and Helicobacter pylori serologies were negative.

Repeat MRI of the spine showed wedge collapse of T6 and a burst fracture of T10. CT of the chest and abdomen revealed left hydropneumothorax, multiple pulmonary nodules, and multiple hypodense enhancing hepatic lesions.

A previously healthy 7-year-old boy presented with 2½ months of fever and bilateral lower-limb pain, progressing over the past week to nearly complete loss of lower-limb movement. He had onset of bilateral foot swelling and noted loss of sensation in the legs and bladder/bowel dysfunction. There was no history of seizures; family and past histories were unremarkable.

On examination, he was pale, with nonpitting edema of the lower limbs, urinary and fecal incontinence, and hepatomegaly 4 cm below the costal margin (no splenomegaly). Meningeal signs were positive. Deep tendon reflexes were absent and muscle power in both lower limbs was 0/5.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL, white blood cell count 11,500/mm3, platelet count 71,000/mm3, and lactate dehydrogenase 3,441 U/L. Chest radiography and echocardiography were unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the brain demonstrated smoothly enhancing masses in the left lateral ventricular atrium (3.8×3 cm), along the anterior falx cerebri (2×1.7 cm), at the left anterior middle cranial fossa base, and in the right lateral extraconal orbital space (15×8 mm). CT of the spine and abdomen revealed an enhancing left paravertebral soft-tissue mass at L3 (2.3×1.0 cm) and extradural deposits at the D4 and D8 levels.

A 36-year-old woman at 33 weeks of an otherwise uncomplicated pregnancy presented with a 4-day history of dry cough, progressive dyspnea and recent orthopnea. She also reported generalized malaise with myalgias and arthralgias. She had smoked five cigarettes per day until pregnancy, denied prior lung disease, and had two prior cesarean deliveries without complications.  
On examination she was alert, diaphoretic and tachypneic with intercostal retractions. Oxygen saturation was 74% on noninvasive oxygen at 10 L/min, blood pressure 130/90 mm Hg, heart rate 100 bpm, respiratory rate 21/min and temperature 36°C. Pulmonary exam showed bilateral crepitant crackles at the bases and decreased breath sounds. Cardiovascular exam revealed tachycardia without murmurs. Fetal heart rate was 158 bpm.  
Arterial blood gas on oxygen showed pH 7.40, PaO₂ 43 mm Hg, PaCO₂ 24 mm Hg and HCO₃⁻ 16.9 mEq/L. Endotracheal intubation and emergency cesarean delivery were performed, and the mother was admitted to the ICU.  
Initial laboratory studies showed no leukocytosis. Chest radiograph revealed bilateral lower-zone opacities. Chest CT demonstrated bilateral alveolar infiltrates and areas of consolidation with right-base predominance. Empiric IV ceftriaxone and oral clarithromycin were started.  
In the ICU, consecutive blood cultures, bronchial secretion cultures, IgG antibodies against Mycoplasma pneumoniae and a galactomannan assay were all negative; serum procalcitonin was 0.02 ng/mL. Immunologic assays to evaluate for autoimmune disease were negative. Forty-eight hours later she was extubated but remained oxygen dependent.  
Transthoracic echocardiography showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 66% with normal systolic function, mild diastolic dysfunction, and a 300 mL global pericardial effusion, excluding decompensated heart failure as the cause of her respiratory failure.

A 15-year-old girl presented with a swelling of her upper left jaw that had been present for 1 year and was gradually increasing in size. There was no pain. On extra-oral examination, there was a single, diffuse, non-tender, hard swelling in the left anterior maxillary region measuring approximately 3 cm × 4 cm. Intra-orally, there was a well-circumscribed, smooth-surfaced swelling involving the buccal and palatal aspects of the left upper anterior maxilla, causing obliteration of the buccal vestibule. The deciduous left maxillary lateral incisor and canine were present; the permanent left maxillary lateral incisor and canine were absent. Bicortical expansion was noted.

An intra-oral periapical radiograph and an orthopantomograph revealed a well-circumscribed, unilocular radiolucency extending from the left maxillary central incisor to the first premolar. The lesion was associated with an impacted left maxillary lateral incisor and a mesially displaced root of the left central incisor. Specks of calcification were visible within the radiolucent area. Additionally, an impacted left maxillary canine was seen superiorly, near the first molar region.

A 68-year-old Japanese man presented with a 1-year history of mild rectal pain and tenesmus without bleeding or weight loss. His only comorbidity was well-controlled hypertension. He denied alcohol or tobacco use. Family history was notable for a father who died of acute myocardial infarction and a mother who died of metastatic gastric cancer. He had an uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy 10 years earlier.

On examination, vital signs were normal. The abdomen was non-tender with hyperactive bowel sounds. Digital rectal examination revealed a firm right-sided mass 3 to 7 cm from the anal verge; no blood was noted. Colonoscopy showed a 5 cm subepithelial, mucosa-covered elevation located 4 cm above the pectineal line. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a well-defined round mass arising from the distal rectum, with low signal intensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images and no invasion of the bladder or prostate. Endoscopic ultrasound revealed a homogeneous hypoechoic mass with areas of necrosis originating from the fourth layer (muscularis propria).

A 19-year-old man with known HIV infection (diagnosed 10 months earlier; CD4 count 610 cells/μL; viral load 150,000 copies/mL) presented with a 4-month history of rapidly enlarging cervical swelling. He reported night sweats but denied fever or weight loss. On examination, he had firm, painless bilateral cervical lymph nodes up to 3 cm in diameter; other lymph node regions were not involved. Laboratory testing showed hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, MCV 84 fL, WBC 7.8 G/L, neutrophils 3.8 G/L, lymphocytes 2.1 G/L, and platelets 189 G/L. No abnormal cells were observed on the peripheral blood smear. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 32 mm/h. Serologic tests for hepatitis B and C viruses and syphilis were negative. A fine-needle aspiration of a cervical lymph node stained with May–Grünwald–Giemsa revealed:  
  • Low-power: diffusely distributed histiocytes with vacuolated cytoplasm.  
  • High-power: histiocytes with single, double, or multiple nuclei, fine chromatin, prominent basophilic nucleoli, and abundant cytoplasm containing several intact plasma cells or lymphocytes (emperipolesis), with occasional halos around phagocytized cells.

A 70-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of horizontal diplopia, most pronounced with lateral gaze, and a constant dull frontal headache partially relieved by NSAIDs. He also reported decreased energy and leg weakness. His medical history included nonmedicated diabetes mellitus, gastroesophageal reflux, hyperlipidemia, and tachycardia. On examination, he had bilateral sixth cranial nerve palsy and intermittent binocular horizontal diplopia.

Initial head CT revealed a sellar mass involving the right cavernous sinus measuring 2.8 × 1.9 × 1.7 cm. MRI confirmed a heterogeneous sellar mass invading the right cavernous sinus with leftward deviation of the infundibulum, small suprasellar extension, and mild mass effect on the optic chiasm. Visual field testing was normal.

Hormonal studies showed possible secondary adrenal insufficiency (AM cortisol 3.3 μg/dL; ACTH 8 pg/mL), secondary hypothyroidism (TSH <0.01 mIU/L; free T4 0.7 ng/dL), secondary hypogonadism (testosterone 47 ng/dL; LH 1.3 mIU/mL; FSH 2.3 mIU/mL), and mild hyperprolactinemia (56.8 ng/mL; normal 4.0–15.2). IGF-1 was normal. No acute surgical intervention was planned, and he was discharged on levothyroxine and hydrocortisone.

Three-month follow-up MRI showed interval increase in tumor size, extension along the infundibulum from 0.4 cm to 0.7 cm in transverse width, mild increased optic chiasm compression, further sellar growth, and suspected right cavernous sinus invasion with clival erosion. Neurosurgical resection was planned.

Days later, he presented with severe headache, nausea, vomiting, polyuria, polydipsia, mild hypernatremia, nystagmus, and reduced right eye abduction. Diabetes insipidus was treated with DDAVP. A repeat MRI was unchanged. He was given stress-dose steroids and underwent emergent endoscopic endonasal transsphenoidal resection. Intraoperatively the tumor was firm and hemorrhagic. Preliminary frozen-section pathology was suggestive of pituitary adenoma, and tumor debulking was performed as safely possible.

A 19-year-old Egyptian woman, recently married, presented with dyspareunia and discomfort for her husband due to a vulvar swelling. She first noticed a small, painless mass in the clitoral region more than 5 years earlier, within a few years after undergoing type-II female genital mutilation/cutting (clitoridectomy with near-total labia minora excision) at age 7 under general anesthesia. The mass gradually increased to approximately the size of a small orange. On examination, there was evidence of type-II FGM/C and a 5 × 5 cm anterior midline cystic swelling at the circumcision scar, partially occluding the introitus. The swelling was soft, fluctuant, mobile, non-tender, not warm, with normal overlying skin, and showed no expansion on Valsalva. Urethral and vaginal orifices were normal; there was no groin hernia or Canal of Nuck hydrocele. Ultrasound of the mass showed a non-septated, hyperechoic cystic lesion measuring 7 × 5 cm. Routine blood tests, urinalysis, and kidney and liver function tests were all normal.

An 18-year-old previously healthy male presented with a 4-week history of progressive ataxia and a 2-week history of diplopia, facial asymmetry, tinnitus, and dysphagia. On examination, he was alert and oriented with stable vital signs. Cranial nerve testing showed bilateral fourth-nerve palsies and left seventh, ninth, and tenth nerve palsies, along with mild cerebellar ataxia. A noncontrast CT scan revealed a posterior fossa mass. MRI showed a well-demarcated, homogeneously enhancing subependymal tumor outlining the fourth ventricle (3×3×3.5 cm), occluding its lumen and extending into the foramen of Magendie, with moderate surrounding edema in the adjacent brainstem and left cerebellum. Two smaller lesions were present: one (12×6 mm) in the floor of the third ventricle anterior to the aqueduct, and another intradural extramedullary lesion at the right C4 level. Laboratory studies including CBC, electrolytes, liver and kidney function, uric acid, and LDH (206 U/L) were normal. Serologies for hepatitis B, C, and HIV were negative. Quantitative immunoglobulins and lymphocyte subsets (CD4+ T cells 1.73×10^9/L) were normal. Peripheral smear showed no abnormal cells. CSF analysis revealed 526 RBCs/µL, 1 WBC/µL, normal protein (0.1 g/L), and no malignant cells on cytology.

A 28-year-old man presented with left testicular pain. On examination, both testes were normal in size, with no palpable mass. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 157 g/L, WBC 7.54 ×10^9/L, platelets 314 ×10^9/L, INR 1.1, urea 5.7 mmol/L, creatinine 91 µmol/L, sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L; tumor markers were within normal limits (AFP 1 IU/mL; hCG <2 IU/L), and hormone levels were unremarkable (FSH 3 IU/L; LH 5 IU/L; prolactin 7.5 µg/L; testosterone 27 nmol/L). Semen analysis showed oligoteratozoospermia. Scrotal ultrasonography revealed a grade 3 left varicocele and incidentally detected a 9 mm calcified lesion in the right testis. Further clinical evaluation was unremarkable, with no gynecomastia or signs of metastasis. Serum AFP and hCG remained normal.

A 21-year-old non-smoking woman, G1P0 at 31 weeks of gestation, presented with a 3-month history of cough productive of sputum, exertional dyspnea, and intermittent fever. She was initially diagnosed with asthma and treated with bronchodilators, with transient relief of cough and dyspnea. However, she continued to experience shortness of breath on exertion while remaining asymptomatic at rest. Four days before transfer, she was hospitalized again for worsening dyspnea that did not respond to asthma therapy. On transfer to the respiratory intensive care unit, she remained hypoxic despite pressurized mask oxygen and was endotracheally intubated and mechanically ventilated. Although oxygen saturation normalized, peak airway pressures exceeded 40 cm H₂O. Urgent bronchoscopy identified an irregular tracheal tumor occluding approximately 80% of the lumen, located about 2 cm above the carina. The endotracheal tube was advanced past the lesion under bronchoscopic guidance, which markedly reduced airway resistance.

A 45-year-old multiparous woman presented with a 6-month history of progressive abdominal distension and fatigue. Menstrual cycles were regular. She had no prior surgeries or major illnesses. On examination, there was a large, semi-mobile, non-tender abdominal mass; the uterus and adnexa were not palpable. Vital signs were normal.  
Abdominal sonography revealed a large cystic mass with multiple septations occupying the entire abdomen; the uterus and endometrium appeared normal, and the ovaries were not visualized. Abdominopelvic CT confirmed a 30×26×17 cm multiloculated cystic mass extending from the pelvis to the upper abdomen, displacing the bladder and uterus superiorly and compressing the small bowel laterally.  
Laboratory studies showed normal electrolytes, liver, and renal function; hemoglobin was 6.79 g/dL, hematocrit 23.6%. Tumor markers (CA-125, CA19-9, CA15-3, CEA, AFP) were all within normal limits.

A 34-year-old woman with no significant medical history reported 3 months of dull, postprandial epigastric pain without systemic symptoms. Examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests including complete blood count, biochemistry, CEA (0.9 ng/ml), and CA 19-9 (2 U/ml) were normal. Upper endoscopy showed extrinsic compression near the lesser curvature. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 5 × 5 × 3 cm retroperitoneal mass thought to arise from the pancreas. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 48 × 50 mm solid, homogeneous, hypervascular, well-circumscribed mass posterior to the pancreatic body, abutting celiac branches without invasion or additional lymphadenopathy. MRI confirmed a 5 × 5 × 4 cm lesion in the lesser sac, hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2, with heterogeneous enhancement. A provisional diagnosis of retroperitoneal gastrointestinal stromal tumor or pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor was made.

A 71-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of right lumbocrural pain and gait disturbance accompanied by paresthesia and right leg weakness. On examination, right leg motor strength was grade 3/5, and sensation was diminished on the right side from the L4 dermatome caudally; deep tendon reflexes were normal. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging revealed a mass lesion involving the L4 vertebral body and extending into the spinal canal with compression of the lumbar spinal cord. Computed tomography demonstrated a slowly growing tumor with severe destruction of the L4 vertebral body.

An 8‐year‐old neutered male Boxer was referred for evaluation of a firm, ovoid mass (3–5 cm in diameter) on the ventral aspect of the neck present for 6 weeks. The primary veterinarian had drained serosanguinous fluid by needle aspiration on two occasions, but the swelling recurred within weeks. The dog had intermittent regurgitation when excited. On examination, the mass was mobile, well circumscribed, nonpainful, and located adjacent to the trachea; there was no lymphadenopathy. Cardiorespiratory and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Complete blood count and serum biochemistry, including liver enzymes, were within reference intervals except for mild hypercholesterolemia. Serum total T4 and TSH were not measured. Ultrasound showed an ovoid, thin‐walled cystic lesion in the region of the right thyroid lobe. Ultrasound‐guided aspiration yielded proteinaceous fluid with mild cell necrosis but no diagnostic cells. Measurement of thyroxine concentration in the cyst fluid was markedly elevated compared to serum reference intervals, confirming thyroidal origin. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the neck revealed a 3.7 × 2.7 cm fluid‐attenuating structure with a thin, uniformly enhancing rim displacing but not invading the trachea or adjacent tissues; there was no lymphadenopathy or pulmonary lesions.

A 16-year-old girl presented with a two-year history of a progressively enlarging swelling over her left elbow. There was no history of trauma, fever, or joint effusion. On examination, there was a firm, slightly tender swelling on the anterior aspect of the upper third of the left forearm without erythema or warmth. Elbow flexion and extension were normal; pronation and supination were each restricted by approximately 15 degrees. The neurovascular examination was unremarkable.

Plain radiographs demonstrated a round, calcified, heterogeneous mass anterior to the proximal ends of the radius and ulna with no apparent cortical or medullary continuity with the underlying bones. CT imaging showed a well-defined, lobulated soft-tissue mass measuring 45 mm × 25 mm with flaky calcifications. MRI revealed a nonenhancing, intermuscular mass lying between the biceps brachii and brachialis muscles, abutting the supinator and medial epicondylar muscles, without any continuity to the ulna or radius. The lesion was heterogeneously low signal on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously high signal on T2 FAT-SAT images, with peripheral low-signal areas consistent with calcification.

On the basis of imaging, myositis ossificans was the leading diagnosis, but a soft-tissue sarcoma could not be excluded.

A 55-year-old man presented with a one-month history of a rapidly enlarging, painful swelling in the left maxillary gingiva that developed shortly after extraction of the left maxillary molar. The lesion measured approximately 4 × 4 cm, was noduloulcerative, firm, tender, bled on touch, and obliterated the left buccal vestibule. A second ulcero-proliferative mass measuring 2 × 2 cm was noted on the right maxillary gingiva adjacent to the canine and first premolar. Examination revealed a fixed, tender left submandibular lymph node and a tender, mobile right submandibular node. The provisional clinical diagnoses were gingival hyperplasia, squamous cell carcinoma, and metastatic disease. Routine blood tests were unremarkable. An incisional biopsy was performed. Shortly thereafter, the patient experienced new-onset seizures; MRI of the brain revealed multiple lesions suggestive of metastases. Cone-beam CT demonstrated lytic lesions in the vertebrae, sacrum, pelvis, femur, and ribs (with a pathological rib fracture), bilateral pleural effusions with basal atelectasis, and moth-eaten bony destruction of the maxilla. Histologic examination of the gingival biopsy showed large clusters and sheets of clear cells with abundant clear cytoplasm, marked pleomorphism, and hyperchromatism within the connective tissue stroma, along with degenerative changes in the overlying oral mucosa.

A 45-year-old premenopausal multiparous woman presented with a 6-month history of lower abdominal pain and progressive abdominal distension. She noted an abdominal mass over the past 3 months, associated with increasing pain and easy fatigability. Her obstetric history was notable for four vaginal deliveries; she had no prior abdominal surgeries. Medical history included 10 years of type II diabetes mellitus and hypercholesterolemia. She denied menstrual irregularities and had no family history of genital malignancy.

Vital signs were within normal limits. On abdominal examination, there was a distended abdomen with a hard, solid mass filling the entire cavity that could not be lateralized; there was no rebound or tenderness. Pelvic examination showed a normal cervix and vagina, but the fornices were full bilaterally.

Transvaginal ultrasonography revealed a large, solid, complex pelvic mass extending to the subdiaphragmatic area; the organ of origin could not be determined. MRI of the abdomen demonstrated a 33 × 17 × 25 cm solid mass containing cystic and fatty components; it appeared inseparable from the uterus, and both ovaries were not visualized. Routine laboratory tests, including complete blood count, liver and renal function, coagulation studies, and electrolytes, were normal. Blood glucose, HbA1c, and cholesterol levels were elevated. Serum CA-125 was 210 mIU/ml (reference range <35 mIU/ml).

In light of the imaging findings and laboratory results, a uterine leiomyosarcoma was considered the most likely diagnosis, and surgery was planned.

A 60-year-old man presented with a two-week history of progressive ataxia, dysarthria, and headache. His past medical history was significant for multiple nonmelanoma skin cancers, including a basaloid squamous cell carcinoma of the scalp in 2017. In December 2018, he underwent wide local excision of a rapidly enlarging 2-cm nodular lesion on the left anterior scalp. Histopathology of that lesion showed an ovoid tumour arising from the basal epidermis, infiltrating into subcutaneous tissue, composed of anastomosing ductal and glandular structures lined by neoplastic cuboidal or columnar cells. Immunohistochemical stains were strongly positive for EMA, focally positive for CEA in ducts, and negative for ER, PR, and SOX10. Margins were negative, and there was no lymphovascular or perineural invasion. A diagnosis of primary pT1N0M0 ductal eccrine adenocarcinoma was made, and he received adjuvant radiotherapy (55 Gy in 25 fractions).

On examination at this presentation, he had bilateral horizontal nystagmus, right-sided limb dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesis, and gait ataxia; other neurologic findings were normal. MRI of the brain revealed a solitary 25-mm peripherally enhancing cystic lesion in the right pons with surrounding edema. Staging PET-CT showed two left-sided pulmonary lesions (45 mm in the lower lobe and 12 mm in the lingula) and ipsilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. The patient underwent resection of the pontine lesion followed by biopsy of the larger left lower lobe lung lesion.  
Histopathological review of both specimens demonstrated metastatic adenocarcinoma that was morphologically similar to his previous scalp tumour. Immunohistochemistry on the metastatic lesions showed CK7 positivity, CK20 negativity, and TTF-1 negativity. PD-L1 expression was <1%, and mismatch repair protein expression in the original scalp tumour was intact.

An 85-year-old man was admitted for evaluation of a splenic mass. Fifteen days earlier, he had been hospitalized in the hematology clinic for thrombocytopenia with tongue bruising. He was 170 cm tall, weighed 68 kg (BMI 22.4 kg/m²), and had been receiving oral prednisolone (80 mg daily) for thrombocytopenia. His history included benign prostatic hyperplasia (surgically treated), appendectomy, and inguinal hernia repair; he had no diabetes, hypertension, coagulopathy, smoking history, or other medications. On examination, the spleen was not palpable. After prednisolone, his WBC was 9,300/mm³, INR 1.02, and platelets 437,000/μL. Carcinoembryonic antigen and CA 19-9 levels were 4.3 ng/mL and 25.5 U/mL, respectively (normal). Abdominal ultrasound showed an 80 mm hypoechoic, exophytic solid lesion in the mid–superior spleen. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed several nodular lesions (largest 50 mm) with heterogeneous, hypodense, expansile involvement of the spleen. Contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated a 67 mm splenic mass with central cystic necrosis and peripheral enhancement. A presumptive diagnosis of splenic metastasis or abscess was made, and splenectomy was planned.

A 61-year-old man noted a progressive, painless swelling in his right inguinoscrotal region of more than 6 months’ duration, with more rapid growth over the past 6 weeks to approximately 8 × 5 cm. There was no cough impulse. On palpation, the swelling was firm, smooth, and mildly tender. The transillumination test was negative, and there was no palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy. Scrotal ultrasonography showed a heterogeneous hyperechogenic mass with mixed echogenicity involving the right spermatic cord; this pattern was highly suspicious for malignancy. A chest–abdominopelvic CT scan revealed a heterogeneous right supratesticular mass of fatty tissue measuring 84 × 78 × 72 mm and no evidence of metastatic disease.

A 66-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with severe right flank pain of 9/10 intensity that had persisted for several hours and radiated to the right lower quadrant. She denied vomiting, changes in bowel habits, or recent trauma. Her medical history was notable for a deceased-donor kidney transplant placed in the right iliac fossa 20 years earlier for end-stage renal disease due to chronic glomerulonephritis; she had returned to hemodialysis 3 years ago because of chronic allograft nephropathy. Additional problems included recurrent biliary colic, chronic deep venous insufficiency, osteoporosis, hypothyroidism, and chronic hepatitis B carriage. Medications were lamivudine, levothyroxine, folic acid, omeprazole, low-dose aspirin, calcium, and vitamin D.

On examination she appeared uncomfortable. Vital signs were: temperature 36.7°C, pulse 66/min, blood pressure 120/60 mmHg. Physical examination showed severe tenderness to palpation over the right lower abdomen and flank. Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 7300 cells/µl (68% granulocytes), blood glucose 4.8 mmol/l, blood urea 12.5 mmol/l, and serum creatinine 470 µmol/l. Chest and abdominal radiographs were normal.

A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen demonstrated a 3 cm round hypodense mass (22 Hounsfield units) in the upper pole of the transplanted kidney with surrounding fatty effacement. Empiric intravenous antibiotics and analgesics were started. A follow-up ultrasound showed a complex hypervascular hypoechoic mass in the same location.

Review of prior imaging revealed that an abdominal CT scan two years earlier had shown a subtle 1 cm hypodense lesion at that site, and an MR cholangiopancreatography from around that time had incidentally captured a 2 cm round mass of low T2 signal intensity in the transplanted kidney.

A 51-year-old woman presented with heavy vaginal bleeding, pelvic pressure, bladder incontinence, and dyspareunia. She had grade 2 obesity and well-controlled diabetes; her medical and surgical histories were otherwise unremarkable. On examination, her uterus was enlarged by fibroids up to the level of the umbilicus. She elected uterine artery embolization and underwent pelvic MRI, which showed an indeterminate 5.5 cm solid enhancing mass inferior to the bladder and inseparable from the superior anterior urethral wall. She subsequently underwent cystoscopy, which ruled out invasion of the mass into the urethra.

A 40-year-old woman at 39 weeks of gestation was admitted for cesarean delivery owing to fetal breech presentation. Her obstetrical history included two first‐trimester abortions and one prior cesarean delivery for breech presentation. Beginning at 20 weeks’ gestation, she noted a progressive, painless swelling of the right flank. Multiple ultrasound examinations demonstrated a rapidly growing, sharply defined abdominal mass with heterogeneous echogenicity and a smooth contour, findings interpreted as highly suggestive of a subserosal uterine leiomyoma. The patient had no other symptoms, denied tobacco and alcohol use, and took only prenatal vitamins. Under spinal anesthesia, a lower-segment transverse uterine incision was made. After delivery of a healthy male infant, inspection revealed that the mass was extra-peritoneal and originated from the right lateral abdominal wall musculature, appearing whitish, firm, and fixed to surrounding tissues. A general surgeon was consulted intraoperatively for further evaluation.

A 31-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of right buttock and posterior thigh pain accompanied by intermittent paresthesia and weakness in the right lower leg and foot. Her medical history was notable for a dysplastic right kidney removed in childhood. On examination, she had lumbar tenderness and an antalgic gait favoring the right side; motor, sensory, and reflex testing were otherwise unremarkable. Her baseline Oswestry Disability Index was 54, indicating severe impairment.

An MRI of the lumbar spine demonstrated a 2.5 cm partially cystic and solid mass along the medial edge of the right psoas muscle near the L4 and L5 nerve roots. A subsequent MRI of the pelvis confirmed a multilobulated lesion measuring 2.6 cm × 1.7 cm medial to the right psoas muscle. On T2-weighted images, the mass was predominantly hyperintense with a region of low T2 signal anteriorly; this T2-dark component demonstrated signal drop-out on out-of-phase imaging, indicating fat. The mass was low on T1-weighted fat-saturated sequences and abutted the right L5 nerve root.

Based on imaging, the differential diagnosis included hematoma, lymphatic structure, nerve sheath tumor, or myxoma. Conservative management failed to relieve her symptoms, and she elected to undergo surgical resection for definitive diagnosis.

A 13-year-old girl presented with a 4-year history of chronic abdominal pain that had worsened over time. Over the preceding weeks she developed lower abdominal pain, new-onset dysuria, terminal hematuria, and purulent mucoid discharge. She noted a progressively enlarging lower abdominal mass over 6 months, associated with gradual weight loss and intermittent fevers. She had been treated empirically for suspected extrapulmonary tuberculosis for 5 months without improvement. There was no menarche or signs of precocious puberty. 

On examination she was pale, cachectic, and tachycardic. Abdominal examination revealed a scaphoid abdomen and an ill-defined, firm, tender mass with a rough surface extending from the hypogastric to the right iliac region and into the pelvis, with dullness to percussion and no shifting dullness.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 6.3 g/dL (12.3–15.3), white blood cell count 15.4 × 10^9/L (<16 × 10^9), C-reactive protein 142 mg/L (0.5–5), negative HIV 1/2 serology, β-hCG <0.1 mIU/mL (<5.3), CA-125 32.45 U/mL (<35), and urine positive for nitrites and leukocytes. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated an abdominal mass originating from the urinary bladder dome, breaching the bladder wall, extending to the distal ileal loop with inflammation and fistula formation, and associated intra-abdominal lymphadenopathy with calcification.

A 52-year-old African American woman with a more than 10-year history of Sjögren’s syndrome treated with corticosteroids was admitted with sudden onset chest pain. Computed tomography of the chest revealed a large anterior mediastinal mass and several enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes; the liver and spleen were unremarkable. HIV serology was negative. At surgery, the mass was found to extend from the right side of midline into the left chest, adhering to the pericardium and left pleura and involving the phrenic nerve; the mass and adjacent lymph nodes were excised. Permanent histologic sections were reported as lymphocyte-predominant thymoma and benign reactive lymph nodes. The postoperative course was uneventful.

Twelve months later, she reported night sweats, low-grade fever, flu-like symptoms, green sputum production, a 14-lb weight loss, and exertional dyspnea. Follow‐up CT showed multiple enlarged lymph nodes throughout the chest and upper abdomen, new noncalcified pulmonary nodules, and bilateral pulmonary consolidation.

A 72-year-old man presented with a one-year history of gait imbalance and two months of headache and vomiting. He had no prior medical or family history of brain lesions. On examination, his visual acuity was mildly reduced (0.6/0.4) with normal visual fields. Brain MRI revealed a 55 × 47 × 44 mm hypo- to isointense mass occupying the entire fourth ventricle with an associated cyst and obstructive hydrocephalus on T1-weighted images, intermediate signal intensity on T2-weighted images with only slight perilesional edema, and intense contrast enhancement. Considering the patient’s age and these MRI characteristics, a provisional diagnosis of metastasis was made.

A 28‐year‐old woman, gravida 2 para 1 at 35 weeks and 2 days of gestation, presented with a 1‐week history of severe hypertension. She had a prior history of moderately elevated blood pressure noted at 25 weeks’ gestation that required no therapy. One week before presentation, she complained of headache and right flank pain; her blood pressure was 165/110 mmHg. Laboratory studies—including complete blood count, electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, liver enzymes, and a random urine protein-to-creatinine ratio—were within normal limits. She was diagnosed with pregnancy‐induced hypertension and started on labetalol 200 mg twice daily. Obstetrical ultrasound and umbilical artery Doppler showed no fetal growth restriction. Her management plan included twice-daily blood pressure monitoring, twice-weekly antenatal visits, and planned delivery at 38 weeks.

Despite labetalol, her blood pressure remained labile and the right flank pain persisted. An abdominal ultrasound, performed to evaluate for renal pathology, unexpectedly revealed a heterogeneous right suprarenal solid mass measuring 6 × 4.5 cm. On transfer to our center, her blood pressure fluctuated between 200/120 mmHg and 110/80 mmHg. Repeat laboratory studies, including complete blood count, coagulation profile, liver panel, electrolytes, urea, and creatinine, remained normal. Twenty-four-hour urinary protein was 165 mg, making the diagnosis of preeclampsia unlikely.

A 70-year-old woman was referred to endocrinology for evaluation of unintentional weight loss of 15.7 kg over 12 months. Her medical history included hypothyroidism, multinodular goiter, type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 6.3%), dyslipidemia, and well-controlled hypertension (96/55 mm Hg) on amlodipine, losartan-hydrochlorothiazide, and low-dose carvedilol. She also described fatigue, infrequent night sweats, and increased anxiety attributed to life stressors. On assessment by geriatrics, she met phenotypic criteria for frailty, including >5% weight loss in a year, fatigue, decreased activity tolerance, and slowing gait speed. Age-appropriate cancer screenings for colon, breast, and bone had been negative within the past year.

On physical examination, she appeared well and in no acute distress; vital signs remained within normal limits. Initial laboratory studies—including complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR), autoimmune serologies, thyroid function tests, and HbA1c—were unremarkable. A chest radiograph showed right middle lobe opacity, but a follow-up chest CT demonstrated no consolidation. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 2.0 × 2.0 cm left adrenal mass with an attenuation of 136 HU. No additional lesions were identified.

An 82‐year‐old Japanese woman underwent routine upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and was found to have a protruding submucosal lesion in the middle esophagus. She had no dysphagia or other symptoms, and laboratory studies, including hemoglobin, liver and renal function tests, and tumor markers for adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, were normal. White‐light endoscopy revealed a 8 mm brownish submucosal tumor 25 cm from the incisors with mild surface reddening and a central depressed area; the lesion was elastic, mobile, and hard on forceps compression. Narrow‐band imaging with magnification showed a central brownish area with slightly dilated, non‐uniform intrapapillary capillary loops. The central depression stained only slightly with Lugol’s solution. Endoscopic ultrasound revealed a hypoechoic, homogeneous 8.0 × 4.2 mm mass involving primarily the second and third layers of the esophageal wall, with a thickened hyperechoic submucosa and slight irregularity of the third layer. Biopsy specimens showed only esophagitis without evidence of tumor. Contrast‐enhanced CT did not demonstrate lymphadenopathy or distant lesions. With these findings, squamous cell carcinoma and gastrointestinal stromal tumor were considered.

A 64-year-old Chinese man presented with a 2-month history of skin jaundice. He denied significant medical, medication, family, or occupational exposure histories and reported no use of herbal supplements. On examination, he had marked jaundice but no palpable lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory testing showed hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, leukocytes 9.5 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 7.1 × 10^9/L, and platelets 73 × 10^9/L. Serum direct bilirubin was 165.24 mg/dL; alkaline phosphatase, 273 IU/mL; aspartate aminotransferase, 156 IU/mL; alanine aminotransferase, 44 IU/mL; and lactate dehydrogenase, 1000 IU/mL. Infectious‐disease testing for hepatitis A, B, and C, Epstein–Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus was negative. Autoimmune hepatitis antibodies (anti–smooth muscle, anti–liver–kidney microsomal, and anti–soluble liver antigen) were negative. An abdominal CT scan was unrevealing. As the jaundice worsened, a PET–CT was obtained and showed diffuse hypermetabolism in both liver and spleen.

A 2-year-old boy presented with progressive abdominal enlargement over 1.5 years and poor feeding, without pain, constipation, fever, or jaundice. Birth and family histories were unremarkable. On examination, he was afebrile and stable, weighing 8 kg. The abdomen was markedly distended with visible vascular markings; it was soft, non-tender, and a large mass was palpable. No peritoneal signs or jaundice were noted. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, white blood cell count 12 000/mm³, platelet count 623 000/mm³, and normal tumor markers (CEA, CA 125, CA 19-9, AFP, β-HCG). Abdominal ultrasound revealed a large multicystic mass extending from the right hypochondrium to the pelvis with multiple fluid-filled locules. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 12.5 cm cystic mass in the right upper abdomen containing multiple thin internal septations.

A 45-year-old woman presented with 1 year of right-sided facial pain and swelling and numbness of the right lower lip. She had undergone enucleation of a similar right mandibular swelling 8 years earlier. Over the past year, she noted recurrence of the swelling, paresthesia, and increasing difficulty with mouth opening and swallowing. 

On examination, there was a firm, tender, diffuse swelling (approximately 4 × 9 cm) on the right side of the face, extending from the zygomatic arch and infraorbital margin to the lower border of the mandible; the overlying skin was stretched but not inflamed. Intraorally, all mandibular teeth were absent; there was a soft-tissue mass obliterating the right buccal vestibule. Palpation revealed buccal and lingual cortical expansion, with perforation of the lingual cortex near the region of the right first molar.

A panoramic radiograph showed a multilocular radiolucent lesion extending from the right mandibular symphysis to the right condylar region, with loss of continuity of the lower mandibular border suggesting a pathologic fracture. Axial CT demonstrated opacification of the entire right hemimandible with destruction of the condyle and lower border of the mandible.

What is your leading diagnosis, and what other entities would you include in your differential?

A 34-year-old male presented with 20 days of jaundice. He had scleral and skin icterus but no abdominal tenderness, rebound, Murphy sign, palpable mass, organomegaly, or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests showed total bilirubin 5.17 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 2.49 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 152 U/L, and CA19-9 58.5 U/mL. Serologies for hepatitis A, B, C, and HIV were negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed soft-tissue nodules in the common bile duct with clear borders, inhomogeneous morphology, heterogeneous density, and luminal bulging; the venous phase showed significant heterogeneous enhancement with gradual strengthening. MRCP demonstrated a localized filling defect in the lower common bile duct with luminal narrowing.

A 52-year-old woman noted a painless swelling in the right buccal mucosa for about two years. The mass had grown gradually but remained asymptomatic. An incisional biopsy at an outside clinic suggested a malignant tumor of minor salivary-gland origin, such as adenoid cystic carcinoma or mucoepidermoid carcinoma. On presentation, she had a smooth-surfaced, nontender, elastic-hard, well-movable 1.5 cm exophytic mass in the right buccal mucosa without mucosal ulceration or cervical lymphadenopathy. Neck ultrasonography showed a 12.5 × 9 mm hypo- to isoechoic lesion with smooth margins. Contrast CT and MRI demonstrated a 1.3 cm internally homogeneous, enhancing lesion in the right buccal mucosa and no evidence of lymph node or distant metastasis. Laboratory studies, including tumor markers, were normal. Complete surgical resection was recommended.

An 88-year-old African American woman presented with a 1-month history of a painful lump in her right breast. She had no prior breast imaging, no personal or family history of breast or ovarian cancer, and an unremarkable medical history. On examination, her breasts were symmetric without skin changes; a tender mass was palpable in the superior-lateral peri-areolar region of the right breast. No axillary lymphadenopathy was noted.  

A diagnostic mammogram showed a dense breast with an ill-defined lobular mass containing coarse internal calcifications in the right breast. Targeted ultrasound of the 7–8 o’clock retroareolar region demonstrated a 1.6 × 1 cm heterogeneous hypoechoic solid mass with internal calcifications; a second 6 × 3 mm irregular hypoechoic mass was seen 3 cm from the nipple at the same clock position. In the left breast at 2 o’clock 2 cm from the nipple, there was a 7 × 2.4 mm irregular solid mass. The axillae were normal. The mammogram was assigned BI-RADS category 4.  

Ultrasound-guided core-needle biopsy of the dominant right retroareolar mass revealed tumor composed of both luminal epithelial cells and small bland myoepithelial cells surrounding pseudoglandular spaces filled with mucin. Immunohistochemical staining for p63 highlighted the basal (myoepithelial) cell component.

A 62-year-old woman underwent total hysterectomy in 2012 for benign uterine fibroids. Two years later, she noted a lump in the left supraclavicular fossa and was referred for evaluation.

On examination, a firm, non-tender 18 × 11 mm lymph node was palpated in the left supraclavicular area; her thyroid gland was unremarkable and vital signs were normal.

Thyroid ultrasonography showed a 6.9 × 4.7 × 3 mm hypoechoic nodule in the left lobe that was taller than wide, without microcalcifications, and with peripheral vascularization. Ultrasonography of the left supraclavicular region revealed a round, predominantly hypoechoic lymph node measuring 18 × 10.5 × 9.5 mm with intense hilar and peripheral vascularization and no calcifications.

Serum thyroid-stimulating hormone, free thyroxine, thyroglobulin antibodies, and thyroglobulin were within normal limits. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the thyroid nodule was reported as Bethesda category Thy 5 (suspicious for malignancy).

Because the lymph node’s ultrasound appearance was atypical for thyroid metastasis, an ^18F-FDG PET/CT scan was obtained. The scan demonstrated low FDG uptake in the left supraclavicular lymph node (SUV lbm max, 2.64) and higher uptake in a left latero-aortic lymph node (SUV lbm max, 4.72) and bilateral external iliac lymph nodes (SUV lbm max, 4.81).

A 43-year-old woman presented with a painless swelling of the right hard palate. Three years earlier, she had noted a small lesion near the second premolar, presumed to be a periodontal abscess; the adjacent tooth was extracted without resolution. Over time, the lesion gradually enlarged to approximately 4 × 3 cm. On examination, the swelling was soft and fluctuant, extending anteroposteriorly from the second premolar to the third molar; the adjacent teeth were intact and firm. An incisional biopsy showed fibrous connective-tissue stroma with a predominance of mucicarmine-positive mucous cells with pale, foamy cytoplasm intermixed with intermediate, epidermoid, clear, and oncocytic cells. Small gland-like structures, engorged blood vessels, and areas of hemorrhage were also noted.

A 37-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 5-year history of intermittent right knee pain aggravated by strenuous activity. He denied instability, locking, systemic symptoms, or weight loss. On examination, flexion was limited to 110° with moderate pain on further flexion.
