There was no swelling, effusion, or palpable mass. Routine blood tests were normal. Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the knee were unremarkable. MRI revealed a 16×15 mm encapsulated nodular lesion within the infrapatellar Hoffa’s fat pad, medially located. The lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images, showed a discrete hyperintense signal on T2-weighted images interrupted by hypointense punctuations, and demonstrated intense homogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. Bone and patellar tendon were uninvolved.

A 60-year-old man presented with generalized abdominal pain and anorexia for several days. The pain was moderate, predominantly in the left iliac fossa, and associated with nausea. He reported mild episodic pain over the previous month, managed with over-the-counter analgesics. He denied bleeding per rectum or weight loss. His surgical history included a right inguinal hernia mesh repair in 2015 and a hemorrhoidectomy two months earlier; there was no other significant medical, family, or social history.

On examination, he appeared pale. The abdomen was mildly distended, with tenderness in the left flank, resonant percussion notes, and sluggish bowel sounds. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin concentration of 7.4 mg/dL, a white-cell count of 15 180 /mm3, and a platelet count of 870 000 /mm3. An erect abdominal radiograph demonstrated air-fluid levels. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed an eccentrically located, heterogeneously enhancing intraluminal mass in the left iliac fossa acting as a lead point for intussusception and resulting in distended, fluid-filled proximal small-bowel loops.

A 6-year-old boy was evaluated for poor growth. He was born at term with normal birth metrics. At age 6 years and 3 months, his height was 107 cm (<3rd percentile), weight 15 kg (<3rd percentile), and growth velocity <4 cm/year. Laboratory tests revealed low IGF-1 (26.2 ng/ml; normal 52–419), delayed bone age, and peak GH of 2.6 ng/ml on provocation testing. He began GH replacement, with growth increasing to 1 cm/month.

After 10 months of GH therapy, he developed polydipsia and polyuria. Twenty-four-hour urine volume was 6200 ml; urine specific gravity 1.004; serum electrolytes and renal function were normal. During admission, he experienced palpitations and vomiting. Laboratory screening showed hypercalcemia (serum calcium >3.49 mmol/l) and elevated PTH (386.9 pg/ml). An ordinary urinary tract ultrasound was normal.

A water-deprivation test followed by arginine vasopressin administration confirmed central diabetes insipidus. Brain MRI demonstrated absence of the posterior pituitary bright spot and thickening of the pituitary stalk. Initial parathyroid ultrasound and SPECT imaging were negative. He was diagnosed with central DI and primary hyperparathyroidism and treated with desmopressin and calcitonin.

Eight months later, repeat neck ultrasound revealed a right upper parathyroid mass. Parathyroidectomy was performed, and histology confirmed a parathyroid adenoma. Postoperatively, serum calcium and PTH normalized, and his growth velocity improved modestly, but polydipsia and polyuria persisted.

A 72-year-old woman with a history of obesity, hypertension, and recently diagnosed moderately differentiated cholangiocarcinoma presented with a painless mass in her right breast that had been present for 1 year. She had no family history of breast cancer and could not recall her last breast imaging examination. On physical examination, there was a palpable mass in the lower-inner quadrant of the right breast without signs of inflammation or nipple discharge.

A diagnostic breast ultrasound revealed a 12 × 4 cm lesion that appeared consistent with a lipoma (BI-RADS 1). Given her oncologic history, she underwent further evaluation with chest computed tomography (CT), which demonstrated a solid, oval, well-defined mass measuring 10 × 6 cm in the same location; it had slightly higher density than fatty tissue, internal vascularity, and heterogeneous postcontrast enhancement. 

Breast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed an oval, well-circumscribed mass isointense to subcutaneous fat on T1- and T2-weighted sequences and signal suppression on fat-saturated images. After gadolinium administration, the lesion exhibited mild, delayed, peripheral enhancement, raising initial suspicion for a low-grade liposarcoma. The lesion was classified as BI-RADS 4, and an ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy was performed for definitive characterization.

A 35-year-old man with hypertension, hydronephrosis, kidney stones, and a desmoid tumor of the knee initially presented three years ago with fatigue, weakness, a 14-kg unintentional weight loss, and left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. Excisional biopsy of the lymph node showed replacement by small round cells with dense fibrous stroma. Immunohistochemical studies showed tumor cells positive for AE1/AE3, CK8, CAM 5.2, and CD99, and negative for desmin, EMA, S-100, germ cell markers (PLAP, HCG, AFP), neuroendocrine markers (chromogranin, synaptophysin), and lymphocytic markers (CD45, CD30, CD3, CD5, CD20, CD138, BCL2, BCL6). FISH for EWSR1 (22q12) break-apart was positive, confirming desmoplastic small round cell tumor (DSRCT). Staging CT showed extensive intra-abdominal disease with liver involvement and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. He underwent multiple lines of chemotherapy over 3 years with intermittent responses, and most recently presented with bowel microperforation requiring antibiotics and planning for salvage chemotherapy. A chest CT demonstrated multiple small bilateral lung nodules and a right pleural effusion. Thoracentesis yielded 1000 mL of clear yellow fluid with negative microbiologic studies. ThinPrep cytology showed a mixture of reactive mesothelial cells, macrophages, lymphocytes, and neutrophils, with rare cohesive cell clusters interpreted as reactive mesothelial cells. Cell‐block H&E sections revealed cohesive groups of cells in “floating island” formations, with central epithelioid cells having bland oval nuclei, minimally to moderately abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm with focal vacuolation, and an incomplete peripheral layer of bland elongated/spindled cells, some with hyperchromatic nuclei and others with preserved tinctorial chromatin similar to the central cells.

A 33-year-old G1P0 woman with a history of infertility presented at 13 weeks and 4 days of gestation for evaluation of heavy vaginal bleeding. Pelvic ultrasonography at that time showed a viable intrauterine pregnancy and a subchorionic hemorrhage. A routine anatomy scan at 19 weeks was normal. At 27 weeks’ gestation, an obstetrical ultrasound identified a large fetal abdominal mass compressing the liver and kidneys, with bilateral hydronephrosis and ascites. The sonographer could not determine the origin of the mass but favored a retroperitoneal source based on displacement of the abdominal organs. At 28 weeks, fetal MRI demonstrated a 9.4×6.8×8.6-cm heterogeneous intra-abdominal mass displacing the liver and kidneys, with restricted diffusion. The liver appeared heterogeneous, raising concern for metastatic disease versus multifocal hepatoblastoma. There was diffuse skin thickening and placentomegaly consistent with hydrops. A biophysical profile score was 2 of 8, and the patient was admitted to the high-risk obstetrical unit. Due to nonreassuring fetal heart tones, a cesarean section was performed. The neonate required intubation for oxygen desaturation. An emergent bedside ultrasound showed sliding of the liver over the mass with respiratory movements, suggesting that the mass did not originate from the liver. A decompressive laparotomy revealed a large tumor arising in the right abdomen and extending into the left side, with multiple nodules on the liver surface suggestive of metastases. Severe coagulopathy precluded biopsy or resection. The infant developed renal failure, refractory acidosis, and ventilatory failure, and support was withdrawn.

A 59-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of persistent hyperparathyroidism. Thirteen years earlier, she had undergone a 3.5-gland parathyroidectomy. Her medical history included autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease with bilateral nephrectomy, end-stage kidney disease managed by transplant (8 years) then dialysis (resumed), a subtotal colectomy for colorectal cancer, and a recent myocardial infarction.  
  
Yearly surveillance CT of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a new 1.5 × 1.3 cm pretracheal lesion abutting the aortic arch, not present on prior imaging. An endobronchial ultrasound with transbronchial needle aspirate (EBUS TBNA) was non-diagnostic. A PET scan showed a left thyroid mass, suspicious for malignancy, with adjacent FDG-avid uptake and an FDG-avid pretracheal node. Repeat EBUS TBNA demonstrated an oncocytic neoplasm; immunostains for TTF-1 and thyroglobulin were negative.  

On referral she was asymptomatic. Laboratory tests revealed a PTH of 1256 pg/mL (15–65), adjusted calcium 2.05 mmol/L (2.21–2.52), phosphate 2.32 mmol/L (0.81–1.45), free T4 19.9 µg/dL (12–22), and TSH <0.01 mU/L (0.27–4.20). A CT scan of the neck again demonstrated a large left thyroid mass with a differential of metastatic lymphadenopathy versus a parathyroid adenoma. An ultrasound‐guided fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid mass revealed a Thy3A lesion with no evidence of malignancy.

A 76-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of pruritic nodules that began around his right elbow and left flank and, despite topical steroids, progressed to involve approximately 75% of his body surface area, including the face. He had no systemic symptoms. Physical examination revealed no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Complete blood count, liver function tests, and renal function tests were within normal limits. Two skin biopsies (an excisional specimen from a right thigh nodule and a punch biopsy from a left flank lesion) showed well-circumscribed dermal nodules extending to the dermal–epidermal junction without epidermotropism. The nodules were composed of large histiocytoid cells with ample eosinophilic cytoplasm, pale polymorphic nuclei, and inconspicuous nuclear grooves. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated positivity for CD1a, lysozyme, fascin, CD14, CD4, CD43, LCA, CD56 (unusual), and variable S100, and negativity for langerin, CD163, CD68, OCT2, TdT, and other lineage markers.

A 52-year‐old woman presented with a 6-week history of an umbilical lump and 5 weeks of overlying redness, swelling, pain, and haemopurulent discharge. She had been treated for presumed infected umbilical hernia with 5 weeks of oral clindamycin, with initial improvement followed by worsening pain and discharge. Her history included endometriosis and hormone-responsive left breast cancer treated 4 months earlier with wide local excision, sentinel lymph node biopsy, and radiotherapy; she was awaiting bilateral oophorectomy and hormone therapy. Surgical history also included two diagnostic laparoscopies 10 and 12 years prior for endometriosis, complicated by keloid scarring (none visible now). She was a non-smoker, non-drinker, had a BMI of 30 kg/m2, and was allergic to penicillin (rash). On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs. There was a firm, tender, 3×2×2 cm umbilical mass with surrounding erythema and a small volume of haemoserous fluid. White blood cell count was 8×109/L (4.0–12.0), and C-reactive protein was 8.7 mg/L (<5.0). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed soft tissue thickening of the umbilicus of uncertain nature without intraperitoneal extension.

An 83-year-old man presented with a several-month history of gradually worsening motor weakness of both lower extremities, worse on the right, leading to gait disturbance. He also reported numbness of both lower extremities with dull thermal sensation below the inguinal region and nocturia. On examination, deep-tendon reflexes were increased bilaterally in the lower extremities, and Babinski signs were present on both sides. Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine disclosed at the T1 vertebral level an intradural extramedullary lesion that demonstrated homogeneous enhancement on gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted images. Associated findings included spinal cord edema extending from C1 to T8 and syringomyelia from C5 to T6. There were no flow voids on T2-weighted images.

A 62-year-old man with hypertension, chronic kidney disease, and treated prostate cancer underwent routine surveillance pelvic magnetic resonance imaging, which revealed a 14.3-mm submucosal mass in the low rectum. His screening colonoscopy 2 years earlier had been normal. He reported no mucous or blood per rectum, no change in bowel habits, and no abdominal or rectal pain. Flexible sigmoidoscopy was unrevealing, but endoscopic ultrasound identified a 9.8 × 10.9 mm hypoechoic lesion arising from the rectal wall and abutting the external sphincter. Because of its proximity to the sphincter complex, fine-needle aspiration was not feasible, and the patient was referred for surgical management. He underwent transanal excision of the lesion without complication.

A female infant was born at 32 weeks’ gestation. On day 2 of life, she was noted to have increased work of breathing and required continuous positive airway pressure. Family history was unremarkable. On physical examination, she appeared well but had a pedunculated mass protruding into the oropharynx from the nasopharynx; the otologic and nasal examinations were normal, and no other head-and-neck abnormalities were found. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head and neck showed a discrete mass in the posterior nasopharynx abutting the uvula and soft palate but not arising from the soft palate. On T1-weighted images, the mass was predominantly hyperintense, suggesting fat content. On short tau inversion recovery images, it was heterogeneous, and on T2-weighted images it was hyperintense. There was no restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging.

A 42-year-old woman was under routine surveillance ten months after total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, omentectomy, appendectomy, para-aortic lymph node dissection, and adjuvant chemotherapy for papillary serous ovarian adenocarcinoma. Surveillance abdominal CT demonstrated a cystic lesion in the midportion of the pancreas, which was confirmed on follow-up MRI. To assess for malignancy, endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration of the cyst yielded fluid containing malignant cells but did not identify the tumor’s origin. 

On referral, she reported vague abdominal discomfort but had an otherwise normal physical examination and unremarkable laboratory studies. At laparotomy, a 4×2-cm cystic mass was found confined to the midpancreas without local invasion or distant spread. Intraoperative fluid cytology again showed malignant epithelial cells without a definable primary source. Operative findings led to a spleen-preserving distal pancreatectomy.

A 47-year-old woman presented with progressive lower back pain for 1 year, fecal incontinence for 2 years, and urinary incontinence for 1 year. She had no history of pulmonary tuberculosis or diabetes mellitus. On examination there was local tenderness over the sacral region without palpable swelling or cervical lymphadenopathy. Routine hematological, biochemical, and thyroid hormone assays were within normal limits. Plain radiographs and cross-sectional imaging revealed a lobulated, expansile 6.5×5 cm mass involving the S1 and S2 vertebrae, encroaching the sacral canal and foramina and extending superiorly to the L5–S1 recess; on imaging, a diagnosis of chordoma was rendered. Sagittal MRI confirmed an extradural mass with spinal canal stenosis. A core-needle biopsy under imaging guidance showed follicles and acini arranged in a compact, back-to-back pattern. Keeping in mind this architectural pattern, a differential diagnosis of metastatic adenocarcinoma (e.g., breast, colon) versus follicular thyroid carcinoma was made on histology alone.

A 29-year-old Asian woman presented with one month of discomfort, pain, and horizontal diplopia in the left eye. She had no significant medical or surgical history; her only relevant family history was a maternal aunt with colon cancer. Routine laboratory tests were normal. On examination, there was left exophthalmos with mild limitations in abduction and supination, resulting in left-inferior strabismus.

Noncontrast CT of the orbits showed a spindle-shaped mass with a well-defined border and smooth margins in the left orbit, without calcification. After contrast administration, the mass enhanced intensely, and there was thinning of the lateral orbital wall adjacent to the lesion.

MRI revealed a 34 × 19 × 20 mm spindle-shaped mass on the lateral side of the left orbit, extending to the superior orbital fissure and involving both intra- and extraconal spaces. On T1-weighted images, the lesion was mildly hyperintense relative to the medial rectus muscle; on fat-suppressed T2-weighted images, it was homogeneously hyperintense with multiple intralesional flow voids. On turbo-spin echo diffusion-weighted imaging (b = 800 s/mm2), the mass showed mildly increased signal, and the minimum apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) of the solid portion was 1.3 × 10–3 mm2/s. The margin between the mass and the lateral rectus muscle was indistinct. Dynamic postcontrast MRI demonstrated early and persistent homogeneous enhancement. 

FDG-PET/CT showed mild FDG uptake in the lesion, with a maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) of 3.2.

A 61-year-old woman presented with a large perianal mass that had been increasing in size over the preceding year. She reported dull pain and discomfort in the right buttock region, without changes in bowel habits. Her medical history was notable only for prior cholecystectomy, thyroid nodulectomy for a benign nodule, appendectomy, and tonsillectomy. There was no personal or family history of neurofibromatosis. 

On examination, a firm, tender, well-circumscribed mass extended from the right perianal area abutting the rectal wall to the right gluteal region; the overlying skin was normal. Digital rectal examination revealed smooth rectal mucosa and an extraparietal palpable mass; anoscopy was unremarkable. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis demonstrated an 8.5 × 5.5 × 10 cm bilobed mass in the right ischiorectal fossa extending into the gluteal region and displacing the uterus to the right without bladder involvement; small (<10 mm) pelvic lymph nodes were noted, and abdominal organs were normal. MRI confirmed these findings. The radiological interpretation was that of a right ischiorectal lipoma.

A 31-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of intermittent, dull aching pain in the left leg. Over the past 3 months he noted a mild, nonprogressive swelling at the site. He denied trauma, fevers, weight loss, or other lesions.

On examination, the skin over the anterior left tibia was normal. There was tenderness and bony irregularity over the anterior tibia; knee and ankle motion was full, and distal neurovascular function was intact. Laboratory tests were within normal limits.

Radiographs of the left tibia showed a 7 × 3 cm multiloculated lytic lesion in the diaphysis with a sclerotic margin, areas of cortical thickening, expansion, and doubtful intralesional calcification; there was no periosteal reaction or cortical breach. MRI revealed a well-defined intramedullary lobular lesion with moderate endosteal scalloping, a focal geographic area of marrow replacement on T1-weighted images, corresponding high signal on T2-weighted images, and no soft-tissue extension.

A 39-year-old woman presented with progressive shortness of breath and a dry, nonproductive cough of 4 months’ duration. She had seen her primary care provider multiple times and was treated with antitussives without improvement. She denied fever, chills, night sweats, arthralgias, myalgias, or leg edema. Outpatient chest radiographs, respiratory viral panels, and laboratory tests had been repeatedly negative. Over the preceding weeks, she developed exertional dyspnea progressing to dyspnea at rest, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.  

She had undergone transthoracic echocardiography 8 months earlier for evaluation of a patent foramen ovale; the study had shown a normal atrium and ventricle. Two weeks before presentation, a chest CT scan performed in the outpatient setting showed a 4.6-cm mass in the left atrium and an enlarged left subcarinal lymph node.  

On arrival to the emergency department she was afebrile, heart rate 103 beats/min, blood pressure 95/63 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Examination revealed sinus tachycardia without murmurs or abnormal heart sounds, normal peripheral pulses, no jugular venous distension, and no peripheral edema. Lung auscultation disclosed bibasilar crackles.  

Laboratory evaluation showed a brain natriuretic peptide level of 303 pg/mL and a normal troponin level. Electrocardiography demonstrated sinus tachycardia at 106 beats/min. A repeat CT scan of the chest revealed a large intracardiac mass measuring 6.3 × 6.0 × 3.0 cm, centered at the mitral valve and extending into the left atrium, with persistent left hilar lymphadenopathy, diffuse ground-glass opacities, and pulmonary edema.  

Transthoracic echocardiography confirmed a pedunculated left atrial mass measuring 6.0 × 3.2 cm, attached to the left inferior interatrial septum, prolapsing through the mitral valve; the left ventricular ejection fraction was 55%. A transesophageal echocardiogram showed a large, echo-dense mass in the left atrium intermittently entering the mitral orifice.  

Differential diagnoses at the time were atrial myxoma, cardiac sarcoma (considering the hilar lymphadenopathy), or intramural blood clot, given the rapid growth rate.

A 31-year-old woman presented with a 7-year history of episodic palpitations, profuse sweating, and severe headaches. Over the same period, she noted a gradually enlarging anterior neck swelling without compressive symptoms or signs of thyroid dysfunction. Four years ago, she also observed a slowly enlarging midline swelling over her chin. She denied any family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, or similar endocrine disorders. 

On examination, blood pressure was intermittently elevated during evaluation. A firm, non-tender anterior neck mass moved with deglutition; a second midline submental swelling was palpable at the level of the hyoid. 

Laboratory studies revealed:
- 24-hour urinary metanephrines >10 000 µg (normal 25–312 µg) and normetanephrines 8791 µg (normal <600 µg)  
- Serum calcitonin 10 506 pg/mL (normal <11.5 pg/mL)  
- CEA 2750 ng/mL (normal 0–5 ng/mL)  
- Intact PTH 128 pg/mL (normal 11.1–79.5 pg/mL)  
- Normal serum calcium, phosphorus, and vitamin D levels  
- Mild elevations in SGOT, SGPT, and ALP; other labs unremarkable  

A high-resolution neck ultrasound showed:
- Right thyroid lobe: 1.5 × 1.8 cm well-defined hypoechoic nodule with calcifications  
- Left thyroid lobe: 1.9 × 3 cm hypoechoic solid–cystic nodule with calcifications  
- Midline submental solid–cystic lesion with internal calcifications

A 76-year-old man was referred for a left-eye pterygium that was suspicious for squamous cell carcinoma. He reported a one-year history of ocular redness and tearing without pain, discomfort, or photophobia. His medical history included diabetes mellitus, hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and coronary artery disease status post–coronary artery bypass graft; he denied any prior ocular history, trauma, or malignancy. On examination, visual acuity was 20/60 in the right eye and 20/100 in the left eye. There was no preauricular or submandibular lymphadenopathy. Intraocular pressures were 23 mm Hg OD and 22 mm Hg OS. Slit-lamp examination of the left eye revealed diffuse conjunctival injection and a large fibrovascular growth with conjunctivalization of the cornea from the 2:00 to 10:00 positions, thickest between 4:00 and 9:00, extending 6 mm onto the cornea; the lesion stained centrally with fluorescein. The presumed diagnosis was ocular surface squamous neoplasia.

A 54-year-old woman with a history of hypertension presented with chronic left upper quadrant abdominal pain for five months, progressively increasing in intensity. She denied fever, weight loss, or night sweats. She had no other chronic illnesses or relevant family history. On examination, she was afebrile, with normal vital signs. The abdomen was soft, non-tender, without palpable masses or splenomegaly. Routine blood tests, including a complete blood count, liver function tests, and tumor markers (CA 19-9, CEA, AFP), were all within normal limits. An abdominal ultrasound showed a 3.9 cm non-vascular mass at the upper pole of the spleen. Contrast-enhanced CT scan demonstrated multiple hypodense, well-defined cystic lesions in the spleen without features suggestive of malignancy. MRI further characterized a dominant cystic lesion measuring 55 × 45 mm surrounded by smaller cysts scattered throughout the spleen, with hyperintensity on T2-weighted images and hypointensity on T1-weighted images. Given her persistent symptoms, diffuse splenic involvement, and concern for complications, a decision was made to proceed with total laparoscopic splenectomy.

A 6-year-old African boy was evaluated for a 6-month history of dull, aching abdominal pain and a progressively enlarging abdominal mass, which worsened over the month before presentation. He had no past medical or surgical history and no family history of similar illness. On examination, he was hemodynamically stable. Abdominal palpation revealed an ill-defined, smooth-surface, fixed, nontender intra-abdominal mass centered in the abdomen and extending into the left upper quadrant, measuring approximately 8 cm × 10 cm. Laboratory tests, including liver and renal function, pancreatic enzymes, and tumor markers, were all within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed multiple adjacent, non-communicating cystic masses, the largest measuring 8 cm × 7.5 cm × 9.5 cm, lying adjacent to the head of the pancreas without a clear plane between the lesion and pancreatic tissue. The initial radiology report listed pseudocyst and duodenal duplication among the possibilities, whereas a senior radiologist raised the possibility of a lymphatic origin for the lesion.

A 70-year-old Indian woman presented with a 6-month history of an insidious, gradually progressive swelling of the left cheek, associated with intermittent dull aching pain. On examination, there was a hard, fixed, tender bony swelling with an ulcero-proliferative lesion in the left upper alveolus extending from the incisor to the upper premolar; cervical lymph nodes were not palpable. Vital signs were within normal limits.

A noncontrast CT scan of the face demonstrated a well-defined, dense, lobulated sclerotic lesion involving the left premolar and first molar alveolar process, with a bony protuberance along the gingiva. An incisional biopsy showed inflammatory exudates with reactive new bone formation, suggestive of a chronic abscess. She underwent wide local excision of the palatal mass and upper alveolectomy; intraoperatively, the maxillary sinus was inspected endoscopically and appeared free of tumor. Histopathology of the surgical specimen was reported as a chronic pyogenic abscess with marked nodular new bone formation. The postoperative course was uneventful.

One year later, she returned with recurrent swelling at the same site. Local examination revealed an ulcero-proliferative growth on the left hard palate, not crossing the midline. CT of the neck again showed a well-defined dense lesion of the left premolar and first molar alveolar process with gingival protuberance. A preoperative biopsy demonstrated epithelial hyperplasia with focal intra-epithelial inflammation and no malignancy; findings were described as consistent with a benign osseous, osteocartilaginous, or infectious lesion including sclerosing osteomyelitis. A total re-excision of the mass was then performed.

A 31-year-old man with a 10-year history of HIV/AIDS, poorly compliant with HAART, presented in November 2019 with three days of worsening dyspnea, an excruciating throbbing headache, photophobia, and spots in his vision. His symptoms had insidiously begun in July with dyspnea, a nonproductive cough, fevers, and chills, leading to an October hospitalization and empiric treatment for presumed PJP pneumonia. He improved briefly on HAART and trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole but was noncompliant, and symptoms recurred twice more with associated nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and a syncopal episode; he required supplemental oxygen but was never intubated.  
Past medical history included neurosyphilis and hypertension. On examination, he was tachypneic, mildly hypoxic, tachycardic, hypotensive, and had a supple neck with no palpable lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed elevated lactate, normal LDH, a CD4 count of 267 cells/μL, and an HIV viral load of 5.27 log copies/mL.  
Bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii and common respiratory viruses. Sputum studies showed no acid-fast bacilli, and urine histoplasma antigen and buffy coat smear were negative. Blood cultures were sterile.  
Chest radiography revealed retrocardiac atelectasis. A CT pulmonary embolism protocol showed no embolus or right heart strain but noted increased soft tissue density in the right lower neck with subcutaneous edema. Nuclear medicine imaging confirmed a low probability of pulmonary embolism.  
Urgent CT and MRI of the head showed no acute abnormalities. Lumbar puncture yielded clear fluid with normal protein, no pleocytosis, and negative studies for cryptococcal antigen, VDRL, treponemal antigen, fungal antibodies, and HSV and VZV DNA.  
Four days later, CT of the neck soft tissue demonstrated an enlarged heterogeneous right sternocleidomastoid muscle and a 7.4 cm heterogeneous right jugulodigastric confluent mass causing transient compression and complete occlusion of the proximal right internal jugular vein.

A 26-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of a growth in the floor of her mouth, with progressive alterations in speech and difficulty swallowing over the past 2 years. On extraoral examination, her neck appeared short and thick, producing a double chin appearance; no cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. Intraoral inspection revealed a smooth, non‐tender, 3×3 cm swelling involving the submental, submandibular, and sublingual regions, adhered to deep planes and displacing the tongue upward such that the soft palate could not be visualized; the overlying mucosa and the orifices of Wharton’s ducts were normal. Upon applying pressure to the submental area, the mass was displaced upward. Ultrasonography demonstrated a cystic area with echogenic material and internal echoes and no flow on color Doppler. MRI showed an encapsulated cystic mass without calcification.

A 63-year-old black woman presented with intense vulvar pruritus of long duration and, three months earlier, noted a purplish lesion with white striae. Her medical history included controlled hypertension; she denied hormone therapy use, smoking, or family history of gynecological cancer. On examination she was afebrile and well appearing. Vulvar inspection revealed a hypertrophic right labium majus with a 4-cm ulcerated purple lesion with hyper- and hypochromic spots near the vaginal fourchette. Inguinal lymph nodes were not palpable. Colposcopic examination and cytologic smear of the vulva showed intense inflammation without neoplastic cells. Bilateral mammography and transvaginal and transabdominal ultrasound were unremarkable. An incisional biopsy of the lesion demonstrated malignant intraepidermal neoplasia composed of large cells with karyomegaly, visible nucleoli, and clear cytoplasm; focal periodic acid–Schiff positivity was present, and black pigment was noted in some basal-layer cells.

A 63-year-old man with heavy tobacco use, COPD, and a history of a left breast leiomyoma presented with a nonhealing left breast “abscess.” He had undergone multiple incision and drainage procedures for a persistent 3 cm retroareolar mass. On examination, the left axillary lymph nodes were unremarkable; the nipple was not inverted but chronically distorted, indurated, and inflamed. Initial concern was for inflammatory breast cancer. Superficial biopsies by dermatology and surgery were equivocal. A diagnostic mammogram and targeted ultrasound revealed a 3.3 × 3.6 × 2.7 cm heterogeneous retroareolar mass. Ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy showed dissociated fragments of cribriform-like and papillary-like carcinoma. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated that the tumor was immunoreactive for CD117 (c-kit), CK5 (basal cytokeratin), and p40, with a low Ki-67 index of 38%; it was nonreactive for CD10 and was triple-receptor-negative. The pathologic differential diagnosis included breast adenoid cystic carcinoma and basal-like ductal carcinoma in situ.

An 86-year-old Asian man was referred for refractory pneumonia of the left upper lung field, unresponsive to broad-spectrum antibiotics. He had a 22 pack-year smoking history and a past medical history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus. On chest radiograph, there was consolidation in the left upper lung field with blunting of the left costophrenic angle. A chest CT scan showed consolidation in segment S1+2 of the left upper lobe with an air bronchogram in B3 and revealed a polypoid endobronchial mass at the B1+2 bronchus nearly occluding the apico-posterior segmental airway. Bronchoscopic examination confirmed a smooth-surfaced polypoid tumor with superficial capillary telangiectasia occluding B1+2 a+b, and the lesion was removed by forceps biopsy. 

Histologic examination (H&E) demonstrated a well-circumscribed solid tumor beneath bronchial epithelium, composed of small, rounded basophilic cells of uniform size arranged in cord-like and alveolar structures, with focal palisading. Immunohistochemical studies showed strong pan-keratin (AE1/3) positivity; CK7 positivity in luminal cells; p40/p63 positivity in abluminal basaloid cells; α smooth muscle actin positivity in myoepithelial cells; and negative staining for CK20, TTF-1, CD56, and synaptophysin. Ki-67 labeling was less than 1%.

A 45-year-old Maasai man presented with a 5-year history of pain localized to the tip of his left ring finger, with no preceding trauma or skin discoloration. He described point tenderness that worsened over time and was exacerbated by cold exposure. He had been treated empirically for gouty arthritis without relief.  
On examination, he was well-appearing with no systemic signs. The distal nail bed of the left ring finger showed focal swelling and sharp central tenderness without erythema. Applying pressure with a pinhead reproduced intense pain (Love’s pin test), application of a tourniquet reduced the pain (Hildreth’s test), and immersion in cold water provoked pain (cold test).  
Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 4.7 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 15.3 g/dL, platelets 280 × 10^9/L, creatinine 98 µmol/L, uric acid 492.6 µmol/L, and negative rheumatoid factor.  
A plain radiograph showed a small depression on the dorsal aspect of the distal phalanx without bony lesion.  
Magnetic resonance imaging of the left hand demonstrated a well-defined soft-tissue mass in the nail bed measuring 0.3 cm × 0.3 cm × 0.5 cm, isointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2/STIR sequences.

A 14-year-old boy presented with a 5-month history of intermittent headache, vomiting, and generalized weakness, accompanied by unintended weight loss. He denied palpitations or syncope. On examination, his pulse was 120 beats/min; blood pressure was 160/110 mm Hg supine and 150/100 mm Hg standing. Airway, cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, white blood cell count 12 200 cells/μL, platelets 225 000/μL, random blood sugar 116 mg/dL, creatinine 0.6 mg/dL, sodium 140 mEq/L, potassium 5.4 mEq/L, and calcium 9 mg/dL. Chest radiograph and thyroid function tests were normal. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia with tall T waves. Echocardiography revealed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy and an ejection fraction of 60%. Abdominal ultrasonography identified a 48 × 45 × 30 mm heterogeneous para-vertebral mass with cystic areas just above the umbilicus, suggestive of pheochromocytoma. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a well-defined, heterogeneously enhancing retroperitoneal para-aortic mass anterior to the inferior vena cava at the level of the inferior mesenteric artery origin and aortic bifurcation, consistent with an extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma. Twenty-four–hour urinary metanephrine excretion was 702.72 μg (reference range, 32–167 μg).

A 70-year-old man presented with 1½ months of constipation, bloody defecation, and pain during defecation. He had no significant past medical or family history. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL; blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin were normal. Digital rectal examination revealed a solid growth in the mid anal canal. Colonoscopy identified a polypoid solid mass at the lower anorectal junction. CT imaging showed irregular mural thickening of the anal canal with heterogeneous enhancement, measuring up to 4.5 cm; there were no lesions in the liver, lungs, or bones. He underwent abdominoperineal resection. Grossly, the 5 × 3 × 2 cm dark-gray polypoid tumor was located 2 cm from the anal margin; the cut surface was gray-white, firm to hard, with foci of ossification. Microscopy revealed sheets of pleomorphic spindle cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and prominent nucleoli in the lamina propria and submucosa, with abundant osteoid formation between tumor cells. No epithelial carcinoma was present. Immunohistochemistry showed tumor cells positive for stabilin-2 and negative for pan-cytokeratin (CK AE1).

A 74-year-old woman (gravida 3, para 2) with a history of ovarian dysgerminoma treated 39 years earlier by bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, hysterectomy, and radiation therapy presented with intermittent heartburn. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests including routine blood counts and chemistries were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed a 5 × 4 cm right retroperitoneal mass adjacent to the aorta and duodenum, with several enlarged paraaortic lymph nodes but no other organ involvement. Radiologic interpretations included gastrointestinal stromal tumor, ganglioneuroma, and other primary retroperitoneal tumors. The mass was surgically resected.

At gross examination, the tumor was a well-circumscribed ovoid mass measuring 6 × 5 × 5 cm; the cut surface was gray-white with areas of hemorrhage and necrosis. Histologically, the lesion consisted of polygonal cells arranged in sheets, with clear or eosinophilic cytoplasm, large round nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and interspersed lymphocytes.

Immunohistochemical studies showed tumor cells positive for D2-40, OCT3/4, and SALL4, and negative for c-kit, AE1/AE3, CK18, DOG1, S-100, HMB-45, and Melan A.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 38-year-old woman presented with a single erythematous nodule on the left helix associated with mild itching. She first noticed a small lesion three years earlier, which enlarged over three months, improved with topical therapy, and recurred on cessation; its size was stable over the past year. She experienced pain for four months but denied weight loss, appetite loss, fevers, night sweats, hemoptysis, hematemesis, melena, or other systemic symptoms.

On examination, vital signs were normal. She was moderately nourished, without lymphadenopathy. Cutaneous exam revealed a firm, nontender, well-defined erythematous nodule measuring 2.0 × 1.5 cm on the left helix; no other skin findings were noted. Routine laboratory studies were within normal limits. Initial clinical differentials included Jessner’s lymphocytic infiltrate, lupus vulgaris, leishmaniasis, and discoid lupus erythematosus.

A punch biopsy showed an atrophic epidermis with mild hyperkeratosis and a dense dermal infiltrate of medium-sized monomorphic lymphoid cells with round to irregular nuclear contours and blastoid chromatin extending into the subcutaneous fat without adipocyte rimming; no epidermotropism or angioinvasion was observed. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated lesional cells positive for CD3, CD5, CD8, and TIA-1 and negative for CD20, CD30, CD56, CD4, and Granzyme B. The Ki-67 labeling index was <5%. Polymerase chain reaction for T-cell receptor clonality was negative.

An 18-year-old girl presented with a 4-month history of a painful right-thigh mass. One month earlier she sustained a femoral fracture after being accidentally dropped. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable.

On examination, there was angulation and shortening of the right femur with tenderness and soft-tissue swelling anteromedially above the knee.

Initial radiographs of the right femur showed an osteolytic lesion in the distal diaphysis with a wide transition zone and periosteal elevation (Codman triangle). Three months later, repeat radiographs demonstrated a pathologic fracture of the distal femoral shaft with bone destruction and a bulky soft-tissue mass. A chest radiograph showed no pulmonary lesions.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the right femur revealed:
• A 6.0 × 3.7 × 13.3 cm soft-tissue mass with bone destruction in the distal diaphysis and a pathologic fracture  
• Intramedullary involvement extending to mid-femoral shaft  
• Multiple skip lesions in the L5 vertebra, right and left pelvic bones, and proximal femora  
• Heterogeneous contrast enhancement with central necrosis  
• Restricted diffusion in solid areas (ADC, 1.15–1.2 × 10⁻³ mm²/s) and higher ADC in necrotic zones (2.05–2.54 × 10⁻³ mm²/s)  
• Early enhancement with a mixed plateau pattern on perfusion imaging  
• Significant lipid–lactate elevation with unremarkable choline increase on MR spectroscopy

From MRI, two leading radiologic diagnoses were synchronous multifocal osteosarcoma and primary bone lymphoma.

A 30-year-old woman presented with a 12-year history of pain and swelling localized to her left medial malleolus. The pain was gradual in onset, intermittent, aggravated by walking, and relieved by rest and analgesics. She had sustained an ankle injury at the onset of her symptoms but reported no fever, weight loss, or other systemic complaints. Examination revealed a firm, tender 3 × 3 cm swelling over the left medial malleolus with normal overlying skin temperature. The swelling was noncompressible, nonreducible, and the ankle’s range of motion was full and pain free. There was no lymphadenopathy, and systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies were within normal limits.

Plain radiographs of the left ankle showed a well-defined, spherical, lytic lesion measuring approximately 2 cm in the medial malleolus. The lesion was non-expansile, eccentric, and without periosteal reaction or cortical breach. A chest radiograph was normal.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the left ankle revealed an intramedullary, lobulated, cystic lesion in the medial malleolus, sub-articular but without involvement of the tibial articular surface. The lesion was surrounded by hyperintense marrow edema, with no cortical breach, periosteal reaction, or soft-tissue extension, and the ankle joint and talar surface were intact. These findings suggested a benign bone lesion, most likely a chondroblastoma. Based on the clinical and radiologic data, the leading diagnostic considerations were chondroblastoma, giant cell tumor, and chondromyxoid fibroma.

A 13-year-old girl presented with 2 weeks of progressive intermittent holocranial headaches without behavioral changes. Brain MRI demonstrated a well-defined lesion adjacent to the floor of the third ventricle with minimal surrounding edema. In 2003, the lesion was resected and diagnosed as an intraventricular meningioma. In 2011, regrowth prompted repeat resection; histopathology was then interpreted as gliosarcoma, and she received 28 sessions of radiotherapy (total dose 50 Gy). Postoperatively, she developed diabetes insipidus and hypothyroidism, managed medically. Three months later, she experienced convulsive seizures. MRI in 2012 showed tumor regrowth in the hypothalamic region, and she developed psychomotor impairment despite preserved performance status (Karnofsky 90, ECOG 1). She was referred for a total transcortical resection guided by neuronavigation, and surgical specimens from the second and third resections were sent for independent histologic review.

A 62-year-old man with childhood-onset asthma and a remote smoking history was evaluated for an intractable cough of three to four months’ duration. His dyspnea remained well controlled on inhaled formoterol and budesonide, but his cough persisted despite the addition of theophylline and montelukast. He described bouts of cough with scant mucoid sputum, particularly when changing posture at night. He denied chest pain, hemoptysis, night sweats, or weight loss. His past medical history was significant only for asthma and gastritis; family history was unremarkable.  

On examination, vital signs were stable. Chest auscultation revealed slightly reduced breath sounds over the right lung and bilateral wheezes; the remainder of the systemic examination was normal. A chest radiograph was clear. Baseline hematological, coagulation, and biochemical studies were within normal limits, as was an abdominal ultrasound.  

To evaluate for possible bronchiectasis or pulmonary infection, a high-resolution CT scan of the chest was obtained. It showed upper-lobe centrilobular emphysema and an incidentally noted mass lesion in the truncus intermedius.

A 27-year-old morbidly obese African American woman, gravida 1, para 0, presented in her first trimester of pregnancy with progressive swelling of the right jaw and loosening of her teeth. She reported localized pain but denied fever, weight loss, or other constitutional symptoms. On examination, there was a tender swelling over the right mandible. An incisional biopsy of the lesion demonstrated mixed inflammation with numerous foamy histiocytes. To assess the extent of disease, a CT scan of the facial bones was performed and revealed a lytic lesion involving much of the body of the right mandible, extending into the mentum and crossing the midline to the left anterior mandibular body. Scintigraphy showed avid radiotracer uptake in the same region. Needle core biopsies of adjacent lymph nodes showed only reactive hyperplasia.

A 65-year-old man with asthma presented initially with several days of bleeding per rectum. Colonoscopy demonstrated irregular thickening with a slightly raised area in the proximal transverse colon. Biopsy was reported as neuroendocrine carcinoma. Abdominal CT showed a solitary mass in the proximal transverse colon without lymphadenopathy or other lesions. He underwent transverse colectomy, which revealed a 2.3 cm ulcerated, infiltrating high-grade malignancy positive for CD56 and focally positive for NSE, but negative for cytokeratins (AE1/AE3, CK20, CK7), synaptophysin, chromogranin A, TTF-1, HMB45, Melan A, S100, and CDX2. Nine months later, he re-presented with right shoulder pain and recurrent rectal bleeding. Whole-body CT showed multiple osteolytic lesions in the ribs, clavicle, and femoral shafts, and a large retroperitoneal mass posterior to the stomach and involving the duodenum that was presumed to be recurrence. Colonoscopy at the anastomotic site revealed a raised lesion. Biopsies showed small to medium oval neoplastic cells infiltrating the lamina propria without crypt destruction; the cells had round nuclei and prominent nucleoli without glandular formation. Immunohistochemical staining of this biopsy was negative for cytokeratins (AE1/AE3, CK8/18), chromogranin A, NSE, and synaptophysin. The tissue was exhausted without confirmation of the original neuroendocrine diagnosis, prompting retrieval of the initial tumor blocks for further evaluation.

A 25-year-old man presented with blurred vision and central metamorphopsia in his left eye of several weeks’ duration. He had no history of systemic disease or ocular trauma. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/200 in the left eye. Intraocular pressure and anterior segment examination were normal bilaterally. Dilated fundus examination of the left eye revealed a macular epiretinal membrane and, in the inferior retinal periphery, a circumscribed, amelanotic, reddish mass surrounded by hard exudates, with prominent feeder and draining vessels. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated a vascularized retinal mass that was hyperfluorescent in both early and late frames, with well-defined feeder and draining vessels. Optical coherence tomography of the macula showed an epiretinal membrane causing full-thickness distortion of the fovea, disorganization of inner and outer retinal layers, cystic spaces, and hyperreflective dots in the outer retina.

A 27-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of an insidious, progressively enlarging, hard swelling in the posterior region of the right mandible. She denied pain, discharge, fever, paresthesia, difficulty chewing, trauma, or local infection. On examination, there was a solitary, nonpulsatile, nontender, approximately 1.5 cm bony hard mass fixed to the right mandibular angle; the overlying skin was normal in appearance and not adherent to the lesion. Computed tomography revealed a well-circumscribed, hyperdense lesion with a lobulated surface at the right angle of the mandible. Three-dimensional reconstruction showed a pedunculated, homogeneous bony mass attached to the buccal cortex at the same site.

A 1-month-old male infant was brought with 10 days of redness and watering in both eyes. Since birth, he had multiple raised lesions on the scalp and trunk, more than six café-au-lait spots (>5 mm) and axillary freckles. His mother has neurofibromatosis type 1, and exome sequencing in the infant revealed a heterozygous pathogenic NF1 deletion. Under anesthesia, intraocular pressures were 34 mmHg OD and 28 mmHg OS, with horizontal corneal diameters of 11 mm OU. Slit-lamp examination showed hyphema and inflammatory membranes in both anterior chambers, preventing fundus view. B-scan ultrasonography of both eyes was anechoic with no optic nerve head cupping. Ultrasound biomicroscopy demonstrated diffuse thickening of the iris, especially of the posterior pigment epithelium.

A 47-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of progressive, intermittent abdominal pain. She had no personal or family history of familial polyposis or colorectal cancer. Physical examination revealed bilateral pitting edema and an elevated jugular venous pressure. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed an ill-defined, hypoattenuating solid mass in the small-bowel mesentery with slight displacement of adjacent loops and mild enhancement. The patient underwent surgical resection of the mass with right hemicolectomy. Pathology demonstrated a mass with clear margins, and the diagnosis was desmoid tumor. No additional treatment was administered.

Four years later, she returned with signs of small-bowel obstruction. Repeat CT showed a recurrent, irregular, solid hypoattenuating mass in the right lower-quadrant mesentery, adjacent to ileal loops, with proximal small-bowel dilation and little colonic gas. MRI demonstrated the mesenteric mass to be low in signal on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously bright on T2-weighted images, and showing slight enhancement after contrast. Over a 4-month interval, the mass had increased from 5×4 cm on CT to 8×7 cm on MRI.

A 35-year-old Hispanic transgender woman with HIV diagnosed two months earlier and HAART-naive presented to the emergency department (ED) with cough, subjective fever, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting for several days, and unintentional weight loss and malaise for three months. 

On her first ED visit, vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination showed laryngeal stridor, bilateral crackles, coarse breath sounds, and left lower quadrant tenderness. Laboratory studies revealed a platelet count of 74,000/μL, an aPTT of 36.3 seconds, sodium 129 mmol/L, and potassium 5.5 mmol/L; CBC and LFTs were otherwise normal. Chest radiograph showed no infiltrates. She was discharged with metoclopramide and esomeprazole.

Six days later, she returned with blood-streaked vomitus and stool, odynophagia, constipation, and generalized body pain. Vital signs remained normal. Examination disclosed epigastric tenderness. Fecal occult blood was positive; hemoglobin had dropped from 12.8 to 9.7 g/dL, hematocrit from 35.9% to 26.9%, and platelets to 43,000/μL. CD4 count was 8 cells/mm3. She was transfused one unit of packed red blood cells and admitted with presumed GI hemorrhage from a gastroduodenal ulcer. On the ward, multiple red maculopapular, nonpainful, nonpruritic skin lesions were noted on the back, thighs, and arms. Oral fluconazole was started for possible Candida esophagitis; a barium esophagram was unremarkable. She improved and was discharged on HAART and opportunistic-infection prophylaxis with outpatient GI follow-up.

Two weeks later, she returned with three days of nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and fever to 102.5°F. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, hematocrit 25.4%, platelets 86,000/μL, and sodium 126 mmol/L. CD4 count had risen to 20 cells/mm3 and HIV-1 viral load had declined. Blood cultures and other infectious studies were negative. An abdominal CT with oral and intravenous contrast showed severe thickening of the gastric antrum.

A 35-year-old Caucasian woman presented with four months of spontaneous, periodic bleeding from her umbilicus. The bleeding began two days before her menses and continued throughout her period; it was accompanied by pain and swelling at the site. She reported regular, heavy, painless menstrual periods, had two prior vaginal deliveries, no history of dyspareunia or infertility, and was not on hormonal contraception. She had no prior abdominal surgeries. On examination, a firm 2 cm × 2 cm umbilical nodule exuded a reddish-brown discharge. Suspecting infection, she underwent swabbing and completed a five-day course of broad-spectrum oral antibiotics, but at follow-up two months later her symptoms persisted. An ultrasound scan then revealed a 15-mm thin-walled cyst located approximately 5 mm below the skin surface at the umbilicus.

A 62-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of a slowly enlarging, mildly tender mass in the anterolateral aspect of her left distal forearm. She had no history of trauma, and the overlying skin was normal without adherence. She reported paresthesia and numbness over the dorsoradial aspect of the left hand, corresponding to the superficial radial nerve distribution. On examination, there was an immobile, nonpulsatile subcutaneous mass in the distal forearm. Percussion over the mass elicited radiating pain, and a positive Tinel’s sign was present in the superficial radial nerve distribution. Sensory testing confirmed hypoaesthesia in the dorsoradial hand. Electromyography and nerve conduction studies demonstrated an isolated sensory deficit of the radial nerve. Conventional radiographs of the forearm were unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging of the distal forearm showed a multilobulated, well-circumscribed mass with homogeneous low isointensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images.

A 76-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and hypothyroidism presented to the emergency department with intermittent left upper back pain for one year that acutely worsened over the past two days. She denied chest pain, dyspnea, fever, chills, or gastrointestinal bleeding but admitted to occasional heartburn and an unintentional 10-pound weight loss over six months. Four days earlier, she had flown into the area and reported a brief episode of pallor with weakness, lightheadedness, and nausea. She had no trauma history.

On arrival, her temperature was 36.9 °C, heart rate 90 bpm, blood pressure 101/76 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. She appeared mildly uncomfortable but non-toxic. Conjunctival pallor was noted. The lungs were clear; cardiovascular exam was normal. The abdomen was soft with mild epigastric tenderness but no guarding or masses. The back was atraumatic with no vertebral, paraspinal, or scapular tenderness and full painless range of motion. Neurologic examination was normal. A rectal exam revealed no gross blood.

Given the severity and chronicity of her pain with non-specific findings, pulmonary embolism, aortic dissection, aortic aneurysm, and acute coronary syndrome were included in the differential. A CT angiogram of the chest showed no pulmonary embolus, aortic dissection, aneurysm, or other acute pathology. CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast demonstrated celiac artery stenosis with post-stenotic dilation but no evidence of ischemia. Laboratory tests revealed a hemoglobin of 8.4 g/dL (normal 13–18) and hematocrit of 26.8% (40–52); the fecal occult blood test was positive. A bleeding peptic ulcer was suspected, she received IV pantoprazole in the ED, and was admitted for further evaluation.

A 61-year-old woman was evaluated for a gradually enlarging nodule on her back. Four years earlier, she had undergone total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid carcinoma. Two years after the thyroidectomy, a local recurrence was excised. Subsequent evaluation for thoracic pain with CT imaging revealed multifocal osteolytic lesions in the sternum and other bones, cervical, axillary, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and nodules in both lungs and both adrenal glands. Two axillary masses were excised; histology showed papillary architecture, and thyroglobulin staining confirmed thyroid origin. On current examination, there was a single, well-circumscribed, firm, nonmobile, painless soft-tissue nodule on the left paraspinal region of the back. The lesion was surgically excised and submitted for histopathological evaluation.

A 4-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of left upper eyelid ptosis and a superonasal orbital mass present since birth. He was otherwise healthy, and the parents denied any pain or change in the size of the lesion. On examination, uncorrected visual acuity was 20/30 in the right eye and 20/70 in the left eye. Mechanical left upper eyelid ptosis was noted secondary to a soft, non-tender, freely mobile superonasal swelling without overlying skin changes, pulsation, discharge, or tear reflux on palpation. Pupillary reactions were normal, with no afferent defect, and extraocular movements were full. Slit-lamp and funduscopic examinations were unremarkable. Autorefraction revealed +0.75–1.00 × 173 in the right eye and −8.75–8.75 × 31 in the left eye. B-scan ultrasonography demonstrated an anechoic, fluid-filled cavity with no internal echoes. Computed tomography of the orbits revealed a well-defined, hypodense cystic lesion in the medial extraconal compartment of the left orbit, with mild orbital compression and minimal adjacent bony remodeling.

A 57-year-old woman with a history of metastatic lung adenocarcinoma presented with increasing shortness of breath, weakness, and intermittent melanotic stools over several days. Four months earlier, she had developed left hip pain; imaging then showed cortical destruction of the lesser trochanter with a soft-tissue mass, and a chest radiograph revealed a large left lung mass. Laboratory studies at that time showed leukocytosis (19.3 × 10^9/L), microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 7.1 g/dL, MCV 71 fL), and thrombocytosis (595 × 10^9/L). Bone-lesion biopsy demonstrated poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma; immunohistochemical stains were CK7+, TTF-1+, CK20–, and GATA3–, consistent with lung origin. CT of the chest confirmed an 8.5 × 6.7 × 10.7 cm left upper-lobe mass with local invasion and an adrenal metastasis. Next-generation sequencing revealed BRAF V600Q and TP53 G245V mutations; no EGFR, ALK, KRAS, NRAS, ROS1, MET, PIK3CA, RET, or RB1 alterations were detected. She received palliative radiotherapy to the femur and two cycles of carboplatin plus pemetrexed.

On return to the emergency department, she was afebrile. Physical examination showed pallor and virtually absent air entry over the left hemithorax. Laboratory tests revealed a white-cell count of 80.2 × 10^9/L (92% neutrophils), hemoglobin 6.0 g/dL, and platelets 519 × 10^9/L. A guaiac test was positive. CT of the chest now showed explosive growth of the left upper-lobe mass to 14.5 × 10.0 × 17.4 cm with progressive mediastinal invasion.

A 73-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of right lower back and gluteal pain of 6 months’ duration that radiated down her right leg with associated numbness and tingling. The pain was minimally responsive to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents and gabapentin. She denied fevers, weight change, trauma, or prior surgery. On examination, there was tenderness over the right gluteal region and at the hamstring origin on the ischial tuberosity. Hip flexion reproduced her pain and was limited; there were no overlying skin changes or deformities, and neurovascular and motor exams were otherwise normal. Anteroposterior pelvic radiographs showed soft-tissue calcification overlying the right ischial tuberosity extending into the muscle belly. MRI of the right hip demonstrated a 6.9×3.1×2.7 cm well-defined, lobulated heterogeneous soft-tissue mass within the proximal hamstring tendon origin. The lesion was isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images with patchy areas of low signal, and postcontrast T1-fat-saturated sequences revealed intermediate signal intensity without surrounding edema. Cortical irregularity of the adjacent ischial tuberosity was noted on coronal and axial views. A CT-guided biopsy was performed; scout and axial images confirmed a lobulated calcified mass within the hamstring tendon origin with cortical irregularity of the adjacent ischial tuberosity.

A 62-year-old woman undergoing presurgical evaluation for resection of an olfactory groove meningioma underwent an abdominal CT in April 2009, which revealed a 2.9-× 2.5 cm round mass in the body of the pancreas with well-defined margins, avid homogeneous enhancement, and mild upstream pancreatic duct dilation but no lymphadenopathy or other lesions. Differential considerations included a neuroendocrine tumor versus a vascular abnormality such as an aneurysm or pseudoaneurysm. Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated a 2.2-cm, well-defined, solid hypoechoic mass in the pancreatic body, suspicious for a neuroendocrine tumor. Fine-needle aspiration at that time showed no evidence of malignancy but only changes of chronic pancreatitis. The patient was asymptomatic—her abdominal examination was normal, and she denied pain, weight loss, diarrhea, or constipation. A repeat CT in October 2013 showed mild interval enlargement of the mass to 3.0 × 3.0 cm. Endoscopic ultrasound in December 2013 confirmed a 3.2 × 2.8 cm hypoechoic mass with internal vascularity on color Doppler. Repeat fine-needle aspiration yielded only atypical epithelial cells. The complete blood count, metabolic panel, and plasma carcinoembryonic antigen level were within normal limits. Urine catecholamine metabolites were never checked presurgically as the patient exhibited no signs or symptoms of catecholamine excess, and metaiodobenzylguanidine scintigraphy was not performed.

An 8-year-old girl, previously healthy, was referred for evaluation of a painless, slowly enlarging swelling of the lower jaw. The lesion had been present for 3 years and was associated with loss of several teeth. There was no relevant personal or family history. On examination, there was a large, tender swelling of the mandible without sensory deficits. The lower third of the face was disproportionately enlarged, and her lower lip protruded with incomplete lip closure. Intraorally, a firm 50 mm, non-pulsatile mass was felt, causing displacement of adjacent teeth and malocclusion. 

A panoramic dental radiograph showed a poorly defined mandibular lesion with tooth displacement and root resorption. Subsequent computed tomography revealed a 34 × 43 mm, isodense, unilocular, destructive cystic mass in an eccentric position of the mandible, with cortical perforation, no peripheral sclerosis, and no internal trabeculation; the mass displaced the tongue posteriorly. 

Laboratory studies including serum calcium, parathyroid hormone, and phosphate were within normal limits.

A 7-year-old boy presented with a 4-year history of gradually worsening right distal forearm and wrist pain. There were no constitutional symptoms or sensory changes. Pain and limited supination (0–20°) interfered with daily activities and schooling. Examination revealed moderate tenderness over the distal forearm without visible mass or skin changes. Pronation was full (0–90°); neurovascular examination was normal. Routine blood tests, including inflammatory markers, were within normal limits. 

Plain radiographs of the forearm showed ring-and-arc calcifications in the interosseous soft tissues near the distal ulna metadiaphysis and remodeling of the medial distal radius; there was no cortical destruction or periosteal reaction. A benign chondroid lesion was initially suggested on X-ray.

Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-defined soft-tissue lesion deep in the forearm muscles. It contained signal voids corresponding to calcifications, was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2/STIR, and showed postcontrast enhancement.

A 65-year-old man presented with an abdominal lump and right flank pain of 4 months’ duration. He reported no hematuria or lower urinary tract symptoms. On examination, a hard, nodular mass was palpable in the right hypochondrium, epigastrium, and right lumbar region. 

Ultrasonography with Doppler study, contrast-enhanced CT scan, and MRI revealed an upper and mid–pole right renal mass measuring 20×16×10 cm, extending from the subdiaphragmatic area to the aortic bifurcation. There was associated retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Areas of doubtful fat density were noted within the mass. A tumor thrombus was seen in the inferior vena cava, extending from the intrahepatic portion to the right common iliac vein. 

On the basis of the imaging findings and caval involvement, a clinical diagnosis of renal cell carcinoma with venous extension was made.

An 84-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of pelvic pain that had significantly worsened over the past month. He denied changes in bowel habits or urinary symptoms. His medical history included conservatively treated bladder cancer, hypertension, and benign prostatic hypertrophy.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis showed a well-encapsulated, lobulated 5-cm mass posterior to the rectosigmoid colon, abutting the sacrum at levels S3–S5. The lesion had a heterogeneous appearance, with mixed fat attenuation (as low as –40 HU) and soft-tissue components, and no calcifications. Pelvic MRI confirmed macroscopic fat by high signal on T1-weighted images and signal loss on fat-suppressed T1 sequences. The soft-tissue component demonstrated low to intermediate signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images and avid enhancement after gadolinium. A thin, intact fat plane separated the mass from the rectosigmoid muscular layer, and there was no evidence of sacral bone or nerve-root invasion. The bladder wall was diffusely thickened, and no pelvic lymphadenopathy was present.

A 22-year-old Brazilian woman was referred for surgical treatment of achalasia. She reported a 10-month history of progressive dysphagia for solids and liquids, postprandial vomiting, nighttime sialorrhea, retrosternal pain, and a 15-lb weight loss over 6 months. She had no history of pancreatitis, abdominal trauma, or significant comorbidities.

On examination, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Cardiopulmonary findings were unremarkable. The abdomen was flat, soft, and non-tender, with no palpable masses or organomegaly.

Esophageal manometry confirmed type 2 achalasia. Upper GI endoscopy showed mild gastritis and initial Helicobacter pylori infection that cleared after eradication therapy. The patient underwent laparoscopic Heller myotomy. Intraoperatively, a mass involving the tail of the pancreas with firm splenic adhesion was noted incidentally.

Postoperatively, her esophageal symptoms improved. Before discharge, a contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan was obtained, revealing a 7.8×8.0×8.0 cm, well-demarcated heterogeneous mass in the pancreatic tail with both solid and cystic components, displacing adjacent structures.

A 78-year-old man with atrial fibrillation underwent an abdominal CT that revealed an incidental 2.2 cm mass at the capsule side of his left kidney. On noncontrast CT, the lesion was faintly hyperattenuating; on contrast-enhanced images, there was intense early peripheral enhancement with washout in delayed phases and a small internal cystic focus. The patient underwent partial nephrectomy. Grossly, the cut surface showed a central cyst surrounded by a solid, dark-brown area. Histologically, the lesion was composed of cells with oncocytic, eosinophilic cytoplasm lining cystic spaces and forming microcystic to tubular structures, with focal papillary areas and occasional dilated blood-filled tubules. Nuclear enlargement was present with only mild atypia, and the MIB-1 labeling index was about 1%. The tumor lacked a well-formed capsule, showed no invasion of surrounding tissue, and was staged as pT1a without vascular invasion. Immunohistochemical stains demonstrated diffuse, strong CK7 positivity and E-cadherin positivity, whereas c-kit, CD10, vimentin, and alpha-methylacyl-CoA racemase were negative.

A 20-year-old male college aviation student presented with chronic pain and a skin lesion on the left fourth toe. His symptoms began at age 7 while playing soccer, with intermittent pain when kicking. At age 15, he was diagnosed with verruca vulgaris and underwent two liquid nitrogen cryotherapy treatments without improvement. At age 20, he attempted self-excision of the lesion, noted significant bleeding, and cauterized it without resolving the lesion. He then saw a podiatrist who, during attempted wart excision, encountered bone under the skin and ordered radiographs.

On examination, there was a 3 × 5 mm ovoid, hyperkeratotic lesion with diffuse borders at the tip of the left fourth toe, immediately beneath the nail, without erythema or drainage. The toe tip appeared bulbous and was firm and nodular on palpation, eliciting sharp pain (8/10) on direct pressure. There was no tenderness on passive toe movement, and neurovascular examination was normal.

Plain radiographs of the left foot showed a pedunculated bony exostosis at the tuft of the distal phalanx with clear cortical and medullary continuity with the parent bone in a skeletally mature patient. Comparison views of the right foot were normal.

A 17-year-old woman was referred by her dentist for evaluation of a solitary, asymptomatic swelling in her left cheek of two months’ duration. She had no significant medical history, took no medications, and denied tobacco or alcohol use. On intraoral examination, there was a 1.5 × 1.0 cm, well-circumscribed, mobile, hard-elastic submucosal mass in the left buccal mucosa. The overlying mucosa and adjacent skin appeared normal, and the lesion was non-tender to palpation. An ultrasound scan of the area demonstrated a hypoechoic, homogeneous mass with well-defined margins. The patient was scheduled for excisional biopsy under local anesthesia.

A 2-year-old boy was evaluated for a gradually enlarging, circumscribed swelling over the left body of the mandible, first noted approximately 1 year earlier. The lesion was painless, although the child cried when it was palpated, and there were no other associated symptoms. On examination, there was a firm-to-hard, mildly tender, 4.0 by 2.5 cm mass over the left mandibular body. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck showed a soft-tissue mass eroding the underlying mandibular bone, suggestive of a neoplastic lesion. The complete blood count and routine biochemical tests were within normal limits. A tru-cut biopsy of the lesion revealed sheets of intermediate-sized mononuclear blast-like cells with round to oval nuclei, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, prominent nucleoli, and scant basophilic cytoplasm. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the blast cells were positive for CD45, CD68, and lysozyme and negative for CD3, CD20, CD99, TdT, MPO, and CD138.

A 4-year-old boy presented with a 2-month history of diffuse left-sided cervical swelling. Multiple eczematous lesions were noted over the swelling. On examination, there were firm, tender, slightly mobile cervical lymph nodes measuring 0.8 × 0.8 to 1.2 × 1.5 cm in the anterior neck on both sides. He also had left ear discharge for 2 weeks but denied fever or weight loss. There was no hepatosplenomegaly and no known tuberculosis exposure.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, leukocyte count 12 080/µL (45% neutrophils, 37% lymphocytes, 15% monocytes, 3% eosinophils), and a normal platelet count. The Mantoux test was negative. Bone marrow biopsy was unremarkable. A skeletal X-ray survey revealed no abnormalities.

PET scan demonstrated a conglomerate nodal mass in left cervical levels II, III, IV/V, and a supraclavicular mass extending to the superior mediastinum and left chest wall; no skeletal lytic lesions were identified. The thyroid gland appeared normal.

Fine-needle aspiration of the left supraclavicular swelling yielded a hemorrhagic whitish aspirate. Smears stained with Papanicolaou and Giemsa stains were highly cellular. They showed numerous atypical histiocytes, both singly and in loose clusters, that were binucleate or multinucleate with abundant dense cytoplasm and eccentric vesicular nuclei. The nuclei exhibited intranuclear pseudoinclusions and prominent indentations or grooves with a kidney- or coffee-bean appearance. The background contained lymphocytes, neutrophils, and a few eosinophils.

A 35-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of swelling in the left cheek region. On examination, there was a smooth, oval, 2×3-cm swelling of the left cheek that was diffuse, firm yet soft on palpation, and became more prominent when he clenched his teeth. Auscultation over the swelling revealed a mild bruit. Intraoral examination showed no mucosal discoloration or intraoral extension. Magnetic resonance imaging and angiography demonstrated an enhancing, well-circumscribed intramuscular mass within the masseter muscle. A provisional diagnosis of a vascular lesion was made, and the differential diagnosis of other soft-tissue lesions, including lipoma, neurofibroma, and pleomorphic adenoma, was considered and subsequently ruled out.

A 30-year-old woman, at 8 weeks’ gestation, presented with severe anal pain and an anal “bump” of a few days’ duration. She noticed a small amount of bright red blood on toilet paper and coating her stools and reported constipation; the pain was worse during and after defecation. Her history included irritable bowel syndrome, recurrent oral ulcers, and anal pruritus; her maternal relatives had inflammatory bowel disease. She denied anal intercourse, instrumentation, abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting.

On initial examination, an atypical fissure with heaped-up skin edges and a central ulcer was noted at the left posterior anal verge. A local anesthetic block and steroid injection were performed; she was prescribed topical lidocaine with diltiazem and fiber supplementation. Two weeks later, her pain recurred and the fissure’s appearance was unchanged. She was admitted for pain control, examination under anesthesia, and flexible sigmoidoscopy. The admitting differential diagnosis was new-onset Crohn’s disease versus a severe anal fissure.

On admission, vital signs were normal. Anal inspection revealed two large skin tags; digital rectal examination was not possible due to severe tenderness. Laboratory studies showed: WBC 3.9×10^3/µL, platelets 133×10^3/µL, hemoglobin 11.0 g/dL, hematocrit 31.5%, MCV 91 fL, and normal electrolytes. In the operating room, a large, deep anal canal ulcer was seen in the left posterolateral position without fistula or abscess. Sigmoidoscopy showed numerous aphthous erosions in the rectum and sigmoid colon, findings considered consistent with inflammatory bowel disease. Biopsies were obtained from the anal ulcer and rectosigmoid mucosa.

A 62-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of insidious, painless, gradually progressive protrusion of the left eye. He denied trauma, systemic illness, prior surgery, or diplopia. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/200 in the right eye and 20/50 in the left. Examination revealed a nontender, nonpulsatile, lobulated, firm mass in the left superotemporal orbit that did not change in size on Valsalva. There was a 2 mm horizontal and 4 mm vertical dystopia displacing the globe inferomedially, and left levoelevation was limited. Pupillary responses and funduscopy were normal. Systemic examination was unremarkable with no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Laboratory studies showed an ESR of 25 mm/1 st hour; all other blood tests, including an immunological profile, were within normal limits and the patient was immunocompetent. Orbital ultrasound B-scan demonstrated a low–internal-reflectivity mass in the lacrimal gland region. Contrast-enhanced MRI showed a well-defined soft-tissue lesion (3.2 × 1.6 × 2.4 cm) in the superolateral extraconal compartment of the left orbit with intraconal extension abutting the lateral rectus muscle; the lesion was isointense on T1, hyperintense on T2 with tiny hypointense foci, and exhibited progressive contrast accumulation with delayed persistence and diffusion restriction. A provisional diagnosis of left solitary encapsulated venous malformation with bilateral immature senile cataract was made, and the patient was scheduled for mass excision via lateral orbitotomy.

A 14-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a “cyst” on his right temporal scalp. He first noticed a bump several weeks earlier, and it had grown rapidly and become tender. On examination, there was a single, fixed, subcutaneous nodule measuring approximately 2.5 cm on the right temporal scalp. No overlying skin changes were noted. Palpation of regional lymph nodes revealed normal size and no tenderness. A noncontrast CT scan of the head was obtained. Imaging demonstrated a lytic lesion of the right parietal bone with full-thickness calvarial destruction, an associated periosteal reaction, and an adjacent heterogeneous soft-tissue mass in the right frontoparietal scalp. The ventricular system was normal in size, and there was no intracranial hemorrhage or infarction. The patient was referred to pediatric neurosurgery and scheduled for excision of the skull lesion.
