A 61-year-old woman with a history of invasive lobular carcinoma of the right breast (T1N0) treated with mastectomy and adjuvant anastrozole presented in November 2017 for routine follow-up. In April 2015, she had developed bone metastases to T6, L2, and the sacrum, treated with radiotherapy, zoledronic acid, and a switch from anastrozole to letrozole. She reported no respiratory symptoms, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable. 

Thoracic CT revealed a new 1.5 cm×1.5 cm subpleural nodule in the left lower lobe with a broad base against the pleura. 18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated that the nodule was hypermetabolic (SUVmax 14.9) with an ill-defined border to the pleura; known vertebral lesions (eg, T6) remained FDG-avid (SUVmax 9.9). 

Laboratory studies showed normal lactate dehydrogenase and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, with a mildly elevated β2-microglobulin (1.84 mg/L; normal 0.7–1.8 mg/L). Serologies for hepatitis B and C, HIV, and syphilis were negative. Bone marrow aspiration showed no malignant involvement.

A 69-year-old man presented with two months of rectal bleeding and pain. He had a history of chronic anal fissures and a remote basal cell carcinoma of the face, along with morbid obesity (BMI 33), hypertension, and a prior anti-reflux procedure. He denied tobacco use and had no family history of colorectal cancer. On examination, there was a large, ulcerated, fungating mass in the posterior midline of the anal canal. Laboratory evaluation showed a carcinoembryonic antigen level of 3.7 ng/mL (normal). Colonoscopy identified four tubular adenomas in the colon and confirmed a fixed, posterior midline fungating lesion extending into the anal canal. Staging MRI of the pelvis (rectal cancer protocol) demonstrated a 4.8 × 3.1 × 1.3 cm mass involving the internal and external anal sphincters without lymphadenopathy. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no distant metastases.

A 45-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 3, presented with a 20-year history of an itch, skin peeling, and pricking sensation of her right nipple. Over time the entire nipple darkened, ulcerated, produced a pus-like discharge, and ultimately the nipple was destroyed. She tried multiple topical medications without improvement. She denied breast trauma, tobacco use, and hormonal contraception; menarche was at 14 years, menopause 1 year earlier; no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. 

On examination, vital signs were normal; BMI was 30 kg/m2. The right nipple-areolar complex showed an eczematous ulcerative lesion measuring 2 × 4 cm with no palpable tenderness; a firm mass was palpable in the right lower outer quadrant of the breast; no axillary lymphadenopathy was detected. 

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography were unremarkable. A chest radiograph revealed multiple round “cannon-ball” lesions. 

Histologic examination of a punch biopsy of the nipple demonstrated clusters of large pale-cytoplasmic cells within the epidermis. A core needle biopsy of the breast mass revealed grade 2–3 infiltrating ductal carcinoma (Nottingham score 7/9), positive for estrogen and progesterone receptors and negative for HER-2.

A man in his early 50s presented with a 20-day history of gradually progressive abdominal discomfort and back pain, associated with early satiety, an unintentional 20-lb weight loss, dark urine, scleral icterus, and acholic stools. He had no prior medical or surgical history and denied tobacco, alcohol, or recreational drug use; his only medication was simethicone for abdominal discomfort. His family history was notable for metastatic lung cancer, undifferentiated leukemia, and breast cancer. 

On examination, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. He had scleral icterus and jaundice, as well as a diffuse, non-blanching petechial rash over the thighs, groin, lower abdomen, buttocks, and axillae. His abdomen was distended but non-tender, with no hepatomegaly or palpable lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory studies showed total bilirubin 23.7 mg/dL (direct 8.07 mg/dL, indirect 14.40 mg/dL), alanine aminotransferase 64 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 63 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 424 U/L, albumin 2.3 g/dL, and C-reactive protein 108.7 mg/L. Tumor markers were elevated (carcinoembryonic antigen 54.4 ng/mL, cancer antigen 19-9 60 721.9 U/mL). The white-cell count was 101.3×10^9/L with an absolute neutrophil count of 49.6×10^9/L and an absolute eosinophil count of 46.6×10^9/L.

Contrast-enhanced CT and MR cholangiopancreatography revealed a 6.2×3.7 cm low-attenuation mass at the splenic hilum, likely arising from the pancreatic tail, multiple hepatic masses (largest 6.1×4.5 cm), mild intrahepatic biliary dilation, and lymphadenopathy in the gastrosplenic and left paraceliac regions.

A 31-year-old woman with a 3-year history of Crohn’s disease, previously treated with azathioprine and intermittent prednisolone after ileocolic resection, presented with a 2-week history of abdominal pain and diarrhoea. Physical examination was unremarkable aside from mild abdominal tenderness. Laboratory studies showed no leukocytosis and normal renal function. 

MRI of the abdomen performed to assess enterocolitis demonstrated active inflammation of the small and large bowel and revealed an incidental mass in the inferior pole of the left kidney measuring 2.5×2.9×2.3 cm. On MRI, the lesion was slightly hypointense to renal cortex on T2-weighted images, isointense on pre-contrast T1, and exhibited a honeycomb appearance after contrast with irregular enhancing septa around small (1–5 mm) non-enhancing foci; diffusion weighted imaging showed restricted diffusion. A dedicated contrast-enhanced CT scan confirmed a well-defined, isodense mass pre-contrast that was homogeneously hypoenhancing in the arterial phase with cystic non-enhancing foci in the portal venous and delayed phases; there was no calcification, adenopathy, perinephric stranding, or vascular invasion. On renal ultrasound, the lesion was slightly hypoechoic with no demonstrable internal vascularity.

A 44-year-old woman underwent an abdominopelvic ultrasound as part of a routine health check. She was asymptomatic, denying pelvic pain, gynecologic symptoms, fever, fatigue, or weight loss, and had no relevant family history. Initial ultrasound revealed multiple uterine fibroids and a mass on the right side of the uterus, suspected to be an ovarian tumor. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed an oval, well-defined, heterogeneous hypoechoic solid mass measuring 42×39×25 mm within the right pelvic fascia between the uterus and the iliac vessels, with peripheral hypervascularity on color Doppler. No free fluid was present in the recto-uterine pouch. Physical examination revealed no palpable lymphadenopathy in the cervical, axillary, or inguinal regions. Laboratory studies, including CA-125 and CA-19.9, were within normal limits, and a chest radiograph was unremarkable. Pelvic MRI at 3.0 Tesla confirmed a well-circumscribed mass in the right extraperitoneal space that was nearly isointense to the uterine wall on T1- and T2-weighted images, with relatively heterogeneous enhancement following gadolinium administration. Multiple uterine fibroids were again noted, and no other masses or lymphadenopathy were identified.

An 81-year-old man with severe COPD on home oxygen presented with mucosuria, urinary frequency, and nocturia. On digital rectal examination, the prostate felt benign and was approximately 60 cc in size. His prostate-specific antigen level was 0.38 ng/mL. Nineteen months earlier, he had undergone transurethral resection of a 2.5 cm pT1 urothelial carcinoma at the bladder dome. Two surveillance urine cytology examinations, at 5 and 2 months before presentation, were negative for malignant cells. On recent cystoscopy, the bladder mucosa appeared normal, but there was white fibrinous material emanating from the prostatic urethra and median lobe; no discrete bladder mass was observed. Prostatic enlargement consistent with benign prostatic hyperplasia was noted, and the patient underwent a greenlight photoselective vaporization followed by bipolar transurethral resection of the prostate. During resection, after vaporization of the median lobe, a white fibrinous exudate near the verumontanum was encountered. Deep to this material, a papillary lesion was visualized and resected.

A 61-year-old man with a history of macrocytic anemia, neutropenia, and a confirmed somatic UBA1 (p.Met41Thr) mutation underwent reduced-intensity allo-HSCT for VEXAS syndrome with busulfan/fludarabine conditioning and ATG, tacrolimus, and methotrexate prophylaxis. On day +46 he developed acute skin and upper-GI GVHD treated with corticosteroids. By day +100, donor chimerism was 80% lymphoid and 97% myeloid, with no residual autoinflammatory symptoms. At day +175 post-transplant, he noted a 1 × 1 × 0.5 cm raised, nonblanching, firm, violaceous, asymptomatic lesion on the buccal gingiva adjacent to teeth 43 and 44. A periapical radiograph showed no mandibular bone or tooth-root changes. Based on the clinical presentation, the differential diagnosis included myeloid sarcoma, giant cell granuloma, or pyogenic granuloma. An incisional biopsy was performed.

A 3-year-old girl was brought by her parents for evaluation of a swelling on the left side of her face noticed over several weeks. On extraoral examination, there was mild asymmetry and a firm swelling over the left mandibular region. Intraorally, the left mandibular mucosa was elevated by a smooth, firm mass; all deciduous teeth were present and intact. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated a well-defined, unilocular radiolucent lesion in the posterior left mandible with scattered radiopaque foci predominantly in its center; the unerupted first permanent mandibular molar was displaced inferiorly. An axial CT scan confirmed a well-circumscribed unilocular radiolucent lesion with a radiopaque center in the posterior left mandible. The clinical impression was of an odontogenic lesion. Under general anesthesia, the second primary mandibular molar was extracted and the lesion, which was adherent to the permanent molar, was enucleated with curettage of the surrounding bone.

A 14-year-old boy presented with a one-month history of progressive paraplegia. Two months earlier, he had developed low back pain radiating to his left lower limb; according to his family, he then became acutely paraplegic. He also had a longstanding history of urinary and stool retention. His past medical and surgical history was otherwise unremarkable.

On examination, he was alert and oriented, with intact cranial nerves. Power was 5/5 in the upper limbs; the lower limbs were paraplegic with preserved sensation and proprioception. Reflexes in the lower limbs were absent.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the entire spine revealed a large left-sided space-occupying lesion at the D12–L1 level extending into the left neural foramen and paraspinal area. On T2-weighted sagittal images the lesion was hypointense; on T1-weighted axial images it was hyperintense, with mass effect on the spinal cord and extension into the retroperitoneal and pleural cavities.

The patient underwent a left D12–L1 hemilaminectomy and resection of the spinal tumor. Intraoperatively, the mass was noted to be highly vascular. Good decompression of the cord and roots was achieved, and the surgeon reported complete removal of the lesion without complications.

On postoperative day 2, CT and MRI of the dorso-lumbar spine confirmed total excision of the mass at D12–L1 with spinal cord decompression and only minimal left-sided fluid collection.

An 81-year-old Japanese woman presented with chest pain at rest for one month. She had a history of papillary thyroid carcinoma treated surgically 30 years earlier and was followed for psychiatric problems and hypothyroidism. On admission, blood pressure was 125/81 mm Hg, heart rate 78 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Physical examination revealed no heart murmurs, jugular venous distention, or pedal edema. An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with an incomplete right bundle branch block. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a heterogeneous, irregular mass–like lesion measuring approximately 45×40 mm on the right ventricular free wall, contacting the tricuspid valve in diastole, with a small pericardial effusion. Transesophageal echocardiography showed part of the mass was mobile. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed a 51 mm lobular mass involving the right ventricle and pericardium with heterogeneous enhancement. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed the mass to be isointense on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images. 18-Fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography demonstrated increased uptake in the anterior lower wall of the right ventricle without evidence of metastasis. Coronary angiography showed normal coronary arteries and an arterial branch supplying the mass.

A 22-year-old man presented with a 4-year history of slowly progressive right-sided hearing loss without symptoms of otitis. He had no significant medical history, no tobacco or alcohol use, and no family history of genetic disorders. On examination, vital signs were normal. Otoscopic inspection revealed a pale, firm mass arising from the inferior wall of the right external auditory canal that completely occluded the canal. Neurologic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and basic metabolic panel, were within normal limits. A CT scan of the temporal bone showed a well-circumscribed soft-tissue mass narrowing most of the external auditory canal, originating from the inferior canal wall in the cartilaginous portion, with no bone erosion and no involvement of the middle ear or mastoid.

A 64-year-old African-Ugandan woman presented with a 1-week history of colicky abdominal pain and partial constipation. One day before admission, she noted mucoid, blood-tinged stools and was unable to pass flatus. She described a 1-year history of intermittent left-sided abdominal ache—cramp-like after meals—with progressive bloating, flatulence, and pellet-like stools; her appetite and weight remained stable. She had a total abdominal hysterectomy 5 years earlier but no other chronic illnesses. On examination, she was afebrile and moderately dehydrated; pulse 82 bpm, blood pressure 115/80 mmHg. The abdomen was grossly distended, tympanitic, with reduced bowel sounds and mild generalized tenderness but no peritoneal signs. Rectal examination revealed an empty rectum with small amounts of bloody mucoid stool. A diagnosis of large-bowel obstruction, presumed secondary to intussusception, was made, and she was taken for exploratory laparotomy.

A 20-year-old man noted asymptomatic scalp lesions for 60 days, which gradually enlarged; new lesions then appeared on the face and trunk. Dermatologic examination revealed nodules and firm, erythematous, infiltrated plaques of varying size on the scalp, left ear, brow, chin, cheeks, right shoulder, left lumbar region, and presternal area. Initial clinical hypotheses included cutaneous lymphoma, Sweet’s syndrome, mycosis fungoides, sarcoidosis, and leprosy. Excisional biopsies of lesions on the right shoulder and left lumbar region showed an infiltrate of immature neoplastic hematolymphoid cells with an interstitial, perivascular, periadnexal, and subcutaneous pattern and numerous mitoses. Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated CD3+, CD4+, CD5+, CD7+, CD8+, CD10+, Ki-67+, TdT+, and CD79A+ staining.

A 79-year-old woman presented with abdominal distention and constipation. Five years earlier, she had undergone an open total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for endometrial serous carcinoma (T1aN0M0, Stage IA with lymph vascular invasion) but did not return for follow-up. On examination, she had abdominal tenderness. Laboratory tests showed a CRP level of 7.9 mg/dL; carcinoembryonic antigen was 3.4 ng/mL and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 was 39.2 U/mL. Enhanced abdominal CT revealed irregularly enhanced wall thickening in the sigmoid colon with regional lymph node enlargement and proximal bowel dilatation. PET–CT demonstrated uptake in the sigmoid colon tumor (SUVmax 9.49) and in two pelvic peritoneal lesions (SUVmax 3.85), with no liver or lung metastases. Colonoscopy showed circumferential stenosis of the sigmoid colon, and two self-expanding metal stents were placed across the obstruction. Biopsy of the lesion revealed a moderately differentiated tubular adenocarcinoma, and the working diagnosis was colon cancer cT3N0M1c, Stage IVc.

A 52‐year‐old man presented with a 1-week history of upper abdominal fullness without pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, hematemesis, melena, or changes in bowel habits. Gastroscopy revealed a sessile mucosal elevation on the anterior wall of the lower gastric body with normal overlying mucosa. A 20-MHz endoscopic ultrasound probe demonstrated a 10.34×7.06 mm hypoechoic mass in the third (submucosal) layer, with uniform internal echoes, distinct margins, and intact remaining layers. Abdominal CT showed an ~8 mm nodular elevation on the greater curvature of the gastric body with mild continuous enhancement and no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests revealed a positive fecal occult blood test; CBC, coagulation profile, renal function, and tumor markers (chromogranin A, CEA, CA 19-9) were within normal limits. There was no family history of gastrointestinal malignancy. A provisional diagnosis of a gastric space-occupying lesion was made.

A 15-year-old girl presented with dull pain in the right maxillary second molar region. A general dentist had performed root canal treatment and prescribed amoxicillin 2 g daily for one week without improvement. She also reported numbness of the right lower lip. Oral examination showed gingival swelling around the right maxillary molars extending onto the right palatal mucosa. There were no apparent lesions of the lower lip. A panoramic radiograph was unremarkable. Owing to persistent symptoms and nonresponse to dental treatment, a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the maxillofacial region was obtained, revealing a solid mass in the right maxilla with strong contrast uptake, osteolysis, and destruction of the floor of the right maxillary sinus.

A 33-year-old woman with neurofibromatosis type 1, hypothyroidism, epilepsy, and learning difficulties presented with a longstanding history of bilateral nipple “skin tags.” She had no family history of neurofibromatosis. On examination, each nipple-areolar complex bore pedunculated, polypoid, fleshy lesions: the right measured 60 × 55 × 35 mm and the left 25 × 25 × 25 mm. 

Microscopic examination showed dermal proliferations of bland spindle-shaped cells with elongated wavy nuclei, with no atypia, pleomorphism, necrosis, or mitotic activity. The spindle-cell proliferation extended close to a mammary duct but did not arise from breast parenchyma; smooth muscle fibers of the nipple were intermingled. 

Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated strong positivity for S100 protein and neurofilament in the spindle cells and negativity for cytokeratins AE1/3 and p63. Desmin and smooth muscle myosin highlighted abundant smooth muscle bundles within the lesion.

A 43-year-old woman presented with a 3–4-month history of a left adnexal cyst and foul-smelling vaginal discharge. She had hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. Vital signs were normal, and the abdominal examination was unremarkable. Pelvic ultrasonography performed for the adnexal cyst incidentally revealed a well-defined, approximately 9 cm hypoechoic lesion in the right hepatic lobe. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 9 × 8.7 × 8.4 cm well-circumscribed hypodense mass in segments VI and VIII of the liver, with arterial-phase enhancement and a central nonenhancing component, followed by progressive enhancement in the portal venous phase. On imaging, focal nodular hyperplasia was initially favored. The patient was admitted and underwent right hemihepatectomy.

A 67-year-old Iranian man presented with a 3-month history of weakness and epigastric pain. On examination, his blood pressure was 115/80 mm Hg and pulse rate was 88 beats per minute; no other abnormalities were noted. Laboratory studies revealed severe anemia (hemoglobin, 3 g/dL), a serum iron level of 65 μg/dL, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 65 mm/h. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a suspicious collection at the lesser omentum. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated an 81 × 73 mm polypoid mass involving the gastric antrum and duodenum, as well as a 54 × 45 mm enhancing lesion in the left posterior mediastinum suggestive of lymphadenopathy. Gastroendoscopy revealed a large, pedunculated duodenal mass. Endoscopic biopsy identified a poorly differentiated malignant neoplasm, suggestive of an epithelioid gastrointestinal stromal tumor, but was deemed inconclusive. The patient underwent total gastrectomy with gastrojejunostomy. Gross examination showed a brownish, polypoid tumor in the duodenum. On hematoxylin and eosin staining, the tumor was highly pleomorphic, composed of bizarre eosinophilic, round, and spindle cells with apparent skeletal muscle differentiation, extending into the submucosa without lymphovascular invasion. Based on morphology alone, the differential diagnoses included lymphoma, mucosal melanoma, undifferentiated carcinoma, epithelioid GIST, and sarcoma. Immunohistochemical stains and molecular studies are pending.

A 70-year-old woman presented with a 10-month history of cough that was initially dry and later productive of white, sticky sputum. She denied fever, chills, hemoptysis, or chest pain. She had no significant past medical history, was a non-smoker, and her family and social histories were unremarkable. Physical examination was normal. Routine laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits.

Four months after symptom onset, chest CT revealed a 5.0 × 2.6 cm irregular patchy shadow in the right lower lobe with obstruction of the superior segment bronchus. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy showed jelly-like material obstructing that bronchus, and bronchoscopic biopsy did not demonstrate malignant cells. The patient was managed conservatively, and six months later a repeat chest CT showed an enlarging irregular mass measuring 5.2 × 2.9 cm in the same location. Subsequent 18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated focal high FDG uptake in the proximal portion of the mass (SUVmax 5.1), with no increased uptake distally. Based on imaging and growth, a clinical diagnosis of pulmonary malignancy was made.

A male Indian adolescent in his mid-teens presented with a brownish lesion in the right eye. The lesion had been present since childhood as a pin-head sized spot and showed progressive enlargement over the past 2 years. There was no history of prior surgical intervention. On examination, the pigmented lesion measured approximately 20 × 12 mm, involved nearly the entire temporal bulbar conjunctiva, and encroached on the temporal limbus; the fornices and lateral canthus were spared. Multiple cystic spaces were visible on the surface of the lesion. Anterior-segment optical coherence tomography showed cystic spaces within the conjunctiva and no involvement of the sclera.

A 73-year-old man presented after a fall with headaches and memory loss over the past year. His medical history included hypertension, hypothyroidism, and prostate cancer treated 22 years earlier. On examination, he was mildly confused but had no focal neurologic deficits. Noncontrast CT of the head showed a well-circumscribed, partially hemorrhagic mass in the left temporal–occipital region causing effacement of the occipital horn and atrium of the left lateral ventricle and trapping of the temporal horn. MRI of the brain demonstrated a heterogeneously enhancing mass with mixed cystic and solid components. At this time, a differential diagnosis of glioblastoma multiforme or metastasis was proposed. A metastatic workup with CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, however, was unremarkable. The patient and his family elected to proceed with a stereotactic biopsy for tissue diagnosis.

A 16-year-old girl presented to the orthopedic clinic with a one-month history of swelling of the right middle finger and occasional pain. The swelling had progressively increased in size. On examination, the middle phalanx was diffusely swollen with mild tenderness and there were no overlying skin lesions. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, were normal. Plain radiographs of the right middle finger showed an expansile lesion of the middle phalanx with thinning of the cortex and intralesional calcifications. A CT scan demonstrated a central, oval area of geographic destruction in the medullary canal at the metaphyseal region of the middle phalanx, with dystrophic calcifications, bulbous expansion of the bone, cortical thinning, and no soft-tissue involvement. Considering her age and the radiological features, a diagnosis of enchondroma was made.

An 18‐year‐old woman presented with a 2-month history of headache and numbness above her right eye that was refractory to medical management. Neurologic examination revealed facial paresthesia in the distribution of the right ophthalmic (V1) division of the trigeminal nerve; the remainder of the cranial-nerve and general neurologic examination was normal. There was no evidence of endocrine dysfunction, and her medical history was unremarkable. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the head showed an ill-defined, enhancing lesion in the infrasellar region extending into the sella and suprasellar compartment, with displacement of the pituitary gland. The mass involved the superficial clivus, bilaterally encased the cavernous sinuses and internal carotid arteries, extended anteriorly into the ethmoidal air cells, and reached the prepontine cistern posteriorly. 

Gadolinium-enhanced MRI demonstrated a large sellar mass that was hypointense on T1- and T2-weighted images with moderate heterogeneous enhancement.

A 3-month-old girl was referred for evaluation of a right mandibular-angle swelling noted by her mother. The mass was soft, noncompressible, without overlying skin changes, more prominent in the evening, and had gradually increased in size. The patient was afebrile and asymptomatic. Laboratory studies showed normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate, normal C-reactive protein level, and normal white-blood-cell count. Ultrasound of the neck demonstrated a large, polylobulated, hypoechoic lesion replacing most of the right parotid gland, with relatively homogeneous internal echotexture, fine hyperechoic septa, multiple coarse intralesional vessels, and marked vascularity on color Doppler. A vascular peduncle was visible at the lesion’s base. A second, smaller lesion with identical sonographic features lay adjacent to the main mass. The left parotid gland appeared normal, and there were no cervical lymphadenopathies.

A 69-year-old Asian man with end-stage renal disease underwent a living-donor kidney transplant nine years earlier and has been maintained on mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus, and low-dose prednisone. He presented with acute encephalopathy and respiratory failure immediately after a witnessed tonic-clonic seizure. Over the preceding month he had episodes of confusion, right-sided twitching, and intermittent speech disturbance described as possible aphasia. One month earlier, he had a fall with a witnessed seizure; head CT was unremarkable but brain MRI demonstrated multiple lesions, and CSF studies were positive for Epstein-Barr virus. On admission, he was afebrile, blood pressure was 130/71 mmHg, pulse 66/min, and respirations 20/min. Lung and cardiac examinations were normal. Neurologic examination after sedation revealed no movement of the right extremities in response to pain. Repeat head imaging showed multifocal parenchymal hemorrhages with surrounding edema and a 5 mm midline shift. Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics and antivirals were started. A whole-body PET scan demonstrated hypermetabolic lesions confined to the central nervous system. Over the next several days, he developed worsening confusion, apraxia, gaze deviation, and right flaccid hemiparesis. Given this progression in an immunosuppressed transplant recipient, the leading considerations were vasculitis, infection, and central nervous system lymphoma.

An 85-year-old woman presented with a painful perianal mass first noted 1 year earlier, which had increased in size. Her medical history included hypertension, angina, and an indeterminate pulmonary nodule detected 3 years ago. On examination, there was a 7.0×3.5 cm exophytic erythematous nodule in the perianal area, some of which was covered with whitish discharge and crusts. 

A biopsy specimen revealed epidermal invaginations and papillary projections lined by a two-layered epithelium with underlying stromal plasma cell infiltrates. Tumor cells forming tubular structures demonstrated nuclear atypia and mitotic figures, and pagetoid cells were present in the overlying epidermis. 

Immunohistochemical staining was positive for periodic acid–Schiff, cytokeratin 7, epithelial membrane antigen, carcinoembryonic antigen, and cytokeratin 5/6, and negative for p63 and gross cystic disease fluid protein 15. The proliferation index (Ki-67) exceeded 50%. 

Routine laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, chemistry panel, and tumor markers (total prostate-specific antigen, alpha-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and carbohydrate antigen 19-9), were within normal limits. Abdominal computed tomography and fluorodeoxyglucose–PET showed no evidence of locoregional or distant metastasis beyond the known pulmonary nodule.

A 19-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of pain, progressive swelling, and facial asymmetry of the left lower face. She denied trauma. Examination revealed a diffuse, tender, bony-hard swelling of the left mandible extraorally. Intraorally, there was swelling of the left mandibular gingiva extending buccally and lingually, with a sunken first molar and a half-sunken second molar; no caries were noted.  
Panoramic radiograph showed a well-defined, relatively round, radiopaque mass measuring approximately 4.5 cm in greatest diameter, partially surrounded by a thin radiolucent halo, in contact with the roots of five teeth from the first premolar to the third molar in the left mandible.  
Unenhanced CT of the mandible demonstrated a 4.40 × 4.02 × 4.75 cm radiopaque mixed-density mass with buccal and lingual extension, thinning and perforation of the cortical bone, continuity of the mass with the root apex of the first molar, and a well-defined hypodense border between the mass and surrounding bone.

A 58-year-old man with a history of HIV on Genvoya and type 2 diabetes presented with a 17-month history of a progressively enlarging fungating anal mass. He reported new onset incontinence, ongoing bleeding, and intermittent fevers. On examination, the mass was cauliflower-like, with erythema and purulent drainage but was limited to the right side of the anal canal and was circumferentially clear of the dentate line. Initial outpatient biopsies repeatedly showed only anal intraepithelial neoplasia I, consistent with condyloma. Laboratory studies revealed a CD4 count of 667 cells/μL. CT of the abdomen and pelvis for staging demonstrated no evidence of metastases or inguinal lymphadenopathy. Given the extent of the mass, ongoing infection, and concern for occult malignancy, the patient underwent wide local excision for definitive diagnosis and source control.

A 50-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a right lateral neck mass. He reported that the mass had been present for many years and had slowly increased in size. He noted a sensation of a lump in his throat but denied pain, dysphagia, odynophagia, or changes in his voice.

On examination, a 3 × 4 cm mass was palpated in the right neck below the mandible. The mass was pulsatile, nontender, and mobile only in the horizontal plane. Auscultation over the mass revealed a bruit. No cervical lymphadenopathy was noted, and cranial nerve examination was normal.

A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the neck showed a well-defined, intensely enhancing retropharyngeal mass located between the right internal and external carotid arteries, with mass effect on the lateral oropharyngeal wall. The common carotid artery bifurcation and its branches were unusually positioned retropharyngeally.

A 50-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with a 5-day history of intermittent lower abdominal pain that worsened over several hours and was associated with nausea, vomiting, and anorexia. She had been constipated for 4 days, which was atypical for her. On examination, her abdomen was distended, with guarding, tenderness to percussion, and rebound; bowel sounds were hyperactive. A per-rectal examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed mild hyponatremia and acute kidney injury; lactate, white-cell count, liver-function tests, and other electrolytes were normal. She was hemodynamically stable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed marked fluid distension of the stomach and small bowel compatible with high-grade obstruction, extending to a 12 mm calcified lesion in the terminal ileum. The terminal ileum telescoped into the cecum at the level of this lesion, with complete collapse of the colon distally, consistent with an ileocolic intussusception with a calcified mass as the lead point; the walls of the distal ileum and cecum were edematous and thickened, without pneumatosis intestinalis or pneumoperitoneum.

A 36-year-old woman in the third trimester of pregnancy noted a progressively enlarging lump in her left breast. A core‐needle (trucut) biopsy revealed features of angiosarcoma. She delivered a healthy infant, then underwent a modified radical mastectomy for a 10-cm left breast mass with 1 of 15 lymph nodes positive for tumor. She received postoperative radiotherapy (60 Gy in 30 fractions) and initiated weekly paclitaxel.

On day 15 of chemotherapy, she developed progressive abdominal distension, bilateral lower-extremity edema, jaundice, and dyspnea on exertion. Examination showed pallor, icterus, bilateral pedal edema, and dullness to percussion at the left lung base. Her Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status was 3. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 4.3 g/dL, leukocyte count 14 100/mm3, platelets 135 000/mm3, creatinine 0.5 mg/dL; total bilirubin 4.46 mg/dL (conjugated 2.49 mg/dL); albumin 2.54 g/dL; aspartate aminotransferase 128 U/L; alanine aminotransferase 82 U/L; alkaline phosphatase 759 U/L.

A PET–CT scan showed a left‐sided pleural effusion with passive collapse of the left lower lobe, no ascites, and multiple hypodense nodules (largest 10 cm) in an enlarged liver. There was no significant uptake on FDG-PET or DOTANOC-PET scans and no intrahepatic biliary-radicle dilatation. Multiple ill-defined lytic lesions were seen in visualized bones.

Ultrasound-guided biopsy of a liver nodule demonstrated features of angiosarcoma. Pleural fluid cytology was negative for malignant cells. Iron studies were within normal limits. Peripheral blood smear showed a leukoerythroblastic picture with myelocytes, nucleated red cells, and tear-drop erythrocytes. A bone marrow biopsy revealed infiltration by tumor cells that stained positive for CD31.

A 50-year-old previously healthy Middle Eastern man presented with a 4-year history of a painless bulge in the left iliac fossa that arose 6 months after repair of a left inguinal hernia. The mass was initially small but grew gradually, becoming more uncomfortable when he walked over the past 5 months. He denied pain, skin ulceration, pigment changes, systemic symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), trauma, or infections. He had no other medical or surgical history, did not smoke or drink alcohol, and had a BMI of 28 kg/m2.

On examination, he was mildly tachypneic with borderline tachycardia; other vital signs were normal. The abdomen moved normally with respiration; there was a fixed, hard, well-demarcated bulge in the left inguinal region that was irreducible, had no cough impulse, and did not change with position. The overlying skin was adherent and mildly erythematous but showed no induration, telangiectasia, ulceration, or pigmentation. There was no tenderness, guarding, or regional lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory studies were within normal limits. Ultrasound of the left iliac fossa demonstrated a 7.0 × 2.7 cm hypoechoic lesion. The radiological interpretation favored a lipoma, although malignant etiologies could not be excluded.

A 16-year-old boy with no prior medical history presented with a 3-month history of progressive suboccipital and axial neck pain that did not respond to conservative therapy. On examination, vital signs were normal. Neurologic evaluation revealed full muscle strength, intact sensation without a sensory level, no sphincter dysfunction, no gait disturbance, and no signs of myelopathy. There was no significant family or social history.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine showed a well-defined cystic lesion in the C2 vertebral body involving the odontoid process, isointense on T1-weighted images, iso- to hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and demonstrating enhancement after gadolinium administration. Computed tomography revealed an expansile osteolytic lesion of the C2 vertebral body with cortical thinning and insufflation.

An interdisciplinary spine team recommended an open curettage biopsy via a retropharyngeal approach with intraoperative frozen-section analysis to establish a diagnosis and plan definitive therapy.

A 3-year-old boy presented with a 2-week history of intermittent abdominal pain and vomiting. On examination, there was a large, non-tender, palpable abdominal mass. Vital signs were normal, and routine blood tests, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits.  
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a large, coarse mass of mixed echogenicity in the left paravertebral region, displacing the pancreas and intestinal loops. Color-Doppler evaluation showed poor intra- and perilesional vascularity, and elastosonography demonstrated predominantly soft consistency, appearing green on the hardness scale.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a well-defined, capsulated mass extending from the subhepatic space to the lower pelvis, composed largely of fat-density tissue with thin internal septations. After contrast administration, there was low overall enhancement, mainly within the septa, and the mass compressed adjacent intestinal loops. The imaging findings suggested a peritoneal lipomatous neoplasm.

A 21-year-old man with no prior medical history presents with a 4-month history of left neck swelling, severe pain, dysphagia to solids, intermittent fever, and marked decline in performance status. On examination, there is a tender left lateral neck mass without overlying erythema, and oropharyngeal inspection reveals a bulge on the posterior pharyngeal wall. He is afebrile on admission, has no motor or sensory deficits, and a WHO performance status of 4. Cervical MRI shows a signal abnormality at C2–C3 with epidural infiltration, significant soft-tissue extension, and spinal cord compression, accompanied by left lateral cervical lymphadenopathy. CT of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis identifies a conglomerate lymph node mass in left level III (63.5 × 26 mm) causing mass effect on the oropharynx and carotid vessels, as well as C2–C3 spondylodiscitis with medullary compression; the chest and abdomen are otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory studies demonstrate normal inflammatory markers and a negative QuantiFERON assay. Empirical anti-tubercular therapy is initiated.

A 48-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of recurrent fever and splenomegaly. Her medical history was notable for right mastectomy with silicone breast-implant reconstruction 4 years earlier for intraductal carcinoma, followed by implant removal and re-implantation due to local inflammation, and a subsequent left breast reduction and bilateral lipofilling.

Eight and five months before admission she had 3-week febrile episodes treated empirically with levofloxacin. Three months later she developed fever, sore throat, fatigue, night sweats, cough, and a 10-kg weight loss over a year. In a peripheral hospital she was found to have:
• Hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, leukocytes 3.6×10^9/L, LDH 638 U/L, ferritin 398 ng/mL  
• Splenomegaly (15-cm span) on ultrasound  
• Chest CT: bilateral apical pleural scarring, subpleural densities  
• Abdominal CT: hepatosplenomegaly, ovarian cysts, pelvic fluid; no lymphadenopathy  
• Bone marrow biopsy: non-diagnostic  
• 18FDG-PET/CT: hypermetabolism of both adrenal glands  

She received azithromycin with defervescence but persistent weakness. Extensive laboratory and imaging evaluations for infection, autoimmunity, and malignancy were unremarkable. On admission she was afebrile with pallor and gait instability. Over the first week her temperature rose to 39 °C. A tuberculosis workup (sputum microscopy, culture, PCR; Mantoux; QuantiFERON) and Leishmania studies were negative. Despite high‐titer anti-Salmonella serologies (Widal Wright O 1:160, H 1:2560), ceftriaxone had no effect. Indomethacin produced transient defervescence, but fever recurred. She then developed transient right hemiparesis and aphasia; brain MRI was normal; CSF protein was elevated without pleocytosis.

She was treated empirically with broad-spectrum antibiotics, anti-tubercular therapy, antifungals, and high-dose corticosteroids, with initial improvement followed by relapse of fever, weakness, anorexia, and confusion. By hospital day 22, laboratory values revealed:
• Leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia  
• Triglycerides 301–442 mg/dL, fibrinogen 94–98 mg/dL  
• Ferritin rising to 1046 ng/mL, sIL-2R 13,190–45,800 U/mL  
• sIL-2R/ferritin ratio >2  
These findings fulfilled HLH/MAS criteria. Because of reports linking silicone breast implants to hyperinflammatory syndromes, her prosthesis was explanted and surrounding tissue debrided. Immunoglobulin and cyclosporine were administered without clinical benefit.

An 80-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of pain and swelling of the left lower face. She had no prior awareness of the swelling. Two years earlier, her impacted left mandibular third molar had been extracted. On extraoral examination, there was an ill-defined, irregular swelling (approximately 2×3 cm) over the left lower face. Intraoral palpation revealed obliteration of the left mandibular ramus. An orthopantomograph showed a multilocular radiolucent lesion in the left angle and ramus of the mandible. Aspiration of the lesion yielded straw-colored fluid. The initial differential diagnosis included odontogenic keratocyst, ameloblastoma, and dentigerous cyst. An incisional biopsy demonstrated a non-keratinizing cystic lining epithelium with mucous cell metaplasia and a connective tissue wall. Correlating the history with the clinical, radiographic, and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of a long-standing dentigerous cyst with mucous metaplasia was made.

A healthy, full–term 20-month-old girl was evaluated for a birthmark on the lateral aspect of her left thigh. The lesion was asymptomatic and present since birth, but the parents noted increasing size and nodularity. On examination, there was an ill-defined, 7.5 cm × 5.0 cm indurated, coarsely reticulated violaceous plaque with subcutaneous, skin-colored nodules palpable within it. The remainder of the skin examination was unremarkable; there was no myokymia, no pseudo-Darier sign, and no limb length discrepancy or other limb abnormality.  
Based on the clinical history and examination, the differential diagnosis included cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita, plaque-type glomuvenous malformation, tufted angioma, plaque-type noninvoluting congenital hemangioma, morphea, and congenital dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans.

A 31-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with a 3-week history of isolated, recurrent right lumbar pain without other complaints. Vital signs were normal: blood pressure 125/75 mm Hg, pulse 75–86 bpm; BMI was 29 kg/m2; hydration status was normal. Physical examination showed no signs of hyperpigmentation, Cushingoid features, or abdominal masses.

An abdominal CT scan revealed bilateral adrenal masses: on the right, 10 × 40 mm; on the left, 35 × 26 mm. Both lesions were heterogeneous with a large fat component and a soft-tissue component of spontaneous density < 10 HU, with minimal enhancement in arterial (20 HU) and portal phases (38 HU) and punctate calcifications in the right lesion.

Laboratory studies showed a normal fasting glucose level and normal urinary metanephrine and normetanephrine levels. Morning serum cortisol was low at 41.2 ng/mL (reference 50–250), and ACTH was elevated at 90 pg/mL (reference 10–50). An insulin-induced hypoglycemia test elicited an insufficient cortisol rise to a peak of 102 ng/mL (< 180 ng/mL). A 17-hydroxyprogesterone level was 1.26 ng/mL (reference < 2 ng/mL), ruling out congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

A 48-year-old man presented with acute onset of nausea and nonbloody, nonbilious vomiting for one day, after two weeks of vague nausea and subjective fevers, and one month of progressive right upper quadrant pain, jaundice, night sweats, weakness, and unintended weight loss. He had a history of diabetes and hypertension. On arrival, his temperature was 36.4 °C, heart rate 110 bpm, respiratory rate 16/min, and blood pressure 125/82 mmHg. Examination showed jaundice and right upper quadrant tenderness without peritoneal signs. Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 18.3 K/mm3 and a total bilirubin of 14.5 mg/dL; other blood chemistries, liver function tests, CEA (1.2 µg/L), and CA19-9 (21 U/L) were normal. An abdominal ultrasound showed a distended gallbladder with a thickened, edematous wall, gallstones, a focal wall defect, and intrahepatic and extrahepatic ductal dilation. MRCP demonstrated a T2-hypointense right hepatic lobe lesion involving the right hepatic artery and narrowing of the common bile duct. Contrast CT of the abdomen confirmed a contained gallbladder perforation, moderate intrahepatic ductal dilation, a possible mass at the porta hepatis, a long segment narrowing of the CBD, and multiple enlarged retroperitoneal and pelvic lymph nodes up to 2.6 cm. Chest CT revealed abnormally enlarged right hilar lymph nodes. 18F-FDG PET-CT showed intensely hypermetabolic activity at the junction of the cystic duct and proximal CBD and in several para-aortic and iliac lymph nodes. Ultrasound-guided biopsy of an iliac lymph node showed lymphoid tissue but was otherwise inadequate for diagnosis.

A 23-year-old man with Mibelli’s porokeratosis presented with an 8-month history of swelling of the left knee and recurrent joint effusions. The pain was insidious, without clear aggravating or relieving factors. Since age 15, he had experienced inflammatory polyarthralgia of the lower-limb large joints, with intermittent joint swelling and talalgia. He underwent multiple knee aspirations and received intra-articular corticosteroids and NSAIDs, with no significant improvement. 

On examination, there was a diffuse, painless suprapatellar swelling of the left knee, a positive patellar tap, and limited hip movements. Laboratory studies showed a normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate, normal rheumatoid factor, normal white-cell count, and normal uric acid level. Aspiration of the left knee yielded 60 cm3 of sterile, citrine-yellow fluid containing 3900 white cells/mm3 and no crystals.

Spine and pelvic radiographs were normal. Knee radiographs demonstrated increased density in the suprapatellar recess consistent with effusion, without bone lysis or osteosclerosis. Ultrasonography confirmed a significant suprapatellar effusion. 

MRI of the left knee showed multiple frond-like projections of the synovium into the joint. These projections exhibited high signal intensity on T1-weighted images and low signal on proton-density fat-saturated sequences, with suppression of their signal on fat-saturation sequences. After gadolinium, these villous projections did not enhance, although the overlying synovial membrane showed diffuse enhancement. Moderately abundant joint effusion was present. Sagittal GRE T2* images showed no low-signal foci to suggest hemosiderin deposition. No meniscal or ligamentous lesions were identified.

A 52-year-old postmenopausal nulliparous woman presented with intermittent crampy lower abdominal pain, bloating, and nausea without fevers, bladder or bowel complaints, weight loss, or vaginal symptoms. Initial CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 3.5 × 2.8 × 4.0 cm indeterminate complex right lower pelvic mass clearly separate from the right ovary. She was lost to follow-up for three years and then re-presented with ongoing intermittent pain, new pelvic pressure, and urinary frequency. Repeat CT showed interval growth to 6.1 × 5.7 × 7.0 cm.  

On examination, there was a firm right-sided paravaginal mass palpable on bimanual exam; the cervix appeared grossly normal and the uterus was freely mobile. Repeat CT confirmed a 6.7 × 5.0 × 7.8 cm heterogeneous right pelvic mass with cystic and solid components, ill-defined margins, abutting the right pelvic side wall, and remaining separate from the uterus and right ovary; there was leftward deviation of the bladder, right ureter, and uterus due to mass effect, without evidence of invasion. Stable pelvic lymphadenopathy was noted. Transvaginal ultrasound showed an unremarkable uterus and left ovary and a septate complex right adnexal mass measuring 7.0 × 4.9 × 7.5 cm. Colonoscopy was unremarkable. Serum CA-125, CEA, and CA 19-9 were within normal limits. MRI and biopsy were considered but deferred, and the decision was made to proceed directly to definitive surgical resection.  

Final preoperative assessment: enlarging complex pelvic mass of uncertain origin in the paravaginal/paravesical region. Surgical oncology and urology teams were consulted for surgical planning.

A 70-year-old woman presented with gross hematuria. A CT urogram revealed a focal linear filling defect in the proximal right ureter and a heterogeneous mass along the inferior bladder border. Positron emission tomography–CT demonstrated multifocal hyperenhancing lesions in the bladder: the largest at the anterior bladder neck and orifice measuring 1.9 × 1.5 cm with probable extension into the urethra, and an additional 1.4 cm lesion near the right posterior bladder base. No hypermetabolic disease was evident outside the bladder. Dermatological examination revealed no suspicious skin lesions or evidence of a non-urologic primary.

A 49-year-old woman was admitted with intermittent dyspnea, palpitations, and dizziness. Four years earlier, she had undergone a myomectomy for uterine leiomyoma. Nine months before admission, she was diagnosed with right iliac vein thrombosis and was receiving warfarin. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits except for bilateral pretibial edema. Chest radiography was unremarkable. Magnetic resonance venography demonstrated a mass originating in the right internal iliac vein and extending into the inferior vena cava. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a mass extending from the inferior vena cava into the right atrium. Transesophageal echocardiography showed two small membrane-like attachments of the mass to the right atrial endocardium. Thoracic, abdominal, and pelvic magnetic resonance imaging confirmed an intravascular mass continuous from the right iliac vein through the inferior vena cava into the right atrium, with venous occlusion.

A 32-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of slowly progressive, painless right-eye proptosis and diplopia on upgaze and downgaze. She had no systemic or prior ocular disease. On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally. Hertel exophthalmometry measured 25 mm on the right and 19 mm on the left. Margin reflex distance 1 was 3 mm in both eyes; margin reflex distance 2 was 7 mm on the right and 5 mm on the left. Right-eye motility was limited in upgaze (–2) and downgaze (–1). Pupillary reactions, relative afferent pupillary defect testing, intraocular pressure, and funduscopic findings were normal.  
Orbital CT scan revealed enlargement of the right inferior rectus muscle. Contrast-enhanced MRI showed a well-circumscribed lesion measuring 5 × 15 × 25 mm within the right inferior rectus muscle, with heterogeneous enhancement, especially peripherally; all other extraocular muscles and orbital soft tissues appeared normal.  
The preoperative diagnosis was a benign tumor arising from the inferior rectus muscle, such as a neurogenic tumor.

A 53-year-old African American woman with diabetes and hypertension, a lifelong nonsmoker, presented with a two-week history of progressive shortness of breath and minimally productive cough associated with subjective fevers and chills. She had been treated with a week of outpatient antibiotics without improvement. She denied hemoptysis, rash, joint symptoms, sick contacts, or recent travel. 

On examination, her temperature was normal, HR 110 bpm, RR 25 bpm, BP 135/82 mm Hg, and SpO₂ 92% on room air. Lung auscultation revealed coarse vesicular breath sounds with bibasilar rales. Cardiac sounds were normal. 

Laboratory studies showed a WBC count of 11,800/mm³ with 79% neutrophils; a comprehensive metabolic panel was unremarkable. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated preserved ejection fraction without wall motion abnormalities. 

A chest radiograph revealed diffuse bilateral infiltrates. Chest CT showed diffuse bilateral confluent nodular and air-space opacities with areas of consolidation. 

The patient received broad-spectrum antibiotics. Sputum and blood cultures were negative. Acid-fast bacilli smear and culture, fungal cultures, and routine viral studies were all negative. Autoimmune serologies and hypersensitivity panels were within normal limits. 

Bronchoscopy revealed only trace mucopurulent secretions and patent airways; bronchial washings for cytology and cultures were negative. Despite treatment, she remained hypoxemic and dyspneic on supplemental oxygen.

Repeat CT of the chest after 12 days of hospitalization demonstrated extensive confluent nodular opacities throughout both lungs, with a focal mass-like consolidation in the left upper lobe and several enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes.

A 56-year-old woman presented for routine annual follow-up in the Breast Unit. Screening mammography revealed a newly developed, non-palpable, solid 0.8-cm lesion in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast without microcalcifications; small axillary lymph nodes were noted. Ultrasonographic examination was negative. 

Her medical history was notable for low-grade, stage I non-Hodgkin lymphoma confined to cervical lymph nodes, treated with radiation therapy 12 years earlier; she had discontinued hematologic follow-up six years ago. Four years ago, she was diagnosed with atypical ductal hyperplasia by excisional biopsy. Her mother had postmenopausal breast carcinoma. She was otherwise healthy, with a BMI of 25, menarche at age 15, drug-induced menopause at age 44, two induced abortions, three full-term pregnancies (total lactation 15 months), and no exogenous estrogen use.

The radiologist assigned a BI-RADS category of 4B (intermediate suspicion of malignancy), and a vacuum-assisted breast biopsy under stereotactic mammographic guidance was scheduled. Under local anesthesia, 24 cores were obtained using an 11-gauge vacuum probe, a clip marker was placed, and post-biopsy mammography confirmed sampling of the target lesion.

A 62-year-old Kurdish man presented with a swelling on his left forearm of 10 years’ duration, which had increased in size over the past 2 months. He had hypertension and a remote inguinal hernia repair. On examination, there was a hard, non-tender 3 × 2 cm mass fixed to the skin on the posteromedial aspect of the mid-forearm. Routine hematologic tests, including an erythrocyte sedimentation rate, were normal. Doppler ultrasound of the left elbow showed an ill-defined intramuscular hypoechoic lesion measuring approximately 32 × 21 mm. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-defined oval mass within the subcutaneous fat with mild post-contrast enhancement and no evidence of surrounding invasion. The working diagnosis was a benign cystic lesion, particularly a dermoid cyst or lipoma.

A 16-year-old girl presented with a 6-month history of chronic pelvic pain. She had menarche at age 12½ with irregular menstrual cycles and no significant past medical history. There were no associated digestive or urinary symptoms. On examination, she had abdomino-pelvic distension and a palpable mass reaching the level of the umbilicus.  
Pelvic ultrasonography showed a suprauterine, multi-compartmentalized mass with irregular solid-cystic contours measuring 12.6 cm in its longest dimension; the ovaries were not visualized, and there was a moderate amount of peritoneal fluid. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis confirmed a 15 × 9.3 cm pelvic solid-cystic mass and moderate intraperitoneal effusion, with no enlarged deep lymph nodes.  
Laboratory studies revealed normal levels of CEA, CA 125, AFP, and β-hCG.

A 25-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a nonhealing, draining extraoral sinus in the submental region that had been present intermittently for one year and was tender on palpation. He reported intermittent pain over the past year and had applied various topical antibiotic ointments without resolution. Intraorally, there was crowding of the lower anterior teeth and evidence of traumatic occlusion with attrition. Pulp testing revealed no response in the lower left lateral incisor. An intraoral periapical radiograph showed a large radiolucency at the apex of that tooth. A provisional diagnosis of an infected periapical cyst was made, and root canal therapy was performed over three appointments with calcium hydroxide medicament, followed by obturation. Three weeks after obturation, the lesion showed no regression. A panoramic radiograph was obtained, revealing:  
• A large radiolucent lesion in the anterior mandible crossing the midline from the right premolar to the left premolar region  
• A radiolucent area in the left mandibular ramus associated with an impacted third molar  
• Additional radiolucencies in both maxillary third-molar regions  
• Impacted right maxillary canine and right mandibular third molar

A 28-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a left breast mass that had enlarged progressively. She first noted a 20 mm mass in her left breast at age 21, which was diagnosed as benign and observed for 6 years. During her pregnancy at age 28, the mass grew rapidly to approximately 70 mm. On examination, a circumscribed, painless 70 mm mass was palpated in the left upper outer quadrant without overlying skin changes or dimpling. She had no medications, allergies, or family history of breast disease; she did not smoke and drank alcohol only occasionally.

Mammography demonstrated a 62 × 42 mm, equal-density, lobular mass in the upper-outer quadrant of the left breast. Ultrasonography showed a circumscribed, hypoechoic lobular mass with cystic regions measuring 61 × 57 × 34 mm in the same location. Breast MRI revealed an approximately 65 mm mass with both solid and cystic components and contrast enhancement in the upper-outer left breast.

Because of concern for malignancy, a core needle biopsy was performed, and the lesion was diagnosed as adenosis. The patient discontinued breastfeeding and was treated with cabergoline for two months; however, the mass did not decrease in size. Although the biopsy showed adenosis, the sample represented only a portion of the mass, and malignancy could not be ruled out completely.

A 39-year-old Greek woman, who works as a nurse, presented with a several-month history of flatulence and epigastric discomfort. She had no significant past medical, surgical, family, or social history and took no regular medications. She did not smoke or consume alcohol. On examination, she was afebrile, with a blood pressure of 126/84 mmHg, a pulse of 75–80 beats/minute, and a normal neurological examination.

Laboratory studies showed mild leukocytosis (11.1 × 10^9/L), thrombocytosis (503 × 10^3/μL), an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 67 mm (reference ≤20 mm), C-reactive protein of 6.8 mg/dL (reference <0.5 mg/dL), and lactate dehydrogenase of 418 U/L (reference 125–220 U/L). Other routine blood chemistries were within reference ranges.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen revealed a large mass measuring 23.7 × 16.5 × 11.5 cm arising from the right adrenal gland, occupying the right abdomen, compressing the right hepatic lobe and inferior vena cava, and abutting the right perirenal fascia.

A functional adrenal work-up, including measurement of serum aldosterone, potassium, renin, adrenocorticotrophic hormone, a dexamethasone suppression test, and 24-hour urinary metanephrine levels, was performed. All results were within the reference ranges.

A 36-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a right adrenal mass discovered on CT during workup for low back pain. She had experienced secondary amenorrhea since age 30 and noted increased forearm and facial hair over the same period; her pre-treatment Ferriman–Gallwey score was 27. On examination, she had class I obesity, acne, male-pattern pubic hair distribution, and clitoromegaly.  

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 35×27 mm solid right adrenal mass with noncontrast attenuation of 40 Hounsfield units (HUs), venous phase attenuation of 90 HUs, delayed phase attenuation of 65 HUs, an absolute washout of 50%, and a relative washout of 28%. A 25×20 mm solid nodular area was noted in the hepatogastric space.  

Endocrine evaluation revealed elevated serum testosterone at 247 ng/dL (reference range, 10–75 ng/dL) and androstenedione >10 ng/mL (reference range, 0.4–3.4 ng/mL), with normal DHEA-S, DHEA, and 17α-hydroxyprogesterone levels. A negative hCG level and transvaginal ultrasound ruled out an ovarian tumor; the ovaries showed polycystic morphology. A 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test yielded a baseline cortisol of 11.52 μg/dL and a post-dexamethasone cortisol of 10.57 μg/dL. Plasma ACTH was 30 pg/mL (reference range, 10–100 pg/mL). Urine and plasma metanephrines were normal, serum potassium was 4.36 mmol/L, and blood pressure was normal.  

Because of the adrenal mass’s imaging features and the hepatogastric adenopathy, an 18F-FDG PET/CT was performed. The adrenal lesion showed focal hypermetabolism (SUV 10.6), and the hepatogastric node also had increased uptake (SUV 10.9); no other lesions were identified.

A 16-year-old woman presented with a several-month history of right knee pain without antecedent trauma. She was otherwise healthy. Physical examination revealed full range of motion of the knee and no other abnormalities. Anteroposterior radiographs of the knee showed an osteolytic lesion surrounded by a sclerotic rim in the lateral femoral condyle. On MRI, the lesion had intermediate signal intensity on both T1-weighted and T2-weighted images. The patient was initially diagnosed with osteochondritis dissecans. Thirteen months later, repeat MRI demonstrated that the lesion had increased in size to 16 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm. She was referred for further evaluation. CT of the knee revealed a well-defined geographic bone destruction demarcated by a sclerotic rim in the lateral femoral epiphysis. Given the benign appearance, an arthroscopic resection biopsy was planned.

A 58‐year‐old woman presented with a self‐palpated left‐breast mass. Her history included a grade‐3 invasive breast carcinoma (pT1cN0M0) in the same breast in 1996, treated by lumpectomy, axillary dissection, adjuvant cyclophosphamide–methotrexate–5‐fluorouracil, and radiotherapy. Family history was notable only for a second‐degree female relative with breast cancer after age 55.  
On examination, there was an irregular 30 × 25-mm nodule at the 3-o’clock position, mobile, without skin changes or lymphadenopathy. Mammography showed an 18 × 14-mm irregular, dense mass highly suspicious for malignancy. Ultrasound revealed a hypoechoic, parallel-oriented mass with irregular borders and heterogeneous composition.  
Core‐needle biopsy demonstrated a high‐grade invasive carcinoma composed of eosinophilic cells suspicious for squamous/epidermoid or apocrine differentiation without a mucinous component, deferring definitive classification pending excision. Staging studies (chest radiograph, abdominal ultrasound, bone scan) were negative for metastasis.  
She underwent simple left mastectomy. Grossly, there was a sharply demarcated, white nodular tumor measuring 20 mm in diameter. Microscopically, a non‐capsulated nodule showed solid nests with necrosis; a composite population of large pleomorphic epidermoid cells and smaller intermediate cells without mature keratinization; cribriform and microcystic structures embedded in large extracellular mucin pools with columnar mucinous epithelium; frequent microabscesses; up to seven mitoses/mm²; and a component of poorly differentiated ductal carcinoma in situ with similar features.

A 47-year-old woman with no significant medical or family history presented with a 2-year history of progressive left-sided facial swelling, associated with mild pain, dysphonia, and dysphagia; symptoms markedly worsened in the past month. On examination, there was a large, firm swelling extending from the left infraorbital region to the mandibular area, apparently originating from the left maxillary (second) quadrant.  

A maxillofacial CT scan revealed a 12 × 11 × 8 cm lesion centered in the left upper maxilla with both cystic and solid components, evidence of bone remodeling, a multilocular appearance, and invasion into the nasal cavity, hard palate, and left upper alveolar arch; areas suggestive of malignant transformation were noted. The radiologic impression was an odontogenic tumor, possibly ameloblastoma with areas of malignant change.  

An incisional biopsy showed an epithelial neoplasm of probable odontogenic origin and without criteria for malignancy, but the sample was insufficient for a definitive diagnosis.

A 28-year-old man presented with an 8-month history of progressive bilateral lower limb weakness and sensory loss from the umbilicus downward, leading to inability to walk. He had no history of trauma, bowel or bladder dysfunction, weight loss, or constitutional symptoms. He reported gradual-onset low back pain worsened by activity and relieved by analgesia, and intermittent dizziness without tinnitus or loss of consciousness.

Two years earlier, he had a painless anterolateral neck swelling with dyspnea and dysphagia. Examination then revealed a firm, fixed, non-tender, pulsatile 12×5 cm mass along the left carotid sheath with palpable lymph nodes. MRI of the neck showed an enhancing left carotid sheath mass encasing the great vessels and compressing the trachea. Excisional biopsies of cervical lymph nodes were repeatedly interpreted as reactive lymphadenitis, and the patient was lost to follow-up.

On current examination, he was afebrile with mild pallor and stable vital signs. Neurologically, cranial nerves and upper limbs were normal. Lower limbs showed reduced bulk, increased tone, grade 3/5 power, hyperreflexia, and a sensory level at the umbilicus. Laboratory studies demonstrated leukocytosis, anemia, and mildly elevated C-reactive protein.

MRI of the thoracic spine revealed an extradural lesion at T6 involving the vertebral body and transverse process with significant spinal cord compression.

A 26-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of a slowly enlarging left neck swelling and progressive dysphagia. She had no significant past medical history. The swelling extended from the lower limit of the left ear to the floor of the neck. She noted discomfort when the mass was palpated. On examination, there was a well-defined, solitary 6×5 cm mass below the left angle of the mandible; it was non-tender at rest but tender to direct palpation. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy and the overlying mucosa appeared normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed a well-circumscribed 6×4×5 cm mass in the left parapharyngeal space with heterogeneous enhancement, displacing the submandibular gland superiorly, pushing the carotid sheath anterolaterally, and impinging on the oropharyngeal airway. Routine blood tests were within normal limits.

A 20-year-old woman presented with a 6-week history of a painless, rapidly progressive swelling on the left side of her face. She reported no visual changes, dysphagia, or dyspnea, and her medical history was unremarkable. On examination, there was a diffuse, bony-hard, nontender expansile swelling of the left maxilla measuring approximately 5 cm by 4 cm, causing facial asymmetry. Intra-orally, a well-defined swelling of the left palate (3 cm by 2 cm) extended from the region of the upper left second premolar to the first molar with slight tooth displacement; the lesion was firm and nontender to palpation.

Laboratory studies showed normal hematologic values and a mildly elevated serum alkaline phosphatase level (125 U/L). Panoramic radiograph revealed a mixed radiolucent–radiopaque lesion with a ground-glass appearance, obliterating the left maxillary sinus. CT imaging demonstrated a hyperdense mid-facial mass involving the left maxillary sinus and palate with mixed density and expansion but no evidence of sinus obstruction. Cone-beam CT confirmed an ill-defined mixed-density lesion with numerous calcific spicules, buccal cortical plate thinning, and slight displacement of adjacent premolars.

Preoperative incisional biopsies were performed. On gross examination, the specimens were multiple grayish-white, firm masses.

A 51-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of swelling and paresthesia in the right body of the mandible. One month earlier he had undergone periodontal treatment and extraction of the first molar at the same site. His medical history was notable for prostate cancer treated surgically 3 years earlier, with no evidence of metastasis on follow-up. 

On intraoral examination, there was an extensive firm mass in the posterior right mandible extending from the canine to the second molar, with mobility of adjacent teeth. Extraoral examination revealed facial asymmetry from swelling over the right mandibular body.

Panoramic radiography demonstrated an extensive radiolucent area in the right mandible from the first premolar to the second molar, with a line of fracture in the posterior region. Facial CT showed a 45 × 11 mm osteolytic lesion centered around the mandibular canal and mental foramen, with erosion of the vestibular cortical bone.

A 67-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a painless left inguinoscrotal mass that had gradually increased in size, causing a sensation of heaviness. He denied gastrointestinal or urinary symptoms. His medical history included uncontrolled type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, stable angina, and mild dyspnea. He was a smoker with occasional alcohol use.

On examination, there was a soft mass in the left inguinoscrotal region that enlarged on standing and decreased in size when supine. Transillumination of the scrotum was negative. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies revealed a hemoglobin concentration of 12 g/dL and a fasting blood glucose level of 160 mg/dL.

Inguinoscrotal ultrasonography showed normal testes and epididymides without focal lesions, but dilation of the left spermatic veins (4 mm) with reflux consistent with grade III varicocele. Ultrasound of the mass demonstrated a heterogeneous echogenic area extending from the left inguinal canal into the scrotum, with a hypoechoic component interpreted as an intestinal loop. Based on these findings, an inguinal hernia was suspected, and surgical repair was planned.

A 61-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of dull, nonradiating anal pain during defecation and occasional frank red rectal bleeding occurring as drops after stool passage. He denied tenesmus, weight loss, dizziness, or weakness. He had no known chronic illnesses but reported alcohol use and smoking. On examination, his vital signs were normal; he appeared moderately built with a Karnofsky performance status >80 and had no pallor, jaundice, or lymphadenopathy. Digital rectal examination revealed a hard, indurated, nontender, bosselated mass extending from the anal verge between the 2- and 9-o’clock positions with tethered overlying mucosa; the upper border was not palpable. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and biochemistry, were within normal limits, and HIV serology was negative. Transrectal ultrasound showed ill-defined mural thickening and hypervascularity of the anorectal canal indenting the prostate. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated an endo-exophytic soft tissue mass at the anorectal junction concerning for a mitotic lesion. Pelvic MRI confirmed a lesion involving the rectum and anal canal with extension into the intersphincteric plane and puborectalis muscle. Colonoscopy suggested anorectal carcinoma, and an endoscopic biopsy showed spindle cell carcinoma. A repeat punch biopsy from the mass suggested leiomyosarcoma.

A 16-year-old virginal female was referred for copious vaginal discharge. One month earlier she had an abnormally heavy menstrual period, soaking seven pads per day for six days, followed by clear vaginal discharge. She had normal monthly menses before this episode and no significant medical or surgical history. Her primary care provider obtained a pelvic MRI, which revealed an 8-cm mass in the lower cervix/upper vagina connected to the left uterine body by a 2.3-cm vascular stalk. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 6.9 g/dL. In clinic, a single-digit vaginal examination revealed a large, smooth, firm mass in the midvagina with a heterogeneous appearance and evidence of internal hemorrhage.

An 18-year-old man reports a one-year history of insidious, intermittent right ankle pain, aggravated by walking and ankle movement and relieved by analgesics. He recalls a twisting injury one year ago and subsequent massage therapy. There is no swelling or constitutional symptoms. Tenderness is present over the anterior talus, and terminal movements of the subtalar and midtarsal joints are restricted and painful. Laboratory studies, including inflammatory markers, are within normal limits. Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the right ankle show an expansile, lytic lesion measuring approximately 2 × 3 cm at the talar neck–body junction, involving the articular surface, with a thin periosteal shell, a clear zone of transition, and a sclerotic rim.

A 10‐year‐old girl presented with an 8‐day history of right upper quadrant abdominal pain unrelated to meals. She had no fever, jaundice, vomiting, diarrhea, or melena. Initial laboratory studies showed normal liver function tests and blood counts; cytomegalovirus IgG was mildly elevated (23.7 U/ml). Urinalysis revealed red blood cells 3+ (294.8/μl) and white blood cells 3+ (422.9/μl). Tumor markers were negative for alpha‐fetoprotein and CEA; CA19-9 was elevated at 247.25 U/ml (normal 2–37 U/ml). 

Abdominal ultrasound showed a 78 × 71 mm vascular mass in the right liver lobe. The main portal vein and intrahepatic portal branches were not visualized; the superior mesenteric and splenic veins drained directly into the inferior vena cava. The left and middle hepatic veins joined and emptied into the inferior vena cava. 

Contrast‐enhanced CT with multiplanar reconstructions confirmed that the splenic and superior mesenteric veins joined and drained into the inferior vena cava; only two hepatic veins drained into the vena cava, and a small 3 mm portal branch supplied the left lobe. A poorly demarcated 55 mm mass in segment 5 showed mild heterogeneous arterial enhancement and iso- to hypoattenuation on portal and delayed phases. Abernethy malformation type II with concurrent hepatocellular carcinoma or hepatoblastoma was suspected.

A 33-year-old woman presented with episodes of flushing and sharp lower abdominal pain below the umbilicus that worsened with movement and urination and improved partially with medication. She had a 4-year history of hypertension managed with oral therapy, which only partially relieved her symptoms. On examination, she was tachycardic and hypertensive (160/90 mm Hg); the abdomen was soft, nontender, and without palpable masses. Routine blood tests, including complete blood count, electrolytes, and liver and renal function, were normal. 

An outside ultrasound showed a normal-sized uterus (6 mm endometrial thickness) and a 6.2 × 5.6 cm mixed echogenicity mass separable from the anterior uterine wall; the differential diagnosis included a subserosal fibroid or an extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma. A 5.7 × 5 cm complex cyst with thick walls and septations was noted in the left adnexa. 

Repeat ultrasound at our institution revealed a well-circumscribed, solid echogenic mass in the right pelvis with marked Doppler flow, a 10.7 × 5.8 cm tubular septated anechoic structure in the left adnexa, and a 1.2 cm Nabothian cyst in the cervix. No fibroids were visualized. 

Twenty-four–hour urine studies showed a markedly elevated normetanephrine level (>4800 µg; normal 110–1050 µg/24 h) with normal metanephrine and dopamine levels. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated an irregular 7.8 × 7.2 × 6.2 cm hypodense prevertebral mass inferior to the aortic bifurcation with central low attenuation, vivid peripheral enhancement, and adjacent fat stranding. A 4.5 × 7.5 cm elongated cystic tubular structure was seen in the left adnexa; the ovaries were not separately visualized.

A 12-year-old right-handed girl was evaluated for a 1-month history of gradually worsening headache. Initially generalized, the headache became localized to the left temporal region, was mild to moderate in intensity, and was not associated with vomiting or identifiable aggravating or relieving factors. Over the same period she noted continuous, dull, left ear pain without fever, discharge, or hearing loss. Fifteen days before presentation she noticed a painful swelling in the left preauricular area that had grown from approximately lemon size to apple size, without redness, discharge, or trauma. She denied difficulty chewing.

On examination, mental status and cranial nerves were intact. Motor strength and sensation in the lower limbs were normal, as were reflexes; plantar responses were flexor bilaterally. Local inspection revealed a 4 cm × 3 cm hard, lobular, tender, nonpulsatile swelling over the left temporal and zygomatic region, with no overlying skin changes or venous distension; jaw movement was normal.
