A skull radiograph demonstrated a multilobulated radiolucent lesion with well-defined margins in the left temporal region. Noncontrast CT of the head showed an expansile 4.1 cm × 3.2 cm mass arising from the squamous part of the left temporal bone at the floor of the middle cranial fossa; the lesion was isodense with small calcific foci. MRI revealed a 4.0 cm × 3.7 cm × 4.4 cm lobulated expansile mass in the squamous left temporal bone with intact cortex and no intracranial extension; it was hypointense on T1-weighted images, isointense on T2-FLAIR, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed strong heterogeneous postcontrast enhancement with nonenhancing areas.

A 52-year-old man presented with a progressively enlarging, mildly tender right-flank subcutaneous nodule noted over two years. He had a history of HBV-positive hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) treated with partial hepatectomy, entecavir, transarterial chemoembolization, sorafenib, regorafenib, and pembrolizumab over the preceding two years. On admission, vital signs were: temperature 37.2°C, pulse 112/min, respiratory rate 19/min, blood pressure 114/78 mmHg. He denied alcohol or tobacco use.

Physical examination revealed an ~8×4 cm subcutaneous mass over the right hypochondriac and flank regions; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed: white blood cell count 8.93×10^3/µl, hemoglobin 13.8 g/dl, AST 55.7 U/l, ALT 55.7 U/l, lactate dehydrogenase 201 U/l, alpha-fetoprotein 157 ng/ml, CEA 7.99 ng/ml, CA19-9 21.6 U/ml, HBsAg reactive, HCV-PCR negative. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules. Abdominal CT showed multiple nodules in liver segments 5 and 7 (largest 3.5 cm) and a right-flank soft tissue mass invading the 12th rib measuring 8×4×4 cm. Based on the clinical history and imaging, extrahepatic metastasis of HCC was suspected, but a primary soft tissue sarcoma could not be excluded. After discussion, surgical excision of the flank mass was performed without complications.

A 12-day-old newborn was referred for respiratory difficulty, most pronounced at night, and difficulty swallowing noted since birth. The infant was alert, with an oxygen saturation of 100% and suprasternal tugging. Examination of the oral cavity revealed a white, pedunculated mass in the oropharynx. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the neck showed a well-circumscribed mass measuring 5.9 × 6.6 × 13.7 mm, exhibiting mixed soft-tissue and fat density, filling the oropharyngeal lumen anterior to the valleculae and sparing the base of the tongue and prevertebral space.

A 56-year-old woman presented with a 7-year history of progressive generalized body pain and weakness. She also reported chronic nasal obstruction with occasional moderate epistaxis. Treatments with analgesics, decongestants, and antidepressants provided little relief, and she became wheelchair-bound after multiple falls due to incapacitating pain.

On examination, her vital signs were within normal limits. Musculoskeletal examination revealed diffuse bone tenderness and proximal muscle weakness; neurologic examination was otherwise unremarkable. Examination of the nasal passages showed bilateral obstruction without a visible mass.

Pelvic radiographs demonstrated diffuse loss of bone mineral density with bilateral comminuted proximal femoral fractures (subcapital and subtrochanteric) and bilateral superior and inferior pubic rami fractures. Radiographs of the hands showed marked cortical thinning, prominent trabeculae, and multiple metacarpal and phalangeal fractures.

Biochemical studies revealed an inorganic phosphate level of 0.57 mmol/L (reference range 0.78–1.42), an alkaline phosphatase level of 420 U/L (42–98), and a parathyroid hormone level of 5.1 pmol/L (1.5–7.6). Urinary studies showed a fractional excretion of phosphate of 56% and decreased tubular reabsorption of phosphate; serum calcium was normal.

These findings led to the conclusion that the hypophosphatemia was secondary to fibroblast growth factor 23 abnormalities.

A 38-year-old man presented with an 8-month history of lower back pain and bilateral leg pain. One month before presentation, after exercise, he noted claudication after prolonged walking. He denied any antecedent trauma. On neurologic examination, muscle strength in the lower extremities was full and symmetric, sensation was intact to all modalities, and reflexes were symmetrical and nonpathological. Plain radiographs of the lumbar spine showed spondylolisthesis at L4–L5. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-circumscribed 1.4-cm soft-tissue mass arising from the right superior articular process of L4 with extension into the spinal canal, forming an extradural mass that compressed the thecal sac.

A 25-year-old African woman presented with a several-year history of progressively enlarging swellings of the right calf and ankle. She was referred for musculoskeletal MRI with a clinical diagnosis of soft tissue sarcoma. On examination, there were ill-defined, warm, firm, and non-tender subcutaneous masses at the posterior right calf and at the right ankle. She had undergone excision of a similar swelling 10 years earlier. Routine hematology and serum chemistry were normal, and there was no personal or family history of neurocutaneous disease. Plain radiographs showed two oval, well-defined, homogeneous soft tissue masses in the posterior calf and at the ankle, with no abnormal calcification or phleboliths; the overlying skin and adjacent bones appeared normal. MRI demonstrated well-defined, oval subcutaneous masses that were iso-intense to muscle on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images; the larger lesion measured 8.3 × 4.0 × 5.3 cm and displaced adjacent muscles; both masses exhibited marked heterogeneous enhancement after intravenous gadolinium.

A 45-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of right-sided anterior pleuritic chest pain radiating to her back and a 7-kg weight loss. She had no fever, cough, orthopnea, or lower-extremity edema and no history of smoking or systemic disease. Initial treatment for presumed right lower lobe pneumonia with antibiotics did not relieve her pain, and she subsequently developed dyspnea on exertion. On examination, breath sounds were diminished and percussion was dull over the right hemithorax. A chest radiograph showed right pleural effusion and right lower lung atelectasis. Thoracentesis yielded exudative fluid with 398 nucleated cells/μL (15.0% polymorphonuclear cells, 16.2% neutrophils, 46.2% lymphocytes, 21.3% monocytes). Chest CT revealed sublobar consolidation, atelectasis with interlobular septal thickening, ground-glass opacities in the right middle and lower lobes, right hilar lymphadenopathy, pleural thickening, loculated right pleural effusion, and an elevated right hemidiaphragm. The patient underwent video-assisted thoracoscopic surgical decortication.

A 10-year-old boy, obese (90th percentile) and tall (75th percentile), presented with a 6-month history of recurrent generalized weakness and episodes of loss of consciousness, followed by multiple generalized tonic–clonic seizures over the past month. He had no significant past medical or family history, and his physical examination was unremarkable.

During an episode of hypoglycemia, laboratory studies revealed:
• Blood glucose: 35 mg/dL  
• Serum insulin: 35.8 mIU/L (normal < 2 mIU/L)  
• C-peptide: 8.9 ng/mL (normal 0.15–2.72 ng/mL)  
• Urine ketones: negative  
• Serum cortisol: 18.4 µg/dL (normal 7–28 µg/dL)  
• ACTH: 28.5 pg/mL (normal 10–60 pg/mL)  
• Growth hormone: 12 ng/mL (normal 0–20 ng/mL)  
• Serum prolactin: within normal limits  

Given the inappropriately elevated insulin and C-peptide during hypoglycemia alongside normal counterregulatory hormones, diazoxide therapy was initiated to prevent further hypoglycemic events.

A 25-year-old primigravida at 24 + 2 weeks of gestation was referred for routine prenatal ultrasound. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable.  
Ultrasound findings:  
- Fetal orbital asymmetry: right globe 10.9 × 8.3 mm (normal ~11.0 mm), left globe 6.8 × 6.0 mm  
- A crescent-shaped, hyperechoic lesion in the left retro-orbital space, maximum thickness ~1.6 mm; confined to the orbit with no evidence of proptosis  
- No calcifications within the lesion  
- Colour Doppler: significant vascular flow within the lesion  
- No other structural anomalies; intracranial anatomy, head circumference, abdominal circumference, and femur length all appropriate for gestational age

A 90-year-old man with no prior significant history underwent a routine CT scan after a motor vehicle collision. The CT scan revealed an incidental, asymptomatic, round, well-defined soft-tissue density lesion in the right ischiorectal fossa measuring 3.5 × 2.5 cm, with variable contrast enhancement.  
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis confirmed a well-defined mass in the right ischiorectal fossa, inseparable from the lateral pelvic sidewall muscles, abutting the rectum medially and superiorly, and displacing rather than invading the pelvic floor muscles. The lesion measured 3.5 × 2.5 cm and exhibited mixed intermediate and hyperintense signal on T2-weighted images, suggestive of a neoplastic process.  
A CT-guided core-needle biopsy showed a spindle-cell neoplasm composed of a patternless proliferation of short spindly cells with mitotically inactive nuclei, inconspicuous nucleoli, pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, and a collagen fibril network admixed with small blood vessels. Immunohistochemical stains revealed that the tumor cells were positive for CD34, BCL2, CD99, and STAT6 and negative for desmin, S100, and pancytokeratin (AE1/AE3).

A 55-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of intermittent abdominal pain, vomiting of ingested matter, and loss of appetite. He reported inability to pass feces but was passing flatus for 2 days. He denied abdominal distension, constipation, diarrhea, or bleeding per rectum. His medical history was unremarkable, with no prior abdominal surgery, comorbidities, or medication use. He had no history of tobacco or substance use. 

On examination, he appeared well, with stable vital signs. The abdominal examination was non-tender and without palpable masses or distension. 

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 21 000/mm3 with 88.3 % neutrophils and a platelet count of 471 000/mm3; other laboratory parameters were within normal limits. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a long segment of small bowel telescoping into adjacent small bowel in the left upper quadrant, with a 3.5 × 3.0 × 3.0 cm intraluminal mass serving as the lead point. 

The working diagnosis was partial small-bowel obstruction secondary to jejunojejunal intussusception. He was admitted for surgical management.

A 26-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of dull aching pain and swelling around the knuckle of the left index finger. The pain was insidious in onset, gradually worsened with movement, and was confined to this site. He reported no trauma, fever, or other systemic symptoms, and there was no family history of bone lesions. 

On examination, a 1×1 cm tender swelling was noted on the dorsal aspect of the left hand, proximal to the second metacarpophalangeal joint; the overlying skin was normal, temperature was not elevated, and range of motion of the index finger was full. 

Plain radiographs of the hand and wrist showed well-defined, homogenous focal lesions in the epiphyseal and metaphyseal regions of all bones of the hand and wrist. A similar pattern of well-defined homogenous lesions was seen in the pelvis. On the left second metacarpal, there was an expansile lytic lesion in the distal metaphyseal-diaphyseal region, with no cortical breach and a well-defined zone of transition. 

Laboratory studies, including serum alkaline phosphatase, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and complete blood count, were within normal limits.

A 34-year-old man presented with left knee pain that began at age 14 and recurred intermittently despite symptomatic chiropractic treatment. He denied any history of trauma. On examination, the left knee had full range of motion, no visible or palpable mass, and slight tenderness at the superior edge of the patella. There was pain over the same area on squatting, but no pain at rest. Thigh circumference was 40.0 cm on the left versus 43.0 cm on the right, indicating quadriceps atrophy. Initial considerations included discoid meniscus, intra-articular loose body, or intra-articular tumor. 
Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a multilocular lesion in the suprapatellar pouch adjacent to the superior patellar border, with scattered low-signal areas. Computed tomography showed an indistinct mass in the patellar pouch without calcification or ossification, blurred cortical margins of the adjacent patella, small lucent areas with peripheral sclerosis suggesting bone erosion. Based on these findings, pigmented villonodular synovitis was suspected.

A 62-year-old woman with a 3-year history of stage IV grade 1 to 2 follicular B-cell lymphoma, managed with observation, presented with a mildly pruritic patch over her frontoparietal scalp and forehead of 3 months’ duration that had not changed. She had stable disease on a “watch and wait” protocol without treatment. Physical examination revealed an approximately 10 cm × 15 cm ill-defined erythematous reticular patch with blanchable telangiectasias over the frontoparietal scalp and forehead. The patient had applied clobetasol 0.05% solution twice daily for 2 weeks, which she discontinued 1 week before presentation due to lack of response, and she noted no change in the rash with steroid use. Given her medical history, cutaneous lymphoma was high on the differential, and a punch biopsy specimen was obtained from the frontal scalp.

A 16-year-old boy presented with a left-sided neck mass. His clinical history was otherwise unremarkable. On examination, there was a firm 4 × 3 cm nonmobile mass medial to the left sternocleidomastoid muscle. Flexible endoscopy revealed a left submucosal mass of the lateral pharyngeal wall impinging on the larynx, with normal vocal-cord mobility. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head and neck showed a 4.8 × 3.3 × 7.0 cm mass displacing the great vessels laterally and pushing the left hypopharynx and larynx medially.

A 25-year-old woman with congenital cytomegalovirus hydrocephalus, severe cerebral and brainstem atrophy, and dependence on mechanical ventilation presented with a gradually enlarging mass around her right distal femur, first noted about 10 years earlier. Her medications included zonisamide, valproate, phenobarbital, furosemide, spironolactone, and levothyroxine. She had restricted communication and ambulation. On examination, there was a tense, baby-head–sized mass over the distal femur with spider telangiectasia and distended overlying skin. Laboratory studies, including alkaline phosphatase, were within normal limits. The anesthesiologist deemed her high risk for general anesthesia despite normal echocardiography, ECG, and ventilatory parameters. 
Plain radiographs showed a large (approximately 20 × 15 cm) osteolytic lesion of the distal femur without clear demarcation and a prominent sunburst periosteal reaction. CT confirmed a destructive lesion of the distal femur with peripheral invasion through the cortex. MRI demonstrated a 192 × 135 mm lesion with high signal intensity on T1‐ and T2-weighted images and marked signal loss on fat-suppression sequences.

A 56-year-old Caucasian man presented with a one-month history of right breast enlargement. He noted an initially small swelling under the right nipple that progressed into a large, painless mass, and over the past week the overlying skin in the lower outer quadrant changed from orange to red. He denied trauma, fever, weakness, weight loss, or anorexia. He did note mild left hip and upper thigh pain for several days. His medical history was unremarkable; family history was notable only for breast cancer in an older sister at age 55. On examination, there was a 13 cm × 15 cm, well-circumscribed, nontender, hard mass fixed to the skin and underlying structures; the overlying skin was pinkish. There was no nipple retraction or discharge, and the left breast was normal. He had mild conjunctival pallor and no palpable lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL, hematocrit 28.7%, platelets 102 × 10^3/μL, and white-cell count 22 × 10^3/μL with 44% neutrophils, 30% bands, 20% lymphocytes, 4% monocytes, and 2% eosinophils. CT of the chest revealed a 13 cm × 9 cm mass involving the right anterior and lateral chest wall, eroding into the thoracic cavity with areas of low density suggestive of necrosis and destruction of the fifth and sixth ribs; no pulmonary lesion was seen. A 1.5 cm nodule was noted in the right adrenal gland. A bone scan showed increased uptake in the proximal left femoral shaft and in the occipital skull.

A 24-year-old man was referred with a 4-month history of neck pain that evolved into cramps and progressive weakness of both hands and feet. He became unable to stand or walk. He denied chronic cough, night sweats, weight loss, or known TB contacts. He had no history of diabetes or hypertension.  
On examination, motor strength was 0/5 in the C5–T1 and L2–S1 myotomes, and there was no hypoesthesia. Physiological reflexes were increased; pathological reflexes were absent.  
Cervical spine radiographs revealed total collapse and destruction of the C3 vertebral body, involving the inferior endplate of C2 and superior endplate of C4. A noncontrast cervical MRI showed anterior translation at C2–C3, spinal cord edema at this level, and bilateral foraminal stenosis.  
Based on these findings, cervical spinal tuberculosis was suspected, and the patient was scheduled for debridement and anterior cervical corpectomy and fusion.

An 84-year-old woman presented with a 9-year history of progressive left-eye protrusion, decreased visual acuity, redness, tearing, and lower eyelid malposition. On inspection, the left globe was displaced superiorly and anteriorly, and a mechanical lower eyelid ectropion was present. Palpation revealed a firm, easily mobile, nonpulsatile mass in the inferolateral left orbit that did not change with posture, eye movements, or Valsalva maneuver. Pupillary reactions were normal, and diplopia was noted in all gaze positions. Best-corrected visual acuity was 9/10 OD and 4/10 OS. Hertel exophthalmometry measured 14 mm OD and 22 mm OS. Biomicroscopy, intraocular pressure, and fundoscopy were unremarkable. Systemic examination was noncontributory.

Computed tomography of the orbits showed a large, well-demarcated, oval intraconal mass in the left inferolateral orbit that was isodense to the extraocular muscles, with discrete bone remodeling. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 33 × 24 mm intraconal lesion in the same location with well-defined margins. On T1-weighted images, the lesion was isointense to muscle; on T2-weighted images, it displayed a heterogeneous but predominantly hyperintense signal. T2* gradient-echo images revealed a central hypointense component suggestive of micro-hemorrhages. Contrast-enhanced sequences showed progressive, heterogeneous enhancement with a more vivid central region. A working diagnosis of cavernous hemangioma was made based on the clinical and imaging features.

A 9-year-old spayed, long-haired Dachshund was referred for evaluation of a 2–3-week history of bilateral mydriasis and right-sided ocular discharge. The referring veterinarian had prescribed neomycin/polymyxin/dexamethasone ophthalmic ointment for 1 week, with only partial improvement of signs.

On presentation, vision was intact bilaterally, but the right eye demonstrated moderate blepharospasm and mild mucoid discharge. Pupillary light reflexes were markedly decreased OU due to severe iris atrophy. Schirmer tear tests measured 16 mm/min OD and 20 mm/min OS. Examination of the right palpebral conjunctiva and nictitating membrane revealed severe chemosis and an irregular, pink, multilobulated mass along the bulbar and medial aspect of the nictitating membrane; its depth of invasion could not be assessed.

Slit-lamp biomicroscopy showed no corneal defects; fluorescein staining was negative OU. Intraocular pressures were 9 mmHg OD and 11 mmHg OS. Funduscopic and posterior segment examinations were unremarkable bilaterally. Palpation of the mandibular lymph nodes was normal, but fine-needle aspiration of the right mandibular node showed a mildly reactive lymphoid population.

An incisional biopsy of the nictitating membrane mass was obtained under topical anesthesia and fixed in 10% neutral-buffered formalin. Histologic examination revealed an unencapsulated, well-demarcated, multilobular neoplasm composed of basal cells within a moderately dense fibrovascular stroma. The pathologist rendered a presumptive diagnosis of a basal cell tumor but noted that “it was difficult to determine whether the neoplasm represented a benign process such as a meibomian epithelioma or a malignant process, such as a basal cell carcinoma.” There was “no evidence of sebaceous or squamous differentiation in the examined sections.”

A 3-year-old boy was referred for a mass on the right side of his back. He was born at 38 weeks’ gestation after an uncomplicated pregnancy. The mass was not present at birth and was first noted at age 1 year. At that time, ultrasonography showed a well-circumscribed, high-flow vascular lesion within the right latissimus dorsi muscle, surrounded by increased fat density. Magnetic resonance imaging identified a well-delineated intramuscular lesion measuring 33 × 21 × 12 mm with flow voids, no phleboliths, sparing of adjacent structures, isointense signal on T1-weighted images, hyperintense signal on T2-weighted images, and early homogeneous enhancement after gadolinium.

No follow-up was performed until age 3, when the lesion had continued to grow. Physical examination revealed an indurated, skin-colored, nonpulsatile, fixed, nontender tumor measuring 45 mm in diameter with superficial telangiectasias; the remainder of the examination was normal. Repeat ultrasonography demonstrated a high-flow vascular lesion of unchanged echotexture, now measuring 41 × 15 × 18 mm, representing a 30% increase in size.

An 80-year-old woman presented with a two-month history of a nonhealing, progressively enlarging lesion in the right posterior mandible, associated with moderate intermittent pain and purulent discharge. She reported a 60-year history of chewing tobacco with slaked lime and a 50-year history of smoking (5–6 cigarettes per day); her medical history was otherwise unremarkable.  

On extraoral examination, there was a localized swelling over the right mandibular body and a single, firm, tender, mobile submandibular lymph node measuring approximately 1.0 × 1.5 cm. Intraoral examination revealed a 2.5 × 2.5 cm soft, erythematous swelling with ulceration extending from tooth sites 44 to 48, involving the vestibule, buccal mucosa, edentulous alveolar ridge, and lingual mucosa toward the floor of the mouth; the lesion had purulent discharge, tenderness, and peripheral induration. A root stump was noted near teeth 42–44, and carious exposure involved teeth 33–41 with edematous gingiva.  

A panoramic radiograph demonstrated a homogeneous radiolucent lytic lesion of the right mandibular body and angle from sites 44 to 46 with irregular cortical margins. A clinical diagnosis of oral carcinoma was made, and an incisional biopsy was obtained for histopathological evaluation.

An 80-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of progressive abdominal pain, weight loss, fatigue, and pallor. Her medical history included hypertension and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. On examination, she had marked pallor and massive splenomegaly (spleen palpable 10 cm below the left costal margin, firm, non-tender) without lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed:
• Hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL with mild microcytosis (MCV 79.3 fL) and reticulocyte count 1.36%  
• White-cell and platelet counts within reference ranges  
• Renal and liver function tests normal; ferritin 206 ng/mL (RR 13–150), transferrin saturation 10% (RR 20–50)  
• Folic acid and vitamin B12 levels normal  

An abdominal CT scan demonstrated a diffusely heterogeneous, massively enlarged spleen (24 × 11 × 18 cm; volume 2470 mL) with hypovascular areas; the liver was unremarkable, and there was no abdominal lymphadenopathy or venous thrombosis. Chest CT showed cardiomegaly and coronary atherosclerosis. Upper endoscopy revealed a small gastric foveolar polyp. Bone marrow biopsy disclosed 60% cellularity with increased granulocytic precursors, retarded maturation, and 1% CD34-positive immature cells; there was no morphological evidence of lymphoma or reticulin fibrosis. The patient was discharged with a working diagnosis of splenomegaly secondary to myelodysplastic syndrome.

One week later, she returned with acute worsening of abdominal pain, hypotension (mean arterial pressure 57 mmHg), pallor, and diffuse abdominal tenderness. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 5.7 g/dL, mild microcytosis (MCV 79.1 fL), and leukocytosis; platelet count and chemistries remained normal. Serologies for HIV, hepatitis B and C, and syphilis were negative. Point-of-care ultrasound and repeat CT scan showed free intraperitoneal fluid consistent with hemoperitoneum from splenic rupture. She underwent emergency laparotomy and splenectomy.

Pathological examination revealed an 18.0 × 13.0 × 6.5 cm spleen weighing 1200 g with multiple disrupted capsular areas and fibrin deposits. On sectioning, the parenchyma contained ill-defined nodules—larger white firm nodules and smaller blue-red spongy nodules. Microscopy showed replacement of splenic tissue by anastomosing, irregularly ectatic vascular channels lined by plump, mildly atypical endothelial cells, interspersed with solid spindle-cell fascicles exhibiting moderate nuclear atypia and frequent mitoses; vascular lumina contained red blood cells, and periodic-acid Schiff staining highlighted small eosinophilic intracytoplasmic globules in the spindle cells. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated diffuse CD31 and FLI-1 positivity in both spongy and spindle areas, CD34 reactivity in the spindle areas only, negative D2-40, and absence of CD8, CD68, lysozyme, and CD21 expression in tumor cells; the Ki-67 index was approximately 50% in spindle areas and 10% in spongy areas.

A 37-year-old man presented with swelling in the lower anterior jaw for one year. He had undergone excision of a previous lesion in the same area. He denied pain or trauma. On extraoral examination there was no facial asymmetry. Both right and left submandibular lymph nodes were palpable, approximately 1.5 × 2 cm, soft to firm, mobile, and non-tender. Intraorally, there was an oval growth on the gingiva buccally and lingually from the lower right canine to first molar, measuring 4 × 2 cm, pinkish white, with diffuse margins, a smooth surface, soft to firm consistency, non-tender, and not fixed. The clinical differential diagnosis included pyogenic granuloma and malignancy of the lingual alveolar mucosa in the 41–46 region. An orthopantomogram showed an ill-defined radiolucent lesion extending from the lower right canine to the distal of the first molar. CT of the mandible demonstrated an ill-defined, intensely enhancing mass lesion in the right buccal mucosa near the alveolar ridge and adjacent to the tongue, measuring 4.5 × 2.2 cm, with bilateral submandibular lymphadenopathy (largest 1 × 0.6 cm). Ultrasound of the neck was unremarkable. A biopsy was performed.

A 49-year-old African man, a non-smoker, presented with acute onset of vomiting and abdominal distension. Plain abdominal radiographs suggested small-bowel obstruction, and exploratory laparotomy revealed adhesions without a clear obstructing lesion; no biopsy was obtained. Three months later he returned with progressive weight loss, anorexia, abdominal distension, cachexia, and ascites. Upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopies were normal. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed free peritoneal fluid and diffuse, mild thickening of the gut wall and mesentery. Routine blood tests were within normal limits. Further history elicited occupational asbestos exposure from ages 23 to 29 while working in pipe insulation.

A 13-year-old girl presented with a nine-month history of rapidly growing, painless lumps in both breasts. She had regular menstrual cycles since menarche at age 11. There was no history of trauma, weight loss, familial cancer, irradiation, or oral-contraceptive use. On examination, the left breast had a 25 cm × 25 cm non-tender, smooth, well-defined, firm, mobile mass without skin fixation or axillary lymphadenopathy. The right breast was asymmetrically enlarged by a 30 cm × 25 cm mass; the overlying skin was dark with excoriations and superficial venous prominence, but there was no nipple discharge. Ultrasound imaging showed large, well-circumscribed solid masses in both breasts. Fine-needle aspiration cytology from both lesions revealed tightly cohesive clusters of benign ductal epithelial cells in a branching pattern against fibromyxoid stroma without evidence of malignancy. Laboratory and biochemical parameters were within normal limits.

A 35-year-old woman presented with left fronto-orbital swelling of 10 years’ duration. She reported progressive deterioration of vision in her left eye over 1.5 years, to the point where she could barely perceive hand movements near her face. The proptosis had become more pronounced over the past month, and the left globe was displaced inferiorly and medially. There was no history of endocrine abnormalities.  
On contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain, there was a heterogeneous enhancing mass in the left orbital roof displacing the globe anteriorly and inferolaterally. An axial CT scan showed an expansive lytic bony lesion involving the superior and lateral walls of the orbit, including the orbital roof, frontal bone, and sphenoid wing.

A 73-year-old woman presented with a painless, palpable mass in her right breast of more than 1 month’s duration. She had no B symptoms and no family history of breast cancer. On examination, there was a hard, 50 mm mass in the outer quadrant of the right breast without palpable axillary lymphadenopathy. Mammography showed a high-density mass with microlobulated margins. Ultrasonography revealed a 47 mm irregular hypoechoic mass with a heterogeneous internal echo and internal blood flow. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a solitary breast mass without evidence of metastases. MRI demonstrated that the margin of the mass was isointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images; the time–intensity curve on contrast-enhanced T1-weighted imaging showed a slow plateau pattern. Serum carcinoembryonic antigen and carbohydrate antigen 15-3 were normal; lactate dehydrogenase was 207 IU/L. Core needle biopsy revealed solid proliferation of atypical cells with rounded nuclei. Immunohistochemical staining was negative for estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2; the Ki67 labeling index was 80%. Based on these findings, the lesion was diagnosed as triple-negative invasive ductal carcinoma (cT2N0M0).

A 6-year-old boy presented with a 2-month history of a nontender swelling in the right posterior mandible. On extraoral examination, there was a diffuse, hard swelling of the right mandibular body causing slight facial asymmetry; there was no skin change, discharge, paresthesia, or trismus. Intraorally, a 2 × 3 cm painless bony swelling involved the region of the primary second molar and erupted first permanent molar, with obliteration of the buccal vestibule; the teeth were noncarious and there was no lymphadenopathy. Panoramic and periapical radiographs revealed a well-defined radiolucent lesion extending from the distal first molar to the anterior ramus, with an intact inferior mandibular border; the permanent first molar was erupted with incomplete root formation and the second molar tooth germ lay within the lesion. Routine blood and urine studies were normal. There was no other skeletal or systemic involvement, and the medical and family histories were unremarkable. The initial differential diagnosis included odontogenic keratocyst, cemento-ossifying fibroma, and central giant cell granuloma. Aspiration yielded only blood with few surface squamous cells. A provisional diagnosis of ossifying fibroma was made.

A 75-year-old man with a history of malignant melanoma of the right chest (with lymphatic spread to the right axilla; right mastectomy performed 1 year earlier) presented for routine surveillance. He was asymptomatic, with no skin lesions or palpable lymphadenopathy. Vital signs were normal. Complete blood count, metabolic panel, and coagulation studies were within normal limits.  

Positron emission tomography–computed tomography showed increased metabolic activity in the proximal pancreas (standardized uptake value, 10.36). Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen revealed a 1.7-cm focal pancreatic mass and a large left upper retroperitoneal lymph node.  

Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated multiple well-demarcated, hypoechoic pancreatic lesions: a 24.6 mm × 21.4 mm mass in the pancreatic body; a 6.9 mm × 6.6 mm nodule in the body; and two lesions (14.1 mm × 11.7 mm and 10.6 mm × 7.2 mm) in the pancreatic head. Endoscopic ultrasound–guided fine-needle aspiration of the pancreatic head lesions was performed with a 25-gauge needle.

A 53-year-old Asian woman presented with a firm, painless, palpable nodule in the right thyroid lobe. She had no symptoms of thyroid dysfunction. On examination, the nodule measured approximately 24 mm in diameter with a smooth surface; no cervical lymphadenopathy was palpable. Thyroid function tests, including T3, T4, and TSH, were within normal limits. Serum thyroglobulin was < 0.20 ng/mL, and antithyroglobulin and antithyroid peroxidase antibody levels were markedly elevated. A radioactive iodine uptake scan demonstrated a cold nodule. Neck ultrasound revealed a well-circumscribed, low echo–level, 24 × 18 mm nodule in the right lobe. The patient underwent right hemithyroidectomy. On frozen-section analysis, the lesion was described as a well-circumscribed spindle cell tumor with an incomplete fibrous pseudocapsule; nuclei of some tumor cells were enlarged and hyperchromatic, and suspicious pseudocapsular invasion was noted in small foci, but mitotic figures and necrosis were absent.

A 12-year-old girl presented with right upper quadrant abdominal pain, progressive jaundice, and fever for two months. She reported dark urine, pale stools, pruritus, anorexia, and weight loss. On examination, she was cachectic and deeply icteric, with tender hepatomegaly; there were no stigmata of chronic liver disease, ascites, or other palpable masses.

Laboratory studies revealed an obstructive cholestatic pattern: total bilirubin 13.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 12.1 mg/dL, and alkaline phosphatase 943 U/L. Bleeding parameters and serum albumin were normal, and viral serologies were negative.

Abdominal ultrasonography showed central intrahepatic biliary dilation, a dilated gallbladder with sludge, and an upper common bile duct diameter of 9.3 mm without gallstones. MRCP confirmed these findings but did not visualize the distal CBD. CT of the abdomen demonstrated central intrahepatic biliary ductal dilation with an abrupt cutoff at the mid to distal CBD by an ill-defined soft tissue lesion; the pancreatic head appeared bulky with a normal main pancreatic duct.

An ERCP attempt failed due to obscured ampullary anatomy, and a percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage (PTBD) was placed. A PTBD dye study confirmed a cutoff at the mid-CBD. A working diagnosis of a long-segment distal CBD stricture due to an unknown mass lesion was made. Differential diagnoses included tuberculosis, lymphoma, primary sclerosing cholangitis, connective tissue disorders, and cholangiocarcinoma. The work-up for tuberculosis and connective tissue disorders was negative, and bile cultures showed no growth. The lesion was not amenable to endoscopic ultrasound biopsy, image-guided biopsy, or cytology.

A 33-year-old Japanese woman was referred after an 8 cm mass in segment 8 of the liver was detected incidentally on screening abdominal ultrasound. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a lobular, cystic lesion containing highly viscous fluid. On MRI, the mass was isointense or hypointense to muscle on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with enhancement of an internal septum on Gd-EOB-DTPA–enhanced sequences. FDG-PET showed no uptake in the lesion or elsewhere. Ultrasound revealed a solid, hypoechoic tumor with slightly indistinct borders and internal inhomogeneity; contrast-enhanced ultrasound depicted a hypovascular lesion with an enhanced internal partition wall. Liver function tests were normal, and serum tumor markers (CEA, α-fetoprotein, CA19-9) were within reference ranges. Serologic tests for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV were negative. From these findings, she was diagnosed with a mucinous cystic neoplasm of the liver and underwent subsegmentectomy of segment 8.

A 14-year-old right-hand-dominant Caucasian male presented with a several-year history of a slowly enlarging mass on the palmar side of the left hand centered over the third metacarpal head. The mass was painless except when batting during baseball. He reported no sensory deficits or motor weakness. On examination, there was a soft, fixed, 3–4 cm mass spanning from the second to fourth metacarpal heads on the palmar aspect of the left hand. Neurologic assessment was unremarkable. Plain radiographs of the hand showed no abnormalities. MRI with intravenous gadolinium revealed a well-defined 3.6 × 1.6 × 2.4 cm soft tissue mass centered at the third metacarpophalangeal joint abutting the flexor tendon sheath of the third digit; the lesion demonstrated mild contrast enhancement, with no osseous erosion or joint effusion. Initial differential diagnosis included infectious process versus soft tissue tumor such as giant cell tumor of tendon sheath, lipoma, leiomyoma, or neuroma.

A 55-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with a 2-month history of progressive left flank pain. She also reported intermittent headaches, sweating, and palpitations. On examination, her blood pressure was 180/90 mmHg, heart rate 90 bpm, and there was a palpable left flank mass. 

An abdominal ultrasound revealed a well-defined, multilocular, anechoic mass measuring 100 × 80 mm in the left retroperitoneum. Contrast-enhanced CT of the adrenals demonstrated a predominantly fluid-density left retroperitoneal mass with a small solid component that enhanced after injection; the mass abutted—but did not occlude—the left renal and splenic veins. 

MRI of the adrenal region showed the lesion to have a cystic component with marked T2 hyperintensity and a solid component with intermediate T2 signal that enhanced post-contrast. There was no fat signal on in-/out-phase images and no diffusion restriction.

A 20-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of progressively worsening pelvic pain, fatigue, occasional urinary frequency, and incontinence. He denied bowel or genital complaints and had no relevant family history. On examination, he was afebrile (37°C) with a blood pressure of 145/100 mmHg, heart rate 80/min, and respiratory rate 22/min. General and neurological examinations were unremarkable, with no skin lesions. Abdominal palpation revealed a partly firm, nonmobile mass in the hypogastric region; the digital rectal examination was normal. Laboratory tests showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 120 mm/h and C-reactive protein of 70 mg/L; complete blood count, blood urea nitrogen, and creatinine were within normal limits. Urinalysis revealed microscopic hematuria (blood 1+, 30–40 red cells per high-power field). Ultrasonography demonstrated normal kidneys without hydronephrosis and a 125×45×65 mm infiltrative heterogeneous hypoechoic mass over the bladder dome extending into the lateral pelvic wall and rectovesical pouch, exerting pressure on the bladder wall. The prostate and seminal vesicles appeared normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed an enhancing soft-tissue density mass superior to the bladder, extending into the rectovesical pouch and invading the posterior bladder wall and dome, without calcification or macroscopic fat, along with a few pre-aortic lymph nodes up to 13 mm in short axis. Soft tissue sarcoma, nerve sheath tumors, and retroperitoneal fibrosis were considered, and image-guided biopsy was planned.

A 16-year-old male presented with a 1-month history of epigastric discomfort radiating to the right flank, which worsened over the 5 days before presentation. The pain was dull and continuous without clear relieving or aggravating factors. He also reported headaches associated with transient loss of sight. He was previously well, with no prior surgeries or significant medical history. 

On examination, blood pressure was 245/152 mm Hg and pulse 91 beats/min. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the right flank extending to the right lower quadrant without peritoneal signs; no masses were palpated. Funduscopic exam showed grade 1 papilledema. Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL, white-cell count 8.3 × 10^9/L, platelet count 521 × 10^3/mm^3, urea 2.17 mmol/L, creatinine 56.9 μmol/L, sodium 143 mmol/L, and potassium 4.49 mmol/L. Twenty-four–hour urine collections revealed metanephrines 1148 nmol/day (reference 167–938) and normetanephrines 15,968 nmol/day (reference 311–1562).

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 3.3 × 3.4 × 4.5 cm para-aortic mass superior to the aortic bifurcation at L3, abutting and compressing the inferior vena cava; both adrenal glands appeared normal. The lesion had heterogeneous enhancement with areas of necrosis and cystic change, measuring 54 HU in the arterial phase, 136 HU in the portal venous phase, and 106 HU in the delayed phase. The initial radiologic differential diagnosis included extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma and conglomerate lymph node masses; there was no vascular communication to suggest an aneurysmal lesion, and no ureteral communication to suggest an atypical urinoma.

A 70-year-old woman presented with a firm, painless mass on the right axilla. It had been stable for a year but recently increased in size, causing friction with her undergarment. She had a history of melanoma in situ. On examination, there was a nontender, orange-pink, 3.2-cm firm plaque with a pitted surface and no secondary changes. The initial differential diagnosis included xanthoma, spontaneous keloid, and adnexal gland neoplasm. A punch biopsy of the lesion showed atypical intradermal epithelioid cells arranged singly and in cords.

A 36-year-old woman with no prior medical or surgical history presented with a 5-day history of subacute small-bowel obstruction characterized by colicky right iliac fossa pain, vomiting, and abdominal distension. She also reported 6 months of chronic watery diarrhea, anorexia, and weight loss but denied rectal bleeding. On examination, she was hemodynamically stable; the abdomen was distended without tenderness or peritoneal signs, and no masses were palpable in the right iliac fossa. Rectal examination was normal. Laboratory tests revealed an inflammatory syndrome without anemia or metabolic derangements. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed circumferential wall thickening of the terminal ileum with a “target” configuration, suggesting active Crohn’s disease. The patient was managed conservatively with bowel rest, nasogastric decompression, and IV fluids; her obstruction resolved within 6 hours. Colonoscopy revealed a normal colonic mucosa and ulcerations in the terminal ileum; the ileocaecal valve was narrow with a fibrotic appearance, and biopsies were nonspecific. After multidisciplinary discussion, a diagnosis of Crohn’s disease with fibrostenotic stricture was made, and surgical resection was recommended.

A 64-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation on warfarin, COPD, active smoking, hypertension, and a history of laryngeal cancer treated 4 years earlier presented with 10 days of generalized weakness and epigastric discomfort. She had a fall 1 week before presentation and noted dark stools and red urine. Medications—including warfarin—had been unchanged for 1.5 years, with a stable INR over that period. 

On arrival, she was alert but lethargic, pulse 160 beats/min, afebrile, normotensive. Examination showed a right subconjunctival hemorrhage; mucous membranes were dry. Cardiopulmonary exam was unremarkable except for tachycardia. The abdomen was soft with mild epigastric tenderness. Rectal exam revealed stool mixed with dark blood. Neurologic examination was nonfocal.

Laboratory results: hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL (baseline ~12 g/dL), WBC 15 × 10^3/µL, platelets 232 × 10^3/µL, PT 169 s, PTT 92 s, INR unrecordable. Chemistry showed BUN 54 mg/dL, creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, bicarbonate 10 mEq/L. LFTs: albumin 2.8 g/dL, ALT 420 U/L, AST 973 U/L, ALP 435 U/L. Other labs: lactate 13.3 mmol/L, LDH 8003 U/L, troponin 0.206 ng/mL, CK 872 U/L, CK-MB 40 ng/mL. Hepatitis A, B, and C serologies were negative; acetaminophen level < 15 ng/dL.

INR two weeks prior was 2.8; LFTs four weeks prior were normal. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. A CT scan of the abdomen showed a markedly enlarged, heterogeneous liver suggestive of an infiltrative process, with no free fluid or obvious bleeding.

A two-year-old boy presented with a 15-day history of progressive weakness of both lower extremities, difficulty standing and walking, and progressive loss of bowel and bladder control. There was no history of trauma, back pain, weight loss, or fever, and developmental milestones were age-appropriate. On examination, there was paraspinal fullness and complete loss of motor power below the knees (hip flexion and knee extension, grade 5; ankle dorsiflexion, great-toe extension, and ankle plantar flexion, grade 0). Muscle bulk was normal, tone was reduced, sensations were decreased below the L3 dermatome with reduced perianal sensation, and both ankle reflexes and plantar responses were absent. Laboratory studies were normal except for an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (48 mm/hour). Plain radiographs of the spine, chest, and abdomen were unremarkable. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography showed marked bladder distension consistent with a neurogenic bladder. Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbosacral spine revealed a soft-tissue mass originating from the right L4 pedicle, invading the spinal canal, posterior elements, and right psoas muscle, with destruction of the L4 vertebral body.

A 39-year-old man presented with recurrent epigastric pain radiating to the back, without gastrointestinal or constitutional symptoms. Examination showed tenderness in the upper abdominal area. Laboratory studies were notable for a C-reactive protein level of 48 mg/L and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 65 mm/h; other blood tests were unremarkable. Gastroduodenoscopy revealed a hiatal hernia. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed a 7 cm mass in the left kidney, ipsilateral retroperitoneal lymph-node enlargement, and bilateral lung lesions. He underwent a left partial nephrectomy with ipsilateral lymph-node dissection. Grossly, the 6.8×7×5.5 cm tumor was confined to the renal capsule, with negative margins and deep pigmentation on slicing. Microscopically, the lesion consisted of sheets, nests, and trabeculae of brown pigment–containing spindle and occasional rounded cells, with nuclei showing prominent small red nucleoli and occasional grooves; focal necrosis and rare mitoses were present. Immunohistochemical studies showed positivity for vimentin, melan A, HMB45, cytokeratin, and CK7, with patchy, weak smooth-muscle actin and BCL2 positivity, and negativity for CK20, CD10, synaptophysin, chromogranin, PAX8, desmin, CD34, and CD99.

A 62-year-old woman presented in January 2018 with one month of malaise, fever, a 4-kg weight loss, and transfusion-dependent anemia. 
Initial evaluation included:
• Chest CT: a 58-mm mass in the right lower lobe of the lung.  
• Fibrobronchoscopy: nondiagnostic.  
• Right lower lobectomy: pathology revealed an inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, fibrohistocytic variant.  

The patient entered surveillance. In June 2018, she developed a lesion at the site of the upper right incisor, prompting extraction of the tooth. A few months later, the lesion recurred; re-excision confirmed recurrent inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor.  

In February 2019, she noted further growth of the oral lesion, associated with facial pain and difficulty with oral intake.  
• CT imaging: a contrast-enhancing nodular lesion measuring 22 × 17 mm in the upper nasal vestibule, an 8-mm nodule in contact with the nasal spine, and multiple smaller nodules extending toward the base of the nasal vestibule.  
• Histopathology: spindle and myofibroblastic cells arranged in fascicles with a dense inflammatory infiltrate rich in plasma cells, histiocytes, lymphocytes, and a few eosinophils.  
• Immunohistochemistry: strong ALK expression, increased FLI1, reduced CD10 and TLE1.

A 6-year-old girl of North-African origin was referred for evaluation of an expansive mass in the left lower jaw. She had a marked, painless swelling of the left mandible without neurosensory deficits or functional impairment. Intraoral examination revealed buccal expansion of the left mandible; the mixed dentition appeared normal. Panoramic imaging showed a mixed radiolucent/radio-opaque lesion in the left mandible with cloudy internal opacities, expansion and erosion of the inferior cortex, and a thin radiolucent rim separating the lesion from surrounding bone. Cone-beam CT demonstrated a voluminous mass in the left ramus extending from the second deciduous molar to the coronoid process, with medial and lateral cortical erosion and focal interruptions. The lesion contained unerupted first and second mandibular molars and numerous plump calcifications with a “ginger root–like” appearance. MRI showed a heterogeneous center with multiple hypointense components on a T1- and T2-isointense background; after gadolinium, the background enhanced while the hypointense components did not. There was no invasion of adjacent structures and no lymphadenopathy.

A 27-year-old woman, at 26 weeks of gestation, presented with a 2-month history of weekly headaches accompanied by blurred vision in both eyes and diffuse left-sided numbness and tingling. Neurologic examination was normal. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the head showed ventriculomegaly and an ill-defined mass in the pineal/thalamic region. Subsequent MRI without gadolinium demonstrated a 1-cm mass in the pineal region with obstructive hydrocephalus and periventricular T2 hyperintensity suggestive of transependymal CSF flow.

A 41-year-old man with a 15-year history of HIV infection, maintained on antiretroviral therapy (tenofovir, lamivudine, lopinavir/ritonavir), presented with a 1-year history of irregular fevers (38–39 °C), progressive dyspnea, an 8 kg weight loss, and asthenia. He noted painless enlargement of cervical lymph nodes over the same period. Six months earlier, he had been started on rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for presumed ganglionic tuberculosis, without clinical improvement. On thoracic CT, there was enlargement of axillary and mediastinal lymph nodes. Abdominal CT showed abundant intra-abdominal fluid, extensive hypertrophied retroperitoneal lymph nodes at the mesenteric root and inguinal regions, and hepatosplenomegaly (splenic index, 590).

A 43-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a small swelling on the anterior dorsal surface of her tongue, just left of the midline. She first noticed the lesion more than 2 years earlier; it remained unchanged and asymptomatic unless inadvertently bitten. Her medical history was notable only for depression treated with desvenlafaxine. She did not smoke and drank little alcohol.

On examination, there were no extraoral abnormalities or cervical lymphadenopathy. Intraorally, there was a small, nonulcerated, sessile mass on the anterior dorsal tongue, not tender to palpation, with otherwise normal mucosa. A provisional diagnosis of fibroepithelial polyp was made, and the lesion was excised.

An elliptical specimen of oral mucosa measuring 10 × 8 × 8 mm was submitted for histopathology. Microscopic examination showed a semipedunculated, nonencapsulated but well-circumscribed submucosal mass covered by stratified squamous epithelium. Centrally, there were lobules of fibromyxoid stroma separated by fibrous septa. Within these lobules, numerous randomly distributed stellate and spindle-shaped cells were seen. Nuclear pleomorphism was minimal, and mitotic figures were inconspicuous.

A 2-year-old boy with a fair complexion was brought for evaluation of multiple light brown skin lesions on his cheeks and forehead. According to his mother, a few small macules had first appeared at age 9 months on the left temple without preceding inflammation; new lesions developed, particularly after summer sun exposure. Family history was negative for skin diseases. On examination, there were multiple symmetrical light brown macules on the face. The Darier sign was negative. Because the lesions were confined to the face and appeared to worsen after sun exposure, xeroderma pigmentosum was considered, but genetic testing for a mutation in the ERCC3 gene was negative. Five months later, the number of lesions had increased, and the macules had evolved into monomorphic flat reddish-brown papules.

A 58-year-old white heterosexual Greek man with no history of abdominal operations presented with a 2-week history of gradually worsening abdominal pain. He reported passage of flatus but no bowel movements for 5 days, along with progressive nausea, vomiting, and abdominal distention leading to inability to tolerate oral intake.

On examination, he was well-nourished, mildly febrile (37.5°C), and hemodynamically stable. His abdomen was soft, distended, and tender in the hypogastrium and right lower quadrant, with scarce bowel sounds. No hernia was apparent. Rectal examination revealed heme-positive stool.

Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 4080/μl with a normal differential, a hematocrit of 30%, and normal electrolytes, liver biochemistry, and amylase levels. Plain abdominal radiographs demonstrated multiple air-fluid levels in distended small-bowel loops and air in the colon, consistent with partial small-bowel obstruction. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed dilated loops of small intestine with a transition point in the mid-ileum and a characteristic “target sign” of intussusception.

A 9-year-old healthy girl was evaluated for congenital skin lesions. The lesions had been stable and asymptomatic until the past 6 months, when she noted increased hair growth and darkening. There was no family history of similar lesions, and review of systems was unremarkable.

On examination, there were multiple well-demarcated, hyperpigmented patches with irregular, “splashed-on” borders and areas of hypertrichosis on the trunk and bilateral lower extremities, extending below the knees. A 4-mm punch biopsy of a patch on the right posterior hip showed epidermal acanthosis, regular elongation of rete ridges, hyperpigmentation of the basal layer, and an increase in the number of arrector pili muscles.

A 36-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of painless protrusion and downward displacement of her right eye. She denied visual disturbance, pain, or double vision, and had no history of trauma or ocular surgery. On examination, Hertel exophthalmometry (110-mm base) showed 26 mm of proptosis in the right eye (18 mm on the left) and hypoglobus on the right. Visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally; ocular motility was full; pupils were normal; intraocular pressures were 18 mm Hg (right) and 16 mm Hg (left); and anterior and posterior segments were unremarkable.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the orbits revealed a well-defined, ovoid intraconal lesion measuring 25 × 17 × 25 mm along the superomedial aspect of the right orbit, displacing the globe inferolaterally. Systemic examination was noncontributory, and there was no lymphadenopathy. Hematological testing showed hemoglobin of 8 g/dL; peripheral smear revealed microcytic, hypochromic red cells; and bone marrow aspiration showed a mildly hypercellular marrow with adequate trilineage hematopoiesis and mild erythroid hyperplasia. 

Based on the clinical presentation and imaging features, a provisional diagnosis of a right orbital soft-tissue tumor of vascular or connective-tissue origin was made.

A 28-year-old man presented with a several-week history of diarrhea and fever that did not respond to antibiotics. On examination he was afebrile, with normal vital signs. Laboratory studies were unremarkable except for mild transaminase elevations (ALT 65 U/L, AST 46 U/L). Two weeks later, abdominal ultrasonography showed a normal liver, biliary ducts, and pancreas, but an enlarged spleen (15 cm) containing a 70 × 77 mm hypoechoic, asymptomatic solid mass at its upper pole. Color Doppler imaging revealed blood flow along the periphery of the lesion, with no significant internal signals. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a round splenic lesion that was hypodense relative to normal parenchyma, with mild arterial-phase enhancement and complete washout in the late venous phase; there were no prominent internal vascular structures. Given the difficulty of obtaining a definitive preoperative diagnosis, the high risk of bleeding with biopsy, and the potential for spontaneous rupture, the patient was referred for a totally laparoscopic splenectomy.

A 66-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of epigastric pain and nausea. He was an ex-smoker and social drinker with no significant comorbidities or family history. On examination, he was jaundiced with hepatomegaly. Routine serum parameters were within normal limits; tumor markers including AFP, CEA, and β-HCG were not assessed. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a thickened posterior gastric wall at the pylorus, periaortic lymphadenopathy, and multiple hepatic and pulmonary metastases; no primary lesions were seen in the testes, mediastinum, or other sites.  

He underwent palliative gastrectomy with partial hepatic resection. The gastric specimen contained a 33×33×15 mm ulcero-vegetative mass; the liver specimen revealed a 30×20×15 mm whitish, necrotic, hemorrhagic tumor. Histologically, there was a proliferation of large, dyscohesive, pleomorphic cells from the mucosa through the muscularis with extensive hemorrhage and vascular emboli. Two cell populations were identified: (1) giant cells with lobulated, bizarre nuclei resembling syncytiotrophoblasts and (2) oval cells with pale cytoplasm resembling cytotrophoblasts.  

Immunohistochemical staining showed that both cell types were diffusely positive for cytokeratin 7, MLH-1, MSH-2, PMS-2, and c-MET. The syncytiotrophoblast-like cells were diffusely positive for inhibin and CD138, whereas the cytotrophoblast-like cells were negative for these markers. A minor adenocarcinoma component (<10% of the tumor) at one margin was diffusely positive for CDX2, cytokeratin 7, CEA, and c-MET, with focal positivity for cytokeratin 20 and CD138. The choriocarcinomatous cells were negative for CEA and CDX2 but positive for cytokeratin 7 and HCG. There was progressive loss of E-cadherin in both components; in vascular emboli, tumor cells were positive for CD138 and β-catenin but negative for inhibin. The choriocarcinomatous component was also present in hepatic metastases.

A 55-year-old woman with no significant past medical or surgical history presented with a large, painless mass in the proximal right thigh noted after recent intentional weight loss. On examination, there was a firm, mobile, 15 cm mass in her right upper inner thigh without Tinel’s sign or inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Ultrasound of the mass demonstrated a lobulated, predominantly hypoechoic solid lesion with circumscribed margins and internal vascularity on Doppler imaging.

MRI revealed a sharply demarcated intermuscular mass located between the sartorius and adductor longus muscles. The lesion was isointense to slightly hyperintense relative to muscle on T1-weighted images and homogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted fat-saturated sequences, with strong homogeneous contrast enhancement. The superficial femoral artery was identified along the posterior aspect of the mass, with more than 180° of its circumference encased, but without luminal invasion or occlusion. The femoral vein was compressed, and there was no evidence of muscular invasion.

Because of the intimate relationship with the artery, the primary imaging consideration was a vascular leiomyoma; a peripheral nerve sheath tumor was also considered given the lesion’s intermuscular location and proximity to the saphenous nerve. Tissue sampling was requested for definitive diagnosis.

A 21-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of burning pain in the right chest, gradually worsening in intensity, and a progressively enlarging bulge on the right thoracic wall. She had no prior medical conditions or history of trauma. On examination, there was a palpable, tender mass over the right fifth and sixth ribs. A chest radiograph showed significant deformity of the right rib cage. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a 10.4 × 3.7 cm expansile, lytic lesion involving the right fifth and sixth ribs, with areas of increased density and a ground-glass appearance; there was no cortical rupture or adjacent soft-tissue mass.

A 55-year-old man with no medical history presented with dyspnea on exertion for 1 month. His temperature was 37.4°C, pulse 105/min, blood pressure 111/63 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Examination was notable only for pallor. Chest radiograph and electrocardiogram were normal.  
Complete blood count showed a white blood cell count of 97,600/µL with 26% blasts and 45% circulating monocytes, hemoglobin 6.6 g/dL, and platelets 23,000/µL. Bone marrow examination revealed hypercellularity with increased myeloblasts. Flow cytometry of bone marrow cells was positive for CD13, CD123, CD7, CD34, CD117, and HLA-DR, and a KMT2A–partial tandem duplication was detected. A diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia was made.  
During hospitalization, the patient developed hyperbilirubinemia and progressive dyspnea. A chest radiograph showed a rapidly growing left-sided pleural effusion. Ultrasound-guided thoracentesis yielded 650 mL of bloody fluid. Pleural fluid analysis indicated an exudative, lymphocyte-predominant effusion (46% lymphocytes, 38% monocytes, 16% neutrophils), protein <3 mg/dL, glucose 84 mg/dL, LDH 922 U/L, and an ADA level of 42 U/L. Given these findings, a diagnosis of tuberculous pleural effusion was considered.

A 28-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of diffuse abdominal pain, postprandial abdominal distension, 3–4 loose stools per day, melena, and a 3-kg weight loss. Symptoms began approximately 2 weeks after treatment for COVID-19. Colonoscopy with biopsy of the terminal ileum was performed, and based on clinical correlation, budesonide (3 mg) was given in three doses over 1 month without clinical improvement. On re-evaluation, physical examination, acute-phase reactants, and liver and kidney function tests were normal. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed multiple scattered millimeter-sized nodular calcifications superficially in the omentum of the right and left lower quadrants, as well as clustered nodular calcifications measuring about 3.5×2 cm and 3×1 cm, with heterogeneous omental appearance; the abdominal viscera were otherwise normal. Diagnostic laparoscopy demonstrated diffuse omental calcific nodules, partial omental adhesions to the small intestine in the pelvis, and a small amount of free serous fluid. Two omental fragments (15×5×2 cm and 8×7×1.5 cm) containing numerous firm, gray-white nodules were resected and sent for further evaluation.

A 39-year-old gravida 1, para 1 woman presented with a positive home pregnancy test. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed no intrauterine gestational sac and a cystic mass in the extrauterine space. Initial serum β-HCG was 142.4 mIU/mL. MRI demonstrated a 7 cm cystic mass extending from the anterior wall of the lower uterine segment into the pelvic cavity, with high signal intensity on both T2- and T1-weighted images, suggestive of subacute hemorrhage. Hysteroscopy and laparoscopy revealed a cystic mass containing old hemorrhagic material in the left paracervical retroperitoneal space, with a fistulous tract from the lower uterine cavity into the mass and otherwise normal adnexa. Pathologic examination of the resected tissue showed necrotic tissue, hemorrhagic material, and decidua without definitive diagnosis. On postoperative day 21, serum β-HCG was 304.6 mIU/mL, and persistent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia was diagnosed; weekly methotrexate was administered for 8 weeks. By postoperative day 88, β-HCG remained elevated at 119.8 mIU/mL. On referral, β-HCG was 132.9 mIU/mL, MRI showed a 21 × 12 × 10 mm mass in the left myometrial portion of the lower uterus, slightly hyperintense on T2-weighted imaging, and CT revealed no metastatic disease.

A 13-year-old girl presented with a 6-month history of intense anterior left knee pain, localized to the anterosuperior aspect. The pain was continuous (VAS score 3 at rest), increased to 7 during sports, and over the last month had worsened at night (VAS 8) without daytime exacerbation. Six months earlier she had been diagnosed with patellofemoral malalignment and completed a course of physical therapy without relief. She had no history of trauma, no fever, and no systemic symptoms. On examination, the Q-angle was normal, range of motion was full and painless, and there was focal tenderness at the superior patella at the quadriceps insertion. Patellar crepitus was absent and the patellar apprehension test was negative. Laboratory studies (erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and basic biochemistry) were normal. A standard knee radiograph in two projections was interpreted as negative. Because her pain was predominantly nocturnal, she was given one aspirin nightly for 10 days, after which she reported significant pain reduction whenever she took the medication.

A 5-month-old male infant was brought with 5–6 days of nonbloody vomiting and decreased oral intake. There was no fever, seizures, loss of consciousness, or lethargy, and the head circumference had not visibly increased. Developmentally, he had lost the ability to hold his neck, roll over, coo, and grasp in the past 8–10 days. 

On examination, he appeared dehydrated with sunken eyes. Neurologic examination revealed a tense, bulging anterior fontanelle with sutural separation and a sunsetting sign; plantar reflexes were decreased, and pupils were dilated and sluggishly reactive. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain demonstrated gross hydrocephalus and a large, well-defined lobulated mass centered in the trigone of the occipital horn and body of the left lateral ventricle, showing intense homogeneous enhancement, along with agenesis of the corpus callosum.

Complete blood count and serum biochemistry were within normal limits. A lumbar puncture yielded 1 mL of clear CSF. Cytopathological smears were highly cellular and showed predominantly singly scattered and syncytial clusters of round-to-oval atypical cells, with occasional papillary fragments. The cells exhibited mild pleomorphism, eccentrically placed nuclei, finely granular chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, nuclear membrane indentations, and moderate to abundant pale cytoplasm. Occasional mitotic figures and a few binucleate forms were noted.

A 45-year-old woman presented with 6 months of increasing abdominal cramping and marked distention despite a 35-pound intentional weight loss. She denied other systemic or gastrointestinal symptoms. Her history was notable only for in vitro fertilization resulting in twin pregnancy 7 years earlier; she was otherwise healthy, with a body-mass index of 27 and no medications. On examination, her abdomen was firm and distended, with a palpable large mass; there was no lower-extremity edema. Laboratory studies, including serum hCG, were normal. CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 27×20×13 cm heterogeneous, hypodense intra-abdominal mass with irregular central solid-enhancing components, distinct from the uterus and without ascites or lymphadenopathy. An ultrasound-guided core-needle biopsy showed an admixture of mature adipocytes and spindle cells. Immunohistochemical staining was diffusely positive for smooth muscle actin, desmin, and estrogen receptor, but negative for HMB-45.

A 10-year-old boy presented with mild lower-quadrant abdominal pain without fever or other symptoms. His medical history was unremarkable. In the setting of suspected acute appendicitis, blood tests were normal (Alvarado score 3). Ultrasound of the right lower quadrant showed a normal-sized appendix with minimal adjacent fat hyperechogenicity, small nearby lymph nodes, and a slight pelvic fluid collection; acute appendicitis was excluded. Liver ultrasound revealed intense hyperechogenicity of the hepatic parenchyma along the portal branches without focal lesions. Between the gallbladder, duodenum, and pancreas, there was a multiseptated cystic mass, homogeneously hypoechoic with thin septa; the largest cyst measured approximately 25 mm. The gallbladder was normally distended with homogeneous content. The following day, contrast-enhanced abdominal MRI demonstrated thin-walled cystic structures clustered along the mid-lower edge of the liver adjacent to the gallbladder and hepatic hilum, continuous with periportal T2-weighted hyperintense signal forming a tissue cuff around the portal axis and its intrahepatic branches, with small septa suggesting clustered cysts rather than solid tissue. Post-contrast images showed mild enhancement of the cystic septa and minimal enhancement of the intrahepatic periportal tissue. The findings were considered suggestive of a mixed type of hepatic lymphatic malformation with both macro- and microcystic components.

A 59-year-old woman was referred from a dental clinic for excessive gingival enlargement that had appeared abruptly 20 days earlier. She had a history of hypertension but was not taking any medications associated with gingival overgrowth. She also reported a severe upper respiratory infection 30 days ago. 

On examination, there was generalized gingival enlargement, most pronounced in the maxillary anterior region. In the anterior maxilla, discrete bulbous enlargements were noted in the interproximal areas; posteriorly, the enlargement was diffuse and extended onto the alveolar mucosa, especially on the palate where it extended beyond the cingula of the anterior teeth. The gingiva was pale blue with a glazed texture, loss of stippling, and was generally friable. Spontaneous bleeding was observed on the palatal surfaces of the canine and premolar regions.

A panoramic radiograph showed generalized horizontal bone loss, most marked in the anterior maxilla, although the clinical enlargement was notably more pronounced than the radiographic bone loss. Extraoral examination revealed a bruise adjacent to the right lower lip without any recalled trauma and mild tenderness and enlargement of the right cervical lymph nodes. The patient also reported ongoing general weakness and headache.

Given the disproportionate gingival findings and systemic symptoms, a complete blood count with differential was obtained.

A 78-year-old man presented with a 4-week history of productive cough, occasional hemoptysis, and epistaxis. His medical history included hypertension and treated tuberculosis; he was an ex–cigarette smoker. Physical examination was unremarkable. A chest radiograph showed a spiculated 3.5 cm mass in the right lower zone. CT of the thorax demonstrated a 5 cm cavitating mass in the right lower lobe with bilateral small cavitating nodules. Laboratory tests revealed a cytoplasmic ANCA titre of 1 / 20 and a PR3 level of 14.6 IU ml−1. CT-guided biopsy of the right lower lobe mass showed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation without evidence of malignancy. The patient was started on subcutaneous methotrexate, and after 3 months a chest radiograph showed reduction of the nodule to 2 cm. He then developed renal impairment attributed to disease progression and/or methotrexate toxicity, and treatment was switched to high-dose intravenous cyclophosphamide with a tapering dose of oral prednisolone. After 3 months of cyclophosphamide, he developed a new cough and chest radiography showed enlargement of the right lower lobe nodule to 4 cm; CT confirmed an increase to a 5 cm cavitating mass at the same location.

A 6-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a painless, progressively enlarging mass in the inferotemporal quadrant of the left eye, first noted more than one year earlier. His ophthalmic history included cataract extraction in the left eye at 6 months of age and placement of an Ahmed tube at 1 year for secondary glaucoma. He subsequently developed a dense vitreous hemorrhage and an intense intraocular inflammation, diagnosed as suspected endophthalmitis, which was treated by pars plana vitrectomy and intravitreal antibiotics; the eye ultimately became blind and atrophic.

At presentation, visual acuity was 20/25 in the right eye and no light perception in the left eye. Examination of the left eye revealed an irregular red–yellow bulging mass at the inferotemporal corneoscleral limbus with prominent sentinel vessels, band keratopathy, corneoscleral thinning, and corneal opacification. The anterior chamber was shallow, and the iris was atrophic with a distorted pupil. The posterior pole was not visible.

B-scan ultrasonography showed heterogeneous dense vitreous opacities, a large highly reflective lesion casting an acoustic shadow over the inferior retina, and a 360° bullous choroidal detachment. Ultrasound biomicroscopy demonstrated an inferotemporal elevated area with underlying dense organized opacities. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed an anterior intraocular mass with a heterogeneous soft-tissue component, scleral thinning, and extra-scleral extension spanning from the 3 to 8 o’clock positions.

Given the lack of visual potential and suspicion of a malignant process, enucleation of the left eye was planned.

A 12-year-old girl presented with a chief complaint of trismus. Several months earlier, she had noticed a bulge in the left maxillary gingiva associated with pain on pressure but no spontaneous pain. She was afebrile, with no history of trauma or medications.  
On examination, her height was 164 cm and weight 54 kg. Extraoral inspection showed a slight bulge of the left cheek with facial asymmetry and severe trismus; maximum mouth opening was 18 mm. No palpable cervical lymphadenopathy was noted.  
Intraorally, there was a firm mass extending from the left maxillary first molar to the maxillary tuberosity, interfering with occlusion on that side.  
Panoramic radiography demonstrated impaction of the left maxillary second molar and resorption of alveolar bone between the left maxillary molar area and the maxillary tuberosity.  
Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a soft-tissue mass extending from the left masticator space into the buccal space and the alveolar regions of the maxilla and mandible, with pressure resorption of the anterior ramus border, the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus, and the lateral pterygoid plate; maxillary sinus involvement was suspected.  
Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI showed a correspondingly high-signal mass and enhancement in the left cervical and retropharyngeal (Rouviere) lymph nodes.

A 47-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a radiolucent lesion adjacent to the left maxillary lateral incisor. She noted no pain. Oral examination revealed a soft‐tissue depression of the left palatal mucosa in the lateral‐incisor and canine region without erythema or swelling. The area was non‐tender to palpation, but percussion elicited a positive response and slight mobility of the adjacent teeth. 

Panoramic radiography showed a poorly defined radiolucent lesion with an irregular border extending from the left lateral incisor to the first premolar and involving the alveolar ridge. Intraoral films demonstrated significant external resorption of the roots of the involved teeth. Cone‐beam computed tomography revealed an osteolytic lesion with an undulating border in the upper left anterior maxilla, destruction of the palatal cortical bone, thinning of the labial cortical plate, external root resorption, and a soft‐tissue shadow corresponding to the palatal depression; no bucco‐palatal expansion was noted.

On the basis of the ill‐defined border and invasive bony destruction, clinicians provisionally considered minor salivary gland malignancy or a benign odontogenic tumor with strong osteolytic activity.

A 58-year-old woman presented with generalized seizures characterized by right-leg cramping, a 1–2-minute collapse while remaining conscious, and upward gaze. She denied vertigo, numbness, weakness, nausea, or vomiting. She had no history of hypertension, renal disease, or von Hippel–Lindau syndrome; there was no family history of similar disorders. On examination, she was fully conscious with normal strength and no visual defects, tinnitus, hematuria, or hyperhidrosis. Laboratory results showed a red blood cell count of 4.31 × 10^6/μL, hemoglobin 13.3 g/dL, and hematocrit 38.7%. 

Noncontrast CT of the brain revealed a 1.4 cm enhancing nodule in the right frontal lobe with surrounding edema. FLAIR MRI showed a mass with a slightly hyperintense mural component, marked perifocal edema, and a leftward midline shift. After gadolinium, T1-weighted images demonstrated a hyperintense heterogeneous nodule, and T2-weighted images showed a hyperintense cystic area. Intense contrast enhancement and prominent serpentine flow voids suggested a highly vascular lesion. Digital subtraction angiography revealed tightly packed, wide vessels fed by branches of the right anterior cerebral artery and a dilated draining vein. 

Preoperative differential diagnoses included hemangioblastoma with an advanced astroglial response, angioglioma (highly vascular anomaly, arteriovenous malformation, and glioma), brain metastasis, lymphoma, and glioblastoma multiforme.

A 65-year-old Caucasian man was referred for evaluation of leukocytosis. Two months of progressive exertional dyspnea prompted a CBC showing WBC >100 K/μL (predominantly lymphocytes) and hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL; a WBC >100 K/μL had been documented two years earlier without further work-up. He reported diminished appetite and fatigue but denied fevers, night sweats, weight loss, headaches, dizziness, blurred vision, or chest pain.
