His history was notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension; medications included amlodipine, valsartan, metformin, and glimepiride. He had no recent infections or new medications.

On examination, blood pressure was 129/76 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. He appeared well, with bilateral supraclavicular lymph nodes ~2 cm and palpable splenomegaly. There were no signs of infection.

Laboratory studies revealed: WBC 593 K/μL (3.9–11.0 K/μL), hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL (12.4–18.0 g/dL), MCV 103 fL (80–99 fL), platelets 85 ×10^3/μL (160–392 ×10^3/μL). Chemistry showed BUN 31 mg/dL (7–25 mg/dL), creatinine 1.0 mg/dL (0.7–1.25 mg/dL), potassium 6.1 mmol/L (3.5–5.3 mmol/L), calcium 10.4 mg/dL (8.6–10.3 mg/dL), uric acid 9.5 mg/dL (4.0–8.0 mg/dL), phosphorus 3.6 mg/dL (2.1–4.3 mg/dL), LDH 301 U/L (120–250 U/L), beta-2 microglobulin 11.5 mg/L (<2.51 mg/L). Peripheral smear showed numerous small lymphocytes and smudge cells without red cell agglutination. Flow cytometry identified a clonal B-cell population (81%) that was CD5+, CD10–, CD19+, CD20+, FMC7+, CD23+. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated diffuse bulky lymphadenopathy (up to 6.2 cm) and hepatosplenomegaly (spleen 22 cm).

A 59-year-old man presented with a 4-week history of a pressure sensation in the rectum and rectal imperiosity. He had no significant personal or family medical history. On rectal examination, a firm, 4-cm pre-rectal mass was palpated on the right side of the pelvis. His performance status was 0, and serum prostate-specific antigen was normal. Pelvic ultrasonography identified a right-sided pelvic mass. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated an 8-cm heterogeneous mass predominantly in the right pelvis, likely arising from the right seminal vesicle and abutting the posterior bladder wall and anterior rectal wall. A CT-guided transperineal core-needle biopsy of the mass revealed a well-differentiated leiomyosarcoma. Pelvic MRI confirmed a mass centred on the right seminal vesicle, displacing the prostate and left seminal vesicle, with loss of the cleavage plane at the right prostate and right obturator muscle, yet preserving a fat interface between the mass and both the bladder and rectum. No lymphadenopathy or distant metastases were detected.

A 6-year-old girl was evaluated for several weeks of dry cough that failed to improve with over-the-counter cold remedies, amoxicillin-clavulanate, and azithromycin. Two years earlier she had been treated for lymphocyte-predominant leukocytosis without a clear diagnosis; at that time, physical examination, blood chemistry, bone marrow biopsy, and abdominal ultrasound were normal, but peripheral blood flow cytometry showed more than 85% mature T-lymphocytes. Hydroxyurea was discontinued after 18 months because of lack of efficacy.

On examination now, she weighed 14 kg (−3 SD) and measured 110 cm (−1 SD). Heart and lung sounds were absent over the left hemithorax; percussion was dull on the left and resonant on the right. The left chest was visibly bulging. There was no respiratory distress or cyanosis. Vital signs: respiratory rate 32/min, heart rate 93/min, blood pressure 120/80 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 92% on room air.

Complete blood count again demonstrated severe lymphocytosis, and peripheral blood immunophenotyping confirmed that 80% of circulating cells were mature T lymphocytes.

A chest radiograph revealed diffuse opacification of the left hemithorax with a shift of the mediastinum to the right. Contrast-enhanced chest CT showed a 130 × 160 × 160 mm heterogeneous, fat-containing soft-tissue mass arising in the anterior mediastinum, causing complete collapse of the left lung and contralateral mediastinal shift, with no invasion of adjacent structures.

An 18-year-old woman presented with right-sided hearing loss and intermittent nonpulsatile tinnitus. She had a history, dating to age 3, of right otitis media with effusion treated medically, and at age 8 underwent right myringotomy with ventilation tube and adenoidectomy. Two years later she received a T-tube, which was removed after two years; symptoms then recurred. She denied otorrhea, otalgia, vertigo, or neurologic symptoms. Examination showed a retracted right tympanic membrane; the left ear was normal. An audiogram revealed moderate right conductive hearing loss, and tympanometry was type A with reduced compliance. CT of the temporal bone demonstrated a right mastoid and middle ear mass with erosion of the floor of the middle cranial fossa and extradural extension elevating the right temporal lobe. MRI of the temporal bone and brain showed a heterogeneous but predominantly hyperintense mass on both T1- and T2-weighted images in the right mastoid and middle ear cavity, elevating the right temporal lobe.

A 45-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a retroperitoneal left adrenal mass that had been discovered incidentally on abdominal ultrasonography 3 months earlier. His medical history was notable only for mild hypertension on medication and an appendectomy 37 years earlier; he had no family history of endocrine or neoplastic disease. On examination, his abdomen was soft, with no palpable masses; there were no cutaneous lesions or lymphadenopathy. Routine blood tests were normal. Twenty-four–hour urinary catecholamines, cortisol, and chromogranin levels were all within normal limits. Ultrasonography showed a heterogeneous, expansive mass measuring 12 cm in maximal diameter adjacent to the left adrenal gland. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen confirmed a 14 cm heterogeneous mass with both solid and cystic components arising from the left adrenal gland.

A 77‐year‐old woman presented with pollakiuria. Ultrasonography showed left hydronephrosis. Contrast‐enhanced computed tomography revealed thickening of the bladder wall and para‐aortic and bilateral external iliac lymphadenopathy. Cystoscopy demonstrated mucosal swelling and redness around the bladder neck without an exophytic tumor. Transurethral biopsy revealed high‐grade invasive urothelial carcinoma. The clinical stage was T2N1M1. She received eight courses of cisplatin (56 mg/m2 on day 2) and gemcitabine (1000 mg/m2 on days 1 and 8), with a 20% dose reduction of cisplatin. Despite therapy, lymphadenopathy persisted. After the eighth cycle, she developed bilateral lower‐leg edema and multiple nodular erythematous lesions on the lower abdominal wall. Follow‐up CT showed new or progressive axillary and inguinal lymph node enlargement.

A 61-year-old obese (BMI 35.2) woman of Maltese background presented with a 5-year history of intermittent, non-specific abdominal pain. Her medical history included hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia; she denied paroxysmal hypertension, flushing, syncope, or palpitations. Physical examination revealed no abdominal masses or tenderness. An abdominal CT scan demonstrated a 9.5 × 8.6 cm right adrenal lesion with fat lobules, calcifications, and heterogeneous progressive enhancement. An adrenal biochemical workup showed normal results: potassium 4.7 mmol/L, plasma renin 6.6 mU/L, plasma aldosterone 228 pmol/L, aldosterone-to-renin ratio 35, 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test 44 nmol/L, plasma normetanephrines 580 pmol/L, plasma metanephrines 150 pmol/L, DHEAS 2.3 µmol/L, and chromogranin A 88 µg/L. Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed a 9.8 × 8.2 × 8.1 cm right adrenal mass with heterogeneous T1 and T2 signal intensity and nodular peripheral enhancement with progressive central fill-in. An ^18F-FDG PET scan showed a predominantly photopenic mass with a mild peripheral rim of uptake (SUV max, 3.4). A technetium-99m–labeled red blood cell scan did not demonstrate delayed pooling of tracer.

An infant boy was born at 40 weeks of gestation to healthy, non-consanguineous parents via forceps-assisted vaginal delivery. His birth weight was 2410 g (small for gestational age), and Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes. At 15 hours of life, he became hypothermic (core temperature, 36°C) and was transferred to the NICU. Laboratory evaluation showed a white-cell count of 15.1×10^9/L, hemoglobin of 185 g/L, platelet count of 323×10^9/L, and a normal differential. A TORCH screen was negative, and empiric antibiotics were started pending blood cultures. By 36 hours of life, he was normothermic, tolerating full feeds, and antibiotics were discontinued after 48 hours of negative cultures.

On day 4 of life, he acutely developed poor respiratory effort, hypotension, and peripheral hypoperfusion, accompanied by abdominal distension and marked hepatomegaly. Initially irritable, he rapidly became lethargic and required endotracheal intubation. Urgent cranial ultrasonography and chest radiography were unremarkable. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed no structural cardiac defects but showed low intraventricular volume, myocardial thickening, and decreased systolic function. Despite aggressive fluid resuscitation and inotropic support, hypotension persisted. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a complex intra-abdominal fluid collection consistent with hemoperitoneum. The infant was taken to the operating room for emergency laparotomy.

A 62-year-old woman with a history of FIGO stage IIB cervical squamous carcinoma treated 32 years earlier with radical hysterectomy, bilateral iliac lymph node dissection, and adjuvant radiation therapy (70 Gy external beam plus 30.5 Gy brachytherapy) presented with rectal bleeding. On digital rectal examination, a solid exophytic mass was palpated 5 cm above the anal verge. Rigid proctosigmoidoscopy revealed a 3 cm anterior wall rectal tumor with irregular margins and swollen mucosa; colonoscopy showed no synchronous lesions. Snare biopsy demonstrated an undifferentiated malignant nonepithelial tumor, and immunohistochemical analysis was inconclusive due to insufficient tissue. Pelvic MRI (1.5 T, MERCURY protocol) showed a 30 mm lower rectal tumor 4 cm above the anorectal junction with mesorectal infiltration up to 3 mm (mrT3b), no mesorectal fascia involvement (mrCRM−), no extramural vascular invasion (mrEMVI−), and no radiologic lymph node involvement (mrN0). The vaginal stump and rectovaginal septum exhibited marked T2 signal fibrosis. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no distant metastases or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies, including blood, serum, and urine tests, and upper GI endoscopy were unremarkable. The working diagnosis was a malignant nonepithelial lower rectal tumor of unknown origin, staged as mrT3a mrN0 cM0.

An 8-month-old male, born full term, was referred to the Emergency Department with a 9-day history of high-grade fevers. There were no vomiting, diarrhea, rash, seizures, sick contacts, or travel history. On exam, he had dry, red lips; temperature was 36.5 °C and heart rate 140 beats/min, with other vitals normal for age. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, MCV 81 fL, WBC 31,500/mm3, platelets 618,000/mm3, CRP 21.53 mg/L, sodium 133 mmol/L, chloride 98 mmol/L, and a normal urinalysis. Blood cultures drawn at the primary care office showed no growth. A chest radiograph was normal. With an initial suspicion of Kawasaki disease, intravenous ceftriaxone was started and the patient was admitted to rheumatology; echocardiography showed no coronary aneurysms. Further exam revealed mild right-sided abdominal pain. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a large, heterogeneous right intra-abdominal mass concerning for neoplasm versus abscess. Serum alpha-fetoprotein, β–human chorionic gonadotropin, urine homovanillic acid, vanillylmandelic acid, liver function tests, and coagulation profile were all normal. A contrast-enhanced CT scan showed a rim-enhancing cystic mass. The lesion was considered most consistent with an abscess or a superinfected duplication cyst and less likely to represent a malignancy. In light of ongoing fevers, antibiotics were switched to piperacillin–tazobactam pending planned surgical exploration.

A 67-year-old man presented to the emergency department with severe pain in his left thigh. His medical history was notable for a prior left inguinal hernia repair. On examination, there was a firm bulge in the left groin that could not be reduced by manual pressure.  
An ultrasound of the groin demonstrated a solid mass with mixed echotexture and intense vascularity.  
Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a well-encapsulated, predominantly adipose mass measuring 20 × 24 × 21 cm. The lesion extended from the mesogastrium and left lumbar region into the left iliac fossa and herniated through the ipsilateral inguinal canal. The internal structure was inhomogeneous, with thin septa and several hyperdense nodules (largest ~30 mm) showing early and intense contrast enhancement. The mass displaced but did not invade adjacent bowel loops, colon, bladder, ureter, major vessels, or other organs.

A 50-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with a 1-week history of rapidly progressive gait disturbance. He reported no back pain, fevers, night sweats, or weight loss and had no history of smoking or known malignancy. On examination, he had full strength throughout all extremities but had decreased sensation from the T3 dermatome downward. He exhibited four beats of clonus bilaterally, hyperreflexia in the lower extremities, and profound ataxia, rendering him unable to walk more than a few steps. 

Contrast-enhanced MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrated a diffusely enhancing lesion centered at T1 with near-circumferential epidural extension causing severe cord compression. CT of the thoracic spine showed an expansile bony lesion of the T1 vertebral body with extension into the left pedicle and posterior elements. CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no evidence of a primary malignancy, and laboratory studies, including inflammatory markers, were within normal limits. 

Given his rapidly progressive neurological decline, the decision was made to proceed urgently with surgical decompression, spinal stabilization, and tissue diagnosis.

A 50-year-old woman presented with a swelling of the gums in the upper front tooth region of 4 years’ duration. It began as a small painless nodule and slowly increased to about 3.0×2.5 cm, causing an obvious bulge of the upper lip. She had no discomfort and no relevant medical history. On examination, there was a firm, ovoid, well-circumscribed swelling measuring 3.0×2.5 cm on the attached gingiva adjacent to teeth 11 and 12, extending from the free marginal groove inferiorly to the buccal sulcus superiorly; the marginal gingiva was uninvolved, and there was no ulceration. The Silness and Löe plaque index was 1.2 (fair). Periapical radiography showed a mild alteration in the trabecular pattern in the region of teeth 11 and 12.

A 55-year-old man presented with a 4-year history of chronic vomiting of food remnants and recent weight loss of 34 kg over 1 month. He also reported chronic partial constipation. Physical examination revealed a distended abdomen but was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory tests were within normal limits. Upper endoscopy showed an enlarged, food-filled stomach and severe edema at the pylorus, preventing passage of the endoscope into the duodenum. The finding was interpreted as gastric outlet obstruction due to pyloric stenosis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a severely dilated stomach and a 4 cm mass in the pyloric region with 1 cm thickening of the pyloric wall.

A 78-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of weight loss and intermittent abdominal pain. Contrast-enhanced CT performed at an outside hospital showed a pancreatic mass occupying the main pancreatic duct (MPD), and he was referred for further evaluation. On examination, his abdominal pain had resolved; bowel sounds were normal, and there was no palpable abdominal mass. Laboratory studies demonstrated normal hepatobiliary enzymes and no elevation in tumor markers (including CEA, CA19-9, and AFP). Transabdominal ultrasound revealed a dilated MPD filled by a diffusely low-echoic lesion. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 9-mm MPD completely occupied by a poorly enhancing tumor. Diffusion-weighted MRI demonstrated high signal intensity throughout the ductal lesion. Endoscopic ultrasonography confirmed a hypoechoic tumor filling the duct, with thinning of the surrounding pancreatic parenchyma and an indistinct duct-parenchyma interface, making EUS-FNA unfeasible. ERCP revealed a dilated, translucent MPD, and an endoscopic biopsy was obtained through the papilla of Vater. FDG-PET showed intense uptake in the pancreatic head (SUVmax 20.1) without evidence of distant metastases.

A 41-year-old woman presented with sudden onset of painless gross hematuria for 1 month. She had no significant past medical or family history. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 113 g/L, hematocrit 34.2%, and platelet count 206 ×10^9/L. Urinalysis revealed >100 red blood cells and 0–3 white blood cells per high-powered field, with no proteinuria or pyuria. 

Cystoscopy at an outside hospital showed a bluish ovoid mass with blood clots on the anterior wall of the bladder, and a transurethral resection of the bladder tumour was performed. The initial biopsy showed gland cystitis and local urothelial hyperplasia with nodule formation, but no clear cancer cells. 

Computed tomography urography demonstrated a 5.0 cm × 3.1 cm × 4.0 cm mass arising from the superior and anterior bladder wall, with multiple punctate calcifications and marked uneven enhancement, which was suspected to be urachal carcinoma.

A 68-year-old man presented with jaundice without abdominal pain. He had a history of an 8 cm × 4.7 cm multilobulated heterogeneous tumor of the parieto-occipital lobes resected 14 years earlier and diagnosed as solitary fibrous tumor, with two subsequent recurrences treated by radiosurgery and craniotomy. Physical examination revealed jaundice only. Laboratory tests showed aspartate aminotransferase 223 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 394 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 762 U/L, total bilirubin 4.18 mg/dL, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 1990 U/L, normal amylase and lipase, normal carcinoembryonic antigen, and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 of 42.2 U/mL. Abdominal CT demonstrated a 3.5 cm mass in the pancreatic head, causing biliary and pancreatic duct dilation (double duct sign); the mass was hypervascular in the arterial phase and isovascular in the delayed phase, with relatively clear boundaries. MRI showed that the lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images and isointense on T2-weighted images compared with the pancreatic parenchyma.

A 24-year-old woman was admitted with sudden headache and left-sided weakness 6 hours earlier. She had no history of hypertension. Initial head CT showed an irregular right frontal lobe hematoma. Laboratory studies revealed a serum β-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-HCG) level of 2266 mIU/mL; CA 19-9 was 37.13 U/mL. She received mannitol and supportive care and was discharged.  

Two weeks later, she was transferred for a generalized seizure. On examination, she was alert; pupils were equal and reactive. She had limited leftward gaze bilaterally, symmetric forehead wrinkles, tongue deviation to the left, and left upper and lower limb strength of grade IV–; right limbs were grade V. Obstetric history included a normal delivery 2 years ago, an abortion 1 year ago, an intrauterine device placed 7 months ago, and regular menses for the last 2 months.  

During hospitalization, she had two more seizures and her serum β-HCG rose from 63 148 to 980 893 mIU/mL. Gynecologic ultrasonography showed a normal uterus and adnexa, with no evidence of intrauterine or ectopic pregnancy. Repeat head CT demonstrated a new hemorrhagic focus at the margin of the chronic hematoma, which had enlarged substantially 10 days later. Head MRA and digital subtraction angiography showed no aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation. Chest radiograph revealed a 6-cm mass in the right lung; abdominal and pelvic CT scans were unremarkable.

A 66-year-old Arab man with diabetes presented with a 5-week history of a rapidly enlarging, tender nodule at the right lateral canthus extending onto the lower eyelid. He reported previous similar lesions: one at the lower lip diagnosed as squamous cell carcinoma 6 years ago and treated surgically, which recurred at the left lateral canthal area and then spontaneously resolved over 5 months; and another on the right nasolabial fold that disappeared within a few weeks. 

On examination, there was a 1.3-cm firm, movable, dome-shaped papule with a smooth, shiny surface and a central crateriform ulceration containing a keratin plug. The lesion was secondarily infected but without regional lymphadenopathy. Vital signs were normal.

A preliminary diagnosis of a secondarily infected keratoacanthoma was made. The differential diagnoses included squamous cell carcinoma, verrucous carcinoma, and metastatic skin carcinoma. Given the risk of malignancy and functional concerns, an excisional biopsy with a 3-mm margin and primary closure was performed under local anesthesia without complications.

A 46-year-old man presented initially with abdominal pain and was found to have an ileal mass causing intussusception. His history was notable for chronic diarrhoea and an elevated 24-hour urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid level (90.3 mg; reference 0.0–14.9 mg). CT of the chest performed for staging showed bilateral subcentimetre pulmonary nodules and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. The patient’s abdominal symptoms resolved, but he was lost to follow-up.

Five years later, he returned with a one-month history of fatigue, cough, and dyspnoea, along with a 40-lb weight loss over six months and persistent diarrhoea. He smoked marijuana daily and had a five pack-year history of tobacco use. Repeat chest CT again showed scattered pulmonary nodules and bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, as well as new left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.

Bronchoscopic biopsy of the hilar lymph nodes revealed non-caseating granulomas. A QuantiFERON-TB Gold assay was negative, and bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and tissue were also negative. Pulmonary function testing demonstrated a moderate obstructive ventilatory defect without bronchodilator response (FEV1 57% predicted, FEV1/FVC 54%, DLCO 59% predicted). On the basis of the clinical presentation, imaging, and histopathology, sarcoidosis was diagnosed. He was treated with oral corticosteroids and inhaled bronchodilators for a concurrent diagnosis of COPD.

Despite therapy, he continued to have weight loss, diarrhoea, wheezing, and shortness of breath. Given that supraclavicular lymphadenopathy and systemic weight loss are atypical for sarcoidosis, further evaluation of the supraclavicular node was planned.

A 71-year-old Hispanic man was referred for a 2-month history of dysphagia and left oropharyngeal fullness. His medical history included hypertension, dyslipidemia, atrial fibrillation, and a left superficial parotidectomy in 2008 for a Warthin tumor, followed by Frey syndrome. He is an active smoker with a 27.5–pack-year history. On examination, there was left soft-palate fullness without ulceration. Review of contrast-enhanced CT images from 2008 showed an enlarged left intraparotid lymph node with central hypodensity and, retrospectively, a small left oropharyngeal nodule. In early 2014, MRI of the head and neck demonstrated a small (8 mm), submucosal, ovoid nodule in the left oropharyngeal airway with a peripheral ring of enhancement.

A 32-year-old woman presented with intermittent, dull left lower quadrant abdominal pain radiating to the left flank for 3 weeks. Her medical history included Crohn’s disease (quiescent on mesalamine), endometriosis, disseminated histoplasmosis, and nephrolithiasis; she denied fevers, night sweats, weight loss, diarrhea, or rectal bleeding. She had no recent changes in bowel habits and denied oral-intake–related pain. 

Thirteen years earlier, she underwent resection of 75 cm of jejunum and 10 cm of terminal ileum for Crohn’s disease; subsequent management included methotrexate and adalimumab, but therapy was modified to mesalamine after an episode of histoplasmosis in 2017. Since then, her Crohn’s disease had been well controlled.

In 2019, contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 5.3 × 3.8 cm heterogeneous solid mass in the left retroperitoneum. Diagnostic laparoscopy confirmed a retroperitoneal mass; further workup was delayed by the pandemic. 

On examination, she had mild suprapubic and left lower quadrant tenderness without palpable lymphadenopathy or masses. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 12.7 g/dL, a white-cell count of 5.0 × 10^9/L (85% neutrophils), a platelet count of 305 × 10^9/L, and a C-reactive protein level of 3.23 mg/L.

Magnetic resonance enterography demonstrated a well-defined, lobulated, avidly enhancing left pelvic sidewall lesion measuring 4.3 × 5.7 × 5.1 cm, described as radiographically consistent with a paraganglioma, peripheral nerve sheath tumor, or desmoid tumor. Follow-up CT showed similar findings without additional lesions. Flexible sigmoidoscopy with endoscopic ultrasound-guided biopsy revealed a polymorphous population of lymphocytes but was nondiagnostic. Due to persistent discomfort, she elected to undergo surgical resection of the mass.

A 31-year-old Dutch man of Turkish origin presented with low back pain. On examination, a marked effusion of the right knee was noted, which the patient reported had been present for two years with intermittent pain. He denied trauma. His medical history included psoriasis; his father had type 2 diabetes mellitus. Aspiration of the knee yielded 113 cc of citrine‐colored fluid, and he was treated with rest and NSAIDs without improvement. Plain radiographs of the knee demonstrated effusion and osteoarthritic changes. One week later, he returned with recurrent swelling. Ultrasonography showed a large suprapatellar fluid collection with synovial villi but no hyperemia; a bony spur was seen on the medial femoral condyle. Laboratory studies revealed normal inflammatory markers and negative rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP antibodies, and HLA-B27 typing. A bone scan with SPECT demonstrated mildly to moderately increased remodeling in both knees, predominantly on the right. MRI showed moderate knee osteoarthritis, a region of chondropathy in the medial tibial cartilage, and a marked joint effusion.

A 45-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of a lump in her left breast, associated with bloody discharge. On examination, there was a hard, tender 8×7-cm mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast and palpable left axillary lymph nodes; the right breast was normal. Routine blood tests were within normal limits. To exclude other primary sites, chest radiograph, abdominal ultrasonography, thoracic computed tomography, and gynecologic examination were performed, and no other primary lesion was detected. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the breast mass revealed carcinoma. The patient underwent a modified radical mastectomy with axillary lymph node clearance.  

On microscopic examination, the tumor was composed of cells with large hyperchromatic nuclei and abundant cytoplasm, multiple foci of keratin pearl formation of varying sizes, and marked mitotic activity. There was no origin from the surface epithelium and no different tumoral components were seen. No axillary lymph node deposits were identified.

A 58-year-old man was referred after routine laboratory studies showed an elevated bilirubin level. He denied abdominal pain, bloating, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Physical examination revealed no jaundice or palpable abdominal mass. His medical history included removal of multiple colonic polyps, which were tubular adenomas on pathology.

Laboratory tests showed:
• White blood cell count 6.84×10^9/L  
• Hemoglobin 147 g/L  
• Aspartate aminotransferase 23.8 IU/L  
• Alanine aminotransferase 20.9 IU/L  
• Alkaline phosphatase 98.6 IU/L  
• Total bilirubin 50.2 μmol/L (direct 7.1 μmol/L; indirect 43.1 μmol/L)  
• Alpha-fetoprotein, carbohydrate antigen 19-9, and carcinoembryonic antigen within normal limits

Contrast-enhanced CT of the liver demonstrated a slightly hypodense mass in segment VI measuring 40×28 mm with indistinct borders. In the late arterial phase, the mass showed uneven and marked enhancement, and in the venous phase it exhibited sustained enhancement.

A 77-year-old man presented with a one-month history of multiple, slightly painful nodules on his lower legs. His past medical history included hypertension, dyslipidemia, and a prior myocardial infarction; medications were aspirin, diltiazem, lovastatin, and valsartan. Two weeks after onset, the nodules increased in number and induration, and his general practitioner referred him to dermatology. A presumptive diagnosis of panniculitis was made, and prednisone 25 mg daily was prescribed without improvement.

On admission, he was afebrile, blood pressure was 160/70 mmHg, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Cutaneous examination revealed multiple, ill-defined, firm, erythematous-violaceous nodules, 2–4 cm in diameter, distributed on both lower legs; one nodule on the left leg showed superficial ulceration.

Laboratory studies showed:  
• Serum lipase 6027 U/L (normal 13–60) with normal amylase  
• Hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL (normocytic anemia)  
• Creatinine 1.26 mg/dL  
• ESR 69 mm/h; CRP 6.07 mg/dL  
• GGT 163 U/L; LDH 489 U/L  
• Tumor markers: CEA, CA 19-9, PSA within normal limits; AFP 202.7 ng/mL

A deep skin biopsy of a nodule demonstrated lobular fat necrosis with liquefaction of adipocytes, anuclear “ghost” cells, and calcium deposits.

A 35-year-old woman presented with neck pain after a motor vehicle accident. She had a 15-year history of migraine headaches; over the past year they had become more severe and positional (worse when lying down). She also reported 3 months of memory impairment and dizziness, and 1 year of gradual-onset tinnitus and dysphagia. Physical examination was unremarkable. 

Noncontrast CT of the head revealed a mass in the left cerebellomedullary cistern isodense to gray matter without calcifications. CT angiography showed displacement of the prepontine vessels without encasement. MRI demonstrated a 3.4×3.3×3.3 cm, well-circumscribed mass in the left cerebellomedullary and premedullary cisterns that was hyperintense to CSF on T1- and T2-weighted images, did not restrict diffusion, showed a focus of susceptibility-related signal loss, had no enhancement, and exerted mass effect on the brainstem and cerebellum without surrounding edema.

A 79-year-old white man presented with a two-month history of multiple asymptomatic, disseminated erythematous papules. On examination, there were symmetrically distributed papules, some clustered, most prominent on the dorsal aspects of the trunk and proximal limbs; the scalp, mucous membranes, palms, and soles were spared. He had no systemic symptoms, and lesion sensitivity was preserved. Laboratory tests for syphilis and leprosy were negative. A skin biopsy showed a dense mononuclear dermal infiltrate without atypia occupying the entire dermis, with perivascular lymphocyte clusters in the superficial dermis. Wade staining was negative. Immunohistochemical staining was positive only for CD68 and negative for CD1a, CD34, and S100.

A 63-year-old woman with hypertension, diabetes, and obstructive sleep apnea noted a new lump in her left breast over 3 months. Her prior mammogram 1 year earlier was normal. She had menarche at age 12, two full-term pregnancies, hysterectomy at 43, menopause at 55, and no personal history of breast, colon, or ovarian cancer.

On examination, there was a firm, rubbery 1.5 cm mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast without skin changes, nipple retraction, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Diagnostic 3D mammography showed a new calcified, lobulated mass in the left upper outer quadrant, suggestive of bone. Targeted ultrasound confirmed a 1.5 cm irregularly calcified mass. An ultrasound-guided core biopsy revealed an atypical biphasic lesion with metaplastic bone formation; “differentials included periductal stromal sarcoma and phyllodes tumor.” MRI was attempted but not completed due to body habitus. The patient underwent lumpectomy.

Histologically, the lesion showed a cellular spindle-cell stroma with osteoid matrix and cytologic atypia, and a mitotic rate of 5 per 10 high-power fields. There was no necrosis or lymphovascular invasion. Immunohistochemical staining was negative for pankeratin, CK5/6, SMA, and desmin, while p53 and Ki-67 were elevated.

A 36-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 3, HIV-positive on antiretroviral therapy, presented for evaluation of extensive vulval and nipple lesions. Two years earlier she had noted progressive warty growths on her vulva and nipples that were never treated. She complained of vulval pain and a malodorous discharge. She denied other sexually transmitted infections. She uses barrier contraception. Her most recent CD4 count was 275 cells/mm3 and HIV viral load was 35 copies/mL. On admission she was pale; hemoglobin was 7.9 g/dL and platelet count was 104 × 10^9/L. Blood pressure was 116/48 mmHg and pulse 110 beats/min. Breast examination revealed bilateral 4 × 4 cm condylomatous-appearing lesions covering the nipples without extension to the areola; there was no bleeding and no palpable axillary lymphadenopathy. Vulval examination showed extensive exophytic warts involving both labia majora and minora, measuring in aggregate 15 × 10 cm, extending to the posterior commissure; the clitoris and clitoral hood were spared. The remainder of the systemic examination was unremarkable.

A 35-year-old man undergoing preoperative evaluation before septoplasty was found to have an asymptomatic lytic lesion in the right sphenoid wing on CT. He had no neurological or systemic symptoms, and general and cranial nerve examinations were normal. Non-contrast CT of the head demonstrated a well-demarcated fibro-osseous lesion in the right sphenoid wing with adjacent bone remodeling and sclerosis. MRI of the head showed a roughly 3 cm lesion centered in the right sphenoid wing, extending inferiorly to the pterygoid plate and involving the foramen rotundum; the lesion was low in signal intensity on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously isointense on T2-weighted sequences, and exhibited prominent contrast enhancement. The preoperative differential diagnosis included intraosseous meningioma, metastatic tumor, and granulomatous infection.

A 56-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of progressive weakness and numbness in both legs, which had worsened over the past 10 months, causing unsteady gait and occasional falls. His medical history was notable for 4 years of hypertension, managed with irbesartan. On examination, neck examination showed no rigidity; muscle strength was grade IV in both lower extremities and grade V in both upper extremities, with normal muscle tone. Sensory testing revealed decreased pain, warmth, and light touch below the inguinal level bilaterally; pathological reflexes were negative. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the thoracic spine demonstrated an intramedullary mass measuring 8.0 × 1.0 × 1.0 cm occupying nearly the entire canal at T10–T12. The lesion was hyperintense on T1-weighted images and hypointense on T2-weighted images. On contrast-enhanced T1-weighted imaging, the signal intensity was similar to that on unenhanced images, rendering enhancement uncertain. Minimal T2 hyperintense edema was noted above the mass.

Based on imaging and clinical presentation, a cavernous malformation with subacute hematoma was initially considered. Additional differential diagnoses included intramedullary melanoma, ependymoma, astrocytoma, and schwannoma.

A 76-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a large liver mass. She had undergone ovariectomy for an ovarian tumor 30 years earlier (details unknown). At age 68, a routine abdominal ultrasound revealed a gallbladder polyp and a 3-cm liver mass, which was “considered to be a hepatic hemangioma showing slow growth”; however, follow-up was discontinued. Five years later, repeat imaging showed the liver tumor had enlarged to 17 cm, and she was referred for further management. 

On examination, she had mild anemia (hemoglobin 10.3 g/dl), low albumin (3.0 g/dl), elevated alkaline phosphatase (557 U/l), lactate dehydrogenase (250 U/l), and C-reactive protein (1.21 mg/dl). Tumor markers—including carcinoembryonic antigen, carbohydrate antigen 19-9, α-fetoprotein, PIVKA-II, and AFP-L3—were all negative. Serologies for hepatitis B and C were negative.

Abdominal ultrasound showed a mass involving the right hepatic lobe, composed of two adjacent masses with mixed high and low echoes and detectable blood flow. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated an 18-cm right-lobe lesion with “uneven and prolonged contrast effect during the early and equilibrium phases.” MRI revealed mixed high- and low–signal intensities on T2-weighted imaging with a mosaic appearance suggestive of bleeding and necrosis, diffusion-weighted hyperintensity, and “prolongation of the internal contrast effect” in the hepatobiliary phase. PET showed no abnormal FDG uptake in the liver or elsewhere. “Thus, the tumor was suspected to be a liver hemangiosarcoma. Malignancy was possible since the tumor had grown over time,” and right trisectionectomy was planned.

A 58-year-old Tanzanian woman presented with a 6-month history of intermittent low-grade fever and bilateral neck masses. She reported no weight loss, night sweats, or other systemic symptoms. On examination, multiple firm, ovoid, mobile, non-tender lymph nodes were palpated in both the cervical and submandibular regions, the largest measuring 5×5 cm. Vital signs were within normal limits except for a temperature of 37.8°C recorded intermittently. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 11.0 g/dL and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 30 mm/h. No imaging studies were performed. Given the constellation of persistent lymphadenopathy and elevated inflammatory markers, a presumptive diagnosis of lymphoma was made, and fine-needle aspiration cytology was obtained.

A 45-year-old G7P4 Micronesian woman presented with one week of heavy intermenstrual vaginal bleeding and symptomatic anemia. Her history included a 32–pack-year smoking history and no prior cervical cancer screening; she had two Cesarean deliveries in 2015–2016. On exam, moderate blood was noted in the vaginal vault, with a foul-smelling discharge and a necrotic upper vaginal mass. 

CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a diffusely enlarged cervix and a distended uterus containing enhancing nodular endometrial masses and fluid, bladder distension with mild bilateral hydroureteronephrosis, and incidental numerous nodules at the lung bases. Chest CT revealed more than 30 round, discrete pulmonary nodules scattered bilaterally, the largest measuring 1.2 cm in the right upper lobe. 

Because of ongoing bleeding and a hemoglobin of 7 g/dL, she received two units of packed red blood cells and was referred to gynecologic oncology. Over the following days, she developed urinary retention requiring catheterization and recurrent severe abdominal pain, bleeding, and malodorous discharge. Pelvic exam showed an immobile, exophytic, friable, necrotic mass replacing the cervix and upper vagina, mimicking parametrial involvement. A portion of the mass was removed for pathology, which showed infarcted smooth muscle without atypia or malignancy. 

She returned a day before planned surgery with fever, leukocytosis, and signs of sepsis; blood cultures were obtained and cefoxitin with doxycycline started for presumed superinfection. Given her origin from a TB-endemic area, tuberculosis was considered but deemed less likely due to the peripheral distribution and radiographic appearance of the pulmonary nodules. Surgery was scheduled for definitive diagnosis. The working differential at that time included locally advanced cervical cancer with lung metastases, metastatic leiomyosarcoma, or leiomyosarcoma with concurrent pulmonary pathology.

A 49-year-old woman was referred for surgical management of a presumed large nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma. She reported a 2-year history of chronic bitemporal headache, unexplained easy fatigability, and very slowly progressive diminution of vision. Her medical history was notable only for well-controlled hypertension. On examination, visual acuity was decreased bilaterally (worse on the left) with bitemporal homonymous hemianopia. Endocrinological evaluation revealed central hypothyroidism, and levothyroxine replacement was initiated. Noncontrast CT of the brain showed a slightly hyperdense large sellar/suprasellar mass extending into both cavernous sinuses with right parasellar extension and bony remodeling of the sella turcica and upper clivus. Contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated a 36 × 41 × 50 mm sellar/suprasellar/parasellar mass with heterogeneous low T1 signal, intermediate high T2 signal, small central areas of diffusion restriction on DWI, and mild patchy postcontrast enhancement. The lesion encased the cavernous and clinoid segments of the right internal carotid artery and partially encased the left cavernous segment. The optic nerves and chiasm were elevated and inseparable from the mass, and the pituitary gland and stalk were not visualized.

A 23-year-old man presented with mild to moderate, dull, nonradiating epigastric pain for 10 days. He denied jaundice, fever, anorexia, weight loss, diabetes, alcohol abuse, and had no prior major surgery. On examination, there was mild epigastric tenderness. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 16 g/dL, negative anti-hemoglobin core, undetectable hepatitis C RNA, normal liver and kidney function tests, CA 19-9 23.13 U/mL, and CEA 1.02 ng/mL.  
Abdominal ultrasound revealed a hypoechoic lesion in the pancreatic neck without internal vascularity. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a low-attenuation, minimally enhancing lesion at the body-neck junction of the pancreas. On MRI, the 4.2 × 3.5 × 3.5 cm mass was hypointense on T1-weighted images and mildly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with a central T2-hyperintense scar. Postcontrast images showed minimal peripheral enhancement and a spoke-wheel–type delayed enhancing scar centrally. The main pancreatic duct and common bile duct were not dilated.  
Based on these findings, a provisional diagnosis of solid serous adenoma with a central scar was made, and the decision was made to proceed directly to surgery without biopsy.

An 11-year-old girl with no significant medical history was referred for evaluation of delayed and complicated eruption of the left maxillary canine and first premolar. A panoramic radiograph revealed marked resorption of the mesial root of the first premolar. On examination, there was marginal gingivitis and 6–8 mm gingival pockets around the adjacent teeth, with tenderness on palpation. The premolar was extracted and granulation tissue enucleated without histologic analysis. Twelve weeks later, repeat imaging showed a persistent osteolytic defect in the left maxilla, infraocclusion of the canine, and external resorption of the lateral incisor and canine roots. Cone-beam CT demonstrated a cystic, osteolytic lesion with palatal cortical perforation from the lateral incisor to the first premolar, and bluish discoloration of the overlying gingiva. There was no extraoral swelling or tooth mobility; adjacent teeth remained vital. Given the locally aggressive osteolytic appearance with multiple root resorptions, the differential diagnosis included aggressively behaving odontogenic tumors, nodular fasciitis, and malignant lesions such as soft tissue sarcomas, bone tumors, and lymphoma.

An 11-month-old male infant with a history of recurrent bronchoalveolitis since age 3 months and progressive thoracic deformation since age 5 months was evaluated for persistent respiratory symptoms. On examination, he had discrete respiratory distress but appeared well perfused and hydrated. Chest radiography showed a large homogeneous mediastinal opacity with mediastinal enlargement.

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a 15-cm mass compressing both atria. Thoracic ultrasound demonstrated a well-circumscribed upper mediastinal process adjacent to the pericardium on the right side, measuring 116 × 79 × 76 mm, with two components: a predominantly cystic, septated component and a vascularized solid component. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest confirmed a combined cystic–solid mass with thick septa and evidence of a fat–fluid level; the mass displaced the heart, thymus, pulmonary veins, aorta, and pulmonary artery. Laboratory studies showed severe anemia (hemoglobin 11 g/L) and normal alpha-fetoprotein levels. The infant was referred for surgical excision of the mass.

A 17-year-old female presented with headache and blurred vision in both eyes for 1 month, bilateral lower limb weakness (more pronounced on the left), and multiple generalized seizures for 20 days. On examination, visual acuity was reduced to counting fingers bilaterally, and funduscopic examination showed papilledema. Motor strength was Grade 5/5 in both upper limbs, Grade 3/5 in the right lower limb, and Grade 1/5 in the left lower limb. 

Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 5.9 cm × 4.6 cm × 2.7 cm bilateral middle-third parasagittal extra-axial mass that was isointense on T1- and T2-weighted images, with mass effect, perilesional edema, and homogeneous contrast enhancement along the falx. Diffusion-weighted images demonstrated restriction, perfusion-weighted images showed increased perfusion, and MR venography indicated obstruction of the mid–superior sagittal sinus by tumor invasion. Spectroscopy displayed a high choline peak. 

On radiologic grounds, meningioma and hemangiopericytoma were the primary considerations. The patient underwent a biparietal parasagittal craniotomy and subtotal excision of the lesion, leaving tumor within the sinus. Intraoperatively, the dura was thickened; the firm, grayish, moderately vascular tumor was attached to both the convexity and falx, with no bone infiltration and no clear arachnoid plane. Postoperative MRI demonstrated residual tumor along and within the superior sagittal sinus, and the patient showed mild improvement in lower-limb weakness.

A 75-year-old woman presented with an eight-month history of continuous lower back pain that was unrelated to activity and without radiation or neurologic deficits. On physical examination, a firm mass was palpable in the lower abdomen. Pelvic ultrasound revealed a well-defined retro-uterine mass separate from the uterus and rectum, measuring approximately 13 cm in greatest dimension, with both anechoic cystic areas and isoechoic solid tissue. Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis demonstrated an oval, encapsulated retro-uterine mass (132 × 126 × 103 mm) with heterogeneous enhancement, internal calcifications, and large fluid-filled regions; the lesion displaced the iliac vessels laterally, the rectum posteriorly, and extended into the left first sacral foramen without overt invasion of adjacent organs. MRI confirmed a well-encapsulated retroperitoneal mass in T1 isosignal and heterogeneous T2 signal with cystic hypersignal areas, diffusion restriction, and heterogeneous gadolinium enhancement. Serum tumor markers including CA19-9 and CA 125 were within normal limits.

A 48-year-old postmenopausal woman (gravida 2, para 2) presented with a 3-month history of brown-yellowish vaginal discharge, fluctuating lower abdominal pain, fever, and progressive abdominal enlargement over 15 years, worsening in the last 5 years. She reported difficulty with defecation and voiding. She had undergone an attempted myomectomy in the past, but removal was aborted due to severe adhesions. There was no relevant drug or family history.

On rectovaginal examination, a smooth, firm pelvic mass was palpated extending to two fingers below the umbilicus, with limited mobility; the cervix could not be visualized or sondaged. Laboratory studies showed an elevated Cancer Antigen 125 level of 115.6 g/dL.

Transabdominal ultrasound revealed a 269 × 529 mm hypoechoic mass within the uterine cavity, suspected to represent infected hematometra, and a separate 126 × 106 mm homogeneous solid mass in the left adnexa with a clear border, raising suspicion for an intraligamentary myoma with cystic degeneration or a left ovarian fibroid.

Abdominal and pelvic computed tomography demonstrated a 145 × 110 × 146 mm multilocular cystic mass with thick septa and enhancing solid components, clearly demarcated from the uterus and bladder, displacing the uterus to the right superior-lateral side. The uterine cavity was distended with fluid and air forming an air-fluid level. No lymphadenopathy was noted.

A 61-year-old man with no prior medical problems presented with a 5-month history of progressive lower-extremity weakness and urinary urgency. On examination, he was unable to walk, had paraparesis (strength 3/5 bilaterally), hyperreflexia, and bilateral Babinski signs. He had been treated previously for presumed lumbar canal stenosis without improvement. A whole-spine MRI with and without gadolinium showed an enhancing T8 vertebral body lesion and a homogeneously enhancing posterior epidural mass at T7–T8, with severe spinal-cord compression and cerebrospinal-fluid blockade.

A 52-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a right parotid-region swelling of six years’ duration. She reported no pain, facial weakness, numbness, skin changes, xerostomia, dysphagia, or dyspnea. On examination, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. There was a single, firm, non-tender, mobile mass approximately 4–5 cm in the right parotid area; no cervical lymphadenopathy was noted and the facial nerve was intact. Laboratory studies were unremarkable.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck demonstrated a well-defined soft-tissue density lesion in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland. MRI showed a 4.5 cm, well-circumscribed tumor with both cystic and solid components surrounded by a thin capsule.  
Fine-needle aspiration of the lesion yielded a monomorphic basaloid cell population with minimal nuclear atypia, mitoses, or tumor necrosis, and was interpreted as a benign basaloid neoplasm.  
The patient was scheduled for surgical excision.

A 15-year-old boy with no prior medical history presented with a 3-week history of a neck mass. He initially experienced a globus sensation and pain on swallowing, which resolved spontaneously after one week. Physical examination revealed a smooth, non-tender, approximately 3 cm mass in the left thyroid lobe. Thyroid function tests were normal (TSH 2.4 mU/L [0.5–5.0 mU/L]; FT4 13.7 pmol/L [12.0–22.0 pmol/L]); calcitonin and thyroglobulin levels were within normal limits.

Thyroid ultrasound showed a solid, homogeneous, hypoechoic lesion in the left lobe measuring 2.0 cm × 2.8 cm × 3.4 cm. The lesion was taller than wide, had a well-defined smooth border, and contained two macrocalcifications; Doppler signal was absent. On compression, the lesion was partially elastic without fluctuation. A left cervical lymph node of normal size lacked a fatty hilum and exhibited internal calcifications with heterogeneous echotexture.

Based on the ultrasound findings, the differential diagnosis included thyroid adenoma, thyroid carcinoma, and a thyroidal epidermal cyst.

A 64-year-old Caucasian woman was referred for evaluation of a gigantic left neck mass. She first noted a small paratracheal node 34 years ago, which grew progressively over the subsequent three decades. Twenty-four years ago, an attempted resection was aborted due to massive intraoperative bleeding; intraoperative findings suggested a glomus tumor. The patient declined further surgery and remained asymptomatic until recent enlargement caused discomfort and mild swallowing difficulties.

On examination, there was a 9 cm pulsatile, slightly tender mass in the left lateral neck, displacing the sternocleidomastoid muscle laterally and the trachea 2 cm to the right. There was no Horner syndrome or abnormal respiratory reflex.

In 2013, MRI showed a hypervascularized mass with a maximum diameter of 4 cm at the left carotid bifurcation, causing forward displacement of the external carotid artery and backward displacement of the internal carotid artery. In 2016, angioMRI confirmed a 9 cm paratracheal mass on the left cervical side with lateral displacement of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and the trachea. A carotid occlusion test and complete angiography demonstrated a patent circle of Willis and corroborated the vascular nature of the lesion.

A 50-year-old man presented with a one-week history of progressive visual loss in his right eye. He had no significant medical or infectious history. On examination, visual acuity was 20/400 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Pupils were round and reactive bilaterally, and extraocular movements were full. Optical coherence tomography of the macula was normal in both eyes. Intraocular pressure measured by tonometry was 27 mm Hg in the right eye and 19 mm Hg in the left eye. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye revealed a yellowish mass involving the iris and covering the iridocorneal angle between the 5 o’clock and 6 o’clock positions; there was prominent tumor vascularization, cells and fibrin in the anterior chamber, and a mild hyposphagma. Ultrasound biomicroscopy demonstrated infiltration of the iris by the lesion, with no extension into the vitreous cavity.

A 29-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of progressive abdominal distension and pain. He had no stigmata of liver disease or lymphadenopathy, but physical examination revealed marked, tense ascites. Cardiac evaluation showed only moderate tricuspid regurgitation. A comprehensive hepatic workup, including abdominal ultrasonography with Doppler, was unremarkable. Paracentesis yielded an exudative fluid with reactive mesothelial cells but no malignant cells. CT scans of the chest and abdomen confirmed isolated ascites without other abnormalities. 

Diagnostic laparoscopy demonstrated an abnormally thickened and shortened greater omentum and mesentery. Laparotomy was performed for safe access, and biopsies were obtained from the omentum and peritoneal nodules. Histopathological examination showed sheets and cords of small, rounded cells embedded in abundant collagenous stroma. The cells had scant to eosinophilic, occasionally vacuolated cytoplasm; nuclei were small with inconspicuous nucleoli and clear or dispersed chromatin. Peripheral areas contained more spindle-shaped cells in fascicular arrangements. Mitoses were infrequent.

Immunohistochemical staining revealed positivity for MNF116 (dot-like pattern), CAM5.2, and occasional EMA. Tumor cells also reacted with MiC2, β2-microglobulin, and Fli-1. Further analyses showed negative staining for LCA, CD43, S100 protein, CD34, CD31, chromogranin, synaptophysin, SMA, and CD56.

A 48-year-old woman (G2P2) was referred for a 4-year history of mucoid vaginal discharge. Ten years earlier, she had undergone a supracervical hysterectomy for uterine fibroids, with pathology confirming multiple leiomyomas. On pelvic examination, the cervix was slightly enlarged with signs of chronic cervicitis. A ThinPrep Pap smear was negative for intraepithelial lesions or malignancy. Colposcopy revealed chronic inflammation and benign nabothian cysts without atypia, and directed cervical biopsies were normal. Transvaginal and abdominal ultrasonography showed only nabothian cysts. Pelvic MRI demonstrated an enlarged cervix (63 × 50 × 44 mm) containing multiple cystic lesions of varying sizes interspersed with solid components, suggestive of a tunnel cluster. There was no evidence of adnexal masses, and the lesion was clinically staged as IB.

A 27-year-old Caucasian woman with untreated hypertension, irritable bowel syndrome, hidradenitis, and ovarian cysts presented with a 3-day history of left flank pain. Seven years earlier, a CT scan had shown a 2.7 × 2.1 cm left adrenal lesion consistent with an adenoma. Noncontrast CT at this presentation showed a 5.6 × 3.7 × 4.0 cm mass contiguous with the left adrenal gland and splenic artery. CT with intravenous contrast revealed a 5.0 × 6.2 cm left adrenal mass with a portal-phase density of 67 Hounsfield units and a 15-minute washout to 42 Hounsfield units. MRI of the abdomen with adrenal protocol demonstrated a 4.7 × 5.9 cm enhancing left adrenal mass, with a differential diagnosis of pheochromocytoma, adrenal carcinoma, and metastatic disease. Biochemical evaluation was unremarkable except for elevated total and free testosterone levels (124 ng/dL and 17.2 pg/mL); she had a prior diagnosis of polycystic ovarian syndrome. On examination in the surgical oncology clinic, she had persistent left flank pain but normal physical findings. Surgical resection was recommended.

A 31-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of a gradually enlarging mass over the left frontal bone and positional headache. On examination, there was a fixed, non-tender 3×2 cm mass in the left frontal region and multiple small, firm, non-tender subcutaneous nodules on the trunk and extremities consistent with lipomas; the overlying skin was intact. Complete blood count, routine biochemistry, and serologic tests for HIV, HBV, HCV, and EBV were normal or negative. Noncontrast CT of the brain showed a 35×22 mm destructive, enhancing soft-tissue mass of the left frontal bone with enhancement of the adjacent meninges. MRI revealed a 34×28 mm skull-vault lesion in the left frontal region with high T2 signal intensity and avid dural enhancement. The patient underwent craniotomy with resection of the mass and cranioplasty. Histopathology demonstrated a high-grade spindle-cell neoplasm invading bone and fibro-adipose tissue, with dural involvement but without skull adhesion; surgical margins were negative. On second pathological review, the lesion was described as a high-grade pleomorphic sarcoma compatible with anaplastic meningioma.

A 14-year-old previously healthy female of Indian descent presented with 3 weeks of mild left posterior auricular, “nummular” headache, gradually progressive left-sided neck pain, and dysphagia without dysarthria. She denied fever, weight loss, vision or hearing changes, weakness, sensory changes, neck stiffness, abdominal pain, or hematuria.  
On examination, she had isolated leftward tongue deviation. Two days into admission, she also developed left-sided uvular deviation. A dysphagia study showed oropharyngeal impairment.  
Laboratory studies revealed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 43 mm/hour and mild normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL); other blood counts, metabolic panel, C-reactive protein, and urinalysis were normal.  
Brain MRI, cervical spine MRI, and CT angiogram of the head and neck (all with and without contrast) were unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed normal opening pressure, cell count, glucose, and protein, with no bacterial growth on culture.  
Given the evolving cranial neuropathies and a high suspicion for a skull-base lesion, an MRI of the brain with and without contrast using a fast imaging employing steady-state acquisition (FIESTA) sequence was performed 2 days after the initial imaging.

A 72-year-old man with a history of hypertension and atrial fibrillation presented with a progressively enlarging, painless swelling of the right hemiscrotum. He denied lower urinary tract symptoms. On examination, there was a 3 cm firm-to-hard mass in the right hemiscrotum that was distinct from the epididymis; the right epididymis and testis appeared normal. Scrotal ultrasound demonstrated a 4 × 3 cm right extratesticular heterogeneous lesion with peripheral vascularity. The patient underwent a radical right inguinal orchiectomy. Gross examination of the 9 cm surgical specimen revealed a 3 cm testis with intact tunicae and a separate white-surfaced mass measuring 2 cm; four satellite nodules (2–5 mm) were noted around the mass.

An 18-year-old woman was referred for orthognathic surgery to correct facial asymmetry and mandibular prognathism. Her medical and dental histories were unremarkable. Extraoral and intraoral examinations revealed no abnormalities: there was no facial swelling, pain, mucosal change, or temporomandibular dysfunction, and no palpable mass or cortical expansion was identified. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated a well-circumscribed radiolucent lesion in the right mandibular ramus with an associated condylar deformity. Cone-beam computed tomography showed a radiolucent, well-circumscribed lesion in the right mandibular ramus, a cortical bone defect on the medial aspect of the ascending ramus, thinning of the cortical bone, and a lesion located posterior to the inferior alveolar nerve canal.

A 71-year-old woman was admitted with a 2-week history of low-grade fever, night sweats, and progressive dyspnea. Chest imaging showed bilateral ground-glass opacities, and brain MRI revealed a subacute infarct in the right corona radiata. On 5 L/min oxygen, her temperature was 37.1 °C, blood pressure 126/71 mm Hg, respiratory rate 24/min, and oxygen saturation 91%. Lung auscultation revealed slight expiratory crackles; cardiac exam showed a soft pansystolic murmur at the apex. Neurologic exam demonstrated mild left-sided dysmetria on finger–nose testing.

Initial laboratory studies demonstrated:
• LDH 1027 U/L (normal 120–220)  
• sIL-2R 1180 U/L (145–519)  
• CRP 3.49 mg/dL (0–0.35)  
• ANA ×1280 (<40) and anticentromere antibody ×1280 (<40)  
• Other serologies, cultures, and markers of infection were negative

Community-acquired pneumonia was suspected, but her hypoxia worsened despite treatment. Given the high-titer anticentromere antibody, rapid renal dysfunction with hematuria and proteinuria, and lung findings, interstitial pneumonia related to systemic scleroderma was diagnosed, and she received methylprednisolone pulse therapy and plasma exchange. Subsequent chest imaging showed improvement of the ground-glass opacities but new bilateral pleural effusions.

A 65-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, chronic neck and back pain, a 10-pack-year smoking history, and a history of robotic-assisted laparoscopic left inguinal hernia repair (with mesh) two years earlier presented with a persistent left groin bulge. He noted the bulge almost immediately after his prior surgery but attributed it to postoperative fluid and did not seek evaluation. He denied pain, nausea, vomiting, changes in bowel or bladder function, or skin changes. His primary concern was avoidance of future complications.

On examination, there was a chronically incarcerated left inguinal swelling extending into the hemiscrotum. The contents were firm and non-tender; both testicles were palpable and the overlying skin was normal. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count and basic metabolic panel, were unremarkable.

A preoperative CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated an 8-cm lipomatous lesion extending from the hernia neck near the repair mesh into the left hemiscrotum, with density similar to subcutaneous fat, well-demarcated borders, and no apparent invasion of adjacent structures. Given the presumed recurrence of a left inguinal hernia containing fat, the decision was made to proceed with an elective open repair.

A 12-year-old Caucasian boy was referred with a presumed diagnosis of a right optic nerve glioma. At age 8, he was noted to have a yellow‐whitish, well‐demarcated papillary cyst with central retinal vessel displacement in the right eye; visual acuity was 20/30 in both eyes, and he was monitored twice yearly without change. Four years later, his right eye visual acuity had declined to 20/80 with concentric visual‐field reduction to the central 10° isopter, but the fundoscopic appearance of the lesion was unchanged. One month later, after a severe headache, vision in the right eye deteriorated to no light perception, with an absolute afferent pupillary defect. A computed tomography scan showed right optic nerve thickening. On admission, contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated elevation and enhancement of the right optic disc. Fundoscopy revealed a well-defined whitish mass at the optic disc without macroscopic calcification, dilated and tortuous retinal vessels, and small superficial retinal hemorrhages. General physical examination was unremarkable.

A 30-year-old G2P2 woman was admitted with headache, nausea, vomiting, and right-sided blurred vision. She had no prior medical history. Neurologic examination showed right optic disc edema. Cranial CT revealed three hyperintense lesions (6 mm right parietal, 16 mm left occipital, 7 mm left temporal), each surrounded by edema. Cranial MRI confirmed multiple lesions suggestive of metastatic cancer. To locate a primary tumor, thoracic and abdominopelvic CT scans were obtained. Upper abdominal CT showed multiple indistinct, heterogeneously enhancing liver lesions (< 15 mm). Pelvic imaging demonstrated a 62 × 53 mm solid-cystic mass in the right adnexa with irregular septations and a 38 × 24 mm solid component; right pelvic lymph nodes were mildly enlarged and there was no ascites. Upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy and breast ultrasonography were normal. Pap smear was negative for malignancy. Serum tumor markers (CA 125, CA 15-3, CA 19-9, CEA, AFP) were within normal limits.

A 67-year-old man presented for evaluation of a small papule at the hairline of his left scalp that had been present for over 40 years without symptoms but had shown rapid growth over the past 6 months. He denied pain, itching, or bleeding. His medical history was notable only for type 2 diabetes mellitus managed for 15 years. He had no history of alcohol use, drug allergies, or similar family skin lesions.

On examination, there was a single, round, 15 mm neoplasm at the left scalp hairline. The lesion was tough, non-tender, with slight hyperplasia of the surrounding skin and minimal brown pigmentation and crusting at the margin. There was no palpable lymphadenopathy.

A skin biopsy was performed. Histologic sections showed a lobulated tumor extending into the dermis and continuous with the epidermis. The lesion consisted of lobules of epithelial cells, some with clear cytoplasm. At the periphery of each lobule were columnar cells with nuclear palisading, surrounded by a thickened, glassy basement membrane. The central stroma was hyalinized and eosinophilic, containing irregular cords and nests of epithelial cells. Scattered lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils were noted in the adjacent dermis.

A 37-year-old woman was referred after a routine health check-up revealed a cystic lesion in her left lower lung field. She reported a 2-year history of vague chest discomfort and heaviness but denied fever, cough, hemoptysis, or weight loss. She had never smoked and had no known comorbidities. Physical examination was unremarkable. Complete blood count with differential, serum chemistry, and electrocardiogram findings were all within normal limits. 

Initial posteroanterior chest radiography showed a roughly 3-cm radiolucent lesion in the left lower zone. Low-dose chest CT confirmed a 35-mm intraparenchymal, thin-walled cyst in the lingular segment without solid components. After multidisciplinary discussion, a course of watchful waiting was chosen.

Twelve months later, follow-up CT demonstrated interval enlargement of the cyst to 90 mm in diameter and a suspected connection between the cyst and an adjacent bronchiole. The patient continued to have intermittent mild chest discomfort but remained otherwise well. Because of the rate of cyst growth and concern for possible complications, the decision was made to proceed with surgical resection.

A 48-year-old man with a history of isolated left parotid gland enlargement presented with a several-month history of a rash on his face, anterior neck, and upper chest. He first noted a single lesion on his anterior neck that gradually expanded superiorly to the face and inferiorly to the chest wall. He was treated empirically with oral antibiotics for presumed cellulitis, but the rash worsened and developed palpable, thick, leathery borders. He also reported progressive dysphagia, odynophagia, and a 40-lb unintentional weight loss. 

Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI of the neck and chest demonstrated diffuse skin thickening extending into the subcutaneous fat of the anterior neck and chest wall, along with scattered sclerotic lesions in the visualized skeleton, concerning for metastatic disease. A punch biopsy of a right chest wall lesion was performed. Immunohistochemical staining showed tumor cells positive for CK7 and CDX2 and negative for p63, TTF1, CK5/6, CD45, S100, and SOX10; the morphologic features favored a poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of luminal upper gastrointestinal origin.

A 58-year-old woman was referred after routine chest CT identified a pulmonary nodule. She reported only occasional cough with phlegm and had no significant past medical, family, or smoking history. Vital signs were within normal limits. Lung examination revealed slightly increased breath sounds without rales.

Tumor markers including CEA, CA125, NSE, CK19, SCC, and pro-GRP were all within reference ranges. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed an 8 mm solid lobulated nodule with blurred edges at the apex of the right upper lobe.

A wedge resection of the right upper lobe nodule was performed. Grossly, the 0.7 cm gray-white nodule was well circumscribed, attached to the pleura, and had a salivary-gland–like appearance.

On hematoxylin-eosin staining, the lesion had a clear boundary with adjacent lung tissue and contained small air spaces and arterioles at its periphery. At low power, the cells formed acinar and papillary-like structures. At higher magnification, most cells were medium sized with pale, homogeneous chromatin; local luminal cells exhibited cilia and occasional nuclear enlargement and atypia. There was no obvious necrosis.

An 18-month-old girl was brought for evaluation of a swelling in her left medial thigh. Over the past six months, the mass had enlarged gradually and was painless, with no history of trauma or infection. On examination, there was a firm, nonpulsatile mass measuring approximately 10 cm, fixed to underlying tissues but mobile relative to the overlying skin. There were no signs of inflammation, neurovascular impairment, or inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory tests were unremarkable. A CT scan of the thigh showed a well-defined, lobulated, hypodense mass in the left anteromedial compartment of the proximal thigh, extending toward the inguinal area. The lesion exhibited internal septations and a density similar to subcutaneous fat, displacing the common and superficial femoral vessels anterolaterally without signs of invasion; it abutted the proximal femoral bone but did not erode it.

An MRI confirmed a fatty-appearing, well-circumscribed mass with internal septations and no encasement of neurovascular structures.

A 35-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, with no significant gynecologic history, was found to have an incidental 10-cm left adnexal mass on abdominal ultrasound. Serum tumor markers (CA-125, CEA, CA19-9) were within normal limits. The patient underwent left salpingo-oophorectomy and omental biopsy. Grossly, the adnexal mass measured 10 cm. On microscopic examination, the lesion consisted of sheets of spindle cells with branching tubules and sieve-like patterns, including cystic spaces. Mitotic figures and nuclear pleomorphism were rare. Tumor invasion of the left fallopian tube serosa and focal omental involvement were identified. Immunohistochemical staining showed strong positivity for calretinin, inhibin, WT1, CD56, vimentin, CK19, and CK7, and negativity for PAX-8, EMA, CD10, AFP, and glypican-3.

A 56-year-old woman presented with acute abdominal pain. Initial CT at an outside hospital demonstrated a 10-cm tumor protruding from the left lateral segment of the liver with surrounding high-density ascites, suggestive of rupture. On transfer, she was hemodynamically stable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, albumin 3.4 g/dL, γ-globulin 18.5%, and an anti–acetylcholine receptor antibody level <0.3 nmol/L. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a well-marginated 10-cm enhancing mass in the left lateral liver and an irregularly marginated 4.5-cm mass in the anterior mediastinum. Hepatic arterial embolization was performed to prevent rebleeding. MRI of the liver lesion revealed a low-intensity focus on T1-weighted images and heterogeneous signal on T2-weighted images. FDG-PET showed increased uptake in both the hepatic lesion (SUVmax 4.8) and the mediastinal lesion (SUVmax 3.9), with no other metastatic disease. A percutaneous biopsy of the liver lesion suggested either malignant T-cell lymphoma or metastatic thymoma.

A 12-year-old girl presented with 2–3 weeks of chest pain, chest tightness, and shortness of breath, accompanied by intermittent cough, nausea, right shoulder pain, and back pain. On examination, she was obese, and lung auscultation revealed decreased breath sounds in the right middle and lower lobes. A chest radiograph showed a large right lower lobe mass localized to the posterior mediastinum. Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated a 10.0 × 9.1 × 9.5 cm heterogeneous soft-tissue mass in the posterior right hemithorax, associated with a 2.8 cm pedunculated osseous excrescence arising from the posterior aspect of the right 10th rib with a continuous medullary cavity. The lesion contained coarse internal calcifications and minimal fat density. There was mild widening of the right T10 and T11 neural foramina. Spirometry revealed a borderline obstructive pattern with no bronchodilator response. Complete blood count and metabolic panel results were within normal limits, and there were no significant constitutional symptoms.

A 22-year-old woman presented with three weeks of progressive shortness of breath, palpitations, and fatigue. She reported a history of multiple blood transfusions, with the last transfusion six years ago. Since birth, she had button-like bluish lesions on her lips, hands, and feet; she noted that these lesions had increased in size and number over the past six years.

On examination, she was pale, with numerous compressible, dark blue cutaneous papules on her lips, hands, and feet. Vital signs on arrival: blood pressure 70/40 mmHg, pulse 100 beats/min, oxygen saturation 65% on room air, temperature 98.6°F, Glasgow Coma Scale score 13/15. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 2.1 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 57.5 fL, and features of hypochromic microcytic anemia on peripheral smear. She was started on packed red blood cell transfusions. Upper endoscopy revealed a vascular hemangioma-like lesion in the esophagus and multiple similar lesions in the duodenum. Colonoscopy showed several hemangioma-like lesions extending to the splenic flexure; colonic biopsy demonstrated acute self-limited colitis. A skin biopsy of one of the cutaneous lesions showed angiokeratoma.

A 40-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of a painless swelling in the left floor of the mouth. Her medical history was unremarkable. On intraoral examination, there was a soft, nontender mass in the left floor of the mouth, extending posteriorly toward the supraglottic region. A computed tomography scan showed a single, homogeneous hyperdense lesion in the lower middle portion of the floor of the mouth. The clinical impression was of a benign salivary gland tumor, and an incisional biopsy was performed.

A one-week-old girl was noted by her parents to have a firm swelling on the right side of her abdomen. She had a good appetite, was gaining weight appropriately, and had no fever. Laboratory evaluation showed an alpha fetoprotein level of 2158.5 IU/mL and a normal β-hCG concentration. Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen revealed a mass in liver segments V and VI. Pathologic evaluation of a percutaneous liver biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of fetal hepatoblastoma. Within days, a tumor-like lesion emerged at the biopsy site in the anterior abdominal wall. The patient was transferred to our hospital, where her white-cell count was 21.0 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 144 g/L, and platelet count 556.0 × 10^9/L. Abdominal ultrasound showed an inhomogeneous, partially cystic, partially solid mass in the liver with color-Doppler signal limited to the periphery. Repeat MRI demonstrated a heterointense T2-weighted mass with a hyperintense cystic component and a small solid component, evidence of hemorrhage in the cystic area on T1-weighted images, and inhomogeneous postcontrast opacification with a hyperintense capsule. Two additional lesions with identical imaging characteristics were identified in the abdominal wall and chest wall. No other metastases were seen on abdominal MRI or chest CT. The abdominal-wall lesion was surgically excised and sent for pathologic analysis.

A 74-year-old man presented with a one-year history of persistent right-sided headache affecting the frontotemporooccipital region. The headache was daily, with an intensity of 4/10, described as a dull ache with occasional brief shooting retroorbital pain once or twice a week and occasional photophobia. There was no nausea, visual dysfunction, or exacerbation by postural changes or Valsalva maneuvers. The headache failed to settle with analgesics. He had a history of migraine in his teens with the last episode 10 years ago and a family history of migraine. His medical history included ischemic heart disease, diabetes mellitus, and COPD. Physical and neurological examinations were normal. The differential diagnosis included hemicrania continua and chronic migraine, and a trial of indomethacin was initiated. A non-contrast CT scan of the brain showed age-related cerebral atrophy with no intracranial abnormality. The patient was treated for migraine, but “The response to the standard prophylactic and therapeutic treatment for migraine was suboptimal and variable.”

A 66-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 24-hour history of rapid, regular palpitations and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, superimposed on a one-year history of progressive dyspnea on exertion, generalized edema, abdominal discomfort after meals, and gradual onset of hirsutism. She had no past medical history, never smoked or used exogenous hormones, and experienced menopause at age 52.  

On examination, blood pressure was normal, heart rate 150 beats/min regular, with enlarged cardiac dullness, a 3/6 pansystolic mitral murmur, jugular venous distension, right basal crackles, diminished breath sounds at the left pulmonary base, massive generalized edema, hirsutism (Ferriman–Gallwey score 14), minimal frontal balding, and a painless left hypochondriac abdominal mass. BMI was 33.3 kg/m^2.  

Electrocardiogram showed typical atrial flutter with 2:1 atrioventricular conduction at 150 bpm and left bundle branch block.
