Laboratory studies revealed hemoconcentration, new-onset diabetes (HbA1c 10.7%), hyperkalemia (K⁺ 5.6 mmol/L), mild hyponatremia (Na⁺ 133 mmol/L), elevated liver enzymes consistent with cardiac stasis, and an INR of 1.5 without anticoagulation. Tumor markers (AFP, CA 19-9, CEA) and viral hepatitis markers were negative. Hormonal analysis demonstrated excess steroid hormones, including markedly elevated androgens.  

Chest radiography revealed cardiomegaly, left pleural effusion, and pulmonary venous congestion. Transthoracic echocardiography showed mild mitral regurgitation, a dilated left ventricle with ejection fraction 28%, enlarged left atrium, and mild pulmonary hypertension.  

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan disclosed a 21 cm × 17 cm × 12 cm well-defined, heterogeneously enhancing mass in the left adrenal region with central calcifications and nonenhancing necrotic areas, displacing the stomach, left lobe of the liver, and left kidney, but without evidence of local invasion.

A 48-year-old woman presented with progressive, painless decreased vision in her left eye for 2 months. Visual acuity was light perception in the left eye and 20/20 in the right eye. Biomicroscopy of the left eye showed no conjunctival hyperemia, a clear cornea, and no inflammation in the anterior chamber; intraocular pressure was normal. Fundus examination and fluorescein angiography revealed a retinal detachment with a large superior brownish mass in the left eye. B-scan ultrasonography demonstrated a dome-shaped choroidal mass measuring approximately 12 × 11 × 11 mm, surrounded by subretinal fluid, without acoustic hollowing or calcification. MRI of the orbits showed an intraocular lesion with high signal intensity on T1-weighted images, low signal intensity on T2, a collar-button extension, scleral thickening, and enhancement after gadolinium administration. A thoracoabdominal CT scan revealed no evidence of metastasis. Given the clinical and radiologic findings highly suggestive of a choroidal melanoma, enucleation of the left eye was recommended and performed with the patient’s consent.

A 75-year-old woman with a history of right-breast high-grade DCIS treated 6 years earlier by lumpectomy, re-excision, chemoradiation (42.6 Gy in 16 fractions), and tamoxifen presented with progressive discomfort and fullness in the right breast and new nipple prominence. She reported menarche at 13 years, first pregnancy at 31 years, 5 years of remote oral contraceptive use, and a maternal aunt with bilateral breast cancer. On examination, there was an intact lumpectomy scar, mild hyperpigmentation with fibrosis, and a palpable 3 cm mass at the 10 o’clock position just superior to the prior incision. Diagnostic mammography showed a new dense oval mass with indistinct margins in the right upper-outer quadrant at 10 o’clock. Ultrasound demonstrated an irregular, hypoechoic mass with indistinct, microlobulated margins at the same location. Ultrasound-guided core-needle biopsy revealed a malignant neoplasm with epithelial-myoepithelial differentiation: nests, trabeculae, and cords of epithelial cells with moderate atypia, cribriform architecture, moderate to abundant eosinophilic to oncocytic cytoplasm, frequent mitoses, and foci of necrosis. Immunohistochemistry showed positivity for CK7 and C-kit, an intermixed myoepithelial component highlighted by smooth muscle myosin, smooth muscle specific actin, and p63, and negativity for ER, PR, HER2, and MUC4.

A 54-year-old woman with a history of left ovarian endometrial adenocarcinoma and childhood partial excision for a gastric duplication cyst and pancreas divisum underwent routine follow-up. She was asymptomatic. On contrast-enhanced CT, there was a 16-mm poorly enhancing mass in the pancreatic body, cystic dilatation of the main pancreatic duct, and a separate cystic nodular lesion beside the diaphragm crus. Initially thought to be a metastatic lymph node, closer review showed that the nodular lesion was connected to the pancreas. Laboratory studies revealed elevated CA19-9 (207.0 U/mL), DUPAN-2 (230.0 U/mL), and SPan-1 (65.0 U/mL), with a normal carcinoembryonic antigen level (2.0 ng/mL). Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography demonstrated a bifurcated main pancreatic duct and a cystic lesion protruding from the ventral pancreas that communicated with the duct and the nodular lesion. An endoscopic ultrasound–guided biopsy and ERCP were deferred due to the risk of cyst rupture and tumor cell dissemination. Clinically, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma was suspected, staged as T1N0M0.

A 63-year-old woman was admitted with a two-year history of intermittent abdominal distension and, over the preceding 10 days, severe abdominal pain accompanied by hematemesis and hematochezia. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 °C, pulse 75/min, respirations 15/min, and blood pressure 80/55 mmHg. On examination, a palpable mass was noted in the left lower abdomen; the liver and spleen were not palpable.

Laboratory tests revealed WBC 3.8 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 62%, hemoglobin 93 g/L, platelets 181 × 10^9/L; total protein 51.3 g/L, albumin 25.2 g/L; CA 12-5 39.4 U/mL; weakly positive fecal occult blood; PT 15.2 s, PTA 76%, INR 1.18. Abdominal ultrasound showed thickening of the left small-intestine wall, mesenteric thickening, and enlarged lymph nodes suggestive of obstruction. Contrast-enhanced CT of the small intestine demonstrated incomplete obstruction, diffuse wall thickening, and local effusion in the left iliac fossa. A barium enema confirmed intestinal obstruction. Before surgery, the working diagnosis was an obstructive space-occupying lesion of the small intestine.

A 23-year-old woman presented with a year of progressively increasing abdominal girth, first noted after the delivery of her second child. She reported mild, generalized abdominal discomfort but no other specific symptoms. Her medical history included two years of oral contraceptive use; prior evaluations at multiple clinics had yielded no diagnosis or relief.

On examination, she appeared slightly pale. Vital signs were notable for a blood pressure of 130/85 mmHg, pulse rate of 125 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation of 98 % on room air, and a random blood glucose of 6 mmol/L. Her weight was 80 kg and height 160 cm. Abdominal examination revealed marked distension with visible superficial veins and an abdominal circumference of 128 cm, corresponding to a 38-week gestation; a fluid thrill was present. The abdomen was smooth, mobile, and firm. Pelvic examination showed a normal-appearing cervix and full fornices. Chest auscultation revealed bilaterally decreased air entry; other systems were unremarkable.

An abdominopelvic ultrasound suggested the presence of ascites. Subsequent CT imaging of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a massive unilocular peritoneal fluid collection measuring approximately 32 × 35 × 39 cm without septations or enhancing solid components, displacing visceral organs posteriorly. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of a large peritoneal cystic mass was made, and the patient was scheduled for exploratory laparotomy.

A 35-year-old previously healthy man presented with a 20-day history of dull, aching, nonradiating low back pain. Over the same period, he noted gradual numbness in both lower limbs and developed urinary and bowel retention. Within one week before admission, he became paraplegic.  
On examination, power in both lower limbs was grade 0 except for grade 1 plantar flexion. There was complete sensory loss below the T10 level. Muscle tone was increased with exaggerated deep tendon reflexes and clonus bilaterally. Sphincter disturbance required catheterization.  
A thoracolumbar spine radiograph was unremarkable except for slight loss of lumbar lordosis.  
Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine revealed an irregular intramedullary lesion behind the body of L1, predominantly on the right side, displacing the cord to the left. On T1-weighted images, the lesion was hyperintense; on T2-weighted images, it was isointense relative to the normal cord. After gadolinium administration, there was only slight enhancement of the lesion’s surrounding wall.

A 42-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of neck pain and progressive spastic hemiparesis, recently worsened, without bowel or bladder involvement. She also reported dysphagia and disturbed sleep. On examination, there was paralysis of the right sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles; motor strength was Medical Research Council grade 3 on the right. Deep tendon reflexes were exaggerated, and bilateral plantar responses were extensor. There were no stigmata of neurofibromatosis. MRI of the cervicomedullary region showed a well-defined, dural-based mass at the foramen magnum, situated anterior to the neuroaxis, extending above and below, severely compressing the spinal cord. The lesion enhanced homogeneously and encased both vertebral arteries.

A 50-year-old woman with stage IV colon cancer (status post total colectomy and multiple lines of chemotherapy) and known metastases to the liver (post three resections) and lung (on monthly systemic therapy) presented to the emergency department with new-onset encephalopathy, generalized weakness, and fatigue. She was receiving folinic acid, fluorouracil, and irinotecan (FOLFIRI). 

A noncontrast CT scan of the brain revealed a new polypoidal mass in the left nasal cavity obstructing the left maxillary sinus infundibulum, with associated mucosal thickening and an air-fluid level in the left maxillary sinus. Dedicated CT of the sinuses confirmed a mass in the left nasal cavity extending into the medial superior aspect of the left maxillary sinus and the inferior portion of the left ethmoid sinus; this was a new finding compared with head imaging obtained two years earlier. Otolaryngology was consulted.

On examination, the patient was somnolent but arousable, followed commands, and answered questions appropriately. She reported 3–4 weeks of nasal obstruction with difficulty breathing through the left naris and one or two episodes of minor left-sided epistaxis that resolved with pressure. She denied changes in smell, postnasal drip, purulent drainage, rhinorrhea, facial pain, numbness or paresthesia, otologic symptoms, dyspnea, dysphagia, dysphonia, odynophagia, oral bleeding or lesions, and neck pain or masses. 

Her medical history included esophageal varices, depression, and a multidrug-resistant organism infection. Surgical history was notable for multiple hepatic wedge resections, hysterectomy, and bladder sling placement. She had no prior sinonasal disease, was a non-smoker, and denied alcohol or illicit drug use.

Two days after the consultation, she underwent bilateral nasal endoscopy. A hypervascular, solid mass was identified, originating from and contiguous with the left middle turbinate and extending into its posterior aspect without definitive invasion into the maxillary sinus. Biopsy was complicated by epistaxis but she remained stable postoperatively. At this time, the differential diagnosis included a primary nasopharyngeal carcinoma versus further metastasis of her stage IV colon cancer.

A 50-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a mass in the vulva that had been detected incidentally 2 years earlier and had gradually grown with only mild tenderness. Her obstetrical history was G3P1 with two abortions; her last menstrual period was approximately 18 months ago, and she had undergone diagnostic dilation and curettage four times for dysfunctional uterine bleeding.  

On examination, there was a soft, movable, cystic, well-circumscribed mass approximately 4.0 cm × 2.0 cm located in the middle to lower part of the left labium majus. The initial clinical diagnosis was a Bartholin gland cyst.  

Transcutaneous ultrasonography demonstrated a 3.6 cm × 1.5 cm unilocular, oval, well-circumscribed mass under the skin of the left labium majus. It was heterogeneous and mildly echogenic with uneven low-echo areas and punctate hyperechoic foci, as well as slight posterior acoustic enhancement. Color Doppler imaging revealed abundant blood flow signals within the mass.  

The patient underwent excision of the mass under lumbar anesthesia. On gross inspection, the specimen was a reddish-gray soft tissue measuring about 3.2 cm × 2.8 cm × 1.6 cm.

A 30-year-old woman presented with a painless swelling on the anterior aspect of her left leg. She reported that a small oval bulge had been present since birth and had gradually enlarged to approximately 10×6 cm. There were no associated symptoms such as fever, warmth, or overlying skin changes. Her medical, family, drug, and allergy histories were unremarkable.

On examination, the mass was smooth, soft, and mobile in all directions. There was no fluctuation, translucency, reducibility, compressibility, or pulsatility. A lateral radiograph of the left leg below the knee showed a localized soft-tissue swelling. MRI of the same region demonstrated a large, solitary, well-defined, heterogeneously isointense lesion measuring 13×9×6 cm in the subcutaneous plane over the diaphysis of the tibia, with an identifiable feeding vessel.

Based on the imaging findings, a subcutaneous hemangioma was diagnosed. The patient was treated with propranolol, but no improvement was observed. Surgical excision and biopsy were then planned.

A 23-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of a gradually enlarging mass on the anterior aspect of his right wrist, along the radial edge. On examination, Phalen’s maneuver and Durkan’s test were positive, indicating median nerve compression. Magnetic resonance imaging of the wrist demonstrated a well-defined, encapsulated mass on the radial side of the wrist that exhibited biphasic (central and peripheral) contrast enhancement (target sign).

A 58-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis and a history of renal lithiasis surgery presented with a 7-month history of low back pain and constipation. On examination, the abdomen was unremarkable. Digital rectal examination revealed a renitent, cystic mass compressing the posterior rectal wall. Pancolonoscopy showed a rounded, extrinsic, nonstenosing tumor compressing the rectum. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a well-circumscribed presacral cystic mass measuring 13×12×10 cm. Pelvic MRI confirmed a presacral cystic formation measuring 13×11 cm compressing the posterior rectal wall. Fine-needle aspiration was not performed to avoid the risk of tumor seeding.

A 54-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension presented with a mass in the anterior left thigh that had been slowly enlarging over 10 years. He recently noted a sensation of heaviness during walking and difficulty fitting clothing over the area. He denied pain, paresthesia, pruritus, or discharge and had no history of trauma, surgery, or radiation to the thigh. On examination, there was a large, dome-shaped, firm, nontender, nonpulsatile mass measuring approximately 24 cm × 15 cm, occupying most of the anterior thigh. The overlying skin was normal, and there was no regional lymphadenopathy. Distal pulses, sensation, and motor function were intact. MRI of the left thigh showed a well-circumscribed lesion measuring 90 mm × 150 mm × 215 mm arising from the anterior surface of the femur, extending from the inguinal region to the femoral condyles. The mass displaced but did not invade adjacent muscles. It was homogeneously hyperintense on T1- and T2-weighted images, contained focal internal calcifications, and there was no peri-lesional vascular proliferation, cortical bone erosion, or marrow invasion.

A 50-year-old East Indian woman presented with a 6-month history of lower back pain, fatigue, and unintentional weight loss. She denied hypertension, headache, palpitations, or excessive sweating and had no family history of cancer. On examination, there was a large, nontender mass in the left upper quadrant that crossed the midline. Laboratory studies were unremarkable except for microcytic anemia (mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration, 7.3 g/dL). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 23.2 × 17.6 × 13.6 cm mass superior to the left kidney, with areas of necrosis, punctate calcifications, and irregular contours; the mass displaced the pancreas anteriorly, compressed the left kidney, and the normal left adrenal gland was not visualized. Mesenteric and para-aortic lymphadenopathy were present without evidence of distant metastases. Tumor markers, including carcinoembryonic antigen, CA 15-3, CA 19-9, and CA 125, were normal.

A 2-year-5-month-old boy was brought to the otorhinolaryngology clinic because of a 2-week history of enlargement and hardening of the left maxillary region. His parents denied fever, weight loss, pain, discharge, prior surgery, dental procedures, or trauma. On examination, there was a 2.5 cm fibroelastic lesion over the left maxilla without signs of infection. Oroscopy, otoscopy, and neck examination were normal. Facial computed tomography revealed a radiolucent maxillary sinus lesion of odontogenic origin with associated bone erosion.

A 45-year-old woman with iron deficiency anemia and untreated stage I papillary thyroid carcinoma presented with chronic fatigue, night sweats, body aches, and joint pain. Hemoglobin was 6.6 g/dL. She denied chest pain, weight loss, hematochezia, melena, or hematemesis. She had a positive fecal occult blood test and a history of Barrett’s esophagus. On hospital day 2, she developed palpitations and was found to be in atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response (heart rate up to 150 bpm), remained hemodynamically stable, and converted to sinus rhythm after intravenous metoprolol. The patient then reported a two-year history of palpitations and occasional syncope, which she had attributed to an experimental immunotherapy she had received. 
CT of the chest showed a 6.6 × 5.2 cm mass inferior to the heart with a moderate to large circumferential pericardial effusion. Transthoracic echocardiography estimated an ejection fraction of 70%, with no signs of tamponade and identified a mass posterior to the heart abutting the right atrium and right ventricle. Cardiac MRI confirmed a heterogeneous mass in the pericardial space measuring approximately 5.9 × 5.8 × 6.2 cm displacing the heart superiorly. Laboratory studies revealed C-reactive protein of 110.0 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 127 mm/h, platelets 686,000/μL, ferritin 144 ng/mL, iron 11 μg/dL (transferrin saturation 4%), and a negative troponin level. She received intravenous iron and red blood cell transfusions with improvement in anemia.

A 30-year-old woman with a 2-year history of systemic lupus erythematosus, treated pulmonary tuberculosis in 2014, and repaired atrial septal defect, presented with a 1-month history of intermittent fevers (up to 102°F), left-sided pleuritic chest pain, and a productive cough with whitish sputum. She noted dyspnea when supine and a 4-kg weight loss over 2 months. She denied rash, photosensitivity, or Raynaud phenomenon; she reported moderate arthralgias and a history of first-trimester abortions.

On examination, she was thin, tachycardic (104 bpm), blood pressure 132/82 mm Hg, respiratory rate 24/min on 4 L oxygen, temperature 37.5 °C. Findings included pallor, pedal edema, non-scarring alopecia, reduced chest expansion, and coarse inspiratory crackles over the left upper lung field. The abdomen was distended with shifting dullness; no organomegaly. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory tests showed Hb 11.2 g/dL, WBC 9,000/µL, ESR 48 mm/hr, CRP 5.9 mg/dL; ANA 3+ homogeneous, anti-dsDNA 27.4 U/mL, C3 0.27 g/L, C4 0.07 g/L; urinalysis with 1+ protein. Chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral pleural effusions. Thoracentesis yielded clear yellow exudative fluid (protein 2.9 g/L, LDH 417 IU/L, lymphocyte-predominant; cultures and AFB negative). Echocardiography revealed a trace pericardial effusion with preserved function. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed bronchiectasis in the left upper and apical segments, collapse of the left upper lobe, and moderate bilateral pleural effusions.

A 22-year-old woman presented with three months of progressive weakness in all four limbs, beginning in the lower extremities and extending to the upper extremities over the last month. She also noted right calf pain one month before weakness onset, but denied numbness, sphincter dysfunction, trauma, headache, fever, or seizures. Her developmental history was significant for delayed ambulation until age 4, with no prior surgery or family history of neurologic disease. 

On examination, there were no cutaneous stigmata of dysraphism. Muscle strength was graded 4/5 in the upper limbs and 3/5 in the lower limbs. Reflexes were normal in the upper extremities and hyperactive in the lower extremities, with positive Babinski and Chaddock signs bilaterally and myoclonus of the lower limbs. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervicothoracic spine revealed an intradural tumor extending from C5 to T4 that was hyperintense on T1-weighted and T2-weighted sequences and hypointense on STIR images. The leading diagnostic considerations at this stage were intratumoral bleeding, dermoid cyst, and a cervicothoracic subpial lipoma.

A 48-year-old woman presented with 2 months of recurrent abdominal pain and weight loss. She had no fever, jaundice, prior liver disease, blood transfusions, tattoos, or alcohol abuse. Her comorbidities included diabetes, hypertension, and obesity; there was no family history of carcinoma. On examination, a palpable epigastric mass was noted; the remainder of the clinical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, serum biochemistry, coagulation profile, and CA19-9, were normal; viral serologies were nonreactive. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a 9.9 × 7.8 cm ill-defined, heterogeneous, hypervascular mass in the left hepatic lobe with central necrosis, partial washout on delayed images, encasement of the left portal vein branch, and compression of the left hepatic vein; there was no cirrhosis and the main portal vein and right branch were uninvolved. PET-CT demonstrated an SUV max of 6.4 in the mass, normal hepatic parenchymal uptake, and no abnormal uptake above or below the diaphragm. Ultrasound-guided biopsy revealed spindle cells with nuclear pleomorphism, up to 10 mitoses per 10 high-power fields, and necrosis, suggesting a spindle cell neoplasm; immunohistochemistry showed tumor cells to be desmin positive, caldesmon negative, DOG1 negative, and CD117 negative.

A 7-day-old male neonate presented with progressive difficulty in breathing and feeding, accompanied by intermittent cyanosis since birth. He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy; no antenatal ultrasonography was performed. On the second postnatal day, he developed irritability with frequent sneezing and worsening respiratory distress during feeding and sleep. On day 6, intermittent cyanotic episodes prompted hospital admission. Examination revealed an irritable, tachypneic neonate with nasal flaring, grunting, suprasternal retractions, and central cyanosis. A lateral cervical radiograph demonstrated a well-defined soft-tissue mass in the nasopharynx. An endotracheal tube was placed to secure the airway, and a nasogastric tube met resistance at the nasopharynx. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a 35×15 mm well-defined pedunculated heterogeneous mass arising from the right lateral wall of the nasopharynx and extending into the hypopharynx. The mass nearly completely obstructed the airway and deviated both tubes to the left. There was no intracranial connection. The lesion had a relatively hyperdense central core surrounded by low-attenuation fatty components, slight peripheral enhancement, and no calcification or lymphadenopathy.

A 56-year-old woman with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis on long-term methotrexate presented in June 2013 with fluctuating cervical spine pain radiating to the occipital region. By early November, pain severity necessitated a 2-week hospitalization for intensive analgesic therapy. On October 27, she abruptly became noncommunicative and fixed her gaze. Examination revealed receptive and expressive aphasia and cervical paravertebral muscle tenderness without meningeal signs. Noncontrast brain CT was normal. Suspecting an acute ischemic stroke within the therapeutic window, she received intravenous thrombolysis, with rapid full recovery. Partial complex seizure was also considered. Neuropsychological testing showed mildly impaired memory and executive function. Internal, ophthalmologic, EEG, carotid/vertebral Doppler ultrasound, and CT angiography were unremarkable. She was discharged for thrombophilia screening and planned MRI.

On December 18, she was readmitted with sudden aphasia, disorientation, and a generalized tonic-clonic seizure, aborted with intravenous diazepam. She reported cervical pain, had no meningeal signs, exhibited lower-extremity hyperreflexia, and a mild paraparetic ataxic gait. MRI of the brain and spinal cord demonstrated diffuse T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in the bilateral hippocampi, brainstem, cerebellum, and spinal cord gray matter extending to T7–T8. Proton MR spectroscopy of the brainstem region showed no definite metabolic abnormalities. CSF flow studies were normal. CSF analysis revealed markedly elevated protein (12.0 g/L), albumin 4.0 g/L, mild lymphomonocytic pleocytosis (monocytes 22/µL, lymphocytes 5/µL), and a CD4:CD8 ratio of 2.94 without oligoclonal bands or red cells. Laboratory evaluation including CBC, coagulation, metabolic panel, tumor markers (CEA, CA 19-9, CA 15-3, CA 125, CYFRA 21-1, SCC antigen), hormone levels (PRL, FT4, TSH), serologies for bacterial, viral, and other pathogens (syphilis, Borrelia, Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, EBV, CMV, HSV1/2, VZV, HIV, tuberculosis, Toxoplasma, rubella), onconeural antibodies, and broad-spectrum autoantibodies were all negative. Whole-body FDG PET showed intense meningeal uptake along the cervical and thoracic spinal cord, infratentorial regions, and partially over the cerebral convexities. The working diagnosis was autoimmune meningoencephalitis with secondary epilepsy, and she received high-dose methylprednisolone (total 5 g), plasmapheresis (3 sessions), IVIG (0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days), acyclovir, and ceftriaxone.

Despite therapy, she developed a central right facial nerve palsy, left upper-limb dysmetria, spastic lower-limb paraparesis, and recurrent seizures despite carbamazepine, levetiracetam, and lamotrigine. In early February 2014, she became progressively somnolent and then semicomatose. MRI revealed hydrocephalus with enlargement of all ventricles; ophthalmologic exam showed bilateral papilledema with hemorrhages. External lumbar drainage yielded transient improvement—she remained somnolent with meningeal signs, was blind, and exhibited an organic psychosyndrome. Repeat CSF showed protein 12.9 g/L with pleocytosis (monocytes 52/µL, lymphocytes 2/µL). Interictal EEG revealed mixed slow and epileptiform activity in both temporal regions. At the end of February, MRI showed mild regression of T2/FLAIR hyperintensities, persistent hydrocephalus, and frontoparietal leptomeningeal contrast enhancement. Her condition continued to worsen with bronchopneumonia, sepsis, left subclavian vein thrombosis, and multiorgan failure. She died on April 26, 2014, approximately 10 months after symptom onset.

A 32-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of headache and, over the preceding week, worsening pain, left ocular proptosis, diplopia, and eye pain, accompanied by hyaline nasal discharge. The headache was throbbing, progressive, and located in the left frontal region, with associated fatigue and myalgia. Her medical history was notable for triple-negative breast adenocarcinoma treated with radical mastectomy and chemotherapy three years earlier, atopic dermatitis treated with prednisone 80 mg daily for the past year, and well-controlled asthma and hypertension. On examination, her vital signs were normal, she had a Cushingoid appearance, and there was left ocular proptosis; nasal endoscopy showed only a discrete hyaline secretion in the nasal vestibule. Noncontrast and contrast-enhanced CT of the skull and sinuses revealed bilateral opacification of the sphenoid and ethmoid sinuses, left intraorbital involvement with contrast enhancement, and extension into the cavernous sinus causing pachymeningeal enhancement.

A 63-year-old woman presented with right-sided nasal obstruction and intermittent epistaxis for 6 months. The obstruction was insidious in onset and gradually progressive, becoming complete over the past 3 months. Epistaxis occurred about once monthly, spontaneous, with each episode involving approximately 250–500 mL of blood. She had no history of systemic disease. On anterior rhinoscopy, there was a pinkish, fleshy mass filling the entire right nasal cavity that bled easily on contact. Contrast-enhanced CT of the nose and paranasal sinuses showed a heterogeneously enhancing mass in the right nasal cavity, likely centered on the middle turbinate, with extension into the right ethmoid sinus superiorly and into the choana and sphenoid sinus posteriorly, associated with erosion of adjacent bone, destruction of the nasal septum, and extension into the left nasal cavity—features suggestive of inverted papilloma. A biopsy of the mass was obtained to confirm the diagnosis.

A 70-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis was hospitalized for worsening anemia, intermittent weakness, and confusion. He also reported several weeks of painful swelling in the left forearm. Over the prior 2–3 months, he had experienced low-grade fevers and persistent leukocytosis, with white-cell counts as high as 28,000/µL, but no source of infection was identified despite blood and urine cultures.

Physical examination revealed a tender, firm swelling over the volar aspect of the mid–left forearm without overlying skin changes. Vital signs showed a temperature of 37.8 °C; other parameters were within normal limits.

Plain radiographs of the left forearm demonstrated prominence of the volar soft tissues without bone abnormality. Magnetic resonance imaging of the forearm revealed a 12.6 × 5.5 × 5.0 cm mass in the anterior compartment. The lesion exhibited high T1 and heterogeneous central T2 signal with peripheral intermediate T1 and high T2 signal and surrounding edema.

To evaluate for occult infection as the cause of his fevers and leukocytosis, autologous Indium-111–labeled leukocytes were injected intravenously, and 24-hour delayed images were obtained. The scan showed focal radiotracer uptake in the proximal to mid–left forearm corresponding to the MRI mass. Whole-body bone scintigraphy and CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no evidence of distant metastatic disease.

A 60-year-old Chinese man presented with one month of persistent right abdominal pain and dark stools, along with recent nausea and vomiting. He denied fever, anorexia, hematemesis, radiating pain, or weight loss. Upper endoscopy showed a malignant‐appearing tumor in the descending duodenum; biopsy suggested poorly differentiated carcinoma but yielded too few cells for immunostaining. Physical examination revealed no visible pigmented lesions or enlarged superficial lymph nodes. Routine hematologic and biochemical studies were normal. Serum tumor markers (AFP, CEA, CA-50, CA-19-9) were within normal limits. Fecal occult blood testing was positive. A barium meal study showed a filling defect in the descending duodenum without mucosal destruction and normal transit of barium. Abdominal CT demonstrated a space-occupying lesion in the descending duodenum causing luminal narrowing. Exploratory laparotomy confirmed a solid duodenal tumor invading the serosa, with enlarged mesenteric and peripancreatic lymph nodes; a palliative segmental resection was performed. On gross examination, the tumor measured 2.5 cm × 1.5 cm × 1.0 cm and appeared gray-red and pliable without pigment; one mesenteric lymph node was involved. Frozen-section histology showed a submucosal, diffusely infiltrative proliferation of epithelioid cells with marked nuclear atypia, prominent eosinophilic nucleoli, abundant mitotic figures, and no visible melanin pigment. Pathologists favored lymphoma or undifferentiated carcinoma.

A 37-year-old man collapsed outdoors from sudden cardiopulmonary arrest and was resuscitated with bystander CPR and two external defibrillator shocks. His only past gastrointestinal history was gastric mucosal erosions diagnosed 9 years earlier. He reported chronic abdominal pain and intermittent reflux despite long-term proton-pump inhibitor therapy. He denied alcohol or tobacco use and had no known allergies.

On arrival, his temperature was 36.2 °C, blood pressure 139/111 mmHg, heart rate 130 beats/min, respiratory rate 32 breaths/min, and Glasgow Coma Scale score was E4V1M4; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory evaluation showed leukocytosis, mild elevations of liver enzymes and creatinine, lactic acidosis (arterial pH 7.118, lactate 8.1 mmol/L), and a D-dimer >100 µg/mL. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen revealed an incidental 8 cm mass in the lesser omentum composed of three fused solid tumors, one with a nonenhancing low-density area suggestive of necrosis or hematoma. 

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed a red, 7 mm submucosal gastric tumor with central depression, prominent gastric folds, and shallow duodenal ulcers despite ongoing intravenous PPI treatment. Endoscopic ultrasound identified three well-circumscribed hyperechoic masses in the lesser omentum, one with a hypoechoic center, and no pancreatic lesions. 

Fine-needle aspiration of both the gastric and omental lesions yielded grade 2 neuroendocrine neoplasms that stained positive for chromogranin A and synaptophysin. 

During laparoscopy, an 83 × 80 × 37 mm omental mass was resected en bloc. Histopathology showed nests of small ovoid cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and dilated capillaries; immunohistochemistry was positive for chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and gastrin. 

Review of the gastric biopsy specimen demonstrated identical morphology and confirmed strong gastrin immunoreactivity in the submucosal tumor.

A 59-year-old woman with osteoarthritis, hypothyroidism, and recently diagnosed follicular B-cell lymphoma presented with a pruritic, erythematous, dome-shaped papular rash with crusting on her back, neck, forehead, and perinasal and periorbital areas. The rash developed during bendamustine and rituximab therapy. Bendamustine was discontinued (due to cytopenia and worsening rash) and chemotherapy was changed to R-CHOP, which improved the rash on her trunk but not on her face.

Initial punch biopsy of a back lesion showed dermal lymphohistiocytic infiltrates, and the differential diagnosis included granulomatous rosacea and granulomatous folliculitis. A trial of minocycline was stopped due to side effects; doxycycline plus topical metronidazole produced minimal improvement.

A second biopsy of a forehead lesion demonstrated a dense superficial perifollicular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate in the superficial and mid dermis, reported as suggestive of granulomatous rosacea. Treatment was switched to oral erythromycin and topical clobetasol, leading to significant improvement in pruritus; clobetasol was later replaced with topical tacrolimus.

Given the persistent facial lesions, the biopsy specimens were reviewed. No morphologic evidence of cutaneous involvement by follicular lymphoma was found. Immunohistochemistry of the dermal histiocytes showed patchy cytoplasmic staining for S100 and no staining for CD1a.

A 68-year-old man with a history of reflux esophagitis and benign prostatic hyperplasia presented with a complaint of abdominal pain. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a round, smooth, elevated submucosal mass with central ulceration in the second portion of the duodenum. Laboratory studies showed normal carcinoembryonic antigen and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels. Dynamic contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 26 mm circumscribed duodenal mass with marked enhancement on arterial and portal phases and persistent enhancement on equilibrium phase, abutting the pancreatic head without biliary or pancreatic duct dilatation. MRI showed hypo-intensity on T1-weighted images, modestly high intensity on T2-weighted images, and slight hyperintensity on diffusion-weighted images. Endoscopic ultrasonography identified a hypoechoic lesion arising from the fourth layer of the duodenal wall. A biopsy from the central ulceration showed no malignancy. Immunohistochemical studies of the biopsy specimen were positive for smooth muscle actin and negative for S100, C-Kit, and CD34.

A 45-year-old right-handed man presented with a 3-month history of partial seizures affecting his right upper limb and right face, accompanied by progressive expressive aphasia. He had well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus. There was no headache, visual disturbance, or fever. On examination, he was afebrile and normotensive. Neurological examination revealed Broca’s aphasia but was otherwise nonfocal, with no sensory, cerebellar, or gait abnormalities.

Brain magnetic resonance imaging and computed tomography demonstrated a mass in the left frontotemporal region extending into the insular cortex. The lesion contained calcifications, areas of necrosis, and solid components, and it produced appreciable mass effect with compression of the left lateral ventricle and surrounding edema.

The patient underwent a left parietal craniotomy and debulking. Intraoperative cytologic preparations showed a hypercellular smear with numerous delicate vascular channels and clusters of monomorphic round to oval cells having fine fibrillary processes, eosinophilic cytoplasm, a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and conspicuous nucleoli. There was no significant nuclear pleomorphism or mitotic activity, and occasional reactive astrocytes were seen. A low-grade glial tumor favoring oligodendroglioma was diagnosed, although focal, ill-formed peritheliomatous arrangements suggested the possibility of an ependymal tumor.

Histopathological examination of the resected specimen revealed a clear cell neoplasm arranged in sheets and nests without definitive perivascular pseudorosettes or ependymal rosettes. Tumor cells had clear cytoplasm, round hyperchromatic nuclei, and inconspicuous nucleoli. There were focal areas of mild nuclear atypia and 4–6 mitoses per high-power field, along with reactive gliosis, calcification, and endothelial proliferation. No necrosis was identified. On the basis of these findings, an anaplastic oligodendroglioma (WHO grade III) was diagnosed.

A 40‐year‐old man presented with a two‐month history of a rapidly enlarging swelling in the palmar aspect of his right hand. On examination, the 3-cm mass was firm, tender, poorly mobile, and caused difficulty making a fist; the overlying skin was tense. MRI of the hand showed a well-defined lobulated T2/STIR hyperintense, T1 hypointense cystic lesion with thin internal septations measuring 28 × 44 × 69 mm encasing the flexor tendons from the distal carpal row to the fourth metacarpophalangeal joint, with no significant adjacent fat edema; it was interpreted as a tendon sheath or synovial cyst. Fine-needle aspiration cytology revealed a dual population of cells—larger cells with vacuolated cytoplasm and vesicular nuclei and smaller cells with scant cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei—arranged in clusters and forming rosettes. Periodic acid–Schiff staining highlighted the large cells. Immunocytochemistry showed positivity for vimentin and negativity for CD45, S-100, and epithelial membrane antigen. A provisional diagnosis of a small round cell tumor was made, with the leading considerations being primitive neuroectodermal tumor/Ewing sarcoma and rhabdomyosarcoma, and a biopsy was advised.

A 33-year-old man underwent CT after a mild traumatic brain injury, which revealed an incidental skull-base mass. He had previously undergone resection of an abdominal para-aortic paraganglioma at age 11 and a right adrenal pheochromocytoma at age 19; medical records were unavailable. He reported periods of elevated blood pressure, chest pain with exertion, intermittent claudication, tachycardia, and diaphoresis during childhood, but had been asymptomatic since the second surgery until the recent trauma. 

On examination, he had right moderate hearing loss, right proptosis, optic nerve atrophy with right temporal hemianopsia, and sensory loss in the V2 and V3 distributions. Blood pressure ranged from 130/90 to 140/100 mmHg. There were no weight changes or other endocrine symptoms.

Brain MRI was interpreted as compatible with a meningioma versus a hemangiopericytoma. Laboratory evaluation showed normal 24-hour urinary metanephrines (208 μg; normal 86–320 μg) and markedly elevated normetanephrines (10,828 μg; normal 120–400 μg; 27× upper limit of normal), with other hormonal tests within normal limits. The diagnosis of a functioning paraganglioma was then established.

A 59-year-old woman underwent total gastrectomy for low-risk gastric GIST (KIT exon 11 mutation) and synchronous advanced gastric adenocarcinoma (pT2bN0M0). She had no personal or family history of FAP or Gardner syndrome and received no adjuvant therapy. Two years after surgery, surveillance CT revealed a new 3.7-cm well-defined, ovoid mass in the right diaphragmatic crus with homogeneous, mild delayed enhancement and no necrosis, hemorrhage, or cystic change. 18F-FDG‐PET showed mild hypermetabolic activity (SUV max 3.5). Physical examination and laboratory tests were unremarkable.

A 21-year-old woman underwent evaluation of a right pelvic mass that had been noted incidentally on routine examination 2 years earlier. She remained asymptomatic, and laboratory tests, including carcinoembryonic antigen, CA19-9, CA125, and α-fetoprotein, were within normal limits.  
Noncontrast and contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 40-mm well-demarcated, low-attenuation mass in the right pelvis, containing both solid and cystic components; the solid portion measured 47 HU on noncontrast images and 77 HU after contrast administration. There were no calcifications or visible fat.  
On MRI, the lesion lay adjacent to the right ovary without a beak sign. The cystic component was isointense on T1-weighted images and markedly hyperintense on T2-weighted images. The solid, papillary nodule projecting into the cyst showed intermediate T2 signal with punctate foci of high intensity, high signal on diffusion-weighted imaging, and an apparent diffusion coefficient of 1.0–1.2 × 10⁻³ mm²/s. On dynamic contrast-enhanced T1-weighted imaging, the nodule demonstrated heterogeneous, prolonged enhancement.  
Based on these radiologic findings, the initial differential diagnoses included ovarian serous borderline tumor, serous adenocarcinoma, and endometrial borderline tumor.

A 58-year-old Asian woman was evaluated at our hospital after routine follow-up imaging revealed multiple pancreatic lesions. She had undergone right nephrectomy for renal cell carcinoma 20 years earlier, followed by resection of soft-tissue and chest-wall metastases and partial left nephrectomy for additional RCC metastases between 2005 and 2007. She had been receiving interferon therapy since 2007. She was asymptomatic on presentation. Laboratory studies showed normal carcinoembryonic antigen and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated multiple hypervascular nodules throughout the pancreas. ^18F-FDG PET/CT revealed FDG accumulation in the tail of the pancreas (standardized uptake value, 2.5) without evidence of uptake elsewhere. MRI of the abdomen showed three enhancing nodular lesions in the head, body, and tail of the pancreas, with no dilation of the main pancreatic or bile ducts. Preoperative differential diagnoses included pancreatic endocrine tumor and metastatic carcinoma.

A 45-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of a slowly growing, dull, intermittent swelling and discomfort in the right upper vestibule. She reported fluctuations in pain intensity and a sensation of heaviness in the area. On examination, teeth #15 and #16 were grossly carious, and there was a firm, mildly tender diffuse swelling of the adjacent vestibular mucosa. There was no tenderness on percussion of the involved teeth. Panoramic radiography demonstrated a mild periapical radiolucency at the affected root apices. A provisional diagnosis of a periapical abscess was made, and extraction of the carious teeth with socket curettage was planned. Preoperative blood tests (CBC, hemoglobin, blood sugar, bleeding and clotting times) were within normal limits. Under local anesthesia, the teeth were extracted, and curettage yielded a gelatinous, soft, mushy tissue, which was sent for histopathological examination with a provisional diagnosis of periapical granuloma.

A 45-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 14-year history of palpitations that had become more frequent and intense over the preceding two months, associated with dyspnea on exertion and unintentional weight loss of 2 pounds per month. Her medications included atenolol 50 mg daily and aspirin 200 mg daily. On cardiovascular examination, the heart rhythm was regular, S1 was split, and there were no murmurs. Findings in other systems were normal.

A chest X-ray showed clear lung fields with right atrial enlargement. Electrocardiography revealed sinus rhythm with right bundle branch block and an anterosuperior divisional block. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a mobile mass in the right atrium attached to the atrial septum, right atrial enlargement, right ventricular volume overload, and a dilated inferior vena cava. 

Abdominal CT after contrast administration showed a normal-size liver with heterogeneous parenchymal enhancement and dilatation of the hepatic veins and inferior vena cava, consistent with cardiogenic changes. Chest CT with contrast revealed an enlarged cardiac silhouette and an intra-atrial hypodense mass measuring approximately 6.1 × 5.6 cm that occupied most of the right atrium and prevented contrast opacification of the chamber.

A 30-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of a slowly enlarging, soft mass in the right upper posterior alveolar mucosa associated with mild pain on chewing. About 18 months earlier he had a mobile tooth extracted from that area; the mass persisted and continued to enlarge. His medical history was noncontributory.

On examination, the lesion measured approximately 3×3 cm, was diffuse, reddish and slightly ulcerated, rubbery to firm in consistency, mildly tender, and bled slightly on palpation. Panoramic radiographs showed no bony changes. An incisional biopsy was performed.

Microscopic examination demonstrated surface epithelium overlying a loose myxoid stroma with a prominent vasculature. The stroma contained scattered spindle- to stellate-shaped cells with distinct borders and oval nuclei; there was no atypia, hyperchromasia, mitotic activity, or necrosis. Small, thin-walled curvilinear blood vessels were prominent throughout, and a mild infiltrate of neutrophils was present. Immunohistochemical staining showed most stromal cells to be immunopositive for vimentin, and the endothelial cells of the blood vessels to be immunoreactive for CD34.

A 49-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of progressive neck stiffness and spasm, left-sided jaw pain, and left-sided headache. Her initial toothache workup was normal. She subsequently noted morning-worse, shooting pain from the superoposterior left neck into the left occiput, aggravated by leaning to the left. She had full neck range of motion, moderate bilateral paraspinous muscle tenderness, negative Lhermitte and Spurling signs, and no neurologic deficits. 

MRI of the cervical spine showed a 3.0 × 2.6 × 2.5 cm heterogeneously T1 hypointense and markedly T2 hypointense, faintly enhancing trans-spatial mass involving the dens and right lateral mass of C2, the anterior arch and right lateral mass of C1, and extending into the prevertebral perivertebral space. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a soft-tissue density, lytic lesion with a sharp zone of transition, thin sclerotic margins, no internal matrix or calcification, and a center at the atlantoaxial joint. Whole-body FDG-PET/CT revealed intense uptake in this mass (maximum SUV 24.5) with no other FDG-avid lesions.

Differential diagnosis included neoplastic causes (metastasis, multiple myeloma/plasmacytoma, giant cell tumour, or pigmented villonodular synovitis), metabolic lesions (brown tumour or amyloid), and inflammatory conditions (gout or calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal deposition).

A 54-year-old man with relapsed angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma underwent an HLA-matched sibling peripheral blood stem cell transplant after reduced-intensity conditioning (fludarabine, busulfan, rabbit ATG) and was maintained on mycophenolate and cyclosporine. On day 7 posttransplant, he developed fever to 38.5°C, profound fatigue, and enlargement of multiple superficial lymph nodes. Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics for 3 days produced no improvement, and quantitative EBV-DNA was markedly elevated. CT imaging revealed enlarged subclavian, axillary, popliteal, inguinal, mediastinal, and abdominal lymph nodes. An excisional lymph node biopsy was performed, and simultaneously lymph node cells were submitted for flow cytometry.  
Flow cytometry showed that lymph node lymphocytes highly expressed the B-cell marker CD20, whereas markers including CD2, CD3, CD5, CD7, HLA-DR, CD10, CD8, CD23, FMC7, CD79a/b, and cyclin D3 were unchanged compared with peripheral blood.

A 37-year-old Iraqi man presented with a 4-year history of an occasionally pruritic eruption on his legs and back. Over the past 4 months, he noted intermittent drainage and swelling of his right ear. He had applied clotrimazole 1% cream with minimal improvement. He denied fevers, night sweats, weight loss, or other constitutional symptoms and had no significant medical or family history.

On examination, the right pinna bore a soft, pink-to-violaceous plaque with a beaded border. Similar pink-to-brown infiltrative plaques were present on his back and right posterior thigh. On the right anterior thigh and right lateral lower leg, there were coalescing 3–5 mm pink, partially blanchable macules forming a patch. There was no lymphadenopathy or mucosal involvement.

A punch biopsy of the right posterior thigh revealed a dense dermal inflammatory infiltrate composed predominantly of plasma cells and histiocytes. Spirochete and acid-fast bacilli stains were negative. Rapid plasma reagin and HIV tests were negative. An interferon-γ release assay (T-spot) was positive.

A 77-year-old woman with a history of ipsilateral triple-negative breast carcinoma treated with mastectomy, sentinel lymph node biopsy, and adjuvant chemotherapy 14 years ago presented with a 4-month history of a palpable, protuberant, ulcerated cutaneous mass in her right axilla. On examination, the lesion was protuberant and ulcerated but without palpable residual mass in the axilla. A shave biopsy of the lesion revealed poorly differentiated carcinoma, with a differential diagnosis that included squamous carcinoma and metastatic breast carcinoma. Given the clinical impression, she was referred to dermatology for wide local excision and possible Mohs procedure. An excisional biopsy was then performed.

A 1-year-old boy was evaluated for a 2-week history of a limp, fever, and difficulty moving his left leg. On examination, there was no deformity, swelling, skin lesion, pitting edema, or focal tenderness of the left leg. He had no weight loss, jaundice, polyuria, or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed a white-blood-cell count of 14.67×10^3/µl; all other values, including red-cell indices, platelets, liver enzymes, lactate dehydrogenase, alkaline phosphatase, and creatinine, were within reference ranges. Plain radiographs of the left tibia revealed a radiolucent lesion in the proximal meta-diaphysis with a laminated periosteal reaction. A diagnosis of osteomyelitis was made, and the patient underwent curettage of the lesion and grafting with a tobramycin-impregnated bone-graft substitute.

A 34-year-old man presented with moderate to severe low back pain that limited ambulation and was partially relieved by NSAIDs. His history was notable only for a prior chemonucleolysis at L5–S1 for discopathy with radicular compression, and MRI at that time had also shown left renal enlargement. 

On examination, the abdomen was soft and non-tender, and lumbar palpation and movement reproduced his discomfort; Valsalva’s maneuver also elicited pain. Both testicles were normal on inspection and palpation. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Review of his prior lumbar spine MRI confirmed a resolved discopathy but persistent retroperitoneal lymph node enlargement. A urotomography scan revealed multiple left paraaortic retroperitoneal masses measuring 10×8×6 cm, with satellite lymph nodes around the left psoas muscle causing lateral displacement of the left kidney and hydronephrosis.

Scrotal ultrasound showed the left testis to have heterogeneous parenchyma with high vascularity and irregular borders (28×23×14 mm; volume 4.9 cm3), whereas the right testis was normal. These findings raised suspicion for a primary testicular germ cell tumor.

Laboratory studies demonstrated an alpha-fetoprotein level of 15 115 ng/dL (normal <20 ng/dL), β–human chorionic gonadotropin of 11 IU/L (normal <0.5 IU/L), and lactate dehydrogenase of 394 U/L (normal <250 U/L).

A middle‐aged man (BMI 38.4 kg/m^2) was evaluated 40 days after detection of a thyroid nodule. He had no significant past medical, surgical, or family history. On examination, the thyroid was firm without palpable enlargement; there was no cervical lymphadenopathy. Thyroid ultrasonography revealed:  
• Right lobe: heterogeneous echotexture with a 2.7 × 1.09 cm hypoechoic area; a 0.61 × 0.60 cm hypoechoic nodule (aspect ratio > 1) with regular borders and punctate hyperechogenicity in the deep layer; and a 0.28 × 0.34 cm anechoic nodule (aspect ratio < 1) in the superficial layer.  
• Left lobe: a 0.54 × 1.01 cm solid hypoechoic nodule (aspect ratio < 1) with regular borders.  
Fine‐needle aspiration of the larger right‐lobe nodule showed atypical cells suggestive of papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
Laboratory tests: TSH 0.862 mIU/L (0.372–4.94); PTH 64.62 pg/mL (15–56); serum calcium 2.42 mmol/L (2.2–2.65); renal function normal; vitamin D not assessed.  
The patient underwent right thyroid lobectomy with isthmusectomy and central neck dissection. After removal of the right lobe and isthmus, two firm, well‐circumscribed masses (1.5 × 0.8 × 0.7 cm and 2.5 × 1.5 × 0.5 cm) were found on the dorsal and lateral aspects of the excised tissue. Intraoperative frozen section showed scattered round cells in fibroadipose tissue, suggesting parathyroid origin. Intraoperative PTH levels fell from 64.62 pg/mL pre‐resection to 29.68 pg/mL at 15 minutes and 35.71 pg/mL at 30 minutes; postoperative day 1 calcium was 2.30 mmol/L.

An 87-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of progressive left-sided weakness. She initially had difficulty ambulating and ascending stairs, and over time became wheelchair-bound. On neurologic examination, she had diffuse 3/5 left-sided strength, a left leg drift, and a left facial droop. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed a large confluent T2-hyperintense lesion in the right frontal lobe with multifocal nodular enhancement throughout the left cerebral hemisphere, as well as enhancement in the cerebellum and leptomeninges. The radiologic differential diagnosis included vasculitis, lymphoma, and CNS sarcoidosis as the most probable causes of the multifocal process, with glial neoplasm, demyelination, and metastases considered less likely.

A 38-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of left knee pain associated with difficulty walking, sitting cross-legged, and bending the knee. On examination, the range of motion was full; McMurray’s test and anterior and posterior drawer tests were negative. There was focal tenderness over the pes anserinus bursa and localized redness and soft-tissue swelling over the proximal medial tibial region. 

Plain radiographs of the knee (AP and lateral views) showed a well-circumscribed sclerotic lesion in the proximal medial and posteromedial tibial metaphysis with disorganized trabeculae and a sharp transition zone to normal bone. 

Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-defined metaphyseal lesion extending to the subarticular margin that was hyperintense on T2-weighted images and moderately hypointense on T1-weighted images, with surrounding bone-marrow edema and associated pes anserinus bursitis. 

The imaging findings were interpreted as suggestive of either an osteoblastoma or a hemangioma.

A 56-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive abdominal distention. She had no abdominal pain, palpable mass, weight loss, respiratory symptoms, or constitutional complaints. Her medical, surgical, travel, family, and social histories were unremarkable; she had worked in an iron factory for 4 years without known asbestos exposure.

On examination, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. There was no lymphadenopathy, anemia, or jaundice. The abdomen was markedly distended, soft, and non-tender, with evidence of massive ascites but no palpable masses.

Laboratory studies showed thrombocytosis, hypoalbuminemia, and elevated C-reactive protein. The white-cell count, hemoglobin, renal function, and electrolytes were normal. Liver tests revealed an alkaline phosphatase level of 292 IU/L and lactate dehydrogenase of 159 IU/L; aminotransferases, γ-glutamyltransferase, and amylase were within normal limits. Serum cholesterol and triglycerides were normal. Tumor markers—including CEA, AFP, CA 19-9, CA 125, and CYFRA—were all within reference ranges. Serum KL-6 was elevated at 9000 IU/mL (normal ≤ 500 IU/mL).

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a thickened greater omentum and massive ascites, with no pulmonary lesions or signs of interstitial lung disease. FDG-PET demonstrated increased uptake in the peritoneum and no abnormal uptake in the ovaries.

Diagnostic paracentesis yielded yellow exudative fluid (protein 5.2 g/dL; specific gravity 1.036) with 3610 total cells (predominantly mononuclear). Ascitic fluid CA 125 was 86 U/L, and ascitic KL-6 was 7500 U/mL. Hyaluronic acid levels were 60 ng/mL in serum and 11 900 ng/mL in ascites. Cytologic evaluation of the fluid suggested the possibility of peritoneal mesothelioma but was insufficient for a definitive diagnosis.

A 60-year-old Persian woman was referred for evaluation of a painless lesion in her right external auditory canal that had been found incidentally. She denied aural fullness, vertigo, tinnitus, otalgia, or otorrhea and had no relevant medical or surgical history. On otoscopic examination, there was a single, round lesion in the cartilaginous portion of the right external auditory canal; the overlying skin was normal without ulceration, discoloration, or bleeding on manipulation, and there appeared to be no attachment to the tympanic membrane. A temporal-bone computed tomography scan demonstrated an external auditory canal soft-tissue mass outside the tympanic membrane with no bone erosion; the middle ear cavity and ossicles were normal, and no lesions were seen in the middle ear.

A 41-year-old woman (G1P1) presented with a left-sided vulvar mass that had increased in size over the past year. She denied fever, vaginal discharge, dyspareunia, urinary or menstrual abnormalities, and had no family history of malignancy. She reported perineal discomfort, especially when sitting or walking. On examination, there was a solitary, firm, partially movable, non-tender swelling measuring 5 × 2 cm in the lower part of the left labia majora at the site of the Bartholin gland, without inguinal lymphadenopathy. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed a solid mass in the posterior vaginal wall; the uterus and myometrium were normal without focal lesions, the ovaries were unremarkable, and there was no pelvic free fluid.

A previously healthy 2-year-old girl was transferred for evaluation of suspected Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis after an upper respiratory illness. Two days before transfer, she received acetaminophen at home and then experienced a seizure, prompting admission at an outside hospital, where she was given levetiracetam, vancomycin, and acyclovir. A few hours after admission, she developed tense blisters that evolved into diffuse desquamation on her chest and back. On hospital day 3, skin examination revealed full-thickness desquamation with underlying erythema and surrounding tense bullae on the chest, back, and neck, involving 20% of her body surface area. There was no mucosal or ocular involvement. An atypical presentation of Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis secondary to viral infection versus acetaminophen was initially favored, although these are uncommon triggers. Linear IgA bullous dermatosis, bullous drug eruption, and staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome were also considered. Intravenous immunoglobulin infusions were initiated, and punch biopsies were obtained for histologic and direct immunofluorescence studies.

A 33-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a left jaw mass. Six months earlier, she had extractions of teeth 36 and 37; she had no complications following previous extractions of teeth 34 and 35. Over the past few months, she noted a painless swelling in the left posterior mandible that enlarged rapidly. She denied infection, sensory disturbance, or difficulty with mastication or speech. On intraoral examination, there was a firm, multilocular swelling measuring approximately 4 × 3 cm on the left alveolar ridge, extending around tooth 33; the overlying gingiva were mildly elevated but intact. The masseter muscle was intact, and there was no facial nerve deficit. A panoramic radiograph showed a well-defined, corticated radiolucent lesion in the left mandibular body measuring about 3 × 4 cm, with minimal displacement of tooth 33, extending from the distal aspect of tooth 32 to the site of the prior extractions, and a fine granular bone pattern at the lower border of the lesion.

A 4½-year-old girl was referred for magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits because of a new ocular motility disorder affecting her right eye. Her history was notable for a relative amblyopia of the same eye, previously diagnosed as Bergmeister’s papilla, a benign epipapillary membrane. The patient was otherwise healthy, with no systemic symptoms.

Orbital MRI was performed with thin-slice coronal T1-weighted, T2-weighted fat-saturated, axial T2-weighted, and postcontrast T1-weighted fat-saturated sequences. Imaging revealed a plaque-shaped lesion immediately anterior to the right optic disc, measuring approximately 6 mm in width and less than 1 mm in thickness. On T1- and T2-weighted images, the lesion was almost isointense to the optic nerve. After administration of gadolinium, a discrete enhancement was observed. A thin, hyperintense layer between the lesion and the optic disc corresponded to normal choroid. There were no signs of calcification. The sizes of both globes were symmetric. The remainder of the right eye, the left eye, optic nerves, and brain parenchyma appeared normal.

A 77-year-old previously healthy woman presented with bloody vaginal discharge. Colposcopic examination revealed a 2.5-cm papillary mass involving the uterine cervix, and a punch biopsy raised the possibility of papillary squamotransitional cell carcinoma or papillary squamous cell carcinoma. She underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. Two years later, she returned with vaginal discharge. Pelvic computed tomography showed a 6-mm enhancing nodular lesion at the right vaginal stump. A cervicovaginal liquid-based cytology smear was obtained.

On the liquid-based cytology preparation, cellularity was moderate to high, with a few small hyperchromatic crowded groups (HCGs) in a background of abundant scattered cells. At higher magnification, the HCGs formed three-dimensional, irregularly shaped papillary fragments containing fibrovascular cores. The lining cells were uniformly distributed, with mild nuclear overlapping; nuclei were round-to-oval, smaller than parabasal cells, with smooth nuclear membranes, inconspicuous nucleoli, and only occasional mitotic figures. Similar-appearing cells were singly scattered in the background; some showed spindle shapes with long, tapered cytoplasmic processes. Interspersed among these were a few cells with increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, hyperchromasia, and irregular nuclear membranes, suggesting high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion. A small cluster of dyskeratotic cells was also present. No tumor diathesis was identified.

A 64-year-old woman presented with 7 days of right-sided epigastric pain and nausea. She had hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and a remote appendectomy. She denied alcohol or tobacco use. On examination, her abdomen was soft with epigastric tenderness. Laboratory tests showed a white-blood-cell count of 12,000/µL; liver function tests, carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (6.39 U/mL), and carcinoembryonic antigen (1.98 ng/mL) were within normal limits. 

Contrast-enhanced CT performed during evaluation for acute appendicitis incidentally revealed a 2.6 × 2.8 cm multilobulated cystic mass with thin septa and eccentric coarse calcification in the tail of the pancreas; the main pancreatic duct was not dilated, and there was marked upstream parenchymal atrophy with collateral vessels around the splenic hilum. A differential diagnosis of mucinous cystic neoplasm (MCN) or intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN) was made, yet the patient deferred further evaluation.

Seven months later, she returned with nausea and diffuse abdominal pain. Repeat CT showed the mass had enlarged to 5.4 × 4.0 cm with an intracystic heterogeneously enhancing solid component occupying most of the lesion. Pancreatic MRI demonstrated an intermediate-to-high T2 signal solid portion with diffusion restriction, small intra-tumoral hemorrhage, and progressive peripheral enhancement on dynamic contrast sequences. FDG PET-CT revealed intense uptake in the lesion without distant metastasis. The imaging findings suggested a possible pancreatic mucinous cystadenocarcinoma.

A 46-year-old woman presented with a six-month history of progressive back pain and bilateral lower-extremity weakness and sensory loss. She had no prior medical problems, no history of trauma, and no family history of tumors. Symptomatic treatments elsewhere had been ineffective.

On examination, pin-prick testing revealed loss of motor and sensory function in both lower extremities.

MRI of the thoracic spine showed a mass posterior to the T11 vertebral body, bulging into the spinal canal with spinal stenosis and indentation of the spinal cord. The lesion was isointense on T1-weighted images, mixed on T2-weighted images, and enhanced homogeneously with contrast.

CT of the thoracic spine demonstrated discontinuity of the T11 bone cortex.

No 68 Ga-PET/CT was performed.

A 66-year-old Caucasian man was referred for colonoscopy after a positive fecal occult blood test during routine screening. He was asymptomatic, denied rectal bleeding, and had no anemia. His history included ischemic heart disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, atrial fibrillation, and hypercholesterolemia; his medications included dabigatran. On colonoscopy, an unusual vascular pattern was seen throughout the rectum up to the rectosigmoid junction: there was confluent circumferential purple discoloration and heaped-up mucosal folds involving the entire rectum with a sharp transition to normal mucosa in the distal sigmoid colon. No mucosal ulceration or active bleeding was present. The appearance resembled extensive rectal varices, although he had no history of liver disease or thromboembolic disease. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed marked thickening of the rectosigmoid wall with multiple small rounded punctate calcifications and an abrupt transition to normal wall at the rectosigmoid junction; there was no other visceral or cutaneous involvement.

A 10-year-old boy had an 11-month history of changes in most fingernails. Initially, subungual purpuric lesions appeared, followed weeks later by a yellowish discharge from the left thumbnail that was treated with antibiotics for presumed bacterial infection, with only partial improvement. Several months later, he was referred for recurrence and worsening of the lesion. On examination, there was a friable tumor with purulent discharge under the left thumbnail and subungual hemorrhages affecting most fingernails. The scalp showed erythematous, scaly papules with crusts previously diagnosed as seborrheic dermatitis. Biopsies from the nail bed lesion and scalp papules revealed a diffuse infiltrate in the upper dermis of medium-to-large mononuclear cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and reniform nuclei admixed with inflammatory cells. Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated positivity for CD1a and S100 protein and negativity for CD68; testing for the BRAF V600E mutation was negative.

A 34-year-old Persian man with sickle cell trait presented with 3 weeks of colicky periumbilical and right lower-quadrant abdominal pain, associated anorexia, nausea, non-bloody vomiting, recent 5-kg weight loss, and 2 days of constipation. He denied fever, night sweats, or melena. He reported 10 years of alcohol use and methadone therapy. On exam he appeared unwell, afebrile, with BP 110/70 mmHg, pulse 105/min, RR 16/min, SpO2 96%, and pale conjunctiva. His abdomen was distended without organomegaly, had active bowel sounds, right lower-quadrant tenderness, shifting dullness, and a positive fluid wave. Initial labs showed WBC 10.1 × 10^9/L, Hb 11.4 g/dL, albumin 2.3 g/dL, CRP 30 mg/L, normal renal and liver enzymes, and ascitic fluid culture showed no growth after 48 hours. Abdominal ultrasound revealed small bowel distention, moderate to severe free fluid, and two small gallstones. Contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed severe abdominopelvic ascites, nodular thickening of the parietal peritoneum with omental infiltration, and a mass-like thickening of the ileocecal region without obstruction. Tuberculosis peritonitis and, less likely, peritoneal carcinomatosis were considered as differential diagnoses.

A 2-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of a gradually enlarging mass on the left side of his neck over several months. The parents noted nighttime stridor, respiratory difficulty during sleep, and some difficulty swallowing. There was no relevant personal or family medical history, and no prior surgeries or drug exposures. The mass had been presumed to be a cystic hygroma; the patient underwent two sessions of sclerotherapy without clinical improvement.

On examination, there was a multilobulated mass measuring approximately 10 × 8 × 8 cm occupying the left neck. Superiorly it extended to the left cheek, posteriorly to the nape, and inferiorly into the supraclavicular area, crossing the anterior midline. Palpation revealed mixed soft and firm areas; transillumination was negative. The trachea was deviated to the right. There were no signs of overlying inflammation. Vital signs were normal, and the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck demonstrated a 10 × 8 × 8 cm enhancing multicystic lesion in the left neck containing multiple flecks of calcification, with displacement of the trachea, esophagus, and carotid sheath to the contralateral side. There were no enlarged cervical lymph nodes.

A 29-year-old man with a 7-year history of fistulizing ileal Crohn’s disease treated with adalimumab every 2 weeks presented with 2 months of gradually onset, dull, intermittent left flank pain without fever, dysuria, or hematuria. He reported 3–4 watery bowel movements daily without blood or mucus and denied rash, arthralgia, eye symptoms, jaundice, NSAID use, or recent antibiotics. On examination he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable; there was no pallor, jaundice, lymphadenopathy, or abdominal tenderness, and no palpable renal masses. Rectal examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed WBC 11.0×10^9/L, hemoglobin 15.2 g/dL, platelets 320×10^9/L, INR 1.0, normal liver and renal function, and CRP 14.5 mg/L. Urinalysis was normal with no nitrites, leukocytes, erythrocytes, or casts. An abdominal CT scan revealed a well-defined, 2.6 cm × 2.6 cm hypodense lesion near the left renal hilum with inhomogeneous enhancement in the arterial phase and partial washout in the delayed phase. Colonoscopy showed normal colonic mucosa to the terminal ileum, and biopsy confirmed acute on chronic ileitis.

A 74-year-old man presented with three days of severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and obstipation. He reported a two-month history of 12 kg weight loss, poor appetite, alternating constipation and diarrhea, and intermittent colicky abdominal pain relieved by flatus and defecation. On examination, his abdomen was distended and soft, with generalized tenderness but no peritonism, organomegaly, or palpable masses; bowel sounds were reduced and rectal examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory tests showed elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 231 mg/L; WBC 17.1 × 10^9/L) and microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL; MCV 71 fL). Abdominal radiography demonstrated distended small-bowel loops, and a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast revealed a 9 cm circumferential wall thickening of the small bowel inferior to the transverse colon, associated with two areas of intussusception and additional abnormal loops of bowel.

A 23-year-old man from The Gambia presented with progressive gait impairment, bilateral lower-limb weakness, and pain of several months’ duration. He denied fever, weight loss, or night sweats. His medical history included drug-sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis treated in 2017 and a chronic ischiatic ulcer treated surgically, with no malignant features on prior biopsy. On examination, mobilisation of the lower limbs was painful, with left-sided hypoesthesia and paresthesia. Laboratory studies showed a stable mild leukopenia (3300 cells/µL, 28.3% neutrophils); ESR and CRP were normal; HIV and hepatitis serologies were negative. Chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable. 

CT of the spine revealed an expansive hypodense lesion extending from L1 to S1, with bilateral psoas involvement, marked vertebral erosion, and posterior vertebral scalloping. MRI of the lumbar and sacral spine demonstrated a multiloculated, intradural, intraforaminal mass that was hyperintense on T2-weighted images, homogeneously hypointense on unenhanced T1-weighted images, without fat or hemorrhage. After gadolinium administration, the cyst walls and intralesional septa showed marked rim enhancement. Serologic tests for cystic echinococcosis (IgG ELISA and IHA) were negative.

A 77-year-old man with a history of angina pectoris and former tobacco use presented with a 6-week history of progressive pain and swelling at the tip of his left ring finger. Initially treated elsewhere for presumed gout without radiographs or laboratory evaluation, he was referred when the swelling grew and became more painful. Examination showed the fingertip two to three times larger than the contralateral side, resembling a drumstick, with marked tenderness and ankylosis of the distal interphalangeal joint. There was no regional lymphadenopathy, and he denied fever, weight loss, or night sweats. Laboratory studies revealed a serum uric acid of 4.3 mg/dL (normal 3.4–7.0), WBC count 8.5 × 10^9/L (4.5–11.0), ESR 10 mm/h (< 15), and CRP 0.3 mg/dL (< 0.5). Radiographs of the hands showed a radiolucent, osteolytic lesion destroying almost the entire distal phalanx of the left ring finger without sclerosis or periosteal reaction. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. The patient declined CT and MRI and agreed only to excisional biopsy.

A 33-year-old woman presented with a 6-year history of a slowly enlarging, painless lump in her right buttock. She had no significant medical or family history and took no medications. On examination, she was afebrile, alert, and well-appearing. A 6 cm smooth, fibroelastic, non-tender, non-adherent mass was palpable in the right gluteal subcutaneous tissue, with overlying skin normal and a normal neurologic examination. MRI of the right gluteal region showed a 6.7×4.5×8 cm subcutaneous mass with stranding but no drainable fluid. Given the firmness of the mass and its attachment to deeper tissues, a soft-tissue malignancy was suspected, and an incisional biopsy was performed; tissue was sent for pathological analysis.

A 50-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of pain in the upper left molar region, after which his first and second left maxillary molars were extracted. Following extraction, he noted progressive diffuse swelling in the left maxillary alveolar region and mobility of adjacent teeth. 

On extraoral examination, there was diffuse swelling obliterating the left nasolabial fold. Intraorally, a sessile, soft, non-pulsatile, non-tender, non-hemorrhagic mass extended from the left maxillary second premolar to the tuberosity region and medially to the midpalatine raphe. No cervical lymphadenopathy was palpable. 

Clinically, carcinoma of the maxillary sinus and metastatic carcinoma were considered. A panoramic radiograph showed an ill-defined osteolytic lesion in the left posterior maxilla with resorption of the hard palate and floor of the maxillary sinus. A postero-anterior skull radiograph demonstrated multiple punched-out radiolucent lesions. Subsequent imaging included an anteroposterior pelvis radiograph and coronal, axial, and sagittal CT sections of the skull, which confirmed multiple punched-out lesions in the skull and a 4.2×4.1 cm soft-tissue density mass in the left maxilla eroding the walls and floor of the maxillary sinus.

A 14-month-old boy was evaluated for 3 months of worsening paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea characterized by episodic respiratory distress, cyanosis, and coughing that interrupted sleep up to three times nightly. His past medical and family histories were unremarkable, with normal growth and development. Vital signs were within normal limits. On cardiac examination, there was a grade III/VI systolic ejection murmur best heard at the upper left sternal border and an S4 gallop. The remainder of the physical examination was normal. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia, right axis deviation, and right ventricular hypertrophy without other abnormalities. A sedated, supine two-dimensional echocardiogram with Doppler revealed a pedunculated mass measuring approximately 4.3 × 2.0 × 1.4 cm occupying most of the right ventricle, attached to the base of the anterior leaflet of the tricuspid valve and to the interventricular septum.
