The mass extended into the right ventricular outflow tract and caused marked systolic obstruction of the pulmonary artery. Estimated right ventricular pressure based on the tricuspid regurgitation jet was 100–110 mmHg. Left ventricular size, morphology, and function were normal.

An 82-year-old woman presented with right flank pain. Her medical history was noncontributory; family history included various solid tumors. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen revealed a 3.3 cm left adrenal indeterminate mass with an absolute washout of 21.9% and a relative washout of 10.1%, which did not meet criteria for an adrenal adenoma. A comprehensive metabolic panel, plasma metanephrines, and a dexamethasone suppression test were all normal, and she had no hypertension or stigmata of Cushing’s disease. Given the small size and negative metabolic evaluation, she was managed with active surveillance. Ten months later, MRI showed significant enlargement of the left adrenal mass, now measuring 6.5 × 5.1 × 5.0 cm. Repeat metabolic testing remained negative. Because of concern for adrenal cortical carcinoma, she underwent an open left adrenalectomy. Laparoscopic or robotic approaches were avoided due to the risk of peritoneal dissemination. Intraoperatively, the mass was densely adherent to the spleen and renal hilum, necessitating splenectomy and left nephrectomy to achieve complete resection. Her postoperative course was notable for a congestive heart failure exacerbation managed with diuretics; she was discharged on postoperative day 5.

A 74-year-old woman with a history of right radical nephrectomy for renal clear cell carcinoma 11 years ago presents with a 4-month history of a hard, painless nodule in the right submandibular region. On examination, the lesion measures approximately 1.5 cm and is firm. Ultrasonography reveals a 16 mm hypoechogenic nodule with central vascularization in the right submandibular gland. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy shows nests of epithelial cells with clear cytoplasm, rounded nuclei with anisocaryosis, and prominent nucleoli. Immunohistochemical staining of the biopsy specimen is positive for paired-box gene 8 (PAX8).

An 18-year-old male presented with progressive difficulty breathing, swallowing, and speaking due to swelling of the floor of the mouth. He first noticed a painless sublingual swelling at age 8. Two years before presentation, swallowing became difficult; one year prior, breathing and speech were also affected. He reported no pain, fever, weight loss, systemic disease, smoking, or alcohol use. On examination, there was a 7-cm, soft, immobile, pedunculated mass on the oral floor, matching the surrounding mucosal color. Ultrasonography showed a solitary, round, isoechoic lesion (5.42 × 4.6 × 4.64 cm), well-demarcated with regular margins, no calcifications, and no prominent vascularization on Doppler imaging. A lateral cervical radiograph showed a round radiopaque mass at the mouth base narrowing the airway. MSCT with contrast revealed a solitary, well-circumscribed, inhomogeneous hypodense lesion (57.99 × 55.33 × 41.41 mm, 10–30 HU) in the oral cavity, with no pathological enhancement. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy yielded 0.05 cc of yellowish-white viscous material; smears showed monomorphic squamous epithelial cells amid basophilic amorphous keratin, with no malignant cells.

A 77-year-old man with a history of high-grade prostate adenocarcinoma (Gleason score 5 + 4 = 9; pT3bN0M0) treated in December 2006 with radical prostatectomy, lymph-node dissection, androgen-deprivation therapy, and radiation presented for routine follow-up. His serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) remained below 1 ng/mL until March 2012 (PSA 0.98 ng/mL). By June 2012, PSA had risen to 3.24 ng/mL, and by October 2012 to 6.16 ng/mL. Physical examination was unremarkable, with no skin changes on the glans and no palpable inguinal nodes. A CT scan showed no abdominal metastases but revealed osteolytic lesions in the L2 vertebral body and left femur; bone scintigraphy confirmed these. The patient began estramustine phosphate. In January 2013, PSA rose to 8.07 ng/mL; repeat CT identified a 21 mm oval subcutaneous nodule along the left margin of the corpus cavernosum with homogeneous, early contrast enhancement, and a left scrotal hydrocele. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a nodular area hypointense on T1- and T2-weighted sequences with early and persistent gadolinium enhancement.

A 30-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of multiple purplish raised spots on the dorsal and left lateral aspects of her tongue. The lesions began as a single raised spot on the dorsum and gradually enlarged and coalesced into a patch covering most of the anterior two-thirds; additional smaller bumps were noted on the left lateral tongue. She reported occasional spontaneous bleeding from the lesions without identifiable trauma. No similar lesions were noted elsewhere on her body, and she denied systemic symptoms.

On examination, several shiny, soft, raised papules on the dorsum and left side of the tongue ranged in color from pink to bluish-purple and did not bleed when touched. Examination of the skin, other mucosal sites, and systemic organ systems was unremarkable. Complete hematological and biochemical investigations were within normal limits.

An excision biopsy of one of the tongue lesions was performed under local anesthesia with minimal bleeding.

A 77-year-old man presented with a two-month history of progressively worsening bilateral vision loss, more pronounced in the left eye. He was initially diagnosed with non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy and referred for neurology evaluation. He denied headache, mandibular claudication, or pain with eye movements. On examination, pupils were hyporeactive; visual acuity was reduced with dyschromatopsia in the right eye and no light perception in the left eye. No other neurologic deficits were noted. Brain and orbit MRI showed nodular thickening with non-uniform enhancement of the optic chiasm and left optic tract, along with FLAIR hyperintensity in the left mesial temporal lobe and left lateral midbrain. There was no diffusion restriction. Given the possibility of demyelinating disease, oligoclonal bands were sent, and intravenous methylprednisolone was administered, with modest clinical improvement. One month later, he returned with complete bilateral blindness but no new neurologic signs. Repeat contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated progressive thickening and enhancement of the same structures and a heterogeneously enhancing mass in the left optic tract.

An 89-year-old woman presented with traces of vaginal bleeding and a foul-smelling yellowish discharge. She had two prior vaginal deliveries, no comorbidities apart from treated hyperthyroidism, and no history of pelvic inflammatory disease or malignancy. On examination, she was cognitively intact, and there were no palpable adnexal masses. Laboratory studies showed an elevated CA-125 level on two consecutive measurements; α-FP, CA 15-3, CA 19-9, and CEA were within normal limits. Transvaginal ultrasound and pelvic MRI revealed a tube-like structure in the vicinity of the right ovary without obvious ovarian lesions.

A 2-year-old boy was referred for reevaluation of a nasal purpuric lesion that persisted 6 months after he fell on his nose. Immediately after the fall, a hematoma formed on the nasal dorsum, but the lesion failed to resolve and even expanded during heat exposure. There was no prior nasal abnormality.

On examination, there was a firm, red-purple swelling of the skin and subcutaneous tissue over the nasal dorsum extending into the paranasal area, with small pearls of clear fluid on the surface. Endonasal inspection revealed congested mucosa and crusting. Vital signs were normal, and laboratory tests showed no thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy.

Magnetic resonance imaging showed subcutaneous infiltration of the nasal dorsum extending into the nasal cavity and anterior ethmoid sinus, with bright heterogeneous enhancement on T1-weighted images after gadolinium and no connection to intracranial dural sinuses. Doppler ultrasound revealed rich vascularization without signs of lymphangioma or traumatic arteriovenous malformation.

An infected, organized hematoma was suspected, and the patient received two weeks of amoxicillin–clavulanic acid without improvement. Surgical exploration was scheduled to rule out a foreign body, dermoid cyst, or lymphatic malformation. While awaiting surgery, the lesion suddenly enlarged and he experienced episodic epistaxis without signs of infection.

A 3-month-old boy was brought for evaluation of a developing mass on the right superior orbital rim that had shown aggressive growth over the prior 3 weeks. On examination, there was a hard, reddish, immobile mass measuring 5 × 5 cm over the right superior orbital margin, causing complete ptosis of the right eyelid. There was no bruit or pulsation over the lesion, and the eyelid mass precluded visualization of the anterior and posterior segments of the eye. 

A spiral orbital CT scan revealed a round lesion along the superior and supratemporal margin of the right orbit, protruding into both the orbital cavity and toward the anterior cranial fossa. The central portion of the lesion had relatively homogeneous density, and there was visible destruction of the orbital rim. The underlying brain parenchyma appeared uninvolved.

Based on these findings, the primary differential diagnosis was Ewing’s sarcoma, with orbital metastases also considered. Further systemic evaluation revealed no additional lesions or evidence of a primary malignancy. Given the patient’s presentation and imaging features, an excisional biopsy was planned.

A 55-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of a gradually enlarging exophytic mass in the left oral cavity. She noted progressive left facial asymmetry due to cheek bulging. Intraoral examination showed poor oral hygiene and a pedunculated, rubbery, nontender, pink gingival-like mass extending from the lower left first premolar to the second molar, occupying the entire buccal vestibule; the lesion measured 5.9 cm in diameter. A soft-tissue radiograph of the region demonstrated calcifications within the mass. On MRI, the lesion was homogeneously isointense on nonenhanced T1-weighted sequences with multiple small hypointense foci suggestive of calcifications; it was iso- to hypointense on T2-weighted sequences. The mass displaced the zygomaticus major muscle and facial artery without fat-plane invasion, and there was slight cortical plate erosion seen as loss of cortical hypointensity on T1. After gadolinium administration, the lesion showed heterogeneous enhancement.

A 65-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of vague left lower abdominal and back pain, abdominal fullness, lethargy, and a non-ballotable lump in the left lumbar and iliac region. She denied genitourinary, gastrointestinal, or gynecological symptoms. Laboratory tests showed microcytic hypochromic anemia, an ESR of 92 mm/hr, and a CRP of 24 mg/L. Serum protein electrophoresis revealed no monoclonal bands. Renal and liver function, 9 AM cortisol, testosterone level, 24-hour urine metanephrine, and vanillylmandelic acid were all within normal limits. Pan endoscopy was unremarkable.  
Abdominal ultrasound identified a 12 × 12 cm solid mass in the left suprarenal area. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 17.5 × 11.5 cm enhancing lesion replacing the left adrenal gland with peripheral coarse calcification, inferior displacement of the left kidney, and no lymphadenopathy; the contralateral adrenal gland and other intra-abdominal organs were normal. Comprehensive screening for extra-adrenal primary malignancies was negative.  
On this basis, a non-secreting left pheochromocytoma was considered, and elective laparoscopic left adrenalectomy was planned.

A 57-year-old woman was referred to our hospital 8 years after a partial resection of a presumed benign hepatic lesion and multiple sessions of transcatheter arterial embolization (TAE) for hemobilia from a right‐lobe tumor. She had experienced six episodes of hemobilia treated with TAE but had progressive enlargement of the right‐lobe mass. 

Her medical history included appendectomy, two Cesarean sections, and lobectomy for lung adenocarcinomas at age 53. She had no history of liver disease, including hepatolithiasis. 

On admission, vital signs were stable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL; total bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL; AST 65 IU/L; ALT 54 IU/L; alkaline phosphatase 819 IU/L; γ-GTP 227 IU/L. Alpha-fetoprotein and PIVKA-II were within normal limits, while CEA was 12.8 ng/mL and CA19-9 was 862 U/mL. Viral hepatitis markers were negative. Physical examination revealed a liver edge palpable four fingerbreadths below the xiphoid process.

Abdominal ultrasonography showed a 10 × 15 cm multilocular oval mass with papillary infoldings in the right hepatic lobe. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 15 cm low-density hepatic tumor occupying the right and caudal lobes, compressing the portal vein, with contrast-enhanced mural nodules. T1-weighted MRI revealed a low-intensity mass except for the nodules, which were hyperintense on T2-weighted images. Superior mesenteric arteriography showed the right hepatic artery arising from the SMA with tumor staining. FDG-PET/CT showed intense uptake in the lesion. 

Endoscopic retrograde cholangiography demonstrated obstruction of the right hepatic bile duct, compression of the left hepatic duct, and dilation of peripheral bile ducts. The cystic lesion was suspected to be a mucin-producing biliary tumor, such as a mucinous cystic neoplasm of the liver or an intraductal papillary neoplasm of the bile duct. Biliary cytology revealed papillary adenocarcinoma in situ or papillary adenoma with severe atypia.

A 7-month-old boy was referred for evaluation of one month of progressive, painless abdominal distention. His prenatal and family history were unremarkable; past history included bilateral inguinal hernia repair and thalassemia minor. Growth and development were normal. On exam, he was well-appearing; his abdomen was distended and tense, with a positive fluid thrill, but there was no organomegaly or palpable mass. There were no clinical, laboratory, or imaging signs of portal hypertension or liver disease. 

Abdominal ultrasound showed free fluid in Morison’s pouch, the left upper quadrant, and Douglas space, without septations or multicystic appearance, and no organ abnormalities. A comprehensive workup excluded hepatic, renal, cardiac, intestinal, pancreatic, inflammatory, or infectious diseases; malignancy; and congenital metabolic disorders. 

Previously, he had a mild pleuro-pericardial effusion during a febrile illness and transient hyperkalaemia, raising concern for stomatocytosis, but PIEZO1 gene testing was negative. A positive interferon-gamma (QuantiFERON®) test prompted evaluation for peritoneal tuberculosis: chest radiograph and Mantoux tests (patient and parents) were negative; gastric aspirate cultures and repeat interferon-gamma assay were negative; atypical mycobacterial infection was excluded.

Abdominal MRI confirmed an abundant fluid collection, centralization of bowel loops, and normal-appearing organs. Paracentesis yielded pale-yellow serous fluid with a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 1.1; triglycerides and leukocyte counts were normal (98% lymphocytes); cytology showed reactive lymphomonocytes, mesothelial cells, and foam cells without malignant cells. Fluid rapidly re-accumulated in days. 

Diuretics (spironolactone and furosemide) provided only transient relief; recurrent paracenteses were required over the following months. Repeated imaging and fluid analyses did not reveal any new diagnostic clues. Eighteen months after symptom onset, repeat ultrasound and MRI again showed free-appearing ascites without additional findings.

A 62-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and osteoarthritis presented with a seven-month history of gradual, dull, constant right lower quadrant abdominal pain radiating to his right groin and anterior thigh. He also reported a ten-month history of mild but persistent epigastric discomfort, dysphagia, and odynophagia for solids and liquids. He denied fever or chills but noted over 10 lb of weight loss and night sweats over the prior six weeks. He had a 50-year, two-pack-per-day smoking history and a remote history of heavy alcohol use. Three months earlier, he had undergone laparoscopic cholecystectomy for similar pain without relief.

On re-presentation, vital signs were within normal limits. He appeared cachectic. The abdomen was soft and nondistended, with moderate tenderness in the right lower quadrant and suprapubic region; there was no peritoneal irritation. Bowel sounds were normal; there was no hepatosplenomegaly. Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL; renal function was normal. Total protein was 5.8 g/dL, albumin 2.9 g/dL, alkaline phosphatase 1619 U/L, ALT 51 U/L, AST 43 U/L, GGT >1200 U/L, C-reactive protein 3.7 mg/dL, and ESR 52 mm/hr. Blood cultures were negative.

An abdominal ultrasound showed a normal-sized liver without intrahepatic biliary dilation and mild extrahepatic dilation (common bile duct 10 mm). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated ill-defined areas of low density throughout the right psoas muscle with surrounding inflammatory changes. Lumbar MRI revealed diffuse thickening and heterogeneous enhancement of the right iliopsoas musculature, with normal appearance of the left side. The radiologist’s differential diagnosis was an infectious process versus neoplastic infiltration.

A 24-year-old male smoker presented to his general practitioner with a 6-month history of right foot pain extending from the base of the first toe to the plantar surface. The pain fluctuated in severity, did not correlate with specific activities, and was only partially relieved with common analgesics. His work involved prolonged standing and heavy lifting. He had bilateral pes planus and valgus heels during childhood but had been asymptomatic for several years. Two abdominal nodules had been excised two years before presentation; histopathology at that time reportedly confirmed a fibroma and a leiomyoma. Apart from a few minor injuries, his medical and surgical history was otherwise unremarkable.

Initially, the pain was attributed to his previous foot deformity and managed conservatively with analgesia. Over the next three months, the pain persisted, and he was referred to orthopedics. Extensive X-ray studies and blood tests including inflammatory and immunological markers were all normal, and he was fitted with arch supports. Despite this, his pain progressively worsened over six months. A foot MRI revealed mild, early degenerative first metatarsophalangeal joint changes with a small amount of fusion but no other abnormalities. Reflex sympathetic dystrophy was considered and supported by a radionuclide isotope scan. Rocker-sole shoes, stronger analgesia including oral morphine, physiotherapy, and multiple guanethidine blocks all failed to control his symptoms, which caused significant disability 18 months after his initial visit.

In the following weeks, he developed progressive weight loss, fatigue, and muscle wasting below the knee. He then noticed a firm, round mass approximately 15 cm in diameter on the lower posterior aspect of his thigh. He was referred back to orthopedics, and an urgent MRI confirmed an oval, smoothly defined heterogeneous mass in the posterior thigh, in addition to signal changes in both right and left femurs, most likely representing metastatic foci. He was referred urgently to oncology.

A 42-year-old hypertensive man presented with a 5-year history of a nodular lesion on the left buccal mucosa. He had no history of tobacco, alcohol, dental extraction, or trauma. On examination, there was a 2.4 × 2.0 cm, well-circumscribed, non-tender, nodular lesion near the left upper alveolus; the overlying mucosa was normal, and there was no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. An outside histopathology report described a salivary gland neoplasm favoring secretory carcinoma. On review, the biopsy showed eosinophilic tumor cells arranged in papillary architecture. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for GATA3 and MUC4 and negative for androgen receptor. Contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated a 2.3 × 1.3 × 1.7 cm lobulated, enhancing nodular lesion arising from the left buccal mucosa near the superior alveolus without bone marrow involvement, and bilateral symmetrical level IIa reactive cervical nodes.

A 24-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of a painless, slowly enlarging swelling of the upper left posterior gingiva. Six months earlier, a similar lesion in the same region had been excised, the associated tooth was extracted, and an adjacent tooth underwent root canal treatment. His medical and family histories were unremarkable.  

On extraoral examination, there was a diffuse, firm, mildly tender swelling of the left cheek. Intraorally, a well-defined, sessile swelling measuring 3 × 2 cm extended from the mesial aspect of the left first premolar to the distal aspect of the first molar. The overlying mucosa was stretched, shiny, and pale, with focal erythematous patches. The lesion was firm, nonreducible, noncompressible, and nonfluctuant; there was no discharge, bleeding, or tooth mobility.  

Radiographs, including periapical, panoramic, and cone-beam CT, revealed a well-defined, mixed radiodense and radiolucent multilocular lesion in the left posterior maxilla measuring approximately 40 × 31 × 41 mm. It extended anteriorly from the premolars to the pterygoid plates, superiorly to the level of the middle meatus, and showed buccal cortical expansion with focal perforation. There was root resorption of adjacent teeth. Routine blood and biochemical tests were normal.  

An incisional biopsy showed connective tissue containing streaming fascicles of benign spindle-shaped cells in a storiform pattern, interspersed with foamy histiocytes, occasional multinucleated giant cells, and areas of hyalinization. The cells lacked atypia. A histopathological diagnosis of a benign spindle cell neoplasm suggestive of benign fibrous histiocytoma was rendered, and immunohistochemistry was advised.

A 38-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of pain localized to the tailbone. She had no significant medical history. On neurologic examination, motor strength was 5/5 in both lower extremities; sensation and deep tendon reflexes were symmetrical and intact. She denied urinary or fecal incontinence. An MRI of the lumbar spine revealed a 17 × 12 × 15 mm intradural lesion posterior to the L3–4 disc and the upper part of the L4 vertebral body. On midsagittal T2-weighted images, the lesion had indistinct hypointense margins; on axial T2-weighted images it was hyperintense and compressed nerve roots against the dura, obliterating CSF signal. The lesion was isointense to vertebral body on T1-weighted images and showed homogeneous enhancement on contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images.

A 51-year-old woman with a 30-year history of ulcerative colitis limited to the colon, maintained in remission on oral 5-aminosalicylic acid, underwent routine surveillance colonoscopy. In July 2011, a 15 mm elevated lesion with an unclear boundary and a small superficial ulcer was identified in the descending colon. Narrow band imaging with magnification revealed a type IIIL pit pattern. Biopsies, including deep (boring) samples, showed only mildly inflamed mucosa with regenerative changes and no dysplasia or neoplasm. Laboratory studies were normal except for a C-reactive protein level of 1.4 mg/dL; carcinoembryonic antigen and CA 19-9 were within normal limits.

Over 14 months of observation, the lesion enlarged and took on the appearance of a type-2 cancer. Abdominal CT demonstrated a 20–30 mm mass in the descending colon without lymphadenopathy or distant metastases. Endoscopic ultrasonography showed the lesion confined mainly to the submucosal layer, with compression of the muscularis propria. Serial colonoscopies and biopsies over the next 4 months remained negative for malignancy. A contrast enema revealed a smoothly elevated lesion with a central depression in the same location.

A 34-year-old man underwent wide resection of a 4.4 cm cutaneous dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans of the lower back, confirmed by biopsy and FISH. For staging, he had a contrast-enhanced CT of the chest. He was asymptomatic with normal vital signs. The CT scan showed no pulmonary nodules but revealed a well-demarcated 4.0×4.9×4.7 cm mass in the prevascular mediastinum. The mass was heterogeneous, containing soft-tissue attenuation, areas of negative Hounsfield units consistent with fat, and small calcifications. A slightly enlarged (11 mm) and mildly heterogeneous right hilar lymph node was also noted. Serum alpha-fetoprotein and human chorionic gonadotropin levels were both <1 µg/L (normal). 
What is your differential diagnosis for this mediastinal mass?

A 66-year-old postmenopausal woman presented to the emergency department with a two-day history of sudden-onset sharp abdominal pain located in the umbilical and suprapubic regions, associated with a low-grade fever. She was gravida 6, para 6, with menopause 20 years earlier and no significant medical or surgical history. On examination, her temperature was 37.8 °C, pulse rate 107 beats/min, blood pressure 107/70 mm Hg, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Urinalysis showed a trace of leukocytes and protein but was otherwise unremarkable. The abdomen was soft, with rebound tenderness over the lower quadrants. Initial differential diagnoses included gastroenteritis, diverticulitis, urinary tract infection, or an ovarian cyst with possible intermittent torsion or malignancy. Laboratory studies revealed a C-reactive protein level of 155 mg/L and a white blood cell count of 13.3×10^9/L with a neutrophil count of 11.8×10^9/L. 

Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 7.4×5.6×5.9 cm mixed-density lesion in the right adnexa containing calcifications and fat and fluid density areas; there was no perilesional fat stranding, free fluid, or bowel abnormality. Pelvic ultrasound showed a 10×3.2×6 cm well-circumscribed complex mixed solid–cystic mass in the right adnexa with a hyperechoic component, posterior shadowing, ground-glass internal echoes, and no increased vascularity. Serum CA125 was 29 U/mL. The patient was discharged with analgesia and scheduled for laparoscopic bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy eight days later.

A 36-year-old woman with no significant medical or family history presented with three months of persistent dyspnea that did not limit her daily activities. Vital signs were stable, and lung auscultation was normal. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, blood chemistry panel, and COVID-19 PCR test, were all within normal limits. A chest radiograph showed mediastinal widening. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed an 84 × 47 mm heterogeneous lesion in the right anterior mediastinum; additional findings included a 5 mm pulmonary nodule in the lateral segment of the left lower lobe, fibrotic bands at the lower lobes, and splenomegaly, with no pleural effusion or chest wall abnormality. The lesion was reported to be suggestive of thymoma or teratoma, and biopsy was not planned because of a high risk of bleeding. Surgical excision through a median sternotomy was recommended.

A 47-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of a painless, verrucous bulge on the plantar side of her left hallux. The lesion’s surface skin exhibited intermittent abrasion and poor wound healing, with granulation tissue formation. Conservative treatments were applied without relief.

Her medical history was notable for tuberculous pleurisy 20 years earlier (treated) and uterine fibroid surgery 1 year ago. She denied smoking, alcohol, drug use, systemic diseases, or a family history of similar lesions.

On examination, vital signs were stable (temperature 36.8 °C; blood pressure 140/80 mmHg; pulse 110 bpm). A 0.8 cm red, solid, verrucous mass with a tough texture was observed on the plantar aspect of the left hallux. The skin over the lesion was of normal temperature, and the dorsalis pedis pulse was palpable and strong.

Laboratory tests showed mild evidence of urinary inflammation, with a neutrophil percentage of 73.9%, a white blood cell count in urine of 99.6/μL, and a bacterial count of 1014.5/μL. Other blood tests were within normal limits.

An ultrasound examination revealed a solid nodule on the plantar side of the left hallux with abundant internal blood flow.

A 57-year-old man, a farmer, presented with a 1-year history of an asymptomatic skin lesion on the right forearm. It began as a single nodule on normal-appearing skin, gradually expanded peripherally, and showed central healing with an intervening scar. On examination, there was a large plaque extending from below the right elbow onto the extensor forearm, with arcuate nodular ulcerated margins and a whitish scar traversed by narrow strips of normal skin. He had been treated empirically with antitubercular therapy without improvement. General examination and routine laboratory tests were unremarkable. Chest radiograph was normal. A Mantoux test and HIV screening were negative.

A 65-year-old man presented with a left breast mass. He had no family history of breast or ovarian cancer, took no medications, and was a nonsmoker. On examination, there was a round, nontender mass of approximately 4 cm in the upper part of the left breast without nipple discharge or retraction; there was no palpable lymphadenopathy, and the contralateral breast was normal.

Ultrasonography of both breasts and axillae with a 10 MHz probe showed a 46 × 18 mm solid, hypoechoic, well-defined, homogeneous mass with small calcification in the upper left breast and no axillary lymphadenopathy.

Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the mass revealed abundant, randomly arranged single and clustered benign spindle-shaped mesenchymal cells with elongated or oval nuclei, finely granular chromatin, and inconspicuous nucleoli. No pleomorphism, mitotic activity, or epithelial component was identified.

The patient underwent a modified radical mastectomy. Gross examination showed a well-defined creamy-white mass measuring 4 × 2 × 2 cm. Histopathology demonstrated nests of cells with spindle to oval nuclei and abundant amphophilic cytoplasm separated by broad bands of hyalinized collagen; mitotic figures and pleomorphism were absent.

Immunohistochemical staining revealed that the tumor cells were positive for desmin, CD34, estrogen receptor, and progesterone receptor, and negative for CD31, cytokeratin, and leukocyte common antigen.

An 84-year-old man underwent abdominal ultrasonography for diabetes screening, which incidentally identified a 15-mm hypoechogenic, lobular nodule in segment 7 of the liver. He was asymptomatic, with a history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension, no alcohol use, no blood transfusions, and an unremarkable family history. Laboratory tests showed a normal blood count, normal liver-function and cholestasis markers, negative viral hepatitis markers, and normal levels of alpha-fetoprotein and des-gamma-carboxy prothrombin; soluble interleukin-2 receptor was mildly elevated at 599 U/mL. Initial color Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated linear blood flow within the nodule and a strand of intermediate echogenicity penetrating the lesion. Low-mechanical-index contrast-enhanced ultrasonography (CEUS) revealed reticular vessels with gradual arterial-phase enhancement, lower enhancement than liver parenchyma in the portal phase, and complete wash-out in the late phase. Noncontrast CT showed a hypodense nodule, and contrast-enhanced CT depicted a homogeneous hypovascular lesion in both arterial and equilibrium phases. The patient declined biopsy and was observed without intervention. Ten months later, CT revealed a 7-cm lobular heterogeneous mass with intermediate peripheral attenuation, central hypoattenuation, and hepatic arteries penetrating the lesion. MRI showed central hyperintensity and peripheral intermediate intensity on T2-weighted images, diffusion-weighted imaging with a high signal and an apparent diffusion coefficient of 0.5 × 10 −3 mm2/s, no fatty component, and no uptake on the hepatobiliary phase of gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI. Follow-up ultrasonography showed a 6.5-cm mass with a hypoechoic periphery, echogenic center, and a cord-like echogenic structure with pulsatile monophasic blood flow corresponding to arterial and portal branches. Repeat CEUS demonstrated evenly distributed linear vessels in the arterial phase and central enhancement in the portal phase. The rapid growth of the mass, the low uptake in the hepatobiliary phase on MRI, and the wash-out after the portal phase on CEUS led to the suspicion of a hepatic malignancy such as lymphoma, cholangiocellular carcinoma, cholangiolocellular carcinoma, and neuroendocrine carcinoma.

A 54-year-old man presented with several weeks of lower abdominal pain, frequent stools with diarrhea and mucus, and recurrent oral ulcers. He also had a 6-year history of a recurrent penile ulcer. CT enterography showed irregular skip thickening of the cecum through the descending colon with marked arterial-phase enhancement. Colonoscopy revealed multiple ulcers of varying sizes and shapes in the ileocecal region and throughout the colon, with surrounding mucosal hyperemia and edema. Biopsies of the colonic ulcers showed only nonspecific inflammation. He was diagnosed with Behçet’s disease and treated with prednisone, leading to initial improvement. One month later, he was hospitalized elsewhere for colon perforation requiring surgery. On transfer, bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy was noted, and a biopsy of the penile lesion was performed for histological examination.

A 36-year-old woman presented with occasional headaches for the past year, which had worsened over the preceding week and were accompanied by blurred vision. She had no significant past medical history and was taking no regular medications. On examination, her vital signs were normal and the neurological and general physical examinations were unremarkable.

A noncontrast brain MRI demonstrated a large, heterogeneous mass in the right frontal lobe extending into the right parietal lobe, with low signal intensity on both T1- and T2-weighted sequences and a significant midline shift to the left. Following intravenous gadolinium administration, the lesion exhibited peripheral, punctate enhancement.

A 76-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a 4-day history of abnormal vaginal bleeding. Her medical history included hypertension, type II diabetes, and prior cerebral infarctions; she was on aspirin and antihypertensive therapy, with no tamoxifen or hormone use. Initial pelvic ultrasound revealed a 3.3 × 3.0 × 2.5 cm mass with heterogeneous echogenicity and well-defined margins in the uterine cavity. Pelvic MRI showed an endometrial thickness of 1.1 cm and an irregular, slightly hypointense T2-weighted lesion adherent to the posterior uterine wall, with low or no contrast enhancement, consistent with an endometrial polyp possibly containing a small blood clot. Given her postmenopausal status and bleeding, hysteroscopic polypectomy with dilatation and curettage was performed; two-week follow-up ultrasound showed no residual lesion. Six months later, the patient again reported vaginal bleeding. Repeat MRI demonstrated a pedunculated mass measuring 7.1 × 3.4 × 2.5 cm in the endometrial cavity with a clear demarcation from the myometrium. The patient subsequently underwent laparoscopic-assisted vaginal total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.

A six-year-old boy presented with a six-week history of a painless, progressively enlarging swelling over the lateral aspect of his left lower eyelid. He denied any other ocular or systemic symptoms. Examination revealed a well-defined, firm, non-tender nodular mass at the lateral edge of the left inferior orbital rim; the lower fornix and overlying skin were uninvolved. There was no globe displacement, proptosis, or restriction of extraocular movements, and visual acuity was normal. The remainder of the ocular and systemic examinations was unremarkable. A chest radiograph and ultrasonography of the abdomen and pelvis were within normal limits. MRI of the orbits demonstrated a well-circumscribed soft-tissue mass abutting the left zygomatic bone; it was hypointense on T1-weighted images with adjacent bony erosion and isointense, relatively homogeneous, and well-circumscribed on T2-weighted images.

A 9-year-old previously healthy girl presented with a several-week history of a progressively enlarging swelling on the posterior ulnar aspect of her right forearm. There was no history of trauma, systemic symptoms, or family history of similar lesions. On examination, a firm, non–tender 4 × 5 cm mass was palpated in the subcutaneous tissues of the distal forearm without overlying skin changes. Neurovascular examination of the hand was normal. 

Plain radiographs of the forearm showed no fracture but demonstrated soft-tissue swelling with cortical irregularity of the adjacent ulna. MRI of the right forearm revealed a mass arising from the bone and extending into the soft tissues. The lesion was isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images and heterogeneous hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with marked enhancement after gadolinium administration. The mass caused cortical bone lysis with medullary involvement.

A 54-year-old woman presented with a right thigh mass. Eight years earlier, a 5-cm mass had been removed from the same site and diagnosed histologically as a lipoma. The current swelling had been present for several years and had gradually increased in size. On examination, two distinct masses, each approximately 20 cm in diameter, were palpable in the right thigh. The lateral mass was soft and superficial; the medial mass was firm and deep, abutting the femur. Both were nontender, without overlying skin changes. There was no history of trauma or family history of malignancy.

Contrast-enhanced multislice CT of the right thigh revealed a 23 × 16 × 27 cm intermuscular lesion extending from the proximal to the distal third of the femur. The lesion contained both fat attenuation and calcific foci; borders were smooth in some areas and irregularly septated in others.

The patient underwent a wide excision under regional anesthesia. Intraoperatively, two encapsulated intermuscular lobules were removed: a soft, lipomatous lateral lobe and a firm, bone-like medial lobe.

A 35-year-old nulliparous woman with a 10-year history of infertility presented with a three-year history of dull, cyclical pain at her umbilicus. She noted an umbilical nodule that bled during menstruation, with pain worsening at menses and relieved by analgesics. She also reported dysmenorrhea, menorrhagia, and dyspareunia. Three years earlier she had a copper intrauterine device placed and had been taking a combined oral contraceptive pill for the last 3–4 months to alleviate her pain. Her menstrual cycles were otherwise regular, and she had no notable medical, surgical, or social history.

On examination, her vital signs were stable. Abdominal inspection revealed a 3×2 cm hyperpigmented swelling at the umbilicus that was firm, immobile, non-tender, non-reducible, and not tethered to underlying structures. 

An abdominal MRI showed an ill-defined, enhancing mass measuring 3×4×6 cm along the right anterior abdominal wall, connected to a sinus tract extending inferiorly to the suprapubic region without communication with the peritoneal cavity. Additionally, bilateral adnexal lesions were seen: the right measured 1.6×1.7 cm and the left 2.0×0.8 cm; both were hyperintense with focal hypointense areas and variable diffusion restriction, consistent with ovarian endometriomas.

“The differential diagnosis was broad, including an umbilical hernia, granuloma, keloid scar, nodular malignant neoplasms and embryological abnormalities.”

A 72-year-old man with hyperlipidemia, retired plumber and veteran, and a 38–pack-year remote smoking history presented with piercing right-sided chest pain worse on inspiration, sometimes with cough but no dyspnea. Vital signs and cardiopulmonary examination were normal. Acute coronary syndrome was excluded by normal ECG and negative troponins, and he was treated for pleurisy with NSAIDs and a brief steroid taper.

Two weeks later, he returned with similar pain. Labs showed mild leukocytosis. Chest radiograph revealed a new small right pleural effusion with right lower lobe infiltrate. Contrast-enhanced chest CT excluded pulmonary embolism and demonstrated a small right pleural effusion, right lower lobe consolidation versus infiltrate, right hilar lymphadenopathy, and minimal pericardial effusion. He was treated as community-acquired pneumonia with intravenous ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and methylprednisolone followed by oral antibiotics and a prednisone taper; his symptoms improved and effusion resolved on imaging.

Within two weeks of completing steroids, he developed recurrent pleuritic pain, tachycardia (111 bpm), tachypnea, leukocytosis (19.6 × 10^3/μL), and a right-sided pleural effusion on chest radiograph. Repeat CT showed worsening effusion and progressive right lower lobe consolidation. He again received broad-spectrum antibiotics and steroids. Echocardiogram was normal. Bedside ultrasound showed only a minimal effusion too small to tap.

Given dramatic steroid responsiveness, connective-tissue disease was considered. Laboratory testing revealed positive rheumatoid factor and strongly positive anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide (>70), with elevated ESR (61 mm/hr) and CRP (260.4 mg/L); ANA, ANCA, and anti–Scl-70 were negative. The effusion cleared with prednisone 40 mg daily.

Over the next two months, tapering prednisone led to recurrent effusions with return of pleuritic pain; each time, imaging showed resolution on steroids and recurrence off steroids. Four months after initial presentation, while on prednisone 30 mg daily, he underwent thoracentesis for the first time. Pleural fluid was exudative (fluid LDH 851 IU/L), with lymphocyte predominance, glucose 137 mg/dL, negative microbiology, and cytology showing atypical but nondiagnostic cells. A second thoracentesis one week later yielded similar inconclusive results.

A 38-year-old previously healthy Asian man presented with a 6-month history of intermittent dull aching pain in the left lumbar region without aggravating or relieving factors. He denied fever, night sweats, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. Physical examination revealed a firm, non-tender retroperitoneal mass approximately 10×7 cm in the left lumbar region. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, metabolic panel, carcinoembryonic antigen, lactate dehydrogenase, and α-fetoprotein, were all within normal limits; HIV testing was negative. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a hyperechoic mass in the left abdomen. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a well-defined enhancing solid mass in the left paravertebral region with small calcifications and necrotic foci, displacing the left ureter anteriorly and abutting the psoas muscle, with preserved fat planes. Chest CT was unremarkable. MRI of the abdomen showed an isointense to hyperintense mass with calcifications and necrosis abutting the psoas muscle and displacing the inferior mesenteric vessels. A retroperitoneal sarcoma and gastrointestinal stromal tumour were considered, and the patient was scheduled for surgical resection without preoperative biopsy.

A 62-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of nasal obstruction, chronic rhinorrhea, and frequent epistaxis. Six months before presentation he developed fever and lower extremity edema. A primary hospital detected renal dysfunction with hematuria, and he was referred for investigation of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. On admission, his temperature was 37.8 °C, blood pressure 140/85 mm Hg, and heart rate 88 beats/min. Physical examination was notable for bilateral lower extremity edema; the remainder was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed: hemoglobin 7.6 g/dL, creatinine 3.05 mg/dL (6 months earlier 0.76 mg/dL), blood urea nitrogen 28.3 mg/dL, C-reactive protein 1.16 mg/dL. Urinalysis showed proteinuria (1.28 g/gCr), occult blood 3+, 50–99 red cells per high-power field, and red-cell casts. Serology was positive for PR3-ANCA (28.5 U/mL) and negative for MPO-ANCA, anti-GBM antibody, and antinuclear antibodies. Complement levels were within the reference range. Chest radiography and computed tomography showed no abnormalities. Renal ultrasonography revealed mildly enlarged kidneys (11 cm longitudinally).

A 12-year-old boy presented with a one-year history of an insidious, slowly progressive swelling in the right lateral cervical region. He had no history of trauma, surgery, or other comorbidities. Physical examination revealed a 3 cm cystic mass in the right parotid gland, situated sublobularly and movable relative to the overlying skin, which appeared normal. There was no fistula in the external auditory canal, no facial or trigeminal nerve dysfunction, and no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. MRI of the parotid region showed a round, well-defined multilobulated cystic lesion measuring approximately 4 cm in the retropatod region without invasion of adjacent tissues. On MRI, the lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, demonstrated no contrast enhancement, and there were no abnormal lymph nodes.

A 12-year-old girl with no significant medical history presented with a 3-month history of a painful swelling of the right thigh, causing a limp. She denied fever, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a prominent, non-erythematous swelling at the distal end of the right femur with restricted knee mobility but no signs of local inflammation.

Plain radiographs of the right femur showed a diaphyseal–metaphyseal periosteal reaction with a sunburst-like appearance at the distal femur. CT imaging revealed a hypodense, septated cortico-medullary lesion extending from the metaphysis into the diaphysis, with medullary hyperdensity, cortical irregularities, periosteal reaction, circumferential peri-osseous extension, and displacement of adjacent soft tissues. 

MRI demonstrated an expansive, osteolytic lesion involving the metaphysis, diaphysis, and epiphysis of the distal femur, infiltrating both cortical and medullary bone and extending into adjacent soft tissues. The mass was isointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted sequences, and showed heterogeneous enhancement after gadolinium. There was an associated knee joint effusion. The lesion compressed and displaced surrounding muscles (gracilis, sartorius, semitendinosus, biceps femoris, vastus intermedius, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis), which appeared atrophic, and displaced the popliteal vascular pedicle without occluding it.

A follow-up MRI obtained three months later revealed significant progression: the lesion had lobulated margins, heterogeneous T1 hyperintensity (suggestive of haemorrhage), invasion of the femoral condyles and distal femoral physis, and extension into the meniscal and ligamentous structures of the knee.

A 34-year-old Caucasian woman presented with 3 months of progressively worsening vision and floaters in her left eye. She had no history of malignancy and no family history of intraocular tumors. Visual acuity was 20/25 in the right eye and 20/150 in the left eye. The right eye was normal. In the left eye, there were 1+ mixed pigmented cells in the anterior vitreous. Fundus examination revealed a 5.5 × 6 mm amelanotic, circumpapillary retinal tumor obscuring the optic disc, extending nasally with foveal involvement, prominent dilated intrinsic vessels, and dense vitreous seeding adjacent to the lesion. B-scan ultrasonography showed a dome-shaped retinal mass overlying the optic nerve and macula, 3.51 mm in height, with low to medium internal reflectivity. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated intrinsic circulation within the tumor, and optical coherence tomography confirmed its primarily intraretinal origin. The case was discussed at a multidisciplinary tumor board. The initial differential diagnosis included retinocytoma with malignant transformation into retinoblastoma, amelanotic uveal melanoma extending into the retina, metastatic cutaneous melanoma, retinal astrocytoma, and combined hamartoma. The patient was lost to follow-up for two months, then returned with further vision loss (counting fingers) and increased vitreous seeding. MRI of the brain and orbits showed a retinal mass near the optic disc without extraocular extension. Given concern for retinoblastoma, poor vision potential, and patient preference, primary enucleation of the left eye was performed.

A 25-year-old man slipped from a five-foot ladder and landed on his right heel, after which he noted pain and swelling. There was no prior history of bone lesions or malignancy. On examination, there was soft, tender swelling over the medial aspect of the right heel with stretched overlying skin. Radiographs of the right ankle showed an eccentric, expansile, cystic lesion of the calcaneus with thin septae traversing the cavity, producing a blown-out or soap-bubble appearance, and a cortical breach suggestive of a pathological fracture.

A 48-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of nonradiating left lower quadrant abdominal pain that worsened with eating. He also reported low-grade fever, malaise, loose stools, and a 10-lb weight loss over 3 months. He denied nausea, vomiting, melena, jaundice, trauma, recent infections or travel, alcohol use, and NSAID use. His father had prostate and colon cancer. On examination, he was tachycardic but afebrile and normotensive; weight was 77 kg, BMI 22.4 kg/m². Abdominal exam showed tenderness in the left lower quadrant without a palpable mass. Laboratory studies revealed neutrophilic leukocytosis (14.3 thou/mcL), microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL, MCV 24.3 pg), an elevated HbA1C (7.1%), elevated alkaline phosphatase (245 U/L), elevated ALT (58 U/L), and a normal CA 19-9. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 6.8 cm complex cystic mass in the tail of the pancreas with mild ductal dilatation. MRI demonstrated a 9.2 cm macrolobulated pancreatic mass without local extension or metastasis, with upstream atrophy and ductal dilatation. PET-CT revealed a large FDG-avid, centrally necrotic pancreatic mass without distant disease. Endoscopic ultrasound showed a 65 × 49 mm round, heterogeneous, hypoechoic mass in the pancreatic body with well-defined borders, upstream ductal dilatation (4.4 mm in the body), and no invasion of the celiac trunk. Fine-needle biopsy yielded malignant spindle cells. Immunohistochemistry was negative for CKAE1AE3, CD163, synaptophysin, CD117, CD34, CD31, SMA, S-100, and SOX-10. In this setting, the differential diagnosis remained broad but included sarcomatoid carcinoma versus primary sarcoma.

A 21-year-old woman presented with a right-sided parietal scalp swelling. She first noticed the mass at age 7, a few months after a fall at home, and it had slowly increased in size since then. She denied headache, neurological symptoms, or skin changes.

On examination, neurological findings were normal. There was a 6.0×6.0×3.0-cm firm, noncompressible, nonpulsatile mass in the right parasagittal region of the scalp, without skin discoloration, thrill, or bruit. Cough impulse and transillumination tests were negative.

A noncontrast CT scan of the brain with bone windows demonstrated a hyperdense mass of the right parasagittal parietal bone with thinning of the cortex, expansion of the involved bone, and a “ground-glass” appearance. Contrast-enhanced MRI showed a nonenhancing bony defect at the same site with a subcutaneous mass but no dural or brain parenchymal invasion.

A 66-year-old man with a history of smoking, arterial hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia underwent an aorto-bifemoral bypass in 2002 for critical right-leg ischemia, at which time a superficial ulcer was noted on the right calf. Over the next 14 years, the ulcer failed to heal and progressively enlarged. In July 2016, angiography for worsening calf pain demonstrated occlusion of the right superficial femoral artery. In October 2016, a right femoro-popliteal bypass was performed, and tissue from the ulcer bed was submitted for histologic examination.

Microscopic examination showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia at the ulcer edges and malignant structures at the base composed of spindle-shaped and epithelioid cells, with focal necrosis, secondary vascular thrombosis, and up to 8 mitoses per 10 high-power fields (French Federation of Cancer Centers Sarcoma Group grade 3).

Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated diffuse positivity for cytokeratins (CK AE1-3) and early growth response protein 1 (ERG-1); negative staining for CD31, CD34, and desmin; and retained expression of INI1. Cyclin D1 was diffusely positive, and BerEp4, calretinin, and HHV8 were negative.

A 54-year-old man with a 48-year, 1.5-pack-per-day smoking history presented with a several-month history of chronic cough. He had childhood asthma, hyperlipidaemia and hypertension. He was afebrile, and the physical examination was unremarkable, with no superficial lymph-node enlargement. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and normal liver and renal function; C-reactive protein was elevated at 8.91 mg/dL. Tumor markers (CEA, cytokeratin-19 fragment, pro-GRP, and sIL-2R) were within normal limits. Antinuclear antibody titer was <40 times, and an interferon-γ release assay was negative. Chest CT demonstrated mediastinal lymphadenopathy and a small subpleural nodule in the right upper lobe. On PET-CT, the nodule had low FDG uptake (SUVmax 2.5), while the mediastinal nodes had intense uptake (SUVmax 10.7). EBUS-TBNA of the mediastinal nodes suggested a lymphoproliferative process but was nondiagnostic. A thoracoscopic lymph-node biopsy revealed no malignant cells; instead, IgG4-positive cells were scattered in the lymph nodes and accumulated in the extranodal area, with an IgG4/IgG ratio of approximately 50%, suggesting IgG4-related disease.

A 53-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a gastric mass that was incidentally discovered during an abdominal ultrasound performed for chest pain. She reported intermittent epigastric discomfort and dysphagia for solids. Her medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, and a hysterectomy 5 years earlier for uterine cancer.

On contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen, there was a homogeneous exophytic mass measuring 4.8 × 4.2 × 3.6 cm arising from the gastric antrum. The overlying mucosa appeared smooth, with a few minute calcifications, and no other abnormalities were noted.

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a submucosal lesion in the gastric antrum with normal-appearing mucosa. Biopsies showed only mild inactive chronic inflammation without malignancy. Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated a hypoechoic, heterogeneous mass with calcifications and cystic spaces arising from the muscularis propria and no perigastric lymphadenopathy. EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration yielded rare spindle-cell tissue fragments with bland cytology, and these findings appeared most consistent with a gastrointestinal stromal tumor.

A 64-year-old healthy man presented with a slowly enlarging scrotal swelling of 2 years’ duration, initially thought to be a hydrocele. On examination, there was a nontender scrotal swelling situated between two normal testicles. Scrotal ultrasonography showed diffuse median swelling with edema and small fluid pockets. Noncontrast CT of the pelvis demonstrated a similar diffuse scrotal mass. The patient was taken for scrotal exploration. At surgery, surgeons found a well-encapsulated lipocystic mass measuring 7 × 11 × 19 cm and weighing 576 g, located adjacent to the bulbar urethra and not involving the testicles; it was discrete and easily removed without adhesions to surrounding tissues.

A 44-year-old black woman was referred for evaluation of an asymptomatic swelling in the vestibular region of the left mandibular canine area. The overlying oral mucosa was normal in color, and needle aspiration of the swelling was negative. Extraoral examination revealed no lymphadenopathy. A panoramic radiograph showed a well-circumscribed lesion measuring approximately 10 cm in diameter, extending from the right lateral incisor to the left second molar. The lesion had a mixed radiopaque and radiolucent appearance and caused radicular resorption of tooth 41.

A 45-year-old man presented to the emergency department with acute colicky abdominal pain. He denied nausea, loss of appetite, changes in bowel habits, or urinary symptoms. His only past medical history was right urolithiasis treated with a double J stent; he had no allergies and no family history of similar conditions. On examination, he was afebrile, with a soft, non-tender abdomen and no palpable masses. Laboratory studies including complete blood count, coagulation profile, metabolic panel, and liver and kidney function tests were all within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed right-sided kidney stones and a 19.5 × 13.6 × 18 cm heterogeneously hypodense retroperitoneal mass composed predominantly of adipose tissue with internal septa and a solid hyperdense nodule, contiguous with the right psoas major muscle. MRI confirmed a large predominantly adipose mass exerting a compressive effect on the inferior vena cava and right renal vein. To establish a definitive diagnosis, a CT-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy was performed, showing “spindle cell mesenchymal neoplasm, not specified, to be further defined at the definitive histological examination after resection.” Immunophenotyping of the biopsy specimen showed CD34 +, SMA −, desmin −, caldesmone −, S100 −, MDM2 −, STAT6 −, EMA −, KIT −, and DOG1 −.

A 20-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of sleeping with an open mouth, snoring, a foreign-body sensation in the throat, and difficulty swallowing. On oropharyngeal and nasal endoscopic examination, there was a medium-hard, semimobile, painless, well-circumscribed mass measuring 2 × 1 cm, originating in the nasopharynx and extending downward from the posterior soft palate. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a vascular-appearing lesion without high-flow characteristics, arising in the nasopharynx and completely filling the choanae. Computed tomography demonstrated a nonhomogeneous lesion that did not erode adjacent tissues and showed no calcifications. Ear, nose, throat, and cranial nerve examinations were otherwise normal.

A 63-year-old Caucasian man presented with a bump on his right earlobe that had been present for several years. He noted that he could often express material from the bump but denied any history of trauma, ear piercing, or prior treatment. His medical history was benign. On examination, there was a 4 mm, skin-colored nodule with a small central opening on the right earlobe. Provisional diagnoses included an epidermal inclusion cyst, a dilated pore of Winer, and a trichofolliculoma. A 4 mm punch biopsy was performed, and the specimen was sent for routine hematoxylin–eosin staining.

An 85-year-old woman presented with a four-month history of a gradually enlarging, nontender mass in her right buttock. Two years earlier she had undergone excision of a retroperitoneal soft tissue tumor. On examination, the buttock mass was firm, mobile, poorly circumscribed, and measured 4.4 × 3.8 cm. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a well-defined, enhancing lesion within the right gluteal musculature.

Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) was performed using 25-gauge needles, with material submitted for air-dried and alcohol-fixed smears and a formalin-fixed cell block. Diff-Quik and Papanicolaou smears revealed loosely cohesive clusters and dyscohesive spindle cells with enlarged, hyperchromatic nuclei, cytoplasmic tails, and coarse chromatin in a background of adipose tissue and dense amorphous matrix. Occasional osteoclast-type giant cells were noted. Cell block sections demonstrated hypercellular fragments of pleomorphic spindle cells with mitotic figures associated with ribbons of dense eosinophilic material consistent with osteoid and areas of adipocytes containing atypical stromal cells. No necrosis was seen.

Immunohistochemical stains on the cell block showed tumor cells positive for vimentin and focally positive for smooth muscle actin, with a Ki-67 labeling index of 20%. The cells were negative for cytokeratin (AE1/AE3, Cam 5.2), S-100, CD34, Melan-A, and HMB-45.

A 37-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of subacute fever, cough, dyspnea, and significant weight loss. On examination, both lungs had inspiratory and expiratory wheezes; cardiac auscultation revealed normal S1 and S2 and a 3/6 systolic ejection murmur at the left upper parasternal border with respiratory variation. There was no peripheral edema. A CT scan of the chest demonstrated a large mediastinal mass and bilateral renal masses. Biopsies of the kidney and bone marrow revealed a high-grade B-cell lymphoma.  
An electrocardiogram showed a heart rate of 75 beats per minute in sinus rhythm with first-degree AV block and markedly abnormal T waves in leads I, aVL, V1, and V2. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, creatinine, and liver-function tests, were within normal limits; tests for HIV and hepatitis B and C were negative.  
Transthoracic echocardiography revealed multiple intracardiac masses involving the right ventricular outflow tract, right ventricular apex, medial right atrium, and posterior left atrium, with mild impairment of right ventricular systolic function. The masses in the right ventricular outflow tract produced partial obstruction (peak velocity, 2.3 m/s), with a right ventricular systolic pressure of 43 mmHg. A mass in the left atrium was obstructing flow from the right upper pulmonary vein. The left ventricular ejection fraction was 60%.

A 24-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of progressive headaches, episodes of syncope, and blurred vision. Her medical history was notable only for an uncomplicated appendectomy and a head injury in a traffic accident at age 6, which had not been investigated or treated. On examination, she was alert and oriented; all neurologic findings were normal except for a firm, non-tender, 5 cm × 5 cm bony mass in the left frontoparietal region. Routine laboratory tests, including a complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. Noncontrast head CT demonstrated focal thickening of the diploic space in the left frontoparietal bone, extending to the orbital roof, without evidence of cortical destruction or periosteal reaction. MRI of the brain and skull showed a heterogeneous bony mass in the same region with no intracranial or dural invasion.

A 4-month-old boy was brought to the urology clinic for evaluation of left scrotal swelling. On examination, a left-sided hydrocele was noted. Scrotal Doppler ultrasonography revealed an 11 × 10 mm solid-cystic lesion within the left testis containing multiple small cystic cavities; the lower aspect of the lesion demonstrated vascular flow. Laboratory studies showed normal serum α-fetoprotein and lactate dehydrogenase levels; human chorionic gonadotropin was 8 IU/L. Given the concern for an intratesticular tumor, the patient was taken for left inguinal exploration with testis-sparing enucleation of the mass.

A 50-year-old woman presented with progressive weight loss and bilateral lower-extremity weakness. Laboratory studies revealed an alpha-fetoprotein level of 17.5 ng/mL and a normal beta-human chorionic gonadotropin level. Neurologic, gastroenterologic, and oncologic evaluations, including fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography, whole-body computed tomography, lumbar spine MRI, esophagogastroduodenoscopy, and colonoscopy, were unrevealing. Retrospective review of the initial brain MRI showed subtle T2 hyperintensity and swelling in the dorsal medulla oblongata. Six months after symptom onset, she developed numbness of the bilateral upper extremities. On examination, muscle strength was 5/5 in all extremities, deep tendon reflexes were brisk, and there were no Babinski or Trömner signs. Repeat whole-spine MRI and contrast-enhanced brain MRI demonstrated a lesion in the dorsal medulla oblongata with high signal intensity on T2-weighted imaging and heterogeneous enhancement on contrast imaging.

A 39-year-old woman (gravida 3, para 2) with no significant medical or surgical history and a normal menstrual cycle presented with isolated pelvic pain. On examination, the uterus was normal in size, and a left latero-uterine mass separate from the uterine corpus was palpated. Serum CA-125 was within normal limits. Pelvic ultrasound showed an oval, well-defined left pelvic mass with regular contours, heterogeneous hyperechoic echostructure, cystic areas, and no vascularity on color Doppler imaging. Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis revealed a predominantly fatty mass containing soft-tissue components without calcifications and heterogeneous enhancement, suggesting initially a mature teratoma. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a round suprauterine mass adjacent to the left ovary with a thin wall, containing a fatty component (hyperintense on T1 and T2, suppressed on fat-saturated sequences) and a solid component (T2 hyperintense, T1 hypointense, diffusion hyperintense, with strong postcontrast enhancement). MRI findings were interpreted as a left ovarian dermoid cyst with a potentially malignant solid component, corresponding to O-RADS MRI category 5.

A 5-year-old boy with no prior medical history was noted by his parents to have a slowly developing limitation in right-eye movement over several weeks. There was no pain, inflammation, fever, trauma, or history of ocular infection, and his overall health was unchanged. On examination, abduction of the right eye was restricted. There were no signs of proptosis, strabismus, visual impairment, or inflammation in either eye; the remainder of the physical examination was normal. Laboratory studies, including an infectious work-up, were negative.  
Noncontrast CT of the orbits showed a well-circumscribed extraconal mass at the right superolateral orbital wall, adjacent to the frontozygomatic suture, with smooth bone remodeling and fluid-attenuating content but no bone invasion. Subsequent MRI demonstrated a cystic mass in the right superior extraconal compartment that was hyperintense on T2-weighted images, hypointense on FLAIR imaging, and exhibited no diffusion restriction or internal enhancement after gadolinium administration. The lesion exerted mild compression on the external and superior rectus muscles, correlating with the abduction deficit, but did not involve the optic nerve, intraconal fat, or show intracranial extension.

A 12-year-old boy presented with a one-year history of a slow-growing, painless mass beneath his tongue. He denied pain, dysphagia, dysphonia, or any other symptoms. There was no relevant personal or family medical history. On oral examination, a solid, non-tender mass measuring 4.5 × 7 cm occupied the sublingual region of the tongue. No cervical lymphadenopathy was noted, and routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging of the tongue showed a well-circumscribed, ovoid nodular lesion in the sublingual region that was homogeneously isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images, homogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and demonstrated uniform enhancement after contrast administration.

A 49-year-old man presented with a 10-day history of intermittent, colicky abdominal pain that worsened after eating, and a reduced appetite. His medical history was significant for a right nephrectomy for a benign tumor and an appendicectomy. He was afebrile, and vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination disclosed a soft abdomen with localized epigastric tenderness; there were no palpable masses and bowel sounds were normal. Laboratory studies were unremarkable except for a mild microcytic anemia. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a bowel-related mass in the epigastric region. A computed tomography scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 3 × 6 cm fatty ovoid lesion within the transverse colon causing colo-colic intussusception. Colonoscopy showed an abnormal dusky grey lesion occupying most of the lumen in the distal transverse colon, with two ulcerated areas on its leading edge.

A 76-year-old woman with bilateral knee osteoarthritis, prior tobacco use, cirrhosis with esophageal varices, and hypothyroidism presented with a one-year history of progressive fatigue, weakness, cold intolerance, and 60–90 lb weight loss. She noted a painful right lateral abdominal wall mass and multiple subcutaneous “bumps” on the abdomen, right axilla, and right knee, previously observed without intervention. On presentation she was tachycardic (heart rate 115 bpm). 

Initial laboratory studies revealed leukopenia (WBC 3.8 × 10^9/L), anemia (Hb 10.6 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (platelets 74 × 10^9/L), elevated alkaline phosphatase (714 U/L), hypoalbuminemia (1.7 g/dL), AST 147 U/L, and lactic acidosis (3.4 mmol/L). 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated gallbladder distension, intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile-duct dilation with 1.5 cm intraductal filling defects (masses vs stones), more than 18 subcutaneous soft tissue masses (0.5–5.5 cm), a 1.7 cm left lower lobe pulmonary nodule, small right pulmonary nodules, endometrial thickening, and moderate ascites. 

She received IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics, and underwent ERCP with biliary stenting. Despite continued antibiotics, incision and drainage of one abdominal wall lesion, and removal of an axillary eschar, her lactic acidosis persisted and multiple wound and fluid cultures remained negative. CT-guided biopsy of the right abdominal wall mass was nondiagnostic; a second core biopsy was obtained from the left abdominal wall. 

MRI of the left knee showed an enhancing fluid collection concerning for abscess vs septic arthritis with osteomyelitis; aspiration revealed monocyte predominance but no organisms. Rheumatology evaluation for polyarteritis nodosa and pyoderma gangrenosum was negative (ANCA negative). Laboratory evaluation argued against tumor lysis syndrome and acute interstitial nephritis. Treatment for hypercalcemia, hypoglycemia, and fluid overload failed to correct her metabolic abnormalities. 

Two weeks into hospitalization, the preliminary pathology of the left abdominal wall core biopsy reported a high-grade hematolymphoid neoplasm with a differential including myeloid sarcoma and blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of intermittent abdominal distension and heartburn. One week before admission, upper endoscopy showed a bulge in the gastric fundus, and chronic nonatrophic gastritis with bile reflux was noted. Her medical history included iron deficiency anemia, menoxenia, and a prior cholecystectomy. She denied tobacco and alcohol use; family history was noncontributory. Physical examination and laboratory tests were unremarkable.

An enhanced abdominal CT scan demonstrated two circular nodules in the fundus of the stomach measuring approximately 1.8 × 1.3 cm and 2.3 × 1.6 cm, suggesting a benign gastric tumor; the differential diagnosis included a stromal tumor and a leiomyoma. Endoscopic ultrasound revealed two connected, spherical bulges on the anterior wall of the fundus, measuring 28 mm and 43 mm. Both lesions were covered by normal mucosa, appeared hypoechoic from the muscularis propria, and grew toward the outer cavity with uniform internal echo and attenuated rear echo. Based on the CT and EUS findings, a diagnosis of gastrointestinal stromal tumors was made preoperatively.

A 54-year-old woman presented with progressive right buccal swelling of 2 years’ duration and headache for 2 months. Empiric anti-inflammatory and analgesic therapy provided no relief. She denied dyspnea, nausea, dysphagia, hoarseness, loss of consciousness, neurologic deficits, or constitutional symptoms. There was no relevant medical or family history, and she was a non-smoker. 

On examination, a non-tender, fixed, non-pulsatile sessile mass approximately 4 cm in diameter was noted on the right cheek; there was no cervical lymphadenopathy. Intraoral evaluation revealed a buccal swelling with mildly erythematous mucosa, predominantly located in the right maxillary sinus and involving the base of the maxilla. Routine hematologic and biochemical tests were within normal limits.

Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-circumscribed heterogeneous lesion with a necrotic center in the right maxillary sinus that was relatively hypointense on T2-weighted sequences. Computed tomography of the paranasal sinuses showed a 7 × 6 × 6 cm soft-tissue mass occupying the entire right maxillary sinus, extending from the roof of the oral cavity to the skull base, causing thinning and destruction of the anterior and lateral sinus walls and erosion of the orbital floor. There was no involvement of the dura mater or intracranial structures and no evidence of metastatic disease.

A 30-year-old man with a history of heavy alcohol use and prior hospitalization for alcohol withdrawal was brought to the emergency department with sudden-onset severe dyspnea, significant hemoptysis, and altered mental status. He had been drinking heavily until the day before presentation and had exercised a few hours earlier. He had an untreated history of hypertension and anxiety.

On examination: temperature 38.4 °C; heart rate 148 beats/min; blood pressure 140/80 mm Hg; respiratory rate 30 breaths/min; oxygen saturation 86% on room air; mottled skin.

Initial laboratory results:  
• White blood cell count 25.5 ×10^3/μL (4–11)  
• Glucose 561 mg/dL (70–99)  
• Creatinine 1.7 mg/dL (0.72–1.25)  
• Lactate 19.3 mmol/L (0.5–2.2)  
• Troponin I 2.21 ng/mL (<0.04)  
• Blood ethanol undetectable; urine toxicology positive for cannabinoids

Noncontrast CT of the chest demonstrated bilateral reticular and airspace opacities, consistent with acute respiratory distress syndrome. He was intubated, sedated, and paralyzed, but remained profoundly hypoxemic despite 100% FiO2 and high PEEP, prompting initiation of veno-venous ECMO for respiratory support. He then developed hemodynamic collapse and cardiac arrest, and was converted to veno-arterial ECMO. Transthoracic echocardiography showed severe biventricular dysfunction with an ejection fraction of 5–10%.

Within 24 hours of VA-ECMO support, cardiac function improved and VA-ECMO was removed on day 4. By day 10, ejection fraction had normalized, but he continued to require 100% oxygen, high PEEP, prone positioning, deep sedation, and neuromuscular blockade for persistent ARDS. He developed acute renal failure requiring continuous renal replacement therapy. He received broad-spectrum antibiotics, stress-dose corticosteroids, and standard management for alcohol withdrawal.

High fevers (>40 °C), sinus tachycardia, mild to moderate systolic hypertension, and leukocytosis persisted, but repeated blood and bronchial cultures remained negative. Once his oxygenation was relatively stable, a noncontrast CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was obtained as part of the work-up for presumed infection.

A male neonate was delivered at 33 weeks’ gestation after a pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios and antepartum hemorrhage. Birth weight was 2085 g. On delivery, he had immediate respiratory distress requiring IPPV and scored 5, 7, and 8 on the APGAR at 1, 5, and 10 minutes, respectively. At 15 minutes of life, he was admitted to the NICU for CPAP and was intubated at 1 hour for worsening distress and CO2 retention. A single dose of surfactant was administered for suspected hyaline membrane disease. On day 1, a trial extubation was attempted, but significant apnea and desaturation led to traumatic reintubation, during which a purple, hemorrhagic mass on the posterior pharyngeal wall was noted, obscuring the airway. Examination revealed a protruding tongue and an oral cavity mass. On day 4, laryngobronchoesophagoscopy showed a vascular, exophytic mass arising from the posterior pharyngeal wall, extending from the postnasal space to the hypopharynx. MRI demonstrated a well-circumscribed heterogeneous mass in the nasopharynx measuring 33×22 mm axially and 32 mm craniocaudally. The radiological appearance, with heterogeneous T1 and T2 signals, was suggestive of a teratoma, with differential diagnoses of rhabdomyosarcoma, haemangioma, hairy polyp, and congenital pleomorphic adenoma.

A 50-year-old Chinese man presented with low back pain, right buttock pain, and radiating pain from the right buttock to the back of the right leg. The right buttock pain was the most prominent symptom, worsened by movement and relieved by lying supine, and caused an abnormal gait. He had no prior treatments or surgeries and no relevant family or social history.

On examination, Lasegue’s sign and its strengthening test were positive on the right, as were the right femoral nerve traction test and FABER test; right hip abduction was limited. Neurological examination of the lower limbs showed no sensory loss or muscle weakness. Abdominal examination was unremarkable.

Plain radiographs of the lumbar spine showed no abnormalities. MRI of the lumbar/sacral spine revealed lumbar disc herniation that did not explain the predominant buttock pain. Musculoskeletal ultrasound of the right sciatic nerve demonstrated an anechoic, lobulated mass within the right piriformis muscle measuring 6.0 × 2.3 × 2.6 cm, with regular margins and no posterior wall enhancement. MRI of the pelvis and right hip confirmed a cystic-appearing lesion in the piriformis region with low T1 signal and high T2 signal, measuring up to 3.1 × 2.2 cm.

A piriformis ganglion was suspected, and the differential diagnoses included hematoma, metastatic tumor, and so forth.

A 56-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a sudden onset of widespread deep purple skin lesions. He reported no new medications or known exposures. On examination, there were numerous discrete to confluent deep purple papules and nodules distributed over the trunk and extremities. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies were notable only for an elevated soluble interleukin-2 receptor level of 672 U/mL; complete blood count and other blood chemistries were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated multiple homogeneous skin nodules extending into the subcutaneous tissue without lymphadenopathy or visceral organ involvement.
