A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman (G1P1, BMI 23) with no prior medical history was diagnosed with invasive breast carcinoma of no special type (IBC-NOS). Pelvic examination was unremarkable; she had no signs of virilization, Cushing’s syndrome, or metrorrhagia.  
Staging computed tomography revealed a 2 cm solid mass in the right ovary. Pelvic MRI showed a solid ovarian lesion that was T1 isointense, T2 hyperintense, with a high-risk enhancement curve.  
She underwent partial mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection; pathology showed a 34 mm grade II IBC-NOS, luminal A, with micrometastasis in 1 of 28 nodes (pT2N1mi).  
Subsequently, diagnostic laparoscopy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and endometrial curettage was performed. No peritoneal masses or enlarged lymph nodes were observed.  
Gross examination of the right ovary revealed a well-circumscribed solid mass measuring 3 × 2 cm. The cut surface was firm, gray-yellowish, and showed no hemorrhage or necrosis. The remainder of the adnexa was unremarkable.

A 32-year-old Pakistani man presented with 2 months of progressive abdominal distention and pain, intermittent low-grade fever, and a 6-kg weight loss. He had no significant medical history and denied tobacco, alcohol, or drug use. On examination, he appeared pale and mildly uncomfortable; the abdomen was distended with mild right-upper-quadrant tenderness and a palpable 20×15-cm mass. There was no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed normal urine metanephrine (160 mcg/24 h; N 140–785), urine dopamine (128 mcg/24 h; N 65–400), blood free metanephrine (73 pg/mL; N 0–90), and blood free normetanephrine (118 pg/mL; N 0–190), with an elevated urine normetanephrine (600 mcg/24 h; N 75–375). Serum alpha-fetoprotein (3.0 ng/mL; N 0–8), CA 19-9 (<2.06 U/mL; N 0–37), and CEA (1.97 ng/mL; N 0–2.5) were normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 24×16×23.8-cm lobulated epigastric mass with cystic and solid components displacing the inferior vena cava, gallbladder, duodenum, pancreas, and hepatic hilum; the right adrenal gland was not visualized separately but the mass was distinct from the right kidney and appeared adrenal in origin. A percutaneous biopsy demonstrated tumor cells positive for synaptophysin, cytokeratin, and S-100, indicating a neuroendocrine origin.

An elderly woman with a history of asthma and hypertension, well controlled on medication, presented with a 4-week history of intermittent left-sided lumbar pain radiating to her back. She also experienced three to four episodes of nonprojectile, non–blood-stained vomiting but denied urinary symptoms or weight loss. She had no relevant drug, family, or genetic history. On examination, she appeared mildly dehydrated. Abdominal palpation revealed mild tenderness in the left hypochondrial and left lumbar regions; pulmonary and spinal examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed hyponatremia (Na+ 128 mEq/L), hypokalemia (K+ 2.8 mEq/L), elevated blood urea nitrogen (50 mmol/L), and creatinine (2.80 mg/dL); urinalysis was normal. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a well-defined, 4.5 × 3.0 × 3.5 cm hyperechoic lesion arising from the left suprarenal gland. Serum cortisol (17.60 μg/dL), urinary vanillylmandelic acid (11.4 mg/24 h), and serum metanephrines (243.26 μg/dL) were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a left suprarenal mass abutting the upper pole of the left kidney, spleen, and psoas muscle; there was no focal enhancement, and the mean attenuation was −28 to +10 HU in arterial, venous, and delayed phases, without calcification, hemorrhage, necrosis, or surrounding fat stranding.

A 29-year-old Caucasian man presented with 3–4 months of right upper-quadrant and right flank discomfort. He denied gastrointestinal, urinary, or endocrine symptoms. His history was notable for latent tuberculosis diagnosed 3 months earlier, for which he was taking rifampicin and isoniazid. On examination, a palpable mass in the right hypochondrium displaced the liver anteriorly; blood pressure was normal. Laboratory evaluation showed normal results on a dexamethasone suppression test, 24-hour urine catecholamine and metanephrine assays, and plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio. Abdominal ultrasound and CT scans revealed a 15-cm heterogeneous right adrenal mass compressing the liver, findings that raised the possibility of a primary adrenal carcinoma. A metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scan with SPECT showed no significant tracer uptake, making a pheochromocytoma less likely. A fluorodeoxyglucose–PET scan demonstrated an intensely metabolically active right adrenal mass measuring 14.5 × 9.5 × 17.2 cm, with dystrophic calcification and central necrosis, features consistent with either adrenal cortical carcinoma or tuberculosis. The left adrenal gland was normal, there were no features to suggest active tuberculosis elsewhere, and there was no evidence of metastatic disease. Because of the large size of the mass, he underwent an open right adrenalectomy; the postoperative course was uneventful.

A 9-year-old boy presented with a 4-month history of recurrent left-sided epistaxis and nasal obstruction. The bleeding episodes were self-limited but had become more frequent. The caregiver noted that just before symptom onset the child had been performing repeated anterior nasal swabs in the left nostril for COVID-19 self-testing. He had no prior nasal surgery, bleeding disorders, or other health issues.

On examination, anterior rhinoscopy revealed a well-defined red mass arising from the anterior nasal septum in the left nostril. Nasal endoscopy showed no additional lesions. Vital signs and routine blood tests were normal. Given the persistent episodes of bleeding and the lesion’s appearance, the patient was scheduled for endoscopic surgical excision under general anesthesia.

A 91-year-old man with nonischemic cardiomyopathy status post dual-chamber implantable cardioverter–defibrillator implantation in 2010 and upgrade to a biventricular device in 2013, permanent atrial fibrillation, and essential thrombocythemia on hydroxyurea presented with 2 weeks of progressively worsening swelling and erythema over his device pocket. He denied pain, fever, or other systemic symptoms. On examination, the left anterior chest wall pocket was erythematous and swollen with overlying telangiectasias. He was afebrile, and laboratory studies showed a mild leukocytosis. Ultrasound of the pocket demonstrated an irregular fluid collection measuring 4.0 × 2.6 × 3.3 cm inferior to the generator. He was treated empirically with broad-spectrum antibiotics for presumed device infection and referred for pocket exploration. Surgical exploration revealed a solid mass with cystic components extending onto the generator, leads, and surrounding tissues, and a biopsy was obtained. Bacterial and acid-fast bacilli cultures of the pocket were negative, as were blood cultures, and antibiotics were discontinued given low clinical suspicion for infection and absence of supportive microbiologic data. Microscopic examination of the biopsy specimen showed fragments of fibrous tissue with focal chronic inflammation and fibrosis but no malignant cells.

A 15-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of a swelling in the upper outer aspect of her right eye. She reported that the lesion had been present for 3 years without any change in size or symptoms and denied any history of trauma. On examination, visual acuity was 6/6 in both eyes, and ocular alignment and extraocular movements were normal. Pupillary reactions and intraocular pressures were within normal limits. Slit-lamp examination revealed a 3 × 3 mm firm, whitish, mobile subconjunctival swelling in the superotemporal quadrant of the right eye, with surrounding vascularization. There were no signs of rapid growth, pigmentation, feeder vessels, necrosis, or ulceration. With a working clinical diagnosis of an epibulbar dermoid and because of her constant discomfort, an excision biopsy of the lesion was performed under topical anesthesia.

A 44-year-old single man presented with a 10-year history of progressively enlarging perianal and lower scrotal warts. He reported pruritus and a bloody, foul-smelling discharge over the past 4 years. He had a history of smoking, alcohol use, chronic hepatitis B infection, and multiple heterosexual partners.

On examination, he was well-nourished with normal vital signs. There were hard, cauliflower-shaped, circumferential perianal warts sparing a 1 cm bridge at 6 o’clock, and an associated exophytic lesion measuring 22 cm involving the lower scrotal skin. Proctoscopic and per-rectal examination showed no intra-anal involvement. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 7.2×10^9/l, hemoglobin 12.3 g/dl, platelets 303×10^9/l, normal liver and renal function tests, and normal coagulation parameters. Treponema pallidum hemagglutination and indirect hemagglutination assays were non-reactive. HIV antigen/antibody testing was negative, and hepatitis B surface antigen was positive.

A 50-year-old man presented with a painless, slowly enlarging epigastric mass over 5 years. He denied fever, night sweats, appetite loss, or weight change. On examination, there was a 4 × 3 cm firm, non-tender mass in the subcutaneous plane over the xiphoid process; the overlying skin was normal, and the lesion was not fixed to underlying structures. The remainder of the abdominal examination was unremarkable, and no lymphadenopathy or other subcutaneous masses were noted. Routine hematological and biochemical tests were within normal limits, and tumor markers (CEA 0.9 ng/ml; CA 19-9 2 U/ml) were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a well-circumscribed, oval 38 × 34 mm subcutaneous lesion anterior to the xiphoid process with soft-tissue density and peripheral calcifications. Based on these findings, a calcified hydatid cyst was suspected.

A 14-year-old girl with no comorbidities presented with a 3-month history of a slowly enlarging, painful swelling at the back of her head. She denied fever, headache, trauma, or systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a 2×2-cm soft, fluctuant, tender swelling in the occipital region without erythema, sinus tract, or discharge. Contrast CT of the head showed an intraosseous lesion with lytic changes of the inner table of the occipital bone and soft-tissue extension externally. Contrast MRI demonstrated multiple rim-enhancing collections (largest 1.9×1.2×1.4 cm) extending through the occipital bone into the subcutaneous fat; the lesions were heterogeneously hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2, and showed peripheral enhancement. Adjacent brain parenchyma was normal, with no edema. MR venography revealed mild narrowing of the right transverse sinus and torcular herophili without thrombosis. Laboratory studies, including white-cell count, C-reactive protein, and blood cultures, were unremarkable. A tuberculous etiology was considered but serum adenosine deaminase levels and a Mantoux test were normal. No predisposing factors for an abscess were identified.

A 4-day-old female neonate was referred with progressive abdominal distention and bilious vomiting after each feed. She was born at 39 weeks and 3 days’ gestation via vaginal delivery, with a birth weight of 3124 g. Passage of meconium occurred soon after birth. On examination she was slightly inactive, mildly dehydrated, and had a distended abdomen; vital signs were within normal limits. An upper gastrointestinal series showed a normal appearance without evidence of malrotation. A gastrografin enema demonstrated that the transverse colon near the hepatic flexure was not delineated on the oral (proximal) side, and application of pressure revealed a “string sign.” No microcolon was observed. Given these findings, exploratory laparotomy was planned under suspicion of intestinal stenosis caused by intussusception or volvulus.

A 15-year-old North Indian, sexually inactive, unmarried girl presented with a painless swelling of the left labia majora that had gradually increased in size over the past year. She denied pain, dysuria, discharge, fever, weight loss, or bowel or bladder symptoms. Menarche occurred at age 12, with regular, normal menstrual cycles. Her medical and surgical histories were unremarkable. 

On examination, she was in no distress. Local inspection revealed a 14 × 10 cm solid, nonpedunculated mass on the left labia majora with superficial vascularity; it was slightly warm, nontender, and not adherent to the overlying skin or surrounding structures. The mons pubis and right labia were normal. There was no inguinal lymphadenopathy. 

Routine hematological and biochemical tests were within normal limits. Transperineal ultrasonography demonstrated a solid vulvar mass with superficial high vascularity; the uterus, ovaries, and adnexa were normal. 

Differential diagnoses included sarcoma, lipoma, Bartholin cyst, aggressive angiomyxoma, and fibroid. With the clinical and ultrasonographic findings suggesting a benign lesion, the decision was made to proceed with surgical excision of the mass.

A 65-year-old woman presented with a 12-month history of progressive right-sided nasal obstruction and tearing (epiphora), associated with a painless lump on the right lateral nose. She had a 2 pack-year smoking history and no constitutional (“B”) symptoms. Medical history included hypertension, mild angina, and hypercholesterolaemia; performance status was 0.

On examination, the right globe was proptosed and laterally displaced by a firm medial canthal mass; the tear lake was elevated. Visual acuity and extraocular movements were intact. Nasal endoscopy showed a mass in the right nasal cavity of unvisualized origin; the contralateral postnasal space was clear. There was a palpable right level 1B neck node. Fine-needle aspiration of that node showed reactive hyperplasia without dysplasia or malignancy.

Contrast CT of the sinuses revealed an extensive soft-tissue mass filling the right maxillary sinus, extending into the right nasal cavity, ethmoid and frontal sinuses, invading the nasolacrimal system, and breaching the lamina papyracea into the right orbit, abutting and displacing the globe. 

The patient underwent endoscopic sinus surgery, with biopsies taken from the right inferior turbinate, lateral nasal wall, lacrimal fossa, and maxillary sinus and preserved in formalin.

A 74-year-old Asian woman with emphysema, hyperlipidemia, Parkinson disease, and stage 1b lung adenocarcinoma in remission underwent surveillance colonoscopy. One year earlier, PET–CT had shown a hypermetabolic focus in the sigmoid colon, and colonoscopy at that time had revealed two large tubulovillous adenomas that were snared. The patient reported chronic constipation but denied weight loss, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, hematochezia, or melena. Physical examination was unremarkable.

Surveillance colonoscopy identified a 10-mm pedunculated lesion in the sigmoid colon, suspicious for a previous polyp stalk. The lesion was lifted with epinephrine (1:10 000) and removed with a hot snare. A 3-mm sessile cecal polyp was also removed and later identified as a tubular adenoma. There was no diverticular disease, and there were no peri- or post-procedural complications.

On histologic examination, the sigmoid lesion was a villiform polyp lined by normal-appearing colonic mucosa. The underlying submucosa contained increased blood vessels and inconspicuous lymphatic channels (detected with D2-40 immunostaining), with no significant inflammation in the lamina propria. No hemosiderin was seen on hematoxylin and eosin stain, and CD31/CD34 immunostains confirmed dual vascularity within the submucosa.

A 70-year-old man with a 40–pack-year smoking history presented with a 3-year history of chest discomfort, cough, and white sputum production, worsening over the past 2 months. He denied dyspnea, fever, chills, or chest pain. On high-resolution CT, there was a 34 × 24 mm ground-glass opacity in the left upper lobe (tumor A) and a 19 × 13 mm irregular solid nodule in the right lower lobe (tumor B), along with scattered small nodular and calcified lesions in both lungs. PET-CT showed hypermetabolism in the left upper lobe lesion, mild hypermetabolism in bilateral hilar lymph nodes, and patchy changes in the right lower lobe. Four months apart, he underwent left upper lobectomy with mediastinal lymph-node dissection and right lower-lobe wedge resection. Pathology of both nodules showed moderately differentiated invasive adenocarcinoma without vascular invasion, perineural invasion, or lymph-node metastasis. Histologically, tumor A was a mixture of acinar and papillary subtypes, and tumor B showed acinar and lepidic patterns. Molecular analysis by ARMS-PCR revealed that tumor A harbored MET exon 14 skipping and a PIK3CA (p.E545K) mutation, while tumor B contained a KRAS exon 2 (p.G12S/D) mutation.

A 54-year-old woman with a history of light chain multiple myeloma treated three years earlier with VAD chemotherapy and autologous stem cell transplant followed by thalidomide maintenance presented with progressive neutropenia over three years. On routine blood work, peripheral smear demonstrated 33% blasts and nucleated red blood cells. She was admitted for further evaluation. Bone marrow aspirate showed 15% blasts, of which many had numerous azurophilic cytoplasmic granules.

A 15-year-old Chinese girl presented with 4 months of chest tightness and exercise-induced shortness of breath. She reported occasional left shoulder and back pain and a mild cough but denied fever, night sweats, or weight loss. She could climb only two or three flights of stairs before resting. On examination, her temperature was 36.5 °C, pulse 95 beats/min, and blood pressure 105/60 mmHg. There was no cyanosis or dyspnea at rest. The left hemithorax appeared full, with flat percussion notes and absent breath sounds; the cardiac apex was displaced to the right midclavicular line. Neurologic examination was normal.

Laboratory tests showed WBC 5.15 × 10^9/L, platelets 118 × 10^9/L, RBC 5.15 × 10^12/L, hemoglobin 144 g/L; liver and kidney function were normal. Serum tumor markers were within normal limits: AFP 0.46 ng/mL, hCG < 1 mIU/mL, ferritin 152 ng/mL, NSE 12.4 ng/mL; 24-hour urinary VMA was 7.82 mg.

Chest ultrasound revealed a large irregular echogenic mass occupying the left thoracic cavity with star-like blood flow on Doppler imaging. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 324 mm × 193 mm × 176 mm mixed-density mass in the left hemithorax, partly of fat density. The solid components showed minimal delayed enhancement; prominent feeding vessels were seen in the arterial phase. The mass caused near-complete collapse of the left lung, rightward shift of the mediastinum, and compression of the right lung. Enlarged vessels from the left eighth intercostal artery and branches of the celiac trunk entered the mass. Airway reconstruction demonstrated compression of the trachea and left main bronchus, with absence of its distal segment; the left hemidiaphragm was depressed. Radiologically, a malignant mesenchymal tumor could not be excluded.

A 69-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a mass on her left frontoparietal skull that had enlarged over 2–3 months and caused radiating pain down the left side of her face. She reported no history of trauma. Her past medical history included arthritis, depression, and hypertension; surgical history was notable only for tonsillectomy and partial hysterectomy. She had a 60–pack-year smoking history. 

The lesion was nonmobile, tender to palpation, and measured approximately 3.3 cm in diameter. Primary care management had presumed a subcutaneous or sebaceous cyst and treated her with a 10-day course of levofloxacin without relief. 

Noncontrast CT of the maxillofacial region and brain, along with plain skull films, revealed a lytic lesion in the left frontoparietal skull. The patient was referred to oncology. On initial workup, the oncologist considered metastatic neoplasm versus multiple myeloma. A contrast CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed a spiculated right hilar lung nodule measuring 2.4 × 2.4 cm and no other sites of metastatic disease. Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation studies were negative. 

Neurosurgical evaluation demonstrated intact cranial nerves, normal motor strength, and preserved sensation in all extremities. MRI of the brain revealed a 2.8-cm lesion extending through the outer and inner tables of the left frontal bone with slight dural encroachment and minimal mass effect.

A 1.7-year-old girl was brought to the hospital with a two-week history of worsening respiratory distress and high fever. She was initially evaluated at an outside facility, where a chest X-ray and noncontrast CT scan revealed a pleural effusion. A chest tube was placed, but no fluid was drained and her condition did not improve. On transfer, she was afebrile, in no apparent distress, with normal oxygen saturation. She had no cyanosis, rib retractions, or jugular venous distention. Auscultation revealed absent breath sounds on the left and heart sounds displaced to the right; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, white blood cell count 12,000/mm3, and platelets 623,000/mm3. Tumor markers—including carcinoembryonic antigen, CA 125, CA 19-9, alpha-fetoprotein, and beta-human chorionic gonadotropin—were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a large mass in the anterior mediastinum extending into the left hemithorax, compressing the entire left lung and shifting the mediastinum to the right.

A 5-year-old boy presented with a 4-year history of progressive right-sided nasal obstruction, recurrent sinusitis, and noisy breathing. His growth and development were normal. Examination showed a smooth, purple, non-tender mass attached to the roof of the right nasal cavity; there was no cervical lymphadenopathy. Non–contrast CT of the sinonasal cavity revealed a 2.5×3.6×4.3 cm, well-defined, homogeneous soft-tissue mass in the right nasal cavity extending through the ethmoid sinus to the cribriform plate and anterior cranial fossa, with erosion of the cribriform plate. The lesion measured 33–36 HU precontrast and enhanced to 64–69 HU postcontrast. MRI demonstrated a well-demarcated mass in the right nasal cavity with low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, mixed high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, and striking inhomogeneous contrast enhancement. There was no calcification, cystic component, or dural enhancement. The mass compressed the middle and inferior turbinates medially and deviated the nasal septum to the left but did not invade adjacent structures.

A 75-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a painless, pedunculated mass on the left side of his tongue. The lesion had grown rapidly over four months. He denied recent weight loss or trauma. He had used one smokeless tobacco pouch daily for 45 years and had a history of coronary artery disease and bronchial asthma.

On examination, there was an approximately 4 cm hard, partially ulcerated, pedunculated mass on the left lateral tongue. There was no regional lymphadenopathy, and the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

An incisional biopsy was performed. Histopathological analysis reported that the lesion was either a spindle cell carcinoma with an unusual appearance or an inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor.

A 23-year-old G0P0 woman was referred at 31 weeks 4 days’ gestation for evaluation of a fetal abdominal mass. Serial prenatal ultrasound examinations showed a heterogeneous echogenic mass in the left hypochondriac region at the upper pole of the left kidney, measuring 45 × 50 × 42 mm at 31+4 weeks, 48 × 58 × 50 mm at 34+3 weeks, and 80 × 74 × 66 mm at 39+0 weeks. The mass contained calcified structures with shapes suggestive of a skull, spine, and femur, which became more apparent as the fetus grew. Color Doppler imaging demonstrated a branch arising from the fetal abdominal aorta with an umbilical arterial waveform supplying the mass.

A 34-year-old woman was admitted for worsening confusion. Two years earlier, she had developed weight gain, irregular menses, elevated blood pressure, and easy bruising. Laboratory evaluation showed ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome, with serum cortisol failing to suppress after a 1-mg dexamethasone test and undetectable ACTH; 24-hour urine-free cortisol and midnight salivary cortisol levels were elevated. Dehydroepiandrosterone-sulfate, plasma aldosterone, renin activity, and plasma metanephrine levels were all within normal limits. A CT scan of the abdomen revealed a 7-cm left adrenal mass with precontrast Hounsfield units of –8 to 31. The patient underwent an uncomplicated laparoscopic left adrenalectomy. Pathology showed a 7.4 × 7.2 × 5.0 cm well-circumscribed, homogeneous, yellow-tan adrenal mass without cystic change, hemorrhage, or calcifications; final pathology was reported as benign adrenal adenoma.

Hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone replacement were initiated and later tapered. Approximately 10 months postoperatively, she developed weight gain and new-onset type 2 diabetes. Two weeks later, she was hospitalized for depression, worsening confusion, and inability to perform activities of daily living. After withholding hydrocortisone, her 8 am serum cortisol was 29.9 µg/dL, and cortisol failed to suppress on both 1-mg and 8-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression tests; 24-hour urine-free cortisol and midnight salivary cortisol levels remained elevated. Abdominal MRI revealed multiple hepatic masses, with no residual lesion in the adrenalectomy bed and an unremarkable right adrenal gland.

A 29-year-old previously healthy woman presented with a 3-month history of treatment-refractory headaches. She was alert, fully oriented, and had no focal neurologic deficits; motor and sensory examinations were normal. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI showed a 41×18 mm extra-axial mass in the left cerebellopontine angle extending into Meckel’s cave and the middle cranial fossa. Three-dimensional CISS sequences demonstrated compression of the left middle cerebellar peduncle, pons, and fourth ventricle without hydrocephalus. On T1- and T2-weighted images the lesion had heterogeneous intensities; postgadolinium T1-weighted images showed heterogeneous solid and cystic enhancement with internal calcification and hemorrhage. Diffusion-weighted imaging revealed areas of restricted diffusion; the mean ADC of the solid component was 0.594×10⁻³ mm²/s and the minimum ADC was 0.460×10⁻³ mm²/s. Complete blood count and serum chemistry results were within normal limits. Chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasound showed no abnormalities.

An 89-year-old Japanese man presented with a three-month history of swelling in his left thigh and a slight fever. Over the preceding three days, the swelling had rapidly enlarged and become painful. He also reported weight loss over the past month but denied night sweats, skin lesions, or inguinal lymphadenopathy. On examination, there was a well-demarcated, elastic, soft mass measuring 7×6 cm in the medial aspect of the left thigh.  
MRI showed two intramuscular soft-tissue tumors between the vastus medialis and adductor muscles with extensive peritumoral inflammatory edema. The distal lesion (4.0×4.0×3.5 cm) was homogeneously low signal on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously low and high signal on T2-weighted images; the proximal lesion (2.0×2.0×1.5 cm), located 9 cm proximal to the distal mass, had similar signal characteristics.  
Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 10.9×10^9 cells/L (neutrophils 80%; lymphocytes 18%; monocytes 6%), an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 100 mm/h (normal <20), and a C-reactive protein level of 10.0 mg/dL (normal <0.3); other biochemical parameters, including lactate dehydrogenase, were normal.  
Because the clinical and radiological findings were suggestive of an abscess, he received antibiotics for two weeks, but his symptoms did not improve.

A 21-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of fatigue, high-grade fevers, and a generalized skin rash. Prior outpatient evaluation revealed pancytopenia without circulating atypical cells, and empirical antibiotics and topical steroids yielded no improvement. On admission, vital signs were notable for persistent fever. Laboratory studies showed:  
• WBC 0.49×10^9/L, RBC 2.98×10^12/L, hemoglobin 87 g/L, hematocrit 25.8%, MCV 86.6 fL, platelets 13×10^9/L  
• Calcium 2.09 mmol/L, urea 3 mmol/L, creatinine 106 μmol/L  
• D-dimer 14.91 mg/L, fibrinogen 3.91 g/L  
• PT 17.9 sec (INR 1.4), PTT 39.5 sec (ratio 1.2)  
Peripheral-blood smear confirmed marked pancytopenia and showed occasional blasts and rare abnormal promyelocytes. Given the finding of abnormal promyelocytes in the context of coagulopathy, all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) was initiated pending urgent fluorescence in situ hybridization for PML-RARA translocation.

A man in his early 30s with a 15-year history of Wilson’s disease treated with chelation therapy presented with an inability to walk and to flex the right knee, along with progressive deformity. On examination, multiple firm to hard swellings were palpable around the right knee joint. Radiographs of the right knee demonstrated multiple radio-opacities, a valgus deformity, and osteoarthritic changes predominantly in the lateral compartment. Ultrasound revealed joint effusion with a few loose bodies. MRI of the right knee showed extensive effusion with multiple loose bodies in the suprapatellar bursa, posterior recess, and Hoffa’s fat pad, suggestive of synovial chondromatosis, along with Kellgren–Lawrence grade III osteoarthritis of the tibiofemoral joint. A standing scanogram revealed a hip–knee–ankle angle of 196° on the right and 188° on the left.

A 38-year-old woman presented for an annual examination with a 3-year history of painless swelling of the left labia majora that began after her last cesarean delivery. She is G2P2 with a surgical history significant for two cesarean deliveries, tubal ligation, appendectomy, and benign breast tumor excision. She has no personal or family history of gynecologic cancer or sexually transmitted infections. She noted numbness over the swollen area and progressive dyspareunia but denied discharge, pruritus, pain on palpation, or urinary symptoms. 

On gynecologic examination, the left labia majora was enlarged, containing an elongated, soft, nonmobile, nontender, sausage-like mass measuring approximately 12 × 6 × 4 cm extending from the mons pubis to the anal verge along the left labial fold. There were no overlying skin changes or drainage. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Abdominal and pelvic CT with oral and intravenous contrast demonstrated left labial edema without ascites or inguinal or pelvic lymphadenopathy. The lesion was confined to the vulva and did not extend beyond the pelvic diaphragm; however, a vulvar mass could not be excluded. The differential diagnosis included a labial neoplasm, cyst of the canal of Nuck, and a hernia.

A 27-year-old primigravida at 38 weeks’ gestation underwent antenatal ultrasonography that demonstrated a multicystic lesion in the left side of the fetal chest with mediastinal shift. The stomach was visualized below the diaphragm, but the lesion was thought to represent a loop of small bowel. A repeat scan suggested the spleen intermittently in the left thorax, and the possibility of a congenital diaphragmatic hernia was raised. The infant was delivered at term by forceps-assisted delivery and was intubated briefly. A postnatal chest radiograph was reported as normal. After extubation, the neonate showed intermittent respiratory distress. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a multiloculated, cystic anterior mediastinal mass. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest demonstrated a predominantly cystic mass in the anterior mediastinum with solid components in its left lateral aspect and more fluid attenuation inferiorly; these findings were interpreted as most consistent with a mediastinal teratoma or congenital cystic adenomatoid malformation.

A 33-year-old woman noted a few millimeters of mass on her left labium majus two years ago, which was presumed to be folliculitis and observed. Over two years the lesion enlarged to 4 × 3 × 3 cm. She had no pain, pruritus, or systemic symptoms. On examination, the mass was mobile, deeply seated in the subcutaneous tissue of the labium majus; the overlying skin was normal and not adherent. There was no inguinal lymphadenopathy and no other lesions. The patient underwent wide local excision under general anesthesia without complication.

Grossly, the specimen measured 3.5 × 3.0 × 2.2 cm with poorly defined borders and white fibrotic areas extending into surrounding adipose tissue. Microscopically, the tumor was composed of sheets and nests of round to polygonal cells separated by thick collagenous bands; the cells had distinct borders, coarse eosinophilic cytoplasmic granules, and small dense nuclei extending into adjacent fat and reaching the surgical margin. 

Periodic Acid–Schiff staining demonstrated PAS-positive large cytoplasmic granules. Immunohistochemical staining showed diffuse positivity for S-100 protein and vimentin, and no staining for smooth-muscle actin or CD34.

A 33-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with a 3-month history of progressively worsening occipital headache, exacerbated by Valsalva maneuvers. On neurologic examination, he had bilateral past-pointing and an intention tremor. Brain MRI revealed a 6.9 × 5.5 × 6.1 cm lobulated mass centered at the left cerebellopontine angle, extending craniocaudally from the left ambient cistern to the premedullary space. The lesion involved and expanded Meckel’s cave, with a small extension into the left infratemporal fossa via the foramen ovale. It contained multiloculated T1-hypointense, T2-FLAIR–partially suppressible nonenhancing cystic areas with interspersed enhancing septa, as well as T1/T2-isointense enhancing solid components. Susceptibility-weighted imaging demonstrated curvilinear signal loss with corresponding T1 hyperintensity consistent with hemorrhagic foci, and diffusion-weighted imaging showed no diffusion restriction. There was compression of the left cerebellum and brainstem, dilation of the third, fourth, and lateral ventricles, anterior displacement of the cavernous sinus, and encasement with mild narrowing of the left petrous internal carotid artery; the masticator muscles were preserved. Noncontrast CT of the head showed smooth remodeling and erosion of the left petrous apex, clivus, carotid canal, and foramen ovale, along with two punctate calcifications; the internal auditory canals and inner ear structures were unremarkable.

A previously well 9-year-old girl presented with an 8-day history of fever, lethargy, and pallor and, over the last 2 days, had experienced syncopal episodes amid coryza and sore throat. She had a background of recurrent tonsillitis and a COVID-19 infection during the prior month but had briefly recovered before becoming unwell again. In the ED she was febrile and moderately dehydrated; other vital signs were normal. Examination revealed marked pallor and mildly enlarged non-exudative tonsils without lymphadenopathy, rash, or bleeding. She was admitted for investigation, and three venepuncture attempts were made because the first two samples were rejected for suspected dilution. The third sample showed: hemoglobin 43 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 78 fL, mean corpuscular hemoglobin 28 pg, platelets 2 × 10^9/L, white-cell count 1.3 × 10^9/L with undetectable neutrophils. Liver-function tests were mildly deranged, albumin was 25 g/L, and C-reactive protein was 262 mg/L.

A 50-year-old woman with a history of hypertension presented with a 6-month history of headache, tinnitus, and vertigo that was empirically treated as otitis media without relief. Ten days before referral, she developed gait imbalance and recurrent vomiting. On examination, she was alert and oriented (GCS 15), with intact cranial nerves. Neurologic findings included positive cerebellar signs, a positive Romberg sign, an ataxic gait, and inability to perform tandem gait. Brain CT and MRI demonstrated a left cerebellar mass of unknown origin.

A 40-year-old man, a nonsmoker and nonalcohol user, presented with a painless, slowly enlarging mass on the soft palate for 4 years. He denied dysphagia, odynophagia, voice changes, weight loss, fever, or sleep apnea. On examination, there was a firm, nontender, nonpulsatile, round, pinkish mass arising from the midline and right side of the soft palate without ulceration or mucosal erosion. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy. A lateral soft-tissue radiograph of the nasopharynx showed a well-defined oropharyngeal mass abutting the posterior pharyngeal wall with significant airway compromise. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a 5.4 × 4.4 × 4.2 cm, well-defined, heterogeneous, mildly enhancing soft-tissue mass in the soft palate, closely abutting but not invading adjacent structures, with maintained fat planes; there was no calcification, cystic component, fat, or lymphadenopathy. Based on imaging, a benign palatal mass was suspected, and an incisional biopsy was performed.

A 9-year-old boy had a 2½-year history of progressive, asymptomatic, monomorphic 2–3 mm tan-brown papules on the trunk and extremities, along with indurated chalky white nodules over the knees and right thumb. He was otherwise healthy.

On examination, numerous uniform tan-brown papules were noted over the trunk, and firm chalky white subcutaneous nodules were palpable over the knee.

An initial 4-mm punch biopsy of a chest papule showed focal calcification with surrounding inflammation in the dermis. A biopsy of a knee nodule demonstrated calcinosis cutis with possible perforation through the epidermis.

Laboratory studies revealed normal serum calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone (PTH), and creatine kinase (CK) levels, and a myopathy antibody panel for dermatomyositis was negative.

A 56-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a painless tongue lesion present for three months. She had no significant medical history, normal lipid levels, did not consume alcohol, and had a 30-year history of smoking 6–19 cigarettes per day. She was taking no medications.

On examination, there was an asymptomatic, pink-white, well-demarcated, sessile lesion with a granular surface and slightly raised margins measuring 1.0 × 0.5 × 0.3 cm on the left lateral border of the tongue extending to its ventral surface. The lesion was soft on palpation. Adjacent to this, and bilaterally on the buccal mucosa, were white striae in a reticular pattern consistent with oral lichen planus. No cervical lymphadenopathy was noted, and extraoral examination revealed no skin or genital lesions.

Given the concern for malignancy arising within oral lichen planus of the reticular/hypertrophic type, an incisional biopsy including both the granular lesion and the adjacent white plaque was performed under local anesthesia.

A 17-year-old female presented with a 3-year history of a slowly enlarging lesion on the posterior tongue, associated only with a persistent foreign-body sensation and no pain, bleeding, dysphagia, voice change, or respiratory symptoms. Her past medical and surgical history was unremarkable, with no family history of malignancy and no tobacco use. On examination, a single, well-defined, smooth-surfaced, white mass approximately 1 × 1 cm was visible on the posterior third of the dorsal tongue with protrusion. The lesion was hard and non-tender on palpation, and there was no cervical lymphadenopathy. A neck ultrasound was normal, and the serum thyroid-stimulating hormone level was within the reference range.

A 42-year-old Taiwanese woman was referred for hepatic tumors found incidentally during a routine check‐up. She denied abdominal pain, weight loss, or anorexia. Her medical history was negative for liver disease, and she took no regular medications. She smoked 2–5 cigarettes daily for ten years, denied alcohol use, and had no family history of malignancy. On examination, she was afebrile, with no jaundice or lymphadenopathy; the abdomen was soft and non-tender without ascites. Laboratory tests showed WBC 9950/µL, hemoglobin 15.0 g/dL, AST 37 U/L, ALT 82 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, albumin 3.5 g/dL, alkaline phosphatase 167 U/L, LDH 180 U/L; HBsAg and anti-HCV were negative; AFP, CEA, CA19-9, and CA125 were within normal limits. Tri‐phasic contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed multiple heterogeneous masses in both lobes of the liver, the largest measuring 8.3 cm in segment 4, with uneven arterial enhancement and washout in the portal venous and delayed phases. An ultrasound‐guided liver biopsy showed epithelioid tumor cells with moderate nuclear atypia and focal intracytoplasmic melanin pigments in solid nests infiltrating the parenchyma. Immunohistochemical staining revealed diffuse positivity for HMB45, Melan-A, SOX10, and BRAF V600E, with negativity for cytokeratin.

A 66-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of nonproductive cough, intermittent dyspnea, and a gradually enlarging lump in the lower right chest. He also reported intermittent chest pain for 2 months and an 8-kg weight loss over 4 months. He denied fevers or hemoptysis. Vital signs were normal. Examination showed decreased movement and tactile fremitus on the right chest, diminished right vesicular breath sounds, and a firm, fixed 10×10 cm mass over the right lower chest wall without overlying skin changes.

An initial chest radiograph showed a cavitating lesion with an air-fluid level in the right lower lung zone and minimal left lower-zone fibrosis, unchanged from a prior film. Four months later, repeat chest radiography demonstrated persistence of the cavitating lesion with air-fluid level, new right pleural effusion, and a left parahilar nodule. Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed a 9.5×8.3×10 cm cavitating lesion with solid and cystic components (air-fluid level) in the anterobasal segment of the right lower lobe, a 1.2×1.2 cm nodule in the left lingula, loculated right pleural effusion, and a 3.4×3.1 cm right peribronchial lymph node enlargement.

A 36-year-old woman awoke with decreased vision in both eyes. Over the preceding 3 days, she had experienced intermittent visual field changes, nausea, and vomiting. On neurologic examination, she had right House–Brackmann grade II facial dysfunction, right ptosis, right horizontal nystagmus, and bilateral dysmetria. She denied gait difficulties, tinnitus, hearing loss, diplopia, or poor coordination. She had no history of anticoagulant or antiplatelet use and no stigmata of neurofibromatosis.

Noncontrast and contrast-enhanced CT of the head showed a 3.8 × 5.1 × 3.2 cm hypodense cystic lesion in the left cerebellar hemisphere with a 0.7 × 1.0 × 0.9 cm mural nodule demonstrating avid homogeneous enhancement. There was mass effect with partial effacement and rightward displacement of the fourth ventricle, resulting in dilatation of the third and lateral ventricles consistent with hydrocephalus.

Subsequent MRI of the brain with and without contrast revealed a 3.4 × 3.7 × 4.0 cm extra-axial mass in the right cerebellopontine angle extending into the internal auditory canal, with acute intratumoral hemorrhage. The lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously mildly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed diffuse heterogeneous enhancement. Susceptibility-weighted imaging demonstrated punctate foci of artifact consistent with hemorrhage and areas of signal loss on phase images indicating microcalcifications. There was significant mass effect on the brainstem and fourth ventricle, with obstructive hydrocephalus and downward tonsillar displacement.

A 73-year-old man with a history of abdominal aortic aneurysm repair and former smoking presented initially with two weeks of rectal bleeding. Abdominal CT showed sigmoid diverticulosis and pericolic hypervascularity; hemoglobin fell from 13.5 to 12.5 g/dL. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and sigmoidoscopy were unrevealing, and he was discharged with a presumed diverticular bleed. One month later, he was readmitted with fatigue, cough, hemoptysis, and dyspnea. He was pale, had bilateral pedal edema, and hemoglobin was 7.0 g/dL. Chest radiography showed bilateral infiltrates interpreted as pulmonary edema, and echocardiography revealed an ejection fraction of 45%. Repeat abdominal CT showed no bleeding source. Contrast CT of the chest excluded pulmonary embolism but demonstrated bilateral airspace disease with large pleural effusions. Thoracenteses yielded hemorrhagic fluid, prompting bilateral chest-tube placement. Bronchoscopy revealed diffuse alveolar hemorrhage. He was treated empirically for pulmonary vasculitis with intravenous steroids and plasma exchange without improvement. Serologic tests for anti–GBM antibody, p-ANCA, and c-ANCA were negative; bacterial, fungal, and viral studies (including HIV) were negative; coagulation studies were normal; and repeated pleural-fluid cytology was negative. CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis did not reveal any lesions amenable to biopsy. Despite multiple transfusions and several weeks of hospitalization, the patient continued to decline.

A 77-year-old woman with type II diabetes, sick sinus syndrome, diastolic heart failure, and dementia presented with 4 weeks of progressively worsening bilateral lower-extremity weakness, orthostatic hypotension, rigors, and night sweats. On admission she was hemodynamically stable, afebrile, alert, and oriented. Examination revealed anasarca to the umbilicus and lower-extremity weakness: hip flexion against gravity 2/5, leg abduction and adduction 4/5; cranial nerves II–XII intact. 

Laboratory studies showed: leukocytosis (11.6 K/mm3) with neutrophil predominance, hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL (previously 12 g/dL), normal platelets, sodium 125 mmol/L, chloride 85 mmol/L, lactate 3.8 mmol/L; TSH normal, T3 41 ng/dL, T4 3.4 μg/dL; random cortisol 31.5 μg/dL; ferritin 619 ng/mL; triglycerides 204 mg/dL; CRP 226 mg/L; LDH 1,016 U/L. 

CT of head, chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed anasarca of the lower abdomen and upper thighs without masses or lymphadenopathy. MRI of the thoracic and lumbar spine with gadolinium showed no canal stenosis, cord compression, or abnormal enhancement. 

Hyponatremia was treated with fluid restriction, diuretics, and salt tablets, with normalization of sodium but no improvement in weakness. Thyroid and cortisol abnormalities were deemed insufficient to explain the weakness. Empiric corticosteroids were initiated for presumed inflammatory myopathy; creatine phosphokinase was normal. A bone marrow biopsy showed no granuloma, atypia, or malignancy. A muscle biopsy was then performed.

An 18-year-old woman presented with a five-year history of right forearm and shoulder pain. The pain began in the forearm as intermittent, nocturnal, progressive discomfort and, months later, involved the shoulder, becoming constant, burning in nature, and aggravated by movement. Pain was relieved by NSAIDs and associated with excessive sweating in the right arm during attacks; severity was 7 of 10. She had been previously diagnosed with regional pain syndrome and had undergone medical treatment and physiotherapy without improvement. Family history was unremarkable. Earlier plain radiographs of the shoulder and cervical spine were normal.

On examination, the right shoulder had a painful range of motion, particularly with abduction, flexion, and extension. There was no swelling, point tenderness, or skin changes.

Plain radiograph of the right shoulder showed an ill-defined lucency at the inferior glenoid with an intact articular surface and no periosteal reaction. Non-contrast CT of the right shoulder revealed a well-defined lytic lesion measuring 1.4 × 1.2 cm in the posterior inferior glenoid, with peripheral sclerosis and cortical thickening forming a central nidus, without periosteal reaction or soft-tissue component. MRI of the shoulder showed a 1.2 × 1.3 × 1.1 cm lesion in the infero-posterior glenoid that was low signal on T1, high signal on T2, and showed avid postcontrast enhancement except for a small anterior nonenhancing portion; mild adjacent bone marrow edema was noted, with no cortical destruction or soft-tissue extension.

A G2P1 woman in her thirties at 18 weeks of gestation presented with progressive dyspnea. Her medications included prenatal vitamins, folic acid, and an occasional bronchodilator inhaler.  
Vital signs were: temperature 36.3 °C, pulse 110 bpm, respiratory rate 22 /min, blood pressure 90/59 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. On cardiac examination, heart sounds were distant with pulsus paradoxus; there was no murmur or pericardial rub. The remainder of her physical examination was unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin concentration of 89 g/L and a platelet count of 223 × 10^9/L; both antinuclear antibodies and anti–double-strand DNA antibodies were negative. Coagulation parameters and thyroid-stimulating hormone were within normal limits. An electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus tachycardia.  
Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a large pericardial effusion with signs of impending tamponade. The patient underwent pericardiocentesis, with removal of 800 mL of blood-stained fluid. Cytopathologic and microbiologic examinations of the fluid showed only red blood cells without evidence of infection, autoimmune disease, or malignancy. Follow-up echocardiograms at two and eight weeks showed resolution of the effusion, and the patient did not return for further follow-up.  

At 38 weeks of gestation, she presented with acute chest pain. Vital signs were: temperature 37.6 °C, pulse 100 bpm, respiratory rate 19 /min, blood pressure 113/85 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Auscultation revealed a few crackles; the abdomen was distended consistent with pregnancy; the skin and lymph nodes were normal. Laboratory tests revealed a hemoglobin concentration of 110 g/L, a platelet count of 324 × 10^9/L, and a troponin level of 0.8 ng/mL. The electrocardiogram showed diffuse ST-segment depression with T-wave inversion.  
A repeat transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated a fragile, echo-dense, mobile structure within a dilated right atrium. Subsequent transesophageal echocardiography confirmed a large right atrial mass.

A 45-year-old man presented with a 1‐month history of a progressively enlarging, hard lesion at the site of a right maxillary molar extraction, associated with oozing and pain on swallowing. Two weeks before presentation, he developed severe pain in the upper right jaw, cheek, and retro-orbital region, accompanied by right cheek swelling and fever. He had no history of tumors or allergies.  
On examination, his general condition was good but notable for right cheek swelling, difficulty breathing, and bleeding from the right nostril. Otoscopic examination showed right tympanic membrane retraction. Nasal examination revealed bilateral inferior turbinate enlargement and a deviated septum to the left. Intraorally, there was a soft, tender 3 × 3 cm mass opposite the first and second upper right molars, extending onto the hard palate. Nasal endoscopy demonstrated a brown, friable, bleeding lesion filling the right middle meatus and extending through the widened maxillary ostium into the nasal cavity and choanae. Trigeminal examination revealed numbness in the V2 distribution. Laboratory studies were within normal limits.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses showed a large mass completely filling the right maxillary sinus, eroding its lateral wall, protruding into the oral cavity, extending posteriorly through the lateral sinus wall into the infratemporal fossa, and causing bone loss at the orbital floor.

A 20-day-old male infant was admitted for evaluation of a growing abdominal mass. The mass had been first noted on his mother’s ultrasound at 39 weeks’ gestation. Postnatal abdominal ultrasound showed a large liver mass initially thought to be a hepatic hemangioma, and routine follow-up was recommended. At 20 days of age, repeat ultrasound demonstrated significant growth of the liver lesion, and the serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) level exceeded 1000 ng/mL. On admission, the infant’s vital signs were stable. Abdominal ultrasound revealed an 8.7 × 6.4 × 8.0 cm mass in the liver involving the first hepatic hilum, with the portal vein and hepatic artery traversing the lesion. Enhanced abdominal CT showed a 7.8 × 7.0 × 8.1 cm hepatic mass occupying the first and second hepatic portals. Chest CT showed no pulmonary lesions. The infant’s AFP was 205,902 ng/mL.

A 50-year-old man was found to have mild elevations in liver enzymes on routine laboratory tests during an annual visit. He underwent an abdominal ultrasound that demonstrated hepatic steatosis and an incidental 6 cm left upper-quadrant mass.  
His medical history included well-controlled hypertension on lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide, obesity (BMI 39), and a 30–pack-year smoking history. He had no prior surgeries. Family history was notable only for uterine cancer in his mother.  
An MRI of the abdomen with contrast revealed a 6.8 cm, well-circumscribed but heterogeneously enhancing mass in the left adrenal gland, raising concern for pheochromocytoma or adrenocortical carcinoma. He then underwent FDG-PET/CT, which showed intense FDG uptake in the adrenal lesion without other areas of abnormal uptake.  
Biochemical evaluation demonstrated normal levels of cortisol, potassium, aldosterone, plasma renin activity, dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate, metanephrine, and normetanephrine, indicating a nonfunctional adrenal tumor.

A 70-year-old woman (BMI 23 kg/m2) was referred with an unclear right-sided retroperitoneal tumor. She reported exercise-related dyspnea, retrosternal pain, and dysphagia. Cardiologic evaluation (ECG, ambulatory blood pressure, echocardiography) and gastroenterologic workup were normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 15×12×14 cm subhepatic retroperitoneal mass with displacing growth but no invasion of adjacent organs or metastases; the inferior vena cava and left renal vein were stretched. The patient’s performance status was WHO 0. Her history included a hemithyroidectomy in 2013 for thyroid follicular carcinoma; echinococcus serology was negative. Medications were limited to thyroid hormone replacement; family history was noncontributory. On further imaging, the mass lay between the aorta and IVC, could not be clearly separated from the right adrenal gland, and appeared predominantly cystic with arterial hyperenhancing septa and solid components. The leading differential diagnoses were sarcoma, retroperitoneal paraganglioma, mucinous cystadenoma/cystadenocarcinoma, and cystic teratoma. The patient was scheduled for surgical resection.

A 37-year-old woman underwent a routine physical examination, including a chest radiograph, which revealed a slightly widened superior mediastinum with a possible mass. She was asymptomatic, had no prior illnesses, was a life‐long non‐smoker, and had no known exposures. Physical examination findings and routine blood tests were normal.

A noncontrast chest CT scan showed a right posterior mediastinal mass with a smooth margin, adjacent to the trachea. On contrast‐enhanced CT, the mass demonstrated slow, progressive enhancement along the course of the azygos venous arch. MRI of the chest revealed mixed signal intensity within the lesion and a partially low‐void area on T2‐weighted images.

A 58-year-old man presented with an 11-day history of right upper abdominal pain, unrelated to food intake or position, without nausea, vomiting, fever, or weight loss. His medical history included right inguinal hernia repair three years earlier; he had no history of hepatitis or relevant family history. On examination his abdomen was flat and soft without tenderness, rebound, or palpable masses; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory tests showed elevated cholesterol (5.3 mmol/L) and LDL (3.78 mmol/L); routine blood counts, liver and renal function, prothrombin time, quantitative hepatitis B tests, alpha-fetoprotein, CEA, and CA19-9 were normal.

Imaging:
• Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 99 × 92 mm right hepatic cystic–solid hypodense mass with multiple septa that enhanced mildly, displacing the right hepatic vein and supplied by the right hepatic artery.  
• Contrast-enhanced MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging revealed a 101 × 98 mm mass in the right liver that was low signal on T1, high on T2, with uneven septa and fluid–fluid levels; solid components and septa enhanced, while cystic areas did not.  
• Ultrasound showed a 123 × 98 mm mixed-echo mass with clear borders; anechoic areas predominated, with uneven septa and punctate flow on Doppler.  
• Contrast-enhanced ultrasound demonstrated hyperenhancement of the peripheral parenchyma and internal septa in the arterial phase, and isoenhancement in the portal and delayed phases; the anechoic areas remained unenhanced.

Based on these findings, the lesion was preliminarily identified as a hepatic cystadenoma.

A 29-year-old woman presented with acute epigastric pain radiating to the back over several hours. She was afebrile, with normal vital signs. Laboratory evaluation showed a serum lipase level of 2,164 U/L and normal liver enzymes. Abdominal ultrasound revealed no gallstones. 
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis on initial presentation demonstrated a 2.8-cm fluid-attenuating lesion in the body–tail region of the pancreas without pancreatic-duct dilatation. On hospital day 2, MRI showed a 2.6 × 2.8-cm simple-appearing cyst with a thin enhancing wall in the pancreatic body–tail and mild distal duct prominence, findings described as suggestive of a pseudocyst or cystic neoplasm. 
She had no history of prior abdominal complaints, reported only one to two beers the night before presentation, and had normal IgG4, serum triglycerides, and CA19-9 levels. No cholelithiasis was identified on any imaging modality. The leading diagnostic considerations were a cystic neoplasm provoking pancreatitis versus an acute pancreatic fluid collection progressing to a pseudocyst. 
Five weeks after the index episode, endoscopic ultrasound revealed a 21 × 17-mm anechoic cyst in the pancreatic tail with a large hypoechoic mural nodule and apparent communication with the main pancreatic duct; no ductal dilatation was seen, and no mucin extruded from the ampulla. Fine-needle aspiration yielded serous, yellow-tinged fluid with amylase >30,000 U/L, CEA 32 U ng/mL, and cytology showing proteinaceous material without intracellular or thick extracellular mucin.

A 44-year-old woman presented with three months of progressive right-sided facial swelling, difficulty opening her jaw, and retro-orbital pressure. Initial treatment for presumed sinusitis failed. Her symptoms then expanded to include severe right temporal headache, retroauricular pain radiating into the neck, and right V2 distribution paresthesia. She had no history of radiation exposure or tobacco use; family history included distant relatives with various malignancies but no neurologic diseases. On examination, she had a firm right temporal mass, mild right proptosis, and hypoesthesia in the V2 distribution, with otherwise intact cranial nerves and neurologic function. CT of the head showed a 6-cm right temporal lobe mass with destruction of the greater wing of the sphenoid bone and extension into the infratemporal fossa. MRI demonstrated further growth over one week, increased mass effect, midline shift, vasogenic edema, and extension through the skull base into the orbit, maxillary sinus, and masticator muscles. A CT-guided biopsy of the temporal extracranial component was performed.

A 64-year-old woman presented with worsening fatigue, low-grade fever, and mild upper abdominal discomfort for three months and reported a 5-kg weight loss over six months. During hospitalization, she experienced afternoon fevers with diaphoresis. On examination, there was a palpable mass in the left upper quadrant. Laboratory tests showed a severe hypochromic microcytic anemia (HCT 18.2%, HGB 5.4 g/dL, MCV 53.4 fL), thrombocytosis (platelets 705 × 10^3/µL), a normal white blood cell count, a C-reactive protein of 170 mg/dL, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 120 mm/h. Abdominal ultrasound suggested a mass adjacent to the spleen. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 13.5 × 7.7 × 8.5 cm mass with heterogeneous enhancement and well-defined margins; it was separate from the spleen, adherent to the stomach, and compressing the pancreas. Based on these findings, the radiologist’s initial differential diagnosis was a gastrointestinal stromal cell tumor (GIST) or sarcoma.

A 60-year-old man was referred for evaluation of pain in his right mandible. He was in good general health, a 10-pack-year smoker, with no significant systemic disease. On intraoral examination, oral hygiene was fair. Multiple teeth were missing, and there was a firm, nonfluctuant swelling with crepitus in the region corresponding to tooth sites 4.4–4.7 and the edentulous area of sites 4.5–4.6.  

A panoramic radiograph demonstrated:  
• Three well-defined, round, unilocular radiopaque lesions each surrounded by a thin radiolucent rim—two in the right posterior mandible adjacent to edentulous sites 3.6 and 4.6, and one in intimate contact with the roots of tooth 4.7.  
• A separate rounded radiolucent lesion with a sclerotic border at the apex of tooth 4.4.  

Thermal pulp testing of teeth 4.4 and 4.7 was nonresponsive. To further characterize the posterior mandibular lesions, a CT scan of the mandible was obtained, confirming three well-circumscribed, round, unilocular radiopaque masses with thin radiolucent margins; one mass was in close contact with the roots of the lower right second molar.

A 50-year-old man presented with a six-month history of a painful nodule on the dorsum of his penis that had gradually increased in pain intensity and interfered with sexual activity. He denied any erectile dysfunction or penile deviation. His medical history was unremarkable. On examination, there was a 5 mm tender, firm nodule at the midshaft of the penis dorsally and no inguinal lymphadenopathy. A penile ultrasound scan showed a well-circumscribed, 6 × 8 mm lesion within the subcutaneous tissue over the dorsal aspect of the penis, superficial to the corpus cavernosum, with inherent blood flow within the lesion.

A 57-year-old woman presented with fever and painful vulvar lesions of 1 week’s duration that had not improved after 6 days of oral doxycycline (200 mg daily). She also reported mild migratory polyarthralgia for 1 month but denied other systemic symptoms. Her past medical history was notable only for dyslipidemia managed with atorvastatin.

On examination, she was febrile (38.0 °C) but hemodynamically stable. Multiple ulcerative lesions with violaceous borders and a friable vegetating center were noted on the labia majora and inner thighs, against a background of indurated vulvar edema. Lesions measured 0.5–3 cm, some with infiltrated borders and superficial skin detachment. Multiple millimetric shallow oral ulcers on an erythematous base were present on the hard palate and gingivae.

Laboratory studies showed C-reactive protein 36.50 mg/dL (normal < 0.50), procalcitonin 1.10 ng/mL (normal < 0.50), D-dimer 71 148 ng/mL (normal < 500), leukocytosis 40.8 × 10^9/L (normal 3.9–10.2), mild normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 11.0 g/dL), and moderate thrombocytopenia (67 × 10^9/L). Serologic tests for syphilis, hepatitis B and C viruses, and HIV were negative; PCR tests in urine for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis and PCR for cytomegalovirus from the base of a vulvar ulcer were negative. Repeated peripheral blood cultures were negative.

She was admitted for further evaluation. The initial working diagnoses were pemphigus vulgaris and Behçet disease, coexisting with presumed herpetic oral infection and a possible leukemoid reaction to infection. Empiric treatment included intravenous meropenem, clindamycin, oral acyclovir, and oral methylprednisolone (32 mg daily). The oral lesions completely resolved in 1 week, but the vulvar ulcers persisted. Repeat peripheral immunophenotyping showed a relative increase in granulocytes, predominantly neutrophils, with no increase in blasts, suggesting a reactive process.

A 44-year-old man with schizophrenia presented with a one-year history of gradually progressive right proptosis, accompanied by right orbital pain for two months. He was uncooperative with detailed examination. On inspection, there was severe right proptosis, marked eyelid swelling, conjunctival congestion, total corneal opacity, and a frozen globe with poor light perception. Palpation revealed a firm orbital mass palpable above the upper eyelid. 

Noncontrast CT of the orbits showed a 41 × 39 × 37 mm extraconal mass in the superotemporal quadrant of the right orbit with erosion of the orbital roof. The mass displaced the superior rectus muscle and the lacrimal gland, causing marked anterior globe displacement. There was no intracranial extension, and the paranasal sinuses were well aerated and clear. 

Based on imaging, the radiologic differential diagnosis included an epidermoid cyst and adenoid cystic carcinoma.

A 44-year-old woman with no significant past medical or family history presented with a 4-week history of progressive abdominal distension. She denied constitutional symptoms and reported only occasional palpitations without pre-syncope, syncope, or dyspnea. On admission, vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed non-tender abdominal distension; there were no additional heart sounds or signs of volume overload. Initial laboratory studies showed an elevated CA-125 level of 70.4 U/mL (reference ≤ 34.9 U/mL); other tumor markers were within normal limits. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated a heterogeneous mixed solid and cystic mass arising from the fundal endometrium, with a large cystic component extending into the epigastric region, and a filling defect extending from the right ovarian vein into the inferior vena cava (IVC), right atrium (RA), and right ventricle (RV). Transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a mobile 3.0 × 3.2 cm mass extending from the IVC into the RA, with a serpentine projection across the tricuspid valve into the RV. 

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with contrast and velocity flow mapping confirmed a 3.8 × 1.5 cm mobile mass in the RA projecting into the RV. The mass was isointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and homogeneous on delayed gadolinium enhancement.

A 46-year-old Japanese man was transferred for evaluation of persistent fever of 8 weeks’ duration. He had hypertension and a 20 pack-year smoking history but no family history of malignancy. He reported anorexia but denied any gastrointestinal symptoms, weight loss, or night sweats. Five weeks before transfer, he had developed sudden paralysis and numbness of both legs. MRI of the spine at that time showed an epidural mass at the T11 level, and he underwent laminectomy (T10–T12) for presumed abscess and osteomyelitis; surgical cultures were negative, and no tissue was sent for pathology. Broad-spectrum antibiotics were restarted without clinical improvement, and he was transferred.

On admission, his performance status was 4; he had fecal and urinary incontinence. Vital signs: T 38.2°C, BP 119/62 mmHg, HR 109 bpm, RR 30/min, SpO2 90% on room air. Examination revealed paraplegia and numbness below L1 without spinal tenderness. Laboratory studies showed normocytic anemia and markedly elevated AST, ALT, ALP, LDH, CRP, and ferritin. PSA was normal, and serum protein electrophoresis showed no paraproteinemia.

Contrast CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated diffuse osteolytic lesions throughout the spine and pelvis and a left adrenal adenoma; there was no colonic wall thickening. MRI of the spine revealed high-intensity lesions from C2 to L5 on STIR and diffusion-weighted imaging, with low intensity on T1-weighted images.

Based on the osteolytic lesions, initial differential diagnoses included hematological malignancies (lymphoma, leukemia, multiple myeloma), metastatic carcinoma, Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, primary hyperparathyroidism, and primary amyloidosis. “Based on the laboratory and imaging findings, multiple myeloma, primary amyloidosis, leukemia, and hyperparathyroidism were unlikely,” and “tuberculosis also seemed to be less likely.” Therefore, intravascular lymphoma and metastatic carcinoma were considered the leading diagnostic possibilities.

A 36-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of progressive pain and swelling of the right wrist extending onto the dorsal hand, associated with difficulty in wrist motion. He denied trauma, fever, or systemic symptoms, and the swelling did not respond to analgesics. On examination, there was tenderness over the wrist and carpometacarpal joints, a restricted range of motion of the wrist, and multiple lobulated swellings on the dorsal aspect of the wrist without overlying erythema.

A plain radiograph of the wrist showed a destructive, ill-defined lytic lesion of the distal radius and additional lytic lesions at the bases of the second and third metacarpals. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 2.5 × 2.4 cm osteolytic lesion of the distal radius with subarticular extension and an extraosseous soft-tissue component breaching the volar cortex; multiple lytic lesions of the trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, and bases of the second and third metacarpals with marrow edema; and an enhancing 2.9 × 2.1 cm soft-tissue mass abutting the carpal bones. Whole-body PET-CT revealed increased FDG uptake (SUVmax 5.0) in the distal radius lesion with soft-tissue extension and involvement of multiple carpal bones.

A 58-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with 7 days of fever, fatigue, cough, and progressive dyspnea. On arrival, his oxygen saturation was 70% on room air, and he was intubated the same day. Chest radiography showed bilateral diffuse pulmonary infiltrates with interstitial thickening and basal consolidation. A nasopharyngeal swab was positive for SARS-CoV-2. Initial laboratory studies revealed pancytopenia (WBC 2.6 × 10^3/µL, ANC 1.8 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, platelets 85 × 10^3/µL), acute kidney injury (creatinine 120 µmol/L), transaminitis (ALT 170 U/L, AST 330 U/L), and elevated LDH (857 U/L). He received hydroxychloroquine, azithromycin, tocilizumab, methylprednisone, and intravenous immunoglobulin. His course was complicated by septic shock requiring vasopressors, broad-spectrum antimicrobials, and dialysis. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a normal‐sized spleen without focal lesions. Despite granulocyte colony‐stimulating factor support, by hospital day 16 his pancytopenia had worsened (WBC 0.5 × 10^3/µL, ANC 0.3 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL, platelets 74 × 10^3/µL).

A 12-year-old boy with type II diabetes mellitus presented with an 8-month history of a gradually enlarging mass on the left lateral nasal wall. He reported a history of nasal trauma approximately one year earlier. He had no nasal obstruction, epistaxis, sinus infections, olfactory changes, or snoring. There was no family history of childhood cancers. On examination, a 1.5 × 1.5 cm firm, nontender, immobile subcutaneous mass was noted over the frontal process of the maxilla without overlying skin discoloration. Limited MRI of the face was nondiagnostic due to artifact but suggested a possible nasal dermoid. Subsequent CT imaging showed a hyperdense, nonlipomatous soft-tissue mass of the left lateral nasal wall. An excisional biopsy was performed; there was no apparent intranasal extension.

A 6-year-old boy presented with 6 weeks of insidious pain, mild swelling, and stiffness of the right index finger that was partially responsive to ibuprofen and ice. He denied preceding trauma or systemic symptoms. On examination, there was mild edema and erythema over the middle phalanx without bruising, angulation, or nail-bed changes; the digit was tender to palpation and had slightly limited end-range flexion. Plain radiographs showed a rounded lucent lesion with sclerotic margins in the middle phalanx abutting the cortex. MRI with and without contrast revealed an eccentric intramedullary lesion along the radial aspect of the proximal metadiaphysis of the middle phalanx that was hyperintense on T2-weighted images and demonstrated solid enhancement on postcontrast sequences. The MRI also showed an extraosseous soft-tissue component crossing the cortex into the intraosseous portion. The patient’s complete blood count and inflammatory markers were normal, and blood cultures showed no growth.

A 46-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of a painless, progressively enlarging swelling of the left external upper lip. He denied trauma and had no relevant medical, dental, or family history. Vital signs were normal. On inspection and palpation, there was a 1.5 × 1.0-cm firm, rubbery, well-circumscribed nodule on the cutaneous aspect of the left upper lip near the philtral column, fixed to the skin without a central punctum. The lesion did not extend into the oral mucosa and lay superficial to the orbicularis oris muscle. Oral motor function was intact, there was no facial asymmetry, and no regional lymphadenopathy. The clinical impression was of a localized sebaceous cyst, and an excisional biopsy under local anesthesia was planned.

A 6-year-old boy with no prior medical history presented with a 6-month history of gradually increasing abdominal swelling; there was no hematuria or fever. On examination, a large, firm, non-tender mass, approximately 10×10 cm, was palpable in the left hypochondrium and flank without overlying skin changes or lymphadenopathy. Initial laboratory studies were normal.  

Abdominal ultrasound showed a well-circumscribed, roughly oval mass arising from the left kidney, with both cystic (anechoic) and heterogeneous tissue components; the thicker portion demonstrated color Doppler flow. The mass abutted the inferior vena cava, which remained patent. A second round, well-defined lesion with cystic and tissue components lay adjacent to the ipsilateral psoas muscle.  

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen confirmed a 10 cm left renal mass with a spur sign, involving the upper and medial pole, containing cystic areas and small hemorrhages, heterogeneously enhancing, displacing—but not invading—the renal vein and inferior vena cava. A similar-appearing 3 cm mass was noted in the left psoas muscle. A 10 mm para-aortic lymph node was present; no pulmonary or bony metastases were identified.  

Abdominal MRI demonstrated both the renal and psoas masses as well-defined, T2 hyperintense, T1 hypointense lesions with areas of T1 hyperintensity (hemorrhage), diffusion restriction, and heterogeneous gadolinium enhancement. Both lesions compressed adjacent structures without frank invasion.

A 27-year-old woman presented with a 17-year history of multiple low-trauma fractures, 12 years of progressive ocular proptosis with binocular visual decline, and 7 years of gradual facial rounding and weight gain. Three years ago she developed amenorrhea; imaging revealed bilateral adrenal nodules and she underwent bilateral adrenalectomy with pathology confirming primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease. 

On examination she was overweight with a full moon facies, thin skin with multiple purple striae over the abdomen, and numerous punctate blackish-brown macules on the lips and buccal mucosa. Family history was notable for similar facial asymmetry in multiple relatives. 

Laboratory evaluation demonstrated loss of diurnal cortisol rhythm, elevated 24-hour urine free cortisol, failure to suppress with both low- and high-dose dexamethasone tests, and a suppressed plasma ACTH level (<5 pg/mL; normal 5–50 pg/mL). 

Skull CT showed marked enlargement of the calvarial and maxillofacial bones with mixed sclerotic and lytic lesions. Brain MRI revealed diffuse bone lesions in the frontal, occipital, and sphenoid bones with heterogeneous T1 and T2 signal intensities, regions of high signal on fat-saturated T1 images, and marked post-gadolinium enhancement. Spine MRI demonstrated flattened vertebral bodies and multiple patchy bone lesions with low T1 signal, mixed T2 signal, high signal on fat-saturated T2 images, and enhancement after gadolinium.

A 72‐year‐old man with hypertension and a history of stage I left renal cell carcinoma was referred for evaluation of a right chest wall mass found incidentally on surveillance chest computed tomography. He had a 20 pack‐year smoking history and no known exposure to environmental fumes or dust. He was asymptomatic. Physical examination and routine laboratory studies were unremarkable. Pulmonary function tests and cardiovascular evaluation were normal. Chest CT revealed a mixed-density mass measuring 8.0 × 5.0 × 3.0 cm along the anterior right thoracic wall in the third through sixth intercostal spaces; a CT from one year earlier had shown a 7.8 × 4.8 × 1.2 cm area of fat in the same location that was not considered abnormal. MRI demonstrated a heterogeneous fatty mass with several high‐signal foci on T2‐weighted imaging and irregular marginal enhancement. FDG‐PET showed a maximum standardized uptake value of 3.78 in the lesion. Based on these radiologic findings, surgical resection was scheduled with suspicion of liposarcoma.

A 66-year-old man presented with unintentional 30-lb weight loss and fatigue. Initial laboratory evaluation showed hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, white blood cell count 3.81 × 10^3/µL, hematocrit 30%, mean corpuscular volume 92 fL, and platelet count 75 × 10^3/µL. A CT scan revealed marked splenomegaly and diffuse soft-tissue masses near the spleen and pancreatic tail. Review of prior records demonstrated persistent thrombocytopenia since 2020, progressive neutropenia (absolute neutrophil count 0.80 × 10^3/µL), and anemia (hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL), with IgM and IgG monoclonal gammopathies and an elevated β2 microglobulin of 11.9 mg/L. These abnormalities suggested a slowly progressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma. The patient’s condition deteriorated, prompting hospitalization for frequent falls, during which bone marrow and inguinal lymph node biopsies were obtained.

A 38-year-old man with a history of unprovoked deep vein thrombosis on rivaroxaban, alcohol use, and 22 pack-year tobacco use presented with right lower-extremity swelling and right groin pain radiating to the right testicle. He was hemodynamically stable and afebrile. Physical examination showed right lower-extremity edema and slight tenderness of the right testicle. 

Given concern for occult malignancy in the setting of recurrent unprovoked DVTs, a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was obtained, which showed diffuse gastric wall thickening, extensive retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, and nodularity with stranding along the peritoneal surfaces.
