Scrotal ultrasound demonstrated a 0.9 × 0.7 × 0.8-cm, well-marginated hypoechoic lesion in the upper pole of the right testicle. 

The patient underwent a right orchiectomy. Histopathological examination revealed infiltrating signet ring cell adenocarcinoma involving both the testicular parenchyma and spermatic cord with angiolymphatic invasion. Immunohistochemical studies were positive for cytokeratin (CK)-7, CK-20, CK AE1/AE3, and CDX2, and negative for Helicobacter pylori.

An 88-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of intensely pruritic erythematous plaques on the trunk and lower limbs that were unresponsive to topical and systemic corticosteroids. On examination, there was erythroderma involving approximately 90% of the body surface area, with ill-defined erythematous and edematous plaques on the back, abdomen, and thighs, and superimposed excoriations. Results of blood chemistry, liver enzymes, electrolytes, glucose, renal function tests, lactate dehydrogenase, and beta-2 microglobulin were within normal limits. Staging ultrasound and total-body computed tomography showed generalized superficial lymphadenopathy without visceral involvement.

After a 1-month treatment washout, a skin biopsy of a thigh plaque revealed psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia with compact hyperorthokeratosis, mild spongiosis, and occasional dyskeratosis. In the superficial dermis, there was a dense perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with eosinophils and plasma cells, exhibiting occasional lichenoid and vaguely nodular arrangements. The infiltrate consisted of small lymphocytes intermixed with atypical medium and large neoplastic cells constituting more than 25% of the infiltrate, with easily detectable mitotic figures and a Ki-67 index of approximately 30%. Focal epidermotropism with Pautrier microabscesses was present.

Immunohistochemical studies showed that the lymphoid cells were positive for CD4 and T-cell receptor βF1, with partial loss of CD7, intact CD3, CD2, and CD5 expression, and focal CD30 positivity. A subset of neoplastic cells coexpressed the TFH markers PD-1 and CXCL13, with focal positivity for BCL6 and CD10. Epstein–Barr virus–encoded RNA was negative. T-cell receptor gene rearrangement studies demonstrated a monoclonal T-cell population. Flow cytometry of peripheral blood revealed a CD4:CD8 ratio >10 and a population of clonal CD3+CD4+CD7±CD5+CD26– T cells comprising 40% of circulating lymphocytes.

A 5-year-old girl presented with a progressively enlarging abdominal mass over 7 months without pain, fever, hematuria, or vomiting. On examination, there was a large right-sided abdominal mass extending from the right lumbar region to the right iliac fossa and into the umbilical and hypogastric areas. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax and abdomen revealed a 16 × 13 × 13 cm minimally enhancing solid mass replacing the right kidney and subcentimetric peripheral nodules in the left lung, with no extension into the adrenal gland, renal vein, or inferior vena cava. A tru-cut biopsy suggested a mesenchymal variant of Wilms’ tumour versus cellular mesoblastic nephroma. A provisional diagnosis of stage IV Wilms’ tumour was made, and the patient received six cycles of AVD-regimen chemotherapy. Post-chemotherapy CT showed resolution of the lung nodules but no significant change in the renal mass. A right nephroureterectomy with lymph node sampling was planned.

A 16-year-old male with no prior medical history noted a small lump in his right hemiscrotum two months earlier during self-examination. He denied any history of scrotal trauma or inflammation, and the lump’s size remained unchanged over two months. He experienced only mild discomfort during exercise, which resolved with rest. On physical examination, there was a painless, round, hazelnut-sized mass localized to the tail of the right epididymis; the testicles and groin were otherwise unremarkable. Scrotal ultrasonography demonstrated a solid, well-demarcated, hyperechoic, hypoperfused 1.3 × 1.1 cm mass at the tail of the right epididymis containing two small hypoechoic foci, with no invasion of adjacent structures. Routine blood tests, coagulation profile, and serum tumor markers (AFP, LDH, CEA, and β-HCG) were all within normal limits.

A 36-year-old HIV-positive man presented with a painless, hard, “pea-size” lump in his left breast that he had noticed for many years, with a perceived increase in size over the past 6 months. There were no overlying skin changes, axillary lymphadenopathy, or family history of breast cancer. Diagnostic mammography demonstrated an oval, circumscribed mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast with smooth borders and multiple pleomorphic calcifications. Gray-scale ultrasound showed a 1.0 × 0.8 × 0.6 cm superficial, isoechoic, circumscribed, oval mass oriented parallel to the skin and chest wall, with internal vascularity and multiple hyperechoic foci correlating with the mammographic calcifications. Despite benign-appearing ultrasound features, the presence of pleomorphic calcifications and recent growth led to a BI-RADS 4B assessment.

A 36-year-old previously healthy man presented with a several-day history of blurred vision and acute onset of aggressive behavior and agitation. In the emergency department, his Glasgow Coma Scale fell to 8, requiring intubation. Noncontrast head CT revealed a large (52 × 37 mm), bifrontal extra-axial mass at the anterior skull base, involving ethmoid air cells, frontal sinuses, and the right orbit, with dural infiltration and extensive peritumoral edema causing significant mass effect. On transfer, he had fixed mid-dilated pupils, minimal flexion to pain, and intact corneal and gag reflexes. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. He received high-dose intravenous dexamethasone and mannitol and underwent emergent bifrontal decompressive craniectomy with tumor debulking and placement of an intracranial pressure monitor. Postoperatively, his intracranial pressure averaged <25 mmHg, but he remained at a Glasgow Coma Scale of 3 with absent brain-stem reflexes; persistent bilateral massive edema was seen on CT, and he died 1 week later.  
Histologic examination showed a tumor composed of small to medium cells, some with clear cytoplasm, no rhabdoid cells, areas of necrosis, and high mitotic and apoptotic activity. Immunohistochemical stains demonstrated loss of INI1 expression; diffuse strong positivity for epithelial membrane antigen and p63; partial positivity for smooth muscle actin, glial fibrillary acidic protein, B-cell lymphoma 2, and vimentin; focal positivity for pan-keratin and keratin 8; negativity for OLIG2, S100, desmin, synaptophysin, NEU-N, and chromogranin; and a Ki-67 proliferative index of 25–30%.

A 59-year-old Chinese Han woman presented with a 10-year history of constant left pulsatile tinnitus that had become unbearable and interfered with sleep. She had seen multiple otologists; each otoscopic exam was normal, and a temporal bone CT 9 years earlier was negative. She had been labeled as having a venous hum and received no effective treatment. Over the preceding 2 years she noted gradual hearing deterioration in the left ear. Her medical history was notable only for treated hypertension.

On examination, the pulsatile tinnitus was completely suppressed by digital pressure over the left internal jugular vein or by turning the head toward the affected side. Cranial, carotid, and chest auscultation were negative. Carotid ultrasonography, electrocardiography, thyroid function tests, and chest radiography were normal. Otoscopy revealed a vague, reddish mass behind the superior- posterior quadrant of an intact left tympanic membrane.

A pure-tone audiogram showed moderately severe conductive hearing loss in the left ear, most pronounced at low frequencies; tympanometry demonstrated a flat left tympanogram. High-resolution CT of the temporal bone revealed a slightly ill-defined soft tissue mass in the left middle ear involving the posterior mesotympanum, epitympanum, and mastoid antrum, with erosive changes of the facial fallopian canal and an indistinct margin between the lesion and the incus; the lateral semicircular canal was intact.

A 24-year-old woman with no significant medical or gynecological history presented with moderate, intermittent suprapubic cramp-like pelvic pain and dysuria. She denied abnormal uterine bleeding. Pelvic MRI revealed a well-demarcated vaginal mass measuring 10 × 8.3 × 5.6 cm, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, hypointense on T1, with areas of high signal on fat-saturated sequences, compressing the bladder; no pelvic lymphadenopathy was seen. On physical examination, she was afebrile and in good condition; the abdomen was soft, with no palpable mass; vulvar and perineal inspection was normal, and there was no inguinal adenopathy. Diagnostic hysteroscopy revealed a large exophytic mass on the anterior cervical lip filling the vagina. Directed biopsy showed moderate cellularity with patches of round cells having irregular hyperchromatic nuclei and mitotic figures, occasional large cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm suggestive of rhabdomyoblastic differentiation, and a loose, edematous, highly vascular stroma.

A 24-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a 6-month history of swelling in the left floor of her mouth. She reported slight difficulty swallowing but denied pain or tongue paralysis. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. 

On intraoral examination, there was a well-defined 3.5 × 3 × 2 cm solid, spherical submucosal nodule adjacent to the sublingual gland. The overlying mucosa was smooth and light bluish in color. The patient experienced slight tenderness on palpation. Tongue mobility and sensation were normal, and there was no palpable lymphadenopathy in the submandibular region. 

All laboratory test results were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the head and neck revealed a 2.8 × 1.8 × 2.1 cm well-defined, solid, heterogeneously enhancing nodule in the left floor of the mouth, without obvious infiltration into surrounding soft tissue or involvement of the lingual cortical bone of the mandible. Three-dimensional reconstruction demonstrated abundant blood flow within the lesion, which was located lateral to the hyoid bone and adjacent to the left sublingual fossa. No enlarged lymph nodes were identified.

The initial clinical impression was a benign salivary gland tumor, dermoid cyst, or benign connective tissue neoplasm.

A 70-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of disseminated, mildly pruritic papules that had progressively increased in number and distribution without regression. An earlier skin biopsy by an outside dermatologist demonstrated granulomas, and he was treated for presumed sarcoidosis with topical steroids and hydroxychloroquine without improvement. His medical history included lumbar spinal stenosis treated surgically and complicated by Pseudomonas osteomyelitis, for which he remains on lifelong ciprofloxacin, and remote bladder cancer treated with intravesical BCG. 

On examination, there were numerous, firm, nontender, erythematous papules 0.5–0.7 cm in diameter on the face, neck, trunk, and extremities. There was no palpable lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. A repeat punch biopsy of a chest lesion showed a diffuse, nodular, nonepidermotropic dermal infiltrate composed of crowded histiocytoid cells with a minor inflammatory component of lymphocytes, histiocytes, plasma cells, and rare eosinophils. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated that the lesional cells were positive for CD1a and S100 but negative for langerin (CD207).

A 25-year-old man with a history of Hodgkin lymphoma presented with a 2-month history of a gradually enlarging mass over the dorsum of his left hand. Six years earlier, he had been diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma on the basis of mediastinal lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms, and he received 13 courses of chemotherapy. Physical examination at this visit revealed a soft-tissue mass over the second metacarpal dorsum, approximately 4 cm in greatest dimension, with mild tenderness and no limitation of movement. The patient underwent surgical excision of the lesion, and two specimens were submitted to pathology. The larger specimen consisted of gray, gelatinous tissue measuring 4 × 2.5 × 0.8 cm and 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 cm. Microscopic examination showed a mixture of inflammatory cells, abundant myxoid stroma, epithelioid and spindle-shaped cells, lipoblast-like cells, and occasional Reed–Sternberg–like cells. Given the presence of Reed–Sternberg–like cells in an inflammatory background, the pathologist recommended immunohistochemical staining to distinguish among possible diagnoses.

A 48-year-old Caucasian man presented with one month of diarrhea, vomiting, and epigastric pain that worsened with coughing or leaning forward. He had sustained a blunt abdominal trauma at work one month earlier. On examination, there was a large palpable mass occupying the epigastric and right hypochondriac regions. Laboratory tests were nearly normal except for a mild elevation in gamma-glutamyl transferase. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed an 18 × 10 cm heterogeneous mass anterior to the pancreas, displacing the left liver lobe, and 5–6 intrahepatic lesions suggestive of hemangiomas. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 20 × 9 × 16 cm prepancreatic mass with predominantly peripheral heterogeneous enhancement and multiple hypodense hepatic nodules, two of which raised concern for possible metastases. Thoracic CT was normal. The case was reviewed by a multidisciplinary board, which suspected a giant pedunculated liver hemangioma and recommended liver MRI. MRI demonstrated multiple classic hemangiomas throughout the liver with typical contrast enhancement; the largest was a pedunculated lesion arising from segment 3, measuring 20 × 8 × 14 cm, displacing the pancreas posteriorly. There was no imaging evidence of rupture, torsion, or hemorrhage.

A 9-year-old girl presented with a 20-day history of progressively worsening headache associated with nausea and vomiting, a one-week history of right-sided weakness, and tonic–clonic seizures beginning 24 hours before admission. She had no prior medical history. On examination, she was alert but had motor aphasia, dysnomia, right hemiparesis, right hemihypoesthesia, and right-sided corticospinal signs. Complete blood count, serum biochemistry, and urinalysis were within normal limits.

Noncontrast CT of the head revealed a well-demarcated, multilobulated lesion in the left frontoparietal region measuring approximately 6 cm in greatest dimension, with both solid hyperdense and cystic components, mixed densities within the cysts, minimal peritumoral edema, and associated midline shift with collapse of the ipsilateral ventricle.

Brain MRI showed a 6.1 × 5.6 cm intra-axial frontoparietal mass that on T1-weighted images was heterogeneous but predominantly isointense to white matter; on T2-weighted images it was multicystic and hyperintense with a striking “bubbly” heterogeneous internal pattern; FLAIR sequences demonstrated minimal surrounding edema; postcontrast images revealed mixed solid and peripheral rim enhancement. MR spectroscopy demonstrated a high choline peak.

An 86-year-old woman with a history of depression presented with sudden-onset, non-radiating precordial pain of 9 hours' duration. She denied dyspnea, nausea, or back pain. Her medications included escitalopram as needed, and she had no family history of gallbladder cancer. On examination, her abdomen was soft, flat, and without scars. An electrocardiogram showed no ST-segment changes. Laboratory tests revealed a hemoglobin level of 6.4 g/dL, with normal cardiac enzymes, white blood cell count, and C-reactive protein. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest and abdomen demonstrated a tense gallbladder containing a heterogeneous, high-density area and increased pericholecystic attenuation on arterial-phase images; there was no evidence of pleurisy, aortic dissection, contrast extravasation, or obvious mass lesions.

A 34-year-old woman presented with a 1-day history of spontaneous nosebleeds, gum bleeding, and dark-red skin spots. Over the preceding 4 years she had intermittent gingival bleeding after tooth brushing and episodes of dark blue-red patches on her limbs. In the prior year she had heavy menstrual flow for five consecutive months requiring specialist care. There was no fever, weight loss, or night sweats. She was the sixth of seven siblings; no similar bleeding history in her sisters.

On examination, she had mild pallor, small cervical and axillary lymph nodes, multiple petechiae and ecchymoses on her forearms and lower limbs, and a slightly enlarged liver tip; the remainder of the examination was normal.

Laboratory studies showed a hematocrit of 27%, a white‐cell count of 4.7 × 10^9/L with relative lymphocytosis, and severe thrombocytopenia. The direct Coombs test was negative; HIV-1 and HIV-2 tests were nonreactive. Coagulation studies, chest radiograph, and abdominal ultrasound were normal. An ANA (LE) preparation was positive.

Bone marrow aspiration demonstrated increased megakaryocytes with budding, normal erythropoiesis and myelopoiesis, and reactive lymphoid cells, without dysplasia or blasts. Treatment with intravenous hydrocortisone followed by high‐dose oral prednisolone was initiated. Over two weeks, her platelet count rose to 95 × 10^9/L and bleeding resolved. She was discharged on tapering steroids.

Thirteen weeks later she reported a missed menstrual period. Off steroids, she had gum bleeding, a hematocrit of 29%, a white‐cell count of 4.8 × 10^9/L, and a platelet count of 65 × 10^9/L. Obstetric examination estimated gestational age at 15 weeks. Steroids were restarted, and her platelet count returned to 113 × 10^9/L.

A 75-year-old man presented with persistent erythema and red spots around the external urethral orifice of the glans penis. Five years earlier, he had undergone radical cystectomy and cutaneous ureterostomy for high-grade urothelial carcinoma in situ of the bladder; preoperative urethral margins were negative, and routine postoperative urethroscopy and upper-tract surveillance had shown no recurrence. Initial treatment with topical medications did not improve the lesion. On urethroscopy three months after presentation, red spots were noted on the urethral mucosa without discrete tumors. A skin biopsy of the glans showed heterotypic cells with clear cytoplasm proliferating in an intraepithelial, alveolar pattern. Immunostaining demonstrated cytokeratin 7 positivity and cytokeratin 20 positivity. Chest and abdominal computed tomography revealed no lymphadenopathy or distant metastases.

A 3-year-old boy was evaluated for dribbling of urine. He had a single episode of hematuria at age 2 but no abdominal pain, fever, weight loss, or appetite change. On examination, there was no palpable abdominal mass.  
Abdominal ultrasonography showed a partly exophytic, hypoechoic mass arising from the interpolar region of the left kidney, measuring 4.7×4.8×5.3 cm, with internal vascularity suggestive of Wilms tumor.  
Ultrasound-guided biopsy revealed sheets of spindle-shaped cells with oval to elongated nuclei, moderate cytoplasm, no atypia or mitoses, and occasional tubules lined by cuboidal cells. Immunohistochemistry on the biopsy specimen showed negativity for WT-1 and S-100.

A 67-year-old man presented with progressive abdominal distention over 3 years. He noted an abdominal mass on examination, received no treatment, and experienced worsening distention. His medical history included laparoscopic appendectomy and surgery for a retroperitoneal tumor 10 years earlier. He was a heavy smoker for over 40 years; he had no known allergies, took no regular medications, and had no significant family history.

On laboratory evaluation, the white-cell count was 9.4 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 8.35 × 10^9/L, lymphocytes 0.49 × 10^9/L, and hemoglobin 136 g/L. Carbohydrate antigen 19-9 was elevated at 594.5 U/mL and carcinoembryonic antigen at 361.9 U/mL; other tumor markers were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a well-circumscribed multilocular cystic mass measuring 35 × 24 × 13 cm, extending from the epigastrium into the pelvis and occupying most of the right abdominal and pelvic cavity. The mass was predominantly hypoattenuating, contained internal septations of isodensity, and demonstrated calcifications. There was extrinsic mass effect on adjacent organs.

MRI showed the lesion to be hypointense on T1-weighted images and markedly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with low-signal internal septations that enhanced intensely after contrast administration. The boundary between the lesion and the lumbar spine was distinct, with no evidence of bony invasion or destruction.

Based on a large retroperitoneal cystic mass with thin septa and calcifications in an elderly man, a preoperative diagnosis of retroperitoneal lymphangioma was considered; cystic mesothelioma or, less likely, a retroperitoneal myxoma were also included in the differential.

An 8-year-old, female intact Black Baldy cow was presented for evaluation of a white, proliferative mass on the left cornea that had been present for approximately 2 weeks. The cow was bright, alert, and responsive, with normal mentation, and on rectal palpation was confirmed to be 45 days pregnant.

Ophthalmic examination of both eyes revealed a positive menace response, dazzle reflex, palpebral reflex, and intact direct and consensual pupillary light reflexes. Schirmer tear test results were 28 mm/60 seconds in the right eye and 27 mm/45 seconds in the left eye. Intraocular pressure by rebound tonometry was 27 mmHg in the right eye and 20 mmHg in the left eye. The right eye had faint, focal, axial, anterior stromal fibrosis.

In the left eye, there was a raised, white, exophytic mass originating from the temporal limbus extending to the medial paraxial cornea, measuring approximately 20 mm long × 10 mm wide × 8–10 mm thick, with 1–2 mm of perilesional corneal edema. Based on the ophthalmic examination, a working clinical diagnosis of suspected limbal squamous cell carcinoma of the left eye was made. Differential diagnoses included papilloma, lymphoma, parasitic infestation, and inflammatory granuloma.

A 15-year-old girl presented with a 3-month history of intermittent abdominal pain, constipation, and spaniomenorrhea. She had menarche at 11 years with previously regular cycles. There was no family history of malignancy. On examination, vital signs were normal and abdominal and pelvic examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed:
– Serum testosterone: 66.5 pmol/L (normal 3.0–37.0 pmol/L)  
– Serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP): 117 ng/mL (normal <14 ng/mL)  
– β-hCG, CA 125, CA 19-9, and CEA: within normal limits  

Pelvic MRI (T2-weighted) demonstrated a 7.8 × 6.4 × 7 cm right adnexal solid mass without ascites; the left ovary and uterus appeared normal. 

Based on the imaging and laboratory findings, the leading preoperative considerations were a germ cell tumor (dysgerminoma or yolk sac tumor) versus a pure sex cord–stromal tumor such as a juvenile granulosa cell tumor. A laparoscopic right salpingo-oophorectomy was performed.

A 43-year-old woman presented with a 10-second syncopal episode without prodrome. Four months earlier, she had dyspnoea and epigastric discomfort. Imaging at that time showed a large pericardial effusion on contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and chest; pericardiocentesis yielded 600 mL of bloody fluid with negative biochemistry, microbiology, and cytology. Autoimmune, thyroid, and tumor-marker studies were negative. FDG-PET-CT demonstrated hypermetabolism only in the right cardiac region. A pigtail pericardial catheter was removed upon discharge without treatment of unknown aetiology.

On current admission, physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed microcytic anaemia; biochemical tests were normal. ECG showed sinus rhythm. Chest radiography revealed an enlarged cardiac silhouette. Transthoracic echocardiography again showed a large pericardial effusion, and pericardiocentesis was performed.

Cardiac MRI demonstrated a 3.8 cm × 5.8 cm × 6.8 cm lesion arising from the right atrium with a thickened pericardium. Repeat echocardiography at our institution showed minimal pericardial effusion without obvious mass. ECG-gated coronary CT angiography and non-ECG-gated chest CT revealed a cauliflower-like tumour mainly in the right atrium with inner thrombus formation, right atrial anterior wall aneurysm, obliteration of the fat plane at the right atrioventricular groove, and epicardial extension encasing the mid-right coronary artery.

Coronary angiography showed multiple feeding arteries originating from the right coronary artery to the tumour.

A 40-year-old man presented for evaluation of left anterior knee discomfort. He reported a small bump over the inferior pole of the patella that had recently increased in size, with extreme sensitivity to touch and pain when kneeling directly on it. He denied systemic symptoms, and there was no history of trauma.

On examination, a 1 cm × 1 cm subcutaneous, fluid-filled mass was palpated over the anterior aspect of the left knee. There were no signs of infection or warmth. The arc of motion was painless, weight bearing was tolerated without pain, and there was no mechanical instability. 

Plain radiographs of the left knee (AP, lateral, and sunrise views) showed preserved joint spaces, no fractures or loose bodies, and a subtle anterior subcutaneous soft-tissue mass without calcification. No further imaging was obtained.

Given the size, location, and sensitivity of the lesion, the patient elected to undergo surgical excision. An open excision under local anesthesia was performed, and the specimen was sent for histopathologic evaluation.

A 34-year-old woman with a history of acute myelomonocytic leukemia (AML-M4) underwent semicompatible allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in July 2019. In January 2020, she noted multiple painless, palpable masses in both breasts. On examination, one left-breast mass measured 3.0 × 1.2 cm and one right-breast mass measured 2.3 × 1.6 cm; there was no axillary lymphadenopathy. Initial breast ultrasound classified the lesions as BI-RADS-3. By March 2020, the masses had grown rapidly; repeat ultrasound showed multiple well-defined, hypoechoic, oval lesions scattered throughout both breasts, classified as BI-RADS-4a, with the largest measuring 3.1 × 1.6 cm on the left and 3.0 × 2.3 cm on the right. In April 2020, ultrasound measurements increased to 4.0 × 1.6 cm in the left breast and 4.4 × 1.2 cm in the right breast, and hypoechoic nodules appeared in both axillae. Breast MRI demonstrated that all lesions were hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed striking enhancement after gadolinium contrast.

A 20-year-old woman presented with right flank pain. An abdominal ultrasound incidentally revealed a contralateral adrenal mass. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a solid left adrenal lesion measuring 11 × 10 × 7 cm, with heterogeneous density (17–40 HU), calcifications, and progressive modest enhancement in the venous phase. She had no clinical stigmata of hormone excess; blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg, pulse 64 beats/min, BMI 20.7 kg/m2. Medical history included patent foramen ovale and focal nodular hyperplasia of the liver; she was an active smoker. Laboratory evaluation showed normal blood count, electrolytes, coagulation studies, and renal, liver, and thyroid function. Urinary metanephrines and normetanephrines were within normal limits; DHEA‐S was 1500 ng/ml (350–4300); aldosterone was 457.2 pg/ml (37–150), renin 1.5 ng/ml/h (1.0–2.4), and aldosterone-renin ratio 30.48. Basal cortisol and 17-OH-progesterone were normal both at baseline and after 250 mcg ACTH stimulation. The patient was on estrogen–progestin contraception at the time of hormonal testing. Given the size of the mass and indeterminate imaging features, she met criteria for surgical resection and underwent transabdominal left adrenalectomy, which required additional nephrectomy due to hilar involvement.

A 33-year-old Asian woman was referred for rapidly growing subcutaneous nodules in her right axilla over 4 weeks. She had no significant medical or family history. Initially, a small non-pustular nodule was excised by her physician without pathological examination. On presentation, she had a swollen, painful, red lump in the right axilla. Laboratory studies showed: white blood cells 6400 μL⁻¹, lymphocytes 2163 μL⁻¹, hemoglobin 11.3 g/dL, platelets 208 000 mm⁻³; serum lactate dehydrogenase 1148 IU/L (normal 105–333), C-reactive protein 1.5 mg/L (normal < 0.3). HIV and Epstein–Barr virus serologies were negative. 
Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a large, poorly marginated, homogeneous soft tissue mass in the cutaneous and subcutaneous compartments of the right axilla with slight enhancement, along with enlarged axillary lymph nodes. MRI showed a homogeneous mass slightly hyperintense to muscle on T₁-weighted images, intermediate signal on T₂-weighted images, and diffuse, homogeneous enhancement on fat-suppressed contrast-enhanced T₁-weighted images, with associated skin thickening and marginal septal enhancement. The subclavian vessels were not invaded. Based on these findings, the differential diagnoses included lymphoma, melanoma, breast cancer, fibrosarcoma, and malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour.

A 10-year-old Hispanic boy was referred for evaluation of 6 months of persistent tearing of the left eye. One month earlier, an ophthalmologist diagnosed left nasolacrimal duct obstruction. He denied vision changes, weight loss, fevers, chills, or other symptoms. Laboratory studies were within normal limits, without leukocytosis, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, or hypergammaglobulinemia. Noncontrast CT of the orbits revealed a soft-tissue mass involving the medial aspect of the left ethmoid and maxillary sinuses with adjacent osseous destruction of the medial orbital wall. Nasal endoscopy did not visualize a mass due to a narrow nasal cavity and enlarged middle turbinate. An initial orbital biopsy demonstrated lymphoid tissue with proliferation of histiocytes.

A 70-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a painful ulcer on the right lateral border of the tongue present for two years. He described dull, continuous pain, a burning sensation with spicy foods, difficulty chewing and swallowing, restricted tongue movements, weight loss, loss of appetite, decreased salivation, and hoarseness of voice. His habits included kharra (smokeless tobacco) chewing two to three times daily for two years and a 20–25–year history of bidi smoking (two to three per day), which he had quit 10 years earlier. 

On extraoral examination, bilateral tender submandibular lymph nodes measuring approximately 3 × 4 cm were palpable. Intraoral examination revealed a 2 × 3 cm ulceroproliferative lesion on the right lateral tongue border extending from the dorsal to ventral surfaces, from the lower right molar region to the retromolar trigone and involving the soft palate. The lesion had everted margins and was indurated on palpation. A provisional diagnosis of tongue malignancy was made.

Contrast-enhanced MRI of the tongue showed a 7.6 × 4.5 × 4.3 cm heterogeneously enhancing mass on the right side of the tongue with areas of necrosis, abutting the lingual septum medially and extending into the infratemporal fossa laterally. Multiple subcentimetric to centimetric heterogeneously enhancing lymph nodes were noted in the submental, bilateral submandibular, and jugulodigastric regions; the largest measured 4.3 × 3.2 cm in the right submandibular region with necrotic areas. The radiologic impression was tongue carcinoma with lymphadenopathy.

An incisional biopsy of the tongue lesion was performed.

A previously healthy six-month-old girl, born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy, presented with a persistent high fever. She was found to have pyuria and bacteriuria. There was no significant past medical or family history, and the physical examination was unremarkable, with no gross malformations.  

Laboratory studies confirmed urinary tract infection, and ultrasonography of the abdomen revealed multilocular cysts in the right kidney; her abdominal ultrasound at four months of age had been normal. Abdominal contrast-enhanced computed tomography demonstrated a multilocular cystic mass occupying the upper pole and midportion of the right kidney. The mass was characterized by septal wall thickening pressing on adjacent normal renal parenchyma. There was no direct infiltration into the renal pelvis and no hydronephrosis. Renal dysplasia was considered unlikely because of the preserved adjacent kidney tissue.

A 15.5-year-old neutered male domestic shorthair cat was evaluated for a 4-month history of progressive right pelvic limb lameness, with left pelvic limb involvement over the preceding 2 weeks. Treatment with meloxicam (0.05 mg/kg q24h) provided no appreciable improvement. On neurologic examination, the cat was ambulatory paraparesis with proprioceptive deficits in both pelvic limbs (right > left) and marked hyperesthesia on palpation over L6. Hematology and serum biochemistry results were within normal limits except for a hematocrit of 25.7% (reference range, 30.3–52.3%).

Orthogonal radiographs of the lumbar spine revealed a right-sided osteolytic lesion affecting the L6 vertebra. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the lumbosacral spine showed a 2.2 × 2.0 × 2.9 cm expansile mass in the dorsal lamina of L6, with bilateral (right > left) pedicle infiltration. The lesion exhibited central soft-tissue attenuation, a thin mineralized peripheral rim, mildly irregular but well-defined borders, and severe spinal canal stenosis. The soft tissue component demonstrated diffuse contrast enhancement. Differential diagnoses based on the CT findings included primary bone tumors such as fibrosarcoma, osteosarcoma, or chondrosarcoma. A fine-needle aspiration of the lesion was non-diagnostic. Surgical excision was planned.

A 40-year-old woman presented with 7 months of mild, nonprogressive fullness over her right cheek. She had no pain or other symptoms. General examination was unremarkable. Extraoral inspection showed an ill-defined 1×1-inch fullness over the right lower two-thirds of the face, with normal overlying skin. Intraorally, there was diffuse expansion of the right posterior maxillary region, from the distal of the upper right second premolar to the tuberosity (about 2.5 cm), causing partial obliteration of the buccal vestibule. The overlying mucosa appeared normal. Palatal expansion was minimal with slight blanching. The swelling was hard and nontender, except adjacent to the buccal aspect of the upper right second molar, where the bone felt “windowed.” The upper right second molar showed grade II mobility; all right upper molars were nonresponsive to pulp testing. Oral hygiene was good, and aspiration was negative. A benign neoplasm of the basal maxillary bone was suspected, with initial differential diagnoses of benign odontogenic, nonodontogenic, and maxillary antral tumors.  
Laboratory studies, including hematologic values, were normal. Rhinoscopy revealed a mass in the middle meatus nearly occluding the right nasal cavity. Intraoral periapical radiography showed a diffuse, hazy radiolucency from the right upper second premolar to the third molar with root resorption and multiple fine calcifications. Panoramic imaging confirmed haziness of the right maxillary sinus. A paranasal sinus view demonstrated nonuniform opacification of the right maxillary sinus with an intact orbital margin.  
CT imaging was then performed. The CT scan revealed an ill-defined expansile mass completely occluding the right maxillary sinus and extending inferiorly to the alveolus, measuring approximately 5.6×3.3×4.2 cm. There was destruction of the medial, anterior, and lateral walls of the sinus, as well as of the maxillary alveolus and turbinates. The middle and posterior ethmoidal air cells were occluded. The lesion contained cystic spaces, calcific specks, and areas of ground-glass appearance.

A 20-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of dyspeptic symptoms including early satiety, postprandial fullness, and heartburn. Two months before evaluation, she noted a nonpainful lump in her upper abdomen. She had no significant past medical or surgical history. On examination, she was mildly pale, and there was a firm, nontender, ill-defined 6 cm × 5 cm mass in the epigastrium with an uneven surface that moved with respiration; the remainder of the abdominal examination was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a well-defined, heterogeneously hypoechoic solid lesion measuring 6.1 cm × 5.8 cm with internal vascularity posterior to the body of the stomach, suggestive of a gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST). Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology showed sheets of neoplastic cells on a hemorrhagic background, also suggestive of GIST. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was normal except for a healed duodenal ulcer scar. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen demonstrated an intensely enhancing, heterogeneous, well-defined, rounded exophytic soft-tissue lesion measuring 7 cm × 6.2 cm × 8 cm arising from the greater curvature of the stomach and abutting the pancreas and superior mesenteric vein, possibly a GIST. On the basis of these findings, a preoperative diagnosis of gastric GIST was made.

A 49-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of sharp, constant epigastric pain rated 8/10, associated with early satiety and nausea, worsened by food intake. She also reported a 15-pound weight loss and intermittent blood-stained stools. She denied dysphagia, hematemesis, fever, or NSAID use. Her medical history included GERD and diabetes mellitus with retinopathy. 

On examination, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. The abdomen was soft and obese, with tenderness in the epigastrium but no guarding or rebound. Neurologic exam revealed decreased lower-extremity sensation and thoracic spine tenderness.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, platelet count 551 ×10^3/mm^3, alkaline phosphatase 111 U/L, albumin 3.2 g/dL, blood glucose 180 mg/dL, AFP 1252 ng/mL, CA 19-9 68 U/mL, CA 125 82 U/mL, and CEA 126 ng/mL; H. pylori stool antigen was negative.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated gastric wall thickening, multiple necrotic lymph nodes in the upper abdomen, and multiple hepatic lesions suggestive of metastases. A bone scan revealed lesions in T11 and L1. Upper endoscopy showed a large fungating, ulcerated mass involving nearly the entire lesser curvature of the stomach.

A 15-month-old boy, a dizygotic twin born via cesarean delivery, was referred for evaluation of an incomplete cleft palate and a residual tongue lesion. At 7 days of age, the patient underwent excision of a tongue dermoid cyst at another hospital. On examination, there was a bifid palate with a firm midline mass at its posterior margin measuring 2.5×1.5 cm, and a residual lesion on the anterior dorsal tongue measuring 2×1.5 cm.  
Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a midline defect of the hard and soft palate and a polypoidal mucosal mass with retention cysts protruding from the right nasal cavity through the palatal defect. Subsequent CT of the facial bones confirmed a cleft lip and palate and revealed a skull-base lesion centered at the clivus extending into the sphenoid sinus, as well as a separate midline nasal mass at the nasion extending to the skin without a sinus tract.  
Given the cleft palate and imaging findings, a combined endoscopic transnasal and transoral approach was planned for resection of the clival mass, with separate resection of the nasal lesion.

A 40-year-old Hispanic woman presented with a 3-month history of neck pain and a bulging lesion in the right retromastoid area. She had no significant medical history. On examination, there was a tender, swollen area over the right lateral occipital bone behind the mastoid process. The neurologic examination was normal without motor, sensory, or visual deficits. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed an extradural, contrast-enhancing lesion destroying both inner and outer tables of the right occipital bone and extending into the scalp and posterior fossa, measuring 42.5 × 33.5 × 39 mm on T1-weighted images with gadolinium. On T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences, the lesion was hypointense with multiple thin septa, fluid–fluid levels, and signs of hemorrhage.

A 36-year-old man was referred after an incidental finding on chest imaging. Five months earlier, his chest radiograph was unchanged; the current film showed a new 5-cm soft-tissue density within a longstanding right apical bulla. He had no respiratory or constitutional symptoms. 

CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated a 4.4 × 5.2 cm intracavitary solid-appearing mass along the wall of the apical bulla, with heterogeneous fluid layering and questionable enhancement; radiologic impression was “concerning for a primary bronchogenic malignancy versus adherent fungus ball with a superimposed infection.” 

Two months later, PET imaging revealed interval growth of the lesion to 3.3 × 6.8 × 5.9 cm, intense FDG avidity in the mass, and several smaller FDG-avid nodules along the inferior bulla; there was no evidence of distant metastasis. 

Past medical history was notable for Type 1 multiple endocrine neoplasia, Noonan syndrome, peptic ulcer disease, intermittent hypercalcemia, and childhood abdominal rhabdomyosarcoma with lung metastasis (both resected). He had undergone pancreatectomy, subtotal parathyroidectomy, and thymectomy. He smoked three-quarters of a pack per day for 20 years, used cannabis daily, and worked as a millwright. Family history included pancreatic and lung cancer. 

On examination, he appeared thin and older than his age; scars from prior thoracotomy and laparotomies were present; otherwise the exam was unremarkable. 

Because of the lesion’s location within a large bulla, percutaneous biopsy was deemed high risk. Our preoperative working diagnoses were metastatic recurrence, primary bronchogenic carcinoma, and infectious process. The patient was taken to the operating room for surgical resection.

A 53-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of progressive cough and chest pressure. She initially expectorated green sputum, which improved after antibiotics from her primary care physician. She received two courses of steroids during emergency-department visits, with transient stabilization. She denied smoking and had no known mold or pet exposures. She reported occasional postprandial bloating but no systemic symptoms. On examination, she was afebrile, with an oxygen saturation of 87% on room air. Auscultation revealed coarse breath sounds bilaterally and decreased breath sounds at the left posterior lung base. A chest CT showed bilateral linear coarse reticulations without peripheral predilection or ground-glass opacities, and a small left pleural effusion; there were no lung nodules, masses, or mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests, including antinuclear antibodies and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, were negative. Based on her symptoms and chest CT findings, we suspected a diagnosis of interstitial lung disease (ILD).

A 9-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a large swelling on the right side of his mandible noticed one month earlier after a fall. He was previously treated at another hospital with incision, drainage, and extraction of a decayed lower right first molar for presumed dentoalveolar abscess. He was otherwise healthy, and prior blood tests were normal. 

On examination, there was a diffuse, tender swelling over the right mandibular region. Intraorally, the extraction socket was healing well without signs of infection. There was bony expansion of the labial cortex extending from the lower right second molar region to the lower left canine region. Facial nerve and inferior alveolar nerve function were normal.

Panoramic radiography revealed two large cystic lesions: one in the right mandibular body and one at the mandibular symphysis, associated with unerupted lower left second molar and bilateral canines. CT imaging confirmed two cystic cavities connected by a canal-like tract through intact bone in the right canine region.

Two separate incisional biopsies—one from the posterior lesion and one from the symphyseal lesion—were performed. Multiple histologic sections of each specimen suggested a dentigerous cyst.

A 25-year-old previously healthy Asian woman was referred for evaluation of an enlarging, subcutaneous mass in her intergluteal fold. She first noticed the lesion 2 years earlier when it measured less than 0.5 cm; it had slowly grown to about 2.5 cm in diameter, and over the past few months it had become tender and occasionally made sitting uncomfortable. She denied urinary or fecal dysfunction.

On examination, there was a 2 × 3 cm, solid, mildly tender, mobile mass over the coccyx, well circumscribed proximally but less so distally. The neurological examination was normal.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the sacrococcygeal region showed a 6 × 3 cm, well‐circumscribed, lobulated subcutaneous mass overlying the coccyx, composed of two ovoid contiguous components, and with no direct invasion of the coccyx. On MRI, the lesion demonstrated low signal on T1‐weighted images and high signal on T2‐weighted images.

To evaluate for metastatic disease, CT scanning of the thorax and abdomen was performed and demonstrated no evidence of lung or liver metastases. An isotope bone scan showed no evidence of skeletal metastases.

A 51-year-old Chinese woman was referred after a routine health examination detected a hepatic mass. She was asymptomatic.  
History of present illness: An incidental, painless right hepatic–lobe mass was noted on imaging.  
Past medical history: Unremarkable.  
Physical examination: No abnormalities.  
Laboratory studies: Serum alpha-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels were normal.  
Ultrasound of the liver showed a 3.8 × 3.6 cm hypoechoic lesion with well-defined borders in the right anterior lobe; Doppler imaging revealed internal vascular flow.  
Contrast-enhanced CT scan demonstrated a 4.1 cm low-density, well-circumscribed mass in the anterior–superior segment of the right lobe, with heterogeneous enhancement and a central ring of enhancement; the right hepatic artery coursed through the lesion, the adjacent portal vein branch was abutted, and there was mild intrahepatic bile-duct dilation.

A 47-year-old woman presented with a two-month history of continuous pain in the neck and bilateral shoulders. She had no history of trauma, fever, weight loss, or appetite change. Her past medical history was notable only for a stable pulmonary nodule under observation. On examination, cervical range of motion was markedly reduced (forward flexion 20°, extension 20°, side bending 25°, rotation 30°) with paravertebral muscle spasm and tenderness; there were no neurologic deficits. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, tumor markers, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, were within normal limits.

Plain radiographs of the cervical spine showed collapse of the C6 vertebral body with mild malalignment, suggesting a pathologic fracture. Contrast-enhanced CT of the cervical spine demonstrated extensive bone erosion involving nearly the entire C6 body, destruction of the upper endplate and anterior and posterior walls, without adjacent disc involvement or significant intraosseous enhancement. MRI with contrast revealed diffuse T1 hypointensity, T2 hyperintensity, and contrast-enhanced infiltration of the C6 vertebral body; the C5–6 and C6–7 discs appeared normal. PET–CT showed focal hypermetabolism in C6 only (SUVmax 11.4).

Based on these findings, a neoplastic lesion with a pathologic fracture of C6 was suspected. Differential diagnoses included giant cell tumor, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, infection, and primary or metastatic bone tumor.

A 54-year-old woman presented with a painless, gross hematuria of three months’ duration. Her medical history was notable for a hysterectomy 24 years earlier for uterine cancer. She also reported urinary frequency, a sensation of residual urine, nocturia, and left leg edema.

On pelvic ultrasonography, there was a 3.8 × 4.3 cm solid mass in the urethra bulging against the bladder wall, with a clear bladder lumen. Computed tomographic urography demonstrated a 4 cm low-attenuation mass with a cystic component adjacent to the vaginal stump, and multiple enlarged paraaortic and pelvic lymph nodes up to 3 cm in diameter.

Voided urine cytology showed moderate cellularity with small clusters of globular or papillary cells in an inflammatory background. Necrotic debris and inflammatory cells were present within some clusters. Tumor cells were enlarged and had abundant clear or granular cytoplasm with cytoplasmic vacuoles; some clusters exhibited hobnail features. The nuclei were round with folded, irregular membranes, vesicular chromatin, and prominent nucleoli, with moderate pleomorphism. Small hyaline bodies were noted in cell clusters, and benign urothelial cells were rare.

A 29-year-old woman presented with one day of periumbilical pain that localized to the right iliac region. The pain was associated with two to three episodes of vomiting and anorexia; there was no fever, dysuria, melena, or hematuria. She had no significant past medical or surgical history. On examination, she had tenderness and rebound in the right iliac fossa. Laboratory tests showed a leukocyte count of 11,300/mm3 with 80% neutrophils and a serum amylase of 98 U/L. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed an enlarged appendix with a wall-to-wall diameter of 8 mm and minimal free fluid in the pelvis and right iliac region. During open appendectomy, the appendix was found to be inflamed, positioned in the pelvis, with approximately 50 mL of pelvic fluid and a 4 × 3 cm swelling at the tip of the appendix. The lesion was removed en bloc with the mesoappendix without lymphadenopathy.

A 34-year-old woman noted a palpable, painless, hard, movable mass (~2.6×3.5 cm) in the upper outer quadrant of her right breast, with no skin changes, nipple retraction, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Three years earlier, she had been diagnosed with AML (M2) on the basis of nasosinal lesions, treated with six cycles of cytosine arabinoside, and attained remission. 

Mammography revealed a 2.5×2.4 cm round mass with irregular, well-defined margins and prominent vessels in the upper outer quadrant, and a second 1.4×1.1 cm mass in the lower outer quadrant; several right axillary lymph nodes measured up to 1.9 cm. Ultrasound showed a lobulated, hypoechoic 3.7×2.6 cm mass with marked vascularity (resistive index 0.60) in the upper outer quadrant and a second 1.8×1.1 cm hypoechoic lesion below the nipple; a 1.8 cm hypoechoic axillary node was also seen. 

Complete blood count, chest radiograph, and abdominopelvic CT were normal. Fine-needle aspiration of both breast lesions revealed inflammatory cell infiltration, granular calcification, and several atypical epithelial cells, suggesting possible malignancy. Bone marrow aspirate showed no evidence of leukemia. A lumpectomy was performed under local anesthesia; frozen section examination revealed a poorly differentiated malignant tumor.

A 32-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 1-year history of progressive swelling of her right hallux. The mass gradually increased in size, causing discomfort when wearing shoes, but there was no history of trauma or systemic symptoms. She ambulated with a slight limp. On examination, there was a firm, slightly tender 2 cm swelling on the dorsal aspect of the hallux at the interphalangeal joint, fixed to both superficial and deep planes, without overlying erythema or skin changes. There was no bone pain, no sensory or motor deficits, and capillary refill was intact. 

Plain radiographs of the toe showed a well-defined osteolytic lesion adjacent to the interphalangeal joint without cortical breach. MRI demonstrated a tissue mass encasing the interphalangeal joint and invading adjacent soft tissues, including the extensor and flexor tendons of the hallux. 

A synovial and bone biopsy via a medial approach revealed whitish tissue and friable bone. Histopathology was inconclusive, showing features “doubtful between a pigmented villonodular synovitis and a giant cell tenosynovial tumor without histological signs of malignancy.”

A 40-year-old woman presented with a 4–5-year history of multiple daily episodes of dry retching and vomiting. Her medical history included hypertension treated with a β-blocker and an angiotensin-receptor blocker. She was a current smoker. Physical examination findings were unremarkable. A computed tomography scan of the abdomen was normal. An oesophago-gastro-duodenoscopy revealed two sessile polyps in the mid-oesophagus, the largest measuring 10 mm. Both lesions were endoscopically resected and sent for histopathologic analysis.

An 85-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of intermittent, sharp left upper quadrant abdominal pain that was unrelated to meals but worsened with movement. She also reported a decrease in appetite and an unintentional weight loss of 5 pounds. Her past medical history was unremarkable; recent upper and lower endoscopic evaluations were normal.

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness confined to the left upper quadrant without detectable organomegaly or palpable masses. No other abnormalities were noted.

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and serum electrolytes, were within normal limits. An abdominal CT scan demonstrated multiple discrete masses within the splenic parenchyma, findings interpreted as suspicious for malignant involvement.

A 33-year-old Chinese man was admitted in January 2019 with an 11-day history of cough with yellow sputum and 5 days of hemoptysis. Eleven days earlier he had developed cough, yellow sputum, and fever to 39.4°C, which resolved with cephalosporin therapy; 5 days before admission he began expectorating blood. He had no prior illnesses and no family history of tumors. On examination, temperature was 36.8°C, respiratory rate 15 breaths/min, heart rate 78 bpm, blood pressure 130/90 mmHg; lung auscultation was normal except for vesicular breath sounds. Laboratory studies showed WBC 6.04×10^9/L (66% neutrophils), hemoglobin 165 g/L, platelets 275×10^9/L, ESR 2 mm/h; urinalysis, stool studies, occult-blood test, electrolytes, blood chemistry, HIV antibody, CEA, NSE, cytokeratin 19 fragment, squamous cell carcinoma antigen, coagulation, and immune indices were all normal or negative. Chest CT revealed a 1.20 cm × 0.88 cm calcified nodular lesion on the compressed posterior wall of the lower left main bronchus and bronchiectasis in the left lower lobe. Bronchial glomus tumor and carcinoid carcinoma were considered. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy showed a yellow–white hard mass obstructing the entrance to the basal segment of the left lower lobe, with multiple nodular ridges and superficial hyperemia laterally; a biopsy was performed and the lesion was prone to bleeding.

A 59-year-old woman was evaluated for a chronic cough. Her only past medical history was gastroesophageal reflux disease. She denied haemoptysis, dyspnea, or weight loss. Pulmonary function tests showed a vital capacity of 4.5 L (130% of predicted), an FEV1 of 3.8 L (130% of predicted), and a diffusing capacity of 105% of predicted. A chest radiograph revealed a mass in the left thoracic wall, identical in size to radiographs obtained in 2005. Chest CT showed a 4.7 cm calcified tumour arising from the left second rib with slight impression of the adjacent lung and no other lesions in the lungs or chest wall.

A 39-year-old man with no known comorbidities presented with a right frontoparietal scalp mass of three years’ duration. The lesion began as a small nodule after head trauma at work, then enlarged rapidly, ulcerated, became painful, and bled intermittently. He smokes (26 pack-years) and drinks 18 units of alcohol per week; he has no prior surgeries. Examination revealed a 15 cm × 13 cm × 9 cm ulcerated, fixed mass of the right frontoparietal scalp, without cervical lymphadenopathy. A punch biopsy of the scalp lesion showed a low- to intermediate-grade spindle cell neoplasm. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated S-100 negativity and CD34 positivity. Staging CT scans of the head, neck, chest, and abdomen showed no bone destruction, intracranial extension, or distant metastases.

A 64-year-old Chinese woman presented with a 7-month history of productive cough, intermittent hemoptysis, dyspnea, and dizziness. She denied any history of skin cancer, and physical examination revealed no pigmented lesions on the skin, scalp, mucosa, anogenital region, or eyes.

Imaging:
– CT scan of the chest showed a large, space-occupying lesion in the lingual lobe of the left lung.  
– PET-CT demonstrated multiple well-demarcated nodules in the apicoposterior segment of the left upper lobe (largest 26 × 19 mm) with bronchovascular involvement and left hilar lymphadenopathy; no hypermetabolic lesions were identified elsewhere in the body.  
– Brain MRI revealed numerous enhancing nodules consistent with metastatic deposits.

To establish a tissue diagnosis, CT-guided percutaneous biopsy was performed.

Pathology:
– Gross: Four gray-taupe cores (1 cm × 0.1 mm). KIT gene mutation detected; no EGFR mutation.  
– Microscopic: Sheets, nests, and discohesive aggregates of medium-sized cells with vacuolated nuclei, prominent nucleoli, frequent mitoses, and focal fine melanin granules; thin-walled blood vessels and collagen fibrosis between nests; occasional plasmacytoid cells.  
– Immunohistochemistry: Tumor cells strongly positive for HMB-45, Melan A, S-100, and vimentin; negative for cytokeratin (pan), CD138, TTF-1, Napsin-A, CK7, P63, P40, synaptophysin, chromogranin A, NSE, desmin, CD99, and LCA. Ki-67 labeling index ~50%.

A 48-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension presented with bilateral breast lumps of one-week duration. She had no family history of breast or ovarian cancer and had previously regular menstrual cycles. On examination, the left breast had a 4 × 4 cm hard lump in the lower inner quadrant fixed to the chest wall; the right breast had a firm, mobile 1 × 1 cm lump in the lower outer quadrant. MRI showed a 3.8 × 3.5 cm irregular spiculated mass in the left breast suspicious for malignancy and a 2.3 × 1.5 cm well-defined lesion in the right breast with a type 1 contrast enhancement pattern (< 6% probability of malignancy) and bilateral axillary lymphadenopathy. Ultrasound and bone scan were negative for metastases. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the left breast lump revealed poorly cohesive clusters of ductal cells with pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, and prominent nucleoli; myoepithelial cells and bare nuclei were absent. FNAC of the left axillary lymph node showed similar malignant cells. FNAC of the right breast lump showed three-dimensional clusters of hyperchromatic cells with prominent nucleoli and scattered pleomorphic cells with mitotic figures admixed with benign ductal cells and myoepithelial cells; a few bare nuclei were seen. Cytologic diagnosis was duct cell carcinoma of both breasts with left axillary lymph node metastasis. A core-needle biopsy of the left breast confirmed infiltrative duct cell carcinoma that was estrogen- and progesterone-receptor positive. On the basis of the physical examination results, the right breast lump was suspected to be a fibroadenoma. Hence, lumpectomy was performed.

A 26-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a right testicular mass noted on self-examination several weeks earlier. He had no significant medical history or prior testicular trauma.  
On examination, the right testis was enlarged without tenderness. Serum tumor markers were obtained, and a testicular ultrasound was performed. The ultrasound revealed a 32 cc right testicle with highly heterogeneous parenchyma containing multiple hypoechogenic, hypervascular nodules and a moderate hematocele. Doppler imaging also showed bilateral varicoceles.  
An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 4 cm superior retroperitoneal lymph node with surrounding fat stranding. A contrast-enhanced thoracoabdominopelvic CT scan confirmed a lateroaortic retroperitoneal lymphadenomegaly and a 2 cm left supraclavicular lymphadenomegaly, without other metastatic lesions.  
The patient underwent right radical orchiectomy. Histologic examination showed a mixed germ cell neoplasm with seminomatous, embryonal carcinoma, and yolk sac components, together with germ cell neoplasia in situ. Pre-chemotherapy serum markers were elevated: AFP 47.9 mg/dL (normal 1–8 mg/dL), hCG 4.3 mIU/mL (normal 0–4 mIU/mL), and LDH 239 U/L (normal 135–225 U/L).  
He received four cycles of bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin. Tumor markers peaked approximately 2 months after surgery and then declined over the next two months to within normal limits, remaining stable thereafter. However, surveillance CT scans performed every 2 to 3 months showed an increasing number and size of cervical and retroperitoneal lymph nodes and new mediastinal lesions characterized by diffuse hypodensity, suggesting a cystic or necrotic nature.

A 60-year-old woman was evaluated for newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus and a year-long history of vague abdominal discomfort with mild epigastric pain. Her medical history included hypertension and tachycardia, and she was a moderate smoker. On examination, vital signs were normal, and there was a palpable upper abdominal mass with mild epigastric tenderness. Laboratory studies showed a normal white-cell count, normal serum amylase and lipase levels, and normal carcinoembryonic antigen and cancer antigen 19-9 concentrations. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed cholelithiasis and a well-defined 11.6-cm cystic lesion adjacent to the upper pole of the spleen and the tail of the pancreas. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a hypodense cystic mass measuring 12.0×9.5×10.0 cm between the pancreatic tail and spleen, with minimal enhancement, no calcifications, no soft-tissue component, and no evidence of infiltration. MRI confirmed microcholelithiasis and normal intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts; it also showed multiple microcystic changes in the body and tail of the pancreas (suggestive of a branch-duct intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm) and a separate multilobulated 12.8×10.2×8.65 cm cystic lesion between the pancreatic tail and splenic hilum, without solid components, pathological signal intensity, lymphadenopathy, or vascular invasion. MRI findings raised the possibilities of an atypical pseudocyst, a mucinous cystic neoplasm, or a cystic lymphangioma.

A 71-year-old woman with 13 pregnancies and menopause at age 36 presented with two months of postmenopausal vaginal bleeding. Her medical history was notable only for well-controlled hypertension; there was no family history of cancer and no clinical features of Peutz–Jeghers syndrome. On examination, vital signs were stable and the physical examination was unremarkable.

Transvaginal ultrasound showed a 1.0 cm endometrial lining thickness, a right ovarian complex cystic mass measuring 5.9 cm in diameter with a thin septum, and a normal-appearing left ovary. The CA-125 level was mildly elevated at 66.5 U/mL; CA 19-9 was normal. The presumptive diagnosis was endometrial hyperplasia, and she underwent laparotomy with bilateral hysterosalpingo-oophorectomy.

Gross pathology revealed:
- Uterus: 1.5 cm endometrial thickening and a 3 × 0.7 cm fundal polyp.
- Right ovary: cystic mass 8 × 5 × 5 cm with citrine fluid; internal surface septate, multilobed, yellowish.
- Left ovary: solid–cystic 3 × 1 × 0.5 cm yellow-brown mass without hemorrhage or necrosis.

Microscopically, both ovarian lesions were predominantly cystic with simple and complex annular tubules in the medullary stroma. Tumor cells were columnar with antipolar nuclear arrangement around central hyaline-like material; nuclei were round with inconspicuous nucleoli. Immunohistochemical stains showed strong inhibin and calretinin positivity in tumor cells.

A 46-year-old previously healthy man presented with a 1½-year history of insidious, progressively worsening intermittent constipation. He reported hard stools with abundant mucus and a sense of incomplete evacuation. He also noted a 7-kg weight loss over 6 months but denied rectal bleeding, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or systemic symptoms. He was a nonsmoker and nondrinker with no significant family history. 

On examination, he appeared in fair condition without cachexia, pallor, jaundice, or lymphadenopathy. Abdominal palpation was soft and non-tender, with no organomegaly. Digital rectal examination revealed normal sphincter tone and no palpable mass, though a small bulge was felt on the anterior rectal wall approximately 4 cm above the anal verge; no blood was noted. Proctoscopy was unremarkable. 

Routine laboratory tests were normal except for mildly elevated transaminase levels; serum CEA and CA 19-9 were within normal limits. Colonoscopy showed no mucosal lesions. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a well-circumscribed, heterogeneously enhancing 2.3 × 3.5-cm mass in the rectovesical space with nonenhancing cystic or necrotic areas. Multiple minimally enhancing lesions were seen in both hepatic lobes and several enhancing soft-tissue density nodules were present in both lungs, suggesting metastatic disease. 

An ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the rectal mass showed a spindle cell neoplasm.

A previously healthy 10-year-old boy presented with 10 days of progressively worsening aching pain in the right lower limb after a trivial fall; he became unable to walk. He had no fever, weight loss, or pain elsewhere. Birth and family history were unremarkable, and immunizations were up to date. On examination, there was tenderness and swelling over the right knee; the remainder of the physical and systemic examination was normal. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10 g/dL, platelet count 67,000/µL, markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase (9587 U/L) and lactate dehydrogenase (3414 U/L), parathyroid hormone at the upper limit of normal for age (169 pg/mL), and normal serum calcium and other biochemical parameters. Serologies for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were negative.  
Radiographs of the right femur demonstrated a sclerotic lesion in the lower metadiaphysis with a wide zone of transition, mild spiculated periosteal reaction, cortical breach at the medial epicondyle, and a soft-tissue component with calcific foci. A second sclerotic lesion with a wide zone of transition and cortical breach was seen in the upper metadiaphysis of the right tibia. Skeletal survey of the pelvis, spine, and ribs revealed multiple similar sclerotic lesions, sparing the skull, forearms, and small bones of the hands and feet. Chest radiograph and CT scan showed no pulmonary lesions but revealed diffuse sclerotic lesions in the vertebrae, sternum, ribs, and humeri. Technetium-99m bone scintigraphy demonstrated abnormally increased tracer uptake at multiple sites.

A 22-year-old man presented with progressive shortness of breath. He was found to have severe superior vena cava syndrome, with pleural and pericardial effusions. CT imaging showed a bulky mediastinal mass compressing the right superior bronchus, displacing the trachea and right intermediate bronchus, and associated pleural and pericardial effusions. PET scan demonstrated supraclavicular lymphadenopathy without hepatic involvement. Laboratory studies revealed an alpha–fetoprotein level of 765 ng/mL (normal < 10.9 ng/mL) and a lactate dehydrogenase level of 14 468 U/L (normal 240–480 U/L). A biopsy of a supraclavicular lymph node showed a poorly differentiated, diffusely necrotic carcinoma. Immunohistochemical staining was weakly positive for AE1–AE3 cytokeratin, TTF-1, p63, synaptophysin, chromogranin A, and CD34; focally positive for epithelial membrane antigen and cytokeratin 7; and negative for PLAP, alpha–fetoprotein, beta–HCG, CD30, CD3, CD20, CD117, Melan-A, S100, ALK, PAX8, and desmin.

A 33-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of a gradually enlarging swelling over the right thigh. The overlying skin showed puckering. On palpation the mass was nontender and hard. Systemic examination was unremarkable. 
Magnetic resonance imaging of the right thigh demonstrated a 3.0 × 2.5 × 1.5 cm T1- and T2-hypointense mass in the posterolateral upper third of the thigh, with significant postcontrast enhancement and extension into the vastus lateralis; there was no bone erosion. A provisional diagnosis of soft tissue sarcoma was made, and fine‐needle aspiration (FNA) was performed. 
Cytologic smears were cellular and showed a bimodal population: clusters of spindle cells with bland, ovoid nuclei separated by fibrovascular septae, and scattered multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells whose oval nuclei resembled those of the spindle cells. The background was hemorrhagic, and mitotic figures were absent.

A 35-year-old man presented with 18 months of gradually progressive difficulty walking, characterized by dragging of the right foot and slippage of footwear, without significant interference in daily activities. Six months after onset, he developed spontaneous painful drawing up of both legs in response to noxious or non-noxious stimuli; these movements became frequent over the past two months and disturbed his sleep. He also noted urinary frequency, urgency, and incontinence for one year. He denied sensory disturbances, headaches, vomiting, seizures, trauma, or fever. He had intermittent low backache for two years, radiating along the posterior right thigh, responsive to analgesics.

On examination, he was of average build with normal vital signs and no cranial nerve or higher cortical deficits. Motor examination of the lower limbs showed grade 3 spasticity on the right and grade 2 on the left; right ankle dorsiflexors, evertors, and invertors were 0/5, plantarflexors 5/5; power was normal elsewhere. Flexor spasms were present bilaterally (spasm score 4). Deep tendon reflexes were brisk at knees and ankles bilaterally; the right plantar response was extensor, the left plantar was not elicitable. Sensory testing revealed a 1-cm decrease in two-point discrimination on the anterior right leg compared with the left, with intact primary modalities and cortical sensations. Gait showed a right high steppage pattern.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and serum biochemistry, were normal. MR imaging of the cervical and thoracic spine was unremarkable. Lumbar MRI revealed a disc prolapse at L4–L5 with minimal thecal sac compression. The presence of an abnormal cortical sensory finding despite normal primary modalities prompted consideration of an intracranial lesion.

A 68-year-old man was evaluated after surveillance imaging incidentally revealed a gallbladder lesion. His history was notable for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the right testis treated 8 years earlier, with subsequent complete remission, and longstanding protein-losing enteropathy managed with steroids. He was asymptomatic with respect to the abdomen. On examination, there was no abdominal tenderness or Murphy’s sign; bilateral lower-extremity edema reflected his hypoproteinemia. Laboratory studies showed CEA 5.7 ng/mL (normal ≤ 5.0), CA 19-9 55.7 U/mL (normal ≤ 37), normal α-fetoprotein, and soluble interleukin-2 receptor 625 U/mL (normal 145–519). He had chronic hepatitis B (Child-Pugh class B). 
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 27 × 10 mm homogeneous, hypoechoic mass at the gallbladder neck and body on the liver-bed side. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed the mass without obvious hepatic invasion and noted pericholecystic lymphadenopathy. MRI demonstrated low T1 and high T2 signal intensity of the lesion relative to liver parenchyma. FDG-PET showed focal uptake in the gallbladder lesion (SUV max 6.9) without other abnormal foci. ERCP revealed lateral deformation with an irregular surface at the gallbladder neck and body; bile cytology was Class I. Endoscopic ultrasound depicted a 25 × 12 mm hypoechoic, trapezoidal protruding lesion with preservation of the outer hyperechoic layer, suggesting no liver invasion.

A 44-year-old obese woman presented with a left-sided abdominal mass of one year’s duration. She denied abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, fullness, diarrhea, flushing, weight loss, anorexia, fatigue, jaundice, fever, or chills. One month earlier, she had undergone an exploratory laparotomy in Haiti that was aborted after a presumptive diagnosis of pancreatic cancer. On examination, a firm mass was palpable in the left upper quadrant. Laboratory studies showed a fasting blood glucose level of 103 mg/dL, with normal complete blood count, electrolytes, and liver-function tests. Tumor markers were within normal limits (CEA, 0.9 ng/mL; CA 19-9, 5 U/mL). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 13 × 13 cm mass arising from the body and tail of the pancreas, with solid and cystic components, calcifications, and irregular heterogeneous enhancement of the cyst walls and solid areas. The mass compressed the stomach and duodenum and abutted the left kidney and spleen, without evidence of local invasion, lymphadenopathy, ascites, or distant metastases. A multidisciplinary tumor board recommended primary resection without preoperative biopsy.

A 16-year-old female presented with a 2-year history of progressive neck pain and left arm abduction weakness (grade III). On examination, there were no long-bone deformities. Plain cervical radiographs revealed an ill-defined calcified mass at the C3–4 level. Three-dimensional computed tomography showed a 3.0×2.4-cm calcified extradural lesion eroding the vertebral body and extending into the left C3–4 neural foramen. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed an extradural, calcified mass compressing the cervical spinal cord. Vertebral angiography demonstrated a hypoplastic left vertebral artery. There was no family history of exostoses.

A 23-year-old student presented with 16 months of left‐sided chest pain and 6 months of progressive bulging of the left anterior chest wall. Examination showed multiple cutaneous neurofibromas and café‐au‐lait spots. The left anterior chest wall was visibly bulging with thoracic kyphoscoliosis. The trachea was deviated to the right, and the cardiac apex was palpable in the fifth right intercostal space at the midclavicular line. Percussion over the entire left anterior chest wall produced dullness, and breath sounds were absent. There was distension of the neck veins with edema of the face and left upper limb.  
A chest radiograph demonstrated homogeneous opacification of the entire left hemithorax with marked mediastinal shift to the right. Computed tomography of the chest showed a nonenhancing, isodense mass completely occupying the left hemithorax.

A 62-year-old man with diabetes presented with 15 days of sudden, acute, severe abdominal pain and vomiting. He was in pain but neither pale nor jaundiced. On examination, Murphy’s sign was positive; the gallbladder was not palpable. Abdominal ultrasound showed a thick-walled gallbladder with multiple stones and thick bile content with a fluid level, suggesting chronic cholecystitis. CT of the abdomen revealed a distended gallbladder with a thick, enhancing wall, pericholecystic inflammatory changes, and a large stone at the neck; adjacent liver parenchyma had ill-defined hypodensity and focal inflammatory changes in the right lobe, consistent with calculous cholecystitis with hepatitis-type changes. MRI confirmed features of acute calculous cholecystitis and a markedly dilated gallbladder. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 11.0 g/dL, white-cell count 8000 cells/mm3, total bilirubin 1.1 mg/dL, albumin 3.2 g/dL, AST 50 IU/L, ALT 33 IU/L; hepatitis B and C serologies were negative. Serum CA19-9 was 914.8 U/mL. After informed consent, an open cholecystectomy was performed via an inverted L-shaped incision. Intraoperatively, the liver appeared cirrhotic; Calot’s node was enlarged; there were adhesions involving the hepatic flexure, duodenum, gallbladder, and colon; no ascites or peritoneal lesions were seen. The right hepatic artery was encased by a mass; intraoperative cholangiography and Doppler ultrasound were used to confirm arterial patency. The cystic artery was identified and ligated, and the patient recovered uneventfully.

A 45-year-old woman presented with a three-month history of a dull, dragging abdominal pain. She denied weight loss, jaundice, fever, pruritus, anorexia, or pale stools. On examination, she had hepatomegaly without a palpable gallbladder mass. Laboratory tests showed mild elevations in total bilirubin (1.5 mg/dL; direct 0.9 mg/dL), ALT 100 IU/L, AST 90 IU/L, and ALP 198 IU/L. Tumor markers were within normal limits (CEA 1.5 ng/mL; AFP 13 ng/mL; CA 19-9 18 IU/mL). The white-cell count was 6000/µL with eosinophils <5%.

Transabdominal ultrasound revealed a large, well-defined cystic lesion in the left biliary segments, with dilated segmental ducts and an irregular isoechoic papillary mural thickening projecting into the lumen; no vascularity was seen. Hydatid (IgG 0.3; normal <0.9) and amoebic (IgG 0.47; normal <0.9) serologies were negative.

Contrast-enhanced MRI of the upper abdomen demonstrated:
 • A well-defined cyst at the hepatic hilum containing an isointense, frond-like soft tissue projecting into the cyst and extending into the common hepatic and common bile ducts.  
 • Mild upstream bilobar intrahepatic ductal dilatation and mild downstream CBD dilatation (7.8 mm).  
 • The mural soft tissue was heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, showed diffusion restriction, and on triple-phase contrast-enhanced sequences exhibited late arterial enhancement with reduced enhancement on porto-venous and delayed phases.

A 64-year-old man presented with several days of worsening left lower quadrant abdominal pain accompanied by nausea and vomiting. He had a history of diverticulitis and colonoscopy findings of internal hemorrhoids and diverticula throughout the colon.  
On examination, he was afebrile, and abdominal palpation revealed mild tenderness and fullness in the left lower quadrant without rebound or guarding.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 12.6 × 10 × 9 cm bilobed mass in the central pelvis abutting the sigmoid colon, as well as a 2.5 cm lesion in the right hepatic lobe concerning for metastasis.  
A CT-guided core biopsy of the pelvic mass showed poorly differentiated epithelioid malignant cells with partial necrosis, scattered mitoses, and marked nuclear atypia.  
Initial immunohistochemical staining revealed that the tumor cells were positive for MART1 (MelanA) and HMB45 and negative for S100.
