Positron emission tomography confirmed hypermetabolic activity in the pelvic mass, in three liver lesions, and in left axillary lymph nodes.  
On the basis of imaging and biopsy, the differential diagnosis included lymphoma, gastrointestinal stromal tumor, and adenocarcinoma.

A 20-year-old man with no significant medical history presented for evaluation before orthognathic surgery. On oral examination, there was a 1.5-cm diameter, exophytic, smooth, regular, and soft lesion on the midline of the dorsal tongue. The patient reported that the lesion had been present since birth and had not changed in size or character. Vital signs were within normal limits. An MRI of the tongue showed a 1.5-cm protuberant mass arising from the dorsal aspect of the tongue in the midline at the junction of the oral component and base; the lesion appeared partly fatty, likely submucosal, demonstrated mild contrast enhancement, had intact overlying mucosa, and showed no involvement of intrinsic tongue muscles. The sublingual space and major salivary glands appeared normal.

An 81-year-old man with a history of primary adrenal large B-cell lymphoma diagnosed 3 months earlier and currently receiving R-CHOP chemotherapy presented with 7 days of decreased vision in the left eye and orbital pain exacerbated by eye movements. On examination, visual acuity was 20/40 in the right eye and light perception in the left eye. Anterior segment examination was unremarkable, and intraocular pressures were 12 mm Hg bilaterally. Pupils were equal and reactive without a relative afferent pupillary defect. Funduscopy revealed vitreous cells in both eyes (more pronounced in the left eye) and edema of the left optic disc. Optical coherence tomography confirmed left optic disc edema. An orbital and brain MRI with gadolinium showed thickening and enhancement of the left optic disc without radiological signs of neoplastic meningitis. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis, including cytology, was normal.

A 46-year-old Caucasian man presented with a several-month history of right proximal thigh pain. He had no significant past medical or family history. Physical examination revealed no neurological deficits. Radiographs and magnetic resonance imaging of the right femur showed a 10 cm permeative, lytic lesion in the proximal femur with cortical destruction and an adjacent soft-tissue mass. Whole-body staging with chest, abdominal, and pelvic CT scans showed no evidence of metastatic disease or a second primary tumor. Core-needle biopsy revealed a malignant fascicular spindle-cell proliferation. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated tumor cells positive for α-smooth-muscle actin, desmin, and caldesmon, and negative for cytokeratin and S-100.

A 15-year-old Caucasian female presented with a 6-month history of swelling in the submental region. On extra-oral examination, there was a painless, mobile, resilient bulge of the submental soft tissues; the overlying skin was intact and the regional lymph nodes were not enlarged. Intra-oral examination showed intact mucosa in the floor of the mouth and a full complement of teeth without signs of dental or mucosal pathology. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a well-defined, unilocular, low-attenuation lesion in the submental space containing multiple granular hyperattenuating foci.

A 32‐year‐old G2P1 Caucasian woman at 40 weeks’ gestation was admitted for elective induction of labor. Her pregnancy had been uncomplicated apart from mild second‐trimester anemia, chronic constipation worsening near 36 weeks, and 17.3 kg weight gain. A 9‐week ultrasound showed normal‐appearing ovaries; a 19‐week anatomy scan noted bilateral choroid plexus cysts and incomplete adnexal visualization. Fundal heights remained appropriate.

On admission she was well appearing; vital signs were normal and fetal heart tracing reactive. Labs showed hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL and platelets 131 × 10^9/L. Cervical exam was challenging: cervix anterior and shifted left, fetal station –2. Induction with misoprostol and Foley balloon yielded no change in station despite contractions and an epidural for pain control. Oxytocin was started 15 h after admission.

Shortly after, she developed fever (38.0 °C), right upper quadrant pain, and intermittent Category II fetal heart tracing with late decelerations. Repeat labs showed hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL, platelets 118 × 10^9/L, LDH 1518 U/L, AST 78 U/L, and normal bilirubin. Urinalysis revealed large blood and 51–100 WBCs. Atypical HELLP syndrome, urinary tract infection, and chorioamnionitis were considered; she received ceftriaxone, then ampicillin and gentamicin.

At 25 h of induction, bedside transabdominal ultrasound demonstrated a cephalic fetus and a poorly defined mass in the posterior cul‐de-sac without Doppler flow. The differential included an adnexal mass, cervical fibroid, or stool from constipation. Fetal heart tracing then showed persistent late decelerations and moderate variability with a baseline of 160 bpm, prompting a primary cesarean delivery for non‐reassuring fetal status.

A 21-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive dysphagia accompanied by nausea and vomiting after meals. Chest CT revealed a 30 × 26 mm spherical soft-tissue mass in the upper thoracic esophagus causing marked luminal narrowing, with mild, uniform enhancement and no mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Abdominal CT, neck ultrasound, brain MRI, and bone ECT were unremarkable. Flexible esophagoscopy showed a large polypoid mass 18 cm from the incisors completely obstructing the lumen; the mucosal surface appeared intact with mucosal bridges. Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated that the lesion arose from the muscularis propria and had a smooth, continuous adventitia. The primary clinical diagnosis was a submucosal lesion of the upper thoracic esophagus, possibly a leiomyoma.

A 69-year-old woman with hypertension, previous thyroidectomy for hyperthyroidism, and hysterectomy for uterine myomas presented with progressive swelling of the dorsal right side of her neck. There were no signs of vascular obstruction, venous stasis, neural deficits in the head and neck, or functional or sensory loss in the right arm. Examination showed no Horner’s syndrome, dysphagia, cough, or dyspnea.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and upper mediastinum revealed a retroclavicular soft-tissue mass extending up to 4.5 cm cranio-caudally, displacing the trachea to the left and compressing the subclavian vein. An adjacent 3.5 × 3.5 cm lesion at the inferior right thyroid lobe compressed the internal jugular vein. Near the confluence of these vessels, subtotal occlusion of the brachiocephalic vein was noted. MRI provided no additional information regarding tumor origin or cause of venous occlusion, and showed no clear invasion of the brachial plexus, brachial artery, esophagus, or trachea. A preoperative chest radiograph demonstrated a right-sided upper mediastinal enlargement.

Venous angiography revealed a filiform stenosis of the subclavian vein, a longitudinal irregular partial displacement of the lumen in the brachiocephalic vein, and extensive collateral cervical and supraclavicular blood flow. Neither CT, MRI, nor angiography could definitively distinguish between intravascular tumor growth and thrombosis.

A 42-year-old woman presented with a 7-month history of painless right-sided neck swelling, drenching night sweats, fever, weight loss, and general weakness. Initial therapy with antibiotics, antivirals, and antituberculosis medications produced only partial regression. Four months later the mass rapidly enlarged, and she was found to be anemic, prompting referral. Examination revealed an 8×6 cm right supraclavicular mass without tenderness, generalized lymphadenopathy (largest 5×3 cm), and, two months later, ulceration of the mass with straw-colored fluid and a pathological fracture of the right clavicle. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 5 g/dL, normal white-cell and platelet counts, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 95 mm in the first hour. A peripheral smear showed few small- and medium-sized mature lymphocytes with cleaved nuclei. HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C tests were negative. Acid-fast bacilli smear of the ulcer fluid and a Mantoux test were negative, and chest radiography was normal. Renal and liver function tests were within normal limits. Ultrasonography revealed cervical, supraclavicular, and infraclavicular lymphadenopathy and hepatomegaly with intra- and retroperitoneal lymph node enlargement.  
Histologic evaluation of an initial biopsy was reported as reactive lymphadenopathy. A second review diagnosed small lymphocytic lymphoma, with sheets of mature lymphocytes effacing nodal architecture. Clinicians questioned this diagnosis given the clavicle fracture. A third histologic opinion identified numerous mononuclear and classic Reed–Sternberg–like cells amid eosinophils and neutrophils and rendered a diagnosis of mixed cellularity Hodgkin’s lymphoma.

A 20-year-old man presented with a 24-hour history of right iliac fossa pain and vomiting. One month earlier, he had similar pain for seven days; laboratory tests and plain radiographs were unremarkable, and he declined laparoscopy. His only medication was lymecycline for acne. On readmission, temperature was 39.6°C, pulse 93/min, respirations 19/min, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, and Glasgow Coma Score normal. Abdominal examination showed diffuse tenderness with generalized guarding, absent bowel sounds, and no distension. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 16.7 g/dL, white-cell count 13.6 × 10^9/L, normal renal function, and normal C-reactive protein. A plain abdominal film was normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated what appeared to be a 50 cm multiseptated collection occupying much of the abdominal and pelvic cavities, containing air pockets, with a small amount of free fluid around the liver and in both paracolic gutters; the appendix was not visualized.

A 51-year-old man presented with progressive right facial fullness over 4 years, accompanied by recent facial pain and serosanguinous drainage. He denied fever, fatigue, weight loss, or facial weakness and had no history of trauma or radiation. On examination, there was a palpable, firm, 4-cm mass in the right parotid region; cranial nerve VII function was intact, and no cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a 3.3 × 2.8 × 3.2 cm, well-defined, cystic and solid mass with peripheral enhancement and internal septations in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland. The patient underwent a right superficial parotidectomy with selective level II and III neck dissection. Grossly, the specimen was a well-circumscribed, unilocular cystic mass with a surrounding solid component. Histologically, the lesion consisted of a large cyst lined by either papillary projections or a single layer of cuboidal cells with mild to moderate nuclear atypia, and adjacent solid tumor nests exhibiting a focal cribriform growth pattern; there was no overt mitotic activity or necrosis.

A 47-year-old perimenopausal woman presented with 3 weeks of worsening abdominal distention, diffuse abdominal tenderness, and constipation. Her medical history was notable for hypothyroidism, latent tuberculosis, and prior cesarean section with bilateral tubal ligation. She had no family history of malignancy.  

Vital signs were normal. On examination, the abdomen was distended and diffusely tender. Pelvic examination revealed a 30 cm left adnexal mass; the uterus was small and difficult to palpate.  

Transvaginal and transabdominal ultrasound with Doppler showed a multiloculated complex pelvic mass with thick septations measuring 24 × 18 cm, likely arising from the left ovary and extending to the first intercostal space, with moderate pelvic free fluid. The uterus was anteverted with a thin endometrial lining. The right ovary measured 3.9 × 3.3 × 3.5 cm and contained a 3 cm simple cyst.  

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a predominantly cystic mass measuring 28.3 × 24.4 × 16.3 cm extending from the pelvis to the upper abdomen, displacing bowel superiorly.  

Serum CA-125 was elevated at 95 U/mL.

A 10-week-old female Rottweiler was referred with a 4-day history of progressive pelvic limb ataxia and lumbosacral pain. On examination, the puppy was bright and alert but non-ambulatory paraparetic; she could stand and bear some weight if supported. There was marked pain on palpation of the lumbar spine. Cranial nerves were normal. Proprioceptive placing was decreased in both pelvic limbs (left worse than right). Spinal reflexes were normal. The puppy could urinate and defecate spontaneously. A T3–L3 spinal cord lesion was suspected.

Complete blood count showed mild anaemia and mild monocytosis; serum biochemistry was unremarkable. Initial differential diagnoses included fracture, haemorrhage, neoplasia, congenital malformation, and discospondylitis. Survey radiographs of the lumbosacral region were unremarkable.

High-field MRI of the spine (T3–S1) revealed an ovoid, well-marginated lesion from the mid L3 vertebral body to the caudal L4 vertebra, centered on the left L4 pedicle, extending into the ipsilateral vertebral foramen and dorsolaterally. The mass was homogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, heterogeneously iso- to hyperintense on T1-weighted images, and showed moderate heterogeneous contrast enhancement with a dural-tail sign. It measured 2.8 × 1.3 × 1.1 cm, occupied ~75% of the vertebral canal, and caused rightward displacement and moderate compression of the spinal cord. The lesion infiltrated the adjacent vertebral arch and pedicle with decreased bone signal. Imaging localization was primarily intradural-extramedullary with an extradural component. The imaging diagnosis was soft tissue neoplasia with osseous invasion.

A 52-year-old woman undergoing routine breast screening had an ultrasound that detected a 1.2-cm lesion in the lower outer quadrant of her left breast, although she felt no palpable mass. She had a history of laser treatment for cervical dysplasia but no breast surgery or trauma. Family history was notable for a sister with breast cancer and a father with gastric cancer. On examination there was no palpable breast mass or axillary lymphadenopathy.  
Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein concentration of 0.16 mg/dL (reference 0.00–0.14 mg/dL), normal carcinoembryonic antigen and cancer antigen 15-3 levels, and a normal serum interleukin-6 concentration.  
Mammography revealed a focal asymmetric density in the lower outer left breast. Ultrasonography showed a smoothly marginated, relatively hypoechoic 1.2-cm mass with scant internal vascularity and partial cystic change. MRI demonstrated a 1.2-cm lesion with mildly high T2 signal, diffusion restriction, and early contrast enhancement with a plateau on delayed imaging. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a solitary heterogeneously enhancing mass without lymphadenopathy or distant lesions.  
A core needle biopsy of the mass showed a fibrosing lesion with proliferation of fibroblastic cells in a storiform pattern accompanied by chronic inflammatory and histiocytic cells. No epithelial neoplasm was observed. Immunohistochemical staining of the spindle cells was diffusely positive for ALK-1 and negative for IgG4.

A 53-year-old man with no significant medical history presented after sustaining an acute traumatic fracture of his right thumb. He was evaluated for operative fixation with Kirschner wire placement when a routine preoperative chest radiograph showed a 9 cm rounded opacity overlying the left mid lung zone, obscuring the anterior portion of the left third rib.  
 
Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a 6.3 × 6.5 × 5.4 cm aggressive-appearing, pleural-based mass along the left anterior chest wall, with erosion and destruction of the underlying left third rib and no additional pulmonary lesions. On physical examination, a diffuse, firm density was palpable in the left hemithorax without overlying skin changes.  

Interventional radiology–guided biopsy was performed, and histologic examination revealed a small round blue cell tumor.

A 67‐year‐old woman was referred for evaluation of a painless right vulvar mass extending into the right inguinal region. She first noted the lesion two years earlier, with gradual enlargement over the past four months. She denied pain, changes in appetite or bowel habits, urinary symptoms, weight loss, infection, or bleeding. Her medical history was notable for hypertension, managed with valsartan/amlodipine, and a hysterectomy in 2016 for abnormal uterine bleeding. She was post‐menopausal, had no history of hormone therapy, and did not smoke or drink alcohol.

On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs. Abdominal exam was unremarkable. Inspection revealed a 12 cm, non‐tender mass of the right labia majora extending to the right groin, without erythema, lymphadenopathy, or signs of inflammation. Pelvic exam was otherwise normal.

Soft‐tissue ultrasound showed a well‐defined, hypoechoic solid mass measuring 90 × 44 × 55 mm in the right labia majora tracking into the inguinal canal, with mild peripheral blood flow on Doppler imaging. Routine laboratory results, including blood counts and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. The leading preoperative impression was a canal of Nuck hernia containing omental tissue.

A 71-year-old man with a 15-year history of diabetes mellitus, hepatic hemochromatosis, and bronchial asthma was referred for evaluation of a pancreatic mass after worsening glycemic control. He had previously undergone a left adrenalectomy for adrenal neuroma. On admission, he was afebrile; abdominal examination revealed no palpable mass. Laboratory studies showed: hemoglobin 9.6 g/dl, WBC 3.1 × 10^3/μl, Fe 23 μg/dl, amylase 89 U/l, trypsin 1171 ng/ml (normal, 100–550), elastase-1 959 ng/dl (0–300), normal liver function, CEA 3.0 ng/ml, CA19-9 20 U/ml, Span-1 39 U/ml (< 30), NCC-ST-439 1.2 U/ml (< 4.5), AFP 2 ng/ml. Pulmonary function was impaired (FEV1% 43.5%). 

Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a 27 mm slightly enhanced mass in the pancreatic tail with dilation of the distal MPD. MRCP showed mild dilation of the cranial MPD (3.5 mm), moderate dilation of the caudal MPD (7 mm), and a cystic lesion in the pancreatic neck suggestive of branch-duct IPMN. Thin-slice MDCT confirmed a homogeneous, slightly enhanced, well-marginated tail mass without infiltration of retropancreatic tissue or the splenic vein, and downstream intraductal tumor progression in the MPD extending to the left side of the portal vein. 

EUS demonstrated a 3 cm lobulated, hypoechoic mass in the tail, upstream MPD dilatation, and an intraductal tumor thrombus downstream from the main tumor.

An 81‐year‐old woman presented with progressive dysphagia, shortness of breath, and stridor. Her past medical history included mediastinal radiotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma 14 years earlier, leading to radiation-induced pulmonary fibrosis treated with long-term azathioprine and prednisolone. One year prior, she had surgical excision and adjuvant radiotherapy for a moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the nasal tip. Five months before this admission, sputum cultures grew Haemophilus influenzae and Mycobacterium kansasii, and she was advised a two-year course of rifampicin, ethambutol, and clarithromycin; due to delays, she received only six weeks of therapy. On nasoendoscopy during the acute admission, there was a left anterior vocal cord granulation and an exophytic pedunculated lesion arising from the right vocal cord causing a ball-valving effect at the glottic inlet, with diminished right vocal cord mobility. With her history, the initial working diagnosis was squamous cell carcinoma, with mycobacterial disease in the differential. She was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics and steroids without response and subsequently taken to the operating room for endoscopic debulking to reestablish the airway; tissue samples were sent for histological and microbiological analysis.

A 43-year-old man presented with an 8-month history of progressive dysphonia and dysphagia. Fibrolaryngoscopy revealed a smooth submucosal swelling in the left pyriform sinus associated with immobility of the left vocal cord. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated an oval, well-circumscribed lesion in the left pyriform sinus extending into the ipsilateral paraglottic space without signs of invasion of adjacent structures. Clinical and radiological features suggested a benign process, and his anatomy was favorable for transoral exposure.

A 56‐year‐old man presented with a 6‐month history of recurrent headaches, vertigo, diplopia, impaired hearing, and gait imbalance. His medical history was notable only for well‐controlled Graves’ disease. Neurologic examination was unremarkable. Noncontrast head CT ruled out acute intracranial pathology, including hydrocephalus. MRI of the brain and spine revealed:  
• A small cystic lesion in the right cerebellar hemisphere.  
• Diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement of the cerebellum, brainstem, and cervical spinal cord with nodular thickening along the entire neuraxis.  
• Multiple punctate subcortical cerebellar lesions.  

Electrophysiologic studies showed evidence of demyelination in the optic and sensory pathways of the right arm and lower extremities. CSF analysis demonstrated markedly elevated protein (3032 mg/dL) and the presence of CD56‐positive cells; cytology was negative for S100, Melan A, and CD138. Genetic testing for common BRAF single‐nucleotide variants and indels was wild‐type. A repeat CSF assay was negative for Listeria and Whipple’s disease. Comprehensive infectious work‐up, including HIV, tuberculosis, Epstein‐Barr virus, syphilis, and echinococcal serologies, was negative. Full‐body imaging showed benign hepatic lesions but no evidence of systemic malignancy. Dermatologic evaluation revealed no cutaneous neoplasms. The patient was referred for a surgical biopsy to obtain a definitive histopathological diagnosis.

A 72-year-old woman with a history of sarcoidosis, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation on apixaban, obstructive sleep apnea, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with sudden onset involuntary movements of her right arm and hand, followed by left-sided facial droop, dysarthria, and expressive aphasia. Noncontrast CT of the head showed a curvilinear hyperdensity in the left central sulcus, left subinsular region, and inferior frontal operculum, worrisome for an acute subarachnoid hemorrhage. CT angiography of the head and neck revealed no vascular abnormalities, and catheter angiography confirmed the absence of aneurysms or contrast extravasation. Brain MRI demonstrated curvilinear hyperintensity filling the left central sulcus without evidence of acute blood and a second area of focal parenchymal abnormality anterior to the left frontal horn with subtle mass effect and vasogenic edema. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis from lumbar puncture did not reveal xanthochromia. Given these findings, intracerebral hemorrhage was felt less likely, raising concern for an underlying inflammatory or neoplastic process. The patient subsequently underwent a left frontal craniectomy with stereotactic biopsy of the abnormal leptomeningeal region.

A 75-year-old man, non-smoker, with a history of controlled hypertension and hyperlipidemia presented for evaluation of large masses overlying the alveolar ridges in both maxillary and mandibular posterior areas. He had received dental implants in the posterior maxilla and the left mandibular first molar seven years earlier with cemented and screw‐retained prostheses functioning without reported occlusal overload.

On initial panoramic radiography, ovoid radiopaque masses were seen adjacent to the implants in both posterior maxillary regions and the left mandibular first molar site. One maxillary lesion showed a radiolucent medullary space within an outer cortical layer, while the mandibular lesion was uniformly radiopaque. One year after placement of two additional implants and prosthetic loading, follow-up panoramic imaging showed more pronounced radiopaque masses at these three sites.

Intraoral examination revealed prominent, dome-shaped masses on the buccal alveolar ridges of the posterior maxilla and mandible, causing difficulty with toothbrushing and mastication. The lesions were non-tender, with no paresthesia or lymphadenopathy.

Three-dimensional cone-beam CT demonstrated well-circumscribed, pedunculated masses arising from the buccal cortical bone of each implant site. The maxillary lesions had a dense cortical shell with internal radiolucent marrow, and the mandibular lesion had a thick cortical layer with minimal marrow space.

A 43-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 4-week history of right upper quadrant and right flank pain radiating to his right testicle. There was no preceding trauma, haematuria, or other systemic symptoms. His medical history included a resected osteoid osteoma of the left femur in 2007 and an L4/5 microdiscectomy. He was a non-smoker with no allergies and took no regular medications. On examination, the right flank was full in contour with minimal tenderness. Laboratory studies showed a haemoglobin concentration of 140 g/L, a creatinine level of 116 µmol/L, and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 66 ml/min.  
An abdominal ultrasound revealed a large right renal subcapsular haematoma measuring 7 × 5 × 7 cm compressing the renal cortex. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed an enlarged right kidney with a mass in the lower pole measuring 7.4 × 7.5 × 9.2 cm and associated paracaval lymphadenopathy causing compression of the right renal vein and inferior vena cava. A repeat CT scan several weeks later demonstrated an increase in tumour size to 11.5 × 11.6 × 11.5 cm. Based on the clinical findings and imaging, a preliminary diagnosis of renal cell carcinoma was made, and the patient was referred for an open radical right nephrectomy.

A 38-year-old woman presented with 2 years of progressive right hallux pain, described as pinching and pressure at the tip and lateral side, worsened by standing and activity. Her history included hypothyroidism, anxiety, Raynaud’s disease, and stage 2 thyroid cancer treated in remission; she also had a right hallux fracture 10 years earlier. She denied smoking or alcohol use. On examination, the medial nail of the right hallux was thinned and dystrophic, and she experienced severe pain on pressure at the acral and lateral nail edges; cold-sensitivity testing was inconclusive. Radiographs showed an eccentric expansile lytic lesion of the dorsomedial distal phalangeal tuft with a well-demarcated sclerotic inner margin. MRI revealed an 8×7×6 mm subungual mass that was hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2 fat-saturated sequences, with homogeneous contrast enhancement, causing more than 50% erosion of the dorsal distal phalanx and associated reactive edema; joints and tendons were uninvolved. The radiologist’s impression was a glomus tumor, with differential diagnoses including squamous cell carcinoma and, less likely, a melanocytic tumor.

A 19-year-old nulligravid woman with no significant medical history presented with two months of lower abdominal pain and irregular menstrual cycles. On gynecological examination, there was a firm, non-tender 3-cm mass with a clear boundary and visible surface vascular pulsations arising from the cervical canal; the vulva, urethra, and vagina were unremarkable. Pelvic ultrasound and contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a 30-mm mass in the cervical canal; the uterine body appeared normal. The patient underwent a cervical lumpectomy. Grossly, the lesion was well-circumscribed with a solid gray-yellow cut surface interspersed with soft cystic areas showing hemorrhage and necrosis. Microscopically, the tumor was unencapsulated and showed nested and trabecular/cord patterns of ovoid to spindle cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, fine chromatin, and fewer than 1 mitosis per 10 high-power fields; a delicate capillary network was present without lymphovascular invasion. Immunohistochemical staining showed that the tumor cells were positive for Calretinin, AE1/AE3, Desmin, progesterone receptors, smooth muscle actin (SMA), and h-caldesmon but negative for CD10, WT1, Myo D1, HMB45, ALK, EMA, and Inhibin.

A 70-year-old man presented to the emergency department with four days of dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. Three months earlier he had required pericardiocentesis for hemorrhagic pericardial effusion causing tamponade; cytology was negative, and chest CT at that time revealed a 4.2×4.0 cm mass in the right atrium, but he declined further evaluation and was lost to follow-up. On this presentation, his blood pressure was 156/85 mmHg, pulse 102 beats/min, and respiratory rate 22 breaths/min. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 5.7 g/dL; liver and renal function were normal. Chest radiography demonstrated diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and cardiomegaly. Gastric and colonoscopic evaluations for gastrointestinal bleeding were normal. Contrast-enhanced chest CT showed the known right‐atrium mass, a moderate pericardial effusion, multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules, and extensive diffuse ground-glass opacities. Initial assessments included acute pulmonary edema, atypical pneumonia, and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage. Empirical antibiotics and antifibrinolytic therapy were started, and bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and PET-CT were performed. A moderate amount of endobronchial bleeding was found on lavage, and PET-CT demonstrated hypermetabolic activity in the right atrium mass, multiple lung nodules, and mediastinal and bilateral hilar lymph nodes.

A 30-year-old man with non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus presented for routine follow-up, during which liver enzymes were elevated (ALT 166 U/L, ALP 116 U/L). He denied abdominal pain, nausea, or changes in bowel habits. Laboratory studies showed a serum CEA of 5.3 ng/mL, with normal AFP and CA 19-9 levels. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed an 8.8 × 7 cm heterogeneous midline retroperitoneal mass with calcified components and indistinct margins relative to the head of the pancreas. A noncontrast CT scan confirmed an 8.8 × 7.2 cm well-defined hypodense mass posterior to the pancreatic head, featuring multiple central calcifications and a small area of fat density, without a clear fat plane between the lesion and adjacent pancreatic structures.

An 83-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a seizure disorder presented with melena. She reported taking ibuprofen twice daily. Laboratory studies on admission showed hypoalbuminemia (2.4 g/dL), hyperbilirubinemia (2.8 mg/dL), aspartate transaminase 88 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 224 U/L. Two years earlier, a CT scan had demonstrated a cirrhotic liver; abdominal ultrasound confirmed cirrhosis and revealed dilation of the common bile duct (CBD) to 19 mm with left intrahepatic biliary dilation. Upper endoscopy identified a clean-based pyloric channel ulcer, and evaluation of the biliary tree was deferred. Abdominal MRI demonstrated abnormal signal in the mid to upper CBD extending into the bilateral hepatic ducts. Endoscopic ultrasound showed CBD dilation to 17 mm with intraluminal congealed sludge or a soft-tissue mass. ERCP revealed a dilated biliary tree with extensive filling defects. After sphincterotomy, balloon sweeps removed several large black stones. A repeat cholangiogram suggested a proximal CBD stricture. Choledochoscopy at the stricture yielded additional stone fragments, and lithotripsy was performed. Subsequent balloon sweeps removed more stones, blood clots, and a large piece of soft tissue, which was sent for histologic analysis. A fully covered metal stent and a double-pigtail plastic stent were placed.

A 48-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 3-month history of low back pain radiating to the left leg, associated with a needle-pin-prick sensation in her lower extremities. She denied any bowel or bladder dysfunction. On neurologic examination, there was a mild decrease in strength of the left foot extensor muscle; sensation was otherwise intact. Vital signs were within normal limits.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine revealed a well-delineated intradural, extramedullary mass extending from T12 to the upper edge of L2, measuring 6 cm in length. The lesion was isointense on both T1- and T2-weighted sequences. On T1-weighted images after gadolinium administration, the mass demonstrated homogeneous enhancement and a few flow voids at its upper pole suggestive of high vascularity.

A 26-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of pain and swelling in the left submandibular region. He denied prior swelling or tooth pain. After a week of empirical antibiotics prescribed by a general dentist, the swelling resolved transiently but recurred two weeks later. Extraction of the left mandibular third molar produced no change. He then noted a mass in the nasal passage, and fine-needle aspiration showed chronic inflammation with fibrous granulation tissue. He reported fever and weight loss over the past two months. He was an occasional alcohol consumer, a nonsmoker, and had childhood asthma; there was no relevant family history. Intraoral examination was unremarkable. Complete blood count, blood sugar profile, and routine biochemistry were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck revealed two enhancing masses lateral to the left submandibular gland (45×30 mm and 16×10 mm) and a 26×27 mm mass in the right submandibular region, with enlarged level II and III lymph nodes bilaterally (largest 27×19 mm on the left). Abdominal CT demonstrated mesenteric lymphadenopathy, and neck ultrasound showed ovoid hypoechoic lesions with internal vascularity in the jugular spaces.  

An excisional biopsy of the left submandibular lesion was planned for definitive diagnosis.

A 30-year-old Black woman from Addis Ababa presented with a slowly enlarging swelling over the left superior inner orbit for 4 years. She denied headaches, diplopia, nasal congestion, or visual changes. Physical examination revealed a hard, nonmobile mass at the left superior medial orbit with slight left proptosis. Nasal endoscopy showed a submucosally covered hard mass above the inferior turbinate on the left lateral nasal wall. There was no history of cutaneous lesions, gastrointestinal symptoms, dental problems, or relevant family history. Fundoscopic and slit-lamp examinations were normal bilaterally. A noncontrast CT scan demonstrated a 45×42 mm fronto-ethmoidal bony mass protruding into the left orbit and intracranial space.

A 21-year-old immunocompetent Caucasian woman presented with a 2-week history of dry cough and swelling of the face, neck, and upper limbs, which worsened when supine. She also noted dyspnea that intensified on standing.  
On examination there was marked swelling of the face, neck, and arms, jugular venous distention, and dilated superficial chest veins; there was no lymphadenopathy and the systemic examination was otherwise unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies showed lymphopenia (790/mm3), C-reactive protein 10.7 mg/L, lactate dehydrogenase 421 IU/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 27 mm/h, and normal coagulation tests. Serum beta-human chorionic gonadotropin, alpha-fetoprotein, and anti-acetylcholine-receptor antibodies were negative, and serologic tests for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were negative.  
Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed a large anterior mediastinal mass compressing the superior vena cava, with small left pleural and pericardial effusions. Subsequent thoracoabdominopelvic MRI demonstrated a 109 × 60 × 105 mm anterior mediastinal mass fully encasing the superior vena cava.

A previously healthy 3-year-old girl presented with a 2-day history of fever, nonproductive cough, and dyspnea. On examination, her temperature was 38.2 °C, respiratory rate 30/min, heart rate 120/min, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. Auscultation revealed absent breath sounds over the left hemithorax. Routine laboratory tests, including a complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits.

A chest radiograph showed complete opacification of the left hemithorax with contralateral mediastinal shift. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and upper abdomen demonstrated a 15.7 × 10.9 × 9.6 cm heterogeneous mass filling most of the left hemithorax, with both solid and fluid-filled cystic components, inhomogeneous enhancement, significant mediastinal displacement to the right, and invasion of the lateral chest wall. The lesion displaced the left hemidiaphragm, spleen, and left kidney inferiorly. The residual left lung appeared completely collapsed, and a large pleural effusion was noted. No systemic arterial supply to the mass was identified on CT angiographic sequences.

Thoracic ultrasound confirmed a complex pleural effusion with densely corpuscular fluid and multiple septations. Abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable, and brain MRI showed no intracranial lesions. A percutaneous ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the thoracic mass was performed.

A 16-year-old male presented with congenitally missing lower left incisors. He was otherwise healthy, with no relevant medical or hereditary history. Extraoral examination was unremarkable. Intraoral examination revealed all maxillary teeth present and absence of teeth 31 and 32 in the mandibular arch. There was no pain, swelling, erythema, ulceration, or tenderness of the overlying mucosa.  
Panoramic radiography showed an approximately 1 cm × 1.5 cm ill-defined lesion in the region of teeth 31 and 32, characterized by mixed radiolucent and radio-opaque components and surrounded by a thin radiolucent band.

A 60-year-old man with no significant medical history had multiple emergency visits over 2 years for weakness, weight loss, leg pain, polydipsia, and polyuria. An initial workup suggested diabetes insipidus, but no definitive diagnosis was made. He later presented with right hemithorax pain and a several-month history of left eye pain. On examination, there was slight exophthalmia. Laboratory tests showed elevated C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate; kidney, liver, and thyroid function tests, viral serologies, autoimmune panels, complement levels, and IgG subclasses were all normal.

Orbital computed tomography revealed a retro-orbital hypodense infiltrative soft-tissue lesion in the intraconal space. Magnetic resonance imaging of the orbit showed that the mass was hypointense on both T1- and T2-weighted images with homogeneous enhancement after contrast.

Contrast-enhanced body CT demonstrated hypodense soft tissue circumferentially involving the thoracic and abdominal aorta and its branches (“coated aorta sign”). There were bilateral irregular hypodense soft tissue masses in the perirenal and posterior pararenal spaces causing moderate hydronephrosis (“hairy kidney sign”). An enhancing soft tissue mass surrounded the right atrium and the right atrioventricular groove, encasing the right coronary artery, with associated pericardial thickening and effusion.

Cardiac MRI confirmed a hypointense mass on balanced steady-state free precession sequences with conspicuous late gadolinium enhancement around the right atrium and atrioventricular groove. Chest CT showed smooth thickening of the interlobular pulmonary septa. Review of a radiograph of the legs from 2 years earlier revealed bilateral cortical sclerosis affecting the metaphyses and diaphyses of the femurs and tibias.

A 38-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with a 20-year history of a slowly enlarging mass of the tongue. Over the past year, she developed progressive dyspnea, dysphonia, and severe dysphagia, losing 10 kg and becoming markedly fatigued. She had a family history of hypothyroidism. On examination, a large, mobile, hard mass was evident at the base of the tongue, obstructing most of the oropharynx and part of the supraglottic area. Thyroid ultrasound showed a gland in its normal position, and Doppler findings suggested thyroiditis. Laboratory studies revealed elevated TSH, low T4 and T3, and high anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody titers, consistent with Hashimoto disease. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an 8.5 × 5 × 6 cm pedicled, bilobed, well-circumscribed, encapsulated basilingual mass.

A 32-year-old man with a history of monostotic fibrous dysplasia of the left maxilla, diagnosed in 2015 by incisional biopsy, had stable lesion dimensions on CT scans in 2015 (32.5×30.6×45.1 mm) and 2017 (34.2×31.3×49.5 mm). Three months after a mild COVID-19 infection in August 2020, he noted rapid enlargement of the left maxillary swelling. On examination, there was a hard, non-mobile, non-tender mass in the left buccal vestibule extending from the left incisor to the tuberosity; the overlying skin and palatal mucosa were normal. Involved teeth were vital, without mobility, displacement, or percussion pain. There was facial asymmetry with interference in occlusion, eating, and speaking. The right maxilla, mandible, tongue, oral mucosa, temporomandibular joint, and regional lymph nodes were normal. Serum calcium, phosphorus, and alkaline phosphatase levels were within normal limits. A CT scan in April 2021 showed the lesion had grown to 46.6 mm (sup–inf) × 46.2 mm (med–lat) × 63.3 mm (ant–post). The lesion was ill-demarcated, mixed opaque-lucent, with homogeneous sclerosis and abnormal trabecular pattern; cortical expansion with thinning but no destruction; no tooth displacement or root resorption; absent lamina dura of involved teeth; intact maxillary sinus floor with mild mucosal thickening.

A 38-year-old woman noted a swelling of her right lower leg 8 years ago that had been stable until 6 months ago, when it enlarged and became painful on walking more than 10 m. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender, 15 × 6 × 3 cm mass continuous with the anterior border of the right tibia; the overlying skin was pinchable and without warmth.  
Plain radiographs of the leg showed an eccentric, expansile, lytic lesion in the distal third of the right tibial diaphysis with scalloping and anterolateral cortical breach; a similar small lesion was noted in the distal fibula.  
MRI demonstrated an irregular, eccentric, expansile lesion of the anterior cortex of the distal tibia measuring 6.5 × 2.2 × 5.8 cm, with a narrow zone of transition; the lesion was isointense on T1, hyperintense on T2 and STIR sequences, showed homogeneous post-contrast enhancement, and extended into the intramuscular and subcutaneous planes. A separate 7 × 2 mm lesion was seen in the lower third of the right fibular diaphysis.  
Tru-cut biopsy revealed a high-grade spindle-cell neoplasm with areas of round blue-cell rests and sarcomatous dedifferentiation. Immunohistochemistry was positive for Ki-67 (30–40%), cytokeratin, p53, and CD99. Cytogenetic analysis demonstrated a t(11;22)(q23;q12) translocation, and FISH confirmed EWSR1 gene rearrangement in 32% of cells.

A 22-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of left-sided nasal obstruction. He had no history of allergy or prior nasal surgery. On examination, there was a soft, compressible bulge of the left septum, and careful inspection revealed a small, round mass in the upper part of the septum. Noncontrast CT of the nasal cavity showed a 1.5 cm thick hypodense mass in the left septum. Subsequent MRI demonstrated an amorphous, heterogeneous 54 × 8 × 94 mm lesion in the left anterior nasal septum that was hyperintense on T2-weighted images and did not enhance after gadolinium administration.

A 19-year-old woman with no significant past medical or family history presents with two weeks of progressive abdominal pain and distention. On examination, there is a palpable mass in the right iliac fossa. Contrast CT and MRI reveal a 23×19×14 cm abdominopelvic mass in the mesogastrium and right iliac fossa compressing the iliac vessels and psoas, with moderate ascites and clustered retroperitoneal lymph nodes. Serum ionic calcium is normal. Ultrasound-guided biopsy shows a neoplasm with a biphasic pattern, partly spindle-shaped and partly epithelioid. Immunohistochemical staining is negative for PAX-8, p53, WT-1, inhibin, estrogen receptor, and progesterone receptor; positive for cytokeratin AE1/AE3; and shows focal calretinin positivity.

A 32-year-old woman with no prior surgeries presented with 5 days of severe colicky right upper–quadrant abdominal pain that began after a large meal. She reported no relief with a liquid diet, secnidazole, or fenoverine. On examination, her abdomen was asymmetrically distended, and palpation elicited 10/10 pain in the right upper quadrant. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 9.9×10^3/μL (68.1% neutrophils), hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL, hematocrit 40.8%, platelets 246×10^3/μL, and normal creatinine and β-hCG. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a distended transverse colon and a classic target lesion of ileocolic intussusception, with a low-density tubular structure at the distal aspect of the invaginated segment. The report noted that this finding “did not rule out the possibility of appendicular mucocele in this location.” Given the imaging findings, the decision was made to proceed to exploratory laparoscopy with possible intestinal resection.

A 49-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of intermittent epigastric pain. She had no past medical or surgical history and no pertinent family history. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits, and abdominal examination revealed mild epigastric tenderness without palpable mass.

Laboratory testing, including complete blood count, metabolic panel, and tumor markers, was within normal limits. Endocrine workup, including catecholamine assays, was negative.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen demonstrated a 90-mm, well-circumscribed, nonenhancing mass in the retroperitoneum, partly situated between the abdominal aorta and the inferior mesenteric artery. Magnetic resonance imaging showed the lesion to be hyperintense on T2-weighted images. On T1-weighted sequences, the mass was hyperintense on in-phase imaging and hypointense on out-of-phase imaging, indicating the presence of fat within the tumor.

At this stage, the differential diagnosis included ganglioneuroma and dedifferentiated liposarcoma. Surgical resection was planned both for treatment and to establish a definitive diagnosis.

A 38-year-old Iranian man was referred for evaluation of an intraoral lesion on the right side of his mandible, first noted 1 year earlier. Nineteen years ago he had received a kidney transplant for end-stage renal disease, but experienced graft rejection 2 years ago and has been on hemodialysis since. He first presented for dental assessment prior to a planned second transplant and reported gradual enlargement of the lesion over the past year. 

On oral examination, there was a sessile, exophytic, pink mass with an erosive surface located distal to tooth #45, measuring approximately 1 × 1 cm. A periapical radiograph of the area revealed focal bone erosion at the alveolar ridge crest just distal to tooth #45 beneath the lesion.

A 45-year-old white woman with no history of smoking presented in 2011 with dyspnea, mild orthopnea, and tachycardia but no fever. Her body mass index was normal. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL, serum iron 31 µg/mL, ferritin 302 ng/mL, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 38 mm/h; C-reactive protein was 0.1 mg/dL. Serologies for coxsackievirus, echovirus, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein–Barr virus were all negative. Electrocardiography showed diffuse ST-segment elevations. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a 1 cm pericardial effusion with normal ventricular function and no masses. Chest radiography demonstrated moderate cardiomegaly. She was treated for presumed acute pericarditis with ibuprofen and a beta-blocker.

Over the next two years, she developed non-erosive polyarthritis, a photosensitive rash, sicca symptoms, and recurrent pericarditis with effusions. Autoantibody testing showed an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:320 (homogeneous pattern) and transient anti-cardiolipin antibodies; complement levels, extractable nuclear antigens, anti-double-stranded DNA, and anti-Smith antibodies were within normal limits. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate remained elevated while C-reactive protein stayed normal. Treatment with prednisone (25 mg/day), hydroxychloroquine, and colchicine led to only partial improvement. Ultrasound-guided pericardiocenteses yielded fluid with repeatedly negative cytology and cultures.

In 2014, she was readmitted for evaluation of recurrent serositis. Her vital signs were normal, but she had lost 7 kg since 2011. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest revealed extensive, irregular thickening of both visceral and parietal pericardial layers completely surrounding the heart, aortic root, pulmonary arteries, and veins.

A 47-year-old Sudanese woman presented with bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy over two months and reported significant weight loss. She denied fever, night sweats, chills, dyspnea, cough, arthralgia, rashes, or other systemic symptoms. Her medical history was unremarkable: no chronic illnesses, malignancies, infections, thyroid disorders, surgeries, radiation exposure, or family history of malignancy. On examination, she had multiple firm, non-tender, mobile bilateral inguinal lymph nodes of varying sizes without overlying skin changes. The thyroid and cervical lymph nodes were not palpable, and there was no hepatosplenomegaly or uveitis. Routine laboratory studies—including complete blood count, inflammatory markers, thyroid function tests, and screening for HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C—were all within normal limits. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed normal ovaries, pelvic organs, and abdominal structures, with no evidence of a primary malignancy.

A 73‐year‐old woman presented with a 5‐month history of a painless vaginal mass that protruded from the introitus on straining. She denied bleeding, discharge, or systemic symptoms. Pelvic examination revealed a soft, well‐defined pink mass occupying the upper vagina. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory tests were unremarkable.

An MRI of the pelvis was performed on a 3.0 T system, including axial T1-weighted, small‐field‐of‐view T2-weighted in three planes, diffusion-weighted imaging, and post-gadolinium fat-saturated T1-weighted sequences in arterial and portal venous phases. Imaging showed a 47 × 40 × 44 mm oval, well-circumscribed mass in the upper vagina. On T1-weighted images, the lesion was intermediate in signal intensity, similar to skeletal muscle. On T2-weighted images, it had two discrete zones: an anteroinferior region of high T2 signal without enhancement and a posterosuperior region of low T2 signal with avid enhancement. There was no restricted diffusion. The lesion appeared to arise from the left posterolateral vaginal wall, with loss of definition of the outer vaginal margin and hazy low T1 and T2 signal changes in the left paravaginal fat. The bladder, urethra, and rectum were uninvolved.

A staging contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis in the portal venous phase demonstrated a mixed fluid and soft‐tissue attenuation mass with patchy enhancement and no evidence of lymphadenopathy or distant metastases. Through multidisciplinary discussion, the lesion remained suspicious for malignancy, and en bloc surgical excision of the uterus, ovaries, cervix, and upper vagina was planned.

An 18-year-old woman with no prior medical history was referred for evaluation of multiple subcutaneous tumors on her right arm, left arm, and upper back. The lesions had been present for approximately 2 years and had enlarged over the past 3–4 months. She denied pain or antecedent trauma until the masses began to grow. On examination, there was a 15.5 × 15.2 cm lesion on the upper back, a 2.5 × 3.5 cm lesion on the right arm, and a 5 × 5.3 cm lesion on the left arm. All lesions had a pseudo-bullous appearance, were firm, painful on palpation, red-brown in color, and lacked ulceration or fixation. Over the last month, the upper-back lesion enlarged further to 18.4 × 17.5 cm due to hemorrhage and assumed a hemorrhagic cystic aspect. MRI of the lesions showed no vascular abnormalities. Excisional biopsy of all lesions was undertaken, and the specimens were sent for microscopic examination with a differential diagnosis that included vascular lesions, neurofibroma, adnexal tumor, and cystic lesions.

An 85-year-old man was referred for a 1-month history of progressive dyspnea. He was a former smoker with no known hematologic or respiratory disorders. His performance status was ECOG 3. On examination, fine crackles were audible bilaterally; no lymphadenopathy was noted. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air showed a PaO₂ of 76.7 mmHg. 

A chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral ground-glass opacities in the lower lung fields. High-resolution computed tomography of the chest revealed perivascular ground-glass opacities with a centrilobular distribution and numerous centrilobular micronodules forming a “tree-in-bud” pattern, predominantly in the lower lobes.

Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 12,200 cells/μL with 67% lymphocytes (absolute lymphocyte count 8174/μL), hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL, platelet count 2.16 × 10^5/μL, lactate dehydrogenase 264 IU/L, C-reactive protein 0.06 mg/mL, KL-6 1050 U/mL, soluble interleukin-2 receptor 2290 U/mL, and β-D-glucan <2.6 pg/mL.

At that time, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, atypical pneumonia, Mycobacterium infection, and a lymphoproliferative disorder were considered. Bronchoscopy was performed. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid contained 53% lymphocytes, and no bacteria or mycobacteria were cultured. A transbronchial lung biopsy revealed infiltration of small lymphocytes in the lung parenchyma; immunohistochemical staining showed positivity for CD5, CD20, and CD23.

A 48-year-old woman presented with a palpable mass in her lower abdomen. She denied abdominal pain, distension, dyspepsia, diarrhea, or weight loss, and her appetite was unaffected. Her medical history was unremarkable, with no hypertension, diabetes, heart disease, smoking, alcohol use, or known hereditary disorders.

On examination, her abdomen was soft, nondistended, and nontender, with no other abnormalities.

Laboratory tests showed normal complete blood count and biochemical parameters. Tumor markers revealed a CA 19-9 level of 251 U/mL (elevated) and a CA 125 level of 412 U/mL (elevated); CA242, CEA, AFP, and CA 72-4 were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated:
- A 5.9 × 4.6 cm low‐density lesion in the tail of the pancreas with a poorly defined margin, hypoenhancement during the pancreatic phase, and progressive delayed enhancement.
- A 15.1 × 12.0 cm cystic‐solid mass in the right ovary and a 5.7 × 4.3 cm cystic mass in the left ovary; both were thin‐walled with multiple enhancing septa.
- No evidence of liver or peritoneal metastases.

A 44-year-old woman was referred by her general dentist for assessment of bilateral temporomandibular myofascial pain syndrome and bruxism. She denied pain, swelling, or sensory changes in the jaws. On panoramic radiography, there was a deeply impacted right mandibular third molar with a well-circumscribed, approximately 3-cm radiolucent area immediately above the crown. Cone-beam CT confirmed an osteolytic lesion in the right posterior mandible lying superior to the inferior alveolar canal; the radiologic appearance was non-pathognomonic. Under general anesthesia, the lesion was surgically excised en bloc and the third molar extracted. The specimen measured about 2 cm in greatest dimension and was firm on palpation. No damage to the inferior alveolar nerve occurred.

A 41-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with left shoulder pain worsened by inspiration. She had no history of trauma or notable findings on clinical examination. Her medical history included ulcerative colitis in remission on mesalazine and mercaptopurine, pyoderma gangrenosum, and a COVID-19 infection six weeks earlier. Blood tests, including liver function tests, serum lipase, and troponin levels, were normal. Electrocardiogram and chest radiograph showed no abnormalities. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen demonstrated a lobulated cystic lesion measuring 7.3 × 6.7 × 4.2 cm between the spleen and diaphragm, with a slightly thickened wall and scattered coarse calcifications; the lesion indented and appeared inseparable from the spleen, and no peritoneal disease was evident.

A 72-year-old woman was referred after detection of a rectal mass on routine endoscopic surveillance. She denied abdominal pain or changes in bowel habits. Her past medical history was remarkable for:
• 1985: hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for early-stage, low-grade endometrioid endometrial carcinoma (FIGO Ib) treated with intravaginal brachytherapy.  
• 1989: left thyroid lobectomy for papillary carcinoma followed by I-131 therapy.  
• 2001: endoscopic resection of bladder papillary carcinoma.  
• 2003: right hemicolectomy for pT3 N1 colonic adenocarcinoma followed by adjuvant chemotherapy.  

Genetic testing revealed microsatellite instability due to a heterozygous somatic MLH1 mutation. In 2013, colonoscopy showed a right-sided extrinsic compression of the rectal wall with intact mucosa. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a 4.7 × 3.5 cm intramural mass located 6.5 cm from the anocutaneous plane and 3 cm from the anorectal junction, with a nearby 11 mm focus in perivisceral fat and an 8 mm mesorectal lymph node. Multidetector CT confirmed a hypodense rectal lesion with a slightly eccentric hypodense area and an intensely enhancing medial component in the arterial phase, without liver or pulmonary metastases. Endoscopic ultrasound revealed a subepithelial hypoechogenic mass in the right paramedian rectal wall, minimal vascularity, and a 6–7 mm lymph node.  

Fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the rectal mass yielded poorly differentiated carcinoma cells. Immunocytochemistry showed CEA (+), CDX2 (−), CA125 (−), and estrogen receptor (+). No endometriosis foci were identified in the specimens. Serum tumor markers were within normal limits.

A 72-year-old woman presented with dyspnea, cough, and chest tightness of two months’ duration. On examination she was tachypneic with orthopnea and use of accessory respiratory muscles. Routine laboratory studies were within normal limits. A chest radiograph showed a homogeneous opacity occupying the lower two-thirds of the left hemithorax with mediastinal and cardiac shift to the right. Thoracentesis yielded 1800 mL of serosanguinous fluid; analysis demonstrated an exudate with no malignant cells on cytology and sterile cultures. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a 7.3 × 2.3 cm solid mass in the left posterosuperior mediastinum associated with pleural effusion. For staging, CT scans of the brain and upper abdomen, a bone scan, and bronchoscopy were performed and were all normal. Serum levels of alpha-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, CA 19-9, neuron-specific enolase, and squamous cell carcinoma antigen were within normal limits. The mass appeared resectable, and surgical resection was planned.

A 41-year-old woman first presented with a left fifth metatarsal base fracture after an inversion sprain; the fracture healed with conservative treatment. Eight months later, she had sudden left forefoot pain without trauma, and radiographs showed a fracture of the left second metatarsal with callus formation. One year after the initial fracture, she returned with spontaneous left fourth toe pain; radiographs demonstrated old fractures of the bases of both fifth metatarsals and proximal phalanges of both third toes, with callus formation of the left second metatarsal and a crack fracture of the proximal phalanx of the left fourth toe. She was newly diagnosed with diabetes mellitus, but there was no sensory or neurological deficit of the feet. A dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry scan showed a T-score of –3.0 at L2–L4. She was premenopausal. To investigate secondary osteoporosis, an overnight dexamethasone suppression test showed a cortisol level of 660 nmol/L (not suppressed), 24-hour urine cortisol was 605 nmol/day, and a low-dose short synacthen test produced a peak serum cortisol of 699 nmol/L; plasma ACTH was <1.6 pmol/L. Computed tomography of the abdomen revealed bilateral adrenal adenomas.

A 62-year-old man underwent evaluation after a subacute left frontal subdural hematoma requiring trepanation. Neurologic examination was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced MRI showed:
  • A 61 × 16 mm left frontal subdural collection with peripheral enhancement.  
  • A 4.0 × 2.5 cm solid mass at the skull base invading the sphenoid and cavernous sinuses bilaterally, with suprasellar extension up to the optic chiasm and invasion into the nasal cavity.
He denied headaches or visual changes but reported 14 years of decreased libido and erectile dysfunction. He was a recreational target shooter.  
Two-dimensional Doppler echocardiography revealed a double aortic valve lesion with moderate stenosis and concentric left ventricular hypertrophy; systolic function was normal.  
Laboratory evaluation demonstrated:
  – Prolactin 14,992 ng/mL (normal < 17 ng/mL)  
  – FSH 0.5 IU/L (normal up to 10 IU/L)  
  – LH 0.5 IU/L (normal up to 9 IU/L)  
  – Total testosterone 260 ng/dL (normal 240–816 ng/dL)  
  – Cortisol 25 μg/dL at 8 h (normal 5.4–25 μg/dL) and 15 μg/dL at 16 h (normal 2.4–13.6 μg/dL)

A 62-year-old woman presented with two weeks of intermittent vaginal bleeding. Her medical history was unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed a heterogeneous 4.6 cm longitudinal mass in the uterine myometrium and a hard, whitish 2.0 cm mass arising from the anterior vaginal wall. A punch biopsy of the vaginal mass revealed a malignant tumor that was immunoreactive for smooth muscle actin but negative for HMB-45, findings reported as suggestive of leiomyosarcoma. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a 4.6 × 5.5 cm heterogeneous, contrast-enhancing mass in the uterine myometrium and a 2.1 × 1.1 cm indistinct, heterogeneous, enhancing lesion in the lower vagina. Chest CT revealed multiple pulmonary nodules consistent with metastatic disease. The patient was taken for exploratory laparotomy and surgical staging.

A 42-year-old woman presented with a firm, tender, palpable lump in her right breast that she first noticed 2 days earlier after minor trauma. Her medical history was notable for acute myeloid leukemia treated with autologous stem cell transplant 2½ years ago; gilteritinib maintenance was stopped 2 years ago after complete remission. She had no skin changes or nipple retraction. Menopause began at age 40; her paternal grandmother had breast cancer at age 85. A screening mammogram 5½ months earlier was normal (BI-RADS 1).

On diagnostic mammography, there was a new spiculated high-density mass in the right breast central to the nipple at anterior depth. Targeted ultrasound showed a 3.9 cm irregular hypoechoic mass with spiculated margins at 7 o’clock, 2 cm from the nipple, and a right axillary lymph node with uniform cortical thickening up to 3 mm. An ultrasound-guided core biopsy of both the breast mass and the axillary node was performed.

A 49-year-old man presented with right-sided chest pain. He had no significant past medical history and no neurologic deficits on examination. Magnetic resonance imaging of the thoracic spine revealed a dumbbell tumor of Eden type III with heterogeneous gadolinium enhancement at the T9–10 levels, in contact with the right pleura through the intervertebral foramen. 

The patient underwent laminectomy of T8–10 and resection of the lesion. Intraoperatively, a grayish, elastic, soft, well-defined neoplastic lesion was identified in the extradural and intradural spaces adjacent to the right T9–10 foramen. The intradural component adhered to the T9 dorsal root, which was amputated to achieve gross total resection.

Histologic examination showed a malignant neoplasm partly composed of rhabdoid cells with necrotic areas. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated the following: pan-cytokeratin (AE1/AE3) strongly positive; Ki-67 labeling index over 80%; cytokeratin profile CK20 positive and CK7 negative; S-100 protein expression not distinctive; focal and faint positivity for vimentin, synaptophysin, and CD56; intact SMARCB1 (INI1) expression; and loss of SMARCA4 (BRG1) expression.

A 55-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a three-week history of productive cough, dyspnea, chest pain, and unintentional weight loss. Her medical history included hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, dyslipidemia, chronic renal failure, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and chronic anemia. She had a 30 pack-year smoking history. Physical examination was unremarkable. A chest radiograph showed a large subcarinal mass. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest revealed a 6.2 × 5.0 cm well-circumscribed lesion in the subcarinal space. Bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy demonstrated suspicious malignant cells without definitive classification. A positron-emission tomography scan showed a hypermetabolic subcarinal mass with a standardized uptake value of 14.3. The differential diagnosis included an infected bronchogenic cyst, an esophageal duplication cyst, and a malignant subcarinal lymph node. Thoracoscopic surgical resection was planned for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. Preoperative esophagoscopy and bronchoscopy confirmed the absence of any communication between the mass and the esophagus or airways.

A 39-year-old man presented with a painless nodule over the anterolateral aspect of his left leg that had been present for 6 months and was slowly increasing in size. There was no history of trauma. On examination, there was a 4×1 cm well-circumscribed, firm, nonpulsatile, nontender deep swelling within the left anterolateral leg, freely mobile and not adherent to surrounding muscle; the overlying skin and muscle were normal, and knee and ankle movements were unaffected. Ultrasonography showed a 4.2×0.9 cm, well-defined, hypoechoic fusiform lesion adjacent to the tibia without internal vascularity. A CT scan demonstrated a well-defined hypodense lesion in the deep aspect of the left anterior tibialis muscle abutting the bone, without bony deformity or contrast enhancement. MRI revealed a 4.4×1.2×1.2 cm, regular-contoured mass with subtle postcontrast enhancement, touching but not invading the lateral tibia; the cruciate ligaments and menisci were normal, with no bone marrow edema. Complete blood count, biochemistry, and other laboratory tests were within normal limits. Both clinical and radiological features were suggestive of a benign process, and intramuscular myxoma was considered as an initial diagnosis.

A 6-month-old boy was brought by his mother after she noticed a mass in his right chest. He had no significant medical history. On examination, there was a hard, immobile mass in the right posterior chest wall, and breath sounds were markedly decreased over the right lung field. The patient was in mild respiratory distress with a respiratory rate of 57 breaths per minute. 

Chest radiography revealed a large right-sided chest wall mass that expanded and disrupted the fourth rib, with displacement of the mediastinum to the left; the lesion had well-defined margins. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest showed a 5.7 × 4.1 cm mass arising from the right posterior chest wall, with well-defined borders, heterogeneous density, and coarse calcifications. The fourth rib was involved and undergoing destruction without any periosteal reaction. There was compression of the right main bronchus, and the mass enhanced heterogeneously after contrast administration.

An 82-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of postmenopausal bleeding. Her gynecological history included a negative hysteroscopy in 1998 and prior hormone replacement therapy. She was otherwise healthy except for hypertension treated with bendroflumethiazide and atenolol. On examination, the uterus was bulky without adnexal masses. A pipelle biopsy yielded only fragments of blood clot. Transvaginal ultrasound revealed a large endometrial mass with calcification; the ovaries appeared normal. In July, hysteroscopic removal of a 6-cm polypoid lesion was performed. Microscopic examination showed polypoid tissue with fibrotic stroma, focal adipose tissue, possible chondroid metaplasia, mucinous and keratinizing squamous epithelial metaplasia, focal nuclear atypia, focal mitoses, and occasional cribriform gland fusion. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated CK7 and TTF-1 positivity in the epithelium, S100 positivity in the chondroid areas, focal estrogen and progesterone receptor staining in glands and stroma, SMA in stroma, and negative thyroglobulin, desmin, CK20, and CDX2. A diagnosis of benign teratoma with thyroid gland and cartilaginous elements was made. Despite polyp removal, bleeding persisted, and ultrasound showed near-complete cavity filling by the mass. MRI revealed a tumour distending the endometrial cavity, extending into the cervix with posterior myometrial invasion, no lymphadenopathy, and normal ovaries. Tumour markers (AFP, CEA, CA19-9) were normal; CA125 was 42 U/ml, and LDH was 372 IU/L. The decision was made to proceed to total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.

A 48-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia presented with a 6-year history of an enlarging right inguinal hernia and increasing discomfort. Physical examination revealed a cystic mass superior to the right testicle and a firm, solid, fully mobile subcutaneous mass in the right groin that was minimally tender and not connected to the external ring. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable. 

A CT scan showed a partially visualized, heterogeneous, enhancing right inguinal mass, raising concern for a peripheral nerve sheath tumor or sarcoma of the spermatic cord. Surgical excision revealed a 7.0×5.5×2.5 cm, 67.5 g mass inside the external cord but outside the internal spermatic fascia, eroding through the external oblique aponeurosis. The cut surface was white, firm, whorled, and contained occasional small cysts; the border was well delineated.

Microscopically, the tumor displayed a pattern-less architecture with alternating hypocellular and hypercellular areas, interstitial hyalinization, ropy collagen bands, and numerous small- to medium-sized vessels showing a spectrum from myocytic proliferation to intimal thickening and mural hyalinization; occasional subendothelial mucoid degeneration and hemangiopericytoma-like channels were noted. Neoplastic cells were ovoid to spindle-shaped with scant cytoplasm and rare mitoses (<1 per 10 high-power fields); margins were negative.

Immunohistochemistry showed tumor-cell expression of CD34, BCL-2, CD99, and focal positivity for estrogen and progesterone receptors, with negative staining for smooth muscle actin and S100.

A 30-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of pain in the lower left jaw. On extraoral examination, there was no facial asymmetry. Intraorally, there was mild swelling from the lower left lateral incisor to the first molar region, with buccal cortical-plate expansion and areas of crepitus. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. A panoramic radiograph showed a well-defined unilocular radiolucency with a corticated border extending from tooth 32 to 36, reaching the inferior mandibular border; an impacted permanent canine and an over-retained deciduous canine were noted. Computed tomography revealed an expansile osteolytic lesion with perforation of the buccal cortical plate.  
Provisional diagnosis: lateral dentigerous cyst associated with an impacted canine.  
Differential diagnosis: keratocystic odontogenic tumor, unicystic ameloblastoma, orthokeratinized odontogenic cyst.

A 30-year-old Japanese woman with no prior pregnancies and no significant medical history was referred for evaluation of a uterine tumor detected incidentally on ultrasonography. Initial transvaginal ultrasound identified a 43 mm uterine fundal tumor containing multiple intratumoral cystic lesions and abundant peripheral blood flow. T2-weighted MRI demonstrated an ovoid heterogeneous mass in the uterine fundus with signal intensity higher than that of the surrounding myometrium, deforming the uterine cavity. The high T2 signal intensity raised concern for tissue degeneration or hypercellularity, including malignant transformation. The patient initially declined surgery to preserve fertility and was monitored. Six months later, the lesion had grown to 59 mm with an increase in cystic components. She elected a gasless laparoscopic-assisted excision. During surgery, en bloc enucleation was difficult due to the tumor’s fragile, myxomatous nature and poorly defined border; fragmented resection was performed with careful irrigation to avoid tissue dispersal and direct palpation through a wound retractor guided the excision margin. The uterine wall was closed in two layers, hemostasis was achieved, and a drain was removed the next day. Surgery lasted 82 minutes with minimal blood loss, and the postoperative course was uneventful.

A 42-year-old Han woman was followed for thyroid nodules first detected in 2018. Over the subsequent years she reported occasional hoarseness, hyperhidrosis, palpitations, and intermittent dysphagia but denied choking with liquids, convulsions, or dyspnea. On examination, the thyroid was bilaterally symmetric without palpable nodules, tenderness, or tremor.  
In December 2022, ultrasound demonstrated heterogeneous thyroid parenchyma and a hypoechoic nodule measuring 1.2 × 1.1 × 1.0 cm in the lower left thyroid lobe with ill-defined margins and an irregular shape. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle biopsy at a local hospital was interpreted as papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
In January 2023, laboratory evaluation revealed a mildly elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration of 4.51 mIU/L, a slightly decreased free triiodothyronine level of 3.56 pmol/L, elevated anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies of 229 IU/mL, normal anti-thyroglobulin antibodies, and a normal carcinoembryonic antigen level.  
The patient underwent left thyroid lobectomy with isthmectomy and central lymph node dissection. Gross examination showed a well-circumscribed, encapsulated lesion. Microscopic examination revealed tumor nests separated by dense fibrous stroma with prominent infiltration of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils. Tumor cells displayed marked atypia with areas of squamous epithelial–like differentiation and keratin pearl formation. Mucin pools were present, and neoplastic cells exhibited ovoid nuclei with vacuolar chromatin, conspicuous nucleoli, occasional nuclear grooves, and a mitotic rate of 0–1 per 10 high-power fields. Surrounding thyroid parenchyma demonstrated lymphocytic thyroiditis–like changes. No lymph node metastases were identified.

A middle-aged patient presented with a 4-month history of right eyelid swelling, diplopia, and excessive tearing that began after cataract surgery. He had mild hypoesthesia on the right side of the face and a palpable mass causing elevation of the right lower lid. Visual acuity, intraocular pressure, and ocular motility were normal.  

Orbital MRI with contrast revealed a T2-intermediate, enhancing mass extending from the right inferior extraconal orbital space through the nasolacrimal duct into the right nasal cavity, with involvement of the inferior oblique muscle. CT of the paranasal sinuses confirmed an infiltrative lesion along the right orbit, nasolacrimal duct, and nasal cavity, with expansile bony destruction of the nasolacrimal duct. PET-CT showed no distant metastases.  

After multidisciplinary discussion, the patient was scheduled for a right medial maxillectomy and partial orbital exenteration, preserving the eyeball and inferior rectus muscle.

A 41-year-old woman presented with several months of nonproductive cough and occasional mild hemoptysis. She had no significant past medical history. On examination, breath sounds were decreased over the right upper lung field. A chest radiograph showed a homogeneous mass in the right upper lobe without pleural effusion or pneumothorax. Routine laboratory studies, including carcinoembryonic antigen, CA 19-9, CA 125, and SCC antigen, were all within normal limits. A whole-body FDG-PET/CT scan demonstrated a well-circumscribed 3.3 cm mass in the medial right upper zone with homogeneous increased uptake (SUV max 8.9). There was mild focal uptake (SUV max 2.0) in a small adjacent right lower paratracheal node and in the right hilum; no other abnormal FDG-avid lesions were identified. Pulmonary function tests revealed an FEV₁ of 2.58 L (88% of predicted) and a KCO of 1.40 mmol/min/kPa/L (82% of predicted).

A healthy 2-month-old boy was brought for evaluation of a newly noted mass over the left cheek in the masseter region. On examination, the lesion was firm, partially mobile, cold, apparently painless, and measured approximately 2 cm in diameter. There was no restriction of neck rotation or lateral movement and no head tilt. Ultrasonography showed a fusiform, inhomogeneous, hypoechogenic mass measuring 17×15 mm within the left masseter muscle; the ipsilateral sternocleidomastoid muscle showed focal thickening to 8 mm. Magnetic resonance imaging of the facial soft tissues demonstrated a 20×15×21 mm enlargement of the left masseter muscle that was minimally hyperintense on T2-weighted images, isointense on T1-weighted images, and showed no contrast enhancement; the proximal sternocleidomastoid muscle was also thickened (13×14×31 mm). Repeat ultrasonography at 2 months showed interval growth of approximately 10 mm in the mass. In view of the growth rate, a decision was made to perform a punch biopsy.

A 31-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of swelling on the left side of the mandible. On examination, there was a localized, tender, soft, fluctuant expansion of the left mandible covered by normal oral mucosa. The left canine and first and second premolars were displaced and mobile but remained vital. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy, and his medical and dental history was unremarkable.

Panoramic radiography showed a unilocular radiolucency with well-defined borders extending from the left canine to the second molar, with root divergence, destruction of the lamina dura, and no root resorption. Cone-beam computed tomography confirmed a radiolucent lesion with destruction of the buccal and lingual cortices. A radiographic differential diagnosis included central giant cell granuloma, ameloblastoma, odontogenic myxoma, and keratocystic odontogenic tumor.

An incisional biopsy was performed. Histologic sections revealed a combination of follicular, plexiform, and desmoplastic patterns characteristic of ameloblastoma, with extensive areas of granular cells in a fibrous stroma.
