Scattered foci of calcified, dentinoid-like matrix and occasional glandular (duct-like) areas were also observed.

A 63-year-old right-handed woman presented with a slowly but progressively growing mass on the volar ulnar aspect of her right wrist. She reported pain worsened with wrist flexion, persistent swelling, and reduced sensation, impeding daily activities. Her medical history was unremarkable; there was no prior trauma or sports-related injury. Physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness palmar to the right distal radioulnar joint and flexor carpi ulnaris tendon. Pain was rated 3/10 at rest and 6–7/10 with movement. Active range of motion of the affected wrist was 50° extension, 50° flexion, 5° ulnar deviation, and 20° radial deviation (compared with 70° extension, 80° flexion, 20° ulnar deviation, and 30° radial deviation on the contralateral side). She also had bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome confirmed by neurographic studies. MRI of the wrist showed a volar-directed mass arising from the distal radioulnar joint measuring 12×17 mm with internal fluid-equivalent signal and peripheral hypointense areas on T2-weighted images.

A 64-year-old white man presented with a one-year history of right-sided facial and nasal pain, progressive ipsilateral nasal obstruction, and occasional epistaxis. He reported no weight loss, anorexia, or fatigue, and his overall health was preserved (Karnofsky performance status 90%). 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated a large, solid mass (3.8 × 3.1 × 5.1 cm) occupying the right nasal cavity, extending into the left nasal cavity, ethmoidal air cells, and cribriform plate with evidence of bony erosion. Incisional biopsy of the right maxillary sinus lesion revealed an undifferentiated carcinoma. Further CT imaging of the brain and paranasal sinuses confirmed a solid lesion involving the ethmoidal cells, nasal cavity, and right sphenoid sinus, extending to the floor of the sella turcica with erosion but without intracranial extension. There was bilateral maxillary sinus mucosal thickening (predominantly right) and septal deviation to the left. CT of the neck showed no cervical lymphadenopathy. The patient was staged as clinical T4aN0M0.

A 45-year-old man was evaluated in the otolaryngology clinic for progressive hoarseness, loud snoring, and episodes of “drowning” or gasping during sleep. He had no significant past medical history. On flexible laryngoscopic examination, the laryngeal inlet appeared narrowed, with an impression of external compression. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the neck showed a retropharyngeal mass measuring approximately 4 × 8 × 12 cm. The lesion was well circumscribed, contained a few thin, regular septae, did not enhance after intravenous contrast administration, and had uniformly low attenuation values (mean –80 HU) throughout the mass.

A 48-year-old Asian woman presented with a 15-day history of headache and intermittent bleeding from her right nasal cavity. She had a history of hypertension treated with amlodipine and enalapril. Anterior rhinoscopy showed a mildly deviated nasal septum and a right-sided nasal polyp. There was no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. A computed tomography scan revealed a low-density lesion with a few soft-tissue–density areas completely filling the right maxillary sinus and extending into the middle meatus and posterior nasal cavity, with widening of the antrum; no bony destruction was noted. The radiologic impression was an antrochoanal polyp. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. The patient underwent endoscopic polypectomy and middle meatal antrostomy. Multiple irregular gray-brown soft-tissue fragments measuring up to 3.0 × 2.0 × 1.5 cm were submitted for histopathology. Microscopic examination revealed mature adipose tissue admixed with hematopoietic cells, including myeloid, erythroid, and megakaryocytic lineages.

A 71-year-old Caucasian man, with a 15–cigarette/day smoking history and no other significant medical or family history, presented with a 1-year history of an asymptomatic lesion on the lateral aspect of his lower lip. On examination, there was a 1.8-cm ulcerated, exophytic, irregularly shaped, indurated mass at the mucocutaneous junction of the right lower lip. The remainder of the oral mucosa was unremarkable. Palpation of the neck revealed no lymphadenopathy or tenderness. Routine laboratory analyses were within normal limits. Clinical differential diagnoses included squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma with sebaceous differentiation, and salivary gland neoplasms. Under local anesthesia, the lesion was excised with 0.5-cm margins in a W-shaped wedge, and the defect was primarily closed without complications.

A 47-year-old Caucasian man presented with rapid-onset blurred vision in his right eye. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/64 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Slit-lamp examination of the anterior chamber was normal. Ophthalmoscopic examination revealed multiple pigmented placoid lesions in the posterior pole and midperiphery of both retinas and a serous macular detachment in the right eye. Optical coherence tomography confirmed the macular neurosensory detachment in the right eye. Fundus fluorescein angiography showed arterial-phase hypofluorescence of the lesions with progressive hyperfluorescence in subsequent phases in both eyes and complete filling of the neurosensory detachment in the late phases in the right eye. On further history, he reported that a cutaneous malignant melanoma on his upper back had been excised 6 years earlier (superficial spreading type, Clark level III, Breslow thickness 0.71 mm). Clinical suspicion of choroidal metastases was raised.

A 67-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of bleeding from the mouth, nose, and skin. Two weeks earlier, imaging had detected a splenic mass. She had no prior medical history. On examination, the spleen was not palpable. Laboratory testing revealed severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count, 1 × 10^9/L), which did not respond to recombinant human thrombopoietin, intravenous immunoglobulin, or methylprednisolone. A contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan showed splenomegaly with a 57 × 58 mm patchy low-density lesion. In the arterial phase, the lesion exhibited moderate peripheral enhancement and central hypoenhancement; in the venous phase, there was slightly reduced enhancement centrally. A preliminary diagnosis of splenic hamartoma was made, and the patient was scheduled for laparoscopic splenectomy.

A 9-year-old girl presented with a 5-day history of ocular redness and periorbital pain following conjunctivitis treated with topical antibiotics. Two days after the initial red eye, she was diagnosed with right anterior uveitis and started on topical steroids. Over the next week she developed headache, malaise, episodes of intense perspiration, blurred vision, ocular pain, and lethargy without respiratory symptoms; repeated SARS-CoV-2 antigen tests were negative.

On admission her best-corrected visual acuity was 0.6 in the right eye and 1.0 in the left eye. Slit-lamp exam of the right eye showed conjunctival hyperemia, perikeratic reaction, corneal edema, endothelial dusting, pigment dispersion, and a sluggish pupil; there was moderate vitreous haze. Funduscopy revealed a hyperemic, moderately elevated optic disc with blurred margins. The left eye was unremarkable. Intraocular pressures were 9 mmHg (right) and 12 mmHg (left). Optical coherence tomography confirmed moderate thickening of the right retinal nerve fiber layer.

Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, an ESR of 110 mm/h, CRP of 95.8 mg/L, fibrinogen of 470 mg/dL, and procalcitonin of 0.038 µg/L. Two days into IV antibiotics and topical steroids, she developed left eye hyperemia and periorbital pain; funduscopy showed mild hyperemia and blurred disc margins. Cranial CT was normal. Infectious studies—including QuantiFERON, serologies for CMV, EBV, toxoplasma, and toxocara—and cultures for resistant organisms were negative. ANA, C-ANCA, p-ANCA, and ACE levels were normal, and there was no history of autoimmune disease, joint pain, or skin rash.

A 48-year-old woman presented with progressive swelling of the left cheek. Three years prior, she noted a painless palpable mass on the left cheek, initially the size of her fifth finger tip. Over the next three years, the mass enlarged to roughly an adult fist and became painful. She also developed left epiphora, exophthalmos, blurry vision, rhinitis, and lost 23 kg in six months. She denied headaches, seizures, prior malignancy, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or surgery. On examination, there was a single 6 × 5 × 10 cm fixed, hard, irregular mass in the left maxillary-nasal-infraorbital region with intraoral ulceration of the left maxillary gingiva. Visual acuity was 5/5 in the right eye and 5/6 in the left, with normal intraocular pressures. Panoramic radiographs showed permeative maxillary sinus destruction with a sunburst periosteal reaction, a broad transitional zone, and a chondroid-type matrix. A CT scan suggested an aggressive primary malignant bone tumor, most likely chondrogenic osteosarcoma, with bilateral maxillary sinusitis and submandibular and posterior trigonum lymphadenopathy. Thoracic radiography showed no pulmonary metastases. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy yielded hypercellular specimens with anaplastic oval-round pleomorphic nuclei, binucleation, hyperchromasia, and an eosinophilic matrix.

A 65-year-old man with a history of mild hypertension began experiencing new throbbing occipital and retro-orbital headaches three months before presentation, without phonophobia or photophobia. Initial vital signs and neurologic examination were normal. He was treated as a primary headache disorder with over-the-counter medications, with no relief. One month later, he developed persistent severe headache and mild intermittent confusion. At an outside hospital, lumbar puncture revealed protein 58 mg/dL, 38 nucleated cells, and 206 RBC; cytology, viral, and bacterial studies were negative, and opening pressure was normal. Noncontrast head CT was unremarkable. CT angiography showed possible diminutive distal MCAs and ACAs bilaterally. Brain MRI with and without contrast and MR venogram were normal. Digital subtraction angiography revealed segmental narrowing of distal MCA branches. A working diagnosis of vasculitic meningitis was made, and he was treated with high-dose prednisone with taper, but symptoms worsened, including encephalopathy and new gait instability.

On transfer for further evaluation, repeat brain MRI with gadolinium demonstrated a new 12 mm mass-like focus of enhancement in the pineal region abutting the tectum, adjacent right midbrain T2 signal abnormality, and prominent leptomeningeal enhancement over the parieto‐occipital sulci and superior cerebellum. Lumbar spine MRI with contrast showed small enhancing foci around the cauda equina. Repeat lumbar puncture revealed 4000 RBC, 126 nucleated cells (lymphocytic predominance), protein 144 mg/dL, and glucose 23 mg/dL; opening pressure was normal. CSF bacterial, TB, and fungal cultures and viral PCRs were negative. CSF cytology identified large plasmacytoid cells with frequent cytoplasmic vacuoles. Flow cytometry showed no monoclonal B-cell population.

A 67-year-old woman was referred in February 2021 for evaluation of an adnexal mass. Her history was notable for HCV-related hepatocellular carcinoma diagnosed in 2009 (Edmonson and Steiner grade 2, pT2 N0 M0, G2, V1), treated with left hepatectomy and cholecystectomy. Preoperative AFP had been 8600 ng/mL and fell to 2.7 ng/mL postoperatively; there was no cirrhosis and no other disease localization at that time.

At routine follow-up in October 2020, serum AFP had risen to 467 ng/mL and CA-125 was borderline at 37.4 U/mL. Liver function tests were normal and imaging of the residual liver showed no lesions. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed bilateral ovarian enlargement, more pronounced on the left (55 × 33 × 58 mm) with solid-cystic features and calcifications; there was a small pelvic fluid collection but no lymphadenopathy or peritoneal disease. Pelvic ultrasound confirmed a left multilocular-solid ovarian cyst measuring 62 × 23 × 34 mm with a color score of 2 (IOTA risk of malignancy 59.6%) and mild pelvic effusion.

After multidisciplinary review, the patient underwent laparoscopic left ovariectomy and peritoneal biopsies. Intraoperative frozen section demonstrated a tumor with solid trabecular architecture and atypical cells with a high mitotic index, requiring further characterization. A laparotomic hysterectomy, right oophorectomy, pelvic peritonectomy, and omentectomy were then performed, with no residual macroscopic disease.

A 70-year-old Caucasian man with no significant medical history presented with a three-week history of headache and right-sided maxillary pain, followed by recent onset of dysphonia and dysphagia for solids.  
On neurologic examination, there was paresis of cranial nerves IX and X, with displacement of the soft palate to the right and difficulty swallowing; paresis of cranial nerves XI and XII, with lowering of the right shoulder, hypotonia of the right trapezius muscle, rightward deviation of the tongue, hypotonia, and muscle twitching on the right. The remainder of the physical examination was normal.  
Laboratory studies showed an alkaline phosphatase level of 350 UI/L; other blood tests were within normal limits.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the larynx and neck demonstrated an asymmetrical union between the clivus and the right occipital condyle adjacent to the jugular foramen, with increased ground-glass bone density and no cortical or soft-tissue lesion.  
MRI of the skull base revealed a bone lesion at the right occipital condyle and adjacent basilar bone that was hypointense on T1- and T2-weighted sequences, with moderate gadolinium enhancement causing slight narrowing of the jugular foramen and condylar canal.  
Therefore, fibrous dysplasia, Paget’s disease and metastasis were considered in the differential diagnosis.

A 27-year-old woman presented with a 10-week history of swelling and intermittent pain in the right cheek, worsening with mastication. She had no significant medical history. On examination, the overlying mucosa was intact, with no inflammation, ulceration, or discharge. Bimanual palpation revealed a 1.5 × 1 cm soft, lobulated, tender mass beneath the mucosal layer of the right buccal mucosa. An orthopantomogram showed no bony pathology. 

Under local anesthesia, the lesion was excised via a horizontal incision on the buccal mucosa. Grossly, the specimen was yellowish, well circumscribed, rubbery, and measured 2.2 × 1.5 cm with a solid, lobulated cut surface. 

Microscopic examination revealed a nodular tumor with lobulated, follicular, and focal invasive areas. The cells were monomorphic epithelioid, with vacuolated eosinophilic cytoplasm, central round nuclei, and small nucleoli. Follicles contained colloid-like eosinophilic secretions, and there was no mitotic activity or necrosis. 

Immunohistochemical staining showed that the tumor cells were positive for SOX-10, GATA-3, and MUC-4, and negative for cytokeratin 7.

A 75-year-old woman presented with a new lump in her left breast. She had undergone right mastectomy, axillary dissection, radiotherapy, and reconstruction for invasive ductal carcinoma 21 years earlier. Her medical history included hypertension, a pacemaker for arrhythmia, and anticoagulation with acenocoumarol for pulmonary embolism. On physical examination, a firm, nodular lesion was palpable in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast without overlying skin changes. Mammography revealed a dish-shaped skin nodule measuring approximately 1.4 cm in the upper outer quadrant. Breast ultrasound confirmed a 14 × 8 mm lesion in the dermal/subcutaneous layer, and Doppler imaging showed marked hypervascularity. Magnetic resonance imaging could not be performed because of the pacemaker. On the basis of these imaging features, a probable diagnosis of angiosarcoma was made.

A 26-year-old woman was referred after the incidental discovery of a liver tumor during a routine medical examination 3 days earlier. She denied pain, systemic symptoms, or localized compressive signs. Her medical history was unremarkable. On admission, temperature was 36.5 °C, heart rate 81 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, blood pressure 121/70 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Physical examination revealed no abnormalities.

Laboratory tests showed a slight increase in gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (70.0 U/L; normal range up to 50 U/L) and total bilirubin (19.2 μmol/L; normal up to 17 μmol/L). Other liver enzymes and blood counts were within normal limits.

Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a well-encapsulated, hyperechoic mass approximately 5.0 cm × 5.0 cm in the left hepatic lobe. Noncontrast computed tomography (CT) revealed a quasi-circular, mixed-density mass measuring 5.0 cm × 6.0 cm × 5.0 cm in segment 4 of the liver. On contrast-enhanced CT, the lesion showed no early arterial phase enhancement, but peripheral and central regions enhanced during the portal and delayed phases. CT angiography confirmed a hypervascular intrahepatic mass with vessels not arising from the main hepatic arterial branches.

An 8-year-old boy was evaluated after two brief episodes of transient loss of consciousness, each preceded by warmth, light-headedness, and chest discomfort. There was no fever, vomiting, abnormal movements, frothing, incontinence, or postictal confusion. On examination, pulse was 100 bpm, regular, with synchronous peripheral pulses and no radiofemoral delay. Blood pressure was 210/140 mm Hg. Cardiovascular examination revealed a heaving apex, a normal first heart sound, a widely split second heart sound, and a short systolic murmur at the apex. 

Baseline blood tests were normal except for a serum potassium level of 2.8 mmol/L. Electrocardiography showed a prolonged QT interval of 0.47 seconds. Echocardiography demonstrated concentric left ventricular hypertrophy. Renal Doppler ultrasonography revealed normal renal vessels with a normal flow pattern. Abdominal ultrasonography identified an 8 × 8 cm mass at the hilum of the left kidney with grade II hydronephrosis. Serum cortisol and 24-hour urinary vanillylmandelic acid levels were within normal limits. 

At laparotomy, an 8 × 8 cm mass was found at the left renal hilum, necessitating nephrectomy for complete excision; a single enlarged para-aortic lymph node was also removed. A presumptive diagnosis of Wilms tumor was made, and left nephrectomy with excision biopsy of the lymph node was performed.

A 36-year-old man presented with atraumatic left lateral thigh, groin, and hip pain of more than 1 year’s duration. On examination, range of motion was preserved but he experienced pain with combined hip internal rotation and flexion. Plain radiographs of the left hip showed preserved joint spaces without obvious bony pathology. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a small anterior superior labral tear of the left acetabulum, moderate joint effusion, and a well-circumscribed lesion with mildly heterogeneous marrow signal at the anterolateral femoral head–neck junction, interpreted as a synovial herniation pit. Joint aspiration yielded no fluid, and intra-articular lidocaine improved his tolerance of FABER and FADIR testing. One month later, computed tomography again showed preserved joint spaces and identified the same well-defined subcortical defect at the anterior femoral head–neck junction, thought to represent a synovial herniation pit. Two months after presentation, he underwent left hip arthroscopy with femoroplasty for presumed cam impingement, acetabuloplasty, labral debridement, and synovectomy. Intraoperatively, frond-like synovitis with marked erythema, chondromalacia beneath the torn labrum, synovitis of the ligamentum teres, and the labral tear were noted. Synovial biopsy revealed no neoplasia or metaplasia; inflammation was attributed to chronic traumatic changes. Two months postoperatively, his pain had improved, and he was progressing with physical therapy. Three months postoperatively, he reported continued discomfort at night but overall improvement in pain. Six months postoperatively, he again complained of significant groin pain similar to his preoperative discomfort and was unable to resume exercise. Plain radiographs showed a presumed synovial herniation pit at the anterior femoral neck. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed moderate increased T2 signal within the left femoral neck and a focal, oval-shaped cortical irregularity measuring approximately 1.3 cm at the anterior head–neck junction, again interpreted as a synovial herniation pit, along with moderate synovial irregularity.

A 4-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of a painless, soft, polypoid nodule on the right chest wall. Over the preceding 3 months, it had enlarged from a pinpoint lesion to approximately 0.9 cm × 0.8 cm × 0.7 cm. On ultrasound, the lesion was heterogeneous and hypoechoic without definitive internal vascularity, findings most suggestive of a hematoma. Because of progressive growth, the lesion was excised. 

Microscopic examination showed a well-circumscribed, unencapsulated dermal nodule extending into subcutaneous adipose tissue, composed of spindle and epithelioid cells with prominent granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and vesicular nuclei. No cytologic atypia was seen, and surgical margins were negative.

Immunohistochemical staining revealed that the tumor cells were positive for CD68 and negative for S100, AE1/AE3/PCK26, SOX10, and neuron-specific enolase (NSE).

A 29-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of cough, intermittent hemoptysis, and progressive exertional dyspnea. He denied fevers, weight loss, rash, joint pains, hematuria, or toxin exposures. His medical history included childhood nephrotic syndrome in remission; he had a 5–pack-year smoking history and no HIV risk factors. 

On examination, he was afebrile, with an oxygen saturation of 90% on room air; the only findings were pallor and bilateral rhonchi. Chest radiography showed patchy bilateral infiltrates. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 6.5 g/dL, white cells 10.7 × 10^3/mm^3, platelets 273 × 10^3/mm^3, and a microcytic, hypochromic anemia; renal and liver functions, coagulation profile, and urinalysis were normal. 

Bronchoscopy demonstrated diffuse oozing of blood from segmental bronchi bilaterally. Serologic tests including antinuclear antibody, anti–ribonucleoprotein, anti–basement membrane, antineutrophil cytoplasmic, and antiphospholipid antibodies, as well as complement and cryoglobulin levels, were all normal. HIV testing was negative. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed peripheral ground-glass and reticular opacities in both lungs and a nonhomogeneous anterior mediastinal mass. A CT-guided biopsy of the mediastinal lesion was nondiagnostic.

A 25-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of left knee pain that worsened after a Judo competition. He had no prior trauma, no relevant family or medical history. On examination, there was slight atrophy of the left thigh (42 cm versus 45 cm on the right) but no tenderness, swelling, warmth, redness, or limitation of motion.  
Plain radiographs of the knee showed a 1.7 × 2.4 cm soap bubble–like radiolucent area in the medial patella without periosteal reaction.  
MRI revealed a lesion in the patella that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed diffuse enhancement after gadolinium; the lesion was multicystic with fluid–fluid levels and no obvious invasion into adjacent muscle or joint.

A 39-year-old Hispanic woman presented with 8 months of atraumatic, nonspecific right ankle pain that worsened at night and was partially relieved with activity modification. She denied fevers, weight loss, or other symptoms. On examination, the right ankle had a limited and painful range of motion but no skin lesions, masses, edema, or lymphadenopathy; neurovascular status was intact. The initial clinical diagnosis was posterior tibial tendonitis, and she was treated with an ankle brace, oral steroids, and physical therapy without improvement.

Conventional radiographs revealed a lytic lesion in the right medial malleolus. MRI showed contrast-enhancing marrow-replacement lesions in the medial malleolus and lateral calcaneus without significant cortical or soft-tissue involvement. A whole-body bone scan demonstrated multiple lesions throughout the bilateral lower extremities. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 54 mm/h and a C-reactive protein level of 32.65 mg/L; the white-blood-cell count was normal. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no evidence of organ involvement.

A CT-guided core-needle biopsy described “lymphoplasmatic infiltrate with fibrosis suspicious for chronic osteomyelitis.” Because of persistent symptoms, an open biopsy was performed; intraoperatively, cysts containing apparent purulence were noted, and a specimen was sent to the laboratory to rule out lymphoma. The osseous lesion was excised and packed with cancellous bone chips.

A 48-year-old man was referred after routine health screening revealed a right retroperitoneal mass. He had a 5-year history of hypertension (up to 180/100 mmHg), managed with telmisartan; he was asymptomatic. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including CA 72-4, α-fetoprotein, CEA, CA 19-9, CA 12-5, and NSE, were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed an 8.0 × 7.0 × 5.0 cm oval mass in the right perinephric space with homogeneous isodensity and a clear margin. In the arterial phase, the lesion demonstrated intense heterogeneous enhancement, followed by rapid homogeneous washout in the portal-venous and delayed phases. There was no evidence of renal invasion, and the tumor compressed the adjacent duodenum. Multiplanar reconstruction revealed that the blood supply arose from the right testicular artery.

MRI of the abdomen demonstrated a perinephric mass with low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, slightly high signal on T2-weighted images, and restricted diffusion on DWI. On dynamic gadolinium-enhanced fat-suppressed T1-weighted sequences, the enhancement pattern mirrored CT, with a conspicuous enhancing capsule. A hyperintense central stellate area on T2-weighted images showed delayed enhancement in the portal-venous and delayed phases.

A 48-year-old woman noted a tender mass inferior to her right inframammary fold 6 weeks after minor trauma. Despite a course of antibiotics for presumed infection, the lesion persisted, and she was referred for surgical evaluation. On examination, there was a 2 × 1 cm superficial mass with an adjacent accessory nipple.  
Ultrasound imaging demonstrated a 15-mm hypoechoic lesion thought to be a sebaceous cyst. A core needle biopsy of the mass was performed.  
Biopsy results revealed Grade 2 invasive ductal carcinoma with strong estrogen and progesterone receptor positivity (Allred scores of ER 7, PR 7) and negative HER2 status.  
Breast MRI showed a 22 × 12 mm spiculated mass deep to the accessory nipple, with overlying skin infiltration and a clear margin between the tumour and the costal fascia. No masses were identified in either native breast.

A 37-year-old woman presented with a 9-month history of diffuse axial and low back pain. On neurologic examination, she had hypesthesia in the left lower limb and bilateral hyperactive deep-tendon reflexes. Spinal MRI with gadolinium revealed an intramedullary lesion at the T8–T9 level with both solid (hypointense) and cystic (hyperintense) components on T2-weighted images, dishomogeneous contrast enhancement after gadolinium administration, and an associated cranial syrinx.

Under intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring, the patient underwent T8–T9 laminotomy and gross total resection of the lesion. Histologic examination showed a neoplasm composed of round to oval cells with finely dispersed chromatin and small nucleoli; ganglion cell differentiation was commonly present among the neurocytic cells. Hyalinized blood vessels were also observed. There were no atypical features such as mitotic activity, microvascular proliferation, or necrosis. Immunohistochemically, the neoplastic cells were positive for synaptophysin, and the MIB-1 labeling index was 1%.

A 7-year-old boy with unremarkable medical history presented with a 3-month history of a gradually enlarging, painless, firm swelling in the right frontal bone region just behind his hairline. On examination, the mass measured 4.0×4.5×4.0 cm, was non-tender, firm to hard, fixed to bone, with a smooth surface and overlying skin that was normal in appearance. There were no neurologic deficits, and systemic examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory investigations were within normal limits. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the skull showed an expansile extraaxial osteolytic heterogeneous mass, 4.5 cm in diameter, involving the right frontal bone with thinning and focal breach of both cortices. The lesion abutted the superior sagittal sinus without evidence of involvement or thrombosis. Internally, it demonstrated septations with a soap-bubble appearance and areas of spontaneous hyperdensity suggestive of hemorrhagic sediment; no solid nodules were seen.

MRI revealed a well-circumscribed, multilocular frontal cystic lesion (58×45×30 mm) with a hypointense capsule on T1 and T2 sequences, laminating both tables of the cranial vault and compressing but not occluding the superior sagittal sinus. The cyst contents were low signal on T1, high on T2/FLAIR, and showed multiple fluid–fluid levels (high T1, intermediate T2). There was heterogeneous enhancement of septa after gadolinium administration, no diffusion restriction, and T2* hypointense areas consistent with hemosiderin deposition.

Selective angiography demonstrated that the mass derived its blood supply predominantly from the anterior and posterior frontal branches of the superficial temporal artery. A frontal craniectomy and en bloc excision were planned without preoperative embolization. However, surgery was postponed due to the SARS-CoV-2 crisis, and the patient was discharged with an outpatient follow-up appointment.

A 54-year-old man was noted to have left proptosis on routine examination. He was otherwise asymptomatic and had no diplopia, nystagmus, or stigmata of neurofibromatosis. Visual acuity was 20/320 bilaterally, and visual fields were normal. Noncontrast computed tomography of the orbits confirmed an intraconal mass causing left proptosis. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a well-demarcated 43 mm mass compressing the optic nerve medially; the lesion was hyperintense on T2-weighted images and showed heterogeneous enhancement on contrast-enhanced T1-weighted fat-suppressed sequences. Digital subtraction angiography revealed no apparent tumor blush or abnormal vessels, though VasoCT demonstrated feeders from the ophthalmic artery encircling the anterior pole of the mass. The differential diagnosis included cavernous hemangioma, schwannoma, and meningioma.

A 43-year-old man was referred with a new-onset 8-minute loss of consciousness at home. There was no seizure activity, mouth frothing, ocular deviation, headache, nausea, or vomiting. Four days earlier, MRI at an outside hospital had shown a right temporofrontal lobe mass with surrounding edema.  

On arrival, he was fully conscious and well oriented (GCS 15). He had no prior episodes, no significant medical or family history, and denied fever, weight loss, or night sweats. Vital signs were within normal limits. Examination revealed no palpable lymphadenopathy; cardiorespiratory and abdominal examinations were unremarkable except for a single spider angioma on the abdomen. Neurologic examination showed symmetric pupils, intact cranial nerves, normal motor strength (5/5), and no pathologic reflexes.  

He was a current smoker and drank alcohol occasionally. A repeat contrast-enhanced brain MRI demonstrated a right temporofrontal lobe mass with subdural extension and perilesional edema. EEG findings were unremarkable. A CT scan of the chest revealed a left lower-lung nodule and changes consistent with chronic inflammation.  

The initial radiologic differential diagnosis included meningioma and glioma.

A 47-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of painful swelling of the left side of her face. She noted a longstanding mass of 15 years’ duration that had grown slowly until accelerating in size over the past 6 months. There was no history of prior biopsy or treatment of the lesion. Physical examination revealed a firm, tender, nonmobile mass over the left zygomatic region. Plain radiographs demonstrated a 3 cm × 2 cm destructive lesion of the left zygomatic bone. A CT scan showed a lobulated, well-demarcated osteolytic lesion of the zygomatic bone with cortical expansion and partial destruction.

An 85-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and dyslipidemia was referred for evaluation of right eyelid droop. She reported a 3-month history of right ptosis and no diplopia. During this time, she experienced back and hip pain; laboratory testing by her family physician showed hemoglobin 95 g/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 94 mm/h, and C-reactive protein 106.6 mg/L. One week before ophthalmology consultation, she fell and underwent head CT, which showed an old right basal ganglia infarct; spine and clavicle X-rays showed only degenerative changes.

On initial ophthalmologic examination:  
• Best-corrected visual acuity: 20/70 OD, 20/30 OS  
• Pupils equal, reactive; mild relative afferent pupillary defect on the right  
• Right ptosis and complete limitation of elevation in the right eye; other ductions full  
• Anterior segment: grade 2 nuclear sclerotic cataracts bilaterally  
• Posterior segment: mild right optic disc edema  

She was diagnosed with a right superior-division third nerve palsy and admitted for further evaluation. MRI of the brain and orbits with contrast showed diffuse heterogeneous osseous lesions throughout the skull and a soft-tissue mass in the right orbital apex involving the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone and orbital canal.

A 20-year-old man presented with a painless left axillary mass of 2 months’ duration. His medical history was unremarkable. On examination, vital signs were stable, and a firm, 8 × 7 cm mass was palpable in the left axilla without hepatosplenomegaly or generalized lymphadenopathy. 

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count with differential and biochemical tests, were within normal limits. Chest radiography and abdominal ultrasonography revealed no abnormalities. Left axillary ultrasonography showed a well-defined superficial mass with punctate calcifications and no evidence of hemorrhage or necrosis, suggestive of an enlarged lymph node.

The mass was surgically excised for further evaluation.

A 63-year-old woman presented in acute respiratory distress with hypercapnic respiratory failure requiring endotracheal intubation. Physical examination revealed a large, firm, immobile mass in the left submandibular region. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a bulky heterogeneous mass centered in the thyroid region, extending into the surrounding soft tissues. Multiple core biopsies showed a malignant mesenchymal neoplasm without the typical cytomorphologic features of a primary thyroid carcinoma. Immunohistochemical stains of the tumor cells were positive for vimentin, CD34, and caldesmon, with focal positivity for smooth muscle actin; type IV collagen staining exhibited a distinctive pericellular membranous pattern. Next‐generation sequencing of the lesion identified mutations in RECQL4, PDGFRB, NRG1, MYC, and MED12.

A 27-year-old nulliparous woman presented with a slowly enlarging lump in the vulvar region over a 2-year period. She denied pain, discharge, bleeding, prior vulvar lesions, or systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a hard, mobile, nodular subdermal mass measuring 30 × 20 mm on the mons pubis, situated about 2 cm superior to the clitoris and 1 cm lateral to the midline. The lesion was fixed to the overlying skin, which had a normal appearance, was nontender, and showed no discharge or bleeding. There were no palpable inguinal lymph nodes. A preoperative ultrasound scan demonstrated a well-defined subcutaneous mass without increased vascularity. An excision biopsy of the lesion was performed under regional anesthesia.

A 3-year-old girl presented with progressive shortness of breath of several months’ duration. She had no fever, night sweats, weight loss, vomiting, flushing, hypertension, or abdominal pain. Physical examination was notable only for low oxygen saturation; routine laboratory tests were normal. A chest radiograph showed opacity of the entire right hemithorax and scoliosis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a well-circumscribed solid mass measuring 10.2 × 9.2 × 11.8 cm in the right posterior mediastinum, extending from the first thoracic vertebra to the level of the heart. The mass was hypodense and mildly heterogeneous, contained punctate calcifications, caused contralateral displacement of mediastinal structures and trachea, demonstrated mild heterogeneous contrast enhancement, and showed no invasion of adjacent organs or the chest wall. There was no evidence of spinal destruction, and nerve involvement could not be assessed.

An 11-year-old girl presented with a 1-month history of a progressively enlarging, painful swelling of the left cheek associated with left nasal obstruction, rhinorrhea, and weight loss. She had no significant medical history or trauma. On examination, there was a hard, well-defined 4×3 cm para-nasal mass on the left, extending into the infraorbital region; ophthalmologic, otologic, oral, and cervical examinations were otherwise normal. Routine laboratory studies were unremarkable. Craniofacial CT revealed a 43×39×41 mm tissue lesion centered in the left maxillary sinus with mixed lytic and sclerotic features, irregular borders, and heterogeneous enhancement. The lesion elevated and thinned the orbital floor, lysed the walls of the maxillary sinus and alveolar bone exposing dental roots, invaded the soft palate, and infiltrated adjacent jugal soft tissues; it also breached the papyraceous lamina into the left nasal cavity and septum. No cervical lymphadenopathy was noted.

A 28-year-old man presented with four weeks of progressive dyspnea—initially on exertion, later at rest—and two weeks of pleuritic chest pain. He had a remote history of treated pulmonary tuberculosis but no prior cardiac disease. On arrival, blood pressure was 90/60 mm Hg, heart rate 114 bpm, respiratory rate 27/min, and oxygen saturation 84% on room air. Cardiac examination showed a regular rhythm, a diminished second heart sound, and a grade III holosystolic murmur best heard at the left upper sternal border. Lung bases had crackles; there was no peripheral edema or jugular venous distension. SARS-CoV-2 antigen test was negative. Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 14.9×10^9/L, metabolic acidosis, and hyponatremia. Electrocardiography showed sinus rhythm, complete right bundle branch block, and signs of right ventricular systolic overload. 

A noncontrast CT of the chest demonstrated fibroatelectatic tracts, traction bronchiectasis and pleural thickening, and a hypodense mass in the right ventricle attached to the interventricular septum. CT pulmonary angiography ruled out pulmonary embolism and instead confirmed a pedunculated intracardiac mass in the right ventricle. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a heterogeneous echogenic mass in the right ventricle. Transesophageal echocardiography showed a 36×46 mm heterogeneous mass with regular borders attached to the basal interventricular septum, causing dynamic obstruction of the right ventricular outflow tract, mild tricuspid regurgitation, and right ventricular dilation. A contrast-enhanced thoracoabdominal and pelvic CT scan showed no other abnormalities.

A 58-year-old woman presented after a single episode of a rounded mass protruding from her anus during defecation, which she manually reduced. She reported normal bowel habits and denied abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, weight loss, or a family history of colorectal disease. Examination revealed no abdominal tenderness or masses; stool testing was positive for occult blood. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 11.6 gm/dL, consistent with mild hypochromic microcytic anemia, and a normal carcinoembryonic antigen level. Other routine blood tests were within normal limits. Colonoscopy revealed a large (approximately 8 cm), smooth-surfaced but highly vascular polyp occupying two thirds of the sigmoid lumen 14 cm from the anal verge; the stalk was not clearly identified. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a well-defined, circumferential arterial enhancing bowel mass measuring 8.1 cm in length arising from the distal descending colon, with entrapped fat attenuations within the lumen and no mesenteric lymphadenopathy; radiographic interpretation suggested a fat-containing mesenchymal tumor (GISTS) of the colon. To avoid hemorrhage, no biopsy was performed, and the patient underwent surgical resection of the sigmoid segment containing the lesion; the resected specimen was sent for histologic examination.

A 47-year-old woman presented with worsening dyspnea over 2 weeks. She denied chest pain, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, hemoptysis, and right-upper-quadrant pain. She had no history of coronary disease, pulmonary disease, cancer, or prior cardiac surgery. Family history was noncontributory.

On examination, temperature was 36.5°C, blood pressure 135/85 mmHg, heart rate 82 beats/min. A 4/6 mid-diastolic murmur was heard at the apex. There was bilateral pitting edema of the lower extremities and expiratory wheezing. The New York Heart Association functional class was III.

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count with differential, cardiac enzymes, and three sets of blood cultures, revealed no evidence of infection. Chest radiography demonstrated displacement and widening of the carina, elevation of the left main bronchus, Kerley B lines, cardiomegaly with a straightened left border, and prominent pulmonary vasculature. Electrocardiography showed atrial fibrillation with right-axis deviation.

Three-dimensional transesophageal echocardiography revealed:  
• Severe rheumatic mitral stenosis (mitral valve area by pressure half-time 0.6 cm2; mean gradient 15 mmHg) with mild regurgitation.  
• A markedly enlarged left atrium with a 40×14 mm heterogeneous semi-mobile thrombus attached to its anterior wall and a 15×17 mm thrombus in the left atrial appendage.  
• Moderate tricuspid regurgitation, severe pulmonary hypertension, and preserved left ventricular systolic function with D-shaped septum.  
• A small (10×4 mm), hypermobile, worm-like mass attached to the arterial side of the aortic valve.

A 21-month-old full-term boy with known lactose intolerance was referred for evaluation of an incidentally discovered left renal mass. His mother noted progressive abdominal distension accompanied by polyuria, polydipsia, and constipation. The parents are consanguineous; two healthy brothers and ten sisters, two of whom died in childhood. 

On examination, vital signs were normal. Height and weight were at the 25th percentile. The abdomen was distended, soft, and lax without palpable masses or ascites. There were clinical signs of active rickets. Genital examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed serum creatinine 37 µmol/L, phosphorus 0.81 mmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 2178 U/L, vitamin D 16.8 ng/mL, blood glucose 8.9 mmol/L with HbA1c 5.5%, and LDH 186 U/L. CBC revealed polycythemia (Hb 18.1 g/dL, Hct 52.6%). Urinalysis demonstrated glucosuria and aminoaciduria. Genetic testing identified a homozygous c.474A>C p.(Arg158Ser) variant in SLC2A2, confirming Fanconi–Bickel syndrome.

Renal ultrasound showed a sharply marginated peripheral hypoechoic hypovascular mass at the upper pole of the left kidney measuring approximately 2.0 × 1.8 × 2.0 cm. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a solitary, partially exophytic, homogeneously enhancing mass at the left upper pole measuring 1.8 × 1.9 × 2.0 cm. The kidneys were mildly enlarged, and there were radiographic signs of rickets in the ribs and femurs.

A 15-year-old boy presented with a 10-year history of pain and progressive sensory and motor deficits in the right median nerve distribution. He noted a slowly growing, soft, non-tender subcutaneous mass over the right thenar eminence. On examination, the mass measured 6 cm in length and 3 cm in width. Thenar intrinsic muscle strength (abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, flexor pollicis brevis) was graded 3/5. Tinel’s sign and Phalen’s test were both positive. Nerve conduction studies showed markedly reduced amplitude and prolonged motor latency of the median nerve; the ulnar nerve was normal. Plain radiographs of the hand and wrist revealed no bony abnormalities. Ultrasound and MRI demonstrated an enlarged median nerve with a “coaxial cable–like” appearance on axial images and a “spaghetti-like” appearance of interspersed fatty tissue on coronal images.

A 39-year-old Asian man presented with a 4-month history of a painless swelling of the left lateral border of the tongue. The lesion began as a pea-sized nodule and gradually increased to 2×1.5 cm. The patient had no significant medical, surgical, or family history. He denied trauma, pain, bleeding, or paresthesia. A complete blood count was normal. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy. Orthopantomography was unremarkable.

On extraoral examination, multiple soft cutaneous nodules—sessile or pedunculated, ranging from a few millimeters to centimeters—were distributed over the face, trunk, and extremities. Approximately 15 café-au-lait macules (>15 mm) were present; the largest measured 22×13 cm on the right arm and exhibited overlying long dark hair. Rubbing this lesion elicited a transient piloerection (pseudo-Darier sign). Neither axillary freckling nor Lisch nodules were observed.

Intraoral examination revealed a firm, fixed, non-tender, lobulated, smooth-surfaced, ovoid sessile lesion, 2×1.5 cm in size, on the left lateral tongue, with well-circumscribed, non-erythematous margins. The slow-growing, asymptomatic nature of the lesion led to a provisional diagnosis of a benign process. Based on the extraoral signs of neurofibromatosis type 1, a neurofibroma was initially favored. Other differential diagnoses included schwannoma (neurilemmoma), granular cell tumour, focal fibrous hyperplasia (giant cell fibroma), leiomyoma, rhabdomyoma, hemangioma, lymphangioma, lipoma, and benign salivary gland tumours. No further imaging was performed given the small size and benign appearance of the lesion.

An 18-year-old previously healthy man presented with right hip pain and inability to ambulate after a low-energy impact while playing basketball; he felt a sudden inaudible “pop.” He reported excruciating right hip pain and occasional numbness and tingling in the right lower extremity. On examination, there was tenderness to palpation over the right proximal thigh; the skin was intact, and distal neurovascular examination was normal. He had a history of right groin pain 4 to 6 months earlier, with a nondiagnostic ultrasonography at that time. Radiographs of the right hip showed an intertrochanteric femur fracture through a 5.4 × 5.6 cm radiolucent lesion with varus angulation, a narrow zone of transition, and a fine sclerotic rim; a ground-glass matrix was noted. MRI of the right hip demonstrated a well-defined lesion in the proximal femur that was hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2, and showed heterogeneous enhancement post-contrast, with extensive surrounding marrow edema, endosteal scalloping, cortical thinning, and intratumoral bone fragments. CT of the lesion showed a lytic intraosseous mass with well-defined margins, high-grade endosteal scalloping, and posterior cortical buckling. Radiological differential diagnoses included fibrous cortical defect, fibrous dysplasia, bone cyst, giant cell tumor of bone, chondroblastoma, and, less likely, metastasis.

An 88-year-old woman presented with a protruding mass in the manubrium that she first noticed 6 years earlier, with progressive chest pain in the same region for the past 3 months. She had no significant past medical, personal, or family history. On examination, a firm, non-tender, protruding mass was palpated over the sternal manubrium. Routine laboratory studies were within normal limits. 

Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated an aggressive, expansile, osteolytic lesion of the manubrium with cortical destruction. Technetium-99m MDP scintigraphy showed moderately increased uptake localized to the right side of the sternal manubrium without evidence of additional lesions. 

Dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI of the chest revealed that the lesion was hyperintense on T2-weighted sequences, isointense on T1-weighted sequences, and demonstrated mild peripheral nodular enhancement in the early post-contrast phase with progressive centripetal fill-in on delayed-phase images.

A 26-year-old healthy Caucasian Moroccan woman presented with a 4-day history of a painless swelling on the left side of her face. She also reported a 1-month history of weight loss and fatigue. On examination, there was a soft swelling causing facial asymmetry over the left maxillary and mandibular regions and a mobile, medium-sized, painless left cervical lymphadenopathy. Paresthesia of the left mandible and lower lip had been present for 1 month and was improving.

Intraoral examination revealed a firm, reddish, partly ulcerated mass in the vestibular and lingual left mandibular ridge from tooth 38 to 43, not involving the floor of the mouth. A similar mass involved the vestibular and palatal aspects of the left maxillary ridge from tooth 28 to 24, covering the left hard palate. Teeth were free of caries or mobility except for palatal displacement of teeth 23–25. Mouth opening was limited to one and a half finger breadths.

Panoramic radiograph showed widening of the periodontal ligament space at teeth 25, 26, 28, 38, 35, and 44, and radiopacity filling almost the entire right maxillary sinus. CT imaging demonstrated near-total filling of the right maxillary sinus through an enlarged ostium, suggestive of an antrochoanal polyp, and mucosal thickening of the left maxillary sinus floor. Complete blood count was normal except for an elevated eosinophil count (453/mm3).

Given the rapid growth, clinical appearance, periodontal ligament widening, and paresthesia, a malignant tumor was suspected.

A 77-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of a painless, soft mass on the left lateral border of the tongue. Her medical history was notable for hypertension; she had no tobacco or alcohol use and no family history of tumors. On examination, the lesion was movable, 15 mm in diameter, with an intact surface; no cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an 18×12×8 mm, well-circumscribed mass in the tongue, slightly hyperintense on both T1- and T2-weighted images, without vascular or muscular invasion. A clinical diagnosis of lipoma was made, and the lesion was excised. Grossly, the specimen was a 13-mm, yellow, partially encapsulated nodular lesion with a soft texture. Microscopic examination revealed relatively uniform spindle cells separated by mature adipocytes in a collagenous stroma; the spindle cells exhibited minimal cytonuclear atypia, lipoblasts, necrosis, and mitoses were absent, and the lesion showed infiltrative growth at the margins. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated diffuse CD34 positivity in spindle cells, negativity for smooth muscle actin and S-100 protein, and focal MDM2 positivity in adipocytes.

A 55-year-old woman presented with an 8-year history notable for a malignant melanoma of the right thigh (1.05 mm thickness, Clark level IV, no ulceration, negative sentinel node) treated with wide excision. She had been asymptomatic until she developed new-onset back pain and generalized fatigue, followed shortly by painless gross hematuria. Urinalysis confirmed hematuria without infection. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed multiple hepatic and splenic lesions, bilateral subcentimeter pulmonary nodules suspicious for metastatic disease, and several intraluminal bladder masses, the largest measuring 1.9 cm. On cystoscopy, three polypoid, spherical, stalked lesions were identified (two ~2 cm on the left anterior bladder dome; one ~1 cm on the left lateral wall), without any gross discoloration. The tumors were excised by monopolar loop electrocautery, and the bases were fulgurated.

A woman in her late 60s was referred in July 2012 for anemia of at least one and a half years’ duration. Her history included type 2 diabetes, hypertension, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and recurrent urinary tract infections, one complicated by urosepsis. She noted fatigue beginning in 2010–2011; hemoglobin (Hb) had fallen from 13.4 g/dL in 2008 to 8.9 g/dL in February 2011. She had received one transfusion without reaction and experienced exacerbations of anemia during febrile infections. There was no history of acrocyanosis or Raynaud phenomena.

On admission, she appeared well; physical examination was unremarkable, without lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, or acrocyanosis. Chest radiography and abdominal ultrasonography were normal. Laboratory data included: Hb 8.2 g/dL, leukocytes 7.8 × 10^9/L, platelets 263 × 10^9/L, MCV 99 fL, reticulocytes 88 × 10^9/L, CRP 11 mg/L. Iron studies, cobalamin, and folate were normal; ferritin was elevated at 1257 µg/L. LDH was 544 U/L, bilirubin 43 µmol/L, and haptoglobin undetectable. Urinalysis was negative for hemoglobin and protein. Serum albumin was 41 g/L; immunoglobulins were normal (IgG 7.0 g/L, IgA 3.2 g/L, IgM 0.69 g/L). Serum electrophoresis revealed a small monoclonal IgAλ spike. Free λ chains were slightly elevated at 53 mg/L with a normal κ/λ ratio. Direct antiglobulin test was strongly positive for C3d and negative for IgG, IgM, and IgA; cold agglutinin titer was 128 at 4 °C. Erythropoietin was 36 IU/L.

She was diagnosed with primary cold agglutinin disease (CAD). A bone marrow biopsy in 2012 showed erythroid hyperplasia and small lymphocytic infiltrates interpreted as lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma; flow cytometry identified two clonal populations: κ-positive B lymphocytes and λ-positive plasma cells. She remained stable (Hb 9.0–10.0 g/dL) on supportive care alone.

By late spring 2016, fatigue and atrial fibrillation worsened. Hb declined to 8.5 g/dL, reticulocytes rose to 191 × 10^9/L, LDH 303 U/L, bilirubin 96 µmol/L, haptoglobin < 0.1 g/L, IgA increased to 12.5 g/L, and cold agglutinin titer rose to 512. She received four weekly doses of rituximab (375 mg/m^2), after which Hb normalized and hemolysis resolved, but IgA rose further to 19.6 g/L by January 2017.

From June 2017, Hb declined again and IgA continued to rise. In January 2018, she had severe lumbar pain. One month later, Hb was 9.5 g/dL, reticulocytes 153 × 10^9/L, LDH and bilirubin unchanged, IgA was 24.5 g/L, and β2-microglobulin 3.5 mg/L. A new bone marrow trephine biopsy showed a hypercellular marrow with 20% infiltration by monoclonal λ-positive plasma cells and residual small lymphocytic infiltrates. A CT scan demonstrated osteolytic lesions of the skull but no other skeletal involvement.

A 70-year-old man with atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease, chronic heart failure, and hypertension presented with chest tightness. He had a remote smoking history (25 pack-years) and possible low-level asbestos exposure during a brief period of industrial work. Two years earlier, chest radiography had shown cardiac enlargement, and initial pericardial drainage yielded class IIIb cytology without a definitive diagnosis. His symptoms improved transiently but recurred every two weeks, necessitating pericardial drainage approximately every three months.

On examination, he was euvolemic with no signs of heart failure. Laboratory tests showed blood urea nitrogen 29.1 mg/dL, creatinine 1.62 mg/dL, and brain natriuretic peptide 103.7 pg/mL; serum lung tumor markers were negative. Chest radiography and echocardiography confirmed massive pericardial effusion with normal ventricular function. CT and 18F-FDG PET-CT demonstrated small nodular FDG uptake along the pericardium around the right ventricle, pulmonary artery, and aortic root.

During the current admission, pericardiocentesis drained over 2000 mL of hemorrhagic fluid. Two months later, effusion recurred to a similar volume. Analysis of the fluid revealed a hyaluronic acid level of 329 000 ng/mL and class III cytology. Cell-block sections showed diffuse proliferation of atypical cells with enlarged nuclei, eosinophilic cytoplasm, and papillary structures. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated that the tumor cells were diffusely positive for calretinin, D2-40, and WT-1; focally positive for epithelial membrane antigen; and negative for carcinoembryonic antigen, TTF-1, and desmin. Loss of BRCA1-associated protein 1 (BAP1) was also observed.

A 57-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive dyspnea and low-grade fever. Initial blood tests showed a red-cell count of 1.46×10^12/L and hemoglobin of 45 g/L. Empiric treatment with piperacillin–sulbactam and levofloxacin produced no improvement, and she was admitted for further evaluation.

On examination she was afebrile, with normal vital signs and an unremarkable cardiopulmonary and abdominal exam. Chest CT demonstrated bilateral multiple pulmonary nodules and masses with air bronchograms in a peribronchovascular and subpleural distribution; some lesions were well circumscribed.

Admission laboratory studies revealed WBC 3.36×10^9/L, RBC 0.95×10^12/L; ANA titer 1:320 (weak U1-snRNP, SSA-Ro60, SSA-Ro52 positive); PR3-IgG 61.2 AU/mL, ACA >300 AU/mL; IgG 25.6 g/L, IgM 4.18 g/L; C4 0.05 g/L, C3 1.09 g/L; T-SPOT and fungal G/GM tests negative; vitamin B12 and folate normal. Despite 13 days of meropenem and voriconazole, symptoms persisted.

Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy showed marked hypercellularity with predominance of lymphocytes. Flow-cytometric immunophenotyping revealed B lymphocytes comprising 57.8% of nucleated cells, all CD19+ and lambda-restricted, with partial FMC-7, CD79a, and CD20 positivity, and negativity for CD5, CD10, CD23, CD25, CD34, CD138, kappa, MPO, and CD3. 

Ultrasound of superficial lymph nodes identified enlarged nodes in the neck, supraclavicular fossa, left axilla, and groin (0.9×0.7 to 2.8×1.8 cm). ^18F-FDG PET/CT showed multiple hypermetabolic lymph nodes in cervical, supraclavicular, mediastinal, retroperitoneal, pelvic, and inguinal regions, as well as uptake in bilateral pulmonary lesions, pleura, and bone.

A 30-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 2-month history of left-sided nasal obstruction, recurrent left epistaxis, and left-sided headache. She denied nasal trauma, nasal picking, or pregnancy. On anterior rhinoscopy, a smooth, reddish-bluish soft-tissue mass filled the left nasal cavity, was attached to the nasal septum, and bled on palpation. Findings on ear, throat, neck examination and fiberoptic nasopharyngolaryngoscopy were unremarkable. Routine blood tests were normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses revealed a 3.5 × 1.2 cm soft-tissue lesion with heterogeneous patchy enhancement, attached to both the lateral and medial nasal walls, causing mild septal deviation but no bone erosions. MRI showed the lesion to be hypointense on non-contrast T1, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2 with multiple flow voids, and to have peripheral inhomogeneous enhancement after gadolinium. Digital subtraction angiography demonstrated a hypervascular left nasal mass receiving 70–80% of its blood supply from bilateral anterior ethmoidal branches and the remainder from the internal maxillary artery.

A 62-year-old woman with IgG kappa plasma cell myeloma (Durie-Salmon IIA, R-ISS II), previously treated with multiple chemotherapy regimens, two autologous stem-cell transplants, thalidomide maintenance, and focal bone radiotherapy, underwent routine surveillance imaging.  
She was asymptomatic with stable vital signs and no hepatosplenomegaly on examination. Liver function tests, including ALT, AST, ALP, GGTP, and bilirubin, were within normal limits.  
On PET/CT, a 35 mm lesion in the right hepatic lobe showed an SUVmax of 6.1. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the abdomen demonstrated a 17 mm lesion in segment VI with moderately increased T2 signal, decreased T1 signal, weak heterogeneous contrast enhancement, and restricted diffusion, favoring a non-characteristic malignant lesion.  
Serial imaging over subsequent months showed a decrease in lesion size to 10 mm, followed by enlargement to 57 × 46 mm.  
Given these findings, a percutaneous liver biopsy was planned to establish a definitive diagnosis.

A 3-year-old boy was admitted with pain localized to the sternum for 10 days. The pain began insidiously, increased with palpation, and was not relieved by over-the-counter medication. Three days before admission, he developed a paroxysmal cough without fever, vomiting, or diarrhea; after 3 days of oral amoxicillin and expectorant therapy, the cough resolved but sternal pain persisted. On examination, he was afebrile with normal vital signs and in good general condition. Routine blood and urine tests were normal. A chest CT scan showed no pulmonary nodules but revealed cortical discontinuity of the sternum and an underlying osteolytic lesion; 3-dimensional reconstruction confirmed focal osteolysis of the sternum. Ultrasound of the anterior chest wall demonstrated an ill-defined, irregular hypoechoic collection overlying periosteal disruption at the site of the lesion. A percutaneous needle biopsy of the sternal lesion was recommended.

A 42-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of elevated blood glucose and blurred vision. Seven years earlier, she had gestational diabetes treated with metformin and developed extremity numbness and progressive visual changes. Three years ago, she underwent resection of a left atrial mass, initially reported as “left atrial mucinous adenocarcinoma.” Her medical history also included hypertension for over 10 years, controlled with enalapril. Menarche occurred at age 15, with prior cycles of 27–30 days; over the past year she noted menstrual cycles of 2–4 months with scant flow. She denied a family history of similar findings.

On examination, she had centripetal obesity, buffalo hump, mild facial plethora, purple striae on the lower abdomen, and multiple spotty pigmented macules on her face and lips.

Laboratory studies:
• Fasting glucose: 5.64 mmol/L (ref 3.90–6.10)  
• HbA1c: 6.9% (4.3–5.7)  
• 8:00 am cortisol: 11.21 µg/dL (4.30–22.40)  
• 8:00 am cortisol after 1 mg dexamethasone: 10.06 µg/dL (<1.8)  
• 8:00 am cortisol after low-dose dexamethasone: 10.02 µg/dL (<1.8)  
• 8:00 am cortisol after high-dose dexamethasone: 11.19 µg/dL (suppression >50%)  
• ACTH (8:00 am): 24.40 pg/mL (5.00–46.00)  
• LH: 7.32 IU/L (1.90–12.50)  
• FSH: 44.01 IU/L (2.50–10.20)  
• Estradiol: 114.87 pmol/L (71.60–529.20)  
• Progesterone, prolactin, testosterone, TSH, free T3, free T4, tumor markers (CA125, CA199, CEA, thyroglobulin) were within or near reference ranges.

Imaging:
• Adrenal CT: multiple small bilateral adrenal nodules, up to 8 mm, suggestive of adenomas.  
• Brain CT: left hemispheric ischemic focus and partial empty sella.  
• Transthoracic echocardiography: mild tricuspid regurgitation; no intracardiac masses.  
• Thyroid ultrasound: two right-lobar hypoechoic nodules (6 × 6 mm, TI-RADS 4a; 8 × 5 mm, TI-RADS 4b); FNA of the 4b lesion was Bethesda V, suspicious for papillary carcinoma.  
• Breast ultrasound: right breast hypoechoic nodule (BI-RADS 4a); left breast multiple hypoechoic nodules (BI-RADS 3).  
• Pelvic ultrasound: cystic mass in left adnexa; cervical inclusion cyst.  
• DXA of lumbar spine: Z-scores −3.2 to −2.4, total −2.8, consistent with osteoporosis.

A 24-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with a 7-month history of cough and blood-streaked sputum and a 1-month history of progressive visual disturbance in the right eye. An ophthalmologic evaluation was normal, but brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated multiple intracranial lesions, and she was referred for further evaluation.

On examination, she was alert and oriented. Visual acuity was counting fingers in the right eye and 30/50 in the left eye; there were no other focal neurologic deficits. A noncontrast head CT scan showed multiple 5–15 mm high-density intra-axial nodules with surrounding edema in both cerebral hemispheres and cerebellum, with obscuration of sulci consistent with increased intracranial pressure. Emergency cerebral angiography excluded vascular malformations and sinus thrombosis but revealed a prolonged intracranial perfusion time. Brain MRI demonstrated that the nodules were hypointense to isointense on T1-weighted sequences, hypointense on T2-weighted sequences, and contained numerous low-intensity foci on susceptibility-weighted imaging, suggestive of old hemorrhage. Postcontrast images showed minimal enhancement of most lesions with weak enhancement of a few nodules.

Given the suspicion of multiple brain metastases, a chest CT scan was performed, revealing multiple small hemorrhagic nodules in both lungs. Abdominal CT showed similarly sized hypodense nodules in the liver without intralesional hemorrhage and with homogeneous enhancement. Serum tumor markers, including carbohydrate antigen 19-9, squamous cell carcinoma antigen, and sialyl Lewis X were within normal limits, and sputum and bronchial lavage cytology were class I. Additional evaluations for melanoma (dermatological inspection; serum 5-S-cysteinyldopa), choriocarcinoma (gynecologic examination), and other neoplasms (thallium scintigraphy) were negative.

Because of the systemic and multiorgan involvement, metabolic, hematologic, and infectious etiologies were considered; laboratory tests revealed only mild anemia. Systemic amyloidosis was ruled out by serum protein electrophoresis and urinalysis. Tests for tuberculosis, including sputum and lavage cultures, acid-fast staining, Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR, and interferon-gamma release assay, were negative.

A 24-year-old man presented with a nasofrontal mass present since birth that had slowly enlarged over the past 2 years. He reported a nonspecific frontal headache but no history of trauma, visual changes, rhinorrhea, epistaxis, or changes in smell. On examination, there was a painless, mobile, 2-cm mass in the glabellar region; the overlying skin was normal and nasal endoscopy revealed a normal endonasal anatomy. A CT scan showed a 2.0 × 1.3 × 2.2-cm well-circumscribed lesion in the glabellar area causing thinning of the anterior frontal sinus wall; the posterior wall of the frontal sinus and the sinus outflow tract appeared normal. Sonography demonstrated a cystic lesion without internal vascular flow.

An otherwise healthy 11-month-old girl was brought with an 8-day history of a painless swelling in the left medial canthal region. She had a mild upper respiratory infection treated 5 days earlier. There was no history of trauma or nasal, ocular, or dental disease. On examination, a nontender, firm, fixed infraorbital mass measuring 2 × 2 cm arose from the left maxillary sinus; the overlying skin was intact. Ophthalmological evaluation showed no involvement of the globe or lacrimal pathway. Orbital ultrasound revealed an ill-demarcated mass with irregular internal structure, medium internal reflectivity (44%), and peripheral bony destruction. CT scan demonstrated a heterogeneous mass in the anterior maxillary sinus, leading to a possible clinical diagnosis of a lacrimal sac tumor.

A 48-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of progressive abdominal distention and weight loss. Six months earlier, she had developed progressive numbness and weakness of the lower limbs; electromyography showed moderate to severe peripheral neuropathy, more pronounced in the lower than in the upper limbs, with sensory disturbances exceeding motor deficits. She is now wheelchair-bound.

On examination, vital signs were normal. There were no stigmata of chronic liver disease, anemia, edema, or lymphadenopathy, but she appeared cachectic. Her hands had hyperpigmented skin and slightly pale nails. The abdomen was markedly distended, with a positive fluid thrill and shifting dullness. Neurologic examination showed normal cranial nerves and full strength in the upper limbs (5/5), but markedly reduced distal power in the lower limbs (0/5) and mildly reduced proximal strength (4/5); tendon reflexes were absent in the extremities, and sensation was diminished in both lower limbs.

Laboratory studies revealed serum IgA 16.20 g/L (0.7–4), λ light chain 4.78 g/L (0.9–2.1), prolactin 1192 μIU/ml (102–497), M-protein 6.05 g/L, and VEGF 252.01 pg/ml (0–160). Other blood tests were unremarkable. Analysis of the ascitic fluid showed an exudative profile; cytologic examination on two occasions revealed no malignant cells.

Contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated hepatosplenomegaly, a widened portal vein, extensive ascites, and severe pelvic effusion without intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Whole-body PET/MR imaging showed increased FDG uptake (SUV max 4.3) at the anterior edge of the third thoracic vertebra.

A 14-year-old boy presented with a 12-month history of painful swelling of his right foot. On examination, there was diffuse tender swelling involving the right ankle joint and foot, with normal overlying skin and restricted joint mobility. Hematological and biochemical studies showed a normal hemogram and normal liver and renal–function tests. Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the foot demonstrated a condensed lesion in the calcaneus with aggressive periosteal reaction and associated soft-tissue swelling. Noncontrast CT of the foot revealed a sclerotic lesion of the entire calcaneus with permeative cortical destruction, aggressive spiculated periosteal reaction, and a large adjacent soft-tissue mass.

A teenage female presented with a 6-month history of mild, dull aching pain on the right side of the chest, without diurnal variation or visible swelling. Physical examination showed mild tenderness over the lateral aspect of the sixth rib on the right. Routine blood tests, including inflammatory markers, were within normal limits. A chest radiograph revealed a nodular, hyperdense lesion on the lateral chest wall adjacent to the right fifth through seventh ribs. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed a 4.4 × 3.9 × 2.7 cm lesion arising from the right sixth rib, characterized by a ground-glass matrix, cortical thinning with a smooth margin, and no soft-tissue component. Fine-needle aspiration cytology demonstrated mostly benign spindle cells.

A 74-year-old woman presented with a slow-growing mass in the upper lip. She first noticed a small lesion 2 years earlier, with more rapid enlargement over the past 6 months. She denied pain but reported difficulty eating and drinking. Her medical and dental histories were unremarkable, except for multiple extractions of upper teeth for periodontitis. 

On examination, the lesion was soft, mobile, non-tender, and well demarcated in the upper lip and labial vestibule. The overlying mucosa was normal, with a small area of leukoplakia likely due to irritation. Panoramic radiography showed no bone involvement.

The differential diagnosis included soft-tissue neoplasms (lipoma, fibroma), salivary-gland tumors (pleomorphic adenoma, canalicular adenoma), and irritation fibroma. Mucocele was also considered but is more common in the lower lip.

An excisional biopsy was performed under general anesthesia with local infiltration of articaine 4% and epinephrine 1:200 000. The mass was bluntly dissected and easily separated from surrounding tissues with clear margins. Primary closure was achieved. The excised specimen was an oval, yellowish, myxoid, soft mass measuring 3.2 cm at its greatest diameter.

Histologic sections revealed a severely hypocellular tumor composed of stellate and spindle cells without atypia or mitoses in abundant myxoid stroma. Immunohistochemical stains showed tumor cells positive for vimentin and CD34 but negative for smooth-muscle actin and S100.

A 55-year-old Nepalese man presented with a 6-month history of vague, generalized, mild central abdominal pain that was nonradiating and relieved by analgesics. He denied weight loss, fever, abdominal distension, or history of trauma. He had no prior surgeries, no family history of malignancy, chewed tobacco for 30 years, and drank alcohol socially.

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs and an unremarkable abdominal exam. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, white blood cells 11 × 10^3/μL, urea 6.9 mmol/L, creatinine 125 μmol/L, sodium 132 mEq/L, and potassium 3.7 mEq/L. Twenty-four-hour urine studies showed vanillylmandelic acid 5.4 mg (normal < 13.6 mg) and metanephrine 82.64 μg (normal 73–808 μg).

Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a heterogeneous mass near the left adrenal gland. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a well-defined heterogeneous left adrenal mass measuring 7.8 × 8.3 × 6 cm with foci of calcification in the left retroperitoneum.

A 59-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and COPD presented with three days of diffuse abdominal pain, distension, obstipation, and brownish vomiting. He had no prior surgeries, travel history, or recent antibiotic use. On exam, he was afebrile, normotensive, and in sinus rhythm at 75 bpm. His abdomen was distended with alternating hyperactive and absent bowel sounds and diffuse tenderness; the rest of the exam was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL, white cells 10.9 ×10^3/µL (74% neutrophils, 13.7% lymphocytes), platelets 262 ×10^3/µL, normal liver tests, and C-reactive protein 115 mg/dL. Contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a small-bowel obstruction with a transition point comprising a moderately thickened jejunal loop approximately 10 cm long.

Initial management included IV fluids, antibiotics, and nasogastric decompression, after which the patient passed flatus and stool. Stool studies showed a negative culture, positive fecal immunochemical test, and fecal calprotectin 214 mg/kg. Entero-MRI confirmed a thickened jejunal loop without evidence of inflammatory bowel disease. A total-body scan revealed no other lesions. Upper endoscopy showed only mild gastritis, and colonoscopy was normal. The patient was referred for laparoscopic oncologic resection. Intraoperatively, a circumferential stricture of the jejunum was found 1 m proximal to the ileocecal valve, tethered to the abdominal wall by a fibrotic band. Segmental resection with wide margins and a side-to-side jejuno-jejunal anastomosis was performed; the postoperative course was uneventful.

A 13-year-old boy presented with four months of a soft-tissue overgrowth in the anterior region of his lower jaw. He was born at term via normal vaginal delivery, has no known allergies or medications, and has no history of dental extractions. On extraoral examination, there was a right-sided cleft lip and bilateral splitting of both hands and feet. His father had similar split-hand and split-foot malformations; no other family members, including an older sister, were affected. Hair density and nail morphology were normal. Intraorally, there was a well-defined, pedunculated, soft, non-tender overgrowth extending from the distal surface of the right mandibular lateral incisor to the right second premolar, cupping over the alveolar ridge. Multiple carious teeth were noted. Panoramic radiography showed no bony abnormality underlying the lesion but revealed multiple congenitally missing permanent teeth, including both maxillary lateral incisors and canines and mandibular incisors and premolars. Radiographs of the hands demonstrated absence of the third metacarpal and its phalanges in the left hand with fusion of the first and second digits, and absence of the second and third metacarpals and their phalanges in the right hand. Foot radiographs showed a cleft between the toes and fourth digit and fusion of the second and third metatarsals on the right side with missing phalanges of the second and fourth digits, and a cross bone fused to the second metatarsal with deviation of the first metatarsal and absence of the middle and distal phalanges of the second digit on the left. The differential diagnosis for the mandibular overgrowth included pyogenic granuloma, peripheral giant cell granuloma, peripheral ossifying fibroma, and peripheral cemento-ossifying fibroma.

A 12-year-old Caucasian girl was evaluated in an allergy clinic for persistent cough and possible environmental allergies. Since age 1, she had seasonal nasal congestion and watery eyes from January to May with minimal relief from oral antihistamines. Between ages 2 and 3 she experienced cough and occasional wheezing after upper respiratory infections, which improved with albuterol. At age 10, she developed persistent posterior nasal drainage, cough, nasal congestion, and rhinorrhea sometimes triggering shortness of breath despite environmental control measures, and was treated with albuterol, inhaled corticosteroids, and an oral leukotriene inhibitor. Five months before presentation, she had worsening wet cough and croup-like symptoms treated with antibiotics and oral and parenteral corticosteroids. She denied shortness of breath or wheezing with activity, reflux symptoms, or dysphagia. She described sleeping upright because of an intermittent sensation of a flap obstructing her throat during inspiration and expiration, which induced coughing and throat clearing and occasionally vomiting. On examination she had loud, grunting, hyponasal breathing; an S-shaped nasal septal deviation with narrowing of the left nasal passage and clear mucus; mild tonsillar enlargement; and inspiratory and expiratory rhonchi bilaterally. Skin testing for environmental allergens was negative. Spirometry was limited by cough but showed an almost complete blunting of the forced expiratory phase with an FEV1 of 36% of predicted and an FEV1/FVC ratio of 28%, suggesting variable extrathoracic obstruction. Chest radiography demonstrated patchy bibasilar infiltrates with mild hyperinflation. Noncontrast chest computed tomography revealed patchy airspace infiltrates in the right middle and lower lobes and a filling defect measuring 1.3 cm in diameter in the proximal trachea attached to the posterior wall, suggestive of a large polyp or obstructive lesion.

A 30-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of left-sided abdominal pain. He denied fever, weight loss, digestive or urinary symptoms. On examination, he was overweight with normal vital signs.
