Abdominal palpation revealed a deep, firm, immobile 10 cm oblong mass in the left hypochondrium and flank; the remainder of the physical examination, including testicular exam, was normal. Laboratory tests, including hemoglobin and renal function, were within normal limits, and urinalysis was sterile. Colonoscopy showed no abnormalities. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a heterogeneous 9 cm retroperitoneal mass in the left flank containing water, fat, and calcium densities, causing mild compression of the left ureter and slight hydronephrosis. Chest radiograph was normal and no other lesions were identified.

A 14-year-old girl presented with a 4–5-month history of a swelling on the palatal aspect of her maxillary right central and lateral incisors. She noted localized bleeding on brushing and slight pain and discomfort when eating. One year earlier, she had undergone excision of gingival enlargement in the same region, but the lesion recurred within two months and then stabilized after 3–4 weeks. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable, and her development was normal. 

Intraoral examination revealed a firm, pedunculated, bright-red bilobulated mass arising from the interdental papilla between teeth 11 and 12 on the palatal side. The lobes measured approximately 5.0 × 4.0 cm and 3.0 × 2.5 cm; the surface was smooth with well-defined margins, and there was no ulceration, secondary infection, or clinical attachment loss. A panoramic radiograph showed no alveolar bone loss.

A provisional diagnosis of pyogenic granuloma was made based on the history and clinical features, with consideration of malignancy, trauma, infection (bacterial, viral, fungal), and drug-induced gingival enlargement. Complete blood and urine studies were within normal limits, ruling out leukemic enlargement and diabetes mellitus. HIV, HBsAg, VDRL, and Mantoux tests were negative, excluding an infectious etiology. An intraoral periapical radiograph confirmed intact lamina dura and no crestal bone loss. After scaling, the lesion was ligated at its stalk to reduce blood flow and was excised under local anesthesia; the specimen was placed in formalin and submitted for histopathological examination.

A 40-year-old man presented with sudden, profuse bright-red hemoptysis while cycling. He denied chest pain, dyspnea, fever, weight loss, or fatigue. His 10–pack-year smoking history was otherwise unremarkable. On examination, he was stable: heart rate 100 bpm, oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Lung bases had decreased breath sounds; cardiac exam revealed a loud S1 murmur; there was no edema. ECG showed sinus rhythm. Laboratory studies revealed normal D-dimer and NT-proBNP levels, without evidence of inflammation, anemia, or renal or hepatic dysfunction. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a 75 × 28 mm mass in the left atrium extending into the left ventricle, with mild mitral regurgitation and moderate to severe functional mitral stenosis; left ventricular ejection fraction was 55% with normal chamber size. Chest CT showed no pulmonary parenchymal or mediastinal abnormalities; CT angiography excluded pulmonary embolism. Bronchoscopy was unremarkable. Cardiac MRI revealed an 80 × 39 × 40 mm heterogeneous, mobile left atrial mass attached to the anterior mitral leaflet and protruding into the ventricle in diastole, with heterogeneous signal characteristics and late gadolinium enhancement “suggestive of a malignant cardiac mass.”

A 30-year-old man in good general health was referred for evaluation of left mandibular pain of unknown etiology. He described dull pain originating from the left basilar border of the mandible and radiating along the hemi-arch, worsening at night. He had recently undergone endodontic treatment on tooth #37 with no relief. 

On extraoral examination, there was a small, firm swelling along the left basilar border, mildly tender on palpation; there was no labiomental hypoesthesia. Intraoral findings included a temporary filling on tooth #37; percussion tests were painless. 

A panoramic radiograph taken with the head in slight extension was nondiagnostic due to superposition of the hyoid bone. A repeat panoramic radiograph with better positioning showed a well-circumscribed, homogeneous radiolucent lesion below the mandibular canal at the left basilar border. Tooth #37 showed a suboptimal endodontic filling but no periapical radiolucency. The tooth was extracted without symptom relief. A periapical film post-extraction confirmed healing alveolar bone but again demonstrated the cortical lesion at the basilar border.

CT imaging revealed a mixed-density, cortical lesion measuring under 1 cm in maximal diameter at the left mandibular basilar border. The lesion contained a central hyperdense nidus surrounded by a hypodense halo and a zone of peripheral sclerosis.

A 53-year-old man initially underwent excision of a 2.0 × 1.5 × 0.7 cm left gingival mass, which was diagnosed at an outside hospital as non-Hodgkin lymphoma and treated with six cycles of cyclophosphamide, adriamycin, vincristine, and prednisone. Nine months later, he presented with a painless left submandibular mass.  
On contrast-enhanced CT of the neck, there was a 3.2 × 2.5 × 2.2 cm enhancing mass with a central low-attenuation area suggestive of cystic or necrotic degeneration, and there was enlargement of cervical lymph nodes at levels IIa and IIb.  
The submandibular mass was excised. Grossly, it was tan-white, well-circumscribed, and on sectioning showed a centrally necrotic and cystic cut surface.  
Microscopic examination revealed two distinct components:  
• A central undifferentiated epithelial component with primitive malignant cells arranged in sheets, cords, nests, and trabeculae.  
• A peripheral neurogenic component composed of mature ganglion cells and Schwann cells within a neurofibrillary stroma.  
Immunohistochemical staining of the undifferentiated component demonstrated diffuse positivity for cytokeratin AE1/AE3, cytokeratin 8/18, S-100 protein, and focal CD56, and was negative for synaptophysin, chromogranin, neuron-specific enolase, melan-A, GFAP, CD45, CD99, CD20, CK5/6, CK7, CK20, EMA, p63, and EBV antigen. The ganglion cells of the neural component were positive for chromogranin and synaptophysin.

A 25-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 4-year history of a lesion on the right index finger. It began as a 5-mm papule that gradually enlarged and became painful. On examination, there was a firm, well-circumscribed, infiltrated nodular lesion approximately 2 cm in its long axis, with an ulcerated center and a hyperkeratotic surface, located at the radial aspect of the metacarpophalangeal joint of the right index finger. A malignant skin tumor was strongly suspected.

A 24‐year‐old man presented with pain in the right mandibular wisdom tooth. His medical and family histories were non-contributory. On examination, oral hygiene was poor, there was malalignment of the mandibular anterior teeth, and the right mandibular third molar was carious. A panoramic radiograph revealed a large, well-circumscribed radiopaque lesion in the right posterior mandible, surrounded by a radiolucent halo, extending from the first to the second molar region. The lesion comprised two components: an assemblage of multiple tooth-like structures and a separate, amorphous radiopaque mass. Cone-beam computed tomography demonstrated that the lesion occupied the right mandibular body, was displaced buccally, and caused expansion and thinning of the buccal cortical plate.

A 3-year-old boy was brought with a 1-year history of progressive torticollis and a left-sided headache over the occipital bone. Over the previous week he had developed vomiting and unsteady gait. On examination, he had bilateral lower-limb weakness; other findings were unremarkable.

Noncontrast CT of the head revealed a large lobulated heterogeneous hyperdense lesion in the left posterior fossa, causing mass effect on the fourth ventricle and brainstem, supratentorial triventricular hydrocephalus, and a permeative bone reaction in the left occipital bone.

MRI of the brain demonstrated an extra-axial infratentorial mass appearing dural-based with invasion of the left occipital bone marrow. On T2-weighted images the lesion was heterogeneous with central areas of high signal suggestive of necrosis. Post-contrast images showed invasion of the inner skull table and intradiploic space, loss of the plane between the mass and cerebellum indicating invasion, and protrusion through the foramen magnum with displacement of the upper medulla.

Routine blood studies and other imaging were unremarkable.

A 51-year-old man of African descent presented with 4 days of constipation and a 4-day history of right-sided, colicky abdominal pain without fever or other symptoms. He was hemodynamically stable and afebrile. Physical examination revealed tenderness in the right iliac fossa without guarding or peritoneal signs. Laboratory tests were within normal limits. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen showed a large, well-circumscribed cystic mass in the right lower quadrant adjacent to the ascending colon and appendix. The mass was initially thought to represent an appendiceal mucocele. Given the risk of rupture, the surgical team planned an open laparotomy for resection of the mass.

A 6-year-old schoolboy presented with a 2-day history of holocranial, progressively worsening headache, multiple episodes of projectile nonbilious vomiting, and new-onset right-sided weakness. Neurological examination revealed right hemiparesis with Medical Research Council grade 3/5 strength in the upper and lower extremity flexors and extensors. Nine months earlier, he had an episode of generalized tonic-clonic seizure; a noncontrast head CT at that time showed a subtle ill-defined hyperdense area in the left high parietal region, and he was treated for presumed viral encephalitis with acyclovir and started on levetiracetam. On current MRI of the brain, there was a large heterogeneous, contrast-enhancing lesion in the left parietal region extending medially to the temporal horn and abutting the dura laterally. Given the short clinical history and aggressive radiographic appearance, a preoperative diagnosis of malignant brain pathology was made and surgical resection was planned.

A 14-year-old girl with a known diagnosis of Sturge–Weber syndrome since age 5 presented with a several-year history of an asymptomatic left mandibular mass that was first noted at age 6 and more recently associated with pain. Her medical history is notable for epilepsy, mental retardation, cerebral palsy, right-sided hemiplegia, and left conjunctival choristoma. There is no family history of similar lesions.

On examination, there were no facial port-wine stains. The left side of the face appeared mildly asymmetric, with a firm, bone-hard bulge over the left mandibular body. Intraoral findings included irregular dentition and thickened, pigmented gingiva.

Noncontrast craniofacial CT showed calcification over the left cerebral surface, hypoplasia of the left frontal and maxillary sinuses, thickening of the left frontal bone, and high-attenuation lesions with surrounding lucent bands in both the left maxilla and mandible. Panoramic radiographs dating from ages 6 to 16 years demonstrated a progressively enlarging hard-tissue lesion in the left mandible—initially without a clear border, then becoming better demarcated over time—and a separate expanding radiopaque mass in the left maxilla that displaced the unerupted second premolar.

A 37-year-old man with a history of cutaneous angiosarcoma of the nuchal region underwent surgical excision with skin grafting and adjuvant doxorubicin chemotherapy. Four months later, chest CT had shown pulmonary nodules (0.5–1.5 cm) and axillary lymphadenopathy. Nine days after his fourth cycle of doxorubicin, he presented with dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, and fever to 38.8 °C. On examination, a residual nuchal mass and poorly healed surgical wound were noted. Laboratory studies revealed a normal white-cell count, mildly elevated ALT, γGT, and LDH, a C-reactive protein level of 125 mg/L (normal ≤5.0), and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 80 mm/hr. Empirical intravenous ceftazidime and levofloxacin were started. Blood, wound, urine, and sputum cultures were all negative. Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral pneumatoceles in the middle and lower lung fields, up to 5.0 cm in diameter, and an obtuse right costophrenic angle. Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed that previous solid nodules had become cysts; numerous new bilateral cysts and cavities measured 1.0–5.0 cm with wall thickness up to 0.8 cm; several new nodules (0.8–1.5 cm) appeared; lesions were predominantly subpleural in the middle and lower lobes; additional findings included ground-glass attenuation, consolidation, septal thickening, bilateral pleural effusion, and a small left pneumothorax.

A 63-year-old white man presented with a 3-month history of headaches, vomiting, and episodes of blurred vision, consistent with intracranial hypertension. On admission, he had papilledema, nystagmus, and lethargy. A T1-weighted MRI of the brain showed a hypointense lesion in the anterosuperior posterior fossa at the falcotentorial junction, displacing the cerebellar vermis inferiorly and compressing the aqueduct of Sylvius, resulting in obstructive hydrocephalus. The mass enhanced homogeneously with gadolinium, and flow voids compatible with vessels were observed around it. MR angiography demonstrated intense tumoral vascularization. MRI of the neuroaxis showed no additional lesions. Whole-body contrast-enhanced CT scans were unremarkable. Serum levels of alpha-fetoprotein, human chorionic gonadotropin, and carcinoembryonic antigen were within normal limits.

A 63-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 2-month history of severe, persistent, gradually worsening sharp pain over her left distal fibula. The pain interfered with sleep and did not improve with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. She denied fevers, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. On examination, there was extreme tenderness to palpation over the lateral distal fibula and a soft-tissue prominence over the mid to lower third of the fibula. Radiographs of the left lower leg demonstrated two ill-defined osteolytic destructive lesions measuring 29 mm and 37 mm in the fibular diaphysis, with a pathologic fracture through the distal lesion. Technetium-99m bone scintigraphy showed avid radiopharmaceutical uptake in both fibular lesions. Laboratory evaluation, including serum protein electrophoresis, alkaline phosphatase, and basic metabolic profile, was unremarkable. CT scans of the chest and abdomen revealed no evidence of primary malignancy or metastatic disease.

A 39-year-old woman (para 2) presented with a 2-year history of progressive vulvar swelling accompanied by intermittent oozing and intense itching. She also reported a 2-year history of right lower-leg swelling. Five years earlier, she had undergone a laparotomy for a benign gynecologic condition. On examination, there was a healed infraumbilical midline scar. Genital examination revealed bilaterally enlarged labia with multiple papular and vesicular lesions; some lesions oozed clear fluid, and the overlying skin was shiny. Musculoskeletal examination showed non-pitting edema of the right lower extremity extending to the thigh. 

Over multiple outpatient visits, she had been diagnosed sequentially with vulvar eczema and genital warts and treated accordingly without improvement. Vulvar cancer was also considered. Basic laboratory investigations were unremarkable, and pelvic ultrasonography was normal. A skin biopsy was then performed prior to definitive management.

A 60‐year‐old man presented with a 1‐month history of a painless, white growth on the right cheek. He reported gradual onset with no change in size since it was first noticed and denied any bleeding or dysphagia. He had no history of topical applications or similar lesions elsewhere. He chewed areca nut and tobacco. On examination, the right submandibular lymph nodes were palpable, about 1 cm in diameter, soft, and movable. Intraorally, there was a well‐defined keratotic mass with finger‐like projections measuring 4 cm × 5 cm, extending from the right buccal mucosa to the hard and soft palate near the faucial pillars, and involving the retropharyngeal area and lingual alveolar mucosa. The lesion was nonscrapable, nontender, nonindurated, and did not bleed on touch. A separate white keratotic patch (2 cm × 3 cm) was present on the right lateral border of the tongue. A provisional diagnosis of verrucous carcinoma was made, and an incisional biopsy showed verrucous hyperplasia.

A 67‐year‐old man with a history of right parotid carcinoma treated one year earlier by parotidectomy followed by chemoradiotherapy was found on surveillance to have a swollen left supraclavicular lymph node. Biopsy of that node confirmed metastatic carcinoma. A contrast‐enhanced CT scan demonstrated focal thickening of the gastric wall, an enlarged perigastric lymph node, and pancreatic enlargement. FDG‐PET–CT showed intense uptake in the left cervical, mediastinal, paraaortic, and cardiac lymph nodes, as well as in the stomach and pancreas. Laboratory evaluation revealed hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL, hematocrit 32.4%, platelets 206 000/µL, alpha‐fetoprotein 2.5 ng/mL, carcinoembryonic antigen 11.1 ng/dL, and CA 19-9 11 U/mL. Gastroduodenoscopy disclosed a large, easily bleeding ulcer in the upper body of the stomach. Biopsy of the lesion revealed poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma. At this point, it was not possible to distinguish primary gastric cancer from a metastatic tumor.

A 67-year-old man presented with progressive fatigue, memory and concentration loss, right-sided neglect, right-sided weakness, and gait disturbance.  
Brain MRI showed an inhomogeneous, contrast-enhancing mass in the left temporo–parieto–occipital region invading the trigone of the left lateral ventricle. He underwent subtotal resection under 5-ALA fluorescence; a small ventricular remnant was left. Histologic analysis revealed glioblastoma multiforme (WHO grade IV). No molecular studies were performed.  
Postoperatively, he received fractionated radiotherapy (62 Gy) with concomitant temozolomide (75 mg/m2 daily for 44 days). Ten weeks after surgery, he experienced vertigo and a transient episode of right visual field restriction and neglect, which resolved with oral corticosteroids. MRI at that time demonstrated new contrast enhancement around the resection cavity, thought to be treatment-related, and a 14-mm-thick left subdural fluid collection causing a 6-mm midline shift. This was interpreted as a subdural hygroma or hematoma.  
One week later, CT showed slight progression of the collection. Burr-hole evacuation yielded a slightly xanthochromic, pressurized subdural hygroma; the dura appeared normal. Three weeks after evacuation, CT again showed recurrence of the subdural collection, which was attributed to post-radiation changes. The patient remained asymptomatic and received two cycles of adjuvant temozolomide (150 mg/m2 and 200 mg/m2).  
Fifteen weeks after tumour resection (four weeks after the first hygroma evacuation), he returned with concentration loss, fatigue, and moderate right hemiparesis. CT revealed a markedly progressive subdural fluid collection with a 3-mm-thick subdural membrane. A second burr-hole evacuation was performed, but drainage remained unsatisfactory and a subduro–peritoneal shunt was placed. A thick greyish subdural membrane was observed intraoperatively, but no tissue was sampled. Although the fluid volume decreased, significant mass effect persisted.  
Several days later, MRI performed as part of tumor follow-up showed an inhomogeneous, contrast-enhancing subdural membrane with irregular contours over the left hemisphere.

A 30-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of mild low back pain that had become severely worse over the preceding 20 days, with radiation to the posterolateral lower limbs and difficulty walking. On examination, palpation of the lumbar spine and sacroiliac joints was painful (positive Patrick’s test). Laboratory studies showed a normal C-reactive protein level. He was a heavy smoker without other comorbidities.  
Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine demonstrated an infiltrative mass involving the vertebral body and pedicles of L4, with extension into the vertebral canal and heterogeneous contrast enhancement. The lesion extended into the distal third of the inferior vena cava and into the left iliopsoas muscle.  
Computed tomography revealed a lytic lesion with indistinct borders in the L4 vertebral body, associated with a soft-tissue component displacing the aorta and inferior vena cava, and a typical “ring-and-arc” pattern of chondroid matrix mineralization.

A 66-year-old man presented with a right scrotal mass that he first noticed 20 years ago as a 3–4 cm nodule. It had grown slowly, causing only a sensation of mild heaviness. On examination, there was a firm, painless 10 × 15 cm mass in the right scrotum with soft contours; it did not transilluminate and was mobile without adherence to the scrotal skin. Serum tumor markers (alpha-fetoprotein, β-hCG, LDH, PSA) were all within normal limits. Scrotal ultrasonography showed a solid hypoechoic lesion with thin echogenic septa. Cross-sectional imaging revealed no evidence of distant spread. The patient was scheduled for a right inguinal orchiectomy.

A 41-year-old man presented to the emergency department after falling while water-skiing at 40–50 km/hr and landing face-first on the water. He did not lose consciousness but noted periorbital swelling and bleeding from both eyes, which resolved over 30 minutes. He complained of neck and right shoulder pain and a frontal headache and had a 2–3-month history of chronic headaches. His medical history was notable for lumbar disc prolapse surgery; medications included dothiepin and sulfasalazine.

On examination, he was alert (GCS 15), blood pressure 123/92 mmHg, pulse 72 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 95%. There was periorbital bruising, a laceration of the right upper eyelid with ongoing bleeding, and bilateral conjunctival hemorrhages. A full ophthalmologic evaluation was normal. Radiographs of the head, pelvis, cervical spine, right shoulder, and lumbar spine showed no fracture or dislocation. A head CT scan revealed a small hyperdense extra-axial collection with a maximum thickness of 1 mm. Differential diagnoses included an arachnoid cyst, haemangioma, meningioma, or a secondary lesion. A subsequent bone scan showed an active lesion.

An 11-year-old boy presented with a 2-year history of left clavicle pain (VAS 6) and swelling following a fall while playing. Initially treated as a clavicle fracture with conservative management, his pain resolved after 3 months but recurred with progressive swelling 6 months later. On examination, there was diffuse, tender, bony-hard swelling extending from the sternal to the lateral end of the left clavicle; the mass was nonmobile, the overlying skin was pinchable, without warmth or sinus formation, and shoulder abduction was painful and terminally limited. 

Plain radiography of the left clavicle showed an expansile lesion with diffuse periosteal thickening, thinning of the cortex, and well-defined margins along the entire clavicle. MRI demonstrated diffuse marrow edema, extensive destructive lysis of the shaft, adjacent periosteal reaction, surrounding soft-tissue edema, and midshaft expansion with sclerotic changes and permeative destruction.

A percutaneous core-needle biopsy suggested a benign fibro-osseous lesion. An open biopsy at the tumor–normal junction revealed caseous material in the medullary canal. Histologic examination showed fibroblastic proliferation and osteoblastic proliferation laying down woven bone. Culture of the biopsy specimen yielded no growth.

A 37-year-old woman presented with lower abdominal pain of 4 months’ duration. Vaginal palpation revealed a hard, adherent, and painless mass. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, serum electrolytes, creatinine, and urea, were within normal limits. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed a 6.0 × 7.6 × 6.0 cm solid mass located between the uterus and the rectum. Contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT demonstrated a 7.4 cm nodular solid mass in the same location, with attenuation values rising from 20 Hounsfield units (HU) pre-contrast to 70 HU on delayed images, and multiple tortuous enhancing vessels at the periphery. The mass indented the posterior uterine wall without invasion of adjacent organs, and no lymphadenopathy was seen. Based on location and imaging features, a subserosal uterine fibroid was suspected.

A 42-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a swelling on the volar aspect of her right wrist that had slowly increased in size over 2 years and caused intermittent pain. She recalled a mild wrist injury preceding the swelling, which fluctuated in size but never fully resolved. She denied systemic symptoms, anticoagulant use, or other swellings. Medical history included hiatus hernia, Barrett’s esophagus, and a benign breast lump. No family history of malignancy was reported.

On examination, there was a well-defined, tender, mobile mass in the volar-radial compartment of the wrist extending toward the first dorsal space. The mass was neither warm nor transilluminating. Neurovascular examination was normal.

Laboratory studies revealed normal inflammatory markers, vitamin D, and calcium levels. Wrist radiographs demonstrated focal soft-tissue calcification anterior to the distal radius with smaller foci anterior to the proximal carpal row, but no bone or joint abnormalities. Ultrasound identified a 14 × 8 mm irregular calcific lesion at the volar-radial aspect of the wrist, sitting adjacent to the flexor pollicis longus and inferior to the flexor carpi radialis, with no involvement of any tendon or tendon sheath. 

At this point, the differential diagnosis was considered.

A 3-day-old male neonate was referred for evaluation of a gingival swelling present since birth. The infant fed and breathed normally, and all vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, there was a single, round, pink, pedunculated, non-tender, fleshy swelling measuring 2 × 2 × 1 cm on the right maxillary anterior alveolar ridge. Abdominal and transfontanelle ultrasound examinations were unremarkable. The baby had been born at term via spontaneous vaginal delivery to healthy parents. To establish a definitive diagnosis, the lesion was excised under general anesthesia, and the specimen was sent for histopathological analysis.

A 61-year-old man was found to have a solitary hypoechoic mass measuring 27 × 24 mm in the right liver lobe on ultrasound one year ago, initially thought to be a hemangioma. He did not pursue regular follow-up. Recently, a chest CT performed for unrelated reasons revealed that the lesion had increased to approximately 101 × 99 mm. He denied abdominal pain, bloating, fever, or jaundice and had no history of chronic hepatitis. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including CBC, electrolytes, liver and kidney function, and coagulation tests, were within normal limits. Serologic screening for hepatitis and other infections was negative. Tumor markers (AFP, AFP-L3, PIVKA-II, CA 19-9, CA 125) were normal; CEA was slightly elevated at 6.00 μg/L (normal 0–4.5). Contrast-enhanced CT of the liver showed a well-defined hypoattenuated lesion in the right hepatic lobe with heterogeneous arterial-phase hyperenhancement and portal- and delayed-phase hypoenhancement. MRI demonstrated a well-circumscribed right-lobe lesion that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, mixed-hyperintense on T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted images, with inhomogeneous arterial-phase enhancement that decreased in the portal and delayed phases, and a hypointense hepatobiliary-phase signal.

A 3-year-old girl recently emigrated from El Salvador presented with a 2-year history of monthly recurrent swelling of her left eyelids, often accompanied by subjective fevers, discoloration, and pain. She had a remote left eye trauma at 8 months of age, asthma, and infancy resection of a benign cystic neck mass. Prior episodes were treated with antibiotics with partial improvement but incomplete resolution. She was otherwise healthy with normal development. On examination, there was a mildly tender, non-erythematous swelling of the left upper and lower eyelids without conjunctival injection. Mild proptosis was noted; extraocular movements were intact, visual acuity was normal, and pupils were equal and reactive. No other abnormalities were found. Laboratory studies showed a normal C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate; the white blood cell count was elevated at 15.4 × 10^9/L. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed a T1- and T2-hyperintense cystic lesion with an enhancing mural nodule centered in the left pterygopalatine and infratemporal fossa. A non-contrast sinus CT demonstrated a 3.1 × 1.7 cm expansile lesion in the left pterygopalatine fossa without aggressive features.

A 46-year-old woman presented with a painless swelling of the right cheek that had been present for 6 years. The lesion was initially small and slowly enlarged; there was no history of trauma. Her medical history was notable for diabetes mellitus and anemia. On extraoral examination, there was no visible asymmetry, but intraoral palpation revealed a firm, compressible mass firmly attached to adjacent tissues, measuring approximately 1.5 cm in diameter, with intact overlying mucosa and no color change. There was no pulsation or bruit. 

Color Doppler ultrasound showed a well-defined, hypoechoic, heterogeneous mass beneath the skin measuring 13 × 18 mm with moderate vascular flow. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a circular, well-defined, homogeneous mass overlying the buccinator muscle. MRI revealed a well-circumscribed lesion between the buccinator muscle and buccal fat that was low signal on T1-weighted images and uniformly high signal on T2-weighted images.

A 65-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of lower abdominal pain of one year’s duration and 3–4 weeks of left leg swelling. Her medical history included hypertension, appendectomy, and a history of smoking; she was 10 years postmenopausal. Family history was notable for ovarian cancer in her mother. On examination, there was a relatively fixed mass in the left iliac fossa. Serum CA-125 was 16 U/mL (reference range, ≤35 U/mL). Pelvic MRI demonstrated a fibroid uterus displaced by a 9 × 7 cm complex cystic mass in the left pelvis. CT imaging showed that the iliac vessels were traversing and displaced by the mass. Diagnostic laparoscopy revealed that the lesion was retroperitoneal, arising from the left obturator fossa rather than the ovary. True-cut biopsy specimens were obtained, and frozen-section analysis showed a myxoid spindle cell tumour possibly reactive but unable to exclude a leiomyosarcoma.

A 56-year-old man presents with a 6-year history of intermittent, sharp pain in the inner posterior aspect of his left thigh that has worsened over the past 2 years. The pain is sudden, brief, and sometimes radiates to the calf. He reports no trauma or other comorbidities aside from well-controlled hypertension treated with amlodipine. He is slightly obese (BMI, 28.1) and smokes two to three cigarettes daily. On examination, vital signs are within normal limits. A tender, deep, indistinct subcutaneous lump is palpated in the posteromedial distal left femur; sciatic-related pain is absent. Lumbar spine MRI performed for low back pain evaluation was normal, and rehabilitative therapy did not relieve his symptoms. Ultrasonography demonstrates a 6 × 5.3 mm subcutaneous cystic lesion in the posteromedial distal femur. Doppler ultrasonography shows an aneurysmal vascular structure originating from the medial genicular artery. Computed tomographic angiography reveals normal muscular and skeletal structures without vascular abnormalities. The working diagnosis is a vascular lesion, suggesting a haemangioma.

A 31-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an incidental mass in the right lower lung field found on a screening chest radiograph. She was asymptomatic, with an unremarkable medical history. Physical examination and routine laboratory tests, including carcinoembryonic antigen and alpha-fetoprotein levels, were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced chest CT showed a 5.5 cm mass abutting the posterior inferior vena cava and the right side of the esophagus, with heterogeneous enhancement in the delayed phase. FDG-PET/CT demonstrated low metabolic activity in the lesion with a maximum standardized uptake value of less than 2.0.

CT-guided percutaneous needle biopsy yielded only nonspecific fibrous tissue without a definitive diagnosis on immunohistochemistry. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed no esophageal abnormalities. Endoscopic ultrasonography localized a well-defined, avascular mass at 35 cm from the incisors, but EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration again failed to establish a diagnosis.

A 66-year-old multiparous woman with a history of total hysterectomy and bilateral adnexectomy 22 years earlier for uterine myomas presented for routine follow-up. She has severe obesity (BMI 40 kg/m^2), hypertension, type II diabetes, and a remote gastric cancer treated by gastroresection. She received hormone-replacement therapy for 6 years after her gynecologic surgery. 

On examination, vital signs were stable. The abdomen was soft, nontender, and non-distended; no mass was palpable. Speculum and vaginal examinations were unremarkable. Serum Ca 125 and HE4 were within normal limits.

Transvaginal ultrasound revealed a 20 × 17 × 21 mm intraperitoneal solid mass in the right pelvic cavity, near the pelvic wall, with a spherical shape, echotexture showing radial stripes and acoustic shadowing. Color Doppler showed no central or peripheral vascularization. No other similar lesions were seen. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a 2 cm, iso- to hypodense, well-circumscribed solid mass in the right pelvic cavity medial to the hypogastric artery, with no peritoneal implants or lymph node enlargement.

A 13-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of two painless swellings, one over the right shoulder and one at the right mid-thigh, both present for 1 month and gradually increasing in size. He reported progressive weight loss and dizziness. His medical history was unremarkable. On examination, he was pale, tachycardic (136 beats/min), but afebrile and normotensive. The right shoulder mass measured 11×5 cm, was firm, round, non-tender, and immobile. The right mid-thigh lesion was circumferential, fixed, and non-tender (12×10 cm). Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL, ESR 28 mm/h, normal leukocyte count, and mildly elevated AST (40.6 U/L); renal function was normal, and bone marrow aspirate was unremarkable.  
Conventional radiography of the right femur revealed a large soft tissue swelling with diffuse permeative lesions in the mid and distal femoral shaft and medial cortical destruction. Imaging of the right shoulder demonstrated a large soft tissue mass with proximal humeral destruction and a pathological fracture. Chest radiograph and abdominopelvic ultrasound were normal, with no evidence of metastatic disease. A diagnosis of sarcoma was suggested, and incisional biopsies were obtained.

A 36-year-old nulligravid woman presented with one month of progressive left flank pain radiating to the left lower quadrant and inguinal region. She denied menstrual abnormalities, gastrointestinal or urinary symptoms, fever, or weight loss. Her medical, surgical, family, and medication histories were unremarkable. On examination, vital signs were normal. There was costovertebral angle tenderness on the left and a firm, bulky abdominal mass extending from the epigastrium to below the umbilicus. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 14.3 g/dL, normal renal and liver function tests, negative beta-hCG, normal ESR, and unremarkable urinalysis. Tumor markers showed normal CEA and AFP but an elevated CA-125 level of 151 U/mL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 26 × 22 × 14 cm solid-cystic mass with multiple calcified foci arising from the right adnexa and a small to moderate amount of ascites. The preoperative differential diagnosis included malignant ovarian tumors (eg, sex cord stromal tumor, ovarian fibrothecoma) and benign masses (eg, ovarian thecoma, pedunculated subserosal uterine leiomyoma).

A 60-year-old Japanese woman presented with a 3-year history of a slow-growing, painless mass in her left parotid region. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. On examination, a thumb-sized, hard, nontender mass was palpated in the left parotid gland; facial nerve function was intact. Endoscopic examination of the nasopharynx showed no tumorous lesions. Ultrasonography revealed a well-circumscribed, lobulated, hypoechoic mass with posterior enhancement measuring 19×12×10 mm in the left parotid gland. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a solid, homogeneously enhancing mass in the posterior part of the left parotid; no abnormal lymphadenopathy was noted. FDG-PET/CT showed uptake only in the parotid lesion, with no other areas of abnormal activity. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the mass revealed numerous irregularly shaped trabecular clusters of relatively large cancer cells with vesicular chromatin and prominent “cherry-red” nucleoli; lymphocytic infiltrate was not conspicuous. Cytologically, a poorly differentiated carcinoma was suggested.

A 70-year-old man presented with a one-month history of persistent right back pain. He had no history of pleural tuberculosis, chronic pyothorax, or dust exposure. On examination, there was no chest wall tenderness or swelling and no palpable lymphadenopathy; a band-shaped sensory disturbance was noted from the right anterior chest to the lateral chest. Laboratory tests showed a soluble interleukin 2 receptor level of 981 U/mL. A chest radiograph revealed a right tumour-like shadow in the upper right lung field. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated an irregularly shaped mass in the right posterior chest wall without bone destruction; the mass formed a dumbbell-shaped lesion extending from the thoracic cavity through the T5 intervertebral foramen into the spinal canal and enveloped the intercostal artery, producing a positive pleural sandwich sign. FDG-PET showed a maximum SUV of 30.6 in the chest wall mass, with no other areas of uptake.

A 40-year-old woman with a history of polycystic ovary syndrome (on metformin) and a strong family history of early breast cancer presented with a 4-year history of a painless “lump” sensation in the outer part of her left breast near the underarm. The sensation had increased in prominence over the past week. On examination, there was an apricot-sized, non-tender, well-circumscribed swelling in the left axillary tail, approximately 3 cm below the axilla, without skin changes or nipple discharge. Mammography showed a partially visualized hyperdense abnormality at the lateral part of the left axillary tail (BIRADS 0). Breast ultrasound revealed a 3.5 cm submuscular/intramuscular oval heterogeneous lesion, predominantly hyperechoic with evidence of fat content, extending into the underlying intercostal space (BIRADS 3). To further characterize the lesion, a contrast-enhanced MRI of the left axilla was obtained. The MRI demonstrated an hourglass-shaped, encapsulated intramuscular fat-signal lesion in the upper mid-lateral left chest wall, mildly insinuating between the lateral aspects of the fourth and fifth ribs, with no suspicious enhancement on postcontrast sequences.

A 39-year-old woman (para 1) was referred from dermatology to plastic surgery for evaluation of a nodular lesion arising from her umbilicus. She first noticed the lesion 18 months earlier; it had remained static in size for the past year and was entirely asymptomatic, with no bleeding, discharge, or cyclical changes during menstruation. She reported no history of trauma to the umbilicus aside from a long-standing peri-umbilical piercing. Her surgical history was notable only for excision of a benign ovarian cyst at the time of a caesarean section 10 years ago; she had no laparoscopic procedures with umbilical cannulation and no prior diagnosis of endometriosis.

On examination, there was a firm polypoid lesion arising from the central umbilicus with a normal overlying skin envelope. The lesion was adjacent to the previous piercing site but appeared to arise separately. The remainder of the abdominal examination was unremarkable, with no signs of hernia.

Differential diagnoses at that time included keloid scarring, neurofibroma, or dermatofibroma. An ultrasound scan of the lesion revealed a superficial soft-tissue nodule measuring 15 × 12 × 12 mm with an identifiable posterior wall and no evidence of deep connections.

A 2-year-8-month-old Mexican girl was referred to a dental clinic for “strongly decayed, painful teeth and gum bleeding.” Her parents denied craniofacial trauma, medication use, allergies, or prior surgeries. Since age 1½ years, she had recurrent skin erythema and rash, otitis media, anemia, and fever.  

On extraoral examination, she appeared in good general health but was markedly uncooperative. She had thinning hair but no other abnormal extraoral findings. Intraorally, she had an almost completely erupted deciduous dentition with mild incisor crowding, poor oral hygiene, excessive plaque, and halitosis. None of the teeth showed abnormal mobility. Deep carious cavities were present in multiple molars and canines, and there were root remnants of one molar. Soft tissues were unremarkable. The parents also recalled a small palatal bulge that had appeared about a year earlier and then resolved spontaneously over a few months.  

A radiographic survey including frontal and lateral skull radiographs and a 3-dimensional cranial‐bone model demonstrated two well-defined, punched-out osteolytic lesions: a 1-cm ovoid defect in the right frontal bone, divided into two cavities by a thin bone ridge, and a 3-mm circular lesion in the left temporal bone, 1 cm from the orbit. Additionally, she had hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and evidence of bone marrow cell infiltration.

A 67-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and rising serum creatinine identified on routine follow-up. She denied fever, weight loss, or urinary symptoms. Her medical history included mild hypertension, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome with prior splenectomy, habitual abortions, and thrombophlebitis. Physical examination was unremarkable except for an impalpable spleen. Approximately four years earlier, an ESR of 75 mm/h prompted treatment with oral prednisolone and azathioprine, and her ESR rose further to 100 mm/h after one year. 

On current admission, laboratory tests showed an ESR of 100 mm/h and creatinine of 1.6 mg/dL. Nonenhanced chest and abdominopelvic CT demonstrated bilateral isodense masses in the renal pelvis measuring 80 × 75 × 92 mm on the right and 90 × 102 × 126 mm on the left, without calcification. Multiple small mediastinal and periaortic lymph nodes (maximum short-axis diameter, 8 mm) were noted; there were no skeletal lesions. 

Abdominal MRI revealed the renal lesions to be hypo- to isointense on T1-weighted images, isointense to hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with mild restricted diffusion on ADC maps and gradual enhancement without washout on delayed phase images. Bilateral hydronephrosis with left-predominant parenchymal loss was present; no perinephric or subcapsular masses were seen. 

A CT-guided core-needle biopsy showed marked lymphoplasmacytic and histiocytic infiltrate without granulomas but was nondiagnostic. The patient then underwent right partial nephrectomy and left radical nephrectomy to obtain a definitive diagnosis.

A 40-year-old hypertensive, non-diabetic woman presented with one month of daily per-oral bleeding noted when spitting, about a teaspoon each episode, which improved with topical tranexamic acid and povidone gargles. She denied hoarseness, dysphagia, hemoptysis, respiratory distress, or neck swelling. She had no smoking or alcohol history but used local snuff for 16 years. Examination of the oral cavity and nose was normal. Indirect laryngoscopy revealed a mass on the posterior surface of the epiglottis. Flexible 70° endoscopy confirmed a well-circumscribed supraglottic mass on the epiglottis; the false and true vocal cords, aryepiglottic folds, and commissures were intact and mobile. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed an isodense supraglottic opacity at the level of the epiglottis, without invasion of adjacent structures.

A 72-year-old man with a history of laryngeal cancer treated in the past, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea, hypercholesterolemia, and long-term tobacco use presented with sudden onset of severe abdominal pain and hematochezia since the prior night. He noted fever and sweats several hours before the abdominal pain. On arrival, he was hypotensive and bradycardic. Physical examination revealed diffuse abdominal tenderness. Laboratory tests showed acute liver injury with markedly elevated transaminases. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated pancolitis with concern for ischemia versus infectious colitis.

He was admitted for supportive care, but his abdominal pain worsened, and plain abdominal radiographs suggested a possible volvulus. Follow-up CT showed thickening of the left colon with possible obstruction, wall dehiscence, and ischemia. Diagnostic laparoscopy revealed extensive adhesions, prompting conversion to open laparotomy. Surgical findings included full-thickness ischemia of the distal transverse colon through proximal sigmoid colon, adhesion of that segment to adjacent small bowel, and widespread fibrous adhesions. A sigmoid resection with transverse colostomy and small bowel resection was performed. Gross examination of the colon specimen showed dusky serosa with focal exudate, multiple transmural defects, and necrotic mucosa. The small bowel specimen had congested serosa with focal exudate and fibrous adhesions but no discrete mucosal lesions. Regional lymph nodes were unremarkable.

A 10-month-old boy was brought for evaluation of progressive abdominal distension over 4 months. There was no vomiting, fever, or changes in bowel habits. Antenatal scans were normal, and the perinatal period was uneventful. On examination, the child appeared pale. Abdominal palpation revealed a non‐tender, firm, irregular mass in the epigastric and right hypochondriac regions; the liver edge was palpable separately. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory testing showed mild anemia; serum alpha-fetoprotein, beta-human chorionic gonadotropin, and lactate dehydrogenase were within normal limits, and urine metanephrines were negative. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a large, well-defined mass with mixed echotexture and minimal vascularity. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 13.3×12.8×6.4 cm lobulated lesion of predominant fat attenuation in the region of the greater omentum, displacing bowel loops posteriorly and abutting the bladder without lymphadenopathy or infiltration. Based on these findings, the clinical team considered a benign lipomatous tumor and decided to proceed with primary surgical excision without preoperative biopsy.

A 67-year-old man from Haiti presented with a 10-month history of nodular lesions on his lower legs. Initially pruritic, the lesions became progressively painful. He denied fevers, chills, or weight loss. His medical history included hypertension and chronic active hepatitis B. On examination, vital signs were stable. Skin examination revealed numerous indurated hyperpigmented and erythematous patches, subcutaneous nodules, and tumors on the trunk and extremities, covering about 21% of the body surface. Bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy was noted; mucosal surfaces were normal.

Four months earlier, an initial skin biopsy showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with an atypical lymphoid infiltrate, predominantly CD3+, CD4+, and CD30–, leading to a provisional diagnosis of mycosis fungoides; peripheral blood flow cytometry and staging CT scan were unremarkable, and no treatment was started.

At a second-opinion evaluation, five new lesion biopsies demonstrated a pan-dermal atypical lymphoid infiltrate with epidermotropism and prominent Pautrier-like microabscesses. The atypical cells were medium-to-large with vesicular chromatin and irregular nuclear contours. Immunohistochemical studies revealed a predominance of CD3+ T cells with a CD4/CD8 ratio >10:1, strong CD5 and CD25 expression, and loss of CD7; CD30 highlighted scattered dermal cells, and CD20 was limited to rare B cells.

A 43‐year‐old man with a history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, asthma, and smoking presented with a 3-year history of intermittent pain over the posterolateral aspect of his left elbow. The pain did not limit his range of motion, was not related to activity or time of day, and he denied any tenderness to palpation over the lateral elbow. He reported that exposure to cold temperatures or cold water worsened the pain. There were no sensory or motor deficits, no palpable mass, and no overlying skin changes or signs of inflammation.

Ultrasonography of the left elbow revealed a small (0.6 × 0.2 cm) oval hypoechoic lesion in the subcutaneous tissue of the dorsal aspect, with posterior acoustic enhancement and no detectable vascularity on color Doppler. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 0.44 × 1 × 0.8 cm subcutaneous oval lesion at the posterolateral elbow. The lesion was hyperintense on both T1- and T2-weighted sequences, was not suppressed on fat-saturated sequences, and showed no definite enhancement.

A 20-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of vague epigastric pain without nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, jaundice, or weight loss. She had no significant medical history. On examination, she had mild tenderness in the epigastrium without peritoneal signs. Laboratory studies, including pancreatic, liver, and renal function tests, were normal. Serum CA19-9 and CEA levels were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a lobulated mass measuring 13 × 6 × 5 cm between the head and inferior portion of the pancreas, compressing adjacent structures. The lesion was predominantly low in density, contained patchy high-density areas, and included a 2 × 5 cm calcification. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a well-defined, solid, hyperechoic midline mass approximately 5 × 5 cm in size with smooth borders, without invasion of surrounding organs or regional adenopathy.

A 73-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and thyroid disease presented with left neck swelling and pain. She denied smoking, and her family history was noncontributory. Physical examination revealed a 2 cm, firm, smooth, palpable mass in the left parotid region. Neck ultrasonography demonstrated a well-circumscribed, heterogeneous, hypoechoic, solid mass measuring 2.9 × 2.9 × 2.2 cm within the superficial portion of the left parotid gland. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the neck confirmed a 2.7 cm solid-appearing lesion in the left parotid gland, and a neoplastic process was favored. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration showed clusters of benign acinar cells in a background of scattered lymphocytes, favoring a benign pathologic process.

A 13-year-old girl was admitted with a 2-week history of progressive dysphagia, dyspnea, facial swelling, pallor, and fatigue. On examination, she had signs of superior vena cava syndrome. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 6×10^9/L (48% lymphocytes, 42% neutrophils), hemoglobin 85 g/L, and C-reactive protein 117. Chest radiography revealed an anterior mediastinal mass extending to the hila. CT scan confirmed multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the anterior mediastinum without other masses. The patient underwent surgical resection of the mediastinal lesions, yielding ten lymph nodes measuring 3–7 cm. Histologic sections showed effacement of nodal architecture by cohesive sheets of large pleomorphic cells with abundant cytoplasm, kidney-shaped nuclei, frequent mitoses, and occasional Reed–Sternberg–like cells. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated strong CD30 positivity in the large and Reed–Sternberg–like cells, with negativity for CD15, CD3, CD20, ALK, CD45Ro, and EMA.

A 69-year-old man with bronchiectasis, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a 13 pack-year smoking history presented with progressive dyspnea (mMRC grade 3) and left chest pain. Three months earlier, chest radiography and CT had shown a 20 mm nodule in the left upper lobe, but further evaluation was deferred. On admission, chest radiography and CT demonstrated a 60 mm mass in the left upper lobe, multiple nodules in both lungs, and a liver lesion suspicious for metastasis. Thoracentesis yielded a bloody pleural effusion; cytologic examination on three separate samples showed only a few atypical cells. Bronchoscopy revealed no endobronchial lesions, and transbronchial biopsy of the left upper lobe mass was nondiagnostic. Over the next 2 weeks, pleural fluid reaccumulated rapidly, and his dyspnea, oxygenation, and performance status worsened markedly.

A 28-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of hip pain following low-impact falls. Initial imaging revealed stress fractures of the left rib, left sacrum, and left femoral neck. Laboratory studies showed an elevated alkaline phosphatase level of 220 U/L (reference range, 30–95), a phosphorus level of 2.1 mg/dL (2.5–5.0), creatinine 0.56 mg/dL, and 25-OH vitamin D 14.8 ng/mL (30–95). Outpatient evaluation demonstrated 1,25[OH]2D3 <8 pg/mL (18–72), calcium 9.3 mg/dL, albumin 4.28 g/dL, parathyroid hormone 37.9 pg/mL, ferritin 16.9 ng/mL, 24-hour urine phosphorus 0.5 g (0.3–1.3 g), urine creatinine 0.9 g/24 h (1–2 g/24 h), thyroid-stimulating hormone 2.54 mIU/L, and fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) 1241 RU/mL (<180). Bone densitometry showed Z-scores of −2.5 in the lumbar spine and −1.9 in the femoral neck, and an octreotide scan was negative. She was treated with calcitriol and phosphate and underwent percutaneous pinning of the femoral neck. She became pregnant; her phosphate and calcitriol were adjusted to maintain normal phosphorus levels, and genetic evaluation for hypophosphatemic disorders, including X-linked hypophosphatemia, was unremarkable. Family history was negative for bone disease. After a planned cesarean delivery, she continued to have disabling bilateral hip, knee, and ankle pain. On re-presentation, examination revealed a slow gait with a limp and lumbar tenderness. Current labs on calcitriol 0.5 mcg daily and elemental phosphorus 500 mg twice daily included alkaline phosphatase 204 U/L, phosphorus 1.6 mg/dL, 25-OH vitamin D 32 ng/mL, 1,25[OH]2D3 32.4 pg/mL, calcium 9 mg/dL, albumin 4.2 g/dL, and parathyroid hormone 74 pg/mL. Phosphate supplementation was increased to three times daily, raising the phosphorus level to 2.3 mg/dL. A gallium-68 DOTATATE PET/MRI showed a 9×8-mm intracortical lesion in the anterolateral right fibular head (standard uptake value [SUV], 65), with additional uptake in a right femoral neck stress fracture (SUV, 5.6) and bilateral calcaneal stress fractures (SUV, 4).

A 5-month-old boy was referred for evaluation of nocturnal coughing, dyspnea, episodic biphasic stridor with apneas, and intense drooling without dysphagia that had been present for 3 months. On examination during crying, using a tongue depressor, a cystic-appearing mass attached to the epiglottis was noted. Flexible laryngoscopy revealed a rounded, pink, pedunculated mass originating in the vallecula; it intermittently obstructed the supraglottic airway and moved synchronously with respiration and crying. A noncontrast computed tomography scan of the neck showed a smooth-edged, homogeneous mass measuring approximately 1.5 cm in diameter in the vallecula.

An 82-year-old multiparous woman was referred for progressive abdominal distension, right iliac fossa pain, and a palpable pelvic mass. Her medical history included hypertension and gastroesophageal reflux; she denied alcohol or tobacco use. Laboratory studies revealed a CA-125 level of 277 U/mL (normal 0–36) and a CA 19-9 of 64.5 U/mL (normal 0–37). Transabdominal ultrasound showed a heterogeneous, multiseptated pelvic mass with solid components and a sclerotic gallbladder with wall thickening and biliary sludge. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a thick-walled gallbladder adherent to the duodenum, moderate ascites, and a 17 × 11.5 cm right ovarian mass containing necrotic and calcified areas. The patient was deemed fit for surgery. At explorative laparoscopy, there was an advanced gallbladder lesion with diffuse peritoneal carcinomatosis and a unilateral ovarian mass showing early vascular compromise; the contralateral ovary was normal. The ovarian mass was resected and peritoneal biopsies were obtained. Peritoneal cytology was positive for adenocarcinoma.

A 71-year-old woman presented with a palpable mass in the left upper outer quadrant of her breast. She had no skin or nipple changes. On examination, there was a firm thickening fixed to the underlying pectoralis muscle (E4/5). 

A mediolateral oblique mammogram was reported as normal (M1), but the full pectoralis muscle shadow was absent on the left side. 

Breast ultrasound showed no lesion in the upper outer quadrant but revealed, deep in the posterior medial breast, an ill-defined hypoechoic expansion measuring 6 × 2 × 4 cm arising from the pectoralis muscle. Three 14-gauge core needle biopsies were obtained under ultrasound guidance. 

Breast MRI performed 3 days later demonstrated a 16 × 12 × 7 cm mass arising from and replacing most of the left pectoralis major, engulfing the lower costochondral area, and extending posteriorly into the thoracic cavity and anterior chest wall. The overlying breast tissue was oedematous but showed no discrete lesion. A moderate left pleural effusion was also noted. 

A subsequent staging CT scan revealed a large soft-tissue mass involving the muscles of the left lateral chest wall, extending inferiorly into the left rectus abdominis; involvement of the costal cartilages and pleura with lobulated pleural thickening and a large left pleural effusion; and additional soft tissue in the left superior mediastinum encasing the left subclavian artery, vein, and brachial plexus.

A 15-year-old teenager presented after inadvertently injuring his left thigh while descending stairs at school. He reported acute onset of pain and was unable to bear weight. On examination, the left thigh was visibly swollen with localized tenderness and palpable crepitus; the overlying skin was intact without ulceration. Routine laboratory studies were within normal limits. Radiographs of the left femur demonstrated a cystic space-occupying lesion in the middle and lower diaphysis with an associated pathological fracture. Computed tomography revealed an ill-defined intramedullary lesion with thinning and discontinuity of the cortical bone and a dense soft-tissue–density shadow filling the medullary cavity; no normal trabecular bone was evident. Magnetic resonance imaging showed uneven signal intensity within the medullary cavity with patchy low-signal areas on multiple sequences.

A 75-year-old man presented with continuous, moderate abdominal pain and progressive distension over two months. On examination, a large, palpable mass was noted in the upper abdominal quadrants. Laboratory studies revealed a mild normocytic, normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL), thrombocytosis (platelets 496 × 10^3/μL), hypergammaglobulinemia (2.4 g/dL), an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (>20 mm/h), and increased fibrinogen (460 mg/dL) with elevated fibrinogen degradation products (440 ng/dL). Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a heterogeneous, vascular mass arising from the omental sheets, displacing the diaphragm and bowel loops. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 32 × 29 × 15 cm, well-defined mass with heterogeneous enhancement and peripheral cyst-like areas compressing adjacent organs. The radiologist’s initial differential diagnosis included gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) and sarcoma. Preoperative gastroscopy revealed a small, reepithelialized ulcerative lesion in the prepyloric region; biopsy showed moderate lymphoplasmacytic and granulocytic infiltration with focal emperipolesis and no Helicobacter pylori. Colonoscopy was unremarkable. Bone scintigraphy showed no evidence of metastatic disease.

A 73-year-old woman presented with a subcutaneous nodule on the right thigh that had been present for about one year and was occasionally irritating. There was no overlying skin lesion. Her medical history included hypertension, atrial fibrillation, prior cerebrovascular accident, aortic valve replacement, total knee replacement, Parkinson’s disease, and recent excision of a squamous cell carcinoma on the forehead. She was wheelchair-dependent and resided in a nursing home. On examination, a firm, elastic 4 cm subcutaneous nodule was palpable without sinus tract. Initial differential diagnoses included lipoma or sarcoma. 

An MRI of the thigh demonstrated a 44 mm nonspecific subcutaneous lesion. An ultrasound-guided needle biopsy was performed, and the histopathological report concluded malignant melanoma (clusters of atypical cells with variable hyperchromic and prominent nuclei, relatively eosinophilic cytoplasm; SOX10 positive, Melan-A positive, HMB-45 negative to weak positive, AE1/AE3 negative to weak positive, P40 negative). Laboratory studies showed S100 of 0.04 µg/L and lactate dehydrogenase of 189 U/L.

To search for another primary or metastatic site, a total body dermatologic examination revealed only seborrheic keratoses and no suspicious nevi. A PET-CT scan showed intense FDG uptake in the right thigh lesion and increased muscle activity around the left supraspinatus, but no lymphadenopathy or other suspicious foci. An ultrasound of the left supraspinatus area demonstrated only degenerative rotator cuff changes and no focal lesions. Hence, it became much more likely that the subcutaneous nodule represented a primary subcutaneous melanoma.

A 57-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a radiolucent lesion in the left mandible. His medical history included hypertension, hemiplegia, dysarthria, and dysphagia; he was taking amlodipine 2.5 mg daily. Three weeks earlier, during dental care for a right maxillary caries, a new, large radiolucent area was noted around the left mandibular wisdom tooth.

On examination, there was no gingival swelling or tenderness over the lesion, and oral hygiene was fair. Panoramic radiography showed an impacted left mandibular third molar with a well-defined, unilocular radiolucency surrounding the crown, consistent with a dentigerous cyst. Under general anesthesia, the cyst and associated second and third molars were removed without complication, and histopathology confirmed a dentigerous cyst.

Follow-up at 1 and 3 weeks was unremarkable. At 6 weeks postoperatively (42 days), a rapidly proliferating, slightly reddish, friable mass measuring 13×8 mm was observed, arising on a stalk from the mesial wall of the second molar extraction socket. The patient was unaware of its onset, and there was no connection to the cystectomy site. Given the rapid growth and bleeding tendency, an excisional biopsy was performed.

A 71‐year‐old man presented with slowly enlarging bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, parotid gland swelling, and night sweats. His medical history was notable for melanoma resected from the nasal bridge in 2015 and a 40-pack-year smoking history. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head, neck, and chest showed multiple enlarged bilateral parotid gland lesions, scattered level I and II cervical lymph nodes, and upper mediastinal (right paratracheal) lymphadenopathy. Ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration and core needle biopsy of a 4.0 × 1.9 cm left cervical lymph node demonstrated cytology consistent with Warthin’s tumor. A level IA neck dissection confirmed Warthin’s tumor without evidence of malignancy or lymphoma. Six-month follow-up imaging showed stable bilateral parotid masses and cervical nodes but enlargement of right upper mediastinal lymph nodes. Endobronchial ultrasound–guided transbronchial biopsy of the paratracheal node revealed absence of malignant cells, and flow cytometry was negative for lymphoma. Six months later, imaging demonstrated stable mediastinal lymphadenopathy and slight enlargement of a left cervical lymph node. Physical examination revealed bilaterally enlarged parotid glands and bulky cervical lymphadenopathy; facial nerve function was intact.

A 42-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of a slowly enlarging, painless mass in the oropharynx associated with progressive dysphagia for 1 year and dyspnea for 3 months. She had no history of smoking or alcohol use. On examination, a large mass arising from the left lateral pharyngeal wall occupied the entire oropharynx, crossed the midline, and nearly touched the opposite lateral pharyngeal wall; neurologic examination was normal. MRI with gadolinium showed a well-defined, heterogeneously enhancing 72 × 44 × 66 mm mass in the left parapharyngeal space with marked mass effect on the naso- and oropharyngeal airway. A CT scan confirmed a heterogeneous mass extending from the level of the nasopharynx to C3 vertebra. On T1-weighted MRI, a fat plane was preserved between the mass and the deep lobe of the parotid gland.

A 21-year-old woman presented with a three-month history of epigastric pain, jaundice, weight loss, and intermittent melena. On examination she was pale and icteric; blood pressure was 120/60 mmHg, heart rate 90/min, and temperature 36.5 °C. Laboratory studies showed a hematocrit of 24%, total bilirubin 7 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 5 mg/dL, AST 100 IU/L, ALT 200 IU/L, LDH 430 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 760 IU/L, and γ-GT 430 IU/L. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a bulging ampulla of Vater that bled on touch; biopsies were negative. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 5 cm hypoechogenic lobulated mass displacing the duodenum, inferior vena cava, and mesenteric vessels, with dilation of the intrahepatic biliary tree, common bile duct (15 mm), and pancreatic duct (4 mm). Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 52 × 35 mm smooth-outlined solid mass in the second part of the duodenum with peripheral enhancement compressing the pancreatic head; the intrahepatic ducts, common bile duct (17 mm), and pancreatic duct (5 mm) were dilated, and there was no lymphadenopathy or metastasis.

A 9-year-old boy was referred with left cheek swelling and hyperglobus of the left eye. Hyperglobus was first noted about 1 year earlier under ophthalmologic observation. Six months later, swelling of the left cheek developed, with marked progression over the preceding 3 months. 

On extraoral examination, there was a painless, bony-hard swelling of the left cheek. The overlying skin was normal, but the patient reported numbness of the left cheek and weakness in movement of the left upper lip. There were no other neurologic deficits, no visual disturbances, and ocular motility was intact. Intraoral examination revealed expansion of the left maxillary ridge with mobility of primary teeth c, d, and e.

A panoramic radiograph and cone-beam computed tomography demonstrated a large, well-circumscribed, expansile, heterogeneous (mixed-density) mass occupying the entire left maxillary sinus. The lesion caused deviation and destruction of the nasal septum, invaded the ethmoid sinus, thinned, displaced, and perforated the anterior wall of the sphenoid sinus, extended into the pterygopalatine fossa with destruction of the pterygoid plates, and elevated and perforated the left infraorbital rim. There was extreme postero-superior displacement of the second molar toward the inferior orbital fissure, resulting in blockage of the fissure, and compromise of the nasopharyngeal space.

Medical history was notable for seasonal allergic reactions and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency; blood pressure was documented as 10/5 mmHg. Coagulation studies were within normal limits. Laboratory evaluation showed WBC 19 × 10³/μl, RBC 3.66 × 10⁶/μl, hemoglobin 10.6 g/dl, hematocrit 33.2%, and MCHC 31.9 g/dl; other serum chemistries were normal.

An intraoral incisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia with mepivacaine to minimize the risk of methemoglobinemia.

A 31-year-old Black woman, nulliparous and obese, presented with a history of pelvic pain and dysmenorrhea. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed an enlarged heterogeneous uterus. In May 2017, she underwent a complete hysterectomy; the specimen weighed 13.9 pounds, and pathology revealed leiomyomas without malignancy. One month later, she developed dyspnea and chest pain. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a mass presumed to be a thrombus in the right atrium. At sternotomy, the lesion was deemed unresectable; biopsy revealed “a fusocellular neoplasm, without atypia, richly vascularized, with areas of stromal fibrohyalinization, and the immunohistochemical analysis revealed angioleiomyoma.” Magnetic resonance imaging of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis identified a vascularized lesion within the inferior vena cava extending 19 cm from the iliac confluence to the right atrium, with an external component around the right gonadal vein. MRI also showed a 2.5-cm lingular lung nodule; percutaneous biopsy of this nodule demonstrated “neoplasm with smooth muscle differentiation of gynecological/Müllerian type without criteria for malignancy.” Intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography confirmed a mass partially filling the IVC and projecting into the right atrium, suggestive of a tumor.

A 60‐year‐old man with metastasized ascending colon cancer diagnosed 18 months earlier (initial hemicolectomy followed by XELOX; later FOLFOX/bevacizumab and FOLFIRI/aflibercept) and comorbid hypertension, dyslipidemia, sleep apnea, primary hypothyroidism, and asthma was hospitalized for febrile neutropenia. During his stay, he reported progressive thirst and polyuria. Initial capillary glucose reached 11.2 mmol/l with a hemoglobin A1c of 6.9%, leading to a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and initiation of insulin therapy. Despite euglycemia, he continued to have fluid intake up to 6.3 L/day and urine output up to 8.4 L/day, especially at night. Endocrine evaluation revealed complete panhypopituitarism: TSH 0.1 mU/l (0.4–4.0), free T4 8.0 pmol/l (10.0–22.7), baseline cortisol <35 nmol/l (>500), testosterone <0.15 nmol/l (5–32), LH <0.2 U/l (1.0–8.6), FSH 2.6 U/l (0.7–11), prolactin 34.5 μg/l (2.7–17), IGF‐1 11.4 nmol/l (7.7–25.5), and copeptin 3.6 pmol/l (1.2–16.4) at a sodium level of 143 mmol/l. After hydrocortisone, desmopressin, and increased levothyroxine, his thirst and urine output decreased to 2–3 L/day. MRI of the brain with contrast showed a round enhancing lesion in the pituitary stalk and another in the pineal gland, with no other intracranial abnormalities. Ophthalmological examination was normal.

A 57-year-old Asian woman with hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and prediabetes presented with a 2-month history of fatigue, fever, night sweats, chills, and abdominal distension, accompanied by an 8-pound weight loss and acute right upper-quadrant pain. On examination, she was jaundiced and had a palpable, centrally located abdominal mass. Laboratory studies showed mild to moderate hypochromic anemia and mild leukocytosis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 16 × 19 cm lobulated, heterogeneously enhancing mass in the pancreatic head and uncinate process, with bulky lymphadenopathy encasing the superior mesenteric vessels. PET scan demonstrated FDG-avid peripancreatic mass and superior mesenteric lymphadenopathy. A mildly enlarged 1.2 cm right inguinal lymph node was also noted. Endoscopic ultrasound–guided fine-needle aspiration of the peripancreatic mass revealed sheets of large atypical lymphocytes with hyperchromatic nuclei, irregular nuclear contours, and scant cytoplasm. Flow cytometry showed kappa-restricted B-cells expressing CD20, CD10, Bcl-2, Bcl-6, and c-myc, and negative for MUM-1, TdT, and CD3. Epstein–Barr virus was negative by in situ hybridization. The Ki-67 proliferation index was approximately 85%.

A 28-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of acute-onset binocular diplopia, most pronounced on left gaze. He denied trauma. On examination, primary gaze alignment was orthophoric by corneal light reflex, with esophoria on the cover–uncover test. Prism measurements demonstrated 16 prism diopters of esotropia when fixating with the right eye. In right gaze there was orthophoria; in left gaze there was 35 prism diopters of esotropia. Duction testing revealed a −3 underaction of the left lateral rectus muscle, consistent with approximately 25% abduction past midline. Diplopia charting showed maximum separation of uncrossed images in left gaze, and Hess charting confirmed underaction of the left lateral rectus with overaction of the right and left medial rectus muscles. Best corrected visual acuity was 6/6 in both eyes; intraocular pressures were 13 mm Hg bilaterally. Dilated fundus examination was unremarkable, with no papilledema. His medical history was notable for neither diabetes nor hypertension. 

Laboratory evaluation showed hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, white blood cell count 5800/mm3 (57% neutrophils, 37% lymphocytes, 6% eosinophils), random blood glucose 108 mg/dL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 5 mm/h. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain and orbits demonstrated a bulky left medial rectus muscle with heterogeneous enhancement and mild diffusion restriction, enhancement of the right sixth cranial nerve, bilateral third cranial nerves, and bilateral trigeminal nerves, and altered signal in the left choroid plexus suggestive of immune complex deposition. 

Lumbar puncture revealed cerebrospinal fluid protein 150.4 mg/dL, glucose 59 mg/dL, and a white cell count of 50 cells/mm3 with 90% lymphocytes. Tuberculous meningitis was suspected, but real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) for Mycobacterium tuberculosis was negative.

A 40‐year‐old man was evaluated for several episodes of brief unresponsiveness lasting approximately 30 seconds. He reported four seizure‐like events triggered by minor stimuli (blood draw, hot tub, minor trauma). He had no family history of neurologic disease. On examination, he was alert and oriented with normal cranial nerve and motor findings; gait was slightly antalgic from a recent ankle sprain. 

An unenhanced head CT showed a 1.7‐cm hyperdense nodule extending from the left tentorium. MRI of the brain with and without contrast revealed a 2.2‐cm lobulated mass along the left tentorium that was T1 isointense, mildly T2/FLAIR hyperintense, and demonstrated homogeneous enhancement. Susceptibility‐weighted imaging showed small punctate areas of hypointensity within the lesion. No surrounding edema or significant mass effect was noted. 

Based on imaging characteristics, the differential diagnosis included meningioma and hemangiopericytoma. The patient was taken for surgical resection of the mass.

A 70-year-old previously healthy man presented with a 3-day history of constant right lower abdominal pain and nausea, without fever or weight loss. Vital signs were normal. On examination, his abdomen was soft and distended, with normoactive bowel sounds and a palpable tender mass in the right lower quadrant. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 6400/μL, hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL, C-reactive protein 0.98 mg/dL, soluble interleukin-2 receptor 790 U/mL, and normal lactate dehydrogenase levels. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated ileocecal intussusception with a mass in the terminal ileum; CT of the neck, chest, and pelvis revealed no other lymphadenopathy or organ involvement. Colonoscopy confirmed ileocolic intussusception and identified a 50 mm submucosal tumor-like protruding mass arising from the terminal ileum, with a smooth surface and multiple irregular ulcerations; the mass reduced back into the ileum with endoscopic manipulation. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy was normal. Multiple biopsies of the mass showed diffuse infiltration of monotonous small-to-medium–sized lymphoid cells. Immunohistochemical analysis of the biopsy specimens demonstrated positive staining for CD20 and CD5; mantle cell lymphoma was suspected.

A 9-year-old boy with known tuberous sclerosis, diagnosed in infancy, presented to the dental clinic for evaluation of left mandibular swelling. He had the Vogt triad of sebaceous adenomas, epilepsy, and developmental delay, with no family history of similar disease. On examination, there was facial asymmetry from a firm, non-tender, 8 mm diameter swelling over the left mandible from the canine to the second primary molar; enamel pitting was noted on the permanent anterior teeth. Vital signs were normal. Panoramic and periapical radiographs revealed a well-circumscribed, unilocular, radiolucent lesion in the left mandibular body. Cone beam CT confirmed a 5.6 × 9.6 × 8.3 mm lesion with an incomplete fibrous capsule and cortical thinning but no cortical breach. The decision was made to perform surgical enucleation and send the specimen for histopathological analysis.

A 41-year-old woman with a history of multinodular goiter was seen in routine follow-up after noting a recent growth on the right side of her neck. She had no other significant personal or family history. On examination, there was a solid, partly exophytic nodule in the right thyroid lobe that was mobile with swallowing and non-tender. There was no dysphonia, dysphagia, or palpable cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed normal TSH, free T4, and free T3; thyroglobulin, calcitonin, thyroid peroxidase antibodies, and thyroglobulin antibodies were negative. Ultrasonography and CT imaging demonstrated a 3.0-cm hypoechogenic, heterogeneous nodule in the right thyroid lobe, abutting the sternocleidomastoid muscle and internal carotid artery. Fine-needle aspiration cytology was reported as TIR 3B (indeterminate follicular lesion). The patient underwent a total thyroidectomy with central compartment (level VI) lymphadenectomy. The postoperative course was uneventful. 

Histopathologic examination revealed a 2.3-cm solid, whitish nodule with irregular margins extending into perithyroid soft tissue. Microscopically, the tumor contained two intermingled components: a mesenchymal spindle-cell proliferation comprising approximately 70% of the lesion with a fibromatosis-like (desmoid) appearance, and an epithelial component comprising approximately 30% of the lesion showing features of papillary thyroid carcinoma. The lesion was staged as pT3b N0.
