A 75-year-old woman presented with sudden-onset flaccid paraparesis of 1 day’s duration. Her medical history was notable for diabetes mellitus and hypertension. She had no fever, cardiopulmonary symptoms, extremity pain, or palpable lymphadenopathy. On neurologic examination, motor strength in both legs was grade 2 to 3, deep-tendon reflexes were decreased, anal tone was lost, and there was numbness below the T4 dermatome. Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine showed an intramedullary mass lesion at T2–T4 that was iso-intense on T2-weighted images and iso- to slightly low-intense on T1-weighted images, with heterogeneous enhancement, associated with cord swelling and edema from C7 to T6. Brain and whole-spine MRI revealed no other lesions. Whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated an isolated lesion at T2–T4 with a maximum standardized uptake value of 3.14 and no systemic abnormality. Before surgery, the patient’s leg weakness progressed to grade 1.

An 84-year-old woman presented with one month of postprandial fullness, nausea, and occasional vomiting. She had a two- to three-year history of intermittent hematemesis, melena, and orthostatic hypotension. Her medical history included hypertension, chronic kidney disease, and hepatitis B infection. She denied tobacco, alcohol, or betel-nut use. On examination, she was alert, afebrile, with normal vital signs. The abdomen was flat, with normoactive bowel sounds, no tenderness, guarding, or rebound. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, WBC 9.37 ×10^9/L, platelets 302 ×10^3/µL, creatinine 1.53 mg/dL, BUN 25.9 mg/dL, CRP 2.04 mg/L, electrolytes within normal limits, and CEA 3.58 ng/mL. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 4.5 cm × 4.6 cm mass with an alternating concentric echogenic “doughnut” sign. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy demonstrated tortuous distortion of gastric folds from the lesser curvature into the duodenal bulb, gastric outlet stenosis, and a friable ulcerated mass barely passed into the second portion of the duodenum. Several differential diagnoses were suspected, including gastroduodenal intussusception, gastric cancer invasion to the duodenum, or pancreatic cancer adherent to the gastric antrum and duodenum. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT was then obtained. It showed gastroduodenal intussusception with a long-stalked, 5.9 cm polypoid mass in the duodenal bulb.

A 15-year-old Hispanic female with a known history of autosomal-dominant neurofibromatosis type 2, first diagnosed in early childhood with vestibular schwannomas and multiple CNS meningiomas, presented with a 2–3-day history of worsening right lower quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and occasional vomiting. She reported a 9-kg weight loss over the preceding months due to decreased appetite.  
On contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen, there was a right renal mass measuring approximately 7 cm. MRI of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a large, solid, peripherally enhancing right renal mass with central heterogeneity measuring 8.1 × 5.4 × 8.7 cm; retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy was present (a 4.1 × 2.0 cm retrocaval node, a 2.6 × 1.6 cm superior retrocaval node, and a 1.5 × 0.9 cm precaval/aortocaval node). A chest CT revealed a small right pulmonary nodule. A baseline PET scan confirmed FDG-avid renal and nodal disease and bilateral pulmonary nodules.  
Ultrasound-guided biopsy of the renal mass showed discohesive cells with rhabdoid morphology (highly atypical nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm). Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated strong positivity for pankeratin and PAX8, negativity for CK7, CK20, GATA3, CDX2, TTF1, CAIX, S100, CD34, CD30, SMA, desmin, OCT3/4, and CD163, and diffuse loss of SMARCB1/INI-1 expression in the nuclei of neoplastic cells (with internal positive controls present). Hemoglobin electrophoresis was negative for sickle cell trait or other hemoglobinopathies.

A 32-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of right ear discharge, pain, and hearing loss. Otoscopic examination revealed a skin-covered mass protruding from the postero-inferior wall of the external auditory canal entrance, significantly narrowing the canal and obscuring the tympanic membrane. After 1 week of topical ciprofloxacin and dexamethasone, his symptoms and clinical findings improved. Pure-tone audiometry demonstrated conductive hearing loss with a mean air–bone gap of 25 dB. A computed tomography scan showed a soft-tissue density mass arising from the postero-inferior wall of the external auditory canal, obstructing the canal without invasion of adjacent tissues. Fine-needle aspiration yielded an insufficient number of specialized cells for diagnosis.

A 4-year-old boy presented with a 3-month history of yellow discoloration of his eyes, dark urine, and pale stools, and 2 months of progressive abdominal distension. On examination, he was pale, had scleral icterus, and a distended abdomen with a large palpable liver.

Admission laboratory tests showed elevated cholestatic liver enzymes, conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, an elevated international normalized ratio, and iron-deficiency anemia.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a heterogeneous periportal mass with internal flow on color Doppler and dilation of the common bile duct (CBD), cystic duct, gallbladder, and intrahepatic bile ducts.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 60 × 45 × 89 mm fusiform-shaped mass with heterogeneous contrast uptake running parallel to the expected CBD course; its superior aspect was inseparable from the porta hepatis and proximal central bile ducts. The portal vein was partially attenuated without thrombosis. The mass deviated and partially compressed the first and second portions of the duodenum without obstruction. Inferiorly, it extended just below the right kidney’s lower pole. The aorta was displaced to the left, and the IVC was partially attenuated without thrombus. There was diffuse intrahepatic ductal dilation, marked gallbladder and cystic duct dilation, and pancreatic duct dilation. Minimal ascites was present, with no liver, lung, or bone metastases, but enhancing para-aortic and mesenteric lymph nodes were noted.

MRI with MRCP showed a fusiform intraductal lesion filling the dilated CBD with asymmetric mural thickening, largely hyperintense on T2 with patchy hypointense regions. The gallbladder was dilated, and a small calculus lay in the dilated cystic duct. Contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated heterogeneous enhancement of the solid components. MRCP revealed a markedly dilated CBD with a large filling defect and no normal-caliber distal duct.

A 34-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of an insidious, painless swelling in the right shoulder associated with gradually progressive restriction of shoulder movement but no trauma or systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a solitary, round, non-tender mass (≈5×5 cm) on the anterior aspect of the right shoulder with limited internal rotation and terminal flexion and abduction. Routine laboratory tests, including electrolytes, renal function, and white blood cell count (6400/μL with normal differential), were unremarkable. Plain radiographs showed a soft-tissue mass without calcification. Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed a well-defined, encapsulated, bilobed fatty-intensity lesion within the anterior deltoid measuring 5.1×7.4×5.6 cm abutting the bicipital tendon and reaching the anterior humeral cortex. The lesion was hyperintense on T1 and T2, showed demonstrable flow voids, exhibited fat suppression, had no diffusion restriction, and demonstrated heterogeneous post-contrast enhancement.

A 44-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with an 8-year history of a painless plantar nodule on the right foot. Over the previous 6 months, he noted discomfort when walking. On examination, there were subcutaneous nodules on the medial aspect of the plantar surface of the right foot. He had no family history of similar nodules, took no medications, and was otherwise healthy. Vital signs and laboratory tests were normal.

Ultrasound of the plantar arch with a 13–5 MHz array transducer showed a hypoechoic, homogeneous nodule within the plantar fascia with increased color Doppler flow. Magnetic resonance imaging of the foot demonstrated a hyperintense nodule on proton density images and a hypointense signal on T1-weighted images at the distal part of the superficial medial plantar fascia, with intense enhancement after gadolinium administration.

A 7-year-old boy was evaluated for a painless, right-sided neck mass that had appeared suddenly several years earlier and had gradually increased in size. On examination, the mass was 2 cm in diameter, soft, mobile, and non-tender. During a Valsalva maneuver, the mass enlarged and became more prominent. There was no dysphagia, stridor, or dyspnea, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI of the neck revealed a well-circumscribed cystic lesion extending from the right cervical region into the right hemithorax, with evidence of a “tail” of tissue in relation to the larynx. Based on these clinical and radiologic findings, a diagnosis of a laryngocele was made, and surgical excision was planned.

A 32-year-old non-smoker woman presented with progressive neck pain, dysphagia, and dyspnea. Her medical history was notable only for prior cesarean section and laparoscopy for adhesiolysis. On examination, there was a solid, tender, and mobile mass occupying the right and central neck. Laboratory studies revealed hypothyroidism. Thyroid ultrasound showed a 4 × 8 cm heterogeneous, hypoechoic lesion in the midline with right-sided predominance, displacing the right cervical vessels laterally and elevating the right thyroid lobe. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy yielded atypia of undetermined significance (Bethesda category III). Staging with neck ultrasound and chest and neck CT showed no evidence of metastases. The patient underwent complete thyroidectomy with mass excision without complications.

A previously healthy 7-year-old Thai girl presented with one month of back pain and progressive paraparesis resulting in inability to walk. On examination, there was no scoliosis; muscle strength in the lower extremities was grade III, with hyperreflexia in both lower extremities and hypoalgesia below the T4 dermatome. Plain radiographs of the spine showed normal alignment and no bony destruction. Magnetic resonance imaging disclosed a well-circumscribed, homogeneous extradural mass measuring approximately 1.0 × 1.4 × 4.0 cm in the posterior spinal canal from T4 to T7. The lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images, intermediate in intensity on T2-weighted images, and showed intense homogeneous enhancement after contrast administration. On axial T2-weighted images, the mass appeared to originate from the left facet joint at T5–T6, with abnormal marrow signal in that joint.

A 12-year-old boy presented with a firm, bulging mass over the plantar aspect of the right first metatarsophalangeal joint that had been present for more than a year. The overlying skin was erythematous but the lesion was non-tender and there were no systemic signs of infection. Ultrasound showed a multilobulated, heterogeneous hypo- and hyperechoic mass with increased internal vascular flow along the flexor hallucis longus tendon. An initial surgical excision yielded a histopathologic diagnosis of localized tenosynovial giant cell tumor without further immunohistochemical testing. Four months later, he returned with a larger recurrent mass at the same location, now associated with throbbing pain and skin erosion. Hematologic laboratory tests were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the right foot revealed a lobulated mass measuring approximately 3.1 × 2.1 × 5.0 cm abutting the flexor hallucis longus tendon; the lesion demonstrated iso- to high signal intensity on T2/proton-density–weighted images, marked homogeneous enhancement, nonenhancing dark signal foci, and partial infiltration into adjacent muscle.

A 35-year-old premenopausal woman presented with heavy, prolonged vaginal bleeding for one year, accompanied by foul-smelling discharge, severe lower abdominal pain, headache, palpitations, and weakness. She had been diagnosed with severe anemia and received three blood transfusions (960 mL) and iron therapy at an outside clinic. She had two term pregnancies, no history of cervical screening, no contraceptive use, no smoking or alcohol, and no personal or family history of gynecologic or breast cancer.

On examination, she was pale, afebrile, blood pressure 131/78 mmHg, heart rate 126 bpm, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Pelvic exam revealed red blood and purulent discharge. The uterus was normal in size, with no palpable abdominal masses but a distended abdomen. On speculum examination, a fungating cervical mass measuring 3 × 4 cm was visible. The parametria were free. Bimanual exam confirmed a cervical-origin mass. Initial clinical impressions included endometrial cancer with cervical infiltration or cervical cancer.

Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 2.2 g/dL, blood group O negative, normal platelet count, normal renal and liver function tests, normal electrolytes and coagulation indices, CA 125 of 19 U/mL, and CEA of 2.9 ng/mL. An abdominal CT scan with contrast revealed a 3.2 × 5.7 × 7.1 cm irregular mass centered in the cervix and infiltrating into the uterine neck, with mild fluid in the endometrial cavity, pelvis, and vaginal canal, and no lymphadenopathy or pelvic wall invasion.

A 43-year-old multiparous woman presented with a 4-month history of a giant, painless mass on the right side of the vulva associated with ulceration and foul-smelling vaginal discharge. She had no fever, regular menstrual cycles, and a history of psoriasis. On examination, she appeared pale without jaundice. Dermatologic findings included scaly, pruritic patches on her hands and feet. Genitourinary examination revealed an ulcerated, pedunculated mass measuring approximately 17×7×17 cm on the right labia majora. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, sodium 129 mEq/L, and calcium 1.28 mg/dL. Transvaginal ultrasonography demonstrated a normal uterus containing an intrauterine device, a normal left adnexa, and an enlarged right ovary. Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis revealed an oval cyst measuring 4×7 cm in the right uterine adnexa, a gallstone, a 15×7×17 cm irregular mass with central necrosis on the right labia majora, and right iliac lymphadenopathy.

A 37-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of a growth in the lower left posterior mandibular gingiva. Three months prior, she had food impaction and mild pain with occasional bleeding after using a toothpick. A small pea-sized nodule appeared in that area and progressively enlarged without pain, spontaneous bleeding, or paresthesia; one adjacent tooth exfoliated during this period. Her medical history was unremarkable.

On intraoral examination, there was a well-defined, exophytic, multilobulated growth on the mandibular alveolar ridge in the region of the lower left first molar, measuring approximately 5 cm × 4 cm × 3 cm and extending from the mesial surface of the left canine to the distal surface of the left second molar. The surface was smooth, shiny, and the same color as surrounding mucosa; a small 1 cm × 2 cm ulceration was noted on the buccal aspect. The lesion was firm, pedunculated, nontender, noncompressible, nonpulsatile, not warmer than surrounding tissue, and freely mobile on its peduncle.

Panoramic radiograph showed the left lower first molar was missing, the adjacent premolars appeared “floating,” and there was generalized moderate interdental bone loss consistent with periodontitis; there was no bone involvement at the site of the lesion. Routine blood tests, including hemogram, blood sugar, HBsAg, and HIV screening, were within normal limits. An incisional biopsy revealed a connective tissue mass lined by parakeratinized stratified squamous epithelium of variable thickness; portions of the stroma demonstrated myxoid areas with delicate fibers and stellate-shaped cells, along with multinucleated giant cells.

A 42-year-old man presented with a 20-day history of progressive dysuria characterized by decreased urinary stream, interrupted urination, and increased nocturia. There was no hematuria, weight loss, or systemic symptoms. On digital rectal examination, the prostate was markedly enlarged with a smooth, spherical contour and a firm, tough consistency. Serum prostate-specific antigen was 0.81 ng/mL (reference <4 ng/mL). Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis demonstrated an abnormally enlarged prostate measuring 6.7 × 6.6 × 5.8 cm, with poor demarcation of the central and peripheral zones. An irregular soft-tissue mass was noted in the right posterior prostate, showing heterogeneous internal signal intensity, protrusion beyond the prostate capsule, close relation to the rectum, and involvement of the right seminal vesicle; the prostatic urethra was compressed anteriorly. Whole-body computed tomography revealed no other masses or metastatic lesions. Ultrasound-guided needle biopsy of the prostate yielded three core specimens. Histologic examination showed densely arranged short strands and fascicles of spindle cells with moderate nuclear atypia, fine granular chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, sparse cytoplasm, and a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. In focal areas, spindle cells formed hemangiopericytoma-like vascular patterns, and the stroma contained variable collagen and mucinous degeneration.

A 67-year-old Japanese man with a history of distal cholangiocarcinoma presented for evaluation of a left lung lesion. Three years earlier, he had been diagnosed with distal cholangiocarcinoma after presenting with obstructive jaundice; percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage was performed, and imaging showed thickening of the distal bile duct. He underwent pancreaticoduodenectomy, which revealed a T3N1M0, stage IIB cholangiocarcinoma, followed by six months of adjuvant S-1 chemotherapy.  

At the time of his initial diagnosis, a chest CT demonstrated a small air-space consolidation in the left upper lobe, which was too small to characterize and thought possibly to represent pneumonia; the lesion was observed. Follow-up chest CTs performed every ~4 months showed gradual enlargement of the lesion, which measured 36.8 mm at 3.5 years after surgery. The patient remained asymptomatic, with unremarkable physical examination and normal routine laboratory tests except for a mildly elevated carcinoembryonic antigen level (5.6 ng/mL). A PET–CT scan revealed focal uptake in the lung lesion (maximum standardized uptake value, 4.30). A transbronchial lung biopsy demonstrated malignant cells, but no definitive diagnosis could be made.

A 26-year-old woman presented with 5 days of left upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She denied fever, weight loss, jaundice, or changes in bowel habits. Her medical, social, and family histories were unremarkable. Vital signs were normal. On examination, she had tenderness in the epigastrium and left upper quadrant without peritoneal signs; there was no palpable mass or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, coagulation profile, and inflammatory markers; serum AST, ALT, and lipase were mildly elevated. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 10 cm × 9 cm × 7 cm multilobulated mass inseparable from the body and tail of the pancreas, filling the lesser sac and partially encasing the gastric fundus. PET-CT demonstrated an FDG-avid pancreatic lesion and a separate 2.2 cm left subdiaphragmatic nodule suspicious for metastasis. A CT-guided core biopsy of the pancreatic mass showed sheets of small round cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and scant ill-defined cytoplasm.

A 13-year-old boy presented with a pruritic skin lesion on his right flank that had first appeared at age 2 and slowly enlarged until stabilizing 1 year before evaluation. His medical history was notable for mild atopic dermatitis and asthma. He reported no family history of similar lesions. On examination, there was a well-demarcated, erythematous plaque with overlying thick white scales arranged in a linear blaschkoid pattern over the right abdomen, flank, and back; multiple discrete papules were noted along the midline of the abdomen. Nails, scalp, mucous membranes, and musculoskeletal examination were normal. A skin biopsy showed parakeratosis with underlying hypogranulosis alternating with orthokeratosis with underlying hypergranulosis and a perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate in the upper dermis. No evidence of porokeratosis was identified on histopathological examination.

A previously healthy 5-year-old Nigerian girl was referred for evaluation of a 1-year history of recurrent abdominal pain. The pain was colicky, localized to the central abdomen, aggravated by feeding, and relieved occasionally by antacids. Episodes occurred 15–30 minutes postprandially, were severe enough to interrupt activities, and were sometimes relieved by vomiting of recently ingested food without blood. She had no abdominal distention, constipation, diarrhea, worms, hematochezia, fever, weight loss, or anorexia. She had a congenital umbilical protrusion (0.5 × 0.5 cm) unchanged during pain episodes. Between colics, she appeared well and participated normally in activities.

She had been evaluated repeatedly and diagnosed in turn with mesenteric adenitis, gastroenteritis, helminthiasis, and peptic ulcer disease, with no relief despite appropriate treatments. After non-specific abdominal pain and attention-seeking were considered and psychotherapy failed, she underwent repair of the umbilical defect without exploration. Two weeks later, pain recurred, now accompanied by hyperactive bowel sounds. Plain abdominal radiographs, ultrasound, and a gastrografin meal and follow-through were all normal. Upper endoscopy and laparoscopy were not available, and CT was unaffordable. Because of ongoing distress for the child and family, a diagnostic exploratory laparotomy was undertaken.

A 14-year-old previously healthy Asian girl was referred for evaluation of a heart murmur detected 5 months earlier. She had no family history of cardiac disease and reported no symptoms. Vital signs were normal. Cardiac auscultation revealed a grade 3 systolic murmur at the apex; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Electrocardiogram showed an incomplete right bundle branch block. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a 26 × 17 mm elliptic, slightly hyperechoic mass adherent to the right ventricular inner wall. A contrast-enhanced gated cardiac CT scan revealed an irregular low-density lesion (∼33 HU on noncontrast, ∼67 HU on enhanced, 74 HU delayed) closely related to the interventricular septum with mild enhancement. PET-CT showed a nodule near the septum in the right ventricle with no increase in glucose metabolism, suggesting a benign process.

A 51-year-old Asian man with no prior abdominal surgery or significant medical history presented with sudden onset of left abdominal pain. On examination, there was a tender, mobile mass the size of an infant’s head in the left abdomen. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a smooth, solid intra-abdominal mass approximately 19 cm in diameter containing cystic components. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen demonstrated a well-circumscribed mass with heterogeneous internal density appearing to arise from the small intestine. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a high-signal region on T1-weighted images, suggestive of intratumoral hemorrhage, and scattered cystic areas on T2-weighted images. Small-bowel endoscopy showed ischemic mucosal changes and slight luminal narrowing 20 cm from the ileocecal valve. Based on these findings, a gastrointestinal stromal tumor was initially suspected, and surgery was planned for diagnosis and treatment.

A 69-year-old woman, never smoker, with a history of hysterectomy for benign uterine fibroids 20 years earlier, presented with back pain. A chest radiograph revealed two pulmonary lesions. Chest CT with contrast showed a well-demarcated right lower lobe mass measuring 4.2×3.8 cm and a left lower lobe nodule measuring 2.8×2.6 cm extending to the left upper lobe; both were hypervascular and caused mild extrinsic compression of the adjacent bronchovascular bundles. The patient denied respiratory symptoms; spirometry showed an FEV1 of 106% predicted and a DLCO of 103% predicted. Abdominal CT revealed a 1.4×1.9 cm slowly growing hypervascular mass in the left adnexa separate from the ovary. She was on estrogen replacement therapy. An image-guided biopsy of the right lung lesion revealed a cellular spindle neoplasm with immunohistochemical findings supportive of a benign smooth muscle neoplasm.

A 10-month-old female infant was evaluated for recurrent hematochezia. The first episode at 7 months was of little quantity and treated empirically as an intestinal infection with antibiotics without resolution. Over the next 2 months, there were two more episodes of rectal bleeding. An abdominal ultrasound excluded intussusception. A possible food allergy was suspected, and she was switched from dairy formula to an elemental diet, but hematochezia persisted. At 10 months, she was referred to pediatric gastroenterology.

On evaluation, vital signs were normal. Physical examination showed a well-colored infant with a soft, nondistended, nontender abdomen and no visceromegaly or masses. Laboratory tests revealed hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, hematocrit 26.8%, leukocytes 9,260/mm³, platelets 243,000/mm³; clotting times were normal (PT 15.8 s, PTT 23.4 s, INR 1.0). She was admitted to the pediatric ICU for transfusion support.

A colonoscopy showed small angiodysplasia lesions in the colon at the splenic flexure and transverse colon extending approximately 5 cm, with no active bleeding or ulceration. A technetium-labeled red-cell scan demonstrated radiotracer uptake at the splenic flexure extending into the descending colon. A CT angiogram of the aorto-iliac vessels revealed irregular hyper-enhancing areas of neovascularization at the splenic flexure and mesentery along the splenic and superior mesenteric arterial territories. Finally, mesenteric angiography confirmed hypervascularity in the splenic flexure and transverse colon in the distribution of the superior mesenteric artery.

A 39-year-old woman with known neurofibromatosis type 1 (diagnosed at age 8, with café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, cutaneous neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules) presented with a painless left abdominal mass noted for one month. She has learning disabilities but was oriented on exam. There was no family history of endocrine tumors. Blood pressure was 105/65 mmHg. Abdominal CT showed a 15×13×11 cm heterogeneous mass with internal necrosis and small calcifications adjacent to the pancreatic tail. MRI localized a 14.6×11.3 cm heterogeneous lesion in the left adrenal gland with cystic areas, internal vessels, and mass effect on the right kidney. Given the NF1 background, biochemical testing for pheochromocytoma was obtained: 24-hour urinary normetanephrine 291 µg (reference <600 µg), vanillylmandelic acid 4.3 mg (reference ≤13.6 mg), morning cortisol 18.1 µg/dL (reference 3.95–27.2), and DHEAS 0.38 µg/mL (reference 0.35–4.2). These findings did not support a diagnosis of pheochromocytoma.

An 11-year-old boy presented with a 2-month history of a progressively enlarging right popliteal mass without other symptoms. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right knee showed a 5 × 4 × 10 cm lesion in the distal posterior thigh and popliteal fossa, isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images, intermediate on T2, with intense, heterogeneous contrast enhancement and surrounding subcutaneous and muscular fascia edema. 

A needle biopsy revealed an undifferentiated malignant tumor composed of small round cells that were positive for vimentin and CD99 and negative for CD45, CD20, and CD3, suggesting Ewing’s sarcoma/pPNET. Ten days later, examination at our hospital showed a painless, hard, fixed mass in the posterior right knee, overlying cutaneous venous prominence, and a 4 cm circumference discrepancy; no lymphadenopathy was noted. Blood tests and bilateral bone marrow aspirates were normal. 

An incisional biopsy demonstrated tumor cells positive for TdT; B-lineage markers CD79a, PAX5, CD19, CD22, CD10; myeloid marker MPO; CD34; CD43; FLI-1; and focally CD33 and CD117; cells were negative for CD38, cytoplasmic µ chains, CD13, CD15, monocyte/macrophage markers (CD68, CD11c, CD14, lysozyme, CD163), T-lineage markers (CD2, CD3, CD4, CD5, CD7, CD8), Myf4, MND116, and EMA. The Ki-67 index was 50%. PCR demonstrated clonal immunoglobulin heavy‐chain gene rearrangements (dominant peaks at 107 bp and 247 bp). Notably, no residual lymph nodal architecture was observed in the specimen.

An 81-year-old man and former heavy smoker presented with a 10-day history of hemoptysis. He denied chest pain, dyspnea, fever, or weight loss. His medical history included type II diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, and atrial fibrillation managed with metformin, atorvastatin, carvedilol, and dabigatran. 

On examination, vital signs were stable and the physical exam was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, coagulation profile, and basic biochemistry panel. 

A chest radiograph demonstrated a retrocardiac opacity on the left side. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a heterogeneous mass lesion in the right upper lobe and multiple bilateral solid pulmonary nodules. Flexible fiberoptic bronchoscopy showed narrowing of the right upper lobe anterior segment bronchus with an abnormal-appearing mucosa and necrosis. Endobronchial biopsies demonstrated chronic inflammation and necrosis without evidence of malignancy. Bronchoalveolar lavage cytology was negative for malignancy and granulomas. 

A PET-CT scan showed intense 18F-FDG uptake in the right upper lobe lesion, multiple pulmonary nodules, and left hilar lymph nodes.

A 49-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of progressively enlarging left subauricular masses. Her history was notable for cervical cancer treated surgically 14 years earlier. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender mass in the left parotid region. Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 2800/μL and a red blood cell count of 3.55×10^6/μL; other tests were unremarkable.  
Ultrasonography showed multiple, round, hypoechoic masses up to 2 cm in diameter with punctate calcifications in both parotid glands; color Doppler imaging showed no significant internal blood flow. The submandibular glands had heterogeneous echotexture with scattered small hypoechoic lesions, suggesting chronic inflammation.  
Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated well-defined masses in the left parotid and right sublingual glands that were hypointense on T2-weighted images and iso- to slightly hyperintense on T1-weighted images. Diffusion-weighted imaging and apparent diffusion coefficient mapping showed no significant diffusion restriction. Gadolinium-enhanced fat-suppressed T1-weighted images revealed peripheral enhancement with faint central enhancement. Atrophy and fatty replacement of both parotid glands were also noted.  
Given the presence of multiple salivary gland nodules in a patient with suspected Sjögren syndrome, MALT lymphoma was considered. However, MRI showed T2-hypointensity with no significant diffusion restriction, which was atypical for malignant lymphoma. Other than MALT lymphoma, cellular type pleomorphic adenoma, Warthin tumor, oncocytoma, malignant salivary gland tumors, IgG4-related disease, and amyloidosis were considered in the differential diagnosis for T2-hypointense salivary gland lesions.

A 46-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 2, with a history of stage pT1N0M0 invasive lobular carcinoma of the left breast treated 2 years earlier with neoadjuvant and adjuvant chemotherapy, breast-conserving surgery, radiation, and 2 years of hormone therapy (goserelin and tamoxifen), presented for evaluation of persistent anemia. Initial breast cancer staging had shown no evidence of metastasis on PET-CT or pelvic MRI. At the completion of tamoxifen therapy, she reported worsening menorrhagia requiring multiple blood transfusions.  
On gynecologic examination 2 years earlier, a 3.5-cm cervical mass had been noted; Pap smear was negative, and the mass was presumed to be a leiomyoma. On current pelvic ultrasound, a solid cervical mass measured over 8 cm in diameter, appearing submucosal at the isthmic portion. Laboratory studies showed:  
• CA-125: 535.4 U/mL  
• CA 15-3: 5.0 U/mL  
• CEA: 1.8 U/mL  
• Estradiol: 39.3 pg/mL  
Given the size, bleeding, and progressive enlargement of the mass, she was scheduled for total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.

A 24-year-old virgo-intacta woman presented with several months of suprapubic crampy abdominal pain, noncyclical vaginal bleeding, urinary frequency, and incontinence. She denied fever, weight loss, vaginal discharge, and gastrointestinal symptoms. She had no prior medical, surgical, or cancer history. On examination, a fungating mass measuring approximately 6 cm × 5 cm was visible at the introitus, arising from the anterior lip of the cervix. Laboratory studies showed microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 8.8 g/dL, MCV 74.5 fL) and normal renal and liver function. Tumor markers (CA-125, CA-19-9, CEA, AFP) were within normal limits. Under anesthesia, an excisional biopsy of the cervical mass was performed. Histopathology revealed primitive mesenchymal elements in hypo- and hypercellular areas with loose myxoid stroma and perivascular condensation. A cambium layer composed of subepithelial condensations of undifferentiated cells was observed, and the tumor cells were small, spindle-shaped, with interspersed strap cells. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for desmin and negative for vimentin and actin.

A 12-year-old boy was evaluated for a 6-month history of intermittent dysphagia and a sensation of food sticking in his throat. His siblings have a confirmed diagnosis of neurofibromatosis type 1. On examination, eight café-au-lait macules larger than 5 mm and several smaller macules were noted on the trunk. Palpation revealed a firm, tender swelling in the right cervical region along the mid–sternocleidomastoid muscle and an indurated cord along the posterior auricular nerve. Oropharyngeal and nasopharyngoscopic examinations were unremarkable. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the head and neck demonstrated a 40.7-mm right retro-mastoid subcutaneous mass and a 59.6-mm lateral pharyngolaryngeal soft-tissue lesion medial to the parotid gland, both traversed by the jugulo-carotid vessels. Laboratory evaluation showed normal urinary catecholamine levels, and blood pressure was within normal limits. Ophthalmologic examination and radiographs of the tibia and fibula were unremarkable.

A 48-year-old woman presented with impaired visual acuity in her right eye. She had a history of elevated prolactin levels (89 ng/mL) that normalized after medical therapy. On examination, visual acuity was decreased in the right eye; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory studies were within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain was performed using high‐resolution coronal and sagittal T1- and T2-weighted sequences with 2 mm slices and a small field of view, as well as T1-weighted images after intravenous gadolinium. Imaging showed a 5 mm round lesion in the suprasellar region that was iso‐intense to brain on T1‐weighted images and hyperintense on T2‐weighted images, with aberrant peripheral enhancement after contrast administration. The pituitary gland within the sella turcica appeared normal. There was no continuity between the lesion and the pituitary gland; the lesion was in contact with the pituitary stalk medially and displaced the optic chiasm superiorly.

A 65-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of epigastric pain and discomfort. Ten years earlier, hepatic cysts had been noted on routine examination. On admission, abdominal CT showed multiple hepatic cysts and a 2.6-cm mass in the gastric body with marked inhomogeneous contrast enhancement in the arterial, venous, and delayed phases. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed multiple gastric polyps and a submucosal eminence in the gastric body. Laboratory studies demonstrated elevated platelet large cell ratio, mean platelet volume, platelet distribution width, uric acid (433.7 µmol/L), β2-microglobulin (3.50 mg/L), cystatin C (1.4 mg/L), neuron-specific enolase (9.77 ng/mL), CA19-9 (37.26 U/mL), and CA50 (33.51 IU/mL); reduced total protein (63.3 g/L) and complement C1q (143.9 mg/L). The gastric lesion was resected, revealing a 1.9 × 1.4 cm submucosal multinodular tumor. Microscopically, one section showed infiltrative multinodular plexiform growth into the muscularis propria with epithelioid and diffuse areas of bland spindle cells in a loose myxoid stroma admixed with smooth muscle. Another section demonstrated diffuse growth with less loose myxoid stroma. Immunohistochemical staining of both sections showed tumor cells positive for smooth muscle actin, vimentin, and H-caldesmon, and negative for desmin, CD117, CD34, DOG1, pan-CK, CD10, and S-100; CD34 highlighted a rich capillary network in the stroma; the Ki-67 index was <5%. Fluorescence in situ hybridization for GLI1 rearrangement was negative, and sequencing of C-kit (exons 9, 11, 13, 17) and PDGFRA (exons 12, 18) showed no mutations.

A 39-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of left flank pain without other complaints. Physical examination was unremarkable. Complete blood count, renal function, and liver function tests were all within normal limits. Renal ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic lesion at the left renal hilum. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a well-defined 45 × 42 × 39 mm mass in the midpole of the left kidney, displacing adjacent renal vessels. A core biopsy revealed tissue cores infiltrated by tumor cells arranged in sheets and a perivascular pattern. The cells were round to polygonal with marked nuclear pleomorphism, irregular nuclear contours, coarse chromatin, prominent nucleoli, and a moderate amount of cytoplasm; some cells had eccentric nuclei, and multinucleated giant cells were present. Immunohistochemical analysis showed focal positivity for RCC antigen and CD10, and a diagnosis of renal cell carcinoma was initially suggested.

A 59-year-old man with chronic alcohol abuse presented with an upper-arm fracture sustained while gardening. Radiography revealed a spiral fracture of the proximal humeral diaphysis with displacement. During evaluation, he reported dyspnea on exertion and progressive abdominal distension, prompting admission for preoperative clearance.

His medical history was notable only for alcohol abuse; he denied tobacco and illicit drugs. Family history was noncontributory. On examination, temperature was 97.1°F, blood pressure 160/65 mmHg, heart rate 60/min, and respiratory rate 18/min. He had a mildly enlarged, nontender liver, a grade IV/VI systolic murmur at the aortic area, and scattered basilar crackles. There was no splenomegaly, jaundice, or lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, WBC 5700/mm3, platelets 115,000/mm3, BUN 14 mg/dL, creatinine 0.62 mg/dL, calcium 8.7 mg/dL, albumin 2.7 g/dL, total protein 8.4 g/dL, alkaline phosphatase 172 IU/L, ALT 71 IU/L, AST 107 IU/L, LDH 224 IU/L, total bilirubin 1.0 mg/dL, prothrombin time 14 sec (control 10–13), aPTT 34 sec (control 27–37), alpha-fetoprotein 8.7 ng/mL, hepatitis C antibody reactive, and HCV RNA 1,626,714 IU/mL.

CT of the right shoulder confirmed an oblique comminuted proximal humeral fracture traversing an ovoid lucency measuring 5.5 × 2.8 cm, without a discrete soft-tissue mass. CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated cirrhosis with portal hypertension and four liver lesions: the largest 3.1 cm lesion was “typical of HCC,” and a 5.8 × 5.2 cm lesion was “hypoattenuating and atypical for HCC.” Staging chest imaging showed no metastases. Based on imaging, the differential diagnosis included a primary bone tumor, skeletal metastasis of unknown primary, or hepatocellular carcinoma.

A 52-year-old Japanese woman with a history of T1cN0M0 invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast (ER-positive, PR-positive, HER2-negative) treated by mastectomy and sentinel lymph node resection presented for routine follow-up 12 months after surgery. She had received tamoxifen for six months with no evidence of recurrence.  
On abdominal contrast-enhanced CT, a solid lesion was noted in the splenic hilum that was slowly enhanced between the portal venous and equilibrium phases. MRI of the abdomen demonstrated a mass with diffuse heterogeneous enhancement. FDG-PET revealed uptake within the splenic mass (SUVmax 2.57).  
Laboratory studies showed a mildly elevated white blood cell count (10 900/µL) with other blood counts, biochemistry, and tumor markers (CEA, CA19-9, CA15-3) within normal limits.

A 65-year-old African American man with end-stage renal disease secondary to hypertension and insulin-dependent diabetes underwent a right nephrectomy for renal cell carcinoma 25 years earlier. In 2010, during evaluation for kidney transplantation, contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed multiple low-attenuation renal cysts and a 3.1×2.6 cm nonenhancing lesion in the upper pole of the left native kidney, consistent with a Bosniak class II renal cyst; no further follow-up was recommended. He received a living-related kidney transplant in 2012 with induction rabbit antithymocyte globulin followed by maintenance tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone. Five months posttransplant, he presented with gross hematuria and swelling of the left leg. Abdominal CT revealed an enlarging, minimally enhancing hypodense 3.3×3.8 cm cystic mass in the left native kidney upper pole (Bosniak class IV) that was “suspicious for RCC.” Venous duplex ultrasonography of the left leg demonstrated deep venous thrombosis extending from the popliteal to the common femoral vein. He underwent thrombolysis, placement of an inferior vena cava filter, systemic anticoagulation, and laparoscopic radical nephrectomy of the left native kidney.

A 1-year 7-month-old boy was brought for evaluation of right scrotal swelling noted by family. On examination, a 7-cm lobulated, rubbery-hard, smooth-surfaced, mobile mass was palpated in the right scrotum, separate from the bilateral testes. Ultrasonography showed a well-circumscribed, hyperechoic, lobulated mass with lobules measuring 1–4 cm in diameter, located outside the tunica vaginalis, and with scant internal blood flow. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated minimal enhancement of the mass. MRI revealed uniformly high signal intensity on T2-weighted images and a mosaic pattern on T1-weighted images, with coexisting low- and high-intensity areas. Serum alpha-fetoprotein and beta–human chorionic gonadotropin levels were within normal limits.

A 76-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 6-month history of progressive skin hyperpigmentation and fatigue. He had applied skin-lightening and sunscreen creams without improvement. On examination, there were brown-to-violet hyperpigmented patches on the face and upper trunk. Mucosal exam revealed violaceous plaques on the hard palate and yellow sclera with red-to-purple patches on the inner aspects of both lower eyelids. Palpable axillary lymphadenopathy was noted. Laboratory studies showed a white-blood-cell count of 4.6×10^3/μL (neutrophils 18%, lymphocytes 50%), hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL, and platelet count 72×10^3/μL.

A 63-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a gradually enlarging mass in the right thigh over five years. He noticed only its increasing size and was primarily concerned about its appearance; he denied pain, weight loss, or systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a 70 mm × 50 mm mobile, non-tender mass in the adductor compartment of the right thigh without overlying skin changes. There was no lymphadenopathy, and the neurovascular examination of the limb was normal. MRI of the right thigh showed an oval, well-defined intramuscular lesion measuring 53 × 38 × 57 mm in the adductor compartment. The mass was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, demonstrated a “bright caps sign,” and showed no enhancement after gadolinium administration. The lesion lay clear of major vascular structures.

A 51-year-old woman noticed a 2-cm palpable right-breast lump in 2019 that grew progressively. By June 2021 the overlying skin ulcerated with straw-colored exudate. She had local pain but no systemic symptoms. She had no chronic medical history. On examination, the right breast was asymmetrically enlarged; a 15×15 cm firm, immobile mass with indistinct borders occupied the entire breast, the overlying skin was erythematous, swollen, and dehiscent, and no axillary or clavicular lymphadenopathy was palpable. Laboratory studies showed mild anemia (hemoglobin 83 g/L) and slightly low albumin; other blood counts and liver function tests were near normal. Breast ultrasound revealed loss of normal architecture with mixed cystic (>90%) and solid echoes. Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI demonstrated a large irregular cystic-solid lesion with internal fluid levels and tortuous vessels; a right axillary lymph node showed slight cortical thickening. Core needle biopsy revealed dilated ducts with broad papillary structures, a mono- to multilayer epithelial covering, and densely packed tumor cells with moderately atypical nuclei. Immunohistochemistry showed ER 90%, PR 90%, HER2 negative, Ki-67 20%, CK5/6 negative, E-cadherin positive, p63 negative, calponin negative, and GATA3 positive. The absence of myoepithelial markers, lack of a fibrous cystic capsule, and presence of fused papillary networks with abundant fibrovascular cores narrowed the differential.

A term neonate girl was delivered by cesarean section to consanguineous parents. Prenatal care was notable only for a second-trimester ultrasound that detected a large sacrococcygeal mass (18×17 cm); first-trimester imaging had been omitted. The mother (BMI 30 kg/m2) had no chronic illness, and there was no family history of genetic disorders. At birth, the infant weighed 5 kg. Her heart rate was 150 beats/min, respiratory rate 50 breaths/min, and she had a brief period of oxygen saturation of 85% with peripheral cyanosis and weak movements. Examination revealed a soft, variably consistent mass weighing 2.5 kg in the sacrococcygeal area. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a completely external mass, consistent with an Altman type I lesion. Preoperative investigations showed a normal complete blood count, negative hepatitis viral markers, and elevated alpha-fetoprotein levels.

A 99-year-old man was admitted with three days of worsening colicky periumbilical pain, vomiting, and constipation. His history included hypertension and atrial fibrillation; he had no prior abdominal surgeries. On exam, his abdomen was distended and diffusely tender without guarding or rigidity. Laboratory tests showed a creatinine of 124 μmol/L, urea 12.7 mmol/L, and an elevated C-reactive protein of 133.48 mg/L; blood counts, liver function tests, and pancreatic enzymes were normal. A plain abdominal radiograph revealed multiple air–fluid levels. Non-contrast CT demonstrated dilated loops of jejunum and proximal ileum (up to 3.4 cm) with air–fluid levels and an abrupt transition to collapsed distal bowel. At the transition, there was a round, well-defined intraluminal mass with a mottled gas pattern and adjacent wall thickening (~1.5 cm), findings interpreted as a phytobezoar causing small-bowel obstruction. The patient underwent emergency exploratory laparotomy. Intraoperatively, a proximal ileal mass was identified; the presumed phytobezoar was removed, and a segment of ileum containing the mass was resected with end-to-end anastomosis. He recovered uneventfully and was discharged on postoperative day 6.

A 55-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of intermittent moderate upper abdominal pain and a 30-pound weight loss. She denied vomiting, changes in bowel habits, melena, or hematemesis. She had no significant medical or family history and was a non-smoker, non-alcoholic. On examination, she had mild epigastric tenderness without palpable masses. Laboratory evaluation revealed microcytic hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin 10.2 mg/dL) with otherwise normal blood counts and tumor markers. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed a 4 cm mass arising from the posterior wall of the stomach along its minor curvature. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy demonstrated a 3 cm protruding submucosal tumor on the posterior wall of the lower gastric body, reported as suggestive of a gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST). An endoscopic biopsy of the lesion showed moderate chronic non-atrophic inflammation with slight intestinal metaplasia.

A 61-year-old Japanese man presented with a 4-year history of a slowly enlarging mass in the midline of his upper lip. He had been treated for chronic hepatitis C years earlier but had no other significant medical history. The patient noted occasional epithelial detachment and bleeding, but did not seek evaluation until referral. On examination, the lesion was a well-defined, elastic, hard, ulcerated mass measuring 9×12 mm in the median upper lip; no regional lymphadenopathy was palpable.  

The lesion was excised under local anesthesia without preoperative imaging because of its clear boundaries. The tumor surface was smooth and covered by a capsule-like structure; the cut surface was solid and pale yellow. Histologically, beneath the erosive epithelium there were small nests of neoplastic cells embedded in markedly hyperplastic fibrous connective tissue. The stroma was heavily infiltrated by eosinophils. Tubular structures contained periodic acid–Schiff–positive mucus in their lumina and goblet cells were present. Venous invasion was also identified.  

Immunohistochemical staining showed positivity of the ductal structures for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), and of the solid areas for cytokeratin. The MIB-1 labeling index was 7.9%. The nearest surgical margin was 1 mm. Subsequent contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and whole-body scintigraphy revealed no metastases. Thyroid function tests, autoantibody panels, and peripheral eosinophil count were all within normal limits. Surveillance was planned with clinical exams every three months and annual contrast-enhanced neck CT.

A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with six months of lower abdominal discomfort and distension. On examination, a hard, non-tender, poorly mobile 20 cm pelvic mass was palpated. She had no significant medical or surgical history. Laboratory studies showed an elevated prolactin level of 30.67 µg/L (normal, 2.74–19.6 µg/L). 

Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated an irregularly shaped, well-defined hyperechoic pelvic mass measuring 169 × 77 mm, with multiple slightly hyperechoic nodules and unclear demarcation from the uterus. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 46 × 17 mm irregular hyperechoic intraluminal mass in the hepatic segment of the inferior vena cava (IVC).

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a long, strip-like mixed low-density lesion within the IVC containing fat-density signals and a filling defect in the pelvic vein extending to the left renal vein and into the IVC. Pelvic MRI demonstrated an irregular mixed-signal mass: areas of high signal on T1-weighted images that were suppressed on fat-suppressed T1-weighted sequences.

Based on these imaging findings, a diagnosis of intravenous leiomyomatosis involving the pelvic veins and IVC was considered.

A 46-year-old woman presented with a 17-day history of dry cough and dyspnea. She denied fever, chest pain, or hemoptysis. She was a lifelong nonsmoker with no significant family history. Vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, breath sounds were diminished with dullness to percussion over the right upper lung field; the remainder of her physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 4.71×10^9/L (67.9% neutrophils), hemoglobin 109 g/L, platelet count 408×10^9/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 78 mm/h, and neuron-specific enolase 20.9 ng/mL. Chest CT revealed an 8.9 cm × 7.1 cm soft-tissue mass in the right lung with multiple spot-like calcifications, heterogeneous internal density, compression of adjacent lung, a clear boundary, multiple vascular regions in the arterial phase, and delayed peripheral enhancement; there was no mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Bronchoscopy demonstrated external constriction of the right mid-lobe bronchus without endobronchial lesion. Endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial lung biopsy yielded only scattered lymphocytes and epithelial cells and was nondiagnostic.

An 18-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of a gradually enlarging, painless swelling in the left posterior mandible. There was no tooth mobility, paresthesia, or history of trauma. On extraoral examination, the left mandibular region showed a diffuse, firm, nontender swelling measuring approximately 4 × 5 cm, with normal overlying skin. Intraorally, the left mandibular third molar was clinically absent, and there was mild buccal and lingual cortical expansion (< 1 × 1 cm) without crepitus, tooth mobility, or displacement.

A panoramic radiograph demonstrated a large, well-defined multilocular radiolucency with long, thin internal septa, extending from the mesial aspect of the left first molar to the posterior ramus and from the sigmoid notch to the inferior border of the mandible, causing cortical thinning. A posterior–anterior skull radiograph confirmed expansion and marked thinning of the buccal and lingual cortices. CT (axial view) revealed a hypodense, well-circumscribed lesion involving the left mandibular body and ramus, with marked buccal and lingual cortical expansion and thinning but no cortical perforation.

A 51-year-old Japanese man (ECOG PS 0) was referred with a one-year history of gradually progressive bilateral nipple retraction and a three-week history of painful breast masses. At age 41, he was diagnosed with ALK-positive lung cancer (cT3N3M1b, stage IV) and treated sequentially with cisplatin/pemetrexed, alectinib, ceritinib, brigatinib, lorlatinib, and most recently with a combination of atezolizumab, bevacizumab, carboplatin, and paclitaxel (ABCP). One year prior, CT had shown bilateral breast enlargement without contrast enhancement, which was attributed to gynecomastia. Four months after initiation of ABCP therapy, CT revealed vertically oriented bilateral breast masses with contrast enhancement despite regression of his other metastatic sites. On examination, blood pressure was 119/79 mmHg, heart rate 92/min, temperature 36.5 ℃, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. His serum albumin was 3.9 g/dL; white blood cell count, hemoglobin, platelet count, liver and renal function tests, CEA (3.4 ng/mL), and cytokeratin fragment 19 (2.1 ng/mL) were otherwise within normal limits. Physical examination showed firm subareolar masses with nipple retraction measuring 2×2 cm on the right and 2×1 cm on the left. Mammography demonstrated bilateral microlobulated round subareolar masses with unclear margins. Breast ultrasonography revealed solid hypoechoic masses of approximately 20 mm beneath each nipple.

A 70-year-old postmenopausal multiparous woman noted a firm, slightly raised nodule on her right labium majus four months earlier; it progressively enlarged to about 3 cm. PET–CT performed externally showed multiple hypermetabolic foci suggesting malignancy. Cystoscopy revealed masses in the bladder trigone and near the left ureteral orifice; biopsy confirmed invasive carcinoma. Colposcopy showed invasive carcinoma involving the cervix and vaginal wall, suggesting cervical malignancy.

On examination, there were firm, non-tender, immobile bilateral inguinal lymph nodes (up to 2.5 cm), more prominent on the left. A 30 mm irregular, hard, fixed subcutaneous mass was present in the right vulva near the symphysis pubis. The vagina was patent but the anterior and lateral walls up to one-third were stiff with contact bleeding. Bartholin, Skene, and vestibular glands were unremarkable. The uterus was small and anteverted; adnexa were normal; anal exam was unremarkable.

A vulvar mass was excised. Histologic examination showed infiltrating adenocarcinoma in the dermis and subcutis without epidermal connection, arranged in nests and cords with pleomorphic cells, prominent nucleoli, 15 mitoses per 10 high-power fields, and lymphovascular invasion. All margins were free. Initial immunohistochemical results: tumor cells were diffusely positive for CK7, E-cadherin, and P53; negative for ER, PR, WT1, PAX8, CDX2, GATA3, P40, HMB45, and S100; Ki-67 index was 80%. The lesion was diagnosed as poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma.

A 30-year-old primipara was transferred on her fourth postpartum day for management of uncontrolled hypertension and intractable vomiting. At her first antenatal visit (8 weeks’ gestation), she was noted to have systemic hypertension (180/100 mm Hg) and was treated with amlodipine and methyldopa throughout pregnancy. The pregnancy was otherwise uncomplicated until 37 weeks, when her blood pressure rose to 220/120 mm Hg, accompanied by headache and multiple episodes of vomiting despite intravenous labetalol and magnesium sulfate. She underwent an emergency cesarean section for failure to progress; intraoperative blood‐pressure spikes were managed with nitroprusside. A healthy female infant was delivered.

During the postpartum period, her blood pressure remained markedly elevated. On arrival at our center she appeared in fair general condition. Temperature was 99°F; blood pressure, 230/130 mm Hg bilaterally; pulse, 120 beats/min; oxygen saturation, 92% on room air. She had no pallor, icterus, lymphadenopathy, or dehydration, but there was 3+ bilateral pedal edema. The breasts and thyroid examination were normal. The abdomen was distended and tender, with a positive fluid thrill, and bowel sounds were normal. Respiratory examination showed decreased air entry at both lung bases.

Laboratory studies revealed a slightly low hemoglobin, significant leukocytosis, and a serum potassium of 2.5 mmol/L; other routine hematologic and biochemical parameters were within normal limits.

A 47-year-old multiparous woman presented with a 12-month history of a gradually enlarging palpable mass in the vulvar region that was causing difficulty in walking. She reported mild discomfort but had not sought previous medical care. Her medical history was otherwise unremarkable, with no history of gynecologic surgery or vulvar trauma. 

On physical examination, vital signs were within normal limits. Inspection and palpation revealed a 6 × 4 × 3.5 cm, regular, mobile, soft mass located in the left labium minus. The uterus, cervix, vagina, and abdomen were normal on examination.

A 57-year-old woman was referred to a dental clinic with severe, generalized pain on the left side of her jaw and decreased sensitivity in certain teeth and adjacent gingiva. She had no facial asymmetry or extraoral findings. Intraoral examination revealed multiple teeth with extensive restorations and recurrent caries; the oral mucosa and alveolar ridges appeared normal. She reported no systemic illnesses and took no medications.

A panoramic radiograph showed several multilocular “punched-out” osteolytic lesions in the mandible, bilateral cortical erosion, and external root resorption of the distal roots of teeth 37 and 38. Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) confirmed multiple hypodense areas reflecting medullary and cortical bone loss with a punched-out appearance, without buccolingual expansion, and revealed a focal rupture of the lingual cortical plate near tooth 37, but no vertical bone expansion.

Following imaging, the clinical diagnosis was suggestive of a neoplasm of lymphoid origin, such as multiple myeloma or lymphoma, or a metastatic process. The differential diagnosis also included ameloblastoma, osteosarcoma, Paget disease, or other fibro-osseous conditions.

A 27-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of what he initially thought was a “callus” on the plantar forefoot of his left foot. Over time the lesion grew to 1.5 cm in diameter, became red, exquisitely tender, and caused sharp pain with walking. He noted occasional fever and chills at home. On examination, he was morbidly obese, and there was a variably hyperkeratotic, ulcerated, small red tender lesion on the plantar surface, resembling an abscess. Foot radiographs showed only soft-tissue swelling. He was treated empirically with antibiotics for presumed cellulitis.

Two months later, he returned with a significantly enlarged, ulcerated, cavitary mass at the same site. The lesion (5.0 cm × 3.5 cm × 3.5 cm) was excised. Intraoperative touch preparation showed loosely cohesive malignant cells with small hyperchromatic nuclei and scant cytoplasm. Histologic sections revealed sheets of poorly differentiated malignant cells with vesicular nuclei, clear cytoplasm, and abundant mitoses.

Immunohistochemical studies showed diffuse positivity for vimentin, CD99, c-MYC, and WT1; focal positivity for CD56; and negativity for CD10, CD45, S100, chromogranin, synaptophysin, pan-cytokeratin, HMB-45, myogenin, CD34, desmin, ERG, and NKX2.2. Next-generation sequencing of tumor RNA and DNA was negative for EWSR1 fusions; comprehensive NGS of 1400 cancer-related genes revealed no fusion RNAs (including CIC, DUX4, BCOR) and FISH was negative for SYT gene rearrangements.

A 62-year-old man with HIV (CD4 641 on therapy) and chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (diagnosed 2 years earlier) presented with 1 week of fatigue and dyspnea on exertion. He had progressive CMML despite prior cycles of decitabine, ruxolitinib and azacitidine, and was receiving hydroxyurea. He was deemed ineligible for transplant because of renal dysfunction. On admission, he had worsening anemia, thrombocytopenia and leukocytosis (WBC 62 K/µl, up from 40 K/µl 3 weeks earlier). A direct Coombs test was positive, and he was diagnosed with autoimmune hemolytic anemia and started on prednisone. He received red-cell and platelet transfusions. Bone marrow biopsy showed dysmegakaryopoiesis and 14% monoblasts, consistent with CMML. He was given prophylaxis with trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, IV fluids, allopurinol and continued hydroxyurea. 

By hospital Day 5, radiation oncology was consulted for palliative splenic irradiation for symptomatic splenomegaly. Over the next days, his respiratory status worsened, requiring nasal-cannula oxygen. A chest X-ray on Day 9 showed bilateral interstitial opacities interpreted as possible pulmonary edema. Two months earlier, his echocardiogram had been normal; on Day 9, his BNP was 71 pg/ml. He was treated with IV furosemide but continued to deteriorate and was started on broad-spectrum IV vancomycin and piperacillin–tazobactam. He required noninvasive ventilation and was intubated on Day 10. 

CT of the chest on Day 8 demonstrated new diffuse interstitial and ground-glass opacities with interlobular septal thickening.

A 3-year-old boy was brought with a valgus deformity of the right middle finger and an ulnar bony swelling at the base of the middle phalanx, first noted at age 1 and enlarging slowly until rapid growth over the past 3 months.

On examination, there was a pedunculated bony mass arising from the dorsoulnar aspect of the base of the middle phalanx of the right middle finger, measuring 2 × 1 × 3 cm, and a second, sessile bony lesion measuring 2 × 1 × 1 cm on the medial aspect of the proximal phalanx of the right second toe, both with mild tenderness and associated valgus deformities.

Radiographs of the right hand demonstrated a pedunculated mass at the proximal metaphysio-diaphyseal junction of the middle phalanx with minimal soft-tissue shadow, irregular areas of dense calcification within the matrix, and continuity of the phalangeal medullary canal with the lesion. Radiographs of the right foot showed a sessile lesion at the medial base of the proximal phalanx with medullary continuity and multiple smaller similar lesions in the hands and feet. The remainder of the skeletal survey was unremarkable.

A 76-year-old man was admitted after 3 weeks of headache, confusion, agitation, difficulty with speech, inappropriate movements, anorexia, and abdominal pain. On examination he was febrile (38.4 °C), cognitively impaired, and weak. Initial laboratory studies including complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, thyroid-stimulating hormone, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, ammonia, vitamin B12, and antinuclear antibodies were unremarkable. Empiric vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam were started for presumed infection. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed tiny diffusion-weighted hyperintensities in the right cerebellum. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal cell count and glucose, elevated protein (102 mg/dl), and negative cultures. Electroencephalography demonstrated a moderate to severe diffuse encephalopathy. Blood and CSF cultures remained negative. A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was obtained to seek an occult source of fever, which disclosed an 8.6 × 6.8 × 13 cm left adrenal mass displacing the left kidney. Adrenal hormone levels were normal, and there was no adrenal insufficiency. CSF testing showed an elevated tau protein (1617 pg/ml), an ambiguous 14-3-3 assay, and N-type calcium channel antibodies on paraneoplastic evaluation; other antineuronal and antiglial antibodies were negative.

A 40-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of a swelling on the right side of the face involving the middle third. The mass was firm, nontender, approximately 5 × 4 cm, and extended from the infraorbital ridge to 2 cm above the mandibular border, and from the right corner of the mouth to 1.5 cm anterior to the tragus. The borders were diffuse, the overlying skin was of normal color, and there was no ulceration; the lesion was mobile. Intraorally, there was no obvious swelling, the mucosa was intact, and scattered Fordyce spots were noted on the right buccal mucosa. A Water’s view radiograph showed a soft-tissue impression on the right cheek. Laboratory evaluation revealed hemoglobin of 7.5 g/dL; other hematologic parameters and a chest radiograph were normal. No lymphadenopathy was present. An incisional biopsy of the buccal mucosa lesion was performed. 

Microscopic examination showed a tumor in the deeper mucosa with pushing margins. Large nests of neoplastic cells with a squamoid appearance were separated by scant stroma. The cells had large vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli, marked pleomorphism, and both typical and atypical mitotic figures. Within some nests, clear cells with foamy cytoplasm were seen, and periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) staining was negative for mucin or glycogen. Intermixed were smaller basaloid cells with oval nuclei and scant cytoplasm.

A 78-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with progressive bilateral leg weakness and numbness over the previous week. On examination, he had deep paraparesis with motor strength of 3/5 in both lower extremities and was unable to walk. MRI of the thoracic spine with and without contrast showed a homogeneously enhancing, dumbbell-shaped extradural mass extending from the T3 vertebral body to the upper margin of T5. The lesion passed through the left T4 intervertebral foramen into the left middle thorax and displaced the thoracic spinal cord to the right on T2- and post-contrast T1-weighted sequences.

A 40-year-old man with a history of heavy tobacco use and HIV infection presented with a 5-day history of cough, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. On arrival, he was afebrile, with a pulse of 104 beats per minute and a blood pressure of 80/60 mm Hg. Chest radiography showed right lower lobe consolidation. Chest CT revealed right paratracheal lymphadenopathy and a 5.8 × 4.5 cm mass occluding the bronchus intermedius. Noncontrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated dense bilateral adrenal masses measuring 5.4 × 4.0 cm on the right and 4.8 × 2.0 cm on the left. Laboratory studies were notable for a white-cell count of 18.5 K/mm3, sodium 131 mmol/L, creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, and a CD4 count of 567 cells/mm3. He was admitted for presumed sepsis, received IV fluids, and was started on vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam. Infectious studies—including serum CMV, influenza PCR, Mycoplasma and Bartonella IgG/IgM, Cryptococcus and Histoplasma serologies, and Legionella urinary antigen—were all negative. Persistent hypotension led to measurement of a random morning cortisol, which was 7.0 μg/dL. A cosyntropin stimulation test yielded cortisol levels of 10.1 μg/dL at 30 minutes and 10.3 μg/dL at 60 minutes, with an elevated serum ACTH level of 83.4 pg/mL. MRI of the brain revealed no pituitary lesion. He was treated with stress-dose IV hydrocortisone, resulting in resolution of hypotension and abdominal pain, and was transitioned to oral prednisone 15 mg each morning and 5 mg each evening.

A 50-year-old man presented with a 9-year history of a right wrist swelling. Initially painless, the lump was soft and non-tender and remained stable in size. In mid-2022, he developed right-hand pain and grip weakness. On examination, there was a soft, non-tender mass at the right distal forearm. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right wrist revealed a lobulated lesion measuring 3.8 × 1.5 × 1.3 cm in the anterolateral distal forearm, located within the sheath of the median nerve. The lesion displaced nerve fascicles peripherally, with one fiber bundle seen centrally. It demonstrated high signal on T1- and T2-weighted images, suppression on fat-saturated sequences, and no significant enhancement on postcontrast images.

A 78‐year‐old woman presented to her general dentist with an enlarging soft‐tissue mass of several months’ duration. She was otherwise healthy, with no history of malignancy, and was not in acute distress. Intraoral examination revealed a fluctuant, exophytic lesion of the maxillary anterior gingiva, extending from the right lateral incisor to the left central incisor. The lesion measured 3.0 cm × 1.5 cm, appeared dark red with secondary tan‐gray ulceration, and the tissue collapsed under pressure from the forceps. A smaller, similar lesion was identified in the right maxillary vestibule adjacent to the labial frenum. A periapical radiograph showed no changes in bone quality or quantity and no evidence of odontogenic infection. A clinical diagnosis of pyogenic granuloma was made, and an incisional biopsy was performed.

Histologic examination showed stratified squamous epithelium with focal ulceration. Beneath the epithelium, tumor cells completely effaced the lamina propria. The cells were arranged in lobular aggregates separated by thin fibrous septa, some with a perivascular pattern, and the lesion exhibited a rich vascular network. On high‐power magnification, the cells displayed pink to vacuolated cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli, marked nuclear pleomorphism, and brisk mitotic activity.

A 30-year-old Caucasian woman with no past medical history presented with a mass in the right orbit but no proptosis. On examination, her right visual acuity was reduced; the left eye was normal. CT of the orbits showed a well-defined ovoid soft-tissue mass in the upper-external quadrant of the right orbit with a central calcified focus displacing but not involving the optic nerve. MRI demonstrated an intraconal mass adherent to the superior rectus muscle, with iso-to-hyperintense signal on T1- and T2-weighted images, central low-signal calcification, and homogeneous enhancement of the soft-tissue component. These findings led to a radiologic differential diagnosis of vascular malformation, cavernous hemangioma, and solitary fibrous tumor.

An 8-month-old boy was evaluated for an enlarging lesion on the left side of his tongue, first noted at 6 months of age and now three times its original size. He had no pain or respiratory symptoms, and his weight gain was appropriate, although he had some difficulty with solid foods.  
On examination, there was a pale mucosal lesion with a firm, submucosal 2-cm mass involving the left tongue and floor of mouth; no cervical lymphadenopathy was present.  
Magnetic resonance imaging of the face and neck revealed three discrete but connected lesions in the left oral cavity:  
 • Floor of mouth lesion measuring 4.4 cm, well-marginated, containing multiple foci of T1-bright fat.  
 • Anterior tongue lesion measuring up to 3.5 cm, with scant fatty signal and more solid enhancement.  
 • Posterior tongue lesion measuring up to 2.0 cm, with even less fat signal and solid enhancement.  
Under the same anesthetic immediately after imaging, an excisional biopsy of the floor of mouth mass and an incisional biopsy of the anterior tongue lesion were performed.  
Histologic examination showed lobules of mature adipose tissue with a myxoid stroma and a paucity of identifiable lipoblasts.

A 69-year-old man with a history of HIV on HAART presented with 2 months of diffuse abdominal pain, abdominal distension, low-grade fever, night sweats, hematuria, nonbloody diarrhea, anorexia, generalized weakness, and a 20-lb weight loss. On examination, his abdomen was distended with left upper and lower quadrant tenderness and fullness; there was no shifting dullness. Laboratory studies showed WBC 3.3×10^3/µL, hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL, hematocrit 34.4%, platelets 282×10^3/µL, creatinine 3.91 mg/dL (baseline 2), LDH 1418 U/L (normal 140–280), HIV viral load undetectable, CD4 count 229 cells/µL, EBV nuclear antigen antibody 130, EBV VCA IgG 679, HHV-8 titer 1:20, and CD20 negative by flow cytometry. Serum and urine protein electrophoresis and light chains were normal. CT of the chest/abdomen/pelvis revealed multiple nodular soft-tissue densities in the mesentery, surrounding the hydronephrotic left kidney, and in the anterior omentum. Noncontrast pelvic CT showed diffuse soft-tissue thickening of the posterior bladder wall with upstream hydronephrosis of the left kidney. A biopsy of an omental nodule showed sheets of undifferentiated plasma cells. Colonoscopy revealed colonic cystic lesions and focal thickening at the hepatic flexure; biopsy of that area showed very immature plasmacytoid cells in the lamina propria.

A 54-year-old man presented with a painful right supraclavicular mass of a few weeks’ duration, noted after swimming. He had hypertension treated with medication, a history of tonsillectomy in childhood, and knee arthroscopy in 2013. Ultrasonography revealed a single thin-walled cystic mass measuring 35 × 17 mm in the right supraclavicular region, superior and lateral to the brachial plexus and subclavian vessels, without associated nodular or tissue formation and without abnormal vascularization. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration yielded small lymphocyte-like cells mixed with lymphedema-like material, but the cyst recurred rapidly after puncture. On examination, the mass was renitent, movable, and nonadherent. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a right supraclavicular cystic lesion anterosuperior to the subclavian vessels measuring 43 × 40 × 27 mm; it was thin-walled, had no fleshy component or nodular formation, and demonstrated no tissue enhancement after gadolinium administration.

A 55-year-old man presented with a 10-month history of a painless ulcer on the left middle finger. Because he was a nail-biter and the lesion discharged pus, an initial diagnosis of paronychia was made; nail removal was performed and antibiotics were administered, but the ulcer failed to heal despite months of wound dressing. On examination, the fingertip was swollen and ulcerated with partial loss of the nail plate; there was no clinical lymphadenopathy. Routine hematologic studies were within normal limits. Radiographs of the left hand revealed a radiolucent lesion in the distal phalanx of the affected finger.

A 59-year-old man was referred after a routine physical examination revealed a mass in the region of the left seminal vesicle. He had no urinary or systemic symptoms. On digital rectal examination, a large, soft mass with indistinct margins was palpated at the base of the prostate. Serum prostate-specific antigen was 0.993 μg/L (reference 0–4 μg/L) and carcinoembryonic antigen was 2.89 μg/L (reference 0–5 μg/L). 

Contrast-enhanced CT urography showed two well-demarcated, round, low-density lesions in the left seminal vesicle measuring 5.4 cm × 5.8 cm (uniform density, no significant enhancement) and 4.3 cm × 3.6 cm (heterogeneous density with mild to moderate uneven enhancement). Pelvic MRI demonstrated cystic components that were hyperintense on T1 and T2 sequences and solid components that were isohypointense on T1 with mixed signal on T2 and small nodular hyperintense areas; the solid components exhibited marked heterogeneous enhancement, suggesting a suspected malignant tumor.

An ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy of the left seminal vesicle mass revealed fibrous connective tissue with muscular blood vessels lined by cuboidal epithelial cells; neither the epithelial cells nor the subepithelial stromal cells showed atypia. Prostatic tissue in the biopsy showed only hyperplasia. Because of the lesion’s large size, cystic-solid nature, and the possibility of under-sampling, the team considered borderline or malignant disease and the risk of torsion or incarceration. To exclude invasion from a prostate malignancy and to obtain a definitive diagnosis, surgical resection of the prostate and seminal vesicle mass was recommended.

A 41-year-old man presented with left-sided scrotal swelling and pain for 15 days without history of trauma or surgery. On examination, there was a firm, tender 2.5-cm nodule in the left testis; the right testis was normal. Clinical considerations included a testicular neoplasm versus an epididymal cyst. Serum α-fetoprotein, β–human chorionic gonadotropin, and lactate dehydrogenase levels were normal. Scrotal ultrasonography showed a 2.5-cm, well-defined, heterogeneous, hypoechoic solitary mass in the left testis. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration using a 24-gauge needle yielded scant grayish-white material. Smears stained with hematoxylin and eosin, Papanicolaou, and May–Grünwald–Giemsa stains were moderately cellular, showing tumor cells in monolayered sheets and loosely cohesive clusters. The cells were round to oval with indistinct borders, moderate to abundant pale vacuolated cytoplasm, and eccentrically placed monomorphic nuclei with fine granular chromatin and small inconspicuous nucleoli; occasional binucleated cells were present. The background contained pink amorphous material, bare nuclei, and a few lymphocytes.

A 79-year-old man with a 20-year smoking history presented with a dry cough of 3 months’ duration. He denied respiratory allergies, reflux symptoms, fevers, dyspnea, or bronchial obstruction. His only comorbidity was well-controlled hypertension.
