On examination, he was afebrile, morbidly obese (BMI 31 kg/m2), with a blood pressure of 135/88 mm Hg, pulse 82 beats/min, respiratory rate normal, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Lung auscultation was clear, and the remainder of the exam was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a normal white blood count without eosinophilia, normal biochemistry (including IgE, AST, ALT, LDH, CRP, and creatine kinase), and negative ANA, anti-dsDNA, rheumatoid factor, complement levels, and ANCA (PR3-MPO). Chest radiography was normal. Given his smoking history, a chest CT scan was obtained, revealing mild centrilobular emphysema and a 6-mm polypoid lesion on the right wall of the proximal trachea. Flexible bronchoscopy identified a firm, pedunculated polypoid lesion with pink mucosa arising from the right lateral wall of the proximal trachea.

A 35-year-old Caucasian woman presented with several months of swelling over the medial margin of her right scapula, associated with local inflammation and intermittent pain on abduction of the right arm. There was no pain at rest, fever, or chills. Her medical history was notable only for chronic asthma; family history was noncontributory. On examination, there was a wing-like prominence of the medial margin of the right scapula at rest. The scapula moved freely, winging was not accentuated by active shoulder maneuvers, and there was no snapping with movement. Neurological examination of the shoulders was normal. A true lateral radiograph of the right scapula revealed an exophytic mass arising from the ventral scapular surface, with continuity of the cortex and medulla with the underlying bone. CT confirmed a large exophytic lesion on the ventral aspect of the scapula. MRI demonstrated a hypointense cartilaginous cap measuring up to 1 cm in thickness with an associated pseudobursa, and no features suggestive of malignancy.

A 38‐year‐old man presented with a 3-month history of a swelling in the right lower posterior tooth region. Seven months earlier, teeth 46 and 47 had been extracted for caries, after which he noted persistent pus discharge but no increase in swelling size and no pain. He reported regular discharge of a creamy viscous fluid from the gingival sulcus of adjacent teeth. His medical history was significant only for asthma, treated with regular medications. Family history was notable for a 9-year-old daughter with similar bilateral mandibular swelling.

On examination, his head circumference was 57 cm with frontal bossing, hypertelorism, and right‐sided strabismus. Intraorally, a diffuse, soft, fluctuant swelling (2 × 4 cm) was noted in the right posterior mandible (teeth 44–46).

Panoramic radiograph showed three cystic lesions in the mandible at the apices of teeth 33–35, 44–45, and 48, with deformation of the right condylar and coronoid processes. The maxillary alveolar region (teeth 14–16) demonstrated a mixed radiolucent and radiopaque “ground‐glass” appearance. A chest radiograph revealed bifid anterior portions of the right fourth and eighth ribs. CT of the brain showed lamellar calcification of the falx cerebri and tentorium, with a mottled appearance of the parietal skull vault. Facial CT demonstrated enlargement of the right mandible with two osteolytic lesions and ground‐glass marrow with internal calcific densities. 

Aspiration of the mandibular lesion yielded a cheesy fluid, which was sent for histopathologic evaluation.

An 85-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a painful palatal lesion present for two weeks. Her medical history was notable for hypertension, diastolic heart dysfunction, and episodes of dizziness. Intraoral examination revealed a 30-mm ulcer with raised, irregular edges and a yellowish-white membrane on the left border of the hard and soft palate. A panoramic radiograph showed no bone changes.

A 30-year-old man presented with a 3-week history of a painful right iliac fossa mass. He had undergone a laparoscopic appendicectomy 7 years earlier. He denied bowel symptoms or constitutional complaints. On examination, there was a 10×10 cm tender, firm, mobile, globular mass in the right iliac fossa without overlying skin changes or lymphadenopathy. Blood tests were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT showed a homogeneous, oval-shaped soft-tissue mass (HU 50–80) measuring 9.8×9.0×10.4 cm arising from the terminal ileum, containing specks of fat but no calcification, and abutting the posterior margin of the right rectus abdominis muscle. The radiologist’s impression was ileal GIST. Colonoscopy showed no intraluminal lesion, and random biopsies of the terminal ileum were normal. The patient underwent a planned laparoscopic limited right hemicolectomy, which was converted to open surgery because of dense adhesions, and an 8×8 cm ileal tumour was resected with ileocolic anastomosis.

A 73-year-old man underwent laparoscopic right adrenalectomy for a rapidly enlarging 3.5 × 2.5 cm right adrenal mass discovered incidentally on CT performed for dyspnea. Over the preceding two years, MRI and PET scans had shown an increasing lesion with imaging features suggestive of adenoma, pheochromocytoma, or tuberculosis, along with splenomegaly. Laboratory tests excluded a secreting lesion and tuberculosis infection. His medical history included hypertension (on beta-blockers), benign prostatic hyperplasia (on silodosin), COPD (on inhaled steroids), and hypothyroidism; he had prior appendectomy and surgery for head trauma.

The adrenalectomy was performed laparoscopically using an open technique for trocar placement. The adrenal vein was coagulated, and the gland was removed; haemostasis was achieved and two drains were placed. Postoperatively, he was monitored in the ICU for COPD. That night he developed hypotension refractory to fluids, tachycardia, and anemia unresponsive to transfusion, with haemorrhagic fluid noted in the drains. An urgent exploratory laparotomy revealed massive haemoperitoneum with clots adjacent to the spleen, in Morrison’s pouch, and at the confluence of the right renal vein and inferior vena cava, but no bleeding source was identified. The abdomen was lavaged, haemostatic agents were applied, and two new drains were placed.

In the postoperative period, his white-cell count rose progressively to 53 000/mm3 with basophilia, monocytosis, and thrombocytosis in the absence of any signs of infection; hemoglobin remained stable and coagulation studies were normal. He then developed spontaneous bleeding from the abdominal wall requiring arteriography and embolization. Because of the marked leukocytosis without evidence of infection, he was referred to hematology for further evaluation.

A 60-year-old man presented with a one-month history of mild intermittent pain and a sudden ulcerated growth on the right maxillary edentulous alveolar ridge; he had undergone tooth extraction in that area one year earlier. Examination showed diffuse, mildly tender swelling of the right cheek with proptosis and watery discharge from the right eye, and palpable discontinuity of the right infraorbital margin. Intraorally, there was a soft, well-defined ulcerated mass covered by yellowish necrotic material extending from the right maxillary first molar region to the tuberosity; it was slightly tender. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included squamous cell carcinoma, minor salivary gland tumor, and carcinoma of the maxillary sinus. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated severe bone destruction of the right maxilla distal to the canine and destruction of the floor of the right maxillary sinus. Contrast-enhanced CT scans revealed a large, noncalcified soft-tissue density lesion centered in the right maxillary sinus, destroying all sinus walls and extending medially into the nasal cavity, laterally into the pterygopalatine fossa, superiorly into the orbit, and inferiorly through the hard palate into the alveolar process. Three-dimensional reconstructions confirmed a large lytic lesion of the right maxilla and palate.

A 67-year-old woman presented with a 10-year history of a progressively enlarging, tender mass in the left parotid region. Her medical history was unremarkable. On examination, a 16 × 18 cm firm, fixed, immobile, smoothly contoured mass was noted over the left parotid area without overlying erythema. There was no facial-nerve palsy, no mass in the pharynx or larynx, no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy, and the oral mucosa was intact. Postcontrast CT of the head and neck showed a well-defined, heterogeneously enhancing mass with prominent intratumoral vascular structures, extending across the pretragal area and over the zygomatic arch, abutting the mandible without bone destruction or masticator-space infiltration. CT angiography demonstrated a rich vascular network within the lesion. Preoperative embolization of the feeding vessels was performed, and the patient underwent total parotidectomy with attempted facial-nerve preservation.

An 8-year-old girl presented with a 1-year history of epileptic seizures, headache, and decreased visual acuity. On examination, she was alert and afebrile; vital signs were normal. Neurologic examination showed decreased visual acuity but was otherwise unremarkable. Cranial MRI revealed a right occipito-temporal, voluminous, well-demarcated mass with a multicystic “bubbly” appearance on T2-weighted images and heterogeneous hypointensity on T1-weighted images; after gadolinium, there was strong contrast enhancement, peritumoral edema, and left lateral ventricular dilation. An incomplete resection was performed because of intraoperative hemorrhage. Histologic examination showed tumor cells forming perivascular rosettes; the cells had indistinct cytoplasmic borders, round to oval nuclei without pleomorphism or mitoses, and the vascular walls were focally thickened and hyalinized. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated diffuse GFAP positivity, negative EMA staining, a Ki-67 labeling index of approximately 7%, and negative p53. IDH1/2 sequencing showed no mutation.

A 35-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of right-sided nasal obstruction. He underwent septoplasty, but symptoms persisted. Three years after surgery, rhinoscopic examination revealed complete obstruction of the right nasal passage by a cystic lesion arising from the nasal septum. The lesion was excised endoscopically, and histopathology showed chronic inflammation without tumor. Two months later, nasal obstruction recurred. Posterior rhinoscopy demonstrated a mass in the posterior upper part of the nasal septum. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the paranasal sinuses showed a soft-tissue mass involving the nasopharynx, ethmoid sinus, and sphenoid sinus, without apparent bony destruction of the maxilla.

A 44-year-old nulligravida woman presented with sudden onset of lower abdominal pain while walking. She had a 10-year history of infertility with no prior abnormal findings on routine ultrasonography. On pelvic examination, a soft, neonatal-sized mass was palpated anterior to the uterus without tenderness. Laboratory studies showed a mildly elevated serum cancer antigen 125 level of 56.3 ng/mL (normal <35 ng/mL); levels of cancer antigen 19-9, carcinoembryonic antigen, human chorionic gonadotropin, α-fetoprotein, and human epididymis protein 4 were all within normal limits. The patient reported no symptoms of hyperthyroidism.

Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a 10 × 8 cm mass in the pelvis with heterogeneous blood flow. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen revealed a smooth, ovoid right adnexal mass measuring 12 × 9 × 8 cm with heterogeneous low density on nonenhanced images, strong enhancement of the solid components, and several nonenhancing cystic areas. Magnetic resonance imaging showed that the mass contained a low-intensity solid component and multiple high-intensity cystic components on T2-weighted images; on fat-suppressed T1-weighted images, the solid portions were isointense to muscle and the cystic portions were low intensity. Dynamic contrast MRI revealed partial strong enhancement of the solid components in the early phase, with the enhancement spreading over the entire solid portion in delayed images.

A 30-year-old woman with no prior medical history was admitted after a motor-vehicle collision. She was hemodynamically stable and all laboratory studies were within normal limits. Her only complaint was tenderness over the thoracic vertebrae. 

Because of persistent back pain, a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest was obtained, which revealed an incidentally noted mass in the left anterior superior mediastinum. The mass was oval, vertically oriented, well defined, and homogeneous, measuring 78 × 64 × 103 mm in the prevascular space and extending anterior to the pericardium. There were no calcifications and no evidence of invasion into adjacent structures. The patient denied any respiratory or systemic symptoms, and there were no other remarkable comorbidities.

A woman in her mid-70s with a history of left-sided diverticulosis presented with 2 months of worsening nonbloody diarrhea, left lower-quadrant abdominal pain, decreased appetite, and fever. She had been treated empirically for diverticulitis without improvement. She denied recent travel, infectious contacts, or medication changes. Outpatient blood tests showed leukocytosis (WBC 23.63 × 10^9/L) and anemia (hemoglobin 81 g/L). The automated differential flagged immature granulocytes; a manual smear revealed a left shift to the blast stage with approximately 6% circulating blasts. She was referred to the emergency department. 

Abdominal computed tomography demonstrated extensive sigmoid diverticulosis but no bowel wall thickening or mass. Blood and urine cultures showed no microbial growth. Stool culture and parasite enzyme immunoassay were negative. Clostridioides difficile serology was negative. Repeat blood counts showed persistent blasts. Bone marrow biopsy revealed 65%–80% myeloblasts, consistent with acute myeloid leukemia; flow cytometry confirmed 47% myeloid blasts.

Because of her persistent severe diarrhea, she underwent flexible sigmoidoscopy without full bowel prep. Endoscopy showed grossly normal mucosa with scattered petechiae and surface friability, but no discrete lesions or masses. Random biopsies were obtained from the rectosigmoid colon.

A 21-year-old woman with a history of psoriasis, urolithiasis, and allergic rhinitis presented with a 4-week history of colicky, intermittent epigastric pain associated with a single episode of vomiting and diarrhea. She was afebrile, with normal vital signs. The abdomen was soft and non­tender; hematologic and biochemical laboratory tests were within normal limits.

Abdominal ultrasonography showed a hyperechoic intraluminal lesion in the jejunum measuring approximately 1.6 × 3.6 cm, raising suspicion for a polypoid tumor and small-bowel intussusception. Magnetic resonance enterography demonstrated a 2 cm well-circumscribed, fat-intensity lesion encircling the jejunum, with approximately 7 cm of telescoped bowel in the left upper quadrant.

A 65-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis treated with low-dose methotrexate for seven years and known hepatitis B carriage was referred for evaluation of a liver mass detected on screening ultrasound. She was asymptomatic. Physical examination and vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies showed normal liver function tests and no elevation in AFP, CEA, or CA19-9. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 16 × 29 mm hypoechoic lesion in segment 6 of the liver. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated slight arterial-phase enhancement of the lesion with sustained delayed-phase tumor staining. MRI showed weak enhancement in the arterial phase and hypointense signal in the delayed and hepatobiliary phases. The differential diagnoses included well-differentiated hepatocellular carcinoma, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, metastatic liver tumor, and primary hepatic lymphoma.

A 20-year-old single male smoker with no prior medical or surgical history presented with a 9-month history of intermittent obstructive urinary and retention symptoms. He reported urgency, dribbling, a weak stream, daytime frequency of about 10 voids, and nocturia of 3–6 times per night. He also described intermittent mild bilateral flank pain and constipation. He denied fever, vomiting, or urethral discharge and had no issues with sexual desire or erection aside from intermittent painful ejaculation. 

Initially treated as a urinary tract infection without improvement, he experienced three episodes of acute urinary retention requiring Foley catheter placement; during the second episode, 1500 mL of clear urine was evacuated. He was managed with antibiotics and tamsulosin between catheter episodes but continued to have bothersome symptoms.

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. Abdominal and genital examinations were unremarkable: there were no palpable masses, no costovertebral angle tenderness, and an inconclusive digital rectal examination.

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, renal function tests, urinalysis with culture, and prostate-specific antigen level, were all within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed diffuse bladder wall thickening and a large, well-circumscribed multilocular cystic pelvic mass with multiple septations and a focal soft-tissue component arising in the expected region of the prostate, displacing the Foley catheter laterally; there was no ascites and other abdominal organs appeared normal. 

Pelvic MRI further characterized the lesion as a large, well-defined multiloculated prostatic mass that was hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2, without diffusion restriction, and demonstrated enhancing soft-tissue components post-contrast but no gross invasion; the mass deviated the prostatic urethra to the left, with no seminal vesicle invasion or significant lymphadenopathy. The imaging differential included prostatic cystadenoma, cystic prostatic carcinoma, and hydatid cyst.

A 10-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a left orbital mass present for 3 years that had become more prominent over the past year, associated with intermittent redness, tearing, inward deviation of the eye, and decreased vision. He had been treated elsewhere for presumed mild infection with analgesics and topical drops. On examination, visual acuity in the left eye was 4/60 (nasal field) with no color plates identified (Ishihara 0/38). Ocular motility was limited (–2) in the superior, superotemporal, lateral, and inferotemporal quadrants and (–1) in the superomedial and inferior quadrants. There was inferonasal displacement of the globe and mild proptosis. Laboratory studies, including hematologic and metabolic panels, were within normal limits.

Computed tomography of the orbits suggested an intraconal mass, with an initial differential diagnosis of optic glioma, lymphoma, and meningioma. MRI demonstrated a left retrobulbar intraconal lobulated mass measuring approximately 3.6 × 2.3 × 2.7 cm displacing the globe anteriorly and widening the optic canal. On diffusion-weighted imaging, the lesion showed low signal intensity consistent with unrestricted diffusion and had well-defined borders. On T1-weighted images, the lesion was isointense to extraocular muscle, slightly heterogeneous, well circumscribed, and did not infiltrate the orbital muscles. T2-weighted and FLAIR images revealed an isointense lesion with a subtle hypointense line suggestive of a “tram-track” sign. After gadolinium administration, there was slight heterogeneous enhancement with a few nonenhancing areas.

A 46-year-old Japanese woman with a history of epilepsy presented with redness and swelling of the right breast. On examination, there was erythema and swelling in the lower right breast. Ultrasound revealed a 54 × 41 × 31 mm low-echo mass with partially unclear margins in the outer right breast. Biopsy showed invasive ductal carcinoma (no special type), high grade, ER+, PgR–, HER2 3+, Ki67 70%. Whole-body PET-CT revealed increased uptake in the right axilla, anterior mediastinum, left pleura, and liver, consistent with cT4dN3M1 stage IV breast cancer. She received four cycles of FEC chemotherapy, after which lesions nearly disappeared, and then trastuzumab plus pertuzumab with docetaxel, achieving a clinical complete response maintained for 23 months. Two years after treatment initiation, she developed a persistent headache. CT and MRI of the head revealed a 30-mm mass lesion in the right temporal lobe.

A 56-year-old woman with paranoid schizophrenia was evaluated for abdominal discomfort, and CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a solid right adnexal mass measuring 7.3 × 6.2 × 4.5 cm, a small amount of ascites, and moderate pericardial effusion. MRI suggested the pelvic mass was mesenchymal or stromal. Tumor markers were within normal limits (CA-125 5.9 U/mL, CA 19-9 24 U/mL, CEA 2 ng/mL). Seven months later, she reported gradual onset of dyspnea. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a large pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology. On presentation to the hospital four days later, her blood pressure was 138/99 mm Hg, heart rate 76 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Examination revealed distant heart sounds and jugular venous pressure of 14 cm but no pulsus paradoxus. Chest radiograph showed an enlarged cardiac silhouette and small bilateral pleural effusions. ECG demonstrated normal sinus rhythm with low-voltage QRS complexes. Initial laboratory tests, including troponin, were unremarkable. Rheumatologic studies showed positive antinuclear antibodies, low double-stranded DNA titer, and normal complement levels; confirmatory assays for connective tissue disease were negative. She underwent pericardiocentesis with removal of 600 mL of transudative serosanguineous fluid; opening pressure was 9 mm Hg. Fluid cytology revealed no malignant cells; gram stain, adenosine deaminase, acid-fast bacilli, and bacterial and fungal cultures were all negative. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed no pericardial thickening or late gadolinium enhancement. The pericardial drain was removed on day 5. A follow-up echocardiogram 48 hours later showed reaccumulation of a moderate pericardial effusion (1.2 cm).

A 25-year-old man presented with an 8-year history of a localized, non-itchy, thickened, hyperpigmented skin lesion on the left side of his chest. He first noticed a small, dark papule that enlarged over five years and then remained stable. There was no preceding trauma, rubbing, or application of topical agents, and he denied use of nicotinic acid derivatives or triazinate. He was otherwise healthy, with no family history of similar lesions.

On examination, there were multiple broad, brown-black, velvety plaques with soft ridges and ill-defined, irregular margins measuring 3×3 to 5×5 cm over the lateral left chest. The lesions merged imperceptibly with surrounding skin and had a few hairs. The remainder of the skin, including the neck, axillae, groin, palms, soles, and mucous membranes, was normal. Hair, nails, and genital exam were unremarkable.

He had a BMI of 21.2. Systemic examination was normal. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, urinalysis, nonreactive VDRL and HIV tests, fasting blood glucose 91 mg/dL, postprandial glucose 103 mg/dL, and fasting insulin 10.7 IU/mL. Liver function tests, T3, T4, TSH, and growth hormone levels were within normal limits. Radiographs of the chest, skull, and hands, as well as abdominal ultrasonography, were normal.

A punch biopsy of the lesion showed hyperkeratosis, papillomatosis, basal-layer hyperpigmentation, and mild acanthosis. The dermal papillae formed upward finger-like projections, and the intervening valleys were filled with keratotic material.

A 33-year-old man noted a mass on his left posterior scalp that had been enlarging over 4 months. He denied pain, paresthesias, or trauma, although the lesion bled intermittently. He had no significant sun exposure or use of alcohol or tobacco. On examination, there was a 5×5×4 cm painless, highly vascular mass over the left parietal scalp with normal overlying skin and no fixation to the calvarium. Multiple enlarged left level V lymph nodes were palpable. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the head showed a well-defined scalp mass without calvarial involvement. MRI demonstrated the lesion to be isointense on T1-weighted images and slightly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with flow voids. Both CT and MRI revealed significant left-sided cervical adenopathy. A PET scan showed abnormal uptake at the left posterior scalp and mid-left lower neck, with no evidence of distant disease. 

An incisional biopsy of the scalp lesion was performed, and histopathology was reported as a malignant adnexal neoplasm.

A 74‐year‐old man underwent routine abdominal ultrasonography, which revealed a mass in the abdominal wall. He had no history of abdominal trauma. On examination, there was a firm, elastic, painless mass measuring approximately 20 × 20 mm in the right lateral abdominal wall. Noncontrast CT demonstrated a low‐density mass within the right internal abdominal oblique muscle, and contrast‐enhanced CT showed mild, nonhomogeneous enhancement. A PET scan revealed low FDG uptake in the lesion (SUV‐max 1.4) and no evidence of distant metastases. The mass had not been present on CT images obtained 5 years earlier. The patient underwent wide en bloc resection of the lesion. Grossly, the tumor was well encapsulated, and its cut surface was pale white and glistening. Histologic examination showed a well‐circumscribed lesion within a thin fibrous capsule, composed of spindle‐shaped fibroblast‐like cells arranged in a whorled collagenous stroma with focal myxoid areas. Occasional areas of increased cellularity and scattered multinucleated or stellate cells were noted. The nuclei were mildly pleomorphic and hyperchromatic but lacked overt malignant features. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated that the tumor cells were negative for desmin, S100, smooth muscle actin, CD34, and CD117 and were positive for MUC4.

A 75-year-old man with a 10-year history of hypertension and recent urinary difficulty underwent a TURP two months ago, which showed adenocarcinoma on prostate biopsy. Two weeks post-procedure, he developed right flank pain and gross hematuria without other symptoms. He has no family history of tumors and takes only antihypertensive medication.  
On presentation, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Abdominal and flank examinations were unremarkable, and he voided without difficulty.  
Laboratory studies were within normal limits.  
Renal ultrasound revealed a 6×6 cm mass in the right kidney; the left kidney was normal.  
Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed a heterogeneous 6×6×5 cm mass in the upper pole of the right kidney without vascular invasion or lesions elsewhere.

A 69-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of progressive neck enlargement that had increased rapidly over the past several months. She reported orthopnea and dyspnea on exertion and was admitted for worsening respiratory distress. Her medical history was notable for hyperthyroidism, managed with suppression therapy. There was no history of systemic amyloidosis. On examination, her thyroid gland was bilaterally nodular and enlarged without cervical lymphadenopathy. Thyroid ultrasonography showed a diffusely enlarged gland with heterogeneous echotexture and multiple echogenic lesions in the right lobe, the largest measuring 1.8 by 1.0 cm. A thyroid radionuclide scan demonstrated asymmetrical enlargement and a prominent cold nodule in the lower right lobe; there was no retrosternal extension. Fine-needle aspiration of the right lobe revealed normal follicular cells and colloid. A clinical diagnosis of multinodular goiter with obstructive symptoms was made, and the patient underwent total thyroidectomy.

A 43-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of a painless swelling in the right preauricular region. On examination, a well-defined, firm, 3-cm mass was palpable in the right parotid area. Facial nerve function was intact, and there was no cervical lymphadenopathy. Ultrasonography showed a 3.6 × 3.4 × 2.0 cm hypoechoic lesion posterior to the angle of the mandible in the right parotid gland. Fine-needle aspiration cytology revealed moderate to high cellularity of epithelioid cells arranged predominantly in discrete forms and cohesive clusters, with rare acinar, papillary, and cylindromatous patterns. The cells exhibited mild anisokaryosis, fine uniformly distributed chromatin, regular nuclear borders, ovoid nuclei, indistinct nucleoli, and moderate amounts of cytoplasm. Some clusters contained fibrillary material without definite chondromyxoid stroma on Giemsa stain, and numerous cyst macrophages were present. There were no tubule formations, mitotic figures, necrosis, or cytologic atypia. Based on the cytomorphology, a diagnosis of low-grade parotid neoplasm was rendered.

A 29-year-old woman presented with right back pain. Nonenhanced CT showed a 10-cm right renal mass with calcifications in its caudal portion. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated tumour thrombus extending into the right renal vein and a 14×8 mm lymph node in the right renal hilum; multiple tiny pulmonary nodules were also noted. On T1-weighted MRI, the mass was slightly heterogeneous and hyperintense with foci suspicious for haemorrhage; on T2-weighted MRI, it was relatively low in signal with mixed hyperintense areas; diffusion-weighted imaging showed hyperintensity. FDG PET-CT performed for staging revealed partially increased uptake in the renal mass (SUVmax, 7.14), mild uptake in the hilar lymph node and thrombus, and no significant uptake in the pulmonary nodules.

A 65-year-old man presented with a 6-week history of right breast swelling that had been insidious in onset but rapidly increased in size. He had no pain or fever. His past history was notable for familial lipomatosis with multiple longstanding subcutaneous nodules. On examination, there was a non-tender, firm, 15 cm hemispherical mass occupying the entire right breast, with peau d’orange of the overlying skin and nipple distortion. The left breast was normal and there was no axillary lymphadenopathy. Multiple soft, non-tender lipomas were palpable on the trunk, and a large right-sided hydrocele was present. Baseline blood tests and chest radiography were normal.  
Breast ultrasound showed an encapsulated mass with areas of decreased echogenicity suggestive of sarcomatous change in a lipoma. MRI of the breast demonstrated mixed signal intensity with areas of enhancement similar to those seen in soft-tissue sarcomas. CT scanning excluded pulmonary metastases. Mammography revealed an enlarged, dense right breast containing a well-circumscribed soft-tissue mass occupying nearly the entire breast, with a rim of normal tissue peripherally. An image-guided core biopsy was inconclusive; the histological appearance was compatible with a wide differential diagnosis including fibromatosis, fasciitis, myofibroblastoma, dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, leiomyoma, or peripheral nerve sheath tumour.

A 24-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of progressively worsening pain and swelling of her left foot. She denied trauma or fevers. Initial management included footwear modification and analgesics without relief. An MRI of the foot showed hyperintensity on short-tau inversion-recovery sequences in the cuboid bone and adjacent soft tissues, and she was started empirically on anti-tubercular therapy. She reported no symptom improvement and noticed increased swelling. 

On examination, the left foot was diffusely swollen, the forefoot was everted with loss of the medial arch, and there was midfoot and medial border tenderness without warmth. Calf muscles were wasted; ankle range of motion was normal. The midfoot AOFAS score was 24. 

Plain radiographs demonstrated diffuse osteopenia and early midfoot arthritic changes. A CT scan revealed an expansile osteolytic lesion eccentrically located in the inferomedial aspect of the cuboid bone. Complete blood counts, alkaline phosphatase, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein were within normal limits; liver and renal function tests were unremarkable. Given the lack of response to anti-tubercular therapy, a core biopsy of the cuboid was performed and sent for histopathology and GeneXpert testing. The GeneXpert result was negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

A 27-year-old man noted a progressively enlarging lesion on his right cheek over two months. He had no pain, pruritus, bleeding, weight loss, appetite changes, trauma, or relevant family history. On examination, there was a dome-shaped, firm, nodular subcutaneous lesion measuring about 2×2 cm on the right cheek; it was painless, non-tender, without pulsation or skin temperature change. Head and neck lymph nodes were not enlarged; other findings were normal.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count with differential, liver and renal function tests, serum electrolytes, and urinalysis, were all within normal limits. Contrast and noncontrast MRI of the face showed an ill-defined subcutaneous lesion in the right cheek, measuring about 16×15×12 mm. The lesion was isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and exhibited vivid contrast enhancement.

Based on these MRI findings, an atypical hemangioma was considered, and the patient was referred for surgical excision.

An 82-year-old man presented with a 4-week history of progressive dry cough, dyspnea on mild exertion, bilateral lower-limb swelling, abdominal distension, early satiety, and unintentional weight loss. He had intermittent dry cough since June 2021 without orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, fevers, or prior edema. He denied known chronic illnesses. 

On examination, he had bilateral non-tender pitting edema to the knees. Vital signs: blood pressure 120/70 mm Hg, pulse 79 bpm, respiratory rate 18 bpm, temperature 36.8 °C, and oxygen saturation 75% on room air (improved to 96% on 7 L oxygen via non-rebreather mask). Cardiovascular exam revealed warm extremities, normal pulses, muffled heart sounds without murmurs. Abdominal exam showed distension, hepatomegaly 4 cm below the costal margin, and shifting dullness; spleen was not palpable. Respiratory and neurologic exams were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed WBC 75.32 × 10^9/L (neutrophils 67.6%, monocytes 24.0%, lymphocytes 6.6%), hemoglobin 12 g/dL, platelets 142 × 10^9/L, and NT-proBNP 4800 pg/mL (normal <125 pg/mL). Renal, liver, and thyroid function tests were normal. Blood cultures showed no growth.

ECG demonstrated low-voltage QRS complexes with electrical alternans. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a large circumferential pericardial effusion (3.0 cm), swinging heart, right atrial and ventricular free-wall collapse, dilated non-collapsing IVC, pulmonary hypertension (RVSP 43 mm Hg), and normal ventricular function. CT of the chest and abdomen showed pericardial and bilateral pleural effusions, moderate ascites, and multiple para-aortic and mesenteric lymph nodes.

A 36-year-old woman presented with a 7-day history of right-sided chest pain and dyspnea without fever or cough. She reported two prior spontaneous pneumothoraces: one right-sided in 2018 managed medically, and one left-sided in 2019 treated surgically. She also noted occasional small-volume hemoptysis. 

On admission, she was alert, with SpO2 97% on room air. Right chest auscultation revealed hypoventilation; no crackles were appreciated. The remainder of the examination, including endocrine and genitourinary systems, was unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies (CBC, chemistry, urinalysis) were within normal limits; microbiological tests for tuberculosis and other bacteria were negative. 

Chest radiography showed lung hyperinflation without focal parenchymal abnormalities. HRCT of the chest revealed a small right pneumothorax and numerous round, thin-walled air cysts (2–5 mm) scattered in both lungs; no irregular cyst shapes were noted. 

Pulmonary function testing demonstrated a 6-minute walk distance of 67% predicted, normal DLCO, and a negative bronchodilator response. 

Thirteen days later, she developed left-sided chest pain and dyspnea. Chest X-ray confirmed a new left pneumothorax; CT again showed a large left pneumothorax with passive atelectasis and persistent small air cysts bilaterally. Thoracoscopic surgery with pleural drainage was performed, and lung biopsies were obtained. 

Three months later, she had bilateral pneumothoraces requiring a third thoracoscopic intervention. One month after discharge, repeat CT showed resolution of pneumothorax, persistent small air cysts, and faint nodular infiltrates in both lower lobes.

A 14-year-old Eastern European male was referred for severe malnutrition and epigastric abdominal pain initially attributed to gastroesophageal reflux. He reported eight months of daily postprandial periumbilical pain. He had been taking omeprazole with some improvement in pain but had nonetheless lost 9% of his body weight over six months, with his weight falling below the 3rd percentile.

His medical history was notable for Nijmegen breakage syndrome diagnosed in infancy, with combined immunodeficiency requiring routine IVIG infusions, and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma at age eight, now in remission for six years on a reduced-dose chemotherapy protocol. Family history included two siblings and a cousin with Nijmegen breakage syndrome.

On examination, he appeared malnourished. The abdomen was soft, non-distended, and non-tender with no palpable masses. There was no significant lymphadenopathy and the oropharynx was clear.

Initial laboratory studies including complete blood count, metabolic panel, C-reactive protein, and celiac antibodies were all within normal limits. Because of his weight loss and elevated inflammatory marker, a fecal calprotectin was obtained and found to be 318.2 mcg/g (normal <50 mcg/g). An upper endoscopy and colonoscopy were then performed. Endoscopy revealed white nummular lesions in the stomach, chronic gastritis without evidence of H. pylori, and focal active ileitis. Colonoscopy showed a <5 mm tubular adenoma in the sigmoid colon.

A 76-year-old man with locally advanced prostate cancer (Gleason score 5 + 3) on hormone therapy presented with persistent rectal pain and new-onset fecal incontinence. Physical examination revealed a hard prostate adherent to adjacent tissues. Laboratory studies showed a prostate-specific antigen level of 8.4 ng/mL. Pelvic MRI demonstrated diffuse neoplastic involvement of the prostate (poorly defined T2 hypointense areas, restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging, and early contrast enhancement) extending into the rectal wall. In the rectum, there was markedly stratified parietal thickening with concentric areas of intermediate signal intensity on T2-weighted images, restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging, and contrast enhancement, involving both the submucosal and muscular layers.

A 54-year-old woman with no significant medical or dental history presented with an expansile swelling on the right side of her face. Panoramic radiography showed a well-defined, unilocular radiolucent lesion with buccal and lingual cortical expansion in the posterior right mandible. There was no pain, paresthesia, or tooth mobility. The initial clinicoradiographic differential diagnosis included unicystic ameloblastoma and developmental odontogenic cysts, especially an odontogenic keratocyst. An excisional biopsy of the lesion was performed, and the specimen was submitted for histopathological examination.

A 62-year-old African American woman presented with a 5-year history of an asymptomatic rash that began under her left axilla and subsequently involved the abdomen, covering less than 10% of her body surface area. She was cosmetically concerned but had no systemic symptoms. Physical examination revealed:
• A large, well-demarcated hyperpigmented thin plaque with a rim of annular erythema extending from the left axilla to the medial upper arm.  
• Multiple subtle hyperpigmented, ill-defined patches with a wrinkled appearance on the lateral right abdomen.  
• No lymphadenopathy.  

Three punch biopsies (left axilla and right abdomen) were performed. Histopathology revealed:
• An interstitial pattern of cells in the dermis with small aggregates of mildly enlarged atypical lymphocytes and a few histiocytes.  
• Mild increase in dermal mucin.  
• Scattered atypical lymphocytes in the lower epidermis.  
• No dermal wiry collagen.  

Immunohistochemical staining showed:
• Atypical dermal lymphocytes positive for CD3 and CD8.  
• Negative for CD4 and CD7.  
• Scattered CD68-positive histiocytes.  
• S100-positive dermal dendritic cells and marked Langerhans cells in the epidermis.

A 32-year-old Moroccan woman presented with a two-year history of a palpable mass in her right breast. She had no personal or family history of malignancy. Physical examination revealed a firm, painless, 1.5-cm mass at the junction of the outer quadrants of the right breast, without skin changes or palpable axillary lymphadenopathy. Mammography showed a dense mass with ill-defined borders. Ultrasonography demonstrated a 17-mm hypoechoic, heterogeneous, irregular, poorly defined lesion at the same location, abutting the latissimus dorsi muscle; these findings were considered suspicious for malignancy.

A 54-year-old woman presented with a 4-year history of exertional dyspnea, palpitations, fatigue, dizziness, and mild pitting edema of the lower extremities. Her initial blood pressure was 125/77 mm Hg. Her medical history was notable for diabetes insipidus, chronic osteomyelitis, well-controlled hypertension, and hyperthyroidism.  

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 100 mm/h, a C-reactive protein level of 42.4 mg/l, a B-type natriuretic peptide of 2137 ng/l, an interleukin-6 level of 61.3 pg/ml, a white blood cell count of 15.7 × 10^9/l, a platelet count of 653 × 10^9/l, and a serum CA 19-9 of 32.9 U/ml. Her daily urine output exceeded 10 000 ml.  

Cardiac computed tomography revealed a soft-tissue lesion of inhomogeneous density with an unclear boundary infiltrating the right atrial wall, interatrial septum, and atrioventricular sulcus, with a small pericardial effusion; the lesion showed slight enhancement after contrast administration. Coronary CT angiography demonstrated encasement of the right coronary artery without luminal stenosis. Perivascular infiltration of the aorta (“coated aorta”) was also present. Cardiac MRI showed a mildly inhomogeneous hyperintense lesion on T2-weighted images and hypointense signal on cine SSFP; after gadolinium administration, the lesion exhibited gradual, heterogeneous enhancement from first-pass perfusion to late gadolinium enhancement. Transthoracic echocardiography identified a hypoechoic mass on the right ventricular wall with contrast enhancement; the left ventricular ejection fraction was 63%.  

Abdominal CT showed a soft-tissue lesion with irregular contour and mild enhancement involving bilateral adrenal glands, kidneys (with a “hairy kidney” appearance), and retroperitoneal fat, as well as mild left hydronephrosis and severe stenosis of the proximal celiac and left renal arteries. MRI of the sella turcica revealed thickening and homogeneous enhancement of the pituitary stalk with patchy enhancement in the clivus. Laboratory tests for tuberculosis, pituitary, adrenal, and thyroid function and for immune diseases were all negative. A biopsy of the lesion had not yet been performed because of the patient’s condition.

A 7-year-old Asian boy was referred for 2 months of persistent mid-back pain that worsened with walking and improved with rest. His respiratory rate was 26 breaths per minute, heart rate 96 beats per minute, and temperature 37.0°C. Examination revealed pale conjunctivae and multiple, mobile, non-tender lymph nodes in the abdominal and inguinal regions. Cardiac auscultation disclosed a grade II/VI innocent murmur, and there was no organomegaly, rash, petechiae, or edema. His weight was 18.5 kg (<3rd percentile) and height 118 cm (10th–25th percentile per CDC growth charts).

Initial laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 11.59 × 10^3/μL, hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 80.2 fL, and platelet count 41 × 10^3/μL. Peripheral blood smear revealed normochromic anemia with thrombocytopenia and no blasts. Results of thyroid, parathyroid, calcium, electrolyte, liver-function, and renal-function tests were within reference ranges. A tuberculin skin test was negative.

Spine radiographs showed multiple compressions of the thoracic vertebrae, and pelvic radiographs demonstrated osteoporosis. Magnetic resonance imaging of the thoracic spine revealed multiple wedge-shaped and biconcave compressions of the vertebral bodies with fatty replacement of marrow in osteoporotic bone.

A 23-year-old Tharu man from a remote village in Nepal presented with a 2-month history of progressive difficulty opening his mouth. The limitation was painless but led to significant weight loss due to restricted oral intake. He denied any history of trauma, fever, joint pain, dental pain, rashes, or other swellings. He had been receiving antitubercular therapy for suspected abdominal tuberculosis for the past 3 months. 

On examination, there was no visible swelling or inflammation around the temporomandibular joints; intraoral examination was unremarkable except for a maximal interincisal opening of one finger breadth. No lymphadenopathy was present, and systemic examination was normal. A radiograph of the temporomandibular joints was normal. CT and MRI demonstrated an ill-defined mass in the right infratemporal region extending into the pterygopalatine fossa and invading the maxillary sinus, with loss of normal pterygoid muscle planes. 

A working differential diagnosis included sarcoma and a fibrous variant of tuberculosis.

A 70-year-old Caucasian man was transferred for management of a large chronic ulcer on his left pretibial area. He reported that 17 years earlier he had noted intermittent lesions on the left upper tibia after minor trauma. Over the ensuing decade the wounds became more frequent, and 10 years before presentation an outside physician diagnosed pyoderma gangrenosum associated with his longstanding Crohn’s disease and recommended nutritional supplements. Despite two surgical debridements, a skin graft attempt 5 years earlier, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, and multiple courses of antibiotics, the ulcer progressively enlarged. He applied wound vacuum dressings and managed his own dressing changes every 2 to 3 days. Four months before admission the tibia became exposed. His pain intensified, requiring high-dose extended-release oxycodone.

His medical history was notable for Crohn’s disease diagnosed in early childhood, managed without corticosteroids after partial colectomy at age 30. He was otherwise active until this lesion progressed. On examination he was cachectic and had a 13 cm by 8 cm ulcer over the proximal left tibia, extending to underlying muscle with desiccated bone visible. Multiple pressure ulcers were present on his back and sacrum.

Consultations were obtained for atrial fibrillation, Crohn’s disease activity, exposed bone osteomyelitis, presumed pyoderma gangrenosum, plastic surgery for wound coverage, nutrition, and chronic pain. The atrial fibrillation was controlled with amiodarone. Gastroenterology noted ileitis on recent imaging and small-bowel narrowing, with a plan to consider anti-TNF-α therapy pending confirmation that the ulcer was inflammatory. Infectious diseases recommended discontinuation of antibiotics given no pathogens and improvement after rehydration. Dermatology performed a bedside punch biopsy. Plastic surgery deferred flap coverage pending improvement of the underlying cause. Nutrition instituted a high-protein diet. Pain management tapered his opioids.

A radiograph of the left tibia showed mottling of the proximal third of the tibia with otherwise normal remaining tibia. MRI of the tibia demonstrated involvement of the entire proximal tibia with air posterior to the bone, without extension into the knee joint or femur.

A 26-year-old gravida 4, para 1 woman at 37 weeks of gestation was admitted for evaluation of a rapidly enlarging left anterior chest wall mass. She first noticed a peanut-sized lesion in her left accessory breast at 10 weeks of pregnancy; it grew progressively and became painful, whereas a similar lesion in her prior pregnancy remained small throughout. On examination, both native breasts appeared normal; bilaterally, small accessory breasts were present. The left accessory breast contained an elastic, mobile, well-circumscribed mass measuring approximately 15 cm × 15 cm, with overlying edema, congestion, and increased local temperature. Breast ultrasound demonstrated a relatively homogeneous solid lesion with short-strip blood flow signals. Abdominal ultrasound confirmed a single live fetus at 37 weeks. Mammography and MRI were deferred, and the patient declined core needle biopsy. Three days after admission, the mass enlarged further, with skin breakdown and bleeding. Given fetal maturity, a combined cesarean section and excision of the mass and accessory breasts was planned.

A 43-year-old Asian man with a 6-year history of hypertension controlled with α- and β-blockers and a diuretic was found on routine abdominal ultrasonography to have a well-defined soft-tissue density lesion in the right adrenal gland. He had a history of myocardial infarction 9 years earlier treated with coronary angioplasty and was taking an antiplatelet agent. On examination, his blood pressure was 150/90 mm Hg. A chest radiograph showed prominent vascular markings in both lung fields and cardiomegaly. MRI of the abdomen demonstrated a 119 × 105 mm, well-defined lesion of altered signal intensity in the right suprarenal region; other organs and lymph nodes were unremarkable. CT confirmed a 116 × 100 mm, well-defined soft-tissue density mass with intrinsic fat density areas in the right adrenal region. Laboratory studies showed a random blood glucose of 82.6 mg/dL; normal renal and liver function tests and serum electrolytes; hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL; normal blood counts; negative serologic tests for HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C virus; unremarkable urinalysis; and a 24-hour urinary vanillylmandelic acid level of 4.7 mg (reference range, 2–8 mg/24 h).

A 48-year-old man presented with several weeks of persistent epigastric abdominal pain that was nonradiating and not associated with nausea, vomiting, changes in bowel habits, or weight loss. He denied jaundice, postprandial vomiting, or early satiety. His medical history was unremarkable, with no prior abdominal surgery, trauma, infections, or congenital disorders. On examination, the abdomen was soft, nondistended, and without masses or tenderness.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver function tests, serum amylase, and lipase, were all within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound showed no biliary pathology. Gastroscopy revealed normal gastric and duodenal mucosa without ulcers or masses.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a well-defined, nonenhancing 36 × 30 mm soft-tissue lesion in the aortocaval (retroduodenal) region with punctate calcifications; there was no lymphadenopathy or ascites. Endoscopic ultrasound confirmed an isoechoic 36 × 30 mm mass between the inferior vena cava and aorta; fine-needle biopsy was deferred because of bleeding risk.

To exclude a paraganglioma, 24-hour urine collections for normetanephrine and metanephrine were obtained and were within normal limits. Gallium-68 PET/CT showed no increased tracer uptake in the lesion. The patient was referred for surgical evaluation.

A 57-year-old woman presented with intermittent lower back pain worsened by activity, occasionally radiating to the left buttock with numbness and tingling in both thighs. She denied weakness, bowel or bladder incontinence, weight loss, fevers, or chills. She had no significant medical or family history and had not improved with physical therapy. 

Plain radiographs of the lumbar spine showed subtle sclerosis in the posterior half of the L2 vertebral body and degenerative changes. MRI of the lumbar spine demonstrated a T1-hypointense, STIR-heterogeneous lesion in the posterior L2 vertebral body with irregular posterior cortex, an epidural soft tissue component causing spinal canal stenosis, and compression of the thecal sac without focal lesions elsewhere. 

CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast revealed an irregular, sclerotic L2 lesion with posterior cortical destruction and no other suspicious lesions. PET/CT showed increased FDG uptake in the posterior L2 lesion (SUV max 4.2) with no other hypermetabolic foci. A Tc-99m bone scan and SPECT-CT confirmed isolated increased uptake at L2 without additional osseous lesions. 

Differential diagnosis based on imaging included metastasis, lymphoma, chordoma, and aggressive hemangioma.

A 42-year-old man presented with occasional pain in his left hip when walking. On examination, he had a full range of motion at both hip joints without tenderness or deformity. Plain radiographs of the left hip showed an osteolytic area in the femoral neck and an adjacent area of osteosclerosis. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-defined lesion in the femoral neck with homogeneous high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, intermediate signal intensity on T1-weighted images, and peripheral gadolinium enhancement. In the adjacent sclerotic region, there was heterogeneous low- to slightly high-signal intensity on both T2- and T1-weighted images, with diffuse gadolinium enhancement.

A 28-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of pain and swelling in the left lower jaw. She had no history of trauma, oncologic disease, or significant medical or dental issues. Physical examination revealed a firm, fixed, tender lesion of the left mandible without lymphadenopathy or dental mobility.   
   
A spiral CT scan showed a bone lesion involving the left mandibular condyle and angle, with a thick, irregular periosteal reaction and an associated soft-tissue mass extending into the lateral pterygoid muscle and infratemporal fossa. No cervical lymphadenopathy was seen.  
   
An incisional biopsy demonstrated neoplastic tissue composed of uniform small round cells with round nuclei, extensive necrosis, and destruction of bony trabeculae. The initial pathology report suggested either Ewing sarcoma/primitive neuroectodermal tumor or small-cell variant osteosarcoma.  
   
Immunohistochemical staining revealed tumor cells positive for vimentin and MIC-2 (CD99) and negative for SATB-2, pan-cytokeratin, CD45, and TLE-1. The Ki-67 proliferation index was 12–15%.

A 62-year-old man presented with an 8-month history of progressive dyspnea, dysphagia, and hoarseness of voice. He had a 50-pack-year smoking history and remote tuberculosis. He reported a 4-5 kg weight loss over recent months. Physical examination revealed no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. Flexible laryngoscopy showed a smooth, white, exophytic mass arising from the anterior two thirds of the right vocal cord with paresis of the right cord and significant airway obstruction. Neck CT with contrast demonstrated an ill-defined enhancing mass measuring 2.3 × 1.5 × 1.7 cm in the right supraglottic larynx extending into pre-epiglottic fat but without cartilage destruction or lymphadenopathy. Chest CT showed bilateral fibrotic changes with traction bronchiectasis, pleural thickening, and calcified apical nodules without mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Under general anesthesia, direct laryngoscopy confirmed an exophytic lesion in the anterior commissure; biopsy was performed.  
Histopathology revealed markedly atypical, pleomorphic spindle cells with hyperchromatic nuclei beneath intact squamous epithelium, consistent with a high-grade malignant spindle-cell neoplasm. Immunohistochemical staining showed positivity for p40 and vimentin and negativity for S100, STAT6, ERG, cytokeratin, and CD31.

A 12-year-old boy from rural northern Ethiopia presented with a 7-month history of swelling over the proximal left thigh that rapidly increased over the last 2 months, associated with pain and limping. The family had applied herbal remedies to the swelling. One week before admission, he developed a dry cough, tachypnea, left-sided chest pain, and high-grade fever. He had no personal or family history of similar illness, surgeries, or allergies.

On examination, his temperature was 38.7 °C and respiratory rate 38 breaths/min. Local examination revealed a 20 × 15 cm firm, tender, erythematous swelling of the proximal left thigh, fixed to underlying structures, with an overlying scar. Other findings were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 5.8 g/dL and elevated LDH (> 1200 U/L). Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral asymmetric nodular opacities, predominantly in the hilar regions. Anteroposterior radiographs of the left thigh and pelvis revealed soft-tissue swelling, irregularity of the iliac bone, and an ill-defined lateral cortical outline of the ipsilateral femur, without evidence of calcification. MRI of the pelvis and left thigh showed a large, relatively well-defined soft tissue mass in the anterior compartment of the thigh extending proximally along the iliopsoas tendon to the pelvic side wall. The mass exhibited heterogeneous signal with focal T1-hyperintense layering, solid diffusion restriction, peripheral postcontrast enhancement with papillary projections and necrosis, and a proximal medial cortical breach with marrow infiltration. Neurovascular structures appeared uninvolved.

A 77-year-old multiparous woman presented with a 2-year history of vulvar discomfort and itching. She noted a pink lesion on her right labia majus that progressed insidiously over this period. Topical corticosteroid and antifungal creams provided no relief. Her medical history was unremarkable for tobacco use, immunosuppression, pelvic radiation, or any personal or family history of skin or internal malignancies. On examination, there was a well-demarcated, erosive plaque measuring 10×4 cm on the right labium majus. No inguinal or femoral lymphadenopathy was palpable, and a full skin examination revealed no other suspicious lesions. Pelvic ultrasonography showed no abnormal inguinal lymph nodes. An incisional biopsy of the lesion was performed.

A 36-year-old man with a history of cervical radiculopathy presented with a 2-month history of lower back pain, saddle anesthesia, and bowel and bladder incontinence. His family history was notable for multiple cancers without specific details. On arrival, his blood pressure was 170/115 mm Hg (attributed to pain); he was awake and alert, with no cranial nerve deficits. Examination revealed paresthesia in the left ulnar distribution and tenderness to palpation over the lumbar spine.  
MRI of the brain demonstrated extra-axial, contrast-enhancing lesions involving the lateral ventricles and posterior fossa, including one lesion with a dural tail. MRI of the spine revealed multiple intradural, extramedullary enhancing lesions in the thoracic and lumbar regions, suggestive of multiple schwannomas. Initial tumor biomarkers, including carcinoembryonic antigen, β-human chorionic gonadotropin, α-fetoprotein, and β2-microglobulin, were all negative.  
What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 71-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of progressive chest pain, worsened by movement and breathing, and an unexplained 22-kg weight loss. His medical history included hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and chronic kidney disease. On examination, vital signs were stable; the chest wall was tender on palpation but without crepitus or deformity. Laboratory studies showed normocytic anemia, elevated C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and a rise in serum creatinine. A chest radiograph was normal. Computed tomography angiography of the chest revealed no pulmonary embolism or parenchymal abnormalities. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a known adrenal adenoma without other findings. Because of concern for malignancy, the patient underwent 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT, which showed disseminated, predominantly osteoblastic lesions in the thoracic and lumbar spine, iliac bones, ribs, humeri, and clavicles, but no identifiable primary tumor. Magnetic resonance imaging was contraindicated due to longstanding lumbar spinal hardware. A CT-guided biopsy of an iliac‐crest lesion was nondiagnostic, showing only fatty marrow without malignant cells.

A 16-year-old girl presented with a 2-week history of aural fullness in her left ear. She had no history of ear infections or prior ear surgery and was otherwise healthy aside from allergic rhinitis. Otoscopic examination revealed a papillomatous-appearing mass on the posterior wall at the inlet of the left external auditory canal. The remainder of the head and neck examination and routine blood tests were normal. A biopsy of the lesion performed under topical anesthesia yielded a diagnosis of papilloma with no evidence of malignancy. Given the small size of the lesion and its benign biopsy result, en bloc excision under local anesthesia was performed.

A 41-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a pancreatic head mass incidentally detected by ultrasonography during a routine health check. She was asymptomatic, with no significant past medical or family history, and her physical examination was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 2.3×1.5 cm well-demarcated mass in the head and uncinate process of the pancreas, showing low attenuation in the early and late arterial phases and high enhancement in the portal venous phase; there was no bile duct or vascular invasion. Serum tumor markers were within reference ranges: CEA 1.8 ng/ml (0–5), CA 19-9 9.2 U/ml (0–37), chromogranin A 45.21 ng/ml (24–97), insulin 5.2 µIU/ml (2–25), and glucagon 28.7 pg/ml (40–130). Owing to concern for a potentially malignant or borderline tumor, a pylorus-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy was performed. On gross examination, a 2×1 cm firm, well-encapsulated, lobulated, whitish mass without hemorrhage or degenerative change was identified in the pancreatic head.

A 69-year-old woman was referred for gait disturbance and urinary incontinence of several months’ duration. Several months prior, she had a transient loss of consciousness; a CT scan then showed a giant solid mass in the middle cranial fossa with density higher than brain parenchyma and no calcification. Over the next year, the lesion grew but the patient had no hydrocephalus symptoms until the new gait and continence issues.

On examination, she had mild right hemiparesis, difficulty walking, urinary incontinence, and mild cognitive dysfunction (Mini-Mental State Examination score 28/30). Her Karnofsky Performance Scale score was 80.

Noncontrast CT showed an extra-axial tumor measuring 64 × 40 × 48 mm extending from the right cavernous sinus and sella turcica into the medial temporal fossa, compressing the midbrain; the lesion was slightly hyperdense without calcification. MRI demonstrated marked hypointensity on T1-weighted images, prominent hyperintensity on T2-weighted images, and uniform enhancement on post-contrast T1-weighted images. The foramen of Monro was obstructed, with disproportionate ventricular enlargement and slight periventricular hyperintensities on FLAIR. No hemosiderin deposition was seen.

Cerebral angiography revealed medial deviation of the right intracranial internal carotid artery, small feeding arteries from the meningohypophyseal trunk and the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery, and gradual contrast filling of the lesion from its inner part.

A 60‐year‐old woman presented with a slowly enlarging, asymptomatic nodular lesion on the dorsal aspect of her left wrist that she had first noticed 10 years earlier. The mass had grown from pea size to approximately 5 × 6 × 18 mm and did not cause pain or numbness, though she noted slight weakness in dorsiflexion of the wrist. There was no history of trauma. Examination revealed a firm, non‐tender mass on the dorsal wrist, free from the overlying skin but adherent to the extensor indicis proprius tendon. The wrist range of motion was 45° of extension and 80° of flexion. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, antistreptolysin O level, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, high‐sensitivity C‐reactive protein level, anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide level, other immune indices, and tumor markers, were all within normal limits. MRI of the left wrist demonstrated an 18 × 6 × 5 mm spindle‐shaped mass encircling the extensor indicis proprius tendon. The lesion was isointense on T1‐weighted images and hyperintense on T1 and T2 fat‐suppressed sequences.

A 28-year-old man presented to the emergency department with acute onset of severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain and associated vomiting that began while lifting weights. His medical history was notable for 6–7 years of anabolic steroids, human growth hormone, and testosterone use to gain muscle mass. He had no prior surgical history. On abdominal examination, the abdomen was nondistended with focal tenderness and guarding in the right upper quadrant. Vital signs included a blood pressure of 190/85 mm Hg, heart rate of 83 beats/min, and oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. Laboratory investigations showed a hemoglobin level of 17.1 g/dL, neutrophilia, and a normal C-reactive protein level. Liver function tests revealed a mixed hepatitic and obstructive pattern: total bilirubin 35 µmol/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 443 U/L, and alanine aminotransferase 848 U/L; the international normalized ratio was normal. Contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography demonstrated a 9.6-cm well-circumscribed abnormality in segment 5 of the liver and a smaller focal lesion in segment 6, findings interpreted as acute hemorrhage into two focal liver lesions, likely hepatic adenomas. Subsequent liver magnetic resonance imaging revealed multiple hepatic adenomas and an increase in the size of the larger lesion to 12 cm.

A 53-year-old man presented with two days of acute periumbilical pain, fever (38.0 °C), and nausea without vomiting. He denied melena, hematochezia, or diarrhea, reporting only a one-day delay in bowel movements. He had no significant medical or family history. On examination, vital signs were stable, and the abdomen was soft and non-tender without palpable masses. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 12.7 G/L (83.4% neutrophils); amylase, CEA, and CA 19-9 were normal. 

Abdominal radiography was unremarkable. Ultrasound of the supra-umbilical region revealed a focal multilocular anechoic cystic mass with internal septa in the transverse colon wall and no hypervascularity. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a low-density (10–12 HU) multilocular mass with thin, poorly enhancing walls and septa in the transverse colon, with upstream submucosal edema but no other abnormalities. The CT was thought to be suggestive of a cystic lymphangioma but did not exclude other more common diagnoses. 

Flexible colonoscopy demonstrated a broad-based, smooth polypoid lesion with glossy pinkish mucosa in the mid-transverse colon, consistent with a submucosal tumor; no biopsy was performed.

A 55‐year‐old Indian man presented with 1½ months of progressive lower abdominal distension and 15 days of continuous, dull aching pain. He denied trauma, weight loss, anorexia, altered bowel habits, fever, vomiting, or urinary symptoms. He was a chronic smoker. On examination, he was moderately built, with visible fullness in the left lower abdomen. Palpation revealed a smooth, ill‐defined, non‐tender mass approximately 20×15 cm, extending from the left iliac and hypogastric regions across midline to the right midclavicular line at the iliac crest. The mass was firm‐cystic with restricted mobility. There was no inguinal lymphadenopathy and digital rectal examination was unremarkable.  
Ultrasonography showed a large septated cystic lesion left of the urinary bladder, with the liver, spleen, pancreas, and kidneys appearing normal. Contrast‐enhanced CT demonstrated a 14.4×14.6×9.2 cm multilocular cystic mass with enhancing septations occupying the left abdomen and pelvis, displacing gut loops and bladder to the right, and encasing the left iliac artery; attenuation was +10 to +15 HU, with no ascites or bowel obstruction.  
Fine‐needle aspiration of the mass yielded red blood cells, neutrophils, and lymphocytes in a proteinaceous background, suggesting a lymphangiomatous process. A provisional diagnosis of retroperitoneal lymphangioma versus mesenteric cyst was made.

A 13-year-old boy presented with a 2-week history of right-sided headache and a 1-week history of vomiting. He was alert, had no focal neurologic deficits, and showed no stigmata of neurofibromatosis (no neurofibromas, café-au-lait spots, Lisch nodules, optic glioma, distinctive bony lesions, or axillary/inguinal freckling). Brain MRI demonstrated a 6.7-cm diameter, well-defined, intensely enhancing mass in the right frontal lobe. The preoperative differential diagnoses included glioblastoma multiforme, anaplastic astrocytoma, and malignant meningioma.

A 53-year-old woman presented with intermittent nocturnal anterior chest pain of several months’ duration. Her medical history was noncontributory.

Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed several variable-sized, oval to lobular, relatively circumscribed, well-enhanced masses in both breasts, an enlarged right internal mammary lymph node, and an enhanced pleural mass in the left hemithorax.

Breast ultrasonography demonstrated, in each breast, an oval mass with an indistinct margin, heterogeneous echogenicity, and posterior acoustic enhancement (located at 2 o’clock in the left breast and 10 o’clock in the right breast). Color Doppler US showed internal vascularity. These masses were assigned BI-RADS category 4A on ultrasound.

US-guided core needle biopsy of both breast lesions was planned.

A 61-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of progressive right periorbital fullness, with worsening vision and pain over the preceding 3 weeks. She denied a history of infectious keratitis, contact lens use, ocular trauma, melanoma, lymphoma, or any other malignancy. Three months earlier, she had noted blurry vision and periorbital swelling for 1 month.  
An orbital MRI showed an area of hyperintensity in the right orbit and an 8 mm fluid collection contiguous with the superior aspect of the optic nerve sheath. These imaging findings were interpreted as consistent with orbital cellulitis and a retrobulbar abscess, and she was treated with intravenous ceftazidime, clindamycin, and vancomycin without improvement. She was then diagnosed with orbital inflammatory syndrome and treated with systemic oral corticosteroids; a biopsy was recommended but the patient was lost to follow-up.  
Three weeks later, she presented with no light perception in the right eye, restricted extraocular motility in all directions, and a tense, inflamed orbit. The cornea was perforated with expulsion of intraocular contents. CT of the orbits demonstrated a large, ill-defined, heterogeneously enhancing mass encasing and compressing the globe.  
She underwent evisceration of the right eye with biopsy of the orbital mass. Intraoperatively, the sclera was nearly collapsed, and the mass appeared dense and white with little vascularity.  
Microscopic examination of the evisceration specimen showed acute and chronic inflammatory infiltrates in the cornea, uveal tissue, vitreous, and retina. A cytokeratin stain of the intraocular contents was negative. Histopathologic examination of the orbital mass revealed atypical basophilic cells in a linear configuration with pleomorphic nuclei and an increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. Special stains (Gram, GMS, and AFB) showed no organisms. Immunohistochemical stains for cytokeratin and estrogen receptor were positive; HER-2 and progesterone receptors were negative.

A 28-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a right breast lump. Her history was notable for childhood hydrocephalus and developmental delay. At age 23, she underwent total thyroidectomy for a 5.6-cm follicular lesion of undetermined significance; pathology revealed papillary thyroid carcinoma, solid/trabecular variant, and she received radioiodine ablation followed by levothyroxine. One year later, ultrasound detected jugulocarotid microcalcifications concerning for thyroid cancer recurrence, but biopsy was not performed at that time.

In November 2017, at 38 weeks’ gestation, she noted a 3-cm right breast mass (BIRADS-2). Six months postpartum, the lesion measured 4 cm and was biopsied (BIRADS-4C). Mammary CT showed a multilobulated mass with coarse calcifications. Histology of the core biopsy demonstrated a high-grade malignant neoplasm composed of atypical spindle cells with areas of rhabdomyoblastic and osteosarcomatous differentiation. Chest CT for staging revealed multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules <1 cm. 

On examination, her head circumference was 58.1 cm (>97th percentile). She had multiple round, keratotic palmar pits and verrucous papules on the face and scalp. Vital signs were normal; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

A 44-year-old Nepali woman with a history of hypertension presented with 1 month of progressive abdominal distension and 7 days of fever (to 101°F) with generalized, dull aching abdominal pain and multiple episodes of non-bloody vomiting. She denied diarrhea, melena, jaundice, or known liver disease. On examination, she was alert; pulse 112/min; BP 130/90 mm Hg; RR 20/min; SpO2 98% on room air; and febrile. The abdomen was distended, tender in both hypochondriac and epigastric regions, with the spleen palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 16,500/mm3, platelets 729,000/mm3, hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, hematocrit 37%. Peripheral smear revealed normocytic normochromic RBCs, neutrophilic leukocytosis, and thrombocytosis. ESR, blood glucose, renal and liver function tests, and iron profile were within normal limits.

Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated normal liver parenchyma, moderate splenomegaly (16 cm), moderate ascites, and nonvisualization of the portal vein, suggestive of thrombosis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis confirmed splenomegaly and a completely occluding thrombus in the main portal vein, right and left portal branches, superior mesenteric vein, and splenic vein. Multiple periportal, perigastric, and splenic hilar collateral vessels were seen, consistent with a portal cavernoma in chronic splanchnic vein thrombosis.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of left hypochondrial pain described as a random mass-like sensation without systemic symptoms. Her surgical history was notable only for cholecystectomy. Family history was unremarkable. Physical examination showed slight tenderness in the left hypochondrium that increased with inspiration; there was no palpable splenomegaly. Bowel sounds were normal, and the rest of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits.  
Abdominal ultrasound revealed a spleen of normal size containing a well-defined heterogeneous lesion measuring 42 × 58 mm in the superior pole. Contrast-enhanced MRI confirmed a non-encapsulated solid splenic mass with regular contours, heterogeneous enhancement, a vascular component, and areas of necrosis.  
Given these findings, the patient underwent a laparoscopic-assisted splenectomy.

A 33-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of intermittent, colicky upper abdominal pain radiating to the flanks. There were no food-related triggers or alleviating factors. Her medical and surgical history was unremarkable, and she had no family history of pancreatic disease. She did not smoke or drink alcohol. 

On examination, her vital signs were normal. The chest was clear, and the abdomen was soft without tenderness or palpable mass.

An abdominal ultrasound and contrast-enhanced CT scan performed at an outside facility showed a 2.3 × 2.1 cm mass at the neck of the pancreas. The lesion was hypodense relative to pancreatic parenchyma, contained multiple septations, showed mottled enhancement after contrast, and there was no pancreatic duct dilatation.  

MRI of the abdomen demonstrated the same lesion at the pancreatic neck, which was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, exhibited mild mottled gadolinium enhancement, and showed no diffusion restriction on diffusion-weighted imaging or apparent diffusion coefficient maps.

Based on her age and gender, the differential diagnosis included pancreatic adenocarcinoma, serous and mucinous cystic neoplasms, and solid pseudopapillary epithelial neoplasm. A Gallium ^68Ga-DOTATATE PET-CT scan was obtained to evaluate for neuroendocrine tumor and was negative.  

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. Pancreatic enzyme levels were normal. Tumor markers (CA 19-9 and chromogranin A) were negative.  

Endoscopic ultrasonography with biopsy was recommended, but the patient declined and elected to proceed directly to surgical resection.

An 87-year-old Caucasian man with a history of type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease stage 4, and cardiac comorbidities was referred for evaluation of right-sided flank pain and possible ureteral stones. A non-contrast abdominal–pelvic CT scan demonstrated a small distal right ureteral stone that did not require surgical intervention. Incidentally, the scan revealed a 4.4 × 4.0 × 4.0 cm mass in the right retroperitoneum, located posterior to and compressing the inferior vena cava and the right renal artery. 

The radiologist interpreted the lesion as a possible neuroendocrine tumor and recommended a ^68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT. This study showed a well-circumscribed retrocaval mass with peripheral radiotracer uptake, described as “compatible with a paraganglioma or a lymph node metastasis of a neuroendocrine tumor.” 

Serum and urine hormone assays, including catecholamines and metanephrines, were within normal limits, effectively excluding hormonally active neoplasms. The only abnormal laboratory finding was an elevated creatinine level consistent with baseline chronic kidney disease. The patient reported no additional symptoms.

A 45-year-old man with no prior medical history noted non-tender, reddish discoloration of both ears about 3 years ago, without B symptoms. He sought evaluation for cosmetic concerns. On examination, there were plum-colored swellings involving the helices of both ears and palpable cervical and axillary lymph nodes. CT imaging confirmed cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy without hepatosplenomegaly.
