Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 19.1×10^9/L (lymphocytes 11.1×10^9/L), hemoglobin 15.5 g/dL, and platelets 122×10^9/L. Punch biopsies of the auricular lesions revealed a dense mononuclear infiltrate, with immunohistochemical stains positive for CD20, a few cells positive for CD3, and negative for CD30.

A 29-year-old Taiwanese man presented with 2 weeks of persistent dull aching pain localized to his right lateral chest wall. He denied fevers, weight loss, respiratory symptoms, or trauma. He had no palpable mass and no changes in his external appearance. On examination, vital signs were normal, and the only finding was mild tenderness over the right lateral chest wall without overlying skin changes.  
A chest radiograph showed a faint patchy opacity in the periphery of the right upper lung zone. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax demonstrated a lobulated mass measuring 5.5 × 4.5 × 4.3 cm in the intercostal space between the right fifth and sixth ribs. MRI of the chest revealed a 5.2 × 4.5 × 4.6 cm lobulated lesion involving the right serratus anterior muscle, fifth intercostal space, and subpleural region; it was isointense to hypointense relative to muscle on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously hyperintense on fat-suppressed T2-weighted images with low-signal foci, and showed inhomogeneous gadolinium enhancement. Malignancy could not be excluded on imaging studies.

A 51-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented after 8 months of progressively worsening headaches refractory to medication, along with a bilateral decrease in visual acuity and recent-onset horizontal diplopia. On examination, her temperature was 36.5 °C, blood pressure 125/70 mm Hg, pulse 77 beats/min, and respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. Ophthalmologic evaluation revealed decreased visual acuity and a right sixth-nerve palsy; there was no papilledema, no visual field defect, and corneal reflexes were intact. Examination of the remaining cranial nerves and motor and sensory neurologic function was normal. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, metabolic panel, thyroid function tests, and pituitary hormonal assays, were all within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the head showed a large, enhancing, expansile, lytic mass centered in the sphenoid sinus measuring approximately 5.0 × 4.6 × 3.9 cm, with extension into the sellar and suprasellar regions, anterior invasion of ethmoidal air cells, erosion of the clivus, posterior displacement of the basilar artery into the prepontine cistern without brainstem compression, and encasement of both cavernous sinuses and the internal carotid arteries.

Gadolinium-enhanced MRI confirmed a sizable mass that was isointense on T1-weighted images, hypointense on T2-weighted images with a prominent cystic component, and showed heterogeneous contrast enhancement.

Given the sellar and suprasellar location of the tumor, initial consideration was given to pituitary macroadenoma, craniopharyngioma, atypical meningioma, or a bone tumor such as chordoma or chondrosarcoma. A tissue diagnosis was planned.

A 70-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive abdominal distension. Pelvic ultrasound revealed an 18-cm solid–cystic mass occupying the pelvic and abdominal cavities with rich intralesional blood flow. Laboratory studies showed a serum CA-125 level of 367.9 U/mL, neuron-specific enolase of 24.83 ng/mL, and CYFRA21-1 of 3.85 ng/mL. At laparotomy, 0.5 L of hemorrhagic ascites was evacuated. Examination revealed a 20-cm right ovarian cystic and solid mass infiltrating the uterus, intestinal loops, and parietal pelvic wall, with diffuse peritoneal implants on the surface of the uterus and intestines; the left ovary, fallopian tube, and pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes appeared normal. A right salpingo-oophorectomy was performed and frozen section analysis demonstrated a poorly differentiated carcinoma. Consequently, a total abdominal hysterectomy with left salpingo-oophorectomy, omentectomy, and resection of visible pelvic metastases was carried out. Grossly, the right ovarian tumor measured 33 × 23 × 5 cm, had a fragile nodular “rotten-flesh” surface, and its cut surface showed gray-white solid areas with hemorrhage and necrosis. The largest pelvic metastasis measured 12 × 10 × 3.5 cm, had an irregular dusty-pink external surface, and showed cystic and hemorrhagic regions on sectioning. Histologic examination of H&E-stained sections revealed predominantly trabecular and rosette-like formations of pleomorphic hyperchromatic tumor cells with moderate cytoplasm, round to oval nuclei (occasionally with conspicuous nucleoli and coarse chromatin), and a high mitotic rate.

A 67-year-old Asian man presented with several weeks of severe fatigue and back pain requiring opioid analgesics. He denied fevers, night sweats, weight loss, gastrointestinal bleeding, and urinary symptoms. His medical history was notable for a remote right middle cerebral artery stroke with residual hemiparesis, diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and a 60 pack-year smoking history. Three years earlier, he had biopsy-proven extramammary Paget disease of the scrotum treated with imiquimod for 1 year, with complete resolution on re-biopsy. Family history was negative for malignancy.

On examination, he had left-sided pyramidal neurologic findings, hepatomegaly, and a diffusely enlarged prostate. Initial laboratory studies revealed pancytopenia with leukoerythroblastic features, and he required repeated red-cell and platelet transfusions. Serum creatinine, calcium, and liver-function tests were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed moderate left hilar and para-aortic lymphadenopathy, multiple liver lesions, bi-lobar prostate enlargement, and left hydronephrosis due to ureteral obstruction, for which a ureteral stent was placed. Transrectal ultrasound–guided prostate biopsy revealed Gleason 3+4 adenocarcinoma in 3 of 8 cores without perineural or extraprostatic extension; the prostate-specific antigen level was 17.7 ng/mL.

Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy demonstrated marrow packed with poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma with signet-ring cells; immunohistochemical staining was positive for keratin 7 (KRT7) and prolactin-induced protein (PIP) and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) but was negative for prostate-specific antigen, prostate-specific acid phosphatase, P504S, CD45, KRT20, vimentin, TTF1, CDX2, S100, and estrogen receptor. Fine-needle aspiration of a liver lesion showed adenocarcinoma cells with signet-ring morphology.

A 53-year-old incarcerated Hispanic man presented with worsening abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, and upper abdominal tenderness with rebound and guarding, four days after being struck multiple times in the abdomen. He reported two months of fatigue, easy bruising, and spontaneous epistaxis with vague abdominal discomfort. His medical history included hypertension and pancreatitis; family history was noncontributory.

On arrival, his white blood cell count was 38.4 × 10^9/L, platelet count was 691 × 10^9/L, and lipase was 55 U/L. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 10.3 cm × 6.5 cm × 10.0 cm hematoma encasing the pancreatic tail, displacing adjacent viscera, with a small hemoperitoneum. He underwent an emergent laparotomy, which revealed a near-severed distal pancreas and devascularized colon; distal pancreatectomy, splenectomy, and colonic resection with primary anastomosis were performed.

Postoperatively, he received piperacillin–tazobactam. Despite this, his leukocytosis peaked at 69.6 × 10^9/L on postoperative day 9 and thrombocytosis peaked at 2293 × 10^9/L on day 12. Aspirin was added. A sepsis workup—including repeat CT with oral and IV contrast—showed no abscess or leak, and procalcitonin remained low (0.11–0.13 ng/mL). Hematology was consulted. Peripheral blood smear confirmed severe leukocytosis and thrombocytosis without circulating blasts.

A 47-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of a painless left scrotal swelling that had enlarged over the past 6 months. He denied trauma or genitourinary infection. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender left scrotal mass associated with a hydrocele; the overlying skin was normal. Serum tumor markers were within normal limits. Ultrasonography revealed a large heterogeneous extratesticular mass on the left side with an associated hydrocele; color Doppler showed abundant internal vascularity. 

A 1.5-T MRI of the scrotum was performed, including T1-weighted, T2-weighted, diffusion-weighted (b = 0 and 900 s/mm2), magnetization transfer, and dynamic contrast-enhanced sequences. The lesion measured 5.5 × 4.8 × 4.3 cm, was well circumscribed, and displaced the ipsilateral testis. On T1-weighted images the mass was isointense to testicular parenchyma; on T2-weighted images it was mildly hyperintense. There was no evidence of restricted diffusion; the apparent diffusion coefficient was high. On magnetization transfer images the mass showed low signal intensity with an MTR comparable to that of the normal testis. After intravenous gadolinium, the lesion enhanced strongly and heterogeneously, reaching a late peak followed by a plateau (type II time–signal intensity curve), whereas the displaced testis showed a gradual linear enhancement pattern (type I curve). 

MRI findings were strongly suggestive of a benign paratesticular tumor.

A 35-year-old man presented with a one-month history of a painless growth on the palate. He was otherwise healthy and reported no trauma, bleeding, tobacco or alcohol use, or systemic symptoms. On examination, there was an exophytic, lobulated, soft mass on the maxillary palatal gingiva extending from the right lateral incisor to the left first premolar, with focal ulceration and bleeding on probing. Extraoral examination was unremarkable. Complete blood count was normal, and HIV testing was negative. Occlusal and periapical radiographs showed interdental bone loss between the maxillary incisors and between the left lateral incisor and canine. An incisional biopsy was performed. Histologic sections showed ulcerated parakeratinized stratified squamous epithelium overlying a diffuse infiltrate of large round cells with open-face nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and occasional eccentric nuclei; macrophages were admixed. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated that the tumor cells were positive for leukocyte common antigen, CD138, and CD56, and negative for CD20, CD30, ALK1, Cyclin D1, and epithelial membrane antigen.

A 67-year-old Brazilian woman presented with 12 months of pain during bowel movements, tenesmus, hematochezia, increased bowel movements, and weight loss. Her medical history included hypertension, hypothyroidism, and osteopenia, treated with hydrochlorothiazide, levothyroxine, and alendronate. She had no history of tobacco, alcohol, or drug use. Her family history was notable for a daughter who died at age 32 from breast cancer and a granddaughter with adrenocortical carcinoma; two siblings died of prostate cancer in their 60s. On examination, she was hemodynamically stable, with a BMI of 20.7 kg/m2 and no neurologic deficits. Digital rectal examination revealed a mass on the anterior rectal wall 7 cm from the anal verge. Anoscopy and proctosigmoidoscopy showed a vegetating, infiltrating tumor. Colonoscopy demonstrated a friable, bleeding, ulcerated, indurated lesion extending 6.5 cm cranially, involving 50% of the circumference and 80% of the lumen, but allowed passage of the scope to the cecum. Biopsy of the lesion revealed a mesenchymal pattern of neoplasm. CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed rectal wall thickening from the mid-rectum to the rectosigmoid transition without liver nodules or other organ abnormalities; chest CT was normal. Pelvic MRI demonstrated rectal wall thickening 7 cm from the anal verge with suspicion of uterine invasion.

An 80-year-old man presented in 2011 with dizziness. He was found to have anemia, thrombocytopenia, and monocytosis (>1000/mm³). His vital signs were normal, and routine studies including renal function and electrolytes were within normal ranges. 

A myelogram showed dyserythropoiesis, dysgranulopoiesis, and dysmegakaryopoiesis; blasts were approximately 2.2%. Cytogenetic analysis revealed a normal karyotype. 

A bone marrow biopsy showed hypercellularity with significant expansion of the granulocytic and megakaryocytic series and mild focal reticulin thickening. The patient had not received any blood transfusions and had no reports of infection.

A 73-year-old man with hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and obstructive sleep apnea presented with 3 days of coffee-ground emesis and melena, accompanied by dizziness, weakness, palpitations, and fatigue. In the emergency department, he was hypotensive and tachycardic; his hemoglobin was 3.4 g/dL and INR 1.29. He received aggressive fluid resuscitation and multiple units of packed red blood cells, with stabilization of vital signs.

An emergent esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed isolated bleeding gastric fundal varices, which were treated with argon plasma coagulation. He was started on intravenous protonix and octreotide drips and transferred for evaluation of presumed cirrhosis and possible transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt placement. He denied any history of liver disease, injection drug use, or current alcohol use, though he recalled one episode of hematemesis 40 years earlier requiring transfusion. He also reported a 38-lb weight loss over the prior 6 months.

Repeat endoscopy at our center confirmed multiple clusters of medium-sized isolated gastric varices (IGV1 by Sarin classification). Laboratory studies showed normal liver function tests; HIV and viral hepatitis serologies were negative. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated patent hepatic and portal veins with no sonographic evidence of cirrhosis. Cross-sectional MRI and CT imaging identified a large, heterogeneously enhancing mass in the pancreatic tail with direct invasion into the spleen, splenic vein thrombosis, and enlarged abdominal lymph nodes; there was no metastatic disease in the liver or thorax.

A 42-year-old woman with a history of stage II mucinous adenocarcinoma of the sigmoid colon (treated by colectomy and 12 cycles of FOLFOX two years earlier) presented with a 3-day history of left upper-quadrant abdominal pain radiating to the back, associated with nausea, chills, and anorexia without fever, diarrhea, or constipation. Physical examination was notable only for tenderness in the left hypochondrium. 

Laboratory tests showed a mildly elevated carcinoembryonic antigen level of 6.33 ng/mL and a hemoglobin concentration of 10.1 g/dL with a hematocrit of 30.7%; other biochemical tests were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 9.3 × 14 cm well-defined cystic mass in the left adrenal gland. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed the adrenal cystic mass with associated grade 2 hydronephrosis and an 8 mm nodule in the left breast; no other abnormalities were seen.

Because of the patient’s symptoms and the size of the adrenal lesion, she underwent left adrenalectomy. Unexpectedly, multiple palpable 1 cm nodules were noted in both breasts during surgical preparation, prompting delayed investigation of the breast nodules. Histopathology and immunohistochemistry of the adrenal specimen revealed mucinous adenocarcinoma of colonic origin.

After recovery, breast examination confirmed a 1 cm nodule at 9 o’clock in the right breast and three similar nodules in the left breast (3 o’clock, 1 o’clock, and the axillary tail). Breast ultrasound demonstrated multiple hypoechoic oval bilateral masses, mostly well-defined, though three had irregular margins with central necrotic changes. Mammography showed multiple round masses without spiculations, calcifications, or skin thickening; three masses were lobulated with irregular margins (BI-RADS 4A). A core-needle biopsy was obtained from the largest lesion.

A 5-year-old boy was referred to pediatric otolaryngology for evaluation of a uvular mass that had been noted incidentally during tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy performed to treat a sleep-related breathing disorder. The patient had no history of feeding or swallowing difficulty, and symptoms of sleep-disordered breathing resolved after the tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy. His birth history and family history were unremarkable; his past medical history was notable only for asthma.

On examination, the child appeared well, with no respiratory distress. Otologic and nasal examinations were normal. In the oral cavity, the tonsils were absent, and the uvula appeared elongated; the tip could not be visualized without a tongue depressor, at which time a mass was seen at the tip of the uvula. No other abnormalities were noted in the head and neck region.

Excision of the uvular mass was performed under general anesthesia. Intraoperative inspection revealed a 0.4 cm × 0.6 cm × 0.6 cm well-circumscribed, white, submucosal cystic lesion at the tip of the uvula. The overlying mucosa was sharply dissected away, and the cyst decompressed, expressing thick, white squamous debris. The entire cyst was removed, and the uvular mucosa was repaired. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the child was discharged.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a rapidly enlarging mass in her right breast. She first noticed a small lump one year earlier, with modest growth until 2 months before presentation, when the lesion expanded markedly. On examination, the mass measured approximately 20 cm in diameter, and the overlying skin appeared darkened with areas of ulceration. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 20 cm heterogeneous, hemorrhagic, well-defined mass in the right breast, with enlargement of ipsilateral axillary and supraclavicular lymph nodes but no evidence of chest wall invasion or distant metastases.

A 25-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of a right-sided facial mass. The lesion had insidious onset, progressive enlargement, intermittent pain, and difficulty chewing on the right side. She denied fever or weight loss. General and systemic examinations were unremarkable.

On inspection, there was a firm, non-tender mass measuring approximately 10 by 6 cm from the zygomatic arch to the submandibular region, causing facial asymmetry. Mouth opening was full. Intraoral examination revealed expansion of both buccal and lingual cortical plates from the parasymphysis to the retromolar pad, with mobility of all involved teeth.

Panoramic radiography showed a multilocular radiolucent lesion on the right side of the mandible extending from the mental foramen toward the condylar neck and causing displacement of adjacent teeth. An incisional biopsy was performed. Histologic sections demonstrated islands of epithelial cells with central edema and loose arrangement, bordered by a rim of palisading columnar cells. In some areas, there were aggregates of eosinophilic granular cells.

An 11-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of syncope. He had no family history of cardiac tumors. On admission, pulse was 100 beats/min, blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg, and there were no signs of heart failure. Cardiac examination revealed a grade 4/6 systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border. Chest radiography was normal. Electrocardiography showed sinus rhythm at 110 beats/min, ST-segment depression in leads V1–V4, right-ventricular hypertrophy, and right-axis deviation. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a mobile 19×19 mm mass attached to the right ventricular outflow tract, sparing the pulmonary valve and causing severe obstruction (RV–pulmonary artery gradient 90 mm Hg). There was right atrial and right ventricular dilation, mild tricuspid regurgitation, and an estimated right ventricular systolic pressure of 105 mm Hg. Abdominal ultrasound and venous Doppler studies of the lower limbs were unremarkable.

A 67-year-old previously healthy Chinese woman presented with diffuse and extensive oral mucosal prominence. On examination, there were velvety, widespread, reddish papillary lesions on the hard palate, buccal mucosa, gingiva, and upper lip mucosa. General examination revealed no evidence of bone damage or perforation. Dermatological assessment showed mild pigmentation around the mouth, nape of the neck, back of the hands, and armpits. She had no significant medical or family history and was not taking any medications. An incisional biopsy of the oral mucosa demonstrated papillary proliferation of the squamous epithelium. Laboratory studies showed elevated tumor markers, including CA125 at 100 U/mL, CA153 at 159.2 U/mL, CYFRA21-1 at 4.97 ng/mL, and NSE at 19.72 ng/mL; levels of CA199, CA724, and SCC antigen were within normal limits. A systemic positron emission tomography/computed tomography scan raised strong suspicions of lymph node metastasis from ovarian cancer.

A 71-year-old man presented with a two-month history of sharp, progressively worsening pain in the left scapular region and the ulnar aspect of the left forearm that intensified when he lay down. Neurologic examination revealed hyporeflexia of the left triceps reflex, slight hypoesthesia in the left ulnar forearm distribution, an accentuated left knee-jerk reflex compared to the right, and a mute left plantar reflex; motor strength and motility were intact. Ten days before admission, MRI of the cervical spine with and without contrast demonstrated at the C7–D1 level an intracanal lesion that was hyperintense on T2-weighted images, iso- to hypointense on T1-weighted images, and showed homogeneous enhancement after contrast. In axial views, the lesion appeared homogeneous and dumbbell-shaped, partly involving the left C7–D1 foramen. One slice suggested that the C8 nerve root was posteriorly displaced by the mass. Radiologists raised the possibility that the lesion was extradural rather than intradural or root-originating.

A 26-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with a 2-month history of intermittent vomiting, headaches, and vertigo, accompanied by progressive visual deterioration. Physical examination was unremarkable without lymphadenopathy. Noncontrast CT of the head revealed bifocal hyperdense, compressive extra-axial masses with surrounding edema in the right parieto-occipital and left frontal regions, causing mass effect on the lateral ventricles and midline. Subsequent MRI confirmed dural-based lesions: T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences showed iso- to hypointense signals with vasogenic edema, diffusion-weighted imaging (b1000) revealed no restriction, and gadolinium-enhanced images demonstrated strong, homogeneous enhancement.

A 51-year-old man presented with a persistent purulent perianal discharge. On examination, an external orifice of an intersphincteric fistula was located 2 cm from the anal verge in the right posterior quadrant. Palpation revealed a well-circumscribed, rubbery, slightly mobile ovoid mass about 3 cm in diameter, located 1 cm proximal to the anal verge in the midline posteriorly, closely abutting the anal sphincter. Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging showed a homogeneous, ovoid mass measuring 3.4 × 3.5 × 2.7 cm in the intersphincteric plane arising from the posterior aspect of the internal anal sphincter. The lesion grew away from the lumen, displacing and stretching the external anal sphincter. On T2-weighted sequences the mass had moderate to low signal intensity, and on post-contrast images there was no internal enhancement, necrosis, lymphadenopathy, or cystic component. The fistula tract passed adjacent to the right lateral border of the mass without evidence of invasion.

A 41-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 3-month history of stable hoarseness and progressive breathing difficulty. On examination, there was a level VI neck mass without palpable lymphadenopathy. Flexible laryngoscopy revealed a large mass occupying the left side of the larynx. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed a 3.5 × 2 × 3 cm soft-tissue lesion at the level of the left vocal cord and anterior commissure, extending into the left laryngeal ventricle, false vocal cord, and aryepiglottic fold, with near-total occlusion of the airway. Additional findings included medial deviation of the left arytenoid cartilage with pyriform sinus dilation (sail sign) suggestive of left vocal cord paralysis, and sclerosing and splitting of the left thyroid cartilage plate with adjacent muscle thickening.

A 46-year-old white man with hypertension and no diabetes presented with a large, painful, malodorous mass on his left heel. He reported that the lesion began as a nonhealing wound after trauma in a motor‐vehicle accident 20 years ago; over the past 4 years it had progressively enlarged. He denied recent trauma, weight loss, night sweats, or systemic symptoms. 

On examination, temperature was 98.5 °F, heart rate 102 beats/min, blood pressure 131/90 mm Hg, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. The left heel had a 15 × 20 cm hypergranular, fungating mass with areas of necrosis, mild erythematous margins, and serosanguinous drainage. The lesion extended proximally to the ankle, distally to the midtarsal region, and medially and laterally to the malleoli. There was severe pain on palpation; ankle motion was limited in a fixed equinus position. Peripheral pulses were palpable bilaterally. There was no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly, and the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Plain radiographs of the left foot showed a lytic lesion in the lateral posterior calcaneus without evidence of bone resorption. CT scans of the chest and abdomen showed no masses, lymphadenopathy, or organomegaly.

A 71-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with chronic epigastric pain that had progressively worsened over several years. She reported no other gastrointestinal symptoms and was in generally good health. On examination, there was slight tenderness in the epigastric region without any palpable mass. Routine blood tests, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed no abnormalities. An abdominal ultrasound revealed a large cystic lesion with a few thin internal septa located superior to the pancreas; the remainder of the abdominal organs appeared unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a well-circumscribed, lobulated, thin-walled cystic mass measuring 9 × 5 × 6 cm within the omental bursa. The lesion displaced the stomach anteriorly and exerted external compression on the body of the pancreas. There was no pathological enhancement after intravenous contrast administration. Tumor markers were within the normal range, and hydatid serology was negative.

A 19-year-old HIV-negative woman was found to have multiple pulmonary nodules on chest radiography obtained during a routine physical examination. She denied chest tightness, cough, or fever. Physical examination was unremarkable. Routine blood tests and serum chemistries were within normal limits. Tumor markers (CEA, AFP, CA19-9, CYFRA21-1, NSE, and SCC) were all negative. Three separate sputum specimens were negative for acid-fast bacilli. Chest CT showed multiple round nodules with smooth borders and homogeneous density scattered throughout both lungs; the largest measured 2.2 × 2.4 × 2.1 cm near the apex of the left upper lobe. No lymphadenopathy or cavitation was noted.

A 56‐year‐old woman presented with a 2‐month history of a slowly enlarging, painless swelling in the left posterior parotid region. She denied systemic symptoms or prior head and neck trauma. On examination, there was a firm, non‐tender parotid mass measuring approximately 1.5 × 2 × 2 cm; no cervical lymphadenopathy was palpable. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the neck revealed a 4.5 × 3.4 × 3.2 cm irregular, lobulated mass involving the deep lobe of the left parotid gland with clear but uneven margins. The mass compressed and displaced the left internal jugular vein anteriorly; there was no cervical lymph‐node enlargement. On coronal images, the lesion extended superiorly toward the left temporal bone. Based on clinical and radiologic findings, a pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland versus a facial‐nerve neurilemmoma was considered, and the patient underwent a left partial parotidectomy with preservation of the facial nerve.

A 53-year-old man presented with a one-month history of worsening right mandibular swelling, pain, and progressive trismus. He had been treated in the emergency department with intravenous cefazolin for a presumed odontogenic infection without improvement. His medical history was notable for resection of a Rathke’s cleft cyst; he took hormone replacements and occasional codeine. He smoked 20 pack-years and used alcohol and marijuana infrequently. 

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. There was mild, firm, nonfluctuant swelling of the right posterior mandible without skin changes. Palpation produced diffuse tenderness in the right submandibular region; no cervical lymphadenopathy was palpable. He had paresthesia and loss of sensation of the right lower lip, trismus (maximum incisal opening, 16 mm), and no other neurologic deficits. Intraorally, dentition appeared healthy; there was minor erythema distal to the right mandibular second molar, which was tender. Flexible nasopharyngoscopy was normal.

An orthopantomogram showed a vertically impacted right mandibular third molar with an ill-defined, “moth-eaten” radiolucency extending to the ramus and obscuring the mandibular canal; no root resorption or periosteal reaction was seen. CT of the facial bones revealed a 12×7.3 mm osteolytic lesion destroying lingual and buccal cortices around the impacted third molar, with adjacent soft-tissue reaction and subcentimeter right perifacial and jugulodigastric lymph nodes. A focal abscess could not be excluded on imaging.

Given the clinical and radiographic findings, the working diagnosis was an odontogenic infection secondary to the impacted right mandibular third molar, and the decision was made to perform incision and drainage under general anesthesia.

A 10-year-old boy presented with a 2-month history of dysphagia, breathlessness, disturbed sleep, and snoring. He had no fever or throat pain. Examination of the oral cavity revealed a large, smooth bulge on the posterior pharyngeal wall with intact mucosa; the swelling was firm and nontender, and its inferior margin could not be palpated. No cervical lymphadenopathy was appreciated on physical exam. For preoperative evaluation, contrast-enhanced MRI and noncontrast low-dose CT were performed.

The studies demonstrated a well-defined, midline retropharyngeal mass measuring approximately 4.8 × 1.5 cm on transverse and anteroposterior views and extending 6.6 cm superoinferiorly. The lesion contained multiple well-defined loculi: cystic areas with fluid-fluid levels, solid components, and a large lipomatous component, confirmed by high signal on T1-weighted images, fat-saturated T2-weighted suppression, and CT attenuation values indicative of adipose tissue. The solid, nonlipomatous portions enhanced homogeneously after contrast administration. There was no calcification or hemorrhage. The mass caused marked anterior displacement of the nasopharynx, oropharynx, hypopharynx, and supraglottic larynx, all of which appeared intrinsically normal. Bilateral, multilevel cervical lymph nodes were noted, each oval, subcentimeter, and with intact fatty hila, radiologically consistent with reactive nodes.

A 67‐year‐old Asian man was referred for evaluation of a rod‐shaped, pedunculated mass at the left inner canthus, present for two months with noted rapid growth. He denied pain, discomfort, systemic symptoms, prior malignancies, or significant medical history. On examination, he appeared well. Vital signs were normal. Cardiac, pulmonary, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. The eyelid mass measured approximately 3.0 cm in length, was dark yellow with a smooth surface and longitudinal texture; the base was soft and pliable, permitting easy twisting, whereas the distal portion was stiff. Routine blood, urine, and stool tests were normal. Chest radiography, electrocardiography, and coagulation studies showed no abnormalities.

A 12-year-old boy with autism spectrum disorder was brought by his parents for evaluation of a 2-month history of intermittent nosebleeds, reduced oral intake, dysphagia, and decreased speech. He has no prior medical or surgical history. Because of his autism, history was obtained entirely from his parents.

On examination, there was a nontender, midline sublingual mass protruding into the oral cavity, displacing the tongue superiorly. No mucosal abnormalities, bluish discoloration, bleeding, or oozing were noted. The patient had no dyspnea or dysarthria. There were no palpable neck masses or lymphadenopathy. He was afebrile and had no weight loss.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed a homogeneous, well-circumscribed, capsulated cystic lesion measuring 6.5 × 5.4 × 4.6 cm, located centrally in the sublingual space anterior to the hyoid bone. MRI demonstrated a thin-walled unilocular cyst with uniformly high protein content and peripheral enhancement after gadolinium administration in the sublingual space. Fine-needle aspiration yielded only squamous cells and was otherwise nondiagnostic.

A 14-year-old girl, previously healthy, presented with a 1-year history of dull left hip pain without progression or constitutional symptoms. On examination, there was tenderness and swelling over the left lower pelvis; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. A pelvic radiograph showed an expansile, well-defined lytic lesion in the left superior pubic ramus. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a multicystic lesion with fluid–fluid levels and enhancement of the internal septations on post-gadolinium images. To obtain a definitive diagnosis, a CT-guided biopsy of the lesion was performed.

A 32-year-old Brazilian woman presented with a 2-year history of diffuse pain in her upper and lower limbs and back, which began during pregnancy and gradually worsened, ultimately limiting her mobility. Magnetic resonance imaging performed after increasing hip pain revealed a femoral neck fracture, and she underwent orthopedic fixation. Despite surgery, her pain persisted, and she was initially diagnosed with fibromyalgia and osteoporosis by neurology and endocrinology. Routine rheumatologic laboratory studies, however, demonstrated persistent hypophosphatemia with a normal serum 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D level. To investigate tumor-induced osteomalacia, somatostatin analog scintigraphy was performed and showed an asymmetric focus of increased radiotracer uptake in the right nasopharynx. On otolaryngologic evaluation, she reported a history of occasional epistaxis since childhood and more recent right-sided nasal obstruction. Nasofibroscopy revealed a reddish polypoid lesion originating from the sphenoethmoidal recess in the right nasal cavity. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the sinuses confirmed a polypoid, contrast-enhancing mass measuring 1.5 × 2.0 × 5.1 cm at the junction of the nasal roof, sphenoethmoidal recess, and posterior ethmoid cell on the right.

A 35-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of worsening headaches, blurred vision, and progressive weakness of both upper and lower extremities. She had been diagnosed at age 12 with a brain mass, when imaging raised a differential of intracranial epidermoid versus dermoid cyst; because of stable symptoms, she was managed conservatively. At age 23, she underwent craniotomy and ventriculoperitoneal shunting for increased headaches, vision changes, and new extremity weakness. Intraoperative pathology showed hair, keratin, and necrotic material. She improved but at age 29 developed recurrent headaches and mild extremity weakness. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. MRI at that time demonstrated a lobulated, fat-fluid-containing mass, measuring 27 × 21 mm, anterior to the right temporal lobe and extending to the prepontine cistern and medulla. The lesion showed high T1 and T2 signal intensity, areas of hyposignal consistent with hemosiderin deposition, no contrast enhancement, and exerted mass effect on the brainstem. Over the subsequent year, her condition deteriorated; examination revealed slurred speech, reduced strength in all extremities, impaired coordination, and hyperreflexia with intact cranial-nerve function. Repeat MRI one month ago showed enlargement of the lobulated fat-fluid mass extending from the right cerebellum into the peripontine and interpeduncular cisterns and the right parietofrontal and temporal lobes, with a 9 mm midline shift, mild-to-moderate fourth-ventricle dilation, and encasement of basilar, right posterior cerebral, and right middle cerebral arteries without occlusion.

A 3-week-old female infant was evaluated for a congenital pigmented lesion on the scalp. On examination, she had a 7-cm, non-tender, soft, well-circumscribed nevus centered on the vertex and extending into the occipital and parietal scalp. The surface had heterogeneous red-purple discoloration and coarse hair growth.

A punch biopsy of the lesion revealed:
• Extensive dermal involvement by small nests and whorls of spindle-shaped melanocytes embedded in a fibrillar matrix.  
• Increased vascularity and clusters of small, round melanocytes tracking around hair follicles and sweat glands, extending into the subcutaneous septa and between adipocytes.  
• Rare pagetoid arrays of melanocytes as single cells and small nests with pale, vacuolated cytoplasm and dusty melanin.  
• No alarming features such as increased mitotic activity or perineural invasion.

Immunohistochemical studies showed:
• Melan-A: diffusely positive in the melanocytic component but negative in areas of spindle cell (Schwannian) differentiation.  
• PRAME: negative in lesional cells.

A 59-year-old Caucasian man with a history of smoking and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease underwent chest computed tomography as part of a COPD clinical trial and was found to have a suprahilar right upper lobe mass. Positron emission tomography demonstrated fluorodeoxyglucose avidity of the mass without mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Bronchoscopic biopsy established a diagnosis of carcinoma, and he underwent right upper lobectomy without complication.

Pathological examination revealed a 5.0 cm poorly differentiated carcinoma with a high Ki-67 proliferation index, positive cytokeratin 5/6, focally positive p63, and negative p53. Incidentally, at the stapled parenchymal margin, there was a 0.2 cm, well-circumscribed, microscopic lesion. Histologically, the lesion was well demarcated and composed of bland cuboidal cells lining irregular spaces; the interstitium contained vaguely spindle-shaped cells. Immunohistochemical studies of the lesion demonstrated positivity for cytokeratin AE1/AE3 and thyroid transcription factor 1, and negativity for p53, synaptophysin, chromogranin, p63, S-100, CD31, calretinin, and Wilms’ tumor 1.

An 11-year-old boy presented with a 3-month history of progressive bilateral scrotal enlargement and a 4- to 5-year history of intermittent palpitations, restlessness, anger, and dizziness. He had no fevers or scrotal pain.  
On examination, blood pressure was elevated at 150/100 mm Hg (left arm) and 144/100 mm Hg (right arm); other vital signs were normal. Weight was at the 75th–90th percentile and height at the 50th percentile for age. Generalized skin hyperpigmentation was noted. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Genital examination revealed firm, non-tender, bilaterally enlarged testes under normal-appearing scrotal skin. Tanner stage was 3 for both genitalia (testis length 3.5 cm, penile length 10 cm) and pubic hair.  
Scrotal ultrasonography showed normal testicular volumes (right 2.9 mL, left 2.8 mL) with multiple well-defined, round to oval, hetero-echoic intratesticular nodules containing calcific foci. Color Doppler imaging demonstrated increased peripheral and internal vascularity of these nodules.  
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed large, triangular hypoechoic lesions in the left suprarenal region and smaller similar lesions in the right suprarenal region, both without internal vascularity.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated homogeneously enhancing, bilaterally enlarged adrenal glands with maintained shape, suggestive of adrenal hyperplasia, and bilateral testicular hypodense lesions with multiple enhancing nodules.  
Serum tumor markers—including alpha-fetoprotein, lactate dehydrogenase, and β-hCG—were within normal limits.  
What is your differential diagnosis?

A 45-year-old nulligravida woman with a history of left breast lobular carcinoma (triple-negative, pT2N1M0) treated 2 years earlier with lumpectomy (6 of 13 positive nodes), adjuvant TAC chemotherapy, and radiotherapy presented for routine follow-up. On examination, a left adnexal mass was palpated. Transvaginal ultrasound revealed a 5-cm left ovarian mass with mixed cystic and solid components and increased Doppler vascularity. Serum CA-125 was 78 IU/ml. The patient underwent explorative laparotomy. Intraoperative frozen section of the left adnexa was positive for malignancy, prompting cytological peritoneal washings (positive for cancer cells), total hysterectomy, contralateral adnexectomy, infracolic omentectomy, and peritoneal biopsies. Clinicians faced the question whether this represented a new primary ovarian cancer or metastasis of her prior breast carcinoma.

A 60-year-old man presented with a palpable right upper quadrant mass and abnormal liver function tests. He had no significant medical history.  
Laboratory studies revealed:  
• AST 406 U/L; ALT 397 U/L; total bilirubin 1.01 mg/dL; direct bilirubin 0.61 mg/dL; ALP 4380 U/L; γ-GTP 1548 U/L; amylase 509 U/L.  
• Elevated tumor markers: CEA 8.6 ng/mL; CA19-9 261 U/mL; SPan-1 100 U/mL; DUPAN-2 750 U/mL; soluble interleukin-2 receptor normal.

Abdominal ultrasonography showed a well-demarcated, heterogeneously solid mass, 8 cm in diameter, in the head of the pancreas. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 7 × 9 × 7 cm exophytic mass in the pancreatic head, hypodense in the arterial phase and becoming uniformly hyperdense in the delayed phase, with biliary stricture, main pancreatic duct disruption, and obstructive pancreatitis but no obvious invasion of adjacent organs or enlarged lymph nodes. MRI revealed the lesion to be hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and diffusely hyperintense on diffusion-weighted imaging; MR cholangiopancreatography showed intra- and extra-hepatic bile-duct and pancreatic-duct dilatation. FDG-PET showed heterogeneous uptake in the pancreatic head mass (SUV max 7.65) without distant or nodal metastases.

Endoscopic ultrasound–guided fine-needle aspiration (EUS-FNA) yielded atypical cells with increased chromatin granularity. Histopathology showed proliferating short spindle-shaped cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and scattered mitotic figures. Immunohistochemical staining of the biopsy specimen was positive for CD34 and CD56, partially positive for cytokeratin AE1/AE3, and negative for synaptophysin, chromogranin A, somatostatin receptor type 2, CD117, DOG1, S-100, smooth muscle actin, desmin, and CD31.

A 63-year-old man presented with a one-year history of gradually progressive gait imbalance, upper-limb incoordination, behavioral changes (anger outbursts, emotional lability, disinhibition), recent memory impairment, lower-limb bone pain, weight loss, and fatigue. On examination, he had generalized wasting, bilateral xanthelasma, bony tenderness, perseveration, immediate and recent memory deficits, broken‐pursuit eye movements, up-gaze restriction, and bilateral cerebellar signs with gait ataxia. Routine blood counts and metabolic panels were normal. Brain MRI T2-weighted images showed diffuse hyperintensity in the pons, medulla, and cerebellar peduncles bilaterally, as well as periventricular white-matter hyperintensities. A 99mTc bone scintigraphy demonstrated symmetric increased uptake in the diaphyseal and metaphyseal regions of the humeri, femora, and tibiae, and in the frontal and maxillary bones. Whole-body FDG PET-CT revealed hypermetabolic cortical thickening and sclerosis of the long bones with epiphyseal sparing, involvement of facial bones, a focal hypermetabolic lesion in the brainstem, small enhancing intraconal orbital nodules, and soft-tissue thickening along the aorta and its branches.

A 69-year-old previously healthy Japanese man was evaluated for a 2-month history of diarrhea and lower abdominal discomfort. Physical examination findings were unremarkable, including digital rectal examination. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 14.5 mg/dL, normal liver and renal function, and a positive fecal occult blood test. 

Colonoscopy revealed a 15-mm Paris class 0-IIa lesion located at the appendiceal orifice. Biopsy demonstrated atypical epithelium with focal suspicion for adenocarcinoma. Surgical resection was planned due to the lesion’s location.

During preoperative staging, chest computed tomography showed multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules measuring 2–10 mm in diameter without pleural thickening or effusion. Serum tumor markers, including CEA and CA19-9, were within normal limits. The appendiceal lesion was not visible on CT, and there was no lymphadenopathy or hepatic lesions. The initial clinical impression was appendiceal cancer with pulmonary metastases, though this was questioned given the small size of the primary lesion.

Fluorine-18-FDG PET/CT demonstrated a maximum SUV of 2.4 in the appendiceal lesion, while the largest (10-mm) lung nodule had an SUV of 1.0.

A 30-year-old woman presented with a three-year history of left knee pain, worsened by walking or climbing stairs and occasionally accompanied by joint locking. The pain, located mainly in the popliteal fossa, initially resolved with rest and self-massage. Over time, she developed similar mild symptoms in the right knee. There was no history of trauma, systemic illness, or family history of joint disease, and constitutional symptoms were absent.

On examination, she was independent in ambulation. The left knee showed tenderness in the popliteal area, mild suprapatellar swelling, and a 5° flexion contracture; the right knee had normal range of motion. Meniscal testing elicited pain and muscle guarding on extension but was normal in passive flexion. There was no ligamentous laxity; the patella was stable; other joints were unremarkable. Routine blood tests were within normal limits.

Plain radiographs of both knees demonstrated multiple nonspecific calcifications. MRI of the knees revealed multiple intra-articular intermediate–signal lesions in the suprapatellar pouch, posterior Hoffa’s fat pad, and posterior joint capsule (up to 8 mm), suggestive of synovial chondromatosis, along with focal cartilage loss in the medial femoral condyle with subchondral irregularity and cystic changes suggestive of focal degenerative joint disease.

A 57-year-old man underwent screening colonoscopy. He had well-controlled hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia and no gastrointestinal symptoms. Physical examination was unremarkable. Bowel preparation was excellent. In the proximal sigmoid colon, the endoscopist found a smooth, semipedunculated polyp estimated at 12 mm in size. A hot-snare polypectomy was performed, and the specimen was retrieved. 

Histopathological examination showed colonic mucosa with a mass-like lesion composed of sheets of plasma cells. Immunohistochemical stains highlighted plasma cells expressing CD138 and BCL2 with kappa light chain restriction, and they were negative for CD3, CD5, CD10, CD43, BCL1, BCL6, and pan keratin.

A 64‐year‐old woman presented with daily fevers up to 102 °F for one month, associated with night sweats, muscle aches, dry cough, headache, fatigue, and an 8-pound weight loss.  
Her medical history included hypertension and anxiety; she denied smoking, alcohol use, recent travel, or pet exposure. Family history was notable for cardiovascular disease in her parents and breast cancer in her twin sister.  

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 14 000/mm³ (neutrophils 10 000/mm³), hematocrit 33.5%, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate >120 mm/hr, and C-reactive protein 238 mg/L. Thyroid-stimulating hormone was 1.19 µIU/mL. Serum and urine protein electrophoresis showed no monoclonal spike.  

Blood and urine cultures were negative, and tests for Lyme antibody, Bartonella IgG/IgM, Anaplasma PCR, and Babesia PCR were negative.  

Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen revealed a 3.8 × 2.9 × 5.0 cm heterogeneous, enhancing lesion in the left adrenal gland; the right adrenal gland appeared normal. A random urine normetanephrine was elevated at 2917 µg per gram of creatinine (reference, 108–524).  

Further evaluation showed serum free normetanephrine 344 pg/mL (≤148) and serum free metanephrine <25 pg/mL (≤57). Twenty-four-hour urine studies revealed normetanephrine 1915 µg (122–676), metanephrine 139 µg (90–315), norepinephrine 133 µg (15–100), dopamine 148 µg (52–480), and a normal urinary free cortisol of 27.4 µg (4–50). MRI of the abdomen demonstrated a 3.4 × 4.0 × 4.7 cm mass in the left adrenal gland with heterogeneous T2 hyperintensity and T1 isointensity.

A 44-year-old woman underwent elective bilateral breast reduction. She was asymptomatic with normal appetite and stable weight; she reported no breast pain, fullness, or nipple discharge. Her prior self-exams and two screening mammograms were unremarkable. Medical history was notable only for Factor XI deficiency; there was no personal or family history of cancer. On examination there was no lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, or skin or mucosal lesions. Complete blood counts were within normal limits (WBC 6.6×10^3/mm^3, RBC 4.62×10^6/mm^3, platelets 257×10^3/mm^3) with a normal differential. Random sections of the left breast tissue showed a diffuse interstitial infiltrate of small, mature lymphocytes with round nuclei, condensed chromatin, indistinct nucleoli, and abundant pale cytoplasm. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated that the infiltrate was composed of CD20- and PAX5-positive B-cells with variable nuclear Cyclin D1 expression, cytoplasmic Annexin-A1 and TRAP positivity, and weak CD25; DBA.44 was inconclusive, and CD3, CD5, CD10, CD21, and CD23 were negative. Fluorescence in situ hybridization for t(11;14) was negative.

A 61-year-old white woman with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidaemia presented with 1 hour of sudden-onset pain and numbness in both legs, associated with lightheadedness, dyspnoea, and diaphoresis. She was afebrile (98.6°F), blood pressure was 160/110 mmHg, heart rate 70 bpm, respiratory rate 24/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. On examination, she was in acute distress due to leg pain. Lungs were clear. Cardiac examination revealed a regular rate and rhythm without murmurs. The abdomen and neurologic examination were unremarkable. Both lower extremities were mottled, pale, and cold from mid-thigh down, with absent right femoral, bilateral popliteal, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses.  
Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with T-wave inversion in leads I, V2–V4. Laboratory tests revealed a leukocyte count of 20.7 × 10^3/µL and a peak troponin of 2.08 ng/mL (normal <0.03 ng/mL). Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated thrombosis of the right iliac and bilateral common femoral arteries. Computed tomography angiography of the abdomen and pelvis showed splenic and bilateral renal infarcts and embolic occlusion of the right external and internal iliac arteries and the left distal common femoral artery. Computed tomography angiography of the chest did not show pulmonary emboli but revealed a 3.4-cm solid ovoid filling defect in the left atrium concerning for thrombus vs. myxoma.

A 19-year-old man with a ten-year history of epilepsy presented with increasing frequency of simple and complex partial seizures, despite high-dose antiepileptic therapy. He also reported transient severe morning headaches with nausea, vomiting, and dizziness since age nine, at which time imaging had revealed a presumed right insular vascular abnormality. Exam showed only distal left upper extremity weakness and hand muscle atrophy from a prior motor vehicle accident. 

One year before planned surgery, MRI of the brain revealed a suspected single right posterior frontal flow void with adjacent cortical foci of susceptibility artifact compatible with calcification or hemosiderin, suggesting an atypical vascular lesion. The flow void resembled a developmental venous anomaly, but the pattern of adjacent hemosiderin deposition was noted to be unusual for a DVA or an associated cavernous malformation. No imaging features were specific for a parenchymal arteriovenous malformation or a dural arteriovenous fistula. The vascular abnormality was not visualized on MRA. Repeat imaging confirmed the same lesion, still felt to represent an atypical vascular malformation.

A 71-year-old woman was admitted with sudden faintness and bilateral leg weakness. Her history included hypertension, osteoporosis, and coronary heart disease treated in 2011 with a DES in the LAD. On admission, troponin I was 189 ng/l (normal <45), rising to 7510 ng/l on hospital day 2, consistent with a NSTEMI treated by PTCA and placement of a DES in the right coronary artery. Dual antiplatelet therapy was started. Initial labs also showed serum calcium 3.35 mmol/l (normal 2.15–2.55), phosphate 0.36 mmol/l (0.81–1.62), vitamin D 47 nmol/l (50–250), and PTH 1156 ng/l (18.4–72). She reported polydipsia, polyuria, and mild dysphagia but denied nephrolithiasis, bone pain, or dyspepsia. Examination revealed a firm, nonmobile right-sided neck node. Neck ultrasound identified a 5 cm right thyroidal mass classified as TIRADS 5. Fine-needle aspiration showed a monomorphic, partially follicular cell population with focal weak PTH immunopositivity. CT and MRI demonstrated a 5 cm tumor at the right caudal thyroid pole compressing the trachea by ~50% without clear extrathyroidal invasion. A 99mTc-sestamibi scan was halted early for pain, but early images revealed nodal uptake at the right tracheal side, suggesting a parathyroid origin. Cinacalcet was started, lowering calcium to near normal over 8 weeks while PTH remained elevated.

A 62-year-old man on maintenance hemodialysis for 11 years was referred after multiple episodes of syncope and retrograde amnesia. He was asymptomatic on arrival. His medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, peripheral arterial disease, bilateral carotid stenosis, and prior coronary artery bypass grafting. Medications included clopidogrel, amlodipine, valsartan, rosuvastatin, and linagliptin.  
Vital signs were stable. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were unremarkable, and there were no focal neurologic deficits. Laboratory tests revealed hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL, BUN 45.5 mg/dL, creatinine 13.9 mg/dL; white blood cell count, platelets, electrolytes, C-reactive protein, and coagulation studies were within normal limits.  
Brain MRI showed multiple small subcortical infarctions in both hemispheres on diffusion‐weighted imaging. ECG demonstrated normal sinus rhythm without arrhythmia. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a 2.5 cm highly echogenic mass attached to the ventricular side of the posterior mitral leaflet, moving synchronously with the valve.  
Contrast-enhanced CT showed a mass with marginal calcification on the mitral valve without significant contrast enhancement. Cardiac MRI demonstrated the mass to be isointense to myocardium on T1-weighted and fat-suppressed T2-weighted images, and gradient-echo cine sequences confirmed firm attachment and mobility of the lesion on the posterior mitral leaflet.

A 10-month-old boy, previously healthy, was noted by his parents to have a gradually enlarging mass in the anterior aspect of his right thigh for three months. He had no fever, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender mass in the right anterior thigh.

Magnetic resonance imaging of both thighs (axial, sagittal, and coronal T1-weighted, PD, and PDFS sequences) demonstrated several fusiform intramuscular and intermuscular lesions measuring up to 15 × 14 mm in each thigh, more prominent on the right; the bone and bone marrow appeared normal, without lytic or sclerotic changes. The radiologic impression was that of neurofibroma.

One week later, the patient underwent radical excision of the right thigh mass. Grossly, the specimen was a 3 × 2 cm grayish tumor with areas of hemorrhage. Histologic examination showed nests of small, dark, round cells with scant cytoplasm and pseudorosette formations, together with foci of hemorrhage.

A 77-year-old woman presented with intermittent hoarseness and episodes of choking when swallowing. Panendoscopy revealed a smooth, cystic mass arising from the right posterior aryepiglottic fold. An initial biopsy showed only mild mucosal dysplasia. An urgent CT scan of the neck was interpreted as showing a malignant-appearing mass arising from the right superior thyroid pole. Ultrasound-guided biopsy of the lesion demonstrated spindle cells, and the differential diagnoses included a spindle cell variant of anaplastic thyroid carcinoma or Riedel’s thyroiditis; however, the sample was too small for a definitive diagnosis. At a multidisciplinary head and neck oncology meeting, concerns were raised about the quality of the initial CT images, so a repeat contrast-enhanced CT was obtained. The new images showed a distinct tissue plane separating the mass from the right thyroid lobe, indicating that the lesion originated in the hypopharynx. A further incisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia and sent to a regional sarcoma panel for analysis.

A 73-year-old Japanese woman presented with a chief complaint of abdominal pain. She had a history of hypertension. On examination, her vital signs were stable and her abdomen was flat and soft without tenderness. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 6730/μL, C-reactive protein of 0.03 mg/dL, hemoglobin of 10.2 mg/dL, carcinoembryonic antigen of 2.2 ng/mL, and CA 19-9 of 11.4 U/mL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a giant tumor measuring 15 cm along its greatest dimension in the left upper abdomen.

A 7-year-old girl presented with a one-month history of pain and swelling in the left posterior mandibular gingiva, with bleeding that worsened during brushing and chewing. Her medical and dental histories were unremarkable. On examination, there was a solitary, well-defined, firm, tender, dark red sessile mass measuring 2.5 × 1.5 cm on the lingual and distal gingiva of tooth 36, extending posteriorly toward the ramus. There was no bony involvement on panoramic radiograph. A provisional diagnosis of pyogenic granuloma was made. The initial clinical differential diagnoses included traumatic fibroma, peripheral giant cell lesion, neurofibroma, schwannoma, and hemangiopericytoma. An excisional biopsy was performed. Histopathologic examination showed anastomosing surface epithelium with elongated rete ridges and a tumor composed of interlacing fascicles of spindle-shaped cells with myofibroblastic features, occasional mitoses, and focal round to polygonal cell areas. To further characterize the lesion, immunohistochemical studies were done, revealing tumor-cell positivity for α-smooth muscle actin and negativity for CD34.

A 27-year-old man presented with progressive abdominal swelling for two years, accompanied by loss of appetite, significant weight loss, and constipation. Over the past month, he noted worsening abdominal distension, new scrotal swelling, and dyspnea. He had no prior surgery, comorbidities, tobacco, alcohol, or drug use. On examination, he was emaciated and tachypneic (24–26 breaths/min); other vital signs were normal. The abdomen was hugely distended, tense, and shiny with visible veins; the umbilicus was everted, percussion was dull throughout, and no discrete mass could be palpated. There was bilateral pedal and scrotal edema. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10 g/dL and albumin 2.5 g/dL; other values were normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a large, multiseptated cystic mass filling the abdominal and pelvic cavities; its origin could not be determined. Differential diagnosis on imaging was a mesenteric cyst.

A 35-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 1-month history of progressively worsening spontaneous pain in the left hip, initially relieved by NSAIDs but later present at rest and exacerbated by weight bearing. Physical examination of the left hip was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 4.1 × 10^3/μl (normal 4.5–11 × 10^3/μl), a C-reactive protein level of 2.6 mg/dl (<0.9 mg/dl), and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 18 mm/h (0–22 mm/h). Tests for infectious organisms, including microscopy, PCR, and culture for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, were negative. MRI of the left proximal femur demonstrated findings suggestive of osteomyelitis. An open biopsy yielded normal tissue with no evidence of osteomyelitis. The patient underwent bone debridement with negative bacterial and fungal cultures and received broad-spectrum antibiotics, with resolution of pain.

Twelve months later, he returned with gradually progressive pain and swelling of the left hip. A PET/CT scan demonstrated markedly increased uptake in the proximal left femur with a soft-tissue mass measuring 164 × 114 × 200 mm (SUVmax 33.9). Involved lymph nodes included left internal iliac (15 × 8 mm) and left inguinal (15 × 9 mm) nodes.

A 68-year-old retired male clerk presented with a 10-year history of slowly progressive, multiple erythematous and hyperpigmented scaly and crusted erosions and plaques on the trunk. Lesions measured 0.5×0.5 cm to 10×10 cm, were mostly on sun-protected sites, and were intermittently itchy or burning; a few were tender. He had no history of alcohol use, smoking, extramarital sexual exposure, immunosuppression, or underlying malignancy; family history was unremarkable. Twenty years earlier, he had taken homeopathic remedies for general well-being for about 10 years but discontinued them after the skin lesions appeared. He had no mucosal involvement or clinical signs of chronic arsenic exposure. He had undergone cryotherapy, topical antifungals, retinoids, steroids, 5-fluorouracil, and imiquimod without improvement. 

Vital signs were stable, and systemic examination was normal. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and urinalysis. HIV serology was negative. Serum arsenic was 15 μg per liter (normal < 60 μg per liter). 

A skin biopsy from a representative plaque showed disorganized proliferation of atypical squamous epithelial cells with disproportionately enlarged, hyperchromatic nuclei; a few cells in the upper epidermis showed vacuolation. The basal cell layer was sharply demarcated from the underlying dermis, and melanin pigment was increased in the basal epidermal layer.

A 1‐year‐old boy was evaluated for difficulty moving his upper extremities. One month earlier, he had developed an upper respiratory infection with fever. Two days after the fever began, he noted progressive weakness of his arms. A week of antibiotics resolved his systemic symptoms, but the arm weakness persisted, prompting referral. There was no prior history of neurologic deficits or similar episodes after vaccinations.

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. He was not febrile, cyanotic, or in respiratory distress. Neurologic assessment revealed decreased muscle strength in the left upper extremity (grade 3/5) with slightly reduced tone in both upper limbs; lower‐limb strength and tone were normal.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL, white blood cell count 11,000/mm3, and platelets 323,000/mm3. A chest radiograph revealed no abnormalities.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine with contrast demonstrated a mass at the level of C2 and C3, extending into the vertebral foramina from C3 to C6. The lesion was located outside the meninges and compressed the anterior aspect of the cervical spinal cord.

A 64-year-old woman with a history of left invasive lobular breast carcinoma (pT1cN3, ER 90%, PgR 80%, HER2-negative), treated with wide excision, axillary dissection, adjuvant chemotherapy and aromatase inhibitor therapy, presented for routine follow-up. She reported no thyroid-related symptoms. Physical examination revealed bilaterally enlarged, multinodular thyroid lobes. Thyroid function tests were normal. Neck ultrasound showed an enlarged gland with retrosternal extension; the right lobe was finely inhomogeneous, and the left lobe was entirely occupied by a large nodule with mixed echogenicity, cystic and colloid degeneration, and calcifications. Fine-needle aspiration of both lobes was performed. Smears from the right lobe showed only colloid and benign thyrocytes. Smears from the left lobe revealed two cell populations in a colloidal background: benign thyrocytes and a second population of small cells, dispersed or in loose aggregates, with a plasmacytoid appearance and occasional vacuoles.

A 13-year-old boy was brought to the clinic for evaluation of a swelling in the left parietotemporal region of the skull. He first noticed a hard, non-tender lump measuring about 5 × 4 cm, which progressively enlarged over several weeks to 10 × 7 cm without accompanying pain or neurological symptoms.  
On examination, the mass was firm, fixed to the underlying bone, and without overlying skin changes. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and basic metabolic panel, were unremarkable.  
A skull radiograph demonstrated permeative, lytic destruction of the outer table with a sunburst periosteal reaction. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and skull showed an exophytic soft-tissue mass arising from the left parietotemporal bone, with erosion of the outer table and extension into surrounding soft tissues.

A 21-year-old woman presented with a painless vulvar mass that she first noticed four years earlier; it had grown progressively larger over time and more rapidly during the past several months. She reported mild discomfort when seated and a localized burning sensation but denied pain, bleeding, or systemic symptoms. Her medical and surgical history was unremarkable.

On examination, there was a pedunculated, bilobulated, tense-elastic mass measuring approximately 10 cm in diameter arising from the left labia minora. The overlying skin was intact without ulceration. There was no inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, liver enzymes, iron studies, renal function, coagulation profile, and tumor markers (CA-125, CA-19-9, CA-15-3, alpha-fetoprotein, and carcinoembryonic antigen), were within normal limits. Vaginal ultrasonography revealed a uterus and adnexa of normal appearance. Ultrasonography of the mass showed a well-demarcated soft-tissue lesion with homogeneous echotexture and normal vascularity.

To exclude a surgical hernia, the patient was evaluated by general surgery; based on her history, physical examination, and ultrasonography, a perineal or inguinal hernia was ruled out.

A 26-year-old woman presented with persistent right knee pain following anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. Sixteen months earlier, she had sustained an acute right knee injury at a dance tryout. Initial radiographs and MRI at injury demonstrated a complete ACL tear, a terminal sulcus impaction injury, and a corner fracture of the posterior lateral tibial plateau. She underwent bone–patellar tendon–bone ACL reconstruction with an uneventful recovery; immediate postoperative radiographs were unremarkable.

Approximately 6 months after reconstruction, she slipped on ice and reinjured her right knee. Radiographs were again interpreted as unremarkable, but her symptoms persisted. MRI at that time showed a new lesion in the anteromedial aspect of the proximal tibia, adjacent to the tibial tunnel. No specific differential diagnosis was offered by the outside radiologist.

At 10 months after reconstruction, repeat radiographs demonstrated a slight interval increase in the size of the medial tibial lesion. The patient was treated with a local steroid injection for symptom relief.

A 14-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of intermittent abdominal pain and vomiting of one year’s duration. On examination, he had tenderness in the left lower quadrant without a palpable mass. His history was notable for rectal and intravesical ulcerations treated 5 years earlier, a tonsillectomy one year earlier, and spotty skin pigmentations not typical of café-au-lait spots.

Routine blood tests, peripheral blood smear, lactate dehydrogenase, ferritin, neuron-specific enolase, adrenocorticotropic hormone, cortisol, and 24-hour urinary vanillylmandelic acid, homovanillic acid, and metanephrine levels were all within normal limits. Chest radiography and bone marrow aspiration and biopsy revealed no abnormalities.

Abdominal ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic 30 × 37 mm solid lesion adjacent to the medial upper pole of the left kidney, causing mild contour change. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a 32 × 40 mm homogeneous, well-circumscribed mass in the left adrenal region. MRI demonstrated a 35 × 37 mm solid, well-defined lesion in the left adrenal area without evidence of invasion into surrounding tissues, suggestive of a benign process.

A 78-year-old nondiabetic woman with a history of remote pulmonary Mycobacterium avium complex infection, Staphylococcus aureus osteomyelitis of the right clavicle, and squamous cell carcinoma in situ of the right thigh presented with progressive ulceration of a long-standing plaque on the right shin that had been present for 40 years. On examination, there was a 9.0 × 25.0 cm atrophic, telangiectatic, yellow-pink plaque with a central 4.5 × 4.0 cm ulcer. The initial differential diagnosis included infection with exuberant reactive epithelial hyperplasia, vegetative pyoderma gangrenosum with or without underlying active necrobiosis lipoidica, and squamous cell carcinoma. Biopsies of the ulcer over time showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with limited keratinocyte atypia, fibrosis, and mixed inflammation. Occult infection was ruled out by tissue cultures, microbial stains, polymerase chain reaction, and gamma-interferon release assay. To avoid pathergy and per patient preference, anti-inflammatory and conservative treatments—including oral and intralesional steroids, pentoxifylline, oral tofacitinib, and intralesional 5-fluorouracil—were administered. The ulcer initially waxed and waned over several years but eventually developed a verrucous appearance and became painful.

A 35-year-old single nulliparous woman was referred to gynecology for evaluation of uterine fibroids. Over four years, she noted progressive abdominal swelling associated with dysmenorrhea and heavy menstrual bleeding. One year ago, she began to notice that her umbilicus increased in size and became painful in a cyclical fashion during menstruation; the swelling subsided after menses, and there was no bleeding or discharge. She had no prior abdominal surgeries and denied dyspareunia, changes in bowel habits, urinary symptoms, or weight loss. 

On examination, the abdomen was distended and moved with respiration. There was a hyperpigmented, firm, nontender umbilical swelling measuring 4 × 4 cm without expansile cough impulse; it was not attached to underlying structures or overlying skin and was not reducible. A non-tender pelvic mass with a nodular surface extended to the size of a 32-week uterus.

Abdominopelvic ultrasonography showed a large uterus with multiple heteroechoic masses, some with rim calcification, the largest measuring 8.9 cm in diameter; the endometrial stripe was distorted. Both ovaries appeared normal; there was no adnexal mass and no fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Preoperative hemogram, biochemical, and coagulation profiles were within normal limits.

A 24-year-old Persian man was referred for evaluation of persistent halitosis following recovery from mild COVID-19. His dentist noted localized interproximal bone loss and bleeding around teeth 18 and 19; scaling and root planing were performed, and halitosis resolved. Two months later, he returned with cold sensitivity in lower incisors; vitality testing showed teeth 23 and 24 to be nonvital. A periapical radiograph revealed a radiolucent lesion in the anterior mandible. Panoramic imaging then demonstrated a large, well-defined, scalloped, lytic lesion extending from tooth 31 on the right to the left ascending ramus. Cone-beam CT confirmed a multilocular lytic lesion with thinning and perforation of both buccal and lingual cortices.

Medical history was notable for mitral valve prolapse; recurrent otitis since infancy; septicemia at age 1; seasonal allergy treated with bronchodilators; and a 4-year history of empty sella syndrome with polyuria and polydipsia managed with levothyroxine, cabergoline, desmopressin, and testosterone. Family history included maternal Hashimoto thyroiditis. He had a BMI of 34.5. Extraoral and intraoral examinations were otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count but elevated ESR and CRP. An incisional biopsy of the anterior mandible was performed. Histologic sections revealed diffuse infiltration of large pale-staining histiocytes with indented nuclei intermixed with numerous eosinophils in a fibrous stroma.

A 40-year-old Haitian man presented with a two-week history of progressive right-sided weakness, dysesthesias, and headaches. He denied dizziness, vision changes, nausea, vomiting, or neck stiffness. On neurological examination, he had upper motor neuron–pattern weakness (4/5) in the right upper and lower extremities, increased temperature sensitivity on the right side, and right lower-extremity gait abnormality; reflexes were intact and cranial nerves were normal.

A noncontrast CT scan of the head revealed widespread cystic lesions throughout the cerebral hemispheres. Brain MRI demonstrated numerous bilateral intraparenchymal cystic enhancing lesions, some with internal hemorrhagic components. The largest was a 5.0 × 3.4 × 4.0 cm cyst in the left frontoparietal region causing mass effect, with additional lesions in the left caudate head, left basal ganglia rimmed with hemorrhage, and the right superior frontal white matter. There was a 5 mm rightward septal shift.

CT of the chest and abdomen showed no primary or metastatic masses. Syphilis serology was nonreactive, and the Quantiferon TB test was reactive; the patient had no prior treatment for latent tuberculosis. CSF analysis revealed 10 WBC/mm3, protein 69 g/L, glucose 70 mmol/L, and cytology showing atypical cells. Other infectious studies—including VDRL, routine blood cultures, AFB smear, serum Cryptococcus antigen, HIV, galactomannan, Fungitell, and toxoplasmosis serology—were negative.

Three days after admission, his right lower-extremity weakness progressed to paralysis, and repeat CT of the head showed hyperdense material layering within a cystic lesion, suggestive of intracystic hemorrhage. He was started on dexamethasone for vasogenic edema, with slight improvement. Despite negative cysticercosis serology, he received empiric albendazole, praziquantel, and levetiracetam. Given the reactive Quantiferon test, he was also treated for latent tuberculosis.

A previously healthy 16-year-old girl presented with 2 weeks of worsening epigastric pain and mild intermittent chest pressure. She denied fevers, cough, jaundice, emesis, diarrhea, constipation, mental status changes, new bruising, or weight loss. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies showed a leukocytosis (white blood cells 11.8 K/μL) and an elevated lipase level (2,524 U/L).  
An abdominal ultrasound, performed because of suspected pancreatitis, revealed a 5-cm mass in the head and uncinate process of the pancreas. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis confirmed a mixed solid and cystic mass in the pancreatic head. MRI of the abdomen demonstrated a 4.2-cm mixed solid/cystic mass at the pancreatic head with mild pancreatic duct dilation and a 2.6-cm hypoenhancing lobulated mass in the inferior pole of the spleen. MR cholangiopancreatography further showed necrosis within the pancreatic head mass as well as solid splenic and upper mediastinal masses.

An 18-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of a painless swelling on the left side of her face. She had a repaired cleft lip from infancy and no significant medical or dental history. On examination, there was a 6×5 cm soft-to-firm, non-tender swelling extending from the corner of the mouth to the tragus and from the lower border of the mandible to the zygomatic buttress. Mild vestibular swelling was noted intraorally on the left. Palmar pits were present on both hands, and a soft-to-hard palpable swelling was noted on the right midline of her back. Sprengel’s deformity was absent.

Orthopantomogram showed missing teeth 18 and 28; impacted 38 and 48; a supernumerary tooth between 22 and 23; rotated 22; and multiple well-defined unilocular radiolucencies with radiopaque borders in the maxilla and mandible. A differential diagnosis of odontogenic keratocyst (OKC), ameloblastoma, dentigerous cyst, and aneurysmal bone cyst was made.

Aspiration yielded a dirty creamy white viscous suspension. Noncontrast CT of the maxilla and mandible demonstrated expansile soft-tissue–attenuation lesions with cortical erosion and extension into adjacent soft tissues. Incisional biopsy of lesions in both jaws showed parakeratinized stratified squamous epithelium without rete ridges.

A chest radiograph revealed bifid ribs, and a skull radiograph showed calcification of the falx cerebri. Pelvic ultrasound demonstrated mildly enlarged ovaries with multiple subcentimetric cysts.

A 50-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 2-week history of forceful, unrelenting vomiting and moderate nausea that did not respond to proton pump inhibitors or antiemetics. Over the preceding 24 hours, he developed worsening headache and a decrease in his level of consciousness. On examination, his Glasgow Coma Score was 12, pupils were equally reactive, and there were no focal neurological deficits. An urgent head CT scan demonstrated obstructive hydrocephalus and a homogeneously enhancing, hyperdense lesion within the fourth ventricle. He underwent endoscopic third ventriculostomy with rapid recovery of consciousness. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal and cytology was negative for malignant cells. MRI of the brain and spine revealed a 20 × 25 × 30 mm strongly enhancing mass occupying the inferior half of the fourth ventricle, molding to the ventricular cavity and extending toward the foramina of Luschka and the obex, with no parenchymal invasion or drop metastases.
