The radiologist’s impression was that of an ependymoma or possibly a subependymoma.

A 52-year-old woman was referred to endocrinology in 2011 for a 2-month history of right-sided neck swelling, worsening dysphagia, and mild pain. Her past medical history was notable for excision of a dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans in the left inguinal–suprapubic region in 1998, with four local recurrences (2000, 2001, 2008, and 2009) treated surgically; she also received external radiotherapy (66 Gy) after the last excision.

On examination, there was a large, firm, mildly tender mass on the right side of the neck without fixation; the Pemberton sign was positive. Laboratory studies showed:
• TSH 0.363 mIU/L (0.32–5.0)  
• Free T4 14.6 pmol/L (9.0–19.0)  
• Anti-thyroglobulin antibody 1 U/mL (< 1)  
• Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody 1 U/mL (< 1)  
• Intact PTH 6 pmol/L (1.48–8.43)

Ultrasound of the thyroid revealed a right lobe volume of 50 mL and left lobe 7.3 mL; the entire right lobe was replaced by a hypo- to anechoic mass measuring approximately 6 × 4 × 6 cm, displacing the trachea 1 cm to the left, with no pathological lymphadenopathy. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the right lobe yielded a hemorrhagic background with isolated clusters of pleomorphic round and oval nuclei; it was classified as category IV/3, suspicious for primary or secondary malignancy.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and thorax confirmed a voluminous right thyroid mass and detected two pulmonary nodules consistent with metastases. MRI showed no lymphadenopathy. Laryngoscopy demonstrated freely mobile vocal cords.

A 27-month-old girl was evaluated for progressive right periorbital swelling of three weeks’ duration without preceding trauma. Two weeks earlier, she had been treated with ophthalmic ointment and eye drops without improvement, and the eyelid became erythematous. An outside pediatrician diagnosed periorbital cellulitis and prescribed oral cefaclor for two weeks, but the swelling and redness persisted. Her medical history was unremarkable, and immunizations were up to date.

On transfer, laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 0.59 mg/dL and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 57 mm/h; other test results were within normal limits. An orbital CT scan revealed a destructive lesion centered on the anterior wall of the right maxillary sinus, forming a large soft-tissue mass that protruded into the sinus; a small fluid-attenuated focus was noted in the anterior portion of the mass. On MRI, the lesion was isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images; within the cystic portion, a fluid-fluid level was identified. The mass demonstrated heterogeneous enhancement after contrast administration and invaded the ipsilateral inferior orbital wall and extraconal space. Adjacent soft-tissue edema and fat infiltration involved the right cheek and periorbital area. The maxillary alveolar processes and teeth were intact. Serial imaging over two weeks showed rapid enlargement of the mass.

A 30-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a lesion on the left posterior hard palate, present for 3 years and slowly enlarging. She was otherwise healthy, with no systemic disease, no smoking or alcohol use, and no family history of similar lesions. On examination, there was a 15 × 25 × 5 mm, firm, sessile, pink, smooth, nonulcerated nodule with well-defined borders near the left first and second molars, not crossing the midline. The lesion was nonfluctuant and asymptomatic. No lymphadenopathy was noted. Teeth mobility was absent, and adjacent teeth were vital. The remainder of the oral and head-and-neck examination was unremarkable.

Cone-beam CT showed a soft-tissue–density mass on the left posterior hard palate extending from the upper left second premolar to the third molar, without evidence of bony invasion. The clinical differential diagnosis included benign mesenchymal tumors (e.g., prior excised benign myxoid tumor, fibroma, fibromyxoma) and salivary gland neoplasms (e.g., pleomorphic adenoma). An excisional biopsy was performed, revealing a 30 × 20 × 5 mm firm specimen. Histologic sections demonstrated fibrous to myxoid connective tissue containing giant fibroblasts, numerous wavy spindle cells with elongated nuclei, scattered mast cells, and chronic inflammatory cells. Islands of muscle fibers, nerve bundles, minor salivary glands, adipose tissue, and reactive bone were present. The lesion was covered by nonkeratinized to parakeratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

A 69-year-old woman presented with chest distress and reduced exercise tolerance for one month. She had no significant past medical history. Laboratory tests showed elevated interleukin-6 (7.3 pg/mL; normal 0–6.4), lactate dehydrogenase (342 U/L; 120–250), high-sensitivity troponin I (556 pg/mL; 0–11.6), and brain natriuretic peptide (1,551 pg/mL; 0–100), with mild anemia (hemoglobin 105 g/L; red blood cell count 3.6×10^12/L). C-reactive protein, anti-streptolysin O, and rheumatoid factor were normal. The patient denied fever or upper respiratory symptoms. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed severe aortic regurgitation and a 9.8×6.6 mm irregular, oscillating, soft-textured echogenic mass on the left coronary leaflet of the aortic valve, along with severe mitral regurgitation, mild tricuspid regurgitation, and an ejection fraction of 47%. Contrast-enhanced CT angiography showed a 6 mm low-density area in the aortic root extending into the proximal ascending aorta. Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis of the aortic valve was suspected, and antibiotics were withheld. The patient received a 7-day course of cardiac and diuretic therapy to optimize function.

A 39-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a one-month history of progressive dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. Her past medical history included anxiety, depression, heavy cigarette and cannabinoid smoking, and one prior term pregnancy 16 years earlier. On examination, she was in respiratory distress, requiring 9 L/min of oxygen to maintain normal saturations. Lung auscultation was clear; there were two discrete masses in the right breast and tenderness in the upper abdomen.

A chest radiograph revealed multiple pulmonary opacities suggestive of metastases and a left pleural effusion. Contrast-enhanced CT showed extensive metastatic lesions in the lungs, liver, spleen, kidneys, pancreas, and subcutaneous tissues of the right chest wall, left flank, and breast, including a dominant 12-cm mass in the lingula amid marked emphysema. The uterus and adnexa appeared normal.

Breast ultrasound identified a 22×8 mm hematoma and a 12×11 mm vascular lesion, which was biopsied. Laboratory studies demonstrated microcytic anemia and a mildly elevated alanine aminotransferase; other routine tests were unremarkable. A urinary pregnancy test was performed and was positive, prompting measurement of tumor markers.

Histopathological examination of the breast lesion showed cohesive sheets of markedly pleomorphic cells with moderate eosinophilic and focally clear cytoplasm, scattered multinucleated giant cells, and extensive necrosis without a prominent biphasic pattern. Immunohistochemical staining revealed strong positivity for pancytokeratin (AE1/3, MNF116), CK7, CD10, and p63, with focal human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) expression; tumor cells were negative for CK20, CDX2, S-100, estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1), gross cystic disease fluid protein-1 (GCDFP-1), and placental alkaline phosphatase.

A 48-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of progressive headache, vomiting, vertigo, and gait instability. Neurologic examination revealed subtle bradypsychia; there were no focal motor or sensory deficits.  
Noncontrast CT of the head demonstrated a large right parietal extra-axial–appearing mass with internal calcifications and a subtle hyperostotic spicule on the inner table of the skull.  
Brain MRI revealed a lobulated right parietal mass with mild adjacent edema. On T1-weighted images, the lesion was hypointense; on T2-weighted images, it was predominantly hyperintense with punctate areas of low signal. A partial cerebrospinal fluid cleft separated the lesion from the cortex. Post-gadolinium T1-weighted images showed heterogeneous “honeycomb” enhancement. Dynamic susceptibility contrast perfusion imaging demonstrated strikingly low cerebral blood volume within the tumor. There was no diffusion restriction.  
MR spectroscopy did not reveal any specific biomarkers: there was no alanine peak, no elevated myo-inositol, and no high mobile lipid signal.

A 77-year-old man presented with a three-month history of left hip and buttock pain accompanied by left foot weakness. His medical history included esophageal adenocarcinoma and testicular seminoma treated with external-beam radiation therapy approximately 40 years earlier, and he had no clinical stigmata of neurofibromatosis type 1. MRI of the lumbar spine with and without gadolinium demonstrated a homogeneously enhancing, well-demarcated intradural extramedullary lesion at the L2–L3 level. MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine was unremarkable. Given the imaging appearance, a benign nerve sheath tumor was suspected, but because of his history of malignancy a metastatic lesion was also considered. A metastatic work-up revealed no evidence of additional lesions.

A 60-year-old Caucasian woman with no significant medical history presented with pharyngitis. On examination, an incidental murmur prompted transthoracic echocardiography, which revealed thrombus in the right atrium and inferior vena cava. She was started on anticoagulation. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed an 18.7 × 14.1 cm left renal mass with extension into the inferior vena cava and renal and splenic veins, with encasement of the small bowel and pancreas. Apart from a sore throat and weight loss, she denied other symptoms. Two weeks later, an open radical nephrectomy was attempted but was aborted due to extensive tumor fixation to surrounding organs. Biopsy demonstrated a highly cellular neoplasm with moderate nuclear pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, and two to three mitotic figures per ten high-power fields. Immunohistochemical staining was diffusely positive for synaptophysin, chromogranin, and GATA-3.

A 44-year-old Hispanic man presented with a 2-month history of worsening abdominal pain and jaundice. He had no significant past medical, family, or social history and denied exposure to vinyl chloride, arsenic, or thorium dioxide. On examination, he appeared icteric and had a distended, diffusely tender abdomen; there were no spider angiomata, palmar erythema, shifting dullness, hepatic bruit, caput medusae, or asterixis.

Laboratory studies revealed:
• WBC 13 400/mm3, hemoglobin 8.8 g/dL, MCV 99 fL, platelets 57 000/mm3  
• Alkaline phosphatase 118 IU/L, total protein 5.4 g/dL, albumin 2.7 g/dL  
• Total bilirubin 6.4 mg/dL (direct 3.1 mg/dL), AST 42 IU/L, ALT 72 IU/L  
• Prothrombin time 29.4 s (INR 2.88), PTT 40.7 s, fibrinogen < 60 mg/dL, d-dimer > 9.999 mg/dL  
Serologic tests for viral hepatitis and autoimmune liver disease were negative. Serum AFP, CA 19-9, and CEA were within normal limits.

Abdominal ultrasound showed multiple heterogeneous hepatic masses with peripheral echogenicity and hypoechoic centers; Doppler study showed hypervascularity. Multiphase CT and MRI demonstrated discrete, multifocal, isodense masses in all liver segments (largest 6.5 cm) with peripheral enhancement in the arterial phase and no enhancement or washout on portal venous and delayed phases—findings not typical of hepatocellular carcinoma or cholangiocarcinoma.

A 49-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a 3-month history of worsening dyspnea on exertion, cough, and sputum. He was a current smoker (2 packs/day for 20 years) and had been treated for presumed bronchial asthma with inhaled bronchodilators for the past 12 months without improvement. On examination, expiratory and inspiratory wheezes were heard over the right chest. There was no weight loss or cervical lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests were notable only for a slightly elevated neuron-specific enolase level of 18.09 ng/mL (normal 0–17.3 ng/mL). Pulmonary function testing showed a severe obstructive defect (FEV1 1.59 L [47% predicted], FVC 3.67 L [80% predicted], FEV1/FVC 43% predicted) with no bronchodilator response. A chest radiograph revealed a low-radiolucent round shadow in the lower trachea. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed a 1.5×1.3 cm homogeneous mass arising from the right lateral wall of the trachea just above the carina, nearly occluding the lumen, as well as a 0.5×0.4 cm nodular lesion in the posterior segment of the right upper lobe and multiple enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes (subcarinal, right hilar, right interlobar). Flexible bronchoscopy demonstrated a broad-based, richly vascular polypoid lesion arising from the right lateral tracheal wall 0.5 cm above the carina and nearly obstructing the right main bronchus. The possible differential diagnoses included benign and malignant tracheal tumors such as carcinoid and tracheal carcinoma with lung and lymph-node metastases. Flexible bronchoscopic biopsy was inconclusive, and surgical resection was planned because of the risk of airway obstruction and bleeding during endoscopic intervention given the tumor’s size and vascularity.

A 16-year-old female with no significant medical history presented with four months of dizziness, frequent vomiting, and weight loss. Four months after symptom onset, she developed right hearing loss and blurred vision, prompting referral. Neurological examination revealed right-dominant resting horizontal nystagmus, right facial nerve palsy, right hearing loss, and headaches triggered by head motion; there was no neck stiffness.

Noncontrast brain CT showed a 7×5 mm iso- to slightly hypodense nodule in the right frontal cortex containing a focal hyperattenuated region. Brain MRI demonstrated diffusely thickened, strongly enhancing leptomeninges over the bilateral cerebral and cerebellar hemispheres, with multiple contrast-enhanced nodules along the meningeal surfaces, including one in the right frontal lobe protruding into the parenchyma. That frontal lesion was heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted imaging, hypointense on T1-weighted imaging, and markedly hypointense on T2*-weighted imaging; diffusion-weighted imaging revealed heterogeneously restricted diffusion with an ADC of 0.9×10⁻³ mm²/s. Spinal MRI showed similarly thickened leptomeninges without intraparenchymal abnormalities. FDG-PET revealed a mean SUV of 3.51 for the frontal nodule—lower than that of normal cortex—and no other sites of abnormal uptake. Detailed blood tests showed no evidence of infectious or autoimmune disease.

A 32-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of progressive dull aching throat pain, a foreign body sensation in the left oropharynx, and gradual left facial asymmetry. She denied dysphagia or dyspnea. On oropharyngeal examination, there was a diffuse swelling occupying the left tonsillar fossa and deviation of the uvula to the right. Palpation of the neck revealed a non-tender, fixed mass in the left submandibular area.  

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed a 4.0 × 4.5 × 6.0 cm, well-defined, dumbbell-shaped mass in the left post-styloid parapharyngeal space, extending into the left prevertebral area. The mass demonstrated heterogeneous enhancement with internal cystic changes and no calcifications. It was separate from the left parotid gland and displaced the left internal carotid artery laterally; there was no adjacent bony erosion.  

MRI revealed that the mass was isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with multiple cystic areas. On contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images, the lesion showed homogeneous, strong enhancement.

A 65-year-old man presented with a one-year history of a dry cough. He had no other respiratory or systemic complaints. On examination, breath sounds were diminished over the right lower hemithorax with dullness to percussion. A chest radiograph showed a right lower-lobe opacity. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest revealed a 6-cm, well-circumscribed, heterogeneous soft-tissue mass along the right lateral basal pleura, connected to the chest wall at an obtuse angle, with no evident infiltration or invasion of adjacent structures.

A 25-year-old woman presented with an eight-month history of painless proptosis and redness of her right eye. Her best-corrected visual acuity was counting fingers at 2 m in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye. On external examination of the right eye, there was severe ptosis, marked proptosis with downward displacement of the globe, and limitation of extraocular movements in all gazes. Slit-lamp examination revealed eyelid erythema and edema, conjunctival injection, and chemosis. The left eye examination was unremarkable.

Orbital computed tomography showed a 5.2 × 2.5 cm homogeneous extraconal mass within the superior rectus–levator complex, causing globe indentation and optic nerve compression. Brain and orbital magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a hyperintense fusiform lesion occupying the superior rectus muscle throughout its length, sparing the origin and insertion, with no extension into the cranial fossa or paranasal sinuses. Systemic evaluation and imaging revealed no evidence of metastasis.

A 52-year-old woman with chronic hepatitis C infection presented with 4 months of right upper‐quadrant abdominal pain, fever, and weight loss. On examination, her temperature was 38.6 °C; she had splenomegaly and no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed normal blood counts, alanine aminotransferase 300 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 150 U/L, alpha‐fetoprotein 5 ng/mL, carcinoembryonic antigen 1.5 µg/L, and lactate dehydrogenase 400 U/L. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a dysmorphic liver with multiple cystic lesions and hypoechoic nodular lesions. Liver MRI showed a cirrhotic liver with portal hypertension, multiple nodular lesions that were isointense on T1-weighted images, of intermediate signal on T2-weighted images, with peripheral enhancement after gadolinium and restricted diffusion, and multiple noncommunicating hepatic cysts (hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2). Thoracoabdominopelvic CT scan demonstrated no lymphadenopathy, no splenomegaly, and no extrahepatic lesions. The radiologic differential diagnosis included atypical hypovascular hepatocellular carcinoma, hepatic metastases, and primary hepatic lymphoma.

A 48-year-old woman presented with six months of progressive lower abdominal and pelvic pain and intermittent constipation relieved by laxatives. She had a history of lateral internal sphincterotomy for anal fissure five years earlier but denied other gastrointestinal, urinary, or neurologic symptoms. On examination, she was hemodynamically stable with no remarkable findings. Laboratory tests, including hemoglobin, leukocyte and platelet counts, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, and serum tumor markers (CA 15-3, CEA, CA 125), were all within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed a 4 × 5 cm hypodense cystic lesion externally compressing the rectum in the presacral region. Pelvic MRI showed a 4 × 4 × 5 cm encapsulated, multiloculated cystic lesion posterior to the rectum without internal septations; it was hypo-intense on T2-weighted imaging, heterogeneously hyper-intense on T1-weighted imaging, and showed no significant post-contrast enhancement. A tiny T1‐ and T2-hypo-intense focus at the dome suggested calcification. The lesion’s main bulk exhibited true diffusion restriction on diffusion-weighted imaging and ADC mapping; small adjacent peripheral cysts were also noted, and the mass displaced the rectum laterally. Colonoscopy confirmed external compression of the rectal wall, and biopsies of the overlying mucosa were nondiagnostic.

A previously healthy 6-year-old boy presented with 7 days of left eyelid drooping, headache, left-sided hearing loss, and nasal blockage. On examination, visual acuity was 6/6 in the right eye and 6/18 in the left. The left eye had complete ptosis, a mid-dilated fixed pupil, absent corneal sensation, limitation of eye movements in all directions, left red–green color deficiency, and reduced contrast sensitivity; the right eye was normal. General examination was unremarkable. Routine blood tests, renal and liver function tests, urine analysis, and chest radiograph were normal. Pure-tone audiometry showed moderately severe mixed hearing loss in the left ear. A limited MRI of the brain and orbits revealed an ill-defined lesion centered in the petrous part of the left temporal bone with extension into the left cavernous sinus and reaching the left orbital apex.

A 44-year-old woman with an 18-year history of antisynthetase syndrome and rheumatoid arthritis overlap, complicated by 5 years of nonspecific interstitial pneumonitis (NSIP), presented with 2 weeks of progressively worsening dyspnea and cough. She had been diagnosed with polymyositis 20 years earlier by muscle biopsy and, at age 38, had developed exertional dyspnea; anti–Jo-1 antibodies were positive and chest CT and transbronchial biopsy had confirmed NSIP. Her regimen included tacrolimus and hydroxychloroquine. 

On arrival, temperature was 38.2°C, blood pressure 149/59 mm Hg, heart rate 103/min, respiratory rate 26/min, and oxygen saturation 79% on room air. She was in mild to moderate respiratory distress, with coarse bibasilar crackles. Chest radiography showed new diffuse bilateral patchy alveolar and interstitial opacities. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 24 500/mm3 (38% neutrophils, 54% lymphocytes), hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, platelets 268 000/mm3, blood urea nitrogen 26 mg/dL, creatinine 1.01 mg/dL, and potassium 5.0 mEq/L. 

Initial differential diagnoses included adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) from infection versus an acute exacerbation of ILD. She was admitted to the intensive care unit on high-flow nasal cannula and received empiric antimicrobials targeting health care–associated pathogens and influenza. Urine antigens for Streptococcus, Legionella, Histoplasma, and Blastomyces; sputum gram stain and culture; sputum fungal culture; respiratory influenza and viral NAATs; serum CMV NAAT; Pneumocystis jiroveci direct fluorescent antibody; and serum Aspergillus galactomannan antigen were all negative. 

On hospital day 2, chest CT revealed bilateral patchy consolidation and multiple enlarged axillary and mediastinal lymph nodes. On hospital day 3, her respiratory status worsened, and she was intubated. Bronchoscopy was unremarkable, and bronchoalveolar lavage for infectious studies was negative. On hospital day 5, video-assisted thoracoscopic biopsies were taken from the right middle and lower lobes.

A 40-year-old man presented with a painful nodule on the lower part of his right leg. He reported that the lesion had been stable in size and painless for 4 years but had enlarged and become tender over the past 6 months. There was no history of trauma or personal or family history of malignancy.

On examination, an irregular, firm, erythematous, mobile, tender mass measuring 3.5 × 2.3 × 1.7 cm was noted just above the lateral malleolus of the right leg. No popliteal or inguinal lymphadenopathy was present, and there were no other suspicious cutaneous lesions. Routine blood tests, including complete blood count, fasting blood sugar, liver and renal function tests, were within normal limits. Tests for hepatitis B surface antigen and HIV were negative.

The patient underwent a local excision. Grossly, there was a lobulated, tan-gray, firm mass partly covered by skin, measuring 3.5 × 2.3 × 1.7 cm. On light microscopy, the dermal tumor extended into the superficial subcutis and was composed of nests and fascicles of spindle-shaped to epithelioid cells with pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, and prominent nucleoli within a collagenous stroma. Mitotic figures, including atypical forms, measured 7–8 per 10 high-power fields. There was no intracytoplasmic melanin pigment, and the overlying epidermis showed no increase in basal melanocytes, junctional activity, or pagetoid spread.

Immunohistochemical staining showed strong positivity for vimentin and focal positivity for Melan-A and HMB-45. The tumor cells were negative for S-100 protein, pancytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, and CD31.

A 43-year-old man presented with a 6-cm × 3.5-cm painless swelling of the left cheek, causing facial asymmetry. The swelling extended from the corner of the mouth posteriorly to the mid-body of the mandible. Intraorally, the lesion involved the region from the mesial of tooth 37 to tooth 33, and tooth 35 was mobile, appearing to “float” within the lesion. On palpation, the mass was soft to firm, non-tender, and had smooth borders. A provisional clinical diagnosis of ameloblastoma was made. Panoramic radiograph showed a multilocular radiolucency with a soap-bubble appearance extending from the distal root of tooth 37 to tooth 41, with tooth displacement, mild root resorption, and erosion of the left mandibular body. CT imaging confirmed the multilocular radiolucency in the same region with perforation of the buccal and lingual cortical plates.

An 18-year-old man presented with a one-month history of discomfort in the right posterior gingiva. On examination, there was slight buccal and lingual expansion with redness over the region of teeth #29, #30, and #31; the overlying mucosa was intact, and there was no spontaneous pain. Periapical and panoramic radiographs revealed a 4–5 mm radiolucency at the apices of teeth #29 and #30 with loss of the lamina dura, widening of the periodontal ligament space, and mild rarefaction of the interdental alveolar bone. The patient denied dental trauma; there were no cracks or restorations on teeth #29 and #30. Pulp testing of these teeth elicited a normal response. Cone-beam computed tomography showed an ill-defined hypodense lesion with internal hyperdense foci, thinning of the buccal and lingual cortical plates, and alterations in trabecular bone associated with the roots of teeth #29 and #30. Based on the location and radiographic findings, a periapical abscess was initially suspected; however, the vital pulps and imaging characteristics also prompted consideration of intraosseous malignancies.

A 53-year-old man presented with an 18-month history of a painless, progressively enlarging nodule of the right shoulder and a new axillary lump. On examination, there was a 10-cm mass in the right deltoid region with overlying skin edema and involvement. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right shoulder showed a necrotic tumor in the lower posterior deltoid and triceps, extending into the axillary region with a suspicious lymph node. 

Microscopic examination of the deltoid lesion revealed normal epidermis overlying dense fibrocollagenous tissue with few perivascular inflammatory cells. The axillary specimen, initially presumed to be a lymph node, lacked lymphoid tissue and showed extensive necrosis; nests and cords of cells with small, round nuclei, dense chromatin, scant cytoplasm, and larger eosinophilic cells forming acinar and alveolar structures; occasional signet-ring–like and plasmacytoid cells; and areas of myxoid stroma containing stellate, myoepithelial-type cells. There was perineural and muscle infiltration, and scattered PAS-positive cells. In summary, the lesion was a biphasic tumor composed of epithelial and myoepithelial elements, raising the possibility of carcinoma or a malignant mixed tumor of the skin.

A 17-year-old male presented with a 4-year history of multiple asymptomatic skin lesions. He reported that the lesions began on his lower limbs and gradually spread to involve his face, trunk, and both upper and lower extremities. He had no relevant personal or family medical history.

On examination, there were numerous well-defined, soft to firm, pedunculated papulonodular lesions ranging up to 15 mm in diameter. The lesions were yellow-brown in color and nearly symmetrically distributed over the entire body, particularly the extensor surfaces of the joints. Examination of the mucous membranes, palms, and soles was unremarkable. A pigmented patch with increased hair growth was noted on his back. He also had a marked kyphosis.

Ophthalmologic assessment, abdominal ultrasonography, and chest radiography revealed no evidence of extracutaneous involvement.

The initial differential diagnoses included histiocytosis, neurofibromatosis, sarcoidosis, and xanthoma.

A 17-year-old student presented with 7 days of upper abdominal pain, loose stools, and occasional bilious vomiting. He had no past medical history. On examination, he was grossly pale, with a temperature of 100.0°F and a pulse of 107/min. The abdomen was mildly distended, and a visible mass was noted in the right hypochondrium; palpation revealed a tender 4×5 cm mass with localized rigidity. Bowel sounds were sluggish. Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin level of 4 g/dL and a leukocyte count of 11×10^9/L; HIV serology was negative. An erect abdominal radiograph demonstrated no air–fluid levels and no free intraperitoneal air. Abdominal ultrasonography and contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen were reported to be consistent with small-bowel intussusception and minimal pelvic fluid.

An 8-year-old Caucasian girl was referred to the Pediatric Ophthalmology Clinic for a 5-day history of a rapidly growing right conjunctival mass. Uncorrected visual acuity was 6/15 bilaterally; intraocular pressures and pupillary examination were normal. Right eye motility showed a –1 abduction deficit without significant proptosis. The right upper eyelid exhibited fullness with approximately 3 mm of blepharoptosis but no erythema or tenderness. On eyelid eversion, a 30 × 10 × 4 mm multilobulated, vascularised, papillomatous lesion arose from the superior conjunctival fornix and involved parts of the bulbar conjunctiva. The remainder of the anterior and posterior segment examination was unremarkable; the left eye was normal. Differential diagnoses based on the clinical findings included pyogenic granuloma, papilloma, lymphoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.

A 64-year-old woman was referred for elective surgery after routine screening detected stones in the intrahepatic bile ducts and gallbladder. She had no abdominal pain or jaundice. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory tests showed: leukocyte count 8230/µL; hemoglobin 15.7 g/dL; total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL; direct bilirubin 0.2 mg/dL; aspartate aminotransferase 19 IU/L; alanine aminotransferase 14 IU/L; lactate dehydrogenase 298 IU/L; alkaline phosphatase 57 IU/L; γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 51 IU/L. Serum CEA and CA 19-9 were within normal limits.  
Abdominal CT revealed mildly dilated intrahepatic ducts containing stones and numerous small gallbladder stones; the distal common bile duct and pancreas appeared normal. ERCP demonstrated a threadlike stricture at the proximal common bile duct with upstream dilation and stones; the gallbladder was filled with stones, and the cystic duct inserted aberrantly into the right intrahepatic duct.  
Surgery was planned because the intrahepatic stones were believed to be secondary to the biliary stricture, and it was difficult to differentiate between a malignant or benign stricture.

A 5-year-old boy presents with a 6-month history of intermittent right knee pain without trauma, fever, or weight loss. On examination, there is tenderness to palpation over the proximal right tibia without swelling, erythema, warmth, or restriction of motion. Plain radiographs show a well-circumscribed metaphyseal lesion of the proximal tibia that is lytic with a thin sclerotic rim, has a mixed lytic–blastic matrix, and lacks periosteal reaction or physeal involvement. CT confirms a cystic, well-demarcated metaphyseal lesion with sclerotic margins and no periosteal reaction or physeal breach. MRI reveals a multilocular cystic lesion in the proximal tibial metaphysis with well-defined margins, surrounding marrow edema, fluid–fluid levels, and heterogeneous contrast enhancement.

A 7-year, 11-month-old boy was evaluated for intractable seizures. He had gelastic seizures beginning in the neonatal period, and epilepsy was diagnosed by EEG at 3 years, 8 months. On admission, his height was 102.4 cm (+0.71 SD), and his weight was 14.8 kg (–0.35 SD). Brain MRI showed a sessile, isointense mass measuring 1.2 × 1.5 cm arising from the tuber cinereum, involving the hypothalamus, and distorting the third ventricle. He was treated with valproic acid and clonazepam without seizure control, and at 4 years, 11 months underwent γ-knife therapy, which ceased drop attacks but not gelastic seizures. Laboratory studies demonstrated a serum testosterone level of 149.0 ng/dl (normal <5.0), and an LH-releasing-hormone stimulation test showed a pubertal pattern (LH rising from 3.7 to 25.0 mIU/ml). At 6 years, 3 months of age, testicular volume was 5 ml, penile Tanner stage II, and bone age was 8 years.

A 61-year-old man presented with a slowly enlarging exophytic mass on the skin of his left upper lip that he first noticed 4 years earlier. The lesion measured about 1 cm, was well circumscribed, firm, and rubbery on palpation, and was not visible from the intraoral mucosa. Lip movement was normal, and there was no associated pain, discharge, ulceration, or history of trauma or dental procedures. The patient had no significant medical history and took no regular medications.

A preoperative computed tomography scan of the head revealed a 1.3 cm protruding mass in the subcutaneous tissue of the left upper lip skin that abutted but did not involve the orbicularis oris muscle or the mucosal surface. No cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. The initial clinical impression was an inclusion cyst, and surgical excision via a skin incision was planned for definitive diagnosis.

A 62-year-old man presented with a two-year history of a slowly enlarging swelling of the lateral wall of his left orbit. The mass had a hard consistency, was slightly painful on palpation, and was associated with mild left proptosis. 

Magnetic resonance imaging showed a large intradiploic lesion involving the lateral orbital wall and greater wing of the sphenoid. On T2-weighted sequences, the lesion was hyperintense, with a non-homogeneous, relatively hypointense round component. On FLAIR sequences the lesion was hypointense. After intravenous contrast, the round component demonstrated a mildly non-homogeneous increase in signal intensity.

Computed tomography of the skull revealed a 23 × 32 mm osteolytic lesion in the same region. Most of the lesion appeared fluid-filled, while a solid portion measuring 8 × 9 mm displayed heterogeneous contrast enhancement.

A 46-year-old woman with a history of generalized tonic–clonic seizures since 1999, managed with carbamazepine and topiramate, was initially diagnosed empirically with neurocysticercosis and treated with albendazole. In 2012 she developed a 2-minute left hemi-body clonic seizure. CT of the brain, chest, abdomen, and pelvis and MRI of the brain revealed multiple lesions in her brain and lungs; she declined biopsy and was lost to follow-up.  
In 2018 she presented with one month of progressive bilateral upper and lower limb weakness, difficulty with activities of daily living, rapid deterioration of vision in her left eye, confusion, and bed bound status. On examination she was disoriented, dysarthric, and had left retinal detachment. Muscle strength was 0/5 on the left and 2/5 on the right.  
Brain CT and MRI demonstrated multiple intra-axial supratentorial and infratentorial lesions of variable size, some with a miliary pattern; extra-axial lesions involved the sellar–suprasellar region and the left globe. The lesions were hemorrhagic, appearing as blooming artifacts on gradient-echo MRI, and resembled metastatic melanoma, metastatic choriocarcinoma, familial cavernous malformations, or amyloid angiopathy.  
Fluorodeoxyglucose-PET CT showed metastases in bilateral lungs, mediastinal lymph nodes, liver, and adrenal glands.

A 70-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of bilateral eyelid drooping, double vision, and eye watering. Initially, eye watering was sudden in onset, progressive, worsened with eyelid rubbing, and improved with cold-water eye washes. Blurring of vision with diplopia developed in the right eye, followed 8 days later by sudden, progressive right-eyelid drooping, reaching complete ptosis within 10 days. After six weeks, blurring and drooping occurred in the left eye, accompanied by periorbital edema. He also noted breathlessness on walking a few steps. He had no history of hypertension, diabetes, or other systemic illness. On examination, there was complete bilateral ptosis, diplopia, and restricted extraocular movements. Bulbar muscle fatigability was demonstrated on the SLURP test. Application of an ice pack to the eyelids produced a 3 mm improvement within 5 minutes, indicating a positive ice pack test. Generalized examination revealed areflexia. A chest x-ray showed a well-defined, lobulated radio-opaque lesion in the right hemithorax adjacent to the mediastinum. High-resolution CT of the thorax revealed a well-defined, round to oval soft-tissue density lesion in the anterior mediastinum—predominantly on the right—partially obliterating the retrosternal space and compressing the lateral border of the right atrium, suggesting a thymic mass.

A 40-year-old man with a 20-year history of a left orbital mass presented with a one-month history of persistent headache. On examination, he was alert, had left exophthalmos and blurred vision, and had no motor or sensory deficits. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, electrolytes, and biochemistry, were within normal limits.

Pre- and post-contrast CT of the head revealed a 76 × 60 × 57 mm mass originating in the left maxillary sinus with extension into the ethmoid and frontal sinuses. The lesion had a thick capsule, multiple internal “ground-glass” nodules, a central fluid-density area, and no post-contrast enhancement. There was nasal septal deviation, compression of the left frontal bone, and 5 mm of midline displacement, but no evidence of bone invasion.

On MRI, the central region was homogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted and FLAIR images, without diffusion restriction, and contained multiple septa. The peripheral cortex was isointense to hypointense on T1-weighted and hypointense on T2-weighted and T2* sequences. Post-contrast sequences showed vivid septal and ring enhancement.

A 50-year-old Indian man presented with headache and blurred vision in his right eye for three months. He denied seizures, vomiting, or dizziness but reported an occasional dry cough for the past four to five months.

Ocular examination revealed best corrected visual acuity of counting fingers at one foot in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Slit-lamp examination, pupil size and reactions, ocular movements, and intraocular pressures were all normal. 

On systemic examination, chest movements were bilaterally symmetrical. Vesicular breath sounds were decreased on the right side from the first to fourth intercostal spaces, with decreased vocal fremitus and resonance; no added sounds or palpable lymphadenopathy were noted.

Fundus examination of the right eye showed an ill-defined, yellow-white elevated choroidal lesion three to four times the disc diameter in size, located superotemporally to the optic disc; the left fundus was normal. Fluorescein angiography of the right eye demonstrated late-phase hyperfluorescence over the surface of the lesion with subretinal fluid. B-scan ultrasound of the right eye revealed a flat-surfaced, elevated choroidal mass with moderate internal reflectivity.

Routine systemic investigations, including complete blood count, platelet count, coagulation studies, urinalysis, serum electrolytes, hepatic and renal biochemistry, carcinoembryonic antigen, prostate-specific antigen, and serum acid phosphatase, were all within normal limits. Bone scan and upper and lower gastrointestinal series were unremarkable. Chest radiography showed a homogeneous right hilar opacity. Mantoux testing and tuberculosis serologies (IgM and IgG) were negative.

A 72-year-old man was referred for evaluation of chronic anemia and leukopenia. Over the past 3 years, his hemoglobin declined from an average of 13.6 g/dL to 12.1 g/dL (reference, 13.5–16.0 g/dL), and his white-cell count decreased to 3.3×10^3/µL (reference, 3.5–11.0×10^3/µL). One year earlier, he began to experience intermittent confusion and memory loss. 

Laboratory studies showed a 24-hour urine protein excretion of 810 mg (reference, 42–225 mg) and normal blood urea nitrogen and creatinine levels. Serum protein electrophoresis demonstrated a hypogammaglobulinemic pattern with a monoclonal gamma paraprotein of 0.83 g/dL. Skeletal radiographs of the skull, spine, humeri, and femora revealed no lytic lesions.

Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy showed a normocellular marrow with trilineage hematopoiesis, a mildly decreased myeloid and erythroid series, and 27% plasma cells (normal ≤3%). A subset of plasma cells contained single or multiple nonbirefringent, translucent rhomboid intracytoplasmic crystals, and scattered extracellular rhomboid crystals were noted. Flow cytometric analysis identified a monotypic, cytoplasmic λ-light-chain–restricted CD38+, CD138+ plasma cell population with dim CD45+, CD56+, and CD117+ expression. A Congo red stain for amyloid deposition was negative.

A 63-year-old Caucasian man with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and hypertension was referred for evaluation of a recurrent mass in the left inguinal region. He had undergone two prior surgical resections of left groin masses with clear margins and no postoperative adjuvant therapy. On examination, there was an oval 9 × 11 cm lobulated, firm, fixed, and nontender mass in the left inguinal area without overlying skin changes. Laboratory studies—including complete blood count, renal, bone, hepatic, and coagulation profiles, as well as tumor markers (CEA, AFP, and CA 12–5)—were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis revealed a large multilobulated heterogeneous mass in the left groin compressing and inseparable from the left common femoral vein and ventral adductor muscles; associated findings included local lymphadenopathy, multiple small subcutaneous nodules, and an enlarged left external iliac lymph node measuring 1 × 1.5 cm. PET imaging demonstrated a hypermetabolic, heterogeneous, lobulated lesion in the left groin measuring approximately 9.6 × 9 cm, with a few adjacent FDG-avid nodal lesions suggestive of regional metastatic involvement.

A 38-year-old woman presented with a one-day history of acute epigastric pain without nausea or vomiting. She had a history of non–insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus diagnosed 18 months earlier. On examination, she was overweight and had epigastric tenderness without a palpable mass. Routine hematologic and biochemical tests, including serum tumor markers, were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a 5 × 3 cm partially cystic mass in the distal pancreas, raising the possibility of a cystic neoplasm. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography confirmed a roughly 2 cm lesion in the pancreatic body. Dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI then showed a 4 cm predominantly cystic lesion in the pancreatic body “suggestive of a mucinous cyst adenocarcinoma.” No liver or other abdominal metastases were detected on imaging.

A 35-year-old woman presented with persistent, moderate right upper-quadrant abdominal pain of several months’ duration without nausea, vomiting, or changes in bowel habits. She had no significant medical or family history of adrenal disease. On examination, she was well-nourished and in no acute distress; abdominal palpation elicited mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant without palpable masses or peritoneal signs, and there was no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy.

A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a homogeneous 4 cm mass in the right adrenal gland. The precontrast attenuation was 1 Hounsfield unit, with an absolute contrast washout of 60%. Review of a CT scan obtained 6 years earlier showed the same lesion measuring 1.5 cm. Biochemical evaluation for adrenal hormone excess was unremarkable: morning cortisol after 1 mg dexamethasone suppression, 1.0 mcg/dL; serum aldosterone, 1.8 ng/dL; plasma renin activity, 1.363 ng/mL/h; serum metanephrines, < 10 pg/mL; serum normetanephrines, 46.6 pg/mL. Given the patient’s symptoms and interval growth of the lesion, she was referred for surgical resection.

A 36-year-old white man presented with a one-week history of a painless mass in his right axilla. He had a history of intravenous drug use (ceased 1 year earlier) and chronic hepatitis C infection. On examination, there was a single enlarged lymph node group in the right axilla; no other lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen showed no additional lymphadenopathy or other abnormalities. Initial differential diagnoses included cat-scratch disease, bacterial lymphadenitis, viral infections (Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, HIV), and lymphoproliferative disorders. Serological tests for Bartonella henselae IgG and IgM were negative. Viral serology was positive for hepatitis C but negative for HIV and herpesviruses.

A 78-year-old man was undergoing routine transthoracic echocardiography for monitoring of an ascending aortic dilation when a mass on the mitral valve was incidentally detected. His medical history was notable for ascending aortic dilation (45 mm), tricuspid aortic valve, nonobstructive coronary artery disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, stage 3A chronic kidney disease, secondary polycythemia, obstructive sleep apnea, benign prostatic hyperplasia, gout, and prior sarcoidosis. Medications included metoprolol, lisinopril, chlorthalidone, aspirin, ezetimibe-simvastatin, fish oil, allopurinol, albuterol as needed, and weekly testosterone injections. He was asymptomatic and in sinus rhythm on electrocardiography. 

Transthoracic echocardiography showed a mobile mass on the atrial surface of the anterior mitral leaflet, measuring 0.5 cm × 0.6 cm, with trivial mitral regurgitation. The ascending aortic dilation measured 46 mm (stable), the aortic valve was sclerotic without stenosis or regurgitation, and the left ventricular ejection fraction was 62%. 

Transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a 0.5 cm × 0.5 cm homogeneous, mobile mass attached by a stalk to the atrial side of the medial aspect of the A2 segment of the anterior mitral leaflet.

A 37-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of epigastric pain and a 45-pound weight loss. She denied nausea, vomiting, changes in bowel habits, melena, or hematemesis. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. On examination, she had cutaneous pallor and mild epigastric tenderness without a palpable abdominal mass. Laboratory studies were notable only for a normocytic, normochromic anemia (hemoglobin, 7.7 g/dL); other blood tests including tumor markers were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography showed cholelithiasis and a 6.8 × 4.8 × 7.3 cm lesion adjacent to the pancreas without internal calcifications, communication with the pancreatic duct, or Doppler flow. Contrast-enhanced CT imaging demonstrated that the lesion arose from the posterior wall of the stomach. Upper endoscopy revealed a submucosal, broad-based, protruding tumor approximately 7.5 cm in diameter, located in the posterior wall of the lower gastric body, resembling a gastrointestinal stromal tumor.

A 70-year-old man with extensive nicotine use and a remote history of laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma (7 years prior) and bladder urothelial carcinoma (10 years prior) underwent dual-chamber pacemaker implantation for sick sinus syndrome 9 months ago. Postoperative checks on days 1, 2, and at 3 months showed normal pacemaker function and a clinically unremarkable pocket. Three weeks before presentation, he tested positive for COVID-19 infection, but his fatigue, dyspnea, and cough persisted and worsened rather than improving. At a routine cardiology visit 9 months after implantation, he reported a new, painless but bothersome swelling over the pacemaker site. On examination, his blood pressure and heart rate were normal, and there were no signs of cardiac decompensation or cachexia. Chest ultrasound revealed a soft tissue mass with increased vascularity surrounding the device. CT imaging confirmed a soft-tissue mass around the pacemaker pocket, and haematoma or infection was excluded.

A 62-year-old African American man with hypertension presented with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. His abdomen was soft, distended, and tender in the epigastrium. Initial complete blood count, urinalysis, and serum lipase were within normal limits. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed a heterogeneous exophytic lobulated solid mass measuring 7.7 × 7.2 × 6.5 cm in the head/uncinate process of the pancreas, with mild pancreatic ductal dilatation and an adjacent eccentric nodal mass. A pancreatic protocol CT performed two days later demonstrated occlusion of the superior mesenteric vein and involvement of the superior mesenteric artery and main portal vein to less than 180°. The lesion was highly vascular, extended into the adjacent duodenum, and was associated with a 1.5-cm peritoneal nodule and isolated distended distal small-bowel loops.

A 50-year-old man with a 25-year history of xeroderma pigmentosum and multiple prior excisions of basal and squamous cell carcinomas on sun-exposed skin presented with a slowly progressive nasal lesion of 2 years’ duration. He noted no neurologic or ophthalmologic symptoms. On examination, there was a 1.6 × 1.3 cm ulcerative, erythematous, non-bleeding plaque on the right nasal ala. A full-thickness excisional biopsy was performed. Grossly, the specimen was hemorrhagic and necrotic. Microscopically, the dermis showed numerous irregularly shaped anastomosing vascular channels with a highly infiltrative, poorly demarcated architecture. The channels were lined by plump, hyperchromatic, pleomorphic endothelial cells with multilayering and increased mitotic activity. Dissecting collagen bundles were noted, and there were frequent intratumoral foamy cells amidst mild stromal lymphocytic aggregates.

A 15-year-old boy presented with a 6-month history of a slowly enlarging, firm nodule within the glans penis. He was asymptomatic and voided normally. There was no history of trauma or systemic disease. On examination, there was a well-circumscribed, firm, whitish, painless mass approximately 1 cm in diameter in the glans; the overlying skin was normal and there was no inguinal lymphadenopathy. Tanner stage was III.  
Penile Doppler ultrasonography revealed a hypoechogenic, hypoperfused, poorly defined area within the glans. MRI of the penis showed a single hyperintense mass in the glans without involvement of the corpora cavernosa.  
An excisional biopsy was performed under general anesthesia. The lesion was not clearly demarcated and lay close to the urethra; the mass was removed under magnification and the defect closed primarily.  
Grossly, the specimen measured 10 × 8 × 5 mm, was pale, light red on the cut surface, and solid. Histologic examination showed a complex, multinodular intravascular proliferation of uniform, elongated spindle cells without hyperchromasia, pleomorphism, mitotic figures, or necrosis. Immunohistochemical studies revealed strong intralesional positivity for alpha-smooth muscle actin, low proliferative activity (Ki-67 < 1%), negativity for desmin in the tumor cells (with desmin positivity in preexisting vessel walls), and no reactivity for S-100 protein, CD34, or ERG.

An 8-year-old previously healthy boy presented with new-onset spells characterized by facial grimacing with whimpering (a mixture of laughing and crying), pupillary dilation, and facial and upper-body flushing. Episodes lasted 5–15 seconds, were followed by a brief period of confusion with uncoordinated running around the room, and resolved to baseline within 2 minutes. He had no recollection of the events. The frequency of spells had increased over the preceding week. He also reported frontal headaches and urinary incontinence. 

On examination, he was mildly encephalopathic; the remainder of the neurologic examination was normal. Video EEG monitoring captured two seizures. Ictal onset for one seizure appeared to be from the right anterior temporal/inferior frontal and mid-temporal regions (F8, T8), and the other from the right anterior temporal/inferior frontal region (F8). Interictal EEG showed predominantly right frontotemporal spikes and waves (F4, F8), less frequent bifrontal spike-and-wave discharges, and rare left frontal sharp waves. Levetiracetam was started, with cessation of clinical seizures. 

MRI of the brain demonstrated a tumor in the anteroventral portion of the right temporal pole with surrounding edema extending to the anterior margin of the fusiform gyrus.

A 75‐year‐old woman presented with long‐standing right‐sided nasal obstruction, dependent mouth breathing, clear rhinorrhea, congestion, and hyposmia unresponsive to intranasal steroids and nasal irrigations. Her history was significant for endoscopic sinus surgery more than 20 years earlier, ambulatory cauterization for nasal polyposis, and nonmelanotic skin cancers of the nose treated with radiation. On examination, there was a fleshy intranasal lesion on the right side. Computed tomography of the sinuses showed complete opacification of the right maxillary sinus, obstruction of the right ostiomeatal complex, and soft‐tissue density within the right nasal passage. An initial biopsy of a mass originating in the right inferior meatus revealed multiple polypoid fragments lined by respiratory‐type epithelium with edematous stroma and mild chronic inflammation. There was invagination of the surface epithelium into the stroma, forming nested aggregates of bland glandular and mucinous cells with focally benign squamous epithelium, and this was interpreted as a benign inverted papilloma. Given her diagnosis of inverted papilloma and chronic rhinosinusitis, she underwent right partial inferior turbinectomy, an extended maxillary antrostomy, and stripping of maxillary mucosa. Intraoperative and postoperative pathology again showed inverted papilloma.

A 21-year-old woman was referred with two gingival enlargements of 2 months’ duration in the left maxilla: one between teeth #21 and #22 on the buccal interdental gingiva (Site A) and one on the palatal aspect between teeth #22 and #23 (Site B). Her dental history included frequent oral ulceration, burning sensations, and erythematous gingiva. Medical history was significant for asthma managed with medication. Hematological studies showed lymphocytopenia. On intraoral examination, both lesions were approximately 5 × 5 mm, soft, non-tender, mulberry-shaped, reddish, and pebbly in surface texture, with bleeding on probing and pseudopocket formation but no ulceration. Periapical radiographs revealed no significant bone changes. A provisional diagnosis of inflammatory gingival enlargement was made, and the differential diagnosis included pyogenic granuloma, plasma cell gingivitis, hemangioma, and fibroma.

A 46-year-old woman underwent routine abdominal sonography, which incidentally revealed a mass adjacent to the right kidney. She was asymptomatic except for one month of night sweats; she denied weight loss, fever, urinary symptoms, or feebleness. Her medical history included 10 pack-years of smoking, irritable bowel syndrome with mild abdominal pain, and excision of a right breast fibroadenoma five years earlier. Physical examination and routine laboratory tests were unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a well-defined, highly vascularized right renal mass measuring 45 × 65 × 102 mm, displacing the kidney laterally and abutting the renal pelvis. CT angiography in the arterial phase revealed extensive tumor vascularization with feeding and draining vessels and arteriovenous shunting. MRI confirmed a hypervascular renal lesion.

The patient underwent an open retroperitonealectomy with en bloc resection of the right kidney. Grossly, the specimen measured 15 × 12 × 6 cm and weighed 468 g. The kidney was almost entirely replaced by a tan-grey, soft tumor with multiple necrotic foci; the perirenal fat was uninvolved, and surgical margins were clear.

Histologic examination showed a highly cellular neoplasm composed of uniform small round cells with round to oval nuclei, very small nucleoli, “smoky” chromatin, slightly irregular nuclear membranes, and scant PAS-positive cytoplasm. Numerous mitotic figures, scattered apoptotic cells, and geographic areas of necrosis were present.

A 36-year-old woman noted a progressively enlarging, painful swelling in the region of her right parotid gland over 4 months. In March 2018, she underwent a superficial parotidectomy with preservation of the facial nerve. Histopathological examination showed a plasmacytoid myoepithelioma. 

In October 2018, she developed an asymmetric, hyperpigmented macular lesion on her right frontal scalp that bled spontaneously. Excisional biopsy revealed a nodular melanoma, non-ulcerated, with a Breslow thickness of 2.1 mm and no lymphovascular or perineural invasion.

Staging with ^18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated right cervical lymphadenopathy at levels IIA and IIB, the largest node measuring 25 × 15 mm. Given these findings, a total parotidectomy with modified radical neck dissection was planned for presumed recurrent plasmacytoid myoepithelioma.

A 76-year-old man with a history of COPD and active smoking presented with a 20-day history of rapidly worsening dyspnea and severe cough, associated with dysphagia and cervical pain. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (19.27 K/µL), an elevated D-dimer level (2994 µg/L), and otherwise normal chemistries; tumor markers were within normal limits. Chest radiography demonstrated an imprint on the right side of the trachea. Thyroid ultrasound revealed a large, heterogeneous gland with a 4.76 × 4.01 cm calcified mass in the right upper pole, showing high vascular perfusion. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and thorax showed a heterogeneous, irregularly bordered lesion extending from the sternoclavicular joints to the upper poles of the thyroid, surrounding the trachea anterolaterally (displacing it to the left) and displacing the right common carotid artery, without lymphadenopathy. Bronchoscopy revealed a fracture of the first tracheal ring but no tumor invasion; bronchial lavage cytology was negative. Due to acute respiratory failure, he was intubated and taken for emergency surgery via a collar incision. A whitish, scleroelastic tumor with moderately regular borders was found adherent to the superior pole of the right thyroid lobe, the sheath of the right common carotid artery, and the anterolateral trachea. En bloc resection with total thyroidectomy and regional lymph node dissection was performed. Frozen section of the thyroid mass showed malignant squamous features with negative margins. Final histology revealed a nonencapsulated, irregularly lobulated tumor with broad fibrous septa, lymphoplasmacytic and eosinophilic infiltration, and neoplastic cells in nests with focal keratinization. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for p63, CD117, CKH, CD5, and CD3 (in the lymphoid component) and negative for thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF1).

A 35-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of progressive swelling of the left maxilla and a 4-month history of swelling of the left mandible. She noted paraesthesia of the left lower lip and chin and left nasal obstruction. On examination, the maxillary swelling was firm to hard, non-tender, measured approximately 7×6 cm, extended from the infraorbital margin to the left lip commissure, obliterated the nasolabial fold, and caused nasal obstruction; the overlying skin was intact. Intraorally, the lesion involved the entire left buccal vestibule with mobility of the involved teeth. The mandibular swelling measured 4×3 cm, was firm to hard, non-tender, and associated with tooth mobility. There was no family history of similar lesions, facial nerve involvement, or cervical lymphadenopathy. CT of the face revealed an expansile lytic mass in the left maxilla (39×37×37 mm) with an exophytic component into the cheek, constricting the posterior nasal cavity, and a similar expansile lytic mass in the left mandibular dental arch (37×35×35 mm). Three-dimensional reconstruction confirmed an osteolytic defect of the left maxilla extending into the nasal cavity and upper dental arch, with a corresponding defect in the left mandibular arch. Orthopantomogram and occlusal radiographs showed multiple poorly defined radiolucent areas in the left maxilla and mandible without root resorption. Serum calcium and parathyroid hormone levels were within normal limits.

A 7-year-old boy was brought with a 6-month history of a swelling in the lower right anterior jaw. On intraoral examination, there was a non-tender, hard mass on the alveolar ridge distal to the right mandibular lateral incisor, with buccal cortical expansion and absence of the right deciduous canine. A panoramic radiograph showed a well-demarcated, radiopaque lesion with the density of a tooth, located distal to the right mandibular lateral incisor, mesial to the right first deciduous molar, and coronal to an impacted deciduous canine, surrounded by a thin radiolucent rim.

A 9-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of a fleshy mass on the superotemporal aspect of her left bulbar conjunctiva. Her mother noted that the eye was sometimes “puffy” on awakening, and on lifting the upper lid she saw the mass. On examination, there was a moderate epibulbar lesion without hairs or inflammation. Vision was 6/4 bilaterally, pupils were normal, ocular alignment and motility were full, and there was no facial asymmetry or microsomia. An orbital MRI showed a high fat signal on T1-weighted images in the superotemporal bulbar region, consistent with a suspected epibulbar dermolipoma, with no posterior orbital extension. The lesion was managed conservatively. 

Two years later, the patient re-presented because the mass appeared larger. Vision remained 6/4 bilaterally, and the lesion now had a small area of conjunctival keratinization and a minimal symblepharon at the lateral canthus. A decision was made to perform surgical debulking under general anesthesia. Only the keratinized surface epithelium was excised, preserving all non-keratinized conjunctiva. The excised specimen was macroscopically consistent with a typical epibulbar dermolipoma.

A 12-year-old Brazilian girl with no systemic illnesses presented with an 8-month history of a painless, slowly enlarging swelling of the lower right face. On extraoral examination, there was a unilateral expansion of the body and angle of the right mandible. Intraorally, the swelling was associated with the lower right third molar region. Panoramic radiography showed a well-defined unilocular radiolucent lesion extending from the mandibular body to the right ascending ramus, displacing the second molar toward the mandibular base and the third molar into the ramus. CT imaging demonstrated buccal and lingual cortical expansion with areas of fenestration. Needle aspiration was negative for vascular contents. An incisional biopsy was performed, and the specimen was sent for histopathologic evaluation. Based on the clinical and radiographic features, two diagnoses were considered: unicystic ameloblastoma or dentigerous cyst.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 15-year history of a painless swelling in the left anterior maxilla. Fifteen years earlier, she sustained trauma to this area, resulting in loss of the upper left anterior teeth and subsequent bridge restoration in that region. On intraoral examination, a firm, non-tender lesion was noted on the left anterior maxillary ridge.

A cone-beam CT scan of the maxilla (9 × 14 cm FOV) was obtained. On the panoramic view, teeth 18, 21, 22, and 28 were missing. Tooth 12 demonstrated a radiopaque crown filling extending to the pulp and widened periodontal ligament space apically. Tooth 11 had undergone root-canal treatment. A radiopaque crown-and-bridge unit spanned teeth 11–23. Adjacent to this, in the left anterior maxilla (region 21–23), there was an ovoid radiolucent lesion containing internal radiopaque septa; its borders were partially well-defined and partially ill-defined with rough, destructive cortical bone edges.

Coronal reformatted images showed a mixed radiolucent–radiopaque lesion measuring approximately 21 × 17 × 18 mm in the edentulous ridge of teeth 21–22, mesial to tooth 23. Its borders were partially well-defined and partially ill-defined with rough, partially destroyed bone margins. Internally, it appeared semi-multilocular with septations and had a density of 129.8–252.9 gray values (consistent with fluid or soft tissue). The labial cortical plate was expanded and partially disrupted, while the palatal plate remained intact.

Sagittal and axial views revealed that the lesion contacted the apex of tooth 23, causing distal displacement without root resorption, and abutted the nasopalatine canal without wall discontinuity. It lay inferior to the nasal cavity and maxillary sinus, neither of which was involved.

A 51-year-old woman presented with abdominal pain. Physical examination was unremarkable.  
Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 1.6 cm hyperechoic mass at the lower pole of the left kidney. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 1.7 × 1.4 × 1.7 cm hypodense, enhancing, mainly endophytic lesion in the left lower pole without perinephric fat invasion or renal vein involvement; the RENAL nephrometry score was 7.  
She underwent robotic-assisted laparoscopic left partial nephrectomy with selective clamping of the lower-pole artery; the warm ischemic time was 25 minutes without complication.  
Gross examination revealed a 2.2 × 2.0 × 1.5 cm pinkish nodule weighing 3.8 g, with no necrosis.  
Microscopically, the tumor was partly covered by a thin fibrous capsule and rim of renal tissue. It consisted of tightly packed tubules and occasional elongated tubular structures set in a myxoid stroma with extracellular mucin highlighted by Alcian Blue. Tumor cells ranged from cuboidal cells with pale eosinophilic cytoplasm to bland spindle cells; mitotic figures and necrosis were absent.  
Immunohistochemical studies showed positivity for EMA, AMACR, CK7, PAX8, and CD56; the MIB-1 proliferation index was less than 1%.

A 77-year-old African-American man presented with a two-month history of a pruritic rash on his left lower abdomen that had not improved with topical corticosteroids. He noted only a mild headache. His medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension; family history was noncontributory. On examination, there was a 7.5 × 8 cm round, well-demarcated, erythematous, mildly lichenified plaque with central excoriation. Within the plaque was a firm 5–6 mm yellowish superficial nodule and several firm 1–2 mm papules along its superior border. A potassium hydroxide preparation was negative for fungal hyphae or spores. A punch biopsy showed nuclear atypia, numerous mitotic figures, and areas of tumor necrosis.

A 52-year-old man presented after a fall with left-sided chest and upper abdominal pain. His history included hypertension and atrial fibrillation treated with ramipril, amlodipine, and apixaban. A chest radiograph showed a fracture of the seventh rib. Because of anticoagulation, a CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was performed and revealed incidental bilateral adrenal masses measuring 6 cm on the left and 5 cm on the right with attenuation of 50 Hounsfield units on portal venous images, and mild splenomegaly (14.5 cm).  
In the endocrine clinic he reported 6 years of tiredness, palpitations, and weight gain. His blood pressure was 116/90 mm Hg, heart rate 97 beats/min, and BMI 32 kg/m2. Examination was normal with no lymphadenopathy or Cushingoid features.  
Baseline adrenal studies were normal, including plasma metanephrines (normetanephrine 830 pmol/L; metanephrine <100 pmol/L), aldosterone 270 pmol/L, random cortisol 230 nmol/L, and ACTH 29.4 ng/L. An overnight dexamethasone suppression test with 1 mg at 11 pm yielded an 8 am cortisol <28 nmol/L, excluding autonomous cortisol secretion.  
Eight days later, a dedicated adrenal CT showed reduction in adrenal masses to 4.5 cm on the left and 3.5 cm on the right, and spleen to 12.5 cm. Noncontrast, portal venous, and delayed-phase Hounsfield units were 35, 54, and 45, respectively, with an absolute washout of 47% and a relative washout of 17%, described as indeterminate adrenal lesions.

A 45-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of a slowly enlarging, painless swelling of the left wrist. On examination, there was a firm, noninflammatory prominence at the distal radius without overlying skin changes. Radiographs of the left forearm demonstrated an expansile, subarticular, lytic lesion with a “soap-bubble” appearance in the distal radial epiphysis extending into the metaphysis. A skeletal survey revealed an asymptomatic osteolytic lesion in the right sacral ala. Biopsy specimens from both sites showed the characteristic histology of a giant cell tumour of bone. The patient underwent resection-reconstruction arthroplasty of the distal radius using an autogenous proximal fibular graft. She was asymptomatic for six months but was then lost to follow-up. Twelve months after the wrist surgery, she returned with three months of progressively disabling low back pain. She denied lower-limb weakness, sensory changes, bladder or bowel dysfunction, or fever. On examination, there was tenderness over the sacrum and right sacroiliac joint without redness, warmth, or swelling; the neurologic examination was unremarkable. A pelvic radiograph showed a large expansile lytic lesion involving the sacral body and right sacral ala with extension into the sacroiliac joint. CT with three-dimensional reconstruction confirmed a destructive sacral lesion.

A 19-month-old boy of Han ethnicity was evaluated for an impalpable undescended left testis. Ultrasound confirmed left cryptorchidism; otherwise, physical examination and routine laboratory tests were normal. During orchiopexy, the left testis (0.8×0.5×0.3 cm) was located in the inguinal canal, adjacent to a firm, nodular mass adherent to the testis and epididymis. Frozen-section analysis of the mass was inconclusive, and a radical left orchiectomy was performed.

On gross examination, the mass invaded testicular tissue but did not extend beyond the testis. Microscopic examination of paraffin-embedded sections showed fibrous stroma with multiple foci of immature glomeruli, tubules, and blastemal cells. Mitotic figures were infrequent, and none were atypical. Another portion of the lesion contained undifferentiated blastemal tissue, abortive glomeruli, and dysplastic tubules intermingled with testicular parenchyma. Seminiferous tubules and rete testis were adjacent to the nephrogenic foci, and overall testicular development was age-appropriate. No definitive invasive component was identified.

A 70-year-old man presented with progressive left-sided hearing loss over several years, with accelerated decline in the preceding months. He denied headache, weakness, numbness, nausea, vomiting, dysphagia, speech changes, dizziness, vertigo, or gait difficulties. Examination was notable only for significant left-sided hearing loss; facial nerve function was intact. Audiometry confirmed profound left-sided sensorineural hearing loss. MRI of the brain with contrast showed a 2.5 cm heterogeneously enhancing, extra-axial, well-defined mass with cystic components in the left cerebellopontine angle, causing mild to moderate mass effect on the left pons, anterior cerebellar hemisphere, and middle cerebellar peduncle. The lesion appeared to involve the proximal segments of cranial nerves VII and VIII without extension into the internal auditory canal.

A 61-year-old man presented with non-healing ulceration of the right buccal mucosa for 9 months; a similar lesion developed on the left side 3 months later. He had a 20-year history of cigarette smoking and occasional alcohol use; his medical history was otherwise unremarkable. On examination, there was an ulcero-proliferative, erythematous lesion measuring 1.5 × 1.0 cm on the right buccal mucosa near the retromolar area with peripheral induration and tenderness, and pain on mouth opening. On the left buccal mucosa near the vestibular area of the second molar region, there was a 0.5 × 0.5 cm heterogeneous white lesion with central ulceration. Complete blood counts and chemistry were within normal limits. An incisional biopsy of the right lesion and an excisional biopsy of the left lesion were performed and sent for histopathological examination.

A 77-year-old man presented with a 15-day history of abdominal pain unresponsive to analgesics, accompanied by chills and a nocturnal fever spike; he denied any change in bowel habits. His past medical history was unremarkable. On examination, blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg and pulse 80 beats/min. The abdomen was tender in the right iliac region without palpable masses; bowel sounds were normal. Digital rectal examination revealed stool on the probing finger. Laboratory testing showed leukocytosis (white blood cell count 91 000/mm3 with 71.6% neutrophils) and an elevated C-reactive protein level (45 mg/L); other laboratory values, including hemoglobin, platelets, renal function, amylase, electrolytes, and coagulation studies, were within normal limits.  
Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a 10-cm dense fluid–filled mass in the right iliac fossa with a nonperfused wall. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 14-cm lobulated cystic mass at the level of the right iliac vessels extending to the upper margin of the pelvis; the lesion had a thick, calcified wall. No free intraperitoneal fluid was observed, and the remaining intra-abdominal organs appeared normal.

A 55‐year‐old Moroccan man with insulin‐dependent type II diabetes presented with right flank pain. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, hemoglobin, urea, and creatinine clearance, were within normal limits. Renal ultrasonography showed right hydronephrosis. Retrograde pyelography confirmed hydronephrosis secondary to calyceal and pelvic stones and revealed a nonfunctional right kidney. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 10-cm, well‐circumscribed mass within the right renal parenchyma that had uniform fat attenuation (–25 to –100 Hounsfield units); the perinephric fat, adrenal glands, and lymph nodes appeared normal.

A 20-year-old man presented with a 6-week history of left hemicranial headache and 10 days of associated vomiting. He also noted drooping of the left eyelid for 1 week. On examination, he had partial ptosis of the left eye and a left sixth-nerve palsy. The remainder of the neurologic and ophthalmologic examinations was normal. His past medical history was unremarkable. 

Noncontrast CT of the brain showed a homogeneous, expansile mass with lytic bone destruction involving the clivus, sphenoid sinus, sella, and nasopharynx; bone-window images demonstrated peripheral “eggshell” calcification. Contrast CT revealed uniform enhancement of the lesion. MRI of the brain demonstrated a well-defined clival and sphenoidal mass that was isointense on both T1- and T2-weighted images.

A 9-year-old boy presented with lower back pain of 3 months’ duration that became worse at night. On examination, he had lumbar percussion tenderness, focal tenderness over the lumbar spine, and a mild lumbar scoliosis. Neurologic examination was normal, and routine laboratory studies were unremarkable.

A 35-year-old G4P2012 woman presented at 9 weeks 0 days gestation for a medication abortion. Her obstetrical history included one prior miscarriage and no hemorrhagic complications. She received mifepristone and misoprostol. She reported heavy bleeding for one day, which then slowed. One week later, office transvaginal 2D ultrasound showed a thickened endometrial complex with no obvious retained products of conception. Bleeding stopped shortly thereafter but recurred six weeks after the abortion. After five days of heavy bleeding, she presented to an outside emergency department where hemoglobin was 12.0 g/dL and quantitative hCG was negative. Transvaginal 2D ultrasound with color Doppler revealed a new 3-cm hypervascular mass in the endometrial cavity, and radiology noted “markedly thickened endometrium with heterogeneous appearance and marked vascularity.” She was discharged with oral misoprostol. The patient reported passage of clots without tissue, and bleeding persisted. Five days later, office transvaginal 2D ultrasound again demonstrated a large hypervascular mass in the endometrial cavity.

A 66-year-old woman with a 3-year history of multiple myeloma in remission after chemotherapy noted a 1.5 cm firm, ill-defined, nodular lesion in her right breast. Clinical laboratory tests, including blood counts and urine studies, were unremarkable, and Bence Jones protein was negative. Breast ultrasonography identified a suspicious solid lesion, and an ultrasound-guided core biopsy was performed.

Microscopic examination of hematoxylin–eosin–stained sections showed chronic lymphocytic infiltrates with rare plasma cells and a separate fragment with massive tumor infiltration. The tumor grew in solid nests and sheets, with peripheral single files of discohesive, equidistant cells with occasional cytoplasmic microlumina, set in a sclerohyaline stroma with diffuse lymphocytic infiltrate. There was no in situ component or necrosis, and mitotic activity was low.

Immunohistochemical staining of tumor cells revealed:
- CD138 positivity in up to 25% of cells (predominantly cytoplasmic with incomplete membrane staining)  
- Aberrant kappa light-chain expression in ~70% of cells and lambda in ~30% (high intensity)  
- Negative staining for CD79a, MUM1, and CD56 in tumor cells  
- CD20 positivity only in scattered interstitial B lymphocytes  
- A T-cell–predominant infiltrate (CD3+, mostly CD4+ with rare CD8+ cells)  
- CD56+ cells restricted to the inflammatory infiltrate, not tumor cells  

Based on these findings, what is your differential diagnosis?

A Chinese man in his early 40s presented with snoring and hoarseness for over 1 year, which had worsened during the previous week. On routine examination, a faint red, non-tender, mobile mass with an uneven surface was noted at the left base of the tongue. Indirect laryngoscopy confirmed a mass in the left tongue base measuring approximately 1.5×1.0 cm.
