Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI of the oropharynx and mandible revealed an uneven oval mass measuring 4.6×3.9 cm in the body and left root of the tongue, with a relatively clear boundary and inhomogeneous contrast enhancement. Chest CT and ECG showed no abnormalities. The patient underwent a radical resection of the lesion. The excised tissue measured 5.5×4×3 cm, had an uneven surface with focal nodularity, was well circumscribed, partly cystic, and appeared grey-red on cut section.

A 24-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of pain and swelling in the right mandibular region. Intraoral examination showed a firm swelling from the right mandibular central incisor to the first molar, obliterating the buccal vestibule; the overlying mucosa was pink and ulcerated. There was no paraesthesia. Aspiration yielded straw-colored fluid. A lateral oblique radiograph revealed a well-defined, unilocular, corticated radiolucency enveloping an impacted right mandibular first premolar and extending almost to the apex of the tooth. On the basis of these clinical and radiographic findings, the differential diagnosis included a dentigerous cyst, unicystic ameloblastoma, odontogenic keratocyst, and adenomatoid odontogenic tumor.

A 39-year-old woman was admitted with acute upper abdominal pain. At laparotomy, a 5 mm perforation of the anterior pyloric wall was closed with omental coverage; no masses or serosal nodules were seen. Postoperatively, endoscopic biopsy revealed adenocarcinoma of the pylorus. Upper endoscopy showed a submucosal tumor-like lesion on the anterior pylorus with irregular nodules on its exposed surface. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a tumor confined to the gastric wall with an intact fat plane to the pancreas and no evidence of distant metastasis; PET-CT showed avidity in the same region (SUV max 4.47). Gastroduodenal barium study revealed an irregular defect on the pylorus extending 1 cm into the duodenum. Laboratory studies showed normal CEA and CA19-9, but elevated Span-1 (220 U/mL; normal < 30 U/mL). Preoperative differential diagnoses included carcinoma arising in a heterotopic pancreatic rest versus primary gastric adenocarcinoma (cT3N0M0, stage IIB).

A 43-year-old woman presented with left-sided ptosis that had progressed over two years. She noticed a gradually enlarging, nontender mass centrally located in the sulcus of the left upper eyelid. She denied visual changes, discharge, bleeding, or prior orbital trauma or surgery. Distance visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left. Ocular motility was full, and pupils were equal, round, and reactive to light. External examination revealed a firm, mobile, subcutaneous mass in the center of the left supratarsal fold with a few overlying feeder vessels but without erythema, warmth, scaling, or ulceration; eyelid eversion was unremarkable. The left margin–reflex distance (MRD1) was 2.5 mm with good levator function. The remainder of the examination was normal. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an 18 × 8 mm circumscribed lesion anterior to the left globe that was bright on T2 and STIR sequences with thin internal septations and trace delayed enhancement, without evidence of bony erosion.

A 3-year-old castrated male domestic shorthair cat, FIV positive, was referred for a 1-week history of progressive tail paresis. On neurologic exam, proprioception was normal in all limbs, cutaneous trunci reflexes were absent on the right, perineal reflex was reduced, and tail tone was markedly decreased. The lesion was localized to the L7–S3 spinal segments. MRI of the lumbosacral spine with contrast showed a homogeneously contrast-enhancing intradural mass extending from the caudal third of L7 to Cd1. Fine-needle aspirates of the lesion contained occasional clusters of plump monomorphic spindle cells; cytology was interpreted as a spindle cell tumour, with the two main differentials being a peripheral nerve sheath tumour and meningioma. Thoracic radiographs showed no metastases. Palliative radiation therapy was delivered to L6–Cd7 (5 weekly fractions of 6 Gy for a total of 30 Gy), and the cat’s tail function returned to normal by week 3. 

Thirty-six months later, the cat presented with a 2-week history of left pelvic limb lameness and a 5-day history of obstipation. Physical examination revealed mild abdominal discomfort, firm feces in the colon, and a large firm intrapelvic mass felt on rectal exam causing narrowing of the pelvic canal. CBC and biochemistry were unremarkable. Three-view abdominal radiographs confirmed a moderate fecal burden without other abnormalities. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen revealed a large irregular pelvic mass with a hypodense nonenhancing center displacing the rectum to the right; there was moth-eaten osteolysis and irregular periosteal new bone on the left ilium, pubis, and ischium. Review of the prior radiation plan confirmed that the ilium and sacrum had been within the irradiated field.

A 45-year-old male manual laborer presented with complete paraplegia for 1 month and loss of bowel and bladder control for 7 days. Four months earlier, he developed progressive weakness of both lower limbs, and over the same period he noticed a right chest wall swelling that was gradually increasing in size. He reported constitutional symptoms. One month before presentation, he was started empirically on antitubercular therapy by a local practitioner based on chest radiograph and clinical impressions; despite this, his condition worsened.

On examination, he was severely dehydrated and cachectic (height 173 cm; weight 45 kg). A 3 × 3 cm variegated, immobile mass with increased local temperature was palpable on the right chest wall. Neurologic examination revealed spastic tone in both lower limbs, muscle power 0/5 in all lower-extremity muscle groups, altered sensation below the D5 dermatome and complete loss below L1, hyperactive knee and ankle reflexes with ankle clonus, and loss of bowel and bladder control.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 70 mm/h, C-reactive protein 80 mg/L, sodium 128 mEq/L, potassium 6.0 mEq/L, urea 75 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.3 mg/dL. A dorsolumbar spine radiograph demonstrated a heterogeneous opacity in the right lung field extending from T7 to T9 with coarse chondroid calcification and non-visualization of the posterior aspects of the T7–T9 vertebrae.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the spine revealed a well-defined heterogeneous enhancing right paravertebral mass with ring-and-arc calcification, destruction of the adjacent ribs and vertebrae, and extension into the paraspinal muscles and spinal canal. MRI confirmed an oval lesion with low to intermediate T1 and high T2 signal intensities involving the right ribs and vertebral bodies, with epidural extension and compression of the spinal cord.

A 22-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of lower left abdominal pain without urinary or bowel symptoms. She had no significant medical or surgical history. On bimanual pelvic examination, there was a well-circumscribed, firm, slightly movable, spherical lesion noted on the left vaginal wall. Urinalysis was normal. Pelvic ultrasonography showed a relatively irregular, heterogeneous mass in the left posterior wall of the bladder. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 3.2 × 2.5 cm soft-tissue mass with mild enhancement near the left posterior bladder wall, protruding into the bladder lumen. Cystoscopy revealed a hemispherical mass on the left bladder wall near the internal urethral orifice with intact urothelium, suggesting an intramural or extravesical lesion. A transurethral resection deep biopsy was performed, which showed normal tissue.

A 46-year-old woman with no significant medical history noted a rapidly enlarging mass on the inner aspect of her left cheek over 3 weeks. On examination, there was an ulcerating, well-circumscribed, flesh-colored mass measuring 4.0 × 3.5 cm, with overlying white surface changes. Multiple submandibular lymph nodes measuring up to 1.5 cm were palpable. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a cheek lesion without involvement of the mandibular bone or sinonasal tract. Chest CT and abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable. An excisional biopsy was performed.

Pathological examination revealed a neoplasm composed of:
• Mature benign epithelial components (intestinal-type, respiratory and squamous epithelium)  
• Mature mesenchymal components (muscle and cartilage) and neuroglial tissue  
• Immature malignant elements, including small blue cells resembling primitive neuroectodermal tumor, adenocarcinoma, and sarcoma with muscle and cartilaginous differentiation  

Immunohistochemical staining showed:
• Epithelial cells positive for pankeratin  
• Mesenchymal cells positive for desmin, myogenin, and S-100  
• Primitive neuroectodermal component positive for NSE, CD99, GFAP, synaptophysin, and focally for chromogranin  
• SALL4 negative  

Resected submandibular lymph nodes showed no malignant infiltrate.

A 29-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of right frontal headache that was localized to that region and refractory to medication. She had no history of systemic disease, meningitis, or head injury. Physical and neurologic examinations were normal. A plain skull radiograph demonstrated an ovoid radiopaque lesion in the right frontal area. Computed tomography revealed a homogeneous high-density lesion isolated from the inner table of the frontal bone. Magnetic resonance imaging showed an extraaxial mass with low signal intensity on T2-weighted images and a broad-based enhancement after gadolinium administration.

A 2-year-old girl presented with a 3-day history of acute abdominal pain, non-bilious vomiting, and decreased urine output. She had experienced intermittent abdominal pain over the previous 6 months that resolved with conservative treatment. There was no history of bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, constipation, blood in the stool, fever, or urinary tract infection. On examination, she was dehydrated and irritable. Her abdomen was distended and tender, and a soft, tender, ill-defined, immobile mass was palpable in the left lumbar region. Following fluid resuscitation and initiation of broad-spectrum antibiotics, ultrasonography revealed a “target sign” in the left lumbar region with fluid collection, interpreted as intussusception with necrotic bowel. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a cystic lesion in the mesentery with a thick enhancing wall resembling a gut signature, evidence of perforation, and a surrounding phlegmonous collection.

A 58-year-old man presented with epigastric pain. He had undergone Helicobacter pylori eradication 4 years earlier and had no current proton pump inhibitor use.  

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed:  
• A Borrmann type II gastric cancer in the antrum.  
• A 10 mm submucosal tumor-like lesion on the lesser curvature of the upper third of the stomach, in mucosa classified as atrophic (O-1).  

Biopsy of the submucosal lesion showed that the superficial foveolar epithelium was intact, but in the deep layer of the lamina propria there were atypical cells mimicking fundic gland cells with mildly enlarged nuclei, suggesting a fundic gland–type lesion.  

Narrow-band imaging with magnification demonstrated a regular microvascular pattern and a regular microsurface pattern, with a central depressed area consistent with prior biopsy.  

Endoscopic ultrasonography showed the lesion predominantly in the second layer with slight invasion into the third layer, and additionally identified a hypoechoic mass in the third layer adjacent to the tumor.  

Tumor markers (CEA 2.2 ng/mL; CA 19-9 14.3 U/mL) were within normal limits. CT of the abdomen confirmed gastric wall thickening at the antrum without nodal or distant metastases.  

Given suspicion for a fundic gland–type adenocarcinoma, endoscopic submucosal dissection was planned as an excisional biopsy prior to gastrectomy for the antral cancer.

A 4-year-old girl of Turkish ancestry was brought to the emergency department for progressive unsteadiness and recurrent falls over the preceding 5 days. Five days earlier she had first noted staggering and grabbing for support to avoid falls; during her initial fall she sustained a nasal bridge laceration that required suturing. There was no prior medical history. On examination she was alert (GCS 15), afebrile, and appeared well; the nasal bridge wound was clean. Both external ear canals were obstructed by effusion and cerumen; the remainder of the neurologic and physical examination, including cranial-nerve testing, was age-appropriate. Routine blood tests were unremarkable.  
 Three-month history of “ear problems” was elicited: initial diagnosis of otitis media with effusion and tympanic perforation treated with antibiotics led to partial resolution. On current otoscopic examination, the left tympanic membrane was intact without effusion; the right external canal was occluded by polypoid tissue and purulent secretion. A Frenzel’s examination showed no nystagmus.  
 Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and temporal bones revealed bilateral osteolysis of the mastoids, superior and lateral semicircular canals, and the right external auditory canal, plus a separate osteolytic lesion in the dorsal left parietal bone. There was also adenoid hypertrophy and mild sinus mucosal thickening.  
 Brainstem evoked response audiometry demonstrated a threshold of 40 dB with normal wave latencies on the left and an 80 dB threshold with prolonged wave I latency on the right, indicating profound right-sided hearing loss.

A 16-year-old female with no prior illness presented with 6 months of low back and bilateral lower limb pain, 3 weeks of inability to walk, and 2 days of bowel and bladder incontinence. She denied fever, night sweats, or trauma. On examination, cranial nerves were intact, lower-limb strength was slightly decreased, and there was no lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, pallor, or icterus. Laboratory studies, including a peripheral smear, abdominal ultrasound, chest radiograph, and CSF analysis, were unremarkable. MRI of the lumbosacral spine showed a soft-tissue mass at the L3 vertebral level. The patient underwent urgent excision with decompressive laminectomy and pedicle-screw fixation. Histopathological examination revealed a small round blue cell tumor.

A 35-year-old woman was referred by her dentist for evaluation of a slow-growing mass on the anterior hard palate. Her medical and family history were noncontributory, and she noted a marked swelling for at least five years. On intraoral examination, a firm, sessile submucosal tumor measuring 2.0 × 1.5 cm was observed in the midline of the hard palate; the overlying mucosa was intact except for a central erythematous area. Panoramic radiographs showed no significant findings. Maxillary occlusal radiography demonstrated a poorly defined, slightly radiolucent area in the midline of the left palatine process. A fine-needle aspiration biopsy was attempted but yielded no tissue due to the lesion’s solid consistency.

A 47-year-old man presented with a one-year history of parietal and occipital headaches, retro-orbital pain, transient blurry vision, fatigue, and difficulty completing routine tasks. He denied symptoms of hyperprolactinemia. His family, medical, surgical, and medication histories were unremarkable. On examination, findings were noncontributory. Laboratory studies showed a serum prolactin level of 269 ng/mL; all other laboratory results were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the sphenoid sinus and pituitary region revealed a 2 cm mass within the clivus extending into the sphenoid sinus, with moderate enhancement and peripheral calcifications; the intrasellar pituitary gland and stalk appeared normal.

A 63-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a right-sided groin bulge noted by his primary care physician. He reported a one-year history of an asymptomatic right groin mass and possible urinary changes. On examination, his abdomen was soft and non-tender. There was a right inguinal canal impulse bulge with mild right testicular tenderness; the left side was normal. Scrotal ultrasound showed a mild right varicocele (3 mm) without testicular lesions or definite bowel-containing hernia. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 10.3 × 7.4 × 18.1 cm predominantly fat-density lesion with small internal foci of soft-tissue density in the right retroperitoneum, extending into the right lower quadrant along the paracolic gutter and anterior to the iliopsoas muscle. The lesion displaced the bladder and bowel and had continuity with the inguinal canal contents, which showed homogeneous fat-density similar to the retroperitoneal lesion. A lobulated nodular focus of intermediate density suggested nonlipomatous tissue within the mass.

A 71-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department by family members because of chronic dyspnea at rest of 2 months’ duration, worsened by minimal exertion. She also reported long-standing generalized fatigue and left lower-limb swelling. She had no other respiratory or abdominal complaints. Her medical history was notable for diabetes mellitus, hypertension, iron-deficiency anemia, and chronic kidney disease requiring hemodialysis; she had been noncompliant with her medications. 

On examination, she appeared pale. Her temperature was 101.3 °F, pulse 110 beats/min, and blood pressure 113/73 mm Hg. Respiratory examination disclosed bilateral basal crackles; the abdomen was distended but non­tender, and there was bilateral pitting edema of the lower limbs. A COVID-19 PCR test was negative. 

An echocardiogram was normal. A frontal chest radiograph showed a large, lobulated, heterogeneously opaque mass in the right posterior mediastinum with splaying of the carina and an unfolded aortic arch. A nonenhanced CT scan of the chest revealed an 8.2 × 7.6 × 12.7 cm mid-thoracic posterior mediastinal mass with mixed fat and soft-tissue attenuation (soft-tissue components mean 34 HU). After hemodialysis, an enhanced CT scan showed homogeneous enhancement of the soft-tissue component (mean 95 HU), with encasement and displacement of the lower azygos vein and right main pulmonary trunk. There was no bony erosion, neural-foraminal narrowing, pleural effusion, surrounding invasion, or calcification.

A 66-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a left-sided nasolacrimal duct mass. Five years earlier, she had undergone a left dacryocystorhinostomy for tear-duct obstruction. Over the past year, she noted progressive nasal obstruction, tearing, and crusting of her left eyelid, accompanied by numbness at the tip of her tongue. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 1.5 × 1.4 × 2.5 cm lobular, frond-like soft-tissue mass centered within and expanding the left nasolacrimal duct, with near-homogeneous contrast enhancement and no evidence of bone destruction. An incisional biopsy proved inconclusive; differential considerations included squamous cell papilloma versus squamous cell carcinoma and other nasolacrimal neoplasms of salivary gland origin. Surgical excision was planned given her symptoms from mass effect on surrounding structures.

A 60-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of an approximately 4 cm lump in the medial aspect of her left breast. On examination, there was no palpable axillary lymphadenopathy. Mammography demonstrated a circumscribed, well-demarcated density in the medial left breast without evidence of lymph node enlargement. Fine-needle aspiration cytology suggested a poorly differentiated carcinoma. A metastatic work-up, including CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, and a bone marrow scan, showed no evidence of disease elsewhere. She underwent total left mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy, which revealed no lymph node involvement. Gross examination of the mastectomy specimen showed a 4.8 × 4.0 × 3.8 cm solid, well-circumscribed, lobulated tumor with central necrosis. Histologic evaluation demonstrated an undifferentiated, high-grade tumor composed of small round blue cells.

A 74-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of dull mid-thoracic back pain radiating to the chest and upper abdomen. The pain, initially intermittent with exertion, had become more frequent and severe, interfering with daily activities. There was no history of trauma. His medical history was significant only for hypercholesterolemia managed with a statin; he also took aspirin. He had undergone varicose vein surgery seven years earlier, had no drug allergies, and smoked 10 cigarettes daily.

On examination, he had a mild thoracic kyphosis. There was marked tenderness and percussion pain over the mid-thoracic spine. Straight leg raising tests were negative bilaterally, and his neurologic examination was normal. The remainder of the systemic examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, electrolytes, and alkaline phosphatase, were within normal limits.

Chest radiography showed widening of the right paratracheal stripe and calcified left hilar lymph nodes. Plain radiographs of the thoracic spine revealed mid-thoracic kyphosis with loss of distinction of the posterior cortices of T7 and T8. MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine demonstrated an infiltrative process involving the vertebral bodies of T6 and T7, with expansion and some destruction, extensive demineralization of T6, extension into T7 crossing the disc space, and involvement of the left superior and inferior articular facets at T5. CT of the thoracic spine confirmed an infiltrative lesion extending into both pedicles of T6 and T7 with mild foraminal compromise, but without definite nerve-root compression. The lesion appeared aggressive and destructive, raising concern for a malignant process, although a sclerotic edge suggested an indolent component.

A 67-year-old man presented with acute urinary retention and left leg swelling. A urinary catheter was placed, and ultrasonography revealed an extensive left femoral vein deep venous thrombosis, for which he received anticoagulation and an inferior vena cava filter. At that time, his prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level was 77.2 µg/L; no prostate biopsy was performed.

Six months later, he developed two days of shortness of breath and productive cough with whitish sputum. Pulmonary embolism was excluded by blood tests and imaging. Chest radiography showed a left-sided mediastinal mass. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen (oral contrast only, no IV contrast because of renal impairment) demonstrated lobulated mediastinal masses extending into both supraclavicular regions (largest 9.8 cm) and large retroperitoneal masses (15 × 15 cm) from the upper abdomen to the aortic bifurcation, with bilateral hydronephrosis and hydroureters. The radiologic impression was lymphoma.

A core-needle biopsy of the mediastinal mass showed an epithelial tumor with nesting patterns and focal acinar formation. The tumor cells had enlarged nuclei, abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, focal necrosis, and scattered mitoses.

A 50-year-old woman presented with a slow-growing nodule over the left cheek for one and a half years. The lesion began as a 2 mm asymptomatic papule and gradually enlarged to approximately 1.5 cm in diameter. There was no history of trauma, pre-existing skin lesion, topical application, or family history of similar lesions. On examination, there was an ulcerated nodule with a peripheral hyperpigmented rim just lateral to the left nasolabial fold. The lesion was firm, mobile, non-tender, and did not bleed on touch. No regional lymphadenopathy was noted. The clinical differential diagnosis included basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, amelanotic melanoma, and keratoacanthoma.

A 19-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 2-week history of progressive headache and two episodes of vomiting. His parents also noted a 12-month history of apathy and declining academic performance. On neurologic examination, he had a right pronator drift; the remainder of his examination was normal. Noncontrast CT of the brain showed a large extra-axial heterogeneous mass over the left frontal and temporal convexity with well-defined lobulated margins and avid enhancement of denser areas; there was erosion of the inner table of the left frontal bone and near-complete erosion of the outer table. Contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated a 6.2×7.1×7.0 cm extra-axial ovoid mass at the left frontal convexity with heterogeneous enhancement and susceptibility artifacts consistent with calcification and/or hemorrhage. There was evidence of calvarial destruction and a small extracranial component. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of hemangiopericytoma was entertained, and surgical resection was planned.

A 55-year-old man presented with 3 hours of crushing central chest pain. He denied hypertension, diabetes, or alcohol use. On arrival, blood pressure was 184/110 mmHg, heart rate 124 beats/min, respiratory rate 25 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and temperature 36.3°C. Electrocardiogram showed the de Winter pattern, and rapid troponin I was 0.44 ng/mL (normal, 0.00–0.30). He was treated for presumed acute myocardial infarction with aspirin, clopidogrel, and intravenous glyceryl trinitrate; his chest pain improved and blood pressure normalized. Coronary angiography revealed no stenosis. Serum amylase was 7021 IU/L (normal, 15–135) and lipase was 175 IU/L (normal, 0–66). Contrast-enhanced CT angiography of the aorta showed no dissection or signs of pancreatitis, but revealed a 74×64×78-mm right adrenal mass with arterial phase hyperenhancement and well-demarcated margins, without metastases. During hospitalization, he developed worsening dyspnea, diffuse crackles on lung auscultation, and oxygen saturation of 79% on room air. NT-proBNP was 3949 pg/mL (normal, 0–300). Echocardiography showed regional septal and posterior wall motion abnormalities with an ejection fraction of 48%. Treatment with morphine, furosemide, deslanoside, and high-flow oxygen led to resolution of heart-failure symptoms and normalization of NT-proBNP, oxygenation, and ejection fraction (68% on day 9).

A 60-year-old woman presented with two months of progressive abdominal pain, abdominal distension, and a 6-kg weight loss. On examination, there was a bulky mass occupying the right abdominal quadrants. Routine laboratory tests showed no evidence of chronic liver disease, and serum tumor markers (AFP, CEA, CA 19-9) were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 15 × 12 × 23 cm expansive mass in the right lobe of the liver, poorly separable from the surrounding parenchyma, with heterogeneous contrast enhancement. The lesion was partially cystic, with thickened walls and an intralesional solid component.

A 15-year-old girl presented with a six-month history of general malaise and weakness, followed sequentially by bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, painless bilateral breast masses, and gradually progressive bilateral proptosis. On examination, the cervical nodes were firm, the largest 1.5 cm, with restricted mobility. The breast masses measured 4.5 cm on the left and 5.0 cm on the right; overlying skin was unremarkable, and the lumps were fixed. Bilateral uniform proptosis was noted without hepatosplenomegaly or other lymphadenopathy.

Fine-needle aspiration cytology of a cervical lymph node and of the breast masses yielded similar smears. Both Papanicolaou- and May–Grünwald Giemsa–stained preparations showed a polymorphous population of large atypical cells in a background of mature and reactive lymphoid cells. The tumor cells were roughly twice the size of mature lymphocytes, with round to oval nuclei containing fine chromatin and 2–3 nucleoli, and pale blue cytoplasm. A fair number of these cells contained Auer rods and fine granules. Smears from the breast did not demonstrate any ductal epithelial cell clusters.

A 73-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of gradual right flank pain, lower back pain, loss of appetite, malaise, and a significant unintentional weight loss. He denied hematuria or fever. He had a 24 pack-year smoking history and social alcohol use. On examination, he appeared cachectic and pale without lymphadenopathy. Abdominal examination revealed a firm, bimanually palpable, minimally mobile mass in the right renal angle. Laboratory tests showed: leukocytes 9.87 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL, platelets 200 × 10^9/L, creatinine 171 μmol/L, potassium 5.83 mmol/L, sodium 124 mmol/L, calcium 3.19 mmol/L, lactate dehydrogenase 478 U/L, and negative HIV serology. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a large hypo‐echoic mass in the right kidney measuring 15.6 × 14.1 cm; the left kidney was normal. A working diagnosis of right renal cell carcinoma was made. Contrast CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a hypo‐enhancing soft‐tissue mass on the medial aspect of the right kidney measuring 17 × 13 × 14 cm with areas of necrosis, extension beyond Gerota’s fascia, para‐aortic lymphadenopathy, and encasement of the right renal vessels, inferior vena cava, and aorta; it was reported as stage IV RCC. In view of vessel involvement, an open biopsy of the renal mass and a para‐aortic lymph node was planned.

A 37-year-old woman with a history of uterine sarcoma underwent surgical resection 2 years ago for primary tumor and pelvic lymph node metastases, radiotherapy for a cervical spine metastasis, and resection of a solitary right lower lobe pulmonary metastasis 1 year ago. She continued chemotherapy but surveillance 18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated new bilateral lung lesions. She was referred for surgical resection of these pulmonary metastases.

The patient had no respiratory symptoms. Physical examination was unremarkable, and routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. A preoperative chest radiograph showed no abnormalities. Chest CT revealed multiple localized thickenings, each ≤3 cm, in both lungs:
• In the right middle lobe, smooth and nodular thickening of the interlobular septa surrounding a lobule.  
• In the right lower lobe, irregular nodular thickenings along the bronchovascular bundle and smooth septal thickenings.  
• In the left upper lobe, well-circumscribed ground-glass opacity along the interlobular septa surrounding a lobule.  

The lung architecture at the sites of these lesions was preserved. There was no pleural effusion, no chest wall invasion, and no hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

A 39-year-old Taiwanese woman presented with a painless mass of the right upper eyelid that had been present for 5 years. In her early 20s, she had undergone blepharoplasty for trichiasis. Two years earlier, at a local clinic, an incision and curettage was performed for a presumed chalazion, but the lesion did not subside after the procedure. 

On examination, there was a firm nodule with a crusted wound at the margin of the right upper eyelid. The fornix, anterior chamber, and fundus were normal. There was no palpable orbital mass and extraocular movements were full. 

Under local anesthesia, the eyelid skin was incised at the wound site, and necrotic tissue along with soft tissue above the tarsus was excised and sent for clinical pathology. The wound healed without complications.

A 40-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an abnormal radiolucency in the right mandible detected on a routine panoramic radiograph. She reported intermittent pain in the right mandibular region. Her medical, surgical, and family histories were unremarkable, and she denied any history of trauma. On extraoral examination, there was no swelling, facial asymmetry, cutaneous changes, or lymphadenopathy; motor and sensory functions were intact. Intraorally, there was buccal cortical expansion of the right mandible from the canine to the anterior border of the ramus; the area was bony-hard and non-tender, with margins blending into surrounding bone and intact overlying mucosa. All teeth in the involved region responded normally to vitality testing.

A panoramic radiograph at presentation showed a well-defined multilocular radiolucent lesion in the right mandibular body and ramus, with coarse radiopaque septa and preservation of the inferior alveolar canal; no tooth resorption or displacement was seen. Review of a panoramic radiograph taken five years earlier revealed a dome-shaped radiolucency in the retromolar area, “ground-glass” radiopacity of the ramus and posterior body, and a mixed radiodensity anteriorly from the first premolar to the second molar.

An incisional biopsy under local anesthesia revealed a thin buccal cortical plate; aspiration yielded yellowish fluid. The specimen comprised a mixture of brittle hemorrhagic-appearing tissue and fibro-osseous tissue. Microscopic examination of the solid component showed dense fibroblastic proliferation of spindle-shaped mononuclear cells without atypia or mitotic figures, interspersed with numerous bone trabeculae and cementum-like calcified spans that were often confluent and lined by regular osteoblastic cells. Smears of the aspirated fluid demonstrated a discretely hematic background with polymorphic inflammatory cells and histiocytes, without any abnormal or neoplastic cells.

A 41‐year‐old G4P4 woman presented with a several‐month history of a left vulvar mass. She had no personal or family history of breast or other malignancies. On examination, there was a 2.0-cm erythematous, ulcerative nodule at the junction of the left labium majus and labium minus. The clitoris, right labia, vestibule, and vaginal wall were unremarkable. Bilateral groin examination revealed enlarged, firm, fixed lymph nodes. 

An excisional biopsy of the lesion showed:
• Neoplastic epithelial cells arranged in cords, trabeculae, and nests within the dermis.  
• Cuboidal to round cells with amphophilic cytoplasm, enlarged slightly pleomorphic nuclei, coarse chromatin, and inconspicuous nucleoli.  
• Rare glandular structures, mitotic rate ≥10/10 high‐power fields, focal coagulative necrosis, and delicate fibrous stroma.  
• Overlying squamous epithelium partially replaced by nests of large atypical cells in the basal and parabasal layers, with clear to amphophilic cytoplasm and frequent mitoses.  

Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated tumor cells that were positive for CK7, EMA, and Her‐2/neu (score 2+), and negative for CK20, HMB-45, Melan-A, estrogen receptor, and progesterone receptor. Chromogenic in situ hybridization for HER2 amplification was negative.

A previously healthy 26-year-old woman presented with four months of progressive left-sided abdominal pain radiating to the back and left flank, associated with fatigue but without gastrointestinal, urinary, or constitutional symptoms. Physical examination was notable for normal vital signs and a firm, round mass of approximately 13 × 10 cm in the left upper and lower quadrants without tenderness. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, metabolic panel, pregnancy test, and tumor markers (CEA, CA 19-9, CA 125, AFP), were all within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 17 × 12 × 10 cm bilobed retroperitoneal mass with cystic components displacing the pancreatic body and tail anteriorly and the upper left kidney posteriorly; the inferior part of the mass was inseparable from the third part of the duodenum, proximal jejunum, and left adrenal gland, with no clear invasion and no evidence of lymphovascular invasion. MRI confirmed a mass measuring 18.7 × 10.7 × 11.1 cm with high T2 signal and moderate T1 signal suggesting a myxoid component, central necrosis, hemorrhagic foci, and peripheral enhancement; it again was inseparable from adjacent bowel and adrenal structures and encased the inferior mesenteric vein and possibly the artery. PET/CT showed hypermetabolic activity confined to this mass without metastatic disease.  
The differential diagnosis included myxoid soft tissue sarcoma, adrenal cortical carcinoma, or, less likely, gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST).

An 82-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a right ventricular outflow tract mass discovered on preoperative echocardiography. Two days earlier, she had fallen and sustained a right femoral neck fracture without loss of consciousness; she was scheduled for surgical repair. Her history was notable for hypertension and remote uterine fibroid surgery. She was asymptomatic from a cardiac standpoint, with an oxygen saturation of 98% on room air and no peripheral edema.

Vital signs were stable. Cardiovascular examination was unremarkable. Electrocardiography showed sinus rhythm. Chest radiography revealed mild cardiomegaly with a cardiothoracic ratio of 0.53. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a 36 × 30 mm mass in the right ventricular outflow tract, mild tricuspid regurgitation with a pressure gradient of 51 mmHg, and no enlargement of the right atrium or right ventricle.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest revealed a contrast defect around the pulmonary valve with a bifurcated morphology; there was minimal staining in the early phase but slight enhancement in the delayed phase. Coronary computed tomography showed no significant stenosis of the coronary arteries. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging revealed a stalked mass attached to the pulmonary valve with mixed high and moderate signals on T2-weighted sequences.

A 10-year-old girl presented with a 2-week history of continuous headache aggravated by nausea. On examination, she was alert, with normal vital signs and no cutaneous stigmata of tuberous sclerosis. Noncontrast head CT showed acute hemorrhage in the region of the right lateral ventricle and evidence of obstructive hydrocephalus. Brain MRI revealed an approximately 3.6-cm, well-defined mass on the body of the right lateral ventricle, exhibiting mixed low and high signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images. After gadolinium administration, there was heterogeneous peripheral enhancement of the solid components, and perfusion imaging showed focally increased cerebral blood volume in the enhanced areas. The lesion contained mixed cystic and solid components with multistage hemorrhages localized at the right-sided foramen of Monro. Radiological differential diagnoses included high-grade glioma, subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, and choroid plexus tumor.

A 43‐year‐old woman with β‐thalassemia presented with an 8‐year history of cutaneous changes on the right fifth toe, without preceding trauma. She reported swelling, partial nail loss, and distal ulceration with occasional bleeding. The lesion was painless in open shoes but became painful and bled when she wore closed shoes. On examination, the distal end of the right fifth toe showed a central ulcer with blood remnants and partial onycholysis. Anteroposterior and oblique radiographs of both feet revealed subluxation of the distal phalanx of the right fifth toe without evidence of bone infiltration. A diagnostic biopsy was performed. Histologic examination showed a neoplastic dermal proliferation of spindle‐shaped cells without significant atypia, embedded in a myxoid stroma with collagenized areas and a prominent vascular network. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated cytoplasmic positivity for CD34 and negativity for S-100, actin, and melanocytic markers. The Ki-67 proliferation index was less than 1%.

A 71-year-old man with a 30-year history of heavy alcohol use (≥90 g/day) and known alcoholic liver cirrhosis presented after detection of a 53-mm liver mass in segment 7. He had mild jaundice and lower‐leg edema; vital signs were stable. Laboratory studies showed cirrhosis (platelets 54×10^9/L, albumin 2.8 g/dL, PT 66.7%), elevated bilirubin (total 2.0 mg/dL), AST 61 IU/L, γ-GT 347 IU/L, mildly elevated AFP (11.6 ng/mL) and CEA (8.36 ng/mL), normal CA19-9, and negative viral hepatitis markers. Dynamic contrast CT demonstrated slight arterial enhancement of the lesion with prolonged wash-in through portal and delayed phases. On Gd-EOB-DTPA–enhanced MRI, the mass was hypointense on T1, showed slight arterial enhancement, and was isointense in the hepatobiliary phase. Ultrasonography revealed a heterogeneous mass with an ill‐defined border. FDG-PET showed uptake in the tumor (SUVmax 4.3) without other lesions. A percutaneous needle biopsy was performed after diuresis of ascites, and the specimen was initially diagnosed as hepatocellular carcinoma with a pseudo‐glandular pattern. Given his limited hepatic reserve and tumor meeting up-to-seven criteria, he was referred for transcatheter arterial chemoembolization and percutaneous radiofrequency ablation.

A 60-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of a slowly enlarging, asymptomatic nodule on the first phalanx of the right index finger. He had no history of pain, cold sensitivity, tenderness, trauma, or systemic disease. On examination, there was a 2.5 cm purplish, soft tumor covered with yellowish and hemorrhagic crusts, deforming and compressing the nail plate. Neurologic and muscular function in the finger were normal. Dermoscopic examination revealed polymorphic vessels in a rainbow pattern with melliciric and hemorrhagic crusts. Radiographs of the hand showed no bony lesions. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 26 × 16 mm mass of low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, marked hyperintensity on T2-weighted images, and vivid enhancement after gadolinium administration.

A 62-year-old man presented with general fatigue and severe dyspnea. He was an ex-smoker with no known asbestos exposure. On examination, his oxygen saturation was 90% on room air, and there were decreased vesicular breath sounds over the left hemithorax. Arterial blood gas on 2 L/min of oxygen showed pH 7.48, PaO₂ 73.9 mm Hg, and PaCO₂ 24.8 mm Hg. Spirometry was not performed because of severe dyspnea. A chest radiograph revealed a large left pleural effusion, and contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 20-cm mass occupying the left thoracic cavity. Thoracentesis produced clear fluid with negative cytology. CT-guided needle biopsy of the mass showed a proliferation of atypical short spindle or oval cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm. Immunohistochemically, the tumor cells were positive for D2-40, BCL-2, CD99, and p53, and negative for TTF-1, WT1, calretinin, CK5/6, CK7, CK20, HBME-1, CEA, and CD34. The biopsy specimen was diagnosed as a sarcomatoid mesothelioma. One month later, repeat CT showed rapid enlargement of the mass and a small right pleural effusion, presumed inflammatory. Given the patient’s severe dyspnea from left lung collapse and a perceived discrepancy between imaging and biopsy findings, pleuropneumonectomy was planned.

A 12-year-old girl presented with one week of nausea and vomiting, four months of intermittent cramping abdominal pain, fatigue, and a 25-pound unintentional weight loss over three months. On examination, she was tachycardic with pale conjunctivae and mild abdominal tenderness. Initial laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL, hematocrit 29.7%, mean corpuscular volume 62 fL, red blood cell distribution width 18.9%, and platelet count 708 K/μL. Iron studies showed serum iron 10 μg/dL, total iron‐binding capacity 304 μg/dL, iron saturation 3%, and ferritin 5 ng/mL. A fecal occult blood test was positive. Six days later, her hemoglobin had fallen to 5.9 g/dL, and she was admitted for transfusion. C-reactive protein was 3.01 mg/dL. Initial considerations included inflammatory bowel disease and NSAID-induced gastritis. Upper endoscopy was normal. Colonoscopy revealed a fungating, nonobstructing, approximately 7-cm cecal mass; the remainder of the colon was normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis confirmed a cecal mass with enlarged pericolonic and mesenteric lymph nodes. CT of the chest showed a 1.1-cm noncalcified subpleural nodule in the left lower lobe; PET scan demonstrated increased uptake in the right colon mass and possible uptake in the mediastinum and left lower lobe. Eighteen days later, a biopsy of the cecal mass was reported as a malignant sarcomatoid neoplasm. Immunohistochemical staining showed tumor cells weakly positive for SATB2 and negative for keratin OSCAR, keratin AE1/AE3, desmin, myogenin, SMA, SOX10, S100, CD34, WT1, SALL4, and EMA.

A 9.8-year-old obese (BMI 24.7 kg/m2, >97th percentile), Tanner stage 3 girl with normal development presented with a 1-month history of painless swelling in the left breast. On examination, there was a firm mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast. Contrast-enhanced MRI performed days earlier demonstrated a well-defined 27 × 18 mm lesion in the laterocranial left breast, with pronounced calcifications, limited diffusivity, and a BI-RADS 4 assessment. Ultrasound confirmed a 28 mm hyperechoic lesion with multiple calcifications, marked hyperemia, and no axillary lymphadenopathy. Core-needle biopsy yielded fibrovascular stroma and bone trabeculae composed of osteoid and osteoblasts, findings suggestive of a bone-forming tumor.

A 58-year-old man presented with a 2–3-month history of progressive abdominal distension, loss of appetite, and weight loss. He had a firm, nodular, non-tender midline neck swelling (4×4 cm) present for 15 years. There was no fever, cough, hematemesis, melena, or history of tuberculosis. He was not diabetic or hypertensive. On examination, he was pale but afebrile, normotensive, and without lymphadenopathy. Abdominal exam revealed moderate hepatosplenomegaly and ascites. Thyroid-stimulating hormone was elevated at 21.005 pg/mL (normal 0.55–4.78); free T3 and T4 were decreased. Other biochemistry was normal. Hemoglobin was 8.8 g/dL, leukocyte count 16,200/μL, platelets 260,000/μL. Peripheral smear showed a leukoerythroblastic picture with myelocytes 17%, metamyelocytes 10%, neutrophils 46%, lymphocytes 21%, monocytes 2%, basophils 2%, eosinophils 2%, and five nucleated red cells per 100 leukocytes; red cells were normocytic to microcytic with anisocytosis and occasional teardrop cells. Bone marrow aspiration was hemodilute; biopsy was inadequate.  
Ultrasonography of the neck showed a multinodular goiter; abdominal ultrasound revealed hepatosplenomegaly, gross ascites, omental caking, and peritoneal thickening suggestive of tuberculosis. Ascitic fluid adenosine deaminase was 10.0 U (normal <40), and the Montaux test was negative. Chest radiography showed bilateral pleural effusions with focal consolidation. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen confirmed hepatosplenomegaly, portal hypertension, thickened peritoneum, gross ascites, bilateral pleural effusions, and moderate pericardial effusion. Fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid was benign. Ascitic fluid was sent for cytological examination.

A 37-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of right facial pain and a 3-month history of progressively painful swelling beneath the right earlobe. Physical examination revealed a smooth, elastic, mobile, tender mass in the anteroinferior auricular area; facial nerve function was intact, and there was no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy or systemic symptoms. Metastatic screening showed no lesions in the lungs or abdomen. Ultrasonography demonstrated a solid echo in the right parotid gland with cervical lymph node enlargement. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a well-defined 40 × 25 mm soft-tissue mass in the deep lobe of the right parotid gland. 

The patient underwent a standard parotidectomy with excision of a 10 × 10 mm deep lateral cervical lymph node. Intraoperative frozen-section analysis indicated a low-grade malignancy in the parotid mass and no nodal metastasis. The tumor was excised with a 1 cm margin, preserving the facial nerve; surgical margins were microscopically negative.

Grossly, the specimen measured 60 × 25 × 30 mm and consisted of a grayish-red collagenous mass intermingled with myxoid areas; the main stem of the facial nerve and the sternocleidomastoid muscle were involved. Microscopically, the tumor was fairly well circumscribed but not perfectly encapsulated, with hypocellular to moderately cellular myxoid or fibromyxoid areas, curvilinear capillaries with perivascular condensation, and fusiform cells ranging from small bland forms to enlarged bizarre pleomorphic multinucleated cells; mitoses were infrequent. 

Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated strong positivity for vimentin and alpha1-antichymotrypsin, a Ki-67 labeling index of 35%, and negativity for desmin, alpha-smooth muscle actin, beta2-microglobulin, and CD34.

A 61-year-old woman presented with one month of worsening back pain and progressive weakness of both lower limbs. She was unable to stand or walk at the time of admission. She had been treated twice with NSAIDs and analgesics without relief. On examination, there was muscle weakness and hypoesthesia in both lower limbs, with a sensory level at the fifth thoracic vertebra. 

Plain radiographs of the thoracic spine showed only cuneiform degeneration of the T4 vertebral body. A CT scan revealed an osteolytic lesion involving the posterior elements of T3 and T4, with extension into the paravertebral space. MRI demonstrated a contrast-enhancing extradural mass causing severe spinal cord compression at T3–T4. The lesion’s radiographic appearance suggested metastatic disease. 

A thorough metastatic workup, including tumor markers, CT of the chest and abdomen, and a bone scintigraphy, failed to identify a primary malignancy.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a two-year history of back pain and progressive bilateral lower limb weakness. Over the preceding two months, she had developed urinary incontinence. On examination, there was bilateral lower limb hypertonia, motor strength graded 0/5 throughout, brisk deep-tendon reflexes, and sensory loss below the T11 dermatome. Magnetic resonance imaging of the thoracic spine revealed an intramedullary mass adjacent to the conus medullaris at the T11–T12 level. Differential diagnosis at that point of time was astrocytoma and ependymoma.

A 24-year-old woman with a history of systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, and sickle cell trait presented with a 5-month history of a slow-growing, mobile mass in her left flank that was tender on palpation. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a subcutaneous mass interpreted as consistent with a lipoma. The lesion was excised, yielding fragments of adipose tissue measuring 10.0 × 6.0 × 2.5 cm. Histologic examination of hematoxylin and eosin–stained sections revealed predominantly univacuolated adipocytic cells with intermixed granular multivacuolated cells. Immunohistochemical stains showed that both cell populations were strongly immunoreactive for S100, while Ki-67 immunoreactivity was virtually absent.

A 94-year-old man with an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 3 and a 5-year history of renal pelvis and bladder cancer under best supportive care noted a bruise-like rash on his forehead without antecedent trauma, which appeared and progressively enlarged over 4 months. On examination, there was a dome-shaped, dark purple, firm mass measuring 8 × 4 cm on the forehead, along with multiple pale-dark infiltrative eruptions on the scalp; no superficial lymphadenopathy was palpable. Given the clinical appearance, the clinician suspected hemangiosarcoma and obtained a skin biopsy from the forehead lesion. Histopathology demonstrated a diffuse proliferation of atypical cells extending from the dermis into subcutaneous tissue. Immunohistochemical staining revealed diffuse strong positivity for CD4, CD56, and CD123 and negativity for CD3, CD34, and lysozyme. A CT scan showed thickening of the skin on the occiput without evidence of other distant lesions. Peripheral blood counts were within normal limits with no abnormal circulating cells, and laboratory studies revealed severe renal dysfunction.

An 82-year-old woman with known neurofibromatosis type 1 presented with a palpable lump in her left breast. She had a history of hypertension and right breast cancer treated by resection 15 years previously (pathology unknown). There was no family history of breast cancer. On examination, an elastic hard mass about 3 cm in diameter was palpated in the upper quadrant of her left breast; multiple cutaneous nodules were also present. Laboratory studies were unremarkable.

Mammography showed a 3 cm oval high-density mass with zonal pleomorphic calcifications in the upper outer quadrant. Doppler ultrasonography revealed a hypo-echoic lesion with irregular margins, indistinct anterior border, and abundant internal vascular flow. Noncontrast CT demonstrated a heterogeneous low-density mass that enlarged from 3 cm to 6 cm over a 3-month interval without evidence of lymphadenopathy or distant metastasis.

Dynamic contrast-enhanced breast MRI showed a well-circumscribed oval mass. On T1-weighted images, there were spotty hyperintense areas; on STIR, there were partially hyperintense regions. The solid component enhanced heterogeneously with a fast initial rise and washout pattern on time-intensity curves. Diffusion-weighted imaging showed restricted diffusion with an ADC of 0.63 × 10⁻³ mm²/s. Multiple enhanced nodules were also seen in the overlying skin.

A 39-year-old man was referred for evaluation of tooth displacement in the left mandibular lateral incisor and canine region. He reported no history of trauma or systemic illness. Extraoral examination was unremarkable. Intraorally, there was no mucosal expansion or inflammation, and the displaced teeth were vital on testing. Cone-beam computed tomography showed a 2-cm unilocular radiolucent lesion with sclerotic borders between the left lateral incisor and canine, causing divergence of their roots without evidence of resorption.  
Lateral periodontal cyst, odontogenic keratocyst, and central giant cell granuloma were considered as differential diagnoses.

An 86-year-old man with a history of stroke, hypertension, and cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma presented with several months of fatigue, dizziness, generalized weakness, and weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable. 

A chest radiograph showed multiple bilateral noncalcified lung nodules. Whole-body CT imaging revealed multiple hypervascular hepatic nodules and a 12.3 × 9 × 8 cm right renal mass that was well-encapsulated and partially necrotic, findings that were interpreted as suspicious for primary renal cell carcinoma with pulmonary and hepatic metastases. 

A CT-guided renal biopsy yielded only scant vascular fragments and was nondiagnostic. A repeat biopsy again showed extensive necrosis with few tissue fragments containing multiple vascular channels lined by pleomorphic endothelial cells with increased mitotic figures. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated positivity for CD34 and CD31 and negativity for AE1/3, CK8/18, CD10, and RCC antigen.

A 47-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of a lesion in the right posterior mandible associated with lower-lip paresthesia and right ear pain. Examination revealed extraoral swelling over the right mandibular angle and, intraorally, a firm mass in the edentulous right posterior mandible covered by intact mucosa. There was no tooth mobility. Her medical history was notable only for hypothyroidism. Panoramic radiography showed an ill-defined unilocular radiolucent lesion in the right posterior mandible. Computed tomography confirmed an ill-defined lytic lesion in the same region without cortical breach or fracture; small (up to 5.5 mm) right submandibular lymph nodes were present.

A 50-year-old woman with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and substance abuse presented with several weeks of right chest pain and discomfort. Her father had lung cancer. On examination, vital signs were normal and physical findings were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed: hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL (anemia), RDW 19.2%, WBC 4.1 k/µL (leucopenia), hemoglobin A2 1.6%, total calcium 9.8 mg/dL, albumin 4.4 g/dL, total protein 9.2 g/dL, LDH 263 units/L, and normal renal function. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a right pleural-based mass eroding the second rib, six enlarged lymph nodes adjacent to the right rib cage, and multiple lytic lesions in the right scapula, the eighth and ninth ribs, the iliac bones, left ischium, sacrum, coccyx, and throughout the thoracic and lumbar vertebrae. She was referred for evaluation of a suspected Pancoast tumor and a right axillary lymph-node biopsy was scheduled; however, she was lost to follow-up.

One month later, she returned with two weeks of left upper-thigh pain and two days of right shoulder pain worsened by movement. There was no trauma, weakness, or numbness.  
– Chest X-ray: right upper-lobe mass-like opacity.  
– Right shoulder X-ray: lytic, permeative lesion of the proximal and mid humeral diaphysis with a pathologic compression fracture and lung opacities.  
– Right elbow X-ray: lytic lesions in the distal humeral diaphysis.  
– Repeat chest CT: a 5.5 cm pleural-based mass in the right upper lobe eroding the second rib, right axillary lymphadenopathy, extensive diffuse lytic lesions in the visualized bones, and multiple pathologic fractures of right ribs, proximal right humerus, and T4–T5 vertebral bodies.  
– CT of the abdomen and pelvis: a large destructive lesion in the left ilium and multiple lytic lesions throughout the pelvis and spine.

A 74-year-old normotensive, nondiabetic man with a 30–pack-year smoking history presented with 2 months of progressively worsening shortness of breath, cough productive of white mucoid sputum, and oppressive retrosternal and right parasternal chest pain that worsened with exertion and was associated with palpitations. He denied sweating, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, hemoptysis, leg swelling, facial puffiness, or radiation of pain. He reported significant weight loss and anorexia. He had chronic bronchitis–predominant COPD treated for 5 years.

On examination, he was afebrile; heart rate 120 bpm; respiratory rate 24/min; blood pressure 94/64 mmHg; SpO2 96% on room air. He had pallor and clubbing, and multiple hard, discrete, nontender left cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes. Lung auscultation revealed vesicular breath sounds with prolonged expiration, bilateral basal crackles, and occasional wheezes; cardiac examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.1 g/dL; other biochemistry was normal. ECG demonstrated atypical ST-segment elevation and T-wave inversion in leads V4–V6. An initial rapid troponin-T test was inconclusive; a repeat at 12 hours was negative. Chest radiograph (PA view) showed cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio >0.5) with clear lung fields.

A 56-year-old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with a 5-year history of asymptomatic skin lesions. On examination, she had multiple orange-to-dark brown papuloerythematous nodules and tumor-like plaques on the trunk, arms, and legs. The lesions were asymmetrically distributed, firm, and non-tender. There was no lymphadenopathy. She denied systemic symptoms, including fever, weight loss, respiratory, neurologic, or ocular complaints.

Routine laboratory tests, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. A contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly.

Punch biopsy of a representative lesion revealed a dense dermal infiltrate of large histiocytic cells with pale eosinophilic cytoplasm. Numerous intact lymphocytes and neutrophils were seen within the cytoplasm of the histiocytes (emperipolesis), and the infiltrate was accompanied by lymphocytes, plasma cells, and fibrosis.

Immunohistochemical staining showed that the histiocytes were positive for S100 protein and CD68 and negative for CD1a and Langerin. Molecular testing for BRAF and KRAS mutations was negative.

A 43-year-old healthy white man presented with a 2-year history of a slow-growing mass on his right upper arm within a tattoo that had been in place for more than 20 years. He reported mild pain and itching at the site, with intermittent bleeding and purulent drainage. He had been treating the lesion at home with 17% salicylic acid liquid wart treatment and 70% isopropyl alcohol. He denied fatigue, fever, chills, night sweats, or weight loss.

On examination, there was a 2.6 × 2.5 cm exophytic, verruciform, ulcerated plaque on the right upper arm with an erythematous rim and a small amount of yellow purulent fluid draining centrally. The deep aspect of the plaque extended 0.5 to 1 cm into the subcutaneous tissue beyond the base of the cutaneous portion. There was no clinically significant axillary lymphadenopathy or additional nodules.

Because of the appearance of the mass, its size, and depth of local invasion, the initial differential diagnosis included dimorphic fungal infections, atypical mycobacterial infections, squamous cell carcinoma, and sarcoidosis.

A 27-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of loss of appetite, mild abdominal distension, and a sense of fullness in the right upper quadrant. She had no significant medical history and a 1–pack-year smoking history. On examination, there was no jaundice. The right upper quadrant was mildly distended, and palpation revealed a tender, smooth-surfaced mass in the region of the liver. Routine blood tests were within normal limits except for a carcinoembryonic antigen level of 6.5 ng/mL. Beta human chorionic gonadotropin and echinococcus serology were negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated an ill-defined, contrast-enhancing, multilobulated cystic lesion measuring 19 × 15 × 10 cm in liver segments II, III, VI, and VIII, containing adipose tissue with calcifications and multiple septations.

A 54-year-old man with a 30 pack-year smoking history presented with one month of asthenia and 14 days of right eyelid drooping and diplopia. On examination, he had palsies of the right cranial nerves III, IV, VI, and the V2 division of V, manifesting as right-sided ptosis, diplopia, and decreased sensation over the right cheek. Both pupils were normal in size and reactive to light. Routine laboratory tests were normal except for a urinary red blood cell count of 14.80/hpf. Noncontrast brain MRI showed an irregularly marginated mass in the clivus invading the sphenoid and cavernous sinuses bilaterally and encasing both carotid arteries; the lesion was isointense on T1-weighted images and slightly hyperintense on T2-weighted images. Brain CT demonstrated osteolysis of the clivus and both petrous apexes, with marked enhancement of the clival lesion after intravenous contrast administration.

A 12-year-old boy presented with a 6-month history of a painless swelling in the right mandible. His medical history was unremarkable. Intraoral examination showed firm buccal and lingual expansion in the mandibular right quadrant, retention of primary lower incisors (8.2 and 8.3), absence of the permanent canine (4.3), and displacement of adjacent teeth without mobility. The overlying mucosa was intact and appeared normal.

A panoramic radiograph revealed a well-demarcated, unilocular radiolucency with a corticated border extending from the region of teeth 3.4 to 4.5, reaching the mandibular base. Cone-beam CT showed a broader hypodense area containing irregular hyperdense foci, displacement of premolar and incisor roots, thinning and expansion of both cortical plates without perforation, and small calcified bodies at the lesion margins.

An intraoral vestibular incision was performed for an incisional biopsy. During surgery, calcified fragments and a whitish, denticle-like mass were removed. A decompression cannula was placed and sutured to maintain communication between the lesion and the oral cavity.

A 39‐year‐old man presented with a one-year history of a progressively enlarging, painless abdominal mass and increasing distension. He had no prior surgeries or medication use and denied smoking or alcohol consumption. On physical examination, his BMI was 26.4 kg/m2; he exhibited central obesity and fusiform purple striae on the inner thighs and buttocks, findings that raised suspicion for Cushing syndrome. Plasma cortisol levels were not assessed. Abdominal CT revealed two well‐circumscribed adrenal‐region masses measuring 25.6 × 16.4 × 33.0 cm on the left and 14.3 × 12.4 × 24.1 cm on the right, with noncontrast attenuation values between –111 and –98 HU and no significant enhancement on arterial, venous, or delayed phases. MRI similarly showed large lipid‐rich lesions without obvious enhancement. Branches of the left renal artery, aorta, and diaphragmatic arteries appeared to supply the left mass. The radiologic impression was highly suggestive of liposarcoma. Fine-needle aspiration yielded findings described as polycystic benign mesothelioma; subsequent immunohistochemical studies ruled out mesothelioma and demonstrated predominantly adipose tissue, suggesting an adipogenic tumor.

A 63-year-old woman presented with two weeks of diplopia and right-sided headache. She had no prior personal or family history of disease. On examination, visual acuity was normal with no exophthalmos. She had bilateral diplopia on upward gaze, with limitation of elevation of the right eye; Hess–Lancaster testing confirmed restricted movement of the right inferior rectus muscle. General examination revealed no other masses. Orbital magnetic resonance imaging showed a fusiform, hypervascularized mass in the right inferior rectus muscle with a fatty signal: it was hypointense on spin-echo T1-weighted images and hyperintense on spin-echo T2-weighted images.

A 72-year-old Japanese man, a heavy smoker of >50 pack-years with a remote history of cerebral infarction, was found on routine follow-up to have a mass in the mid-zone of the right lung. Sputum culture grew Mycobacterium gordonae, but serial chest radiographs demonstrated progressive enlargement of the lesion over 18 months. He had no history of malignancy or immunosuppression. Laboratory studies were notable only for mild renal dysfunction (BUN 38 mg/dL; Cr 1.87 mg/dL). Tumor markers were modestly elevated: CEA 4.3 ng/mL, SCC 5.3 ng/mL, CYFRA 5.3 ng/mL, NSE 13.5 ng/mL, and pro-GRP 78.8 pg/mL; CA 19-9 and SLX were normal. Chest CT revealed a well-demarcated 37 × 30 × 23 mm mass in the right upper lobe, with central, thin-walled cavitation. No lymphadenopathy or distant metastases were seen on head and abdominal imaging. Bronchial brushing cytology showed clusters and three-dimensional sheets of cohesive small to medium (12–20 μm) tumor cells with scant cytoplasm, hyperchromatic granular nuclei, inconspicuous nucleoli, and occasional mitoses. Rosette formation and necrotic background were absent. Based on these findings, the lesion was interpreted as suspicious for carcinoma, such as atypical carcinoid, and a right upper lobectomy was performed.

An 89-year-old Japanese man was referred for evaluation of a gallbladder lesion detected on surveillance imaging. He had a history of papillary adenocarcinoma of the left upper lobe (pT3N2M0, Stage IIIB), for which he underwent lobectomy 3 years earlier; mediastinal lymph node and right-lobe pulmonary metastases developed 2 years later and have been stable after chemoradiotherapy. His comorbidities included left internal carotid artery stenosis, early colorectal and bladder cancers, hypertension, and hyperuricemia. He reported no abdominal symptoms, and physical examination findings were unremarkable.

Surveillance 18F-FDG PET-CT showed focal uptake in the gallbladder fundus (SUVmax 4.2) and in hepatoduodenal lymph nodes (SUVmax 3.2), as well as in mediastinal lymph nodes (right carinal node SUVmax 11.0; para-aortic node SUVmax 6.1). On PET-CT, the gallbladder lesion measured 15 mm in diameter, and the hepatoduodenal lymph nodes measured 12 mm. There was no appreciable change in size of the known pulmonary lesions.

A 46-year-old Asian man was referred to the endocrine clinic after sustaining a subacute atraumatic fracture of the left femoral diaphysis, for which he underwent surgery. In the months before surgery, he had progressive atraumatic left thigh pain, muscle cramps, and loosening of his lower teeth requiring dental implants. On examination, he used a walker but had no palpable bony abnormalities. 

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and renal function. His parathyroid hormone level was elevated at 84.3 pg/mL, serum phosphorus was low at 1.8 mg/dL, and 25-hydroxy vitamin D was mildly decreased at 25 ng/mL. Alkaline phosphatase was elevated at 160 U/L; bone-specific alkaline phosphatase was elevated at 74.8 mcg/L. Serum and urine calcium levels and thyroid function were normal. The urine phosphate-to-creatinine ratio was 0.168, which was inappropriately high for his degree of hypophosphatemia.

Given the elevated PTH, low phosphorus, and insufficiency fracture, normocalcemic primary hyperparathyroidism was considered. The patient was started on ergocalciferol; his PTH normalized but his serum phosphorus remained severely low. Paget’s disease was also considered because of elevated alkaline phosphatase levels but was felt to be inconsistent with his hypophosphatemia and atraumatic fracture. Because of persistent severe hypophosphatemia without hyperparathyroidism as a cause, serum FGF23 was obtained to rule out oncogenic osteomalacia.

A 74-year-old man was referred for evaluation of hypertension, proteinuria, and hematuria. On examination, his blood pressure was 146/92 mm Hg. Laboratory studies showed a serum creatinine level of 5.47 mg/dL, uric acid 11.6 mg/dL, and potassium 6.1 mEq/L. Serum tumor markers were elevated (CEA 7.4 ng/mL, CYFRA 5.7 ng/mL, proGRP 178.9 pg/mL). His history was notable only for hypertension; family history was unremarkable. Abdominal CT revealed a 9.7 × 7.0 cm mass in the lower pole of the right kidney and multiple small nodules in the lower lobes of the lungs, suggestive of metastases. He underwent a laparoscopic right nephrectomy. 

Gross examination showed a 55 × 94 mm white-to-tan tumor in the lower portion of the kidney with marked hemorrhage and necrosis. Microscopically, the lesion consisted of solid sheets of polygonal to ovoid cells with round nuclei, clear to eosinophilic cytoplasm, indistinct cell borders, and 5 mitoses per 10 high-power fields. Immunohistochemistry revealed positivity for CD10, MUC1, vimentin, WT-1, smooth muscle actin, caldesmon, and CD34, and negativity for cytokeratin AE1/AE3, CAM5.2, EMA, PAX8, S-100, HMB45, c-kit, and STAT6; a few cells were renin-positive, and the MIB-1 labeling index was 4%. Electron microscopy demonstrated near-rhomboid crystalline structures within tumor cells.

A 17-year-old man was referred after an orthodontic evaluation revealed an incidental mixed radiolucent–radiopaque lesion in the right anterior maxilla. He was asymptomatic, with no history of trauma, pain, paresthesia, or lymphadenopathy. Extraoral examination was normal. Intraorally, there was slight hard swelling from the right maxillary central incisor to the first molar; the anterior portion was slightly tender and fluctuant. All teeth in the area responded normally to cold testing. A panoramic radiograph showed a well-defined mixed radiolucent–radiopaque lesion extending from tooth 11 to tooth 16 with root resorption of teeth 11, 12, 14, and 15. CT scan demonstrated a 2.7 × 2.1 cm hypodense lesion displacing the floor of the right maxillary sinus, containing internal hyperdense foci and confirmed the root resorption. Under local anesthesia, cyst decompression was performed. Fine-needle aspiration yielded lemon-yellow fluid. An incisional biopsy was obtained and a decompression tube placed. Based on the history, clinical and radiographic findings, and aspiration results, provisional diagnoses included adenomatoid odontogenic tumor; calcifying odontogenic cyst; calcifying epithelial odontogenic tumor (Pindborg tumor); and juvenile cemento-ossifying fibroma in the intermediate stage.

A 74-year-old Spanish-speaking man visiting the United States from Honduras presented with a 2-month history of postprandial abdominal pain, nausea, night sweats, early satiety, and a 10-kg weight loss. One week earlier, an abdominal and pelvic CT scan had shown distal ileitis, and he had received a course of antibiotics without improvement. On re-presentation, he reported worsening symptoms and difficulty tolerating oral intake. He denied hematochezia, diarrhea, or fevers. His medical history was notable for prior appendectomy and recently treated helminth infection.

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. There was no abdominal tenderness or palpable masses, and no evidence of perianal disease. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 42 mm/hr, a C-reactive protein level of 35 mg/L, and a fecal calprotectin of 94 μg/mg. Stool studies were negative for enteric pathogens. Repeat CT imaging demonstrated persistent distal ileitis.

Ileocolonoscopy revealed a normal terminal ileum, but a nontraversable distal ileal stricture, cecal ulcers, and patchy loss of vascularity throughout the colon. Segmental biopsies of the ileum and colon were obtained. QuantiFERON-TB Gold was positive. Hepatitis B serologies showed a reactive core total antibody, a reactive e antigen, negative surface antigen, and undetectable HBV DNA. He was started on isoniazid for latent tuberculosis.

An 11-month-old girl was evaluated for a swelling of the left side of the face present since birth. The parents noted no pain, feeding or hearing difficulty, mouth-opening limitation, or neurologic deficits. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender 10 cm × 7 cm mass involving the left lateral face, extending superiorly to the temporoparietal region, medially to the mid-cheek and lateral upper eyelid, and posteriorly displacing the ear; the overlying skin was normal, and neurologic examination was unremarkable. Routine blood tests were normal, and the serum α-fetoprotein level was 7.3 ng/mL (reference range, 0–10 ng/mL). Ultrasonography demonstrated a solid-cystic mass with septations in the left temporoparietal region. Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed a well-defined, extracranial, multicystic mixed-intensity mass measuring approximately 8 × 6 × 9 cm along the left skull vault, with internal areas of fat intensity and a focal scalp defect with curvilinear communication to the extradural space. CT of the lesion showed no calcifications.

A previously healthy 10-year-old girl presented with a 6-month history of swelling of the right little finger. The swelling began as a small painless lesion and was associated with fever and chills. An initial radiograph showed a cystic and lytic lesion of the proximal phalanx of the little finger. She was treated with analgesics and antibiotics for presumed osteomyelitis, but the swelling and pain progressed. 

On referral, examination revealed a 6 × 6-cm tender, pulsatile, firm mass over the proximal phalanx of the right little finger. A radiograph showed destruction of the entire proximal phalanx with a large soft-tissue component and areas of calcification. MRI of the hand demonstrated an ill-defined expansile lesion centered in the proximal phalanx with T1 hypointense and T2/STIR hyperintense marrow signal, cortical erosion, and an adjacent juxtacortical soft-tissue mass. 

Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the lesion showed features of a “small blue round cell tumor.” CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no abnormalities.

A 29-year-old well-nourished man presented with a 2-month history of a gradual, asymptomatic swelling of the right lower face. He denied trauma or past medical illness. Vital signs were normal. Examination revealed one nontender, soft, freely movable right submandibular lymph node. Facial inspection was unremarkable, but palpation showed an ill-defined, bony hard, 2.5×3 cm swelling in the right parasymphyseal mandible, 2 cm above the inferior border; there was no crepitus, paresthesia, or warmth. Intraoral examination was normal; all teeth in the region were vital. Provisional diagnosis was central giant cell granuloma; keratocystic odontogenic tumor and ameloblastoma were also considered.

Laboratory studies showed anemia, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, leukocytosis with eosinophilia, and alkaline phosphatase of 145 IU/L. Endocrine, liver, and renal evaluations were normal. A true-occlusal radiograph demonstrated an ill-defined radiolucency in the premolar regions bilaterally and the right parasymphyseal area without cortical perforation or tooth displacement. Panoramic imaging showed scalloping of the mandibular cortex and multiple bilateral radiolucencies in the ramus and basal bone: larger lesions were well defined and nonsclerotic, smaller ones poorly defined; the internal structure was clear, with discontinuity of the lamina dura and no root resorption or tooth displacement. PA mandible views were similar, and a skeletal survey was normal.

CT-guided fine-needle aspiration of the mandible yielded osteoclast-like giant cells with scant inflammatory cells and no atypia, suggestive of a giant cell tumor.

A 72-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of left-sided nasal obstruction, frequent epistaxis, and facial pain. Her medical history was notable only for hypertension. Nasal endoscopy revealed a reddish mass occupying the left nasal cavity. MRI of the paranasal sinuses showed a mass filling the left nasal cavity and extending along the olfactory fissure area, with involvement of the osteomeatal complex but preservation of sinus aeration. The lesion was isointense relative to nasal mucosa on T1-weighted images and isointense to hyperintense on T2-weighted images.

A 78-year-old woman presented with a four-month history of a painless swelling in the right sub-brow region of her forehead, which had progressively increased in size. On examination, there was a 3.0 × 3.5 cm mass that was elastic, firm, relatively mobile, non-tender, non-pulsatile, and non-transilluminant, with normal overlying skin. MRI of the head with intravenous contrast revealed a cystic-appearing mass that was hypo-intense on T1-weighted images, hyper-intense on T2-weighted images, partially suppressed on FLAIR sequences, and showed heterogeneous enhancement after contrast administration. A distinct dark rim was noted surrounding the lesion, delineating it from the adjacent normal adipose tissue.

A 26-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of a painless, progressively enlarging swelling on the dorsum of her tongue, associated with mild difficulty swallowing and speaking but no bleeding. She denied trauma, fever, cough, or weight loss. Medical and surgical history were unremarkable. 

On examination, there was a single pale-pink exophytic growth, 2.5 × 2.0 cm in size, with a pedunculated base on the anterior dorsum of the tongue. The lesion was soft, non-tender, with a smooth surface that did not bleed on touch; there was no discharge, tongue mobility was normal, and there was no cervical lymphadenopathy. Oral hygiene was poor.
