Routine laboratory studies, including complete blood count, coagulation profile, serology, and biochemistry, were within normal limits. Based on the history and physical findings, hemangioma and papilloma were considered as the leading provisional diagnoses.

A 63-year-old woman, G5P5, menopausal for 15 years, with no comorbidities, presented with severe intermittent pelvic pain for 2 months. She denied vaginal bleeding or gastrointestinal symptoms. On examination, a well-defined, mobile, tender right suprapubic mass was palpated on abdominal and vaginal examination. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a normal uterus and a purely anechoic, thick-walled cystic lesion in the left parametrium measuring 59 × 53 mm without Doppler flow; the right ovary contained a small anechoic cyst of 25 × 22 mm. Abdominopelvic CT scan revealed a rounded, unilocular cystic formation above and left of the uterus, 66 × 50 mm in size, with a thick, regular wall and homogeneous, slightly dense fluid content without septations or vegetations, showing mild contrast enhancement. Tumor markers were within normal limits (CA 19-9 2.06 IU/ml; CA 125 7.6 IU/ml). Given her age, imaging findings, and tumor marker levels, an ovarian serous cystadenoma was diagnosed, and the patient was scheduled for surgery.

A 60-year-old woman with a 30–pack-year smoking history presented with 3 weeks of worsening posterior headache, right upper extremity dysmetria, and truncal ataxia without nausea. Vital signs were stable. Neurologic examination confirmed dysmetria and ataxia; the remainder was unremarkable.  
Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed a 1.1 cm lesion in the right cerebellum and a 0.6 cm lesion in the right parietal lobe. Chest CT detected a 2.8 cm right upper lobe mass. Paratracheal lymph node biopsy showed metastatic lung adenocarcinoma (KRAS G12C+, PD-L1 > 50%).  
Both brain metastases were treated with stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS), and she began a trial of niraparib plus pembrolizumab. Between December 2018 and June 2019, new brain lesions appeared, including a second right temporal lesion, which also received SRS. In July 2019, systemic therapy was switched to carboplatin, pemetrexed, and pembrolizumab for extracranial progression.  
From August to December 2019, headaches worsened despite steroids for presumed radiation necrosis, and MRI showed enlargement of the right temporal and cerebellar lesions. MR spectroscopy in December 2019 showed prominent lipid peaks in both lesions, favoring necrosis. The primary lung tumor and mediastinal nodes regressed. Therapy was changed to pemetrexed and bevacizumab.  
From January to May 2020, she developed new right-hand tremor, blurry vision, dysarthria, and personality change. Follow-up MRI showed improvement of the cerebellar lesion with resolution of tremor, while the right temporal lesion further enlarged despite steroids and bevacizumab. MRI with perfusion in April 2020 displayed hyperperfusion in the right temporal lobe but not in the right cerebellum.  
She was hospitalized in May 2020 for altered mental status and underwent decompressive resection of the right temporal brain mass.

A 15-year-old Japanese girl was referred with a 1-year history of a painless, slowly enlarging swelling on the dorsum of her tongue and mild throat discomfort. Her medical history was unremarkable. Intraoral examination showed a 5 mm, pedunculated, well-circumscribed nodule on the left posterior dorsal tongue near the foramen cecum. The overlying mucosa appeared normal, and the lesion felt elastic-hard and granular on palpation, suggesting a fibroma. An excisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia, and healing was uneventful.

A 64-year-old woman with a 32-pack-year smoking history underwent a screening chest CT scan, which revealed multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules up to 7.8 mm in size. A needle core biopsy of a right lower lobe nodule demonstrated moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for cytokeratin 7, cytokeratin 20, SATB2, and PAX-8, and negative for TTF-1 and estrogen receptor; GATA3 staining appeared cytoplasmic. Serum tumor markers showed markedly elevated carcinoembryonic antigen and cancer antigen 19-9 levels. Colonoscopy and abdominal/pelvic CT scans revealed no evidence of colorectal or gynecologic primary tumors. On follow-up, repeat CT imaging showed enlarging pulmonary nodules, scattered ground-glass opacities, and new sclerotic lesions in the right ilium and vertebral body concerning for osseous metastases. The patient then developed hematuria and intermittent urinary retention. Cystoscopy demonstrated an irregular, thickened bladder wall. Pelvic examination revealed a firm, fixed 4 × 3 cm urethral mass invading the anterior vaginal wall; cystoscopy showed that the mass circumferentially involved the urethra up to the bladder neck without intrinsic bladder lesions. Urethral and vaginal tumor biopsies were performed.

A 55‐year‐old man presented with a 3-month history of insidious onset diplopia when looking to the right and when focusing on distant objects. He reported no visual blurring, facial asymmetry, hearing changes, headache, vomiting, seizures, limb weakness, gait disturbance, or bowel or bladder dysfunction. On examination, his vital signs were stable, and higher mental functions were intact. Cranial‐nerve testing revealed a right sixth‐nerve palsy and nystagmus on right gaze; visual acuity and visual fields were normal. No other cranial‐nerve, motor, or sensory deficits were observed, and the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain disclosed an expansile, contrast-enhancing mass involving the entire clivus that was isointense on T1- and T2-weighted images, with erosion of the posterior wall of the sphenoid sinus and bulging of the lesion into the sinus; the pituitary gland appeared normal. With a working diagnosis of clival chordoma infiltrating the sphenoid sinus, a subfrontal trans-basal approach was planned for decompression.

A 53-year-old man was referred for evaluation of massive hemoptysis, estimated at approximately 200 mL per day for 1 week. His vital signs were stable, and his hemoglobin level was 11.5 g/dL. Two months earlier, he had undergone left nephrectomy for a 76 mm clear-cell renal carcinoma. His medical history was otherwise unremarkable, with no known bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, or exposure to tuberculosis, nontuberculous mycobacteria, or Aspergillus species. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest revealed a 16 mm nodule in the right middle lobe associated with a peritumoral hematoma. The nodule demonstrated intense enhancement in the arterial phase and washout in the venous phase. Right bronchial arteriography showed enhancement of the nodule but no evidence of contrast extravasation, arteriovenous shunting, or vascular malformation.

A 61-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of intermittent, vague abdominal pain. He had no history of hepatitis B or C, alcohol abuse, or prior surgery. He was hemodynamically stable and physical examination revealed no palpable abdominal mass or tenderness. Laboratory studies showed normal α-fetoprotein and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels, but an elevated protein induced by vitamin K absence or antagonist-II (PIVKA-II) level of 83.99 mAU/mL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen in the portal venous phase and enhanced MRI demonstrated a 7.2-cm heterogeneous, lobulated, exophytic soft-tissue mass in the left subphrenic space adjacent to the gastric fundus. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a large subepithelial lesion at the gastric fundus. A subepithelial gastric tumor such as a gastrointestinal stromal tumor or leiomyoma was suspected. Laparoscopic resection was performed and the specimen measured 7.3 cm × 6.8 cm × 4.5 cm; it appeared as a gray-to-yellow-brown solid mass within a thin fibrous capsule. The specimen was sent for pathological examination.

A 26-year-old woman, 14 weeks pregnant, was found on routine antenatal ultrasound to have a complex cystic mass in the right kidney. MRI showed a well-defined unilocular cystic lesion with multiple mural nodules at the inferior pole, radiologically suspicious for renal cell carcinoma. There was no prior chemotherapy and all blood tests were normal. At 15 weeks’ gestation, she underwent right radical nephrectomy; the tumor was confined to the kidney. 

Grossly, the specimen revealed a 5.5 × 4.5 × 3.5-cm well-encapsulated unilocular cystic tumor with multiple friable tan-gray mural nodules up to 2.0 cm in size. Microscopically, the lesion consisted of malignant epithelial cells in papillary, trabecular, and nested/alveolar patterns. The cells had discrete borders and abundant eosinophilic or finely vacuolated clear cytoplasm, mildly enlarged nuclei with occasional prominent nucleoli (Fuhrman grade 2). The stroma contained hyaline nodules, numerous psammoma bodies, and areas of hemorrhagic necrosis with hemosiderin-laden macrophages. No lymphovascular invasion was identified, and margins were clear.

A 26-year-old right-hand-dominant male warehouse worker presented with 3 months of atraumatic ulnar-sided left hand pain. The pain was aggravated by heavy lifting with ulnar deviation and often awakened him at night. On examination, there was tenderness over the hypothenar aspect of the hand and pain at end ranges of wrist flexion and extension. He had discomfort with ulnar deviation but was non-tender over the ulnar fovea. There was no instability or pain with lunotriquetral manipulation. He was tender to palpation over the pisiform but not over the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon. Capillary refill time was 2 seconds through the radial artery and 11 seconds through the ulnar artery, symmetric to the contralateral hand. Standard posteroanterior and lateral wrist radiographs were normal. An unenhanced MRI of the left wrist demonstrated marrow edema in the distal pole of the pisiform and the distal portion of the hamate, including the hook, with surrounding synovitis and overlying subcutaneous edema. These findings were concerning for an occult fracture. A CT scan of the wrist was obtained for further evaluation.

A 58-year-old man with hypertension, dyslipidemia, peripheral arterial disease, and a 40-pack-year smoking history presented with persistent exertional dyspnea. His father had a myocardial infarction at age 56. He previously underwent surgery for a pituitary adenoma. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a round, oval, mobile tumor (approximately 11 mm in diameter) attached to the pulmonary valve on the right cusp, with an estimated ejection fraction of 55%, no segmental wall-motion abnormalities, and no signs of pulmonary thromboembolism. Coronary angiography demonstrated chronic occlusion of the circumflex artery, severe distal right coronary artery stenosis, and severe stenosis of the intermediate branch. To further characterize the mass, cardiac MRI was performed and showed a 1.1 × 0.8 cm lesion that was iso- to hypointense on T1-weighted images, mildly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and displayed peripheral enhancement without central enhancement on delayed post-contrast sequences.

A 27-year-old Filipino man was admitted after generalized tonic-clonic seizures associated with documented hypoglycemia. His medical history was notable for a painless nodular mass in the right temporo-zygomatic region first noted 10 years earlier, for which he underwent five resections and postoperative radiotherapy. The lesion was diagnosed histologically as hemangiopericytoma. He remained well for two years until three months ago, when he experienced malaise and was found to be hypoglycemic during a prior hospitalization. One month later, he had new-onset generalized tonic-clonic seizures; evaluation again revealed hypoglycemia, and he was discharged for outpatient oncologic work-up. 

On the day of his current admission, he had another seizure with transient deterioration of consciousness. He had no history of diabetes, hypertension, insulin or other glucose-lowering drug use, alcohol ingestion, herbal remedies, or illicit drug use. On examination, he was drowsy but oriented, with a heart rate of 108 bpm, blood pressure of 110/60 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 20/min, and temperature of 36.1°C. He was obese (BMI 30.8 kg/m2), had a depressed surgical scar over the right temporo-zygomatic area, and hepatomegaly (liver span 15 cm at the midclavicular line). The remainder of the physical and neurologic examinations was unremarkable.

A 72-hour fasting protocol was initiated. At six hours, he developed neuroglycopenic symptoms with a capillary blood glucose of 42 mg/dL, prompting termination of the fast. Post-fast laboratory studies showed decreased insulin and C-peptide levels, excluding endogenous pancreatic insulin hypersecretion. Cranial CT showed no recurrent intracranial mass. Abdominal CT revealed multiple well-defined, heterogeneously enhancing ovoid lesions in the right hepatic lobe (largest measuring 10.2×9.1×10.7 cm) and a right adrenal lesion measuring 3.7×4.4×6.4 cm, compatible with metastases. Chest CT demonstrated bilateral pulmonary nodules without skeletal involvement. Histologic review of prior resections of the temporo-zygomatic mass showed sheets of atypical pericytes surrounding thin-walled, ramifying vessels with scant connective tissue.

A 34-year-old man with autism presented with a 2-year history of progressive abdominal distension. On examination, there was a large, tender mass spanning the midline in the middle and lower abdominal quadrants. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated an 18 × 13 cm hypomesogastric mass composed of two components: a predominantly hyperechoic solid portion and, superiorly, multiple cystic-appearing cavities. Duplex and color Doppler imaging showed the mass surrounding the celiac trunk and mesenteric vessels without flow alterations.

Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a 25 × 13 cm abdominal mass extending from the hepatic hilus to the pelvis. The lesion abutted the great vessels posteriorly and displaced the small bowel downward and the transverse colon upward. It contained a fatty area with attenuation of −85 HU adjacent to the mesentery and a hyperdense dorsal portion measuring 32 HU.

Magnetic resonance imaging before and after gadolinium demonstrated a mass with fat-signal intensity in the ventral portion and a multicystic-appearing area dorsally. Fat-suppressed sequences confirmed adipose tissue in the ventral segment and cystic characteristics of the dorsal segment. There was no significant enhancement after contrast administration and no evidence of invasion of adjacent organs or vessels.

An 84-year-old woman presented with a right breast mass that she first noticed more than 1 year earlier. She reported intermittent pain and discomfort in the lump for the past 12 months. Her personal and family histories were unremarkable.  

On examination, there was a 3.0 cm × 2.0 cm × 2.0 cm firm, well-circumscribed mass in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast without overlying skin or nipple changes and without axillary lymphadenopathy.  

Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits.  

Breast ultrasound showed a mixed echogenic mass with clear margins, uneven internal echo, and disordered blood-flow signals (BI-RADS category 4C). Chest CT demonstrated a nodular soft-tissue density in the right breast measuring approximately 2.0 cm in diameter, with no axillary lymphadenopathy.

A 19-year-old female presented with 9 months of insidious right wrist pain and swelling without antecedent trauma. Examination revealed swelling and tenderness on the ulnar aspect of the right wrist, with intact pulses, sensation, and a full range of motion.  
Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the right forearm showed an expansile, mixed lytic lesion with a broad zone of transition in the distal ulna. A provisional diagnosis of giant cell tumor was made, with fibrous dysplasia and Ewing’s sarcoma also considered.  
MRI of the right forearm demonstrated a 7.07 × 2.63 × 1.92 cm lobulated intraosseous mass in the distal ulna that was iso- to hypointense to muscle on T1-weighted images and heterogenous on T2-weighted images with a triple signal pattern. Postcontrast images showed avid enhancement with areas of cystic necrosis.  
A tru-cut biopsy of the distal ulna revealed spindle-shaped cells arranged in a whorled pattern, with occasional large ganglion-like cells, and a diagnosis of nodular fasciitis was made.

A 55-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of epigastric pain and a palpable lump. She denied nausea, vomiting, weight loss, jaundice, gastrointestinal bleeding, or constitutional symptoms. She had no history of pancreatitis or prior surgeries. On examination, there was a firm, minimally mobile mass in the epigastric and right hypochondrial regions extending into the right lumbar area. Routine blood tests were unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a well-defined exophytic cystic lesion measuring 15 × 8 × 10 cm arising from the second and third parts of the duodenum, with a small solid component at its origin and luminal narrowing. Upper endoscopy revealed a polypoid lesion in the distal second part of the duodenum adjacent to an apparent diverticular opening. Multiple attempts at endoscopic biopsy, including with a pediatric scope, were unsuccessful due to the lesion’s angulation.

A working preoperative diagnosis was a duodenal diverticulum with possible malignant transformation. The patient was scheduled for exploratory laparotomy with a tentative plan for pancreaticoduodenectomy.

A 61-year-old man presented with an 11-month history of a progressively swollen left cheek. He denied any history of trauma or prior surgical procedures. On examination, there was noticeable swelling of the left buccal mucosa without overlying skin changes.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the face showed a lobulated cystic lesion measuring 3.0 × 3.8 × 4.6 cm, located in the left masticator space and extending along the anterior border of the mandibular ramus. The lesion had low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, and exhibited thin peripheral rim enhancement after gadolinium administration.

A 25-year-old woman presented to a student health clinic with several months of increasing abdominal fullness, left-sided lower back pain, and left lateral thigh numbness. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. On examination, there was a large, fixed mass in the left upper and lower abdominal quadrants. Laboratory testing revealed a carcinoembryonic antigen level of 49 ng/mL. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis showed a large retroperitoneal mass with both cystic and solid components. Ultrasound-guided biopsy of the solid portion demonstrated well-differentiated adenocarcinoma with intestinal morphology. Subsequent colonoscopy and gynecologic examination revealed no abnormalities. Positron-emission tomography showed uptake in the primary lesion without evidence of distant metastatic disease.

A 66-year-old man with a history of diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia presented with sudden-onset difficulty walking. He was alert and fully oriented (GCS 15), with fluent speech, intact comprehension and repetition, and no cranial nerve deficits. Motor strength was 5/5 in all extremities, sensation and deep tendon reflexes were normal, and there was no dysmetria or dysdiadochokinesia. The Romberg and tandem gait tests were positive, with a tendency to sway to the left. A noncontrast head CT was negative for intracerebral hemorrhage. Diffusion-weighted MRI of the brain showed no acute infarct. Cervical MRI revealed no pathology to explain the ataxia. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography excluded peripheral neuropathy. The patient was admitted for further evaluation of the etiology of acute ataxia.

A 66-year-old non-Hispanic white man presented with a 3-month history of a self-palpable, slowly enlarging, nontender lump in his left groin. He reported intermittent dull pain at the site but denied fevers, night sweats, weight loss, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, dyspnea, or weakness. His medical history included hypertension, dyslipidemia, and obesity (BMI 32 kg/m2). 

Ultrasound-guided needle biopsy of the groin mass demonstrated a stage III malignant melanoma. Immunohistochemical staining showed diffuse, strong positivity for S-100, SOX10, and MART-1. 

On further questioning, he recalled that 2 years earlier he had accidentally scraped off a “mole” on the medial aspect of his left ankle with his toenail; although the superficial lesion healed, he noted a new deep, rock-hard nodule in that same area. 

A PET scan revealed a 1.4 × 0.9 cm nodule in the left medial ankle (SUV 21) and an enlarged left inguinal lymph node (SUV 84). MRI of the brain was negative for metastases. Ultrasound-guided biopsy of the ankle nodule confirmed nodular malignant melanoma with an 8.9 mm Breslow depth, without an epidermal component, ulceration, or lymphovascular invasion.

A 42-year-old man was brought to the emergency department in a comatose state (Glasgow Coma Scale score of 4). Relatives reported sudden onset of headache followed by several episodes of vomiting. On arrival, he was sedated, intubated, and unresponsive to verbal or painful stimuli; pupils were bilaterally dilated and nonreactive.  
 
An urgent noncontrast head CT revealed a large right frontal intraparenchymal hemorrhage with severe surrounding edema, significant mass effect, compression of the right lateral ventricle, and evidence of tonsillar herniation.  

An external ventricular drain was placed in the left lateral ventricle, and an intraparenchymal pressure monitor was inserted in the right frontal perilesional region; intracranial pressure exceeded 40 mmHg. The patient underwent bilateral decompressive craniectomies and evacuation of the hematoma. Intraoperatively, after clot removal, a cherry-like, round, lobulated lesion was identified in the edematous right frontal lobe and was completely resected.

A 41-year-old man presented with one month of left lumbar pain and gross hematuria. He had no significant medical or family history and no alcohol use; he chewed tobacco daily for 10 years. On examination, vital signs were normal, and his ECOG performance status was 1. There was a non-tender, firm, smooth 5×5 cm mass in the left lumbar region and conjunctival pallor; no lymphadenopathy or jaundice was noted. Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin concentration of 6.7 g/dL, serum creatinine of 2.1 mg/dL, and blood urea nitrogen of 25 mg/dL; other values were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed an enlarged left kidney almost completely replaced by a heterogeneous hypodense mass, with a filling defect extending from the left renal vein into the inferior vena cava. A percutaneous core biopsy of the mass demonstrated sheets of round-to-spindle cells in a hemangiopericytoma-like pattern with areas of hyalinization; at high power, entrapped normal renal tubules were seen. Immunohistochemical studies showed tumor cells positive for CD99, BCL2, and vimentin, and negative for pan-cytokeratin (AE1), epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), and leukocyte common antigen (LCA).

A 72‐year‐old man with hypertension and reflux esophagitis presented with three years of progressive dysphagia. In June 2022, he developed respiratory distress in the left lateral decubitus position. Fiberscopic examination showed a pedunculated mass arising from the right aryepiglottic fold that swung pendulum‐like during phonation and breathing, nearly obscuring the glottis. Narrow‐band imaging revealed no mucosal abnormalities. Contrast‐enhanced CT demonstrated a 25×12×25 mm homogeneous, oval soft‐tissue mass bordering the right lamina propria with enhancement similar to pharyngeal mucosa. Contrast‐enhanced MRI showed uniform early enhancement. The preoperative differential diagnosis included cancer, lymphoma, soft‐tissue tumour, and amyloidosis. A tracheotomy was performed under local anaesthesia, and the mass was completely excised via direct laryngoscopy. 

Histologic examination revealed diffuse proliferation of plasma cells in the submucosal stroma with germinal centres. Immunohistochemistry showed CD138 positivity, IgG+, IgA–, IgM–, and focal CD20+ cells. In situ hybridization demonstrated kappa light‐chain restriction. DFS staining was negative for amyloid, and AE1/AE3 cytokeratin staining was negative. Flow cytometry of the tumour cells was CD19+, CD10–, and CD56–. Bone marrow biopsy showed no tumour infiltration. Serum levels of IgG, IgA, IgM, and the κ/λ ratio were within normal limits. Cytogenetic analysis of the lesion revealed a normal karyotype.

A 66-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of headaches and light-headedness. Her medical history was notable for invasive ductal breast cancer treated with breast-conserving surgery, adjuvant hormonal therapy, and radiation approximately 10 years earlier. 

On non-contrast CT of the skull base, there was a quadrangular, lytic lesion within the clivus with internal foci of calcification; the sella was not expanded but had focal areas of bone erosion. MRI showed a well-circumscribed clival mass that was isointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and demonstrated avid heterogeneous enhancement. There was no extension into the sella, and the native pituitary gland appeared normal with a midline infundibulum. On bone scan the lesion was photopenic.

Serum biochemistry revealed prolactin levels between 4.6 and 8 times the upper limit of normal without significant macroprolactin. Follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone levels were lower than expected for her postmenopausal state, while thyroid, adrenal, and growth hormone axes were intact.

A 45-year-old man was referred after a routine chest radiograph showed an abnormal shadow in the right lower lung field. He reported slight dyspnea on exertion for 3 months but no other symptoms. He had no smoking history or prior medical conditions. 

Chest CT revealed a well-defined 13 × 10 cm mass in the anterior-inferior mediastinum abutting the diaphragm, pericardium, right inferior pulmonary vein, and superior vena cava, with heterogeneous contrast enhancement. FDG-PET showed uptake in the mass (maximum SUV, 4.2). 

Laboratory studies demonstrated normal serum alpha-fetoprotein (2.4 ng/ml), normal beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (<0.2 ng/ml), and a negative anti-acetylcholine-receptor antibody. 

Differential diagnosis included thymoma, thymic carcinoma, and a germ cell tumor; surgical resection was thus recommended.

A 32-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of insidious pain over the lateral aspect of his left foot and pins-and-needles sensation in the plantar surface. He denied any history of trauma. Six months earlier he had noted a small, peanut-shaped swelling behind his left knee, which gradually increased in size.

On examination, there was an oval, firm, nonpulsatile, nonfluctuant, nontransilluminating mass measuring approximately 2×3×1 cm in the left popliteal fossa. The mass was mobile in both directions and the overlying skin was pinchable. Neurologic examination revealed decreased sensation over the lateral plantar aspect of the left foot; motor strength was preserved. Distal pulses in the left popliteal and dorsalis pedis arteries were palpable.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the left popliteal fossa showed an encapsulated, round to oval lesion eccentrically placed within the intermuscular space posterior to the knee joint. The lesion was homogeneously isointense on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with focal hypointense areas suggestive of a fascicular sign. Sagittal images demonstrated continuity of the mass with the tibial nerve and a fat-split sign. The lesion measured 2×3×1 cm.

A 37-year-old Filipino man presented with a 3-month history of a progressively enlarging fleshy, fibrovascular mass in his right eye, associated with blurred vision, foreign-body sensation, redness, and intermittent tearing but no pain. He worked as a tricycle driver with prolonged sun exposure and had no history of ocular trauma or surgery. On examination, an 8.5 mm × 8.0 mm elevated, pedunculated fibrovascular lesion was noted at the superonasal limbus, encroaching onto the peripheral cornea. The surface was irregular and covered with whitish-gray plaques, and feeder vessels were visible around the base. There were no other lesions on the eyelids or adnexa, no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy, and dilated fundus examination was normal. The patient was HIV-seronegative. 
Given the clinical appearance and the patient’s age, ocular surface squamous neoplasia was the leading diagnosis. He underwent wide excision of the lesion using a no-touch technique under local anesthesia, and the specimen was sent for histopathological examination.

A 21-year-old woman presented with a 7-day history of a reddish-bluish swelling on the left inner cheek that had appeared after an accidental bite. She reported occasional similar episodes of cheek biting and bleeding, but no marked change in the lesion’s size. Her mother recalled a mild left-cheek swelling at age 5, which was monitored without intervention. 

On extraoral examination, there was slight left facial asymmetry with asymmetric nasolabial folds on smiling; facial movements were normal. Intraorally, a solitary 2 cm × 1 cm reddish-bluish swelling with a translucent yellow surface was noted on the left buccal mucosa, extending from the occlusal plane to 1 cm above the retromolar trigone and 2 cm from the corner of the mouth. The surface was irregular, showed tooth-indentation marks, and multiple pinhead-sized clear vesicles were seen near its superior border. Palpation revealed a soft, slightly tender, nonindurated, nonpulsatile submucosal mass that was not adherent to the skin; the surrounding mucosa was normal. A 1 cm × 1 cm nontender, movable left submandibular lymph node was palpable.

A provisional diagnosis of traumatic hematoma was made, with lymphangioma and hemangioma considered in the differential. After informed consent, the lesion was excised under local anesthesia without identification of a feeder vessel, and the specimen was sent for histopathological examination.

A 27-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of chronic gastrointestinal symptoms that had progressively worsened over several years, including nausea, vomiting, bloating, diarrhea, and epigastric pain radiating to the back. The pain was precipitated by motion and relieved at rest. She denied fevers, fatigue, or weight loss. Her past medical history was notable only for recurrent urinary tract infections; she took ondansetron and had a hormonal intrauterine device. Family history was noncontributory.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Abdominal exam revealed epigastric tenderness without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies, including amylase, lipase, liver enzymes, and catecholamine levels, were within normal limits.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a lobulated, hypoechoic retroperitoneal mass measuring 29 × 33 × 28 mm. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a well-defined, noninvasive hypodense mass (37 × 24 × 29 mm) abutting the portal vein, celiac axis, common hepatic artery, and caudate lobe of the liver; fat planes were preserved and there was no vascular encasement. MRI confirmed a 26 × 37 × 36 mm retroperitoneal lesion with an enhancing capsule, preserved fat planes, and no evidence of invasion into adjacent vessels or organs.

A 39-year-old woman underwent resection of a dorsal surface lesion on her right third metacarpal that had been diagnosed elsewhere as an osteochondroma. Within months she noted rapid recurrence of a firm, painful mass with increased swelling and progressive limitation of metacarpophalangeal motion (0° to 40°). She had no history of trauma. On examination, there was a well-healed dorsal incision overlying a prominent, non-tender, firm 2- to 3-cm mass; neurovascular function was intact. 

Plain radiographs showed an ossified mass bordering the dorsal aspect of the distal third metacarpal. CT scanning demonstrated continuity between the medullary cavity of the lesion and that of the underlying bone. MRI revealed a juxtacortical mass with mature ossification, containing both cortical and medullary components. Review of imaging obtained before the initial resection showed an exophytic lesion with a corticated rim and a cartilaginous cap and no medullary continuity. 

The differential diagnosis at this point included osteochondroma, periosteal osteosarcoma, and periosteal chondrosarcoma.

An 11-year-old Japanese boy was referred for evaluation of painless bone expansion of the right maxillary alveolus, delayed eruption of the permanent second molars, and altered occlusion. He had no significant medical or family history. A panoramic radiograph showed a unilocular cystic lesion in the right maxilla containing a calcified mass associated with an impacted tooth. CT imaging revealed a 3.6 × 3.1 × 2.7 cm cystic lesion with internal calcified structures and expansion of the right maxillary bone.

A 26‐year‐old man presented with a several‐month history of pain and swelling in his left heel. On examination, there was localized tenderness over the anterior aspect of the calcaneus without overlying skin changes or neurovascular compromise.  

Plain radiographs of the left foot showed a 2.0‐cm intraosseous, eccentric, expansile, well‐demarcated osteolytic lesion in the anterior calcaneus. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated that the lesion was subcortical and predominantly solid with a small cystic component and distinct internal septations; there were no fluid–fluid levels. The cortical bone varied in thickness and was focally disrupted, but there was no peripheral shell of bone.

An 89-year-old woman was referred with a 2–3 week history of a right chin swelling and tenderness, and a firm intraoral lump. She had no response to a 1-week course of doxycycline. Medical history was notable for cardiovascular disease and advanced dementia. Medications included clopidogrel and psychotropic agents. She was a lifelong non-smoker and non-drinker. Examination revealed a moderate-sized, firm swelling on the right chin with an intraoral component fixed to bone. An orthopantomogram showed an ill-defined radiolucency in the right mandible from the left lower lateral incisor region to the right lower canine region. Computed tomography was not performed due to the patient’s dementia. Under local anesthesia, surgical exploration revealed a pale cystic lining adherent to mucosa and brown fluid within the cavity; the cyst was enucleated with curettage. Cytopathological analysis of the aspirate showed numerous neutrophils, foamy macrophages, and cholesterol clefts, consistent with cyst contents.

A 15-year-old girl presented with a 6‐month history of painless swelling below her right eye, gradually enlarging to 4×3 cm. There was no medical or surgical history of note. Examination showed a firm, non‐tender swelling extending from the infraorbital rim to the maxillary roof, medially to the lateral nasal wall, and laterally to the zygomatic body, with focal skin thinning and ulceration. Ophthalmologic evaluation revealed normal vision and extraocular movements without proptosis. There was no facial paraesthesia and intraoral examination was unremarkable. CT of the face demonstrated a well‐circumscribed 2×2 cm lesion of mixed hyperdense and hypodense areas involving the infraorbital rim, without involvement of the maxillary sinus or nasal septum. A provisional diagnosis of ossifying fibroma was made, and an excisional biopsy was planned.

A 3-year-old Nigerian boy was evaluated for 4 months of left flank swelling and recurrent fever. The swelling had progressively increased but was painless. There was no hematuria, no change in urine output, no peripheral edema, and no weight loss or anorexia. There was no family history of similar disease.

On examination, the abdomen was distended with fullness of the left flank and distended anterior abdominal wall veins. A firm, nontender mass occupied the left flank. Vital signs showed tachycardia at 140 beats per minute and blood pressure of 100/60 mm Hg. The external genitalia were normal.

Laboratory studies revealed a packed cell volume of 30% with normal white-cell differentials. Blood urea nitrogen and serum creatinine were normal. Urinalysis was unremarkable.

A plain abdominal radiograph (KUB) showed abdominal distension with fullness of the left flank and rightward displacement of bowel loops by a left-sided soft-tissue mass. 

Ultrasonography demonstrated that the left kidney was enlarged (15.6 cm × 10.4 cm) with a heterogeneous mass in the mid and lower poles measuring 12.5 cm × 11.3 cm. The mass distorted the renal parenchyma, showed increased flow on Doppler interrogation, and had no calcifications. There was moderate hydronephrosis of the upper pole calyx and pelvic moiety. The mass crossed the midline and displaced—but did not encase—the aorta and inferior vena cava. The right kidney was mildly enlarged (8.1 cm × 3.6 cm) with preserved corticomedullary differentiation and mild pelvicalyceal fullness. The liver, spleen, gallbladder, pancreas, and para-aortic area appeared normal, and no ascites was seen.

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed a large heterogeneous mass with solid and cystic components occupying most of the left kidney, with a rim of normal tissue in the upper pole. The mass measured 15 cm × 13.1 cm, enhanced heterogeneously, and contained no calcifications. The upper-pole calyceal system was dilated and the left ureter was not visualized. There was mass effect displacing bowel loops, aorta, and inferior vena cava to the right without encasement. No intraluminal filling defect was seen in the left renal vein. The right kidney measured 8.6 cm × 4.1 cm with normal parenchymal density, prompt contrast excretion, and mild pelvicalyceal dilatation. The right ureter, urinary bladder, lung bases, and visualized bones were normal.

A 14-year-old girl with no significant past medical history presented with four months of progressive exertional dyspnea. On examination she had signs of superior vena cava syndrome, including facial and neck edema with engorged supraclavicular fossae. Multiple café-au-lait spots were noted on her trunk and lower limbs; no palpable lymphadenopathy or peripheral masses were found. A chest radiograph showed opacification of the left hemithorax with mediastinal shift to the right. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a heterogeneous anterior mediastinal mass measuring 120 × 109 × 142 mm with cervical extension, displacement of the heart, great vessels, and trachea to the right, scalloping of the anterior vertebral bodies at T3–T5, a small left pleural effusion, and atelectasis of the left lower lobe and lingula. Serum alpha-fetoprotein and beta-human chorionic gonadotropin levels were within normal limits.

A 73-year-old woman with a 20-year history of diabetes and hypertension presented with 12 days of new-onset inflexibility of her left limbs. Seven days before admission, she experienced transient convulsions involving her left upper limb and face, accompanied by dizziness, nausea, and headache. She remained conscious and afebrile, with no incontinence. On examination, she was alert and fluent. Cranial nerves were intact. Muscle strength was grade V on the right and grade IV on the left. Reflexes and coordination were normal. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed an irregular, 2.8 × 2.3 cm right frontoparietal parenchymal lesion with mixed T1 and T2 signal intensity, clear boundaries, finger-cuff edema, and ringlike enhancement after gadolinium. Staging computed tomography demonstrated multiple lesions: mildly hypoattenuating, ring-enhancing nodules in the liver; nodular high-density lesions with uneven mild enhancement in the adrenal glands; soft-tissue-density destruction in the iliac bone; a solid pulmonary nodule in the right upper lobe; and focal rib destruction.

A term African American male infant was delivered by spontaneous vaginal delivery at 39 weeks 1 day, birth weight 3.03 kg. The mother’s prenatal care included a fetal echocardiogram at 32 weeks 5 days for suspected fetal arrhythmia, which showed two small (4.0 mm × 2.6 mm) echogenic masses in the right ventricular apex and septal aspect, suspicious for rhabdomyomas. Third-trimester ultrasound demonstrated oligohydramnios (AFI 4.86), and the mother was GBS positive, receiving intrapartum penicillin.

After an uncomplicated birth, the infant was admitted to the NICU for postnatal cardiac evaluation and concern for tuberous sclerosis. He had one episode of brown emesis managed with gastric lavage and IV fluids; he then tolerated full enteral feeds. An ECG showed normal sinus rhythm for age. Postnatal transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated that the two masses were smaller than on prenatal imaging, with no inflow or outflow obstruction and normal cardiac structure and function; no arrhythmias were observed.

During a 4-day NICU stay, the infant remained hemodynamically stable on room air, with normal vital signs, tone, reflexes, and no seizure activity. Pediatric cardiology recommended repeat imaging in 3–4 months unless instability occurred. Pediatric neurology examination was normal. Dermatologic inspection revealed no hypo- or hyperpigmented lesions. Cranial and renal ultrasounds were unremarkable. Brain MRI showed no intracranial manifestations of tuberous sclerosis. Pediatric ophthalmology found well-formed eyes with normal anterior segment, disc, macula, vessels, and zone 3 retinal vascularization, recommending follow-up in one month. The infant was discharged with outpatient follow-up arranged with pediatrics, genetics, cardiology, neurology, ophthalmology, and dermatology.

A 58-year-old woman presented with one week of right ankle pain. MRI of the right distal tibia revealed a mass, and open biopsy showed osteoblastic conventional osteosarcoma. Baseline chest radiography and CT showed no pulmonary lesions but identified two discrete calcified nodules: one in the right breast and one in the anterior mediastinum. Given her planned neoadjuvant intra-arterial chemotherapy, the differential included benign granuloma versus metastasis, and short-term follow-up was recommended. Three weeks later, repeat chest CT demonstrated interval enlargement of both calcified masses. The patient was referred for breast imaging. Diagnostic mammography showed a dense calcified mass in the right upper breast with spiculated margins. Breast ultrasound revealed a 1.5 cm dense calcified mass with posterior acoustic shadowing. Percutaneous core biopsy was deemed difficult because of dense calcifications, and excisional biopsy was planned for definitive diagnosis.

A 60-year-old woman with hypertension presented with intermittent postprandial bloating and was known to have an atrophic right kidney with hydronephrosis. Physical examination revealed left lower quadrant abdominal tenderness without costovertebral angle tenderness. Laboratory tests showed an elevated serum creatinine level; urinalysis and autoimmune studies were unremarkable. Non–contrast CT of the abdomen demonstrated wall thickening of the descending duodenum and left-sided hydronephrosis with renal atrophy. Because of allergies to procaine and iodine, contrast enhancement was avoided. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and small-bowel endoscopy revealed circumferential stenosis at the junction of the descending and inferior duodenum. Multiple mucosal biopsies showed only duodenitis. To further evaluate the lesion, endoscopic ultrasound–guided fine-needle aspiration (EUS-FNA) of the thickened duodenal wall was performed using a 22-gauge needle. Endoscopic ultrasound revealed a duodenal wall thickness of 15 mm. On-site cytologic evaluation demonstrated increased cellularity and markedly atypical clusters suggestive of a poorly differentiated carcinoma.

A 21-day-old female infant, born at 38 weeks’ gestation after an uncomplicated pregnancy and spontaneous vaginal delivery (Apgar scores 9 and 10), was discharged home on day 2 of life. There was no family history of genetic disease and no prenatal abnormalities. The mother noted frequent post-feed vomiting that was initially milky but progressed to bilious vomitus despite anti-reflux positioning and medication. At 3 kg and 21 days of age, the infant was brought to the hospital with dehydration, jaundice, irritability, and marked abdominal distension. A nasogastric tube immediately returned large volumes of bilious fluid.  
Plain abdominal radiography demonstrated distended small-bowel loops. A contrast study showed complete failure of contrast progression beyond the proximal jejunum, suggesting a type I jejunal atresia (in membrane). After correction of fluid and electrolyte imbalances, the infant underwent a supraumbilical transverse laparotomy. Intraoperatively, the only abnormality was a stenotic segment of proximal jejunum with a purplish hue; the remainder of the small intestine and colon appeared normal without additional areas of stenosis. A 7 cm segment, located 15 cm distal to the ligament of Treitz, was resected, and an end-to-end anastomosis was performed, along with placement of a post-pyloric jejunostomy tube.

A 42-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of right knee pain. She described a sharp, shooting pain triggered by pressure over a point just medial to the patellar ligament at the joint line. She was apprehensive during the examination and resisted repeated palpation because of the severity of pain. Deep knee flexion, such as squatting or sitting cross-legged, reproduced the pain. She had no history of temperature-related exacerbation. She had seen multiple physicians without a diagnosis. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 7800 cells/mm3 and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 10 mm/hr. A plain radiograph of the knee was normal. MRI of the knee revealed a 1 × 1 cm nodule in Hoffa’s fat pad inferior to the patella, which was hyperintense on T2-weighted images and hypointense on T1-weighted images. An ischemia test (Hildreth sign) was performed and was positive.

A 36-year-old woman presented with 5 days of intense, colicky left lower abdominal pain radiating to the groin and lower back, accompanied by nausea. She denied fever, genitourinary symptoms, or bowel changes. Over the preceding 6 months, she noted palpitations, heat intolerance, a 7-kg unintentional weight loss, insomnia, and tremor.  
Vital signs: temperature 36.5°C, blood pressure 105/60 mmHg, heart rate 110 bpm, respiratory rate 20/min. She appeared anxious but was in no acute distress. Cardiac exam revealed a hyperdynamic precordium. The thyroid gland was nonpalpable. Abdominal exam was soft with localized tenderness in the left iliac fossa without rebound.  
Her medical history was unremarkable; she had two prior term pregnancies, regular menstrual cycles, no medications, and occasional weekend alcohol use. Family history included primary hypothyroidism in a maternal grandmother.  
Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, metabolic panel, liver function tests, and urinalysis. Thyroid function tests demonstrated a thyrotropin level <0.01 mIU/mL and a free T4 of 2.6 ng/dL.  
Pelvic ultrasound revealed a solid left adnexal mass, confirmed by CT scan. A 99mTc thyroid scan showed complete absence of uptake, and dedicated thyroid ultrasonography was unremarkable.

A 57-year-old man presented with profuse blood-streaked mucous drainage from his penis. He had sustained a T12 spinal cord injury in a motor vehicle accident in 1971, and in 1975 underwent ileal conduit urinary diversion for intractable incontinence and vesicoureteral reflux, with the native bladder left in situ. On examination, a right prostatic nodule was palpated; the prostate-specific antigen level was 1.5 ng/mL. Transrectal prostate biopsies showed mucinous adenocarcinoma in six of eight cores, with large pools of mucin dissecting the parenchyma and nests of columnar cells floating within mucin. Immunohistochemical studies revealed positivity for carcinoembryonic antigen, cytokeratin-7, and cytokeratin-20, and negativity for prostate specific antigen and prostatic acid phosphatase. Colonoscopy identified multiple adenomatous polyps without invasive carcinoma. Cystoscopy showed a massive amount of mucoid material within the bladder associated with a mass. Bladder washings and biopsies demonstrated copious mucin with malignant glandular nests and single cells consistent with mucinous adenocarcinoma.

A 4-year-old boy was referred after an incidental liver cyst was discovered on abdominal ultrasound performed for congenital hydronephrosis. He was asymptomatic, with no history of hepatic disease, biliary obstruction, infection, or abdominal pain. 

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a 5.3 × 4.8 × 2.2 cm minimally complex, partially exophytic cyst in the right hepatic lobe, with minimally enhancing septations. 

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, α-fetoprotein level, prothrombin time, hepatic function panel, and Echinococcus antibody titers, were within normal limits. 

Annual surveillance ultrasound demonstrated an increase in cyst size over 3 years to 7.4 × 6.1 × 3.0 cm. The patient remained asymptomatic. 

What is your differential diagnosis, and what diagnostic or therapeutic steps would you take next?

A 30-year-old man who worked as a manual laborer presented with a 6-month history of low back pain (VAS 8) and restriction of spinal movement. He also reported numbness and paresthesias in the right lower limb. His pain acutely worsened after recent trauma, preventing him from working. He denied fever, weight loss, night sweats, or appetite loss. His past medical history was unremarkable. On examination, he had an antalgic gait, localized tenderness over the lumbosacral junction, and limited lumbar motion. Neurological examination revealed hypoesthesia over the right L5 and S1 dermatomes and weakness of the right extensor hallucis longus and extensor digitorum longus (4/5). Laboratory studies showed an ESR of 33 mm/h and a CRP of 43 mg/L; blood count, liver, and renal tests were normal. A plain radiograph of the lumbosacral spine demonstrated a lytic, non-expansile lesion with collapse of the L5 vertebral body. CT revealed a well-defined osteolytic lesion involving the entire L5 vertebral body with pathological fracture and intact posterior elements, without reactive osteoblastic activity. MRI showed hypointense signal on T1-weighted and hyperintense signal on T2-weighted sagittal images at L5, with normal discs at L4–L5 and L5–S1. PET scan revealed metabolically active lesions in the L5 vertebral body and the right ischium, but no primary lesion was identified. A CT-guided biopsy of L5 was performed, but the histopathological report was inconclusive owing to an inadequate sample.

A 50-year-old man with a history of recurrent urethritis and multiple sexual partners presented with a 10-year history of progressive swelling of the penis. On examination, there was a massive, grayish-pink, papillomatous, irregular, cauliflower-like lesion of the penis, multiple tender inguinal lymphadenopathies, and a general deterioration of health. HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis serologies were all negative. Pelvic MRI showed a lobulated, cauliflower-like mass encasing the penis in intermediate T2 signal with diffusion restriction and marked post-gadolinium enhancement, sparing the corpora cavernosa and scrotum. A second perineal mass demonstrated low T2 signal, mild enhancement, and infiltration of both internal and external anal sphincters, extending toward the scrotum.

A 6-month-old boy presented with an episode of gross hematuria. The parents denied fever, trauma, or other symptoms. Renal ultrasound showed a right lower-pole, predominantly solid, well-defined lesion measuring 3.2×1.8×2.6 cm with multiple small cystic components and a 2.1 mm linear calcification with shadowing. MRI of the abdomen with and without contrast revealed a right lower-pole lesion measuring 2.8×2.5×1.8 cm with multiple T2 hypointense, nonenhancing cystic areas and mild enhancement of intervening septa. On examination, the abdomen was soft, nondistended, and nontender, with no palpable masses. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 10 800/µL, hemoglobin 12.0 g/dL, creatinine 0.44 mg/dL, urinalysis positive for blood, and a negative urine culture. Liver-function and electrolyte panels were normal, and the mass had no hormonal function.

A 37-year-old healthy woman presented with a painless nodule in her left labia majora of 6 years’ duration that had progressively enlarged over the past few months. She denied pain or bleeding. On local and colposcopic examination, there was a 3.5 cm, freely mobile, nonreducible nodule in the left labia majora. Pelvic ultrasonography revealed a superficial, well-demarcated, solid soft-tissue mass. Surgical excision was planned.

A 48-year-old man with a history of hypertension presented with a 1-year history of a gradually enlarging, painless mass on the volar aspect of his left wrist. He denied trauma and had no relevant family history. On examination, the mass was firm, non-tender, without skin changes, and the neurovascular examination of the hand was normal. He had full range of motion of the wrist (flexion, extension, supination, pronation) and fingers. 

Plain radiographs of the left wrist showed a calcified, ill-defined mass on the volar cortex of the distal ulna. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 3.0 × 1.8 × 1.3 cm ossified mass with multiple calcified foci on the volar ulnar side; the volar cortex of the ulna was intact, there was no cortical or medullary continuity with the ulna, and the ulnar artery and nerve were not involved. 

Because of cosmetic concerns and mild limitation of wrist flexion, the patient consented to an excisional biopsy.

A 43-year-old woman presented to the oral and maxillofacial clinic in January 2023 with a 3-year history of a painless, slow-growing mass on her chin. It began as a small nodule that gradually enlarged and then ulcerated; she reported mild discomfort when eating but no history of trauma. She consumes alcohol but does not smoke and is otherwise healthy. On examination, there was no facial asymmetry or lymphadenopathy, and speech and swallowing were normal. Extraoral inspection revealed a fungating, whitish-pink, cauliflower-shaped lesion with an uneven surface, measuring 8 × 6 cm over the submandibular region and lower border of the mandible. Intraoral examination showed an ulcer on the lower border of the mandible in the chin area. An orthopantomogram and chest radiograph were normal.

A 60-year-old woman presented with progressive hoarseness and shortness of breath over 2 months. Fourteen years earlier, she had undergone resection of a laryngeal tumour, which was diagnosed as chondroma. She has long-standing hypertension, does not smoke or drink, and has no family history of malignancy. On examination, an approximately 6-cm, fixed, oval-shaped mass was palpated on the left side of the neck, with no palpable lymphadenopathy. Indirect laryngoscopy showed displacement and immobility of the left hemilarynx and reduced respiratory space; the mucosa was intact. Laboratory tests were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a 5.6-cm, hypodense mass containing calcifications in the left subglottic laryngeal wall, with infiltration and partial destruction of the cricoid and thyroid cartilages and significant subglottic luminal narrowing. No pathologic lymphadenopathy or distant metastases were identified on chest x-ray or abdominal ultrasound.

A term male infant (birth weight 4.17 kg) was delivered by cesarean for antenatally detected fetal ascites and abdominal distension. At 20 weeks’ gestation, ultrasound showed fetal ascites with normal morphology; amniocentesis and karyotype were normal, and viral studies (cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis) were negative. At 23 weeks, ultrasound demonstrated increased ascites, peritoneal thickening, and an irregular solid mass arising from the left posterolateral peritoneal surface. Fetal MRI showed a T1- and T2-isointense soft‐tissue mass in the left lower quadrant, without cystic or fatty components, separate from visceral organs but inseparable from the left peritoneal lining, along with a large amount of ascites. At 35 weeks, ultrasound showed enlargement of the mass and multiple subdiaphragmatic peritoneal deposits. These findings raised suspicion for a malignant soft‐tissue tumor of peritoneal origin, with differential diagnoses of fibrosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, and peritoneal neuroblastoma.

The infant was born at term with marked abdominal distension and respiratory distress requiring mechanical ventilation; he was extubated on day 2. A postnatal CT scan revealed a large multilobulated enhancing mass (5.8×4.3×8.6 cm) along the left paracolic gutter extending to the left iliac fossa, a tortuous draining vein into the inferior vena cava, and multiple small (up to 1.6 cm) avidly enhancing subphrenic and perihepatic lesions. The bowels were displaced, and no lymphadenopathy was seen. These features were described as suggestive of a malignant soft‐tissue tumor with peritoneal deposits. Tumor markers, including alpha-fetoprotein, HCG, and urine catecholamines, were unremarkable. Ultrasound‐guided paracentesis yielded chylous exudate without malignant cells. The infant was fed a medium-chain triglyceride–based formula. On day 13 of life, a laparoscopic biopsy was performed to obtain tissue for histologic diagnosis.

A 60-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of a progressively enlarging swelling in the right gluteal/pararectal region associated with dull aching pain radiating to the right lower limb and urinary urgency. She noted that the swelling reduced completely when she lay down. Her medical history included long-standing hypertension; surgical history was notable for a lower-segment cesarean section 25 years earlier, hysterectomy for fibroids 10 years ago, and ventral hernia repair 9 years ago.

On examination, there was a 5×5 cm non-tender, compressible swelling in the right pararectal area with a positive expansile cough impulse. Vaginal vault was intact; the mass was palpable on the right side. Rectal and proctoscopic examinations were normal.

With a working diagnosis of a sciatic or posterolateral perianal hernia, a local ultrasound scan was performed and was reported as an ischiorectal abscess herniating through the sciatic foramen (approximately 130 cc in volume). Because this did not correlate with the clinical picture, a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was obtained; it showed a 4.2×5.7×7.9 cm collection abutting the right rectal wall with posterior extension and a 3.5×4.5×3.9 cm cystic lesion posterior to the bladder, raising the possibility of supralevator abscess extension. Given the discrepancy between clinical and radiologic findings, diagnostic laparoscopy was planned.

A man in his 70s presented with 2 months of fatigue, dyspnea on exertion, dull posterior headache, decreased appetite, and a 10-lb weight loss. He denied fevers, cough, hemoptysis, chest pain, leg swelling, hematemesis, or melena. His history included hypertension, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease, and non-invasive bladder cancer >10 years earlier. He had a 50-pack-year smoking history, chronic alcohol use, and a family history of smoking-related lung cancer.

Vital signs were unremarkable. Physical examination showed no focal neurologic deficits or hepatosplenomegaly.

Chest radiograph revealed a left upper lobe (LUL) nodule. Chest CT showed two irregular LUL masses (2.9 cm and 1.6 cm). PET/CT demonstrated those masses (SUVmax 18.4 and 15.9) and an infiltrative mass at the right clivus (SUVmax 8.5). Brain MRI showed a 3 mm enhancing lesion in the left cerebellar hemisphere and a T1/T2 hypointense infiltrating mass in the right clivus.

Endobronchial ultrasound–guided biopsy of the larger LUL mass showed metastatic poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma. Immunohistochemical stains were positive for AE1/3, CAM5.2, glypican-3, SALL-4, HepPar-1, and focally positive for glutamine synthetase and arginase-1. Tumor cells were negative for OCT3/4, napsin, TTF-1, CK7, CK20, p40, GATA3, CDX2, RCC, PSA, and NKX3.1.

Serum studies showed AFP 112.9 ng/mL (elevated), LDH 143 IU/L (normal), CEA 2.8 ng/mL (normal), β-hCG <5 mIU/mL, and PSA 1 ng/mL (normal). Dedicated liver and testicular imaging showed no mass lesions. 

Next-generation sequencing (FoundationOne CDx) revealed KEAP1 R320Q, TSC2 loss (exons 3–26), CDKN2A/B loss (exons 1–2), STK11 splice-site variant, and TP53 frameshift. Tumor mutational burden was 6 muts/Mb, PD-L1 TPS was 0%, and MSI was stable. Fluorescence in situ hybridization for isochromosome 12p was negative.

A 62-year-old man presented with a two-week history of an asymptomatic swelling in the right lower half of the face and reduced mouth opening. He reported two prior similar episodes over eight years: the first, five years ago, was treated as a buccal-space infection with incision and drainage; the second, two years ago, resolved spontaneously. He had no pain or fever and was a known diabetic on regular medication. 

On examination, there was gross right facial asymmetry. Extraorally, a 6 × 6 cm ovoid subcutaneous swelling extended from the level of the right lateral canthus to 1 cm below the corner of the mouth and from the corner of the mouth posteriorly to the mandibular ramus. The borders were ill-defined, the consistency ranged from soft to firm, and the overlying skin was normal. There was no lymphadenopathy, paresthesia, or facial palsy. Intraorally, the right buccal mucosa was elevated and glistening, with no vestibular obliteration; mouth opening was restricted by the mass.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the face showed a well-defined soft-tissue mass with cystic areas in the right buccal space. Intracystic loculations with dense cystic content were noted, and there was erosion of the posterior buccal cortex without perforation of the maxilla; the maxillary antrum was compressed.

A clinical diagnosis of a nonspecific chronic abscess with buccal-space involvement was made. Under general anesthesia, an intraoral approach was used to excise the lesion in toto with a margin of fibrous tissue. The lesion shelled out easily, with no involvement of buccinator muscle or bone. The excised specimen measured 4.8 × 4.5 cm, was creamish-brown, firm, irregular, and had a leathery pouch-like appearance, entirely within the soft tissue of the buccal space.

A 37-year-old woman at 20 weeks of gestation, with no past medical history, presented initially with left shoulder pain, palpitations, and a productive cough. Vital signs were notable for tachypnea but were otherwise unremarkable. An ECG and spirometry were normal. One week later she developed chest tightness and worsening tachypnea. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 31 000/µL and a C-reactive protein level of 143 mg/L. Given suspicion for pulmonary embolism, a lung perfusion scan was performed, which ruled out pulmonary thromboembolism but demonstrated marked diffuse hypoperfusion of the left lung. Chest radiography revealed complete opacification of the left hemithorax with blunting of the left costophrenic angle and no significant mediastinal shift. An abdominal ultrasound suggested a suprarenal mass. Subsequent MRI of the abdomen and chest showed heterogeneous iso-intense lesions in the upper pole of the right kidney and both adrenal glands. Chest MRI revealed a 140 × 100 × 95 mm lobulated mass in the left mediastinum with diffusion restriction, extension into the left hilum and upper and lower lobes, multiple nodules in the right lung lobes, prominent right supraclavicular lymph nodes with central necrosis, and thickening and irregularity of the left pleura.

A 7-year-old boy presented with a 4-month history of swelling in the upper left anterior maxillary region. He reported no pain or systemic symptoms. On extraoral inspection, there was swelling of the left upper lip and slight protrusion of the left nasal ala. Intraorally, a non-tender, firm mucosal swelling extended from the primary left central incisor (61) to the primary left canine (63), obliterating the buccal vestibule; a minor palatal swelling with normal mucosa and a fistula near the root of 63 were noted. Tooth 61 was geminated. Vitality tests were inconclusive, and there was no sensory disturbance.

Panoramic and CT imaging revealed a well-defined, unilocular radiolucent lesion measuring approximately 2 × 3 cm in the left anterior maxilla. The lesion extended from the midline to the mesial root of the left first deciduous molar, encompassed the crowns of the unerupted permanent left central (21) and lateral (22) incisors, and had displaced them superiorly and posteriorly.

Based on the patient’s age, lesion location, and its association with an impacted tooth, an initial diagnosis of a dentigerous cyst involving tooth 21 was made. Marsupialization under local anesthesia was attempted but was not well tolerated. The team proceeded with enucleation of the cystic lesion under general anesthesia. Teeth 61 and 62 were extracted, the cystic lining was removed in toto along with the impacted central incisor (21), and that tooth was immediately reimplanted into the bony cavity. The surgical specimen was sent for pathological examination.

A 63-year-old white man presented with a 3-week history of redness of the left eye and extensive bilateral lymphadenopathy. He reported blurred vision and loss of vision in the left lower quadrant, with supraorbital pain in both eyes, all worsening over 3 weeks. His lymph nodes (preauricular, submandibular, cervical, supraclavicular, and axillary) had progressively enlarged. He denied fever, chills, weight loss, rash, or joint pains, but noted several weeks of malaise.

Initial treatment for presumed viral and bacterial conjunctivitis included erythromycin ointment three times daily for 2 weeks, followed by topical prednisolone, tobramycin/dexamethasone ointment, and cyclopentolate without improvement. On presentation, visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/125 in the left. Intraocular pressure was 11 mm Hg in the right eye and 32 mm Hg in the left. Slit-lamp examination showed 1+ cell in the right eye, 4+ cell in the left, and a gelatinous layered hypopyon with red-blood-cell layering in both eyes, consistent with a hemorrhagic hypopyon. Dilated exam revealed 1+ vitreous haze and optic-nerve pallor in the left eye; the right eye was unremarkable. B-scan ultrasonography showed no retinal detachment or masses.

He was diagnosed with panuveitis, with malignancy or infection strongly suspected. An anterior chamber paracentesis of the left eye yielded only acellular, dense, proteinaceous material.

A 45-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of palpitations and right-sided exophthalmos. He had no history of neck irradiation or family thyroid disease. On examination, a solitary 3 cm nodule was palpated in the left thyroid lobe, and mild exophthalmos was noted on the right; there were no dermopathy signs. Thyroid function tests showed elevated free T4 of 1.8 ng/dL (normal 0.9–1.7), T3 of 6.4 pg/mL (normal 2.0–4.4), and a suppressed TSH of 0.005 mIU/mL (normal 0.27–4.2). Thyroid ultrasound revealed a 3 cm solid left-lobe nodule with necrotic-appearing areas. Technetium-99m pertechnetate scanning demonstrated diffusely homogeneous uptake throughout the gland and a hyperfunctioning focus in the left lobe containing centrally hypoactive foci corresponding to the nodule. TSH-receptor antibodies were positive at 2.36 U/L (normal <1.0), while antithyroglobulin and antiperoxidase antibodies were undetectable. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of Marine–Lenhart syndrome was made.

A 63‐year‐old woman presented with right‐sided hearing loss that had been present since early childhood. She had no history of congenital anomalies, trauma, or ear surgery. Otoscopic examination showed a moderate‐sized tympanic membrane perforation of the right ear and a small perforation of the left ear. Pure‐tone audiometry demonstrated mixed‐type hearing loss in both ears. Computed tomography of the temporal bones revealed a soft‐tissue density with massive calcification in the right middle ear and suspected erosion of the tegmen tympani.

The patient underwent a canal‐wall‐down mastoidectomy and tympanoplasty. Intraoperatively, a well‐cleavable, vascular mass resembling a schwannoma was identified in the middle ear and mastoid antrum. A frozen section yielded differential diagnoses of an inflammatory lesion with fibrous stroma, a benign spindle‐cell lesion (such as schwannoma), and possibly a neuroglial tissue. The incus and stapes were fixed by massive tympanosclerosis, and after separation of the incudostapedial joint, the incus and sclerotic material were excised. Although erosion of the tegmen was observed, there was no cerebrospinal fluid leak or connection with intracranial structures. The mass was completely separable from the intact facial nerve canal.

A 47-year-old woman with a history of delayed gastric emptying presented with daily migratory paresthesias ascending her right side, each lasting about 20 minutes and accompanied by headache and confusion. During the preceding month, she had been admitted elsewhere with right-sided paresthesias, worsening migraines with visual aura, and intermittent somnolence. An initial contrast-enhanced brain MRI showed only minimal nonspecific subcortical T2/FLAIR hyperintensities. Transferred for concern of focal motor seizures, she had no lymphadenopathy, skin lesions, or edema. On examination, she was somnolent but arousable, and when alert scored 22/30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, with deficits in attention, language, and abstraction. The remainder of the neurologic exam was unremarkable.

Laboratory evaluation, including cerebrospinal fluid analysis, was unrevealing. Repeat MRI of the brain 13 days later revealed two new diffusion-restricted foci in the left centrum semiovale consistent with infarcts, progression of FLAIR hyperintensities in frontal regions, and petechial hemorrhages on T2* sequences. Continuous EEG showed encephalopathic slowing without epileptiform activity. Cerebral angiography demonstrated an irregular, beaded appearance of the cervical carotid arteries, initially thought to represent fibromuscular dysplasia. High-resolution vessel wall MRI showed no arterial wall enhancement to suggest vasculitis. FDG-PET of the brain and CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis were unrevealing.

With an extensive negative workup (including CSF oligoclonal bands, flow cytometry, viral studies, autoantibodies, paraneoplastic panels, and toxicology), she was diagnosed with idiopathic encephalitis and treated with a five-day course of IV methylprednisolone followed by a prednisone taper. She improved for one month but then developed worsening headache, vomiting, lethargy, and episodic left facial droop. Repeat MRI showed new areas of infarction, vasogenic edema, and a moderate right temporoparietal hemorrhage with midline shift, along with additional petechial hemorrhages. CSF protein was elevated to 140 mg/dL without pleocytosis. Catheter angiography revealed a new right cervical internal carotid artery dissection and progressive luminal irregularities. MRA of the head and neck demonstrated new bilateral vertebral artery dissections and narrowing of the temporal arteries.

The differential diagnosis expanded to include atypical vasculitides, inflammatory amyloid angiopathy, complicated posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, and intravascular lymphoma. Laboratory testing revealed an elevated serum LDH of 450 U/L.

A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a 5-month history of gradually enlarging, painful bilateral vulvar masses. She also reported increased thirst and polyuria (>5 L/day). Her past history was notable for an isolated right maxillofacial lesion diagnosed in October 2021 as Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH), treated with local excision; immunohistochemistry at that time was positive for CD1α, Langerin, S100, and CD21. Her medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus controlled with NovoMix 30.

On gynecological examination, the right vulvar mass measured 3.0×3.0×2.0 cm with a 0.5×0.5 cm superficial vesicular area and yellowish discharge; the left mass measured 3.0×3.0×3.0 cm with intact overlying skin. The vagina, cervix, uterus, and adnexa were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed low triiodothyronine and thyroxine with elevated TSH, hyperglycemia (fasting 10–13.8 mmol/L, HbA1c 10.7%), reduced lymphocyte subsets, and negative viral serologies; routine blood counts, liver and kidney function, and coagulation were normal.

PET/CT revealed a hypermetabolic soft-tissue mass in the left neck (7.7×3.4 cm, SUVmax 14.5), bilateral sternocleidomastoid muscle thickening (SUVmax 12.7), and striated nodular soft-tissue shadows in the perineal area with a “figure-of-eight” pattern (SUVmax 9.6) involving the bilateral vulva and obturator internus muscles. Pelvic MRI demonstrated bilateral pelvic floor involvement along the obturator internus muscles and perineal region, with striated T2 slightly hyperintense signals, unclear margins, and significant enhancement (thickness ~2.5 cm). Enhanced MRI of the saddle region was normal.

A biopsy of the right vulvar mass showed clusters of medium-sized cells with dense eosinophil infiltration. Immunohistochemistry revealed: “Langerin positive, CD1a positive, CD68 partially positive, CD163 partially positive, CD45 positive, vimentin positive, and Ki-67 (hotspot area approximately 40% positive).”

A 21-year-old woman presented with acute headache and a visual field defect. She had a history of recurrent headaches diagnosed as migraine but had never experienced visual changes before. She denied any other medical or surgical history, including personal or family history of neurofibromatosis type 1. Ophthalmological assessment revealed a junctional scotoma on visual field testing. She was referred for urgent MRI to rule out pituitary apoplexy.

MRI of the brain and orbits on a 3-T scanner demonstrated isointense thickening of the optic chiasm on T1-weighted images with extension into the left prechiasmatic optic nerve and a normal pituitary gland. Postcontrast T1-weighted images showed mild heterogeneous enhancement of the lesion. On T2-weighted images, there was central hyperintensity without evidence of hemosiderin deposition, and FLAIR sequences revealed a subtle increase in signal intensity at the lesion site. No other intracranial cavernous malformations were identified. A presumptive diagnosis of optic nerve glioma was made, and screening MRI of the entire neuraxis showed no evidence of neurofibromatosis. Over the next 48 hours, her vision improved, returning to baseline within one week. Expectant management with repeat imaging in two months was planned.

A 72-year-old man presented with a 15-day history of a large ulceroproliferative lesion over the left gluteal region. He reported a small nodular swelling at the same site for 10 years that had gradually increased in size and then ulcerated 15 days ago, after which the lesion grew rapidly. He also had a chronic discharging sinus on the right buttock, with purulent and occasionally bloody discharge but no rectal bleeding. There was no clinically significant lymphadenopathy. 

On systemic examination there were no abnormalities; routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. Perirectal examination and sigmoidoscopy were unremarkable. 

Local examination of the left gluteal region revealed an oval ulceroproliferative lesion measuring approximately 10 × 7 cm near the natal cleft. The lesion was non-tender, not fixed to underlying muscle, had everted edges, and an indurated margin; its floor was covered with blood-stained purulent discharge. On the right buttock was a chronic discharging sinus from which purulent material could be expressed. Additionally, three to four nodular swellings each about 12 cm in diameter were noted over both buttocks.

A 42-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an incidentally discovered lung mass and multiple pulmonary nodules on chest radiography performed during a routine medical inspection one month earlier. She had undergone a myomectomy seven years ago for a benign uterine leiomyoma. She was asymptomatic, and physical examination was unremarkable. Chest radiography showed a right perihilar mass with tiny peripheral nodules in the right mid-lung field. Chest CT revealed a 4.5-cm well-demarcated right perihilar mass and multiple variably sized peripheral nodules in both lungs.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and blood biochemistry, were within normal limits. Tumor markers (CEA, SCC antigen, alpha-fetoprotein, and β-hCG) were also normal. The imaging features suggested either a primary lung malignancy with intrapulmonary metastases or metastatic disease from an extrathoracic origin.

Given her history of uterine surgery, a gynecologic evaluation was performed. Pelvic examination revealed a firm, non-tender, smooth intrapelvic mass palpable at the symphysis pubis. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a mixed echogenic mass approximately the size of a 16-week gestation. Abdomen–pelvis CT demonstrated a 6.9×5.8-cm heterogeneously enhancing pelvic mass with possible attachment to adjacent pelvic structures. Pelvic MRI showed moderate enhancement on T1-weighted images with an internal fibrovascular septum, and the mass appeared to partially abut the uterine fundus, raising the possibility of a subserosal myoma or fibrous tumor such as malignant fibrous histiocytoma.

A PET-CT scan showed no hypermetabolism in either the pulmonary lesions or the pelvic mass (SUV max values of 1.02 in the lung lesion and 1.32 in the pelvic mass), a finding inconsistent with typical malignancy and suggesting a common pathology. To establish a definitive diagnosis, simultaneous biopsy of both the lung and pelvic masses was planned.

A boy in his second decade presented with mid-back pain for 1 month, radiating to his right chest, and progressive right-sided spinal deformity. He denied trauma, fever, weight loss, appetite changes, chronic cough, neurologic symptoms, or bowel/bladder issues. On examination, he had tenderness over the dorsal spine, normal neurologic findings and reflexes, and right thoracic scoliosis with the right shoulder elevated.  

A plain radiograph showed right thoracic scoliosis with increased radiopacity at the sixth dorsal vertebra. MRI revealed a lesion occupying the D6 vertebral body and extending into both pedicles that was hyperintense on T2-weighted images and hypointense with vertical striations on STIR images, with mild collapse of the vertebral body. Axial MRI sections demonstrated an epidural “honeycomb” mass causing anterior spinal cord compression.
