A 93-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department after an episode of altered consciousness and hypotension at home, though she had fully regained consciousness by the time of evaluation. She had a history of cerebral infarction with residual dysphagia requiring gastric tube feeding, hypertension, atrial fibrillation, chronic renal insufficiency, and constipation. Her medications included an antiplatelet agent, antihypertensives, and a cathartic.

On examination, she was mildly drowsy (Japan Coma Scale 1), afebrile, and had an irregular pulse. Blood pressure was within normal limits. Mild pitting edema was noted in both lower extremities. There was no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Urinalysis revealed asymptomatic bacteriuria. Laboratory tests showed normocytic anemia, hypoalbuminemia, and elevated C-reactive protein, lactate dehydrogenase, creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, potassium, ferritin, and soluble interleukin-2 receptor levels. Electrocardiography confirmed atrial fibrillation, and carotid ultrasonography demonstrated moderate arteriosclerosis.

Computed tomography of the head, neck, chest, and abdomen showed multiple lacunar infarctions, bilateral pleural effusions, pericardial effusion, and bilateral renal atrophy, without any mass lesions, lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly. Echocardiography revealed massive pericardial effusion. Heart failure, infection, and connective tissue disease were excluded clinically.

Analysis of the pleural fluid showed an exudative effusion containing hemophagocytosis and numerous atypical lymphoid-like blast cells that were positive for CD19, CD20, and CD25. Flow cytometry did not demonstrate monoclonality in the B-lymphocyte fraction. Tests for HIV and Epstein–Barr virus were negative. Cytogenetic analysis for HHV-8 was not performed.

Bone marrow examination revealed similar atypical lymphoid-like cells without formation of discrete tumor masses. Immunophenotyping of bone marrow cells showed a marked deviation toward the γ-chain side in the B-lymphocyte fraction, and approximately 70% of cells were CD20-positive.

An 18-year-old previously healthy woman presented with a toothache. Intraoral examination revealed a large, soft, fluctuant, solitary swelling in the midline of the floor of the mouth. Despite its size, the lesion was asymptomatic.  
Ultrasonography demonstrated a well-circumscribed hypoechoic cystic lesion.  
Contrast-enhanced CT showed a well-defined hypodense lesion in the sublingual space.  
MRI revealed a well-circumscribed lesion that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, showed no enhancement after contrast administration (T1W+C), and exhibited diffusion restriction on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI).  
The lesion measured 24 × 40 × 48 mm.

A 63-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with a 3-month history of chronic cough, chest pain, and purulent sputum, accompanied by fatigue, intermittent fever, and night sweats. On examination, he had enlarged bilateral cervical lymph nodes. Chest CT showed multifocal patchy consolidations with multiple nodules in both lungs and necrotic lymphadenopathy in the cervical, paratracheal, and hilar regions. A cervical lymph-node biopsy demonstrated epithelioid cell granulomas with giant cells and caseating necrosis. Tuberculin skin testing was positive (11 mm). He was started on rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol.

After 5 months of directly observed therapy, he returned with persistent and enlarging cervical nodes, erythematous papular skin lesions over the nodes, diffuse abdominal pain, and further weight loss. Examination revealed multiple painless, voluminous cervical lymphadenopathies causing drooping of the right corner of the mouth, confluent erythematous papules overlying these nodes, bilateral axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathies, a tender abdominal mass, and splenomegaly. Abdominal CT showed multiple confluent enlarged lymph nodes forming lobulated masses with heterogeneous enhancement and an enlarged spleen. FDG-PET revealed extensive hypermetabolic lymphadenopathy (SUV 9.8–12.1), hypermetabolic costodiaphragmatic lesions, splenomegaly (SUV 3), focal liver uptake (SUV 4.17), and bilateral pleural effusions. Laboratory studies showed a normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL), elevated LDH (806 U/L), elevated CRP (221 mg/L), and hypoalbuminemia (20 g/L).

A Japanese premenopausal woman in her early 30s with known stage IV (cT4bN3M1) estrogen receptor–positive, progesterone receptor–positive, HER2-negative breast cancer (Ki-67, 42.9%) diagnosed in December 2018 presented to the emergency department in December 2022 with impaired consciousness.  

Her oncologic history included:  
• Nine cycles of FEC (5-fluorouracil, epirubicin, cyclophosphamide) every 3 weeks (best response: partial response)  
• Weekly paclitaxel for 13 cycles (stable disease; discontinued for neuropathy)  
• Tamoxifen and leuprorelin for 13 months (progression of liver metastases)  
• Fulvestrant, abemaciclib, and leuprorelin for 14 months  

Head CT and subsequent whole-brain MRI revealed contrast enhancement along the cerebral sulci consistent with CNS involvement, and she received whole-brain radiotherapy (30 Gy in 10 fractions). Systemic therapy was then switched to capecitabine, which was interrupted 3 months later due to disseminated herpes zoster. One month after stopping capecitabine, she experienced an absence seizure.  

Repeat whole-brain MRI showed multiple small and large enhancing lesions along the cerebral and cerebellar sulci, and abdominal imaging revealed enlarging liver metastases. There was no evidence of recurrent disease in the left breast.

A 59-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of severe right shoulder pain. She was initially diagnosed with shoulder periarthritis at a primary clinic and treated with oral analgesics and monthly intraarticular corticosteroid injections over 4 months without relief. On examination, active range of motion was markedly restricted, with flexion to 80° and abduction to 70°. Laboratory studies were unremarkable, including normal levels of matrix metalloproteinase 3, anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, and rheumatoid factor. Plain radiographs revealed only mild degenerative change of the humeral head. Ultrasonography with color Doppler identified a cyst-like mass with internal blood flow in the subdeltoid bursa; needle aspiration yielded no fluid. MRI demonstrated a lobulated, tumor-like mass invaginating into the subacromial and subdeltoid bursae, with high signal intensity on both T1-weighted and T2-weighted sequences and complete suppression on fat-suppression images. A possible partial tear of the supraspinatus tendon at its humeral attachment was also noted.

A 67-year-old woman with a 7-year history of well-controlled diabetes was referred for evaluation of a liver mass discovered on ultrasonography performed for elevated serum γ-glutamyl transpeptidase. She had no family history of liver disease. Laboratory tests showed normal levels of α-fetoprotein and PIVKA-II. Hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody were negative. AST was 21 IU/L, ALT 20 IU/L, ALP 184 IU/L, γ-GTP 109 IU/L, total bilirubin 0.75 mg/dL, albumin 4.6 g/dL, and INR 0.93.  
Ultrasonography revealed a 14 mm well-defined, hypoechoic mass in segment 7 of the right hepatic lobe. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 17 mm lesion with arterial-phase enhancement and portal- and delayed-phase washout. On MRI, the lesion was low intensity on T1-weighted fat-suppressed images, high intensity on T2-weighted images, and showed arterial-phase enhancement with low signal in the hepatobiliary phase of Gd-EOB-DTPA-enhanced imaging.

A 27-year-old Caucasian man presented with an eight-year history of progressive nasal obstruction. His past medical and family histories were unremarkable. Endoscopic nasal examination revealed a smooth-surfaced mass arising from the left posterior nasal septum, completely filling the nasopharyngeal cavity. Findings on other systemic examinations were normal. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, activated partial thromboplastin time, and prothrombin time, were within normal limits. Computed tomography of the paranasal region demonstrated an approximately 4 cm × 3 cm soft-tissue mass with lobulated margins and calcifications in its septa, extending from the posterior nasal septum into the nasopharynx and abutting the left inferior turbinate; there was no evidence of adipose tissue or cystic components. A punch biopsy of the lesion was reported as sinonasal papilloma. The mass was then completely resected under local anesthesia via an endoscopic approach without perioperative complications.

A 39-year-old healthy woman (BMI 19.0) presented with a 5-month history of progressive left infraumbilical abdominal pain that worsened with exercise or physical strain. One month before presentation, she noted a painful, hard mass in that region. Her gynecologic history was notable for three cesarean sections (10, 7, and 6 years earlier); she had no known endometriosis or other comorbidities.  
On examination, there was a 3-cm, painful, firm, fixed mass in the left infraumbilical region, 10 cm above the cesarean scar, without overlying skin changes. Routine blood tests, including inflammatory markers, were normal.  
She was referred to general surgery with a suspicion of muscle injury. Ultrasonography revealed a heterogeneous, predominantly hypoechoic 2.0 × 1.5 cm lesion within the left rectus abdominis muscle; Doppler showed internal vessels without high flow. US-guided fine-needle aspiration yielded scant atypical cells but was inconclusive for a definitive diagnosis, prompting recommendation for biopsy.  
Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a 2.1 × 0.9 cm focal lesion within the left rectus abdominis muscle of unknown etiology; there were no other intra-abdominal lesions or connections to the cesarean scar.

A 4-year-old girl was admitted with a right-sided abdominal mass of 3 months’ duration, intermittent fever for 3 weeks, and hematuria for 1 week. There was no dysuria or associated anomalies, and her blood pressure was normal. On examination, a firm 11 × 10 cm mass was palpable in the right lumbar region, not crossing the midline. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 9.7 g/dL, sterile urine culture with microscopic hematuria, and normal renal and liver function tests. Serum alpha-fetoprotein and vanillylmandelic acid levels were within normal limits. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. Ultrasonography of the abdomen demonstrated a large heteroechoic mass measuring 11.6 × 10.2 × 8.9 cm arising from the lower pole of the right kidney; the left kidney was normal, and the renal vessels appeared uninvolved. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a heterogeneous mass in the mid and lower pole of the right kidney measuring 11.7 × 10.3 × 9 cm, with good excretion of contrast and splaying of the pelvicalyceal system, and no lymphadenopathy.

A 65-year-old man presented with a 10-year history of cough and sputum production that worsened in winter, and one year of exertional dyspnea. One month before presentation, he noted dark-colored skin lesions that subsequently spread, accompanied by increased dyspnea and weight loss. He had no comorbid conditions, including diabetes mellitus, and no relevant family history. He was a 60–pack-year smoker. 

On examination, blood pressure was 120/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, temperature 36.5°C, weight 64 kg, height 170 cm (BMI 22.1 kg/m²). Skin examination revealed hyperpigmented, hypertrophic, symmetric, verrucose plaques on flexor surfaces of the upper and lower extremities, face, palms, and in the axillary regions. Lung auscultation revealed bilateral infrequent expiratory rhonchi; other findings were normal.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 64 mm/h, fasting blood glucose 74 mg/dL, and compensated respiratory acidosis on arterial blood gas analysis; other labs were within normal limits. 

Chest CT demonstrated a 5.0 × 5.5 cm hypodense mass at the ostium of the basal segment bronchi of the left lower lobe, with indistinct margins blending into adjacent consolidation. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy revealed near-complete obstruction of the left lower lobe bronchus by an endobronchial lesion. Abdominal CT, esophagogastroduodenoscopy, and colonoscopy showed only erosive gastritis and no evidence of malignancy.

A 42-year-old man presented with a two-month history of a gradually enlarging right lateral neck swelling. He noted a single febrile, painful episode treated successfully with antibiotics. He had no history of smoking, alcohol use, or prior radiation. On examination, there was a solitary 5×3 cm firm, non-tender mass below the angle of the mandible, deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle at the junction of its upper and mid thirds. The mass had well-defined borders, a smooth surface, normal overlying skin, and was nonpulsatile and noncompressible. Examination of the oral cavity and other systems was unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a well-defined predominantly cystic lesion measuring 3.8×3.7×3.9 cm with smooth margins and minimally enhancing eccentric solid areas, located inferomedial to the parotid gland between the sternocleidomastoid muscle laterally and the carotid space medially. On MRI, the cystic component showed a fluid-fluid level that was hyperintense on both T1- and T2-weighted images, suggestive of hemorrhagic or proteinaceous content. The eccentric solid component was heterogeneous and isointense on T2-weighted images. Fine-needle aspiration yielded hemorrhagic fluid, and cytology was inconclusive.

A 35-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with nonspecific abdominal pain without urinary symptoms. His physical examination, including abdominal and genital exams, was unremarkable. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. 

A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a well-defined, homogenous, hypodense lesion in the right renal cortex measuring 22 × 27 × 18.6 mm, with an attenuation of 17 Hounsfield units, no enhancement, and no calcifications or septations. The lesion was classified as a Bosniak class I cortical cyst.

One month later, an abdominal ultrasound showed a well-defined hyperechoic lesion in the right lower pole measuring 26 × 18 × 27 mm. Subsequent MRI of the abdomen demonstrated a right lower pole parenchymal lesion measuring 25 × 19.6 × 22 mm; it was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed internal nodular enhancement consistent with a Bosniak class IV cyst.

A 64-year-old man presented with a three-month history of gradually worsening gait disturbance and blurred vision while watching television or reading. His medical history was notable for hypertension, urolithiasis, and prior right-eye retinal detachment. On examination, he had a wide-based gait with short strides, taking 20 seconds on the 3-meter up-and-go test. There was no motor or sensory deficit. Ophthalmologic evaluation revealed left lateral hemianopsia; visual acuity in the right eye was limited to hand-motion perception. Cognitive impairment and urinary incontinence were also present. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a 24×20×24-mm heterogeneously enhancing suprasellar mass compressing the optic chiasm and severe communicating hydrocephalus. Routine blood tests were normal, but a hypothalamic stimulation test demonstrated insufficient GH, FSH, and LH responses. Cerebrospinal fluid obtained by lumbar puncture had a mildly elevated protein level (143 mg/dL), and gait performance improved to 14 seconds after the procedure. A preoperative diagnosis of craniopharyngioma with normal-pressure hydrocephalus was made, and ventriculo-peritoneal shunting resulted in significant improvement in gait stability.

A 67-year-old woman presented with 3 months of general malaise, slight fever, and elevated C-reactive protein (2.54 mg/dl) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (93 mm/h). Initial treatment with levofloxacin provided no improvement. She then developed bilateral shoulder pain and jaw claudication. On examination, her temperature was 37.0°C, pulse 102/min, blood pressure 134/74 mmHg; shoulder tenderness was noted, but the rest of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, renal function, calcium, and liver enzymes; rheumatoid factor was 41.8 IU/ml, soluble interleukin-2 receptor 518 U/ml, and all other serologies, including ANA and ANCA, were negative. Two sets of blood cultures were also negative. Contrast-enhanced CT showed no significant abnormalities. Based on Bird’s criteria, she was diagnosed with polymyalgia rheumatica, possibly complicated by giant cell arteritis, and started on prednisolone 15 mg daily, with marked symptomatic relief and normalization of CRP and ESR. However, when the prednisolone dose was reduced to 12.5 mg daily, CRP and ESR rose again despite the absence of recurrent clinical symptoms. To exclude malignancy or vasculitis, whole-body PET/CT was performed.

A 22-year-old woman presented with a 20-day history of headache, vomiting, diplopia, gait unsteadiness, and tremor of the left upper limb. There was no fever, seizures, altered sensorium, or focal weakness. On examination, vital signs were normal. Neurologic examination revealed bilateral papilledema, left sixth cranial nerve palsy, action tremor, and left-sided cerebellar signs; meningeal signs were absent. Brain MRI with gadolinium showed diffuse, thick leptomeningeal enhancement with a few nodular enhancing lesions in the right cerebellomedullary cistern; the brain parenchyma and ventricles were normal. Four lumbar punctures revealed elevated protein (up to 1.2 g/dl), normal glucose, red blood cells (200–2000 cells/dl), and lymphocytic pleocytosis (0–100 cells/dl). Smears and cultures for acid-fast bacilli, DNA PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Gram stain, bacterial cultures, and fungal studies were repeatedly negative. CSF cytospin preparations showed no malignant cells, and CSF angiotensin-converting enzyme levels were normal. Serum complete blood count, liver and renal function tests were unremarkable. Serologic markers for vasculitis were negative, Mantoux test was non-reactive, contrast CT scans of the chest and abdomen were normal, and HIV and hepatitis B serologies were negative.

A 3-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of painful gingival growths in the upper and lower jaws, present for 1 month. The pain was sudden in onset, intermittent, nonradiating, worsened with chewing, and self-resolving. He had been treated with analgesics and antibiotics at a local clinic without improvement. His medical and family histories were unremarkable.

On examination, he was healthy in general appearance. Extraorally, there was a firm, tender, diffuse 4×2 cm swelling over the left mandible from the inferior border of the body to the superior ramus, with palpable, firm, nontender left submandibular lymph nodes (~0.5×2 cm). Intraorally, there were diffuse, erythematous, ulcerated gingival swellings covered with necrotic slough and bleeding spots adjacent to teeth 55, 65, 75, and 85, with Grade II mobility of those teeth.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL with microcytic hypochromic anemia on peripheral smear; normal liver and urine tests; creatinine 0.3 mg/dL; C-reactive protein 2.5 mg/dL; negative HIV and hepatitis B surface antigen.

An orthopantomogram revealed multiple areas of bone loss in the left mandible. Axial and coronal CT showed multiple soft-tissue density lesions with irregular, punched-out bony destruction of the left mandible, left occiput, right maxilla, and right temporal bone. Three-dimensional CT confirmed multiple osteolytic lesions in the maxillary alveolar process and the body and ramus of the left mandible.

A 43-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of intermittent headaches, progressive visual deterioration, and dizziness accompanied by nausea and vomiting. A few days after symptom onset, she experienced generalized tonic-clonic seizures. She denied fever, weight loss, or recent travel. At age 19, she had an episode of left-sided weakness and facial droop; CT then demonstrated a right hemispheric white-matter lesion suggestive of infarction, MRI showed no multiple sclerosis, and CSF and visual evoked potentials were normal. She recovered fully with no residual deficits and had been well since.

On current examination, vital signs were normal and a full neurologic exam was unremarkable: there was no focal deficit, neck stiffness, or meningism. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits.

Noncontrast head CT showed a 2.7-cm low-density lesion in the right parietal region without enhancement or mass effect. Brain MRI confirmed mature changes consistent with an old infarct and revealed leptomeningeal enhancement in several regions. Differential diagnoses included diffuse leptomeningeal disease secondary to sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, or malignancy (primary or metastatic).

Chest radiography and CT of the chest and abdomen revealed no malignancy. A vasculitic screen, including ANCA, was negative. Serologies for syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were all negative. A specialist neuroradiologist and neurologist favored neurosarcoidosis and recommended steroids and lumbar puncture.

Lumbar puncture demonstrated an elevated opening pressure of 41 cm H₂O, a mixed lymphoid pleocytosis without malignant cells, and elevated protein (12.90 g/L). CSF culture was negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Serum ACE and calcium were normal. The patient reported transient visual improvement and a decrease in opening pressure after steroids.

Given the lack of fever, weight loss, lymphadenopathy, and a normal serum LDH, lymphoma was considered unlikely. Fundoscopy showed no papilledema. After 2–3 weeks of steroids, her vision worsened to blindness in the left eye and only light perception in the right. Serial CSF studies remained abnormal. MRI of the spine showed diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement coating the entire spinal cord to the conus and involving the cauda equina nerve roots, while the cord parenchyma was normal.

A 49-year-old female teacher with no history of chronic illness was referred for evaluation of a swelling on the sole of her left foot of 2 months’ duration. The swelling was painless initially and had gradually increased in size. There was no history of trauma. A Doppler ultrasound showed a fluid collection in the subcutaneous tissue of the plantar surface of the left foot with mixed echogenicity measuring 2.6 × 2.5 × 1.8 cm and surrounding soft tissue inflammatory changes; an abscess was suspected and a hematoma was also queried. An x-ray of the left foot was unremarkable. On examination, there was a 5 × 3 cm soft, tender swelling at the medial arch of the left foot that was not mobile and was attached to the overlying skin, with hyperkeratosis of the overlying skin. There were no palpable inguinal lymph nodes.

A 68-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an expanding anterior left leg soft-tissue mass. Fifteen years earlier, after a motor-vehicle accident, she had developed mild left knee pain that progressed within a year to severe burning pain with episodes of allodynia preventing active extension. Five neurologists and an outside orthopaedic surgeon had diagnosed complex regional pain syndrome and pursued physical therapy, oral pain medications, intravenous lidocaine/ketamine/midazolam infusions, and an offered sympathetic block, all without relief. 

Her medical history included prior pancreatic cancer treated with distal pancreatectomy and splenectomy, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, osteoporosis, and a remote transient ischemic attack. Surgical history also included resection of carotid body and adrenal lesions 12 years earlier.

On examination, there was a 5-cm ovoid, firm mass in the proximal anterolateral left leg, mildly tender to palpation, without overlying skin changes, and with intact distal neurovascular status. She refused palpation of the anterior knee region because of extreme sensitivity related to her presumed CRPS. 

Plain radiographs of the left knee showed no fracture or destructive bony changes. MRI of the left lower extremity with and without contrast demonstrated a heterogeneous solid subcutaneous mass along the anterolateral calf concerning for soft-tissue sarcoma and a small T2-hyperintense nodule in the subcutaneous tissues overlying the patella that could “represent a number of pathologies, including prepatellar bursitis, ganglion cyst, glomus tumor, or even potentially be a part of the sarcoma itself.”

A 43-year-old woman presented with a 20-year history of a left-breast lump that had gradually increased in size, associated with tenderness and nipple discharge. She had no significant laboratory abnormalities and no family history of breast cancer. On examination, there was a mobile, elastic, hard mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast. Mammography showed a heterogeneous breast density and an approximately 5-cm oval, homogeneous, high-density mass with well-defined borders and no calcifications. Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated a regularly shaped, hypo-echoic mass containing irregular cystic areas, posterior acoustic enhancement, and detectable flow. CT revealed the mass to contain separate low-density and high-density regions, with no evidence of metastasis. On dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI, the lesion was an oval mass with a smooth margin comprising solid and cystic components: the solid part was hypo-intense on T1-weighted imaging, hyper-intense on STIR imaging, showed heterogeneous enhancement with dark internal septation, exhibited a fast/plateau enhancement pattern, and had no restricted diffusion (ADC, 1.83 × 10^−3 mm^2/s); the cystic part was slightly hyper-intense on T1, slightly hypo-intense on STIR, and demonstrated neither restricted diffusion nor contrast enhancement. Based on these imaging findings, phyllodes tumor, complex fibroadenoma, mucinous carcinoma, intracystic papilloma, and encapsulated papillary carcinoma were considered as differential diagnoses.

A 57-year-old woman presented with postmenopausal bleeding and hot flushes. Physical examination and transvaginal sonography showed no abnormalities. Endometrial sampling with a pipelle revealed syncytial metaplasia. After additional episodes of bleeding, hysteroscopy disclosed an endometrial polyp, which was resected. Grossly, the polyp measured 9×8×2.5 mm and was pale gray and elastic. Microscopic examination showed fragments of uterine wall infiltrated by malignant-appearing, nonpleomorphic tumor cells with pale chromatin, small nucleoli, minimal nuclear contour variation, rare mitoses, and mostly scant cytoplasm (with occasional epithelioid cells containing foamy cytoplasm). These cells formed solid areas, glomeruloid structures, and small nests resembling ovarian sex cord tumors. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated tumor cell positivity for calretinin, MART-1, inhibin, CD99, desmin, actin, vimentin, and pankeratin, and negativity for EMA, chromogranin, synaptophysin, S100, CD30, CD31, CD34, CD117, Myf-4, AFP, oct3/4, and PLAP. A computed tomography scan of the abdomen and pelvis was unremarkable.

A man in his 50s presented with several months of unstable gait and dizziness that interfered with his work. He had no significant medical, medication, or family history. On admission, he was conscious and had no focal neurological deficits. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the head revealed a cystic lesion in the left cerebellar hemisphere that was low intensity on T1-weighted imaging, high intensity on T2-weighted imaging, and low intensity on diffusion-weighted imaging. Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images showed no nodular enhancement, and there was no surrounding edema or brainstem compression. 

Digital subtraction angiography demonstrated no enhancing mural nodules or abnormal vessels. Given the recent onset of cerebellar symptoms and the indeterminate imaging, a cystic neoplasm was suspected but unconfirmed. Differential diagnosis included other cystic lesions such as an arachnoid cyst. To establish a diagnosis and treat the lesion, a minimally invasive keyhole craniotomy with endoscopic cyst puncture and inspection was planned.

A 39-year-old woman with Philadelphia-positive acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, in remission for 6 months after two allogeneic stem cell transplants and donor lymphocyte infusion, presented with 2 days of fevers, malaise, and central dull chest pain that was neither pleuritic nor positional. She had no known cardiovascular disease. On examination she was dehydrated, tachycardic (heart rate up to 130 b.p.m.), hypotensive (90/65 mmHg), and febrile (38.5 °C), with an otherwise unremarkable cardiovascular exam. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein of 72.7 mg/L (normal <10), a Troponin T of 2490 ng/L (0–14), and a white-cell count of 10.4 × 10^9/L with no precursor cells on peripheral smear; other biochemistry was within normal limits. Blood cultures were negative. Chest radiography was normal. Electrocardiography demonstrated sinus tachycardia and new deep T-wave inversion in leads V3–V6. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed mild–moderate left ventricular hypertrophy, anterior and anteroapical hypokinesis, a small circumferential pericardial effusion, and an ejection fraction of 45%, with no significant valvular abnormalities. Coronary angiography showed no obstructive coronary disease. She received intravenous fluids, piperacillin–tazobactam, and pulsed high-dose methylprednisolone for presumed severe myopericarditis but continued to have fevers, tachycardia, and hypotension. Differential diagnoses including infiltrative, tachycardic, and catecholaminergic cardiomyopathies were considered, and an urgent cardiac magnetic resonance imaging study was obtained, showing severe patchy increased signal intensity involving the basal anteroseptum, anterior wall, mid-lateral wall, distal interventricular septum, and pericardium on oedema-weighted and late gadolinium sequences, with regional wall motion abnormalities.

A 47-year-old Caucasian man with a 33-year history of penetrating Crohn’s disease (Montreal L2, B3+P) presented with two weeks of painless jaundice, unintentional weight loss, and malaise, without fever. His Crohn’s disease had been in remission for five years on azathioprine (150–200 mg daily) following prior budesonide, mesalamine, and limited infliximab exposure; he had undergone right and left hemicolectomies and later a permanent ileostomy. 

On examination, he was afebrile, icteric, and had palpable hepatosplenomegaly without lymphadenopathy. 

Laboratory tests showed:  
• Hemoglobin 7.7 mmol/L (8.5–11.0)  
• White blood cell count 4.6×10^9/L (4.0–10.0)  
• Platelet count 42×10^9/L (150–400)  
• Bilirubin 175 μmol/L (0–17)  
• Alkaline phosphatase 265 IU/L (0–125)  
• γ-Glutamyl transferase 154 IU/L (0–45)  
• Aspartate aminotransferase 250 IU/L (0–34)  
• Alanine aminotransferase 437 IU/L (0–44)  
• Lactate dehydrogenase 701 IU/L (0–247)  

Contrast CT and PET–CT confirmed hepatosplenomegaly with increased metabolic activity in the liver, spleen, and bone marrow, without bile-duct dilation or focal obstructive lesions. Viral serologies, including Epstein–Barr virus, were negative.

A 34-year-old man presented with persistent pain and mild effusion of the left first metatarsophalangeal joint, gradually increasing in size over the previous year. He began to have difficulty fitting into shoes over the last 2 months. He denied any history of foot trauma, gout, or other inflammatory diseases. On examination, there was a solid, mobile, palpable soft-tissue mass around the first MTPJ. Blood tests were normal. Plain radiographs of the foot showed no bony erosions or calcifications. 

Based on the clinical findings, joint synovitis and/or possible extensor hallucis longus tenosynovitis was initially diagnosed, and the patient was treated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, activity restriction, and a course of physiotherapy. After slight transient improvement, his pain recurred to its initial intensity, and the joint effusion persisted. As a 3-month nonoperative treatment failed to achieve symptom relief, an MRI of the foot was obtained.

MRI depicted a diffuse periarticular mass, measuring 4 cm in length, with a lobulated contour surrounding the first MTPJ and extending into the soft tissues of the dorsal and plantar aspects of the metatarsal head and neck. The lesion demonstrated homogeneous intermediate signal intensity on T1-weighted images (similar to muscle), intermediate signal intensity on T2-weighted scans (higher than muscle), and high signal intensity on short tau inversion recovery sequences (lower than water). There was no muscle edema or osseous involvement. A small amount of joint effusion was present. There were no areas of decreased signal intensity on any sequence to suggest calcification or ossification. After intravenous gadolinium, there was marked diffuse enhancement of the mass. These findings were strongly suggestive of joint synovitis.

A 41-year-old woman with a history of asthma and gastroesophageal reflux disease presented with 2–3 days of a choking sensation and shortness of breath and 4 months of gradually worsening voice changes with aspiration of thin liquids. She had no history of tobacco or alcohol use. On examination, she had inspiratory stridor but normal oxygen saturation on room air. Fiberoptic laryngoscopy revealed a large, pink, pedunculated ball-valving polypoid lesion arising from the anterior glottic commissure, obstructing approximately 75% of the airway. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the neck demonstrated a well-defined, partially enhancing 1.5-cm soft-tissue mass at the anterior commissure with moderate compromise of the laryngeal lumen. The patient was admitted for continuous respiratory and pulse oximetry monitoring, and definitive management was planned.

A 55-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a progressively enlarging mass in the left thigh over 6 months. He denied fever, weight loss, or inflammatory symptoms, and his general condition was preserved. On examination, there was a palpable, firm, nonfluctuant, non-tender mass on the anteromedial aspect of the thigh; there was no overlying skin change and no regional lymphadenopathy. Hip mobility was normal.

Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 16-cm lesion deep in the thigh, located between the sartorius and adductor longus muscles. The mass was iso-intense on T1-weighted images, hyper-intense on T2-weighted images, and showed heterogeneous enhancement after contrast. The lesion extended toward the femoral neurovascular bundle in the femoral triangle.

The patient underwent complete surgical excision through an anteromedial thigh incision. Intraoperatively, the mass was well-circumscribed and encapsulated, without invasion of adjacent muscles or skin. Macroscopically, the specimen was soft, well-circumscribed, encapsulated, and had a red-brown cut surface.

Microscopic examination showed a benign proliferation of spindle-shaped cells arranged in a storiform pattern, with oval to elongated, wavy nuclei, fine chromatin, and small nucleoli; there was no cytologic atypia or mitotic activity, and the stroma contained abundant collagen bundles.

Immunohistochemical analysis showed strong, diffuse positivity for CD34 and focal positivity for Desmin. The tumor was negative for β-catenin, H-caldesmon, actin-smooth muscle (AML), S100, SOX10, MDM2, CDK4, CD31, HHV8, STAl6, and Myogenin.

A 73-year-old woman presented with a four-year history of a painful swelling of the left knee that had grown slowly and became increasingly painful, especially with weight bearing or sitting. She had no significant past medical history and maintained full range of motion without systemic symptoms. Conservative management for presumed osteoarthritis, including nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs, provided no relief. On examination, there was local tenderness and a small, firm, well-defined swelling over the medial proximal tibia, without erythema or warmth.  
Plain radiographs of the knee showed a small, well-defined osteolytic lesion in the medial proximal tibial metaphysis with cortical thinning and a thin sclerotic margin. A CT scan demonstrated a radiolucent, cortex-eroding lesion with central calcification. MRI revealed a hypointense mass on both T1- and T2-weighted images that did not suppress on fat-suppressed sequences, showed gadolinium enhancement, lacked fluid–fluid levels, and extended extraosseously. A technetium-99 bone scan revealed increased uptake at the lesion. Laboratory studies, including inflammatory markers and serum chemistries, were within normal limits.  
A CT-guided core biopsy of the lesion was performed, and specimens were submitted for histopathological and immunohistochemical evaluation.

A 69-year-old woman presented with two months of progressively worsening upper abdominal pain. Her past medical history was notable for a cutaneous malignant melanoma resected in 1997 and a germline CDKN2A codon 59 mutation in a kindred with familial atypical multiple mole melanoma. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including CA 19-9, were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen revealed a 30 mm solid–cystic mass in the body of the pancreas with ill-defined borders, pancreatic tail atrophy, encasement of the splenic vessels, and partial involvement of the superior mesenteric artery and vein; the celiac axis and its branches were spared. A CT performed three years earlier showed no pancreatic lesion. Radial and linear endoscopic ultrasonography confirmed the solid–cystic mass. Transgastric EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration demonstrated malignant cells with both glandular and squamous differentiation.

A 56-year-old Ivorian man with no significant past medical history presented with a 2-day history of abdominal pain and sudden obstipation of solids and gas. He was in good general condition. Physical examination revealed abdominal distension with tympanism; the rectal examination was normal and there was no lymphadenopathy. Abdominal radiographs demonstrated dilated bowel loops with fluid levels consistent with descending colonic obstruction. At exploratory laparotomy, numerous polypoid lesions were palpated in the left colon and sigmoid, with the largest lesion occluding the lumen; a subtotal colectomy with ileocolostomy was performed. Gross examination of the colectomy specimen showed multiple polypoid formations in the colonic mucosa. Microscopic examination (H&E) of the colonic submucosa revealed a diffuse proliferation of small lymphoid cells with hyperchromatic, crenelated nuclei.

A 76-year-old woman with a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension, both well controlled on oral medications, noted sudden swelling of the right side of her neck while swimming. She presented to the emergency department with a one-day history of right neck enlargement but no pain, dysphagia, dyspnea, or voice changes. On examination, she was hemodynamically stable. Inspection and palpation revealed a localized, non-tender right neck mass that did not move with swallowing and was not associated with overlying erythema or warmth. 

Laboratory studies were unremarkable. An unenhanced computed tomography (CT) scan of the neck demonstrated marked enlargement of the right thyroid lobe, replaced by a 9.2 × 5.2 × 5.5 cm heterogeneous, predominantly hyperdense mass causing leftward tracheal deviation. Subsequent CT angiography revealed active contrast extravasation along the posterior aspect of the right thyroid lobe mass and a tortuous vessel arching over the collection, suggesting an arterial source of bleeding.

A 20-year-old woman with no smoking history underwent a chest radiograph at a routine employment checkup, which revealed a round shadow in the right middle lung field; an image 2 years earlier had been normal. She was asymptomatic and had no comorbidities. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed a lobulated solid mass in the hilum of the right lung measuring 3.5 × 3.0 cm, with homogeneous enhancement in the early phase and no intratumoral fat or calcification. ^18F-FDG PET demonstrated intense uptake in the lesion (SUV max 7.1 early, 8.4 delayed). Serum lung-cancer tumor markers (CEA, cytokeratin 19 fragment, pro-gastrin-releasing peptide) were within normal limits. Based on imaging, the leading considerations were invasive lung cancer, lymphoma, Castleman’s disease, solitary fibrous tumor, or inflammatory pseudotumor. A transbronchial biopsy specimen was insufficient for diagnosis. The lesion was staged clinically as T2aN0M0 (stage IB NSCLC), and the patient underwent right S3 segmentectomy. Intraoperative frozen-section analysis showed branched gland ducts and columnar epithelial cells with mild nuclear atypia in papillary arrangements, and the lesion was diagnosed as a benign pulmonary tumor (e.g., papilloma or adenoma). The operation was concluded without further resection.

A 92-year-old man was referred for assessment of a tongue ulcer. He reported a painful ulcer on the left posterior dorsum of the tongue present for two months, with associated odynophagia and a 7-kg weight loss in one month. His medical history was unremarkable; he had a long history of pipe smoking and moderate regular alcohol use. On examination, there was a 3-cm indurated ulcer on the left posterior dorsum of the tongue and an ipsilateral 4-cm lymph node in the level 3 region. An incisional biopsy of the tongue lesion was performed under local anaesthesia. Histopathological examination showed an adenocarcinoma. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated that the tumour cells were positive for cytokeratin 20 and CDX2 and negative for cytokeratin 7, TTF1, thyroglobulin, and PSA.

A previously healthy 4-year-old girl was evaluated for a 6-week history of non-specific cough. Growth and development were normal. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits; auscultation revealed diminished breath sounds over the right lung. Chest radiography demonstrated a mass in the right upper and middle lobes with central calcification. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a well-circumscribed, heterogeneous, solid mass in the right upper and middle lobes with a central calcified focus and no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 10 mm/h, hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, leukocyte count 8.8×10^9/L, and otherwise normal hematological and biochemical results. Sputum microscopy, culture, and cytology were unremarkable. Serologic testing for Echinococcus and a Mantoux test were negative. The patient did not improve after a course of antibiotics, and surgical resection was planned for definitive diagnosis and treatment.

A 27-year-old woman noticed a palpable swelling in her right flank associated with dull pain. On examination, an elastic-hard, fixed mass occupied the right abdomen. Abdominal computed tomography revealed a solid, encapsulated retroperitoneal mass measuring approximately 11 × 9 cm compressing the right kidney caudally. Contrast-enhanced CT showed early staining predominantly on the dorsal aspect of the tumor, with feeding vessels traced to lumbar muscles including the latissimus dorsi, quadratus lumborum, and psoas major. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-circumscribed retroperitoneal lesion of relatively smooth margins with high signal intensity on both T1- and T2-weighted sequences. Chest radiography and CT showed no lymphadenopathy or distant metastases.

A 57-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of two asymptomatic abdominal masses identified on enhanced abdominopelvic CT at an outside hospital. Imaging showed (1) a 3.3-cm hypervascular mass with internal cystic changes in the uncinate process of the pancreas and (2) a 1.6-cm enhancing, fat-containing lesion in the right adrenal gland. Her medical history was notable for hypertension and dyslipidemia on medication. Family history included pancreatic cancer in her father and sister, gastric cancer in her brother, and type 2 diabetes mellitus in her mother.  

Laboratory testing revealed elevated plasma aldosterone (399.38 pg/mL; reference 37.82–388) with suppressed renin (<0.07 ng/mL/h; reference 0.30–4.88), while serum sodium and potassium were within normal limits. MRI confirmed the CT findings of a hypervascular pancreatic uncinate mass and an enhancing adrenal lesion. PET–CT showed equivocal fluorodeoxyglucose uptake at the pancreas head/duodenum region and focal uptake in the right adrenal gland.  

With these findings, the team planned a pylorus-preserving pancreatoduodenectomy for presumed pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor with cystic changes. The adrenal lesion, measuring less than 4 cm, was managed conservatively with spironolactone and deferred further intervention.

A 73-year-old woman was found to have an incidental mass in the right external auditory canal during a routine examination. She had no ear-related symptoms and no history of cold-water swimming or sauna use. On otoscopic inspection, there was a 2 mm, firm, white, round mass covered by normal-appearing epithelium located at the medial portion of the anterior wall of the bony external auditory canal, just anterior to the short process of the malleus. The tympanic membrane appeared normal and was not contacted by the mass. Palpation with a Rosen needle revealed that the lesion was firm and nontender. A computed tomographic scan of the temporal bone showed a small lesion emanating from the anterior bony external auditory canal; the canal wall was flat with well-defined boundaries and showed no cortical erosion or invasion.

A 5-year-old girl presented with a one-year history of a left eye inferior nasal conjunctival lesion measuring 10 × 10 mm. The mass was nonpigmented, cystic, mobile, and not fixed to the sclera; it had increased in size over the preceding two months. There was no history of ocular trauma or surgery, and systemic evaluation was unremarkable.

On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally. The conjunctiva was not red, and extraocular movements were full in both eyes. There was no strabismus, nystagmus, or abnormal head posture. Cyclorefraction was +3.00 – 1.00 × 180 in both eyes. Slit-lamp and fundus examinations were within normal limits.

Ultrasonographic microscope imaging of the left eye revealed a large conjunctival lesion in the inferior nasal fornix without evidence of scleral invasion.

An 88‐year‐old woman presented with iron deficiency anemia, fatigue, occasional vague right‐sided abdominal discomfort, and 10 lb of unintentional weight loss over several months. Her medical history was unremarkable, and her family history included prostate cancer in a brother and unspecified cancer in a sister. Vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination was notable only for mild right lower‐quadrant tenderness without peritoneal signs.

Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a large (11.0 × 15.7 × 15.5 cm), heterogeneous, partially necrotic mass in the right lower quadrant. The mass contained multiple vessels, extended from the anterior pararenal space adjacent to the inferomedial right hepatic lobe and the junction of the second and third segments of the duodenum, and produced complete effacement of most of the ascending colon with anterior displacement of the proximal ascending colon and cecum. There was no extension into the right adnexa or uterus. A retroperitoneal origin was favored.

Subsequent MRI showed that the lesion abutted the ascending colon/cecum, with heterogeneous T2 hyperintensity, T1 isointensity to hypointensity, predominantly peripheral contrast enhancement, and no significant signal dropout on in-/out-of-phase images, indicating a lack of fatty content. Diffusion-weighted sequences were degraded by susceptibility artifacts. At this stage, the main considerations were colon carcinoma, a mesenteric tumor such as sarcoma, or a large GIST; an enlarged mesenteric lymph node was also included in the differential.

A 27-month-old boy presented to the emergency department with cough, fever, and decreased oral intake. He had received a diagnosis of autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease at another hospital based on a renal ultrasound. On examination, he had a wheezy chest, a distended abdomen, and bilaterally palpable kidneys. His temperature was 38.0°C, and blood pressure was 130/83 mm Hg. Liver-function tests, urinalysis, and renal-function tests were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed bilaterally enlarged kidneys (right, 8.9 cm; left, 8.4 cm) with increased cortical echogenicity, loss of corticomedullary differentiation, multiple bilateral subcapsular cysts, and large multiseptated perirenal fluid collections. The liver was normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed enlarged kidneys with heterogeneous cortical enhancement, bilateral perinephric fluid collections with multiple septations, multiple small subcortical cysts, and subtle renal sinus cysts splaying the collecting systems; no hydronephrosis was observed, and a small amount of ascites was present. MRI of the kidneys demonstrated increased cortical signal and decreased medullary signal on T2-weighted images with poor corticomedullary differentiation; perinephric fluid was hypointense on T1 and hyperintense on T2 with septal enhancement, along with small subcortical and renal sinus cysts splaying the collecting systems.

A 57-year-old Pakistani man presented with dull right flank pain of 4 years’ duration. He had been clinically diagnosed with a right ureteric stricture and had undergone three ureteroscopic dilations with double-J stenting and one laser incision with stenting at other institutions. His medical history was notable for well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and an appendectomy in his twenties, complicated by an incisional hernia repaired with mesh.

He also reported chronic polyuria, averaging 5 L of urine output daily, without prior endocrinologic evaluation. 

Laboratory studies showed microscopic hematuria on urinalysis; blood glucose, renal function tests, and urine pH were repeatedly within normal limits. Serum antidiuretic hormone levels were normal preoperatively; serum potassium was at the upper limit of normal but later fell postoperatively.

Renal ultrasonography demonstrated moderate right hydronephrosis with proximal ureteral dilation. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed an 11 × 5 mm narrowing in the mid-ureter at the level of the common iliac vessels, with peri-ureteral soft-tissue enhancement, irregular ureteral lumen, and upstream dilation of the ureter and renal pelvis; the lesion was located approximately 15 cm distal to the renal pelvis.

Diagnostic ureteroscopy showed a focal luminal narrowing without an intraluminal mass. Laparoscopically, the stricture segment was excised with a 1 cm proximal margin. The proximal ureter was mobilized, straightened, and reimplanted into the bladder via a Boari flap with placement of a 5 Fr double-J stent.

In the immediate postoperative period, the patient developed abdominal distension and polyuria exceeding 7 L/day accompanied by hypokalemia; he was diagnosed with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Electrolytes were corrected, bowel function resumed, and he was discharged on postoperative day 10 on oral potassium supplementation and his diabetes medications.

A 27-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of progressive jaundice. On examination, he was icteric and had a palpable 7 × 7 cm mass in the right hypochondrium; the external genitalia were normal. Laboratory studies showed total bilirubin 16.2 mg/dL (conjugated 11.7 mg/dL), AST 118 U/L, ALT 40 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase 180 U/L, α-fetoprotein 120 000 U/L, and human chorionic gonadotropin <1.2 mIU/mL. Ultrasound of the abdomen revealed multiple ill-defined heteroechoic lesions in both liver lobes with central necrosis and intrahepatic biliary radicle dilatation. MRI of the abdomen demonstrated a 13.6 × 10.6 × 10.6 cm lobulated mass in the right hepatic lobe, extending into the left and caudate lobes, with T2 hypointense areas corresponding to necrosis and intrahepatic biliary dilation.

A 63-year-old woman presented with a 10-month history of paresthesia and neuropathic pain involving the left tongue and left mandibular distribution. She was treated with standard neuropathic pain agents for presumed trigeminal neuralgia, with only marginal relief. An MR scan of the head with gadolinium contrast showed abnormal enhancement in the left Meckel cave along the course of the mandibular nerve, extending through the foramen ovale into the inferior temporal fossa and medial pterygoid muscle. CT scans of the head/neck, thorax, and abdomen/pelvis with contrast did not reveal malignancy. On examination, she had numbness of the left tongue and left mandibular area without changes in taste or hearing. Cranial nerve motor function was intact, with no facial droop. Intraoral inspection showed no mucosal lesion, but palpation revealed a 1 × 2 cm rubbery mass deep to the mucosa of the left tongue without overlying changes. No head or neck lymphadenopathy was noted.

A 38‐year‐old man presented to the emergency department with bladder tamponade and gross hematuria. He underwent cystoscopy, which was unremarkable apart from the hematuria. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 10‐cm mass in the lower pole of the left kidney. The patient proceeded to radical nephrectomy. On gross examination, the renal specimen showed partly brown‐beige nodular discoloration and areas of necrotic, cystic, disintegrating tissue in the region of the lower pole.

A 37-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of a right facial swelling that had recurred twice and been excised 14 years earlier. The mass was painless, firm, nonfluctuant, immobile, and measured approximately 3×2×2 cm at the right nasolabial fold, with no cervical lymphadenopathy. CT of the face showed a subcutaneous lesion without bone or muscle invasion. FNAC suggested a benign spindle cell lesion. At surgery, two well-encapsulated oval masses overlying the buccinator muscle were excised en bloc, measuring 7×4×2.5 cm. 

Histopathology revealed spindle cells arranged in storiform to whorled patterns, with moderate eosinophilic cytoplasm, oval to elongated nuclei, and five mitoses per ten high-power fields. The tumour infiltrated subcutaneous fat in a honeycomb pattern with perivascular myoid spindle cell proliferation. There was no nuclear atypia, pleomorphism, or necrosis. Immunohistochemistry showed tumour cells positive for CD34 and myoid areas positive for alpha-smooth muscle actin; the myoid areas demonstrated weak CD34 staining. Tumour cells were negative for S100, STAT6, and TLE1.

A 36-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident in which she sustained right eye trauma. She reported right-sided blurry vision but no loss of consciousness or other injuries. Examination and imaging of the head were unremarkable apart from traumatic uveitis. A chest radiograph, obtained to evaluate possible rib fractures, revealed a 1.1 cm pulmonary nodule in the right midlung. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest confirmed two well-circumscribed nodules in the right upper lobe (1.1 cm and 1.0 cm), consistent with benign-appearing lesions, and unexpectedly demonstrated a large filling defect in the right ventricle extending toward the outflow tract, presumed to be thrombus.

The patient was started on anticoagulation. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography showed a large mobile mass arising from the interventricular septum with turbulent flow through the right ventricular outflow tract. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging revealed an oblong 4.9 cm soft-tissue mass occupying the entire right ventricular outflow tract and abutting the pulmonary valve. The patient denied chest pain, dyspnea, syncope, and weight loss. Physical examination was notable for a systolic murmur.

On further history, she disclosed a hysterectomy 12 years earlier for “myomas” and denied any personal or family history of malignancy. Abdominal and pelvic CT confirmed the absence of a uterus and identified a 2.2 × 1.7 cm soft-tissue nodule at the left aspect of the vaginal cuff, initially interpreted as an ovary. Serum CA-125 was within normal limits.

A 57-year-old man had chronic headaches and progressive bilateral visual loss for over 2 years and 10 months of recurrent pain and swelling around his left eye. Two years earlier, he underwent gamma-knife treatment for a presumed left orbital cavernous hemangioma without improvement. He also had a 1-year history of heart failure and pulmonary infection.  

On examination, there was left-sided proptosis, restricted eye movements, eyelid lag, bulbar conjunctival congestion and edema, and a corneal ulcer of the left eye. The right eye had conjunctival congestion, restricted motility, and an intraocular pressure of 28 mmHg; vision was 1.0 in the right eye and hand movement in the left.  

Orbital MRI demonstrated bilateral intraconal masses, more pronounced on the left. Whole-body CT revealed ascites, pleural effusion, pericardial thickening with effusion, and bilateral hydronephrosis with perinephric fat stranding. Echocardiography showed right ventricular enlargement, left ventricular hypertrophy, pulmonary hypertension, and dilation of the aorta and pulmonary artery.  

Laboratory studies showed normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 98 g/L), thrombocytosis (platelets 536×10^9/L), normal white-cell count, hypokalaemia (K+ 2.81 mmol/L), and hypoalbuminaemia (albumin 33.7 g/L).  

He underwent bilateral orbital mass resection. Histopathology showed fibrous tissue hyperplasia with chronic inflammatory infiltration and numerous histiocyte reactions, leading to a diagnosis of inflammatory pseudotumor. His corneal ulcer and conjunctival edema improved, and left vision partially recovered.  

One year later, he returned with 2 weeks of recurrent orbital pain and swelling, now involving the right eye. Exam revealed bilateral motility restriction, corneal haze, and conjunctival hyperemia and edema of the right eye. Visual acuity was 0.02 in the right eye and light perception in the left. Orbital CT again showed bilateral intraconal masses. Echocardiography findings of left ventricular hypertrophy and vascular dilation persisted. Laboratory tests again demonstrated hypoproteinaemia and hypokalaemia.

A 42-year-old man underwent transthoracic echocardiography as part of a routine medical checkup, which revealed a left ventricular mass. He had no prior medical history and denied fever, weight loss, dyspnea, or other symptoms. On admission, his temperature was 36.5 °C, blood pressure 120/80 mm Hg, and electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm. A chest radiograph revealed no active lung lesions. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a mobile, smooth, oval, pedunculated mass originating from the left ventricular lateral wall, measuring 1.34 × 1.9 cm. Contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography showed the mass attached to the interventricular septum with focal contrast enhancement.

A 37-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of intermittent small-volume hematochezia and a 4-month history of watery diarrhea up to five times daily associated with left lower quadrant pain relieved by bowel movements. She endorsed nocturnal diarrhea twice weekly without dietary triggers and reported no improvement with fiber supplements. She denied alcohol, tobacco, or drug use and had no family history of gastrointestinal disease. Vital signs and physical examination were normal. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, metabolic panel, and stool infectious workup, were unremarkable. An esophagogastroduodenoscopy was unremarkable. Colonoscopy revealed a 5-cm pedunculated polyp with villous features in the descending colon and a 1.5-cm pedunculated polyp in the sigmoid colon; both were excised. Histopathology showed tubulovillous adenomas. The colonic mucosa showed no evidence of colitis, and biopsies were negative for microscopic colitis and celiac disease.

A 54-year-old woman presented with acute urinary retention and reported irregular menses for the past four years. She was a former smoker, had a remote history of myomectomy, and no family history of cancer. On examination, she had a distended abdomen and suprapubic tenderness. Pelvic examination revealed a large cervical mass appearing to originate from the endocervical canal. Laboratory studies showed CA 125 127 U/ml, CEA 0.7 ng/ml, and CA 19-9 52 U/ml. Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis demonstrated an 8 cm heterogeneous mass involving the cervix without extension into the bladder or rectum and no significant lymphadenopathy. Under anesthesia, the cervix was occupied by an 8 cm smooth, firm, hemorrhagic mass with a broad base; the parametria were free, and a prominent left ovary was palpated. Cystoscopy and proctoscopy were unremarkable. Cervical biopsy specimens revealed only fibrovascular tissue with severe hemorrhage.

A 70-year-old man was referred after abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 48-mm tumor in the gallbladder. He was asymptomatic. Laboratory studies showed mild elevations in AST (67 U/L) and ALT (64 U/L), an ICG R15 of 20%, and normal carcinoembryonic antigen and CA 19-9 levels.  
Ultrasonography demonstrated a 50-mm hypoechoic mass in the gallbladder neck without obvious blood flow. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 48-mm, well-circumscribed mass on the right side of the common bile duct, with no invasion but with mass effect displacing the bile duct. MRI revealed a sharply demarcated lesion containing hyperintense cystic and reticulated areas on T2-weighted images and a hyperintense region on diffusion-weighted imaging. FDG-PET demonstrated high FDG uptake in the early phase without increase in the delayed phase.  
With a high suspicion of malignancy based on imaging, the patient underwent open cholecystectomy with wedge resection of the gallbladder bed.

A 60-year-old man was referred for further evaluation of a nodular shadow in the left middle lung field on screening chest radiography. He had hypertension diagnosed at age 55 and was on antihypertensive therapy. On examination, his blood pressure was 137/80 mm Hg, and the rest of the physical examination was normal. Serum sodium and potassium levels were within the reference range. Repeat chest radiography and noncontrast chest CT showed no pulmonary lesions. However, an incidental, well-defined, homogeneous, low-density mass measuring 2.3 × 2.3 × 2.1 cm (15 HU) was found in the right renal hilum, partially abutting the renal cortex. Dynamic contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated slight arterial‐phase enhancement and delayed‐phase washout. Both adrenal glands appeared normal, with no connection to the mass. On MRI, a T1-weighted gradient-echo sequence showed a uniform signal drop on out-of-phase images compared with in-phase images, indicating microscopic fat within the lesion. On diffusion-weighted imaging (b = 1000 s/mm2), the lesion was slightly hyperintense, and the ADC map showed lower signal than the renal cortex. Based on these imaging characteristics, a diagnosis of renal cell carcinoma was made.

A full-term male neonate (4110 g) was delivered by emergency cesarean section for pelvic insertion, polyhydramnios, ascites, and meconium in the amniotic fluid. Apgar scores were 1, 2, and 4 at 1, 5, and 15 minutes. He required immediate intubation and mechanical ventilation for bradycardia (heart rate 85 bpm) and hemodynamic instability and received vasoactive support, surfactant, and empirical ampicillin and gentamicin.

A chest radiograph disclosed multiple round lesions up to 8 mm in diameter diffusely involving both lungs. Lung ultrasonography demonstrated that these nodules were solid and there was no pleural effusion. Head ultrasonography showed mild cerebral edema. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed normal abdominal organs.

Laboratory studies showed elevated aspartate transaminase and γ-glutamyl transferase, prolonged coagulation studies with elevated D-dimer, thrombocytopenia, metabolic acidosis (pH 7.11) with elevated lactate, and anuria. Bicarbonate was administered and peritoneal dialysis was initiated. 

Examination of the skin revealed multiple bluish papular nodules, approximately 4 mm in size, covering the trunk and limbs. One of the skin nodules was biopsied and sent for histopathological assessment.

A 55-year-old woman presented with a painless, gradually enlarging mass in the right superior orbit over 4 years. She denied vision loss or field defects but reported occasional diplopia on up gaze for 6 months. Visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally. Examination of the right eye revealed a solid, non-tender, freely mobile 20 × 15 mm mass in the superior orbit causing proptosis; pupillary reactions, color vision, and visual fields were normal. Supraorbital, infraorbital, and corneal sensation were intact, and cranial-nerve and neurologic examinations were otherwise unremarkable. Slit-lamp and fundus examinations showed no optic-nerve involvement. Subjective diplopia in up gaze correlated with inferior globe dystopia, but ocular motility was full, and no compensatory head posture was noted. The left eye and general physical examination were normal. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the orbits showed a well-defined, homogenous, nonenhancing mass measuring 20 × 12 mm in the right superior orbit displacing the globe. Based on these findings, a provisional diagnosis of an orbital dermoid or cyst was made, and the patient was scheduled for excisional biopsy.

A 71-year-old woman presented with several weeks of fatigue. Her medical history was notable for a hysterectomy and oophorectomy in the 1980s for menorrhagia. A surveillance contrast-enhanced CT scan performed for a right lower lobe lung mass revealed a 3.6×2.5 cm right adnexal solid mass involving the right gonadal vein with extension into the inferior vena cava (IVC). A repeat chest CT at an outside facility showed that the mass reached the IVC–right atrial junction without clear intracardiac involvement. An abdominal MRI demonstrated tumor propagation to the confluence of the infrahepatic veins, but the level of termination remained unclear. The patient denied symptoms of renal, bowel, or cardiac compromise. Surgical resection via laparotomy and sternotomy was planned under possible cardiopulmonary bypass. After induction of anesthesia, intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) in a modified bicaval view unexpectedly revealed a thin-walled cystic structure in the right atrium close to the IVC junction, confirmed by color Doppler and bubble study. Advancing the probe into the IVC demonstrated a mass filling approximately half the lumen. As the probe was further maneuvered toward the IVC–atrial intersection, the mass was seen to divide into a tubular component leading into the cyst and a separate solid head abutting the interatrial septum. The remainder of the echocardiographic examination was unremarkable.

A 73-year-old man with known bilateral presbycusis and hearing aids presented with right-sided hearing impairment. He denied otorrhea, vertigo, or facial weakness. On examination, tone audiometry showed combined hearing loss on the right with a 20 dB conductive component and sensorineural loss on the left. The Weber test lateralized to the right ear, and Rinne’s test was positive bilaterally. Otoscopic inspection of the right ear revealed a smooth, white mass behind an intact tympanic membrane, causing a lateral bulge. Vestibular testing was normal. Given the intact tympanic membrane and inconsistent history, a high-resolution CT scan of the temporal bone was obtained. The scan showed a lesion at the handle of the right malleus with high-density values (mean, 930 ± 115 Hounsfield units), no adjacent bone erosion, and, on comparison with the temporal squama (1100 ± 95 HU), bony composition. Three-dimensional reconstruction demonstrated a small bony connection to the malleus.

A 61-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of low-grade fever, dry cough, and breathlessness. Medication reduced his fever, but cough persisted. Cardiovascular, neurologic, and abdominal examinations were normal. A chest radiograph showed multifocal bilateral consolidation and cardiomegaly. Transthoracic echocardiography was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed bilateral consolidation and demonstrated a large, broad-based soft-tissue mass along the left heart border extending to the left hilum; the fat planes between the mass and adjacent myocardium, pleura, and lung were preserved, with no evidence of invasion. On delayed imaging, the lesion showed heterogeneous enhancement with internal hypodense (necrotic) areas. Cardiac MRI was not available. CT-guided fine-needle aspiration and biopsy of the mass revealed “proliferation of fibrous tissue in a sheet-like pattern, which were elongated, spindle shaped with elongated bland nuclei. No mitotic activity was seen.”

A 22-year-old man presented with a swelling on the left side of his left eye that had been present for 1 year. He first noticed a small, quiescent nodule approximately 1 year earlier, which gradually increased to its present size. He denied trauma to the area, paresthesia, or recent weight loss. On extra-oral examination, there was a well-defined oval swelling measuring about 4 cm anteroposteriorly and 5 cm superoinferiorly, located 1 cm lateral to the outer canthus of the left eye and extending to approximately 6 cm anterior to the external auditory meatus. The overlying skin was smooth and normal in color. On palpation, the mass was firm, non-tender, and freely mobile relative to both skin and underlying tissues. No cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. Radiographic and sonographic evaluations of the region revealed no abnormalities.

A 73-year-old man presented with a rapidly growing, painful mass in his left thigh for the past few days. He reported difficulty walking due to pain but denied fever, weight loss, or systemic symptoms. His medical history included COPD, hypertension, and peptic ulcer disease, managed with theophylline, omeprazole, valsartan, aspirin, salmeterol, and ipratropium. Five days before symptom onset, he received an intramuscular Sinopharm COVID-19 vaccine in his left deltoid. He had no history of trauma.

On examination, he was afebrile with normal vital signs. In the lateral mid–portion of the left thigh, there was a firm, round, tender intramuscular mass measuring approximately 4 cm, without overlying skin changes or lymphadenopathy. The remainder of his physical examination was unremarkable.

Soft‐tissue ultrasonography showed an oval, well-defined 15 × 41 mm intramuscular mass in the vastus lateralis, hypoechoic with a striated pattern and increased vascularity on color Doppler, without extra‐fascial extension or bony invasion. MRI of the left thigh revealed a well-circumscribed 19 × 39 mm intramuscular lesion in the mid–vastus lateralis muscle that was homogeneously low signal on T1-weighted images, high signal on T2/proton-density sequences, and exhibited extensive surrounding vasogenic edema and intense homogeneous contrast enhancement. Based on imaging, neoplastic lesions such as sarcoma, nerve‐sheath tumors, and metastasis were considered.

An 11-year-old boy presented with one month of low-grade fever and decreased appetite. Three weeks before admission, he noted a mass in the right iliac fossa, approximately 10×10 cm, mobile, firm, and globular, associated with localized pain. He had no history of abdominal trauma or prior surgery. On examination, vital signs were stable; a firm, mobile mass was palpated in the right iliac fossa. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7 g/dL and an ESR of 140 mm in the first hour; all other routine tests were normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a well-defined soft-tissue mass in the peritoneal cavity in the region of the right iliac fossa without obvious lymphadenopathy. The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy, which revealed a well-vascularized 10 cm mass arising from the mesentery of the proximal ileum and adherent to the bowel wall. Ten centimeters of ileum were resected en bloc with the mass, and an end-to-end anastomosis was performed. On gross inspection, the lobulated mass was firm and, on sectioning, had a gritty texture.

A 58-year-old Asian man presented in 2022 with a painless subcutaneous nodule on the left cheek. He first noted a sesame-seed–sized black superficial lesion at that site in 2017 and underwent laser therapy without biopsy. The lesion recurred in 2019 and gradually enlarged over 3 years. On examination, there was a 0.6 cm × 0.6 cm round, reddish nodule with medium texture, clear borders, and a smooth intact surface; regional lymph nodes were not palpable. He was afebrile, with a heart rate of 80 beats/min and blood pressure of 116/72 mmHg. His medical, family, and exposure histories were unremarkable. 

An excisional biopsy performed on June 8, 2022, revealed heterogeneous epithelial cells floating in mucinous lakes within subdermal fibrous tissue. Immunohistochemical staining showed tumor cells positive for cytokeratin 7, with a few cells positive for synaptophysin and chromogranin-A, and negative staining for CD117, p63, cytokeratin 20, p40, MUC5AC, and CDX2. A total-body PET-CT scan showed no evidence of a primary visceral malignancy.

A 15-year-old boy presented with intermittent abdominal pain for 2 years. He had no significant past medical history, no family history of gastrointestinal tumors, and denied smoking, alcohol use, or allergies. Vital signs were normal. Physical examination of the chest, lungs, and abdomen was unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including routine blood, urine, stool, biochemical studies, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, were within normal limits except for an alkaline phosphatase level of 197 U/L and uric acid of 431.6 µmol/L. CT of the chest and abdomen revealed a 5 cm space-occupying lesion in the gastric fundus without other abnormalities. Gastroscopy showed a semicircular bulge approximately 5 cm in size on the lesser curvature near the cardia with surface erosion and shallow ulcers. Endoscopic ultrasonography demonstrated a heterogeneous, hyperechoic lesion originating from the submucosal layer with an intact muscularis propria and serosa and abundant Doppler flow. Biopsy revealed spindle cell proliferation with interstitial mucinous changes and chronic inflammatory surface mucosa. Immunohistochemical staining of the biopsy specimen showed smooth muscle actin positive, CD117 negative, CD34 negative, DOG-1 negative, S-100 negative, and Ki-67 labeling index < 1 %.

A 68-year-old man was referred for rapidly deteriorating mental status and persistent fever. Over the preceding two months he had experienced low-grade fevers, fatigue, lethargy, and a 7-kg weight loss. On examination he was febrile but had no focal neurologic deficits, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, and no skin rash. Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 2560/µL (absolute neutrophils 1430/µL), hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL, platelets 108,000/µL, and a markedly elevated C-reactive protein (4.48 mg/dL) with a normal procalcitonin level (0.26 ng/mL). Blood cultures were negative. Serum calcium was 20.6 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 2668 IU/L, blood urea nitrogen 43.3 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.39 mg/dL. A noncontrast brain CT scan showed no intracranial hemorrhage or mass. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen showed mild splenomegaly but no lymphadenopathy, no masses, and no osteolytic lesions in the chest wall, pelvis, or vertebrae.

A 38‐year‐old gravida 2 para 1 Japanese woman at 37 weeks 1 day of gestation was admitted for elective cesarean section because of a low‐lying placenta. On hospital day 6, she developed massive vaginal bleeding and underwent emergency cesarean delivery. Following the operation, she experienced rapidly worsening dyspnea and was transferred to the ICU.

Vital signs on ICU admission: temperature 36.3°C; pulse 83 beats/min, regular; blood pressure 116/50 mmHg; respiratory rate 15 breaths/min; SpO₂ 98% on room air. Physical examination revealed only lower‐abdominal pain. Laboratory studies showed a drop in hemoglobin from 10.1 g/dL pre‐delivery to 6.1 g/dL post‐delivery.

On postoperative day 1, chest X‐ray demonstrated cardiomegaly and bilateral lower‐zone opacities. Non‐invasive positive‐pressure ventilation and intravenous diuretics were initiated, with transient improvement. On postoperative day 2, contrast‐enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed:
• Bilateral pleural effusions  
• Multiple small nodules throughout both lungs  
• Multiple masses in the liver  
• Multiple osteolytic lesions in the bones  
• Thrombi in the splenic vein, abdominal inferior vena cava, and left common iliac vein  
Importantly, there were no filling defects to suggest pulmonary embolism.

A 35-year-old multiparous woman presented with a 15-day history of an abdominal mass and intermittent acute lower abdominal pain. She was noted to have severe pallor on examination. 

On pelvic and rectal examination:
• Uterus and cervix: normal  
• A 15×15×15 cm mobile, tender abdomino-pelvic mass arising from the right adnexa, extending into the left iliac fossa and lumbar regions  
• Bilateral parametria supple; rectal mucosa free  

Laboratory studies revealed:
• Hemoglobin: 8.0 g/dL  
• Other hematologic parameters and serum biochemistry: within normal limits  
• Serum CA-125: 178 U/mL (elevated)  
• Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH): 899 U/L (elevated)  
• β-hCG, carcinoembryonic antigen, and α-fetoprotein: within normal limits  
• HIV and HBsAg serologies: negative  
• Chest radiograph: normal  

Transvaginal ultrasound showed a 10.9×10.8 cm solid heterogeneous right adnexal mass with increased vascularity on Doppler.  

At laparotomy, findings included:
• Minimal hemorrhagic ascites  
• A very vascular right ovarian mass (14×15×6 cm) with solid and cystic areas and deposits on the bladder peritoneum  
• Normal uterus, left adnexa, appendix, omentum, and upper abdominal viscera  
• Palpable bulky para-aortic and iliac lymph nodes  

An intraoperative frozen section was reported as a poorly differentiated neoplasm carcinoma. The patient underwent extrafascial hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, bilateral pelvic lymphadenectomy, para-aortic node dissection, excision of peritoneal deposits, and omentectomy.  

Postoperatively, she developed rapidly accumulating ascites, right-sided pleural effusion, and paralytic ileus. Therapeutic paracenteses and pleurocenteses provided symptomatic relief; pleural fluid cytology showed reactive mesothelial cells without malignancy. Final histopathology remained inconclusive, describing a poorly differentiated neoplasm; all lymph nodes and omentum were reactive. The clinical stage was assigned as FIGO IIC.
