Weekly carboplatin (AUC 2) was initiated to control effusions and her general condition. By day 7 after the first infusion, pleural fluid had nearly resolved; she completed three additional weekly cycles, and her CA-125 and LDH normalized.  

Immunohistochemical analysis of the tumor demonstrated:  
• Positive: CD138, lambda light chain, cytokeratin, focal EMA  
• Negative: CK7, CD99, inhibin, CD117, synaptophysin, chromogranin, MIC2, LCA, HMB45, CK20, SMA, desmin, CD34, S100, CD79a, kappa light chain

A 60-year-old woman presented with a 2-day history of cough and hemoptysis. She had well-controlled diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia and was a lifelong non-smoker. On examination, she was afebrile, SpO2 was 97% on room air, and there were no adventitious lung or heart sounds. Laboratory tests showed a leukocyte count of 11,700 cells/μl (80.2% neutrophils), C-reactive protein 2.22 mg/dl, and hemoglobin A1c 6.5%. Liver and renal function were normal. Serum carcinoembryonic antigen, cytokeratin-19 fragment, pro-gastrin-releasing peptide, β-D-glucan, aspergillus antigen, and cryptococcus antigen were within normal limits. An interferon-γ release assay for tuberculosis was negative. 

Chest radiography and contrast-enhanced CT revealed a non-enhanced, oval, well-circumscribed 5 × 6 × 10 cm mass in the right lower lobe, containing air bubbles and surrounded by a ground-glass halo. Review of a chest radiograph from one year earlier identified a 1-cm right hilum nodule. PET/CT showed no FDG uptake in the lesion. Bronchoscopy on hospital day 7 demonstrated active bleeding from the superior segmental bronchus of the right lower lobe without visible endobronchial lesions; lavage fluid cytology and bacterial cultures were negative, and biopsy was not obtained. 

Clinical differential diagnoses included lung cancer, rare benign hemorrhagic neoplasms, lung abscess, mycetoma, and congenital malformations such as congenital cystic adenomatoid malformation and bronchopulmonary sequestration.

A 37-year-old woman with polysubstance abuse history and generalized anxiety disorder presented with sudden onset of abdominal pain for 1 day. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a 12.5 cm heterogenous, enhancing mass in the left adrenal gland with mild to moderate hyperdense fluid throughout the abdomen, consistent with prior hemorrhage. The patient was hemodynamically stable; heart rate was 112 bpm, blood pressure 114/92 mmHg, temperature 98.6 °F, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. She denied histories of hypertension or diaphoresis but reported occasional headaches, palpitations, and an unintentional 10–15 lb weight loss over 4 months. She initially denied current substance use and was taking suboxone and bupropion; there was no family history of endocrine disorders.

On examination, she had abdominal distention, diffuse tenderness, and anasarca without cushingoid features. Initial biochemical tests revealed plasma cortisol six times the upper limit of normal, plasma metanephrines 25–30 times the upper limit of normal, and urine metanephrines 30–100 times the upper limit of normal. A urine toxicology screen was positive for amphetamines, and she then admitted to amphetamine use one week before admission. After two weeks drug washout, plasma cortisol declined by more than 50%, and urine metanephrines remained elevated at 20–40 times the upper limit of normal.

A 41-year-old woman, gravida 7, para 7, presented with a six-month history of lower abdominal pain and abnormal vaginal bleeding. Her menstrual history was unremarkable. She had undergone a cesarean section three years earlier and an appendectomy one year earlier. On examination, a palpable pelvi-abdominal mass was noted. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin concentration of 10.1 g/dL, a random blood glucose level of 80 mg/dL, and normal liver and renal function tests. Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a normal-sized uterus displaced to the right by an 8 cm left ovarian mass; there was no free pelvic fluid. The initial clinical impression was a left ovarian cyst.

At laparotomy, the left ovarian mass appeared as a hemorrhagic solid tumor. A frozen section was interpreted as an undifferentiated neoplasm, with benign versus malignant nature indeterminate. The patient underwent a left salpingo-oophorectomy and an incisional biopsy of the right ovary. Gross examination of the left ovarian mass showed a 7.0×6.0×2.0 cm brownish, hemorrhagic lesion with both solid and cystic areas. Permanent sections demonstrated a vascular neoplasm with adjacent compressed ovarian parenchyma at the periphery, showing arborizing channels of variable sizes and shapes lined by atypical endothelial-appearing cells. Areas of necrosis were present, and the mitotic count was four to five mitoses per 10 high-power fields.

A 40-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of left facial nerve paralysis, a 3-month history of dysphagia manifested by coughing when drinking water, a 2-month history of dysarthria, and a 1-month history of headache. She had no significant medical or family history. On examination, she had left facial hypalgesia, leftward deviation of the tongue with ipsilateral tongue atrophy on protrusion, and otherwise normal cranial nerve function. Routine blood, urine, and biochemical studies were within normal limits. 

Computed tomography of the skull base showed a lobulated soft-tissue mass in the left mastoid region with a sclerotic rim, scalloped margins, and intratumoral calcification. The lesion eroded the left mastoid air cells, invaded the mastoid segment of the facial nerve canal and the jugular foramen, and involved the ipsilateral hypoglossal canal. 

Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 4.4×2.3×4.0 cm lobulated mass that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and demonstrated peripheral gadolinium enhancement with a nonenhancing central area.

A 53-year-old man was referred for evaluation of left-sided neck swelling of seven months’ duration. Ultrasound examination revealed an echo-free, well-circumscribed mass measuring 24.1×36.4 mm, located 3.9 mm beneath the skin over the left parotid region, with no adhesions to surrounding tissues and a leading consideration of a benign mass or lymphadenopathy. He had a lifelong history of photosensitivity and multiple skin lesions; at age 51, he was diagnosed with basal cell carcinoma of the zygomatic region and lip, metatypical carcinoma of the frontal skin, and keratoacanthoma-like squamous cell carcinoma of the nose. Family history was unremarkable. He underwent radical lymph node dissection; the submandibular specimen measured 4×2.5×1 cm and was effaced by a malignant mesenchymal tumor with a storiform pattern. Neoplastic cells were spindle-shaped with hyperchromatic, pleomorphic nuclei, vesicular chromatin, prominent nucleoli, and eosinophilic cytoplasm; mitotic figures were frequent (≈15 per 10 high-power fields), and areas of hemorrhage and necrosis were present. Review of hematoxylin and eosin– and trichrome-stained slides confirmed near-total effacement of the nodal architecture by fascicles and sheets of large pleomorphic cells with abundant pale eosinophilic cytoplasm and bizarre, grooved nuclei, accompanied by mitotic figures and a narrow rim of small lymphocytes. Immunohistochemical studies were recommended to establish a definitive diagnosis.

A 57-year-old man was referred 4 weeks after transurethral resection of a 2 cm × 2 cm bladder tumor, histologically confirmed as nested-variant transitional cell carcinoma. He reported 2 months of painless hematuria and, more recently, lower-limb weakness and progressive dyspnea with a nonproductive cough. 

On examination, he appeared pale, was febrile to 99.5°F, tachycardic, and tachypneic, and had motor weakness of both lower limbs. Oxygen saturation was 82% on room air, improving to 95% with 6 L/min of supplemental oxygen. Digital rectal examination revealed a normal prostate and decreased rectal tone. Despite a 22-Fr three-way Foley catheter, suprapubic fullness persisted; bladder washout yielded 200 mL of old clots.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.5 g/dL, leukocyte count 14 500/mm3 (neutrophilia), creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, albumin 2.5 g/dL, alkaline phosphatase 300 IU/L, and PSA 4.2 ng/mL. Urinalysis revealed numerous pus cells, red blood cells, and leukocyte esterase positivity; culture grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated diffuse bladder-wall thickening with a right-sided diverticulum, intraluminal air, bilateral external iliac and para-aortic lymphadenopathy, and osteolytic lesions in the sacrum, right acetabulum, bilateral iliac bones, L5 vertebra, T4 and T9 vertebrae, and the right eighth costovertebral angle.

CT of the chest revealed thickened, nodular interlobular septa and polygonal arcades in both upper lobes and the right middle lobe.

A 50-year-old woman with a >10-year history of mid-dorsal back pain noted progressive lower-limb weakness and stiffness over 8 months, worse on the right, requiring a walker. She also reported bilateral thigh paresthesias and urinary hesitancy. On examination, she had right hip and knee flexion 3/5, foot dorsiflexion and plantar flexion 2/5; left lower-limb strength was 4/5. There was a sensory level at T8 with hypoesthesia below, severely impaired position sense in the right leg, absent abdominal reflexes, hyperreflexia, and bilateral Babinski signs. Anal tone was preserved with weak voluntary contraction. MRI of the thoracic spine showed a fusiform posterior epidural mass spanning T6–T9, compressing the cord. The lesion was inhomogeneous, hyperintense on T1- and T2-weighted images, and showed inhomogeneous enhancement on postcontrast T1-weighted images with and without fat suppression. It tapered at both ends and extended through the neural foramina into the thoracic cavity.

A 95-year-old man with long-standing bilateral, symmetric, age-related hearing loss developed new-onset, sharp intermittent left ear pain and asymmetric hearing loss. He denied vertigo, tinnitus, aural pressure, drainage, or facial weakness. His medical history included prostate cancer treated 12 years earlier with androgen deprivation therapy and brachytherapy, as well as Parkinson’s disease, hypertension, type II diabetes, and gout. At an outside hospital his symptoms were attributed to Eustachian tube dysfunction or temporomandibular joint arthritis, and he was treated with ciprodex otic drops, fluticasone nasal spray, and acetaminophen; an MRI was recommended but declined. Two weeks later, his ear pain had resolved but the asymmetric hearing loss persisted. On examination, both ear canals, tympanic membranes, and middle ears were normal. Audiometry showed bilateral sensorineural hearing loss worse on the left (Speech Recognition Threshold: right ear 40 dB HL, left ear 55 dB HL; Speech Discrimination: right ear 88% at 85 dB HL, left ear 80% at 90 dB HL), compared with a 2012 audiogram that demonstrated milder thresholds (speech recognition thresholds 35 dB HL bilaterally). He declined steroid treatment. Laboratory studies showed PSA levels rising from 4.22 ng/mL in 2012 to 6.43 ng/mL in 2014; alkaline phosphatase and lactate dehydrogenase were within normal limits. MRI of the brain with internal auditory canal protocol revealed an extensive skull base tumor involving the clivus and petrous temporal bone, with extension into the posterior-inferior mastoid air cells, bordering the foramen lacerum, obliterating the left jugular foramen, and involving the hypoglossal canal. A fine-cut CT of the temporal bones confirmed an infiltrative bony lesion at the left skull base. Differential diagnosis included metastatic multiple myeloma, glomus tumor, and most likely metastatic disease.

A 52-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of painful swelling of the left upper jaw, associated with decreased vision and watering of the left eye. His medical and family histories were noncontributory; he had a 30-year history of smoking and alcohol use. Extraoral examination showed a non-tender, hard swelling of the left midface. Intraorally, there was a well-defined, firm-to-hard, non-tender swelling of the left maxillary alveolus in the region of the first through third molars, with obliteration of the buccal vestibule. 

Periapical radiographs revealed a “ground glass” appearance and symmetric widening of the periodontal ligament space around the left canine and first and second premolars. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated complete destruction of the walls of the left maxillary antrum and zygomatic process, with numerous central calcifications. CT (bone algorithm) showed a hypodense mass occupying the left maxillary antrum, with destruction of all walls and invasion into the nasal fossa, orbit, and hard palate; the inferior aspect was micro-multilocular, and the rest contained haphazard calcifications. CT (soft-tissue algorithm) confirmed diffuse calcifications in the left maxillary alveolar process and antrum. 

Based on these radiologic findings, differential diagnoses of osteosarcoma and osteoblastic metastatic malignancy (such as prostate cancer) were considered.

A 58-year-old African-American woman presented with several months of left lower quadrant abdominal pain. She had no jaundice or weight loss. Vital signs were stable. Physical examination was unremarkable except for mild tenderness in the left lower quadrant. Laboratory studies showed carcinoembryonic antigen 6.5 ng/mL (normal 0–5.0) and CA 19-9 of 39 U/mL (normal 0–37). Functional endocrine hormone studies revealed a gastrin level of 214 pg/mL (mildly elevated) with normal insulin, glucagon, and vasoactive intestinal peptide levels. Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI of the abdomen demonstrated a 3.8 cm hypervascular, well-circumscribed mass in the head of the pancreas without evidence of vascular invasion or distant metastasis. Endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle aspiration was nondiagnostic.

A 68-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of intermittent cough productive of yellow viscous sputum. He had smoked 20 cigarettes daily for over 50 years. On examination, respiratory sounds were weakened over the left upper lung; no rales were heard. Serum tumor markers showed an elevated CYFRA21-1 level of 4.67 ng/mL; NSE, AFP, PSA, CEA, CA12-5, CA19-9, CA15-3, and ferritin were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed in the left upper lobe a large high-density mass with surrounding band-like opacities and bronchial wall thickening with luminal narrowing, suggestive of obstructive pneumonia. In the right middle lobe, there was a 3.2 × 2.8 cm lobulated, spiculated high-density mass. Bronchoscopy demonstrated an abnormal hyperplastic bulge of the left upper lobe bronchial mucosa with a thickened, firm wall and narrowed lumen. Biopsy of the left upper lobe lesion showed small cell lung cancer, with positive immunostaining for CK, CK7, CD56, Villin, CgA, Syn, partial TTF-1 and CD117, negative CK20, NapsinA, P40, P63, and ~80% Ki-67 positivity. CT-guided needle biopsy of the right middle lobe lesion revealed moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma with positive CK, CK5/6, P40, P63, negative CK7, TTF-1, NapsinA, and ~20% Ki-67 positivity.

An 80-year-old man presented with one month of nonproductive cough, fatigue, low-grade fevers, a 2.5-kg weight loss, and a syncopal episode. His history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, nephrolithiasis, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and treated Lyme disease one year earlier. He had a remote 22 pack-year smoking history. Three months before admission he noted a tick bite treated with amoxicillin; his symptoms transiently improved but recurred, and he was prescribed doxycycline, which he did not complete.

On admission he was febrile (38.2 °C) with a platelet count of 66 000/mm3. During his stay at an outside hospital he developed progressive anemia and thrombocytopenia. CT scans of the head, chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no central nervous system lesions, lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly; small bilateral pleural effusions were noted. Bone marrow biopsy was unrevealing, and flow cytometry showed no clonal cell population.

After transfer to the intensive care unit on hospital day 16, labs showed elevated glucose, lactate, D-dimer, BUN, AST, and unconjugated bilirubin; hyponatremia, low CO2, ionized calcium, albumin, prealbumin, total protein, total T3, free T4, and amylase. Hemoglobin was 12.2 g/dL, white blood cell count 6 870/mm3 (76% neutrophils, 16% lymphocytes, 8% monocytes, 1% nucleated red cells), and platelets 13 000/mm3. Peripheral smear demonstrated mild anisocytosis, ovalocytosis, and macrocytosis.

Physical examination revealed a blanching, tan-pink maculopapular rash on the right lower extremity. He required platelet transfusions to maintain counts. Lyme titers, HAV, HBV, HIV, syphilis, and rheumatologic serologies were negative. Cardiac function was normal. Although TSH and free T4 were low, pituitary imaging was normal. With concern for ehrlichiosis or other tick-borne infection, serologies for Ehrlichia and CSF studies (HSV, Cryptococcus, Lyme) were obtained. He was started on vancomycin, doxycycline, and piperacillin-tazobactam.

By hospital day 3 he required 14 L of fluid over 18 hours for worsening lactic acidosis and hypotension. Abdominal CT revealed diffuse anasarca and possible peritonitis. Given his rapid decline and poor prognosis, care was withdrawn, and he died on hospital day 4.

A 20-year‐old man with no prior medical history presented with a 2‐week history of severe frontal, pulsatile headache (lasting 30 minutes every 3 hours), nausea, vomiting, malaise, and nonbloody sputum, along with 15 kg of weight loss over 2 months. He had no family history of tuberculosis or lung cancer. Vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, his conjunctiva were pale, and he had cervical and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy; other findings were unremarkable.

Because of the headache, an MRI of the brain was performed, demonstrating multiple hyperdense lesions. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a large pericardial effusion (~750 cc), leading to pericardiocentesis; pericardial fluid and a myocardial biopsy were sent for analysis.

Spiral CT of the chest and abdomen showed innumerable small pulmonary nodules in a miliary pattern, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and bilateral adrenal lesions. An infectious disease work‐up was undertaken, including sputum smear and culture for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, blood and sputum MTB‐PCR, cytology MTB‐PCR, technetium‐99 m–ethambutol scintigraphy, and interferon‐γ release assay. Sputum smear and culture, blood, and sputum MTB‐PCR were negative, but Tc‐EMB scintigraphy was positive. On the basis of the clinical picture and positive scintigraphy, an anti‐tuberculosis regimen (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) with dexamethasone was initiated.

A 54-year-old Caucasian man with hypertension and chronic lower-extremity pain was referred for evaluation of a suspected choroidal melanoma in the left eye. He reported photopsias in that eye. On examination, visual acuity was 20/25 in the right eye and 20/70 in the left. Slit-lamp evaluation of the left eye revealed stellate keratic precipitates and 1+ anterior chamber cells; fundus examination showed 1+ vitreous cells, blunting of the foveal reflex, and a yellow–gray choroidal lesion along the inferior arcade with surrounding subretinal fluid. B-scan ultrasound measured the lesion at 6 mm thickness and 11 mm in basal diameter with a hyper-echoic, dome-shaped appearance. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated early staining and late leakage corresponding to subretinal fluid. Enhanced-depth OCT confirmed a domed choroidal elevation with effaced choroidal vessels, preserved choriocapillaris, overlying hyperreflective subretinal exudation, and cystoid macular edema (central thickness 533 μm). Indocyanine green angiography showed persistent hypocyanescence of the lesion. A chest radiograph showed only smoking-related changes. Laboratory tests revealed normal ACE levels and a negative Quantiferon GOLD. Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated eccentric, noncalcific thickening of the aortic arch and the origin of the left subclavian artery.

A 75‐year‐old woman was brought to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident, during which evaluation revealed a right neck lymphadenopathy. She reported that the right neck swelling had progressively increased in size over several weeks. She had no facial asymmetry, erythema, or tenderness externally, but a single enlarged, fixed, non‐tender cervical lymph node was palpated. Panoramic radiograph showed an ill‐defined radiolucent lesion distal to tooth #31 without root resorption. Intraoral examination revealed intact mucosa over tooth #31 that was tender to palpation but without mobility or purulence. A CT scan demonstrated a 23‐mm mandibular radiolucency with erosion of the lingual cortical plate, thinning of the buccal cortex, and no bucco‐lingual expansion. An incisional biopsy was performed. Histopathologic examination revealed an epithelial‐lined cyst wall with infiltrating nests composed of both epidermoid and mucous cells, with a predominant mucinous component.

A 16-year-old girl with no significant past medical history presented with a 2-month history of insidious left occipital headaches that had recently increased in intensity. She also noted a painless swelling over the frontal scalp first noticed by friends. She denied fever, seizures, photophobia, visual disturbances, weight change, or constitutional symptoms. Approximately 3 months earlier she had slipped in the bathroom without loss of consciousness or vomiting. Over the past 2 months, NSAIDs no longer relieved her headaches.  

On examination, vital signs were normal. Neurologic and systemic examinations were unremarkable except for a tender, firm swelling over the frontal scalp. Routine laboratory studies, including biochemical and electrolyte tests, were within normal limits.  

Noncontrast and contrast-enhanced CT of the head revealed a large extra-axial cystic-solid lesion in the left frontal region with multiple calcifications in the solid component and peripheral rim, erosion of the adjacent frontal bone, and extension into the overlying scalp. Fifteen days later, contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain showed a large, well-defined, heterogeneously enhancing extra-axial mass in the bilateral frontal regions (predominantly on the left) with calvarial extension and surrounding signal-intensity changes. The radiologist suggested a malignant lesion with two leading differentials: hemangiopericytoma or anaplastic meningioma.

A 5-year-old girl presented with 1 month of right-sided chest pain and cough. On examination she was mildly febrile (38°C) and had dullness to percussion over the right chest near the heart border. Initial blood tests showed a neutrophil count of 12 G/L and a C-reactive protein level of 6 mg/L. A chest X-ray demonstrated consolidation in the right middle lobe outlining the inferior margin of the horizontal fissure, with an obscured right heart border but a visible right hemidiaphragm. She was treated with cefotaxime and linezolid for 1 month without clinical or radiographic improvement. Repeat chest X-ray showed persistent consolidation. A chest CT scan then revealed a homogeneous, well-defined mass in the right middle lobe causing occlusion of the right middle lobe bronchus and necrosis of the residual parenchyma.

A 40-year-old G2P2 woman presented with a 5-month history of umbilical swelling, cyclic umbilical pain, and bleeding. Her menstrual cycles occur every 29 days, lasting 5 days with moderate flow. She denied lower abdominal pain, trauma to the abdomen or umbilicus, bleeding from other sites, and urinary or bowel symptoms. She had two prior spontaneous vaginal deliveries without complications and had stopped using levonorgestrel implants two years earlier. She had no other relevant medical, surgical, or gynecologic history.

On examination, her vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination revealed a 2.0 × 1.5 cm brownish umbilical nodule that was non-tender. Speculum and bimanual examinations were unremarkable. The remainder of her physical examination, including cardiovascular, respiratory, lymphatic, and neurologic assessments, was normal.

An abdominopelvic ultrasound showed a 10.3 mm endometrial thickness. Chest radiography, complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, and urinalysis were all within normal limits.

A 35-year-old Caucasian man presented with an intraoral swelling that had been growing for 8 years. The lesion was asymptomatic until its size began to impair his speech. On examination, there was a firm, mushroom-shaped mass with bony consistency, covered by smooth mucosa, spanning almost the entire right alveolar border of the mandible. The area was edentulous; according to the patient, the growth had begun shortly after the extraction of a lower molar, and over time the remaining adjacent teeth (28 through 32) had been extruded until they fell out. There were no extraoral abnormalities. The patient was otherwise healthy, with no history of systemic disease, smoking, or substance use. Computed tomography showed a well-defined pedunculated mass attached to the right mandibular body, with a central area of moderate radiopacity resembling medullary bone and a surrounding thin, more radiopaque rim comparable to cortical bone.

A 62-year-old postmenopausal Japanese woman presented with progressive abdominal distension and a palpable pelvic mass.  
She had a known history of uterine leiomyomata diagnosed over 20 years earlier, treated briefly with gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists. Her menopause occurred at age 51. At age 55, she underwent partial resection of a right breast mass diagnosed as invasive lobular carcinoma (pT2N1M0, stage IIA). Immunohistochemical staining of the breast tumor was positive for estrogen receptors, progesterone receptors, and cerbB2, with a Ki-67 index of 20%. She received adjuvant radiotherapy (50 Gy plus a 10 Gy boost), six cycles of fluorouracil, epirubicin, and cyclophosphamide, and took anastrozole for five years.  
Twenty months after completing hormonal therapy, routine blood tests revealed elevated tumor markers: cancer antigen 15-3 at 87.9 IU/mL, carcinoembryonic antigen at 15.6 ng/mL, and NCC stomach 439 at 120 IU/mL.  
Pelvic imaging with computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, and transvaginal ultrasonography showed an irregularly enlarged uterus measuring 23 × 12 cm, with marked growth of presumed leiomyomata since two years earlier. On positron emission tomography–computed tomography, the uterine mass demonstrated intense fluorodeoxyglucose uptake, and systemic evaluation, including bone scintigraphy and upper endoscopy, revealed no other lesions. Endometrial sampling was not technically feasible because of the size of the mass.  
Given the concern for uterine malignancy, she underwent total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, although it was unknown whether the tumor represented a primary uterine cancer or a metastasis.

A 60-year-old Ethiopian woman (para VI) presented with a progressively enlarging swelling of the right vulva that had been present for 25 years. Over the past 3 months, she developed a dull aching pain and difficulty with micturition and dysuria. There was no discharge or bleeding. She reported genital cutting and sewing during childhood; her other medical and surgical histories were unremarkable. She was a non‐smoker, did not consume alcohol, and had not sought prior medical care for this issue.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Abdominal and cardiopulmonary examinations were unremarkable. Genitourinary examination revealed an 18 cm × 12 cm fluctuant, multilobulated, mobile, non‐tender mass of the right labia majora extending to the mons pubis and stretching the ventral skin over the urethra. The overlying skin was intact, and the labial edges were fused at the cranial aspect. Speculum and bimanual examinations of the vagina, cervix, and uterus were normal. Inguinal lymph nodes were not enlarged. Musculoskeletal and neurological examinations were normal.

Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 13 g/dL, white blood cell count 6500/mm³, platelet count 250 000/mm³, and blood group B +. Urinalysis was unremarkable. A pelvic ultrasound showed an atrophied uterus with no additional pelvic masses.

A 35-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 1-year history of gradually progressive left-sided hearing loss and a sensation of ear fullness. He denied trauma, noise exposure, or family history of deafness. Examination revealed a normal left external auditory canal and a bulging, thickened tympanic membrane. Pure-tone audiometry showed moderate conductive hearing loss on the left. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the temporal bones demonstrated a soft-tissue-density mass filling the left middle ear and extending into the attic, displacing the ossicles without evidence of bone erosion. The patient underwent endoscopic exploratory tympanotomy, which revealed a polypoid bony mass free from the surrounding middle ear walls; the stapes was absent, and the long process of the incus was eroded. The lesion was completely excised endoscopically, and a type III tympanoplasty was performed using a tragal chondral perichondrial graft.

A male neonate was delivered vaginally at 38 weeks’ gestation to a 29-year-old G1P1 woman; birth weight was 3750 g. At birth, he had no significant respiratory distress but was noted to have feeding difficulties. Examination revealed a polypoid mass arising within the oral cavity, partly covered with skin and likened in shape to a human foot. Associated findings included a cleft tongue and cleft palate. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a mixed-density tumour in the oropharynx, probably attached to the palate. Computed tomography confirmed the cleft palate.

A 45-year-old woman presented with a several-month history of fluctuating blood pressure and generalized abdominal pain localized to the right hypochondrium and flank, accompanied by postprandial nausea and discomfort after fatty meals. On examination, there was tenderness in the right hypochondrium with a positive Murphy’s sign; there was no weight loss or other systemic symptoms.

Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a hyperechoic mass measuring 13.7 × 15.8 cm in the right hypochondrium, displacing the right kidney inferiorly. The mass had irregular borders, poor color Doppler perfusion, and no calcifications, suggesting a fatty lesion likely originating from the right adrenal gland. The gallbladder was enlarged and contained multiple small to medium-sized stones.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a well-defined heterogeneous mass measuring 17 × 14 × 11 cm, with fatty and soft-tissue components and a 2 × 3 cm nodular density in the upper medial region, without calcifications; the lesion displaced the liver superiorly and the kidney inferomedially. The gallbladder wall was thin and regular, containing multiple low-density cholesterol stones of approximately 6 mm in diameter. No other abnormalities were noted.

Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, electrolytes, renal function, and coagulation profile, were within reference ranges. Hormonal studies showed normal morning cortisol levels and normal 24-hour urine metanephrines and normetanephrines. A dexamethasone suppression test yielded an 8 a.m. cortisol of 0.8 ng/dL, indicating no autonomous hormone secretion.

A 41-year-old Caucasian woman noticed left cheek swelling and pain in the corresponding upper premolars and molars lasting more than a week. Her medical history included a prior ischemic cerebrovascular accident treated with anticoagulants. On extraoral examination, there was a firm swelling of the left cheek without lymphadenopathy or sensory loss. Intraorally, there was severe periodontal disease, pain on percussion of the left upper premolars and molars, buccoalveolar sulcus bulging, and a floating tumefaction adjacent to the left upper molar roots. The lesion was initially managed as a dental abscess with drainage and antibiotics, and a multislice CT was requested. The patient returned three weeks later with new-onset paresthesia, severe left facial pain, and progressive cheek swelling. She was admitted, and noncontrast multislice CT showed, on axial images, a hypodense soft-tissue mass filling the left maxillary sinus with discontinuity of the anterior and lateral sinus walls extending toward the orbital floor; frontal images revealed involvement of the nasal cavity. A repeat CT scan demonstrated enlargement of the lesion, greater nasal cavity extension, and more extensive bony destruction. Routine blood counts, coagulation studies, lymphocyte immunophenotyping (CD3+/CD4+), and parathyroid hormone levels were all within normal limits.

A 60-year-old woman presented with a three-year history of a painless gingival growth in the upper left anterior mouth. The mass had slowly increased in size to approximately 2.5 × 3 cm and was associated with occasional bleeding when brushing; there was no history of trauma. On intraoral examination, there was a solitary, sessile, lobulated growth on the residual ridge of the missing left canine (tooth 23), between teeth 22 and 24. The lesion was the same color as the adjacent gingiva, with the mesial half slightly more reddish, and extended from the marginal gingiva of teeth 22 and 24 down about 1–2 cm. On palpation, it was firm, nontender, nonfluctuant, nonreducible, with mild bleeding on probing. An intraoral periapical radiograph of the left maxillary anterior region showed faint, irregular radiopacity in the area of the missing canine and slight mesial tipping of tooth 22 and distal tipping of tooth 24. A maxillary occlusal radiograph demonstrated an irregular soft-tissue radiopacity interspersed with areas of bone-like density, suggesting ossification.

A 71-year-old man with a 25–pack-year smoking history and a remote left parotidectomy for Warthin tumor presented with a painless, palpable right parotid mass. Physical examination revealed a soft, 0.5-cm right parotid nodule without facial nerve deficits or cervical lymphadenopathy. CT imaging showed a 1.4 × 1.3 cm superficial right parotid mass. He underwent right superficial parotidectomy; intraoperative frozen section reported an intermediate-grade malignancy, and the operation was extended to include deep-lobe parotidectomy with facial nerve preservation and right neck dissection.

Gross examination of the superficial parotidectomy specimen revealed a firm, tan-white, ill-defined intraparenchymal nodule measuring 1.3 × 1.1 cm and, 1.1 cm away, a separate 0.6-cm cyst. Histologic sections of the main nodule demonstrated two well-demarcated components without a transition zone. The first component was a multinodular proliferation of small basaloid cells in nests with peripheral palisading and surrounding eosinophilic hyaline stroma. Immunostains highlighted an abluminal p63- and CK5/6-positive population and scattered CK7-positive luminal cells. The second component showed mucin-containing glandular spaces and solid nests composed of mucous cells, polygonal epidermoid cells, and intermediate cells; mucicarmine stain highlighted intra- and extracellular mucin, and immunostains showed p63 and CK5/6 in epidermoid cells and CK7 in mucinous cells. The Ki-67 proliferation index was approximately 3–4%. Eighteen lymph nodes were negative.

A 57-year-old man presented with a 15-day history of a growth in the lower left back-tooth region. The lesion began insidiously, was painless, and had no discharge. There was no weight loss or appetite change.  
On examination:  
• A solitary, oval, sessile mass in the left retromolar area measuring 3.0×1.5×1.0 cm with distinct borders  
• Superficial ulcerations and indentations from opposing teeth  
• Tooth 38 was missing; teeth 36 and 37 were present without mobility  
• The mass was firm, non-tender, and non-fluctuant; no regional lymphadenopathy  
Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and HIV testing, were normal. Panoramic radiography showed no bony changes.  
The lesion was excised with removal of teeth 36 and 37.  
Two months later, the patient returned with a similar growth at the same site, noted 10 days prior and rapidly enlarging to its current size.

An 86-year-old man was referred for evaluation of an intraoral mass that his dentist discovered beneath the left buccal mucosa. He was asymptomatic and unaware of the lesion. His medical history was notable for transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder; his family history was unremarkable. On examination, there was a round, 12 mm diameter mass in the left buccal mucosa that was soft, nontender, nonadherent to surrounding tissue, and covered by normal-appearing mucosa. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left buccal region revealed a well-circumscribed lesion with signal intensity lower than skeletal muscle on T1-weighted images and higher than adipose tissue on T2-weighted images. A clinical diagnosis of a benign buccal soft-tissue tumor was made, and the mass was excised under local anesthesia.

A 21-year-old healthy right-handed nurse presented in November 2012 with a several-month history of right‐hand symptoms, including limited active extension of the fourth finger, pain in the palm, and a triggering phenomenon. By December 2012, the symptoms had worsened, particularly the triggering and pain, and she was referred to a hand surgeon. Physical examination revealed a sizzling noise with movement of the fourth flexor tendon, and tenosynovitis was suspected. In February 2013, she underwent open trigger‐finger release and synovectomy. Intraoperatively, a 10×7×4 mm multilobulated, firm, white mass adherent to the deep flexor tendon of the ring finger was found and excised entirely. Histologic examination showed a well‐circumscribed lesion composed of synovial‐type cells in a collagenous stroma without mitotic atypia, consistent with a fibroma of the tendon sheath; margins were clear. Postoperatively, she regained full motion and returned to work. She remained asymptomatic until May 2017, when over three weeks she noted identical symptoms and a new swelling in the surgical scar area. On examination, active extension of the metacarpophalangeal joint of the fourth finger was 30° and of the proximal interphalangeal joint 60°, with full passive motion and tenderness in the palm.

A 65-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a six-week history of lethargy, loss of appetite, and progressive pedal edema. She had no significant past medical history.

On examination, she was pale, hypotensive (blood pressure 98/60 mmHg), and had significant peripheral edema.

Laboratory studies showed:
• Serum sodium 118 mmol/L  
• Albumin 25 g/L, alkaline phosphatase 244 U/L, alanine transaminase 61 U/L, aspartate transaminase 61 U/L  
• Hemoglobin 11 g/dL, white blood cell count 3.0 × 10^9/L, platelet count 99 × 10^9/L  

A 250-μg short tetracosactrin test demonstrated cortisol levels of 93 nmol/L at 0 minutes, 43 nmol/L at 30 minutes, and 315 nmol/L at 60 minutes, suggesting adrenal failure. Baseline plasma adrenocorticotropic hormone was 4 ng/L (reference range 10–40 ng/L). She was started on hydrocortisone replacement with slight improvement.

Further endocrine evaluation revealed secondary hypothyroidism (TSH 0.35 mU/L, free T4 7.1 pmol/L, free T3 <1.7 pmol/L), secondary hypogonadism (FSH 6.3 U/L, LH 1.2 U/L), serum prolactin 343 mIU/L, and IGF-1 34 nmol/L. There was no evidence of diabetes insipidus.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary revealed no mass lesions.

Abdominal and pelvic ultrasound showed multiple intra-abdominal lymph nodes, multiple solid liver lesions, and a 2-cm right groin lymph node. A full-body CT scan confirmed these findings and demonstrated involvement of the base of the skull.

A 2-year-old girl was brought by her parents with a one-year history of a mass at the right medial canthal area, noted to enlarge during upper respiratory infections. There was intermittent purulent discharge from the right eye, and she had been treated several times for presumed bacterial conjunctivitis. There was no change in size or color of the mass with crying or feeding. 

Her past medical and developmental histories were unremarkable. On examination, she appeared well, vital signs were normal, and growth parameters were at the 50th percentile. A 2 × 2 cm noncompressible, nonpulsatile mass was present at the right medial canthus without obscuration of vision, and the Furstenberg sign was negative. The remainder of the eye examination was normal. 

Nasal endoscopy revealed healthy mucosa in both nasal cavities, mild bilateral inferior turbinate hypertrophy, and no intranasal masses. 

Noncontrast CT of the paranasal sinuses showed homogenous opacification of the right anterior ethmoid cells with erosion of the lamina papyracea and extension into the extraconal orbit. MRI demonstrated a well-defined expansile cystic lesion in the right agger nasi cell, with intermediate T2 and low T1 signal intensities, no contrast enhancement, no intracranial extension, and measurements of 29 mm (AP) × 13 mm (ML) × 23 mm (CC).

A 50-year-old man was referred after an abnormal chest radiograph noted during a routine medical checkup. He had a 20 pack-year smoking history (ages 15–35) and hypertension. He was asymptomatic, with normal vital signs, an unremarkable physical examination, and no laboratory abnormalities. Initial chest radiography revealed a nodular shadow in the left upper lung field. Chest CT showed a 6-mm nodule in the left lower lobe (segment 6) without features suggestive of malignancy. The patient declined surgical intervention, and the nodule was followed with serial CT scans. Over 6 years, the lesion slowly increased to 8 mm in diameter. Positron emission tomography–CT showed no fluorodeoxyglucose uptake. Given the gradual growth, thoracoscopic partial resection of the left lower lobe was performed; intraoperative rapid pathology was inconclusive.

A 19-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of intermittent bloody sputum; she had not previously sought care. Five days before presentation she expectorated approximately 5 mL of blood and underwent evaluation at an outside center. She had no chronic illnesses, no prior surgeries or trauma, and was a non-smoker. Physical examination was unremarkable. 

Chest CT showed an irregular 43 × 35 mm soft-tissue–density lesion in the mediobasal segment of the left lower lobe with adjacent ground-glass opacities. Dynamic MRI was recommended “for further evaluation with preliminary diagnoses of sequestration and bronchogenic cyst.” 

Laboratory studies, including CBC, coagulation profile, liver and renal function tests, vasculitis markers, connective-tissue markers, sputum AFB smear, and mycobacterial culture, were all normal or negative. 

Bronchoscopy demonstrated generalized bronchial hypervascularity and significant narrowing of the posterobasal segmental bronchus of the left lower lobe from external compression; the mucosa appeared smooth but densely vascularized. Lavage cytology showed no malignant cells, and cultures were negative. 

PET imaging revealed intense hypermetabolism in the lesion (SUVmax, 32.1). MRI displayed a T2-weighted hypointense lesion with a suspected central membrane, “adding stage II–IV hydatid cyst to the differential diagnosis.” Indirect hemagglutination testing for hydatid cyst was negative, and abdominal ultrasound was normal. IgG4 level was 2.73 g/L. Pulmonary function tests showed FEV1 2.30 L (64 % predicted), FVC 2.74 L (67 % predicted), and FEV1/FVC 99 %. 

After multidisciplinary discussion, a left lower lobectomy was planned for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes with a working diagnosis of a mesenchymal tumor.

A 51-year-old Asian man with a history of alcoholic liver cirrhosis presented one month after a diagnosis of poorly differentiated esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (cT2N2M1; PD-L1 10%) with mediastinal lymph node, lung, bladder, and bone metastases. He had undergone palliative radiation to the primary esophageal lesion. He now reports progressive blurred vision in the left eye.

On examination, visual acuity was 20/320 in the left eye and 20/25 in the right eye; intraocular pressures were 10 mmHg and 8 mmHg, respectively. Fundus examination of the left eye revealed a large, submacular, yellowish-white choroidal mass. B-scan ultrasonography demonstrated a large choroidal mass in the superior temporal quadrant with moderate-to-high internal reflectivity. Optical coherence tomography showed an elevated choroidal lesion with shallow subretinal fluid. Fluorescein angiography displayed late-phase hyperfluorescence with dye staining of the lesion.

A 33-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of a growing, painless nodule in the lower outer quadrant of the left breast. On examination, the lesion was firm, mobile, well defined, and without skin changes. There was no nipple discharge or palpable lymphadenopathy; the right breast was normal. Mammography showed a well-defined 33 × 26 mm mass with multiple pleomorphic calcifications that had increased in number compared with a prior study. Ultrasonography revealed a 3.5 cm hypoechoic, subcutaneous, poorly circumscribed nodule with marked posterior acoustic shadowing from microcalcifications and no locoregional lymphadenopathy. The lesion was classified as ACR BI-RADS IV.

An man in his early eighties presented with sudden severe abdominal pain and vomiting, on a background of multiple self-limiting episodes of similar pain for which no radiologic or endoscopic cause had been identified. His medical history included therapeutic anticoagulation for bilateral lower-limb deep-vein thrombosis, a cardioembolic stroke, and a diagnosis of bladder carcinoma in situ (T1) eight years earlier treated by transurethral resection and intravesical Bacillus Calmette-Guérin, with no recurrence on annual surveillance cystoscopy and biopsy (last performed eight months before presentation). 

On examination, he had an acute abdomen with generalized peritonism. A computed tomography angiogram of the abdomen demonstrated a thrombus in a distal branch of the superior mesenteric artery without evidence of bowel compromise. The provisional diagnosis was mesenteric arterial occlusion by thrombosis; differential diagnoses included mesenteric venous thrombosis, arterial embolism, and non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia. 

The patient was started on a therapeutic intravenous heparin infusion and underwent diagnostic laparoscopy, which showed macroscopically normal and viable small and large bowel. He remained on anticoagulation. Thirty-six hours later, he reported worsening abdominal pain and developed tachycardia. A repeat CT angiogram revealed resolution of a large component of the superior mesenteric artery thrombus but persistent occlusion with changes suggestive of ongoing distal small-bowel ischaemia.

A 32-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with several years of worsening pain and swelling in the medial proximal aspect of his left thigh. On physical examination, there was a palpable, firm mass in the adductor compartment without overlying skin changes. Radiographs of the left femur showed a dense, well-circumscribed soft-tissue lesion with mineralization adjacent to the medial cortex of the femur. Subsequent MRI demonstrated a 9.6 × 7.3 × 13.0 cm extraskeletal mass centered in the adductor magnus muscle, with no signal abnormality within the femur to suggest osseous involvement. The lesion was intermediate in signal on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with multiple tiny central hypointense foci corresponding to calcification. Post-gadolinium sequences revealed moderate peripheral enhancement, most prominent at the superior and inferior margins, and displaced muscle fibers around the mass. There was no evidence of fascial breach or neurovascular invasion.

A 12‐year‐old neutered male Jack Russell terrier (5.4 kg) presented for routine vaccination and follow‐up abdominal ultrasonography after multiple prior cystotomies for calcium oxalate uroliths. The dog had a history of asymptomatic primary hypoplasia of the portal vein discovered on liver biopsy 2 years earlier. 

Physical examination was unremarkable. Temperature was 38.2 °C, heart rate 102 bpm, and respiratory rate 20 breaths/min. 

Laboratory studies showed mild elevations in alanine aminotransferase (217 U/L; RI 20–99 U/L) and alkaline phosphatase (712 U/L; RI 49–298 U/L); all other hematologic and biochemical tests, coagulation profile, echocardiography, thoracic and abdominal radiographs, and urinalysis were within normal limits. 

Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 14 × 17 mm well‐circumscribed mass in the dorsal retroperitoneum, adjacent to the caudal vena cava and abdominal aorta; bladder stones were also noted. Twelve days later, whole‐body contrast‐enhanced CT confirmed a 14 × 17 × 19 mm retroperitoneal mass with heterogeneous arterial‐phase enhancement and no evidence of local vessel invasion or distant metastases. 

Under ultrasound guidance, fine‐needle aspiration of the mass yielded numerous degenerate cells with naked nuclei. Cytologic interpretation led to a differential diagnosis of lymphoma, neuroendocrine tumour, or metastatic tumour.

A 38-year-old man with no cardiovascular risk factors was referred for evaluation of progressive dyspnoea and pulmonary hypertension. Twelve months earlier he noted exertional dyspnoea that gradually worsened until he could walk <100 m. On admission he was normotensive, heart rate 76 bpm, O₂ saturation normal on room air. Examination revealed jugular venous distension, hepatomegaly, and bilateral lower‐limb oedema.  

An ECG showed sinus rhythm, borderline right‐axis deviation (+90°), and an S1Q3T3 pattern. Twelve months prior he had a severe pleural and pericardial effusion at the referring hospital; a pericardial window and biopsy yielded haematic fluid with lymphomononuclear cells and inflammatory tissue without malignancy. The initial differential diagnosis included heart failure with pulmonary hypertension, biventricular dysfunction, and chronic pulmonary thromboembolism.  

During this admission, repeat ECG showed complete right bundle‐branch block. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a dilated right atrium and ventricle; left ventricular ejection fraction was 60%; right ventricular systolic function was reduced (TAPSE 15 mm, s′ 8 cm/s); tricuspid regurgitant velocity was 4 m/s; estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure was 85 mmHg; and there was supravalvular stenosis without valvulopathy.  

Cardiac CT confirmed severe extrinsic compression of both pulmonary arteries. Thoracic MRI showed mild fibrotic changes in the anterior and middle mediastinum with vascular compromise but no discrete mass. FDG-PET demonstrated hypermetabolic activity at the anterior and middle mediastinum and pleural surfaces.  

He then developed superior vena cava syndrome; venography revealed total obstruction of the superior vena cava and innominate vein, managed with balloon dilation and stent placement in the pulmonary arteries and innominate vein. A small pericardial effusion was observed and managed conservatively.  

Because of the hypermetabolism on FDG-PET, a thoracoscopic pleural biopsy was performed; no malignant neoplasia was found. An initial diagnosis of fibrosing mediastinitis of unknown aetiology was made after exclusion of primary causes.

A 28-year-old Arab woman presented with a 3-year history of chronic left-sided chest pain that recently worsened, accompanied by dyspnea and pain radiating to her neck and left arm. She reported weight loss and anorexia. Her medical history was notable only for a salpingectomy for ectopic pregnancy two years earlier; she denied tobacco use and had no significant family history.  
On examination, breath sounds and vocal fremitus were decreased on the left; the remainder of her physical examination and routine blood tests were unremarkable.  
A chest radiograph showed a homogeneous opacity occupying nearly the entire left hemithorax with loss of the left diaphragmatic silhouette. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed an enormous anterior mediastinal mass with a central area of necrosis and rightward displacement of mediastinal structures.  
An anterior left mediastinotomy demonstrated a pink, smooth-surfaced tumor in the anterior mediastinum that adhered to mediastinal structures and appeared to invade the left lung. Because resection was not feasible, a biopsy was obtained.

A 72-year-old Japanese woman presented with epigastric pain and nausea of 3 days’ duration, with gradual worsening. Laboratory results revealed serum amylase of 838 IU/l, pancreatic amylase of 778 IU/l, and CA 19-9 of 86.4 U/ml; other tumor markers were within normal limits. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed localized inflammation in the pancreatic head, dilation of the main pancreatic duct (MPD), and a cystic lesion with slightly high density in the head. Transabdominal ultrasonography and MRCP confirmed a 14 mm cystic lesion in the pancreatic head, dilation of the MPD from body to tail, and obstruction of the MPD at the lesion without demonstrable communication. 

Endoscopic ultrasonography revealed a 15 mm mass in the pancreatic head consisting of a hypoechoic heterogeneous solid component and an anechoic cystic component; the MPD was dilated to 5 mm and abruptly cut off at the mass. ERCP demonstrated a >12 mm stenosis of the MPD at the head, precluding passage of a cytology brush. 

Endoscopic ultrasound–guided fine-needle aspiration (EUS-FNA) of the solid component was performed.

A 71-year-old woman presented with right upper quadrant discomfort and epigastric pain. She was a smoker with treated type 2 diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis. On examination, she had pallor, right upper quadrant tenderness, and palpable hepatomegaly.  
Abdominal ultrasound revealed two hypoechoic liver masses (60×75 mm in segment VII and 60×55 mm in the hilum). CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed:  
• Hepatomegaly (24 cm)  
• A 53×77 mm mass infiltrating the head of the pancreas and duodenum, extending to the liver hilum  
• A 75×70 mm hypodense lesion in segment VII with contrast enhancement  
• Significant gallbladder dilatation without wall thickening  
• A 28×44 mm asymmetrical hyperperfused nodule adherent to the anterior bladder wall  
Ultrasound-guided liver biopsy demonstrated poorly differentiated carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry was positive for CK20, focally positive for CK7, and negative for GATA3, TTF-1, Pax-8, and Hep-Par 1. Serum CA-125, CEA, AFP, and CA19-9 were within normal limits. Cystoscopy with curettage of the bladder dome nodule was performed to obtain tissue for diagnosis.

A 57-year-old woman with a history of stage T2aN1MX pulmonary adenocarcinoma resected 10 years earlier underwent routine oncologic follow-up. One year ago, an incidental 3-cm lesion was noted in the central spleen on CT; serial scans showed progressive enlargement.  
On recent evaluation, she was asymptomatic, denied tobacco, alcohol, or drug use, and had unremarkable vital signs. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, metabolic panel, cancer antigen 19-9, and carcinoembryonic antigen, were all within normal limits.  
Abdominal CT revealed a 55 × 65 × 59 mm lobulated, irregular, centrally located splenic mass with a density of –50.3 Hounsfield units and well-enhancing intralesional vessels. MRI confirmed a hyperintense T2 lesion with fat suppression. PET/CT showed no radiotracer uptake in the spleen.  
Given the lesion’s unknown etiology, risk of rupture, and concern for metastasis, a diagnostic and therapeutic laparoscopic splenectomy was planned.

A 6-year-old boy presented with a 3-day history of a painless, rapidly growing swelling in the right axilla. There was no history of trauma, infection, discharge, erythema, discoloration, fever, dilated veins, or sinus tracts. On examination, he was well and alert. A 7×5 cm, globular, soft, non-tender mass was palpable in the right axilla; it was movable with arm elevation, not fixed to the skin, and there was no axillary lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed: WBC 9.2 K/µL, neutrophils 56%, RBC 4.31×10^6/µL, hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, hematocrit 34.3%, MCV 79.5 µm^3, MCH 26.9 pg, MCHC 33.8%, RDW 12.8%. Ultrasonography of the right axilla revealed a unilocular cystic mass measuring 6×5.5×4 cm anterior to the axillary vessels, with no septae, no calcifications or soft-tissue component, no enlarged lymph nodes, and no abnormal flow.

A 40-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of an insidiously progressive swelling over the dorsum of his left foot and 4 months of dull, aching pain aggravated by activity and relieved by rest and analgesics. He denied constitutional symptoms or trauma. On examination, there was a well‐defined, firm, tender, ovoid swelling measuring 7 × 4 cm over the first and second metatarsal region of the dorsal left foot; the overlying skin was mobile. Radiographs of the left foot showed an expansile osteolytic lesion of the entire first metatarsal extending to the tarsometatarsal and metatarsophalangeal articular surfaces, with cortical thinning and the classical “soap-bubble appearance.”

A 38-year-old woman noted a right upper cervical nodule when extending her neck. She denied dysphagia, phonation changes, pain, paresthesia, or neurologic symptoms. On examination, there was an approximately 4 cm elliptical, fibroelastic, mobile nodule in the right posterior triangle anterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle, extending to the angle of the mandible; Tinel’s sign was negative. Oropharyngeal and cranial-nerve examinations were normal, and there were no skin lesions. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the neck revealed a fusiform, well-defined expansive lesion in the right carotid space measuring 4.5 cm × 3.0 cm × 1.7 cm. The mass showed increased signal on T1- and T2-weighted sequences, intense and progressive contrast uptake—particularly centrally—and no restriction on diffusion imaging. It was located along the expected course of the vagus nerve, displacing the internal carotid artery anteromedially and the internal jugular vein laterally, with maintained planes adjacent to the parotid gland, pterygoid muscles, mandibular ramus, vertebral elements, and sternocleidomastoid muscle.

A 38-year-old woman presented to the periodontology clinic with a painless swelling of the gingiva between her maxillary right canine and first premolar. She was systemically healthy, not taking any medications, and not pregnant. Intraoral examination revealed a 0.7×0.6×0.4 cm fibrotic, sessile, smooth-surfaced gingival overgrowth interdentally between teeth #13 and #14, with slight plaque accumulation, mild gingival inflammation, and edema. The adjacent teeth were vital, nonmobile, and non-tender to percussion. Periapical radiographs showed no abnormalities. Full-mouth periodontal indices were: mean plaque index 1.09, gingival index 1.11, and mean probing depth 2.92 mm. The patient received oral hygiene instruction and scaling/root planing, but the lesion persisted with minimal change.

A 12-year-old Malay girl presented with a 9-month history of progressive hoarseness that began after a sore throat. She had no airway distress, feeding problems, or weight loss, and no history of vocal abuse, loud talking, or singing. There was no relevant family history. Perceptual voice evaluation (GRBAS) scored G 3, R 3, B 0, A 3, S 1.

Flexible nasoendoscopy revealed a well-circumscribed lesion with a smooth mucosal surface on the right true vocal cord; vocal cord mobility was normal. The initial working diagnosis included vocal cord polyp, granuloma, and recurrent respiratory papillomatosis.

Under microlaryngoscopy, a firm, broad-based lesion involved the anterior two-thirds of the right true vocal cord and ventricle; the left cord appeared normal. A biopsy was taken and sent for histopathologic examination.

Pathological analysis of the biopsy revealed chronic inflammation with stromal myxoid degeneration and hyalinization. The lesion was composed of ovoid to spindle-shaped cells admixed with plasma cells; the cells had vesicular to hyperchromatic nuclei and abundant eosinophilic to lightly basophilic cytoplasm.

A 62-year-old woman presented with a 7-year history of a right palatal swelling that had gradually increased in size over the past 2 years, associated with intermittent toothache and occasional facial swelling. Initial examination showed a firm, non-tender mass over the anterior palate without buccal or lingual expansion and no cervical lymphadenopathy. Dental panoramic tomogram revealed a radiolucent lesion with a well-defined sclerotic border of the right maxilla extending into the right maxillary sinus and significant root resorption of the upper right central and lateral incisors and first molar. An excisional biopsy of the anterior palate was performed intraorally; hematoxylin and eosin sections demonstrated small epithelial tumor cell cords in a densely collagenized stroma without obvious dysplastic features. Contrast-enhanced CT scan showed an expansile, enhancing osteolytic mass of the right maxilla with marked buccal and palatal bone perforation, extension into the right inferior turbinate, and breach of the nasal septum; there was no evidence of cervical lymphatic spread.

A 47-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of painless swelling around the right orbit. Her past medical history included completely resected cervical and renal cancers with no recurrence. On examination, there was slight proptosis and periorbital swelling of the right eye; visual acuity and extraocular movements were normal.

Noncontrast CT of the brain demonstrated an isodense mass in the superolateral orbit without adjacent orbital wall erosion. MRI showed an extra-conal, intensely enhancing tumor that was isointense on T1-weighted images and of mixed intensity on T2-weighted images, displacing the lateral rectus muscle inferomedially.

The patient underwent gross total resection via lateral orbitotomy. The lesion under the periorbita was whitish, elastic-hard, and minimally vascular. It was easily dissected from surrounding structures except for focal adhesions to the lacrimal gland.

Microscopic examination revealed a mixture of squamous and epithelioid cells alongside cells with clear, plump cytoplasm arranged in alveolar and gland-like patterns. No necrosis, neural invasion, or mitotic figures were noted. Immunohistochemical staining was intensely positive for cytokeratin 7, negative for cytokeratin 20, and periodic acid–Schiff and mucicarmine stains highlighted mucin in a subset of cells. The MIB-1 labeling index was 8%.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of a neck mass, sore throat, hoarseness, and intermittent dysphagia. On examination, there was a “woody” hard swelling arising from the right thyroid lobe without cervical lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory studies showed hypothyroidism (T4 0.8 pmol/L; TSH > 100 mIU/L) and anti–thyroid peroxidase antibody > 1000 U/mL. Flexible laryngoscopy demonstrated bilateral Reinke’s edema of the vocal cords without suspicious lesions.

Thyroid ultrasound revealed a diffusely enlarged, heterogeneous, low-echogenicity gland with a 4.0 × 1.5 cm abnormal nodule extending across the isthmus and no calcifications. MRI of the neck showed diffuse thyroid enlargement with marked contrast enhancement and no focal nodules. Several prominent but reactive-appearing jugular lymph nodes were present bilaterally.

A fine-needle aspiration of the nodule was nondiagnostic, so an open core biopsy was performed. Histologic examination showed dense sclerotic fibrosis punctuated by nodular mononuclear inflammatory cells that obscured follicular epithelial cells.

A 42-year-old man presented with a 1½-year history of progressive abdominal discomfort and distension. He had quit smoking 4 years prior. On examination, there was a large, non-tender mass in the right hypochondrium. Testes were descended and normal. Routine blood tests and serum CA 19-9 were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated what appeared to be a unilocular cystic lesion in the right lobe of the liver, thought to represent a hydatid cyst. At an initial laparotomy, the liver was normal; instead, five cystic, multilocular masses were found in the median retroperitoneum between the inferior vena cava and aortic bifurcation. The pancreas, spleen, and kidneys were unremarkable. Three masses were excised; two were left in situ due to dense vascular adhesions. Contrast-enhanced CT showed residual hyperdense retroperitoneal masses with both cystic and solid components and no enhancement. MRI revealed multiple retroperitoneal processes from behind the pancreas to the aortic bifurcation, adherent to vessels; they were hyperintense on T1 and T2 with fat suppression (consistent with mucinous content) and exhibited slight enhancement of some solid areas after gadolinium. The pancreas was homogeneous without focal lesions. At re-exploration, four additional encapsulated, multicystic masses filled with mucinous material were removed; none was attached to any intra-abdominal organ.

A 62-year-old woman was referred to the breast clinic after routine screening mammography identified a mass in her left breast. Her oncologic history included an ileal carcinoid tumor resected in 2001, a right breast metastasis treated with lumpectomy and radiation in 2005, and liver metastases managed with transarterial chemoembolization and cryoablation in 2011, with stable subsequent scans. At this visit, she was asymptomatic and physical examination was unremarkable; she denied palpable masses, pain, nipple discharge or retraction, skin changes, and lymphadenopathy. Diagnostic mammography revealed a 0.6 × 0.5 × 0.5 cm BI-RADS 4 mass at the 6:30 position, 4 cm from the nipple. The mass was biopsied and tissues were sent for pathologic evaluation.

A 15-day-old dizygotic twin girl was referred for ventriculomegaly noted on prenatal ultrasonography. She was born at term via uncomplicated vaginal delivery. On examination, the anterior fontanelle was soft but full, scalp veins were dilated, and head circumference was above the 97th percentile for gestational age. Neurologic examination was nonfocal. Postnatal cranial ultrasonography showed progressive hydrocephalus and a midline echogenic mass in the posterior fossa compressing the cerebellum. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a large, well-circumscribed, dural-based extraaxial mass along the dorsal posterior fossa that was mostly T1 isointense and T2 hypointense, contained flow voids and areas of prior hemorrhage, and demonstrated avid contrast enhancement. There was marked mass effect on the cerebellum, fourth ventricle, and brainstem, with resultant obstructive hydrocephalus and transependymal flow.

An 8-year-old healthy boy presented with a 2-month history of a gradually enlarging, painful swelling around his right shoulder, associated with mild restriction of motion. He denied trauma or systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a tender, firm mass over the proximal anteromedial aspect of the shoulder that was not fixed to bone or skin, with reduced mobility in the longitudinal direction. Shoulder abduction and forward flexion were painfully restricted. 

Plain radiographs of the right shoulder showed multiple well-defined swellings on the anteromedial proximal humerus, each with a calcified wall; one measured approximately 2 cm × 2 cm. “This picture was suggestive of calcified hydatid cyst or chondrocalcinosis.” 

Laboratory testing revealed a total white-cell count of 12 000 per mm3 with a normal eosinophil count. Ultrasound of the abdomen and chest showed no evidence of hydatid cyst. Ultrasound-guided aspiration of the lesion demonstrated inflammation without evidence of infection. 

Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-defined lesion with a calcific wall containing multiple loose bodies, arising from the biceps tendon sheath, with normal glenohumeral articular cartilage and no intra-articular loose bodies. The radiologist opined in favor of synovial chondromatosis and noted a differential diagnosis of calcified hydatid cyst.

A 33-year-old nulliparous woman with a body‐mass index of 19.4 kg/m2 and no significant medical or family history underwent a routine gynecologic examination. She was asymptomatic and her physical examination was unremarkable. A transvaginal ultrasound revealed a multilocular solid mass measuring 20 × 20 × 16 mm adjacent to the left ovary, with an internal solid component 13 mm in diameter and 7 mm in height. Color Doppler showed no blood flow in the solid component, although one septation demonstrated vascularity. Serum CA-125 was 13.3 U/mL and other laboratory tests were within normal limits. An International Ovarian Tumor Analysis (IOTA) risk assessment using the ADNEX model yielded a 9.1% risk of malignancy. Pelvic MRI showed a cystic mass of uncertain origin adjacent to the left ovary, measuring 18 × 15 × 20 mm, with high signal intensity on T2-weighted images and low signal on T1-weighted images; a nodular solid element was present, and postcontrast images demonstrated enhancement of the cyst wall. The uterus and right adnexa appeared normal.

A 55‐year‐old man presented with a several‐month history of progressive dyspnea, right chest pain, and unintentional weight loss.  
He was a two‐pack‐per‐day smoker with no known asbestos exposure.  
On examination, he was tachypneic but hemodynamically stable; there were signs of respiratory distress, and routine laboratory studies were unrevealing.  
Contrast‐enhanced CT of the chest revealed a 7.2 × 8.8 × 5.2 cm pleural‐based mass (40 HU noncontrast; 72–90 HU postcontrast) with destruction of the right posterior–lateral rib and multiple enlarged lymph nodes (perivascular, left peribronchial, right lower paratracheal, and left supraclavicular).  
No parenchymal lung lesions or nodules were identified.  
The mass appeared confined to the pleural cavity, raising suspicion for a primary pleural tumor.

A 55-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a palpable left-sided neck lump. Four years earlier, she had been diagnosed with thyroid nodules; her medical history was notable for hypertension and vertebrobasilar insufficiency. She had no family history of malignancy. On ultrasound, the thyroid gland was normal in size with hypoechogenic nodules, and a heterogeneous, ovoid 2.6 × 1.4 cm mass was identified in the left side of the neck. The lesion was thought to represent a lymph node, and a malignant process was suspected. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the mass was inconclusive. On examination, her blood pressure was 150/90 mmHg and heart rate 88 beats/min in sinus rhythm. Laboratory tests were normal. Clinical evaluation revealed a firm, non-tender, approximately 3 × 2 cm mass in the left lateral neck. The patient was referred for surgical excision of a presumed malignant lymph node.

A 5-year-old girl was evaluated for a mass in the right parapharyngeal region present since birth. On examination, the lesion was firm, solid, non-tender, and measured 4 × 3 cm; the overlying skin was normal. Routine laboratory studies were within normal limits. Ultrasonography revealed a solid, well-circumscribed lesion. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy was performed under ultrasound guidance, yielding five smears. The aspirates were moderately cellular without a fibrillar or necrotic background. Two distinct cell populations were noted: the first consisted of spindle-shaped cells with wavy nuclei; the second consisted of large oval to polygonal cells with abundant granular cytoplasm, one to three large round vesicular nuclei often eccentrically placed, and prominent nucleoli.

A 63‐year‐old Japanese man was referred for evaluation of a hepatic cystic lesion first detected 14 years earlier, which had grown from 16 mm to 4.2 × 4.1 cm. He was asymptomatic. Laboratory tests, including liver function and tumor markers, were within normal limits. Contrast‐enhanced abdominal CT showed a well‐demarcated multicystic lesion with a thick septum in segment 8 of the liver, with slight contrast enhancement. T2‐weighted MRI demonstrated high‐signal multicystic fluid content. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiography revealed no communication between the lesion and the biliary tree, which was confirmed by post‐procedural CT showing no residual contrast in the lesion.

A 67-year-old man with stage IIIa cutaneous melanoma (back lesion with inguinal nodal spread) excised three years earlier (no adjuvant therapy) presented with one month of intermittent confusion, fatigue, daily nausea and vomiting, occasional headaches, unintentional weight loss, and hyponatremia. On neurologic examination he was alert but disoriented without focal deficits. Brain MRI showed a contrast-enhancing mass occupying the lateral, third, and fourth ventricles with mild diffusion restriction and a diffuse ependymal pattern. Lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 55 cm H₂O; CSF analysis showed 87 WBCs/mm³ (86% lymphocytes), 5893 RBCs/mm³ with xanthochromia, protein 524 mg/dL, glucose 20 mg/dL, cytology with rare atypical cells, and flow cytometry demonstrating a mixed inflammatory exudate without a monoclonal subset. Over two weeks, he developed acute obstructive hydrocephalus requiring bilateral external ventricular drains, and a frameless needle biopsy under neuronavigation guidance was planned.

A 24-year-old man presented with a more than two-year history of a right cheek mass. He noted mild swelling and intermittent pain that worsened when eating. Ultrasonography at an outside hospital showed a hypoechoic mass thought to be benign, and the lesion was excised. 

Grossly, the 30 mm mass was solid and reddish-yellow. Histologic examination revealed an infiltrative lesion composed of nests of polygonal cells arranged in both acinar (“alveolar”) and solid organoid patterns, separated by fibrous septa containing slit-like capillaries. Tumor cells showed variable cytoplasm—some clear, some with eosinophilic granules—and occasional nuclear atypia without conspicuous mitoses. 

Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated nuclear TFE3 positivity, MyoD1 negativity, partial Desmin positivity, negative S100, focal SMA positivity, weak CD56 staining, and a Ki-67 index of 8%. Periodic acid–Schiff staining showed intracytoplasmic, amylase-resistant rod-shaped crystals.

A 40-year-old Caucasian man with a history of familial adenomatous polyposis presented with an asymptomatic, slow-growing nodule on his left thigh. On examination, there was a solitary, erythematous, firm nodule measuring 5.0 × 4.0 cm on the lateral proximal thigh; the surface showed an ulcer with scarring, and there was no locoregional lymphadenopathy. A CT scan of the thigh, with and without contrast, revealed a well-defined, enhanced subcutaneous lesion measuring 3.7 × 3.5 × 1.7 cm, containing microcalcifications. Initial differential diagnoses included a complicated skin appendage lesion, sebaceous cyst, and pilomatrixoma.

A 49-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of a gradually enlarging, mildly tender lump in her left lower abdominal wall. She had no significant medical or gynecologic history and reported no weight loss. She had undergone a cesarean delivery 15 years earlier. Recent pelvic ultrasonography was normal. On examination, a firm, 5 cm mass was palpated in the left lower quadrant, approximately 3 cm below the umbilicus, with tenderness only on deep palpation. Routine laboratory tests, including tumor markers, were within normal limits. Abdominal CT and MRI showed a 6.7 × 4.9 × 3.5 cm mass within the left rectus abdominis muscle and no other intra-abdominal abnormalities. The mass was excised with clear margins; intraoperative inspection revealed both ovaries of normal size and no ascites or peritoneal lesions. Histologic examination demonstrated a high-grade carcinoma with strong cytokeratin 7 and CA-125 positivity and weaker estrogen receptor staining.

A 9-year-old boy with no prior medical history presented with a 2-year history of visual obscurations and, over the past 6 months, progressive holocephalic headaches and gait imbalance. On examination, he had an ataxic gait on tandem walking without lateropulsion, globally increased muscle tone, dysdiadochokinesia, and bilateral ankle clonus. His Glasgow Coma Scale score was 15, but his verbal responses were delayed. There was no relevant family, social, or medication history. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed multiple bilateral intraventricular masses that were hypointense on T1-weighted images with homogeneous contrast enhancement. Additional enhancing foci were noted along the posterior straight sinus, confluence of sinuses, and in the right cerebellum. The patient was admitted for neuromonitoring and supportive care, and a staged surgical resection was planned.

A 37-year-old Mandarese woman presented with recurrent right-sided epistaxis and nasal obstruction over several years. She had no history of trauma, radiation exposure, smoking, alcohol use, or family history of cancer. On nasal endoscopy, lacerations and a mass were noted in the right nasal cavity; the pharynx, larynx, oral cavity, and nasopharynx were normal, and no cervical lymphadenopathy was present. Laboratory studies were notable for hemoglobin 8 g/dL and leukocytosis (13.3 × 10^9/L); other biochemical and hematological tests were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head showed an isodense 4.4 × 3.3 × 2 cm mass filling the anterior right nasal cavity and extending into the right ethmoid and sphenoid sinuses, without bone erosion or involvement of the orbit, cranial fossa, or other paranasal sinuses. After a blood transfusion, a biopsy was obtained under local anesthesia. Histopathology revealed a dense proliferation of spindle-shaped fibroblasts with hyperchromatic nuclei arranged in a herringbone pattern and mitoses of 1–2 per 10 high-power fields. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for Ki67, P53, and vimentin.

A 54-year-old man presented with two months of mild, intermittent, diffuse lower abdominal pain without nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, or hematochezia. He had a history of well-controlled hypertension and a 20-year, 10–12 cigarettes/day smoking history; he denied alcohol use. Vital signs were normal. The abdominal examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies—including complete blood count, liver enzymes, protein, albumin, electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, glucose, urinalysis, and stool examination—were within normal limits. Chest and abdominal radiographs and abdominal ultrasonography showed no abnormalities. Upper endoscopy revealed chronic superficial gastritis. 

After bowel preparation, colonoscopy revealed a single, 15-mm semi-pedunculated lesion in the sigmoid colon with a smooth surface. The lesion was firm (cushion sign negative) and lifted easily after submucosal injection of epinephrine/saline (lifting sign positive).
