A snare polypectomy was performed, and the lesion was removed without bleeding or perforation.

A 51-year-old man presented with a several‐month history of a gradually enlarging, painful right scrotal mass. On examination, there was induration of the scrotum without overlying skin changes. Laboratory tests, including carcinoembryonic antigen, squamous cell carcinoma antigen, carbohydrate antigen 19-9, and α-fetoprotein, were within normal limits.

Unenhanced CT of the scrotum demonstrated a 39 × 27 × 23 mm lobulated heterogeneous mass with hyperattenuation and tiny calcifications. Multiphasic contrast-enhanced CT showed a well-defined lesion with cystic areas, solid components, and septations that exhibited progressive enhancement. There was no lymphadenopathy or distant metastasis.

MRI revealed a 37 × 25 × 24 mm lobulated scrotal mass separate from the testes and epididymis. On T2-weighted images, the mass had predominantly intermediate signal intensity with low-signal reticular structures and focal high-signal areas on fat-saturated T2 images. On T1-weighted images, regions of markedly and slightly high signal intensity were seen relative to muscle; fat-sat T1 sequences showed no fat. Dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated gradual enhancement of the low- and intermediate-signal regions (solid parts and septa), whereas the cystic and high-signal T1 areas showed no enhancement. Diffusion-weighted imaging revealed mild hyperintensity in the solid portions with an ADC value of approximately 0.61 × 10^−3 mm^2/s, indicating diffusion restriction.

A 38-year-old woman with clinical stage IIIC (cT2N3M0) infiltrating ductal carcinoma of the left breast, negative for ER, PR, and HER2 and treated with neoadjuvant docetaxel–doxorubicin followed by curative resection (pathologic stage ypT2N3M0) and adjuvant cyclophosphamide–methotrexate–5-fluorouracil chemotherapy, presented during her third cycle with sudden-onset right chest pain and cough. At that visit, a chest radiograph was normal. Ten days later, she returned with right inspiratory chest pain, dyspnea on exertion, cough, and mild febrile sensation but denied high fever, sputum, pitting edema, or orthopnea. Her temperature was 36.5°C, blood pressure 133/68 mmHg, heart rate 97/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Fine crackles were auscultated in the right upper lung field without pleural friction rub. A chest radiograph showed patchy consolidation in the right upper lobe. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed right upper lobe consolidation with ill-defined small ground-glass opacities in the right upper and lower lobes and no evidence of pulmonary thromboembolism. Laboratory values included a white blood cell count of 5800/mm3 (76.4% neutrophils) and a C-reactive protein level of 0.86 mg/dL. Under the impression of community-acquired pneumonia, she was started on a third-generation cephalosporin plus a macrolide. One week later, follow-up CT showed progression of the right upper lobe consolidation, and her dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain had worsened. Initial respiratory cultures were negative. Although the imaging suggested a fungal pneumonia, she had not experienced severe neutropenia for several months and had no predisposing clinical factors favoring a fungal etiology. We considered the probability of lymphangitic metastatic carcinoma or a fungal infection such as aspergillosis or mucormycosis.

A 56-year-old Vietnamese woman presented with prolonged fever and fatigue. Initial laboratory evaluation showed severe anemia (hemoglobin 60 g/L), microcytosis (MCV 72.9 fL), WBC 9.65 G/L with 55% neutrophils and 20% monocytes, and platelets 193 G/L. HIV antibody, ANA, anti–dsDNA, rheumatoid factor, and Coombs tests were negative. Triglycerides were 565 mg/dL, ferritin 3154 ng/mL, soluble CD25 3317 U/mL, and LDH 592 U/L. EBV PCR was positive. Lumbar puncture yielded 14 WBC, 6 RBC, protein 32.6 mg/dL, and glucose 3.58 mmol/L; MTB PCR was negative. Bone marrow aspirate demonstrated red cell and platelet phagocytosis. Abdominopelvic CT scan revealed hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. Brain MRI showed subacute bilateral pontine infarction. Gastrointestinal endoscopy was unremarkable. The patient was diagnosed with HLH probably secondary to EBV infection and pontine infarction and was treated with dexamethasone and aspirin, resulting in partial improvement.

Three months later, she was admitted with acute left-sided weakness and slurred speech. Examination disclosed expressive aphasia, memory deficits, left central facial palsy, and quadriparesis. CBC showed WBC 13.39 G/L, hemoglobin 96 g/L, platelets 142 G/L. Brain MRI revealed multifocal infarcts in the left frontal lobe and bilateral corona radiata. MRA was normal. Holter monitoring, echocardiography, carotid and lower-extremity Doppler studies were unremarkable. CSF analysis showed 19 WBC, 2000 RBC, protein 95 mg/dL, glucose 3.6 mmol/L, lactate 4.14 mmol/L; cultures and PCRs for bacteria, fungi, HSV, and MTB were negative. She was treated with dexamethasone and clopidogrel.

Ten days after discharge, she was readmitted with quadriplegia, decreased consciousness, agitation, visual hallucinations, and low-grade fever. Laboratory tests revealed WBC 9.01 G/L, hemoglobin 78 g/L, platelets 122 G/L, and LDH 300 U/L. Brain MRI showed new small subcortical infarcts in the left frontal lobe. HR-vwMRI post-contrast T1W demonstrated vessel wall thickening with moderate enhancement of the left PCA and bilateral MCA segments, suggesting vasculitis. Repeat CSF showed 13 WBC (90% lymphocytes), 0 RBC, protein 111 mg/dL, glucose 5.2 mmol/L, lactate 4.14 mmol/L; cultures and PCRs were negative. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed splenomegaly; multiple bilateral lung nodules; liver lesions; bilateral renal masses; gastric wall thickening; and omental nodules. Bone marrow aspirate again demonstrated hemophagocytosis. Gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsy was performed and sent for analysis.

A 40-year-old man presented with 1 week of difficulty voiding and was catheterized for urinary retention. Ultrasonography revealed a large prostatic mass, and his prostate-specific antigen level was 0.62 ng/mL (normal <4.0). He denied pain, fever, or abdominal distension. Physical examination was unremarkable, and complete blood count, routine chemistries, and tumor markers (CEA, CA19-9, CA-125, SCC antigen, CYFRA) were all within normal limits. Digital rectal examination revealed an enlarged prostate with palpable nodules and an ill-defined border. Pelvic ultrasound confirmed a heterogeneous prostatic mass. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a 5.5-cm heterogeneous lesion in the right prostate lobe, and cystoscopy raised suspicion for bladder invasion. Positron emission tomography–CT and colonoscopy suggested rectal invasion. A provisional diagnosis of prostatic sarcoma was made, and a transrectal needle biopsy was performed. The biopsy result was interpreted as either prostatic stromal sarcoma or prostatic stromal tumor of uncertain malignant potential.

A 71-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a left adrenal mass that had been incidentally discovered on abdominal ultrasonography performed 3 months earlier. She reported a 6-month history of intermittent, vague left flank pain radiating posteriorly. Her medical history was significant only for well-controlled hypertension and an appendectomy decades earlier; there was no relevant family history. On examination, her abdomen was soft, with no palpable masses, and there were no cutaneous lesions or lymphadenopathy. Routine blood tests were normal, and 24-hour urinary catecholamines, cortisol, and chromogranin levels were within normal limits. Ultrasonography showed a 6 cm heterogeneous mass adjacent to the left adrenal gland. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen confirmed an 8.2 cm, well-circumscribed, heterogeneous mass with both solid and cystic components arising from the left adrenal gland.

A 28-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of right scrotal enlargement and discomfort, accompanied by intermittent chest pain and progressive dyspnea. Six months earlier, he had noted a 1 × 1 cm mass over his right scrotum. He was treated empirically for tuberculosis for one month, during which his dyspnea worsened. He had no history of smoking or other comorbidities. On examination, the right scrotum was enlarged and swollen, with a tender, fixed mass measuring 5 × 6 cm and an immobile nodule in the right inguinal canal. A thoracic CT scan showed bilateral pleural effusions, segmental atelectasis, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Scrotal ultrasound revealed enlargement of the right testis (5.0 × 3.5 × 3.4 cm) with increased blood flow. Serum tumor markers were as follows: AFP 1.57 ng/ml (normal), CEA 13.00 ng/ml (elevated), CA-125 1437 U/ml, CA 74-4 68.37 U/ml, CYFRA21-1 13.57 ng/ml, NSE 16.83 ng/ml, and β-HCG 7.19 mIU/ml. Thoracentesis provided symptomatic relief and samples for cytology. Pleural fluid analysis showed β-HCG 7.19 mIU/ml, CEA 3.90 ng/ml, NSE 34.89 ng/ml, and CYFRA21-1 (not quantified). Immunohistochemical studies on pleural fluid cells demonstrated positivity for calretinin, D2-40, WT1, EMA, pancytokeratin, glut-1, and desmin, and negativity for P16, CEA, GPC-3, CD117, CD30, AFP, HCG, PLAP, OCT3/4, and SALL-4. PAS and Alcian blue stains were negative. A diagnosis of malignant pleural mesothelioma was made, and the right testicular mass remained suspicious for metastasis.

A 58-year-old African American man with a 5-year history of chronic hip pain was referred to neurology for 9 months of progressive right upper-extremity weakness and numbness. He described burning, electric-shock pain from the right shoulder to the hand, awakening him at night, accompanied by swelling of the right hand and decreased proximal strength. On examination, the right arm was adducted with forearm externally rotated; there was extensive muscle wasting of proximal and distal muscles. Strength in the right upper extremity was 2/5 (with 0/5 wrist flexion and finger movements); the left upper extremity was 5/5. Sensation was absent in a C8–T1 distribution on the right. Thenar, hypothenar, lumbrical, and interossei muscles were grossly atrophied. The patient had right-sided miosis; cerebellar function, speech, and cognition were normal; lower extremity strength was 4+/5 bilaterally. 

MRI of the cervical spine demonstrated a right apical soft-tissue mass and mild cervical spondylosis. MRI of the right shoulder showed a glenohumeral effusion and axillary fullness suggestive of lymphadenopathy. Chest x-ray revealed extensive bullous changes in the right upper lung. CT of the chest confirmed a heterogeneous right apical mass extending into the right supraclavicular region.

A 16-year-old male presented in August 2012 with a 1-year history of progressive left knee pain at rest and with activity, associated with decreased range of motion. He denied any history of trauma. On examination, the left knee had reduced flexion and extension; there was focal tenderness over the medial femoral condyle but no erythema or warmth. Radiographs obtained at an outside facility showed a lobulated, well-defined epiphyseal lesion with sclerotic margins and no stippled calcifications. A CT scan of the left knee demonstrated a low-attenuation lesion in the medial femoral condyle measuring 13 × 16 mm, with well-defined sclerotic margins and depression of the subchondral bone at the lesion border. Differential diagnosis at this time included chondroblastoma, giant cell tumor, clear cell chondrosarcoma, and osteomyelitis. Because of the delayed presentation and concern for metastatic disease, a CT of the chest was obtained, which showed no evidence of metastasis.

A 67-year-old Caucasian man was referred for evaluation of a recurrent mass in the left posterior neck. One year earlier, at a nonreferral center, he had undergone surgical excision of a neck lesion; pathology then showed a pleomorphic sarcoma with 30% of tumor cells positive for Ki-67 and positive microscopic margins. No adjuvant therapy was given.

On examination, there was a firm, fixed, painless 5-cm mass in the left posterior neck. Neck magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 50 × 20 mm mass with early invasion of the left paravertebral muscle. Positron-emission tomography/computed tomography showed no distant metastases. A pathological re-examination of the original specimen was performed, and the lesion was reclassified as myxofibrosarcoma.

A 33-year-old woman, G2P2A1 at 8 weeks’ gestation, was referred for evaluation of 2 months of vaginal spotting and a mass protruding through the introitus. She had not had a gynecologic examination in 2 years and had no significant family or genetic history. An abdominal ultrasound confirmed a live intrauterine embryo with no other abnormalities. On speculum examination, three firm masses, each measuring approximately 10 cm in greatest diameter, were seen in the vagina; the surfaces were superficially ulcerated. She underwent outpatient polypectomy without anesthesia.

A 15-year-old girl with no significant medical history presented with a slowly growing mass in her right axilla over the preceding 6 months. On examination, there was a 5 cm firm, nonmobile, painless palpable lesion without tenderness, erythema, or fluctuance. She denied any prior trauma. Laboratory studies, including white blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein, were all within normal limits. Frontal and lateral chest radiographs were unremarkable. MRI of the right axilla revealed a well-defined, well-circumscribed 4 × 5 × 6 cm solid mass within the subcutaneous fat that was slightly hyperintense to muscle on T1-weighted images and homogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images. There was marked diffuse homogeneous enhancement after intravenous contrast. The surrounding fat and adjacent muscle appeared normal without inflammatory changes. Adjacent ribs were normal, and a few small reactive lymph nodes were present without lymphadenopathy. Given the nonspecific imaging appearance and inability to exclude malignancy, tissue sampling was recommended.

A 29-year-old right-hand dominant woman presented with a 6-month history of progressive swelling, pain, tingling, and numbness of the right palm. She had no recent trauma and a normal cervical spine examination. One year earlier, she underwent carpal tunnel release elsewhere for moderate wrist pain and mild paresthesia without swelling; she was symptom-free for 1 year before the current recurrence. The present symptoms were refractory to analgesics, gabapentin, icing, and elevation.

On examination, there was a diffuse, tender volar wrist swelling measuring approximately 3×4 cm in Zone 5. Finger range of motion was normal; wrist flexion and extension were limited to 20° each, with painful radial and ulnar deviation. Tinel’s, Phalen’s, and Durkan’s tests were positive. Sensation was reduced in the median nerve distribution; the radial pulse was intact.

Hematologic studies and plain radiographs of the right wrist and hand were normal. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a tenosynovial mass encircling the flexor tendons at the level of the distal radioulnar joint, suggestive of pigmented villonodular synovitis. Nerve conduction studies revealed reduced conduction in the median nerve distribution.

A 36-week-gestation female infant was born by cesarean section to a 32-year-old G3P2 mother after premature rupture of membranes. Prenatal course was uncomplicated until 25 weeks, when ultrasound showed a relatively homogeneous echogenic mass (34 × 30 × 55 mm) in the region of the fetal pancreas causing compression of the inferior vena cava. Amniotic fluid volume and appearance of the fetal lungs, liver, and kidneys were normal.

At birth, weight was 2800 g (appropriate for gestational age), and Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes. Physical examination revealed a firm abdominal mass spanning both right and left quadrants. The infant developed mild respiratory distress syndrome requiring supplemental oxygen and had episodes of hypoglycemia and hypocalcemia managed with intravenous glucose and calcium. Laboratory studies demonstrated an elevated carcinoembryonic antigen level and a normal alpha-fetoprotein level.

On day 2, a chest radiograph showed elevation of the diaphragm on the right, attributed to mass effect from the pancreatic lesion. On day 6, contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a large, 113 × 70 × 60 mm pancreatic mass with contrast-enhancing solid areas and cystic or necrotic components encasing the superior mesenteric artery and vein, splenic vein, and portal vein; an 8 × 6 mm hypodense, hypoenhancing nodule in hepatic segment IV; normal spleen and kidneys; and thrombosis of the subhepatic inferior vena cava and renal veins.

A 10-year-old girl was referred with 6 months of progressive, intermittent projectile vomiting of semidigested food, occurring almost always after meals, accompanied by nonspecific epigastric pain, weight loss, fatigability, and bone aches. There was no fever, diarrhea, hematemesis, or family history of peptic ulcer disease, tuberculosis, or gastric carcinoma. On examination, she appeared emaciated, pale, and dehydrated. Vital signs were: temperature 37.0 °C, pulse 110 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, blood pressure 90/60 mm Hg. Her weight was 18.9 kg (<5th percentile) and height 137.5 cm (50th percentile). Abdominal examination revealed a soft, lax abdomen with epigastric fullness and no palpable masses or organomegaly. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 14 g/dL, WBC 9.2 × 10^9/L, platelets 459 × 10^3/mm^3, ESR 30 mm/hr, arterial blood gas with pH 7.59, PCO2 50 kPa, HCO3 55 mmol/L, hyponatremia (122 mmol/L), hypokalemia (1.87 mmol/L), hypochloremia (62 mmol/L), elevated urea (13 mmol/L) and creatinine (69 mmol/L), and normal liver enzymes and pancreatic enzymes. A clinical diagnosis of gastric outlet obstruction was made. Barium meal confirmed gastric outlet obstruction and revealed a cratered ulcer along the lesser curvature. Abdominal ultrasound showed marked thickening of the antral wall (12 mm) and pyloric channel and moderate pelvic free fluid. Upper endoscopy demonstrated markedly reddened, friable lower esophageal mucosa; a markedly thickened antral mucosa occluding the pylorus; and a clean-based 2.0 × 1.5 cm ulcer at the lesser curvature. Balloon dilation of the narrowed antrum and pylorus permitted passage of an 8.6 mm scope into the duodenum, which appeared normal, and a nasojejunal feeding tube was placed.

A 59-year-old postmenopausal woman (gravida 2, para 2) presented with vaginal bleeding. Initial cytological tests of the cervix and endometrium were negative. On referral, vaginal examination revealed an enlarged uterus. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a large heterogeneous mass occupying the entire endometrial cavity. Repeat endometrial cytology remained negative, and fractional curettage yielded only fibrous tissue with epithelial-like cells. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 77 × 76 mm heterogeneous solid tumor filling the uterine cavity, and degenerated myoma, leiomyosarcoma, or endometrial stromal sarcoma was suspected. Serum CA125 was mildly elevated at 41.4 U/mL, whereas CA19-9 and CEA were within normal limits. The patient underwent total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and pelvic lymphadenectomy. At laparotomy, the uterus was fist-sized without serosal invasion, both ovaries appeared normal, and a tumor arising from the uterine body occupied the entire cavity.

A 37-year-old woman, gravida 6 para 3 abortion 2, at 41 weeks of gestation was admitted for induction of labor. Four months earlier, she had developed intense right knee and lower-leg pain; deep-vein thrombosis was excluded by a negative Doppler examination. Over the preceding 2 weeks, she had progressive loss of function with difficulty standing and walking. On admission, the right knee was swollen, warm, and tender. Laboratory tests revealed a C-reactive protein level of 44 mg/L, a white-cell count of 11,300 cells/µL, and neutrophils of 8803 cells/µL. Ultrasonography of the knee and lower leg showed a necrotic or inflammatory collection at the proximal tibia, with an irregular periosteal and cortical surface. Osteomyelitis was suspected, and treatment with flucloxacillin was initiated. Labor and delivery were uneventful, and she delivered a healthy male infant.

On the first postpartum day, examination revealed multiple palpable breast masses, the largest measuring 4 cm in the right breast. Blood tests showed normal renal function, mildly elevated hepatic enzymes, a CA 15-3 level of 14 IU/mL, and a CA 125 level of 121 IU/mL. Radiographic imaging of the right leg demonstrated an infiltrative, destructive lesion of the proximal tibial metaphysis with cortical destruction. Chest radiography and computed tomography of the chest and abdomen revealed bilateral pulmonary nodules and peritoneal and multiple bony lesions. Mammography and breast ultrasonography confirmed two large masses with 12 lesions in the right breast and 7 in the left. Whole-body bone scintigraphy and positron-emission tomography confirmed metabolically active lesions at all these sites.

A 75-year-old woman was transferred for evaluation of an abnormal complete blood count. She reported anorexia, night sweats, and weight loss. On examination, she had mild splenomegaly with right upper quadrant discomfort. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL, white blood cell count 72×10^9/L with 2% blasts and 29% granulocytic precursors, and platelets 359×10^9/L. The peripheral blood smear demonstrated dysplastic features in the granulocytic series. Bone marrow aspirate revealed granulocytic proliferation with dysplasia, increased megakaryocytes, and focal fibrosis. Chromosome analysis showed a karyotype of 47,XX,+14/46,XX. Molecular studies for BCR-ABL1, PDGFRA, PDGFRB, and FGFR1 rearrangements and for JAK2, CALR, and MPL mutations were all negative.

A 39-year-old woman presented with anal pain and protrusion during defecation. Her medical and family history were unremarkable. On examination, there was an approximately 1-cm, well-circumscribed, umbilicated, reddish nodule on the anus, in association with prolapsed internal hemorrhoids. Laboratory studies, including white-cell count, hemoglobin, platelet count, alanine aminotransferase, and aspartate transaminase, were within normal limits. Viral markers for hepatitis B and serologic studies for immunocompromise were negative. Anoscopy confirmed multiple internal hemorrhoids. Endoanal ultrasound showed normal findings with no evidence of abscess or fistula. The patient underwent hemorrhoidectomy and excisional biopsy of the mass under caudal block.

A 59-year-old woman presented with a 1-week history of progressive, pruritic, pink, lacy patches on her trunk and extremities. She reported associated fevers, abdominal pain, dyspnea, and episodes of hypotension. On examination, there were generalized erythematous papules, macules, and patches arranged in a netlike, reticular pattern over the chest, abdomen, back, and upper and lower extremities. The lesions blanched on pressure without scaling, and mucosal surfaces were spared. Laboratory studies showed an elevated lactate dehydrogenase level, leukocytosis, anemia, hyperbilirubinemia, and hypofibrinogenemia. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed prominent lymphadenopathy in the cervical, axillary, mediastinal, hilar, retroperitoneal, and inguinal regions. Her recent medical history was notable for recurrent pericardial effusions and pneumonia, but she had not received any antibiotics or new medications in the preceding 2 weeks.

A 69-year-old man with a history of hypothyroidism and hypertension presented with a 2-week history of nausea, vomiting, generalized weakness, and left-sided discomfort. He also reported an unintentional 80-lb weight loss over the past year but denied fevers, chills, or night sweats. On examination, he was cachectic with dry mucous membranes; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Vital signs were within normal limits. Initial laboratory studies revealed:  
• Serum calcium, 16.1 mg/dL (8.5–10.5)  
• Blood urea nitrogen, 67 mg/dL (5–25)  
• Creatinine, 3.25 mg/dL (0.61–1.24)  
• Thyroid-stimulating hormone and thyroid function tests within normal limits  
• Intact parathyroid hormone (iPTH), 6.8 pg/mL (15–65)  
• PTH-related peptide (PTHrP), 3.7 pmol/L (0.0–2.3)  
• 25-Hydroxyvitamin D, 168 pg/mL (19.9–79.3)  
• β2-Microglobulin, 9.8 mg/L (1.1–2.4)  

Given the combination of severe hypercalcemia, renal dysfunction, and anemia, serum and urine protein electrophoreses were performed to evaluate for multiple myeloma, both of which were negative. Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, pelvis, and head was unremarkable, and a skeletal survey showed no lytic lesions. To further evaluate for a hematologic malignancy, a bone marrow biopsy was performed.

A 71-year-old woman presented for routine follow-up 1.9 years after adjuvant radiotherapy for synchronous bilateral breast cancer. Her initial cancer treatment had included wide excision of a right invasive lobular carcinoma (pT1cN0, ER/PR positive, HER2 negative) and management of left ductal carcinoma in situ, followed by bilateral whole-breast irradiation (50 Gy each with a 10 Gy boost to the right tumor bed). Treatment was well tolerated, and she was maintained on letrozole. 

At follow-up, she was noted to have a small, discolored patch of skin surrounding the right surgical scar without pain, pruritus, systemic symptoms, or signs of lymphedema. Mammography and ultrasound were unremarkable. A punch biopsy of the area was performed.
 
Histologic analysis of the biopsy specimen demonstrated changes consistent with a radiation-associated atypical vascular lesion.

A 25-year-old woman with HIV infection since birth, on antiretroviral therapy, presented with bilateral upper and lower extremity pain and progressive lower limb weakness leading to wheelchair dependence for 2 years. She had prior radiographs at multiple centers showing lytic bone lesions but no definitive diagnosis. On examination, she was normotensive, pale, and had digital clubbing. Multiple soft-tissue swellings and deformities were noted at the left elbow, dorsum of the left hand, both knees, and just above the right medial malleolus. Laboratory studies showed normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 5.6 g/dL, MCV 85.5 fL, RBC count 2.3×10^12/L), WBC 11.4×10^9/L, platelets 489×10^9/L; C-reactive protein was normal. Renal function was normal (creatinine 86 μmol/L). HIV viral load was undetectable and CD4 count was 733 cells/μL. A skeletal survey revealed multifocal lytic expansile lesions with gross bone destruction and associated soft-tissue swelling, resembling vanishing bone syndrome.

A 71-year-old woman presented to her primary physician with dyspnoea, cough, and fever, treated as a lower respiratory tract infection. One month later, she developed painful erythematous lesions on both lower limbs with pedal edema, clinically consistent with erythema nodosum, along with tenderness of the hands, wrists, and ankles. An audiogram, head MRI, and ENT evaluation for concurrent hearing impairment were unremarkable. Initial routine blood tests, including liver function, were normal.

Three months after initial presentation, rheumatology evaluation revealed tender, edematous ankles; tenderness of metatarsophalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints; nodal arthritic changes in the hands; and erythema nodosum–like lesions. Laboratory studies showed eosinophilia of 1.7 ×10^9/L (normal 0.0–0.6), ALP 205 U/L (50–140), GGT 112 U/L (<38), ALT 50 U/L (<34), total bilirubin 5 μmol/L (<20), ESR 69 mm/hr (<20), and CRP 26 mg/L (<5). Autoimmune and infectious studies were negative. Chest radiograph was normal; hand x-rays showed erosive interphalangeal arthritis. A presumptive diagnosis of sarcoidosis was made, and oral prednisolone (15 mg daily) was started.

One month later, she deteriorated with worsening ankle pain and lower limb lesions, including a discharging lesion on the left heel; prednisolone was increased to 50 mg daily. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a complex liver mass. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a heterogeneous irregular mass filling liver segments 2 and 3, bulging into segment 4A, involving the left hepatic vein, abutting the middle hepatic vein, and a bulky but uniformly enhancing pancreatic tail. Tumor markers showed chromogranin A 844 μg/L (<102) and lipase 10 825 U/L. MRCP revealed a T1-hypointense, well-circumscribed hypervascular liver mass in segment 2 and a lobulated hypervascular mass in the pancreatic tail that was T1-hypointense, mildly T2-hyperintense, and showed restricted diffusion. Whole-body CT revealed no additional lesions.

A 48-year-old white woman with a 12-year history of primary Sjögren’s syndrome presented with progressive enlargement of all peripheral lymph nodes. On exam, conglomerates up to 6.0 cm in the left supraclavicular area caused tracheal compression and stridor, and up to 5.0 cm in the left femoral-inguinal area caused lymphostasis of the left leg. There were no fevers, night sweats, or weight loss.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 89 g/L, total protein 120 g/L, normal lactate dehydrogenase, and blood viscosity 7.9 mPa·s (normal <5.3). Serum immunochemistry revealed an M-spike of IgAκ at 72 g/L, with reduced polyclonal IgG and IgM. Urine electrophoresis detected Bence-Jones κ-type light chains. HIV serology was negative.

Contrast CT of the chest and abdomen revealed multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the mediastinum, pulmonary hila, abdominal cavity, and retroperitoneum, forming confluent conglomerates up to 6.5 cm, with hepatosplenomegaly. Skeletal radiographs showed no bone destruction.

Bone marrow myelogram showed 1.6% plasma cells and 7.6% lymphocytes; histology demonstrated no plasma cell or lymphocyte infiltration.

Biopsies of cervical and inguinal lymph nodes showed effacement of the nodal architecture with expanded interfollicular areas infiltrated by plasmacytic cells. Immunohistochemistry revealed plasma cells positive for CD138, MuM1, CD43, expressing IgAκ; some co-expressed CD20 and CD79a; negative for CD56, BCL2, cyclin D1, CD23, HHV-8, and EBV-encoded RNA. The Ki-67 index was 10%.

A 47-year-old man noted a gradually enlarging, painful soft-tissue mass on the inner aspect of his right thigh over 7–8 months. Physical examination revealed a 4 × 3 cm firm subcutaneous lesion without overlying skin changes. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the pelvis demonstrated an enhancing lesion in the perianal region; there was no bowel wall thickening, free fluid, abdominal lymphadenopathy, or visceral organ abnormalities. He underwent a marginal excision elsewhere, and the initial biopsy was reported as a poorly differentiated carcinoma. On referral, his carcinoembryonic antigen level was 1.8 ng/mL (normal 0.3–2.7 ng/mL). Six months after recommendation for wide local excision, he re-presented with local recurrence, difficulty walking, and had received interim chemotherapy and radiotherapy. 

Real-time B-mode high-frequency ultrasonography of the right upper inner thigh showed an oval, hypoechoic solid lesion measuring 2.9 × 2.2 × 2.1 cm in the deep subcutaneous tissue, adjacent to the scar of the prior excision, along with two smaller hypoechoic nodules (10 mm and 8 mm). The main lesion had an ill-defined echogenic wall, peripheral linear echoes suggesting a lymph node, and distorted cortical architecture; there was no significant internal Doppler flow.

Gross examination of the original specimen revealed gray-white soft tissue fragments totaling 3.5 × 2 × 2 cm. Histologically, there were multinodular sheets of oval to polygonal cells separated by thin fibrous septa, focal areas of cellular disintegration with hemorrhage producing a pseudoangiosarcomatous pattern, moderate nuclear pleomorphism, interspersed large cells with vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli, abundant cytoplasm with intracytoplasmic inclusions (“rhabdoid” morphology), and focal necrosis. Reticulin staining highlighted the nodular growth pattern.

Immunohistochemical studies showed diffuse strong positivity for cytokeratin, vimentin, CK7, epithelial membrane antigen, and CD34; desmin was focally positive. Tumor cells were negative for smooth muscle actin, MyoD-1, CK20, CEA, S-100, HMB-45, CD31, C-KIT, leukocyte common antigen, and calretinin.

A 46-year-old woman presented with several weeks of worsening gastroesophageal reflux, a pressure-like sensation in the upper abdomen, early satiety, intermittent nausea, and bloating. Her medical history was notable for seronegative neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder complicated by bilateral optic neuritis and transverse myelitis, treated with low-dose prednisone and azathioprine for 12 years, as well as chronic kidney disease, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and obstructive sleep apnea. On examination, she had moderate tenderness in the epigastrium and right upper quadrant.  
Laboratory studies were unremarkable. A right upper quadrant ultrasound showed increased hepatic echogenicity consistent with steatosis and a 1.9 × 2.4 × 1.9 cm hypoechoic solid mass in the right hepatic lobe. An MRI of the abdomen demonstrated an ill-defined, lobulated T2-hyperintense lesion of corresponding size with heterogeneous restricted diffusion and no central fat signal. Gastroenterology review concluded that “imaging was compatible with an inflammatory adenoma,” and she was advised to lose 20–25 lb and to have repeat abdominal imaging in six months.

A 59-year-old man presented with a painless mass on the anterior aspect of his upper thigh, slowly enlarging over 5 years. On examination, there was a firm, mobile, 5 × 3 cm nodule covered by normal skin. He was otherwise healthy. Laboratory studies—including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, urinalysis, aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, blood urea nitrogen, and creatinine—were normal. 

Sonography revealed a mixed echogenic solid mass measuring approximately 4.5 × 3 × 2 cm. Doppler ultrasound showed vessels predominantly at the periphery of the mass. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-circumscribed, lobular, subcutaneous 4.7 × 2.9 × 2.2 cm mass with heterogeneous enhancement, predominantly in its peripheral portion, after intravenous contrast administration. Diffusion-weighted imaging showed areas of increased signal intensity compatible with a highly cellular tumor.

Based on these imaging findings, the differential diagnosis included benign subcutaneous lipomatous tumors with cystic and solid components—such as angiolipoma or fibrolipoma—as well as a well-circumscribed low-grade soft tissue liposarcoma without extension into surrounding tissues. Because of the lesion’s vascularity and heterogeneous pattern of contrast enhancement, a simple lipoma was excluded.

A 35-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of dysuria, bladder tenesmus, suprapubic pain, and urinary urgency that had been treated as recurrent urinary tract infections with broad-spectrum antibiotics without symptomatic relief. Urine cultures were repeatedly negative. Physical examination, including abdominal and genital evaluation, was unremarkable. Renal and bladder ultrasound demonstrated a mass at the dome of the full bladder. Cystoscopy revealed a solitary 4.0 cm polypoid mass with mucoid characteristics arising from the bladder dome. Contrast-enhanced CT of the lower abdomen showed a 60 × 40 mm mixed cystic and solid mass with a density of 30 HU and peripheral calcifications located on the anterior and superior edge of the bladder. Transurethral resection yielded a pathological diagnosis of moderately differentiated, muscle-invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma. Subsequent upper endoscopy, colonoscopy, and mammography showed no evidence of malignancy. Given the midline location, calcifications, and cystic and solid components, a diagnosis of urachal adenocarcinoma was proposed.

A 23-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of right facial swelling. The mass remained stable in size for the first 3 months, then became more prominent, and she began experiencing intermittent pricking pain over the last 3 months. She had no significant medical history. On examination, there was a diffuse 2×2 cm warm, tender, soft swelling over the right mandibular body; it was mobile horizontally but limited in vertical movement, and the overlying skin was pinchable. The swelling became more prominent on clenching. Intraoral examination was unremarkable. Routine hematological tests were within normal limits. A posteroanterior mandibular radiograph showed no abnormalities. Ultrasonography revealed a 2.2×0.6 cm mixed echogenic lesion within the right masseter muscle with a speck of calcification. Colour Doppler ultrasound demonstrated dilated vascular channels with good flow and no interarterial or venous communications. MRI showed a well-defined T2-weighted mixed hypo- and hyperintense lesion measuring 2.1×2.5×1.8 cm along the anteroinferior aspect of the right masseter.

A 42-year-old woman with no medical comorbidities presented with a 9-month history of lower back pain. Following a minor fall, she developed radicular pain in the right lower limb but denied motor weakness or changes in bladder or bowel function. On examination, gait and lower-limb motor strength were normal. Sensation was decreased over the right medial thigh, and the right Achilles tendon reflex was absent. Babinski reflexes were equivocal bilaterally, and anal sphincter tone was intact. MRI of the lumbosacral spine with gadolinium revealed a 1.3 × 1.1 × 1.2 cm intradural, extramedullary lesion at L4–L5 with mild heterogeneous enhancement. The lesion contained tiny high T1-signal foci, caused splaying of the cauda equina nerve roots, and resulted in severe spinal canal stenosis. MRI of the brain and cervicothoracic spine was normal. Initial radiological differential diagnosis included myxopapillary ependymoma of the cauda equina.

A 24-year-old man presented with acute urinary retention and fever. He reported 10 days of diffuse myalgia followed by painful dysesthesia in the left arm, for which he received corticosteroids. On examination, there was marked weakness of the upper extremities (worse on the left), light spastic paraparesis, and decreased pain, position, and touch sensation below the T1 level. Deep tendon reflexes were weak, Babinski signs were negative bilaterally, and gait was slightly unsteady. Abdominal palpation elicited pain in the hypogastric region. After Foley catheter placement, urinary microscopy showed a normal leukocyte count and no erythrocytes. Because of sudden gait instability and worsening neurologic status, emergency MRI of the spine was obtained. Imaging revealed a 27×8 mm intradural, extramedullary mass posterolateral to the spinal cord at the C7–T1 level, causing compression without signal changes in the cord. The lesion was homogeneously hyperintense on T1- and T2-weighted images and showed heterogeneous hyperintensity on STIR sequences, suggesting a highly vascularized nature.

A 16-year-old girl presented with a 2-month history of a slowly enlarging swelling in the left anterior maxilla. She had no pain, neurological symptoms, or nasal discharge. On examination, there was marked deformation of the left cheek with intact overlying skin, and egg‐shell crackling of the expanded buccal and palatal cortical plates from the central incisor to the first molar. The oral mucosa was healthy, the left canine was unerupted, and a supernumerary tooth occupied the midline. A panoramic radiograph revealed a well-defined, unilocular radiolucency of the left maxilla with thinning of all bony walls, displacement of the canine, and root resorption of the first and second premolars; no calcifications were noted. A clinical diagnosis of dentigerous cyst and adenomatoid odontogenic tumor was made, with additional considerations including keratocystic odontogenic tumor, ameloblastic fibroma, odontogenic myxoma, central giant cell tumor, and unicystic ameloblastoma. Under local anesthesia, the lesion was enucleated along with removal of the impacted canine, supernumerary, and first premolar, yielding yellowish‐brown fluid.

A 21-year-old woman, two years after resection of papillary thyroid carcinoma, presented with new-onset seizures. She experienced secondarily generalized tonic–clonic seizures lasting 1–2 minutes with a brief postictal period. There was no personal or family history of neurofibromatosis or other genetic disorders. On admission, vital signs were normal and physical examination, including a detailed neurologic exam, was unremarkable.

Noncontrast CT of the head showed a 2.6 × 2.4 cm heterogeneous mass in the left frontal lobe with a hyperdense peripheral rim and surrounding vasogenic edema but no calcification. Brain MRI revealed an intra-axial left frontal lobe lesion that was hypointense with an isointense rim on T1-weighted images, mixed isointense and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and demonstrated extensive vasogenic edema. The mass exhibited heterogeneous ring enhancement with a central nonenhancing region and restricted diffusion in the enhancing wall. There was no evidence of hemorrhage or calcification on susceptibility-weighted MRI or CT.

Given her history of thyroid cancer and the imaging characteristics, the initial diagnostic considerations included metastatic thyroid carcinoma, primary high-grade glioma, and lymphoma.

A 35-year-old man with no significant comorbidities presented with a 5-month history of a slowly enlarging swelling on the right upper back. He reported mild discomfort when lying supine but denied pain, fever, or weight loss. He also noted three smaller, stable subcutaneous swellings (each ~1×1 cm) on the right arm, right thigh, and left anterior chest wall. There was no history of chest pain, dyspnea, cough, rash, itching, or skin discoloration. He previously used anabolic steroids for bodybuilding (2.5 years, discontinued 3 months ago) and denied trauma or radiation exposure.

On examination, he was normotensive and afebrile. No lymphadenopathy was present. The three small swellings were soft, mobile, had a smooth surface, and demonstrated a positive slip sign. A larger 15×12 cm mass on the posterior right chest was firm, smooth, well-defined, nonfluctuant, noncompressible, mobile in all directions, with pinchable overlying skin. It lateralized on overhead abduction of the right arm and became fixed with shoulder extension/adduction. Percussion was dull without bruit. Lung fields were clear bilaterally.

Laboratory studies (CBC, LFTs, RFTs, electrolytes) were normal. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. Ultrasound of the back mass showed a large echogenic subcutaneous lesion suggestive of a lipoma. Fine-needle aspiration cytology revealed atypical cells with moderate pleomorphism, irregular nuclear membranes, and hyperchromasia against a chondromyxoid background, suggestive of a spindle cell neoplasm. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated a 15×10×5 cm well-circumscribed lesion in the intermuscular plane beneath the latissimus dorsi, displacing but not invading muscle, with intact underlying bone, no lymphadenopathy, and no distant metastases.

A 61-year-old man was brought to the emergency department late at night after working a 12-hour night shift. He developed general fatigue, nausea, multiple episodes of vomiting, and progressive breathlessness. On arrival, his blood pressure was 170/110 mmHg (later rising to 202/132 mmHg), heart rate 132 beats per minute, and he subsequently became febrile with clouded consciousness. His respiratory status rapidly declined, necessitating endotracheal intubation.

Laboratory tests on admission showed a white blood cell count of 19,800/μL, C-reactive protein 6.93 mg/dL, creatine kinase 741 IU/L (MB isozyme 57 IU/L), and troponin-I 7.867 pg/mL. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated diffuse severe hypokinesis of the mid-apical segments with basal hyperkinesis. Coronary angiography revealed normal coronary arteries. 

Chest radiography revealed bilateral pulmonary congestion and interstitial shadows. Chest computed tomography showed patchy ground-glass opacities with bilateral infiltrative and interstitial shadows. The patient was diagnosed with acute lung injury, considered to represent interstitial pneumonia or severe bacterial pneumonia, and was treated with methylprednisolone (1,000 mg) and meropenem (1 g). Upon transfer to the intensive care unit, his blood pressure was 220/110 mmHg. Two hours later, he developed arrhythmia, profound hypotension (systolic blood pressure 40 mmHg), and subsequent cardiac arrest; resuscitative efforts failed, and he died six hours after arrival.

A 37-year-old man presented with a 1‐year history of a progressively enlarging exophytic lesion on the left buccal mucosa. He reported slight bleeding but no pain, numbness, or functional impairment. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. On examination, there was a well‐circumscribed, 2×2 cm pedunculated mass covered by smooth, light blue mucosa. The lesion was soft to rubbery and bled easily on palpation. No cervical, submandibular, or submental lymphadenopathy was noted. Routine laboratory tests, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included a benign vascular neoplasm, a benign neural tumor, or inflammatory hyperplasia. The patient underwent excision of the lesion under local anesthesia with a high‐power CO₂ laser, and the specimen was fixed in 10% formalin and sent for histopathological evaluation.

An 87-year-old woman with known bilateral sensorineural hearing loss was referred for evaluation of a mass in her right external auditory canal (EAC). She was asymptomatic, without otalgia, otorrhea, facial paralysis, or taste disturbance. Five months earlier, a superficial biopsy of a 1.2 × 0.4 cm spherical lesion at the transition from the cartilaginous to the bony part of the right EAC had been performed externally. The lesion grew, and a second, more extensive biopsy of the now 1.3 × 1.0 × 0.6 cm mass was obtained. The initial biopsy revealed a ceruminous adenoma, but pleomorphic adenoma or ceruminous adenocarcinoma could not be excluded because of its superficial nature. The second biopsy demonstrated a basaloid biphasic neoplasm with chondromyxoid stroma; ceruminous pleomorphic adenoma and ceruminous adenoid cystic carcinoma were both considered. On otoendoscopy, a discrete mass was seen on the posterior wall of the right EAC, with otherwise normal ear findings. Computed tomography of the temporal bones showed a soft-tissue–density exophytic mass in the right EAC without evidence of bony erosion. An exclusive endoscopic resection of the lesion was planned, with removal up to the cartilaginous and bony canal walls.

A 3-year-old boy who had undergone distal hypospadias repair 1.5 years earlier was brought to the clinic for evaluation of a slowly enlarging mass on the ventral aspect of his penis and an abnormal urinary stream. On examination, he was afebrile, with a pulse of 96 beats/min and blood pressure of 85/54 mmHg. The distal urethra was dehisced, and urine flow was deviated. A firm, painless mass measuring 2 × 2.5 cm was palpable on the ventral distal penis. Bilateral testes were descended and normal in size. Neurologic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a WBC count of 6.9 × 10^3/mm^3, hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, ALT 14 U/L, AST 18 U/L, and creatinine 0.6 mg/dL. Urinalysis revealed normal red cells and no signs of infection.

A 72-year-old man with a history of systemic angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma, recently completing six cycles of brentuximab-CHP and two cycles of ICE therapy one week before presentation, was admitted with worsening dyspnea and a new pruritic rash of two weeks’ duration. He denied pain, oral lesions, fevers, chills, or weight loss. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 18.2 × 10^3/µL with 49% lymphocytes and a hemoglobin level of 8.8 g/dL; the metabolic panel and respiratory viral panel were unremarkable, and blood cultures showed no growth. On examination, red-pink macules and thin papules coalesced into thin plaques and patches on the chest, arms, abdomen, and back, some with trailing scale and islands of sparing; a diffuse red patch with scale involved the face and frontal scalp. Given the exam findings of plaques with intermittent trailing scale and recent chemotherapy initiation, diagnoses of morbiliform drug eruption, pityriasis rubra pilaris, psoriasis, and pityriasis rosea–like drug eruption were considered. A punch biopsy of a lesion on the right abdomen was performed.

A 55-year-old man with diabetes, hypertension, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and chronic kidney disease presented with painless frank hematuria for 2 months. Cystoscopy revealed a 5 cm posterior bladder wall tumor; biopsy showed infiltrating high-grade urothelial carcinoma, pT2. He underwent transurethral resection and contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis, which showed no metastatic disease. After a prolonged postoperative hospitalization with multiple complications, serial CT scans remained negative. Seven months later, he reported lower back pain and was found to have elevated serum calcium. Bony metastasis was suspected, but repeat CT scans again showed no local recurrence or distant metastasis. Two months thereafter, he developed left knee pain and swelling. 
Plain radiography of the left tibia–fibula demonstrated a lytic destructive lesion in the proximal fibula. Ultrasound of the left calf showed a 2.0 × 3.2 × 3.9 cm oval heterogeneous intramuscular hypoechoic lesion in the proximal lateral gastrocnemius muscle with peripheral vascularity. MRI of the left knee revealed an ill-defined enhancing soft tissue mass in the proximal lateral gastrocnemius muscle that was isointense on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, measured 2.5 × 4.3 × 4.2 cm, and was associated with surrounding muscle edema and adjacent fibular marrow hyperintensity with postcontrast enhancement.

A 27-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease on thrice-weekly hemodialysis for 11 years and hypertension presented in May 2013 with a 1-week history of a mass of the hard palate. Examination showed a 40 × 50 mm pink-to-purple, firm-to-hard, nontender, dome-shaped lesion at the mid–hard palate. A panoramic radiograph revealed bony rarefaction in the right maxilla in the canine–premolar region and an incidental, well-defined, unilocular radiolucent lesion with scalloped borders in the right mandibular body from the central incisor to the second premolar. Laboratory tests demonstrated elevated parathyroid hormone levels, and a parathyroid scan identified an adenoma in the lower left thyroid lobe. Parathyroidectomy was performed, and a whole-body bone scan showed multiple foci of increased uptake in the nasofacial bones, spine, humerus, ribs, pelvis, and tibiae, with a pattern favoring metabolic bone disease. Six months later, she reported progressive swelling and new pain in the right maxilla. On examination, there was a bony hard mass of the right maxilla with nasal deformity and obstruction, infraorbital nodular purple swelling with superior displacement of the right globe, a firm mass in the right buccal sulcus, and displacement and loosening of the right upper teeth. Panoramic radiograph showed a large, poorly marginated radiolucent lesion of the right maxilla with tooth displacement. Coronal contrast-enhanced CT revealed a heterogeneous, expansile osteolytic mass of the right maxilla crossing the midline and invading the left maxillary sinus and alveolar process, and a separate osteolytic lesion of the right mandibular body with cortical thinning and buccal displacement of teeth. According to her history and imaging, Brown tumor and central giant cell granuloma were suspected.

An 80-year-old woman with a remote central facial fracture in childhood presented in May 2014 with progressive right eye bulging and epiphora. She had previously undergone partial resection of a right orbital/nasal bridge/sinus bony tumor in 1999 and again in 2010. Histopathology from 2010 reportedly showed “dense hyalinized and myxoid fibrous tissue associated with cartilage and bone, consistent with fibroma of the cortex of the orbital bone, and was not suspicious of malignancy.” 

On examination in 2014, she had 3 mm of right axial globe proptosis, 2 mm of right hypoglobus, complete right nasolacrimal duct obstruction, and a palpable bony prominence spanning the right medial orbit across the nasal root to the left medial orbit. Visual acuity was 20/25 bilaterally; intraocular pressures were 21 mm Hg (right) and 22 mm Hg (left). 

Non-contrast CT of the orbits demonstrated a well-circumscribed 20 × 36 mm lobular ossified mass extending from the right ethmoid sinus and medial orbital wall to the left nasal bone. In October 2014, she underwent partial resection, restoring normal bony contours and alleviating proptosis. Histology showed “cartilage with endochondral ossification with mature trabeculae of bone and osteoid without mitotic activity,” consistent with benign sino-orbital osteochondroma.

In June 2015, tumor progression caused diplopia and difficulty wearing spectacles. The patient elected repeat debulking, and histology again demonstrated benign osteochondroma. She remained asymptomatic until May 2018, when she returned with renewed diplopia. Vision was 20/40 bilaterally with full motility. Repeat CT showed a 42 × 39 × 25 mm bony lesion involving the right orbit, ethmoid sinus, frontal sinus, and floor of the anterior cranial fossa.

A 44-year-old man with a 13-year history of untreated HIV infection presented with a 3-week history of persistent, dull bilateral back pain, fever, fatigue, and weight loss. He declined antiretroviral therapy and on admission had a CD4+ T-lymphocyte count of 6 cells/µL and an HIV RNA load of 10 001 391 copies/mL. Physical examination was notable only for costovertebral angle tenderness. Laboratory studies showed mild anemia (hemoglobin 103 g/L), elevated aspartate transaminase (79 U/L) and γ-glutamyltransferase (207 U/L), and hypoalbuminemia (30.7 g/L). There was no serologic or microbiologic evidence of cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, fungi, or tuberculosis. Renin, angiotensin, aldosterone, adrenocorticotropic hormone, cortisol, and catecholamine levels were within normal limits. Unenhanced abdominal computed tomography revealed two large (67 × 38 mm on the left, 56 × 58 mm on the right), heterogeneous, hypodense masses adjacent to both adrenal glands. Contrast enhancement was moderate and heterogeneous, with associated retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy compressing the adrenals. Given the imaging appearance and the patient’s profound immunodeficiency, lymphoma was initially suspected; adrenal carcinoma and pheochromocytoma were also considered. A CT-guided core-needle biopsy of the right-sided lesion was performed.

An 82-year-old man first presented in 2008 with mild anemia, bilateral flank pain, and night sweats. Initial noncontrast abdominal CT showed nonobstructive right renal calculi, minimal peri-renal and peri-aortic fat stranding, and mild bilateral hydronephrosis. Two years later, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated progression with a “hairy” appearance of the kidneys and a concentric peri-aortic soft-tissue cuff (“coated” aorta). A peri-renal biopsy revealed non-specific retroperitoneal fibrosis with numerous CD68-positive histiocytes. He was treated with corticosteroids followed by methotrexate.

In 2015, a follow-up abdominal CT angiogram showed stable to minimally progressive retroperitoneal fibrotic changes. FDG-PET/CT revealed active uptake in those retroperitoneal lesions and new uptake in the left pleural region, with no skeletal involvement. The patient later required hospitalization for acute renal failure and pneumonia.

In 2016, chest CT demonstrated new pleural, fissural, and some interlobular septal thickening with ground-glass opacities. A pleural biopsy showed chronic inflammatory infiltrates with histiocytes morphologically similar to those in the peri-renal biopsy; immunostaining was CD68-positive, CD1a-negative, and S-100-negative. BRAF V600E mutation testing on the pleural specimen was negative.

Three years later, repeat FDG-PET/CT showed no skeletal lesions but revealed mild focal uptake (maximum SUV 2.6) in the right atrium. Transthoracic echocardiography confirmed a 1.8×3.0 cm mass attached to the anterolateral wall of the right atrium; the left ventricular ejection fraction was normal, and the patient remained asymptomatic from a cardiac standpoint.

A 52-year-old man was referred for a several-week history of cough, mild dyspnea, and pleuritic chest pain. He had a 36–pack-year smoking history and drank approximately 50 g of alcohol per day. On examination, he had hepatomegaly without cutaneous lesions. Laboratory tests showed AST 90 U/L, ALT 89 U/L, GGT 63 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 128 U/L; albumin and total bilirubin were normal. The complete blood count was unremarkable. Chest radiography revealed multiple nodules, some cavitated, with upper-lobe predominance. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed multiple infracentimetric centrilobular nodules, some cavitated, and cysts predominantly in the upper lobes, sparing the lower segments. Abdominal CT demonstrated hepatomegaly with multiple hypodense hepatic nodules up to 15 mm, some confluent; bile ducts were not dilated and there were no other abdominal abnormalities.

A 48-year-old Syrian woman, G0P0, presented with one week of diffuse abdominal pain varying from mild to severe, fatigue, debility, high fever, vomiting, and urinary retention. She had been treated empirically for cystitis without improvement. Her last menstrual period was 5 years ago. There were no night sweats or weight loss. On examination, her abdomen was distended with periodic tenderness; other systems were normal. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 11 mg/dL (normal 12–14) and CA-125 333.75 U/mL (normal 1.7–32). Pelvic ultrasound revealed a heterogeneous lobulated mass on the anterior and superior uterine walls extending to both ovaries with mixed echogenicity and high perfusion on Doppler, and moderate free fluid in the abdomen. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated a 112 × 191 × 160 mm irregular, heterogeneous, lobulated uterine mass extending to both ovaries, enlarged lymph nodes along the abdominal aorta and right iliac vessels with mesenteric involvement, moderate ascites, and a large right pleural effusion with right lower lobe atelectasis.

A 7-year-old girl was brought for evaluation of skin lesions on the sole of her left foot. The lesions were present at birth and have been asymptomatic. She has no significant medical history; family history is notable only for atopic dermatitis. Prior treatments with over-the-counter topical antifungal agents and salicylic acid produced no improvement. On examination, there are unilateral hyperkeratotic, verrucous papules coalescing into plaques in a linear configuration following the lines of Blaschko along the lateral border of the left sole.

A 3-year-old Syrian boy presented with 2 months of gradual, painless swelling of the left lower eyelid and ptosis that worsened over 2 weeks. There was no vision loss, trauma, or systemic symptoms except 1 week of decreased appetite. Family history was unremarkable.

On examination, the left globe was displaced superomedially with limited upward gaze. What appeared to be left upper-lid ptosis was pseudoptosis from globe displacement. Palpebral fissure measured 5 mm on the left (9 mm on the right). A hard lesion was palpable at the left inferior orbital rim and lateral orbit, measuring 3.5 cm × 1.5 cm. There was no proptosis, skin changes, or lymphadenopathy.

CT of the orbits showed a 9.5 mm osseous defect at the left inferior lateral orbital margin with an associated soft-tissue mass 1.9 × 2.1 × 1.9 cm extending into the orbit and a 7.8 × 7.8 × 9.7 mm component toward the subcutaneous zygoma. MRI revealed a solid, enhancing mass involving the lateral and inferior left orbital walls, displacing the globe superiorly and medially, with medial displacement of the inferior rectus; the optic nerve and contralateral orbit were normal.

An incisional biopsy showed diffuse sheets of atypical cells infiltrating bone. Many cells had clear cytoplasm resembling Reed–Sternberg cells, with pleomorphic nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and numerous mitoses. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated strong positivity for CD3, CD4, CD8, and CD43, and negativity for CD20, CD21, CD30, CD56, granzyme B, and TdT.

A 48-year-old man with a 25-year history of left-sided ulcerative colitis presented with four days of fever, nausea, diarrhea, and hematochezia. Over the past year he had multiple steroid-dependent flares despite attempts to taper off prednisone, and azathioprine was added eight months ago. His home medications included prednisone and pantoprazole. 

On examination, he was afebrile, heart rate 62 bpm, blood pressure 143/84 mmHg. His abdomen was soft and non-tender, without rebound or guarding, and there were no skin rashes. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, white cells 10.1×10^9/L, and a negative HIV antibody test. 

Contrast CT of the abdomen revealed sigmoid wall thickening, luminal narrowing, surrounding inflammatory stranding, and a 3-cm fluid collection consistent with an abscess. Blood cultures grew Klebsiella pneumoniae, and he received a 14-day course of antibiotics. 

After resolution of the diverticulitis, a colonoscopy was performed, which revealed a discrete tumor in the rectum.

A 34-year-old woman presented with a painful, firm swelling on the distal anterolateral aspect of her right fibula. Ten months earlier she underwent excision of a similar lesion, which was reported as an osteochondroma. She had no history of trauma. On examination, she had a well-healed longitudinal scar and a non-tender, firm mass over the distal fibula. Ankle motion was full, weight-bearing was unrestricted, and neurovascular status was normal.  
Plain radiographs showed a well-marginated ossified mass projecting from the anterolateral cortex of the fibula. CT scanning confirmed an ossified outgrowth without corticomedullary continuity. MRI demonstrated a focal osteocartilaginous lesion arising from the lateral cortex that was isointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense at the surface on T2-weighted images, and contained deep heterogeneous areas. All routine laboratory studies were normal.

A 44-year-old woman was referred with postoperative headache and confusion. Three days earlier, she had undergone a transabdominal hysterectomy and left salpingo-oophorectomy for abnormal uterine bleeding. Postoperatively she developed a decreased level of consciousness (GCS 12) and severe headache; a noncontrast brain CT performed at the outside hospital showed multiple hemorrhagic lesions with surrounding edema. 

On arrival, her level of consciousness and headache had normalized (GCS 15), but she complained of paresthesia and numbness of the left face and body. Her medical history was unremarkable. She was afebrile, and her blood pressure remained 110/70 mm Hg throughout hospitalization. Neurologic examination revealed decreased pinprick and touch sensation on the left side; the remainder of the exam was normal.

Brain MRI revealed multiple hyperintense lesions on T1- and T2-weighted sequences in supra- and infratentorial regions with surrounding edema, consistent with late subacute hemorrhage in the subcortical white matter. FLAIR images showed asymmetrical hyperintense signals in the frontal and parietal lobes. Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images demonstrated ring enhancement of the lesions, and diffusion-weighted imaging showed restricted diffusion in some. Magnetic resonance venography was normal.

Laboratory studies including ESR, CRP, thyroid and liver function tests, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, vasculitis markers, an extractable nuclear antigen profile, blood cultures, anti-toxoplasma antibodies, and viral markers were all within normal limits or negative.

Abdominopelvic CT identified a heterogeneous 60×40 mm solid-cystic mass in the left adrenal gland. Twenty-four-hour urine collections showed metanephrine and normetanephrine levels exceeding 2000 and 3000 µg/d, respectively (normal values substantially lower). ^131I-MIBG scintigraphy demonstrated marked uptake in the left adrenal lesion.

A 19-year-old woman presented with intermittent, moderate dull pain in the right hypochondrium for 9 months. She had no history of smoking, alcohol use, or hepatitis. On examination, her vital signs were stable, and abdominal examination revealed mild tender hepatomegaly without other findings. Routine hematology and liver function tests, including alpha-fetoprotein, were within normal limits; hepatitis B and C serologies were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography showed two hypoechoic lesions in both lobes of the liver. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated an enlarged, irregular liver with mild caudate-lobe hypertrophy and two hypodense lesions: a 100×80 mm mass in segments VI–VIII and a 30×25 mm mass in segments III–IV.

A 29-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with a 1-year history of right hip pain. On examination, there was tenderness over the right anterior hip joint.  

Plain radiographs of the pelvis showed an ill-defined expansile lytic lesion centered in the right acetabulum. CT imaging confirmed an expansile lytic lesion of the posterior column of the right acetabulum with cortical breaches medially, laterally, and involving the articular surface. MRI demonstrated that the lesion was isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images, showed intermediate signal on STIR sequences, and exhibited mild diffuse enhancement on post-contrast fat-saturated T1-weighted images. FDG PET/CT revealed intensely increased tracer uptake at the acetabular/iliac lesion (SUV max 12) without evidence of distant uptake.  

A CT-guided core biopsy revealed a proliferation of xanthomatous histiocytes admixed with smaller fibrohistiocytic cells, isolated epithelioid cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and moderate nuclear atypia, and occasional osteoclast-type giant cells; no significant pleomorphism, necrosis, or atypical mitoses were seen, and there was no overt inflammatory infiltrate.  

Immunohistochemical studies showed focal keratin expression in the epithelioid cells, negativity for CK7, CK8/18, and CK CAM5.2, diffuse CD68 and factor XIIIa positivity in the xanthomatous cells, negative smooth muscle, vascular, and neural markers, and retained nuclear INI-1 expression.  

The initial morphological differential diagnoses included a fibrohistiocytic lesion of bone, non-ossifying fibroma, and an exuberant reaction to an adjacent neoplasm.

A 45-year-old woman was admitted with a one-month history of seizures, altered consciousness, incoherent speech, irritability, and urinary incontinence. On examination, she was disoriented and exhibited intermittent agitation but had no focal motor deficits. Brain MRI showed multiple patchy and punctate hyperintense signals in the bilateral frontal lobes, left insular cortex, and left basal ganglia on both T1-weighted and T2-weighted sequences; corresponding areas were hyperintense on T2 FLAIR, with no contrast enhancement. Laboratory studies revealed anti-NMDAR antibody IgG titers of 1:300 in serum and 1:100 in cerebrospinal fluid. CA19-9 was 48.44 U/mL (elevated); CA125 was 21.9 U/mL (normal). A diagnosis of anti-NMDAR encephalitis was made. Given the strong association with ovarian teratoma, a bedside transvaginal ultrasound was performed, revealing a 54 × 37 mm oval mixed echogenic lesion in the left adnexa with a thin cyst wall, homogeneous punctate hyperechoic foci, and internal anechoic areas, suggesting an ovarian teratoma. No peritoneal lesions were identified.

A 70-year-old man presented with urgency, urinary incontinence, and nocturia for five days. He had a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia treated with tamsulosin and a longstanding history of anemia. Physical examination revealed no palpable abdominal mass. Laboratory evaluation showed anemia (hemoglobin 8.5 mg/dL; MCV 80 fL; MCHC 30.9 g/dL), leukocytosis (WBC 14×10^3/µL), creatinine 90 µmol/L, and platelets 156 ng/mL. Renal ultrasound demonstrated a right renal mass. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed an ill-defined, infiltrative 4 cm mass in the mid to lower pole of the right kidney involving the parenchyma, hilum, and renal pelvis. MRI confirmed these findings and showed a tumor thrombus extending through the right renal vein into the inferior vena cava.

A 62-year-old man was referred with a 2-year history of a painless mass in his right external auditory canal. He had undergone excision of a small keratoacanthoma from the same ear in 2001. The lesion was first noted on routine examination in 2005 and remained asymptomatic; he deferred treatment until retirement. On examination, a myringoscope revealed a smooth, flesh‐colored mass approximately 1 cm in diameter, located deep in the right external auditory canal near the tympanic membrane, with no bleeding. A CT scan showed a well‐circumscribed, slightly enhancing solid lesion in the inferior wall of the right external auditory canal without bony erosion. Facial electromyography, vestibular function tests, and pure‐tone audiometry were all normal. The mass was excised under microscopic guidance, preserving the canal wall and tympanic membrane, and the specimen was sent for pathologic evaluation.

A 48-year-old man presented with rapidly worsening headache and nausea. On noncontrast CT of the head, there was a left frontal variegated lesion with mass effect, surrounding edema, and midline shift. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain demonstrated a heterogeneous mass in the left frontal lobe that was hyperintense on T1-weighted images, relatively hypointense on T2-weighted images, and showed contrast enhancement with associated perilesional edema. A provisional diagnosis of meningioma was made preoperatively.

A 24-year-old woman presented with several months of constant, nonradiating right hypochondriac pain that progressed from mild to moderate intensity over 3 weeks and was temporarily relieved with analgesics. She also reported abdominal fullness and dyspepsia. She denied use of oral contraceptives or herbal medications and had no significant medical or surgical history. On examination, her liver border was palpable below the right costal margin; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed normal liver function tests (AST 27 IU/L, ALT 24 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 97 IU/L, GGT 40 IU/L), a normal serum alpha-fetoprotein level, and negative hepatitis B and C serologies.

A triphasic dynamic CT scan of the liver demonstrated a smoothly marginated, well-defined lesion in segments V, VI, and VII, with an inferior exophytic component, central coarse, chunky intralesional calcifications, no convincing washout in the venous or delayed phases, and tumor thrombus in the right posterior portal vein. Subsequent MRI revealed a 9.8 × 9.4 × 12 cm solid lesion with a cystic component in the same segments, showing heterogeneous arterial enhancement that persisted through the venous and delayed phases.

Major differential diagnoses based on these radiologic findings included cholangiocarcinoma, atypical hepatocellular carcinoma, neuroendocrine tumor, and hepatic adenoma. An ultrasound-guided biopsy of the lesion was performed for tissue diagnosis.

An 18-year-old woman presented with a 10-day history of acute onset right leg pain and swelling that progressively worsened and limited her ability to walk. On examination, there was a 2 cm × 2 cm tender, warm swelling on the anterior aspect of the mid-shaft of the right tibia; she had no constitutional symptoms. Plain radiographs of the right tibia (anteroposterior and lateral views) showed a well-defined expansile osteolytic lesion with sclerotic margins in the mid-shaft. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-circumscribed cystic lesion at the same site.

A 34-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a large, painless growth on the dorsum of his right foot that had been present for approximately 10 years without pain, tenderness, neurological symptoms, or functional deficit. He also noted two smaller lesions of similar appearance on the dorsum of his left foot. There was no history of trauma, ill-fitting footwear, or relevant occupational exposure. 

On examination, the right lesion measured 4 cm × 4 cm and was dome-shaped; the two left lesions measured 1 cm × 1 cm. All were well defined, smooth, firm and rubbery (not fluctuant), non-transilluminating, non-fixed to underlying structures, and the same color as acral skin but distinct from surrounding skin. Routine blood tests including glucose and serum lipids were normal.

A 43-year-old man presented with a 5-month history of progressive, painless swelling of the left hand. During this period, the first metacarpal appeared enlarged and deformed. One month before presentation, minor trauma to the area led to a marked increase in swelling. 

On radiography, there was lytic destruction of the left first metacarpal bone with adjacent soft-tissue swelling. Noncontrast CT confirmed an ill-defined soft-tissue mass surrounding the first metacarpal, with heterogeneous density (31–60 HU) and cortical bone destruction. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated obvious heterogeneous enhancement (up to 106 HU) and focal areas of nonenhancement suggestive of necrosis.

MRI findings included:
• T1-weighted images: slightly hyperintense signal in the lesion.  
• T2-weighted and fat-suppressed T2-weighted images: mixed hyperintense signal.  
• Both T1 and T2 sequences: multiple hypointense linear septations within the mass.  
• Post-contrast MRI: pronounced heterogeneous enhancement with patches of nonenhancement.

A 24-year-old man presented with a painless swelling in the anterior hard palate that had gradually enlarged over five years. He denied trauma or infection. On examination, there was a well-defined, firm, non-tender mass along the left anterior maxillary wall, extending into the floor of the left nasal cavity and displacing the nasal septum to the right. Intraorally, the lesion bulged on the anterior hard palate without pulsation or signs of infection. Nasal endoscopy confirmed a cystic-appearing swelling on the left nasal floor with septal deviation. A CT scan showed a 51 mm, oval, well-defined radiolucent lesion in the midline of the maxilla with bony remodeling, bulging into the hard palate and left nasal cavity. A vitality test was positive for all anterior teeth and fine-needle aspiration cytology was performed to exclude malignancy.

A 56‐year‐old previously healthy man presented with a 2‐week history of abdominal pain and jaundice. He was initially diagnosed with acute cholecystitis and underwent endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography and cholecystectomy, but his symptoms persisted. Subsequent imaging revealed common bile duct narrowing and a 20 × 3.5 cm perihepatic fluid collection, which was drained percutaneously. Laboratory studies showed:  
• WBC 51.4 × 10^9/L (4.5–11.0)  
• Hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL (13.5–17.5)  
• Sodium 129 mEq/L (135–145)  
• Potassium 3.4 mEq/L (3.5–5.0)  
• Albumin 2.1 g/dL (3.5–5.0)  
• Lipase 303 U/L (0–50)  
• AST/ALT 93/97 U/L (8–20/8–20)  

He was discharged on antibiotics but returned one week later with fever, chills, and leukocytosis. Abdominal CT showed multiple fluid collections in the liver parenchyma, the largest measuring 2.2 × 2.0 cm. A CT‐guided biopsy of the presumed abscess revealed an epithelioid to spindle‐cell neoplasm infiltrating hepatocytes, featuring marked nuclear atypia, prominent necrosis, and a pleomorphic pattern. Extensive immunohistochemical staining—including hepatocellular carcinoma markers (AFP, HepPar1, Glypican-3, pCEA, ARG1), epithelial antigens (CK7, CK20, AE1/AE3, CAM5.2, EpCAM, EMA), germ cell, melanoma, endothelial, muscle, hematolymphoid, and histiocytic markers—was uniformly negative. Based on the imaging, morphology, and immunophenotype, a primary liver sarcoma was favored.

A 9-year-old Indian boy presented with a 1.5-year history of subtle but progressive pain and swelling in his right ankle, which had intensified over the past 6 months and altered his gait. There was no preceding trauma or relevant medical history. On examination, he had an antalgic gait, restricted dorsiflexion of the right ankle, a firm non-tender swelling over the anterior ankle, and a 20° equinus deformity. Other systemic examinations were unremarkable. Routine blood tests and immune and infection markers were within normal limits. A plain radiograph showed osseous masses over the anterior talus with intra-articular loose bodies. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-defined osseous projection arising from the anterior aspect of the talar neck, described as suggestive of osteochondroma, without obvious thickened cartilage, and two well-defined osseous fragments in the tibiotalar joint consistent with loose bodies. Based on these clinical and imaging findings, a provisional diagnosis of ankle synovial chondromatosis was made, and surgical excision was planned.

A 9-year-old boy presented with persistent headache and was found to have hypertension. He had no other constitutional symptoms. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a well-circumscribed 11.0 × 10.0 × 8.0 cm heterogeneous mass arising from the upper pole of the left kidney. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a solid, disproportionately enhancing lesion with clear borders and no lymphadenopathy or tumor thrombus. T2-weighted MRI demonstrated necrosis and hemorrhage within the mass; a bone scan showed no metastases. A left radical nephrectomy was performed through an anterior subcostal approach. Grossly, the tumor was solid, elastic-soft, light yellow, with areas of degenerative necrosis, hemorrhage, and cystic change; the resected kidney weighed 630 g.  
Microscopic examination showed a high nuclear-to-cytoplasm ratio with sheets of short spindle-shaped cells intermingled with foci of cells containing scant clear cytoplasm and round nuclei. Immunohistochemical staining was negative for cytokeratin and positive for vimentin, Bcl-2, CD-56, and CD-99.

An 80-year-old woman was referred for management of a chronic superficial sacral wound present for approximately 2 years. She reported progressively worsening sacral pain and local skin irritation but denied purulent discharge, altered bowel habits, rectal bleeding, or rectal discharge. Her history was notable for inverse psoriasis affecting the natal cleft, prior coccygectomy 20 years earlier, multiple cutaneous nonmelanoma skin cancers, ischemic heart disease status post coronary artery bypass grafting, hypertension, dyslipidemia, mild asthma, and splenectomy. Medications included aspirin, rosuvastatin, valsartan, and topical corticosteroids as needed.

On examination, she was afebrile and systemically well.
