The coccygectomy scar was slightly indurated and surrounded by a broad area of excoriated skin with plaques and focal ulceration in the upper natal cleft. A small superior sinus tract without obvious pits and mild serous discharge were noted. The lesion was located more than 5 cm from the anal verge. There was no exophytic mass, no underlying abscess cavity, and no palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis with contrast demonstrated a 6 × 13 × 28 mm area of nonspecific, irregular superficial enhancement in the natal cleft without invasion of underlying structures, no visible sinus tract, and no regional nodal or bony metastases. A staging CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no metastatic disease.

A 47-year-old man presented with recurrent episodes of epigastric pain, melena, and a sensation of epigastric fullness. Two prior upper and lower endoscopies had been reported as normal. He had no notable medication, family, or psychosocial history. On examination, he appeared pale; conjunctivae, palms, and oral mucosa were pale without jaundice or cyanosis. Blood pressure was 100/60 mm Hg, pulse 95 beats/min, temperature normal, and BMI 38. The abdomen was soft, non-tender, without organomegaly or stigmata of chronic liver disease. Laboratory studies revealed a hemoglobin level of 8 g/dL with normal electrolytes, liver, and renal function tests. He received two units of packed red blood cells. Repeat upper endoscopy demonstrated a large pedunculated polyp with ulceration arising from the second part of the duodenum just distal to the ampulla of Vater. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed no additional lesions or abnormalities.

A 77-year-old woman with hypertension, type II diabetes, dyslipidemia, and stage II chronic kidney disease presented after a mechanical fall without loss of consciousness. On admission, hemoglobin was 10.8 g/dL (baseline 12.5) with normal red-cell indices, WBC count 9.8 × 10^9/L (lymphocytes 1.4 × 10^9/L; granulocytes 7.8 × 10^9/L), normal platelets, serum creatinine 2.01 mg/dL (baseline 1.03) with GFR 29 mL/min, and normal electrolytes. CT of the cervical spine revealed multiple lytic lesions in C2, C5, and T2 spinous process. MRI of the brain and cervical spine showed multiple focal lesions in the calvarium, clivus, C2, C5, and T1 spinous process, with spinal-cord compression at C3–C7. A whole-body bone scan demonstrated numerous bony abnormalities in the left femoral shaft, left acetabulum, L1–L2 vertebrae, and bilateral ribs. Physical examination and trauma workup also identified a palpable 7.5 × 3.7 × 7.8 cm irregular mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast. Mammography and ultrasound confirmed this mass at the 2:00 position, 15 cm from the nipple. Core-needle biopsy of the breast mass revealed invasive, well-differentiated ductal carcinoma with mucinous features that was positive for estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and HER2.

A 45-year-old woman presented with a 1½-year history of recurrent episodes of profuse hematemesis, each involving 1–1.5 L of fresh blood, accompanied by melena and symptoms of anemia. Her first episode occurred at 8 months’ gestation and led to intrauterine fetal demise; subsequent episodes recurred at 8 months, then at 1 and 1½ years later with decreasing intervals. She denied epigastric pain, dysphagia, odynophagia, abdominal pain, fever, jaundice, or hematochezia. She reported unintentional weight loss from 90 kg to 70 kg over one year.

Her medical history was notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed 6 years earlier and well controlled on metformin and glibenclamide. She denied liver disease, alcohol use, or NSAID use.

On examination after an episode, she was tachycardic (120 beats/min), hypotensive (100/60 mmHg), and pale. Abdominal, respiratory, cardiovascular, and neurologic examinations were otherwise unremarkable. Rectal examination confirmed melena. After resuscitation, vital signs stabilized.

Laboratory studies showed microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 4.17 g/dL; MCV 76.1 fL), normal white-cell and platelet counts, normal coagulation profile, liver and renal function tests. Viral serologies (HBsAg, HCV, HIV) and VDRL were negative. Hemoglobin A1c was 6.1%.

Upper endoscopy revealed a 5 × 6 cm broad-based mass in the fundus extending to the proximal body, with intact overlying mucosa that bled easily on contact. Multiple punch biopsies were non-diagnostic. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a well-enhancing intragastric mass causing luminal narrowing without evidence of metastases. Endoscopic ultrasound was unavailable.

A 48-year-old Asian man with a history of resected gastric carcinoma underwent routine follow-up including ^18F-FDG PET/CT one year after surgery. He reported a painless soft mass on the upper right arm present for several years. The PET scan revealed a 12×10 cm mass in the upper right arm with intense FDG uptake (SUVmax 9.6). On examination, the mass was soft, non-tender, and not warm; there were no neurological deficits. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the arm showed a well-circumscribed lesion with heterogeneous hyperintensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images and intense enhancement after gadolinium administration, including linear areas of marked signal within the mass. The leading imaging impression was a lipid-containing tumor, with concern for possible malignancy.

A 60-year-old man noted a painless lump beneath his right nipple for four months. He reported no pain, itching, or nipple discharge and had no personal or family history of cancer. At a local hospital, a core-needle biopsy showed aggressive-appearing tumor cells. Immunohistochemical stains were negative for ER, PR, HER2, E-cadherin, P120, CK5/6, and P40, and Ki-67 staining showed high proliferative activity. A diagnosis of triple-negative invasive breast carcinoma was made. Seeking additional opinions, he was referred to our institution. On admission, ultrasound of the right breast revealed a 4.4 cm × 4.4 cm × 1.4 cm hypoechoic lesion beneath the nipple with internal striped blood-flow signals and a small area of low echoes in the superficial fat layer (1.1 cm × 0.5 cm). On the basis of imaging, the lesion was assigned BI-RADS category 4C.

A 62-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of decreased visual acuity in both eyes. He had no prior systemic or ocular history. Visual acuity was 20/200 bilaterally, and intraocular pressures were 15 mm Hg OD and 17 mm Hg OS. Slit-lamp examination showed no conjunctival injection, a normal anterior chamber, mild cataract without significant refractive error, and trace anterior vitreous cells in both eyes. Fundus examination revealed pink optic discs without atrophy and markedly reduced foveal reflexes. The patient reported no auditory, integumentary, neurological, or systemic symptoms.

Optical coherence tomography demonstrated multilobulated bilateral exudative retinal detachments with a visibly thickened choroid and compressed choriocapillaris. Fluorescein angiography showed hypofluorescent areas corresponding to subretinal fluid and multiple pinpoint hyperfluorescent and hypofluorescent dots primarily around the periphery of the detached retina, sparing the central macula.

Given these findings, the initial differential diagnoses included Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome, central serous chorioretinopathy, lymphoma, and choroidal metastasis. As VKH is a diagnosis of exclusion and the visual acuity was worsening, the patient was empirically started on oral prednisolone 50 mg daily while awaiting further workup.

A 4-month-old girl was brought for evaluation of a swelling over the left angle of the mandible that had been present for several weeks. The lesion was noted to be painless, soft, and nontender, with normal overlying skin and no regional lymphadenopathy. An ultrasound examination of the left parotid region using a 4–7-MHz linear transducer demonstrated a largely homogeneous, isoechoic mass replacing the parotid gland, with lobulated margins and internal echogenic septae. Color Doppler imaging revealed multiple dilated vascular channels within the lesion. Subsequent magnetic resonance imaging of the neck showed a lesion in the left parotid gland that was hyperintense on fat-suppressed T2-weighted and STIR sequences, contained thin internal septae, and demonstrated prominent flow voids. On post-contrast T1-weighted images, the mass enhanced homogeneously, with thin nonenhancing septae. The right parotid gland and overlying skin appeared normal.

A 19-year-old unmarried woman presented with a one-year history of a painless mass in the left vulvar region that had progressively increased in size over the past year and caused difficulty in ambulation. She had no significant medical history or family history of vulvar masses. On examination, there was a single irregular, cauliflower-like pedunculated mass measuring 10 cm by 10 cm arising from the left vulva. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed a large exophytic, lobulated, heterogeneous mass originating from the left vulval area, described as “suspicious of malignancy,” along with multiple subcentimetric enhancing left external iliac and bilateral inguinal lymph nodes, “which raised the suspicion of metastasis.” A two-step surgical management plan was made: first, wide local excision for diagnosis; second, if malignant, revision surgery for lymph node dissection.

A 21-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a painless, gradually enlarging swelling in the right mandibular premolar region. He had no significant medical history. On intraoral examination, there was a firm, non-tender swelling extending from the right mandibular canine to the second premolar, with a central area of eggshell crackling. The right mandibular first premolar was clinically absent; the adjacent canine and second premolar were vital and non-mobile. A panoramic radiograph revealed a well-circumscribed, unilocular radiolucency involving the impacted right mandibular first premolar and displacing the roots of the canine toward the lateral incisor and the second premolar toward the first molar. The lesion pushed the impacted tooth toward the lower mandibular border. A working differential diagnosis included a dentigerous cyst, unicystic ameloblastoma, and an adenomatoid odontogenic tumor.

A 69-year-old Caucasian man presented to the emergency department with a year-long history of episodic lightheadedness. He described a sensation beginning in his feet, spreading upward, and then feeling lightheaded, hot, and clammy; each episode lasted a few minutes, occurred randomly without identifiable triggers, and was not associated with focal neurologic symptoms. He also reported general malaise over the past year, including fatigue, weakness, and reduced appetite without weight loss.

His medical history was significant only for hypertension, treated with ramipril. He had previously undergone evaluation for ischemic heart disease; an exercise‐tolerance test was negative for ischemic changes, and echocardiography demonstrated good global systolic and diastolic function. Outpatient monitoring with a 7‐day ECG recording showed sinus rhythm with 12 episodes of bradycardia in 24 hours (lowest rate, 23 bpm), ventricular ectopic beats, and pauses in cardiac activity of up to 2.5 seconds; these events occurred at random times, with no ischemic changes, and were not further investigated.

He was a nonsmoker, a social drinker, and lived independently. On examination, temperature was 36.9 °C, blood pressure 170/100 mm Hg, pulse 54 bpm, respiratory rate 12 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Cardiovascular, pulmonary, abdominal, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable, and there was no chest pain.

Initial investigations included normal full blood count, electrolytes, renal and liver function tests, inflammatory markers, thyroid function, and serum calcium. Lying and standing blood pressures were 170/100 and 160/100 mm Hg, respectively, with a heart rate of 54 bpm and no orthostatic changes. Urinalysis and chest radiograph were normal.

A 12‐lead ECG on admission showed sinus bradycardia at 54 bpm with occasional premature ventricular complexes and no features of an acute ischemic event.

A 60-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of left-sided epiphora and nasal obstruction that failed to improve after multiple courses of systemic antibiotics and topical therapy. He subsequently noted swelling over the left medial canthus and episodes of epistaxis. On examination, there was a firm, painless mass at the left internal canthus; no other systemic abnormalities were found.

Computed tomography dacryocystography revealed a well-defined lobulated mass in the left lacrimal fossa causing proximal nasolacrimal duct obstruction with absence of contrast beyond the lesion. After intravenous contrast, the mass enhanced intensely, extended through the nasolacrimal duct, and produced discrete bony erosion; there was no orbital or sinus involvement.

Magnetic resonance imaging showed that the mass was hyperintense on T1-weighted images, hypointense on T2-weighted images, and exhibited intense, homogeneous enhancement after contrast administration; no enlarged lymph nodes were identified.

A 65‐year‐old woman presented with a 2‐year history of pelvic pressure and anorectal pain, as well as difficulty with urination and altered bowel habits. On examination she had mild tenderness on palpation of the posterior pelvis. Laboratory studies showed a carcinoembryonic antigen level of 3.7 ng/mL (normal <5 ng/mL) and a carbohydrate antigen 19-9 level of 266 U/mL (normal <37 U/mL). Abdominal and pelvic computed tomography revealed a 17 cm cystic retrorectal mass. Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a 17.3 × 11.4 × 7.7 cm retrorectal cystic lesion with a solid mural nodule.  
What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 51-year-old man with a 3-month history of progressive dyspnea, dysphagia, and obstructive sleep symptoms presented with worsening shortness of breath when supine and a 10-kg weight loss. On examination he was dyspneic with inspiratory stridor; oxygen saturation was 96% and other vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 14.9 g/dL, white blood cells 7640/μL, serum glucose 117 mg/dL, creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, and normal liver tests. Flexible transnasal endoscopy revealed a smooth, pedunculated, rounded mass covered with mucosa arising from the posterior hypopharyngeal wall, moving freely over the laryngeal vestibule and causing subtotal obstruction of the supraglottis by a valve effect. An urgent tracheotomy was performed under local anesthesia to secure the airway. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a fusiform, well-defined 7.8 × 2.0 × 1.0 cm mass in the visceral space posterior to the right thyroid lobe, with a heterogeneous density predominantly of fat attenuation, partial contrast enhancement, slight displacement of the esophagus, extension through the pharyngeal constrictor muscles into the supraglottis, and no effacement of adjacent fat planes, vessel invasion, bone erosion, or abnormal lymphadenopathy.

A 60-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of girdle-type epigastric and left hypochondrial pain radiating to the left lumbar region, associated with anorexia and an 8-kg weight loss. She had no significant medical history, but smoked (30 pack-years). Her father had recently been treated for pancreatic adenocarcinoma. On examination she appeared fatigued and depressed; abdominal examination revealed no masses, hepatomegaly, ascites, or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed anicteric cholestasis (2× upper limit of normal) and a C-reactive protein level of 34 mg/L (normal <5 mg/L). Tumor markers were within normal limits (CEA 2.7 ng/mL; CA 19-9 32 IU/L). A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated extensive involvement of the pancreatic tail with locoregional extension to the posterior wall of the stomach and a subcentimeter lesion in liver segment VI. Endoscopic ultrasound revealed a 5.3×4 cm, well-defined, hypoechoic homogeneous lesion at the junction of the pancreatic body and tail, with small intralesional hyperechoic foci, multiple mural nodules, a fine vascular network on Doppler, and posterior echogenic enhancement. Fine-needle aspiration was performed with a ProCore 20-gauge needle; the lesion did not display the typical hardness of a primary adenocarcinoma, and samples were nonbloody.

A 50-year-old Japanese woman noted a gradually enlarging, painful mass in her left posterior thigh over 8 months. Her medical history was notable only for hepatitis C virus carrier status. On referral, magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-defined posterior thigh soft-tissue mass with high signal intensity on T2-weighted images. Differential diagnoses included undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, pleomorphic liposarcoma, dedifferentiated liposarcoma, and other high-grade sarcomas. A needle biopsy of the thigh lesion established a diagnosis of pleomorphic liposarcoma. Staging computed tomography revealed a solitary liver mass measuring 140 × 80 × 120 mm, while chest CT showed no lesions in the lungs or pleura. Liver function tests showed normal bilirubin, mildly elevated transaminases, and a low serum albumin level.

A 68-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of painless outward protrusion of the left eye, progressive vision deterioration, limited upward gaze, and partial loss of vision in that eye. She had no other medical or family history of similar disorders.  

On ophthalmologic examination, the left eye showed exophthalmos, ptosis, optic nerve atrophy, senile macular degeneration, and vitreous destruction. Visual acuity was +2.75 diopter sphere bilaterally, and movement of the left eye was restricted.  

Ocular ultrasonography revealed a tissue‐type echoic mass measuring 1.3 cm × 1.4 cm behind the left eye. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated thinning of the macular retina and reduced retinal nerve fiber layer thickness in all quadrants of the left eye, consistent with ganglion cell axon loss.  

Noncontrast CT of the orbits showed a 1.5 cm × 2.5 cm × 1.5 cm intraconal mass occupying most of the left orbit, with thinning and depression of the extraocular muscles.  

Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain and orbits revealed a smoothly contoured retrobulbar mass extending along the left optic nerve through the prechiasmal region into the optic chiasm, measuring approximately 5.2 cm × 2.0 cm × 1.9 cm. The lesion demonstrated peripheral contrast enhancement, cystic changes, restricted diffusion on DWI (ADC value 1500 × 10^−6 mm^2/s at b = 1000 s/mm^2), and high T2 signal intensity.

A 20-month-old girl with normal psychomotor development presented with one month of progressive limb weakness and difficulty turning her head. On examination, she had bilateral upper and lower limb weakness progressing over weeks. Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine showed an intramedullary, oval, well-defined solid mass extending from C7 to T2 with associated syringohydromyelia. The lesion was isointense to spinal cord parenchyma on T1-weighted images, slightly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed homogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain and entire spine revealed no additional lesions.

A 22-year-old woman presented with 5 months of increasing abdominal girth. Pelvic examination and ultrasonography revealed a 15 cm solid mass in the right ovary. She underwent exploratory laparotomy with right salpingo-oophorectomy, lymph node and omental biopsies, appendectomy, and peritoneal washings. Initial histology suggested FIGO stage IA grade 2 endometrioid adenocarcinoma. Upon referral, slide review raised the possibility of a Sertoli cell tumor. Immunohistochemical stains and additional gross sampling were performed. A thyroid scan, chest radiograph, and abdominal CT scan showed no thyroid lesion or metastases.

Fifteen months later, she developed a dry cough, and chest CT showed multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules. Her serum thyroglobulin was 247.3 ng/mL (normal ≤ 40 ng/mL). Malignant struma ovarii was suspected; she underwent total thyroidectomy (histologically unremarkable) and high-dose radioactive iodine therapy. Forty-two months after initial surgery, hemoptysis and dyspnea led to chemotherapy. Five years after surgery, pulmonary nodules enlarged and intramedullary spinal metastasis developed; she died 7 years after the original operation.

Grossly, the ovarian mass was solid, yellow-white, with necrosis and hemorrhage; the capsule was intact. Serial sections showed gelatinous tan foci and a 1 cm sebaceous area.

Microscopically, the tumor consisted of uniform cuboidal to columnar cells arranged predominantly in tubular structures; focal dilated gland-like spaces with papillary-like infoldings; solid tubules; trabecular areas; and an insular pattern comprising about 20% of the lesion. Mitotic figures ranged up to 11 per 10 high-power fields in solid regions. Coagulative tumor necrosis was observed. No true papillae with fibrovascular cores or ground-glass nuclei were seen. Scattered areas of typical thyroid tissue and a focus of mature cystic teratoma were identified. There was no capsular invasion or lymphovascular space involvement.

Immunohistochemistry showed diffuse positivity for pancytokeratin (AE1/3), cytokeratin 7, and thyroglobulin; focal epithelial membrane antigen and vimentin positivity; and negativity for calretinin, CD99, chromogranin A, and synaptophysin.

A 27-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with a painful locked right knee. He denied trauma but reported two years of mild activity-related knee pain and decreased range of motion without swelling or locking until the current episode. Examination showed marked knee swelling, tenderness along the joint line, and pain with active and passive motion; specific ligament or meniscal tests could not be performed because of pain. Laboratory studies, including erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and blood counts, were normal. Plain knee radiographs were unremarkable. MRI of the knee revealed a well-circumscribed, lobulated intraarticular mass measuring 4 × 2 × 1.5 cm, originating from the distal one third of the patellar side of the ligamentum mucosum, without evidence of meniscal, ligamentous, or cartilaginous injury. Due to the imaging findings, a giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath or fibroma was considered.

A 10-year-old girl presented with a 3-year history of recurrent swelling, pain, and deformity of her right knee. She had undergone excision of a similar swelling at another center and remained asymptomatic for one year before the swelling recurred. On examination, there was a soft, 3×4-cm lump in the suprapatellar region and a fixed flexion deformity of 10°.

Plain radiographs of the knee showed a poorly defined soft-tissue density over the infrapatellar fat pad without joint changes. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a lobulated hyperintense lesion involving Hoffa’s fat pad, extending from the anterior margin of the patella to the anterior cruciate ligament and menisci, with mild cortical irregularity and subchondral marrow edema in the patellofemoral joint. These MRI features were suggestive of a hemangioma or a venous malformation.

A focused ultrasound examination demonstrated anechoic spaces in Hoffa’s fat pad that exhibited vascularity on augmentation. Other differentials considered included pigmented villonodular synovitis.

What is your differential diagnosis?

A 62-year-old Asian man presented with a 13-year history of an enlarging, painful mass in his right shoulder. He reported no systemic symptoms, and examination revealed no palpable lymphadenopathy. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a poorly defined soft-tissue mass within the posterior neck muscles of the right shoulder. The lesion measured approximately 8 cm by 6 cm and was homogeneous on imaging. An extended local excision was performed.

Grossly, the intramuscular mass was poorly circumscribed and homogeneous. Histologic examination showed a diffuse proliferation of large, isolated cells with rhabdoid features—mild nuclear atypia and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm—interspersed with clusters of small lymphoid cells. Initial immunohistochemical stains revealed that the large cells were negative for desmin, muscle actin (HHF35), α-smooth muscle actin, and myoglobin, but showed strong positivity on periodic acid–Schiff stain with diastase digestion.

An 80-year-old man was admitted with severe, progressive dyspnoea without chest pain. On examination, blood pressure was 75/54 mmHg, heart rate 57 beats/minute, and oxygen saturation 95% on 15 L/min via non-rebreathing mask. Heart sounds were muffled and extremities were cold, pale, with early marbling; jugular veins were not distended. His history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and recurrent paroxysmal atrial fibrillation after failed pulmonary vein isolation, treated with a factor Xa inhibitor, a beta-blocker, an angiotensin receptor blocker, and a beta2-agonist. The electrocardiogram showed sinus bradycardia with ST-segment elevation in leads V2–V3 and T-wave inversions in leads II, III, and aVF. Troponin T was elevated at 0.044 µg/L, and lactate was 3.0 mmol/L. Initial transthoracic echocardiography performed by the emergency physician revealed a pericardial mass, raising suspicion of a covered perforation or left ventricular free-wall rupture due to myocardial infarction or aneurysm. A subsequent cardiologist-performed echocardiogram confirmed cardiac tamponade with a 4.6 cm solid mass compressing both ventricles and causing biventricular dysfunction. Contrast-enhanced aortic computed tomography excluded aortic dissection and left ventricular free-wall rupture but suggested a haemopericardium. Pericardiocentesis was deemed unfeasible and a sternotomy was performed, yielding 400 mL of haemorrhagic pericardial fluid; active bleeding and the origin of the fluid were not identified, and a vascular mass was noted intraoperatively. One week later, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed that the apical pericardial mass did not enhance on perfusion or late gadolinium images, findings interpreted as consistent with a haematoma rather than a neoplasm. A multidisciplinary team judged complete excision unsafe, and with the patient’s clinical decline, no further diagnostic or therapeutic interventions were pursued.

A 74-year-old woman presented with a dark-brown papule on the anterior middle third of her left leg that had appeared one year earlier and had slowly increased in size. She reported no pain, pruritus, trauma, or other preceding injury. She had severe venous insufficiency with a superficial hypertrophic and congested venous capillary network but no other relevant medical history.

On examination, the lesion was an oval, ulcerated papule measuring 30 mm in diameter. It was fixed to surrounding soft tissues, with ill-defined margins, and no palpable lymphadenopathy in the draining fields. The lesion was excised under local anesthesia; the specimen measured 30 × 20 × 12 mm.

Histologic examination of hematoxylin–eosin–stained sections showed a dermal lesion composed of a variable admixture of fibroblast-like cells and histiocytes, with more than 85% of cells exhibiting large eosinophilic cytoplasm filled with granules or microvacuoles. The stroma was loose and vascular, with a predominantly lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate and globular collagen bundles at the periphery. The lesion had defined margins with a pseudocapsule. The overlying epidermis was atrophic, with basal hyperpigmentation and melanin deposition. No mitotic figures were identified.

Immunohistochemical studies revealed diffuse CD68 positivity in the lesional cells. The lesional cells were negative for S-100 protein, CD34, Melan-A, and CD10. Ki-67 proliferation index was less than 1%.

A 14-year-old girl presented with a 2-month history of localized swelling and pain over the proximal lateral aspect of her left fibula. The pain was insidious in onset, most severe at night, and was not related to physical activity. There were no systemic symptoms such as fever or weight loss. On examination, there was focal tenderness and mild soft-tissue swelling over the proximal fibular shaft; distal neurovascular findings were normal. Plain radiographs of the left leg demonstrated a small, well-circumscribed lucent focus in the proximal lateral fibula, surrounded by a zone of reactive sclerosis. A trial of acetylsalicylic acid led to immediate pain relief; however, her symptoms recurred within days of stopping the medication.

A 45-year-old woman (BMI 33.6) presented with 6 months of upper abdominal pain, anorexia, malaise, mild jaundice, and pruritus. Examination showed scleral icterus but was otherwise unremarkable. Liver function tests were normal; CA 19-9 was 37 U/ml. Contrast CT of the abdomen revealed a 4.2×3.6 cm multiloculated cystic lesion in segments I, V, and VIII of the liver, communicating with the right hepatic duct; there was biliary dilation with thickening of the common hepatic duct and extrinsic compression at the biliary confluence. An additional hemangioma-like lesion was noted in segments V/VIII. MRI confirmed a hypodense cystic lesion with internal septations. Preoperative right portal vein embolization increased the future liver remnant from 26.8% to 45.4% over 4 weeks. Intraoperative cholangiography via the cystic duct confirmed communication between the cyst and the bile ducts, along with extrinsic biliary compression; ultrasound showed no macrovascular invasion.

A 63-year-old multiparous woman, postmenopausal for 15 years, presented with 2 months of progressive abdominal bloating, increased abdominal girth, and difficulty with urination. She denied fever, chills, weight loss, night sweats, nausea, vomiting, or bowel or bladder symptoms. Her medical and surgical history was unremarkable. On vaginal examination, a mass the size of a 10-month pregnancy was palpated, fixed to the posterior cervix; the remainder of the examination was normal. An abdominal and pelvic ultrasound revealed a 15.9 cm × 12.0 cm × 8.6 cm mass without definite evidence of local infiltration or lymphadenopathy, which was highly suspected as a subserosal uterine leiomyoma.

A 12-year-old previously healthy boy presented with a slowly growing lump on the lateral side of the left arm, 14 cm proximal to the elbow joint. The lesion was painless, subcutaneous, mobile, and soft, measuring 2 × 2 cm, with no overlying skin discoloration or attachment to deeper structures. Clinically, it resembled a benign lump, possibly a lipoma. However, because of certain atypical characteristics, excision of the lump was planned under local anesthesia, with histopathological analysis to provide further insights.

A 46-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of a pelvic mass, increased menstrual volume, and prolonged menstrual periods. She had undergone laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy and myomectomy 10 years earlier. Six months after surgery, ultrasound showed a 13×12 mm hypoechoic uterine lesion, for which she declined treatment. On re-evaluation in February 2023, ultrasound revealed multiple uterine fibroids, bilateral ovarian cysts, and a 26×33×15 mm mass in the anterior cervix. An 83×88×63 mm anechoic structure was noted adjacent to the uterus. She underwent total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. Intraoperatively, bilateral ovarian cystic tumors and a firm 2.5 cm nodule on the sigmoid mesentery were found; the family requested frozen sections without further intervention.

Frozen-section microscopy of ovarian and mesenteric tissues showed:
• Cyst walls partially lined by small blue round cells with mild dysplasia, infiltrating adjacent stroma.  
• Variable thickness of cell proliferation, with focal nodularity.  
• Cells were small, spindle-shaped with round or oval nuclei, scant cytoplasm, indistinct nucleoli, and rare mitoses.  
• Stroma contained numerous thin-walled, spiral blood vessels.  
• Mesenteric lesion cells were histologically identical and contained intravascular tumor thrombi.

A 48-year-old Chinese woman presented with a several-week history of abdominal distension, generalized weakness, and fatigue. She had undergone a right oophorocystectomy 11 years earlier for an ovarian cyst. She denied weight loss, fever, or changes in bowel habits. On examination, the only notable finding was splenomegaly. 

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and liver-function tests, were within normal limits. Serologic tests for hepatitis A, B, and C were negative.

Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated an enlarged spleen with multiple well-defined hyperechoic lesions throughout the parenchyma. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed marked splenomegaly and multiple round, hyperdense splenic lesions that showed early hypoattenuation on arterial and early portal phases, followed by heterogeneous to homogeneous enhancement on late portal and delayed images; some lesions demonstrated complete contrast washout to isoattenuation on delayed scans. 

On the basis of the imaging findings, a splenic hemangioma was favored, and the patient was scheduled for splenectomy.

A 45-year-old man presented with a 10-year history of a midline anterior neck swelling that had recently increased in size over 2 months and was associated with a change in his voice. He was a chronic smoker for 15 years and denied weight loss. On examination, the swelling was firm, measured 7 cm × 3 cm, moved with deglutition, and was otherwise non-tender. Thyroid–stimulating hormone and thyroid hormone levels were within normal limits. Ultrasonography was not performed. Fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid swelling was performed under palpation guidance. Air-dried smears were stained with May-Grünwald–Giemsa; alcohol-fixed smears were stained with hematoxylin and eosin and Papanicolaou. A cell‐block preparation was also made. The smears revealed sheets, clusters, and scattered malignant squamous cells with moderate anaplasia, hyperchromatic nuclei, and scant dense cytoplasm; orangeophilic cytoplasm was noted on Pap stain. Admixed benign follicular epithelial cells, macrophages, and bare nuclei were present. The cell‐block showed keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma. A cytologic diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma, likely metastatic, was rendered.

An 82-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of gross hematuria. His vital signs were within normal limits. Cystoscopy revealed an ulcerated lesion in the bladder trigone. A bladder washing and cell-block preparation were performed.

The specimen was hypercellular and contained two distinct populations of malignant cells. The predominant population comprised small cells seen singly and in clusters, with scant cytoplasm, moderate pleomorphism, nuclear molding, finely granular hyperchromatic chromatin, irregular nuclear contours, occasional rosette formations, and a background of blood and necrosis. A minor population consisted of larger atypical cells with a moderate amount of cytoplasm, small nucleoli, and irregular nuclear contours.

Immunohistochemical staining on the cell block showed that only the small-cell population was positive for synaptophysin.

A 67-year-old woman presented with an asymptomatic right-sided neck swelling for 2 months, gradually progressive, followed by 1 month of subacute pelvic pain, abdominal distension, and weight loss. She had no history of surgery, central venous catheter placement, chemotherapy, diabetes, hypertension, or ischemic disease.

On examination, vital signs were normal. A 2×2 cm superficial, movable, nontender, nonpulsatile mass was palpable on the right side of the neck. Abdominal examination revealed two lower abdominal masses measuring approximately 5×6 cm and 7×7 cm, with associated ascites. Gynecologic examination confirmed bilateral adnexal masses.

Laboratory studies showed normal blood chemistry (including AFP, beta-HCG, LDH), lipid profile, and antinuclear antibody. A coagulation profile (including homocysteine, PT, aPTT, fibrinogen, fibrinogen degradation products, D-dimer, protein C, protein S, and antithrombin III) was within normal limits. Genetic testing for Factor V Leiden G1691A, prothrombin G20210A, and MTHFR C677T mutations was negative. Testing for antiphospholipid antibodies (anticardiolipin, anti–β2-glycoprotein I) and lupus anticoagulant was negative.

Venous Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated an expansile thrombus in the right internal jugular vein without atherosclerotic plaque or calcification. Computed tomography of the thorax confirmed right internal jugular vein thrombosis with no evidence of lung metastasis, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, or compressive lesions. Abdominal CT showed large bilateral adnexal masses that were predominantly cystic with internal septations and enhancing solid components (98×88×107 mm on the right and 110×52×94 mm on the left).

A 67-year-old man was hospitalized with recurrent left lumbar pain, increased fatigability, and intermittent macroscopic hematuria. On examination, a large mass was palpable in the left flank. Laboratory tests showed anemia and hypercalcemia. Renal ultrasonography revealed a giant, heterogeneous left retroperitoneal mass with poor vascularity and multiple hyperechoic areas. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 30-cm left renal tumor with no excretory function in that kidney, absence of retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, no renal-vein thrombus, and no evidence of metastasis. Chest radiography showed no lung lesions. A CT-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the renal mass was performed to guide management.
Pathological examination of the biopsy specimen showed well differentiated, benign-appearing cartilaginous tissue, raising the suspicion of a chondrosarcoma, osteosarcoma or another cartilage producing tumor.

A 57-year-old white man presented with a 3-month history of new-onset, severe bifrontal headaches and a 30-lb weight loss. Initial head CT was normal. Laboratory studies showed an ESR of 80 mm/h and a CRP of 55.3 mg/L. Over the next weeks, he developed bilateral jaw pain and left facial numbness and was started on prednisone 60 mg/day for presumed giant cell arteritis, with partial headache improvement. Bilateral temporal artery biopsies performed 3 days later were negative, and prednisone was discontinued.

Two weeks later, headaches worsened and he developed right‐eye horizontal diplopia and perioral numbness. Brain MRI was interpreted as normal. He received pulse‐dose steroids (1000 mg daily for 3 days), which resolved visual symptoms, and was discharged on prednisone 60 mg/day. Attempts to taper below 50 mg/day resulted in rising inflammatory markers, return of diplopia, and progression of headache. He also developed severe left hip pain; plain radiographs were negative.

On referral after 6 weeks of high-dose glucocorticoids, he continued to have headaches and left jaw numbness. He reported no tobacco or alcohol use. His medications included warfarin and diltiazem. Family history was negative for autoimmune disease. Laboratory evaluation showed: ESR 72 mm/h; CRP 53 mg/L; hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL; platelets 110×10^9/L; INR 2.3; calcium 11.6 mg/dL; AST 64 U/L; ALT 106 U/L; alkaline phosphatase 360 U/L. Autoimmune serologies were negative.

Vital signs: BP 94/44 mm Hg; HR 95 bpm; RR 12 breaths/min; O2 saturation 96%; BMI 48.6 kg/m^2. Examination revealed Cushingoid features and morbid obesity. Temporal arteries were non-tender without nodularity. Neurologic exam showed 20/20 visual acuity, mild right esotropia, and decreased sensation in the left V3 distribution. Hip exam showed marked pain with range of motion.

Given the persistent headache despite high-dose glucocorticoids and atypical features, alternative etiologies were suspected.

A 60-year-old woman presented with two months of left abdominal pain radiating to the midline, moderate in intensity, without aggravating or alleviating factors. She also reported intermittent postmenopausal vaginal bleeding, dysuria, and generalized weakness, but denied fever, night sweats, or headache. Her surgical history included right radical nephrectomy for renal cell carcinoma 6 years ago, a cesarean delivery, and tubal ligation. Six months earlier she had been diagnosed with a plasma cell neoplasm, and one month earlier her nephrologist noted anemia. 

An outpatient ultrasound had shown an enlarged left kidney with a multifocal mass thought to be neoplastic. A follow-up CT scan demonstrated near‐complete replacement of the left kidney by an enhancing mass with internal neovascularity. The patient did not complete a scheduled renal biopsy and presented three weeks later to the emergency department. 

On admission, hemoglobin was 6.9 g/dL with a mean corpuscular volume of 79.2 fL. Fecal occult blood was negative; urinalysis showed 6+ red blood cells. CT imaging confirmed a multifocal left renal malignancy and lesions in the left hepatic lobe; there was also a hypervascular mass in the vagina. 

On pelvic examination there was active, life‐threatening vaginal hemorrhage. Under anesthesia, a 3.5 × 1 cm necrotic mass on the left vaginal sidewall was identified, bleeding briskly and not amenable to suture ligation or electrocautery. The mass was biopsied and the vagina was packed. While still intubated, the patient underwent transcatheter embolization of pelvic arteries to control the bleeding. Two biopsy specimens were submitted for pathologic evaluation.

A 60-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of foul-smelling nasal discharge, headache, and progressive nasal obstruction that worsened in the supine position, accompanied by snoring and mouth breathing. He recently noted a swelling of the left lower eyelid causing difficulty in opening that eye. He denied trauma, diabetes, hypertension, or immunocompromise. On examination, he appeared chronically ill but was well-nourished; vital signs were within normal limits. HEENT examination revealed a 5 × 4 cm non-tender diffuse swelling over the left lower eyelid. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, and total protein, were all within normal limits. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the head and paranasal sinuses showed a 7 × 6.6 × 5 cm midline mass with mild heterogeneous enhancement extending into the left nasal cavity, the upper oropharynx pushing the soft palate, and the maxillary sinus. On the basis of this CT impression, a provisional diagnosis of advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma was made.

A 51-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of gradually progressive pain and swelling below his left knee, accompanied by intermittent fevers. Three months before presentation, the swelling ulcerated. He remained ambulatory without assistance.  
On examination, there was a firm mass measuring 30 × 18 × 12 cm over the distal tibia extending into the calf, with an anterior discharging ulcer 12 cm in diameter and areas of necrosis. The discharge was yellow and thick. Knee range of motion was reduced, and there was tenderness over the left knee and proximal tibia. Distal pulses (dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial, popliteal) were intact and lower-limb neurologic examination was normal. Other systemic examination findings were unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. Chest radiograph showed no abnormalities. Plain radiographs of the left leg demonstrated a large metadiaphyseal lesion of the tibia with soft-tissue opacity, bone erosion and destruction of the tibia and adjacent fibula, and linear and ring-like calcifications, with extension into the proximal leg soft tissues. A Tc-99m bone scan revealed increased tracer uptake in the shaft of the left tibia and proximal soft tissue, without evidence of distant skeletal metastases. MRI was not obtained due to financial constraints.  
Based on the clinical presentation and radiographic appearance, the leading considerations were osteosarcoma and chondrosarcoma of the tibia. On admission, the patient received intravenous antibiotics and analgesics and was counseled regarding treatment options. Taking into account lesion size, secondary infection, prosthesis cost, and prognosis, the patient elected transfemoral amputation with plans for postoperative chemotherapy.

A 31-year-old Asian woman presented with a pelvic mass and a six-month history of infertility. She had undergone laparoscopy and a subsequent laparotomy elsewhere for a presumed right ovarian cyst. Intraoperatively, a 9 × 7 cm hemorrhagic, dark red–brown, soft-to-firm mass arising from the pelvic colonic mesentery was excised; the uterus, tubes, ovaries, and bowel lumen appeared normal, and there was no peritoneal endometriosis or tuberculosis.

On referral, her performance status was ECOG 1. Examination revealed no lymphadenopathy, abdominal masses, or ascites; pelvic and rectal examinations were normal. Over the six months before the initial surgery, she had noted new-onset facial hair, a deepening voice, and shortening of menses to one-day spotting every 35–40 days; immediately after removal of the mass, her hirsutism resolved, her voice normalized, and menstrual cycles returned to a regular 3/28-day schedule.

Laboratory studies showed normal hemogram, chest radiograph, serum hCG 0.29 mIU/mL, alpha-fetoprotein 3 ng/mL, and lactate dehydrogenase 458 IU/L. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated normal liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, and kidneys; both adrenal glands and ovaries were normal without mass lesions; there was no para-aortic lymphadenopathy or ascites.

A 26-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a swelling on the left lower attached gingiva adjacent to the first and second mandibular molars. She first noticed the lesion two years earlier, with gradual, continuous enlargement; there was no pain, bleeding, trauma, or fever. Medical history was unremarkable. On examination, the lesion was a dome-shaped, smooth-surfaced exophytic mass measuring 1.5 × 1 × 0.7 cm with pale pink-red and focal yellow coloration. It was soft to palpation, non-fluctuant, and non-mobile. Intraoral examination revealed no other lesions and no lymphadenopathy. Aspiration was negative. Adjacent teeth were vital and showed no periodontal problems. Periapical radiography was unremarkable. At this point, what is the most likely diagnosis?

A 60-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of sore throat, progressive dysphonia, dysphagia to solids, choking and aspiration episodes. She also noted left-sided otalgia and weight loss but denied dyspnoea. There was no personal or family history of cancer.  
   
On flexible nasoendoscopy, a left pyriform fossa mass was seen invading and compressing the left hemilarynx; the larynx was fixed, the airway significantly narrowed but no stridor was present. The neck laryngeal framework appeared broadened with loss of the laryngeal click.  
   
MRI of the neck demonstrated a large necrotic mass centred on the left pyriform fossa extending superiorly along the posterolateral pharyngeal wall, invading the left glottis and strap muscles, crossing the midline into the retrovisceral space and abutting the right carotid sheath. Enlarged, rounded, heterogeneously enhancing cervical lymph nodes were present bilaterally in level II, left level III and IV.  
   
FDG PET–CT confirmed high metabolic activity in the hypopharyngeal mass and a right level II lymph node, and detected focal uptake with sclerotic changes in the left femoral neck, suggesting bony metastasis.  
   
Neck ultrasound revealed a large ill-defined hypoechoic mass involving the upper pole of the left thyroid lobe with internal coarse calcification contiguous with the hypopharynx. Multiple morphologically abnormal lymph nodes were seen in left levels II–IV and right level II, appearing rounded, hypoechoic, lacking hilum and containing coarse calcification.  
   
Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration of the left neck mass and right level II lymph node showed a poorly differentiated malignant tumour on rapid onsite evaluation.

A 61-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer presented with a 1-year history of progressive facial swelling and the development of a typical Cushingoid appearance. On examination, she was mildly hypertensive and centrally obese. Laboratory studies showed a 9:00 am plasma cortisol of 1652 nmol/L (reference, 180–800 nmol/L) and a plasma ACTH of 454 ng/L (reference, < 50 ng/L). Plasma cortisol failed to suppress after both a 1 mg overnight and an 8 mg high-dose dexamethasone suppression test. She declined inferior petrosal sinus sampling.  

Chest radiography revealed a small peripheral nodule in the right lower lobe that had remained unchanged over six years. MRI of the pituitary gland was normal. CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed only mild bilateral adrenal hyperplasia and no other masses. Whole-body 111In-octreotide scintigraphy and FDG-PET failed to identify any abnormal uptake. A gut peptide panel was within normal limits.

A 17-year-old Asian high-school senior presented with an intermittent protruding mass in her left upper quadrant for several months. The mass varied in size—becoming palm-sized at its largest, especially after consuming dairy products—and persisted for hours to days. She also reported intermittent epigastric pain and episodes of vomiting but had no history of pancreatitis, weight loss, or systemic symptoms. Laboratory studies, including hematology, biochemistry, coagulation profiles, and tumor markers (CA 19-9, CEA, hCG, and AFP), were all within normal ranges. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 6.99 × 6.52 cm hypoechoic cystic lesion posterior to the stomach and pancreas. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a 6.3 × 7.1 × 7.1 cm unilocular cystic lesion in the tail of the pancreas without splenic vessel involvement or peripancreatic lymphadenopathy. Because of the size of the lesion and her symptoms, laparoscopic resection of the cystic pancreatic tumor was planned.

A 2-day-old girl was referred for a swelling in her mouth noted since birth. The mother reported that the lesion prevented complete closure of the mouth and interfered with breast-feeding; it did not change in size. Pregnancy and vaginal delivery at 37 weeks were uncomplicated, and prenatal ultrasound was normal.

On examination, the infant had a 1.5 × 1.5 cm, smooth, pinkish-red, pedunculated mass on the left side of the maxillary gingival ridge. The lesion was soft, freely mobile, non-compressible, non-pulsatile, and partially blocked the oral cavity. There was mild surface erythema at the attachment site, but no ulceration, bleeding, or other mucosal abnormalities.

Point-of-care ultrasonography with a high-frequency linear probe revealed a well-defined, hypoechoic, oval lesion measuring approximately 1.17 × 1.33 cm arising from the left upper gingiva. It extended from 2 cm below the nasal aperture to 1.5 cm above the submental region. There was no internal vascularity, no signs of infection or abscess, and no enlarged regional lymph nodes. Based on these findings, the radiologist suggested a diagnosis of “epulis.”

The team planned an excisional biopsy under local anesthesia.

A 14-year-old girl presented with a three-year history of right-sided nasal obstruction and severe headache, most pronounced over the right forehead. Over the past three months, the headaches intensified to the point that she could not attend school. She also reported anosmia and occasional epistaxis from the right nostril. Physical examination revealed right middle-turbinate fullness without overt purulence or signs of acute infection. Neurologic examination was otherwise normal.

An MRI of the brain revealed a mass arising from the right middle turbinate. To characterize the bony anatomy, a multislice CT scan of the paranasal sinuses was obtained. It showed a clearly delineated, heterogeneous tumor with an inhomogeneous central portion and marginal mineralization. The lesion involved the right middle turbinate, the complete anterior and partial posterior ethmoidal cells, and the frontal sinus ostium. The cribriform plate was largely eroded by the mass, while the skull base appeared intact. The lamina papyracea was free of involvement and clearly demarcated from the tumor. The nasal septum was deviated to the left without perforation.

A 28-year-old man presented with severe radiating pain and swelling in the right leg for more than one year. The pain was continuous, worse at night, and disrupted sleep. He had progressively worsening gait difficulty and numbness over the right foot and leg. The pain radiated from the lower back to the posterior thigh. He denied fever or trauma. 

On examination, the right lower limb was oedematous with palpable distal pulses. Muscle strength was 3/5 in dorsiflexion, inversion, and eversion, with reduced ankle reflexes. Sensory loss was noted along the S2 dermatome; anal tone was normal. The left lower limb was normal.

Basic laboratory tests and lumbosacral spine radiographs were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the lumbosacral spine revealed a 7.2 × 10 × 8.7 cm mass, possibly arising from the right proximal sciatic nerve, infiltrating adjacent muscles, extending laterally through the greater sciatic notch and superiorly through the S1 and S2 neural foramina. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed a mass exiting the S1–S2 intervertebral foramen, extending laterally into the pelvis and buttocks, with no evidence of metastasis.

Diagnostic possibilities such as lymphomas, nerve sheath tumour, and neurosarcoma were suggested.

A 31-year-old woman from West Africa was referred after routine blood tests showed marked inflammation (C-reactive protein, 352 mg/l) and anemia (hemoglobin, 7.2 g/dl). Over the preceding 2 weeks, she had experienced malaise, fatigue and night sweats, as well as palpitations and persistent headaches. In the emergency department, she was tachycardic, and examination revealed a painful, palpable infraumbilical mass.  
Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 5 cm prevertebral, smoothly rounded soft-tissue mass with smooth edges and internal vascularization on color Doppler. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen in arterial and portal venous phases showed a heterogeneously enhancing nodular mass caudal to the aortic bifurcation, without evidence of invasive growth or distant metastases.  
Positron emission tomography–CT one hour after injection of 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose revealed inhomogeneous intense uptake within the lesion, with a maximum standardized uptake value of 12.2, and no FDG-avid locoregional lymph nodes or distant lesions.

A 72-year-old man was referred for evaluation of xerostomia and bilateral upper eyelid and salivary gland swelling that had persisted for eight months. He had no significant past medical history or medication use. On examination, both the lacrimal and salivary glands were swollen. Laboratory tests revealed: white blood cell count 7.8×10^3/μL, hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 139 U/mL, total protein 8.8 g/dL, soluble interleukin-2 receptor 5295 U/mL, C-reactive protein 1.30 mg/dL, total IgG 3880 mg/dL, and IgG4 3580 mg/mL, with the IgG4 subclass accounting for 92% of total IgG. Labial salivary gland biopsy showed lymphocytic infiltration, but anti–SS-A and anti–SS-B antibodies were negative, and a definitive diagnosis of Sjögren’s syndrome could not be made. Lip biopsy and excisional biopsy of the left submandibular gland confirmed MALT lymphoma. To assess disease extent, ^18F-FDG PET/CT was performed, showing abnormal uptake in the bilateral lacrimal and salivary glands, duodenum, pancreas, retroperitoneum, and multiple lymph nodes (mediastinal, bilateral bronchopulmonary, abdominal para-aortic, and mesenteric), with SUVmax values ranging from 2.5 to 6.8. Elevated serum IgG4 raised the possibility that these lesions could represent either MALT lymphoma or IgG4-related disease.

A 47-year-old African-American man with a history of T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia presented with a 2½-week history of a widespread rash. Nine months earlier he had been diagnosed after a 2-month history of fatigue, abdominal discomfort, a leukocyte count exceeding 150,000 per cubic millimeter, and generalized lymphadenopathy; bone marrow biopsy then showed 85% involvement, and cytogenetic studies revealed trisomy 8 and a TCRAD gene rearrangement at 14q11. He has been treated with alemtuzumab and pentostatin, with no other notable medical history. On examination, there were multiple skin-colored to violaceous or red-brown papules and nodules distributed over the trunk, extremities, and groin, each with central vesicles or small crusted erosions.

An 80-year-old man (Fitzpatrick skin type III) presented with a 7-month history of progressive brown pigmentation affecting the nail plate of the right middle finger. He denied pain or trauma. Examination of the nail unit revealed onycholysis, mild distal hyperkeratosis, and a 3-mm longitudinal brown band. Dermatoscopic evaluation of the nail plate (onychoscopy) demonstrated onycholysis and distal hyperkeratosis, with irregular parallel brown longitudinal lines of varying thickness and color, interrupted by parallel breaks, without bleeding.

A 29-year-old woman, 4 months postpartum, presented with a 4-month history of right groin pain that occasionally radiated to the hip and anterior thigh. The pain was intermittent but progressive, worsened by standing and lifting her infant, and was refractory to a trial of physical therapy and ibuprofen. She denied any history of trauma, fever, chills, night sweats, weight loss, or nocturnal pain.

Plain radiographs of the right hip and femur were unremarkable. An MRI of the right hip revealed a large marrow-replacing lesion extending from the intertrochanteric region into the proximal femoral diaphysis, with surrounding edema of bone and adjacent soft tissues. A CT scan of the right hip confirmed a focal lesion in the same region with cortical irregularity.

A 54-year-old man with a 2-year history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia under active surveillance presented with 3 weeks of progressive fatigue, exertional dyspnea, and enlarging cervical and inguinal lymph nodes. He had hypertension, chronic headaches, fatigue, and a recently excised dermal squamous cell carcinoma. On examination, he appeared unwell, was obese (BMI 34.9), and had diffuse lymphadenopathy and marked splenomegaly. Laboratory studies showed normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 72 g/L), thrombocytopenia (platelets 74 × 10^9/L), and leukocytosis (white blood cell count 135 × 10^9/L) with an absolute lymphocyte count of 130 × 10^9/L. Peripheral-blood smear demonstrated numerous smudge cells. Computed tomography of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed multiple enlarged lymph nodes (2.2–3.2 cm) and splenomegaly (16.4 cm).

A 45-year-old multiparous woman presented with a painful umbilical mass that worsened during menstruation. She had no history of abdominal surgery. Three years earlier, she developed progressive dysmenorrhea that was diagnosed clinically as endometriosis and treated sequentially with dienogest for 14 months and oral contraceptives for 18 months. She then noted gradual enlargement and increased tenderness of an indurated subcutaneous nodule at her umbilicus.  
 
Ultrasonography and magnetic resonance imaging revealed a solitary 1.0 × 1.5 cm nodule in the caudal umbilicus. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy showed adenomatous cells with a high nucleus–to–cytoplasm ratio, atypical cells, and hemosiderin-laden macrophages; adenocarcinoma was suspected. A PET-CT scan demonstrated slight fluorodeoxyglucose uptake, but metastatic carcinoma was ruled out by the pathologist.  

On examination, the lesion was a rigid, discolored, nonbleeding mass that could not be reduced by digital pressure. Transvaginal ultrasonography revealed a 4 cm uterine fundal myoma; abdominal MRI showed no pelvic endometriotic lesions. Serum CA 125 and squamous cell carcinoma antigen levels were within normal limits, and there was no sign of infection or bleeding at the umbilicus.  

Based on these findings, the differential diagnosis included urachal cancer, urachal remnant, umbilical endometriosis, and malignant transformation of umbilical endometriosis.

A man in his fifties with type II diabetes, dyslipidemia, and chronic hepatitis C presented two months earlier with odynophagia and neck swelling. Examination revealed a left para-tonsillar mass; CT and MRI confirmed a large pharyngeal mass and cervical lymphadenopathy. Excisional biopsy showed medium-to-large lymphoid cells positive for CD20, CD79a, PAX-5, CD10, BCL-2, and BCL-6, consistent with germinal-center–type DLBCL. Baseline labs were notable for platelet count 102×10^3/µL and LDH 274 U/L; bone marrow staging was inconclusive. He completed six cycles of R-CHOP plus intrathecal methotrexate, achieving a complete metabolic response on PET/CT. 

Two months after completing therapy, he developed subacute bilateral upper-limb weakness that progressed to dense right-sided arm paralysis, complete left facial weakness, blurred vision, altered consciousness, and intermittent tonic-clonic seizures. He had no headache or meningeal signs. Brain CT and MRI were unremarkable. CBC showed platelets 94×10^3/µL and WBC 3.6×10^3/µL; LDH was 257 U/L. Whole-body PET/CT showed only mild subfrontal uptake. Lumbar puncture revealed WBC 651/μL with lymphocytic predominance and CSF cytology demonstrated numerous malignant lymphoid cells. Bone marrow biopsy showed 40% infiltration by medium-to-large atypical lymphoid cells with dispersed chromatin, irregular nuclear contours, occasional cytoplasmic vacuoles, and hypocellularity with interstitial infiltration.

A 61‐year‐old man with hypertension and ischemic heart disease (status post-CABG 7 years earlier) noted a keloid at the surgical scar site, treated over the past 2 years with monthly intralesional triamcinolone for 3 months. Six months after his last injection, he developed an enlarging pruritic erythematous, indurated, scaly plaque with sharp borders on the center of his chest extending to the left side; discrete crusts were present on the upper lesion. He denied fever, weight loss, or anorexia. His medications included losartan and atorvastatin. On examination, there was no cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy and no organomegaly. Routine laboratory tests, chest radiograph, and CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis were normal. Digital dermoscopic examination showed follicular keratinization and plugging, reticulated and linear blood vessels, yellow dots and scales, multiple discrete ulcers, and an elongated white fibrous band. Based on a review by Piccolo and colleagues, these dermoscopic signs favored a lymphoproliferative disorder, especially mycosis fungoides. Skin biopsy was performed, and the differential diagnosis included cutaneous T‐cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides, pagetoid reticulosis), seborrheic dermatosis, Bowen’s disease, keloid, and psoriasis.

A 15-year-old boy presented with a 3-month history of right elbow pain and swelling without antecedent trauma or systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a firm, nonerythematous swelling over the distal humerus without neurovascular deficit.

Laboratory studies showed a normal serum alkaline phosphatase level. 

Plain radiographs of the right distal humerus demonstrated a lytic, expansile epiphyseometaphyseal lesion with blown-out appearance, thinned cortices, and a wide zone of transition.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the lesion revealed:
– On coronal T1-weighted images, an expansile lesion involving the metaphysis and epiphysis of the distal humerus that was isointense to hyperintense, with areas of thinned or indistinct cortex.  
– On coronal STIR images, a multi-cystic lesion with fluid-fluid levels and associated joint effusion.  
– On axial T1 post-gadolinium images, intense heterogeneous enhancement of the lesion with cortical breach and extension into adjacent soft tissue.

A 38-year-old woman with morbid obesity and chronic hypertension, at 36 weeks of gestation, presented with a 1-week history of mild headache, nausea, epigastric and right upper quadrant pain, and dark urine. On examination, she was jaundiced with hepatomegaly; the neurologic examination was normal. Laboratory values showed a leukocyte count of 12.0 × 10^9/L, platelet count of 450 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, total bilirubin 6.4 mg/dL (direct 5.0 mg/dL), AST 83 U/L, ALT 87 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 319 U/L, glucose 66 mg/dL, LDH 679 U/L, uric acid 4.2 mg/dL, and total serum bile acids 71 μmol/L. Coagulation studies showed a prothrombin time of 17 seconds (INR 1.4). Viral hepatitis serologies, autoimmune markers, and ceruloplasmin level were unremarkable. A 24-hour urine protein was elevated at 1300 mg (baseline 180 mg prior to pregnancy). Ultrasonography revealed marked hepatomegaly (≈27 cm), fatty infiltration of the liver, a right hepatic hypoechoic 2.8 cm lesion, and heterogenous echotexture with areas of nodular contour.

A 52-year-old woman with no significant past medical or surgical history and no family history, who is a nonsmoker, presented with an 8-month history of progressive increase in abdominal circumference, epigastric pain, early satiety, and weight loss. On examination, she had a slightly tender hepatomegaly with an abdominal perimeter of 98 cm; the remainder of her examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests including alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, total bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyl transferase, albumin, total proteins, lactate dehydrogenase, prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C virus serology were all within normal limits. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest and pelvis showed no abnormalities. Abdominal MRI demonstrated an enlarged liver due to a 16.9 × 9.4 cm lobulated mass involving segments IV through VIII, which was slightly hyperintense on T2, slightly hypointense on T1, exhibited restricted diffusion, and showed minimal arterial and portal-phase enhancement. The mass infiltrated the gallbladder and right portal vein, while the bile ducts and other vascular structures appeared unremarkable.

A 16-year-old female presented with a 12-month history of a slowly enlarging, asymptomatic swelling in the left anterior maxillary region. She was undergoing orthodontic treatment, and a cyst-like radiolucency was noted incidentally on imaging adjacent to an impacted maxillary lateral incisor. On extraoral examination, there was a well-defined, hard, non-tender swelling of the left nasal ala region causing mild facial asymmetry. Intraorally, there was a smooth, bony-hard, non-fluctuant swelling measuring approximately 1.5×2 cm in the left maxillary buccal vestibule, with expansion of the buccal cortex. Teeth #22 and #23 were clinically absent; adjacent teeth were vital. Cone-beam CT demonstrated a well-circumscribed, unilocular radiolucent lesion with a corticated border extending from the midline to the second premolar and associated with the crown of the impacted lateral incisor. The radiolucency enveloped the entire crown and overlapped its root. Based on imaging, a dentigerous cyst, an adenomatoid odontogenic tumor, or a calcifying odontogenic cyst was considered.

A 34-year-old woman with a history of psoriasis, celiac disease, and penicillin allergy presented with 2 weeks of worsening inflammatory mid-back pain that was unrelieved by analgesics. She reported gait difficulties and a sense of heaviness in both lower limbs without bowel or bladder dysfunction. She denied trauma, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. 

On examination, she had a spastic gait and proximal paraparesis, most pronounced in hip flexion and knee extension bilaterally. There was hyperreflexia in the lower limbs and bilateral Babinski signs; sensation was intact. The remainder of the systemic examination was unremarkable. 

Initial laboratory studies, including complete blood count, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, metabolic panel, serum calcium, alkaline phosphatase, and parathyroid hormone levels, were all within normal limits. Blood cultures and tuberculosis screening were negative. 

Given the progressive neurological deficits, urgent spinal imaging was obtained. Magnetic resonance imaging of the thoracic spine revealed a lesion arising from the T11 vertebral body with extension into the spinal canal and significant spinal cord compression. Computed tomography confirmed an osteolytic T11 lesion associated with spinal instability and kyphotic deformity. 

The radiologic features initially raised suspicion of metastatic epiduritis, and urgent decompressive surgery was planned.

A 57-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a 4-month history of dyspepsia, a 4-kg weight loss, and one episode of coffee-ground emesis. Physical examination was unremarkable, and routine laboratory studies were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a round, soft-tissue–density lesion in the proximal duodenum measuring approximately 2 × 4 cm. Upper endoscopy showed a freely mobile, polypoid submucosal mass in the first portion of the duodenum that intermittently prolapsed through the pylorus and back, causing intermittent gastric outlet obstruction. Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated a heterogeneous, hypoechoic submucosal lesion measuring 2.9 × 2.8 cm. Multiple standard endoscopic biopsies of the lesion were nondiagnostic. The patient then underwent laparoscopic transduodenal excision. Frozen-section examination revealed a submucosal nodular glandular proliferation with mild architectural distortion, scattered irregular duct-like structures, and focal equivocal mild cytonuclear atypia; a definitive diagnosis could not be rendered intraoperatively.

A 13-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of irregular maxillary teeth. He had undergone limited orthodontic bonding of selected incisors and the primary maxillary right canine without prior radiography. Extraoral examination was unremarkable. Intraoral examination revealed a retained primary maxillary right canine; its permanent successor was not visible, and there was no canine bulge or cortical expansion. The left maxillary quadrant showed a full set of permanent teeth to the second molar. Mandibular dentition was complete to the first molars, with second primary molars near exfoliation. A panoramic radiograph showed a supernumerary tooth-like structure between the roots of the permanent maxillary right lateral incisor and the primary maxillary right canine, enclosed within a unilocular cystic space that caused divergence of those roots. A mesially rotated, impacted permanent maxillary right canine overlaid this space. Radiologically, the lesion resembled a compound odontoma or a dentigerous cyst. The primary canine was extracted, and the embedded tooth-like structure with its cyst-like lining was surgically enucleated and sent for histopathological examination.

A 52-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with slow-growing, painless swellings in the palmar area of his left hand and the right middle finger. He denied numbness, tingling, or functional deficits. He recalled a mass at the same site on his right middle finger 22 years ago, which was excised 15 years ago and diagnosed as a schwannoma; it recurred in the same location and a new painless swelling appeared on the left palm 7 years ago. There was no history of trauma, infection, or family history of similar lesions. 

On examination, there were two mobile, nonpulsatile, soft masses measuring 20 mm × 10 mm on the left hand and 15 mm × 10 mm on the right middle finger. Neither was tender, and Tinel’s sign was negative; sensory testing was normal.

Magnetic resonance imaging of both hands demonstrated well-defined, sharply demarcated, heterogeneously hyperintense lesions on T2-weighted images; a thin peripheral rim of fat on T1-weighted images (split fat sign); multiple small ring-like structures with peripheral hyperintensity (fascicular sign); and a low-signal-intensity core surrounded by hyperintensity (bull’s eye sign).

A 43-year-old man presented with a 15-day history of mild, intermittent, dull aching pain in the upper lip. His medical history was unremarkable. He had sustained a lip laceration and anterior tooth fractures in a motor-vehicle accident 15 years earlier; the laceration was sutured, and root-canal treatment with crowns was later performed. Two years after the accident, he underwent a minor surgical procedure to remove a tooth spicule from the same region. 

On general examination, vital signs and review of systems were normal. Intraorally, inspection of the upper lip and labial mucosa revealed no visible abnormalities, but palpation identified a firm, tender, 5-mm mass in the upper lip, 0.5 cm lateral to midline adjacent to the crowns on teeth 11 and 12. A soft-tissue periapical radiograph of the upper lip showed a single, well-defined, radiopaque mass measuring approximately 3 × 2 mm. Blood tests were within normal limits.

A 24-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of a painless, progressively enlarging right neck mass. She denied dyspnea, dysphagia, voice changes, weight loss, fevers, night sweats, or tuberculosis exposure. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender, well-demarcated 4 × 3 cm mass in the right level II that was mobile on the horizontal plane, did not move with swallowing, and did not elicit a cough impulse. Oral, ear, and systemic examinations were normal. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration was performed, with samples sent for histopathology, tuberculosis smear and culture, and GeneXpert. Smears and cultures were negative for tuberculosis. Histopathology showed spindle cells staining positive for IH558 and S-100. Routine blood tests and chest radiograph were unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging of the neck revealed a 2.4 × 2.4 × 2.8 cm oblong lesion that was isointense on T1, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2/STIR, displacing the internal carotid artery and internal jugular vein anteriorly without luminal narrowing.

A 45-year-old man in good general health presented with a five-month history of a right maxillary swelling. He reported no pain or paresthesia. On extra-oral examination, there were no abnormalities and no palpable lymphadenopathy. Intra-orally, there was a 2-cm diameter round, firm swelling of the mucosa in the right upper premolar–molar region, covered by normal mucosa. The vitality test of the adjacent teeth was positive, and no tooth mobility was noted. Panoramic radiography showed a radiolucent area in the middle third of the roots of the right first molar and second premolar.

A 60-year-old woman presented with chronic mechanical cervicobrachial neuralgia and intermittent paresthesia of the three ulnar fingers on the right, progressively worsening over a few weeks. She had no motor weakness and an otherwise unremarkable physical examination. MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine showed no disc herniation but revealed a lesion at the T8 level. Subsequent CT of the thoracic spine demonstrated an osteolytic lesion of the T8 vertebral body extending into both pedicles and laminae, containing thickened vertical trabeculae and showing mild expansion of the vertebra in the anteroposterior dimension. There was only mild paravertebral soft-tissue extension, and no other vertebral lesions were identified. Laboratory studies were normal except for an IgM κ monoclonal gammopathy. Initial differential diagnoses included aggressive hemangioma, plasmacytoma, and, to a lesser extent, Paget’s disease.

A 9-year-old boy presented with a swelling on the right anterior chest that had first appeared as a pea-sized nodule three years earlier. The lesion had gradually increased to approximately 0.5 cm in diameter before remaining stable in size. He had no pain, tenderness, or respiratory symptoms, and no other swellings. On examination, the mass was lobulated, smooth-surfaced, bony hard, fixed to the underlying rib, and non-tender; the overlying skin was normal and freely mobile. A tangential chest radiograph showed a bony outgrowth arising from the lateral aspect of the right sixth rib. Osteochondroma was suspected.

A 20-year-old man presented for a routine eye examination as part of a university health screening program.  
- Habitual corrected Snellen visual acuities were 6/5 −2 in each eye; unaided visual acuities were 6/6 −2 (right eye) and 6/12 (left eye). Near acuity was N5 at 40 cm bilaterally.  
- Anterior-segment slit-lamp examination was unremarkable.  
- Dilated fundus examination (1% tropicamide) revealed in the right eye a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.2, blot and dot hemorrhages in the perifoveal area approaching the posterior pole, Roth’s spots, cotton wool spots, and venous dilation in the superior quadrant. The left eye had a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.3 and similar hemorrhages located more in the mid-periphery.  

Further questioning disclosed a 3-month history of night sweats, occasional bone pain, fatigue, and exercise intolerance, which the patient had attributed to academic stress. He had no known systemic disease; family history was notable only for hypertension and diabetes.  
- Blood pressure and pulse rate were consistently normal on four separate occasions.  
- Fasting blood sugar was 5.1 mmol/L; glycosylated hemoglobin was 6.2%.  

Initial complete blood count (CBC) showed: hematocrit 37.1% (normal 40–52%), RDW 15.9% (10–14%), RBC 4.0 × 10^12/L (4.4–5.9), WBC 56.8 × 10^9/L (3–10.6), lymphocytes 18.6 × 10^9/L (0.8–3.9), granulocytes 35.5 × 10^9/L (1.1–7.8), MID cells 2.7 × 10^9/L (0.0–1.5).  
Repeat CBC one week later revealed: hematocrit 33.2%, RDW 19.8%, RBC 3.96 × 10^12/L, WBC 160 × 10^9/L, lymphocytes 17.4 × 10^9/L, granulocytes 35.5 × 10^9/L, MID cells 47.0 × 10^9/L, MCHC 39.2 g/dL (32–36), platelets 157 × 10^9/L (150–400).  
- ESR was elevated at 16 mm fall/h (0–10).  
- Blood cultures showed no growth after 5 days.  
- Peripheral blood smear revealed mainly normocytic, normochromic cells along with numerous myeloid cells and neutrophilic band cells.

A 23-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with a 4-year history of a painless midline neck mass that had enlarged dramatically over the past 3 months and was now causing difficulty swallowing and shortness of breath. He denied fevers, weight loss, pain, or other masses and had no family history of thyroid or neck malignancy. On examination, vital signs were normal. There was a 4×5 cm hard, irregular, non-tender central neck mass that moved slightly with tongue protrusion and swallowing; there were no skin changes, no intraoral extension, and no palpable cervical lymph nodes. Laboratory studies showed normal hemoglobin, white-cell count, C-reactive protein, and procalcitonin. Thyroid function, renal function, liver function, and coagulation tests were all within normal limits. Neck ultrasound revealed a 5×5 cm irregular cystic mass with a solid component and increased vascular flow; the thyroid gland appeared normal without nodules and there was no lymphadenopathy.
