A thyroid uptake scan showed normal uptake in both lobes and no cold nodules. MRI of the neck demonstrated a 5×5 cm mixed cystic and solid soft-tissue mass anterior to the hyoid bone, compressing the trachea, with no thyroid nodules or enlarged lymph nodes. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration of the solid component was performed.

A 28-year-old nonpregnant woman with three prior term deliveries presented with menorrhagia for 2½ years. She had no significant past medical, surgical, medication, or family history. On examination, vital signs were stable and pelvic and speculum exams were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.6 mg/dL) and a negative β-hCG. Transabdominal ultrasound revealed a well-defined hypoechoic area measuring 34 × 27 mm within the endometrial cavity. Transvaginal sonography confirmed a 35 × 23 mm hypoechoic lesion attached to the anterior endometrial wall. The leading considerations were endometrial polyp, submucosal leiomyoma, and blood clot. The patient underwent dilation and curettage, but bleeding persisted. Given her completed childbearing, a supracervical hysterectomy was performed.

A 53-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of left-sided abdominal pain and multiple episodes of bilious vomiting. During the first week she had diarrhoea that responded to oral antibiotics. She had no history of immunosuppression. On examination, vital signs were normal, and the abdominal and general physical examinations were unremarkable. Routine blood tests were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed concentric wall thickening of small-bowel loops in the left lumbar and paraumbilical region, measuring approximately 9 mm, with loss of wall stratification. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 4-cm segmental stricture of the proximal jejunum with thick, enhancing walls, surrounding fat stranding, hyperemia with dilated mesenteric vessels, dilated proximal loops, and collapsed distal loops. These findings were suggestive of an inflammatory process, with a differential diagnosis of Crohn’s disease or a chronic infectious process such as tuberculosis. Colonoscopic examination was unremarkable. The patient was scheduled for surgical resection of the jejunal stricture.

A 14-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of a slowly enlarging, asymptomatic swelling on the left side of her nose and malaligned teeth. She sought orthodontic treatment for the malocclusion; a nasal twang in her voice was noted. 

On extraoral examination, there was a firm, non-tender 3 cm swelling over the left nasal region. Intraorally, a hard swelling of similar size was palpable in the left maxillary canine–premolar area. The permanent left maxillary canine was absent, and the first premolar was tilted mesially into the canine space.

Panoramic radiography showed an impacted left maxillary canine enclosed within a well-circumscribed unilocular lesion that contained both radiolucent and radiopaque components. The maxillary sinus floor and adjacent premolar roots were displaced posteriorly. 

Computed tomography of the maxilla confirmed a well-defined cystic lesion encasing the impacted canine, containing focal radiopaque material, with posterior and distal displacement of the sinus floor.

A 31-year-old Brazilian woman was referred for evaluation of a diffuse 20 mm radiolucent lesion in the right maxilla associated with teeth 13 and 15 and an overlying painless swelling. She reported prior endodontic treatment of teeth 13 and 15 without regression of the lesion. Teeth 14 and 24 had been extracted previously for orthodontic reasons. Panoramic radiography and CT confirmed a unilocular radiolucency involving the apices of teeth 13 and 15. The initial working diagnosis was an inflammatory periapical cyst. Preoperative laboratory tests were obtained, and the patient underwent excisional biopsy of the lesion under general anesthesia.

A 41-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of recurrent lower abdominal pain. Her medical history included epilepsy managed since age 17, obesity (WHO grade I), arterial hypertension, and a prior ovarian cyst removal (side unspecified). Family history was notable for a sister with systemic sclerosis and an uncle with lung cancer. On previous gynecologic sonography, a cystic lesion measuring 44×27×30 mm was reported, located cranial to the uterus and separate from the adnexa.

At admission, she was asymptomatic. Vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination revealed a soft, non-distended abdomen with normoactive bowel sounds and no palpable masses or organomegaly. Laboratory studies, including tumor markers and thyroid function tests, were within normal limits.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen demonstrated a multicystic solid retroperitoneal mass ventral to the left psoas muscle and iliac artery. The ventral portion was polycystic (37×26×45 mm), and the dorsal portion was lobulated with both cystic and solid components (36×15×33 mm), showing vascular contact. There was no connection to the ovaries or to a presumed horseshoe kidney.

A 56-year-old man with hypertension and chronic renal failure presented with a 3-year history of chronic lower back pain localized to the sacral region that worsened with sitting and improved on standing. Over the past 3 months he noted progressive lower-limb weakness. He also had occasional episodes of constipation and abdominal cramps.

On examination, general and systemic findings were unremarkable. Local palpation elicited tenderness over the sacrum.

Plain radiographs of the pelvis showed a large, rounded radiolucent lesion with multiple calcifications and destruction of the lower sacral vertebrae and coccyx. Ultrasound of the sacral region demonstrated a large heterogeneous hypoechoic mass with areas of calcification. Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis revealed a 16 × 13 × 13.8 cm, well-circumscribed lytic expansile soft-tissue mass with intralesional calcifications centered on the lower sacrum and coccyx; the mass displaced and compressed the rectum anteriorly and extended posteriorly into the subcutaneous tissue and gluteal musculature, with destruction of the sacrum and coccyx on bone windows. Contrast MRI showed a large lobulated mass in the same region, hypointense on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with heterogeneous post-contrast enhancement, intralesional calcifications, and foci of hemorrhage.

A 58-year-old woman presented with a painless mass in her left thigh of 3 years’ duration. She had no history of trauma. On examination, a firm 3×4 cm mass was palpated in the anterior aspect of the left thigh. A lateral plain radiograph of the thigh showed irregular mineralization within the soft tissue. Axial MRI revealed a well-circumscribed intramuscular mass in the rectus femoris muscle that was predominantly high in signal intensity on both T1-weighted and T2-weighted images, with interspersed areas of intermediate signal intensity. The medial border of the lesion was poorly defined, and no enhancement was seen after administration of gadolinium-DTPA. On sagittal images, the lesion showed irregular intermediate-signal areas surrounding regions of high signal intensity on T1-weighted sequences, and on T2-weighted sequences it was heterogeneous, with both high and intermediate signal intensities.

A 6-year-old boy presented with a 2-year history of progressively worsening headaches and a 1-year history of left hemiparesis. He had no seizures, fever, or history of trauma. On examination, he was alert and oriented; pupils were equal and reactive. He had macrocephaly (head circumference 57 cm, >99th percentile), an open anterior fontanelle, frontal bossing, sunset eyes, and left-sided hemiparesis (MRC grade 5/2) with paresis of cranial nerves III, IV, and VI on the left. Noncontrast CT of the head showed a lobulated isodense mass in the posterior third ventricle infiltrating the left lateral ventricle and obstructing the cerebral aqueduct, resulting in hydrocephalus. Postcontrast CT demonstrated strong enhancement of the lesion. After ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement, MRI revealed a lobulated mass in the posterior third ventricle arising from the roof of the ventricle, measuring 32.4 × 30.2 × 21.1 mm. The lesion was hypointense on T1 and T2, did not suppress on T2-FLAIR, and showed signal loss on SWI consistent with microhemorrhages. Contrast-enhanced T1 images showed heterogeneous strong enhancement without parenchymal invasion. Diffusion-weighted imaging demonstrated restricted diffusion with a mean ADC value of 0.978 × 10⁻³ mm²/s.

A 15-year-old girl presented with multiple swellings of five months’ duration. She noted progressive enlargement of bilateral neck masses and one each on her back and anterior abdominal wall, without pain. There was no significant past medical, personal, or family history. 

On examination, there were seven subcutaneous, nontender, mobile swellings measuring 1×1 to 3×3 cm in the cervical regions, right paraspinal area, and anterior abdominal wall. The lesions were firm to hard without changes in the overlying skin. 

Complete blood count, metabolic panel, and skeletal survey were all normal. With a clinical impression of lymphoreticular malignancy or metastatic disease, fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) was performed on the most prominent swellings (two cervical, one paraspinal, one abdominal). 

Cytology smears from all sites showed moderate cellularity with similar features: predominantly plump spindle cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, fragments of collagenous matrix, and occasional small cells with scant cytoplasm. The spindle cells had bipolar cytoplasmic extensions and round-to-oval nuclei with fine granular chromatin; nucleoli were inconspicuous. Nuclear hyperchromasia, pleomorphism, or atypicality was not seen, and mitoses were sparse. There was no necrosis or inflammatory cells. 

Ultrasonography confirmed that all lesions were confined to the subcutaneous tissue, with no lymphadenopathy or deeper masses.

A 39-year-old man with Fitzpatrick skin type II presented with a 3-year history of a slowly enlarging “soft lump” on the right side of his forehead at the exact site where he sustained minor blunt trauma from a baseball. He noted more rapid growth over the past 12 months but denied pain, sensory changes, or functional deficits. He was otherwise healthy and took no medications. On examination, there was a 2.0-cm rubbery, nontransilluminant, slightly mobile subcutaneous nodule without overlying skin changes. There was no weakness of the frontalis muscle and intact sensation over the area. Targeted ultrasound revealed a subdermal hypoechoic lesion measuring 1.7 × 1.4 × 0.3 cm immediately anterior to the outer table of the calvarium, with a prominent superficial artery coursing over the mass.

A 50-year-old man presented with a 5-month history of a painless, slow-growing swelling in the right maxillary teeth region. There was no history of trauma, pain, smoking, or other deleterious habits. His medical history was noncontributory. 

On extraoral examination, there was a diffuse, firm, nontender swelling extending from the tip of the nose to 3 cm lateral to the right ala and from the ala-tragus line to the lower border of the upper lip, causing mild nasal tip deviation and obliteration of the right nasolabial fold. A single, firm, fixed, tender right submental lymph node was palpable. 

Intraoral examination revealed a 5 × 4 cm lobulated, purplish-black pigmented growth between the maxillary right central incisor and first molar, involving the marginal, attached, and interdental gingiva on the labiobuccal aspect without palatal extension. The lesion was firm, bled on probing, and the right canine and first and second premolars were missing, with slight lateral displacement of the right lateral incisor. Oral hygiene was poor. 

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, biochemical tests, and urinalysis, were within normal limits. A panoramic radiograph showed a partially edentulous right maxilla with an irregular radiolucent lesion with ill-defined margins from the canine to the first molar. 

Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a mass lesion involving the anterior wall of the right maxillary sinus and the right maxillary alveolar arch up to the second molar, with extension into the gingivobuccal sulcus, buccinator muscle, and zygomatic prominence laterally, showing heterogeneous postcontrast enhancement.

A 55-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of intermittent dull epigastric pain associated with acid regurgitation and belching. She had no history of smoking or relevant medications. On examination, the abdomen was soft without palpable masses. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 89 g/L, ferritin 10.4 ng/mL, vitamin B12 2170 pg/mL, and normal serum tumor markers. Gastroscopy revealed chronic atrophic gastritis with bile reflux and a 5 × 3 cm smooth-surfaced protuberant lesion in the gastric antrum. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 5 × 4 cm mass in the gastric antrum with heterogeneous high attenuation and uneven enhancement.  
What is your differential diagnosis?

A 76-year-old woman presented with 4 days of severe right lower quadrant abdominal pain. She reported mild fever but no other gastrointestinal symptoms. On examination, she had localized tenderness and rebound at the right iliac fossa. She was afebrile to 38.0 °C, with stable vital signs otherwise. She had no history of ganglioneuromatosis, neurofibromatosis, or multiple endocrine neoplasia. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 6000/mm3 with 79% neutrophils; other blood tests were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a dilated vermiform appendix in the right lower fossa with a peri-appendiceal fluid collection. A clinical diagnosis of acute appendicitis was made, and she underwent an appendectomy. The resected specimen was sent for pathologic examination.

A 44-year-old woman with a history of lupus and asthma underwent a partial mastectomy for a cT1N0 infiltrating ductal breast carcinoma. A perioperative chest radiograph revealed a large posterior mediastinal mass. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a 5 × 6.4 cm posterior mediastinal mass encasing the distal esophagus and the aorta. Because of concern for an esophageal tumor, endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle aspiration was performed, which suggested a sarcoma. After multidisciplinary review, a CT-guided core biopsy was obtained, revealing a neuroendocrine tumor. At this point it was decided to perform laboratory studies.

A 45-year-old man with a history of systemic lupus erythematosus, well controlled without immunomodulatory therapy, presented with a 30 × 20 mm painless, slowly progressive mass on his left forehead over 1 year. He had undergone excision of a similar frontal bone lesion diagnosed as fibrous dysplasia 2 years earlier. He denied headaches or neurologic symptoms.  
On CT scan, the lesion showed a ground-glass appearance with homogenous matrix expansion of the frontal bone, predominantly affecting the external cortex. Fine-needle aspiration cytology with immunostaining excluded multiple myeloma (no CD138+ cells). A core biopsy demonstrated diffuse sclerosis, complete bone resorption, and intra-trabecular fibrosis; the bone was not uniformly mineralized, and these findings were reported as suggestive of fibrous dysplasia.  
Preoperative laboratory tests, including inflammatory markers, renal function, and blood counts, were within normal limits. The patient underwent complete surgical excision of a 40 × 50 mm portion of frontal bone, including the lesion with a 15 mm margin of normal bone, via a coronal approach. The bone defect was repaired with an autologous calvarial graft using piezoelectric osteotomies.

A 26-year-old Afro-descendent woman presents with a several-month history of asymptomatic swelling on the left side of her mandible. Her only notable past surgical history is resection of a fibro-osseous lesion from the right hemimandible two years earlier. On extraoral examination, there is mild left facial asymmetry with submandibular fullness but no lymphadenopathy. Intraorally, there is expansion of the buccal and lingual cortical plates from tooth 33 to 37 without tooth mobility or tenderness to palpation or percussion. A panoramic radiograph demonstrates a single, extensive multilocular lesion of the left mandible with thinning of both cortical plates and a “ground-glass” appearance. Cone-beam CT with sagittal and axial views confirms an unencapsulated, expansile lesion with irregular margins, marked cortical thinning, and no root resorption; 3D reconstruction shows a destructive lesion abutting the basal mandibular edge. Based on these findings, a fibro-osseous lesion is the leading consideration; initial differential diagnoses include ameloblastoma, keratocystic odontogenic tumor, and central giant-cell lesion.

A 67-year-old Filipino man with hypertension presented with upper abdominal pain and bloating. He underwent a routine colonoscopy that showed diverticulosis, and subsequently an esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) that revealed a gastric cardia/fundus mass. At our center, EGD with endoscopic ultrasound showed a 3.5 cm subepithelial hypoechoic gastric mass arising from the muscularis propria with central umbilication and ulceration; the remainder of the stomach, duodenum, and esophagus was unremarkable. Fine-needle aspiration demonstrated groups and single enlarged atypical cells with anisonucleosis, pleomorphism, and prominent nucleoli consistent with adenocarcinoma. Immunostains on the cytologic specimen were positive for CK7, Villin, and CDX2 and negative for CK20, CD117, and CD56, indicating an upper gastrointestinal or pancreatobiliary primary adenocarcinoma. A PET/CT scan showed increased hypermetabolic activity confined to the gastric mass with no evidence of metastases or lymph node involvement.

A 78-year-old woman presented with an 8-year history of a slowly enlarging, painless mass in the right parotid region. She has a 10–pack-year smoking history and no alcohol use. On examination, there was a mobile, elastic, hard, ovoid lesion in the right preauricular area. MRI of the head and neck showed a 29×27×27 mm superficial parotid nodule with well-defined edges, a fibrous capsule, hypointensity on most sequences, heterogeneous hyperintensity on T2, and contrast enhancement with papillary-like internal projections. Fine-needle aspiration yielded neoplastic cells with moderate atypia, macrokaryosis, occasional nucleoli, and scant cytoplasm arranged in three-dimensional strips with nuclear superimposition in a bloody background; few lymphocytes were seen (Milan Classification V).

A 33-year-old woman was referred to an orthodontist for evaluation of mandibular anterior crowding. Screening panoramic radiography revealed a unilocular radiolucent lesion with a well-defined sclerotic border extending from the left mandibular canine to the right canine. The patient had no relevant medical history. Intraoral and extraoral examinations were unremarkable, with no visible swelling or bony expansion and no tenderness on palpation. All mandibular anterior teeth responded normally to electrical pulp testing. She was referred to a maxillofacial surgeon, and cone-beam computed tomography demonstrated a well-circumscribed radiolucent lesion with a smooth border, with no cortical expansion, root resorption, or tooth displacement.

A 26-year-old woman presented with a two-week history of prolonged, heavy menstrual bleeding during her last period and episodes of postcoital bleeding. She had regular menses and a negative pregnancy test. On general examination, findings were unremarkable. Speculum examination revealed a 4-cm polypoid lesion in the upper vagina; the cervix was not distinctly identified. Abdominal ultrasound showed a normal uterus without intrauterine masses. An incision biopsy of the vaginal lesion suggested a blue nevus with a differential diagnosis of schwannoma. The patient underwent examination under anesthesia and an attempted excision of the tumor, which proved incomplete. Colposcopic examination then demonstrated a residual 2.5-cm tumor in the posterior vaginal wall; the adjacent cervix appeared normal. Two months later, a second procedure achieved complete excision of the residual mass, measuring 6 cm at its widest diameter. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day three.

A 25‐year‐old man presented with a massive, asymptomatic enlargement of the right side of his face, noted since childhood. The prominence increased until age 18, then stabilized. He was an orphan with no available family history and reported no other health issues.

On examination, there was diffuse enlargement of the right hemiface extending from the facial midline to the preauricular region, superiorly to the frontal bone, and inferiorly to the mandible’s inferior border. The nasal and chin midlines were deviated to the left, creating an arched midline from nasion to gnathion. The right corner of the mouth was slightly drooped, and the right lips appeared fuller. The skin on the right cheek was coarser; the right pinna was larger. Soft‐tissue overgrowth was pronounced over the zygoma, infraorbital region, and symphysis, causing partial closure of the right eye. Palpation revealed a nontender soft tissue swelling over the right parietal bone. Temporomandibular joint function and mandibular range of motion were normal.

Intraorally, the right maxillary and mandibular alveolar ridges were enlarged compared to the left. The right gingiva and hard palate had a granular surface. The right half of the tongue was enlarged to midline, with polypoid fungiform papillae. The right buccal mucosa was pendulous. Tooth‐size measurements showed that the right permanent maxillary canine, premolars, and molars and the right permanent mandibular lateral incisor, canine, and premolars exceeded their left counterparts by 57–337% in volume. The dental midline was shifted left, there was a generalized crossbite due to mandibular prognathism, and the right occlusal plane was canted downward.

A panoramic radiograph demonstrated enlargement of the right mandibular body with widening of the right inferior alveolar canal. A PA skull view confirmed enlargement of the right mandible, maxilla, zygoma, and overlying soft tissues.

Facial CT showed enlargement of right‐sided bony structures, including the maxilla, mandible (body, condyle, glenoid fossa), zygoma, external auditory canal walls, and pterygoid bone. The right glenoid fossa showed bony overgrowth with articular surface irregularity; the right condyle was irregular and flattened, though the joint space was maintained. The external auditory canal was stenosed by bony overgrowth. Right frontal and parietal bone inner tables were thinned and irregular. The right foramen ovale, spinosum, rotundum, mental and infraorbital foramina, vidian canal, and palatine canals were widened relative to the left. An intracranial lipoma was noted in the right quadrigeminal cistern. The right orbit was deformed but globe and orbital contents were normal. Deviation of the nasal bones and chin to the left was apparent. The right parotid gland was enlarged and heterogeneous with prominent vessels and nodular areas. The right submental, submandibular, parapharyngeal, and pterygopalatine spaces; soft palate; tongue; and floor of mouth showed soft‐tissue overgrowth with fat attenuation. All right muscles of mastication and the anterior belly of the digastric were enlarged with fatty infiltration.

An 18-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an asymptomatic radiopaque lesion in the right mandibular bone, discovered incidentally on routine imaging. Her medical history was unremarkable. On extraoral examination, the facial contour was normal, and mouth opening was within normal limits. Intraorally, the mucosa appeared healthy, teeth in the posterior right mandible were vital, and there was no evidence of bone deformity or cortical expansion.  

Panoramic radiography and cone-beam computed tomography revealed a well-defined, unilocular radiopaque lesion measuring in the region of the right canine and first premolar (tooth 43–44) on the lingual aspect. The lesion contained irregular tooth-like structures. There was no buccal or lingual cortical expansion or thickening, and adjacent teeth showed neither displacement nor root resorption.

A 56-year-old woman presented with a 5–6-month history of persistent headache and new-onset slight diplopia. The headache was initially NSAID-responsive but progressively worsened. On neurologic examination, she had peripheral right facial-nerve and right abducent-nerve palsies. Vital signs and routine blood tests were normal.

Noncontrast CT of the brain with 2D multiplanar reconstructions and 3D volume rendering revealed a large expansile lesion in the right posterior cranial fossa extending through the foramen magnum into the middle cranial fossa. The mass displaced the right temporal lobe upward and laterally and shifted the brainstem to the left; the cerebellar vermis and fourth ventricle were compressed, resulting in hydrocephalus. Bone windows demonstrated erosion of the right petrous apex and greater wing of the sphenoid with widening of the right inferior orbital foramen. Attenuation measurements showed a cranial portion of the lesion at −5 to −10 HU and a caudal portion at −50 to −60 HU, suggestive of a fatty component. Numerous additional markedly hypodense foci (−150 to −180 HU) were scattered throughout the supratentorial cisternal and cortical spaces.

MRI, including T1-weighted, T2-weighted, FLAIR, T1-fat-suppression, postcontrast T1, and 3D-TOF angiographic sequences, showed the caudal portion of the mass to be homogeneously hyperintense on T1 and T2. The cranial portion exhibited heterogeneous hyper- and hypointense signals with internal dark areas consistent with hemosiderin. There was no contrast enhancement of the mass or the extra-axial foci. 3D-TOF angiography revealed displacement and stretching of the basilar artery, the right posterior cerebral artery, and the right posterior communicating artery.

A 65-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a massive frontal scalp lesion that had been slowly enlarging over 22 years and had become ulceronecrotic and prone to bleeding for 4 months, with rapid enlargement after an attempted incision and drainage. On examination, there was a 17-cm dome-shaped mass on the forehead with central necrosis and active bleeding; there was no palpable regional lymphadenopathy and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the head revealed a heterogeneous large soft-tissue mass with multiple foci of calcification and numerous concentric vessels demonstrating marked enhancement; there was no intracranial extension and no lymphadenopathy.

A 23-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of progressive abdominal distension accompanied by early satiety and urinary urgency. She denied pain, weight loss, or systemic symptoms. Her menstrual cycles were normal, and her mother had a history of ovarian cysts. On examination, the abdomen was distended with dull percussion notes but without tenderness or guarding.

Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a cyst measuring 16 × 24 cm that compressed adjacent abdominal organs. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography showed a large midline intraperitoneal cyst, 30 × 25.6 × 16.8 cm in size, extending from the liver to the pelvis and involving the uterus and ovaries. The lesion had a fluid density of 20 Hounsfield units and demonstrated no calcifications, soft-tissue components, or enhancing septations, suggesting a benign etiology.

Laboratory studies, including α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, cancer antigen 19-9, and cancer antigen 125, were all within normal limits; the Risk of Malignancy Algorithm (ROMA) score was 4.1 %. Serological testing for Echinococcus granulosus was negative. A giant intra-abdominal cyst was diagnosed preoperatively, and laparoscopic cyst aspiration with exploration under general anesthesia was planned.

A 56-year-old woman with a decades-long history of type 2 diabetes mellitus complicated by non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia was admitted with progressive limb edema, dyspnea, dizziness, nausea, and oliguria. She was found to have blood urea nitrogen of 106 mg/dL, creatinine of 17.77 mg/dL, and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 2 mL/min/1.73 m2. C-reactive protein was elevated at 5.508 mg/dL; hemoglobin was 11.0 g/dL, and platelets were 119×10^3/μL. She underwent emergent hemodialysis, with improvement of BUN to 44 mg/dL and creatinine to 5.29 mg/dL, and then was transitioned to regular dialysis.

During her admission, abdominal ultrasonography incidentally revealed a 1.6 cm hypoechoic hypervascular nodule in the right renal parenchyma. Noncontrast MRI showed the lesion to be isointense to renal cortex on T1- and T2-weighted images with restricted diffusion on DWI and ADC sequences. The patient declined further evaluation at that time. Eight months later, contrast-enhanced CT performed as part of transplant assessment demonstrated no increase in lesion size, early homogeneous enhancement in the arterial phase, and no regional lymphadenopathy or invasion; “the possibility of renal cell carcinoma could not be completely excluded.” The patient was scheduled for laparoscopic nephroureterectomy.

A 54-year-old woman presented with 3 weeks of dull, diffuse abdominal pain, bloating, and early satiety. She reported fatigue, night sweats, and a 5 lb weight loss over 4 weeks but denied palpitations, anxiety, headaches, hot flashes, or tremors. Her medical history included obesity, diet-controlled hyperlipidemia, and well-controlled hypertension on hydrochlorothiazide. Vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination revealed right upper-quadrant tenderness without peritoneal signs. Complete blood count, liver function tests, and renal function tests were normal.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a 6.6 cm heterogeneous, hypervascular mass in the caudate lobe of the liver, with mass effect on the inferior vena cava and left hepatic vein. Multiphasic MRI demonstrated a T2-hyperintense lesion with punctate T1-hyperintense foci and avid arterial enhancement with delayed washout. Given the risk of bleeding and tumor seeding, surgical excision was recommended instead of biopsy.

On the day of surgery, her blood pressure was 127/85 mm Hg. General anesthesia was induced uneventfully, and initial tumor exposure did not alter hemodynamics. Upon manipulation of the mass, however, her systolic blood pressure acutely rose to the low 200 mm Hg. This was treated with increased anesthetic depth, nitroglycerin, esmolol, and labetalol, bringing systolic pressures to the 150 mm Hg range. Blood pressure normalized when tumor manipulation ceased. Concurrently, her blood glucose spiked to 400 mg/dL, requiring insulin infusion. These findings led the anesthesia team to suspect a catecholamine-secreting tumor.

A newborn male was noted on prenatal ultrasound at 28 weeks of gestation to have a cyst on his left eye. He was delivered at 38 weeks and 2 days without complications. On ophthalmic examination, the lesion was a 9 mm cyst, translucent and vascularized, protruding from the left globe. It was attached to the limbus nasally and temporally and to the inferior sclera. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits revealed a unilocular cyst arising from the left globe; no other abnormalities were seen. The lesion was thought to be an atypical dermoid cyst. Erythromycin ointment was prescribed, and close follow-up was arranged.

At two months of age, the cyst had regressed slightly but persisted as a firmly attached, pink infratemporal mass that completely occluded the pupil, with little potential for useful vision. After discussion with the parents, the decision was made to excise the lesion and perform corneal graft placement. Intraoperatively, the cyst wall was fully excised, revealing a corneal defect with uveal tissue protrusion; the lens was uninvolved and retained, and a donor cornea was sutured into place. The patient tolerated the procedure well. On postoperative day 1, the graft was in good position. By two months postoperatively the graft had become diffusely cloudy, and by three months it showed peripheral vascularization. The eye was asymptomatic. Given the extensive limbal involvement, a repeat graft was considered unlikely to succeed. The excised tissue was sent for histopathologic evaluation.

A 65-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with a 2-year history of progressive joint pain and difficulty walking. He initially noted right ankle and right hip–thigh pain when walking uphill, and over time he developed multiple falls. Eight months before presentation, evaluation demonstrated sacral, vertebral, and rib fractures, vitamin D deficiency, and a femoral bone T-score of –4.3; he was diagnosed with osteoporosis and started on calcitriol. Despite rehabilitation, calcitriol, and analgesics, his pain persisted, and he was referred for further evaluation.

On examination, neurologic findings were normal, muscle strength was 5/5 in all limbs, and he walked with a walker but could not ambulate long distances. Laboratory studies revealed serum phosphate 1.58 mg/dL (2.7–4.6), alkaline phosphatase 724 U/L (38–113), bone-type alkaline phosphatase 70.6% (25–59%), 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D 21 pg/mL (20–60), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 9.7 ng/mL (>20), and TmP/GFR 1.6 mg/dL (2.3–4.3). Intact PTH (46 pg/mL; 10–65) and renal function (eGFR 115 mL/min/1.73 m2) were normal, and serum FGF23 was elevated at 108.0 pg/mL (<30).

Upper and lower endoscopy were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the torso showed a 6 × 4 mm lesion on the anterior surface of the right scapula and a 13 mm lesion in the right parotid gland. ^18FDG PET/CT demonstrated uptake at both sites (SUVmax 3.5 in the scapula and 6.3 in the parotid). Somatostatin receptor scintigraphy was negative. A needle biopsy of the parotid lesion was nondiagnostic, and surgical removal of either lesion was deemed high risk.

A 65-year-old woman (gravida 0, para 0) underwent a chest radiograph for routine health screening, which revealed multiple pulmonary nodules. She reported no symptoms. Thoracic–pelvic CT confirmed multiple bilateral lung lesions and revealed uterine enlargement. She had a history of benign goiter (surgery in her 20s) and hypertension. Menopause occurred at age 50. 

On pelvic examination, the cervix was replaced by a palpable mass; the uterus was the size of an adult head with poor mobility, suggesting parametrial invasion. Contrast-enhanced pelvic MRI showed a 15×8.5×10 cm mass involving the uterine cervix and corpus, with heterogeneous low signal intensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images, areas of hemorrhage, and suspected serosal invasion. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed multiple lung metastases; no other distant lesions were seen. Serum tumor markers (SCC, CA125, CA19-9, CEA) were within normal limits.

Histologic examination of a cervical biopsy specimen showed no atypia of the superficial stratified squamous epithelium, but the deep stroma contained numerous nests of atypical small cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and coarse chromatin. Immunostaining was p16 negative and partially synaptophysin positive. Endometrial cytology likewise revealed a population of bare-nucleus cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios. As the tumor involved both the cervix and corpus, the primary site was difficult to identify.

A 62-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of a soft-tissue swelling in the interdental papilla between the upper left canine and first premolar (teeth 23–24). She reported two prior excisional biopsies at the same site over the past year, without follow-up on the pathology reports. She maintained good oral hygiene, and dental records indicated that oral prophylaxis had been performed as part of treatment after each previous excision. 

On examination, the 1.0 × 1.5 cm lesion had an irregular, pebbly surface; the periphery was erythematous, grading to a bluish center. It was nontender, did not bleed spontaneously, but bled on gentle probing. An intraoral radiograph showed a well-demarcated radiolucency in the interdental bone between teeth 23 and 24. 

An excisional biopsy was performed; hemostasis required approximately 20 minutes, and a periodontal dressing was placed. At the conclusion of the procedure, a provisional diagnosis of pyogenic granuloma was ruled out based on the patient’s good plaque control and prior prophylaxis, and a vascular tumor was suspected. The excised tissue was sent for histopathologic evaluation.

An 11-month-old boy was referred for evaluation of a growing left suprascapular mass noted by his parents. There was no history of trauma or other symptoms. On examination, a firm, well-circumscribed, painless 3 × 3 cm mass with normal overlying skin was palpated in the left suprascapular region. Laboratory studies including α-fetoprotein, β-hCG, carcinoembryonic antigen, and urinary catecholamine metabolites were within normal limits. Ultrasound with Doppler imaging demonstrated a heterogeneous mass with a hyperechoic component extending into deeper tissues with poorly defined borders. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed a fatty mass with well-defined septa and focal densities corresponding to myxoid regions. MRI revealed a well-circumscribed mass arising from the suprascapular soft tissues, with signal characteristics consistent with adipose tissue, extending through the ribs into the left chest cavity.

A 17‐day‐old female neonate, born at 38 weeks’ gestation by cesarean delivery (birth weight 3100 g), had an uncomplicated prenatal course. From day 7 of life she developed stridor, tachypnea, and respiratory distress. She was admitted to a local NICU, where an AP chest radiograph showed opacity in the right upper lobe consistent with collapse consolidation and atelectasis. She received ampicillin, cefotaxime, oxygen by oxyhood, inhaled Pulmicort, and salbutamol without clinical or radiographic improvement and was transferred to our NICU. Repeat chest radiography showed persistent right upper‐lobe opacity. Given concern for tracheoesophageal fistula or other obstructive lesion, an upper gastrointestinal study with thin barium was performed. The study showed no evidence of tracheoesophageal fistula but demonstrated esophageal regurgitation during contrast ingestion and a 35 × 34 mm mass adjacent to the upper intrathoracic esophagus with mild mass effect. On hospital day 3 she developed respiratory failure requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. After relative stabilization, a contrast‐enhanced thoracic CT scan was planned for further evaluation.

A 46-year-old white woman was referred after routine abdominal CT to evaluate an incisional hernia at the midline incision from a prior colectomy revealed multiple small splenic lesions. She was asymptomatic and reported no abdominal pain, weight loss, fever, or other complaints. Her medical history was significant for classic familial adenomatous polyposis diagnosed 20 years earlier, treated by restorative proctocolectomy, cranial osteoma excision, and hysterectomy for benign ovarian cysts with uterine myomatosis. She also has congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium and dental anomalies. On examination, vital signs were normal, the abdomen was soft and non-tender, and no masses were palpable. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and chemistries, were within normal limits. Upper and lower endoscopy were unremarkable, and abdominal ultrasonography showed no primary lesions. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a dysmorphic, inhomogeneous spleen with multiple millimeter-sized nodular hypodense areas that appeared almost isodense to the adjacent splenic parenchyma during arterial and portal phases (maximum diameter 11 mm).

A 63-year-old man presented with an 8-month history of painless scrotal swelling. Physical examination revealed bilateral testicular enlargement without tenderness. Scrotal ultrasound showed large, solid masses in both testes. Serum β-human chorionic gonadotropin, α-fetoprotein, and lactate dehydrogenase were all within normal limits. To evaluate for lymphoid malignancy, a positron emission tomography–computed tomography scan was performed and showed no evidence of lymphadenopathy or extranodal lymphomatous masses. After multidisciplinary discussion, a left radical inguinal orchiectomy was performed. The specimen contained a 7.0 × 6.0 × 4.2 cm tumor confined to the testis with lymphovascular invasion. Histologic examination demonstrated a pleomorphic tumor composed of three distinct cell types: small cells, medium cells, and large cells.

An 81-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of constipation and a pelvic mass. Her surgical history included a total hysterectomy for uterine myoma and left salpingo-oophorectomy 40 years earlier. She had hypertension, dyslipidemia, and ischemic enteritis. On examination, a pelvic mass was palpable. Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a 10-cm round pelvic mass. Serum CA-125, CA19-9, and carcinoembryonic antigen levels were within normal limits. Unenhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 10 × 10 cm well-circumscribed mass in the central pelvis with areas of isodensity and hypodensity relative to skeletal muscle. MRI demonstrated that the mass was isointense to skeletal muscle on T1-weighted imaging and had mixed low and high signal intensity on T2-weighted imaging. On dynamic gadolinium-enhanced fat-suppressed T1-weighted imaging, there was mild enhancement of the peripheral area in the early phase and increased enhancement in the delayed phase, with central areas of abundant intratumoral vessels. Diffusion-weighted imaging (b = 800 s/mm²) showed heterogeneous high signal in the peripheral enhanced areas, with apparent diffusion coefficient values of 0.60–0.80 × 10⁻³ mm²/s. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen revealed no distant metastases.

An 11-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a 5-month history of a small nasal conjunctival mass in the left eye that did not resolve with topical corticosteroid drops. He had a history of epilepsy treated with carbamazepine for four years; he had no ocular history and no known allergies. On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in each eye. The anterior and posterior segments were normal bilaterally except for an elevated pinkish mass on the nasal bulbar conjunctiva of the left eye. Excisional biopsy under general anesthesia yielded an irregular tan-gray mucosal fragment measuring 0.8 × 0.6 × 0.3 cm. Histologic examination showed a dense nodular lymphoid infiltrate composed of small lymphocytes with irregular nuclear contours and large transformed lymphoid cells with multiple prominent nucleoli; increased tingible body macrophages were present. Immunoperoxidase studies demonstrated that the lymphoid cells were positive for CD20, paired box 5, CD10, and BCL6 and negative for BCL2; Ki-67 immunostaining showed an abnormal nodular pattern with a proliferation index of approximately 30%; T cells appeared morphologically unremarkable, and plasma cells were polytypic.

A 19-year-old warmblood mare was referred for evaluation of her left eye. The owner noted ocular discomfort with blepharospasm and tearing for 14 days; a mass in the anterior chamber was first observed 4 days before referral. The horse’s general health was otherwise unremarkable. On ophthalmic examination, the left pupil was mildly miotic; palpebral reflexes and menace responses were normal bilaterally. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy of the left eye revealed a pink, nonpigmented, rounded, partly lobulated mass arising from the ventrolateral anterior surface of the iris and extending into the anterior chamber, abutting the corneal endothelium ventrally and temporally. The cornea was clear except for mild edema and neovascularization overlying the mass. Conjunctiva and episclera showed mild vascular congestion. Posterior synechiae were present at the margin of the mass, with mild aqueous flare and a cortical equatorial cataract contiguous with the synechiae. Fundic examination was unremarkable. The right eye and adnexa were normal. Schirmer tear tests were 22 mm/min (right) and 25 mm/min (left). Intraocular pressures were 21 mmHg (right) and 12 mmHg (left). Fluorescein staining was negative in both eyes. Transcorneal ultrasonography of the left eye showed a rounded, smooth, well-defined, homogeneous echoic mass (8 mm diameter) arising from the ventrolateral iris and extending into the anterior chamber, with moderate internal vascularization on power Doppler. The lens exhibited a thin echoic line consistent with early cataract; the vitreous and retina were normal.

A 17-year-old woman was admitted with an 8-month history of dyspnea, a 10-day history of dry cough, and a 2-day history of periodic fever without an obvious cause. She had a history of rheumatic disease of unknown origin treated with colchicine and prednisolone for the past 2 years. There was no relevant family history.

On admission, vital signs were: blood pressure 120/90 mmHg, pulse 81 beats/minute, respiratory rate 17 breaths/minute, and temperature 37 °C. Cardiovascular examination revealed a tumor plop at the apex and mild edema of the lower extremities. The remaining examination findings were normal.

Laboratory studies showed: white blood cell count 11,300/µL, hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, hematocrit 35.8%, platelet count 350,000/µL; sodium 141 mmol/L; potassium 4.0 mmol/L. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a pulmonary artery pressure of 45/25 mmHg (mean, 26 mmHg) and right ventricular pressure of 45/26 mmHg, with normal coronary arteries on angiography. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed a moderate pericardial effusion and features of constrictive pericarditis, but this was not felt to be the definitive diagnosis. CT of the chest and brain MRI showed no evidence of metastatic disease. An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm. Chest radiography revealed bilateral pleural edema and a left-sided pleural effusion.

After multidisciplinary consultation, a standard median sternotomy was performed. Upon opening the pericardium, extensive adhesions were noted between the pericardium and the right atrium, which required careful separation. A 4-cm section of pericardial tissue was excised and sent for histopathological analysis.

A 70-year-old woman presented with progressive right upper-eyelid swelling of 6 months’ duration. She had undergone two prior resections of a right upper-eyelid mass at the same site over the preceding 3 years, each followed by local recurrence; adjuvant radiotherapy was administered after the second surgery. On examination, her right visual acuity was count-fingers at 40 cm and 0.6 in the left eye; intraocular pressures were normal. The right upper eyelid was swollen and ptotic, and a firm, 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm movable mass was palpated in the medial aspect of the lid. Slit-lamp examination disclosed a 6 mm × 2 mm ulcer on the temporal cornea and a non-round pupil with extensive posterior synechiae and absent light reflex; the left eye was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced orbital CT revealed a well-defined cystic to solid mass measuring 1.9 cm × 1.9 cm in the superolateral orbit, compressing the lateral aspect of the globe.

A 37-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of fullness and progressive hearing loss in the left ear. She denied tinnitus, otalgia, otorrhea, vertigo, or facial weakness. Otomicroscopy revealed a reddish, easily bleeding hypotympanic mass extending to the medial third of the external auditory canal. Examination of the facial nerves, nasopharynx, oral cavity, larynx, and neck was normal. There was no personal or family history of von Hippel-Lindau disease. Pure-tone audiometry showed moderate pantonal conductive hearing loss in the left ear. CT of the temporal bone demonstrated an irregular, hypodense, expansile lytic lesion of the mastoid portion of the left petrous bone extending into the middle ear, with subtotal erosion of the ossicular chain and tegmen tympani; the semicircular canals, facial nerve canal, and internal auditory canal were spared. MRI showed a lesion of increased signal on T1-weighted images with nonhomogeneous contrast enhancement of the medial middle ear and tubaric region. The patient underwent a canal wall-down tympanoplasty with complete removal of the mass; the postoperative course was uneventful.

A 48-year-old premenopausal woman presented with a 3-month history of distal hypesthesia and pricking paresthesia in the upper extremities that progressed to severe distal-accentuated weakness (Medical Research Council grade 3/5 in upper and 2/5 in lower extremities). All extremities were affected by severe hypesthesia; vibration sense was preserved. She became wheelchair bound and required assistance for activities of daily living (modified Rankin score 4).  

Her medical history was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed normal electrolytes, coagulation profile, renal and liver function, thyroid‐stimulating hormone, C‐reactive protein, and homocysteine, with elevated lipase (68 U/L) and leukocytosis (20.6 G/L). Extended immunologic tests were negative for antinuclear antibodies, anti–double-stranded DNA, ANCA, AMA/LKM-1, cryoglobulins, cold agglutinins, and antineuronal antibodies (anti-Yo, ‑Hu, ‑Ri). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed mild protein elevation (0.59 g/L; normal 0.21–0.42 g/L) without evidence of active infection.  

Nerve conduction studies demonstrated absent sensory potentials in the radial and sural nerves and reduced conduction velocities with decreased compound muscle action–potential amplitudes in the tibial and median nerves. Electromyography of the anterior tibial muscle showed no spontaneous activity. Cranial and spinal MRI and CT of the chest and abdomen were unremarkable.  

To further evaluate, a sural nerve biopsy was performed, revealing advanced axonal neuropathy with moderate microangiopathy. High-dose corticosteroid therapy (75 mg daily) and pregabalin were initiated.

A 53-year-old man with hypertension presented with progressive enlargement of the left testis. He had no history of cancer or cryptorchidism. On examination, the left testis was enlarged and palpated as a mass with irregular borders. Scrotal ultrasound demonstrated a well-circumscribed, hyperechoic lesion measuring approximately 6×6×4 cm within the left testis lobules without evidence of extension to the tunica albuginea or tunica vaginalis. Laboratory studies including lactate dehydrogenase, human chorionic gonadotropin, and alpha fetoprotein were within normal limits.

A 42-year-old Ethiopian woman presented with a 1-year history of dull, aching pain and a slowly enlarging swelling in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen. She denied trauma, changes in bowel or urinary habits, and had no significant past medical or surgical history. On examination, vital signs were normal. There was a tender, nodular mass in the left upper quadrant. 

An abdominopelvic ultrasound scan showed an enlarged spleen (20 cm × 17 cm × 7 cm) containing multiple hypoechoic, variably sized cystic lesions with internal septations and peripheral calcifications. No abnormalities were identified in the pancreas, appendix, liver, bowel, both ovaries, or the peritoneal cavity. Routine laboratory investigations were within normal limits.

A 77-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of persistent right knee pain without recalled trauma. He was suspected to have a degenerative meniscus lesion and, after an intra-articular steroid injection yielded no substantial improvement, underwent arthroscopic partial medial and lateral meniscectomy. Shortly thereafter, he noted a dramatic increase in pain intensity accompanied by soft-tissue swelling, skin color change, and hyperhidrosis of the right knee. On examination, he was afebrile, used two crutches, and walked about 30 m with pain. The right knee showed slight rubor, locally increased skin temperature, and hyperhidrosis. Active and passive range of motion was limited to 40°–20°–0° (flexion/extension). There was tenderness over the medial femoral condyle. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 12.2 g/dl (14.0–18.0), ESR 83 mm/h (≤8), alkaline phosphatase 106 U/l (40–129), and CRP 38.9 mg/l (<5). Plain radiographs showed moderate degenerative changes and an intra-articular effusion. CT demonstrated nonspecific trabecular changes in the medial and lateral femoral condyles. A triple-phase bone scan with Tc-99m-DPD revealed increased activity in the distal femoral diaphysis and epiphysis during the perfusion phase and multiple enhancements in the distal femur, right tibia, and right hemipelvis during the blood-pool and delayed phases.

A 1-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of multiple swellings on the anterior and lateral borders of the tongue. The patient’s mother noted the lesions at birth; they had slowly enlarged without pain, though he was irritated by their presence and had difficulty chewing. There was no history of trauma, infection, or systemic illness. The patient was born to consanguineous parents.

On intraoral examination, there were multiple polypoid masses on the lateral and anterior tongue margins, each 0.5–1.5 cm in diameter, covered with intact mucosa. The lesions were doughy in consistency, non-tender, and showed no pulsations on palpation. Erupting molars and early childhood caries were also noted in the maxillary anterior region. Extraoral examination was normal, and there was no cervical or submandibular lymphadenopathy.

Fiberoptic pharyngeal imaging revealed multiple lipolytic granules. No other abnormalities were detected on general physical examination. After multidisciplinary consultation, the preliminary differential diagnosis included angioedema, neurofibroma, lipoma, fibrolipoma, glandular cell tumor, schwannoma, and dermoid cyst of the tongue.

A 48-year-old man presented with a 5-year history of progressive difficulty urinating and acute urinary retention. On digital rectal examination, his prostate was enlarged, hard, fixed, and nodular, especially on the left. His serum PSA was 0.29 ng/mL (reference range, 0–4 ng/mL). Transrectal prostate biopsy showed sheets of basaloid cells with large pleomorphic nuclei, scant cytoplasm, peripheral palisading, and solid nests infiltrating between benign glandular elements. Immunohistochemical stains demonstrated tumor cell positivity for 34βE12, bcl-2, p63, p53, and a Ki67 labeling index of approximately 70%, with negative staining for PSA, cytokeratin 7, and cytokeratin 20. Pelvic MRI revealed extraprostatic extension with invasion of the bladder wall and rectum.

A 9-year-old healthy girl presented with a 6-month history of a painless, gradually enlarging swelling of the left mandible. She had undergone extraction of the left primary mandibular first molar for the same reason, without trauma, pain, or fever. Medical history was unremarkable. On intraoral examination, there was diffuse buccal expansion from the distal of the left primary canine to the distal of the left primary second molar; the swelling was firm, nontender, and the overlying mucosa appeared normal. There was no lymphadenopathy. An orthopantomogram showed a unilocular radiolucency with well-defined sclerotic borders extending from the left permanent mandibular canine to the mesial of the left permanent first molar, root resorption of the left primary second molar, and displacement of the developing permanent canine, first premolar, and second premolar. 

Initial differential diagnosis: dentigerous cyst, radicular cyst, odontogenic keratocyst, ameloblastoma, odontogenic myxoma, and odontogenic fibroma.

An 11-year-old female neutered domestic shorthair cat was evaluated for a mass on the rostral aspect of the tongue that had been causing difficulty with eating, drinking, and grooming. On oral examination, the lesion was partly exophytic, well demarcated, partially lobulated, and measured approximately 1 cm in diameter. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable, and the owner declined further staging investigations. An excisional biopsy was performed and submitted for histopathological assessment.

A 62-year-old man, lifelong nonsmoker with no history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, or coronary artery disease, presented with a 6-week history of episodic midsternal “burning” chest pain radiating intermittently to his back and associated with dysphagia, abdominal bloating, and palpitations. The pain initially responded to antacids but became persistent and unresponsive. On the day of admission, his prolonged chest discomfort resolved before arrival. 

On presentation, blood pressure was 138/89 mm Hg, heart rate 68 bpm, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with lateral ST-segment and T-wave abnormalities consistent with a non–ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Serial high-sensitivity troponin T levels rose from 84 ng/L to a peak of 123 ng/L before trending to 104 ng/L. Physical examination was unremarkable. 

A chest radiograph was normal. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60% with no regional wall motion abnormalities. Coronary angiography demonstrated an 80% proximal left anterior descending artery stenosis with TIMI-3 flow and no other significant coronary disease. 

The patient was admitted for monitoring. Initial laboratory studies revealed a platelet count exceeding 1,000,000/μL. Prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, and fibrinogen levels were within normal limits, and inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR) were mildly elevated.

A 19-year-old woman with a history of right temporal lobe surgery for a dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor at age 16 presented with recurrent seizures. She had initially experienced focal seizures at age 13 and underwent complete resection of a right temporal tumor in 2019. Serial MRIs over the next two years showed no residual or recurrent lesion.  
Three years after surgery, she developed pharmacoresistant epileptic seizures characterized by loss of consciousness and right-sided limb paresthesia.  
Noncontrast head CT and cerebral MRI demonstrated a right hemispheric intra-axial mass measuring 11 cm in height, with ringlike temporal enhancement and serpiginous neovascular structures. There was no significant perilesional edema, but subfalcine and temporal herniation were noted. Proton MR spectroscopy revealed moderate peaks of myoinositol, N-acetyl aspartate, and lactate, interpreted as favoring an infiltrating glioma with areas of degeneration. Preoperative diffusion tensor tractography showed distortion of the right arcuate fasciculus and rarefaction of adjacent white matter fibers, with displacement but preservation of corticospinal tracts; interhemispheric and pontine fibers were intact.

A 6-year-old boy presented with 30 hours of acute abdominal pain, fever, and vomiting. He was hemodynamically stable. On examination, he had right lower quadrant tenderness, a positive McBurney sign, and signs of peritoneal irritation. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, hematocrit 34.6%, mean corpuscular volume 72.7 fL, mean corpuscular hemoglobin 24.7 pg, leukocyte count 15,110/μL, platelet count 279,000/μL, and C-reactive protein 3.81 mg/dL; electrolytes and coagulation were normal.  
Ultrasonography demonstrated a well-defined, hypoechogenic solid mass measuring 6 × 2 cm in the right iliac fossa; the appendix, liver, and kidneys appeared normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a nonenhancing, solid fusiform mass measuring 6 × 2.4 cm, abutting the ascending colon at one end and the small bowel at the other. Imaging excluded acute appendicitis and Meckel’s diverticulum.  
Emergency laparoscopy revealed a pedunculated solid mass attached to the antimesenteric edge of the ileum, 8 cm proximal to the ileocecal valve, covered by inflammatory omentum and appearing ischemic from torsion. The omental covering was resected, and the mass with adjacent ileum was exteriorized and separated; the ileal wall was normal.

A 47-year-old premenopausal, nulliparous woman was referred for evaluation of an abdominal mass and intermittent abdominal pain. Her medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and fatty liver; she was under treatment for diabetes and hypertension. Physical examination was unremarkable, and no rebound tenderness was noted. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed a 77 × 60 × 51 mm multilocular mass adjacent to the right side of the uterus and moderate ascites; the right ovary was not visualized. Serum tumor markers, including CEA, CA 72-4, CA 19-9, and CA 125, were normal. Cytologic examination of bloody ascites showed no malignant cells. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a heterogeneous mass next to the uterus with isodense peripheral and septal components and hypodense central areas. MRI revealed a lesion with low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, high-signal areas on T2-weighted images, and enhancement of peripheral and septal portions on fat-saturated, gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted images; no fat component was identified. The right ovary remained unseen, and the left ovary appeared enlarged. Based on imaging, a right ovarian mucinous tumor was suspected. Two weeks later, the mass size decreased to 50 × 47 × 46 mm with resolution of ascites; two months after onset, it increased slightly to 60 × 50 × 50 mm without new symptoms, and surgical resection was planned. One week later, the patient developed sudden severe abdominal pain, and emergency surgery was scheduled for presumed torsion of the tumor pedicle.

A 50-year-old para 2 woman with a history of stage I breast cancer treated 8 years earlier (lumpectomy, axillary lymph node dissection, adjuvant chemotherapy, radiation, and 5 years of tamoxifen) presented with several weeks of abdominopelvic pain and soreness. She denied abnormal uterine bleeding and was thought to have no evidence of breast cancer recurrence.

Pelvic ultrasonography revealed a 15-cm complex mass in the right lower quadrant. Contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT demonstrated a markedly enlarged uterus with an ill-defined mass in the right adnexa contiguous with the uterine fundus, findings suggestive of possible sarcoma. Serum CA-125 was elevated at 407 U/mL.

She underwent diagnostic laparoscopy followed by exploratory laparotomy, radical hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, omentectomy, and debulking. Intraoperatively, a 15-cm necrotic mass was noted arising from the uterine fundus; frozen-section analysis reported a poorly differentiated carcinoma of unknown etiology. The omentum was grossly and microscopically negative for malignancy.

Histologic sections of the uterine mass showed a poorly circumscribed, infiltrative tumor composed of epithelioid and spindle cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, scant cytoplasm, extensive geographic necrosis, and angiocentric areas forming pseudorosettes. Immunohistochemical staining was strongly positive for CD99, Fli-1, and Vimentin.

A 34-year-old G4P3003 woman presented with a 1-week history of vaginal bleeding and right lower abdominal pain that intensified a day before admission. Her last menstrual period was 2 months earlier. Vital signs: blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, pulse 98/min, respiratory rate 18/min, temperature 37°C. Abdominal examination showed mild right lower-quadrant tenderness with rebound. Speculum exam revealed active bleeding from the cervical os. Bimanual exam demonstrated cervical motion tenderness and right adnexal tenderness without a palpable mass. Laboratory studies: serum β-hCG 14 000 IU/L (normal 0–5 IU/L), hemoglobin 8.0 g/dL (normal 12.1–15.1 g/dL). Transvaginal ultrasonography showed a 7-week gestational sac in the right adnexa, moderate free pelvic fluid with internal echoes, and no fetal pole. A presumptive diagnosis of ruptured right tubal pregnancy was made, and the patient underwent an emergency laparotomy. Intraoperatively, there was 500 cc of clot and fresh blood in the pelvis; the uterus and left adnexa appeared normal. A right salpingectomy was performed, and one unit of packed red blood cells was transfused. The patient was discharged in good condition on postoperative day 1. Two weeks later, her β-hCG level was 12 000 IU/L.

A 48-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of progressive headache and blurring of vision. Physical and neurologic examinations were unremarkable. Routine laboratory studies, including a pituitary hormonal profile, were normal. Non-contrast CT of the brain demonstrated a large, extra-axial, sellar and left parasellar mass that was isodense to slightly hyperdense without calcification or necrosis. It effaced the prepontine cistern and caused smooth bone remodeling with erosion of the medial sphenoid wing, but no hyperostosis. MRI with gadolinium revealed a well-demarcated, dumbbell-shaped extra-axial lesion measuring 5.2×4.3 cm, displacing the temporal lobe laterally and extending into the sellar and suprasellar regions. The mass was hypointense on T1, markedly hyperintense on T2, showed initial heterogeneous enhancement on axial post-contrast images followed by homogeneous intense enhancement on subsequent coronal and sagittal sequences, exhibited no diffusion restriction or GRE blooming, and encased the cavernous internal carotid artery without occlusion. The preoperative neuroradiologic differential diagnosis included trigeminal schwannoma, meningioma, and pituitary macroadenoma with parasellar extension.

A 77-year-old woman presented with a two-week history of progressive shortness of breath and acute-onset palpitations and chest pain, and with acute confusion for two days before admission. Her history included a chest infection treated five months earlier, a transient ischemic attack four years ago, rheumatoid arthritis, and osteoarthritis. On examination she was afebrile, normotensive, and had an irregularly irregular pulse at 150 beats per minute. Cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable. An electrocardiogram showed fast atrial fibrillation. She was started on digoxin, warfarin, and a beta blocker. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a mobile mass in the left atrium. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed a 2.7 cm × 3.5 cm mobile mass attached to the fossa ovalis region of the inter-atrial septum, prolapsing into the left ventricle through the mitral valve in diastole.

A 64-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after being found unconscious at home with “generalized shaking,” without trauma or incontinence. He recovered spontaneously, was hemodynamically stable and afebrile, and had a normal neurologic examination. Arterial blood gas testing showed normoglycemia and no acid–base or electrolyte disturbances. Laboratory studies revealed a mildly elevated serum creatine kinase level of 762 U/L (reference <145), with normal renal and hepatic function and a normal complete blood count. Noncontrast brain CT demonstrated a well-defined hyperdense lesion measuring 20.8 × 14.5 mm in the right temporal fossa, producing mass effect on the adjacent temporal lobe, without ventricular involvement, edema, structural deviation, skull fracture, or hemorrhage. An electroencephalogram showed generalized epileptiform activity arising from the right temporal lobe.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of a right breast mass. She had undergone augmentation mammoplasty with textured implants 15 years earlier. Her family history was significant for leukemia in a paternal aunt. She had smoked one cigarette daily for 5 years but had quit one year ago. Her only medication was an antihistamine as needed for seasonal allergic rhinitis. 

On examination, bilateral periareolar scars were noted. In the right breast, a 5-cm palpable mass was present in the lower medial quadrant, along with right axillary lymphadenopathy; the overlying skin was normal. The left breast and axilla were unremarkable. 

Diagnostic imaging with mammography and ultrasound identified a 5-cm lesion in the lower medial quadrant of the right breast classified as BI-RADS 5 (high suspicion of malignancy). A breast MRI demonstrated a right periprosthetic breast mass.

An 11-month-old girl, meeting developmental milestones, was brought with a 1-month history of a subcutaneous mass in the sacrococcygeal region. The overlying skin was stretched but mobile; the mass was firm with limited mobility. There was no urinary or bowel dysfunction.  
Ultrasonography revealed a 6.5 × 6 × 5.5-cm solid mass with cystic components in the sacrococcygeal area.  
Pelvic MRI (T2-weighted axial and coronal images) showed a 6 × 5.8 × 5-cm midline posterior pelvis mass straddling the sacrococcyx in a dumbbell configuration, with nearly equal pre- and post-sacral portions. The lesion insinuated around the rectum and extended posteriorly and laterally to the urinary bladder. No pelvic lymphadenopathy was noted.  
Provisional clinical and radiological diagnosis: sacrococcygeal teratoma, Altman type II.

A 55-year-old woman with a history of primary ovarian insufficiency treated for osteoporosis presented after a routine test showed severe hypercalcemia. She was dehydrated but alert, with a blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg and a pulse of 70 beats per minute; ECG findings were normal. Laboratory studies revealed a serum calcium of 3.43 mmol/L (normal 2.2–2.6), phosphate 0.53 mmol/L (0.74–1.50), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 12.5 ng/mL (30–50), albumin 43 g/L, and PTH 1325.6 pg/mL (10–55). Renal function was normal; 24-hour urine calcium was 6.44 mmol (normal ≤5.7). Neck ultrasound demonstrated a 2.05 × 3.97 × 3.18 cm heterogeneous hyperechoic mass near the left thyroid lobe, and a ^99mTc-sestamibi scan localized uptake to the left inferior parathyroid region. Given the large lesion and biochemical severity, markers of malignancy were checked: alkaline phosphatase 420 IU/L (44–147) and βHCG 4.09 mIU/mL (<5).

A 68-year-old man with obesity, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, gout, diabetes mellitus, nephrolithiasis, and benign prostatic hyperplasia treated with dutasteride presented with an elevated serum prostate-specific antigen level of 6.68 ng/mL without urinary symptoms. His family history was notable for breast cancer in a maternal grandmother at age 92. Digital rectal examination revealed no suspicious nodules. Prostate multiparametric MRI showed a PIRADS 5 lesion in the right transition zone; subsequent MRI/transrectal ultrasound fusion biopsy demonstrated Gleason score 5+4=9 (grade group 5) prostate cancer. One month after diagnosis, staging with 18F-PSMA-PET/CT showed intense uptake in the prostate (SUVmax 32.6) and an additional focus along the right anterior chest wall (SUVmax 7.7). Physical examination of the breasts was unremarkable. A diagnostic bilateral mammogram showed no masses, calcifications, or other abnormalities. Targeted ultrasound of the right breast revealed a 1.5 × 2.1 × 1.8 cm irregular hypoechoic mass with spiculated margins, posterior shadowing, and abutment of the pectoralis muscle; no internal vascularity or axillary adenopathy was observed. The lesion was characterized as suspicious, and a core needle biopsy was recommended.

A 65-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of progressively worsening dysphonia and a 3-month history of mild dysphagia. He had no respiratory distress or constitutional symptoms. Flexible laryngeal fiberscopy revealed a reddish, pedunculated, voluminous mass arising from the left false vocal cord and extending into the ventricle, without compromise of the airway. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy on neck examination. Under general anesthesia, direct suspension laryngoscopy with a CO2 laser was performed, and the lesion was widely excised, preserving the true vocal cord.

A 64-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a longstanding mass and progressive weakness of his left upper extremity. More than 30 years earlier, he had undergone surgery and was told he had a brachial plexus tumor, but no records were available. He was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus 2 years ago. Five years ago, he noticed muscle weakness in his left arm that gradually worsened until, 2 years ago, the arm was nearly nonfunctional and he was referred to our hospital.

On examination, there was a biloculate, palpable mass in the left supraclavicular region. Tinel’s sign over the mass elicited paresthesia in the left arm. There were no café-au-lait spots or other cutaneous stigmata of neurofibromatosis type I, and no other masses were palpable. Manual muscle testing of the left upper extremity revealed marked weakness in muscles innervated by the axillary, musculocutaneous, and median nerves; the ulnar-innervated muscles were preserved. Sensory examination showed loss in distributions of the axillary nerve, the lateral brachial cutaneous nerve, and the median nerve. A cervical spine radiograph was unremarkable.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brachial plexus showed a continuous, multinodular, plexiform mass extending from the left C5–C7 nerve roots along the course of the brachial plexus into the arm. The lesion was isointense with muscle on T1-weighted images, slightly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed no enhancement after gadolinium administration. There was no involvement of the spinal canal.

A 45-year-old Caucasian woman was referred for evaluation of a left groin mass. She reported two months of aching, soreness, and heaviness in both lower extremities. Her medical history included thyroidectomy for multinodular goiter (on levothyroxine) and hypertension (on amlodipine and valsartan). She denied trauma and tobacco use.  
 
Lower-extremity venous duplex ultrasonography performed for venous insufficiency revealed on the right side saphenofemoral junction insufficiency and on the left side a 50×55 mm solid hypoechoic mass of heterogeneous texture, 11 mm beneath the skin, with minimal blood flow, abutting but not compressing the femoral vessels; no lymphadenopathy was noted.  

On examination, she had a painless, fixed, solid left groin mass; both legs had normal symmetry and motility.  

Pelvic MRI showed a lobulated 78×59×45 mm mass situated between the pectineus anteriorly, the adductor muscles posteriorly, the obturator laterally, and the innominate bone medially. The lesion had heterogeneous low signal on T1-weighted images, heterogeneous high signal with internal low-signal areas on T2-weighted images, relatively well-defined margins, and no enhancement after intravenous gadolinium.  

Chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasonography of the upper and lower abdomen were unremarkable.  

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, metabolic panel, liver and kidney function tests, electrolytes, amylase, coagulation profile, and thyroid function, were within normal limits. Tumor markers were obtained: α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, CA 15-3, CA 19.9, and CA 125; CA 19.9 was elevated at 39.51 U/mL (reference 0–35 U/mL) on three separate measurements.

A 79-year-old man was admitted with a 1-month history of progressive bilateral lower-limb weakness and a several-day history of dysuria. He had undergone total gastrectomy for gastric cancer 7 months earlier, followed by adjuvant chemotherapy with S-1 and cisplatin. On examination, muscle strength was Medical Research Council grade 3/5 in bilateral iliopsoas, quadriceps, tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, and flexor hallucis longus muscles. Sensation was diminished to 1/10 below the T4 dermatome. Deep-tendon reflexes were normal; plantar responses were flexor bilaterally. A bladder catheter drained 1400 mL of urine. 

Laboratory tests showed WBC 4,200/µL, CRP 0.6 mg/dL, hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, platelets 109,000/µL, LDH 275 IU/L, AST 33 IU/L, ALT 59 IU/L, ALP 355 IU/L, calcium 8.0 mg/dL, CEA 15.2 ng/mL, CA19-9 1420 U/mL, and AFP 1034 ng/mL. 

Cerebrospinal fluid was clear, with 32 cells/µL (polymorphonuclear leukocytes 81%, mononuclear cells 19%), glucose 104 mg/dL, protein 181 mg/dL, CEA <0.50 ng/mL, and cytology Class I. 

Plain thoracic spine radiographs were unremarkable. Thoracic MRI revealed a low-to-isointense lesion on T1 and an iso-to-high-intensity mass dorsal to the dura at T2–4, causing posterior cord compression. Head, chest, and abdominal CT and PET showed no other mass lesions.

A 19-year-old man was admitted with a 2-week history of headaches, episodes of hyperventilation, and new-onset focal seizures. He had no significant medical or family history and no prior radiation exposure. On examination he was in postictal recovery; higher mental functions were intact, and he had a left upper-extremity paresis. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed a 5×6×6-cm mass in the right precentral gyrus. Corticospinal fibers and motor areas were displaced anteriorly and posteriorly around the lesion. The mass was of intermediate signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, with heterogeneous, honeycomb enhancement after contrast. The patient underwent a right parietal craniotomy. The overlying dura was irregularly distended but not adherent to bone; the inner table was drilled without full removal. The tumor was dissected easily from the cortex and was entirely removed in piecemeal fashion. Grossly, the specimen was multinodular, ivory-colored, and had a distinctly cartilaginous consistency.

An 18‐year‐old man presented with a painless mass of the left hard palate. He had noticed a slowly enlarging palatal swelling over 2 years, with recent rapid growth. His medical history was notable only for febrile seizures in infancy; family history was unremarkable. Examination showed facial symmetry, no cervical lymphadenopathy, and a dome‐shaped, partially ulcerated, elastic‐hard mass measuring 4.0×3.0 cm on the left hard palate, extending posteriorly toward the soft palate.  

Panoramic radiograph revealed left maxillary sinus opacity, an impacted posterior tooth, and descent of the sinus floor. CT showed a well‐demarcated, multilocular expansile radiolucent lesion in the left maxillary sinus with the impacted tooth in the posterior wall, without cortical perforation. MRI demonstrated a nonhomogeneous, mildly enhancing lesion in the left hard palate and alveolar process, and a separate highly enhancing homogeneous lesion in the left maxillary sinus. No cervical, thoracic, or abdominal lymphadenopathy or lesions were identified.  

An incisional biopsy of the palatal mass showed epithelium composed primarily of squamous cells with focal clear cells, ghost cells, and calcifications. These findings, combined with the impacted tooth, led to consideration of calcifying epithelial odontogenic tumor or calcifying odontogenic cyst.

A 16-year-old previously healthy male noted right-sided nasal obstruction for 3 months, worse at night, with hyposmia, intermittent bloody rhinorrhea, and retronasal discharge.
