He subsequently developed right hemicranial headache, facial heaviness, retro-ocular pressure with movement, hyponasal speech, nighttime snoring, and occasional mild epistaxis. He also reported months of cough, fatigue, and one month of episodic nausea, vomiting, and dizziness. Prior evaluations by general practitioners, gastroenterology, and otoneurology were non-diagnostic. Six months after symptom onset, he was referred for otolaryngology evaluation.

On endoscopic nasal examination, there was left septal deviation and turbinate hypertrophy. A pinkish-pearl, smooth, vascularized ovoid mass hung from the posterior middle meatus on the right, occupying the choana; early nasopharyngeal extension was seen on retrograde endoscopy. Oral cavity, pharynx, and otoscopic examinations were normal. Complete blood count and basic chemistry were within normal limits.

Contrast CT of the skull and paranasal sinuses showed a right-sided hypervascular mass in the depth of the nasal passage insinuating into the sphenoparietal (pterygopalatine) fossa, with associated inflammatory changes in the maxillary sinuses. MRI of the skull and facial soft tissues confirmed a 2 × 3 × 5 cm right nasal and nasopharyngeal mass without intracranial invasion.

A 33-year-old Japanese woman presented with two months of right upper quadrant abdominal pain. She had no significant medical history. Laboratory studies showed slightly elevated γ-glutamyl transpeptidase and C-reactive protein levels; serum levels of CEA, CA19-9, AFP, and PIVKA-II were within normal limits. Tests for hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody were negative.  
Conventional abdominal ultrasonography revealed multiple low-echoic liver nodules with vague margins, some coalescing at the periphery. Contrast-enhanced CT in the arterial phase demonstrated multiple low-density liver nodules suggestive of hypovascular tumors. Chest CT showed multiple small lung nodules. On MRI, the hepatic lesions were hyperintense centrally on T2-weighted imaging; on diffusion-weighted imaging (b = 1000 sec/mm2), the peripheral portions were hyperintense, while the centers were hypointense on the ADC map. Gastrointestinal endoscopy and colonoscopy showed no evidence of primary malignancy.

A 41-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of right upper quadrant abdominal pain and a palpable mass. The pain was constant, worsened when seated, and associated with periodic nausea, vomiting, and dyspnea when supine. She reported an 8.8-kg weight loss over this period. Her medical history was notable for appendectomy and empirical treatment with albendazole (400 mg twice daily) for a presumed hydatid cyst. Family history was noncontributory. 

On examination, vital signs were stable (heart rate 83 beats/min, temperature 37.4 °C, blood pressure 125/69 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min). Abdominal palpation revealed a firm, well-defined, horizontally mobile subhepatic mass measuring approximately 10 cm without point tenderness. Laboratory studies, including liver function tests, were within normal limits. 

Abdominopelvic ultrasonography showed a single subhepatic cyst measuring 76 × 87 × 15 cm with internal septations and an estimated volume of 523 cm3; the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 130 × 80 × 54 cm cystic mass in the left hepatic lobe with internal septations. Given the imaging findings and the high regional prevalence of echinococcal disease, the patient was scheduled for laparoscopic resection of a presumed hydatid cyst.

A 76-year-old man presented with one month of progressive lower extremity weakness leading to falls and two days of bladder and bowel incontinence. He also reported chronic intense back pain, lower extremity numbness and tingling, and unquantified weight loss over six months. He had emigrated from Peru seven years earlier and had limited medical care. His history included iron deficiency anemia, cholecystectomy, hernia repair, and prostatectomy for presumed benign prostatic hyperplasia.

On examination, lower extremity strength was 1/5 with absent reflexes and absent pain, temperature, and proprioception. Upper extremity strength was 3/5 with intact sensation except mild paresthesia. He had mild saddle anesthesia and spinal tenderness. Other findings were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, BUN-to-creatinine ratio 28:1.2 mg/dL, total protein 5.8 g/dL, albumin 3.2 g/dL, alkaline phosphatase 142 U/L, and normal calcium and coagulation parameters.

Imaging included a normal chest radiograph and noncontrast head CT. MRI of the lumbar spine with gadolinium revealed L2–L3 and L4–L5 disc protrusions and multiple foci of abnormal bone marrow signal. MRI of the cervical spine showed a large mass at C7–T1 with destruction of three vertebral bodies, epidural extension, severe cord compression, and cord edema. CT of the neck, thorax, and abdomen did not identify a primary neoplasm but confirmed the cervicothoracic mass with hemorrhagic areas and numerous well-defined lytic lesions throughout the axial and appendicular skeleton. Common tumor markers (CEA, CA 19-9, PSA) were normal.

A 68-year-old woman with a history of chronic hepatitis C, hypertension, hypothyroidism, and diverticulosis presented with 4 weeks of belching and abdominal bloating and an unintentional 5-lb weight loss over several months. She had no fever, night sweats, or pain. On examination she was icteric; the abdomen was soft without masses or organomegaly. Initial laboratory tests showed:  
• Chemistry: Na 134 mEq/L, K 4.1 mEq/L, creatinine 0.87 mg/dL, glucose 66 mg/dL  
• Liver tests: ALT 133 U/L, AST 207 U/L, ALP 203 U/L, total bilirubin 12.1 mg/dL (direct 8.0 mg/dL), albumin 3.5 g/dL  
• CBC: WBC 11.7×10^9/L, hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, platelets 288×10^9/L  
• CA19-9: 57 U/mL (modestly elevated)  

Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a heterogeneous right hepatic lobe mass and a 2.8-cm hypoechoic mass in the adjacent pancreatic head. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 7.5×4.9×12.7 cm periportal solid mass that obstructed the central hepatic ducts and encased the main portal vein, appearing inseparable from the pancreatic head.  
Attempts at ERCP were unsuccessful; IR placed a transpapillary biliary drain, but persistent leakage around the drain led to internalization of biliary stents.

A 71-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of ulcerated tumors on her face that had increased in number and size.  
Her medical history was notable for rheumatoid arthritis concurrent with polymyositis for 17 years. She had received methotrexate, 10 mg weekly, since the onset of rheumatoid arthritis and, 3 years ago, tofacitinib, 5 mg daily, was added; she had been off systemic prednisolone for 3 years.  
She complained of severe pruritus. On examination, there were partially ulcerated, crusted tumors measuring 2–5 cm in diameter on the forehead, left cheek, philtrum, and chin.  
A skin biopsy showed diffuse proliferation of atypical lymphocytes in the dermis and subcutaneous tissue. Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated positive staining for CD20, CD79a, CD30, and Epstein–Barr virus–encoded RNA in situ hybridization.

A 17-year-old male presented with a 6-year history of episodes beginning with an aura of blurred affect followed by involuntary movements of the lips and tongue lasting 4–5 seconds, accompanied by postictal confusion and headache. Seizure frequency increased from once monthly to 4–6 times daily. He denied generalized convulsions, tongue bite, incontinence, or symptoms of raised intracranial pressure. Neurologic examination was normal. Brain MRI revealed a 5.8 × 5.5 × 5.2 cm right temporal lobe mass that was T1 hypointense, T2 heterogeneous hyperintense, cystic with thin septations, showed mild patchy diffusion restriction, lacked a solid component, and exhibited peripheral wall enhancement with mass effect on adjacent sulci and the ipsilateral temporal horn.

A 26-year-old man presented with a 5-year history of dysuria and progressive abdominal distension, along with rectal mucosal prolapse. Over the past year, he developed difficulty walking and impaired leg movement. He had no history of urinary tract infection. On examination, he was anemic and had multiple café-au-lait macules over the abdomen. The prostate-specific antigen level was 1.74 ng/mL (normal). 

Abdominal ultrasound revealed multiple well-defined, oval hypoechoic lesions with a hyperechoic center and hypoechoic rim (“target sign”) extending from the abdominal to pelvic cavity. In the pelvis, a large heteroechoic, hypovascular mass filled the abdominal and pelvic cavities. 

Contrast-enhanced CT scans showed bilateral, symmetrical, lobulated low-attenuation masses occupying intraperitoneal, extraperitoneal, intramuscular, and intermuscular spaces with vascular encasement. A large pelvic mass arising from the prostate demonstrated variable contrast enhancement and displaced the bladder anterosuperiorly. 

On MRI, the prostate mass extended into the pelvic cavity; there was extensive enlargement of a fusiform mass at the lumbosacral nerve roots and multiple plexiform lesions in intramuscular and extraperitoneal areas compressing adjacent organs. The masses were heterogeneous on T2-weighted images, exhibited the target sign, and were low-signal on T1-weighted images. The prostate lesion had solid and necrotic areas with heterogeneous enhancement on gadolinium-enhanced sequences.

A 28-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of continuous right posterior chest pain that responded poorly to analgesics. On examination, there was a right-sided pleural friction rub; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a platelet count of 511 000/mm3, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 79 mm, and a C-reactive protein level of 9.24 mg/dL; hepatic and renal function and the rest of the blood count were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography and a chest radiograph were normal. Computed tomography of the thorax demonstrated right posterior pleural thickening, a small pleural effusion, and adjacent passive atelectasis. Further investigations revealed negative interferon‐gamma release assay in peripheral blood and negative sputum and blood cultures. Tests for HIV antibodies and autoantibodies (ANA, ANCA, and anti–double‐stranded DNA) were negative. Quantitation of IgG subclasses was within normal limits, with an IgG4 level at the lower limit of normal (6.0 mg/dL). Culture of fluid obtained by CT-guided thoracentesis was negative for bacteria (including Legionella), Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and fungi. Cytology and histology of a percutaneous pleural biopsy showed nonspecific inflammatory cells without evidence of malignancy. The patient underwent surgical resection of the pleural mass, which measured 3 × 9 cm. Histopathological examination revealed an inflammatory hypocellular sclerosing process with scattered lymphoid aggregates and no granulomas, calcifications, or neoplastic cells. Immunohistochemical studies showed strong focal positivity for vimentin and nonspecific actin, focal positivity for factor XIIIa, and negativity for anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK), CD34, and calretinin.

A 70-year-old man presented with fatigue, headache, and arthralgia of recent onset. He had no fever, weight loss, night sweats, adenopathy, splenomegaly, or bone pain. Vital signs were normal. Neurologic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed total serum protein 10 700 mg/L, IgM 7665 mg/L, and an M-spike of 4600 mg/L (43.3%) on protein electrophoresis. Serum creatinine and calcium were normal. Hemoglobin was 9.5 g/dL (macrocytic anemia); platelet and leukocyte counts were normal. β2-Microglobulin was 3.15 mg/dL. Bone marrow biopsy revealed 65–70% clonal plasma cells that were CD138+, CD79a+, monoclonal κ-light chain–restricted, IgM+, cyclin D1+, CD20−, CD45−/+, CD56−. Testing for MYD88 L265P mutation was negative, and fluorescence in situ hybridization showed translocation t(11;14). Low-dose CT of the skeleton and chest/abdomen showed no lytic bone lesions, lymphadenopathy, or organomegaly.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of a gradually progressive, painless swelling of the left lower eyelid. She had undergone incision and curettage twice for a presumed chalazion elsewhere, but the swelling recurred and increased in size after each procedure. There was no history of similar lesions elsewhere and no significant family history. On examination, there was a firm, nontender, nonmobile nodular mass measuring 10 × 10 × 8 mm, fixed to the underlying tarsus, with normal overlying skin. Eversion of the eyelid revealed scarring of the tarsal conjunctiva. The remainder of the anterior and posterior segment examinations of both eyes and the systemic examination were unremarkable. A full-thickness excisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia, and the eyelid defect was repaired with a Tenzel semicircular flap. The specimen was sent for histopathological examination.

A 21-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a painful lesion arising within a black tattoo on his right arm. The tattoo had been placed 2 years earlier. He had no other significant medical history. On examination, there was a single, light-red, firm, tender, mobile nodule measuring 10 mm in diameter embedded in the black-inked dermis. A punch biopsy of the lesion was performed. Microscopic examination showed a nodular proliferation in the dermis consisting of numerous collagen and fibroblastic-like cells in an irregular arrangement, with no cytological atypia. Extracellular deposits of black ink pigment were evident within the lesion, and the overlying epidermis was acanthotic with basal hyperpigmentation. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for factor XIIIa and CD68 and negative for CD34, S-100, and actin.

A 48-year-old woman with a penicillin allergy presented with a progressively enlarging right cheek mass. Five years earlier, a similar soft-tissue lesion had been excised and diagnosed as a lipoma. Eight months after that excision, she noted recurrence of a firm, rounded, well-circumscribed, non-tender mass of about 4.5 cm in the right lower jugal region, causing facial asymmetry but with normal overlying skin and mucosa. No regional lymphadenopathy was present. Facial CT showed a well-defined, oval, fat-density lesion in the right jugal soft tissues, measuring 44 × 20 mm and extending 48 mm, crossed by linear septa, abutting the superficial cervical fascia and contacting the masseter without invasion.

A 60-year-old man presented with a 5-year history of low back pain radiating to his right leg, with aggravation over the past month. He had been previously diagnosed with lumbar disc herniation. He reported no urinary or fecal incontinence. On examination, lumbar motion was limited; there was tenderness and percussion pain over the L2–L4 spinous processes. Lower-extremity muscle strength was grade 4 bilaterally, with normal tone. There were no superficial or deep sensory deficits in the hips, anterior thighs, knees, or below. The right straight-leg–raising test was positive at 60°, and the right femoral-nerve stretch test was positive. His preoperative Japanese Orthopedic Association lumbar score was 8, Oswestry Disability Index score was 27, and visual-analogue scale scores were 6 for lumbar pain and 7 for leg pain. MRI of the lumbar spine demonstrated an oval, well-circumscribed, dorsal epidural mass at L2–L3 causing marked spinal-cord compression. The lesion was isointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, occupying approximately 75% of the spinal canal and located on the right.

A 29-year-old woman with a history of breast fibroadenoma and an ovarian juvenile-type granulosa cell tumor at age 14 presented after two episodes of disorientation, global aphasia, and left-sided facial and lower extremity numbness with paresthesias. She remained conscious during both episodes, was briefly somnolent afterward, and then returned to baseline. She reported two weeks of intermittent headaches and denied trauma, prior seizures, visual changes, gait instability, or systemic illness. Her last menstrual period was 2 days earlier. She drank alcohol socially, never smoked, and denied drug use.  
On examination, temperature was 99.0°F, blood pressure 125/77 mm Hg, pulse 98/min, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO₂ 99%, and BMI 31.8. She was alert, oriented, and had no focal neurologic deficits.  
MRI of the brain with and without contrast revealed a 1.5-cm intra-axial anterior left temporal lobe mass that was isointense on T1, hyperintense on T2, showed ring enhancement on postcontrast T1, and had surrounding vasogenic edema on FLAIR. A continuous EEG showed no epileptiform discharges.  
Given her oncologic history, a metastatic workup was performed. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed a 1.4 × 2.2 cm left breast fibroadenoma. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated physiologic ovarian cysts in the remaining ovary. Serum tumor markers were all within normal limits (CA-125 17 U/mL, CEA 1.4 ng/mL, inhibin A 4 pg/mL, inhibin B 32 pg/mL).

A 39-year-old woman presented with periodic left facial convulsions for more than 3 months, accompanied by a mild headache, twitching of the left masticatory muscle, and difficulty opening her mouth during episodes. There was no dizziness, facial numbness, nausea, or vomiting. Her medical history was notable for a partial thyroidectomy 2 years earlier for papillary thyroid cancer with lymph node metastases. Vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, she was alert and cooperative, with normal heart, lung, abdominal, and neurologic findings. Facial electromyography, lateral spread response, and somatosensory evoked potentials were approximately normal.

Noncontrast CT of the head showed a circular, well-circumscribed mass in the left parasellar region that was predominantly hyperdense with patchy hypodense areas, without surrounding edema. Bone-window images demonstrated compression of adjacent bone without destruction.

Multimodal MRI revealed that the lesion was heterogeneously hyperintense on T1-weighted sequences and heterogeneously hypointense on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences. The patchy hypodense areas on CT corresponded to regions that were hypointense on T1 and hyperintense on T2 and FLAIR. There was no contrast enhancement. Arterial spin labeling showed decreased perfusion within the lesion. On diffusion-weighted imaging, most of the tumor was hypointense relative to normal brain parenchyma and demonstrated an elevated apparent diffusion coefficient, while a small portion had DWI and ADC values similar to normal tissue. Susceptibility-weighted imaging showed no areas of signal reduction. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy was unsuccessful due to field inhomogeneity. Digital subtraction angiography and magnetic resonance angiography showed no tumor staining or vascular abnormalities.

A 24-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of right nasal obstruction, right eye pain, and lower eyelid swelling with orbital fullness. Endoscopic examination revealed an obstructive, soft-tissue mass occupying the right nasal cavity. Cranial-nerve examination was intact. Hematologic and biochemical tests were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses showed an enhancing soft-tissue lesion in the right ethmoid sinus eroding the medial wall and orbital floor. MRI demonstrated an infiltrative soft-tissue mass in the right ethmoid sinus with erosion of the inferomedial orbital wall and extension into the extraconal space. PET imaging revealed an ill-defined 4.5 × 4.2 cm mass in the right nasal cavity and ethmoid sinus extending to the medial orbital floor, without evidence of lymphadenopathy.

A 53‐year‐old woman presented with a two‐year history of a gradually enlarging mass in her right breast. She had no comorbidities or family history of cancer but had undergone right hemimandibulectomy with bone grafting for ameloblastoma 15 years earlier. 

On examination, the lesion measured 16 × 13 cm, involved the upper chest wall and the right side of the neck, and there was no palpable lymphadenopathy. 

Contrast‐enhanced computed tomography of the chest demonstrated a heterogeneous solid and cystic mass in the superior region of the right breast measuring 15 × 15 × 10 cm, with extension into the pectoralis major muscle but no other masses or lymphadenopathy. 

A punch biopsy of the breast lesion was performed, yielding a spindle‐cell neoplasm.

A 53-year-old woman with a history of hypertension presented with episodic holocranial headaches associated with vomiting. Neurologic examination was unremarkable, with no focal deficits. A noncontrast CT scan of the brain showed a well-defined extra-axial lesion measuring approximately 6.0×2.2×4.4 cm in the left frontal parasagittal convexity region, with peripheral specks of calcification and hyperostosis of the overlying bone, causing effacement of the left frontal lobe. MRI revealed that the lesion was isointense on T1-weighted images, hypointense on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences, and showed peripheral rim and central foci of enhancement on postcontrast images. There was no diffusion restriction, and arterial spin labeling perfusion imaging demonstrated hypoperfusion. The mass was abutting the superior sagittal sinus. A working diagnosis of a meningioma or a solitary fibrous tumor was made.

A 26-year-old woman presented with dyspnea of 3 weeks’ duration. Three days earlier, a chest CT at an outside hospital had shown a 3.3-cm, well-circumscribed mediastinal mass with tracheal invasion and stenosis. Her history was notable only for thyroidectomy 6 years earlier; she had no smoking or alcohol history. On transfer, vital signs were: BP 115/65 mm Hg, pulse 100/min, respiratory rate 24/min, temperature 37.0 °C. She appeared acutely ill but was alert; there was no pallor, facial or cervical swelling, or jugular venous distention. Stridor was audible over both upper lung fields; cardiac examination was normal. Abdominal and neurologic examinations were normal. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL, WBC 11,820/mm3 (77.4% neutrophils), platelets 249,000/mm3, and CRP 1.2 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air revealed pH 7.404, PCO2 38.7 mm Hg, PO2 52.9 mm Hg, HCO3– 23.7 mEq/L, and SaO2 87.7%. Biochemistry was within normal limits. Chest radiography demonstrated right upper-lobe volume loss, rightward tracheal deviation, and a suspected tracheal wall mass. On hospital day 2, bronchoscopy revealed a polypoid tumor obstructing the mid-tracheal lumen. Endoscopic biopsy showed only chronic inflammation with fibrin exudation. A repeat bronchoscopy on day 3 again yielded chronic inflammation with granulation tissue but no definitive diagnosis.

A 43-year-old white man was referred after a routine abdominal ultrasound, performed by his general practitioner 8 weeks earlier, revealed a splenic mass. He had a history of superficial spreading malignant melanoma of the left instep, treated 7 years ago with wide excision (pT1a, Clark level II, thickness 0.2 mm, R0). He was asymptomatic, and his physical examination, family history, psychosocial history, and laboratory values were unremarkable.

Over the next 3 weeks, the following evaluations were performed:

• Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed chronic type C gastritis and was treated with a proton pump inhibitor.  
• Abdominal ultrasound confirmed a 2 cm hypoechoic lesion in the inferior pole of the spleen with blurred margins and inhomogeneous echotexture.  
• Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (SonoVue®) showed only discrete contrast enhancement and accentuated nodular borders in the arterial phase.  
• Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated two hypodense splenic lesions measuring 2.3 cm and 3.5 cm, highly suspicious for metastases.  
• MRI of the upper abdomen revealed two splenic lesions (2.5 cm and 4.0 cm), hyperintense on T1-weighted images and inhomogeneous hypointense on T2-weighted images. MRI of the head and bone scintigraphy were normal.  
• The first ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration was nondiagnostic. A second aspiration showed atypical, hyperchromatic, polymorphic cells highly suspicious for malignancy.  
• Immunohistochemical analysis of the second specimen revealed overexpression of HMB45, S100, and vimentin, strongly indicating metastatic melanoma.

The case was reviewed by the tumor board, and a splenectomy was recommended.

A 59-year-old man, a non-smoker, was under surveillance eight months after completion of chemoradiotherapy for stage II anal carcinoma. He was asymptomatic when a surveillance CT scan demonstrated diffuse omental thickening and moderate-volume ascites. Analysis of ascitic fluid revealed fragments of fibroadipose tissue with marked desmoplastic stroma, ducto-glandular structures lined by cuboidal and low columnar epithelium, and rare psammoma bodies. A subsequent diagnostic laparoscopy found approximately 2–3 L of straw-colored ascites and numerous small peritoneal implants over the bladder, small bowel serosa, mesentery, and right hemidiaphragm. Biopsy specimens showed multiple nests of medium-sized malignant cells infiltrating fibroadipose stroma with a micropapillary architecture, characteristic retraction artifacts, moderate cytoplasm, hyperchromatic nuclei, numerous psammoma bodies, and a prominent desmoplastic response.

A 53-year-old man presented with several weeks of fevers, joint pain, and abdominal pain. On admission, his temperature was elevated, and laboratory tests showed a total bilirubin of 1.8 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 171 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 265 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 466 U/L. An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a thickened gallbladder wall without gallstones and a normal common bile duct. A CT scan of the abdomen was reportedly unremarkable. By hospital day 2, his white blood cell count had risen to 15,000/μL, and he was diagnosed clinically with acute cholecystitis. Because no biliary dilation was seen on imaging, he underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy with intra-operative cholangiogram, which showed no choledocholithiasis. Gallbladder pathology revealed chronic cholecystitis without gallstones and no evidence of lymphoma. Postoperatively, his bilirubin rose to 10.2 mg/dL, white blood cell count increased to 16,000/μL, hemoglobin fell below 9 g/dL, and he had daily fevers above 101°F. A postoperative CT scan showed no acute complications, and an MRCP demonstrated normal biliary drainage with intact ducts and no residual stones. Given these findings, the gastroenterology team recommended a percutaneous liver biopsy.

A 65-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of right iliac fossa pain that had gradually worsened, and he noted a growing mass in the lower right abdomen. On examination, rebound tenderness was present, and there was a hard, tender lump approximately 50 × 40 mm in size. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 16,500/µL and a C-reactive protein level of 21.3 mg/dL; carcinoembryonic antigen and CA19-9 were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a heterogeneous, contrast-enhancing mass measuring 55 × 50 mm in the lower right quadrant, with an indistinct border from the iliopsoas muscle. The lesion was thought to represent an abscess from retroperitoneal perforation of the appendix, and percutaneous drainage was performed. Contrast injection via the drainage tube demonstrated continuity between the abscess cavity and the appendix. One month later, after reduction of the abscess and normalization of inflammatory markers, an appendectomy was performed. Gross examination of the specimen showed a perforated appendiceal diverticulum and an adjacent small nodule measuring 14 mm in diameter.

A 48-year-old woman was brought to the hospital after an episode of loss of consciousness. She had no significant past medical history. On examination, vital signs were stable, and the physical examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory tests, including complete blood count and basic metabolic panel, were within normal limits. 

Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated a 35 mm mass in the right posterior mediastinum at the level of T7–T8. The mass showed heterogeneous enhancement, with no apparent extension into surrounding structures or into the spinal canal. Three-dimensional CT reconstruction identified a feeding vessel arising from the right eighth intercostal artery supplying the mass. 

Magnetic resonance imaging revealed low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted images. Within the mass, there was a localized area of high signal on T1-weighted images, suggesting a fatty component. 

Preoperatively, the differential diagnosis included schwannoma, hemangioma, or lipoma. Given the evidence of hypervascularity, preoperative embolization of the feeding intercostal artery was planned to reduce intraoperative bleeding risk, followed by video-assisted thoracoscopic surgical resection.

A 5‐year‐old boy was evaluated for a 3‐year history of a swelling over the lumbosacral region, medial rotation of the right foot, and progressive difficulty walking. There was no history of trauma, sensory symptoms, bowel or bladder dysfunction, or other complaints. Developmental milestones were normal. On examination, he was alert and oriented. Motor strength was 5/5 in the upper limbs and left lower limb, and 4/5 in the right lower limb; sensation was diminished over the right lower limb. Reflexes and plantar responses were normal; rectal tone was intact without saddle anesthesia. Inspection of the back revealed a 4 × 4 cm soft, non‐tender, non‐pulsatile swelling in the lumbosacral area without a tuft of hair. 
MRI of the spine demonstrated a 1.6 × 1.4 × 1.1 cm well‐circumscribed intradural nodular lesion posterior to the cord at L2, cord tethering, diastematomyelia below D12, and a dorsal dermal sinus at L4–5. CT of the spine showed defects in the posterior arches of L2–L5 and the sacrum, partial fusion of the right L4–5 facet, and a thin linear tract between the spinal canal and skin at L4–5. Craniospinal screening ruled out hydrocephalus and Arnold–Chiari malformation.

A 64-year-old woman presented with a slowly enlarging mass in the left labia majora over 10 years. Her vital signs were normal. On examination, the mass was firm, painless, immobile, and measured approximately 7 × 4 cm, extending toward the mons pubis. Routine laboratory tests were normal. 

Surgical history:
– In 2000, a mass in the Bartholin’s gland was excised; histopathology in 2007 showed chondroid syringoma.  
– One year later, a recurrence in the labia majora was resected; histology showed clear cell hidradenoma (“lobular glandular proliferation of cuboid cells with no anaplasia”).  
– Most recently, ultrasound revealed a 4.2 × 8 cm heterogeneous, hypervascular subcutaneous mass; CT scan demonstrated a 3.8 × 7.2 cm heterogeneous, contrast-enhancing lesion in the left labia majora extending to the anterior perineum, and a low-density focus in the liver suggestive of a simple cyst.  
– The vulvar mass was excised; on gross examination it measured 7 × 3 × 4 cm, was gray and well-circumscribed, and was reported again as chondroid syringoma.  

Three months later, the patient noted another recurrence near the fourchette. The lesion was excised and submitted for histopathologic evaluation.

A 12-year-old boy was seen in the surgical outpatient clinic for evaluation of a swelling on the left side of his lower jaw. His mother first noticed the lesion 2 years earlier when it was much smaller; the swelling had been painless and had slowly enlarged to approximately 4 × 5 cm. On examination, there was a firm, rough-textured, rounded mass over the left hemimandible. The overlying skin appeared normal, and there was no tenderness or dermatologic abnormality. 
A panoramic radiograph demonstrated a well-circumscribed radiolucent area in the left body and ramus of the mandible. Ultrasonography revealed a complex cystic lesion partly superficial and partly deep to the ramus, suggestive of an osseous cystic process. Contrast-enhanced CT of the maxillofacial region showed a 4.6 × 4.5 × 5 cm, well-defined, expansile lytic lesion in the left angle, ramus, condylar, and coronoid regions of the mandible. The lesion had corticated margins, underlying bone erosion with periosteal elevation, and a homogeneously enhancing soft-tissue component. It was exerting mass effect on the adjacent parotid gland and medial pterygoid muscle.

A 51-year-old woman presented with a two-month history of progressive dyspnea, fatigue, unintentional weight loss, and fevers. On examination, breath sounds were diminished over the right lung, and there was bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. A right-sided pleural effusion was drained; fluid analysis showed an exudate containing CD30+ lymphoma cells. Excisional biopsy of a cervical lymph node revealed CD30+, CD20–, ALK– large cell lymphoma, with coexpression of CD79a, PAX-5, and MUM-1. Initial laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 178×10^9/L, hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL, and platelets 56×10^9/L. Differential counts demonstrated 4% neutrophils, 90% eosinophils (absolute count 160×10^9/L), 1% monocytes, 1% basophils, and 4% lymphocytes. Despite several weeks of hydroxyurea at 3000 mg/day, the eosinophil count remained elevated. Lactate dehydrogenase was 2450 U/L. PET/CT imaging showed extensive FDG uptake in the spleen, liver, and cervical, axillary, and mesenteric lymph nodes. Review of travel, medications, past medical history, and allergic exposures was unrevealing for secondary causes of eosinophilia. Peripheral-blood smear demonstrated marked eosinophilia with partial degranulation and hypersegmentation. Bone marrow biopsy was hypercellular (90%) with increased eosinophilic precursors and eosinophils, plus dyserythropoiesis and dysmegakaryopoiesis; there was no increase in blasts or lymphoma involvement. Cytogenetic analysis revealed a complex karyotype with dup(1q), monosomy 7, and other abnormalities, but no FGFR1 rearrangement. Interphase FISH was negative for PDGFRB (5q33) and PDGFRA (4q12) rearrangements. Bone marrow tryptase staining was normal and PCR was negative for KIT Asp816Val; FISH for BCR-ABL fusion was negative. Flow cytometric analysis and T-cell–receptor gene rearrangement studies did not identify an aberrant T-cell clone.

A 45-year-old man presented with recent-onset dry cough and exertional dyspnea. He had no significant past medical history. Initial contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a 12 cm mass in the anterior superior mediastinum and multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules suggestive of metastatic disease. A few weeks later, he developed neck edema, distended neck veins, and facial plethora. Repeat CT confirmed invasion of the superior vena cava above the azygos vein and thrombus extending into the left brachiocephalic trunk. He was treated with heparin and high-dose corticosteroids, with rapid symptomatic relief; stenting was deferred. Video-assisted thoracoscopy yielded a wedge resection of a pulmonary lesion and biopsy of the mediastinal mass. Histopathology showed a multinodular proliferation of small, round, monomorphic cells with clear cytoplasm. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated diffuse strong WT1 positivity and moderate, patchy CD99 positivity.

A 54‐year‐old man presented with a 7‐month history of right‐sided lower‐facial swelling. On examination, there was a non‐tender, bony hard, smooth‐surfaced extraoral swelling over the right mandibular body, with intraoral buccolingual expansion and obliteration of the buccal vestibule. He was a habitual tobacco chewer and occasional smoker; other findings were noncontributory. A CT scan showed an expansile mandibular lesion with multiple cortical perforations extending from the right parasymphysis to the subcondylar region, with thinning of the lower border and moderate cortical expansion. Aspiration with a wide‐bore needle was negative. Based on these findings, the differential diagnosis included ameloblastoma, ameloblastic fibroma, central ossifying fibroma, central giant cell lesion, and myxoma.

A 57-year-old Caucasian man with a history of Crohn’s disease, colon cancer, bilateral deep vein thromboses, and a 13-year chronic nonhealing skin lesion over the right lateral tibia was evaluated. The lesion had been biopsy-proven pyoderma gangrenosum and was refractory to multiple treatments, with waxing and waning severity; the patient was maintained on Humira. Surgical history included venous thrombectomy, colon resection, splenectomy, cholecystectomy, and hernia repair.

On examination, there was an irregularly shaped, raised, fungating, exophytic lesion over the right lateral tibia measuring 12.0 cm × 12.0 cm × 1 cm, without bleeding or overt infection. Bilateral lower-extremity hyperpigmentation suggested chronic venous stasis. Abdominal exam was unremarkable. The patient denied tobacco or drug use and had ceased alcohol 30 years earlier.

Four years prior, a punch biopsy of this area showed “lobular vascular proliferation within the dermis with associated hemosiderin and spongiosis of the epidermis consistent with stasis dermatitis.” 

One month before presentation, a limited extremity venous ultrasound demonstrated “new partial compressibility of the proximal femoral vein and partial compressibility of the popliteal vein … unable to distinguish between acute nonocclusive thrombus within the proximal femoral vein versus manifestations of chronic DVT.” A right tibia/fibula X-ray showed no acute osseous injury or aggressive destruction. A PET/CT scan from skull base to thigh revealed “a large, intensely hypermetabolic lesion along the skin of the right calf … no clear delineation between the two suspected processes, pyoderma gangrenosum and squamous cell carcinoma,” and hypermetabolic right inguinal and external iliac lymph nodes without evidence of distant metastasis.

A 65-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an intraoral lesion. She reported no pain or systemic symptoms. Her medical history was unremarkable. 

On examination, there was a 1-cm, asymptomatic, exophytic lesion of the alveolar mucosa adjacent to the maxillary right lateral incisor; the keratinized gingiva was not involved. The involved tooth responded normally to vitality testing.

Panoramic radiography revealed a well-circumscribed unilocular radiolucency in the right anterior maxilla at the apex of the lateral incisor. Cone-beam CT with 3D reconstruction confirmed a solitary radiolucent lesion without cortical perforation. A periapical radiograph demonstrated a round radiolucency contiguous with the tooth root.

Given the radiographic appearance, the patient underwent root canal therapy of the right lateral incisor. One week later, an excisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia. Intraoperatively, the lesion appeared cribriform and was surrounded by intact cortical bone. The specimen was fixed and sent for histologic and immunohistochemical analysis.

A 27-year-old transgender woman presented with a self-detected right breast lump that she had noticed for 12 months, becoming more apparent after an intentional weight loss of approximately 5 kg. She reported no skin changes, dimpling, pain, nipple discharge, or history of trauma. Her medical history included depression and male-to-female gender transition, which she began at age 21; she has been on a stable dose of oral estrogen for 3 years. She had not undergone any gender-affirming surgery or breast augmentation. There was a family history of breast cancer in a maternal aunt in her mid-30s.

On examination, she had B-cup breasts with a firm, mobile 3 cm lump palpated at the 10-o’clock position, deep to the areolar edge; there was no axillary lymphadenopathy. The contralateral breast was unremarkable.

Breast ultrasound demonstrated a lobulated lesion measuring 31 × 14 × 19 mm with minimal calcifications and no suspicious lymph nodes. Ultrasound findings were otherwise normal.

A core biopsy of the lesion revealed a fibroepithelial lesion with low cellularity and mitotic figures. A low-grade phyllodes tumour could not be excluded based on the core biopsy. After discussion of surveillance versus repeat biopsy versus excisional biopsy, the patient elected to proceed with excision of the lesion.

A 51-year-old Filipino man presented with a one-week history of hemorrhagic swelling in the right mandibular region. He denied pain, fever, night sweats, weight loss, tobacco use, or alcohol use. His history included hypertension (on amlodipine) and chronic kidney disease, with planned hemodialysis.

Intraoral examination revealed an exophytic, hemorrhagic, ulcerated mass (~3 cm) surrounding the buccal and lingual gingiva of the right mandibular premolars, extending posteriorly to the edentulous alveolar mucosa. The adjacent teeth showed terminal mobility, 1 cm pocket depths, and bleeding on probing. Additional gingival enlargement was noted in the left posterior mandibular buccal gingiva and the left posterior maxillary palatal gingiva. Extraoral examination found a painful, nearly fixed right submandibular lymph node.

Panoramic radiograph demonstrated alveolar bone loss near the right mandibular premolars. Cone-beam computed tomography revealed superficial resorption of the alveolar ridge and buccal cortex measuring ~7 mm by 3 mm.

The differential diagnosis included hematologic malignancies (e.g., lymphoma, leukemic infiltrate), sarcomas, squamous cell carcinoma, calcium-channel blocker–induced gingival enlargement with pyogenic granuloma–like lesions, peripheral giant cell granuloma, and brown tumor of secondary hyperparathyroidism. Incisional biopsies of all gingival lesions were performed.

A 61-year-old woman was evaluated for iron-deficiency anemia noted by her primary care physician. Two years earlier, upper endoscopy was normal. She had mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL) without abnormalities in liver, biliary, or pancreatic enzymes and normal tumor markers. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed a 10 mm tumor protruding into the lumen of the descending duodenum with weaker contrast enhancement than the pancreas and a clear plane separating it from the pancreatic parenchyma; there was no dilatation of the main pancreatic duct or common bile duct. Upper endoscopy revealed a submucosal tumor–like lesion with a central concavity just proximal to the major papilla. Endoscopic ultrasound showed a well-defined hypoechoic 10 mm mass adjacent to but indistinct from the pancreas. Biopsy of the lesion demonstrated neoplastic cells with round nuclei, granular cytoplasm, and focal small gland-like structures. Immunohistochemical staining was negative for Synaptophysin and Chromogranin A and positive for Trypsin and BCL10; the Ki-67 index was 80%.  
What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 6-year-old girl presented with a new-onset seizure and hearing loss. Her past medical history was unremarkable. On examination, she had no focal neurologic deficits, and routine laboratory studies were within normal limits. Brain MRI with gadolinium revealed a well-defined, homogeneous solid mass in the right cerebellopontine angle measuring 27 × 38 × 34 mm. On T2-weighted imaging, the mass was hyperintense; it was isointense on FLAIR, hyperintense on diffusion-weighted imaging, and hypointense on the apparent diffusion coefficient map, with a mean ADC value of 0.40 × 10⁻³ mm²/s (compared with 0.62 × 10⁻³ mm²/s in normal parenchyma). Intravoxel incoherent motion analysis showed diffusivity of 0.35 × 10⁻³ mm²/s, perfusion fraction of 0.05, and pseudo-diffusivity of 5.40 × 10⁻³ mm²/s in the tumor (versus 0.68, 0.11, and 5.00, respectively, in normal tissue). Fractional anisotropy on diffusion tensor imaging was 0.507 in the lesion and 0.506 in normal parenchyma. Semiquantitative T1-perfusion imaging demonstrated a relative enhancement of 25.00% (vs. 1.88% in parenchyma); maximum enhancement of 98.06 (vs. 24.76); maximum relative enhancement of 6.31% (vs. 2.01%); time to peak of 63.27 s (vs. 145.52 s); wash-in rate of 18.34 s⁻¹ (vs. 5.89 s⁻¹); wash-out rate of 10.21 s⁻¹ (vs. 7.82 s⁻¹); and area under the curve of 4730.40 (vs. 215.75) in the lesion. MR spectroscopy showed a choline-to-N-acetyl-aspartate ratio of 1.30 in the mass. Based on these clinical and radiologic data, a diagnosis of schwannoma was made preoperatively.

A 35-year-old man presented with a painless, solitary mass over his left proximal tibia. The lesion had been insidious in onset and grew slowly over two years from pea-sized to approximately 9×8 cm. There was no warmth, tenderness, crepitus, discoloration, or regional lymphadenopathy. The swelling was firm and adherent to underlying structures.

Plain radiographs of the left tibia showed a large lytic lesion with well-defined margins and a narrow zone of transition in the metaphyseal–diaphyseal region without cortical breach or periosteal reaction. A skeletal survey was otherwise unremarkable. MRI of the tibia demonstrated ill-defined serpiginous areas of heterogeneous T2 hyperintensity and T1 hypointensity with heterogeneous postcontrast enhancement in the proximal tibial marrow. A subcutaneous T2 hyperintense, T1 hypointense collection communicated with the marrow through a cortical defect. FDG-PET revealed a circumscribed sclerotic lesion in the left proximal tibia with high fluorodeoxyglucose uptake and no other abnormal foci. A core biopsy was then planned.

A 22-year-old woman was admitted with six months of worsening lower back pain and progressive lower limb weakness, culminating in paraparesis and loss of bladder and bowel control. She had no prior history of neurological deficits after surgical repair of a congenital lipo-myelomeningocele in infancy. On examination, vital signs were stable. Neurologic assessment showed flaccid paralysis of both lower limbs, absent deep tendon reflexes, and diminished sensation in the lower extremities. Spinal MRI revealed a well-defined intramedullary mass measuring 6 × 5 × 3 cm at the L4–S1 level, appearing hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images. Considering her history, the differential diagnosis included primary spinal cord tumors and secondary lesions.

A 55-year-old man presented with left upper abdominal pain, spiking fever, and night sweats. He had a 16-year history of myasthenia gravis (MGFA class IIa) treated with thymectomy at age 39 (pathologically normal thymus) followed by tacrolimus and prednisolone. On examination, he had tenderness in the left upper abdomen, palpable splenomegaly, and lymphadenopathy in the cervical, submandibular, and right inguinal regions; neurologically, he had bilateral ptosis and diplopia.  
Laboratory evaluation showed a normal white-cell count, thrombocytopenia (93×10^3/µL), elevated lactate dehydrogenase (432 U/L), anti–acetylcholine receptor antibody positivity (0.6 nmol/L), and a markedly elevated soluble interleukin-2 receptor level (16 600 U/mL). Contrast-enhanced CT revealed right inguinal lymphadenopathy and low-density lesions in an enlarged spleen.  
An excisional biopsy of a right inguinal lymph node demonstrated diffuse proliferation of atypical small- to medium-sized lymphoid cells. Immunohistochemistry showed that these cells were positive for CD3 and CD5, expressed both CD4 and CD8, had diminished CD7 expression, and were negative for CD20 and CD79a.

A 61-year-old man presented with a two-year history of worsening diarrhea, six months of fatigue, weight loss, and three weeks of abdominal pain. His medical history included coronary artery disease, hypertension, mitral valve repair, congestive heart failure, COPD, and a 40-pack-year smoking history. He was a Navy veteran with no documented asbestos exposure. A fecal occult blood test was positive. Colonoscopy revealed a 5 cm circumferential mass in the ascending colon, and biopsy showed adenocarcinoma arising in a tubulovillous adenoma. 

Abdominal CT demonstrated a 5.8 cm partially obstructing cecal mass, ascites, two left renal masses (2.1 cm and 4.5 cm), fat stranding around the cecum and splenic flexure, and focal irregularity of the left peritoneal lining; “these findings were thought to represent peritoneal implants from the adenocarcinoma.” PET confirmed uptake in the cecal mass and a focus in the descending colon but showed no distant organ metastases. He was staged clinically as T4, M1 colonic adenocarcinoma. Laboratory studies showed a WBC of 14.5 K/cmm, CEA of 12.7 ng/mL, and BUN of 3 mg/dL.

Two months later, due to obstructive symptoms, he underwent a palliative hand-assisted laparoscopic right hemicolectomy. Intraoperatively, diffuse peritoneal implants presumed to be carcinomatosis were noted, and 800 mL of thick peritoneal fluid was evacuated. The resection specimen included the right colon, terminal ileum, appendix, and omentum. Grossly, a tan-red polypoid mass measuring 6.5 × 5.3 × 4.9 cm extended through the muscularis propria to the serosa, with overlying serosal puckering. The remaining serosa of the ileum, appendix, and colon and the surrounding mesenteric fat were diffusely red, gritty, and nodular (0.2–0.6 cm). The omentum was “bumpy,” tan to yellow, and nodular.

An 88-year-old man noted abrupt-onset, exquisitely tender nodules on the dorsum of his penis at the midshaft. He denied trauma. His urologic history included left orchiectomy and groin radiation, BPH treated with two TURPs, overactive bladder on oxybutynin, low testosterone on replacement, recurrent prostatitis, and irritative voiding symptoms. A previous prostate biopsy for elevated PSA and palpable nodule was negative, as were all TURP specimens. Eighteen months prior, he had intermittent pelvic pain responsive to prostatitis treatment. His medical history also included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, arthritis, and chronic diarrhea. On exam, hard nodules were palpated in the corpus spongiosum and corpora cavernosa, tender to touch. Given that the lesions were not clearly consistent with Peyronie’s disease, pelvic MRI was obtained and showed multiple nonenhancing low-signal lesions in the corpus spongiosum and bilateral corpora cavernosa suggestive of metastatic disease.

An 18-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with a one-month history of fatigue and lethargy and 2–3 days of progressive dyspnoea. She reported presyncope, severe dyspnoea on minimal exertion, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, chest tightness, and palpitations. She was a non-smoker without relevant family history. On examination, she was afebrile; respiratory rate, 22 breaths per minute; oxygen saturation, 98% on room air; heart rate, 140 beats per minute in sinus rhythm; blood pressure, 120/80 mmHg. There was no peripheral oedema or jugular venous distension. Cardiac auscultation revealed a grade II/VI pan-diastolic murmur; breath sounds were decreased at both lung bases. Laboratory tests showed a d-dimer of 6.6 μg/mL (normal <0.5 μg/mL) and haemoglobin 13.7 g/dL; other blood counts and biochemistry were normal. An ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia with a normal P-wave axis and a narrow QRS complex. Chest radiography revealed mild bilateral costophrenic-angle blunting. Computed tomography pulmonary angiography excluded pulmonary embolism but identified bilateral pleural effusions and a 60 × 38 mm filling defect in the left atrium. Transthoracic echocardiography confirmed a large, mobile left atrial mass arising from the interatrial septum that partially prolapsed into the left ventricle during diastole, causing anterior displacement of the mitral leaflet and obstruction of mitral inflow; there was no pericardial effusion or associated thrombus. A full-body CT scan showed no evidence of distant metastases.

A 44-year-old primiparous woman presented with a 4-week history of light vaginal bleeding. Four years earlier, she had undergone endometrial ablation for heavy menstrual bleeding and had been amenorrheic until this episode. On abdominal and pelvic examination, the uterus was normal in size, and no adnexal masses were palpable. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed a cystic lesion near the cervix and an endometrial thickness of 1 cm. An endometrial biopsy yielded fragments of benign mature adipose tissue and scant benign smooth muscle, along with keratin debris; no malignancy or myometrial invasion was identified, although sampling was limited by her prior ablation. The patient was counseled about possible diagnoses, including uterine lipoma, lipoleiomyoma, uterine teratoma, and uterine perforation as a complication of biopsy. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis revealed a complex, cystic, fat-containing mass in the lower uterine segment measuring 2.0 × 3.5 × 2.3 cm, with no evidence of adjacent infiltration or lymphadenopathy.

A 54-year-old man presented with a several-week history of a painful anal swelling. He denied overt drainage but noted occasional moisture. He reported regular bowel movements with intermittent pain and no bleeding. Six weeks earlier, his white-cell count was 11.4×10^3/µL. In clinic, his heart rate was 106 beats/min, blood pressure 145/87 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and temperature 98.2°F. Examination revealed a large, firm, tender posterior anal mass; a digital rectal exam yielded a small amount of presumed pus. Differential diagnoses included perirectal abscess, presacral mass, malignant neoplasm of the rectum, and pelvic abscess.

Under general anesthesia in the prone jackknife position, a rigid proctoscope showed a posterior mass indenting the rectal wall, extending 11 cm from the anal verge, with normal overlying mucosa and no pus. Fine-needle aspiration through the posterior perianal skin produced red, gelatinous material, which was sent for cytology, biopsy, and culture. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 10×9×16 cm mass located between the rectum and sacrum. A CT scan of the chest showed no evidence of metastases.

A 73-year-old Caucasian woman with hypertension presented with 2 weeks of intermittent subjective fevers, anorexia, weakness, fatigue, and night sweats. Her weight was stable. She reported a persistent nonproductive cough but no sore throat or rash. One month earlier she had transient left knee pain after hiking; knee and femur x-rays then were unremarkable, and the pain resolved without intervention. She had no sick contacts, sexual partners, insect or tick bites, tuberculosis exposure, or animal contacts. She took only enalapril and had no relevant family history.

On examination, her temperature was 38.6 °C, heart rate 96 bpm, blood pressure 130/65 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. She appeared non-toxic. There were no rashes, lymphadenopathy, or thyroid enlargement. Heart and lung examinations were normal, with no murmurs or crackles. Abdominal and neurologic exams were unremarkable. Her knees showed no redness, warmth, effusion, or tenderness.

Initial investigations showed WBC 11.9×10^9/L, hemoglobin 125 g/L, platelets 373×10^9/L, alkaline phosphatase 179 U/L, gamma-glutamyltransferase 84 U/L, albumin 24 g/L, CRP 153.8 mg/L, ferritin 883.7 μg/L, with other chemistries and enzymes near normal. ANA, ANCA, anti-smooth muscle, anti-mitochondrial antibodies, and rheumatoid factor were undetectable. Serum free light chains and SPEP were normal; peripheral smear was unremarkable. Five sets of blood cultures, a urine culture, and Lyme serology were negative. Chest x-ray and CT scans of the head, neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis were unremarkable. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed a normal heart with no vegetations. Empiric piperacillin-tazobactam was started and then discontinued when cultures were negative. 

After an 8-day admission, she was discharged for outpatient follow-up. One month later she remained febrile with persistent fatigue and reported recurrence of left leg pain. Her CRP was 207 mg/L. On examination, there was a large, warm mass on the left thigh.

A 13-year-old girl with no prior medical history had a 2-year history of chronic diarrhea unresponsive to symptomatic treatments, accompanied by growth retardation (weight and height −2 SD; bone age 10 years). Celiac disease was suspected; antitransglutaminase and antiendomysium antibodies were negative, and a jejunal biopsy showed villous atrophy II. She was placed on a gluten-free diet for 6 months without improvement. Over the next several months, she developed intermittent fevers (37.8–38.5 °C), asthenia, anorexia, weight loss, night sweats, and overall decline in health.

Approximately six months later, an insidiously enlarging abdominal mass was noted. On transfer and admission, her temperature was 38.5 °C. She appeared pale, in poor condition, with weight 24 kg (−3 SD) and height 138 cm (−3 SD). Examination revealed hepatomegaly 4 cm below the costal margin, splenomegaly two fingerbreadths below the left costal margin, and a painless, mobile paraumbilical mass ~6 cm in diameter. Lenticular inguinal and cervical lymph nodes were palpable.

Abdominal ultrasound and contrast-enhanced CT showed hepatosplenomegaly, multiple enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes (largest 19 mm), and a well-defined, moderately homogeneous soft-tissue mass measuring 40 × 65 × 56 mm abutting the gallbladder and gastric antrum with surrounding fat infiltration. Chest radiograph was normal.

Laboratory studies demonstrated microcytic hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin 7 g/dL), thrombocytosis (489 000/mm3), elevated inflammatory markers (ESR 145 mm/h; CRP 252 mg/L; fibrinogen 7.1 g/L), hyperferritinemia (528 µg/L) with low serum iron, hypoalbuminemia (22 g/L), increased alpha1, alpha2, and beta2 globulins, and hypergammaglobulinemia (37.5 g/L). IGF-1 was low (26.5 ng/mL) with normal growth-hormone response; liver enzymes and LDH were normal. Bacteriological cultures, viral serologies (EBV, CMV, HIV, hepatitis B and C, HHV-8), and parasitology were negative. Immune and thyroid function tests were normal.

A scan-guided biopsy of the abdominal mass was performed.

A 70-year-old man with acute myeloid leukemia in remission for six years was referred for progressively worsening shooting pain in the left posterior calf and sole, rated 7/10, described as spontaneous, lancinating, and accompanied by extreme cold sensation. Examination showed mild atrophy of the left calf, decreased strength (3/5) of left ankle plantar flexion and inversion, and absent left ankle reflex. Electromyography and nerve conduction studies revealed reduced response of the left posterior tibial nerve. Lumbar spine MRI demonstrated diffuse disc degeneration and mild left-sided L2–3 foraminal bulging, deemed insufficient to explain his symptoms. Infrared thermography showed hypothermia of the left leg. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, were all normal. Pain persisted despite nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs, high-dose gabapentin, tricyclic antidepressants, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, and lumbar epidural and piriformis injections. A left sciatic nerve block under ultrasound guidance provided only temporary relief.  
On ultrasound examination of both sciatic nerves, an enlarged, hypoechoic, edematous segment was identified on the left sciatic nerve at the mid-thigh level.

A 43-year-old woman noted a rapidly enlarging mass in her right breast. Ultrasonography revealed a well-circumscribed, middle- to high-echoic lesion. Core-needle biopsy showed hypocellular myxoid stroma with small spindle cells and non-atypical mammary ducts, suggesting a benign fibroepithelial process. Two weeks later, the lesion was excised. On gross examination, the tumor measured 4.0 × 3.0 cm and was well circumscribed and predominantly cystic, with an intracystic polypoid component and areas of hemorrhage.

A 67-year-old woman with obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and a remote cholecystectomy presented with three years of progressively worsening dyspnea and right lower-chest discomfort. Vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination and routine laboratory studies were unremarkable. A chest radiograph demonstrated elevation of the right hemidiaphragm suggestive of eventration. An abdominal ultrasound showed a heterogeneous mass beneath the right hemidiaphragm. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 20 × 18 × 10 cm encapsulated, predominantly fatty subdiaphragmatic mass with scattered soft-tissue nodules, septations, and coarse calcifications, causing mass effect on the liver and diaphragm. A CT-guided 18-gauge core-needle biopsy of the mass showed adipose tissue containing pleomorphic lipoblasts.

A 9-year-old boy presented with a 3-month history of a painless swelling in the right upper posterior tooth region that had grown progressively, causing facial asymmetry. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. Examination revealed a 4.0×3.5 cm diffuse, well-defined, hard, nontender swelling on the right middle third of the face, extending from 1 cm below the infraorbital margin to the inferior border of the mandible and from the ala of the nose posteriorly to the anterior border of the ramus. The overlying skin was normal. Intraorally, there was a 4.0×3.0 cm ovoid, hard, nontender swelling in the right buccal vestibule with buccal cortical expansion and slight palatal expansion but no mucosal changes. A provisional clinical diagnosis of juvenile ossifying fibroma was made, with fibrous dysplasia as a consideration. 

Panoramic and periapical radiographs showed a ground-glass trabecular pattern with radiolucency around the roots of deciduous teeth and erupting premolars. A maxillary occlusal film demonstrated increased radiopacity, buccal cortical expansion, and a ground-glass appearance without palatal involvement. Cone-beam CT revealed expansion of the buccal and palatal cortical plates, involvement of more than half of the right maxillary sinus, a well-defined margin, and a ground-glass internal pattern. Based on these images, a radiological diagnosis of juvenile ossifying fibroma of the right posterior maxilla was made, with fibrous dysplasia considered less likely because “the margin of the swelling was well-defined and well demarcated from the surrounding areas which was very much unlike FD whose margin is ill-defined and merges with the surrounding areas.”

A 31-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of a growing, firm mass in his left flank. He noted a sharp, constant pain rated 7/10, radiating to the abdomen and left groin. There were no gastrointestinal or genitourinary symptoms, and review of systems was otherwise unremarkable. He had no relevant family or social history. On examination, the abdomen was soft but tender around a firm, deep 5 cm ovoid mass in the left lumbar region. The mass was nonreducible; there was no organomegaly or hernia. Laboratory tests, including white cell count, hematocrit, electrolytes, and liver function, were all normal.  
Abdominal ultrasound showed a 56×28×27 mm homogenously hyperechoic mass within the abdominal wall musculature with mild internal Doppler flow. A provisional diagnosis of a fat-containing lumbar hernia was made, and a portal-venous-phase CT scan was obtained. CT demonstrated an ovoid mass within the external oblique muscle with heterogeneous attenuation, without calcification, inflammation, or invasion. The appearance was deemed inconsistent with a simple lipoma, so an MRI was performed to exclude sarcoma.  
On MRI, the lesion was well circumscribed within the external oblique muscle, hypointense to muscle on T1, hyperintense on T2, with avid enhancement, diffusion restriction, and prominent feeder vessels. Differentials of undifferentiated sarcoma, fibroma, or desmoid tumour were considered.

A 76-year-old woman with a history of appendicitis, torsion of an ovarian cyst pedicle, and uterine myoma presented with a rapidly enlarging right parietal mass behind the ear over one month. She had no neurological deficits or systemic symptoms. Laboratory studies, including complete blood counts, metabolic panel, and viral serology for HIV and Epstein-Barr virus, were all normal or negative. Noncontrast CT of the head revealed a 5-cm hyperdense meningeal mass with parietal bone invasion. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI showed a heterogeneously enhancing lesion in the right parietal region. Cerebral angiography demonstrated a vascular tumor supplied by the middle meningeal artery. Thus, a clinical diagnosis of osteoblastic meningioma was made, and the differential diagnosis included primary lymphoma, metastasis, and sarcoma. The patient underwent endovascular embolization of the feeding artery followed by surgical resection. Intraoperatively, the tumor was extradural, caused skull destruction, and had no intradural involvement. Histology showed a malignant spindle cell neoplasm with positive immunostaining for α-smooth muscle actin, vimentin, and desmin, and negative staining for Epstein-Barr virus.

18-year-old male with no comorbidities presented with a 6-month history of a small, painless right scrotal mass that had gradually increased in size. He denied trauma, systemic symptoms, or relevant family history. On examination, vital signs were stable; cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurological exams were unremarkable. Local scrotal exam revealed an approximately 2×3 cm well-defined, nodular, firm mass adjacent to the head of the right epididymis; there were no signs of inflammation, and the mass was indistinct from the testis, scrotal skin, spermatic cord, and regional lymph nodes. Scrotal ultrasonography showed a 25.5×24.4 mm well-defined heterogeneous extratesticular solid lesion adjacent to the head of the right epididymis that was initially avascular; on repeat imaging, peripheral vascularity was noted with mild right hydrocele. Routine preoperative laboratory tests, including β-hCG, LDH, and α-fetoprotein, were within normal limits.

An 11-month-old girl, with no significant prenatal or family history, was brought for evaluation of a 1-month history of progressive abdominal distension. Physical examination confirmed hepatomegaly without splenomegaly. Initial laboratory studies showed serum alpha-fetoprotein of 653 ng/ml, rising to 1000 ng/ml 2 days later and 783 ng/ml a week thereafter. Aspartate and alanine aminotransferase levels were mildly elevated at 111 U/L and 55 U/L, respectively. Viral hepatitis and other infectious markers were negative. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a large, multiseptated cystic lesion in the liver with no flow on color Doppler. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated a well-defined multicystic mass occupying segments IV, V, and VIII of the liver, with a thick enhancing wall, multiple thick septa, and a single hyper-enhancing nodule within. No additional hepatic lesions, lymphadenopathy, or distant metastases were identified.

A 24-year-old woman, gravida 0 para 0, received routine obstetrical care and presented at 38 weeks of gestation for an elective cesarean section because of cephalopelvic disproportion. She had no abdominal pain, gastrointestinal symptoms, or other complaints throughout her pregnancy, and prenatal sonography showed normal fetal development without adnexal abnormalities.

Under combined spinal–epidural anesthesia, a live female infant was delivered uneventfully. During the routine intraoperative survey, the uterus and uterine adnexa appeared normal. However, the appendix was noted to be markedly enlarged, measuring approximately 10 cm in length and 3 cm in diameter, with a sausage-like shape and elastic hardness; the appendiceal root appeared normal, and no other abnormalities were seen in the abdominal cavity. A general surgeon was consulted, and an appendectomy was performed by ligation and transection of the mesoappendix and appendix root. On gross inspection, the resected specimen was a unilocular cystic structure whose lumen was filled with a white, jelly-like mucinous substance. Routine preoperative laboratory tests and prenatal sonography were unremarkable. Pathological examination was pending.

A 45-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of right knee pain. Several months earlier, her symptoms had been attributed to osteoarthritis, and a high tibial osteotomy was being considered. She had a body-mass index of 29.8 and no other relevant medical history.

On examination, she walked with a valgus-thrust gait and had a partially correctable 5–10° valgus deformity of the right knee. There was a mild effusion on patellar-tap and sweep tests. Quadriceps bulk was symmetrical. She reported anterior knee pain but had no medial or lateral joint-line tenderness and no ligamentous instability. She had a full range of motion and was neurovascularly intact. The left knee was normal.

Laboratory testing showed a C-reactive protein level of 14 mg/L (reference, 0–5) and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 72 mm/hr (reference, 0–20). Rheumatoid factor and anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide levels were within normal limits.

Weight-bearing radiographs of the right knee showed approximately 15° of genu valgum, severe patellofemoral joint-space loss with subchondral sclerosis, and minimal medial compartment narrowing.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the right knee confirmed severe patellofemoral arthropathy with full-thickness cartilage loss, cortical irregularity, underlying cystic change, marrow edema, and mild medial compartment degeneration with preservation of the lateral compartment. There was no patella alta, trochlear dysplasia, or patellar maltracking. The MRI also demonstrated a large joint effusion with frond-like synovial proliferation in the prepatellar space; the synovial masses were hyperintense on T1-weighted images and suppressed on fat-saturated sequences.

A 63-year-old man presented with a more than 2-year history of right groin and back pain unresponsive to analgesics. Over the preceding year he noted swelling and increasing pain in the right gluteal region.  
On lumbar-spine radiographs there was mild left convex scoliosis and a partially visualized osteolytic lesion of the right iliac wing.  
Pelvic radiographs revealed a large osteolytic lesion involving the right iliac crest and wing with sclerotic margins and no obvious gross matrix calcifications.  
MRI of the pelvis showed a saddle-shaped mass (approximately 176 × 129 × 94 mm) arising from the superior aspect of the right iliac wing. The lesion was homogeneously hypointense on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with internal fluid-equivalent signal and a peripheral nodular hypointense margin. The mass overhung the iliac crest, with an internal limb displacing and attenuating the right iliopsoas muscle and an external limb extending into the gluteal region between the gluteus medius and minimus. There was no evidence of invasion or encasement of the iliac vessels and no regional lymphadenopathy.

A 45-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a right axillary mass of six months’ duration. He noted thickening of the overlying skin and purulent discharge but denied fever, chills, weight loss, or systemic symptoms. His brother had lymphoma at age 28. He had no chronic illnesses, no known tuberculosis exposure, and no significant travel or occupational exposures. He reported prolonged use of a topical hair-removal preparation in both axillae and a 15-year, 1.5-pack-per-day smoking history.

On examination, he was well-appearing, without lymphadenopathy elsewhere or organomegaly. The right axilla showed hyperemic, thickened skin over a 5-cm irregular, firm mass. The left axilla had redness, warmth, tenderness, and a draining sinus. Other systems were normal.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, and electrolytes, were within normal limits. An enhanced CT scan of the neck, chest, and abdomen showed matted right axillary lymph nodes measuring 5.0 × 2.5 cm with central necrosis and small skin thickening in the left axilla without discrete masses. No other lymphadenopathy or organ lesions were identified.

The radiologic findings were interpreted as most consistent with tuberculosis and, less likely, lymphoma. Because the patient had no tuberculosis contacts and a negative tuberculin skin test, lymphoma was considered most likely. He was referred for excisional biopsy of the right axillary mass.

A 16-year-old girl was referred with a 6-month history of gradual visual decline and metamorphopsia in her left eye. She had no relevant medical or ocular history. On examination, visual acuity was 6/6 in the right eye and 6/18 in the left eye. Fundoscopic examination of the left eye revealed a well-defined orange lesion at the macula with overlying pigmentary changes. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography showed subretinal fluid, a dome-shaped retinal pigment-epithelium detachment with choroidal enlargement, and a central retinal thickness of 297 μm. Fundus fluorescein angiography demonstrated retinal pigment-epithelium mottling, gradually increasing hyperfluorescence of the lesion in the venous phase, and late persisting hyperfluorescence with no evidence of pinpoint leakage or late phase leakage. Indocyanine green angiography revealed a well-defined mass with no evidence of hot spots, staining, or leakage of the inner choroid. B-scan ultrasonography showed an elevated choroidal mass of high reflectivity and acoustic shadowing.

A 15-year-old Sri Lankan girl presented with a 2-year history of a painless, progressively enlarging lump in her left thigh. She was otherwise healthy. On examination, there was a soft, non-tender mass arising from the anterior compartment of the thigh, without neurovascular compromise, and both hip and knee joints were normal. Initial hematological investigations were within normal limits. MRI of the left thigh revealed a 6 cm, thickly septated mass in the subcutaneous tissue of the anterolateral and medial aspects of the thigh; there was no contrast enhancement and no involvement of underlying muscle or bone. An incisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia.

A 63-year-old man presented with one day of stretching, continuous abdominal pain that partially improved with hyoscine but persisted, accompanied by hyporexia. He reported early satiety and a 10-pound weight loss over the past month. He had a 50-year smoking history, no other comorbidities, surgeries, or relevant family history.

On examination, his abdomen was flat, with superficial tenderness in the epigastrium, no rebound tenderness, and a palpable 12 cm mass in the left abdominal quadrant. Laboratory studies were within normal limits.

An upright abdominal radiograph showed elevation of the left hemidiaphragm. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a large, hypodense mass with central necrosis and heterogeneous enhancement, located posterior to the stomach and abutting the spleen and left kidney, without a clear plane between the mass and the left hepatic lobe or the body of the pancreas; the lesion compressed adjacent organs and appeared to invade the posterior gastric wall.

Upper GI endoscopy demonstrated an extrinsic bulge with overlying gastric mucosal edema.

An 18-year-old woman with McCune–Albright syndrome diagnosed at age 6 (tibia fracture, café-au-lait spots, ovarian cysts) and known polyostotic fibrous dysplasia presented after minor trauma to her left leg with acute left hip pain and inability to bear weight. On examination, she had antalgic limitation of left hip motion without neurovascular deficit.  
Plain radiographs of the left femur showed an impacted fracture at the base of the femoral neck in the context of an expansile lytic lesion with partial ground-glass density and a rind sign, as well as multiple well-defined expansile lesions with ground-glass density in the left femur and tibia. Comparison with radiographs from 36 months earlier demonstrated progressive expansion of the lesion and development of multiple low-density areas within it.  
Magnetic resonance imaging of the left femur revealed a lesion with well-defined margins, low T1 and intermediate-to-high T2 signal involving the femoral neck, trochanteric, and subtrochanteric regions, surrounding a multicystic lesion with fluid levels and foci of spontaneous T1 hyperintensity. A complete transverse fracture with impaction and varus angulation was present. Additional lesions with similar signal characteristics were noted in the proximal and distal femoral epiphyses, proximal and distal tibial epiphyses, and patella.

A 73-year-old man with a history of Hodgkin lymphoma treated decades earlier and renal cell carcinoma resected at age 60 was hospitalized in November 2016 for pneumonia. Laboratory evaluation revealed anemia and bone marrow aspiration showed multilineage dysplasia consistent with treatment‐related myelodysplastic syndrome (International Prognostic Scoring System: low risk). Serum protein electrophoresis and immunoelectrophoresis demonstrated a small IgM κ monoclonal spike, and flow cytometry of marrow cells identified approximately 2.5% clonal B cells, leading to a diagnosis of IgM monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS).

In August 2017, he developed a transient fever above 38°C in the setting of neutropenia (neutrophil count 286/μl), which was treated as febrile neutropenia. No infectious focus was found on examination, cultures, or FDG-PET/CT imaging, and autoimmune serologies were negative.

Beginning in February 2018, he experienced recurrent fevers unresponsive to antibiotics or low-dose steroids. Repeat bone marrow aspiration revealed hypercellular marrow with dysplastic features (including pseudo-Pelger–Huët anomalies and micromegakaryocytes) and 2.4% abnormal lymphocytes. Flow cytometry now showed 2.7% clonal B cells with κ light-chain restriction. Allele-specific PCR on marrow cells detected the MYD88 L265P mutation. CT imaging showed no lymphadenopathy.

A 32-year-old woman presented with several years of vague neck discomfort. Thyroid ultrasonography revealed two lesions in the right thyroid lobe: a 0.5 cm hypoechoic nodule with ill-defined margins and a taller shape (suspicious for malignancy), and a separate 1.8 cm anechoic, oval cystic lesion with a well-defined margin located posteriorly, superior to the smaller nodule. To evaluate both lesions, ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration was performed. The aspirate from the cystic lesion yielded 1 cc of thick, yellowish, pus-like fluid; the cyst collapsed after aspiration. Fluid cytology showed no follicular cells and only a few squamous cells. The parathyroid hormone level in the cyst fluid was normal, and bacterial cultures were negative.

An 80-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with a 3-year history of a gradually enlarging mass on the left side of her neck. She reported mild dysphagia but denied any dysphonia or dyspnea. On examination, there was a firm, smooth, pulsatile left laterocervical swelling measuring 6 × 5 cm with regular margins; no cranial-nerve palsies were noted.

A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the neck demonstrated a 3.7 × 3.0 × 5.7 cm hypodense, heterogeneous mass that did not enhance, displacing the common, external, and internal carotid arteries anteriorly and the internal jugular vein anterolaterally.
