On MRI, the lesion was low in signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high in signal intensity on T2-weighted images. These radiological findings aligned most closely with a diagnosis of vagal nerve schwannoma, although cervical sympathetic chain schwannoma could not be excluded.

A 54-year-old virgin woman presented with urinary retention and dysuria. She had been treated for a presumed severe urinary tract infection. Her medical history included meningitis at age 4, secondary hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine, and mild intellectual disability. She had no prior surgeries, trauma, or genital procedures. On examination, there was a large, painless mass covering the labia, and the urethral meatus appeared reduced to a pinhead opening. Pelvic ultrasound with Doppler showed a well-defined cystic mass without vascularity and no clear relationship to the urethra or vagina. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a superficially placed, midline fluid-density lesion above the vulva measuring 54 × 40 mm, with no invasion of adjacent structures.

A 71-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of appetite loss, weight loss, and fatigue and a 1-week history of cough that did not improve with levofloxacin. He denied fever or night sweats. On examination, he was afebrile, and there was a palpable right cervical lymph node swelling. Laboratory studies showed:
• White blood cell count 15,900/mm3 (93.5% neutrophils)  
• C-reactive protein 15.9 mg/dL  
• Lactate dehydrogenase 380 U/L (normal 118–223)  
• Calcium 11.3 mg/dL  
• Pro–gastrin-releasing peptide 89.1 pg/mL (normal 0–81.0)  
• Soluble interleukin-2 receptor 7910 U/mL (normal 0–613)

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen revealed:
• A large cavitary mass in the right hilar area measuring 8.4 × 6.3 cm  
• Two smaller satellite nodules in the left lower lobe (1.4 × 1.1 cm and 1.1 × 0.9 cm)  
• Lymphadenopathy in right cervical, mediastinal, and intra-abdominal regions  
• A splenic mass measuring 9.0 × 8.3 cm with a low-density central area suggestive of necrosis

A 41-year-old man presented with a 5-month history of progressive right-sided nasal obstruction, facial pain, and intermittent epistaxis. He had no fever, rhinorrhea, or loss of smell. His past medical and family histories were unremarkable, and he was a cigarette smoker. On examination, vital signs were normal. Anterior rhinoscopy revealed a well-circumscribed soft tissue mass filling the right nasal cavity and displacing the septum to the left; the oral cavity and oropharynx were normal, and there was no cervical lymphadenopathy. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. CT of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses showed a homogeneously enhancing ovoid mass (27 × 14 × 24 mm) in the right nasal cavity, extending into the right ethmoid sinus with erosion of adjacent bone. MRI demonstrated a tissue process in the right nasal cavity with extension into the ipsilateral anterior ethmoid sinus, showing heterogeneous T2 hyposignal and homogeneous intense enhancement after gadolinium, with no evidence of intracranial or intraorbital extension.

A 36-year-old Indonesian woman presented with an 8-month history of a painful, palpable nodular mass in the umbilical region of her abdomen. She reported that the pain and occasional bleeding from the lesion occurred in a cyclic pattern coinciding with her menstrual period. She denied any history of abdominal or pelvic surgery, menstrual abnormalities, hormonal therapy, or use of birth control. On examination, there was a well-defined, tender nodular mass measuring 2 × 2 cm at the umbilicus. Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed an inhomogeneous hypoechoic, hypovascular lesion measuring 2.12 × 1.46 × 1.96 cm with posterior shadowing in the umbilical region, suggestive of umbilical endometriosis.

A 51-year-old Asian-Japanese man with no past medical history was referred for evaluation of an incidentally discovered retroperitoneal mass. The lesion was first noted during an abdominal ultrasound at a routine health checkup. He denied abdominal pain, weight loss, fevers, or neurologic symptoms. Physical examination was unremarkable. 

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen showed a well-defined 45×48×53 mm mass between the aorta and left adrenal gland, flanked by the left renal artery and vein, with a hypodense center and mild peripheral enhancement. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated central cystic degeneration or necrosis with slightly low T1-weighted signal, slightly high T2-weighted signal centrally, and high signal intensity on diffusion-weighted images at the periphery. 

Fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography–CT revealed an SUVmax of 5.5 in the lesion without other areas of abnormal uptake. 123I-metaiodobenzylguanidine scintigraphy showed no uptake in the mass. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, metabolic and endocrine panels, and plasma catecholamines, were all within normal limits.

A 56-year-old nulliparous woman presented 14 months after a supracervical laparoscopic hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for menorrhagia, pelvic pain, and large uterine leiomyomas. Her preoperative evaluation included a normal Pap smear; no chest radiograph or endometrial biopsy was obtained. At surgery, an 18–20-week–size uterus (1518 g) was removed via prolonged mechanical morcellation without a containment bag; superficial pelvic endometriosis was noted and cauterized. Final pathology on six uterine fragments demonstrated weakly proliferative endometrium without atypia, adenomyosis, and leiomyoma; the ovaries showed benign parenchyma and endosalpingiosis. 

On presentation, she reported left lower quadrant pain, persistent cough, and shortness of breath. Examination revealed a firm left lower quadrant abdominal mass and a fleshy lesion at the vaginal apex; the cervix was not visualized. PET–CT showed multiple hypermetabolic masses in the pelvis, abdomen, and chest. A core-needle biopsy of a 9 cm left pelvic mass revealed poorly differentiated epithelioid cells with hyperchromatic nuclei in necrosis. Immunohistochemical stains were positive for cytokeratin, vimentin, and CD138, and negative for SMA, EMA, ER, TLE1, HMB45, desmin, myogenin, CD117, BCL2, inhibin, MDN2, CD4, CA125, WT-1, CD45, calretinin, DOG-1, p16, CEA, CK20, HPV, and CD99. A vaginal biopsy showed grade 3 endometrioid adenocarcinoma. Pathology re-review of the hysterectomy and oophorectomy specimens showed no evidence of malignancy.

A 75-year-old man presented with a three-month history of left-sided headaches and diplopia. He also noted altered taste and paresthesia in the left maxillary region but denied epistaxis. His medical history included fast atrial flutter (on bisoprolol), hypertension, polymyalgia rheumatica, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and a previously excised papillary squamous cell carcinoma of the left thigh. He was an ex-smoker (quit 40 years earlier) and had a performance status of WHO 1.  
On examination, there was no cervical lymphadenopathy. Flexible nasoendoscopy revealed a mass extending to the left inferior turbinate, obscuring the left nasal cavity. The left eye showed approximately 3 mm of proptosis and diplopia on lateral gaze; visual acuity was 6/30 bilaterally, with no afferent pupillary defect or papilledema.  
CT of the head demonstrated an aggressive lesion in the left ethmoidal and frontal sinuses, with invasion of the left orbit and anterior cranial fossa and destruction of the left lamina papyracea. MRI confirmed bone erosion and dural breach adjacent to the left orbitofrontal cortex, without intraparenchymal brain invasion. A PET scan showed no distant lesions but progressive involvement of the frontal sinus.
Our initial differential diagnoses were squamous cell carcinoma, carcinosarcoma, lymphoma, teratocarcinosarcoma, olfactory neuroblastoma, small cell carcinoma and alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma.

A 23‐year‐old G3P2 woman at 38 weeks’ gestation underwent emergency Cesarean section after an unremarkable antenatal course and three normal obstetric ultrasounds. She had no abdominal complaints. Intraoperatively, numerous gray‐white, rubbery nodules of varying sizes were noted on the anterior and posterior uterine surfaces, omentum, and peritoneum, extending over bowel loops with finger‐like projections and unilateral adhesions to the left adnexa; precise measurements were not possible. Three tissue fragments (1.0–2.5 cm) were submitted for histopathology. Grossly, they were firm, homogeneous, white, and fibrous without hemorrhage or necrosis. Hematoxylin–eosin sections revealed low‐grade spindle‐cell proliferation in fascicular arrangements forming small and large nodules, with no cytologic atypia, mitotic figures, hemorrhage, or necrosis; focal decidual change was present. All specimens showed similar benign features and no evidence of malignancy.

A 45-year-old woman underwent gross total resection of a 2.5 cm nonfunctioning pituitary adenoma in August 2013. Pathology showed pleomorphic cells positive for synaptophysin, chromogranin, CAM5.2, and AE1/AE3. By March 2014, MRI revealed recurrence in the sella with left cavernous sinus invasion. Debulking resection demonstrated ACTH-positive cells with nuclear pleomorphism, prominent nucleoli, mitotic figures, and a Ki-67 index of 8–12%, leading to classification as an atypical adenoma. She received postoperative CyberKnife radiation (25 Gy in 5 fractions). Over the next 18 months, she developed left cranial nerve III, IV, and VI palsies with ptosis, diplopia, and headaches. In December 2015, she had salivary cortisol four times normal and began pasireotide and cabergoline. MRI two months later showed tumor growth (3.0 × 1.9 × 2.1 cm) with persistent cavernous sinus invasion. In February 2016, she received stereotactic radiosurgery (14 Gy). Follow-up MRIs at 1, 3, 5, 7, 10, and 14 months showed a stable large lesion abutting the left optic nerve and new CN-III enhancement but only minimal size change. ACTH levels rose from 155 to 269 pg/mL post-SRS, with normal cortisol. Starting at 12 months, ACTH climbed to 667 pg/mL with subsequent cortisol elevation and clinical Cushing’s (weight gain, psychotic episode, anxiety, and paranoia) requiring hospital admission, despite 2 mg cabergoline twice weekly. Repeat MRI showed only mild tumor progression (2.9 × 1.8 × 2.6 cm).

A 7-year-old girl presented with a 2-year history of an enlarging, intermittently painful, purplish lump in her left ear canal. Approximately 18 months earlier, she had developed cracking and pus-filled sores at the site and received antibiotics and analgesics before referral. On examination, there was a 3.5 × 2.5 cm purplish-red mass in the left external ear canal, with an irregular, friable surface and bleeding on minimal contact. Contrast-enhanced CT of the mastoids showed a lobulated mass in the cutis and subcutis of the left auricle extending into the external acoustic canal and into the left parotid space, with bilateral level II–IV cervical lymph nodes up to 0.6 cm in diameter. CT angiography demonstrated marked vascularity of the mass, supplied by branches of the left superficial temporal and posterior auricular arteries. Incisional biopsy revealed atypical cells and granulomatous inflammation, leading to a provisional diagnosis of an auricular malignant tumor without a clear histopathological subtype.

A 39-year-old Ukrainian immigrant woman presented with approximately 1 year of upper gastrointestinal bleeding. She had no prior evaluations and was referred for upper endoscopy, which revealed a large antral mass; a mucosal biopsy was obtained, but she declined endoscopic ultrasound and was lost to follow-up during pregnancy. She later returned with ongoing anemia and new epigastric pain. Repeat esophagogastroduodenoscopy with endoscopic ultrasound identified a 6 cm mass arising from the muscularis propria of the gastric antrum. Preoperative computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 9.7 × 7.8 × 4.8 cm heterogeneous mass adherent to the posterior wall of the gastric antrum, with predominantly fat attenuation, internal septations, and no pathologic lymphadenopathy. She then presented with melena; a repeat endoscopy showed mucosal ulceration overlying the mass, and biopsy results were consistent with adipose tissue.

A 57-year-old man presented with multiple painful tumors on the chest, right shoulder, and neck. Eleven months earlier, he noted right-sided cervical lymphadenopathy; one month later, multiple marble-sized skin tumors developed over these nodes. Over the next two months, the tumors spread to the chest and neck, accompanied by cough and hoarseness of voice. In the two months before presentation, the skin lesions increased in number and became painful, and he also developed dyspnea and weakness.

On examination, he was tachypneic. He had pale conjunctivae, elevated jugular venous pressure, and asymmetric chest expansion with diminished vesicular breath sounds over the left hemithorax. Multiple non-tender, immobile lymphadenopathies were palpable in the anterior and posterior cervical regions. Dermatologic examination revealed multiple, well-defined tumors on the chest, right shoulder, and neck, some with serous crust.

A chest radiograph showed a right pleural effusion; pleural fluid cytology revealed a lymphocytic effusion. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a solid mass in the anterior mediastinum infiltrating the superior vena cava, with bilateral pleural effusions. Histopathologic examination of a right supraclavicular lymph node revealed metastatic carcinoma, and immunohistochemistry was positive for CK7. Histopathology of a skin lesion showed round, hyperplastic, hyperchromatic cells in the dermis consistent with metastasis. Immunohistochemical staining of the skin specimen was positive for CK7 and negative for CD5, CD117, p63, CK20, P40, and TTF-1.

A 55-year-old man with a long-standing history of schizophrenia, who had repeatedly claimed that he was pregnant, was referred to general surgery for evaluation of progressive abdominal pain, coffee-ground emesis, and distension. He was cachectic with bilateral temporalis muscle wasting. His abdomen was markedly distended, and palpation revealed a large, firm, ill-defined, mobile mass occupying the entire abdomen. Mild tenderness was noted in the epigastrium without rebound. Bowel sounds were diminished, especially in the left upper quadrant. According to family members, he had recurrent coffee-ground vomiting and chronic low frequency of bowel movements; for the past 11 days he had passed only flatus.  
Abdominal ultrasonography showed a large cystic hypoechoic mass filling the abdominal cavity. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 21 cm×33 cm nonenhancing monolocular cyst in the right abdomen displacing intestinal loops to the left, and a separate 67 mm×93 mm heterogeneous mass in the left adrenal gland. Although he had no clinical features of pheochromocytoma, 24-hour urinary metanephrines, vanillylmandelic acid, and catecholamines were within normal limits.

A 47-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a right scrotal mass that had progressively increased in size over several months. He denied dysuria, incontinence, straining during urination, or other urinary symptoms. He had no family history of urological malignancy. On examination, there was a painless, firm 5.9 cm mass palpable adjacent to the right testis. Scrotal ultrasonography demonstrated a heterogeneous extratesticular mass on the right side, with borders distinct from the testicle and epididymis, along with a reactive hydrocele.

A 65-year-old man presented to the oncology clinic with a 2-week history of low-grade fever, a gradually progressive swelling on the left side of his neck, malaise, and easy fatigability.  

On examination, he was pale and febrile (100 °F). Bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy (levels IB, II, III, and V) and axillary lymphadenopathy were present; the largest node measured 3 cm × 3 cm at left level IB. The nodes were firm, non-tender, mobile, and discrete. The chest and cardiac examinations were unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed moderate splenomegaly.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, platelet count 206 × 10^9/L, and leukocyte count 19 × 10^9/L. Peripheral blood smear revealed 5% large pleomorphic lymphoid cells with a high nuclear-to–cytoplasmic ratio, sparse basophilic cytoplasm, irregular nuclei, and clumped chromatin. Bone marrow aspiration was hypercellular with similar abnormal lymphoid cells. Trephine biopsy demonstrated marrow spaces replaced by a monotonous population of medium-to-large lymphoid cells with scant-to-moderate cytoplasm; some cells had cleaved nuclei. Serum lactate dehydrogenase was elevated at 1053 mg/dL, with normal renal function, uric acid, and serum electrolytes.

Neck ultrasound showed multiple enlarged hypoechoic cervical lymph nodes, the largest 2.5 cm × 1.8 cm at left level II. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax and abdomen revealed bilateral mild pleural effusions (left > right), subsegmental collapse of the left lower lobe, multiple non-necrotic homogeneous lymph nodes in the mediastinum, axillae, retroperitoneum (largest 3.6 cm × 2.7 cm), and inguinal regions, as well as splenomegaly. Cerebrospinal fluid examination was normal.

Excisional biopsy of a cervical lymph node showed complete effacement of nodal architecture by a monotonous infiltrate of medium-to-large lymphoid cells with scant cytoplasm, irregular nuclei, and clumped chromatin. Adjacent small nodes contained areas of necrosis surrounded by histiocytes; acid-fast bacilli stain was negative.

A 42-year-old Japanese woman with iron deficiency anemia was brought to the emergency department 36 minutes after a high-energy head-on motor-vehicle collision while wearing a seatbelt and airbag. On arrival, she was alert; respiratory rate 30/min, heart rate 74/min, blood pressure 148/64 mmHg, temperature 36.2°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on 10 L/min via reservoir mask. She complained of anterior chest pain and had a laceration on the left lower thigh and a contusion on the right groin. On abdominal examination she had mild to moderate tenderness in the right lower quadrant without guarding or rebound. Focused ultrasonography showed fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Laboratory tests revealed a white-cell count of 14,030/mm3, hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL, normal lactate (1.8 mmol/L), and normal coagulation parameters. Noncontrast CT of the torso identified fractures of the right clavicle, sternum, and left 6th–8th ribs, and complex fluid (mean attenuation 28 HU) around the Douglas fossa extending to the ileocecal area. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a slightly dilated appendiceal tip containing a coprolith and an unclear appendiceal wall at the tip, without pneumoperitoneum, solid-organ injury, or contrast extravasation. Her vital signs remained stable and hemoglobin did not decrease over one hour; however, serial CT scans showed an increase in peritoneal fluid extending from the appendix through the pelvis. Emergency laparotomy was then considered because of localized peritonitis and possible intraperitoneal hemorrhage.

A 56-year-old Japanese man presented with eczema and redness of the right nipple and an 11 mm firm lump in the right subareolar area. He had no family history of breast cancer and his medical history was notable only for surgery for a cerebral hemorrhage 2 weeks earlier. On examination, there was erosion and erythema of the right nipple–areolar complex and a palpable, firm 11 mm mass beneath the areola. Ultrasonography revealed a 13 mm cystic mass below the right areola with a “rippling‐water” appearance and no obvious invasive component. Contrast‐enhanced computed tomography showed only the cystic right breast lesion and no lymphadenopathy or distant metastasis.

A 71‐year‐old white woman with no history of skin cancer presented for her annual skin examination and evaluation of facial lesions. She was adopted, and her family history of skin cancer was unknown. On examination, there was a 3 mm translucent papule on the left nasal ala and a separate 4 mm pink papule on the right side of her nose. Both lesions were shaved for clinicopathologic evaluation to rule out cyst versus basal cell carcinoma (BCC). 

Histologic examination of the right‐sided papule demonstrated clusters of basaloid cells in the dermis with palisading nuclei and retraction spaces, and a diagnosis of BCC was made; Mohs surgery was scheduled. 

The 3 mm × 1 mm shave biopsy of the left nasal lesion showed expression of epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) and pankeratin, but not leukocyte common antigen (LCA). The laboratory reported a neoplasm of epithelial‐structure origin and recommended a second opinion. 

On review, the pathologist noted cells of interest staining against AE-1/AE-3 in a perinuclear dot-like pattern, focal perinuclear EMA positivity, and negative LCA. Features were described as suspicious for Merkel cell carcinoma, and additional immunohistochemical studies and complete re-excision were recommended.

A 26-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of headache and gait unsteadiness. Over the past month, he noted left facial deviation, drooling from the left mouth corner, a change in voice, nasal regurgitation, and difficulty swallowing. On examination, visual acuity and funduscopic findings were normal, without papilledema. He had left cranial nerve VII, IX, X, and XI palsies, left cerebellar signs, and nystagmus. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed a heterogeneous extra-axial lesion in the left cerebellopontine angle that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed heterogeneous enhancement after gadolinium. The mass appeared attached to the posterior petrosal dura, extending from the sigmoid sinus to the medial internal acoustic meatus and along the inferior tentorial surface, with marked dural enhancement. Diffusion-weighted imaging demonstrated restricted diffusion, with corresponding low signal on the apparent diffusion coefficient map. Multiple additional intracranial lesions with similar diffusion restriction were seen in the periventricular regions. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest and abdomen showed no evidence of a primary malignancy or systemic metastases.

A 40-year-old woman with Eisenmenger syndrome, without gynecologic or gastrointestinal symptoms, was found to have an abdominal mass on routine examination.  
A CT scan revealed two abdominopelvic masses: a solid mass in the right adnexa and a cystic mass in the left adnexa.  
Pelvic ultrasound showed a unilocular, homogeneous cystic mass in the left adnexa (14.0 × 19.3 × 10.6 cm) with low-level internal echoes, a well-defined wall, no solid areas, and no internal blood flow; the left ovary could not be visualized. In the right adnexal region, a solid-appearing mass measuring 8.4 × 6.0 × 8.5 cm had echogenicity similar to myometrium; the right ovary was identified.  
Because of the size of the lesions, an MRI was obtained. In the right adnexa, a mass showed a bridging-vessel sign, consistent with a uterine leiomyoma. In the left adnexa, a 17.0 × 9.8 × 13.0 cm cystic mass showed a claw sign indicating ovarian origin; on T1-weighted images it was homogeneously hyperintense without solid components, and in the retrocervical region there was hypointense tissue on T2 with focal T1 hyperintensity.  
Serum tumor markers were as follows: CA 125, 70.4 U/mL; CA 19-9, 383.1 U/mL; CA 15-3, 19.7 U/mL; β-hCG, 0.29 IU/mL; AFP, 1.6 ng/mL; CEA, 3.5 ng/mL.

A 66-year-old African-American woman presented with a two-year history of a “raw,” non-healing ulcer on her right nipple with intermittent serous and bloody discharge. Her medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, congestive heart failure, and uterine fibroids. In February 1998, she underwent lumpectomy for a 3-cm ductal carcinoma in situ (nuclear grade II/III micropapillary type) located in the inferomedial quadrant of the right breast; margins were negative. She then received whole-breast radiation therapy (total dose 6000 cGy) followed by five years of tamoxifen. 

On examination, the right nipple showed an irregular excoriation partially eroding through the nipple; the surrounding areolar skin was effaced, retracted, and indurated without odor or cellulitis. There was no palpable axillary lymphadenopathy. Mammography was negative for recurrent breast cancer, and magnetic resonance imaging showed abnormal enhancement confined to the nipple–areolar region.

A 61-year-old obese man with a history of hypertension underwent laparoscopic partial nephrectomy after an incidental left renal mass was detected during evaluation of his blood pressure. Histopathology revealed a chromophobe renal cell carcinoma. One year later, routine surveillance imaging demonstrated a new lesion in the left seminal vesicle.  
Magnetic resonance imaging showed a 32 mm, well-circumscribed, heterogeneous solid mass in the left seminal vesicle with well-defined planes separating it from the rectum and bladder. The patient underwent laparoscopic excision of the left seminal vesicle.  
The resected seminal vesicle measured 6 × 3 × 2 cm. On sectioning, there was a 30 mm, solid, well-circumscribed, brownish, smooth nodule; surgical margins were free of tumor.  
Microscopic examination revealed well-defined nests of cuboidal cells separated by vascular fibrous septa without vascular invasion, mitotic figures, or necrosis. Focally, gland-like structures were present. Individual cells had a large central nucleus, small to medium nucleoli, and granular eosinophilic cytoplasm.  
Diagnostic considerations included metastasis of the previous chromophobe renal cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma of the seminal vesicle, and paraganglioma.

A 32-year-old woman presented with menstrual irregularities and pelvic pain for 3 months and abdominal distension for 1 month. On examination, a large abdomino-pelvic mass was palpable. Ultrasonography revealed a 15 cm heterogeneous, predominantly solid pelvic mass with some cystic foci. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a large, well-defined inhomogeneous solid and cystic lesion inseparable from the right ovary, without calcifications, and with moderate enhancement of solid areas; the fat planes with the urinary bladder were partially effaced. Radiologic interpretation was suggestive of a malignant ovarian tumor. Serum CA-125 was 843 IU/mL. All hematological investigations and serum hormonal assays were normal, and ascites was absent. The patient was hospitalized with a presumed diagnosis of a malignant ovarian tumor.

A 78-year-old man with diabetes mellitus type II, hypertension, hypothyroidism, and recurrent urinary tract infections presented with fatigue, left upper abdominal pain, urinary frequency for 1 week, and an unintentional 10-kg weight loss over 3 months. On examination, vital signs were stable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL with a normocytic normochromic anemia on peripheral smear, normal white-cell count, lactate dehydrogenase 1266 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 434 IU/L. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a mildly enlarged liver with normal attenuation and hypodense, wedge-shaped splenic lesions suggestive of infarcts. For evaluation of possible neoplasm, a whole-body FDG PET-CT was performed and showed diffusely increased FDG uptake in the liver (SUVmax, 4.5) with no significant FDG uptake in the splenic lesions or elsewhere.

An 8-year-old boy presented with a 1-month history of a painless, diffuse swelling of the left cheek. On extraoral examination there was facial asymmetry with a bony hard, non-tender swelling extending from 3 cm below the left infraorbital margin to the lower border of the mandible, and from the ala of the nose to the tragus of the ear; the overlying skin was normal. Intraorally, there was a diffuse bony hard swelling of the left posterior mandible from the deciduous first molar to the retromolar pad, with buccal and lingual cortical plate expansion; the deciduous second molar and permanent first molar were absent, there was no mucosal change, tooth mobility, or lymphadenopathy. Cone-beam CT showed a well-defined mixed radiolucent–radiopaque lesion with sclerotic borders in the left mandibular body and ramus, containing coalescent hyperdense foci and causing expansion and thinning of buccal and lingual cortices, with posteroinferior displacement of the unerupted left first molar into the angle region.  
Based on these clinical and radiographic findings, a provisional diagnosis of calcifying odontogenic cyst, ameloblastoma, calcifying epithelial odontogenic tumour, metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma, metastatic lung adenocarcinoma, and ossifying fibroma was considered.

A 50-year-old woman (P3L3) presented with a 1½-month history of a painless right breast lump and a 30-year history of circumferential hyperpigmentation of the same breast. She reported no nipple discharge, skin contractures, or eczema, and had no personal or family history of breast or ovarian cancer. On ultrasonography, there was a well-defined, mildly hypoechoic lobulated lesion measuring 4.3×2.4×4.1 cm at the 7 o’clock position of the right breast; the contralateral breast and axillary lymph nodes were normal. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the lesion revealed multiple fatty fragments composed of adipocytes without ductal epithelial cells or atypia, suggestive of benign breast disease. With clinical suspicion of a giant fibroadenoma versus a phyllodes tumor, she underwent a wide local excision. Histopathological examination of the excised specimen demonstrated atypical oval to spindle cells with moderate to marked pleomorphism, enlarged and irregular nuclei, and more than 10 mitoses per high-power field; adipocytes were interspersed among the atypical cells, myxoid areas were present, and benign ductal components lined by intact myoepithelium were entrapped at the periphery. No leaf-like pattern was noted, and margins were negative for malignancy.

An 18-year-old man with no significant medical history presented after a motor-vehicle collision. He reported chest pain following the trauma but denied dyspnea. Vital signs were stable, and oxygen saturation was 98% on room air. On examination, chest movement was limited on the right; tactile vocal fremitus was decreased over the right hemithorax, with dullness to percussion and diminished breath sounds on the right. 

A chest CT scout view showed an opacity in the right lower hemithorax with minimal shifting of the heart to the left. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a well-circumscribed, predominantly fat-containing mass with interspersed soft-tissue components, measuring 13 × 23 × 15 cm, arising from the anterior mediastinum and extending into the right hemithorax. The lesion did not cross below the diaphragm nor markedly shift the mediastinum, and it was associated with near-complete collapse of the right lower lobe.

A 47-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of dull left chest pain and progressive dyspnea (MRC Grade III). He also reported a productive cough without hemoptysis. He was a non-smoker with no known environmental or occupational exposures.

On examination, his body mass index was 20 kg/m2. There was no clubbing or lymphadenopathy. Chest-wall excursion and breath sounds were diminished over the left hemithorax.

A chest radiograph showed a homogeneous opacity in the lower left hemithorax obliterating the left cardiac border with rightward mediastinal shift. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax revealed a large, well-defined, heterogeneous mass in the anterior mediastinum with central areas of necrosis, abutting but not infiltrating the chest wall, and without mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

Abdominal ultrasonography was unremarkable. Routine blood tests, including serum cortisol, were within normal limits. Fibreoptic bronchoscopy revealed no endobronchial lesions. Bronchial washings, brushings and transbronchial needle aspiration were non-diagnostic. A CT-guided transthoracic tru-cut biopsy showed small round tumor cells, but a definitive histologic diagnosis could not be made.

An 88-year-old Caucasian woman presented with several months of upper back pain and, over the past 4 weeks, progressive bilateral lower-extremity weakness requiring a walker. She denied fevers, night sweats, or weight loss. Physical examination revealed no lymphadenopathy, a positive Romberg sign, decreased pinprick sensation in both legs to the L2 level, loss of proprioception in all extremities, normal rectal tone, and extensor left toe and equivocal right toe responses. Laboratory studies showed mild anemia and thrombocytosis; all other values were normal. Plain radiographs of the spine were unremarkable. MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrated a dorsal epidural lesion from T2 to T4 with involvement of the posterior left T4 vertebral body and extension through the left T2–3 and T3–4 neural foramina, causing significant cord compression and mild cord edema.

A 58-year-old woman presented with chronic, nonspecific bilateral lower rib pain. She had a history of cholecystectomy and gastroesophageal reflux disease. Physical examination was normal. A chest radiograph showed a questionable retrocardiac opacity. Routine laboratory tests, including hemoglobin, hematocrit, white blood cell count, and platelet count, were all within normal limits.

A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest and upper abdomen during the portal venous phase demonstrated a hiatal hernia correlating with the radiographic opacity and incidentally revealed splenomegaly with a solitary 6.6 cm × 6.0 cm mass. On CT, the lateral aspect of the mass enhanced homogeneously, whereas the medial aspect remained hypoenhanced.

To further characterize the lesion, multiphasic MRI of the abdomen was performed. The mass was isointense to normal splenic parenchyma on both T1-weighted and T2-weighted images. During the arterial phase, there was mild peripheral nodular and internal septal enhancement, and during the portal venous phase the enhancement became complete, diffuse, and mild, persisting on delayed images.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 45-year-old woman presented with 3 weeks of progressive epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting, which worsened over the 3 days before admission. She also reported fatigue, anorexia, and weight loss but denied diarrhea, hematemesis, or melena. Her medical history included convulsions treated with valproate sodium for 2 years, hypothyroidism on levothyroxine, and secondary amenorrhea. On examination, her vital signs were stable, and the only notable finding was hyperpigmentation of the skin, particularly on the face and in skin folds. Laboratory testing showed a normocytic anemia with a normal iron profile; serum amylase and lipase were within normal limits. An abdominal ultrasound revealed gallbladder sludge. Upper endoscopy demonstrated three mass-like lesions in the stomach, each with central mucosal ulceration; biopsy specimens were non-diagnostic. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen was unremarkable except for mild antral wall thickening. Endoscopic ultrasound showed three round, hypoechoic submucosal lesions measuring 13 mm at the proximal lesser curvature, 4 mm just distal to that lesion, and 10 mm in the antrum.  
What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 50-year-old woman (G1P1) was referred for evaluation of uterine prolapse. Her medical history was notable for a resected spinal schwannoma one year earlier; there was no family history of cancer. 

On transvaginal ultrasound, a 54 × 37 mm solid, hypoechoic pelvic mass with irregular margins and color Doppler score 3 vascularity was identified in the right adnexa; the left ovary appeared normal except for two tiny (< 1 mm) anechoic areas. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis confirmed a lobulated right adnexal lesion with heterogeneous post-contrast enhancement.

The patient underwent laparoscopic evaluation. A round, reddish, easily bleeding mass was noted in the pelvis; it originated from an ileal loop displacing the right ovary, which appeared covered by the mass. The left ovary had a 1 cm exophytic, reddish vascular lesion on its surface despite normal overall volume. Multiple small nodules with similar appearance were seen on the peritoneum in the pouch of Douglas. There was no gross lymphadenopathy.

A 53-year-old man was referred after an asymptomatic radiolucent lesion was noted in the right maxilla during routine dental planning. He had normal overlying mucosa and slight buccal cortical plate swelling in the edentulous region of the upper right premolars. The upper right canine, premolars, and molars had been extracted about 10 years earlier, and a partial removable appliance was in place. Panoramic and periapical radiographs revealed a 1.0 cm well-defined, round, unilocular radiolucency in the edentulous premolar area, adjacent to the superficial cortical bone. The lesion was at the level of the apical third of the remaining upper right lateral incisor, with areas suggestive of cortical fenestration due to ridge resorption. Provisional clinical diagnoses included a residual cyst and an odontogenic keratocyst, and the patient was scheduled for surgical removal of the lesion.

A 71-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of a painless lump in the right lateral neck that became more prominent with Valsalva manoeuvre. He denied other symptoms and had no prior medical history of note. On examination, there was a 20-mm, non-pulsatile, non-tender, solid subcutaneous mass in the right supraclavicular fossa between the two heads of the sternocleidomastoid muscle; it was mobile, not adherent to skin, with no overlying skin changes or regional lymphadenopathy. Routine blood tests, including tumour markers, were within normal limits. Ultrasound of the neck showed a heterogeneous solid mass measuring approximately 22 × 22 × 25 mm at the base of the right neck, with marked internal vascularity; the lesion lay superficial to the carotid and visceral space and was closely associated with the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck confirmed a well-circumscribed, hypervascular mass measuring 22 × 19 mm in the right supraclavicular fossa at the origin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, external to the carotid and visceral space with no bony erosion.

A 50-year-old man with a history of bilateral gynecomastia and sarcoidosis on low-dose corticosteroids for 20 years presented to the emergency department with hemoptysis that resolved spontaneously. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest performed to evaluate the hemoptysis revealed an incidental 0.6-cm, well-circumscribed soft-tissue density mass in the left breast. On further questioning, he reported a 1-year history of a tender, palpable mass in that location. 

Diagnostic mammography confirmed a round, circumscribed, subareolar 0.7-cm hyperdense mass without calcifications or architectural distortion. Targeted ultrasound demonstrated a round, circumscribed, nearly isoechoic 0.8-cm nodule with minimal internal vascularity on color Doppler and no posterior shadowing. There was no axillary lymphadenopathy.

A 79-year-old man with no prior relevant medical history presented with two asymptomatic tumors on the medial aspect of the lower left leg that had arisen over 3 months. There was no palpable lymphadenopathy. Complete blood count and peripheral blood examination were within normal limits.  
Skin biopsy showed a kappa-monotypic blastoid proliferation with a Ki-67 index greater than 90%. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated positivity for CD79a and MUM-1, heterogeneous expression of MYC, and weak positivity for CD123; the cells were negative for CD20, PAX5, immunoglobulin M, BCL6, and CD138. Fluorescence in situ hybridization revealed no MYC, BCL2, or BCL6 rearrangements. Next-generation sequencing identified a class 5 pathogenic TP53 variant (exon 5).  
A positron emission tomography–computed tomography scan showed no extracutaneous abnormalities.

A 55-year-old woman with hypertension presented with two days of abdominal pain, distension, inability to pass gas or stool, nausea, vomiting, and near syncope. She was pale, hypotensive (90/45 mmHg), tachycardic (115 bpm), tachypneic (24/min), and mildly hypoxemic (SpO₂ 91% on room air). Temperature was 37.2 °C. She had no regular medications, was a smoker, and had no relevant family history. On examination, the abdomen was distended, with deep tenderness in the right quadrants without guarding, and a giant non-tender mass palpated in the left and midline quadrants. Laboratory studies showed neutrophilic leukocytosis (WBC 18.8 × 10³/μL) and anemia (Hb 7.5 g/dL). She received IV fluids, three units of packed red blood cells, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and bowel rest. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated a heterogeneous, hypodense giant retroperitoneal mass measuring 36 × 32 × 28 cm, compressing and displacing surrounding intra- and retroperitoneal organs, and was suspected to represent a retroperitoneal soft-tissue sarcoma.

A 13-year-old girl presented with a 5-month history of swelling over the dorsum and medial aspect of her right hand. The mass had gradually increased in size without antecedent trauma, pain, fever, or systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a firm, nonwarm, mobile swelling over the dorsal and inner side of the fifth metacarpal. Deep palpation elicited tenderness, and range of motion at the fifth metacarpophalangeal joint was restricted. Routine hematological tests were within normal limits. Radiographs of the right hand showed an osteolytic, fusiform, expansile lesion involving the distal two-thirds of the fifth metacarpal and its articular surface; the cortex was paper-thin, breached, with no periosteal reaction, and the lesion displayed a “soap-bubble” appearance. A provisional clinicoradiological diagnosis of aneurysmal bone cyst versus giant-cell tumor was made. A chest radiograph was normal.

A 48-year-old woman underwent screening esophagogastroduodenoscopy and was found to have an elevated lesion in the esophagus. She was asymptomatic, drank 10 g of ethanol daily, and smoked 10 cigarettes per day. Her family history was unremarkable, and carcinoembryonic antigen, CA19-9, and routine blood tests were within normal limits.

Ten days later, repeat endoscopy confirmed circumferential long‐segment Barrett’s esophagus extending >3 cm from the esophagogastric junction. Within this segment at the mid-esophagus was a 15 mm submucosal tumor with a central depression, covered by Barrett’s mucosa.

Narrow-band imaging of the lesion showed enlargement of the mucosal pattern and dilation of mucosal microvessels without irregular glandular arrangement or tortuous vessels.

Miniprobe endoscopic ultrasonography (20 MHz) revealed a homogeneous hypoechoic mass confined to the lamina propria mucosa and submucosa.

Biopsy specimens demonstrated clusters of histiocytoid cells with abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm. Immunohistochemical studies were negative for pancytokeratin (AE1/AE3) and positive for S-100 and CD68.

CT scan showed no evidence of metastasis.

A 40-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of a sensation of fullness in her right ear, progressive hearing loss, and intermittent ipsilateral tinnitus. She had no significant past medical history. On otoscopic examination, there was a smooth, pink, firm, well-circumscribed mass attached to the posterosuperior wall of the right external auditory canal that bled on contact. Weber and Rinne tuning-fork tests were negative and right-lateralized, respectively. Pure-tone audiometry revealed an average right conductive hearing loss of 37.5 dB. A noncontrast CT scan of the temporal bone showed a 17-mm, well-defined, soft-tissue–density lesion (61 HU) occupying the outer two-thirds of the right external auditory canal, with erosion of the middle-ear structures and partial opacification of nearby mastoid air cells.

A 64-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a two-day history of bleeding from her left breast. She reported a slowly enlarging growth on the left nipple–areolar complex over two years, which recently became ulcerated with serous discharge. She denied weight loss, fever, systemic symptoms, or risk factors such as excessive sun exposure, radiation, arsenic, or immunosuppression. 

Vital signs were within normal limits except for blood pressure of 164/85 mm Hg. On examination, there was a >10 cm fungating ulcerative mass occupying most of the mid and outer left breast with distortion of the nipple–areolar complex, open bleeding wounds, foul odor, surrounding erythema, and palpable left axillary lymph nodes. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed a large heterogeneous enhancing mass in the left breast and mildly enlarged left axillary lymph nodes, with no evidence of distant metastasis. Brain MRI and bone scintigraphy were negative for metastatic disease. A core-needle (Tru-cut) biopsy of the mass was performed.

A 40-year-old man presented with a three-week history of progressive swelling on the left side of his face and neck, associated with pain, dysphagia, and dysphonia. On extraoral examination, there was firm, extensive edema over the left mandible without skin involvement or palpable lymphadenopathy. Intraorally, a large, tender mass extended from the left mandibular premolar region to the ascending ramus, with associated tooth mobility. Needle aspiration yielded a viscous, yellowish fluid under high internal pressure, and the swelling immediately diminished after decompression. Three-dimensional CT reconstruction demonstrated destruction of the left buccal cortical plate of the mandible with projecting osseous spicules. A panoramic radiograph revealed a well-defined radiolucent lesion bounded by a radiopaque corticated margin, involving the left mandibular premolar and molar region. The clinical, radiologic, and tomographic findings raised the possibility of a keratocystic odontogenic tumor or an ameloblastoma.

A 71-year-old woman was referred after an incidental finding of an anterior mediastinal mass on routine health examination one month earlier. She was asymptomatic. Her medical history included hypertension and prior surgery for an intraspinal meningioma. On admission, her blood pressure was mildly elevated; other vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies showed normal levels of alpha-fetoprotein, human chorionic gonadotropin, carcinoembryonic antigen, C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, and interleukin-6. Non-contrast chest CT revealed a 5.0 cm × 4.0 cm right anterior mediastinal mass with heterogeneous density and punctate calcifications, abutting the right lung and pericardium without aortic invasion. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a well-defined lesion with solid and multilocular cystic components. No mediastinal lymphadenopathy was noted. The patient could not undergo PET-CT for financial reasons. Based on the CT appearance of soft tissue, cystic areas, and calcifications, a mediastinal teratoma was considered most likely. A subxiphoid video-assisted thoracoscopic approach was chosen for resection. Intraoperatively, the mass was found to be soft, encapsulated, and contained opaque fluid with necrotic debris. The lesion was densely adherent to the right middle lobe of the lung but was otherwise separable from surrounding structures. En bloc resection of the mass and thymus was performed, along with a partial right middle lobectomy.

A 48-year-old South Asian man presented with sudden onset of slurred speech, episodes of vomiting, and complete motor aphasia of 10 hours’ duration, which had begun to improve over the preceding hour. He had experienced a similar self-limited episode 5 months earlier. He had no history of hypertension or diabetes. On examination, he was afebrile; blood pressure was 106/74 mm Hg; heart rate, 104 beats per minute with a regular rhythm; and all distal pulses were palpable. Cardiac examination revealed a faint, short mid-diastolic murmur. Neurologic examination showed motor aphasia without peripheral deficits. Computed tomography of the brain demonstrated multiple infarcts in the left parietal lobe, right occipital lobe, right caudate nucleus, left internal capsule, left thalamus, and bilateral cerebellar hemispheres. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed multiple foci of high signal on diffusion-weighted imaging in the right corona radiata, left thalamus, and bilateral cerebellar hemispheres, consistent with acute infarction. These findings suggested a cardio-embolic source, although the patient had no known cardiac history.

A 34-year-old North African woman with no significant past medical history was referred for management of obstructive jaundice. Two months earlier, she had undergone laparotomy and resection of the protruding dome of a segment I hepatic cyst thought to be a hydatid cyst compressing the biliary convergence. She now presented with fever to 38.5 °C, mucocutaneous jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools. On examination, she was febrile and icteric; there was no abdominal tenderness, hepatomegaly, or palpable mass. Laboratory studies showed moderate hepatocellular enzyme elevations and cholestasis. Hydatid serology and serum carcinoembryonic antigen and carbohydrate antigen levels were negative. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a cystic lesion in segment I with parietal and septal enhancement and rupture into the biliary convergence. MRI demonstrated a multiloculated lesion that was hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2, communicating with the biliary bifurcation, with dilatation of intrahepatic ducts (predominantly left) and of the common bile duct containing heterogeneous signal material. At laparotomy via a subcostal incision, the liver appeared micronodular; on opening the common bile duct, mucinous fluid and membranes were extracted, raising questions about the presumed diagnosis.

A 28-year-old Ethiopian woman presented with a 3-year history of a left axillary swelling that was initially small but had progressively increased in size. She reported mild local discomfort but denied cough, fever, weight loss, night sweats, or other constitutional symptoms. Her medical history was unremarkable; she had no surgeries, no use of hormonal contraception, and no family history of cancer or chronic disease. She had regular menstrual cycles and no pregnancies.

On examination, vital signs were normal. In the left axilla there was a solitary 5 × 4 cm firm, nontender, well-defined, mobile mass completely separate from the breast; overlying skin was normal with no nipple, areola, or ulceration. Examination of the breasts, right axilla, other lymph node regions, chest, cardiovascular system, abdomen, genitourinary system, musculoskeletal system, and neurologic system was unremarkable.

A provisional clinical impression of axillary lymphadenopathy due to either lymphoma or tuberculosis was considered. Laboratory studies including complete blood count (WBC 5900/mL with normal differential, hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, platelets 247 000/mL), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (13 mm/h), renal and liver function tests, urinalysis, and chest radiograph were within normal limits.

A 39-year-old woman presented with painless swelling in the left groin of several years’ duration. The mass had gradually increased in size. She reported no fever, groin trauma, discharge, or change in size with straining or coughing. There were no urinary or defecatory symptoms and no personal or family history of malignancy. On examination, there was a non-tender, soft, mobile nodular mass measuring approximately 10 cm × 5 cm in the left groin region extending to the superior thigh, without overlying skin changes. The mass remained unchanged with coughing, standing, or straining, and transillumination was negative. Ultrasonography showed a large ill-defined iso- to hyperechoic lesion measuring 13 cm × 4.1 cm, with no deeper muscular extension, calcifications, cystic components, or central vascularity. Findings were deemed consistent with a benign lesion. With a provisional diagnosis of lipoma, no tumor markers, biopsy, or aspiration cytology were performed, and surgical exploration was planned.

A 53-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of a slow-growing, painless nodule in her right upper arm. She denied pain, sensory changes, or trauma. On examination, there was a hard, well-defined mass within the right deltoid muscle; it was non-tender, did not limit range of motion, and there was no neurologic deficit. Her medical history was unremarkable.
  
Ultrasound of the upper arm showed a sharply delineated fusiform mass measuring 8.5 × 6.5 × 3.0 cm with heterogeneous echogenicity, limited internal Doppler flow, and close association with the lateral humeral cortex beneath the deltoid muscle; “A soft tissue tumor such as a sarcoma or desmoid was suspected.”  
   
MRI demonstrated a well-circumscribed ovoid lesion abutting the humerus without evidence of bone or neurovascular invasion. The mass was heterogeneous isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images and heterogeneous hyper- and isointense on T2 fat-suppressed images, with multiple T1 and T2 hypointense foci. There was limited peripheral enhancement with a slow initial phase and plateau on dynamic contrast–enhanced sequences, and no diffusion restriction was noted.  

Plain radiographs of the right shoulder confirmed a 9 × 5 cm soft tissue mass without calcifications, periosteal reaction, or cortical invasion. Non–contrast CT of the upper arm showed a well-circumscribed isodense mass beneath the deltoid muscle, again “without embedded calcifications or ossification.”

An 8-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a conjunctival nodule in the right eye. His parents first noted the lesion three months earlier; it had not changed in size, and he reported no pain, visual disturbance, or other ocular symptoms. There was no history of trauma, ocular surgery, or systemic disease.

On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes, and intraocular pressures were within normal limits. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye revealed a pale-yellow, firm nodule approximately 5 mm in diameter beneath the bulbar conjunctiva in the superotemporal quadrant. The lesion had clear borders, was immobile, mildly congested, and non-tender. There was no proptosis, and extraocular movements were full. Funduscopic examination of the right eye showed a normal posterior segment.

Computed tomography of the right orbit demonstrated a crescent-shaped calcified nodule on the temporal scleral surface without involvement of the extraocular muscles. To exclude systemic causes of tissue calcification, laboratory studies were obtained: serum calcium, phosphate, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and angiotensin-converting enzyme levels were all within normal limits.

A 74-year-old woman presented with a two-month history of a rapidly enlarging, painless mass in the left preauricular region. Her medical history was notable for a colon ascendens adenocarcinoma treated with hemicolectomy in 2003 (pT3 N1 G2 L1 V0 R0 M0, stage IIIB) and a clear cell renal cell carcinoma treated with nephrectomy seven years ago (pT1 NX G2 L0 V0 R0 M0, Fuhrmann grade 2). Follow-up for both cancers had been unremarkable, with the last renal cell carcinoma review one year before the current presentation. On examination, there was a mobile 3 cm lesion in the left parotid region. Ultrasonography showed a 3 cm polygonal hypoechoic lesion with well-defined smooth margins. Fine-needle aspiration was not performed. The patient underwent a left parotidectomy with preservation of the facial nerve. Grossly, the specimen contained a yellow tumour surrounded by a fibrous pseudocapsule, embedded in otherwise normal parotid parenchyma.

A 34-year-old woman presented with 6 months of progressive left proptosis, with recent ecchymosis and subconjunctival hemorrhage after a sudden rise in blood pressure. She had intact ocular motility, a best-corrected visual acuity of 0.9 in the left eye, and normal anterior and posterior segment examinations without optic nerve signs. The right eye was anophthalmic following enucleation in 2010 for a large choroidal melanoma confirmed by histopathology and metastatic workup; she received no adjuvant therapy and was lost to follow-up after 2 years of disease-free status. Orbital CT showed a well-defined isodense intraconal lesion measuring 2.6 × 2.5 × 2.4 mm with intrinsic high-density areas, located inferomedially between the optic nerve and inferior rectus, displacing them and scalloping the lamina papyracea. MRI demonstrated a hyperintense mass on T1-weighted images and hypointense signal on T2-weighted images. General physical examination and systemic metastatic evaluation were negative. An incisional biopsy via anterior inferomedial transconjunctival orbitotomy was planned.

An 18-year-old Asian woman presented with a 3-month history of fluctuating swelling and ptosis of the left upper eyelid. She reported mild discomfort at times of increased swelling but no visual changes or diplopia. On examination, a well-defined, soft, non-tender lesion was palpable in the left upper eyelid just below the superior orbital rim; there were no signs of inflammation. Visual acuity was normal, extraocular movements were full, and intraocular pressures were 17 mmHg OD and 20 mmHg OS.

Noncontrast computed tomography of the orbits revealed a homogeneous, well-circumscribed lesion in the left superior orbit molding to the globe and adjacent structures, with no bony erosion. “The findings favored the diagnosis of a lymphoid lesion,” and a transpalpebral biopsy was performed.

Histopathological examination showed structures resembling lymphoid follicles surrounded by loose connective tissue. At higher magnification, numerous blood vessels lined by plump endothelial cells with oval nuclei protruding into the lumen were seen, surrounded by a chronic inflammatory infiltrate rich in lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils. Immunohistochemical staining for Factor VIII highlighted the marked vascularity of the lesion and confirmed that the atypical “epithelioid” endothelial cells were of vascular origin. Blood counts and urinalysis were normal.

A 77-year-old man with a diagnosis of stage III multiple myeloma presented for evaluation of worsening anemia. He had been treated with radiation to cervical and thoracic spine lesions and sequential chemotherapies (bortezomib-based regimens, melphalan, prednisolone, then lenalidomide plus dexamethasone). His hemoglobin fell to 6 g/dL despite ongoing therapy. On Day 114 of treatment, upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was performed and revealed a 5-mm, submucosal tumor-like elevated lesion in the upper thoracic esophagus. On white-light observation, the lesion appeared whitish with a central area of redness. After iodine staining, the lesion was only faintly stained. On narrow-band imaging, the central part of the elevated lesion appeared green with an unclear boundary of elevation and showed small submucosal tumor-like findings.

A 63-year-old woman, gravida 7, para 3, postmenopausal for 10 years, presented with 2 months of vaginal bleeding. Physical examination was unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed a mass-like submucous degenerated myoma nodule in the uterine cavity. An endometrial biopsy performed elsewhere was reported as endometrial hyperplasia with cellular atypia; a Papanicolaou smear was normal. The patient underwent laparoscopic hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. 

Gross examination revealed a 4.0 × 2.5-cm polypoid mass in the lower left lateral uterine segment, pressing on the myometrium. Histologic examination showed a diffuse proliferation of relatively uniform small neoplastic cells with scant cytoplasm, hyperchromatic nuclei, frequent mitoses, numerous apoptotic bodies, and large areas of necrosis. The tumor had fully penetrated the uterine wall, with histologic evidence of lymphovascular and cervical invasion. There was no associated endometrial lesion in the hysterectomy specimen.

A 5-year-old boy presented with 10 days of pain and swelling in the left mandibular posterior region. His parents had noted mild swelling of the lower left face for 1 week. On examination, there was a diffuse, firm, tender swelling of the left lower face and intraoral obliteration of the buccal vestibule near the left deciduous mandibular second molar. Palpation revealed mild expansion of the buccal cortical plate, and the molar was tender to percussion. A panoramic radiograph showed a well-circumscribed, globular radiopaque mass continuous with the mesial root of the involved molar, surrounded by a thin, uniform radiolucent halo, and displacing the second premolar tooth bud distally. Based on these findings, cementoblastoma, osteoblastoma, osteoma, and odontoma were included in the differential diagnosis. The tooth with the attached mass was extracted for histopathologic confirmation.

An 18-year-old man presented with a one-month history of recurrent swelling and dull aching pain in the upper left posterior region of the jaw. Four years earlier, he had first noted a slowly enlarging swelling in the same area, which had been operated on twice at his native hospital, with partial reduction but persistent residual lesion. He had no other significant medical, personal, or family history. 

On extraoral examination, there was a diffuse, bony-hard swelling (7×5 cm) on the left side of the face, extending from the left ala of the nose to the anterior border of the ramus and from the infraorbital rim to the corner of the mouth; the overlying skin was normal, and a 2×2 cm left submandibular node was palpable. Intraorally, there was an ovoid, smooth, bony-hard swelling from the distal of tooth 22 to the mesial of 26, obliterating the buccal vestibule; it was slightly tender and fixed to the underlying bone.

CT scanning revealed a mixed hypodense-hyperdense unilocular lesion in the left maxilla, from the distal aspect of tooth 21 to tooth 26 and from the alveolar ridge to the floor of the orbit. The lesion had a partly corticated periphery and multiple intermittent hyperdense flecks internally. There was expansion, thinning, and focal perforation of the buccal cortical plate, thinning of the maxillary sinus walls, and invagination toward the orbital floor. 

On these findings, a benign odontogenic tumor was suspected, and, given the size and recurrence, a calcifying cystic odontogenic tumor (CCOT) was provisionally considered. An incisional biopsy was performed. Histopathological examination of H&E-stained sections showed a cystic lumen lined by odontogenic epithelium of variable thickness, with a basal layer of tall columnar cells with polarized hyperchromatic nuclei, overlying stellate reticulum–like cells, and superficial clusters of pale eosinophilic ghost cells. The connective-tissue wall was fibrous, densely collagenous, and non-inflamed; there were active odontogenic rests and focal globular calcifications.

An 84-year-old woman presented with abdominal pain, pruritus, and laboratory evidence of cholestasis, including an alkaline phosphatase level of 241 U/L (normal range, 55–142 U/L) and a total bilirubin level of 1.48 mg/dL (normal range, 0.3–1.0 mg/dL). Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography revealed a mass involving the entire thickness of the mid-portion of the duodenal wall, measuring approximately 12 mm, with no involvement of the ampulla of Vater. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen confirmed the presence of the duodenal wall mass and showed no regional lymphadenopathy.

A 15-year-old otherwise healthy Korean boy presented with a 6-year history of multiple papules on his fingers that were recalcitrant to laser treatments and cryotherapy. On examination, there were punctate pits and hyperkeratotic papules in a linear arrangement on the first and second fingers of his right hand. The keratotic papules had comedo-like plugs that coalesced to form linear verrucous plaques. Based on a clinical diagnosis of palmoplantar wart, he received periodic intralesional bleomycin injections and cryotherapy without improvement. A punch biopsy was then taken from one of the papules. 

Histologic examination revealed an epidermal invagination with a parakeratotic column (cornoid lamella) centered on an acrosyringial duct. The granular layer was absent at the base of the invagination, and dyskeratotic keratinocytes and vacuolization were observed. Intraepidermal eccrine ducts below the cornoid lamella were slightly tortuous and dilated but showed no other morphologic abnormalities.

A 46-year-old Chinese man with no prior medical or surgical history presented with a 6-month history of vague abdominal discomfort. He localized the pain to the left upper quadrant; it was dull in character and associated with nausea, dyspepsia, and early satiety. On examination, there was a smooth, non-tender, palpable mass in the left upper quadrant. Routine laboratory investigations were within normal limits.

He underwent esophagogastroduodenoscopy, which showed no abnormalities. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a well-circumscribed 5.5 × 5.5 × 5.6 cm mass projecting from the mesenteric fat adjacent to the transverse colon without a clear cleavage plane and without pathological lymphadenopathy. Subsequent colonoscopy was normal.

At a gastrointestinal multidisciplinary meeting, the differential diagnoses included primary colorectal carcinoma, a large gastrointestinal stromal tumour, and a desmoid tumour. The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy. Intraoperatively, the mass was noted to infiltrate the small bowel, encase the superior mesenteric artery and vein, and compromise small-bowel blood supply; it was also adherent to the cecum. An extended right hemicolectomy and segmental small-bowel resection with primary anastomoses were performed. The mass could not be fully excised, and a specimen was sent for histologic analysis.

A 38-year-old gravida 2, para 1 woman was referred at 37 weeks of gestation for evaluation of a fetal abdominal mass. Her medical history was unremarkable. Detailed ultrasonography showed a 45×45 mm left suprarenal cystic mass with homogeneous content and intracystic septations suggesting hemorrhage; color Doppler imaging demonstrated peripheral vascularization without internal flow. The fetal spleen and left kidney appeared normal, and no other structural anomalies were identified. Maternal urine homovanillic acid and vanillylmandelic acid levels were within normal limits. Two weeks later, follow-up sonography revealed a mass of unchanged size, and the fetal biophysical profile was 8 of 8. The infant was delivered by cesarean section for breech presentation at 39 weeks 4 days, weighing 3100 g, with Apgar scores of 8 and 10 at 1 and 5 minutes. Postnatal sonography confirmed a 48×50 mm left adrenal mass; one week later, the lesion had increased to 65×70 mm in size.

A 30-year-old woman presented with one month of painless vision loss in her right eye. She reported fever and a severe headache at symptom onset. She had no past ocular or systemic disease.  
On examination, right-eye best-corrected visual acuity was 6/18 (with +8.0 D) and left eye 6/6; intraocular pressures were 12 mm Hg in both eyes. Pupils were reactive, anterior segments were quiet, lenses clear, and there were no vitreous cells. Fundus examination of the right eye showed a neurosensory detachment at the posterior pole involving the fovea and extending inferiorly, with a few retinal hemorrhages; the left fundus was normal.  
Ultrasound B scan of the right eye revealed a localized retinal detachment temporal to the optic nerve head involving the macula and increased peripapillary choroidal thickness. Swept-source OCT showed intraretinal and subretinal fluid with shadowing of the choroidoscleral interface, photoreceptor-layer fibrin, and hyperreflective dots in the superficial choroid. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated early stippled pinpoint hyperfluorescence, placoid pooling in the late frames, and late disc staining in both eyes.  
Based on the prodromal systemic symptoms and these imaging findings, a provisional diagnosis of unilateral Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada disease was made, and routine blood tests and physician clearance for systemic steroids were planned.

19-year-old woman at 33 weeks’ gestation presented with 1 week of progressive dyspnea. Over the prior 3 months she had noted an 8-cm painful mass on the left side of her neck and developed dysphonia. On indirect laryngoscopy, a left hemilaryngeal tumor occupied >50% of the glottic lumen, with left vocal cord fixation and displacement of the right vocal cord. An urgent tracheotomy was performed, and labor was induced successfully the same day. Core needle biopsy of a left cervical lymph node and biopsy of the laryngeal mass revealed densely packed cells with uniform laminar invasive growth, nuclear hyperchromasia, nuclear molding, scant cytoplasm, a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, necrosis, and a high mitotic rate; the overlying laryngeal epithelium showed no dysplasia. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated strong diffuse positivity for p63, synaptophysin, CD56, CD57, and p16; focal positivity for vimentin and CD99; and negativity for CD45, chromogranin, TTF-1, desmin, myogenin, p40, CK5/6, CK20, TdT, and S-100 protein. Ki-67 was 100%. Cervical CT showed a 3.5-cm mass in the left glottic and supraglottic region extending to the epiglottis and pyriform sinus, with airway narrowing, and an adenopathic conglomerate measuring 7.2 × 3.5 cm in left cervical level II. Thoracoabdominal CT and bronchoscopy revealed no additional lesions.

A 5-year-old boy presented with a 1-year history of gradual flexion of his left little finger. There was no history of trauma, pain, or crying, and no family members had similar deformities. On examination, the left little finger exhibited a mallet deformity with ulnar angulation and an active extension lag of approximately 45° at the distal interphalangeal joint. The joint remained mobile. A lobulated, hard mass was palpable just proximal to the DIP joint. Plain radiographs demonstrated cortical irregularity and metaphyseal widening of the dorsal middle phalanx head. MRI of the finger revealed an exophytic bony lesion with continuity of both cortex and medullary cavity with the parent bone.

A 24-year-old man presented with a 9-month history of a slowly enlarging swelling in the anterior lower jaw. One month before onset, he had trauma to the region with extraction of several teeth. On examination, there was a firm, asymptomatic 4×4 cm swelling in the mandibular midline with a scar overlying the skin. Intraorally, the mucosa was intact, and a 4×3 cm soft-to-firm, nontender, nonfluctuant mass extended from the region of teeth 34 to 43, obliterating the labial vestibule; teeth 31, 32, 33, and 41 were missing, and tooth 42 exhibited grade II mobility.  
Orthopantomogram showed a well-defined unilocular radiolucency crossing the midline, root resorption of tooth 42, and a tooth-like radiopaque mass within the lesion. Cone-beam CT demonstrated a round unilocular lesion with complete destruction of the labial cortical plate and an irregular resorption front on the lingual side; three-dimensional reconstruction confirmed nonuniform bone resorption and a tooth-like calcification.  
Routine blood tests were normal. During an incision biopsy, thick yellow fluid was expressed; an H&E-stained smear of the fluid revealed large oval to round cells with vesicular and hyperchromatic nuclei against a background of red blood cells.

A 4-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of a 2-month history of profuse night sweats involving the head, neck, and upper body, followed by progressive abdominal pain. Despite analgesic and antiparasitic therapy, her pain worsened and was soon accompanied by difficulty walking and progressive lower-limb weakness. There was no history of trauma, fever, or significant weight loss. Her prenatal and postnatal histories were unremarkable, and developmental milestones were normal. Family history was notable only for an aunt with early breast cancer.

On examination, she was alert and in no acute distress. Temperature and vital signs were normal. Neurologic examination revealed decreased muscle tone and reduced range of motion in the lower limbs with inability to bear weight; sensation was intact. The abdomen was soft and mildly distended but non-tender. Findings in other systems were unremarkable.

Initial laboratory studies showed a normal blood cell count (Hgb 11.2 g/dl, platelets 249 000/mm3), an ESR of 40 mm/hr, negative CRP, normal liver and renal function, and a rising lactate dehydrogenase (from 536 to 3520 U/l). Total serum protein declined from 6.0 to 2.9 g/dl. Urinalysis and cultures were negative, and abdominal ultrasonography was unremarkable.

Lumbar puncture revealed CSF with 10 white cells/mm3 (100% monocytes), protein 44.1 g/dl, and normal glucose. Electromyoneurography showed reduced amplitude and velocity of M waves in the peroneal and tibial nerves bilaterally. She was treated for suspected acute polyradiculoneuritis with corticosteroids and IVIG without improvement.

In the second week, she developed dry cough, chest discomfort, and worsening dyspnea. Chest radiography showed a large homogeneous mass occupying the right hemithorax with slight leftward mediastinal shift. Chest CT confirmed a well-defined hypodense mass filling the right hemithorax, likely arising from the posterior mediastinum, causing mediastinal displacement, bronchial compression, and minimal pleural effusion. Further contrast CT showed a 95 × 75 × 70 mm heterogeneously enhancing mass with central necrosis, no mediastinal or axillary adenopathy, no bony destruction, and no connection to the spinal canal.

A 71-year-old woman presented with a firm swelling at the base of her tongue of unknown duration, which had progressively increased in size. She noted distortion of the tongue but no pain or ulceration. Her medical history was notable for controlled hypertension and a thyroid gland tumor. On examination, there was a 3 × 2 cm well-encapsulated, nodular mass at the left tongue base; there was no ulceration, no lymphadenopathy, and no neurologic deficits. Magnetic resonance imaging of the tongue showed a well-defined, solid, soft tissue lesion with heterogeneous enhancement, without evidence of invasion into surrounding structures.

A 64-year-old woman with end-stage pulmonary small cell carcinoma presented with a four-week history of a painless lump on the anterior tongue that had grown rapidly and was causing difficulty with speech and swallowing. On examination, there was a firm, well-defined, nontender 5 cm lesion in the midline of the anterior tongue, just beneath the mucosa. An incisional biopsy showed polygonal cells with clear cytoplasm arranged in a richly vascular stroma. Immunohistochemical staining revealed positivity for pan-cytokeratin (AE1/AE3), epithelial membrane antigen, vimentin, and CD10, and negativity for RCC antigen, cytokeratins 7, 19, and 20, and TTF-1.

A 34-year-old Caucasian man with a history of neuroblastoma (resected in infancy, followed by 18 months of chemotherapy) presented with abdominal pain and constipation. He had no other symptoms. On examination, there was a large, firm, mobile mass in the lower abdomen. Laboratory studies, including inflammatory markers, were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a heterogeneously enhancing mass arising from the small-bowel and sigmoid mesentery. The patient was hemodynamically stable and underwent an elective exploratory laparotomy, which revealed a >15 cm solid pelvic mass originating from the small-bowel mesentery of the mid-ileum and the wall of the sigmoid colon. The mass was well-circumscribed, tan-gray, encapsulated, and had a smooth, shiny external surface. A 22 cm segment of attached small bowel was resected en bloc with the mass.

A 59-year-old woman was found to have a palpable mass in her right midabdomen during a routine physical examination. She reported intermittent abdominal pain but denied hematuria or other urogenital symptoms. Her medical history was unremarkable, and she had no prior renal disease or trauma. Family history was notable for a brother who underwent nephrectomy for renal cell carcinoma at age 62.

An abdominopelvic CT scan revealed a 14 × 13 × 12 cm solid mass arising from the mid and upper poles of the right kidney, with significant enhancement of its solid components and finger-like areas of absent enhancement suggestive of necrosis or acute inflammation. The mass displaced the right lobe of the liver and the inferior vena cava anteriorly. No tumor thrombus was seen in the renal vein or IVC. Several hypoenhancing lesions in the liver were noted and deemed suspicious for metastases. A focal, slightly lucent lesion with a sclerotic rim in the T10 vertebral body was felt to represent either a small hemangioma of bone or a metastatic lesion, but a subsequent bone scan was negative. CT of the thorax showed no metastases.

Given the presumed diagnosis of RCC with potential metastases, the patient underwent percutaneous biopsy of the liver lesions; pathology revealed liver parenchyma with fatty deposits and no malignancy. In light of the negative liver biopsies and normal bone scan, an open radical nephrectomy with right retroperitoneal lymph node dissection was performed for suspected localized RCC.

A 36-year-old man presented with a 6-year history of a slowly enlarging, painful swelling on the sole of his right foot that caused a limp on walking. He denied any history of trauma. On examination, there was a single, 5 × 3 cm mobile mass on the plantar surface with normal overlying skin and no lymphadenopathy. Face and profile radiographs of the foot were normal. Ultrasound revealed a well-circumscribed, nonvascularized, heterogeneous mass measuring 48 × 30 × 26 mm that was isoechoic relative to fat. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a multilobulated lesion with fat signal intensity on all sequences, located in the extra-aponeurotic subcutaneous soft tissue of the sole without deep extension.

A 65-year-old man presented with a 3½-month history of an ulcer in the right lower posterior tooth region. He reported difficulty in mouth opening and swallowing. His habits included bidi smoking (12 per day for 50 years), and he had completed treatment for tuberculosis one year earlier.

On intraoral examination, there was a nontender, well-defined ulceroproliferative lesion distal to the right mandibular molar with an irregular white projection on its surface. The right submandibular lymph node was palpable but not tender. A panoramic radiograph showed slight erosion of the underlying bone in the right posterior mandible.

On the basis of clinical and radiographic features, a provisional diagnosis of tuberculous ulcer was made. An incisional biopsy demonstrated full-thickness epithelial dysplasia—altered nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, pleomorphism, hyperchromatism, and mitotic figures—without stromal invasion, and was reported as carcinoma in situ.
