A middle‐aged African American man presented with lower urinary tract obstructive symptoms and right groin pain. Eight years earlier, he had a similar episode thought to be a right seminal vesicle abscess or cyst on transrectal ultrasound, which was treated with aspiration; pathology, cytology, and culture reports were unavailable. He was lost to follow‐up until recurrence of right groin pain, when a CT scan showed a retroperitoneal mass measuring 12.7 × 8.9 cm, felt to be a seminal vesicle cyst. He again was lost to follow‐up and presented four years later with discomfort; CT imaging demonstrated growth of the mass to 15.4 × 9.9 × 16.8 cm. Follow‐up MRI showed a 17.7 × 12.0 × 11.1 cm non‐enhancing, fat‐containing cystic lesion thought to arise from the right seminal vesicle. In clinic, he reported incomplete bladder emptying, frequency, intermittency, urgency, weak urinary flow, and nocturia twice nightly despite 0.4 mg of tamsulosin daily. His American Urological Association symptom score was 20 and quality‐of‐life score 5. On digital rectal examination, findings were unremarkable but limited by a body mass index of 35.1. Serum creatinine and other laboratory values were within normal limits. Given his persistent obstructive symptoms and discomfort, he elected to undergo robotic‐assisted laparoscopic seminal vesiculectomy.

A 59-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of progressive swelling, pain, anesthesia of the left lateral lower leg, and loss of extension of the left great toe. Physical examination revealed a 2.0 cm tender, palpable mass at the posterolateral aspect of the proximal lower leg over the fibular head and a positive Tinel sign. Radiographs of the left leg showed a lytic lesion with irregular cortical thinning in the upper fibula and slight surrounding soft-tissue swelling. Additional X-rays revealed similar osteolytic lesions in the distal tibia and cuboid. Routine blood tests were within normal limits. MRI of the left lower extremity demonstrated multiple solid lesions in the gastrocnemius muscle at the level of the fibular head and multifocal lesions with irregular borders in the upper fibula, distal tibia, cuboid bone, and calcaneus; the right leg was normal, and the chest radiograph showed no abnormalities. Needle-aspiration biopsies from the cuboid bone and tibia revealed neoplastic infiltration composed of vascular structures of varying caliber lined by mildly atypical endothelial cells in a myxoid stroma; the epithelioid cells were polygonal or spindle-shaped with vesicular nuclei, inapparent nucleoli, and eosinophilic cytoplasm containing intracytoplasmic vacuoles. Immunohistochemical studies showed immunoreactivity for smooth muscle actin (SMA), CD31, CD34, CD68, and vimentin, and no immunoreaction for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA).

A 38-year-old woman (gravida 2, para 2) presented with a left-sided vulvar mass that she first noticed one year earlier; it was initially small and slowly enlarged. On examination, there was a 3×3-cm, nontender, well-defined, soft-to-firm swelling in the left labium majus; the overlying skin was unremarkable, and systemic examination was noncontributory. Fine-needle aspiration cytology revealed moderately cellular smears composed of tissue fragments of cells with indistinct cell margins, a moderate amount of eosinophilic cytoplasm, and spindly nuclei of varying size. Scattered mature adipocytes were entrapped within the spindle-cell fragments against a hemorrhagic background. The cytological interpretation was a benign spindle-cell lesion with a differential diagnosis of spindle cell lipoma and leiomyoma. Complete excision was advised for histopathological confirmation.

A 28-year-old woman, 10 months postpartum, was referred with a 3-month history of excessive thirst, polyuria (≈12 L/day), mild headache, and fatigue. She had breastfed for 4 months and experienced two menstrual cycles after weaning, followed by amenorrhea coincident with the onset of polyuria. Physical examination showed no signs of hypopituitarism or visual-field defects. Laboratory evaluation demonstrated mild hyperprolactinemia and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism; other anterior pituitary axes were intact (Table 1). A water-deprivation test revealed serum osmolality 310 mmol/kg, sodium 148 mmol/L, and urine osmolality 107 mmol/kg, all of which normalized with desmopressin, confirming central diabetes insipidus. Pituitary MRI showed an enlarged gland and a uniformly enhancing thickened stalk (5.2 mm). Screening for systemic causes, including markers for sarcoidosis and vasculitis, was negative. A presumptive diagnosis of lymphocytic hypophysitis was made; she declined glucocorticoid therapy and was managed with desmopressin.

Two months later, she presented with a persistent cough. She was an occasional smoker. Chest radiograph and high-resolution CT showed bilateral upper-zone thin-walled cystic lung disease. Respiratory medicine consultants favored pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis based on clinical and radiologic correlation, but the coincidence of hypophysitis with this finding raised consideration of Langerhans cell histiocytosis or sarcoidosis. Bronchoalveolar lavage, transbronchial biopsy, skeletal survey, and calcium studies were inconclusive, and an open-lung biopsy was planned.

A 68‐year‐old woman with no history of breast disease underwent screening mammography, which revealed subtle inversion of the left nipple and suspicious microcalcifications measuring 0.8 cm in the left areolar‐nipple complex. She reported occasional nipple discharge and pruritus but denied any palpable mass. Ultrasound demonstrated calcifications within a flattened left nipple, and an ultrasound‐guided core needle biopsy was performed. Review of the biopsy revealed atypical ductal proliferation favoring a cutaneous adnexal origin in a background of breast tissue with keratin cysts, associated calcifications, and a foreign body–type giant cell reaction. The differential diagnosis included syringomatous adenoma of the nipple versus low‐grade microcystic adnexal carcinoma, and surgical resection was recommended to make a definitive diagnosis.

A 78-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of multiple papular lesions around the anus. He reported no pruritus or pain. His medical history was notable for hypertension, glaucoma, and urinary tract obstruction. On examination, there were several flesh-colored, wart-like papules, each measuring less than 1 cm in diameter. Under polarized contact dermoscopy, the lesions displayed a hyperkeratotic, callus-like surface without the characteristic features of warts. Skin punch biopsy and human papillomavirus (HPV) staining were performed for accurate diagnosis.

A 71-year-old man was admitted with sudden-onset epigastric pain. Laboratory tests showed a lipase level above 2000 U/L, cholestatic jaundice (bilirubin 103 µmol/L), and hepatic cytolysis (ALT 154 U/L; AST 131 U/L). Abdominal CT demonstrated a heterogeneous infiltration around the pancreatic head without biliary duct dilatation. Endoscopic ultrasound confirmed a heterogeneous hypoechoic lesion in the pancreatic head extending to the hepatic hilum and in contact with the portal vein. There was no evidence of biliary stones or recent alcohol use.

His medical history was notable for an immunoglobulin A plasmacytoma diagnosed 3 years earlier (t(4;14) positive, del(17p) negative) treated with lenalidomide and dexamethasone, with an extramedullary relapse at L4 one year ago. On admission, his platelet count was 41 000/mm3. Lenalidomide toxicity was suspected, and viral hepatitis serologies were negative. A transjugular liver biopsy showed centrilobular and portal polymorph infiltrates with eosinophils, suggesting drug-induced hepatitis or hepatitis related to biliary obstruction. High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone was initiated, but bilirubin increased to 346 µmol/L over 10 days. Repeat CT showed mild-to-moderate biliary duct dilatation and a small volume of ascites. Given the appearance of a mass in the pancreatic head, a second EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration was performed; cytology revealed only benign ductal epithelial cells.

A 28-year-old healthy Saudi woman presented in January 2020 with an asymptomatic lesion on her forehead that had been present for eight years without change in size or appearance and without other lesions. She had no significant medical or surgical history and no family history of similar lesions. On examination, there was a solitary, nontender, firm, skin-colored to pink nodule with overlying telangiectasia on the left forehead, measuring 3.0 × 3.4 mm. Dermoscopy revealed a pink-orange homogeneous background with fine linear vessels. Clinical differential diagnoses included trichoepithelioma, syringoma, and basal cell carcinoma. A 4-mm punch biopsy was performed. Histologic examination showed a well-circumscribed dermal tumor composed of irregular, variably sized nests of uniform basaloid epithelial cells with peripheral palisading and pale to clear cells centrally, set in a fibrotic stroma with moderately dense lympho-histiocytic infiltrates. There were no retraction artifacts, cytologic atypia, mitotic figures, or necrosis.

A 23-year-old woman presented with a 9-month history of a painless swelling of the right posterolateral chest wall. She denied any preceding trauma and had no history of genetic disease or cancer. On examination, there was a hard, nontender mass over the posteroinferior lateral thoracic region. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. A plain chest radiograph revealed a calcified opacity projecting over the ninth rib without evidence of underlying bone destruction. Computed tomography showed a 6 cm × 5 cm × 2.5 cm ossified mass arising from the outer surface of the ninth rib, with preservation of cortical integrity and no medullary involvement. Whole-body scintigraphy and CT of the chest did not demonstrate skip lesions or pulmonary metastases.

A 74-year-old woman presented with a 4-week history of bilateral leg pain and numbness, followed by progressive leg weakness beginning in the third week. She denied bowel or bladder incontinence. She had a 45-year history of smoking one pack per day. On examination, there was paraparesis and hypoesthesia below the T10 level. Routine preoperative craniospinal MRI and chest radiograph were unremarkable. Thoracic MRI demonstrated a solitary intramedullary lesion at the T9–T10 level with homogeneous contrast enhancement. The initial differential diagnosis included neoplasms such as ependymoma, astrocytoma, intramedullary lymphoma, and infectious processes.

A 35-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of intermittent headache and blurred vision, with severe diplopia on left lateral gaze that had rapidly worsened over the past 3 months. On examination, visual acuity was 6/24 in both eyes, and there was a left sixth cranial nerve palsy. Routine blood, urine, and stool analyses, including a full hormone profile, were within normal limits. Contrast MRI of the brain showed a large clival-based, homogeneously enhancing lesion involving the entire clivus and invading the sphenoid sinus, without calcification. Based on the radiologic appearance, a provisional diagnosis of pituitary adenoma, clival chordoma, or plasmacytoma was considered.

A 25-year-old woman presented with an on-and-off frontal headache for a few weeks, accompanied by occasional vomiting and blurred vision for several days. She had no fevers, loss of consciousness, seizures, or focal neurologic deficits. Two months postpartum after an uneventful vaginal delivery, she reported that her symptoms began during pregnancy and had recently worsened. There was no history of trauma, surgery, tuberculosis, diabetes, hypertension, or other systemic disease.

On noncontrast CT of the brain, there was a well-defined hyperdense mass in the right frontal region with small hypodense areas and calcific foci, associated with adjacent white matter hypodensity, mass effect, and focal erosion of the right frontal bone.

Subsequent contrast MRI of the brain showed a lobulated extra-axial lesion in the right frontal region that was T1 hypointense, T2 and FLAIR hyperintense, with a CSF cleft sign. There was no restricted diffusion. SWI demonstrated round and linear blooming foci corresponding to calcification and vascular channels. The lesion exhibited predominantly homogeneous postcontrast enhancement with a few nonenhancing areas, produced significant mass effect with midline shift and subfalcine herniation, and caused focal frontal bone erosion. MR venography was normal.

Imaging differentials for a solitary, well-defined extra-axial, predominantly homogeneously enhancing lesion in a young adult woman included hemangiopericytoma, atypical meningioma, histiocytosis, and dural metastases.

A 64-year-old man presented with a six-month history of a nonpainful lump in the temporal conjunctiva of his left eye that had enlarged over the past two months. He had initially been told it was a pterygium. On examination, there was a slightly elevated, inflamed, granular, mobile, non-tender, non-ulcerated, non-hemorrhagic, non-pigmented nodule measuring 3 mm × 2 mm × 2 mm, extending from the temporal mid-conjunctiva to the limbus, not adherent to the sclera. Uncorrected visual acuity was 6/36 bilaterally and corrected to 6/6 in each eye. Extraocular movements were full and painless. Anterior segment and dilated fundus examinations were unremarkable in both eyes, and the lacrimal apparatuses were normal. The clinical differential diagnosis included phlyctenulosis or a soft-tissue tumor. The lesion was completely excised under local anesthesia with a 2 mm conjunctival margin. Grossly, the surgical specimen was a white tissue fragment admixed with mucus, measuring 6 mm × 5 mm × 3 mm.

A 62-year-old woman with essential thrombocythemia diagnosed at age 36 (JAK2 V617F–positive) was treated with hydroxyurea until 1994 and then with pyrimethamine. In February 2012, she noted a 3-month history of intermittent fevers, unintentional weight loss, and lethargy. She also developed discomfort and brownish discoloration of her left leg, initially managed as venous insufficiency. Peripheral blood film showed leukoerythroblastic changes. A bone marrow biopsy again demonstrated megakaryocytic hyperplasia consistent with essential thrombocythemia, without fibrosis or leukemic transformation.

While hospitalized for atypical pneumonia, she observed multiple nodular lesions on her left lower leg. On examination, there were numerous firm nodules from mid-shin to ankle without ulceration, bleeding, discharge, lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly. A punch biopsy of one lesion revealed a diffuse dermal infiltrate of large pleomorphic cells with both plasmacytic and immunoblastic features. Immunohistochemistry showed negativity for CD20 and positivity for CD138, Bcl-2, CD45, and weak CD79a, with a Ki-67 proliferation index of approximately 50%. Staining was negative for pan-cytokeratins, S-100, Melan-A, CD2, CD56, CD30, Bcl-6, and TdT. In situ hybridization for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV EBER-ISH) revealed positive nuclear staining.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the left leg confirmed subcutaneous nodules with adjacent tibialis anterior myositis but no bone involvement. MRI of the spine showed a known T8 compression fracture and no new lesions. A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated mild splenomegaly (16.2 cm) and no other disease sites. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 106 g/L, platelets 123 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 8.7 × 10^9/L, lactate dehydrogenase 1151 IU/L, β2-microglobulin 6.51 mg/L, an IgA kappa monoclonal protein of 7 g/L, and IgG kappa < 1 g/L. Serologic tests were negative for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV; there was evidence of past EBV and CMV exposure.

A 25-day-old male infant, born at 34 weeks’ gestation, was referred with a one-month history of an enlarging abdominal mass. Antenatal ultrasonography had detected the mass in utero. After birth, the infant developed progressive abdominal distension and was initially thought to have a teratoma on ultrasound at a local hospital. 

On examination, there was a 5 cm×4 cm palpable mass in the right upper abdomen; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed total bilirubin 98.7 μmol/L (reference 5.0–28.0), direct bilirubin 17.9 μmol/L (reference <8.8), indirect bilirubin 80.0 μmol/L (reference <20), alpha-fetoprotein >1210 ng/mL (normal for age 1164–118 850), and neuron-specific enolase 21.48 ng/mL (reference <15). Echocardiography revealed a patent foramen ovale; chest radiography was normal.

To further characterize the lesion and its blood supply, the infant underwent multimodal abdominal ultrasound (grayscale high-frequency US, color Doppler flow imaging, and contrast-enhanced ultrasound) and a plain CT scan. Grayscale US revealed a 5.5 cm×5.0 cm heterogeneous complex cystic and solid mass in the right upper abdomen, with the solid portion resembling a head and body and multiple small hyperechoic spots arranged in a vertebral column–like structure, all surrounded by a membranous capsule. Color Doppler imaging identified an aorta-like arterial vessel within the solid component (peak systolic velocity 58.4 cm/s) and a separate umbilical vessel-like structure at the lesion’s edge. Contrast-enhanced US confirmed the aorta-like structure with 2 mm limb branches and a 3 mm umbilical vessel connecting to the patient’s abdominal aorta. Plain CT demonstrated a 5.6 cm×4.6 cm retroperitoneal mass with a hyperattenuating axial skeleton corresponding to the vertebral-like structure on US. No abnormalities were seen in the liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, or kidneys on either modality.

A 34-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of infertility despite unprotected marital relations and reported noticing left‐sided scrotal swelling. His medical and family history were unremarkable. On examination, both testes were normally positioned within the scrotum and had normal size and consistency. In the left hemiscrotum, a soft, elastic mass was palpated; it transilluminated and could not be reduced without pain. These findings were interpreted as a Grade 3 varicocele. Semen analysis showed a sperm concentration of 11 million per cc, motility of 15% at 30 minutes, and 4% normal morphology by Kruger strict criteria. His body-mass index was 32 kg/m2.

A 46-year-old man presented with a 6-week history of progressive visual loss. He first noticed gradual visual decline in his left eye, progressing to complete blindness, and partial vision loss in his right eye. He denied headaches, jaw claudication, or pain with eye movement. On examination, there was reduced pupillary reactivity to light in the left eye and discoloration of the right eye; no other neurologic deficits were present. Brain MRI with intravenous contrast revealed a diffuse lesion involving the left optic nerve and optic chiasm, extending along the optic tract, optic radiation, and pituitary stalk. The lesion demonstrated hyperintensity on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences, heterogeneous enhancement on postcontrast T1-weighted images, and an apparent diffusion coefficient of 1.049 × 10−3 mm2/s. These findings were interpreted as consistent with a high-grade optic pathway glioma (modified Dodge grade 3).

A 67-year-old man presented with acute-onset spastic quadriparesis. He had a 2-year history of follow-up after decompressive laminectomy for lumbar spinal canal stenosis and fusion for thoracic ligamentum flavum ossification. In April 2016, he suddenly noted weakness in all four limbs, with inability to stand or walk. Two weeks later, on evaluation:

• Manual muscle testing revealed right-dominant quadriparesis.  
• Patellar and Achilles tendon reflexes were hypoactive.  
• Gait was spastic, broad-based, and steppage; he required a walker.

Emergent MRI of the cervical spine showed an epidural mass in the right ligamentum flavum at C4–C5 that was isointense on T1-weighted images and low to isointense on T2-weighted images. CT of the cervical spine showed no ossification within the mass. Review of a cervical MRI obtained 2 years earlier for neck pain demonstrated a smaller lesion at the same site that did not compress the spinal cord.

Based on the acute and rapidly deteriorating presentation and imaging, two main diagnostic considerations were entertained.

A 46-year-old woman presented with a 20-day history of idiopathic upper abdominal pain. She denied weight loss, viral hepatitis, drug abuse, and had no family history of cancer. Her medical history was notable for systemic lupus erythematosus diagnosed 2 years earlier and treated with prednisone 10 mg daily. On examination, she was well nourished, afebrile, and had no jaundice, icteric sclera, spider naevi, or palmar erythema. The abdomen was soft and non-tender without palpable masses, although deep palpation of the right hepatic region elicited pain. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, coagulation profile, and hepatitis B and C serologies, were within normal limits. Carcinoembryonic antigen, α-fetoprotein, and CA19-9 were normal. Antinuclear antibody was positive at 1:320; complement levels (C3, C4) and immunoglobulin levels (IgA, IgM, IgG) were within reference ranges, and specific autoantibodies (anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, anti-SSA/Ro, anti-SSB/La, anti–Scl-70, anti–Jo-1) were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed a 6.3 × 5.5 cm inhomogeneous solid lesion with iso- and hypoechoic areas in the right hepatic lobe. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a 6.0 × 5.0 cm irregular hypodense lesion in the right anterior lobe that enhanced less than surrounding liver in arterial and delayed phases. Colonoscopy, gastroscopy, chest radiograph, and whole-body bone scan were unremarkable. A working diagnosis of primary liver neoplasm was made, and the patient was referred for surgical resection.

A 60-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of intermittent gastric discomfort triggered by solid foods. Her medical history was notable only for depression treated with paroxetine. Physical examination was unremarkable. Upper endoscopy revealed an incidentally discovered submucosal exophytic mass in the gastric antrum with normal overlying mucosa. Mucosal biopsies showed only mild inactive chronic inflammation without evidence of neoplasia. Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated a 1.6 × 1.3 cm hypoechoic, exophytic lesion arising from the antrum. EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology revealed spindle cell tissue fragments interpreted as consistent with a gastrointestinal stromal tumor. An abdominal CT scan provided no additional diagnostic insight. After multidisciplinary discussion, the patient elected to undergo elective laparoscopic wedge resection of the gastric mass.

A 30-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of a localized gingival swelling between the mandibular left canine and first premolar. The lesion had grown slowly, causing displacement of the teeth and widening of the interdental space. She recalled a similar growth in the same region 11 years earlier that had been excised, but no records were available. On examination, there was an approximately 0.8 × 1.0 cm sessile, nonlobulated mass with sharp margins, covered by mucosa of normal color and of firm, fibrotic consistency. Full-mouth periodontal examination revealed generalized 3–4 mm pockets with subgingival calculus and poor oral hygiene. A clinical diagnosis of chronic periodontitis with focal fibrous hyperplasia (irritation fibroma) was made. An intraoral periapical radiograph showed horizontal bone loss in the involved area. The lesion was removed by excisional biopsy with an internal bevel incision and open-flap debridement; healing was uneventful. Five weeks later, the surgical site appeared well healed. Microscopic examination of the excised tissue revealed a partially circumscribed lesion composed of interlacing fascicles of collagen fibers and abundant islands and strands of odontogenic epithelium; the connective tissue contained focal chronic inflammatory infiltrates (predominantly plasma cells) and occasional multinucleated giant cells. The overlying epithelium was hyperplastic, parakeratinized stratified squamous with elongated rete ridges.

A 20-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with a 2-day history of right flank pain and constipation. Her mother had a history of Hodgkin’s lymphoma. Vital signs were normal. Physical examination revealed a palpable pelvic mass. Laboratory studies showed a CA-125 level of 62.1 U/mL; β-hCG and AFP were negative. 

Abdominal and pelvic CT revealed an 18 × 11 × 13 cm heterogeneous pelvic mass, suggestive of an immature teratoma; chest CT was unremarkable. The patient underwent right salpingo-oophorectomy and peritoneal washing. Intraoperative consultation confirmed malignancy, and an omentectomy, peritoneal biopsies, bilateral pelvic and para-aortic lymphadenectomy, and appendectomy were performed with no residual macroscopic disease.

Microscopic examination showed a neoplasm with a diffuse growth pattern and focal follicle-like spaces containing eosinophilic fluid, composed of small round cells with scant cytoplasm, hyperchromatic nuclei, small nucleoli, and brisk mitotic activity. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated patchy cytokeratin positivity, diffuse CD56 and WT1 expression, and loss of SMARCA4 expression. There was no expression of inhibin, SF1, desmin, or actin.

An 8-year-old Yemeni boy with no prior medical history presented with dark skin discoloration over a slow-growing, mobile subcutaneous mass on the mid-lateral aspect of his left thigh that had been present for 6 months and enlarged most over the prior 2 months. The lesion appeared after a suspected penetrating trauma. He reported intermittent low-grade fevers, predominantly at night, along with weakness and fatigue. On examination, there was a 5×5 cm dark brown patch with a central hypopigmented, scaly area over a firm, non-tender, mildly warm swelling. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL, C-reactive protein 102 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 42 mm/h, and a normal white-cell differential. Plain radiographs of the left femur revealed a subtle soft-tissue opacity without radiopaque foreign body or gas. Ultrasound demonstrated a 3.6×2.4×1.9 cm complex predominantly cystic lesion with interspersed vascular channels showing arterial spectral Doppler waveforms and occasional fluid-fluid levels. MRI of the thigh showed a heterogeneously hyperintense T2 fat-suppressed and isointense T1 lesion with fluid-fluid levels, a peripheral low-signal fibrous pseudocapsule, central intense enhancement, peripheral variegated enhancement, perilesional edema and enhancement, a feeding artery from the left profunda femoris, and enlarged ipsilateral inguinal lymph nodes. The initial differential diagnosis included a post-traumatic infected hematoma, a vascular malformation, or a vascular tumor.

A 32-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a single painless red nodule on the middle of his upper lip. He noted that the lesion began as a corn-sized papule, bled easily when touched, and caused no discomfort. On examination, there was a solitary, hemispherical, red nodule measuring approximately 8 mm in diameter, with a smooth, moist surface, telangiectasia, clear boundaries, and a soft texture that bled easily. Reflectance confocal microscopy of the lesion revealed extensive proliferation of capillaries within the dermis, abundant blood flow, markedly dilated capillary lumens containing erythrocytes, and a small number of inflammatory cells around the vessels.

A 20-year-old man with a history of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) diagnosed at age 1, who discontinued treatment at age 4, presented with a gradually enlarging left testicular swelling of 1 year’s duration. He denied other symptoms and had deferred medical care due to socioeconomic factors and fear of a poor prognosis.

On examination, there was a large, hard, indurated swelling of both epididymes, more pronounced on the left. The left testis was ill-defined and measured approximately 3.5 cm in diameter. 

Scrotal ultrasonography demonstrated bilateral enlargement of the testes and epididymes, with the right testis measuring 6.6 × 3.7 × 2.3 cm (41 ml) and the left testis measuring 6.2 × 4.5 × 3.6 cm (52.1 ml). Bilateral grade II varicoceles were also noted. Semen analysis revealed azoospermia.

A biopsy of the right epididymis was performed. Histologic examination showed nodules of cells separated by dense fibrous septae. The nodules consisted of nests and cords of polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, uniform round nuclei, small nucleoli, distinct cell borders, and a lymphoid infiltrate in the stroma. Adjacent testicular tissue exhibited seminiferous tubules with thickened basement membranes, germ cell aplasia with occasional spermatogonia, and tubules containing only Sertoli cells; spermatocytes, spermatids, and spermatozoa were absent. Collections of similar polygonal cells were observed between seminiferous tubules. Intratubular germ cell neoplasia or malignancy was absent. Special stains with Mason trichrome did not reveal Reinke crystals.

A 41-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented in June with headache, generalized weakness, and chills. Physical examination was unremarkable. A noncontrast CT scan of the head showed no abnormalities, and she was treated empirically for a presumed viral infection. One week later she developed dysphasia and a right facial droop. MRI of the brain with gadolinium revealed a 1.5×2.0 cm mass in the left temporal lobe with nonuniform vasogenic edema; the lesion appeared dural-based, suggesting a meningioma. CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no extracranial disease. In July, a left frontal craniotomy was performed, and the dural mass was completely excised. Grossly, the lesion measured 3×2 cm. Histologic examination revealed a diffuse, noncohesive proliferation of large neoplastic cells with abundant foamy eosinophilic cytoplasm, frequent neutrophils within the cytoplasm, phagocytosis, irregular multilobulated nuclei with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli, and a background of lymphocytes and neutrophils.

An 8-year-old girl with known neurocutaneous melanosis—history of multiple congenital pigmented nevi, early-onset seizures, neuromotor delay, tetraventricular hydrocephalus treated with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt, and prior stable neuroradiology—presented with several weeks of intractable headache, vomiting, and generalized seizures. Noncontrast CT of the head showed a 1 cm faintly hyperdense, round intraparenchymal lesion in the left cerebellar hemisphere. Brain MRI demonstrated a 1 cm focal lesion that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, mildly hyperintense on T2-weighted and FLAIR images, surrounded by edema, with restricted diffusion on DWI/ADC and inhomogeneous enhancement after gadolinium. No spinal abnormalities were detected. Lumbar puncture yielded cerebrospinal fluid positive for Cryptococcus neoformans var. gattii, raising concern for a cerebellar abscess, although neoplasm was not excluded.

A 51-year-old woman with a 17-year history of common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) had been receiving intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) every 45 days, maintaining IgG levels > 700 mg/dL until 2012, when treatment adherence lapsed. In 2017, she noted bilateral laterocervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy and progressive splenomegaly. She reported fatigue, fevers, and night sweats. Laboratory studies revealed hypochromic microcytic anemia, mild neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and an inverted CD4/CD8 T-cell ratio due to expansion of CD8+ T cells. Immunoglobulin levels were low: IgG 345 mg/dL, IgA 2 mg/dL, and IgM 4 mg/dL. A Wright agglutination test; markers for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, and HHV-8; tumor markers; serum and urine immunofixation; and fecal antigen for H. pylori were all normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly (22 cm), splenomegaly (> 30 cm) with a 26 mm lesion at the splenic pole, portal‐vein ectasia, thickened gastric and mesenteric walls, and small volume ascites. Contrast-enhanced thoracic and abdominal CT revealed numerous irregular pulmonary nodules with parenchymal thickening and bronchiectasis; multiple paraaortic, iliac‐obturator (short axis ~ 12 mm), celiac, and gastric‐curvature lymph nodes; and marked hepatic enlargement without focal liver lesions. Surgical consultation recommended splenectomy.

A 57-year-old woman with diabetes and a remote appendectomy presented with a one-year history of right-sided sciatica that progressively worsened, associated with intermittent claudication and reduced walking distance. She had no sphincter dysfunction. On examination, she had a mild right lower-limb motor deficit, absent right patellar and Achilles reflexes, and stiffness of the lumbar paravertebral muscles; there was no sensory deficit or overlying skin changes. Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine revealed a right paramedian intradural extramedullary mass at the L4–L5 level, compressing the right L4 nerve root and the cauda equina, along with grade I L5–S1 spondylolisthesis and bilateral foraminal stenosis.

A 61-year-old woman was referred for characterization of an incidentally discovered left adrenal mass. She was asymptomatic, and physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including serum catecholamines, were within normal limits. 

MRI with and without gadobenate dimeglumine showed a 9 × 6 × 7 cm, well-circumscribed solid heterogeneous mass in the left adrenal gland. The mass had low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously high signal intensity on T2-weighted images with cystic components, and progressive contrast enhancement of the periphery and septa. There was no signal drop on T1 opposed-phase imaging. The lesion abutted adjacent structures (kidney, bowel, pancreas, renal vein, aorta, diaphragm) without signs of invasion.

Unenhanced CT performed during FDG PET/CT revealed a heterogeneous adrenal mass with hypodense foci (<20 HU) and no calcifications. PET demonstrated increased FDG uptake in the mass.

A 71-year-old man with a 20-year history of insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus presented with a 2-month history of meteorism and a subjective feeling of abdominal enlargement. He denied diarrhea, anorexia, weight loss, fever, night sweats, headaches, anxiety, gastric ulcer disease, or rash. He had no prior history of pancreatitis or gallstones and no known malignancy. His medications included insulin glargine, two antihypertensives, two diuretics, and acetylsalicylic acid; he reported an allergy to metformin. He did not smoke or drink alcohol.

On examination, he was afebrile and normotensive, appeared well nourished (BMI 26.8), and had a soft, non-tender abdomen without masses. There was no jaundice or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL, hematocrit 25%, MCV 78 fL, uric acid 10.2 mg/dL, creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, random glucose 148 mg/dL, and HbA1c 6.9%. Liver enzymes, cholestasis markers, CEA, and CA 19-9 were normal. Serum pancreatic lipase was mildly elevated at 88 U/L; pancreatic elastase was normal.

Abdominal ultrasound revealed a mass in the uncinate process of the pancreas. Endoscopic ultrasound confirmed a 24 mm lesion between the neck and body, compressing the splenic vein but without invasion. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 3 cm, well-defined, homogeneous, slightly hypervascular mass with central dot-like calcification at the pancreatic neck and an absent pancreatic body and tail.

A 39-year-old healthy woman presented with a one-month history of subacute blurred vision in her right eye. She had no significant family or medical history and took no medications. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity in the right eye was counting fingers, and intraocular pressure was 18 mmHg. External inspection showed dilated temporal scleral sentinel vessels overlying a clear cornea and a normal lens. After pupil dilation, a large pigmented mass was noted in the ciliary body with a basal diameter of 18 mm and height of 13 mm; there were no orange pigment deposits or drusen, but there was extensive subtotal exudative retinal detachment. Ultrasound biomicroscopy demonstrated an isoechoic lesion that transmitted light completely on transillumination. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy by an ocular oncologist ruled out ciliary body melanoma based on lack of expression of HMB45 and Melan-A. The differential diagnosis included glomus tumor and angioleiomyoma, but no definitive diagnosis was reached. Over the next two weeks, the mass grew rapidly and vision deteriorated to light perception. The decision was made to proceed with enucleation of the right non-seeing globe.

A 71-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of slowly enlarging swelling and diffuse pain in the left posterior mandibular region. She had undergone mastectomy for breast cancer 15 years earlier and had insulin-dependent diabetes. On examination, there was a smooth-surfaced, soft, well-defined mass in the left mandibular region that was tender but not fixed to the overlying skin or underlying bone. Panoramic radiography showed a retained root fragment in the left maxillary molar area. For further evaluation of possible metastasis, inflammatory swelling, or benign salivary-gland tumor, ultrasonography of the neck was obtained. Ultrasonography revealed normal thyroid and submandibular glands but showed a 40 × 18 mm, well-defined, hypoechoic solid lesion in the superficial lobe of the left parotid gland with echogenic septa and posterior acoustic enhancement. Hence, a pleomorphic adenoma was suspected, and contrast-enhanced CT was requested.

A 21‐year‐old woman presented with a semihard, painless submental swelling that had been slowly enlarging over 5 years. Over the past 6 months, she reported progressive dysphagia and dysarthria. On intraoral examination, there was a nodular, fluctuant‐feeling mass in the floor of the mouth. Extraorally, there was a small submental swelling with intact overlying skin. Vital signs were within normal limits.

An ultrasonic scan of the submental region showed an infrasonic, well‐defined lesion. Contrast‐enhanced computed tomography demonstrated a semitransparent, cystic mass with distinct borders. A thyroid scintiscan using Tc-99m revealed no evidence of ectopic thyroid tissue in the area.

A 5-year-old boy was brought by his parents for evaluation of a slowly enlarging swelling in the right anterior lower jaw. The swelling was first noticed several months ago and had increased in size; there was no pain, discharge, or other symptoms. On examination, there was a well-defined, hard, non-tender swelling of the right buccal cortical plate in the region of the unerupted primary canine. The permanent canine (tooth 43) was palpable apically, and the primary canine (tooth 83) was clinically absent. No draining sinus or mucosal changes were noted. 

An intraoral periapical radiograph, panoramic radiograph, and mandibular occlusal radiograph were obtained. Imaging demonstrated multiple dense radiopaque structures within a radiolucent cavity surrounded by a corticated border in the region of the missing primary canine, with expansion of the buccal cortical plate. A separate radioopaque structure representing the unerupted primary canine was seen inferior to the radiopaque mass.

A 45-year-old man presented with a 5-month history of a growing palpable mass in the right anterior chest wall. He had no history of medication use, congenital anomaly, trauma, or prior surgery. On examination, there was a large, soft, non­tender mass in the right anterior chest wall. Laboratory findings, including complete blood count, were normal. A chest radiograph showed a mass-like opacity in the right chest wall. Ultrasonography revealed a huge, well-circumscribed, anechoic mass with thin septations and posterior acoustic enhancement in the right anterior chest wall; color Doppler showed no internal vascularity. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 15 × 11 cm thin-walled, homogeneously low-attenuation mass without definite enhancement in the right anterior chest wall, extending from beneath the pectoralis minor and latissimus dorsi muscles to the apex of the axilla and abutting the ribs, with no intra-thoracic or intra-abdominal extension.

A 25-year-old woman, gravida 2, was referred at 36 weeks of gestation for further management of suspected fetal encephalocele and preeclampsia. She had been diagnosed with preeclampsia at 32 weeks during routine antenatal care; a target scan at 19 weeks had been reported as normal. On examination, her blood pressure was 140/90 mm Hg, and systemic findings were unremarkable. Obstetric examination revealed a single live fetus in breech presentation corresponding to 36 weeks; the amniotic fluid index was 14. Ultrasound showed two echogenic masses measuring 4×5 cm and 3×4 cm arising from the fetal surface of the placenta near the occiput; one mass was cystic and the other lobulated with septations. There was no detectable skull defect, and the attachments of the masses to fetal or placental structures could not be traced. Fetal intracranial anatomy appeared normal. Doppler imaging demonstrated minimal vascularity on the surface of the masses. Magnetic resonance imaging was not performed due to the patient’s financial constraints.

A 75-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of recurrent chills, nausea, and vomiting. She had no significant past medical history and denied tobacco or alcohol use. On examination, she had slight scleral icterus; the abdomen was soft without tenderness or palpable mass. Laboratory studies showed total bilirubin 40.0 μmol/L (normal 0–17.1), direct bilirubin 31.4 μmol/L (0–5.1), AST 99 IU/L (0–40), ALT 85 IU/L (0–40), γ-GT 377 U/L (6–71), CA19-9 25.4 IU/mL (0–37), WBC count 13.67×10^9/L (3.5–9.5) with 89.8% neutrophils, and CRP 80.25 mg/L (0–10). Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 12×13 mm area of localized wall thickening with iso–low density nodules in the mid–common bile duct, with heterogeneous enhancement. MRI revealed dilation of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic ducts and a soft-tissue mass with rough margins at the lower end of the common bile duct, demonstrating restricted diffusion and low ADC signal.

A 34-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 0 at 26 weeks’ gestation, presented with severe epigastric pain and inadequate weight gain. She has a history of multiple sclerosis and cholecystectomy. Her mother died of pancreatic cancer at age 47. She denies alcohol or tobacco use.  
On admission:  
  • AST 68 U/L, ALT 100 U/L, ALP 227 U/L, total bilirubin 0.3 mg/dL, lipase 364 U/L, bile acids 25 µmol/L  
  • Abdominal ultrasound: common bile duct 7.4 mm, pancreatic duct 9.6 mm  
  • MRCP at 26 weeks: ill-defined space-occupying lesion in pancreatic head, mild CBD dilation, peripancreatic edema  
She was treated conservatively for presumed acute pancreatitis with pain control and pancreatic enzyme replacement.  
One week later she returned with ongoing epigastric pain, weight loss, and vomiting. Liver enzymes were similar; bilirubin rose to 3.0 mg/dL.  
MRCP at 30 weeks showed a persistent pancreatic head lesion and further dilation of the CBD.

A 56-year-old man first presented in September 1991 with back pain managed conservatively. In April 1992, he developed sudden paraplegia. Myelography and post-myelography CT revealed three tumors at L1–L3; all were resected via laminectomy. Histology at that time was reported as “atypical ependymoma,” and his paraplegia, saddle anesthesia, sphincter disturbance, and leg weakness persisted. In December 1992, two new tumors at L5–S1 were excised, again labeled as atypical ependymoma. His neurologic deficits remained stable thereafter.

In December 2006, he noted numbness and pain radiating into his upper body and arms. Spinal MRI showed space-occupying lesions at C7–T1 and T8–T9. The C7–T1 lesion, intradural extramedullary and contacting the left T1 root, was fully resected via laminectomy without new deficits. In March 2007, the T8–T9 lesion—also extramedullary, arising from a cauda equina nerve root—was removed uneventfully.

Because of recurrent “ependymomas,” a cranial MRI was obtained, revealing a contrast-enhancing mass in the third ventricle. The patient was asymptomatic from the intracerebral lesion, with no visual field or hormonal abnormalities. He declined surgery. Follow-up MRIs in 2010 and 2012 showed no new lesions or growth of the third-ventricle mass.

A term female infant was noted at birth to have a mass over the right parietal region of the scalp. Antenatal ultrasounds had been unremarkable, and there was no family history of dermatologic lesions. At 6 weeks of age, magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed a 3-cm-diameter exophytic right parietal scalp mass that appeared superficial and was separated from the cranial vault by a layer of scalp fat; there were no underlying bone or intracranial abnormalities, and the radiologic impression was of a benign-appearing scalp mass. Differential diagnoses at that time included an epidermoid tumour or another benign tumour. The patient was seen in the plastic surgery clinic at 5 years of age. Examination revealed a well-circumscribed, pink, cerebriform-like plaque measuring 5 × 2 cm over the right parietal scalp, camouflaged by her hair. The remainder of her physical examination was unremarkable, with normal developmental milestones and no dysmorphic features.

A 69-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of a progressively enlarging right supraclavicular mass. He had no prior medical history. On examination, his temperature was 37.3℃, blood pressure 130/90 mmHg, and pulse 75/min. Head and neck examination revealed a firm, fixed, non-tender, 8-cm mass in the right supraclavicular area; no other lymphadenopathy was noted, and the abdomen was normal on palpation. Laboratory studies showed normal complete blood count, chemistry panel, and renal function; urine dipstick and microscopy revealed no hematuria or abnormal cells. Computed tomography of the neck demonstrated enlargement of the right supraclavicular lymph node. An incisional biopsy of the node was performed. Hematoxylin and eosin staining showed polygonal tumor cells with clear cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, and prominent nucleoli. Immunohistochemical staining revealed that the tumor cells were positive for pancytokeratin, vimentin, and CD10, but negative for thyroid transcription factor 1, cytokeratin 7, cytokeratin 20, and hepatocyte specific antigen.

A 17-year-old nulliparous female presented with 4 weeks of gradually worsening abdominopelvic pain radiating to the lower abdomen. She denied abnormal vaginal bleeding or discharge. Her medical, surgical, social, and family histories were unremarkable, with no personal or family history of gynecologic disorders. Menarche occurred at age 13; she has regular monthly 6-day menses without heaviness. She is sexually inactive. On examination, her Tanner stage was V, vital signs were stable, body mass index was 22.1 kg/m2, and there was tenderness in the lower abdomen. A urine pregnancy test was negative. Laboratory studies, including CBC, inflammatory markers, and renal and liver function tests, were all within normal limits. Transabdominal pelvic ultrasound showed massive uterine enlargement with a heterogeneous 9.8-cm structure in the fundus; both ovaries were normal. Pelvic MRI revealed an enlarged uterus containing a 10.78 × 8 cm heterogeneous complex mass compressing but not attached to the endometrium. The findings from the radiology review were concerning for leiomyoma.

A 59-year-old man presented with a 5-month history of gait disturbance and memory impairment. On neurologic examination, he was alert but showed mild postural instability. A noncontrast CT scan of the brain revealed a 3.5×2.8 cm lobulated mass in the pineal region with uniformly high attenuation. MRI of the brain showed that the lesion had a dense hypointense rim on T2-weighted images and was hyperintense on T1-weighted images, with heterogeneous enhancement of the central portion. Mild ventricular enlargement was noted without other intracranial abnormalities. Based on neuroimaging, the initial preoperative differential diagnosis included densely calcified pineal masses such as teratoma, less likely germinoma, and meningioma with dense calcification. Additional studies included MR spectroscopy, which showed that the choline/creatinine ratio was not elevated, and perfusion MRI, which demonstrated that regional cerebral blood volume was not elevated.

A 43-year-old Filipino man first noted an indurated mass on the right breast 12 years before presentation. Over the next 2 years the lesion enlarged, followed by erythema and the development of slowly enlarging pendulous indurated masses on the left breast and in the lower abdominal fold. A biopsy at that time showed granulomatous dermatitis, and he was treated with three full courses of antituberculosis therapy without improvement. In the ensuing years he developed diffuse erythema and areas of induration on the neck, with reticulated violaceous and hypopigmented patches, atrophy, and telangiectasia. Prominent engorged veins with punched-out necrotic ulcers were noted, accompanied by severe skin pain. At presentation, he had bulky, indurated, sagging skin folds on the inframammary areas and lower abdominal fold.  

Multiple skin biopsies showed:
- A nodular-to-diffuse infiltrate of lymphocytes and histiocytes around dilated telangiectatic blood vessels, with granulomas composed of lymphocytes, histiocytes, Touton, Langhans, and foreign-body giant cells throughout the dermis.  
- Granulomatous vasculitis of small- to medium-sized vessels, with fibrin deposition and swollen endothelial cells infiltrated by lymphocytes, histiocytes, and giant cells.  
- Broad areas of sclerotic collagen within the reticular dermis.  

Verhoeff Van Gieson elastic tissue staining demonstrated absence of elastic fibers in the infiltrative areas, scattered fibers at the periphery, and fragmented elastic fibers within giant cells, consistent with elastophagocytosis.

A nine-month-old female infant presented with a two-month history of progressively increasing abdominal distention. She had a good appetite, no vomiting or symptoms of intestinal obstruction, and no fever or weight loss. On examination, the abdomen was distended with fullness in the right renal angle. A large mass was palpable in the right upper quadrant; it moved with respiration, was ballotable, and dull to percussion. Routine laboratory tests, including complete blood count and renal and liver function tests, were normal. Urine vanillylmandelic acid, serum alpha-fetoprotein, and human chorionic gonadotropin levels were all within normal limits for age. Abdominal ultrasound showed a large heterogeneous right suprarenal mass with multiple cystic areas. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a well-defined 12.0 × 10.5 × 8.5 cm mass in the right adrenal region with fatty hypodense cystic components, calcifications, multiple enhancing septations, and small enhancing soft-tissue nodules. The mass was inseparable from the right adrenal gland, displaced the right kidney posteroinferiorly, and exerted mass effect on the right liver lobe. It crossed the midline, slightly displacing the aorta and inferior vena cava to the left without vessel encasement. There was no abdominal wall infiltration, intraspinal extension, or ascites.

A 21-year-old man with no past medical history noted a multinodular back mass at the scapular level that increased rapidly in size over 2 months. On examination, there were multiple ulcerated, centimetric nodules with a crusty surface. Wide local excision was performed. Grossly, the specimen showed multiple ulcerated nodules with crusted surfaces. Microscopically, there was a multinodular proliferation arranged in clusters sometimes delimiting slit-like spaces, composed of spindle and epithelioid cells with brightly eosinophilic cytoplasm, at times mimicking rhabdomyoblasts. Tumor cells had nucleated nuclei with variable atypia; mitotic figures were rare and no necrosis was observed. The lesion ulcerated the epidermis, extended through the dermis and subcutaneous fat, and infiltrated underlying skeletal muscle. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated tumor cells positive for cytokeratin AE1/AE3, ERG, and INI-1, and negative for EMA, CD34, and CD31.

A 67-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a gradually widening nasal columella over 10 months and nasal pain for 5 months. She reported only bilateral nasal obstruction otherwise. On examination, both nostrils were partially obstructed by enlargement of the columella, and the overlying skin was hypervascular. A smooth, soft, well-circumscribed submucosal mass was palpable around the superior labial frenulum. Nasal endoscopy showed a normal septum and nasal cavities. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the nose and paranasal sinuses demonstrated a heterogeneous soft-tissue density mass without contrast enhancement in front of the anterior nasal spine and no invasion of adjacent structures.

A 21-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of a gradually enlarging swelling in the right inguinal region following a trivial fall while playing football. He reported dull aching pain localized to the inguinal area without radiation and denied weight loss. On examination, there was a palpable bony-hard mass fixed to the underlying bone in the right inguinal region. The hip had full range of motion, and strength and sensation in the right lower limb were normal. Peripheral pulses, including the right femoral pulse, were normal. There was no warmth or erythema over the swelling. 

Plain radiography of the pelvis showed a large expansile lytic lesion of the right superior pubic ramus. Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis demonstrated a 5 × 6 cm expansile lytic lesion with multiple cavities arising from the right superior pubic ramus. CT angiography revealed compression and displacement of the femoral vessels with reduced flow in the femoral artery.

A 15-year-old girl presented with a 3-day history of fever, cough, and lethargy. She had no prior medical illness. On examination, she was febrile (38.3°C), mildly tachypneic with normal oxygen saturation, and hemodynamically stable. Breath sounds were diminished over the left lung with crepitations at its base. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 17.6×10^3/µL and a platelet count of 487×10^3/µL; she was started on oral antibiotics without improvement. A chest radiograph demonstrated homogenous opacification of nearly the entire left hemithorax, obscuring the left heart border, aortic knuckle, and left hemidiaphragm, with contralateral mediastinal shift. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax revealed an 11×13×16 cm low-attenuation enhancing mass in the left thoracic cavity, thought to originate from the left upper lobe, causing collapse of the left lung. The mass contained nonenhancing areas suggestive of necrosis, with narrowing and occlusion of distal bronchi, and compression of the pulmonary trunk and left pulmonary artery. There was loss of the fat plane between the mass and pericardium, with associated pericardial and left pleural effusions. The chest wall was intact, and no mediastinal lymphadenopathy or liver lesions were seen. These findings raised concern for an aggressive left lung tumor, and CT-guided tissue biopsy was subsequently performed.

A 30-year-old woman presented with sudden onset of severe, constant right upper–quadrant abdominal pain that began the previous day in the epigastrium and later localized to the right upper quadrant. She had anorexia, nausea, and vomiting. Two months earlier she had been diagnosed by MRI with a hepatic hydatid cyst and had been taking mebendazole for 2 weeks. She had used oral contraceptives for six months previously.  
On admission her temperature was 39.0°C, pulse 96 beats/min, blood pressure 100/70 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. The abdomen was distended with absent bowel sounds; there was tenderness, guarding, and rebound in the right upper quadrant and epigastrium.  
Laboratory studies showed hematocrit 30%, hemoglobin 10 g/dL, red blood cell count 3.3 × 10^3/mm^3, white cell count 13.7 × 10^3/mm^3 with 84.4% neutrophils; other tests were normal.  
Abdominal ultrasound and contrast-enhanced CT scan revealed a 9 × 11.8 × 10 cm cyst involving segments IV, VII, and VIII of the liver. The lesion was multiloculated with multiple smaller internal cysts, demonstrated detachment of the wall from hepatic parenchyma suggesting hemorrhagic leak, compressed the inferior vena cava and right and middle hepatic veins, and showed perihepatic hematoma in the adipose tissue posterior to the hepatic pedicle.

A 44-year-old woman presented with 12 hours of moderate, colicky pain in the left flank without radiation. She reported similar mild, intermittent pain over preceding months. She denied fever, urinary or gastrointestinal symptoms, and had no history of trauma. Her medical history was unremarkable except for obesity (BMI 39 kg/m²).  
On examination she was hemodynamically stable. Abdominal findings included a flaccid, nondistended abdomen with normal bowel sounds and mild tenderness on palpation of the left flank and left hypochondrium. There was no hepatomegaly, no signs of peritonitis, and Giordano sign was negative bilaterally.  
Laboratory studies showed mild leukocytosis and elevated C-reactive protein. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed an 11 × 10 cm oval intraparenchymal hypodense splenic lesion containing areas of increased density, with small amount of free fluid in the abdomen. A repeat CT after three days showed no change in size but a change in the shape of the lesion.  
Given persistent pain and imaging findings suggestive of a splenic hematoma, a laparoscopic splenectomy was planned. Intraoperatively, there were no macroscopic signs of malignancy.

A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with gradually increasing abdominal distension and postmenopausal genital bleeding. She had a history of a uterine myoma treated medically at age 45 with stable size on follow-up. Her past medical history included myocardial infarction, sleep apnea, diabetes mellitus, and dyslipidemia. Family history was unremarkable.

On examination, an abdominal mass was palpable to the level of the umbilicus. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a 17 × 16 cm, well-circumscribed uterine corpus mass. The lesion was hyperintense on both T1- and T2-weighted images and hypointense on fat-suppressed T1-weighted images, indicating a substantial fat component. Within the mass, a septum of nonuniform thickness appeared hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on fat-saturated T1-weighted images, and showed contrast enhancement on fat-saturated, gadolinium-enhanced sequences. Diffusion-weighted imaging showed no regions of restricted diffusion, and the ADC map had predominantly high signal. Cervical and endometrial cytologic evaluations were negative for malignancy.

Based on these findings, the radiologic impression was a uterine lipoma or lipoleiomyoma.

A 33-year-old man with a 1-year history of multiple myeloma was referred for evaluation of chronic headache. One year earlier, he had presented with back pain; radiographs showed multiple osteolytic lesions and laboratory testing was positive for Bence Jones protein. He had since begun capecitabine chemotherapy. On examination, he was alert and had no focal neurologic deficits. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain (0.5-T) revealed a well-demarcated, extra-axial mass in the posterior fossa measuring 31.3×31.2×23.0 mm, situated beneath the occipital bone. The lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images and enhanced homogeneously after contrast administration, and on sagittal views a hyperintense line appeared to divide the mass in half.

A 65-year-old Caucasian man with Child-Pugh class A alcoholic cirrhosis, diagnosed after an esophageal variceal bleed, was seen in routine follow-up. He was asymptomatic and on propranolol for portal hypertension.  
On abdominal ultrasound, his liver was cirrhotic, and there was a hypoechogenic, heterogeneous nodule in the left lobe measuring about 7 cm, with several gastrohepatic omental lymph nodes (largest 24 mm). Physical examination revealed hepatomegaly without ascites; the spleen and peripheral lymph nodes were not palpable.  
Initial labs showed hemoglobin and leukocyte counts within normal limits, mild thrombocytopenia (107 × 10^3/μl), and INR of 1.3. Liver tests showed AST 37 U/L, bilirubin 1.56 mg/dL, and albumin 3.3 g/dL. Serologies for HBV, HCV, and HIV were negative. Serum AFP, CA 19-9, and CEA were all within normal limits; LDH was normal, and β2-microglobulin was slightly elevated at 3.49 mg/L.  
Abdominal MRI demonstrated a cirrhotic and enlarged liver with a 15.6 × 10.9 cm nodular lesion in the left lobe that was isointense on both T1- and T2-weighted images, showed minimal heterogeneous enhancement after contrast, and had central necrosis.

A 3-year-old girl presented with right knee pain and swelling for 3 months. Six weeks earlier, she had sustained a fracture of the left femoral diaphysis. There were no fevers, weight loss, or night sweats. She received antibiotics for presumed osteomyelitis without improvement. On examination, she was mildly pale but without lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, rash, or edema. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 105 g/L, white-cell count 7.4×10^9/L (neutrophils 52%, lymphocytes 33%, monocytes 5%, band forms 10%), platelet count 445×10^9/L; peripheral smear showed no blasts. Serum uric acid was 350 μmol/L, lactate dehydrogenase 368 U/L, and urinary vanillylmandelic acid was not elevated. Radiographs of the lower limbs revealed an expansile lytic lesion in the right supracondylar femur and multiple lytic areas in the diaphyses and metaphyses of both femora and tibiae. A bone scan demonstrated patchy radiotracer uptake in multiple long bones and the right superior pubic ramus. CT of the torso showed numerous well-defined expansile lytic lesions in the femora, iliac blades, ischial tuberosities, vertebral body of D9, scapulae, and humeri, as well as multiple hypodense lesions in both kidneys and a poorly enhancing lesion in the left adnexal region. Bone marrow aspiration showed occasional abnormal cells, and bilateral bone marrow biopsy revealed no infiltrative disease.

A 68-year-old man underwent abdominal ultrasonography during evaluation for vascular insufficiency of the lower limbs, which revealed a large cystic mass in the right hypochondrium. He had no abdominal pain or other gastrointestinal symptoms. On examination, there was a palpable mass in the right upper quadrant. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. Ultrasonography showed a well-defined 12-cm cystic lesion with multiple membranous septa. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a large cystic mass adjacent to the right hepatic lobe, gastric antrum, and pancreatic head without evidence of vascular supply. MRI confirmed markedly high signal intensity consistent with fluid content, but no clear connection to liver, stomach, or pancreas was identified. Malignancy could not be excluded, and surgical resection was planned.

A 79‐year‐old man with chronic kidney disease and a history of high‐grade invasive urothelial carcinoma of the bladder (stage pT4b N0 M0) treated with transurethral resection, neoadjuvant gemcitabine–cisplatin, cystoprostatectomy, and immunotherapy presented with a 5‐week history of a painful, pruritic rash in the right inguinal region. He had been treated empirically with oral valacyclovir and topical clotrimazole without improvement and denied fevers or night sweats. On examination, there were firm papulonodules forming confluent hyperpigmented to violaceous plaques in the right inguinal fold, extending to the proximal anterior thigh. A punch biopsy showed a dermal proliferation of neoplastic cells in irregular nests with focal glandular differentiation, high‐grade nuclear features, and no involvement of the overlying epidermis. Immunohistochemical studies revealed that the tumor cells were positive for cytokeratin 20 and GATA3 and negative for cytokeratin 7.

A 57-year-old woman presented with a 10-year history of a slowly enlarging, painless swelling of the vulva. She denied fever, weight loss, appetite changes, discharge, or pigmentation. Twenty years earlier she had had a similar lesion at the same site, which was excised. A biopsy performed elsewhere had diagnosed dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans.

On examination, her BMI was 25 kg/m2. Inspection revealed an 8 × 10 cm irregular lesion over the left labia majora and mons pubis, composed of multiple confluent nodules (0.5–2 cm each), crossing the midline to involve the clitoris. On palpation, the lesion was firm to hard, indurated, non-tender, and well demarcated. No inguinal or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy was noted.

Ultrasonography showed a lobular solid subcutaneous tumor. Serum markers including CA-125, carcinoembryonic antigen, desmin, and epithelial membrane antigen were negative.

She underwent a wide local excision with clear margins under frozen-section control, followed by a thigh skin graft. Grossly, the resected mass was smooth and white on cross-section. Microscopic examination demonstrated patternless sheets of fibroblastic spindle cells embedded in a hyalinized collagenous stroma.

A 30-year-old man reported a right ankle distortion at work seven months earlier. He experienced persistent pain and saw a general practitioner, and ankle radiographs were normal. The joint was immobilized in a plaster cast for six weeks, followed by physical therapy, but his pain did not improve. Six months later, magnetic resonance imaging of the right ankle showed a well-circumscribed localized tumor anterior to the ankle, with focal bulging and erosion of the tibia and talus but no damage to the fibular collateral ligaments. On examination thirteen months after the injury, there was tenderness to pressure at the ventral aspect of the ankle adjacent to the medial malleolus, and painful dorsal extension; the collateral ligaments were intact and repeat radiographs remained unremarkable. An ultrasound examination revealed a solid, homogeneous hypoechoic mass measuring 3.5 × 2.5 × 2 cm, with uncertain relation to the joint. An impingement syndrome of the right ankle caused by synovial hypertrophy was diagnosed preoperatively.

A 56-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with intermittent, vague left-sided abdominal pain of one year’s duration. He denied urinary symptoms, hematuria, or fever. On examination, his abdomen was soft and non-tender. Laboratory studies—including a complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, serum chemistry, and urinalysis—were all within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a large exophytic mass in the upper pole of the left kidney measuring 12 × 11 × 8.6 cm, appearing heterogeneous and hypodense, with no invasion beyond the renal capsule; these findings were reported as suspicious for renal cell carcinoma. The patient underwent a left robotic radical nephrectomy. Gross examination showed a well-circumscribed, encapsulated 12 × 11.5 × 8 cm mass occupying most of the kidney without penetration of the capsule, featuring a lobulated gelatinous/myxoid cut surface and scattered firm white-yellow areas. Histologic sections demonstrated a hypocellular tumor arranged in lobules separated by delicate fibrous strands, composed of bland spindle cells in an abundant myxoid stroma with thin-walled blood vessels and no cellular atypia, lipoblasts, mitotic figures, or necrosis. Immunohistochemical staining revealed diffuse strong positivity for vimentin, patchy positivity for CD34, and negativity for Pan-cytokeratin, desmin, smooth muscle actin, S100, and MUC4. Ki-67 labeling was <1%. FISH analysis for CHOP (12q13) and FUS (16q11.2) rearrangements was negative.

A 13-year-old girl with a known history of neurofibromatosis type 2 (bilateral vestibular schwannomas, prior optic nerve glioma resection, and cutaneous neurofibromas; positive family history) presented with a 3-year history of a left-sided tongue mass that had gradually increased in size and recently caused dental issues and difficulty chewing. On examination, there was a well-circumscribed, nontender, nonerythematous 2.0 × 2.0 cm mass at the left anterior tip of the tongue, clinically suspected to be a neural tumor related to NF2. She underwent transoral excisional biopsy under general anesthesia with 2 mm margins. Grossly, the specimen measured 1.7 × 1.4 × 0.5 cm and on sectioning revealed multiple well-circumscribed white fibrous nodules, 0.1 to 0.7 cm in size, the largest abutting a margin.

An 85-year-old man presented with a 9-month history of a tender, violaceous subcutaneous nodule over the right upper quadrant at the site of his ventriculoperitoneal shunt, inserted 9 months earlier for normal-pressure hydrocephalus. He also reported malaise, reduced appetite, and a 5-kg weight loss over 5 months but denied rectal bleeding or melena. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL (normal 13–17 g/dL). On examination, multiple smaller subcutaneous nodules without epidermal changes were noted tracking along the shunt, including a prominent lesion near the right clavicle.

A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis performed 2 months before admission had attributed the right upper quadrant lesion to scar tissue of indeterminate significance. Ultrasonography of the abdominal and sternal nodules demonstrated echogenic soft-tissue masses surrounding the shunt. A biopsy of the main abdominal lesion was performed. Histologic examination revealed an intradermal malignant neoplasm with features of adenocarcinoma. Immunohistochemical staining showed positivity for CK cocktail, CK19, EMA, CDX2, and mCEA, and negativity for CK5/6 and D2-40. Serum tumor markers were elevated: CA 19-9 at 1545 kU/L (normal ≤37), CA 125 at 181 kU/L (0–35), and CEA at 19.1 μg/L (0–3.0).

A 36-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of left chest pain, predominantly between the shoulder blades, that worsened with physical activity. He had no significant medical, family, or social history. 

A noncontrast spiral computed tomography scan of the chest revealed a 130 × 110 mm heterogeneous solid–cystic mass in the left lung apex, causing dislocation of the T4 and T5 vertebrae and destruction of the posterior segment of the left fourth rib. 

Magnetic resonance imaging showed a solid–cystic lesion with heterogeneous enhancement in the left upper thorax and posterior mediastinum extending into bone and the epidural space at T4 and T5, with compression of the spinal cord. No abnormal signals suggestive of malignant nerve-sheath tumor or sarcoma were detected on MRI.

A 55-year-old woman was evaluated for a 4-year history of episodic psychiatric symptoms, headache, and seizures. In June 2016, she developed irritability, auditory hallucinations, and delusions; a brain CT showed left frontal dural hyperdensity. Her symptoms improved with risperidone. In November 2016, she had acute severe headache, drowsiness, dullness, and seizures; MRI with contrast showed linear dural enhancement over the left frontal convexity and falx cerebri. Pachymeningitis was favored, and differential diagnoses included meningioma, lymphoma, neurosarcoidosis, Rosai-Dorfman disease, and Erdheim-Chester disease, but the patient refused a dural biopsy. Over the next 4 years, her episodic symptoms remitted with intermittent mannitol and diazepam; annual MRIs showed no change until December 2019, when CT and contrast MRI revealed a growing left frontal dural mass with more diffuse enhancement. 
In April 2020, on admission, she was alert and oriented but slightly apathetic; cognitive function was intact and a right Chaddock sign was present. Laboratory tests were unremarkable except for an elevated serum IgG level of 18.1 g/L (reference range 7.51–15.6 g/L). Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 200 mm H₂O; cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal cell count, glucose, protein, and chloride, undetectable CSF IgG4, and no malignant cells.

A 9‐year‐old boy presented with a 1½‐month history of excessive thirst and urination. At age 2, he had a biopsy-proven Langerhans cell histiocytosis lesion in the left femur, which resolved after 3 months of orthopedic follow-up; no further imaging or endocrine evaluation was performed. On examination at age 6 years 5 months, his height was 117.5 cm (+0.3 SD) and weight 21.25 kg (+0.1 SD); height velocity was normal but he had lost weight since onset of symptoms. Laboratory tests showed serum sodium 148 mEq/L, chloride 113 mEq/L, and serum osmolality 298 mOsm/kg, with urine osmolality of 205 mOsm/kg and a 24‐hour urine volume of 7570 mL/m2. A water deprivation test followed by vasopressin confirmed complete central diabetes insipidus. MRI of the brain demonstrated an enlarged pituitary stalk with gadolinium enhancement and absence of the posterior pituitary bright spot on T1‐weighted images. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed undetectable levels of alpha-fetoprotein, β‐human chorionic gonadotropin, and placental alkaline phosphatase. Stimulation tests of the anterior pituitary (L‐arginine, CRH, TRH, and LHRH) were normal. A skeletal survey showed no evidence of active bone lesions.

A 74-year-old man with age-related macular degeneration presented with sudden marked visual loss in his left eye. He had developed a choroidal neovascular membrane in the left eye in March 2011 and was managed with a treat–extend–stop protocol of intravitreal bevacizumab, receiving 58 injections by April 2018, when his vision measured 20/50. In July 2018, his left-eye vision declined to 20/800. An extensive ophthalmic workup showed no evidence of glaucoma or optic neuropathy on fundus examination. Fluorescein angiography showed a stabilizing choroidal neovascular membrane without increased exudation. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography demonstrated no progression of the membrane and an intact ellipsoid zone. A subjective brightness test was 100% in the right eye versus 70% in the left. Humphrey visual fields revealed greater central loss in the left eye. Given his dialysis history and potential hypotensive episodes, a posterior ischemic optic neuropathy was considered. To evaluate for a neurological cause of the unexplained vision loss, an MRI of the brain and orbits was recommended.

A 23-year-old woman presented with a two-week history of right upper quadrant abdominal pain and a palpable mass. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. Abdominal computed tomography revealed a large, well-circumscribed mass measuring 17.5 cm × 15.9 cm displacing the liver. At surgery, a tumorous mass arising from the peritoneum was found compressing the liver, along with multiple peritoneal nodules and right pleural nodules. No ovarian or other pelvic lesions were identified. The index lesion and peritoneal nodules were excised.

On gross pathology, the peritoneal nodule was circumscribed, firm to soft, with a fleshy tan cut surface and no hemorrhage or necrosis. Microscopically, the lesion was cellular, composed of elongated cells with oval, mildly pleomorphic nuclei. Both perivascular pseudorosettes and true rosettes were present, and mitotic figures were rare. Immunohistochemical staining showed strong positivity for glial fibrillary acidic protein and EMA with a cytoplasmic and paranuclear dot-like pattern; the Ki-67 proliferation index was less than 1%.

A 71-year-old Portuguese man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and gout presented with an 8-week history of persistent right lower quadrant abdominal pain, anorexia, and a 20-lb weight loss. Vital signs were stable. On examination, there was a firm, tender, fixed mass in the right lower quadrant. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed multiple peritoneal and mesenteric masses. A necrotic 10-cm mass on the right side of the abdomen communicated with the small bowel and suggested a walled-off perforation. 

CT-guided core-needle biopsy of the abdominal mass showed mixed spindle and pleomorphic cells with focal rhabdoid features, high-grade nuclear atypia, brisk mitotic activity, and Ki-67 expression up to 70%. 

Initially, a differential diagnosis of poorly differentiated synovial sarcoma of the colon was considered, but fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) studies for Ewing sarcoma and synovial sarcoma were negative. 

On immunohistochemistry, tumor cells showed patchy weak S100 immunoreactivity, with Melan A and CD34 positivity and negative stains for HMB45, chromogranin, synaptophysin, and myogenin. Ki-67 proliferation index was 70%. FISH testing of the surgical masses was negative for EWSR1 and SS18 (SYT) genes.

A 57-year-old man was evaluated for a splenic mass. One year earlier, imaging had revealed a 41-mm lesion in the spleen that was presumed benign and followed expectantly. He was admitted for dental surgery, and on the day after the procedure he developed fever and left upper-quadrant abdominal pain. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed acute calculous cholecystitis and an incidental 85-mm, irregularly shaped, heterogeneously enhancing mass in the spleen that had increased in size since prior imaging. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL, leukocyte count 5.2 × 10^9/L, platelet count 328 × 10^9/L, and soluble interleukin-2 receptor 322 U/mL. Further evaluation with MRI confirmed a large, irregular splenic mass with heterogeneous enhancement and suggestions of involvement of the left kidney, pancreatic tail, transverse colon, and left diaphragm. PET–CT demonstrated an SUVmax of 4.1 in the splenic lesion without evidence of lymphadenopathy or distant metastases. Colonoscopic examination showed an easily bleeding area with mucosal irregularity at the splenic flexure.

A 50-year-old Hispanic man with obesity and hypertension presented with a 3-month history of abrupt episodes of weakness and altered mental status. He described anxiety, aggressiveness, agitation, diaphoresis, visual blurring, and a burning sensation throughout his body, sometimes leading to loss of consciousness; symptoms occurred at any time of day and improved with eating. He reported worsening frequency and severity of attacks, which disrupted his work as a truck driver and led to suicidal thoughts. He had no tobacco or excessive alcohol use and took candesartan and hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension.

He was hospitalized briefly at a local hospital for recurrent irritability and aggression; psychiatric evaluation yielded no diagnosis. A subsequent 3-hour postprandial test revealed a blood glucose level of 58 mg/dL, prompting transfer. On admission, he was afebrile, heart rate 93 beats/min, blood pressure 161/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 19 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Examination was normal, including a neurologic evaluation.

Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 15.7 g/dL, white blood cell count 9.51 K/µL, and calcium 9.6 mg/dL.
