During a supervised 72-hour fast, he became symptomatic after 20 hours; laboratory testing revealed a blood glucose level of 29 mg/dL, insulin 426 mIU/L, and C-peptide 12.83 ng/mL. Sulfonylurea levels were undetectable. Abdominal ultrasound and contrast magnetic resonance imaging of the pancreas showed no abnormalities. Prolactin, parathyroid hormone, albumin, and calcium levels, as well as brain MRI, were normal, effectively ruling out multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1.

A 24-year-old Bangladeshi woman presented with a swelling on the lower right side of her face of four years’ duration and associated pain for two months. The swelling developed slowly with no prodromal symptoms; the pain was dull, intermittent, aggravated by chewing, and relieved by medication. Her medical, dental, family, and personal histories were noncontributory. 

On examination, she was well nourished, with normal vital signs and no anemia, icterus, or clubbing. Extraorally, there was mild facial asymmetry from parasymphysis to the ramus on the right, with a single 2 × 3 cm hard, non-tender, immobile swelling and paresthesia of the region. Temporomandibular joint function was normal, and there were no enlarged lymph nodes or skin pigmentations. Intraorally, there was hard, non-compressible, non-tender expansion of the buccal cortical plate from the right first premolar to second molar; the contralateral side was normal. Teeth were non-mobile and percussion tests were negative.

Laboratory investigations showed a normal complete blood count and serum levels of calcium, alkaline phosphatase, T3, T4, and thyroid-stimulating hormone. 

Panoramic radiography revealed a mixed radiolucent and radiopaque lesion on the right mandible with loss of the normal trabecular pattern and obliteration of the mandibular canal. An intraoral periapical radiograph demonstrated a “ground-glass” appearance of the trabeculae with loss of the lamina dura and narrowing of the periodontal ligament space. An occlusal radiograph confirmed buccal cortical plate expansion in the right second and third molar regions.

A 55‐year‐old woman was referred for evaluation of fever, weakness, and abnormal liver tests. Three years earlier, she had presented with fever, generalized weakness, and elevated liver enzymes. At that time she had positive anti‐nuclear antibody (ANA), anti–smooth muscle antibody (ASMA), and elevated IgG; a liver biopsy showed bridging fibrosis with mild ductular changes. She was treated for presumed autoimmune hepatitis with azathioprine and prednisolone for two years without clinical improvement, then empirically received anti‐tubercular therapy without benefit.

On current examination she was febrile and pale, with generalized lymphadenopathy and a spleen palpable 2 cm below the costal margin. Laboratory studies showed: 
 • AST 69 IU/L (normal 5–40); ALT 44 IU/L (7–35); total bilirubin 6.7 mg/dL (0.3–1.2); alkaline phosphatase 299 IU/L (32–92); albumin 2.0 g/dL (3.5–5.2).  
 • Prothrombin time 11.5 sec; INR 0.96.  
 • ANA and ASMA were now negative; IgG 9.12 g/dL (6.39–13.49).  
 • Hemogram: Hb 8.8 g/dL, WBC 2,700/mm3 (neutrophils 87%, lymphocytes 4%), platelets 50,000/mm3.

Serologic tests for hepatitis A–E, HIV, dengue, leptospira, malaria, and blood and urine cultures were negative. IgM antibodies for CMV, EBV, and HSV types 1 and 2 were negative. Quantitative viral loads showed EBV 5.0 log10 copies/mL; CMV and HSV undetectable. 

Ultrasonography revealed parenchymal liver disease, splenomegaly, no biliary dilation, and multiple small aortocaval and mesenteric lymph nodes. The patient was provisionally diagnosed with EBV‐related infectious mononucleosis with hepatitis and splenomegaly and received valganciclovir for one week. Repeat EBV viral load remained 5.0 log10 copies/mL and her symptoms persisted. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen with MR cholangiopancreatography demonstrated hepatosplenomegaly with heterogeneous hepatic signal, multiple tiny T1‐ and T2‐hypointense lesions, no biliary dilation, and numerous enlarged peripancreatic, portocaval, gastrohepatic, mesenteric, and retroperitoneal lymph nodes.

A 21-year-old woman with ventriculoperitoneal shunt–dependent hydrocephalus since infancy for myelomeningocele presented with an 8-day history of mild nausea and fevers up to 39 °C. She reported no headaches or neurologic symptoms. On examination, vital signs were notable only for fever; the neurologic exam was unchanged from her baseline. Abdominal examination revealed a firm, non-tender mass in the right lower quadrant. 

Noncontrast CT of the head showed stable ventricular size, appropriate proximal catheter placement, and no transependymal flow. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a multiseptated fluid collection in the right lower quadrant extending into the lower abdomen, separate from bowel, ovary, and uterus; a segment of the shunt catheter was seen adjacent to the fluid, but the tip could not be identified. Because of her history of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt and the new cystic abdominal mass, she was initially diagnosed with a CSF pseudocyst, and neurosurgery was consulted for further evaluation, including an abdominal CT.

A 64‐year‐old man was referred to oral and maxillofacial surgery for a mass on the right mandible associated with paresthesia of the right lower lip. Intraoral examination revealed a 5 cm bony‐hard expansion of the right mandible causing facial asymmetry. CT scans of the mandible showed a lesion with periosteal reaction displaying sunray spicules, along with both bone destruction and bone formation in the ramus of the right mandible; there was no cortical perforation or mandibular canal destruction. An incisional biopsy of the jaw lesion reported “clear cell carcinoma” which may primarily originate from genitourinary tract such as kidney, bladder, and prostate gland.

A woman in her 50s with no significant medical history presented with a 6-month history of an intensely pruritic rash and gradually enlarging sores on her scalp, trunk, and extremities. She had been treated for presumed contact dermatitis with systemic prednisone and topical steroids without improvement. She denied weight loss, night sweats, or fevers. She reported a 25-year history of occupational exposure to ammonium nitrate fertilizer.

On examination, there were multiple annular, ulcerated, erythematous-violaceous plaques ranging from 1 to 20 cm in diameter on the breasts, axillae, lower abdomen, back, groin, and proximal extremities; several lesions showed concentric rings of ulceration. A 20-cm ulcerated plaque with fibrinopurulent exudate was present on the posterior scalp. A pink fleshy plaque was noted on the bulbar conjunctiva of the left eye.

Initial laboratory evaluation (while on prednisone) showed a white-cell count of 9,700 cells/µL with 17% eosinophils (absolute count 1,649 cells/µL), which rose off prednisone to a white-cell count of 39,000 cells/µL with 56% eosinophils (absolute count 21,840 cells/µL). Peripheral-blood flow cytometry showed no aberrant myeloid or lymphoid population, but a clonal T-cell receptor gene rearrangement was detected. Serum lactate dehydrogenase was elevated at 308 U/L.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the head, neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a 3-cm nodular consolidation in the left lower lobe of the lung without lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Bone marrow biopsy demonstrated hypocellular marrow (20%) with trilineage hematopoiesis and eosinophilia; marrow flow cytometry was negative for aberrant populations, but a matching clonal T-cell receptor gene rearrangement was present.

Several skin biopsies over 4 months were interpreted as eosinophilic spongiosis, and direct immunofluorescence was negative. Wound cultures grew abundant Staphylococcus aureus and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia.

A 58-year-old woman reported intermittent right upper‐quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, and fever for approximately 3 years, often triggered by high‐fat or spicy food. She had known gallstones on prior ultrasound. The most recent symptomatic episode occurred 3 months before admission. On examination, she was afebrile, with mild right upper‐quadrant tenderness and a negative Murphy’s sign; no lymphadenopathy was noted. Laboratory studies were normal except for a white-cell count of 10.89 × 10^9 cells/L (reference 3.5–10.5 × 10^9 cells/L). Ultrasound showed hepatic steatosis and a folded gallbladder with thickened walls, blurred outlines, and small stones within the lumen. With a presumptive diagnosis of acute exacerbation of cholecystitis, she underwent surgery. Intraoperatively, there were severe pericholecystic adhesions, an almost intrahepatic gallbladder with thickened walls, and palpable small stones. The infundibular wall was extremely thickened and ocher colored, raising suspicion for gallbladder carcinoma. A cholecystectomy and atypical resection of segments IV and V of the liver were performed. The express histological examination rejected malignancy.

A 64-year-old right-hand–dominant woman with hypertension presented with a 9-month history of progressive swelling of the left thenar eminence. She reported reduced sensation and paresthesia predominantly in the radial three digits and decreased thumb range of motion. On examination, there was a non-tender, soft, palpable mass measuring approximately 3 × 3 cm over the volar aspect of the left thenar eminence, and flexion at the interphalangeal joint of the thumb was limited. Neurologic examination showed decreased sensation in the radial three and a half digits of the left hand and reduced grip strength compared with the right. Nerve conduction studies suggested a lesion at the left carpal tunnel. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left hand confirmed a large, lobulated, well-defined fatty lesion in the palm centered between the flexor tendons and metacarpals, with both dorsal and volar extensions, and a proximal component within the carpal tunnel causing median nerve compression.

A 27-year-old woman with a history of a marginal excision of a hidradenoma from the sole of her right foot in 2015 noted in August 2019 a 1 cm, nonmobile lump at the same site. It grew slowly over months, causing discomfort on walking, and occasionally discharged a small amount of serous fluid. In early 2020 she developed a painless right inguinal lymph node enlargement. Vital signs were normal. On exam, a firm right inguinal lymph node was palpable; the foot mass was noninflamed. Plain radiographs of the right foot showed no bone involvement. MRI revealed a 24 × 11 × 17 mm cutaneous and subcutaneous soft-tissue lesion in the central sole with a spiculated contour abutting the plantar fascia and flexor digitorum brevis; it was hypointense on T1, heterogeneously intermediate on T2, and showed significant peripheral post-contrast enhancement. No adjacent nerve or vascular invasion was seen.

A 52-year-old woman noted a right breast lump of one month’s duration, accompanied by nipple erosion and bloody discharge. She had no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. On examination, a firm 28 mm mass was palpated in the right breast, and a separate 15 mm mass was found in the left breast. Fine-needle aspiration cytology from both lesions was suggestive of ductal carcinoma. Dynamic computed tomography showed no evidence of distant metastasis. The patient underwent bilateral total mastectomy with sentinel lymph node resection. Adjuvant chemotherapy was administered, and the postoperative course was uneventful.

A 65-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and bronchial asthma presented with mild headaches of several months’ duration and no focal neurologic deficits. He had undergone cranial MRI 4 years earlier for unrelated reasons, with no significant change in the identified lesion since then. Laboratory studies were normal. Noncontrast CT of the head revealed a well-defined, 19-mm mass in the left parietal bone near the squamosal suture, centred in the diploic space, with sparse but preserved trabeculae and a slight bony bulge, without disruption of the inner or outer tables. MRI showed the lesion to be isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images, with multiple internal hyperintense foci, heterogeneous signal on T2-weighted images, and restricted diffusion. The hyperintense foci on T1 images were presumed to represent bone marrow fat, and the preserved trabecular architecture suggested that pre-existing structures were not destroyed.

A 36-year-old man presented with 2 weeks of dizziness. On examination, vital signs were normal and neurologic findings were nonfocal. MRI of the brain revealed a 1.6 cm intraventricular mass in the fourth ventricle that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed homogeneous enhancement on contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images. Preoperative cerebral angiography showed no vascular staining of the lesion. The tumor was resected via a midline suboccipital craniotomy with a telovelar approach. Intraoperatively, it was noted to be a soft, well-circumscribed mass attached to the choroid plexus of the rhomboid fossa and was removed en bloc. Histologic examination showed spindle-shaped cells with scant eosinophilic cytoplasm embedded in abundant myxoid stroma. Immunohistochemical staining was negative for the glial markers isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 and glial fibrillary acidic protein.

A 30-year-old army officer noted a two-year history of gradually progressive swelling of his right knee. He reported night pain severe enough to awaken him, but paradoxically stated that the pain lessened as the swelling increased. He denied any history of trauma, surgery, or infection.  
On examination, there was diffuse, nontender swelling in the suprapatellar area, full range of motion, intact meniscal and ligamentous tests, and normal distal neurovascular status.  
Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and inflammatory markers, were within normal limits.  
Plain radiographs of the knee revealed a dense soft-tissue opacity in the suprapatellar pouch with preserved joint spaces and no bony abnormalities.  
CT of the knee demonstrated a low-density intra-articular mass resembling fat with multiple villous projections, surrounded by joint fluid and without bone erosion.  
MRI showed a large joint effusion and multiple frond-like synovial villi with signal intensity identical to fat on T1- and T2-weighted sequences; after intravenous gadolinium, only the overlying synovial lining enhanced, while the subsynovial fat did not. There was no evidence of meniscal or ligament injury.  
Based on these imaging findings, a benign intra-articular synovial lesion was suspected, and the patient was scheduled for a synovial biopsy.

A 68-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of intermittent periumbilical pain without vomiting, obstruction, or change in bowel habits. He was haemodynamically stable. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the left iliac fossa without distension; bowel sounds were present. An abdominal ultrasound showed a bowel mass in the left iliac fossa, and CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a “bowel within bowel” configuration in the pelvis involving the sigmoid colon into the rectum, with sigmoid wall thickening and pericolonic fat stranding, findings suggestive of colorectal intussusception. The lead point was not visualized. Colonoscopy revealed a mass 20 cm from the anal verge; biopsy demonstrated mucinous adenocarcinoma. On further evaluation, the abdomen was soft and nontender with no palpable masses; digital rectal examination was normal. CT of the chest showed no metastases. Bone scan was recommended. Urea, electrolytes, liver function tests, and complete blood count were normal. The carcinoembryonic antigen level was 13.20 ng/mL (normal, 0.00–5.00). The patient was referred for surgical resection.

A 53-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of progressive nasal obstruction and frequent epistaxis. His medical history included well-controlled hypertension and diabetes. On examination, no café-au-lait spots or other cutaneous lesions were observed; HIV serology was negative.

Endoscopic evaluation demonstrated a polypoid mass extending from the midportion of the right inferior turbinate to the choana. Paranasal sinus CT showed a 2.5 cm heterogeneously enhancing mass filling the right nasal cavity, extending into the right choana and nasopharynx, with erosion of the nasal septal bone. MRI revealed a well-demarcated 2.5 × 1.5 cm fungating mass with gadolinium enhancement, internal hemorrhage, and increased vascularity.

The lesion was removed endoscopically in a piecemeal fashion. Grossly, the specimen was a soft, pinkish, friable mass originating from the right choana and the posteroinferior aspect of the nasal septum; the adjacent septal mucosa was resected, and the septal bone was preserved.

A 7-year-old girl presented with months of aching and swelling on the left side of her mandible. She had no significant medical history. Initial evaluation by a local maxillofacial surgeon led to incision and intravenous amoxicillin–clavulanic acid for presumed abscess, but only significant soft-tissue edema was noted, with no pus drainage. Intraoral exam demonstrated superficial cheek necrosis from molar friction. A panoramic radiograph revealed an osteolytic zone in the left mandibular angle and ramus, with absence of the thin circumferential cortical layer around the developing second molar. Ultrasound showed an inhomogeneous, relatively well-defined soft-tissue mass above the left submandibular gland invading the mandible. CT and MRI confirmed a mass in the left masseter region fixed to the ascending mandibular ramus with osteolysis. For staging, PET-CT demonstrated abdominal hypermetabolic lesions consistent with metastases.

A 72-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a gingival enlargement in the mandibular anterior region that had developed over one month. His medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, a remote basal cell carcinoma, alcohol use, and former smoking; he denied known hepatitis or HIV infection. Extraoral examination revealed no lymphadenopathy. Intraorally, he had poor oral hygiene, generalized periodontal disease, and a 2 cm sessile, lobulated, dark-red nodular lesion on the buccal and lingual gingiva of the mandibular incisors, extending to the floor of the mouth; the adjacent teeth had heavy biofilm, calculus, and mobility. Panoramic radiography showed significant horizontal bone loss around the anterior teeth, extending to the left first premolar, and calculus accumulation consistent with chronic periodontal disease. Given the rapid growth and appearance, an incisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia.

A 31-year-old man with HIV infection diagnosed 16 years earlier, who had discontinued HAART and follow-up for the past 3 years, presented with 20 days of high-grade fever, diaphoresis, and cough productive of scant whitish sputum. He also reported a 20-kg weight loss over 8 months, intermittent epigastric pain, and progressive dysphagia.  
On admission, vital signs were notable for fever; examination revealed epigastric tenderness without palpable lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, chemistries, liver and renal function tests, electrolytes, and lactate dehydrogenase. The CD4 count was 261 cells/mm3 and the HIV viral load was 163 597 copies/mL.  
Upper endoscopy demonstrated a 20-cm narrowing of the distal esophagus with intact-appearing mucosa, and in the posterior wall of the gastric antrum a 4-cm ulcer with elevated, well-circumscribed borders and a clean base. Biopsies of both lesions were obtained.  
Histologic examination of the esophageal biopsy showed chronic esophagitis with Candida species. Gastric biopsy revealed a high-grade, poorly differentiated neoplasm composed of atypical, poorly cohesive cells in a solid growth pattern with frequent mitoses and conspicuous nucleoli.

A 32-year-old man noted a right mid-abdominal mass for 1 month, associated with intermittent pain but no fever, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. He presented after sudden severe abdominal pain. On examination, vital signs were stable; the abdomen was soft without palpable lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Abdominal CT revealed an 8.5×7.4×4 cm mass at the jejunoileal junction involving the adjacent intestinal wall and mesenteric fat; the colon and rectum were normal, and there was no enlargement of mesenteric or mediastinal lymph nodes; the liver and spleen appeared normal. Laboratory studies showed negative serum tumor markers (AFP, CEA, CA125, SCC antigen, CA19-9) and a normal complete blood count, including white cells (5.42×10^9/L), lymphocytes (1.5×10^9/L), hemoglobin (142 g/L), and platelets (350×10^9/L).

A 26-year-old man with a history of intracranial germinoma treated successfully three years earlier with chemotherapy and whole-brain radiation presented with vacillating paresthesia in his right hand and both legs. He had no focal motor deficits on examination. Serum β-hCG and α-fetoprotein levels were within normal limits, and CSF cytology was negative. CSF studies showed a positive oligoclonal IgG band, an IgG index of 0.66, and elevated myelin basic protein (45.8 pg/mL). Cervical MRI revealed a heterogeneously enhancing, expansile intramedullary lesion at the C1–C2 level with marked T2 hyperintense edema extending from the medulla oblongata to the C4 level. There were no lesions in the thoracic or lumbar spine.

A 42-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of exertional dyspnea and retrosternal chest pain (NYHA Functional Class II). He had no cardiovascular risk factors or prior medical history. On examination, there was a systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border, a diastolic murmur, an accentuated P2, and a right‐sided S4. ECG showed sinus tachycardia. Laboratory studies were notable for a troponin level of 0.2 ng/mL, NT-pro-BNP of 1350 pg/mL, and a venous blood gas demonstrating mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis (pH 7.32, pCO2 5 mmHg, pO2 35 mmHg, HCO3 20 mEq/L).

Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography revealed a semimobile, multilobulated mass measuring approximately 2.7 × 5.7 cm in the right ventricular outflow tract and main pulmonary artery, extending into the pulmonary valve and causing significant RVOT and pulmonary valve stenosis (peak gradient 59 mmHg). Right ventricular ejection fraction was 30% and left ventricular ejection fraction was 55%.

Multislice CT angiography showed a 3.1 × 6.1 cm intraluminal filling defect extending from the right main pulmonary artery into the right pulmonary artery and its upper lobar branch, with mild right ventricular enlargement.

Cardiac MRI demonstrated the lesion to be isointense on T1, hyperintense on T2‐STIR, with mild perfusion vascularity and scattered late gadolinium enhancement alongside hypointense areas suggestive of necrosis or thrombosis. The mass encased the pulmonary valve and caused severe RVOT stenosis.

A PET–CT scan revealed no hypermetabolic lesions outside the pulmonary artery.

A 54-year-old woman presented with a 1-day history of proptosis, lid swelling, diplopia, and retro-orbital pain in her left eye. Her past medical history was significant for poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the stomach, with known metastases to the ovary, mesentery, subcutaneous tissue of the neck, and thoracic bone marrow; she had undergone multiple chemotherapy regimens and was on palliative care. On examination, external inspection showed left eyelid swelling, erythema, and proptosis. Ocular motility testing revealed an adduction deficit of –4.0 and an abduction deficit of –1.0 in the left eye. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally, and intraocular pressures were normal in both eyes. Anterior segments were unremarkable. Pupils were equal and reactive without a relative afferent pupillary defect. Funduscopic examination of the left eye showed partial optic disc edema without choroidal masses or striae. Review of a CT scan performed 10 days before presentation demonstrated enlargement of the left medial rectus muscle; comparison with imaging from 3 months earlier showed progressive enlargement, while a scan from 6 months earlier was normal. There was no enlargement of other extraocular muscles or other orbital abnormalities.

A 73-year-old woman undergoing routine surveillance CT for a history of pulmonary MALT lymphoma was found to have a 2.0 cm × 1.1 cm peripancreatic lymph node adjacent to the pancreatic head. She denied abdominal pain, weight loss, nausea, or vomiting. Her medical history was notable for breast cancer, hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and MALT lymphoma. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including fractionated metanephrines, chromogranin A, and gastrin levels, were within normal limits. Endoscopic ultrasonography demonstrated a 19 mm × 11.5 mm hypoechoic lesion near the pancreatic head. Two transduodenal EUS-FNA passes were performed. Direct smears showed tumor cells with neuroendocrine features. Initial immunoperoxidase stains on a cell block were positive for synaptophysin and chromogranin. The pathologist was informed that the lesion was peripancreatic without a definite pancreatic parenchymal mass.

A 76-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a history of scattered nodules over her body for 18 months. She first noticed a few lesions on the neck, with subsequent lesions in the inframammary region, abdomen, back, and later the limbs and face, including the nose and ears. The lesions were reddish or brown, dome-shaped, painless papules of firm consistency, 1–5 mm in size, that occasionally ulcerated. She had no fever, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms, and applied topical corticosteroid cream over her face with subjective improvement. Her medical history included hypertension treated with valsartan, levanlodipine, clopidogrel, and simvastatin, and a remote myocardial infarction treated with angioplasty. On examination, she appeared depressed, had normal vital signs, and multiple nonpruritic, nontender papules and nodules were noted on the face, trunk, and extremities. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, electrolytes, renal and liver function tests, calcium, thyroid function, protein electrophoresis, β2-microglobulin, immunoglobulin levels, and serologies for HIV, hepatitis B and C, syphilis, ANA, and anti-DNA, were all within normal limits or negative. A bone radiologic survey was unremarkable. Chest CT showed signs of pulmonary emphysema. PET–CT demonstrated multiple hypermetabolic cutaneous lesions but no other suspicious foci. Brain MRI was normal. The patient was scheduled for a skin biopsy of a representative lesion.

A 34-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of persistent dry cough and intermittent dyspnea. She denied sputum production, fatigue, or chest discomfort. Vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed clear bilateral breath sounds without wheezes or crackles. 

Enhanced chest CT showed a 2.3×2.0 cm hypervascular nodule on the posterior tracheal wall at the thoracic inlet, occupying approximately two-thirds of the lumen, with no regional lymphadenopathy (cT2N0M0). Routine blood counts, biochemistry, and LDH (186 U/L; normal range 120–250 U/L) were unremarkable.

Bronchoscopy revealed a broad-based, lobulated mass seven cartilage rings below the glottis, causing significant luminal obstruction. A preoperative endobronchial biopsy showed small round tumor cells infiltrating the submucosa in trabecular and nest-like patterns within fibrous stroma, with mild nuclear atypia, uniform size, occasional clear cytoplasm, no keratinization, and rare mitotic figures. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated diffuse strong positivity for p40 and p63, partial positivity for CEA, negativity for CD56, TTF-1, Napsin A, and Synaptophysin, a low Ki-67 index (<10%), and weak p53 positivity. Based on these findings, a working diagnosis of poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma was made.

An 8-year-old girl was brought with a three-year history of a slowly enlarging swelling of the right upper posterior maxilla. The lesion was initially asymptomatic but caused pain over the past year when the lower teeth contacted it at jaw closure. There was no history of trauma or toothache. Her past medical history was unremarkable, and vital signs were normal.

On extra-oral examination, there was a large right facial swelling causing displacement of the right nasal base, cranial displacement and protrusion of the right eye, and lateral and ventral displacement of the zygoma with gross facial asymmetry; mouth opening was normal. Intra-orally, the swelling was solitary, well defined, non-ulcerated, firm, and non-tender, extending from the right maxillary tuberosity to the left central incisor and up to the infra-orbital rim, with slight palatal expansion. The patient had infra-orbital paraesthesia, difficulty chewing and speaking, marked alveolar asymmetry, and the adjacent teeth were firm without root resorption. There was no lymphadenopathy.

A panoramic radiograph showed a unilocular radiolucency with well-defined borders and central opacification in the right maxilla. A 3-D CT scan demonstrated a well-circumscribed mixed-density lesion with a ground-glass appearance involving the right maxilla and hard palate, with mass effect on the maxillary sinus.

A 66-year-old woman with a history of endometrioid endometrial carcinoma presented with abdominal and pelvic pain. Physical examination was unremarkable, and laboratory studies, including a creatinine level of 0.81 mg dl–1, were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a right renal mass with areas of fat attenuation located in the upper pole, creating a defect in the renal parenchyma. The lesion contained visible vessels extending into the renal cortex, a finding known as a “renal parenchymal vascular pedicle.” Additionally, there was a fatty tumor thrombus within the right renal vein extending to its confluence with the inferior vena cava. No other masses or enlarged lymph nodes were identified.

A 48-year-old woman presented with sharp, severe left lower quadrant pain. Transabdominal ultrasound showed an enlarged uterus with multiple masses suggestive of leiomyomas, an 8.7 cm complex left adnexal mass, and minimal pelvic fluid; a CT scan confirmed these findings. Pelvic examination revealed a posterior cervix and an enlarged, boggy uterus without tenderness; the cervix could not be visualized on speculum exam. No inguinal lymphadenopathy was noted. Laboratory studies showed an elevated CA-125 level of 125.9 U/mL. Her medical history was notable for breast cancer treated with lumpectomy, radiation, and tamoxifen; her gynecologic history included a laparoscopic myomectomy 12 years earlier. She denied abnormal bleeding, weight loss, or urinary or gastrointestinal symptoms.

The patient underwent total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. Gross examination of the cervix revealed a 0.9 × 0.4 × 0.3 cm rubbery nodule in the posterior endocervical canal with a homogeneous gray-white cut surface, and a 1.3 × 0.4 × 0.4 cm tan-white soft polyp on the anterior endocervical canal. 

Histologically, the rubbery nodule was well circumscribed, composed of spindle cells with localized nuclear palisading and abundant thick-walled hyalinized blood vessels; mitotic activity was minimal, confirmed by scant Ki-67 staining. Immunohistochemical studies showed strong S-100 protein positivity and negative staining for neurofilament protein, CD34, desmin, actin, chromogranin, synaptophysin, and pan-melanoma.

A 17-year-old woman presented with one month of progressively worsening pain in the left hypochondrium and epigastrium, accompanied by vomiting without bleeding or changes in bowel habits. She was afebrile and her general condition was preserved. Physical examination revealed a 20 cm firm mass occupying the left hypochondrium and epigastrium; it was mobile in the superficial plane and fixed to the deep plane. Laboratory studies, including hemoglobin and renal function, were normal, and tumor markers CA 19-9 and ACE were negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax and abdomen showed a 20 cm necrotic tissue mass in the omental bursa, possibly arising from the stomach or pancreas. Endoscopic ultrasonography demonstrated a heterogeneous solid mass abutting the corporocaudal region of the pancreas without loss of the intervening fat plane and indenting the portal vein and splenomesenteric confluence.

A 44-year-old man from Afghanistan presented with a 6-week history of initially dry cough that became productive, followed after 2 months by daily hemoptysis of approximately two tablespoons. He also reported low-grade fevers with sweating (no rigors), an 8% weight loss over 2 months, moderately severe epigastric pain radiating to the right upper quadrant for 1.5 months, and vague mild lower back pain for 1 month. His past medical history was notable only for enteric fever 15 years earlier.  

Initial investigations in Afghanistan showed a leukocyte count of 12,000/μL with 20% eosinophils, hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL, and platelets 210,000/μL. High-resolution CT of the chest revealed bilateral nodular infiltrates and mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy. He received steroids for presumed eosinophilic pulmonary disease without response. Tuberculosis tests, including GeneXpert PCR and interferon-γ release assay, were negative, but he was treated empirically with anti-tuberculous therapy for 1 month, during which his respiratory symptoms and weight loss worsened.  

On presentation to our hospital, he had diffuse crackles on lung exam, mild tender hepatomegaly, and lower back tenderness. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed innumerable bilateral pulmonary nodules, extensive mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy (the largest subcarinal node 16 mm), small hypodense lesions in liver and spleen, and lytic expansile lesions in L2 and L5 vertebral bodies.  

An endoscopic ultrasound–guided biopsy of the subcarinal lymph node was performed and sent for histopathology and immunohistochemistry. Meanwhile his hemoglobin fell to 8.2 g/dL and platelet count to 57,000/μL. Coagulation studies showed a prothrombin time of 30 s, activated partial thromboplastin time of 66 s, peripheral smear with 6–8 schistocytes per high-power field, lactate dehydrogenase 312 U/L, and fibrinogen 112 mg/dL. All this workup suggested DIC with consumptive coagulopathy and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.

A 73-year-old woman, lifelong non-smoker, presented with a 4-week history of progressive dyspnea and dry cough. On examination, breath sounds were reduced with dullness to percussion over the left hemithorax. A painless, poorly defined mass with overlying skin redness was noted in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast, along with palpable left axillary lymph nodes.  
Chest radiography showed a massive left pleural effusion with mediastinal shift to the right. Contrast CT of the chest confirmed compression atelectasis of the left lung by a large pleural effusion, with a few deep left axillary and paratracheal lymph nodes.  
Mammography demonstrated diffuse asymmetrical density and skin thickening in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast without calcifications.  
Bronchoscopy revealed submucosal infiltration at the secondary carina, with approximately 70% obstruction of the lingula orifice. Pleural fluid re-accumulated rapidly, prompting medical thoracoscopy with biopsy of the parietal pleura. An excisional breast biopsy was also performed.

A 72-year-old woman with chronic renal failure on continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis was admitted with acute onset of abdominal pain. On admission, she had a low-grade fever. Physical examination revealed generalized abdominal tenderness, and her peritoneal dialysis fluid appeared turbid. Laboratory testing showed a mildly elevated white-cell count. An urgent contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was obtained to evaluate for peritoneal dialysis–associated peritonitis. The scan showed no evidence of peritonitis or intra-abdominal sepsis. Incidentally, there were bilateral perirenal lesions composed of mixed fat and soft tissue surrounding both kidneys and predominantly involving the renal sinuses. Prominent enhancing soft-tissue nodules were noted bilaterally, larger on the left. Multiple enlarged retroperitoneal lymph nodes in the aortocaval and retrocaval regions were also seen, some containing areas of macroscopic fat. There was no evidence of renal vascular invasion.

A 19-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of a painless swelling in the lower right mouth. On examination, there was a small, hard swelling in the right mandibular buccal and lingual sulci. Tooth 47 was absent; the patient denied any prior extraction and reported that the tooth had never erupted. In the opposing arch, tooth 37 was erupted and tooth 38 was impacted. The overlying mucosa was normal, nerve function was intact, and tooth 46 adjacent to the swelling had no pathologic mobility or periodontal pockets. There was no draining sinus or fistula. Aspiration was performed and was negative for vascular contents. An incisional biopsy report of odontomes was received. Cone-beam CT showed a large, well-defined radiolucency measuring approximately 6 cm×3 cm, extending from the mesial root of 46 to the inferior aspect of the ramus and reaching the inferior mandibular border. Teeth 47 and 48 were contained within the radiolucency, and the inferior alveolar canal was displaced inferiorly. A mild buccolingual cortical expansion was noted. The lesion was predominantly radiolucent but contained well-defined radiopaque areas. The patient reported no pain or neurologic symptoms.

A 51-year-old man presented with three weeks of right facial weakness. He was unable to close his right eye and had deviation of the mouth on the same side (House–Brackmann grade 5/6). He had no hearing loss, tinnitus, or ear fullness. 

Pure-tone audiometry showed mild bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. Tympanometry was type A bilaterally, but ipsilateral and contralateral blink reflexes were absent on the right. Otoacoustic emissions were absent in both ears, and brainstem auditory-evoked potentials demonstrated morphologically normal waveforms. Videonystagmography revealed no spontaneous nystagmus, and caloric testing was normal.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed a 0.8 × 0.4 mm enhancing mass within the right internal auditory canal.

A 69-year-old man with a 9-year history of recalcitrant idiopathic pyoderma gangrenosum affecting his shins and ankles had stable disease on prednisone, mycophenolate mofetil (1 g twice daily), and monthly intravenous immunoglobulin (2 g/kg). Two months before presentation, he noted a 4 × 3 cm friable, fungating nodule arising within a chronic ulcer on his right anterior shin. To exclude squamous cell carcinoma, a 4.0-mm punch biopsy was performed. Light microscopy revealed a diffuse dermal infiltrate of plasmacytoid malignant cells with numerous mitoses and surrounding necrosis. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated positivity for CD38, CD138, and MUM1 and negativity for CD45RB, CD20, CD56, CD79a, CD117, HHV8, PAX5, and ALK. Ki-67 expression was 90% of the tumor cells, and in situ hybridization showed diffuse positivity for Epstein-Barr virus–encoded RNA.

A 35-year-old Palestinian woman, lifelong non-smoker and previously healthy, presented with a six-month history of progressive cough, mild hemoptysis, fatigue, and dyspnea on mild-to-moderate exertion without weight loss. On admission, her vital signs were stable and her BMI was 23.4. She had no chronic illnesses, surgeries, drug use, or known environmental exposures; family history was unremarkable. Physical examination was normal: lungs were clear with good bilateral air entry; there was no lymphadenopathy, clubbing, cyanosis, or peripheral edema. High-resolution chest CT showed bilateral reticulonodular infiltrates with cystic changes. Pulmonary function tests demonstrated an FVC of 1.63 L, FEV₁ of 1.64 L, and an FVC/FEV₁ ratio of 1.01. Bronchoscopy revealed normal airways without endobronchial lesions or active bleeding. Laboratory tests, including CBC and metabolic panel, were normal except for a CRP of 8.9 mg/L. Bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial biopsies were obtained, and a subsequent chest X-ray showed a right-sided pneumothorax requiring chest-tube placement.

A 30-year-old non-smoking woman was referred after a routine chest radiograph detected a left-sided pleural effusion. She denied cough, sputum, or dyspnea. Her history included endometriosis, an ovarian cyst, and left breast fibroadenomas treated two years earlier with polypectomy and hormone therapy. She travelled monthly for business, including over 15 visits to an Indonesian coal mine. Vital signs were: T 37.1°C, BP 108/70 mmHg, HR 70/min, RR 16/min, SpO2 96% on room air. Exam revealed diminished breath sounds and dullness to percussion at the left lower lung; otherwise normal. Laboratory values were unremarkable, including leukocytes 5500/µL, CRP <0.04 mg/dL, soluble IL-2 receptor 293 U/mL, CEA 0.5 ng/mL, SLX 34.9 U/mL, and CA 19-9 7.9 U/mL. Chest radiograph showed homogeneous opacity in the left lower lung field. HRCT demonstrated multiple strongly and heterogeneously enhancing pleural-based masses along the medial aspect of the left lower lobe (largest 27×15×33 mm) fed by the musculophrenic branch of the left internal thoracic artery. A 15-mm hypoattenuating lesion with peripheral enhancement in the right liver anterior segment suggested a hepatic hemangioma. Thoracentesis yielded lightly yellow fluid with 162 cells/µL (10% lymphocytes, 8.5% neutrophils), ADA 4.9 U/L, protein ratio 0.6, LDH ratio 0.5; cultures were negative and cytology showed no malignant cells. PET–CT performed one week later showed no FDG uptake in the chest and an increase in pleural effusion.

A 16-year-old Asian male presented with a 2-year history of insidious anterior left knee pain. Initially intermittent and mild, the pain had progressively worsened and become continuous, with nocturnal exacerbations. He reported only modest relief with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. On examination, there was no focal point of tenderness; a small suprapatellar effusion was noted. Knee range of motion was full, but there was wasting of the ipsilateral quadriceps. Vital signs and serum biochemistry were within normal limits. Plain radiographs of the knee were unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed, at the medial aspect of the patella near the articular surface, a hypointense punctate focus surrounded by a small hyperintense zone of marrow edema. A thin-slice CT scan of the patella demonstrated a small central nidus surrounded by a sclerotic rim.

A 50-year-old right-hand-dominant woman presented with a 3-month history of swelling around the A1 pulley of the right third finger and snapping on flexion. She had been treated for presumed trigger finger with a tendon sheath injection without improvement. On examination, there was an approximately 2 cm elastic, firm mass on the ulnar side of the right third metacarpal head with tenderness and audible snapping, but full range of motion was preserved. Routine laboratory results were unremarkable. Plain radiographs of the hand showed a focal radiolucency in the head of the third metacarpal. CT imaging demonstrated cortical destruction of the same metacarpal head. MRI revealed a well-circumscribed mass of low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high signal intensity on STIR sequences, extending into the metacarpal head. Based on these findings, a giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath was suspected, and surgical resection was planned.

A 38-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of gradually enlarging, painless neck swellings. The initial left-sided pea-sized swelling grew and was later joined by bilateral cervical nodes, similar swellings on her cheeks and anterior chest, nasal congestion, recurrent headaches, and sinusitis. She had two self-limited episodes of epistaxis in the past 6 months, intermittent dysphagia without odynophagia, and undocumented intermittent fevers over the past year. She denied weight loss, night sweats, respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms, visual changes, or neurologic deficits. 

Her medical and family histories were unremarkable, and she had no known tuberculosis exposure. She was afebrile, with blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg, pulse 70 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Physical examination showed mild pallor and multiple firm, smooth, freely movable, non-tender cervical lymph nodes (largest 2.5 × 2.5 cm). Oral examination revealed bilateral tonsillar enlargement without exudate. Nasopharyngolaryngoscopy demonstrated adenotonsillar hypertrophy and bilateral nasal polyps. 

Initial laboratory studies showed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Neck magnetic resonance imaging revealed a lobulated isointense lesion in the right nasal cavity and an enlarged nasopharyngeal tonsil with homogeneous postcontrast enhancement, homogeneously enhancing palatine tonsils, and bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy.

A young, previously healthy patient presented with a two-week history of severe headache and vomiting that recurred despite transient relief from analgesics and antiemetics. There was no history of trauma, surgery, smoking, drug use, or relevant family history. On examination, vital signs were stable, Glasgow Coma Scale score was 14 (E3, V5, M6), and there were no focal neurologic deficits. Routine blood tests were normal. Noncontrast head CT demonstrated a left parasagittal frontal space-occupying lesion with mass effect, cerebral edema, and asymmetric ventricular enlargement. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a hyperdense lesion measuring approximately 60 × 52 × 38 mm with similar mass effect and edema. Sagittal views revealed the lesion abutting the sphenoid wing. CT angiography revealed multiple enlarged vascular channels and several larger feeding vessels within a vascularized left frontal lesion. Upon radiologic interpretation, these findings were concluded to represent a large left frontal arteriovenous malformation.

A 45-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of dull, aching pain in the left side of his abdomen that radiated to the back. There were no associated symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, or changes in bowel habits, and he denied weight loss, trauma, chronic illness, or prior surgery. He was a nonsmoker with an unremarkable medical and family history. 

On examination, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. His abdomen revealed a freely mobile, well-defined, firm mass measuring approximately 20 × 20 cm in the left abdomen; the remainder of the examination was normal.

Laboratory tests, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits.

Abdominal ultrasonography showed an intra-abdominal (mesenteric) mass without hydronephrosis or free fluid. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a well-defined, lobulated, heterogeneously enhancing mass arising from the mesocolon.

A 37-year-old man was involved in a minor rear-end collision and immediately noted neck pain and abnormal sensations in both forearms. On neurologic examination, he had allodynia in both hands and increased deep-tendon reflexes in the lower extremities without motor weakness, gait disturbance, or bladder dysfunction. Cervical CT showed normal alignment and no fracture, but revealed an oval extradural mass at the C6–C7 facet level with a high-density rim clearly separate from the adjacent bone. T2-weighted MRI demonstrated a well-circumscribed mass of high signal intensity surrounded by a low-intensity rim compressing the dural sac without spinal cord signal change. On T1-weighted images, the mass exhibited high signal intensity, suggesting fatty content. After 3 months of conservative treatment, his allodynia resolved but he continued to experience neck pain and dysesthesia in both hands. Repeat examination revealed isolated ulnar-hand dysesthesia, worsened by rightward neck rotation with extension. Imaging was unchanged. The leading preoperative considerations were a calcified synovial cyst or ossification of the ligamentum flavum, but the MRI characteristics did not align with either entity.

A 5-year-old boy presented with a 2-month history of torticollis and pain radiating to his left upper limb. He had no previous medical history. On examination, he had decreased sensation in both upper limbs, bilateral lower-extremity weakness (motor strength 4/5 in distal muscle groups), and hypoactive reflexes in all four extremities. There was no bowel or bladder dysfunction. Cervical CT and MRI revealed a 75 × 36 × 24 mm extradural, dumbbell-shaped mass with extra-spinal extension at the left C1–C6 level, containing calcifications and showing heterogeneous signal intensity with homogeneous intermediate enhancement after gadolinium administration. No other spinal cord lesions or osseous abnormalities were identified.

A 43-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of pelvic floor weakness, during which an incidental liver mass was palpated. She denied gastrointestinal symptoms, changes in bowel habits, weight loss, fevers, or night sweats. She reported drinking one bottle of wine nightly for 10 years but had no stigmata of cirrhosis and no family history of liver disease or malignancy.

Laboratory studies showed:
• Normal complete blood count and platelet count of 224×10^9/L  
• International normalized ratio 0.9  
• Plasma ammonia 32 μmol/L  
• Normal liver function tests: albumin 50 g/L, bilirubin 17 μmol/L, transaminases, alkaline phosphatase 63 U/L, γ-glutamyl transferase 32 U/L  
• Tumor markers (CEA, CA15-3, CA125, CA19-9) all within normal limits  
• Negative hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibodies

Contrast-enhanced CT of the liver demonstrated a large exophytic mass in segment 5/6 with multiple central hypodense areas. On arterial phase, there was hypervascular curvilinear and nodular internal enhancement with hypoenhancing components. During the portal venous phase, the hypodense areas showed gradual enhancement, and on delayed imaging the solid component was hyperenhancing relative to liver parenchyma. The biliary ducts were not dilated, and hepatic vessels appeared patent. The initial imaging differential included atypical focal nodular hyperplasia and hemangioma.

Subsequent MRI of the liver with gadoxetic acid showed:
• A heterogeneous mass with intermediate T1 and low T2 signal septations, areas of diffusion restriction, and circumscribed T2 hyperintense foci  
• No definite fat or lipid content; mild signal increase on T1 opposed-phase consistent with possible haemosiderin  
• Dynamic sequences revealed moderate peripheral arterial enhancement, minimal centripetal filling in the portal venous phase, and no washout  
• On 20-minute hepatobiliary phase imaging, there was uptake of gadoxetic acid throughout both the low and high T2 signal regions of the mass

An 11-month-old male with a history of nasolacrimal duct stenosis and a small thyroglossal duct cyst was evaluated for left facial swelling of 9 months’ duration. Six months earlier, a mass was noted on the left cheek, which had enlarged progressively over the preceding 2 months. The patient had intermittent fevers in the week before presentation but was otherwise well. Baseline laboratory studies, including a platelet count, were within normal limits.

On examination, there was a firm, mobile, non-tender mass just inferior to the left zygomatic arch. Ultrasonography demonstrated a vascularized, solid lesion measuring 12 × 15 × 16 mm, confined to the superficial soft tissues. MRI of the face revealed a multilobular mass with high T2 signal centered within the left masseter muscle and with infiltrative signal extending into the adjacent subcutaneous tissue.

The patient underwent an ultrasound-guided core-needle biopsy. Histologic examination was interpreted initially as consistent with tufted angioma, showing fibrovascular tissue containing compact nests of variably sized and ill-defined vascular channels. Immunohistochemical stains revealed that the endothelial cells were diffusely positive for CD34 and CD31, partially positive for D2-40, and negative for GLUT-1.

A 41-year-old Hispanic woman with no history of smoking presented with a 3-year history of predominantly dry cough and dyspnea. Three years earlier, while living in Arizona, she was treated for Chlamydia pneumoniae with a 3-month course of doxycycline without symptom resolution. Her past medical history was notable only for well-controlled gastroesophageal reflux disease.

On examination, her temperature was 98°F, blood pressure 122/90 mmHg, pulse 70 bpm, respirations 15/min, SpO₂ 95% on room air, and BMI 32. Head and neck examination showed no lymphadenopathy. Cardiovascular exam was unremarkable. Lung auscultation revealed mild late-end expiratory wheezes bilaterally. The abdomen was non-tender without organomegaly. There was no cyanosis, clubbing, or edema.

Current medications included albuterol, montelukast, pantoprazole, tiotropium, calcium, and cyanocobalamin. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count with differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, and serum total immunoglobulin E, were normal. Pulmonary function tests demonstrated severe obstruction without bronchodilator response, mild restriction, and a reduced DLCO that normalized when corrected for alveolar volume. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. High-resolution chest CT showed diffuse bilateral micronodules and a mosaic pattern consistent with air trapping. A bronchoalveolar lavage from the lingula was performed, yielding fluid with 62% lymphocytes.

A 70-year-old Syrian woman presented with 10 days of intermittent, localized epigastric pain accompanied by diarrhea, nausea, and weight loss; she denied fever. Six days before presentation, she noticed dark-colored urine. Twenty-five days earlier, she had been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus during a routine examination. Her medical history included a partial thyroidectomy 20 years earlier and hip replacement 7 years earlier; family history was notable for type 2 diabetes in her father and brother. On examination her blood pressure and electrocardiogram were normal; abdominal examination was unremarkable.  

Laboratory studies showed WBC 5 × 10^3/µL (lymphocytes 47%, neutrophils 50%), hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.3 mg/dL, amylase 42 U/L, glucose 237 mg/dL, C-reactive protein 120 mg/L, and thyroid-stimulating hormone 8.22 µIU/mL with normal free T4 and free T3.  

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated cystic dilation of the main pancreatic duct in the body of the pancreas, associated with an irregular mass. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography revealed a “fish-mouth” ampulla of Vater and a 15 mm cystic dilation of the main pancreatic duct surrounding an irregular mucinous lesion at the junction of the pancreatic head and body, with connection to multiple small cleft-like cysts in branch ducts.  

The primary radiographic differential diagnosis included intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm and mucinous cystic neoplasm. The patient was referred for surgical management.

A 31-year-old man with no significant past medical history or family history of cancer presented to the emergency department with four weeks of clot-forming gross hematuria. Five weeks earlier, he had an episode of asymptomatic gross hematuria that was treated as a urinary tract infection. On this admission he was in hypovolemic shock from ongoing hematuria. Vital signs showed tachycardia and diaphoresis. Lung auscultation revealed bilateral rales; the abdomen was soft with no palpable masses or peritoneal signs. Genital examination showed a normal penis and descended testes, but there was an indurated, painless mass in the left scrotal sac without erythema or warmth.  
Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 7560/μL, hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, platelets 204 000/μL; prothrombin time 16 s, partial thromboplastin time 33.2 s, INR 1.3; serum glucose 116 mg/dL; blood urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL; creatinine 1.3 mg/dL; sodium 134 mmol/L; potassium 3.5 mmol/L; chloride 102 mmol/L. Tumor markers were remarkable for a β-hCG of 483 100 mIU/mL, an α-fetoprotein level of 1.05 ng/mL, and an LDH of 386 IU/L.

A 48-year-old Caucasian man with a history of type 2 diabetes underwent an abdominal ultrasound for chronic abdominal discomfort, which revealed a large mass in the left kidney. He denied flank pain, weight loss, hematuria, or other symptoms. His medical and family histories were otherwise noncontributory. On examination, vital signs were normal and a firm mass was palpated in the left upper abdominal quadrant. Laboratory studies showed normal renal and liver function, with the exception of hyperglycemia; urinalysis and a chest radiograph were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen demonstrated a well-defined heterogeneous mass measuring 16.5 × 13.9 cm at the lower pole of the left kidney, containing both cystic and solid components. Magnetic resonance imaging of the renal vasculature showed no evidence of thrombus in the renal vein or inferior vena cava. Given the concern for a renal malignancy, a radical nephrectomy was planned.

A 61-year-old woman, nonsmoker, presented with a 1-month history of nonproductive cough and a 5-kg weight loss. She had no prior hospitalizations and did not require supplemental oxygen. On examination, breath sounds were diminished over the left lung; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level <10 mg/L, a white-cell count of 4.1 × 10^9/L, and normal fasting glucose. A chest radiograph demonstrated opacification of the left hemithorax with rightward tracheal deviation. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a large, heterogeneously enhancing mass measuring 10.2 × 9.0 × 14.8 cm in the left upper lobe without sparing of the lingular segments, along with two pleural-based nodules in the posterior basal segment of the left lower lobe (largest, 2.8 × 2.6 cm). Flexible bronchoscopy showed extrinsic compression of the left main bronchus 2 cm from the carina. CT-guided biopsy of the left upper-lobe mass yielded multiple grey-white fragments. Histologic examination revealed two cell populations: neoplastic epithelial cells that were round to oval without nuclear atypia, and a highly proliferative immature lymphocytic population. Immunohistochemical analysis showed that the epithelial cells were diffusely positive for cytokeratin AE1/AE3, cytokeratin 5/6, cytokeratin 7, cytokeratin 19, and p40, and negative for CD5 and CD117. The lymphocytes were positive for CD3 and TdT and negative for CD20.

A 43-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of a progressively generalized pruritic skin eruption. He denied viral infections, contact allergies, systemic illness, or recent drug intake. On examination, he had generalized infiltrated erythematous plaques on the trunk and extremities covering most of his body surface area. The plaques were studded with multiple flaccid and tense vesicles and bullae arranged in an annular pattern. Some blisters were ruptured, with exudative superficial erosions; there was no mucosal involvement. The patient appeared well and had no systemic symptoms.

Skin biopsies from the plaques and bullae were performed. Histologic examination showed both intraepidermal and subepidermal blisters, with infiltration of the upper dermis and dermo-epidermal junction by atypical lymphocytes demonstrating epidermotropism. High-power views revealed large lymphoid cells with convoluted nuclei. Immunohistochemical staining showed a predominantly T-cell infiltrate that was CD3+, CD4+, and CD8–. Direct immunofluorescence testing for IgG, IgA, IgM, and C3 was negative.

A 42-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with a 3-month history of progressive left ankle pain and swelling, associated with low-grade fevers, night sweats, and weight loss. He denied any trauma. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. He ambulated with a cane and had marked swelling, warmth, dark skin discoloration, and moderate-to-severe tenderness over the left ankle and distal leg. No lymphadenopathy was palpable. Ankle range of motion was limited by pain.

Laboratory studies showed normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, white-cell count, procalcitonin, and hemoglobin. Plain radiographs of the left ankle demonstrated soft tissue swelling around the joint and abnormal bone density at the distal tibia. Magnetic resonance imaging of the ankle revealed extensive bone marrow and soft tissue edema in the distal tibial metadiaphysis with a reactive joint effusion and a subchondral fluid collection measuring 2.5 × 2.0 × 1.5 cm, indicating an aggressive lesion most likely representing osteomyelitis. A three-phase bone scan showed increased uptake over the left ankle with intense hypervascular activity suggestive of bone infection. A gallium scan with SPECT/CT revealed multiple areas of intense uptake in popliteal and inguinal lymph nodes, raising the possibility of a neoplastic process. Computed tomography of the chest demonstrated two ground-glass pulmonary nodules in the left upper lobe and the apical segment of the left lower lobe. A tissue biopsy was strongly recommended.

A 42-year-old Arab woman presented with progressive abdominal heaviness. She was a mother of three (two vaginal deliveries and one cesarean section 14 years earlier), unemployed, of low socioeconomic status, and had no formal education. She had used a copper intrauterine device until its removal 2 years ago and had not undergone any gynecologic cancer screening. Her medical history included hypertension managed with bisoprolol 2.5 mg daily, and she had undergone kidney-stone removal 20 years ago. She reported no significant family history. On examination, she had marked abdominal distention; vital signs were stable. Laboratory tests were within normal ranges. Transabdominal ultrasonography was limited by the size of the mass, which appeared septated. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis identified a complex ovarian cyst measuring 30 × 30 × 10 cm with internal septations. At this point, the differential diagnoses included serous ovarian tumor, mucinous ovarian tumor, tubo-ovarian abscess, and fibroids. Tumor marker assays were unavailable, and there was no ascites for sampling.

A 62-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an incidentally detected intra-abdominal mass. She reported a 20-year history of chronic constipation and intermittent abdominal discomfort without weight loss. She had no cardiopulmonary symptoms. Her past history included a total hysterectomy eight years earlier for uterine leiomyoma and a diagnosis 12 years ago of retroperitoneal sarcoma with lung metastases treated with chemotherapy; CT scans in 2005 and 2007 showed no change in disease extent.  

On examination, blood pressure was 140/90 mmHg; lungs were clear; the abdomen was soft and obese without palpable masses or organomegaly; no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests revealed hemoglobin 15.6 g/dL, WBC 7600/µL, platelets 205 000/µL, LDH 564 U/L, and normal CA 125, CA 19-9, and CEA.  

Abdominal CT showed multiple large, well-defined, hyperenhancing masses in the retroperitoneum and pelvis unchanged since 2005. Chest CT demonstrated multiple tiny cavitary and cystic nodules in both lungs, also stable. FDG PET/CT showed bulky retroperitoneal and pelvic masses with heterogeneous uptake (SUVmax 4.0). Pulmonary lesions were too small for biopsy, so a 12.2 × 6.3 × 4.5 cm retroperitoneal mass was resected.  

Grossly, the 283 g mass had a pale brown capsule and a whitish homogeneous cut surface. Microscopically, there was spindle cell proliferation with mild to focally moderate nuclear atypia, mitotic activity <1 per 50 HPFs, and no coagulative tumor cell necrosis. Immunohistochemistry was negative for pancytokeratin, CD117, PDGFR, and CD34; positive for actin and desmin; Ki-67 labeling index <5%; p53 negative; estrogen receptor and progesterone receptor positive.

A 68-year-old Caucasian man presented with macroglossia that had developed from a slight swelling on the right lingual border noted 3 years earlier. The lesion involved the lateral edge of the ventral surface of the tongue, measured 20 mm in maximum diameter, had a sinuous shape and soft consistency, was movable on superficial and deep planes, and was covered by normal mucosa. He reported difficulty swallowing and changes in tongue sensation, with occasional numbness at the tip. Examination of the neck and cervical lymph nodes was normal. Sensory testing with a sharp instrument revealed hypesthesia and dysesthesia in the anterior third of the tongue. Oral magnetic resonance imaging with contrast confirmed the suspicion of a lipomatous lesion.

A 66-year-old man with a history of prostate cancer was referred for evaluation of an enlarging intra-abdominal mass. He reported 12 months of increasing abdominal girth, early satiety, and new-onset discomfort. On examination, there was a non-tender, firm mass filling the abdominal cavity. Laboratory studies were unremarkable except for a total bilirubin of 1.3 mg/dL; hepatitis serologies and tumor markers were negative. Cross-sectional imaging showed a liver mass measuring 10 × 25 × 37 cm (previously 10 × 21 × 27 cm one year earlier). On dynamic CT, the lesion exhibited progressive peripheral nodular enhancement but was heterogeneous, containing large unenhanced cystic components and lacking centripetal fill-in. It involved most of the liver—sparing only the right posterior section—and extended into the pelvis.

A 50-year-old man presented with right leg and low-back pain. His history was notable for cholecystectomy and essential hypertension. On examination, a fixed, hard mass was palpable in the right lower abdominal quadrant. Laboratory studies, including CEA and CA 19–9, were normal. Abdominal CT showed a 10×10 cm thick-walled, multilocular cystic mass anterior to the right psoas and iliopsoas muscles, adjacent to the iliac vessels. Nonenhanced CT revealed spotty calcification in the hyperdense wall; on contrast-enhanced images, neither the wall nor the septae enhanced. Doppler ultrasound demonstrated no vascular flow in the wall or septae but revealed fluid–fluid levels. Based on these imaging findings, a retroperitoneal type CE5 hydatid cyst was diagnosed preoperatively.

A 64-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of a gradually enlarging scalp mass over the left parietal bone. He noted recent paresthesia in the area but denied pain, drainage, redness, weight loss, fever, chills, weakness, fatigue, vision changes, infections, or head trauma. His medical history was notable only for anxiety and hypercholesterolemia; he took no medications. He was a non‐smoker, minimal alcohol use, and no illicit drugs.

On examination, vital signs were normal. There was a 4-cm fluctuant, mobile mass over the left parietal scalp; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. In the office, aspiration of the mass yielded no fluid, raising suspicion for a solid lesion. Surgical excision was scheduled. Under general anesthesia, dissection revealed soft hemorrhagic tissue and a defect extending through the left parietal bone into the cranial cavity; the wound was packed and the patient transferred for imaging.

Noncontrast CT of the head showed a 3.3-cm lytic lesion of the left parietal bone with soft-tissue extension to the dura. Contrast MRI of the brain demonstrated an enhancing mass eroding the left parietal bone with scalp and dural involvement, as well as additional small enhancing lesions of the frontal calvarium. Laboratory studies revealed a serum calcium of 10.6 mg/dL and hemoglobin of 11.5 g/dL.

A 60‐year‐old woman presented with a 10‐year history of bilateral knee pain, worse on the right, and an inability to fully flex her knees. She first noticed a mass below her right patella 10 years ago, which had gradually increased in size. There was no history of trauma or rheumatologic disease. On examination, a bony‐hard mass was palpable just inferior to the patella and moved with patellar motion. The right knee had a range of motion from 25° to 90°, Grade II varus instability, and a varus deformity. Neurovascular status was normal. Plain radiographs of the right knee showed a well‐defined bony mass posterior to the patellar tendon just below the patella; skyline view demonstrated a medial mass displacing the patella laterally. There was collapse of the medial joint space, widening of the lateral joint space, and marginal osteophytes consistent with advanced osteoarthritis. CT of the knee revealed a well‐circumscribed mass with a pedicle attached to the inferior pole of the patella. Laboratory studies were within normal limits.

A 41-year-old Chinese man presented with a 1-year history of dry stool and a 1-month history of rectal bleeding. He had undergone perianal abscess surgery in 2009. He had hearing impairment and a remote history of pulmonary tuberculosis. On examination, he appeared well and had no lymphadenopathy. Anorectal examination revealed circumferential mucosal erosion and hard, tender, granular or nodular protrusions extending from the anus to 3 cm into the anal canal, predominantly on the right side. Routine blood counts, liver and kidney function tests, and urinalysis were all within normal limits. Colonoscopy showed annular mucosal erosion with granular or nodular elevations covered by fragile white tissue around the anal verge. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis demonstrated a round, hyperintense lesion on fat-suppressed T2-weighted images within the anal canal, with an enhancing wall, extending into the perianal skin on the left side and measuring approximately 3.1 cm in length.

A 50-year-old woman with a history of mild idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy (NYHA class III), chronic atrial fibrillation, and hypertension was admitted for worsening heart failure. On examination, her blood pressure and heart rate were normal, and her temperature was 36.5 °C. The external jugular veins were distended; there was mild hepatomegaly; and a systolic murmur was heard at the fourth intercostal space along the left sternal border. Laboratory studies were unremarkable, with no elevation in inflammatory markers. A chest radiograph showed an enlarged cardiac silhouette, and the ECG confirmed atrial fibrillation. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed mild dilated cardiomyopathy, severe biventricular dysfunction, and a small (1.3 × 1.0 cm) mass adherent to the noncoronary cusp of the aortic valve. Because of atrial fibrillation, the mass was initially presumed to be a thrombus, and the patient received thrombolysis and intravenous heparin; however, the lesion did not change in size. She was referred for further evaluation. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a highly mobile, homogeneous, echodense mass with a smooth surface attached by a pedicle to the closing margin of the noncoronary aortic cusp; all three cusps appeared normal in thickness, and there was no valvular regurgitation. These findings raised suspicion for a valvular tumor rather than a thrombus or vegetation. Cardiac MRI was performed and revealed a mobile nodular mass with slightly lower signal intensity than the myocardium on a single-slice breath-hold segmented turbo fast low-angle shot sequence.

An 86-year-old man presented with a 4-week history of skin lesions on his abdomen and lower back. He reported occasional blurry vision and joint aches but denied weight loss, chills, abdominal pain, bleeding, or healing problems. His medical history was notable only for a 20–pack-year smoking history (quit 50 years ago) and no history of skin cancer. On examination, there were numerous moderately severe, irregular, erythematous papules and nodules on the abdomen and lower back. Laboratory results from 1 month earlier showed leukopenia (white cells 1,900/μL), anemia (3.24 million RBC/μL), mild thrombocytopenia (128,000/μL), and neutropenia (766/μL). C-reactive protein was elevated at 19.5 mg/L, and alkaline phosphatase was 249 U/L. A panel for sexually transmitted infections was negative. A shave biopsy of a representative papule revealed in the dermis a dense infiltrate of monotonous neoplastic cells with dispersed chromatin and a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio.

A 52-year-old man with a history of heavy alcohol use and smoking, and no prior medical problems, presented with a left submandibular swelling that had been present for 1 year. He denied pain, fever, or weight loss. On examination, there was a 1.5 cm soft, non-tender mass beneath the left mandible without overlying skin changes. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy, and the remainder of the physical examination—including lung and neurologic findings—was unremarkable. Routine blood tests were within normal limits. Cervical ultrasonography demonstrated a poorly circumscribed, hypoechoic nodule measuring approximately 9.9 × 13.6 mm at the outer edge of the left submandibular gland.

A 74-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a painless lump in the left neck. He had hypertension but no other relevant history. Physical examination revealed a firm 2×2 cm left upper cervical swelling with slightly restricted mobility and no palpable primary lesion. Ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic 16×14×20 mm mass with a regular border, enhanced back echoes, and heterogeneous internal echoes. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated an enhancing lesion in the left upper neck adjacent to the carotid bifurcation and jugular vein. Fine-needle aspiration cytology suggested a possible malignant tumor, such as epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma or basal cell adenocarcinoma, without a definitive diagnosis. PET-CT showed FDG uptake only in the level II left cervical lymph node (21×16 mm) and no primary lesion in the salivary or mammary glands. The patient underwent a left modified radical neck dissection. Intraoperative frozen section indicated poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma. Grossly, the lymph node contained a yellow-white lobulated nodule. Histologic sections showed tubular structures with intraluminal secretion, papillary-cystic structures featuring microcysts, and a solid proliferation, suggesting acinic cell carcinoma or mammary analogue secretory carcinoma. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated tumor cells negative for p63 and DOG1 but positive for S100 protein and GATA3.

A 60-year-old man presented with six months of progressively worsening right foot pain and difficulty with ambulation. He denied trauma, systemic symptoms, or other joint involvement. His medical history was unremarkable. On examination, vital signs were normal. There was mild tenderness over the right calcaneus without overlying skin changes, masses, or lymphadenopathy. Distal pulses were intact.

A plain radiograph of the right foot showed a large heterogeneous lytic lesion involving the anterior calcaneus without a sclerotic border or periosteal reaction; the remainder of the foot and ankle appeared normal. Noncontrast MRI of the right ankle demonstrated a 3.1×3.2×3.3 cm lesion in the calcaneus that was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted and STIR images, with mild adjacent marrow edema. There was no obvious cortical breach or associated soft-tissue mass.

Given these findings, a CT-guided core needle biopsy of the calcaneal lesion was performed.

A 49-year-old woman presented with a three-month history of a slowly enlarging, painful lower-abdominal mass. She denied respiratory symptoms, had no smoking history, and no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. On examination, multiple large, non-tender masses were palpable in the lower abdomen; cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were normal.  
An abdominal CT scan showed a solid, contrast-enhanced tumor of the left ovary measuring 48 × 58 mm, peritoneal thickening and nodules up to 55 × 100 mm, and moderate ascites. Thoracic CT images revealed multiple round nodules and masses of varying sizes in the right lung, suggesting metastatic lesions. Laboratory studies demonstrated CA125 117 ng/mL, HE4 256 pmol/L, CA15-3 15 ng/mL, CEA 14.1 ng/mL, and CYFRA 21-1 1.67 ng/mL. Gastroscopy and colonoscopy were unremarkable.  
A transvaginal biopsy of the pelvic mass showed carcinoma, and a working diagnosis of FIGO stage IV ovarian carcinoma with lung metastasis was made.

An 18-year-old woman at 36 weeks’ gestation presented with progressive right-sided visual impairment over several years. Examination revealed right optic nerve pallor and atrophy without other neurologic deficits. A noncontrast brain MRI showed a right supraclinoid mass measuring 2.5 × 2.2 × 2.5 cm. Following delivery, a contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated an extra-axial mass in the right clinoidal region measuring 2.9 × 3.0 × 2.0 cm, with homogeneous enhancement, a dural tail, encasement of the right internal carotid artery, mild mass effect on the right aspect of the optic chiasm, and possible extension into the right cavernous sinus.

A 33-year-old woman, with no prior medical history, presented with intermittent mild anterior pain of the right knee for 18 months. Initially, she was “clinically diagnosed as pb. Hoffitis/tendinitis” and treated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and electro-physical therapies, which relieved her pain until mid-pregnancy, when acetaminophen and physical therapy again provided temporary benefit. One and a half years after symptom onset, she developed severe shooting pain and local swelling; no palpable mass was noted. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a discretely lobulated ovoid lesion, with well-defined borders, located below the patella and involving the patellar tendon sheath. The lesion measured approximately 22 mm × 14 mm × 28 mm and showed “discrete heterogeneous behavior of frank hyperintense predominance in density of protons with fatty saturation…slightly hypotensive in T2 and hypotensive in T1; with the contrast medium, its enhancement is homogeneous.” The MRI report also noted minimal proximal patellar tendinosis, lateral patellar inclination, and mild Hoffa’s fat-pad edema, and concluded that a “giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath was suggested.” On preoperative physical examination, there were no meniscal signs or ligamentous instability. The knee had full range of motion, with pain at maximal flexion. Muscle strength and tone were normal. There was a modest increase in anterior knee volume and tenderness over the joint line, but no neurovascular compromise.

A 35-year-old previously healthy man presented with a 3-month history of an incidentally discovered mass in his right neck. He reported no fever, cough, tingling, itching, testicular pain, or any other symptoms. Physical examination revealed an isolated, firm but soft, 6–7 cm mass in the right upper neck; no other abnormalities were noted, and testicular examination was normal.
