Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the neck showed a 50 × 29 mm soft-tissue mass in the right upper neck, encasing the right internal jugular vein. Neck ultrasonography revealed a hypoechoic, irregular mass approximately 68 × 18 × 50 mm in size, located deep to the right sternocleidomastoid muscle and lateral to the common carotid artery and internal jugular vein, with a clear boundary but multiple small nodular components; Doppler imaging showed no obvious internal blood flow. 

Contrast-enhanced ultrasound of the mass demonstrated heterogeneous hyperenhancement during the arterial phase and hypoenhancement during the venous phase.

A 75-year-old man presented with increasing abdominal distension that progressed over several months and was recently accompanied by abdominal discomfort and constipation. He denied hematuria or any other genitourinary symptoms. On examination, his abdomen was markedly protuberant with dullness to percussion and hyperactive bowel sounds. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen revealed a giant retroperitoneal mass, possibly arising from the left kidney, measuring 32.6 × 27.7 × 32.4 cm.

A 28-year-old woman was referred for extraction of a right impacted mandibular third molar. She was in good general health, with no history of trauma, systemic disease, or medication use. Extraoral and intraoral examinations were unremarkable. A panoramic radiograph showed no clear lesion or root resorption around the third molar. Under local anesthesia, the tooth was extracted without complication. On inspection of the surgical site, the dentist noted a yellowish, soft mass measuring 12 × 10 × 6 mm that was not attached to the crown or root of the extracted tooth and without signs of infection.  
Dentigerous cyst was excluded because the lesion was not associated with a tooth crown. Odontogenic keratocyst was excluded due to its non-cystic appearance.

A 21-year-old man with stage IIIB microsatellite-instability-high sigmoid colon adenocarcinoma, recently completing eight cycles of adjuvant XELOX chemotherapy, presented with atypical chest pain and shortness of breath. On examination, he was tachypneic (RR 24/min), hypertensive (150/90 mmHg), and tachycardic (HR 108 bpm), with oxygen saturation 93% on room air. Lung auscultation revealed decreased breath sounds bilaterally, and cardiac auscultation revealed a grade II systolic ejection murmur at the left sternal border. ECG showed sinus tachycardia with nonspecific ST-T changes, and troponin was normal. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a 2.7 × 4.7 cm hyperechoic mass with irregular borders in the basal to mid interventricular septum and an ejection fraction of 35%. Contrast echocardiography revealed a well-defined vascular mass within the septum. Cardiac MRI confirmed an intramyocardial septal mass measuring 2.5 × 3.8 cm that was iso-intense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted fat-saturated images, exhibited hypervascularity on first-pass perfusion, and showed enhancement on late gadolinium images.

A 57-year-old man presented with a 5-month history of coughing without hemoptysis, dyspnea, or chest pain. He was a former smoker (quit 14 years earlier) and had no history of weight loss, fever, or tuberculosis exposure. Physical examination and vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, metabolic panel, and coagulation profile, were within normal limits. A chest radiograph showed an opacity in the right middle lobe. After a 10-day course of antibiotics with only partial symptom relief, a follow-up chest radiograph demonstrated persistent middle-lobe opacity. A CT scan revealed right middle-lobe consolidation and a small, round lesion in the right intermediate bronchus that contained calcification and fat and exhibited low enhancement. The next day, bronchoscopy demonstrated a smooth, round, yellowish mass subtotally occluding the intermediate bronchus without hypervascularization. Multiple endobronchial biopsies were obtained, and the histopathological examination showed chronic inflammation without evidence of malignancy.

A 39-year-old man presented with worsening dyspnea over 10 days and a 6-month history of asthenia and progressive exercise intolerance. He had no significant past medical history. On examination, heart rate was 70 beats/min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Heart sounds were normal except for a diastolic murmur at the apex; jugular veins were not distended. Breath sounds were decreased bilaterally without rales, and there was no peripheral edema. Electrocardiography was normal. 

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a large (36 × 21 mm), nonhomogeneous mass in the left atrium, adherent to the mitral annulus and extending into the left ventricle, causing severe mitral stenosis, with mild pericardial effusion. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed the mass to be isointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with predominantly peripheral gadolinium uptake, heterogeneous late gadolinium enhancement, and hypoperfusion on first-pass perfusion sequences. 

A total-body contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan confirmed a large, irregular, hypodense mass without evidence of extracardiac metastases or invasion of the epicardial vessels.

A 24-year-old nulliparous woman presented with gradual abdominal distention over one year, early satiety, and a 10-kg weight loss over six months. She denied pain, anorexia, fatigue, prior surgeries, or medical illnesses. Vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination revealed a large, firm, regular-margined mass extending from the epigastrium to the hypogastrium, non-tender, with an unpalpable lower border. Speculum examination showed a healthy vagina and cervix, deviated to the right. Bimanual examination revealed a firm, mobile uterus with left forniceal fullness. Transabdominal ultrasound demonstrated a huge hypoechoic midline mass displacing the uterus to the right; Doppler showed high blood flow. The ovaries were not visualized, and there was no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a heterogeneous left pelvic retroperitoneal mass, superior to the pubic symphysis and extending up to the splenic hilum, with increased central vascularity; the uterus was normal but displaced posteriorly and to the right. No lymphadenopathy or free fluid was noted. Laboratory tests, including CA-125 (18.7 U/ml; normal 0–35 U/ml), were within normal limits.

A 40-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of sharp, pleuritic right-sided chest pain radiating to the right neck and associated dyspnea. He denied fever, weight loss, prior asbestos exposure, smoking, and previous radiotherapy. His medical history was otherwise unremarkable. 

On admission, he was hemodynamically stable and the physical examination was unremarkable. Routine hematologic and biochemical tests were within normal limits. A chest radiograph showed a right-sided pleural effusion. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed right-sided pleural effusion with diffuse pleural thickening and passive collapse of the adjacent lung, without underlying parenchymal abnormalities. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated normal cardiac function (ejection fraction, 63%) and no pericardial effusion.

Diagnostic thoracentesis yielded an exudative pleural effusion; cytological examination of the fluid was unremarkable. Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery disclosed right pleural thickening, visceral pleural nodularity, and a large effusion. A pleural biopsy was obtained and processed for histology and immunohistochemistry.

Microscopically, the pleural tissue showed single cells, cords, and nests of atypical polygonal cells with round to reniform nuclei, occasional vesicular chromatin, and abundant pale eosinophilic vacuolated cytoplasm; intracytoplasmic vacuoles sometimes contained erythrocytes. There was no increased mitotic activity, necrosis, or prominent pleomorphism. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated strong positivity for vimentin, CD31, and CD10; a subset of cells reacted with CD34 and EMA; WT1 and calretinin were negative. The Ki67 proliferation index was up to 15%.

A 14-year-old male presented with a swelling in the right axillary region that had been present for 5 years. He noted that it started small and gradually increased in size. It was painless, with no history of trauma or swellings elsewhere. His past medical and surgical histories were unremarkable. 

On examination, there was a 10 × 5 cm soft, non-tender, non-reducible, mobile mass in the right axilla, extending to the lateral chest wall. The overlying skin was normal, and the mass transilluminated brilliantly. 

Routine laboratory investigations were within normal limits. Ultrasonography revealed a multicystic lesion with internal septations. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the right axilla showed a well-defined, multiloculated cystic lesion with five septations in the muscular plane, measuring approximately 15.8 × 7.1 × 4.8 cm, with a multi-fascial distribution extending to the right shoulder.

A 78-year-old man presented with a pigmented lesion over the left nipple and areola, associated with itching and a burning sensation for 4 months and noted gradual enlargement. He denied any exposure to radiation, arsenic, tar, prior burns, surgery, trauma, nipple disease, or a personal or family history of skin cancer. On examination, there was a pigmented macular lesion confined to the left nipple–areola complex and no palpable lymphadenopathy; no other skin lesions were observed. Mammography and breast ultrasound were unremarkable.

A 53-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with a 2-month history of progressive dyspnoea, nonproductive cough, fevers, night sweats, anorexia, nausea, and fatigue. He was a 30 pack-year former smoker. Initial evaluation at a local hospital revealed:

– Vital signs: on Bilevel Positive Airway Pressure for respiratory distress; oxygenation improved transiently.  
– Physical examination: clear lungs, normal heart sounds, no jugular venous distention, no peripheral oedema.  
– ECG: sinus tachycardia with non-specific ST–T changes.  
– Chest radiograph: mild pulmonary oedema.  
– Laboratory studies: WBC 6 300 cells/μL, haemoglobin 13.3 g/dL, platelets 226 000/μL, creatinine 1.2 mg/dL; arterial blood gas on BiPAP showed pH 7.44, PaCO₂ 30 mmHg, PaO₂ 145 mmHg.  
– Treated empirically for pneumonia with ceftriaxone and azithromycin.

His respiratory status worsened over the following days. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed mild RV enlargement and an estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 65 mmHg. A CT pulmonary angiogram demonstrated multifocal pulmonary infiltrates and small pleural effusions but no pulmonary embolism; the main pulmonary artery measured 25 mm in diameter. Broad-spectrum antimicrobials were administered without clinical improvement.

He then developed acute liver injury (AST 450 U/L, ALT 302 U/L, total bilirubin 20 mg/dL), encephalopathy, oliguric renal insufficiency (creatinine 1.9 mg/dL), microcytic anaemia (haemoglobin 9.7 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (platelets 101 000/μL), and an elevated lactate dehydrogenase level of 756 U/L. He was transferred to the intensive care unit for further management.

On arrival to the ICU: afebrile, heart rate 124 b.p.m., blood pressure 124/79 mmHg, O₂ saturation 85% on 5 L nasal cannula. He appeared ill, with temporal wasting, scleral icterus, and confusion. Pulmonary examination revealed coarse anterior rales and tachypnoea with accessory-muscle use. Cardiac examination showed a jugular venous pressure of 10 cm H₂O, a prominent P₂, and a soft holosystolic murmur at the right sternal border. He had hepatomegaly without ascites or splenomegaly.

Investigations in the ICU included:  
– ECG: incomplete right bundle-branch block with right axis deviation.  
– Echocardiogram: severe RV dilation (5.3 cm annulus) with hypokinesis of the free wall and apex, septal flattening in systole and diastole, estimated RV systolic pressure 60 mmHg, mild tricuspid and mitral regurgitation, small pericardial effusion.  

Despite maximal supportive measures, his shock worsened.

A 50-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of right-sided otalgia, aural fullness, and hearing loss. He had no significant past medical history. Otoscopic examination revealed a rounded red mass completely filling the right external auditory canal, soft, non-tender, and non-friable on manipulation. Rinne’s test was negative on the right, and Weber’s test lateralized to the right, indicating right conductive hearing loss. Facial nerve function was normal bilaterally. Pure-tone audiometry confirmed a 40-dB air-bone gap in the right ear. High-resolution CT of the temporal bone showed opacification of the right middle ear cavity and external auditory canal; the auditory ossicles and facial canal were intact with no evidence of bony erosion. Six days later, he developed House-Brackmann grade II right facial palsy with mild forehead and oral asymmetry, prompting administration of intravenous steroids and planning of an urgent right ear exploration.

A previously healthy 14-year-old boy presented with a 2-month history of constipation and intermittent per rectal bleeding, accompanied by dull, non-specific lower abdominal discomfort. He had been diagnosed with subacute bowel obstruction at a peripheral hospital and managed conservatively before transfer. On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. Abdominal examination was unremarkable, and the perianal region appeared normal. Digital rectal examination revealed a firm, irregular mass approximately 3 cm above the anal verge without blood on the examining finger. Laboratory studies showed normal serum carcinoembryonic antigen and CA 19-9 levels. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen demonstrated circumferential thickening of the rectum without locoregional spread or distant metastases. Pelvic MRI confirmed a 5.7 cm long segment of rectal wall thickening 3.7 cm above the verge, with maximal thickness of 1.8 cm and effacement of the fat plane between the lesion and the urinary bladder, but no bladder muscle invasion. A well-targeted colonoscopic biopsy was obtained.

A 73-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis and celiac sprue presented with two weeks of right upper quadrant abdominal pain radiating to the back, associated with nausea without emesis. On examination she was hemodynamically stable; abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the right upper and left upper quadrants without rebound or guarding. Laboratory testing showed hyponatremia (Na 123 mmol/L), hypochloremia (Cl 88 mmol/L), and an elevated lactate dehydrogenase level (LDH 505 IU/L). 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated significant retroperitoneal inflammation and fat stranding at the level of the third and fourth portions of the duodenum and pancreatic head, abutting the superior mesenteric artery and vein. An upper GI series with KUB showed a small collection of contrast at the junction of the fourth portion of the duodenum and the ligament of Treitz, findings overall suspicious for a sealed duodenal perforation. The patient was managed non-operatively with bowel rest, intravenous antibiotics, and proton-pump inhibitors, and was discharged in stable condition after a repeat CT confirmed a contained duodenal perforation.

She returned the next day with severe left upper quadrant pain. Repeat CT showed relatively stable phlegmonous changes centered within the mesentery adjacent to the third and fourth portions of the duodenum, involving the head and body of the pancreas and encasing the superior mesenteric vessels, without evidence of vascular thrombosis. Scattered reactive mesenteric lymph nodes were noted without discrete masses. Given her marked pain and diffuse tenderness, the decision was made to proceed with an urgent exploratory laparotomy.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of severe occipital and temporal headaches that were paroxysmal, aggravated by changes in position, and associated with bilateral blurry vision and morning projectile vomiting. Neurological examination showed a kinetic and static cerebellar syndrome with ataxia, imbalance, uncoordinated movements, bilateral nystagmus, and stage I bilateral papilledema. Routine blood tests were unremarkable.

Noncontrast CT of the head showed no abnormalities. Brain MRI revealed an inferior median oval lesion of the cerebellar vermis measuring 40 × 31 × 29 mm, hypointense on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with heterogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. The lesion filled the foramen of Magendie, exerted mass effect on the medulla, and showed no surrounding edema on FLAIR. Diffusion-weighted imaging demonstrated increased signal, and GRE T2* sequences showed no hemorrhage or calcification. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy showed an elevated choline peak and reduced N-acetyl aspartate signal.

A 56-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with one day of severe right lower-quadrant abdominal pain. Six months earlier she had sustained blunt abdominal trauma. Since then she had experienced intermittent mild to moderate right-sided abdominal and groin pain radiating to the right leg nightly. Her medical history was notable only for hepatitis B; she reported no bleeding disorders.

On examination, she was afebrile, and vital signs were stable. Abdominal examination showed tenderness in the right lower quadrant without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. An abdominal ultrasound revealed a mass in the right iliac fossa. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 7.6 × 11.0 cm heterogeneous mass in the right iliac fossa displacing the uterus, bladder, and rectum, with appearance suggestive of retroperitoneal hematoma; there was no contrast extravasation.

The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy. A well-circumscribed 8 × 10 cm mass composed of old blood clots was removed from the retroperitoneum. Histologic examination showed blood clots admixed with fragments of a high-grade malignant mesenchymal tumor, with small to medium-sized atypical cells, light nuclei, eosinophilic nucleoli, and frequent mitoses. Immunohistochemical staining revealed strong CD117 positivity, moderate plasmin positivity, and negative staining for DOG1, CD31, CD34, smooth muscle actin, S100P, EMA, and other markers, suggesting a malignant gastrointestinal stromal tumor.

A 19-year-old woman presented with excessive gingival display on the right side when smiling. She first noticed a firm, non-tender swelling of the gums around the upper right canine-premolar region at age 15 that had slowly enlarged. She had no significant medical, family, or psychosocial history. Panoramic radiography showed a mixed radiolucent–radiopaque lesion with a “ground-glass” appearance that blended into adjacent bone and loss of the lamina dura around the involved teeth. An incisional biopsy of the maxillary lesion demonstrated irregular trabeculae of mature bone containing osteocytes in lacunae and rimmed by osteoid within a cellular, vascular fibrous connective tissue, consistent with a hamartomatous fibro-osseous lesion.

A 28-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of progressive shortness of breath and swelling of her right arm. She had recently recovered from a severe upper respiratory tract infection and was taking oral contraceptives; her medical and family histories were otherwise unremarkable. On examination she was hemodynamically stable. Duplex ultrasonography of the right arm and axilla revealed a deep vein thrombosis in the right subclavian vein extending into the proximal internal jugular vein. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest confirmed a pulmonary embolus in the right lower lobe pulmonary artery and demonstrated a large right pleural effusion. Mediastinal and right supraclavicular lymph nodes were enlarged and lacked a normal fatty hilum. Pelvic MRI showed a heterogeneous 13.5-cm mass arising from the left ovary. Serum tumor markers revealed normal levels of human chorionic gonadotropin and alpha-fetoprotein, with a moderately elevated CA-125 of 368 U/mL (reference range, 0–35). She was treated with anticoagulation and placement of a prophylactic inferior vena cava filter.

A 75-year-old Caucasian man presented with a several-month history of recurrent left lower quadrant abdominal pain, weight loss, and progressive asthenia. He reported occasional diarrheic stools without visible blood. He had no significant medical history. On examination, he appeared pale and had tenderness in the left lower quadrant without palpable masses, ascites, or peripheral edema. Laboratory studies revealed mild iron deficiency anemia (hemoglobin 10.2 g/dl; serum iron 33 μg/dl) and an inflammatory syndrome (positive C-reactive protein; erythrocyte sedimentation rate 42 mm/h). 

In the prior month, he underwent upper endoscopy, which found no lesions, and two unsuccessful colonoscopy attempts that failed to pass the sigmoid colon. A barium enema demonstrated diverticulosis, and his symptoms were managed as diverticulitis with anti-diarrheics, spasmolytics, and a fluoroquinolone, yielding only partial and temporary relief. He was referred for further evaluation.

Colon capsule endoscopy (Pillcam Colon2) was performed, revealing multiple diverticula without surrounding mucosal inflammation and a submucosal mass approximately 3 cm in diameter in the sigmoid colon. Subsequent CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed multiple colonic diverticula and a 5 cm soft-tissue mass in the sigmoid colon with a necrotic center, increased sigmoid wall thickness, indistinct margins relative to the urinary bladder, and densification of the perisigmoid fat.

A 70-year-old woman presented after a syncopal episode with mild head trauma. She reported a two-year history of similar episodes (two to three per year) without seizures or other neurologic symptoms. On examination, she was alert (GCS 15), bradypsychic, with facial bruising but no focal motor or sensory deficits.  
Noncontrast head CT showed a rounded subcortical lesion in the left frontal lobe with extensive vasogenic edema, mass effect, rightward midline shift, and subfalcine herniation.  
Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain demonstrated a well-defined intra-axial left frontal lesion that was isointense on both T1- and T2-weighted images, showed homogeneous contrast enhancement, had no diffusion restriction, and was surrounded by extensive perilesional edema with midline shift.

A 28-year-old man with a history of migraine disorder presented with several months of pain and swelling in the right mastoid area, with a recent subjective enlargement of the mass and increased pain. Noncontrast CT of the head demonstrated a 3.0 × 3.0 × 1.1 cm hyperostotic lesion of the outer table of the right calvarium without intracranial extension or adjacent soft-tissue mass. Because of the new-onset pain and subjective growth of the lesion, surgical excision was planned, and MRI with and without contrast was obtained. MRI revealed a densely calcified mass measuring 3.6 × 1.5 × 3.0 cm involving the inferior squamosal portion of the right temporal bone, with low signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images, mild patchy internal enhancement, thickening of the inner table, and no soft-tissue component beyond the bone or dural involvement. A small amount of fluid was noted in the right mastoid air cells, and mucosal thickening was present in the right ethmoid air cells. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and free T4, were within normal limits.

A 32-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 2, presented with a 2-month history of vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal discomfort. She had undergone a laparoscopic uterine myomectomy with power morcellation 5 years earlier for an 8×7-cm uterine fibroid. She had no medication use and an unremarkable family history.

On examination, her uterus was enlarged to approximately 16-week size, and there was mild rebound tenderness over the left adnexa. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 151 g/L, red-cell count 4.72×10^12/L, and a serum CA-125 level of 553 U/mL. 

Transvaginal ultrasonography revealed an indeterminate left adnexal mass measuring 11×9.5 cm with normal Doppler flow. Pelvic MRI demonstrated multiple pelvic tumors closely attached to the uterus and peritoneum, the largest measuring 13 cm in maximum diameter, with no radiologic features suggestive of malignancy.

A 75-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of a swelling in the left submandibular region. He had sustained trauma to the lower jaw 2½ years earlier. On examination, there were two firm, nontender masses in the left submandibular area: an anterior 3×4-cm node that was immobile with ill-defined margins, and a posterior 3×3-cm node that was mobile and firm to hard. The overlying skin was normal. No other lymphadenopathy was detected in the axillary or inguinal regions; intraoral examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory tests, including complete blood count, blood chemistry, Mantoux test, and chest radiograph, were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography was normal. Ultrasonography of the submandibular region revealed two lymph nodes with internal echoes; the anterior node was fixed, the posterior node mobile, and there was no increased vascularity. The ultrasonographic findings were suggestive of chronic inflammatory pathology.

A 70-year-old Japanese man presented with a 9-month history of progressive swelling in the left parotid region. On examination, a soft, non-tender mass was palpable in the left parotid gland. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed an irregularly shaped, well-circumscribed mass with a low-density central area in the left parotid gland. The patient underwent partial parotidectomy under general anesthesia. Intraoperatively, a 3.0 × 2.0 cm soft, cystic mass was located deep in the parotid lobe, immediately beneath the buccal branch of the facial nerve; there was no facial nerve weakness postoperatively.  
Gross histologic examination demonstrated closely packed ductal structures in close contact with a unilocular cystic space, both components showing a double-layered arrangement. The luminal cells had eosinophilic cytoplasm, and the outer layer comprised basaloid cells with scant cytoplasm. Secondary stromal fibrosis was present, and no definitive fibrous capsule separating the lesion from surrounding parotid parenchyma or fat was identified. In areas of the lesion, diastase-resistant PAS-positive inclusions were observed on the luminal surfaces of the ducts, and a direct transitional zone was seen between native acinar units and the proliferating small ducts.

A 47-year-old woman, G5P1041, with regular menstrual cycles presented with hip pain. Her only surgical history was a cesarean section 13 years earlier. On pelvic examination, the uterus was anteverted and enlarged to approximately 18 weeks’ size, and a 5-cm left adnexal mass was palpable; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen and pelvis revealed an enlarged uterus with multiple myomas, a 3-cm complex right ovarian mass, a separate left adnexal mass, and a 7-cm complex solid mass anterior to the rectum; no lymphadenopathy was present. The serum CA-125 level was 88.8 Units/mL (normal < 38 Units/mL). Because of concerns for a peritoneal process, the patient was referred to gynecologic oncology for further management.

A 67-year-old man underwent colonoscopy after a positive fecal occult blood test and was found to have two distinct colorectal masses, one well-differentiated adenocarcinoma and one moderate-to-poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma. His serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) level was 15.1 ng/mL (normal for a healthy smoker < 5.5 ng/mL). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 1.0-cm left adrenal nodule and a 6-cm heterogeneous, ill-defined splenic mass. On portal venous phase images, the splenic lesion measured 42 Hounsfield units (HU) and was unchanged on 4-minute delayed images. A noncontrast CT later measured the lesion at 28 HU, suggesting mild enhancement. The adrenal nodule was subsequently characterized as a benign adenoma. Assuming metastatic colorectal cancer, systemic chemotherapy was initiated; the CEA level dropped to 0.9 ng/mL, and follow-up CT showed that the splenic mass remained stable in size.  
A fluorodeoxyglucose PET scan showed no abnormal uptake in the splenic lesion. Tc-99m–labeled red blood cell scintigraphy demonstrated a photopenic region in the spleen corresponding to the mass. MRI of the abdomen with gadolinium revealed a well-defined splenic lesion with heterogeneously high T2 and low T1 signal intensity and centripetal contrast fill-in on delayed images, but without complete homogeneous enhancement. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound showed a mildly hyperechoic splenic mass with peripheral vascular flow on Doppler. Immediately after intravenous microbubble contrast, straight vessels feeding the mass were seen, with heterogeneous early enhancement and early wash-out; the enhancement pattern was not typical for either a hemangioma or a lymphangioma.

A 60-year-old Asian man with a 120–pack-year smoking history presented with intermittent dry cough, hemoptysis, chest tightness, and dyspnea for 3 months. He denied fever, weakness, or weight loss. Two months before admission, he received a 2-week course of antibiotics without improvement. On presentation he was afebrile (36.5 °C), blood pressure 105/60 mmHg, pulse 65 beats/min, respiratory rate 19 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 92 % on room air. Arterial blood gas analysis showed PaCO₂ 43 mmHg, PaO₂ 66 mmHg, and SaO₂ 92 %. Chest auscultation revealed decreased breath sounds and fine crackles bilaterally, more prominent in the left lower lung. He had no evidence of suspicious pigmented lesions on skin, mucosa, or eyes. 

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, white blood cell count 10.46 × 10⁹/L (neutrophils 7.72 × 10⁹/L), and potassium 2.89 mmol/L. Metabolic panel was otherwise normal. Serum tumor markers (CEA, SCC, CYFRA21-1, NSE, AFP, CA19-9, CA72-4) were all normal. Tests for ANA, ANCA, thyroid function, ESR, T-SPOT, hepatitis, syphilis, and HIV were negative. Pulmonary function tests, including DLCO, were within normal limits. Fractional exhaled nitric oxide was 3.6 ppb.

Chest radiograph showed bilateral nodules with surrounding reticular fibrotic lesions. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed bilateral consolidations: a 28 × 24 mm nodule in the right upper lobe and a 33 × 43 mm subpleural mass in the left lower lobe, each surrounded by intralobular septal thickening and ground-glass opacity (“crazy-paving” pattern). Enlarged right hilar, mediastinal, and left axillary lymph nodes, bilateral pleural thickening, fibrotic changes, and small bilateral pleural effusions were also noted. A similar CT performed 2 months earlier demonstrated smaller nodules with the same surrounding paving pattern. 

He was treated empirically with cefoperazone/tazobactam and levofloxacin for presumed bacterial infection, without clinical or radiographic improvement.

A 12-year-old boy with a history of acute myeloid leukemia treated with chemotherapy and bone marrow transplantation 4 years earlier, now in complete remission, presented with a recently noted, hard, non-tender mass in his right thigh. Vital signs were normal. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right thigh demonstrated a 3.8×2.8 cm enhancing soft-tissue mass in the subcutaneous layer on the posteromedial aspect of the mid-thigh, suggestive of leukemic infiltration. The mass was excised; grossly it appeared irregular and tan-white with areas of sclerosis. Microscopic examination showed dense lymphoplasmacytic and histiocytic infiltration within sclerotic stroma involving deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue. Numerous dilated sinuses contained large histiocytes with engulfed intact lymphocytes (emperipolesis). Immunohistochemical staining revealed that these histiocytes were positive for CD68 and S100 protein, with no CD117- or CD34-positive atypical blastic cells identified. Up to 70 IgG4-positive plasma cells per high-power field were noted, and the IgG4/IgG ratio was 25% in the area with the most IgG4-positive cells.

A 10-year-old previously healthy girl presented with a 1-year history of recurrent occipital headaches. Physical and neurologic examinations were unremarkable. Noncontrast head CT showed a small, rounded, hyperdense lesion anterior to the pontomedullary junction. On MRI, the lesion appeared extra-axial and was mostly hyperintense on T1-weighted and T2/FLAIR images, showed facilitated diffusion, had no chemical-shift artifact, and did not enhance with gadolinium. A small intracystic nodule was low signal on T1, T2, and T2* sequences. The lesion measured 10 × 9 × 8 mm (280 mm3), with no surrounding edema and slight mass effect on the brainstem. A watch-and-wait approach was adopted.  
Two-year follow-up MRI showed progressive growth to 19 × 28 × 23 mm (5400 mm3), increased lobulation, and extension into the prebulbar and prepontine cisterns, with significant mass effect. The prepontine vasculature was displaced anteriorly but not encased. These findings prompted the decision to proceed with neurosurgical treatment.

A 10-year-old Ethiopian boy presented with a 10-day history of sudden-onset weakness of both lower extremities and new urinary and fecal incontinence. He also reported long-standing epigastric pain but denied fever, cough, trauma, or neurologic events. He had received all routine childhood vaccines except hepatitis B, as he was born one year before its introduction into the national schedule.

On examination, his temperature was 38.0 °C, pulse 115 beats/min, and he had a hard, tender hepatomegaly measuring 16 cm in span (10 cm below the right costal margin). Neurologic examination showed a sensory level at T10, 0/5 motor strength in both lower extremities, areflexia, and a hypotonic anal sphincter.

Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood count, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 25 mm/hr, alanine aminotransferase 160 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 136 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 761 U/L, and serum albumin 3.4 mg/dL. Renal function, electrolytes, coagulation profile, blood and urine cultures, HIV and hepatitis C serologies were unremarkable. Hepatitis B surface antigen was positive.

Thoracolumbar magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated collapse of the T9 vertebral body with T1 isointense and T2 heterogeneous hyperintense marrow signal, and an enhancing epidural and paravertebral soft-tissue mass from T7 to T11 causing marked spinal-cord compression.

A 21-year-old man of African descent presented with 6 months of progressive shortness of breath, awareness of heartbeats, easy fatigability, bilateral lower-limb swelling, and left-sided chest discomfort, worsening over the past 3 months. He had osteosarcoma of the left calcaneus diagnosed in 2004 by biopsy, treated with radiotherapy and chemotherapy, and declared cured after 5 years of surveillance. On examination, he had bilateral pedal edema, a grade 3 pansystolic murmur at the left sternal border (fourth intercostal space), hepatomegaly (liver span 17 cm), a positive fluid wave, and shifting dullness. Brain natriuretic peptide was elevated, and electrocardiography was abnormal. A chest radiograph showed cardiomegaly, increased interstitial pulmonary markings, and right pleural effusion. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed cardiomegaly with right atrial and right ventricular enlargement and a nonenhancing mass (5.99×5.59 cm) in the right ventricle; the aorta was normal. There was marked pericardial effusion without septations, right pleural effusion, hepatic congestion with ascites, and suspicious filling defects in the inferior vena cava. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a medium-echogenic mass in the right ventricle with rich blood flow, measuring 4.32×6.60 cm, occupying the right ventricular outflow tract and encroaching on the interventricular septum; left ventricular systolic function was preserved (ejection fraction 65%). An X-ray of the left calcaneus showed bone erosion. Pleural fluid cytology revealed benign epithelial cells in small clusters.

A 32-year-old Han Chinese man, a professional driver, presented with a 4-year history of a slowly enlarging pigmented lesion on the upper left lip vermilion. He first noticed a 1 cm × 0.5 cm macule, which progressively increased in size without symptoms. After 3 years, he noted brownish discoloration of the skin above the vermilion. He had no significant medical or family history, and he did not smoke or drink.

On examination, multiple pigmented papules of various sizes involved the vermilion of the upper left lip, with brownish skin discoloration extending from 0.5 cm medial to the left angle of the mouth to the left philtral ridge. The lip was slightly swollen. Intraorally, a 1.5 cm lesion extended from the labial frenum to 0.5 cm medial to the left angle of the mouth; it was non-tender, non-indurated, and exhibited focal ulcerations. No cervical lymphadenopathy or other skin lesions were found.

Results of a complete blood count, biochemical profile, and urinalysis were within normal limits. Chest radiography was unremarkable. A computed tomography scan of the head and neck was performed to assess local extent of the lesion and to evaluate regional lymph nodes.

A man in his 40s with no prior medical history presented with a one-year history of a painful, slowly enlarging swelling on the plantar surface of his left second toe. The pain was moderate, worsened by standing and walking, and he noted a pins-and-needles sensation and reduced range of motion of the second toe. He recalled a trauma to that foot more than a year earlier when a car ran over it, but no fracture was diagnosed at the time. He denied systemic symptoms.

On examination, there was a 3×3 cm firm, well-circumscribed mass over the plantar aspect of the second metatarsal head. The overlying skin was mobile and intact. Movement at the metatarsophalangeal joint of the second toe was limited, but perfusion and sensation were preserved. There was no erythema or tenderness.

Plain radiographs of the foot showed an ossified lesion with irregular margins related to the proximal phalanx of the second toe and a second smaller ossified lesion arising from the medial aspect of the second metatarsal head. Laboratory tests were unremarkable.

A CT scan demonstrated a well-defined, heavily calcified lesion attached to the cortex of the second proximal phalanx without medullary continuity and mild focal cortical thickening. It closely surrounded the flexor digitorum longus tendon.

MRI revealed a heavily calcified mass along the plantar aspect of the second proximal phalanx that elicited low signal intensity on all sequences, showed minimal enhancement, lacked a cartilage cap, and had no medullary involvement. The lesion encased the flexor tendon without invading it, and there was surrounding soft-tissue edema and fat stranding.

Based on the MRI appearance, the main diagnostic considerations for the lesion were bizarre parosteal osteochondromatous proliferation and heterotopic ossification.

A 54-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of insidious onset left knee pain and diffuse swelling. He had undergone analgesic therapy, therapeutic knee aspiration, and compression bandaging at multiple centers without relief. There was no history of trauma, locking sensation, fever, constitutional symptoms, or night pain. On examination, the left knee showed diffuse swelling and a positive patellar tap. Range of motion was 0° to 100° with pain on terminal flexion; ligamentous testing was unremarkable. Plain radiographs of the knee were normal. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 2.5×4.5×2.5 cm T2-hypointense lesion arising from the synovium in Hoffa’s fat pad, associated with a large joint effusion and synovial hypertrophy. Routine hematological, biochemical, and immunological studies were within normal limits. Differential diagnoses at this stage included loose body, synovial chondromatosis, hematoma, and localized pigmented villonodular synovitis.

An 82‐year‐old man presented with a 4–5-month history of progressive dysphagia and a 17-pound weight loss. He denied throat pain but noted voice changes, frequent nasal regurgitation of liquids, episodes of food sticking, and repeated coughing spells. After one severe coughing episode, he received an analgesic with transient improvement, yet his dysphagia worsened until even water provoked choking. He had no family history of cancer. 

Evaluation by upper endoscopy showed no esophageal lesions, but flexible laryngoscopy revealed a benign-appearing mass in the hypopharynx. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the neck demonstrated a 3.5-cm hyperdense mass originating from the left dorsal hypopharyngeal wall and a 1.7-cm lesion on the right posterior hypopharynx. 

A biopsy of the larger mass was interpreted as a benign fibroepithelial polyp. Because of persistent airway obstruction, the patient underwent a transoral robot-assisted pharyngectomy with removal of the mass, which was submitted for comprehensive pathologic evaluation.

A 13-year-old boy with no prior medical history presented with six months of progressive left knee pain. He denied any trauma or constitutional symptoms. On examination, there was a moderate left knee effusion with warmth but no erythema, tenderness along the medial joint line, and a decreased passive range of motion of 40° to 90°. Neurovascular examination was intact without lymphadenopathy or instability.

Computed tomography of the left knee showed a mixed radiolucent and sclerotic permeative lesion in the left posterior medial femoral epiphysis with cortical destruction and an associated suprapatellar effusion; the physis was intact. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an infiltrative process in the left distal medial femoral epiphysis, extending proximally along the posterior cortical surface, appearing hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on STIR and T2-weighted images.

The radiographic differential diagnosis included chondroblastoma, osteomyelitis, and eosinophilic granuloma. A metastatic workup with CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis; three-phase bone scintigraphy; and FDG-PET was unremarkable.

A 15-year-old Hispanic boy with no significant past medical history was found to have a scrotal nodule during a routine physical examination. He recalled the lesion had been present for 3–4 years, was nonpainful, and had shown no significant change in size. On examination, there was a firm, nodular lesion immediately beneath a yellowish, discolored area of scrotal skin; no other mucosal or cutaneous lesions were noted.

He underwent complete surgical enucleation of the lesion without complications. Grossly, the specimen was a 1.0 × 0.8 × 0.6 cm firm, nonencapsulated mass covered by loose fibrous tissue; on sectioning, it showed a whitish, homogeneous cut surface without hemorrhage or necrosis. Low-power histology demonstrated a poorly circumscribed nodular lesion that appeared completely excised. On higher-power hematoxylin and eosin staining, the lesion comprised polyhedral cells with abundant granular cytoplasm and small, uniform, dark nuclei arranged in nests and as single cells within fibrous connective tissue.

A 31-year-old man presented with asymptomatic skin lesions overlying his implanted cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) that had gradually developed over 4 years. He had Brugada syndrome diagnosed at age 27 after a cardiac arrest, and an ICD was placed without postimplant complications. He denied infection, allergic dermatitis, or repeated trauma at the device site. On examination, there was a solitary 13 × 5 cm brown, verrucous plaque directly over the left-chest ICD, with smaller satellite lesions on adjacent skin. The remainder of the skin, hair, nails, mucous membranes, and regional lymph nodes was normal, and review of systems was unremarkable. Complete blood count and renal and liver function tests were within normal limits. A punch biopsy of the lesion showed extensive hyperkeratosis, papillomatosis, and papillary dermal fibrosis.

A 27-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of right shoulder pain. The pain was initially dull, activity-related, and relieved intermittently by oral analgesics. Over the last 6 months, her pain progressively intensified, and she became a daily user of analgesics. She had no history of trauma, strenuous activity, or family history of masses.

On examination, there was no erythema or warmth over the right scapular area. Palpation revealed a tender, 2 × 2 cm mass over the scapula. Active range of motion of the shoulder was painful in all directions; passive motion was full. The neurologic examination was normal.

Laboratory studies were within normal limits: calcium 10.2 mg/dL, phosphorus 3 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 117 U/L, parathyroid hormone 30.5 pg/mL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 5 mm/h, and C-reactive protein 3.3 mg/L.

Plain radiographs of the right shoulder revealed a trabeculated, lucent, expansile lesion with cortical destruction in the body of the scapula, accompanied by an adjacent soft-tissue mass. CT confirmed an expansile lytic lesion in the scapular body extending to the coracoid process. MRI showed an infiltrative lesion with posterior cortical disruption and extension into posterior soft tissues; the coracoid process was involved. Whole-body bone scintigraphy demonstrated irregular increased tracer activity along the lateral border of the right scapula, suggestive of a primary bone lesion and less likely a malignant tumor.

A 61-year-old woman presented with several years of intermittent epigastric discomfort. Initial gastroscopy showed slight superficial mucosal erosion of the gastric antrum; testing for Helicobacter pylori was negative. Abdominal ultrasonography detected a mass in the upper abdomen. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a solitary, lobulated nodule measuring 29 × 27 mm above the neck of the pancreas, with a clear boundary, uniform density, and slow contrast enhancement; these radiologic features were interpreted as benign. The patient’s discomfort improved with a 2-week trial of omeprazole, and she deferred biopsy or surgery. Three months later, repeat CT showed slight growth of the nodule to 32 × 25 mm without other abnormalities. She remained afebrile, without weight loss; examination was unremarkable, and no superficial lymphadenopathy was present. Laboratory studies revealed mild hyperglycemia and hypertriglyceridemia; carcinoembryonic antigen, CA 19-9, CA 125, and CA 242 were normal, and immunologic panels were within normal limits. An endoscopic ultrasonography–guided biopsy of the nodule was performed, and histology showed suspicious adenocarcinoma cells.

A 32-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of a progressively enlarging, painful swelling of the left scrotum. He denied trauma, infection, or other tumors. On examination, the left hemiscrotum was markedly enlarged, and a firm 8.0 cm mass was palpable; the right scrotum and penis were normal. Serum tumor markers (CEA, AFP, PSA, β-HCG) and hormone levels were within normal limits. Scrotal ultrasound revealed a 7.7 × 6.7 × 4.8 cm hypoechoic mass in the left scrotum with well-defined borders. The lesion was extratesticular—compressing the left testis—and was attached to the scrotal wall by a thick pedicle containing visible blood vessels. Color Doppler ultrasonography showed minimal internal flow but abundant arterial signals within the pedicle and an associated hydrocele. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated an irregular solid mass with continuous significant enhancement and a thickened left testicular artery extending into the lesion, so “the possibility of a malignant lesion could not be excluded.”

A 45-year-old woman presented with a 24-hour history of 9–10 watery, nonbloody stools and intermittent vomiting. She denied fever, chills, prior similar episodes, nor medication or dietary changes. She reported mild abdominal discomfort, anorexia, and fatigue. Her medical history was notable only for a uterine leiomyoma resection; family history was noncontributory.

On examination she appeared dehydrated but alert; vital signs were within normal limits. The abdomen was soft and nontender with normal bowel sounds. Admission ECG showed sinus tachycardia and repolarization abnormalities.

Laboratory studies revealed: potassium 2.1 mEq/L, sodium 123 mEq/L, calcium 11.1 mg/dL, glucose 159 mg/dL, creatinine 4.2 mg/dL, and arterial pH 7.25 with bicarbonate 5.3 mmol/L. Abdominal radiographs were unremarkable; ultrasound showed gallbladder enlargement.

She was treated with intravenous fluids, potassium, antibiotics, and fasting, yet diarrhea persisted at 8–9 episodes per day. The diarrhea was classified as secretory based on high stool volume and nonresponse to fasting. Stool ova and parasite exams, cultures, and C. difficile toxin assays were negative. Serologic testing for salmonellosis, brucellosis, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV was negative. Thyroid-stimulating hormone and intact parathyroid hormone levels were normal. Inflammatory markers were not elevated. A 24-hour urine potassium excretion was low (7.2 mmol), confirming gastrointestinal potassium loss. After 7 days, serum potassium remained at 2.2 mEq/L.

An urgent contrast-enhanced MRI of the abdomen demonstrated a 63 × 51 mm lesion in the pancreatic tail with heterogeneous enhancement and central necrosis; there were no hepatic lesions or pathological lymphadenopathy.

A 47-year-old man presented with two painless masses on the plantar aspect of the lateral side of his right great toe. The larger proximal mass had been present for 5 years and measured approximately 13 cm × 8 cm; the smaller distal mass appeared 1 year prior and measured about 2.5 cm in diameter. Both masses had grown gradually and now affected his gait and prevented him from wearing shoes. Examination showed the masses to be globular, tense but soft, free from the skin and underlying tissues, and transilluminated positively. Application of pressure caused the distal mass to slip under the edge of the proximal mass and nearly reduce into it. There were no other masses or abnormal skin findings, neurovascular examination of the toe was normal, and inguinal lymph nodes were not enlarged. Plain radiographs of the foot revealed soft tissue shadows without bony involvement. MRI was not available.

A 40-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with painless palpable lesions in both testes. Initial scrotal ultrasound demonstrated small inconspicuous cystic lesions bilaterally. Serum alpha-fetoprotein was 2.5 ng/ml (normal <7.0) and beta-human chorionic gonadotropin was <0.1 IU/l (normal <2.6). Three months later, examination showed a distinctly palpable mass in the right testis. Repeat ultrasound revealed two hypoechoic intratesticular tumors suspicious for malignancy. The patient underwent right orchiectomy. On gross examination, two well-circumscribed bright-colored intratesticular masses, the larger measuring 3 cm, were identified; the remaining parenchyma appeared normal. Histologic examination of paraffin-embedded tissue showed a well-demarcated proliferation of spindle-shaped cells in an irregular storiform pattern with loosely admixed collagen fibers, bland nuclei, and very few mitoses, accompanied by focal dense infiltrates of lymphocytes and plasma cells and scattered ganglion-like cells. Adjacent seminiferous tubules were markedly atrophic with a Sertoli-only pattern; the epididymis showed moderate chronic inflammation with ductal cystic dilation. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated diffuse smooth muscle actin positivity; S100 was positive only in dendritic cells; desmin, CD34, Pankeratin MNF116, and EMA were negative. Among inflammatory cells, CD5-positive T lymphocytes outnumbered CD20-positive B lymphocytes; isolated CD30-positive activated cells were seen. PLAP staining was negative, excluding germ cell neoplasia in situ.

A 68-year-old man with a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia presented with a one-year history of chronic headaches, dizziness, gait imbalance, and incoordination. Three years earlier, a brain MRI had shown a cystic lesion in the right cerebellum; no follow-up was performed until recent imaging demonstrated interval enlargement. On examination, he had a positive Romberg sign, dysmetria on the left, mild right pronator drift, left V1–V2 hypoesthesia, and an abnormal tandem gait. A head CT and subsequent MRI of the brain revealed a right posterior fossa lesion with both solid and cystic components. Given the lesion’s size increase and the nonspecific radiologic appearance, the differential diagnosis included ependymoma, hemangioblastoma, and other cystic cerebellar lesions with CSF trapping. Surgical intervention was recommended to establish a definitive diagnosis and provide therapy.

A 9-year-old previously healthy boy presented with a 2-day history of right periocular swelling, foreign-body sensation, and watery discharge. He reported intermittent diplopia that had resolved by the time of evaluation. Two days prior, he had a single axillary fever of 39°C that spontaneously resolved. Initial treatment for presumed preseptal cellulitis with IV antibiotics at a rural hospital led to clinical worsening. 

On arrival at a tertiary pediatric center, his temperature was normal. Ophthalmic examination showed visual acuity 20/20 OU, mild right periocular edema, eyelid tenderness, decreased palpebral fissure height, and proptosis (Hertel OD 19 mm, OS 13 mm, base 97 mm). Posterior segment examination revealed slight nasal elevation of the right optic disc without vessel obscuration and mild peripheral vessel tortuosity. Pupillary responses, intraocular pressures, color vision, extraocular movements, and visual fields were normal in both eyes.

Laboratory studies showed leukocytes 8.1 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 115 g/L, normal potassium and uric acid, and C-reactive protein elevated at 91.8 mg/L. A contrast CT scan of the head revealed an extracranial sphenoid wing mass with erosion of the temporal and sphenoid bones. MRI of the head demonstrated a 5.4 × 6.8 × 7.0 cm right-sided soft tissue mass centered on the sphenoid bone with extension into the right orbit, displacing the lateral rectus muscle and optic nerve, with low–intermediate T1 signal, mild T2 hyperintensity with foci of higher signal, and restricted diffusion. MRI of the spine showed multiple bilateral solid renal lesions and diffuse T2 hyperintensity and enhancement in vertebral bodies (L1 and S1), the left sacroiliac joint, and right iliac crest.

A 2-year-old girl was referred to the emergency department for bilateral optic‐nerve edema after her mother noted progressive deterioration in vision over the preceding week. Her past history included congenital left upper‐lid ptosis but was otherwise unremarkable. On admission, visual behavior was limited to fix-and-follow in both eyes. Pupils were equal, round, and reactive without anisocoria or afferent pupillary defect. The anterior segments were normal except for the existing 2 mm left upper‐lid ptosis. Dilated fundus examination revealed bilateral optic disc margin blurring, nerve‐head elevation, disc hemorrhages, dense peripapillary cotton‐wool spots, arterial narrowing, and retinal exudates including a macular star in the right eye. There was no proptosis, periorbital ecchymosis, or abnormal eye movements.

Review of systems was notable for five months of weight loss, decreased appetite, irritability, polydipsia, and polyuria. Physical examination disclosed cervical, auricular, and inguinal lymphadenopathy and a palpable left upper‐quadrant abdominal mass. MRI of the brain and orbits with contrast showed bilateral prominence of the optic discs and superior ophthalmic veins; there were no other signs of increased intracranial pressure (no empty sella, no perineural fluid distension, no optic-nerve tortuosity, and no flattening of the globes). Initial blood pressure was 104/76 mm Hg; during hospitalization, systolic pressures ranged from 140 to 208 mm Hg and diastolic pressures from 86 to 151 mm Hg. Echocardiography demonstrated mild left ventricular hypertrophy, mildly depressed systolic function, and mild to moderate coronary artery dilation.

A 5-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of rapid linear growth and penile enlargement over 3 months. His mother also noted pubic hair development, deepening of his voice, and adult body odor during that time. He denied headache, visual changes, or balance problems.

On examination, his height and weight were both above the 99th percentile, with a recorded height velocity of 16.25 cm/year (97th percentile for age). He had a muscular habitus, a deep voice, mature male facial features, a thin scrotum, and Tanner stage 3 pubic hair. The stretched penile length was 12 cm with a diameter of 2.5 cm. Testicular volumes were 2 mL on the left and 5 mL on the right.

Laboratory studies showed:
• β-hCG: 695 mIU/mL (reference 0–3)  
• 17-Hydroxyprogesterone: 633 ng/dL (0–90)  
• Estradiol: 81.3 pg/mL (0–20)  
• Total testosterone: >1500 ng/dL (after dilution, 2700; reference 0–19)  
• LH: <0.2 mIU/mL (undetectable)  
• FSH: <0.2 mIU/mL (undetectable)  
• Dehydroepiandrosterone: 62.8 µg/dL (18–194)  
• Alpha-fetoprotein: 6.9 ng/mL (0.0–9.0)

Bone age was advanced at 11 years 6 months, compared with a chronological age of 5 years 6 months.

An 8-year-old girl presented with a 2-week history of an atraumatic “bump” on her right cheek. Examination revealed a non-tender, firm nodule on the right zygomatic arch without overlying skin changes. Plain facial radiographs showed a sclerotic lesion with a central lucency in the right zygomatic bone. Non-contrast maxillofacial CT demonstrated a well-defined, round, expansile, soft-tissue–density lesion arising from the right zygomatic bone, measuring 1.7 × 1.6 × 1.6 cm, with variably thinned cortex, a narrow zone of transition, scalloping of the zygoma, and bulging into the orbit, but no cortical breach or adjacent soft-tissue invasion. Facial MRI with and without contrast showed a lobulated expansile lesion that was homogeneously hypo- to isointense relative to muscle on T1, showed avid peripheral enhancement with a central non-enhancing focus on postcontrast fat-suppressed T1, intermediate signal with a central curvilinear hyperintense focus on STIR, and heterogeneous DWI signal without restricted diffusion.

A 47-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension presented with progressive muscle weakness and weight gain. On examination, she had a rounded “moon face,” dorsocervical fat pad, and central obesity with thin extremities. Laboratory studies showed an elevated serum cortisol level of 489 nmol/L and an adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) concentration of 11.1 pmol/L (reference range, 2–11 pmol/L). Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary gland revealed a 5-mm nonenhancing nodule in the left adenohypophysis, suggestive of a microadenoma.

A 60‐year‐old tailor with no significant medical history presented with a 3‐year history of macerated skin between his toes. He complained of a painful, fissured ulcer at the base of the fourth interdigital space of the right foot, which had been progressively enlarging over the past 18 months. He had received multiple antifungal regimens—including topical sertaconazole for 6 weeks and oral terbinafine 250 mg daily for 6 weeks—without improvement. On examination, there was a verrucous, infected ulceration with infiltrated, hyperkeratotic edges and a whitish, fissured base measuring 3 cm in diameter, extending onto the dorsum of the foot. Dermoscopy revealed unstructured whitish areas and hyperkeratosis. Popliteal and inguinal lymph nodes were not palpable, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

A 54-year-old gravida 3, para 2 woman, 2 years postmenopausal, presented to the emergency department with severe right lower abdominal pain of sudden onset. She reported two months of postmenopausal uterine bleeding and three months of progressive abdominal distension. On examination, her vital signs were stable. Abdominal palpation revealed tenderness and signs consistent with an acute abdomen. Pelvic examination identified a right adnexal mass estimated at 15 cm in diameter. Initial laboratory testing showed a hemoglobin level of 11.7 g/dL, which fell by 1 g/dL over the next three hours. Transabdominal ultrasound and contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT confirmed a right adnexal mass measuring 13 × 12 × 8 cm with multiple septations, along with free fluid in Morrison’s pouch and the cul-de-sac. Because of the acute presentation and hemoglobin drop, an immediate exploratory laparotomy was planned.

A 54-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a painless, palpable lump in her right breast, noticed for one year. On examination, there was a soft, deep-seated mass measuring 4.5 × 4.0 cm in the upper inner quadrant, without skin changes, nipple discharge, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Her history included diabetes mellitus and nonobstructive coronary heart disease with a pacemaker. Mammography and ultrasound showed a well-marginated oval lesion measuring 4.1 × 2.9 × 2.7 cm at the same location, with an inhomogeneous isoechoic-hyperechoic signal, a small hypoechoic halo, and minimal peripheral vascularity (BI-RADS 4). A core-needle biopsy was performed. Histologically, the lesion consisted of short fascicles of bland fusiform cells in a patternless architecture around branching vascular spaces within a fibrous stroma with wispy collagen and scattered mast cells; the stroma contained mature adipose tissue without atypia or lipoblasts. No ductal epithelial component was observed. On immunohistochemistry, the tumor cells were negative for pancytokeratins (CKAE1/AE3, CK5/6, CK7, CK19), EMA, p63, SMA, desmin, and S100-P; they were strongly positive for vimentin, CD34, and nuclear STAT6.

A 61-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of right flank pain, dysuria, urinary urgency and frequency, and occasional hematuria, associated with fever, chills, and rigors. Over the preceding 3 months, he had a 40-pound weight loss, drenching night sweats, and intermittent low-grade fevers. His history was notable for nephrolithiasis treated conservatively 3 weeks earlier and multiple past episodes of renal colic treated with lithotripsy. He was a 30 pack-year smoker and drank alcohol occasionally.

On arrival, his blood pressure was 78/49 mmHg (MAP 59 mmHg), temperature 97.3°F, heart rate 80 beats/min, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 98–99% on room air. Hypotension did not improve after 3 L of normal saline. He was diagnosed with urosepsis and admitted to the ICU, where he received norepinephrine and broad-spectrum antibiotics.

Examination showed mild pallor, no icterus or edema, and right costovertebral angle tenderness. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL (MCV 77.6 fL), WBC 5.1 k/µL (77% neutrophils), alkaline phosphatase 212 U/L, ALT 80 U/L, AST 96 U/L, total protein 3.6 g/dL, albumin 1.5 g/dL. Urinalysis showed 1+ blood, protein 30, glucose 50; microscopy revealed 109 RBC and 12 WBC. A random cortisol level was 182.6 mg/dL. Two sets of blood and urine cultures remained negative after 5 days.

CT of the abdomen demonstrated numerous ill-defined hepatic lesions not present on a CT performed 3 weeks earlier, along with a staghorn calculus without obstruction or abscess. After two days of pressor support, his MAP rose above 70 mmHg, but he had recurrent hypotensive episodes requiring fluid boluses. On hospital day 5 he developed fluid overload treated with intravenous furosemide.

He declined liver biopsy and was discharged with oral levofloxacin. Three days later he returned with acute weakness, fatigue, and a single fever. His temperature was 94.1°F, blood pressure 84/49 mmHg (MAP 60 mmHg), heart rate 59/min, respiratory rate 18/min, and SpO2 97% on room air. Examination was unremarkable. Repeat blood and urine cultures again showed no growth, and he was restarted on vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam.

A 75-year-old man presented with a 3-week history of anorexia, abdominal fullness, and chills, and a 3-day history of jaundice. His medical history was notable only for AV nodal reentrant tachycardia treated six months earlier; he was taking diltiazem and aspirin, and liver tests were normal two months before admission. On examination he was afebrile, with scleral icterus and mild epigastric tenderness without hepatomegaly or ascites. Laboratory tests showed total bilirubin 9 mg/dL, albumin 4.0 g/dL, alkaline phosphatase 383 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 701 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 104 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 206 U/L, and lactate dehydrogenase 451 U/L. Carcinoembryonic antigen and alpha fetoprotein were normal; CA19-9 was 38.8 IU/mL. HIV and hepatitis panels were negative. A chest radiograph was unremarkable, and ECG showed sinus tachycardia. Abdominal ultrasound showed no gallstones or cholecystitis. Contrast-enhanced triple-phase CT of the abdomen revealed a 13×11×10 cm hepatic mass with small peripheral bile-duct dilatation and no common bile duct dilation. Initial differential diagnoses included liver abscess, metastases, atypical hepatocellular carcinoma, and hepatic cystadenocarcinoma.

A 53-year-old man with hypertension presented with a 1-year history of penile pain during erections, progressive curvature, and a sensation of a lump. He denied any trauma. A previous urologist had diagnosed Peyronie’s disease. On examination, there was a firm, 1.0 cm dorsal nodule at the root of the penis, not clearly attached to the tunica albuginea. Penile color Doppler ultrasonography revealed a well-defined, hypervascular, hypoechoic nodule in the dorsal corpora cavernosa, measuring 13×4×3 mm, without calcifications. Sagittal T2-weighted MRI confirmed a small dorsal corpus cavernosum nodule without evidence of additional lesions. No regional lymphadenopathy was noted.

A 55-year-old Chinese woman was referred after multiple pulmonary nodules were incidentally found on a health checkup. She was asymptomatic. Her medical history was notable for a total hysterectomy for uterine leiomyoma 14 years earlier. She was a lifelong non-smoker, with no family history of malignancy, no occupational exposures, and no recent weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory tests, including lung cancer tumor markers, were within normal limits.

High-resolution chest CT showed multiple well-circumscribed nodules in both lungs, the largest measuring 7 mm in the right lower lobe. To clarify the etiology, she underwent CT-guided percutaneous biopsy of the largest nodule, complicated by a small pneumothorax that resolved after aspiration. Cytologic smear revealed neither malignant cells nor organisms suggestive of tuberculosis.

Histologic evaluation of the biopsy showed a few spindle cells. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated Desmin(+) and SMA(+), consistent with smooth-muscle origin, and also showed Bcl-2(+), CD99(+), CD34(+), Vim(+), S-100(–), STAT-6(–), and CR(–).

Subsequent ^18F-FDG PET-CT revealed multiple pulmonary nodules with no FDG uptake and no abnormal uptake elsewhere.

A 28-year-old man with a history of acute myeloid leukemia (M4 subtype) treated successfully two years earlier presented with a two-month history of headaches and visual disturbances without seizures or vomiting. On examination, neurologic findings were normal. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed a 6.5 × 8 × 7 cm left intra-axial parieto-occipital mass that was isointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed homogeneous contrast enhancement with marked surrounding edema and midline shift. Preoperative differential diagnoses included brain lymphoma, glioma, and hematoma, but none of these were well correlated with his clinical, biological, or radiological characteristics. Because of mass effect and the risk of herniation, he underwent emergent left parieto-occipital craniotomy and gross total resection of the lesion.

A 37-year-old Caucasian woman, at 33 weeks of gestation (third pregnancy), presented with a 3-week history of progressive abdominal pain, distension, and alternating diarrhea and constipation. She had taken antibiotics for 4 days without relief. Her medical, family, and social history were unremarkable; she denied tobacco or drug use. On examination, vital signs were normal, Glasgow Coma Scale was 15/15, and she was moderately dehydrated with diffuse abdominal tenderness. Obstetric assessment was normal: uterine size and cervicometry were appropriate for gestational age, active fetal movements and a normal fetal heart rate were noted, and the placenta and amniotic fluid appeared unremarkable. Abdominal palpation revealed evidence of ascites and overdistension of intestinal loops, and a mobile 8–10 cm mass was palpated in the right abdomen.  
Abdominal ultrasound showed diffuse ascites around the liver, spleen, and pelvis; the liver was of normal echogenicity without focal lesions. In the right pelvis, multiple overdistended loops with reduced peristalsis, uneven echogenicity, and indistinct margins were noted within a large fluid collection.  
Laboratory studies revealed aspartate aminotransferase 236 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase 160 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 337 U/L, and lactate dehydrogenase 1171 IU/L; hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL, hematocrit 32.5%, white blood cell count 12,300/mcL with lymphopenia; fibrinogen was elevated at 948 mg%. Serologies for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were negative.  
Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated moderately overstretched jejunal loops with fluid and thickened wall segments on the left, and on the right, collapsed jejunal loops forming a conglomerate mass without clear planes of separation. There was thickening of the posterior peritoneum and irregular omental thickening delineating the intestinal mass, with displacement of the uterus to the left by mass effect.

A 65-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of intermittent epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and weight loss. Her medical history was notable for poor mobility, type II diabetes, and hypercholesterolemia. Eight years earlier, she had been admitted with Escherichia coli sepsis; an abdominal ultrasound at that time had incidentally shown a partially calcified gallbladder without signs of inflammation, and benign fatty changes in the liver. No intervention was pursued given her comorbidities.

On this admission, vital signs were within normal limits and general examination was unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed no organomegaly or palpable mass. Laboratory studies showed: ALT 45 U/L, ALP 775 U/L, total bilirubin 20 µmol/L, albumin 27 g/L, GGT 553 U/L, adjusted calcium 2.73 mmol/L, and a leukocyte count of 10.8×10^9/L. 

Ultrasound of the abdomen demonstrated a distended gallbladder with poor delineation of the posterior wall, appearing large, solid, and heterogeneous with posterior dense shadowing and calcific components. The common bile duct was normal in calibre, with no intrahepatic duct dilatation. There was also a large, ill-defined heterogeneous mass within the liver.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a 10-cm calcified gallbladder wall invading liver segments 4 and 5, enlarged coeliac, peri-pancreatic, and para-aortic lymph nodes, and multiple pulmonary nodules consistent with metastatic disease (T4 N1 M1).

A 26-year-old man presented with new-onset swelling and persistent pain (numeric rating scale 3/10) over the right superior orbital rim. He had a history of monostotic fibrous dysplasia of the right fronto-orbital region diagnosed at age 9, for which he underwent excision of dysplastic bone and reconstruction of the orbital roof with split autologous rib graft. He remained asymptomatic with stable appearance until the current symptoms began. 

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. There was localized tenderness and swelling at the right orbital rim without erythema or fluctuance. Laboratory studies, including inflammatory markers, were all within normal limits.

Noncontrast CT of the orbits revealed a newly appearing 2.3 cm low-attenuation cystic lesion adjacent to fibrodysplastic bone at the right superior orbital rim, with resorption of the previously reconstructed orbital roof. MRI demonstrated central diffusion restriction, T2 hyperintensity, an internal fluid–fluid level, and peripheral contrast enhancement of the lesion.

A 45-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of progressive swelling in the left cheek region. The mass gradually enlarged, resulting in facial asymmetry, significant pain, nasal obstruction, and impaired vision in the left eye. He reported difficulty chewing and discomfort on palpation over the area. His medical history was unremarkable.

On examination, there was a large (≈15 cm), firm, immobile, nontender swelling of the left maxillary region with mild overlying erythema. Intraoral inspection revealed slight displacement of the upper molar teeth without mucosal ulceration. No cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. Neurologically, cranial nerves were intact except for complete loss of vision in the left eye.

Facial CT showed a large, poorly circumscribed soft-tissue mass with irregular margins centered on the left maxillary sinus, with extensive infiltration into adjacent ethmoid and sphenoid sinuses and invasion of the orbital cavity. Marked osteolysis involved the bony structures of the left hemiface and skull base.

MRI demonstrated a poorly defined mass in the left maxillary sinus that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and exhibited diffusion restriction and heterogeneous enhancement postgadolinium. The lesion extended into the ethmoid–maxillary and sphenoid sinuses, encroached on the left nasal cavity, and showed aggressive osseous invasion into orbital structures.

A 64-year-old Caucasian man with a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia, recurrent prostatitis, and multiple negative transrectal ultrasound–guided prostate biopsies presented for evaluation of a persistently rising serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA). Over five years, his PSA had ranged from 8 to 10 ng/mL despite two 12-core biopsies and a 42-core saturation biopsy, all showing no malignancy. He reported 1–2 years of intermittent night sweats without fevers or chills. 

Multiparametric pelvic MRI was performed to evaluate his prostate and revealed suspicious intraprostatic lesions suitable for targeted biopsy, as well as left iliac chain and perivesical lymphadenopathy. MRI-ultrasound fusion–guided prostate biopsy yielded two cores of Gleason 3 + 3=6 prostate adenocarcinoma (5% involvement each) and was otherwise negative. Active surveillance was discussed.

To further characterize the pelvic lymphadenopathy, a ferumoxytol-enhanced MRI was obtained. This showed bilateral pelvic nodes with iron uptake but a left perivesical lymph node without significant uptake. Given the uncertain etiology and concern for malignancy versus other causes, an 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET-CT scan was performed, demonstrating only mild metabolic activity in the left perivesical node.

A 68-year-old woman presented with shortness of breath, fatigue, and abdominal symptoms, including nausea, vomiting, and poor appetite. She reported an unexplained weight loss of 5 kg over several months. Her surgical history was notable for a hysterectomy 20 years earlier and multiple incisional hernia repairs. On examination, she was alert and oriented, with normal vital signs, and her abdomen was distended. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin concentration of 6.5 g/dL (reference range, 12.0–15.5 g/dL) and a mean corpuscular volume of 72 fL (reference range, 80–100 fL); stool tests were positive for occult blood. Upper and lower endoscopic evaluations revealed chronic active gastritis with Helicobacter pylori infection, and she received triple therapy and iron supplementation. Despite treatment, her anemia and abdominal symptoms persisted. An abdominal radiograph demonstrated multiple air-fluid levels and dilated small-bowel loops, and magnetic resonance enterography showed dilated proximal loops with a 5-cm narrowed segment in the distal ileum with circumferential wall thickening, consistent with a stricture. Given her history of prior abdominal surgeries, adhesions were initially suspected as the cause of her chronic small-bowel obstruction.

A 65-year-old man was referred for evaluation of cervical lymphadenopathy detected during an ultrasound screening program. He was asymptomatic.  
Ultrasonography of the thyroid revealed an enlarged gland with homogeneous increased echogenicity and:  
  • A mixed polylobate isthmic nodule (13.5×7.3×14.2 mm) with peripheral vascularization (pattern 2).  
  • Two solid left-lobe nodules; the smaller measured 3.1×4.1×3.5 mm with irregular margins and internal and peripheral hyperechoic spots.  
According to ACR TIRADS 2017, the isthmic and larger left-lobe nodules were classified TR3; the smaller left-lobe nodule was TR4 (total score 5).  
In the left lateral cervical area (Level IV), ultrasound showed:  
  • A lymph node measuring 17.6×21.4×27.7 mm.  
  • Caudally, a block of nodes measuring 9.8×19.4×17.5 mm.  
Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration of the suspicious lymph nodes showed metastasis of carcinoma morphologically compatible with a differentiated thyroid tumor, while cytology of the TR4 left-lobe nodule was non-neoplastic (THY2).  
Medical history included hypertension (on a beta-blocker), gastroesophageal reflux disease (on omeprazole), mild COPD confirmed by spirometry, and a 30 pack-year smoking history. A chest radiograph was unremarkable.

A 7-year-old boy presented with a 10-day history of right lateral leg pain after a blow. He was afebrile, and there was no swelling, redness, or warmth. He had a limp and point tenderness over the middle third of the right fibula. His only notable history was periodontitis with fever 2 years earlier, treated with antibiotics. Laboratory studies, including a C-reactive protein level, were normal.

Ultrasound of the right leg showed a diaphyseal subperiosteal hematoma of the fibula with cortical irregularities. Radiographs revealed a pathological fracture through the proximal diaphysis at the upper end of a cortical lesion of mixed osteolytic and osteosclerotic character, with early callus formation. MRI demonstrated multifocal cortical osteolysis around a narrowed medullary canal, cortical thickening, and no soft-tissue mass. The surrounding soft tissues were hyperintense on T2-weighted images and enhanced after gadolinium administration.

Based on the patient’s age, mixed radiographic appearance, local inflammation, and a remote history of periodontitis, chronic osteomyelitis was initially suspected.
