A 35-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of rapidly progressive swelling of the left side of her scalp, followed by weakness of her right hand and, 30 days later, her right lower limb. Fifteen days before presentation, she had a simple partial seizure affecting her right upper limb. She was anemic but had no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. On examination, there was a tense, globular, fixed swelling over the left frontal scalp measuring 10 × 10 × 6 cm, with a 2-cm ulcer and surrounding inflammation; no cough impulse, pulsation, or bruising was seen. Laboratory studies were normal except for an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 60 mm/h and a hemoglobin level of 8 g/dL. 
 
Skull radiography showed a large bony erosion in the left frontoparietal region with overlying soft-tissue swelling. Contrast-enhanced CT of the brain revealed a solid lesion in the left frontal region with bone erosion and scalp involvement. Contrast MRI demonstrated a left frontosuperior extra-axial mass that was T1-isointense, T2-isointense to heterogeneous, with homogeneous enhancement and a dural tail. MR angiography showed a highly vascular tumor with a patent superior sagittal sinus. Workup for metastatic disease from the breast, thyroid, kidney, and lungs was negative.

A 67-year-old woman receiving inpatient chemotherapy for alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma noticed an enlarging, asymptomatic nodule on the right parietal aspect of her scalp, first observed 3 months earlier. Nine months before presentation, she had several months of sinus congestion, facial swelling, numbness, and pain that progressed to right-sided vision changes and occipital head and neck pain. MRI of the orbits demonstrated an enhancing mass centered in the right ethmoid air cells with extension into the right maxillary sinus, orbital apex, anterior and middle cranial fossae, and cavernous sinus. She underwent right maxillary antrostomy, ethmoidectomy, and sphenoidotomy; surgical pathology showed diffusely infiltrative small round cells positive for desmin, myoD1, and myogenin, with a PAX3-FOXO1 fusion, consistent with alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma. Staging CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was negative for metastatic disease. She then completed two cycles of alternating vincristine-cyclophosphamide-doxorubicin and ifosfamide-etoposide chemotherapy, followed by radiotherapy. MRI of the orbits one month ago revealed a 9 × 6 mm focus of abnormal enhancement and restricted diffusion in the right frontal scalp. On examination today, there is a 15 mm, mobile, erythematous nodule on the parietal aspect of the right scalp.

A 30-year-old man presented in 2000 with a several-week history of pain, swelling, and redness in the left third toe. On examination, the toe was tender and erythematous without ulceration. Radiographs showed a fracture at the base of the proximal phalanx underlying an intraosseous lesion with mixed lytic and sclerotic areas. MRI demonstrated bone-marrow edema in the proximal phalanx with minimal adjacent soft-tissue reaction and no extracortical extension. A biopsy revealed cortical and cancellous bone with reactive changes and damaged cells; the findings were interpreted as osteomyelitis, and his symptoms resolved without antibiotics. Follow-up radiographs four months later were normal, and he was discharged.

Eight years later, at age 38, he returned with a six-week history of recurrent pain and swelling of the same toe. Physical examination again showed swelling and tenderness without ulceration. Radiographs revealed a diffuse, moth-eaten lesion of the proximal phalanx with cortical destruction and surrounding soft-tissue swelling. Technetium-99m bone scintigraphy showed intense uptake only in the left third toe. A clinical diagnosis of osteomyelitis was made, and surgical resection of the proximal phalanx was planned.

A 41-year-old North African Caucasian woman presented with a 2-week history of right lower back pain without hematuria or urinary symptoms. She had no personal or family history of malignancy or tuberous sclerosis. On examination, her abdomen was soft and non-tender, with no palpable masses or lymphadenopathy. Routine biochemical studies were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a suspicious right renal mass. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed a 4.0 × 1.2 cm heterogeneous, exophytic mass arising from the inferior pole of the right kidney with a predominant fatty component and no calcifications, intratumoral necrosis, or aneurysm. A continuous tumoral thrombus extended from the right renal vein through the inferior vena cava to the right atrium. The left kidney appeared normal.

A 16-year-old girl was referred to the emergency unit for abdominal pain and distention. Her gynecologic history was unremarkable; menarche at 13 with regular menses. Family history: mother with diabetes mellitus.
Vital signs were within normal limits.
On physical examination, a relatively firm pelvic mass, likely of uterine origin, was palpated.
Laboratory tests showed mild anemia and a slight elevation of CA 125 (40 U/mL). A pregnancy test was negative.
Transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasonography revealed globular enlargement of the uterus with multiple hypoechoic or heterogeneous masses distorting the endometrial echo.
Contrast-enhanced multidetector CT of the abdomen demonstrated an enlarged uterus with a lobular, deformed contour extending to the level of the lower poles of the kidneys. Multiple heterogeneously enhancing uterine masses were seen without ascites, lymphadenopathy, or hydronephrosis.
Pelvic MR imaging showed an enlarged, posteriorly inclined uterus with innumerable intramural masses up to 13 cm in diameter. The masses were well circumscribed, low signal intensity on T2-weighted images, isointense to myometrium on T1-weighted images, and enhanced after contrast administration. Both ovaries appeared normal.
Imaging findings were diagnostic for a fibromatous uterus.

A 20-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of progressive, sustained pain in her left forearm, radiating to the fourth and fifth fingers, and a slowly enlarging bulge on the dorsal aspect of the lower forearm. Physical examination revealed a 1.5 × 1.5 cm firm, tender mass on the lower dorsal surface of the left forearm; the overlying skin was normal. The elbow had a full range of motion, wrist and forearm strength were 5/5 bilaterally, and sensory testing (light touch, temperature, crude touch, two-point discrimination) was normal in all digits. There were no signs of paresthesia or neurologic deficit. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, were within normal limits.

Plain radiographs of the left forearm (anteroposterior and lateral views) showed a well-defined, eccentric osteolytic lesion in the distal diaphysis of the ulna with cortical thinning and expansion but no cortical destruction, calcification, or marginal sclerosis. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-circumscribed, ovoid intramedullary lesion measuring approximately 2 × 1 cm in the distal ulnar diaphysis, exophytically protruding from the medial cortex. The lesion was low signal on T1-weighted images and high signal on T2-weighted and fat-saturated fast spin-echo T2-weighted sequences.

A 69-year-old man with a 7-year history of a painless ulcerative lesion in the perianal region presented with 2 months of upper abdominal pain and constipation, worsened over the past week. He had type 2 diabetes mellitus and no significant family history. On examination, there was a 3 cm × 2 cm irregular, non-tender ulcer between the 7- and 9-o’clock positions around the anus, with hard raised edges, hyperpigmented margins, and surrounding induration. Per-rectal and proctoscopic examinations were normal. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and basic chemistry panel, were within normal limits. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed Grade 1 reflux esophagitis. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a small gallbladder calculus without wall thickening. Flexible sigmoidoscopy was normal. A dermatologist was consulted, and differential diagnoses for the perianal ulcer included tuberculous ulcer, severe candidial erosive ulcer, Crohn’s disease, and fistula in ano.

A 50-year-old Asian Indian woman, menopausal for two years, presented with three to four months of postmenopausal bleeding. On per speculum examination, there was a 10×8-cm vascular, congested mass abutting the introitus. On bimanual examination, a polypoidal mass with a thick pedicle was felt protruding from the endocervix. Cervical polypectomy was performed, and histopathology showed a small round cell tumor. Despite removal of the polyp, the patient continued to have vaginal bleeding. Ultrasonography and magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen and pelvis revealed an irregular, infiltrative mass lesion involving the uterine corpus and cervix, without parametrial invasion or significant lymphadenopathy.

A 29‐year‐old primigravida was referred at 33 weeks of gestation after fetal ultrasonography detected fluid collection in the thoracic cavity. Fetal MRI showed a large cystic lesion with water‐density fluid, no solid component, in the anterior mediastinum surrounding the heart and great vessels, and compressing both lungs posteriorly. Fetal ultrasonography demonstrated a few internal septations within the cyst. Serial fetal echocardiography revealed a decline in cardiac output from 504 mL/kg/min at 33 weeks to 246 mL/kg/min at 36 weeks; mild pleural effusion and ascites were also noted. A multidisciplinary team planned delivery by Caesarian section at 37 weeks’ gestation with immediate postnatal airway management and ultrasound‐guided percutaneous drainage of the mediastinal fluid. The neonatology and surgical teams stood by in a single operating suite with equipment prepared for both drainage and, if needed, thoracotomy under ECMO. At 37 weeks and 2 days, a male infant was delivered; he was apneic and bradycardic, and while neonatal resuscitation was under way, two surgical teams performed ultrasound‐guided percutaneous tube placement in the left and right anterior axillary lines under local anesthesia at 2 and 6 minutes after birth, respectively, using 6-Fr Argyle™ Trocar Aspiration Kits.

A 24-year-old graduate dental student presented with a 1½-month history of pigmentation on the left buccal mucosa. He first noticed a 5 mm round brown area that had rapidly enlarged. There was no pain, but the surface texture was altered. He smoked one filtered cigarette daily for the past 4 years. 

Intraoral examination showed a carious tooth 28 and multiple class V glass ionomer cement restorations on teeth 36, 37, 38, 46, and 47. He reported undergoing these restorations 3 months earlier during which he sustained a mild bur injury to the left buccal mucosa that healed uneventfully.

Adjacent to the molar region, there was a well-demarcated brownish-black macular lesion on the left buccal mucosa. The lesion extended from the mandibular first molar to the left canine, measured 25 mm anteroposteriorly and 16 mm superoinferiorly, had regular borders, was non-tender, did not blanch on pressure, and was not fixed to underlying tissues.

A 40-year-old woman presented with multiple raised growths over both feet for four years. The lesions began on the soles and progressively involved the dorsum of both feet. They were neither painful nor pruritic. There was no history of trauma, irritant exposure, diabetes, or other systemic disease. On examination, symmetrical, well-defined, firm nodules coalescing into lobulated plaques were noted over the dorsum of both feet, extending from the bases of the 2nd through 5th toes to the midfoot. The overlying skin was non-pinchable, and the nails were normal. Routine blood counts and biochemical tests, including HIV and HBsAg, were within normal limits or negative. Radiographs of both feet showed no bony deformity, and ultrasound imaging revealed no significant soft tissue thickening. An elliptical biopsy of one lesion was performed for histopathologic examination.

A 73-year-old Asian man was referred after preoperative screening TTE revealed an intracardiac mass. He had presented 4 months earlier with bilateral knee pain and was diagnosed with osteoarthritis. He denied palpitations, dyspnoea, or constitutional symptoms. His medical and family histories were unremarkable.

On examination, vital signs were stable, and there were no cardiac murmurs or peripheral stigmata of endocarditis. Laboratory studies, including a coagulation panel, tumour markers, and immune serologies, were within normal limits. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm without ST-T changes.

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a 32 × 24 mm mass adherent to the left atrial septum: the basal portion was solid and isoechoic, and the apical portion was cystic and hypoechoic, with a jet of flow from the cyst toward the mitral valve.

Transoesophageal echocardiography confirmed a highly mobile, pedunculated “light-bulb” tumour. Colour Doppler imaging revealed feeding arteries entering the cyst from its base and twin drainage jets from the cyst toward the mitral valve, observed throughout all phases of the cardiac cycle.

Coronary angiography identified feeding arteries arising from the right coronary artery conus branch and the left circumflex artery; twin jets draining toward the mitral valve were again visualized.

Contrast CT and FDG–PET showed no evidence of extracardiac disease and only mild FDG uptake in the left atrial lesion (maximum SUV 2.4).

A 90-year-old woman presented with a 6-week history of progressively worsening dysphonia, inspiratory stridor, and left-sided otalgia. On examination, she had a firm 2×3 cm left level III neck mass without overlying skin changes. Flexible fiberoptic nasolaryngoscopy demonstrated a large exophytic supraglottic mass causing near-complete airway obstruction. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed a 3.3×3.7×3.1 cm mass involving the left supraglottic larynx, extending inferiorly to the glottis and laterally through the thyrohyoid membrane into the strap musculature. Eight years earlier, she had Stage IA mixed cellularity Hodgkin lymphoma of a left cervical node treated with 3500 cGy in 20 fractions. Her medical history included mild cognitive impairment and a prior hip fracture. An emergency awake tracheostomy was performed, and a biopsy of the mass was obtained.

A 43-year-old woman with an uneventful pregnancy was referred after failure to progress in the second stage of labor for 4 hours. Her medical and family history were unremarkable, with no known genetic disorders. Vital signs were within normal limits. Obstetric examination revealed a full-term uterus, longitudinal lie, cephalic presentation in occipitoposterior position, head fully engaged, fetal distress, and complete cervical dilation. An emergency cesarean section was performed, and a healthy 3.0-kg infant was delivered with Apgar scores of 8 and 9.

During the operation, a right ovarian mass was found incidentally. A right oophorectomy was performed. On gross examination, the mass was encapsulated, ovoid, gray-brown, and firm, measuring 11.9 × 7.0 × 3.8 cm. The cut surface was heterogeneous, fibrous, and yellow-tan in appearance, without cystic changes.

A 12-year-old previously healthy boy presented with 2 weeks of continuous headache, vomiting, and progressive bilateral visual impairment. He denied seizures, limb weakness, or altered consciousness. On examination he was alert with normal cognition. Visual acuity was reduced bilaterally. Cranial nerve testing revealed left facial paresis, left nasolabial fold loss, and tongue deviation to the right; other cranial nerves were intact. Motor strength was 5/5 throughout, with normal tone and no cerebellar or meningeal signs.

Brain MRI showed a heterogeneously enhancing space-occupying lesion in the pineal region. The patient underwent a midline suboccipital craniectomy and gross total excision of the pineal mass. The submitted specimen consisted of multiple gray-white fragments totaling 1.5 × 1 × 0.3 cm.

Microscopic examination demonstrated a highly cellular tumor with two components: sheets of small round cells with scant cytoplasm, elongated hyperchromatic nuclei, brisk mitoses, necrosis, and calcification; and foci of larger cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and multinucleated giant cells. On morphology, a pineal parenchymal tumor was initially favored, but areas of abundant cytoplasm and giant cells suggested rhabdomyoblastic differentiation, leading to consideration of a pineal anlage tumor and rhabdomyosarcoma.

A 53-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a tracheal mass incidentally found during routine health screening. He reported no respiratory or systemic symptoms. His medical history was unremarkable. Vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver and thyroid function tests, inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR), and urinalysis, were all normal. Electrocardiography and pulmonary function tests showed no abnormalities.

Chest radiography was normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a 1.4 × 1.3 × 1.2 cm mass on the right posterior wall of the mid trachea, approximately 3 cm above the carina, demonstrating contrast enhancement similar to adjacent blood vessels; there was no evidence of airway obstruction, lymphadenopathy, or other pulmonary parenchymal lesions.

Flexible bronchoscopy demonstrated a 1.5 cm polypoid endotracheal lesion with a hyperemic mucosal surface at the same location as the CT finding. Rigid bronchoscopic biopsy was performed under general anesthesia; significant bleeding occurred during the procedure and was controlled with topical epinephrine. Biopsy specimens were obtained for histologic analysis.

A 48-year-old woman presented with a painless mass in her left breast. On palpation, there was a relatively soft, 40 mm tumor in the upper inner quadrant; no axillary lymphadenopathy was noted.  
Mammography was normal (category 1) with no mass or calcification.  
Ultrasonography showed an irregular hypoechoic mass, 23 mm in diameter, with angular and indistinct margins, suggestive of malignancy.  
Contrast-enhanced whole-body CT revealed a 22 mm enhancing tumor in the left breast without axillary lymphadenopathy or other lesions.  
Breast MRI demonstrated a 37 mm irregular, heterogeneously enhancing mass with irregular margins; the lesion showed fast initial-phase enhancement and washout in the delayed phase, suggesting invasive ductal carcinoma such as scirrhous carcinoma.

An 81-year-old man was admitted with acute onset of abdominal pain. He reported loss of appetite and general weakness for several weeks without fever. His medical history was notable for stage IIIC ascending colon cancer treated by right hemicolectomy, partial duodenopancreatectomy, splenectomy, and adjuvant chemotherapy in 2006; he remained disease-free until March 2010. On examination, he had multiple purpura on the trunk and lower extremities and gum bleeding; there was no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL, white blood cell count 15 × 10^9/L (70% neutrophils, 15% lymphocytes, 9% monocytes, 4% eosinophils), and platelet count 11 × 10^9/L. Serum biochemical tests were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated massive ascites, diffuse peritoneal and omental thickening, and bowel wall thickening. Diagnostic paracentesis yielded turbid fluid with a white blood cell count of 52,210/mm^3, protein 2.6 g/dL, ascitic albumin 2.5 g/dL (serum albumin 3.5 g/dL), and a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 1.0 g/dL.

A 64-year-old right-handed woman presented with a 3-week history of progressive speech difficulty, initially mild and insidious but evolving to an inability to name objects or family members. She also reported unilateral fronto-temporal headaches, worse in the early morning and occasionally at night, gait unsteadiness, and episodes of urinary incontinence. There was no vomiting, seizures, visual disturbance, or other focal neurologic deficits. Her medical, surgical, family, and medication histories were unremarkable. 

On examination, she was alert and oriented but had anomic aphasia and agraphia. Pupils were equal and reactive. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal examinations were normal. On the right, there was hyperreflexia in both upper and lower extremities, a positive pronator drift, and motor strength of 4/5. The left side was normal.

Brain imaging with contrast-enhanced CT and MRI revealed a 4×4×4 cm extra-axial cystic lesion in the left fronto-temporal region. On MRI it was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, surrounded by vasogenic edema, and causing a midline shift.

A 68-year-old man was found on a routine health check to have an asymptomatic mass in the uncus of the pancreas. He had no history of chronic pancreatitis or other relevant medical conditions, and tumor markers (CEA, CA19-9) were within normal limits. Enhanced abdominal CT showed a well-demarcated 4.2 × 3.9 cm lesion comprising cystic areas of iso- to low-density surrounded by an area of extremely low density resembling adipose tissue. MRI and MRCP demonstrated multilocular cysts 1–several millimeters in diameter within the uncus; the main pancreatic duct was not dilated, and there was no communication between the lesion and the duct. On this basis, a benign tumor such as lipoma, dermoid cyst, or another rare benign cystic lesion was initially suspected. The patient developed a contrast allergy, so surveillance with plain CT and MRI was undertaken. Twenty-one months later, CT showed a slight decrease in overall size (3.9 × 3.6 cm) with smaller cysts and a larger solid component, and endoscopic ultrasound revealed a honeycomb-like appearance. At 28 months, plain CT showed an increase in size to 4.2 × 3.3 cm and MRCP revealed more and larger cysts without ductal invasion. On MRI at that time, the cystic component was low intensity on T1-weighted imaging, iso-intense on T2, and high on T2 fat-saturation, whereas the surrounding solid tissue was iso-intense on T1, iso- to high on T2, and suppressed on fat-saturated sequences—suggesting fluid-filled cysts enveloped by fat. Coronal T2 imaging showed ringed multilocular cysts with a smooth outer margin and a small internal nodule, findings that raised concern for malignant transformation of an intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm.

A 61-year-old woman with no prior thyroid disease noted a progressively enlarging right neck mass over 6 months. She was euthyroid and asymptomatic apart from local discomfort. Initial thyroid ultrasound showed a 32 mm right-lobe nodule (EU-TIRADS 4); fine-needle aspiration was nondiagnostic. Six weeks later, ultrasound revealed rapid growth to 46 mm and multiple cervical lymphadenopathies. Neck CT demonstrated a 4.6 cm right-lobe mass invading the strap muscles and abutting the carotid artery, displacing the trachea. PET–CT showed intense uptake in the thyroid mass but no other hypermetabolic lesions. A surgical core biopsy revealed sheets of pleomorphic and spindle-shaped cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm, blurred cell borders, small hyperchromatic nuclei, and up to 5 mitoses per high-power field; there was infiltration of adjacent striated muscle and no residual thyroid epithelium. Immunohistochemical stains showed the tumor cells to be negative for AE1–AE3, EMA, CK5/6, TTF1, PAX8, and thyroglobulin, but diffusely positive for MyoD1, desmin, and myogenin; Ki-67 was approximately 40 %. A focused NGS panel for BRAF, HRAS, NRAS, KRAS, and TP53 was negative.

A 57-year-old man with a history of hypertension presented with a 1-year history of vague right hypochondrial pain radiating posteriorly. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed lymphopenia, neutrophil predominance, and elevated C-reactive protein; tumor markers were normal; HIV, HHV-8, and Epstein–Barr virus tests were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a retroperitoneal nodular mass of approximately 4 cm. Contrast-enhanced CT scan demonstrated a 40 × 70 mm polylobate mass in the right perirenal space abutting the duodenum with a thin fat plane, intense early contrast enhancement that increased in the portal phase, and a vascular structure posterior to the mass. PET scan showed increased metabolic activity at the lesion site.

A 50-year-old woman presented with a rash that had gradually increased in extent over one year, confined to the chest wall and upper back. She denied systemic symptoms such as dyspnea, arthralgia, gastrointestinal complaints, or constitutional signs. On examination, there were multiple discrete reddish-brown macules and papules on the chest wall and upper back, along with telangiectasia and a positive Darier’s sign. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, renal function, and electrolytes; an elevated serum globulin level of 3.7 g/dL; serum protein electrophoresis revealing a gamma-globulin level of 1.83 g/dL without monoclonal gammopathy; and an IgG4 level of 148 mg/dL. Serologic testing for syphilis (VDRL and TPHA), HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C was negative. Antinuclear antibody testing was negative. A bone survey showed no lytic lesions. Bone marrow aspiration revealed a normal proportion of plasma cells, and karyotype was 46,XX. Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen demonstrated no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. A skin biopsy of a representative lesion showed superficial perivascular and periadnexal plasma cell infiltration with admixed small lymphocytes, and immunohistochemical staining confirmed CD38- and CD138-positive polyclonal plasma cells.

A 28-year-old woman presented with a palpable, painless lump in her left breast. Eight years earlier, a 1 cm nodule was biopsied elsewhere and deemed benign. During lactation for her second child, she noted growth of the lesion. She had no family history of breast or ovarian cancer and no significant past medical history. On examination, there was a well-circumscribed 2 × 1 cm mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast, 7 cm from the nipple, without skin changes, nipple discharge, or axillary lymphadenopathy.  
Bilateral mammography showed no significant findings. Breast ultrasound revealed an oval, hypoechoic mass with partially obscured anterior and lateral borders, internal heterogeneity, posterior echo enhancement, and poor blood flow. Contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated low T1 signal, uniform high T2 signal, and high diffusion-weighted signal; the lesion was categorized as BI-RADS 3.  
Fine-needle aspiration cytology showed small clumps of degenerated ductal cells, adipocytes, and stromal cells without evidence of malignancy. Core needle biopsy revealed proliferation of spindle cells with mild atypia in a fibrous stroma, arranged without a specific pattern; hypercellular areas showed bundled arrangements and some infiltration into surrounding fat in a storiform-like pattern. Immunohistochemical staining of the core biopsy showed tumor cells positive for CD34 and STAT6. We suspected a solitary fibrous tumor and planned an excisional biopsy.

A 71-year-old man presented to the emergency department with dyspnea and epigastric pain and reported non-specific abdominal symptoms. He had no known exposure to carcinogens. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory tests revealed elevated alanine and aspartate transaminase levels, thrombocytopenia, and anemia; α-fetoprotein was negative, and renal function was normal. An unenhanced thoracic CT performed to evaluate his dyspnea incidentally demonstrated hypoattenuating masses in both hepatic lobes on native and contrast-enhanced images, without a definitive diagnosis. He was referred for further evaluation with abdominal MRI. 

On T2-weighted HASTE images, multiple rounded hepatic lesions exhibited heterogeneous internal architecture and hyperintensity, the largest measuring 5.1 cm in segment VII. On T1 in- and out-of-phase images, the lesions had heterogeneous areas of high signal consistent with hemorrhage. Diffusion-weighted imaging (b = 800 s/mm²) showed marked hyperintensity of these lesions with corresponding low signal on the ADC map. 

Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted fat-suppressed VIBE sequences were obtained in the late arterial, portal venous, and parenchymal phases using a hepatocyte-specific agent. In the arterial phase, the lesions showed intense peripheral-to-central rim enhancement. During the portal venous phase, there was progressive, rapid enhancement. In the parenchymal phase, the lesions maintained homogeneous gadolinium uptake.

A 50-year-old woman with a history of papillary thyroid cancer treated by resection and radioactive iodine 10 years earlier, scleroderma, Raynaud syndrome, polymyositis, and pericarditis presented after new-onset seizures characterized by right arm jerking, drooling, and altered mentation. She was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and had an unremarkable neurologic examination. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, chemistry panel, urine drug screen, and urinalysis, were all normal. Noncontrast CT of the head showed multiple supratentorial and infratentorial hyperdense lesions up to 8 mm, the largest in the left parietal lobe, concerning for hemorrhagic metastases. Brain MRI with susceptibility-weighted imaging demonstrated numerous foci of signal dropout in the cerebral hemispheres, cerebellum, and brainstem. Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed peripheral enhancement of some lesions, with one left parietal lesion exhibiting surrounding vasogenic edema and internal hyperperfusion on cerebral blood volume perfusion imaging. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and inpatient colonoscopy showed no evidence of recurrent or metastatic disease.

A 72-year-old man presented with right calf pain and swelling that began while doing roof maintenance. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender 10 cm mass in the medial right calf without warmth, erythema, inguinal adenopathy, and distal neurovascular status was intact.  
Initial MRI of the right calf showed diffuse increased signal intensity in the medial gastrocnemius muscle with a central 3 cm area of abnormal signal, possibly due to contusion and muscle injury. A repeat MRI two months later demonstrated enlargement of the lesion to 11.5 × 6.0 × 8.5 cm, described as suspicious for sarcoma, with intact adjacent bone.  
A whole-body FDG-PET scan revealed intense uptake confined to the right gastrocnemius muscle, with no abnormal activity elsewhere.

A 58-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of a gradually enlarging swelling in the left anterior maxilla. He denied pain, numbness, dysphagia, weight loss, or systemic symptoms. Eighteen years earlier, a similar lesion in the same region had been excised and diagnosed histologically as an ossifying fibroma, after which he was asymptomatic until the current presentation. His medical history was otherwise noncontributory; he used smokeless tobacco for 20 years. 

On examination, he was well-nourished and afebrile. Extraorally, there was a subtle bulge elevating the left ala of the nose; no cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. Intraorally, there was a solitary, well-defined, oval, lobulated, pink, bony-hard, nontender swelling in the premaxillary region extending from the midline to the mesial aspect of tooth 26, obliterating the labial vestibule and extending onto the hard palate. A grayish-brown mucosal patch lay adjacent to the lesion.

Intraoral periapical and occlusal radiographs and a panoramic radiograph showed a roughly ovoid mixed radiopaque–radiolucent lesion measuring approximately 46 × 32 × 20 mm. Some margins exhibited a wide zone of transition blending with normal bone, while others were well defined with a thin radiolucent halo. The internal structure had ill-defined irregular radiopaque areas amid lytic regions, resembling a cotton-wool pattern, and a peripheral periosteal “sunray” appearance. 

CBCT demonstrated lobulation of the mass, thickening of the maxillary sinus membrane, anterior and rightward displacement of the nasopalatine canal, breach of the left nasal floor with mucosal thickening of the nasal cavity and antrum, and widening of the periodontal ligament space around tooth 26.

A 49-year-old man with lifelong congenital lymphoedema of the left lower extremity and a history of multiple erysipelas presented after two non-radical resections of a vascular tumour in his edematous limb that had been diagnosed as angiosarcoma. He had no adjuvant therapy and a PET/CT after the first resection showed no recurrence or metastasis, but local progression occurred one year later. After the second R1 resection, early relapse prompted referral.

On examination, there were purple papules at the edges of a dermo-epidermal mesh graft in the popliteal area, scattered ecchymoses on the left leg, and multiple small nonspecific purple lesions in the left gluteal region. PET/MR revealed multiple small subcutaneous nodules in the left gluteal area, calf, and hamstring, each with low metabolic activity. 

Excisional biopsy of a gluteal lesion showed a dermal cavernous vascular tumour with peripheral papillary protrusions containing hyalinized cores and covered by columnar endothelial cells with hobnail features. No mitoses or severe atypia were seen. Immunohistochemistry revealed diffuse positivity for CD31, ERG, and FLI-1; focal D2-40 positivity; and negativity for CD34, HHV-8, CK-KL1, and smooth muscle actin. 

A subsequent excision of two popliteal lesions and biopsies of calf and gluteal nodules demonstrated a dermal-based vascular tumour with a retiform arrangement of branching channels lined by bland hobnail endothelial cells, occasional papillary protrusions, absence of mitoses or atypia, diffuse CD31 positivity, CD34 negativity, low Ki-67 (~10%), and no lymphatic vessel association.

A 41-year-old Caucasian man was referred for evaluation of chronic and progressively worsening left nasal obstruction over the past year, accompanied by two episodes of self-limited left anterior epistaxis. He denied anticoagulant use, trauma, and other sinonasal symptoms. Vital signs were within normal limits. Anterior rhinoscopy and nasal endoscopy revealed an exophytic, multilobulated, well-defined mass obstructing the left nasal cavity. Contrast-enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses showed a polypoid, non-enhancing lesion in the anteromedial left nasal cavity measuring 31 mm × 15 mm. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Under general anesthesia, endoscopic resection with 1-cm margins was performed without complication.

A 7-year-old boy was admitted with a 3-day history of diffuse abdominal pain, subjective fever, and vomiting, followed by an inability to pass feces or gas. His medical history was notable only for orchiopexy two years earlier. On examination, he was pale but hemodynamically stable, afebrile, and had localized tenderness in the right iliac fossa without peritoneal signs.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 15.7 × 10^9/L with 84.9% neutrophils and a C-reactive protein level of 16 mg/L. Abdominal radiography suggested small-bowel intussusception, and ultrasonography confirmed the “target sign” of intussusception along with findings concerning for appendicitis.

The patient underwent laparotomy. Exploration revealed an ileo-ileal intussusception approximately 70 cm proximal to the ileocecal valve. After reduction, a segmental enlargement of the ileum with a focal depression in the mesentery was noted, and a firm, sessile intraluminal mass was palpated. The affected bowel segment and the appendix were resected.

A 27-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with severe right-sided abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and a fever of 40 °C. She had no significant medical or medication history and reported regular menstrual cycles without symptoms of steroid excess. Vital signs were otherwise normal. On examination, there was a tender, immobile mass in the right hypochondrium, with positive McBurney’s, Rovsing’s, and Murphy’s signs. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, neutrophils 73.1 %, prothrombin time 98 s, albumin 2.6 g/dL, and C-reactive protein 58 mg/dL. Other tests, including serum adrenocorticotropic hormone and adrenocortical hormones, were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a normal gallbladder and could not definitively characterize the mass or exclude appendicitis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a well-defined, hyperdense cyst measuring 12 × 10 cm in the right hypochondriac region, adherent to the head of the pancreas and adjacent to the inferior vena cava. The patient underwent an exploratory laparotomy. An inflamed appendix was resected, and surgical exploration revealed a large cyst in the anterior abdominal wall, which ruptured intraoperatively, releasing necrotic debris and resulting in significant bleeding. Hemostasis was achieved, and a specimen was obtained for pathologic evaluation.

A 63-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of left orbital swelling, ocular pain, and progressive globe displacement. Examination of the left eye revealed conjunctival chemosis, limitation of ocular motility, proptosis, lid edema, conjunctival injection, and vision loss. MRI of the orbits with contrast showed proptosis with thickening of the extraocular muscles and ipsilateral lacrimal gland, findings thought to be inflammatory in origin. Initial treatment with analgesics and high-dose methylprednisolone produced transient symptom relief, but headache, swelling, and pain recurred.  
Her medical history was significant for invasive lobular carcinoma of the right breast and invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast diagnosed 10 years earlier, treated with neoadjuvant therapy, bilateral mastectomy, adjuvant chemotherapy and radiotherapy, and 5 years of tamoxifen.

A 39-year-old Black man from South Africa, living in Doha, Qatar, noted a painless, slowly enlarging right lower thigh skin nodule over 3 months without trauma or functional limitation. Excisional biopsy of the lesion revealed a poorly differentiated tumor. Initial differential diagnosis included Merkel cell carcinoma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, squamous cell carcinoma, cutaneous alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma, and melanoma. He did not follow up until 3 months later, when he presented with a rapidly enlarging right inguinal mass. Biopsy of an inguinal lymph node again showed a poorly differentiated tumor, described as either malignant lymph node metastasis or lymphoma. Examination revealed healed scars at prior biopsy sites and no other palpable lymphadenopathy. PET-CT showed FDG-avid lymph nodes in the right inguinal, right external iliac, upper retroperitoneal, mediastinal, and left supraclavicular regions; axillary nodes had FDG uptake but negative biopsy results. Immunohistochemical analysis of the lymph node specimens demonstrated positivity for CK-20 and negativity for CK-7, TTF-1, and S-100. HIV testing was positive, and the patient was started on antiretroviral therapy.

A 29-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of intermittent right lower abdominal pain. She had no significant past medical history. On examination, her abdomen was soft without palpable masses. Laboratory tests showed a normal carcinoembryonic antigen level but elevated cancer antigen 19-9 and cancer antigen 125 levels. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed an 8.5-cm, well-defined, cystic mass with enhancing and septated components located posterior to the ascending colon. MRI demonstrated the lesion to be iso-intense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images. Incidentally, an 8-cm bi-cystic right ovarian mass and uterine fibroids were also noted. There was no evidence of local invasion or distant metastasis on imaging. Based on these findings, the preoperative differential diagnosis included neurogenic tumor, leiomyosarcoma, malignant fibrous histiocytoma, and other primary retroperitoneal tumors. She was scheduled for surgical exploration with a provisional diagnosis of an unknown retroperitoneal tumor alongside a benign right ovarian cyst and uterine fibroids.

A 60-year-old woman was referred with a 3-year history of complete bilateral nasal obstruction and 6 months of right-sided epiphora. She had a septal perforation from nasal cautery more than 30 years earlier, no other medical history, and was a non-smoker. On examination, her inferior turbinates were massively enlarged bilaterally, completely obstructing the nasal cavity, and there was a 2 cm anterior septal perforation. A biopsy performed elsewhere showed benign cartilage and reactive-looking bone. CT of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated hypertrophic bony change confined to the inferior and middle turbinates bilaterally, with a leftward deviated septum. The radiological features were suggestive of a benign enchondroma involving both inferior turbinates.

A 2.5-year-old neutered male Boxer (36.3 kg) was evaluated for a 2-day history of coughing, lethargy, and decreased appetite. Physical examination revealed increased bronchovesicular sounds; other findings were normal. CBC showed leukocytosis (26,100 cells/µl; ref 6000–17 000) with marked eosinophilia (14,090 cells/µl; ref 100–1000). Venous blood gas and remaining CBC values were unremarkable.

Thoracic radiographs showed a mixed pulmonary pattern: a consolidated alveolar pattern in the right caudal lung lobe with two soft tissue–opaque masses, and a multifocal unstructured interstitial pattern coalescing to patchy alveolar opacity in the left cranial and caudal lobes. Differentials included eosinophilic granuloma, parasitic or fungal pneumonia, or neoplasia. Bronchoalveolar lavage from three lobes was consistent with marked eosinophilic inflammation. Mycoplasma PCR and aerobic culture of lavage fluid were negative. A percutaneous transthoracic fine‐needle aspirate of the right caudal masses was inconclusive.

The dog was treated for presumptive eosinophilic bronchopneumopathy with fenbendazole, prednisone, and amoxicillin/clavulanic acid. One month later, minimal radiographic improvement prompted addition of cetirizine. Two months after presentation, repeat radiographs showed resolution of the right caudal masses but a new, well‐defined 4.3 cm diameter mass in the left caudal lung lobe. Thoracic CT confirmed a 6 × 6.5 × 6 cm contrast‐enhancing mass in the left caudal lobe, a 1.6 mm nodule in the same lobe, and tracheobronchial and cranial mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Lobectomy was recommended.

A 47-year-old man was referred for mechanical circulatory support for severe cardiogenic shock with multiorgan failure of unknown cause. One day earlier, he had undergone excision of a benign thyroglossal duct cyst, during which he experienced recurrent hypertensive episodes. After extubation, he developed profound hypotension and pulmonary oedema. Transthoracic echocardiography showed severely impaired left ventricular (LV) systolic function. Coronary angiography revealed no evidence of relevant coronary artery disease, and toxicological screening was negative. His medical history included chronic polyarthritis and treated arterial hypertension.

On transfer, he was invasively ventilated (PaO2/FiO2 30 mmHg), receiving norepinephrine at 2.5 µg/kg/min. Blood pressure was 75/49 mmHg, heart rate 180 b.p.m., with bilateral rales and basal dullness on chest percussion. He experienced pulseless electrical activity requiring 5 minutes of resuscitation. Bedside echocardiography demonstrated akinesia of all basal and mid LV segments with preserved apical contraction (left ventricular ejection fraction, 15%); right ventricular function was preserved (TAPSE 17 mm). On the basis of these findings, reverse takotsubo cardiomyopathy was suspected. A percutaneous LV assist device (Impella CP®) was implanted immediately. Endomyocardial biopsy revealed moderate chronically active myocarditis with diffuse interstitial remodelling, and PCR testing showed no evidence of acute or persistent myocardial infection.

A 32-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, was referred at 20 weeks’ gestation for evaluation of a fetal neck mass identified on routine ultrasound. Family history was unremarkable, with no consanguinity. Detailed ultrasonography showed a fetus consistent with 20 weeks’ gestation, estimated weight 372 g, and a left lateral neck mass measuring 49 × 38 mm, extending from the preauricular region to the left mandible. The lesion was hyperechoic and mainly solid, with a few cystic components. Destructive lesions were noted in the left mandible, maxilla, and sphenoid bone. The mass appeared to extend into the cranial cavity. The mother’s blood pressure remained within normal limits throughout pregnancy; she denied medication use, alcohol, or teratogenic exposures, and screening tests for fetal anomalies were normal.

A 48-year-old woman presented with lower abdominal pain and menorrhagia. Transvaginal ultrasound revealed multiple uterine myomas, and she underwent contrast-enhanced abdominal CT for preoperative evaluation. CT showed an approximately 14-cm multiseptated cystic mass with irregular enhancing septa in the right hepatic lobe. Gadoxetic acid–enhanced MRI demonstrated that the mass was T1-hypointense and T2-hyperintense, consistent with fluid, with some locules showing T1-hyperintensity and T2-hypointensity suggestive of hemorrhage. Irregular septa exhibited enhancement, but no solid enhancing nodules were identified. The patient had no symptoms referable to the liver lesion. Liver function tests and tumor markers (CA-125, CEA, AFP, CA 19-9) were within normal limits, and no metastases were detected on chest or abdominal CT. Based on these imaging features, a mucinous cystic neoplasm of the liver was suspected.

A 66-year-old woman presented with a slow-growing, painless left laterocervical mass. On examination, there was an elastic, mobile, well-demarcated, non-inflamed 5 × 3 × 2 cm mass in the left parotid region; facial nerve function was intact and there were no systemic symptoms. Contrast-enhanced MRI showed a large, polylobulated mass arising from the deep lobe of the left parotid gland, extending into the parapharyngeal and masticatory spaces. The lesion was isointense on T1-weighted images, mildly hyperintense on T2-weighted and STIR sequences with focal hypointense areas, and demonstrated early, strong, homogeneous enhancement on post-gadolinium T1 fat-saturated sequences.

The patient underwent total parotidectomy with excision of the parapharyngeal extension. Grossly, the specimen was a multinodular whitish mass measuring 5 × 3 × 2 cm. Histologically, there was a spindle-cell neoplasm with alternating hypercellular and collagenous areas and numerous thin-walled, tortuous vascular channels in a hemangiopericytoma-like pattern; mitotic activity was 2 per 10 high-power fields and there was no necrosis. Immunohistochemical stains showed diffuse positivity for CD34 and vimentin, focal positivity for EMA and Bcl-2, tenuous positivity for CD99, and negativity for cytokeratin, S100, HMB45, desmin, actin, CD117, and CD31. The Ki-67 proliferation index was 20–30%.

A 56-year-old Malaysian woman with a history of anemia presented with 1 month of bilateral lower extremity swelling, early satiety, and abdominal discomfort. She reported worsening edema when standing and had gained 10 pounds from fluid retention despite feeling thinner. She denied chest pain, dyspnea, alcohol or tobacco use, and had no significant family history. She was on oral iron and omeprazole; a colonoscopy 1 year earlier was normal. A positive H. pylori breath test led to triple therapy and an endoscopy at an outside hospital that was suggestive of a gastric mass.

On admission, temperature was 37°C, blood pressure 134/78 mmHg, pulse 79/min, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Cardiovascular examination revealed a grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur at the left lower sternal border. The abdomen was soft, non-tender, with normoactive bowel sounds. Both lower extremities had 2+ non-pitting edema to the thighs. No lymphadenopathy or skin rashes were noted.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL (MCV 71.2 fL), reticulocyte count 4.36%, ferritin 32 ng/mL, transferrin 403 μg/dL, transferrin saturation 3%, serum iron 13 μg/dL, platelets 519,000/μL, normal white-cell count, sodium 134 mmol/L, AST 122 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 478 U/L, and albumin 2.3 g/dL.

Electrocardiogram demonstrated T-wave inversions in leads V1–V4 and an S1Q3T3 pattern; troponin was negative. A duplex ultrasound of the lower extremities revealed no deep vein thrombosis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed severe intrahepatic narrowing of the inferior vena cava due to mass effect and an ill-defined 3.0×2.9 cm necrotic mass in the gastric antrum, with omental implants, nodular extension into the lesser sac, and a small amount of ascites.

A 4-year-old boy presented with a diffuse swelling of the left cheek and left upper lip since birth, which had gradually enlarged with his growth. There was no pain or bleeding. On examination, the lesion was diffuse, ill-defined, soft, non-compressible, and involved the left cheek and upper lip; overlying skin showed hyperpigmented spots, and no bruit was heard. Doppler ultrasonography revealed a vascular lesion with questionable communication to the left facial vein. Clinically, hemangioma and arteriovenous malformation were considered. Propranolol was initiated (up to 2 mg/kg), and three cycles of intralesional bleomycin were administered over 8 months, but the swelling persisted. Surgical exploration and debulking were then planned.

A 1-day-old boy was brought in with a large neck mass and difficulty breathing. He required urgent endotracheal intubation and was transferred to the neonatal intensive care unit. The mass had not been detected in utero, although gestational ultrasonography had noted polyhydramnios. The pregnancy was otherwise uncomplicated. 

On examination, a large, irregularly lobulated mass extended from the auricles to the clavicles bilaterally. Chest radiography, abdominal ultrasound, and echocardiography were unremarkable. Neck ultrasonography showed a mass with hypoechoic, cystic areas measuring approximately 80 × 55 mm in the middle and left side of the neck. 

A neck MRI revealed a well-defined, multiloculated complex mass with solid components of intermediate T1 and T2 signal intensity and cystic components of high T2 and low T1 signal intensity, displacing the esophagus and airway.

A 46-year-old man was referred after an incidental finding on ophthalmic examination. He reported photopsia and flashes in both eyes for several weeks. Visual acuity was 20/20 OU, and the anterior segments were unremarkable. Right-eye fundus examination was normal. Left-eye fundoscopy revealed a mid-peripheral temporal lesion approximately one disc diameter, partially hyperpigmented with a small surrounding area of exudation; there was no vitreous inflammation.  
Spectral-domain OCT of the macula showed no abnormalities. An OCT scan through the lesion demonstrated subretinal hyperreflective material, thickening of the retinal pigment epithelium, and a shallow serous neurosensory detachment. B-scan ultrasonography showed a flat detachment without evidence of prominence. Fundus autofluorescence revealed hyperautofluorescent areas corresponding to central hyperpigmentation and a surrounding hypoautofluorescent ring. Fluorescein angiography showed central hypofluorescence and peripheral hyperfluorescence with pinpoint leakage. Indocyanine green angiography demonstrated a hypofluorescent lesion without visible tumor vessels.  
History was notable for living on an animal farm with close contact with sheep and pigeons, several months of nasal corticosteroid use for sinus inflammation, and a history of light blunt trauma to the left eye years earlier. MRI of the brain, orbits, and chest was unremarkable. Laboratory evaluations for hepatitis B and C viruses, HIV, herpesviruses, tuberculosis, Lyme disease, syphilis, toxoplasmosis, rickettsiosis, Bartonella henselae, sarcoidosis, and lupus were negative.

A 42-year-old man presented with six weeks of suboccipital headaches that progressed to holocranial headaches, accompanied by a 10-kg weight loss, dizziness, unsteady gait, and behavioral changes. His medical history was notable for HIV infection diagnosed at age 35, treated with efavirenz, emtricitabine, and tenofovir disoproxil, with consistently undetectable viral loads. On examination, he was alert but exhibited truncal ataxia and dysmetria. Brain MRI with contrast showed an intra-axial mass in the midline posterior fossa, centered in the cerebellar vermis, measuring 48 × 40 × 35 mm. The lesion had two well-defined components: a predominant solid, hypervascular upper component and a lower cystic component that was T2-hyperintense and T1-hypointense. There was obstructive hydrocephalus with markedly enlarged lateral ventricles, obliteration of the cerebellopontine angle cisterns, and tonsillar herniation. Diffusion-weighted imaging and ADC mapping showed no diffusion restriction within the solid component, although prominent vascular flow voids were present.

A 33-year-old woman (gravida 5, para 3, abortus 1) at 19 weeks of gestation presented with 3 months of severe, progressive left shoulder pain radiating to the lateral arm and associated with restriction of movement. The pain was worse with motion and at night. There was no history of fever, weight loss, trauma, or local swelling, and no family history of malignancy. On examination, there was severe tenderness around the proximal humerus, with a markedly reduced range of motion but normal distal neurovascular status; no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Initial blood investigations, including complete blood count and inflammatory markers, were within normal limits. A single anteroposterior radiograph of the left shoulder showed an aggressive lytic lesion of the medial aspect of the surgical and anatomical neck of the proximal humerus with a wide zone of transition and cortical destruction. MRI of the left shoulder demonstrated a 5.3-cm marrow-replacing lesion extending from the anatomical neck to the proximal diaphysis, with multifocal cortical destruction and peri-osseous soft-tissue extension along the medial aspect (9 to 11 o’clock position); no skip lesions were seen. Noncontrast CT of the chest showed no metastatic lesions or other abnormalities.  
  
What is your differential diagnosis, and what would be your next step in evaluation?

An 18-year-old woman was transferred to our outpatient clinic after an appendectomy performed 3 months earlier for acute appendicitis. A preoperative CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis, obtained at that time, revealed three presacral masses. On axial images, a well-marginated 5.5-cm mass in the left retrorectal space extended into the ischiorectal fossa; it contained heterogeneous tissue, including fatty areas, fluid, and calcifications. On the right side, a 6-cm high-density mass lay in the retrorectal region, and a separate 3-cm nodule was identified inferior to it on coronal images. All three masses were individually encapsulated and contiguous, with no evidence of bone destruction or invasion of adjacent structures. On digital rectal examination, a non-tender posterior rectal mass was palpated. Routine laboratory values, including hCG, alpha-fetoprotein, CEA, CA 19-9, and CA 125, were within normal limits. No congenital anomalies were noted on clinical evaluation or imaging.

A 69-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of feculent vomiting. His past medical history included appendicular peritonitis, coronary bypass surgery, hypertension, chronic renal failure, hypercholesterolemia, and insulin-dependent diabetes. He reported nocturnal and diurnal vomiting without abdominal pain, along with months of eructation and burping; his appetite was preserved. On examination, vital signs were normal; the abdomen was soft and non-tender. Laboratory testing revealed a creatinine level of 1.8 mg/dL and a C-reactive protein level of 19.1 mg/L. Given his renal impairment, a non-contrast abdominal CT scan was performed, which demonstrated a distended stomach without duodenal or intestinal abnormality and an infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring > 3 cm in diameter. He was admitted for further evaluation, placed on nil per os with parenteral nutrition, intravenous fluids, high-dose proton-pump inhibitors, and nasogastric decompression. An upper gastrointestinal series revealed severe pyloric stenosis with absent gastric emptying. Gastroscopy was performed, during which the pyloric stenosis was traversed by the endoscope; no lesion or ulcer was visualized, and mucosal biopsies were obtained. Analysis of these biopsies suggested a well-differentiated duodenal adenocarcinoma. Endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle biopsy then yielded findings highly suggestive of an antro-pyloric adenocarcinoma. Additional biopsies analyzed at an external laboratory raised suspicion for infiltration of the gastric wall by a large intestinal adenocarcinoma. Serum tumor markers, including carcinoembryonic antigen and carbohydrate antigen 19-9, were within normal limits. A PET-CT scan showed a hypermetabolic mass confined to the pyloric region without evidence of metastatic disease, raising the possibility of either a primary gastric malignancy or a gastrointestinal stromal tumor.

A 40-year-old woman presented with a few months’ history of self-noticed cheek biting on the right side. On examination, there was an elevated, lobulated, whitish submucosal mass on the right buccal mucosa at the level of the occlusal plane, approximately 1.5 cm in radius, nontender, and mobile on bimanual palpation. No regional lymphadenopathy or other head and neck lesions were present. Neurologic examination of the oral and maxillofacial sensory and motor function was normal.

An excisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia. The lesion was removed with 0.5 cm margins, and the defect was reconstructed with a buccal fat pad. Grossly, the surgical specimen was a well-circumscribed, encapsulated mass measuring 2.0 × 2.0 × 1.5 cm, with a solid, homogeneous, reddish cut surface.

A 13-year-old Saudi girl presented with 6 months of right lower-quadrant abdominal pain without relief from multiple clinic visits. She had an appendectomy 2 years earlier, so appendicitis was not considered. Initial ultrasound examinations were unremarkable. A recent abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a mass in the right iliac fossa arising from the pelvis. On examination, there was no tenderness or palpable swelling in that region. Laboratory studies revealed normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate, complete blood count, and C-reactive protein. An anteroposterior radiograph of the pelvis showed no significant bony abnormalities. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis revealed a soft tissue mass along the right iliac bone, most likely a soft tissue sarcoma with focal bony involvement. Technetium-99m bone scintigraphy was negative for multifocal skeletal metastases and showed no local osseous invasion. Computed tomography of the thorax and abdomen showed no evidence of metastatic disease.

An 84-year-old Caucasian woman was referred for a second opinion on glaucoma management. She was asymptomatic and had no vision complaints. Her medical history was notable only for systemic hypertension; there was no history of trauma, intraocular inflammation, renal disease, or parathyroid disorder. She had undergone bilateral cataract surgery 4 years earlier and was pseudophakic in both eyes. Current medications included timolol 0.5% twice daily; intraocular pressure was 12 mm Hg in each eye. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes.

On dilated fundus examination, the optic discs had cup-to-disc ratios of 0.7 bilaterally. In each eye there was a well-demarcated, yellowish-white lesion located superotemporally, away from the macula, measuring approximately 8.5 mm × 5 mm × 2 mm in the right eye and 7 mm × 4 mm × 2 mm in the left eye. No choroidal neovascularization or subretinal hemorrhage was observed. Fundus autofluorescence showed corresponding hypoautofluorescent areas. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated a subtle elevation of the retina with slight retinal thinning and underlying choroidal thickening with some large choroidal vessels. Automated perimetry (24-2 SITA Standard) revealed a diffuse mild sensitivity reduction in the right eye and a superior arcuate defect in the left eye.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 5-year-old girl was admitted with fever (40 °C), dyspnea, and right-sided chest pain radiating to the right shoulder and arm. She had a history of recurrent pneumonia since 6 months of age, each episode treated with antibiotics. On examination, heart rate, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation were within normal limits. Respiratory examination revealed diminished breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the right lower lung field. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 22,100/mm3 with 74% neutrophils, a platelet count of 764,000/mm3, and hemoglobin of 10.4 mg/dL; electrolytes were normal. A chest radiograph demonstrated diffuse opacification in the middle and lower right lung zones. A contrast-enhanced CT scan showed alveolar consolidation of the right middle lobe consistent with pneumonia and, adjacent to this area, a fluid-density lesion abutting the heart suggestive of a cyst. The patient received broad-spectrum antibiotics but had no radiographic improvement. A follow-up contrast CT revealed a 5-cm cystic mass near the heart with calcified walls and decreased surrounding infiltrates. She was transferred for further management; antibiotics were adjusted, and the leading considerations were a hydatid cyst versus a lung abscess. Serologic testing for Echinococcus antibodies returned negative results, and surgery was planned.

A 37-year-old previously healthy white man presented with acute chest pain and dyspnea that markedly limited his exercise tolerance. He denied cough, infective symptoms, deep-vein thrombosis symptoms, syncope, or constitutional complaints. He had no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism and no identifiable risk factors. His medications were fluoxetine and promethazine; he was a nonsmoker, drank within recommended limits, and worked as a light technician.

On examination, temperature was 37.8 °C, oxygen saturation 92% on room air, respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, heart rate 120 beats/min, and blood pressure 132/84 mm Hg. He appeared pale but was alert; cardiac and pulmonary examinations were normal. Abdominal and neurologic examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 15 g/dL, white-cell count 16.9 × 10^9/L (neutrophils 15.3 × 10^9/L), lymphocytes 0.8 × 10^9/L, platelets 290 × 10^9/L, sodium 145 mmol/L, potassium 3.7 mmol/L, creatinine 105 µmol/L, and C-reactive protein 45 mg/L. Prothrombin time was 11.9 seconds, activated partial thromboplastin time 30.9 seconds, and troponin T level 374 ng/L. Arterial blood gas on room air revealed pO2 7.6 kPa, pCO2 7.6 kPa, and lactate 1.36 mmol/L. SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative.

Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia, right-axis deviation, ischemic changes in the anterior leads, and an S1Q3T3 pattern. He was treated empirically with subcutaneous tinzaparin and underwent CT pulmonary angiography, which confirmed a major pulmonary embolism with right-heart strain and pulmonary trunk dilation. Echocardiography confirmed right ventricular dilation and impaired function with mild tricuspid regurgitation.

To screen for occult malignancy, a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was performed. It demonstrated extensive thrombus extending from the left external iliac vein into the left common iliac vein and along the inferior vena cava to the level of the renal veins. Several prominent paraaortic lymph nodes were noted at the level of the renal veins, which were suggested to be reactive, and a small left pleural effusion was seen.

A 51-year-old woman, gravida 0, with a recent diagnosis of mucinous breast carcinoma, was referred for evaluation of a right pelvic mass. She had undergone a myomectomy 10 years earlier and was receiving treatment for hypertension. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed an 11.2 × 10.3 cm multiseptated cystic adnexal mass. During breast‐cancer staging, CT revealed a 12 cm abdominopelvic cystic tumor with a thick septum, located behind the bladder and anterior to the uterus. On pelvic MRI, the mass was slightly hypointense on T1 with gadolinium enhancement and markedly hyperintense on T2 with curvilinear dark signal, raising suspicion for borderline ovarian cancer. The patient was postmenopausal, asymptomatic, and on pelvic examination a firm, mobile, non-tender mass was palpated. Serum CA-125 and HE4 values corresponded to a low ROMA score for epithelial ovarian cancer. She underwent breast-conserving surgery with concurrent total laparoscopic hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. Intraoperatively, the multiseptated cystic tumor was found to be attached by a stalk to the anterior uterine body rather than the ovary. The mass was aspirated, resected, and sent for frozen biopsy, which reported a benign lesion.

A 29-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of progressive neck pain radiating to his left hand. The pain was described as electrical in nature and was associated with numbness in the C8–T1 dermatomes. Over the preceding week, he noted weakness in fine movements and a weak grip of the left hand. His medical and surgical history was unremarkable.

On examination, there was marked atrophy of the hypothenar and interosseous muscles of the left hand. Motor testing of the left hand revealed muscle strength of 3/5.

Preoperative computed tomography of the cervical spine showed marked osteolysis and collapse of the T1 vertebra, with an extensive paravertebral soft tissue component. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated that the lesion was intermediate to low signal on T1-weighted images, intermediate on T2-weighted images, and showed heterogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. The lesion involved the anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments but did not significantly compromise the thecal sac.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of a rash at the base of her left thumb. The lesion consisted of petechial patches with hyperpigmentation and lichenification, confined to the thumb without involvement of the trunk or proximal extremities. She denied pain, itching, systemic symptoms, and had no history of lymphadenopathy, environmental exposures, or significant comorbidities. Vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed only the localized thumb rash. Dermoscopic evaluation demonstrated fine, abbreviated linear vessels, dotted vascular structures, and orange-yellow patchy areas within the lesion. Routine blood tests, including complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, lactate dehydrogenase, and serologic assays for HTLV-1 and hepatitis B virus, were all within normal limits.

A 45-year-old Caucasian woman with stage IVB cervical cancer treated 8 months earlier with six courses of combined radiochemotherapy and brachytherapy presented with 5 months of progressive dysuria, pollakisuria, and lower-abdominal cramps. She had a 45 pack-year smoking history and remote history of cocaine and heroin use. Her surgical history included gastric banding, abdominoplasty, and recurrent breast abscess excision. On examination, vital signs were stable; pelvic examination was unremarkable. Urinalysis showed sterile leukocyturia. Cystoscopy revealed three small nonspecific mucosal lesions and one ulceration compatible with postradiation changes. To exclude cancer recurrence and investigate her symptoms, a CT scan of the thorax, abdominal wall, and pelvis was performed, which demonstrated multiple bilateral micronodular and cystic lung lesions and diffuse hypodense lesions in the liver. An ELISPOT assay for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, an HIV screening test, and ANA/ANCA testing were all negative.

A 35-year-old woman presented with one month of vague upper abdominal discomfort and mild nausea. She had three prior normal vaginal deliveries and was receiving medroxyprogesterone acetate injections every three months for contraception. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, liver biochemistry, inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), and serum tumor markers (α-fetoprotein, CEA, CA19-9, CA125), were all within normal limits. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed Los Angeles grade B reflux esophagitis. Abdominal ultrasound showed three hypoechoic subcapsular nodules in the right hepatic lobe, the largest measuring 25 mm, against otherwise normal parenchyma. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated two hypodense lesions of 10 mm and 12 mm in the anterior right lobe and one 25 mm lesion with relatively higher density in the posterior segment. To evaluate for a vascular lesion, red blood cell single-photon emission CT was performed to rule out hemangioma. An ultrasound-guided liver biopsy was then obtained for definitive diagnosis.

A 35-year-old man with no significant medical history and a ritual childhood circumcision presented with a left-sided penile mass first noted in 2019. Over the past 8 months, the lesion had gradually enlarged to approximately 2.5 cm × 1.8 cm and was associated with intense pruritus and discomfort during intercourse; there was no pain, discharge, or infection. He denied multiple sexual partners. On examination, the lesion was firm, mobile, non-tender, well-circumscribed, and superficial in the subcutaneous tissue of the middle third of the penile shaft. There was no erythema, ulceration, or inguinal lymphadenopathy, and the corpora cavernosa and spongiosum were freely palpable. Serological tests for HIV, HBV, HCV, VDRL, and TPHA were negative, excluding common infectious causes. At this stage, the differential diagnosis included epidermoid carcinoma, Bowen’s disease, adnexal tumor, leiomyoma, and cutaneous tuberculosis. A biopsy was necessary to confirm the diagnosis.

A 24-year-old man presented with inability to walk after a trivial fall. He reported one year of mild pain and swelling in the right knee. On examination, there was tense swelling and tenderness over the right patella; knee motion was painful and straight-leg raising was not possible. Radiographs of the right knee showed a transverse fracture through the patella with a lytic lesion occupying most of both halves of the patella; a thin sclerotic rim and fine matrix calcification were present, with no periosteal reaction. A chest radiograph was normal. Solitary bone cysts, aneurysmal bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and chondroblastoma were considered as clinicoradiological differential diagnoses. Fine-needle aspiration of the lesion revealed a few osteoclastic giant cells and occasional osteoblasts against a hemorrhagic background.

A 14-year-old boy was referred for a firm, painless swelling of the left cheek and palate. Extraoral examination showed left facial asymmetry with ill-defined jugal swelling, normal overlying skin, and hard, non-tender palpation. Intraorally, there was marked enlargement of the left hemipalate with intact mucosa, no tooth mobility, displacement, or abscess. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the face revealed a well-defined osteolytic lesion in the left maxilla bounded by a thin bony wall, predominately radiolucent with irregular central calcifications, extending into the left maxillary sinus. 

Under general anesthesia, an excisional biopsy was performed; the mass was cohesive, whitish, chondroid, and easily detached. Initial pathology suggested osteoblastoma. On re-examination, microscopic sections showed a lesion composed mainly of spindle cells without atypia (fibroblasts), separated from adjacent bone by large bony trabeculae set in a cellular fibrous stroma. Long, slender strands of osteoid were present within the stroma, with reactive bone lamellae bordered by non-atypical osteoblasts and multinucleated osteoclastic giant cells.

A 59-year-old woman with a family history of breast cancer presented with a 5-month history of a superficial lump in the left breast without nipple discharge. Her medical history included hypertension, dyslipidemia, and diabetes. On examination, there was a 3×3 cm raised polypoid lesion at the left periareolar region and palpable left axillary lymphadenopathy. Bilateral mammography showed a 3.7 cm circumscribed opacity in the left periareolar region. Ultrasound revealed a 3.3×3.0×0.9 cm oval hypoechoic mass at the same site along with enlarged axillary lymph nodes. A punch biopsy demonstrated an infiltrative carcinoma involving the dermis and epidermis. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for p63 and CK5/6 and negative for mammaglobin, estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and HER-2. Core biopsy confirmed nodal involvement, and CT imaging showed no distant metastases. These findings suggested a primary skin cancer rather than a breast carcinoma.

A 25-year-old man presented to the emergency department with acute abdominal pain that began that morning and progressed to severe intensity, unrelieved by analgesics. The pain was diffuse, most pronounced in the epigastrium. He had no past medical, surgical, or familial history and denied trauma or infection. On examination, blood pressure was 100/80 mm Hg, heart rate 110 beats/min, temperature and respiratory rate were normal. The abdomen was soft, non-tender, with no palpable mass; there was no nausea or vomiting. Examination of other systems was unremarkable. An erect abdominal radiograph was normal. Ultrasonography demonstrated a cystic mass in the pelvis; further imaging was unavailable. Laboratory tests, including serum amylase, were within normal limits. Because the cause of severe pain remained unclear, an exploratory laparotomy was performed. Intraoperatively, a large mass arising from the small-bowel mesentery approximately 50 cm distal to the ligament of Treitz was identified, compressing adjacent bowel but without volvulus or ischemia. The mass and involved intestinal segments were resected, and an end-to-end anastomosis was performed.

A 50-year-old woman, gravida 5 para 5, with no significant past medical history and regular menstrual cycles until the onset of perimenopause two years ago, presented with a four-month history of diffuse lower abdominal and pelvic pain. She noted a progressive, symmetrical increase in abdominal girth without urinary or gastrointestinal symptoms and denied any prior similar episodes.

On examination, abdominal palpation revealed a mass in the lower left quadrant. Pelvic examination showed a normal-sized uterus and a palpable mass in the left adnexal region; there was no vaginal bleeding or abnormal discharge.

Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a well-defined, hyperechoic tissue mass measuring 65 × 91 × 113 mm, apparently arising from the left ovary, with absent Doppler flow; the right ovary was unremarkable. Pelvic MRI showed a solid left ovarian mass (64 × 98 mm) abutting the right ovary, with T1 hypointensity, pronounced T2 hypointensity, internal cystic areas, and enhancement after gadolinium; moderate pelvic fluid was noted.

Preoperative laboratory evaluation revealed normal serum CA-125 and HE4 levels. The calculated ROMA score was 11%, suggesting a low probability of ovarian malignancy.

A 59-year-old man presented with acute urinary retention. He reported a 6-month history of chronic hypogastric pain, lower urinary tract symptoms, and constipation. On examination, the bladder was distended, requiring transurethral catheterization. Digital rectal examination revealed a bulging pelvic mass; the prostate itself was not palpable. Laboratory studies showed a serum creatinine of 123 μmol/L, leukocytosis, a normal prostate-specific antigen level, and a sterile urine culture. Contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT revealed a 13×10×9 cm multilocular heterogeneous cystic mass in the rectovesical and supravesical spaces, compressing the bladder and ureters, with bilateral upper-tract dilation; there were no nodular solid components or lymphadenopathy. Hydatic cyst was suspected, but hydatic serology was negative on two occasions. Urethrocystography demonstrated a 12-cm mass projecting over the bladder area. Pelvic MRI showed a 13×10 cm supra-rectal, retro-vesical multilocular cystic lesion of heterogeneous signal with fluid levels, areas of T1 hyperintensity and T2 hypointensity, and thin-walled septa mildly enhancing after gadolinium, findings “evoking a hemorrhagic cystic retro-peritoneal mesothelioma or cystic lymphangioma.”

A 3-year-old boy was noted at birth to have a right parotid region mass that grew slowly. At 4 months of age he underwent excision of the mass and surrounding parotid tissue; histology showed a well-circumscribed, soft yellow lesion composed of mature adipose tissue and normal salivary gland elements with clear margins. Four months later the mass recurred in the same site. On examination, there was a soft, non-tender, mobile, 10-cm mass in the right parotid and ipsilateral cervical region, with several small ipsilateral lymph nodes palpated. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a well-defined subcutaneous mass measuring 90 × 70 × 32 mm in intimate contact with the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland, showing fat attenuation (−108 HU) and nonenhancing septa.

A 60-year-old man presented with a 5-month history of a painless swelling on the right anterior palate. He had no significant medical history and took no medications. Intraoral examination revealed a non-ulcerated, red-purple, pedunculated mass approximately 2 cm in diameter arising from the gingival margin of the right anterior palatal region. The lesion extended from the distal aspect of the maxillary right lateral incisor to that of the maxillary right canine. Five years earlier, the right lateral incisor had been replaced with a dental implant. The patient’s oral hygiene was poor, and a 10-mm probing depth was recorded on the vestibular aspect of the implant. There was no tooth or implant mobility, and the patient reported no symptoms. A periapical radiograph showed a large radiolucent area involving the implant site and the adjacent tooth (tooth 1.3). Based on these findings, the diagnostic hypotheses of peri-implant infection, granuloma, and trauma reaction were carried out, and an excisional biopsy was planned with preservation of the implant.

A 55-year-old woman presented with an 8-month history of a gradually enlarging, painful swelling of the left eye and periorbital area, accompanied by progressive loss of vision over 6 months, culminating in no perception of light. There was no prior ocular disease, surgery, or family history of similar illness. Examination showed an intraorbital mass protruding from the left eye, axial proptosis with stretched sclera, dilated conjunctival vessels, and a hyperemic, keratinized conjunctiva covering the cornea.
