The mass was tender and soft; corneal and fundus examination of the left eye was not possible. The right eye was normal. Systemic, breast, and gynecological examinations were unremarkable. Hematologic, biochemical, and urine studies were within normal limits. Noncontrast CT of the orbits and paranasal sinuses revealed marked left proptosis with expansion of the globe by a hyperdense mass containing cystic components, destruction of the left orbital walls and sphenoid bone, and extension into the left anterior cranial fossa and adjacent sinuses. The radiologist’s provisional diagnoses included primary intraocular tumor, metastatic carcinoma, malignant melanoma, and lymphoma.

A 52-year-old man noted progressive swelling of the left preauricular area over the past year. He denied pain, facial weakness, or systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a non-ulcerated, non-exophytic, hyperemic, firm mass measuring approximately 7.0 × 2.3 cm extending from the left preauricular to mid-parotid region.  

In September 2021, soft-tissue ultrasonography of the left parotid showed a well-circumscribed, apparently capsulated lesion with a homogeneously hypoechogenic pattern, multiple septa of medium echogenicity, and mixed vascular signals on Doppler. Several reactive lymph nodes up to 1 cm were noted in peripolar parotid sites.  

A noncontrast CT scan of the facial skeleton confirmed marked enlargement and asymmetry of the left parotid gland with peri- and subcentimetric reactive lymph nodes in the left submental, submandibular, and laterocervical regions.  

An initial ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) yielded a blood-rich background and a monomorphic basaloid cell population in 3D solid groups with no metachromatic matrix or cribriform features, interpreted as a basaloid cell neoplasm or spindle cell myoepithelioma and classified as category IV-B (SUMP) by the Milan System.  

A repeat ultrasound-guided FNAC in October 2021 again demonstrated cohesive small basaloid cells with scant cytoplasm, confirming a category IV-B SUMP diagnosis.

A 53-year-old man underwent a routine endocrinology consultation after a neck ultrasound detected a small thyroid nodule. He was asymptomatic initially and advised to observe the nodule. Over time, the nodule grew and he developed neck discomfort and mild compressive symptoms. On re-evaluation, he was in good general condition. Examination revealed an enlarged left thyroid lobe extending toward the mediastinum; no cervical lymphadenopathy was palpable. Serum FT3, FT4, and TSH levels were normal.  
Neck ultrasound showed a normal right thyroid lobe and a markedly enlarged left lobe containing a large heterodense, vascularized nodule measuring 78 × 50 × 40 mm that extended caudally to the aortic arch. Two small left lateral cervical lymph nodes (11 × 5 mm and 7 × 3 mm) were noted.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and upper thorax demonstrated an 80 × 50 mm heterogeneous lesion arising from the left thyroid lobe, with its lower pole in the upper mediastinum displacing the trachea contralaterally and pushing the left brachiocephalic vein ventrally. A few borderline-sized pretracheal lymph nodes were visualized.  
Fibro-optic bronchoscopy was normal. A transcutaneous ultrasound-guided core-needle biopsy of the thyroid lesion showed poorly differentiated carcinoma.

A 63-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of productive cough and dyspnea. His medical history was notable for treated pulmonary tuberculosis and a 15–pack-year smoking history. He had multiple outpatient visits and received only symptomatic treatment until a chest radiograph showed mild mediastinal enlargement with a bulge along the right atrial contour, prompting hospital admission. On examination he was afebrile with normal vital signs, no peripheral edema, and a raised jugular venous pressure. Lung fields were clear. Cardiac auscultation revealed an ejection murmur. Hepatomegaly was present, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Baseline laboratory tests were within normal limits. Transthoracic echocardiography showed pericardial thickening with a small effusion and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60%. Contrast-enhanced thoracic CT revealed a soft-tissue–attenuation mass infiltrating the pericardium and anterior wall of the right atrium, along with multiple bilateral solid pulmonary nodules up to 2.6 cm in diameter. Cardiac MRI confirmed a heterogeneous mass diffusely involving the pericardium with invasion and compression of the right ventricular outflow tract, pulmonary artery, and superior vena cava.

A 25-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a painless, slowly growing gingival mass in the lower left anterior region that had increased in size over more than five years. She reported no medical history, medications, or genetic conditions. The lesion had caused adjacent tooth displacement, lip incompetence at rest, and changes in her facial proportions, leading to social embarrassment. Extraoral examination confirmed lip incompetence. Intraoral examination revealed an asymptomatic, mobile, pedunculated, irregular, rubbery, pinkish-red soft-tissue growth arising from the gingiva between teeth #32 and #33, extending from the alveolar mucosa and spanning teeth #34 through #42, with ulcerated mucosa at the site of occlusion and bleeding on palpation. Radiographic imaging demonstrated displacement of teeth #34–41, bone loss around these teeth, and a faint radiolucent area superimposed on normal bone. Blood tests showed a serum calcium level of 8.5 mg/dL and a parathyroid hormone level of 5.2 pmol/L.

What is your differential diagnosis?

A 12-year-old boy presented with a 6-month history of cough, recurrent pneumonia, and progressively worsening dyspnea. He had no significant past medical history. On examination, there was decreased air entry over the right lung field. A contrast-enhanced chest CT scan demonstrated a dense endobronchial lesion in the right lower lobar bronchus, surrounded by inflammatory changes and resulting in subtotal atelectasis of the right lower lobe.

A 68-year-old man with a 20-year history of hypertension and 10 years of chronic bronchitis presented with progressive dyspnea and intermittent headaches for 1 month. On examination, he appeared euvolemic and afebrile with a blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg. A firm, non-tender 7 × 6 cm mass was palpated in the anterior neck; there was no hoarseness or signs of thyrotoxicosis. Neurologic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed mild anemia (hemoglobin 124 g/L), elevated lactate dehydrogenase at 480 U/L (reference 15–240), and mild hyperbilirubinemia. Thyroid function tests, calcitonin, and thyroid antibodies were normal. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the head revealed a 1.5 cm slightly hyperdense nodule in the cerebellum with minimal mass effect. CT of the neck showed a markedly enlarged left thyroid lobe containing a 5.8 × 4.7 × 8.4 cm inhomogeneously enhancing mass with scattered calcifications and necrotic areas, displacing the trachea to the right. The right lobe contained a 1.3 × 1.2 cm nodule without calcification or significant enhancement. No cervical lymphadenopathy was seen. Thyroid ultrasound confirmed a giant hypoechoic mass with heterogeneous echotexture in the left lobe and a smaller solid nodule in the right lobe. 

Given the size of the lesion and tracheal compression, the patient underwent surgical resection of the thyroid masses for definitive diagnosis and relief of symptoms.

A 54-year-old Chinese man under active surveillance for clonal B-cell lymphocytosis of marginal zone origin (CBL-MZ) presented initially with livedo reticularis. Skin biopsy showed perivascular IgM deposition and fibrin thrombi; bone marrow biopsy identified a CD5– CD10– kappa-expressing B-cell clone, and serum IgM-k paraprotein was 3.9 g/L. CT of neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis was unremarkable.

Nine months after diagnosis, he experienced episodic nonpositional giddiness and transient visual darkening. Neurologic and ocular exams were normal; brain MRI demonstrated chronic subcortical infarcts, attributed to increased plasma viscosity. He was managed with aspirin.

Seven months later, he was admitted for daily 1-minute episodes of giddiness and visual blurring. He denied systemic symptoms; exam remained unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including lipid and glucose profiles, and hematologic parameters were unchanged. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI revealed multiple acute and subacute subcortical infarcts in a deep perforator distribution. MRA and CT angiography showed no large-vessel stenosis or occlusion.

A workup for stroke etiology was unremarkable: tests for antiphospholipid antibodies, protein C and S, antithrombin III, and prothrombin G20210A mutation were negative. Extended cardiac monitoring and transthoracic echocardiography were normal; transesophageal echocardiography revealed a 7-mm filamentous aortic-valve mass and a small patent foramen ovale without shunt. Transcranial Doppler ultrasonography detected no microembolic signals.

CSF analysis showed lymphocytic pleocytosis (19 WBC/µL) and elevated protein. Microbiologic studies (HSV-1/2 PCR, Gram stain and culture, fungal and AFB studies) were negative. Oligoclonal bands were absent; CSF cytology, flow cytometry, and MYD88 mutation analysis were negative.

His strokes were classified as cryptogenic, and he was started on antiplatelet and statin therapy.

A 39-year-old multiparous woman presented with a 10-month history of a painful umbilical mass. She reported that each month, one week before menstruation, she developed pain and slight swelling at the umbilicus; the discomfort persisted throughout her cycle. Two years earlier, she had been diagnosed clinically with endometriosis because of worsening dysmenorrhea. She had never undergone abdominal surgery. 

On abdominal-wall ultrasound, there was a 1.15 × 1.07 cm heterogeneous hypoechoic umbilical mass containing cystic areas and hyperechoic spots, with slightly indistinct margins, without invasion of the abdominal fascia or increased angiogenesis. 

Pelvic MRI demonstrated an umbilical lesion with low signal intensity areas on T1-weighted images, high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, and punctate hyperintense foci on T1 and fat-suppressed T1 images consistent with hemorrhage; the lesion showed subtle enhancement after gadolinium. MRI also revealed a right hematosalpinx, a left ovarian endometrioma, adenomyosis, and thickening of the uterosacral ligaments and torus uterinus.

A 51-year-old man with a 10–pack-year smoking history and no significant past illnesses presented with a one-month history of progressive exertional dyspnea and a dry cough. On examination, his vital signs were within normal limits, and pulse oximetry showed an oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. Chest auscultation revealed fine bibasilar crackles without wheezes. 

High-resolution CT of the chest demonstrated large-volume mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy and asymmetrical multilobar alveolar infiltrates. Pulmonary function testing showed a mixed ventilatory deficit: FEV1 2.39 L (69.6% predicted), FVC 3.76 L (88.7% predicted), FEV1/FVC ratio 0.64, total lung capacity 5.31 L (79.7% predicted), and DLCO 66.2% predicted.

A malignant etiology was first suspected, but bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage, transbronchial needle aspiration, CT-PET, bone marrow aspirate, and mediastinal lymph node biopsy failed to reveal malignancy or infection. Serum IgG4 was elevated at 8 g/L (normal 0.03–2.01 g/L), but surgical biopsy of lung and lymph node tissue showed no histological features of IgG4-related disease. Empiric treatment with high-dose glucocorticoids, methotrexate, and propranolol was initiated without clinical or radiographic improvement.

Because the patient’s condition progressed, a surgical wedge resection of the right middle lobe and MRI lymphangiography were performed, revealing focal organizing pneumonia and thoracic lymphatic dilatation. A subsequent CT-guided core biopsy of mediastinal tissue demonstrated immunohistochemical positivity for CD31, establishing the diagnosis.

A 29-year-old woman presented with a 12-day history of black, tarry stools and intermittent hematemesis, totaling one episode per day over the preceding 3 days, followed by altered sensorium for 1 day. She denied jaundice, abdominal distension, chronic alcohol use, or regular analgesic intake. She had received a depot medroxyprogesterone acetate injection 3 months earlier and initially reported no significant gynecological history. On examination, she was pale; blood pressure was 110/70 mm Hg, and pulse rate was 80 beats per minute. There was no supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. A neurologic examination was unremarkable. A provisional diagnosis of upper gastrointestinal bleeding secondary to peptic ulcer disease or gastritis was made, and laboratory tests were ordered. Laboratory results revealed a white-cell count of 15,000/mm3, platelet count of 137,000/mm3, sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 3.5 mmol/L, hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.1. Because the cause of her altered sensorium was not evident, a noncontrast CT scan of the head was performed, revealing a heterogeneously hyperdense mass with disproportionate perilesional edema in the left parietal lobe, suggestive of a hypervascular metastatic lesion.

A 47-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of chronic headache, mood depression, left-sided weakness, and two generalized tonic–clonic seizures. He had no significant past medical history. On examination, he was afebrile with normal vital signs, and neurologic examination revealed left hemiparesis. Noncontrast CT of the head showed a homogeneous, isodense right frontal brain mass without calcification or hyperostosis. Brain MRI demonstrated a right frontal lobe lesion that was hyperintense on coronal T1-weighted sequences and isointense on sagittal T2-weighted sequences, with significant mass effect, surrounding edema, and parenchymal invasion. Gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted images showed homogeneous enhancement of the lesion. With a presumed diagnosis of a high-grade primary brain tumor or metastasis, the patient was referred for neurosurgical evaluation.

A 28-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of a swelling on the posterior lingual aspect of the mandibular gingiva in the region of teeth 34–36. It had been asymptomatic, gradually increasing in size, and he noted occasional interference with tongue movement and occlusion. He denied any trauma or prior surgery at the site. Intraoral examination revealed a solitary, well-defined, ovoid swelling measuring approximately 3.5 cm × 2.5 cm on the lingual gingival aspect, firmly attached by a stalk, nontender, firm in consistency, and covered with pale yellowish mucosa without bleeding or ulceration. Mild dental stains and calculus were present. An occlusal radiograph showed an oblong soft-tissue density shadow on the lingual floor of the mouth at the 34–36 region, with no underlying bony changes but with two small radiopaque spicules emanating from the cortical bone.

A 53-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with several months of epigastric pain. He denied jaundice, anorexia, or weight loss. Physical examination findings were normal. Laboratory studies, including liver function tests, were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography showed no pathologic features. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen revealed a 5 × 4 cm solid–cystic lesion in the body and tail of the pancreas.

A 30-year-old woman with no prior hematologic, autoimmune, or endocrine history presented with several weeks of exertional dyspnea, fatigue, and near-syncope due to severe anemia, requiring ~15 RBC transfusions. She took no medications, had no recent viral illness, and had no family history of blood disorders. Examination revealed conjunctival pallor without hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy.

Initial laboratory studies showed:
- Hemoglobin 4.2 g/dL, MCV 106.8 fL  
- Reticulocyte count 0.8%, absolute retic count 19 × 10^9/L  
- WBC 4.03 × 10^9/L, platelets 213 × 10^9/L  
- Erythropoietin 1504 mIU/mL  
- Ferritin 324 ng/mL, CRP 6.97 mg/dL, ESR 69 mm/hr  
- Workup negative for hemolysis, autoimmune disease, nutritional deficiencies, and parvovirus B19

Peripheral smear: normocytic, normochromic RBCs without rouleaux or schistocytes; occasional plasmacytoid lymphocytes; normal platelets.  

Serum protein electrophoresis: M-spike 1.87 g/dL; immunofixation: IgG λ.  
IgG 2338 mg/L; κ free light chain 14.0 mg/L; λ free light chain 774.9 mg/L; κ/λ ratio 0.018; PET-FDG scan showed no hypermetabolic lesions.  

Bone marrow biopsy: 80% cellularity with virtually no erythroid islands; maturing myeloid cells; adequate megakaryocytes; no lymphoid aggregates. Aspirate: 7% atypical plasma cells, rare erythroid precursors. CD138 staining: 15% λ-restricted plasma cells; negative for CD56, CD117, BCL1. Cytogenetics: 46,XX; FISH unsuccessful. NGS: CREBBP S302N mutation (VAF 47.3%). Flow cytometry: ~0.9% monoclonal plasma cells (CD38+, CD138+, λ light chain), negative for CD19, CD117, CD28; polytypic B cells; CD4:CD8 ratio 1.2; myeloblasts ~0.8%.

A 44-year-old woman presented to the emergency department after multiple syncopal episodes, dyspnea, and progressive non-radiating right flank and epigastric pain. She reported a 3-week history of non-bloody emesis and chronic irregular menstrual bleeding. Her medical history was notable for obesity, hypothyroidism, and anemia treated with prior blood transfusions; she had undergone a cholecystectomy and one Caesarean section. On examination, she was hypotensive and dyspneic. The abdomen was soft, diffusely tender, and distended, with a large, ill-defined, firm, fixed mass palpable. Laboratory testing revealed a hemoglobin level of 4.9 g/dL, and she received three units of packed red blood cells. Due to ongoing hemodynamic instability and concern for intra-abdominal hemorrhage or gastrointestinal perforation, a non-contrast abdominal and pelvic CT scan was obtained, demonstrating a large hyperdense pelvic mass extending into the abdomen, diffuse hemoperitoneum, and possible capsular splenic rupture.

A 49-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of feeling a mass in his upper abdomen accompanied by mild tenderness, abdominal distention, 2–3 soft stools per day, and decreased appetite. In mid-May, he developed worsening abdominal pain and distention and was referred for further evaluation. His past medical history was unremarkable. On examination, there was a 70 × 80 mm mass in the upper abdomen and a 60 × 80 mm mass in the right lower abdomen; both had poorly defined borders and were tender. Routine laboratory studies showed elevated fibrin degradation products (139.2 μg/mL), D-dimer (>50 μg/mL), lactate dehydrogenase (782 U/L), procalcitonin (0.11 ng/mL), and CA 125 (124 KU/L).  
Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an irregular, well-demarcated 103 × 71 mm mass between the stomach and pancreas with heterogeneous T1/T2 signal intensity and uneven arterial enhancement; multiple nodules of varying sizes with similar enhancement were seen in the right abdominal wall, greater omentum, lower abdomen, and pelvis. MRI also revealed multiple liver lesions beneath the capsule, the largest measuring 73 × 55 mm, some protruding beyond the liver surface. Contrast-enhanced CT showed uneven enhancement of the abdominal mass without necrosis and mild to moderate heterogeneous enhancement of hepatic lesions; coronal reconstructions confirmed a lobulated mesenteric mass compressing adjacent bowel and bladder.  
Ultrasound-guided core biopsies of the upper abdominal and liver masses were performed. Hematoxylin and eosin staining showed sheets and nests of oval cells with abundant cytoplasm, eccentric nuclei, plasmacytoid morphology, and fine nuclear chromatin.

A 29-year-old man was referred for evaluation of an asymptomatic, slowly enlarging swelling in the anterior mandible of one year’s duration. His medical history was unremarkable. Extraoral examination was normal. Intraorally, there was vestibular expansion between the mandibular canines and a slight lingual bulge; the overlying mucosa was intact without inflammation. A panoramic radiograph showed a well-defined, unilocular radiolucent lesion extending bilaterally from canine to canine and reaching the mandibular base, with slight displacement of the left canine root. Based on the clinical and radiographic appearance, initial diagnostic hypotheses included central giant cell granuloma and ameloblastoma. An incisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia, and the patient was referred for CT scanning to delineate the lesion’s borders and its relationship to adjacent anatomic structures.

A 32-year-old woman was admitted to the emergency department with hemorrhagic shock. She reported a 5-month history of bilateral back pain without radiation. On examination, she appeared in poor general condition, with hypotension that required urgent fluid resuscitation and noticeable pallor. Abdominal palpation elicited painful, poorly defined masses bilaterally without hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. There were no signs of Cushing syndrome or lymphadenopathy. The evaluation for a primary neoplasm was negative. Laboratory studies showed normal plasma levels of adrenal hormones. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed bilateral adrenal masses. Noncontrast CT of the abdomen demonstrated hypodense masses measuring 7 cm on the right and 10 cm on the left, along with retroperitoneal lymph nodes measuring 10–20 mm. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed enlargement of these adrenal masses.

A 60-year-old man presented with a 5-year history of intermittent shortness of breath that had recently worsened and become persistent over several days. He denied dysphagia. On examination, he was tachypneic. An indirect laryngoscopic evaluation did not reveal any lesion in the oropharynx, supraglottis, glottis, or accessible subglottis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a 30.9×23.1 mm lobulated lesion with “popcorn-like” calcifications arising from the endolaryngeal surface of the posterior lamina of the cricoid cartilage, significantly narrowing the subglottic airway without evidence of invasion into adjacent structures. With these findings, an initial imaging impression of cricoid chondroma was made.

A 36-year-old unmarried Syrian woman presented with recurrent abdominal pain and slight weight loss. She was in good general condition and had no significant medical, surgical, or family history. On examination, there was a palpable mass around the umbilical region with mild tenderness. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a well-defined oval mass with mixed content posterior to the peritoneum, extending from behind the stomach wall to the anterior surface of the pancreas and measuring approximately 15×17×20 cm, with moderate to high turbid fluid in the abdomen and pelvis. The ultrasound differential diagnosis included a hematoma, a pancreatic pseudocyst, or a developmental lesion. The right kidney appeared atrophic, measured 4 cm in length, had irregular edges, diminished corticomedullary differentiation, and multiple coarse foci. The remainder of the abdomen and pelvis was unremarkable except for a small cystic cavity with clear content. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 20×16×10 cm mass occupying the left hypochondrium and lower epigastrium, crossing the midline to the right and compressing mesenteric vessels and intestinal loops. The mass was heterogeneous and necrotic with well-defined non-perfused edges, radiologically suggestive of sarcoma. There was a moderate amount of free fluid and a 48-mm homogeneous accessory cyst with a thin wall on the left side.

A 25-year-old obese African-American woman, gravida 1, who had delivered twins by cesarean section, was admitted one week after an otherwise uncomplicated delivery because she collapsed at home and was found unresponsive with bloody, frothy fluid at the mouth. Her social history was notable for tobacco and marijuana use. On arrival, she required intubation for respiratory distress; the initial clinical differential diagnosis included eclampsia and postpartum cardiomyopathy. Over the next 12 days, she remained ventilator-dependent with respiratory failure, developed systemic hypertension, had methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus cultured from tracheal secretions, leukocytosis, and recurrent asystole. She was treated empirically with gentamicin, ampicillin, clindamycin, phenytoin, enoxaparin, lorazepam, hydralazine, and morphine. Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) was attributed to an infectious source, and multiple antibiotics were administered. A transabdominal ultrasound examination showed heterogeneous, thickened, and irregular products in the endometrial canal. Laboratory studies revealed prolonged prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time, elevated ferritin levels, and a decreased hemoglobin concentration. Despite maximal supportive care, she died; the clinical cause of death was cited as ARDS.

A 46-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with a 6-month history of gross hematuria. She denied dysuria, frequency, fever, or weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable.
  
Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan showed a 6.8 cm exophytic mass arising from the anterior wall and dome of the urinary bladder, with invasion into the anterior abdominal wall.
  
Cystoscopy revealed mucosal erosion over the mass, and a bladder biopsy demonstrated enteric-type adenocarcinoma in the bladder wall, partially covered by urothelium with reactive changes.
  
To evaluate for a possible metastatic source, a thoracic CT scan and virtual colonoscopy were performed, which showed no distant metastases and no evidence of primary colonic neoplasm.

A 33-year-old healthy man presented with two subcutaneous nodules on his vertex scalp and the right postauricular neck. Both lesions had arisen in adolescence and had slowly increased in size; the scalp lesion had been excised several years earlier and had recently recurred, while the postauricular lesion had never been treated. Both nodules were asymptomatic, with no history of inflammation or fluid drainage. On examination, there was a 7-mm, firm, nontender, mobile subcutaneous nodule on the vertex scalp and a 9-mm, firm, nontender, partially mobile subcutaneous nodule on the right postauricular neck; neither lesion had an overlying punctum or any skin discoloration.

Under local anesthesia, both lesions were excised. The scalp specimen was firm, round, and pearly in color, consistent with a cyst. The postauricular specimen, in contrast, was irregularly shaped, inelastic, and yellow to violaceous in color.

A 46-year-old Caucasian man was referred for evaluation of fever, nonproductive cough, and dyspnea of two months’ duration. He had no significant past or family history and had smoked 1.75 pack-years before quitting. On examination, a left lateral cervical lymph node was palpable, and crackles were heard over the left lower lung field. Laboratory studies showed neutrophilic leukocytosis, a C-reactive protein level of 17.58 mg/dL, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 115 mm/h. Serum tumor markers including CEA, CA 19-9, CYFRA 21-1, and neuron-specific enolase were within normal limits. Chest radiography demonstrated an area of consolidation in the left mid-lower lung zone. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed an 8 mm smoothly enhancing intraluminal lesion in the left main bronchus at the origin of the lingular segmental bronchus, with atelectasis of the lingular segment and ground-glass opacities in the apicoposterior segment of the upper lobe. What is your differential diagnosis and next step in evaluation?

An 89-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a prolonged cough. His medical history included hypertension, a subdural hematoma, and lumbar canal stenosis; he denied any intraoral trauma. On oral and pharyngeal examination, the patient forcefully coughed and expectorated a small mass. He reported no awareness of the lesion before this event. The mass measured approximately 10 mm in diameter and was covered by normal-appearing mucosa. Fiberoptic examination of the oral cavity, pharynx, and larynx revealed only mild bleeding at the base of the tongue and no other abnormalities. Six months earlier, a cervical spine CT scan (performed for unrelated reasons) showed a well-defined, rounded, high-density mass with a tiny pedicle arising from the base of the tongue.

A 25-year-old woman presented with an 8-month history of right cheek swelling and right-sided nasal obstruction. Examination revealed a firm, non-tender intraoral swelling extending from the upper right central incisor to the second premolar; the right maxillary canine was absent, and the overlying mucosa was intact. Computed tomography of the maxilla showed a 6 cm × 5 cm unilocular lesion of the right maxillary sinus with expansion and thinning of the sinus walls and an unerupted canine near the mesial wall. Aspirated straw-colored fluid (15 mL) was obtained. On this basis, the differential diagnosis included dentigerous cyst, adenomatoid odontogenic tumor, and odontogenic keratocyst. A small labial bony window was created, and an incisional biopsy revealed a non-keratinized epithelial lining supported by fibrous connective tissue, consistent with a dentigerous cyst.

A 20-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a progressively enlarging, painful swelling of her left shoulder over the past 2 years. On examination, there was an 8-cm mass on the anterior aspect of the left shoulder without overlying erythema or warmth; the mass was tender, adherent to deep tissues, and mobile relative to the skin. Active shoulder movement was impossible; passive extension of the arm was limited to 90°. There was no axillary lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits.

Plain radiographs of the left shoulder revealed marked deformity of the scapula by a mixed lytic and sclerotic process involving the entire bone, with preservation of the humeral head and clavicle. Contrast-enhanced CT of the scapula demonstrated an expansile osteolytic lesion with thin sclerotic margins and internal bony septa delineating multiple cavities, each containing fluid–fluid levels, and cortical breaches without soft-tissue extension; the lesion measured 116 × 56 mm. MRI confirmed a multiloculated mass involving the coracoid process, glenoid cavity, neck, body, and spine of the scapula, with a surrounding rim of low T1 and T2 signal, internal fluid–fluid levels, and septal and peripheral enhancement after gadolinium administration.

A 19-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a two-year history of nocturnal right lumbar paravertebral radicular and low back pain unresponsive to anti-inflammatory medications. He denied trauma, systemic symptoms, or neurological deficits.

On examination, he was in good general condition with a stable gait and no limping. A left-sided gibbosity was noted. The Sonnette sign was positive on the right at L3–L4 and L4–L5. The straight leg–raising test was negative, and there were no focal neurologic deficits.

Six months earlier, lumbar spine radiographs had shown a lytic lesion on the right inferior articular process of L3 and a left-convex scoliotic posture. Because his pain persisted, an MRI was obtained, demonstrating an edematous signal abnormality in the right lateral and posterior arches of L3 and L4, hyperintense on T2 and STIR, hypointense on T1, and showing homogeneous enhancement after gadolinium. The lesion centered on the right posterior zygapophyseal joints, extended into the right L4 joint space, and tracked into the right psoas and paravertebral muscles without fluid collections.

A CT scan revealed a well-defined lytic lesion centered on the right inferior articular process of L3, extending to the inferior articular surface of L3 and the superior articular process of L4. A calcified nidus caused cortical disruption and was surrounded by osteocondensation with indistinct borders.

A 48-year-old woman presented with a 4 × 3 cm well-defined, irregular, non-ulcerated, non-erythematous, firm swelling over the left shoulder, arising from the superficial plane. Three years earlier, fine-needle aspiration cytology of a smaller lesion had led to a diagnosis of sebaceous cyst, but the patient was lost to follow-up. She now reported a rapid increase in size over the past 6 months without pain or other symptoms. Routine physical examination was otherwise normal. Magnetic resonance imaging of the shoulder revealed a solid-cystic mass lesion with hemorrhagic areas involving the superficial and deep subcutaneous planes without intramuscular or bony involvement and no evidence of regional lymphadenopathy; radiologic interpretation raised the possibility of a soft tissue sarcoma.

A 42-year-old woman presented with progressive numbness in her right lower limb. Four years earlier, she had developed low back pain with right-sided radicular pain, which worsened over the past 2 years despite nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs; she had deferred workup for financial reasons. More recently she noted urinary hesitancy and increasing calf numbness but denied saddle anesthesia, incontinence, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. On examination, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 15/15; motor strength in both lower limbs was 5/5, straight‐leg‐raise and Patrick’s tests were negative, plantar responses were downgoing, and proprioception was intact. Knee and ankle reflexes were slightly decreased bilaterally; the rest of the examination was unremarkable. Spinal magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 3 × 10 cm epidural mass extending from L4 to the coccyx with low T1 and heterogeneous T2 signal and apparent involvement of the L5–S2 vertebral bodies.

An 11-year-old boy presented with a 9- to 12-month history of nonpruritic, hypopigmented maculopapular patches. The lesions began in the axillae and progressively spread to involve most of the trunk and extremities. There was no history of myalgia, radiation, chemical exposure, lymphadenopathy, or bleeding into the skin. His past medical history was unremarkable, with no atopy, recent infections, or other inflammatory dermatoses. Family history was notable only for leukemia in a paternal uncle and two paternal cousins. Initial treatment with emollients produced no improvement. Multiple punch biopsies were obtained from hypopigmented patches on the trunk and inguinal region.  
Histopathology showed a superficial dermal and perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate and an epidermis containing scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes with a few intraepidermal hyperchromatic atypical lymphocytes. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for CD3 and partially lost CD7; there was a mixture of CD4 and CD8 positive cells, with CD8 positive T lymphocytes predominating in neoplastic epidermotropism.

A 63-year-old Korean woman with no significant medical history presented with a 1-year history of swelling in her right parotid region. Physical examination revealed a fixed, non-tender, round mass in the right parotid area. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. Neck CT showed a 3.2-cm heterogeneously enhancing mass lateral to the mandibular ramus adjacent to the right masseter muscle. Neck MRI demonstrated a well-demarcated, 2.5×3.0-cm gadolinium-enhanced fungating lesion with internal hemorrhage and increased vascularity. Ultrasonography revealed a heterogeneous hypoechoic mass in the right parotid gland suspicious for a parotid gland tumor. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy yielded fragments of relatively short spindle cells in a myxoid and bloody background; cytologists suggested that pleomorphic adenoma could not be excluded.

A 46-year-old Spanish man with no significant medical history, a former smoker and nondrinker, was referred after his primary care physician identified bilateral adrenal masses on CT. He reported 4 months of evening fevers and an unintended 5-kg weight loss following a SARS-CoV-2 infection. He denied abdominal pain, had a normal appetite, and regular bowel and urinary function. On examination he was afebrile, with a heart rate of 107 bpm, blood pressure 140/70 mmHg, and respiratory rate 20/min; cardiac, pulmonary, abdominal, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, MCV 78.5 fl, MCH 26.0 pg, INR 1.3, CRP 140 mg/L, and endocrine testing excluded hormone-producing tumors. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated an 11.5 × 10.5 cm heterogeneous mass in the right adrenal gland with central calcification and a 2.5 cm lesion in the left adrenal gland without features suggestive of malignancy; there was no evidence of metastases.

An 81-year-old man was referred for evaluation of lung nodules. Four months earlier, routine chest CT had shown multiple small nodules in both lungs. He was asymptomatic, received a short course of oral antibiotics, and did not follow up. Two months later he developed paroxysmal cough with scant white sputum and progressive dyspnea without fever, chills, chest pain, or hemoptysis. Repeat chest CT showed progression to multiple patchy and nodular high-density shadows, suggestive of an infectious or inflammatory etiology. 

On admission to a community hospital, he was afebrile with pH 7.46, pCO2 36.7 mmHg, pO2 63.5 mmHg on room air. Laboratory studies showed WBC 7.6×10^9/L, neutrophils 68.7%, hemoglobin 123 g/L, platelets 225×10^9/L, and CRP 16.5 mg/L. Immunological tests, D-dimer, liver and kidney function, ESR, CEA, CA19-9, AFP, and rheumatologic panels were normal. Sputum AFB smear and bacterial and fungal cultures were negative. T-SPOT.TB and antinuclear antibodies were nonreactive. 

Bronchoscopy was unremarkable. Brush cytology from the right lower lobe showed no malignancy. mNGS of BALF detected no pathogens. BALF β-D-glucan and galactomannan tests were negative. With no pathogens identified and imaging findings, a presumptive diagnosis of secondary organizing pneumonia was made, and methylprednisolone 40 mg IV daily was started. Within 3 days, cough and dyspnea improved. A follow-up CT one month later showed partial resolution of opacities. He was discharged on oral methylprednisolone 20 mg daily.

Four weeks after discharge, cough and dyspnea recurred. Repeat CT showed increased patchy shadows and nodules in both lungs compared to prior imaging. He was readmitted with a preliminary diagnosis of pneumonia. He was afebrile, heart rate 63, respiratory rate 21, blood pressure 139/88 mmHg, and mildly labored respirations. Lung auscultation revealed coarse breath sounds without crackles or wheezes. Laboratory tests showed WBC 9.7×10^9/L, neutrophils 6.1×10^9/L, and LDH 378.9 U/L. Enhanced CT of the chest confirmed multiple patchy shadows and nodules plus hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Superficial lymph node ultrasound was normal.

A 55-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 3, presented with intermittent postmenopausal spotting for 6 months, cough with expectoration, and significant weight loss over 2 months. She received 2 months of empirical antitubercular therapy elsewhere without improvement; instead, her vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal pain increased. She had no history of diabetes, hypertension, or estrogen exposure and had been postmenopausal for 3 years.

On examination, she appeared cachectic (weight 27 kg, BMI 15 kg/m2). Chest auscultation revealed decreased bilateral air entry with rhonchi. Abdominal examination showed a scaphoid abdomen and a hard, nonmobile, nontender mass corresponding to a 14-week gravid uterus in the suprapubic region. On speculum exam, the cervix could not be visualized. Bimanual exam confirmed the hard uterine mass. Hemoglobin was 7.1 g/dL; other blood tests were within normal limits.

Transvaginal ultrasonography demonstrated a well-defined heterogeneous hypoechoic 20 mm × 17 mm intramural lesion in the fundal myometrium, suggestive of a fibroid, with a bulky uterus. Pelvic MRI was interpreted as endometrial carcinoma with more than 50% myometrial invasion. A CT scan of the chest showed traction bronchiectasis and discrete random nodules with feeding vessel signs in the right lower lobe, likely metastases.

Two weeks later, the uterine mass had grown to a 20-week size, her abdominal pain had worsened, and hemoglobin had fallen to 5.2 g/dL. Repeat ultrasonography revealed a large lobulated heterogeneous mass measuring 13.7 cm × 7.3 cm with increased Doppler vascularity, obscuring the uterus and adnexa. She also developed severe left leg pain with unilateral edema; Doppler ultrasonography was normal, excluding deep vein thrombosis. Given the rapid tumor growth and progressive anemia, a presumptive diagnosis of leiomyosarcoma was made, and she was scheduled for exploratory laparotomy.

A 51-year-old man with a 5-year history of HIV infection (most recent CD4 count, 32/mm3) and poor adherence to antiretroviral therapy presented with left-sided weakness and altered mental status. He was intermittently somnolent during the interview. Vital signs were notable for blood pressure of 150/92 mm Hg; temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate were normal. On examination, there was an 8-cm fixed, subcutaneous mass over the left frontoparietal skull; the overlying skin was intact, without erythema or ulceration. The remainder of the dermatologic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 10.7×109/L with neutrophilia (6.4×109/L). 

Noncontrast CT of the head revealed multiple intra-axial masses in both frontal lobes (largest, 2.8 cm), associated with marked surrounding vasogenic edema, and a left frontal infiltrative osseous lesion with overlying soft-tissue swelling. Brain MRI confirmed a 2.5-cm destructive bone lesion in the left frontal skull with a large scalp soft-tissue mass and multiple enhancing cerebral masses up to 2.8 cm, consistent with metastatic disease. Chest radiography showed a 4.3-cm left hilar mass. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated a 6.2×3.8-cm lobulated left hilar mass, bilateral pulmonary and liver nodules, and a right lower-lobe pulmonary embolus.

A 52-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of progressive swelling of the right mandible, initially asymptomatic but associated with diffuse pain for 3 months and paresthesia of the right lower lip. His medical history included hypertension on atenolol and deafness.  
On examination there was a mildly tender, bony-hard, diffuse swelling of the right mandible from the midbody to the angle; intraorally a smooth, indistinct, soft but tender mass extended from the right first premolar to the second molar, with displacement and mobility of the first and second molars and pus around the first molar. Buccal and lingual cortical expansion and thinning were palpable. Aspiration yielded a small amount of blood anteriorly and was negative posteriorly.  
Panoramic radiograph showed a 7.0 × 3.5-cm ill-defined, multilocular radiolucent lesion from the canine to the third molar region with a soap-bubble appearance, mild root resorption, and erosion of the inferior alveolar canal. Occlusal view revealed buccal cortical perforation. Cone-beam CT confirmed an invasive radiolucency resorbing the buccal cortex, alveolar bone, and roots, with minimal fine intralesional calcifications.  
A differential diagnosis was made of odontogenic myxoma, ameloblastoma, and central giant cell granuloma.

A 12-month-old boy sustained second-degree burns to both lower limbs after spilling boiling milk. He was admitted to a burn center, received intravenous antibiotics, and underwent daily silver sulfadiazine dressings. Two weeks later, as the burn wounds were healing, multiple red lesions appeared abruptly at the margins of the burn sites on both knees and shins. The lesions were easily traumatized and bled with minor contact. On examination, there were numerous erythematous, pedunculated papules and nodules ranging up to 2.5×2.5 cm in diameter clustered around the healing scars. A punch biopsy of one nodule revealed an intact epidermis overlying a proliferation of capillary-sized blood vessels in an edematous stroma.

A 63-year-old woman presented with epigastric pain of one month’s duration. Her medical history was notable for pancreatic carcinoma treated four years earlier with distal pancreatectomy and splenectomy, hypertension, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. She denied headache, palpitations, or diaphoresis. On examination, she was mildly hypertensive but otherwise stable; the abdomen was soft without masses or organomegaly. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, serum electrolytes, thyroid, liver, and renal function tests, and urinalysis were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed a 52×29×27 mm, well-circumscribed, vividly enhancing soft-tissue mass on the right side of the aorta, near the aortic bifurcation. MRI showed the lesion to be hypointense on T1-weighted images, markedly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with vivid enhancement after gadolinium administration. Diffusion-weighted imaging demonstrated high signal intensity with low apparent diffusion coefficient values, consistent with restricted diffusion. The mass showed no signal loss on out-of-phase imaging, and multiple punctate flow voids were present on T1- and T2-weighted sequences.

A 49-year-old man presented with nocturnal chest pain, fever, and sweating of one week’s duration. He had a 7-year history of poorly controlled hypertension and an 8-year history of poorly controlled diabetes mellitus. At an outside hospital three days prior, ECG showed ST-segment elevation in leads aVL and V1–V6; leukocytosis and elevated liver enzymes were noted. Echocardiography revealed decreased cardiac output with regional wall motion abnormalities. Abdominal CT showed hepatic parenchymal abnormalities and a 5×5 cm left adrenal mass with heterogeneous enhancement. 

On admission, blood pressure was 140/90 mm Hg, pulse 66 beats/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and temperature 36.8 °C. Examination was unremarkable except for mild right upper quadrant tenderness. Laboratory values were: WBC 59 360/µL, hemoglobin 15.8 g/dL, platelets 244 000/µL, ESR 4 mm/hr, CRP 3.446 mg/L; BUN 22.7 mg/dL, creatinine 0.76 mg/dL; AST 156 IU/L, ALT 317 IU/L, ALP 289 IU/L, total bilirubin 1.05 mg/dL; total protein 5.5 g/dL, albumin 2.7 g/dL; calcium 7.2 mg/dL, phosphate 2.0 mg/dL, Na 134 mmol/L, K 4.4 mmol/L. Hemoglobin A1c was 10.7%. Fasting C-peptide was 0.40 ng/mL (0.48–3.3) and 2-hour postprandial C-peptide was 0.66 ng/mL. LDH was 1240 IU/L. CK-MB was 5.99 ng/mL (0.6–6.3), and troponin-T was 0.073 ng/mL (0.0–0.1). Chest X-ray was normal. Repeat ECG showed sinus rhythm with T-wave inversion and QT prolongation in leads II and V1–V6. Echocardiography demonstrated an ejection fraction of 69% with severe mid-ventricular hypokinesis sparing the basal and apical segments. 

Twenty-four–hour urine studies revealed VMA 33.93 mg/day (0–8.0), metanephrines 20.45 mg/day (0–1.3), epinephrine 2034 µg/day (0–40), norepinephrine 978 µg/day (0–80). Serum epinephrine was 1221 pg/mL (0–120) and serum norepinephrine 778 pg/mL (100–410). Aldosterone, plasma renin activity, and cortisol were all normal.

A 67-year-old man with stage IVA right lung adenocarcinoma (cT3N0M1a) was receiving induction immunochemotherapy. His history included right upper lobectomy 19 years earlier for squamous cell carcinoma and a 30 pack-year smoking history. Molecular testing of the current adenocarcinoma revealed no driver mutations and a PD-L1 tumor-proportion score of 20–30%. Beginning in April, he received nivolumab every 3 weeks (11 cycles to date) combined with ipilimumab every 6 weeks (6 cycles to date); carboplatin and pemetrexed were given for the first two cycles. The serum carcinoembryonic antigen level fell from 23.8 ng/mL at baseline to 5.2 ng/mL at the 10th nivolumab cycle, and CT after the 11th cycle showed stable disease.  

On the scheduled day of his 12th nivolumab dose, he developed dyspnea and acute respiratory failure (SpO₂ 85% on room air). Chest CT showed diffuse ground-glass opacities predominantly in the left lower lobe; the known right lung lesion was unchanged. Serum carcinoembryonic antigen was 6.2 ng/mL.  

Immunotherapy-related interstitial pneumonitis was provisionally diagnosed, although infection and pulmonary lymphangitis carcinomatosa were considered less likely and in need of exclusion. The next day, bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage was performed.

A 55-year-old man presented with a 5-year history of a painless swelling of the soft palate, gradually increasing in size. He reported snoring, obstructive sleep apnea, dysphagia, and hypernasal speech. There was no weight loss or fever. Examination revealed a firm, immobile, well-circumscribed submucosal mass in the soft palate obstructing the nasopharyngeal port; no cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck showed a well-defined, uniformly enhancing solid mass measuring 50 × 35 mm arising from the right posterior soft palate, without infiltration of adjacent fat planes or involvement of the underlying bone.

A 41-year-old man presented with abdominal distension and intermittent discomfort for 1 month. He reported absolute constipation for 3 days, nausea, feculent vomiting, and weight loss, but denied rectal bleeding or tenesmus. On examination he was dehydrated and tachycardic (pulse, 105 bpm; blood pressure normal), with a distended abdomen and high-pitched bowel sounds. Laboratory studies showed acute kidney injury (urea, 15 mmol/L; creatinine, 115 µmol/L) with normal blood counts and coagulation. Abdominal radiography demonstrated centrally located valvulae conniventes consistent with small-bowel obstruction. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a target-shaped soft-tissue mass with a layering effect in the distal ileum, suggestive of ileoileal intussusception.

A 25-year-old woman presented with pelvic pain of four months’ duration. She reported no menstrual irregularities, hypermenorrhoea, or virilizing symptoms. On examination, a large, palpable abdomino-pelvic mass was noted. Transvaginal ultrasound revealed a 15 cm left ovarian mass that was heterogeneous and predominantly solid, with several loculated cystic areas. Laboratory studies, including serum tumor markers and hormonal assays, were within normal limits.

A 25-year-old right-handed man presented after a generalized convulsion. He had experienced focal seizures for several years without treatment and noted slight numbness in the left fourth and fifth fingers. There were no other symptoms or neurologic deficits on examination.

Noncontrast CT of the brain revealed a mass in the right central region that appeared to be a meningioma. A 3-Tesla MRI of the brain demonstrated a solid, well-demarcated homogeneous mass in the same region, which seemed to have a dural attachment. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy showed a 125% increase in choline; N-acetyl-aspartate and keratin/phospho-keratin peaks were absent, there was no increased resonance in the lipid area, and no alanine peak was detected. These spectroscopic features suggested an extra-axial lesion and were felt to exclude metastatic disease.

A 42‐year‐old man noted a left‐sided neck mass 2 months before evaluation. He had no significant medical or family history. On examination, there was a 3.5‐cm, elastic, firm, mobile mass in the left thyroid region; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed: TSH 1.78 µIU/mL (0.50–5.00); FT4 1.38 ng/dL (0.90–1.70); FT3 3.50 pg/mL (2.3–4.0); thyroglobulin 10.60 ng/mL (< 33.7); anti-TPO Ab < 9 IU/mL; anti-Tg Ab < 10 IU/mL; alkaline phosphatase 197 U/L (106–322); calcium 9.7 mg/dL (8.8–10.1); intact PTH 63.0 pg/mL (10–65); CEA 1.7 ng/mL (≤ 5); and calcitonin 2.54 pg/mL (≤ 5.15).

Neck ultrasonography revealed a 46 × 29 × 24 mm irregular, hypoechoic mass in the left thyroid lobe without a clear halo. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a poorly enhancing mass on the posterior aspect of the left lobe, with no extrathyroidal extension or lymphadenopathy. PET-CT showed intense uptake in the left thyroid region (SUVmax 23.9) without other lesions.

Fine-needle aspiration cytology initially suggested medullary thyroid carcinoma. Upon review, cytology exhibited granular, short spindle-shaped atypical cells with clear nucleoli, and a follicular thyroid tumor was suspected.

A 16-year-old boy presented with a 4-week history of bilateral pain and swelling along his Achilles tendons, worse during and after walking. He was not involved in any sports. Two weeks earlier he had transient hematuria. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. On examination, he had tenderness and swelling over both Achilles tendons; otherwise, findings were normal. Height and weight were at the 50th percentile; Tanner stage was 4; blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg. Laboratory tests showed:  
• Serum calcium 14.4 mg/dL (normal 8.4–10.6)  
• Phosphate 2.4 mg/dL (normal 2.3–4.7)  
• Alkaline phosphatase 245 U/L (normal 40–360)  
• Magnesium 0.8 mmol/L (normal 0.5–1.1)  
• Creatinine 0.8 mg/dL  
• Urinary calcium/creatinine ratio 0.2  
• Parathyroid hormone 512 pg/mL (normal 5–65)  

Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of both ankles were normal. A Doppler ultrasound of the Achilles tendons showed calcific nodules with increased blood flow surrounding the nodules in both tendons.

A 74-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of mildly elevated tumor markers on routine blood tests: carcinoembryonic antigen 7.4 ng/mL (normal 0–5.0) and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 44.2 U/mL (normal 0–37.0); all other markers were within normal limits. She was asymptomatic, with unremarkable glucose tolerance. Abdominal ultrasonography was limited by overlying gas. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 15 mm hypodense mass with a clear boundary in the pancreatic tail, containing multiple septal structures and demonstrating contrast enhancement in the portal venous phase; there was no calcification or main pancreatic duct dilation. On MRI, the lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images, nonuniformly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and exhibited mild diffusion restriction without hypercellularity. Dynamic MRI revealed lower early enhancement compared with surrounding pancreas and gradual enhancement thereafter. MR cholangiopancreatography did not visualize the lesion, effectively excluding a cystic pancreatic tumor. Endoscopic ultrasound depicted a 14×16 mm well-demarcated hypoechoic solid mass in the pancreatic tail. EUS-guided FNA was performed twice with 22-gauge needles. Based on imaging, a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor with poor perfusion was initially suspected. Cytopathologic examination revealed atypical cells varying in size, a high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio, chromatin-rich macronuclei, and acidophilic vesicles mixed with interstitial blood clots; periodic acid–Schiff staining was negative. Immunohistochemical staining showed positivity for cytokeratin AE1/AE3 and negativity for synaptophysin, chromogranin A, and leukocyte common antigen; a small subset of cells was CD56-positive. On the basis of these findings, a diagnosis of poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the pancreatic tail was made, and the patient was scheduled for distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy and lymph node dissection.

A 39-year-old man presented with a several-month history of headache and nausea. He had no other medical history, took no medications, and had no family history of tumors. On examination, vital signs and a complete neurologic assessment—including cranial nerves, motor and sensory function, reflexes, coordination, gait, and stance—were normal. Routine laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, and C-reactive protein, were within normal limits.

Noncontrast computed tomography of the head showed an ill-defined, slightly hypointense lesion measuring 39 × 37 × 29 mm in the right cerebellar hemisphere. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed the lesion to be hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences, with only faint contrast enhancement on postcontrast T1-weighted images. There was no evidence of hydrocephalus.

A 9-year-old boy presented with a 3-year history of a painless left scrotal mass that had gradually increased in size. He was otherwise well, with unremarkable early childhood development. On examination, there was a non-tender, fixed, 5 cm mass in the left hemiscrotum with intact overlying skin and no palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy. A complete blood count showed a hemoglobin level of 12.3 g/dL and a white-cell count of 7600 cells/mm3; liver and renal function tests were within normal limits. Enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a heterogeneously enhancing mass (30–55 Hounsfield units) occupying the scrotal region, extending into both inguinal canals and the pelvis, with no bone erosion or evidence of abdominal metastasis. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. An ultrasound-guided Tru-Cut biopsy was performed. Histologic examination of H&E-stained sections revealed sheets of bland cells with spindle-shaped nuclei, pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, and a storiform growth pattern, diffusely infiltrating underlying adipose tissue; prominent myxoid stroma with thin-walled vessels was also noted. Immunohistochemical staining showed diffuse, strong positivity for CD34.

A 72-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of a pruritic eruption on his right thigh and left flank, which had recently progressed over the previous 3 months to include smaller lesions on the arms, legs, and trunk. He denied constitutional symptoms, a personal history of cancer, and recent medication changes. Examination revealed multiple large, indurated, hyperpigmented to violaceous plaques on the medial right thigh and left flank, along with smaller reddish-brown macules and papules on the trunk and extremities. No lymphadenopathy was noted. Laboratory testing showed a hemoglobin concentration of 11.9 g/dL, a C-reactive protein concentration of 4.6 mg/L, and multiple M spikes on protein electrophoresis. A whole-body CT scan was negative for lymphadenopathy but revealed an asymptomatic solitary renal mass of less than 3.0 cm. Initial differential diagnoses included histiocytosis, sarcoidosis, and cutaneous lymphoma.

An 18-year-old college student presented with a one-month history of easy fatigability, postural dizziness, palpitations, and dyspnea, along with a 30-kg weight loss over six months. He was referred for severe anemia (hemoglobin 4.7 g/dL). On examination he was pale; vital signs were normal except for a pulse of 98 beats/min. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 5.1 g/dL, iron < 10 µg/dL, and a positive fecal occult blood test. Bone marrow biopsy revealed normocellular marrow with normal trilineage hematopoiesis. Upper endoscopy showed erosive antral gastritis with patchy ulcerative inflammation. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a rounded echogenic lesion in the right liver lobe (suggestive of hemangioma) and mild splenomegaly. CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a well-defined soft tissue mass in the anterior upper pelvis engulfing jejunal loops and causing bowel wall thickening. 

The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy and excision of an 11 × 8 × 2 cm annular mass within the jejunal wall, ulcerating the mucosa and extending to the serosa. Microscopic examination showed a tumor centered in the muscularis propria, extending to mucosa and serosa; neoplastic cells were arranged in a predominantly pseudoalveolar pattern, polygonal with eosinophilic to clear cytoplasm, oval nuclei with vesicular chromatin and inconspicuous nucleoli; scattered osteoclast-like multinucleated giant cells were present, with frequent mitoses and necrosis; lymph nodes were negative. 

Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated strong, diffuse S100 protein and vimentin positivity in tumor cells. Neoplastic cells were negative for HMB-45, Melan-A, chromogranin A, synaptophysin, CD56, smooth muscle actin, desmin, CD34, CD117, cytokeratin, and LCA.

A 44‐year‐old woman presented with a 10-year history of a painless, slowly enlarging mass in her left thigh. She had no significant medical or family history. On examination, there was a firm, well‐demarcated, approximately 9.0-cm mass in the anteromedial compartment of the left thigh, without tenderness or overlying skin changes. Routine laboratory studies were within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left thigh demonstrated a discrete, homogeneous, well‐defined 8.0 × 3.5-cm tumor displacing the muscles of the medial compartment. The lesion was isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, suggestive of myxoma.

A 54-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of progressive dysphagia, dyslalia, and a sensation of an oropharyngeal foreign body. She reported no pain, had no tobacco use, and no personal or family history of tumours. On examination, there was a firm, nontender 3.0 × 3.5 cm mass on the right side of the base of the tongue, covered by normal mucosa. She exhibited stomatolalia and difficulty protruding the tongue, with deviation to the right. 

Magnetic resonance imaging showed a well-capsulated, solid oval mass measuring 31 × 28 × 21 mm with well-defined margins on T1-weighted images without contrast; it was hyperintense and slightly inhomogeneous on T2-weighted images, and demonstrated marked enhancement after gadolinium. 

Fine-needle aspiration cytology yielded epithelioid cells, either isolated or in nests, occasionally with a three-dimensional appearance. Immunohistochemical staining of the cytology specimen was positive for pan-cytokeratin, high-molecular-weight cytokeratin, and S-100 protein, and negative for α-smooth muscle actin.

A 45-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer treated with radiotherapy 3 years earlier presents with a 1-month history of severe headache refractory to medication. Noncontrast CT of the head shows several hypodense lesions in the cerebral parenchyma. Brain MRI reveals multiple rounded cystic lesions, hypointense on T1 and hyperintense on T2 sequences, each containing an internal nodular structure resembling a scolex, with peripheral contrast enhancement that is most pronounced around the mural nodules. The patient receives a 5-day course of albendazole without clinical or radiographic improvement.

A 43-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive headache, behavioral changes, right facial paresis, and left-sided paresthesia. She denied fever; there were no signs of meningism. Hematologic studies were normal. Brain MRI showed in the right frontal lobe a hypointense lesion on FLAIR with marked vasogenic edema and no diffusion restriction on DWI. On T1-weighted imaging, the lesion exhibited a large, irregular, thick ring of contrast enhancement. Arterial spin labeling perfusion showed increased relative cerebral blood flow at the lesion periphery, and dynamic susceptibility contrast perfusion demonstrated markedly elevated cerebral blood volume at its margins. Multivoxel MR spectroscopy over the lesion margin revealed an increased choline-to-creatine ratio, decreased N-acetylaspartate peak, and an inverted lactate–lipid peak; the peritumoral FLAIR abnormality beyond the enhancing component showed a similar pattern. Based on these imaging findings, a preliminary diagnosis of glioma was made.

A 47-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 1-day history of retrosternal burning chest pain, diffuse abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and fatigue. Her blood pressure was 200/100 mmHg and heart rate 88 b.p.m.; examination revealed right hypochondriac tenderness but no murmurs, no jugular venous distension, and clear lung fields. She had a history of hypertension treated intermittently with amlodipine and indapamide, and 6 months earlier had presented with similar chest pain, ST changes, mildly elevated troponin, global left ventricular hypokinesis (EF 36%), and a normal coronary angiogram; that episode was labeled “acute myocarditis.” Her mother and aunt had polycystic kidney disease.  

Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 18×10^3/L and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 46 mm/h; electrolytes, troponin I, and renal function were normal. Electrocardiography demonstrated 1.0–2.5 mm ST depression in leads II and V2–V6 and >0.5 mm ST elevation in aVR. Chest radiography was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed multiple cysts in both kidneys and a multicystic mass in the right liver lobe; the adrenal glands were not visualized. Transthoracic echocardiography showed global myocardial hypokinesis.  

During her admission, she experienced several transient episodes of sweating, pallor, nausea, and vomiting accompanied by hypertensive crises with blood pressure exceeding 200/100 mmHg. Based on these recurrent sympathetic surges and her prior evaluations, the team decided to measure 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines.

A 17-year-old girl was referred by her dentist after detection of a large sublingual mass elevating her tongue and restricting movement. She and her mother had not noticed the swelling; her only complaints over several years were a lisp and snoring. She denied difficulties with eating, swallowing, or breathing. Her body-mass index was 31, and there was no history of trauma or oral/neck surgery. 

On examination, there was a well-defined, firm, painless mass in the submental region that elevated the floor of the mouth and the ventral surface of the tongue. Beneath the tongue, a symmetrical yellowish dense mass was visible through a thin mucosal covering. Tongue mobility testing revealed inability to protrude the tongue and markedly restricted upward and lateral movements. 

Magnetic resonance imaging showed a well-defined cystic lesion measuring 5.8 × 8.4 cm, with low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, located above the mylohyoid and geniohyoid muscles. The lesion extended from the submental area into the floor of the mouth and superiorly into the tongue, causing slight displacement of the tongue base and narrowing of the upper airway.

A 34-year-old woman with no significant medical or family history noted weakness and numbness in her left arm. Three weeks after symptom onset, brain MRI at an outside hospital suggested a demyelinating process, and she received a 3-day course of high-dose intravenous steroids, but her symptoms progressed and imaging showed lesion enlargement. She was transferred 2 months after onset.

On admission, she was alert, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Neurologic examination demonstrated severe left hemiparesis (muscle strength grade 2/5) and left-sided sensory loss; her Karnofsky Performance Status was 50%.

Non-contrast head CT showed a mildly hyperdense area in the center of a right hemispheric lesion without obvious calcification. Brain MRI revealed a FLAIR-hyperintense lesion involving the cortex and white matter of the right parietal and frontal lobes, extending into the splenium of the corpus callosum. Gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted images showed only faint enhancement in part of the lesion. By contrast, arterial spin labeling demonstrated markedly increased blood flow throughout the entire FLAIR-hyperintense area, with a tumor-to-normal white matter cerebral blood flow ratio of 3.30.

A 47‐year‐old man with a 10‐year history of chronic alcoholism presented with a giant scrotal mass that had grown over 5 years and was now interfering with sexual activity and daily function. He also reported numerous painless, slowly enlarging soft masses in the anterior neck, supraclavicular fossae, nape, bilateral arms, and shoulders. 
On examination, he had poorly defined, soft masses symmetrically distributed in the anterior neck, nape, shoulders, upper back, and a massive scrotal swelling causing expansion of scrotal skin and burying of the penis. A short portion of the penis was only palpable on erection; the prepuce and meatus were normal. Normal‐sized testes were palpable independent of the scrotal mass. Body-mass index was 26.
Thyroid ultrasound and thyroid hormone levels were normal. Blood lipid levels, including cholesterol and triglycerides, were within normal limits. Liver function tests were abnormal, with decreased factors II, V, and VII leading to reduced platelet count and prolonged PTT; he received fresh‐frozen plasma and vitamin K preoperatively. 
Magnetic resonance imaging of the scrotum showed non-encapsulated adipose tissue on both sides of the scrotum. An excision biopsy of the scrotal lesion revealed benign lipomatous tissue.

A 50-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on maintenance dialysis was admitted in January 2017 for living-donor kidney transplantation. Two days before the planned surgery he developed fever. Blood and urine cultures were repeatedly negative, and antinuclear antibody (ANA) and vasculitis markers were negative; C-reactive protein was initially normal. Ultrasonography showed bilaterally contracted kidneys without hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, or ascites. Chest radiograph and whole-body PET-CT did not identify any focus of infection or malignancy. Because he also complained of severe back pain, magnetic resonance imaging of the spine was performed and showed discitis; transpedicular disc biopsy grew Staphylococcus aureus but was negative for tuberculosis. His fever resolved with six weeks of intravenous flucloxacillin and four weeks of oral rifampicin. 

When he was re-evaluated in August 2017, chest CT showed bilateral mild pleural effusions (left greater than right), moderately enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes, left axillary lymph nodes, and small bilateral supraclavicular nodes. Repeat PET-CT showed mediastinal nodes with poor FDG uptake; both erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein remained elevated, and he had severe anemia. Excision of an axillary lymph node revealed vascular transformation of sinuses without evidence of infection or malignancy. Video-assisted thoracoscopic excision of a mediastinal node showed areas of suppuration, but all cultures were negative. He received eight weeks of intravenous antibiotics followed by six weeks of oral antibiotics. His persistent left pleural effusion was exudative but tested negative for tuberculosis and malignancy. He was treated empirically with antitubercular therapy until February 2018 without improvement, and left pleurodesis was planned.

A 36-year-old man presented with a five-year history of a left scrotal swelling. The mass was stable in size but painful and interfered with daily activities. He denied lower urinary tract symptoms, fever, weight loss, prior masses, or sexually transmitted disease. On examination, there was a 2 cm tender swelling attached to the left penoscrotal junction without skin changes. Routine blood tests, liver and renal function, human chorionic gonadotropin, and alpha-fetoprotein levels were all within normal limits. Pelvic MRI showed a 3.1 cm well-circumscribed mass at the left inferolateral base of the penis; the corpora cavernosum and spongiosum were unremarkable. The patient underwent surgical excision of the mass. Histologic examination revealed a neoplasm composed of monophasic spindle cells arranged in intersecting fascicles and devoid of necrosis, with a mitotic count of 3 per 10 high-power fields. Immunohistochemical staining showed the lesion was positive for pancytokeratin (AE1/AE3), epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), TLE-1, CD99, and BCL-2, and negative for smooth muscle actin, desmin, S100, calretinin, CK5/6, and CD34.

A 48-year-old man presented for evaluation of an incidental abnormality on brain imaging performed for a mild headache. He denied focal weakness, sensory changes, or speech disturbances. He had no family history of intracranial lesions. On neurologic examination, he had no focal deficits. Noncontrast head CT and MRI revealed a single 16 mm cystic lesion in the left basal ganglia with an internal fluid–fluid level, without peri-lesional edema. On T1- and T2-weighted MRI, there was no nodular component, rim enhancement, capsule-like appearance, or calcification of the lesion. To exclude vascular malformations or tumors, cerebral angiography was performed and showed no abnormal vascular staining or malformation.

A 2-year-old Caucasian girl was referred to pediatric dentistry for management of totally intruded lower right primary incisors. On initial exam, an asymptomatic tissue growth was noted on the lingual gingiva adjacent to the intruded incisors. The mother had not observed the lesion previously. The child was otherwise healthy. Six months later, the patient returned; oral hygiene was poor with gingivitis. On exam, a firm, nonhemorrhagic, pedunculated fibrous lesion measuring approximately 5 mm × 5 mm × 3 mm was attached to the lingual gingiva of the lower right primary central and lateral incisors. The overlying mucosa was intact and white. The adjacent primary teeth remained in their original positions. No other oral abnormalities were present. Based on its appearance, the clinical differential diagnosis included reactive and benign neoplastic lesions such as fibroma, fibrous hyperplasia, peripheral ossifying fibroma, peripheral odontogenic fibroma, giant cell fibroma, and odontogenic hamartoma. The lesion was excised under local anesthesia and submitted for histopathological analysis.

A 4½-year-old boy, previously healthy, presented with two weeks of fever, progressive lethargy, and abdominal distension. On examination, he was febrile, pale, and irritable. He had generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. His family history was notable for a maternal cousin who died of a lymphoproliferative disorder in childhood. Initial laboratory studies showed pancytopenia, elevated ferritin, and hypertriglyceridemia. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed lymphocytic pleocytosis, and biopsies of a lymph node and bone marrow demonstrated hemophagocytosis. Epstein–Barr virus was detected in the cerebrospinal fluid, lymph node, and bone marrow. Brain magnetic resonance imaging at presentation showed widespread T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions in the cerebral white matter, basal ganglia, and cerebellum; some lesions demonstrated contrast enhancement, and one temporal lesion contained hemorrhage. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy revealed lactate and lipid peaks, a decreased N-acetyl aspartate peak, and a mild elevation of choline.

A 77-year-old man presented with a palpable abnormality in his right breast. His history was notable for a complicated parapneumonic effusion treated with right thoracotomy and pleural decortication 11 months earlier, with benign pathology. He also had prior squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma in situ of the skin, and an occupational history of asbestos exposure. Two siblings had breast cancer and a BRCA1 mutation; his own BRCA status was unknown. On examination, there was a fixed, firm mass in the right breast measuring approximately 5 cm.

A posteroanterior chest radiograph showed pleural thickening along the right lateral chest wall and blunting of the right costophrenic angle. Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated a contracted right hemithorax with an irregular pleural-based process that extended through the intercostal muscle into subcutaneous adipose tissue, suggesting direct spread rather than a discrete metastasis. There was also evidence of bronchiectasis, right middle lobe atelectasis, and changes consistent with prior granulomatous disease. A diagnostic mammogram revealed predominantly fatty breast parenchyma without abnormal axillary lymph nodes. Breast ultrasound demonstrated an irregular, hypoechoic mass with angular margins measuring 5.6 × 2.9 × 3.6 cm, with apparent involvement of the pectoralis muscle and possible extension into the intercostal muscles. Fine-needle biopsy of the breast mass was recommended.

A woman in her 50s presented with a 1-year history of progressive swelling of the left hypothenar eminence and persistent paresthesias in the fourth and fifth digits. There was no history of trauma, neurofibromatosis, or other tumors. On examination, Tinel’s sign over Guyon’s canal and the cubital tunnel was negative. Radiographs of the left wrist showed a well-defined oval soft-tissue density in the hypothenar region. Ultrasonography revealed a slightly hyperechoic mass with a fibrillated pattern contiguous with the proximal ulnar nerve and no internal flow on spectral Doppler. MRI demonstrated thickening of the ulnar nerve extending through Guyon’s canal into a 32×29×70 mm polylobulated volar wrist mass that was moderately hyperintense on T1- and T2-weighted images, lost signal on fat-saturated sequences, and had mild peripheral enhancement after gadolinium. Electromyography showed mild myelinic dysfunction of the ulnar nerve at the wrist, confirming a sensory deficit.

A 45-year-old man presented with a 2–3 month history of recurrent, self-limited left-sided epistaxis, each episode lasting up to 10 minutes. He also noted intermittent dull pain over the left side of his nose and a sensation of a slowly enlarging intranasal mass, without nasal obstruction or facial numbness. An attempt at excision under local anesthesia was aborted because of brisk bleeding, and he was referred to our clinic. On arrival, bleeding had ceased. Medical history was notable only for well-controlled hypertension; there was no tobacco, alcohol, or drug use, and no family history of cancer. Examination revealed a healthy, obese man with marginally elevated blood pressure. Nasal inspection, after removal of a nosepad and suction, showed a well-circumscribed 10 mm mass on the anterior face of the left inferior turbinate; the surface had several incision marks from the prior procedure. Anterior and posterior rhinoscopy otherwise were unremarkable. External examination revealed a slight palpable swelling between the lateral cartilage and nasal bone on the left. Contrast-enhanced CT of the nasal cavity demonstrated a 24 mm lesion of the inferior turbinate with only marginal enhancement, no bony erosion, and uncertain involvement of the adjacent lateral nasal cartilage. Subsequent MRI showed a 9 × 11 × 8 mm nodular, contrast-enhancing lesion arising from the lateral nasal wall at the level of the piriform aperture without any sign of infiltrative growth.

A 59-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of abnormal liver function tests. She had a history of a nonfunctional pituitary tumor and had previously consumed 360–540 mL of sake daily until age 50. She denied smoking or exposure to known hepatic carcinogens. She reported taking several dietary supplements with steroid-like effects. On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs and no stigmata of chronic liver disease.

Initial laboratory studies revealed thrombocytopenia (131 × 10^3/μL), elevated AST (52 IU/L), ALT (75 IU/L), ALP (497 IU/L), and GGT (244 IU/L).
