Viral hepatitis serologies, autoantibodies, and tumor markers (CEA, CA 19-9, AFP, PIVKA-II) were all negative or within normal limits; fibrinogen and coagulation parameters were unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed multiple low-density hepatic lesions with peripheral enhancement in the arterial phase, centripetal fill-in in the portal phase, and near-uniform enhancement in equilibrium. Gd-EOB-DTPA MRI demonstrated these lesions to be hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and hypointense in the hepatobiliary phase; some lesions had peripheral diffusion restriction. FDG-PET revealed no abnormal uptake.

Because vascular tumors were suspected, a percutaneous liver biopsy of a right-lobe lesion was performed. Histology showed sinusoidal dilation with sporadic CD31-positive cells in dilated sinusoids without cytologic atypia. To exclude malignancy, diagnostic laparoscopy with wedge biopsy of a lateral-segment lesion was done two months later; irregular sinusoidal dilation with CD31- and CD34-positive cells was confirmed, again without atypia or fibrosis. A diagnosis of peliosis hepatis was made, and the patient discontinued all dietary supplements.

Four months later, she developed progressively worsening epigastric pain. Six months after the initial evaluation she was readmitted; labs now showed worsening cholestatic and hepatocellular enzyme elevations, anemia (Hb 8.4 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (71 × 10^3/μL), prolonged PT, low fibrinogen, and elevated fibrin degradation products, consistent with disseminated intravascular coagulation. Tumor markers remained within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT revealed two large hepatic tumors (46 mm and 60 mm) with peripheral arterial enhancement progressing centripetally to equilibrium, along with additional smaller lesions. Repeat Gd-EOB-DTPA MRI showed these tumors were hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with intratumoral areas suggestive of hemorrhage on T2*-weighted images, and were hypointense in the hepatobiliary phase.

A 35-year-old man presented with 2 months of progressive dyspnea and weight loss. His history included acute myeloid leukemia treated with allogeneic bone marrow transplant, subsequent relapse managed with chemotherapy, and complete remission on azacitidine and venetoclax. On admission: temperature 37.1°C; heart rate 87 bpm; blood pressure 130/80 mmHg; oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Physical examination showed bilateral lower-extremity pitting edema and normal heart sounds without murmur. ECG demonstrated Q waves in inferior leads, diffuse T-wave inversion, and low-voltage QRS complexes. Laboratory studies revealed leukopenia (2.9 × 10^3 /µL), normal renal and liver function, no blasts on peripheral smear, and elevated high-sensitivity troponin I. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography showed inferior and septal hypokinesia (LVEF 45%), circumferential pericardial effusion without tamponade, abnormal right ventricular wall thickening, and a mobile LV apical thrombus that resolved with anticoagulation. Cardiac MRI confirmed diffuse thickening of the RV free wall (up to 30 mm), isointense on T1-weighted images, without late gadolinium enhancement, extending into the RA and LV, and subendocardial LGE of the inferior LV wall. Coronary angiography showed no atherosclerotic disease. Chest CT revealed incorporation of the right coronary artery by the pathological tissue. FDG-PET scan demonstrated hypermetabolic tissue in the heart, ascending aorta, and aortic arch. A percutaneous endomyocardial biopsy was inconclusive.

A 72-year-old man with a history of clinical T2N0M0 high-grade urothelial carcinoma of the bladder treated two years earlier with radical radiotherapy and neoadjuvant cisplatin presented with worsening back pain and acute kidney injury.  
An ultrasound of the renal tract revealed a soft-tissue mass at the base of the bladder causing bilateral ureteric obstruction, and bilateral nephrostomies were placed with improvement in renal function.  
Biopsies of the bladder and prostate showed neuroendocrine carcinoma with extensive crush artefact and predominantly small cells. His prostate-specific antigen level was 5.9 µg/L, and chromogranin A was 214 U/L.  
CT staging demonstrated a locally advanced bladder malignancy with possible involvement of the mid-rectum but no evidence of metastatic disease. He was treated with androgen-deprivation therapy and neoadjuvant chemotherapy (carboplatin and etoposide).  
After three cycles, PET-CT showed no reduction in tumour volume and no metastatic lesions. Because of severe local symptoms, he underwent radical cysto-prostatectomy; the tumour was dissected from the rectum.  
Histopathological examination revealed a large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma, positive for synaptophysin, chromogranin, and CD56. The tumour invaded through the bladder wall into adipose tissue and was present at the posterior perivesical margins (pT4a). Obturator and external iliac lymph nodes were involved.  
Additionally, there was a separate Gleason score 9 prostatic adenocarcinoma that lacked neuroendocrine immunohistochemical positivity. Peritoneal fluid sampled during surgery was negative for malignancy.

A 24-year-old right-handed man presented with a 4-year history of a slowly enlarging right forearm mass. He reported vague forearm pain and weakness but no numbness or hand dysfunction. Examination revealed an oval, 7 × 4 cm, firm–elastic mass over the extensor compartment of the forearm; the neurovascular exam of the distal extremity was normal. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. Anteroposterior radiography of the distal forearm showed lamellar periostosis of the radius, diffuse changes in bone structure, and an area of reduced bone density in the distal radius. Ultrasonography demonstrated a highly vascularized mass overlying the radius, poorly demarcated from surrounding tissues. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed an inhomogeneous tumor with irregular contours, diffuse postcontrast enhancement, and evidence of osseous invasion of the distal radius.

A 42-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a left buttock mass discovered incidentally on a routine health examination. He had no pain or neurologic symptoms. On examination, a non-tender, deep-seated, elastic soft-tissue mass was palpable in the left buttock; there was no lymphadenopathy and Tinel's sign was negative. MRI demonstrated a well-circumscribed, slightly heterogeneous 12-cm mass between the gluteus medius and maximus muscles. On both T1- and T2-weighted images, the lesion was hyperintense relative to skeletal muscle but slightly hypointense to subcutaneous fat; fat-suppressed T1-weighted images showed mixed low- and intermediate-signal areas consistent with fatty elements. Diffuse enhancement was noted after gadolinium administration. FDG-PET/CT revealed focal increased uptake in the mass with a maximum standardized uptake value of 4.1; there were no other sites of abnormal uptake.

A 48-year-old woman with a history of left invasive ductal breast carcinoma (T1N1M0, ER negative, PR negative, HER2 positive) underwent modified radical mastectomy followed by adjuvant chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Fourteen months postoperatively, she presented with a 1-month history of continuous irregular fever. Empiric antibiotics for 1 week produced no improvement, and common infectious causes were excluded. Laboratory studies showed a carcinoembryonic antigen level of 7.29 ng/mL (reference <3.4 ng/mL). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed low-density lesions in the right hepatic lobe. MRI of the abdomen demonstrated space-occupying lesions in the same region. Cerebral MRI and whole-body bone scan showed no evidence of metastases elsewhere.

A 33-year-old Japanese man noted a diffuse swelling of the right cheek and right maxillary alveolar region associated with mobility of the first premolar and first and second molars. Intraoral examination revealed a soft, nonpulsatile, nontender, nonhemorrhagic mass extending from the right first premolar to the tuberosity region. A panoramic radiograph showed an ill-defined osteolytic lesion in the right posterior maxilla with resorption of the floor of the maxillary sinus. An axial CT scan demonstrated a 45 × 35 mm soft-tissue–density mass in the right maxilla eroding the anterior and lateral walls of the maxillary sinus and extending into the buccal space. MRI of the face revealed a right maxillary mass with low T1-weighted and moderate T2-weighted signal intensity.

A 29-year-old woman with a lifelong history of left-sided deafness presented with 9 days of left ear and neck pain and left facial weakness. On examination, she was afebrile. Otoscopic findings were normal; there was a tender and swollen posterior auricle without erythema. She had left hemifacial paresis (House–Brackmann grade IV). Laboratory studies were inconsistent with infection. Audiometry demonstrated profound sensorineural hearing loss on the left side and normal hearing on the right. Fine-cut bone-window CT of the head showed a 7 mm complex cystic mass in the left temporal bone with a well-defined bony defect extending posteriorly to the mastoid margin and medially to the posterior genu of the facial nerve canal. The lateral semicircular canal was absent, and the cochlea appeared hypoplastic. MRI of the head demonstrated a cystic mass involving the left temporal bone and extending into the soft tissues below the mastoid tip. The lesion was nonenhancing on T1-weighted images with gadolinium and bright on T1-weighted images without gadolinium and on T2-weighted images, suggesting proteinaceous fluid content. Fine-needle aspiration near the sternocleidomastoid muscle yielded 30 mL of beige, cloudy fluid containing macrophages, calcifications, and a few epithelial cells.

A 31-year-old man with a 1.5-year history of poorly controlled hypertension (on an angiotensin-converting–enzyme inhibitor and a calcium-channel blocker) and a 6-month history of diabetes mellitus (on insulin and metformin) was referred for evaluation of suspected hypercortisolemia. He reported an 18-kg weight loss over 6 months, lower-limb swelling, proximal muscle weakness, mood changes, and lower back pain. On examination, his BMI was 20 kg/m2 and WHR 0.86; he had conjunctival hyperemia, facial and neck erythema with papulopustular eruptions, dilated neck veins, purple striae over the hips and thighs, and proximal muscle atrophy. No lymphadenopathy was detected. Laboratory studies showed lymphopenia, persistent hypokalemia despite supplementation, elevated plasma cortisol and ACTH with loss of diurnal variation, failure to suppress cortisol after an overnight 2-mg dexamethasone suppression test, markedly increased 24-hour urinary free cortisol, elevated chromogranin A, low urinary 5-HIAA, and no significant increase in ACTH or cortisol after CRH administration. Chest CT revealed a 90×66×140 mm smooth-contoured anterior mediastinal mass with central calcifications. Abdominal and cranial CT scans were unremarkable. MRI of the pituitary gland demonstrated a 5×3×3 mm hypointense focus in the posterior part of the anterior lobe.

A 21-year-old woman presented with a gradually enlarging, painless mass in her lower abdomen. Physical examination revealed a firm, non-tender, non-movable mass measuring 8 × 9 cm, protruding through the anterior pelvic wall. Hematology and biochemistry indices were within normal limits. She had no history of trauma, surgery, or relevant family history.

Pelvic MRI demonstrated a well-defined, lobulated mass measuring 12 × 10 × 9 cm in the mid-pelvis. On fat-suppressed T1-weighted images, the lesion was isointense relative to muscle. On fat-suppressed T2-weighted images, it showed heterogeneous hyperintensity with small stippled and patchy hypointense areas, and a surrounding rim of low signal intensity consistent with a capsule or pseudocapsule. Sagittal T2-weighted images showed splaying of the rectus abdominis muscle in an umbrella shape. Diffusion-weighted imaging revealed heterogeneous hyperintensity, with corresponding hypointensity on the ADC map, indicating restricted diffusion. Following gadolinium administration, fat-suppressed T1-weighted images demonstrated heterogeneous enhancement, with greater enhancement in areas of higher T2 signal.

A 73-year-old man was treated for pneumonia when routine chest imaging revealed an incidental mass in the right posterior mediastinum. He had no compressive symptoms or systemic complaints. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed hematocrit 25.7% (normal 38–52%), hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL (normal 13–18 g/dL), red-cell count 3.84 × 10^6/mm^3 (normal 4.0–5.5 × 10^6/mm^3), platelet count 88,000/mm^3 (normal 160,000–410,000/mm^3), and white-cell count 7000/mm^3 (normal 3800–8500/mm^3) with 58.3% neutrophils, 9.0% lymphocytes, and 25% eosinophils (normal 0–7%). A bone marrow smear revealed dysplastic megakaryocytes and erythrocytes without an increased number of blast cells, consistent with refractory cytopenia with multilineage dysplasia. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed a 38-mm oval, well-encapsulated mass in the posterior mediastinum. On MRI, the lesion had moderate signal intensity on both T1-weighted and T2-weighted images. Because the radiographic findings were not typical for neurogenic tumors, the mass was surgically removed.

A 12-year-old boy presented with a 6-month history of a slowly enlarging swelling on the left side of his face. He had no significant medical, family, or developmental history. Extraoral examination revealed a diffuse, hard, noncompressible, nontender swelling over the left cheek and mandibular region, extending from the zygomatic arch to the lower border of the mandible and from the angle of the mouth to the retromolar area; the nasolabial fold was intact. Intraoral examination showed firm, nontender expansion of the left retromolar trigone and molar regions with obliteration of the buccal vestibule and buccolingual cortical expansion. An orthopantomogram demonstrated a unilocular radiolucent lesion extending from the last erupted molar to the retromolar region.

A 48-year-old man with a 12-year history of perianal fistula presented with recent mucinous discharge, pain, and perianal induration. One year earlier, he had undergone incision and drainage of a recurrent perianal abscess. 

On examination, there were two indurated, ulcerative lesions each 7 cm in diameter and three external fistula openings around the anus; there was no inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Upper endoscopy was unremarkable. Colonoscopy showed the internal fistula opening at the right side of the dentate line, with otherwise normal mucosa in the rectum and colon on digital and endoscopic examination.

Abdominopelvic CT and MRI demonstrated a well-defined mass at the level of the anorectal junction extending into the right ischiorectal fossa, with enlarged pelvic lymph nodes but no inguinal nodal or distant metastases.

Histological examination of a biopsy specimen from the indurated area revealed mucinous adenocarcinoma. A serum carcinoembryonic antigen level was within the normal range.

A 75-year-old man with an 80–pack-year smoking history presented with 6 months of progressive chest pain radiating to the back. On examination, he had sharp tenderness along the costovertebral angles; lung auscultation and neurologic examination were normal. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, liver and renal function, and C-reactive protein, were normal. A posteroanterior chest radiograph showed a homogeneous opacity without air bronchograms above the carina, vertically oriented along the right lateral aspect of the thoracic vertebrae, with an obtuse mediastinal border and upper extent above the clavicle, suggestive of a posterior upper mediastinal mass. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a posterior mediastinal tumor with heterogeneous enhancement and extension into the spinal canal. MRI demonstrated a well-defined oblong mass (30×20×35 mm) in the right costovertebral gutter from T1 to T3. The lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with interspersed areas of high signal on both sequences that suppressed on fat-saturation images, confirming a fatty component. Post-contrast fat-suppressed images showed early, intense, heterogeneous enhancement, indicating a highly vascular tumor. The mass extended through the right and left T1–T2 intervertebral foramina, widening both foramina and scalloping the posterior vertebral body and arches without cortical destruction; it filled the anterior epidural space, slightly compressing but not invading the spinal cord. These MRI features were interpreted as consistent with a nonaggressive, mixed mesenchymal, fatty, highly vascular tumor, and an angiomyolipoma was suspected.

A 78-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of progressive swelling on the left side of his face and difficulty opening his mouth, accompanied by paresthesia in the same region for 2 months. He also reported a productive cough and exertional dyspnea for 4 years and had been using inhaled steroids. His smoking history included 5–6 chuttas per day for 50 years.

On examination, there was a diffuse, firm, slightly tender swelling over the left body and angle of the mandible, with smooth overlying skin. A 2.0 × 1.5 cm hard, non-tender, level I submandibular lymph node was palpable on the left. Intraorally, the interincisal opening was limited to 24 mm, jaw movements were restricted, and teeth #36–38 exhibited grade 2 mobility. A provisional diagnosis of a malignant neoplasm of the left mandible was made, and a differential of metastatic jaw tumor, osteosarcoma, and chondrosarcoma was proposed.

Panoramic and PA skull radiographs showed a radiolucent lesion with irregular borders in the left mandibular body and ramus extending to the condylar head. TMJ tomography demonstrated osseous destruction of the left condyle.

Given his respiratory history, a chest radiograph was obtained, revealing a homogeneous opacity occupying the mid and lower zones of the left lung. CT of the chest identified a 12 × 7 × 6 cm mixed-density mass in the left lung with bronchial stenosis and distal collapse. CT of the mandible confirmed osteolytic areas from the left first molar region through the ramus to the condylar head, associated with an adjacent soft-tissue mass.

An abdominal ultrasound scan showed no evident pathology. Laboratory studies revealed a raised ESR, while serum calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, and acid phosphatase levels were all within normal limits.

A 5-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a progressively painful mass under his left upper eyelid. His ophthalmic history included left-eye cataract extraction at age 1, glaucoma drainage–device placement and endocyclophotocoagulation at age 2, scleral patch grafting, and chronic posterior ocular inflammation in a blind eye. On examination, a firm mass involved both the palpebral and bulbar conjunctiva of the left upper eyelid. B-scan ultrasonography showed a large intraocular mass with extrascleral extension and no calcification. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed an intraocular lesion with extrascleral extension but without optic nerve involvement. An incisional biopsy of the conjunctival mass revealed sheets of poorly differentiated neuroepithelial cells with rosette-like structures. To evaluate for metastatic disease, a whole-body PET scan was performed.
PET imaging demonstrated uptake in the left parotid gland consistent with regional metastasis.

A 72-year-old man presented with intermittent, mild right upper-quadrant abdominal pain for 1 year. The pain was episodic, did not limit his activities, and was not associated with fever, jaundice, or weight loss. He had a 6-year history of hypertension treated pharmacologically; otherwise, his medical history was unremarkable.

On examination, vital signs were stable and his abdomen was soft, nontender, with normal bowel sounds. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and liver-function tests, were within normal limits.

Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 10 × 5 mm echogenic, nonmobile lesion in the gallbladder fundus with detectable vascular flow on Doppler, suggestive of a polyp. The common bile duct was fusiformly dilated to 3 cm in diameter without evidence of obstruction.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 13 × 8 mm enhancing intraluminal polypoidal lesion in the gallbladder fundus without extraluminal extension. The extrahepatic bile duct was fusiformly dilated to 38 mm over a 4.8 cm length, with no obstructing lesion. MRI confirmed these biliary findings and also noted 3.2 mm of symmetrical thickening of the distal common bile duct.

Incidentally, CT revealed a well-defined, longitudinal, hyperdense left infradiaphragmatic paraaortic mass measuring approximately 5 cm. The lesion demonstrated heterogeneous enhancement with a central nonenhancing area and was supplied by a branch of the celiac artery. It abutted the gastric fundus anteriorly, the left adrenal gland inferiorly, and the left diaphragmatic crus posteriorly. The mass had a mean noncontrast attenuation of +40 HU and a maximum postcontrast attenuation of +90 HU, with absolute and relative washout of 56.8 % and 29.8 %, respectively. 

On MRI, the mass was iso- to hypointense on T1-weighted images and low to intermediate signal on T2-weighted and fat-suppressed images, with a central cystic area. The solid component showed diffusion restriction. There were no intralesional fat or flow voids.

A 24-year-old woman presented with a progressively enlarging, asymptomatic mass just above her right eyebrow that she first noticed at age 22. She had no prior medical history. On examination, the skin over the lateral right eyebrow was slightly distended by a 2.5 cm dome-shaped, smooth, elastic, soft mass. The lesion was mobile relative to the skin but appeared fixed to deeper tissue; it became more prominent with forceful jaw closure and there was no facial palsy. One month later, MRI showed a 2.0 cm mass between the superficial and deep temporal fascia. The lesion had homogenous high signal intensity relative to muscle on both T1- and T2-weighted images, and the signal was uniformly suppressed on fat-suppressed T2-weighted images. Based on these findings, the tumor was diagnosed as a lipoma or an angiolipoma.

A 74-year-old man with a history of interstitial pneumonia presented with one month of right-sided chest pain that worsened with inspiration and severe sweating confined to his right arm and thoracic area, accompanied by a cold sensation. He denied abnormal sensation or muscle weakness. Six months earlier, chest CT had shown dense infiltrates in the ventral subpleural regions of the right upper and middle lobes; on admission these shadows had enlarged. Oral antibiotic therapy failed to improve the infiltrates, and he was admitted for further evaluation.

On examination, he was sweating profusely on the right arm and right thorax. Vital signs were blood pressure 150/78 mmHg, pulse 71/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. A pleural friction rub was heard over the right chest. The skin on the right arm, chest, and back was moister and cooler than the left. Thermography revealed decreased surface temperature over the right arm and right thorax corresponding to dermatomes C5–T12. Pupils were equal and reactive; eyelids were not droopy. Neurological examination showed no sensory deficits or abnormal reflexes.

He had no history of smoking, trauma, or asbestos exposure. His medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and varicose veins, treated with candesartan and ezetimibe. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 9,000/μL and C-reactive protein of 1.14 mg/dL. Intravenous antibiotics were started on admission, but his symptoms, inflammatory markers, and imaging findings did not improve. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage revealed macrophages 65.1%, lymphocytes 4.8%, neutrophils 29.9%, and eosinophils 0.2%, with no microorganisms or malignant cells. A transbronchial lung biopsy showed no malignancy or specific inflammation.

A 43-year-old man presented with an 8-month history of a painless swelling on the buccal mucosa of his lower lip. He reported no history of trauma. On examination, the lesion was soft, well circumscribed, freely mobile relative to surrounding tissues, and covered by intact mucosa. There were no overlying ulcerations or discoloration. Vital signs were within normal limits, and the remainder of the head and neck examination was unremarkable. With a provisional clinical diagnosis of a benign neoplasm of the oral mucosa, excisional biopsy was planned under local anesthesia.

A 66-year-old woman was referred after presenting with chest pain and dyspnea. She was diagnosed with cardiac tamponade and underwent pericardial tap, yielding 90 mL of thick, bloody fluid. Her surgical history included cholecystectomy and tonsillectomy; there was no known history of malignancy.  

Pericardial fluid cytology (cell-block) showed:  
- Clusters of highly malignant-appearing cells with focal glandular arrangements  
- Many cells with vacuolated (clear) cytoplasm, some resembling signet-ring cells  
- Mitotic rate >10 per 10 high-power fields  

Immunocytochemical and special stains on the cell block demonstrated:  
- CK7 positive, EMA positive, CK20 negative  
- Mucicarmine negative; PAS with diastase positive in nonvacuolated cells  
- Focal positivity for CA 19.9, CA 125, E-Cadherin, BER-EP4, CK5/6  
- Negative staining for TTF-1, Calretinin, B72.3, ER, P63, CDX-2, CD99, CD117

A 68-year-old man with a history of a parathyroidectomy in 2011 (operative details unavailable) underwent routine laboratory testing in 2019, which revealed an albumin-corrected serum calcium level of 16.3 mg/dL (normal albumin) and an ionized calcium of 1.93 mmol/L. He denied fatigue, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, constipation, or neuropsychiatric symptoms; his only complaint was difficulty hitting high notes when singing. Additional laboratory results were significant for a PTH level of 2692 pg/mL, alkaline phosphatase of 165 mg/dL, magnesium of 1.3 mg/dL, creatinine of 1.65 mg/dL (clearance 44 mL/min/1.73 m^2), and 25-hydroxyvitamin D of 24.7 ng/mL. After initial medical management, he was transferred for further evaluation.

On transfer, a neck ultrasound demonstrated two thyroid nodules (1.4 and 0.4 cm) without evidence of parathyroid gland enlargement. A Tc-99m sestamibi SPECT/CT scan revealed a 7.2-cm right-sided mass extending from the lower neck into the posterior mediastinum, displacing the esophagus, with only mild, nonspecific sestamibi uptake. Endoscopic ultrasound–guided fine-needle aspiration of the mass showed hypercellular parathyroid tissue, and the aspirate PTH level was >5000 pg/mL. No distant disease was detected on PET/CT. Other laboratory tests typical in the workup for primary hyperparathyroidism, such as 24-hour urine calcium, were foregone given that suspicion for familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia was low and the severity of the hypercalcemia met criteria for definitive surgical management.

A 64-year-old man with diabetic nephropathy underwent an ABO-incompatible living-donor kidney transplantation in August 2011. He received induction with basiliximab and maintenance immunosuppression with cyclosporine (target trough 150–200 ng/mL initially, tapering to 30–50 ng/mL long-term), mycophenolate mofetil (1500 mg daily), and methylprednisolone (maintenance 4 mg daily). His postoperative course was uncomplicated, with a serum creatinine of 1.3 mg/dL and an eGFR of 48 mL/min/1.73 m2 at six years.

Seventy-two months after transplantation, he presented with right colic pain, abdominal distention, and diarrhea. Noncontrast abdominal CT revealed a solitary 11 cm well-circumscribed, lobulated mass in the lower abdomen without evidence of distant metastasis. CT colonography demonstrated the mass arising from the small intestine, extending extraluminally, with internal low-attenuation areas suggestive of necrosis and a trapped air bubble, raising concern for mucosal ulceration. On MRI, the lesion was moderately hyperintense on fat-suppressed T2-weighted images, showed high signal intensity on diffusion-weighted images, and exhibited weak enhancement on contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images.

The preoperative differential diagnosis included a gastrointestinal stromal tumor or post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder of the small intestine.

A 40-year-old woman with no known past medical history presented with a left-breast nodule discovered on self-examination. On physical examination, she had diffuse café au lait spots over her body. Breast examination revealed multiple café au lait macules, and in the left upper-inner quadrant a 20 × 10 mm, well-circumscribed, firm, painless, mobile nodule without overlying skin changes; the axilla was free of lymphadenopathy. Mammography demonstrated very dense breasts with thin, even skin and no architectural distortion. Breast ultrasound showed two oval, anechoic, well-defined masses in the left breast: one in the superomedial quadrant measuring 20 × 10 × 6 mm and a second 6 mm lesion in the inferolateral quadrant.

A previously healthy 3-year-old boy presented with a 6-week history of cough, fever, and vomiting refractory to multiple courses of antibiotics. Sequential chest radiographs demonstrated persistent right middle and lower lobe consolidation. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 9 mm, mildly enhancing, exophytic endobronchial mass arising from the right bronchus intermedius, with associated right lower lobe consolidation, bronchiectasis, and air trapping.

An 8-year-old boy presented with a 6-month history of progressive headache and visual loss in his left eye. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 4 m in the right eye and no light perception in the left eye; the left pupil had no light reflex. A noncontrast CT scan showed an isodense mass in the sellar and suprasellar regions measuring 19 mm × 30 mm, with extension into the sphenoid sinus. Contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated a 2.0 cm × 1.5 cm × 1.0 cm solid mass centered in the anterior pituitary gland, with a large suprasellar component compressing and displacing the optic chiasm and extending toward the floor of the third ventricle; there was invasion of the right cavernous sinus. Pituitary function tests revealed a prolactin level of 96 ng/mL (normal range, 2–17 ng/mL) with all other pituitary hormones within normal limits, suggesting pituitary stalk compression by a nonfunctional tumor. In view of possible macroprolactinoma, the prolactin assay was repeated after 1:100 serum dilution and yielded 27.2 ng/mL. A tentative diagnosis of a nonsecreting pituitary adenoma was made, and the patient was scheduled for an extended endoscopic endonasal transtuberculum/transplanum approach for tumor resection.

A 47-year-old man presented with a 10-month history of pain and swelling over the posterior aspect of his left shoulder. The pain worsened with arm movement, particularly on raising the arm overhead, and he noted mild weakness of the left shoulder. He was otherwise healthy and had no respiratory symptoms.

On examination, there was a hard, tender swelling over the posterior left scapula measuring 11×15×8 cm, with a rough texture and diminished sensation in the left suprascapular nerve distribution. Active flexion and abduction at the left glenohumeral joint were painful. Distal neurovascular examination of the left upper limb was normal. Pain was rated 8/10 on a visual analog scale, and his Revised Musculoskeletal Tumor Society Score was 13/30.

Serum investigations were normal except for an elevated alkaline phosphatase level of 178 IU/L.

Conventional radiographs of the left shoulder showed a large, homogeneous, expansile lesion of the scapula with irregular but well-defined margins and a ground-glass matrix; internal septations compartmentalized the lesion. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-defined expansile scapular mass with intact overlying cortices, endosteal scalloping, high central signal intensity, and scalloped low-signal rims.

A 78-year-old man was referred for evaluation of an ulcerated lesion of the left retromolar trigone. He reported feeling “a hole in his gums” behind his lower left teeth; the duration was unknown. His medical history was notable only for glaucoma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. On examination, there was a 0.4-cm round papule with mixed red and white coloration and indurated borders on the left retromolar pad. Portions of the lesion had a vaguely verruciform (warty) white appearance. The lesion was mildly tender but otherwise asymptomatic, and the rest of the oral mucosa was unremarkable. A panoramic radiograph showed no bone involvement. The clinical differential diagnosis included chronic ulcer, exuberant granulation tissue, irritated papilloma, and squamous cell carcinoma. A biopsy of the lesion and surrounding mucosa was performed.

Histologic examination showed soft tissue covered by benign-appearing stratified squamous epithelium with overlying keratotic material. Within the surface epithelium, there was suprabasilar (intraepithelial) clefting and elongated, test-tube–shaped rete ridges. The lesion also exhibited basilar hyperplasia and dyskeratosis. A slender, keratin-filled crevice extended from the epithelial surface to the region of suprabasilar clefting.

A 3-year-old girl presented with a 1½-month history of a painful, ulcerated swelling in the upper outer quadrant of her right breast. On examination, there was a soft-to-firm, ill-defined, ulcerated mass measuring 3.0 × 2.2 × 1.5 cm. Doppler ultrasonography showed a well-circumscribed, hypoechoic lesion with scant internal vascularity. Fine-needle aspiration cytology revealed cellular clusters and single cells with round, centrally placed nuclei, bland chromatin, abundant granular cytoplasm, and indistinct cytoplasmic borders; the background contained occasional macrophages. The cytologic impression was a fibrocystic lesion of the breast with apocrine metaplasia. The skin nodule was excised. Grossly, the specimen measured 4.5 × 2.5 × 1.4 cm with a central 1 × 1 cm skin ulceration; on sectioning, there was a solid, light-gray, well-circumscribed subcutaneous nodule measuring 3.0 × 2.2 × 1.5 cm. Histologic examination showed sheets of polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm and vesicular nuclei. Mitoses were sparse (<1 per 10 high-power fields), and there was no necrosis. The tumor cells were Periodic Acid–Schiff positive and diastase resistant.

A 59-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of anemia. Over the prior month, she had experienced progressive fatigue and malaise but denied fever or weight loss. Her medical history included mild mitral and aortic valve insufficiency and atrial fibrillation, managed with digitalis, an ACE inhibitor, and acenocoumarol (target INR, 2.5). 

On examination, she was pale and afebrile, with no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. 

Laboratory studies revealed:  
– Hemoglobin, 7.2 g/dL; mean corpuscular volume, 94.8 fL  
– White blood cell count, 3,400/µL (56% neutrophils, 38% lymphocytes, 5% monocytes, 1% eosinophils)  
– Platelet count, 756,000/µL; peripheral smear showed giant platelets without dysplastic features or leukoerythroblastic changes  
– Serum ferritin, 12× upper limit of normal; lactate dehydrogenase, 1.8× upper limit of normal; other chemistries within normal limits  

Bone marrow aspiration yielded a “dry tap.” Core biopsy showed a hypercellular marrow with marked reticulin fibrosis; prominent megakaryocytic hyperplasia with clustering and dysplastic under- or non-lobulated nuclei; few (<5%) small CD61-positive cells with prominent nucleoli lacking CD34 expression; myeloid hyperplasia with left shift and normal blast count; and diminished erythroid precursors.  

Molecular testing for BCR-ABL and JAK2 V617F mutations was negative.

A 50-year-old man with stage II nonkeratinizing nasopharyngeal carcinoma treated one year earlier with intensity-modulated radiotherapy and concurrent chemotherapy developed multiple lung metastases, managed with palliative cisplatin-based chemotherapy, maintenance anlotinib, and stereotactic body radiotherapy to the pulmonary lesions. Three months after lung SBRT, routine magnetic resonance imaging of the head showed a solitary, irregularly shaped, cystic lesion with rim enhancement in the left frontal lobe.

A 62-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of burning sensation and discomfort in her left breast without fever or systemic symptoms. She had hypertension and a remote history of hemorrhoidectomy, dilation and curettage, colonoscopy, and gastroscopy; she was a heavy smoker. On examination, there was a 3 × 3 cm palpable mass in the upper quadrant of the left breast without overlying skin changes. No axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy was noted. Routine blood tests, chest radiograph, and ECG were unremarkable. Breast MRI revealed an ill-defined, deep retroareolar spiculated lesion measuring 3 × 1.5 cm with an early enhancement peak and associated architectural distortion; no axillary lymphadenopathy or skin thickening was identified (BIRADS IV). An excisional biopsy showed breast tissue containing cohesive nests of neoplastic epithelial cells within a dense lymphoid infiltrate. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated that the epithelial cells were positive for cytokeratin AE1/E3 and negative for estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and HER2/neu; the background lymphocytes stained positive for CD3 and CD20.

A 48-year-old man with no history of smoking or betel-nut use and a prior right-tongue squamous cell carcinoma treated by partial glossectomy 9 years earlier presented with progressive dysarthria of 6 months’ duration. Physical examination and initial head and neck CT revealed no obvious mass. Four months later, MRI showed a lesion in the left tongue. Biopsy of that lesion revealed an intermediate-grade adenocarcinoma. On referral, examination at our hospital disclosed a 4×4-cm left ventral tongue mass. 18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated a hypermetabolic process confined to the tongue, without regional lymphadenopathy or distant metastases. The patient underwent wide excision of the left tongue lesion with bilateral selective neck dissection.

A 15-year-old male presented with a 9- to 10-month history of swelling on the left side of the lower jaw. The swelling began small and gradually enlarged; it was initially painless but later became mildly and intermittently painful. Multiple courses of antibiotics and analgesics provided minimal relief. 

On extraoral examination, there was a diffuse, roughly oval, bony-hard swelling (2 cm × 3 cm) over the left mandibular ramus; the overlying skin was normal in color, slightly warm, and a single, tender, mobile left submandibular lymph node (1–1.5 cm) was palpable. Intraorally, there was buccal and lingual cortical expansion in the left retromolar area and a deep periodontal pocket distal to tooth 37. 

Provisional diagnosis was a benign odontogenic lesion. Clinical differential diagnoses included ameloblastoma, odontogenic keratocyst, dentigerous cyst (associated with tooth 38), calcifying odontogenic cyst, calcifying epithelial odontogenic tumor, and ameloblastic fibroma. 

Panoramic radiograph showed a well-defined unilocular radiolucency with corticated borders, extending from the distal of the left second molar to the posterior border of the ramus, superiorly from the coronoid notch to the inferior border of the mandible; root resorption of the second molar was noted. CT and 3D CT scans confirmed a unilocular osteolytic lesion with expansion of both cortical plates and perforation of the lingual cortex. The left third molar was absent, effectively ruling out an associated dentigerous cyst. Routine blood tests were normal. 

An incisional biopsy was performed. Histopathologic examination revealed a cystic cavity lined by odontogenic epithelium with a palisaded basal layer of ameloblast-like cells and a superficial stellate reticulum–like layer. The capsule was dense and fibrous, with numerous engorged blood vessels.

A 36-year-old right-handed man presented with 3–4 months of difficulty flexing his right ring finger. Forming a fist was associated with a palpable “clunk” in the palm and pain and heaviness over the thumb through ring fingers, which resolved on opening the hand. He denied trauma and had no comorbidities. On examination, there was triggering of the right ring finger at the palm without visible swelling or thenar wasting. With the finger extended, deep palpation elicited a firm swelling along the ring-finger flexor tendon that moved proximally and disappeared on flexion; in that position, he experienced pain and heaviness over the radial three and a half digits, and Tinel’s sign was positive at the wrist only during extension. Phalen’s test and transillumination were negative. Plain radiography was unremarkable. High-resolution ultrasonography demonstrated a well-defined, hypoechoic, partially compressible oval lesion (19 × 8 mm), without internal vascularity, arising from the flexor digitorum profundus tendon of the ring finger just distal to the palmar aponeurosis; the lesion glided longitudinally with finger movement, and the median nerve appeared normal. These findings were suggestive of a lipoma or giant-cell tumor of the FDP tendon.

A 4-year-old female spayed Siberian husky was evaluated for a 2-week history of right-eye redness and mild blepharospasm that had worsened over time. The dog remained visual OU with intact menace and dazzle reflexes and had normal direct and consensual pupillary light reflexes OU. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy OD revealed temporal iris thickening with an irregular pupillary margin from 7 to 12 o’clock and rubeosis iridis. Rebound tonometry showed an IOP of 5 mmHg OD (12 mmHg OS). Schirmer tear tests and fluorescein staining were normal OU. Fundic examination OD was unremarkable.

The dog was treated for anterior uveitis with topical diclofenac and artificial tears, with recheck recommended. Three months later, recurrent OD uveitis was noted despite ongoing therapy. Examination revealed temporal iris thickening with rubeosis, mild aqueous flare, and a newly visible iridociliary cyst from 9 to 11 o’clock OD; IOP was 9 mmHg OD and 25 mmHg OS. Topical prednisolone acetate replaced diclofenac.

One month after that, iris thickening had progressed from 7 to 3 o’clock OD with persistent pupillary margin irregularity; there was no flare, IOP was 15 mmHg OD, and fluorescein staining remained negative. Medical therapy was continued. Given disease progression and concern for an intraocular mass, enucleation of the right eye was recommended for definitive diagnosis and therapy.

A 2-year-9-month-old boy was brought for reluctance to use his right upper limb for 5 months and morning discomfort. He was born at term without perinatal complications; development and family history were unremarkable. He received BCG vaccination in the left arm at 7 months. On examination, the right arm was thinner than the left with marked tenderness; passive range of motion at the shoulder and elbow was full. He used only his left hand when playing. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies, including white blood cell count (7.6×10^3/μL) and C-reactive protein (0.01 mg/dL), were within normal limits. Plain radiographs of the right humerus showed an 8×3 mm oval lucent lesion in the proximal metaphysis with surrounding osteosclerosis and unilateral cortical thickening. CT demonstrated an intramedullary lucent area with adjacent cortical thickening and very fine internal calcification. MRI revealed the lesion to be isointense on T1-weighted images and iso- to hyperintense on STIR, surrounded by diffuse bone marrow edema. Given the age, metaphyseal location, imaging findings, and history of BCG vaccination, subacute osteomyelitis (including BCG osteomyelitis) was initially suspected, and osteoid osteoma was also considered.

A 15-year-old boy with salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia diagnosed in childhood and maintained on glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement presented with progressive, painless enlargement of both testes. On examination, he was of normal stature (BMI 21.2 kg/m2). There was a firm, painless 8 cm mass in the right testis and a 10 cm mass in the left testis. Semen analysis showed azoospermia. Laboratory studies demonstrated elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone at 24.1 nmol/L (reference 1.5–6.4 nmol/L). Serum tumor markers were not elevated: α-fetoprotein 1 ng/mL (0–44), β-human chorionic gonadotropin <12 IU/L (<5). Scrotal ultrasonography revealed bilateral, hyperechogenic, hypervascular lesions measuring 8.6×3.5 cm on the right and 8.4×5.5 cm on the left. Given concern for malignant testicular neoplasm, bilateral incisional biopsies were performed. Frozen sections showed complete replacement of normal testicular parenchyma by sheets and nests of large round to polygonal cells with well-defined borders, abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, round central nuclei, and intervening dense fibrous stroma. Reinke crystals were not identified. At this point, the differential diagnosis included Leydig cell tumor or mass-forming testicular adrenal rest tumor.

A 37‐year‐old man presented with a two‐year history of gradually progressive pain and swelling of the right wrist. Initially the pain was dull and intermittent but over six months became continuous and throbbing, worse with movement and relieved by rest. He denied trauma, constitutional symptoms, or prior interventions. On examination, there was a nonpitting, tender swelling over the extensor and supinator aspects of the wrist with tense overlying skin; wrist motion was restricted and painful but there was no warmth, erythema, or transillumination. Examination of other joints and systems was normal.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, coagulation profile, electrolytes, renal and liver function tests, and HIV serology, were all within normal limits. 

Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the right wrist showed lytic lesions of the carpal bones and the bases of the third and fourth metacarpals. Subsequent MRI of the wrist demonstrated ill-defined, moderately hypointense signals throughout all carpal bones except the pisiform, with involvement of the bases of the second through fifth metacarpals, minimal cortical thinning, and near-obliteration of the intercarpal joints. Based on these imaging findings, the leading considerations were primary lymphoma of bone and giant cell tumour of the tendon sheath.

A 69-year-old man was referred for evaluation of hilar bile duct stenosis. His history was significant for laparoscopic sigmoidectomy 4 years earlier for stage IV sigmoid colon adenocarcinoma with synchronous liver metastases. He underwent partial hepatectomy of segment 7 and radiofrequency ablation of segment 8 lesions, and, two years later, resection of a local post-RFA recurrence. He had received no adjuvant chemotherapy.

On presentation, vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies showed cholestatic liver enzyme elevation. Enhanced CT demonstrated wall thickening and enhancement of the hilar bile duct. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography, endoscopic retrograde cholangiography, and intraductal ultrasound revealed a mass protruding into the lumen of the hilar bile duct. Brush cytology returned class IV cells. Based on imaging and cytology, a hilar cholangiocarcinoma (Bismuth type II) was diagnosed. The patient underwent right portal vein embolization followed by extended right hemihepatectomy with extrahepatic bile duct resection.

Gross examination revealed a 3 cm tumor in the hilar bile duct wall. Microscopic evaluation showed a moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma involving the common hepatic duct wall with perineural invasion, but without vascular invasion, lymph node metastasis, or intraepithelial neoplasia at the tumor margin.

A woman in her mid-30s presented with a 2-year history of recurrent pain and swelling in the left proximal leg. She had undergone resection of a biopsy-proven chondromyxoid fibroma of the left proximal tibia 4 years earlier and was asymptomatic for 2 years postoperatively. The current swelling had a rapid onset and was accompanied by pain.

On examination, there was a 20 × 15 cm globular, hard, tender mass over the proximal tibia, adherent to bone. The previous surgical scar was healthy, and distal neurovascular examination was intact.

Plain radiographs of the left tibia showed a lytic, eccentric, expansile meta-diaphyseal lesion with cortical breach and a sunburst periosteal reaction. MRI revealed a T2 hyperintense, lytic, expansile lesion with chondroid matrix and periosteal elevation, with focal invasion of the tibialis anterior and posterior muscles and the medial gastrocnemius head. PET-CT demonstrated a metabolically active lesion in the proximal tibial shaft and subcentimetric left popliteal lymph nodes.

Core-needle biopsy of the lesion showed abundant cartilaginous matrix with chondrocytes in lacunae, moderate nuclear atypia, coarse hyperchromatic nuclei, mitoses, myxoid change, and areas of necrosis.

A 50-year-old man with chronic glomerulonephritis underwent a living-donor renal transplant in 1998. He received prednisolone, cyclosporine (withdrawn after 1 year), and azathioprine, developing posttransplant diabetes mellitus but no rejection episodes. In 2007, nine years post-transplant, he noted 12 days of progressive left-eye protrusion associated with pain, redness, and diminished vision. He denied fever, weight loss, headache, vomiting, or focal neurologic symptoms. On examination, he was afebrile, blood pressure 120/80 mm Hg, with no lymphadenopathy. The left eye showed proptosis, conjunctival redness, hemorrhagic chemosis, and lid edema; the right eye was normal. Visual acuity was limited to light perception with inaccurate light projection; ocular movements were restricted in all directions. Intraocular pressure was 24 mm Hg. Fundoscopy revealed blurred disc margins, ischemia of the superior nasal retina, and macular chorioretinal folds. MRI of the brain demonstrated a 2.5 × 1.6 × 2 cm, mildly irregular, isointense lesion in the superior left orbit, predominantly extraconal with intraconal extension, abutting and partially encasing the optic nerve, displacing extraocular muscles, and with areas of bony erosion. Radiologists considered possibilities of lymphoma, metastasis, or orbital pseudotumor.

A 70-year-old man presented to ophthalmology with sudden bilateral vision decrease (BCVA 20/40 OD, 20/50 OS). He had type 2 diabetes with mild non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages, macular edema). Over several months, he developed intermittent blurry vision; over the past 2 months, he awoke with subjective total color vision loss lasting 1.5–2 hours (now up to half a day) and experienced occasional white-out vision lasting up to 7 hours. He reported jaw claudication, fevers to 101°F once or twice weekly for weeks, and drenching night sweats for years, but denied fatigue, weight loss, anorexia, headache, or focal neurologic deficits. Examination showed BCVA 20/50 OU, no afferent pupillary defect, normal Ishihara plates, normal Humphrey Visual Field 30-2, and normal anterior segment and ocular motility. Fundoscopy revealed mild temporal optic nerve pallor, bilateral macular edema, and multiple intraretinal hemorrhages with white centers (Roth spots) in both posterior poles. Given these findings, a complete blood count with differential, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level were ordered.

A 34-year-old Filipino man presented with a 4-month history of left eye proptosis, diplopia, and chemosis without epistaxis, headache, or nasal obstruction. Endoscopic nasal examination revealed a mass at the level of the left middle turbinate extending into the left nasal roof and eroding the upper nasal septum. Ophthalmologic evaluation showed mild left proptosis with full extraocular movements, no papilledema, and normal visual acuity. Contrast-enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated an expansile, mildly enhancing soft-tissue mass in the anterosuperior nasal cavity encroaching on the left orbital cavity, with remodeling of the left medial orbital wall and extension to the level of the cribriform plate, along with retention of secretions in the left frontal sinus. MRI (T1-weighted postcontrast) showed an enhancing mass reaching the nasal vault without dural enhancement or intracranial extension; T2 and non–contrast T1 sequences revealed no intratumoral hemorrhage or cystic change. The patient underwent endoscopic endonasal resection, which disclosed a cystic mass occupying the left fronto-ethmoid region with destruction of the anterior skull base and erosion of the left lamina papyracea; the dura was exposed but intact, and no cerebrospinal fluid leak was noted. A routine functional endoscopic sinus surgery was completed after tumor excision.

A 3-month-old male infant was referred for evaluation of pallor, abdominal distension, petechial rashes, and recurrent respiratory infections since birth. Previous records documented persistent anemia and thrombocytopenia. On admission, hemoglobin was 6.3 g/dL, the total leukocyte count was 83,000 cells/mm3, and platelets were 35,000 cells/mm3. A skeletal survey was obtained to assess for congenital infections. Radiographs of the lower limbs showed diffuse osteopenia with prominent calcific zones at the metaphyseal ends of the long bones. A dorsolumbar spine film demonstrated osteopenia with pronounced vertebral end plates. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed hepatomegaly with diffusely increased hepatic echogenicity. Facial features were unremarkable, and chromosomal analysis by karyotyping showed no anomalies. Liver and renal function tests were within normal limits. TORCH serologic testing (IgG antibodies for toxoplasmosis, rubella, cytomegalovirus, and herpesvirus) was negative. Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbosacral spine and pelvis demonstrated abnormal marrow signal intensities in both iliac bones.

A 40-year-old right-handed man with no significant past history presented with a 2-week history of a painless swelling of the left thumb following a wooden-splinter injury. He noted profuse bleeding with minimal touch and failed a trial of topical antibiotics. On examination, there was a firm, well-circumscribed, exophytic red mass measuring approximately 2×3×4 cm arising from the eponychial fold of the left thumb, with an irregular surface, areas of ulceration, and necrosis. The lesion bled easily but was non-tender. Thumb interphalangeal motion was normal, and there was no regional lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. Plain radiographs showed a soft-tissue–dense swelling over the interphalangeal joint without bony involvement. MRI of the thumb demonstrated a large hypervascular exophytic lesion of the distal thumb, highly suspicious for malignancy, with no osseous invasion but inseparable from extensor tendon fibers. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed multiple enlarged left axillary lymph nodes but no abdominal or pelvic metastases. An incisional biopsy showed extensively ulcerated and necrotic skin with bacterial colonies and tiny foci of capillary proliferation; immunohistochemistry for HHV8 was negative, yet “malignancy, namely, squamous cell carcinoma could not be ruled out from this specimen.”

A 74-year-old woman was admitted with melena that began several weeks after a Roux-en-Y cystjejunostomy performed for a presumed pancreatic pseudocyst. Initial upper endoscopy showed multiple gastric erosions and a positive urease test for Helicobacter pylori; she received proton-pump inhibitor and antibiotic therapy. Despite healing of the erosions on repeat endoscopy, melena persisted and she required transfusion of 20 units of packed red blood cells. Colonoscopy revealed diverticulosis in the ascending and transverse colon without stigmata of recent bleeding. An abdominal CT scan and a technetium-99m–labeled red-blood-cell scan were nondiagnostic. A small-bowel barium study demonstrated a retro-gastric lesion causing extrinsic compression of the stomach.

A 55-year-old Pakistani woman presented with a painless, freely movable, irregular outgrowth behind her left shoulder. The lesion began as a small nodule approximately 35 years earlier during her first pregnancy and had grown slowly since. She had no history of similar lesions and no family history of skin tumors. Vital signs were within normal limits, and systemic examination, including lymph nodes, was unremarkable. A sonogram of the shoulder revealed a 7 × 6 cm solid, heterogeneous mass. The patient underwent surgical excision of the lesion with preoperative intravenous fluids, followed by defect coverage using a rhomboid flap and drain placement.

A 25‐year‐old woman reported one month of progressive pain, swelling, and decreased movement (flexion and extension) of the left third finger without trauma or other comorbidities. On examination, there was focal tenderness over the proximal phalanx and limited flexion and extension at the metacarpophalangeal joint of that finger. Initial radiographs showed a lytic, hypertranslucent lesion with cortical expansion of the proximal phalanx. One month later, the lesion had enlarged significantly on repeat radiographs. An incisional biopsy revealed a mesenchymal proliferation of uniformly distributed osteoclast‐type giant cells interspersed with mononuclear cells lacking cytologic atypia and showing mitotic activity. MRI demonstrated a large, well-marginated, expansile lesion involving the proximal two-thirds of the third proximal phalanx, measuring 27.0 × 24.0 × 24.0 mm, with low T1 signal, high T2 signal, and central cystic areas; cortical destruction was evident, and adjacent extensor tendons and joint structures were preserved.

A 6-year-old boy presented with a 1-month history of progressive, bilateral neck swelling. Six months earlier, a lymph node biopsy at a peripheral hospital had shown a lymphoproliferative process, and he had been treated with prednisolone (30 mg daily for 5 months) without improvement. On presentation, he was in fair general condition and denied fever, night sweats, weight loss, cough, or other systemic symptoms. Examination revealed multiple firm, mobile, non-tender cervical and submandibular lymph nodes bilaterally, the largest measuring 8 × 10 cm, with biopsy scars and limited neck mobility; there was no hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, white-cell count 17 700/mm3 (87% neutrophils, 10% lymphocytes, 2% eosinophils, 2% monocytes), platelet count 548 000/mm3, sodium 129.2 mmol/L, magnesium 1.7 mg/dL, calcium 7.9 mg/dL, ALT 5 U/L, and normal values for random blood glucose, urea, creatinine, lactate dehydrogenase, alkaline phosphatase, coagulation tests, and serologies for HIV, hepatitis B and C, and SARS-CoV-2. Ultrasound of the neck revealed multiple enlarged lymph nodes bilaterally, the largest measuring 46 × 26 mm. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated multiple enlarged lymph nodes at cervical levels IB through VI, bilateral supraclavicular and mediastinal regions, bilateral axillae, and retroperitoneum.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of an anterior neck swelling that fluctuated in size. She reported mild fatigue but denied symptoms of thyroid or parathyroid dysfunction and had no compressive symptoms. On examination, the mass measured approximately 5 × 5 cm, was soft, smooth, non‐tender, and there were no palpable cervical lymph nodes. Her weight was stable, and vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies showed normal triiodothyronine, thyroxine, and thyroid-stimulating hormone levels; the serum adjusted calcium was 2.37 mmol/L. Fine‐needle aspiration of the swelling yielded clear fluid; cytology demonstrated “scanty foamy histiocytes.” A neck ultrasound revealed a 7.5 cm cystic lesion inferior to the thyroid gland with no internal vascularity and appearances “not consistent with a thyroid cyst,” and the origin of the cyst could not be determined. Subsequent MRI showed a pretracheal, pyramidal‐shaped, bilobed cystic lesion measuring 5.3 × 2.9 × 5.8 cm in continuity with the lower portions of both thyroid lobes. Differential diagnosis at this stage included a thymic cyst extending into the neck.

A 66-year-old woman with a history of hypertension presented with a 4-week history of progressive breathlessness and ankle swelling. Initial measurement of N-terminal pro B-type natriuretic peptide was elevated at 2829 ng/L (normal <125 ng/L). On Day 10 she was assessed by the heart failure service. Vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed mid-shin oedema, a grade III mid-diastolic murmur, raised jugular venous pressure, and clear lung fields. The ECG showed normal sinus rhythm. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a large, mobile, echo-dense, heterogeneous mass arising from the right atrium, attached to the interatrial septum, and extending into the right ventricle, measuring 90 × 42 mm. The tricuspid valve was held open by the mass; the basal right ventricular dimension was 43.5 mm and the tricuspid annular dimension was 49.7 mm. The inferior vena cava measured 19.1 mm with minimal respiratory variation. Chest radiography showed a dilated right atrium and a small left pleural effusion. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis confirmed an isolated mass within the right atrium extending into the right ventricle and superior vena cava, with no evidence of distant metastases or remote thromboembolism. Coronary angiography showed moderate proximal left anterior descending atheroma and normal right and circumflex arteries.

A 68-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of a slowly evolving, asymptomatic, raised, slightly pigmented skin lesion measuring 25–30 mm in diameter on the dorsum of her left hand. She was in otherwise good health, with no predisposing conditions or medications. Cutaneous examination was otherwise normal. Clinically, the lesion was first regarded as a squamous cell carcinoma. Because of its size and appearance, a wide local excision of the skin and underlying subcutaneous tissue was performed, and the defect was reconstructed with a full-thickness skin graft harvested from the anterior surface of the left forearm. The donor site was closed primarily. The surgical specimen was submitted for pathological evaluation.

A 48-year-old farmer with a history of hypertension presented with diaphoresis, epigastric pain, and lower-extremity edema for 2 months. He was afebrile and normotensive. Examination revealed xanthelasmas of the eyelids, muffled heart sounds, and mild peripheral edema. Chest radiography showed cardiomegaly. Electrocardiography demonstrated sinus tachycardia with low voltages. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed preserved biventricular systolic function, no valvular disease, and massive pericardial effusion with hemodynamic compromise. Pericardiocentesis yielded a mononuclear exudate without malignant cells. A Quantiferon-TB Gold test was positive. Laboratory studies showed normal renal and lipid profiles and elevated acute-phase reactants. He was treated empirically for acute pericarditis with ibuprofen and colchicine. A follow-up echocardiogram showed recurrent large pericardial effusion without tamponade and possible ascending aortic dilation. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed soft-tissue encasement of the aorta from the arch through the iliac arteries (“coated aorta”) and a retroperitoneal soft-tissue mass causing right hydronephrosis and renal atrophy.

A 25-year-old man with a 9-year history of focal seizures involving involuntary right arm tremors presented with recent aggravation of seizure activity and new right arm weakness. Neurologic examination was unremarkable at initial presentation. He had no stigmata or family history of neurofibromatosis. Initial brain MRI showed a 1.5×1.0×1.1 cm mass in the left precentral gyrus that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and exhibited intense gadolinium enhancement with surrounding edema but no cystic change or calcification. The initial radiologic differential diagnosis included pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma, ganglioglioma, and dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor. The patient declined surgery and remained stable on antiepileptic therapy; follow-up MRI 2 years later showed no change. Nine years after the initial MRI, he reported prolonged seizures and progressive right arm weakness with grade IV motor strength. CT and MRI at that time revealed an increase in the enhancing mass to 2.3×1.9×1.6 cm and the development of a 5.5 cm peritumoral cyst without calcification or cyst-wall enhancement.

A 13-month-old girl was evaluated for a 4-month history of bilateral parotid gland swelling, 2 weeks of intermittent fever, and loss of appetite. She had no history of skin rash, diarrhea, otorrhea, exophthalmos, polyuria, or polydipsia. On examination, she was icteric without rash. The left parotid measured 5×7 cm, the right 6×7 cm; both were tender and firm with ill-defined borders. Cervical lymph nodes were palpable, each about the size of a soybean. Lung auscultation revealed coarse breath sounds without rales. The liver edge was 6–7 cm below the right costal margin, and the spleen edge was 3 cm below the left costal margin. One week later, scattered red-brown papules and macules with light scaling appeared on the trunk, occasionally coalescing into patches.

Laboratory studies showed a normal white-cell count and platelet count, hemoglobin 91 g/L, total bilirubin 128.5 µmol/L, conjugated bilirubin 61.2 µmol/L, aspartate aminotransferase 136.0 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 1025 U/L; other indices were normal. Bone marrow aspiration was normal, and flow cytometry showed no evidence of lymphoproliferative disease. Ultrasound demonstrated obvious bilateral parotid enlargement with multiple cervical lymph nodes, splenomegaly, and hepatomegaly with diffuse nodular-like lesions. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the head showed homogeneous enlargement of both parotid glands and confluent cervical lymph nodes. High-resolution CT of the lungs revealed randomly distributed nodular or reticulonodular opacities with ill-defined margins and cysts of variable wall thickness, size, and shape. Abdominal CT showed multiple round and oval hypodense nodules in the liver. Although bone scintigraphy showed an abnormality in the left temporal bone, head MRI and skeletal radiographs revealed no osteolytic lesions.

A 45-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of a gradually enlarging, asymptomatic swelling of the left maxilla. She denied pain, bleeding, sensory changes, or trauma. Medical and dental histories were unremarkable. On examination, there was facial asymmetry from a smooth, oval, bony-hard, non-tender swelling of the left cheek and intraoral expansion of the left maxillary alveolus extending from the central incisor to the first premolar, buccally and palatally. The overlying mucosa and skin appeared normal. The maxillary canine on that side was congenitally missing. Percussion tests were negative and all adjacent teeth were vital except the left lateral incisor, which was nonvital. There was no mobility or lymphadenopathy.

Panoramic and periapical radiographs showed a diffuse, ill-defined, mixed radiolucent and radiopaque lesion measuring approximately 2.5 × 3.0 cm, with small flecks of calcification, loss of the lamina dura, and divergence but no resorption of the lateral incisor root. The floor of the maxillary sinus was intact. Occlusal radiographs demonstrated buccal cortical expansion. Axial CT revealed a predominantly lytic, expansile, multiloculated lesion 3.3 cm mediolaterally by 2.9 cm anteroposteriorly by 1.0 cm superoinferiorly, containing internal calcifications producing a “soap-bubble” appearance.

Based on the clinical and radiographic findings, a provisional diagnosis of odontogenic myxoma was made. Aspiration was non-productive, and hematologic studies were within normal limits. An incisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia to establish a definitive diagnosis.

A 77-year-old woman from a neuropsychiatric dementia clinic presented with a several-month history of headaches, memory disturbance, and a swollen left periorbital area. Vital signs were within normal limits. On neurologic examination, she was alert but demonstrated mild short-term memory impairment; there were no focal motor or sensory deficits. Laboratory tests revealed:  
• Serum protein electrophoresis demonstrating an IgA-κ monoclonal gammopathy  
• β2-Microglobulin 1.8 mg/L (normal)  
• Kappa free light chain 23.5 mg/L (elevated)  
• IgA 2408.7 mg/dL (elevated)  
• Serum albumin persistently <3 g/dL  
• Remaining serum and urine studies unremarkable  

Brain MRI and CT showed a large heterogeneous signal mass with central necrosis and pial involvement in the left frontal lobe, with adjacent bony destruction and parenchymal edema. Multiple smaller, well-enhancing nodular lesions were noted in both frontal and parietal bones. Skull radiographs demonstrated multiple punched-out radiolucent lesions in the frontal and parietal bones.

A 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed 5 months earlier and treated with metformin and dietary counseling presented with a 2-month history of a gradually enlarging ulcer on the tip of the right second toe. On examination, the toe was swollen, indurated, and discharged fluid, without systemic signs of infection. Diabetic foot evaluation, including assessments for peripheral neuropathy and vascular insufficiency, yielded normal results. An X-ray of the foot showed no bony abnormalities. Lower extremity CT angiography revealed a mass-like lesion with feeding vessels at the toe tip. MRI of the foot demonstrated a cystic lesion at the same site, raising suspicion for a soft tissue tumor rather than a simple diabetic ulcer.

A 32-year-old nulliparous woman presented for routine gynecologic care. She reported no symptoms, had regular menstrual cycles, and was taking combined oral contraceptives. On pelvic examination, the cervix and uterus were normal. Transvaginal ultrasound revealed a 45 mm intracervical mass with heterogeneous multicystic components and well-defined margins. Diagnostic hysteroscopy identified a firm, pale, broad-based polypoid lesion projecting from the endocervical canal; the mass contained multiple cystic spaces and scattered areas of hemorrhage.

A 44-year-old woman underwent MRI of the right shoulder for chronic tendinopathy. Incidentally, an oval axillary mass measuring 4.5 × 2.5 × 1.0 cm was identified. On MRI, the lesion had a slightly lobulated wall, was isointense on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images with low-signal rows, and contained round millimetric hypointense foci; there was marked contrast enhancement on T1-weighted images after gadolinium, without invasion of adjacent structures. On examination, the mass corresponded to a mobile, well-demarcated, painless axillary lymph node. Ultrasound confirmed an oval, regularly circumscribed lesion with heterogeneous echotexture, a hypoechogenic focus in its caudal portion, small intralesional calcifications, and hypervascularity on Doppler imaging. Bilateral mammography was normal.

A 23-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of a gradually enlarging swelling of the right maxilla. On examination, there was asymmetry of the right midface due to a 4 cm × 3 cm hard, nontender bony expansion of the right maxilla. Intraoral inspection showed buccal and palatal cortical expansion from the right central incisor to the first premolar, with intact overlying mucosa and obliteration of the maxillary vestibule. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated a well-circumscribed unilocular radiolucency extending from the right central incisor to the second premolar region, containing focal radiopaque material. CT imaging confirmed a large expansile lytic lesion arising from the right maxilla, extending into the right maxillary antrum and the anterior portion of the right nasal cavity.

A 4-year-old boy presented with unsteady standing since age 1. Over three years, he developed gradually worsening restriction of movement in the right knee and a slowly enlarging mass on the inner aspect of the right distal femur and adjacent soft tissues. On examination, there was a 3 × 3 cm firm, tender mass at the medial right knee.  
Plain radiographs of the right femur showed irregularly reduced medullary density in the metaphysis. CT imaging confirmed asymmetrical medullary hypodensity with multiple small cystic areas, irregular cortical thickening, and proximal soft-tissue swelling, without an obvious periosteal reaction.  
The lesion was curetted. Seventeen months later, MRI revealed a local recurrence at the operative site.

A 12‐year‐old boy presented with 3 months of intermittent painful swelling of his right knee. Three months earlier he had fallen and hit the anterior knee, at which time bloody fluid was aspirated in a primary care unit. One month later, swelling recurred after minimal activity. He denied fever, myalgia, or chills and had no significant medical or family history. On examination, there was mild tenderness over the anterior knee, an effusion, and a range of motion of 0° to 130°. There was no palpable mass, instability, redness, or warmth. Arthrocentesis yielded 85 mL of reddish, slightly turbid fluid, with 1200 polymorphonuclear cells per milliliter. T2‐weighted MRI of the right knee showed both (1) an irregularly marginated mass spreading through the suprapatellar pouch, posterior compartment, and intercondylar space and (2) a well‐circumscribed mass confined to the anterior compartment with low‐to‐intermediate heterogeneous signal intensity. Scattered foci of low signal on both T1‐ and T2‐weighted images suggested hemosiderin deposition. With an impression of localized pigmented villonodular synovitis and reactive synovial proliferation, further diagnostic evaluation was planned.

A 24-year-old previously healthy man was referred with a 3-week history of visible, painless, total hematuria. He also reported urinary frequency, straining, and significant weight loss and anorexia. Vital signs were within normal limits. Abdominal examination was unremarkable. Digital rectal examination revealed a lobulated extraluminal mass at the anterior rectal wall; the upper limit could not be reached. Laboratory studies showed neutrophil leukocytosis; all other results were within normal limits.  
Pelvic ultrasound demonstrated a large echogenic mass in the retrovesical area measuring approximately 69 × 69 mm that appeared to invade the posterior bladder wall. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a well-defined hypodense mass measuring 79 × 73 mm between the bladder and rectum, with slight post-contrast enhancement and no enlarged lymph nodes. The radiologist’s impression was a pelvic tumor, “lymphoma probably NHL,” with a differential diagnosis of teratoma.  
Because imaging was inconclusive, a multidisciplinary team performed cystoscopy, revealing a large solid tumor (approximately 80 × 80 mm) occupying the bladder neck and trigone, obscuring the ureteral orifices. Transurethral resection of the tumor was undertaken for diagnostic purposes.

A 38-year-old woman with a recently diagnosed, untreated mucinous borderline ovarian tumor was referred for emergency evaluation. Initial staging studies performed several weeks earlier included:  
• Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showing a large, heterogeneous, lower pelvic cystic mass with a solid component along its superior margin.  
• MRI of the abdomen confirming a multilocular cystic mass (hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images) with a solid component.  

She presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of worsening lower abdominal pain, fever to 38.5 °C, and several episodes of nonbloody vomiting. On examination, she had diffuse abdominal tenderness with signs of peritoneal irritation. Laboratory tests revealed leukocytosis and an elevated C-reactive protein level.

An urgent contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen demonstrated:  
• Large-volume ascitic fluid.  
• Peritoneal enhancement and hyperdensity of the adjacent abdominal fat.  
• On comparison with the CT performed one month earlier, a decrease in the size of the known ovarian mass.

A 67-year-old man underwent contrast-enhanced multidetector CT of the abdomen after an incidental mass was noted in the upper abdomen. He was asymptomatic; physical examination and routine laboratory tests, including liver biochemistry, were unremarkable.

Initial CT (September 2014) showed a 4.2×3.9 cm mass near the head of the pancreas compressing the portal vein. The patient was lost to follow-up and returned 12 months later; repeat CT demonstrated growth of the mass to 4.8×5.0 cm and cavernous transformation of the portal vein.

Exploratory laparotomy revealed a tumour at the upper border of the pancreas and duodenum compressing the portal vein and a 1 cm subcapsular lesion in segment II of the liver. Multiple biopsies of the pancreatic-border lesion and resection of the liver lesion were performed. Histologic examination of both samples showed a spindle cell tumour.

Positron emission tomography–CT showed the lesion to be hypermetabolic (SUVmax 7.3) with no evidence of distant metastases. The patient remained asymptomatic with normal levels of bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, alanine aminotransferase, and aspartate aminotransferase.

A repeat multidetector CT performed two months later showed a soft-tissue–density mass measuring 5.3×5.9×6.4 cm, extending from the superior mesenteric vein/splenic vein confluence to the porta hepatis. On arterial-phase images, it exhibited heterogeneous enhancement with feeding vessels within and around the mass. On portal-venous–phase images, numerous perilesional collaterals surrounded the mass, and a sharp interface (“beak” sign) was seen between the mass and the opacified portion of the main portal vein at the porta hepatis. The pancreatic duct was mildly dilated (3 mm); the biliary tree was not dilated. There was splenomegaly (13.5 cm craniocaudal), but no gastroesophageal varices or ascites.

A 3-year-old boy presented with a 1-week history of nausea, vomiting, and ataxia. His history was notable for extreme prematurity (25 weeks), Chiari I malformation (status post posterior fossa decompression), posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus managed with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt, syringo-pleural shunt for cervicothoracic syringomyelia, autism spectrum disorder, sleep apnea, and CFTR-related metabolic syndrome. 

On initial evaluation, noncontrast head CT showed no shunt malfunction or mass, and he was discharged. He returned the next day with worsening ataxia.
