Contrast MRI of the brain revealed a 29 × 23.9 mm mass near the left foramen of Luschka and diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement throughout the brain and spine; an MRI 4 months earlier had been unremarkable. 

He underwent cervical laminectomy and biopsy of subarachnoid tissue. Histopathology demonstrated numerous apoptotic nuclei and mitotic figures; immunohistochemical staining showed tumor cells positive for Melan-A, HMB-45, and S100, negative for BRAF VE1; Ki-67 was elevated at 10–15%; and PD-L1 staining was negative. Molecular profiling identified an NRAS Q61R mutation and no BRAF V600E mutation.

A 61-year-old woman with cirrhosis secondary to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis presented with a one-month history of increased intermittent confusion and emotional lability. Three months earlier, she had been started on lactulose 30 mL three times daily for presumed hepatic encephalopathy, yet she continued to have episodes of confusion, anxiety, and emotional instability. She also reported occasional shakiness and episodes in which she did not recognize her husband or children. 

On examination, she was awake, alert, and oriented to person, place, and date but was confused about why she was in the hospital and exhibited a tangential thought process. A full neurologic examination showed no cranial nerve deficits, no focal motor or sensory deficits, normal deep tendon reflexes, and no asterixis. 

Laboratory studies revealed an ammonia level of 98 µmol/L and a MELD-Na score of 14. She was continued on lactulose, and rifaximin was added.

An 85-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of gradually increasing painless swelling of the right hemiscrotum and vague abdominal discomfort with intermittent pain. On examination, the right scrotum was visibly enlarged with normal overlying skin. Palpation revealed a firm-to-hard mass measuring approximately 12 × 10 cm in the right scrotal sac, extending superiorly into the right inguinal canal along the spermatic cord; the right testis could not be delineated separately. The left testis was normal.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen and pelvis showed a large heterogeneous mass arising from and completely replacing the right testis, measuring 7 × 7.5 × 5 cm. The lesion was T1 hypointense, T2 iso-to-hypointense, STIR hyperintense, and demonstrated strong diffusion restriction with mild homogeneous postcontrast enhancement. The mass extended along the right epididymis and spermatic cord into the inguinal canal, then tracked continuously along the right gonadal vein to its insertion into the inferior vena cava. No significant iliac, para-aortic, or mesenteric lymphadenopathy was identified, and abdominal visceral organs appeared normal.

A 27-year-old African woman was referred for chronic pelvic pain and right lumbar pain. She denied genitourinary symptoms. Her history included a loop electrosurgical cervical procedure, two normal vaginal deliveries, progestogen-only contraception, and newly discovered hypertension. Family history was noncontributory.

Vital signs were normal. Gynecologic examination was unremarkable; rectal examination revealed a firm, painful 2 cm nodule below the right sacrospinous ligament. Abdominal examination was normal.

An abdominal ultrasound showed severe right hydroureteronephrosis without calculi and diminished right renal parenchyma. Pelvic CT confirmed the hydroureteronephrosis and identified an 11 mm oval, solid, heterogeneous lesion fixed to the right pelvic sidewall near the iliac vessels, compressing the right ureter, and appearing adherent to the right ovary. The radiologist suggested deep pelvic endometriosis.

Transvaginal ultrasound revealed a spiculated, infiltrative 17 mm nodule lateral to the right ovary. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a spiculated 28 × 22 × 29 mm nodule with low signal on T1‐ and T2‐weighted images and minimal enhancement adjacent to the psoas muscle, causing right ureteral stenosis and severe hydroureteronephrosis; endometriosis was again suspected, though invasive characteristics could not be excluded.

A nuclear medicine renogram showed that the right kidney provided only 19% of total renal function. Given progressive renal impairment and uncertainty of diagnosis, exploratory laparotomy for histologic diagnosis and treatment was recommended.

A 67-year-old woman presented with a 7-month history of a left-sided neck “lump” and mild discomfort on palpation. She denied odynophagia, dysphagia, or hoarseness. Her medical history was notable for hypertension and age-related cataracts; she was a non-smoker with a BMI of 34 kg/m2 and no family history of malignancy. Physical examination revealed an elastic, tender, mobile mass in the left lateral cervical region; the remainder of the head and neck examination was unremarkable. Prior fiberoptic laryngoscopy, bronchoscopy, and esophagoscopy were normal. Neck ultrasonography showed a 3.0 cm × 2.06 cm well-defined, hypoechoic mass with no intratumoral vascularity on Doppler imaging. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a well-circumscribed 4.5 cm × 3.2 cm × 2.7 cm mass located deep to the internal jugular vein, carotid artery, and vagus nerve. An ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration was performed, but the result was non-diagnostic.

A 72-year-old woman was referred for an enlarged preauricular mass on the right side of her face that had been slowly growing over 3 years. She denied any history of facial trauma. Her medical history was notable only for hypertension and type II diabetes. On examination, there was a solitary, smooth, nontender, firm, bony swelling over the right zygomatic arch measuring approximately 3 cm in diameter. There was no trismus and temporomandibular joints were normal. CT scans demonstrated a 3 cm pedunculated, well-circumscribed, radiopaque, lobulated mass attached to the lateral border of the right zygomatic arch.

A 52-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 3-month history of an asymptomatic nodule on the fourth finger of her left hand. On examination, there was a 3-cm, firm, noninflamed subcutaneous nodule, and regional lymph nodes were not enlarged. The lesion was completely excised. 

Histologic examination revealed a poorly circumscribed, lobulated dermal mass with scalloped borders extending into subcutaneous fat and connecting to the epidermis. The tumor lobules contained nodules, focal tubular lumina, and cystic spaces. The cells were predominantly polygonal or fusiform with basophilic elongated nuclei, with rare clear-cell change. There was marked cytologic atypia, numerous mitotic figures, and focal necrosis. Angiolymphatic and perineural invasion were absent. Immunohistochemical studies showed positivity for epithelial membrane antigen and a high proliferative index on Ki-67 staining.

A 68-year-old healthy woman presented with a slight increase in volume of the left zygomatic region and an 8/10 intermittent, lacerating pain radiating to the ipsilateral temple, unrelieved by common analgesics. On examination, there was a firm, diffuse swelling over the left zygoma. An incisional biopsy via an intraoral approach was reported as odontogenic myxoma. Maxillofacial CT revealed a 3 cm × 3 cm well‐demarcated lesion of mixed density in the body of the left malar bone, extending into the zygomatic arch with internal cortical erosion.

A 73-year-old man noted, over 2 months, difficulty tracking a golf ball along with a narrowed field of vision and metamorphopsia in his right eye. On ophthalmologic examination, the right eye showed a large nonpigmented, dome-shaped choroidal mass in the superotemporal midperiphery with associated serous subretinal fluid extending to the macula; the vitreous and anterior chamber were clear, and the left eye was unremarkable. Best-corrected visual acuity was 0.4 in the right eye and 1.2 in the left; intraocular pressures were 15 mm Hg and 17 mm Hg, respectively. His medical history included chronic renal failure on thrice-weekly hemodialysis; he was asymptomatic systemically and was taking antihypertensives, clopidogrel, phosphate binders, cinacalcet, vitamin D analogues, and erythropoietin. Whole-body FDG-PET revealed abnormal uptake in the right eye, prostate (SUVmax 4.75), vertebral bones (SUVmax 8.01), bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes (SUVmax 5.77), and bilateral lung fields (SUVmax 3.31). A combined CT scan showed multiple bilateral lung-field nodular lesions indicative of metastatic deposits.

A 40-year-old Caucasian woman with a history of chronic bilateral low back pain, worse with activity and without systemic symptoms, underwent routine imaging. On examination, there was no tenderness over the sacrum. 
– MRI of the lumbar spine showed in the left S2 segment:  
  • Axial T1-weighted image: a 21-mm round, homogeneous lesion of low signal intensity interforaminally.  
  • Axial STIR image: a well-defined lesion with inhomogeneous signal and a high-intensity peripheral rim.  
  • Post-contrast T1 with fat saturation: moderate enhancement throughout the lesion and in the rim.  
– Plain pelvic radiograph: no visible abnormality.  
– Bone scan: solitary focus of increased uptake in the left sacrum.  
– PET-CT: a well-defined sclerotic lesion in S2 with mild FDG avidity (average SUV 2.5) and no other lesions.  
Given the atypical imaging appearance, the patient was referred for an image-guided biopsy.

A 65-year-old African American man with no prior medical history presented with a 6-month history of a slowly enlarging subcutaneous nodule in the left chest wall. He has a 20-pack-year smoking history, does not drink alcohol, and has an unremarkable family history. On examination, there was a 2 cm × 2 cm mobile, non-tender, soft but rubbery, non-pulsatile subcutaneous nodule in the left chest wall; the remainder of the skin examination was normal. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and metabolic panel. Ultrasound of the lesion revealed a 1.9 × 0.8 cm oval, solid, well-circumscribed, vascular subcutaneous nodule. Fine-needle aspiration of the nodule yielded abundant malignant epithelial cells in loosely cohesive clusters; the cells had multivacuolated cytoplasm, eccentrically placed nuclei, and prominent nucleoli, suggestive of renal origin. Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated that the tumor cells were positive for carbonic anhydrase IX, CD10, and RCC antigen, and negative for Sox10, PLAP, GCDFP-15, cytokeratin 7, and CD31.

A 12-year-old girl presented with a one-month history of left hip and proximal thigh pain. Physical examination was notable for pain on movement but no neurological deficits. Initial imaging with X-ray revealed a cystic lesion in the proximal left femur. MRI demonstrated a mixed long T1 and long T2 signal in the same region. The lesion was thought to represent an aneurysmal bone cyst. She underwent curettage, bone grafting, and fixation with a proximal femoral plate. Postoperative pathology showed a giant cell–rich lesion, supporting the diagnosis of aneurysmal bone cyst.

Two months later, she returned with recurrent left hip pain, inability to stand or walk, and imaging showed progression of the lesion with hardware displacement and aggressive bone changes. MRI revealed cortical expansion with resorption and a soft-tissue mass. During repeat surgery, the intertrochanteric bone was found to be destroyed, with blood clot–like tissue and loose bone particles cleared. Pathological examination with immunohistochemical staining revealed SATB2 (+), CD68 (+), and Ki-67 positive in approximately 70% of cells. The lesion contained numerous giant cells with areas of necrosis, numerous mitoses, and focal osteoid formation. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) was performed for USP6, H3F3A, and H3F3B. PET-CT showed hypermetabolic activity at the femoral lesion, multiple small hypermetabolic lung nodules, and hypermetabolic left iliac lymph nodes.

A 27-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of sharp, continuous pain in his left fourth toe that was refractory to conservative measures and prevented wearing closed shoes or playing indoor soccer. His medical history included well-controlled type I diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 6.5%) and depression; he took insulin via pump and sertraline. He had no allergies. Examination showed moderate edema of the entire left fourth toe with tenderness along its length and mild discomfort at the metatarsal head; alignment was normal. Diagnostic ultrasound demonstrated a small amount of soft-tissue edema but no ganglion cyst, tenosynovitis, or bursitis. Plain radiographs of the foot revealed a well-defined lucent lesion measuring 15 mm × 7 mm within the proximal phalanx of the fourth toe. MRI confirmed an expansile lesion breaching the inferior and lateral cortex without a soft-tissue mass or features suggestive of malignancy.

A 41-year-old man with a history of IgG kappa multiple myeloma diagnosed 10 months earlier (bone marrow plasma cells >60%), treated with four cycles of bortezomib/lenalidomide/dexamethasone followed by autologous stem-cell transplantation and in clinical remission, presented with progressive weakness of the lower extremities (strength 2/5), loss of deep tendon reflexes, and urinary and fecal incontinence. Vital signs and routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. MRI of the thoracic and lumbar spine revealed an intradural mass extending from the level of the second thoracic vertebra to the sacrum, with marked infiltration of the cauda equina and a high suspicion for astrocytoma. Cerebrospinal fluid obtained by lumbar puncture demonstrated atypical plasmatic cell infiltrates, raising concern for a plasma cell neoplasm.

A 33-year-old gravida 3, para 2 woman at 38 weeks of gestation presented to the emergency department with active left nasal bleeding. Her vital signs were stable, she denied trauma or nose picking, and she reported a one-month history of persistent left-sided nasal obstruction. She had no known medical conditions, bleeding disorders, or relevant family history. Initial hemoglobin was 9.9 mg/dL, and anterior nasal packing achieved hemostasis.  

Ten days later, she returned with recurrent left-sided epistaxis; hemoglobin was 9.4 mg/dL, and bleeding was managed conservatively. On the same day, she re-presented with moderate epistaxis and then a third time within 48 hours with active left nostril bleeding; hemoglobin had dropped to 8.7 mg/dL. Bedside examination showed the right nasal cavity clear; the left contained a large clot and moderate bleeding. Nasal endoscopy revealed a large, red, smooth, rounded mass in the left nasal cavity that bled on contact. Bleeding ceased with anterior packing.  

After spontaneous vaginal delivery two days later, the nasal pack was removed and bleeding recurred; hemoglobin fell to 7.8 mg/dL. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated a 3.2 × 2.2 × 1.5 cm heterogeneously enhancing soft-tissue mass involving the middle and inferior meatus of the left nasal cavity, with normal adjacent bony structures.

A 59-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a left cheek lesion that had begun as a small papule and progressively enlarged over 6 months. On examination, there was a well-demarcated, 5 cm × 7 cm, erythematous to red-brown, indurated, bosselated plaque with superficial telangiectasia and minimal epidermal changes. The lesion was firm, pruritic, and tender without exudate or bleeding. There was no lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, or constitutional symptoms. Laboratory studies showed a mild normocytic anemia (hemoglobin, 101 g/L) and mild thrombocytosis (platelet count, 462 × 10^9/L). Chest radiography was unremarkable. Immunofixation electrophoresis and urine albumin–creatinine ratio were normal. Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, pelvis, and head revealed only indeterminate bilateral upper-lobe pulmonary opacities. Serum vitamin B12 was elevated at 1368 pmol/L, and calcium was mildly elevated at 2.63 mmol/L. An incisional wedge biopsy was performed, and tissue was sent for bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal cultures.

A 60-year-old woman presented with a 5–6-month history of a progressively enlarging, painful swelling over the left cheek. The lesion began as a small, intermittently painful mass over 3 years, transiently responsive to antibiotics and analgesics, but after extraction of a carious lower left molar it rapidly enlarged. An outside fine-needle aspiration found malignant epithelial cells in sheets and clusters with squamous differentiation, suggesting mucoepidermoid carcinoma. On examination, there was a 10×6.5×4.5 cm diffuse, firm-to-hard, moderately tender swelling over the left parotid extending into the submandibular region, with erythematous overlying skin and ipsilateral cervical lymphadenopathy; intraoral exam was unremarkable. MRI of the head and neck demonstrated a 50×52×63 mm solid mass involving the superficial and deep lobes of the left parotid and the submandibular gland, with an obscure boundary and no bony involvement, suggestive of salivary gland malignancy. One week later, a modified radical neck dissection with parotidectomy and submandibulectomy (facial nerve preserved) was performed. Histologic examination (H&E) revealed sheets of round to ovoid noncohesive cells with marked cellular and nuclear pleomorphism, atypical mitoses, stromal destruction, necrosis, hemorrhage, and mixed inflammation. A preliminary diagnosis of “round cell malignant neoplasm” involving both glands was made.

A 21-year-old woman, virgin and with no significant medical history, presented with abundant vaginal bleeding. A pelvic examination was not possible due to her virginity. Abdominal and perineal ultrasound revealed a cervical mass. MRI showed a 44 × 47 × 47 mm, well-delimited, solid, inhomogeneous mass with small cystic areas and intense contrast enhancement, occupying the vaginal cavity and appearing to arise from the cervix (4 mm stalk). The uterus, ovaries, and other pelvic organs were normal, and no lymphadenopathy was seen.

After surgical defloration, examination under anesthesia confirmed a pedunculated tumor filling the vaginal canal. The mass was excised at its pedicle. Grossly, it measured 4.9 × 4.6 × 4.5 cm, had an irregular bosselated surface, and on section showed a white-gray cut surface with microcystic spaces and hemorrhagic, gelatinous areas.

Microscopically, the lesion was a well-circumscribed, biphasic proliferation. There were endometrioid-type glands—some crowded into lobules, others with irregular contours—lined by simple or pseudostratified epithelium with hyperchromatic nuclei, eosinophilic metaplasia, and squamous morules. The stroma consisted of cellular fibromyomatous tissue with edematous areas, thin blood vessels, and thick smooth-muscle bundles interspersed with myxoid change.

A 36-year-old Caucasian woman (G2P2) underwent laparoscopic right salpingo-oophorectomy for a right ovarian mass. The mass was fragmented intra-abdominally, and the outside pathology report described a Sertoli–Leydig–cell tumor. She had no history of hirsutism, virilization, or other endocrine symptoms. Her medical and surgical history was otherwise unremarkable. 

Six months later, she was referred for suspected metastatic disease. Laparoscopy revealed multiple 3–4-mm subperitoneal fatty nodules on the pelvic peritoneum, diaphragm, and previous trocar site; the left ovary appeared solid. Peritoneal washings were negative. 

Laboratory studies showed normal levels of follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone, prolactin, estradiol, progesterone, testosterone, dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate, and cortisol. Ovarian tumor markers—including HE4, β-hCG, and α-fetoprotein—were within normal limits. CA-125 was mildly elevated at 48.8 kU/L but normalized to 24.8 kU/L three weeks later. 

Ten months after the initial surgery, she underwent total abdominal hysterectomy, left salpingo-oophorectomy, omentectomy, pelvic and diaphragmatic peritonectomy, and pelvic lymphadenectomy with optimal cytoreduction. 

Microscopic examination showed diffuse tumor cells with abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm and vacuolization, no nuclear atypia, and a mitotic count of 5 per 10 high-power fields. No Reinke crystals were identified. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated positive expression of inhibin A, calretinin, and synaptophysin but negative expression of pan-cytokeratin, CD68, epithelial membrane antigen, chromogranin A, and estrogen receptor/androgen receptor. The Ki-67 labeling index was up to 15%.

A 37-year-old woman presented with a sacrococcygeal mass that she first noticed 6 months earlier. Initially the size of a pigeon egg and asymptomatic, the mass gradually enlarged and was associated with a sense of lumbosacral fullness. She had no prior medical history and no family history of similar lesions. On digital rectal examination, a large, hard, fixed mass was palpated anterior to the rectal wall, with indistinct borders. Routine blood tests and tumor markers, including CEA, AFP, CA 19-9, and CA125, were all within normal limits. 

Preoperative pelvic MRI demonstrated a sharply demarcated paracervical mass measuring 9.5 × 8.1 cm with a layered appearance on T2-weighted images, displacing the uterus cephalad. Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis showed a mass between the cervix and rectum with nonenhancing areas, pushing the anterior vagina and right posterior rectum. 

Transrectal ultrasonography with a biplane probe revealed an irregular left pelvic mass with an internal layered pattern of alternating hyperechoic and hypoechoic areas and a clear interface with the rectal wall. Color Doppler imaging showed scattered intratumoral vessels corresponding to the lamellar pattern. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) via the transrectal probe demonstrated a laminated distribution of contrast agent within the mass.

A 27-year-old woman presented with a 12-month history of dull aching pain localized to the proximal phalanx of the left great toe. She reported no history of trauma, no other joint pain, and no systemic symptoms. The pain was worse at night and was partially relieved by NSAIDs or aspirin. Physical examination revealed slight pain with motion at the metatarsophalangeal joint but no erythema, swelling, or neurovascular deficits. Laboratory studies, including inflammatory markers, were within normal limits. Plain radiographs of the left foot showed no abnormalities. Subsequent CT and MRI demonstrated a focal 2.5-mm lesion with a central hypodense area surrounded by a sclerotic rim in the proximal phalanx. Technetium-99 bone scintigraphy revealed a small area of hypermetabolic activity at the same site.

A 55-year-old Chinese man presented with a six-month history of cough, sputum production, and anorexia, accompanied by a 15-kg weight loss over one month. His only comorbidity was hypertension. He was a lifelong non-smoker, had no recent travel, and no history of tuberculosis or known exposure.

On examination, vital signs were normal, and he appeared comfortable at rest. Auscultation revealed decreased air entry over the left lower chest; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory tests, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits.

A chest radiograph demonstrated new collapse of the left lower lobe compared with prior imaging. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax confirmed complete collapse of the left lower lobe, subcentimeter mediastinal lymph nodes, and an oval endoluminal lesion measuring 0.8 × 1.1 cm at the origin of the left lower lobe bronchus. Endobronchial ultrasound bronchoscopy revealed a ball-like lesion completely occluding the left lower lobe bronchus and lymph nodes at stations 4R and 11L. Biopsies of the endobronchial mass and transbronchial needle aspirates of the lymph nodes were obtained.

Staging studies included CT of the abdomen, pelvis, and brain, which showed no evidence of metastatic disease. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy was normal. A bone scan revealed no conclusive evidence of metastases.

A 35-year-old nulliparous woman presented with a one-year history of a progressively enlarging, painless swelling extending from her left groin into her left leg. One month earlier, she had undergone surgery elsewhere for presumed incarcerated femoral hernia, but the mass persisted. She reported no gastrointestinal or urinary symptoms. On examination, there was a left groin incision scar and a firm, immobile, non-tender mass filling the lower abdominal quadrants and extending to the upper third of the left thigh. Rectal examination was normal, and external genital examination was unremarkable.  
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a large intra-abdominal solid mass entirely filling the pelvis and extending into the left groin, displacing adjacent organs but with unclear origin. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a well-defined, hypoattenuated pelvic mass with mass effect on the bladder, ureter, uterus, and iliac vessels. MRI showed the lesion to be isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images and of high signal intensity on T2-weighted images. An exploratory laparotomy was planned.

A 26-year-old woman was admitted with a 4-day history of upper abdominal pain. She had no history of hepatitis B or C, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, or relevant family history. On examination, her abdomen was soft, lax, non-distended, and without palpable masses. Laboratory studies showed: AFP 7529.2 ng/mL (normal ≤ 20), CA-125 99.4 U/mL (normal 0–35), creatinine 42 μmol/L (normal 45–84), sodium 131 mmol/L (normal 136–145), GGT 103 U/L (normal 7–32), fibrinogen 4.45 g/L (normal 2.00–4.00), and D-dimer 9611 μg/L (normal 0–700). Unenhanced CT revealed a well-defined low-density, fat-containing mass in the right liver lobe measuring 4.2 × 4.1 cm, and two inhomogeneous low-density masses in the left lobe measuring 8.6 × 7.7 cm and 2.6 × 2.6 cm. On contrast-enhanced images, all lesions showed heterogeneous enhancement. Based on imaging, the right-lobe lesion was preliminarily considered a hamartoma, and the two left-lobe lesions were thought to represent hepatocellular carcinomas.

A 31-year-old woman was referred for persistent dyspnea on exertion (NYHA class II) and presumed chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension. Four years earlier, she had acute chest pain and dyspnea; a second similar episode occurred three months ago and was attributed to pulmonary embolism. She had a history of hookworm infection; she used oral contraceptives and smoked.

On examination, she had digital clubbing, a prominent pulmonary component of the second heart sound, and a left parasternal systolic ejection murmur; blood pressure was 99/60 mmHg bilaterally, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory tests showed no inflammation; ECG was normal.

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a thickened mitral valve, moderate tricuspid regurgitation with an estimated systolic pulmonary arterial pressure of 60 mmHg, and a markedly dilated, mildly hypocontractile right ventricle. Right-heart catheterization showed a mean pulmonary arterial pressure of 28 mmHg, a cardiac index of 2.91 L/min/m2, and a pulmonary vascular resistance of 450 dyn·s·cm−5. Six-minute walk distance was 553 m (69% predicted) with oxygen saturation falling from 96% to 90%. Lung volumes were normal but diffusion capacity was reduced to 46% of predicted.

Chest radiograph revealed enlarged pulmonary arteries and a right parahilar nodule. A ventilation–perfusion scan showed multiple lobar and segmental perfusion defects. Pulmonary angiography demonstrated cutoffs of the right lower lobe and left upper lobe arteries and multiple aneurysmal dilatations of branches of the right upper lobe artery. Contrast-enhanced chest CT confirmed a right upper lobe nodule, and PET imaging showed that the nodule was metabolically active.

A 40-year-old woman was referred after an incidental finding on routine dental radiography. She was asymptomatic. Intraoral examination revealed mild, bony-hard swelling in the anterior mandible; the overlying mucosa was normal, and there were no signs of infection. The anterior mandibular teeth were displaced but not mobile.  
Panoramic radiograph showed a well-defined, unilocular radiolucency with a corticated rim extending from the right to left mental foramina. The roots of the left lateral incisor and canine were deviated and resorbed, and the cervical spine shadow was superimposed over the central lesion.  
CBCT axial images demonstrated expansion of both buccal and lingual cortical plates with perforation of the outer cortex on the left side.  
Differential diagnosis included calcifying odontogenic cyst, central giant cell granuloma, adenomatoid odontogenic tumor, and ameloblastoma.

A 20-year-old previously healthy nonsmoking man presented with acute onset of respiratory stridor accompanied by a sore throat and painful swallowing. On flexible nasendoscopy, there was a large, well-circumscribed mass arising from the left aryepiglottic fold, causing partial obstruction of the laryngeal inlet. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a 7.5 cm × 3.6 cm cystic mass centered in the left supraglottic larynx, extending through the cricothyroid membrane into the left thyroid lobe, with deviation of the laryngotracheal axis. An emergency tracheostomy was performed, and an open biopsy of the left thyroid mass was obtained for pathologic evaluation.

A 31-year-old Chinese woman was incidentally found to have multiple liver lesions. One month earlier, chest CT performed after an upper respiratory infection revealed two hypodense solid lesions in segment VII of the liver, measuring 36 × 31 mm and 21 × 16 mm. She had a 10-year history of chronic hepatitis B infection without antiviral therapy. She was asymptomatic, and vital signs and abdominal examination were normal.

Laboratory studies showed a low neutrophil count (1.53 × 10^9/L; 40.6%), with normal white blood cell, red blood cell, platelet counts, hemoglobin, liver function tests, and tumor markers including AFP, CEA, CA 125, and CA 19-9. Hepatitis B surface antigen, core antibody, and e antibody were positive.

Unenhanced ultrasound demonstrated two heterogeneous hypoechoic lesions without internal blood flow in the same region. Triple-phase contrast-enhanced CT showed both tumors to be well-defined, hypodense on noncontrast images, with heterogeneous sustained hypoenhancement and internal necrosis on arterial, portal venous, and equilibrium phases, remaining hypoattenuating relative to liver parenchyma. On gadoxetic acid–enhanced MRI, the lesions were hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, exhibited heterogeneous sustained hypoenhancement on dynamic phases, and showed patchy hyperintense signal on hepatobiliary phase.

Imaging interpretation favored metastatic lesions or hepatocellular carcinoma, and the patient was referred for further evaluation and management.

A 50-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of persistent cough without other respiratory or systemic symptoms. Her body-mass index was 28.5; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a 2.7×1.3-cm posterior superior mediastinal lesion with a well-circumscribed margin and intense enhancement (approximately 122 HU). Bronchoscopy showed an external mass compressing the membranous portion of the trachea just above the carina, causing elevation of the tracheal wall; there was no intraluminal lesion.

A 37-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of a rapidly enlarging mass on the left first toe. He denied trauma or infection; a prior dermatologist had treated the lesion as a viral wart without improvement. On examination, there was a 9.5×8 cm polypoid, necrotic mass with irregular margins, ulceration, and intermittent bleeding. Ambulation was limited by pain and tumor bulk. Radiographs of the foot showed no bony involvement. There was no palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy, and ultrasound of the groin was normal. Routine blood tests were within normal limits. The patient underwent wide local excision, which was extended to amputation of the toe to achieve clear margins. 
Histological examination of the excised specimen revealed a tumor in the dermis and subcutis composed of cohesive sheets and trabeculae of uniform small to medium round cells with hyperchromatic nuclei, scant pale cytoplasm, indistinct borders, prominent mitotic activity (30–35 mitoses per 10 high-power fields), a Ki-67 index of approximately 80%, numerous apoptotic cells, focal rosette formation, lobulated growth separated by fibrovascular septa, and extensive necrosis and hemorrhage. The overlying epidermis was ulcerated, and the lesion infiltrated deep margins without bone involvement.

A 67-year-old man was referred to surgical oncology for progressive abdominal pain and a growing portocaval mass. He reported one year of aching abdominal discomfort, nausea, and a 10-lb weight loss. His history included hepatitis C treated two decades earlier and hypertension; he had no known cirrhosis. On exam, he appeared well, was overweight, with no abdominal tenderness, distension, jaundice, or scleral icterus. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, creatinine 1.36 mg/dL, AST 61 U/L, normal ALT, ALP, and bilirubin, CEA 2.9 ng/mL, and CA 19-9 52 U/mL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated an enlarging mixed cystic–solid portocaval lesion (from 3.6×2.0 cm eight months earlier to 5.2×3.2 cm), hepatic steatosis, and no focal liver, pancreatic, biliary, or duodenal lesions. Upper endoscopy showed duodenal erythema, ulceration, and a possible submucosal mass. Endoscopic ultrasound confirmed a mixed cystic–solid mass between the pancreas and inferior vena cava, with otherwise normal pancreas, biliary tree, and liver. Fine-needle aspiration of the mass revealed rare fragments of cytokeratin 8/18 and arginase-1 positive atypical cells and was negative for CD34, SOX-10, synaptophysin, chromogranin, DOG-1, and CD117.

A 37-year-old woman with a 20-year history of cigarette smoking and a family history of lung cancer presented with symptoms of bronchitis. A chest radiograph followed by CT scanning revealed an incidental 2.0 cm mass in the posterior mediastinum abutting the T9 vertebral body. The lesion was clinically and radiologically most consistent with schwannoma. A minimally invasive resection showed no pleural thickening or multifocal nodules, and the mass was completely excised.

On gross examination, the lesion was an ovoid, tan-white, completely encapsulated, rubbery mass measuring 2.3 × 2.2 × 1.7 cm. Frozen-section microscopy demonstrated cytologically bland epithelioid cells arranged in cords and luminal configurations. On permanent sections, the neoplasm was confined to a fibrous pseudocapsule and composed of epithelioid cells forming cords and gland-like lumina, with areas of hypercellularity and focal hypocellularity. The cells exhibited mildly pleomorphic nuclei with vesicular chromatin, prominent nucleoli, and vacuolated eosinophilic cytoplasm. No mitotic figures were seen, the Ki-67 proliferative index was <2%, and there was no evidence of infiltration.

Immunohistochemical studies showed strong, diffuse positivity for pancytokeratin, calretinin, and nuclear WT1, and negativity for TTF-1, CD31, CD34, PAX8, p53, and chromogranin.

A 53-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 1-year history of progressively worsening constipation, early satiety, and epigastric fullness. Her past medical history included anxiety, depression, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, fibromyalgia, and hiatal hernia; she had undergone umbilical hernia repair and multiple prior cutaneous lipoma resections. She was a former 35–pack-year smoker who quit 1 year earlier and denied alcohol or drug use. On examination, she had mild epigastric tenderness without rebound or guarding. Initial management with oral polyethylene glycol, followed by lubiprostone and then plecanatide, provided no relief. Colonoscopy with removal of three small rectal polyps did not improve her symptoms. A computed tomographic scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a mass obstructing approximately 75% of the duodenal lumen adjacent to an enlarged gallbladder. The differential diagnosis included duodenal lipoma, duodenal stricture, and irritable bowel syndrome. Six months later, esophagogastroduodenoscopy confirmed an intraluminal mass in the third portion of the duodenum.

A 41-year-old woman presented with a slowly growing palpable lump in the left anterior chest wall that had been noted 3 years earlier. On examination, the mass was soft, movable, non-tender, measured approximately 3 cm initially, and there were no overlying skin changes. Initial ultrasonography showed a 3-cm oval, circumscribed, hypoechoic mass with internal echoes and multiple microcystic spaces, a triangular hyperechoic area at one pole, a peripheral hyperechoic rim, and posterior acoustic enhancement. Three years later, the mass had increased to 3.9 cm; at an 18-month follow-up it measured 5.5 cm, with no change in internal sonographic features. The lesion lay within the subcutaneous fat layer of the left anterior chest wall, unattached to the skin. Color Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated no vascularity, and there was no axillary lymphadenopathy. Mammography revealed a large, oval, circumscribed, hyperdense mass without calcification in the retromammary fat layer of the upper inner quadrant of the left breast.

A 13-year-old boy presented with a large, solitary, painless, progressively growing ovoid mass in the right posterior triangle of the neck for more than five years. On examination, the mass extended from behind the angle of the mandible to the supraclavicular region, deflected the sternocleidomastoid muscle medially, and abutted the trapezius laterally. The trachea was deviated medially, and the external jugular vein was stretched. The mass had very little intrinsic mobility, and the ipsilateral tonsil was pushed slightly medially.

A radiograph of the neck showed a large soft-tissue shadow deviating the trachea anteriorly and to the left. A contrast-enhanced CT scan revealed a hyperdense lesion measuring 15 × 12 × 11 cm, with minimal enhancement, extending from the base of the skull to the clavicle. The lesion pushed the common carotid artery and internal jugular vein medially and extended laterally up to the trapezius.

A 36-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of low back pain and mild motor dysfunction. The pain was persistent, dull, worse at night, without radiation to the lower limbs, and had gradually increased in intensity. She noted new subcostal pain 1 month ago. Previous physical therapy provided no relief.  
On examination, there was tenderness over multiple thoracic vertebrae with a slight rightward curvature; Lasegue, Bragard, Thomas, and Patrick signs were negative. A single 10×10 mm non-tender, mobile cervical lymph node was palpated; the thyroid exam was normal.  
Laboratory studies showed serum phosphorus 0.50 mmol/L (normal 0.96–1.62), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 55.1 nmol/L (75–250), alkaline phosphatase 227 U/L (40–150), and parathyroid hormone 121 pg/mL (15–65); urine phosphorus was within the normal range.  
MRI of the spine demonstrated a slight right lateral curvature at T3, multiple thoracic and lumbar vertebrae with double-concave deformities, and multiple compression fractures.  
SPECT bone scan revealed diffusely increased uptake throughout the skeleton and a solitary mildly active lesion in the right femoral head.  
Parathyroid gland ECT showed multiple low-density regions but no typical MIBI-positive lesions.

A 48-year-old man presented with upper abdominal pain. Laboratory testing showed elevated liver enzymes and cholestatic parameters. Abdominal ultrasound was inconclusive for the gallbladder due to overlying bowel gas. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen was performed to exclude gallbladder perforation; it confirmed acalculous cholecystitis and incidentally revealed a 5.5 × 1.5 × 5.5 cm retroperitoneal mass between the right psoas and iliac muscles, with mean attenuation values of 10–15 HU and minimal heterogeneous enhancement. Subsequent MRI demonstrated that the mass was slightly hypointense to mesenteric fat on T1- and T2-weighted images, markedly hyperintense on T2-weighted inversion recovery sequences, and showed strong heterogeneous enhancement after intravenous contrast. 18F-FDG PET/CT showed intense FDG uptake in the lesion (SUV max 12.3). The working diagnosis was a potentially malignant mesenchymal tumour.

A 62-year-old woman presented with right flank pain. Her medical history was notable for hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine and bilateral knee osteoarthritis; her family history was unremarkable. On examination, she was afebrile with a heart rate of 71 beats per minute and blood pressure of 128/75 mm Hg; the abdomen was soft, nondistended, and without palpable masses. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and serum biochemistry, were within normal limits. Endocrine evaluation showed normal 24-hour urinary catecholamines, plasma renin activity, plasma aldosterone concentration, and cortisol levels. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a well-circumscribed, uniform, hypodense, fat-containing lesion measuring 4.8 cm in the right adrenal gland. The lesion’s attenuation was 12 Hounsfield units (HU) on unenhanced images, 10 HU in the portal-venous phase, and 15 HU on a 15-minute delayed scan, with absolute and relative washout values exceeding 55% and 35%, respectively, findings interpreted as consistent with an adrenal adenoma. Given its size, the patient underwent a right laparoscopic adrenalectomy.

A 67-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a peripheral opacity in the left lower lobe discovered incidentally on chest radiography. She had undergone a radical left mastectomy for breast cancer 13 years earlier, followed by three years of tamoxifen; there had been no recurrence. She was a lifelong non-smoker, drank no alcohol, had no known toxic exposures, and denied a family history of malignancy. She was asymptomatic, in good health, and her physical examination was unremarkable except for a healed chest scar.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, standard biochemical tests, urine analysis, c-ANCA, p-ANCA, tumor markers, and arterial blood gases, were within normal limits. A chest radiograph showed a well-demarcated, non-cavitating, 3-cm opacity in the left lower lobe with obtuse angles to the pleura; this lesion was new compared to imaging one year earlier. Chest CT confirmed a 3 × 4 cm oval, homogenous, well-delineated peripheral mass abutting the pleura, with no mediastinal or axillary lymphadenopathy. CT scans of the brain and abdomen showed no abnormalities. Pulmonary function tests were normal. Bronchoalveolar lavage and bronchial brushing during bronchoscopy were negative for malignancy. A CT-guided fine-needle aspirate revealed clusters of neoplastic cells of unclear affiliation that were strongly positive for vimentin and negative for carcinoembryonic antigen and epithelial membrane antigen.

A 69-year-old Chinese woman was referred for evaluation of a 5-month history of postmenopausal vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal pain. In May 2020, she noted intermittent episodes of vaginal bleeding lasting 4–5 days, and occasional blood in her stool without hematuria. Her last menstrual period was over 14 years ago. On gynecologic examination, the vulva appeared hypopigmented and atrophic; the vagina was smooth. The uterine cervix was mobile and had a roughly 5-cm cauliflower-like mass on the anterior lip; the cervix felt friable, and the shallow vaginal fornix was atrophic. No adnexal masses were palpated. Pelvic color Doppler ultrasound showed an enlarged cervix measuring 5.7 × 4.0 cm with heterogeneous echotexture, suggestive of cervical malignancy. A cervical cone biopsy demonstrated high-grade glands lined by columnar cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and pseudostratified nuclei, forming papillary and micropapillary structures with marked nuclear atypia. Immunohistochemical studies revealed focal positivity for progesterone receptor and estrogen receptor, and diffuse positivity for p16, p53, EMA, CK7, WT-1, and Ki-67. Stains for MUC6, CK20, vimentin, Napsin A, HNF-1β, and CEA were negative. An HPV test was negative. Pelvic MRI showed an irregular anteverted uterine cervix mass measuring 3.0 × 5.0 × 4.1 cm with mild heterogeneous diffusion signal; bilateral adnexa appeared normal, and small lymph nodes were seen adjacent to the right iliac vessels. Pathologic stage was assigned as FIGO IIA.

A 56-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of a palpable mass in her left breast. Mammography and ultrasonography revealed two separate lesions in the upper medial and upper lateral quadrants, each suspicious for malignancy. The overlying skin was unremarkable and there was no nipple discharge. Core biopsy of one lesion confirmed invasive ductal carcinoma. Staging CT of the chest, abdomen, and bones showed no distant disease. She underwent a left biquadrantectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy. Intraoperative frozen section demonstrated positive margins and metastases in two of three sentinel nodes, prompting conversion to simple mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection. Gross examination of the mastectomy specimen identified two tumors, measuring 18 mm and 25 mm, located 3 cm apart; the smaller tumor was solid and yellowish, and the larger contained cystic spaces with a slurry-like content. Microscopically, the larger lesion consisted of poorly differentiated invasive ductal carcinoma with high-grade cytologic atypia, numerous mitotic figures, geographic necrosis, and lymphatic invasion. The smaller lesion was composed of large polygonal cells arranged in infiltrating solid and micropapillary patterns, with abundant eosinophilic, vacuolated, and foamy cytoplasm, marked nuclear atypia with prominent nucleoli, and scattered microcalcifications; no in situ component was seen, and lymphovascular invasion was present in adjacent breast tissue.

A 26-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of a painless, gradually enlarging lump in her left breast. She had no family history of breast cancer, no prior breast surgery, and no hormonal therapy. On examination, the left breast was larger than the right, with a freely mobile, soft mass measuring approximately 12 × 9 cm in the lower outer quadrant; there was no skin tethering or axillary lymphadenopathy. Two-view mammography of the left breast showed a large, well-circumscribed, encapsulated mass with variable densities, including areas of fat lucency subjacent to the capsule and regions of fibroglandular density. Breast ultrasound of the mass demonstrated different echogenicities with peripheral isoechoic fat and central echogenic fibroglandular tissue.

A 16-year-old girl presented with 2 years of progressive right-eye proptosis and intermittent mild to moderate headache. She denied visual loss or diplopia. Examination showed axial proptosis of the right eye with full extraocular movements. Visual acuity was 6/6 bilaterally, visual fields and funduscopic exam were normal, and the neurologic examination was otherwise unremarkable. Routine hematologic and biochemical tests were normal.  
Orbital CT with thin cuts revealed a 4 × 5 cm hyperdense lesion in the right orbital roof, causing splaying of the inner and outer tables of the skull, enlargement of the orbit, and anterior-medial displacement of the globe. The lesion extended medially to the olfactory groove and posteriorly to the planum sphenoidale, encroached on the ethmoid, sphenoid, and frontal sinuses without bony destruction, and showed slight hyperostosis of the anterior and lateral orbital roof. After contrast, it enhanced homogeneously and intensely.  
MRI demonstrated an iso- to hypointense mass on T1-weighted images and a heterogeneous signal on T2-weighted images at the right orbital roof, with intense enhancement after gadolinium administration.

A 10-month-old South Asian boy was brought for evaluation of a limp in his right leg when walking with support. The parents denied any history of trauma. His birth and perinatal course were uneventful, and developmental milestones were normal. Vaccinations were up to date. Family history was unremarkable. 

On examination, he was afebrile and appeared well. There were no bruises, café-au-lait spots, or other dermatologic findings. Systemic examination was normal. In the right leg, there was no overt swelling, tenderness, deformity, or ulceration, but a bony hard lump was palpable over the mid-tibia and fibula with tibia vara and internal rotation. 

Plain radiography of the right leg showed a callus from a previous stress fracture and multiple expansile lytic lesions of the tibia with cortical erosions and sclerotic areas in adjacent bone; a pathological fracture was seen in the fibula. Laboratory studies—including serum alkaline phosphatase, calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone, and 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol levels—were all within normal limits. 

Given the unexplained long-bone lesions and fracture in a non-ambulant infant, the possibility of child abuse was considered, and the child was referred for further assessment.

A 21-year-old woman presented with a six-month history of a slow-growing, painless swelling on the left side of her lower lip. On examination, there was a 1 cm × 1 cm dome-shaped, non-tender, firm-to-soft, mobile mass with a smooth surface and well-demarcated margins. There was no sensory deficit and no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. The patient denied any history of changes in lesion size, local trauma (including habitual lip biting), or paraesthesia. Because the lesion was thought to represent a benign fibrous overgrowth or an organizing mucocele, no imaging or preoperative biopsy was performed. Under local anesthesia, a curvilinear incision and blunt dissection were used to excise the lesion. Intraoperatively, the mass was ovoid, well-encapsulated, and easily separable from surrounding tissues, and the surgical specimen was an ovoid soft tissue mass with a thick capsule.

A 33-year-old HIV-negative man presented in April 2020 with a 5-month history of progressive left blepharoptosis and a 4-month history of numbness and weakness of the right limbs. His past medical history was notable for non-insulin-dependent type 2 diabetes mellitus and pulmonary tuberculosis, for which he was receiving rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, and moxifloxacin. Neurologic examination revealed grade 4 strength of the right upper and lower limbs and hypoesthesia of the right distal extremities. Laboratory studies showed C-reactive protein 21.6 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 33 mm/h, blood glucose 6.8 mmol/L, and a positive T-SPOT.TB test. Brain MRI demonstrated a 1.9 cm × 1.8 cm homogenously contrast-enhancing mass in the left midbrain with surrounding edema. CT confirmed a hyperdense lesion at the same site. Fluorodeoxyglucose PET revealed a maximum standardized uptake value of 7.48 in the midbrain lesion and 5.70 in a right third rib lesion.

A female Aboriginal Australian in her 30s was brought to the emergency department after acute-onset confusion and bilateral lower-limb paralysis noted 1 hour earlier. Her history was notable for systemic lupus erythematosus with class IV lupus nephritis and previous necrotising fasciitis requiring free-flap reconstruction complicated by a postoperative deep-vein thrombosis. Medications included mycophenolate 1 g twice daily and prednisolone 7.5 mg daily. She denied tobacco, alcohol, or drug use.

On examination, respiratory rate was 24 breaths per minute, heart rate 165 beats/min (sinus tachycardia), temperature 39.0 °C, and Glasgow Coma Scale score 14 (E4 V6 M4). Both lower limbs were cold, pulseless, insensate, and flaccid.

Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 112 g/L, white blood cell count 7.61 × 10^9/L, platelet count 134 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 8.2 mg/L, INR 1.2, aPTT 49.3 s, fibrinogen 1.7 g/L, and lactate 4.8 mmol/L. Four hours later, platelet count fell to 93 × 10^9/L and white blood cell count rose to 19.9 × 10^9/L, consistent with sepsis and consumptive coagulopathy.

Computed tomography angiography of the abdomen and pelvis revealed distal abdominal aortic occlusion extending bilaterally into the common and external iliac arteries and the right internal iliac artery, with occlusion of the left profunda femoris and popliteal arteries. Additional findings included low-density lesions in the left ventricle and segmental infarcts in the spleen and kidneys.

A 29-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 45 days of gestation, was admitted with a 9-day history of sudden-onset fever, chills, and widespread pustular skin eruption accompanied by vaginal bleeding. Nine days earlier, she noted erythematous rash beneath both breasts, which spread to her torso and extremities. Pinpoint pustules formed at the margins of annular erythematous patches and merged into larger pustular lakes. She reported severe pain and burning in affected areas, disrupting her sleep.

Her past medical history was notable for a suspected antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, for which she had been taking aspirin 25 mg three times daily. Two weeks later, pregnancy was confirmed and hydroxychloroquine 100 mg three times daily, cyclosporine 50 mg three times daily, and prednisone 7.5 mg once daily were added. At symptom onset, dydrogesterone 10 mg three times daily was given for vaginal bleeding. Empiric cefoperazone–sulbactam and increased prednisone (up to 20 mg twice daily) were administered in the 2 days before admission, but her rash continued to progress.

On admission, she was febrile (38.7 °C) and tachycardic. Skin examination showed widespread confluent erythematous plaques studded with tiny peripheral pustules, most pronounced in intertriginous areas; some pustules had merged into larger bullae. Palms, soles, nails, and oral mucosa were spared. Laboratory studies revealed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 49 mm/h, C-reactive protein 99 mg/L, leukocyte count 21.3 × 10^9/L with neutrophilia, hypoalbuminemia, elevated fibrinogen (6.4 g/L), d-dimer (3750 μg/L), and CA 125. Serum calcium was normal. Repeated blood cultures and pustule swabs were sterile.

A 48‐year‐old woman with fibromyalgia, migraines, and a history of polysubstance abuse presented with several months of fatigue, abdominal pain, and progressive dyspnea. She also reported night sweats, weight loss, early satiety, and nausea. On the morning of presentation, her shortness of breath was severe and did not improve after administration of diuretics in the emergency department.  
On examination, she was tachycardic. Laboratory studies including a complete blood count with differential, basic metabolic panel, and cardiac enzymes were within normal limits.  
A chest radiograph showed an increased cardiac silhouette with vascular congestion and bilateral perihilar and lower-lung opacities, findings interpreted as consistent with congestive heart failure.  
Contrast‐enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated innumerable new bilateral pulmonary nodules, predominantly peripheral and in the lower lobes in a perilymphatic distribution; the largest measured 1.2 × 0.9 cm. Attenuation values ranged from 5 to –30 Hounsfield units, consistent with fluid density. These nodules were new compared with CT imaging one year earlier, suggesting a nodular pattern of pulmonary edema.  
An infectious etiology was considered unlikely given the absence of leukocytosis, fever, or changes in sputum. Gastrohepatic lymphadenopathy was also noted, and gastrointestinal evaluation was recommended. A short‐interval follow-up CT was planned to exclude a neoplastic process after stabilization of heart failure.  
The patient was admitted for management of new-onset heart failure and received further diuresis. Pulmonology recommended a CT-guided lung biopsy to evaluate for an infectious, malignant, or inflammatory process.

A man in his early 70s with metastatic clear-cell renal carcinoma was referred for worsening renal function and nephrotic-range proteinuria. One year after a left nephrectomy (pathologic stage pT3b pN0 M1, Fuhrman grade 3), he began sunitinib. He tolerated therapy for 8 years, with prior side effects of gastrointestinal intolerance, mucositis, hand–foot syndrome, and hypothyroidism managed with levothyroxine. He also received stereotactic radiation to pulmonary nodules. His history included hypertension (on irbesartan and chlorthalidone) and a non-massive pulmonary embolism treated with low–molecular–weight heparin.

On examination, blood pressure was 168/83 mm Hg and heart rate 70 beats/min. He had significant bilateral lower-extremity and facial pitting edema.

Laboratory studies revealed a serum creatinine of 260 µmol/L (eGFR 21 mL/min/1.73 m2), up from a baseline of 110–151 µmol/L over the prior 7 years. A urine protein:creatinine ratio was 857 mg/mmol, and albumin:creatinine ratio was 251 mg/mmol. Serum C3 and C4 levels were normal, serum albumin was 34 g/L, and there were no monoclonal proteins. His hemoglobin was 96 g/L; platelets were 328×10^9/L; white cells were 5.4×10^9/L. A peripheral smear showed polychromasia with occasional schistocytes. Total bilirubin was 6 µmol/L, and lactate dehydrogenase was mildly elevated at 382 U/L. Coagulation studies (PTT, INR) were normal.

Given the nephrotic-range proteinuria, rising creatinine, and presence of schistocytes despite normal platelet counts, a renal biopsy was performed.

A 20-year-old woman presented on postpartum day five with gradually worsening right lower back and lower abdominal pain that began on day three. She was primiparous, had an uncomplicated term vaginal delivery with epidural anesthesia, and was discharged on day one post-delivery. She described the pain as sharp and positional and denied fever, malodorous vaginal discharge, dysuria, incontinence, or trauma. Her medical history included idiopathic osteochondromas and benign thyroid nodules; there was no personal or family history of hypercoagulability.  

On examination, she appeared uncomfortable but was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Vital signs were: temperature 37.1 °C, heart rate 119 beats/min, blood pressure 135/82 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Abdominal examination revealed right lumbar tenderness and right suprapubic tenderness without rebound or guarding.  

The initial differential diagnosis included ascending infection or sepsis, muscular strain, and post‐epidural hematoma or abscess. Laboratory studies—complete blood count, metabolic panel, lactate, and blood cultures—were obtained. Intravenous morphine and topical lidocaine provided pain relief.  

Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 10,400/µL without a left shift; other labs were unremarkable. A contrast‐enhanced CT of the lumbar spine, abdomen, and pelvis was performed. The lumbar spine images revealed no mass effect or soft‐tissue abnormality. Abdominal CT demonstrated an “ill‐defined tubular structure with extensive fat stranding” tracking along the expected course of the right ovarian vein to the inferior vena cava confluence. A subsequent pelvic ultrasound identified a complex right adnexal structure but was otherwise indeterminate.

A 27-year-old man presented with severe epigastric and left hypochondriac pain of 1-day duration radiating to the left shoulder, worse on inspiration and when lying down. He reported drinking approximately 1.5 L of alcohol over 2 hours, followed by multiple episodes of vomiting, after which his abdominal pain intensified. There was no history of trauma, surgery, or significant past medical problems.

On examination, he was afebrile (35.7 °C), with stable vital signs: heart rate 69 beats/min, blood pressure 115/77 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, SpO₂ 100% on room air, and Glasgow Coma Scale 15/15. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the epigastric and left hypochondriac region without guarding or rebound; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 13.7 g/dL, hematocrit 42.6%, leukocyte count 11.2 × 10⁹/L, and normal prothrombin time, aPTT, and INR. Liver function tests and serum amylase were within normal limits.

Given his presentation, differentials included acute alcoholic pancreatitis, acute gastritis, Boerhaave’s syndrome, and Mallory–Weiss tear. Chest and abdominal radiographs were normal. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis in the portal venous phase demonstrated a 13 × 12 × 10 cm hyperdense collection (50–60 HU) in the left hypochondriac region adjacent to the greater curvature of the stomach, with active contrast extravasation (230 HU) within the collection. Delayed images showed contrast pooling (140–145 HU) within the haematoma (110–115 HU), and maximum intensity projection images revealed contrast leak from smaller branches of the splenic artery. These findings raised concern for intraperitoneal hemorrhage secondary to rupture of a vessel, probably one of the short gastric arteries.

A 12-year-old boy presented with a 2-month history of progressive abdominal distension with flank fullness and 15 days of lower-limb swelling. His mother reported dark urine for the past 3 months. He denied abdominal pain, fever, gastrointestinal bleeding, pruritus, neurological symptoms, or features of autoimmune disease. There was no family history of liver disease. 

On examination, he was underweight and stunted, with mild pallor, icterus, bilateral pedal edema, tense ascites, and firm hepatosplenomegaly (liver 3 cm below xiphisternum, span 7 cm; spleen 5 cm below costal margin). 

Laboratory studies showed total/direct bilirubin 3.3/2.8 mg/dL, AST 128 U/L, ALT 137 U/L, ALP 486 U/L, GGT 188 U/L, albumin 1.89 g/dL, INR 2.92, hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL, WBC 3200/mm3, and platelets 30,000/mm3. 

Abdominal ultrasound with Doppler revealed a small right lobe, irregular margins, heterogeneous echotexture, caudate-lobe hypertrophy, splenomegaly, periportal collaterals, and moderate-to-large ascites. Endoscopy showed grade 2 esophageal varices and mild portal hypertensive gastropathy. Transient elastography measured liver stiffness at 75 kPa, consistent with cirrhosis. 

Workup for chronic liver disease showed normal immunoglobulin G levels; autoimmune and viral hepatitis serologies were negative. Ceruloplasmin was low at 9 mg/dL; slit-lamp examination for Kayser–Fleischer rings was negative; 24-hour urine copper excretion was elevated at 182 μg/day. The family declined liver biopsy. 

With a Leipzig score of 4, an initial diagnosis of Wilson disease was made, and D-penicillamine was started, titrated to 20 mg/kg/day. After 3 months of adherence, he had no clinical or biochemical improvement, and repeat ATP7B genetic analysis was negative.

A 31-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks’ gestation presented with sudden dizziness and three generalized tonic-clonic seizures over 20 minutes, each lasting about 15 seconds, followed by transient loss of consciousness. Her obstetrical history was notable for gestational hypertension treated with labetalol 5 mg daily. On arrival, blood pressure was 170/110 mm Hg, pulse 138/min, and she had bilateral pedal edema. Fetal heart rate was 142/min. Urine dipstick showed 3+ protein. Initial management included intravenous diazepam and magnesium sulfate. She was admitted to the obstetrics ICU with a working diagnosis of eclampsia and a differential that included intracranial hemorrhage and posterior reversible leukoencephalopathy syndrome. Despite treatment, she had further seizures, and an urgent noncontrast head CT was obtained, showing low-density shadows in the bilateral parietal lobes and a focal high-density shadow near the cerebral sulcus.

A 33-year-old woman with a body mass index of 34 and no prior liver or respiratory disease was admitted with one week of malaise, fever, and rapidly worsening shortness of breath. Seven days before admission she tested positive for SARS-CoV-2. On arrival, she was severely hypoxemic, requiring endotracheal intubation, mechanical ventilation, and veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (vvECMO) for COVID-19–related ARDS, along with continuous catecholamine support. Hemodialysis was initiated on day 4, vvECMO was discontinued on day 14, and ventilator weaning was completed on day 15.  

During her 154-day hospital course, laboratory tests revealed persistent cholestatic liver dysfunction: bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL, γ-glutamyl transferase 1299 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 1883 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 162 U/L, and alanine aminotransferase 119 U/L. On day 10, contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the upper abdomen showed no parenchymal damage or biliary dilation.

A 38-year-old man with hypertension and a heavy smoking history presented with 10 days of productive cough that began with blood-tinged sputum and progressed to massive hemoptysis. He also reported arthralgias and noted a diffuse purpuric rash on his lower limbs. On examination, he had tenderness of the right first, second, and third proximal interphalangeal joints and the left second proximal interphalangeal joint, along with scattered nonblanching purpura on his lower extremities. Laboratory studies revealed a falling hemoglobin concentration, acute kidney injury, and microscopic hematuria. A chest radiograph showed extensive bilateral ground-glass opacities. High-resolution CT of the chest demonstrated diffuse patchy ground-glass opacities in all lobes except the apical segments of the upper lobes and subpleural areas, and a linear lucency in the left mediastinum consistent with pneumomediastinum. A preliminary diagnosis of pulmonary–renal vasculitis was made, and an autoimmune panel was sent.

A 9-year-old girl with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia presented with epistaxis. Before chemotherapy, her chest radiograph was normal and a tuberculin skin test measured 0 mm. She received induction chemotherapy but required augmented consolidation. One week after augmented consolidation, she developed febrile neutropenia (absolute neutrophil count 0) unresponsive to 4 days of IV piperacillin/tazobactam. Blood and urine cultures and a serum Aspergillus galactomannan assay were negative. Chest CT revealed an air-crescent sign in the anterior segment of the right upper lobe and multiple pulmonary nodules. Intravenous voriconazole was initiated. Two days later, she developed a progressive right-sided headache and neck stiffness. CT angiography of the brain showed an outpouching lesion of the right posterior cerebral arteries. Surgical resection of the aneurysm was performed; Gomori methenamine silver stain of the tissue demonstrated thin septate dichotomous branching hyphae. Voriconazole trough level was 2.1 mg/L. After 2 weeks of antifungal therapy, her neutrophil count normalized, but fever and cough persisted for 4 weeks. Bronchoalveolar lavage revealed no organisms and a negative galactomannan assay. Repeat chest CT again demonstrated an air-crescent lesion in the right upper lobe, contacting the chest wall and costal cartilage. Possible diagnoses included aspergillosis, Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and anaerobic bacteria. She received IV piperacillin/tazobactam. A wedge resection of the lung lesion showed caseous necrosis; Gram stain, bacterial culture, and modified acid-fast bacilli testing of the tissue were negative.

A 4-year-old girl was admitted with a 2-month history of asthenia, weight loss, neck pain, difficulty walking, and frequent falls, and a 1-week history of fever and progressive weakness in all four limbs. On examination, she was alert (Glasgow score 15), had dysbasia, axial and appendicular ataxia, and signs of upper-motor-neuron involvement including spastic tetraparesis, bilateral Hoffmann and Babinski signs, and global hyperreflexia. MRI of the neuroaxis revealed multiple intramedullary contrast-enhancing expansile lesions with diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement along the spinal cord and intraparenchymal enhancement in the brainstem, suggestive of cerebritis. Given the lack of specificity of these findings, surgical decompression and biopsy of the spinal lesion were planned.

A 31-year-old primipara at 39 weeks’ gestation noted bilateral painless bloody nipple discharge when expressing milk, first observed at 36 weeks. She denied trauma, infection, or direct infant suckling and had no family history of breast disease. Physical examination revealed no inflammation, engorgement, palpable masses, tenderness, nipple cracks, or ulcers. Breast ultrasound showed lobular hyperplasia and mild ductal ectasia without cysts, solid nodules, or lymphadenopathy. Cytological analysis of the milk demonstrated numerous inflammatory cells, polynuclear macrophages, a few epithelial cells, and no atypia.

A 46-year-old man presented with a 3-week history of gradually enlarging, stiff, erythematous skin lesions on the right buttock, ipsilateral thigh, and left shin, accompanied by pain in the right leg, lower back, right hand, and neck. He also reported worsening low back and pelvic pain on walking, resulting in a significant gait disturbance. His history was notable for cervical disk herniation surgery 2 years earlier, ongoing acetaminophen use with minimal relief, former cigarette smoking (20 pack-years, quit 8 years ago), and occasional inhalational opioid use. 

On examination, vital signs were stable. A surgical scar was present on the neck; neck movement elicited pain. Right leg straight-leg raise (Lasegue) was positive. There was painful induration with erythema (8 × 15 cm) over the right buttock and an erythematous maculopapular lesion (6 × 18 cm) on the left shin. Proximal muscle strength in the right upper and lower limbs was 4.5/5. Deep tendon reflexes were +3 in the right upper limb and +4 with clonus at the right Achilles.

Imaging studies revealed:
• Cervical MRI: Lordosis alteration with posterior bulging disks at C3–C4, C4–C5, and C5–C6 compressing the thecal sac; myelomalacia at C4; a hemangioma in T1.  
• Pelvic MRI: Numerous low-signal foci in both femoral heads compatible with benign sclerotic lesions.  
• Brain MRI: Normal.  
• Lumbar spine MRI: Decreased lordosis, disk dehydration, bulging at L4–L5 with uncovertebral involvement at L4–L5 and central protrusion at L5–S1.  
• Triphasic Tc-99m bone scan: Uptake consistent with enthesopathy in the right sacroiliac joint, left anterior superior iliac spine, right pelvic brim, bilateral patellae, right tibial tuberosity, and bilateral medial malleoli.

A 4-year-old girl presented to the dermatology department with a 6-month history of multiple grouped asymptomatic raised skin lesions on bilateral axillae, upper back, and face. The lesions appeared on normal skin without preceding inflammation or trauma. There was no history of epilepsy, developmental anomalies, delay in milestones, or pertinent family history.

On examination, there were multiple symmetrically distributed brownish papules and plaques with a leathery surface, ranging in size from 0.2 × 0.2 cm to 2.5 × 2.5 cm. In the axillae, there were a few skin-colored firm non-tender nodules with an irregular thickened surface giving a peau d’orange appearance. No neurocutaneous stigmata, thickened nerves, or systemic abnormality were detected.

Considering a differential diagnosis of connective tissue nevus, histoid Hansen’s disease, and neurofibromatosis, the patient underwent further investigations.

A 60-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of right testicular pain and a palpable lump at the superior aspect of the testicle. He also noted dysuria and debris in his urine but denied fevers or suprapubic pain. Four weeks earlier, he had undergone holmium laser enucleation of the prostate for benign prostatic hyperplasia, followed by a trial without catheter one week before presentation. On that day, a urine culture grew Staphylococcus aureus, and he completed a seven-day course of antibiotics. 

Physical examination revealed a tender, non-reducible lump in the right groin that descended into the hemiscrotum; there was no cough impulse. Laboratory studies showed a mild inflammatory response and a slight rise in creatinine. Scrotal ultrasound demonstrated a 5.3 × 2.2 cm heterogeneous mass in the right inguinal canal, interpreted as presumed herniated peritoneal fat, and a mild septated right hydrocele.

The general surgical team assessed the patient, noted the tender lump without cough impulse, and considered an incarcerated inguinal hernia, leading to a request for CT imaging.

A 65-year-old man was admitted with progressive jaundice, muscle wasting, and abdominal distension. His past history included portal hypertension attributed to cryptogenic cirrhosis diagnosed 4 years earlier on the basis of thrombocytopenia and large non-bleeding esophageal varices; no liver biopsy was performed at that time. On examination he was icteric and had tense ascites.

Laboratory studies showed an alkaline phosphatase level of 674 U/L, total bilirubin of 6.8 mg/dL, and transaminases of 60 U/L. An abdominal CT scan revealed a low‐attenuation lesion in the right hepatic lobe measuring 3.7 × 6.4 × 5.1 cm with peripheral nodular enhancement, suggestive of hemangioma. Both intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts were dilated, with the common bile duct up to 1.5 cm in diameter.

MRCP demonstrated intra- and extrahepatic biliary dilatation and an irregular narrowing of the common bile duct at the porta hepatis, surrounded by an ill-defined soft-tissue lesion. Endoscopic ultrasonography revealed a hypoechoic mass in the pancreatic head region with associated distal bile duct obstruction and extensive collateral circulation. ERCP showed a localized biliary stricture with a malignant appearance, and a self-expandable metal stent was placed via sphincterotomy.

Fine-needle aspiration of the peripancreatic lesion and brush cytology of the bile duct stricture were negative for malignancy. A liver biopsy showed nodular regenerative hyperplasia with minimal fibrosis and intact bile ducts without injury. After stent placement, the patient’s jaundice, ascites, bilirubin level, and alkaline phosphatase level all improved.

A 60-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of dull, aching abdominal pain that began insidiously in the right hypochondrium and gradually worsened, radiating to the left hypochondrium, with intermittent vomiting but no clear triggers. He also noted a swelling in the left inguinal region over the same period. His medical history was notable for transurethral resection of a low-grade bladder papillary urothelial carcinoma followed by intravesical BCG. He had no history of diabetes, tuberculosis, asthma, or hypertension and had ceased alcohol use one year earlier.

On examination, he appeared well nourished and in no distress. Abdominal palpation elicited mild tenderness in the right hypochondrium without organomegaly or peritoneal signs. In the left inguinal region there was a 3 × 2 cm soft, non-tender, non-reducible swelling with a positive cough impulse. The testes were normal.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed multiple 9–10 mm calcified nodules in the left diaphragm, bilateral intercostal muscles, left erector spinae, right psoas, and bilateral gluteal and thigh muscles. A 12 × 8 mm hypodense splenic lesion was also noted; all other abdominal organs were normal. An AP X-ray of the upper thighs showed multiple radiopaque soft-tissue lesions in the gluteal and thigh muscles.

A 74-year-old Caucasian man was admitted with 2 days of malaise, dyspnea, and cough. On presentation, temperature was 37.6°C, blood pressure 124/70 mmHg, pulse 135/min and irregular, and oxygen saturation 91% on 6 L/min oxygen. He had bilateral crackles and basal interstitial infiltrates on lung auscultation, and atrial fibrillation on electrocardiogram. A nasopharyngeal swab confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection; he was started on remdesivir and dexamethasone.

On hospital day 5, he developed acute chest pain, ST-elevation in leads II, III, and aVF, and troponin I elevated to 116 ng/L. Coronary angiography revealed only chronic thrombotic occlusion of marginal branches of the left circumflex artery. He was admitted to the ICU in cardiogenic shock (cardiac index 1.2 L/min/m², pulmonary capillary wedge pressure 27 mmHg, mean pulmonary artery pressure 33 mmHg). Echocardiography showed a normal-size left ventricle with severely reduced ejection fraction (15%) and global akinesia, and severely reduced right ventricular function. He required high-flow oxygen and inotropic support.

Within the first week, platelet count fell from 265 × 10⁹/L to 12 × 10⁹/L. He developed Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia (hemoglobin drop from 153 to 98 g/L, LDH 2844 U/L, haptoglobin <0.10 g/L) with 12% schistocytes on peripheral smear, acute kidney injury requiring renal replacement therapy, and intermittent neurological symptoms including delirium and drowsiness. This combination raised suspicion for a thrombotic microangiopathy. He had no diarrhea, stool tests were negative for Shiga‐toxin–producing bacteria, and ADAMTS13 activity was 52%.

A 57‐year‐old man with a history of urothelial carcinoma (status post resection), psoriatic arthritis, and chronic cigarette smoking sustained burns after an accidental spill of methylene chloride while refinishing furniture at a residence. He had 13% total body surface area burns involving the face (including both eyes), anterior trunk, and right upper extremity. He immediately returned home, showered, and sought medical help approximately 8½ hours after the incident.

On arrival at the burn center, he was hemodynamically stable and in no respiratory distress. Examination confirmed superficial partial‐thickness burns in the described areas and epithelial defects of both corneas. He received warm-water hydrotherapy and topical wound care; ophthalmologic evaluation led to irrigation and placement of Prokera rings in both eyes.

Laboratory studies on admission showed a blood carboxyhemoglobin level of 12%, hemoglobin 14 g/dL, white blood cell count 11.7 K/mm3, and creatinine 0.8 mg/dL. He was placed on 100% oxygen; however, the carboxyhemoglobin level rose to 13.5% five hours later before declining to 2.5% at 27 hours. A chest radiograph obtained on hospital day six was unremarkable. He remained clinically stable without respiratory, circulatory, or neurologic compromise.

A 25-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of a right-sided, palpable inguinolabial swelling that had gradually increased in size and was associated with pain. She denied any history of hernia or trauma. On examination, there was a 5 × 4 cm right inguinolabial bulge that was tender, irreducible, without overlying skin changes, and with a negative cough impulse. Routine blood tests were unremarkable.  
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a well-defined, septated cystic lesion measuring 5.8 × 3.1 cm in the right inguinolabial region without internal or peripheral vascularization. A contrast-enhanced CT scan confirmed a comma-shaped, cystic structure in the same location, without obvious communication to the peritoneal cavity.
