Based on the clinical presentation and imaging, a working diagnosis of femoral hernia was made, and elective surgical exploration was planned.

A 43‐year‐old woman presented with a two‐month history of back pain radiating to both lower extremities that was unresponsive to conventional therapy. Physical examination showed mild splenomegaly. Neurologic examination revealed motor strength of 4/5 in the distal lower extremities, absent deep‐tendon reflexes in the lower extremities, limping gait, and sensory deficits in the L4 and L5 dermatomes; sphincter function was intact. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbosacral spine showed an extradural, contrast‐enhancing mass extending from L3 to S3. Thoracic spine MRI revealed a second contrast‐enhancing epidural lesion from T3 to T11 with mild cord compression. Cervical spine and brain MRI were normal. Abdominal and pelvic CT scans were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed: 
• Red‐cell count 7.66 × 10^6/mm^3, hemoglobin 20.5 g/dL, hematocrit 67.3%, MCV 67 fL, MCH 17.6 pg, MCHC 26.3 g/dL  
• Reticulocyte count 3.5%  
• Platelet count 246,000/mm^3; WBC count 14.6 × 10^3/mm^3 (46% polymorphonuclear cells, 1% band cells, 3% myelocytes)  
• Peripheral smear: nucleated red cells, anisocytosis, microcytosis, hypochromia, poikilocytosis, teardrop spherocytes, and target cells  
• Hemoglobin electrophoresis: normal  
• Coagulation profile: normal  
• Serum erythropoietin: 11 mU/mL (normal)  
• Arterial blood gas: normal oxygen saturation, no hypoxia  

A bone marrow aspiration showed normal megakaryocytes and normoblasts, a mild left shift in myeloid precursors, and increased lymphocytes, consistent with elevated hematopoietic activity.

A 40-year-old gravida 0 woman with a history of Behçet’s disease (prednisone discontinued to pursue conception) and prior laparoscopic myomectomy for uterine fibroids was referred for infertility. She reported regular menses, but ultrasound monitoring revealed irregular cycles and an elevated anti-Müllerian hormone level (5.45 ng/mL). Baseline serum LH 5.6 mIU/mL, FSH 6.8 mIU/mL, prolactin 22.1 ng/mL, TSH 1.9 μIU/mL, free T3 3.13 pg/mL, and free T4 1.17 ng/mL were normal. Tumor markers CA19-9, CA125, and HE4 and the ROMA index were within low-risk ranges. Ovulation induction with clomiphene citrate revealed on cycle day 11 an anechoic 48×41 mm right ovarian mass, initially interpreted as a follicle. By cycle day 16 the mass measured 61×40 mm with mixed echogenicity and a solid component; serum estradiol was 595 pg/mL and progesterone 1.21 ng/mL, and 5000 IU hCG was administered. On cycle day 6 of the subsequent cycle, the mass enlarged to 90×68 mm with distinct solid areas. The patient remained asymptomatic.

A 26-year-old male cook presented with a 1-month history of insidious posterior left ankle pain without preceding trauma. One month after onset, he noted difficulty bending his left great toe and experienced a snapping sensation at the posterior ankle during active and passive motion. He had received local anesthetic injections into the posterior ankle space without relief.

On examination, there was tenderness on the posteromedial aspect of the left ankle. Active flexion of the great toe resulted in locking in the flexed position; passive dorsiflexion corrected the position but reproduced local pain, clicking, and popping sounds. Neurovascular examination and the range of motion of the foot and ankle were otherwise normal.

Plain radiographs and computed tomography of the left foot and ankle showed no remarkable osseous lesions. T2-weighted MRI of the left ankle revealed effusion in the flexor hallucis longus tendon sheath and the possibility of a partial tear of the tendon.

An 8-year-old boy was referred for persistent, superficial corneal opacities noted two months after an episode of mild conjunctivitis treated with ofloxacin drops; there had been no response to subsequent topical hydrocortisone. He had no ocular complaints, no prior eye disease, and no family history of corneal disorders.  
Best-corrected visual acuity was 1.0 bilaterally. Cycloplegic refraction showed high hyperopia with astigmatism (+7.0 Dsph −4.75 Dcyl axis 170° in the right eye; +7.0 Dsph −4.0 Dcyl axis 175° in the left eye). Intraocular pressures were 14 mmHg OU. Axial lengths measured 20.94 mm (OD) and 21.12 mm (OS).  
Slit-lamp examination revealed multiple, diffuse, grayish, indistinct superficial corneal opacities extending from limbus to limbus with subepithelial haze in both eyes. Fundus examination was normal.  
Anterior-segment swept-source OCT demonstrated bilateral generalized corneal thinning (central corneal thickness ~360 μm), inferotemporal thinnest points, with-the-rule astigmatism, a prolate corneal shape, and an ectasia screening index of 0% OU. High-definition OCT scans showed very discrete, diffuse hyperreflective opacities located just beneath the epithelium.  
In vivo confocal microscopy revealed normal epithelium but, starting at Bowman’s layer, multiple, differently oriented dark striae throughout the stroma and a granular, hyperreflective appearance of keratocytes and extracellular matrix; endothelial morphology was not documented due to poor cooperation.

An 83-year-old man presented with a one-month history of progressive yellow discoloration of the eyes associated with dark urine, clay-colored stools, and pruritus. He reported anorexia but denied weight loss, fever, abdominal pain, vomiting, distension, gastrointestinal bleeding, or steatorrhea. His medical history was significant for hypertension; he was a 30 pack-year smoker and a chronic alcoholic. On examination, he was icteric, and his abdomen was soft, non-tender, and without organomegaly. Laboratory studies showed conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 4.09 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 2.10 mg/dL), elevated alanine aminotransferase (93 U/L), aspartate aminotransferase (105 U/L), and alkaline phosphatase (534 U/L); hematologic parameters and serum amylase and lipase were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a narrowed lumen with mild thickening of the distal common bile duct at the pancreatic head and dilation of the upstream common bile duct and bilateral intrahepatic biliary ducts. Due to concern for distal cholangiocarcinoma, serum CA 19-9 (8 U/mL), carcinoembryonic antigen (3.91 ng/mL), and alpha-fetoprotein (5.24 ng/mL) were obtained and found to be within normal limits. An ERCP attempt failed owing to a markedly narrowed ductal lumen.

A 78-year-old man presented with fever, dysphagia, right‐sided neck swelling, and hoarseness. He developed fever 3 days earlier, dysphagia 2 days earlier, and right cervical swelling with hoarseness 1 day earlier. His history was notable for nephrotic syndrome on low-dose prednisolone, prior radiotherapy for glottic carcinoma, and diabetes mellitus. Two days before referral, he received ceftazidime for presumed infection.

On examination, there was swelling of the right side of the tongue, floor of the mouth, and submandibular area. Laryngoscopy showed redness and swelling of the right pharyngoepiglottic fold and edema of the arytenoid and right supraglottic regions. No tongue trauma was seen. A dental examination ruled out odontogenic infection.

Laboratory tests two days before referral showed WBC 4.97×10^3/µL (77.1% neutrophils), CPK 758 U/L, CRP 1.51 mg/dL, and amylase 107 U/L. On presentation, WBC was 4.76×10^3/µL (80.5% neutrophils), CPK 2301 U/L, and CRP 6.15 mg/dL. Blood cultures were negative.

Contrast‐enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated: (1) diffuse inflammation of the right tongue parenchyma, sparing the anterior tongue and crossing the lingual septum; (2) marked thickening of the right hyoglossus muscle from the sublingual space to the hyoid bone; and (3) extension of inflammation into the submandibular and visceral spaces with resultant laryngeal edema.

A 57-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of swelling in the left leg and a sensation of heaviness after walking. He had no history of trauma or surgery and no comorbidities other than alcoholic liver cirrhosis (Child–Pugh class B). On examination, the left leg was swollen without tenderness. To evaluate for deep vein thrombosis and possible extrinsic venous compression, lower extremity CT venography was performed and revealed two separate cystic lesions compressing the distal portion of the left superficial femoral vein without evidence of thrombosis. The proximal cyst encircled the vein from the posterior aspect to the medial and anterior aspects, and the distal cyst lay posteriorly, extending to the level of the adductor hiatus; the two cysts were not interconnected.

A 52-year-old woman with a history of long-standing diplopia was evaluated in clinic for persistent vertical misalignment. In 2005, MRI of the orbits revealed an anomalous band in the right orbit, which was surgically excised without improvement in motility; her diplopia remained stable in primary gaze. On examination in 2023, she was orthotropic in primary position but had an elevation deficit of the right eye. MRI of the orbits with and without gadolinium was obtained. The globes were unremarkable with no measured proptosis. The retroocular fat, optic nerves and sheaths, optic chiasm, and brain parenchyma appeared normal. A right orbital linear soft-tissue lesion was noted medial to the medial rectus muscle, parallel to it, with enhancement and signal-intensity characteristics identical to those of extraocular muscle, and it was unchanged from the previous study.

A healthy 5-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of a subcutaneous nodule on her right superolateral forehead that had appeared spontaneously 7 months earlier. There was no history of trauma or insect bite. She reported intermittent episodes of swelling with erythema and mild tenderness. On examination, the lesion was a firm, nonmobile, non-tender subcutaneous nodule with normal overlying skin. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 5 mm subperiosteal lesion without deep extension. Doppler ultrasound showed absence of vascularization.

A 66-year-old nonsmoking woman was referred for evaluation of slightly tender swelling, erythrocyanotic discoloration, and occasional spontaneous ulceration of her right hand. The symptoms had been present for 6 years, occurring periodically in autumn and winter, and were slowly progressive. One year before symptom onset, she sustained a dog bite to the right hand with extensive soft tissue injury requiring surgical reconstruction. She had no signs or symptoms of cutaneous or systemic lupus erythematosus. Her history included right-hand metacarpal fractures 20 years earlier and treated Lyme disease 10 years ago. There was no family history of autoimmune disease.

Before referral, acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans was suspected, and antibiotics, highly potent topical steroids, and prednisolone were administered without improvement; Borrelia IgG and IgM antibodies were subsequently negative. Arterial Doppler examination was normal. To exclude underlying disease, a punch biopsy was obtained from the dorsal side of the fourth finger of the right hand, and laboratory studies were ordered.

A 17-year-old male was referred for evaluation of bilateral impalpable testes. He had no significant past medical history. On examination, he appeared as a normally developed adult male; the scrotum was hypoplastic and empty, and no gonads were palpable in the inguinal or paragenital regions. Ultrasonography did not detect any gonadal structures in the scrotum, inguinal canals, pelvis, or abdomen. Laboratory evaluation revealed azoospermia, normal luteinizing hormone, normal testosterone, and mildly elevated follicle-stimulating hormone. 

With informed consent for possible gonadectomy, the patient underwent laparoscopic exploration. On the right side, a 35 mm abdominal testis with normal vas deferens, epididymis, and vessels was found at a high iliac position and was successfully mobilized and fixed into the right hemiscrotum. Intraoperative biopsy confirmed arterial flow.

On the left side, a smaller 20 mm gonad was found in the pelvis, completely disconnected from hypoplastic vasoepididymal structures and supplied only by the internal spermatic vessels. During mobilization along the spermatic vascular bundle, a second off-white ovoid structure resembling a “third testis” appeared, and further dissection revealed a third identical ovoid structure. The three tandem structures were connected proximally by a cord-like band.

A 55-year-old Southeast Asian woman presented with a 6-week history of an intensely pruritic rash on her face and torso and a 1-week history of progressive proximal muscle weakness. The rash began 2 days after she received the first dose of the Pfizer BNT162b2 COVID-19 vaccine. Her medical history included type II diabetes mellitus, stage IV chronic kidney disease, and asthma; she took amlodipine, omeprazole, aspirin, sodium bicarbonate, insulin, semaglutide, and iron supplements. She denied new medications, family history of autoimmune disease, smoking, or significant alcohol use.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Proximal muscle strength in the shoulders and hips was 4/5 on the Medical Research Council scale with preserved distal strength and normal sensation. There was an erythematous rash on the face, upper torso, lateral arms, and lower back. Cardiac and pulmonary examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a creatine kinase level of 11 330 IU/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 111 mm/hr, and C-reactive protein of 14.1 mg/L. Other results included hemoglobin 110 g/L, leukocytes 12 × 10^9/L, creatinine 170 μmol/L (baseline), alanine transaminase 132 IU/L, and albumin 33 g/L. A myositis antibody panel was positive for anti–Mi-2a and anti–Ro-52 antibodies.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis and thighs demonstrated edema in the vastus lateralis and gluteus muscles, most pronounced on the right, consistent with inflammatory myositis. Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no evidence of malignancy.

A 26-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 0, presented at 40 weeks and 6 days’ gestation in early labor and underwent an emergency cesarean section after failure to progress, with an estimated blood loss of 450 mL. Twelve hours postoperatively, she developed pain and swelling in her right lower leg.

Timeline of events:
– 14 hours post-op: Complained of right shin pain; exam showed extreme pain on weight bearing, worsened pain over the tibialis anterior with plantar flexion, decreased right foot range of motion, decreased great toe extension, minimal pitting edema, normal capillary refill and pedal pulses, a small painful lump on the anterior midshin, no calf tenderness, normal sensation and temperature, afebrile. Impression: muscle-related pain; started on analgesia, encouraged to mobilize and elevate the leg, applied heat pack and antiembolism stockings.
– 23 hours: Worsening swelling, burning sensation in the muscle, unable to bear weight.
– 28 hours: Removal of stockings precipitated sudden extreme pain and further swelling; right foot inwardly curved, painful to touch; inability to move toes or lift foot; exam revealed marked swelling and tenderness of anterior leg and foot, palpable pedal pulses, erythema, persistent nodule; afebrile. Diagnosed with cellulitis; started on IV antibiotics, prophylactic enoxaparin, and analgesia; stocking could not be reapplied due to pain.
– Day 2: Persistent swelling and pain on mobilization; Doppler ultrasound to exclude DVT was unremarkable; leg more inflamed and reddened; unable to bear weight.
– Day 3: Some improvement in pain/redness but ongoing great toe weakness; liver function tests more deranged; Clexane dose adjusted; antibiotics changed; afebrile. Differential: neurological problems, cellulitis, or gout.
– Day 4: Slight improvement in erythema but limited mobility due to pain; neurologic exam showed tenderness below the knee, severe pain on inversion, decreased sensation in peroneal region; differential by neurologist: right peroneal nerve palsy, pressure effect, compartment syndrome, and cellulitis; surgical review stated symptoms were not diagnostic of compartment syndrome.
– Day 5: Increased redness and loss of sensation in the first web space; diagnosis: worsening cellulitis with secondary neurological symptoms; antibiotics changed; continued on enoxaparin.

A 39-year-old mother of six presented with a 3-year history of progressive exertional dyspnoea and prominent orthopnoea. She could not tolerate lying supine because of severe breathlessness within minutes. She also noted excessive breathlessness when swimming. Over the preceding 2 months, she developed significant daytime somnolence with pounding morning headaches. She was known to snore but had no witnessed apnoeas; her Epworth Sleepiness Scale score was 21 of 24. There was no history of antecedent illness or trauma. Six years earlier, she had unprovoked pulmonary emboli and was on long-term anticoagulation for pelvic venous congestion syndrome. Family history was noncontributory.

On examination, oxygen saturation was 97% on room air, body-mass index 21 kg/m2, neck circumference <40 cm, and Mallampati score II. Craniofacial and upper-airway anatomy appeared normal. She was euvolaemic. Heart sounds were normal, and the chest was clear. Neurologically, she had a mildly waddling gait and slight weakness on hip flexion. Reflexes and sensation were normal. There were no signs of muscle wasting, fasciculations, or fatigability.

Laboratory tests showed a normal full blood count, C-reactive protein, thyroid function, vitamin B12, and renal and liver biochemistry except for minimally elevated transaminases. Creatine kinase was 624 U/L. Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme was normal. Antinuclear antibodies were weakly positive (1:160, speckled), but extractable nuclear antigens and a vasculitic screen were negative. Antibodies to acetylcholine receptor and muscle-specific tyrosine kinase were negative.

Chest radiograph, electrocardiogram, and transthoracic echocardiogram were unremarkable. Pulmonary function tests were normal except for positional spirometry, which showed a 60% decrease in sitting-to-supine forced vital capacity. A daytime arterial blood gas revealed pH 7.39, pCO2 54 mmHg, pO2 85 mmHg, and HCO3 32 mmol/L. Overnight polysomnography demonstrated moderate obstructive sleep apnoea (apnoea–hypopnoea index 27.1/h), an arousal index of 32/h, and severe desaturation during REM sleep (nadir 68% on room air). Continuous positive airway pressure failed to control sleep-disordered breathing, with persistent desaturation and daytime hypercapnia. She was commenced on bilevel ventilation in spontaneous timed mode with significant improvement.

An 18-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a one-month history of recurrent epigastric pain radiating to the back. The pain was unrelieved by over-the-counter medications, associated with a sensation of abdominal fullness and heartburn that worsened when lying down and improved slightly when leaning forward. She also reported occasional nausea, vomiting, difficulty swallowing solid food, and gradual, unintentional weight loss over the past month. She denied changes in bowel habits, fever, chills, or night sweats.

On examination, she was hemodynamically stable and in no apparent distress. Deep palpation elicited mild substernal tenderness; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and normal liver and pancreatic enzyme levels.

Upper endoscopy revealed a subepithelial, well-circumscribed, non-ulcerated, intramural mass in the gastric fundus along the greater curvature, with overlying normal mucosa. Endoscopic ultrasonography identified a 30 × 28 mm anechoic, thin-walled cystic lesion adjacent to the gastric wall, without solid components or septations, and no Doppler flow. Fine-needle aspiration of the lesion yielded highly viscous fluid with a positive string sign of 15 mm. Cytologic examination of the aspirate demonstrated mucoid material with mucinophages and no malignant cells.

A 71-year-old woman presented with a 10-day history of cough and dyspnea but no fever or chest pain. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine for 15 years and no known drug allergies or TB contacts. On examination her vital signs were normal. Chest radiography showed a large right pleural effusion. Pleural fluid analysis revealed a lymphocyte-predominant exudate (sugar 149 mg/dL; protein 5.4 mg/dL; albumin 1.4 g/dL; ADA 92 IU/L; LDH 983 U/L; lymphocytes 94%, neutrophils 6%), with negative AFB and cytology. Chest CT showed right upper lobe pneumonia and a moderate, loculated right pleural effusion. Initial CBC: WBC 11 740/mm³ (neutrophils 80%, lymphocytes 11%, eosinophils 0%), Hb 12.8 g/dL, platelets 64 500/mm³; ESR 98 mm/hr. She was diagnosed with pleural tuberculosis and started on isoniazid (300 mg), rifampicin (450 mg), pyrazinamide (1 000 mg), and ethambutol (800 mg) daily.

Five weeks later she returned with fever (101.5 °F), vomiting, dizziness, and a generalized itchy rash disrupting sleep. There were no rigors, chills, or lymphadenopathy. Skin exam showed multiple erythematous maculopapular lesions (4 mm to 2 cm) on the thighs, legs, arms, and abdomen; palms and soles were spared; scratch marks were present. Repeat labs showed Hb 12.1 g/dL, platelets 408 000/mm³, WBC 15 550/mm³ with eosinophils 21% (absolute 3094/mm³); peripheral smear: eosinophils 36%, lymphocytes 17%, neutrophils 44%, monocytes 3%, no atypical lymphocytes. Liver and renal function tests were within normal limits. Urinalysis was unremarkable.

A 13-year-old girl presented with a 4-month history of insidious, painless, gradually progressive right-sided neck swelling. She had a history of hydrocephalus at birth treated with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt at 6 months of age and no subsequent revisions. There was no fever, trauma, headache, vertigo, or neurologic deficit. Examination revealed a 12 cm × 4 cm tortuous swelling along the right sternocleidomastoid from the mastoid tip to just below the clavicle. The skin was normal without inflammation, the mass was well-defined, cystic, compressible, nonfluctuant, and nontender, and there were no dilated veins or pulsations. A hard, mobile, cord-like structure was palpable from the postauricular region to the swelling. Transillumination was positive, showing a brilliant glow with a cord shadow. Ultrasonography of the neck showed the intracervical portion of the shunt with a large peri-shunt fluid collection. Fine-needle aspiration yielded clear colorless fluid. Biochemical analysis revealed glucose 73 mg/dL and protein 45 mg/dL; culture showed no growth at 48 hours. Computed tomography of the brain demonstrated the proximal end of the shunt lying external to the cranium with persistent hydrocephalus. CT of the neck revealed a cystic lesion within the right sternocleidomastoid muscle containing the radiopaque shunt catheter.

A 38-year-old Indian man with no comorbidities presented with persistent right-sided nasal pain and intermittent epistaxis responsive to conservative measures. He denied visual disturbances, arthralgias, fever, weight loss, or weakness. He had undergone endoscopic sinus surgery on the right side 6 months earlier. On examination, the right nasal cavity showed absence of the inferior turbinate, crusts, and adhesions; the left nasal cavity was clear. Contrast-enhanced CT of the sinuses demonstrated postoperative changes of right uncinectomy, medial maxillectomy, and inferior turbinectomy, with a mass occupying the right maxillary sinus and destruction of the lamina papyracea without orbital herniation. Contrast-enhanced MRI confirmed an enhancing lesion filling the right maxillary sinus. Laboratory studies showed a serum IgG4 level of 257.00 mg/dL (reference range, 3.00–201.00), a total IgE level of 976.00 IU/mL (reference range, 0.00–114.00), and a CD19+ B-cell count of 1.00 cells/μL (reference range, 107.00–698.00). FDG PET-CT revealed increased metabolic activity confined to the walls of the right maxillary sinus and no abnormal uptake elsewhere.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of progressive dyspnea, tachycardia, and jugular venous distension. She was in New York Heart Association functional class III. Vital signs were notable for tachycardia; blood pressure was normal. Cardiac examination revealed no aortic murmur, and the electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm. A chest radiograph demonstrated cardiomegaly with enlargement of the right atrium. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a pericardial effusion measuring approximately 35 mm and a large extracardiac mass above the left atrium that appeared to communicate with the ascending aorta. Transesophageal echocardiography identified a 61 × 77 mm unruptured aneurysmal sac arising from the noncoronary sinus of Valsalva, without thrombus or intracardiac shunting; the aortic valve was competent and there was no annular dilation. Contrast-enhanced CT angiography confirmed a 74 × 60 mm aneurysm of the noncoronary sinus of Valsalva, free of thrombus, compressing the right atrium. Given the substantial pericardial effusion and concern for rupture or pseudoaneurysm, emergent surgical repair was recommended.

A 19-year-old Omani woman presented with upper abdominal discomfort localized to the epigastric region, jaundice, and dark urine. She denied fever, night sweats, or travel. On examination, she was jaundiced; the remainder of the physical exam was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count; liver function tests revealed total bilirubin 52 µmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 302 IU/L, and ALT 457 IU/L. QuantiFERON-TB Gold was positive. CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 2.4×3.9 cm lobulated, heterogeneous liver hilar mass with central necrosis, obstructing the proximal common hepatic duct and causing intrahepatic biliary dilation. Multiple peripancreatic, porta hepatis, and hepatoduodenal lymph nodes up to 1.2 cm were noted without central necrosis, and “features were suggestive of a cholangiocarcinoma of the common hepatic duct.” MRI redemonstrated a T2 hyperintense, T1 hypointense porta hepatis mass with moderate postcontrast enhancement and marked diffusion restriction. MRCP showed severe narrowing of the proximal 1.8 cm of the common hepatic duct with moderate intrahepatic biliary dilation. Additionally, MRI revealed multiple foci of diffusion restriction scattered throughout the liver, some with subtle postcontrast enhancement suggestive of microabscesses. Chest radiograph was normal. Tumor markers (CA 19-9, CEA, AFP, and chromogranin A) were within normal limits.

A 32-year-old white woman presented with a 1-week history of two lumps on her right thigh and one on her left flank, first noticed one week after returning from a holiday in The Gambia. She was otherwise well, with no significant medical history. Her general practitioner treated her for presumed skin abscesses with a course of amoxicillin. Two days later, she reported expressing two live maggots from the thigh lesions and was referred to the emergency department.

On examination, she was systemically well and apyrexial. There were two lesions on the right thigh and one on the left flank, each approximately 2 × 2 cm, with a central punctum surrounded by an erythematous ring and no obvious discharge. There was no tracking cellulitis or lymphadenopathy. When firm pressure was applied to the flank lesion, a live maggot about 6 mm in length was expressed. Microbiology culture samples were taken, and she was discharged on flucloxacillin, with outpatient follow-up arranged.

A 32-year-old man from a malaria-endemic region presented with 7 days of dull, aching left-sided upper abdominal pain associated with intermittent fever, rigors, night sweats, anorexia, and generalized aches. He denied cough, dyspnea, chest pain, diarrhea, jaundice, itching, epistaxis, or trauma. He had a history of prior uncomplicated P. falciparum infections treated with oral therapy.  
On examination, he was confused and pale, with a temperature of 39.8 °C, pulse rate of 110 beats/min, blood pressure of 90/55 mmHg, and oxygen saturation of 91% on room air. Chest auscultation was normal. Abdominal examination showed localized left upper quadrant tenderness and guarding without generalized peritonitis.  
Initial management included high-flow oxygen, intravenous fluids, analgesia, blood cultures, and empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 8 g/dL, white cell count 5,000/mm^3, platelets 170,000/mm^3, normal coagulation profile, and normal renal, liver, and electrolyte panels. Chest radiograph and urinalysis were unremarkable. A peripheral blood smear showed ring stages of P. falciparum with high parasitemia (>5%). He was started on IV quinine and received two units of packed red blood cells.  
Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 9.6×7.9 cm pelvic fluid collection and a perisplenic hematoma. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 3 cm subcapsular splenic hematoma with free peritoneal fluid indicating a grade II splenic rupture; no active bleeding or contrast extravasation was seen. The liver appeared normal, there was no ascites, and the splenic, mesenteric, and portal veins were patent.

An 11-year-old boy with no significant past medical or family history presented with a 6-week history of gradually worsening periumbilical pain, and 2 weeks of nonbilious vomiting, nonbloody diarrhea, and fever. He denied extraintestinal symptoms. On examination he had diffuse abdominal tenderness without guarding or distention.  
Initial CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated inflammation of the ascending and transverse colon with a contained bowel perforation. Laboratory studies showed:  
• White blood cell count 6.0 × 10^3/μL (normal 4.5–13.5)  
• Hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL (11.5–15.5)  
• C-reactive protein 221 mg/L (0–5)  
• Albumin 2.5 g/dL (3.5–5.2)  
• Ferritin 9 ng/mL (24–336)  
• Fecal calprotectin >1250 μg/g (0–50)  
• PCR stool studies for viral, bacterial, and parasitic pathogens negative  

He was treated with 14 days of broad-spectrum antibiotics, with complete symptom resolution.  
Subsequent EGD and colonoscopy showed grossly normal mucosa; biopsies revealed focal active ileitis and colitis, nonspecific and insufficient for IBD. QuantiFERON-TB was negative, and imaging and histology did not support intestinal tuberculosis. A 4th-generation IBD diagnostic panel was negative, and repeat labs (including fecal calprotectin, inflammatory markers, CBC, and albumin) normalized without IBD therapy.  

The patient then developed daily bloody stools and, based on symptoms and ileal inflammation on MRE, was started on infliximab (capsule endoscopy was planned). Several weeks later, he returned with worsening abdominal pain and fever. A repeat CT scan revealed a 7.6 × 4.3 × 7.0 cm phlegmon adjacent to the bowel in the right lower abdomen.

A 13-month-old girl from rural Cruzeiro do Sul in the Brazilian Amazon was admitted with a 30-day history of worsening shortness of breath, productive cough, and intermittent fever. Two months earlier, she had been hospitalized at 11 months of age for presumed pneumonia; microscopy-confirmed Plasmodium vivax infection was treated with chloroquine and primaquine. She was born at term by Caesarean section (birth weight 3.695 kg), and her mother had no prenatal care.

On admission she had respiratory distress with wheezing, crackles, and nasal flaring. Heart rate was 129 bpm, respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, and axillary temperature 37.0 °C; weight was 9 kg, length 72 cm, and there was mild hepatomegaly. Over the next three days her heart rate rose to 162 bpm, respiratory rate to 50 breaths/min, and temperature to 37.8 °C. She was treated empirically for pneumonia with intravenous ceftriaxone.

Electrocardiography showed sinus rhythm with left ventricular and atrial overload. Chest radiography demonstrated pulmonary congestion and cardiomegaly. A thick smear for malaria on hospital day 3 (September 11th) was negative after examination of 100 high-power fields.

On September 13th she was transferred to a referral hospital for cardiac failure of unknown origin. Examination revealed severe dyspnoea (50 breaths/min), tachycardia (140 bpm), and muffled heart sounds. Echocardiography on September 14th showed dilated cardiomyopathy with severe systolic dysfunction (left atrial diameter 27.2 mm, left ventricular diameter 60×50 mm, ejection fraction 35%), severe mitral regurgitation, and mild aortic regurgitation; no structural cardiac malformation was noted.

Laboratory studies revealed a normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate, negative C-reactive protein, normal CPK, elevated CK-MB (42 U/L), AST 42 U/L, ALT 21 U/L, haemoglobin 9.7 g/dL, white-cell count 10,900/mm³ with 57% neutrophils, and platelet count 370,000/mm³. A repeat thick blood smear on September 13th was again negative. Ceftriaxone was continued, and she was started on carvedilol, digoxin, furosemide, captopril, spironolactone, and oxacillin.

Between September 13th and 17th she remained stable, with gradual reductions in heart and respiratory rates. On September 17th she developed nine days of watery diarrhoea (up to seven stools per day) with low-grade fever. Ceftriaxone was stopped on September 20th, but fever persisted, and on September 23rd she was started on ceftazidime and vancomycin. Diarrhoea resolved after three days of vancomycin, but fever continued, reaching 38.5 °C. On September 29th she received dipyrone and her haemoglobin decreased to 8.3 g/dL.

On October 3rd her haemoglobin fell to 6.6 g/dL, prompting a red-cell transfusion. After transfusion she remained anicteric but experienced worsening dyspnoea (respiratory rate 42 breaths/min) and tachycardia (124 bpm).

A 3-year-old girl was referred for 18F-FDG PET/CT to stage newly diagnosed Hodgkin lymphoma.  
History:  
• Born after a complicated delivery with documented birth asphyxia  
• Congenital hypothyroidism  
• Clinical cerebral palsy, neurodevelopmental delay, cortical blindness  
• Seizures onset at age 3 months, treated with phenobarbital and primidone; no seizure on day of scan  
• No prior brain surgery or known metabolic disorder or infection; Epstein–Barr virus studies negative  
• Consanguineous parents; neonatal glucose nadir 40 mg/dL but no recurrent hypoglycemia during lymphoma treatment  

Neurologic exam:  
• Increased muscle tone in all extremities; deep-tendon reflexes reportedly normal but variably assessed due to agitation  
• No pathologic reflexes  
• Microcephaly  

Cranial CT (prior to lymphoma diagnosis):  
• Occipital volume loss and hypodensity without mass lesion or hemorrhage  

PET/CT findings:  
• Marked bilateral occipital hypometabolism  
• Uptake in known malignant lymphatic regions in the neck and abdomen  

Brain MRI:  
• Cystic area in the occipital region with surrounding gliosis  
• Bilateral occipital cortex hyperintense on axial T2-weighted images  
• Posterior parasagittal increased signal on T2 and FLAIR in both occipital lobes  
• Millimetric subcortical cystic changes and thinning of the occipital cortex on FLAIR  
• Identical, nonprogressive findings on repeat MRI one year later

A 38-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of increasing dizziness, binocular diplopia, and limited lateral gaze in his left eye. He also complained of an orthostatic headache. One week earlier, he had undergone endoscopic urological surgery under spinal anesthesia. He had no significant medical history. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. Neurologic examination showed binocular diplopia and impaired abduction of the left eye, consistent with a unilateral sixth cranial nerve palsy; the remainder of the neurologic and fundoscopic examinations was normal. Noncontrast brain computed tomography, diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging, and magnetic resonance venography showed no intracranial lesions, hemorrhage, or venous thrombosis. The following day, lumbar puncture was performed: opening pressure was 2.8 cm H2O; cerebrospinal fluid glucose was 61 mg/dL with a simultaneous blood glucose of 134 mg/dL; protein was 26.4 mg/dL; albumin was 12.3 mg/dL; and viral and bacterial serologic studies were negative.

A 30-year-old primigravid woman at 38 weeks and 3 days of gestation presented with 24 hours of abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She continued to pass flatus and had a bowel movement the previous day. Her history was notable for polycystic ovarian syndrome and a right donor hepatectomy performed 6 years earlier. She took no regular medications and had no allergies.

On examination she appeared uncomfortable. Her abdomen was tympanitic and generally tender but soft, with scant bowel sounds. Vital signs were normal, and fundal height was appropriate. A chevron scar extended to the xiphoid. Urinalysis was negative for infection, pelvic examination was unremarkable, and cardiotocography showed a reassuring fetal trace. Rectal examination revealed an empty vault without masses and no occult blood. Laboratory studies showed a high-normal white-cell count of 16 × 10^9/L with mild neutrophilia; hemoglobin, electrolytes, renal and liver function tests, and lactate were within normal limits.

A provisional diagnosis of adhesive partial small-bowel obstruction was made. A nasogastric tube provided marginal relief, and a rectal enema was unsuccessful. Plain abdominal radiography showed colonic fecal loading with superolateral displacement of bowel loops by the gravid uterus, without clear evidence of obstruction or free air. Obstetric ultrasound confirmed a viable fetus and showed no specific intra-abdominal pathology.

Labor was induced at 38 weeks and 4 days, and a vaginal delivery was achieved. Symptoms initially improved but worsened again 24 hours postpartum; she was no longer passing flatus and had absent bowel sounds. A repeat abdominal radiograph demonstrated large-bowel obstruction with cecal dilatation up to 13 cm and small-bowel dilatation up to 5 cm.

A term male infant was born at 41 weeks’ gestation via uncomplicated vaginal delivery to a healthy 20-year-old mother. Family history was noncontributory for endocrine or midline defects. Birth weight was 3.71 kg, and Apgar scores were 9 and 9. The infant was vigorous but admitted briefly for suspected sepsis due to maternal fever.

On physical examination, stretched penile length was 1.5 cm. Neither testis was palpable in the scrotum or inguinal canal. There were no cleft lip, cleft palate, or other dysmorphic features.

Initial laboratory studies showed normal serum sodium (137 mmol/L), potassium (3.5 mmol/L), and glucose (4.5 mmol/L). Scrotal ultrasound confirmed both testes in the inguinal canal and no Müllerian structures.

An endocrine evaluation revealed an undetectably low morning cortisol level. A high-dose ACTH stimulation test produced cortisol levels of 24.8 nmol/L at both 30 and 60 minutes, indicating adrenal insufficiency. Insulin-like growth factor 1 and binding protein levels were low, suggesting growth hormone deficiency. Thyroid studies showed a borderline low free T4 with an inappropriately normal TSH, consistent with central hypothyroidism. There was no evidence of diabetes insipidus, with serum sodium 137–143 mmol/L and urine output 1.3 mL/kg/hour.

The patient was started on hydrocortisone, levothyroxine, and growth hormone replacement.

A 10-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of early pubertal development. He noted adult-type body odor at 9.1 years and pubic hair at 10 years. At 9.11 years, he developed right arm pain, and imaging of the right humerus showed a 6.7×2.2×2 cm expansile diaphyseal lesion. Leading differentials included fibrous dysplasia, eosinophilic granuloma, and chronic osteomyelitis; biopsy of the lesion demonstrated fibrous dysplasia. He also had a history of left forearm fractures at age 5 years. There was no family history of precocious puberty. At presentation, his height was 148.7 cm (SDS +1.45). On examination, there were no café-au-lait spots; Tanner stage 2 pubic hair; testicular volumes were 15 mL (left) and 12 mL (right); and stretched penile length was 5 cm (Tanner stage 2 genitalia). Bone age was 13 years, with a predicted adult height of 175 cm (midparental height, 173 cm). Laboratory studies were: LH 0.745 mIU/mL (0.2–4.9), FSH 0.933 mIU/mL (1.8–3.2), testosterone 42 ng/dL (18–150), inhibin B 436.6 pg/mL (41–238), anti-Müllerian hormone 36.1 ng/mL (45.3–191.3), β-hCG <2 mIU/mL, IGF-1 within normal limits, and TSH within normal limits. A whole-body nuclear scan showed increased uptake in the right humerus, distal right radius, and right scapula; testicular ultrasound was unremarkable.

A 70-year-old man was admitted with a 4-day history of fever and diffuse pain, initially in the cervical area and right shoulder. Soon after, he developed polyarthritis involving the elbows, wrists, hands, knees, and ankles. Three weeks prior he had self-limited rotavirus diarrhea. He had no remarkable family history. On examination, he was bedridden from pain, with tachycardia and fever (38°C). He had evident polyarthritis of the right wrist, knees, elbows, shoulders, right ankle, and right midfoot; the rest of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 14 mg/dL, white-cell count 26 690 cells/mm3 without a left shift, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 120 mm/h, and C-reactive protein 5.14 mg/dL (normal ≤ 0.5). Serologic tests for dengue, hepatitis B and C, HIV, and syphilis were negative, and urine culture was negative. Serum uric acid, renal function, electrolytes (including calcium, phosphorus, and magnesium), thyroid function, and parathyroid hormone levels were all within normal limits. Transesophageal echocardiography showed no vegetations. Plain radiographs demonstrated chondrocalcinosis in the knee menisci, wrist fibrocartilage, metacarpophalangeal joints, and elbow cartilage, as well as joint-space narrowing and glenohumeral irregularity of the right shoulder resembling Milwaukee shoulder syndrome.

A 24-year-old Aboriginal woman with class IV lupus nephritis on hydroxychloroquine, mycophenolate mofetil, and low-dose prednisone presented with 3 days of fever, productive cough, and worsening dyspnea. Her history included rheumatic heart disease, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and triple-positive lupus antiphospholipid antibodies without prior thromboses. On examination, her respiratory rate was 28/min, temperature 38.6 °C, and oxygen saturation 88% on room air (improving to 92% with supplemental oxygen). Auscultation revealed bibasilar crackles and a pansystolic murmur.  
Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 63 g/L, white cell count 6.8 × 10^9/L, platelets 91 × 10^9/L, creatinine 146 μmol/L, ANA positive with dsDNA > 667 IU/mL, and low C3 (0.32 g/L) and C4 (0.04 g/L).  
Chest radiography and high-resolution CT demonstrated bilateral pulmonary infiltrates with upper-lobe predominance. A CT pulmonary angiogram excluded pulmonary emboli but revealed extensive ground-glass opacities and areas of consolidation. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for infectious pathogens and malignancy and showed no hemosiderin-laden macrophages.

A 4-year-old girl with eczema and absence seizures on ethosuximide presented with 3 months of recurrent fevers, migratory joint pain, joint swelling, and hematuria. During this time she had three hospitalizations for pneumonia and impetigo. More recently she developed abdominal pain, sore throat, cough, and behavior changes. On transfer, vital signs were T 37.5°C, HR 115/min, RR 20/min, BP 121/84 mmHg. She appeared uncomfortable and was “not herself.” Examination revealed diffuse polyarthritis and tender generalized lymphadenopathy; there were no skin rashes, mucosal changes, murmurs, or pleurodynia.

There was no travel or sick contacts. Family history was significant for SLE in her paternal grandmother’s sister. Admission labs showed anemia (Hb 10.5 g/dL), ESR >145 mm/h, CRP 1.12 mg/dL, and a positive direct Coombs test; WBC, platelets, and TSH were normal. HIV and tuberculosis tests were negative. Urinalysis revealed 30 mg/dL protein and 15 RBCs per high-power field, and the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio was 1790 mg/g. Urine culture had no growth. CK was normal. Complement levels were low (C3 48 mg/dL, C4 6 mg/dL), and C1q binding protein was elevated at 61 mcg Eq/mL. She was positive for lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies. Recent outpatient rheumatology labs showed an ANA >1:1280 and positive anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith, and anti-RNP antibodies.

Brain MRI with contrast was normal. Abdominal ultrasound revealed bilateral grade 2 pelviectasis, mild hepatomegaly, increased mesenteric echogenicity, and trace pelvic free fluid. Bone marrow biopsy showed mildly hypocellular marrow with no blasts or other pathology.

A 50-year-old man presented with sudden-onset, severe pain and vision loss in his left eye, accompanied by headache and nausea. He reported intermittent, milder episodes of red eye in that eye over the past few months, which had been treated as conjunctivitis. His past medical history was notable for an 8-year history of psoriasis treated with brodalumab injections every 15 days.

On examination, his uncorrected Snellen visual acuity was 8/10 in the right eye and 4/10 in the left eye. Intraocular pressure measured by applanation tonometry was 15 mm Hg in the right eye and 37 mm Hg in the left eye. The right eye examination was unremarkable. Findings in the left eye included marked conjunctival injection and edema, a clear cornea, convex iris configuration, a very shallow anterior chamber with angle closure in all quadrants on gonioscopy, few cells in the chamber, and a round mid-dilated pupil; the patient was phakic.

Funduscopic examination without pharmacologic dilation revealed a normal optic disc (cup-to-disc ratio 0.3–0.4) and a normal fovea in both eyes. A diagnosis of acute angle closure crisis in the left eye was made, and the patient received topical timolol, latanoprost, dorzolamide, brinzolamide, and oral acetazolamide, followed by Nd:YAG laser peripheral iridotomy. Thirty minutes after iridotomy, the intraocular pressure decreased to 25 mm Hg, and the patient’s symptoms improved slightly. He was discharged on maximal topical anti-glaucoma therapy and daily oral acetazolamide.

The next day, the patient reported persistent ocular pain in the left eye. Visual acuity remained 4/10 OS, intraocular pressure was 25 mm Hg OS, conjunctival edema had increased, injection persisted, and the anterior chamber was only slightly deeper. The peripheral iridotomy was patent. Anterior-segment optical coherence tomography showed a shallow angle and a patent iridotomy in the left eye.

A 64-year-old woman with a history of orthotopic heart transplantation and end-stage renal failure on hemodialysis presented with six weeks of progressive dyspnea, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, and a 5-kg weight loss. An outpatient chest radiograph showed a left upper-lobe infiltrate. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 16.5 Gpt/l and a C-reactive protein level of 245 mg/l. She was treated sequentially with oral amoxicillin and then ciprofloxacin without clinical or radiographic improvement. On hospital admission, her white-cell count was 18.2 Gpt/l and C-reactive protein was 278 mg/l. Chest computed tomography demonstrated an 8 × 8 cm mass in the left upper lobe. Bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy and bronchoalveolar lavage showed no evidence of malignancy on histology, yet lung cancer remained the leading diagnosis. She was transferred for further evaluation. At this point, the microbiologic results of the bronchoalveolar lavage were still incomplete.

An 11-year-old sub-Saharan African girl presented with a 9-month history of left-sided neck swelling and pain. The lesion began as a small, painless, mobile nodule over the left infra-auricular region that gradually enlarged over 6 months, became immobile and intermittently painful, and developed a sinus tract discharging thick, cream-white non-offensive pus. She reported weight loss and intermittent fever but denied anorexia or night sweats. She had received multiple courses of oral antibiotics and anti-inflammatory drugs without improvement. There was no history of dental infection or extraction, but two weeks before onset she recalled a thorn prick injury to the left infra-auricular area. During the last 6 days, the swelling ulcerated, pain increased, and malodorous purulent discharge prompted presentation. She had no known chronic disease and normal socioeconomic status.

On examination, she appeared frail but was afebrile with normal vital signs. A 13 × 14 cm ulcerated mass below the left ear discharged yellowish pus; there was tenderness, trismus, and firm induration of surrounding tissues, but no palpable lymphadenopathy. Intraoral examination was normal.

Laboratory studies showed a normal full blood count and biochemistry. HIV serology and Mantoux test were negative. Cervical radiograph ruled out bone involvement. Ultrasonography and CT were not performed. A wet mount of the pus demonstrated granules, and Gram stain revealed gram-positive filamentous bacteria. Aerobic cultures on blood agar and MacConkey agar remained sterile after 24 hours; pus was sent for anaerobic culture.

A 72-year-old man was followed annually after resection of a small cell carcinoma of adrenal origin at age 66. He noted progressive discomfort in the left lower abdomen. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 0.44 mg/dL (normal <0.30 mg/dL) and a soluble IL-2 receptor level of 619 U/mL (normal <483 U/mL). Glycated hemoglobin was 7.2% (normal <6.2%). Serum tumor markers (CEA, CA 19-9, NSE, and ProGRP) were within normal limits. Stored preoperative serum revealed an IgG4 concentration of 50.8 mg/dL (reference 4.8–105 mg/dL) and a mildly elevated total IgG of 2056 mg/dL (reference 870–1700 mg/dL). Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated a 6-cm lobulated mesenteric mass in the left lower quadrant with mild enhancement. PET–CT showed significant FDG uptake in the lesion (SUV max, 6.5). Clinically, sclerosing mesenteritis versus recurrence of small cell carcinoma was considered.

A 24-year-old man presented with acute onset of left knee pain and inability to flex the knee. He denied any history of trauma or precipitating event. On examination, there was no palpable lesion in the popliteal fossa. Ultrasonography with Doppler imaging demonstrated patent popliteal vessels without thrombosis or flow abnormalities and normal muscle architecture. Electroneurography of the posterior tibial, peroneal, and sural nerves showed normal latencies, amplitudes, and conduction velocities. Needle examination of the left gastrocnemius muscle was normal. A lumbar MRI showed no nerve-root compression, masses, spinal cord compression, or disc herniations. MRI of the left knee—including T2-weighted, T1-weighted, and gradient-echo sequences—excluded meniscal and cartilaginous lesions and revealed an additional muscle arising near the lateral head of the gastrocnemius, coursing deep within the popliteal fossa, and inserting on the posteromedial articular capsule. MRI of the right knee showed no similar muscle.

A 66-year-old woman with mixed connective tissue disease (Fitzpatrick skin type II) presented with a 7-year history of a pigmented band on her left thumbnail. She had received hydroxychloroquine for 18 years, which was discontinued 4 years before presentation due to progressive hyperpigmentation of the lower legs. Skin hyperpigmentation first appeared 3 years after hydroxychloroquine initiation (cumulative dose 438 g), and the nail pigment band developed 15 years after initiation (cumulative dose 2190 g). A prior biopsy of leg skin showed dermal intracellular and extracellular yellow-to-brown granules that were positive on Fontana-Masson and Perl’s stains. Current medications included clopidogrel, prednisone, bupropion, diltiazem, gabapentin, and levothyroxine. On examination, there were hyperpigmented macules and patches on the lower legs and a 1–2 mm central longitudinal gray-brown band of the left thumbnail, without pigment in the nail folds or hyponychium. Dermoscopy of the nail showed a gray-brown background with regular gray-brown parallel lines of uniform color, spacing, and thickness. A tangential shave biopsy of the nail matrix demonstrated brown nonrefractile, coarsely granular pigment in the superficial dermis, both extracellularly and within macrophages and fibroblasts; Fontana-Masson stain highlighted these granules, and Perl’s iron stain was negative.

A previously healthy 1-year-old boy was referred with a 15-day history of 6–7 mucoid, nonbloody diarrheal stools per day, abdominal distension, irritability, and fever spikes up to 39.8 °C. On examination, he appeared ill, with marked abdominal distension, a palpable abdominal mass, decreased bowel sounds, and diffuse abdominal tenderness. Initial laboratory tests showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, thrombocytosis, a C-reactive protein level of 97.1 mg/dL, and mild hyponatremia; liver and renal function, electrolytes (apart from sodium), and blood glucose were within normal limits, and stool examination revealed no parasites. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a multiseptate fluid collection occupying the right abdomen and displacing bowel loops; plain abdominal radiography showed opacification of the right hemiabdomen with displacement of bowel loops to the left without air-fluid levels or calcifications.

A 13-month-old boy and his 5½-year-old sister were evaluated for abnormal head shapes noted since infancy. Both parents were nonconsanguineous, phenotypically normal, with no family history of craniofacial disorders and no exposure to teratogens during pregnancy. Both pregnancies were full-term, and birth weights were within normal limits.

On examination, the boy had dolichocephaly with a wide, high forehead, a small low-bridged nose, and midface hypoplasia. His neurological, cognitive, and motor development were appropriate for age, and there were no signs of increased intracranial pressure or systemic anomalies. The sister had a wide, high forehead, low nasal bridge, midface hypoplasia, and bilateral proptosis, with similarly normal development and no systemic findings.

Three-dimensional CT reconstruction of the skull revealed in the boy complete fusion of the sagittal suture with early closure of bilateral lambdoid, occipitomastoid, and squamosal sutures; the sister had fusion of the sagittal, bilateral coronal, lambdoid, spheno-frontal, squamous, and occipitomastoid sutures with partial spheno-squamous fusion. MRI of the brain showed no Chiari malformation or ventriculomegaly in either child, although the sister demonstrated optic nerve tortuosity, prominence of perioptic CSF, posterior orbital scleral flattening, and an empty sella suggestive of elevated intracranial pressure.

A 26‐year‐old man presented with a 7‐day history of insidious, low‐grade fever without chills or rigors and a 5‐day history of watery diarrhoea (4–5 episodes per day) associated with diffuse abdominal discomfort but no blood or mucus. Three days before admission, he noted jaundice and dark urine without oliguria or dysuria. He denied alcohol excess, hepatotoxins, IV drug use, blood transfusions, or high‐risk sexual behaviour.

On examination, he was febrile (temperature not specified), blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg, pulse 108 beats/min, icteric, and without stigmata of chronic liver disease. There was no rash, lymphadenopathy, or edema.

Initial laboratory results: hemoglobin 12 g/dL, white-cell count 11 330/µL, INR 2.69; total bilirubin 4.5 mg/dL (direct 3.0 mg/dL); AST 452 IU/L; ALT 2750 IU/L; alkaline phosphatase 254 IU/L; GGT 169 IU/L; albumin 2.2 g/dL; globulin 2.7 g/dL. Blood urea 132 mg/dL; creatinine 9.37 mg/dL; electrolytes normal. IgM anti-HEV was positive; serologic tests for hepatitis A, B, C, HIV, dengue, and Leptospira were negative. Peripheral smear and rapid malaria test were negative. He required two sessions of slow low-efficiency dialysis; renal function then improved and dialysis was discontinued.

On hospital day 6, he developed recurrent fever, left-sided pleuritic chest pain, and sudden dyspnoea. He was restless and tachypneic, with an audible S3 gallop. He was intubated for respiratory distress. Arterial blood gas analysis showed type I respiratory failure; ECG revealed sinus tachycardia with dynamic ST-T changes; chest radiography showed pulmonary congestion. Urgent two-dimensional echocardiography demonstrated global hypokinesia with normal chamber size and a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 25–30%. Troponin I was 0.5 ng/mL (elevated) and CK-MB was 68 IU/L (28% of total CK).

A 7-year-old boy with normal development and growth, born to consanguineous parents, was transferred for evaluation of serial generalized tonic–clonic seizures and subsequent coma. Two days earlier he had been admitted locally for febrile seizures, treated with bolus phenobarbital and phenytoin, and then required endotracheal intubation for decreased consciousness. On arrival, he was in a deep coma, with normal vital signs. Examination revealed dilated pupils with sluggish light response, hepatomegaly (4 cm below the costal margin), marked hypotonia, and absent deep tendon reflexes. Routine laboratory studies showed profound hypoglycemia (blood glucose <20 mg/dL) without ketonuria and elevated liver enzymes (AST 234 U/L; ALT 86 U/L). An endocrinology evaluation demonstrated a normal triglyceride level (92 mg/dL), cholesterol 73 mg/dL, LDL 37 mg/dL, lactate 13 ng/dL, cortisol 62.4 µg/dL, ACTH 411 pg/mL, and insulin 0.7 µIU/mL. Viral and immune hepatitis panels were negative, and urine toxicology screening was unremarkable. His older brother had died at a similar age with comparable symptoms.

A 22-year-old woman with poorly controlled type I diabetes mellitus was transferred for evaluation of right-sided facial pain, swelling, and diplopia that developed after extraction of her upper right third molar three days earlier. One week before transfer, she had visited an ear-nose-throat specialist for diffuse midface pain; dental evaluation led to extraction of the upper right third molar, and amoxicillin was prescribed. Postoperatively, her facial pain worsened, and she was hospitalized for generalized facial edema and pain. She was transferred 24 hours later because of double vision caused by paralysis of the right lateral rectus muscle.  
On examination, the patient was undernourished with normal vital signs. There was slight hemifacial edema on the right side, inward gaze of the right eye from right abducens-nerve palsy, and decreased sensation over the maxillary (V2) distribution on the right. Intraoral examination revealed a 1 cm ulcer on the right side of the palate near the second upper molar. Laboratory studies showed elevated blood glucose, mild dehydration, and a glycated hemoglobin level of 12.3%. Ophthalmologic evaluation confirmed right palpebral edema without retinal or optic-nerve lesions and diplopia on rightward gaze. Computed tomography demonstrated thickening of the mucosal lining of the paranasal sinuses, and magnetic resonance imaging showed involvement of all right paranasal sinuses without central nervous system extension.

An 11-year-old female presented with 8 months of intermittent swelling of the bilateral upper eyelids and neck. Examination revealed bilateral swollen upper eyelids with palpable masses in the lacrimal fossae; submandibular and sublingual glands were enlarged, tender, and movable without erythema or signs of acute skin infection. She denied dry eyes or dry mouth and had no family history of bleeding disorders. Neck ultrasound showed enlarged bilateral parotid, submandibular, and sublingual glands with irregular hypoechoic parenchyma. Maxillofacial MRI revealed enlargement of both lacrimal glands and homogeneous enlargement of bilateral submandibular and parotid glands, measuring up to 4.7 × 3.9 cm; bilateral maxillary sinusitis was also noted without abnormal lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed serum IgG 42.31 g/L (normal 6.5–12.3), IgE 271.5 IU/mL (0–170), IgG4 1005.68 mg/dL (1.6–115), an isolated prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time of 80.9 s with normal platelet count and prothrombin time, factor VIII activity of 0.6% (60–150), and a factor VIII inhibitor titer of 480 BU/mL. The patient underwent complete surgical biopsy of the left submandibular gland and subsequently developed a prolonged subcutaneous hematoma and bruising at the biopsy site.

A 36-year-old man presented with a 10-day history of epigastric pain, constipation, and vomiting. He had no prior episodes, surgeries, peritoneal dialysis, chronic medications, or comorbidities. On examination, he appeared well, but his abdomen was distended, diffusely tender on deep palpation, with guarding and dullness in the left hypochondrium and flank. There were no palpable organomegaly, no rebound tenderness, and bowel sounds were reduced. Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin level of 15.6 g/dL and a leukocyte count of 11,700 cells/mL (86% segmented neutrophils, without left shift). An abdominal ultrasound and routine laboratory workup were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a central conglomeration of small-bowel loops, some with air–fluid levels, all enclosed by a thick membranous structure. There was slight enhancement of the intestinal wall, mild engorgement of the mesenteric vessels, and a small amount of free intraperitoneal fluid.

A 41-year-old man presented with right groin pain and apprehension. He had undergone bilateral hip arthroscopy for femoroacetabular impingement three years earlier; operative notes did not describe any capsular repair. In 2016, after a ground-level fall, he sustained an anterior dislocation of the right hip that was reduced closed in the emergency department. He recovered with physiotherapy, but 10 months later sustained a second anterior dislocation of the right hip while pivoting on a standing leg; this too was reduced closed. On examination, he ambulated with crutches, complained of groin pain and pain with hip extension, and had no neurovascular deficits. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right hip demonstrated disruption of the anterior hip capsule. Three-dimensional CT reconstruction showed irregularity of the anterior-superior acetabular rim with adjacent bone fragments and a reduced center-edge angle (15.7° on the right, 25.2° on the left). MRI arthrography revealed rupture of the anterior capsule with deficiency of the anterior ligaments and leakage of contrast antero-superiorly.

A 32-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of a nonhealing nodule on the right side of her face, causing discomfort and cosmetic concern. Several courses of oral antibiotics and topical dermatologic ointments had been prescribed without improvement. On examination, there was a 5 mm × 5 mm soft, erythematous nodule with minimal purulent discharge located over the right nasolabial fold. No intraoral vestibular swelling was evident, but a firm, cord-like tract could be palpated running from the skin lesion toward the apex of the maxillary right canine (tooth 13). A periapical radiograph of tooth 13 demonstrated a roughly round, poorly demarcated radiolucency, approximately 0.5 mm in diameter, surrounding its apex.

A 48-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of a swelling in the palm of her left hand at the level of the index-finger ray. She denied any history of trauma, pain, neurological symptoms, triggering phenomena, or vascular complaints. Her medical history was otherwise unremarkable. 

On examination, there was a 3.5 × 3.0 cm, soft, non-tender, subcutaneous mass in the mid-palm, without overlying skin changes. Distal sensation and perfusion were normal, and there were no palpable thrills or bruits. 

Ultrasound imaging demonstrated a well-circumscribed lesion enveloping both flexor tendons in the palm. Magnetic resonance imaging was not performed because of a documented allergy to gadolinium contrast.

A 2.5-year-old cachectic Afghan boy was referred for evaluation of recurrent vomiting and abdominal distention. Since 1 year of age, he had forceful, non-bilious vomiting 4–5 times daily, occurring 30–60 minutes after feeds; solid foods worsened his symptoms, and his diet was largely restricted to milk and semisolid foods. He also had constipation, painful defecation, fever, and progressive weight loss. Two older siblings had died during surgery for duodenal web. On examination, he was malnourished, and his abdomen was distended with normal bowel sounds; there was no hepatosplenomegaly. An upright abdominal radiograph showed marked distension of the stomach and duodenum with a “double bubble” sign and gas in the distal intestinal loops, indicating partial obstruction. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated severe dilation of the stomach and duodenum, with a focal narrowing at the distal third-to-fourth portions of the duodenum and passage of contrast into distal loops.

A 29-year-old Nepalese man with no prior surgery or comorbidities presented with progressive abdominal distension and dull, nonradiating abdominal pain for one year. He denied fever, cough, jaundice, trauma, nausea, vomiting, altered bowel or bladder habits, significant weight loss, and had no known dog contact. On examination his abdomen was distended with dullness to percussion; otherwise the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL, white blood cell count 11 500/µL with 4 % eosinophils, and normal C-reactive protein; liver and renal function tests were within normal limits. An ELISA test for Echinococcus granulosus was positive. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed multiple well-defined hypoechoic masses with echogenic septations. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed multiple well-defined cystic lesions of variable size throughout the peritoneal cavity, some containing floating membranes. Chest radiography was normal, and there were no similar lesions in the liver, lungs, or other organs.

A 28‐year‐old man with no past medical history, born and raised in Lebanon with no travel outside the country in the past 23 years, presented with fatigue and night sweats of 6 months’ duration. He denied fever, cough, dyspnea, joint pain, or rash. On examination, he was afebrile with normal vital signs. Lung, cardiac, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed a spleen palpable to the pelvis and crossing the midline, without venous collaterals.

Laboratory studies showed thrombocytopenia; liver‐function and renal‐function tests were within normal limits. A chest radiograph was normal. Abdominal ultrasonography confirmed splenomegaly without hepatomegaly. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a spleen measuring 46 × 20 cm with multiple hypodense lesions, and there was neither hepatomegaly nor lymphadenopathy. A peripheral blood smear and bone marrow examination were normal. A PET scan demonstrated multiple hypermetabolic lesions in the spleen (SUV, 15) and no abnormal uptake elsewhere.

A 54‐year‐old woman was referred for binocular diplopia that began 2 weeks earlier. She denied headache, vomiting, recent trauma, pregnancy, childbirth, vaccination, or personal/family history of thrombosis. Her blood pressure was 120/85 mm Hg; other vital signs were normal. On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes; intraocular pressures were 19 and 20 mm Hg. Pupillary responses were normal without an afferent defect. Ocular alignment showed mild esotropia at near, and Hess charting demonstrated bilateral abduction deficits. Slit‐lamp biomicroscopy was unremarkable. Fundoscopy revealed marked bilateral optic disc swelling with peripapillary hemorrhages (Frisén Grade 3). Optical coherence tomography confirmed disc edema; visual fields showed enlarged blind spots. Noncontrast head CT was normal. Contrast‐enhanced brain MRI showed no mass lesions or hydrocephalus, but T2‐weighted axial images demonstrated flattening of the posterior globes and enlargement of the cerebrospinal fluid spaces in the optic nerve sheaths, consistent with intracranial hypertension.

A 59-year-old man presented after an unwitnessed syncopal event in which he stood up, felt dizzy, fell backwards striking his head, and had a brief (<3 seconds) loss of consciousness. He reported three prior unexplained syncopal episodes over the past year, including one resulting in a motor-vehicle collision. His medical history included severe bilateral carotid stenosis, severe mitral stenosis, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes, and stage III chronic kidney disease.

On admission, supine blood pressure was 122/52 mm Hg with a heart rate of 54 bpm; upon standing, blood pressure fell to 95/48 mm Hg and heart rate rose to 59 bpm. Electrocardiogram revealed sinus bradycardia with first-degree atrioventricular block (PR interval 328 ms). Physical examination was notable for bilateral harsh carotid bruits. While auscultating the left carotid sinus and applying pressure, the patient experienced dizziness and his heart rate transiently decreased by more than 10 bpm.

A 14-day-old boy was referred by his anxious parents for evaluation of a left lower-limb deformity. He was the first child of healthy, non-consanguineous parents (mother 32 years, father 33 years), born at term by vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 2600 g. APGAR scores were 2 and 6 at one and five minutes, respectively. The antenatal history was unremarkable for rash, teratogen exposure, radiation, or fever.

On inspection, the left leg was short and thin compared with the right. The left foot appeared short due to absence of the fourth ray, and there was syndactyly between the second and third toes. There was no bowing or skin dimpling. Palpation revealed a normal left ankle joint but medial and lateral laxity of the left knee compared with the right. Examination of the right lower limb, both upper limbs, face, pelvis, and spine was normal. Systemic examination was unremarkable.

Radiographs of the left lower limb showed absence of the proximal tibial epiphysis, absence of the talus, and absence of the fourth ray; the tibia and fibula were shorter than on the right side. A skeletal survey of the remainder of the body was normal. Ultrasonography of the abdomen and pelvis was unremarkable. Peripheral blood karyotyping showed a normal 46,XY result.

A 19-year-old woman presented in January 2024 with primary amenorrhea. Her developmental milestones were normal, and she had been developing phenotypically. She had not commenced sexual activity. There was no family history of genital ambiguity.

On examination, height was 177 cm, weight 53 kg, and the upper-to-lower segment ratio was 1 to 1. Waist circumference was 88 cm and hip circumference was 103 cm. She had a feminine voice with sparse axillary hair. Breast development was Tanner stage 3 and pubic hair Tanner stage 4. The external genitalia appeared normal; vaginal examination was not performed.

Laboratory studies revealed hypergonadotropic hypogonadism with an elevated FSH of 274 mIU/mL and LH of 35 mIU/mL, normal 17-hydroxyprogesterone (0.57 ng/mL), and normal testosterone (0.14 ng/mL). Pelvic ultrasound showed an anteflexed uterus with a normal endometrial stripe and no evidence of ovarian pathology, findings incongruent with the hormonal profile. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a hypoplastic uterus with absent ovaries.

A 4-year-old girl from Kenya, weighing 18 kg, presented with 6 months of persistent pounding of the precordium and clinical features of heart failure despite treatment with diuretics, digoxin, and beta-blockers. On examination she had tachycardia and signs of low cardiac output. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a dilated heart with severe left ventricular dysfunction; no obvious structural cause was identified. A 12-lead ECG revealed a regular narrow-QRS tachycardia at 280 beats per minute, a RP interval of 90 ms, and upright P waves in the inferior leads. Administration of adenosine resulted in continuation of the tachycardia with transient atrioventricular block, seen as rapid P waves without QRS complexes. The differential diagnosis at this point included atrial tachycardia with 1:1 atrioventricular conduction and clockwise atrial flutter. Medical therapy failed to control the arrhythmia or improve heart failure, leading to consideration of radiofrequency ablation.

A 32-year-old Caucasian woman presented with two weeks of throbbing right-sided neck pain radiating to her jaw, acutely worse for two days, along with transient nonspecific visual changes and bilateral upper-extremity paresthesia. An outpatient carotid Doppler ultrasound showed 50–69% stenosis of the right carotid artery. Clinic laboratories revealed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 67 mm/hr and a C-reactive protein level of 2.7 mg/dL. She was started on methylprednisolone 125 mg every six hours and admitted for further evaluation.

Her history included anxiety (on escitalopram), hyperlipidemia (on atorvastatin), and a prior massive transfusion for placental abruption. She denied fevers, chills, chest pain, abdominal pain, headaches, or limb claudication.

On examination, temperature was 36.6 °C, pulse 81/min, blood pressure 109/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, and SpO₂ 100% on room air. She was alert and without distress. The neck was supple but exquisitely tender to light palpation over the right carotid distribution without erythema, induration, lymphadenopathy, or bruits. Cardiopulmonary and neurologic examinations were normal; peripheral pulses were 2+ bilaterally.

Laboratory studies showed ESR 36 mm/hr and high-sensitivity CRP 0.71 mg/dL; complete blood count, metabolic panel, and autoimmune markers (rheumatoid factor; ANA; anti-DNA; and anti-ENA subtypes) were unremarkable. Carotid CT angiography revealed 0% stenosis of the extracranial internal carotid arteries, no dissections, and no pseudoaneurysms. Head CT angiography showed no intracranial vascular abnormalities. Chest magnetic resonance angiography demonstrated normal caliber and patency of the aorta and its major branches without evidence of inflammation.

Given persistent carotidynia and elevated acute-phase reactants despite unremarkable imaging, an early large-vessel vasculitis was considered, and corticosteroid therapy was continued.

A 78-year-old Caucasian woman presented with an 8-day history of nausea, multiple bilious vomiting episodes, anorexia, right hypochondrial and epigastric discomfort, and fevers up to 38.5°C. On examination, she appeared ill, with pale skin and mucous membranes, signs of dehydration, tachypnea, tachyarrhythmia, and a temperature of 39°C. The abdomen was soft, mildly distended, and tender in the epigastrium and right upper quadrant.

Her medical history included chronic hepatitis C infection, hypertension, atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes mellitus, prior stroke with left hemiparesis, hypothyroidism, hyperlipidemia, and recent NSAID use. Laboratory studies showed WBC 10.72×10^9/L (neutrophils 88.5% with toxic granulation), CRP 72.7 IU/L, glucose 139 IU/L, urea 73.4 IU/L, creatinine 1.38 IU/L, γ-GT 87 IU/L, total bilirubin 1.37 IU/L, direct bilirubin 1.10 IU/L, and LDH 517 IU/L.

A chest radiograph suggested possible aspiration pneumonia. Abdominal radiography raised suspicion for air within the gallbladder. Ultrasonography showed a poorly visualized gallbladder with suspected intrahepatic biliary pneumobilia, no biliary dilation, and a dilated, fluid-filled stomach. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a calculus within the second to third portion of the duodenum, dilatation of the first part of the duodenum, mild gastric dilatation, and air and contrast within the gallbladder.

A 15-year-old female was referred for evaluation of recurrent hypoglycemia. She was born at term (birth weight 2980 g, length 50 cm) after a pregnancy complicated by hypertension; Apgar scores were 8 and 9. There were no neonatal complications or developmental delays. At age 13, she lost consciousness; a glucometer reading after recovery was 1.87 mmol/L (33.7 mg/dL). There were no reports of tremor, sweating, palpitations, or seizures. She was not evaluated again until age 14, when routine labs for community-acquired pneumonia revealed hypoglycemia.

On referral at age 15, she had no acute symptoms. Laboratory results showed:
• Glycated hemoglobin: 3.4% (reference 4–6%)  
• Serum glucose: 1.94 mmol/L (34.9 mg/dL) (reference 3.3–6.1 mmol/L)  
• Insulin: 30.29 μU/mL (reference 2.6–24.9 μU/mL)  
• C-peptide: 4.81 ng/mL (reference 1.1–4.4 ng/mL)  
• Anti-insulin antibodies: 2.54 U/mL (reference 0–10 U/mL)  
• No detectable sulfonylureas in serum.

Endoscopic ultrasound, CT, and MRI of the abdomen showed no pancreatic mass. Continuous glucose monitoring revealed persistent asymptomatic hypoglycemia (2.8–3.2 mmol/L) on a complex-carbohydrate diet, with further drops immediately after fast-carbohydrate ingestion. The patient’s father had normal blood glucose; her mother’s fasting glucose was 3.0 mmol/L (54 mg/dL).

A 43-year-old right-handed man was electrocuted after contact with a 440-V line while working on a roof. He lost consciousness and was intubated in the field. He sustained second- and third-degree burns over 21% of his body, with an entry wound on the scalp and an exit wound on the left foot. No spinal fractures were identified. Initially, he was alert and could move all four limbs, but over the ensuing days he moved his legs less than his arms. On hospital day 10, after sedation was held, he was awake, followed simple commands, and had intact cranial nerves. Motor examination revealed flaccid tone with only intermittent trace movement in the left fingers; deep tendon reflexes were diminished and plantar responses were equivocal. He reported pain with light pressure to all limbs. Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine on admission showed edema from the C3 to T2 levels with an intact spinal cord. A repeat MRI was suggested.

A 65-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of left-sided headache, left ear pain, and ear discharge. Three weeks earlier, he had had an ischemic stroke with right-sided hemiparesis and was noted to have a ruptured left tympanic membrane. His medical history was notable for nasopharyngeal carcinoma in complete remission, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus (average HbA1c, 8.1%), hypertension, and hypothyroidism. On examination, he was alert (GCS 15), with dysarthria and right upper- and lower-limb weakness (motor power 3/5). Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 3.5×10^3/mm^3, hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, platelet count 323×10^3/mm^3, HbA1c 8.1 mmol/L, and TSH 17.3 IU/mL; other chemistries were normal. Noncontrast CT of the brain revealed an abnormal density in the left posterior temporal, occipital, and parietal regions with foci of hyperdensities consistent with ischemic infarction and hemorrhagic transformation, as well as a subtle low-density area in the right pons.
