On hospital day 11, gadolinium-enhanced MRI showed lobulated, fluid-containing lesions in the left parietal and occipital lobes with interval enlargement, mass effect on the left lateral ventricle, and dural extension; the largest lesion measured 4.0×3.4 cm. Imaging also demonstrated fluid in bilateral mastoid air cells. CT angiography revealed occlusion of the left internal carotid artery from its origin to the cavernous segment with reconstitution via collaterals, and opacification of mastoid air cells and middle-ear cavities compatible with chronic otomastoiditis.

A 25-year-old Nigerian woman presented with a 1-month history of recurrent low-grade fever associated with chills and rigors, partially relieved by paracetamol and NSAIDs. Two weeks before presentation, she noted bilateral anterior neck swellings, initially peanut-sized, nonpainful, stable in size, and without compressive symptoms. She denied cough, hoarseness, dysphagia, odynophagia, or stridor. Additional symptoms included night sweats, headaches, nausea, anorexia, and a 5-kg weight loss. She had received multiple courses of antimalarial therapy and various antibiotics without symptom resolution.

On examination, her temperature was 37.8 °C, pulse 96 bpm, and blood pressure 112/78 mmHg. There were bilateral lumps at the bases of the right and left anterior triangles of the neck, each measuring approximately 2 cm by 4 cm, mildly tender, fixed to underlying structures, and not attached to overlying skin. The remainder of her neurological, respiratory, cardiovascular, and abdominal examinations was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin concentration of 11 g/dL (PCV 34%), WBC count 4900/mm3 with normal differential, ESR 44 mm/hr, scanty malaria parasites on blood film, and negative HIV I/II and HBsAg tests. A Mantoux test showed no induration after 72 hours, and chest radiography was normal. Neck ultrasonography revealed bilateral septated complex cystic masses measuring 3.86 × 2.31 cm on the right and 3.19 × 1.31 cm on the left, adjacent to the cervical vascular bundles.

A 14‐year‐old intact female mixed‐breed dog (8.5 kg) was referred for eight days of progressive dyspnea despite treatment with antibiotics, prednisolone, dexamethasone, benazepril, and furosemide. The dog had chronic generalized alopecia, polyuria/polydipsia for 11 months, and reduced appetite in recent days. Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 120 bpm with heart sounds of varying volume, RR 24 breaths/min, SBP 80 mm Hg. Physical examination revealed pink mucous membranes, no murmur but an unequal heartbeat, mild mandibular lymphadenopathy, senile cataracts, and prominent, non‐painful abdomen. Thoracic radiographs showed a moderately enlarged left atrium. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a moderate left atrial dilation (LA/AO 1.91) and a 1.63 cm round, hyperechoic mass floating between the left atrium and mitral valve leaflets, with no visible attachment to the atrial wall. Additional findings included moderate mitral regurgitation, low‐grade pulmonary insufficiency, and minimal aortic and tricuspid insufficiency. An ACTH stimulation test showed a basal cortisol of 9.1 µg/dL and post‐stimulation cortisol of 61.6 µg/dL, consistent with hyperadrenocorticism. The owner declined further hematologic, biochemical, abdominal ultrasound, and repeat echocardiographic evaluations. Therapy with benazepril, furosemide, and clopidogrel was instituted.

A 46-year-old man presented with an acute episode of hemoptysis. He reported mild-to-moderate intermittent hemoptysis triggered by exertion and denied smoking, chest trauma, or prior lung disease. Laboratory tests were within normal limits. A chest radiograph showed a homogeneous tubular opacity in the left lower lobe. Bronchoscopy was unremarkable aside from evidence of bleeding. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest revealed a high-flow vascular connection: a tortuous, dilated artery (maximum diameter 11 mm) originating from the proximal descending thoracic aorta and draining into the left lower pulmonary vein. The vessel wall showed calcification, and there were patchy ground-glass opacities in the left lower lobe. The bronchial tree and pulmonary arteries of the affected lobe appeared normal.

A 75-year-old Caucasian man presented with a two-week history of progressively severe diffuse myalgia, localized to the lower back and proximal lower limbs, associated with generalized weakness and reduced power in all four extremities, rendering him bedridden. He denied recent vigorous exercise or alcohol overuse and reported no sensory disturbances, headache, or paresthesia. His medical history included hypertension, atrial fibrillation (on rivaroxaban), hyperlipidaemia (on atorvastatin 80 mg daily for several years), and an infected endovascular aortic aneurysm managed with lifelong prophylactic oral fusidic acid 500 mg twice daily and moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for six days prior to admission. He had no prior personal or family history of muscle disorders or statin intolerance.

On examination, he was afebrile, blood pressure 103/42 mmHg, heart rate 75 beats/min, with normal cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal exams. He had moderate discomfort due to myalgia. The quadriceps were tender, and hip flexor and quadriceps strength was 3/5 bilaterally; all other muscle groups were 5/5. Cranial nerves and sensation were intact.

Initial laboratory studies showed: hemoglobin 6.4 mmol/L, leukocytes 7.8×10^9/L, creatinine 128 μmol/L, urea 16.8 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, sodium 140 mmol/L, glucose 6.5 mmol/L. Muscle enzymes were elevated: CK 328 U/L (40–208), LDH 266 U/L (115–255), BNP 607 pmol/L (<28.9); liver tests showed ALT 125 U/L (10–70), ALP 232 U/L (35–105), normal bilirubin.

Urinalysis showed no significant hematuria or proteinuria. Autoimmune screening revealed p-ANCA (IgG) medium positive (nonconclusive), c-ANCA and ANA negative. A lumbar puncture to evaluate for Guillain–Barré syndrome showed normal protein, glucose, and no pleocytosis. MRI of the cervical spine demonstrated a nonsignificant C5–C6 spinal stenosis. Anti–HMG-CoA reductase antibodies (IgG) were negative.

An 8-year-old girl presented with a 3-day history of postprandial projectile vomiting of recently eaten food, associated with nonradiating colicky upper abdominal pain, slight abdominal distension after feeds, generalized malaise, and constipation. She had a similar, self-limited episode 2 months earlier managed conservatively. There was no history of abdominal trauma. 

On examination, she was underweight and mildly dehydrated but hemodynamically stable. Abdominal examination showed slight distension with symmetrical contours, epigastric and left hypochondrial tenderness, and a firm, regular, non-mobile palpable mass in the epigastrium extending toward the right hypochondrium. Rectal and other system examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (25.45 × 10^9/L, 89.1% neutrophils), hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL, platelets 331 × 10^9/L, ESR 90 mm/h, mild hyponatremia (127.6 mmol/L), normal potassium, normal liver and pancreatic enzymes, and normal renal function. 

Abdominal ultrasound showed a lobulated, septated cystic lesion with internal echogenic material in the epigastrium measuring 6 × 5 cm without Doppler flow. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a cystic lesion in the peritoneum measuring 12.8 × 11 × 5.7 cm compressing the second and third parts of the duodenum, with gastric distension and imaging features suggestive of a pancreatic pseudocyst.

A 61-year-old Hispanic man presented with one month of vague abdominal pain, a 20-lb weight loss, generalized weakness, and malaise, accompanied over the last week by an occasional productive cough. He also reported intermittent nausea and nonbloody diarrhea, denied fevers or chills, and noted arthralgias. He had lived in El Paso, Texas, for decades and worked in a ceramic and tile factory with high dust exposure; he had no recent healthcare encounters until a community physician prescribed ciprofloxacin and metronidazole without diagnostic testing and observed no improvement.

On presentation, his temperature was 98.3 °F, blood pressure 84/61 mmHg, pulse 128 /min, respiratory rate 27 /min, and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. He appeared acutely ill but was alert. Lung examination revealed decreased breath sounds without rales. The abdomen was benign. He had large, firm lymph nodes (>3 cm) in the cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, and inguinal regions.

Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 8,900/mm3 (80% neutrophils, 0.5% bands, 11% eosinophils), hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, platelets 447,000/mm3, bicarbonate 17 mmol/L, BUN 54 mg/dL, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, albumin 2.2 g/dL, lactic acid 2.5 mmol/L, ALT 57 U/L, AST 139 U/L, and procalcitonin 6.1 ng/mL. Chest radiography showed a diffuse micronodular pattern. CT of the chest demonstrated extensive bilateral micronodules in a miliary pattern, mediastinal and axillary lymphadenopathy, and pericardial thickening. CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed enlarged para-aortic, gastrohepatic, inguinal, external, and internal iliac lymph nodes.

He received IV fluids, empiric vancomycin and cefepime, and methylprednisolone, and was admitted to the ICU. Initial infectious workup included HIV testing, which returned positive for HIV-1 with a viral load of 309,000 copies/mL and a CD4 count of 38 cells/mm3.

A 35-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of tender, palpable masses in her right axillary and supraclavicular regions. She first noticed a neck mass 6 months earlier and an axillary mass 2 months earlier. For the week before presentation, she experienced general weakness and fevers of 38–39 °C two to three times daily. She denied respiratory or urinary symptoms. On examination, multiple movable, round, tender masses were palpated in the right axilla and anterior neck. Her temperature was 38.5 °C. Laboratory studies showed normal complete blood count, liver function tests, and urinalysis; erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 25 mm/hr, C-reactive protein 28.3 mg/L, and lactate dehydrogenase 662 IU/L. She had undergone bilateral cosmetic silicone breast augmentation 11 years earlier.  
 
Breast ultrasonography showed intact implants bilaterally and multiple hyperechoic lesions with diffuse posterior acoustic noise in the right axilla and supraclavicular area. CT of the neck and chest demonstrated multiple round to oval nonenhancing lymph nodes extending from the right axilla to the anterior neck. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration of a lymph node revealed reactive lymphoid tissue without malignant cells. Mammography confirmed a hyperdense silicone implant and an enlarged right axillary lymph node with dense internal material. MRI showed a “teardrop sign” of intracapsular rupture of the right implant without extracapsular silicone and oval circumscribed right axillary lymph nodes isointense to the implant material.  

After four days of first-generation cephalosporin and NSAIDs, fever and tenderness persisted, and concern remained for malignancy versus implant-related lymphadenopathy.

A 25-year-old Laotian woman, resident in Thailand for 10 years, presented with a 5-day history of low-grade fever, sudden onset of headache, and rapidly progressive visual loss in both eyes. She denied prior headache, chronic cough, weight loss, prolonged fever, or known exposure to tuberculosis. Two years earlier, she had an uncomplicated second pregnancy and breast-fed for 9 months.

On examination, she was alert but appeared acutely ill. Temperature was 37.8 °C, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, pulse 60 beats/min, and respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. Best corrected visual acuity was hand movements in the left eye and 20/40 in the right eye, with a right temporal hemianopia by Goldmann perimetry. Other cranial nerves and neurologic findings were normal.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed a 1.4 × 2.5 × 2.2 cm rim-enhancing lesion in the sellar region with suprasellar extension; it was hypointense on T1, mixed hypo- and hyperintense on T2, with meningeal enhancement, thickened enhancing pituitary stalk, absence of the posterior bright spot, and compression of the optic chiasm. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. HIV and VDRL tests were negative.

Anterior pituitary evaluation showed panhypopituitarism: TSH 0.081 µIU/mL (0.35–4.94), free T4 0.71 ng/dL (0.70–1.48), morning cortisol <1 µg/dL, prolactin <0.6 ng/mL (5.18–26.53), IGF-1 81 ng/mL (117–329). Serum sodium was 124 mmol/L. After initiation of IV hydrocortisone for adrenal insufficiency, polyuria developed, consistent with central diabetes insipidus.

Because of the acute visual loss and mass effect on the optic apparatus, she underwent urgent endoscopic transsphenoidal pituitary surgery.

A 50-year-old journalist presented with a one-month history of sudden-onset left-sided tinnitus, hearing loss, and general dizziness without true vertigo. He had been treated empirically by an ENT physician with oral prednisolone, betahistine, magnesium, and flunarizine for presumed “acute idiopathic vestibulocochlear loss,” with no improvement in hearing but resolution of dizziness. He also noted a pressure sensation in the left ear. His only notable medication was aspirin 100 mg daily for borderline elevated hematocrit. Otoscopic examination was normal bilaterally. There was no spontaneous or gaze-evoked nystagmus; the head impulse test was inconclusive. Head-shaking elicited a right-beating nystagmus. Pure-tone audiometry revealed a marked left-sided sensorineural hearing loss. Video head impulse testing showed complete loss of left semicircular canal function; dynamic visual acuity was highly pathological on the left. Cervical VEMPs were borderline on the left, and ocular VEMPs showed 100% left-sided loss. Caloric testing demonstrated a 77% left-sided weakness.  
An MRI of the petrous bones demonstrated normal anatomy but unenhanced T1 images showed high-intensity signal in the left cochlea and vestibule.

A 16-year-old previously healthy boy presented with a 6-month history of progressive blurring of distance vision. Initial examination at a local clinic revealed degenerative lesions in the macular area, raising suspicion for Stargardt’s disease. On referral, best-corrected visual acuity was 0.9 in each eye (1.0 with minor astigmatic correction). Static perimetry (24-2) showed subtle central depression (RE MD −2.36 dB; LE MD −2.55 dB, both p < 5%). Anterior segment examination, intraocular pressures (16.5 mmHg RE; 17.2 mmHg LE), Ishihara color testing, and Farnsworth D-15 were normal.

Funduscopic examination with indirect ophthalmoscopy and a Volk lens revealed symmetrical, bilateral circular foci of RPE rearrangement around the optic disc and hypertrophic hyperpigmentation encircling the macula, extending peripherally into a reticular “fishing-net” pattern. Retinal vessels appeared normal. Macular OCT showed no structural anomalies (central thickness 282 μm RE; 279 μm LE). Autofluorescence imaging demonstrated numerous patchy, mosaic areas of hypofluorescence corresponding to the pigmented lesions. Fluorescein angiography revealed blocked choroidal fluorescence in the same reticular distribution.

Multifocal ERG was abnormal in the right eye—with increased P1 implicit times in rings R1–R3—but normal in the left eye. Pattern ERG responses were normal bilaterally. Electro-oculography showed Arden ratios of 3.3 in the right eye and 1.8 in the left eye, indicating significant interocular asymmetry and a near-lower-limit value in the left eye. Flash ERG revealed only slight increases in a- and b-wave implicit times of the rod-cone response, effectively excluding cone and cone-rod dystrophies.

Next-generation sequencing of 317 genes associated with retinal diseases (RetNet panel) detected no pathogenic variants in known retinal dystrophy genes; it identified a C2 gene variant (c.841_849+19del, rs9332736) not previously linked to retinal pathology.

A 16-year-old female presented with a 4-year history of a snapping sound in the hips, elbows, and knees, accompanied by noninflammatory polyarthralgia and a persistent headache. She also reported recurrent syncopal episodes since age 12, with spontaneous recovery and no residual deficits.

On examination, she had marked joint hyperlaxity of the hands, elbows, wrists, knees, and hips, with a Beighton score of 7/9, and increased skin laxity. Supine blood pressure was 70/54 mmHg with a heart rate of 80 bpm; after five minutes seated, blood pressure was 64/52 mmHg with a heart rate of 110 bpm. Radiography of the elbow showed radial head dislocation. Twenty-four–hour Holter monitoring and blood pressure monitoring were normal. A tilt-table test was compatible with mixed neurocardiogenic syncope and orthostatic intolerance syndrome.

A 32-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, was referred at 13 weeks of gestation after an incidental finding on abdominal ultrasonography. At 11 weeks, she had been admitted for back pain and fever; pyelonephritis was diagnosed and treated with intravenous cefalexin. A routine abdominal scan revealed solid, hyperechoic material within a dilated portal vein, with increased caliber and multiple serpentine channels. She was hemodynamically stable and asymptomatic at presentation.

On examination, blood pressure was 100/50 mm Hg, heart rate 65 bpm, and respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute. There was mild splenomegaly; the abdomen was nontender with normal bowel sounds and no ascites. Obstetrical ultrasound confirmed a single viable fetus consistent with 13 weeks of gestation, and first-trimester aneuploidy screening was low risk. The patient’s history was notable for a gastric sleeve procedure one year earlier for obesity; there was no history of liver disease.

Laboratory tests showed:
- Hemoglobin 10 g/dL (normochromic, normocytic anemia)
- AST 81 U/L, ALT 84 U/L
- Normal platelet count, prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time, and bleeding time

Thrombotic risk–factor screening was negative for factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A mutation, hyperhomocysteinemia, antithrombin III deficiency, protein C or S deficiency, and antiphospholipid antibodies. Autoimmune markers (antinuclear, smooth muscle, LKM, SLA, and mitochondrial antibodies) were negative, and viral serologies for hepatitis A–E, herpes simplex, cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, and yellow fever virus were negative.

Transabdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly with right-lobe hypertrophy and a nonhomogeneous echotexture. Gray-scale and color Doppler imaging demonstrated thrombosis of the main portal vein with cavernomatous transformation.

A 48-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of expanding eroded plaques involving his upper lip and bilateral anterior nares, causing nasal obstruction and difficulty breathing. He had no constitutional or gastrointestinal symptoms, no significant past medical history, and no family history of inflammatory bowel disease. On examination, well-demarcated erythematous eroded plaques with a characteristic “snail track” surface were present on the upper lip and around the nares. There was no other mucocutaneous involvement and no cervical lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed peripheral eosinophilia (1.3 × 10^9/L), negative HIV serology, and negative anti–neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies. Chest radiography was normal. CT of the nasal passages showed narrowing of the airways without involvement of the nasal cavity or bone. A skin biopsy revealed a dense mixed inflammatory infiltrate with numerous plasma cells and eosinophils, destructive changes to the epidermis and hair follicles, and no granulomas; the lymphoid cells showed no atypical histologic or immunophenotypic features. Stains for fungal organisms, tissue cultures, and direct immunofluorescence were negative. Further investigations, including liver transaminases, endoscopy, and fecal calprotectin, showed no evidence of liver disease or inflammatory bowel disease.

A 19-year-old Asian woman was referred for recurrent episodes of loss of consciousness. She reported that each event occurred immediately upon rising to an upright posture from supine, during which she turned pale, fell, and developed tonic posturing of her limbs lasting a few seconds before regaining consciousness as soon as she lay flat again. There was no postictal drowsiness. These episodes occurred several times daily for three months and persisted despite treatment with phenytoin, phenobarbitone, and sodium valproate. Over the same period, she experienced fatigue, malaise, myalgia, giddiness, fever, decreased appetite, and weight loss. 

On examination she appeared thin, frail, and anxious but was afebrile. Radial and carotid pulses were very feeble, whereas lower-limb pulses were normal. In the supine position, blood pressure in both upper limbs was 72/58 mmHg, falling to 50/48 mmHg on standing, consistent with orthostatic hypotension; lower-limb pressures were 130/70 mmHg bilaterally. Cardiac, neurologic, and funduscopic examinations were unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 42 mm/h, total leukocyte count 13,400/mm3, and C-reactive protein 26 mg/L. Tests for plasma glucose, liver and renal function, HIV, hepatitis B and C, Venereal Disease Research Laboratory, p-ANCA, and c-ANCA were negative. Chest radiography, electrocardiography, echocardiography, and electroencephalography findings were normal.

A 30-year-old single Thai man with a history of allergic rhinitis and well-controlled hypercholesterolemia (simvastatin 10 mg) was evaluated for persistent insomnia and daytime fatigue.

History of present illness: Two years earlier his mother noted loud snoring. He reported nasal congestion but denied choking, gasping, or nocturnal awakenings; he described a dry throat, clear nasal discharge, and morning headache. Despite 8–9 hours of sleep, he felt fatigued during the day without unintended naps.

Six months before psychiatric evaluation he developed low mood, anhedonia, work-related anxiety, restlessness, difficulty concentrating, and self-blame. He cut back on evening exercise, experienced initial and maintenance insomnia, and gained 4 kg in one month from increased eating. He denied suicidal ideation or hypomanic symptoms. He was diagnosed with major depressive disorder with anxious distress and started on escitalopram 10 mg and clonazepam 2 mg nightly. After two months his mood improved, but he continued fragmented sleep with nocturnal choking sensations, louder snoring, and prolonged re-sleep latency (>60 minutes). He self-titrated clonazepam to 2–4 mg daily, leading to next-day drowsiness and a 5–6 pm nap. His psychiatrist referred him to a sleep disorders center.

Family history: Both parents snore and have hyperlipidemia and type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with oral medications.

Sleep history and evaluation: On weekdays he slept 11 pm–7 am (12 am–10 am on weekends) with 20 minutes of sleep latency. He described himself as an intermediate chronotype. At the sleep center his body-mass index was 26.8 kg/m2, and his STOP-BANG score was 3/8 (intermediate risk of OSA). Upper-airway examination showed swollen inferior turbinates with clear discharge, Friedman tongue position III, tonsillar grade I, a high-arched palate, and overbite malocclusion. The specialists suspected OSA and offered overnight polysomnography; however, he did not return for testing.

A 48-year-old man was initially diagnosed in September 2006 with a posterior fossa grade II ependymoma after presentation with headaches. He underwent craniotomy and biopsy, developed obstructive hydrocephalus requiring a ventriculostomy and, one month later, an occipital ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt. He received 54 Gy of cranial radiotherapy. In late 2007, he developed back pain and was found to have diffuse spinal leptomeningeal enhancement on MRI; drop metastases were presumed and he received whole-spine radiation (41 Gy).  
Over the next two years, surveillance MRI showed progressive leptomeningeal enhancement in the brain and spine, and a large enhancing intrathecal mass extending from L3 to S1. He received multiple courses of temozolomide, carboplatin with etoposide, and radiation to the lumbosacral spine. A VP shunt revision was performed in April 2010 for hydrocephalus management.  
Between May and July 2010, he developed lower extremity weakness, urinary incontinence, and foot drop. In September 2010, brain MRI showed stable leptomeningeal disease, and spinal MRI confirmed persistent leptomeningeal enhancement with a 9 cm intradural soft-tissue mass from L3 to S1. A lumbar puncture from October 2010 demonstrated CSF pleocytosis (WBC 179 cells/µL, neutrophils 78%), elevated protein (125 mg/dL), normal glucose (73 mg/dL), and negative bacterial, fungal, and AFB cultures.  
In September 2010, he underwent spinal decompression for the L3–S1 intradural mass, which intraoperatively appeared as a dense tangle of nerve roots with scant fibrous tissue.

A 16-year-old previously healthy female presented with syncope. Six days earlier she developed malaise, fever, and fatigue, later noting chest pain and shortness of breath. She experienced dizziness, visual changes, and sweating, followed by a true syncopal episode during which she chipped a tooth but regained consciousness within seconds. 

On arrival to the emergency department she was afebrile. Blood pressure was 93/72 mmHg, pulse 90–100 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. She appeared well, with mild pain from her fall, no head or facial bruising, was tachycardic but had normal heart sounds without murmurs, clear lungs, and no hepatosplenomegaly. 

An ECG showed normal sinus rhythm with low-voltage QRS complexes and T-wave inversions in the inferior and anterior leads. Laboratory studies revealed normal electrolytes, blood counts, and inflammatory markers (ESR and CRP). Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated mildly depressed left ventricular function (EF ≈50%), a small pericardial effusion, and moderate-to-severe concentric LV hypertrophy with septal and posterior wall thicknesses of 1.4 cm, without outflow obstruction. 

Initial differential diagnosis included hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (with dysfunction or arrhythmia) and myocarditis. Serial troponin I measurement on admission was 0.977 ng/mL (upper limit of normal <0.029 ng/mL).

A 63-year-old woman with obesity and a history of sleep apnea, hypothyroidism, hyperlipidemia, Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, anxiety, depression, and tardive dyskinesia was admitted after a mechanical fall causing right type VI tibial and fibular fractures. Her medications included levothyroxine, atorvastatin, sertraline, quetiapine, hydroxyzine (Atarax), gabapentin, and benztropine (Cogentin). Preoperatively, she was alert and oriented, with chronic upper-extremity intention tremors.

Before urgent open reduction and internal fixation, she received 2 mg of IV midazolam for anxiolysis. As she entered the operating room, she became agitated, disoriented, and developed diffuse tremulousness with myoclonus. Due to the urgent nature of surgery, general anesthesia was induced with propofol, fentanyl, rocuronium, and a dexmedetomidine infusion. The 2.75-hour surgery proceeded without intraoperative desaturation or hypotension. After reversal with sugammadex, she was extubated.

In the postanesthesia care unit, she exhibited tangential thoughts, agitation, anxiety, and was oriented only to name. Neurologic examination revealed paratonia, asterixis, and diffuse myoclonus of the upper extremities and left lower extremity. The neurology service was consulted. Thyrotropin, electrolytes, ammonia, and gabapentin levels were within normal limits. Urine toxicology and noncontrast head CT scan were negative. Fat embolism was less likely due to lack of clinical symptoms such as petechial rash, hypoxemia, retinal changes, or jaundice, and the patient did not meet Gurd’s criteria for fat embolism.

A 45-day-old girl, the second child of nonconsanguineous parents (an older sibling died at 3 months of unknown cause), was brought with 2 weeks of progressive abdominal distension and a generalized skin rash. Her growth parameters were age-appropriate. On examination she was pale and had scattered petechiae. The liver edge was palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin, and the spleen edge was 7 cm below the left costal margin. Other systems, including a normal funduscopic examination, were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed: hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, white-cell count 43,900/mm3 (30% neutrophils, 57% lymphocytes, 3% eosinophils, 9% monocytes), platelets 30,000/mm3; peripheral smear demonstrated leukoerythroblastosis; reticulocyte count 6%. Liver and renal function tests were normal. Serum calcium was 9.0 mg/dL, phosphorus 3.7 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 370 U/L, and lactate dehydrogenase 640 U/L. Retroviral studies and TORCH titers were negative; blood cultures were sterile. Abdominal ultrasonography confirmed hepatosplenomegaly.

On hospital day 3 she developed a cough. A chest radiograph incidentally showed diffuse skeletal sclerosis, and dedicated skeletal films revealed a characteristic “bone-in-bone” appearance in the femora, tibiae, humeri, radii, ulnae, and iliac bones.

A 47-year-old woman with no significant past medical history other than recurrent migraines presented with a 5-year history of progressive decreased vision in her left eye. She denied fever, altered mental status, or other neurologic symptoms, and she had no history of intravenous drug use or recent infections. She recalled a head injury at age 19 but was uncertain whether it involved orbital trauma. Her metabolic profile was within normal limits.

Optical coherence tomography showed thinning of the peripapillary nerve fiber layer, more pronounced on the left than the right, consistent with optic nerve atrophy. MRI of the orbits demonstrated a decreased caliber of the left optic nerve and increased T2 signal within the left perioptic nerve sheath. MRI of the brain revealed a T2-hyperintense signal along the course of the left optic radiations.

A 73-year-old woman with hypertension presented with a 4-month history of progressive speech difficulty, voice changes, dysarthria, slurred speech, dysphagia to liquids and solids, and constant drooling. She denied respiratory symptoms. On neurologic examination, there were tongue fasciculations (more prominent on the left), muscle atrophy in the left thenar and hypothenar eminences and interossei, fasciculations in the biceps brachii and quadriceps femoris, and muscle strength graded 4/5 on the right and 3/5 on the left. Deep tendon reflexes were brisk in all four limbs; bilateral palmomental reflexes (more on the left), a snout reflex, Hoffman and Babinski signs on the left, and bilateral ankle clonus were present. Pharyngeal examination revealed an absent gag reflex, slight left-sided palatal droop, and uvular deviation to the right.  
Laboratory studies showed a normal white-cell differential and erythrocyte sedimentation rate; serum creatine phosphokinase was 380 U/L. MRI of the brain and spine was unremarkable. Electromyography revealed spontaneous fibrillations, positive sharp waves, fasciculations, and increased polyphasic motor-unit potentials in the biceps, pronator teres, spinal cord–innervated muscles, and tibialis anterior. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis demonstrated albumin-cytologic dissociation (protein 151 mg/dL, 2 cells/mm3) with negative oligoclonal bands. Antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor and muscle-specific kinase were negative. Serologic testing for cytomegalovirus IgM and IgG was negative.

A 34-year-old gravida 4, para 3 woman at 39 weeks’ gestation was admitted for induction of labor because of suspected fetal macrosomia. Her medical history was notable only for obesity (BMI 34) and mild depression. Amniotomy yielded clear fluid, and oxytocin augmentation was used for 4 hours. She delivered a 4230 g male infant vaginally with Apgar scores of 7 and 10. The mother and infant were well, and she was discharged 4 hours postpartum.

Approximately 24 hours after delivery, she returned with chills and lower abdominal pain. On examination, temperature was elevated, blood pressure was 96/72 mmHg, pulse 112 beats/min, and urine output was decreased. Abdominal palpation revealed guarding in both lower quadrants, peritoneal signs, and an enlarged uterus palpable to the umbilicus. Transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasound showed an empty uterus without free fluid. After blood and urine cultures were obtained, intravenous metronidazole and cefuroxime were started. Laboratory tests revealed elevated C-reactive protein and creatinine; white-cell count, hemoglobin, and platelets were normal.

Eight hours after readmission (36 h postpartum), contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed a grossly enlarged uterus with ascites. The patient became hemodynamically unstable during imaging and was transferred to the intensive care unit for vasopressor support and further management.

A 67-year-old man underwent mini-open posterior lumbar interbody fusion with percutaneous screw fixation for spinal stenosis at L4–L5. He was discharged on postoperative day 9 but returned on day 18 with severe lower back pain and fever. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 52 mm/h (normal, 0–20), C-reactive protein (CRP) of 66.04 mg/L (normal, 0–5), white blood cell (WBC) count of 11 600/µL (normal, 4000–10 000), neutrophils 9270/µL (normal, 1500–7500), and eosinophils 80/µL (normal, 40–500). Contrast-enhanced CT of the lumbar spine revealed an abscess along the screw heads and rods. Abscess aspiration cultured Staphylococcus caprae, and he received intravenous vancomycin. Over 2 months, his ESR decreased to 16.1 mm/h and CRP to 10.52 mg/L, and his back pain resolved. Subsequently, his ESR rose to 45 mm/h, CRP to 62 mg/L, and eosinophils to 6130/µL. Repeat CT showed nearly complete disappearance of the abscess. The patient developed whole-body pruritus and a diffuse skin rash.

A 44-year-old woman with a 5-month history of granulomatosis with polyangiitis involving the respiratory tract (c-ANCA positive, nasal biopsy) had been treated first with cyclophosphamide and methylprednisolone with minimal response, then initiated on rituximab. Despite therapy, her symptoms progressed to worsening exophthalmos, drowsiness, and apathy. On admission she was dehydrated but afebrile, with no respiratory or cardiac findings on exam. On hospital day 1 she became drowsy and had a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting one minute. Postictally, she was bradycardic (32 bpm) and hypotensive (84/48 mmHg). In the cardiovascular ICU, ECG revealed complete atrioventricular block with multiple episodes of sustained ventricular tachycardia. Bedside transthoracic echocardiography showed no significant structural abnormalities except mild mitral regurgitation and an ejection fraction of 62%, with no thrombi or wall motion abnormalities. Troponin I and pro-BNP levels were normal. Laboratory testing showed no evidence of infection, electrolyte disturbances, or other organ dysfunction, but C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were markedly elevated. A provisional transvenous pacemaker was placed, with immediate hemodynamic improvement.

A 33-year-old man with known HIV/AIDS not on antiretroviral therapy (CD4 count <20 cells/µL), prior intravenous drug use, and active tobacco dependence was brought from his nursing home after abnormal laboratory results. He reported one month of poor appetite, weight loss, and subjective fevers, and several days of diarrhea without abdominal pain, vomiting, cough, or dyspnea. On examination, he was febrile (39.4 °C), hypotensive (91/60 mmHg, improved with IV fluids), tachycardic (130 bpm), and lethargic. Initial labs showed leukocytosis (31 151/µL) and hyponatremia (Na 121 mEq/L). A chest radiograph was clear. Abdominal ultrasound revealed hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, and enlarged peripancreatic lymph nodes. He was admitted to the ICU with presumed sepsis and started on vancomycin, piperacillin–tazobactam, and metronidazole. He then developed acute hypoxic respiratory failure and septic shock requiring intubation; post‐intubation chest radiograph showed new bilateral infiltrates. Blood cultures remained negative. Lumbar puncture demonstrated an opening pressure of 35 cm H₂O, 1825 RBCs/dL, 1 WBC/dL, glucose 65 mg/dL, and protein 36 mg/dL, and acyclovir was started empirically. Bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for bacterial, viral, fungal, and Pneumocystis jirovecii cultures. Initial sputum smears for acid‐fast bacilli were negative.

A 43-year-old woman presented with severe right-sided exertional lower extremity pain for more than one year, which resolved with rest. She had been an avid cyclist but switched to long-distance running 2 years earlier, averaging 50–75 miles per week. She had no history of diabetes, smoking, or other risk factors for premature atherosclerosis.

Electromyography and lumbar spine magnetic resonance imaging were normal. On vascular examination, femoral pulses were normal bilaterally, with slightly diminished dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses bilaterally; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

A resting ankle–brachial index (ABI) was normal. Exercise ABI on the right was 0.19, rising only to 0.22 six minutes after exercise, whereas the left ABI remained normal. Duplex ultrasonography and magnetic resonance angiography of the lower extremities revealed no significant vascular abnormalities, including no evidence of popliteal artery entrapment. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein were normal.

A 55-year-old woman with no significant medical or family history presented with a 1-year history of right upper abdominal pain, altered bowel habits, weight loss, and low-grade fevers with chills. The abdominal pain was dull, intermittent, and non-radiating. On exam, her abdomen was soft with mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant. Vital signs: pulse 84/min, temperature 99 °F, blood pressure 125/85 mmHg. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL, hematocrit 29.8 %, WBC count 18.83 ×10^3/μL (78.3 % neutrophils), CRP 131.41 mg/L, alkaline phosphatase 337 U/L, LDH 441 U/L, and a positive fecal occult blood test; liver enzymes, bilirubin, albumin, and tumor markers (AFP, CEA, CA 19-9) were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated multiple solid iso-hypoechoic lesions in both liver lobes (up to 30 mm). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed extensive non-enhancing hypodense nodules (1–3 cm) throughout both liver lobes, subcapsular and parenchymal deposits (“frosted liver”), para-aortic lymphadenopathy, and a thickened rectal wall. Colonoscopy to the cecum and upper endoscopy were normal.

A previously healthy 2.5-year-old girl was brought to the hospital with two brief generalized tonic-clonic seizures. She had a 2-day history of vomiting, diarrhea, and a maximum temperature of 37.8°C. The first seizure lasted 30 seconds while she was crying at home; the second lasted 1 minute in the emergency department. Her past history included one febrile convulsion at 13 months; development was normal. On examination she was alert with mild abdominal distension and slightly hyperactive bowel sounds; neurologic examination was normal. Laboratory tests showed a leukocyte count of 5600/µL, hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, platelets 227 000/µL, sodium 138 mEq/L, potassium 3.6 mEq/L, chloride 108 mEq/L, bicarbonate 17 mmol/L, BUN 8.0 mg/dL, creatinine 0.6 mg/dL, glucose 83 mg/dL, ammonia 21 µmol/L, and calcium 9.1 mg/dL. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was not performed. A rotavirus stool antigen test was positive. Electroencephalography was normal. Brain MRI performed on admission showed no abnormalities on T1-, T2-, or FLAIR-weighted images, but diffusion-weighted images demonstrated a linear area of high signal intensity in the splenium of the corpus callosum with decreased apparent diffusion coefficient values.

A 22-year-old woman presented with inability to pass feces and flatus for 2 days, accompanied by 20–25 episodes of vomiting, progressive abdominal distension, and pain. She had chronic constipation since birth managed with laxatives and manual de-impaction, with her last hospital visit 9 years earlier, and continued regular oral laxative use. On examination, she was afebrile, hemodynamically stable but appeared ill, with a markedly distended, firm, nontender abdomen and tympanic percussion note. A provisional diagnosis of large-bowel obstruction was made. Abdominal radiograph showed a markedly dilated colon occupying the abdominal cavity with a mottled gas appearance. Bedside ultrasound revealed a distended rectum but was limited by intraluminal air. After an enema, her distension and symptoms improved. Contrast CT scan demonstrated massive dilatation of the sigmoid colon (maximum diameter, 23 cm) and rectum with internal mottled gas and a large fecaloma; the colon compressed and displaced the liver, spleen, and stomach. Smooth funnel-like tapering was noted approximately 2.4 cm from the anal verge, corresponding to a transition zone; perirectal fat planes were normal, and there was no intraluminal pathology, wall thickening, or abnormal contrast enhancement.

A 43-year-old woman presented with 24 hours of subxiphoid pleuritic chest pain radiating to her left shoulder tip and flank. She reported a 6-week history of intermittent fevers, night sweats, and a 7-kg weight loss. Her medical history included nephrolithiasis managed conservatively and obesity; she denied dysuria, hematuria, frequency, or urgency. She had no diabetes or immunosuppression, no recent travel, and no family history of autoimmune or malignant disease.

On examination, temperature was 36.2 °C, blood pressure 138/96 mmHg, heart rate 130 bpm, respiratory rate 22/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. She appeared volume-depleted with dry mucous membranes, reduced jugular venous pressure, and resting tachycardia. There was no focal source of infection and no palpable abdominal mass.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 15.8 × 10^9/L with neutrophilia, CRP 17.9 mg/dL, hemoglobin 88 g/L with microcytosis, and a chronic thrombocytosis of 400–600 × 10^9/L. Urinalysis revealed pyuria without hematuria; urine cultures were negative, and prior records documented sterile pyuria since 2009. Serial ECGs and high-sensitivity troponins ruled out acute coronary syndrome.

A chest CT performed to exclude pulmonary embolism showed no emboli but did demonstrate a small left pleural effusion and a 10.3 × 3.4 × 5.6 cm loculated fluid collection in the subcapsular region of the spleen.

A 27-year-old man with recently confirmed autosomal-dominant hyper-IgE syndrome (STAT3 mutation) was referred for evaluation of incidental pulmonary infiltrates. As a child, he had recurrent otitis media and pneumonia, retention of primary teeth, typical facies with a broad nasal bridge, and fungal nail infections but no mucosal fungal disease or asthma. 

He reported mild productive clear sputum in the mornings over several years without dyspnea, weight loss, or fever. Pulmonary-function tests were normal. 

High-resolution CT of the thorax showed multiple cavitating lesions in the right upper lobe, one containing a spheroid mass suggestive of a fungal ball. PET/CT demonstrated increased FDG uptake in the cavitary area. 

Bronchoalveolar lavage grew Streptococcus pneumoniae and Achromobacter species; PCR was positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii (treated with sulfamethoxazole–trimethoprim). BAL was negative for Aspergillus species by culture, microscopy, and PCR. Serum Aspergillus IgG was 0.0 AU/mL, and galactomannan antigen was negative. BAL was also negative for mycobacteria by microscopy and culture, and interferon-γ release assay was negative. Total serum IgE was 158 IU/mL (reference < 115 IU/mL); IgA was elevated; IgG2 was low. 

Given the radiographic appearance and the patient’s predisposition, empiric oral voriconazole was initiated and maintained at therapeutic levels for 11 months. Serial CT and PET/CT scans showed progression of the cavitary lesion and new infiltrates despite therapy. A repeat BAL grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa (treated with IV tazobactam and ciprofloxacin), but again was negative for Aspergillus, mycobacteria, and other fungi. A superdimension bronchoscopy with brush biopsy revealed normal cells. CT-guided transthoracic needle biopsy demonstrated chronic inflammation without malignant or fungal elements.

What is the most likely diagnosis underlying his persistent pulmonary lesions?

A 16-year-old female high school basketball player presented with right medial knee pain. Three months earlier, radiographs at initial presentation were interpreted as normal. She continued to play despite persistent pain. One month later, during a game, she felt a cracking sensation in the right knee but completed play. Two days later, repeat radiographs demonstrated a displaced patellar fracture with sclerosis at the margin of the fracture site. On examination at that time, she had point tenderness over the patella but retained full active knee extension.

A 37-year-old woman with HLA-B27–positive spondyloarthropathy treated with methotrexate and daily prednisolone presented with a 2-week history of an itchy, painful pustular rash on her left hand and intermittent fevers. The rash began as a single pustule on the thumb and spread to involve the entire palm. She reported recent cactus-sap exposure and punctures while working in a plant nursery. On initial examination in the emergency department, there were small erythematous pustules over the first dorsal web space and scattered across the palm; the nails were uninvolved, and she had no other skin lesions. Two days later, dermatology review showed increased pustules coalescing into small pustular lakes. The initial impression was contact dermatitis to cactus sap with secondary pyoderma; pustular psoriasis was also considered given her HLA-B27–positive spondyloarthropathy. A swab was obtained for bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal cultures, and she was treated with oral amoxicillin–clavulanate, topical betamethasone dipropionate, gentamicin, and miconazole, plus potassium permanganate compresses, with advice to avoid gardening. Six days later, new pustules continued to develop, and a skin biopsy was planned.

A 35-year-old gravida 5 para 1 woman with three prior in-utero fetal deaths at 5 months and one living child was referred at 19 weeks 4 days of gestation for severe hypertension. She reported headache and epigastric pain. On arrival, blood pressure was 170/110 mmHg. Physical examination showed a closed cervix and no vaginal bleeding. Fetal heart rate was 145 beats per minute, and obstetrical ultrasound demonstrated a single live fetus with no abnormalities. Laboratory studies revealed: hemoglobin 14 g/dL, platelets 142 × 10^3/mm^3, AST 1550 IU/L, ALT 938 IU/L, LDH 2251 IU/L, creatinine 5.2 mg/L, total bilirubin 5.21 mg/dL, and a urine protein–creatinine ratio of 600 mg/g. The patient was started on antihypertensive therapy and magnesium sulfate.

A 34-year-old man was admitted for 8 hours of lower gastrointestinal bleeding. He had no other symptoms and a history only of an appendectomy 3 years earlier; there was no family history of gastrointestinal malignancy. Vital signs were normal. Digital rectal examination confirmed hematochezia. Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin of 7.7 g/dL, and he received 2 units of red blood cells. Colonoscopic examination revealed a 4 × 3 cm submucosal mass in the cecum with a central erosion near its base; the lesion was firm on palpation and showed no active bleeding. Endoscopic biopsies were obtained. Abdominal computed tomography demonstrated a 4 × 3 cm cecal mass with apparent irregular contrast uptake. The endoscopic biopsies were nondiagnostic; however, because malignancy remained a concern, the patient was scheduled for surgical resection.

A previously healthy 5-year-old girl presented with a one-day history of high fever (39°C), sore throat, stridor, and shortness of breath. She was intubated for airway obstruction due to epiglottitis, and a lateral neck radiograph confirmed a grossly swollen epiglottis. Throat swab and blood cultures grew Haemophilus influenzae type f. 

On hospital day 2, she developed anemia (hemoglobin 63 g/L), thrombocytopenia (platelets 53,000/mm³), acute renal failure (creatinine 143 μmol/L), hypertension (BP 123/80 mmHg), and evidence of hemolysis (positive direct antiglobulin test) with elevated APTT (41 sec) and D Dimer. Urinalysis showed microscopic hematuria, proteinuria (0.3 g/L), and casts. Supportive care included antibiotics and blood-product transfusions.

On day 7, she developed seizures associated with severe hypertension (BP 170/100 mmHg). CT of the brain showed multiple subcortical white-matter hypodensities bilaterally, and MRI demonstrated extensive T2 hyperintense changes with diffuse cerebral edema. A diagnosis of probable posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) was made.

A previously healthy 10-month-old girl from the Mekong Delta presented with a 3-day history of high-grade fevers, frequent nonbloody vomiting, and progressive lethargy. There was no history of trauma, sick contacts, or known freshwater exposure. Antenatal and postnatal courses were unremarkable. On arrival, she received empirical ceftriaxone for presumed sepsis.

Within 8 hours, she developed multiple generalized seizures and a decreased level of consciousness (U on the AVPU scale), requiring intubation. After intubation, she progressed to a deep coma without response to stimuli. She was managed in the intensive care unit with mechanical ventilation, intravenous meropenem and vancomycin, intracranial pressure control (mannitol and hypertonic saline), and emergency external ventricular drainage.

Brain ultrasound and computed tomography scan showed acute hydrocephalus. Laboratory studies revealed a C-reactive protein level of 151 mg/L. Urinalysis and urine cultures were negative. Chest radiography and abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable. 

Cerebrospinal fluid obtained at presentation was turbid yellow, with 4,032 white cells/mm3 (88% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), lactate 11.8 mmol/L, protein 6.9 g/L, and normal plasma glucose. Serial CSF and blood bacterial microscopy and cultures were negative. PCR assays for herpes simplex virus, Japanese encephalitis virus, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis were negative. Autoimmune markers (antibody and complement levels) and HIV testing were normal or negative.

A 72-year-old man presented with a 10-day history of fever and progressive shortness of breath. He had been diagnosed 5 months earlier with stage IV bronchogenic carcinoma and lymphangitic carcinomatosis. On examination, he appeared cachectic, tachypneic, and dyspneic. His blood pressure was 140/85 mmHg, heart rate 124 beats/min, oxygen saturation 79% on room air, and temperature 37.7 °C. Chest expansion was reduced on the left side, with decreased air entry there and coarse crackles on the right. A chest radiograph showed a massive left pleural effusion and multiple opacities on the right. A left-sided thoracostomy tube was placed, yielding clear serous fluid. He was admitted for gradual decompression and received antibiotics and analgesia. Because of the COVID-19 pandemic, he underwent RT-PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2 (nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal) and a CT scan of the chest. The RT-PCR test was positive for SARS-CoV-2. CT of the chest revealed multiple ground-glass opacities in both lungs, a left pleural effusion, and an irregular hilar mass.

A 15-year-old boy with no significant medical history was transferred after a motorbike accident. On admission, he was intubated and agitated, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 11, blood pressure stable, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Examination revealed severe head and maxillofacial trauma and a left tibia‐fibula fracture. Abdominal ultrasound raised suspicion for hemoperitoneum in Morrison’s pouch. To assess for abdominal organ injury, a contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan was planned. Before imaging, 5 mg of midazolam was administered for sedation because of patient agitation. During the arterial phase of the CT scan, there was intense contrast opacification of the right atrium, right ventricle, inferior vena cava, and hepatic veins, whereas the left heart chambers and descending aorta were poorly opacified.

A 79-year-old woman with a history of atrial fibrillation (status post–left atrial appendage closure) was admitted for elective mitral valve replacement for asymptomatic severe primary mitral regurgitation due to anterior leaflet prolapse. One month earlier, echocardiography showed a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 56% with normal chamber dimensions, and preoperative CT angiography revealed no coronary lesions. Her only home medication was acetylsalicylic acid. 

The patient underwent implantation of a biological mitral valve without intraoperative complications; intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography confirmed normal prosthetic function, and low-dose noradrenaline (0.05 μg/kg/min) was required after cardiopulmonary bypass. 

On arrival to the intensive care unit, she developed cardiogenic shock with cold extremities, oliguria, systolic blood pressure of 80 mmHg, metabolic acidosis, and elevated lactate. Vasoactive support with noradrenaline (0.1 μg/kg/min) and dobutamine (5 μg/kg/min) was initiated. An electrocardiogram showed atrial flutter at 150 bpm, which was electrically cardioverted; a subsequent ECG demonstrated inverted T waves in the precordial leads. Chest radiography revealed pulmonary congestion. 

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed severe LV dysfunction (LVEF 20%) with mid to distal diffuse hypokinesis, most pronounced in the anterior and septal walls, with relatively preserved basal segment contractility; the mitral prosthesis functioned normally. Urgent coronary angiography showed normal coronary arteries. Troponin I was mildly elevated at 0.12 ng/mL (normal <0.08).

A 13-year-old girl presented with a 3-month history of malaise, dyspnea, diarrhea, and weight loss. Three months earlier, she had been diagnosed with allergic asthma and treated with inhaled formoterol/budesonide. Over the ensuing months, she developed progressive fatigue, occasional nasal bleeding, painful joint swelling, small transient skin ulcerations, and tingling with numbness of the right foot. She received two short courses of prednisolone for presumed asthma exacerbations, with only temporary relief. A few days before admission, watery diarrhea worsened her symptoms.

On examination, she was tachypneic with rales and mild expiratory wheezing. Dark purple lesions were noted on the extremities. Both hands showed arthritis of the proximal interphalangeal joints with interdigital pustules on the right hand. There was slight proptosis of the left eye.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 80 mm/h and a white-cell count of 65.8×10^9/L with 67% eosinophils (absolute count 44×10^9/L). Urinalysis was normal. To exclude a leukemic process, a bone marrow aspiration was performed, which showed, apart from numerous normal eosinophilic granulocytes, no abnormalities.

Chest radiography revealed interstitial and peribronchial infiltrates. Thoracic CT demonstrated bronchiectasis with mucus impaction and multiple granulomatous nodules. Electrocardiography, echocardiography, and abdominal ultrasonography were normal. Head MRI and CT identified a lesion in the left orbit. Neurologic examination was consistent with mononeuritis of the left median nerve, although EMG findings were normal. Extensive cultures and serologic tests for bacterial, viral, parasitic, and fungal infections were negative.

A 42-year-old woman, gravida 4, para 1, presented to the emergency department seven days after an uneventful cesarean delivery with severe shortness of breath.  
On examination, jugular venous pressure was elevated, there was bilateral pitting edema of the lower extremities, and bibasilar crackles were heard on lung auscultation.  
Chest radiographs showed bilateral pleural effusions and perihilar airspace opacities consistent with pulmonary edema.  
A thoracic CT pulmonary angiogram was performed, which ruled out pulmonary embolism but confirmed pulmonary edema and demonstrated asymmetric thickening of the interventricular septum measuring up to 22 mm.  
Transthoracic echocardiography revealed normal left ventricular systolic function, an elevated E/E′ ratio of 19 mmHg indicating raised left atrial pressure, and a mild provocable left ventricular outflow tract gradient of 33 mmHg with amyl nitrate.

A 69-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder and grade 1 hypertension was referred for evaluation of progressive renal dysfunction. She had been treated with lithium for 44 years until routine laboratory monitoring revealed a decline in her estimated glomerular filtration rate, prompting her prior psychiatrist to switch her to lamotrigine. Her bipolar disorder remained in remission after the change, but she reported occasional polyuria and polydipsia. She had been taking lisinopril for hypertension. On examination, she had 2+ bilateral lower-extremity edema. Laboratory studies showed an eGFR >20 mL/min, blood urea nitrogen 48 mg/dL, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, and calcium 10 mg/dL. Point-of-care renal ultrasound demonstrated multiple anechoic, well-circumscribed cystic structures and scattered echogenic foci in both kidneys. Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen with a renal mass protocol revealed normal-sized kidneys with numerous 1–2 mm T2-hyperintense cysts distributed throughout the renal cortex and medulla.

A 76-year-old man with well-controlled HIV (undetectable viral load; CD4 count >200 cells/mm^3 on antiretroviral therapy) presented after an unprovoked syncopal episode. He reported a 10 lb weight loss over several months, decreased appetite, and a general sense of malaise. Family history was notable for cardiovascular-related deaths but no liver disease.  
On examination he was afebrile, blood pressure was normal, and he had mild hepatomegaly on abdominal palpation. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (11.44 × 10^3/µL) with neutrophilia, macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL; mean corpuscular volume 101.8 fL), elevated ferritin (1,403 µg/L), elevated alkaline phosphatase (227 IU/L) and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase (129 IU/L) with normal transaminases. Tumor markers and viral and autoimmune hepatitis serologies were unremarkable, apart from an elevated α1-antitrypsin level.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed an 11.2 cm heterogeneous mass in the right hepatic lobe with areas of solid enhancement and central necrosis, and thrombosis of the right posterior portal vein concerning for tumor in vein. The initial differential included hepatocellular carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, liver abscess, metastatic disease, lymphoma, and hemangioma.  
He was started empirically on a 2-week course of metronidazole for presumed liver abscess and referred for hepatology evaluation.

A 34-year-old man with a 10-year history of immunoglobulin G4–related disease affecting the liver, biliary tract, and pancreas (controlled with prednisone 5 mg daily) and type 2 myotonic dystrophy presented with recurrent episodes of sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT). His VT initially responded transiently to antiarrhythmic agents (amiodarone, sotalol, flecainide) but recurred despite multiple radiofrequency catheter ablations and a stellate ganglion block. He received a primary-prevention implantable cardioverter-defibrillator; at each VT episode, transthoracic echocardiography showed an LVEF of 25% that normalized within 48 hours of VT termination.

Over two years, VT became refractory to medical and interventional therapies. During a recent VT episode unresponsive to defibrillation, he developed cardiac arrest requiring extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation and was placed on peripheral venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). Initial echocardiography on ECMO showed severe biventricular failure without pericardial involvement. Endomyocardial biopsy from the right ventricle revealed areas of fibrosis but was inconclusive for myocarditis; immunohistochemical staining demonstrated only occasional IgG4-positive plasma cells.

A 50-year-old woman presented with an erythematous, pruritic rash over her upper chest and neck of one month’s duration. The lesions appeared one week after the second dose of the inactivated SARS-CoV-2 vaccine and were preceded by similar but milder lesions three weeks earlier after the first vaccine dose. Her history was notable for left-sided invasive ductal breast carcinoma treated 15 years ago with radical mastectomy, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy, with no recurrence since.

On examination, there was a relatively ill-defined, erythematous plaque with focal scaling and mild lichenification over the upper chest in the area corresponding to her prior radiation field, as marked by a tattoo.

A punch biopsy of the lesion revealed epidermal hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, mild irregular acanthosis, mild spongiosis, focal basal cell degeneration with Civatte bodies, and numerous apoptotic keratinocytes. The upper dermis showed perivascular lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltrates, dilated blood vessels, and scattered mast cells.

• A woman in her thirties presented with left occipital–temporal headache, rotational vertigo, and vomiting.  
• Her history included depression and prior episodes of floating dizziness, which had resolved; no family history of inherited vascular disease.  
• On the morning of symptom onset, she experienced sudden rotational vertigo; that afternoon, she developed left occipital–temporal head pain while driving; that night, she vomited.  
• On day 2, a local neurology clinic obtained a head CT and neck radiographs showing no abnormalities and made a “diagnosis of suspected herpes zoster,” prescribing valaciclovir, pregabalin, and acetaminophen without improvement; carbamazepine and aspirin were added, also without effect.  
• Referred to a pain clinic, she reported throbbing pulsatile headache (VAS 100 mm) recurring every few hours, preventing sleep and oral intake. Examination revealed no allodynia, trigeminal paresthesia, cranial or spinal nerve deficits, skin rash, conjunctival injection, fever, or meningeal signs; blood pressure was 160/100 mmHg.  
• Her presentation met the ICHD-3 β diagnostic criteria for migraine without aura, and she received zolmitriptan 2.5 mg; the first dose was inadequate but a second dose improved her symptoms. Migraine treatment was initiated.  
• Because the headache was sudden and unprecedented, a secondary headache was also considered. She was hospitalized, started on lomerizine, and given zolmitriptan and loxoprofen as needed.  
• By hospital day 2, VAS fell to 50 mm but severe recurrences (VAS 100 mm) persisted every few hours; loxoprofen provided superior relief. Persistent hypertension led to cardiology consultation on day 3 and initiation of a calcium antagonist.  
• Although intracranial disease had been ruled out by CT, the inadequate response to triptan and atypically prolonged headache duration prompted MRI and MRA on day 8.

A 5-year-old boy was transferred after 30 days of fever, diarrhea, vomiting, and weight loss. On day 10 of illness he developed progressive abdominal distention and persistent fever. An initial CT of the abdomen showed a large retroperitoneal mass with mesenteric lymphadenopathy. On transfer, temperature was 37.5 °C, heart rate 110 bpm, respiratory rate 28/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. He appeared cachectic and pale, with weight below the fifth percentile. The abdomen was markedly distended, with visible dilated veins and a palpable mass in the left lower quadrant. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 29.9 × 10^9/L (eosinophils 0.27 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 22 × 10^9/L), platelets 1014 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 5.6 g/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate >140 mm/hr, and C-reactive protein 269 mg/L. Repeat CT imaging demonstrated circumferential thickening of the terminal ileum, cecum, and ileocecal valve with proximal small-bowel dilation and collapsed distal colon, plus a 7.9 × 8.2 cm hypodense infiltrative mass in the epigastric region infiltrating the pancreas, portal vein thrombosis, and multiple enlarged retroperitoneal lymph nodes. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy showed no malignant cells.

A 48-year-old woman presented with 6 months of amenorrhea and intermittent lower abdominal pain. The pain was colicky, moderate in intensity, radiated to the back, and was associated with nausea and vomiting. She denied any history of abnormal vaginal or intermenstrual bleeding prior to this time. Eight months earlier, she underwent surgical repair of a cystocele, during which she experienced blood loss requiring 2 units of transfused blood. She has four prior uncomplicated vaginal deliveries and has not used any contraceptive methods. Her medical history includes hypertension diagnosed 8 months ago, managed with amlodipine and candesartan; she has no history of diabetes or asthma. On examination, she appeared uncomfortable but was afebrile, with a blood pressure of 100/60 mmHg, heart rate 80 bpm, and respiratory rate 24 bpm; there was no pallor or jaundice. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL (12–16), total white blood cell count 3.8 × 10^9/L (4.0–11.0), platelets 257 × 10^9/L (150–450), urine microscopy with 10–12 pus cells per high-power field, blood urea nitrogen 15 mmol/L (2.1–8.5), and serum creatinine 0.6 mg/dL (0.59–1.04). Viral screening was negative. Transabdominal ultrasound revealed fluid within the uterine cavity and pelvic area, with upward displacement of the uterus.

A 5-year-old girl presented with two weeks of left thigh swelling, general weakness, poor oral intake, and low-grade fever. She had no history of trauma, bruising, or petechiae. Her past medical history was significant for cerebral palsy with severe developmental delay, generalized tonic–clonic seizures treated with long-term anticonvulsants, and swallowing difficulties with vomiting for over one month. On examination, her weight was below the third percentile, and the left thigh was swollen and warm without erythema; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 17,500/µL (79% neutrophils), platelet count of 528,000/µL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 11 mm/hr, C-reactive protein of 6.05 mg/dL, and hemoglobin of 9.2 g/dL. 

Plain radiographs of the knees demonstrated osteopenia, a thick sclerotic metaphyseal line above a widened physis, small beak-like metaphyseal excrescences on both femora, and disruption of the distal femoral physis on the left. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the left thigh revealed diffuse heterogeneous bone marrow signal changes in the femoral shaft, a large subperiosteal fluid collection with fluid–fluid levels, displacement of the distal epiphysis, surrounding soft-tissue edema, and moderate enhancement of the periosteum and adjacent muscles. 

On hospital day 7, bone scintigraphy showed no increased uptake in the left femur and decreased uptake in the epiphyseal plate of the left distal femur.

A 46-year-old man with hypertension, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus (hemoglobin A1c 10.3%), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and current tobacco use presented with 3–4 weeks of fever, malaise, productive cough with yellow-green sputum, and a 30-pound weight loss over 3 months. He reported self-limited diarrhea and vomiting earlier in the course. He had been treated as an outpatient with cephalexin for 7 days without improvement. 

On presentation, he was febrile and hypoxic, requiring supplemental oxygen. Chest radiography showed bilateral perihilar and right middle lobe consolidation. He was admitted and started on piperacillin–tazobactam, linezolid, and azithromycin. Chest CT on hospital day 0 revealed bilateral patchy consolidations with an evolving cavitary lesion in the right middle and lower lobes. 

Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) on hospital day 1 grew Pseudomonas species; antibiotics were de-escalated and he was discharged on levofloxacin. One week later, he returned with worsening dyspnea at rest and leukocytosis and was readmitted. CT chest showed stable infiltrates. Meropenem was initiated, and a workup for fungal infection was ordered. Laboratory studies included β-D-glucan and serum and urine Histoplasma and Blastomyces antigens. Repeat bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound–guided fine-needle aspiration of mediastinal lymph nodes was performed.

On hospital day 17, Histoplasma antigen was positive in serum and urine, and Blastomyces antigen was detected in both serum and urine. Antinuclear antibodies and anti–U1-RNP antibodies were also positive, but there was low clinical suspicion for mixed connective tissue disease.

A 61-year-old Japanese woman was referred for evaluation of multiple abnormal opacities on her annual chest radiograph. She had no respiratory symptoms. Vital signs were: temperature 35.7 °C, blood pressure 150/90 mm Hg, pulse 97 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Breath sounds were normal. Her medical history was notable only for hematuria and nephritis at age 59. For the past 6–7 months, she had taken choreito (7.5 g/day) for hematuria; she also used Seihaito intermittently. She smoked one pack per day for 31 years and drank 700 mL of beer five times weekly. BMI was 29.2 kg/m2. 

Chest CT showed multiple nodules predominantly in the bilateral lower lobes and a small peribronchial ground-glass opacity in the left lingular lobe. Laboratory studies revealed a mildly elevated CRP (0.33 mg/dL) and positive ANA (1:80 speckled; 1:40 nucleolar). Tests for proteinase 3 ANCA, myeloperoxidase ANCA, T-SPOT tuberculosis, anti-Mycobacterium avium complex antibody, Aspergillus antigen, Cryptococcus neoformans antigen, β-D-glucan, tumor markers, and soluble IL-2 receptor were all negative. Complete blood count, liver function tests, and urinalysis were unremarkable except for slight hematuria. Spirometry was normal. 

Bronchoscopy revealed no visible bleeding. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) from the left B5 segment became serially and increasingly hemorrhagic. Bacterial and mycobacterial cultures of BALF were negative, and cytology showed no malignant cells; no hemosiderin-laden macrophages were seen. A transbronchial biopsy of a subpleural nodule in left S8 demonstrated alveolitis and intraluminal polypoid structures with chronic inflammatory infiltrates, consistent with organizing pneumonia.

A 44-year-old white woman was referred for a second opinion on chronic cystoid macular edema of the left eye. She had a 10-year history of chronic intermediate uveitis in both eyes managed with prednisolone drops. Initial macular edema improved after a sub-Tenon triamcinolone injection but recurred 18 months earlier and failed to respond to intravitreal bevacizumab. She had no other medical history but was undergoing evaluation for possible breast cancer after routine screening mammography detected new right axillary lymphadenopathy with calcifications, which was confirmed on diagnostic mammogram and ultrasound. A chest CT performed five weeks later showed no axillary lymphadenopathy or pulmonary nodules. 

On ophthalmic examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 bilaterally. There was no anterior chamber inflammation; vitreous haze was trace with 1+ vitreous cells in both eyes. The right eye exhibited a mild nuclear sclerotic cataract; the left eye was pseudophakic. Fundus examination showed small patches of perifoveal atrophy. Optical coherence tomography confirmed bilateral cystoid macular edema, more pronounced in the left eye. Fluorescein angiography revealed optic disc leakage and diffuse peripheral leakage in both eyes without vasculitis. There were no cutaneous lesions, pulmonary symptoms, or other systemic complaints. 

Laboratory studies demonstrated HLA-B8 positivity and an angiotensin-converting enzyme level of 67 U/L (reference 12–68). Tests for syphilis, Lyme disease, and tuberculosis were negative. The uveitis was initially labeled idiopathic, although sarcoidosis was suspected. Methotrexate was considered but contraindicated due to alcohol use; mycophenolate mofetil was recommended, but the patient chose to await the results of her breast workup.

A 69-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, gout, and former tobacco use presented to the ED with worsening shortness of breath, productive cough, and dyspnea on exertion. One day earlier, at an urgent care center, he had a normal chest radiograph and was diagnosed with bronchitis; he was started on oral steroids, antibiotics, and a metered-dose inhaler. His symptoms worsened, prompting this ED visit. He reported chronic sinusitis but felt these symptoms were similar to prior respiratory infections. On arrival, his blood pressure was 124/94 mmHg, pulse 108/min, respiratory rate 36/min, temperature 97.4°F, and oxygen saturation 87% on room air. He was placed on 2 L oxygen by nasal cannula, and his vital signs subsequently normalized.

A 59-year-old previously healthy man was referred for evaluation of a one-month history of rapidly progressive cognitive and motor symptoms. He initially developed akinetic mutism, constructional apraxia, and spatial disorientation, which progressed over weeks to delirium with hallucinations, severe cerebellar ataxia rendering him unable to walk, erratic myoclonus, and rigidity. There was no family history of neurological disease, no substance use, and no recent travel or infections. Neurologic examination on admission showed mild gait ataxia with multidirectional oscillations and cognitive deficits. Routine laboratory studies—including complete blood count, metabolic panel, liver function tests, inflammatory markers, autoimmune antibody panels, viral and bacterial serologies, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis—were all within normal limits. Repetitive electroencephalograms showed no specific abnormalities. Brain MRI with T1, T2, and diffusion-weighted sequences was unremarkable. To further evaluate his condition, a brain 18F-FDG PET/CT scan was performed.

A 30-year-old man presented with right lower quadrant abdominal pain of 9 months’ duration. He described severe, dull aching pain in the right lower quadrant with intermittent piercing peri-umbilical pain, occurring once or twice weekly, lasting a day, and resolving without intervention. The pain was sometimes accompanied by vomiting of ingested matter. He denied fever, urinary symptoms, changes in bowel habits, or weight loss. He had multiple prior evaluations with a diagnosis of nonspecific abdominal pain.

On examination, his vital signs were within normal limits. Abdominal examination revealed direct tenderness over the right lower quadrant without rebound tenderness. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 6.6 × 10^3/L, hemoglobin 14 g/dL, and platelets 284 × 10^3/L. C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were within normal range. Stool examination and urinalysis were unremarkable.

An initial abdominal ultrasound demonstrated an echogenic appendiceal wall measuring 7 mm in diameter that was partially compressible, with slight probe tenderness. Two days later, a repeat ultrasound by a different operator showed diffuse appendiceal wall thickening with a prominent hyperechogenic submucosa; the partially compressible appendix measured 6.3 mm wall-to-wall, with no free fluid, findings interpreted as suggestive of chronic appendicitis.

A 2-year-old, 1.8 kg intact female pet rabbit presented for a routine check-up. The owner reported only mild lethargy. The diet was regular, and vaccinations and parasite prevention were up to date.

On examination, the rabbit was bright and alert. Temperature was 39.3 °C. A large, solid, oval intra-abdominal mass was palpated in the right abdomen, eliciting mild discomfort. Popliteal and submandibular lymph nodes were normal; all other parameters were within reference intervals.

Laboratory studies (CBC and biochemistry) were within normal limits.

Abdominal ultrasound (right lateral recumbency) revealed a 5.5 × 6.7 cm hypoechoic ovoid structure with homogeneous parenchyma in the region of the right ovary. There was no peritoneal effusion or reactivity, and Color Doppler showed no peri- or intranodular blood flow. The left ovary and both uterine horns appeared normal.

Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 7.6 × 4.3 cm oval mass occupying much of the right abdomen. The mass had inhomogeneous parenchyma with twisted intralesional vessels and demonstrated a “whirlpool sign.” The right ovary was not visualized; the left ovary and uterus were mildly displaced; no metastatic lesions were noted.

A 55-year-old woman with a remote history of ovarian cancer and no recent vaccinations or infections reported a one-month history of fatigue, mild bilateral retroorbital discomfort, and progressive visual loss—first in the right eye, then the left. On examination she had a right homonymous hemianopia and tetrahyperreflexia. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory tests including routine blood work were unremarkable. A brain MRI revealed a single 3.7 × 2.4 × 1.8 cm expansile lesion in the left temporo-occipital region extending into the splenium of the corpus callosum. On T1-weighted images the lesion was hypointense; on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences it was hyperintense. There was significant perilesional vasogenic edema and no diffusion restriction. After contrast administration, there was peripheral enhancement in an open-ring configuration, with the incomplete portion directed toward the cortex.

A 15-year-old girl with no personal or family medical history presented to the emergency department in deep coma after several tonic–clonic convulsions. Two minutes into a left-sided intraoral injection of 1.5 mL of 2% lidocaine with epinephrine (1:100 000) for endodontic anesthesia—administered without prior aspiration—she collapsed and experienced intermittent convulsions for approximately 30 minutes, followed by unresponsiveness.

On examination, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 3 with intact brainstem reflexes and no fever. Vital signs were within normal limits. The left cheek and gingiva were edematous, and a large gingival hematoma was noted. Fundoscopic examination showed no papilledema.

Electrocardiography demonstrated sinus tachycardia at 120 beats per minute. Electroencephalography revealed diffuse slow activity, predominantly theta rhythms, with no evidence of ongoing status epilepticus.

Noncontrast head CT showed reduced gray–white matter differentiation and effacement of cerebral sulci, consistent with cerebral edema. MRI of the brain with venography and angiography revealed bilateral, symmetric T2-hyperintense lesions with restricted diffusion in the frontal and occipital lobes, with patent cerebral veins and arteries.

Lumbar puncture yielded 10 lymphocytes/mm3, protein 50 mg/dL, no red blood cells, and a negative Gram stain; blood glucose was 50 mg/dL and CSF glucose was 70 mg/dL.
