Serum electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, liver and renal function tests, complete blood count, coagulation profile, and troponin level were all within normal limits.

A 30-year-old woman was admitted with diffuse headache, nausea, diplopia, and gait instability. One week earlier she had an occasional cough without fever. Neurologic examination revealed a lag of the left eye on upward gaze, right abducens nerve paresis, horizontal nystagmus on vertical gaze, vertical nystagmus on upward gaze, diplopia in all gaze directions, and truncal ataxia. She became somnolent with psychomotor agitation and had spontaneous extensor seizures. Noncontrast head CT was normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed pleocytosis (316 cells/µL; normal 0–5), elevated lactate (4.3 mmol/L; normal 1.1–2.4), and elevated total protein (1780.5 mg/L; normal ≤450). PCR for herpes simplex virus types I and II was negative, and oligoclonal bands were absent. Serologic tests of CSF for neurotropic viruses and Borrelia burgdorferi were also negative. Brain MRI demonstrated multiple hyperintense lesions on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences in the cerebellum, brainstem (medulla, pons, midbrain), bilateral posterior limbs of the internal capsules, thalami, subcortical frontotemporoparietal white matter, and optic radiations.

A 21-day-old Black African female, born at 39 weeks by normal spontaneous vaginal delivery to a healthy 19-year-old primigravida mother who had no antenatal complications or ultrasounds, was noted at birth to have asymmetric enlargement of the left lower and left upper extremities. On examination, the left foot had macrodactyly and ectrodactyly, and there were numerous port-wine stains over the left thoracoabdominal region and the anteroposterior aspect of the left lower limb. Vascular lesions were also visible on the abdomen. Heart sounds were normal, and there were no respiratory, abdominal, or neurologic abnormalities. Laboratory studies showed thrombocytosis and a prothrombin time of 16 seconds (reference range, 11–15). A color Doppler ultrasound of the left lower limb and abdomen demonstrated varicose veins without evidence of an arteriovenous fistula.

A 44-year-old woman from a rural area presented with a 12-month history of progressive right elbow pain, swelling, and declining function. Over the same period, she noted fatigue, night sweats, low-grade fevers, and weight loss. There was no history of trauma, immunosuppression, or known tuberculosis exposure. Six months into her illness, a draining sinus tract with purulent discharge developed over the posterior elbow.

On examination, the right elbow was diffusely swollen (10 cm in circumference), warm, erythematous, and tender, with a 30°–80° range of motion. No other joints were involved. Vital signs were notable for a low-grade fever (37.8 °C); other systems were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 40 mg/L (normal 0–5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 37 mm/h (normal 0–20), and white blood cell count of 11 × 10^9/L (normal 4.5–11). Plain radiographs of the right elbow revealed marginal periarticular osteolysis and subluxation.

A sample of purulent fluid from the sinus tract was obtained and sent for bacterial culture, including acid-fast bacilli studies.

A 52-year-old woman with achondroplasia presented with an 8-month history of progressive weakness and numbness in both upper extremities and a spastic gait. On examination, she had grade 3/5 weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles, hyperreflexia of the upper and lower extremities, a positive Hoffmann sign, decreased sensation in the arms, and clumsiness of the hands without bowel or bladder dysfunction. Lateral cervical radiographs showed C1 hypoplasia. CT of the cervical spine revealed congenital canal stenosis due to the C1 posterior arch and the occipital bone. Sagittal and axial MR imaging demonstrated spinal-cord atrophy and a high-intensity intramedullary lesion at C1. 

She underwent posterior decompression at the craniovertebral junction, including resection of the C1 posterior arch and part of the occipital rim. Intraoperative ultrasonography confirmed adequate bone removal. A reactive fibrous band compressing the dura was noted, and a longitudinal durotomy was performed, leaving the dura open without patch graft; the arachnoid appeared intact. Motor strength and gait improved immediately postoperatively, but suction drainage indicated cerebrospinal fluid leakage.

On postoperative day 7, she developed severe headache and nausea. MR imaging showed a moderate CSF collection at the surgical site, and brain CT revealed bilateral infratentorial subdural fluid collections. She was neurologically stable and managed conservatively with intravenous hydration. On day 17, she became drowsy and unresponsive. Emergency brain CT showed increased infratentorial fluid collections and marked enlargement of the lateral ventricles with obstruction at the cerebral aqueduct.

A 38-year-old woman presented to the emergency gynecologic unit with 9 weeks of amenorrhea, inconstant pelvic pain, and vaginal bleeding for 2 days. She had three previous term cesarean deliveries without complications. Her medical and family history were unremarkable. Vital signs were within normal limits (heart rate 90 bpm, blood pressure 105/60 mmHg). On examination, the abdomen was tender on deep palpation in the hypogastric region; the uterus felt pasty, the cervix was closed, and there was no adnexal tenderness or pelvic mass. Speculum examination revealed no active bleeding from the cervix. Transvaginal ultrasound showed an enlarged uterus (96 × 61 × 48 mm), normal adnexa with a corpus luteum in the left ovary (25 × 20 mm), and no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Within the thickness of the anterior uterine wall at the cervico-isthmic site, a gestational sac measuring 16 mm (corresponding to six gestational weeks) was identified, without embryonic echoes suggestive of cardiac activity. Serum β-hCG was 12,770 mU/mL (normal range for nine gestational weeks, 22,075–227,000 mU/mL).

A 61-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of a right tonsillar mass. He denied throat pain, fever, or weight loss. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. On examination, there was a 3 × 2 cm nontender, mobile mass arising from the right lateral wall of the oropharynx; a few lymph nodes were palpable at right levels III and IV. Hematological investigation revealed mild eosinophilia (9%). Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the neck showed a well-defined, minimally enhancing isodense soft-tissue mass measuring 31 × 27 mm in the right oropharynx. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the cervical lymph nodes revealed reactive lymphadenitis.

A 43-year-old Asian man with a 10-year history of type 2 diabetes presented with one month of fever and five days of a painful swelling below the left submandibular region. He also reported weight loss and poor appetite. On examination, he was febrile with a tender 2 × 1 cm left submandibular lymph node; bilateral axillary nodes were palpable up to 0.5 × 0.5 cm. Vital signs and the remainder of the physical examination were normal.

Laboratory studies showed neutrophilic leukocytosis, an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and poorly controlled blood glucose levels. A chest radiograph revealed widening of the right paratracheal stripe. He was started empirically on intravenous amoxicillin–clavulanic acid and subcutaneous insulin.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the thorax demonstrated a 4.2 × 3.7 × 3 cm anterior mediastinal mass in the right paratracheal region, described as suggestive of malignancy, along with a few upper lobe pulmonary densities. An excisional biopsy of the left submandibular lymph node revealed a non-caseating granuloma composed of lymphocytes and plasma cells, interpreted as suggestive of tuberculosis. A tuberculin skin test was negative. Bone marrow examination showed neither acid-fast bacilli nor granulomas. Anti-tuberculosis therapy was withheld.

A 77-year-old woman underwent right total knee replacement for osteoarthritis. Her medical history was notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus (oral therapy), glaucoma, and osteoarthritis of her hips and left knee; she had no history of gout or pseudogout. Her postoperative course was unremarkable, and at 4 weeks she was mobilizing well without wound problems. Five weeks after surgery, she presented with a 3-day history of increasing pain, swelling, and stiffness of the right knee and difficulty bearing weight. On examination, the knee was swollen, warm, and very tender, with a range of motion limited to 10° by pain. Her recorded temperature was 38.0 °C with slight tachycardia. Laboratory studies showed C-reactive protein 98.9 mg/L and white-cell count 16.2 ×10⁹/L (neutrophils 13.92 ×10⁹/L). Plain radiographs showed a well-fixed prosthesis without loosening. An ultrasound was performed to rule out deep vein thrombosis. The knee was aspirated under sterile conditions, yielding 60 mL of cloudy, straw-coloured fluid; the joint was aspirated to dryness. Fluid analysis revealed a high white-cell count and no organisms on Gram stain.

A 31‐year‐old Arab man with no significant medical history presented with a 4‐day history of diffuse cervico‐facial edema and odynophagia. He denied fever, dyspnea, or dysphonia. On examination, there was bilateral, symmetrical, soft, poorly limited, nonpitting edema extending from the submandibular to the supraclavicular and suprasternal regions, with no erythema or lymphadenopathy. Chest examination revealed collateral venous circulation across the upper anterior chest wall; cardiopulmonary auscultation was normal. Oropharyngeal inspection showed multiple painful aphthous ulcers on the tongue and a regular, symmetrical bulging of the posterior oropharyngeal wall without tonsillar involvement or trismus. Laboratory studies demonstrated a C‐reactive protein of 70 mg/L and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 40 mm/h; the complete blood count was normal. Contrast‐enhanced cervico‐thoracic CT revealed retropharyngeal soft‐tissue thickening extending into the parapharyngeal spaces and thrombophlebitis of the superior vena cava and left internal jugular vein. Cervical MRI confirmed a hyperintense retropharyngeal lesion on diffusion‐weighted sequences consistent with edema. Laboratory thrombophilia testing was normal.

A 30-year-old woman with B-cell acute lymphocytic leukemia, who had relapsed after initial chemotherapy and radiotherapy, underwent an allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant one week ago. She now reports pruritus and swelling confined to the red portion of a tattoo on her lower back; the black and peach portions are unaffected. She also notes the onset of diarrhea that has continued for nearly one week. On examination, the red-pigmented area of the tattoo shows erythematous, elevated, indurated papules and plaques. A punch biopsy of the affected tattooed skin reveals interface dermatitis with scattered apoptotic keratinocytes containing deeply eosinophilic, smudged cytoplasm at all levels of the Malpighian layer, basal vacuolar degeneration, and rare satellite cell necrosis characterized by lymphocytes with pyknotic nuclei adjacent to necrotic keratinocytes near the basal epidermis. In the dermis, there is tattoo pigment within perivascular macrophages and a sparse lymphohistiocytic infiltrate without eosinophils. Rare satellite cell necrosis is also observed in a pilosebaceous unit.

A 28-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of progressively enlarging left posterior neck swelling associated with dull pain and restricted neck motion. He had no history of trauma or surgery. On examination, he appeared well, vital signs were normal, and there was a deep, smooth, nontender mass in the posterior neck with unremarkable overlying skin. Sensory and motor examination of the upper limbs was normal. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, were within normal limits. A lateral cervical radiograph showed an ill-defined increased opacity in the suboccipital region. MRI of the cervical spine revealed a 5.3 × 4.3 × 3.4 cm round, well-defined lesion in the suboccipital paravertebral compartment posterior to the spinous processes of C1 to C3. The lesion contained multiple variably sized internal cystic structures, demonstrated homogeneous T1 hypointensity and T2 hyperintensity, had a sharply demarcated thin dark capsule, and showed no contrast enhancement, perilesional fat stranding, or neural foraminal extension.

A 60-year-old woman presented with a three-week history of a painful lump in her right iliac fossa that had worsened over the three days prior to presentation. She also reported abdominal distension, multiple episodes of vomiting, and inability to pass stool or flatus. She denied fever, anorexia, or weight loss. She had no prior surgeries, comorbidities, or known immunosuppression. On examination, there was an 8 cm × 4 cm hard, irregular, immobile, tender mass in the right iliac fossa. 

Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL, leukocyte count 13 690/μL with 88 % neutrophils; serum CEA and CA 19-9 were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a complex heterogeneous, irregular lesion measuring 27.7 mm × 34.4 mm at the ileocecal junction with minimal vascularity and probe tenderness; the initial differential was appendicular lump with localized inflammatory changes. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed asymmetric circumferential thickening of a 9 cm segment of the transverse colon (maximal wall thickness 17 mm) with marked contrast enhancement and luminal narrowing, and a lobulated ill-defined mesenteric mass in the right iliac fossa measuring approximately 4.7 cm × 4 cm × 3 cm with heterogeneous enhancement and adjacent fat stranding. The liver was normal and lymph nodes were not significantly enlarged. These findings were interpreted as carcinoma of the transverse colon with mesenteric metastasis. 

With a provisional diagnosis of complete bowel obstruction secondary to transverse colon carcinoma with mesenteric metastasis, exploratory laparotomy was planned.

An 80-year-old man with pancreatic cancer in remission, previously treated with chemotherapy, radiation, and a Whipple procedure, presented with a one-month history of intermittent melena and bright red blood per rectum. At an outside hospital, CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis, esophagogastroduodenoscopy, colonoscopy, push enteroscopy, and capsule endoscopy failed to localize a bleeding source; a tagged red blood cell scan showed tracer around the stomach. He was transferred for further evaluation. Over the subsequent month, he had ongoing melena, hematemesis, and bright red blood per rectum with hemodynamic instability requiring frequent transfusions and intensive care support. A balloon-assisted enteroscopy could not traverse the efferent jejunal limb but revealed fresh blood refluxing into the stomach from the afferent jejunal limb. Emergent angiography showed no active bleeding. Two weeks later, repeat push enteroscopy with endoscopic ultrasound identified the choledochojejunostomy site approximately 100 cm from the incisors; after dislodging a large clot, multiple large varices with red wale signs and no active bleeding were visualized in the afferent jejunal limb. Endoscopic ultrasound with Doppler confirmed multiple grape-like clusters consistent with varices.

A 49-year-old homosexual man was referred to the colorectal clinic with a 2-week history of perianal pain, peri-anal skin changes, altered bowel habit with diarrhea and fecal incontinence, and occasional fresh blood on toilet paper. He also reported loss of appetite but no weight loss. His past medical history was unremarkable, and he took no medications.

On examination, there was a 3 × 1 cm ulcerated lesion at the 12 o’clock position in the perianal region and a firm nodule at the 9 o’clock position. A colonoscopy to the terminal ileum was normal. Abdominal CT scan revealed only a simple liver cyst; pelvic MRI confirmed an anal nodule without clear distal extent.

An initial biopsy under local anesthesia showed ulcerated, plasma cell–rich inflammation without a definitive mass effect, raising suspicion for a syphilitic lesion. After multidisciplinary discussion, a repeat biopsy demonstrated reactive epithelial changes with ulceration, fibrin deposition, acanthosis, prominent intraepithelial neutrophils, and a dense dermal plasmacytic infiltrate. There was no evidence of granulomas, fungal hyphae, herpetic viral inclusions, or definitive obliterative endarteritis, but the marked plasma cell infiltrate suggested syphilis as a likely possibility.

A 7-year-old girl sustained a second-degree burn (3 × 4 cm) on the posterolateral right elbow after boiling water. One hour later, she presented with impaired consciousness and difficulty breathing. She was unresponsive to painful stimuli, had pinpoint pupils, and apneustic respirations (respiratory rate 6/min); her pulse was 90 bpm, blood pressure 90/60 mm Hg, and temperature 36.5 °C. The burn was covered with a zinc-oxide– and fish-oil–based ointment. Suspecting opioid poisoning, clinicians gave IV naloxone (0.2 mg every 2–5 minutes, total 0.8 mg), after which her consciousness improved. A noncontrast brain CT scan and lumbar puncture were performed; laboratory studies showed hyperglycemia with normal CSF findings. She was transferred to a tertiary pediatric intensive care unit, arriving four hours later in a light coma with miosis and apneustic respirations. A bolus of 0.8 mg IV naloxone again improved her status. Additional management included fluid therapy, a continuous naloxone infusion (0.01 mg/kg/hour), ranitidine, ceftriaxone, and topical silver sulfadiazine. Laboratory tests revealed leukocytosis and an elevated C-reactive protein; a chest x-ray and repeat brain CT were unremarkable.

A 61-year-old right-handed man with no known medical history presented with a 5-month history of progressive unprovoked episodes of dysarthria lasting 10–15 seconds and occurring up to 30–40 times daily. His awareness and comprehension remained intact; there were no triggers or diurnal variation. He denied constitutional symptoms and extra-neurological signs, including mouth or genital ulcers and visual changes. There was no family history of episodic ataxia or dysarthria. 

Vital signs were normal. Neurologic examination revealed right-sided dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and inability to tandem walk. During the evaluation, episodes of 10–20 seconds of stereotyped ataxic dysarthria with dysprosody were observed. Cognitive testing was unremarkable (MMSE 29/30).

MRI of the brain with contrast showed a 5 × 8 × 6 mm homogeneously enhancing midline midbrain lesion at the brachium conjunctivum, with high T2-FLAIR signal, facilitated diffusion, minimal edema, and subtle thickening of the left third cranial nerve. The differential diagnosis included lymphoma, glial tumor, metastasis, solitary demyelinating lesion, neuro-sarcoidosis, and neuro-Behçet’s disease. 

A full-body PET and skeletal survey demonstrated uptake only in the midbrain lesion, with no other hypermetabolic foci, excluding systemic malignancy. Three-month follow-up MRI showed interval regression of the lesion with decreased T2 signal and contrast enhancement, favoring an inflammatory process and making glioma and metastasis less likely.

Lumbar puncture revealed no pleocytosis, normal biochemistry, negative bacterial cultures, negative multiplex viral PCR, and no malignant cells; oligoclonal bands were absent. Blood tests, including an autoimmune panel and angiotensin-converting enzyme level (61 U/L; reference 16–85), were within normal limits. A brain biopsy was deferred due to location and risk. Ophthalmologic examination showed no anterior or posterior uveitis.

The patient was treated with intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 5 days with taper), but there was no notable reduction in the frequency of his paroxysmal ataxia and dysarthria episodes.

A 23-year-old African American man presented with sudden onset of generalized weakness. He went to bed 4 hours earlier and on waking was unable to move his arms or legs. He reported a 40-lb weight loss over the past year, heat intolerance, palpitations, and tremors. Six months ago, he had a similar episode lasting 8 hours; at that time, marked hypokalemia was noted. He had multiple nocturnal, self-resolving episodes of weakness over the past 6 months. He denied alcohol use, laxative or diuretic abuse, and there was no family history of hypokalemia or paralysis.

On examination, the heart rate was 134 bpm and blood pressure 162/87 mm Hg. He had bilateral exophthalmos and a smooth, bruiting thyroid gland. Neurologic examination showed 1/5 strength in all extremities with diminished deep-tendon reflexes; cranial nerves and sensation were intact.

Laboratory studies revealed severe hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia. Thyroid-stimulating hormone was suppressed, and free thyroxine was elevated. Spot urine potassium was low, and the urine potassium/creatinine ratio was low.

A 63-year-old non-smoking man presented with a 10-day history of daily fever, progressive dyspnea (mMRC grade 2), and productive cough. His only medical history was depression treated with sertraline 50 mg daily for several years. On examination, he had crackles over the right upper chest.

Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis (22 480/μL) and C-reactive protein 168 mg/L. Rapid influenza and RSV PCR tests were negative. Chest radiography demonstrated a right upper-zone consolidation. A high-resolution CT scan showed multiple bilateral consolidations—predominantly right, subpleural and peribronchial in distribution—with diffuse patchy ground-glass opacities and a right pleural effusion.

All bacterial analyses were negative. Bronchoscopy appeared normal, and bronchoalveolar lavage revealed a mixed cell pattern (40% lymphocytes, 20% neutrophils, 20% monocytes, and 20% eosinophils; CD4 84.4%, CD8 7%). Cardiac echocardiography was unremarkable. Despite broad-spectrum antibiotics, he deteriorated, requiring mechanical ventilation. A subsequent CT scan showed new left-lung consolidations and worsening diffuse ground-glass opacities.

A surgical lung biopsy from multiple lobes showed intra-alveolar buds of granulation tissue composed of fibroblasts, consistent with organizing pneumonia. High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (1 mg/kg/day) was started, with initial improvement followed by clinical relapse each time the dose was reduced.

A 56-year-old man was admitted to the medical ICU with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure. He reported progressive shortness of breath over the past year, with three prior hospitalizations and extensive workup that was unrevealing. On current admission, he was febrile to 38.9 °C, hypotensive (82/54 mmHg), bradycardic (51 bpm), and required FiO2 95% to maintain SpO2 91%. Chest radiography revealed bilateral extensive multifocal nodular opacities. He was treated empirically for suspected healthcare-associated pneumonia with vancomycin, piperacillin–tazobactam, and methylprednisolone.

Laboratory studies showed pancytopenia (WBC 1.6×10^3/µL, ANC 0.7×10^3/µL, hemoglobin 11.3 g/dL, platelets 99×10^3/µL), elevated creatinine of 1.07 mg/dL (baseline 0.38 mg/dL), and hypoalbuminemia (1.8 g/dL). Urinalysis demonstrated new microscopic hematuria and nephritic-range proteinuria (70.2 mg/dL). Serum ferritin was markedly elevated at 7512 ng/mL, and abdominal ultrasound showed splenomegaly (17.7 cm).

Prior evaluations included chest CT scans demonstrating scattered pulmonary nodules and cavitary lesions; four lung biopsies and a VATS wedge resection revealed only chronic inflammation and necrotizing debris without malignancy. A bronchoscopy a month earlier grew pan-sensitive Pseudomonas aeruginosa and yielded only partial symptomatic improvement with antibiotics. Several months earlier, he developed a diffuse erythematous maculopapular rash and oral ulcers; skin biopsy showed superficial and deep lymphocytic infiltrates with vacuolar interface changes. Despite an exhaustive negative autoimmune workup, granulomatosis with polyangiitis remained under consideration, and a trial of high-dose prednisone led to modest clinical improvement.

A 31-year-old woman with epilepsy had been treated with topiramate 100 mg/day for several years. She continued this treatment unchanged throughout pregnancy and during breastfeeding. To reduce infant exposure, two daily breast-feedings were replaced with formula one week after birth, and the infant initially thrived. At 40 days of age (weight 4735 g), the infant developed 8–10 watery, foamy stools per day. No other family member had diarrhea or gastrointestinal upset. The infant’s rate of weight gain declined, and she was referred to the hospital outpatient clinic. Relevant differential diagnoses such as infection or somatic causes of diarrhea were excluded; however, the infant continued to have frequent, watery stools.

A 7-month-old boy was referred for evaluation of a congenital pin-hole fistula in the right sternoclavicular joint region, first noted at age 1 month. The lesion intermittently discharged clear mucous fluid without signs of infection. On examination, there was a small skin opening but no palpable subcutaneous mass. Because the patient had no infections and the lesion was stable, excision was deferred until imaging could be safely performed under sedation. At 1 year 11 months of age, magnetic resonance imaging revealed a small tubular structure continuous with the skin surface and extending deep into the tissue anterior to the sternal head of the right sternocleidomastoid muscle.

A 4-year-old boy from rural Nepal presented with a 1-month history of acute, nonprogressive right-sided weakness. Six months earlier, he had a similar episode of left-sided weakness for which he received conservative care and was started on aspirin (3 mg/kg/day). There was no history of seizures, facial deviation, loss of consciousness, fever, trauma, or prior radiation exposure. 

On examination, Glasgow Coma Scale score was 15; pupils were equal and reactive. Muscle bulk was decreased bilaterally (more on the right), with power 3/5 in the right upper limb, 2/5 in the right lower limb, and 4/5 on both sides of the left. Deep tendon reflexes were normal; plantar responses were bilaterally upgoing.

Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 15,100/mm3 with lymphocytosis (54%) and eosinophilia (10%), a prolonged prothrombin time of 16 s, and low mean corpuscular volume (78 fl), mean corpuscular hemoglobin (24.7 pg), and mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (31.7%). Serologies for HIV, HCV, and HBsAg were negative; renal and liver functions were within normal limits.

Head CT revealed an ill-defined hypodense area in the left frontoparietal lobe, consistent with a subacute infarct, and a hypodense area in the right frontal lobe, consistent with a chronic infarct. Digital subtraction angiography of the head and neck showed reduced caliber of both internal carotid arteries from their origins to the cavernous segments, with multiple tortuous collateral vessels supplying the distal anterior circulation in a net-like pattern encircling the circle of Willis.

An 81-year-old Caucasian woman with hypertension, coronary artery disease, and heart failure (with AICD) presented with episodes of hypoglycemia occurring mainly after meals. Her vital signs were stable and physical examination was unremarkable, without neurologic deficits. She had no history of diabetes mellitus or prior exposure to insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents. A finger-stick glucose measurement was 39 mg/dL. Laboratory evaluation showed normal beta-hydroxybutyrate, cortisol, and ACTH levels. A plasma screen for sulfonylureas and meglitinides was negative. During hypoglycemia, her plasma insulin concentration was elevated at 1345 pmol/L (reference 111–1153 pmol/L) with a C-peptide of 2.64 nmol/L. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen showed no pancreatic mass. On a subsequent episode of hypoglycemia, insulin rose to 2247 pmol/L and C-peptide to 4.14 nmol/L.

A 26-month-old girl was referred for evaluation of gross motor developmental delay noted from about 12 months of age. Before 1 year, her development was unremarkable. She achieved head control at 8–9 months and independent sitting at 12 months. She was initially treated for suspected refractory rickets without clinical improvement. She was born at term after an uneventful pregnancy to non-consanguineous parents; birth weight 2.8 kg, length 58 cm. She was exclusively breastfed until 7 months and now has a normal diet. Fine motor and social skills were appropriate, but gross motor development remained delayed (developmental quotient 62). Jargon speech suggested mild language delay. Family history was unremarkable.

On examination, weight was 11 kg, length 78 cm, and head circumference 40 cm (all below the 3rd percentile). Vital signs were stable. There was no pallor, lymphadenopathy, cyanosis, or icterus. Facial examination revealed a broad forehead with frontal bossing. Neck and upper limbs were normal. Lower limbs showed pes planus and genu recurvatum. Skin was moderately hyperextensible, and joints were hypermobile; muscle tone was normal. Neurologic, cardiovascular, and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. Brain MRI was normal. Laboratory tests showed serum calcium 9 mEq/L, phosphate 2.0 mEq/L, and alkaline phosphatase 380 IU/L. She received multiple doses of oral and intramuscular vitamin D and calcium supplementation without improvement.

A 57‐year‐old man presented with a 20‐year history of progressive neuropsychiatric and motor symptoms. His symptoms began at age 37 with right leg numbness and gait disturbances that gradually worsened over 2 years, eventually requiring assistance with daily activities. He reported no substance use. Family history was notable for his mother with obsessive‐compulsive disorder, a sister with infantile seizures and borderline intelligence, and an uncle with rapid neuropsychiatric decline.

On examination, he had mild impairment in attention and concentration but was fully oriented. His gait was slow and shuffling without spasticity or ataxia. He demonstrated severe motor slowness, markedly reduced gait velocity, and pronounced bradykinesia. His voice was very soft with low pitch and resonance. Neuropsychiatric features included depressed mood, abulia, anhedonia, paranoid ideation, psychomotor retardation, visual hallucinations of shadows, obsessive thoughts about cleanliness, and frequent headaches. Mental status showed poor eye contact, masked facial expression, a stooped posture, restricted affect, impaired short‐term recall, reduced concentration, and partial insight.

He was initially diagnosed with early‐onset Parkinson’s disease and treated with Levodopa and Amantadine, but his motor and psychiatric symptoms showed minimal improvement over several follow‐up visits. Neurological examination revealed rigidity, reduced arm swing, a positive glabella tap, and no tremor or dystonia. An electroencephalogram was unremarkable.

A 48-year-old man with no history of liver disease, alcohol use, surgery, or metabolic disorders was referred to the emergency department for subacute cognitive decline. Five weeks earlier, he had been treated with gabapentin and paracetamol for a lumbar disc herniation. His family noted progressive behavioral changes and difficulty performing simple tasks; he spoke only in short, simple sentences. He denied headache, nausea, or vomiting.

On examination, his temperature was normal and Glasgow Coma Scale score was 15, though he required repeated prompts to cooperate. Neurological examination was otherwise unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (16.3 × 10^9/L), normal C-reactive protein, and normal liver enzymes. A noncontrast head CT was normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed no pleocytosis, normal protein, and no oligoclonal bands. Over the next three days, his cognition worsened (Montreal Cognitive Assessment 21/30). Tests for thyroid function, HIV, and syphilis were negative. Serum ammonia was elevated at 116 µmol/L; AST, ALT, GGT, bilirubin, LDH, and INR were within normal limits. Repeat CSF studies remained normal. Brain MRI with gadolinium was unremarkable. EEG demonstrated diffuse theta activity with intermittent rhythmic delta bursts consistent with moderate, diffuse cerebral dysfunction.

A 76-year-old man with essential hypertension, treated daily with lercanidipine and valsartan, presented after 8 days of progressive dyspnea preceded by blood-tinged sputum. He denied fever, chills, night sweats, chest pain, or toxic exposures. On examination: T 36.6 °C; HR 108 bpm; RR 26 /min; BP 125/72 mmHg; SpO₂ 89% on room air. Bilateral basal fine moist rales and unilateral lower limb swelling were noted; there were no signs of right-sided heart failure. Laboratory studies showed WBC 4.3×10⁹/L (neutrophils 69.9%), hemoglobin 115 g/L, CRP 36.7 mg/L, NT-proBNP 525 pg/mL, and D-dimer 2.25 mg/L (upper limit 0.05 mg/dL). Arterial blood gas on FiO₂ 35% revealed PaO₂ 78 mmHg, PaCO₂ 38 mmHg, and SaO₂ 94%. Immunological tests and tumor markers were normal. CTPA demonstrated extensive bilateral pulmonary emboli in the main, lobar, and segmental pulmonary arteries. Bedside transthoracic echocardiography revealed a 5.85×4.32 cm mobile mass attached to the posterior wall of the right atrium, partially prolapsing through the tricuspid valve in diastole. Lower-limb compression ultrasound identified thrombosis in the left femoral vein. He was started on low-molecular-weight heparin 5000 IU once daily; he remained hemodynamically stable. Further diagnostic evaluation was refused. A preliminary diagnosis of venous thromboembolism with right atrial myxoma was made. Surgery was recommended but declined. He was discharged on rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 3 weeks, then 20 mg once daily, with planned outpatient follow-up.

An 18-year-old woman presented for evaluation of long-standing seizures and developmental delay.  
History: Pregnancy and delivery were uneventful. She had bilateral congenital cataracts removed at 5 months. She began having focal seizures with secondary generalization at 6 months. Developmental milestones were delayed; she attends a special‐needs school. No family history of stroke, cataracts, epilepsy, or extra‐CNS disease; parents and a younger brother are healthy.  
Examination: Right hemiparesis with stable gross and fine motor deficits over time. Visual acuity corrected with spectacles.  
Brain MRI: FLAIR images show volume loss with gliosis in the left fronto‐parietal periventricular white matter, centrum semi‐ovale, and ganglio‐capsular regions, with ex‐vacuo dilation of the left lateral ventricle. Confluent hyperintense signal in the right fronto‐parietal periventricular white matter and centrum semi‐ovale suggests chronic ischemic changes. GRE sequences show no blooming to indicate hemorrhage or hemosiderin. DWI is negative for acute diffusion restriction.  
MR angiography (Time‐of‐Flight): Paucity of insular and opercular branches of the left middle cerebral artery; no evidence of aneurysm or dolichoectasia.  
There is no history of perinatal complications or neonatal illness to explain these findings.

A 13-year-old girl presented with a 2-year history of intermittent headaches that improved with rest and a 1-year history of irregular menstrual cycles. Three months before admission, her family noted short stature, and an MRI of the sellar region revealed a space-occupying lesion measuring approximately 1.1 × 1.7 × 1.8 cm with clear boundaries. The lesion was dumbbell-shaped, uniformly enhanced on T1 and T2, slightly constricted in the saddle plane, with compression of the pituitary stalk and depression of the sella turcica floor; the optic chiasm was mildly compressed. She had no significant past medical or family history. Vital signs were normal. On examination, her height was 139 cm (<3rd percentile), weight 50 kg, BMI 25.88 kg/m2; visual acuity was 0.8 OS and 0.5 OD with no field defects; the thyroid gland was non-tender and grade II in size; cardiopulmonary, abdominal, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable.

A 5-year-old girl was brought for evaluation of a 10-week history of fever, central abdominal pain, and anorexia. Ten weeks before presentation, she had developed high-grade continuous fever. After two weeks of persistent fever and nontender abdominal lymphadenopathy, she was started on empiric three-drug antituberculous therapy. By week 8 of therapy there was no clinical improvement, and she had lost 2.5 kg.

Her medical history was unremarkable; immunizations, including BCG, were up to date. There was no known exposure to tuberculosis or travel outside her hometown. On examination, she was febrile, icteric, and pale, with hepatomegaly; there was no peripheral lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory studies showed normochromic, normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL), progressive leukocytosis (from 21 to 32 ×10^9/L over 12 weeks), elevated ESR (135 mm/hr), CRP 29 mg/L, and direct hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 4.6 mg/dL, direct 3.7 mg/dL). An episode of Escherichia coli urinary tract infection had been treated.

Imaging studies revealed lymphadenopathy at the lung hila on chest radiograph and enlarged mesenteric (3.9 × 7 cm) and porta hepatis (4 × 5 cm) lymph nodes on abdominal CT. Workup for malaria, typhoid (blood and bone marrow cultures), malignancy (bone marrow smear and trephine), and autoimmune disease (dsDNA, rheumatoid factor, Coombs) was negative. After two months of antituberculous therapy, chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasound showed no change in lymphadenopathy.

A CT-guided mesenteric lymph node biopsy was performed, and tissue was sent for histopathology and AFB culture.

A 53-year-old man with refractory mixed‐cellularity classical Hodgkin lymphoma began nivolumab at 3 mg/m2 every two weeks after progression on multiple lines of therapy. The medication was well tolerated until after the sixth infusion, when he noted new skin lesions.

On examination, there were raised, non‐itchy, erythematous, scaly papules with a silver-white coating and some annular plaques with collarettes of scale of varying sizes on the anterolateral shins, dorsae of the hands, distal forearms, and both tibias. The Köbner phenomenon was not observed.

The clinical differential diagnosis included psoriasis vulgaris, erythema annulare, and tinea circinata. To confirm the diagnosis, a 5 mm punch skin biopsy was obtained from the right tibia.

A 26-year-old woman had an 11-year history of progressive proximal muscle weakness and intermittent dysphagia. In 2009, she presented with lower-limb weakness, elevated serum creatine kinase (6890 U/L), negative inflammatory autoantibodies, and electromyography consistent with myogenic damage; a muscle biopsy then led to a diagnosis of polymyositis based on improvement with prednisone. She received prednisone and methotrexate with relapsing weakness on dose tapering. In 2017, she again had severe proximal weakness, elevated CK and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and a trial of tacrolimus plus prednisone and methotrexate, with relapses upon steroid reduction and improvement when the dose was increased. 

In August 2021, she developed worsening proximal weakness causing difficulty turning over, squatting, climbing stairs, and breathing. On examination, she had stable vital signs, a moon face, humped back, purple striae on the abdomen and thighs, muscle strength graded 3/5 in the legs and 4/5 in the arms, and no other abnormalities. Her parents were consanguineous; there was no family history of muscle disease. Laboratory studies showed WBC 9.86 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 6.84 × 10^9/L, ALT 318 U/L, AST 254 U/L, CK 1772 U/L, and LDH 2727 U/L. Tests for fungal infection, tuberculosis (T-SPOT), respiratory pathogens, and Epstein–Barr virus were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed fatty liver. Muscle MRI revealed abnormal signals in the back, buttocks, and lower extremities. EMG of the legs demonstrated shortened motor-unit potential duration, decreased amplitude, and increased polyphasic potentials. Chest CT suggested interstitial changes in the lower lobes. 

A repeat muscle biopsy showed multiple vacuoles with aggregates of lipid droplets and numerous atypical broken red fibers, findings suggestive of a metabolic myopathy. Genetic testing was planned.

A 54‐year‐old man presented with 2½ hours of acute chest pain. An ECG showed sinus tachycardia, first‐degree AV block, narrow QRS complexes, and marked ST‐segment elevations in leads V3–V6 and I. Blood tests revealed haemoglobin 6.4 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 68 fl, mean corpuscular haemoglobin 20 pg, platelet count 530×10^9/L, and C‐reactive protein 93 mg/L. On arrival in the emergency department, he was pale, febrile (39.4°C), tachycardic (103 bpm), blood pressure 120/60 mmHg, respiratory rate normal, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated mildly reduced left ventricular function with apical akinesia, anteroseptal hypokinesia, and a mean transaortic gradient of 20 mmHg. Point‐of‐care testing showed an international normalized ratio >8. His history was notable for mechanical aortic valve replacement 3 years earlier (for severe aortic stenosis) with normal coronaries on preoperative angiography, an episode of alcohol‐induced hepatitis with melena 14 months ago (gastroscopy showed type C gastritis), and risk factors including diabetes and dyslipidaemia.

A 45-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease secondary to focal segmental glomerulosclerosis underwent preemptive kidney transplantation from his mother 5 years ago. He was maintained on tacrolimus (4.0 mg daily; trough level < 5 ng/mL), methylprednisolone (2 mg daily), and mycophenolate mofetil (750 mg daily). Two and a half years after transplantation, he developed more than 10 bowel movements per day with visible blood. 

On examination, his vital signs were within normal limits. Abdominal examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 4.9 × 10^3/µL, C-reactive protein level of 0.1 mg/dL (reference < 0.3 mg/dL), hemoglobin 12.0 g/dL, platelets 260 × 10^3/µL, and serum creatinine 1.36 mg/dL (baseline). Urinalysis was normal. 

Stool cultures were negative for Shigella, Escherichia coli, and Campylobacter. Tests for Clostridium difficile toxin were negative. Cytomegalovirus infection was excluded by negative antigenemia assay and absence of inclusion bodies on colonic biopsy. 

Colonoscopy demonstrated edematous mucosa, erythema, and patchy pigmentation throughout the colon. Histologic examination of colonic biopsy specimens revealed severe inflammation with decreased goblet cells, crypt abscesses, diffuse stromal lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, and irregular glandular architecture.

A 38-year-old previously healthy Caucasian man presented with a three-week history of dark urine, two weeks of malaise and weakness, and a ten-day history of high-grade fevers to 39°C and a nonproductive cough. He denied weight loss, sick contacts, recent animal exposures, tobacco use, or illicit drugs. He was a social drinker, worked as a driver, and had no significant past medical history.

On examination, temperature was 38°C, pulse 110 bpm, blood pressure normal. Cardiac and lung examinations were unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed hepatomegaly and splenomegaly extending 3 cm below the left costal margin. There was no lymphadenopathy, tonsillar enlargement, or meningismus; mild lower-limb edema was present.

Laboratory tests on admission showed WBC count 13 660/μL (63.8% lymphocytes) with activated lymphocytes on smear; ALT 119 U/L, AST 67 U/L; γGT, ALP, and LDH were elevated. An abdominal ultrasound showed hepatosplenomegaly with a suggestion of splenic infarction. CT angiography confirmed a low-density area in the outer left spleen consistent with an infarct and no arterial or venous occlusion.

Blood and urine cultures were sterile, and transesophageal echocardiography showed no vegetations. Serologic testing for EBV, hepatitis B and C, and HIV was negative. CMV IgM and CMV PP65 antigenemia assays were positive. A thrombophilia screen revealed PT 15.5 s (INR 1.25), aPTT 43.6 s, D-dimer 5.20 μg/mL; homocysteine was normal; antiphospholipid antibodies and anticardiolipin antibodies were negative; antithrombin III 88%, protein C 74%, protein S 52%; Factor V Leiden and prothrombin G20210A mutations were not detected.

A 51-year-old Caucasian man was admitted after home nursing services noted sudden onset dysarthria and unilateral facial nerve paresis. His history included hypothyroidism, peptic ulcer disease, and prior alcohol-related polyneuropathy. He was brought by air ambulance as a possible thrombolysis candidate. 

On arrival he was fully conscious but perplexed and disoriented to date and time. Examination showed equal, reactive pupils; intact corneal reflexes and visual fields; and dysconjugate midline gaze with bilateral abduction weakness causing diplopia on lateral gaze. There was no nystagmus, facial asymmetry, or tongue deviation. Strength testing revealed generalized weakness without focal paresis. Deep tendon reflexes were 2+ with flexor plantar responses, and sensation was intact bilaterally. 

Blood pressure was 170/110 mmHg. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm with T-wave inversion in inferior and lateral leads. Urgent unenhanced head CT demonstrated bilateral hypodense changes in the thalami. CT perfusion revealed hyperperfusion in these areas, while CT angiography of the posterior circulation was normal. 

Laboratory studies showed glucose 7.9 mmol/L and C-reactive protein 14 mg/L; electrolytes, renal, and liver function tests were normal. Toxicology screening was negative. Lumbar puncture yielded normal CSF (protein 0.45 g/L, 2 WBCs/µL, glucose 5 mmol/L). Chest X-ray and transthoracic echocardiogram showed no abnormalities.

A 29-year-old woman presented with sudden onset of anterior chest pain. She had two prior episodes of left pneumothorax at ages 18 and 23. Her vital signs were: blood pressure 113/82 mmHg, pulse 96 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. She was not menstruating at presentation. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and blood chemistry, were within normal limits. A chest radiograph demonstrated a large left pneumothorax and a small pleural effusion. A chest tube was inserted, and after full lung re-expansion a CT scan revealed multiple pulmonary cysts measuring up to 22 mm in maximum diameter, localized at the base of the left lung.

A 27-year-old Iranian woman was admitted with a 4-week history of productive cough, weakness, anorexia, weight loss, and fever. Five years earlier, she had undergone a living-unrelated renal transplant for chronic pyelonephritis. Six weeks before admission, her immunosuppressive regimen was changed from cyclosporine to sirolimus, and the dose of mycophenolate mofetil was reduced; prednisolone was continued.  
On examination, temperature was 38°C, blood pressure 110/60 mm Hg, pulse 92 beats/min, and respiratory rate 20 breaths/min. Chest auscultation revealed fine crackles in the lower lung fields.  
Laboratory studies showed: WBC 5.1×10^9/L, hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, hematocrit 22.4%, MCV 75 fL, MCH 24 pg, MCHC 32%, platelets 213×10^9/L, BUN 62 mg/dL, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, AST 37 IU/L, ALT 45 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 1106 IU/L, total bilirubin 1 mg/dL; urinalysis was unremarkable.  
A chest radiograph showed fine miliary nodules throughout both lung fields. A chest CT scan confirmed widespread miliary nodules. A tuberculin skin test yielded 6 mm of induration. Sputum and bronchial aspirate were positive for acid-fast bacilli.  
On hospital day 4, she developed acute right lower quadrant abdominal pain with diffuse tenderness and rebound. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a small fluid collection in the right lower quadrant and two ovarian cysts. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed normal pancreas and spleen, colonic wall thickening (4 mm), and free intraperitoneal fluid.  
At laparotomy, there was widespread peritonitis and a perforated, inflamed appendix; a cecostomy and drain were placed.

A 27-year-old incarcerated African-American man with a history of polysubstance abuse was transferred for evaluation of pancytopenia after 5 weeks of fevers and abdominal pain. He had been treated with NSAIDs in prison, developed acute renal failure requiring intermittent hemodialysis, but continued to have fevers. Two weeks before transfer, he noted asymmetric polyarthralgias with suprapatellar tenderness and tightness bilaterally, and an identical 2-day history of tightness and tenderness in the right lateral upper extremity. 

On examination, there were mildly hyperpigmented, tender, indurated dermal plaques over both suprapatellar regions and the right lateral upper arm. Review of systems was negative for weight loss, cough, dysphagia, heartburn, and cold‐induced distal extremity pain or numbness.

Laboratory studies on admission showed:  
• White blood cell count 4.66 K/µL, hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL, hematocrit 24.2%, platelets 138 K/µL.  
• ESR 37 mm/h, CRP 2.78 mg/dL.  
• Blood CMV allele-specific quantitative PCR positive on two separate tests; CMV IgM nonreactive, CMV IgG reactive.  
• Negative serologic testing for HIV, hepatitis B and C, syphilis, EBV, HTLV, tick-borne and parasitic infections.  
• Negative ANA, anti-Smith, anti–double-stranded DNA, anticentromere, anti–SCL-70, anti-CCP, and ANCA; normal immunoglobulins and C3/C4.  
• PCR for BCR-ABL and JAK2 V617F negative.  
• Mildly elevated serum ACE level.  
• Chest radiograph unremarkable; CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated mild mediastinal, axillary, inguinal, and external iliac lymphadenopathy.

A punch biopsy of a right upper arm plaque was performed. Hematoxylin-eosin staining showed sclerosing dermatitis with localized sclerodermoid change and a sparse superficial lymphocytic infiltrate with few melanophages, but no granulomatous inflammation. Immunoperoxidase staining of the specimen for CMV was negative.

A 36-year-old woman, gravida 6 para 6 at 13 weeks of gestation, presented with a 2-week history of a painful, enlarged cervical lymph node on the right side of her neck, accompanied by rigors, difficulty in moving her right arm, fatigue, and anorexia. Her medical history was notable for Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (TSH 9.7 μIU/ml) for the past 6 years, and a cesarean delivery 7 years ago. Family history included a father with colon cancer and a mother with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. 

On examination, multiple enlarged posterior cervical lymph nodes were palpated lateral to the right sternocleidomastoid muscle. A complete blood count and chemistry panel were within normal limits. A tuberculin skin test was negative. Serologic testing revealed an elevated anti-toxoplasma IgG titer of 112 IU/ml. 

Ultrasonography of the neck demonstrated several right posterior triangle lymph nodes measuring 10–20 mm with loss of the fatty hilum. Given her pregnancy, computed tomography was deferred. Although active tuberculosis and toxoplasmic lymphadenitis were deemed unlikely, other serious conditions—including malignancies such as Hodgkin’s lymphoma—remained under consideration.

A 12-year-old boy was admitted for precipitous weight loss eight weeks into COVID-19 lockdown. He had no prior eating concerns and denied any desire to lose weight or change body shape, stating that he felt “too thin.” During lockdown, he maintained his usual food intake—estimated at 1300–1500 kcal/day—but began an intense, self-initiated exercise regimen: daily runs of 10–11 km, brother-led cycling 10–20 km, and 1–2 h on the family trampoline, for an estimated expenditure of 2600 kcal/day (reference 1800–2200 kcal/day for his age). Pre-morbidly he played competitive soccer and had eaten a bland, consistent diet without issues.

Before admission his weight fell from 33.1 kg (BMI 15.6, 15th percentile) to 27.5 kg (BMI 12.9, 0.03rd percentile), representing 70% of ideal body weight. He reported no change in appetite or food variety. Developmentally and socially he was popular, academically able, with no history of anxiety, depression, obsessive traits, autism spectrum disorder, or other psychiatric contact. Family history was notable only for parental dieting behavior and a paternal family history of bipolar disorder.

On mental status examination he was cachectic, with poor eye contact and low-volume speech. He endorsed feeling “sad” and “bored” without anxiety or self-harm ideation. He denied fear of fatness but acknowledged becoming “obsessed” with exercise for mood boosting. Physical exam showed hypothermia (35.8°C), nocturnal bradycardia (30s), orthostatic tachycardia (ΔHR ≈22 bpm), and variable hypotension. ECG revealed sinus bradycardia with normal QTc.

Laboratory results revealed mild pancytopenia (WCC 2.8 ×10^9/L, platelets 140 ×10^9/L, Hb 107 g/L), electrolyte disturbances (Na 130 mmol/L, K 2.9 mmol/L, phosphate 0.61 mmol/L), elevated liver enzymes (AST 42 U/L, ALT 53 U/L, LDH 788 U/L), and normal thyroid and parathyroid function.

Psychometric assessment showed no behavioral concerns on the CBCL, a Rosenberg self-esteem score of 40/40 (no low self-esteem), an EDE-Q global score of 0.39 (minimal eating-disorder pathology), and an Exercise Addiction Inventory score of 29/30, exceeding the clinical threshold of 24.

A 19-year-old previously healthy Caucasian man was brought to the ED after being unresponsive for 5 hours. The night before, he had injected 3×2.5 mL of liquid methadone intravenously (his first IV use); he was amnestic for the event, but witnesses reported unconsciousness, urinary incontinence, and ocular deviation. On awakening, he noted partial bilateral hearing loss, gait impairment, and numbness of both inner thighs. He and friends admitted to prior intermittent oral methadone and cannabis use but denied other drugs in the preceding days.

On exam, the patient was intermittently somnolent with psychomotor slowing, slowed speech, and concentration deficits. He had mild paraparesis of the lower limbs, left patellar clonus, and bilateral hypoesthesia of the inner thighs. Vital signs: HR 76 beats/min, BP 121/73 mmHg, O2 sat 97% on room air, T 36.8 °C. ECG showed nonspecific ST changes in V2–V3. FAST ultrasound was normal.

Laboratory tests revealed CRP 5.2 mg/dL (ref <0.5), AST 400 U/L (ref <30), ALT 118 U/L (ref <40), CK 7104 U/L (ref <174), LDH 563 U/L (ref 117–217), normal electrolytes. Urine screen was positive for methadone (2.55 mg/L) and THC-COOH (29 μg/L), negative for other opioids and common drugs of abuse.

Brain MRI on day 1 demonstrated bilateral diffusion-restricted and FLAIR-hyperintense lesions in the basal ganglia, posterior limbs of the internal capsules, and cerebellar hemispheres. TOF angiography was normal. Initial lumbar puncture showed blood–brain barrier disruption but normal protein (542 mg/L), 4 lymphocytes/μL, and no intrathecal antibody synthesis. EEG revealed intermittent slowing without epileptiform activity.

A 41‐year‐old nonsmoking woman was referred for presumed asthma. She reported sudden episodes of breathlessness, wheezing, and a choking sensation triggered by moderate exercise or psychological stress. Each episode lasted about 5 minutes and had increased in frequency over the past 3 years despite treatment with inhaled formoterol/budesonide 320/9 μg twice daily and as needed rescue therapy. Her history included obesity, snoring (with prior polysomnography excluding OSAS), and a remote hemithyroidectomy for a colloid nodule. There was no rhinitis, atopy, or family history of asthma. She had multiple pets but noted no pattern of symptom provocation. 
Physical examination was unremarkable. Chest radiograph, lung volumes, diffusion capacity, arterial blood gas analysis, and serum IgE were all normal. Skin testing to common allergens was negative. A bronchoprovocation test with methacholine was negative (PC20 > 8 mg/mL). Cardiopulmonary exercise testing showed mild exercise limitation attributable to obesity and deconditioning; at the end of the test she developed sudden dyspnea with audible stridor. Spirometry obtained during symptoms demonstrated a flattened inspiratory loop on the flow‐volume curve, suggestive of variable extrathoracic obstruction.

A female office clerk with a body mass index of 31 kg/m2 ate 2–3 bites of cedar-plank salmon at a business dinner and immediately noted a peppery burning sensation in her mouth, facial flushing, choking sensation, chest tightness, dizziness, and palpitations. She had previously consumed salmon without adverse effects. She self-administered 50 mg oral diphenhydramine and, in the emergency department, received intravenous corticosteroids followed by a tapering course of oral prednisone; she was diagnosed with an unspecified allergic reaction. No public-health authorities were notified, and no toxicologic or microbiologic analysis of the fish was performed.

On day 3 after exposure, she was hospitalized and treated with intravenous corticosteroids, ranitidine, and cetirizine. Laboratory studies showed moderate microcytic hypochromic anemia (hematocrit, 31.8%). On day 4, she returned to the emergency department with persistent symptoms. Over the next 4 months, she experienced extreme fatigue and consulted multiple specialists. An otorhinolaryngologist diagnosed new-onset asthma and prescribed beclomethasone and albuterol inhalers along with environmental allergen avoidance measures. From day 28 onward, a pulmonologist recorded normal clinical examinations and spirometry but continued bronchodilator therapy. A psychotherapist diagnosed severe anxiety disorder, documenting excessive wariness, obsessions, compulsions, sleeplessness, and anticipatory fear of fatal reactions, and provided weekly psychotherapy.

On day 191, a neurologist evaluated her dizziness and paresthesiae with magnetic resonance imaging of the brain (showing a single hyperintense periventricular lesion of uncertain significance), electroencephalography (intermittent nonspecific focal transient theta waves over the temporal lobes), normal electromyography and nerve conduction studies, and normal auditory evoked responses; gabapentin was prescribed. A repeat brain MRI 5 months later was unchanged, yet further neurodiagnostic testing was recommended. She then reported dizziness and chest tightness triggered by exposures to hair dyes, foods (potato chips), iron supplements, toiletries, and cleaning chemicals; monosodium glutamate sensitivity was suspected. The neurologist recommended hair analysis for neurotoxins and suspected immune dysfunction.

An immunologist found negative extractable nuclear autoantibodies, a negative antinuclear antibody test, normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate, normal thyroid-stimulating hormone, and normal immunoglobulins A, E, G, and M. On days 133 and 193, a defense-hired allergist diagnosed hypertension, anxiety, and nonoccupational allergies; reported normal plasma norepinephrine, dopamine, and vanillylmandelic acid levels; normal urine 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid; normal serum tryptase; normal immunoglobulin E; a normal comprehensive metabolic panel; blood mercury below 3 µg/L; and sensitization only to dust mites on serum testing for 49 allergens including salmon. A toxicology evaluation showed normal blood levels of lead, arsenic, mercury, and cadmium. Repeat testing for 21 respiratory and 10 food allergens was mildly positive for dust mites only. Helicobacter pylori antibody was negative.

A 39-year-old woman with pigment dispersion–related glaucoma underwent sequential trabeculectomies: the right eye with intraoperative mitomycin-C and, one week later, the left eye with insertion of an Ologen™ porcine collagen implant. Postoperatively, intraocular pressures were 8 mmHg (OD) and 6 mmHg (OS), and visual acuities were 6/18 and 6/12, respectively. Three weeks after the left-eye surgery, she awoke with sudden, severe agonizing left-eye pain that prevented sleep, accompanied by photophobia and difficulty opening the eye. Her visual acuity fell to 6/36 OS, and intraocular pressure was 10 mmHg. Examination revealed marked injection and vascularization of the sclera, episclera, and conjunctiva at the trabeculectomy site; the Ologen implant had disappeared, and an 11 × 6 mm area of sclera was partially dissolved with exposed choroid. The pupil was peaked, and manifest refraction changed from –3.5 DC to –10 DC. There was no conjunctival discharge; the anterior chamber and cornea were clear; and the fundus examination was unremarkable. Conjunctival swabs and Tenon’s tissue were obtained for Gram staining, cultures, and histopathology. Serologic tests for rheumatoid factor, ANCA, ANA, and antiphospholipid antibodies were ordered.

A 10-year-old boy presented with a slowly progressive deformity of the right ankle. He had sustained a foot injury at age 5, which caused medial ankle pain and limping, treated by unknown orthopedic measures. Over time, a varus deformity and medial swelling of the right ankle developed. On examination, there was swelling on the medial aspect of the right ankle with marked varus alignment of the foot, limited ankle motion, and an antalgic gait. Palpation elicited severe pain over the medial tibio-talar joint. The remainder of the musculoskeletal and systemic examination was unremarkable.

A standard radiograph of the right ankle demonstrated an exophytic, intra-articularly oriented bony mass arising from the anteromedial aspects of the distal tibial epiphysis and the talus.

A CT scan with multiplanar reconstructions revealed multiple epiphyseal osteocartilaginous outgrowths—some pedunculated, others broad-based—arising from the medial portions of the talar epiphysis, navicular, medial cuneiform, and inferomedial tibial epiphysis, with extension into and adjacent to the talocalcaneal and talonavicular joints.

A 25-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 1-day history of right lower quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting but no fever or diarrhea. Vital signs were within normal limits. His medical and family histories were unremarkable; he was a smoker and took no medications. On examination, there was mild abdominal distention, right lower quadrant rebound tenderness with guarding, and hypoactive bowel sounds. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 115.5 mg/L and a white-cell count of 15.6 × 10^3/μL with neutrophilia. His Alvarado score was 7. Initial management included intravenous fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and bowel rest. Abdominal ultrasound was negative for appendicitis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated an inflamed subhepatic retrocaecal appendix containing an appendicolith, with surrounding fat stranding and a small pelvic fluid collection.

A 58-year-old man with a history of stage 4 lung adenocarcinoma, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypertension was brought to the emergency department by his oncologist one day after starting chemotherapy because of generalized weakness and dyspnea. He had completed five weeks of radiation therapy and had a newly placed chemotherapy port.

Review of systems revealed weakness, shortness of breath, decreased appetite, polydipsia, polyuria, and chronic leg swelling. He denied fever, chest pain, cough, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, dysuria, weight loss, and sick contacts.

Home medications included empagliflozin 10 mg once daily, insulin aspart, insulin lispro, sitagliptin, dexamethasone, and supportive therapies.

On examination, temperature was 97.3 °F, blood pressure 76/50 mmHg, heart rate 103 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. He appeared lethargic yet was oriented. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with an S3 gallop. Lungs were clear. The abdomen was soft and non-tender. Skin was warm and dry. He had 3–4+ pitting edema to mid-calf bilaterally. The chemotherapy port site showed no signs of infection.

Laboratory studies revealed:
• CBC: pancytopenia  
• Serum chemistry: anion gap 20; bicarbonate 13 mEq/L; glucose 113 mg/dL  
• Serum acetone: large  
• Urinalysis: marked glucosuria and ketonuria  
• Lactate 1.4 mmol/L; procalcitonin 0.05 ng/mL; proBNP 496 pg/mL  
• Influenza A/B swabs negative  
• Nasal swab positive for MRSA; blood, port, and sputum cultures pending  

An electrocardiogram showed an incomplete right bundle branch block. Chest radiograph demonstrated a known cavitary lesion in the left lung, a nodularity in the right lung consistent with his malignancy, and a left-sided vascular access device in good position.

A 61-year-old woman from a rural area presented with a 2-year history of progressive movement and speech difficulty. Two years before presentation, she developed a slow walking pace. Over the following year, she noted a resting tremor in her right hand that impaired her ability to hold utensils, frequent dropping of objects, and mild balance difficulty. Six months before presentation, she developed progressively slow, slurred speech and solid-food dysphagia with choking episodes. She denied mood or behavioral changes, memory loss, toxin exposure, head trauma, seizures, weight loss, loss of consciousness, or stroke. Her father had early-80s–onset dementia. Her medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin.

On examination, she had a right-hand resting tremor, bradykinesia in all limbs, and difficulty with fine motor tasks in the right hand. Speech was slow, dysarthric, and hard to comprehend. There was no spasticity, motor weakness, sensory abnormality, or cognitive impairment; she was alert and oriented. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL, white cells 9600/cm3, platelets 236,000/cm3, fasting glucose 126 mg/dL, HbA1c 7.5%, calcium 9.9 mg/dL, phosphorus 3.8 mg/dL, parathyroid hormone 36 pg/mL, and otherwise unremarkable routine studies. Noncontrast CT of the head revealed symmetric calcifications in bilateral subcortical white matter, caudate and lentiform nuclei, thalami, and dentate nuclei without mass effect, edema, or atrophy.

A 42-year-old woman with a history of chronic migraine treated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and ergotamine–caffeine presented with a sudden, diffuse “thunderclap” headache that began immediately after swimming. The headache was described as explosive and unusual and resolved spontaneously over 8 hours. On initial examination, her vital signs, general physical examination, and neurologic examination were all normal. 

A noncontrast head CT scan was normal. Lumbar puncture revealed oxyhemoglobin and 290 red blood cells per mm3, and a diagnosis of subarachnoid hemorrhage was made. A cerebral angiogram was scheduled for the next day.

On hospital day 1, she developed severe headache with acute hypertension, followed by aphasia and right hemiplegia. Her level of consciousness declined rapidly, necessitating endotracheal intubation. An emergent CT scan showed a left rolandic intracerebral hemorrhage.  
 
Urgent cerebral angiography revealed diffuse segmental narrowing of the cerebral arteries without evidence of an aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation. Intravenous nimodipine therapy was initiated.

A 65-year-old woman with metastatic melanoma presented three weeks after her second pembrolizumab infusion and second dose of the BBIBP-CorV COVID-19 vaccine with a two-day history of bilateral diplopia and ptosis that worsened as the day progressed. She had received her first pembrolizumab infusion and first BBIBP-CorV dose without incident. On examination, there was bilateral ocular weakness without limb weakness. Brain MRI showed no evidence of metastases, and repeat neck MRI demonstrated significant reduction in the size of her known cervical soft-tissue mass. Laboratory testing revealed a creatine kinase (CK) level of 4704 U/L (normal 26–192 U/L) and an aldolase level of 98.6 U/L (normal 1.0–7.5 U/L). Transthoracic echocardiography showed an ejection fraction of 57 %, and the CK-MB to total CK ratio was 4 %. Electromyography demonstrated notable decremental changes in the compound muscle action potentials during repetitive nerve stimulation at low rates of 2–4 Hz.

A 40-year-old woman with a remote history of treated pulmonary tuberculosis and a 20-year history of hemoptysis underwent video-assisted thoracoscopic right upper lobectomy for bronchiectatic and fibrocavitatory disease identified on contrast-enhanced CT of the chest. She remained clinically stable on postoperative day 1. On postoperative day 2 she developed unexplained fever, tachypnea, and leukocytosis. Serial chest radiographs demonstrated progressively increasing opacity in the right upper zone.

A 39-year-old Tunisian woman, at 16 weeks of a twin pregnancy, presented with a 1-month history of left breast pain and induration. Vital signs were within normal limits. A breast ultrasound demonstrated a 43-mm heterogeneous mass with irregular, ill-defined margins in the left outer quadrants. Ultrasound-guided core biopsy showed marked inflammatory infiltrate predominantly of neutrophils, with some lymphocytes and plasma cells centered in the lobules, with destruction of acini and ducts. 

Two weeks later, she returned with worsening breast pain and local inflammatory signs. Repeat ultrasound revealed multiple confluent hypoechoic loculations with ill-defined contours, some communicating with the skin, consistent with mastitis and multiple abscesses. Concurrently, she noted tender, erythematous nodules with erythema and fluctuance on the elbows and anterior tibial surfaces; a clinical diagnosis of erythema nodosum was made. She declined chest radiography and was discharged on amoxicillin–clavulanic acid for 2 weeks.

On follow-up in the breast clinic, local inflammation had progressed with abscess formation. Surgical drainage was performed, and she received piperacillin–tazobactam for 10 days. During hospitalization, the skin lesions improved. A repeat ultrasound-guided biopsy showed pronounced macrophagic infiltrate with scattered multinucleated giant cells forming epithelioid granulomas predominantly within lobules, along with numerous neutrophils. Periodic acid–Schiff and Ziehl–Neelsen stains were negative for pathogens. Abscess cultures grew multisensitive Staphylococcus epidermidis. An extensive infectious and autoimmune workup, including serologies, blood cultures, and interferon-γ release assay, returned negative.

A 45-year-old man with a history of gout (on allopurinol 300 mg daily and colchicine 0.6 mg daily), morbid obesity, and osteoarthritis was admitted for unexplained new-onset nonischemic heart failure (ejection fraction 10–15%), cardiogenic shock, and sustained ventricular tachycardia. Dermatology was consulted for a single multinodular, asymptomatic plaque on the upper left arm present for 1 year. Examination revealed lesions covering approximately 25% of the body surface area, with multiple morphologies:
- Numerous 5–12 cm skin-colored to light brown indurated dermal/subcutaneous plaques on the arms, chest, back, and legs, many palpable but not visible.
- A slightly hyperpigmented plaque on the upper left back with multiple 5–10 mm punched-out depressions, giving a moth-eaten appearance.
- Scattered mildly erythematous plaques studded with 2–4 mm firm, rough-surfaced aggregates of whitish gritty material.
- A 2 cm superficial ulceration on the lower left leg extruding a whitish gritty substance.
Additional findings included ventral pterygia of most fingernails and bilateral lacrimal gland enlargement. There were no joint tophi or deformities, and the patient denied gout flares since the skin lesions appeared. Laboratory studies showed a serum uric acid level of 12.6 mg/dL. Hand radiographs demonstrated periarticular erosions consistent with gout arthropathy; foot radiographs were suggestive of gout. Punch biopsies were obtained from representative lesions.

A 53-year-old man presented with a 5-year history of gradually progressive protrusion of his left eye. He recalled blunt trauma to his left forehead and temporal region years earlier. He had no history of nasal or sinus surgery. On examination, left exophthalmos measured 4 mm; visual acuity was 1.0 in both eyes; intraocular pressures were 20 mm Hg bilaterally; and funduscopic and visual fields were unremarkable. Orbital CT showed a 2.2 × 2.8 cm mass in the superior temporal quadrant at the frontozygomatic suture without contrast enhancement. T2-weighted MRI demonstrated a central area of high signal intensity with heterogeneous peripheral signal and no dural invasion. T1-weighted postcontrast MRI showed homogeneous enhancement of the lesion.  
What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 40-year-old woman with polycystic ovarian disease and a history of resected endometrial polyps presented with 2 days of right lower quadrant and right lower back pain. She was afebrile, had no abdominal guarding, and Blumberg’s sign was negative. Laboratory tests were within normal limits, and transvaginal ultrasonography ruled out gynecologic pathology. An abdominal ultrasound showed a homogenous hypoechoic, thick-walled tubular lesion with regular borders in the pericecal area and no internal vascularity. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a non-specific focal mass in the distal third of the appendix without any evidence of inflammation. Endoscopic evaluation confirmed a 3 cm endoluminal protruding appendiceal mass with a hard consistency and smooth overlying mucosa. Biopsies obtained at endoscopy were inconclusive.

A 26-year-old female farmer from a rural region presented with a one-year history of a gradually enlarging anterior neck mass associated with dysphagia and shortness of breath that worsened as the mass grew.  
On examination, there was a 5 × 4 cm midline anterior cervical mass, slightly inclined to the right, extending to the base of the neck; it was not mobile with deglutition.  
Neck ultrasound showed a large septated cystic lesion with a well-defined wall in the midline, extending into the retrosternal region (approximately 5 cm), with suspected relation to the right thyroid lobe. Two additional small hypoechoic lesions were noted in the thyroid gland (8 mm in the right lobe and 10 mm in the left lobe). A diagnosis of multinodular goiter with a large thyroid cyst was made.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a large, well-walled cystic lesion measuring 7.5 × 5 × 5 cm, compressing the trachea and esophagus and extending into the mediastinum to the level of the aortic arch; the remainder of the chest and abdomen appeared normal.  
Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, thyroid function tests, renal function tests, and blood glucose, were all within normal limits.  
Differential diagnoses included multinodular goiter, malignant thyroid neoplasm, large thyroglossal duct cyst, branchial cleft cyst, cold abscess, and hydatid cyst disease.

A 55-year-old woman presented with a one-day history of colicky epigastric and right-upper-quadrant pain accompanied by vomiting. She had known cholelithiasis and noted that the pain resembled her previous biliary colic; she had no prior episodes of pancreatitis. She was a nonsmoker, consumed nine units of alcohol per week, and had no family history of bleeding or clotting disorders. Her only regular medication was combined hormone replacement therapy.

On admission, vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination revealed point tenderness in the right upper quadrant without organomegaly or peritonism. Laboratory studies showed: alanine aminotransferase 275 U/L, bilirubin 54 μmol/L, amylase 1900 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 80 U/L, C-reactive protein <6 mg/L, and white-cell count 18 × 10^9/L.

An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated cholelithiasis without evidence of common bile duct obstruction. She was treated for presumed gallstone pancreatitis with intravenous fluids and analgesia.

Three days after admission, she developed fever to 38.2 °C with elevated inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein 255 mg/L; white-cell count 19 × 10^9/L). Empiric intravenous amoxicillin, metronidazole, and gentamicin were initiated for possible biliary sepsis or necrotizing pancreatitis. Liver tests improved (bilirubin 20 μmol/L; ALT 81 U/L; amylase 143 U/L).

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed a thin-walled gallbladder, fat stranding adjacent to the pancreatic tail, and a 3 cm reduced-attenuation structure within the falciform ligament thought to represent acute thrombosis of the umbilical vein; there was no pancreatic or peripancreatic collection. Subsequent MRCP confirmed these findings and showed no biliary duct stones. Intravenous antibiotics were discontinued as no source of sepsis was identified on imaging.

A 70-year-old man with a 20-year history of type 2 diabetes, poorly compliant with medications and glucose monitoring, presented with 2 days of severe involuntary movements of the right lower extremity. He had no ketonuria. Non-fasting plasma glucose was 9.08 mmol/L, serum osmolality 307.10 mOsm/L, and urinary ketones were negative. Noncontrast CT of the brain showed increased attenuation in the left putamen and caudate nucleus. MRI revealed heterogeneous hyperintensity in the same regions on T1-weighted images, an irregular hyperintense lesion with mild mass effect on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences, and a ring-like enhancement on contrast-enhanced T1-weighted imaging. The lesion was iso- to hypo-intense on diffusion-weighted imaging. Single-voxel short-echo time 1H magnetic resonance spectroscopy demonstrated markedly increased lactate and lipid peaks, a slightly elevated choline peak, a slightly decreased N-acetylaspartate peak, and stable creatine, with a Cho/NAA ratio of 0.675, Cho/Cr of 1.04, NAA/Cr of 1.54, and (Lac + Lip)/Cr of 1.34.

A 41-year-old man presented with severe bilateral leg pain and a 2-week history of flu-like illness with fever up to 39 °C treated as an outpatient. On initial evaluation at an outside hospital, he was tachycardic (102 bpm), hypotensive (65/50 mmHg), and appeared severely dehydrated. He received 15 L of intravenous fluids on hospital day 1. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 22.3 g/dL, hematocrit 60.4%, serum total protein 2.3 g/dL, creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 37 mg/dL, white blood cell count 15,900/µL, C-reactive protein 1.2 mg/dL, and procalcitonin <0.5 µg/L. Electrolytes and liver-function tests were within normal limits. Arterial blood gas revealed pH 7.06 and bicarbonate 11.9 mmol/L. Creatine kinase was 124 U/L on day 1, rising to >7000 U/L on day 2. Chest radiography showed a small right pleural effusion; echocardiography and abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable. Lower-extremity duplex ultrasound showed no thrombosis. Compartment pressures measured 100 mmHg in the lower legs and 44 mmHg in the thighs, and bilateral decompressing fasciotomies were performed. 

He was transferred to our ICU on hospital day 2, intubated and mechanically ventilated (RR 20/min, PEEP 8 cmH₂O, FiO₂ 0.65). He remained hypotensive (95/50 mmHg) with tachycardia (120 bpm) on norepinephrine 0.13 µg/kg/min.
