Admission labs showed hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, hematocrit 37.4%, WBC 19,620/µL, platelets 174,000/µL, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, BUN 21 mg/dL, CRP 2.1 mg/dL, procalcitonin 0.8 µg/L, lactate 4.6 mmol/L, pH 7.37, and CK 7,624 U/L. Transpulmonary thermodilution monitoring revealed a global end-diastolic volume index of 459 mL/m² (normal 680–800) and stroke volume variation of 19% (normal <10%), indicating intravascular hypovolemia. Aggressive fluid resuscitation and vasopressor support were continued. Urine output improved without need for dialysis, and renal function recovered.

Extensive infectious workup (blood, urine, pleural fluid, wound, and catheter cultures) was sterile. Serologies and PCR for HIV, Leptospira, and influenza A/B were negative. Antinuclear and anti-DNA antibodies were negative. Muscle biopsy revealed normal fibers without necrosis, myolysis, myositis, or fasciitis; electromyography and mitochondrial enzyme assays were normal. During resuscitation, extra-vascular lung water index rose, and pulmonary edema developed on day 4, prompting diuresis. The patient was extubated on hospital day 11 and transferred to the ward on day 14.

A 65‐year‐old man with stage IV gastro‐oesophageal junction adenocarcinoma diagnosed 8 months ago presented after a 2‐minute witnessed syncope at home. He had received FOLFOX chemotherapy since diagnosis and nivolumab 240 mg every 2 weeks for the past 7½ months (12 doses, no prior immune‐related adverse effects). Over the preceding 4 weeks, he noted progressive dyspnoea with minimal exertion. 

On admission, vital signs were: heart rate 85 beats/min, blood pressure 128/70 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 90% on 5 L/min supplemental oxygen. Examination revealed clear lungs and bilateral pitting oedema of the legs. 

An electrocardiogram showed a right ventricular strain pattern with new right bundle branch block. High‐sensitivity troponin I was negative. B‐type natriuretic peptide was elevated at 115 pmol/L (normal < 9.5 pmol/L). A CT pulmonary angiogram showed no pulmonary embolism or lung disease. After diuresis, his oxygen requirement improved to 2 L/min. 

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 29%, a severely enlarged right ventricle (base diameter 6.5 cm, mid‐cavity 4.6 cm) with reduced systolic function (fractional area change < 25%), a D‐shaped septum, moderate tricuspid regurgitation, and an estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 74 mmHg.

A 24-year-old woman (G1P1001) with a history of inflammatory colonic Crohn’s disease and complex perianal involvement presented with one week of vaginal pain and swelling. Three years earlier, she underwent proctocolectomy for medically refractory disease, complicated by partial perineal wound dehiscence requiring multiple debridements and a perineal flap. She has not been on maintenance therapy since surgery and takes valacyclovir for recurrent genital herpes simplex virus. 

On pelvic examination, she had diffuse labial edema and erythema with friable tissue and purulent discharge coating the labia majora; no vesicular lesions were seen. A wet mount was positive for bacterial vaginosis, and tests for gonorrhea, chlamydia, and syphilis were negative. Pelvic CT showed cellulitis without abscess, and she was started on piperacillin–tazobactam, linezolid, and valacyclovir. After 4 days without symptomatic improvement, pelvic MRI demonstrated a 1 cm labial abscess that was not identified during examination under anesthesia.

A 38-year-old man with no prior ocular history presented after an air-hammer injury to his left eye, two days earlier, causing a ruptured globe. Initial exam showed visual acuity of count fingers OS, intraocular pressure of 14 mmHg OU, a corneal laceration, a white traumatic cataract, and an intraocular metallic foreign body confirmed by CT. He underwent corneal laceration repair, pars plana lensectomy, pars plana vitrectomy, and foreign body removal, resulting in aphakia and an uneventful postoperative course. Three months later, a Gore-Tex sutured scleral-fixated MX60E IOL was placed without complication; there was no pre-, intra-, or postoperative inflammation, and his vision was 20/20. Five months after IOL placement, he remained asymptomatic with BCVA 20/20, but was noted to have temporal conjunctival erosion over the Gore-Tex suture, with exposed black pigmentation but no surrounding inflammation. It was attributed to an overly mobile suture. He was started on topical antibiotics and underwent a scleral groove and corneal graft to cover the suture. At one month, conjunctiva was intact except for a pinpoint black focus on the suture; cultures yielded no bacterial or fungal growth. Five months after graft placement, the suture again eroded with a pinpoint of black material, still without inflammation or symptoms. The suture was resecured and cultured intraoperatively, revealing dark skip-lesions on its surface.

A 50-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a two-month history of right upper quadrant abdominal distension and discomfort and two weeks of worsening dyspnea. She had no history of smoking, alcohol use, trauma, recent travel, or exposure to asbestos, animals, or the farming community. She denied fever, night sweats, weight loss, arthralgias, arthritis, rashes, cardiac, neurologic, or other gastrointestinal symptoms. There was no family history of polycystic kidney or liver disease.
On examination, chest radiography showed a large right pleural effusion. Abdominal examination revealed gross hepatomegaly; there was no lymphadenopathy or signs of cardiac failure or chronic liver disease.
Laboratory studies showed normal renal function (eGFR >60 mL/min), an alkaline phosphatase of 145 U/L, albumin 29 g/L, total bilirubin 12 μmol/L, alanine transaminase 9 U/L, total protein 57 g/L, globulin 28 g/L, and a platelet count of 474 × 10^9/L; hemoglobin, white-cell count, and coagulation studies were normal. A serum hydatid ELISA was negative.
Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis confirmed a large right pleural effusion with mediastinal shift to the left, elevation of the right hemidiaphragm, and no intra-thoracic cystic lesions, fistulae, or pulmonary embolism. The liver was polycystic, with one dominant cyst measuring 20 × 21 × 18 cm displacing the right hemidiaphragm and adjacent abdominal structures.
Two thoracenteses yielded exudative fluid (protein 47 and 38 g/L), pH 8.0, glucose 6.1 mmol/L, LDH 321 U/L, and amylase 16 U/L. Microscopy showed no organisms, acid-fast bacilli, ova, cysts, or parasites; all cultures remained sterile; and cytology revealed no malignant cells.

A 32-year-old Japanese woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 28 weeks of gestation, awoke with acute right buttock pain and subsequently developed a fever over 38 °C. She had a 2-year history of rheumatoid arthritis treated with certolizumab pegol (Steinbrocker stage II, no sacroiliac lesions) and was under evaluation for Sjögren’s syndrome. Two weeks prior, she experienced self-limited upper respiratory symptoms. 

On arrival, her temperature was 37.8 °C and heart rate 107 bpm. She denied respiratory or abdominal complaints. Examination revealed sharp tenderness over the right sacroiliac joint. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 17,800/μL (normal < 7800) and a C-reactive protein level of 2.63 mg/dL (normal < 0.3). Obstetric ultrasonography demonstrated a normal placenta without retroplacental collection and an estimated fetal weight of 1245 g. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the sacroiliac joints revealed a high-intensity signal in the right sacroiliac joint on both T2-weighted and STIR sequences, consistent with arthritis. She was diagnosed with right infectious sacroiliitis and admitted; intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g daily) was initiated.

A 51-year-old man presented with new-onset crushing substernal chest pain. He was tachycardic (117/min), hypotensive (89/57 mm Hg), afebrile, and had normal respiratory rate and oxygen saturation on room air. He denied dyspnea and chills.

Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia. Chest CT revealed hydropneumopericardium. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a moderate circumferential pericardial effusion with right atrial systolic collapse and right ventricular diastolic collapse, consistent with tamponade physiology. Urgent pericardiocentesis drained 320 mL of serosanguinous fluid with intermittent air bubbles, and a pericardial drain was placed.

His history was notable for Siewert III gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma diagnosed 4 years earlier, treated with chemoradiation, aborted esophagectomy for liver metastases, further chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and definitive chemoradiation. Eight months earlier he underwent EGD with dilation and esophageal stent placement for dysphagia. Restaging 2 weeks ago showed no active disease.

Given the CT findings, the differential diagnoses included malignant pleural-pericardial effusion, chylopericardium, bronchopericardial or tracheopericardial fistula, and esophagopericardial fistula. EGD and a gastrografin esophagram showed no obvious leak on fluoroscopy but demonstrated tissue invasion into the stent, prompting placement of a second stent within the original. The pericardial drain then had persistent high output of brown, murky fluid with occasional food particles.

Contrast-enhanced CT and repeat endoscopy again showed no evidence of contrast extravasation.

A 27‐year‐old African American man with a 2‐year history of cigarette use and tetrahydrocannabinol vaping presented with two weeks of nonproductive cough, subjective fever, rhinorrhea, chills, myalgia, diarrhea, and vomiting. He had been seen two days earlier for presumed viral upper respiratory infection and discharged. On return, he was tachypneic and tachycardic with leukocytosis and lymphopenia. Chest radiography showed patchy infiltrates in the right upper lobe and bilateral lower lobes. A respiratory pathogen panel was positive for Influenza A, and sputum cultures later grew methicillin‐sensitive Staphylococcus aureus; tests for other pathogens were negative. Admission laboratory values included a white blood cell count of 9.8 k/µL (92.4% neutrophils, 3.8% lymphocytes), platelet count of 97 k/µL, creatinine 2.34 mg/dL, AST 343 U/L, ALT 144 U/L, lactate 9.8 mmol/L, procalcitonin 26.86 ng/mL, and ferritin 5181 ng/mL. Bronchoscopy revealed copious airway secretions, a thick, sloughing, erythematous mucosa, and severely denuded airways throughout the tracheobronchial tree.

A 52-year-old man presented with 1 month of progressive generalized swelling beginning in the legs and later involving the abdomen and face. He reported prolonged fever, malaise, anorexia, fatigue, productive cough, dyspnea on mild exertion, and reddish discoloration of urine, without chest pain, hemoptysis, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, palpitations, flank pain, or change in urine volume. He denied intravenous drug use. His only medical history was hypertension managed with hydrochlorothiazide.

On examination, temperature was 38.3 °C, blood pressure 140/90 mmHg, pulse 104 bpm, respiratory rate 26/min, and oxygen saturation 90% on room air. He appeared ill with conjunctival pallor. Lungs had reduced air entry and crackles at both bases. Cardiovascular exam revealed jugular venous distension, a displaced apical impulse, an early diastolic murmur at the left upper parasternal area, and a holosystolic murmur at the left lower parasternal area without gallops. There was ascites and bilateral pitting edema. No peripheral stigmata of infective endocarditis were present.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 4600/µl, hemoglobin 7 g/dl, platelets 244 000/µl, ESR 93 mm/hr, serum creatinine 2.9 mg/dl, BUN 54 mg/dl, albumin 3.5 g/dl, positive rheumatoid factor, negative ANA, and urinalysis with proteinuria, hematuria, and granular casts. Serologies for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV were negative. Three sets of blood cultures remained negative.

Chest radiography demonstrated cardiomegaly and bilateral pleural effusions. ECG showed sinus tachycardia at 110 bpm. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a 10 × 12 mm mobile vegetation on the pulmonic valve, thickened scalloped pulmonic leaflets with moderate stenosis and regurgitation, right atrial and ventricular enlargement with normal right ventricular function, and preserved left ventricular ejection fraction of 65%. Abdominal ultrasound confirmed ascites.

A 79-year-old woman with hypertension and hypercholesterolemia presented with a 3-hour history of sudden left upper quadrant abdominal pain radiating to her back and left shoulder. She denied any history of trauma but recalled sneezing three times just before pain onset. Emergency medical services found her initially normotensive, then hypotensive (blood pressure 61/38 mmHg) with near syncope; she received intravenous fluids en route. In the emergency department, she was alert, with blood pressure 101/56 mmHg, pulse rate 74 beats/minute, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Physical examination showed a soft abdomen with tenderness in the left upper quadrant without guarding or rigidity. There was no jugular venous distension, heart murmurs, abnormal lung sounds, or focal neurologic deficits; extremities were well perfused. A bedside ultrasound limited by bowel gas showed no obvious abdominal aortic aneurysm, no definite free fluid, and no evidence of pericardial tamponade. Vascular and general surgery were consulted, and a CT angiogram of the abdomen and pelvis was performed. The radiologist reported findings concerning for a splenic laceration and hematoma with hemorrhagic abdominal and pelvic ascites.

A 44-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented to the gynecological emergency department, reporting intermittent pelvic pain, yellowish vaginal discharge, dysuria, fever, and a 5-kg weight loss. She had used an intrauterine device continuously for 10 years without follow-up. On examination, her temperature was 38.5 °C, and there was pelvic tenderness. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 15,300 cells/mm3 (reference range 1700–7000) and a C-reactive protein level of 60 mg/L (reference < 5 mg/L). Pelvic ultrasonography revealed a heterogeneous hypoechoic right tubo-ovarian complex. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a roughly oval, well-defined right tubo-ovarian complex measuring 96 mm in height, with heterogeneous T1 hypointensity, heterogeneous T2 hyperintensity, restricted diffusion, and peripheral enhancement after gadolinium. An intrauterine device was seen in situ and was subsequently removed. Serum tumor markers were negative: angiotensin-converting enzyme 0.8 µg/L (normal < 2.5 µg/L) and CA-125 20 µg/L (normal < 35 µg/L). Vaginal swab and urinalysis were also negative.

A 14-year-old boy was referred from a mission hospital for postoperative wound sepsis after right scrotal exploration and orchidectomy for testicular torsion. He had 24 h of scrotal pain and swelling before surgery. On arrival he was tachypneic, tachycardic (124 bpm), febrile (38.7 °C), and diaphoretic, with pallor of mucous membranes. Blood pressure was 109/68 mmHg, neck veins were flat, and heart sounds were normal. The tips of his fingers and toes appeared cyanosed bilaterally with peripheral oxygen saturations fluctuating between 20% and 30% on room air, despite no severe dyspnea. Ecchymoses were present over the extremities, and he bled easily from puncture sites. The right groin wound appeared necrotic and septic. He had no chronic illnesses or medications and denied smoking.  

Initial laboratory studies showed white blood cells 16 × 10^3/µL with neutrophils 10.8 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 4.8 g/dL, and platelets 26 × 10^3/µL; liver and renal function tests, electrolytes, malaria smear, and hemoglobin electrophoresis were normal. A diagnosis of severe sepsis complicated by DIC and anemia was made, and he received broad-spectrum antibiotics, blood and platelet transfusions, and surgical debridement.  

Despite improvement in systemic parameters and extubation on day 6, cyanosis of fingers and toes progressed to well-demarcated gangrene below the elbows and knees. A contrast angiogram of the aorta and its branches showed patent thoracic and abdominal aorta and no filling defects in major limb arteries.

A 65-year-old man was admitted with high fever and acute aphasia. Laboratory tests showed a C-reactive protein level of 119.8 mg/L. He denied any pain. Physical examination revealed aphasia, complete paraplegia (from a T11 fracture and T8–L2 fusion after spinal cord injury 49 years earlier), and erythema in the right groin. Aside from the known paraplegia and aphasia, the neurologic exam was unremarkable. Cranial CT excluded intracranial pathology. Plain radiographs, abdominal CT, and MRI demonstrated extensive destruction of the L3 and L4 vertebrae with marked instability, along with large abscess formations in the paravertebral tissues, bilateral psoas muscles, and a spinal empyema extending toward the groin.

A 9-month-old girl was referred for evaluation of a midline neck mass. She had a 5-month history of a non-tender, asymptomatic swelling at the level of the thyroid gland. Physical examination revealed a mobile, cystic midline neck mass. MRI of the neck demonstrated a hyperintense lesion in the anterior neck slightly left of midline and a second cystic structure within the floor of the mouth. The anterior neck lesion appeared to be connected to the floor-of-mouth mass, but neither communicated with the foramen cecum. The initial differential diagnosis included dermoid cyst, epidermoid cyst, and rare intestinal foregut cyst. Ultrasonography revealed a midline cystic mass extending into the floor of the mouth with features suggestive of a dermoid cyst. Repeat examination confirmed a small floor-of-mouth cyst without airway compromise. Surgical excision of both lesions was recommended.

A 10-month-old infant was referred for evaluation of asymptomatic red raised lesions present for 1 month during the winter. The infant has a history of congenital pelviureteric junction obstruction with hydronephrosis. Six months earlier, similar lesions on the extremities resolved with topical steroid creams. There is no consanguinity. The mother has autoimmune hypothyroidism on thyroxine; the infant was diagnosed with non-autoimmune hypothyroidism at 2 months and has been on levothyroxine 25 μg daily.

On examination, the patient was afebrile. Dysmorphic facies with a depressed nasal bridge were noted; the thyroid gland was impalpable. Cutaneous findings included multiple skin-colored to erythematous papules coalescing into infiltrated annular plaques over the occipital scalp, neck, ear helices, proximal and distal extremities, elbows, knees, buttocks, and the dorsum of hands and feet, with few lesions on the trunk. There was no scaling. Hair was dry and sparse; nails were normal.

Laboratory tests showed negative hepatitis B surface antigen and nonreactive VDRL. Thyroid function tests revealed an elevated TSH of 7.16 mIU/L with normal T3 and T4 levels and normal anti–thyroid peroxidase antibody levels.

A 65-year-old woman presented with two months of epigastric pain without vomiting, hematemesis, or weight loss. Her medical history was notable for total thyroidectomy for a thyroid nodule and laparoscopic cholecystectomy. On examination, she was neither anemic nor icteric, and there was no palpable abdominal mass. Routine blood tests and tumor markers were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound showed a heterogeneous subdiaphragmatic lesion (6 × 7 cm) adjacent to the medial spleen with an echogenic center. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a well-defined 7 × 8 cm mass at the gastric cardia with regular borders and heterogeneous enhancement. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy demonstrated large ulcerated fundic folds bulging into the lumen consistent with extrinsic compression and congestive gastropathy; the esophagus was normal. Biopsy of the fundic mucosa showed moderately active chronic gastritis without H. pylori, intestinal metaplasia, or malignancy. Based on these findings, a gastrointestinal stromal tumor was suspected, and surgical excision was planned.

A 32-year-old woman, G1P1001, presented with a 2-year history of progressive abdominal distension accompanied by poor appetite and weight loss. Her menses were regular without dysmenorrhea or pelvic pain at presentation. Six years earlier, she had chronic pelvic pain treated empirically with injectable progestin. One year prior, a CT scan at another hospital showed large ascites, peritoneal nodules, and pleural effusion; paracentesis and pleural tapping yielded exudative fluid without malignant cells. A subsequent CT scan suggested circumferential mid‐ to upper‐rectal wall thickening “suggesting rectal cancer” plus ascites and right pleural effusion, but colonoscopic biopsy revealed only acute colitis without malignancy. 

On examination at our institution, she appeared chronically ill and emaciated (BMI 14.9 kg/m2). Her abdomen was markedly distended without tenderness or palpable masses. Vaginal examination showed anterior vaginal‐wall bulging from ascites but no adnexal masses. 

Laboratory tests showed a CA-125 level of 112 IU/mL; CA 19-9 and CEA were normal. A CT scan revealed massive loculated ascites with internal septation and infiltrative enhancing lesions in the cul-de-sac and perirectal region; the uterus and ovaries appeared unremarkable. Chest X-ray demonstrated bilateral pleural effusions and lower‐lobe atelectasis. 

Repeat abdominal paracentesis produced clear yellowish fluid; cytologic examination indicated inflammation without malignant cells. Ascites fluid was negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis by PCR and acid-fast bacilli staining. An exploratory laparotomy was scheduled for tissue diagnosis.

A 65-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with acute abdominal pain, emesis, chronic constipation, and significant weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable. Serum CEA and CA19-9 levels were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed a well-defined, irregularly contoured pre-pancreatic mass in the greater omentum (mesocolon), measuring 54 × 66 × 99 mm. The lesion had heterogeneous density, central liquid areas, and peripheral enhancement. It infiltrated the transverse colon, the head of the pancreas, and the adjacent gastric wall, without evidence of vascular invasion. A few satellite lymph nodes were noted.  
“Following the imaging results, a GIST or complicated duodenal diverticula was suspected.”

A 20-year-old healthy, active-duty US Army man presented with a 2-month history of a painful lump on his right leg that had doubled in size. Baseline pain was 2 of 10 and worsened with daily physical training. A radiograph obtained to evaluate for shin splints showed multiple osteosclerotic foci in the metaphyses of the tibia and fibula. On referral to dermatology, examination revealed a raised, 3-cm, slightly erythematous, immobile nodule on the right distal lateral lower extremity and a 5-cm confluent plaque of yellow 1- to 2-mm papules on the right lumbar region. Punch biopsies of both the lumbar plaque and the leg nodule were performed.

A 19-year-old otherwise healthy boy presented with a 1-year history of pain and a spontaneously discharging wound over the dorsum of his right foot. The discharge was intermittently ‘watery’ and transiently improved with courses of antibiotics. There was no history of trauma or constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, or night sweats.

On examination, five active discharging sinuses were clustered over the dorsum around the first and second metatarsal rays. 

Laboratory studies were unremarkable: hemoglobin 9.1 g/dl, total leukocyte count 10.4 × 10^3/µl, ESR 19 mm/h, CRP 7.1 mg/l, normal glucose and liver‐function tests, and negative HIV testing. A chest radiograph was normal.

Plain radiographs of the right foot showed an expansile osteolytic lesion of the first metatarsal shaft with cortical thinning. MRI demonstrated a 26 × 22 mm lytic lesion involving the head, proximal shaft, and base of the first metatarsal and a sequestrum within the bone.

With a provisional diagnosis of chronic osteomyelitis (pyogenic, tubercular, fungal, or parasitic), open biopsy and wound debridement were planned.

A 1-year-old boy presented with a 2-day history of worsening sore throat, loss of appetite, vomiting, difficulty swallowing, and fever. On examination he was afebrile, with normal vital signs. Inspection of the oropharynx showed enlarged, inflamed tonsils and a bilaterally congested, bulging soft palate—more pronounced on the right—with a midline uvula. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 10 060/mm3 with 54.6% lymphocytes and a C-reactive protein level of 93.1 mg/L. A monospot test was negative. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the neck demonstrated bilateral hypodense collections consistent with peritonsillar abscesses.

A 39-year-old man was admitted with low back pain and dyspnea 3 days after being caught between a motor vehicle and a wall. He had a history of ankylosing spondylitis treated with corticosteroids. On arrival, he was alert (GCS 15) with stable vital signs. Neurologic examination was normal, and he had intact light-touch sensation in all extremities; movement of the lower extremities was limited by pain. Radiographs showed fractures of three left lower ribs, hemothorax, and subcutaneous emphysema. Lumbar–sacral imaging revealed fractures of the L2, L3, and L4 vertebrae, with no cervical spine injury. CT of the thorax confirmed bilateral pleural effusions, fractures of ribs 8, 9, and 10 on the left, fractures of vertebrae L2–L4, and multiple air bubbles within the upper thoracic spinal canal.

A 71-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of low back pain and a 3-week history of right lower extremity paresthesia and pain. He also noted hypesthesia in the perineal and perianal regions, bladder dysfunction with frequent urination and a feeling of residual urine, and intermittent claudication. His medical history was notable for a cerebral infarction 8 years earlier, for which he was taking clopidogrel. He denied any history of spinal trauma. Laboratory studies, including platelet count, prothrombin time, and partial thromboplastin time, were all within normal limits. On examination, patellar reflexes were normal bilaterally; the right Achilles tendon reflex was diminished, with normal left Achilles reflex. There was no Babinski sign and no motor weakness.  
Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a space-occupying lesion extending from the right intravertebral region into the spinal canal at the level of L4. The lesion had heterogeneous intensity on T1-weighted images, low intensity on T2-weighted images, and exhibited heterogeneous enhancement on gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted images.  
Myelography demonstrated a contrast defect of the spinal subarachnoid space at L4–L5, predominantly on the right. Computed tomography after myelography showed a right-sided epidural mass with severe scalloping of the posterior wall of the L4 vertebral body and sclerotic bone at the scalloped margins.

A 39‐year‐old woman with a 14‐year history of adult‐onset Still’s disease, maintained on hydroxychloroquine and intermittent low‐dose prednisone, was admitted with sudden onset of widespread spontaneous ecchymoses on all four limbs, gingival bleeding, and heavy menstruation. On examination, large bruises were visible on the forearms and lower limbs; there was no hemodynamic instability. Initial laboratory tests showed:
• Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT): 68 seconds (ratio 2.36), with normal prothrombin time and platelet count  
• Mixing study: failure to correct the aPTT after addition of normal plasma and 2‐hour incubation at 37 °C (Rosner index 57%)  
• Factor VIII activity: <1%  
• Factor IX activity and von Willebrand factor activity: within normal ranges  
• Lupus anticoagulant screen by dilute Russell’s viper venom test: negative  
There was no personal or family history of bleeding disorders and no recent drug exposures or pregnancies. An acquired factor VIII inhibitor was suspected.

A 64-year-old man presented after a motor vehicle collision with right chest pain. He had no history of systemic disease. Vital signs were T 36.9°C, BP 131/91 mmHg, HR 77 bpm, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. On examination, the chest was clear bilaterally, trachea midline, no crepitus, and there was marked right posterolateral chest wall tenderness with decreased breath sounds. The abdomen was soft, non-tender, non-distended, with no palpable masses or organomegaly. Rectal examination was negative for gross blood. Extremity examination was unremarkable. Chest radiography revealed fractures of the right fifth through eighth ribs and raised concern for free air beneath both hemidiaphragms.

An 85-year-old man with a history of essential hypertension, a remote myocardial infarction, chronic kidney disease, and gout presented with 10 days of generalized, dull abdominal pain (6/10), constipation, early satiety, nausea, and a low-grade fever. There was no prior abdominal surgery. One week earlier he had completed a 10-day course of antibiotics for a urinary tract infection. On examination, temperature was 38.4 °C, blood pressure 127/73 mm Hg, pulse 86/min, and respiratory rate 18/min. The abdomen was soft, moderately distended, and diffusely tender to light palpation with normal bowel sounds. Digital rectal examination revealed hard, brown stool without blood.  
Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 12,000 cells/mm3 with 79% neutrophils and a serum creatinine of 2.13 mg/dL. Urinalysis demonstrated 30–50 white blood cells per high-power field and positive nitrites.  
A plain abdominal radiograph showed a large, well-defined, high-density shadow in the left upper quadrant displacing the descending colon centrally without bowel dilatation. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed multiple, variably sized (3.5–13.0 cm), thin-walled, well-marginated cysts in both kidneys with internal hyperdensity (16–20 HU); both kidneys were normal in size with preserved parenchyma and no solid components.

A 58-year-old woman presented with chronic right lumbar pain that began after a subperitoneal ureterolithotomy 20 years earlier. She reported recurrent episodes of fever and worsening pain, treated empirically with antibiotics and analgesics. On examination, she was afebrile but had tenderness in the right lumbar fossa and peri-umbilical region, and a hard, non-mobile mass was palpated in that area. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 50 mg/L and a white-blood-cell count of 11,000 per microliter. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a well-defined right retroperitoneal cystic mass adjacent to the psoas muscle, independent of the kidney, adrenal gland, and urinary tract, with relatively homogeneous hypodense contents and peripheral enhancement. MRI confirmed the cystic nature of the mass, which exhibited a heterogeneous T2 signal with internal septations enhanced after gadolinium, and no fatty components. The radiologists’ leading impression was an undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma.

A 44‐year‐old man from rural Somalia presented with a 10‐year history of a slowly enlarging, painless swelling of the left buttock extending toward the perineum. After 18 months of unsuccessful treatments, the lesion developed an opening that discharged blood, pus, and dark granules resembling black grains. The patient denied fever, malaise, or other systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a left gluteal mass over 10 cm in diameter with sinuses exuding dark fluid, blood, and black granules. Laboratory studies showed a mildly elevated C‐reactive protein (56 mg/L) with normal white cell and platelet counts; renal and liver function tests were within reference ranges. Viral serologies for HIV, hepatitis B, and C were negative. Hemoglobin was 11.5 g/dL. A wound swab grew Escherichia coli. Ultrasound of the left gluteal region demonstrated hypoechoic collections strongly suggesting an abscess. A CT scan confirmed subcutaneous thickening in the left gluteal and proximal thigh areas consistent with soft‐tissue infection and revealed a tumefied mass with draining sinuses. Based on these findings, differential diagnoses included epidermal cyst, hidradenitis suppurativa, pilonidal cyst, cutaneous tuberculosis, cutaneous mycosis, leprosy, botryomycosis, and metastatic cutaneous lesions.

A 75-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of progressive left lower-limb edema and pain. His medical history included atrial fibrillation, degenerative joint disease, and coronary artery bypass graft surgery 13 years earlier using the left great saphenous vein, without subsequent lower-limb surgery or trauma. He had experienced several episodes of cellulitis in the affected leg. During the first year of symptoms, he was treated with diuretics for presumed congestive heart failure despite a stable ejection fraction on serial echocardiograms; the swelling did not improve. He reported increasing leg pain that disturbed his sleep and quality of life. 

On examination, there was nonpitting edema of the left lower limb, a positive Stemmer sign, fibrotic skin changes, and a well-healed scar from saphenous-vein harvesting. Tape measurements showed a 24% increase in limb volume compared to the right side. His body-mass index was 27.7 kg/m2, and the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests and echocardiography showed no new abnormalities. Four Doppler ultrasonographic studies of the left lower limb over the past two years, most recently three months ago, revealed no evidence of arterial or venous thrombosis and normal arterial and venous flow. 

He described severe leg pain (8/10 on a visual analog scale) and an inability to sleep, exercise, or perform daily activities. He expressed frustration and despair at not having a diagnosis despite multiple consultations.

A 72-year-old man with known COPD collapsed at home and was brought to the emergency department. He reported baseline shortness of breath without activity-induced worsening, intermittent left iliac fossa discomfort, and a single episode of vomiting. He denied fever, nausea, diarrhea, or constipation. His medical history included COPD, type 2 diabetes, osteoarthritis, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, atrial fibrillation, and polymyalgia rheumatica. Medications: apixaban, lercanidipine, duloxetine, omeprazole, bumetanide-senna, allopurinol, empagliflozin, linagliptin; allergy to opioids and NSAIDs. He was a current smoker; family history was negative for gastrointestinal disease.

On examination, he was alert and oriented, breathing comfortably. Vital signs: BP 170/90 mm Hg, T 36.9 °C. Chest auscultation revealed bilateral crepitations. Abdominal exam showed a soft, non-distended abdomen with mild tenderness in the right iliac fossa; bowel sounds were present without rebound or guarding.

Laboratory studies: positive COVID-19 test; WBC 8.2 × 10^9/L (neutrophils 6.38 × 10^9/L); CRP 47 mg/dL; arterial blood gas pH 7.47, PCO2 3.4 kPa, PO2 10.2 kPa; lactate 1.9 mmol/L; platelets 67 × 10^9/L; albumin 37 g/dL; ALP 70 U/L.

Chest X-ray showed air under the right hemidiaphragm.

A 12‐year‐old girl was evaluated after a minor motor‐vehicle collision. She reported transient loss of consciousness, headache, and mild dizziness. On examination, she was alert (GCS 15), hemodynamically stable, with no scalp lacerations or visual deficits. Her medical history included thymoma and pollen allergy; laboratory studies were unremarkable. Noncontrast head CT showed no intracranial hemorrhage or fracture. Incidentally, bilateral pneumatization of the middle turbinates (concha bullosa) was noted. The left concha bullosa was markedly enlarged and contained high‐density material with coarse calcifications. Associated mucosal thickening, bony wall thickening with mild rarefaction, and opacification of adjacent ethmoidal air cells were present. There was no obstruction of the ipsilateral osteomeatal complex.

An 11-year-old girl presented with a 2-month history of lower abdominal pain, anorexia, and a 2-kg weight loss. Her medical history was notable only for chronic constipation; prenatal ultrasonography had been reportedly normal. She appeared well. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits, and blood pressure was below the 50th percentile for age, sex, and height. Growth parameters were at the 81st percentile for weight, 83rd for height, and 78th for body-mass index. Abdominal examination revealed a well-defined, nontender, 9×6-cm periumbilical mass and evidence of stool-filled dilation of the descending colon. Laboratory evaluations were unremarkable. Given the palpable abdominal mass, an ultrasound examination was performed. It demonstrated a left kidney located in the right hemiabdomen, not fused to the right kidney; both kidneys had normal parenchymal thickness, echogenicity, and parenchyma-sinus differentiation, and the ectopic kidney had an anteriorly facing hilum.

A 34-year-old woman with a 5-year history of nephrolithiasis was referred after endoscopic treatment. She reported no family history of hypercalcemia or features of multiple endocrine neoplasia. Serum studies revealed a calcium level of 3.15 mmol/L (normal 2.12–2.75) and a PTH level of 109 ng/L (normal 6.5–36.5), with low serum phosphate (1.6 mg/dL). Genetic testing excluded a MEN1 mutation. On examination, no neck mass was palpable. Neck ultrasound showed a 10 mm nodule in the right thyroid lobe; a 99mTc-sestamibi scan and SPECT-CT showed no pathological parathyroid tissue. Bone density Z-scores were −1.2 at the spine and −1.3 at the hip. Abdominal ultrasound confirmed bilateral kidney stones. She was started on oral hydration, cholecalciferol (600 U/day), vitamin C, and cinacalcet, which was poorly tolerated. Seventeen months later, she became pregnant while on therapy.

A 66-year-old woman was referred to neurology for evaluation of complex symptoms. Her history began in her 20s with a motorcycle collision (no diagnosed TBI), followed by lifelong migraine headaches and syncope with transient vision loss on standing, confirmed by positive tilt-table testing. In 2007, she developed nocturnal whole-body shaking without loss of consciousness, diagnosed as nonepileptic seizures, refractory to levetiracetam. She also experienced intermittent right-sided shaking events associated with prolonged postictal sleep. Over subsequent years, she complained of progressive memory and comprehension difficulties, notably in doing laundry and operating familiar appliances. She denied mood symptoms. Examination revealed a positive Romberg sign and impaired tandem gait but preserved heel-to-toe walking. Video-EEG captured multiple nonepileptic spells without ictal discharges. By 2011–12, she reported worsening headaches and depth-perception problems; MRI showed frontal lobe atrophy. 

In May 2013, she began experiencing nightly complex visual hallucinations of people conversing with each other (never addressing her) accompanied by nonthreatening auditory hallucinations only during visual episodes. She retained insight—“I know these people aren’t really there, and they disappear when I turn on the lights.” She also saw “blue spots” over her left eye and hands and “cracks” on white walls. Fundoscopy revealed floaters. Her husband noted increasing forgetfulness. Neurologic examination found no cogwheel rigidity, no bradykinesia, no shuffling gait, and no gait instability. Cognitive testing yielded a MoCA score of 20/30. Routine labs including B12 and folate were unremarkable.

A male neonate, 15 minutes old, was delivered by emergency cesarean section at an estimated gestational age of 34 weeks for abruptio placentae, severe oligohydramnios, and breech presentation. His birth weight was 2.01 kg, and APGAR scores were 5 and 6 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively; he required 5 minutes of resuscitation. On admission to the NICU he was in respiratory distress with a pulse rate of 160 beats/min, respiratory rate of 70 breaths/min, temperature of 33.4 °C, and oxygen saturation of 60% on room air. On examination, the anterior fontanelle measured 2 × 2 cm. There was micrognathia and a short neck. Respiratory examination revealed intercostal and subcostal retractions with grunting. Cardiac examination showed normal S1 and S2 without murmurs. Musculoskeletal examination revealed bilateral markedly shortened upper limbs with hands appearing directly attached near the trunk; the right lower limb was normal in position and structure, while the left leg was internally rotated at the knee with a normal foot. Neurologically he was lethargic; muscle tone was normal in the right lower extremity and the Moro reflex was difficult to elicit. Laboratory studies showed blood group A+, C-reactive protein reactive, WBC 30,000/mm3, neutrophils 54%, lymphocytes 21.1%, hemoglobin 8 g/dL, and platelets 150,000/mm3. Radiographs demonstrated extreme shortening of the upper extremities and internal rotation of the left lower limb. Echocardiography was normal.

A 36-year-old woman from the Philippines, living in the UAE, presented with a 2-week history of epigastric pain radiating to both upper quadrants, worsened by food and exertion. She also reported anorexia, progressive abdominal distention, night sweats, fatigue, and two episodes of non-bloody vomiting. There was no change in bowel habits, fever, weight loss, or jaundice. One year earlier she had been diagnosed with hyperthyroidism and had been taking carbimazole 5 mg daily; she discontinued it two weeks after symptom onset. A trial of pantoprazole and antibiotics provided no relief. She denied smoking or alcohol use.

On examination, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Abdominal examination showed epigastric tenderness and generalized distention with shifting dullness; there was no peripheral edema or elevated JVP. Chest and thyroid examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 14.6 × 10^3/µL with an absolute eosinophil count of 2.2 × 10^3/µL (15%), and a platelet count of 482 × 10^3/µL. Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) and liver and thyroid function tests were within normal limits. Serum sodium was 130 mmol/L and chloride 95 mmol/L; other electrolytes and renal function were normal.

Contrast CT of the abdomen revealed diffuse circumferential wall thickening with mural edema involving the gastric antrum, pylorus, duodenum, and proximal jejunum, along with moderate to severe ascites. Ultrasound-guided paracentesis yielded 2 L of clear, slightly turbid fluid: total nucleated cell count 1749 cells/mm^3 with 77% eosinophils; fluid protein was 4.6 g/dL and LDH 137 U/L. Gram stain and culture were negative. PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex was negative, and cytology showed no malignant cells.

Additional tests, including tumor markers (CEA, CA 19-9, AFP) and serologies for Ascaris, Strongyloides, Echinococcus, and Schistosoma, were normal. The autoimmune panel, including ANA, ANCA, ENA profile, anti-dsDNA, anti-tissue transglutaminase, and thyroid antibodies, was unremarkable.

A 55-year-old woman presented with 6 months of progressive dyspnea, fatigue, and proximal muscle pain. Her only allergies were to house dust mite; she had no significant exposures. On admission: temperature 37.7 °C, pulse 93 bpm, blood pressure 119/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. Examination revealed bilateral basal crackles and digital clubbing; skin and joint examination were unremarkable.

Pulmonary function testing showed a restrictive pattern (FVC 58% predicted, TLC 56% predicted) and reduced diffusion capacity (DLCO 41% predicted). Six-minute walk distance was 335 m with desaturation to 81%.

Laboratory studies demonstrated leukocytosis (14.3 × 10^9/L) with eosinophilia (1.22 × 10^9/L), C-reactive protein 13.1 mg/L, creatine kinase 305 U/L, IgE 263 kU/L, and a mildly positive ANA (1.2 ratio). Fifteen myositis-specific autoantibodies and a broad microbial panel were negative. Allergy testing was positive only for house dust mite.

High-resolution CT of the chest showed bibasilar peribronchial consolidations suggestive of organizing pneumonia and nonspecific interstitial pneumonia. Transbronchial lung biopsy demonstrated inflammation with eosinophilia, and bronchoalveolar lavage revealed 79% eosinophils. Cultures and PCR for infectious agents were negative.

She was started on oral prednisolone 37.5 mg daily, with rapid improvement of respiratory and muscle symptoms. During steroid tapering, her dyspnea recurred, and a follow-up CT scan showed progression of the interstitial changes. Increasing the dose of oral corticosteroids had no significant effect.

A 44-year-old man with allergic rhinitis, asthma, and gastroesophageal reflux disease presented with a 7-day history of neck pain that had acutely worsened, causing difficulty with neck movement and swallowing, with radiation of pain to the left face and ear. He denied fevers or other systemic symptoms. He was hemodynamically stable. Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 11 × 10^3/μL and a C-reactive protein level of 16.6 mg/L; the basic metabolic panel was normal. Blood cultures were obtained. Noncontrast CT of the brain showed no acute process. Contrast-enhanced CT of the soft tissues of the neck demonstrated a 9 mm fluid collection in the right retropharyngeal space extending from C1 to C5, without rim enhancement or loculation, and a focal calcification of the left longus coli tendon. Flexible laryngoscopy showed moderate edema of the posterior pharyngeal wall without airway obstruction.

A 23-year-old man presented for evaluation of elevated liver enzymes found on routine health screening. He was asymptomatic. Laboratory results showed:  
• AST 410 IU/L (reference 10–45), ALT 209 IU/L (5–45)  
• Alkaline phosphatase, GGT, and total bilirubin normal  
• Prothrombin time, INR, and albumin normal  

History: He drinks 2–4 units of alcohol per week for the past 1.5 years; last binge drinking episode was 6 days before initial tests. He denies recreational drugs, is a nonsmoker, and has no family history of liver disease.  

Physical examination: Average build, normal vital signs, and no stigmata of liver disease.  

Initial investigations:  
• CBC, renal function, lipid profile, urine microscopy – within normal limits  
• Serologic tests for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV – negative  
• Abdominal ultrasound – unremarkable  

He was advised to abstain from alcohol. Three days later, repeat testing showed:  
• AST 580 IU/L, ALT 277 IU/L  

He then underwent further testing:  
• Serology for hepatitis A and E, dengue – within normal limits  
• ANA, anti‐LKM antibody, anti–Smith antibody – negative  
• Thyroid function tests – normal  
• Serum ceruloplasmin – normal  

The AST and ALT remained markedly elevated with no clear hepatic etiology.

A 30-year-old Maasai woman, G4P3 at 30 weeks of gestation, presented with a 3-month history of progressive shortness of breath, dry cough, right-sided chest pain, nausea, vomiting, and fever. She had attended two antenatal visits with no prior medical or obstetric complications.

On examination, she appeared ill, pale, and cachectic. Notable findings included facial edema, grade 2 pitting edema of the lower limbs, and dilated superficial veins on the right side of the neck. Traditional scarification marks were present on her back. Vital signs were blood pressure 110/67 mmHg, pulse rate 120 bpm, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 84% on room air, and temperature 36°C.

Respiratory examination revealed dullness to percussion at the right lung base, diminished breath sounds throughout the right lung, and reduced chest wall movement on that side. Abdominal examination showed a fundal height of 30 cm, right upper quadrant tenderness, and caput medusae. Other systems were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 67 mm/hr, C-reactive protein 100,000 ng/mL, alpha-fetoprotein 310 IU/mL, and albumin 1.12 g/L. Hepatitis serologies, renal function, liver enzymes, coagulation profile, and platelet count were within normal limits.

Obstetric ultrasound confirmed a single live intrauterine fetus at 30 weeks 5 days with a normal biophysical profile.

Due to financial constraints, a noncontrast chest and abdominal CT scan was performed. It revealed a large, complex cystic lesion occupying the right hemithorax, causing atelectasis and mediastinal shift to the left. Dilated, tortuous superficial veins were also noted on the anterior abdominal wall and right neck.

A 26-year-old man with a history of oral opium addiction presented with a 3-day history of a painful skin lesion on his right lower extremity. He reported that while working on his farm, he was bitten by an insect on his right leg, which caused immediate pruritus, redness, and mild swelling. The following day, he developed a painful red blister at the site; the blister ruptured on day 3 and progressed into a black lesion. He denied fever, chills, myalgia, nausea, vomiting, or other systemic symptoms. 

On examination, his temperature was 37.2 °C, blood pressure 125/80 mmHg, heart rate 85 beats/min, and respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. The medial aspect of the middle third of his right leg had a 3 × 5 cm necrotic wound with surrounding erythema, swelling, and warmth extending to the dorsum of the foot; the area was tender. There were diffuse bruises and blisters from the right dorsum of the foot up to the buttock region.

Laboratory studies showed mild renal impairment (creatinine 1.4 mg/dL), leukocytosis (19 × 10^3/mm^3), elevated CPK (713 IU/L), and a slightly prolonged INR (1.5). Radiography of the right lower extremity demonstrated diffuse subcutaneous swelling with fat stranding but no fracture or dislocation. Color Doppler ultrasound showed no deep or superficial vein thrombosis, only soft-tissue swelling.

A 10-year-old, 35 kg girl with no prior medical history underwent outpatient foot surgery under general anesthesia. Premedication included midazolam 10 mg orally. Anesthesia was induced with sevoflurane, and after IV access was obtained, propofol 30 mg and alfentanil 0.125 mg were given for laryngeal mask airway placement. Maintenance was with sevoflurane. Intraoperative medications included fentanyl 0.01 mg, morphine 4 mg, ketorolac 15 mg, and dexamethasone 4 mg; the surgical site was infiltrated with 4 mL of 0.5% ropivacaine at closure. Emergence and recovery in the PACU were uneventful. 

Approximately two hours after emergence, she received ondansetron 3 mg IV for nausea. Thirty minutes later, each time she drifted off to sleep, she developed jerking movements of her arms and torso lasting several seconds; over the next hours these evolved into shaking, seizure-like movements of her upper body and head lasting several minutes. She was easily arousable, asymptomatic while awake, and fully oriented. Diphenhydramine 25 mg IV was administered without effect. She was discharged home on postoperative day one at 0930 h. The nocturnal movements persisted at home, gradually improving over four days until she returned to her baseline state.

A 23-year-old woman presented with a 1-week history of worsening blurry vision and mild headache that progressed to ataxia and difficulty ambulating. On examination, she had nystagmus, left-eye ophthalmoplegia, and diplopia; the remainder of her neurologic examination and a CT scan of the brain were normal. She was admitted to neurology for further workup to exclude multiple sclerosis. Her medical history was notable for fibromyalgia and pityriasis lichenoides et varioliformis acuta, for which she had been taking prednisone (30–50 mg/day) for 2 years and dapsone (150 mg/day). 

Three days into her admission, she developed ongoing hypoxia with pulse-oximetry saturations of 88%–92% while receiving 8 L of oxygen via Hudson mask. She complained of dyspnea and appeared tachypneic but denied cough, hemoptysis, chest pain, or any history of deep-vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, or asthma. Examination revealed mild central cyanosis of the lips and fingertips. Lung auscultation was clear, heart sounds were dual without murmurs, and there was no lower-limb swelling or tenderness. Blood pressure was 103/66 mm Hg, and heart rate was 90–105 bpm in sinus rhythm.

An arterial blood gas performed on 8 L/min of oxygen showed pH 7.56, PaO₂ 178 mm Hg, SaO₂ 98%, PCO₂ 20 mm Hg, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, lactate 2.9 mmol/L, and hemoglobin 98 g/L. Because she had not received DVT prophylaxis for 3 days, a CT pulmonary angiogram was obtained; both pulmonary embolism and pneumonia were excluded. She was transferred to the ICU and placed on high-flow nasal prongs. Repeat arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated a marked discrepancy between the pulse-oximeter saturation (88%–90%) and the calculated arterial oxygen saturation with a PaO₂ in the normal range.

A 69-year-old Caucasian man with well-controlled type 2 diabetes presented with rectal bleeding and tenesmus. On examination, a circumferential, friable mass was palpated at 7 cm from the anal verge; the remainder of the physical examination was normal. Colonoscopy confirmed an ulcerative, exophytic lesion 7 cm from the anal verge with no other colonic lesions. Biopsy showed a well-differentiated, infiltrating Lieberkühnian adenocarcinoma. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a circumferential and irregular thickening of the middle rectum with a heterogeneous, exophytically developing mass infiltrating the mesorectum and abutting the right mesorectal fascia. A thoracoabdominopelvic CT scan showed no distant metastases. Laboratory tests were notable only for a hemoglobin level of 10.8 g/dL.

An 82-year-old woman with a history of chronic hypertension, ischemic stroke without sequelae, and hypothyroidism was admitted for nephrotic syndrome. She was started on prednisone at 1 mg/kg/day. Her hospital course was complicated by multiple intercurrent infections, a right renal infarction, and progressive renal failure requiring initiation of hemodialysis. Three weeks after admission, she developed multiple painful genital and inguinal ulcers. The largest lesion, on the left labia majora, measured 1.5 cm in diameter, had a well-defined erythematous border, and a base with scant fibrin. Over the next days, the ulcers rapidly increased in size and number, extending to the perianal region, thighs, and right leg. Dermatology was consulted. PCR assays for herpes simplex viruses 1 and 2, varicella zoster virus, Epstein–Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus, as well as HIV serology and VDRL, were all negative. Biopsies of the vulvar and right leg lesions were performed. On periodic acid–Schiff staining of the leg lesion, septate hyphae with acute-angle branching and invasion of blood vessels were observed.

A 26-year-old Chinese man presented with recurrent chest pain and self-noticed lymph node enlargement for over one month, with worsening over three weeks. He had been diagnosed with Hodgkin’s lymphoma by lymph node puncture in the UK but sought further evaluation after returning to China. He was otherwise healthy, with no significant medical or family history. He received a third dose of the Pfizer–BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine six weeks prior and reported a month-long habit of staying up past 3 AM before and after vaccination.

On examination, there were multiple non­tender, firm, mobile lymph nodes: four in the right neck and similar nodes in the left neck, axillae, and groin. There was no sternal tenderness, and pulmonary and other systemic examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed normal liver and renal function, lactate dehydrogenase, coagulation profile, autoantibodies (including ANA, anti-GBM, ANCA), immunoglobulin levels (including IgG4), complement, tumor markers, viral hepatitis panel, and thyroid function. Elevated findings included thyroglobulin antibody 12.07 IU/mL, thyroid peroxidase antibody 197.43 IU/mL, WBC 10.63×10⁹/L, neutrophils 7.53×10⁹/L, C-reactive protein 36.1 mg/L, ESR 58 mm/h, and IgE 119 KU/L. Procalcitonin, T-lymphocyte and NK cell levels were normal; B-lymphocyte count was decreased at 66 M/L. Serology showed increased CMV IgG and HSV-1 IgG; EBV and rubella serologies were normal. Urinalysis was unremarkable.

Ultrasound of the liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, and kidneys was normal. Chest and abdominal CT revealed multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the retroperitoneum (largest 2.0×1.8 cm), right axilla, and mediastinum.

A 17-year-old female with no prior medical history presented with left thigh pain and swelling. Thirteen months earlier, she collided with a tree while riding an all-terrain vehicle. The day after the accident, she noted marked swelling and tenderness of the lateral thigh and underwent plain radiographs, which were interpreted as negative for fracture or bony injury. Over the ensuing month, persistent pain and fluctuance prompted an MRI, which demonstrated a well-demarcated fluid collection between the subcutaneous tissue and the fascia of the lateral thigh that measured approximately [size not specified], with internal heterogeneity and a thin enhancing capsule. Initial management consisted of ice, compression dressings, NSAIDs, and physical therapy. Over the following year, she reported waxing and waning symptoms despite high compliance with compressive dressings, anti-inflammatory medications, and physiotherapy. A repeat MRI obtained 13 months after the injury showed a slight decrease in the overall size of the fluid collection but confirmed formation of a persistent pseudocapsule around the lesion.

A 19-year-old Iranian man presented with a 2-month history of dyspnea on exertion (NYHA Class II). He had a past history of hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. There were no known familial genetic disorders. On examination, his height was 135 cm and weight 53 kg; vital signs were normal. Cardiac auscultation revealed a III/VI mid-systolic, high-pitched crescendo–decrescendo murmur at the base consistent with aortic stenosis, and a IV/VI holosystolic murmur at the apex in the left lateral decubitus position suggestive of mitral regurgitation. Pulses were symmetrical. Abdominal examination showed a spleen palpable 4 cm below the costal margin.

Laboratory studies demonstrated thrombocytopenia (platelet count 62 000 × 10^3/µL), with normal red and white cell counts and normal thyroid function. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm with high-voltage QRS complexes and secondary ST-T changes, consistent with left ventricular hypertrophy.

Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 65%, moderate concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, severe calcific aortic valve stenosis (maximum velocity 5.6 m/s, valve area 0.84 cm^2), severe supra-valvular aortic stenosis with a small aortic root (≈14 mm), moderate mitral stenosis (mean gradient 10 mmHg) with severe degenerative mitral regurgitation (vena contracta 7.4 mm, regurgitant volume 84 mL, EROA 0.43 cm^2).

Abdominal ultrasound confirmed splenomegaly (span 180 mm). Multidetector CT angiography showed hypoplasia of the ascending, arch, and descending aorta (≈15 mm diameter), patent aortic arch branches, cervical and cerebral arteries, and patent abdominal vasculature. Coronary CT angiography revealed left circumflex artery calcification without significant luminal stenosis. A heart team recommended surgical intervention.

A man in his mid-20s with no prior ENT history presented ten days after recovering from mild COVID-19. Three days before presentation, he awoke with his left eye remaining closed and noticed a pungent odour; both symptoms worsened over the day. By evening, he developed a bilateral frontal headache aggravated by head movement and progressively worsening over three days. He denied vomiting, photophobia, focal neurologic symptoms, trauma, visual or auditory changes.

On examination, he was alert, afebrile, and hemodynamically stable. He had partial left-sided ptosis. Ophthalmic exam showed equal, reactive pupils, no periorbital swelling or discharge, and normal fundi. ENT exam revealed no nasal deformity, haematoma, or discharge; ears and throat were normal. The neurologic examination was otherwise unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 10.7×10^9/L (normal 3.7–9.5), neutrophils 8.1×10^9/L (normal 1.8–7.5), and C-reactive protein 61 mg/L (normal <4 mg/L); renal and liver function were normal. SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative.

Noncontrast CT of the head demonstrated no infarction, haemorrhage, aneurysm, or mass lesion. There was complete opacification of the left maxillary, frontal, and ethmoid sinuses, partial opacification of the right ethmoid and frontal sinuses, and no sphenoid involvement. There was no evidence of levator palpebrae superioris injury or orbital inflammation.

An 18-year-old Japanese man was referred for evaluation of progressive respiratory discomfort and recurrent joint pain. 

History of present illness and past medical history:
• Since age 2, he had swelling, pain, and limited range of motion in hand, knee, and foot joints; radiographs at that time were normal, and he was observed without treatment.  
• At age 5, he developed contractures of the bilateral hand joints, left shoulder pain, neck pain, and dyspnea.  
• At age 6, chest radiography and CT showed interstitial pneumonia; serum KL-6 was elevated at 2743 U/mL. He was diagnosed with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA)–associated interstitial pneumonia and treated with glucocorticoids (GC) and methotrexate (MTX); joint symptoms improved but lung disease progressed.  
• At age 11, a synovial cyst on the hand dorsum prompted suspicion of early-onset sarcoidosis; no granulomas were found and genetic testing for EOS was negative.  
• From ages 11 to 17, additional therapies including azathioprine, GC pulse therapy, and adalimumab were used; despite these, interstitial changes and emphysematous progression continued, and joint pain flared when GC doses were reduced.

Examination on admission (age 18):
• Height 140.6 cm; weight 36.3 kg; temperature 36.4 °C; SpO₂ 95% on room air.  
• Fine crackles heard in bilateral mid-lower lung fields; no joint tenderness, swelling, or rash.

Laboratory data:
• WBC 11,400/μL; CRP 0.15 mg/dL  
• KL-6 4597 U/mL; IgG 2117 mg/dL; ANA 1:320 homogeneous  
• MPO-ANCA 81 U/mL; PR3-ANCA 23 U/mL  
• RF 25.7 U/mL; anti-CCP antibody negative; no other disease-specific autoantibodies

Imaging:
• Hand and foot radiographs: no joint space narrowing, bone erosion, or destruction  
• Chest radiograph: linear opacity in right mid-lower field, hyperlucency in left mid-lower field  
• Chest CT: marked bilateral emphysematous changes, with progression compared to prior studies

A 38-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of progressive swelling of the left vulva. She had previously undergone excision and reconstructive surgery for a 6×7-cm vulval mass in 2002, with subsequent restoration of normal genital anatomy, but noted gradual re-enlargement. Her menstrual history was normal; she was para 1 (LSCS 15 years earlier). There was no history of genital ulceration, inguinal swelling, tuberculosis, pelvic surgery, or irradiation.

On examination, she was afebrile with no lymphadenopathy. The left vulva had a hypertrophied, pendulous, multilobed mass extending to the upper third of the thigh. The overlying skin was thickened, rugose, ulcerated in areas, pigmented, and malodorous. Palpation revealed a firm, irregular, nonpitting, nontender mass. No inguinal lymph nodes or scar/sinus tracts were present. Systemic examination was unremarkable.

Fine-needle aspiration cytology showed a hypocellular smear with lymphocytes on a proteinaceous background. Biopsy revealed interlacing bands of fibroblasts and collagen, perivascular lymphocytes and mononuclear cells, myxoid stromal changes, and foreign-body granulomas, consistent with superficial chronic inflammation. ZN staining was negative. PAS staining showed no fungal hyphae. Buffy-coat examination for microfilaria was negative. The ESR was 50 mm/h; the Mantoux test was negative. Pelvic ultrasonography was normal. A smear of the vulval discharge grew mixed bacterial flora.

A 17-year-old Vietnamese American male presented to the emergency department after a syncopal episode, generalized muscle weakness, and difficulty breathing. Two months prior, he had been diagnosed with Graves’ disease based on a TSH of 0.007 mIU/mL, free T4 > 7 ng/dL, and positive thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin, and was started on atenolol and methimazole 10 mg three times daily. Thyroid ultrasonography showed markedly increased internal vascularity. On the morning of presentation, he was found on the floor 30 minutes after a thud; he recalled his legs “gave out” and he struck his face. In the emergency department, his heart rate was 116 bpm, blood pressure 131/50 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 24 breaths/min. Examination revealed diffuse and significant muscle weakness in all extremities, including grip strength; he was alert with no headache or papilledema. Laboratory studies showed potassium 1.6 mmol/L (reference 3.5–5.2) and magnesium 1.6 mmol/L (1.6–2.3); the remainder of the basic metabolic panel was unremarkable. Electrocardiography showed U waves, atrial rhythm with first-degree atrioventricular block, intraventricular conduction delay, and a prolonged QTc of 588 ms (normal < 450 ms). A chest radiograph was normal.

A 27-year-old African-American woman with a history of systemic lupus erythematosus complicated by lupus nephritis (diagnosed at age 13 via kidney biopsy), asthma, two miscarriages at 10 weeks’ gestation, antiphospholipid syndrome, heart failure (October 2017), and ischemic stroke (December 2017) was admitted to the intensive care unit with a 48-hour history of shortness of breath and 2 weeks of progressive lower-extremity swelling. She also noted mild rectal bleeding of unclear duration. Home medications included mycophenolate mofetil, hydroxychloroquine, labetalol, isosorbide, and prednisone.

On examination, her blood pressure was 204/131 mm Hg, respiratory rate 21 breaths/min, pulse 91 beats/min, and body-mass index 39.35 kg/m2. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 5.5 g/dL, hematocrit 16.1%, white-cell count 2.8 × 10^9/L, platelets 48 000/mm^3, haptoglobin < 30 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 432 U/L, D-dimer 7884 µg/L, fibrinogen 182 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.43 mg/dL rising to 2.32 mg/dL. A peripheral-blood smear demonstrated schistocytes.

Noncontrast head CT showed no acute hemorrhage but a remote basal ganglia encephalomalacia. Chest radiograph revealed mild pulmonary edema. Renal ultrasound and transthoracic echocardiogram were unremarkable. Doppler ultrasonography of the lower extremities demonstrated bilateral deep venous thromboses.

A 64-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of mucus and blood on formed stools and a weight loss of approximately 9 kg. He had no abdominal pain, distension, tenesmus, fever, or night sweats. He had a 5-year history of diabetes managed with acarbose. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies were normal except for a platelet count of 95 G/L. Colonoscopy disclosed multiple nodular projections in the segmental mucosa of the sigmoid colon, some with a transparent appearance. Endoscopic ultrasound revealed multiple cystic lesions in the submucosa, exhibiting ringing artifacts. An intestinal CT scan demonstrated intramural gas confined to the sigmoid colon.

A 43-year-old woman presented with multiple erythematous, edematous, infiltrated plaques—some annular with raised borders—distributed on the trunk and extremities. She reported severe pruritus. Her medical history included hypothyroidism, hyperlipidemia, obesity, and resection of an appendiceal carcinoid tumor. Nineteen years earlier, she had been diagnosed with eosinophilic cellulitis but had been lost to follow-up; prior treatments with topical and oral corticosteroids, dapsone, and azathioprine provided no relief, after which she experienced spontaneous remission for nearly 20 years. Several months before this presentation, widespread annular plaques reappeared, accompanied by intense itching. On admission, a 4-mm punch biopsy was performed. The pathologic examination revealed throughout the dermis a dense perivascular and interstitial infiltrate of mononuclear cells and numerous eosinophils, with several “flame figures.” Laboratory evaluation showed normal blood eosinophil counts and IgE levels. Serum protein electrophoresis, immunoglobulins, complement levels, antinuclear antibodies, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were within normal limits. Pulmonary function tests and echocardiography were normal. The differential diagnosis included eosinophilic annular erythema and a recurrence of eosinophilic cellulitis.

A 55-year-old man was referred for evaluation of chronic hypercalcemia. Eight years earlier, he had an episode of presyncope, during which an electrocardiogram showed a shortened QTc interval; serum calcium was 11.5 mg/dL (RR, 8.5–10.5 mg/dL). One month before presentation, laboratory studies again showed a serum calcium of 11.5 mg/dL and an intact PTH level of 106 ng/L (RR, 10–65 ng/L). He denied bone pain, kidney stones, abdominal pain, or neuropsychiatric symptoms, and he had no history of lithium or hydrochlorothiazide use. Family history was notable for PTH-dependent hypercalcemia in his mother and half-brother, and his half-brother remained hypercalcemic after removal of three parathyroid glands. 

On examination, vital signs were normal. Repeat labs showed serum calcium 11.6 mg/dL, ionized calcium 1.63 mmol/L (RR, 1.16–1.31 mmol/L), and PTH 144.2 ng/L. Twenty-four-hour urine calcium excretion was 91.7 mg/day (RR, 100–300 mg/day), and the fractional excretion of calcium was 0.004.

A 63-year-old man with a 3-day history of abdominal pain presented in shock. His medical history was notable for atrial fibrillation, stroke, and popliteal and internal iliac artery aneurysms, for which he was taking cilostazol and rivaroxaban. On arrival his heart rate was 102 beats/min, blood pressure 73/48 mmHg, and he was alert but in distress. The abdomen was diffusely tender without peritoneal signs or external trauma. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL, lactic acid 5.7 mmol/L, and C-reactive protein 1.18 mg/dL; other values were unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 95 × 250 mm mass along the sigmoid colon mesentery with heterogeneous internal hyperdensity compressing the colon; there was no obvious extravascular contrast leakage, no identifiable responsible vessel, no aneurysm in or around the hematoma, and no free air. After initial stabilization with transfusions, the patient was managed conservatively.

On hospital day 1 he developed peritoneal irritation signs, white blood cell count rose to 19,600/µL, and C-reactive protein increased to 8.32 mg/dL. Repeat contrast-enhanced CT showed no enlargement of the hematoma or free air but demonstrated poor contrast enhancement of the compressed sigmoid colon wall and increased ascites.

A 1.5-year-old female Scottish Terrier was referred for severe acute bilateral kerato-uveitis. Fifteen days earlier, mild perilimbal corneal edema and diffuse episcleral hyperemia had developed. Initial blood counts and serologies for Leishmania infantum, Toxoplasma gondii, Ehrlichia canis, Leptospira spp., and Borrelia burgdorferi were normal or negative. The dog received topical neomycin-dexamethasone three times daily and oral amoxicillin/clavulanic acid (12.5 mg/kg twice daily) plus prednisolone (1 mg/kg once daily) for two weeks, but lesions worsened with visual impairment.

On presentation, the dog was systemically well. Ocular examination showed bilateral conjunctival and episcleral hyperemia with brown, melting areas of scleromalacia (three lesions OS; one lesion OD), perilimbal corneal edema extending centrally, and deep corneal neovascularization. Menace response was absent OS and decreased OD; pupillary light responses were intact. Intraocular pressure was unmeasurable OU due to hypotony. After pharmacologic mydriasis, the vitreous was cloudy OU with OS hemorrhages, preventing fundoscopy. Ultrasonography revealed dense vitreous hemorrhage OS, hyalitis with vitreous deposits OD, no retinal detachment, and dense retrobulbar tissue OS.

Because of impending scleral perforation and pain, the left eye was enucleated. Histopathology of the globe showed severe chronic suppurative to pyogranulomatous infiltration of the sclera with fibrinous congestion, hemorrhages, and multiple necrotic collagen areas extending into the cornea, choroid, ciliary body, periocular muscles, and orbital fat. Numerous neutrophils, histiocytes forming pyogranulomas, lymphocytes, and plasma cells were present. Periodic Acid Schiff and Fite–Faraco stains revealed no fungal elements or acid-fast organisms, and Onchocerca spp. were absent. The pathologist concluded severe idiopathic pyogranulomatous necrotizing scleritis.

A 19‐year‐old man with a four‐year history of sinusitis and allergic rhinitis and a two‐year history of episodic wheezing and dyspnea was admitted for two months of fever, productive cough, and worsening dyspnea. Two weeks earlier he noted blood‐streaked sputum and gradual paresthesia of his right lower leg. On examination, he was in respiratory distress with coarse crackles, generalized rhonchi, and wheezes at both lung bases. His SpO2 was 74% on room air, rising to 91% with 6 L/min of 40% oxygen via a Venturi mask. He was tachypneic but afebrile and hemodynamically stable. 

Laboratory studies showed a WBC count of 18,000/mm3 with 23% eosinophils and normal hemoglobin and platelet counts. ESR was 14 mm/h (previously 3 mm/h), and liver and renal function tests, coagulation studies, and electrolytes were normal. Blood cultures at one week were negative, and urinalysis was unremarkable. Tests for RF, ANA, cANCA, pANCA, C3, C4, and CH50 were negative. A PPD skin test was negative. Echocardiography was normal.

On hospital day 2, he developed hyperesthesia and severe pain in his right lower leg, progressing to foot drop the next day. EMG and nerve conduction studies showed neuritis and axonopathy of the common peroneal nerve below the right knee. Bronchoscopy with transbronchial lung biopsy revealed eosinophilic infiltration with a few multinucleated giant cells; there was no histologic evidence of vasculitis in the bronchi or lung parenchyma. Bronchoalveolar lavage showed no mycobacteria or malignant cells. Further history revealed that he had undergone allergen desensitization vaccination twice weekly for four months and again for three months this year.

A 67-year-old Han Chinese man with metastatic squamous cell carcinoma of the lung—treated with ten cycles of sintilimab and platinum-based chemotherapy—presented with a 5-day history of nonproductive cough and progressive dyspnea without fever. Symptoms began 15 days after close contact with his son, who had returned from Wuhan. On examination, rales were heard bilaterally and breath sounds were diminished over the left hemithorax. Chest CT showed peripherally subpleural lattice opacities in the right lower lobe and bilateral pleural effusions. Laboratory tests revealed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, lymphopenia, a C-reactive protein level of 97.68 mg/L, and a normal procalcitonin level. Two consecutive SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR tests on nasopharyngeal swabs, performed 72 hours apart, were negative. No pathogens grew from sputum cultures.

A 28-year-old multiparous woman was referred at 24 weeks of gestation after a routine ultrasound at 22 weeks showed a large cystic mass in the fetal pelvis. Ultrasound confirmed a persistently enlarged fetal bladder with a maximum diameter of 5.1 cm in an appropriately grown female fetus. Mild bilateral hydronephrosis was noted, and the amniotic fluid volume was normal. The parents declined prenatal genetic testing. Monthly follow-up ultrasounds demonstrated no progression of hydronephrosis, but the amniotic fluid gradually increased, with an amniotic fluid index of 32 at 36 weeks. In the third trimester, the fetal bowel appeared dilated on ultrasound. Fetal growth and Doppler studies remained normal. Delivery was planned by cesarean section at term.

An 86-year-old man was admitted for generalized weakness and dyspnea on exertion after noting a new nonpruritic petechial rash on both feet. Fifteen days earlier, he had undergone placement of a WATCHMAN left atrial appendage occlusion device and was converted from rivaroxaban to apixaban and aspirin, and from flecainide to amiodarone. His medical history included diverticulosis with partial bowel resection, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation complicated by gastrointestinal bleeding, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage IIIb, major depressive disorder, and obstructive sleep apnea. Home medications also included trazodone, citalopram, sitagliptin, metoprolol, pravastatin, oxybutynin, and tamsulosin. He denied chemical exposures, insect bites, or prior allergic reactions.

On examination, he was afebrile, normotensive, with an irregularly irregular rhythm and no respiratory distress. He had a nonblanching, nonpainful petechial rash on the feet that later spread to the thighs and arms, accompanied by diffuse myalgias. Laboratory studies revealed:  
• WBC 11.3×10^9/L with 0.3% eosinophils (0.3–5.0%)  
• Hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, platelets 289×10^9/L  
• Creatinine 2.14 mg/dL (baseline 1.5)  
• ESR 63 mm/h, CRP 11.7 mg/dL  
• ANA titer 1:40 (borderline), antihistone antibody 4.4 U (strongly positive)  
• C3 147 mg/dL, C4 72 mg/dL  
• Negative double-stranded DNA, ANCA, anti-GBM antibodies  
• Negative serologies for SARS-CoV-2, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, syphilis, coxsackievirus, and ehrlichia

Apixaban was discontinued, and prednisone 30 mg twice daily was initiated. A skin biopsy of a fresh lesion demonstrated superficial and deep perivascular neutrophilic infiltration consistent with leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

A 69-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, peripheral arterial disease, and femoral–popliteal bypass presented with 2 months of recurrent abdominal pain, an 11-kg weight loss, nausea, and vomiting. Two weeks before transfer, an EGD at an outside hospital showed a “blue stomach,” and abdominal CT demonstrated gastric wall emphysema. He improved enough to eat minimally and was discharged to a rehabilitation facility, but his symptoms worsened and he was transferred for further evaluation.

On arrival, he complained of constant mild right upper–quadrant abdominal pain, nausea with retching, nonbloody emesis, and episodic intense epigastric pain with dysphagia around meals. He was afebrile and hemodynamically stable throughout hospitalization, with no history of hypotension. Physical examination showed a soft abdomen with deep palpation tenderness in the right upper quadrant; no bruits were heard.

Laboratory tests revealed a leukocytosis of 21,500 cells/μL (73% neutrophils), normal lipase, normal liver function tests, and a normal lactate level of 1.4 mmol/L.
