Repeat abdominal CT with IV contrast showed resolution of prior gastric emphysema and no acute ischemia. On hospital day 2, EGD revealed a normal esophagus and duodenum; in the proximal gastric body and fundus, there were excavated lesions and a large contiguous area of pale scarring with deep central ulceration, sharply demarcated from normal mucosa in the antrum and cardia. Multiple biopsies from the scarred area and the central ulcer showed ulceration and necrosis.

A 35‐year‐old healthy man presented with two weeks of blurred vision, progressive paracentral scotomata, and photopsias in his right eye. Visual acuity was 20/20 in each eye, with no relative afferent pupillary defect; slit‐lamp examination was unremarkable. Fundus examination of the right eye revealed mild temporal peripapillary retinal thickening and whitening extending to the fovea; the left eye was normal.

Multimodal imaging of the right eye showed hyperautofluorescence corresponding to the area of whitening; fluorescein angiography demonstrated early hypofluorescence and late hyperfluorescence with subfoveal pooling and nasal macular staining; indocyanine green angiography showed hypocyanescence in all frames; OCT‐angiography revealed a choriocapillaris flow deficit corresponding to the area of hypocyanescence; spectral‐domain OCT disclosed an intraretinal (bacillary layer) detachment, minimal subretinal fluid, and a thickened choroid. B‐scan ultrasound confirmed mild macular thickening.

One week later, the patient’s right‐eye uncorrected visual acuity had worsened to 20/60 with increased subretinal fluid and perifoveal hyperautofluorescence. Laboratory testing, including a complete blood count, chest radiograph, Quantiferon assay, rapid plasma reagin, and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption test, was unremarkable. The patient was started on oral prednisone 60 mg daily. Two weeks after initiation of corticosteroids, his right‐eye visual acuity improved to 20/40 − 1 with reduced retinal whitening and resolution of subretinal fluid. Prednisone was tapered, and at a two‐month follow‐up, visual acuity was 20/25 + 2 with reconstitution of the ellipsoid zone and normalization of multimodal imaging.

Nine months after the initial presentation, the patient reported decreased vision in his left eye. On examination, visual acuity was 20/25 + 2 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye; slit‐lamp examination remained unremarkable with no relative afferent pupillary defect. Fundus examination of the left eye revealed mild whitening in the nasal macula. OCT of the left eye showed loss of the ellipsoid layer, disruption of the interdigitation zone, retinal pigment epithelium loss in the nasal macula, and a thickened choroid. Fluorescein angiography of the left eye demonstrated early hypofluorescence with late perifoveal staining; indocyanine green angiography showed hypocyanescence in the same distribution; OCT‐angiography confirmed a choriocapillaris flow deficit in the nasal macula. Imaging of the right eye remained stable without recurrence.

A 30-year-old primigravida underwent a routine second-trimester anomaly scan at 24 weeks of gestation. The pregnancy had progressed uneventfully, with no maternal illnesses, teratogenic exposures, or family history of congenital anomalies. 

Ultrasound (Voluson S6) revealed a solitary, well-circumscribed, anechoic, nonvascular, fluid-filled structure in the fetal cranial region measuring approximately 15.1 mm in diameter. Adjacent brain structures showed no significant mass effect. 

Based on these imaging findings, the prenatal differential diagnosis included an arachnoid cyst, porencephaly, an intracranial cystic tumor, or congenital malformations such as Dandy-Walker malformation. 

Genetic testing via amniocentesis (karyotype and chromosomal microarray) was performed and returned normal results. Additional maternal serological tests for infections, including toxoplasmosis and cytomegalovirus, were negative.

A 69-year-old man with end-stage COPD and pulmonary hypertension underwent bilateral lung transplantation. Induction immunosuppression was with basiliximab and high-dose methylprednisolone, followed by tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone. Seven months post-transplant, he developed lethargy, gait instability, delayed speech, and declining pulmonary function tests. Empiric high-dose steroids for presumed acute rejection were given after a non-diagnostic bronchoalveolar lavage.

Over the next 2–3 weeks, he developed short-term memory loss, behavior changes, episodes of staring with confusion, limited verbal responses, and acute worsening of gait and aphasia. Neurologic examination showed inattention, delayed responses to questions, intermittent command following, tremors, and bilateral clonus; strength was preserved.

Head CT demonstrated bifrontal and right-greater-than-left temporal deep and subcortical white matter hypoattenuation, suggestive of a subacute white matter process. Brain MRI with and without contrast revealed abnormal T2/FLAIR hyperintense signals in bilateral frontal, parietal, and temporal white matter (predominantly right frontal). 

On hospital Day 2, lumbar puncture showed 2 nucleated cells/μL, glucose 52 mg/dL (blood glucose 80 mg/dL), and protein 74.9 mg/dL. CSF cytology, Toxoplasma gondii PCR, EBV PCR, HSV-1 and HSV-2 PCR, and VDRL were negative.

A 22-year-old G1P1 woman at 38 weeks’ gestation, with no comorbidities, was admitted for labor. Four days before delivery she tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 by RT-PCR but remained asymptomatic. She delivered a female infant vaginally; Apgar scores were 10 and 10 at 1 and 5 minutes. Birth weight was 2670 g.

At 11 minutes of life the neonate developed tachypnea, nasal flaring, chest retractions, grunting, and an oxygen saturation of 90%, requiring noninvasive ventilation. The Silverman score was 3. Heart sounds were normal and peripheral perfusion was intact. Arterial blood gas showed pH 7.30, PCO₂ 60 mmHg, PO₂ 65 mmHg, and bicarbonate 20 mmol/L. At 30 minutes a nasopharyngeal swab was positive for SARS-CoV-2; IgM and IgG were negative. The infant was isolated and transferred to the NICU for continued noninvasive ventilation.

A chest radiograph at 30 minutes showed bilateral opacities consistent with respiratory distress syndrome. Intravenous penicillin and gentamicin were started. After 5 days, blood and cerebrospinal fluid cultures remained negative and C-reactive protein levels were low; antibiotics were discontinued. On day 6 of life, respiratory distress persisted. A chest CT scan showed bilateral parenchymal ground-glass lesions involving 10–20% of lung volume. Laboratory tests at that time revealed elevated liver enzymes (ALT 60 IU/L, AST 540 IU/L), elevated LDH, and a pro-BNP level >350 ng/L; echocardiography showed no coronary dilation.

A 30-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with a 3-week history of worsening crampy abdominal pain, nausea, and bloody diarrhea. She denied smoking or alcohol use. Her only medication was a progesterone-only contraceptive, which she had been taking for 2 months.

On examination, her temperature was normal, blood pressure 104/64 mm Hg, heart rate 114 bpm, and BMI 32.3. Abdominal palpation revealed diffuse tenderness without guarding or rigidity; bowel sounds were normal.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, metabolic panel, and coagulation studies; C-reactive protein was 4.8 mg/dL. Stool cultures and assays for Clostridioides difficile toxins were negative. Fecal calprotectin was elevated at 2006 µg/g (reference 10–50 µg/g).

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated mild thickening of the mid- and distal descending colon with adjacent inflammatory stranding; there was no evidence of perforation, abscess, or diverticulosis.

She was treated with intravenous fluids, antiemetics, and pain medications, and received a single dose of ciprofloxacin and metronidazole. 

Colonoscopy revealed segmental erythema and ulceration in the descending and sigmoid colon, with normal-appearing mucosa in the ascending colon, transverse colon, and rectum. 

Biopsy specimens from the affected segments showed subepithelial edema, hemorrhage, mild crypt architectural distortion, and an acute inflammatory infiltrate without granulomas or dysplasia.

A 56‐year‐old man with metastatic upper-tract urothelial carcinoma had been receiving pembrolizumab for 26 months (33 cycles) after progression on chemotherapy. He presented with a 2-day history of fever and general fatigue. On examination, he had pale eyelid conjunctiva, yellowish ocular conjunctiva, and mild subcutaneous bleeding on the lower extremities. Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin concentration of 4.7 g/dL (baseline 10.5 g/dL), a platelet count of 81×10^3/μL (baseline 195×10^3/μL), an elevated lactate dehydrogenase level of 223 U/L (baseline 110 U/L), total bilirubin 2.7 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL, indirect bilirubin 1.0 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 69 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 113 U/L, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 223 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 518 U/L. Coagulation studies were notable for a prothrombin time–international normalized ratio of 1.13 and activated partial thromboplastin time of 31.2 seconds. Immunologic testing revealed a cold agglutination reaction of 256, a positive direct Coombs test, a positive indirect Coombs test, and a negative Donath–Landsteiner test. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen demonstrated hepatosplenomegaly and enlarged mesenteric and hepatic‐hilum lymph nodes but no evidence of bleeding or infection. Bone marrow puncture revealed no malignant findings.

A 60-year-old chronic alcoholic man presented with a 3-day history of self-induced vomiting (5–6 episodes/day), cough with expectoration, hiccups, altered behavior, and dizziness, followed by a fall in the washroom one day prior. Ten days earlier, he had been hospitalized for symptomatic hyponatremia (serum sodium 123 mEq/L, potassium 4.9 mEq/L) and treated with 3% hypertonic saline at 0.5 mEq/L per hour, rising to 129 mEq/L over 12 hours; he improved and was discharged on day 6. He re-presented with imbalance, slurred speech, drowsiness, fever, and cough for 2 days. On examination, his GCS was E4 V1 M1; he had hypertonia and hyperreflexia in all limbs, bilateral extensor plantar responses, nystagmus, and restricted extraocular movements. He was intubated for airway protection. All routine blood, urine, and radiological studies were normal. MRI of the brain (coronal FLAIR T2-weighted) showed central pontine hyperintensities with peripheral sparing forming a trident pattern in the upper pons, plus involvement of the midbrain tegmentum, bilateral thalami, and parts of the globus pallidus.

A 7-month-old girl was referred for evaluation of neurodevelopmental delay and progressive, pharmacoresistant myoclonic seizures. She was the second child of healthy, nonconsanguineous parents. Pregnancy was uneventful; at 39 + 1 weeks she was delivered by cesarean section for placental detachment (birth weight 3.4 kg; Apgar scores 6 and 8). In the neonatal period she exhibited myoclonic movements, cyanosis, and hypotonia, prompting admission to the NICU. 

By day 23 of life she developed recurring focal motor seizures of the upper limbs with apnea. Physical examination showed marked global hypotonia and dysmorphic features, including midfacial hypoplasia, bilateral strabismus, tongue protrusion, and dysplastic, overfolded helices. 

Metabolic testing (urinary organic acids, plasma amino acids) was normal, and empiric biotin and pyridoxine therapy produced no benefit. Brain MRI was unremarkable, and EEG remained normal even during the myoclonic movements. Targeted investigations excluded Prader–Willi syndrome, Pompe disease, and congenital disorders of glycosylation. Karyotype was normal; chromosomal microarray revealed a 1p31.3 duplication of uncertain significance. Laryngomalacia was treated with supraglottoplasty without effect on the spasms. She was discharged with a working diagnosis of sleep myoclonus. 

At 7 months of age she had profound truncal hypotonia with inability to lift her head and worsening myoclonic epilepsy triggered by auditory and visual stimuli.

A 27-year-old Togolese student presented with an 8-month history of a chronic, nonhealing ulcer of the glans penis. Two weeks before presentation, he noted dysuria and burning on urination. The ulcer began as painless erythematous nodules (≈1 × 1 cm) on the glans that evolved into multiple enlarging ulcers around the urethral meatus. He denied trauma, surgery, weight loss, fever, cough, or other constitutional symptoms. He had received BCG vaccination at birth and had tried various herbal treatments without benefit.

On examination, he appeared in good general condition with well-colored conjunctivae. Genitourinary exam revealed a circumferential ulcer of the glans measuring 6 × 4 × 3 cm with irregular margins, a dirty, hemorrhagic, and necrotic base, and a poorly defined urethral meatus. Bilateral inguinal lymph nodes (0.5–2 cm) were firm and mobile. The remainder of the genital exam and systemic examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (54 mm/hr), normal blood glucose, urea, and creatinine levels, and negative HIV and VDRL serologies. Microscopic examination and cultures of urine showed no abnormalities; no acid‐fast bacilli were seen in ulcer scrapings, urine, or sputum. Ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder was normal, and a chest radiograph showed no abnormalities. A biopsy of the lesion was obtained and sent for histopathologic evaluation.

A 68-year-old woman (162 cm, 52 kg) underwent elective total elbow arthroplasty under general anesthesia. Her history included well-controlled diabetes, Parkinson’s disease, depression, anxiety, and dementia. Home medications were valproate, olanzapine, quetiapine, donepezil, diazepam, levodopa, pregabalin, and rasagiline (discontinued two weeks preoperatively). She had experienced delusions and intermittent drowsiness two years earlier but had five prior uneventful general anesthetics.

Preinduction, she was alert and oriented without parkinsonian tremor. Vital signs: BP 145/86 mmHg, HR 78 beats/min. Anesthesia was induced with propofol, remifentanil, and rocuronium and maintained with desflurane, remifentanil, and intermittent rocuronium targeting MAP > 70 mmHg, BIS 40–60, and TOF < 30%. Total anesthesia time was 510 minutes; 3100 ml crystalloid given; urine output 540 ml. Hemodynamics were supported with ephedrine and phenylephrine as needed. 

At the end, anesthetics were discontinued and neuromuscular block was reversed with sugammadex. Although TOF returned to ≥ 90% and spontaneous breathing resumed, her BIS repeatedly fell to 50–60. On examination, her eyelids were tightly closed with left- or downward-deviated eyes; she was semi-comatose with neck and right arm stiffness and no response to painful stimuli. Temperature was 37.1 °C and arterial blood gas results were normal. One hour postoperatively there was no change in mental status. A neurologic consultation was obtained, and computed tomographic angiography of the head showed no evidence of acute stroke.

A 60-year-old man was brought by ambulance for acute right back pain of 5 hours’ duration. The pain was constant and sharp, initially localized just inferior to the tip of his right scapula, and then radiating to his right chest. He denied fever, cough, dyspnea, hemoptysis, falls, or other trauma. His medical history was notable for hypertension for 4 years without treatment.

On examination, temperature was 36.4 °C, heart rate 105 beats/min, blood pressure 98/53 mm Hg, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Conjunctival pallor was noted. Breath sounds were diminished over the right lung field and normal on the left, without rales. Cardiac examination was unremarkable. There was no midline spinal or paraspinal tenderness.

Laboratory evaluation revealed a hemoglobin level of 74 g/L, a D-dimer of 6.08 mg/L, and fibrin degradation products of 16.50 mg/L. Contrast-enhanced chest CT showed a large right hemothorax and an 8.1 × 5.9 × 7.5 cm well-circumscribed, contrast-enhancing mass within the right hemithorax. A distinct feeding vessel arose from the thoracic aorta to supply the mass.

A 9-year-old boy presented with a 10-day history of left heel pain and inability to bear weight, without antecedent trauma. 

First presentation (day 1):  
• Unable to walk on the left foot but otherwise well.  
• Diagnosed clinically with Sever’s disease and discharged with community physiotherapy.  

Second presentation (day 5):  
• Increased pain; exam showed a hot, swollen, erythematous left heel and ankle.  
• Plain radiographs of the foot and ankle showed soft-tissue swelling, sclerosis and fragmentation of the calcaneal apophysis, and widening of the subtalar joint.  
• Again diagnosed as Sever’s disease and discharged.

Third presentation (day 10):  
• Constitutional symptoms: pyrexia, dehydration, severe foot pain.  
• Marked soft-tissue swelling around the ankle and extending lymphangitis up the lower leg.  
• Laboratory studies: WBC 11.1×10^9/L, neutrophils 8.0×10^9/L, ESR 68 mm/hour, CRP 198 mg/L.  
• Orthopedic consultation was obtained, and the patient was admitted for suspected osteomyelitis.

A 46-year-old South Asian woman presented with gradually progressive black pigmentation of her lower lip and tongue over 10 years. She has a history of interstitial lung disease associated with mixed connective tissue disease. She is a nonsmoker, works as a teacher, and has no relevant drug exposures or family history of hyperpigmentation, skin disease, or gastrointestinal disorders.

On examination, confluent lenticular brown-black macules involved the lateral borders of the tongue, lower lip, buccal mucosa, gingivae, and hard and soft palate. Multiple fingernails and toenails had pigmented longitudinal striae; after removal of varnish and acrylic nails from two toenails, true longitudinal melanonychia was evident.

Her body mass index, blood pressure, fasting blood glucose, and full blood count were normal. Plasma cortisol and adrenocorticotrophic hormone levels were normal. There was no history of heavy metal exposure or malnutrition. A prior endoscopic evaluation showed no evidence of gastrointestinal polyposis.

An 85-year-old Japanese man was brought to the emergency department with one hour of excessive diaphoresis and drowsiness. Three days earlier, he had started oral cefcapene pivoxil hydrochloride for suspected urinary tract infection. His history included subtotal gastrectomy with Billroth II reconstruction for gastric cancer four months earlier, total laryngectomy for laryngeal chondrosarcoma, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and neurogenic bladder requiring intermittent catheterization. He had become withdrawn, ate only carbohydrates since losing his teeth, and rarely consumed meat or dairy products.

On arrival he was cachexic and drowsy but arousable with stimulation. Vital signs were stable. A finger-stick glucose measured 47 mg/dL; intravenous 50% dextrose transiently improved his symptoms. He was admitted and started on a 10% glucose infusion plus empirical piperacillin-tazobactam.

Initial laboratory studies showed: blood glucose 58 mg/dL, normal insulin (9.5 μU/mL) with slightly elevated C-peptide (6.21 ng/mL), negative urinary ketones, mild anemia, hypokalemia, respiratory alkalosis with secondary non-anion gap metabolic acidosis, elevated C-reactive protein (2.13 mg/dL), and lactate (22.8 mg/dL). Head CT was unremarkable, and chest/abdominal CT without contrast showed no infection focus or pancreatic lesion. Anti-insulin antibodies were negative.

During hospitalization his glucose stabilized with fluids, and antibiotics were stopped after two doses when sepsis was deemed unlikely. He was discharged on day six with nutrition counseling for small, frequent meals and a tentative diagnosis of late dumping syndrome based on his history and laboratory findings. Despite adherence to dietary modifications, he continued to experience postprandial hypoglycemic episodes with diaphoresis over the next four weeks.

A 27-year-old woman with a 9-month history of systemic lupus erythematosus was admitted with 4 days of worsening pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, and arthralgias in the setting of an acute SLE flare. She noted a 1-day history of a burning, annular eruption on her trunk, palms, and soles. Her medications included hydroxychloroquine, prednisone, and atovaquone. 

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and metabolic panel. Anti–double-stranded DNA antibody titer was 266 IU/mL (elevated), C3 was 41.4 mg/dL (low), and C4 was 6.62 mg/dL (low). Antinuclear antibody was 1:640 with a speckled pattern; anti-Smith and anti-ribonucleoprotein antibodies were positive. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 45 mm/h.

On examination, there were blanchable, erythematous macules and annular urticarial papules and plaques bilaterally on the palmoplantar surfaces, and faint, blanchable erythematous macules on the chest and back. A shave biopsy of a lesion on the left plantar surface showed neutrophils aligned along the dermoepidermal junction with vacuolar alteration and rare dyskeratosis, and a superficial interstitial and perivascular predominantly neutrophilic infiltrate with lymphocytes and leukocytoclasia, without vasculitis or a significant increase in dermal mucin.

A 15-year-old Malay male with T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia diagnosed at age 13 presented during the ninth cycle of maintenance chemotherapy with fever, lethargy, and new-onset jaundice. His chemotherapy regimen (modified DCOG ALL-9 high-risk) included dexamethasone, high-dose methotrexate, 6-mercaptopurine, triple intrathecal therapy, vincristine, daunorubicin, and cytarabine/cyclophosphamide. He had previously experienced febrile neutropenia, vincristine-induced myopathy, and ileus, all managed appropriately. 

On examination, his temperature was 38.5 °C; he appeared pale and jaundiced, with fair hydration and mild hepatomegaly (2 cm below the costal margin). There were no signs of abdominal pain, bleeding, pruritus, or other infection foci. Laboratory tests showed isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal transaminases, albumin, and prothrombin time. The dose of oral 6-mercaptopurine was reduced; bilirubin levels fell but remained elevated. 

Subsequently, after fasting for two days during Ramadan, he developed neutropenia, Escherichia coli septicemia, and abdominal distension; infection resolved with antibiotics, yet severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia recurred. Two months later, during an Acinetobacter baumannii septic episode, his bilirubin rose to 487 µmol/L. Jaundice worsened during both infection and fasting. 

Further investigations, including tests for viral hepatitis, metabolic disorders, hemolysis, and autoimmune disease, were negative. Abdominal ultrasound and CT scans demonstrated hepatosplenomegaly and early portal hypertension. A liver biopsy showed periportal hepatitis with stage 4 fibrosis, likely methotrexate-induced.

A woman in her late 60s presented with difficulty and pain when walking and wearing shoes. She had a history of abnormal enlargement of the right second toe that had been present since childhood. During adolescence, the second toe was similar in size to the great toe, but it progressively increased in size with advancing age. Her medical history was notable for hypertension and diabetes mellitus. On examination, there was macrodactyly of the right second toe without skin changes or signs of infection. Plain radiographs of the feet showed soft-tissue hypertrophy and osteoarthritis of the right second metatarsophalangeal joint, with osseous overgrowth displaying a mushroom-shaped appearance. T1- and T2-weighted MRI of the right foot demonstrated enlargement of the second toe, osteosclerotic findings from the second metatarsophalangeal joint to the distal phalanx, and a proportional increase in soft-tissue and bone volume. Brain MRI revealed a 7 × 5 mm cystic pituitary microadenoma, but hormone tests showed no abnormalities, and the possibility of acromegaly was considered low.

A 69-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of recurrent pain and swelling of the left third finger. One year earlier, the finger had been punctured by wire during agricultural work; after the injury the swelling was mild but gradually worsened over the past 6 months despite several courses of empirical antibiotics. He had no notable medical history. 

On examination, his temperature was 36.6°C, blood pressure 140/100 mmHg, heart rate 81 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute. The left third finger was swollen and tender; there was no involvement of other joints and no systemic symptoms. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the left hand demonstrated a large fluid collection with diffuse synovial thickening and enhancement extending from the proximal to the distal third metacarpal bone, and multiple small intra-synovial bodies (“rice bodies”) along the third flexor tendon. 

Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin of 13.1 g/dL (reference 13.5–17.5), C-reactive protein 0.87 mg/dL (reference <0.5), normal white-cell count and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and normal liver and renal function. An antinuclear antibody titer was <1:80; rheumatoid factor was negative. Tests for hepatitis B and C, HIV, syphilis, and interferon-gamma release assay for tuberculosis were all negative. 

On hospital day 2, incision and drainage of the left hand yielded numerous small whitish granules along the flexor tendon. Histopathology showed acute and chronic inflammation. Stains and cultures for bacteria, fungi, and acid-fast bacilli and PCR assays for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and NTM were negative. 

Subsequent histopathologic review of the rice bodies demonstrated chronic granulomatous inflammation with caseous necrosis.

A 39-year-old woman with well-controlled hypertension had a mild SARS-CoV-2 infection confirmed by PCR one month earlier. She now presents with a 3-day history of worsening generalized body aches, chills, fever, watery diarrhea, nausea, mild dry cough, mild dyspnea, and nonspecific chest pain. On admission, her blood pressure was 82/44 mmHg, heart rate 132 beats per minute, temperature 101.5°F (38.6°C), and oxygen saturation remained above 90% on 2 L nasal cannula. Cardiovascular examination revealed an S3 gallop, 2+ peripheral pulses, warm extremities, and bilateral pitting edema. Pulmonary examination was unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies showed positive SARS-CoV-2 RNA by PCR, troponin-I 4.295 ng/mL, B-type natriuretic peptide 2291 pg/mL, and elevated inflammatory markers including LDH, ferritin, C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, and interleukin-6. Blood cultures were negative. Electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus tachycardia without ST-segment changes. Chest radiograph and CT angiography of the chest were unremarkable.  
Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 20–25%, left ventricular end-diastolic diameter of 6.1 cm, and apical akinesis; there was no pericardial effusion or significant valvular abnormality.

A 67-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of persistent subretinal fluid in her left eye despite 29 consecutive monthly intravitreal aflibercept injections for presumed neovascular age-related macular degeneration. She first noted visual symptoms at age 40 but received no treatment until the anti-VEGF regimen. No intraretinal fluid had ever been observed on OCT.

Her right eye history included foveal pigment epithelial changes, a shallow pigment epithelial detachment, and transient subretinal fluid that completely resolved after a single ranibizumab injection 22 months earlier. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/80 in the left eye and 20/32 in the right eye. Anterior segments were notable only for early corticonuclear cataracts; intraocular pressures were normal. She had arterial hypertension, hypothyroidism, arthritis, and psoriasis on ramipril, bisoprolol, torasemide, and levothyroxine. No family history of retinal disease was reported.

Fundoscopy showed pigment epithelium alterations at both maculae, with a slight foveal prominence on the left. Multimodal imaging was performed:

– Right eye: Near-infrared and SD-OCT revealed pigment epithelium mottling and a shallow pigment epithelial detachment. OCT-angiography showed a type 1 choroidal neovascularization without leakage on fluorescein or indocyanine green angiography. Indocyanine green angiography demonstrated multifocal choroidal hyperpermeability. Enhanced-depth OCT measured subfoveal choroidal thickness at 371 µm.

– Left eye: Near-infrared and SD-OCT showed a serous neurosensory detachment of the fovea with elongated photoreceptors and an underlying shallow, irregular, vascularized pigment epithelial detachment. Subfoveal choroidal thickness was 266 µm. Blue-autofluorescence revealed an ill-defined gravitational tract approximately 4,300 µm by 4,800 µm. The presence of a type 1 choroidal neovascular membrane was confirmed on fluorescein angiography, indocyanine green angiography, and OCT-angiography, with only faint leakage observed.

An 83-year-old woman, previously healthy except for hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia, and overactive bladder on long-term rosuvastatin, febuxostat, vibegron, and vonoprazan, presented 2 days after her fourth dose of BNT162b2 COVID-19 vaccine with fever and immobility. She had mild local reactions after her prior three vaccinations. On examination, her Glasgow Coma Scale was 14 (E4V4M6), temperature 37.9 ℃, pulse 92 beats/min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg. There was discharge and redness around both eyelids; the thyroid gland, chest, and abdomen were unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed an elevated C-reactive protein of 2.89 mg/dL. Morning serum cortisol was low at 4.4 µg/dL (reference 6.4–21.0 µg/dL) with an adrenocorticotropic hormone level of 21.6 pg/mL (7.2–63.3 pg/mL). Thyroid-stimulating hormone was 0.46 µIU/mL (0.38–4.31), free triiodothyronine 1.86 pg/mL (2.10–3.80), and free thyroxine 0.48 ng/dL (0.82–1.63). Prolactin was elevated at 55.45 ng/mL (6.12–30.54). Immunoglobulin G, IgG4, and angiotensin-converting enzyme levels were within normal limits. Computed tomography of the head showed enlargement of the sella turcica with suprasellar extension. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a pituitary gland enlarged for age with a thickened pituitary stalk and loss of the posterior pituitary bright spot.

A 77‐year‐old man with a 15‐year history of rheumatoid arthritis treated with iguratimod and low‐dose prednisolone and diabetes mellitus presented with a cough and sputum production. He had a 40‐year history of smoking 20 cigarettes per day. On examination, he was afebrile (37.1°C), blood pressure was 135/67 mmHg, heart rate 87 bpm, and respiratory rate 20/min. Neurologic examination was normal. Laboratory tests showed an elevated C‐reactive protein level of 6.9 mg/dL (normal 0.03–0.17 mg/dL) and reduced creatinine clearance of 45.5 mL/min. Serum β‐D‐glucan, myeloperoxidase‐ANCA, proteinase‐3‐ANCA, Aspergillus antigen, interferon‐gamma release assay for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and anti–Mycobacteria antibody tests were negative. HIV antibody was negative. Chest computed tomography revealed multiple cavitary lesions in the right lower lobe. Infectious causes such as Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, acid‐fast bacillus infection, and staphylococcal pneumonia, follicular bronchiolitis, and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis were considered.

An 81-year-old man from northeast Thailand presented with a 1-month history of progressive shortness of breath, nonproductive cough, left-sided pleuritic chest pain, and decreased appetite. He denied fever or hemoptysis. His medical history was notable only for hypertension; he had no history of tuberculosis, no high-risk exposures, was a lifelong nonsmoker, and had no family history of lung cancer.

On examination, he was afebrile, with a respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute and an oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. Percussion of the left hemithorax revealed dullness, breath sounds were decreased, and egophony was present over the left lower lung field. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 10.9 g/dL; other hematologic and biochemical tests were within normal limits. Ultrasound-guided thoracentesis yielded 1.2 L of bloody pleural fluid. Analysis of the fluid revealed a pH of 7.439, glucose 104 mg/dL, protein 4.4 g/dL, LDH 1606 U/L, red blood cells 930 000/μL, and white blood cells 2730/μL (51% lymphocytes, 25% eosinophils, 24% neutrophils). The adenosine deaminase level was 24.7 U/L. Cytologic examination of the fluid was negative for malignancy. A closed Abrams needle biopsy of the parietal pleura demonstrated chronic pleuritis without evidence of granuloma or malignancy.

A 77-year-old White woman presented with chest pain, abdominal discomfort, nausea, and vomiting for one day. Her medical history included bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement for calcific aortic stenosis, hyperlipidemia, hypothyroidism, and obstructive sleep apnea. The chest pain was intermittent, nonexertional, and pressure-like, accompanied by four episodes of nonbloody bilious vomiting and dull, poorly localized abdominal discomfort. Vital signs were notable only for a blood pressure of 175/84 mm Hg. On examination, she appeared ill and diaphoretic. A systolic murmur was heard at the aortic area. The abdomen was tender diffusely without peritoneal signs, and bowel sounds were present. 

An initial electrocardiogram showed ST-segment elevations in leads II, III, and aVF with Q waves and reciprocal ST-segment depressions in leads I and aVL. High-sensitivity troponin I was 111 ng/L (normal < 54 ng/L). She was given aspirin, unfractionated heparin, ticagrelor, and a high-intensity statin, and underwent urgent coronary angiography. Angiography revealed a 50% ostial right coronary artery stenosis with thrombolysis in myocardial infarction grade 3 flow; intravascular ultrasound confirmed no hemodynamically significant stenosis. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed normal left ventricular systolic function (ejection fraction 60%) with no regional wall motion abnormalities and noted bioprosthetic aortic valve stenosis. In the absence of critical coronary stenosis and normal wall motion, cardiology concluded that the electrocardiographic changes were of noncardiac origin and recommended discontinuation of heparin and ticagrelor.

A 46-year-old woman was referred to outpatient psychiatry with a 7-year history of a structured delusion of triplet pregnancy. She believed her unborn “babies” were pressing on her stomach and blocking food passage, causing gastric discomfort. Over the previous year, she began self-inducing vomiting and restricting intake, losing 20 kg in 9 months. She denied fear of weight gain or other purging methods.  
Initial evaluations, including upper gastrointestinal endoscopies, were normal. Laboratory tests revealed subclinical hypothyroidism and iron-deficiency anemia. She had no hallucinations, partial affective blunting, and no insight. She did not meet criteria for anorexia nervosa. Food refusal and vomiting were attributed to her delusional beliefs. She was diagnosed with delusional disorder and hypothyroidism, treated with olanzapine and levothyroxine, and gained 2 kg in 2 weeks. After 20 days of involuntary hospitalization, she left treatment.  
One year later, she returned voluntarily, still delusional, weighing 25.1 kg (BMI 10.8). She was readmitted and started on clozapine. After 45 days of hospitalization, she developed fever and cough. A chest radiograph revealed marked esophageal dilation. Chest computed tomography confirmed esophageal dilatation, and subsequent esophageal manometry and a barium swallow study showed delayed esophageal emptying.

A 72-year-old woman with cT1N0M0 stage IA primary right upper lobe lung cancer and poor pulmonary function underwent stereotactic body radiotherapy (48 Gy in 4 fractions). She was a heavy smoker (Brinkman index 900). Before SBRT, serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) was 14.7 ng/mL; KL-6 was 230 U/mL and SP-D was 72.8 ng/mL. Follow-up CT at 2 months showed irregular patchy consolidation in the irradiated field; at 6 and 9 months the consolidation retracted and CEA declined. At 12 months, CT demonstrated a mass-like consolidation around the treated area, and at 13 months it had increased in size; no air bronchograms were seen, and the right 3b bronchus was displaced. Serum CEA, KL-6, and SP-D were unchanged. FDG-PET showed high uptake in the consolidation (SUVmax = 5.61). CT-guided biopsy yielded class II cytology and no histologic evidence of malignancy.

A 48-year-old man, a hepatitis B carrier, presented with sudden onset of left lower limb weakness (3/5 MRC) and numbness, accompanied by acute urinary retention (>1 L residual). He denied trauma or back pain. Neurologic examination showed isolated left lower limb hyperreflexia, L1–S1 motor weakness (3/5), and diminished sensation over those dermatomes; there was no saddle anesthesia and anal tone was normal. He ambulated with a walking stick. Whole-spine MRI revealed only mild spinal canal stenosis at L2–L5 and C3–C6 without cord signal changes. The patient left against medical advice.  

The next day, he returned with new left upper limb C5–T1 weakness (2/5) and hypo-reflexia, plus worsening neck pain; there was no contralateral involvement and Hoffman’s sign was negative. Brain CT and MRI showed no infarct or hemorrhage, and routine blood tests were unremarkable. Repeat whole-spine MRI demonstrated mild cord signal changes at C3–C6, suggestive of early myelomalacia.

A 38-year-old man with a 4-year history of hypertension treated with valsartan 160 mg daily was admitted for elective L5–S1 spinal fusion. He had undergone two prior surgeries before his hypertension diagnosis without complications. He denied drug intolerance, atopy, or family history of angioedema and had not received nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs in the perioperative period. Preoperative vital signs, airway examination, physical examination, and laboratory tests were unremarkable. 

On the day of surgery, anesthesia was induced with intravenous fentanyl and propofol, and tracheal intubation was facilitated with atracurium. The patient was placed prone, and anesthesia was maintained with isoflurane and fentanyl. Intraoperatively, he received 10 mg of morphine and 1 g of cefazolin. At the end of a 305-minute procedure, after turning the patient supine, marked swelling of the face and neck was noted, involving the eyelids, cheeks, and lips. Direct laryngoscopy revealed an edematous tongue, floor of the mouth, glottis, and supraglottic tissues without any associated rash. Auscultation was clear, and vital signs remained within normal limits.

A 14-year-old girl presented nine months after a motor vehicle accident with frontal sinus fractures, intermittent CSF rhinorrhea, and meningeal symptoms treated empirically for meningitis and herpes simplex. She underwent surgical debridement of the sinuses, dural repair, and placement of a lumbar CSF drain. During her perioperative course she had a pruritic fine papular rash attributed to ceftriaxone, which resolved after changing antibiotics. After removal of the lumbar drain, she developed a severe postural headache with nausea, vomiting, and refusal to ambulate. Head CT showed a bifrontal extradural CSF collection. Under anesthesia, an epidural blood patch (15 mL autologous blood) was performed one level above the lumbar drain site. The headache resolved, and she had only mild backache. Eighteen hours later she was noted to be flushed and febrile (maximum temperature 38.8 °C) but was no longer orthostatic, had no nausea, vomiting, or meningeal signs, and her neurologic examination and complete blood count were normal. A repeat head CT showed a significant decrease in the extradural CSF collection. Approximately three hours thereafter, she developed pruritus of the arms and legs with a fine maculopapular rash similar to her earlier eruption.

A 69-year-old woman presented with two months of progressive bilateral hand pain, numbness, and tingling that occurred with exertion. She denied headaches, visual changes, jaw claudication, or shoulder or hip girdle stiffness. She had no history of coronary or peripheral vascular disease, never smoked, and was a vegetarian. Her medications were lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide and a statin. Twenty-five years earlier she had bilateral mastectomies for breast cancer with chemotherapy but no radiation; she had no history of axillary lymph node dissection, radiation, or trauma.

On examination, she appeared well. Radial and ulnar pulses were nonpalpable bilaterally, and upper extremity blood pressures were unobtainable. Temporal arteries were normal in appearance and palpation; range of motion of shoulders and hips was full without stiffness.

A CT angiogram of the neck showed a left subclavian artery irregularity with stenosis proximal to its crossing of the first rib, a focal dilation in the proximal left axillary artery, and severe axillary and brachial artery stenosis; the right subclavian artery was irregular and the right axillary artery was occluded. In the hospital, laboratory studies revealed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 40 mm/h (normal 0–30 mm/h) and a normal hemoglobin of 12.3 g/dL. Catheter angiography demonstrated a 3–4 cm focal occlusion of the right axillo-brachial artery with distal reconstitution, occlusion of the left subclavian artery just past the vertebral takeoff, and reconstitution of the left axillary artery distal to the clavicle. A high-sensitivity C-reactive protein level was 118.4 mg/L (normal <7.4 mg/L).

A 61-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, and hypertension presented with 48 hours of left scrotal pain and swelling. The pain was constant, throbbing, worsened by movement, and localized to the posterior left hemi-scrotum with radiation to the right. He also reported a 3-day history of subjective fevers, chills, dysuria, urgency, frequency, and urinary retention. He denied trauma and any history of sexually transmitted infections.

On arrival: temperature 98.7°F, blood pressure 156/60 mm Hg, heart rate 69 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He appeared comfortable. Cardiac, respiratory, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Urogenital examination showed swelling and erythema of the left hemi-scrotum, marked tenderness over the left epididymis, and a swollen, erythematous penis. There was no crepitus, bullae, blisters, or skin discoloration. Prehn sign was negative, cremasteric reflexes were absent bilaterally, and blue dot sign was negative.

Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 29 600/μL (91% neutrophils), hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL, glucose 244 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 39 mg/dL, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, C-reactive protein 27.2 mg/dL, and creatine kinase 345 U/L. Urinalysis was cloudy, negative for leukocyte esterase and nitrites, with 4+ protein, 2+ glucose, 1.0 EU/dL urobilinogen, 3+ blood, and rare red and white blood cells. HIV and RPR tests were negative, and initial blood and urine cultures showed no growth.

Scrotal ultrasound demonstrated an extremely complex, hypervascular left epididymis, while a testicular duplex scan was normal. The Fournier’s Gangrene Severity Index was calculated at 7. He was started on levofloxacin for presumed acute epididymitis, and urology was consulted 22 hours after admission.

A 17-year-old boy with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome on long-term immunosuppression (prednisolone 10 mg daily, mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg daily, tacrolimus 5 mg twice daily) and 8 months of isoniazid preventive therapy presented with focal seizures of his left arm, secondarily generalizing to status epilepticus. He remained afebrile throughout and denied headache or photophobia. After initial convulsions, he developed choreiform movements of the left arm, persistent despite anticonvulsants, followed by left upper-limb weakness without sensory loss; on day 10 he exhibited continuous seizure-like movements of the left arm lasting hours, consistent with epilepsia partialis continua. 

On examination, he was hemodynamically stable with a Cushingoid appearance, slurred speech, and an upper-motor-neuron pattern of left arm paresis. There was no neck stiffness, rash, or funduscopic abnormality. 

Laboratory studies showed normal complete blood count, liver function tests, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein. Serum anti–nuclear antibody and double-stranded DNA tests were negative. Renal function, calcium, and magnesium were within normal limits. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal protein and glucose with a scant lymphocytic infiltrate; bacterial cultures of blood, urine, and CSF were negative. ELISA testing of CSF for Japanese encephalitis virus, herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2, and cytomegalovirus IgM was negative. 

Nonenhanced head CT on day 1 was unremarkable. On day 3, T2-weighted brain MRI demonstrated high-intensity signals in the right hippocampal gyrus, right putamen, and head of the caudate nucleus, suggestive of multiple infarctions; MR angiography and venography were normal, excluding macrovascular occlusion. Repeat MRI one month later showed enlargement of these lesions and new areas of right cerebral cortical involvement with vasogenic edema, and repeat CT revealed new cortical infarctions without basal ganglia involvement.

A 52-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus (diagnosed at age 17, treated chronically with low-dose prednisolone) and muscle-specific kinase–positive generalized myasthenia gravis was admitted to the intensive care unit for respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation. She had received high-dose steroids, plasmapheresis, and intravenous immunoglobulin for an SLE flare with CNS involvement and her myasthenic crisis.

During her ICU stay, she developed a ventilator-associated pneumonia treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics, then presumed hepatitis E infection treated with ribavirin (complicated by agranulocytosis treated with G-CSF), and subsequently a severe pneumonia with pneumothorax leading to septic shock. Blood cultures grew multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae and Staphylococcus epidermidis, and she received appropriate antibiotics.

Despite a transient decline in procalcitonin levels, she remained febrile with elevated C-reactive protein, ongoing leukocytosis, and persistent requirements for norepinephrine support. A disseminated intravascular coagulation picture developed. Repeated whole-body CT scans, white-cell scans, microbiologic testing (including fungal serology), and blood cultures failed to demonstrate an active infection except for elevated Epstein–Barr virus copies, which were attributed to reactivation. CT imaging showed resolution of the prior lung infiltrates. Laboratory studies at this point demonstrated pronounced leukocytosis with 75% eosinophils and coagulopathy consistent with DIC.

A 32-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of persistent, gray-to-blue-brown patches with underlying telangiectasias on the face, ears, and lateral and posterior neck in sun‐exposed areas. He initially received diagnoses of erythematotelangiectatic rosacea and melasma and was treated with broad-spectrum sunscreen; oxymetazoline/ivermectin/niacinamide cream; and a hydroquinone/kojic acid/vitamin C/niacinamide cream. Three months later, only slight improvement on the cheeks was noted. Hydroquinone was discontinued, and oxymetazoline cream was continued. Due to persistent pigmentation, melasma was favored, and tranexamic acid 325 mg twice daily was prescribed. After 4 months without improvement, he reported regular sunscreen use and wearing a sun-protective hat, noting that unexposed areas under the hat remained spared. Further history revealed 1 year of outdoor work for a water company involving meter reading and digging. Riehl’s melanosis was considered, and a punch biopsy was performed. Histologic examination (H&E) showed brown pigment in the superficial papillary dermis and within epithelioid histiocytes. A Fontana-Masson stain was positive for melanin pigment.

A 56-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of progressively severe low back pain and new-onset urinary incontinence. There was no history of trauma, tumor, or infection. On examination, she had bilateral radicular pain and saddle anesthesia. Motor strength was preserved, and plantar responses were normal. Urodynamic studies demonstrated neurogenic overflow incontinence. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis with eosinophilia; other routine blood tests were within normal limits. 

Plain radiographs of the pelvis revealed an expansile lytic lesion of the right iliac wing with near-complete cortical destruction of the sacrum. Pelvic CT demonstrated a well-circumscribed cystic mass in the right pelvis tracking along the lumbosacral plexus roots. MRI of the lumbosacral spine showed sacral bone destruction replaced by a multiloculated cystic mass extending into the spinal canal, producing cauda equina compression. These findings were described as suggestive of infection or tumor such as echinococcosis or chordoma. The patient was diagnosed with a slow-onset cauda equina syndrome, and further investigations were undertaken to determine the etiology of the lesion.

A 41-year-old man who works in a diesel workshop and smokes daily was referred for sudden bilateral hearing loss. Three weeks earlier, he developed red eyes, photophobia, and gait instability. Three days after symptom onset, he received topical prednisolone without improvement. Eight days later, he experienced bilateral sudden hearing loss, progressive vertigo, tinnitus, headache, and worsening gait instability; three days later, he was given acyclovir (750 mg every 8 hours) and referred for further evaluation.

On examination, he had anterior uveitis, episcleritis, vertigo, bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, and gait instability. Audiologic testing showed a normal type A tympanogram, “no pass” transient evoked otoacoustic emissions at 75 dB, vestibular dysfunction on nystagmography (abnormal saccadic eye movements, altered optokinetic response, bilateral hyporeflexia on caloric testing), and pure-tone audiometry with moderate-severe bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (average 64 dB). An auditory steady-state response confirmed the 64 dB hearing loss.

Laboratory studies revealed creatinine clearance 50.9 mL/min, leukocytes 10.4 k/µL, monocytes 1.12 k/µL, mean corpuscular hemoglobin 31.6 pg, red-cell distribution width 15.4%, lactate dehydrogenase 245 U/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 39 mm/h, positive C-reactive protein, and IgG for rubella. HIV, hepatitis B and C, rheumatoid factor, VDRL, lupus erythematosus cells, anti-SSA/SSB, antinuclear antibodies, anticardiolipin antibody, and ANCA were negative.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a two-week history of abnormal behavior, decreased concentration, and postural instability. She had a history of insomnia and irritable bowel syndrome and was taking vitamin D3, vitamin K, manganese, and activated charcoal. She and her parents denied other medications. She had been started on lorazepam by her general practitioner without improvement.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Teeth had a greyish discoloration. Neurologic exam showed confusion, impaired attention, and disorientation. Muscle tone and strength were normal; coordination, sensation, and cranial nerves were intact; there were no pyramidal signs.

While in the emergency department, she became more somnolent and developed frequent myoclonic jerks. Laboratory tests including CBC, renal, hepatic, and thyroid function, CRP, vitamin B12, and folate were normal; syphilis and HIV tests were negative. Noncontrast brain CT was unremarkable. Lumbar puncture showed protein 47 mg/dL (15–45) and 10 WBC/μL (<5). Empiric IV acyclovir and ceftriaxone were started for possible infectious encephalitis.

On the neurology service, she remained moderately drowsy with exuberant generalized myoclonus at rest and on action. EEG revealed generalized background slowing without focal or periodic features. Brain MRI on hospital day 5 was normal. She clinically worsened despite antivirals and antibiotics, so intravenous immunoglobulin was given empirically for presumed autoimmune encephalitis. A trial of levetiracetam 1000 mg/day failed to improve the myoclonus.

A 48-year-old man with a history of hypertension presented with 3 months of progressive skin tightening, difficulty clenching his fists and opening his mouth, and mild shortness of breath. Physical examination showed numerous waxy, 2 to 3-mm papules on the upper arms, chest, post-auricular scalp, and eyebrows. A skin biopsy demonstrated stromal fibroblast proliferation and mucin deposition in the upper dermis. Thyroid function tests were normal. Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation revealed an IgG λ paraproteinemia. He was treated with prednisone and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) 1 g/kg every 4 weeks, with improvement in his cutaneous findings.

Seven years later, he developed several days of fatigue, myalgia, sore throat, and cough. A chest radiograph showed a small lung infiltrate, and he received azithromycin for presumed pneumonia. Days later, he presented with altered mental status, aphasia, and tonic-clonic movements in all extremities. On admission, he developed fever and seizures that electroencephalography confirmed as status epilepticus. He was intubated, and neurologic examination revealed left-sided motor weakness and right-sided gaze deviation. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging of the head were unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed 10 white blood cells/µL (reference, 0–5), protein 47 mg/dL (reference, 15–45), and an opening pressure of 29 cm H₂O. CSF testing was negative for bacteria by culture. PCR testing of the CSF was negative for herpes simplex virus 1 and 2 and varicella zoster virus. A nasal swab PCR test confirmed influenza A infection. Complete blood count, metabolic panel, urinalysis, chest radiograph, and blood cultures were unremarkable.

A 36-year-old Hispanic man with no significant past medical history presented with two weeks of cough, shortness of breath, and persistent sore throat. He was treated outpatient with azithromycin and prednisone; a rapid strep test was negative. He then developed spastic back pain radiating to his left leg, followed days later by 8/10 substernal chest pain and exertional dyspnea. Over the next week he spiked fevers to 38.9–40 °C daily. On the third day of fever he presented to an outside emergency department, declined lumbar puncture, and returned two days later with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, chest pain, and dyspnea at rest.  
Initial studies showed a neutrophilic leukocytosis of 44 × 10^3/µL, C-reactive protein of 41 mg/dL, elevated troponin, and an electrocardiogram concerning for an ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction. He underwent left and right heart catheterization, which revealed clean coronary arteries, but he developed severe hypotension requiring vasopressors. Computed tomography of the chest demonstrated bilateral lower-lobe infiltrates, and he was treated empirically for septic shock. He was found to have myopericarditis and was started on colchicine 0.6 mg daily and prednisolone 60 mg daily.  
An extensive infectious workup including respiratory viral panel (SARS-CoV-2, influenza, adenovirus, RSV, etc.), HIV, CMV, blood and urine cultures, fungal antigens, syphilis serology, tick- and mosquito-borne panels, Lyme serology (ELISA positive, Western blot negative), Leptospira antibodies, and CSF testing was unrevealing. Laboratory abnormalities included lactate dehydrogenase 1089 U/L, ferritin > 15 000 ng/mL, triglycerides > 354 mg/dL, and a negative direct Coombs test. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain was normal.  
On hospital day 7 he was transferred to our facility. On arrival he was tachycardic to 120 beats/min, normotensive, and febrile to 40 °C. Repeat EBV serology was negative. He experienced episodes of hemoptysis. Liver function tests showed ALT 233 U/L, AST 226 U/L, ALP 328 U/L, GGT 232 U/L, and total bilirubin 3.5 mg/dL. Inflammatory markers peaked with an ESR of 91 mm/hr and CRP of 30 mg/dL. Triglycerides were 385 mg/dL, and soluble interleukin-2 receptor was 5531 pg/mL. Hepatitis B and C serologies and hepatic vein Doppler were negative.  
Peripheral smear revealed normocytic anemia with neutrophilic leukocytosis, no spherocytes or schistocytes, and no blasts. A CT-guided iliac bone marrow biopsy showed a hypercellular marrow without hemophagocytosis, blasts, or evidence of malignancy; genetic testing for JAK2, BCR-ABL, FLT3, IDH1/2, and NPM1 mutations was negative. Rheumatologic studies revealed an ANA titer of 1:320 with a negative extractable nuclear antigen panel and normal complement levels.  
CT chest showed small bilateral pleural effusions and dependent consolidations consistent with atelectasis. Transthoracic echocardiogram and brain MRI were normal. Serial ECGs demonstrated diffuse PR-segment depression consistent with pericarditis.

A 43-year-old healthy Caucasian woman presented with 7–10-day recurrent flares of lower extremity tenderness, swelling, and redness over several months. She also reported upper back and neck myalgias and a one-year history of headaches with transient, curtain-like visual disturbances in her right eye that ophthalmology diagnosed as ocular migraines. Initial laboratory testing showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 31 mm/H, a positive antinuclear antibody, and elevated ribonucleoprotein antibodies (2.4 AI). Double-stranded DNA, antichromatin, anti-Smith, SM/RNP, and Lyme disease antibodies were negative. She received a presumptive diagnosis of undifferentiated connective tissue disease, was started on prednisone for flares, and was referred to rheumatology.

Two months later, she experienced erythema nodosum of the lower extremities, Raynaud’s phenomenon, chest pain, and visual disturbances suggestive of amaurosis fugax. She kept a diary of transient fatigue and painful hand and finger swelling with petechiae and purpura. Brain MRI revealed a 6 mm lacunar infarct in the left cerebellum and a 12 mm cortical sulcal hemorrhage in the right frontal lobe. Magnetic resonance angiography of the head and ophthalmologic assessment were unremarkable. Carotid ultrasound and stress echocardiogram showed no vascular disease or ischemia. At a second rheumatology consultation, concern was raised for evolving mixed connective tissue disease, but undifferentiated connective tissue disease was retained due to a negative ANA.

Seven months after initial presentation, neurology evaluated her for worsening lightheadedness and 6–7/10 bifrontal and apical headaches lasting hours to days. Neuro-ophthalmology found no retinal vasculitis and attributed her right homonymous visual field defect to the known brain lesion rather than amaurosis fugax. Neurology ordered a contrast-enhanced brain MRI and MR venogram to rule out thrombosis and assess for new lesions.

A 20-year-old Middle Eastern woman, gravida 3 para 2, with two prior uneventful pregnancies, presented at 38 weeks’ gestation in early labor. Her antenatal course was unremarkable, and she had a normal vaginal delivery of a healthy male infant. On the morning of postpartum day 1, she developed a sudden, nonpruritic maculopapular rash over her upper limbs, abdomen, and back; the face, neck, palms, and lower limbs were spared, and there were no striae. She denied allergies and had received no new medications. Twelve hours later, she complained of increasing generalized abdominal pain, nausea, and occasional vomiting. Her vital signs were normal (BP 120/70 mmHg; pulse 83 beats/min; temperature 37.1 °C). Urinalysis disclosed yellow turbid urine with 3+ proteinuria and numerous white cells but no glycosuria; a Foley-catheter specimen confirmed these findings. A dermatologist diagnosed a nonspecific maculopapular rash and recommended observation without specific therapy. Initial laboratory tests—including liver and renal function, complete blood count, serum glucose, lactate dehydrogenase, and coagulation profile—were all within normal limits.

A nine-month-old female presented with a one-week history of cough, catarrh, and fever and was admitted and treated for pneumonia. After two weeks, respiratory distress persisted, and over the next two months she had recurrent and worsening dyspnea with repeated admissions. A chest radiograph showed left upper-lobe consolidation and collapse, and she was started on anti-Koch’s therapy. Mantoux test was 5 mm, erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 65 mm/hr, and tests for HIV I and II were negative. There was no history of contact with tuberculosis, vaccinations were up to date, and there was no family history of asthma or atopy; poor weight gain was noted. Echocardiography performed for persistent dyspnea showed a small secundum atrial septal defect, which subsequently closed after six months. After 12 months of anti-Koch’s therapy, at 2 years of age she remained dyspneic with poor weight gain (8.5 kg). Chest auscultation revealed widespread rhonchi and crepitations without cyanosis. A repeat chest radiograph showed a hyperinflated right lung, left upper-lobe collapse, and left mediastinal shift. Anti-Koch’s therapy was discontinued, and diagnoses such as bronchial asthma, foreign-body aspiration, or congenital lung malformation were entertained. A chest CT scan showed collapse consolidation of the left upper lobe with extensive air bronchogram and compensatory hyperinflation of the right upper lobe. A decision was made to perform a left upper lobectomy.

A 33-year-old man with known arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy presented with palpitations, tachycardia, and multiple shocks from his dual-chamber implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for ventricular tachycardia (VT) with left bundle branch–block morphology and inferior axis (cycle length, 375 ms). Despite amiodarone and lidocaine infusions, VT recurred with hypotension and signs of volume overload. Transthoracic echocardiography showed biventricular dysfunction: left ventricular ejection fraction of 14% and a severely enlarged right ventricle with reduced systolic function.

He underwent VT ablation under general anesthesia (propofol and fentanyl) with phenylephrine and epinephrine infusions to maintain blood pressure. Epicardial and endocardial mapping identified targets in the right ventricular outflow tract and inferolateral tricuspid valve annulus; ablation terminated VT. Because of hemodynamic instability during induced VT, an Impella CP device was placed prophylactically and provided maximal support throughout the procedure. Heparin (5000 U) was given after epicardial access, maintaining activated clotting times of 170–190 s. The procedure lasted 4 hours, after which the Impella device was removed without alarms or technical issues.

Dark-tinged urine was noted at the end of the procedure. Soon thereafter, the patient became anuric. His serum creatinine rose from 1.0 mg/dL preprocedure to 3.8 mg/dL, and he developed metabolic acidosis (pH, 7.17). Hemoglobin decreased from 13.5 g/dL to 11 g/dL.

A 31-year-old Japanese-American man presented with a five-day history of new-onset dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, and nonproductive cough. One year earlier, a “heart murmur” was noted but never evaluated. His sister had a spontaneous pneumothorax, and both siblings were taller than their parents. He had no known family history of cardiac disease. On examination, he was a thin, tall man (185 cm) with a 2/6 systolic murmur and a 2/4 diastolic murmur. An ECG showed normal sinus rhythm, evidence of left atrial enlargement, and left ventricular hypertrophy with strain, with no ischemic changes. A chest X-ray revealed marked cardiomegaly. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated global hypokinesis with an LVEF of 28%, an LVEDV of 479 mL, a trileaflet aortic valve with severe aortic regurgitation, mild-moderate pulmonary hypertension, mild atrial and right ventricular enlargement, and a 9.4 cm ascending aortic aneurysm without dissection at the level of the sinuses of Valsalva. A CT angiogram confirmed aneurysmal dilatation of the ascending aorta up to 8.7 cm in diameter and severe four-chamber cardiomegaly with an asymmetrically enlarged left ventricle; the coronary arteries were patent.

A 30-year-old woman presented with a 7-month history of intermittent bright red rectal bleeding associated with constipation and perianal pain. She had no weight loss or abdominal pain and no significant medical history. Family history was notable only for a benign colonic polyp in her mother and various cancers in grandparents. Physical examination was unremarkable, and flexible sigmoidoscopy revealed a sessile malignant‐appearing polyp in the lower rectum. Pelvic MRI staged the lesion as T3 N0 M0, and biopsy confirmed moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma. She received long-course neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy with oral capecitabine, with only transient angina-like chest pain. Restaging MRI showed tumor downstaging to T2, and she underwent laparoscopic ultra–low anterior resection with defunctioning loop ileostomy; pathology demonstrated a complete response (pT0 pN0 R0). 

At 3 months postoperatively, surveillance CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis identified four new subcapsular wedge‐shaped low‐attenuation lesions in the liver, reported as suspicious for metastases. Liver‐specific contrast–enhanced MRI (Primovist) showed four corresponding foci of low T1 signal, none of which were of high T2 signal or exhibited hepatic steatosis; postcontrast images demonstrated minimal arterial enhancement, no rim enhancement, and low signal on the delayed hepatobiliary phase. A subsequent PET–CT scan showed no FDG‐avid liver lesions or extrahepatic disease. The lesions were not visible on ultrasound, and the multidisciplinary team agreed to perform a CT‐guided core biopsy of the most accessible lesion.

A 15-year-old right-handed boy presented with a 3-month history of a gradually enlarging, firm swelling over the anterior aspect of his right thigh. The lesion appeared after a direct trauma sustained during a soccer match. He reported mild pain but no limitation of hip or knee motion. On examination, the mass was tender, firm, and distinct, with no overlying skin changes. Hip and knee ranges of motion were full, and neurovascular examination of the right lower extremity was normal.  

Plain radiographs of the femur demonstrated a well-circumscribed lesion abutting the cortex with peripheral calcification and a multilamellar periosteal reaction. CT imaging revealed a zonal lesion characterized by peripheral ossification surrounding a nonmineralized central area. MRI showed an oblong mass within the vastus intermedius muscle with heterogeneous T1 and T2 signal, a hypointense rim on both sequences, no enhancement after gadolinium administration, underlying cortical irregularity and thinning, and a periosteal reaction with displacement of adjacent muscle fascia.

The patient is a 3-year-old girl from China who presented with a congenital left upper extremity deformity. Previous radiographs showed a deformity within the left forearm and hand, but left radial aplasia was excluded. Holt–Oram syndrome was previously excluded due to the lack of cardiac malformations and, more definitively, the lack of mutations within the TBX5 gene. Klippel–Trenaunay syndrome was previously excluded due to the lack of a port-wine stain or other vascular malformations and the absence of limb or tissue overgrowth; prior genetic testing revealed no mutations within the PIK3CA gene, making Klippel–Trenaunay syndrome unlikely.

On physical examination, the left hand had only four digits, likely from congenital fusion of the first and second digits, which functioned as a thumb opposing the fifth digit with very good strength. The left forearm measured 2 cm shorter than the right with apparent synostosis of the proximal radioulnar joint, and the left humerus measured 3 cm shorter. The patient was unable to undergo passive pronation or supination of the left hand but had preserved flexion and extension at the elbow. Examination of the back demonstrated a symmetrically higher left scapula with a hard prominence palpable at the cervicothoracic junction.

Initial radiographs of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine demonstrated mild cervical scoliosis. Further imaging revealed partial fusion of the left cervicothoracic spine from C4 to T1 and elevation of the left scapula with an associated omovertebral bone. Additional imaging of the left upper extremity confirmed a proximal radioulnar synostosis. Incidental findings included a left cervical rib and a tracheal bronchus. The patient had normal hearing and no congenital cardiac or genitourinary defects on further workup.

A 67-year-old man with dementia was referred for recurrent right-sided gluteal swelling and anaemia after a minor fall 28 days earlier. He was non-communicative and had no obvious external bleeding. On day 2, 500 mL of clotted blood was evacuated through a 4 cm incision; no bleeding point was identified, and he received 2 units of packed red cells (pre-evacuation hemoglobin [Hb] 6.3 g/dL, post-evacuation Hb 8.7 g/dL). He remained haemodynamically stable on day 3. On day 4, the haematoma recurred, and his Hb fell from 8.7 g/dL to 4.9 g/dL, prompting 4 units of red cells. On day 5, his Hb fell again to 6.4 g/dL; he received plasma and 3 units of red cells and underwent a second surgical evacuation, which again revealed no active bleeding. He remained stable on day 6. Because of a history of haematemesis, gastroscopy and colonoscopy were performed on day 6, revealing no recent or active bleeding.

A 12-year-old, left-limb–dominant boy presented with a 2-month history of right groin pain and a limp. Laboratory studies showed a normal white blood cell count, an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and a positive C-reactive protein; antistreptolysin O titer and rheumatic factors were within normal limits. On examination, there was no swelling or local increase in temperature, but deep tenderness was noted over the right groin. Plain radiographs of the pelvis revealed a sclerotic, cherry-sized shadow in the ischiopubic region extending toward the obturator foramen, without periosteal reaction or soft-tissue shadows. A CT scan demonstrated an enlarged, unfused ischiopubic synchondrosis with a lytic lesion and no periosteal reaction or inflammatory changes. MRI showed a hyperintense signal on T2 with fat saturation, a hypointense signal on T1, fusiform swelling with fibrous bridging, and signal alteration of the adjacent soft tissue.

A 30-year-old woman, two weeks postpartum, was admitted with fever, palpitations, erythema, inflammation, and purulent discharge around her cesarean wound. Vital signs: temperature 37.3 °C, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, pulse rate 89 bpm. Initial labs: RBC 4.4×10^6/µL, hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, hematocrit 36%, WBC 11.6×10^3/µL (neutrophils 73%, lymphocytes 18%), platelets 213×10^3/µL. She was diagnosed with a wound infection and treated with cefazolin, gentamicin, and metronidazole. On day 5, she developed hearing loss and gentamicin was discontinued. She has a history of substance use and is on methadone maintenance.

On hospital day 9, she developed nausea, vomiting, aphasia, loss of consciousness, hearing disturbances, extreme rigidity, and gaze deviation and was transferred to a tertiary center. Repeat labs: RBC 4.7×10^6/µL, hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL, WBC 15.4×10^3/µL (neutrophils 92%), AST 29 IU/L, ALT 18 IU/L, Na⁺ 136 mEq/L, K⁺ 4.4 mEq/L, CRP 33 mg/L, arterial blood gas pH 7.307, PCO₂ 26.9 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 13.2 mmol/L. Viral serologies and blood cultures were negative.

CSF analysis: clear fluid, WBC 0–1/µL, RBC 2/µL, protein 202 mg/dL, glucose 99 mg/dL; Gram stain and cultures negative; oligoclonal bands negative; IgG index 0.6; albumin index 5.4. A CSF viral pathogen panel was negative for EBV, CMV, HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, HHV-6, HHV-7, parvovirus B19, and enterovirus.

Brain MRI (axial T1, T2, FLAIR, DWI; sagittal and coronal T2) showed diffuse T2 hyperintense signal changes in the bilateral periventricular white matter and the corpus callosum.

A 43-year-old man presented via video consultation with a chief complaint of worsening, painful oral lesions that began 6 weeks earlier and rated 10/10 in severity. He reported rinsing his mouth with hydrogen peroxide and brushing his tongue with both manual and electric toothbrushes for 5 minutes multiple times daily to “get rid of the mouth infection.” His past medical history included a Staphylococcus aureus infection at age 2 and multiple recurrent skin infections he also attributed to S. aureus. He recently saw his primary care provider for a skin rash thought to be another S. aureus flare, who prescribed cefalexin and mupirocin. He denied any psychiatric history and reported therapeutic marijuana use and occasional alcohol consumption.

Extraoral examination by video revealed a maculopapular rash on the neck and around the right ear. He had provided intraoral photographs showing multiple large ulcers on the buccal mucosa bilaterally, on the right retromolar trigone and hard palate, and in the lower right buccal vestibule. He also suspected exposed bone in the left mylohyoid ridge. During the consultation, he insisted he had an “active S. aureus infection” in his mouth.

He was prescribed chlorhexidine 0.12% rinse twice daily and 2% viscous lidocaine for pain relief and was advised to discontinue hydrogen peroxide. An in-person visit for incisional biopsy was scheduled, and he was referred to dermatology and infectious disease for further assessment. One week later, at the in-person visit, he reported persistent pain (8–9/10) and demonstrated large erosions and ulcers on the right buccal mucosa, hard palate, and left mylohyoid ridge, fewer than in his photographs. He brought zip-lock bags containing material he described as foreign bodies and bacteria removed from his mouth. Our initial differential included self-induced injuries, and an incisional biopsy of the right buccal mucosa was recommended.

A 13-year-old boy was evaluated for a 1-day history of constant, nonradiating abdominal pain that worsened with light activity and an associated fever. He had a 2-year history of headache and seizures. He lived in a rural area and had no prior hospitalizations or medications.

On admission, his temperature was 40 °C, blood pressure 110/75 mm Hg, heart rate 92 beats/min, and respiratory rate 18 breaths/min. General and abdominal examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory tests showed a white-blood-cell count of 7400 cells/mm3, hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, platelets 275 000 cells/mm3, and an elevated alkaline phosphatase level of 548 IU/L. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 16 mm/h, and C-reactive protein was negative. Blood and urine cultures and serological tests were negative. Chest radiography, electrocardiography, and abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography were normal.

Cranial computed tomography revealed a left parieto-occipital, hypodense, cystic, well-demarcated lesion. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a mass containing membranous structures with cerebrospinal-fluid intensity in the left paraventricular region.

A 3-month-old male infant was referred for evaluation of anemia. He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy. At 5 days of age he developed neonatal jaundice, and at 1 and 2 months he had two episodes of acute anemia following febrile upper respiratory symptoms, each requiring red-cell transfusion. During the second episode he received paracetamol and a 5-day course of amoxicillin; a malaria smear was negative, hemoglobin electrophoresis showed no hemoglobin S, and the hemoglobin F fraction was 12% (normal for age). 

At 3 months of age, he was in good general condition but pale, with a palpable spleen; there was no jaundice. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies showed anemia with evidence of hemolysis. A thin blood smear demonstrated parasite inclusions in 11% of red cells identified as Plasmodium falciparum, and a rapid test was positive for P. falciparum. The mother’s smear was also positive. Intravenous artesunate was given to both mother and infant for 3 days, then extended to 7 days when the infant’s parasitemia remained 1%. Further testing showed a normal hemoglobin electrophoresis, a negative direct antiglobulin test, and a glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase level of 3.1 U/gHb (reference, 6.6–17.2). A diagnosis of G6PD deficiency was made, with malaria as the initial trigger. 

At follow-up four weeks later, his hemoglobin remained low at 6.9 g/dL and laboratory markers of hemolysis persisted. The family denied any new fevers, medications, or exposures.

A 42-year-old woman from upstate New York, previously healthy, first noted fatigue, hair loss, paresthesia, and light sensitivity in 2013. Four to six weeks later, she was found to have complete heart block with a junctional escape rhythm; testing was positive for IgG and IgM antibodies against Borrelia burgdorferi, and she was treated with antibiotics. The block persisted, and she underwent placement of a dual-chamber pacemaker. Cardiac MRI at that time was unremarkable.

In 2015 she developed pacemaker syndrome and progressive heart-failure symptoms, prompting upgrade to a cardiac resynchronization therapy pacemaker with a His-bundle lead. Later that year she underwent successful cavotricuspid isthmus ablation for typical right atrial flutter. 

In early 2017 she presented with one year of exertional palpitations and a rapid decline in exercise tolerance. A 12-lead electrocardiogram showed frequent premature ventricular contractions with a morphology suggesting an origin in the basal right ventricle. During a stress test she developed sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed a moderately dilated right ventricle with moderate hypokinesis and mild left ventricular dilation with a normal ejection fraction (55%). Beta-blockade did not reduce her PVC burden (33%), and she was referred for catheter ablation.

During the procedure two distinct PVC morphologies were induced and mapped. Radiofrequency ablation at the right ventricular outflow tract abolished PVC 1, after which PVC 2 was no longer seen. Given the right ventricular dilation, an electroanatomical endocardial activation and voltage map of the right ventricle was created; this revealed extensive fibrosis in the anterolateral and inferolateral right ventricular wall, with a unipolar voltage map suggesting a larger epicardial substrate.

A 55-year-old woman with no past medical history presented with sudden onset of pain in her left middle finger. Examination revealed bruising on both aspects of the finger, sparing the distal phalanx, accompanied by pain and coldness. There was no history of trauma or similar episodes.
