Finger plethysmography showed a pressure of 110 mmHg in the affected finger versus 108 mmHg in the contralateral middle finger.

A second 55-year-old woman with a history of psoriatic arthritis, not on treatment, presented with two days of swelling and bluish discoloration of the right index finger. She denied trauma and was a non-smoker. Examination of the remaining limb and digits showed normal perfusion, and the discoloration involved the finger with sparing of the tip. Finger plethysmography showed a pressure of 123 mmHg in the affected finger versus 118 mmHg in the contralateral index finger.

An 81-year-old woman presented with a 3–4-month history of left maxillary pain. Five months earlier she had undergone extraction of the left maxillary lateral incisor. She denied nasal obstruction, fever, diabetes, or recurrent infections. On examination, there was mild swelling of the left side of the face. Laboratory studies showed no evidence of immunosuppression. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated opacification of the left maxillary sinus. Contrast-enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses revealed a soft-tissue–density mass filling the left maxillary sinus with bone erosion of the anterolateral wall, findings suggestive of a malignancy. A biopsy of the lesion was obtained via a left Caldwell-Luc procedure under local anesthesia.

A 67-year-old woman was evaluated for chronic diarrhea and occasional abdominal pain of several years’ duration, with worsening since July 2021. She denied bleeding or weight loss. Prior evaluations had ruled out bacterial and parasitic infections, inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, and pancreatic disease. A complete laboratory workup was unremarkable, including a normal peripheral eosinophil count (180 cells/μL). 

Colonoscopy showed normal‐appearing mucosa throughout. Random biopsies from the ascending, transverse, descending, and sigmoid colon revealed preserved architecture without lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate but a marked increase in eosinophils (>60 per high-power field; transverse colon: 197/HPF; descending colon: 147/HPF) with focal eosinophilic cryptitis. 

Upper endoscopy with gastric, duodenal, and esophageal biopsies was normal, excluding eosinophilic gastroenteritis. Skin allergy testing excluded atopic disease. Her medications included levothyroxine, bisoprolol, teriflunomide, and clopidogrel, the latter of which had been initiated in April 2021. A temporal association between the start of clopidogrel and onset of diarrhea was noted.

A 30-year-old woman with a 5-year history of infertility presented with progressively worsening lower abdominal pain and distension over 3 months. Initially intermittent, the pain became constant and severe, accompanied by bloating and mild nausea. Eight months earlier, she had undergone a laparotomy for a myometrial mass diagnosed as a smooth muscle tumor of uncertain malignant potential. The prior surgery was uncomplicated. She had no family history of malignancy or gynecological disorders and no known hereditary conditions.

On examination, she appeared uncomfortable because of abdominal distension but was hemodynamically stable. Abdominal palpation revealed diffuse tenderness without rebound or guarding. There was no palpable mass or signs of peritonitis, and bowel sounds were normal. Laboratory studies showed a normal white-cell count (8.5 × 10^3/µL), normal inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, 5 mg/L; erythrocyte sedimentation rate, 15 mm/hr), normal liver and renal function, and normal tumor markers (CA-125, 18 U/mL; CEA, 2.5 ng/mL). A pregnancy test was negative.

Abdominopelvic ultrasound demonstrated a complex intraperitoneal fluid collection with multiple septations and internal debris. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis revealed a large, well-defined cystic lesion in the inter-uterorectal space measuring 14 × 8 cm, exhibiting T2 hyperintensity, T1 hypointensity, thin septa, and no solid components.

A 68-year-old woman presented with a 1-day history of colicky lower abdominal pain, abdominal distention, and vomiting. She had a history of diverticular disease and no prior abdominal surgeries. On examination, her vital signs were normal; she was mildly dehydrated, with tenderness in the right lower quadrant and mild abdominal distention. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 15.9×10^9/L; other results were within normal limits. A nasogastric tube was inserted, intravenous fluids were started, and bowel rest was instituted. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed multiple dilated small-bowel loops in the pelvis with a transition point in the right iliac fossa, consistent with small-bowel obstruction. The surgical team proceeded with diagnostic laparoscopy on the assumption of a congenital band adhesion.

A 55‐year‐old man was referred for evaluation of a palpable mass in the right abdomen. He reported mild discomfort when lying at night but denied pain, trauma, fever, weight loss, nausea, or vomiting. His past medical history and medications were unremarkable. On examination, vital signs were normal. A non-tender, firm mass measuring approximately 20×20 cm occupied the right upper and lower quadrants. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, WBC 8.2×10^9/L, and normal renal, hepatic, and adrenal function. Serum tumor markers and coagulation studies were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 23×20 cm, well-circumscribed, cystic lesion between the liver and right kidney with an enhancing capsule; no metastatic lesions or lymphadenopathy were seen. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI revealed a multicystic lesion in the right adrenal region with a thick capsule and peripheral septations, displacing adjacent organs; large peripheral veins drained into the IVC. After multidisciplinary discussion, the patient was scheduled for surgical resection.

A 49-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of recurrent, painless frank terminal hematuria accompanied by urinary frequency, urgency, and nocturia (three times nightly). He denied urinary tract infections or stone disease; he was a non-smoker with no family history of malignancy. On examination, he had mild suprapubic tenderness but was otherwise unremarkable. Urine microscopy showed 3 white blood cells and 206 red blood cells per high-power field. Urine cytology revealed atypical urothelial cells. Flexible cystoscopy demonstrated a cystic, hyperemic growth on the left lateral bladder wall. Two days later, contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed focal thickening of the left lateral bladder wall, suspicious for an inflammatory or malignant lesion. The patient was scheduled for transurethral resection of the bladder tumor.

A 25-year-old Japanese man presented with hematemesis, nausea, epigastric discomfort, and severe epigastralgia. He had an identified Dieulafoy’s lesion on the lesser curvature of the gastric body. Vital signs were stable. Physical examination showed marked epigastric tenderness without rebound or guarding. 

Laboratory studies, including liver and renal function tests, were within normal limits. Upper endoscopy revealed multiple map-like ulcerative lesions and scars on the greater curvature of the body to the fornix, together with atrophic gastritis and Helicobacter pylori infection. Magnifying narrow-band imaging showed no abnormal microsurface pattern and only a microvascular pattern raising concern for a possible malignant lesion. Endoscopic ultrasonography demonstrated an irregular thickening of the second layer of the gastric wall without invasion of the third layer.

Biopsy specimens from the ulcer edge disclosed multiple noncaseating granulomatous lesions in the mucosal layer. There were no histopathological features suggestive of Crohn’s disease, Whipple’s disease, reaction to malignancy or foreign body, tuberculosis, histoplasmosis, or syphilis. Chest CT showed an infiltrative shadow and a pulmonary nodule, without involvement of the heart, skin, eyes, or nervous system.

He was treated with a proton pump inhibitor and underwent H. pylori eradication with lansoprazole, amoxicillin, and clarithromycin. However, over the ensuing three to six months, his gastrointestinal symptoms and endoscopic findings showed no improvement.

A 50‐year‐old man presented with a 6-year history of progressive pain and swelling in his left thigh. Six years earlier, he had undergone a needle biopsy of a suspicious lesion in the left femoral shaft at another hospital. On examination, there was a large, immobile, and painless mass over the anterolateral aspect of the left thigh. Laboratory studies were within normal limits: erythrocyte sedimentation rate 12 mm/h (reference, 8–12 mm/h), hemoglobin 14.9 g/dL (12.7–17.2 g/dL), leukocyte count 9800/mL (4600–10 200/mL) with 3.2% eosinophils, and an indirect hemagglutination test for Echinococcus that was negative. Plain radiographs of the left femur showed moderate expansion of the diaphysis, cortical thinning, and a focal cortical defect at the anterolateral upper third of the shaft. Abdominal ultrasonography and thoracic computed tomography revealed no abnormalities. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left femur demonstrated a lesion filling the entire intramedullary canal from the intertrochanteric region to the distal metaphysis with heterogeneous signal characteristics, and a 6 × 3 cm cystic lesion destroying the lateral cortex of the proximal diaphysis and extending into the adjacent vastus lateralis and vastus intermedius muscles.

A 22-year-old Hispanic woman with a history of deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism at age 16, systemic lupus erythematosus, acquired protein S deficiency, and secondary antiphospholipid syndrome presented with generalized weakness, malaise, recurrent fevers, and elevated blood pressure. She had a motor-vehicle accident and a diagnosed viral upper respiratory infection one week earlier and was noncompliant with fondaparinux and prednisone. On examination, temperature was 101.3 °F, blood pressure 140/115 mm Hg, and heart rate 130 beats/min. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 6.5 g/dL, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 95 mm/h. She was treated empirically with broad-spectrum antibiotics without clinical improvement. Renal function worsened, hemoglobin fell further, and thrombocytopenia developed requiring transfusion. She then developed livedo reticularis, right upper-extremity weakness, memory loss, cyanotic left toes with diminished dorsalis pedis pulses, and an absent right radial pulse. Arterial Doppler revealed absence of flow in the distal right radial artery. Brain MRI showed multifocal embolic infarcts. Transthoracic echocardiography showed new mitral regurgitation without thrombus or vegetation. Splenic infarcts were also noted incidentally. Blood cultures were negative. Peripheral blood smear showed no significant schistocytosis, and ADAMTS13 activity was normal. Immunologic studies revealed low C3 and C4, elevated CH50, high-titer anti–double-stranded DNA antibody, positive lupus anticoagulant, positive anticardiolipin antibody, and negative anti–β2-glycoprotein I antibody. Infection screening was negative for syphilis, HIV, and hepatitis C virus, but cytomegalovirus PCR was positive with a viral load of 2300 IU/mL. Renal biopsy demonstrated class II lupus nephritis and thrombotic microangiopathy with glomerular capillary and arteriolar thromboses.

A 32-year-old woman, gravida 4 para 3, was referred at 28 weeks of gestation for evaluation of suspected fetal abdominal pathology. Her pregnancies have been non-consanguineous and prior obstetric history was unremarkable. She was diagnosed with gestational diabetes in the first trimester, currently managed without complication. First and second trimester ultrasounds were within normal limits.

A targeted ultrasound at 28 weeks revealed:
• Intestinal dilation to 20 mm without vascular structures  
• Hyperechogenic bowel  
• Multiple linear calcifications throughout the peritoneum  
• Subdiaphragmatic ascites  
Estimated fetal weight was at the 80th percentile for gestational age. These isolated findings raised concern for intrauterine intestinal rupture with meconium peritonitis. 

Given the suspicion for cystic fibrosis, amniocentesis was performed and a CFTR gene mutation panel was ordered.

A 48-year-old woman with an 11-year history of rheumatoid arthritis, well controlled on etanercept since mid-2005, began in December 2008 to experience progressive bilateral numbness and tingling in her lower limbs and along the ulnar border of her left hand. She also noted perineal numbness and bowel urgency. On neurologic examination, muscle tone, strength, reflexes, and coordination were all normal. Sensory testing revealed reduced vibration sense up to the waist, diminished joint position sense at the feet, and decreased temperature sensation to the knees bilaterally; temperature sensation was also reduced in the ulnar fingers of her left hand. Initial laboratory studies showed a slightly reduced folate level (2.2 ng/mL) and a normal vitamin B12 level. She was seronegative for rheumatoid factor and tested negative for aquaporin-4 antibodies. Antinuclear antibody testing was positive at 1:160 with a speckled pattern, but anti–double-stranded DNA antibody was negative. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal biochemistry and microbiology and no oligoclonal bands. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head was normal, whereas MRI of the cervical spine demonstrated abnormal signal intensity extending from the C3 level to the upper border of T1.

A 10-year-old girl presented with 4 days of colicky epigastric pain that became severe the day before admission. She had no fever, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or other symptoms. She was pale and undernourished. Vital signs were within normal limits. Abdominal examination showed severe tenderness and rigidity in the epigastric and left hypogastric regions and mild hepatomegaly without ascites or splenomegaly.

Laboratory studies on admission revealed hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL, leukocyte count 10.15×10^9/L (neutrophils 79%), C-reactive protein 63 mg/L, serum amylase 274 U/L, and serum lipase 351 U/L. Liver and renal function tests were normal. 

Hepatobiliary ultrasound showed hepatomegaly and a mildly dilated common bile duct (0.8 cm). The gallbladder, pancreas, kidneys, and spleen were normal in size and shape, and no gallstones were seen. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a bulky pancreas with surrounding fat stranding and retention of its contour, consistent with mild acute pancreatitis. There was no peripancreatic fluid collection or necrosis. The liver was enlarged, the CBD remained mildly dilated, and no calculi were identified. Linear hypodense areas were noted in the left proximal jejunum.

An 86-year-old Cameroonian man presented with a 4-week history of low-grade intermittent fever and a 2-week history of mild burning hypogastric pain and watery diarrhea, which became blood-streaked. He had self-medicated with amoxicillin, metronidazole, and ibuprofen without relief. Over the subsequent 2 weeks, he developed worsening headache, anorexia, and weakness. His medical history included well-controlled hypertension and chronic low back pain treated intermittently with NSAIDs.

On examination he appeared frail and dehydrated. Vital signs were: temperature 39.0°C, blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg, pulse 124 bpm, and respiratory rate 29 /min. The abdomen was distended with guarding and rebound tenderness in the hypogastrium; bowel sounds were hypoactive. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis (16,000 cells/mm3, 72% neutrophils) and hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL. A Widal test was positive at a titre of <1/160 for both somatic and flagellar antibodies. An erect chest radiograph demonstrated free air beneath the right hemidiaphragm and distended small-bowel loops. 

A diagnosis of localized peritonitis with severe sepsis was made. After fluid resuscitation and commencement of broad-spectrum antibiotics, the working diagnosis was intestinal perforation due to typhoid fever; perforated peptic ulcer and perforated appendix were also considered. The patient was scheduled for emergency exploratory laparotomy.

A 33-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of atypical abdominal pain, intermittently associated with vomiting and hematemesis. The pain was localized to the left hypochondrium, nonradiating, and described as a feeling of heaviness. Her past medical history was notable for a splenectomy performed 18 months earlier; she reported no other health issues or systemic symptoms.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Abdominal palpation revealed mild epigastric and left hypochondrial tenderness without peritoneal signs. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, coagulation profile, blood electrolytes, liver function tests, C-reactive protein, serum lipase, fasting glucose, and tumor markers (alpha-fetoprotein, CA19-9, CEA), were all within normal limits.

A plain abdominal radiograph showed a mass with internal gas bubbles in the left hypochondrium but no radiopaque marker. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated a 4.2-cm hypodense, spongiform-appearing mass in the splenectomy bed with a mildly enhancing wall, communication with the gastric fundus, and surrounding fat stranding. MRI revealed the lesion to be heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, uniformly hypointense on T1-weighted images, and with mild peripheral enhancement after gadolinium administration.

A 34-year-old man presented with a 3-week history of blurred vision and a 3-month history of progressively worsening, moderate-to-severe, pulsatile headache accompanied by nausea and vomiting that did not improve with migraine therapies. He had no significant past medical history. On examination, his blood pressure was 160/90 mmHg; heart rate and temperature were normal. He was underweight (BMI 18.4 kg/m2). Neurological examination was notable for mild nuchal rigidity; fundus examination revealed bilateral papilledema. Visual acuity was 20/20 in the left eye and 20/22.5 in the right eye; visual fields and pupillary responses were normal. Routine blood tests, including complete blood count, inflammatory markers, electrolytes, and chemistries, were within normal limits. Gadolinium-enhanced brain MRI showed bilateral posterior scleral flattening but no parenchymal lesions or meningeal enhancement. Lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 30.0 cm H2O; CSF cell count, protein concentration, and glucose ratio were normal. He had no history of obesity, recent weight gain, drug exposure, or systemic illness. Further evaluation for secondary causes included hormonal studies, brain MR venography, chest and abdominal CT, autoimmune assessment, and tumor markers. Abdominal CT demonstrated a large (14.7 × 10.6 × 16.4 cm) cystic mass in the right retroperitoneal space causing right hydronephrosis.

A 65-year-old man presented with 4 months of dry cough, progressive dyspnea, intermittent fever with chills and night sweats, minimal sputum production, redness of the eyes, and a 15-kg weight loss. He was an ex-smoker and had a 30-year history of hypertension and poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus. Family history was notable for a son with a gastrointestinal stromal tumor. 

Initial evaluation showed a chest radiograph with right lower zone nonhomogeneous opacity. Sputum smears were negative for acid-fast bacilli (AFB). Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed multiple discrete and conglomerating heterogeneous mediastinal and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (some with calcification), ill-defined right lower lobe ground-glass opacities, and minimal right pleural effusion. Empirical anti-tuberculosis treatment (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, and levofloxacin) was initiated, but sputum and bronchoalveolar lavage studies remained negative for AFB and Mycobacterium tuberculosis by culture and gene Xpert. 

After 2 months, he remained symptomatic, and pulmonary function tests showed a mild restrictive pattern. Repeat chest radiographs demonstrated new bilateral lower zone infiltrates. A PET-CT scan revealed multiple FDG-avid lymph nodes in prevascular, aortopulmonary, bilateral paratracheal, subcarinal, paraesophageal, and hilar regions, FDG-avid perilymphatic nodules in both lungs, bilateral pleural thickening, and a right pleural effusion. Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme was elevated; Mantoux test was negative and interferon-gamma release assay was positive. 

Endobronchial ultrasound–guided fine-needle aspiration of lymph nodes and transbronchial lung biopsy showed nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation without atypical cells. A diagnosis of pulmonary sarcoidosis was made. 

To investigate the pleural effusion, medical thoracoscopy was performed. One hundred milliliters of frankly hemorrhagic fluid were aspirated from the right pleural space. Analysis revealed a lymphocytic exudate (total leukocyte count 24,000/mm3; 98% lymphocytes; protein 6.1 g/dL; LDH 643 U/L; ADA 53.2 U/L), with occasional large atypical and binucleate cells.

A 32-year-old woman with no chronic medical illnesses presented with a 2-week history of a left breast lump and breast pain, which had resolved by the time of presentation; the lump persisted. There was no nipple discharge, trauma, or prior breast surgery. On examination, she was healthy-appearing. A 6×6 cm mobile, non-tender mass was palpable in the left breast between the 2 and 4 o’clock positions, 4 cm from the nipple; the right breast and axilla were normal. Initial breast ultrasound was reported as normal. Ten days later, a repeat ultrasound showed architectural distortion with dilated ducts up to 0.3 cm at the 3 to 4 o’clock position without a discrete mass or significant axillary lymphadenopathy, findings interpreted as consistent with mastitis; inflammatory breast carcinoma was also considered. The patient received oral amoxicillin–clavulanate, with partial reduction in swelling but persistence of the mass. Two weeks later, a third ultrasound demonstrated a 1.3 cm hypoechoic mass with indistinct borders at the 4 o’clock position. A decision was made to proceed with a biopsy.

A 46-year-old woman presented to her general practitioner with a painless left supraclavicular mass that she had noticed several weeks earlier. On examination, there was a soft, oblong mass measuring approximately 11 cm in the left supraclavicular fossa. The left breast appeared slightly smaller than the right, but no other masses or abnormalities were detected. 

An ultrasound examination of the neck demonstrated a hypoechoic, approximately 11-cm oblong lesion in the left supraclavicular fossa. A noncontrast CT scan of the neck was then performed at the patient’s request; interpretation was limited by the lack of intravenous contrast, and the preliminary differential diagnosis from the ultrasound included lymphangioma or cystic hygroma.

The patient was referred to interventional radiology for further evaluation. On targeted questioning, she reported that she had undergone an elective mastopexy in Russia three years earlier. Unsatisfied with the cosmetic result, she subsequently received free liquid silicone injections for breast augmentation; details regarding the volume and grade of silicone were not available. She denied any history of breast trauma or additional relevant medical history.

A 33-year-old Hispanic man with no known past medical history presented with a 1½-week history of headache and blurred vision. MRI of the brain demonstrated a 2.7-cm ring-enhancing lesion in the right temporal lobe with mass effect. He underwent craniotomy with biopsy and resection. Postoperatively, he was found to have HIV infection with a CD4 count <20 cells/µL and an HIV viral load of 191 000 copies/mL. Serum toxoplasma IgG was elevated, and CSF studies showed 48 cells/µL (97% lymphocytes) with positive toxoplasma IgG and DNA-PCR for Toxoplasma gondii (286 copies/mL). Other CSF studies, including fungal cultures, cryptococcal antigen, and AFB smear/culture, were negative. Histopathologic examination of the brain tissue revealed bradyzoites and tachyzoites. He was treated with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and started on antiretroviral therapy; empiric antibiotics for bacterial abscess were discontinued.

Two weeks after discharge, he returned with fever to 39.6 °C, generalized weakness, and a 1-day history of productive cough. Chest radiograph showed a new left upper lobe opacification with diffuse reticulonodular interstitial prominence. CT scan of the chest confirmed extensive reticulonodular interstitial infiltrates with focal consolidation in the left upper lobe. He was started on vancomycin, piperacillin/tazobactam, and fluconazole and placed on airborne precautions. His respiratory status worsened, and intubation was planned pending further diagnostic evaluation.

A 12-year-old girl was referred by her family doctor with a suspicion of peritonsillar abscess after presenting with severe neck pain, odynophagia, and sore throat. Three weeks earlier, she had pharyngitis with fever. On examination, there was an asymmetrical prominence of the left palatino-lingual arch, enlargement of the left palatine tonsil, and tenderness on palpation of the left neck. Laboratory studies showed a mildly elevated C-reactive protein level (13.61 mg/L), leukocytosis (19,650 cells/μL), and neutrophilia (16,330 cells/μL). Serologic testing for Epstein–Barr virus revealed positive IgG anti-VCA and IgG nuclear antigen antibodies, with negative IgM antibodies. The patient was started on intravenous fluids and cefuroxime. Ultrasound of the neck demonstrated enlargement of lymph nodes up to 6 mm with surrounding fat-tissue edema on the left side. Magnetic resonance imaging of the neck revealed soft-tissue infiltration measuring 40 × 35 × 90 mm in the left retropharyngeal space, displacing adjacent pharyngeal structures, and a central collection measuring 15 × 10 × 40 mm consistent with an abscess.

A 34-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease on chronic hemodialysis presented after a first‐time generalized tonic-clonic seizure that stopped spontaneously after a few minutes. Her blood pressure and other vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory analysis revealed urea of 0.60 g/L and creatinine of 20 mg/dL, consistent with her known renal failure; other blood tests were unremarkable. Brain MRI demonstrated atypical signal abnormalities: on FLAIR images there was hyperintensity in the left putamen, and on T1-weighted post‐gadolinium sequences there was gyriform cortical enhancement in adjacent regions.

A 62-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of left flank pain. Her medical history was unremarkable. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits and the physical examination was unremarkable. Complete blood count, electrolytes, eosinophil count, serum biochemistry, and urinalysis were all within normal limits.

A plain abdominal radiograph showed a 3-cm round opacity with evidence of calcifications in the left upper quadrant. Chest radiography was normal. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a calcified heterogeneous cystic mass in the retroperitoneal area between the superior pole of the left kidney and the spleen. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a solitary cystic mass with a calcified wall within the left adrenal gland that showed no enhancement after intravenous contrast. No other intra-abdominal or intrathoracic masses were identified.

MRI of the abdomen with T2-weighted imaging demonstrated a lesion within the left adrenal gland characterized by a hypointense rim corresponding to wall calcification and a peripheral hyperintense nodular focus at the upper pole of the cystic lesion.

A 64-year-old woman with a history of well-controlled epilepsy and no tobacco use presented with a six-month history of productive cough with whitish sputum and three episodes of hemoptysis. She denied fever, weight loss, or night sweats. Initial evaluation at a primary care clinic considered tuberculosis, but a Mantoux test and three sputum acid-fast bacilli smears and cultures were negative. Her symptoms persisted despite courses of oral amoxicillin, azithromycin, and moxifloxacin.

On examination, she appeared thin (BMI, 19.3 kg/m2) but was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and had an oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. There were no digital clubbing, palpable lymph nodes, or oral lesions. Respiratory exam revealed reduced breath sounds at the lung bases. Laboratory studies showed a normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin, 10.3 g/dL), normal leukocyte and platelet counts, an elevated C-reactive protein (3.24 mmol/L), and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 66 mm/hr. Other routine blood tests were within normal limits.

A chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral pleural effusions with bibasal consolidations. A thoracentesis was deferred because the effusions appeared minimal. Bronchoscopy revealed an edematous, white-coated bronchial mucosa, with an area of infiltrative appearance in the right lower lobe.

A 34-year-old woman presented with persistent vaginal bleeding for 2 weeks after undergoing a dilation and curettage for abortion. Her vital signs were stable, and hemoglobin was 11.6 mg/dL. Internal examination was deferred because of active bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a linear defect in the right anterior uterine wall, interpreted as uterine wall perforation, and endometrial thickening, thought to be reactionary to the procedure. Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis demonstrated a partial-thickness defect in the same uterine wall without hematoma or free air; she was discharged for conservative management.

Four weeks later, she returned with ongoing vaginal bleeding. Hemoglobin was 10.8 mg/dL. Repeat transvaginal ultrasound again showed a thickened endometrium. Color Doppler imaging revealed tortuous vessels in the myometrium extending into the endometrium. Spectral Doppler demonstrated high vascularity with a peak systolic velocity of 45 cm/s.

A 53-year-old obese man presented with sudden-onset, pressure-like chest pain and lightheadedness lasting one hour. This was his first episode of chest pain and was not exertional. He had a history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation diagnosed one year earlier, but was not on anticoagulation because his CHA2DS2-VASc score was 0. He was a lifelong nonsmoker and had no notable family history. 

On admission, vital signs were stable. Physical examination showed an irregularly irregular rhythm with a borderline tachycardic rate and normal heart sounds without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. An electrocardiogram revealed coarse atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular rate and premature ventricular contractions. Chest radiography was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed mild thrombocytopenia, normal coagulation tests, mild hyperglycemia, and sequential troponin T levels of 0.02, 0.03, and 0.80 ng/ml (upper limit of normal, 0.10 ng/ml). ProBNP was 1104 pg/ml. Thyroid testing revealed an undetectable TSH, FT4 of 3.79 ng/dl, and FT3 of 6.9 pg/ml. Hemoglobin A1c was 5.6% and LDL cholesterol was 58 mg/dl.

Transthoracic echocardiography with contrast showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 45–50%, apical wall akinesis, normal right ventricular function, mild biatrial dilation, mild-to-moderate mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, and moderate pulmonary hypertension.

He was treated with aspirin, a statin, a beta blocker, and a heparin infusion. A left heart catheterization revealed a thrombotic occlusion of the distal left anterior descending artery without any evidence of obstructive epicardial atherosclerotic coronary disease.

A 34‐year‐old woman presented with pain and slight mobility of the mandibular right second premolar and first molar. Her medical history was unremarkable. On examination, percussion of both teeth was tender, and slight mobility was noted, but the overlying mucosa and skin were normal with no erythema, ulceration, or warmth. Intraoral palpation revealed bony‐hard consistency of the buccal and lingual cortices, and the mucosal integrity was intact.

An initial orthopantomogram showed a unilocular radiolucent lesion engulfing the apices of the right mandibular second premolar and a previously endodontically treated first molar, extending to the superior border of the inferior alveolar nerve canal; its irregular shape was atypical for routine periapical cysts or granulomas. Cone beam CT further demonstrated buccolingual expansion with almost complete obliteration of the lingual cortex, measuring approximately 23.4 × 14.2 × 6.6 mm.

Based on the radiographic findings, the preliminary differential diagnosis included odontogenic keratocyst, radicular cyst, and unicystic ameloblastoma.

A 49-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of a slowly enlarging lump in the right mandibular buccal vestibule. The lesion appeared several weeks after extraction of the lower right molars and was asymptomatic, with no weight loss or systemic symptoms. Her medical history was unremarkable. On extraoral examination, there was no facial asymmetry, edema, or erythema. Intraorally, a soft, non-tender, fluctuant mass with ill-defined borders was palpable between the first and second molar regions on the right buccal vestibule; there was no lingual extension. Tooth 48 was mobile; the roots of the first molar and second premolar were not mobile. Other teeth were intact. Vital signs were normal. 

A panoramic radiograph demonstrated a well-circumscribed radiolucent lesion with a sclerotic border in the edentulous area of the right second molar extending toward the third molar region. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy yielded straw-colored fluid; cytology showed a benign cystic lesion, “that might be seen in a radicular cyst.”

A 41-year-old Haitian woman was referred for evaluation of lifelong, treatment-refractory seizures. She had normal cognitive and motor development and no family history of epilepsy. At age 13, she began experiencing unprovoked myoclonic jerks and generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Within one year, she had nearly daily tonic-clonic seizures and essentially continuous, low-amplitude myoclonic jerks involving the face and all extremities. The myoclonus was markedly worsened by voluntary movement and emotional stress, leading to frequent falls, wheelchair dependence, and difficulty eating and drinking. Cognition remained intact, but her seizures forced her to leave school. Multiple antiepileptic regimens—including phenobarbital, carbamazepine, and topiramate—provided little benefit. 

On examination, she had nearly continuous perioral and hand myoclonus but no ataxia; independent ambulation was impossible. Complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel were normal. Brain MRI was normal. In 2012, serum testing for lysosomal storage diseases was performed and yielded negative results.

A 74-year-old Caucasian woman presented with retrosternal chest pain that developed after emotional stress; the pain resolved spontaneously by the time of arrival.  
Vital signs were within normal limits: oxygen saturation 97% on room air, blood pressure 105/57 mmHg, respiratory rate 17/min, heart rate 75/min, temperature normal. Physical examination was unremarkable, with no signs of heart failure.  
Initial troponin was elevated at 2008 ng/L, peaking at 2232 ng/L (reference <18 ng/L). Bedside echocardiography showed apical ballooning of the left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 45%.  
Her past medical history included systemic sclerosis, hypoparathyroidism, hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, a body mass index of 14, and remote colon cancer resection leading to short bowel syndrome. Medications included flecainide, prednisolone, omeprazole, and calcium/vitamin D replacement; she had a history of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia managed in the past.  
Given concern for a non–ST-elevation myocardial infarction, she underwent CT coronary angiography, which demonstrated minimal ostial left main disease, mild stenoses of the left anterior descending and circumflex arteries, and moderate right coronary stenosis. Coronary anatomy was deemed nonobstructive, and she was managed conservatively with beta-blockade and ACE inhibition.  
One month later, non-stress cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed an improved ejection fraction of 59%. However, there was apical segment wall thickness of 15 mm (normal <12 mm) compared with 7 mm basally, with a spade-like apical cavity. T1 mapping times were elevated at 1219 ms mid-ventricle and 1322 ms apically (normal <1060 ms). Late gadolinium enhancement demonstrated no focal scarring and no evidence of prior infarction.

A 15-year-old boy presented with a 3-week history of intensifying upper abdominal pain and acute bright-red hematemesis. He had no significant medical history apart from lactose intolerance and tonsillitis and was taking no medications. There was no history of splenomegaly, anemia, thrombocytopenia, omphalitis, umbilical vein catheterization, or travel to schistosomiasis-endemic regions. Family history was unremarkable. On examination, he was hemodynamically stable but pale, with palpable splenomegaly and sinus tachycardia. Vital signs: BP 115/80 mm Hg, pulse 98/min, temperature 36.7 °C, BMI 21.6 kg/m2. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.8 mg/dL, platelets 90 000/mm3, and normal CRP and ESR. Echocardiography was normal. Tumor markers (alpha-fetoprotein, CA 19-9, carcinoembryonic antigen, human chorionic gonadotropin) were negative. Lipase levels were normal. Abdominal ultrasound with Doppler revealed absent flow in the portal vein at the bifurcation, dilation of the proximal portal vein to 14 mm, splenomegaly (18 × 12 cm), and no liver parenchymal lesions, masses, or cavernoma; hepatic venous pressure gradient was >10 mm Hg. Magnetic resonance angiography confirmed portal vein thrombosis. Liver function tests, viral serology (HBV, HCV, CMV, EBV), FibroScan (F0), ceruloplasmin, copper, iron studies, and lipid profile were normal. Coagulation tests were within normal ranges, and thrombophilia testing (Antithrombin III, Protein S, Protein C, Factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation, MTHFR, PAI-1) was negative.

An 84-year-old European woman (weight 39.5 kg, BMI < 18.5 kg/m2) with COPD on home oxygen, atrial fibrillation, and congestive cardiac failure presented with 2 days of right groin pain, associated constipation, and reduced mobility. Her medications included warfarin, inhalers, diuretics, and antihypertensives. She had prior open appendectomy and a laparoscopic right totally extraperitoneal inguinal hernia repair. On examination, vital signs were normal (heart rate 67 bpm, blood pressure 145/67 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, temperature 36.2 °C, SpO2 100% on 2 L nasal prongs). The abdomen was soft, with normal bowel sounds and no palpable masses. Right groin pain was exacerbated by extension and abduction of the right hip, with tenderness over the medial adductors. Initial labs (CBC, electrolytes, renal and liver function, coagulation) were normal. A pelvic X-ray showed no fracture or bowel obstruction. The initial differential diagnoses were adductor strain and occult right hip fracture. She was admitted for management of constipation and mobility assessment.

A 51-year-old nonsmoking woman with a history of allergic asthma since age 40, chronic sinusitis, and allergic rhinitis presented with intermittent abdominal cramping pain and generalized pruritic erythematous patches and plaques over her trunk and extremities. She reported urticaria-like rashes precipitated by hot baths and by certain medications (eg, clarithromycin). She also had chronic cough and mild dyspnea; her asthma control test score was 18 of 25, indicating uncontrolled asthma. On examination, bilateral wheezing was noted. Pulmonary function testing showed mild obstructive ventilatory dysfunction and elevated fractional exhaled nitric oxide. Thoracic computed tomography revealed localized bilateral ground-glass opacities. Sinus computed tomography confirmed sinusitis. A gastric mucosal biopsy showed infiltration by lymphocytes and eosinophils. Routine blood tests were notable for an eosinophil count of 2100/μL and a total immunoglobulin E level of 373 IU/mL; hemoglobin concentration and platelet count were normal. Screening for perinuclear and cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies was negative. There was no evidence of parasitic or other infectious pathogens. Physical examination, serum tumor markers, and imaging of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no solid tumors, hepatosplenomegaly, or lymphadenopathy.

A 53-year-old man was admitted for progressive dyspnea (NYHA class III). His history included a congenital ventricular septal defect repaired in childhood, subsequent aortic valve and septal patch replacements, permanent atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, chronic hepatitis C–related liver disease, and prior admission for heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. On examination, he had jugular venous distension, irregular rhythm, a 2/6 systolic murmur at the aortic and mitral areas, decreased breath sounds at the right lung base, and peripheral edema.  
ECG showed atrial fibrillation with left bundle branch block. Chest radiography demonstrated pulmonary congestion and a right basal pleural effusion. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed: a dilated left ventricle with preserved ejection fraction (60%), a dilated right ventricle with normal systolic function, no residual septal shunt, a normally functioning mechanical aortic prosthesis but elevated transprosthetic gradients (mean 33 mmHg) with an effective orifice area index of 0.4 cm2/m2 (suggesting severe prosthesis–patient mismatch), moderate mitral regurgitation, severe tricuspid regurgitation, and estimated systolic pulmonary artery pressure of 50 mmHg. The inferior vena cava was dilated with poor inspiratory collapse.  
An initial diagnosis of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction was made, and intravenous diuretics led to reduction of edema and resolution of radiographic congestion, but the patient remained dyspneic with low exercise tolerance and still required supplemental oxygen.  
A contrast CT scan of the chest and abdomen showed a small right pleural effusion, no lung parenchymal disease or pulmonary embolism, cirrhotic liver with a focal lesion suspicious for hepatocellular carcinoma, splenomegaly, and signs of portal hypertension.  
Right heart catheterization revealed a high cardiac output state, normal pulmonary vascular resistance, and only a slight elevation of mean pulmonary and wedge pressures.

A 42-year-old Thai male ophthalmologist with well-controlled dyslipidemia received his second dose of CoronaVac vaccine at 12:50 pm. Thirty minutes of post-vaccination observation were uneventful, but ten minutes later he noted blurred, foggy central vision that expanded over minutes to obscure the entire left visual field without darkening. There was no headache, weakness, or other neurologic symptoms. He presented to ophthalmology 10 minutes after onset. Visual acuity was 20/20 OU. Anterior segments and fundi were normal. There was no intraocular inflammation or relative afferent pupillary defect. Macular OCT was unremarkable. Automated perimetry (24-2) demonstrated a left congruous homonymous hemianopia respecting the vertical midline. Stroke evaluation was initiated; neurologic examination was normal except for a blood pressure of 150/90 mmHg. Brain MRI with DWI showed no evidence of acute infarction, hemorrhage, significant stenosis, arteriovenous malformation, or aneurysm. Approximately two hours after onset his vision returned to normal and repeat perimetry was normal.

A 66-year-old man was transferred from the neurology ward to the emergency department because of progressive loss of consciousness. His medical history included poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus, atrial fibrillation, and recent myocardial infarction treated with percutaneous coronary intervention 17 days earlier. Twelve days after admission he suffered a focal pontine stroke, resulting in dysarthria, hemiparesis, limb ataxia, and a modified Rankin scale score of 4. He was bedridden and required assistance with drinking. Three days into his hospital stay, empagliflozin (10 mg once daily) was initiated for glycaemic control.

On arrival to the ED–critical care unit, he was stuporous (GCS 10), febrile (38.5 °C), hypotensive (95/50 mmHg), tachycardic (180 bpm), tachypnoeic (RR 26/min), oxygen saturation 94% on 2 L O2, and clinically dehydrated. Laboratory results included: serum sodium 164 mmol/l, potassium 3.3 mmol/l, glucose 322 mg/dl, creatinine 2.1 mg/dl, osmolality 355 mosmol/kg; arterial pH 7.45, PCO2 34 mmHg. Urinalysis revealed osmolality 758 mosmol/kg, glucose 3935 mg/dl, sodium 20 mmol/l, potassium 57 mmol/l, ketone bodies 50 mg/dl. Chest radiograph showed patchy consolidations in the upper lung fields. His regular medications included metformin, insulin, empagliflozin, antihypertensives, antiplatelet agents, and others.

A 66-year-old man under surveillance for non–muscle-invasive bladder cancer (pathology T1G2) treated with intravesical BCG presented for routine follow-up. He was asymptomatic, denied pain with ejaculation or perineal discomfort, and had fathered two children without fertility issues. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including renal function and PSA, were within normal limits. Digital rectal examination revealed a normal, fibroelastic prostate.  
Ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis showed absence of the left kidney and a 7.0 × 3.5 cm multilobed lesion in the left posterolateral pelvic region at the expected location of the seminal vesicle, with cystic areas and internal echogenic content. Cystoscopy demonstrated absence of the left ureteral orifice without other findings.  
Pelvic MRI confirmed absence of left renal parenchyma and identified a tubular structure in the left retroperitoneum dilated to 12 mm, compatible with a remnant ureter and renal pelvis. This structure emptied ectopically into an enlarged, multicystic left seminal vesicle measuring 6.9 × 3.5 cm. Both the seminal vesicle and the ureteral remnant displayed high T1 and T2 signal intensity with thin walls and septa and no significant contrast enhancement. The left vas deferens was patent and mildly thickened near the seminal vesicle, and there was cystic dilatation of the left ejaculatory duct.

A 17-year-old right-handed high school senior and varsity softball pitcher with 11 years of experience presented with a 2-month history of right upper-extremity discomfort. She initially noted vague right elbow pain during overhand throwing, right knee pain previously attributed to plica syndrome, and shoulder tightness. Initial examination revealed:
• Right knee: full range of motion, vague patellar discomfort, negative flexion pinch and Lachman tests  
• Right shoulder: capsular tightness with 125° external rotation and only 5–10° internal rotation in abduction  
• Right elbow and forearm: full range of motion, 5/5 strength, stable ligaments, and no pain on resisted movements  

Plain radiographs of both knees and the right elbow were normal. The knee received a cortisone injection, and she began a capsular stretching program for her shoulder and elbow with good relief in those areas.

Six weeks later, she returned with persistent, worsening right volar forearm pain, now present for over a year and acutely worse after a recent tournament, when she also noted forearm swelling. Examination of the forearm showed:
• No swelling or ecchymosis  
• No pain on bony palpation  
• Pain only with resisted wrist flexion and pronation  
• No pain with wrist extension or supination, and normal hand and elbow examination  

A working diagnosis of flexor tendonitis was made, and an MRI of the forearm without contrast was ordered. The patient declined immobilization.

A 61-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 5-year history of progressive, painless dimpling of her forehead. There was no family history of hereditary bone disease. On examination, there was a symmetric depression approximately 3 cm in diameter in the frontal region, with normal overlying skin.

A plain skull x-ray showed multiple irregular defects in both frontal bones. Noncontrast brain CT demonstrated focal thinning of the frontal calvarium, with a minimal thickness of 2.76 mm at the site of greatest dimpling. SPECT-CT revealed heterogeneous radiotracer uptake with decreased uptake in the frontal bone dimplings and no areas of increased uptake. DXA scanning showed osteopenia with a femoral neck T-score of −2.3.

Laboratory studies were within normal limits except for a mild vitamin D deficiency: calcium 8.6 mg/dL, phosphate 4.1 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 71 IU/L; C-telopeptide 0.503 ng/mL; procollagen type 1 N-terminal propeptide 36.5 ng/mL; 25-OH-vitamin D 18.5 ng/mL; and parathyroid hormone 41.6 pg/mL.

An 82-year-old woman was hospitalized for mild congestive heart failure and left lower lobe pneumonia with bacteremia. Her medical history included a myocardial infarction and a left nephrectomy via a flank incision for renal-cell carcinoma. After one week of intravenous antibiotics, she developed diarrhea; Clostridium difficile tests were negative, and she was diagnosed with antibiotic-associated diarrhea. Over the next days, her diarrhea became blood-tinged and her hemoglobin fell by 3 g/dL.

A colonoscopy was performed without difficulty to the cecum. No acute source of bleeding was identified; findings included severe diverticulosis in the left colon and internal hemorrhoids. No biopsies or polypectomies were performed.

In the postprocedure period, she developed left upper quadrant abdominal pain accompanied by hypotension. She did not report left shoulder pain. Abdominal examination revealed left-sided tenderness without peritoneal signs. Laboratory tests showed a drop in hemoglobin from 9.6 g/dL to 6.8 g/dL and a significant leukocytosis. She was transfused, and a computed tomographic scan of the abdomen and pelvis was ordered.

A female infant was born at term (3.1 kg) to a 30-year-old gravida 3, para 2 mother by vaginal breech delivery. The mother had no per vaginal leak, bleeding, or premature rupture of membranes before labor and was VDRL negative. At birth, the neonate was well appearing and hemodynamically stable. On examination, there was a generalized erythematous maculopapular eruption over the face, trunk, back, and extremities; in many areas the rash was papulovesicular. The palms, soles, and mucous membranes were spared. The umbilical cord, membranes, and placenta appeared grossly normal. Laboratory evaluation showed a white-blood-cell count of 17 000/mm3 with 45% neutrophils, 6% bands, and 30% lymphocytes. Blood and urine cultures obtained on admission were negative. A chest radiograph was normal.

A 76-year-old woman presented with one week of right hip pain and difficulty walking. She had received denosumab for osteoporosis for five years and had undergone total hip arthroplasty for a left femoral neck fracture two years earlier. On examination, her Japanese Orthopaedic Association (JOA) score was 96 on the right and 76 on the left. Initial plain radiographs at an outside clinic were reportedly normal. Repeat radiographs at our hospital demonstrated an incomplete transverse fracture in the lateral cortex of the right femoral neck. Computed tomography confirmed a lateral cortical fracture without comminution, and T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a high-signal bend in the same region. Bone mineral density was 0.840 g/cm2 in the lumbar spine and 0.899 g/cm2 in the right femoral neck. Laboratory studies revealed calcium 9.7 mg/dL, phosphorus 3.9 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 47 IU/L, tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase-5b 104 mU/dL, type I procollagen N-terminal propeptide 21.9 μg/L, and osteocalcin 4.9 ng/mL.

A 22-year-old primigravida at 26 weeks' gestation was referred for fetal echocardiography after routine obstetric ultrasonography detected pericardial effusion. The mother's medical history was unremarkable, and prenatal care had been irregular. Fetal echocardiography revealed pericardial, pleural, and abdominal free fluid, skin edema, an increased cardiothoracic ratio (heart one-half the thoracic cavity), severe holosystolic tricuspid regurgitation, and a dilated coronary sinus. Severe fetal bradycardia was present throughout the examination. These findings suggested hydrops fetalis and severe fetal heart failure, prompting immediate referral for emergency cesarean delivery. The newborn male weighed 1050 g, had no spontaneous respirations, a heart rate < 60 bpm, and was hypotonic. He underwent cardiopulmonary resuscitation, was intubated, and transferred to the neonatal ICU. On examination, he was pale with generalized edema; lung auscultation revealed fine rales; heart sounds were muffled, bradycardic at 100 bpm without murmur; peripheral pulses were weak, and blood pressure was unmeasurable; the liver was palpable 3 cm below the costal margin. Mechanical ventilation and inotropic support with dopamine and dobutamine were initiated. Blood gas analysis showed severe metabolic acidosis. A transthoracic echocardiogram was then performed to identify the cause of heart failure.

A 70-year-old man from Quito, Ecuador, presented with a 16-day history of productive cough, sore throat, headache, dysphonia, arthralgia, myalgia, rhinorrhea, fever, profuse sweating, dyspnea on moderate exertion, listlessness, and fatigue. He initially received IV dexamethasone and ceftriaxone without improvement. On day 16, SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed by PCR, and on day 17 he was admitted to the ICU with acute respiratory distress syndrome requiring invasive ventilation and pronation. His treatment included dexamethasone, hydrocortisone, and broad-spectrum antibiotics (carbapenems, glycopeptides, aminoglycosides, quinolones). On day 22, blood cultures were obtained, and on day 24 a carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (NDM type) was isolated. On day 30, two aerobic blood culture bottles signaled positive; Gram stain of the positive cultures revealed septated hyphae along with macroconidia and microconidia.

A 46-year-old Vietnamese-born man with no significant past medical history presented with 2 months of a draining right neck mass, fatigue, and 20-lb weight loss. He then noted 2 weeks of a left neck mass, central chest pain over a tender mid-sternal mass, and diminished sensation in his right upper and lower extremities. He denied fever, night sweats, cough, dyspnea, dysphagia, or gastrointestinal symptoms. He immigrated from South Vietnam at age 20 and currently smokes one pack of cigarettes per day. 

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. He had a 3 × 1 cm erythematous, indurated, firm right neck mass with signs of recent drainage, left posterior neck fullness, and a fixed 6 × 3 cm mildly tender mass over the lower sternum. Neurologic examination revealed decreased sensation in the right upper and lower extremities and mildly reduced strength in the left lower extremity. 

Laboratory studies showed a normal white blood cell count (7.16 k/μL), normal lactate dehydrogenase (215 U/L), normal uric acid (6.1 mg/dL), elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (>111 mm/h), and elevated C-reactive protein (90.8 mg/L). Blood cultures, fungal serology, and QuantiFERON-TB Gold testing were negative. 

Fine-needle aspiration of a left neck nodule yielded abundant necrotic debris. Attempts to sample less necrotic areas were unsuccessful. A portion of the specimen was sent for cultures. 

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the neck and chest demonstrated multiple large masses throughout the neck, posterior mediastinum, mid sternum, adjacent to ribs and vertebral elements, and in the presacral space. Many of these masses caused osseous destruction with pathologic fractures of the sternum, ribs, and multiple thoracic vertebral processes. Diffuse osseous lesions were seen in the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine. A large prevertebral mass was noted anterior to C3, with an adjacent paraspinal mass from C4 to T2. Lytic and sclerotic lesions affected C1–C6, but the intervertebral disc spaces were preserved. 

Based on these imaging features, the differential diagnosis included malignancy versus systemic infection.

A 5-year-old Saudi girl presented to dermatology with asymptomatic skin lesions on the left hand and left foot that had been present since birth and were spreading gradually. Her parents noted exclusive hyperhidrosis of the left hand and foot. There was no history of excessive sun exposure, trauma, or similar lesions in the family. She had previously used topical calcipotriol without improvement. 

On examination, multiple yellowish hyperkeratotic papules coalescing into verrucous plaques were arranged in a linear distribution along the marginal surfaces of the left hand and foot. On the palm, lesions extended from the thenar eminence to the proximal aspect of the fourth finger; on the foot, lesions involved the lateral side and fifth toe. A 4-mm punch biopsy was obtained from a foot papule.

A 28-year-old Moroccan woman presented with an 8-week history of symmetric polyarthralgia and swelling involving the proximal interphalangeal joints, metacarpophalangeal joints, wrists, knees, and ankles. She denied respiratory symptoms, gastrointestinal complaints, fever, or other constitutional signs. Past medical and family histories were unremarkable, and prior treatment with corticosteroids and NSAIDs for 1 month produced no relief.

On examination, temperature was 37°C, heart rate 70/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and blood pressure 120/10 mmHg. Joints were warm, swollen, and tender with restricted movement. No axial arthritis, enthesopathy, or other systemic findings were noted.

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 7.6 g/dl, MCV 68 fl, normal leukocyte and platelet counts, C-reactive protein 126 mg/l, ESR 100 mm/h, polyclonal increase in beta and gamma globulins, elevated IgA, IgG, and IgM, ferritin 7 ng/ml, and vitamin D 10 ng/ml. Liver, renal, electrolyte, albumin, total protein, LDH, glucose, and thyroid function tests were normal.

Arthrocentesis of the left knee yielded an inflammatory, sterile fluid rich in white blood cells without microcrystals. Streptolysin O antibody titers and procalcitonin levels were normal. Cultures of blood, urine, and stool and serologic tests for hepatitis B and C, syphilis, HIV, and CMV were all negative. Antinuclear antibodies, anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were all negative. HLA-B27 testing was negative.

Ultrasound of the hands showed synovitis without erosions. Radiographs of the hands, knees, ankles, spine, and sacroiliac joints were normal, and MRI of the sacroiliac joints was unremarkable. Echocardiography, electrocardiogram, and abdominal–pelvic ultrasound were normal.

A 9-year-old obese African-American boy with a 9-month history of nephrotic syndrome secondary to focal segmental glomerulosclerosis presented with 1 week of prolonged staring, mutism, unusual arm posturing, insomnia, and abnormal gait. His home medications included cyclosporine A 125 mg QAM and 100 mg QHS, prednisolone 60 mg daily, amlodipine, and lisinopril. Seven days before this admission, routine testing revealed a cyclosporine A plasma concentration of 1224 ng/mL (therapeutic range 100–200 ng/mL), after which he became increasingly anxious with somatic delusions of “a hole in my neck.” He was evaluated at an outside emergency department: rapid strep test positive, head CT unremarkable, treated with penicillin G, then discharged.

On arrival at our hospital, he was alert and oriented. Examination showed generalized volume overload (2+ pitting edema), significant negativism (eyes clenched shut, refusing oral exam), and active resistance (biting a tongue depressor). Vitals were normal. Initial laboratory studies—including blood chemistry, CBC, blood cultures, HSV PCR, urine toxicology, and thyroid function tests—were remarkable only for hypoalbuminemia; cyclosporine A level was 64 ng/mL. A serum autoimmune encephalitis panel was obtained. Chest x-ray was unremarkable. Head CT and brain MRI with and without contrast showed mild-to-moderate prominence of CSF spaces and slight thinning of the corpus callosum without focal lesions. The patient’s oral cyclosporine A was discontinued, oral prednisolone was changed to IV methylprednisolone, and empiric acyclovir, vancomycin, and ceftriaxone were started for possible meningitis.

A 64-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a 6-month history of mucoid to foul-smelling white vaginal discharge. She had no postmenopausal bleeding. Her obstetrical history was G5 P5 L5 A1, including a medical termination of pregnancy at 16 weeks 30 years earlier by dilatation and evacuation complicated by excessive bleeding requiring transfusion. Her medical history was notable for well-controlled hypertension and coronary artery disease treated with percutaneous angioplasty and stenting 5 years ago.

On examination, vital signs were normal. The abdomen was soft, with no masses or organomegaly. Pelvic examination showed an atrophic vulva and vagina; per speculum there was purulent-appearing discharge and a normal ectocervix. Bimanual examination revealed a uterus enlarged to approximately parous size, mobile, with free adnexal regions. A Pap smear was inflammatory and negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy.

Transvaginal ultrasonography showed an enlarged uterus measuring 10.7 × 7.5 cm, with linear echogenic structures filling the endometrial cavity to the level of the cervix and surrounding fluid, consistent with pyometra. Differential diagnoses included retained bone fragments or dystrophic calcification. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a fluid collection measuring 39 × 26 × 31 mm consistent with pyometra and bone-like echogenic foci in the endometrial cavity.

The patient underwent hysteroscopy, which revealed multiple shredded bony-appearing fragments embedded in the endometrium; all were removed under direct visualization. The endometrial surface appeared without abnormal vascularity or hyperplastic change. Endometrial sampling was performed, and tissue specimens were sent for histopathological examination.

A woman in her 50s was brought to the emergency department by ambulance with a 4-day history of worsening intermittent chest tightness, dyspnoea, vomiting, and lethargy. Her medical history included a 30-pack-year smoking history, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) treated with tiotropium bromide and as-required salbutamol, chronic low back pain, and anxiety. She had no known thyroid or autoimmune disease and a strong family history of acute coronary syndrome. 

Prehospital treatment included nebulised salbutamol (10 mg), nebulised ipratropium bromide (500 µg), and intravenous dexamethasone (8 mg) for presumed COPD exacerbation. In the emergency department, she received sublingual glyceryl trinitrate and a 300 mg loading dose of aspirin for possible acute coronary syndrome. 

On examination, she was normotensive with a heart rate of 110–130 beats/min, alert, with clear lung fields and dual heart sounds without murmurs. A fine tremor was noted. The thyroid gland was slightly enlarged and non-tender. Proximal muscle strength was 5/5 bilaterally, with brisk patellar and Achilles reflexes. 

Initial investigations showed mild neutrophilia (8.5×10^9/L), lymphopaenia (0.6×10^9/L), and a C-reactive protein level of 6 mg/L. Thyroid function studies were performed. A chest radiograph demonstrated clear lung fields. She was admitted and managed initially for a non-infective COPD exacerbation. 

A high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T was elevated at 151 ng/L (normal <16 ng/L). An initial ECG showed sinus tachycardia without ST-segment elevation or depression. She was started on aspirin, ticagrelor, rosuvastatin, and therapeutic enoxaparin for a presumed non–ST-elevation myocardial infarction. 

Prior to planned coronary angiography, she developed acute-onset dyspnoea and chest tightness. A repeat ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia with dynamic ST-segment elevation in leads V1–V2.

A 20-year-old G2P1 woman at 29 weeks of gestation presented in the second stage of labor with regular contractions for 6 hours. She had a 5-year history of untreated hyperthyroidism and poor antenatal care. On arrival, she was agitated with a Glasgow Coma Score of 12. Vital signs were: temperature 38.4°C, blood pressure 220/120 mm Hg, heart rate 156 /min, respiratory rate 40 /min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Examination revealed bilateral exophthalmos; a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland without bruit; bilateral lung rales; warm extremities; and 2+ pitting edema. Obstetric examination showed a fully dilated cervix with fetal feet at station +2 and a fetal heart rate of 140 /min. Laboratory studies demonstrated an arterial blood gas pH of 7.455 with HCO3– 17.8 mmol/L and pCO2 25.1 mm Hg; urinalysis with 2+ protein and 1+ blood; a blood glucose of 143 mg/dL that decreased on reassessment; LDH 547 U/L; and ECG with sinus tachycardia. Liver transaminases and platelet count were within normal limits. A SARS-CoV-2 antigen test (IgG/IgM) was nonreactive. A chest radiograph demonstrated cardiomegaly with pulmonary edema and bilateral pleural effusions.

A 60-year-old man with well-controlled hypertension underwent resection of a left acoustic neuroma via left retromastoid suboccipital craniotomy. Preoperative evaluation was unremarkable except for decreased hearing. In the operating room, he had two peripheral IVs: an 18-gauge in the right hand (primary line) and a 20-gauge in the left hand (heplocked). General anesthesia was induced via the 18-gauge IV with midazolam 2 mg, thiopental 375 mg, fentanyl 150 μg, lidocaine 60 mg, and cis-atracurium 10 mg. Anesthesia was maintained with desflurane (initially 0.5 MAC) in oxygen/nitrous oxide and a remifentanil infusion (0.15 μg·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹) via the 20-gauge IV. Additional medications (vancomycin, mannitol, dexamethasone, furosemide, metoprolol, morphine) were administered via the 18-gauge IV.  

Forty-five minutes after incision, anesthetic requirements increased; within two hours, 1 MAC desflurane plus nitrous oxide and remifentanil were needed. At 2.5 hours, tachycardia was treated with metoprolol. Train-of-four monitoring showed a 4/4 ratio 60 minutes after the single dose of cis-atracurium. Three hours after induction, the patient resumed spontaneous ventilation (tidal volumes 300–400 mL; rate 18–19 breaths/min) and received morphine 3 mg via the 18-gauge line. Remifentanil infusion was discontinued 12 minutes later. Surgery concluded just over three hours after induction; nitrous oxide, desflurane, and remifentanil were discontinued sequentially.  

When the surgical drapes were removed, the 20-gauge IV site was found to be infiltrated and the hand was swollen. The patient had adequate circulation to the limb and maintained stable ventilation and hemodynamics but remained unresponsive and did not respond to painful stimuli.

A 32-year-old man, status post renal transplantation 3 years earlier for focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, maintained on tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil, presented with a 2-month history of anorexia, marked weight loss, and recent dyspnea. Over the preceding week, he had productive cough and high-grade intermittent fevers with rigor and chills. His past 6 months included recurrent admissions for presumed Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia and a nonhealing left elbow ulcer. On admission, he was febrile; chest examination revealed bilateral crackles without pleural effusion; abdominal examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed platelets 34,000/mm3 (later falling from 175,000/mm3), urea 89 mg/dL, creatinine 2.23 mg/dL, leukocytes 20,000/mm3 with 94% neutrophils, and a deranged coagulation profile. Chest CT demonstrated multiple 4–9 mm cavitary nodules scattered in both lungs (left greater than right). Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and sputum were positive for acid-fast bacilli; HIV and hepatitis B serologies were negative. He was started on first-line antitubercular and antifungal therapy but failed to improve. He then developed dull, continuous right iliac fossa pain with localized tenderness; abdominal ultrasonography showed a minimal collection in that region. Based on clinical and laboratory data, a provisional diagnosis of acute on chronic graft rejection was made. Over the next 2 days, his condition deteriorated further, and he died.

A 26-year-old man presented with a 6-year history of gradual digital clubbing of his fingers and a 5-year history of progressive furrowing of the facial skin. He also noted excessive facial oiliness. He denied hyperhidrosis, arthralgia, visual disturbances, and any similar family history. His parents were not consanguineous. 

On examination, there was thickening and deep furrowing of the forehead and cheeks, bilateral eyelid ptosis, drum-stick clubbing of the fingers, and non-tender enlargement of the wrist, elbow, knee, and ankle joints. 

Laboratory studies showed: 
•   Thyroid-stimulating hormone 2.910 mU/L (normal 0.27–4.2)  
•   Free triiodothyronine 5.10 pmol/L (3.60–7.50)  
•   Free thyroxine 16.90 pmol/L (12.0–22.0)  
•   Growth hormone 0.09 ng/mL (0.03–2.47)  
•   Adrenocorticotropic hormone 48.72 ng/L (5.00–78.00)  
•   Cortisol at 8:00 h 507.00 nmol/L (133.0–537.0)  
•   Insulin-like growth factor-1 64.83 ng/mL (137–278)  

Computed tomography of the chest and echocardiography were unremarkable. Radiographs of the long bones demonstrated cortical thickening along the diaphyses. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary gland revealed a 3 mm × 5 mm hypointense lesion on T2-weighted coronal images.

A 38-year-old Japanese woman was referred for suspected hyperthyroidism. Over one year she experienced tremor, insomnia, diarrhea, anxiety, and a 12-kg weight loss. She had no known thyroid disease in her family and no significant past medical history except psychiatric evaluation for family‐related stress.

On examination, her BMI was 24.6 kg/m^2 and pulse was 93 beats per minute; blood pressure, temperature, and respiration were normal. There was no exophthalmos, tremor, skin moistness, goiter, or thyroid tenderness. Thyroid ultrasound showed a normal gland (volume, 18.5 mL) with low blood flow.

Laboratory studies revealed:  
• Free T4 >8.0 ng/dL (normal 0.8–1.9)  
• Free T3 5.0 pg/mL (normal 2.2–4.1)  
• TSH 0.73 μIU/mL (normal 0.4–4.0)  
• Negative thyroid autoantibodies  
• Thyroglobulin 196.8 ng/mL (slightly elevated)  

Thyroid ^99mTc uptake was 2.2% (normal 0.5–3.5). Thiamazole was initiated but thyroid function did not improve; TSH rose to 23.63 μIU/mL, so thiamazole was stopped after three months. Levothyroxine was started, and thyroid function returned to baseline. Her symptoms resolved with antipsychotic therapy, and levothyroxine was discontinued. Subsequent tests showed persistent elevation of free T4 and T3 with a normal TSH. Pituitary MRI was unremarkable, and sequencing of exons 4–10 of the thyroid receptor β gene revealed no mutations.

A 27-year-old man presented with severe low back pain and right leg numbness. He had an 8-year history of intermittent low back pain (3–4/10) without further treatment until 4 months ago, when the pain intensified to 8/10 with numbness extending to the right leg. Initial lumbar MRI showed findings interpreted as herniated intervertebral disc and cauda equina compression at L4–5, and he underwent emergent open discectomy. Intraoperatively, a large mass compressing the right L5 nerve root was excised. Postoperatively, his pain improved to 4/10, and leg numbness persisted mildly. 

Two weeks later, his back pain worsened gradually, and one week after that he presented to the emergency department with pain 9–10/10, numbness in the L5 dermatome, extensor hallucis motor strength 4/5, and 1–2 seconds of right ankle clonus. Emergency lumbar MRI showed a 1.2 × 2 cm cystic lesion at the previous surgical site compressing the right L5 nerve root and cauda equina.

A 25-year-old otherwise healthy woman presented with acute onset of epigastric pain, nausea, and bilious vomiting. Results of liver function tests and an abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable, showing no evidence of biliary or gallbladder pathology. Within hours of discharge, her symptoms worsened. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a soft-tissue mass posterior to the gallbladder. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography demonstrated a complex cystic structure of indeterminate etiology at the porta hepatis without evidence of communication with either the biliary or vascular structures. The differential diagnosis included a ruptured hepatic adenoma, a biliary cystic lesion, or an enteric cyst.

A 32-year-old Indian male farmer presented with an 8-month history of a painless, gradually enlarging swelling in the left axillary region. He denied fever, weight loss, or other swellings. On examination, there was a 10×8 cm, soft-to-firm, well-defined, non-tender mass in the left axilla; no other abnormalities were noted. Ultrasonography revealed a thick-walled lesion containing multiple cysts with no color uptake. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed a multiloculated mass in the left axilla without evidence of involvement of other organs. MRI demonstrated an 11×5.6 cm heterogeneous T2-hyperintense cystic lesion with internal hypointense membranes and small intralesional cysts in the intermuscular planes of the axilla.

A 49-year-old woman with active intravenous heroin use presented with a 2-month history of fever, chills, night sweats, malaise, nausea, and a 15-lb weight loss. One month earlier, she had a foul-smelling, draining skin abscess in her left arm at a heroin injection site that resolved after a course of trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole. She denied cough, gastrointestinal symptoms, and urinary symptoms. She used heroin daily and had a 20 pack-year smoking history. She was HIV-negative and hepatitis C-positive.

On examination, she was cachectic, temperature 39.4°C, blood pressure 115/69 mm Hg, heart rate 127 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. The previous injection site was healed; needle track marks were present. The lungs were clear. Cardiovascular examination revealed a regular tachycardia without murmurs. Abdominal examination showed mild right upper-quadrant tenderness and a liver span of 14 cm.

Laboratory studies demonstrated leukocytosis (11.2 × 10^9 cells/L), alkaline phosphatase 1210 U/L, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 957 U/L, AST 125 U/L, ALT 55 U/L, and total bilirubin 1.5 mg/dL. Chest radiography showed a left lower-lobe nodule. Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed a 1.7 cm peripheral cavitary nodule in the left lower lobe and a 3 cm mass-like infiltrate in the right lower lobe. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly without focal lesions.

She was started empirically on vancomycin for suspected staphylococcal endocarditis and placed in respiratory isolation for possible tuberculosis. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage yielded negative AFB smear and cultures. Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal systolic function and no vegetations. Despite vancomycin, she remained febrile and became hypotensive on hospital day 3, prompting the addition of piperacillin/tazobactam and intravenous fluids. Although initial blood cultures were negative, gram-positive rods that appeared to be branching grew in multiple aerobic culture bottles on day 5.

A 67-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of severe, generalized abdominal pain, more than 20 kg of weight loss, fatigue, and anorexia. Over the past 2 months, he also experienced nausea, vomiting, constipation, and mild-to-moderate fever, with worsening of symptoms during the preceding 3 days. His medical history was notable for 20 years of type 2 diabetes mellitus (recent fasting plasma glucose, 217 mg/dl; HbA1c, 9.1%). He denied any history of abdominal surgery, trauma, foreign-body insertion, or poor oral hygiene.

On examination, his temperature was 38.9 °C; other vital signs were within normal limits. The abdomen was distended, with generalized guarding, severe tenderness, and rebound tenderness. The pulmonary examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (16.6 × 10^9 cells/L; 82% neutrophils), anemia (hemoglobin, 9.5 mg/dl), and a normal platelet count (180 × 10^9 cells/L). Because of the clinical picture of an acute abdomen, a diagnostic laparotomy was performed.

At surgery, multiple tumors ranging from 2 to 10 cm in diameter with irregular, poorly defined borders and inflammatory adhesions were identified on the peritoneum, stomach, and intestinal walls. There was moderate clear free fluid in the abdominal cavity, and multiple biopsies were obtained. A postoperative abdominal CT scan demonstrated multiple intra-abdominal masses without liver involvement. A chest radiograph was normal.

A 58-year-old woman was evaluated for recurrent episodes of left-sided “bronchopneumonia” characterized by high fever, chills, productive cough with mucopurulent sputum, left chest pain, dyspnea on exertion, and wheezing. Her medical history was notable for smoking (20 pack-years), obesity, and hypertension treated intermittently; she had been asymptomatic in childhood and early adulthood aside from a pulmonary infection at age 19 that was treated empirically for tuberculosis. Previous chest radiographs had been interpreted as left basal pleural thickening and chronic pneumopathy.  

On examination, blood pressure was 180/100 mm Hg. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis with a left shift and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 46 mm/hr (first hour) and 68 mm/2 hr. Electrocardiography demonstrated a leftward axis deviation (QRS +50°), low-voltage QRS complexes, and T-wave inversions in leads V3–V6. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography were unremarkable.  

A posteroanterior chest radiograph revealed an opacity in the left lower pulmonary zone, hypoaeration of the left upper lobe, and leftward mediastinal shift without marked retraction of the left hemithorax. Multidetector CT of the chest showed a small left lung composed of multiple cystic spaces, hyperinflation of the right lung with herniation across the midline, and mediastinal deviation to the left. Multiplanar reconstructions demonstrated depression of the right hemidiaphragm facilitating right lung hypertrophy, with a normally positioned left hemidiaphragm. Three-dimensional volume renderings showed a disproportionate right pulmonary lobation and vascularity filling the thorax, whereas the left lung appeared as a cluster of small cysts with scant vasculature.

A 21-year-old gravida 1, para 0 woman at 34 weeks’ gestation was admitted in labor. Routine prenatal visits had been unremarkable. On admission, her blood pressure was 170/100 mm Hg, heart rate 88 bpm, and temperature 36.1 °C. Cervical examination revealed 8 cm dilation with the fetal head at +2 station.
