Laboratory studies showed aspartate transaminase 100 U/L, alanine transaminase 80 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase 450 U/L, hematocrit 33%, platelet count 100,000/mm3, and 3+ proteinuria on a spot urine sample, consistent with severe preeclampsia. She delivered a live male infant vaginally; Apgar scores were 9 and 10 at 1 and 5 minutes. Within the first postnatal hour, she developed tonic–clonic seizures and a severe headache and was treated with magnesium sulfate and antihypertensive therapy. Over the next several hours, she became somnolent and was noted to have a positive Babinski sign on the left and weakness of the left upper and lower extremities. Noncontrast cranial CT showed hemorrhagic foci on an edematous background in the bilateral frontal and parietal regions, consistent with hemorrhagic infarcts, with a mass effect most pronounced in the left posterior parietal region.

A 40-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of fever, mild headache, and abdominal pain. She was 3 weeks post–cesarean section and had been residing in a postpartum care center. Eleven days before presentation, she had neck swelling and underwent fine-needle aspiration at a private facility, which revealed no abnormalities of the thyroid gland. She had no other medical history and no family history of malignancy.

On examination, temperature was 40.6 °C, blood pressure 100/48 mmHg, heart rate 100 bpm, and respiratory rate 18 breaths/min. There was no thyroid tenderness or swelling, no neck stiffness, no tonsillar enlargement, and the surgical sites (cesarean section and needle aspiration) showed no signs of infection. Abdominal examination was unremarkable, and colposcopy performed to exclude endometritis showed no abnormalities.

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 14.0 g/dL, platelets 133 000/μL, absolute neutrophil count 2512/μL, total bilirubin 0.3 mg/dL, AST 65 U/L, ALT 35 U/L, thyroid function tests within normal limits, and urinalysis with one white blood cell per high-power field. C-reactive protein was elevated at 4.46 mg/dL. Chest radiograph and abdominal CT scan showed no focus of infection.

Her fever subsided after antipyretics, vital signs stabilized, and she was discharged on broad-spectrum antibiotics with outpatient follow-up.

Four days later, she returned with fever of 38.0 °C and hypotension (60/30 mmHg). Repeat labs showed platelets 94 000/μL, total bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL, AST 202 U/L, ALT 444 U/L, blood urea nitrogen 42.1 mg/dL, creatinine 3.35 mg/dL, ferritin 3429 μg/L (normal 13–150 μg/L), and triglycerides 957 mg/dL (normal 10–150 mg/dL).

A 58-year-old man with high-grade B-cell lymphoma underwent systemic chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide and rituximab and CNS prophylaxis consisting of intrathecal methotrexate, cytarabine, and dexamethasone (three doses of intrathecal methotrexate, total 36 mg, given on nonconsecutive days). Ten days after the last lumbar puncture, he noted progressive lower-limb weakness that evolved over hours into flaccid paraplegia with urinary retention. On neurologic examination, deep tendon reflexes were absent in both lower limbs, and there was a sensory level at T1. A lumbar puncture showed normal cell count and normal protein and glucose. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography performed one week after onset revealed absent F waves in peroneal and tibial nerves with minimal decrease in CMAP amplitudes and normal distal motor latencies; sensory studies and upper-limb conductions were normal. A lumbosacral MRI with gadolinium showed no abnormalities.

A 36-year-old Caucasian man presented with 15 days of low-grade fever, weight loss, nonproductive cough, and progressive dyspnea. He had no significant past medical history, did not smoke, and reported frequent respiratory infections over the previous 5 years without hospitalization. On examination, he had bilateral crackles and rales but no lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, skin lesions, or cardiovascular findings. Initial laboratory studies showed a normal white-cell count with severe lymphocytopenia (<200 cells/μL), which progressed to a total lymphocyte count of <60 cells/μL along with declines in platelets and hematocrit. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein were elevated; lactic dehydrogenase was 1485 U/L; ferritin was normal; and fibrinogen was 687 mg/dL. A bone marrow biopsy revealed a hypercellular marrow with mild dysplasia and macrophages exhibiting hemophagocytosis. Chest radiography showed bilateral diffuse perihilar infiltrates. Initial sputum Gram stain and cultures were negative, and empiric antibiotics for community-acquired pneumonia were started. As his respiratory status worsened, he was intubated, and bronchoalveolar lavage grew Pneumocystis jiroveci. High-dose trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole plus corticosteroids were initiated. HIV-1 and -2 serologies were negative. Serum immunoglobulin levels were markedly reduced (IgG 3.9 g/L [normal 7–17 g/L], IgM 0.259 g/L [0.4–2.8 g/L], IgA below normal). Adenosine deaminase activity in erythrocytes was normal. Immunophenotyping showed total lymphocytes 320 cells/μL with CD4+ 16.4%, CD8+ 8%, CD19+ 1.5%, and NK cells 60.3%.

A 6-year-old child presented to the emergency department with left wrist pain 3 weeks after falling onto an outstretched hand. On examination, the wrist was tender and slightly swollen, with mild restriction of movement but no visible deformity or fever; vital signs were normal. Plain radiographs showed a greenstick fracture of the distal radial metaphysis with slight dorsal angulation and adjacent sclerosis consistent with early healing. In addition, there was a well-defined ovoid lucency just proximal to and continuous with the fracture line. Two faint areas of sclerosis in the distal ulnar metadiaphysis suggested undisplaced fractures. Because the nature of the lucency was unclear—including the possibilities of a Brodie’s abscess or an underlying primary bone cyst—MRI was performed 2 days later. On MRI, the lesion demonstrated homogenous high signal on T1-weighted images, complete signal loss on fat-suppressed sequences confirming intralesional fat, and a subperiosteal location on short-axis proton-density fat-suppressed images. There was no enhancement after gadolinium administration.

A 27-year-old previously healthy African male medical intern sustained a needlestick injury to his little finger while performing a lumbar puncture on an HIV-infected patient. He immediately washed the site and commenced 28 days of postexposure prophylaxis with zidovudine, lamivudine, and lopinavir–ritonavir. Initial HIV testing was negative, and PCR at the end of prophylaxis remained negative.

Two weeks after the injury, the finger became swollen and painful. Pus was aspirated, and incision and drainage were performed; culture grew Staphylococcus aureus sensitive to flucloxacillin, and he was treated accordingly. Despite this, the wound remained open for months despite debridement and multiple antibiotic regimens, including levofloxacin, clindamycin, ceftriaxone, and vancomycin.

Six weeks after the injury, he developed painless ipsilateral axillary lymphadenopathy. Over the next six months, the finger swelling persisted and extended into the hand, accompanied by low-grade fever, night sweats, and subjective weight loss. Radiographs showed no bony involvement. Serial blood counts revealed persistent lymphocytosis and an elevated ESR; liver and renal function tests were normal.

Ten months after the injury, repeat surgical debridement was performed. Histologic examination of the tissue revealed a chronic inflammatory process with granulomatous tubercles composed of epithelioid cells, Langerhans giant cells, and a mononuclear infiltrate. No acid-fast bacilli were demonstrated on Ziehl–Nelson staining.

A previously healthy 31-year-old Japanese man presented with 7 days of fever and headache. He was afebrile except for a temperature of 38.3 °C; other vital signs and general physical examination were unremarkable. Initial laboratory testing showed hyponatremia (serum sodium 130 mEq/L), and SARS-CoV-2 NAAT was negative. Five days later, he reported new tremor of the right hand, constipation, sweating, and lightheadedness. On re-presentation, he was alert and cooperative. Neurologic examination revealed bilateral postural tremors of the upper limbs; otherwise, it was normal.  
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed 57 cells/µL (96% mononuclear), protein 103 mg/dL, glucose 41 mg/dL, and ADA 15.0 U/L. CSF PCR for herpes simplex virus and Mycobacterium tuberculosis were negative; CSF bacterial and AFB cultures were negative. Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted brain MRI demonstrated linear enhancement perpendicular to the lateral ventricular walls and along perivascular spaces in a radial pattern. Thoracoabdominal CT showed no abnormal findings.  
Additional studies revealed normal TSH, free thyroxine, C3, C4, CH50, and ACE levels. Serologies including ANA, anti-CCP, anti-dsDNA IgG, anti-SSA/Ro, β-D-glucan, cryptococcus antigen, hepatitis B and C, syphilis serology, Treponema pallidum antibody, and HIV antigen/antibody were all negative. Anti-aquaporin-4, anti–myelin-oligodendrocyte glycoprotein, paraneoplastic syndrome–related antibodies, and anti–glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies were absent; soluble IL-2 receptor was normal.  
Based on these findings, he was managed symptomatically for presumed aseptic meningitis with NSAIDs or acetaminophen as needed.

A 15‐year‐old boy presented with a 6-month history of intermittent fever, weight loss, and arthralgia. For the past 2 months, he also noted pain in both calves that worsened during fever episodes. On examination, temperature was 37.8 °C, pulse 90 /min, blood pressure 116/72 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 16 /min. All peripheral pulses were palpable; there was no rash or erythema of the skin. Abdominal examination and 2D echocardiography were unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.96 g/dL, leukocyte count 12 600 /mm3 (71% neutrophils), serum urea and liver and renal function tests within normal limits, and ionic calcium 1.18 mmol/L. Urinalysis revealed microscopic hematuria (6 RBCs per high-power field). ESR was 55 mm/h, CRP mildly elevated, and ACE level 55.8 mg/L (reference 12–68). Serologic tests for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV were negative. Cold agglutinins, ANA, and ANCA were all negative. High-resolution ultrasound of both legs demonstrated multiple ill-defined hypoechoic lesions centered around intramuscular vessels in the gastrocnemius, soleus, and tibialis anterior muscles, suggesting perivascular inflammation; Doppler ultrasound showed no thrombosis or luminal narrowing. MRI of both legs revealed multifocal patchy high signal on T2-weighted, STIR, and proton density fat-suppressed sequences in the same muscles; on postcontrast T1-weighted images there were small, ill-defined enhancing areas centered on blood vessels with a fuzzy, “cotton-wool” appearance.

A 44-year-old man was referred for sudden painless decreased visual acuity in his left eye since the day before presentation. He reported binocular diplopia one week earlier; brain MRI at that time was unremarkable. Three weeks before referral, he had been hospitalized for one week with fever, dry cough, progressive dyspnea, and 81% oxygen saturation; COVID-19 was confirmed by positive nasopharyngeal RT-PCR, and chest CT showed ground-glass opacities involving 50% of pulmonary parenchyma. He was treated with favipiravir, remdesivir, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and did not receive systemic corticosteroids.

On ophthalmic examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and light perception in the left eye, which progressed to no light perception over four days. A relative afferent pupillary defect was present in the left eye. Intraocular pressures were 12 mm Hg bilaterally. Slit-lamp examination of the left eye revealed 1–2+ cells in the anterior chamber and 2+ cells in the anterior vitreous. Funduscopic examination of the left eye showed multiple cotton-wool-like geographic white patches in the posterior pole and equatorial retina; the right eye was normal. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated delayed retinal arterial filling after 40 seconds and vascular filling defects corresponding to the white patches. Optical coherence tomography of the left eye revealed increased reflectivity and thickness of the inner retinal layers.

A vitreous sample was obtained for PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2, varicella zoster virus, herpes simplex virus, cytomegalovirus, and Toxoplasma gondii. Serum biochemistry was normal except for an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 60 mm/h and 2+ C-reactive protein. Neurology and cardiology consultations to evaluate the carotid arteries and heart as sources of emboli were normal.

A 20-month-old boy was referred for evaluation of a chest-wall deformity. He had no relevant family history. At 6 months, his primary care physician noted left rib protrusion; at 18 months, left torticollis was noted. At 20 months, he was found to have pectus carinatum and referred for further assessment.

On initial examination, his height and weight were at the 60th percentile for age. Physical findings included genu valgum, kyphosis, and pectus carinatum. There was no joint contracture, no coarse facial features, and no respiratory or sleep symptoms. A quantitative urine mucopolysaccharide test showed an elevated glycosaminoglycan level of 97.7 µg/mL (normal, 5.3–34.0 µg/mL). 

At 22 months, on admission, vital signs were normal. Examination again revealed genu valgum, kyphosis, and pectus carinatum. There were no adventitious lung sounds, heart murmurs, organomegaly, neurological deficits, macroglossia, tonsillar hypertrophy, or corneal clouding. Routine blood tests were unremarkable.

Radiographic studies showed flattening of the ribs (“oar-like” ribs), kyphoscoliosis with ovalization of thoracolumbar vertebral bodies, and short, stubby phalanges with mild metaphyseal cupping and proximal coning of the metacarpals. Echocardiography revealed only trivial tricuspid, pulmonary, and mitral valve regurgitation. Brain MRI was normal.

A 24-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with 2 weeks of fever and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. She was born and raised in Batam, Indonesia, and had been working in Singapore; she denied travel elsewhere, raw or undercooked seafood, and direct tap-water consumption. On examination, her temperature was 39.5 °C, pulse 110 beats/min, blood pressure 98/58 mmHg; she appeared lethargic, with marked hepatomegaly and right upper quadrant tenderness. Laboratory studies showed haemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, white blood cell count 33.5 × 10^3/µL, C-reactive protein 302.8 mg/L, procalcitonin 7.03 µg/L, total bilirubin 45.4 µmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 310 U/L, alanine transaminase 324 U/L, and aspartate transaminase 264 U/L. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 15.2 × 17.3 × 21.7 cm cystic lesion in the right hepatic lobe with rim enhancement and multiple peripheral septations. Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone and metronidazole were initiated. Two sets of blood cultures obtained before antibiotics showed no growth. The patient underwent percutaneous drainage; purulent fluid was aspirated, but Gram stain and aerobic and anaerobic cultures of the aspirate were negative. Three consecutive stool microscopic examinations showed no ova, cysts, or parasites.

A 23-year-old female professional runner presented with a 2-week history of insidious left medial mid-calf pain that began after a run, without any specific inciting event. She noted only general calf tightness at rest and had no pain with daily activities but was limited to short runs before developing focal pain. She had been diagnosed elsewhere with a calf strain and underwent dry needling to the calf musculature with only mild improvement. On examination, strength, sensation, and range of motion of the left leg and knee were intact. There was tenderness to palpation at the left medial mid-calf. Ultrasonography of the left calf showed no injury or tear to the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles and demonstrated a patent, compressible popliteal vein. However, there was a focal, hypoechoic swelling of the plantaris tendon of the left calf, which was markedly larger than the remainder of the tendon and larger than that in the asymptomatic right calf.

A 53-year-old woman with well-controlled hypertension and hypothyroidism presented with sudden-onset dyspnea and palpitations. On arrival, her blood pressure was 60/40 mmHg, pulse 160 beats per minute, and she was cyanosed. Respiratory examination was unremarkable. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia, a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound, and a tricuspid regurgitation murmur. 

An electrocardiogram revealed supraventricular tachycardia, which was terminated by synchronized electrical cardioversion. The post-conversion ECG demonstrated right-axis deviation, an S₁Q₃T₃ pattern, a qR pattern in lead V₁, T-wave inversion in leads V₂–V₄, and p-pulmonale. 

She was started on low-molecular-weight heparin and intravenous amiodarone, and admitted to the intensive care unit. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a dilated right ventricle with severe tricuspid regurgitation and an estimated pulmonary artery pressure of 120 mmHg; the left atrium and ventricle were normal with an ejection fraction of 73%. Pulmonary‐function testing revealed a diffusion capacity of 45% with normal FEV₁, FVC, and FEV₁/FVC ratio. 

Given her supraventricular tachycardia and marked pulmonary hypertension, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension was initially suspected. Chest radiography showed oligemia and reduced volume of the right lung field with an empty right hilum, and compensatory hyperinflation and plethoric left lung field with an enlarged left pulmonary artery. A ventilation–perfusion scan demonstrated absent perfusion in the right lung field with preserved ventilation.

A 54-year-old man with glioblastoma treated by surgical resection began a clinical trial with M7824 (a bifunctional fusion protein targeting PD-L1 and TGF-β). Four weeks after initiation of M7824, he presented with a severely pruritic, nontender, erythematous papular and macular eruption on his back, bilateral ankles, and upper extremities. He was not receiving any other new medications. The oncology team initially classified the eruption as a grade I rash and prescribed hydrocortisone 1% cream and oral diphenhydramine, but the rash and pruritus progressed. One month later, the rash reached grade II severity, and doxycycline was started for a suspected acneiform eruption. On dermatologic evaluation, the consensus was that the eruption represented a drug reaction to M7824. Laboratory evaluation showed no elevations in liver enzymes, no eosinophilia, and no lymphadenopathy. The patient was treated with triamcinolone 0.1% ointment and hydroxyzine, but over the following two weeks the rash progressed to grade III with worsening pruritus. M7824 infusions were held, and prednisone at 40 mg per day was initiated according to guidelines, but his symptoms failed to improve.

An 8-month-old, previously healthy female (9 kg) underwent emergent drainage of a retropharyngeal and anterior mediastinal abscess and thoracoscopic decortication of a right-sided empyema. Intraoperatively, she had brief episodes of hypoxia with associated bradycardia that resolved with manual ventilation. At the conclusion of the procedure, her oxygen saturation fell to 40% and she developed minimal breath sounds and progressive hypercarbia. Ventilator settings were adjusted without improvement; tidal volumes remained at 15–30 mL despite peak inspiratory pressures > 50 cm H₂O. Attempts to pass a suction catheter through the 4.0 mm endotracheal tube were unsuccessful. The available fiberoptic scope and exchange catheters could not be advanced through the tube. An intraoperative chest radiograph confirmed correct placement of the endotracheal tube.

A 28-year-old woman with hypertension and systemic lupus erythematosus diagnosed 14 months earlier had been treated with captopril, hydrochlorothiazide, prednisone, and hydroxychloroquine 400 mg/day. She reported daily fevers up to 39 °C for 3 months, generalized erythema, photosensitivity, and asthenia.  
Laboratory studies showed: BUN 8.87 mg/dL (6–21), serum creatinine 0.8 mg/dL (0.4–1.1), eGFR 116 mL/min/1.73 m2 (>90), positive HEp-2 ANA titer 1:160, and ANA 1:640 (both negative reference). Other causes of proteinuria were excluded. Renal ultrasound was normal. A 24-hour urine protein was 600 mg (no hematuria or leukocyturia).  
A renal biopsy was performed.  
• Light microscopy: eight glomeruli with mild mesangial hypercellularity; tubular, interstitial, and vascular compartments were normal.  
• Immunofluorescence: granular mesangial IgM and mild C3 in the vascular wall.  
• Electron microscopy: intralysosomal, osmiophilic, lamellar, and sometimes concentric inclusions in podocytes resembling “zebra bodies.”

A 66-year-old woman presented with chronic asymptomatic bilateral conjunctival hyperaemia for over 1 year, unresponsive to topical therapies. Her medical history included treated arterial hypertension, dyslipidaemia, atrial fibrillation, and type 2 diabetes.  
On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OU. Biomicroscopy revealed prominent bilateral episcleral corkscrew vessels. Intraocular pressures by Goldmann applanation were 27 mm Hg OD and 28 mm Hg OS; pachymetry measured 501 µm OD and 499 µm OS. There was no proptosis; ocular motility was full; pupils were equal and reactive. Gonioscopy showed open angles with blood in Schlemm’s canal OD. Funduscopy revealed healthy optic nerves (cup-to-disc ratios ~0.2 OD, 0.1 OS) and no vascular abnormalities. No carotid or ocular bruits were heard. The patient denied headache, diplopia, pulsatile tinnitus, orbital pulsation, head or neck trauma, and had no family history of glaucoma.  
Optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fiber layer and macular ganglion cell layer were within normal limits. Standard automated perimetry was normal. A diagnosis of ocular hypertension related to elevated episcleral venous pressure was made, and topical timolol was started.  
To identify the cause of elevated episcleral venous pressure, brain and orbital CT scans were performed and were normal, excluding extraocular muscle hypertrophy, orbital masses, or intracranial lesions. Thyroid function and antibody tests were normal. Magnetic resonance angiography showed bilateral dilation of the superior ophthalmic veins. Cerebral digital subtraction angiography revealed no carotid–cavernous fistula. Thoracic CT angiography demonstrated mild signs of pulmonary hypertension and no superior vena cava obstruction.

A 38-year-old woman at 20 weeks of gestation was referred after screening for hydroxychloroquine therapy revealed bilateral multifocal pigment epithelial detachments. Her medical history included mixed connective tissue disease (positive ANA and rheumatoid factor), polycystic ovary syndrome, hypothyroidism, and a resolved dengue infection one year earlier. She had no visual symptoms.  
On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes with myopic correction; Amsler grid and color vision testing were normal. Pupils were equal and reactive with no afferent defect. Anterior segments were unremarkable, and intraocular pressures were 20 mmHg OD and 21 mmHg OS.  
Dilated fundus examination revealed multiple serous PEDs in the macula extending beyond the vascular arcades in both eyes, with no hemorrhage, exudate, drusen, or subretinal fluid. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated multiple dome-shaped serous, nonvascularized PEDs without neurosensory detachment. OCT angiography showed no choroidal neovascularization. Subfoveal choroidal thickness measured 380 µm in each eye.  
Laboratory testing showed persistently positive ANA consistent with her connective tissue disease. QuantiFERON-Gold, reactive plasma reagin, protein electrophoresis, complete blood count with differential, free kappa and lambda light chains, and chikungunya antibody testing were within normal limits.

A 53-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and depression presented with 6 months of progressive bilateral proximal muscle weakness, beginning in the lower extremities and later involving the shoulders. She denied sensory symptoms, fevers, rashes, or joint pain. Medications included metformin, glyburide, aspirin, sertraline, and a high-intensity statin for the past year. 

On examination, she had reduced strength of the neck flexors, deltoids, and quadriceps bilaterally; gait was slightly widened but coordination and sensation were intact. 

Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (12 500/µL), AST 773 U/L, ALT 763 U/L, ESR 35 mm/hr, CRP 24 mg/L, and CK 28 000 U/L. ANA was 1:80 with a nucleolar pattern; anti-dsDNA was negative. 

MRI of the pelvis demonstrated symmetric proximal muscle edema consistent with myositis. Electromyography revealed a diffuse irritable myopathy. A biopsy of the vastus lateralis showed muscle fiber necrosis with minimal inflammatory infiltrate and upregulation of MHC class I.

A 28-year-old woman was referred by her dentist with an 8-month history of left submandibular swelling aggravated by eating—particularly citrus fruits—and pain radiating to her tongue. She noted fluctuations in the size of the mass and occasional fever and extraoral swelling; her most recent flare persisted for two weeks. On examination, there was a tender left submandibular swelling with palpable, mobile lymph nodes. Intraorally, a bluish, fluctuant sublingual swelling on the left side of the lingual frenum slightly elevated the tongue. Bimanual palpation confirmed tenderness and revealed a hard structure within the swelling. The ostium of Wharton’s duct was erythematous, salivary flow was reduced, and aspiration yielded pale yellow fluid; microbiologic testing confirmed infection. A mandibular occlusal radiograph showed an ovoid radiopaque mass near the lower first molar extending toward the third molar.

A 28-year-old primigravida at 23 + 1 weeks gestation presented with lower abdominal pain and minimal vaginal bleeding. She had two known subserous uterine fibroids (35 × 39 × 50 mm and 49 × 81 × 100 mm), was heterozygous for MTHFR, had elevated factor VIII, and was on daily aspirin. She was a Group B Streptococcus carrier and had two treated urinary tract infections (one with a cephalosporinase-producing Escherichia coli). On examination she had preterm premature rupture of membranes, received antenatal steroids, erythromycin, and IV antibiotics; her WBC was 11.18 × 10^9/L and CRP rose from 95.5 mg/L to 151.3 mg/L. She remained apyrexial but tachycardic (110–120 bpm) and developed a maculopapular rash. Four hours later she delivered a live 560 g female infant. During placenta delivery she collapsed with a 1750 mL postpartum hemorrhage due to uterine atony and sepsis. In theatre, retained placental fragments were removed and the uterine cavity was confirmed empty by ultrasound; a Rusch balloon then controlled the hemorrhage. She received seven days of broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, cultures grew the same E. coli, and she was discharged eight days postpartum.  

Three days after discharge she re-presented with fever, lethargy, and lower abdominal discomfort. The uterus was tender and inflammatory markers were elevated. She was started on IV co-amoxiclav. Pelvic ultrasound showed a thickened endometrium, unchanged fibroids, and an apparent 19 × 33 × 46 mm collection suggestive of retained products. She underwent evacuation of retained products of conception; histology confirmed placental tissue and a follow-up ultrasound showed an empty uterus.  

Despite this, she continued to spike fevers. Blood and urine cultures were negative, and IV teicoplanin was added. Three days after the evacuation, a contrast CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated multiple thick-walled, low-attenuation cystic adnexal lesions, most marked on the left (11 × 7 × 7 mm), similar in size to her larger fibroid. A differential diagnosis of complex ovarian cyst or tuboovarian abscess was proposed, but a repeat transvaginal ultrasound showed normal ovaries, no evidence of a pelvic collection, and unchanged fibroids.

A 4-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of bowed upper and lower limbs. He had sustained multiple fractures after minor trauma over the past 2–3 years. His elder sibling had a similar history of fractures and limb deformities, and his parents were consanguineous. On physical examination, he had growth deformity, an abnormally large head with frontal bossing, and discoloration of the deciduous teeth. Intraoral examination revealed yellowish to brownish teeth with complete chipping of enamel and delayed eruption of several deciduous teeth. Chest radiography showed a long, narrow thorax with anterior compression. Radiographs of the upper limbs demonstrated malunion and bowing of the radius and ulna.

A 40-year-old man with a history of anxiety, depression, hypertension, and substance abuse was brought by emergency medical services for agitation, auditory and visual hallucinations, and one seizure-like episode. His mother reported that over the preceding 3–5 days he had experienced hallucinations after taking a supplement purchased online identified as phenibut. His regular medications included hydroxyzine, gabapentin, and trazodone. On arrival, a urine drug screen and blood alcohol level were negative. In the emergency department, he became increasingly agitated and belligerent, requiring intravenous lorazepam and physical restraints; he had incoherent speech, profuse sweating, and a heart rate above 140 beats per minute. A decreased Glasgow Coma Scale score prompted endotracheal intubation for airway protection and sedation. Initial laboratory tests showed a lactate level of 9.1 mmol/L, creatine phosphokinase of 5422 U/L, serum creatinine of 2.03 mg/dL, a white blood cell count of 15,000/µL that peaked at 23,700/µL on hospital day two, and mildly elevated transaminase levels. Urinalysis was positive for 3+ ketones and 2+ blood despite normal blood glucose and no history of diabetes.

A 29-year-old man with no significant medical history was referred for scleral icterus. Six months earlier he developed shortness of breath, dry cough, nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, fatigue, night sweats, and an unintentional 60-lb weight loss. For 3 weeks he experienced intense nocturnal pruritus unrelieved by antihistamines; he noted yellow discoloration of his eyes 3 days before presentation. He denied medication, alcohol, tobacco, or drug use. 

On examination he was afebrile; blood pressure 132/82 mm Hg; heart rate 87 bpm. Physical findings were notable only for icteric sclera. 

Initial labs showed alanine aminotransferase 98 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 124 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 790 U/L, total bilirubin 11.1 mg/dL (direct 8.1 mg/dL), cholesterol >600 mg/dL, triglycerides 305 mg/dL, HDL 13 mg/dL, LDL >526 mg/dL, and albumin 3.1 g/dL. 

Chest radiograph revealed bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Right upper quadrant ultrasound showed no gallstones, a 0.2-cm common bile duct, and no intrahepatic biliary dilation. Autoimmune serologies were negative (ANA, PR3-ANCA, anti–liver-kidney-microsomal, AMA, smooth muscle antibody), and IgG4 was normal. Angiotensin-converting enzyme level was 104 U/L; soluble interleukin-2 receptor was 2576 U/mL. 

Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography demonstrated peripheral intrahepatic biliary ductal strictures and dilatation consistent with changes of primary sclerosing cholangitis.

A 38‐year‐old woman with a history of migraines presented with neck pain and stiffness, stating, “I can’t turn my head.” Five days earlier, her son reached over and, using two fingers, quickly pulled her chin toward her left side; she then developed severe right‐sided lateral neck pain extending posteriorly into her skull. Two days before presentation, she was seen at an urgent care center, given a diagnosis of “neck spasm,” and prescribed a nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drug, a muscle relaxant, and steroids with minimal relief.

In the emergency department, she denied severe headache, vision or hearing changes, speech changes, focal weakness, numbness or tingling, fever, or chills. She was afebrile with normal vital signs. She appeared uncomfortable, sitting with her head tilted to the right and her chin rotated to the left, and she had severely restricted, painful neck motion. Her trachea was midline; there was no submandibular gland tenderness or swelling and no hypertonicity of the sternocleidomastoid muscles. Oropharyngeal examination was limited by pain and mild trismus but showed no abnormalities. There was mild upper midline cervical tenderness to palpation, and no focal neurologic deficits were present.

A computed tomography (CT) scan of the neck with contrast and of the cervical spine without contrast, including three‐dimensional reconstruction, was performed. The CT scans demonstrated asymmetry of the odontoid lateral‐mass interspaces with posterior displacement of C1 on C2 on the left, as well as prevertebral soft‐tissue edema from C3 to C5. These findings suggest a lateral axial rotatory subluxation.

A 42-year-old man presented with two weeks of chest pain and worsening exertional dyspnea. Four years earlier he had undergone total thyroidectomy for Graves’ disease and had been maintained on levothyroxine, but he self-discontinued the medication two years ago. He noted mild exertional dyspnea over the past year, which acutely worsened along with chest pain two weeks before presentation. He had no family history of thyroid or heart disease, a 22 pack-year smoking history, and no alcohol use.

On examination: height 180 cm; weight 118 kg (BMI 35.2 kg/m2); blood pressure 155/103 mm Hg; heart rate 79 beats/min; temperature 36.3 °C; SpO2 78% on room air. Lung auscultation revealed attenuated breath sounds bilaterally; heart sounds were weak without friction rub; no peripheral edema.

Laboratory studies showed TSH 25.5 µU/mL, free T3 1.6 pg/mL, free T4 < 0.40 ng/dL; WBC 25,280/µL; CRP 18.66 mg/dL; AST 90 U/L; ALT 71 U/L; CK 888 U/L; creatinine 1.61 mg/dL; plasma glucose 247 mg/dL. Chest radiograph demonstrated pleural effusion. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a large pericardial effusion with preserved ejection fraction (~60%). Chest and abdominal CT confirmed large pleural and pericardial effusions and showed left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia.

A 23-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of a central scotoma in his left eye. Seven days earlier he had developed fever, sore throat, and a rash on the palms, soles, and perioral area. On examination, the best-corrected visual acuity in the left eye was 0.9, and intraocular pressure was 19 mmHg. Dilated fundus examination revealed a grayish-white patch at the superotemporal macula. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated heterogeneous hyperreflective thickening at the level of the outer retina and retinal pigment epithelium in the foveal region, a central subfield thickness of 318 µm, loss of the ellipsoid zone, increased choroidal thickness, and reduced reflectivity of the interstitial tissue. Fluorescein angiography showed irregular hyperfluorescence at the level of the retinal pigment epithelial lesion with complete late staining; there was no pinpoint leakage or other signs of central serous chorioretinopathy. Laboratory studies revealed normal complete blood count, unremarkable mycoplasma pneumoniae immunoglobulin M, unremarkable serological test for syphilis-rapid plasma, and a positive pan-enterovirus RNA PCR.

A 20-year-old Nepalese man presented with a 1-week history of fever (max 39.6 °C), anorexia, episodic headache, and vomiting. He had no photophobia, rash, joint or abdominal pain, weight loss, or new lumps. He moved to Qatar 18 months prior and had not traveled since. He worked as a farmer without animal contact and denied unpasteurized dairy consumption. On exam he appeared underweight, was febrile, blood pressure 97/49 mm Hg, pulse 82 bpm, and respirations 18/min; meningeal signs were absent and the only positive finding was splenomegaly. Laboratory studies showed pancytopenia (Hb 8.2 g/dL, WBC 1.6×10^6/µL, platelets 53×10^6/µL), elevated liver enzymes (ALT 69 U/L, AST 129 U/L), C-reactive protein 83 mg/L, ferritin 26 294 µg/L, and borderline low vitamin B12. Screening tests for malaria, brucella, tuberculosis, CMV, EBV, parvovirus, and autoantibodies were negative. Ultrasonography of the abdomen and CT of the chest and abdomen confirmed hepatosplenomegaly (liver 18 cm, spleen 23 cm) and diffuse axial skeletal sclerosis; chest radiograph and echocardiogram were normal. The patient received vitamin B12 replacement. On hospital day 9, he remained febrile despite broad-spectrum antibiotics and negative blood cultures, and a bone marrow aspirate and biopsy were performed.

A 70-year-old man with a longstanding history of polyarticular joint pain, soft tissue swelling, diabetes, hypertension, and chronic renal failure presented with sudden onset of upper- and lower-limb weakness. On examination, findings were consistent with spinal cord compression.  

A lateral cervical spine radiograph showed partial collapse of the C5 and C6 vertebral bodies with complete loss of the C5–6 disc space. Contrast-enhanced CT of the cervical and thoracic spine (bone window and postcontrast images) demonstrated:  
• A bulging soft tissue mass at C5 causing narrowing of the spinal canal and obliteration of bilateral neural foramina, with avid enhancement  
• A similar enhancing soft tissue lesion at the left T10 pedicle narrowing the canal  
• Multilevel extradural soft tissue deposits on sagittal reformats  

MRI of the whole spine with contrast revealed:  
• Collapse of C5 and C6 vertebral bodies with an intermediate T1- and T2-weighted signal lesion centered at the C5–6 disc space  
• Heterogeneous contrast enhancement and bony expansion at C5–6  
• Extradural cord compression and obliteration of the anterior subarachnoid space  
• Multiple additional lesions of similar signal intensity affecting posterior elements at multiple levels, some para-articular or juxta-articular to the facet joints  

A 99mTc bone scan showed background polyarthritis in the feet and knees, abnormal tracer uptake at C5–6, and multiple foci of elevated uptake in the posterior elements of the thoracic spine, which is atypical for osseous metastases.

A 73-year-old Iranian man with a 24-year history of uncontrolled diabetes mellitus presented in January 2022 with a 3-month history of a large right-foot ulcer overlying the Achilles tendon. His medical history included heart failure with an ejection fraction of 30%, prior coronary angiography, and pacemaker insertion. He had been self-administering metformin 500 mg twice daily for the past 7 years and had scars from multiple previously healed foot ulcers.

On examination, he had a Wagner grade II, non-infected ulcer measuring 10 cm in length and 4.2 cm in width, with 9.5 cm of the Achilles tendon exposed beyond the sheath. The ulcer had minimal granulation tissue at its edges, and most of the wound surface was occupied by the tendon. An ankle-brachial index was 0.7, indicating poor perfusion. The patient had been using dry sterile gauze dressings, and the tendon was at risk of dehydration and necrosis. Surgical repair was considered but deemed unsuitable because of his cardiovascular comorbidities.

A 23‐year‐old woman presented with a 7‐day history of persistent high fever (maximum, 39°C), sore throat, and joint pain affecting her elbows, fingers, and knees, accompanied by abdominal pain. She denied recent travel or known sick contacts.  
On examination, she was alert and oriented; vital signs were otherwise unremarkable except for fever. There was no lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or joint swelling. A faint, flagellate erythematous rash appeared on her abdomen and neck during hospitalization.  
Initial laboratory studies showed: WBC count 13,800/µL with 89% neutrophils; hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL; platelets 162,000/µL; ESR 98 mm/h; CRP 79 mg/L; LDH 1207 IU/L; ferritin 1760 ng/mL; ALP 410 IU/L; AST 120 U/L; ALT 170 U/L; total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL; INR 1.1. Urinalysis showed 2–3 WBCs per high‐power field.  
Serologic tests for EBV, CMV, hepatitis A, B, and C, and HIV were negative. Wright, Coombs Wright, and 2‐mercaptoethanol tests for brucellosis were negative. Rheumatologic markers, including rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibodies, were within normal limits. Ceruloplasmin was normal.  
Abdominal and pelvic ultrasound was unremarkable. Doppler ultrasound demonstrated thrombosis of small hepatic veins, consistent with Budd–Chiari syndrome. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis confirmed splenomegaly (spleen size, 126 mm) without other abnormalities.

A 51-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of progressive difficulty swallowing solid foods, a pulling sensation in her throat, coughing with excessive mucus after eating, and shortness of breath.  
Her modified barium swallow study was normal except for stasis of solids at the level of the epiglottis.  
Transnasal flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy showed bilateral pharyngeal wall fullness with narrowing from the nasopharynx to the larynx, effaced pyriform sinuses, enlarged adenoid pad, and copious mucus. The mucosa overlying the posterior and lateral pharyngeal walls appeared smooth, and the nose, epiglottis, and larynx were otherwise normal.  
Noncontrast CT of the paranasal sinuses was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed diffuse submucosal thickening of the pharyngeal wall extending from the oropharynx to the cervical esophagus, with involvement of glottic and supraglottic structures (including the epiglottis and aryepiglottic folds), and no cervical lymphadenopathy or abscess.  
Subsequent contrast-enhanced MRI of the neck confirmed diffuse submucosal pharyngeal and supraglottic thickening with low T2/STIR signal intensity, heterogeneous postcontrast enhancement, and mild restricted diffusion.  
Laboratory studies were notable for an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 42 mm/h and an elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level; other results were within normal limits.

A 95-year-old woman with dementia, severe hypokinetic syndrome, hypertensive heart disease, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease presented with a 1-week history of fever (maximum 38 °C), upper abdominal pain, mild dyspepsia, and a rapidly enlarging mass in the anterior abdominal wall. She denied prior surgeries or bleeding disorders. On examination, her temperature was 38 °C, heart rate 86 beats/min, and blood pressure 110/65 mmHg. There was no jaundice. Abdominal palpation revealed an 8 cm diameter tender, tense, warm, and erythematous mass in the epigastric–umbilical region without peritoneal signs.  
Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 14.5 × 10^3/µL (normal 4.1–10 × 10^3/µL), hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL (12.5–15.5 g/dL), C-reactive protein 12.53 mg/dL (0–0.5 mg/dL), and normal liver function and coagulation tests.  
Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a complex‐appearing mass >12 cm within the anterior abdominal wall displacing the stomach posteriorly; the gallbladder appeared normal without stones. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 3.5 cm fluid collection in the anterolateral portion of segment 3 of the left hepatic lobe that was contiguous through a subtle fistulous tract with a 12 × 14 × 7 cm necrotic collection in the subcutaneous tissues of the abdominal wall; the anterior fascia was disrupted, and there was intrahepatic and common bile duct dilatation with a regular outlet into the duodenum.  
Tumor markers and serologic tests for amebiasis and tuberculosis were negative.

A 50-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a painless swelling in the mental region of the mandible. She had no significant medical comorbidities. On intraoral examination, there was bony expansion in the right vestibular mandibular region and a sinus tract with purulent drainage in the vestibular mental area; submental lymph nodes were palpable. The patient had bilateral mandibular implant-supported prostheses without any clinical mobility.

Panoramic radiography and cone-beam CT revealed a well-defined, circular, unilocular radiolucent lesion measuring 2.5 cm in diameter, extending from the left lateral mandibular incisor to the right mandibular first premolar. The lesion enclosed the implant fixture in the region of tooth 4.4 and showed no adjacent root resorption. Radiographic review also noted:
• Implant-supported prostheses in regions 3.4–3.6 and 4.4–4.6  
• A prosthetic overdenture on natural teeth from 3.3 to 4.3  
• Metallic endocanal posts in teeth 3.3, 4.2, and 4.3  
• Previous endodontic treatments of teeth 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 4.1, 4.2, and 4.3, with the obturations in 4.1–4.3 not reaching the apices  

On the basis of these clinical and radiographic features, the preliminary diagnosis was an odontogenic cyst of inflammatory origin.

A 25-year-old male student and active footballer presented with ten days of progressive dyspnea on exertion that progressed to dyspnea at rest, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, easy fatigability, abdominal and leg edema, right upper-quadrant discomfort, early satiety, and productive cough with frothy sputum. He denied fever or urinary symptoms. On examination, he was mildly tachypneic with an O2 saturation of 91% on room air, blood pressure 100/80 mmHg, heart rate 104 bpm, jugular venous pressure ~8 cm, bilateral pitting edema to the shins, displaced apical impulse, a third heart sound, a loud component of S2, a grade IV holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, and a grade III holosystolic murmur over the left lower sternal border. Lung bases had bilateral crepitations. The abdomen revealed soft, tender hepatomegaly 12 cm below the right costal margin and mild ascites. There were no skeletal anomalies or clubbing. Chest radiography showed cardiomegaly, pulmonary venous congestion, and a small left pleural effusion. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia with a complete right bundle branch block and left posterior hemiblock. Laboratory studies revealed a WBC count of 11.6×10^9/L (neutrophils 8.3×10^9/L, lymphocytes 2.6×10^9/L), hemoglobin 16.3 g/dL, hematocrit 54.9%, platelets 522×10^9/L, and normal renal function (creatinine 92 µmol/L).

A 17-year-old healthy boy had been diagnosed in 2016 with severe left-eye uveitis complicated by central retinal vein occlusion and iris rubeosis. Initial workup—including chest radiography and laboratory evaluations—found no infectious, granulomatous, or systemic autoimmune cause. He was managed with immunomodulators and topical steroids, with complete resolution of vein occlusion and rubeosis. His last mild left anterior uveitis occurred in November 2020, treated with a 5-week taper of topical steroids. He remained quiescent at quarterly visits through spring 2021, with best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of 20/16 in both eyes.

In June 2021, he received his first dose of the BNT162b2 (BioNTech-Pfizer) COVID-19 vaccine. The next day, he noted sudden vision loss in the left eye and presented to the ophthalmology clinic. On examination, BCVA was 20/16 in the right eye and 20/500 in the left eye. Findings in the left eye included corneal precipitates; 50 cells per slit in the anterior chamber with fibrin formation; widespread iris rubeosis; 16–25 vitreous cells per slit; and cystoid macular edema on optical coherence tomography.

A 54-year-old man with a 36–pack-year smoking history presented with five days of right-sided pleuritic chest pain and a one-month history of productive cough with white sputum. He denied fever, dyspnea, night sweats, weight loss, or other constitutional symptoms. His medical history included metabolic syndrome and ischemic heart disease. Physical examination was unremarkable.

A chest radiograph showed a 3.6-cm spiculated mass in the right lower zone. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a 3.7 × 2.7 cm right middle lobe mass with central low attenuation suggestive of necrosis, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and a left adrenal nodule. These findings were highly suspicious for metastatic lung carcinoma. Sputum smears for acid-fast bacilli and GeneXpert PCR for tuberculosis were negative.

Endobronchial ultrasound–guided transbronchial needle aspiration of subcarinal and right paratracheal lymph nodes showed moderate lymphocytes without malignant cells. Transbronchial lung biopsy of the mass revealed intra-alveolar foamy macrophages with fibrin, suspicious for lipoid pneumonia. Further history elicited no use of e-cigarettes, no episodes of aspiration, and no ingestion of oil-based traditional medicines. He did report recent do-it-yourself renovation work involving paint and industrial glue, both containing oil-based additives.

A 33‐year‐old woman with a 5‐year history of recurrent abdominal pain and intermittent jaundice was referred for imaging. At age 30, she had been diagnosed with cholelithiasis at another center. Liver function tests showed a slight elevation of bilirubin. 

Abdominal ultrasound revealed an intussusception involving the duodenum and proximal jejunum, with an anechoic cystic lesion within the intussuscepted segment; the biliary tree was dilated. Contrast-enhanced CT in the portal venous phase and MR imaging—including axial and coronal T2-weighted sequences, MR cholangiopancreatography, and dynamic sequences with hepatocyte-specific gadolinium ethoxybenzyl DTPA—confirmed invagination of the distal duodenum, surrounding fat, vessels, and pancreatic head into the proximal jejunum. A simple cystic lesion was again noted within the intussusception, and the stomach was not distended. MR cholangiopancreatography showed slight dilatation of the extrahepatic bile duct, displaced leftward toward the cyst mass. During the hepatocytic (delayed) phase, contrast filled the biliary tree and bowel lumen but did not enter the cyst lumen.

A 34-year-old G5P3 woman presented with acute right lower quadrant abdominal pain one week after laparoscopic bilateral salpingectomy and right ovarian dermoid cystectomy complicated by intra-abdominal sebaceous spill and extensive irrigation. Two days postoperatively she re-presented with significant incision-site pain; a pelvic ultrasound at that time showed an 8.0 cm × 7.0 cm × 4.7 cm complex right adnexal mass, initially suspicious for a hematoma, and she was admitted overnight for pain control. Her pain resolved, and she was discharged. On the current presentation she reports sudden onset of right lower quadrant pain without nausea or vomiting. A Doppler ultrasound of the pelvis shows an enlarged right ovary measuring 7.2 cm × 5.2 cm × 6.2 cm with a swirling vessel (whirlpool) sign.

A 19-year-old woman presents with a lifelong, nonprogressive decrease in hearing on both sides. She has no history of ear infections, trauma, or previous otologic surgery. There is no family history of hearing loss or congenital ear anomalies. Examination reveals normal external ears and intact tympanic membranes bilaterally. Pure-tone audiometry shows bilateral conductive hearing loss at all tested frequencies (250–4000 Hz) with an average air–bone gap of 60 dB. Rinne tests are negative bilaterally, and Weber’s test is heard in the midline. With a presumptive diagnosis of otosclerosis, a right exploratory tympanostomy is planned.

A 6‐year‐old girl with no relevant medical history presented with intensely pruritic skin lesions on her anterior thighs. The lesions first appeared 2 weeks earlier in recurrent 3‐day outbreaks, always at the same locations, and resolved spontaneously without residual injury. She had no systemic symptoms, preceding infection, topical exposures, sunburn, bites, animal contacts, or recent medications.

On examination, there were well‐defined, confluent, erythematous papules and plaques with annular, arciform, and polycyclic morphology, central clearing, and purpuric edges. Lesions were symmetrically distributed on the anterior thighs in a mirror‐image pattern.

Laboratory studies were within normal limits, including complete blood count, biochemistry, urinalysis, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C‐reactive protein, complement levels (C3, C4, C1q), immunoglobulin levels, rheumatoid factor, and acute‐phase reactants. Antinuclear, anti–double‐stranded DNA, antineutrophil cytoplasmic, anti–Ro, anti–La, and transglutaminase antibodies were negative. Serologies for syphilis, hepatitis B and C viruses, HIV, cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, and parvovirus B19 were negative. A chest radiograph was unremarkable.

An 18-month-old Saudi girl was referred for evaluation of recurrent hypoglycemic episodes. She was born at term via cesarean section with a birth weight of 1.0 kg after a pregnancy complicated by maternal gestational diabetes and required 2 months of NICU care for respiratory distress. She met developmental milestones appropriately until age 9 months, when she developed generalized tonic–clonic seizures without fever, lasting 2–3 minutes. A 6-year-old brother has epilepsy.

At 13 months, she became lethargic, drowsy, and irritable; blood glucose measurement revealed hypoglycemia, and she was discharged on dietary recommendations. She then had another seizure and decreased consciousness; a local hospital PICU admission showed a blood glucose level of 30 mg/dL treated with intravenous fluids. On referral, she required high concentrations of dextrose (up to 25%), frequent high-dose octreotide, and glucagon.

Multiple samples during hypoglycemia demonstrated serum glucose 4.0 mmol/L, insulin 3744 pmol/L, and C-peptide 0.02 ng/mL. Physical examination revealed a swelling with needle-insertion marks on the upper lateral right thigh and bilateral deltoid needle marks; the child remained calm during needle pricks. The mother insisted on pancreatectomy. All other investigations—including genetic testing, PET imaging of the pancreas, brain MRI, and EEG—were unremarkable. All hypoglycemic episodes occurred while the mother was present, raising suspicion of an exogenous cause of hypoglycemia.

A 29-year-old Hispanic woman presented with 2 weeks of persistent fevers up to 38.9 °C, arthralgias, and a new stationary “black spot” in her right eye with bilateral floaters. One week earlier she had pharyngitis treated with amoxicillin. Physical examination showed a maculopapular torso rash; the remainder of her exam was unremarkable. She had no significant medical or ophthalmic history, no recent travel or sick contacts, and lived in the suburbs with multiple household pets.  
Initial labs revealed elevated transaminases (ALT 375 U/L, AST 313 U/L), GGT 97 IU/L, ESR 53 mm/hr, and CRP 82.9 mg/L. A chest CT scan was normal. Rickettsial serologies were pending. Rheumatology evaluation led to methylprednisolone 80 mg IM and prednisone 20 mg daily for presumed adult-onset Still’s disease, but ferritin levels and tests for C3/C4, ANA, rheumatoid factor, ANCA, and CCP IgG were within normal limits.  
Ophthalmic examination showed best-corrected visual acuity 20/20 bilaterally, normal intraocular pressures and pupillary responses, and clear anterior segments. Fundus exam revealed bilateral scattered white pre- or inner-retinal spots and a cotton-wool spot in the left eye. OCT demonstrated vitreous opacities anterior to both foveae without ellipsoid-zone disruption. Widefield fundus autofluorescence showed multiple hyperautofluorescent spots, and late-phase fluorescein angiography demonstrated retinal vascular leakage with optic-disc hyperfluorescence in both eyes.

A 31-year-old white woman with a history of menorrhagia, anemia, and recurrent calcium nephrolithiasis presented for preoperative evaluation before ureterolithotomy. She reported a daily pattern of consuming ice chips from a cup and multiple spoonfuls of salt directly from a shaker; these cravings had been present for many years, interfered with her daily life, and acutely worsened after her most recent childbirth. She described menstrual bleeding lasting 5 days per cycle and denied cravings for chalk, clay, or dirt as well as symptoms of lightheadedness, syncope, near-syncope, or melena. On examination, her temperature was 36.7 °C, blood pressure 119/70 mm Hg, pulse 88 beats/min, respirations 20 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 100% on room air, and body‐mass index 26.3 kg/m2. She appeared well-nourished and well-developed, with no pallor, stomatitis, glossitis, or splenomegaly; mentation, mood, and affect were normal. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, hematocrit 33.9%, mean corpuscular volume 74.2 μm3, total iron 22 μg/dL, total iron‐binding capacity 431 μg/dL, iron sat­uration 5%, and ferritin 3 ng/mL. Analysis of a previously passed kidney stone revealed 55% calcium oxalate monohydrate, 30% calcium phosphate hydroxyl form, 7% calcium oxalate dehydrate, 5% calcium phosphate carbonate, and 3% protein.

An 18-year-old woman with no relevant medical history presented with altered mental status and agitation that began earlier that day. She was confused, irritable, and noted to have left-sided upper and lower limb weakness. Cranial-nerve examination was unremarkable. Vital signs were within normal limits (blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, pulse 66/min, temperature 37.3°C). 

Initial laboratory testing, including a complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel, was unremarkable. Brain MRI showed extensive, confluent hyperintensities in bilateral supratentorial periventricular and subcortical white matter on FLAIR and T2-weighted images, with involvement of the frontal and parietal centrum semiovale. There was no diffusion restriction on diffusion-weighted imaging, and no enhancement on postcontrast T1-weighted images. 

Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal protein, normal glucose, and a normal total cell count. Microbiological studies, including PCR for HSV-1, HSV-2, and JC virus as well as a meningitis/encephalitis panel, were negative. Further investigations—HIV and CMV serology, syphilis screening, vitamin B12 levels, and autoimmune and vasculitis antibody panels—were normal or negative. Urine toxicology was positive for cocaine.

A 12-year-old girl was referred to rheumatology at age 9 for management of progressive lower‐leg deformities. 

History of present illness:
• Surgically repaired bilateral developmental dysplasia of the hips at 17 months  
• At age 2, painless left ankle deformity; imaging showed osteonecrosis of the talar body, os calcis, and cuboid  
• At age 4, idiopathic osteonecrosis of the left third metatarsal; biopsy confirmed aseptic osteonecrosis  
• At age 6, atraumatic fracture of the right first metacarpal  
• By age 7, bilateral talar involvement and distal fibular osteolysis with tibial sparing on radiographs  

Family history: Two younger siblings developing similar bone lesions.

Examination at age 9:
• Well-appearing child with gross bilateral deformities of ankles and feet  
• No dysmorphic features; normal growth and development  
• Mild subjective decrease in pain sensation; otherwise normal neurologic exam  

Laboratory and imaging findings:
• ESR 20 mm/hr; full blood picture, urea and electrolytes, ANA, and CRP normal  
• Metabolic studies normal  
• Nerve conduction: intact motor, borderline delayed sensory  
• Mutation analysis for MMP2 gene negative

A 27-year-old woman who works as an agricultural laborer was referred with fatigue, malaise, anorexia, and epistaxis. On examination, she was pale, with eczematous plaques on her chest and proximal right arm, and had splenomegaly 6 cm below the costal margin. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL, white-cell count 4.0×10^9/L, and platelets 23×10^9/L. A peripheral-blood smear revealed lymphoblasts. Flow cytometry was positive for TdT, CD34, CD19, CD10, CD22, and HLA-DR, and bone marrow evaluation confirmed acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The eczematous plaques were treated as contact dermatitis with topical methylprednisolone, resolving rapidly, and induction chemotherapy with hyper-CVAD was initiated. 

On day 8, she developed febrile neutropenia and received piperacillin–tazobactam. Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species grew in blood cultures, prompting addition of teicoplanin. Persistent fever led to repeat cultures, which grew Enterococcus species, and teicoplanin was replaced with daptomycin. High-resolution chest CT showed nonspecific nodules under 1 cm, and serum galactomannan antigen was negative. After 10 days of fever with an absolute neutrophil count of 20/μL, she reported severe pain in her right arm radiating to her shoulder, suggesting herpes zoster; however, no vesicles were present. On examination, there was a very tender point in the upper lateral scapular region with an underlying vague mass. MRI of the right shoulder demonstrated a focal cystic necrotic lesion between the teres minor and teres major muscles.

A 32-year-old North African man presented with a 3-week history of low mood, insomnia, and fatigue. He had no medical comorbidities, was not taking any medications, and had unremarkable physical examination and laboratory tests (including CBC, metabolic panel, thyroid, vitamin D) and ECG. He was diagnosed with moderate-to-severe major depressive disorder and started on Escitalopram 5 mg daily, increased to 10 mg on day 5, with improvement in mood, appetite, and concentration but persistent initial and middle insomnia. After 3 weeks, Zolpidem 10 mg at bedtime was added without benefit, so 25 mg of Agomelatine at night was introduced and Zolpidem stopped (Escitalopram was continued). Two days later, he began experiencing “tingling and crawling” sensations deep in his legs each evening, partially relieved by walking or moving them in bed. By day 7 of Agomelatine treatment, he reported “agonizing electricity and tingling sensation running non-stop through my legs,” predominantly at night with an intense and continuous urge to walk or move his lower limbs and only limited relief.

An 84-year-old man presented with an intermittently painful skin lesion on his forehead. Three months earlier, he had noted a progressive swelling that reached a 3 cm elevation. His history was significant for chronic sinusitis, recurrent purulent rhinorrhea, and sporadic headaches; he denied fever and head trauma. The lesion had been diagnosed as an epidermoid cyst at another hospital, and a minimal amount of pus was released in an attempt to relieve it. Three weeks later, a larger amount of pus drained spontaneously, and clindamycin was started; the wound was left open for drainage. After five weeks without resolution, he was referred for surgical intervention. On examination, there was a small purulent wound in the central forehead with slight bloody effusion, minimal erythema, and no residual swelling; palpation was nonpainful. Under local anesthesia, the skin lesion was excised, revealing chronic inflammatory tissue involving the frontalis muscle. Deep palpation exposed a round opening with smooth bony edges in the frontal bone, with an apparent connection to the left frontal sinus.

A 66-year-old man with a history of complete C7 tetraplegia since a 1974 rugby injury presented with a 3-month history of intermittent hypertension (up to 240/135 mm Hg) triggered by changes in position. He also reported severe headaches, blurry vision, and hyperhidrosis of the left arm and face. These symptoms persisted despite trials of clonidine, hydralazine, chlorothiazide, hemorrhoid excision, colostomy, and colon resection. Bladder distention, catheterization issues, anal fissure, and skin ulcers were all ruled out as causes of autonomic dysreflexia.

On examination, he had no voluntary function below C7, preserved biceps and deltoid strength, normal reflexes at C6 and above, and a sensory level a few inches above the nipple line. Inspection of the thoracic spine revealed an audible, palpable, and visible dynamic kyphosis.

Laboratory studies, including blood and urine analyses, showed no signs of sepsis or urinary tract infection. CT-guided aspiration of the T8–T9 interspace yielded fluid that was negative on Gram stain, bacterial culture, acid-fast bacilli testing, and fungal culture.

Plain radiographs showed mild spondylosis, a well-healed C5–C6 fusion, mild lumbar spondylosis, and anterior osteophytes at multiple thoracic levels without spondylolisthesis or acute fractures. CT of the thoracic spine demonstrated marked fluid collection in the T8–T9 interspace with destruction of the disc space and degradation of the adjacent vertebral bodies. MRI revealed marked kyphotic deformity and high-grade compression of the spinal cord at T8–T9, destruction of the disc space with a central cystic component, and vertebral body fractures; additionally, a nonenhancing expansile lesion extending from C4–C5 to mid-body T2 was noted.

A 43-year-old woman presented in July 2013 with a several-month history of weight gain, central obesity, moon facies, facial plethora, easy bruising, muscle wasting and weakness, skin thinning, headache, menstrual irregularity, depressive mood, acne, hirsutism, and osteopenia. An overnight 1-mg dexamethasone suppression test showed serum cortisol levels of 22.5 and 27.1 μg/dL on two separate days (reference <1.8 μg/dL). Late-night salivary cortisol measurements were 14.5 and 24.7 nmol/L (reference <1.0 nmol/L), and 24-hour urinary free cortisol levels were 472 and 455 μg/24 h (reference <250 μg/24 h). Morning ACTH was 45 pg/mL (reference <46 pg/mL), and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate was 641 ng/mL (reference 61–337 ng/mL). Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary gland revealed an 8-mm lesion in the left side of the gland; CT of the chest and MRI of the abdomen and pelvis were unremarkable. After an 8-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test, cortisol levels decreased by 83%. At that time, she experienced spontaneous weight loss, return of regular menses, and normalization of late-night salivary cortisol (76 ng/dL; reference <100 ng/dL) and urinary free cortisol (25.1 and 70.0 μg/24 h; reference 3–43 μg/24 h), prompting cancellation of scheduled pituitary surgery. By February 2014, her clinical features and hypercortisolism had recurred. She underwent transsphenoidal surgery in June 2014; no adenoma was identified on pathology. On postoperative day 10, cortisol was 23.4 μg/dL (8–9 AM; reference 6.0–18.4 μg/dL) and ACTH was 41 pg/mL. A bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling was planned but was postponed because of another spontaneous clinical and biochemical remission.

A 26-year-old woman from Manila presented with a 5-month history of jaundice associated with intermittent epigastric pain, weight loss, pruritus, and tea-colored urine. She had no comorbidities or prior surgeries. On examination, she was normotensive (110/70 mmHg), heart rate 80 bpm, afebrile, with icteric sclerae and generalized jaundice; the abdomen was soft, nondistended, and nontender. Transabdominal ultrasound showed a nondilated common bile duct, intrahepatic ductal dilatation with segmental areas of dilation, and biliary sludge. A diagnosis of choledocholithiasis with possible biliary stricture secondary to hepatobiliary tuberculosis was made. 

ERCP revealed a patulous ampulla, a nondilated CBD tapering at the common hepatic duct over 13.9 mm, dilated intrahepatic ducts (right 10.1 mm, left 7.3 mm), and no filling defects. After graded dilation of the common hepatic duct stricture and partial sphincterotomy, a 17-cm Fr 8.5 plastic biliary stent was placed with good bile egress. TB-PCR testing of bile was positive for tuberculosis. 

On the first postprocedure day, she reported episodic epigastric pain (VAS 8/10) relieved by analgesics. On the second day, she developed fever, tachycardia, and epigastric tenderness; the impression was post-ERCP pancreatitis. Labs showed amylase 125 U/L, lipase 234 U/L, creatinine 43 μmol/L, albumin 35 g/L, hemoglobin 101 g/L, WBC 5.3×10^9/L, platelets 185×10^9/L, PT 13.9 s, INR 1.11. 

On the third postprocedure day, she remained febrile with new generalized abdominal pain, hypotension to 70/40 mmHg (partially responsive to fluids), abdominal distension, and diffuse direct and rebound tenderness. Chest and abdominal radiographs were negative for pneumoperitoneum. Abdominal ultrasound showed nondilated intrahepatic ducts and common bile duct with the stent in place. Labs now showed WBC 12.9×10^9/L, PT 22.7 s, INR 1.83, aPTT 43.9 s. Broad-spectrum antibiotics, vitamin K, FFP, and norepinephrine were started, and urgent exploratory laparotomy was planned.

A 74-year-old man who smokes presented to the emergency department with 2 days of heavy rectal bleeding and intense pain during defecation. He had no clinical signs of anemia. His medical history included coronary artery disease treated 6 years earlier with angioplasty and placement of three stents; he was taking clopidogrel 75 mg daily and aspirin 75 mg daily. He reported no prior history of hemorrhoids or similar symptoms. 

On initial physical examination, three nodules were seen protruding outside the anal canal and required manual reduction. Two of these nodules, located at the 3 o’clock and 7 o’clock positions, were thrombosed and bleeding; a smaller nodule was present at 11 o’clock. 

A colonoscopy was performed to exclude any other anorectal disease or sources of bleeding; the findings were normal.

A 78-year-old woman presented with a 4-week history of intermittent diarrhea, vomiting, fatigue, and malaise beginning after a course of antibiotics. Her past medical history included atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, gout, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Medications on admission included edoxaban, digoxin, bisoprolol, amiodarone, allopurinol, ferrous fumarate, lansoprazole, metformin, gliclazide, furosemide, atorvastatin, inhalers, mirtazapine, and supplements.

On examination, heart rate was 40 beats per minute with bradycardic atrial fibrillation on ECG, blood pressure 103/57 mm Hg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 92% on room air; she had cool peripheries and was afebrile. ECG demonstrated diffuse down-sloping ST depressions and T-wave inversions, consistent with digoxin effect. Laboratory studies revealed acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease (creatinine 396 µmol/L, eGFR 10 mL/min/1.73 m²), hyperkalaemia (6.2 mmol/L), and a markedly elevated digoxin level of 8.1 nmol/L (reference 0.8–1.2 nmol/L). Other electrolytes and blood counts were within or close to normal limits. Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal ejection fraction and no regional wall motion abnormalities.

She received calcium gluconate, insulin–dextrose, five vials of digoxin-specific antibody fragments, IV fluids, magnesium sulfate, and dobutamine, and was transferred to the coronary care unit for monitoring. While in the CCU, she developed generalized, symmetrical choreiform movements with myoclonus of the fingers, dyskinetic movements of the oral muscles and tongue, diffuse hypertonia, and hyperreflexia. An urgent CT scan of the brain showed no new abnormalities but revealed old bilateral basal ganglia infarcts.

A 72‐year‐old man presented with occasional episodes of abdominal fullness and epigastric pain for 4 years. The discomfort was mainly noted after meals, and he denied vomiting, dysphagia, or weight loss. On examination, vital signs were normal and the physical examination was unremarkable. Serum biochemistries, including amylase, lipase, and liver‐function tests, were within normal limits. Upper endoscopy showed slight hyperemia of the gastric mucosa but no ulcers or mass lesions. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated mild fatty infiltration of the liver and moderate dilation of the stomach and duodenum. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed an incomplete ring of pancreatic tissue arising from the head of the pancreas and partially encircling the second part of the duodenum, creating a “crocodile jaw appearance.” Peripancreatic fat planes were preserved.

A 54-year-old man with a 14-year history of Parkinson’s disease (PD) was admitted for bilateral subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation (DBS). His regimen consisted of levodopa 600 mg/day, carbidopa 125 mg/day, entacapone 1200 mg/day, and pramipexole 0.54 mg/day, all of which were discontinued 18 hours before surgery to optimize intraoperative testing. The DBS electrodes were placed uneventfully. Three hours postoperatively, he developed tremor, muscle rigidity, and a fever unresponsive to acetaminophen. Clinicians initially attributed these findings to PD and administered levodopa 200 mg three times daily via a nasogastric tube. Systemic and central nervous system infection were considered, but cerebrospinal fluid analysis, chest radiography, and blood and urine cultures were normal. Brain MRI showed no intracranial pathology and confirmed optimal lead placement. Twelve hours after surgery, he exhibited severe axial and appendicular rigidity, a coarse resting tremor, prolonged spasms of the extremities, a temperature of 40 °C, and blood pressure of 165/94 mmHg. Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 19.4 × 10^9/L with left shift, a creatine kinase level of 1500 U/L with a normal CK-MB fraction, and normal cardiac troponin levels.

A previously healthy 14-year-old boy first presented with a 5-day history of stabbing left ankle pain and jaundice without fever. Two days earlier, left ankle radiographs and CT were normal. He denied trauma, animal contact, drug use, or sexual activity; he had recently returned from camping in Italy. On exam, he was in good general condition, afebrile, and hemodynamically stable but markedly jaundiced, with localized ankle pain without swelling, warmth, or erythema. Laboratory studies showed total bilirubin 103 µmol/L, platelet count 84 G/L, ALT 178 U/L, AST 129 U/L, C-reactive protein 195 mg/L; full blood count and coagulation tests were otherwise normal. An abdominal ultrasound showed hepatosplenomegaly without biliary obstruction. He was discharged with a preliminary diagnosis of viral hepatitis.

Five days later, he returned in poor general condition with tachycardia (220 bpm), normotension, and persistent jaundice. He had increased tenderness, swelling, and erythema of the left ankle, bilateral wrist and forearm swelling and erythema, diffuse allodynia, inability to walk, and a non-blanching purpuric rash on both legs and the left forearm. Laboratory tests revealed CRP 223 mg/L, leukocytes 29.7 G/L, platelets 53 G/L, total bilirubin 328 µmol/L, acute kidney injury (creatinine 166 µmol/L), ALT 189 U/L, AST 268 U/L, and GGT 168 U/L. He was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit with a preliminary diagnosis of systemic vasculitis versus bacterial sepsis and started on empiric broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics.

A 58-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with acute chest pain radiating to the left arm and dyspnea. Her medical history included hypertension, right upper-lobe lung carcinoma with lymph node metastasis and secondary left-lung involvement, and prior endovascular treatment of a high-flow pelvic varicocele and large pelvic arteriovenous malformation. She also reported chronic dysphagia with pain on swallowing and left-upper-limb functional limitation with paresthesia.

On admission, cardiac markers were within normal limits, but the D-dimer concentration was elevated at 1153 ng/mL (reference ≤500 ng/mL). CT pulmonary angiography demonstrated an occlusive defect in a segmental arterial branch of the right lower lobe, confirming pulmonary embolism. Incidentally, the aortic arch was anomalous: a right aortic arch of normal caliber gave rise independently to the right subclavian and right common carotid arteries; a smaller (9 mm) left arch, stenotic and hypoplastic in its posterior segment, connected to a sacciform dilatation (45 mm) of the descending aorta, together forming a complete vascular ring compressing the esophagus. The left common carotid and left subclavian arteries originated independently from the left arch, with the left subclavian artery showing an 80% focal stenosis from a mixed atherosclerotic plaque. Duplex ultrasound of the left epiaortic and upper-limb arteries revealed increased peak systolic velocity in the left subclavian artery and reversed flow in the left vertebral artery, consistent with subclavian steal syndrome.

A 64-year-old man with a 60-pack-year smoking history was diagnosed with stage IV undifferentiated large-cell lung carcinoma after bronchial biopsy. Initial brain CT showed an edematous, non–contrast-enhancing area in the left temporal lobe, but he had no neurologic symptoms and declined MRI. He underwent four cycles of carboplatin, etoposide, and epirubicin, with a 50% reduction in the primary lung mass and mediastinal lymphadenopathy after three cycles. Twenty days after the fourth cycle, he was admitted for self-limiting complex partial seizures manifesting as motionless staring and facial twitching without secondary generalization. Relatives reported a two-week history of short-term memory loss, temporary confusion, anxiety, and depression. Treatment with levetiracetam and alprazolam was initiated. Brain MRI demonstrated findings of cerebral gliomatosis, and magnetic resonance spectroscopy supported this interpretation. Clinical and laboratory evaluations were not indicative of metabolic, infectious, vascular, drug-induced, or chemotherapy-related disease. Serum testing for anti-Hu antibodies was negative. A stereotactic brain biopsy revealed lymphocytic infiltration and gliosis without evidence of tumor cells.

A 79-year-old man (169 cm, 79 kg) with a history of acute myeloid leukemia in remission, thoracic aortic aneurysm repair, and coronary artery bypass grafting was scheduled for total cystectomy and ileal conduit diversion for bladder cancer. Preoperative vital signs were blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, heart rate 90 bpm, and SpO₂ 98% on room air. A chest radiograph showed a cardiothoracic ratio of 58% with clear lung fields, and transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated normal cardiac function (LVEF 50%). Laboratory tests revealed hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL and platelets 1.0 × 10⁵/μL.  

During anesthesia induction and maintenance, intraoperative platelet transfusion was started. Forty minutes later, the patient’s SpO₂ fell to 92–95% on FiO₂ 0.5, and large volumes of foamy sputum were suctioned from the endotracheal tube. Hypotension ensued, requiring noradrenaline. He received packed red blood cells (560 mL), platelets (400 mL), and albumin (1000 mL). At the end of surgery, a chest radiograph revealed bilateral pulmonary edema, and arterial blood gas showed a PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio of 70.1. He was transferred sedated and mechanically ventilated to the ICU.  

Persistent postoperative bleeding prompted emergency reoperation 1 hour after ICU admission. During the procedure, foamy endotracheal secretions continued, requiring bronchoscopic suctioning and periodic recruitment maneuvers. TRALI was suspected intraoperatively. After surgical hemostasis, arterial blood gas at FiO₂ 1.0 showed pH 7.06, PaCO₂ 96.1 mmHg, and PaO₂ 67.9 mmHg. VV-ECMO support was then initiated for severe hypoxemia and hypercapnia.
