A middle-aged man presented with severe right inguinal and lower abdominal pain that worsened with walking and Valsalva’s maneuver. He denied fever or chills. His medical, surgical, family, and social histories were unremarkable, with no recent trauma, travel, heavy lifting, or high-risk sexual behaviors. On examination, there was tenderness and swelling in the right inguinal region. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (11.39 × 10^3/uL), an elevated C-reactive protein level (35.4 mg/L), and leukocyturia; urine culture was negative. To exclude an incarcerated inguinal hernia, a noncontrast CT scan was obtained, revealing diffuse edematous changes of the right spermatic cord and vas deferens with peripheral fat stranding and no herniated bowel loop.

A 36-year-old man with no significant medical history presented to the emergency department with severe left scrotal pain. He reported one month of left testicular discomfort, with pain worsening over the past few hours. He had no fever or dysuria. On examination, the upper pole of the left testicle was tender and slightly swollen; abdominal palpation was normal. Urinalysis was normal. Laboratory tests showed a C-reactive protein level of 13.4 mg/L, creatine kinase 368 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase 664 U/L, and a white-cell count of 12 100/mm^3 with 83% neutrophils. Viral epididymitis was suspected; oral anti-inflammatory therapy and scrotal support were prescribed, and he was discharged. He returned the next day with worsening pain and swelling despite medication. His white-cell count had risen to 15 100/mm^3 and CRP to 16.4 mg/L. Color Doppler ultrasound of the scrotum demonstrated reduced vascularization of the left testicle; the right testicle was normal. Surgical exploration was performed to exclude torsion. At surgery, there was no torsion; instead, the upper pole of the left testicle had a pale white discoloration with a faint purple aspect. A bilateral orchidopexy was performed, and the testicle was spared.

A 38-year-old man presented with new episodes of transient loss of consciousness, progressive headaches, and tinnitus in his left ear. He also described sharp, electric-shock–like pain affecting the left cheek, jaw, teeth, gums, lips, and forehead, consistent with trigeminal distribution pain that worsened over several months. His medical history was notable for chronic otitis media; there was no history of trauma, malignancy, or significant alcohol or tobacco use. Family history included prostate cancer in his father and hypertension in his mother.

On examination, vital signs were stable and physical findings were unremarkable, including a normal neurologic examination. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. Electroencephalography showed mixed slow delta waves and eight focal spikes over the left frontotemporal region, consistent with focal epilepsy. He was started on carbamazepine.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain (T1-weighted axial) revealed a large, well-demarcated, lobulated expansile mass in the left petrous apex that was uniformly hyperintense on T1-weighted images. The lesion extended anteriorly into the sphenoid sinus and caused mass effect on the pons and left cerebellum. There was no evidence of hydrocephalus.

A 56-year-old woman with no prior medical history received the AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine. Ten days later, she noted gradual generalized weakness predominantly involving proximal and distal lower extremities, accompanied by myalgias. Initial examination and laboratory tests, including a COVID-19 PCR assay, were normal, and she was discharged with symptomatic therapy. Over the next several days, her lower-limb weakness worsened, she developed dysarthria, anorexia, and required assistance to ambulate. There was no history of sensory loss, urinary or fecal incontinence, polydipsia, or upper respiratory symptoms.

On re-presentation to the emergency department, she was afebrile, blood pressure was 190/95 mm Hg (later improving to 156/74 mm Hg), pulse was 95 beats/min, and oxygen saturation was 94% on room air. Body-mass index was 28.3 kg/m^2. Cardiac, respiratory, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Neurologic examination revealed: Glasgow Coma Scale 15; normal pupils; bilateral adduction-gaze deficit; neck stiffness; motor strength 4/5 in upper limbs and 3/5 in lower limbs; diminished deep-tendon reflexes; intact sensation. Gait assessment was limited by weakness.

Laboratory studies showed serum sodium 116 mEq/L, serum osmolality 236 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 64 mEq/L, and urine osmolality 700 mOsm/kg, consistent with the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion. Thyroid and cortisol levels were normal. Lumbar puncture revealed clear cerebrospinal fluid with protein 1.76 g/L, glucose 4.62 mmol/L, 1 WBC, 7 RBC, differential 20% segmented cells, 64% monocytes, and 16% lymphocytes. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. Brain MRI demonstrated large, multifocal, bilateral, asymmetric hyperintense lesions in the subcortical and deep white matter and basal ganglia on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences without gadolinium enhancement.

A 25-year-old previously healthy woman from Lima, Peru, presented with a one-month history of gradual, global headache. Three days before admission, the headache worsened and was accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and sleep interruption. She also noted right-sided weakness and paresthesia, and new abnormal sensation on the left side of her face and neck. She reported a 20 kg weight loss over 3 months. She denied sick contacts, travel, or drug use, but consumed dairy products, possibly unpasteurized, and lived with a dog and a cat.

On examination, temperature was 37.1°C, heart rate 70/min. She was somnolent. Abdominal exam revealed hepatomegaly. Neurologically, she had photophobia, mild right hemiparesis, and paresthesia of the right arm and leg. Cranial nerves, pupils, reflexes, and plantar responses were normal.

Laboratory studies showed leukopenia (1.3×10^3 cells/µL) without other hematologic or metabolic abnormalities. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI revealed a mass in the left temporal lobe with marked vasogenic edema, midline shift, and ventricular compression. A primary or secondary brain tumor was suspected, and mannitol was started for intracranial hypertension.

Given the imaging and clinical picture, serologic tests for infection were performed. Brucella abortus IgM and IgG ELISA were elevated (3.1 U/mL and 2.9 U/mL; normal <2). Bengal rose, Brucella latex agglutination, and tube agglutination were positive at titers of 1:160 and 1:80 (normal <1:40), respectively; serum Brucella PCR was negative. Other infectious studies—including blood cultures; Toxoplasma IgM and IgG; Cysticercosis ELISA; HIV and HTLV ELISAs; and an interferon-γ release assay for M. tuberculosis—were negative.

What is your differential diagnosis?

The patient is a 7-month-old boy, the only child of healthy, nonconsanguineous Chinese parents. Pregnancy was notable for gestational diabetes mellitus managed by diet and progressive oligohydramnios, leading to cesarean delivery at 39+ weeks. The newborn weighed 3000 g with Apgar scores of 10 at 1 and 10 minutes. At birth, he had long fingers and toes, suggesting arachnodactyly, but was otherwise in good condition.

At 2 months of age, he was noted to have a widened forehead, depressed nasal bridge, blue sclerae, short neck, arachnodactyly with long toes, and a slightly adducted thumb posture. Echocardiography showed an increased aortic-sinus diameter of 12.6 mm, with normal arch and descending aorta.

At 5 months of age, examination revealed flexion contracture of the right elbow, scoliosis, long fingers with slightly adducted thumbs, foot deformities, and a body length of 66 cm. Skin examination showed reticular marble pattern over the thoracoabdominal region and dorsum of the hands, without cutis laxa-like features. Head circumference was 45 cm.

At 7 months of age, brain MRI demonstrated external hydrocephalus with enlarged cisterns and frontotemporal sulci. Radiographs showed left elbow dislocation, radioulnar synostosis, vertebral instability at T11–T12, bilateral hip dislocations, and scoliosis. Repeat echocardiography revealed aortic-sinus diameter of 16 mm (Z-score, 2.55).

A 65-year-old man presented with progressive shortness of breath and persistent rhonchi over two years despite treatment for presumed asthma. He had a childhood diagnosis of bronchial asthma controlled with inhaled bronchodilators and steroids, but experienced minimal improvement when courses of systemic steroids were added. He was a former smoker (20 pack-year history, quit 20 years earlier) and had no known allergen sensitivity; radioallergosorbent testing and serum IgE levels were normal, and there was no eosinophilia. Pulmonary function testing showed mild obstructive physiology without significant bronchodilator reversibility (%FEV1/FVC 76%, %FEV1 74%, %FVC 97%, %FEF25–75 38%). CT of the chest revealed left upper lobe bronchial wall thickening with calcification and moderate luminal stenosis. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy demonstrated a yellowish, nodular, tumor-like lesion obstructing the left upper lobe bronchus.

A healthy 3-year-10-month-old Asian boy was first seen for routine dental care in August 2016. At his exam in August 2017, a small inflamed area was noted on the attached gingiva adjacent to the mandibular right primary lateral incisor (tooth #Q, FDI #82). A periapical radiograph showed a subtle radiolucency along the mesial aspect of the periodontal ligament space of that tooth. The area was monitored and in March 2018 was labeled possibly traumatic in origin. Later that month, on limited examination for a “sore” near tooth #Q, the lesion was described as very stable with no change reported by the father, and “based on clinical appearance the lesion may have been a fibroma.” At the next routine exam in September 2018, the gingival nodule remained present and unchanged in size and appearance. At that time, a differential diagnosis of gingival cyst, hemangioma, pyogenic granuloma, or peripheral giant cell granuloma was established. Because complete removal would require reflection of a mucoperiosteal flap and general anesthesia was deemed necessary in this young child, excisional biopsy under general anesthesia was planned.

A 65-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of swelling and a discharging sinus over the anterolateral aspect of the middle third of his left leg. Ten years earlier, he had undergone open reduction and internal fixation of a tibial-plateau fracture with a plate and screws; he remained asymptomatic until the current presentation. His medical history was notable for a 10-year history of diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, and hypertension. On examination, there was localized swelling, erythema, multiple draining sinuses, a surgical scar, dilated veins, and muscle wasting over the anterolateral middle third of the left leg. Local temperature was elevated, and there was tenderness, bony irregularity, and cortical thickening, with sinuses adherent to the underlying bone. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis, elevated C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and hyperglycemia. Pus cultured from the sinus grew Staphylococcus haemolyticus. Plain radiographs of the left leg demonstrated osteolysis and sclerosis with irregular, unsharp cortical borders and multiple sequestra in the midshaft of the fibula. A sinogram revealed a tract communicating with the midshaft of the fibula.

A 14-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of 5 days of sudden-onset excessive thirst and urine output. She reported extreme craving for cold fluids, consuming approximately 10 L of mostly cold water daily, and passing large volumes of urine both day and night. She denied fever, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, or other neurological symptoms. Her appetite and weight had remained stable.

Her medical history was unremarkable, with no medications. There was no family history of renal, endocrine, or psychiatric disorders. Two days earlier, outpatient tests had shown normal plasma glucose and normal serum electrolytes; dipstick urinalysis was negative for glucose and protein.

On examination, she appeared well and euvolemic. Blood pressure was 105/76 mm Hg, pulse 70 beats/min, temperature 37.2 °C. Height was 154 cm (25th percentile), weight 52.3 kg (50th percentile), and BMI 22.0 kg/m2 (75th percentile). Neurologic examination—including cranial nerves, muscle tone, and reflexes—was normal.

Laboratory studies revealed:  
 Serum sodium 133 mmol/L (135–145), serum osmolality 261 mOsm/kg (275–295), urine sodium 12 mmol/L (20–40), urine osmolality 47 mOsm/kg (500–800).  
Basal endocrine studies—including ACTH, TSH, thyroxine, IGF, cortisol, and prolactin—were within normal limits. Brain MRI demonstrated a normal posterior pituitary and pituitary stalk. Renal ultrasonography was unremarkable.

A 77-year-old woman with carotid artery stenosis, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and hypothyroidism presented with sudden-onset dyspnea over several hours, orthopnea, and nausea. She reported poorly controlled blood pressure for 4 years. On examination, her blood pressure was 250/96 mm Hg, heart rate 91 bpm; a right carotid bruit, an ejection systolic murmur over the aorta, and bilateral inspiratory crackles were noted. Abdominal auscultation revealed faint bilateral bruits. Laboratory testing showed a BNP of 384 pg/mL, sinus tachycardia on ECG (102 bpm), and chest radiograph with bilateral vascular congestion. She was treated with a labetalol infusion, IV furosemide, and oxygen, with marked improvement. Further evaluation revealed renin 7.1 ng/mL/h and aldosterone 48.2 ng/dL with an appropriate ratio; she was normokalemic. Renal ultrasound was unremarkable, and renal duplex ultrasound demonstrated patent bilateral renal arteries. Autoimmune studies were negative, and plasma metanephrine and normetanephrine levels were normal.

A 25-year-old primigravida, at 25 weeks and 6 days of gestation by last menstrual period, presented with a 3-week history of involuntary abdominal movements. She described the movements as sudden in onset, rhythmic, and painful, lasting 30–120 seconds and occurring 3–5 times per day. Episodes often began while she was eating and abated with deep breathing or distraction; no other triggers or relievers were identified. She denied the use of any medications other than routine ferrous sulphate, and she had no prior gynecologic procedures. 

On examination, vital signs were normal. Abdominal inspection revealed rhythmic involuntary contractions of the abdominal wall over a 26-week-sized gravid uterus; a fetal heartbeat was present. Results of renal and liver function tests, thyroid function tests, electrolytes, HIV serology, VDRL, and complete blood count were all within normal limits. Obstetric ultrasound confirmed a singleton intrauterine pregnancy measuring 27 weeks without anomalies. Advanced neuroimaging (MRI), EEG, and EMG were not performed due to local unavailability. 

A diagnosis of belly dancer dyskinesia was made, and diazepam was prescribed; the patient declined treatment.

A 68-year-old man with a 15-day history of progressive dyspnea, chills, and productive cough presented to the emergency department. He had a history of smoking, herpes zoster, and inguinal hernia repair but no thoracic trauma or surgery. On admission, temperature was 39.0 °C, heart rate 141 beats/min, blood pressure 174/107 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 77% on room air. Examination revealed decreased breath sounds, wheezing, and rales over the right lung. Laboratory values included white blood cell count 20 000/mm3, hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, platelets 455 × 10^3/µL, C-reactive protein 34.6 mg/dL, and procalcitonin 59.42 ng/mL. HIV testing returned positive with an HIV viral load of 1.11 × 10^5 copies/mL and a CD4+ T-lymphocyte count of 308 cells/µL (15%). Chest radiograph showed complete opacification of the right lung. Chest CT revealed a large right pleural effusion with diffuse pleural enhancement and multifocal low-density lesions in the right lobe. On hospital day 3, percutaneous drainage yielded exudative pleural fluid with 3860 white cells/µL and an adenosine deaminase level of 179 IU/L; cell differential was unobtainable due to lysed cells. Cytology of pleural fluid and sputum showed acute inflammatory cells and necrotic debris without microorganisms, and no malignant cells were identified. Given the high ADA and HIV infection, the patient was started on anti-tuberculosis therapy.

A 33-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of gradual-onset periumbilical abdominal pain, nausea, and nonbloody vomiting. Her medical and surgical history was unremarkable, and she took no medications. She denied tobacco, alcohol, and illicit drug use. On examination, she was mildly tachycardic; abdominal examination revealed periumbilical tenderness without guarding or rigidity. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 10.8×10^3/μL and a hemoglobin level of 9.3 g/dL; serum lipase was normal, and a pregnancy test was negative. Contrasted CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed small-bowel wall thickening with minimal ground-glass changes in the mesentery, suggestive of enteritis. Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy were unremarkable. Magnetic resonance enterography demonstrated persistent small-bowel wall thickening with jejunal distention up to 4 cm. The patient was treated with ciprofloxacin and metronidazole and was discharged home after partial improvement.

She returned several days later with worsening abdominal pain and recurrent nausea and vomiting. Vital signs and laboratory values were unchanged. Push enteroscopy revealed a jejunal bezoar causing an almost complete small-bowel obstruction. Two months after her initial presentation, she was transferred to our facility for repeat enteroscopy and bezoar removal. On push enteroscopy at our center, multiple clean-based jejunal ulcers were seen, along with a foreign body that could not be dislodged despite multiple attempts. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 29.8 mg/dL. Based on these findings, Crohn’s disease was suspected, and methylprednisolone (30 mg intravenously twice daily) was initiated. The patient initially noted improvement in pain, tolerated a full liquid diet, and had loose bowel movements.

A 30-year-old previously healthy woman presented to the emergency department with a two-day history of severe, cramping periumbilical abdominal pain and diarrhea. She also reported chills, nausea, and a nonproductive cough. On examination she was tachycardic and hypertensive, and her abdomen was diffusely tender with rebound. Laboratory studies showed a white-blood-cell count of 18,800/mm3 with 92.9% segmented neutrophils and a total bilirubin level of 2.5 mg/dL (direct bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL). Urinalysis was normal, and a urine β-hCG test was negative. The initial differential diagnosis included appendicitis, acute colitis, and gastroenteritis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated perisigmoid fat-stranding, multiple foci of intraperitoneal air, and a linear hyperdense density within the lumen of the sigmoid colon.

A Caucasian man in his late 60s with a 4-year history of TP53-negative chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) presented with 2 weeks of reduced mobility and confusion and 2 months of subtle memory decline. He had completed six cycles of ofatumumab and chlorambucil 2 months earlier. Comorbidities included fatty liver, gout, and recurrent respiratory infections with hypogammaglobulinaemia. On presentation, his Glasgow Coma Scale was 14/15 due to confusion; initial neurologic examination was normal. Routine blood tests, including full blood count, metabolic profile, thyroid function, and vitamin levels, were unremarkable. Chest radiography and noncontrast CT of the head showed no acute pathology. Microbiological cultures of blood, urine, and stool were negative. A CT scan of neck, thorax, abdomen, and pelvis showed stable splenomegaly and improvement in lymphadenopathy. During admission, he developed worsening cognitive impairment, loss of independence, and right extensor plantar response. Brain MRI demonstrated asymmetric bilateral frontal white-matter hyperintensities on T2-weighted and FLAIR images, no enhancement with contrast, and a thin rim of diffusion restriction at the advancing edge of the lesions.

A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman with uncontrolled type II diabetes mellitus (HBA1C 11.8%), neuropathy, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, morbid obesity (BMI 43.3 kg/m2), and a 15-pack-year smoking history presented with a 4-week history of left breast swelling and associated nipple retraction. She denied pain, erythema, or tenderness and had no family history of cancer. A screening mammogram one year earlier was normal. 

On diagnostic mammography, there was a new retro-areolar mass in the left breast measuring 2.5 cm with associated nipple retraction. Complete left breast ultrasound demonstrated an irregular, complex cystic and solid mass measuring 2.7 × 2.3 × 1.3 cm at the 3:00 axis retro-areolar location; left axillary lymph nodes appeared normal. These imaging findings were highly suggestive of malignancy. 

An ultrasound-guided biopsy yielded thick, odorless, nonpurulent brown fluid.

A 27-year-old man with a 6-year history of hypertension and 2 years of chronic kidney failure on thrice-weekly hemodialysis presented for pre–kidney-transplant evaluation. He reported no fever, cough, night sweats, or weight loss. There was no known exposure to tuberculosis. Vital signs were normal, and physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed a normal complete blood count, urea 23.8 mmol/L, creatinine 1248 µmol/L, and C-reactive protein 13.6 mg/L. The interferon gamma release assay (IGRA) was positive. Sputum tests for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (direct microscopy and GeneXpert MTB/RIF) were negative. Chest radiograph was normal. Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed multiple enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes in stations 2R, 4R, 5, and 7 with clear borders, little contrast enhancement, and uniform density, and no pulmonary parenchymal abnormalities.

A 55-year-old man was brought in as a stroke call with sudden-onset left-sided cheek, arm, and hand sensory loss, visual blurring, and worsening headache. His NIHSS score was 3. His medical history included coronary artery bypass graft surgery, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypercholesterolemia. An urgent noncontrast head CT showed no intracranial hemorrhage, and he received intravenous alteplase. Two hours after thrombolysis, his visual disturbance, headache, and confusion worsened. Repeat CT of the head revealed multiple intracerebral hemorrhages with bilateral posterior hemispheric predominance. Neurosurgical intervention was considered but not pursued. Despite intensive multi-organ support, he developed a chest infection and died four days after the initial presentation. The case was referred to the coroner, and a detailed neuropathological examination was planned.

A 39-year-old G8P6M1 Pacific Islander woman at 15 weeks and 5 days’ gestation was brought by ambulance after a witnessed out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Her family initiated CPR, and prehospital resuscitation involved approximately 40 minutes of downtime, intubation, and multiple direct-current cardioversions. In the emergency department, she had fixed, dilated pupils. Arterial blood gas showed pH 6.7 and lactate 26 mmol/L; serum potassium was 2.1 mmol/L (reference 3.5–5.2). Initial management included a potassium infusion (up to 40 mmol/hr), infusions of adrenaline and noradrenaline, four units of packed red blood cells, and four units of albumin. Four hours later in the ICU, she developed ventricular fibrillation and arrested again; a pre-arrest venous blood gas showed potassium 1.8 mmol/L. Intravenous thiamine 300 mg daily was started on ICU day 1.  
Obstetric ultrasound on day 1 showed a viable fetus with a heart rate of 150 bpm; on day 2, fetal demise occurred, and she underwent dilation and curettage for retained products. Her hospital course was complicated by ischaemic hepatitis, mild encephalopathy requiring rehabilitation, and anuric renal failure requiring temporary dialysis.  
The patient reported significant nausea and vomiting from early gestation, with emesis after almost every meal, limited oral intake, and approximately 10 kg weight loss (9% of body weight). On the day of arrest, she tolerated a small lunch without new symptoms. She denied any episodes of muscle weakness, paralysis, palpitations, presyncope, or syncope. Her personal and family history was negative for cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, renal tubular disorders, thyroid disease, or sudden cardiac death. Serial serum electrolytes before and after pregnancy were normal, and postpartum urine electrolytes showed no renal potassium wasting. Pre-pregnancy and antenatal thyroid-stimulating hormone levels were within normal limits. She was normotensive, had normal cortisol screening, and took no regular medications.

A 31-year-old man was referred urgently for evaluation of significantly elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) in the left eye, initially presumed to be uveitic glaucoma. Four months earlier, he had an episode of left eye pain and photophobia; at that time his IOP was 40 mm Hg and he was treated with topical pressure-lowering drops and steroids, with symptomatic improvement. One week before this visit, his symptoms recurred. At presentation he was using brimonidine tartrate twice daily and dexamethasone once daily in the left eye. He had a history of myopia and astigmatism but denied any prior ocular surgery or trauma. 

On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left eye. The left pupil was sluggish with an afferent pupillary defect; the right pupil was normal. Applanation IOP was 21 mm Hg in the right eye and 64 mm Hg in the left eye, rechecked at 19 mm Hg and 70 mm Hg, respectively. Gonioscopy showed open angles bilaterally with slightly more trabecular pigment in the left eye. Central corneal thickness was 596 µm OD and 581 µm OS. Anterior segment exam of the left eye revealed 2+ anterior chamber cells, no keratic precipitates, and a posterior subcapsular cataract; the eye was otherwise white and quiet. 

Dilated fundus examination of the left eye demonstrated a superior retinal detachment and an increased cup-to-disc ratio of 0.6; the detachment had been previously diagnosed as retinoschisis but lacked typical features, suggesting a chronic rhegmatogenous retinal detachment with a small, unidentified break. The right eye examination was normal.

An 18-year-old woman, a 45-year-old man, and a 25-year-old man presented with 2, 8, and 6 months, respectively, of multiple skin-colored papules interspersed with occasional pustules over the anterior and lateral aspects of the neck, upper chest, and shoulders. The lesions began on the anterior neck and gradually extended over 8–10 weeks. Two patients were asymptomatic; one reported mild pruritus. None had fever, history of atopy, or recent drug intake. On examination, there were multiple monomorphic, skin-colored, follicular papules arranged linearly along the creases of the anterior and lateral neck and upper chest, with occasional pustules. There was no perilesional erythema, pigmentary change, or involvement of other body areas. Mucosa, hair, and nails were normal. Routine blood counts, liver and renal function tests, and urinalysis were within normal limits. Gram stain and culture of pustular material were negative.

A previously healthy 7-year-old boy presented after recurrent episodes of prolonged generalized tonic–clonic seizures without recovery of consciousness. He was intubated, given lorazepam and phenytoin, and weaned off the ventilator under continuous EEG monitoring. On detailed history, parents reported that 6 months earlier he had developed decreased visual acuity with left exotropia. Over the next 2 months he exhibited worsening concentration, inability to follow directions, and loss of basic reading and math skills. In the following 4 months he developed hearing impairment, need to repeat instructions, pseudobulbar affect, social withdrawal, frequent falls, and increasing difficulty walking. His teachers noted academic decline, and he dropped out of school. 

On examination, his skin showed diffuse hyperpigmentation over the joints, perioral area, gums, and knuckles. Neurologic examination revealed that he was alert but inattentive, with impaired reading and calculation, poor abstraction, visual acuity 20/150 bilaterally, spasticity and hyperreflexia in all limbs with bilateral extensor plantar responses, and a spastic gait without ataxia. 

MRI of the brain with contrast showed bilateral parieto-occipital white matter hyperintensities on T2-weighted and FLAIR images, with involvement of periventricular and subcortical regions and no significant contrast enhancement.

A 12-year-old boy was referred with a 1-week history of bloody diarrhea (8–10 times per day) and a 2-week history of vomiting (initially clear, then bilious, 3–5 times per day), high-grade intermittent fever with chills and rigors, arthralgias, and unquantified weight loss. He had swum in a pond and experienced a transient pruritic skin rash. At a local health center, he was treated with metronidazole, ceftriaxone, cimetidine, vitamin B complex, and vitamin K for presumed fulminant viral hepatitis, schistosomiasis, and acute kidney injury and then referred for further evaluation.

On examination, he appeared acutely ill. Temperature was 37.8 °C; other vital signs were normal. Abdominal palpation revealed epigastric tenderness and hepatomegaly (liver span 11 cm); the rectal examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed:  
• Negative serologies for HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C antibody.  
• Total bilirubin 2.33 mg/dL (subsequently 1.84 mg/dL); direct bilirubin 1.69 mg/dL (later 1.53 mg/dL).  
• AST 137 U/L (subsequently 35 U/L); ALT 110 U/L (subsequently 41 U/L).  
• Coagulation: PTT 68.2 s, PT 21.1 s, INR 2.41 (PT later 16.4 s, INR 1.17).  
• Renal: BUN 85 mg/dL, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL (BUN/Cr 26.5).  
• CBC: WBC 12,000/mm3 (neutrophils 67.8%, lymphocytes 22.5%, eosinophils 9.7%), platelets 92,000/mm3.  
• Stool microscopy: Schistosoma mansoni ova and Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites; H. pylori antigen negative.  
• Fecal calprotectin normal.  
• Abdominal ultrasound: hepatomegaly with hypodense hepatic nodules and marked colonic and small-bowel wall thickening and edema consistent with enterocolitis.  
• Urinalysis: leukocytes +1, WBCs 7–10/HPF, protein +2, ketones +1.  
• Electrolytes and blood glucose were normal.

Video pan-colonoscopy to the cecum showed diffuse colonic mucosal inflammation, intense rectal involvement, extensive ulceration, exudates, and loss of vascular pattern. A rectal biopsy was obtained with the clinical impression of ulcerative colitis versus inflammatory bowel disease.

A 27-year-old woman presented with her father for evaluation of recurrent seizures and poor scholastic performance. She was born at term without complications. At age 2 years, she experienced a febrile seizure characterized by focal clonic movements of the left side that evolved to a bilateral convulsion and was followed by three days of unconsciousness. On discharge, she had residual left hemiparesis. Approximately 15 years ago, she developed recurrent generalized tonic–clonic seizures. She demonstrated impaired cognition and poor academic performance, preventing completion of secondary education. Her medication history included trials of phenobarbital, carbamazepine, and phenytoin with persistent poor seizure control and gingival hyperplasia.

On examination, her weight was 43.7 kg and height 1.56 m (BMI 17.9 kg/m²). Her score on Raven’s Standard Progressive Matrices was 11/60 (below the 5th percentile). Neurologically, she had left facial hemiatrophy, left hemibody atrophy, and spastic hemiparesis (4/5 strength in left upper and lower limbs) with a left extensor plantar response. The remainder of the examination was normal. Based on these findings, Rasmussen encephalitis was suspected, and cranial magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalography were requested.

A 62-year-old man was evaluated for a 30-year history of a gradually evolving papulonodular eruption involving the face, flexural areas, and trunk. On examination, there were multiple, well-defined, yellowish-brown papules and nodules symmetrically distributed on the upper and lower eyelids, cheeks, and perioral region. On the anterior neck, lesions were confluent, forming a diffuse plaque. Numerous red-brown papules were symmetrically present in the axillae, genitalia, popliteal fossae, and trunk, with some coalescing into plaques or tumor-like lesions. Small papules and nodules were also noted on the nasal mucosa.  

He reported no polyuria or other systemic symptoms. Urine osmolality testing was normal. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 10,300 cells/mm3 (74% neutrophils), a C-reactive protein level of 7 mg/dL (reference <0.5), a fasting cholesterol level of 148 mg/dL, and a triglyceride level of 141 mg/dL. A chest radiograph and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and pituitary gland were unremarkable.  

Skin-biopsy specimens revealed a dense, diffuse dermal infiltrate of histiocytes with intermixed inflammatory cells and giant cells, abundant foam cells, and no neural involvement. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for CD68 and negative for S-100 protein.

A 51-year-old man presented for evaluation of a recently dislodged porcelain-fused-to-metal crown on the right maxillary first molar; the crown had been placed 5 years earlier. His medical and social histories were noncontributory. On routine oral examination, a well-defined submucosal mass was observed in the mucobuccal fold near the lower right second premolar. Retraction of the cheek revealed a 5 mm × 3 mm yellowish-white nodule. The lesion was soft to rubbery-firm, minimally compressible, with well-defined margins, mobile on palpation, and asymptomatic; the patient was unaware of its duration. An intraoral periapical radiograph was obtained, and vitality testing of the adjacent teeth was inconclusive. Based on clinical and radiographic findings, the differential diagnosis included lipoma, granulation tissue, scarred parulis, fibroma, leiomyoma, neuroma, schwannoma, and foreign body granuloma. The decision was made to perform excisional biopsy under local anesthesia for definitive diagnosis.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of left temporomandibular joint (TMJ) pain that extended to the left eye and was accompanied by daily migraine symptoms. She had no history of trauma. Her pain score ranged from 5 to 9 on a visual analogue scale despite daily tramadol and paracetamol. Examination showed tenderness of the masticatory muscles, maximal mouth opening of 45 mm with pain throughout, crepitus in the left TMJ, and clicking in the right TMJ. Oral examination revealed normal occlusion and no intraoral pathology.  

Computed tomography of the mandible demonstrated irregular bony surfaces with subchondral cysts in both condyles, most prominent on the left. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 9 mm fluid-filled, cyst-like structure anterior to the left external auditory meatus adjacent to the mandibular neck, with high T2 signal and no described degenerative changes.  

The patient underwent bilateral arthroscopy and arthrocentesis, which showed a left disc perforation, right anterior disc displacement with chondromalacia stage II, and modest synovial changes bilaterally. Hyaluronic acid and bupivacaine were injected, and she was discharged with structured TMJ exercises.  

At 2-month follow-up, her pain was unchanged, and repeat MRI showed no change in the diameter of the cyst.

A 74-year-old right-handed woman was brought to the psychiatry clinic with a 5-month history of abrupt onset of disorganized speech, severe anxiety, and self-harm behaviors that began after a family trip. Her speech was rapid, fluent, and nonsensical—exemplified by the phrase “Our neighbor has gone to the cobbler to buy Ghormeh Sabzi”—consistent with Wernicke’s aphasia. Over the ensuing months, she developed agitation, persecutory delusions, visual and auditory hallucinations, urinary and fecal incontinence, and a persistent urge to flee her home.

Her psychiatric history included a 10-year history of depression treated with sertraline. There was no prior cognitive impairment or neurological disease. On examination, she was disoriented to time, demonstrated anomia, and had marked perseveration on the Clock Drawing Test, impaired performance on Luria’s three-step test, and defective crossed-pentagon drawing. Cognitive testing revealed an MMSE score of 2/30 and an ACE-R score of 2/100, likely confounded by comprehension deficits.

An initial brain MRI performed 2 months after symptom onset was reported as normal. She was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease and started on memantine and quetiapine, without clinical improvement. Because of the acute presentation and prominent frontal and temporal features, she was referred to neurology for further assessment.

A 24-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of insidious onset left knee pain that gradually worsened. She denied any history of trauma, fever, cough, or night sweats. On examination, there was localized tenderness over the proximal tibia just below the joint line without swelling or effusion; both active and passive range of motion were normal, and McMurray’s and drawer tests were negative. 

Plain radiographs of the left knee (anteroposterior and lateral views) revealed a well-defined, 2.0 × 1.5-cm lytic lesion in the epiphysis of the proximal tibia with a narrow zone of transition; the remaining bones appeared normal. MRI T2-weighted images suggested a Brodie’s abscess.

The differential diagnosis included Brodie’s abscess, tuberculosis, giant cell tumor, chondroblastoma, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, metastasis, aneurysmal bone cyst, osseous lipoma, osteomyelitis, and subchondral cyst. Fine-needle aspiration cytology was inconclusive. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 9400 per cubic millimeter with 60% neutrophils and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 25 mm/h. 

Given the MRI findings and the inconclusive cytology, the plan was to drain the presumed abscess cavity and fill it with bone graft substitutes.

A 32-year-old man with a recent diagnosis of AIDS presented with a 2-month history of progressive shortness of breath and a 40-lb unintentional weight loss. Chest radiography and sputum studies confirmed Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia. On hospital day 7, he developed painful stomatitis involving the upper lip, the vermilion border of the lower lip, and the middle and anterior thirds of the dorsal tongue. Examination of the oral mucosa showed numerous 3-mm painful papules clustering into vegetative plaques measuring 0.6 to 1.2 cm with defined, scalloped borders and ulcerated, bleeding surfaces on a background of a fissured tongue. The remainder of the cutaneous examination was unremarkable. Venereal disease research laboratory and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption tests were negative. A Tzanck smear of the lesions revealed multinucleated giant epithelial cells with basophilic and pale cytoplasm.

A 29-year-old man presented with 16 months of progressive weight gain (5 kg), facial acne, and violaceous striae in the axillae and inner thighs. In July 2019, he experienced lower-limb weakness; his potassium level was 3.0 mmol/L, which normalized after supplementation. He sustained compression fractures of the thoracic and lumbar vertebrae in January and March 2020 without significant trauma. He reported no use of medications, traditional remedies, or health supplements before symptom onset.

On examination, blood pressure was 151/100 mm Hg; height 166 cm; weight 68.5 kg (BMI 24.9 kg/m²). He had a moon face, acne, dorsocervical fat pad, central obesity, thin skin, and wide purple striae on the axillae and inner thighs.

Endocrine studies showed a preserved cortisol circadian rhythm with morning cortisol levels that were normal or decreased. Two 24-hour urinary free cortisol measurements and urinary 17-hydroxycorticosteroid and 17-ketosteroid levels were below normal. Corticosteroid-binding globulin was 17.1 mg/L (reference 15–20 mg/L), and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate was 101.3 µg/dL (reference 160–449 µg/dL). A 250-µg cosyntropin stimulation test elicited a poor cortisol response (peak 15.7 µg/dL; reference >18 µg/dL). Plasma renin activity, aldosterone, and potassium were within normal limits. Thyroid and gonadal hormone levels were unremarkable. An oral glucose tolerance test indicated impaired glucose tolerance (2-hour glucose 10.54 mmol/L). Bone metabolism studies revealed low 25-hydroxyvitamin D and elevated bone alkaline phosphatase. Adrenal CT and pituitary MRI were normal. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry showed severe osteoporosis (lumbar Z-score −4.2), and spine radiographs confirmed multiple compression fractures. The rubella virus IgM antibody was positive, and both the erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein were elevated.

A 59-year-old woman was transferred for evaluation of ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome. Two years earlier, she developed a 50-lb weight gain, facial plethora, thinning hair, easy bruising, severe proximal muscle weakness, new hypertension, and type 2 diabetes on multiple medications. Her history included obesity, hyperlipidemia, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, nephrolithiasis, severe osteoporosis with vertebral fractures, and a recent NSTEMI; she had a remote 30 pack-year smoking history. 

On examination, her BMI was 48 kg/m^2. She had moon facies, facial plethora, supraclavicular and dorsocervical fat pads, an obese abdomen with wide purple striae, lower extremity edema, proximal muscle weakness, and ecchymoses.

Laboratory studies confirmed ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism: baseline ACTH 96 pg/mL (7.2–63.3), serum cortisol 19.6 mcg/dL (4.8–19.5), 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression cortisol 18.5 mcg/dL, 24-hour urine free cortisol 192 mcg (<45), late-night salivary cortisol 436 and 464 ng/dL (29–101), and high-dose dexamethasone suppression cortisol suppressed to 7.2 mcg/dL (>50% suppression). 

Pituitary MRI (3T) showed a possible 0.5-cm anterior lesion and acute/subacute strokes, precluding inferior petrosal sinus sampling. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a 1.5-cm right adrenal lipid-rich adenoma (2.3 HU), with radiographic appearance excluding adrenocortical carcinoma; biochemical evaluation ruled out pheochromocytoma and hyperaldosteronism. 

Serum proopiomelanocortin was 154 fmol/mL (<40) and chromogranin A was 538 ng/mL (0–103). A 68 Ga-DOTATATE PET-CT scan revealed a 7-mm DOTATATE-avid lesion in the pancreatic tail (SUV max 14.5), suspicious for a somatostatin receptor–expressing neuroendocrine tumor.

A 59-year-old white man presented with bilateral blurry vision of two weeks’ duration, which began shortly after discharge from a prolonged hospitalization for COVID-19 pneumonia. His medical history was notable for coronary artery disease, insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. Six weeks earlier, he had been admitted with fever, cough, and progressive dyspnea; SARS-CoV-2 testing was positive, and chest radiographs showed bilateral infiltrates. He required intubation for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure and was supported with extracorporeal membrane oxygenation for 11 days. His course was complicated by encephalopathy, coagulopathy requiring full-dose anticoagulation, and labile blood pressure requiring multiple antihypertensive agents; blood glucose levels remained well controlled.

On ophthalmic examination, visual acuity was 20/50 in the right eye and 20/60 in the left eye. Anterior segment examination revealed mild nuclear sclerotic cataracts without inflammation. Intraocular pressures were 15 mm Hg in both eyes. Funduscopic examination showed multiple cotton wool spots in the posterior pole of both eyes but no retinal hemorrhages, no arteriolar narrowing, and no arteriovenous crossing changes. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated no retinal edema, and B-scans through the lesions revealed thickening and hyperreflectivity of the retinal nerve fiber layer. Fluorescein angiography showed mild obscuration of the retinal vasculature by a peripapillary cotton wool spot in the left eye and was otherwise unremarkable. Optical coherence tomography angiography of the superficial capillary plexus revealed flow voids corresponding to the location of the lesions in both eyes.

An 81-year-old man with hypertension and obesity was admitted for management of acute pancreatitis. On hospital day 7, in the setting of narcotic-induced hypoventilation and noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV), he noted a new, mildly tender, 1.5 cm × 2.0 cm necrotic ulcer on the bridge of his nose. The ulcer had an erythematous base with a slightly indurated, erythematous border. He denied headache, visual changes, epistaxis, cough, hematemesis, fevers, chills, night sweats, ocular pain, rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, dysphagia, odynophagia, stomatodynia, recent travel, insect bites, or animal exposures. He had no history of HIV or tuberculosis. Several infections were included in the differential diagnosis, including bacterial infections and mycobacterial infections. Because of the rapid progression of the lesion, aggressive angioinvasive fungal infections such as zygomycosis were also considered, as were vasculitic and vasculopathic causes. Two 3-mm punch biopsy specimens were obtained from the indurated, inflamed edge of the lesion. Routine histology showed deep epidermal erosion, fibrin deposition, necrosis of hair follicles and sebaceous glands with neutrophils, and evidence of bacteria within the erosion and papillary dermis. Tissue culture from the ulcer border grew heavy β-lactamase–negative Moraxella species and heavy Staphylococcus epidermidis. Blood cultures were negative, and the patient had no fever, bacteremia, or lymphadenopathy.

A 42-year-old Caucasian woman was admitted with one day of high-grade fever, yellow productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, and resting shortness of breath. She reported 15 years of chronic dyspnea and fatigue and 10 years of chronic loose stools. One week earlier she had been discharged from the ICU after septic shock with multiorgan failure requiring two weeks of ventilatory support and temporary hemodialysis.

Her past medical history included asthma (15 years), COPD (5 years), recurrent sinus and ear infections since adolescence (mastoidectomy 4 years ago), GERD, IBS (10 years), migraines, and bipolar disorder. She was a 20–pack-year smoker. Medications included levalbuterol, montelukast, fluticasone/salmeterol, lansoprazole, loratadine/pseudoephedrine, hydrocodone, quetiapine, and topiramate.

On examination, she appeared chronically ill. Temperature was 99.8°F, pulse 137/min, respirations 26/min, BP 109/59 mmHg, and O2 saturation 88% on 2 L nasal oxygen. Bibasilar rhonchi were present; there was a central venous catheter in the left IJ vein. No clubbing or nasal polyps were noted.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 15,800/mm³ (8,000/mm³ at discharge) and BUN/creatinine 24/1.6 mg/dL trending downward. ABG on 2 L O₂ revealed pH 7.50, PCO₂ 32 mmHg, PO₂ 48 mmHg, HCO₃ 25 mEq/L, and an A–a gradient of 104 mmHg. Cardiac enzymes were normal. Chest X-ray showed improving bibasilar infiltrates. A CT pulmonary angiogram excluded pulmonary embolism. High-resolution CT of the chest demonstrated bronchial wall thickening and dilatation predominantly in the lower lobes. CT of the sinuses showed chronic maxillary sinusitis.

Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae. She was started on IV levofloxacin and vancomycin.

Given her history of recurrent respiratory infections since adolescence and bronchiectasis, a wide differential diagnosis was considered, including cystic fibrosis, immotile cilia syndrome, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, and immunodeficiency. Initial tests revealed a negative sweat chloride test, normal alpha-1 antitrypsin levels, and a negative HIV screening test.

A 46-year-old man presented with sudden onset of severe chest pain, progressive dyspnea, and diaphoresis. He was a current smoker with no other coronary risk factors and no history of radiotherapy or chemotherapy. On examination, he was tachypneic (26 breaths/min), tachycardic (160 beats/min, regular), blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg, and oxygen saturation was 83% on room air. Cardiac auscultation was unremarkable, but bilateral crackles were present. He was intubated for acute pulmonary edema.  

Electrocardiography showed sinus rhythm with ST-segment elevations in leads I, aVL, aVR, and V1–V5, and ST depressions in leads II, III, and aVF, consistent with anterolateral myocardial infarction. Aspirin and clopidogrel were administered, and the patient underwent emergent coronary angiography, which revealed a severely stenotic ostial lesion of the left main coronary artery with a normal distal coronary bed; subtle aortic regurgitation was also noted. A drug-eluting stent was successfully deployed, though the patient transiently required dobutamine and norepinephrine for cardiogenic shock.  

Peak cardiac troponin I was 29.6 ng/mL (upper limit 0.1 ng/mL) and CK-MB peaked at 114 IU/L (reference <25 IU/L). Transthoracic echocardiography showed moderate left ventricular systolic dysfunction with hypokinesia of mid and basal anterior and septal segments, and mild dilation of the ascending aorta.

A 50-year-old woman was evaluated for severe postprandial hypoglycaemia. Seven years earlier, she had undergone Roux-en-Y gastric bypass for morbid obesity (preoperative BMI 44.7 kg/m2). Two years later, following a 57-kg weight loss, she began experiencing episodes 1–2 hours after meals, with loss of concentration, severe fatigue, and visual and auditory impairment that resolved with carbohydrate intake. An oral glucose tolerance test at that time confirmed symptomatic hypoglycaemia (2.9 mmol/L). Dietary modifications and off-label treatment with acarbose, saxagliptin, and metformin reduced but did not resolve her symptoms.  

Her medical history included orthostatic dysregulation, migraine, and a left-sided hemihepatectomy. Examination was unremarkable (BMI 25.5 kg/m2; BP 127/67 mmHg; HR 80 bpm). Routine laboratories were within reference ranges. Continuous glucose monitoring showed a pattern consistent with postbariatric hypoglycaemia without fasting or nocturnal hypoglycaemia. A mixed-meal test (300 mL Ensure Plus, 60 g carbohydrate) after a 10-hour fast provoked symptomatic hypoglycaemia (sweating, drowsiness, odd behaviour, incoordination) at 2.5 mmol/L, requiring intravenous glucose.  

To exclude an insulinoma or focal nesidioblastosis as a surgical target, a 68 Ga-DOTA-Exendin-4 PET/CT was performed and showed a homogeneous signal in the pancreas (SUV 5.7–8.3) but intense uptake in the first and second parts of the duodenum (SUVmax 10.0).

A 36-year-old Black woman was brought to the emergency department for agitation and alcohol intoxication after her family called 911 for what they described as a “nervous breakdown.” On arrival, her blood alcohol level was 255 mg/dL, and a urine drug screen was positive for cannabinoids. She was admitted for medical management of alcohol withdrawal with the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol Scale and oral lorazepam.

Her past medical history included alcohol use disorder, nonfunctional pituitary macroadenoma, adrenal insufficiency, and hypothyroidism. She had undergone four transsphenoidal pituitary tumor resections, the most recent five months earlier, followed by postoperative radiation therapy. Two years before admission, “heavy alcohol use” was noted in her record but was not addressed. Six months before admission, “Alcohol Abuse” was added to her problem list without counseling or follow-up.

On addiction psychiatry consultation, she reported a long history of social drinking that sharply increased five months earlier—immediately after her last surgery—when she felt depressed and anxious due to ongoing postoperative medical needs and social isolation. Since then, she had been drinking one pint of vodka on most days and felt distress and guilt about her drinking. Her reported impairment from alcohol use met the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition criteria for moderate alcohol use disorder, and her mood and personality changes were thought to be substance-induced from the central nervous system effects of acute alcohol intoxication superimposed on chronic excessive alcohol use. 

The differential diagnoses considered also included abnormal hormone levels status postpartial pituitary resection, medication nonadherence for hormone replacement, adjustment disorder, major depressive disorder, and substance-induced depressive disorder.

A 12-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of a radiolucent lesion in the left mandibular premolar–molar region identified on routine orthodontic panoramic imaging. She was asymptomatic but reported generalized fatigue. On examination, there was buccal cortical plate expansion measuring approximately 18 × 22 mm; the overlying mucosa was intact, there was no tooth mobility or caries, no cervical lymphadenopathy, and no neurosensory deficits. A panoramic radiograph showed a well-defined, unilocular ovoid radiolucency with a thin sclerotic rim extending from the distal aspect of the mandibular second premolar to the distal root of the first molar, without root resorption. A preliminary differential diagnosis included inflammatory and developmental odontogenic cysts, giant cell lesions, and odontogenic tumors. Laboratory tests revealed a serum parathyroid hormone level of 81.3 pg/mL (reference 15–68), a low-normal calcium of 2.17 mmol/L (2.15–2.60), and a vitamin D level of 32 nmol/L (75–200); renal function was normal. Thyroid ultrasonography showed no evidence of parathyroid adenoma.

A 65-year-old Tibetan woman presented with a 3-month history of mild cough and occasional hemoptysis, recently worsened by right chest pain. She had been treated empirically with oral penicillin without full resolution of symptoms. She had no history of surgery, trauma, or known infectious disease and lived in a farming region where occasional raw meat consumption is customary. 

On examination, temperature was 36.5 °C, blood pressure 115/65 mmHg, heart rate 73 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min. Breath sounds were diminished over the left lung with collapse; moist rales were heard bilaterally. No rash or subcutaneous nodules were noted.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 10.4 × 10^9/L with 37.2% eosinophils and elevated serum IgE (1650 IU/mL). Tumor markers (CA-125, neuron-specific enolase) were mildly elevated; other blood chemistries were unremarkable. Bone marrow aspirate was hypercellular with marked eosinophilia.

Left-sided thoracentesis yielded yellow-cloudy exudative fluid with >20,000 cells/μL, 100% multinuclear cells, and eosinophil predominance; glucose was low and LDH high. Cytology showed no malignant cells or parasites. Gram stain, acid-fast stain, fungal smear, TB-DNA, and cultures were negative.

Chest CT demonstrated a left hydropneumothorax with partial compressive atelectasis and patchy consolidation in the right lung.

A 50-year-old Eritrean man presented with a six-month history of intermittent moderate- to high-grade fevers (38–39 °C), productive cough, an 8- to 10-kg weight loss, dizziness, and fatigue. He had no significant past medical history. On examination, he was febrile (39 °C) with relative bradycardia (heart rate 74 bpm), mild hepatosplenomegaly, no superficial lymphadenopathy, and no meningeal signs.

A provisional diagnosis of tuberculosis was made. Differential diagnoses included leishmaniasis, brucellosis, hepatitis B and C, AIDS, hematologic and solid tumor malignancy, and connective tissue disease. Initial investigations showed:
- Chest radiograph: slightly widened anterior mediastinum.
- CBC: hemoglobin 2.3 g/dL (14.0–17.5), leukocytes 337/µL (1000–4800), platelets 297 × 10^3/µL (150–450).
- LFTs, renal function, electrolytes: within normal limits.
- Malaria film, autoimmune profile, peripheral blood film: unremarkable.
- LDH 902 U/L (100–190); ESR 72 mm/h (1–20); CRP 132 mg/L (0–3).
- Triglycerides 2.94 mmol/L (0.30–2.30); ferritin 19 948 ng/mL (30–400).
- Mantoux test: negative.
- Repeated sputum and blood cultures: no growth.
- Hepatitis profile and HIV serology: negative.
- Parasite serology: high titer for schistosomiasis.
- Echocardiography: no pericardial effusion or vegetations.
- Chest CT: multiple subcentimeter lymph nodes, not amenable to biopsy.
- Abdominal CT: multiple splenic infarcts, no abdominal or pelvic lymphadenopathy.

During hospitalization, he developed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 2.0 g/dL, leukocytes 266/µL, platelets 23 × 10^3/µL) and hepatic derangement (direct bilirubin 12.6 µmol/L; ALT 256 IU/L; AST 277 IU/L; ALP 440 IU/L).

A 73-year-old woman with no significant medical history initially presented with cervical and lumbar pain. Lumbar MRI showed severe L4–L5 stenosis with grade 2 spondylolisthesis and right-sided nerve root compression. She first underwent C5–C6 anterior cervical discectomy and fusion, followed by physical therapy. On follow-up, her lumbar pain had worsened. She was admitted and underwent an uneventful L4–L5 laminectomy with pedicle screw fixation and fusion; no intraoperative cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage was noted. A 7-Fr Jackson–Pratt drain was placed and later removed. 

Postoperatively, she was extubated in the operating room. In the postanesthesia care unit, she had shallow breathing but stable vital signs (SpO2 99% on nonrebreather). An arterial blood gas and chest radiograph were unremarkable; electrolyte levels were normal. Sugammadex was given for possible residual neuromuscular blockade, and naloxone was given for suspected opioid effect, but her depressed mental status persisted with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) of 6. She vomited on BiPAP, received flumazenil for midazolam reversal, had a brief seizure treated with lorazepam, was intubated, and taken for neuroimaging.

Initial noncontrast head CT showed diffuse cerebral edema and findings suggestive of hypoxic/anoxic brain injury. CT angiography and venography demonstrated normal intracranial arterial and venous circulation. Six hours later, repeat CT showed stable mild cerebral edema. On postoperative day 1, noncontrast CT remained similar, and MRI brain without contrast revealed increased signal and enlargement of the basal ganglia surrounded by a hyperintense rim delineating the lentiform nucleus.

A 50-year-old Caucasian man presented with sudden vision loss and a scotoma in his left eye without pain. He had no prior ocular history. Two months earlier, he began using 0.2% glyceryl trinitrate ointment three times daily for a painful anal fissure; over the preceding 15 days, he had increased use to as many as six applications per day and experienced recurrent headaches, dizziness relieved by analgesics, and, in the last 3 days, episodes of transient postural hypotension. He took no other medications.

Best-corrected visual acuity was 85 ETDRS letters in the right eye and 75 letters in the left. Intraocular pressures were normal, there was no relative afferent pupillary defect, and color vision by Ishihara plates was intact in both eyes. Anterior chambers were unremarkable. Dilated fundus examination showed no abnormalities in the right eye. In the left eye, there was mild retinal venous dilation and tortuosity, scattered blot hemorrhages, and subtle parafoveal whitish lesions in the outer retina.

Swept-source optical coherence tomography demonstrated diffuse hyperreflective bands involving the inner plexiform, inner nuclear, and outer plexiform layers. OCT angiography revealed a focal area of capillary dropout in the deep capillary plexus, with normal superficial plexus, outer retina, and choriocapillaris. Fluorescein angiography showed normal arteriovenous transit time, masking from blot hemorrhages, and early punctate inner-retinal leakage.

A 24-year-old Caucasian woman with a 14-year history of type 1 diabetes mellitus presented with a 10-week history of right ankle pain without antecedent trauma. Her glycemic control had been poor, with a mean glycated hemoglobin of 11.6% over the past 7 years and prior proliferative diabetic retinopathy treated with panretinal photocoagulation, as well as microalbuminuric nephropathy. On examination, the right ankle was warm, tender, and swollen. Plain weight-bearing radiographs of the right ankle showed a displaced fracture of the anterior talus with surrounding bony resorption and callus formation. T1- and T2-weighted magnetic resonance images of the right foot demonstrated significant collapse of the talar head, marked marrow edema in the talar neck, and extensive edema of adjacent midfoot bones and small intrinsic foot muscles.

A 67-year-old woman with a 31-year history of recurrent depressive disorder presented with depressed mood, anhedonia, nervousness, fatigue, decreased appetite, and poor sleep beginning 5 months after COVID-19. She had two severe episodes responsive to escitalopram (up to 20 mg/d) and duloxetine (up to 60 mg/d), and intolerance to venlafaxine, bupropion, and trazodone. Her mother had mania; she denied iron deficiency anemia, hypothyroidism, or substance abuse. Physical and neurologic examinations and routine laboratory tests were unremarkable. On admission, she was receiving escitalopram 10 mg/d, duloxetine 80 mg/d, and clonazepam 1.5 mg/d. On hospital day 3, she reported new deep itching and creeping sensations in her bilateral shoulders and arms, worse at rest, partially relieved by movement, and predominantly occurring in the evening, causing night-time sleep disturbance. Escitalopram was discontinued and duloxetine increased to 100 mg/d while clonazepam was reduced. One week later, the paraesthesias persisted despite reducing duloxetine to 90 mg/d and clonazepam to 0.5 mg/d.

A 31-year-old G1P0 woman was noted at 22 weeks’ gestation to have polyhydramnios (amniotic fluid index, 11.5 cm; normal < 8 cm). She delivered a male infant at 29 weeks’ gestation. Birth weight was 1480 g (85th percentile), length 38.5 cm (50th percentile), and head circumference 26.5 cm (61st percentile).  
Immediately after birth, the infant had polyuria (mean 5.8 mL/kg/h) with dehydration and a 25% weight loss by day 4. Laboratory studies showed hyponatremia (Na+ 129 mmol/L), hypokalemia (K+ 2.95 mmol/L), hypochloremia (Cl– 94 mmol/L), and marked elevations in plasma renin activity (> 12 ng/mL/h; normal 0.05–0.79 ng/mL/h) and angiotensin II (> 800 pg/mL; normal 16.2–64 pg/mL). A urine calcium-to-creatinine ratio was 1147.8 mg/g Cr, and renal ultrasonography demonstrated medullary nephrocalcinosis. Metabolic alkalosis developed (pH 7.521, HCO3– 31.1 mmol/L). Serum magnesium was normal. Hearing screening by otoacoustic emissions and auditory brainstem response was normal. There was no family history of similar findings.  
Antenatal Bartter’s syndrome was suspected.

A 45-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of painless swelling of the left mandibular body, causing facial asymmetry.  
On examination:  
• Well-demarcated, hard swelling of the left mandibular body and angle with palpable submandibular lymphadenopathy  
• Intraoral hard bulge in the left posterior buccal vestibule; the left second premolar was Grade 3 mobile; no sensory deficits  
History: the left mandibular first and second molars had been extracted for mobility without bleeding.  
Panoramic radiograph: well-defined multilocular radiolucent lesion from the mental region to the ramus, containing small loculations and fine trabeculae.  
Laboratory studies: bleeding time 2 min; platelet count 322 × 10^3/μL (both normal).  
Biopsy via the extraction socket of the mobile premolar revealed no hemorrhage, and histology showed thin-walled dilated vascular spaces of variable diameter lined by a single layer of endothelial cells with mild inflammatory infiltrate.  
CT scan: expansile multilocular lesion in the left mandible with buccal cortical periosteal reaction and internal trabeculation.  
MRI (1.5 T): lesion involves the left mandibular body and ramus with buccal cortical breach and soft-tissue extension; T1-weighted images are hypointense without signal voids; T2-weighted images are hyperintense.

A 27‐year‐old woman, G2P0, at 33 weeks 4 days of gestation by last menstrual period presented with a 1‐hour history of severe, generalized abdominal pain and vomiting. She had no prenatal care after recent immigration and a prior first‐trimester termination. On examination, her blood pressure was elevated, heart rate was tachycardic, and she had bilious emesis. Abdominal palpation revealed generalized tenderness with guarding and rebound; fundal height was 34 cm. Continuous fetal monitoring showed a category III tracing with absent variability and repetitive late decelerations. Pelvic examination demonstrated a bulging pouch of Douglas, a presenting part deep in the pelvis, and a short, firm, closed cervix displaced anteriorly behind the pubic symphysis. A limited bedside ultrasound showed a cephalic fetus and a placental location that could not be clearly defined. A tentative diagnosis of uterine rupture versus concealed placental abruption was made, and the patient was taken for immediate laparotomy.

A 22‐year‐old Syrian man presented with a 2‐week history of recurrent fever, intermittent vomiting, aphthous ulcers, fatigue, polyuria, and polydipsia. He had no significant weight loss or anorexia. His medical history was notable for low birth weight, sparse subcutaneous tissue, short stature, high‐pitched voice, orchiopexy for undescended testes at age 10, recurrent chest and middle‐ear infections, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. His parents are first cousins; a sister has proportionate short stature and similar facial features.  

On examination, he weighed 33 kg and was 146 cm tall (BMI 15.5 kg/m2). Vital signs were normal except for a respiratory rate of 26 breaths/min and temperature 37.5 °C. He had dolichocephaly, a prominent nose, and pale conjunctivae. Ophthalmologic findings included right‐sided lateral strabismus, amblyopia, and bilateral lower‐eyelid ectropion; pupils, lenses, media, and fundi were unremarkable. A sun‐sensitive malar rash with telangiectasias, cheilitis with peeling vesicles, a missing upper incisor, café‐au‐lait spots, hypopigmented areas, and chest telangiectasias were noted. Chest auscultation revealed decreased breath sounds; no lymphadenopathy, purpura, or petechiae were present.  

Chest radiograph, ECG, and urinalysis were normal. Laboratory studies showed glucose 237 mg/dL, hemoglobin 6.4 g/dL, hematocrit 18.9%, MCV 85 fL, platelets 19 × 10^3/μL, LDH 692 IU/L, ALP 273 IU/L, CRP 145 mg/dL, and ESR 105 mm/h. White‐cell count was normal. ANA, ANCA, RF, tuberculin skin test, and QuantiFERON were negative. Spirometry showed FEV1/FVC 75%. An islet‐cell antibody test confirmed type I diabetes mellitus. Endocrine studies (GH, testosterone, FSH, LH) were normal; semen analysis revealed azoospermia.  

Peripheral smear showed hypochromic microcytic anemia with anisocytosis, spherocytes, elliptocytes, tear‐drop cells, giant platelets, and hyposegmented granulocytes. Bone‐marrow aspiration and flow cytometry demonstrated hypercellular marrow with an inverted CD4/CD8 ratio, 6% myeloblasts, dysplasia in erythroid and megakaryocytic lineages, and ringed sideroblasts. These findings were consistent with myelodysplastic syndrome with excess blasts‐1.

A 21-year-old African American man was referred for evaluation of progressive forgetfulness and inattention over several months, which had begun to impair his academic performance. His medical history was notable for gastroesophageal reflux disease, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, and learning disabilities. One year earlier, at age 20, he had presented with upper abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting and was found to have an elevated serum ammonia level of 96 µmol/L. An abdominal CT scan demonstrated a large portosystemic shunt with the portal vein draining into the inferior vena cava via the middle hepatic vein just below the cavo-atrial junction and cardiomegaly. On current evaluation, his serum total bilirubin was 1.1 mg/dL, serum potassium 3.4 mEq/L, and prothrombin time 14.4 seconds; all other laboratory studies were within normal limits.

A 17-year-old Middle-Eastern male adolescent was brought to the child and adolescent psychiatric emergency department by his mother and stepfather because of mutism, bizarre postures, salivary drooling, urine and fecal incontinence, and asymmetric convulsions of his arms and legs. He had been living in Sweden with his mother, stepfather, and younger brother since age 12, following his parents’ divorce. He had no family history of psychiatric disease and normal psychomotor development. 

He began using illicit drugs before age 13; over the past 4 years he had smoked cannabis daily (up to 3 g per day) and over the past 2 years had used tramadol (200–1000 mg daily). He had also tried LSD, cocaine, hallucinogenic mushrooms, ecstasy, inhalants, and various analgesics. Three weeks before presentation, he entered a youth programme for a conviction and abstained from cannabis and tramadol, but still tested positive for THC five days before admission.

On examination he was mute, unresponsive to questions, and displayed a depressed mood. A urine toxicology screen on admission was negative for THC and other illicit substances. Physical examination showed motor immobility with bizarre postures, asymmetric convulsions, and incontinence. Vital signs were within normal limits (blood pressure 130/60 mmHg; heart rate 80 bpm). Results of blood tests, a brain MRI, and an EEG were all normal. A pediatric neurological consultation found no signs of a primary neurological disorder.

Possible differential diagnoses included substance‐induced psychosis, depressive stupor, catatonic schizophrenia, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS).

A 55-year-old man was found unconscious in front of his home and brought to the emergency department. He had no significant medical history and took no long-term medications. On arrival, his Glasgow Coma Scale score was 4. He was afebrile, blood pressure was 100/55 mm Hg, pulse 45–55 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, and temperature 32.5 °C. Pupils were poorly reactive bilaterally, with a dilated right pupil. He flexed his arm and extended his leg to pain. Routine laboratory tests, including complete blood count, electrolytes, renal and liver function, and arterial blood gases, were all within normal limits. Cardiovascular exam and ECG were unremarkable. A noncontrast head CT showed no hemorrhage or ischemia. Transcranial Doppler demonstrated patency of the carotid, basilar, and vertebral arteries. He was admitted to the ICU for respiratory support. Four hours later, he regained consciousness but remained somnolent. He had bilateral ptosis, and examination revealed vertical gaze palsy. On hospital day 2, repeat CT showed bilateral paramedian thalamic hypodensities (~15 × 11 mm). CT angiography was unremarkable. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral hyperintense T2 and FLAIR signals in the paramedian thalami and rostral midbrain, with corresponding restricted diffusion on DWI and low ADC values.

A 26-year-old woman presented to the emergency department approximately 2 hours after ingesting about 10 mL of a pesticide (chlorantraniliprole) in a suicide attempt. She was initially asymptomatic. She had no past medical history, no cardiovascular disease, and no family history of coronary artery disease or sudden cardiac death.  
On arrival, temperature was 98.2 °F, blood pressure 100/70 mmHg, heart rate 70 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Cardiac and other systemic examinations were unremarkable.  
A gastric lavage was performed. Initial laboratory results showed normal complete blood count, metabolic panel, coagulation profile, and thyroid function tests. Chest radiograph was normal.  
During observation, the cardiac monitor intermittently dropped P waves. She then complained of lightheadedness; heart rate was 47 beats/min and systolic blood pressure was 90 mmHg.  
An electrocardiogram demonstrated a Mobitz Type I atrioventricular block with progressively prolonging PR intervals followed by nonconducted P waves, a corrected QT interval of 384 ms, and a QRS duration of 86 ms.

A 26-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of decreased vision in her left eye. She was in good health and had undergone femtosecond LASIK in both eyes 2 years earlier for myopic astigmatism, with clear, well-fitting flaps and 20/20 uncorrected visual acuity at her last visit one year ago. One month before presentation, she tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 by RT-PCR and completed a 7-day course of oral hydroxychloroquine (200 mg twice daily). Approximately 1 week after the onset of COVID-19, she noted blurred vision in her left eye. At presentation, her nasopharyngeal RT-PCR was negative for SARS-CoV-2. Visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/32 in the left eye. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye showed a clear LASIK flap interface. In the left eye, there was anterior stromal opacity along the LASIK flap interface without epithelial involvement; the anterior chamber was quiet, and there were no keratic precipitates. She denied pain or photophobia. Corneal sensation was normal in the right eye but reduced in the left eye. Posterior segment examination was unremarkable bilaterally.

A 58‐year‐old woman with protein C and S deficiency, a history of deep‐vein thrombosis on warfarin, systemic lupus erythematosus, and hypothyroidism presented with 3 days of right flank and right upper‐quadrant abdominal pain. An urgent‐care urinalysis showed blood and leukocyte esterase; she was treated for presumed urinary tract infection without improvement. In the emergency department, an abdominal CT scan was interpreted as consistent with a recently passed renal calculus, and she was discharged. Twelve hours later, she returned with worsening pain.

On examination, blood pressure was 154/80 mm Hg, heart rate 85/min, respiratory rate 17/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. The abdomen was diffusely tender with right costovertebral‐angle tenderness. Laboratory results showed white blood cell count 9.1×10^9/L, hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL, platelets 257×10^9/L, and an INR of 4.4. The basic metabolic panel was unremarkable. Liver enzymes were significantly elevated from 12 hours earlier: aspartate aminotransferase 658 U/L (previously 104 U/L) and alanine aminotransferase 772 U/L (previously 82 U/L); bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and albumin were normal. An extensive infectious and rheumatologic evaluation, including inflammatory markers, was unremarkable.

Contrast‐enhanced CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 6.5×6.5 cm infarct in the right hepatic lobe, a hypervascular lesion of the right hepatic artery suspicious for a pseudoaneurysm, and occlusion of the anterior right portal vein adjacent to the lesion. MRI of the abdomen confirmed a wedge‐shaped ischemic area in segments 5 and 8 of the liver and identified a 3 cm intrahepatic pseudoaneurysm compressing the anterior portal vein.

A 13-year-old Iraqi-born boy, unimmunized against measles, presented with a one-year history of progressive vision loss. Two months before evaluation he developed myoclonic jerks of all extremities every 10 seconds and atonic episodes causing falls. He subsequently had difficulty with fine motor tasks and became unable to ambulate without assistance. Over several months he had frequent urinary incontinence and a gradual, then accelerated, decline in memory and school performance. He also exhibited aggressive outbursts, including hitting and biting. His mother recalled a febrile rash illness in early childhood, though measles was never confirmed.

On examination, visual acuity was 20/200 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left, with macular retinopathy on fundoscopic exam. Mental status testing revealed impairment in simple calculations, recall, comprehension, and orientation. Pupils were sluggishly reactive to light, with normal convergence, and oculomotor apraxia. There was diffuse spasticity and hyperreflexia in all limbs, bilateral resting and action tremor, and an unsteady, wide-based gait.

Electroencephalography showed significant frontal slowing during wakefulness and recurrent periodic generalized epileptiform discharges approximately every 10 seconds, with preservation of the posterior basic rhythm. The differential diagnosis included baltic myoclonic epilepsy, Lafora body disease, Unverricht-Lundborg disease, neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, sialidosis, myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers, and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis.

A 40-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with 20 days of heavy per vaginal bleeding with clots, recent unexplained bruises, shortness of breath on exertion, malaise, and light-headedness. She also reported dental pain. She had no significant past medical or family history.

On examination, there were multiple areas of bruising, gingival hyperplasia, left submandibular lymphadenopathy, and petechiae on the palate and lips. She was febrile to 38.0 °C; the abdomen was soft and non-tender.

Initial laboratory tests revealed pancytopenia with a white-cell count of 1 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 89 g/L, platelets 11 × 10^9/L, and neutrophils 0.23 × 10^9/L. A bone marrow biopsy showed hypocellular marrow with erythroid-dominant, dysplastic hematopoiesis, marked reduction in granulo- and megakaryopoiesis, no excess blasts, and stromal edema.

Serum folate and vitamin B12 levels were notably reduced; both were supplemented without any improvement in the blood count. A repeat bone marrow examination again showed a hypocellular sample with erythroid-dominant hematopoiesis and markedly reduced granulopoiesis. Giemsa, Periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott’s methenamine silver, and Ziehl–Neelsen stains did not show any intracellular parasites, fungal elements, or acid-fast bacilli. Bone marrow DNA testing found no copy-number abnormalities or loss of heterozygosity of clinical significance. Screening for myeloma; antinuclear antibodies; anti–double-stranded DNA; anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide; rheumatoid factor; gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase; parvovirus IgG/M and PCR; beta-2-microglobulin; vitamin D; immunoglobulins; reticulocytes; and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase was negative.

A 29-year-old man from North Africa presented with a 3-month history of a right anterior chest wall mass and pleuritic chest pain. He noted loss of appetite without significant weight loss. On examination, vital signs were stable. Head, neck, ear, nose, and lymphatic examinations were unremarkable. Heart sounds were normal.
