The right anterior thorax showed an elliptical 8 × 5 cm mass without fluctuation and with mild tenderness; breath sounds were normal.  
Chest radiography revealed soft-tissue thickening over the right hemithorax, a blunted right costophrenic angle without obvious fluid, and fibrotic changes in the right apex.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a peripherally enhancing, cystic lesion in the right chest wall enveloping the fifth and sixth ribs, communicating with an ipsilateral pleural collection; there was rib erosion and pleural thickening. The right upper lobe contained centrilobular nodules and micronodules with apical retractile consolidation and associated pleural and bronchial retraction.  
Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and electrolytes; C-reactive protein was 60 mg/L.

A 38-year-old G2P1 woman with a dichorionic twin pregnancy at 35+5 weeks was brought for an emergency cesarean section because of failure to progress. She had a 7-year history of hyperthyroidism treated with propylthiouracil 50 mg twice daily throughout pregnancy; her free T4 level had ranged from 1 to 3 ng/dL, and 6 days before surgery it was 2 ng/dL. She was diagnosed with gestational hypertension at 24 weeks, with systolic pressures rising from 145 mmHg to 175 mmHg by 35 weeks; proteinuria was absent. 

On arrival in the operating room, she reported abdominal pain and mild nausea. Vital signs were notable for heart rate 124 beats/min, blood pressure 210/117 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. During preparation for spinal anesthesia she developed dyspnea; oxygen saturation fell to 90% despite 10 L/min via mask, and arterial PaO2 was 58 mmHg. Electrolytes were within normal limits. Blood pressure acutely rose to 240/120 mmHg with heart rate 200 beats/min, and she became irritable with altered consciousness. General anesthesia was induced with propofol and succinylcholine, and a cesarean delivery was performed; two infants were delivered with 1- and 5-minute Apgar scores of 7 and 9, respectively. 

Postoperatively, she was transferred to the ICU. She developed fever, persistent tachycardia, and diarrhea. Chest radiography showed bilateral pulmonary edema, and echocardiography revealed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with acute decompensated heart failure and a preserved ejection fraction.

A 45-year-old Nepalese man presented with a 1-month history of intermittent, colicky pain in the left iliac fossa and blood-mixed stool. He also noted passage of large amounts of mucopurulent discharge per rectum. He denied weight loss, appetite changes, past medical illness, smoking, alcohol use, or family history of gastrointestinal disease. On examination, vital signs were stable and both abdominal and digital rectal examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 11.8 g/dL and normal serum biochemistry. Colonoscopy revealed a 5 × 5 cm exophytic mass at the descending–sigmoid junction occupying half of the lumen, with surface exudates and erosions; the scope could not be advanced beyond the lesion. Carcinoembryonic antigen was 1.69 ng/mL (within normal range). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a well-defined hypodense lesion measuring 4.6 × 3.4 cm with fat density in the sigmoid-colon wall protruding into the lumen, along with invagination of the descending colon into the sigmoid colon consistent with intussusception.

A 41-year-old HIV-1–infected male farmer presented with a 5-day history of right hypochondriac abdominal pain associated with decreased appetite, nausea, vomiting, and 2 days of scleral icterus. He denied fever, diarrhea, visual changes, odynophagia, or dysphagia. 

His HIV infection was diagnosed in 2000. He had previously been treated with zidovudine/lamivudine/nevirapine and later tenofovir/lamivudine/atazanavir/ritonavir after virologic failure in 2011. In September 2016, he developed Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia treated with co-trimoxazole and prednisone; at that time his CD4 count was 109 cells/µL and viral load was 4.89 log copies/mL. Four weeks before this presentation, his regimen was switched to raltegravir/darunavir/ritonavir.

On examination he was afebrile, with normal vital signs, but had icterus and tender hepatomegaly. Laboratory studies showed normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL), normal white-cell count, total bilirubin 9.2 mg/dL, AST 109 U/L, ALT 41 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 906 U/L. Tests for hepatitis B and C were negative.

Abdominal ultrasonography revealed hepatomegaly (liver span 18 cm), grade I–II intrahepatic biliary dilatation with a focal parenchymal lesion, and a common bile duct dilated to 14 mm without a definitive mass. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography showed an edematous, stenotic papilla and a prepapillary common bile duct stricture with upstream dilation. Sphincterotomy was performed and a 7-Fr stent was placed.

Bile aspirate was negative for Cryptosporidium, Microsporidium, Cyclospora, and Mycobacterium. Brush cytology of the stricture showed inflammatory cells, pigment-laden macrophages, and red blood cells, with no acid-fast organisms.

A 28-year-old woman with a history of gastritis, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and known hyperthyroidism (noncompliant with antithyroid therapy) presented with 2 weeks of nausea, vomiting, epigastric burning, and poor appetite. In the days before presentation, she developed persistent malaise and shortness of breath. She smokes and reported recent work stress and high coffee intake.  
On arrival: temperature 37.1 °C; respiratory rate 29 breaths/min; pulse 120 beats/min; blood pressure 123/71 mmHg; oxygen via nasal cannula at 3 L/min.  
Laboratory studies: serum potassium 1.2 mEq/L, sodium 136 mEq/L; other values notable for albumin 2.2 g/dL and antithyroid peroxidase antibody pending.  
Arterial blood gas on O₂ showed pH 7.25, PaCO₂ 22 mmHg, PaO₂ 116 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 9.6 mmol/L.  
Electrocardiogram: sinus tachycardia, T-wave flattening/inversion, ST depression, prominent U-waves, T–U fusion, prolonged QU.  
Chest radiograph: right lower lung infiltration.  
Thyroid function tests: TSH 0.021 μIU/mL; free T₄ 2.01 ng/dL.  
She was transferred to the ICU, where she developed progressive dyspnea, sudden drowsiness, and use of accessory muscles. Respiratory rate 33 breaths/min. Repeat arterial blood gas revealed pH 7.11, PaCO₂ 72 mmHg, PaO₂ 206 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 22.9 mmol/L.

A 40‐year‐old Sudanese woman presented with a 2‐week history of facial skin rash, hair loss, and diffuse arthralgias involving both small and large joints. She also reported palpitations, shortness of breath, and pleuritic chest pain. On admission, she developed acute, severe, cramping periumbilical abdominal pain with distension, vomiting, and infrequent episodes of bloody diarrhea.

Vital signs were notable for blood pressure 150/100 mm Hg, pulse 100 beats/min, and temperature 37.5 °C. Examination revealed a malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds with hyperpigmented patches, broken hair in the frontal and temporal regions, and no nail changes. Cardiac auscultation identified a short, localized systolic murmur at the mitral area. Chest examination showed decreased air entry bilaterally with dullness to percussion. The abdomen was distended with a tender left periumbilical mass. Musculoskeletal examination demonstrated active synovitis of the metacarpophalangeal joints bilaterally, painful knees, and shoulder pain on both active and passive movement.

Laboratory results included hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL, platelet count 127 × 10^9/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 60 mm/h, C‐reactive protein 20 mg/L, serum albumin 2.9 g/dL, positive antinuclear antibodies, positive anti–double‐stranded DNA antibodies, positive antihistone antibodies, and positive anti–ribosomal P protein antibodies. Abdominal CT scan demonstrated a rounded lumbar mass with a double‐layer configuration consistent with intestinal intussusception.

A 44-year-old Nepalese man was referred for management of severe anemia. He had no significant past medical history, took no medications, and denied smoking or alcohol use. He reported 10 days of fatigability and swollen ankles, without fever, night sweats, weight loss, cough, dyspnea, chest pain, or palpitations. He noted a single episode of a small amount of fresh rectal bleeding 2 days prior.  
On examination, blood pressure was 120/56 mmHg, pulse rate 86/min, respiratory rate 19/min, temperature 36.7 °C, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. He appeared markedly pale with clubbing and mild bilateral pedal edema. Heart sounds were normal with a systolic murmur at the tricuspid area. There was no lymphadenopathy.  
Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 1.8 g/dL, hematocrit 8%, mean corpuscular volume 58 fL, normal white-cell and platelet counts, and normal CRP, haptoglobin, and liver and renal function tests. Iron studies showed ferritin 4.2 μg/L, serum iron 2 μmol/L, total iron-binding capacity 93 μmol/L, transferrin 3.7 g/L, and iron saturation 2%. Reticulocyte count was low at 36×10^3/μL. Peripheral blood film demonstrated severe hypochromia, microcytosis, anisopoikilocytosis, rouleaux, dimorphism, few target cells, and teardrop cells.  
Proctoscopy revealed a small internal hemorrhoid without active bleeding. Stool tests were negative for ova and parasites; fecal occult blood test was positive. Further tests for vitamin B12, folate, anti-transglutaminase IgG antibody, and hemoglobin electrophoresis were noncontributory. CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was unremarkable.  
A chest radiograph showed cardiomegaly. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a high cardiac index (6.77 L/min/m^2), mild left ventricular dilation with ejection fraction 41%, moderate pericardial effusion without tamponade, severely elevated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 80 mmHg, moderate tricuspid regurgitation, and TAPSE of 2.2 cm. Thyroid-function tests were within normal limits.

A 69-year-old man with a 120–pack-year smoking history and known GOLD D COPD, diabetes, hypertension, and ischemic heart disease was admitted with RT-PCR–confirmed COVID-19. He had a 3-day history of cough and dyspnea, was tachypneic (RR 28/min), and had type I respiratory failure requiring high-flow nasal cannula (FiO2 0.6 at 60 L/min). His C-reactive protein was 20 mg/L, white-cell count was 7 × 10^9/L, and chest radiography showed bilateral lower-zone ground-glass opacities. CT pulmonary angiography on day 10 revealed moderate organizing pneumonia on a background of emphysema and no pulmonary embolism. He received baricitinib and corticosteroids, underwent pulmonary rehabilitation, and was discharged on supplemental oxygen after 22 days.

Two weeks later, he returned with a 3-day history of cough and shortness of breath. He was febrile (38.0 °C), tachypneic, and had an SpO2 of 92% on room air. Lung examination revealed minimal bibasilar fine crackles. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 16 × 10^9/L and a C-reactive protein of 45 mg/L; renal and liver function were normal, and sputum and blood cultures were negative. Repeat CT pulmonary angiography demonstrated worsening ground-glass opacities with reticulation, a crazy-paving pattern, reduced lung volumes, and displaced fissures, but no organizing pneumonia or pulmonary embolism. Multidisciplinary discussion concluded post–COVID-19 progressive pulmonary fibrosis with concomitant secondary bacterial infection. He was treated with intravenous piperacillin–tazobactam, corticosteroids were stopped, and he improved clinically and was discharged after one week on dual long-acting bronchodilators with outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation.

A 69‐year‐old African American woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and elite control HIV (off antiretrovirals, undetectable viral load) initially presented with worsening lower back pain of 1 month’s duration. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis, anemia, mild renal impairment, and a paraprotein gap. Skeletal survey revealed lytic lesions; spine MRI demonstrated vertebral compression, deformities, and epidural extension. Bone biopsy showed >80% blast cells with marked circulating plasma cells, consistent with plasma cell leukemia. She also had findings of cauda equina syndrome. An abdominal CT scan at that time showed a markedly dilated ascending colon, suggestive of obstruction, although she continued to have bowel movements. She underwent induction chemotherapy and was discharged in stable condition.

She was readmitted for a second cycle of chemotherapy with cisplatin and bortezomib. On admission, serum potassium was 1.8 mmol/L with a U wave on ECG; serum magnesium remained within normal limits. She reported progressive abdominal distension, diarrhea, and bilateral lower extremity edema. Multiple stool studies, including tests for Clostridioides difficile, were negative. Several abdominal CT scans with intravenous contrast showed markedly dilated loops of bowel without evidence of mechanical obstruction. She developed acute kidney injury, raising concern for abdominal compartment syndrome; measured bladder pressure was 29 mm Hg and decreased to 21 mm Hg after placement of a rectal tube.

A 54-year-old Filipino man presented with a 6-month history of painless blurred vision and a white subretinal lesion centered on the optic nerve head in his right eye. He had been treated elsewhere with oral prednisone and five intravitreal bevacizumab injections for presumed inflammatory choroidal neovascular membrane, resulting in temporary resolution of subretinal fluid but not the mass; fluid recurred when steroids were tapered. His past history included type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, steatohepatitis, prior gastric sleeve surgery, and remote herpes zoster ophthalmicus without ocular involvement. 

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 OD and 20/20 OS; intraocular pressures were 9 mmHg OD and 10 mmHg OS. There were no signs of anterior uveitis, vitritis, or retinal vasculitis. Fundus examination OD showed a large white subretinal lesion peripapillary with speckled autofluorescence. EDI-OCT revealed a hyperreflective subretinal mass without choroidal thickening or macular edema. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated optic nerve hyperfluorescence, staining of the lesion, and blocked fluorescence at its margin without retinal vasculitis. ICG angiography showed absolute blockage by the lesion and multiple small hypofluorescent satellite spots. B-scan ultrasonography revealed an echodense lesion at the optic nerve head. Visual field testing OD showed an inferotemporal scotoma.

Laboratory tests including CBC, ESR, QuantiFERON Gold, autoimmune screen, syphilis, Toxoplasma, and Bartonella serologies were normal or negative. Serum ACE was 55 U/L initially and 82 U/L on repeat. MRI of the brain and orbits showed increased intraneural signal in the right optic nerve without optic nerve sheath tumour or glioma. CT chest revealed no hilar lymphadenopathy. PET scan identified metabolically active lymph nodes in the pulmonary hila, para-aortic, iliac, and inguinal regions and lesions in bone, heart, and liver. A core biopsy of a right deep inguinal lymph node showed non-necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis.

Three months later, vision in the right eye declined to 20/100 with new subfoveal fluid on OCT. Given persistent diagnostic uncertainty, the team elected to perform a 27-gauge pars plana vitrectomy and subretinal biopsy of the peripapillary lesion.

A 69‐year‐old obese woman with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia presented with midsternal chest pain radiating to her right arm and right jaw, accompanied by dyspnea. Physical examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, chemistry panel, TSH, and coagulation studies, were within normal limits except for elevated cardiac enzymes: CK 248 IU/L, CK‐MB 32.6 ng/mL, and troponin I 1.18 ng/mL (normal <0.04). She was diagnosed with a non–ST‐segment elevation myocardial infarction and treated with dual antiplatelet therapy, anticoagulation, a beta blocker, an ACE inhibitor, and a statin. Overnight, her chest pain resolved and cardiac enzymes down‐trended.

The next morning, left heart catheterization demonstrated no angiographic evidence of disease in the epicardial coronary arteries, but revealed mid‐cavitary akinesis with apical and basal hyperkinesis and an ejection fraction of 37%, along with a mildly elevated left ventricular end‐diastolic pressure. The patient reported significant emotional stress that peaked 48 hours before presentation. Her antiplatelet agents, anticoagulation, and statin were discontinued, and she remained on the beta blocker and ACE inhibitor. A transthoracic echocardiogram performed later the same day showed severe mid‐cavitary hypokinesis, an ejection fraction of 35–40%, and mild mitral regurgitation. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging the following day confirmed mid‐ventricular hypokinesis with an ejection fraction of 38% and demonstrated no delayed gadolinium enhancement in the epicardium, myocardium, or endocardium.

A 16-year-old Albanian girl with a 4-year history of epilepsy was referred for progressive neurological deterioration. She initially presented in early adolescence with generalized tonic–clonic seizures treated with valproic acid; levetiracetam was later added due to continued seizures. Over the past year she developed visual hallucinations, emotional disturbances, and irritability, for which fluoxetine was prescribed. Subsequently, she experienced cognitive decline, behavioral changes, dysarthria, and difficulty walking.

On admission, she weighed 40 kg, was disoriented, irritable, and nonverbal, and required assistance to stand. The remainder of her neurologic and systemic examinations was notable only for unsteady gait. Routine blood tests, including hemoglobin, platelet count, ESR, CRP, liver enzymes, urea, creatinine, acid–base status, and urinalysis, were all normal. Serum and cerebrospinal fluid analyses excluded infectious and immune-mediated etiologies. Electroencephalography showed diffuse low-voltage activity initially and, on follow-up, severe epileptic paroxysms bilaterally. Brain magnetic resonance imaging was normal. Owing to progressive decline and lack of response to antiepileptic drugs, plans were made for advanced genetic testing and an axillary skin biopsy.

A 70-year-old man was referred for evaluation of recurrent urticaria and suspected repaglinide hypersensitivity. His medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and persistent rhinitis. He is a hunter and dog owner in continental Croatia, with multiple tick bites over the years. His chronic medications were metformin, insulin glargine, lercanidipine, and pantoprazole.

Seven years before referral, he experienced urticaria 6–8 h after ingesting simethicone, which was attributed to a drug allergy. Two months later—2 weeks after a tick bite—he had a second urticarial episode without an obvious trigger. He also reported generalized pruritus without rash after tamsulosin and mild urticarial rash after eating sausages. Notably, he regularly ate cooked red meat (beef, pork, and lamb) without any symptoms.

In the month before referral, he had three short-lived urticarial eruptions following fresh tick bites. The first two occurred 6–8 h after taking repaglinide and resolved with chloropyramine and methylprednisolone. The last episode, accompanied by left-sided facial angioedema, began one day before referral and worsened after taking fexofenadine. He had no respiratory, cardiovascular, or gastrointestinal symptoms.

On examination, he had generalized urticaria and left facial angioedema, which quickly resolved with chloropyramine and methylprednisolone. Initial laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (10.6×10^9/L) with neutrophilia (9.62×10^9/L), lymphopenia (0.72×10^9/L), and an elevated C-reactive protein (21.8 mg/L); other studies were pending.

A 52-year-old woman presented with an 8-year history of asymptomatic hypopigmented macules interspersed with hyperpigmented macules and patches confined to her upper back.  She had no lesions on her extremities or anterior trunk.  Her medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and lichen simplex chronicus of the right lower extremity managed with tacrolimus 0.1% ointment.  She denied any family history of dermatologic conditions, photosensitivity, blistering, itching, erythema, dysphagia, or muscle weakness.  A 2-mm punch biopsy of a lesion on the right superior back was performed.  Hematoxylin and eosin sections revealed amorphous material and a significant accumulation of melanophages in the papillary dermis.  A subsequent crystal violet stain was positive for amyloid.

A 15-year-old boy presented with multiple painless nodules over the dorsal aspects of the proximal interphalangeal joints of the left hand (fifth finger spared) and similar lesions on all toes of both feet, first noted in autumn 2011. He had no history of trauma, and his personal and family histories were unremarkable for fibrosing disorders. From July 2012 to August 2013, dermatologists and a hand surgeon confirmed the diagnosis of knuckle pads and offered various treatments: 5% urea cream for 3 months, 25% urea cream for 40 days, wart-removal products (lactic, glycolic, and salicylic acids) for 40 days, and cryotherapy; all yielded no improvement. The patient discontinued therapy in mid-2014, and the nodules remained unchanged in size and shape. Physical examination revealed well-circumscribed, noncompressible, freely movable, wartlike subcutaneous nodules over the affected joints, without tenderness, erythema, or functional limitation.

A 22-month-old boy was referred for evaluation of short stature. He was born at term to first-cousin parents after an uncomplicated pregnancy and had a 5-day neonatal intensive care stay for meconium aspiration and jaundice treated with phototherapy. His birth weight was 3.12 kg. He experienced early failure to thrive that resolved with supplemental feeding, but his linear growth remained poor. Developmental milestones were appropriate. On examination, his supine length was 74.5 cm (<0.01th percentile, −4.05 height SDS) and weight was 10.44 kg (14th percentile, −1.06 SDS). He appeared disproportionate, with a relatively large head, a patent anterior fontanelle, marked lumbar lordosis, and short limbs. A clinical diagnosis of skeletal dysplasia was made.  

A skeletal survey demonstrated:  
• Diffuse increased bone density with preserved corticomedullary differentiation  
• Wormian bones and widening of the parieto-occipital sutures with open fontanelles  
• Frontal bossing and an obtuse mandibular angle with otherwise normal dentition  
• Acro-osteolysis of the small bones of the hands and feet, short stubby metacarpals, and mild symmetrical shortening of the long bones

A 46-year-old woman presented with a several-month history of intermenstrual bleeding. She reported two prior cesarean deliveries but no other pelvic surgery. She had not used hormonal contraception for years, had a regular menstrual history until the onset of bleeding, denied dysmenorrhea or dyspareunia, and had no history of infertility. She was not sexually active.

On pelvic examination, a 2-cm soft, polypoid lesion was noted on the posterior vaginal cuff; it bled easily on contact. The cervix and remaining vaginal walls appeared normal. A Papanicolaou smear was negative for intraepithelial lesions or malignancy. Transvaginal ultrasound showed small uterine fibroids, normal adnexa, and no sonographic evidence of endometriosis.

Given ongoing bleeding, she was scheduled for an ambulatory polypectomy with electrocoagulation of the lesion’s pedicle.

A 14-year-old girl presented with a 3-month history of a pruritic, painless lesion in her intermammary region. The lesion began as a papule, gradually enlarged to a pustule, and then ulcerated with purulent drainage. She denied fever, weight loss, appetite change, cough, hemoptysis, trauma, or similar lesions in family members. Multiple courses of antibiotics prescribed empirically had failed to improve the lesion.

On examination, there was a single 3.0 cm × 0.5 cm ulcer with a suppurative surface and surrounding crusting over the intermammary area. Mobile, painless, anterior cervical lymph nodes measured 2 × 2 cm bilaterally. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Investigations revealed a normal chest radiograph. A tuberculin skin test was positive, with 15 mm of induration. Three sputum specimens were negative for acid-fast bacilli on direct smear.

A 36-year-old man presented with chronic fatigue, night sweats, and increased susceptibility to infections over several years. Twenty years earlier, he had sustained splenic rupture in a motorbike accident and underwent splenectomy; he received only pneumococcal vaccination at that time. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count with differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, and carcinoembryonic antigen, were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced multidetector CT of the thorax and abdomen revealed soft-tissue–attenuation nodular formations within the mesorectal fascia without enlarged lymph nodes or other suspicious masses. Subsequent contrast-enhanced MRI of the pelvis demonstrated multiple perirectal nodules with low signal intensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images, homogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration, and no diffusion restriction; the nodules appeared separate from the intestinal lumen, and the rectal wall was normal.

A 94-year-old woman was evaluated for functional decline secondary to longstanding right knee pain. Her history included osteoarthritis and a right total knee arthroplasty in 1996. On examination, she was afebrile; her right knee was red, warm, swollen, and effusion was present. Orthopedic surgery was consulted to help determine whether a prosthetic joint infection was present. Initial blood tests showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 54 mm/h, a C-reactive protein level of 52.6 mg/L, and a white-cell count of 6.2 × 10^9/L. A plain radiograph demonstrated loosening of the tibial component with a large effusion believed to represent metallosis. An aspirate of the knee revealed calcium pyrophosphate crystals, a total nucleated cell count of 11.3 × 10^9/L, and 97% neutrophils. She was discharged with a tentative diagnosis of pseudogout. Six weeks later, an enrichment broth subculture of the initial aspirate grew a Gram-positive bacillus identified as a Lactobacillus species (unidentifiable RapID™ ANA II profile; catalase-negative; PYR-negative; LAP-negative; vancomycin resistant). She then presented with Escherichia coli bacteremia from a urinary tract infection. Reassessment of her right knee showed increased swelling, pain, and tenderness. A second aspirate grew the same organism, with no calcium pyrophosphate crystals, a nucleated cell count of 3.1 × 10^9/L, and 96% neutrophils. The isolate was sent for 16S ribosomal RNA sequencing.

A 50-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of recurrent distending pain in the right upper abdomen, paroxysmal and accompanied by nausea and vomiting without diarrhea, hematochezia, fever, or chills. On examination, she had tenderness and rebound pain in the middle and upper abdomen without palpable masses, mucocutaneous ulcers, or perianal lesions. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 97 g/L, albumin 29.6 g/L, CRP 10.47 mg/L, ESR 28 mm/h, and platelets 305×10^9/L. Fecal occult blood was positive. Tuberculosis antibody, T-SPOT.TB, and PPD tests were positive; acid-fast bacilli smear was negative. Abdominal CT showed thickening and enhancement of the cecum and ascending colon with enlarged lymph nodes. Colonoscopy revealed a large circumferential ulcer from the proximal ascending colon to the ileocecal region, with a narrow lumen. Biopsy demonstrated acute and chronic mucosal inflammation with crypt abscesses, exudation, necrosis, and granulation tissue but no granulomatous inflammation. After conservative management failed, she underwent right colon resection; pathology showed a 7×4 cm ileocecal ulcer with acute and chronic inflammation and reactive lymphoid hyperplasia. One month later she was readmitted with intestinal obstruction, treated conservatively, and improved. Six months after surgery she returned with 5 days of right upper abdominal distension. Examination was unremarkable. Labs again showed anemia (hemoglobin 100 g/L), hypoalbuminemia (albumin 33.7 g/L), elevated CRP (13.77 mg/L) and ESR (50 mm/h), and platelets 320×10^9/L; tuberculosis tests remained positive, and other serologies including autoantibodies and tumor markers were negative. CT showed perianastomotic exudation, lymph nodes, and edema of the gastric pylorus. Colonoscopy found a deep ulcer at the anastomosis too narrow to pass; gastroscopy revealed a 3.0×4.0 cm ulcer in the duodenal bulb with a sinus tract. CT angiography confirmed an intestinal wall sinus tract between the transverse colon and duodenum. Further history elicited recurrent oral ulcers 3 years earlier and eye inflammation 5 years earlier, neither of which had recurred. Specimens from her prior colon resection were sent for further pathological evaluation.

A 10-year-old boy presented with a 3-week history of drooping of his right upper eyelid and vertical diplopia that worsened on up-gaze. Three weeks earlier he had sustained a blunt impact to the right forehead with a badminton racket without loss of consciousness or other neurologic symptoms. There was no history of fever, recent vaccination, drug intake, or systemic illness.

On examination, visual acuity was 6/6 in both eyes. He held a chin-elevated head posture. There was moderate right ptosis with right frontalis overaction and limitation of elevation of the right eye. A constant, small-amplitude horizontal jerk nystagmus was noted. Pupils were equal and reactive to light and accommodation. Orbital rims were intact, infraorbital sensation was normal, and funduscopic examination was unremarkable. In primary gaze there was a 30-prism-diopter right hypotropia. Diplopia charting confirmed vertical diplopia in primary gaze, increasing on dextroelevation, suggestive of right superior rectus involvement. Forced-duction testing was negative. Levator palpebrae superioris function measured 12 mm on the right and 15 mm on the left.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the orbits revealed isolated atrophy of the right superior rectus–levator complex without other extraocular muscle, orbital apex, bony wall, cavernous sinus, or midbrain pathology. Paranasal sinuses were normal. Routine hematological and biochemical investigations were within normal limits.

A 53‐year‐old African American man with untreated asthma and polysubstance use presented with 3 days of shortness of breath, subjective fevers, chills, generalized lethargy, and diffuse muscle fatigue without pain. He denied sick contacts or recent travel. He reported that shortly after cleaning a basement bathtub filled with dirty standing water, he developed fatigue that progressed to his current symptoms. 

On examination, he was afebrile (97.2 °F), tachycardic (heart rate 130 beats/min), and tachypneic (respiratory rate 22 breaths/min). He later developed a fever of 102 °F. Oxygen saturation was 86–88% on room air, improving to 94–96% with 2 L of nasal-cannula oxygen. He appeared lethargic, disheveled, and dehydrated. Cardiac auscultation was normal. Pulmonary auscultation revealed bilateral wheezes, decreased breath sounds, and crackles in the left posterior lung zone. Abdominal and neurological examinations were unremarkable except for 4/5 strength in all extremities.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 12.1 × 10^9/L (80% PMNs, 17% bands), procalcitonin 34.3 ng/mL, sodium 128 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 75 mg/dL, creatinine 3.32 mg/dL (baseline 0.7 mg/dL), ALT 496 U/L, AST 1393 U/L, LDH 412 U/L, and glucose 246 mg/dL. Urinalysis revealed large blood with 2–3 red cells per high-power field. Urine toxicology was positive for cannabinoids and cocaine. Serum creatine kinase exceeded 25,000 U/L. Chest radiograph demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation. Electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia.

He was diagnosed with sepsis due to community-acquired pneumonia complicated by hypoxemic respiratory failure and acute kidney injury likely secondary to rhabdomyolysis. Given the hyponatremia, elevated LDH and transaminases, confusion, and possible water-source exposure, atypical pathogens were considered. He was started on intravenous fluids (125 cc/hour), IV azithromycin 500 mg daily, and IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily.

A 41-year-old woman with a history of non-Hodgkin’s follicular lymphoma and deep venous thrombosis on chronic warfarin therapy presented with three weeks of upper respiratory–type symptoms. She reported nonexertional sharp chest pain radiating to her back and left arm that improved with leaning forward, associated fever, chills, nonproductive cough, shortness of breath, dyspnea, and palpitations. 

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. Lung auscultation revealed mildly decreased breath sounds at both bases without wheezing. Initial laboratory studies showed a normal basic metabolic panel, complete blood count, hepatic function panel, and lipase. Cardiac markers were elevated with a troponin level of 1.26 ng/mL and creatine kinase-MB of 5.1 ng/mL. Coagulation studies demonstrated an INR of 2.1, a prothrombin time of 22.7 seconds, and a PTT of 48.8 seconds. An electrocardiogram showed no ST-segment changes or PR-segment prolongation. 

She was treated for non–ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction and pericarditis with metoprolol, atorvastatin, aspirin, and clopidogrel; warfarin was continued. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a circumferential pericardial effusion and normal systolic function without tamponade physiology. Treatment for pericarditis was initiated with high-dose aspirin (975 mg twice daily). 

Within 48 hours of aspirin therapy, she developed right upper quadrant abdominal pain without encephalopathy. Repeat laboratory tests revealed an AST of 7,946 U/L, an ALT of 5,684 U/L, an alkaline phosphatase of 84 U/L, and a total bilirubin of 0.8 mg/dL. Her INR rose to >13.8 with a prothrombin time >100 seconds and PTT of 46.2 seconds; vital signs remained stable. Right upper quadrant ultrasound showed a normal-appearing liver, vasculature, and biliary system. Viral hepatitis serologies were all negative.

A 50-year-old woman was admitted with dyspnea (New York Heart Association class IV) and orthopnea of 5 days’ duration. She had been taking neurotonic medication for dizziness for 2 months. On examination, blood pressure was 100/60 mm Hg, pulse 82 beats/min, and there was no cardiac murmur; bilateral lung rales were present, but there was no jugular venous distension or peripheral edema. Neurologic examination was unremarkable. Electrocardiography showed a prolonged QT interval (432 ms) with nonspecific ST-T changes. Chest radiography revealed marked cardiomegaly and pulmonary congestion. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated global hypokinesia, left ventricular ejection fraction 36.5%, left ventricular diastolic and systolic dimensions of 59 mm and 47 mm, and moderate mitral and tricuspid regurgitation. Serum creatine kinase-MB and troponin-I levels were normal, whereas the brain natriuretic peptide level was 1,855.1 pg/mL. She had no history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or smoking, and her chronic medication was not felt to affect cardiac function. Further evaluation included measurement of electrolytes and hormones, which showed total serum calcium 3.7 mg/dL (normal 8.4–10.2), ionized calcium 0.6 mmol/L (1.12–1.30), magnesium 1.7 mg/dL (1.9–2.5), phosphorus 8.5 mg/dL (2.5–4.6), and creatinine 1.5 mg/dL (0.6–1.2). Thyroid function tests (free T4 and TSH) were normal. Intact parathyroid hormone was 8.17 pg/mL (15–68), and 25-hydroxyvitamin D was 10.1 ng/mL (11–70). Coronary angiography showed no significant stenotic lesions.

A 16-year-old boy presented with 5 months of progressive jaundice and recurrent episodes of diffuse severe abdominal pain, each lasting 7–10 days and requiring hospitalization for intravenous analgesics. He reported photosensitivity since age 5 but denied fever, skin blisters, oral ulcers, musculoskeletal, or neuropsychiatric symptoms. On examination, he had icterus; atrophic scarring and hyperpigmentation of the face, hands, and feet; and nontender hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, white cells 9 × 10^9/L, platelets 174 × 10^9/L, total bilirubin 8.65 mg/dL (direct 4.3 mg/dL), AST 462 IU/L, ALT 256 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 262 IU/L, and INR 1.2. An extensive workup for liver disease was unrevealing, including negative viral markers (hepatitis B surface antigen; anti-hepatitis C; IgM against hepatitis A, hepatitis E, cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, and herpes simplex virus), negative autoimmune markers (ANA; anti–smooth muscle; anti–liver kidney microsome 1; anti–soluble liver antigen), normal ceruloplasmin, and negative IgA tissue transglutaminase. Given his photosensitivity, systemic lupus erythematosus and porphyrias were considered, but anti–double-stranded DNA, anti–Smith antibody, and urinary porphobilinogen were absent. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed small, low-risk esophageal varices. Triple-phase abdominal CT confirmed hepatosplenomegaly without other evidence of portal hypertension, and MRCP revealed no biliary abnormalities.

A 45-year-old man with no past medical history presented with a 3-day history of epigastric pain. The pain was gradual in onset, sharp, progressive, and not relieved by over-the-counter medications. There was no associated fever, diarrhea, nausea, or vomiting, and no history of travel or sick contacts. He denied any other symptoms.

On examination, his temperature was 36.2 °C, blood pressure 167/90 mm Hg, heart rate 62 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He appeared well. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness localized to the epigastrium without guarding or rebound. Bowel sounds were present. Rectal examination was normal without melena. Cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable.

Initial laboratory studies showed:  
• White-cell count 5 × 10^9/L (normal 4–10 × 10^9/L)  
• Lymphocytes 1.3 × 10^9/L (normal 1–3 × 10^9/L)  
• Hemoglobin 15.1 g/dL (normal 13–17 g/dL)  
• Platelets 179 × 10^3/µL (normal 150–400 × 10^3/µL)  
• C-reactive protein 15 mg/L (normal 0–5 mg/L)  
• Serum creatinine 416 µmol/L (normal 62–106 µmol/L)  
• Blood urea 11.9 mmol/L (normal 2.8–8.1 mmol/L)  
• Lipase 21 U/L (normal 13–60 U/L)  
• Amylase 38 U/L (normal 13–53 U/L)

An abdominal CT scan with contrast showed no abnormalities. A chest X-ray was normal.

A 27-year-old woman, 28 weeks pregnant, was admitted 1 hour after a focal-onset generalized tonic–clonic seizure. Her first seizure occurred at 19 weeks of gestation; levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily was initiated, and an EEG at that time was normal. On examination in the emergency department, she had 0/5 strength in the left upper extremity, 0/5 proximal and 2/5 distal strength in the left lower extremity, and mute plantar reflexes bilaterally. Brain MRI showed DWI hyperintensity and corresponding ADC hypointensity in the right temporoparietal region. MR angiography revealed no evidence of major arterial occlusion, and MR venography showed a hypoplastic left transverse sinus but no venous thrombosis. Forty-five minutes after arrival, her left-sided weakness had almost completely resolved. A repeat brain MRI immediately after clinical improvement demonstrated disappearance of the prior diffusion restriction on DWI and normalization of ADC.

A 69-year-old woman with a body mass index of 31.2 kg/m² and a history of diabetes and hypertension underwent bilateral total knee arthroplasty. Her postoperative course was unremarkable until the night before planned discharge (postoperative day 1), when she received an intramuscular injection of diclofenac in her right buttock for pain control. Immediately after the injection, she complained of intense pain at the site. On examination, the skin was swollen and diffusely erythematous with central blanching. 

The following morning, the area was exquisitely tender to palpation. Cutaneous findings included scattered erythematous macules and a livedoid, violaceous patch with dendritic extensions at the injection site. 

Initial differential diagnoses included an allergic reaction to diclofenac, acute bleeding, hematoma, and acute compartment syndrome.

A 59-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of left-knee swelling and occasional pain. The swelling was gradual in onset, progressively increasing in size, and unaccompanied by trauma or constitutional symptoms. On examination, there was a 10 cm × 5 cm anterolateral swelling of the knee; it was cystic, firm, non-tender, not fixed to overlying skin, and the knee had a full, pain-free range of motion. Plain radiographs of the knee were normal. Magnetic resonance imaging of the knee showed a multilobular, complex cystic lesion measuring 22 mm × 27 mm × 41 mm within the lateral Hoffa’s fat pad; it was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, without any connection to the lateral meniscus, and no other intra-articular pathology was noted on the scan.

A 67-year-old Japanese woman presented with a 5-day history of central visual field loss and photopsia in her right eye. One day before symptom onset, she had received a second dose of the BNT162b2 mRNA COVID-19 vaccine, after which she experienced mild fever and general fatigue. She denied prior COVID-19 infection; her medical, drug, and family histories were unremarkable.

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/100 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye; intraocular pressures were 13 mmHg OD and 14 mmHg OS. Pupils were equal and reactive; extraocular movements were normal. Slit-lamp examination showed bilateral mild cataracts; the right eye had moderate vitritis (1+ haze, 2+ cells) with small white balls in the mid to posterior vitreous. Fundus examination of the right eye revealed multifocal deep retinal white dots around the posterior pole and optic disc; the left eye was unremarkable.

Fundus autofluorescence of the right eye showed multiple hypofluorescent spots surrounded by hyperfluorescent circles and scattered hyperfluorescent lesions concentrated around the optic disc and posterior pole. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated early punctate hyperfluorescence in a wreath-like pattern with late staining. Indocyanine green angiography revealed multiple late hypofluorescent spots. Optical coherence tomography of the right eye showed variable hyperreflective lesions in the outer retina and disruption of the ellipsoid zone at the macula. Goldmann visual field testing revealed a central scotoma and paracentral islands of sensitivity loss in the right eye. 

Her laboratory evaluations were negative for syphilis, tuberculosis, or toxoplasma, and selected autoimmune diseases.

A 24-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a persistent purulent discharge from her right lower-abdominal wound, 6 weeks after an appendectomy performed for presumed acute appendicitis. Two weeks before that surgery, she had developed right lower-quadrant abdominal pain. She also reported 6 months of general ill health and occasional changes in bowel habits. 

At her initial presentation for acute appendicitis, she was febrile, tachycardic, and dehydrated. Examination revealed diffuse abdominal tenderness with maximal guarding in the right lower quadrant. Her white-cell count was 24 × 10^9/L. Abdominal radiography showed a few fluid levels, and ultrasonography demonstrated free intraperitoneal fluid and a right-iliac-fossa mass. After resuscitation, she underwent an open McBurney-incision appendectomy. Intraoperatively there was pus and an inflamed appendicular mass; the appendix appeared oedematous and congested. A drain was left in place and removed on postoperative day 3.

Despite broad-spectrum antibiotics, she continued to have wound infection, fever, and a persistent purulent discharge. Histopathological examination of the resected appendix revealed “transmural inflammation with granulomas suggestive of Crohn’s disease.” A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen showed a pericaecal collection with an inflammatory mass anterior to the caecum.

A 25-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with 3 days of high fever (up to 39 °C), left flank pain, and gross hematuria. She had left costovertebral angle tenderness on examination. Urinalysis showed 2055 red blood cells per high-power field; dipstick was negative for leukocyte esterase and nitrites and positive for albuminuria (2+). Microscopy revealed minimal pyuria (6 white blood cells per high-power field) and no bacteriuria. She had not taken antibiotics prior to presentation. Urine and blood cultures were obtained. Laboratory tests showed C-reactive protein 28 mg/dl, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 107 mm/h, creatinine 1.21 mg/dl, and blood urea nitrogen 16 mg/dl. She was admitted with a provisional diagnosis of acute pyelonephritis and started on intravenous ceftriaxone. On the following day, contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen revealed a hypoenhancing region in the upper pole of the left kidney, suggestive of pyelonephritis.

A 12-year-old right-handed girl was evaluated for a long-standing inability to flex her left thumb at the interphalangeal joint. She had no history of recent or remote trauma. On examination, there was an absence of active flexion at the interphalangeal joint, but passive flexion was full. The flexion crease over the interphalangeal joint was absent. Thenar muscles were normal in bulk and strength, and movements of all other hand joints were normal. A plain radiograph of the hand showed no abnormalities.

A 29-year-old man presented with one month of progressively worsening low back pain. He had no history of hyperuricemia, gout, hypertension, or kidney disease. On examination, he had significant tenderness over the lower lumbar spine that was exacerbated by movement. Neurologic examination was unremarkable, with normal lower limb strength and sensation, and a negative straight leg–raising test. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 11.3×10^9/L (reference range 4–10×10^9/L), neutrophils 70.5% (40–75%), C-reactive protein 81.04 mg/L (0–10 mg/L), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 61 mm/h (0–15 mm/h), and serum amyloid A >550 mg/L (0–10.08 mg/L). Serum creatinine was 103.5 μmol/L (57–97 μmol/L) and serum uric acid was 557.0 μmol/L (202–416 μmol/L). Computed tomography of the lumbar spine demonstrated erosions in the left L5–S1 facet joint with adjacent soft tissue masses and sclerotic margins. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 1.8×1.1 cm extradural mass at the left L5–S1 facet joint that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed heterogeneous enhancement with gadolinium.

A 51-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of dyspnea and retrosternal chest pressure that had worsened over the past 4 weeks. Two nights before admission, she experienced acute shortness of breath, chest tightness, nocturnal panic attacks, dyspepsia, and general weakness, primarily when lying down. She had no cardiovascular risk factors except a family history of aortic aneurysms; her only surgical history was a remote hysterectomy. Serial ECGs and a stress test were unremarkable. Two weeks earlier, CT of the chest showed no pulmonary embolism, mediastinal pathology, or aortic aneurysm. On admission, blood pressure was 130/70 mmHg, oxygen saturation 97–100%, and ECG was normal. Laboratory studies, including troponin, CK, D-dimer, liver, kidney, and infection markers, were all within normal limits. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated normal left-ventricular function and no valvular abnormalities but revealed external compression of the right ventricle. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a subdiaphragmatic cyst measuring 9 × 7 cm.

A 77-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease (including bypass surgery in 2009), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease on inhaled steroids, dyslipidaemia, and hypertension presented with persistent left-sided chest pain on exertion for one week and mild dyspnoea. On examination, heart and lung sounds were normal. An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm at 79 b.p.m., a right bundle branch block, and isolated ventricular extrasystoles. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) revealed mildly reduced left ventricular systolic function and moderate tricuspid regurgitation. Cardiac biomarkers were elevated (troponin I 22 114 pg/mL [normal < 57 pg/mL], CK 707 U/L [normal < 190 U/L], CK-MB 44 ng/mL [normal < 3.6 ng/mL]), and a diagnosis of non-ST-segment–elevation myocardial infarction was made. Coronary angiography showed stenosis in the proximal and mid–right coronary artery, treated with drug-eluting stent implantation, and an ostial left anterior descending artery stenosis that was left untreated. Post-procedure TTE was normal. On the following day, repeat TTE showed an unidentified mass occluding the right ventricular cavity. Main differential diagnoses were an intraventricular thrombus or an overlooked myocardial tumour such as sarcoma or metastasis. Computed tomography confirmed a mass and demonstrated widening of the ventricular septum to 40 mm.

A 49-year-old man with a 12-year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus on insulin therapy presented with a 3-day history of bilateral proximal upper extremity and upper back pain, weakness, and stiffness. The pain began as moderate in intensity and over one week became excruciating, was associated with swelling, and limited shoulder movement. He denied trauma, abnormal exercise, fever, arthralgia, or skin changes. He had known diabetic neuropathy, nephropathy, peripheral arterial disease with prior right toe amputation, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. He denied tobacco or illicit drug use but reported a 2-year history of heavy alcohol consumption. 

On examination, he was afebrile, blood pressure 98/56 mmHg, pulse 94/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. He was alert and oriented. Fundoscopic exam showed moderate bilateral preproliferative diabetic retinopathy. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. On inspection of the upper extremities, there was nonpitting edema, local tenderness, and induration around the proximal muscles without erythema or crepitus; peripheral pulses were intact and symmetric. Neurologic exam revealed decreased sensation to 10-g monofilament on the plantar aspects of both feet.

Laboratory studies showed: random blood glucose 292 mg/dL; leukocytes 7.1 × 10^3/µL; hemoglobin 12 g/dL; creatinine 1.9 mg/dL; potassium 6.9 mEq/L; CO2 19.9 mEq/L; creatine kinase 225 U/L (normal 60–110 U/L); HbA1c 11.2%; ESR 76 mm/hr; urinalysis with proteinuria. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia with peaked T waves, treated for hyperkalemia. 

Shoulder radiographs showed no fractures or gas but soft-tissue swelling. He was admitted and treated with a one-week course of corticosteroids for suspected polymyositis without improvement. Two weeks after presentation, he developed similar pain and swelling in both thighs while upper-extremity pain began to improve. Venous Doppler of the upper extremities excluded deep venous thrombosis. MRI of the left arm revealed T2-weighted hyperintensity of the deep biceps, brachialis, and brachioradialis muscles with heterogeneous, patchy contrast enhancement.

A 75-year-old woman presented in July 2015 with a 5-month history of irregularities on her Amsler grid. Five months earlier, at a routine visit, visual acuity was 0.6 in the right eye and 0.8 in the left eye, and fundus examination had shown scattered drusen in both eyes. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) at that time had shown no neovascular membrane. 

On return in July, visual acuity remained 0.6 in the right eye. Fundus examination revealed persistent drusen and a small juxtapapillary hemorrhage in the superior temporal arcade of the right eye. OCT now showed subretinal fluid and a pigment epithelial detachment beneath the superior temporal arcade. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated significant pigment epithelial detachments in the perifoveal capillary network during the venous phase but no obvious polypoidal lesions. An indocyanine green angiogram was scheduled to clarify the diagnosis, and intravitreal ranibizumab was begun at 4-week intervals.

A 43-year-old man presented with fever, chills, and headache. One month earlier, he had noted a painless ulcer on the prepuce that was healing when he developed fever and fatigue. Ten days before admission, he developed a disseminated maculopapular rash on the trunk and extremities. He reported multiple unprotected sexual contacts over the past three months. He is a man who has sex with men and was diagnosed with HIV infection 10 years ago; he takes abacavir, lamivudine, darunavir, ritonavir, and dolutegravir with an undetectable viral load and a CD4 count of 1144 cells/μL. One year ago, he was treated with intravenous penicillin G for suspected otosyphilis and had a full clinical and serologic response. 

On examination, he was ill-appearing but not dehydrated. He had painless enlargement of inguinal, axillary, and cervical lymph nodes (up to 3 cm) and a maculopapular rash on the trunk and extremities. He had a headache but no nuchal rigidity or Kernig or Brudzinsky signs.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 63,300/mL with a lymphomonocytic predominance. Blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, and urine specific gravity were within normal limits. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed 19 white cells (95% lymphocytes) with normal glucose and protein concentrations. Blood cultures were repetitively negative.

A 60-year-old woman with a history of anterior myocardial infarction treated with stenting of the proximal left anterior descending artery in September 2018, poorly controlled type II diabetes (HbA1c 9%), and dyslipidemia began experiencing recurrent episodes of syncope in August 2023. On initial evaluation, her cardiorespiratory examination was unremarkable. A 12-lead ECG demonstrated a bifascicular block, and she underwent implantation of a dual-chamber pacemaker with leads positioned in the right atrium and in the interventricular septum targeting the left bundle branch; no cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was performed prior to device implantation.

In February 2024, she was admitted with suspected ST-elevation myocardial infarction after poorly defined chest discomfort, intermittent dyspnea, and syncope. On arrival, she no longer reported chest pain, and the cardiac and pulmonary examination remained normal. ECG revealed a paced ventricular rhythm with narrow QRS complexes, but frequent premature ventricular contractions originating from an anterobasal left ventricular focus were noted. Pacemaker interrogation showed stable parameters compared with those at implantation and did not reveal any sustained ventricular arrhythmias; however, the detection zone was set below the threshold for slow ventricular tachycardia. Review of ambulatory monitoring from August 30–31, 2023, revealed a PVC burden of 21% with episodes of bigeminy and trigeminy. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a preserved left ventricular ejection fraction of 61% with basal and mid anteroseptal hypokinesis. Coronary angiography showed no significant stenoses and a patent stent in the proximal left anterior descending artery. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging identified two areas of late gadolinium enhancement: a subendocardial scar in the basal anterior wall corresponding to the prior infarction and an intramyocardial scar in the mid inferoseptal wall at the site of the pacing lead, consistent with a non-ischaemic pattern.

A 30-year-old otherwise healthy man presented to the emergency department with bilateral flank pain, nausea, and vomiting after regular cocaine use over the preceding 2 to 3 weeks. He took no medications and had no significant past medical history. On examination, his blood pressure was 153/95 mmHg and other vital signs were normal; he had bilateral costovertebral angle tenderness, more pronounced on the right. Laboratory data revealed a leukocyte count of 12.9 K/µL and a serum creatinine of 1.51 mg/dL; hemoglobin, platelets, electrolytes, liver enzymes, and lactate were within normal limits. Intravenous fluids were administered for acute kidney injury, and contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis was performed 65 seconds after injection of 125 mL of iopamidol. Images demonstrated bilateral heterogeneous, mottled, and striated nephrograms with mild symmetric stranding of the perinephric fat; there were no urinary calculi, no collecting-system dilatation, and the renal arteries and veins were widely patent.

A 60-year-old man was referred for a 30-month history of generalized bone pain without trauma or systemic symptoms. He had chronic hepatitis B treated with adefovir dipivoxil (10 mg daily) for 5 years and no family history of nephrolithiasis or metabolic bone disease. Eighteen months after onset of pain, a whole-body bone scan showed multiple areas of increased tracer uptake in bilateral ribs, sacroiliac joints, and tibias, consistent with fractures. Serum intact PTH and tumor markers were normal, and he was diagnosed with osteoporosis and treated with alendronate, calcitriol, and calcium carbonate; his pain improved only slightly after 6 months.

At the referring hospital, laboratory studies revealed a serum phosphate of 0.51 mmol/L (0.8–1.6), calcium 2.01 mmol/L (2.17–2.75), potassium 3.38 mmol/L, and alkaline phosphatase 109 U/L. Urinalysis showed pH 6.5, protein 1+, and glucose 2+. Twenty-four-hour urine studies showed phosphate excretion of 11.0 mmol and calcium excretion of 5.60 mmol. Renal ultrasonography demonstrated stones in both kidneys and left ureteral obstruction with hydronephrosis. Noncontrast CT confirmed bilateral renal stones and left hydronephrosis. A DXA scan showed a femoral neck T-score of −2.60. A bone marrow biopsy was normal. He underwent extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy and ureteral stent placement and discontinued his bone therapy.

A 67-year-old Japanese man, an apple farmer with no significant medical history, was admitted with difficulty moving and a several-day history of right inguinal swelling.  
CT imaging showed a right inguinal incarcerated hernia without signs of bowel obstruction. Manual reduction failed, and he underwent inguinal hernia repair with ileal resection.  
Postoperatively, he was admitted to the ICU for acute kidney injury and tachycardic atrial fibrillation attributed to dehydration; both improved after blood transfusion, and he was transferred to the general ward on postoperative day (POD) 1.  
He developed prolonged ileus managed with fluids and ileus-tube decompression. On POD 8, psychological disturbance prompted a presumptive diagnosis of delirium; mild spasm-like movements were noted but he remained alert with no focal neurologic deficits.  
On the night of POD 9, he was readmitted to the ICU for hypoxemia and difficulty clearing sputum. His respiratory status improved after bronchoscopy, but he then exhibited marked muscle rigidity throughout his body in response to minimal stimuli.  
At ICU readmission, arterial blood gas under 6 L/min O2 showed pH 7.32, PaO2 139 Torr, PaCO2 45 Torr, and base excess –2 mmol/L. He was in sinus tachycardia at 110–120 beats/min.  
Shortly after starting tazobactam–piperacillin, he developed sudden hypotension (systolic blood pressure 40 mmHg), desaturation (SpO2 50%), and a diffuse rash, leading to a diagnosis of anaphylactic shock requiring intubation and continuous intravenous adrenaline (up to 0.15 μg/kg/min).  
On POD 10, adrenaline was weaned, but muscle rigidity worsened with tapering of propofol (2–3 mg/kg/h) and dexmedetomidine (0.4 μg/kg/h), hindering ventilator weaning.  
Blood cultures, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, and electroencephalography were negative. His irritability increased, tidal volumes dropped from 8 to 3 mL/kg, and respiratory rate rose above 25 breaths/min during awakenings.  
He developed labile blood pressure with systolic peaks of 180 mmHg on awakening, managed with noradrenaline (0.1 μg/kg/min). Despite severe rigidity, he remained able to communicate and reported intense pain from muscle stiffness, necessitating repeated propofol boluses.

A 25-year-old woman, gravida 3, presented to the gynecology clinic with 6 weeks of amenorrhea, right lower–quadrant abdominal pain, and vaginal bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed an empty uterine cavity and a gestational sac in the right adnexa without fetal cardiac activity. The serum β-hCG level was 585 mIU/mL. She received intramuscular methotrexate (50 mg/m2) on day 1, with a decline in β-hCG to 19.1 mIU/mL on day 4 and 9.8 mIU/mL on day 7; because of persistent low levels, a second dose of methotrexate was administered.  

Shortly thereafter, she noted pain and swelling in both knees. On examination, she was afebrile and appeared well. Both knees were diffusely swollen and tender to palpation. Laboratory tests revealed a hemoglobin concentration of 12 g/dL, a white-cell count of 13,600/L, and a platelet count of 576,000/L. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 100 mm/h, and the C-reactive protein level was 43 mg/L. A plain radiograph of both knees was unremarkable. Joint ultrasonography revealed anterior soft-tissue swelling with a thickened synovium and fluid collections measuring 1.0×0.9×2 cm in the right knee and 1.1×0.9×1.8 cm in the left.

A 6-year-old boy presented with a 3-month history of recurrent nonproductive cough, occasional resting shortness of breath, and on-and-off fever for 2½ months. On examination, bilateral diffuse wheezing was noted. He was initially treated for bronchial asthma.  
Laboratory studies showed a peripheral eosinophil count >10%; renal and liver function tests and urinalysis were normal. Antinuclear antibody, proteinase-3 ANCA, and myeloperoxidase ANCA were all negative.  
Chest radiography revealed a lobulated opacity in the right hilar region with otherwise normal lung fields. High-resolution CT of the chest showed a soft-tissue density in the right hilum causing narrowing of the right main bronchus. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a heterogeneously enhancing right hilar mass without fat or calcifications.  
Mantoux testing and GeneXpert assay for tuberculosis were both negative.

A 63-year-old Caucasian man, a dentist with a 6-year history of well-controlled hypertension, was referred for vision changes in his left eye secondary to an epiretinal membrane and cataract. His preoperative visual acuity was 20/30; examination showed a ++ nuclear cataract, macular edema on OCT, and epiretinal membrane with microfolds. He underwent phacovitrectomy under general anesthesia without any nerve block.

On postoperative day 1, he was pain-free, visual acuity was 20/50, and examination showed corneal edema, a well-positioned intraocular lens, Tyndall +, and an attached retina. By postoperative day 7, he remained pain-free, visual acuity improved to 20/20, and the retina remained attached.

On postoperative day 20, he awoke with severe eye pain rated 10/10. He described the pain as paroxysmal, lancinating, lasting 10–30 seconds, radiating within the distribution of the first division of the trigeminal nerve on the right side, and triggered by light facial stimulation; there was no contralateral pain. Neurologic examination was intact. Ocular examination revealed visual acuity of 20/20, pseudophakia, and nasal choroidal detachment. Complete blood count and liver function tests were unremarkable. Normal findings on both CT and MRI were reported.

A 62-year-old man of Bangladeshi origin presented with 2 weeks of lethargy, fever, productive cough and weight loss. His medical history included well-controlled ulcerative colitis managed with long-term prednisolone and azathioprine, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia and chronic hepatitis B. He admitted to taking higher than prescribed doses of prednisolone for the preceding 2 months. He had travelled to Bangladesh 6 months earlier without illness.

On examination, his temperature was 34.8 °C; there was a non-tender, erythematous left calf overlying a saphenous vein harvest site. Initial laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 116 g/L, white-cell count 6.2 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 138 mg/L. A lower-limb ultrasound excluded deep venous thrombosis, and CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a rectal mass and a right basal pneumonia.

Empirical intravenous flucloxacillin was started for presumed cellulitis. Over the first week, fever rose to 40 °C, C-reactive protein increased further, and the erythema extended to the scrotum, abdomen, flanks and right leg. Dermatology suggested multifocal cellulitis, panniculitis or migratory thrombophlebitis. A tender right testicle prompted ultrasound confirmation of epididymo-orchitis, and oral ciprofloxacin with doxycycline was added. Despite broadening to ceftriaxone, linezolid and amikacin, vasculitic, autoimmune and sexual-health screens (including HIV, chlamydia, gonorrhea and mycoplasma serology) were negative; blood cultures and echocardiography were unrevealing.

On day 12 he was admitted to intensive care for ventilatory support and noradrenaline for septic shock, and antibiotics were changed to meropenem and linezolid. No necrotizing fasciitis was seen by surgical teams. He remained febrile, developed coagulopathy and bloody diarrhea, and on day 15 a skin biopsy was performed. A rectal biopsy showed CMV inclusion bodies with plasma CMV DNA of 15 304 copies/mL; ganciclovir (later switched to foscarnet) was given, but the rash progressed. Empirical fluconazole and then micafungin were added for Candida in the urine without cutaneous improvement. On day 28, histopathology of the skin biopsy demonstrated septal/lobar panniculitis, and methenamine silver staining revealed small, round yeasts of 3–5 µm within well-circumscribed areas of inflammation in the dermis and subcutaneous fat.

A 3-year-old spayed British Shorthair and a 1-year-old neutered Maine Coon were each referred for evaluation of focal skin lesions. 

British Shorthair: A round, well-demarcated, exudative area of complete alopecia and intense erythema was noted immediately adjacent to the left orbit. Surrounding desquamation was present but inconspicuous under the coat. The owner first noticed the lesion 3 days earlier; the cat was pruritic and groomed the area excessively. The cat is indoor-only, was taken to a country house in summer where it hunted rodents, was dewormed once at 2 months of age, and received a single vaccination series.

Maine Coon: An ill-defined red macule with branny scale was observed on the ventral tail, equidistant from its base and tip. The hair was sparse and thinned, with no characteristic broken “stipes.” The lesion appeared 2 days before presentation. The cat lives indoors with two regularly walked dogs, has been dewormed biannually, and had a prior episode of feline viral rhinotracheitis.

Neither cat had prior treatments for dermatophytosis. On day 0, hairs and skin scrapings were collected from the lesion margins after cleansing with 70% alcohol. Samples were cultured on standard medium at 28 °C for 10–14 days, yielding colonies with pronounced zonality—fluffy at the periphery and powdery in the center—reminiscent of Microsporum canis. A luminescent (Wood’s lamp) examination did not confirm M. canis infection.

A 50-year-old Iranian woman was admitted for surgery to treat abnormal uterine bleeding. Over the preceding three months she had lost 10 kg, with anorexia, night sweats, nausea, vomiting, and intermittent fever and cough. Her only past medical history was primary biliary cirrhosis treated with ursodeoxycholic acid. On admission she was febrile. Initial laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 8700/mm³, hemoglobin 8.3 g/dL, C-reactive protein 95 mg/L (normal < 6 mg/L), glucose 190 mg/dL, and sodium 130 mmol/L. HIV testing was negative. Chest CT demonstrated bilateral pleural effusions, diffuse ground-glass opacities, and small centrilobular nodules. Sputum acid-fast bacilli were positive, and she was started on isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide. Three days later she underwent hysterectomy. 

On postoperative day 1 she became disoriented, had impaired awareness, and exhibited bizarre behavior. By the next day she was unresponsive. Neurologic examination revealed no neck stiffness or focal signs; cranial nerves were intact, and she moved all limbs symmetrically without convulsions. One week after starting anti-tuberculosis therapy a lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 25 cm H₂O, 0 leukocytes, protein 36.1 mg/dL, and glucose 57 mg/dL (blood glucose 130 mg/dL). CSF PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis was negative, but nested PCR was positive; adenosine deaminase was 32.4 IU/L (normal < 10 IU/L). 

Electroencephalography revealed generalized 1.5–2 Hz continuous sharp and slow-wave activity, which improved markedly after intravenous diazepam and normalized with further antiepileptic treatment. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated multiple ring-enhancing lesions at the subcortical white–gray matter junction in both supra- and infratentorial regions. On T1-weighted images the lesions were isointense; on T2-weighted images they showed central low signal with surrounding vasogenic edema.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of pustular skin lesions on the shoulders, axillae, flanks, and upper arms, accompanied by a burning sensation. She reported unintentional weight loss but denied night sweats, joint pain, or pleuritic pain. Her medical history included cirrhosis and chronic pain; she had no personal history of dermatologic conditions but a family history of psoriasis. On examination, there were multiple erythematous papules and flaccid pustules with visible fluid levels, as well as desquamated areas with geographic and serpiginous borders in the affected regions. Two punch biopsies were performed on the left shoulder. Laboratory studies showed:  
- ANA negative at 1:80, rheumatoid factor <10 IU/mL, ENA panel negative, and anti-skin antibody panels (including basement membrane and intercellular antibodies) negative at 1:10  
- Elevated IgA level of 4.67 g/L; total protein 87 g/L; alpha-2-globulin 10.7 g/L; beta globulin 13.7 g/L; gamma globulin 15.1 g/L; normal albumin and alpha-1-globulin  
- Negative hepatitis A, B, and C serologies; normal G6PD screen  
- Creatinine 105 µmol/L; AST and ALT within normal limits  
- Hemoglobin 114 g/L; leukocyte count 15.74 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 11.07 × 10^9/L; platelets 482 × 10^9/L  
Histological examination revealed superficial perivascular dermatitis and subcorneal pustules. Histological features suggesting psoriasis were not identified.

A 64-year-old white English man presented with a one-year history of a lump behind his right ankle. He denied pain, trauma (violent or repeated), or other symptoms. His medical history included diet-controlled type II diabetes mellitus and gout; he had no history of tobacco use and was not on antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy. On examination, there was a 3×3 cm non-tender, non-pulsatile mass just posterior to the right medial malleolus. Peripheral pulses were normal bilaterally, and no other aneurysms were detected on clinical review. A Doppler ultrasound study revealed a 1.4 cm aneurysm of the posterior tibial artery with a mural thrombus; the proximal and distal segments of the posterior tibial artery, the anterior tibial artery, and the popliteal artery were normal.

A 28-year-old Japanese man was admitted in November 2016 with a 1-week history of fever up to 40.0°C. He had dermatomyositis treated with prednisolone (50 mg daily since October 2014, tapered to 10 mg daily by October 2016). He was a never-smoker with no history of trauma or family lung disease. On examination his temperature was 37.6°C, heart rate 80 beats/min, blood pressure 117/64 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Respiratory sounds were diminished over the right lower lung field. Dermatomyositis findings (facial erythema, Gottron-like eruption, Raynaud phenomenon of the fingers) were unchanged from baseline. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 6400/µL, C-reactive protein 10.79 mg/dL, creatine kinase 62 IU/L, interferon-gamma–release assay for M. tuberculosis negative, anti–Mycobacterium avium complex antibody negative, β-D glucan normal, and C7-HRP negative. Chest radiograph and CT revealed a right pleural effusion without pulmonary infiltrates or lymphadenopathy. Thoracentesis yielded purulent pale-yellow fluid with 1995 cells/µL (54% lymphocytes), total protein 5.5 g/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 1919 IU/L, and no organisms on bacterial culture or Ziehl–Neelsen staining. One week later, the pleural-fluid adenosine deaminase level was 132.7 U/L.

A 58‐year‐old man presented with a 1‐month history of diarrhea, fever, weight loss, and pruritus. He had a history of orthotopic liver transplantation 12 years earlier and type 2 diabetes managed with tacrolimus and oral hypoglycemic agents. On examination, he was icteric and emaciated. Laboratory studies showed a total bilirubin of 15.9 mg/dL (direct 8.3, indirect 7.6), an alkaline phosphatase level of 2052 U/L, and mildly elevated gamma‐glutamyltransferase and aminotransferases. Viral serologies were negative. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated marked dilatation of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts and occlusion of the hepatic artery. MR imaging confirmed the arterial occlusion and showed peripheral hepatic infarcts. He underwent biliary drainage and received antibiotics for cholangiolitic abscesses, with transient improvement, but continued to have impaired liver function and recurrent episodes of cholangitis.

An 84-year-old man presented with progressive exertional dyspnoea 3 years after surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) with a 19 mm bioprosthetic valve for severe aortic stenosis. His medical history included hypertension and hyperuricaemia managed without medication. Preoperative echocardiography had shown an annulus diameter of 19 mm; a 19 mm valve was implanted after a 21 mm sizer would not pass through the annulus, yielding an effective orifice area index of 0.97 cm2/m2 in a patient with body surface area (BSA) 1.52 m2.

On postoperative day 11, transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) showed a trans-prosthetic peak velocity of 3.0 m/s and a mean pressure gradient (PG) of 20.8 mmHg. Two years later, TTE demonstrated a peak velocity of 4.7 m/s and mean PG of 54 mmHg but no paravalvular leakage. The patient was treated with oral furosemide and spironolactone, yet his dyspnoea progressed.

At readmission, he had a harsh systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border, bilateral lung crackles, and mild leg oedema. His weight was 46 kg (BSA 1.41 m2), heart rate 124 b.p.m., blood pressure 134/98 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 93% on 2 L oxygen. He was New York Heart Association Functional Class III. Chest radiograph showed bilateral pulmonary congestion. Blood tests revealed normal renal function and a brain natriuretic peptide level of 1236 pg/mL. TTE now showed a left ventricular ejection fraction decreased from 63% to 45%.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) revealed hypertrophic tissue overhanging the bioprosthetic aortic valve leaflets.

An 8-year-old African boy presented with a 3-month history of progressive left flank pain, malaise, and dysuria. He denied fever, anorexia, vomiting, or bowel symptoms. His history was notable for nephrolithiasis and multiple treated urinary tract infections. On examination, there was left-sided lower abdominal distension with percussion tenderness. Vital signs were: blood pressure 106/69 mmHg, pulse 98/min, temperature 37.8 °C, SpO₂ 96%. He had albinism, no pallor or lymphadenopathy, and the remainder of the exam was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL, ESR 28 mm/h, white-cell count 6.13 × 10⁹/L, creatinine 94 μmol/L, AST 40.6 U/L, ALT 11 U/L. Urinalysis revealed 10–15 WBCs/HPF but sterile culture. Chest radiograph was normal. Renal ultrasound showed an enlarged left kidney (13 × 9 cm) with a tumorous appearance. Contrast CT of the abdomen revealed a complex left renal mass with a hypodense fluid component and peripheral hyperdense calcifications, entirely within the renal capsule, associated retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly; the right kidney was normal. The CT impression was clear cell sarcoma of the left kidney with calcification, with differential diagnoses of congenital mesoblastic nephroma and cystic nephroblastoma.

A 26-year-old previously healthy woman presented with a 6-month history of papules and nodules on her right arm. Despite a short course of systemic antibiotics early in the course, the lesions enlarged and spread to her forearm, hand, and fingers. The patient denied fever, prior illnesses, immunosuppressive medications, or cat exposure. She reported severe pruritus of the lesions and occasional bleeding. On examination, there were multiple tender, erythematous, angiomatous papules and nodules in a grouped distribution on the extensor aspect of the right arm and hand, each measuring 1–2 cm in diameter. Painful right axillary lymphadenopathy was noted. The remainder of her skin, mucous membranes, and systemic examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory studies, including a CD4 count, were within normal limits, and HIV ELISA testing was negative.

A 39-year-old African American woman with a 2-month history of systemic lupus erythematosus (class III and V lupus nephritis on prednisone, mycophenolate, and hydroxychloroquine) was brought to the emergency department with a 1-week history of lethargy, progressive confusion, and a generalized rash over both lower extremities. Two months earlier, she had presented with left lower quadrant pain and nonbloody diarrhea and was found to have photosensitive facial rash, proteinuria, pedal edema, and pancytopenia; a renal biopsy then confirmed proliferative and membranous lupus nephritis.

On examination, temperature was 97.5°F, pulse 102/min, blood pressure 136/79 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 22/min. The oral mucosa was dry without lesions; the neck was supple. The skin was warm, with a nonblanching, erythematous, desquamating rash from hip to ankles, and the Nikolsky sign was positive. The abdomen was soft with mild epigastric tenderness; there was bilateral pitting pedal edema. Neurologically, she was arousable to verbal and tactile stimulation and moved all extremities. There was no organomegaly.

Laboratory studies showed severe pancytopenia and marked metabolic acidosis. She received 2 units of packed red blood cells and 6 units of platelets. She developed hypotension, was given intravenous fluids, and sepsis was suspected; broad-spectrum antibiotics were initiated.
