Portable chest radiography revealed right basilar atelectasis, and a portable X-ray of the lower extremities showed soft-tissue edema.

A 30-year-old man, with a living-related kidney transplant 7 years earlier for end-stage renal disease of unknown etiology, was found on routine follow-up to have rising serum creatinine and nephrotic-range proteinuria. His native kidney disease had been undetermined despite a prior biopsy in adolescence. He had immediate graft function posttransplant and was maintained on tacrolimus, azathioprine, and prednisolone; trough tacrolimus levels were therapeutic. On evaluation, serum creatinine was 2.7 mg/dL. Urinalysis showed heavy proteinuria, with a spot protein/creatinine ratio of 8. Complement levels were normal; antinuclear antibody, HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C serologies were negative. A transplant kidney biopsy revealed global sclerosis in more than half of glomeruli, mesangial hypercellularity with matrix expansion in all viable glomeruli, segmental endocapillary hypercellularity in two glomeruli, and segmental sclerosis in four. Immunofluorescence demonstrated smudged granular positivity for IgG (3+) and C3 (2+) in capillary loops and mesangium, without light-chain restriction. Immunohistochemical staining for DNAJB9 was positive.

A 56-year-old Japanese woman with a 5-year history of chronic upper abdominal pain and discomfort presented to the emergency department with sudden severe epigastric pain. One day before presentation, she had mild epigastric pain that resolved spontaneously; two hours before arrival the pain recurred after defecation, was severe, and waxed and waned. She also reported sweating but denied chest pain, back pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, melena, or hematochezia. Her medical history included well-controlled hyperlipidemia treated with omeprazole, domperidone, and rosuvastatin. She had no history of recent trauma, never smoked, and consumed alcohol occasionally. On admission, temperature was 35.4°C, blood pressure 115/74 mm Hg, heart rate 63/min, and respiratory rate 28/min. She was in acute distress; examination revealed epigastric tenderness without peritoneal signs. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis, elevated liver enzymes, and hyperlactatemia (white blood cell count 14 200/mm3; aspartate transaminase 792 IU/L; alanine transaminase 682 IU/L; lactate 3.29 mmol/L). Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen demonstrated a retroperitoneal hemorrhage surrounding the pancreas and duodenum and focal narrowing of the celiac artery.

A 19-year-old woman was evaluated for recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding since early childhood. Soon after birth, she underwent repeated resections of vascular skin tumors on the right thoracic wall. At age 4, she developed persistent anemia and positive fecal occult blood tests; colonoscopy revealed a vascular malformation in the right colon. At age 5, exploratory laparotomy identified one lesion on the lesser curvature of the stomach, seven in the small intestine, one at the hepatic flexure of the colon, and one in the liver; the small intestinal lesions were resected, and pathology showed cavernous hemangiomas. Four months later, she suffered superior mesenteric artery thrombosis requiring partial small-bowel resection. Thereafter, mild anemia was managed with oral iron for 10 years. At age 15, her hemoglobin decreased to 7–8 g/dL. Capsule and double-balloon endoscopy, along with contrast-enhanced CT, demonstrated numerous venous malformations in the stomach, duodenum, jejunum, ileum, and colon, as well as lesions in the right pleural space, hepatic hilum, liver, and spleen; a right ovarian cyst was also noted. Despite β-blocker therapy, by age 18 her hemoglobin fell to 4 g/dL with ongoing bleeding requiring frequent transfusions. Recent CT shows enlargement of her known lesions.

A 51-year-old woman presented with a two-week history of progressive left breast swelling and tenderness that began just before her menstrual period. She was a nonsmoker with regular menses, no prior breast disease, trauma, implants, medications, or foreign travel; family history was notable only for a grandmother with breast cancer at age 78.  
On examination, the upper half of the left breast was red, indurated, and swollen, extending to the nipple; there was no nipple discharge, axillary lymphadenopathy, or fever.  
A mammogram was normal (M1), and ultrasonography showed nonspecific inflammatory changes without focal lesions (U3). Core needle biopsy revealed chronic mastitis with mixed inflammatory lobulitis, fat necrosis, and fibrosis but no vasculitis or malignancy (B2).  
Laboratory tests, including full blood count, renal and liver function, thyroid function, and glucose, were within normal limits.  
She was treated sequentially with oral flucloxacillin and co-amoxiclav, but after two weeks her breast findings worsened, with increased swelling, induration, cellulitis, and a discharging sinus. Fluid from the sinus grew no bacteria, including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.  
High-dose oral flucloxacillin was started, and three weeks after presentation, ultrasound identified two loculated fluid collections. Outpatient incision and drainage was performed, and specimens were sent for routine bacterial, acid-fast, Gram, and fungal cultures. Routine cultures remained sterile, and she was started on intravenous flucloxacillin and oral rifampicin.  
After two more weeks, the cellulitis improved but multiple sinuses persisted, and ultrasound showed multiloculated abscesses. Five weeks after presentation, she underwent surgical incision and drainage with drain placement; histology again showed chronic mastitis with granuloma formation and no malignancy.

A 68-year-old man with a history of severe COVID-19 (75% pulmonary involvement treated with remdesivir) received his first dose of the Sinopharm (BBIBP-CorV) COVID-19 vaccine without complication. One month later, he received the second dose. Three days after the second injection, he developed edema of the left foot and ankle, which progressed to involve the entire left leg. Color-Doppler sonography (CDS) showed extensive soft-tissue swelling and fat edema in both legs, suggesting a lymphatic drainage disorder, with no evidence of clot or deep vein thrombosis and normal flow in the popliteal and femoral veins; a small Baker’s cyst was noted in the right popliteal fossa. Five days later, he developed similar edema, redness, and warmth in the right foot and ankle. Examination revealed bilateral pitting edema confined below the knees, without ischemia, ecchymosis, arthritis, or trauma; distal pulses were normal. He had no history of diabetes, heart disease, hypertension, thyroid disease, rheumatologic disease, or prior DVT. He was active and otherwise healthy. A vascular surgeon suspected lymphangitis and cellulitis and prescribed oral levofloxacin 500 mg daily for 2 weeks. Laboratory tests showed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 68 mm/h and a positive C-reactive protein; albumin was 3.9 g/dL. Complete blood count, liver and kidney function tests, thyroid function tests, rheumatoid factors, and echocardiography were all normal. Repeat CDS again showed no deep vein thrombosis, no varicose veins, all veins compressible, no arterial obstruction, and persistent subcutaneous edema of the ankles and feet. After 2 weeks of levofloxacin, aspirin, and apixaban, the redness and warmth resolved but the bilateral leg edema remained unchanged.

A 53-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and obstructive sleep apnea presented with acute right lower extremity pain. Arterial duplex and angiography revealed thrombosis of the right superficial femoral and popliteal arteries, and he underwent an uncomplicated thrombectomy. He denied any preceding chest pain or other cardiac or neurologic symptoms. He had no history of coronary artery disease, peripheral arterial disease, trauma, hypercoagulability, or malignancy, but reported several days of intense emotional stress before presentation. On examination, cardiac findings were normal. Electrocardiography showed nonspecific ST–T wave abnormalities. Laboratory studies, including cardiac troponin levels, were within normal limits. On hospital day 1, transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated left ventricular apical akinesis, an ejection fraction of 40 to 45%, and a large (2.4 × 2.0 cm), pedunculated, mobile apical mass suggestive of thrombus. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging on day 2 confirmed a large apical left ventricular thrombus. Coronary angiography revealed only luminal irregularities without obstructive disease.

A 59-year-old man presented with a 40-year history of stiffness, swelling, and pain affecting his neck, back, and bilateral hips (right hip worse than left). Over the past four years, these symptoms have worsened. He also reports pain in his knees, ankles, shoulders, and interphalangeal joints. Climbing stairs and rising from a seated position aggravate his pain; relief is obtained with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), continuous movement, yoga, and meditation. He has intermittent constipation and disturbed sleep due to pain.

His medical history includes:
• Ankylosing spondylitis diagnosed at age 27, with HLA-B27 positivity.  
• Long-term use of low-dose steroids, NSAIDs, a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (sulfasalazine), and a proton-pump inhibitor.  
• Hypothyroidism diagnosed in 2017, currently on levothyroxine.  
• No notable family history beyond a mother with unspecified arthritis.  
• Reports work-related stress and anxiety related to chronic pain.

On examination, he is overweight (BMI 29.0). The skin over his joints is normal; there is no soft-tissue swelling or synovial thickening. Neck muscle spasm is present without wasting. Deep palpation of the cervical spine elicits tenderness and pain on motion. He has a forward-bent posture with limited lateral flexion and rotation of the neck, scoliosis, and kyphosis. Both knees and hips are tender (right > left) with crepitation, but there is no effusion. He ambulates without aids, demonstrating a short-striding gait. Sacroiliac joint tenderness is noted.
  
Laboratory studies reveal HLA-B27 positivity. Early inflammatory markers and hemoglobin are pending.

A 33-year-old man presented with progressive low back pain that did not improve with symptomatic pharmacotherapy. He had no significant past medical history. On admission, he reported reduced touch sensation in both lower limbs, more pronounced in the right leg, and diffuse paresthesia in the L2–L3 dermatomal distribution. Neurologic examination revealed marked weakness (Medical Research Council grade 3/5 in the left leg and 4/5 in the right leg) with present, though diminished, deep-tendon reflexes. Anal sphincter insufficiency and urinary retention were also noted. No other neurologic deficits were observed.  
Magnetic resonance imaging of the entire spine demonstrated a 16 × 10 × 15 mm intradural cystic lesion at the L2–L3 level involving the conus medullaris. The lesion was homogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images. A solid nodule in the posterior part of the cyst did not enhance after gadolinium administration.

A 60-year-old woman with chronic hepatitis B, schizophrenia, and a history of left nephrectomy presented with acute abdominal pain. On examination, she had low abdominal tenderness with rebound pain and hypoactive bowel sounds. Laboratory results showed a white-cell count of 9.65×10^3/µL with 74.7% neutrophils. Abdominal sonography demonstrated ileus and stool impaction. CT scan revealed a sigmoid colon perforation with pneumoperitoneum. She underwent an emergent Hartmann procedure, and a perforated sigmoid colon with fecal contamination was resected. Grossly, the resected colon measured 24.2 cm with a 4.1×2.5 cm perforation. The serosa was coated with fecal material; on sectioning, no polyp, diverticulum, or tumor was identified, and there was focal thinning of the colonic wall around the perforation.

A 53-year-old man with hypertension and dyslipidemia presented with transient attacks of left monocular blindness on 19 Feb 2021, with complete recovery 2 days later. He denied other symptoms. His medications included atorvastatin and candesartan. He was a tobacco smoker. On examination, he was alert and oriented; blood pressure was 158/93 mm Hg and other vital signs were stable. Cardiac and neurological examinations were unremarkable. ECG showed sinus rhythm. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed normal chamber sizes, mildly impaired left ventricular diastolic function, and an ejection fraction of 60–65%. Carotid Doppler ultrasonography and contrast-enhanced cerebral CT angiography were negative for stenosis, atherosclerotic changes, or occlusions. Brain MRI demonstrated chronic ischemic periventricular changes without acute infarction. Laboratory tests, including coagulation profile, inflammatory markers, and blood cultures, were normal.

An 18-year-old Iranian woman was admitted with a 2-week history of anorexia and yellow discoloration of the conjunctiva and urine. She had been taking tofacitinib, 5 mg daily, for treatment of alopecia areata for the past 5 months and reported no use of other medications, alcohol, or toxins.

On examination, she was icteric but hemodynamically stable. Initial laboratory tests showed:  
• Total bilirubin 16.4 mg/dL (normal 0.3–1), direct bilirubin 6.3 mg/dL (normal 0.1–0.3)  
• Serum transaminases elevated: SGOT 1179 IU/mL (normal 7–55), SGPT 960 IU/mL (normal 8–48)  
• Alkaline phosphatase 398 IU/mL (normal 40–129)  
• Normal blood cell counts  
• Prothrombin time 14.9 s (normal 11–13.5), INR 1.43 (normal 0.8–1.1)  

Three months after starting tofacitinib, routine labs showed SGOT 335 IU/mL, SGPT 414 IU/mL, and ALP 253 IU/mL. At the end of month 4, she stopped tofacitinib, and within days developed anorexia and icteric sclera. Repeat labs revealed SGOT 1239 IU/mL, SGPT 805 IU/mL, ALP 198 IU/mL, total bilirubin 8.42 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 7.15 mg/dL, PT 17.7 s, INR 1.34, and normal blood counts. She was diagnosed with drug hepatitis and hospitalized.

During the first week, liver dysfunction progressed, with INR rising toward acute liver failure. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a normal‐sized liver with reduced echogenicity, periportal echogenicity, and gallbladder wall thickening; the portal vein measured 8 mm with peak hepatorenal flow velocity of 15 cm/s. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a uniformly normal liver parenchyma without masses, normal bile ducts, and thickened gallbladder wall. Echocardiography was unremarkable. MRCP revealed normal intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts without stenosis, dilatation, or filling defects, with a contracted gallbladder and mild periportal edema.

A 46-year-old African American man was referred for treatment of gingival recession on the facial aspect of the mandibular left canine. His medical history was unremarkable. Clinical examination revealed approximately 3 mm of Miller Class I gingival recession and less than 1 mm of attached gingiva on the tooth. Periodontal diagnosis was plaque-induced gingivitis, for which he had received prophylaxis. 

He underwent a subepithelial connective tissue graft (SCTG) under local anesthesia. A full-thickness envelope flap was elevated, and connective tissue was harvested from the ipsilateral palatal premolar area. The graft was secured at the recipient site and partially covered by the flap. Hemostasis was achieved, and the patient was discharged with analgesic and antimicrobial rinse prescriptions and standard postoperative instructions.

At the 1-week postoperative visit, healing was within normal limits, and the patient was asymptomatic. At 3 weeks, examination revealed an asymptomatic, slightly indurated, 5 mm swelling at the mesioapical corner of the recipient site. The overlying tissue appeared normal, no drainage was present, the tooth tested vital, and radiographs showed no change from baseline. 

At the 6-week postoperative visit, the lesion persisted and had slightly increased in size.

A 74-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer, carotid atherosclerosis, hypertension, and a 40-pack-year smoking history presented with a 5-month history of postprandial abdominal pain and vomiting associated with a 10-kg weight loss. Physical examination showed sarcopenia and tenderness in the epigastrium without guarding or rebound; examination of the heart, lungs, and extremities was unremarkable. Laboratory studies revealed vitamin D deficiency and a modest elevation in transaminases; other values, including pancreatic enzymes, were within normal limits. An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated gallbladder calculi without signs of acute cholecystitis. Because of her oncologic history, an esophagogastroduodenoscopy was performed; it showed diffuse gastric mucosal hyperemia, multiple ulcers with signs of recent bleeding, and no mass lesions. Histopathology revealed chronic active gastritis with negative staining for Helicobacter pylori, and the patient denied any use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Subsequently, contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen revealed marked atherosclerotic disease of the abdominal aorta with aneurysmal dilations infrarenally and significant stenoses of the celiac artery and superior mesenteric artery.

A 72-year-old woman with a history of scleroderma, previously treated with azathioprine and low-dose steroids, presented with frequent urination. Two months after transurethral resection of a Grade 3 pT1 plus pTis urothelial carcinoma, she underwent intravesical administration of 80 mg BCG (Tokyo 172 strain) after discontinuing azathioprine 2 months and steroids 2 days earlier due to stable scleroderma (baseline KL-6 level, 651 U/mL).

The day after BCG instillation, she noted urinary frequency, gross hematuria, low-grade fever, and oxygen desaturation. Five days later, she developed dyspnea at rest. Chest CT showed scattered frosted-glass opacities centered on the pulmonary hila in the upper lung fields, along with known interstitial changes in the lower lung fields attributed to scleroderma.

On day 7 after BCG, her respiratory status worsened: SpO2 fell below 90% on 15 L/min of oxygen, arterial blood gas analysis revealed a PaO2 of 55.6 mmHg and PaCO2 of 34.0 mmHg, and KL-6 remained at 621 U/mL. She was intubated with a working diagnosis of drug-induced interstitial pneumonia.

A 12-month-old boy was referred for failure to thrive. He was born to consanguineous parents with a birth weight of 3.4 kg but gained only to 6 kg by 12 months. He had held his head at 6 months and sat at 9 months. He had 8–9 bowel movements per day, sometimes steatorrheic. No similar family history was reported.

On examination, growth parameters were below the 5th percentile; the only abnormal finding was widened fontanels. There was no organomegaly. 

Laboratory studies revealed:
- Cholesterol 43 mg/dL, triglycerides 6 mg/dL  
- ALT 17 U/L, AST 60 U/L  
- Total protein 5 g/dL, albumin 3.8 g/dL  
- Stool fat droplets:  +  (< 40 drops/HPF)  
- TSH 6.5 mIU/L, T4 135 nmol/L (consistent with subclinical hypothyroidism)  
- Sweat chloride test normal  

Abdominal ultrasound showed normal liver and spleen but multiple small kidney stones. Brain MRI revealed an intraventricular cyst. Wrist radiograph demonstrated osteopenia and a bone age of ~2 months. Retinal examination was normal.

Upper endoscopy showed normal esophageal and gastric mucosa but a “snow-like” appearance in the duodenal bulb. Duodenal biopsy demonstrated tall villi, fine vacuolation of enterocytes, mild lymphoplasmacytic and eosinophilic infiltration (3–16 cells/HPF), and edema of the lamina propria.

A 41-year-old man with no vascular risk factors presented with acute stuttering right upper extremity weakness and paresthesias, mild slurred speech, and right facial droop. He reported intermittent right arm numbness and tingling over the past month and denied trauma. His past history was notable for rectal bleeding; he took no medications. Family history was negative for neurologic or hematologic disease.

On examination, he was afebrile, blood pressure was 139/82 mm Hg, and heart rate was 54 beats/min regular. Conjunctival pallor was noted, and stool testing was hemoccult-positive. Neurologic examination yielded an NIH Stroke Scale score of 2 (mild right lower facial droop and right upper extremity pronator drift). 

Noncontrast head CT revealed an old right frontal wedge-shaped embolic infarct. CT angiography of the head and neck showed a 1.5 × 0.8 cm thrombus adhering to the wall of the left common carotid artery 4 cm proximal to the bifurcation without evidence of atherosclerosis or dissection. Brain MRI demonstrated acute and subacute cortical infarcts in the left middle cerebral artery territory and the old right frontal embolic infarct.

Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 6200/μL, hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, hematocrit 30.8%, mean corpuscular volume 59.6 fL, and platelets 355,000/μL. Peripheral smear revealed red blood cell hypochromia and microcytosis. Iron studies were consistent with severe iron-deficiency anemia (serum iron 14 μg/dL, ferritin 2.1 ng/mL, total iron-binding capacity 480 μg/dL, transferrin saturation 3%). He had mild hyperlipidemia.

Additional testing—including comprehensive hypercoagulable and rheumatologic panels; chemistry panels; hemoglobin A1C; urine drug screen; serum protein electrophoresis; prothrombin time; partial thromboplastin time; electrocardiogram; chest radiograph; transesophageal echocardiography; lower-extremity venous Doppler; pelvic magnetic resonance venography; and CT of the abdomen and pelvis—did not reveal thrombophilia, cardiac or venous thrombus sources, rheumatologic disease, or malignancy. The severe iron-deficiency anemia was attributed to a gastrointestinal source.

A 4½-year-old boy was brought in because of constant peer harassment due to his “old man” appearance and bleeding from his upper right and left posterior teeth during brushing. His mother reported that his primary teeth had always shown abnormal color and continuous chipping of the tooth structure; he denied pain or sensitivity. He was born at term with normal developmental milestones. There was no history of bone fragility, systemic illness, or drug use. His mother has a diagnosis of Shields type II dentinogenesis imperfecta and has worn an overdenture for 6 years.

On extraoral examination, the child had an edentulous appearance with loss of vertical dimension of occlusion, decreased lower facial height, a prognathic profile, and diminished lip support. Intraorally, all deciduous teeth were attrited to the gingival level; teeth 54, 64, 81, 51, and 61 appeared as mobile root stumps. All remaining teeth were yellow-brown and translucent.

Panoramic and intraoral periapical radiographs showed bulbous crowns with marked cervical constriction of teeth 55, 65, 74, 75, 84, and 85; total obliteration of pulp chambers and root canals of 52, 62, 71, 72, and 82; partial obliteration in the other teeth; and apical resorption with periapical radiolucencies at the root stumps. Developing permanent tooth buds were present, and the dental age matched the chronological age.

A 20-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of worsening bloody diarrhea, crampy abdominal pain, and a 4-kg weight loss. On examination he was hemodynamically stable, with mild tenderness in the left lower quadrant. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL, hematocrit 33.5%, platelets 568,000/mm3, iron level 25 µg/dL, and normal C-reactive protein; stool studies were negative. Colonoscopy revealed left-sided colitis with marked erythema, loss of vascular pattern, friability, and erosions (Mayo score 2); biopsy showed chronic active colitis consistent with ulcerative colitis. He was treated with oral and topical 5-ASA without response, then high-dose corticosteroids with improvement and relapse during taper. Infliximab was initiated but after 4 months there was persistent bloody diarrhea and severe iron-deficiency anemia; repeat colonoscopy showed severe inflammation with deep ulcerations and multiple pseudopolyps at the splenic flexure and distal left colon, and biopsies showed chronic active colitis without cytomegalovirus. He was switched to adalimumab plus azathioprine, with partial relief of diarrhea but ongoing nocturnal colicky pain; adalimumab dosing was increased. Two months later he had severe colicky pain, distension, and weight loss. A colonoscopy showed complete mucosal healing but two large polypoid lesions—one in the left colon and one obstructing at the splenic flexure; biopsies revealed chronic inflammation with architectural distortion and crypt abscesses. Abdominal CT confirmed two large polypoid masses causing obstruction at the splenic flexure.

A 34-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, and a history of mitral valve replacement on chronic warfarin therapy presented with right breast pain. Ten days earlier, she had received antibiotics at an outside hospital for similar pain. On arrival, her INR was 7.0, and she was found to be in diabetic ketoacidosis with an acute kidney injury. 

On examination, there was a tender, firm, immobile mass at the 8 o’clock position of the right breast with overlying skin ulceration, erythema, scabbing, blistering, and peeling. The nipple was eroded. No axillary lymphadenopathy was noted.

Laboratory studies showed calcium 8.8 mg/dL (8.6–10.6), phosphorus 6.8 mg/dL (2.5–4.5), BUN 105 mg/dL (6–20), and creatinine 6.89 mg/dL (baseline ~6.30).

Surgical Oncology recommended a diagnostic mammogram and breast ultrasound to evaluate for a possible breast abscess versus Paget’s disease. The bilateral mammogram demonstrated extensive vascular calcifications and additional amorphous calcifications throughout the right breast with asymmetric, slightly increased density; no discrete mass was seen. Right breast ultrasound revealed an irregular, hypoechoic, suspicious mass with indistinct margins in the subareolar region extending to the nipple, measuring 7.4 × 3.7 × 7.3 cm. On clinical inspection, the breast appeared hard with extensive skin ulceration, mimicking an advanced malignancy.

A 33-year-old woman presented with episodic burning pain and flushing of her face, ears, upper chest, and occasionally her upper extremities. She provided photographs showing bright erythema extending from her lower neck to her face and scalp. Episodes were precipitated by lying down or exposure to warm temperatures and were relieved by cooling; she maintained her home at 60°F. There was no family history of similar symptoms.  

The patient’s symptoms began in 2001 and progressively worsened over several years. At presentation, she experienced multiple daily episodes, each lasting from minutes to hours, which interfered with her ability to work.  

Physical examination during episodes showed normal vital signs except for a core temperature of 94°–95°F. She had dry skin, diffuse blanching erythema over her face, and nail dystrophy (loss of the fingernails).  

Laboratory studies included a normal comprehensive metabolic panel and complete blood count with differential. Thyroid studies revealed a low free thyroxine level and mildly elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone; treatment with levothyroxine did not alter her symptoms. Approximately one year after symptom onset, she developed oligomenorrhea that progressed to amenorrhea; hormonal evaluation showed low estradiol with elevated luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone. Ovarian ultrasound and pituitary MRI were normal. An autoimmune panel, including antiperoxidase, anti-adrenal, anti-ovarian, gastric parietal, antinuclear, anti-Smith, and anti-DNA antibodies, was negative. Serum tryptase was mildly elevated. Skin biopsy showed nonspecific changes. Bone marrow biopsy was normal, excluding systemic mastocytosis and myeloproliferative disorders.  

She underwent trials of antihistamines with a mast cell stabilizer, high-dose corticosteroids, and intense pulsed light therapy; none provided relief.

A 50‐year‐old man presented with progressive left wrist pain and swelling that began after a fall onto his left arm one year earlier. He had undergone percutaneous pinning for an extra‐articular distal‐radius fracture. The postoperative course was initially uneventful, but when the cast was removed at 6 weeks he noted fullness around the wrist, and the pins were found to be loose and subsequently removed. Over the next 9 months, he had gradual, progressive loss of wrist motion and increasing pain. He was treated as having complex regional pain syndrome with nonsteroidal antiinflammatory agents, but without improvement.

He had no history of tuberculosis, immunosuppression, rheumatic disease, or constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, or fatigue. He was not taking any regular medications. On examination, he had considerable pain and severely restricted range of motion of the left wrist; the remainder of the musculoskeletal examination was normal.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and metabolic panel, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 42 mm in the first hour (normal <20), and a C‐reactive protein level of 8.93 mg/L (normal <5). Serological tests for antinuclear antibodies and hepatitis viruses were negative; tests for tumor markers, HIV, and Brucella antibodies were also negative. A tuberculin skin-test result was strongly positive, with 17 mm of induration. A chest radiograph was normal.

An anteroposterior radiograph of the left wrist demonstrated soft-tissue swelling, loss of joint space, gross articular destruction with erosions and cavities throughout the carpus, distal ulna, and radius, and diffuse osteopenia of the carpal bones. A CT scan of the wrist showed near-total loss of bony trabeculae, marked osteoporosis, cortical cysts, and erosions in the carpal and metacarpal bones and in the distal radius and ulna.

A 50-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of a mass on the medial aspect of her right dorsal forefoot. She recalled minor trauma from a hard object to this area; the lesion became painful, then gradually firm and less painful. She denied weight loss, fevers, or systemic symptoms. Examination revealed a well-demarcated, firm 2-cm subcutaneous lump with minimal tenderness. Great toe flexion and extension were slightly restricted. Laboratory studies, including white blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level, were normal. Plain radiographs of the foot showed no bony abnormalities. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a well-defined 18×9 mm nonenhancing soft-tissue mass anterior to the first metatarsal head and metatarsophalangeal joint, with “dystrophic appearing subcutaneous calcifications scattered throughout the outlines” of the lesion and no cortical or marrow involvement.

A 74-year-old woman presented with two weeks of progressive, painless, bilateral proximal muscle weakness involving her legs, shoulders, and arms. Two weeks earlier, she had received a five-day course of azithromycin for a sinus infection. Her medical history included hypertension, hypothyroidism, hyperlipidemia (on atorvastatin 40 mg daily), and remote transient ischemic attacks. Medications were otherwise stable. A sibling had limited scleroderma.

On examination, blood pressure was 155/61 mm Hg and temperature 97.6 °F. She was unable to lift her proximal legs against gravity or to ambulate. Admission laboratory values were: hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, white blood cell count 4.34×10³/μL (50.3% neutrophils), platelets 165×10³/μL, blood urea nitrogen 44 mg/dL, creatinine 1.34 mg/dL. Liver tests showed ALT 545 IU/L, AST 975 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 621 IU/L, total bilirubin 5.0 mg/dL (direct 3.5 mg/dL). Creatine phosphokinase was 2597 IU/L and aldolase 20.8 IU/L. Thyroid function was normal. Immunoglobulins were elevated (IgG 1661 mg/dL; IgA 771 mg/dL; IgM 456 mg/dL). ESR was 98 mm/hr and CRP 19.4 mg/L.

Autoantibody testing revealed ANA 1:80, elevated anti-Ro/SSA, and negative anti-La/SSB, myositis-specific antibodies (including anti–HMGCR), anti-striated muscle, and acetylcholine-receptor antibodies. Chest CT showed no thymoma. Electromyography was nondiagnostic. Muscle biopsy demonstrated focally necrotizing myopathy with chronic inflammation, without features of polymyositis, dermatomyositis, inclusion-body myositis, mitochondrial or glycogen storage disorders, connective-tissue disease, or vasculitis.

She received intravenous fluids for acute kidney injury, and on hospital day 5 was started on prednisone 80 mg daily. Her CPK peaked at 29 210 IU/L on day 5, then declined and her strength improved. On admission her absolute neutrophil count (ANC) was normal, but on day 3 it fell to 860/μL, declined further to zero by day 8, and persisted despite high-dose prednisone.

A 4-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of a mass in her left external auditory canal (EAC). The parents first noted a 5 mm, skin-colored, painless lesion without history of trauma or surgery. Empiric treatment for presumed insect bite included oral amoxicillin/clavulanic acid, oral betamethasone, and topical tobramycin for 7 days. At follow-up one week later, the lesion had rapidly enlarged to 15 mm, was purple-red, ulcerated, and bled easily. Routine blood tests were normal. 

Ultrasonography of the left auricle showed a 12 mm ovoid subcutaneous lesion with regular margins and inhomogeneous echotexture that extended 30 mm along the EAC and abutted the parotid gland without signs of infiltration. Contrast CT and MRI revealed a 17 × 21 × 24 mm lobulated, well-defined solid mass involving the cartilage of the tragus and lateral EAC, extending into the parotid space, compressing but not invading the gland. On MRI, the lesion was hyperintense on T2-weighted and isointense on T1-weighted images, demonstrated high-to-moderate diffusivity on ADC maps, and showed irregular peripheral enhancement. There was associated fluid in the EAC but no bone erosion.

A 25-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 10-day history of intense, persistent lower abdominal pain, fever, vomiting, and urinary frequency. His temperature was 39.5 °C. On abdominal examination, he appeared ill, with diffuse tenderness in the lower abdomen and a 5 cm midline suprapubic mass; the umbilicus appeared normal and there were no peritoneal signs. Rectal examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 13,000/µL with 82% neutrophils; blood chemistries and urinalysis were normal, and urine culture yielded no growth. A standing abdominal radiograph was normal.  
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a hypoechoic tract extending from the umbilicus to the abdominal wall and a hypoechoic mass with heterogeneous contents situated between the peritoneum, the muscle layer, and the bladder, without free peritoneal fluid.

A 30-month-old boy with an unremarkable perinatal history was referred for evaluation of a 6-month history of decreased sensation in the gluteal region and persistent urinary dribbling. He walked, but more slowly than before; power could not be reliably graded. Neurological examination was otherwise normal except for decreased perianal sensation. Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine revealed a well-defined intramedullary cystic lesion measuring 12×8×8 mm within the conus medullaris at the T12–L1 level. The lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with no perilesional edema, no solid component, and no contrast enhancement.

A 6-year-old boy presented with severe pain on the medial side of his left elbow after falling on the lateral aspect of the flexed elbow while skateboarding. He had a history of a lateral condyle fracture of the left humerus treated surgically one year earlier. On examination, the left elbow was slightly swollen with restricted range of motion, and peripheral neurovascular status was normal. Plain radiographs of the elbow showed a solitary bony fragment anterior to the distal humerus. Computed tomography revealed a 7.5 × 9.5 mm fragment displaced anteromedially from the superior border of the trochlea, with intact humeroulnar joint congruity and a normally positioned ossification center of the capitellum. Ultrasonography demonstrated that the fragment was continuous with the cartilaginous trochlea, was unstable with elbow motion, and had a clear border at the midportion of the trochlea without any other associated fracture.

A 50-year-old woman presented with proptosis and restricted movement of her right eye. She reported intermittent eye pain, nasal obstruction, and frontal headache for 1½ years and noted that attempting to blow her nose produced pressure on her eyeball. She had no history of sinus surgery or tumor but was a past intranasal cocaine abuser for many years.  
On examination, there was marked inferolateral proptosis of the right eye; the fundus and pupillary responses were normal. An anterior nasal septal perforation was present, and the nasal cavity was obstructed by a large soft-tissue mass. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy, and examination of the ears and oral cavity was unremarkable. Routine blood tests were normal.  
CT of the brain and sinuses showed an anterior septal perforation and a large soft-tissue mass occupying the nasal cavity and right ethmoid air cells that extended into the right orbit, with destruction of the medial orbital wall. The expansile orbital component measured 5.6 × 4.6 × 4.3 cm and contained thin bony septations.  
Contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated rim enhancement of the sinonasal soft tissues, a persistently hypointense central focus in the nasal cavity indicating fibrotic or scar tissue, proteinaceous fluid in the maxillary sinus, and an orbital mass of variable low signal with mild peripheral enhancement.

A three‐year‐old girl was brought with a 1-month history of gradually increasing abdominal distension and 3 days of periorbital and bilateral lower‐limb swelling. There was no history of hematuria, dysuria, rash, joint pains, chronic illness, or family history of genetic disease. Growth parameters were within normal limits for age. Examination showed periorbital edema, bilateral pitting edema of the lower limbs, a distended abdomen with flank fullness, fluid thrill, and shifting dullness, but no hepatosplenomegaly. Vital signs were normal. Initial laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, lymphocytes 15%, platelets 668 000/mm3, serum calcium 8 mg/dL, normal C-reactive protein, liver and kidney function tests, electrolytes, lipid profile, and thyroid function. Peripheral smear showed microcytic hypochromic anemia with thrombocytosis. Iron level was 54 µg/dL and vitamin D was 13.6 ng/mL. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated moderate ascites, multiple enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes, and mild diffuse mucosal thickening of the bowel without hepatosplenic abnormalities. Urinalysis, culture, and 24-hour urinary protein were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography was unremarkable. Analysis of ascitic fluid revealed an exudative, triglyceride-rich chylous ascites.

A 48-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of low back pain of 4 years’ duration. She described the pain as sharp and stabbing, non-radiating, worsened by activity, and relieved by rest, tramadol, and gabapentin. She had minimal relief from nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs and no benefit from physical therapy. The pain was accompanied by muscle cramps and leg paresthesia. She denied trauma, bowel or bladder incontinence, saddle anesthesia, weakness, fever, night sweats, or weight changes. Her body-mass index was 41.

On examination, there was tenderness over the lower back at the sacroiliac joints with reduced range of motion and a positive FABER test on the left. No arthritis was evident in other joints.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and metabolic profile, a borderline elevated C-reactive protein (1.1 g/dL; reference, <1.0 g/dL), and a normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate (15 mm/h; reference, <20 mm/h). HLA-B27 and hepatitis serologies were negative.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis demonstrated erosions of the bilateral sacroiliac joints and marrow edema, suggesting an inflammatory process. A computed tomographic scan was obtained for further evaluation and revealed sclerosis of the iliac side of the sacroiliac joints with sparing of the joint spaces and a vacuum phenomenon bilaterally, without erosions.

A 43-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 3-year history of persistent right lower rib pain. She described a popping, grinding, and clicking sensation in the right upper quadrant, worsened by activities such as heavy lifting. Prior evaluation at an outside facility included CT of the abdomen, a HIDA scan, and transvaginal ultrasound, all reported as negative. She underwent diagnostic laparoscopy to rule out endometriosis or other intra-abdominal pathology, which was unremarkable. Conservative measures—including over-the-counter analgesics, muscle relaxants, medical marijuana, and intercostal nerve blocks—failed to relieve her symptoms. On examination, there was focal tenderness to palpation over the right lower ribs. A chest ultrasound with Valsalva maneuver was ordered for further assessment.

A 14-day-old boy, the second child of nonconsanguineous Caucasian parents, was brought to the emergency department with a 1-week history of poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, and failure to thrive; his weight had declined by 20% since birth. Two maternal great-uncles had died in early infancy of unknown causes. On arrival he required intraosseous access and endotracheal intubation. Initial laboratory studies demonstrated hyponatremia, marked hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, and elevated blood urea nitrogen and creatinine. The complete blood count showed leukocytosis, bandemia, and thrombocytopenia (platelet count, 18,000 per cubic millimeter). Cardiac monitoring revealed widened QRS complexes and peaked T waves. 

He was treated with sodium polystyrene sulfonate, calcium chloride, sodium bicarbonate, insulin, and dextrose-containing intravenous fluids, along with empiric hydrocortisone and intravenous antibiotics. Urinalysis revealed pyuria, and urine culture grew >100,000 colonies per milliliter of Escherichia coli; blood and cerebrospinal fluid cultures were negative. Renal ultrasonography showed moderate ureteropelvicaliectasis with debris, and voiding cystourethrography demonstrated posterior urethral valves and grade IV vesicoureteral reflux. Hydrocortisone was discontinued after a normal 17-hydroxyprogesterone level. Electrolytes and acid–base status normalized over several days with fluids and antibiotics. 

At 26 days of age, the serum aldosterone concentration was elevated. At 20 days of age, the patient underwent cystoscopic transurethral resection of posterior urethral valves, with subsequent improvement in renal function. Persistent feeding difficulties and aspiration prompted placement of a gastrostomy tube; otolaryngologic evaluation revealed a submucous cleft palate and bifid uvula. At 5 months of age, repeat serum aldosterone remained elevated, plasma renin activity was normal, growth and weight gain were good, and he maintained normal electrolytes without salt supplementation.

A 17-year-old female with a history of migraine presented with fever, headache, and bilateral visual loss. Three days of daily fevers (101.4°F–102°F) occurred in late March, with a negative SARS-CoV-2 test. Two weeks after her febrile illness, she received a first dose of the Pfizer SARS-CoV-2 vaccine. Two days post-vaccination, she developed severe headaches (8/10), initially intermittent then constant; a repeat SARS-CoV-2 test was negative. At an optometry visit nearly three weeks later, visual acuity was 20/20 OU with correction, extraocular movements were full, and slit-lamp exam was normal. Dilated funduscopy revealed bilateral optic disc edema, a peripapillary flame hemorrhage, and multifocal, well-circumscribed, deep chorioretinal white lesions in the periphery of both eyes.

On hospital admission, ESR was 30 mm/hour (reference 0–20), and HSV-1/2 IgM was 1.07 IV (reference <0.89). Blood cultures, cryptococcal antibody, Rickettsia typhi antibody, Borrelia burgdorferi antibody, syphilis antibody, CRP, ANA, ANCA, RF, HIV antibodies, and AQP4-IgG were all negative. MRI of the brain and orbits with contrast showed minimal papilledema but was otherwise unremarkable. Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 55 cm H2O (reference <20), CSF WBC 48 cells/μL, protein 23 mg/dL (15–45), and glucose 56 mg/dL (40–70). CSF CMV PCR was positive, although the patient had no clinical evidence of ocular or systemic CMV infection. 

Fluorescein angiography demonstrated severe optic disc leakage in the right eye, mild leakage in the left eye, and a wreath-like pattern of choroidal hyperfluorescence in the posterior poles of both eyes. Optical coherence tomography revealed bilateral optic nerve edema.

A 67-year-old woman with a history of well-controlled hypothyroidism (on levothyroxine) and remote excised benign skin melanoma presented with acute right-sided weakness and neck pain. She had received her first Sinopharm COVID-19 vaccine 2 days earlier; about 24 hours after vaccination, she developed burning neck pain radiating to her right arm and leg with tingling, followed by weakness more pronounced in her right hand and elbow than her right knee and ankle. On examination, vital signs were stable, GCS 15, mild right facial paresis, right upper-extremity strength 3/5, right lower-extremity strength 4/5, and right‐sided hypoesthesia–dysesthesia. She was on no anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents. Laboratory studies showed normal PT, PTT, INR, D-dimer, and platelet counts. Ten minutes after admission, she developed acute abdominal pain, seizure-like movements, loss of consciousness, and bradycardia, necessitating intubation and resuscitation. Brain CT and MRI showed no acute intracranial process or stroke. Incidentally, cervical spine edema was noted on brain MRI, so a full spine MRI was obtained. It revealed T1, T2, and STIR hyperintensity within the spinal cord from the brainstem to T2, with the hemorrhagic segment corresponding to C3–C5, and no CSF blockage on myelography.

A 45-year-old Caucasian man with a history of chronic back pain and erectile dysfunction, social alcohol use, and occasional smoking presented with 3 days of progressively worsening right lower–quadrant abdominal pain and headaches. Initial vital signs were notable for a blood pressure of 124/86 mmHg; serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL (eGFR 90 mL/min/1.73 m2). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a right lower–pole renal infarct and perivascular inflammation around the celiac artery. Workup for thromboembolism (ECG, transthoracic echocardiography with bubble study, D-dimer, coagulation studies) revealed no abnormalities. Serologic evaluation for systemic vasculitis (ESR, CRP, ANCA, ANA) was negative. He was discharged on apixaban.

Sixteen days later, he returned with recurrent right flank pain, blood pressure 151/88 mmHg, creatinine 1.3 mg/dL (eGFR 65.7), ESR 32 mm/h, CRP 12.3 mg/dL. Urinalysis was bland. CT angiography showed extension of the right renal infarct into the mid pole, acute dissection of anterior and posterior divisions of the right renal artery with multiple branch occlusions, and persistent perivascular inflammation of the celiac and main right renal arteries without new end-organ damage. He underwent catheter-directed thrombolysis, which was complicated by fever and a culture-negative urinary infection; thrombolysis was stopped, and dual antiplatelet therapy was initiated. He was discharged with creatinine 1.0 mg/dL (eGFR 89).

Twelve days later, he was readmitted with gross hematuria, passage of tissue, creatinine 1.63 mg/dL (eGFR 50.1). CT angiography revealed a new left lower–pole renal infarct and segmental dissection of a left renal artery branch, along with persistent perivascular inflammation of the celiac and right renal arteries; the right infarct was stable. Genetic testing including COL3A1 was unrevealing. Hypovolemia, postrenal obstruction, and glomerular or tubulointerstitial nephropathies were considered but deemed unlikely given the absence of obstruction on imaging and bland urine microscopy. Urine output remained adequate at 120–200 mL/h.

A 42-year-old woman with a history of hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine presented with a gradually progressive neck swelling that impaired her ability to swallow solid food. She had no history of other autoimmune diseases or malignancy. On examination, there was a large anterior neck mass that was stony hard in consistency, moved with swallowing but was stationary with tongue protrusion, and multiple enlarged cervical lymph nodes were palpable.

Laboratory studies showed a suppressed TSH level, elevated free T4, and markedly increased antithyroglobulin and anti–thyroperoxidase antibodies. A thyroid ultrasound revealed a diffusely enlarged heterogeneous gland: the right lobe measured 3.9 × 2.7 × 6.5 cm and the left lobe 3.4 × 1.8 × 5.2 cm, with mild tracheal deviation to the left and microcalcifications. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration of the calcified area yielded a mixture of lymphoid cells, rare Hurthle cells, and no colloid; the result was consistent with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, Bethesda category II.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated bilaterally enlarged, heterogeneous, multinodular thyroid lobes extending to the isthmus, causing mild tracheal shift, with no evidence of extrathyroidal calcifications; multiple small cervical lymph nodes with preserved fatty hilum were noted.

A 94-year-old man presented to the emergency department with acute onset, rapidly progressive dyspnea and fatigue. His symptoms began two days after receiving his first dose of the ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 (AstraZeneca) vaccine and worsened over four days before presentation. He had a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia treated with amlodipine and olmesartan; he had no history of heart failure, coronary artery disease, renal disease, cirrhosis, autoimmune disease, or malignancy.

On examination, he was hypotensive (blood pressure 99/51 mmHg), heart rate 61 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94% on 3 L of nasal cannula oxygen, and afebrile (35.5 °C). Cardiac examination revealed distant heart sounds; pulmonary examination showed decreased breath sounds over the bilateral lower lung fields.

Laboratory studies demonstrated a white blood cell count of 4500 /µL, blood urea nitrogen 26 mg/dL, creatinine 1.11 mg/dL, C-reactive protein 0.19 mg/dL, procalcitonin 0.05 ng/mL, and N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide 172 pg/mL. A nasopharyngeal swab for SARS-CoV-2 by RT-PCR was negative.

Chest radiography showed an enlarged, “water bottle” cardiac silhouette and bilateral costophrenic angle blunting. Contrast-enhanced chest CT confirmed moderate pericardial effusion and bilateral pleural effusions. Electrocardiography revealed sinus rhythm with low QRS voltage. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated preserved biventricular systolic function but signs of impending cardiac tamponade.

A 53-year-old woman from a nonconsanguineous family presented with a 20-year history of progressive unsteady gait, slurred speech, and uncoordinated movements. Neurologic examination revealed pure cerebellar signs, including gaze-evoked nystagmus, saccadic pursuit with hypometric saccades, scanning speech, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and a wide-based gait. Cranial nerve function was normal, and the Mini-Mental State Examination was within normal limits. Nerve conduction studies, electromyography, and electroencephalography were all normal. Laboratory tests, including renal and liver function, were within normal ranges. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed diffuse cerebellar atrophy.

An 87-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of blurry vision and optic disc hyperemia in the left eye. She had a history of systemic hypertension and stroke. On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 with correction in both eyes. The right eye showed mild hypertensive retinopathy. In the left eye, there was mild hypertensive retinopathy, a posterior vitreous detachment, and a lesion on the optic disc with mild prepapillary hemorrhage. Biomicroscopic fundus examination revealed that the lesion expanded in size and demonstrated increased filling during systole of the cardiac cycle. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) of the optic disc demonstrated an abnormal saccular dilatation of an artery in the center of the optic disc. Evaluation of the macula by biomicroscopy and SD-OCT showed no intraretinal or subretinal fluid, exudates, or hemorrhage.

A 17-year-old single Arab female presented with a 2-day history of binocular horizontal diplopia in primary gaze and on left gaze, resolving on right gaze or with one eye closed. Over the preceding week, she experienced multiple brief episodes of bilateral transient visual obscurations precipitated by changing from lying to sitting or standing. She also reported mild left shoulder pain for one week. She denied headache, decreased visual acuity, photophobia, vomiting, tinnitus, dizziness, neck pain, or sensory or motor deficits. 

Her medical history was notable for polycystic ovary syndrome diagnosed one year earlier, for which she took metformin. She denied use of tetracycline, hormones, vitamins, cosmetic supplements, or herbs. She was a nonsmoker, denied recent trauma, and had no family history of similar complaints.

On examination, vital signs were normal, and her body mass index was 31. She was alert and oriented. Visual acuity and visual fields were normal. Funduscopic examination showed bilateral moderate papilledema (Frisén grade 3). Ocular motility testing revealed esotropia with limited abduction of the left eye; other cranial nerves were intact. Motor, sensory, cerebellar, reflex, and gait examinations were unremarkable.

Noncontrast head CT and CT venography were normal with no masses, structural abnormalities, or venous thrombosis. Lumbar puncture in the lateral decubitus position revealed an opening pressure of 550 mm H₂O; cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed normal cell count and differential, glucose, and protein. Laboratory studies including complete blood count, electrolytes, blood glucose, liver and renal function tests, and thyroid-stimulating hormone were within normal limits.

A 29-year-old African American woman was referred for a 6-month history of left lower quadrant abdominal pain and a soft-tissue mass at the same site. The pain was sharp, cramping, nonradiating, positional, and worsened during menstruation. Her medical history included three cesarean deliveries and obesity (BMI, 38.66). She took a combined oral contraceptive (norgestimate-ethinyl estradiol).

On examination, there was a non-tender, palpable mass beneath the lateral aspect of her prior cesarean scar in the left lower quadrant.  
Ultrasound showed a 19 × 19 × 9 mm extra-fascial macrolobular hypoechoic mass with internal color flow at the anterior margin of the left rectus muscle.  
CT of the abdomen revealed a poorly delineated ∼2.5 cm mass just medial to the left anterior superior iliac spine, lying superficially over the fascia.  
An ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy was attempted, but Interventional Radiology was unable to perform it due to her body habitus.

A 19-year-old Caucasian woman with Down’s syndrome and hypothyroidism presented with a 4-day history of progressively worsening jaundice, pruritus, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. She also noted poor appetite, dark urine, pale stools, and a 1-month history of fatigue. She denied fevers, alcohol use, recent travel, sick contacts, or herbal supplements. Her medications included levothyroxine, fexofenadine, and combined levonorgestrel-ethinyl estradiol oral contraceptive pills, which she had started 6 months earlier. She was otherwise healthy, non-smoking, and had no family history of liver or biliary disease.

On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs. She had scleral icterus and right upper quadrant tenderness with a positive Murphy’s sign and no peritoneal signs. Laboratory studies showed a total bilirubin of 8.0 mg/dL with a direct bilirubin of 5.1 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 245 IU/L, AST 50 IU/L, ALT 100 IU/L, ESR 10 mm/h, INR 1.1, and lipase 23 IU/L. Over the next several days, alkaline phosphatase rose to 500 IU/L, AST to 78 IU/L, and ALT to 195 IU/L.

An extensive workup for hepatobiliary disease was negative, including tests for acetaminophen toxicity; serologies for viral hepatitis, Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and herpes simplex virus; autoimmune hepatitis; primary biliary cirrhosis; primary sclerosing cholangitis; Wilson’s disease; hemochromatosis; α1-antitrypsin deficiency; and HIV infection. A urine toxicology screen was negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed no cholecystitis, cholelithiasis, choledocholithiasis, or biliary obstruction. CT of the abdomen and MRCP were unremarkable. Given the progressive cholestatic liver-test abnormalities and nondiagnostic imaging and laboratory studies, a liver biopsy was planned.

A 43-year-old man presented 2 hours after a motor vehicle collision with abdominal pain. He was well before the accident. Airway was intact; breathing normal with RR 12/min; no chest injury. BP was 130/80 mm Hg; HR 96/min; capillary refill normal; GCS 15; blood glucose 6 mmol/L. No external bleeding was noted. Secondary survey revealed tenderness in the right iliac fossa with a seat belt mark overlying it; bowel sounds were audible. FAST ultrasound showed no free fluid in the abdominal cavity. Laboratory tests showed a white cell count of 11 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance; renal and liver function tests were normal; urine dipstick was negative. CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated an 8 mm diameter appendix with minimal adjacent fat stranding and subcutaneous fat stranding of the anterior lower abdominal wall consistent with bruising.

A 72-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department with sudden onset of posterior neck discomfort that spread to both shoulders, after which she became unable to move her neck. She had no history of trauma, no history of anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, and no relevant family history. Her medical history was notable only for dyslipidemia and past appendicitis. On arrival, her temperature was 37.5°C, pulse 87 beats per minute, respiratory rate 21 breaths per minute, and blood pressure 182/88 mmHg. Neurologic examination revealed full strength and sensation in all extremities without signs of paralysis. Noncontrast cervical CT at the referring hospital demonstrated a high-density mass in the right posterior epidural space. Sagittal T2-weighted cervical MRI showed a heterogeneous high-signal epidural mass posterior to the spinal cord extending from C2 to C5.

A 34-year-old man presented to the emergency department with an 8-hour history of progressive weakness and paralysis of all four limbs, more pronounced in the lower extremities. The symptoms began several hours after receiving a single 4 mg intramuscular injection of betamethasone for seasonal allergic rhinitis unresponsive to topical nasal corticosteroids. He had no other past medical history, denied gastrointestinal symptoms or urinary complaints, and reported no alcohol or drug use. On examination, he was alert and oriented but unable to stand or walk. Vital signs were within normal limits. Cardiovascular examination was unremarkable. Neurologic examination revealed hypotonia with muscle strength graded as 3/5 in both proximal and distal upper limbs and 1/5 in both proximal and distal lower limbs. Deep tendon reflexes were decreased in the lower limbs, plantar responses were flexor, and sensory, cranial nerve, and higher cortical functions were intact. An electrocardiogram showed occasional premature ventricular contractions. Laboratory studies revealed a serum potassium level of 2.5 mmol/L, with all other electrolytes, complete blood count, metabolic panel, arterial blood gas, and toxicology screen within normal limits.

A 24-year-old man was evaluated for a progressively enlarging, painless swelling in the lumbar region. His parents first noted a protuberant mass three months earlier. He denied trauma, liver disease, coagulation abnormalities, and anticoagulant use. He was an amateur soccer player (1–2 matches per week) with no recent injuries.

On examination, there was a well-demarcated, soft, fluctuant mass measuring 28 cm × 10 cm extending from the sacral spine to the lower thoracic area; the overlying skin was normal. Abdominal, pelvic, and spinal examinations were unremarkable. Neurologic and vascular examinations of the lower extremities were normal.

Laboratory studies showed normal red-cell counts, platelets, clotting factors, and liver function tests. Sagittal T2-weighted MRI demonstrated a large, homogeneous, expansile soft-tissue mass in the lumbar region with signal characteristics compatible with a hematoma; intraspinal and extraspinal structures were intact.

A 54-year-old man with a background of right tibial non-union complicated by chronic osteomyelitis (methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus and occasional gram-negative organisms) underwent surgical debridement with external fixation. His past medical history included well-controlled asthma, obstructive sleep apnea, hypertension, deep vein thrombosis, and pericarditis. Preoperatively, he had been treated for S. aureus bacteremia with intravenous flucloxacillin (increased postoperatively to every 4 hours) and oral rifampicin. A transthoracic echocardiogram had shown a mobile echogenic structure near the mitral valve. On postoperative day 5, because of poorly controlled pain, he was started on pregabalin 75 mg twice daily (later increased to 150 mg twice daily) and a single dose of tapentadol 100 mg extended release. His home medications included sertraline 150 mg daily, amitriptyline 25 mg daily, and ketamine as needed.

On the following day, he developed acute deterioration with hyperthermia (up to 41 °C), tachycardia, and tachypnea. Neurologic examination revealed agitation, tremor, hyperreflexia, and bilateral inducible ankle clonus.

A 25-year-old woman with a 5-year history of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis on glatiramer acetate presented with paresthesia and paraparesis. Vital signs on admission were: pulse 83/min, respiratory rate 16/min, temperature 37 °C, blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg. She was started on intravenous methylprednisolone succinate, 1 g daily for 3 days, for MS exacerbation.  
On day 1 of therapy, she developed mild dyspnea; vital signs remained stable and cardiac examination was unremarkable. On day 2, she developed severe dyspnea, respiratory distress, and oxygen saturation dropped to 65%. She was admitted to the ICU and intubated for mechanical ventilation.  
Chest radiography showed multifocal parenchymal opacification with normal cardiac size. Chest CT revealed diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities without interlobular septal thickening or pleural effusion. Empiric intravenous co-trimoxazole, meropenem, vancomycin, and furosemide were initiated.  
Endotracheal secretion Gram stain and bronchoalveolar lavage evaluation, including bacterial and fungal cultures, PCR for Pneumocystis jirovecii, and acid-fast staining, were all negative. D-dimer testing was negative, and echocardiography showed no cardiac dysfunction.  
By day 6, she was extubated with stable vital signs, and she was discharged on day 12.

A 28-year-old woman was referred to orthopedics for 4 months of persistent right outer thigh pain. She described soreness aggravated by prolonged walking and associated with weight loss of 10 kg and insomnia; there was no history of trauma. On examination, gait and lower-extremity strength were normal. Magnetic resonance imaging of the femur showed increased signal intensity in the right upper and middle femoral diaphysis with cortical destruction and periosteal reaction, findings suggestive of a malignant bone tumor. An open biopsy of the right femur was performed; histopathological examination demonstrated nonsuppurative osteitis and chronic osteomyelitis. Blood cultures for bacteria and fungi were negative. Laboratory tests at two weeks showed a C-reactive protein of 55.5 mg/L (normal <3.48) and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 50 mm/h (normal <20). Conventional anti-inflammatory therapy yielded no improvement. The patient then noted lesions on both soles; dermatologic evaluation led to a diagnosis of palmoplantar pustulosis, and she reported soft toenails and skin changes over the past 4 months.

A 53-year-old man with hypertension, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, pulmonary embolism, and type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with increasing dyspnea, malaise, low-grade fever, and signs of heart failure. Blood pressure was 123/71 mm Hg, heart rate 72 beats/min, and peripheral oxygen saturation 97%. He was afebrile and had no cutaneous signs of endocarditis or skin infection. Electrocardiogram showed an anterior myocardial infarction of indeterminate age with abnormal ST-segment and T-wave changes suggesting lateral ischemia. Chest radiograph revealed a right pleural effusion, cardiomegaly, and interstitial edema. White blood cell count was 5,200 ×10^9/L (normal 4.5–11), C-reactive protein 88 mg/L (normal <0.3), and procalcitonin 0.09 µg/mL. Complete blood count, creatinine, and cardiac enzymes were normal. Blood cultures were negative. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% with apical and anterolateral akinesia and pleuro-pericardial effusions. Coronary angiography revealed a large aneurysm of the left anterior descending artery with a fistula draining into both ventricles. Positron emission tomography indicated an inflammatory process in the anterolateral right ventricle with a hypodense central zone concerning for abscess. Cardiac computed tomography demonstrated multiple pseudoaneurysms in the left anterior descending and right coronary arteries, the largest arising from the distal left anterior descending artery with a biventricular fistula communicating with both the right and left ventricles.

A 71‐year‐old man with persistent symptomatic atrial fibrillation underwent elective repeat catheter ablation under general anesthesia. His medical history included hypercholesterolemia; he had previously maintained sinus rhythm for 9 months after his first ablation and had taken amiodarone for 6 months in 2015 without complications. Medications on admission included warfarin, bisoprolol, and atorvastatin.

In July 2017, the ablation lasted 2 ½ hours with pulmonary vein re‐isolation, complex fractionated electrogram ablation, and linear roof and mitral lines. Two hours postprocedure, amiodarone was started at 200 mg three times daily, planned to taper to 200 mg daily over three weeks.

That night, he developed cough, chest pain, and hemoptysis with clots. He was afebrile, blood pressure and oxygen saturation were normal on room air, and physical examination was notable only for blood‐stained sputum. Laboratory studies showed:  
– Hemoglobin 120 g/L (preprocedure 159 g/L)  
– White blood cell count 11.2×10^9/L  
– Platelets 159×10^9/L  
– CRP 15 mg/L  
– INR 1.8  
– Normal urea, creatinine, and electrolytes  

Chest radiograph revealed bilateral hilar and lower zone consolidation with small pleural effusions. High-resolution chest CT with contrast showed patchy nodular and confluent ground-glass opacities in the left lower lobe, lingula, and posterior right lower lobe; the main pulmonary veins were patent, and there was no esophageal injury or pneumomediastinum. Findings were described as bilateral pulmonary hemorrhage of unclear cause. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated normal left ventricular systolic function and no significant valvular disease.

On hospital day 2, he remained symptomatic with frank hemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain, hypoxia, and fevers. Blood and sputum cultures (including acid‐fast bacilli) were sent, and he began empirical IV co-amoxiclav, continued warfarin, and received a trial of furosemide. A respiratory consult favored pulmonary vein trauma, but serial chest radiographs showed progression of bilateral infiltrates. An autoimmune screen (ANCA and anti–GBM) was ordered.

By hospital day 4, he continued to have hemoptysis and required 3 L/min of oxygen to maintain saturations. Examination revealed bilateral fine inspiratory crackles without signs of heart failure. Repeat labs showed CRP rising to 143 mg/L, with persistently normal white cell and eosinophil counts. Blood and sputum cultures remained negative, and autoimmune tests returned normal.

A 73-year-old woman was evaluated for a persistent dry cough that began 2 years earlier and progressive exertional dyspnea over the past week. She had a history of hypertension, chronic urinary tract infections, hyperlipidemia, and hypothyroidism. For recurrent UTIs, she had been taking nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for about 3 years. Her lisinopril had been changed to valsartan several months before, with no improvement in the cough. She had no history of smoking, lung disease, or occupational exposures.

On examination, she was afebrile, mildly distressed, and fatigued, with a nonproductive cough. Her respiratory rate was 20/min, blood pressure 157/94 mmHg, pulse 102 bpm, and oxygen saturation 90% on room air. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 8.82 × 10^3/mm^3 without eosinophilia; serum chemistry was normal. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 18 mm/h, and the d-dimer level was <150 ng/mL. Thyroid function tests were normal, HIV test was negative, and ANA, ANCA, and rheumatoid factor were within normal limits.

A chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral reticular opacities with areas of atelectasis. High-resolution CT of the chest revealed subpleural reticular opacities with minimal honeycombing. Pulmonary function tests showed a severe restrictive defect (FVC 36.6% predicted; FEV1/FVC 95.2%; FEV1 45.2% predicted) with a markedly reduced diffusing capacity (DLCO 17.3% predicted; DLCO/VA 49.4% predicted). Total lung capacity was 53.5% predicted, and residual volume was 78.9% predicted. Electrocardiography and echocardiography were normal.

A 61-year-old woman with a history of diabetes mellitus presented with a six-month history of a mass in her left breast. She denied fever, pulmonary symptoms, dental problems, facial or skin lesions, tonsillitis, gingivitis, and breast trauma. On examination, there was an indurated 5×6 cm subareolar mass in the left breast with skin fixity but no draining sinuses or axillary lymphadenopathy. She was afebrile and appeared in good health. A chest radiograph was normal. Mammography suggested an abscess. Given a clinical suspicion of breast malignancy, fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) was performed. Repeated aspirations yielded only pus. Smears showed collections of neutrophils, histiocytes, and fluffy areas, and were negative for malignant cells. A diagnosis of chronic suppurative inflammation was made. The patient was already receiving antibiotics.

An 18-year-old woman was referred to Hematology for investigation of a 3-week history of severe internal bleeding. She reported regular menstrual cycles, no personal or family history of bleeding disorders, and at age 15 had an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. Five days postpartum, she developed hemorrhage, epistaxis, and ecchymoses, which resolved after dilation and curettage and two months of transfusions.

Twenty days before referral, she presented with acute abdominal pain, malaise, fatigue, and vomiting. Examination revealed generalized abdominal tenderness, and hemoglobin was 3.5 g/dL; she received blood transfusion.

Ten days before referral, she developed hypovolemic shock and abdominal distention. Ultrasonography showed intra-abdominal free fluid and a left ovarian cyst. At exploratory laparotomy, blood and clots were evacuated; a right ovarian torsion cyst and a left hemorrhagic cyst were removed, and hemostasis was achieved with ovarian drilling and drain placement. 

Laboratory studies:
• aPTT 92.6 s (normal 25–36 s), PT 18.9 s (normal 12.3–14 s), INR 1.38 (normal 0.8–1.2)  
• Mixing test: aPTT remained prolonged; PT and INR normalized after mixing  

Her condition then deteriorated with recurrent abdominal bleeding, prompting a second laparotomy for suspected disseminated intravascular coagulation.

On transfer to Hematology, vital signs were: heart rate 130 bpm, blood pressure 130/80 mmHg, temperature 38 °C, oxygen saturation 99%. Physical examination showed severe pallor, multiple ecchymoses on the limbs and feet, and active bleeding from the surgical drain and sutures.

A 25-year-old African American man with asthma, hypertension, and a documented CD4 T-lymphocyte deficiency presented with progressive shortness of breath and musculoskeletal chest pain. He was initially treated for Pseudomonas pneumonia with meropenem, but his dyspnea persisted. Video-assisted thoracoscopic lung biopsy revealed necrotizing granulomas and yeast on tissue culture. He received two weeks of fluconazole and a steroid taper for presumed sarcoidosis. He returned weeks later with worsening dyspnea, productive yellow cough, vision changes, night sweats, a 30-lb weight loss, and fevers to 102 °F. Blood cultures grew yeast (identification pending), and he was started on vancomycin, aztreonam, levofloxacin, and micafungin. On transfer, he reported working as a customs official and recent Caribbean travel. Physical examination showed papular rashes on the face and chest. High-resolution CT of the chest demonstrated cavitary consolidations in the right upper and lower lobes with diffuse bilateral lymphadenopathy. HIV testing was negative. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage, skin biopsy, and bone marrow biopsy were performed, and all showed fungal elements on preliminary examination.

A 19‐year‐old woman was referred for evaluation of dental and orofacial abnormalities. She was born at term to healthy nonconsanguineous parents after an uneventful pregnancy, with an Apgar score of 8. Immediately after birth, three subdural hematomas were noted; she was hypotonic but had no feeding or breathing disorders. Her growth parameters remained between the 25th and 50th percentiles, but she exhibited delayed developmental milestones. At age 1 year, genetic evaluation was initiated because of persistent hypotonia and developmental delay.

On examination, there was no facial or neck asymmetry, and lymph nodes were not palpable. Temporomandibular joint examination revealed no crepitus, but mouth opening was limited with slight left deviation. Palpation suggested bruxism. The lips showed an excessive lower vermilion and a cupid-bow upper vermilion. Oral mucosa was normal; tonsils had been removed. The tongue was enlarged (macroglossia) and moist, with absence of lingual and inferior labial frenula; the superior labial frenulum caused a large diastema between the upper central incisors. Saliva was thick and sticky. There was an anterior open bite and mandibular prognathism. Generalized moderate gingival enlargement and heavy plaque were noted. Several molars had extensive carious lesions. Panoramic and periapical radiographs demonstrated taurodontism, supernumerary roots in premolars, and root resorption of first mandibular molars.

A 47-year-old woman presented with an 8-hour history of subacute, progressive dizziness, diplopia, dysarthria, and bilateral ptosis. Cranial CT and MRI were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was unremarkable. Over the next hours, she developed complete bilateral ptosis with inability to open her eyes, descending quadriparesis, and paralysis of her respiratory muscles; approximately 24 hours after admission, she required intubation and mechanical ventilation. 

Her 51-year-old husband presented one day later with nausea, dizziness, progressive dysarthria, and diplopia. On examination, he had bilateral ptosis, ophthalmoparesis with diplopia in all directions, dysarthria, dysphagia, and moderate bilateral facial paralysis, but full strength in his extremities.

Further history revealed that both had consumed home-canned green beans of unknown age 2 days before the wife’s admission; their son, who noted an odd odor from the beans, had declined to eat them.

A 75-year-old woman presented with abdominal pain and an altered general condition. Her history included left colectomy for localized colonic adenocarcinoma 12 years earlier, radiotherapy for anal epidermoid carcinoma 3 years earlier, type II diabetes, and a known IgG-kappa monoclonal gammopathy. She reported a year of intermittent abdominal discomfort followed by weight loss over the past 6 months. One year earlier, both a CT scan and colonoscopy had been normal.

On admission, a CT scan showed pseudotumoural thickening of the right colonic wall with diffuse peritoneal effusion. A repeat colonoscopy without biopsies revealed no mucosal abnormalities. Surgical exploration demonstrated a mass infiltrating the right colon, the cecum, and the peritoneum, prompting a right hemicolectomy. The initial histological diagnosis was desmoid-type abdominal fibromatosis, and on review was reclassified as a fibroblastic/myofibroblastic tumour of intermediate malignancy. No further treatment was initiated, and the patient was referred to our institution for evaluation.

A 2-year-old boy was referred for a 2-year history of recurrent lip dermatitis. Two previous dermatologists had prescribed topical tacrolimus 0.03% ointment, hydrocortisone 2.5% ointment, desonide ointment (for presumed atopic cheilitis), and, later, the same regimen for lip-licker’s dermatitis, all with minimal improvement. He had tried aloe vera supplements and a gluten-free diet for 6 months without benefit and resumed a normal diet. His mother reported occasional flares with brown rice, citrus foods, candies, and bread. He used a hypoallergenic lip balm twice daily and fluoride-free toothpaste. Medical history was otherwise unremarkable, with no personal history of atopy. Family history included an older brother with asthma and a father with eczema and psoriasis. On examination, pink fissured plaques with mild yellow crust involved the perioral skin, including both lips; the remainder of the skin examination was clear. A differential diagnosis of lip-licker’s dermatitis and allergic contact dermatitis was made. The patient received a 10-day course of cephalexin and combination topical tacrolimus 0.03% with alclometasone twice daily, and he was referred for patch testing.

A 47-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and ongoing alcohol abuse was brought to the emergency department after a syncopal episode. He reported 7/10 epigastric pain and nonbloody emesis but denied melena. On arrival, his heart rate was 108 bpm, blood pressure 64/34 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air.
