He was alert (GCS 14) but in severe distress, diaphoretic, tremulous, with cold, clammy skin. The abdomen was distended and diffusely tender; a rectal exam was negative for gross blood. A focused abdominal ultrasound (FAST) showed moderate ascites; chest radiography was unremarkable.

Laboratory results included a white-cell count of 7600/mm3 with 38% bands, hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, platelets 149 000/mm3, INR 2.5, AST 213 U/L, ALT 309 U/L, venous pH 7.23, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, and lactate 6.62 mmol/L. Despite 4 L of crystalloid, his blood pressure remained low (75/58), prompting initiation of norepinephrine (30 µg/min) and vasopressin (0.04 U/min). Broad-spectrum antibiotics (vancomycin and piperacillin–tazobactam) were started for presumed septic shock, with spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) suspected based on abdominal pain, ascites, and bandemia. He was electively intubated for airway protection as agitation increased, and transfer for CT imaging was deferred due to hemodynamic instability. He was then admitted to the medical ICU for further management. 

On arrival in the ICU after initial stabilization, a diagnostic paracentesis was performed.

A 63-year-old man presented with a 5-year history of episodic syncope or near-syncope. He described clusters of events in late summer, often preceded by a sense of warmth and mild nausea, and noted that drinking cold water reproducibly precipitated symptoms. He initially had frank syncope but now experiences prodromes and avoids injury. He had no other medical history and was not on any medications.

On presentation, his baseline electrocardiogram was normal. In the emergency department, when he drank cold water, he reproducibly developed second-degree atrioventricular (AV) block. During hospitalization, intermittent periods of advanced AV block correlated with his symptoms. Vital signs and physical examination were unremarkable.

Initial laboratory studies, including thyroid-stimulating hormone, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and Lyme serology, were within normal limits or negative. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging and positron-emission tomography showed normal cardiac function without structural abnormalities or late gadolinium enhancement. Sleep evaluation demonstrated no evidence of sleep apnea, and tilt-table testing yielded a normal hemodynamic response.

An 89-year-old man with previously normal cognition was brought to the emergency department after his wife found him unresponsive on awakening. His medical history included hypertension, prior cerebral infarction, coronary artery disease (post–percutaneous coronary intervention), chronic pleuritis, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He smoked half a pack of cigarettes daily for 60 years.  
 
Medications: aspirin, ticlopidine, candesartan, benidipine, diltiazem, nicorandil, allopurinol, famotidine.  
 
On arrival: temperature 37.8°C; heart rate 104/min; respiratory rate 32/min; blood pressure 167/106 mm Hg; oxygen saturation 100% on 6 L/min O₂. Glasgow Coma Scale score was 9 (E4 V1 M4). He opened his eyes without stimulation but did not respond to pain. Neurologic examination was limited; deep tendon reflexes were normal and plantar responses were downgoing bilaterally.  
 
Cerebrospinal fluid (day 0): WBC 2 cells/mm³; RBC 238 cells/mm³; protein 41.6 mg/dL; glucose 80 mg/dL.  
 
Laboratory studies: WBC 12,040/mm³ (94.6% neutrophils), C-reactive protein 1.84 mg/dL (mild aspiration pneumonia), serum ammonia 53 μg/dL, LDH 379 U/L; other liver enzymes normal. Autoimmune vasculitis panels (eg, anti–double-stranded DNA, MPO-ANCA) were negative. Urine toxicology was negative.  
 
Initial brain MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging showed abnormal signal in the hippocampus with mild reduction in the apparent diffusion coefficient; FLAIR imaging showed no hippocampal abnormality.

A man in his twenties with chemorefractory primary T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma was admitted for disease progression. Two days before admission, he had a fall and complained of weakness and lethargy. A few days after starting dasatinib, he developed sudden, compressing chest pain unrelieved by rest.  
On examination, he was alert but distressed; blood pressure 92/55 mm Hg; pulse 96 beats/min; oxygen saturation 100% on room air.  
Laboratory studies showed a normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 71 g/L), severe thrombocytopenia (platelets 14×10^9/L), and an absolute eosinophil count of 51.9×10^9/L (73% of leukocytes; baseline 0.8×10^9/L). High-sensitivity troponin-I was 2718 pg/mL. COVID-19 PCR was negative.  
Electrocardiography revealed diffuse ST-segment depression over inferolateral leads, compared with a normal baseline ECG.  
Chest radiography demonstrated clear lung fields with no pneumothorax or widened mediastinum.  
Transthoracic echocardiography showed diffuse thrombus deposition along the endocardium, preserved left ventricular ejection fraction of 65% with no regional wall-motion abnormalities, and a moderate pericardial effusion.

An 11-month-old boy was evaluated for a soft, expansile swelling (3 cm × 3 cm) at the nape of the neck, present since birth. Neurologic examination was normal. MRI of the brain and spine showed a meningocele at the C2–C3 level. The child underwent excision of the redundant sac and primary skin closure under general anesthesia (propofol, atracurium; intubated with a 4.5 mm uncuffed tube; maintained with O2/N2O/sevoflurane). The procedure was performed in the prone position without complications. Intraoperative vital signs remained stable. The patient was reversed, extubated with a train-of-four ratio of 90%, and transferred to the PACU at 10:40 am, conscious and breathing on supplemental oxygen. On arrival, heart rate was 110 beats/min, SpO2 100%, blood pressure 90/46 mmHg, and end-tidal CO2 37 mmHg. At approximately 12:30 pm, the patient suddenly developed tachycardia to 205 beats/min, then bradycardia to 30 beats/min, followed by asystole. The patient became unresponsive. CPR was initiated immediately, and 100 µg of intravenous epinephrine was administered. After one cycle, spontaneous circulation returned. The patient was reintubated and ventilated. A CT scan of the brain and spine showed no significant abnormalities.

A 25-year-old man underwent left anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction under general anesthesia with ultrasound-guided femoral and sciatic nerve blocks (0.5% ropivacaine, 25 ml each). Blocks were uneventful, with no paresthesia or high injection pressure. The leg was positioned supine in a thigh holder with 90° knee flexion, and a pneumatic tourniquet was inflated to 250 mmHg for 32 minutes. On postoperative day 2, he developed shock-like pain, tingling, and numbness in the plantar aspect of his foot and along the left lateral leg, with no initial motor deficits. His neuropathic pain worsened over subsequent weeks. He had no systemic inflammatory symptoms. On postoperative day 23, neurologic examination demonstrated decreased sensation to light touch, vibration, and pinprick in the sciatic nerve distribution; toe flexion and extension strength of 3/5; foot dorsiflexion and plantar flexion of 4/5; and absent left Achilles reflex. Nerve conduction studies showed decreased motor responses of the left peroneal and tibial nerves and absent sensory responses of the left sural and superficial peroneal nerves, consistent with a sciatic neuropathy without radiculopathy. Conservative management was recommended. On postoperative day 42, lumbar spine MRI revealed left L5–S1 disk extrusion with nerve compression, and left L5 and S1 foraminal steroid epidural injections were performed without relief. The patient’s hyperesthesia prompted consideration of complex regional pain syndrome, although he had no vasomotor or sudomotor changes. On postoperative day 52, a lumbar sympathetic block and distal ankle block provided significant pain relief.

A 37-year-old woman underwent left skin-sparing mastectomy with immediate subpectoral implant reconstruction and SurgiMend acellular dermal matrix (ADM) in 2016 for high-grade ductal carcinoma in situ with microinvasion (ER positive, PR negative, HER2 negative). In 2020, she presented with a 1 cm subcutaneous lump adjacent to the mastectomy scar. Ultrasound was indeterminate and biopsy was deemed high risk for implant perforation. Breast MRI demonstrated an 11 mm low-signal lesion with mild type 1 enhancement. A narrow‐margin excision biopsy confirmed invasive high-grade DCIS (ER positive, HER2 negative). She underwent wide local excision with a 1 cm margin, reconstruction of the capsule defect with an ADM patch, and adjuvant chest‐wall radiotherapy. 

Three months after surgery, she noted a new nodule deep to her wide-excision scar on the reconstructed breast. Ultrasound revealed an indeterminate nodule with a bright echogenic centre. Dynamic contrast breast MRI did not demonstrate any abnormal enhancement.

A 65-year-old woman was referred with a 3-month history of behavioral and personality changes and progressive cognitive decline. Initially, she had increasing forgetfulness and difficulty with activities of daily living, which progressed to not recognizing family members. She later developed generalized stiffness and visual hallucinations, seeing random people. Over the 2 weeks before presentation, her condition worsened rapidly: she became unable to ambulate and had new urinary and fecal incontinence. She had no relevant past medical or psychiatric history and no family history of neurologic disease.

On examination, she was mute and appeared ill. There was increased muscle tone and brisk reflexes in all extremities, a prominent jaw jerk, bilateral palmomental reflexes, paratonia, bilateral extensor plantar responses, and intermittent forced eye gaze deviation. Continuous myoclonic jerks affected all limbs, and she was unable to stand because of ataxia.

Routine laboratory tests, including serology for hepatitis B, HIV, and syphilis, were negative. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed 2 lymphocytes per cubic millimeter, glucose 3.5 mmol/L, total protein 62 mg/dL, and adenosine deaminase 2.32 U/L. Thyroid function tests, vitamin B12, and folate levels were normal. Chest radiography, electrocardiography, and abdominal–pelvic ultrasonography were unremarkable.

Electroencephalography revealed continuous periodic complexes and generalized slow waves. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated diffusion-weighted high signal intensity in the bilateral frontal (right > left) and occipital cortices, and T2-weighted images showed subtle high signal in the pulvinar nuclei of the bilateral thalami, giving a “hockey-stick” appearance. An autoimmune encephalitis panel, including antibodies against NMDA, AMPA (GluR1 and GluR2), GABA-B, LGI1, and CASPR2 receptors, was negative.

A 72-year-old woman with multiple myeloma on her twelfth cycle of carfilzomib infusion presented with a 3-month history of intermittent central chest tightness radiating to her right arm and right neck, lasting 5–10 minutes and occurring at rest or with exertion. She also reported dyspnoea on exertion without orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, or peripheral oedema. She had no traditional cardiovascular risk factors. Medications included carfilzomib, dexamethasone, thalidomide, and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole. On examination she was slim, normotensive, with a normal cardiopulmonary exam. In the emergency department, an ECG performed while she was pain-free showed sinus rhythm at 70 b.p.m., poor R-wave progression, and T-wave inversion in the anterior leads. High-sensitivity troponin T was 8 ng/L (normal <16). Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated normal left ventricular size and function without regional wall motion abnormalities. She underwent invasive coronary angiography, which showed minor irregularities but no obstructive stenoses.

A 22-year-old woman with no significant medical history was brought to the emergency department after an acute deterioration in mental status. Over the preceding three weeks she developed mood swings, anxiety, depression, and progressive bradykinesia. On the day of admission she was found agitated and delirious, with a suicide attempt by jumping from a moving car. 

On arrival she was involuntarily held by psychiatry for altered mental status, uncooperativeness, agitation, and impulsive aggressive behavior. Initial noncontrast head CT and MRI of the brain showed no acute intracranial abnormalities. She was started on sodium valproate for presumed bipolar disorder with psychotic features, along with olanzapine and clonazepam. 

She was admitted to the medical ICU. Neurologic examination was limited by agitation and confusion, but cranial nerves II–XII appeared grossly intact. Her working diagnoses included encephalopathy (viral, fungal, bacterial, spirochetal, toxoplasmal, paraneoplastic antibody–mediated, and anti-NMDAR encephalitis), sepsis versus systemic inflammatory response syndrome from aspiration, and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. 

An extensive infectious, metabolic, autoimmune, and neurologic workup was initiated. Initial laboratory panels returned negative. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed a white blood cell count of 14.4/mm3 with lymphocytic pleocytosis; protein and glucose levels were normal. Empiric acyclovir was started pending herpes simplex virus (HSV) testing; preliminary HSV-1 and HSV-2 PCR results were negative.

A 35-year-old man presented with swelling, pain, and a discharge from the right upper quadrant of the abdomen for 2 years. He denied fever, nausea, or vomiting and had no other medical comorbidities. His surgical history was significant for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy converted to an open procedure 2½ years earlier and an excision of a sinus tract 1½ years earlier. On examination, his vital signs were normal. Local inspection revealed a discharging sinus in the right upper abdomen along the previous subcostal scar, with purulent material expressed on pressure. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 14,000 per cubic millimeter.  
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 13.1-mm echogenic focus in the superior gallbladder fossa, suggestive of a calculus, surrounded by a 17 × 15.3-mm collection, with an elongated tract extending to the skin surface. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 5.1 × 1.9 × 1.6-cm walled fluid collection in the gallbladder fossa, penetrating segment 4a of the liver, with a small calcific density on its wall and a soft-tissue–density tract extending anteriorly toward the subcutaneous plane of the right upper abdominal wall.

A 44-year-old obese white man with end-stage renal disease secondary to childhood hemolytic-uremic syndrome underwent a deceased-donor renal transplant in 1998. He was found to have an asymptomatic rise in serum creatinine to 3.4 mg/dL from a baseline of 2.0 mg/dL. He denied any symptoms. On examination, a left inguinal hernia was palpable. Renal ultrasonography revealed moderate to severe hydronephrosis of the transplanted kidney with nonvisualization of the distal ureter and no bladder abnormalities. Despite intravenous hydration and adequate bladder emptying, his urine output remained marginal and his serum creatinine remained elevated at 3.1 mg/dL. A noncontrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis was obtained.

A 30-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of low back pain radiating to the right lower limb and 20 days of right lower-limb weakness. On neurologic examination, the right lower limb had Medical Research Council (MRC) strength grade III proximally and IV distally, the left lower limb was grade V, sensation to fine touch and pain was impaired in the right L5 and S1 dermatomes, the right knee and ankle reflexes were absent, and plantar responses were mute bilaterally. A thoracic spinal cord lesion was localized on clinical grounds. Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine showed cord swelling from the D4 to D12 vertebral levels and an intramedullary ring-enhancing lesion measuring 1.1 × 0.9 cm at D11 that was hypointense on T1 and hyperintense on T2; no scolex was identified. MRI of the brain was normal. Differential diagnosis included spinal neurocysticercosis and tuberculoma.

A 79-year-old Caucasian woman with a history of systemic hypertension, heart failure, chronic snoring, sinus bradycardia, and a congenitally absent left arm was admitted in March 2010 with a 3-week history of gait ataxia. Over the subsequent days she developed dyspnea, brief episodes of unconsciousness, right-arm myotonia, and audible stridor. On admission, arterial blood gas analysis showed hypercapnia (pCO₂ 60 mmHg), respiratory acidosis (pH 7.29), and hypoxemia (pO₂ 111 mmHg); respiratory rate was 8 breaths/min. She was admitted to the intensive care unit and treated successfully with noninvasive ventilation.

To evaluate the episodes of unconsciousness, an electroencephalogram and head CT scan were performed; both studies were reported as normal. Otolaryngologic examination by laryngoscopy revealed diminished vocal-cord motility with intermittent midline paresis. Pulmonary function testing demonstrated a restrictive pattern (FVC 46%, FEV₁ 50%, FEV₁/FVC 89%). Polysomnography revealed severe sleep apnea (apnea–hypopnea index 50.2/h), predominantly obstructive events, with no central or mixed apneas.

After respiratory stabilization, she was transferred to the internal medicine ward. There she was noted to have orthostatic hypotension and worsening stridor with recurrent spells of respiratory insufficiency, agitation, and tachypnea, again requiring noninvasive ventilation. Repeat nasal endoscopy confirmed persistent vocal-cord paralysis in the midline. To exclude an extrinsic compressive cause, a chest CT and bronchoscopy were performed; both were unremarkable. Because of recurrent respiratory crises, she underwent tracheostomy in the ICU and, once stable, returned to the ward.

A nearly 7-year-old boy with no relevant medical history presented with abdominal pain and swelling after a fall from his bicycle during which his abdomen struck the handlebar. Immediately after the accident, his mother noticed a swelling at the site of impact. He had no other complaints. On examination, he appeared well and was hemodynamically stable. The abdomen showed a circular contusion several centimeters below the umbilicus, just to the right of midline. On palpation, a clear defect of the rectus fascia was felt. There were no signs of peritonitis. He was admitted for observation and discharged the following morning; surgery was scheduled one week later.

A 36-year-old man with moderate intellectual disability and severe obsessive–compulsive disorder was referred for inpatient psychiatric care because of a two-month history of worsening mental status characterized by increasing tension, irritability, ritualized behaviors, and episodes of stupor and mutism. He had been treated with fluvoxamine (200 mg daily) and risperidone (4.5 mg daily), but, because of lack of improvement and signs suggestive of serotonin syndrome, risperidone was tapered and olanzapine (10 mg daily) was started.

On admission, he was oriented but psychomotor sluggish, hypomimic, tense, and anxious. He intermittently became motionless, answered questions selectively with delayed, stereotyped grimacing, and denied hallucinations. Physical examination was limited by poor cooperation; notable findings were severe obesity (BMI 31.95 kg/m2), bilateral ankle swelling, and gynecomastia. He refused an ECG. His history included repeated psychiatric hospitalizations since age 12 for catatonic stupor with refusal to eat or drink, active negativism, muscle stiffness, and psychosis. Internal medicine records documented dyslipidemia, impaired glucose tolerance, chronic liver-function abnormalities, and hypertension treated with simvastatin and propranolol.

He was diagnosed with organic catatonia; risperidone was discontinued, and he continued fluvoxamine and olanzapine. While on the ward, he lay in bed most of the time, required diapers and assistance with all activities, and engaged intermittently in compulsions. On hospital day 15, he reported feeling worse, claimed he had pneumonia, and demanded antibiotics. Examination revealed minor basal rales, a temperature of 37.3 °C, and a dry, intermittent cough. Two days later, his temperature normalized and vesicular breath sounds were normal; infection was excluded. On hospital day 21, he was noted to have a productive cough and symptoms of upper respiratory congestion.

An 11-year-old Hispanic girl presented with a 2-month history of rapidly enlarging, painful masses in both breasts. She had no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. On examination, there were large, solid, well-circumscribed masses measuring 8 cm in the right breast and 5 cm in the left breast. Ultrasound of both breasts showed multiple oval, solid nodules with well-defined margins and homogeneous hypoechoic texture. Color-Doppler evaluation demonstrated mild vascularity; no cystic collections, acoustic shadowing, signs of tissue invasion, or axillary lymphadenopathy were seen. The ultrasound findings were not considered suspicious for malignancy, and the working diagnosis was a benign breast lesion such as fibroadenoma, PASH, or hamartoma.

A 64-year-old Caucasian woman was admitted for progressive fatigue, slurred speech, nausea, and vomiting. In the emergency department she received IV saline for hyponatremia (serum sodium 121 mEq/L). Her past history was notable only for a hysterectomy at age 34 for postpartum complications; she had three prior uncomplicated pregnancies. Over the preceding months she had experienced fatigue, mental lethargy, myalgias, and leg cramps, which partially improved with multivitamins. 

On examination, she was afebrile, normotensive, and euvolemic. Speech was dysarthric but there were no focal neurologic deficits. The skin was dry and axillary hair was thin. Cardiac, pulmonary, and abdominal exams were unremarkable. No peripheral edema or mucosal dehydration was noted.

Laboratory studies showed:  
• Serum sodium 129 mEq/L; potassium 4.75 mEq/L; plasma osmolality 277 mOsm/L  
• Blood urea nitrogen 28 mg/dL; creatinine 0.83 mg/dL  
• Creatine kinase 1377 U/L; myoglobin 1150 ng/mL  
• Arterial blood gas normal  
• Urine sodium (24 h) 93 mEq/L; specific gravity 1005 N/m³; urine osmolality 175 mOsm/L  
• Autoantibody panels negative  

Endocrine studies revealed:  
• Free T3 0.6 pg/mL (2.0–4.4); free T4 0.06 ng/dL (0.93–1.7); TSH 1.56 µIU/mL (0.27–4.2)  
• Cortisol 1.4 µg/mL (6.2–19); ACTH 17 pg/mL (7.2–63.3)  
• Prolactin 1.41 ng/mL (4.79–23.3); LH 7.04 mIU/mL (25.8–134); FSH 3.0 mIU/mL (7.7–58.5)

A 66-year-old woman, a life-long non-smoker, presented with hemoptysis. Seven years earlier, chest CT had shown a pyramid-shaped pulmonary hemorrhage in the right upper lobe (segment 1). She was well until a second episode of hemoptysis, when chest CT revealed a 9-mm, well-demarcated, round nodule in segment 4 of the right middle lobe against a background of interstitial pneumonia. She underwent further evaluation. Sputum cultures showed no bacterial pathogens, including Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Serum tumor markers, including carcinoembryonic antigen and cytokeratin 19 fragments, were within normal limits. A complete blood count did not reveal eosinophilia. During 3 months of observation, the nodule increased in size to 11 × 10 × 8 mm. An ^18F-FDG PET/CT scan showed low uptake in the nodule, with a maximum standardized uptake value of 0.94.

A 12-year-old boy with a history of epilepsy and ectodermal dysplasia presented with a 4-day history of continuous, progressively worsening colicky abdominal pain. He developed yellowish, food-content vomiting on day 3 and reported chronic intermittent constipation with preserved passage of flatus. There was no significant surgical or family history. 

On examination, he was alert and hemodynamically stable. Abdominal inspection revealed distention; palpation showed a soft, lax abdomen with no significant tenderness. Digital rectal examination demonstrated an empty rectal vault. 

Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 14.54 × 10^3/mm^3 (reference 4.5–13.0 × 10^3), hemoglobin 15.4 g/dL, pH 7.32, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, and an elevated alkaline phosphatase of 265 U/L; other electrolytes and renal and liver indices were within normal limits. 

An abdominal x-ray (AP and lateral views) showed “a large gas filled distended viscus pointing towards the right lower quadrant measuring 12.5 cm with small bowel loops in the right upper quadrant.” A contrast enema demonstrated “the presence of a stricture/stenotic area at the level of the splenic flexure and contrast was not passing beyond that stricture, there was absent opacification of the cecum, ascending colon, and transverse colon.”

A 5-year-old Caucasian girl presented with an 18-hour history of generalized abdominal pain, fever (39 °C), vomiting, and constipation. Her past medical history was unremarkable. On examination, she was febrile, with a rigid abdomen and diffuse severe tenderness. Digital rectal examination revealed soft stool without blood. Chest examination was normal. Laboratory studies showed normal hemoglobin, white-cell and platelet counts, prothrombin time, INR, glucose, creatinine, urea, sodium, and potassium; C-reactive protein was elevated at 134.5 mg/L. An erect abdominal radiograph demonstrated air–fluid levels in the small bowel and dilated large-bowel loops. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 5-cm hyperechoic mass in the hypogastric region surrounded by intestinal loops. Non-contrast abdominal CT demonstrated a hyperdense midline mass above the bladder.

An 8-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of multiple café-au-lait macules (six, each ≥5 mm) and several light-brown lentigines on his face, neck, and thorax. He had coarse facial features, hypertelorism, down-slanting palpebral fissures, epicanthus, large low-set ears, pterygium colli, cubitus valgus, pectus excavatum, and an umbilical hernia. His weight and height were at the 50th percentile, and cephalic perimeter was at the 95th percentile. No genital or hearing anomalies were noted. Cranial MRI performed for headache showed no unidentified bright objects. Ophthalmologic examination showed no Lisch nodules, and skin examination revealed no neurofibromas. At age 9, ECG was normal. Molecular testing for NF1 was negative, and at age 11 SPRED1 testing was also negative. On re-evaluation at age 12, the lentigines had become darker and more widely distributed, and his dysmorphic features and macrocephaly persisted. Echocardiography in the boy showed thickening of the interventricular septum with an ejection fraction of 70% and mitral-valve prolapse. His 50-year-old father, previously reported as healthy, was found on examination to have hypertelorism, ptosis, coarse facial features, large low-set ears with lobe creases, low posterior hairline, pectus excavatum, multiple lentigines, café-au-lait macules, a large café-au-lait macule on the leg, height at the 5th percentile, head circumference >95th percentile, a history of benign arrhythmia, and postnatal growth retardation. Echocardiography in the father revealed mild dilation of the ascending aorta and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Audiometry demonstrated mixed mild deafness in the father; the son had no auditory deficit.

A 51-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis for over 10 years secondary to nephrotic syndrome initially presented with progressive numbness of the extremities, clumsy hands, and difficulty walking without assistance. Examination revealed spastic gait disturbance and increased muscle tone. His serum creatine kinase (CK) was slightly elevated at 315 U/l. Cervical laminoplasty was performed for cervical myelopathy attributed to destructive spondyloarthropathy, and his neurologic symptoms improved postoperatively.

Two months later, he developed intractable, cramp-like muscle pain throughout his body, occurring paroxysmally with severe spasticity. His pain was rated 10/10 on the numerical rating scale, with painDETECT and Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory scores of 28 and 79, respectively. Ketamine provided only partial relief, and conservative measures failed to control his symptoms.

Plain radiographs revealed progressive destructive changes at C4–C5 and C5–C6 and marked kyphosis of the subaxial spine with a C2–7 angle of –53°. Laboratory studies showed a markedly elevated CK of 999 U/l. Neurology and nephrology consultations were obtained, and the differential diagnosis included myopathy, electrolyte imbalance, and adverse drug reactions, but no clear cause was identified.

A 72-year-old woman with hypertension presented with a few days of word-finding difficulty and expressive aphasia. She denied headache, weakness, or visual changes. In the emergency department, her temperature was 38.3 °C, heart rate 96 bpm, and blood pressure 126/74 mmHg. She was alert and oriented. Lung examination was clear; dental exam was normal; there was no lymphadenopathy. Naming was impaired (e.g., she called a stethoscope “football”). She could spell “world” forward without error and made one error backward. Registration was 3/3, recall 2/3; remote and recent memory were intact. Speech was fluent and coherent. Cranial nerves were intact. Strength was 5/5 in all extremities. Tone and bulk were normal; reflexes were 1+; toes were downgoing. Coordination and gait were normal. 

Noncontrast head CT revealed a left temporal-lobe mass-like lesion with surrounding vasogenic edema. Initial differential diagnoses included metastatic disease, brain abscess, cerebral infarction, lymphoma, high-grade glioma, toxoplasmosis, demyelinating disease, and resolving cerebral contusion or hematoma. Empiric vancomycin, ampicillin, and ceftriaxone were started. 

Brain MRI with gadolinium demonstrated a 5.5×4.3 cm left temporal-lobe septated rim-enhancing lesion with bright restricted diffusion, a dark rim on T2, and extensive surrounding vasogenic edema. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 11.3 K/µL. HIV testing was negative. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography showed no vegetations and a normal ejection fraction. Chest radiograph showed no pulmonary infection. Dental evaluation confirmed intact teeth without decay.

A 57-year-old woman was referred for new retinal hemorrhages in the left eye. One week earlier, she experienced acute onset of “spots” in her left eye, similar to transient episodes she had for years that typically resolved within hours; this episode persisted, prompting evaluation in the emergency department. Neuroimaging, carotid Doppler ultrasound, and cardiac echocardiography were unremarkable. An optometrist diagnosed central retinal vein occlusion and referred her for retinal evaluation.

Her medical history included well-controlled hypertension and hyperlipidemia; she had no diabetes, smoking history, obesity, or other cardiovascular disease. On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally; pupillary responses, intraocular pressures, extraocular motility, and anterior segment examination were all normal.

Dilated fundus examination of the left eye revealed multiple flame-shaped and round hemorrhages in the posterior pole. Late-phase fluorescein angiography demonstrated blockage by hemorrhages with otherwise normal vasculature and normal transit times in both eyes. Optical coherence tomography of the left macula showed hyperreflective lesions immediately deep to the internal limiting membrane corresponding to the hemorrhages.

A 78-year-old man was scheduled for resection of a cT4NxM0 left upper lobe lung adenocarcinoma. His history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, former smoking, and ulcerative colitis managed with sulphasalazine; he had no corticosteroid or neoadjuvant therapy. Preoperative spirometry was normal. CT of the chest showed a left upper lobe mass with pleural tethering and consolidation adjacent to the left mainstem bronchus, and calcified lymph nodes in the right hilar and subcarinal regions; the left mainstem bronchus measured 13.1 mm by 14.0 mm two centimeters distal to the carina. The plan was mediastinoscopy with lymph node sampling, followed by left upper lobe wedge resection if nodes were negative.

General anesthesia was induced with propofol, remifentanil, and atracurium. A 7.5 mm single-lumen endotracheal tube was placed and secured at 23 cm. Pressure-control ventilation (peak 20 cmH2O, PEEP 4 cmH2O) delivered 8 mL/kg tidal volumes with a 2 L/min air–oxygen mix. Mediastinoscopy was performed supine; lymph nodes were negative and surgery proceeded via left thoracotomy.

With the patient supine, a 9Fr Fuji Uniblocker endobronchial blocker was introduced into the left mainstem bronchus under bronchoscopy. The balloon was inflated to 7 mL (manufacturer maximum 8 mL), deflated, and after repositioning to lateral decubitus was reinspected and reinflated with no irregularity or bleeding noted. Initial balloon pressure was 31 cmH2O. One-lung ventilation was instituted (peak 24 cmH2O, PEEP 8 cmH2O), and an air leak of approximately 100–150 mL per breath was noted but managed by increasing fresh gas flows to 4 L/min, maintaining tidal volumes of 6 mL/kg. There was no desaturation, abnormal capnography, or abnormal airway pressures or flows.

A 39-year-old man presented with several months of bilateral darkening and pigmentation of both upper and lower eyelids. He reported no history of trauma, sun exposure, new medications, or cosmetic use. His medical history was notable only for keratoconus managed with hard contact lenses and grade 1 fatty liver. On examination, there was purple-black discoloration of the upper and lower eyelids, extending to the medial and lateral canthi of both eyes, without ulceration, telangiectasia, or pruritus. A skin biopsy of a palpebral lesion showed epidermal atrophy, vacuolar degeneration of the basal cell layer, and prominent melanin incontinence.

A 66‐year‐old man with hepatitis C–related cirrhosis and chronic kidney failure was admitted to the surgical intensive care unit with sepsis and oxacillin‐sensitive Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia. His course was complicated by acute tubular necrosis requiring continuous venovenous hemofiltration. A chest radiograph showed mild pulmonary congestion; bronchoscopy was not performed. He received appropriate antibiotic therapy and was treated for an Escherichia coli bacteremia with piperacillin‐tazobactam, with clearance of blood cultures.

While hospitalized, a donor became available. The donor was a 41‐year‐old previously healthy man who had suffered a near‐drowning event in a freshwater lake. Return of spontaneous circulation was achieved after 20 minutes of resuscitation; chest radiographs then demonstrated worsening bilateral opacities suspicious for pneumonia. Three days later brain death was declared, and his kidney and liver were procured. The explanted liver of the recipient was cirrhotic without malignancy.

The recipient underwent combined kidney and liver transplantation. Intraoperative induction immunosuppression included methylprednisolone 500 mg and mycophenolate mofetil 1000 mg. Continuous venovenous hemofiltration was performed intraoperatively and discontinued on postoperative day 1 when renal graft function improved. Postoperative complications included a contained urine leak from the ureteroureterostomy, managed with drains and stents. On postoperative day 8, he was transferred out of the ICU, and on day 14 to an inpatient rehabilitation unit as graft function improved.

On postoperative day 25, he was readmitted to the surgical intensive care unit with signs of peritonitis. Immunosuppression was reduced to prednisone 5 mg daily. On postoperative day 28, he underwent exploratory laparotomy and peritoneal washout; intraoperative findings included purulent ascitic fluid, and fluid specimens were sent for bacterial and fungal cultures.

A 43-year-old man presented with a 30-year history of productive cough, beginning after a childhood whooping-cough outbreak at age 10. The cough had worsened over the past year, producing copious purulent sputum, and was accompanied by progressive dyspnea, left-sided chest pain, and 3 months of weight loss. He denied hemoptysis, fever, night sweats, or allergic history. He had been treated empirically for pulmonary tuberculosis at age 19 (no bacteriologic confirmation) without improvement. He had no history of smoking or alcohol use and no family history of similar illness.

On examination, he was severely wasted (BMI 14.4), afebrile, with grade 3 digital clubbing, central and peripheral cyanosis, and pretibial edema. Respiratory rate was 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation was 99% on room air. Auscultation revealed widespread harsh breath sounds, bilateral crepitations, and rhonchi. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia (108 bpm), a third heart sound, and a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound. Abdominal examination demonstrated moderate ascites, tender hepatomegaly, and a positive hepatojugular reflux.

Laboratory studies revealed normal renal and liver function, hemoglobin 16.9 g/dL, hematocrit 58.5%, low serum albumin (30.2 g/dL), negative HIV serology, and negative Aspergillus IgG/M. Sputum studies were negative for acid-fast bacilli and Mycobacterium tuberculosis by Xpert/Rif assay. Abdominal ultrasound suggested congestive hepatopathy. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia, right-ventricular hypertrophy, and extreme right-axis deviation. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated gross right-heart enlargement, moderate tricuspid regurgitation, and elevated right ventricular systolic pressure (~45 mmHg), consistent with pulmonary hypertension; left ventricular ejection fraction was normal.

Chest radiography revealed marked dilatation of the trachea and main bronchi with diffuse reticulolinear and ring-like opacities, predominantly in the mid and lower lung zones bilaterally. Inspiratory high-resolution CT of the chest showed a tracheal diameter of 38.4 mm, right main bronchus 42.5 mm, left main bronchus 38.1 mm, multiple tracheal diverticula, cystic and varicose bronchiectasis, ground-glass opacities, and mucus-filled bronchi with air-fluid levels.

A 16-year-old male from Iran presented with multiple episodes of vomiting and reduced oral intake. His medical history included seizures and type II diabetes mellitus. On examination, he was afebrile; blood pressure was 120/70 mmHg, heart rate 130 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. The chest was clear bilaterally. 

Abdominal ultrasonography showed a borderline enlarged liver with a hypoechoic lesion measuring 6.7×6.1 cm in the portal confluence region involving segments 5, 6, and 7, with mild internal color flow. MRI revealed hepatomegaly (17 cm) and a heterogeneous right-lobe lesion (8×7×6.7 cm) with areas of diffusion restriction, central nonenhancing zones, and mass effect on the central intrahepatic bile ducts, leading to nonvisualization of the hepatic duct confluence. 

Coronal post-contrast images demonstrated thickening and enhancement of the cecum and ascending colon, along with heterogeneously enhancing hepatic lesions. PET-CT showed a large FDG-avid hypodense lesion in hepatic segments 5–8 and ulceration with irregular mural thickening of the cecum, distal ileum, and ascending colon, with several FDG-avid paracecal lymph nodes.

Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage was performed, and a liver biopsy specimen was obtained. Colonoscopy revealed a deformed, edematous ascending colon and cecum with multiple 1 cm ulcers. Multiple biopsies were taken from the ulcerated lesions.

A 15-year-old boy with primary adrenal insufficiency due to a known hemizygous ABCD1 mutation was referred to neurology after an unrelated screening brain MRI showed T2 FLAIR hyperintense lesions in the cerebral peduncles without gadolinium enhancement. He had mild lower-extremity spasticity, nonsustained ankle clonus, and a mildly spastic gait (neurologic function scale 1). Neuropsychiatric testing revealed a full-scale IQ of 86 and a verbal comprehension index of 89.  
Given his evolving leg symptoms, an MRI of the entire spine with gadolinium was performed. This showed enhancement of the cauda equina nerve roots, predominantly at L1 and L3, with a normal spinal cord signal and anatomy of the conus medullaris.  
Two weeks later, he developed bilateral gastrocnemius pain, hypoesthesia and paresthesia in his right foot and left hand, and severely diminished patellar and Achilles reflexes. There was no cranial nerve involvement or respiratory compromise.  
Lumbar puncture results: total nucleated cell count 3/mm3 (normal 0–7), protein 65 mg/dL (normal 15–45), glucose 53 mg/dL (normal 40–70), negative culture and stain; CSF myelin basic protein 1.63 ng/mL (normal 0–5.5).  
Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy was initially suspected, and he received IVIG (2 g/kg over 5 days).  
EMG/NCS of the left upper and lower extremities revealed a length-dependent polyneuropathy with demyelinating features and multiple sensory and motor conduction blocks. He reported improvement in pain and was ambulatory after IVIG, but continued to have mild lower-extremity pain and a spastic gait.

A 14-year-old boy collapsed during a soccer game three days before presentation. He had gripping anterior chest pain immediately before losing consciousness and developed generalized tonic seizures with median ocular fixation lasting about 10 minutes, which resolved spontaneously without bystander resuscitation. On arrival by ambulance, he was nearly alert; vital signs were stable. At a nearby hospital, physical examination revealed no trauma, dehydration, or respiratory, circulatory, or neurological abnormalities. Electrocardiogram showed no arrhythmias or ST-T–wave changes. Head magnetic resonance imaging and general blood tests, including cardiac enzymes, were unremarkable. He was discharged after overnight observation but referred to our facility for further evaluation because a full cardiovascular workup was not performed at the first hospital.

His medical history included mild asthma and no known cardiac disease, arrhythmia, or family history of sudden death. He reported brief episodes of chest discomfort during exercise over the previous few days. Because of the exertional syncope with preceding chest pain, cardiogenic causes were suspected. Transthoracic echocardiography failed to identify the origin of the left coronary artery in its normal position.

A 50-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of bilateral lower-extremity edema and progressive proteinuria. Four years earlier, routine testing had revealed microscopic hematuria and proteinuria of less than 1 g/day, and she was treated with losartan and atorvastatin for presumed IgA nephropathy based on reports of IgA nephropathy in her family. She had no regular follow-up and remained asymptomatic until several months before presentation when she developed swelling of both lower legs.

Her medications included atorvastatin, losartan, and pentoxifylline. Family history was notable for three brothers who developed kidney failure before age 30 and underwent transplantation (one biopsy inconclusive, another reported as IgA nephropathy), and two of her five sons who also underwent transplantation with one pre-transplant biopsy showing IgA nephropathy. Some affected relatives had hearing loss.

On examination, temperature was 37 °C, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, and there was 2+ pitting edema of the lower extremities. Other findings were unremarkable. Laboratory studies—including complete blood count, electrolytes, liver function tests, thyroid function tests, lipid profile, complement levels, ANA, ANCA, and viral serologies—were normal. Urinalysis showed 4+ blood with numerous red cells and 3+ protein. A 24-hour urine collection demonstrated 1542 mg of protein. Renal ultrasonography revealed normal-sized kidneys with mildly increased echogenicity and an 11 mm cortical cyst in the left kidney. Ophthalmologic examination and audiometry were unremarkable. A kidney biopsy was performed for diagnostic clarification, and prednisolone at 1 mg/kg was initiated pending histopathological results.

A 23-year-old nulliparous woman with no prior medical history presents to the gynecology emergency department with sudden-onset, intense right pelvic pain that began 2 hours earlier. She reports similar but milder episodes over the past year without any vaginal bleeding. Vital signs are normal. On examination, there is right lower-quadrant tenderness; pelvic examination shows a tender right adnexal mass without uterine bleeding. Laboratory tests reveal hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, leukocyte count 15 000/mm³, normal C-reactive protein, and a negative pregnancy test (hCG <5 mIU/mL). Transabdominal ultrasound shows a 65 mm hypoechoic, heterogeneous right ovary with peripherally displaced follicles and decreased Doppler flow. Adjacent to the ovary is a 10 cm cystic adnexal mass. The left ovary appears normal.

A 39-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of a purpuric rash on the lower limbs and left testicular pain. The day before admission he developed persistent lower abdominal pain without fever, gastrointestinal bleeding, dysuria, or urethral discharge. He denied recent infection or trauma. Medical history was notable only for obesity and dyslipidemia; he was on no medications.

On examination, temperature was normal. He had bilateral, symmetrical palpable purpura on the lower extremities. Abdominal examination showed tenderness in the lower quadrants without peritoneal signs. Genitourinary exam revealed a tender, enlarged left testicle with elastic consistency; there was no erythema, fluctuance, or mass. The right testis was normal.

Laboratory tests showed a normal complete blood count and normal coagulation studies. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 22 mm/h (normal ≤20 mm/h) and C-reactive protein was 3.92 mg/dL (normal <0.50 mg/dL). Serum creatinine, urea, liver enzymes, and urinalysis were within normal limits.

Scrotal ultrasound demonstrated enlargement of the left testis with heterogeneous parenchyma and areas without Doppler signal; the right testis had smaller regions of reduced Doppler flow. Abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable.

A 35-year-old man presented with scrotal pain. He first noticed a painless midline scrotal mass two years earlier, which had grown slowly and remained asymptomatic until two days before presentation. He described progressive enlargement, increasing pain, and a sensation of fullness. He denied urologic trauma or infection. 

On examination, there was a 5-cm irregular, tubular structure in the midline scrotum extending from the top of the scrotum to its base, with surrounding erythema, warmth, and marked tenderness. The lesion was nonfluctuant and without discharge. Both testicles were normal without tenderness. There were no signs of Fournier’s gangrene or deep-space infection.

Laboratory evaluation showed a normal white-cell count. Scrotal ultrasound revealed a 7.5 × 1.5 × 1.2 cm avascular fluid-filled tubular structure with thickened walls along the posterior scrotum; testicular morphology and flow were normal. The ultrasound impression was “an unusual complex tubular structure … most likely occlusion of superficial vein.” A CT scan confirmed an avascular tubular structure along the scrotal midline with no deep fat stranding; the CT impression was “most likely a thrombosed vessel.” 

He was diagnosed in the emergency department with septic thrombophlebitis associated with overlying cellulitis and was started on vancomycin, clindamycin, and ceftriaxone.

A 67-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of progressive right proptosis, conjunctival injection, and left frontal headache. During the COVID-19 pandemic, her condition was initially diagnosed via virtual visits as thyroid-associated orbitopathy, although she was biochemically euthyroid. She had no history of smoking, hypertension, or head trauma; her ocular history included mild hyperopia treated with bilateral laser iridotomies.

Over several months, she developed right-eye vision loss, persistent redness, and diplopia on eccentric gaze. She reported hearing an intracranial bruit. Best-corrected visual acuities were 20/140 (right) and 20/40 (left). She could not identify any Ishihara plates with the right eye but read all with the left. Pupils were equal, with a right 2/4 relative afferent pupillary defect. There was no eyelid retraction. Examination revealed 2 mm of right-sided proptosis, a 25 percent reduction in right abduction, and prominent 360° dilated episcleral veins extending to the limbus. Intraocular pressures were 20 mm Hg (right) and 13 mm Hg (left), with pulsatile tonometry mires in the right eye. Fundoscopy showed mild retinal venous tortuosity and subtle optic disc edema. Optical coherence tomography measured average retinal nerve fibre layer thickness of 153 μm (right) versus 113 μm (left).

Noncontrast CT and CT angiography of the orbits demonstrated mild right proptosis, enlargement of the right medial rectus muscle, only slight prominence of the right superior orbital vein, and subtle increased vascularity around the right cavernous internal carotid artery. The neuroradiologic differential diagnosis included thyroid-associated orbitopathy, orbital myositis, and IgG4-related disease. The imaging findings were not sufficiently conclusive for a low-flow carotid–cavernous fistula.

A 47-year-old man with end-stage renal disease from acute pyelonephritis was evaluated for living-related kidney transplantation from his sister. He had received a unit of PRBCs 38 days before evaluation. Both donor and recipient were blood group O Rh(D) positive. Low-resolution HLA typing showed a 5/6 mismatch (HLA-A, ‑B, and ‑DR loci). 

During initial pretransplant work-up (day –27), both complement-dependent cytotoxicity crossmatch (CDC XM) and donor-specific antibody (DSA) lysate crossmatch were negative. As per protocol, a routine CDC XM was repeated 14 days before the scheduled transplant (day –14). The CDC XM showed 40% positivity. A DTT-modified CDC XM to distinguish IgM from IgG antibodies also showed 40% positivity. The transplant was postponed, and repeat samples were sent for blood grouping, antibody screening, and crossmatches.

A 28-year-old G2P1 woman presented 31 days after an elective cesarean delivery under spinal anesthesia with worsening headache and easy fatigability for 3 days. The headache was continuous, global, and had become severe over 24 hours, associated with nausea and malaise. Eight days postoperatively she had developed a mild global headache managed with rest and paracetamol. By day 31 the headache was severe, nonpositional, and unrelieved by rest or analgesics. Vital signs were normal. She was fully conscious and oriented, all meningeal signs were negative, and motor function was intact. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, prothrombin time, partial prothrombin time, and international normalized ratio. Noncontrast CT of the head revealed a layered hypodense crescent-shaped extra-axial collection over the left frontoparietal convexity with areas of linear and crescentic hyperdensity, measuring 15 mm in width with a 13-mm midline shift.

A 33-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 2-year history of progressive bilateral hip pain that was insidious in onset and persisted at rest. He described radiation of the pain to both lower extremities. He denied any history of injury and had no significant medical or surgical history. On examination, both internal and external rotation of the hips exacerbated the pain, but there was full range of motion in both hip joints.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the hips was obtained:
• T1-weighted axial and coronal images showed a mild decrease in the right ischiofemoral space (11 mm) and quadratus femoris space (10 mm), and a mild decrease in the left ischiofemoral space (12 mm) and quadratus femoris space (10 mm).  
• T2-weighted axial and coronal images confirmed similar mild narrowing of both ischiofemoral and quadratus femoris spaces.  
• Short tau inversion recovery sequences demonstrated hyperintense signal (edema) in the proximal iliopsoas and quadratus femoris muscles bilaterally.  
• Diffusion-weighted imaging and apparent diffusion coefficient maps showed no areas of restricted diffusion or altered signal intensities.

A 33-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis diagnosed in 2009 had been treated with interferon-β-1b for 2½ years. She then developed painful erythematous nodules on the anterior aspects of both legs. One week later she noted pain, swelling, and erythema of her left breast, accompanied by dry cough, chills, and fever. On examination, there was a 7×7-cm erythematous tender mass in the left breast; pulmonary and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Multiple 4×5-cm erythema nodosum lesions were present on both legs. She had no history of breast trauma. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 123 mm/hr. Vasculitis tests, including antinuclear antibody, anti–double-stranded DNA, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and complement levels (C3, C4) were normal. Results of angiotensin-converting enzyme level, thyroid function tests, Mantoux test, pulmonary function testing, and abdominopelvic sonography were normal. Serum and urine calcium levels and hand radiographs were normal. A chest CT scan revealed left unilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Bronchoscopy findings were normal. Breast ultrasonography demonstrated a 5×2-cm abscess with peripheral fat inflammation. The abscess was drained, and histopathologic sections showed multiple granulomas composed of epithelioid histiocytes, mononuclear infiltration, and multinucleated giant cells. Bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures of the specimen were negative, and an acid-fast bacillus stain was negative.

A 14-year-old previously healthy girl presented to the emergency department with nausea and headache. Examination revealed only poor oral hygiene; ear, nose, and throat evaluation was otherwise normal. Chest radiography, urinalysis, and a complete blood count were within normal limits, and she was discharged with analgesics.

Three days later she developed right tooth pain. Dental evaluation showed an abscess around the right inferior first molar, and she was prescribed oral amoxicillin and paracetamol.

Two days into therapy, she worsened with submental swelling, dysphagia, and chest pain. On examination her temperature was 39.0°C. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 20 700/mm3 and a C-reactive protein level of 35.7 mg/L. A posteroanterior chest radiograph demonstrated a minimal increase in the cardiothoracic index. Neurologic examination was normal.

An otolaryngology consultation noted purulent secretion from the right inferior first molar, pain-limited mouth opening, and multiple tender lymph nodes in the submental, bilateral submandibular, and anterior cervical regions. Throat and blood cultures were obtained, and she was admitted and started on intravenous ceftriaxone and metronidazole. On hospital day 3, extraction of the right first molar and placement of a Penrose drain were performed. All cultures remained negative.

Despite continued antibiotics, her condition did not improve, and on day 4 vancomycin was added. Immunologic evaluation revealed normal levels of IgA, IgM, IgG, and IgE, and serologic tests for hepatitis and HIV were negative. Cervical magnetic resonance imaging disclosed multiple abscesses in the left carotid sheath extending from the skull base to the level of the carina, with obliteration of the aortopulmonary window, and multiple lymphadenopathy in submental and anterior cervical regions. Ultrasonographically guided percutaneous drainage was attempted but was unsuccessful because of the density of the abscess contents.

A 39-year-old man reports episodes of muscle weakness beginning at age 6, with one attack per month. Attacks ranged from mild weakness to complete paralysis. Early crises occurred with normal potassium levels; in adulthood, attacks worsened with moderate exercise and febrile illness. He required brief hospitalizations; electrocardiograms, brain MRI, and toxicology screens were normal. Renal, thyroid, and liver function tests, Pompe‐disease screening, and lactic acid and pyruvate levels were within normal limits. During his most recent attack, serum CPK ranged from 209 to 873 U/L, and potassium reached 5.3 mEq/L. Electromyographic study (multiMUP) was unremarkable. At age 16, a muscle biopsy showed isolated muscle necrosis with reparative changes; a second biopsy in adulthood revealed denervation changes, regenerating fibers, increased lipid deposition, and intracytoplasmic glycogen. An NGS panel for glycogen storage diseases (PYGM, PGAM1, PFKM, LDHA) was negative. On examination, there was proximal weakness (4+/5) in the shoulders, elbows, hips, and knees, four‐limb hyporeflexia, normal tone, and marked gastrocnemius hypertrophy. A genetic panel for periodic paralysis—including CACN1S, KCNA2, KCNJ2, KCNJ5, and SCN4A—was ordered.

A 24-year-old man was referred for a nonhealing ulcer under the third metatarsal head of his left foot. Two months earlier, he had sustained a skin laceration while walking near a coral reef in Thailand. Abroad, he underwent two courses of antibiotics and surgical debridement, but the ulcer failed to heal.

On examination, the left foot was erythematous, swollen, and warm. Wound cultures grew Proteus species, Providencia species, and Proteus mirabilis; antibiotic therapy was adjusted to sensitivities, resulting in a reduction in erythema and swelling but continued enlargement of the ulcer. MRI of the left foot showed increased uptake at the third toe and metatarsal head, consistent with osteomyelitis. Surgical exploration required amputation of the third toe and metatarsal head.

After tourniquet deflation at the end of surgery, the left foot was noted to be slow to reperfuse. A vascular consultation was obtained. The ankle–brachial pressure index was 0.46 on the left compared with 0.82 on the right. CT femoral angiography demonstrated a short-segment occlusion of the left popliteal artery with reconstitution of the tibio-peroneal trunk through small collateral vessels. On further questioning, the patient acknowledged intermittent claudication with a walking distance of approximately 100 meters.

A 54-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of dull mid-back pain and a two-month history of insidious, progressive weakness and paresthesias in both lower limbs. She noted difficulty holding her footwear in place, although slipping was perceived (suggesting intact posterior column sensation). There were no bowel or bladder disturbances and no history of trauma. On examination, the upper limbs were normal. The lower limbs showed spastic weakness (Medical Research Council grade 4/5 in all major muscle groups), brisk reflexes, and bilateral upgoing plantar responses. Sensation to pinprick, touch, and temperature was decreased below the T12 level, with preserved sacral sensation. Routine hematological and biochemical investigations were within normal limits. MRI of the thoracic spine revealed an intramedullary lesion extending from T9 to T11 that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and nonenhancing after contrast administration. There was no evidence of communication with the central canal. Preoperatively, the leading diagnostic considerations were a syrinx or a cystic teratoma.

A 20-year-old woman presents with a 1-month history of yellow discoloration of the skin over her face, forearms, palms, and soles associated with yellow staining of her clothing. The discoloration is aggravated by exertion. She denied ingestion of carotene-rich foods or new medications, and she has not used cosmetics, dyes, or colored deodorants. She reports no odor and has no psychiatric or family history of similar issues.

On examination, yellowish discoloration is noted over the palms, forearms, toe webs, and face; axillae and groins are unaffected. Under Wood’s lamp examination, there is yellow fluorescence over the face and palms. Blotting sweat onto a white cloth produces a yellow stain, and her clothing exhibits odorless yellow discoloration.

Routine laboratory investigations are normal. Microscopy and culture of skin scrapings are negative for fungus and bacteria.

A 49-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of a left-foot lesion. She first noted a small callus on the plantar surface that repeatedly ruptured and spread until nearly the entire foot was involved. Treatment with antibiotics after three months provided no benefit. Six months later, the foot became swollen, painful, and produced mucopurulent discharge that precluded weight bearing. She walked barefoot habitually but recalled no penetrating injury. She had no history of immunosuppression, diabetes, tuberculosis, or weight loss. 

On examination, the left foot was markedly swollen and deformed, with numerous nodules and draining sinuses over the plantar, medial, and dorsal surfaces. Deep palpation was tender; distal neurovascular function was intact. Ankle and toe movements were painful and restricted. 

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and metabolic panel; the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 93 mm/hr. Blood glucose was normal, and HbA1c was 6.4%. Plain radiographs demonstrated lytic lesions of the tarsal bones and first metatarsal, with disuse osteopenia of the remainder of the metatarsals. On T2-weighted MRI of the foot, there was a “dot-in-circle” appearance adjacent to the tarsal bones and base of the first metatarsal.

A 72-year-old man with hypertension presented to the emergency department with acute chest tightness and a feeling of impending doom. He reported several days of shortness of breath, cough, fatigue, and intermittent diarrhea, and had not sought regular medical care. En route, paramedics noted an afebrile but distressed patient with chest pain and hypoxemia; a field electrocardiogram was interpreted as an acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction. On arrival, his blood pressure was 158/110 mm Hg, and he was placed on high-flow oxygen and moved to a respiratory isolation room while preparations were made for emergent cardiac catheterization. Minutes later, he became unresponsive and pulseless. During resuscitation, he was intubated and briefly regained spontaneous circulation, at which time a second electrocardiogram was obtained. He remained hypotensive, became pulseless again, and after 45 minutes of resuscitative efforts was pronounced dead. A postmortem nasopharyngeal sample tested positive for SARS-CoV-2. No additional laboratory studies were obtained before hemodynamic collapse, and autopsy was not performed.

An 80-year-old woman was referred for bilateral intermittent ear pain. She described mild, left submandibular neck swelling with tenderness that resolved within 2–3 days; these episodes were long-standing but had worsened over several months. Her medical history included hypertension managed with enalapril and amlodipine and hyperlipidemia managed by diet. On examination, her blood pressure was 161/88 mmHg; other vital signs were normal. Physical examination and laryngoscopy were unremarkable except for subtle fullness in the left submandibular region without a discrete mass. A contrast-enhanced CT scan showed a 1.8 × 1.4 × 1.8 cm hyperdense lesion within the left submandibular gland. Because of the discrepancy between imaging and exam, an ultrasound of the neck was performed, and during real-time ultrasound, the lesion was found to be vascular.

An 83-year-old man presented with acute epigastric pain, vomiting, and a sensation of abdominal distention. His past surgical history included appendectomy and cholecystectomy. He had longstanding hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine and, three months earlier, required nine days of mechanical ventilation for aspiration pneumonia during a hypothyroid coma; since then he had been fed via a nasogastric tube. On examination, he was afebrile, with blood pressure 128/79 mmHg, pulse 98 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. The abdomen was distended with mild epigastric tenderness but no peritoneal signs. Laboratory tests showed WBC 12 800/μL, CRP 1.27 mg/dL, BUN 41.7 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.59 mg/dL. A chest radiograph showed no subdiaphragmatic free air; an abdominal radiograph suggested paralytic small bowel. CT scan demonstrated extensive intramural gas within the stomach wall, IFG around the stomach, and HPVG, predominantly in the left hepatic lobe, without ascites. Arterial blood gas analysis was normal (pH 7.40). An upper gastrointestinal series with water-soluble contrast revealed no perforation in the stomach.

A 29-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 2, was admitted to the emergency department 7 days after an elective repeat cesarean section at term for breech presentation. She reported severe lower abdominal pain that began as mild discomfort 1 day earlier and worsened, with colicky exacerbations. Three days after surgery, she noted a marked decrease in lochia and on day 4 a sudden cessation of vaginal bleeding and discharge.

On examination, she was alert and oriented. Vital signs: temperature 37.4 °C, blood pressure 140/80 mm Hg, heart rate 105 beats/min. There was a painful, palpable swelling on the right side above the pelvis without abdominal distension or peritoneal signs. The Pfannenstiel incision was healing well; no vaginal bleeding was noted.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, hematocrit 35%, platelets 280 × 10^9/L, white cells 10.5 × 10^9/L. Urinalysis was unremarkable.

Transabdominal ultrasound revealed a centrally involuted uterus and, on the right lower abdomen, a 25 cm × 8 cm oval mass with thickened walls and complex internal echoes, apparently suggesting an organized hematoma. No free fluid or active bleeding was seen in the pouch of Douglas. After inadequate pain relief and new signs of peritoneal irritation two hours later, an exploratory laparotomy was planned.

A 57-year-old woman was referred for an enlarging neck mass and hoarseness of 5 days’ duration. She reported a very hard, fixed lump on the right side of her neck that had been present for months. She had intermittent treatment for hyperthyroidism over the past 30 years but no recent follow-up, and she denied symptoms of thyrotoxicosis.  
On examination, she was afebrile, blood pressure 130/90 mm Hg, pulse 76 beats/min, and respirations 20 breaths/min. A firm, non-tender thyroid nodule approximately 5 × 4 cm was palpated on the right. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 6460/mm^3, hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, platelets 295 × 10^3/mm^3, ESR 19 mm/hr, CRP <0.2 mg/dL. Thyroid studies: TSH 0.07 µIU/mL (0.4–4.5), free T4 3.86 ng/dL (0.7–2), TBII 51% (0–15), thyroglobulin 493 ng/dL (2–60), antithyroid microsomal antibody 3.1 U/mL (0–8), thyroglobulin antibody 22 U/mL (negative).  
Chest radiograph showed a right-to-left tracheal shift. Thyroid ultrasound revealed a 4 cm irregular, hypoechoic nodule with scattered dense calcifications in the right lobe and no lymphadenopathy.  
Fine-needle aspiration with aspiration technique yielded scant cytologic material; no malignant cells were seen, and an adenomatous goiter was suspected.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a 4.3 × 4.0 cm nodular lesion occupying most of the right thyroid lobe with peripheral calcification and severely calcified margins. The right vocal cord was fixed in a paramedian position, consistent with paralysis.  
Given the large, solid lesion with evidence of recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement, a surgical approach was planned for diagnosis and treatment.

A 23-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of heavy menstrual bleeding, requiring pad changes every 3–4 hours. She reported working long hours without rest and had taken excess acetaminophen for body pain over the preceding 4 months. She had no personal or family history of bleeding disorders, no gynecological abnormalities, and no weight loss. On examination, she was pale; the rest of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, leukocytes 5.4×10^3/µL, and platelets 268×10^3/µL. Bleeding time was prolonged at 9 minutes 11 seconds (Ivy method). Coagulation studies revealed a partial thromboplastin time of 59.2 seconds and a prothrombin time of 33.1 seconds (INR 5.97), both of which corrected on a mixing test without incubation. von Willebrand factor antigen and activity and fibrinogen were normal; factor X activity was 8%. She was started on iron and folic acid and acetaminophen was discontinued. Two weeks later, bleeding time normalized but PT and PTT remained prolonged.

She then developed acute severe dizziness with gait instability and was admitted. Repeat studies showed PTT 38.5 seconds and PT 21.2 seconds (INR 2.51), with normal liver-function tests. A full coagulation factor assay demonstrated factor II 41%, factor VII 3%, factor IX 24%, and factor X 52%; no inhibitors were detected. On further history, she disclosed six months of consuming primarily high-energy drinks with inadequate nutritional intake.

A 62-year-old man underwent colonoscopy for investigation of anemia and positive fecal occult blood tests, which revealed a 4-cm adenocarcinoma at the rectosigmoid junction. Staging studies—including CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis; MRI of the liver; and FDG PET—showed a solitary segment 8 hepatic lesion highly suspicious for metastasis. After multidisciplinary discussion, he was scheduled for laparoscopic anterior resection followed by chemotherapy and planned resection of the liver lesion.

His medical history included type 2 diabetes, hypertension, asthma, and a sleeve gastrectomy performed 4 years earlier for obesity. That procedure had been complicated by spillage of gastric contents into the peritoneal cavity, although details of intra-operative decontamination are unknown.

At laparoscopy, multiple peritoneal nodules with the gross appearance of metastatic disease were observed throughout the abdomen, including in the right upper quadrant, right flank, and pelvis, where they were fusing the rectosigmoid colon to the anterior abdominal wall. The largest lesion measured 2 × 3 cm. The anterior resection was aborted, a diverting colostomy was fashioned proximal to the tumor, and biopsies of the peritoneal nodules were obtained.

A 37-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 16 2/7 weeks of a spontaneously conceived pregnancy presented with a 2-day history of left lower abdominal pain radiating to her back and left thigh. She denied vaginal bleeding, urinary symptoms, or bowel changes. Her only prior obstetrical history was a normal vaginal delivery 16 months earlier.

On examination, her temperature was 37.3 °C, blood pressure 100/55 mm Hg, and heart rate 84 beats/min. The abdomen was tender without guarding or rebound. Pelvic examination revealed a small amount of vaginal blood and no palpable adnexal mass; the uterine size was appropriate for 17 weeks’ gestation.

Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 114 g/L, white cell count 6.6×10^9/L, C-reactive protein 12.7 mg/L, and normal renal function. Abdominal ultrasonography excluded nephrolithiasis and appendicitis. Obstetrical ultrasound confirmed a single viable intrauterine fetus consistent with dates; the adnexa were not commentated on. She was discharged with outpatient management for presumed constipation.

Four days later, she returned with severe abdominal pain and signs of peritoneal irritation. Repeat labs showed a hemoglobin drop to 101 g/L; the white cell count remained stable. Ultrasonography again confirmed a viable intrauterine pregnancy and demonstrated a poorly vascularised left para-uterine mass measuring 7×5 cm that was tender on transducer pressure.

A 16-year-old male was referred for orthodontic treatment. He was in good general health, with an unremarkable medical and family history and no history of trauma. Oral examination showed moderate hygiene and mild gingivitis but no soft-tissue lesions. Intraoral inspection revealed an unusually large tooth in the right lower lateral incisor–canine region, with a developmental groove separating the crown and extending into the gingival sulcus. Percussion was non-tender, warm and cold tests elicited no pain, and electrical pulp testing showed normal vitality. There was no mobility of any teeth and all other teeth appeared normal. A panoramic radiograph of the mandible demonstrated that teeth 42 and 43 shared a single root and single root canal.

An 8-year-old girl presented with a 5-month history of brief (5–20 sec) paroxysmal episodes of altered consciousness and postural instability, occasionally accompanied by facial grimacing, upper-limb tremors, and falls. Each event was always preceded by stereotyped head tilting against one shoulder, back and neck hyperextension, and stretching of the arms. Episodes occurred only during wakefulness, were followed by prompt and complete recovery, and increased in frequency over time. There was no family history of neurologic disorders or syncope. Two prior hospital admissions with blood chemistries, neurologic and cardiovascular assessments, and brain MRI (showing only a quadrigeminal cistern lipoma) were unremarkable; standard supra-aortic trunk and transcranial Doppler were normal.

On a 4-day video-polysomnography (EEG, electrooculography, electromyography, ECG, respiratory monitoring, oximetry), 50–100 typical events were recorded daily and could be voluntarily provoked. Each began with head tilt (more often to the right), neck hyperextension, and arm stretching, followed by a grimacing smile or behavioral arrest with variable loss of tone. During events, EEG showed bursts of monomorphic 2–3 Hz slow-wave activity lasting 3–12 sec, predominantly frontotemporal and mainly ipsilateral to the head tilt. Mild sinus tachycardia was noted; oximetry and blood pressure were not measurable due to artifacts. Provocative maneuvers including Valsalva and passive head movement did not trigger episodes. The patient described a compulsive urge to stretch to relieve a numbness sensation in her chest, shoulders, and head, which she sought rather than resisted.

Extracranial and transcranial color-coded duplex sonography at rest was normal. During head rotation and declination tests, transcranial duplex revealed a reversal of flow with a holosystolic pattern in the right vertebral artery V4 segment when the head was turned 45° to the left (supine and sitting), and a milder mirror-pattern in the left vertebral artery with right rotation. Upon return to neutral, flow normalized within 1–2 minutes, with gradual restoration of diastolic flow.

A 21-year-old man was found unconscious at home. Paramedics documented severe hypoglycemia, which normalized after IV glucose. On arrival at the emergency department he was tachypneic (30/min), SpO₂ 98% on a face mask, heart rate 135/min, blood pressure 96/67 mmHg, temperature 39.6°C, and Glasgow Coma Scale 9. There were no meningeal signs; pupils were equal and reactive, but both eyes were deviated to the left. He had right-sided hemiparesis, pressure sores on the right flank and sacrum, and scant, concentrated urine. Arterial blood gas analysis showed severe metabolic acidosis and hyperkalemia. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia. CT of the head and cervical spine was unremarkable. Because of agitation and airway compromise he was intubated and transferred to the ICU. 

In the ICU, broad-spectrum antibiotics (imipenem and amikacin) were started after samples were obtained for CSF, blood, urine, and bronchial cultures. CSF analysis showed no leukocytosis, normal protein and glucose ratios, clear appearance, and negative rapid tests for N. meningitidis, S. pneumoniae, and H. influenzae. Toxicology revealed amphetamine in urine (no ethanol). Laboratory tests showed acute kidney injury (creatinine 395 μmol/L, BUN 21.5 mmol/L), very high creatine kinase, and procalcitonin elevated to 1640 ng/mL.

A 52-year-old woman presented with severe, continuous, dull epigastric pain aggravated by left lateral decubitus position and food intake. She denied prior similar episodes but reported vague discomfort with fatty foods. She had no comorbidities, no medications, and no allergies. She was a former light smoker and occasional alcohol drinker, with three prior cesarean deliveries. On examination, her abdomen was soft with tenderness in the epigastrium and right upper quadrant; there was no jaundice. Labs showed: ALT 859 µ/L, AST 195 µ/L, conjugated bilirubin 21.38 mg/dL, unconjugated bilirubin 1.38 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 337 µ/L; lipase and coagulation studies were normal. Transabdominal ultrasound revealed a large gallbladder with multiple sub-centimeter stones, a slightly thickened wall, and a smaller saccular structure beside it, suspicious for gallbladder duplication; the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts were not dilated. An endoluminal ultrasound confirmed a double gallbladder and detected a 0.4 cm common bile duct stone, which was removed by ERCP. The second gallbladder was not seen on ERCP. To map the biliary tree before surgery, an MRCP was performed and “clearly demonstrated the 2 gallbladders, one filled with stones and the other without filling defects,” each with its own cystic duct draining separately into the bile duct.

An 8-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of an unaesthetic appearance of her maxillary central incisors, which were positioned behind the lower anterior teeth. Her medical and dental history was non‐contributory, and there was no family history of Class III malocclusion. On examination, the permanent maxillary right and left central incisors were both in crossbite; the maxillary lateral incisors had not yet fully erupted. She was in the early mixed dentition stage and had a bilateral Class I molar relationship, with a 2 mm overjet and 100% overbite. The maxillary dental midline was coincident with the facial midline, whereas the mandibular midline deviated 2 mm to the left. Mild spacing was present in the maxillary arch, with sufficient mesiodistal space for labial movement of the maxillary central incisors. A panoramic radiograph showed no bone or dental pathology. A lateral cephalometric radiograph showed no evidence of a basal skeletal discrepancy between the maxilla and mandible.

A 7-year-old boy, the second child of healthy nonconsanguineous Lebanese parents, was referred for evaluation of lifelong hypotonia and failure to thrive. Pregnancy was notable for placental abruption and unexplained polyhydramnios. At 35 weeks’ gestation, he was delivered by emergency cesarean section for fetal distress. Birth weight was 2340 g (25th percentile), length 47 cm (50th percentile), and head circumference 36 cm (>97th percentile). 

At birth, he exhibited generalized hypotonia, absence of spontaneous movements, intermittent lower-limb tremors, and severe respiratory distress requiring intubation and transfer to the NICU. Initial metabolic and infectious evaluations were normal. Cardiac examination was unremarkable.
