Brain MRI showed slowed flow in superficial cortical veins and asymmetric flow in both transverse sinuses without thrombophlebitis. Continuous EEG monitoring revealed slowed cerebral activity with intermittent burst suppression. CSF neurotransmitter analysis showed L-dopa 31 nmol/L (reference <30 nmol/L), low homovanillic acid (<543 nmol/L; reference 601–1397 nmol/L), and low 5-hydroxy-indole acetic acid (<383 nmol/L; reference 382–949 nmol/L).

At one month of age, he remained hypotonic and areflexic, with no visual tracking or blinking and absent intercostal muscle activity. He had marked plagiocephaly, persistent upper-limb contractures, epicanthal folds, thickened nares, and thick lips. He developed recurrent generalized clonic seizures treated with valproic acid. Ophthalmologic examination disclosed a right anterior subcapsular cataract. He underwent tracheotomy and gastrostomy. Repeat metabolic testing, including amino acid and organic acid chromatography, was normal. Muscle biopsy demonstrated hypertrophy with mitochondrial and neurogenic features. Congenital disorders of glycosylation and Prader-Willi syndrome were excluded by genetic and metabolic studies. 

Despite maximal supportive care, tracheotomy weaning remained impossible and nutrition was provided exclusively by gastrostomy. By age seven, he continued to have profound hypotonia, failure to thrive (weight 16 kg and height 102 cm, both <1st percentile), and macrocephaly (head circumference 56 cm, >97th percentile). He had no recurrent infections and was up-to-date with immunizations.

A 62-year-old woman presented in March 2017 with recrudescence of severe, deep throbbing headache localized to the right retro-orbital region and new-onset posterior nasal drip. One year earlier, she had persistent right retro-orbital headache unresponsive to NSAIDs. Neurologic examination was normal. Ophthalmic examination revealed a normal fundus and eye pressure. Initial brain CT showed obliteration of the right sphenoidal sinus without brain tissue abnormalities; she was treated for presumed sinusitis with oral antibiotics and corticosteroids, with partial improvement but persistent latent headache.

To better characterize the sinus lesion, MRI was obtained. The right sphenoid sinus contained a soft-tissue mass with mucosal thickening that was hyperintense on T2-weighted images with a central T2 hypointense core, showed low signal on T2* GRE, and was hyperintense on T1-weighted images. After intravenous contrast, the mucosa enhanced but the central mass did not. The left sphenoid sinus had only minimal reactive mucosal thickening.

A subsequent dedicated CT scan of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated complete opacification of the right sphenoid sinus with internal streaky calcifications and a sclerotic, bowed bony wall without cortical erosion. Other sinuses showed minimal mucosal thickening without sclerosis, erosion, or calcifications. Laboratory studies including immune and inflammatory markers were within normal limits.

A 16-year-old US-born Hispanic female with no past medical history presented with 4 weeks of right breast swelling and an additive pattern of pain and swelling in the left wrist, left elbow, bilateral knees, and ankles. She had been treated with multiple courses of antibiotics without improvement and developed painful red nodules on her shins and thighs 2 days after starting clindamycin. She denied fever, weight loss, night sweats, cough, shortness of breath, or gastrointestinal symptoms.

On examination, her right breast had an 11 cm area of firm, poorly circumscribed induration in the outer quadrants, with a 3 cm tender fluctuant patch above the areola; the left breast was normal. She had active arthritis of both knees and ankles. There were erythematous, tender nodules on the lower extremities consistent with erythema nodosum.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11 g/dL, WBC 10.6×10^3/µL with 77% neutrophils, ESR 37 mm/h, and IgE 447 kU/L. HIV testing, QuantiFERON-TB, TSH, vitamin D levels, and cultures of blood and breast fluid were negative. Rheumatologic workup including ANA, p-ANCA, c-ANCA, rheumatoid factor, complements, and ACE/lysozyme levels was within normal limits.

Right breast ultrasound demonstrated a 3.3 cm-thick complex area with internal vascularity. Sonographically guided needle aspiration fluid was sent for bacterial, fungal, and AFB studies. Vacuum-assisted core biopsy revealed chronic lobular inflammation with noncaseating granulomas and neutrophilic microabscesses. Chest radiograph was normal. Ophthalmologic exam revealed no uveitis or episcleritis. Cultures of breast aspirate were negative for bacterial, fungal, and AFB organisms.

A 76-year-old woman with diabetes presented with progressive abdominal enlargement below the umbilicus and purulent discharge from a cutaneous fistula on the left side of the umbilicus. She was afebrile and had mild tenderness over the lower abdomen. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 9800/μL; C-reactive protein and tumor markers (carcinoembryonic antigen 0.50 ng/mL, CA19-9 6.39 U/mL, α-fetoprotein 1.3 ng/mL) were within normal limits. Urinalysis revealed pyuria (10–19/hpf). Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a well-enhanced mass in the lower umbilical area involving the rectus abdominis muscle. FDG-PET–CT showed high uptake in the mass (SUV max 16.49). MRI revealed the mass to be isointense on T2-weighted imaging, hyperintense on diffusion-weighted imaging, and connected medially to a fibrous structure presumed to be the urachus; the lateral border of the mass was irregular and appeared contiguous with small-bowel loops. Cystoscopy revealed no apparent tumor or swelling suggestive of a submucosal lesion, and urine cytology was class 2.

A 77-year-old man presented with hematemesis associated with nausea and epigastric pain. He had a history of hypertension, bilateral hip and knee replacements, and chronic non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug and aspirin use. On arrival, his blood pressure was 104/63 mmHg, heart rate 71 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 37°C, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Abdominal examination revealed a non-distended abdomen with epigastric tenderness without guarding, rebound tenderness, or palpable mass. Laboratory tests showed a lipase level of 50 U/L (reference range 0–60 U/L); bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyl transferase, aspartate aminotransferase, and alanine aminotransferase levels were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated inflammatory stranding around the second and third segments of the duodenum and an abnormal course of the proximal duodenum, which traveled posteriorly and superiorly before the third segment crossed the midline at an unusually high position. MRI of the abdomen was performed to exclude a pancreatic head lesion and was negative. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy confirmed duodenitis.

A 20-year-old woman was admitted with a 1-week history of high fever, altered sensorium, psychosocial withdrawal, minimal speech, immobility, and urinary and fecal retention. She had a 1-year history of polyarthralgias, oral ulcers, and alopecia but had not sought medical care. Seven months earlier she was diagnosed with hypertension and treated with losartan. She had two remote episodes of pulmonary tuberculosis, treated successfully. 

On examination, temperature was 100°F, blood pressure 150/110 mmHg, pulse 130/min. She was conscious but mute, unresponsive to commands, with waxy flexibility and variable increased tone. She made no spontaneous movement except brief eye tracking. Neck rigidity was present without meningeal signs. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal exams were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL, WBC 12 ×10^3/μL, platelets 235 ×10^3/μL, ESR 76 mm/hr, creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, and 24-hr urinary protein 720 mg. Serum electrolytes, liver function tests, calcium, phosphate, and uric acid were normal. CSF analysis was normal. Chest radiograph showed patchy consolidation and calcified hilar nodes. Head CT was normal. She was treated empirically with ceftriaxone and acyclovir; cultures (blood, urine, CSF, sputum) remained negative. 

Given persistent symptoms, an MRI of the brain was obtained, showing central white-matter nodular demyelination, most likely post-inflammatory.

A 76-year-old Indian woman with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus (hemoglobin A1c 11.2%) and baseline dementia presented with 4 weeks of worsening confusion and 1 week of falls toward her left side. Her family reported increased visual hallucinations and loss of conversational ability. She also had a dry cough that began 1 month earlier. On examination, she was oriented only to self, had left-sided neglect, 5/5 strength on the right and 2/5 strength in the left upper extremity and 3/5 in the left lower extremity; sensory examination and cranial nerves were intact. Lungs were clear. Laboratory studies showed serum glucose 268 mg/dL and white blood cell count 6200 cells/µL with 87% neutrophils. CT of the head revealed a subacute right subdural hematoma and multiple right-sided ring-enhancing lesions. MRI of the brain demonstrated multiple enhancing lesions with vasogenic edema in the right parietal lobe, the largest measuring 1.4 × 1.9 × 2.1 cm. She was started on intravenous vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and metronidazole, and received levetiracetam. Lumbar puncture showed low opening pressure, CSF glucose 79 mg/dL, protein 105 mg/dL, and WBC 225 cells/µL with neutrophil predominance. Chest CT revealed a necrotic mediastinal soft tissue mass involving the esophagus and multiple bilateral upper lobe pulmonary nodules. She was placed on airborne precautions, and three sputum AFB smears, cultures, and PCR attempts were inadequate. Bronchoscopy with lavage and transbronchial fine needle aspiration was performed.

A 40-year-old woman presented with intermittent right lower abdominal pain of 1 year’s duration, associated with constipation. Her obstetric history was notable for multiple pregnancies and a cesarean section 25 years earlier; there was no other significant medical or surgical history.

On examination, an oval swelling, 6 cm by 5 cm, was palpated in the right flank. The mass had a smooth surface, firm consistency, and was partially reducible; a cough impulse was present. Mild tenderness was elicited on palpation of the right flank; no other abdominal masses were found.

Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a heterogeneously hyperechoic lesion measuring 55 mm × 44 mm × 11 mm with an internal linear strand in the lower right infra-umbilical abdominal wall. The lesion lay between the lateral margin of the right rectus abdominis and the medial border of the right internal oblique muscle, extending superficially toward the external oblique, with a neck measuring 11 mm × 10 mm. The lesion was partially reducible on compression. A CT scan was not feasible.

A 30-year-old man with no comorbidities and a body-mass index of 31.2 kg/m2, living in Dhaka, presented on hospital day 4 of a confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection with an 11-day history of fever (maximum 39.4 °C), 2 days of headache and generalized body ache, and one episode of vomiting fresh blood at home. He had been treated as an outpatient with paracetamol, ivermectin, doxycycline, famotidine, zinc, and vitamins C and D. On admission his temperature was 38.6 °C, pulse 76/min, blood pressure 110/79 mm Hg, respiratory rate 24/min, and SpO2 99% on room air. Examination was unremarkable without signs of dehydration. Chest X-ray showed ill-defined ground-glass opacities in the lower lung zones bilaterally, with an overall radiographic score of 2. Complete blood count revealed a leukocyte count of 5560/µL, platelet count of 170,000/µL, hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL with a mean corpuscular volume of 60 fL and mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration of 30.3%, consistent with microcytic hypochromic anemia. Given the endemic season, a blood specimen for dengue serology was sent, and hemoglobin electrophoresis was ordered to evaluate the anemia.

A 15-year-old healthy female presented with a 6-month history of a slowly progressing eruption on her upper arms. The lesions began on the right arm and extended to the left arm; they were not pruritic but were sometimes tender. Her medical history was notable only for a nevus sebaceous excised 4 years earlier. On examination, clusters of erythematous, keratotic papules coalesced into arcuate plaques on both upper arms. A punch biopsy of a lesion on the right arm showed short eosinophilic elastic fibers penetrating the epidermis and follicular infundibulae. She completed a 2-month course of triamcinolone 0.1% cream and a 4-month course of tretinoin 0.05% cream without improvement.

A 63-year-old man presented with an 8-week history of chronic cough and hemoptysis. He emigrated from India 21 years ago, last visited there 5 months ago, and denied any occupational or industrial exposures, including mining, soot, or biomass fuels. He was a lifelong nonsmoker.  

Vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, there were no remarkable findings in the head, neck, or chest; breath sounds were slightly decreased in the left lower lung field without crackles or wheezes.  

Laboratory testing included a blood QuantiFERON-TB Gold assay, which was positive.  

Chest CT showed a 4-cm area of consolidation in the superior segment of the left lower lobe, abutting the hilum, with prominent left hilar and para-aortic lymph nodes. A CT scan from 3 years earlier had been normal.  

Flexible bronchoscopy revealed an area of raised, velvety, black mucosal discoloration with narrowing of the superior segmental bronchus of the left lower lobe. An adult bronchoscope could not be negotiated past the stenosis, so a pediatric bronchoscope was used.  

Endobronchial biopsies and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) were obtained from the lesion. Endobronchial ultrasound–guided fine-needle aspiration of the left hilar and subcarinal lymph nodes was also performed.  

Cytology from the lymph-node aspirate was negative for malignancy. Histologic sections of the bronchial biopsies showed a submucosal collection of macrophages/histiocytes containing abundant intracytoplasmic black pigment; no granulomas or malignant cells were identified. Immunohistochemical staining for S100 and Melan-A was negative.

A 35-year-old man from rural north India presented with a one-month history of a progressively enlarging, central abdominal lump. Three weeks after the lump appeared, he developed intermittent high-grade fever and dull, aching abdominal pain. He had no significant past medical history. On examination, there was a moderately tender mass in the umbilical region. There was non-tender thickening of the right spermatic cord without scrotal or testicular abnormalities; inguinal nodes were barely palpable, and there was no lower-extremity edema. Complete blood counts and blood chemistry were within normal limits, and blood cultures were sterile. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a large, well-defined, unilocular cyst measuring 20 × 14 × 23 cm located behind the right colon and terminal ileum, without features suggestive of an abscess; the remainder of the abdominal organs appeared normal. Contrast-enhanced CT scan confirmed these findings but did not clarify the origin or etiology of the cyst. Because of diagnostic uncertainty and ongoing symptoms, the abdomen was explored surgically, revealing a large retroperitoneal cyst posterior to the right colon, mesocolon, and terminal ileum that stretched adjacent structures; a well-defined avascular plane allowed complete excision of the cyst, and a conglomeration of grossly dilated lymphatics near its upper pole was also removed.

An 81-year-old Caucasian man with hypertension and hyperlipidemia presented with one day of complete right-eye vision loss, jaw claudication, and bitemporal headaches. He also reported 1–2 months of weight loss, progressive fatigue, decreased oral intake, and severe bilateral lower extremity pain and edema. On examination, he appeared cachectic and ill, with severe anasarca and tenderness over both temporomandibular joints; visual testing confirmed right-sided vision loss. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 64 mm/hr and a serum creatinine level of 11.9 mg/dL. Urinalysis revealed moderate hematuria (10–20 red cells per high-power field) and proteinuria (urine protein–creatinine ratio, 1.15). Serologic testing was notable for a high-titer p-ANCA anti–myeloperoxidase IgG (79 AU/mL; normal <19 AU/mL) and a weakly positive antinuclear antibody titer (1:80); c-ANCA anti–proteinase-3 and complement levels were within normal limits. A right temporal artery biopsy demonstrated vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis and leukocytoclasis in a branch of the temporal artery. Chest computed tomography revealed multiple ground-glass opacities in the right upper and middle lobes and lingula, consistent with interstitial lung disease.

An 8-year-old boy with known β-thalassemia intermedia presented with 6 days of generalized body swelling, 3 days of fever, and 1 day of seizures.  
- Vital signs: temperature 39.0°C, blood pressure 145/76 mmHg, heart rate 115 beats/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.  
- General: pale child with “chipmunk” facies, periorbital and generalized edema.  
- Chest and cardiovascular exams were unremarkable.  
- Neurologic: Glasgow Coma Scale 12 (E4V3M5), no neck stiffness; motor tone normal, strength 4/5 in all limbs, reflexes 2+.  
- Growth parameters: weight −3 SD, height −2 SD for age.  
- History: untreated sore throat in the preceding week; up-to-date vaccinations except no COVID-19 vaccine.  
In the emergency department, he experienced a brief tonic–clonic seizure with urinary incontinence and postictal drowsiness, treated with IV diazepam and levetiracetam.  
A working differential diagnosis included hypertensive encephalopathy in the setting of thalassemia, renal artery stenosis, meningoencephalitis, and acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.

A 44-year-old previously healthy man was referred for evaluation of fever and fatigue. Over the prior 10 days, he had daily fevers up to 38.5°C without chills or sweats, and fatigue for 30 days. He also reported chronic constipation that had worsened over the past month. He denied weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratories showed normal blood counts, mild elevations of C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and trace protein on urinalysis. Tests for mononucleosis-like agents were negative. The patient was hospitalized; fever (38–38.5°C) was confirmed but abated with naproxen. Echocardiography, blood cultures, and eye funduscopic examination were all unremarkable. Colonoscopy showed no abnormalities. Abdominal and pelvic CT scans revealed mural thickening of the sigmoid colon with nodular densities in the adjacent adipose tissue and numerous lymph nodes up to 1.0 cm near the inferior mesenteric vessels. An intestinal lymphoma was initially suspected, and laparoscopic rectosigmoidectomy with lymph node sampling was planned.

A 30-year-old man presented with progressive dyspnea, bilateral lower-limb swelling, and abdominal pain beginning three days after a honey bee sting on the dorsal aspect of his right foot. His only past medical history was a stab wound to the heart repaired two years earlier. On examination, blood pressure was 80/50 mmHg, pulse 120 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 89% on room air. Heart sounds were muffled, and breath sounds were decreased at both lung bases. The abdomen was distended with generalized tenderness and shifting dullness. The sting site was red with central necrosis. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 12,000/mm3; other studies were normal. Contrast CT of the chest and abdomen demonstrated massive pericardial effusion, bilateral pleural effusions, and ascites. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a normal left ventricular ejection fraction and massive pericardial effusion with signs of cardiac tamponade.

A 37-year-old primiparous woman presented with a 1.5-year history of a slowly enlarging, asymptomatic lesion in her umbilicus. She denied prior piercing or trauma. Her medical history was notable for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy with ovarian dermoid cystectomy 10 years earlier. Menstrual cycles were regular with normal flow. On examination, there was a well-circumscribed, firm, bilobulated, 20 × 22 mm nodule in the umbilicus that was nontender. An incisional biopsy was performed with a differential diagnosis of adnexal tumor, umbilical granuloma, and metastasis. Histopathologic assessment demonstrated a few dilated glands lined by stratified columnar epithelium in a secretory phase, surrounded by a hypercellular stroma. Immunohistochemical staining showed estrogen-receptor positivity in glandular nuclei and diffuse CD10 positivity in the stroma, with Ki-67 positivity below 1% in epithelial cell nuclei.

A 2-year-old girl was brought for evaluation of inability to walk and increased urinary frequency since birth. She was delivered at home without prenatal care. Apart from ambulation, all developmental milestones were normal. On examination, vital signs were stable. The spine had levoscoliosis. There was spastic paralysis of both lower limbs with reduced knee and ankle reflexes and muscle atrophy.  
Spinal radiography (anteroposterior view) showed levoscoliosis centered in the dorsal spine and a butterfly vertebra at T7.  
MRI of the brain was normal. MRI of the spine demonstrated:  
• A butterfly vertebra at T7 and partial fusion of posterior elements of D9–D11 on the right.  
• Marked narrowing of the spinal canal from D9–D12, with complete obliteration at D10–D11.  
• An empty dural sac without spinal cord or nerve roots from D5–D9 and from D12 to the upper border of L2.  
• A relatively thickened spinal cord extending from L2–L4.  
• No exiting nerve roots at D7–D8 and D11–D12.  
• Mild levoscoliosis at D9–D10 and partial sacralization of L5.  
• A partially visualized, overdistended bladder with irregular luminal outline and mild left hydroureteronephrosis.  
Blood tests, echocardiography, abdominal ultrasound, ophthalmic and audiological examinations were all normal. Genetic testing revealed no specific syndrome. Urine culture grew bacteria consistent with cystitis.

A 55-year-old HIV-positive man presented with a one-day history of spontaneous left hip pain. He had a similar, self-limited episode in the right hip 10 years earlier. His HIV infection had been diagnosed 6 years before, and he was taking emtricitabine/tenofovir and ritonavir-boosted darunavir. He also had hypercholesterolaemia and treated syphilis. He was a non-smoker and drank alcohol only infrequently. 

On examination, his temperature was 38.1 °C, and he was unable to weight-bear on the left side. Active and passive left hip flexion was limited to 20–75°, and rotation was 10° in each direction; the hip rested in 30° of flexion. The remainder of his musculoskeletal and neurological examination was unremarkable.

Initial blood tests showed a white-cell count of 8.3 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein < 3 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 10 mm/h, creatine kinase 88 U/L, and negative ANA and ANCA. Plain radiographs of the pelvis demonstrated only mild bilateral osteoarthritis.

He was admitted for analgesia and observation, but over the next 48 hours his C-reactive protein rose to 109 mg/L and his erythrocyte sedimentation rate to 90 mm/h; the white-cell count remained 8.1 × 10^9/L. MRI of the hips showed a large left hip effusion and a moderate right hip effusion. An aspiration of the left hip was performed under local anaesthetic and yielded turbid yellow fluid, which was sent for microbiological culture and cytological analysis.

A 33‐year‐old woman presented with a 4‐month history of a palpable right thyroid mass. She denied symptoms of thyroid dysfunction, airway compromise, or family history of thyroid disease. Thyrotropin was 1.4 mIU/L (0.4–4.5 mIU/L).  
Ultrasound revealed a 1.7 × 2.2 × 1.7 cm solid hypoechoic nodule with irregular margins in the lower pole of the right lobe. CT of the neck showed a partially calcified right thyroid nodule measuring 2.2 × 1.8 × 1.5 cm. Ultrasound‐guided fine‐needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) was read as a follicular neoplasm (Bethesda IV) with abundant Hürthle cells and occasional macrophages; Afirma GSC was negative for mutations.  
Three weeks after FNAB, she developed progressive right thyroid pain, enlargement, and mild odynophagia without fever. On examination, vital signs were normal and the right lobe was exquisitely tender. Repeat ultrasound showed enlargement of the nodule to 3.9 × 3.4 × 3.5 cm with surrounding edema. CT demonstrated a 4.7 × 3.1 × 2.8 cm heterogeneous right lobe lesion with suspected intranodular hemorrhage, tracheal displacement, and reactive cervical lymph nodes.  
She was treated with amoxicillin–clavulanic acid for one week, with partial relief of pain and size reduction but persistent swelling. Two months after the FNAB, because of ongoing pain and concern for persistent infection or malignancy despite the negative Afirma result, a right thyroid lobectomy was recommended.

A 12-year-old boy presented with decayed upper and lower anterior teeth. His first two years of life were unremarkable, but he subsequently exhibited poor weight and height gain, scalp and eyebrow hair loss, progressive skin tightening, and difficulty walking; mental development was normal. He had been treated for acute hepatitis and was the second-born of nonconsanguineous parents, with a healthy sibling and no family history of similar features.

On examination, he appeared a wizened old person, with a thin build, poor nutrition, short stature, abnormal gait, coarse, shiny, atrophic skin, and loss of subcutaneous fat over the extremities. He had pectus carinatum. Systemic findings included impaired vision, slurred speech, memory loss, dyspnea, palpitations, and restricted joint mobility with inability to stand or walk. Extraoral examination revealed frontal bossing, a beaked nose, prominent eyes, a high-pitched voice, hypoplastic maxilla and mandible with midfacial flattening giving a “plucked bird” appearance, an interincisal opening of 21 mm, and limited lateral temporomandibular joint movements. Intraorally, the teeth appeared normal in size relative to the small jaw, with multiple carious and fractured teeth, a high-arched palate, and partial anodontia.

Laboratory studies showed a serum cholesterol of 228 mg/dL and increased urinary hyaluronic acid. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated hypoplastic maxilla and mandible with an obtuse infantile mandibular angle, multiple missing teeth, and altered condylar morphology.

A 5-year-old castrated male domestic shorthair cat was evaluated for a 3-month history of weight loss, chronic vomiting of food material, and diarrhea. Initial tests by the referring veterinarian showed:  
• CBC: mild eosinophilia (1.75 × 10^9 cells/L; RI 0.16–1.81)  
• Biochemistry: slight increase in ALT (195 IU/L; RI 15–123)  
• Abdominal ultrasound: diffuse thickening of the proximal duodenum (up to 6.2 mm) with preserved layering, pancreaticoduodenal lymphadenopathy (8.1 mm), and slight colonic thickening (2.3 mm) without loss of layering  

Trials of fenbendazole, marbofloxacin, maropitant, and a hypoallergenic diet were unsuccessful; prednisolone yielded partial improvement. On admission at our institution, the cat was thin (BCS 3/9) with tense cranial abdomen. Repeat testing showed:  
• CBC: marked eosinophilia (2.908 × 10^9 cells/L)  
• Biochemistry: mild ALT elevation (207 IU/L) and slight hypercreatininaemia (159 µmol/L; RI 46–157)  
• Abdominal ultrasound: severe focal thickening of the proximal duodenum (5.8 mm) with loss of intestinal layering and discrete pancreaticoduodenal lymphadenopathy (3.4 mm)  

Based on eosinophilia and the duodenal mass, the differential included high-grade lymphoma, mast cell tumour with paraneoplastic eosinophilia, gastrointestinal eosinophilic sclerosing fibroplasia, inflammatory granuloma, and parasitic lesions.  

Gastroduodenoscopy revealed partial obstruction of the pyloric antrum by grass fibers (removed), and a proliferative lesion of the proximal duodenal mucosa with multiple ulcerative areas showing yellow–green discoloration. Colonoscopy showed diffuse edema in the distal colon and numerous white-to-grey, circumscribed mucosal areas. Endoscopic biopsies were obtained from both sites for histologic evaluation.

A 23-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented in early September 2021 with fever and malaise and was confirmed by PCR to have SARS-CoV-2 infection (Delta variant). She was not vaccinated. On day 8 of illness, she received remdesivir for pneumonia. On day 9, she suddenly developed severe right hip pain and diffuse body aches. On examination, she had tenderness in Scarpa’s triangle without erythema, warmth, or swelling. Right hip flexion was limited by pain (80° on the right vs. 120° on the left). 

On day 15, laboratory studies showed C-reactive protein 14.6 mg/dL (reference, 0.00–0.23) and a white blood cell count of 18.0 × 10^3/μL (reference, 3.9–9.8 × 10^3). Rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies, HLA–B27, hepatitis panels, and HIV testing were negative. Urine culture was negative; blood cultures grew β-lactamase–producing Staphylococcus aureus. 

On day 21, contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the pelvis showed an expanded low-density area in the capsule of the right hip joint. Arthrocentesis yielded cloudy yellowish-white fluid. Joint-fluid cultures were negative. 

On day 23, intravenous cefazolin was initiated.

A 74-year-old man with a history of IgG kappa smoldering myeloma diagnosed in 2006 was monitored until 2014, when he developed back pain and was found to have a T9 vertebral fracture with biopsy‐proven plasma cell neoplasm and 21% bone marrow plasma‐cell involvement. He received palliative radiation to T9 and was treated with lenalidomide and dexamethasone for 18 months without significant toxicity.  

In March 2018, progressive disease was documented with 30% marrow involvement, and he started lenalidomide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone (RVd). He tolerated RVd for six months but switched to an all‐oral regimen of lenalidomide 25 mg on days 1–21, ixazomib 4 mg on days 1, 8, and 15, and dexamethasone 20 mg on days 1, 8, 15, and 22 (IRd) due to difficulty with clinic visits.  

One week after initiating ixazomib, he noted multiple small lesions on his neck and chest. He held ixazomib and was referred for dermatologic evaluation, and a skin biopsy was performed.

An 18-year-old man presented with severe abdominal pain, distension, and repetitive vomiting that began shortly after a buffet meal. He had no prior medical history or recent weight loss; his BMI was 22 (weight 71 kg; height 181 cm). On arrival he was tachycardic (>120 bpm), febrile (38.9 °C), and normotensive (110/80 mm Hg). Examination revealed lethargy and a grossly tympanic, distended, and tender abdomen. Laboratory studies showed a severe lactic acidosis (pH 7.13; lactate 13.7 mmol/L), leukocytosis (white cell count 21 × 10^9/L), and acute kidney injury (creatinine 203 μmol/L; estimated GFR 40 mL/min/1.73 m^2). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated massive gastric dilatation measuring 35 × 19 × 12 cm, gastric pneumatosis, and portal venous gas. There was a clear transition point in the third portion of the duodenum between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta. The aortomesenteric angle was 5° and the aortomesenteric distance was 6 mm.

A 65-year-old man was referred to the Urology Department for evaluation of a right renal mass. Three years earlier, he had undergone transurethral resection of urothelial carcinoma of the bladder followed by six weekly instillations of intravesical Bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG) immunotherapy. Surveillance CT performed two years after therapy showed no evidence of recurrence. 

On recent dynamic contrast-enhanced CT, a 1-cm dorsal lesion in the right kidney demonstrated gradual and weak enhancement at the periphery. Fat-saturated T2-weighted MRI revealed slightly low signal intensity in the lesion, and diffusion-weighted imaging showed strong high intensity with a correspondingly low apparent diffusion coefficient value. 

The initial radiologic differential diagnosis included papillary renal cell carcinoma, a complicated cyst, and an angiomyolipoma. However, only the tumor periphery enhanced, a pattern that did not seem typical of papillary renal cell carcinoma.

An 11-year-9-month-old boy was admitted with an 11-day history of recurrent fever, headache, and progressive projectile vomiting. One month earlier, he had undergone deep supratentorial abscess resection and craniotomy decompression for a left frontal lobe brain abscess. On admission, mental status was normal. Dark red pinpoint rashes were noted on the neck, trunk, and upper limbs; mild lumbosacral tenderness was present. Cardiopulmonary, abdominal, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable.

Day 1 labs: WBC 12.3×10^9/L; neutrophils 69.0%; lymphocytes 23.9%; HGB 120 g/L; platelets 361×10^9/L; CRP 10.7 mg/L. Liver and renal function, electrolytes, coagulation profile, and immune panels were normal. Day 2 CSF: nucleated cells 495×10^6/L (83% neutrophils), protein 819.4 mg/L, glucose 0.98 mmol/L; CMV PCR positive; smear and culture negative. EEG was normal. Cranial CT on day 5 showed residual abscess in the left frontal lobe.

Empiric ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, and vancomycin were started. On day 6, mNGS of CSF identified Streptococcus intermedius, and antibiotics were adjusted to penicillin plus vancomycin. The fever resolved over the next week, and follow-up imaging showed marked reduction of the abscess.

One week after penicillin therapy, fever recurred. Day 22 studies: blood and CSF cultures were negative. Blood count: WBC 1.1×10^9/L; ANC 0.25×10^9/L; HGB 123 g/L; platelets 74×10^9/L. ALT 127 U/L; AST 778 U/L; triglycerides 9.2 mmol/L; fibrinogen 0.70 g/L; ferritin >16,500 ng/mL. He developed a skin rash, bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, conjunctival injection, red cracked lips, and swelling of the hands and feet. A single high-dose IVIG (2 g/kg) was administered, and the fever temporarily resolved.

A 76-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic atrial fibrillation, and alcohol overconsumption was admitted after persistent focal-complex seizures, presenting in a soporous to comatose state (Glasgow Coma Scale score 5). Emergency CT of the head showed a peripherally contrast-enhancing mass lesion in the left frontal lobe. 

Advanced MRI characterization revealed:
• Two confluent, centrally necrotic lesions in the left middle frontal gyrus (7 mm and 14 mm), each with an irregular peripheral contrast-enhancing rim, hypointense on T2-weighted imaging, double-rim sign on susceptibility-weighted imaging, and extensive surrounding edema on FLAIR and T2-weighted images.  
• On diffusion-weighted imaging, the necrotic centers were hyperintense with corresponding severe diffusion restriction (mean ADC 0.4 × 10⁻³ mm²/s) and a central FA of 0.28 on diffusion tensor imaging.  
• DSC perfusion showed no hyperperfusion of the rim (rCBV 0.86).  
• DCE perfusion demonstrated k-trans values of 22–41 × 10⁻³ /min in the rim (vs. 2.3 × 10⁻³ /min in contralateral white matter), with a maximum relative enhancement of 81% and an ascending curve without wash-out.  
• Single-voxel spectroscopy (TE 30 ms) showed a very high lipid peak (Lip/Cr 11.8), a small lactate peak (Lac/Cr 0.316), decreased NAA (NAA/Cr 1.51), slightly increased choline (Cho/Cr 1.12, Cho/NAA 0.741), and no elevation of myoinositol or acetate.  
• APTw imaging measurements yielded the following (max/mean/min): necrotic center 2.6%/2.3%/2.1%; contrast-enhancing rim 3.1%/2.8%/2.2%; immediate perifocal edema 3.3%/2.9%/2.2%; distant edema 2.4%/2.0%/1.6%; normal frontal white matter 1.4%/1.2%/0.9%. Histogram analysis of the entire enhancing rim revealed a bimodal distribution with peaks at 2.4% and 2.9%.

A 70-year-old man presented with a one-month history of insidious-onset pain and swelling at the medial end of his right sternoclavicular region. He reported intermittent fevers but denied weight loss, night sweats, or loss of appetite. He had no history of trauma, prior tuberculosis, or immunosuppressive conditions, and HIV testing was negative. On examination, there was a tender, warm, nonpulsatile, boggy swelling over the right sternoclavicular joint without limitation of shoulder range of motion.  
Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 55 mg/L (reference 0–5), an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 116 mm/h, and a normal total leukocyte count.  
A chest radiograph demonstrated clear lung fields. Ultrasonography of the area revealed a 2.2 × 1.4 cm fluid collection with internal echoes. Magnetic resonance imaging of the sternoclavicular joint showed moderate joint fluid, mild synovial thickening, irregularity of the articular cartilage on both the manubrial and clavicular aspects, articular and subarticular erosions, and diffuse subchondral marrow signal changes.

A 32-year-old woman with relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis presented with severe ataxia and diplopia requiring prolonged hospitalization. Examination showed rotary nystagmus on upgaze to the right, incomplete abduction of the right eye, decreased sensation on the right face, left hemibody deficits, and severe truncal ataxia requiring bilateral assistance to stand. MRI of the head revealed a new T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesion in the right superior cerebellar peduncle. She was treated with intravenous solumedrol, plasmapheresis, and mitoxantrone, leading to clinical improvement. Three months later, follow-up MRI demonstrated persistence of the right cerebellar peduncle lesion and a new T2/FLAIR hyperintense, expansile lesion in the left inferior medullary olive. At that time, she had no new clinical symptoms or signs, including palatal clonus.

An 11-year-old boy with no prior medical history was admitted with a 7-day history of fever, abdominal pain, and vomiting. On presentation his temperature was 36.8 °C, respiratory rate 32 /min, blood pressure 108/70 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. He appeared drowsy and ill; abdominal examination revealed diffuse tenderness, distention, and rigidity. Laboratory studies showed a white-blood-cell count of 30 400/mm3 with 32% bands. CT of the abdomen demonstrated a large perihepatic collection consistent with abscess, and he was diagnosed with complicated appendicitis. He underwent open laparotomy, appendectomy, and drain placement; intra-abdominal cultures grew Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Streptococcus constellatus, and Bacteroides species. He improved and was weaned off vasopressors. His wound was closed by delayed primary closure.

On post-operative day 7, his blood pressures began rising; on day 9 the highest recorded blood pressure was 164/117 mm Hg (95th percentile for age/height/gender, 118/78 mm Hg). On day 10, he became drowsy and had two generalized tonic-clonic seizures treated with intravenous lorazepam. Noncontrast head CT showed hypodensities in the bilateral subcortical parietal regions. Brain MRI with FLAIR, MRA, and MRV revealed abnormal hyperintense signal predominantly in the bilateral parietal regions, extending into frontal and occipital lobes in the subcortical white matter, with associated gyral and leptomeningeal enhancement. There was no evidence of diffusion restriction, venous sinus thrombosis, intracranial hemorrhage, ring-enhancing lesions, or septic emboli.

A 66-year-old Caucasian man with bipolar disorder resided in a psychiatric facility. Baseline mental state was normal: ambulatory gait, no tremor or movement disturbances. His medications included valproic acid extended release 1000 mg nightly and clonazepam 0.25 mg twice daily; olanzapine had been discontinued 8 weeks earlier.

Five days before admission he developed fever and became bedridden, with continuous sleep, a fixed stare, intermittent rigidity, and eye movements described as similar to oculogyric crises. Valproic acid was held, and lorazepam was given for presumed catatonia without improvement.

On presentation to the hospital his blood pressure was in the 100s/70s mm Hg, heart rate in the 110s beats/min, and oxygen saturation 99–100% on 2 L nasal cannula. He remained unresponsive, rigid, and disoriented. Examination disclosed a mild resting tremor, hypertonia in all extremities, intact reflexes, and no focal weakness.  

Initial workup included:
  • Head CT: no acute intracranial findings  
  • EEG: generalized background slowing, no seizures  
  • Brain MRI: no acute abnormalities  
  • CSF analysis: clear fluid, normal protein, minimal cells, negative cultures  
  • Comprehensive labs, cultures, and toxicology: unrevealing  

Broad-spectrum antibiotics were discontinued when cultures were negative. On hospital day 7, a trial of carbidopa/levodopa 25/100 mg every 8 hours was initiated.

A 49-year-old woman with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and presumed transient ischemic attack presented with a 1-year history of an anterior neck mass. Initial thyroid function testing was normal. Fine-needle aspiration cytology at an outside hospital showed scant follicular cells consistent with nodular goiter. On examination, a 3 × 4 cm right thyroid nodule was palpable without lymphadenopathy, tracheal deviation, or Pemberton’s sign. Ultrasound revealed a 4.7 × 3.1 × 1.7 cm mixed solid–cystic nodule in the right mid–lower pole with comet-tail artifact and peripheral vascularity. Repeat ultrasound-guided aspiration (February 7) showed a benign colloid nodule with cystic degeneration. One month later, she returned with 1 day of fever (to 39°C), right thyroid pain, and upper respiratory symptoms; she received oral cloxacillin and clarithromycin. One week later, she was admitted for persistent fever and neck pain. Examination showed a tender right thyroid nodule without skin changes or airway compromise; vital signs were stable. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (13.85 × 10^9/L with neutrophilia), ESR 105 mm/hr, fT4 25.7 pmol/L, TSH 0.04 mIU/L; TRAb, anti-TPO, and anti-Tg antibodies were negative. A thyroid uptake scan showed generalized reduced uptake with a large cold nodule in the right mid–lower pole. Ultrasound demonstrated interval enlargement of the cystic nodule to 5.0 × 4.1 × 3.0 cm with new isoechoic debris. Under strict aseptic conditions, 30 mL of nonpurulent reddish-brown fluid was aspirated and sent for Gram stain and culture. She was treated with intravenous amoxicillin–clavulanate, NSAIDs, and propranolol for presumed infected thyroid cyst with destructive thyroiditis.

A 41-year-old woman with a 3-month history of sacroiliac pain, arthralgias, and lower-limb myalgias partially responsive to NSAIDs was diagnosed with seronegative spondyloarthropathy (negative HLA-B27) after MRI confirmed bilateral active sacroiliitis. Two months later, she began weekly subcutaneous etanercept 50 mg with significant improvement in her joint symptoms. After the third dose, she developed a dry cough and dyspnea on moderate exertion without fever, hemoptysis, chest pain, or other systemic symptoms. She denied tobacco use, recent travel, or exposures to animals, dusts, or sick contacts. 

On examination in the emergency department, she was afebrile, blood pressure 118/84 mmHg, pulse 96 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygenation normal on room air. Pulmonary auscultation revealed scant basal “Velcro”-like crackles. Other exams were unremarkable apart from positive sacroiliac provocation tests. 

Laboratory studies: Hb 13 g/dL, WBC 4,100/mm³ (neutrophils 2,000, lymphocytes 1,400), eosinophils 50/mm³, platelets 325,000/mm³; AST, ALT, bilirubin, creatinine, and BUN were within normal limits. 

High-resolution chest CT showed ground-glass interstitial infiltrates with a centrifugal distribution, predominantly in the upper lobes, and a mosaic pattern of disseminated attenuation without lymphadenopathy or pleural effusion. An echocardiogram was normal, and ECG showed sinus rhythm. 

Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage revealed no endobronchial lesions; GeneXpert for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and methenamine silver stain were negative.

A 37-year-old woman presented 3 months after total laparoscopic radical hysterectomy with bilateral pelvic lymphadenectomy and ovarian transposition for stage IB1 cervical squamous cell carcinoma, with sudden severe pelvic pain. Examination revealed a peritonitic abdomen. Transabdominal ultrasound showed a 6.5×5.2 cm mass in the right mid abdomen corresponding to a transposed ovary, with absent color Doppler flow and marked tenderness. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated both ovaries located in the epigastrium; the more lateral ovary measured 7×6×6 cm, there was pelvic free fluid, and no surrounding inflammatory change.

A 52-year-old man presented with six months of progressively cloudy vision and a more rapid decline in visual acuity over the past six weeks. He denied headaches, seizures, or sexual dysfunction. He was a smoker. On ophthalmologic examination, there was bilateral temporal cloudiness and a left inferotemporal visual field defect; visual acuity was rapidly deteriorating. Routine laboratory studies, including a white blood cell count and C-reactive protein level, were within normal limits. Noncontrast CT of the sinuses and contrast-enhanced MRI of the sellar region demonstrated an intra- and suprasellar homogeneous mass with intense gadolinium enhancement and hyperintensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images. The clinical and radiologic impression was of a pituitary macroadenoma, and the patient was referred for surgical management.

A 20-year-old African American active-duty servicewoman presented with 3–4 days of “static” in her vision and mild intermittent headaches. She recalled receiving a smallpox vaccination (ACAM2000) 10–11 days earlier. Her past medical history was unremarkable, and review of systems was otherwise negative.  
On examination, visual acuity was 20/15 in each eye. External and slit-lamp examinations were notable only for diffuse conjunctival hyperemia; the remainder of the anterior segment was normal. Dilated fundus examination demonstrated profound bilateral vascular sheathing, predominantly of veins with some arteriolar involvement.  
Automated perimetry revealed para-central visual field defects bilaterally, and optical coherence tomography showed corresponding macular edema. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated diffuse vessel sheathing without any leakage.  
Laboratory studies—including ACE level, ANCA, QuantiFERON-TB Gold, HIV rapid test, VDRL, RPR, FTA-ABS, complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, ESR, and CRP—were all within normal limits or negative; antinuclear antibody testing was positive. MRI of the brain was unremarkable.

A 45-year-old man with well-controlled hypertension presented with a one-week history of four to six non-bloody diarrheal stools per day associated with subjective fevers, sore throat, and dizziness. He denied recent travel, intravenous drug use, or alcohol use and was monogamous with his wife. On examination, his temperature was 38.0 °C, blood pressure 163/100 mm Hg, heart rate 76 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. He had erythematous tonsils without exudate, clinical oral candidiasis, mild gum bleeding, and a fluctuant, purulent draining mass on his left upper thigh. No rash, lymphadenopathy, or oral ulcers were noted; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 159 g/L, white blood cell count 3.0 × 10^9/L, platelets 50 × 10^9/L, creatinine 160 µmol/L, creatine kinase 25 000 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase 1739 U/L, ferritin 69 717 µg/L, D-dimer >10 mg/L, fibrinogen 2.0 g/L, and triglycerides 4.36 mmol/L. There was no evidence of hemolysis. Peripheral smear confirmed thrombocytopenia without schistocytes. Abdominal ultrasound showed mild splenomegaly (13.3 cm).

On hospital day 3, one of two blood culture sets grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and two of two grew Streptococcus mitis. Syphilis EIA and urine chlamydia and gonorrhea tests were negative. Anti-nuclear antibodies and C3/C4 complement levels were normal. Hepatitis A IgG was reactive; hepatitis B core antibody/antigen and surface antigen were negative; surface antibody was positive; hepatitis C antibody was non-reactive. EBV IgM was negative and IgG positive. Parvovirus B19 IgM and CMV IgM were negative. A rapid HIV antibody test was negative.

An 80-year-old woman with recurrent right cheek nodular melanoma and new lung metastasis presented with one month of progressive dysphagia, odynophagia, and malnutrition. Six cycles of pembrolizumab had been completed before symptom onset; pembrolizumab was held and oral prednisone was started with initial improvement. Two months later, she developed throat swelling, hoarseness, and new oxygen requirement.

Her past melanoma history included right cheek resection (2015), parotidectomy and neck dissection (2017), radiation therapy and ipilimumab (discontinued for colitis and rash), then pembrolizumab with near resolution of a right upper lobe lung lesion. In October 2018, PET/CT revealed FDG-avid soft tissue fullness in the right supraglottic fold with airway narrowing.

Physical examination showed copious thick oropharyngeal mucus. CT of the neck demonstrated near-complete airway occlusion from supraglottic and epiglottic soft tissue thickening. Direct laryngoscopy revealed massive swelling of the posterior supraglottic larynx threatening airway patency and diffuse inflamed granular mucosa in the supraglottic and lower pharyngeal regions; an open tracheostomy was performed.

Biopsies of the pharyngeal, supraglottic, and glottic mucosa showed fibrinopurulent exudate and granulation tissue with acute and chronic inflammation. Periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott-Gomori’s methenamine silver, gram, Fite, Kinyoun, and Wright-Giemsa stains were all negative for bacteria, acid-fast organisms, and fungi.

A 66-year-old man presented with a 4-week history of progressive balance difficulty and neck and bilateral shoulder pain. On examination, he had diffuse hyperreflexia with normal strength in all four extremities. Sensation was intact in the arms but decreased to light touch, vibration, and proprioception in both legs; pinprick sensation was preserved. His gait was markedly ataxic; visual examination was unremarkable. MRI of the cervical spine showed an eccentric, heterogeneously gadolinium-enhancing intramedullary mass lesion from C2 to C4, with diffuse surrounding cord edema. MRI of the thoracic and lumbar spine and brain revealed no other lesions. Lumbar puncture demonstrated mild pleocytosis (red cells 48/µL; leukocytes 13/µL with 93% lymphocytes), normal glucose (54 mg/dL), normal protein (93 mg/dL), and was negative for oligoclonal bands and myelin basic protein. The patient’s symptoms improved partially with oral dexamethasone (6 mg every 6 hours), but repeat MRI 3 weeks after initiation of steroids showed no change in the size or enhancement of the lesion. A multidisciplinary tumor board recommended surgical biopsy and possible resection.

A 35-year-old man with no past history of trauma or splenectomy underwent screening colonoscopy because of a family history of colorectal neoplasia. He was asymptomatic, and the physical examination was unremarkable. Colonoscopy revealed a 30 mm bulge in the proximal descending colon covered by normal-appearing mucosa. Endoscopic ultrasound showed an oval, regular, hypoechoic, homogeneous lesion measuring 2.6 cm × 1.7 cm with an indeterminate layer of origin (submucosa vs muscularis propria), raising concern for a mesenchymal neoplasm. Endoscopic ultrasound–guided puncture was performed with a 22-gauge fine-needle biopsy needle.

A 74-year-old Japanese woman presented with a left-axillary mass that she had first noticed several weeks earlier. Her medical history was unremarkable, and she was taking no medications. On examination, a thumb-sized, hard, elastic, freely movable mass was palpated in the left axilla; there were no overlying skin changes and no palpable breast masses. 

Laboratory studies showed a normal leukocyte count with 6% eosinophils, an alkaline phosphatase level of 326 IU/L (normal, 60–200), a soluble interleukin-2 receptor level of 605 U/mL (normal, 122–496), and an immunoglobulin E level of 3032 IU/mL (normal, < 173). Serum immunoglobulin G4 was 47.7 mg/dL (normal, 4.8–105.0). Tumor markers, including CEA and CA15-3, were within normal limits. 

Ultrasonography of the left axilla revealed multiple lymph nodes with irregular margins and loss of central hyperechogenicity (largest, 2.2 × 1.5 cm). A CT scan of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed lymphadenopathy confined to the left axilla, with no other masses or enlarged nodes. 

To exclude malignancy, a core needle biopsy of the axillary lymph nodes was performed. Histologic examination demonstrated lymph nodes with rich eosinophilic infiltration but no atypical cells. Immunohistochemical staining was negative for cytokeratin 7, cytokeratin 20, and CD117, with no evidence of lymphoma cells or metastatic carcinoma.

A 12-year-old boy was admitted with extreme fatigue, a 2.6-kg weight loss over three weeks, intermittent fever, worsening respiratory symptoms, and abdominal pain. He had a diagnosis of asthma for 11 months, treated with ipratropium and salbutamol nebulizations and maintenance salmeterol/fluticasone. Initial evaluation then showed an IgE of 228 kU/L, positive grass and tree pollen allergy tests, reversible airway obstruction on spirometry, and an elevated FeNO of 38.5 ppb that normalized on inhaled steroids.

During his summer holidays abroad, his general condition progressively deteriorated. Laboratory studies revealed a leukocytosis of 26.5 × 10^9/L with nearly 50% eosinophils and an IgE of 2901 kU/L. One day after returning, he presented with respiratory distress and was hospitalized.

On examination, he appeared cachectic with scattered skin lesions on the elbows, back, and feet and two firm subcutaneous nodules on the back. Respiratory rate was 23 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation was 97% on room air. Lung, heart, abdominal, and neurologic examinations were otherwise normal; there was no hepatosplenomegaly.

Laboratory findings on admission included a WBC count of 31.9 × 10^9/L with 39% eosinophils (12.4 × 10^9/L), elevated C-reactive protein (66 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (64 mm/h), IgG 27.7 g/L, and IgE 2445 kU/L. Complement C3 and C4 were normal. Tests for ANA, ASO, anti-DNAse B, p-ANCA, c-ANCA, MPO-ANCA, and PR3-ANCA were negative. Rheumatoid factor was 22 U/L. Urinalysis and renal and liver function tests were normal.

Chest radiography and CT scan showed bilateral lower-lobe predominant infiltrates with peripheral consolidations and a small pericardial effusion. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid contained 1.8 × 10^9 leukocytes/L, of which 76% were eosinophils.

A 64-year-old woman with a 20-year history of systemic lupus erythematosus presented with progressive right lower neck pain, painful swelling of the right shoulder for 3 days, and fever without chills for 1 day. Two days before fever onset, she had received acupuncture over her right shoulder. She denied trauma, strenuous exercise, or sick contacts. Her SLE had been managed with azathioprine 25 mg daily for the past year.

On admission: temperature 39.9 °C, pulse 120 bpm, blood pressure 83/47 mm Hg, respiratory rate 26/min. Physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness without erythema over the right lower neck and shoulder with limited range of motion; the overlying skin was warm. No active lupus rash, arthritis, or lymphadenopathy was noted.

Laboratory results showed WBC 2.8×10^3/µL, hemoglobin 8.8 g/dL, platelets 613×10^3/µL, albumin 2.6 g/dL, creatine kinase 587 U/L, lactate 19.8 mg/dL, CRP 24.3 mg/dL, and procalcitonin 42.5 ng/mL. Anti-dsDNA, complement C3 and C4, and lupus activity markers were within normal limits.

Chest radiograph and ultrasound demonstrated a right pleural effusion; thoracentesis showed exudative fluid without bacterial growth. Noncontrast CT of the neck and chest revealed a small heterogeneous low-density lesion at the right lower neck and diffuse edematous changes in the right anterior and lateral chest wall with fat stranding. Musculoskeletal ultrasound showed decreased echogenicity and loss of normal texture in the anterior scalene muscles. Image findings were consistent with pyomyositis without a liquified abscess.

A 68-year-old woman was admitted with a 2-day history of acute onset, progressively worsening sharp epigastric and left-sided “gripping” chest pain of severe intensity. The pain was pleuritic in nature, worsened by deep breaths, had no radiation, and was not relieved by positioning. She denied trauma, recent travel, or similar symptoms in family members. Her medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and hypothyroidism; medications were aspirin, amlodipine, lovastatin, and levothyroxine.

On examination, she appeared uncomfortable, clutching her left chest and epigastrium. Blood pressure was normal; heart rate was 105 beats per minute; temperature 99.9°F; and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. The pain was not reproducible with palpation, and there was no rash. Lung examination revealed a left-sided pleural rub; the right lung and the remainder of the examination were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 9.4 × 10^3/µL with 54% neutrophils, normal hemoglobin and hematocrit, creatinine 0.75 mg/dL, and normal liver-function tests. Cardiac biomarkers were unremarkable: troponin T was <0.030 ng/mL on three measurements 6 hours apart, creatine kinase 122 U/L, and CK-MB 3.7 ng/mL. An electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm without ST-T wave changes. Chest radiograph demonstrated small bilateral pleural effusions without airspace disease. 

Because of persistent pleuritic pain and sinus tachycardia, a CT scan of the chest was performed; it was negative for pulmonary embolism, pulmonary infarction, aortic abnormality, or gastroesophageal pathology, and revealed no muscular edema. Inflammatory markers were elevated: erythrocyte sedimentation rate 65 mm/hr and C-reactive protein 17.2 mg/L. Complement levels (C3 161 mg/dL, C4 16 mg/dL) were normal. Testing for vasculitis and connective-tissue disease showed negative C-ANCA, p-ANCA, and antinuclear antibodies.

A 50-year-old African-American woman with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, diabetic peripheral neuropathy, hyperlipidemia, chronic kidney disease stage 3, and gastroesophageal reflux disease presented postoperatively after elective anterior lumbar interbody fusion for spinal stenosis. In the postanesthesia care unit, she developed sudden shortness of breath with mild hypoxemia but denied chest pain, palpitations, hemoptysis, wheezing, leg pain, or swelling. Temperature was 98.1°F, blood pressure 164/86 mmHg, heart rate 96 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 88% on room air. Examination showed an obese woman in mild distress with fine inspiratory crackles at both lung bases and no jugular venous distension. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm with nonspecific ST changes. Laboratory studies revealed a WBC count of 13,700/µL, hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL, platelet count 293 K/mm³, creatinine 1.47 mg/dL (baseline 1.72 mg/dL), and bicarbonate 24 mg/dL. A chest radiograph demonstrated widening of the mediastinum compared with a film obtained 10 days earlier. Since aortic dissection was a major concern, a labetalol infusion was initiated and an emergent chest CTA was performed.

A 74-year-old man presented with jaundice and recurrent mild epigastric pain for 3 weeks. He had a history of idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis and right-sided hydronephrosis. On examination, there was a palpable, nontender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) without abdominal tenderness. Laboratory studies revealed cholestasis and mild transaminase elevation (ALP 448 IU/L, GGT 541 IU/L, total bilirubin 10.8 mg/dL, ALT 93 IU/L, AST 69 IU/L), new-onset hyperglycemia, an elevated CA 19-9 level (303.4 U/mL; normal < 37), and a markedly elevated serum IgG4 level (3.100 g/L; normal < 2.0), with rheumatoid factor of 79.2 IU/mL (normal < 20). Abdominal MRI showed diffuse pancreatic enlargement with low T1 signal intensity, dilatation of the extra-pancreatic common bile duct and intrahepatic ducts, and a focal stricture of the intrapancreatic bile duct with a ‘beak sign.’ The gallbladder contained stones but appeared otherwise normal. ERCP was unsuccessful due to severe stenosis of the intrapancreatic bile duct. Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated heterogeneous pancreatic parenchyma with lobularity and hyperechoic foci, severe intrapancreatic bile-duct stricture, and extra-pancreatic ductal dilation with wall thickening. EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration of the stricture site revealed fibrosis and lymphoplasmacytic infiltration without evidence of malignancy.

A 32-year-old woman was brought by her husband with a 6-month history of increasingly erratic behavior. Over the preceding 4 months she had slept 2–3 hours per night, lost 15 kg, and experienced palpitations. She reported racing thoughts, long hours of unproductive work, and intermittent paranoid ideas, including believing that her mobile telephone was sending messages directly into her brain. She had worsening anxiety, difficulty caring for her child, and episodes of wandering behavior. She was previously healthy, took no medications, and had no family history of thyroid disease.

In the emergency department she was easily distracted, made intermittent eye contact, paced the room, and had pressured speech without hallucinations or intent to self-harm; her paranoid ideas were not held with delusional intensity. Routine laboratory tests revealed a suppressed TSH level (<0.01 mU/L), an elevated free thyroxine level (97.5 pmol/L), and an elevated free triiodothyronine level (32.3 pmol/L). Other blood tests, including full blood count, C-reactive protein, electrolytes, and liver function tests, were normal. 

Her vital signs showed a temperature of 36.7 °C, heart rate of 120 beats/min, blood pressure of 162/85 mm Hg, and respiratory rate of 23 breaths/min. On physical examination she had a visible, smooth, non-tender goitre and lid lag but no tremor, ophthalmopathy, dermopathy, or other skin changes.

A 23-year-old man presented with sudden onset post‐tussive pleuritic chest pain and left‐sided neck pain. He also noted dyspnea and rhinolalia. Three days earlier he had developed coryzal symptoms. He had no significant medical or family history, took no medications, did not smoke or use recreational drugs, and drank minimal alcohol. He was physically active.

On examination he was tall, of medium build, in mild discomfort, and tachycardic but hemodynamically stable and not hypoxic. There was no jugular venous distention or muffled heart sounds. Surgical emphysema was palpable in the left supraclavicular fossa. The trachea was central, and the lung fields were clear to auscultation with normal resonance.

Laboratory testing showed a white cell count of 13×10^9/L with mild neutrophilia. An ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia. A chest radiograph revealed surgical emphysema extending into the neck from the left lung apex and evidence of pneumomediastinum. An urgent contrast‐enhanced CT scan with an esophagogram confirmed surgical emphysema, pneumomediastinum, and pneumopericardium. No pneumothorax was identified, and no source of free air was seen.

A 28-year-old man with a 22-year history of Wilson disease, managed with chelation therapy, presented with a 4-day history of weakness in all four limbs and speech difficulties. He had intermittent seizures over the past 2 months, with the most recent episode 7 days earlier. His sister had also had Wilson disease and died from it. Laboratory studies showed increased 24-hour urinary copper and spot urinary copper levels, low serum ceruloplasmin, and proteinuria. On examination, Kayser-Fleischer rings were noted, along with signs consistent with an upper motor neuron lesion. Brain MRI revealed an intra-diploic lesion adjacent to the left cavernous sinus measuring approximately 14 × 7 mm. The lesion was isointense to cerebrospinal fluid on T2-weighted images, hypointense to isointense on T1-weighted and FLAIR sequences, showed no diffusion restriction on DWI with corresponding high ADC signal, and exhibited no blooming on gradient-echo sequences. The lesion appeared to communicate with the greater wing of the left sphenoid bone.

A 31-year-old woman presents with a 4-year history of recurrent painful ulcerations on both legs and feet. She has no personal or family history of vascular or autoimmune disease, denies arthralgia or other dermatologic symptoms, and takes no medications. She also denies tobacco or illicit drug use. On examination, a reticular purplish livedo pattern is noted over both lower limbs. Multiple chronic, nonhealing ulcers are present over the lateral malleolus and the dorsum of the left foot, along with white atrophic scars on the lower legs and ankles. Preliminary diagnostic considerations included thrombophilia, hematologic malignancies, immune-mediated vasculitis, connective tissue diseases, arterial disease, vascular proliferations, diabetes, and medication-induced ulcers. A lesional skin biopsy was performed.

A 13-year-old boy was brought unconscious to the emergency department after a bicycle collision. He had no prior hospitalizations or lung disease. On initial assessment, he had laboured breathing and severe facial swelling. Emergency physicians suspected a Quincke oedema and administered intravenous glucocorticoids. During transport, his respiratory status worsened, and he was intubated. In the emergency department, examination revealed a firm “bounce mark” below the thyroid gland and extensive subcutaneous emphysema of the neck and chest wall. A chest radiograph demonstrated a right-sided pneumothorax, and despite mechanical ventilation his oxygenation declined. A CT scan of the chest showed bilateral pneumothorax and massive pneumomediastinum.

A 10-year-old boy of Iraqi descent presented with a 2-week history of lethargy, weight loss, polydipsia, and polyuria. He was born in the UK to healthy parents of Iraqi origin, had a history of nocturnal enuresis and adenotonsillectomy, and took no regular medications. On examination his weight was 56.6 kg; vital signs were normal. Initial laboratory studies showed:  
• Blood glucose, 42.9 mmol/L  
• Venous pH, 7.38; bicarbonate, 21.3 mmol/L; base deficit, 3.3 mmol/L  
• Urine ketones, negative  
• Hemoglobin, 130 g/L; WBC count, 8.1 × 10^9/L; platelets, 274 × 10^9/L  
• Serum sodium, 127 mmol/L; renal and liver function, and thyroid function, normal  
• Positive islet cell antibodies; GAD antibodies > 2000 U/mL  
• HbA1C, 116 mmol/mol  

He was diagnosed with new-onset type 1 diabetes without ketoacidosis, started on subcutaneous insulin, and discharged on day 5 on a basal–bolus regimen. Eleven days later, a home visit noted normal blood glucose but new jaundice and extreme lethargy. He was referred to hospital. On arrival, he had icteric sclera but no hepatomegaly and no stigmata of chronic liver disease; vital signs were normal. Laboratory tests revealed:  
• Hemoglobin, 81 g/L; RBC count, 2.65 × 10^12/L  
• Normal urea, electrolytes, ALP, ALT, CRP, and albumin  
• Total bilirubin, 88 μmol/L; conjugated fraction, 6 μmol/L  

Peripheral blood film showed anisocytosis, spherocytes, polychromasia, and occasional red cell fragments. Further studies showed lactate dehydrogenase 243 U/L and haptoglobin < 0.08 g/L, consistent with acute hemolysis.

A 36-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of colicky epigastric pain radiating to the back, associated with nausea, non-bloody vomiting, night sweats, fevers, chills, fatigue, and an 11-kg weight loss. She had no history of immunosuppression, chronic illness, or family history of gastrointestinal malignancy. On examination she appeared pale and in pain; vital signs were notable for heart rate 110 beats/min and temperature 37.3 °C. The abdomen was soft, with a palpable 16 × 10 cm mass in the left upper quadrant; bowel sounds were increased. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 17.5 × 10⁹/L (67.8% neutrophils), C-reactive protein 320 mg/L, and otherwise normal renal and liver function tests; HIV and hepatitis tests were negative. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed circumferential thickening of a 16 cm segment of the transverse colon with pericolic fat stranding, a 6 × 6 cm necrotic lymph node posterior to the pancreatic head, and multiple enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes. After multidisciplinary consultation, lymphoma involving the colon was considered the most likely diagnosis, with colon cancer and pancreatic cancer in the differential. The patient underwent colonoscopy, which showed an ulcerated, fungating mass in the transverse colon approximately 70 cm from the anal verge, with luminal narrowing. Eight biopsy samples were obtained from the mass.

A 16-year-old man with a history of crustacea allergy and childhood bronchial asthma presented with severe cough, fatigue, and shortness of breath. The symptoms began immediately after he started using heat-not-burn cigarettes and progressively worsened over two weeks. On arrival at the initial hospital, his Glasgow Coma Scale score was E1V3M5. Vital signs were: blood pressure 109/50 mmHg, heart rate 136 bpm, respiratory rate 30 breaths/min, temperature 37.3 °C, and SpO2 81% on room air. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 28 000/μL (neutrophils 98%, lymphocytes 1.5%, eosinophils 0%), C-reactive protein 32.3 mg/dL, normal renal and liver function, and lactate 2.0 mmol/L. Toxicology screening was negative. Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral ground-glass opacities, and CT of the chest revealed consolidations in a mosaic pattern from the mid to distal lungs bilaterally. He received 500 mg of methylprednisolone and was started on oxygen, but respiratory failure progressed, necessitating intubation and mechanical ventilation. The following day, after further deterioration, he was transferred to our ICU. On arrival, ventilator settings were FiO2 1.0, respiratory rate 15/min, PEEP 15 cmH2O, and plateau pressure 30 cmH2O. Arterial blood gas analysis showed pH 7.188, PaO2 76 mmHg, PaCO2 79.3 mmHg, and base excess –1.8 mmHg, with a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 76. Despite optimized ventilation, there was no improvement, and veno-venous ECMO was initiated with drainage via the right internal jugular vein and reinfusion via the right femoral vein at 4.0 L/min. Ventilator settings were reduced to FiO2 0.4, PEEP 10 cmH2O, and plateau pressure 20 cmH2O, at which time the lungs were virtually collapsed with no measurable tidal volumes.

A 19-year-old female presented with a 2-week history of progressive pitting edema in both lower legs and a 2-kg weight gain after intense dance practice. She had allergic rhinitis but no family history of similar disease. She reported mild knee and ankle pain without notable tenderness. She denied fever, dyspnea, chest pain, or urinary symptoms. Examination showed moderate bilateral pretibial pitting edema without redness, induration, skin thickening, joint contractures, or muscle weakness.  
CT angiography of the lower extremities showed no venous obstruction; heparin and compression stockings provided no relief. Initial laboratory studies revealed WBC 8090/µL with 28.9% eosinophils (2340/µL), which rose to 4880/µL; hemoglobin, platelets, ESR, CRP, renal function, liver enzymes, albumin, protein electrophoresis, and urinalysis were normal. Serum IgE was 786 kIU/L (unchanged). Tests for parasitic infection were negative. Thyroid function, ECG, and pulmonary function tests were normal. Rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibody were negative. Abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable.  
MRI of the lower thighs demonstrated increased signal in the subcutaneous fat layer and superficial fascia on fat-saturated T2-weighted images, suggesting inflammation, along with mild synovitis of both knees but no deep fascia thickening.

A female infant was born at 37 2/7 weeks’ gestation to a 29-year-old mother with cutaneous lupus erythematosus and positive ANA, anti-ENA, anti-SSA, and anti-SSB antibodies. Pregnancy was complicated by fetal bradycardia at 20 weeks from complete AV block; dexamethasone was given without improvement. At birth, the infant weighed 2330 g (5th percentile) with APGAR scores 9 and 10; ECG confirmed third-degree AV block with junctional escape at 50 bpm. On day 6, an epicardial VVI pacemaker was placed due to circulatory insufficiency.

On day 8, the patient developed fever and erythema around the pacemaker wound. Blood and wound cultures were repeatedly sterile, but C-reactive protein rose to 80 mg/L (ref < 5). She received flucloxacillin and gentamicin, then ceftazidime after surgical exploration showed purulent infiltrates. Despite improving wound appearance, fever persisted and CRP normalized.

On day 22, a generalized non-pruritic eruption of round-to-oval erythematous papules and plaques appeared on the face, trunk, and extremities; mucosa, palms, soles, liver, spleen, and lymph nodes were normal. Laboratory studies showed ferritin 4162 µg/L (ref 10–150), hemoglobin 7.1 mmol/L (ref 8.5–12.5), normal leukocytes and platelets, fibrinogen 3.6 g/L, D-dimer 3996 ng/mL (ref < 500), AST 84 U/L (ref < 31), ALT 33 U/L (ref < 34), LDH 909 U/L (ref < 600), triglycerides 343.7 mg/dL (ref < 77.3), soluble IL-2 receptor 21 803 pg/mL (ref < 2500). Autoimmune serology remained positive for ANA, anti-ENA, anti-SSA, and anti-SSB. 

Our differential diagnosis consisted of persistent infection (systemic candidiasis, CMV, EBV, varicella), complex neonatal lupus, auto-inflammatory disease (MAS, primary HLH), or primary immunodeficiency.

A 42-year-old right-hand-dominant manual laborer presented 2 days after a trivial hammer injury to his right thumb. He reported mild, constant, dull aching pain and slight swelling since the trauma; there was no prior history of pain, trauma, or infection in that area. His medical and family histories were unremarkable.

On examination, there was minimal swelling on the dorsum of the thenar eminence without erythema or increased warmth. The thumb was moderately tender, and range of motion was achieved with difficulty. Sensation, motor function, and distal vascular examination were normal, and no deformity was visible.

Plain radiographs of the right hand revealed an expansile lytic lesion involving the metaphyseal–diaphyseal region of the first metacarpal, with cortical thinning and a cortical breach at the mid-shaft. There was no periosteal reaction or soft-tissue mass, and adjacent joints and other bones appeared normal.

Magnetic resonance imaging with T1, T2, and STIR sequences demonstrated a lesion of the first metacarpal that was isointense on T1 and hyperintense on T2/STIR. The lesion spanned the entire bone, with incomplete cortical fractures of the shaft, and there was no involvement of the periosteum, surrounding soft tissues, or articular surfaces.

On percutaneous aspiration of the lesion, a reddish-tinged fluid was obtained. Routine blood investigations, including a coagulation profile, were within normal limits.

A 28-year-old G2P0101 woman at 37 weeks’ gestation presented with progressive bilateral breast enlargement that began at 3 months’ gestation. She complained of severe back pain, dyspnea, and marked breast tenderness. Her first pregnancy was uncomplicated until a cesarean delivery at 36 weeks for preeclampsia. Baseline breast size was 34B; she estimated a fivefold increase and now required a 44-DD brassiere, which remained tight. Examination revealed massively enlarged breasts with distended indurated superficial veins over the upper thorax and altered spinal curvature. Measurements of the right breast showed a circumference of 75 cm, axilla to nipple 45 cm, and nipple to midline 37 cm.  
Laboratory studies demonstrated a prolactin level of 103.3 μg/L (reference in pregnancy, 36–372 μg/L) and, on postpartum day 6, 40.4 μg/L (normal up to 100 μg/L). White blood cell count, hemoglobin, hematocrit, platelet count, metabolic panel, alkaline phosphatase, and coagulation studies remained within normal limits.  
She was started on bromocriptine 2.5 mg twice daily and underwent breast sonography, which showed skin thickening and linear hypoechoic areas corresponding to dilated ducts and vascular structures, with no abnormal growth—findings consistent with breast hypertrophy.

A 70‐year‐old man with a history of multivessel coronary artery disease, multiple prior stents, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus was admitted electively for coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). Over the preceding three months, he had progressive chest pain and exertional dyspnea. A nuclear stress test demonstrated anterior and anterolateral reversible defects with a drop in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) from 47% at rest to 31% on stress and a blood pressure decrease from 125/77 to 106/44 mmHg. A limited echocardiogram showed an LVEF of 40%–45% with anterior and lateral wall hypokinesis.

On admission, he was afebrile, blood pressure 130/84 mmHg, heart rate 87 beats/min, and in sinus rhythm. Physical examination was unremarkable. An initial electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with frequent premature ventricular contractions and an atypical left bundle branch block.

He underwent triple‐vessel CABG (LAD, OM1, RPL1) with cardiopulmonary bypass, systemic cooling to 34°C, and cardioplegia every 15–20 minutes. Postoperatively, he was transferred to the cardiac ICU with temporary epicardial pacing wires and brief norepinephrine support. Routine chest tube removal occurred on postoperative day 1.

On postoperative day 1, telemetry recorded a 4‐second run of high‐grade atrioventricular block with ventricular standstill. The patient remained fully alert and asymptomatic without syncope. Over postoperative day 2, multiple additional 3–5 second episodes of ventricular standstill were noted, all asymptomatic and without capture by the epicardial pacer wires. Serum electrolytes were within normal limits (potassium 3.6–4.1 mEq/L; magnesium 2.1–2.5 mg/dL; calcium 7.8–8.4 mg/dL; sodium 134–140 mEq/L). On postoperative day 3, a rhythm strip showed atrial flutter with loss of capture from the epicardial pacemaker; the patient remained asymptomatic.

A 60-year-old male Ethiopian farmer presented with an 8-day history of recurrent colicky abdominal pain followed by progressive abdominal distension, vomiting, and constipation. Six years earlier, he had undergone sigmoid resection and anastomosis for sigmoid volvulus. He had no other medical, psychiatric, or family history of note and took no regular medications. 

On examination, he was afebrile; pulse, 88/min; blood pressure, 100/72 mmHg; respiratory rate, 22/min; and oxygen saturation, 96% on room air.
