The abdomen was markedly distended, soft, and non-tender, with hyperactive bowel sounds. Rectal examination revealed an empty rectum. Laboratory studies, including hematological and biochemical tests, were unremarkable.

An erect plain abdominal x-ray showed dilated small and large bowel loops with multiple air-fluid levels and multiple radio-opaque stones in the right iliac fossa that were mobile on follow-up films; a distal rectal gas shadow was present. A CT scan had been planned but was not available at the time.

A 31-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of progressive right ankle pain and paresthesia along the medial plantar foot. She had no history of trauma. Her past medical history was notable only for Raynaud’s syndrome, managed by a rheumatologist for eight years. She had gained weight in the past year due to medications and reduced activity.  

Initial evaluation in the emergency department yielded no diagnosis; she was referred back to her rheumatologist. Her symptoms persisted despite conservative therapy with NSAIDs and rest. She was treated with high-dose intravenous corticosteroids and later with sulfasalazine, but her ankle pain and foot paresthesia did not improve. A three-phase bone scan and ankle ultrasound were unremarkable. A musculoskeletal MRI of the right ankle was reported as normal. She was diagnosed with complex regional pain syndrome and managed with lidocaine patches, opioids, pregabalin, and hyperbaric chamber therapy, with no sustained relief.  

At presentation to our outpatient clinic, a plain radiograph of the right ankle showed a dense area in the calcaneus. Computed tomography of the right ankle demonstrated a 10×4 mm insula compacta in the calcaneus with no other abnormalities. Her American Orthopaedic Foot & Ankle Society (AOFAS) Ankle-Hindfoot score was 18, and her visual analog scale (VAS) for pain was 10 at rest and with movement.  

On examination, ankle range of motion was limited by pain; there were no signs of instability or impingement. Heel rise was not possible due to pain. Palpation of the posteromedial ankle was painful. Percussion over the tibial nerve proximal to the tarsal tunnel elicited posteromedial ankle pain along with numbness and tingling in the medial plantar foot (positive Tinel’s sign). A lateral radiograph showed obliteration of Kager’s fat pad, with no other bony abnormalities.

A 16-year-old woman with stage IIIb malignant melanoma was receiving adjuvant nivolumab (6 mg/kg every 4 weeks). After the sixth dose, she developed anorexia, nausea, recurrent vomiting, upper abdominal pain, and a 3 kg weight loss over 2 weeks. She had no prior gastrointestinal history. On examination she appeared pale and dehydrated, with epigastric tenderness; the remainder of the abdominal examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed a mild elevation of alanine transaminase (91 U/L; reference 10–45 U/L) and normal thyrotropin and cortisol; albumin was within the reference range at this time. A PET-CT scan demonstrated increased fluorodeoxyglucose uptake throughout the gastric wall, most prominently in the corpus-antrum region. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed erythematous gastric mucosa with severe fibrinous erosions in the fundus, corpus, and antrum, and endoscopic ultrasound showed diffuse thickening of the gastric wall to 13 mm without focal masses. Gastric biopsies from fundus, corpus, and antrum showed diffuse chronic active pangastritis with ulceration, crypt abscesses, increased intraepithelial lymphocytes (45 per 100 epithelial cells), and apoptosis. The lamina propria contained a full-thickness lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate. There was no evidence of epithelial granulomas, thickened subepithelial collagen, prominent eosinophils, Helicobacter pylori, CMV infection, or malignancy. Epstein-Barr virus nuclear antigen IgG was positive, consistent with prior infection.

A 51-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and ischemic heart disease noted a 2-week history of a painful left breast lump. She denied trauma. Examination revealed a firm 30 mm lesion at the 10 o’clock position, 7 cm from the nipple, without axillary lymphadenopathy. 

Mammography showed a poorly circumscribed 40 × 24 mm mass in the lateral left breast with irregular, stranded contours and no suspicious calcifications. Breast ultrasound demonstrated a lobulated, heterogeneous, hypoechoic mass measuring 31 × 17 × 21 mm, with distortion of surrounding structures, edema, and skin thickening; the lesion was considered suspicious for malignancy.

Five days later she returned with increased erythema, swelling, and purulent discharge from the upper inner quadrant; she was started on oral clindamycin for presumed cellulitis and referred for biopsy. Ultrasound showed marked enlargement of the lesion with skin thickening and erythema, thought to represent an inflammatory lesion. Aspiration was attempted but no pus could be drawn due to high viscosity; oral antibiotics were continued.

A few days later she presented to the emergency department with ongoing discharge. Examination revealed an open wound with central necrosis, surrounding purulent discharge, erythema extending to the nipple, and peau d’orange changes. She was hemodynamically stable. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 13.0 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein of 123 mg/L, and a blood sugar level of 25.2 mmol/L.

A 65-year-old man presented with a 10-day history of worsening abdominal pain and vomiting. He had a prior history of recurrent episodes of pancreatic-type abdominal pain that had not been evaluated.  
On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. Abdominal palpation revealed generalized tenderness without guarding or rebound.  
Initial laboratory tests showed:  
• Lipase 357 IU/L (normal <60 IU/L)  
• Leukocyte count 13,090/mm³  
• C-reactive protein 80 mg/L (normal <5 mg/L)  
Liver function tests and serum bilirubin were within normal limits.  
Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a swollen, hypoechoic pancreas and bilateral triangular hypoechoic lesions in the renal cortices. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed diffuse pancreatic enlargement with loss of normal lobulations (a “sausage-like” appearance) and a small simple cyst in the pancreatic tail; there were also bilateral peripheral renal lesions and enlarged lymph nodes in the peripancreatic and mediastinal regions.  
MR cholangiopancreatography showed pancreatic enlargement with homogeneous signal and the tail cyst, hypointense peripheral renal lesions on T2-weighted images, peripancreatic lymphadenopathy on diffusion-weighted imaging, and multiple areas of stenosis and dilation of the right intrahepatic bile ducts with filiform stenosis of the distal common bile duct.  
Further laboratory evaluation revealed:  
• Serum IgG4 3.76 g/L (normal <1.35 g/L)  
• Antinuclear antibodies, extractable nuclear antigen antibodies, and ANCA negative  
• Tumor markers CA19-9, AFP, and CEA within normal limits  
• Tests for hepatitis B and C viruses negative

A 71-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of intermittent headaches relieved by analgesics and an abrupt loss of vision over the same period. He reported weakness of his left extremities for 1 year, after which he required assistance to walk. He denied seizures, vomiting, anosmia, hearing loss, weight loss, or systemic symptoms. His past medical history was notable only for a stroke 1 year earlier; there was no history of tuberculosis, hypertension, diabetes, or malignancy. On examination, vital signs were stable and neurologic and general physical examinations were unremarkable. Routine laboratory tests and immunoserologies, including HIV antibody testing, were within normal limits. 

Noncontrast and contrast-enhanced CT of the brain demonstrated multiple well-defined calcified nodules in the right subcortical parietal lobe, left thalamus (largest 1.20 cm), and left basal ganglia; additionally, a 0.90 cm calcified nodule in the right occipital cortex showed surrounding hypodensity suggesting vasogenic edema. No contrast enhancement was observed.

MRI of the brain revealed a 0.90 cm spherical lesion in the right subcortical occipital lobe that was hypointense on T1, had a hyperintense T2 rim, showed ring enhancement post-contrast, and demonstrated a blooming artifact on SWI without diffusion restriction. Similar lesions without T2 signal or enhancement but with SWI blooming were seen in the left temporal juxtacortical region, right parietal juxtacortical region, and left thalamus.

MR spectroscopy of an intralesional voxel showed decreased choline, creatine, and N-acetylaspartate peaks, elevated lactate and lipid peaks, and NAA/Cr and Cho/Cr ratios of 0.38 and 1.21, respectively.

A 46-year-old man with no history of diabetes, uveitis, or retinal disease underwent standard phacoemulsification with acrylic posterior-chamber intraocular lens implantation under topical anesthesia. Preoperative best-corrected visual acuity was 0.1 in the right eye and 1.0 in the left eye; intraocular pressure in both eyes was 16 mmHg. Preoperative OCT of the right macula was unremarkable, and the vitreous was attached. At the end of surgery, 0.1 mL of a 10 mg/mL intracameral cefuroxime solution was administered.

On postoperative day 1, the patient complained of painless vision loss and a central scotoma in the right eye. Best-corrected visual acuity was 0.02; intraocular pressure was 15 mmHg. Slit-lamp examination showed a clear anterior chamber without inflammation. Dilated fundus examination revealed diffuse macular edema without retinal hemorrhages or cotton-wool spots. Swept-source OCT demonstrated a serous macular detachment with subretinal fluid predominantly in the foveal area and intraretinal edema in the outer nuclear layer; the central macular thickness was 697 µm. There was no posterior vitreous detachment or vitreomacular traction. Fluorescein angiography showed an early nonfluorescent zone adjacent to the optic disc surrounded by an irregular fluorescent band, late diffuse leakage into the optic disc area, multiple nonfluorescent spots corresponding to RPE changes, and a parafoveal hyperfluorescent spot; the foveal avascular zone was normal.

A 27-year-old gravida 2 para 0 woman with an uncomplicated spontaneous pregnancy was referred at 36 weeks’ gestation for suspected fetal renal anomalies. Prenatal ultrasound showed:
• Bilateral renal enlargement and hydronephrosis  
• A markedly dilated fetal bladder  
• A left perirenal fluid collection measuring 64 × 34 mm that displaced the left kidney anteriorly; the collection contained multiple light bands, flocculent echoes, and slightly echogenic material  
• Oligohydramnios

An emergency cesarean delivery produced a male infant (weight 2530 g) with Apgar scores of 8, 8, and 10 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes. His vital signs were stable, and physical examination was normal. Blood and urine routine studies were unremarkable, but serum creatinine was elevated at 156.1 µmol/L, indicating impaired renal function.

On postnatal MRI, the left perirenal collection demonstrated mixed long and short T1 and T2 signals with internal light bands. Magnetic resonance urography revealed bladder wall irregularity and thickening, bilateral ureteral dilation, and urinary retention.

A 41-year-old New Zealand European man was admitted after a car-versus-bicycle collision in which he was ejected from his bicycle. He sustained multiple injuries, including a right tripod facial fracture; a CT scan of the face performed at initial trauma evaluation showed a hyperdense lesion within the posterior segment of the right globe. Ophthalmology was consulted to assess for a retained intraocular foreign body.

His ocular history included bilateral keratoconus, with three prior right penetrating keratoplasties; the left eye was managed with a rigid gas-permeable contact lens. On examination, uncorrected visual acuity was counting fingers in the right eye (improving to 6/15 with pinhole) and 6/7.5 in the left eye with the contact lens. Intraocular pressures were 10 mm Hg in the right eye and 6 mm Hg in the left eye. Extraocular movements, color plate testing, confrontational visual fields, and pupillary responses were normal; there was no relative afferent pupillary defect. Exophthalmometry measured 15 mm on the right and 16 mm on the left. Slit-lamp examination revealed a clear right corneal graft, moderate keratoconus in the left cornea, deep and quiet anterior chambers, clear crystalline lenses, and quiet vitreous in both eyes.

Dilated fundus examination of the left eye was normal. In the right eye, there was a white, raised lesion located superotemporal to the optic disc, approximately 4 disc diameters from the disc margin and 1.5 disc diameters in greatest dimension. Enhanced-depth optical coherence tomography (EDI-OCT) through this lesion demonstrated a double “rocky and rolling” elevation of the outer retina without subretinal fluid.

A 101-month-old boy was brought for evaluation of a deformity and restriction of movement in his right forearm that had developed over the preceding 5 months. He had no other skeletal deformities. He had been followed for structural short stature (weight 20 kg [1.44th percentile], height 119 cm [2.68th percentile]). On examination, there was a prominent varus angulation of the right forearm. Elbow and wrist flexion and extension were normal; forearm supination was full, but pronation was limited by 25 degrees. Plain radiographs of the elbow and forearm demonstrated shortening of the ulna, varus angulation of both the ulna and radius, subluxation of the radial head, and cortical irregularity in the distal one-third of the ulna.

A 42-year-old man was referred for evaluation of an abnormal chest shadow. He had undergone partial resection of tongue carcinoma 15 years earlier, was an ex-smoker (4 pack-years), and had no known dust or drug exposures. Three maternal uncles had malignancies. Chest radiography showed a reticular shadow and volume loss in the lower lung fields. High-resolution CT demonstrated reticulation with lower lobe predominance and traction bronchiectasis, consistent with a “probable UIP pattern.” On examination, he had nail dystrophy, oral leukoplakia, reticulated hypopigmentation, mild hair loss, and dental abnormalities; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed elevated KL-6 (881 U/mL), surfactant protein-D (221 ng/dL), and total IgE (9,556 IU/mL), mild thrombocytopenia, and elevated transaminases; autoantibodies were negative. Pulmonary function testing revealed mild restrictive impairment (FVC 3.48 L [77.9% predicted]) and reduced DLCO (66.1% predicted). Bronchoalveolar lavage from the right middle lobe yielded 5.1×10^5 cells/mL (80% macrophages, 14% lymphocytes, 3% neutrophils, 3% eosinophils). Skin biopsy of a pigmented forearm lesion showed epidermal thinning, basal epithelial cell loss, and melanin pigmentation. MRI of the abdomen revealed enlargement and blunting of the left hepatic lobe; liver biopsy demonstrated A2/F3 fibrosis (pre-cirrhosis). Video-assisted thoracoscopic lung biopsy showed subpleural and perilobular fibrosis with fibroblastic foci, homogeneous centrilobular fibrosis with cellular infiltration, bronchiolitis, lymphoid follicles, and macrophage accumulation; multiple pathological findings suggested a differential diagnosis including UIP, fibrotic non-specific interstitial pneumonia, desquamative interstitial pneumonia, and bronchiolitis.

A 57-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a cranial bone lesion incidentally found on brain CT during workup for a thyroid tumor. Two months earlier, he had undergone facial nerve decompression for right facial palsy. He was asymptomatic and alert. On examination, there was a hard, non-tender protuberance over the left parietal region without skin discoloration or hair changes. Laboratory tests, including blood counts and tumor markers, were within normal limits. Noncontrast brain CT showed a 3 cm iso-dense lesion involving the left parietal bone with cortical thinning and a lytic appearance. MR imaging demonstrated that the lesion was isointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, hypointense on diffusion-weighted imaging, and showed uniform, faint enhancement after gadolinium.

A 14-year-old African American girl (BMI 21.5 kg/m2) began taking oral minocycline 100 mg daily for acne 6 weeks before presentation. Four weeks into therapy, she developed a generalized, palpable, nonblanching erythematous rash and mild anasarca, accompanied by fever, myalgia, nausea, vomiting, sore throat, and generalized weakness. She denied flank or lower abdominal pain and used diphenhydramine with only partial relief.

On examination she was alert, nontoxic, and normotensive. She had a widespread erythematous rash, mild anasarca, erythematous tonsils with exudate, and bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. The lungs, heart, abdomen, and costovertebral angles were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 26 × 10^9/L with 1% eosinophils and 1.29 × 10^9/L atypical lymphocytes; hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL; platelets 156 × 10^9/L; prothrombin time 16.3 s. Serum creatinine was 12.9 mg/dL, urea nitrogen 75 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 378 U/L, and aspartate aminotransferase 146 U/L. Complement levels were C3 0.89 g/L and C4 0.08 g/L.

Urinalysis revealed leukocyte esterase positivity, 0–2 red cells/hpf, 6–15 leukocytes/hpf, leukocyte casts, granular casts, and few eosinophils; protein-to-creatinine ratio was 44.1 mg/mmol. Urine, blood, and throat cultures were negative. EBV IgM was positive but EBV PCR and Monospot were negative. Renal ultrasound showed bilateral enlarged, echogenic kidneys.

A 33-year-old primiparous woman at 15 weeks and 5 days of gestation presented with a 1-day history of acute-onset bilateral frontotemporal headache associated with dizziness, blurred vision, and two episodes of non-projectile vomiting without blood. She then developed reduced responsiveness, impaired vocalization with incomprehensible speech, and sudden weakness in her left upper limb that progressed to her left lower limb. There was no history of head trauma, urinary incontinence, respiratory or cardiac symptoms, or vaginal bleeding. Her past medical history was unremarkable; she had one prior cesarean delivery. 

On examination, temperature was 97.2°F, pulse 102/min, blood pressure 130/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO₂ 96% on room air, and body-mass index 18.2 kg/m². Glasgow Coma Scale was 10 (E3 V2 M5); she was disoriented with sluggish left pupil reaction and impaired speech but no facial palsy. Motor testing revealed increased tone, hyperreflexia, and bilateral upgoing plantar responses on the left, with decreased strength in the left upper and lower extremities.

Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (13 500/mm³; normal 4 000–11 000) with neutrophilia (81%; normal 45–75), hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL (normal 12–18), hyponatremia (128 mEq/L; normal 134–146), hypokalemia (3.5 mEq/L; normal 3.6–5.0), and elevated fibrinogen (533 mg/dL; normal 200–400). Dengue serologies and antiphospholipid antibodies were negative or within normal limits. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed acute hyperintense lesions on T2/FLAIR in the right pons and right cerebellar peduncle. Magnetic resonance angiography demonstrated occlusion of the basilar artery and obstruction of the V3 segment of the right vertebral artery. A noncontrast head CT showed no acute intracranial abnormality.

A 19-year-old Caucasian woman, G5P0040, with a documented COL7A1 mutation and a history of autosomal dominant dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa presented for routine prenatal care. Her pregnancy was otherwise uncomplicated. She had occasional cutaneous blistering with mechanical stress but no genital or vaginal mucosal lesions. After counseling, she elected an elective low transverse cesarean delivery under spinal anesthesia at 39 weeks’ gestation. A male infant weighing 3000 g was delivered with Apgar scores of 8 and 9. 

On postpartum day 1, the neonate developed erythema and small blisters on the back, inguinal region, and right buttock. By day 3, diffuse erythematous and bullous lesions had appeared on the chin, forearms, face, thumbs, fingers, left buttock, the remainder of the back, and both legs, covering approximately 30% of the total body surface area. There were ruptured bullae but no secondary bacterial infection. Supportive skin care measures for suspected epidermolysis bullosa were initiated.

A 4-year-old Caucasian boy was brought with a 6-month history of persistent purulent discharge from the distal dorsum of his penis following circumcision. He had been treated with various antibiotics without improvement and had no prior complaints before the procedure. His medical, developmental, and social histories were unremarkable; there was no family history of inherited disease.  

On examination, temperature was 36.4 °C, pulse 98 beats/min, and blood pressure 80/50 mmHg. Genital examination revealed a small pinhole opening at the distal dorsal aspect of the penis and a firm, cylindrical tract extending toward the penile base.  

Laboratory studies showed a white-blood-cell count of 6.1×10^3/mm^3 with normal hemoglobin, liver enzymes, and creatinine; serologies for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV were negative. Urinalysis suggested a possible urinary tract infection, but swab cultures from the lesion grew no bacteria. Genitourinary ultrasonography was normal.  

Fistulography performed with contrast injected into the sinus demonstrated a tract extending toward the prepubic area with no communication between the sinus and the urinary tract.

A 44-year-old Caucasian woman with a history of hypertension and preeclampsia who had taken oral contraceptive pills for 15 years presented with two weeks of intractable colicky abdominal pain that worsened with oral intake and was associated with diarrhea and nonbilious vomiting. The diarrhea was sometimes watery and hemoccult positive; gastroccult testing of vomitus was negative. On examination, she had stage III hypertension out of proportion to her risk factors and diffuse periumbilical tenderness without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 16.1×10^9/L with 91% neutrophils, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 79 mm/hr, and a C-reactive protein level of 100 mg/L. An abdominal CT scan demonstrated nonspecific colitis. She received intravenous metronidazole and ciprofloxacin, but all microbial cultures, including three for Clostridium difficile, were negative. Urinalysis revealed nephritic-range proteinuria. Tests for P-ANCA, C-ANCA, ASCA, ANA, celiac serologies, lactate, CA-125, and TSH were all negative. Colonoscopy showed diffuse colonic lymphoid reactive hyperplasia; a small-bowel series and indium scan were unremarkable. Contrast CT scans of the chest, abdomen, pelvis, head, and a transvaginal ultrasound showed no evidence of malignancy. Although she remained normotensive off oral contraceptives, mesenteric ischemia was considered, and magnetic resonance angiography of the abdomen revealed proximal superior mesenteric artery stenosis, which was confirmed by CT angiography to be severe in both the proximal and distal segments.

A 55-year-old Japanese man with a 13-year history of diabetes was brought to the hospital after a sudden loss of consciousness and bilateral convulsions (day 0). On examination, he was afebrile (temperature 36.8 °C), hypertensive (blood pressure 142/92 mmHg), and tachycardic (heart rate 108 beats/min). He had left-sided hemiparesis that was unresponsive to painful stimuli. Laboratory evaluation showed a pH of 6.95 and a blood glucose level of 486 mg/dL, consistent with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). He was treated with fluid resuscitation, insulin infusion, and potassium supplementation; consciousness returned after 12 hours and hemiparesis diminished by day 1.  
Given concern for cerebral infarction, MRI of the brain with FLAIR sequences was performed, revealing bilateral lesions in the right temporal lobe, right parietal lobe, and left temporal lobe that did not conform to a vascular distribution. The most prominent lesion shifted from the right temporal lobe on day 0 to the right parietal lobe by day 9. Serial measurement of the lactate-to-pyruvate ratio was repeatedly above 20 (reference <15). Convulsions are rare in DKA but are frequently associated with metabolic encephalopathy, particularly in mitochondrial disorders.

A 75-year-old woman presented with an almost 2-year history of intermittently pruritic pink, scaly plaques on the bilateral shins. Over time, she received diagnoses of guttate psoriasis, verruca vulgaris, irritated seborrheic keratoses, lichen planus–like keratoses, and was evaluated for nonmelanoma skin cancer. She was treated with triamcinolone 0.1% ointment for presumed psoriasis and with topical salicylic acid, fluorouracil, and cryotherapy for presumed warts, but the lesions persisted and sometimes ulcerated. Over the preceding year, she underwent seven punch biopsies. Some specimens were reported descriptively or as verruca vulgaris, demonstrating digitated acanthosis with hypergranulosis and sparse lichenoid inflammation; other biopsies showed nonspecific papillomatosis and parakeratosis but no malignancy. Immunohistochemical staining and polymerase chain reaction studies for human papillomavirus on two biopsies were negative. One pathology report suggested a differential diagnosis of hypertrophic lichen planus.

A 32-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a “bump” on her left eye, noted 2 months earlier. She denied pain or discharge but reported a subjective decrease in vision OS. She had no history of trauma or systemic illness. The lesion was initially elevated and white but became flatter and yellow with increased vascularity over time.

On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/40 OS. Slit-lamp examination OS showed a 7.0 × 5.3 mm oval yellow elevated conjunctival lesion at the inferior limbus with overlying conjunctival injection and dilated vessels. The lesion was nontender and immobile; the remainder of both eyes was normal.

The patient was treated with a 2-week topical prednisolone taper without improvement. At follow-up, the lesion measured 5.8 × 5.8 mm, and vision remained 20/40 OS. Steroids were discontinued, and excisional biopsy was planned.

A 72-year-old Japanese man presented with a one-month history of dyspnea on exertion and bilateral shoulder pain, progressing to difficulty in raising both upper limbs. He denied headache, jaw claudication, visual loss, or fever. On admission, blood pressure was 147/90 mm Hg, pulse 110 beats/minute, respiratory rate 12 breaths/minute, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Examination showed no temporal artery tenderness and mild shoulder tenderness. The right arm could not be elevated to shoulder level and the left arm could not be elevated at all. Laboratory tests revealed a C-reactive protein level of 13.99 mg/dL and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 31 mm/hour. Rheumatoid factor, anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, antinuclear antibody, and anti-SSA antibody were negative; matrix metalloproteinase-3 was normal. Musculoskeletal ultrasound of both shoulders showed no tenosynovitis, bursitis, or glenohumeral synovitis. He scored 3 points on the 2012 provisional classification criteria for polymyalgia rheumatica and 2 points on the 2010 rheumatoid arthritis classification criteria, below the thresholds for diagnosis. Because passive elevation of the arms did not elicit pain, neurological disease was considered. Neurological examination revealed absent biceps and brachioradialis reflexes bilaterally, preserved reflexes elsewhere, and weakness of C5–C6-innervated muscles predominantly on the left. Ultrasound showed absence of left diaphragmatic movement during breathing. Cervical magnetic resonance imaging showed no evidence of mechanical compression, suggesting cervical radiculopathy of unknown origin.

A 28-year-old woman presented with a slowly enlarging, intermittently painful mass over the medial aspect of her proximal right leg for three months. She denied trauma, locking, clicking, loss of motion, warmth, constitutional symptoms, or functional limitation. On examination, there was a 4.0 × 3.0 cm firm, tender mass over the pes anserinus insertion on the proximal tibia. The lesion was fixed to bone, noncompressible, and had no overlying warmth, erythema, induration, bruit, dilated veins, or lymphadenopathy. Distal neurovascular examination was normal. The knee had a full, painless range of motion without instability or meniscal signs. Plain radiographs were normal. MRI of the right knee revealed a 4.5 × 3.0 × 2.0 cm soft-tissue mass at the pes anserinus insertion with areas of low to intermediate signal intensity on all sequences and heterogeneous contrast enhancement; there was no bone or joint involvement. Laboratory studies, including a coagulation profile, were noncontributory.

A 51-year-old man presented with a one-day history of increasing fatigue and malaise, preceded by nausea, vomiting, myalgia, and arthralgia. This was his sixth similar presentation over six months. His past medical history included mild obstructive sleep apnea, prior intracranial hemorrhage, and two hospital admissions for undefined “septic shock.” He took aspirin and vitamin B12, had no allergies, was a nonsmoker, and reported a long history of heavy alcohol use. Family history was notable for a brother with lymphoma.  

On examination, he was tachycardic at 103 bpm and had an oxygen saturation of 92% on room air; other vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies showed: hemoglobin 224 g/L, red-cell count 6.66×10^12/L, hematocrit 64%, albumin 34 g/L, white-cell count 19.7×10^9/L, and evidence of acute kidney injury (creatinine 121 µmol/L, eGFR 59 mL/min/1.73 m^2). A 130-mL venesection was performed, and the patient was admitted.  

Despite aggressive fluid resuscitation, his blood pressure fell to 83/41 mmHg, and he was transferred to the ICU. After further fluids, blood pressure normalized but urine output remained low (26 mL/h). He developed pitting edema to the knees, mild bilateral basal crackles, and sacral edema. Mixed metabolic acidosis with elevated lactate was noted. Blood and urine cultures were negative.  

Within 24 hours in the ICU his urine output increased to 200–500 mL/h, his hemoglobin normalized, and he left by his own request. Twelve hours later he returned with dyspnea; he was tachypneic and hypoxic and had pulmonary edema. He received intravenous furosemide and improved rapidly.

A 35-year-old Hispanic woman presented with 48 hours of severe hypogastric abdominal pain and lower GI bleeding characterized by diarrhea with clots and hematochezia unrelieved by over-the-counter medications. Her history included childhood episodes of lower GI bleeding that resolved spontaneously, hypothyroidism, and polycystic ovary syndrome treated with hormonal contraceptives for five months. On examination, she was tachycardic (112 bpm), normotensive, and 90% on room air; she had diffuse abdominal tenderness and a clear systolic murmur. Laboratory tests revealed hypoalbuminemia (3.1 mg/dL) and an elevated D-dimer (10 000 μg/mL) with a normal thrombophilia and autoimmune workup. Colonoscopy demonstrated tortuous hemorrhoidal veins and dilated vessels in the colon and terminal ileum, raising suspicion for mesenteric venous thrombosis versus ischemia. Contrast-enhanced thoracoabdominal CT showed segmental pulmonary emboli with bilateral infarctions, portal vein atresia, a shunt from the left mesenteric vein to the right colonic vein, marked varicose dilatation of the inferior mesenteric and splenic veins, and engorgement of the inferior vena cava and iliac veins. Echocardiography revealed preserved ejection fraction and elevated pulmonary venous pressure (62 mmHg). She was started on therapeutic enoxaparin but developed worsening GI bleeding requiring transfusions and temporary anticoagulation cessation, followed by angiographic embolization of mesenteric and colonic veins. She then developed acute dyspnea from new pulmonary artery obstruction necessitating thrombolysis, thrombectomy, inferior vena cava filter placement, and heparin infusion. Persistent vaginal bleeding prompted angiography that identified three splenic artery aneurysms, which were coiled successfully.

A 63-year-old woman with developmental cognitive delay and a history of sleep apnea on BiPAP presented with persistently irritated, red left eye for several months. She had already failed a trial of olopatadine eye drops and topical polymyxin B/trimethoprim, then was referred to optometry. There, she reported burning, tearing, and blurred vision. Examination showed 1–2+ inferior bulbar conjunctival injection OS and reduced tear volume OU. Over two follow-up visits, she used aggressive lubrication with erythromycin ointment, cyclosporine 0.05% drops, 1000 mg oral fish oil, and increased oral hydration without improvement. 

On ophthalmology referral, visual exam revealed persistent 2+ conjunctival injection and 2+ punctate keratopathy OS, with peripheral corneal vascularization and subepithelial haze in the inferior one-fourth of the left cornea. Retraction of the upper eyelids demonstrated a normal tarsal plate in the right eye but profound flaccidity of the left upper eyelid, which could be stretched 15 mm above the superior orbital rim. There was approximately 1.5 mm of lagophthalmos OS only. Schirmer 2 testing revealed 21 mm of wetting OD and 22 mm OS.

A 28-year-old man presented 10 days after liposuction performed abroad with increasing abdominal discomfort, nausea, fevers, and chills. He had lost 20 kg and weighed 63 kg; he had no prior intra-abdominal pathology or surgery. He became septic from an abdominal collection. On examination, he was febrile to 38.5 °C, heart rate 104 bpm, blood pressure 137/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min. His abdomen was distended by a large, fluctuant mass with generalized tenderness and maximal guarding in the left iliac fossa. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed three subcutaneous cystic collections in the left flank (12.5 × 3.5 × 10.7 cm), right flank (5.9 × 1.2 × 7 cm), and left rectus muscle (1.2 × 1.8 × 2 cm), and a large cystic intra-abdominal mass displacing the bladder to the right, measuring 18 × 14 × 7.6 cm. He was treated with broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and percutaneous drainage of the subcutaneous collections, then discharged for preoperative optimization prior to planned surgical resection of the intra-abdominal lesion.

A 51‐year‐old woman was referred for evaluation of proteinuria (1.97 g/24 h) and an eGFR of 36 mL/min/1.73 m2 (CKD stage G3b/A3). Her history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, depression, and chronically elevated alkaline phosphatase. Medications were amlodipine, valsartan, atorvastatin, fluoxetine, omeprazole, and occasional amitriptyline. Blood pressure was 116/85 mm Hg; BMI 32.6 kg/m2. Examination showed normal strength, impaired tandem gait, no skin or nail abnormalities, and no patellar or abdominal masses. Renal ultrasound revealed slightly echogenic kidneys and a simple left cyst. Serologies were unremarkable: normal complement levels, negative viral hepatitis serology, and ANA <1:80. Automated urinalysis showed 1+ hematuria (3–8 RBCs/HPF) without casts. A kidney biopsy was performed. Light microscopy showed occasional foamy enlarged podocytes, 12 of 13 glomeruli globally sclerotic, severe intimal fibrosis, and arteriolar hyalinosis. Immunofluorescence was essentially negative except for equal kappa and lambda in tubulointerstitial casts. Electron microscopy revealed numerous lamellar bodies in podocytes. The initial pathology differential diagnoses were Fabry disease, iatrogenic cationic amphiphilic agent–associated phospholipidosis, and nail–patella syndrome.

A 61-year-old man with a 13-year history of elevated creatine kinase levels and a 10-year history of positional tremor noted progressive right fifth-finger abduction weakness over 1 year, followed by bilateral paresthesias in all fingers and toes. Six months before admission, he developed low back pain radiating to both legs (more on the left). Two months before admission, he experienced anginal chest pain; cardiac evaluation showed only hypertension and mild left ventricular hypertrophy, and a stress test was halted at 80 W because of muscle weakness.  

On neurologic examination at admission, he had weakness of head flexion, tongue atrophy with fasciculations, bulbar speech, diffuse mild muscle weakness (M4) and wasting, hypotonia, positional tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, absent upper-limb tendon reflexes, bilateral gynecomastia, hip flexion weakness (M4–), absent lower-limb reflexes, and calf fasciculations. Abdominal ultrasound revealed hepatic steatosis. Lumbar spine MRI showed canal stenosis at L4/5, osteochondrosis at L3/4 and L5/S1, spondylarthrosis L2–5, and spondylosis.  

Two months later, he was admitted after a fall due to leg weakness. Examination revealed bilateral peripheral facial palsy, tongue atrophy with fasciculations, quadruparesis (M3–4), stocking-type sensory loss, and a broad-based ataxic gait. Nerve conduction studies showed a sensorimotor polyneuropathy with conduction blocks in the median, ulnar, and left peroneal nerves. Brain CT was unremarkable. Laboratory studies found CK 1340 U/L, normal TSH, vitamin B12, immunofixation, antiganglioside antibodies, and Borrelia serologies; CSF showed 24 cells/µL with normal protein and glucose. Intravenous immunoglobulins were administered, leading to partial remission of the conduction block in the left median nerve and modest gait improvement, with no other clinical changes.

A woman in her mid-20s who is a professional basketball player presented with a 7-hour history of sharp, worsening abdominal pain rated 7/10, initially epigastric then migrating to the right lower quadrant. She had nausea and vomiting in the emergency department, for which she received IV ondansetron and a bolus of lactated Ringer solution. She denied diarrhea, constipation, fever, chills, dysuria, or vaginal discharge. Her last menstrual period was within the past month, and she reported a low likelihood of pregnancy. She had no history of abdominal surgery, inflammatory bowel disease, or other gastrointestinal disorders. Medications, alcohol, tobacco, and drug use were denied.

Vital signs: temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 131/65 mm Hg, heart rate 60 bpm, respiratory rate 16/min, oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Physical examination revealed a nondistended abdomen with normal bowel sounds in all quadrants and tenderness in the right lower quadrant without guarding or rebound.

Laboratory studies, including a comprehensive metabolic panel, complete blood count, and lipase, were within normal limits. A serum pregnancy test was negative, and urinalysis showed only trace ketones. CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast demonstrated distended loops of small bowel with wall thickening and enhancement, decompressed distal loops, and fecalization of the small bowel.

A 2½-month-old female infant, born to nonconsanguineous parents, was referred for evaluation of gradual abdominal distension noted since 1 month of age. Her weight was 4.2 kg and length 52 cm, both below the third percentile. On examination, she had tense ascites causing severe respiratory distress but no pedal edema. Ultrasonography of the abdomen showed massive ascites without other abnormalities. Approximately 200 mL of thick milky turbid fluid was obtained by paracentesis, which temporarily relieved her respiratory distress. Biochemical analysis of the ascitic fluid showed a triglyceride concentration of 5896 mg/dL, total protein of 4.8 g/dL, lactate dehydrogenase of 341 U/L, and a white-cell count of 200 cells/mm³ with 80% lymphocytes. Serum electrolytes, liver-function tests, and renal-function tests were normal.

A 69-year-old man with upper lobe–dominant pulmonary fibrosis and chronic cough was referred for evaluation of an enlarging mediastinal air cyst seen on CT. He had no smoking history and worked in iron casting; he was taking antitussives. On admission, white blood cells were 4000/μL, lactate dehydrogenase 193 IU/L, C-reactive protein 0.04 mg/dL, and KL-6 363 U/mL. Pulmonary function tests showed a restrictive pattern (vital capacity 2.16 L [60.7% predicted], FVC 2.33 L, FEV1/FVC 96.6%). Chest CT revealed a 30 mm air cyst adjacent to the left main bronchus with subpleural fibrotic changes in both upper lobes. A frontal‐plane reconstruction demonstrated that the cyst lumen was connected to that of the left main bronchus through a thin tunnel and that multiple tiny air spaces extended from the bronchial wall. Flexible bronchoscopy showed a round left main bronchial lumen with bubbling from slits in the mucosa, findings absent in the right main or lobar bronchi. Comparison with imaging from four years earlier showed progressive right upper–lobe volume loss and enlargement of the cyst.

A 2-year-old boy was evaluated for an 8-month history of persistent vomiting. Initially the episodes occurred 1–2 times every 2–3 days but gradually increased to 6–8 nonbilious, nonprojectile episodes per day containing food particles, particularly after large meals. Despite multiple outpatient visits and symptomatic treatment with antiemetics, proton pump inhibitors, and domperidone, his symptoms progressed over the month before admission to complete intolerance of solid foods, with nutrition limited to liquids. He lost 4 kg over 3 months. His parents also noted a sense of abdominal fullness with a nontender, nonmobile lump in the left hypochondriac and epigastric regions.

He was born after an uncomplicated pregnancy to nonconsanguineous parents and had been healthy until symptom onset. On examination he was vitally stable but appeared cachectic, with severe wasting and stunting (weight 5.5 kg, height 78 cm, both <3 SD for age). He had pallor and grade 3 digital clubbing but no peripheral edema or lymphadenopathy. Abdominal examination revealed upper abdominal distension and a palpable 4.5×7.5 cm lump in the epigastric and left hypochondriac area without tenderness, visible peristalsis, ascites, or organomegaly. Other systems were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed mild microcytic hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin 98 g/L), a total leukocyte count of 9.48×10^9/L, platelets 456×10^9/L, and a slightly reduced serum albumin level of 33 g/L. Renal and liver function tests were otherwise normal. He had hypokalemia (2.8 mmol/L), hypochloremia (85 mmol/L), and a metabolic alkalosis (pH 7.52, bicarbonate 32 mmol/L).

Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated diffuse smooth thickening of the gastric wall with luminal narrowing but no obstructing mass. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a grossly distended stomach with intensely enhancing mucosal thickening up to 18 mm displaying a polypoidal appearance, without any extraluminal mass or organomegaly.

Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed complete narrowing of the gastric cavity owing to giant polypoidal gastric folds predominantly in the body of the stomach, impeding passage of a standard 9.2 mm endoscope; an ultra-thin 5.2 mm scope was then advanced, showing similar hypertrophic folds in the antrum causing pyloric narrowing. Multiple mucosal biopsies were obtained from the gastric folds.

A 75-year-old white man presented with 3 months of fatigue, evening fevers, night sweats, an unexplained 5-kg weight loss, worsening dyspnea, cough, and mucopurulent sputum. He was a current smoker (30 pack-years) and had worked in a stone quarry until 12 years earlier. His medical history included chronic catarrhal bronchitis, benign prostatic hypertrophy, and an intestinal polypectomy. He denied ever having spirometry or taking systemic or inhaled corticosteroids; a chest radiograph 3 years earlier showed rarefaction of the bronchovascular tree.

On examination, he was afebrile. Chest auscultation revealed reduced vesicular sounds and widespread rhonchi; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a neutrophilic leukocytosis (white-cell count, 16 500 per µL [70% neutrophils]), mild anemia (hemoglobin, 11.4 g/dL), an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (72 mm/h), and a C-reactive protein level of 20 mg/L. Plasma immunoglobulins, liver and renal function, and an HIV antibody test were normal or negative. 

Spirometry revealed a severe obstructive defect with a post–β₂ agonist forced vital capacity of 72% and a forced expiratory volume in one second of 46% of predicted. Chest radiography showed bilateral apical and subclavian sclerosis with multiple cavitary nodules. High-resolution CT of the chest demonstrated multiple nodular opacities with small central cavitations in both upper lobes and apical segments of the lower lobes, tree-in-bud foci, and cystic bronchiectasis in both lung apices; there was no significant mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and the findings were interpreted as “consistent with chronic TB.” 

Three sputum samples were obtained on different days and submitted for the search for Mycobacteria spp.

A 39-year-old African American woman with chronic focal epilepsy presented with three days of fevers (>38°C) and a mildly pruritic, erythematous maculopapular rash. The rash began two weeks earlier on her left arm and gradually spread to the trunk, face, oropharynx, periorbital area, and legs. Her medications included long-term carbamazepine, a tapering course of lamotrigine started one year ago, and a recent course of amoxicillin initiated for unilateral neck lymphadenopathy and exudative pharyngitis.  

Vital signs were notable for fever; skin examination showed a diffuse maculopapular eruption with periocular edema. Initial laboratory studies revealed a neutrophil count of 10.47 K/µL, mild eosinophilia (6–8%), and mildly elevated transaminases (AST 48 IU/L; ALT 42 IU/L).  

Dermatology consultation raised an initial differential of acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) secondary to amoxicillin versus drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome (DIHS) from lamotrigine or carbamazepine. A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no source of infection. Blood cultures were negative, and skin cultures grew only normal flora. Skin biopsy showed nonspecific findings most consistent with AGEP. CT of the abdomen demonstrated multiple wedge-shaped lesions in the spleen suspicious for focal infarction and ischemia.

A 65‐year‐old right‐handed Ethiopian man was referred to neurology for diffuse, symmetrical fat deposition. Fifteen years earlier, he noted gradual accumulation of abdominal fat, which later extended to involve his anterior chest with bilateral breast enlargement and, over time, his torso, upper arms, and thighs, sparing his face and distal limbs. During the past six months, he developed deep aching pain in both knees and ankles, and more recently low back pain, resulting in difficulty standing and walking. He had been told at a nearby clinic that his symptoms were due to excess body weight (114 kg) and was treated with oral analgesics and advised weight loss, without improvement. He denied significant alcohol, tobacco, or illicit drug use. 

He found it difficult to fit his clothing but otherwise had no dyspnea, dysphagia, abdominal pain, or distal sensory or motor symptoms. He had lost his driving job because of mobility issues. He had no family history of similar illness.

On examination, BMI was 39.6 kg/m2; vital signs were normal. There was diffuse, bilateral, symmetrical, non-tender, soft swelling of the trunk, shoulders, upper arms, thighs, and bilateral breast enlargement. Skin folds over the back and torso were thick and redundant, with large lipomatous masses sparing the neck. The forearms and shins appeared normal. Neurologic exam revealed mild lumbar tenderness; motor and sensory exams were normal. No joint swelling or crepitus was noted.

Laboratory tests showed hyperuricemia (10.6 mg/dl) but were otherwise within normal limits, including blood glucose, lipid panel, liver and thyroid function, renal function, rheumatoid factor, and HIV serology.

Sagittal T1-weighted MRI of the cervical and lumbar spine demonstrated diffuse subcutaneous fat deposition in the posterior neck and lower back, along with multilevel degenerative disc prolapse and osteophytic changes.

A 65-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of tooth sensitivity. Her medical, dental, and personal histories were noncontributory. On extraoral examination, multiple warty lesions were observed on the face, scalp, and trunk. Intraoral examination revealed multiple coalescent papillary projections involving the labial gingiva of the anterior maxilla, extending through the interdental papilla to the palate, and similar lesions on the lower labial gingiva, dorsum of the tongue, and bilateral buccal mucosa. The lateral borders of the tongue were fissured with loss of papillae and melanin pigmentation. The patient reported that these asymptomatic lesions had been present and gradually spreading over 6–7 months. Radiographs showed no underlying bony invasion. Routine blood tests were unremarkable, and HIV testing was negative. Based on the clinical appearance, a provisional diagnosis of HPV-associated multifocal papillomatosis was made, with verrucous leukoplakia, Cowden’s syndrome, and verrucous carcinoma included in the differential diagnosis.

A 23-year-old woman at 37 weeks of gestation was bitten on the left leg by a horned viper (Cerastes cerastes). She developed local pain and blisters. She received polyvalent antivenin, then was transferred to a hospital in Tobruk. On presentation she was fully conscious. Vital signs: blood pressure 110/70 mmHg; heart rate 130/min. Initial labs: hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL, WBC 9.3×10^3/μL, platelets 105×10^3/μL, INR 2.7. After fresh frozen plasma, a cesarean section was performed. Over the next week she became febrile and obtunded, with gradual vision loss and no seizures, headache, or focal weakness. A noncontrast brain CT was unremarkable. The left leg ulcer turned gangrenous. She remained normotensive; urine testing showed no proteinuria. She was transferred to our center. On admission she was stuporous (GCS 12), febrile (38°C), tachycardic (120/min), and dehydrated. Neurologic exam showed bilateral visual acuity reduced to hand motion, sluggish pupils. Labs: hemoglobin 8.3 g/dL, WBC 8.1×10^3/μL, platelets 63×10^3/μL, INR 1.1, Na+ 142.6 mmol/L, K+ 3.21 mmol/L, Mg2+ 0.9 mg/dL, creatinine 0.76 mg/dL, urea 35.3 mg/dL. Procalcitonin 0.2 ng/mL, CRP 13.7 mg/L. Hypercoagulability panel: positive for Factor V Leiden and MTHFR mutations; negative for protein C, protein S, ANA, and antiphospholipid antibodies. Follow-up noncontrast CT showed a faint hypodense area in the posterior parietal and occipital lobes. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral, symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in the posterior parietal regions and the genu and splenium of the corpus callosum, with patchy diffusion restriction on DWI/ADC. MR venography was normal.

A 65-year-old woman was referred to the emergency department for evaluation of a rapidly evolving swelling of the left side of her face and neck. Earlier the same day, during an airflow cleaning procedure by her dental hygienist in the region of a dental implant (tooth 34), she felt pain in the left submandibular region. She presented with:

• Large swelling extending from the left upper eyelid down the neck  
• Dysphagia and dyslalia  
• Diffuse subcutaneous crepitus, without pain on palpation  
• Intraoral examination: no visible mucosal incision; slight bleeding around the implant site  

Her vital signs were: heart rate 65 beats/min, blood pressure 145/90 mmHg, respiratory rate 19 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air.

To evaluate the dysphagia and dyslalia, a CT scan was obtained from the maxillofacial region through the thorax, revealing extensive soft-tissue emphysema tracking from the left face into the bilateral neck paraspinal muscles, pharynx, superior mediastinum surrounding the trachea and esophagus, and terminating at the upper diaphragm.

A 12-month-old girl with a history of repaired gastroschisis at birth was brought to the emergency department with high-grade fever, cough, and dyspnea. She was previously healthy after an uneventful abdominal closure. On examination, her temperature was 39.0 °C, heart rate 170 beats/min, respiratory rate 70 breaths/min, blood pressure 70/30 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 80% on room air. She appeared drowsy and in respiratory distress with suprasternal and subcostal retractions, mild cyanosis of the lips, chest crepitations, and paradoxical abdominal respiration. A provisional diagnosis of ARDS and septic shock due to bacterial pneumonia was made. She was intubated and placed on conventional mechanical ventilation (pressure control, PEEP 12 cm H₂O, inspiratory pressure 30 mmHg), but remained hypoxemic (PaO₂ 82 mmHg) and was switched to high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV) after 6 hours. During the first 2 days on HFOV (mean airway pressure 32 mmHg), her oxygen saturation remained above 88% and her condition initially improved. On day 7 of HFOV weaning, she developed abrupt worsening of ventilation and oxygenation. Chest radiography showed a left tension pneumothorax, which was treated with an intercostal drain. A few hours later, her abdomen became markedly distended and subcutaneous emphysema appeared over the upper torso. Thoracoabdominal radiographs demonstrated persistent pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, and a large pneumoperitoneum. Her abdominal circumference increased from 40 to 50 cm. Bedside abdominocentesis released approximately 1 L of free air, partially improving hemodynamics, but the abdomen remained tense and she was still unstable. She was taken to the operating room to exclude diaphragmatic injury from the chest tube, hollow viscus perforation, or abdominal compartment syndrome.

An 18-year-old nulliparous woman was referred from urology with a 1-year history of recurrent urinary tract infections and persistent left iliac-fossa discomfort. Initial intravenous pyelography revealed a left pelvic kidney. During two admissions for hypogastric pain and urinary infection, she was diagnosed with pyelonephritis and treated with ciprofloxacin and tobramycin; pelvic ultrasound and CT scan showed bilateral hydrosalpinx and a suggested bicornuate uterus.

On gynecologic evaluation, the uterus was retroverted with a bicornuate appearance on transvaginal ultrasound. Both ovaries appeared normal, but there were elongated 6–7 cm anteuterine masses, “suggesting endometriomas or mucinous tumors by their appearance.” Cervicovaginal cultures were negative. Laboratory studies showed an ESR of 36 mm/hour and CA-125 of 98 U/mL. Repeat IVP confirmed the pelvic kidney.

The patient received doxycycline and anti-inflammatory agents, followed by hysterosalpingography, which again demonstrated a bicornuate uterus and bilateral hydrosalpinx. She then developed low-grade fever (37–37.5 °C), an ESR of 66 mm/hour, and was treated for presumed PID with clindamycin and doxycycline. Transvaginal ultrasound continued to show bilateral solid-cystic adnexal masses with increased Doppler flow (resistance index = 0.7). One month later, ESR was 44 mm/hour and CA-125 had risen to 424 U/mL.

In December 2005, laparotomy revealed large pelvic abscesses anterior to the uterus, converged fallopian tubes adherent to bladder and sigmoid colon, a large left pyosalpinx, and a floating right pyosalpinx. The ovaries and uterine fundus (septate) appeared normal. Drainage, adhesiolysis, and bilateral salpingectomy were performed, and samples were sent for microbiological and histopathological analysis.

A 46-year-old Ghanaian woman with a 4-year history of hypertension and poor medication adherence awoke with inability to move her right arm and leg. She denied slurred speech, dysphagia, headache, seizures, sensory loss, bladder or bowel dysfunction, diarrhoea, vomiting, heat intolerance, or excessive sweating. She had no history of laxative or diuretic use, strenuous exercise, or high-carbohydrate intake before bed, and no personal or family history of stroke or muscle weakness. At a referring health center her blood pressure was 172/130 mmHg, and she received nifedipine 30 mg orally before transfer.

On arrival, temperature was 36.7 °C, pulse 94 bpm, blood pressure 165/120 mmHg. She was alert and oriented, with a supple neck and negative Kernig’s sign. Neurologic examination showed muscle strength of 3/5 in the right upper limb and 2/5 in the right lower limb, with reduced tone and reflexes and flexor plantar responses. Sensation and cranial nerves were intact.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, lipid profile, and a fasting blood glucose of 5.8 mmol/L; HIV test was negative. A noncontrast CT scan of the brain was normal, and a contrast-enhanced CT scan showed no space-occupying lesion.

A 70-year-old woman presented with gradually bilateral decreased vision. Best-corrected visual acuity was 0.50 logMAR in the right eye and 1.0 logMAR in the left eye. Ocular motility and alignment were normal without proptosis. Both eyes were aphakic from prior cataract surgery. Fundus examination was unremarkable in the right eye. In the left eye, there was a dome-shaped orange mass beneath the superotemporal vascular arcade in the macular area.  

An orbital CT scan demonstrated bilateral calcification of the dural optic nerve sheaths and posterior globe walls, as well as calcifications in the trochlear apparatus and the brain. B-scan ultrasonography revealed a highly reflective echogenic lesion with posterior acoustic shadowing. Spectral-domain OCT showed that the mass was located within the sclera, causing marked elevation that displaced the choroid and retina inward, associated with thinning of the outer nuclear layer, absence of the external limiting membrane and inner segment–outer segment junction, and no subretinal fluid.  

The patient was referred for systemic evaluation. All metabolic investigations, including serum calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, vitamin D, thyroid-stimulating hormone, calcitonin, and parathyroid hormone levels, were within normal limits.

A 79-year-old Caucasian male field worker from São Paulo, Brazil, presented with a six-month history of irritative lower urinary tract symptoms—urgency, frequency, nocturia—and difficulty initiating urination that progressed to urinary retention requiring a catheter. His medical history included Chagas disease with cardiac impairment, coronary disease treated with a stent in the anterior interventricular artery, and dyslipidemia. Digital rectal examination revealed a 40-cm3 prostate, slightly hardened at the apex with no nodules. Prostate-specific antigen was 1.2 ng/mL. Examination of the penis, testicles, and epididymides was unremarkable. Initial treatment with an α-blocker failed to allow catheter removal, and transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) was performed. During hospitalization, laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, hematocrit 36%, leukocytes 9300/µL, urinalysis with leukocytes 33 000 cells/mL and erythrocytes >500 000 cells/mL, and a negative urine culture. Serum sodium was 133 mEq/L, potassium 4.3 mEq/L, glucose 128 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.4 mg/dL. Postoperatively, he was discharged with normal urinary function. Anatomopathological analysis of the TURP specimen revealed chronic granulomatous prostatitis of fungal etiology with extensive necrosis.

An 80-year-old man with atrial fibrillation, prior myocardial infarction, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with emphysema, and a 15-year history of a reducible right inguinoscrotal hernia presented with 24 hours of acute abdominal pain, a painful right groin mass, nausea, constipation, and abdominal distension. Medications included antihypertensives, antiarrhythmics, oral anticoagulants, and bronchodilators. On examination, blood pressure was 140/90 mm Hg, irregular pulse 110 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute with oxygen saturation of 94%, and temperature 37.4 °C. The abdomen was soft with tenderness in the right lower quadrant but no rebound. The right groin mass was erythematous and nonreducible. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis of 10 200/mm^3 with neutrophil predominance, C-reactive protein of 83.1 mg/L, and an INR of 2.13. A nasopharyngeal swab for SARS-CoV-2 was negative. A clinical diagnosis of right incarcerated inguinoscrotal hernia was made, and the patient was taken for emergent open inguinal exploration under locoregional anesthesia.

A 20-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of intermittent evening fevers, headache, and vomiting, without cough, chest pain, dyspnea, hemoptysis, or weight loss. On examination, she was afebrile, and vital signs and systemic findings were normal. Neurologic examination showed neck stiffness; Kernig and Brudzinski signs were negative. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, white-cell count 7300 cells/µL (81% neutrophils, 15% lymphocytes, 1% monocytes, 0% eosinophils), and platelets 450 × 10^3/µL. Renal and hepatic function tests were normal, and HIV ELISA was negative. A chest radiograph showed soft-tissue enlargement along the right paratracheal stripe. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis supported tuberculous meningoencephalitis (Gram stain negative; adenosine deaminase 8 U/L). Brain MRI demonstrated ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding edema consistent with tuberculomas, and antitubercular therapy was initiated. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed an ill-defined, heterogeneously enhancing 4 × 4-cm mass in the anterior mediastinum, raising the possibility of a thymic lesion or confluent, necrotic lymph nodes.

A 44-year-old woman with no prior thyroid disease presented with progressive anterior neck pain, headache, asthenia, insomnia, hand tremor, hyperhidrosis, diarrhea, weight loss of 8 kg, and palpitations. These symptoms began 14 days after a mild SARS-CoV-2 infection confirmed by PCR one month earlier and had initially regressed with symptomatic therapy. She had delivered a child one year ago and denied recent iodine exposure. On examination, palpation of the neck was painful without discrete nodules; the thyroid gland was slightly enlarged and tender. The skin was warm and moist, and a fine finger tremor was noted. Laboratory studies showed:  
• TSH 0.005 mIU/L (reference 0.27–4.20),  
• fT3 15.5 pmol/L (3.1–6.8),  
• fT4 51.8 pmol/L (12–22),  
• ESR 98 mm/h,  
• CRP 78 mg/L (≤ 5).  
Thyroid ultrasonography revealed a 50 ml gland with an inhomogeneous, predominantly hypoechogenic structure and mild hyperperfusion throughout the organ.

A previously healthy 2-year-old boy was brought to the emergency department with sudden onset of left‐sided weakness and a right‐sided headache. He had no recent infections or vaccinations beyond his routine immunizations. Family history was unremarkable. On examination, he was alert, with complete left hemiplegia and a decreased left patellar tendon reflex; there was no neck stiffness. 

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, electrolytes, renal function, glucose, and urinalysis, were normal. A lumbar puncture revealed normal cerebrospinal fluid. Noncontrast head CT showed no hemorrhage. Brain MRI likewise showed no intracranial hemorrhage, but a varix on the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) was noted; this finding was not thought to explain his clinical presentation.

A 19-year-old African American woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus since age 10 and multiple admissions for diabetic ketoacidosis (most recently 4 months earlier) presented with 1 day of generalized weakness and fatigue. She denied abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, fever, diarrhea, or other systemic symptoms. Home insulin regimen was degludec 30 U nightly and aspart 5 U before meals (0.85 U/kg/day). Vital signs: T 36.6 °C; pulse 116 bpm; BP 109/84 mm Hg; RR 22 bpm; O₂ saturation 98% on room air. She appeared ill; examination revealed a firm liver edge palpable 7 cm below the right costal margin without stigmata of chronic liver disease; BMI was 21.5 kg/m². Initial labs: glucose 510 mg/dL; Na⁺ 130 mmol/L; K⁺ 4.9 mmol/L; HCO₃⁻ 10 mmol/L; anion gap 24; creatinine 0.65 mg/dL; AST 1129 U/L; ALT 766 U/L; ALP 216 U/L; total bilirubin 1.0 mg/dL; albumin 3.8 g/dL; GGT 274 U/L; β-hydroxybutyrate 8.86 mmol/L; ABG pH 7.25, PCO₂ 40 mm Hg. Urine tox screen was negative. She received IV fluids and insulin; the anion gap closed within 24 hours, and she was transitioned to subcutaneous insulin.  
On hospital day 1, elevated liver tests were attributed to hypotension in DKA and managed conservatively. Despite hemodynamic stabilization, labs on day 4 showed AST 1089 U/L; ALT 529 U/L; ALP 204 U/L. Further evaluation revealed: negative acute viral and mononucleosis panels; acetaminophen level < 2 μg/mL; abdominal ultrasound with hepatomegaly (22 cm) and diffuse fatty infiltration without gallstones or bile duct dilatation; Doppler ultrasound without Budd–Chiari syndrome or portal vein thrombosis; negative autoimmune serologies (ANA, anti-smooth muscle, antimitochondrial, LKM); and negative ceruloplasmin, 24-hour urine copper, and iron studies.

A 20-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of asymptomatic discoloration and thickening of both areolas. It began as a pink, scaly, eczematous plaque on the areola that gradually darkened, with notable worsening over the past 2 months. She denied atopy, bloody nipple discharge, personal or family history of breast malignancy, and was not taking any medications. On examination, there was diffuse brownish pigmentation and verrucous thickening of the entire right areola and the upper part of the left areola with overlying scale-crust. No palpable breast masses, lymphadenopathy, nipple retraction, or discharge were noted. The remainder of the skin examination was unremarkable, her body mass index was within the normal range, and routine laboratory tests were unremarkable. A skin biopsy of the areolar lesion showed marked epidermal thickening with slight papillomatosis, filiform downward anastomosing rete ridges, basal-layer hyperpigmentation without melanocytic proliferation, and slight fibrosis of the upper dermis.

A 51-year-old woman presented with gingival bleeding, pain on eating, and difficulty with oral hygiene. She reported similar episodes over the past two years, each following periods of psychological stress. She had no systemic illnesses, was postmenopausal without climacteric symptoms, and was under hormonal follow-up. On examination, there was heavy dental biofilm accumulation, erythematous swollen gingiva, and mild pain. Initial management on June 15 included a diagnosis of necrotizing periodontal disease with amoxicillin 500 mg and metronidazole 400 mg three times daily for seven days and chlorhexidine 0.12% mouthwash twice daily. After 14 days, there was no satisfactory improvement; the gingiva remained erythematous and ulcerated, and the patient reported new “blood blisters” that burst and caused pain. An air jet elicited a positive Nikolsky’s sign on the oral mucosa. Due to this blistering and lack of response to therapy, an incisional biopsy of the gingival lesion was performed.

An 80-year-old man presented with progressive shortness of breath. Six months earlier, bilateral pleural and pericardial effusions had been noted on chest CT. His medical history was notable for λ-type Bence-Jones–protein multiple myeloma (stage IIIA) in his sixties, treated with vincristine, doxorubicin plus dexamethasone, high-dose etoposide, autologous peripheral blood stem-cell transplantation, and combination chemotherapy, with remission for 16 years. He also had atrial fibrillation treated with edoxaban; family history was noncontributory. Five thoracenteses and one pleural biopsy at the initial hospital were inconclusive, and effusions proved difficult to control.

On referral, chest radiography showed moderate to large bilateral pleural effusions. PET-CT showed no obvious 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose accumulation in the thoracic cavity. Laboratory studies revealed a serum total protein of 5.9 g/dL and LDH of 168 U/L; serum immunoelectrophoresis showed no obvious M protein, and urine immunoelectrophoresis showed no obvious Bence Jones protein. Chest CT confirmed large bilateral pleural effusions, and a left-sided drain yielded clear yellow fluid with total protein 3.8 g/dL and LDH 74 U/L (exudate by Light’s criteria). A few days later, right-sided drainage yielded fluid with total protein 2.9 g/dL and LDH 60 U/L (transudate). Cytology and cell-block examination of both effusions showed no malignancy. Echocardiography showed no significant systolic or diastolic dysfunction.

A 58-year-old Chinese woman (G4P3) with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma (cervical lymph nodes, brain, bone) was admitted for lumbosacral pain on April 29, 2022. She had completed pemetrexed/carboplatin/bevacizumab and was on oral dacomitinib. On admission, vitals were normal (T 36.6 °C, BP 122/76 mmHg, HR 80 bpm, RR 20/min), and exam showed only lumbosacral tenderness. Lumbar radiotherapy began on hospital day 1; by day 9 her pain improved but she developed increased stool frequency without fever or abdominal pain. Procalcitonin and C-reactive protein were normal; urine and stool studies were unremarkable. She was treated empirically for radiation enteritis.

On day 15 at 08:58, she had breakthrough abdominal pain (NRS 5) and received tramadol 100 mg IM with inadequate relief. At 13:36 she received morphine 10 mg intrathecally; her pain improved (NRS 2) but she then developed nausea, vomiting, dizziness, and a fever of 38.0 °C by 18:00. Physical cooling normalized her temperature. At 00:29 on day 16, she again received morphine 10 mg for pain (NRS 6) and by 05:00 her temperature rose to 39.2 °C. During the fevers her pulse increased to 100 bpm, and eosinophil count rose from 0.08 × 10^9/L on day 8 to 0.17 × 10^9/L on day 16.

A 39-year-old healthy nulligravida woman presented to the emergency department with significant vaginal bleeding and hemodynamic instability. She had undergone a laparoscopic supracervical hysterectomy 18 days earlier for symptomatic uterine myomas; preoperative cervical cytology and endometrial biopsy were benign, and final pathology confirmed benign fibroids with no endometrial pathology. On admission, her temperature was 37.0 °C, pulse 118 beats/min, and blood pressure 70/55 mm Hg. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 7.7 g/L, white blood cell count 14.2 × 10^9/L, platelets 180 000/µL, C-reactive protein 13.7 mg/L, and normal coagulation studies. Vaginal examination revealed two actively bleeding ulcerative lesions, each approximately 1 cm in diameter, at the 1- and 5-o’clock positions of the remaining cervical stump; the adnexa and parametria were unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a 3 cm residual cervical stump, with no free peritoneal fluid, hematoma, or adnexal mass.

A 67-year-old woman underwent breast cancer screening during which she detected a left axillary, fingertip-sized palpable mass. She reported no breast masses or cervical lymphadenopathy. Her height was 147 cm and weight was 45 kg. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies showed a normal white blood cell count and normal C-reactive protein level.

Screening mammography of both breasts was unremarkable. Ultrasound of the left axilla revealed multiple, markedly hypoechoic ovoid lymph nodes, some containing coarse calcifications. Targeted mammography of the left axillary tail demonstrated irregularly shaped macrocalcifications and dense tissue nodes.

Noncontrast CT of the chest showed a cluster of 12 well-circumscribed dense nodes measuring up to 3.0 × 2.8 × 1.7 cm, distributed around vessels in the left deep axilla, supraclavicular, and infraclavicular regions. Some nodes contained large and dotted calcifications; noncalcified areas measured 54–62 HU. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated homogeneous enhancement of these nodes to 98–102 HU. CT also revealed calcification in a right parabronchial lymph node and small pulmonary nodules at the right lung apex consistent with a primary tuberculous complex.

A 58-year-old man with a deceased donor renal transplant 3 years earlier for unknown end-stage renal failure presented with a 2-week history of watery diarrhea, occurring 10–14 times per day, without abdominal pain, blood, or mucus. He was afebrile, tachycardic (110 bpm), hypotensive (92/68 mm Hg), and dehydrated by tongue exam; abdominal, cardiac, and respiratory exams were otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed normal inflammatory markers; serum urea 8.3 mmol/L; creatinine 138 µmol/L (baseline GFR 60–62 ml/min; current GFR 49 ml/min); potassium 3.4 mmol/L; and tacrolimus level within the target range. Fecal assay was negative for routine bacterial, viral, and protozoan pathogens. The dose of mycophenolate mofetil was split from 720 mg twice daily to 360 mg four times daily, resulting in symptom improvement and return of renal function to baseline. Two weeks later, he reported persistent diarrhea, now 16 bowel movements per day, with maintained hydration and stable hemodynamics. He was readmitted and referred for inpatient colonoscopy and biopsy.

An 80-year-old Caucasian man was referred for evaluation of asymptomatic skin lesions on his arms and legs that had been present for at least two years. He had been diagnosed elsewhere with late-onset plaque psoriasis and treated with topical calcipotriol/betamethasone for three months followed by clobetasol for four months without improvement. His medical history included hypertension, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and hyperlipidemia; family history was negative for chronic skin conditions. On examination, there were well-demarcated, irregularly shaped erythematosquamous plaques on the upper and lower extremities. Dermatoscopic evaluation showed yellow-orange clods intersected by fine, horizontal telangiectasias.

A 27-year-old man presented with 20 days of periumbilical abdominal pain, 10 days of progressive abdominal distension, and 3 days of loose stools. The pain was a dull ache around the umbilicus, becoming intermittent with bloating relieved by passage of flatus. He denied vomiting, fever, jaundice, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. Outside laboratories showed an absolute eosinophil count of 11 400/μL. He had no history of allergies, atopy, new medications, or B symptoms, and no relevant family history.

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs and a BMI of 22 kg/m2. Nailfold inspection revealed splinter hemorrhages; abdominal examination showed distension with shifting dullness and sluggish bowel sounds, without organomegaly. Systemic examination was otherwise unremarkable.

Laboratory studies demonstrated a leukocyte count of 33 000/μL with an absolute eosinophil count of 25 000/μL; hemoglobin and platelet counts were normal. Renal and liver function tests were within normal limits. Total IgE was elevated at 830 kUA/L. Midnight diethylcarbamazine provocation test and multiple stool examinations were negative for parasites. Ascitic fluid analysis revealed an exudative fluid (SAAG 0.7 g/dL) with 95% eosinophils. Abdominal ultrasonography confirmed septated ascites. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed diffuse bowel wall thickening with submucosal edema. Upper and lower endoscopy revealed erythematous mucosa; biopsies from the antrum, duodenum, terminal ileum, cecum, and rectum demonstrated dense eosinophilic infiltration in the lamina propria and muscularis mucosa.

A 16-year-old girl was referred after an incidental posterior-pole finding in the left eye during a routine ophthalmologic examination. She was asymptomatic, with best-corrected visual acuity of 20/20 in both eyes. Slit-lamp examination was unremarkable in both eyes; intraocular pressure was 12 mmHg in the right eye and 14 mmHg in the left eye. The right fundus appeared normal. In the left eye, fundus examination revealed a large, solitary, whitish-yellowish flat lesion with fringe-like scalloped margins adjacent to the optic nerve, extending to the superotemporal vascular arcade. The central area of the lesion showed thinned, atrophic retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), while midperipheral lacunae exhibited fibrosis and RPE hyperplasia. A fibroglial proliferation was noted overlying the retina and the optic nerve head. The patient denied any history of ocular trauma or inflammation; her only systemic history was a febrile illness of unknown origin requiring hospitalization three months earlier. Physical examination and chest radiography were normal. Blood tests—including full blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein—and a Quantiferon test were all negative. Fundus autofluorescence demonstrated a hypoautofluorescent central zone with clearly demarcated hyperautofluorescent borders and patches corresponding to RPE hyperplasia. Optical coherence tomography showed disruption of the outer retinal layers, a shallow nasal RPE detachment, choroidal thinning, and an incomplete posterior vitreous detachment with vitreomacular adhesion at the fovea and optic nerve head. Optical coherence tomography angiography showed no evidence of choroidal neovascular membrane. The patient was advised close observation.

A 24-year-old Vietnamese man living in Switzerland for 3 years presented with unremitting pain in his right knee. Two months earlier he had sustained a right knee contusion. Since that injury he reported occasional night sweats with chills and a weight loss of 5 kg. He was otherwise in good health, did not smoke, and took no medications.

On examination there was a painful, red, nonulcerating induration measuring 3 × 4 cm over the right fibular head. The lesion was fluctuating and appeared adherent to the deep subcutaneous tissues. Right knee range of motion was preserved, and the neurovascular examination was normal.

Laboratory studies showed a microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 76 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 61 fl), no leukocytosis, and a C-reactive protein level of 4 mg/L. Plain radiography of the knee revealed a 1 × 1 cm lytic lesion with an ill-defined margin in the proximal right fibula, breaking through the outer cortex. MRI demonstrated a T2 hyperintense lesion at the fibular head with cortical disruption and an adjacent soft-tissue abscess, findings thought to be consistent with focal osteomyelitis rather than a bone tumor.

Surgical debridement was performed, and tissue fragments were sent for bacteriologic culture and pathology, with a special request to evaluate for tuberculosis. Empiric intravenous amoxicillin–clavulanate was initiated. Pathologic examination revealed acid-alcohol resistant bacilli within an inflammatory process, but standard cultures were noncontributive. A tuberculin skin test was negative at 72 hours.

A 28-year-old man with autism and a seizure disorder treated with phenytoin presented with bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy and 4 kg of unintentional weight loss over two months. On examination, he had palpable bilateral cervical nodes; the largest node (right level V) measured 2.9 × 2.0 cm on CT. His abdomen was soft without hepatosplenomegaly, and his skin showed no rash.
