Laboratory studies revealed a WBC count of 6,400/μL, hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, platelets 324,000/μL, and an LDH level of 429 U/L. A whole-body PET/CT scan demonstrated multiple moderately enlarged cervical lymph nodes with moderate to marked fluorodeoxyglucose uptake and no other hypermetabolic foci. Flow cytometry of peripheral blood identified a small T-cell population (1.5% of analyzed cells) lacking CD7 and weakly expressing CD5. T-cell receptor gene rearrangement studies of peripheral blood showed a clonal TCR β rearrangement; the TCR γ rearrangement was negative. A bone marrow biopsy revealed normocellular marrow with adequate trilineage hematopoiesis and 14% atypical lymphocytes on differential; cytogenetics showed a 46,XY karyotype. TCR β gene rearrangement in marrow cells revealed an identical clonal fragment to that in peripheral blood.

A septuagenarian man with a history of hypertension controlled on medication presented with 4 days of malaise, gait unsteadiness, left arm weakness, fever, vomiting, and headache. On admission, he was lethargic but opened his eyes to voice; pupils were reactive, extraocular movements were full, and corneal reflexes were intact. Initial computed tomography (CT) of the brain and blood cultures were unremarkable. Within 24 hours, oculocephalic movements were lost, but pupils remained small and corneal reflexes intact. Two days after admission, he developed severe lethargy, left hemiplegia, a right gaze preference, and a poor gag reflex, and he was intubated for airway protection. Repeat CT showed a linear band of low attenuation in the right external capsule, suggestive of a lenticulostriate infarct. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed 73% neutrophils, 17% lymphocytes, 9% monocytes, glucose 91 mg/dL, and protein 96 mg/dL; CSF and blood cultures remained negative. Empirical treatment included ceftriaxone, ampicillin, doxycycline, and acyclovir. Electroencephalography demonstrated right frontotemporal periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges, and he received phenytoin. His neurologic status progressively declined with loss of brainstem reflexes. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain on hospital day 4 showed diffuse enhancement of the leptomeninges, brainstem, basal ganglia, and medial temporal lobes, consistent with meningoencephalitis. Serological studies of blood and CSF were obtained and sent for arboviral panel testing.

A 71-year-old man with hypertension and prostate cancer, and no prior ocular surgeries, presented for pars plana vitrectomy and epiretinal membrane peel in his left eye. Preoperatively, he received topical cyclopentolate and phenylephrine in the left eye. Under monitored anesthesia care with propofol, a left retrobulbar block was performed using a 25-gauge, 1.5-inch needle to inject 6 mL of a 1:1 mixture of 0.75% bupivacaine and 2.0% lidocaine. Intraoperatively, vital signs remained stable, and the 25-minute procedure was uneventful.

After surgery, with the left eye patched, the patient sat up and noted that he could not see from his right eye. His right visual acuity was hand motion (baseline 20/20), and the right pupil was dilated to 7 mm with minimal reactivity. Intraocular pressure in that eye was normal, extraocular movements were intact, and indirect ophthalmoscopy showed a well-perfused retina with a normal fundus. One drop of 1% pilocarpine in the right eye constricted the pupil to 1.5 mm. A stroke code was activated, and the neurologic examination was normal.

Noncontrast CT of the brain showed no acute intracranial pathology but did reveal an air bubble within the left optic nerve sheath. MRI and MRA of the brain and orbits demonstrated no intracranial abnormalities but confirmed abnormal enhancement along the left intraorbital optic nerve and the same air bubble within the left optic nerve sheath. Ninety minutes after surgery, right-eye vision returned to 20/20. On postoperative evaluation, vision remained normal, and both fundus examination and macular optical coherence tomography were unremarkable.

A 60-year-old Caucasian woman with a 30–pack-year smoking history, well-controlled hypertension, prior partial thyroidectomy, and a maternal history of osteoporosis presented with 6 months of left lower-limb pain. The discomfort began after minor trauma and initially involved her knee with difficulty walking. It progressed to severe left hip pain that worsened with movement, did not respond to analgesics, and radiated to the medial calf and toes. She developed a limping gait with palpable crackles in the hip and knee.

On examination, the left lower limb was 2 cm shorter than the right, and there was swelling over the posterolateral right hip. Pelvic radiographs showed decreased bone density, complete absence of the left femoral head with articulation of the femoral neck against the iliac bone, regions of osteolysis in the pubic rami and left sacroiliac joint, upward displacement of the right hemipelvis, and a small avulsion fracture at the T12 vertebral body. CT and MRI confirmed absence of the left femoral head, replaced by cystic heterogeneous soft tissue, and focal osteolytic lesions in the right pubis and sacroiliac joint.

Laboratory studies revealed ionized calcium 2.31 mg/dL (reference 4.5–5.6 mg/dL), total calcium 7.6 mg/dL (8.4–10.2 mg/dL), 25-OH vitamin D3 17.5 ng/mL (30–80 ng/mL), and a DEXA T-score of −3 with a Z-score <−2.

An 8-month-old Asian Indian girl with a history of atopic dermatitis presented with 4 days of fever (to 38.7°C) and a rapidly spreading rash. One day after fever onset, an acute rash appeared on her neck and was treated with oral cephalexin, clotrimazole cream, and triamcinolone cream for presumed bacterial and fungal infection. Despite this, the rash progressed to her face and trunk. There was no cough, rhinorrhea, vomiting, eye redness, or discharge. She was fully immunized and had no sick contacts.

On examination, T 38.7°C, BP 112/72 mm Hg, HR 178 bpm, RR 38 bpm; she was irritable and tearful. Skin exam showed diffuse crusted papules over areas of chronic eczema on the anterior neck, upper trunk, and face. Some lesions were clustered vesicles, and confluent areas of denudation exposed pink dermis over about 10% of body surface. 

A swab of an unroofed vesicle was sent for HSV PCR. Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood count and a comprehensive metabolic panel with AST 47 U/L (normal 10–37) and ALT 31 U/L (normal 3–30). She was started on intravenous acyclovir and intravenous vancomycin. She was admitted to the pediatric unit, and ophthalmology evaluation revealed no evidence of herpetic keratitis.

A 63-year-old man with a history of familial Mediterranean fever treated with colchicine presented with a several-day history of pain and swelling in his left knee that extended to the mid-thigh, causing difficulty bending the joint. He denied fever, trauma, or involvement of other joints. On examination, the left knee and the distal third of the thigh were warm, tender, and markedly swollen, with an 8-cm greater circumference above the patella than on the right. Arthrocentesis yielded turbid synovial fluid containing 19,850 white blood cells per microliter (94% neutrophils), 5% lymphocytes, and 850 red blood cells per microliter. Synovial fluid culture was negative for organisms, and microscopic examination revealed no crystals. Magnetic resonance imaging of the knee demonstrated multiple cystic collections in the interfascial planes of the hamstring muscles, the largest measuring 7.9 by 4.6 cm, with extensive edematous infiltration of the posterior thigh and calf surrounding these collections, findings described as compatible with a perforated cyst leaking into the soft tissue, along with mild to moderate joint effusion.

A 25-year-old man from Uttar Pradesh presented with a painless left cheek swelling that had gradually enlarged over the past year. He noted that the mass transiently increased in size while eating and then returned to baseline after meals. On examination, there was a 2.0 × 1.5 cm, firm, non-tender, mobile, globular swelling below the left malar prominence, with normal overlying skin. The swelling became more prominent when he clenched his teeth. He was afebrile, and there was no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Laboratory studies showed an absolute eosinophil count of 1100 cells/mm3; the peripheral smear was otherwise unremarkable. Ultrasonography of the cheek revealed cystic dilatation of the mid-portion of the left Stensen’s duct with minimal lobulated soft-tissue contents and mild ductal wall thickening. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a well-defined, hypodense cystic lesion superficial to the anterolateral aspect of the left masseter muscle, indenting its surface and communicating with a tubular hypodense structure continuous with the parotid gland, consistent with a dilated Stensen’s duct and sialocele formation.

A 69-year-old woman with ischemic cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction 25–30%), coronary artery disease (status post–coronary artery bypass graft), atrial fibrillation, and a HeartMate 3 left ventricular assist device (LVAD) placed 48 days earlier for refractory heart failure presented with recurrent low-flow LVAD alarms. Her hospital course had been complicated by right ventricular failure requiring temporary right ventricular assist device support, acute renal failure requiring continuous renal replacement therapy, respiratory failure necessitating tracheostomy, and decubitus ulcers. 

On postoperative day 48, the LVAD emitted multiple low-flow alarms. She was hypotensive with increased vasopressor requirements. A bedside transthoracic echocardiogram showed an underfilled left ventricle, which improved after administration of intravenous fluids and reduction of LVAD speed. Right ventricular function remained unchanged from baseline, and there was no pericardial effusion. Despite these interventions, the low-flow alarms persisted. An arterial-contrast computed tomography scan was performed to rule out hemorrhage, device obstruction, and pump thrombosis. After switching to a different monitor, periods of intermittent pump shutdowns lasting several seconds were confirmed. Despite replacing the LVAD controller, verifying all connections, and inspecting the power cable for disruptions, the alarms continued.

A 45-year-old man with gastroesophageal reflux disease and a history of alcohol-induced pancreatitis complicated by a pseudocyst presented with a one-week history of upper abdominal pain, anorexia, hematemesis, and coffee-ground emesis. His pain was mild, nonradiating, and worsened with vomiting; he noted nausea and coffee-ground emesis mixed with food shortly after eating. Four weeks earlier, he had undergone successful embolization of a gastroduodenal artery pseudoaneurysm at the origin of the pancreaticoduodenal artery. He denied NSAID use, recurrent alcohol use, caustic ingestion, and had no known history of Crohn’s disease, tuberculosis, gastric polyps, annular pancreas, diabetes, or gastroparesis.

On examination, his temperature was 37 °C, blood pressure 105/55 mm Hg, heart rate 76 beats/min, and respiratory rate 18 breaths/min. He appeared in moderate distress. Abdominal examination revealed mild epigastric tenderness without guarding or rebound. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 7400/µL, hemoglobin 13.3 g/dL (down from 15.5 g/dL), hematocrit 40.6%, and platelet count 165,000/µL.

A CT angiogram of the abdomen demonstrated edema along the posterior wall of the stomach and the medial wall of the duodenum adjacent to the pancreatic head, with no extrinsic compression of the gastric outlet and no residual flow in the embolized vessels. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed intense edema, inflammation, and friability in the duodenal bulb causing near obstruction of the gastric outlet; the second portion of the duodenum appeared normal. Biopsies of the duodenal bulb mucosa showed no evidence of malignancy and were negative for Helicobacter pylori. A contrast upper gastrointestinal series demonstrated compression of the gastric antrum without evidence of obstruction.

A 60-year-old man with coronary artery disease and dyslipidemia suffered an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest due to ventricular fibrillation. After 26 minutes of resuscitation, including defibrillation and 1 mg of intravenous adrenaline, he underwent coronary angiography and stenting of the left main trunk. Despite cardiac recovery, he remained comatose and received therapeutic hypothermia under midazolam sedation for two days. Sedation was stopped on day 5, but he did not regain consciousness. On day 10, cerebral hypoxia was diagnosed based on his clinical course, examination, brain MRI, and EEG. On day 20, tracheostomy and continuous positive airway pressure were initiated; enteral feeding via a nasogastric tube was started. His neurological and general status remained stable. He was transferred on day 37 with a Glasgow Coma Scale of E4 VT M1, requiring mechanical ventilation. Examination showed aimless movements and limb hypertonus; vital signs, laboratory tests, and head CT were normal. EEG revealed poorly organized background activity with sporadic theta and intermittent delta waves over bilateral frontal regions, without paroxysmal discharges. Rehabilitation led to gradual improvement in consciousness and motor function. On approximately day 50, he developed episodes occurring three to four times daily of sudden high fever, tachycardia, hypertension, tachypnea, profuse sweating, and specific posturing such as hypertonia with left lower limb torsion. Laboratory studies and a chest radiograph were unremarkable. Neuroimaging and EEG could not be obtained because of patient restlessness. We then considered paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity as the underlying cause.

A 60-year-old woman with chronic hypertension was brought to the emergency department by her family after suddenly losing consciousness at home approximately 1 hour earlier. On arrival, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was E1V1M4. She had bilaterally dilated, nonreactive pupils (7 mm on the right, 5 mm on the left). She was intubated for airway protection. Initial vital signs were blood pressure 130/90 mmHg, heart rate 88 beats/min, oxygen saturation 85% on room air, and random blood glucose 158 mg/dL.

Neurologic examination revealed left-sided hemiplegia and left facial droop. The left plantar response was upgoing; the right was mute. Motor strength was 1/5 in the left upper and lower limbs and 2/5 on the right. There were no meningeal signs. Cardiovascular, pulmonary, and other systemic examinations were unremarkable.

A noncontrast head CT scan was obtained within 30 minutes of arrival.

A 75-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of several migratory ecchymotic 2- to 3-cm nodules on his lower extremities, mainly the thighs, without associated symptoms. Each lesion lasted approximately 2 weeks before resolving, after which new lesions arose in different areas. He denied recent illnesses or new medications.  

His medical history was significant for chronic lymphocytic leukemia refractory to prior chemotherapy; he had been treated with ibrutinib, 420 mg daily, for 1 year. Six months before starting ibrutinib, he completed treatment for miliary tuberculosis with rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, and levofloxacin. He denied pulmonary or constitutional symptoms at presentation.  

On examination, multiple subcutaneous 1- to 2-cm nodules with overlying ecchymosis were observed on the thighs. There was no erythema or warmth. A deep punch biopsy of a right-leg nodule showed a brisk mixed acute and chronic inflammatory infiltrate involving both the septa and lobules of adipose tissue, with fibrinoid necrosis of small-vessel endothelium, associated neutrophils, and erythrocyte extravasation. Chest radiographs were negative for granulomatous disease. Interferon-γ release assay was not performed. Sterile punch biopsies of a left-thigh lesion for acid-fast bacilli culture and Mycobacterium tuberculosis polymerase chain reaction were negative.

A 44-year-old previously healthy Sri Lankan man presented with a 6-month history of progressive left ankle swelling, restricted movement, and pain on weight-bearing. He denied respiratory symptoms, fever, weight loss, or night sweats and reported no history of trauma or surgery. On examination, the left ankle was swollen but not tender or warm, with global restriction of motion; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 35 mm in the first hour, and a positive Mantoux test (18 mm induration). A Ziehl–Neelsen stain of sputum was negative, and the chest radiograph was normal. Serologic tests for rheumatoid factor, anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, and antinuclear antibody were negative. Fasting glucose and HIV testing were also normal/negative.

Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the ankle revealed an irregular outline of the ankle mortise, loss of joint space, and irregular articular changes of the subtalar joint. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated marked loss of articular cartilage, bone marrow oedema in the distal tibial subarticular and metaphyseal regions, and chronic inflammatory changes in the subtalar joint. Joint aspiration was not possible owing to minimal effusion. Because the initial workup, including imaging, was inconclusive, the patient underwent an open synovial biopsy.

A 60-year-old woman was admitted with one week of progressive dyspnea and general weakness. She had a 20-year history of diabetes, hypertension, and daily alcohol use (≈14 g). On exam she appeared mildly ill; blood pressure 132/80 mmHg, pulse 76/min, respiratory rate 20/min, temperature 36.8°C. Lung exam revealed decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the lower one‐third of the right hemithorax; heart exam was unremarkable. There was no hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, palmar erythema, spider angiomata, or peripheral edema.

Laboratory studies: albumin 3.2 g/dL, total protein 6.4 g/dL, AST/ALT 33/24 IU/L, ALP 801 IU/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, BUN/Cr 12.5/0.89 mg/dL, WBC 3430/mm3, hematocrit 38.4%, platelets 150,000/mm3, INR 1.08, CRP 0.07 mg/dL, NT-proBNP 257 ng/mL. Urinalysis showed no proteinuria. Viral hepatitis serologies were negative.

Chest radiograph showed a large right pleural effusion. Thoracentesis removed 1500 mL of yellowish fluid. Analysis: pH 7.3, glucose 212 mg/dL, LDH 105 IU/L, protein 3.0 g/dL, RBC 330/mm3, WBC 1/mm3, ADA 11.9 IU/L; fluid met transudative criteria. Cultures—including bacterial and AFB—and cytology were negative. Chest CT showed no lung parenchymal disease or pleural thickening. Abdominal ultrasound showed a normal‐sized liver with slightly increased echogenicity (suggestive of fatty change) and no ascites. EGD revealed gastric erosion without varices. Echocardiography was normal. Despite diuretics and repeated thoracenteses over two weeks, the right pleural effusion persisted.

A 35-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with an 18-month history of a pigmented patch on her right breast. She denied any application of topical agents, tight clothing, pre-existing erythematous lesions, systemic illness, or trauma. She and her first-degree relatives had no history of malignant tumors. Her skin phototype was IV. On examination, there was a rounded 2.5-cm hyperpigmented macular plaque on the right areola with irregular borders extending onto the surrounding skin. Dermoscopic evaluation showed white structureless areas and heterogeneous pigmented areas with a reticular network at the periphery.

A 17-year-old man was admitted with a 10-day history of cough, low-grade fevers, and progressively worsening dyspnea. Symptoms began 3 days after discharge following ankle reconstruction surgery. He had no prior medical or respiratory history, no recent travel or sick contacts. His 14-year-old brother had a recent cough and dyspnea, and his mother had a three-month persistent cough.

On examination, he was tachypneic with exercise-induced hypoxemia (SpO2 82% on ambulation) requiring 3 L/min of supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula to maintain saturations >90%. Chest auscultation revealed extensive bilateral crackles without signs of heart failure.

Laboratory studies showed mild neutrophilia (8.6 × 10^9/L), eosinophilia (1.17 × 10^9/L), and mildly elevated C-reactive protein (10 mg/L). An extensive infectious workup, including blood cultures; respiratory virus PCR; urinary Legionella and Streptococcus pneumoniae antigens; Mycoplasma, Chlamydia psittaci, and Chlamydia pneumoniae serologies; and Aspergillus and avian precipitins, was negative. An autoimmune screen was negative.

Pulmonary function tests revealed a restrictive pattern: FEV1 2.52 L (64% predicted), FVC 3.42 L (72% predicted), no bronchodilator reversibility, and DLCO 19.54 mL/min/mmHg (67% predicted).

Chest CT showed bilateral, symmetrical, diffuse patchy ground-glass opacities with small-volume mediastinal adenopathy, without micronodularity.

Further history revealed that the family’s indoor swimming pool had recently switched from chlorine to a perox-and-ozone system. Occupational hygiene assessment found molds (Scedosporium spp. and Cladosporium spp.) in the home and a pet cockatiel in the kitchen.

A preliminary diagnosis of hypersensitivity pneumonitis was made. Specific precipitins for Micropolyspora faeni, terrestrial actinomycetes, pigeon serum IgG, Penicillium, Cladosporium, Candida albicans, Alternaria, and Setomelanomma were negative. No elevation in specific IgE or IgG to Aspergillus was detected.

Bronchoalveolar lavage showed lymphocytosis (36%) without eosinophilia (0%) and standard cultures grew no pathogens.

A 47-year-old man with long-standing, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 10.1%) presented to the emergency department after three consecutive generalized tonic-clonic seizures and a postictal state. He reported 24 hours of nocturia, polyuria, and polydipsia. He was hemodynamically stable (BP 130/80 mmHg; HR 85 bpm; RR 20/min; T 36.5°C; SpO2 98% on room air) and had dry mucous membranes. His BMI was 32.2. He was lethargic (GCS 11/15), with muscle strength 4/5 in the lower extremities and diminished deep tendon reflexes; cranial nerves and sensation were normal. Finger-stick glucose could not register; venous blood gas showed pH 7.36, PCO2 42 mmHg, PO2 32 mmHg, lactate 1.2 mmol/L, and bicarbonate 23.7 mEq/L. Urinary and plasma ketones were negative.

Initial laboratory studies:
• Plasma glucose 838 mg/dL; blood urea nitrogen 21 mg/dL; creatinine 1.1 mg/dL (eGFR 71 mL/min)  
• Serum sodium 133 mmol/L; chloride 89 mmol/L; calcium, potassium, phosphorus, magnesium normal  
• Serum albumin 2.1 g/dL; alkaline phosphatase 192 U/L; ALT 19 U/L; AST 21 U/L; total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL  
• Calculated serum osmolality 320 mOsm/kg  

Head CT, ECG, and chest X-ray were unremarkable. He was started on IV normal saline at 500 mL/h and insulin infusion at 0.14 U/kg/h. After 24 hours, despite gradual glucose reduction (30–40 mg/dL/hr; glucose now 200–300 mg/dL), he remained lethargic and developed worsening paraparesis (strength 3/5). Serum osmolality had decreased to 305 mOsm/kg; sodium remained within normal limits throughout admission.

Brain MRI performed 24 hours after admission demonstrated increased T2/FLAIR signal intensity with restricted diffusion in the central pons and medulla, with sparing of the thalami, mamillary bodies, and cerebral hemispheres. Lumbar puncture results were normal; EEG showed nonspecific slowing; toxicology screens were negative.

A 45-year-old woman from the Caribbean with a history of right invasive mucinous breast cancer (pT1c pN0 Mx, G2) treated 6 months earlier by nipple-sparing mastectomy and sentinel node excision presented after a mild thoracic trauma with a painful swelling over her right chest wall. Physical examination revealed a solitary 4×5 cm soft, tender, fluctuating lesion with defined margins over the eighth rib, not attached to underlying structures. She was afebrile with normal vital signs and an unremarkable respiratory examination.  
Chest CT showed a fracture of the eighth rib with an adjacent tumefaction. PET-CT demonstrated an FDG-avid lesion next to the fractured rib, highly suspicious for a necrotizing metastasis, and several axillary and infraclavicular nodes with lower FDG uptake.  
Repeated fine-needle aspirations of the chest wall lesion and of axillary lymph nodes revealed granulomatous inflammation without malignant cells. Bacterial cultures remained all negative. Laboratory studies showed mild normocytic, normochromic anemia (Hb 119 g/L), normal leukocyte and platelet counts, normal electrolytes, creatinine, and liver enzymes except for elevated alkaline phosphatase (109 U/L) and γ-glutamyltransferase (203 U/L) without clinical symptoms. The lesion continued to enlarge, and the patient was admitted for operative excision of the mass.

A 74-year-old man with a history of generalized anxiety disorder had been treated sequentially with escitalopram and sertraline, both discontinued due to adverse effects. Two weeks after starting low-dose venlafaxine (9.375 mg daily), his anxiety and myoclonic symptoms improved. Approximately 1 month after venlafaxine initiation, he developed a nonpruritic, erythematous, papular rash involving the distal lower extremities, bilateral buttocks, one elbow, and the oral mucosa. He had no fever, arthralgia, or other systemic symptoms. His vital signs were within normal limits. His medical history included ischemic heart disease, hypertension, and benign prostatic hyperplasia, and his medications included aspirin, clopidogrel, metoprolol tartrate, rosuvastatin, losartan, tamsulosin, and pantoprazole. No laboratory tests or skin biopsy were performed.

A 32-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of a painless, slowly enlarging swelling in the anterior maxillary region. He denied trauma or pain, and his medical history was unremarkable.  
Extraoral examination showed diffuse swelling over the anterior maxilla, extending from the tip of the nose laterally toward the left ala and from just below the left inner canthus to the superior border of the upper lip. There was mild deviation of the nasal tip to the right and effacement of the left nasolabial fold. The swelling was firm and nontender.  
Intraorally, there was a well-circumscribed vestibular swelling measuring approximately 3.5 cm × 3 cm, extending from the right central incisor region to the distal line angle of the left canine, obliterating the labial mucobuccal fold. The overlying mucosa was intact, and the swelling was firm at its periphery but yielded centrally to pressure.  
All maxillary anterior teeth were vital on testing. A provisional diagnosis of nasolabial cyst was made.  
A maxillary occlusal radiograph revealed a well-defined, corticated, unilocular radiolucency extending mediolaterally from the right to the left central incisor region and anteroposteriorly from the apices of the incisors into the palate. An inverted impacted supernumerary tooth (mesiodens) was seen, with the radiolucency circumscribing its cemento-enamel junction. There was slight root resorption of the central incisors.  
Fine-needle aspiration yielded blood-tinged cystic fluid, and microscopy demonstrated cholesterol crystals.

An 11-year-old boy was admitted after two generalized tonic–clonic seizures over 2 days. Two days before admission he had subfebrile temperature (37.5 °C), abdominal pain, and one episode of vomiting. On presentation he was somnolent (GCS 9), pulse 111 beats/min, blood pressure 130/69 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, oxygen saturation 71% on room air, with perioral cyanosis. Neurologic exam (post-midazolam) showed intact cranial nerves, symmetric low muscle tone, symmetric reflexes, no focal deficits, and no meningeal signs.  
Laboratory tests showed neutrophilic leukocytosis (16.87 × 10^9/l), respiratory acidosis (pH 7.248), lactate 8.1 mmol/l, glucose 6.9 mmol/l, and normal electrolytes, CRP, liver, and kidney function. SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative; IgG antibodies were positive.  
Brain CT was normal. EEG showed focal intermittent theta and delta slowing in the left frontal region. Brain MRI (T2-FLAIR) demonstrated cortical thickening with hyperintense signals in both hippocampi and a 10 mm hyperintense focus at the base of the right frontal lobe.  
Suspecting encephalitis, CSF analysis revealed no pleocytosis, normal IgG, IgM, and albumin levels, no intrathecal IgG synthesis, and elevated glucose (4.3 mmol/l). PCR testing of CSF was negative for herpes simplex virus 1/2, human herpesvirus 6, and human herpesvirus 8. Serum and CSF IgM and IgG for varicella-zoster virus, Lyme disease, and tick-borne encephalitis were negative. HHV-7 DNA was detected in the CSF.

A 34-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with a 9-day history of progressive painful swelling of the penis. The symptoms began shortly after vigorous sexual intercourse. He denied any trauma, urinary symptoms, or use of medications. He reported having frequent and intense sexual relations. Physical examination revealed a soft swelling of the entire penis and an indurated, filiform, tender subcutaneous cord palpated at the dorsal root of the penis. The remainder of the genitourinary examination was normal. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, renal function, and urinalysis, were all within normal limits and showed no evidence of infection. Based on the history, there was no “popping” sound or sudden loss of erection to suggest penile fracture.

A 28-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of right shoulder pain radiating into the hand, which was worse at night and with elevation of the right upper limb. She reported episodes of paresthesia, loss of fine and crude touch sensation in the C8 and T1 dermatomes, and intermittent coldness and swelling of the right arm. On examination, right-hand interossei muscle strength was 4/5 (Medical Research Council scale). An anteroposterior radiograph of the cervical spine showed bilateral elongation of the transverse processes of the seventh cervical vertebra, more pronounced on the right. Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine demonstrated a short-segment syrinx at C2–C3 and focal compression of the right brachial plexus in the lower trunk region.

A 32-year-old Pakistani woman presented to the eye outpatient department with pain, photophobia, and blurred vision in her right eye one week after evisceration of the left eye.  
History of present illness: Two months earlier, she had worn contact lenses for a few hours and developed left‐eye keratitis unresponsive to topical Moxifloxacin and Brolene, leading to corneal perforation, no light perception vision, and pain. An evisceration was performed, and a prosthesis placed; pain resolved.  
Current examination of the right eye:  
- Visual acuity: 6/60  
- Slit‐lamp: mutton‐fat keratic precipitates; +2 cells in the anterior chamber; posterior synechiae  
- Fundus: +3 vitritis; optic‐disc swelling; normal retina  
Other medical, family, and social history noncontributory; no immunocompromise.

A 70-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of progressive dizziness, pre-syncope, and malaise. On arrival: hemoglobin 62 g/L, hematocrit 0.16 L/L, mean corpuscular volume 105 fL, leukocytes 13.6 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 9.6 × 10^9/L, and C-reactive protein 18.95 mg/L; electrolytes, thyroid-stimulating hormone, INR, aPTT, and creatinine were within normal limits. Her history included COPD, hypertension, irritable bowel syndrome, a 45 pack-year smoking history (quit 3 years prior), and daily alcohol use. She received two units of packed RBCs. A direct antiglobulin test was positive for IgG and C3 with a pan-reactive eluate. Chest radiograph was normal. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no lymphadenopathy or mass. Upper endoscopy revealed a 3.0 × 2.0 cm moderate-grade gastric adenocarcinoma at the gastroesophageal junction; PET scan confirmed no metastases. She began neoadjuvant FLOT chemotherapy, and one week later developed painful acrocyanosis of the feet. Repeat labs: hemoglobin 88 g/L, total bilirubin 86 µmol/L, direct bilirubin 14 µmol/L, lactate dehydrogenase 487 U/L, and undetectable haptoglobin (<0.10 g/L). Prednisone 60 mg daily was initiated. Hematology consultation yielded a positive cold agglutinin screen (thermal amplitude 30°C, titer 1:256), confirming mixed warm and cold AIHA. Bone marrow biopsy showed normal trilineage hematopoiesis and a monoclonal B-cell population (<1%) with a CLL-like phenotype. Serum protein electrophoresis detected IgG kappa 3.0 g/L and trace IgM kappa. Viral (hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV) and rheumatological (rheumatoid factor, ANA, ENA) workups were negative.

A 23-year-old white man was admitted with a 2-week history of suddenly enlarged left cervical lymph nodes unresponsive to multiple antibiotics. One week before admission, he developed fever up to 39 °C, fatigue, weight loss, and night sweats. His medical history was notable for over 20 episodes of bacterial tonsillitis in the past 2 years; his brother died young of a nasopharyngeal malignancy. He denied travel to endemic regions. Physical examination revealed a few separate, slightly tender left cervical lymph nodes with normal overlying skin and asymmetric left palatine tonsillar enlargement without exudate. His temperature reached 39.5 °C, responsive only to intramuscular metamizole; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed leukopenia (2.2–3.3 × 10^3/μL), anemia (hemoglobin 12 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (127 × 10^3/μL), granulocytopenia, monocytosis, and 1% lymphoid cells on smear. Coagulation studies revealed aPTT 39.8 s and D-dimer 1.9 μg/mL. Inflammatory markers were elevated (CRP 17.6 mg/L, ESR 40 mm/h; procalcitonin negative), and LDH was 463 U/L, with both CRP and LDH rising further during hospitalization.

Serologic tests for toxoplasmosis (IgG, IgM), syphilis (VDRL), hepatitis B and C, EBV (VCA IgG, IgM), HIV, anti-streptolysin O, and ANA were negative; anti-HBs was positive from prior vaccination; CMV IgG positive, IgM negative. Blood and urine cultures and a tuberculin skin test were negative. Chest radiograph was normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck showed multiple left cervical lymph nodes up to 2 cm, mostly supraclavicular, without other masses; chest CT revealed small axillary nodes but no mediastinal or pulmonary lesions. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of a lymph node was non-diagnostic.

A 41-year-old man was evaluated for 2 years of infertility. His height was 1.58 m, weight 65 kg (BMI 23.9 kg/m²). On examination, both testes were atrophic (9 mL by Prader orchidometer) with pea-sized indurations palpable at the epididymal heads bilaterally. Scrotal ultrasound revealed bilateral heteroechogenic, hypovascularized masses near the testes. Semen analysis showed oligoasthenozoospermia (volume 2.6 mL; concentration 7 × 10^6/mL; motility 14%). Serum follicle-stimulating hormone was 2.7 mIU/mL, luteinizing hormone 1.3 mIU/mL, testosterone 4.3 ng/mL, and estradiol 13 pg/mL. Tumor markers, including human chorionic gonadotropin, alpha-fetoprotein, and lactate dehydrogenase, were within normal limits. Pelvic MRI (T2-weighted) showed irregular, heterogeneous low-signal-intensity lesions with surrounding high-signal normal parenchyma in both testes. Contrast-enhanced CT scan demonstrated diffuse, irregular enlargement of both adrenal glands without other abnormalities.

A 60-year-old man presented in April 2016 with progressive jaundice that began during a trip to Cuba. He had a 10-year history of intermittent pruritus and minimal scleral icterus, and 1 year earlier had developed bilateral deep-vein thromboses. His medical history was notable for type I diabetes mellitus (since 1998) treated with insulin, and hypertension treated with an angiotensin II receptor blocker. During the first hospitalization, he experienced an acute upper gastrointestinal bleed.

Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed intrahepatic bile-duct strictures described as PSC-like lesions with bile-duct dilation and findings strongly suspicious for a Bismuth type IV hilar cholangiocarcinoma. MRI also showed an irregularly configured and accentuated pancreatic duct. ERCP-guided biopsy of the common hepatic duct demonstrated fibrosis and a nonspecific inflammatory reaction without malignant cells. Laboratory tests revealed an elevated carbohydrate antigen 19-9 level of 148.4 IU/mL (normal <39.0 IU/mL). Serologic testing for antimitochondrial antibodies (AMA), anti–liver-kidney microsomal antibody (LKM), soluble liver antigen (SLA), smooth muscle antibody (SMA), cytoplasmic ANCA (c-ANCA), and perinuclear ANCA (p-ANCA) were all negative.

A 55-year-old Caucasian man with type 2 diabetes treated with oral agents and a history of cigarette smoking presented with left-sided community-acquired pneumonia and acute renal failure. He reported no recent use of nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs or antibiotics. On admission, temperature was 38.0 °C, blood pressure 120/60 mmHg, and urine output was diminished and concentrated. Pulmonary examination disclosed diffuse crackles in the left lung, a dry cough, and exertional dyspnea. Chest radiography showed alveolar opacities in the left lung. A Legionella urinary antigen test was positive. He was treated with erythromycin and ofloxacin. Laboratory studies showed serum creatinine 614 μmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 28 mmol/L, C-reactive protein 360 mg/L, leukocyte count 13×10^9/L, lactate dehydrogenase 408 IU/L, and creatine phosphokinase 2000 IU/L. Arterial blood gases on room air revealed pH 7.44, PaCO2 29 mmHg, PaO2 65 mmHg, and HCO3– 22 mmol/L. Urinalysis demonstrated aseptic leukocyturia (684 cells/mm^3), hematuria (56 cells/mm^3), urinary sodium <20 mmol/L, urinary urea 13 g/L, proteinuria 2.48 g/L, and albuminuria 0.4 g/L. Renal ultrasound was normal. Despite saline infusion, his renal function worsened and he became anuric, with a serum creatinine of 1000 μmol/L on day 3, prompting initiation of hemodialysis.

A 60-year-old man sought extraction of remaining teeth and evaluation for regenerative treatment. He had stage 4 squamous cell carcinoma of the right submandibular gland with mandibular involvement and lung metastasis diagnosed in 2018; he underwent cisplatin/docetaxel chemotherapy and 70 Gy of fractionated radiotherapy to the submandibular region, achieving complete remission. Follow-up from 2015 to 2021 showed no recurrence. He experienced occasional post-therapy pain managed with methadone and complained of oral burning, xerostomia, and gingival recession.

Extraoral examination revealed normal mouth opening and mandibular movements. Intraoral examination showed normal saliva, no soft-tissue ulceration or dehiscence, no exposed bone, infection, or fistulae, but evidence of periodontal bone loss and radiation caries. Panoramic and CBCT imaging demonstrated ill-defined patchy bone destruction of the posterior mandible bilaterally, surrounded by sclerotic bone with a wide transitional zone, sequesters within the lesions, cortical bone resorption, and a fistula extending to the right lingual cortex. 

Differential diagnosis included osteoradionecrosis, chronic osteomyelitis, and diffuse sclerosing osteomyelitis. An incisional biopsy of the right mandibular lesion was performed.

A 46-year-old woman with a 5-year history of hypertension and hypothyroidism presented for preoperative assessment after the diagnosis of a left breast mass on screening mammography. She reported progressive shortness of breath and dry cough for 2 years, with orthopnea developing over the past 6 months. She denied palpitations, syncope, hemoptysis, chest trauma, or prior thoracic surgery. Her medications included levothyroxine and metoprolol; she was a nonsmoker without known allergies. Vital signs were normal. Cardiac examination revealed regular rhythm and normal heart sounds; physical examination was otherwise unremarkable except for grade 2 bilateral lower-limb edema. Electrocardiography showed normal sinus rhythm. A preoperative chest radiograph demonstrated a well-defined, oval opacity at the right cardiophrenic angle. Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed a homogeneous mass measuring 7.2 × 9.1 cm in the right lower thorax, most consistent with a pericardial cyst, although a bronchogenic cyst could not be ruled out. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a 7.5 × 7 cm cystic structure adjacent to the right atrium, mild tricuspid regurgitation, and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60%. Complete blood count, liver function tests, serum creatinine, and electrolytes were within normal limits. An ELISA test for hydatid disease was negative. Urinalysis showed no microscopic hematuria, and abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated normal kidneys.

A 33-year-old primigravida at 40 weeks’ gestation presented after spontaneous rupture of membranes. Labor was augmented, and 2 hours later fetal bradycardia prompted emergency cesarean delivery; intraoperatively, 50% placental abruption was noted without significant hemorrhage. A healthy female infant was delivered, weighing 3.3 kg (Apgar scores 8 and 9). Fourteen hours postoperatively, the patient became jaundiced, oliguric, and hypoglycemic (glucose 40 mg/dL). She was alert and hemodynamically unstable without evidence of obstetric bleeding. Vital signs were: heart rate 120 bpm, blood pressure 74/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.3 °C. Laboratory evaluation showed: total bilirubin 7.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 5.149 mg/dL, indirect bilirubin 2.7 mg/dL, AST 170 U/L, ALT 149 U/L, prothrombin time 27 s, INR 2.56, fibrinogen 71 mg/dL, creatinine 2.7 mg/dL, ammonia 126 μmol/L, platelets 95 000/μL, white-cell count 33 030/μL, hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, hematocrit 27.8%, and LDH 432 IU/L. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated an echogenic liver with fatty infiltrates consistent with mild hepatic steatosis. The patient had no prior symptoms of liver disease and no history of viral exposures or hepatotoxic medication use.

A 32-year-old man presented with a gradual-onset, severe right-sided headache that resolved spontaneously within 24 hours, followed by dysphagia, dysphonia, and right-sided neck pain. He reported a recent upper respiratory infection with frontal sinus pain, fevers, and mucopurulent nasal discharge. He had no significant medical history, denied illicit drug use, was a non-smoker, and drank alcohol moderately.

On examination, the right neck was tender along the deep cervical chain without lymphadenopathy. Ear, nose, and neck movements were normal. Neurologic examination revealed dysfunction of the right cranial nerves IX, X, and XII: absent right gag reflex, right soft palate paralysis with uvula deviation to the left, hypotonic right tongue deviated to the right on protrusion, and right vocal cord palsy with pooling of saliva in the hypopharynx. The trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles had normal strength, and the remainder of the neurologic examination was normal. Audiometry was normal.

Laboratory studies showed a normal white-cell count and C-reactive protein, with mild lymphopenia. HIV testing was negative. A computed tomography scan of the neck suggested an abscess in the right carotid space ascending into the jugular foramen. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a focal thrombus in the superior part of the right internal jugular vein extending through the jugular foramen into the sigmoid sinus; there was no deep cerebral venous thrombosis.

A 65-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on twice-weekly hemodialysis (4 months), diabetes, hypertension, and receiving isoniazid plus rifampicin for pulmonary tuberculosis noted a 2-day history of a vesicular rash in a thoracic dermatome. He was conscious, oriented, and was prescribed oral acyclovir 400 mg three times daily. Two days after starting acyclovir, he presented with dysarthria, drowsiness, and disorientation. Blood pressure was 150/90 mm Hg. Neurologic examination revealed slow speech and cerebellar signs, including bilateral upper-limb past pointing and rebound. The rash was crusting. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL, elevated blood urea and serum creatinine, and otherwise normal biochemistry. Brain MRI revealed only age-related cerebral atrophy without acute infarction. Empiric intravenous acyclovir (5 mg/kg once daily) was initiated. Blood cultures were negative. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed no cells, protein 65.3 mg/dL, glucose 50 mg/dL, adenosine deaminase 1.9 IU/L, and a straw color. CSF quantitative PCR for varicella–zoster virus and a multiplex viral encephalitis panel were negative. Bacterial, fungal, and tuberculosis cultures and CSF cytology were also negative.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a 9-month history of gradual swelling and stiffness of her right thumb, which extended to her hand and wrist after returning from Jamaica. She had no fever, and laboratory markers were within normal limits. Over this period, she was diagnosed sequentially with idiopathic carpal tunnel syndrome, De Quervain’s tenosynovitis, rheumatoid arthritis, and complex regional pain syndrome type II, and received NSAIDs, sulfasalazine, local and systemic corticosteroids without improvement. She denied major trauma but performed gardening and sometimes had minor unnoticed injuries. Tests for HIV and diabetes were negative.

Ultrasound of the hand revealed marked diffuse synovitis with low vascular flow and tenosynovitis of the common flexor tendons extending into the thumb and the fifth finger’s flexor tendon sheath. She underwent drainage of a collection in the fifth finger and limited debridement of the flexor tendon sheath. Histopathological analysis of synovial tissue disclosed intense chronic inflammation with both necrotizing and non-necrotizing granulomas. Cultures from perioperative samples grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus, and mycobacterial liquid culture became positive after eight days. Ziehl–Neelsen staining showed acid-fast bacilli. She was diagnosed with chronic nontuberculous mycobacterial flexor tenosynovitis complicated by MSSA cellulitis.

A 28-year-old woman from the Philippines presented with a one-month history of right upper quadrant pain, suprapubic pain, abdominal bloating, and night sweats. Her medical history was notable for chronic hepatitis B under specialist follow-up. On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs; her abdomen was distended with mild, diffuse tenderness. Laboratory studies showed a normal white-cell count and liver-function tests; hepatitis B serology was consistent with chronic infection. Her CA 125 level was elevated to 218 U/mL, whereas carcinoembryonic antigen, CA 19-9, and α-fetoprotein levels were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a 16 mm left para-ovarian cyst, thickened fallopian tubes, and moderate free fluid. Computed tomography of the abdomen revealed moderate ascites with diffuse peritoneal thickening encasing loops of small bowel. An ascitic fluid tap yielded lymphocyte-predominant fluid without malignant cells. A tuberculosis screening test performed six years earlier was negative. She underwent diagnostic laparoscopy, which showed a physiologic left ovarian cyst, numerous peritoneal and omental nodules, reactive serous fluid, and extensive adhesions; biopsies were taken. Histologic examination revealed granulomatous inflammation, although polymerase chain reaction testing for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex DNA was negative.

A 55-year-old man with metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma (lungs, liver, bone, and multiple lymph nodes) had previously received 34 cycles of axitinib plus pembrolizumab without severe adverse events, followed by everolimus and then cabozantinib. He was rechallenged with nivolumab, and on day 11 after the first dose he noted difficulty closing his left eyelid and mouth. Four days after onset, physical examination revealed paralysis of the upper and lower left facial muscles consistent with peripheral facial nerve palsy. There were no facial paresthesia, hearing loss, dizziness, tinnitus, auricular rash, dysphagia, dysarthria, or other cranial nerve abnormalities. Contrast-enhanced cranial MRI demonstrated abnormal enhancement of the left facial nerve but showed no brain metastasis or cerebral infarction. Serological antigen tests for herpes simplex virus and varicella zoster virus were negative. The patient had no history of diabetes mellitus or neurological disorders.

A 12-year-old boy from Ethiopia presented with 2 months of progressive lower extremity weakness. The weakness began distally and spread proximally. He also reported tingling and numbness in his legs and developed bladder and bowel incontinence. He denied fever, headache, cough, nausea, vomiting, or recent illnesses. Although he frequently contacted river water, he had no history of bloody diarrhea or prior treatment for schistosomiasis.

On examination, he was well-nourished and in no acute distress. Vital signs were normal. He was awake, alert, and fully oriented. Cranial nerves were intact. Upper extremity strength and reflexes were normal. Lower extremities had 0/5 strength, hypotonia, hyperesthesia, and absent knee and ankle reflexes. Sensation to pain, light touch, vibration, and proprioception was intact.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count without eosinophilia. Organ function tests, stool, and urine examinations were unremarkable. MRI of the spine revealed a 2.4 × 1.1 × 1.6 cm eccentrically located intramedullary mass at the conus medullaris that was T1 isointense, T2 hyperintense, and demonstrated avid homogeneous postcontrast enhancement, with cord expansion and superior cord edema. No vertebral or disc abnormalities were noted.

Based on these findings, a diagnosis of myxopapillary ependymoma was made, and the patient underwent T1–L1 laminectomy with myelotomy and mass excision.

A 45-year-old man presented with 3 days of right-sided abdominal pain, fever, myalgias, anosmia, ageusia, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. His temperature was 103.0°F, and he was tachycardic. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the epigastrium, right upper and lower quadrants, McBurney’s point, and positive psoas and obturator signs. He had a positive tuberculin skin test two years earlier with a negative chest radiograph and was born and raised in a TB-endemic country. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis, elevated lipase, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein. Chest radiography demonstrated bibasilar atelectasis and a small left pleural effusion. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed thickening of the distal ileum and cecum, hypodense lymphadenopathy in the retroperitoneal, mesenteric, and porta hepatis regions, a small volume of ascites, and mild gallbladder and duodenal wall thickening. Right upper quadrant ultrasound confirmed gallbladder wall thickening and porta hepatis adenopathy. He was started on IV fluids, antipyretics, and empiric antibiotics. Influenza and COVID-19 tests were negative. An interferon‐gamma release assay was negative, but concern for a false-negative result prompted HIV testing, which returned positive with a CD4 count of 10 cells/μL. CTA of the chest showed no pulmonary embolism but revealed bilateral subcentimeter randomly distributed pulmonary nodules, worsening pleural effusions, and atelectasis. Paracentesis demonstrated mildly elevated adenosine deaminase but negative acid-fast smears. Exploratory laparoscopy with mesenteric wedge biopsy was nondiagnostic. Bronchoscopy with biopsy and bronchoalveolar lavage was initially nondiagnostic, but a send-out test revealed rare acid-fast bacilli. Due to clinical deterioration, he was empirically started on quadruple antitubercular therapy and prophylaxis for Pneumocystis jirovecii.

A 65-year-old Gurung Nepalese woman from a remote hilly area, a farmer by occupation, presented with painless bulging of her left eyeball for 2 months and progressive diminution of vision for the past 15 days. She had no significant past medical or family history. On examination, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 15/15. Vital signs were within normal limits. There was no lymphadenopathy. Ocular examination revealed proptosis of the left eye with visual acuity of 6/18; extraocular movements were intact. The right eye and the remainder of the neurologic examination were unremarkable.

Routine laboratory studies were within normal limits, including hemoglobin 110 g/L, WBC count 6.5×10^9/L, renal and liver function tests, electrolytes, and chest radiograph. 

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the head and orbit showed a multiloculated cystic lesion in the left infratemporal fossa extending into the extraconal orbital space through the infraorbital fissure, with erosions of the adjacent orbital bones. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-defined multiloculated lesion that was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, eroding the lateral wall of the maxillary sinus and the floor of the medial cranial fossa and displacing the globe anteromedially.

Radiological differentials included a soft tissue mass and ameloblastoma.

A 44-year-old Caucasian man presented with one week of fever (up to 39°C), general weakness, headache, dry cough, and diarrhea. He was a 20 pack‐year smoker with no other comorbidities or travel. He had been treated empirically with oral amoxicillin–clavulanate without improvement.

On admission: temperature 38.9°C; pulse 100/min; respiratory rate not recorded; oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Chest examination revealed reduced vesicular breath sounds and crackles over the left upper lung field. 

Initial laboratory studies showed WBC 2020 cells/mm3, total bilirubin 1.6 mg/dL, albumin 2.7 g/dL, alkaline phosphatase 382 U/L, γ-glutamyl transferase 69 U/L, and CPK 422 U/L. Serologies were negative for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C. Blood cultures were negative. 

A chest radiograph demonstrated extensive consolidation of the left upper lobe without pleural effusion. The patient was started on IV piperacillin–tazobactam and oral clarithromycin. On hospital day 3, a urine antigen test was positive for Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1; clarithromycin was replaced with IV levofloxacin, and piperacillin–tazobactam was continued.

By day 6, his respiratory status worsened, and rifampicin was added. On day 9, he developed respiratory distress (40 breaths/min); arterial blood gas on room air showed PaO2 50 mmHg, PaCO2 30 mmHg, pH 7.50, and SaO2 86%. Chest CT revealed extensive left upper lobe consolidation with ground-glass opacities and pleural effusion, and patchy ground-glass areas in the right lung. On day 10, PaO2/FiO2 was 101 and he was transferred to the ICU and placed on CPAP, improving to a PaO2/FiO2 of 254.

Levofloxacin was held on day 17 for washout and resumed with IV fluconazole on day 19. On day 21, he again developed respiratory distress; CT showed increased bilateral consolidation and a left-sided pneumothorax. On day 22, he was intubated and underwent bronchoalveolar lavage, which revealed 32% macrophages, 26% lymphocytes (CD4/CD8 ratio 0.8), 40% neutrophils, and 2% eosinophils; no protozoa, fungi, or malignant cells were seen. 

On day 23, IV methylprednisolone 120 mg/day was initiated for presumed ongoing ARDS.

A 59-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with acute right upper quadrant pain and a low-grade fever (maximum temperature, 37.8°C). On examination, she had localized signs of peritoneal irritation in the right upper quadrant. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a normal liver, gallbladder, and bile ducts; the appendix was not visualized. In the subhepatic region, there was a 4-cm, noncompressible, heterogeneous, hyperechoic mass with a thin hypoechoic rim and absent internal blood flow on color Doppler imaging. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen demonstrated a 43×33×56-mm ovoid lesion between the right colic flexure and the inferior margin of hepatic segment IVb, characterized by a heterogeneous adipose matrix with dense internal branching and a surrounding hyperdense enhancing rim. No other significant abdominal abnormalities were identified.

A 15-year-old girl with no prior medical history was brought to the emergency department after a high-speed front-end motor-vehicle collision. She was a restrained passenger; airbags deployed. On arrival, her Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) was 15, though she had brief loss of consciousness and amnesia. Injuries included a displaced comminuted fracture of the left femur, bilateral tibia/fibula fractures (left side comminuted), multiple pelvic fractures, a small left apical pneumothorax (<5%), a grade 2 liver laceration, two left rib fractures, and scattered ecchymoses. Initial head and cervical-spine CT scans showed no intracranial hemorrhage or edema. The left lower extremity was placed in traction, and she was admitted to the ICU.

Nine hours after arrival, her GCS fell to 7 (eyes open to pain only, extensor posturing). She was intubated for airway protection. Repeat CT angiography of the head, neck, and thorax showed no new hemorrhage, edema, or central pulmonary embolism. Laboratory studies were notable for leukocytosis (WBC 22.11 ×10^9/L), lactic acidosis (4.6 mmol/L), and elevated creatine kinase (3,216 U/L).

The patient was empirically loaded with levetiracetam and an EEG was obtained. On ICU day 2, brain and brainstem MRI demonstrated innumerable, multifocal bilateral foci of restricted diffusion with associated cytotoxic edema, possibly representing fat embolism. EEG monitoring showed no seizures or epileptiform activity. On ICU day 3, transthoracic echocardiography revealed a patent foramen ovale; left ventricular ejection fraction was 55–65% with no valvular lesions.

A 25-year-old medically fit man presented to a dental emergency clinic with a 7-day history of constant aching pain localized to the left mandible. Extraoral and intraoral soft-tissue examinations were unremarkable. Periodontally, there were no pathological pockets, and oral hygiene was good. Dentally, he had an unrestored adult dentition with absent third molars and no detectable caries. The lower left first premolar was markedly tender to percussion, and a long-cone periapical radiograph demonstrated a significant periapical radiolucency. A diagnosis of acute apical periodontitis was made, and the tooth underwent pulp extirpation, dressing with ledermix, and temporary restoration. The patient was referred to a general dental practitioner for completion of root canal treatment.

Two weeks later, he reattended with constant aching pain in the lower right mandible. Clinical examination again revealed no decay or periodontal pathology. A periapical radiograph of the lower right quadrant showed periapical pathology associated with the right first premolar. Acute apical periodontitis was diagnosed, and pulp extirpation was performed.

A 66‐year‐old woman presented with 2 days of shortness of breath and chest pain. Her medical history included rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus, for which she took prednisolone (6 mg/day) and hydroxychloroquine (200 mg/day). She frequently worked with potting soil in her garden and reported orange‐coloured sputum. On admission, temperature was 36.1 °C; blood pressure, 109/69 mmHg; pulse, 111/min; respiratory rate, 30/min; and oxygen saturation, 96% on 9 L/min via reservoir mask. She was alert and had coarse crackles bilaterally. Laboratory tests showed WBC 30,510/μL (99.5% neutrophils), hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL, platelets 5.0 × 10^4/μL, LDH 341 U/L, BUN 30 mg/dL, creatinine 1.21 mg/dL, and CRP 41.06 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas on room air revealed pH 7.397, pCO2 34.4 torr, pO2 46.5 torr, and HCO3– 21.8 mEq/L. Chest radiography showed bilateral consolidation in the upper and middle lung fields, and CT revealed consolidation of the right upper, middle, and lower lobes, left upper lobe, and atelectasis of the left lower lobe. Sputum Gram stain was not diagnostic. Both pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigen tests were negative. Empiric IV levofloxacin and meropenem were started. Given her immunosuppressed state, differential diagnoses included viral or fungal infection, alveolar hemorrhage, and interstitial pneumonia. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) performed under intubation yielded orange‐coloured fluid with a neutrophil predominance (90%), a negative Gram stain, and cytology showing numerous neutrophils and a few macrophages without hemosiderin.

A 46‐year‐old male marathon runner presented with one week of localized right lower quadrant pain. The pain was excruciating when seated or upright, worsened with movement, and was relieved only in the supine position; he also experienced nausea. His only surgical history was orchidopexy in childhood. On examination, there was guarding and rigidity at McBurney’s point, rebound tenderness, and a positive psoas sign; the Rovsing sign was negative. No masses or cutaneous lesions were palpable. Hip flexion beyond 90° elicited pain, but internal and external rotation were pain‐free. Neurologic examination was normal. Laboratory studies were within normal limits except for a mildly elevated C‐reactive protein level of 12.5 mg/L; the Alvarado score was 4. A contrast‐enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed no abnormalities and excluded the classic causes of right lower quadrant pain. The patient was admitted for monitoring and NSAID pain management, but symptoms persisted despite stable laboratory values. Given the movement‐dependent pain, an MRI of the lumbar spine and neurologic evaluation were performed, revealing no pathology.

A 34‐year‐old Tibeto‐Burman Nepalese woman presented with a 3‐week history of low‐grade fever, painful right‐sided neck swelling, and fatigue. On examination, there were discrete, tender lymph nodes in the right posterior cervical triangle; the largest measured 2×1 cm without overlying skin changes. She denied night sweats, anorexia, weight loss, or other systemic complaints. She had no history of tuberculosis or known tuberculosis exposure. ENT and dental examinations were unremarkable, and there were no rashes, photosensitivity, joint pain, or alopecia.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 13.0 g/dl and leukopenia (2800 cells/mm3; neutrophils 52%, lymphocytes 40%). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 25 mm/h, and C‐reactive protein was positive. Renal and hepatic function tests were normal. There was no growth on blood culture or throat swab after 72 hours, and peripheral blood smear showed no atypical lymphocytes. Rheumatoid factor, anti‐cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies, antinuclear antibodies, anti‐neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and anti‐double‐stranded DNA antibodies were all negative. A chest radiograph was normal.

Neck ultrasonography demonstrated multiple enlarged, round lymph nodes with hypoechoic centers and hyperechoic rims. An incisional biopsy was performed, and gray‐white to gray‐brown lymphoid tissue was obtained.

A 10-year-old spayed female Labrador retriever was referred for acute hepatopathy and urinary retention. The dog had a 1–2-day history of anorexia, vomiting, and stranguria with decreased urine output. Exposure to unidentified mushrooms in the yard was reported, although ingestion was not observed. Four months earlier, routine laboratory tests had been normal.

On presentation (day 0), the patient was alert, with normal heart and respiratory rates. The abdomen was tense, and a large bladder was palpated. Point-of-care ultrasound showed a distended urinary bladder without mechanical obstruction; a urinary catheter was placed. Blood gas analysis revealed a normal pH (7.407) with moderate respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis due to mild hyperlactatemia (3.4 mmol/L; RR 0–1.0 mmol/L).

Day 1 laboratory tests showed polycythemia (hematocrit 62.3%; RR 40–55%), thrombocytopenia (70,000/μL; RR 150,000–400,000/μL), and an inflammatory leukogram with bands (485). Biochemistry revealed severe mixed hepatocellular hepatopathy (ALT 13,288 IU/L, AST 1830 IU/L, ALP 1508 IU/L, GGT 17 IU/L), hyperbilirubinemia (1.4 mg/dL), panhypoproteinemia (albumin 3.3 g/dL, globulin 1.6 g/dL), and hypoglycemia (73 mg/dL). Coagulation testing showed prolonged PT and aPTT, hypofibrinogenemia, and elevated D-dimers.

Abdominal ultrasound noted mildly hyperechoic hepatic parenchyma with small nodules, lymphadenomegaly, gallbladder wall edema, a distended bladder with thickened proximal urethra, and bilaterally enlarged adrenal glands (left 1.1 cm, right 1.1 cm with a hypoechoic region).

On day 2, a urine toxicology assay detected alpha-amanitin, confirming amanitin intoxication. The dog was hospitalized with intravenous fluids, dextrose, acetylcysteine, vitamin K, antiemetics, antibiotics, and analgesia. The patient’s hepatic enzymes and function improved, and she was discharged on day 8 with supportive medications.

On day 24, the dog returned with anorexia, vomiting, and a 4.7-kg weight loss since initial presentation. Vital signs were normal. CBC showed eosinophilia (1806/μL; RR 0–1500/μL) and thrombocytopenia. Chemistry revealed hyponatremia (131 mmol/L; RR 143–151 mmol/L), hyperkalemia (5.1 mmol/L; RR 3.6–4.8 mmol/L), Na:K ratio 25.7, hypercalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, severe hypoglycemia (43 mg/dL), hypoalbuminemia, hypocholesterolemia, mild hyperbilirubinemia, and a mixed primarily cholestatic hepatopathy.

Abdominal ultrasound showed mild small-bowel wall thickening and bilateral adrenal nodules similar in size and appearance to those previously seen. The liver was diffusely hypoechoic with rounded margins; gallbladder wall edema had resolved.

A 48-year-old Vietnamese man presented after an out-of-hospital ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest following a low-speed single-vehicle collision. Emergency medical services defibrillated him in the field and administered potassium and amiodarone. He was unresponsive, intubated, and found to have bilateral pneumothoraces managed with chest tubes. On admission to the intensive cardiac unit, his vital signs and electrolytes were normal, and he was started on postarrest cooling.

On hospital day 2, he developed multiple ventricular arrhythmias—including paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, and premature ventricular complexes—in the setting of severe hypokalemia (serum potassium, 1.9 mmol/L). He remained hemodynamically stable during these episodes.

He had no prior medical history, did not use alcohol, tobacco, or illicit drugs, and had no family history of cardiac disease. Initial differential diagnoses included acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, hemorrhage, electrolyte abnormalities, and cardiac contusion.

Investigations included cardiac catheterization, which showed normal left ventricular function and no coronary artery disease. Computed tomography of the chest was negative for pulmonary embolism but confirmed a large left pneumothorax. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a left ventricular ejection fraction of 55–60% with no wall motion abnormalities or signs of cardiac contusion. Thyroid function tests revealed thyroid-stimulating hormone <0.01 μIU/mL, free thyroxine >5 ng/dL, and free triiodothyronine 8.9 ng/dL.

A 23-year-old Afro-Jamaican woman presented with a 7–8-month history of generalized lymphadenopathy. She reported progressive fatigue, malaise, unintentional weight loss of 40 pounds, nausea, intermittent headaches, and bilateral lower-extremity edema. She denied fever, chills, night sweats, anorexia, rash, sore throat, cough, or dyspnea. Her medical history included an episode of left facial palsy at age 15, tonic–clonic seizures two years earlier managed with sodium valproate, and an ischemic stroke two years prior with residual left-sided weakness. There was no known history of infections, sarcoidosis, malignancies, or relevant family history.

On examination, she appeared well with normal vital signs. Cardiac and pulmonary exams were unremarkable. Abdominal exam revealed hepatomegaly and mild splenomegaly. There was 2+ pitting edema of the lower extremities to the shins. Multiple painless, soft, non-tender, freely movable lymph nodes were palpable in cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions, the largest measuring 5×4 cm. Neurologic findings reflected her prior stroke, with left facial droop, decreased strength (3/5) and sensation on the left, and slowed coordination on the left side.

Laboratory studies showed pancytopenia (WBC 3,700/μL, hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, platelets 96/μL), hypoalbuminemia (1.5 g/dL), proteinuria (≥500 mg/dL on urinalysis), hyperlipidemia (cholesterol 364 mg/dL, triglycerides 580 mg/dL), elevated inflammatory markers (ESR 132 mm/h, CRP 0.50 mg/dL), and elevated LDH (964 U/L) and ALP (169 U/L). Contrast-enhanced CT scans revealed widespread lymphadenopathy in the cervical, axillary, mediastinal, hilar, abdominal, pelvic, and inguinal regions, hepatomegaly (17.7 cm), mild splenomegaly (12.9 cm), and a hypodense splenic lesion measuring 1.4×3.4×3.6 cm. An excisional biopsy of an inguinal lymph node showed reactive follicular hyperplasia with prominent germinal centers and no evidence of lymphoma. Flow cytometry and immunophenotyping were negative for malignancy. Acid-fast stain and bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal cultures were all negative.

A 41-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of visual loss and ocular pain in her right eye. She had no significant systemic or family history. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/50 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Slit-lamp examination of the anterior segment was unremarkable bilaterally, and intraocular pressures were within normal limits.

Dilated fundus examination of the right eye revealed an amelanotic subretinal mass beneath the superior temporal arcade, associated with surrounding subretinal fluid. B-scan ultrasonography demonstrated a hyperechoic, dome-shaped mass. Optical coherence tomography showed an elevated retina with normal-appearing choroidal tissue beneath and adjacent subretinal fluid.

Fluorescein angiography did not reveal dual circulation but showed pooling-type hyperfluorescence around the lesion. Indocyanine green angiography demonstrated a central area of intense hypofluorescence surrounded by a mild hypofluorescent halo.

A 72‐year‐old man presented with a 4‐hour history of fever, chest tightness, and dull precordial chest pain unrelieved by rest or nitroglycerin. His temperature was 39.7 °C, pulse 136 beats/min, respiratory rate 23 breaths/min, and blood pressure 98/67 mmHg. He had a history of right upper lobectomy for stage IIB lung adenocarcinoma in 2016, adjuvant chemotherapy, nodal recurrence treated with chemotherapy in 2018, tracheal tumour involvement treated with cryotherapy and radiotherapy in early 2024, and most recently three cycles of pemetrexed, carboplatin, and bevacizumab for progressive disease. On examination, lung sounds were slightly coarse without rales; heart rate was 136/min with distant, dull heart sounds and no murmurs. Laboratory tests showed WBC 10.05×10^9/L with 93.2% neutrophils, hemoglobin 110 g/L, platelets 187×10^9/L, CRP 130 mg/L, D‐dimer 7.83 mg/L, and normal cardiac enzymes including troponin I and BNP. ECG showed sinus tachycardia, abnormal Q waves, and ST‐segment elevation (> 0.1 mV) in leads II, III, and aVF, with ST-segment changes in leads I and aVL. He received aspirin, clopidogrel, and intravenous nitroglycerin. Four hours later, repeat ECG still showed ST‐segment elevation without dynamic change, cardiac biomarkers remained normal, and chest pain persisted. At that time, he was taken for coronary angiography.

A 36-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a suspected lung cancer. He had a 6-week history of dull, aching left anterior chest pain, cough with scanty sputum, anorexia, and weight loss. He denied fever, hemoptysis, abdominal symptoms, or neurologic complaints. He had no history of lung disease, diabetes, illicit-drug use, or immunosuppressive therapy. He worked as a mason, had a 10-pack-year smoking history, and lived in a rural area of Tamil Nadu, India.

On examination, vital signs were normal. General examination was unremarkable. Chest auscultation revealed dullness to percussion and diminished breath sounds over the left hemithorax. A chest radiograph showed a large homogeneous opacity occupying the left hemithorax. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 22,500/mm3 with neutrophil predominance; serum electrolytes, liver function, and renal function were within normal limits. HIV serology was negative. Serum immunoglobulin levels and a CD4 count (618 cells/μL) were normal.

Chest CT confirmed an 11.9 cm × 8.2 cm mass in the left upper lobe with central hypoattenuation. On hospital day 3, the patient developed mild headache and nausea. He was alert, without neck stiffness or focal neurologic deficits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the brain showed mild meningeal enhancement; the ventricles and brain parenchyma appeared normal.

A 32-year-old man with no prior medical or surgical history presented to the emergency department with a 3-week history of a pulsatile mass at the lateral aspect of his left knee. Three weeks earlier, he had undergone an uncomplicated arthroscopic medial meniscectomy. Since then, he had noticed that the mass was becoming increasingly painful and appeared to be enlarging. On examination, he was hemodynamically stable, and routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. 

Point-of-care CT angiography of the left lower extremity demonstrated a nonspecific blush of contrast in the region of the lateral left knee, but the study was limited by motion artifact. Concerned about a possible arterial injury, clinicians obtained dedicated anterolateral color Doppler ultrasound (CDU) of the lateral left knee. CDU revealed a heterogeneous, echogenic collection measuring approximately 2.9 cm × 2.3 cm × 1.5 cm with an adjacent small vessel. Spectral Doppler imaging showed pulsatile, to-and-fro flow within the collection. These findings were interpreted as consistent with a vascular outpouching in the distribution of the left lateral inferior genicular artery.

A 78-year-old woman with a history of thyroid cancer treated by thyroidectomy and bilateral breast cancer treated by mastectomy underwent primary debulking surgery for suspected ovarian cancer, which included hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, omentectomy, rectal resection, and lymphadenectomy. Twenty-three days after surgery, she began adjuvant chemotherapy with paclitaxel (175 mg/m2) and carboplatin (area under the curve, 6) administered on day 1. On day 8, she experienced dizziness, nausea, and vomiting. Laboratory studies revealed:  
• Serum sodium, 114 mEq/L  
• Plasma osmolality, 231 mOsm/kg  
• Urine osmolality, 352 mOsm/kg  
• Urinary sodium excretion, 90 mEq/L  
• Antidiuretic hormone, 5.3 pg/mL  
• Creatinine, 0.52 mg/dL  
• Cortisol, 22.7 μg/dL  
Physical examination showed no signs of hypovolemia or hypervolemia.  
What is the most likely cause of her hyponatremia?

A 10-year-old Afro-descendant girl was referred with a chief complaint of a painless gingival swelling that had caused difficulty in mastication and aesthetic concerns. The patient’s mother reported that the enlargement was first noted at age 5 during the deciduous dentition and became more pronounced with the eruption of permanent teeth. There was no history of systemic illness or chronic medication use. Family history revealed a similar gingival enlargement in her father; her mother was unaffected.

On extraoral examination, there was an open-mouth posture, elevated lips, marked open bite, and inability to achieve a passive lip seal. Intraorally, there was a generalized gingival enlargement covering most of the maxillary and mandibular crowns, with a rough, pink, fibrous texture, areas of melanic pigmentation, and gingival margin hyperemia. In the palate, the overgrowth extended toward the midline, partially obliterating the palatal vault. Several teeth were displaced, with crowns partially or completely immersed in the fibrotic tissue. The gingiva was firm and painless on palpation.

Hematological tests were within normal limits. A panoramic radiograph showed normal development and positioning of all permanent teeth. An incisional biopsy was performed at two sites. Histopathological examination revealed a hypocellular, hypovascular, dense fibrous connective tissue covered by stratified squamous epithelium with acanthosis and elongated rete ridges. Picro-sirius red staining demonstrated a marked increase in collagen fiber bundles.

A 35-year-old woman presented with a 7-hour history of sudden-onset, crampy periumbilical abdominal pain, associated with repeated vomiting that initially contained ingested matter and later bilious fluid. She also reported mild abdominal distension. Her obstetric history was notable for three cesarean deliveries, the most recent 4 months earlier; she had no prior similar episodes, no history of trauma, and no family history of abdominal disorders. She continued to pass flatus and stool. 

On examination, her pulse was 108/min, blood pressure 120/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, and she was afebrile. Mucous membranes were dry. The abdomen was mildly distended, hyperresonant, and had hyperactive bowel sounds; it was soft and non-tender. Digital rectal examination revealed stool without masses or bleeding. 

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 16.4×10^3/μl with 84.8% granulocytes. An erect abdominal radiograph demonstrated dilated, centrally located small-bowel loops with prominent valvulae conniventes. 

The patient was kept NPO, received intravenous fluid resuscitation, and had a nasogastric tube and urinary catheter placed pending further management.

A 30-year-old healthy man presented with a 4-month history of a slowly enlarging, painless mass in the right lateral neck. He denied any history of trauma, surgery, or neck manipulation, and had no personal or family history of connective tissue disease. He noted that the mass swelled when he performed a Valsalva maneuver. On examination, there was a 4-cm soft, compressible, nonpulsatile, mobile mass along the anterolateral right cervical region that increased in size with Valsalva but did not change with respiration or swallowing. There was no ecchymosis, skin discoloration, inflammation, or surrounding lymphadenopathy, and upper-extremity arterial pulsations were normal. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. Ultrasonography showed a 4.3-cm hypoechoic, compressible structure in the subcutaneous tissues between the platysma and cervical fascia, connected to the external jugular vein. Color Doppler ultrasonography revealed internal flow with alternating positive and negative waveforms, consistent with a to-and-fro pattern in the neck of the lesion.

A 41-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after being punched and kicked multiple times in the head during an assault. He was comatose on arrival (GCS score of 3).
