Vital signs were: temperature 36.8 °C, heart rate 90/min, blood pressure 140/85 mm Hg, respiratory rate 14/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Physical examination showed facial bruises, fractures of the bilateral mandible and left mastoid process, and tenderness over several left ribs.

Toxicology on admission revealed cocaine at 0.224 mg/L and ethanol at 1.35 g/L in the blood. Noncontrast head CT demonstrated diffuse subarachnoid and subdural hemorrhages, areas of contusion, and skull fractures. CT angiography revealed a blister-like aneurysm of the left posterior communicating artery with active contrast extravasation. Given the high surgical risk, he was treated pharmacologically and underwent endovascular coiling of the left internal carotid artery and branches of the left posterior and anterior communicating arteries on the following day.

A 61-year-old woman presented with gradual‐onset epigastric pain radiating to the back and exertional dyspnea of 1 month’s duration. She had no history of alcohol consumption or pancreatitis, and her medical and family histories were unremarkable. On examination, she was in mild respiratory distress; oxygen saturation was 92% on room air, blood pressure was 124/71 mmHg, pulse 78 beats/min, and temperature 36.9°C. Chest auscultation revealed dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds over the right hemithorax. Abdominal examination showed epigastric tenderness without rebound or guarding.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 7000/μL, hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, total protein 6.4 g/dL, albumin 2.5 g/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 199 IU/L, serum amylase 1288 IU/L (pancreatic isotype), C-reactive protein 19.4 mg/dL, and CA19-9 104 ng/mL. A chest radiograph demonstrated a large right-sided pleural effusion. Thoracic CT confirmed massive right pleural fluid. Diagnostic thoracentesis yielded black, exudative fluid. Pleural fluid analysis revealed pH 7.35, protein 3.9 g/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 546 IU/L, glucose 101 mg/dL, albumin 1.8 g/dL, amylase 55,128 IU/L, and CA19-9 586 ng/mL. Cytology was negative for malignant cells, and cultures showed no pathogens. A chest tube was placed, after which her symptoms improved. Repeat thoracic and abdominal CT after drainage showed only a small encapsulated pleural collection, no pulmonary masses, and a pancreas of normal appearance. Given the black color of the fluid and marked pleural and serum amylase elevations, a pancreatic source was suspected.

A 6-hour-old full-term male infant was referred shortly after birth for evaluation of a fleshy perineal mass and abnormal genitalia. The pregnancy was uncomplicated and the infant was born vaginally at term, weighing 2.5 kg. On examination, there was a mucosa-lined patch protruding from the perineal region, extending up to the penoscrotal area. Genital anomalies included penoscrotal hypospadias, penoscrotal transposition, and an ectopic right hemiscrotum. The anal opening was located in the orthotopic position, but the anterior half of the opening was replaced by the mucosal patch, which appeared to continue internally into the rectum. Ultrasonography revealed a solitary right kidney without hydronephrosis, and a voiding cystourethrogram was normal. There were no cardiac or spinal anomalies.

A 44-year-old white woman with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with right lower quadrant abdominal pain and was found to have acute appendicitis. Review of systems was negative for fever, cough, chest pain, dyspnea, arthralgias, changes in bowel habits, or weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable except for tenderness in the right iliac fossa without guarding or rebound. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 9130/μL, and normal liver and renal function tests. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed appendicitis and incidentally revealed multiple lytic lesions in the vertebral bodies. She underwent appendectomy and recovered uneventfully. Follow-up CT of the spine and chest demonstrated numerous lucent lesions throughout the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar vertebrae, along with bilateral lower-lobe noncalcified pulmonary nodules. A purified protein derivative (PPD) skin test for tuberculosis was negative. Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine showed diffuse bone-marrow heterogeneity throughout the cervico-thoracic and thoraco-lumbar regions with preserved disk spaces and no fractures.

A 10-year-old Tibetan girl presented with a 2-month history of moderate to severe headache and nonprojectile vomiting. She had no fever, seizures, or weight loss. Six schoolmates had similar symptoms and were under evaluation for parasitic infection. Her diet included cooked yak and pork.  
On admission, her vital signs were normal, and general and neurologic examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 7.5×10^9/L with 7.8% eosinophils.  
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a protein concentration of 696.4 mg/L (normal 80–430), a white-cell count of 25×10^6/L (normal <15×10^6/L), and normal glucose. Gram and India ink stains and bacterial cultures of CSF were negative.  
C-reactive protein, serum IgE, HIV and syphilis serologies, T-SPOT.TB, tuberculin skin test, stool examination, abdominal ultrasound, chest CT, and ocular and spinal MRI were all unremarkable.  
Brain MRI showed numerous cystic lesions throughout the cerebral hemispheres, brain stem, and cerebellum. Some lesions demonstrated the so-called “hole-with-dot” appearance.

A 29-year-old man presented for a routine ocular examination. He had no history of ocular or systemic disease, trauma, or surgery. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye; intraocular pressure was 12 mm Hg bilaterally by Goldmann applanation tonometry. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye after full dilation revealed posterior capsular haze with surface vascularization of the temporal half of the posterior capsule extending from the 6- to 12-o’clock positions. There were no cells or flare in the anterior chamber or anterior vitreous, and gonioscopic evaluation of the angles was unremarkable in both eyes. Fundus examination of the right eye by slit-lamp biomicroscopy and indirect ophthalmoscopy was normal; the left eye examination was normal throughout.

B-scan ultrasonography of the right eye showed a normal retinochoroidal complex and optic nerve head, with a few medium-reflective dot echoes in the vitreous cavity. The axial length was 22.17 mm in the right eye. Ultrasound biomicroscopy of the right eye was unremarkable. Anterior segment optical coherence tomography demonstrated a thickened intact posterior capsule centrally adhered to another thickened membrane posteriorly (interpreted as neovascular tissue), with separation of the two layers peripherally, and hyperreflective signals behind the ciliary body in the quadrant corresponding to the vascularization.

The patient had an allergic reaction to a test dose of sodium fluorescein, precluding fundus fluorescein angiography. Routine blood tests, including antinuclear antibody titers and a tuberculin skin test, and carotid Doppler ultrasonography were all within normal limits. A cardiovascular evaluation was unremarkable. Given the excellent visual acuity and the asymptomatic, nonprogressive nature of the lesion, biopsy was deferred and the patient was followed closely.

A 67-year-old man with a history of hypertension presented with right knee pain for more than 2 months without injury. He had no history of autoimmune disease, HIV, cancer, chronic steroid use, recreational drug use, smoking, or alcohol use. Initial right knee radiograph showed early osteoarthritic changes, and he was treated for degenerative osteoarthritis. One year later, he returned with acute right knee pain, joint effusion, and erythema in the absence of fever or systemic symptoms. He denied any prior intra-articular injections or procedures. A follow-up radiograph demonstrated progression of osteoarthritic changes without bone destruction. Laboratory evaluation revealed an ESR of 23 mm/h (reference <20) and a CRP level of 2.85 mg/dL (reference <0.5). Arthrocentesis yielded 70 mL of yellowish, turbid fluid with a WBC count of 247,200/mm3 (90% neutrophils). Gram stain, AFB stain, and fungal cultures of the synovial fluid were negative. Arthroscopic irrigation and synovectomy were performed.

A 67-year-old man with a history of chronic systolic and diastolic heart failure, coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, and atrial fibrillation was admitted with shortness of breath and diarrhea. Chest radiograph showed bilateral infiltrates. N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide was 24 591 pg/mL (normal <350 pg/mL), and troponin was 0.15 ng/mL (reference 0.03–0.10 ng/mL). Electrocardiography showed no ST-segment changes. C-reactive protein was 5.3 mg/dL (normal 0.1–0.4 mg/dL), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 37 mm/hr (normal 0–15 mm/hr). Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 24%. SARS-CoV-2 PCR testing was positive. He was treated with ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and intravenous diuretics. He had a brief episode of atrial fibrillation that resolved spontaneously. Thyroid-function tests showed a thyroid-stimulating hormone level of 0.029 µIU/mL (normal 0.27–4.2 µIU/mL) and a free thyroxine level of 2.1 ng/dL (normal 0.8–1.7 ng/dL). He reported weight loss, fatigue, and diarrhea but denied neck pain. Examination of the thyroid was unremarkable, and there were no ophthalmic findings. There was no use of biotin, levothyroxine, or amiodarone. It was initially unclear whether he had early Graves’ disease, a toxic nodule, or thyroiditis. Methimazole, 20 mg daily, was started, and thyroid autoantibody testing was ordered.

A 54-year-old man presented with a 4-year history of Sweet’s syndrome, characterized by tender ulcers on his fingers and cutaneous lesions on all extremities, and progressive numbness, paresthesias, and hearing loss. He was initially diagnosed by skin biopsy showing a neutrophilic dermal infiltrate with papillary dermal edema and no evidence of vasculitis. Despite treatment with oral and intralesional corticosteroids and topical agents, he underwent amputation of a finger for ulceration and infection. Over subsequent months, he noted new lesions and worsening distal numbness and paresthesias in his feet and hands. Neurologic examination revealed decreased pinprick, vibratory, and position senses in the distal lower extremities. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography demonstrated severe sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy with mixed axonal and demyelinating features. Laboratory evaluation showed a leukocyte count of 13.8×10^3/μL with 90% neutrophils, hemoglobin of 13 g/dL with an MCV of 131 fL, a TSH of 0.254 μIU/mL, and a monoclonal IgG κ spike on serum immunofixation. Hemoglobin A1C, vitamin B12, ANA titer, and rheumatoid factor were within normal limits. Heavy-metal levels were normal. A sural nerve biopsy revealed moderately severe axonal neuropathy with approximately 40% loss of myelinated fibers. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed a protein of 177 mg/dL, red cells 12/mm^3, albumin 141 mg/dL, and IgG 12.6 mg/dL, with normal glucose, white cells, and myelin basic protein. He also reported rapidly progressive bilateral hearing loss, positional dizziness, and tinnitus; trial of hearing aids was unsuccessful. Audiometry showed profound bilateral sensorineural hearing loss with 0% word recognition. Magnetic resonance imaging of the internal auditory canals and brain showed no mass or other abnormalities.

A 68-year-old man presented with sudden right-sided hemiparesis, aphasia, fever, and progressive loss of consciousness. His history included hypertension, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and prior coronary artery bypass grafting. Home medications were atorvastatin, carvedilol, aspirin, and allopurinol, with no recent changes.

On examination, temperature was 38.2 °C, heart rate 90 bpm, respiratory rate 14/min, blood pressure 150/86 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis (17 000/μL with granulocytosis), platelet count 266 000/mm³, hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, serum creatinine 2.18 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 30 mg/dL, INR 1.11, aPTT 21 s, ESR 46 mm/h, and CRP 29 mg/L. Chest CT revealed gravitational ground-glass opacities, and noncontrast brain CT demonstrated acute ischemia.

He was started on vancomycin (25 mg/kg IV loading dose, then 1000 mg every 12 h) and meropenem 1000 mg IV every 12 h for presumed sepsis, with a 30-minute interval between the two antibiotics. Within 4.5 hours of symptom onset and with no contraindications, alteplase (rTPA) was administered as a 0.1 mg/kg bolus followed by 0.8 mg/kg infusion over 1 h via the right cubital vein.

Sixty minutes after completion of the rTPA infusion, small vesicles appeared at the injection site. Over the next 12 hours, these lesions enlarged into tense hemorrhagic bullae with underlying ecchymoses extending proximally and distally on the right upper limb. There was no mucosal involvement, angioedema, bronchospasm, or blood-pressure fluctuation. The Nikolsky sign was negative.

Radiographs of the right upper limb showed no fractures. Compartment pressures measured 15–20 mmHg (with simultaneous blood pressure 130/80 mmHg). Ultrasound and radiologic studies revealed no subcutaneous or fascial involvement. Blood and urine cultures were negative.

A 69-year-old Caucasian man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes was admitted with progressive dyspnea and new-onset diarrhea. He had orthopnea and bilateral pleural effusions on chest radiograph. Examination revealed a grade 2 systolic murmur at the apex, bilateral lower-extremity edema, and lung crackles. ECG showed new-onset atrial fibrillation with inverted T waves in the inferior and lateral leads. NT-proBNP was 35 000 pg/mL; troponin I was ∼200 ng/L. In the emergency department, he was tachypneic (RR 21/min), hypoxemic (SpO₂ 89% on room air), febrile (37.5 °C), with AF and a median heart rate of 65 b.p.m., and blood pressure of 100/65 mmHg. Laboratory tests revealed WBC 11 750/mm³ (95.7% neutrophils), hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL, platelets 32 000/mm³, CRP 166.7 mg/L, procalcitonin 9.43 ng/mL, INR 2.04, fibrinogen 80 mg/dL, D-dimer 13 380 ng/mL, normal liver function, and creatinine 2.06 mg/dL. Blood and urine cultures grew Morganella morganii. An ISTH DIC score was 6, consistent with overt DIC. Transthoracic echocardiography showed left ventricular dilation (EDV 155 mL), EF 35% (previously 55% one year prior), global hypokinesia, elevated filling pressures, and biatrial enlargement (LA end-systolic volume 90 mL). A highly mobile, rounded, hyperechoic mass was seen in the left atrium. Three days later, transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a highly mobile mass in the left atrial appendage and another mass in the right atrial appendage.

A 14-year-old girl presented with a 6-month history of exertional dyspnea, right-sided chest pain, and nonproductive cough. Symptoms were worse when supine, prompting her to sleep sitting or prone. She had intermittent low-grade fevers responsive to outpatient treatment.  
On examination, breath sounds were absent over the right lung fields, chest expansion was reduced on the right, and percussion revealed dullness. Breath-holding time was 10 seconds, and pulmonary function tests showed a restrictive pattern. Systemic and laboratory evaluations were normal.  
A chest radiograph demonstrated a large mass occupying nearly the entire right thoracic cavity. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax revealed a well-defined, thin-walled cystic lesion (8.2 × 8.4 × 13.5 cm) in the right anterior hemithorax, containing an air–fluid level and no internal septations, with compression of the right middle lobe bronchus and collapse of the right middle lobe.  
A provisional diagnosis of bronchogenic versus pleuro-pericardial cyst was made, and surgical excision via right lateral thoracotomy was planned.

A 59-year-old woman with no significant medical history underwent minimally invasive mitral and tricuspid valve repair via mini-thoracotomy for severe myxomatous mitral regurgitation and moderate tricuspid regurgitation. The immediate postoperative course was uneventful, and she was discharged home. Ten days later, she returned with progressive shortness of breath. 

On examination, she was in mild respiratory discomfort; vital signs were within normal limits, and oxygen saturation was 93% on room air. Cardiac auscultation revealed normal heart sounds without murmurs; the lungs were clear. A chest radiograph showed a right hydropneumothorax. An electrocardiogram revealed normal sinus rhythm without acute changes. 

Transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department demonstrated a small pericardial effusion without right ventricular diastolic collapse on subcostal imaging. When the patient was placed in the left lateral decubitus position, parasternal and apical views revealed a substantially larger pericardial fluid collection and the presence of air bubbles within the pericardial space. 

Noncontrast computed tomography of the chest confirmed a large hydropneumothorax on the right and a large hydropneumopericardium. A computed tomography pulmonary angiogram was negative for pulmonary embolism.

A 10-year-old previously healthy girl presented with several months of morning back pain accompanied by gait stiffness. Initially mild and self-limited, her symptoms gradually increased in intensity and duration, causing her to cease gymnastics. She was afebrile without night sweats, lymphadenopathy, or skin changes. On examination, there was slight tenderness to palpation over the C7 spinous process; the neurologic examination, including lower-limb strength, was normal. Laboratory evaluation, including inflammatory markers, fecal occult blood tests, and stool S-100, was normal or negative. HLA-B27 testing was negative, and electromyography of the lower limbs was normal. Spinal radiographs were unremarkable. Initial MRI of the brain, entire spine, and pelvis showed a T2-hyperintense lesion in the C7 vertebral body suggestive of hemangioma, along with bilateral acetabular bone marrow edema. Skeletal scintigraphy revealed an inhomogeneous distribution without focal pathological uptake of Tc-99m diphosphonate.

An 11-year-old boy presented with sudden breathlessness, throat tightness, abdominal pain, and vomiting. He had a 2-week history of polydipsia, polyuria, abdominal pain, and fatigue. On examination, he appeared clinically dehydrated (~10%), had Kussmaul breathing with tachypnea and tachycardia, hypertension, and a room-air oxygen saturation of 96%. Finger-prick blood sugar was incalculably high, and blood ketones were 6.0 mmol/L. A venous blood gas confirmed severe diabetic ketoacidosis. Blood urea and serum creatinine were elevated. He received an intravenous normal-saline bolus and insulin infusion. Because of throat tightness, anaphylaxis was considered and IM adrenaline was administered. He was transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit. Twelve hours later, after transition to subcutaneous insulin, he reported mild inspiratory chest discomfort. Vital signs were normal on room air. Examination revealed bilateral neck crepitus and a precordial “crunching” sound on auscultation. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm. Review of his initial chest radiograph revealed subcutaneous emphysema of the neck and pneumomediastinum.

A 70-year-old man was admitted for renal dysfunction and hypertension. He had a 10-year history of Raynaud’s phenomenon and had been treated for dyslipidemia. Seven months before admission, his serum creatinine was 1.04 mg/dL. Five months before, his systolic blood pressure rose to 180 mmHg, and irbesartan and amlodipine were started. Despite adjustments, creatinine climbed to 1.5 mg/dL at 5 months, 2.4 mg/dL at 3 months, 3.8 mg/dL at 2 months, and 6.91 mg/dL two weeks before admission.

On admission, blood pressure was 168/83 mmHg, pulse 79/min, and he was alert. He had puffy fingers with mild skin thickening of the fingers (mRSS 1) but no fingertip lesions or telangiectasia. Chest examination revealed bilateral fine rales in the lower lung zones; heart, abdominal, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed BUN 76 mg/dL, creatinine 8.41 mg/dL, sodium 129 mEq/L, potassium 4.7 mEq/L, and uric acid 9.7 mg/dL. Urinalysis showed protein 2+ with 0.51 g/day proteinuria and 1–3 RBCs/HPF. Hematocrit was 27.2%, hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, WBC 10,100/µL, and platelets 329,000/µL.

Serologic testing revealed an ANA of 1:1280 (centromere type) and an anticentromere antibody level of 131 IU/mL. Tests for anti–topoisomerase I, anti–RNA polymerase III, anti–U1-RNP, anti–double-stranded DNA, anti–single-stranded DNA, anti-Sm, anti–mitochondrial M2, rheumatoid factor, and anti–CCP antibodies were all negative. While on angiotensin receptor blockade, plasma renin activity was >20 ng/mL/h and aldosterone was 608 pg/mL.

Chest CT showed reticular shadows in the lower lung fields and esophageal dilation; echo suggested mild pulmonary hypertension. Kidney ultrasound showed a slightly atrophic left kidney and normal right kidney without hydronephrosis. He had hypertensive retinopathy (Keith–Wagener grade 3).

The presence of Raynaud’s phenomenon, limited finger skin thickening, interstitial lung disease, and positive anticentromere antibodies indicated limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis. As he had severe hypertension with rapidly progressive renal failure, he was clinically diagnosed with scleroderma renal crisis. Because SRC in anticentromere antibody–positive limited cutaneous SSc is extremely rare, a renal biopsy was scheduled for differentiation of other renal diseases.

A 53-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of progressive genu valgum and knee pain. Her family noted widening of the knees from age 8, which had gradually worsened without functional disability. Over the past year, knee pain increased and was unrelieved by analgesics. She had no visual, auditory, cognitive, or neurologic symptoms. Physical examination showed marked genu valgum, mild facial dysmorphism (prognathism, prominent ears, frontal bossing), and poor dental condition with caries and partial edentulism. There were no signs of anemia, jaundice, organomegaly, fractures, or neurologic deficits. Family history was notable for parental consanguinity and two of eight siblings with similar phenotypes; the parents were unaffected. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. A plain radiograph of the knees demonstrated marked femorotibial metaphyseal flaring with cortical thinning, consistent with an Erlenmeyer flask deformity.

A 23-year-old G2P1 woman at 39 weeks and 6 days gestation underwent induction of labor with oxytocin followed by cesarean delivery under spinal anesthesia for fetal tachycardia. Intraoperatively, she received 2000 mL of normal saline and 30 IU of oxytocin after fetal delivery. Thirty minutes after transfer to the recovery room, her blood pressure was 80/56 mmHg, heart rate 64 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and SpO2 on room air was 99%. One hour later, she acutely developed shortness of breath and chest discomfort. Her respiratory rate was 40 breaths/min, blood pressure 142/90 mmHg, heart rate 90 bpm, and SpO2 90% on room air. She was alert and oriented. Lung examination showed reduced breath sounds and bilateral crepitations; cardiac examination showed a regular rate without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.  
Chest radiograph showed prominent bilateral interstitial pulmonary opacities consistent with pulmonary edema without cardiomegaly. ECG revealed sinus tachycardia with normal QRS complexes and no ST-segment or T-wave changes. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL, white blood cell count 9000/µL, platelet count 124,000/µL, and creatinine 0.65 mg/dL.

A 21-year-old man presented with insomnia, loss of appetite, weight loss, memory impairment, reluctance, malaise, and fatigue of several weeks’ duration. He had no prior history of hair loss, no substance use, and no medical or psychiatric disorders. On psychiatric examination, he was conscious, cooperative, fully oriented, with decreased self-care, depressed mood, and impaired vegetative symptoms (initial insomnia; reduced appetite and libido). The Beck Depression Inventory score was 41. He was diagnosed with major depressive disorder and started on sertraline, 50 mg daily. Fifteen days after initiation of sertraline, he reported active diffuse hair loss. A dermatology consultation was obtained. Laboratory studies—including thyroid, liver, and kidney function tests; levels of vitamin B12, iron, folate, iron-binding capacity, sodium, potassium, calcium, chloride, magnesium, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, urinalysis, total testosterone, dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate, zinc, and copper—were all within normal limits. A gentle hair-pull test yielded more than 6 hairs. The patient returned to clinic one week later and continued to have progressive hair loss.

A 51-year-old man presented with progressive enlargement of a left thigh mass. He had sustained a gunshot wound to the same thigh one year earlier, treated initially with debridement. Two months after surgery he noted gradual, painless swelling that became tense, warm, and tender, prompting evaluation.

On examination, the left thigh circumference was 73.5 cm. Hip and knee range of motion were limited by severe pain and weakness. The left lower extremity was edematous, and distal pulses were weak.

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 99 g/L, hematocrit 0.29, and a coagulation profile prolonged by 1–2 seconds. Plain radiographs of the femur showed permeative lytic lesions and cortical erosion with an associated large soft tissue mass. Ultrasound demonstrated a noncompressible mass with areas suggestive of necrosis. CT of the left thigh revealed diaphyseal bone lysis, cortical erosions, and an enlarged anterior muscle compartment measuring 34.2 × 16.4 × 13.7 cm.

Considerations based on imaging were chronic osteomyelitis versus a primary aggressive new growth.

A 44-year-old man was admitted with one month of progressive dyspnea, cough, and fever. He initially had mild fever, dry cough, and night sweats without treatment. Two weeks later he developed shortness of breath and yellow sputum. A bronchoscopy at a local hospital showed negative bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) for acid-fast bacilli and Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR. He was treated for community-acquired pneumonia with antibiotics for 10 days without improvement and was transferred.

On arrival, temperature was 37°C, pulse 84/min, respirations 28/min, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, and he required 10 L/min of oxygen by bag-valve mask. Arterial blood gas showed pH 7.38, PaO2 70 mmHg, PaCO2 32.7 mmHg, HCO3– 19.4 mmol/L. Examination revealed dullness to percussion, fine crackles, and decreased breath sounds at the right lower lung field. Laboratory tests showed WBC 8.84 G/L (77.5% neutrophils, 13.3% lymphocytes), hematocrit 38.2%, C-reactive protein 78.4 mg/L, mildly elevated liver transaminases, and negative HIV testing. Chest radiograph demonstrated consolidation in the right lower hemithorax. Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed consolidation with small necrotizing cavities.

He was treated with meropenem, ciprofloxacin, and vancomycin for four days without defervescence. Intravenous methylprednisolone (40 mg daily) was then started, resulting in rapid clinical and radiologic improvement. On hospital day 14, however, fever recurred, and repeat CT showed significant regression of the consolidation.

A 68-year-old man with primary myelofibrosis underwent matched unrelated–donor hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) after conditioning with busulfan, fludarabine, and thiotepa. Post-transplant prophylaxis included caspofungin, levofloxacin, valacyclovir, letermovir, tacrolimus, and mycophenolate mofetil. Nine days after HCT, he had a fever attributed to a transfusion reaction. On day 13, he developed constant right-sided chest pain at rest. CT of the chest without contrast showed right lower lobe consolidation, scattered bilateral nodules, and small pleural effusions. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) cultures were negative; an Aspergillus antigen index was 7.69, and Pneumocystis jirovecii PCR was mildly positive. He was treated with amphotericin B and voriconazole, later switched to posaconazole; P. jirovecii was deemed colonization. He improved and was discharged on day 30.

Over the next 3 weeks he developed progressive exertional dyspnea and dry cough. On day 53, evaluation revealed an enlarging, multiloculated right pleural effusion. Thoracentesis yielded 1650 mL of serosanguinous fluid, exudative by protein and LDH; bacterial, fungal, and AFB cultures were negative, and cytology was nondiagnostic. Twelve days later, his dyspnea and cough worsened. CT chest showed presumed worsening fungal pneumonia and an increased multiloculated effusion. He was started on cefepime and caspofungin. A second thoracentesis removed 1100 mL of hazy fluid; glucose was 115 mg/dL and LDH was less than three times serum; pH was not obtained. Chest CT showed new nodules and progression of prior opacities, prompting a repeat BAL; bacterial cultures were negative. He was discharged on oral posaconazole, IV caspofungin, and intermittent amphotericin B. Subsequent BAL Aspergillus antigen index was 0.18 and fungal cultures were negative, but the patient did not improve.

A 13-month-old previously healthy Saudi boy presented with a 2-day history of fever and cough. During coughing episodes, his mother noted transient lip darkening. There was no known exposure to SARS-CoV-2. He had no history of asthma or chronic illness. On examination, he was afebrile (37.2°C), heart rate 110 bpm, respiratory rate 38/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. There were mild suprasternal and subcostal retractions. Breath sounds were reduced bilaterally, with scattered crepitations in the left lung. Laboratory studies showed normal electrolytes, inflammatory markers, and liver and kidney function. SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR was negative; adenovirus PCR was positive. Anteroposterior supine chest radiograph demonstrated a left-sided mediastinal shift, right-lung hyperinflation, and left-lung consolidation or collapse. He was treated with salbutamol nebulization and intravenous cefuroxime.

A 42-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a large perineal swelling, fever, and dysuria. Two years earlier, he had acute urinary retention and perineal swelling; emergency ultrasound at that time showed a perineal cystic collection (122 cc) with normal prostate and bladder. Incision and drainage yielded serous fluid that proved to be urine on chemical analysis. Two weeks later, voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) revealed a rounded cystic outpouching from the ventral aspect of the proximal bulbar urethra measuring 2.5 × 2.5 × 2.3 cm. The patient did not follow up for 2 years and returned with similar symptoms. Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated large, well-defined, multiloculated, tortuous tubular cystic structures measuring 7.5 × 3.0 × 2.7 cm, encircling the proximal bulbar urethra, extending to the urogenital diaphragm, and coursing anteriorly parallel to the ventral distal bulbar urethra. The lesion was hyperintense on T2-weighted and T2-fat-saturated images and showed wall and septal enhancement on postgadolinium T1-weighted images.

A 44-year-old man with nephrolithiasis and well-controlled HIV presented with 5 days of left flank and lower abdominal pain radiating into the left testicle, achy to sharp in nature. He also reported painful ejaculation, nausea, vomiting, decreased appetite, subjective fever, and chills. He noted that over the prior week he began using a prostate vibrator for the first time.  
On arrival: temperature 101.2 °F, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 21 breaths/min, SpO2 98% on room air. He appeared ill, diaphoretic, and in distress. Oral mucosa was dry. Cardiovascular: sinus tachycardia without murmur. Lungs: clear. Abdominal: tenderness at the left costovertebral angle, left upper and lower quadrants with voluntary guarding. Genitourinary: tenderness along the left inguinal canal and left epididymis; no abscess, cellulitis, or crepitus.  
Laboratory studies: white-cell count 18.2×10^3/mm^3 (neutrophil predominant), hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, platelets 220×10^3/mm^3. BUN 27 mg/dL, creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, glucose 130 mg/dL. Lactate 3.2 mmol/L (1.5 mmol/L two hours later). Urinalysis: 2+ blood, +nitrites, 3+ leukocyte esterase, >50 WBCs, 3+ bacteria, 25–50 RBCs. C-reactive protein 7.1 mg/dL (0.0–0.8 mg/dL). The remainder of the laboratory evaluation was unremarkable.

A 65-year-old man with hypertension and type II diabetes mellitus presented with sudden interscapular pain followed by motor weakness in his left arm and leg. He was not taking antiplatelet or anticoagulant medications and had no history of trauma. Earlier that day he had performed repetitive deep bows at a funeral ceremony. At a local hospital, noncontrast brain CT was unremarkable, and he was treated with thrombolytic therapy for presumed acute cerebral infarction. His left-sided weakness worsened, and on transfer, diffusion-weighted brain MRI showed no acute infarction. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, coagulation profile, and chemistry panel, were within normal limits. Cervical spine MRI revealed a longitudinal epidural collection extending from C2 to C6, causing compression of the spinal cord.

A 40-year-old African-American woman presented with a 3-year history of worsening headaches, episodes of altered awareness, fatigue, back and neck pain, and progressive visual loss. The headaches were initially thought to be migrainous but did not improve with treatment. Visual acuity was 20/300 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye, and an MRI of the brain showed bilateral optic nerve enhancement. A biopsy of the sclera, optic nerve sheath, and lacrimal gland was non-diagnostic. Initial chest CT and serum ACE levels were normal. Lumbar puncture revealed 9 white cells per microliter, protein 86 mg/dL, glucose 37 mg/dL, positive oligoclonal bands, and normal CSF ACE; cytology was negative. Daily prednisone (60 mg) was started, and the patient received a one-year trial of interferon-β1a for presumed atypical multiple sclerosis, but her neurologic status continued to decline and left-eye vision worsened to 20/200. Prednisone was continued (60–80 mg every other day) and azathioprine (50–100 mg/day) was added for six months without improvement. Repeat chest CT showed grade I hilar adenopathy, and gallium scintigraphy revealed bilateral increased activity in the hilum, orbits, and mediastinum. A lung biopsy then demonstrated non-caseating granulomas, leading to a diagnosis of neurosarcoidosis. Over the next seven months, despite four intravenous steroid pulses, two cycles of cyclophosphamide, and oral cyclosporine (25 mg twice daily) in addition to prednisone, she lost all functional vision, experienced worsening headaches, severe radicular neck and back pain, migratory paresthesias, and developed complex partial seizures treated with levetiracetam. Repeat MRI showed further thickening and enhancement of the optic nerves (up to 6 mm), enlargement of the infundibulum (6 mm), and diffuse meningeal enhancement.

A 65-year-old man presented with right perineal pain that worsened when sitting and during kneeling. He reported gnawing pain radiating to the right testicle and inferior inguinal area, which over time led to difficulty maintaining a strong erection. Initially thought to have pudendal neuralgia, he underwent pelvic imaging.  
A frontal pelvic radiograph revealed a 2-cm corticated, cannulated bony protuberance attached to the right ischiopubic ramus via a pseudoarthrotic articulation and oriented toward the right perineal soft tissues.  
Subsequent pelvic MRI demonstrated an oblong cortico-spongious structure arising from the antero-inferior margin of the right ischiopubic ramus, with signal characteristics identical to adjacent bone (high T1, low T2, and low STIR); a single joint at its base; extension toward the ipsilateral corpus cavernosum insertion; hypertrophy of the right corpus cavernosum; deformation of the pubic insertion of the right adductor magnus; and no peripheral high T2 signal to suggest a cartilage cap.

A female preterm infant was delivered at 30 + 2 weeks’ gestation by cesarean section for maternal fever and fetal tachycardia. Prenatal ultrasound at 20 + 1 weeks had shown fetal bowel dilatation, microcephaly (< 5th percentile), and mild hydrops fetalis with ascites and pericardial effusion, prompting amniocentesis (results pending). Antenatal betamethasone was given seven and eight days before birth. Birth weight was 1240 g (29th percentile), length 34 cm (4th percentile), head circumference 26.5 cm (19th percentile); Apgar scores were 6, 8, and 9, and cord pH was 7.3. Continuous positive airway pressure was initiated and less-invasive surfactant was administered in the first hour.

On day 1, laboratory studies showed C-reactive protein 8 mg/dL (normal < 0.5), WBC count 24 400/µL (normal 6000–13 300), and interleukin-6 136 pg/mL (normal < 7). Chest and abdominal radiography on day 2 demonstrated markedly distended intestinal loops without free air or pneumatosis. Laparotomy revealed partial obstruction of an ileal segment by adhesions and scar tissue without perforation or malrotation; a segmental ileal resection and ileostomy were performed. Histopathology of the resected segment showed mucosal necrosis, mesenteric edema with congestion, and focal neutrophilic infiltration with endothelial proliferation.

Postoperatively, enteral nutrition was slow to establish due to recurrent liquid stools and vomiting, requiring partial parenteral nutrition and multiple dietary modifications without improvement. On day 8, a maculopapular rash developed on the thorax, face, and extremities, lasting about one week. From birth, conjugated bilirubin was elevated at 3.44 mg/dL (normal < 1.0), rising to 28.52 mg/dL by day 75. Liver enzymes peaked at AST 402 U/L (normal < 79) on day 50, ALT 115 U/L (normal < 48) on day 50, and GGT 515 U/L (normal < 200) on day 46. Sonography revealed hepatosplenomegaly, a small gallbladder with irregular wall structure, hypoplastic bile ducts, and massive ascites necessitating drainage on days 40–45.

Hematologic complications included anemia, coagulopathy, and thrombocytopenia requiring multiple transfusions, and ultrasound on day 33 demonstrated thrombi in the left subclavian vein and inferior vena cava treated with enoxaparin and antithrombin III. Despite recurrent elevations of CRP and multiple courses of broad-spectrum antibiotics, blood cultures remained sterile.

A 55-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder (on lithium for 10 years), hyperlipidemia, and a stroke 3 months earlier (with right-sided residual weakness) was transferred from his nursing home to the emergency department because of altered mental status and syncope. On examination, he was somnolent, disoriented, and had dry oral mucous membranes with reduced skin turgor. He had persistent right-sided weakness from his prior stroke; the remainder of the cardiac and respiratory examinations was unremarkable.

Initial laboratory studies showed:
• Serum sodium 157 mmol/L, chloride 119 mmol/L  
• Serum calcium 14.3 mg/dL (ionized calcium 1.71 mmol/L)  
• Serum creatinine 2.25 mg/dL  
• Leukocyte count 15.85×10^9/L, creatine kinase 203 U/L  
Urinalysis revealed WBC esterase, 6–10 white blood cells, and hyaline casts. His serum lithium level on admission was within the therapeutic range, and prior levels had often been subtherapeutic. A renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis, and head CT was normal. Serum and urine protein electrophoreses were unremarkable. 

The patient received intravenous fluids, with improvement of creatinine toward baseline. Calcium-lowering therapy (calcitonin and zoledronic acid) was initiated, but serum sodium remained elevated. He required 5% dextrose infusion for hypernatremia, and he continued to have polyuria, with urine outputs of 4–6 L per day despite poor oral intake and an estimated free-water deficit of 6 L.

A 57-year-old man, previously healthy and physically active, presented with sharp, non-radiating low back pain of 1 week’s duration after minor weight lifting. He denied fever, chills, or recent travel. He had no radicular symptoms. Physical examination showed localized tenderness over the lower lumbar spine. Neurologic examination was normal with intact strength, sensation, and reflexes in both legs. Laboratory studies, including CBC, CRP, and Brucella serology, were sent.

Given persistent pain despite NSAIDs and absence of neurologic deficits, an MRI of the lumbar spine was obtained. On post-contrast MRI, there was a 2.5 × 2 × 2 cm nodular lesion within the right psoas muscle at the L3–L4 level, surrounded by moderate edema and demonstrating rim enhancement, raising concern for a psoas abscess.

Seven days later, CT-guided aspiration was performed; no material was obtained, and cultures of lavage fluid showed no growth. CBC and CRP remained within normal limits. The patient continued NSAIDs with close clinical monitoring.

An 18-year-old woman with a history of Graves’ disease treated with methimazole presented with sharp chest pain at rest, radiating to the left arm and trapezius ridge. The pain was relieved by sitting up and leaning forward and worsened when supine, with deep inspiration, or coughing. She denied fever, respiratory symptoms, or recent systemic illness. 

On examination, blood pressure was 141/63 mmHg and temperature 36.5 °C. Heart sounds were normal without friction rub; there was no jugular venous distension or pulsus paradoxus. 

Electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia at 128 b.p.m. and diffuse, concave ST-segment elevations with PR-segment depression in all leads except aVR and V1. Laboratory tests revealed normal cardiac markers, D-dimer, complete blood count, C-reactive protein, and procalcitonin. Thyroid‐stimulating hormone was suppressed (< 0.0008 mIU/L) and free thyroxine 4 was elevated (61.24 pg/mL); methimazole was increased and propranolol was initiated. 

Autoimmune serologies—including antinuclear antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, ANCA, AMA, ENA, anti–smooth muscle, and anti–topoisomerase I antibodies—were all negative. Viral studies for SARS-CoV-2, Epstein–Barr virus, HIV, hepatitis C, enterovirus, Parvovirus B19, and adenovirus were negative. 

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a normal left ventricular ejection fraction (65%) and no pericardial effusion. A non-ECG-gated CT angiogram excluded acute aortic or pulmonary disease and showed a pericardial effusion with slightly increased density (maximum thickness 15 mm) in the upper mediastinum. 

Cardiac MRI with gadolinium revealed a 73 × 51 mm extrapericardial mass in the upper mediastinum, with a minimal adjacent pericardial effusion but no pericardial infiltration, late gadolinium enhancement, or surrounding lymphadenopathy.

A 55-year-old man presented in April 2020 with sudden-onset, left-anterior chest pain of 4 hours’ duration. The pain was 5/10, radiated to the left arm, and was not accompanied by dyspnea. He also reported a 2-week history of dry cough and fever. He is a police officer; two coworkers tested positive for SARS-CoV-2.

His medical history is notable for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease status post–percutaneous coronary intervention with a drug-eluting stent in 2005 and quadruple coronary artery bypass grafting in 2008, untreated type II diabetes mellitus, and polycythemia.

On presentation, he was diaphoretic; heart rate was 100 bpm, blood pressure 148/100 mm Hg, and he was hypoxic on room air. Initial laboratory testing showed a cardiac troponin I level of 0.02 ng/L (reference < 19 ng/L). Reverse transcription–polymerase chain reaction testing for SARS-CoV-2 was positive.

Chest radiography demonstrated severe diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates with air bronchograms. Electrocardiogram showed acute inferolateral ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction with ST-segment depression in leads V1 and V2.

A 4-month-old male presented with a 4-day history of fever (maximum 39 °C). He was not in respiratory distress (respiratory rate 35/min, heart rate regular). He had no vomiting, loss of consciousness, or convulsions. On exam he appeared ill and hypoactive; later he developed abdominal distension and a rigid abdomen. A septic workup was performed. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was turbid with WBC 1200/mm3 (normal < 8), glucose 40 mg/dL (50 – 80), and protein 210 mg/dL (15 – 45), leading to an initial diagnosis of bacterial meningitis; he received ampicillin and gentamicin for 7 days. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis (WBC 15.8 ×10^3/µL; normal 6 – 14), neutrophils 56% (54 – 62%), platelets 250 ×10^3/µL (150 – 450), and hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL (10.5 – 14). Abdominal ultrasound revealed a distended appendix measuring 8 mm with surrounding fat stranding. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a mural-enhanced subhepatic inflamed appendix with inflamed mesenteric fat and surrounding fluid.

A 1.5-year-old boy was admitted with a 4-day history of fever, diarrhea, and vomiting. On the first hospital day he had a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. On hospital day 4 his level of consciousness declined and he was transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit. He is the first child of a healthy family and resides in a village. His past history was notable only for pneumonia at 6 months of age; there was a family history of febrile seizures. He was initially treated with ceftriaxone, vancomycin, phenytoin, and acyclovir. 

On examination he appeared toxic. Temperature was 39.0°C, heart rate 160 beats/min, respiratory rate 45 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Glasgow Coma Scale was 8. The abdomen was soft but there was mild tenderness in the right lower quadrant; rectal examination was unremarkable. 

Initial laboratory studies showed normal electrolytes, blood gases, coagulation profile, and liver and kidney function. Peripheral white-cell count was 1100 per cubic millimeter with 49.9% neutrophils, 40.1% lymphocytes, and 13% band forms; hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL; platelet count 45,000 per cubic millimeter; erythrocyte sedimentation rate 74 mm/hr; C-reactive protein positive. He also had hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia. He was managed for presumed sepsis with aggressive fluid resuscitation and broad-spectrum antibiotics (meropenem and vancomycin).

During his ICU stay he developed bilious gastric drainage, episodes of bloody diarrhea, and progressive abdominal distension. An abdominal ultrasound was obtained to evaluate for obstructive processes versus intra-abdominal pathology.

A 74-year-old man with hypertension presented with 4 days of low-grade fever and 2 days of severe global headache. He had anomic aphasia but no vomiting, seizures, or focal deficits. He had no history of immunosuppression, freshwater exposure, or recent travel. Initial treatment included intravenous ceftriaxone and dexamethasone. On day 4, brain MRI showed a left temporal-lobe lesion that was T1 hypointense, T2 hyperintense with microhemorrhages, suggestive of hemorrhagic encephalitis. Intravenous acyclovir (10 mg/kg three times daily) and phenytoin were started, and dexamethasone was stopped. CSF analysis showed 95 cells/mm3 (86% lymphocytes), protein 100 mg/dL, glucose 132 mg/dL; Gram, AFB, KOH stains and PCRs for HSV and TB were negative; ADA was low. That day, he developed altered sensorium and agitation. Over the next 5 days, he developed bilateral lower-limb weakness and truncal weakness; repeat MRI showed enlargement of the temporal lesion with confluent hemorrhage and increased edema. Dexamethasone was restarted, producing rapid improvement in strength, but his sensorium continued to fluctuate. A second CSF was obtained. Because of persistent non-improvement, empirical antitubercular therapy and meropenem were initiated. Over the following week, he improved and was discharged after completing 21 days of acyclovir and 14 days of meropenem. Apart from anomic aphasia, he was neurologically stable and was managed for intermittent hypertension and headache. Ten days later, he developed vomiting (one episode of hematemesis) and returned with agitation and altered sensorium. Repeat MRI showed further enlargement of the left temporal lesion and a new right high-parietal lesion. His Glasgow Coma Scale deteriorated to E1M5V1, and he was electively intubated.

A 28-year-old man presented with 2 months of progressively worsening dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and bilateral leg swelling. He also reported a 2-week history of cough productive of whitish, frothy sputum. There was no fever, facial swelling, or reduction in urine output, and no history of recurrent sore throats. He denied hypertension or diabetes. He consumed approximately 120 g of alcohol daily for 5 years and did not smoke.

On examination, he was dyspneic and cyanotic (respiratory rate 30/min, SpO₂ 78% on room air). Pulse was 110/min and regular; blood pressure was 110/60 mmHg. He had bilateral pitting edema to the knees and jugular venous pressure elevated to the angle of the jaw. The apex beat was heaving and displaced to the 7th left intercostal space, anterior axillary line. A left parasternal heave and palpable P₂ were present. Auscultation revealed an S₃, a grade 3/6 pansystolic murmur at both the mitral and tricuspid areas, a systolic ejection murmur in the pulmonary area, a widely split and fixed S₂, and a loud P₂. Bibasal fine crackles were heard. The abdomen showed tender, soft, pulsatile hepatomegaly with ascites. Other findings were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies demonstrated mild elevation of total and conjugated bilirubin; liver enzymes, glucose, renal function, complete blood count, clotting profile, lipid profile, and serologies for hepatitis B, C, and HIV were normal. Chest radiography showed plethoric lung fields, a prominent pulmonary conus, and cardiomegaly with a cardiothoracic ratio of 0.80. ECG revealed left atrial enlargement, right ventricular hypertrophy, and incomplete right bundle branch block.

Transthoracic echocardiography showed:
• A large ostium secundum atrial septal defect measuring 27 mm with left-to-right shunt  
• Mild mitral stenosis (mitral valve area 3.0 cm² by planimetry and 2.4 cm² by pressure half-time; mean gradient 0.74 cm²) with thickened, partly calcified leaflets and uniformly restricted motion, plus bicommissural calcification  
• Severe mitral and tricuspid regurgitation and moderate pulmonary regurgitation  
• Pulmonary hypertension (estimated mean pulmonary arterial pressure 51 mmHg)  
• Preserved left ventricular systolic function (ejection fraction 67%) and impaired right ventricular systolic function (TAPSE 15 mm)  
• Biventricular diastolic dysfunction, dilated right ventricle, left and right atria, and spontaneous echo contrast in all chambers

A 71-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of worsening cough, anorexia, and exertional dyspnea. He had no history of asthma or atopic disease. He lived in an unsanitary environment with moldy food, had a 35-pack-year past smoking history (quit at age 55), and no known sick contacts.  
On examination: temperature 37.4 °C; oxygen saturation 89% on room air.  
Laboratory studies: WBC 17,000 cells/μL with 26.6% eosinophils (4500 cells/μL), CRP 8.0 mg/dL, IgE 180 IU/mL; negative specific IgE to common molds; negative myeloperoxidase- and proteinase 3-ANCA.  
Pulmonary function tests: VC 73.4% predicted, FEV1% 73.0%.  
Chest CT: consolidation and heterogeneous ground-glass opacities with multiple cystic lesions, predominantly in the left lung.  
Bronchoalveolar lavage from left B5 showed 95% eosinophils; cultures negative.  
Transbronchial lung biopsy demonstrated eosinophilic infiltration of alveolar spaces and walls, mild interstitial fibrosis, and intraluminal organization.  
Video-assisted thoracic surgery biopsy revealed diffuse eosinophilic infiltration and massive exudation into airspaces with numerous tiny eosinophilic abscesses; lung architecture was largely preserved; no evidence of vasculitis.

A 68-year-old woman presented with a sudden, temporary loss of vision in her left eye 1 day earlier. She described a “black window shade” pulled over the bottom half of her vision while reading; the episode lasted approximately 1 minute and resolved spontaneously. She denied chest pain, palpitations, headache, flashes, floaters, or recent illness. Her medical history included rheumatoid arthritis and migraines without aura; she took low-dose aspirin daily. She had an uncomplicated cataract extraction in both eyes 2 years ago. Family history was notable for cardiovascular disease but no personal history of atrial fibrillation or glaucoma. She did not smoke and drank alcohol socially.

On examination, blood pressure was 140/80 mmHg and pulse was 80 beats per minute, regular. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25+2 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left. Pupils were equal and reactive without an afferent pupillary defect. Extraocular movements and confrontational visual fields were full. Intraocular pressures were 14 mmHg bilaterally. Slit-lamp examination revealed dry eyes and well-positioned posterior chamber intraocular lenses. Fundoscopic examination showed clear vitreous, sharp optic discs with cup-to-disc ratios of 0.2 bilaterally, and normal maculae, vessels, and retinal periphery without Hollenhorst plaques or occluded vessels. Carotid auscultation revealed no bruits.

A differential diagnosis of amaurosis fugax, transient ischemic attack (TIA), atrial fibrillation, papilledema, and migraine was considered. The patient had no cardiac abnormalities at presentation or in her history, so attention turned to vascular causes. Given the history of a brief, monocular vision loss without headache, postural changes, or exertion and a normal optic disc appearance, amaurosis fugax due to retinal hypoperfusion was deemed most likely. To search for an embolic source, CT angiography with three-dimensional reconstructions of the aortic arch, great vessels, cervical vessels, and intracranial vessels was performed.

A 52-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes (HbA1c 9.7%) and hypertension presented with a 3-month history of pain in the upper right posterior teeth. During the past month, he experienced spontaneous loosening and loss of multiple teeth and noted watery nasal discharge when drinking. He had a self-limited febrile illness one month earlier, for which he was not tested for COVID-19. He also had a 15-year history of betel leaf and tobacco chewing.

On extraoral examination, there was mild left-sided facial asymmetry without tenderness and right-sided facial paresthesia. Intraoral examination revealed extensive necrotic bone from tooth regions 13 to 18 with pus discharge, an oroantral communication with watery discharge, and multiple pseudomembranous, scrapable areas on the buccal mucosa, tongue, and soft palate. Panoramic radiography demonstrated significant erosion of the right maxilla with loss of dentition. CT imaging showed necrosis of the bilateral palate, maxillary alveolus, and the right zygomatic body. A provisional diagnosis of fungal osteomyelitis of the maxilla was made, with actinomycosis and aspergillosis included as differential diagnoses. An incisional biopsy was performed.

A 48-year-old man with squamous cell carcinoma of the maxilla and no history of diabetes presented with sudden-onset left-sided facial paralysis. He had completed 6 weeks of radiotherapy (total dose 67.5 Gy) with four weekly doses of cisplatin; symptoms began 33 days after the final chemoradiation session. On examination, he had asymmetric facial muscle tone with inability to close the left eye and an asymmetric smile. Two days after onset, laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 4.43 × 10^3/µL, a glucose level of 89 mg/dL, and an hs-CRP of 0.37 mg/dL, with no signs of acute viral infection or diabetes. Six days after symptom onset, MRI of the head demonstrated marked reduction in the known maxillary carcinoma but showed increased swelling at the orifice of the left Eustachian tube, with severe mastoiditis and otitis media.

A 67-year-old single Caucasian woman with no prior psychiatric history was followed for major depressive disorder with psychotic features from January 2016 onward. She initially responded to citalopram but, in May 2016, was hospitalized for worsening depressive symptoms, nonspecific fears, weight loss, irritability, anhedonia, and lack of energy. In the hospital, she developed persecutory delusions and was treated sequentially with clomipramine and olanzapine, then risperidone, without symptom remission. After 14 sessions of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), she improved and was discharged on clomipramine 225 mg daily and risperidone 6 mg daily.

In November 2016, she was readmitted for recurrent mood worsening and psychotic symptoms; 21 sessions of ECT were discontinued for lack of response, and lithium 400 mg daily plus quetiapine 100 mg daily were added to risperidone. On March 10, 2017, parkinsonian gait and bradykinesia prompted discontinuation of risperidone. Twelve days later, she developed fever up to 38°C, diaphoresis, tachycardia (105 bpm), hypertension (195/115 mmHg), and leukocytosis (16 100 WBC/µL). Examination revealed stiffness of the extremities, poverty of speech, stupor, mutism, negativism, and mannerism. A cranial computed tomography scan, a lumbar puncture, and blood tests were performed, without revealing any abnormality.

A 70-year-old man with persistent atrial fibrillation refractory to drugs underwent radiofrequency catheter ablation with pulmonary vein isolation, roof and bottom lines in the left atrium, and cavo-tricuspid isthmus ablation. Preprocedure CT angiography of the pulmonary veins was normal. Baseline echocardiography showed an ejection fraction of 56%, left atrial diameter 40 mm, a calcified aortic valve, and mild mitral and tricuspid regurgitation.

He was discharged on rivaroxaban and remained in sinus rhythm. On postablation day 5 he developed progressive dyspnea, fatigue, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea without fever. Heart rate was < 110 bpm. Examination revealed a pansystolic murmur at the left sternal border and decreased breath sounds at the lung bases.

Labs showed normal leukocyte and neutrophil counts but 79.6% neutrophils, ESR 18 mm/h (0–15), CRP 13.8 mg/L (0–6), IL-6 126.6 pg/mL (0–7), NT-proBNP 2200 ng/L (0–125), and negative high-sensitivity troponin T. Oxygen saturation was normal.

ECG in sinus rhythm demonstrated increased P-wave amplitude in V1–V4, PR-segment depression, and ST-segment elevation. CT angiography revealed no pulmonary embolism and no pulmonary vein stenosis; chest CT showed bilateral patchy flocculent densities in the right lower lobe, small pleural effusions, and localized pericardial thickening. Echocardiography revealed EF 53%, severe TR (max gradient 75 mmHg), severe PAH (est. 85 mmHg), and mild pericardial effusion. Tuberculosis spot test and autoimmune panel were negative.

Tumor, tuberculosis, autoimmune disease, acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary vein stenosis, and pulmonary embolism were excluded. He was treated for acute heart failure with diuretics, vasodilators, and anticoagulation, but symptoms and severe PAH with TR persisted, and the cause remained unexplained.

A 49-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of persistent weight gain and central obesity. Her history included hypertension, prediabetes, dyslipidemia, and biopsy-confirmed nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (80% diffuse steatosis with pericellular inflammation).

Two years earlier, an abdominal CT scan performed for nephrolithiasis had revealed a left adrenal adenoma. At that time and on current examination, she had no phenotypic features of Cushing syndrome (no moon facies, purple striae, or dorsocervical fat pad).

A follow-up noncontrast CT showed a stable, lobulated left adrenal mass measuring 2.9 × 1.9 × 2.5 cm with an attenuation of 14 Hounsfield units and high fat content.

Laboratory evaluation included negative studies for pheochromocytoma and primary aldosteronism. Testing for cortisol excess revealed mildly elevated urinary free cortisol levels, failure to suppress cortisol on multiple 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression tests, elevated late-night salivary cortisol, suppressed adrenocorticotropic hormone levels on repeated assays, and low dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate.

A 66-year-old African-American man with a 4-year history of metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma presented with a 1-week history of bilateral lower extremity weakness, lethargy, several falls, hyperthermia, confusion, and gait abnormalities. His cancer history included a partial nephrectomy for papillary RCC with clear cell component, excisional biopsy confirming metastatic CCRCC, treatment with pazopanib and sunitinib, and ultimately a left radical nephrectomy. A positive QuantiFERON TB Gold test had excluded him from earlier immunotherapy trials. He then received seven cycles of nivolumab (240 mg) without prior complications.

On this admission, he became hypothermic, was transferred to the ICU, and required endotracheal intubation. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a lymphocytic pleocytosis (white blood cell count 27/mm3, 78% lymphocytes; protein 70 mg/dL). CSF virus culture and Gram stain showed no growth; a CSF pathogen panel and cryptococcal antigen were negative. Blood cultures and AFB smear were negative. Brain MRI demonstrated diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement and a 1.7 × 1.0 × 1.0 cm focus of T1-hypointensity at the midbrain–pons junction that had been stable for four years. A CSF MTB PCR test was negative.

A two-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of progressive, bilateral, painless swelling of the jaws over several months. On examination, he had symmetrical enlargement of the mandible and maxilla with intact, bluish-gray oral mucosa. Vital signs were normal, there was no lymphadenopathy, and routine hematologic tests were unremarkable. Panoramic radiography revealed well-defined, multilocular radiolucent areas involving the mandibular bodies, angles, ascending rami, and the maxillary tuberosities. Computed tomography of the jaws showed bilateral, expansile, multilocular lesions with thinning of the cortical plates of the maxilla and mandible, mild anterior displacement of an unerupted first molar, and no cortical breaches or soft-tissue extension.

A 65-year-old woman was admitted with a 3-day history of progressive shortness of breath at rest and on exertion, productive cough, and fever to 103°F. She had no history of asthma, COPD, or smoking. Her medical history was notable for coronary bypass grafting, ascending aortic aneurysm repair, and bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement one year earlier, complicated by MRSA sternal osteomyelitis and mediastinitis requiring debridement. She completed a 6-week course of vancomycin but had recurrent MRSA bacteremia; antibiotic susceptibilities showed a vancomycin MIC of 2 µg/mL and a ceftaroline MIC of 0.5 µg/mL. Five weeks into a planned 6-week course of intravenous ceftaroline (600 mg every 12 h), she developed her current respiratory symptoms.

On examination, she was dyspneic, tachypneic, and orthopneic. Diffuse inspiratory crackles were present throughout both lung fields. Arterial blood gas on 8 L nasal cannula showed a PaO₂ of 64.8 mmHg. She was transitioned to high-flow nasal oxygen, improving O₂ saturation to 98%. Laboratory tests revealed a leukocyte count of 23,000/mm³ with an absolute eosinophil count of 3,200/mm³; renal and hepatic panels and serum procalcitonin were normal. Chest radiography showed bilateral multifocal infiltrates. CT of the chest demonstrated extensive bilateral pulmonary infiltrates without pulmonary embolism.

Ceftaroline was discontinued; linezolid was started and levofloxacin was added for empiric coverage of Pseudomonas and atypical pathogens. Nasopharyngeal PCR for influenza A and B and a multiplex respiratory virus panel were negative. Sputum cultures showed no growth, sputum Legionella culture and urine Legionella antigen were negative, and urine pneumococcal antigen was negative. Levofloxacin was then discontinued. HIV serology was nonreactive. There was no history of environmental or allergen exposure, parasitic risk factors, or clinical evidence of autoimmune disease.

A 49-year-old Hispanic man with essential hypertension and a remote history of treated syphilis presented with 1 week of severe, dull right upper quadrant abdominal pain rated 6–7/10, persistent and nonradiating. He reported progressive jaundice, dark urine, fatigue, nausea, and anorexia. He denied fevers, rashes, other medications, alcohol use, illicit drugs, tattoos, transfusions, or toxin exposures. On examination, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. He had icteric sclerae and generalized jaundice without rash and was alert and oriented. Laboratory tests showed AST 1280 U/L, ALT 1652 U/L, ALP 147 U/L, total bilirubin 19.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 15.5 mg/dL, and INR 1.6. Platelets were 100 × 10^9/L, with otherwise normal blood count and metabolic panel. Abdominal ultrasound and MRCP demonstrated normal liver size, no steatosis, no bile duct dilatation, mild splenomegaly, and no masses. Viral hepatitis panel showed immunity to hepatitis B with undetectable HBV DNA; HSV1/2 IgM, CMV IgM, EBV IgM, and HIV tests were negative (HSV2 IgG positive). An autoimmune panel was positive only for ANA (1:80). Ceruloplasmin and iron studies were normal. Serologic tests for syphilis—rapid plasma reagin and fluorescent treponemal antibody-absorption—were reactive.

A 26-year-old woman presented with two hyperkeratotic prominences on the lateral surfaces of the main nail of each fifth toe. These small accessory nails had arisen during childhood, grew at the same rate as her normal nails, caused mild pain when walking, and were cosmetically distressing. Her medical history included epilepsy and paroxysmal tachycardia. There was no history of trauma to the feet. Three other female relatives (her sister, her mother, and her niece) had the same finding since early childhood. 

On examination, each accessory nail was 3–6 mm in diameter at the base and 4–7 mm long, grayish-yellow, and separated from the main nail by a vertical groove extending from the cuticle to the hyponychium; the perionychium was normal. Dermoscopy of an accessory nail showed a proximal nail fold, lateral nail fold, hyponychium, and transverse bands reminiscent of barrel staves. A silicone cast scanned by electron microscopy revealed a stumpy nail with a wrinkled surface. Ultrasonography of the right fifth toe demonstrated two distinct nail plates and two matrices: a main central matrix and a smaller lateral matrix appearing as a hypoechoic area connected by an isthmus to the primary matrix. Karyotype analysis was normal, and radiographs of the feet and distal phalanges showed no bony abnormalities.

A 63-year-old man with metastatic EGFR-L858R–positive non–small-cell lung adenocarcinoma, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and prior light tobacco use presented after four months of first-line osimertinib therapy. Pre-treatment echocardiography showed a normal LVEF (65%) and a small pericardial effusion. During therapy, he remained asymptomatic despite a large, free-flowing pericardial effusion. Four weeks after declining elective drainage, he developed progressive dyspnea, abdominal distension, and weight gain, and underwent emergent pericardiocentesis with removal of 1.1 L of serosanguinous fluid. The following day he reported new-onset orthopnea. On examination, blood pressure was 90/68 mmHg, heart rate 125 bpm, jugular venous pressure was 13 cm H₂O, and he had bilateral crackles. Furosemide was initiated. After clamping of the pericardial drain, limited transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a small-to-moderate pericardial effusion and newly reduced biventricular function with an LVEF of 30–35%, with akinesis of the mid-left ventricle and anteroseptal wall motion abnormality. Initial troponin was 1.4 µg/L, peaking at 2.2 µg/L six hours later, and brain natriuretic peptide was 666 pg/mL. Coronary angiography showed mild, non-obstructive coronary artery disease and an elevated left ventricular end-diastolic pressure of 17 mmHg.

A 26-year-old previously healthy woman presented with a 2-year history of cyclic right hip pain without a history of trauma. She had a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device placed 3 years earlier, resulting in light, irregular menstrual periods. Physical examination of the pelvis and right lower extremity was unremarkable. Symptoms persisted despite 12 months of over-the-counter analgesics, muscle relaxants, and physical therapy.

Over time, she developed peripheral neuropathic symptoms, including right foot and lateral thigh weakness and paresthesia. MRI of the right hip revealed an ill-defined T1 isointense, T2 hypointense lesion in the right sciatic notch with gadolinium enhancement and mild increased signal on fat-saturated T1 images. Surrounding this lesion was diffuse intramuscular edema and atrophy of the right piriformis, gluteal, and quadratus femoris muscles; the sciatic nerve was not well visualized. Foci of T2* gradient-echo hypointense signal suggested mineralization. These findings were initially interpreted as post-traumatic denervation of the sciatic nerve with possible myositis ossificans, and desmoid tumor was also considered.

Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a heterogeneously enhancing mass-like density involving the same musculature, with faint hypodense foci thought to represent mineralization versus hemorrhagic products. Electromyography showed a right L5–S1 plexopathy.

A 62‐year‐old woman with a 1‐year history of stage IVB lung adenocarcinoma (EGFR L858R) treated with gefitinib presented with progressive dyspnea and bilateral upper‐extremity edema. Although her pulmonary and metastatic lesions had markedly regressed on therapy, she continued to have bilateral pleural effusions. Vital signs were: T 37.4 °C, HR 85 bpm, BP 110/60 mmHg, RR 24/min, SpO₂ 94% on room air. Examination showed bilateral upper‐extremity pitting edema, dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds over both lung fields, and digital clubbing. Laboratory results revealed WBC 8820/mm³ with left shift, Hb 12.4 g/dL, platelets 182 000/mm³, LDH 204 U/L, AST/ALT 18/11 U/L, albumin 3.1 g/dL, BUN 19 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, CRP 0.24 mg/dL, BNP 6.1 pg/mL, and normal TSH and free T4. Her CEA had declined from 931.7 to 20.3 ng/mL. Chest radiography showed massive bilateral effusions, larger on the right. ECG and echocardiography were unremarkable. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the chest revealed thrombosis extending from the superior vena cava to the left brachiocephalic and subclavian veins, confirmed by Doppler ultrasonography. Anticoagulation with heparin and warfarin was initiated, and thoracenteses were performed every 4–5 days. All pleural fluid samples were lymphocyte‐predominant transudates with negative cytology and microbiology, and the effusions persisted despite therapy.

A 35-year-old woman from southern Ethiopia presented with one day of intermittent, colicky right upper–quadrant abdominal pain associated with anorexia and nausea but no fever or vomiting. On examination, vital signs were normal, scleral icterus was present, and there was tenderness in the right hypochondriac region. Laboratory studies showed neutrophilic leukocytosis, conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and elevated alanine transaminase. Stool microscopy revealed ova of Ascaris lumbricoides. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated worms in the distal common bile duct with partial obstruction, a dilated gallbladder, and dilation of the right and left hepatic ducts.

A 78-year-old woman presented for evaluation of a newly identified pelvic mass. Three years earlier, she had undergone an extended right hepatic lobectomy and biliary reconstruction for hilar cholangiocarcinoma, followed by one year of adjuvant S-1 chemotherapy. She had been monitored with blood tests every 3 months and contrast-enhanced abdominal CT every 6 months.  

On routine follow-up, her carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) level had risen to 10.6 ng/mL (reference range, 0.1–5.0 ng/mL), whereas her carbohydrate antigen 19-9 level was 16.0 U/mL (reference range, <37.0 U/mL). She denied abdominal pain, fever, or other new symptoms. Vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed no abdominal tenderness. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 6200/μL, and a C-reactive protein level of 0.06 mg/dL.  

Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 37 × 30 mm irregular mass with a heterogeneous contrast enhancement and a partial liquid component in the right lateral pelvis, appearing to infiltrate adjacent ileum. Colonoscopy revealed a raised lesion at the appendiceal orifice; biopsy specimens showed no evidence of malignancy. At this point, disseminated recurrence of hilar cholangiocarcinoma and a newly emergent appendiceal carcinoma were suspected, and diagnostic laparoscopy was planned to establish a definitive diagnosis.

A 27-year-old Hispanic woman presented with sudden-onset shortness of breath and increased difficulty moving her right arm. Over the preceding two months she had noted progressive right-arm weakness with limited strength and range of motion. On the evening before admission, while lying down, she developed acute shortness of breath, worsening right-arm weakness, and substernal chest pressure described as non-radiating, with associated nausea, palpitations, and lightheadedness. She denied headache, loss of consciousness, vomiting, diarrhea, or vertigo. Two months earlier, she had been evaluated for right-arm weakness and dysphasia; brain MRI was unremarkable, and cervical MRI showed only mild canal narrowing; she had been diagnosed with hemiplegic migraine headache. 

On examination, her vital signs were stable, and she was afebrile. She appeared anxious. Cardiac and pulmonary exams were normal. Abdominal palpation revealed a firm abdomen. The right upper extremity was rigid on active and passive movement; the fingers were clenched in a fist and recoiled to flexion after passive extension. She had mild dysarthria; cranial nerves and position sense were intact. Muscle strength was 5/5 globally, with pain on testing the right hand; deep tendon reflexes were 1+ throughout.

Initial routine laboratory tests and chest radiography were unremarkable. A computed tomography angiogram of the chest was negative for pulmonary embolism. Cardiac stress testing and serial troponins were negative. A psychiatric consultation ruled out factitious disorder, conversion disorder, malingering, and adjustment disorder. Neurology was consulted because her presentation was atypical for hemiplegic migraine. To evaluate a possible vascular cause, magnetic resonance angiography of the neck (with and without contrast), two brain MRIs (with and without contrast), head MRA without contrast, and head CT angiography were obtained; these studies revealed no explanation for her right-arm spasticity but did show incidental intracranial findings. 

Coagulation studies—including protein C and S levels, factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation, antiphospholipid antibodies, antithrombin III, and fibrinogen—were all within normal limits. Rheumatologic tests—erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and rheumatoid factor—were normal. Autoimmune serologies revealed an anti–double-stranded DNA level slightly above normal and a positive antinuclear antibody titer of 1:320 (speckled).

A 15-year-old girl presented with irregular teeth, nasal obstruction, and an unaesthetic facial appearance. She was referred for correction of her malocclusion before planned rhinoplasty. Her medical and natal history was unremarkable except for delayed developmental milestones, and there was no consanguinity. Her mother (45 years) had similar facial features; the elder sister was unaffected. There was no history of birth trauma or prenatal exposure to warfarin, alcohol, or phenytoin. The patient had normal intelligence, no hearing or olfactory loss, and normal menarche and hormonal profiles.

On examination, both patient and mother had a small narrow face with a concave profile from midfacial hypoplasia, hypertelorism, flattened nasal bridge, short columella, wide alar wings, a flattened nasal tip, an acute nasolabial angle, and a wide frontonasal angle. Nostrils were triangular on basal view. The upper lip was slightly everted with a short philtrum. On tongue protrusion, there was a central groove and heart-shaped tip, consistent with moderate ankyloglossia, but no feeding or speech difficulties other than a nasal twang.

Intraorally, multiple deciduous teeth were retained; there was a high-arched V-shaped palate, rotated malposed upper incisors, and several missing permanent teeth. A panoramic radiograph confirmed retained deciduous teeth, malposed and impacted teeth, and missing maxillary lateral incisors. There were no other skeletal, digital, or cervical abnormalities.

A 64-year-old man from Northern Morocco with poorly controlled diabetes presented with 8 months of progressive dyspnea, pericarditis-like chest pain, night fevers, sweats, asthenia, and 10% weight loss. On examination, he was afebrile, blood pressure 117/63 mm Hg, heart rate 82 beats/min, respiratory rate 17/min, O₂ saturation 99% on room air. Signs of right heart failure included jugular venous distension, hepatomegaly, moderate ascites, and bilateral lower extremity edema. ECG showed low QRS voltage in peripheral leads and negative T waves from V1 to V6. Laboratory studies revealed cholestatic liver enzyme elevations (alkaline phosphatase 314 U/L, GGT 161 U/L, total bilirubin 36 mmol/L), negative sputum AFB, positive Quantiferon (TB1-Nil and TB2-Nil >0.35 IU/L), and elevated CA-125 at 1325 U/mL. Full blood count, renal function, and other liver tests were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated pericardial thickening around both ventricles, a septal bounce, moderate tricuspid regurgitation, significant respiratory variation in transvalvular flows, and preserved biventricular systolic function. Chest CT showed pericardial thickening of 17 mm. Cardiac MRI confirmed pericardial thickening and revealed pericardial calcifications, particularly adjacent to the right ventricle.

A 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 11.2%) presented with a one-week history of worsening right hand pain, swelling, and erythema, most prominent in the distal palm. Two weeks earlier, a concrete bench had fallen on the dorsal base of his right fourth digit without skin break; over the following week, he noted a bruise at that site. On examination, there was a 1.5-cm painful, fluctuant mass extending from the palmar web space to the A2 pulley of the fourth digit, with focal tenderness over the flexor sheath and limited active digit motion. He was afebrile; WBC count was 17.5 × 10^9/L.
