Plain radiographs of the right hand showed diffuse soft-tissue swelling throughout the palm and into the distal interphalangeal joints of the third and fourth digits with intact bony anatomy and no fracture or dislocation.

A 50-year-old man with no history of cardiovascular disease and no medications experienced a witnessed out-of-hospital collapse. Bystander CPR was started immediately, and EMS found him pulseless in ventricular fibrillation. After 2 minutes of CPR and one defibrillation, he achieved return of spontaneous circulation (downtime ~10 min) and was intubated. In the emergency department he developed recurrent VF requiring five additional shocks and amiodarone boluses without ROSC, prompting initiation of veno-arterial ECMO; ROSC was then achieved (total downtime ~30 min). Post-ROSC ECG showed normal sinus rhythm with ST elevations in the inferior leads. Bedside transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35%. Head CT was negative for anoxic injury. Initial laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 22 200/µL, creatinine 1.41 mg/dL, troponin-I 0.04 ng/mL, lactic acid 11.5 mmol/L, and an anion gap of 19 mmol/L.

A 33-year-old previously healthy Sri Lankan woman, on postpartum day 6 after an uncomplicated elective cesarean delivery, presented with acute breathlessness (MRC dyspnoea scale grade 4) for 1 day and a nonproductive cough for 3 days. She had low-grade fever on postpartum day 1 that resolved spontaneously and was afebrile on admission. She works as a clerk whose duties include field visits to paddy fields with exposure to surface water and mud. 

On examination, BMI was 28 kg/m^2. She was afebrile, tachypneic, and in respiratory distress with occasional coarse crepitations in the right lower lung zone. Pulse was 130 beats/min, blood pressure 100/70 mmHg, and JVP was not elevated. There was mild bilateral pitting edema of the lower limbs. No organomegaly or neurological deficits were noted.

Within hours, she developed type I respiratory failure requiring intubation. Chest radiograph showed right lower lobe consolidation. ECG revealed sinus tachycardia; echocardiography showed mild to moderate pulmonary hypertension with an ejection fraction of 60%. Laboratory tests on admission: Hb 10.2 g/dl; WBC count 11 × 10^9/l (90.6% neutrophils); platelets 74,000/µl; CRP 96 mg/l; ESR 100 mm/hr; D-dimer 4.8 mg/l; normal blood sugar; blood picture consistent with sepsis. CTPA excluded pulmonary embolism; HRCT chest demonstrated bilateral ground-glass opacities with focal consolidations.

She was started on ceftriaxone and clarithromycin. By day 3, she had high-grade fevers and multilobar consolidation on chest radiograph. Abdominal ultrasound showed bilateral pyelonephritis with multiple renal abscesses. Sputum culture grew coliform species; blood and urine cultures were negative. BALF culture grew Stenotrophomonas maltophilia; BALF was negative for fungi, mycobacteria, and PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Retroviral, RPR, treponemal, influenza A/B PCR, and autoimmune panels were negative.

On day 6, she developed focal seizures, hemoglobin fell to 7.3 g/dl, platelets to 47,000/µl, and blood smear showed microangiopathic hemolytic anemia; LDH was 1240 U/l with a normal coagulation profile. NCCT brain was unremarkable. A presumptive diagnosis of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura was made and plasmapheresis initiated.

Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen revealed bilateral pyelonephritis with a 1.6 cm right upper pole renal abscess and early abscess formation in the left lower pole.

A 63-year-old woman presented with dyspepsia in February 2010. She was otherwise well but found to have a blood pressure of 150/90 mm Hg. She was started on omeprazole 20 mg once daily and lisinopril 10 mg once daily. Baseline blood tests showed a haemoglobin concentration of 13.9 g/dL, a white-cell count of 7.37 × 10^9/L (eosinophils 0.07 × 10^9/L), and platelets of 303 × 10^9/L. Shortly after starting lisinopril, she developed a dry cough, which was attributed to the medication but continued.  

By July 2010, her gastro-oesophageal reflux symptoms had worsened, and an upper endoscopy was performed. Biopsy of the oesophageal mucosa revealed marked mucosal thickening with prominent intraepithelial eosinophils forming microabscesses, without dysplasia or malignancy. A diagnosis of eosinophilic oesophagitis was made; no specific therapy was initiated.  

In November 2010, she reported anorexia, a 7-kg weight loss, generalized malaise, and ongoing dyspepsia. Serial blood tests since February showed the development of a normocytic, normochromic anaemia, a modest eosinophilia, elevated ESR and ferritin, and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia. Iron supplementation produced no haematologic response.  

In January 2011, she was referred for further evaluation. History and examination were unremarkable. A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis excluded occult malignancy and infection. Liver, renal, thyroid, and bone profiles were normal, and tissue transglutaminase antibodies were negative. The patient observed that her systemic and gastrointestinal symptoms began after starting lisinopril.

A 45-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of an abrupt onset of an asymptomatic cutaneous eruption on the neck and both forearms. The lesions began small and progressively enlarged over 5 days. He denied fever, malaise, or other constitutional symptoms, and reported no contact with cattle or sheep. He took no medications and had no significant medical history.

On examination, there were multiple papules and plaques of varying sizes on the dorsal forearms and nape of the neck, each showing a striking central depression that mimicked vesiculation; some neck lesions had an overlying crust. All lesions were firm and nontender. 

A Gram stain of fluid from one lesion was inconclusive. A punch biopsy showed no epidermal changes and revealed a dense inflammatory neutrophilic infiltrate within the dermis, marked dermal edema, and no evidence of vasculitis. 

Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 14 g/dL, a white-cell count of 13,000/mm3 with 89% neutrophils, and a normal peripheral smear. Renal and liver function tests were within normal limits. Imaging of the abdomen and pelvis was unremarkable. Urine testing for Bence–Jones protein was negative. A throat swab grew only normal flora.

A 33-year-old African American woman with D-transposition of the great vessels repaired by Mustard procedure presented with a one-month history of elevated liver enzymes. She had recurrent atypical atrial flutter treated intermittently with oral amiodarone (400 mg daily) and was also taking lisinopril, metoprolol, and warfarin. She denied alcohol use. Her medical history included hypothyroidism, anemia, and a prior pilocytic astrocytoma with stroke.

On evaluation, alanine aminotransferase was 188 U/L (reference, 5–50), aspartate aminotransferase 162 U/L (5–50), and alkaline phosphatase, total bilirubin, total protein, and albumin were normal. Antinuclear antibodies were elevated at 1:260; anti–smooth muscle and anti–mitochondrial antibodies were negative. Serum protein electrophoresis disclosed a mildly elevated beta-2 globulin fraction; quantitative immunoglobulins were within normal limits except for a slightly elevated IgA.

Abdominal ultrasonography was unremarkable. A percutaneous liver biopsy was performed. Histologic examination revealed portal tracts with minimal inflammation and a subtle ductular reaction. There were ballooned hepatocytes and Mallory-Denk bodies. Trichrome and reticulin stains showed extensive perisinusoidal fibrosis with zone 3 to 3 bridging. Notably, there was no steatosis or phospholipidosis; Periodic acid–Schiff–diastase and iron stains were negative. Electron microscopy showed no lamellar lysosomal inclusions.

A 54-year-old woman with occult anemia was scheduled for screening gastroscopy and colonoscopy under sedation. She had no known drug allergies, no significant cardiac history, and was a heavy smoker but had no other coronary risk factors. Baseline vital signs were normal (BP 112/65 mm Hg; HR 72 beats/min; RR 12/min; SpO₂ 100% on room air). Sedation was induced with meperidine 50 mg, midazolam 2 mg, and propofol 40 mg IV, with continuous monitoring and oxygen by nasal cannula.

Ten minutes into gastroscopy, she developed bradycardia (SpO₂ 97%) that progressed to asystole without any rash. She received IV lidocaine 60 mg, atropine 2 mg total, epinephrine 0.01 mg, and hydrocortisone 250 mg, with 100% face-mask ventilation. She then converted to sinus tachycardia (HR 112 beats/min) with BP 70/42 mm Hg and maintained spontaneous breathing.

A few minutes later, she regained consciousness with acute chest pain, dyspnea, pulmonary edema, and hypoxia (SpO₂ 60%). The procedure was aborted, and she was transferred to the ICU. An ECG showed no acute ST-T changes. Chest radiography revealed diffuse bilateral infiltrates. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated global hypokinesia of the left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 20–29%. Arterial blood gas analysis showed respiratory acidosis.

A 52-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a 15 pack-year smoking history, moderate alcohol use, and no significant family history presented after a presyncopal episode. He was found to have pancytopenia. Vital signs were normal and the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory testing showed a normal metabolic profile and urinalysis. Complete blood count confirmed pancytopenia; peripheral smear demonstrated a myeloid left shift with 5% blasts. Bone marrow biopsy revealed erythroid dyspoiesis, left-shifted granulopoiesis, and grade 3+ fibrosis consistent with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) with fibrosis. Genetic testing showed wild-type JAK2 and MPL, normal karyotype, absence of BCR-ABL1 translocation, and a negative MDS FISH panel. His hemoglobin was 7.8 g/dL, platelet count was 32×10⁹/L, and absolute neutrophil count was 11.3×10⁹/L, yielding a high-risk IPSS-R score. He received multiple transfusions and was treated with ruxolitinib. 

Three months later, during evaluation for bone marrow transplantation, abdominal ultrasound detected a 4 cm hypoechoic lesion in the right hepatic lobe with internal vascularity and hepatosplenomegaly (spleen 19 cm). Contrast-enhanced MRI showed diffuse hepatic iron overload. A segment 7 lesion was T1-hypointense, T2-isointense, exhibited mild heterogeneous arterial phase enhancement, and washed out to isointensity on portal venous and delayed phases. The lesion was not visible on T2*-weighted gradient-echo images or on diffusion-weighted imaging. The differential diagnosis included focal nodular hyperplasia and adenoma, with hepatocellular carcinoma being less likely and metastasis unlikely.

An 85-year-old man with severe aortic stenosis (valve area 0.8 cm², mean gradient 47 mmHg, peak gradient 91 mmHg, peak velocity 4.76 m/s), mild mitral regurgitation, moderate mitral stenosis with annular calcification, chronic anemia requiring biweekly red blood cell transfusions and monthly IV iron for recurrent small-bowel angiodysplasias, and New York Heart Association class II–III dyspnea, was awaiting transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI). He presented to a peripheral emergency department with orthopnea.  
Vital signs: blood pressure 113/54 mmHg; heart rate 93 bpm; respiratory rate 18 breaths/min; oxygen saturation 95% on 2 L/min; temperature 35.1 °C.  
Cardiac exam: late-peaking systolic murmur at the aortic area radiating to the carotids, absent S2. Pulmonary exam: bibasilar crackles. Extremities: 2+ bilateral pitting edema.  
Laboratory studies: white blood cell count 15.2 × 10⁹/L (normal 4.0–11.0), hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL (post–2 units transfused the prior day), troponin 1.610 µg/L (normal < 0.012), negative COVID-19 nasopharyngeal swab.  
Chest radiograph: bilateral patchy opacities emanating from the mediastinum and moderate bilateral pleural effusions consistent with pulmonary edema. ECG: sinus rhythm at 92 bpm, incomplete left bundle branch block, left ventricular hypertrophy, no acute ischemic changes.  
He received diuresis, bilevel airway pressure support, and empiric ceftriaxone plus azithromycin for possible community-acquired pneumonia. Both pleural effusions were drained and were transudative. He stabilized and was transferred for TAVI planning.

A 50-year-old woman (BMI 39.1 kg/m^2) with type II diabetes mellitus (on insulin and metformin) and hyperlipidaemia (on atorvastatin) presented with pain and discoloration of her left breast three days after starting warfarin 10 mg daily for newly diagnosed antiphospholipid syndrome (initial INR 1.0, target 2.5). She had been admitted previously with ischaemic changes of the toes and was otherwise asymptomatic. On examination, the left breast was swollen with darkening of the skin beginning at the nipple–areola complex and spreading centrally. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies showed: complete blood count normal; prothrombin time 22.9 s (normal 11 s) with INR 2.0; partial thromboplastin time 48 s; cardiac markers, ECG, and chest radiograph were normal. Two days after discharge with a diagnosis of bruising and ecchymosis, she returned with worsening pain, increased ecchymosis, central breast necrosis, and swelling.

A 29-year-old woman presented in autumn 2017 with fever and severe pharyngitis one week after completing a 7-day course of doxycycline prescribed for a swollen posterior auricular lymph node and subjective fever following a 3-week trip to Southeast Asia. She had received atovaquone–proguanil prophylaxis and noted multiple mosquito bites but no tick bites. Two days after returning, she developed lymphadenopathy and fever, treated with doxycycline, which transiently improved her fever but was followed by a torso rash. Three days after finishing doxycycline, she had fever to 38.9°C; the rash resolved over 6 days. The following week, she had a fever of 39.4°C, severe pharyngitis, and tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, prompting ED evaluation.

On presentation, temperature was 38.1°C, heart rate 86 bpm, blood pressure 106/55 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16 bpm, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Examination revealed tonsillar enlargement with purulent exudate, an aphthous lip ulcer, and tender subcentimeter anterior cervical nodes; there was no organomegaly. Laboratory studies showed WBC 0.9 × 10^3/µl, ANC 0.0 × 10^3/µl, ALC 0.8 × 10^3/µl, hemoglobin 12.2 g/dl, platelets 201 × 10^3/µl, MCV 87.1 fl, and RDW 11.7%. ESR was 41 mm/h and CRP 6.1 mg/dl. Blood and fungal cultures, urinalysis, and urine culture were negative; pregnancy test was negative. An extensive hematologic, rheumatologic, and infectious workup was unrevealing except for ANA 1:640 homogeneous, low vitamin B12 at 219 pg/ml with positive intrinsic factor antibody, and throat culture positive for non–group A beta-hemolytic streptococci. Flow cytometry showed no malignancy. She declined bone marrow biopsy. Treatment included piperacillin–tazobactam, acyclovir (later discontinued), fluconazole, two doses of filgrastim, and cyanocobalamin. By hospital day 5, ANC rose to 1.0 × 10^3/µl, and she was discharged with amoxicillin–clavulanate and B12 supplementation. One month later and at a 2-year follow-up, her blood counts and vitamin B12 and folate levels were normal.

In August 2020, she re-presented with fever, hand arthralgias, and tender cervical lymphadenopathy. Three weeks earlier, she had begun a course of doxycycline for recurrent perioral dermatitis. The day after starting doxycycline, she developed fever and arthralgias; ten days after her final dose, she noted low-grade fevers to 37.8°C and tender 1 cm bilateral cervical nodes. In the ED, vital signs were within normal limits except for fever up to 38.9°C. Examination showed mild tonsillar swelling and faint periorbital dermatitis without organomegaly. CBC revealed WBC 2.9 × 10^3/µl, ANC 0.0 × 10^3/µl, and ALC 2.3 × 10^3/µl. ESR was 39 mm/h, CRP 3.4 mg/dl, and ANA 1:1280 homogeneous. Repeat flow cytometry was similar to prior reactive findings. Vitamin B12, LDH, TSH, and respiratory viral panels (including SARS-CoV-2) were normal or negative. She was treated with piperacillin–tazobactam and filgrastim; by hospital day 2, ANC rose to 2.9 × 10^3/µl, and she was discharged on day 3.

A 71-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history presented with several weeks of progressive abdominal distension and weight loss. He was alert (GCS 15), afebrile, but appeared malnourished and was bedridden. Skin examination revealed painless flesh-colored papules and nodules in the pelvic area and purpuric ecchymoses on the hands. He had bilateral lower-limb edema. On abdominal examination there was fluid wave with dullness to percussion. Lung examination showed decreased vocal fremitus and diminished breath sounds at the bases.  

Diagnostic paracentesis yielded an exudative ascitic fluid (albumin 35 g/L) with 569 leukocytes/mm3 (60% lymphocytes). Cultures and assays, including quantiferon and antinuclear antibodies, were negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen demonstrated right pleural effusion, moderate ascites, diffuse peritoneal thickening, and infiltration of the abdominal fat. Thoracentesis revealed a transudative pleural effusion (albumin 24 g/L). Investigations for pleural fluid etiology, including 24-hour urinary protein excretion and liver function tests, were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography showed biventricular hypertrophy, a subnormal ejection fraction, a “granular and sparkling” myocardial appearance, interatrial septal thickening, and a small pericardial effusion.

A 22-year-old woman from Madagascar, living in Germany for two years, presented to the psychiatric emergency department with acute auditory hallucinations of seven days’ duration and visual hallucinations beginning on the day of admission. She reported hearing a repetitive voice telling her to “go to the sea” and seeing an old, faceless woman—the presumed source of the voice. She had no prior psychiatric history and denied altered consciousness or orientation; she was notably frightened by the hallucinations. She also experienced episodic severe headaches that intensified the hallucinations. One week before onset of psychiatric symptoms, she had several days of severe diarrhea while working as an elderly care nurse in a retirement home experiencing an outbreak of diarrhea.

On examination, her vital signs were normal; there was no fever or neck stiffness. Neurologic and internal examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including C-reactive protein and lymphocyte counts, were within normal limits. Cranial MRI and EEG showed no abnormalities. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a normal cell count (1.0 cells/µl), normal blood–CSF barrier function (albumin ratio, 6.64; total protein, 474 mg/l), no intrathecal IgG, IgA, or IgM synthesis, and no CSF-specific oligoclonal bands. Tests for antineuronal and autoimmune encephalitis antibodies in serum and CSF were negative. PCR assays and antibody-specific indices for cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, Epstein–Barr virus, and varicella–zoster virus were negative.

A 27-year-old woman presented with an 8-year history of chronic neck pain and cervicogenic headache following a whiplash injury in a motor vehicle collision. She described suboccipital cramping, burning, and aching pain radiating to her jaw and posterior neck, worse on the right, aggravated by postural changes and neck rotation, and rated 9/10 on the visual analog scale. Relief was minimal with NSAIDs, sleep, and neck manipulation. Associated symptoms included temporomandibular joint clicking, neck stiffness, teeth clenching, bilateral periorbital headaches, numbness and tingling, anxiety, and fatigue; she denied fever, visual changes, motor weakness, and weight loss. She had undergone a C4–C6 laminectomy, multiple occipital nerve blocks, cervical epidural steroid injections, and C2–C5 facet joint injections without lasting benefit. Medications included anxiolytics, tricyclic antidepressants, topical analgesics, and opioids.

On examination, there was tenderness over the proximal right sternocleidomastoid and suboccipital regions, mild scapular winging, and pain with active neck rotation. The cervical flexion–rotation test was positive, and maximal ipsilateral side bending with contralateral rotation reproduced pain at the atlantoaxial joint. Neurologic examination, including cranial nerves, reflexes, and Hoffman’s sign, was normal. The Sharp Purser test, Spurling’s, and lateral shear tests were negative except for bilateral finger paresthesias. The Neck Disability Index was 25/50. MRI of the cervical spine showed multilevel disc desiccation at C2–C5, C2–C3 and C3–C4 disc bulges, uncovertebral joint hypertrophy with bilateral neural foraminal narrowing, and spinal canal stenosis.

Initial differential diagnoses included cervical facetogenic pain, cervical radiculopathy, and degenerative zygapophyseal joint arthropathy. Diagnostic medial branch blocks at C2–C3 and C3–C5 provided no pain relief. Given the clinical findings, bilateral C1–C2 intra-articular diagnostic blocks with 1% lidocaine were performed, resulting in 75–80% reduction in pain. A second confirmatory block reproduced a similar degree of relief.

A 48-year-old woman presented with urgency, dysuria, dyspareunia, and vaginal discharge. She had completed 5 days of ciprofloxacin without symptom relief, and urinalysis was negative. She was febrile (temperature not specified) and had lower abdominal tenderness. Laboratory studies revealed a white-blood-cell count of 13.2×10^3/mm^3 (normal 4.2–10.5), neutrophils 84.9% (normal 40–75), and a C-reactive protein level of 12.64 mg/dL (normal 0.0–0.5); hemoglobin, hematocrit, and creatinine were within normal limits. A Foley catheter was placed and clamped for imaging. 

Transabdominal ultrasound showed mild left calico-pelvic dilation and, inferior to the mildly distended bladder, an inhomogeneous fluid-filled mass measuring up to 6.4 cm with a thick central septum, thick walls, and surrounding fat inhomogeneity. After bladder emptying, the catheter balloon lay against the upper pole of the lesion, and the catheter line traversed the midline septum. 

Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a bilocular cyst with low-level internal echoes, regular walls, and a nonvascularized septum, located below the bladder and anterolateral to the urethra; there was no communication between the cyst and the urethra. 

Pelvic MRI with contrast revealed an oval fluid collection lateral to the external urethral meatus and inferior to the pubic symphysis. The lesion was hyperintense on T2-weighted images, had thickened walls, perilesional fat stranding, lower T2 signal, higher T1 signal, and smooth peripheral wall enhancement.

An 8-year-old girl underwent surgical closure of an atrial septal defect via a right minithoracotomy. Two months after surgery, she presented with a 15-day history of fever without chills or rigors. On examination, she was febrile; percussion over the right basal hemithorax was dull, and auscultation revealed decreased breath sounds with bronchial breathing in that area. A chest radiograph (posteroanterior view) showed an inhomogeneous radio-opacity in the right lower zone without definitive signs of volume loss or air bronchogram; thin, radio-dense lines were noted centrally within the opacity. An unenhanced CT scan of the thorax demonstrated a large extrapulmonary, intrapleural hypodense lesion in the basal right hemithorax containing entrapped air bubbles. Thin, coiled hyperdense structures (average density 440 HU) were present in the core of the lesion. The adjacent right lower lobe was partially collapsed.

A 12-year-old girl presented with a 3-month history of a burning sensation in her mouth when eating spicy foods, lasting a few minutes and resolving spontaneously. There was no history of toothpaste or mouthwash changes, no new medications, no dental procedures, and no systemic symptoms such as skin eruptions, pruritus, eye lesions, or joint pain. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable.

On examination, her oral hygiene was fair and there were no decayed or restored teeth. Soft-tissue inspection revealed bilateral, irregular 2×2 cm grayish-white patches with peripherally radiating white striae on the gingiva and vestibular areas of the permanent mandibular molars. These lesions were non-scrapable, non-tender, non-indurated, and did not bleed on manipulation. The buccal mucosa, tongue, floor of mouth, hard palate, soft palate, skin, nails, and scalp were all normal. Cervical lymph nodes were not palpable.

An incisional biopsy was performed. Histopathology showed hyperplastic parakeratinized stratified squamous epithelium with acanthosis, basal cell degeneration, saw-tooth rete ridges, areas of basement-membrane disruption, intraepithelial lymphocytes, and a juxta-epithelial band of lymphocytic infiltration. Routine hematological and liver‐function tests were within normal limits.

A 2.5-year-old boy was brought to the emergency department with a one-day history of high fever and frequent vomiting followed by decreased level of consciousness. He had two similar episodes at ages 10 and 21 months, previously treated as febrile seizure and meningitis. Born to consanguineous parents, he had normal growth and development and no family history of liver disease. On examination, his temperature was 38.8°C, pulse 125 bpm, and he was drowsy (modified Glasgow Coma Scale score 6) with flexor posturing to pain; there was mild hepatomegaly without splenomegaly. Initial laboratory tests showed hypoglycemia (16 mg/dL), which corrected with glucose; a serum ammonia level of 650 µg/dL; elevated transaminases (ALT 429 U/L, AST 65 U/L); hypoalbuminemia (2.8 g/dL); and coagulopathy (PT 20.7 s, INR 1.65). Metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap resolved with hydration. CSF analysis and cultures of blood, CSF, and urine were normal. Brain CT demonstrated bilateral symmetric low focal attenuation in the thalami and focal lesions in posterior parietal and occipital white matter. EEG showed no seizure activity. Initial differential diagnoses included genetic metabolic disorders, acute necrotizing encephalopathy of childhood, and Reye’s syndrome.

A 30-year-old woman, 31 weeks pregnant, noted visual distortion (“dented road surface and distorted lines”) in her left eye for one week and in her right eye for one day. She also reported a mild headache without tinnitus or hearing loss. She had no significant past medical history except one prior uneventful delivery and was taking no medications. She declined COVID-19 vaccination.

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 1.0 in both eyes and intraocular pressure was 9 mmHg bilaterally. There were no keratic precipitates or aqueous cells. Fundus examination revealed multifocal serous retinal detachment in the posterior poles of both eyes, and the optic discs appeared normal.

A 64-year-old Caucasian man presented with one day of left arm pain and numbness. He was not taking any medications and had no family history of coronary artery disease or sudden death. Physical examination was unremarkable. An electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with T-wave inversions in leads II, III, and aVF; chest radiography was normal. He was started on aspirin, intravenous heparin, nitroglycerin, and eptifibatide. Initial troponin I was 0.47 ng/mL, rising to 2.28 ng/mL, and he underwent left heart catheterization. Angiography of the right coronary artery revealed >90% stenosis, and a drug-eluting stent was placed with TIMI grade III flow. He received a 600-mg loading dose of clopidogrel. 

Fifteen hours later, he developed left-sided chest pain and ST-segment elevations in leads II, III, and aVF. Repeat catheterization showed acute thrombosis of the stent; thrombectomy was performed and a second drug-eluting stent was placed. His platelet count fell from 145,000/µL to 74,000/µL, prompting suspicion for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia; heparin was stopped and argatroban initiated. Heparin platelet factor 4 antibody testing returned mildly elevated (0.419 OD) but did not meet criteria for HIT. Two hours later, he again developed chest pain with recurrent inferior-lead ST elevation; before repeat catheterization, he became unresponsive, hypotensive, and developed ventricular tachycardia. After cardioversion and initiation of vasopressors, a transvenous pacemaker and intra-aortic balloon pump were placed. Angiography showed 100% thrombosis of the recently placed stent; intra-arterial tPA and thrombectomy partially restored flow. Clopidogrel was switched to prasugrel. Further workup showed a rise in creatinine to 2.02 mg/dL, a platelet count of 46,000/µL, generalized petechiae, bleeding from his nasogastric tube, and free intraperitoneal fluid on abdominal ultrasound.

An 11-year-old child was admitted after a high-speed car–scooter collision. Initial examination: Glasgow Coma Scale score 14/15; no other abnormal clinical findings. Past medical history unremarkable. Head CT showed a nondisplaced comminuted fracture of the left temporal bone and a 2×5×8 cm temporoparietal epidural hematoma with 4 mm midline shift, radiologic signs of subarachnoid hemorrhage, and minor temporoparietal contusions. Chest CT revealed diffuse minor pulmonary contusions; abdominal CT was normal. An emergency craniotomy evacuated the hematoma. Intraoperatively, lactate was 3.2 mmol/L and hemodynamic instability required high-dose vasopressors. Postoperatively, an intracranial pressure monitor showed ICP 7–10 mmHg and cerebral perfusion pressure 60–65 mmHg; head CT confirmed hematoma evacuation. In the pediatric ICU, the patient was ventilated with low oxygen support. A few hours later, they developed worsening hemodynamic instability with a gallop rhythm, increasing norepinephrine requirements, and an episode of ventricular fibrillation that resolved with increased vasopressors. Despite support, profound shock persisted. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction with regional wall-motion abnormalities, an ejection fraction of 40%, and fractional shortening of 28%. Troponin rose to 5000 mg/dL, and ECG showed ST-segment elevations, repolarization abnormalities, and Q waves in leads V2–V6. Continuous cardiac output monitoring (PiCCO) showed a cardiac index of 2–2.5 L/min/m2, global ejection fraction of 8%, and systemic vascular resistance index of 1500 dyn·sec·cm−5·m2. An initial trial of dobutamine was ineffective, and the patient was stabilized on milrinone and adrenaline infusions.

A 57-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of abdominal pain, diarrhea, and passage of bloody mucus stools more than ten times daily. The periumbilical pain was relieved by defecation; she denied fever, cough, or chest tightness.

Two years earlier, she was diagnosed with dermatomyositis after hospitalization for eyelid edema, limb weakness, and swallowing difficulty. Findings included Gottron’s papules, V-neck sign, facial erythema, periorbital edema, electromyography showing myogenic damage, muscle-biopsy evidence of interstitial vascular dilatation with lymphocytic infiltration, and MRI consistent with myositis. She has remained on prednisone, methotrexate, and cyclosporine, with persistent proximal muscle weakness but no new rash.

Her history also includes hypertension and depression; she had an appendectomy 25 years ago and does not smoke or drink.

On examination, she was 160 cm tall, weighed 45 kg (BMI 17.6). Blotchy pigmentation was noted on the neck, legs, and hips. Abdomen was tender without rebound. Muscles of the neck and limbs were tender; distal strength was 4/5, proximal 3/5; tone was normal.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 5.03 × 10^9/L, RBC 2.42 × 10^12/L, hemoglobin 70.7 g/L, albumin 32.6 g/L, D-dimer 742 ng/mL. Stool occult blood was positive with red and white cells; no parasites or bacteria were detected. Autoantibodies were positive for ANA, anticentromere antibody, anti-Ro52, and centromeric immunofluorescence (1:320). Cardiac enzymes, tuberculosis, viral serologies, and tumor markers were normal.

Colonoscopy revealed diffuse hyperemia, erosions, and 0.3–0.6 cm ulcers with yellow-white exudate throughout the colon and rectum; the terminal ileum showed hyperemia and erosions; multiple 0.3–0.7 cm broad-based and pedunculated polyps were seen in the ileocecal region. Mucosal biopsy of the transverse colon showed moderate chronic inflammation with neutrophil infiltration and appendageal changes.

CT enterography demonstrated mild thickening of the splenic flexure, descending colon, sigmoid colon, and rectum walls, with shallow colonic pouches and a “sausage-like” appearance.

A 66-year-old man with no prior neurologic disease was referred for evaluation of subacute cognitive and neurologic symptoms. Over the preceding weeks, he developed memory impairment, progressive speech difficulties, dizziness, fluctuating awareness, balance problems, apraxia, twitching of the extremities, mood changes, and visual hallucinations. On examination, he had mild aphasia and dysarthria, bilateral resting tremor, truncal instability, myoclonus, severe bilateral apraxia, and dysdiadochokinesia; the Mini–Mental State Examination score was 25/30. Neuropsychological testing revealed a dysexecutive/subcortical cognitive profile, fulfilling formal criteria for dementia.

Cerebral CT excluded subdural hematoma, and supplemental MRI was normal. Chest radiography and full-body PET showed no extra-cerebral malignancy; paraneoplastic antibodies in blood were negative. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis demonstrated elevated protein and a mild pleocytosis; biomarkers for Alzheimer’s disease (Aß42, F-tau, P-tau) were negative. Testing for Lyme disease was negative. Brain ^18F-FDG–PET showed globally decreased cortical glucose metabolism, interpreted as more consistent with metabolic or toxic effects than with a neurodegenerative process.

A 59-year-old man presented with blurred vision in his left eye. He reported a 15-year history of itching nodules on his hands and legs. Six years ago, dermatologic evaluation revealed petechiae on the trunk and confluent purpura with ulceration on the lower legs; a skin biopsy of the hand confirmed leukocytoclastic vasculitis, clinically consistent with erythema elevatum diutinum. He has since been treated with Tripterygium Glycosides (20 mg three times daily) and Sulfasalazine (50 mg three times daily). Ophthalmic history included cataract surgery in the right eye and a pterygium in the left eye, both 6 years earlier.

On examination, there were multiple well-demarcated, red, firm nodules and plaques on the dorsum of the hands, some superficially eroded and crusted. Best-corrected visual acuity was 1.0 in the right eye and hand motion in the left eye. Slit-lamp examination of the left eye showed nasal conjunctival thickening with stromal infiltration (~3 mm), central corneal thinning with perforation, corneal edema, and absence of the anterior chamber; a senile nuclear cataract was also present. The right anterior segment was normal.

The patient underwent conjunctival flap covering of the left cornea and received postoperative topical gatifloxacin ophthalmic gel three times daily, recombinant bovine basic fibroblast growth factor three times daily, fluorometholone 0.1% eye drops twice daily, and cyclosporine 0.05% eye drops three times daily. One week later, the perforation had sealed, leaving a vascularized pseudopterygium and central scar; vision remained hand motion.

Six months after the left-eye surgery, he returned with pain, redness, photophobia, and tearing of the right eye. Visual acuity was 0.6 in the right eye and limited to counting fingers in the left eye. Anterior-segment examination of the right eye revealed conjunctival hyperemia and marginal corneal guttering from 11 to 1 o’clock with ulceration; the posterior segment was normal.

He underwent conjunctival flap covering of the right cornea, with resection of adjacent conjunctiva and ulcer edges, and the same postoperative topical regimen. Two months later, dense stromal inflammatory cell infiltrates were noted at the ulcer margin. Tobramycin and dexamethasone ointment were added once daily. One week thereafter, the cornea cleared without infiltrates. Three months postoperatively, vision stabilized at 0.6, and the ulcer had healed.

A laboratory workup including routine blood and urine tests, liver and kidney function, infectious disease serologies (hepatitis, syphilis, HIV), cryoglobulins, immunoglobulins (IgA, IgG, IgM), complement components (C3, C4), erythrocyte sedimentation rate, rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and serum protein electrophoresis showed only elevated C-reactive protein, IgA, and D-dimer; erythrocyte sedimentation rate, rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, and ANCA results were unremarkable.

A man in his early 60s presented with a 1.5-month history of a painful ulcer on the left edge of his tongue that had not responded to topical steroids. His medical history included type 2 diabetes managed with ipragliflozin, and he had a 37-year history of heavy cigarette smoking, now switched to e-cigarettes. He did not consume alcohol. 

On examination, he was well-nourished. Facial asymmetry was noted due to left submental swelling without facial nerve deficits. Palpation revealed multiple elastic, firm, mobile lymph nodes in the left submandibular region (one ~tip-of-index-finger size, tender; two ~soybean size, non-tender) and a tender node of similar size in the right submental area. The tongue lesion measured 23 × 14 mm on the ventral surface near the floor of the mouth, with indurated and hemorrhagic surrounding tissue.

Laboratory studies showed mild anemia (hemoglobin 122 g/L), elevated γ-glutamyl transpeptidase (142 U/L), hyperglycemia (blood glucose 8.6 mmol/L), elevated C-reactive protein (50.1 mg/L), and HbA₁c of 68 mmol/mol.

Panoramic radiography demonstrated vertical bone resorption mesial to the left mandibular second molar and multiple dental caries without other bony lesions. Contrast-enhanced CT showed no destructive change in the tongue or mandible, but bilateral submandibular and upper internal jugular lymphadenopathy (minor axis 2–19 mm) without rim enhancement. Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed an enhancing area from the left tongue margin to the mylohyoid muscle, with variably swollen lymph nodes exhibiting heterogeneous interiors and rim enhancement. ¹⁸F-FDG PET showed mild uptake in the left tongue margin (SUVmax 3.6) and bilateral submandibular nodes (SUVmax 2.8–5.2) with no other abnormal foci.

Based on these clinical, laboratory, and imaging findings, the tongue lesion was thought to be tongue cancer with cervical lymph node metastases (T2N2cM0).

A 60‐year‐old man with a history of childhood poliomyelitis and residual right‐sided weakness presented with a 6‐year history of left lower quadrant abdominal pain, a painful left groin mass, and left lower extremity swelling. He grew up in Montenegro and moved to the United States as a teenager. On examination, he ambulated with a cane, had a right leg limp, and asymmetric lower‐extremity size. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and basic metabolic panel, were within normal limits. 

Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a large complex cystic collection in the left retroperitoneum along the iliopsoas muscle, extending into the left pelvis and thigh. The initial differential diagnosis included benign lymphatic malformation, malignancy such as myxoid liposarcoma, and multiloculated abscess; infection was considered less likely given the absence of sepsis. The patient was lost to follow‐up and returned 6 years later for repeat CT, which showed no change in the lesion’s size. 

MRI of the pelvis and left thigh, with and without intravenous contrast, demonstrated a large nonenhancing multicystic mass along the left iliopsoas muscle extending into the thigh, with multiple hyperintense cysts within and along the sartorius on STIR sequences and no enhancement post‐contrast. Incidentally, there was severe fatty atrophy of the right pelvic musculature and a shallow right acetabulum consistent with chronic poliomyelitis. The leading considerations remained lymphatic malformation and myxoid liposarcoma.

A 61-year-old man of Taiwanese descent presented with a painful, diffuse maculopapular rash on the face and trunk. One year earlier, he had fevers, chills, and weight loss and was found to have diffuse mediastinal, hilar, and axillary lymphadenopathy. Bronchoalveolar lavage grew Mycobacterium avium complex, and he was treated with clarithromycin, ethambutol, and rifampin. Three months into therapy, he stopped ethambutol because of a new rash. On examination, 3–6 mm erythematous maculopapular lesions involved the face and trunk. Punch biopsy showed mixed granulomatous and neutrophilic inflammation with plasma cells, sheets of histiocytes, and focal emperipolesis. Ophthalmology evaluation revealed bilateral anterior uveitis. Repeat sputum cultures were negative, and CT imaging showed stable lymphadenopathy. He continued clarithromycin and rifampin but was lost to follow-up.

Seven months into MAC therapy, he re-presented with fevers, profound weakness, and leukocytosis of 50 000 cells/µL with lymphocytic predominance. CT imaging showed progression of lymphadenopathy. Core biopsy of an axillary lymph node demonstrated lymphocytic infiltration with up to 70 IgG4+ plasma cells per high-power field and an IgG4+/IgG ratio of < 30%; AFB stain, flow cytometry, and molecular studies were negative. Excisional biopsy revealed effacement of nodal architecture by mixed inflammatory cells, storiform fibrosis, histiocyte collections, microabscesses, rare acid-fast bacilli on careful review of AFB stain, and variable IgG4+ plasma cells (10–130 per high-power field) with an IgG4/IgG ratio of 30–40%. Serum IgA, IgE, and IgG were elevated, with an IgG4 level of 308 mg/dL.

A 52-year-old man who works as a cattle rearer in rural India presented with a 2-year history of a slowly enlarging swelling in his left thigh. He first noticed a small, painless lump that insidiously grew to approximately 18 × 12 cm without periods of rapid change. There was no history of trauma, fever, or other medical conditions. On examination, vital signs were normal. The left thigh showed a firm, non-tender mass occupying the upper two thirds; the overlying skin was unremarkable. No other masses were detected. Routine blood tests were normal. Ultrasonography revealed a large multiloculated complex cystic mass measuring 31 × 29 × 19 cm in the subcutaneous plane of the anterior and medial upper thigh (volume, 236 mL). Magnetic resonance imaging showed well-encapsulated cystic lesions containing multiple daughter cysts in the anterior (vastus medialis and adductor muscles; approximately 17.2 × 10.6 × 8.7 cm) and posterior (approximately 25 × 17 × 7 cm) compartments of the left thigh, with mild peripheral enhancement and compression of adjacent muscles and the neurovascular bundle; there was no bony involvement. Chest radiography and contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no other organ lesions.

A 16-year-old Black female secondary-school student from Nigeria presented with a 6-month history of bilateral leg swelling and failure of menarche. She denied jaundice, abdominal pain, dyspnea, or gastrointestinal symptoms. There was no significant past medical history and no family history of liver disease. On examination, she had grade 2 bilateral pitting edema but was otherwise comfortable. Abdominal examination revealed a liver span of 10 cm without splenomegaly or ascites. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable, with no encephalopathy. 

Laboratory studies showed:  
• Total bilirubin 34.2 µmol/L (normal <17), conjugated bilirubin 17.1 µmol/L (<5.1)  
• AST 287 IU/L (15–40), ALT 139 IU/L (13–34), ALP 697 IU/L (<240)  
• Serum sodium 141 mmol/L, potassium 2.6 mmol/L  
• Total protein 88.5 g/L (62–80), albumin 10.2 g/L (30–50), globulin 78.3 g/L (18–30)  
• Serum protein electrophoresis showed reduced albumin fraction, elevated gamma fraction with beta-gamma bridging  
• HBsAg negative, anti-HCV negative  

An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a coarse hepatic echotexture with reduced periportal markings consistent with cirrhosis and an echogenic gallbladder mass with shadowing. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed grade 2 esophageal varices.

A 47-year-old Caucasian man with a history of substance abuse presented with four days of nausea, vomiting, watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, anuria, fatigue, and paresthesia of the extremities. His only outpatient medications were trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole and clindamycin for an arm rash. On examination, he was hypotensive (67/48 mm Hg), tachycardic (115 beats/min), and had altered mental status. Petechiae were present on all extremities, and he had diffuse abdominal tenderness. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (35.2×10^3/μL), anemia (hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL), acute kidney injury (BUN 64 mg/dL; creatinine 5.3 mg/dL), and thrombocytopenia (21×10^3/μL). Stool tests and blood and sputum cultures were negative. Further evaluation revealed microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with an elevated lactate dehydrogenase (4,473 U/L), decreased haptoglobin (<10 mg/dL), indirect hyperbilirubinemia (2.2 mg/dL), and schistocytes on peripheral smear. A diagnosis of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura was presumed, and he underwent five days of therapeutic plasma exchange without clinical improvement.

A 16-year-old boy was admitted after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting 2 minutes. He had projectile vomiting and new right-sided motor weakness with hypoesthesia post-ictally. His history was notable for 3 years of severe headaches; an MRI performed 1 year earlier was normal. Two weeks before presentation, he experienced fever, myalgia, and upper respiratory symptoms. 

On evaluation, his height was 179 cm (90th percentile) and weight 106.3 kg (>97th percentile). Brain MRI revealed T2-weighted hyperintense lesions in the left parietal, right frontal, and right temporal lobes with patchy contrast enhancement. Laboratory testing showed a white blood cell count of 10 420/mm3, C-reactive protein of 0.99 mg/dL (0–0.5), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 31 mm/hr (0–9). 

CSF analysis revealed 4 WBC/mm3 and a protein level of 35 mg/dL; cytospin showed no malignancy. Serum studies were negative for antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, rheumatoid factor, antiphospholipid antibodies, anti–aquaporin-4 and anti-MOG antibodies; complements C3 and C4 were normal. CSF PCR for Epstein–Barr virus, herpes simplex viruses 1 and 2, and human herpesvirus 6 was negative. Serum immunoglobulin G antibodies to Taenia solium and Sparganum species were negative. 

Under the impression of an acute demyelinating syndrome, he received methylprednisolone 1 000 mg/day for 3 days followed by oral steroid maintenance. His headaches improved and no further seizures occurred. However, a 1-month follow-up MRI showed enlargement and increased enhancement of the lesions.

A 64-year-old Italian man was referred in November 2017 for gingival bleeding. He had undergone dental fillings in 2016 and subsequently noted erythematous, hyperplastic gingivitis of the upper arch interfering with eating. He denied allergies, tobacco or other habits, and systemic symptoms including weight loss, fever, Raynaud’s phenomenon, photosensitivity, xerostomia, or xerophthalmia. Medical history included hypertension treated with nebivolol and diuretics; family history was negative for psoriasis or rheumatic diseases.  
On examination, there was intense edema and bright-red erythema of the adherent vestibular gingiva from tooth numbers 1.5 to 2.5, with probing depths <3 mm, no loss of attachment, and marked bleeding on probing. Blood tests showed isolated positivity for proteinase 3 antibodies.  
Two incisional biopsies of the affected gingiva were performed. Microscopic evaluation revealed a dense inflammatory infiltrate predominantly composed of plasma cells in the lamina propria, with edema and intraepithelial spongiosis. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated no restriction of immunoglobulin light chains.

A 25-year-old man with celiac disease underwent orthotopic heart transplantation in 2011 for giant cell myocarditis. His maintenance immunosuppression consisted of tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisolone, later intensified with everolimus after recurrent acute cellular rejection episodes. In 2013, he received a pacemaker for complete heart block. Graft function remained stable until early May 2017, when he developed fever and malaise without focal symptoms. After 7 days at home without improvement, he was admitted for evaluation.

On admission, laboratory studies demonstrated a marked inflammatory reaction, but real‐time PCR assays for multiple viruses and bacterial cultures were all negative. An electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia at 108 beats per minute, supraventricular extrasystoles, right bundle branch block, left anterior fascicular block, and signs of left ventricular hypertrophy. Chest radiography was unremarkable, and abdominal ultrasonography showed no hepatosplenomegaly. Drug levels of tacrolimus and everolimus were within therapeutic range. Intravenous hydrocortisone was started to counteract inflammation.

Further laboratory tests revealed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 97 g/L [reference 134–170], white cells 2.1×10^9/L [3–7], platelets 139×10^9/L [145–348]), elevated ferritin (1378 µg/L [30–400]), hypertriglyceridaemia (4.1 mmol/L [0.45–2.6]), and hypofibrinogenaemia (1.37 g/L [1.8–3.8]). Haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) was considered, and a bone marrow biopsy was performed. It showed normal histiocyte numbers and no evidence of haemophagocytosis. Empiric broad‐spectrum antibiotics were initiated, but the patient’s condition continued to worsen.

A 64-year-old man was referred for evaluation of severe lower urinary tract symptoms (dysuria, urgency, frequency) and recurrent urinary tract infections. One year before presentation, he was diagnosed with benign prostatic hyperplasia and underwent transvesical prostatectomy at an outside hospital. Three months after surgery, he continued to have severe symptoms and was treated repeatedly with oral antibiotics for presumed UTIs. He subsequently developed acute urinary retention and had a suprapubic catheter placed.

On examination, he was a well-appearing adult with a suprapubic Foley catheter in place and a well-healed lower abdominal scar. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, normal renal function, and normal urinalysis; the urine culture revealed no growth. Abdominopelvic ultrasonography was unremarkable. 

A cystourethroscopy was performed with the impression of urethral or bladder neck stenosis and revealed a large whitish spongiform structure impacted within the urethral lumen.

A 47-year-old man with no smoking history and previously good health presented with a 1-year history of progressive dyspnoea, presyncope, and leg swelling. One year earlier, he had undergone complex spinal surgery including L5–S1 discectomy, laminectomy, and bilateral nerve reconstruction. Since then, he had multiple admissions for right-sided heart failure requiring intravenous diuresis.

Echocardiography revealed preserved left ventricular function, a severely dilated right ventricle and right atrium, normal left atrial size, severe tricuspid regurgitation, and a small pericardial effusion. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed a D-shaped left ventricle consistent with right ventricular pressure and volume overload and pulmonary hypertension.

On examination, jugular venous pressure was elevated, the second heart sound was loud, and a systolic murmur was heard diffusely. There was peripheral oedema, ascites, and an abdominal bruit. Laboratory studies showed haemoglobin 11.7 g/dL, normal liver and thyroid function, and NT-proBNP 3600 pg/mL. Pulmonary function tests revealed normal spirometry and a diffusion capacity of 75%. Chest radiography demonstrated cardiomegaly and central pulmonary vascular congestion.

CT pulmonary angiography revealed a dilated main pulmonary artery (35 mm), normal lung parenchyma, dilated right-sided chambers with normal left chambers, reflux of contrast into the inferior vena cava, and large-volume ascites; there was no pulmonary thromboembolism. These findings were felt to be consistent with severe right heart failure, likely secondary to pulmonary arterial hypertension.

Right heart catheterisation showed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 30 mm Hg, a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 24 mm Hg, a cardiac output of 13.5 L/min, and a pulmonary vascular resistance of 0.4 Wood Units. Left heart catheterisation demonstrated normal coronary arteries and a left ventricular end-diastolic pressure of 24 mm Hg. Mixed venous oxygen saturation was 86.3%, raising the possibility of left-to-right shunting. Invasive saturation monitoring revealed saturations of 72.3% in the superior vena cava, 91.4% in the inferior vena cava, 84.6% in the right atrium, 84.2% in the right ventricle, and 86.3% in the pulmonary artery. There was a significant discrepancy between the superior vena cava and inferior vena cava saturations, suggesting the possibility of a sub-diaphragmatic shunt.

A 27-year-old Filipino man with no prior medical history presented with acute bilateral leg weakness of 2 hours’ duration and milder arm weakness. He denied pain or numbness and reported a 5-kg weight loss over the past month. Vital signs were normal except for a heart rate of 117 beats per minute. On examination, muscle strength was 4/5 in the upper limbs and 3/5 in the lower limbs, and there was a diffuse goiter. ECG showed sinus tachycardia. Head CT performed to exclude stroke demonstrated bilateral basal ganglia and dentate nuclei calcifications. Laboratory tests revealed a free thyroxine level >100 mIU/L (reference, 11.0–23.3), a thyroid-stimulating hormone level <0.01 mIU/L (0.30–4.20), a potassium level of 3.0 mmol/L (3.5–5.3), and elevated TSH receptor antibodies.

A 28-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of left facial asymmetry and a scar at the left mandibular angle, resulting from a fall and laceration. His chief complaint was an enlarging left-sided facial “growth” without pain. He had no systemic illness.

On extraoral examination, there was a unilateral swelling centered over the left mandibular angle. Palpation revealed that the tissue was of normal tone and nontender. Mandibular movements were within normal limits. When asked to clench his teeth, the swelling became more prominent and firm. The patient reported preferential use of the left side when chewing. There was no temporomandibular joint clicking and no family history of similar findings.

Intraoral examination revealed bilaterally distoangularly impacted mandibular third molars. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated a prominent left mandibular angle without evidence of osseous lesion.

A 22-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1 at 30 weeks 5 days of gestation, was brought to the emergency department after a witnessed tonic-clonic seizure at home, followed by loss of consciousness and fixed dilated pupils. Six days earlier she had developed progressive shortness of breath, and her husband reported recent use of inhaled opioids in a patient without prior addiction. On arrival, her Glasgow Coma Scale was low and she was intubated; she required eight rounds of cardiopulmonary resuscitation with atropine, calcium gluconate, sodium bicarbonate, and epinephrine. Emergency transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a markedly dilated right atrium and right ventricle with interventricular septal flattening; estimated systolic pulmonary artery pressure was 50 mm Hg, and left ventricular ejection fraction was 30%, consistent with a massive pulmonary embolism and biventricular failure. She received an intravenous infusion of alteplase (100 mg) and was transferred to the intensive care unit. A repeat echocardiogram showed severe right ventricular dysfunction with McConnell’s sign, moderate tricuspid regurgitation (systolic pulmonary artery pressure 35 mm Hg), dilated pulmonary artery and inferior vena cava, mild pulmonary insufficiency, and a normal left ventricle. Laboratory studies were notable for leukocytosis with lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia (platelet count 103 × 10^3/mm^3), prolonged prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time (PT 69.1 sec, PTT 82 sec, INR 5.6), elevated D-dimer (+3), low fibrinogen (81 mg/dL), and negative antiphospholipid, anticardiolipin, and lupus anticoagulant antibodies. Chest radiography revealed diffuse bilateral consolidative opacities, more pronounced on the left side.

A 44-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with 2 days of sharp, stabbing right-sided chest pain (8/10) worsened by exertion and relieved by leaning forward, accompanied by shortness of breath on minimal activity. She also reported chronic right lower-leg swelling and six months of symmetric wrist stiffness that improved during the day. Her history included heavy menstrual bleeding, a miscarriage at age 14, chronic warfarin-refractory deep vein thromboses, and placement of a nonretrievable inferior vena cava filter. She denied fevers, chills, or intravenous drug use.

On examination she was obese and mildly tachypneic, sitting forward. Vital signs: temperature 98.6°F, blood pressure 116/91 mm Hg, heart rate 88/min, respiratory rate 20/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. She had a malar rash, jugular venous distension, tender anterior chest wall, bibasilar Velcro crackles, and a grade 2/6 pansystolic murmur at the left sternal border that increased with inspiration.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, platelets 71 × 10^3/mm^3, ESR 55 mm/h, CRP 90.9 mg/L, D-dimer 3.7 µg/mL, and prolonged PTT of 49 s with normal PT/INR/fibrinogen. Blood cultures were negative. CT pulmonary angiography demonstrated small bilateral pleural effusions and multifocal atelectasis without pulmonary embolism. Lower-extremity duplex ultrasound was negative for DVT. Chest radiograph revealed cardiomegaly, blunting of the right costophrenic angle, and elevated bilateral hemidiaphragms. Transthoracic echocardiography showed an ejection fraction of 55–60%, moderate-to-severe tricuspid regurgitation, a 1.6 × 0.9 cm tricuspid-valve vegetation, and mild pericardial effusion. Transesophageal echocardiography confirmed vegetations on all three tricuspid leaflets.

Based on these findings, rheumatic heart disease and nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis were considered in the differential diagnosis.

A 37-year-old Chinese woman was referred for nausea and oliguria. About 20 days earlier, she noted progressive bilateral visual acuity loss with periorbital swelling. Over the preceding 2 weeks, she had gained 4.5 kg and developed worsening anasarca.

Five years ago, routine labs revealed leukopenia, but she underwent no further workup. There was no family history of autoimmune or ocular disease.

On examination, she appeared fatigued and malnourished. Vital signs revealed a heart rate of 91 beats/min, respiratory rate of 17 breaths/min, and blood pressure of 145/87 mmHg. Findings included periorbital swelling, conjunctival chemosis, decreased breath sounds at both lung bases, and bilateral ankle pitting edema. Visual acuity was “count fingers” at 20 cm in the right eye and “hand motion” in the left eye, with formal ophthalmologic testing showing 2/100 OD and 1/100 OS.

Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 1.69 × 10^9/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 60 mm/h, total protein 61.7 g/dL, serum albumin 30 g/dL, normal BUN and creatinine, and normal serum potassium. Urinalysis revealed 0.81 g protein in 24 h. D-dimer was elevated at 4.86 µg/mL. Serologies were positive for antinuclear, anti–Smith, anti–SSA, anti–nRNP, and anti–Ro52 antibodies; complement levels were low (C3 19.5 mg/dL, C4 2.5 mg/dL). Brain MRI demonstrated small bilateral frontal lobe ischemic foci; lumbar puncture was declined. Thoracentesis yielded exudative fluid by the Rivalta test.

Slit-lamp examination showed a normal anterior segment and mild optic-disc swelling. Optical coherence tomography and ophthalmoscopy demonstrated bilateral serous retinal detachment. Fundus fluorescein angiography and indocyanine green angiography were deferred due to concerns about contrast nephrotoxicity.

A 32-year-old man noted a swelling of the right testicle over 1 month, which became painful over the 10 days before presentation. He was afebrile and denied trauma. On examination, the right testis was mildly enlarged, with a 1 cm × 1 cm ill-defined tender nodule at the lower pole. The epididymis, spermatic cords, and the left testis were normal. Complete blood count, including differential, was normal (no eosinophilia). A chest radiograph was normal. Serum tumour markers were not obtained due to cost. Scrotal ultrasonography showed the right testis larger than the left, with a 1.5 cm × 0.6 cm hypoechoic lesion in the lower-pole parenchyma and an echogenic speck within it, suggestive of a testicular neoplasm. The patient was counselled that the lesion could be benign but that malignancy could not be ruled out with certainty. Since the swelling was painful, the patient consented to an inguinal orchiectomy.

A 66-year-old Indian man presented with headache and a three-day history of painful vision loss in his left eye that rapidly progressed to no light perception. On examination, the left eye had no light perception, papilledema, and an afferent pupillary defect; extraocular movements were full and vision was normal in the right eye. CT of the skull base and brain showed bilateral pneumatization of the anterior clinoid processes and a 10×16×9 mm soft-tissue density lesion expanding the left anterior clinoid process, causing compression of the left orbital apex and the left optic nerve canal. MRI revealed an expansile lesion in the left anterior clinoid process with hyperintense signal on T1-weighted images, intermediate signal on T2-weighted images, lack of suppression on T1 fat-saturated sequences, and peripheral rim enhancement after intravenous gadolinium.

A 90-year-old man with known myelodysplastic syndrome with refractory anemia and myelofibrosis, transfusion- and thrombapheresis-dependent, underwent implantation of a right subclavian totally implanted central venous access device. On postoperative day 7, he developed dyspnea and fever to 38.6 °C and was admitted to the hospital. He had positive troponin levels, anterolateral ischemic changes on ECG, and severe anemia (hemoglobin 68 g/L) prompting a diagnosis of ischemic left ventricular dysfunction. Examination of the device insertion site revealed marked skin inflammation with a central necrotic ulcer and violaceous, undermined edges. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (11.8 × 10^9/L) with neutrophilia and a C-reactive protein level of 175 mg/L. On postoperative day 8, the device was removed and cultures were obtained. The patient was started on cefepime and vancomycin, later switched to imipenem and teicoplanin because of persistent fever and progressive renal impairment. All cultures remained sterile. Despite prolonged antibiotic therapy, the patient remained febrile, systemic inflammatory markers remained elevated, and the necrotic ulcer rapidly extended across the right upper chest wall.

A two‐year‐old boy with a history of panhypopituitarism, hydrocephalus, developmental delay, and obesity was referred for evaluation of recent severe visual deterioration. He had no headache, vomiting, or other signs of raised intracranial pressure. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed Chiari malformation, ventricular dilatation, and a small pituitary gland, with no mass lesion. Bedside fundoscopy was difficult due to patient movement, so an examination under anaesthesia was performed, revealing severe papilloedema in the right eye and a hypoplastic optic disc in the left eye.

A 42-year-old woman with a history of treatment–resistant cycloiriditis was referred for evaluation to rule out inflammatory bowel disease. She denied dysuria and reported no difficulties with defecation. Gastroscopy and colonoscopy showed no abnormalities. MR enterography detected a pelvic mass. Abdominopelvic CT imaging revealed a well-circumscribed, rounded presacral mass lying left of the midline at the level of the fourth sacral vertebra, measuring 3.4 × 2.8 cm. The lesion had a central liquid component, a peripheral tissue density of 31 HU, and a fine calcification at the right rim; there was no osseous destruction. On physical examination, anal sphincter tone was normal, the perianal soft tissue was supple, and the rectal vault was empty. Digital rectal examination elicited an extrarectal fullness posteriorly that was reachable with the fingertip.

A 19-year-old Iranian woman was referred for evaluation of progressive, painless thoracolumbar kyphosis that began at age 10. She reported no other symptoms and had no family history of spinal deformity. On examination, her neurologic status was normal. Laboratory tests were within normal limits. A lateral radiograph of the spine showed anterior narrowing of the disc spaces at T8–L1 and L2–3 with a kyphotic angle measuring 85°. Sagittal T1-weighted MRI demonstrated loss of anterior disc height and fusion at the same levels. A bone scan revealed increased uptake corresponding to those spinal segments.

A 76-year-old woman with a history of chronic low back pain radiating to her right thigh and lower leg, accompanied by tingling, was admitted for further evaluation. She had well-controlled hypertension but no history of trauma or prior spinal surgery. Physical examination showed increased tenderness in the paraspinal region and over the back of the right thigh and lower leg, a positive straight-leg raise on the right, mild paravertebral muscle hypertonia, and limited lumbar flexion (Schober test, 2 cm). Motor strength in both legs was normal, but sensation was decreased in the right thigh and lower leg; reflexes were symmetric.

Lumbar imaging revealed osteoporosis, lumbar spondylosis with compression fractures of L1 and L3, and an annular tear at L5–S1. She underwent vertebroplasty at L1 and L3. On hospital day 3, because of persistent symptoms attributed to L5–S1 disc herniation, she received an epidural steroid injection (1% lidocaine plus Diprospan) at L5–S1 without evident cerebrospinal fluid leak. The next day, she developed new tingling in the buttocks and perineum with increased pain but no motor weakness, reflex changes, or urinary or fecal retention. These findings raised concern for cauda equina syndrome, and lumbar CT and MRI were ordered.

A man in his 60s was referred for evaluation of new, progressive skin lesions on his back. He noted that the lesions began 1 year after he began a rigorous indoor swimming program (75 minutes per session, 30–35 laps in a 25 m pool, five days per week), and they were asymptomatic. He denied endocrine disorders, recent weight changes, corticosteroid use, or any preceding rash or striae. His history included hyperlipidemia and benign prostatic hypertrophy managed with long-term atorvastatin and aspirin. 

On examination, there were yellow, horizontally layered, symmetric, linear papules and cords on the mid-upper and lower back; intertriginous areas were clear. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, metabolic panel, lactate dehydrogenase, immunofixation electrophoresis, and lipid panel, were all within normal limits. 

Punch biopsies of the cords showed a normal epidermis and increased elastic fibers throughout the dermis. Verhoeff–Van Gieson staining highlighted intact and fragmented elastic fibers with aggregation in the papillary dermis. von Kossa staining was negative for calcified elastic fibers.

A 23-year-old man, previously healthy army personnel, presented with intermittent postprandial vomiting and leg cramps for one month, which worsened over two days to about ten episodes per day. He denied loin pain or hematuria. On examination, he was alert, not pale, not jaundiced, and without cachexia; vital signs were: blood pressure 130/73 mmHg, pulse 92 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Initial laboratory studies revealed severe metabolic alkalosis (venous pH 7.56, bicarbonate 62 mmol/L), hypokalemia (K⁺ 1.6 mmol/L), hyponatremia (Na⁺ 126 mmol/L), and acute kidney injury (serum creatinine 218.3 μmol/L, eGFR 35.5 mL/min/1.73 m²); corrected calcium was 2.04 mmol/L. Shortly after arrival, he had a generalized tonic seizure followed by pulseless electrical activity cardiac arrest; return of spontaneous circulation was achieved after 70 minutes of CPR and 14 defibrillation shocks. He was intubated, required inotropic support, and became anuric, necessitating renal replacement therapy. A nasogastric tube drained approximately 2 L of gastric contents, but he remained intolerant of feeding. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis showed a markedly distended, elongated stomach with an air–fluid level; no lesion or compression at the pylorus or gastric antrum; significant narrowing of the third part of the duodenum in the precaval and preaortic region with loss of intervening fat; an aortomesenteric angle of 21° (normal 25–60°) and a distance of 8 mm (normal 10–28 mm).

A 59-year-old man with a history of diabetes was hospitalized on day 12 of COVID-19 illness for oxygen therapy. He received methylprednisolone (2 mg/kg/day), remdesivir, and heparin; oxygen was discontinued after 3 days, and the steroid was tapered and stopped after a total of 13 days (day 24). He was discharged but on day 34 developed fatigue and fever. On day 36, blood tests showed an elevated inflammatory response, and chest radiography and CT revealed a localized infiltrative shadow in the left lower lobe. Empirical amoxicillin/clavulanic acid therapy was initiated without improvement, and he was readmitted on day 39. A saliva PCR test for SARS-CoV-2 was negative. On day 40, transbronchial lung cryobiopsy was performed. Photomicrographs showed prominent airspace obliteration by fibrinous exudate admixed with lymphohistiocytic accumulation, diffuse and mild thickening of the alveolar septa, few neutrophils or eosinophils, and no intra-alveolar fibromyxoid plugs.

A 54-year-old woman presented with a 20-day history of throat foreign-body sensation and dysphagia. One month earlier she had developed an intermittent cough, and her oropharyngeal symptoms gradually worsened until she also noted sleep apnea. She had a 2-year history of hypertension managed with oral lisinopril–hydrochlorothiazide. 

On examination, there was a tender, smooth-mucosal mass palpable at the right base of the tongue. There were no palpable cervical lymph nodes and no thyroid tissue was palpable in the normal anterior neck region. 

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, and thyroid function tests, were all within normal limits. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the oral and maxillofacial region showed a 2.3 cm × 2.0 cm right-sided nodule at the base of the tongue with homogeneous enhancement. Laryngoscopic examination revealed a 4 cm × 3 cm submucosal bulge at the tongue base. Ultrasonography of the neck demonstrated absence of thyroid tissue in the normal anatomical location. Tc-99 thyroid scanning showed radiotracer uptake at the base of the tongue and none in the normal thyroid bed.

A 66-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of acute left cheek and pre-auricular pain that began after a forceful facial acupressure massage. He described tenderness over the left masseter and pain on clenching his teeth, opening his mouth, and moving his jaw laterally. He reported no fever or other systemic symptoms. 

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. Maximum mouth opening was 35 mm. There was tenderness of the left masseter region but no visible swelling of the cheek or temporomandibular joint (TMJ) area. A panoramic radiograph and TMJ tomography showed no abnormal findings. He was tentatively diagnosed with temporomandibular disorder and discharged with conservative treatment.

Five days later, he returned with increased pain radiating beyond the TMJ area and reduced mouth opening. He was again diagnosed with temporomandibular disorder and received an intravenous analgesic.

Two days after that, he presented with severe pain and trismus. Maximum interincisal opening had decreased to 25 mm, and he had tenderness in the left masseter, temporalis, and pre-auricular regions without overt swelling. 

Contrast-enhanced facial CT revealed a 4.2 × 1.9 × 2.3 cm lobulated fluid collection in the left masticator space with peripheral enhancement, raising suspicion for either an abscess or an organized hematoma.

A 72-year-old man presented with a 9-month history of right prepatellar swelling that began 3 days after striking his knee against a post while horse riding. He was otherwise healthy. His general practitioner diagnosed prepatellar bursitis, and over six months he underwent four aspirations of clear synovial fluid and steroid injections without relief. He subsequently had a surgical excision of the prepatellar bursa, but the swelling recurred. Elastic compression bandaging reduced knee swelling but caused lower-leg edema. 

The patient reported discomfort and annoyance but no pain, instability, or functional limitation aside from reluctance to kneel. On examination, he appeared well with a normal gait. The right knee had full extension and flexion to 130°, and there was an 8 × 7 cm area of soft fullness over the patella. The contralateral knee was normal.

MRI of the right knee revealed a large prepatellar fluid collection extending from the distal quadriceps expansion to the patellar tendon insertion over a craniocaudal length of 10 cm; the only other finding was an incidental free-margin tear of the posterior horn of the medial meniscus. 

Under ultrasound guidance, 18 mL of serous fluid was aspirated, and 25 mg of hydrocortisone acetate in lignocaine was injected, followed by a pressure dressing. Two weeks later, 22 mL were aspirated to dryness under identical conditions, and one week later 25 mL were removed. Three further aspirations were performed; the last included an injection of 6 mL of 25% dextrose, but the collection persisted.

A 47-year-old man presented with acute epigastric pain radiating to the back and profuse sweating. He was obese, a smoker, with known hypertension but no regular medications. On examination, blood pressure was 210/120 mm Hg; other vital signs were normal. The abdomen was distended without rebound tenderness. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (white blood cell count 12 000/µL with 55% neutrophils) and normal hematocrit, platelet count, coagulation profile, and serum biochemistry. Abdominal ultrasonography was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen revealed a large retroperitoneal hematoma at the site of the left adrenal gland, with minimal contrast extravasation.

A 70‐year‐old man presented with proximal upper‐limb weakness for several years and, over the past 2 months, progressive lower‐limb weakness with gait disturbance and falls. He had no significant medical history. Examination revealed bilateral shoulder‐girdle muscle atrophy and a kyphoscoliotic spine; vital signs were normal. Neurologic examination showed MRC strength 0/5 in deltoids bilaterally, 3/5 in biceps and triceps, normal wrist strength, 3/5 hip flexors and knee flexors, and preserved ankle strength. Deep tendon reflexes were absent in the upper limbs and present in the lower limbs; abdominal reflexes were depressed on the left; bilateral Babinski signs; tactile hypoesthesia of the left upper limb; muscle fasciculations in the upper limbs; and urinary incontinence. Cranial nerves were intact; there was no family history of neurodegenerative disease. Nerve conduction studies were normal. Needle EMG showed a chronic, slowly evolving neurogenic pattern. Cervical spine MRI revealed multilevel disc protrusions and herniations from C2 to C6 with significant spinal‐cord compression (70% stenosis at C3‐C4, 40% at C4‐C5, 50% at C5‐C6) and spinal‐cord edema. Head CT showed cerebral atrophy without acute lesions. Laboratory tests revealed mild hypoproteinemia and hypoalbuminemia; urine culture was negative.

A 77-year-old man was evaluated for acute dyspnea and tachyarrhythmia. He had a 150 pack-year smoking history and past occupations as a tailor and metalworker. His medical history included hypertension (on olmesartan), partial gastrectomy for peptic ulcer, and a recent stroke treated with aspirin. He denied heart disease, diabetes, fever, cough, or chest pain. 

On presentation, heart rate was 166 beats per minute in atrial fibrillation, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, and arterial blood gas showed PaO₂ 57 mmHg with normal PaCO₂ and pH. He reported several months of exertional dyspnea. Laboratory tests revealed macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin 11 g/dL, MCV 104 fL), leukocytes 10.5 × 10⁹/L (80% neutrophils), and CRP 28.7 mg/L. An electrocardiogram confirmed paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, managed with amiodarone and anticoagulation.

Chest radiography showed a right, organized pleural effusion. Chest CT confirmed a right pleural effusion with thickening of the right parietal and mediastinal pleura, suggestive of malignant pleural disease, without lymphadenopathy and with compressive atelectasis of adjacent lung.

Medical thoracoscopy was performed, obtaining multiple pleural biopsies and draining 850 mL of pleural fluid. The fluid was orange-colored, corpusculated, and fibrinous. Analysis showed pH 7.18, lactate 9.9 mmol/L, LDH 7849 IU/L, and protein 5.7 g/dL, consistent with an exudate. Cytology revealed an inflammatory pattern (60.9% neutrophils, 36.5% lymphocytes) with no malignant cells.  
Mycobacterial culture of the fluid was negative. Peripheral lymphocyte subset typing by flow cytometry excluded lymphoid malignancies.

A term neonate presented with acute respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation after 3 days of worsening cough and apnea. She had an unvaccinated sibling with upper respiratory symptoms. A sepsis evaluation was initiated; a pertussis PCR returned positive on hospital day 2. Her lung compliance worsened with refractory hypercarbia, right ventricular failure from severe pulmonary hypertension, hemodynamic instability, and fluid overload, prompting cannulation to venoarterial ECMO within 30 hours of admission. Due to abdominal distention and feeding intolerance, total parenteral nutrition was started on day 3. On hospital day 9, a new, progressive lactic acidosis (lactate >3 mmol/L and climbing) was noted. A septic workup, multiple abdominal evaluations, and attempts to clear lactate by increasing ECMO circuit flows and CRRT did not improve lactate levels.
