Liver dysfunction and inborn errors of metabolism were considered and ruled out. Carnitine and coenzyme Q10 were supplemented without benefit. Lactate remained elevated, peaking at 10.4 mmol/L.

A 49-year-old woman presented with painless swelling in her right inguinal region. She had a history of a cesarean section and no history of infantile inguinal hernia. On physical examination, there was a soft, egg-shaped mass extending from the right inguinal region to the labia majora; the mass was visible when she stood and disappeared when she lay down. Ultrasonography revealed a well-defined, hypo-echoic, elongated mass that extended from the superficial inguinal canal, with no solid component. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 55 × 34 × 95 mm oval fluid collection in the right inguinal region adjacent to the cecum and retroperitoneum. Total colonoscopy demonstrated no mucosal abnormalities but revealed an extrinsic mass pushing against the cecal wall.

An 18-year-old white woman presented with progressive, painless bilateral facial swelling of several years’ duration. She reported difficulty opening her mouth, with maximal interincisal opening of approximately 2 cm. On examination, there was bilateral mandibular enlargement and eversion of the lower vestibule. The eruption pattern was notable for full eruption of the right lower third molar, partial eruption of the left lower third molar, and full eruption of both upper third molars; the overlying mucosa appeared normal.

Laboratory studies revealed:
– Alkaline phosphatase: 20 IU/L (normal adult 13–43 IU/L)  
– Serum calcium: 8.6 mg/dL (normal 8.8–11.0 mg/dL)  
– Serum phosphorus: 4.1 mg/dL (normal adult 2.5–4.8 mg/dL)  
– Parathyroid hormone: 21.3 pg/mL (normal 13–54 pg/mL)

Maxillofacial CT with 3-D reconstruction showed bilateral, multilocular, osteolytic lesions of the mandibular rami and angles with thin, eroded vestibular and lingual cortical plates and multiple deep depressions; the condyles and mandibular bases were spared. Panoramic radiograph demonstrated “soap‐bubble” cavities in both mandibular rami.

An incisional biopsy of the left mandibular lesion was performed. Histologic sections demonstrated loosely arranged fibrous connective tissue, a discrete number of blood vessels, various bone trabeculae, osteoid tissue, and relatively few multinucleated giant cells.

A 47-year-old man with homelessness, chronic hepatitis C, active intravenous drug use, and a 30 pack-year smoking history was admitted with respiratory distress and septic shock. He had no history of liver or gastrointestinal disease and reported no significant alcohol intake. On admission, he was hypotensive (mean arterial pressure <65 mm Hg), tachycardic (heart rate 130/min), and hypoxemic (oxygen saturation 80%). Laboratory evaluation showed leukocytosis (18 000/µL), elevated C-reactive protein (250 mg/dL; reference <5 mg/dL), elevated procalcitonin (2.2 ng/mL; reference <0.5 ng/mL), and markedly elevated transaminases (ALT ~50× normal, AST ~100× normal). Bilirubin, γ-glutamyltransferase (GGT), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and albumin were within normal limits. Chest CT demonstrated bilateral pneumonia; abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable. He required mechanical ventilation and high-dose catecholamines and developed a renal infarction and paralytic ileus, both of which resolved. After one week, his transaminases normalized. Ten days later he was transferred for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation for worsening respiratory failure; after 30 days on ECMO, he returned to the ward. At that time, liver tests were normal except for mildly elevated GGT. During his ward stay, GGT rose to ~30× normal and ALP to ~10× normal, while bilirubin remained normal. Abdominal ultrasound now showed extrahepatic biliary dilation (common bile duct 12 mm) with hyperechoic longitudinal material within the duct.

A 21-year-old woman of Philippine descent was referred for evaluation of right upper quadrant abdominal pain of one year’s duration. She had no prior medical history. Physical examination and laboratory tests were normal. An abdominal ultrasound showed cholecystolithiasis and incidentally revealed a cystic lesion in the tail of the pancreas. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 24 mm cystic lesion in the pancreatic tail abutting the spleen, with thickening and enhancement of the caudal cyst wall. MRI of the pancreas showed a 31 mm cystic lesion that was hyperintense on T1-weighted images, consistent with prior hemorrhage; the cyst wall enhanced in the venous phase, with focal central enhancement in the arterial phase, and the rim exhibited diffusion restriction on diffusion-weighted imaging. At a multidisciplinary conference, a solid pseudopapillary neoplasm with prior hemorrhage was considered most likely; cystic neuroendocrine tumor and mucinous cystadenoma were also included in the differential. Endoscopic ultrasound was not performed, and a spleen-preserving distal pancreatectomy was planned.

A 54-year-old previously healthy farmer from rural Sri Lanka presented with 10 days of fever with chills and rigors and painful right leg swelling after a cut injury. Twelve days earlier, he sustained a laceration on his right leg while walking in a paddy field; the wound became painful with purulent discharge and was associated with a tender right inguinal lymph node, loss of appetite, and malaise. He was an occasional alcohol consumer and a nonsmoker.  

Initially, he received oral antibiotics from a general practitioner. He then was hospitalized locally for five days and treated for presumed wound sepsis with intravenous cefotaxime and flucloxacillin, with incision and drainage—without clinical improvement.  

On transfer, he was febrile. Examination showed a superficial purulent wound on the anterior right leg (5 cm proximal to the ankle), surrounding cellulitis, and tender right inguinal lymphadenopathy; cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal exams were otherwise normal.  

Laboratory studies on admission: WBC 14,000 cells/mm3 (88% neutrophils), hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, platelets 204,000/mm3; blood smear with neutrophil leukocytosis, left shift, and toxic changes; CRP 173 mg/L; ESR 18 mm/hr; normal liver and renal function. Abdominal ultrasound showed an enlarged right inguinal lymph node without abscess. Blood and urine cultures were negative; a wound swab grew an organism pending further identification. He was started on intravenous ceftriaxone and local wound care.  

Five days later, he developed worsening dry cough, dyspnea, intermittent fever (99°F), and oliguria. He was tachypneic (25 breaths/min), tachycardic (144 beats/min), blood pressure 116/60 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. Bibasal crackles were noted; heart and abdominal exams remained unremarkable.  

He was admitted to the ICU with type 1 respiratory failure and vasodilatory shock, intubated, ventilated, and started on inotropes. Repeat studies showed: WBC 23,000 cells/mm3 with persistent left shift; platelets 112,000/mm3; CRP 420 mg/L; ESR 20 mm/hr; creatinine 356 μmol/L; blood urea 81 mg/dL; oliguria; lactate 8 mmol/L; rising AST, ALT, ALP; prolonged PT, aPTT, INR; hyperkalemia; CPK 94 U/L. Chest radiograph revealed heterogeneous opacifications at the lung bases. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed no vegetations. Renal ultrasound demonstrated increased echogenicity. A repeat blood culture grew coagulase-negative staphylococci (thought to be a contaminant), and all cultures remained pending further identification. He was treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics including meropenem, teicoplanin, metronidazole, and doxycycline.

A 28-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of diarrhea, vomiting, high fevers, sore throat, and skin flushing. She had no recent travel, toxin or drug exposure, or gynecologic complaints, and she had not used tampons, as she was on intramuscular Depo-Provera contraception and not menstruating. Six years earlier, she had a toxic shock–like illness requiring intensive care. On examination, her temperature was 39.6°C, pulse 120/min, and blood pressure 110/70 mmHg; she appeared distressed and flushed with widespread erythema of the skin. Cardiac and other system examinations were normal; pelvic examination was normal. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 9.4×10^9/L with a left shift, C-reactive protein 250 ng/mL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 45 mm/hr, and arterial blood gases with a respiratory alkalosis (pH 7.57, PaO2 13.8 kPa, PaCO2 2.2 kPa). A chest radiograph was normal. She received aggressive intravenous fluids and, after blood cultures were obtained, cefuroxime and clarithromycin were started for presumed bacterial sepsis. The rash initially resembled severe sunburn and over two days exfoliated and desquamated; dermatology agreed it was consistent with toxic shock syndrome, and supportive care was recommended. Serum albumin fell to 20 g/L, and she remained febrile at 38–39°C. Blood and stool cultures were repeatedly sterile; cultures of throat, skin, and high vaginal swabs yielded no growth; paired serologic titres for streptococcal and staphylococcal antibodies showed no rise; rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies, and other autoantibodies were negative; C1 esterase inhibitor and complement levels were normal; and screens for viruses, toxic metals, cardiolipin antibody, urinary porphyrins, and porphobilinogen were all negative. Five days after admission, her fever rose to 40°C, she became delirious, her pulse increased to 140/min, and an echocardiogram was normal. She was transferred to the intensive care unit, and because she had not responded to antibiotics and no bacteria had been cultured after five days, a decision was made to administer empirical corticosteroids.

A 67-year-old woman with a history of right-sided colon adenocarcinoma underwent an uncomplicated laparoscopic-assisted extended right hemicolectomy and was discharged on postoperative day 5. On postoperative day 10, she returned with diffuse abdominal pain, hematemesis, and subjective fevers. Abdominal CT showed free intraperitoneal fluid and pneumoperitoneum; broad-spectrum antibiotics were started, and she underwent an exploratory laparotomy. A small anastomotic leak was found and resected; an end ileostomy was created. Intraoperative vital signs were stable except for a low-grade tachycardia. She was extubated after surgery but remained obtunded. Her oxygen saturation stayed above 95% on supplemental oxygen with airway adjuncts, yet she failed to regain consciousness and developed apnea requiring bag-valve-mask ventilation. Naloxone, glycopyrrolate, and neostigmine were administered without improvement. Blood glucose was normal. Arterial blood gas revealed pH 7.03, PCO2 107 mm Hg, and PaO2 375 mm Hg. She was re-intubated for hypercapnic respiratory failure, and sedating medications were held. Given persistent unresponsiveness, a noncontrast head CT was obtained, showing diffuse cerebral edema with tonsillar herniation and hydrocephalus, most pronounced in the parietal and occipital regions. An external ventricular drain was placed, and measures to control intracranial pressure—including hypertonic saline, head elevation, normotension, and seizure prophylaxis—were initiated.

A 17-year-old boy from a village in Saudi Arabia presented with a 2-week history of fever, vomiting, and malaise, followed by 5 days of left upper-quadrant abdominal pain. He reported ingesting unpasteurized milk and had lost 9 kg over 2 months. He had been treated with antibiotics at another hospital without improvement. 

On examination, he appeared ill and in pain; temperature was 38.4 °C, pulse 116 bpm, blood pressure 111/68 mmHg, and respiratory rate 21 breaths/min. Abdominal examination showed moderate tenderness in the left hypochondrium without palpable organomegaly; bowel sounds were normal.

Laboratory tests revealed WBC 4.12 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, platelets 364 × 10^9/L, ESR 61 mm/H, CRP 66.5 mg/L, amylase 509 U/L, lipase 471 U/L, ALT 45 U/L, AST 32 U/L, ALP 162 U/L, γ-GT 86 U/L, total bilirubin 0.2 mg/dL, albumin 39 g/L, creatinine 0.5 mg/dL, urea 3.2 mmol/L, and LDH 303 U/L. Chest X-ray and abdominal X-ray were unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed multiple irregular peripheral hypodense splenic lesions suggestive of splenic infarcts and borderline splenomegaly, with patent splenic veins and no evidence of acute pancreatitis.

A 62-year-old Caucasian man with a history of follicular non-Hodgkin lymphoma presented in June 2020 with progressive vision loss. He had been treated initially with R-CHOP in 2010 and, after recurrence in 2017, with R-bendamustine followed by rituximab maintenance until February 2020. During maintenance he experienced recurrent urinary tract infections, gingivitis, and herpes zoster reactivation. On examination he was afebrile with normal vital signs and had a right homonymous hemianopia; the remainder of the neurological and general examinations was unremarkable.

Noncontrast head CT revealed an uneven hypodense cortical and subcortical lesion in the left posterior temporal and occipital lobes without enhancement. MRI demonstrated a left parenchymal lesion with two components: a periventricular area of inhomogeneous T1 hypointensity and T2 hyperintensity, and a more uniform white-matter region of T2 and FLAIR hyperintensity with T1 hypointensity. Both components showed restricted diffusion, and there was no gadolinium enhancement. MR spectroscopy showed decreased N-acetyl aspartate, elevated choline, and a double lactate peak. Total-body contrast CT showed no evidence of active lymphoma and only two stable lymph nodes.

Brain biopsy revealed numerous CD68+ macrophages, isolated reactive astrocytes, and mild perivascular T-lymphocyte infiltrates; no neoplastic cells were identified. No microbiological studies were performed on the tissue. The patient was discharged but returned with worsening vision, mental confusion, and psychomotor slowing. Laboratory studies including CBC, CRP, electrolytes, renal and liver function tests were unremarkable. Repeat MRI showed marked enlargement of the left temporal–parietal–occipital and peritrigonal lesion, now crossing the corpus callosum with vasogenic edema and slight mass effect; there remained no contrast enhancement, and DWI again showed restricted diffusion at the lesion edges.

A 14-year-old girl presented with a 1-year history of persistent diffuse swelling of the upper lip and a 2-month history of diffuse anterior gingival enlargement with bleeding. She also reported a 1.5-year history of craving and eating clay, mud, and paint flakes. Her past medical history was notable for elevated serum IgE levels and menorrhagia for the past year. There were no respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms, no family history of atopy or Crohn’s disease, and she was not taking any medications.

On examination, the upper lip showed a localized, symmetrical, pale pink swelling with a uniform smooth surface; it was firm, nontender, and without nodules. Intraorally, there was diffuse enlargement of the marginal, interdental, and attached gingiva in the maxillary and mandibular anterior region, covering two-thirds of the labial tooth surfaces. There was no facial nerve palsy, fissured tongue, cobblestone mucosa, or oral ulcers, and regional lymph nodes were not enlarged.

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, neutrophilic leukocytosis, elevated eosinophil count, and serum IgE above the reference range. Peripheral smear showed dimorphic anemia (iron deficiency and macrocytic features), with vitamin B12 at the low end of normal. Hormonal assays, including thyroid function, FSH, and LH, were within normal limits. Pelvic ultrasonography was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasonography showed no hepatobiliary or intestinal abnormalities. Panoramic radiograph revealed mild interdental horizontal bone loss in the maxillary anterior region.

Incisional biopsies of the upper lip and gingiva demonstrated hyperplastic parakeratinized stratified squamous epithelium overlying connective tissue with perivascular aggregates of lymphocytes and plasma cells, and well-formed noncaseating granulomas composed of lymphocytes, macrophages, and multinucleated giant cells.

A 28-month-old girl was referred for evaluation of a 3-month history of persistent cough, wheeze, and increased work of breathing despite oral antibiotics and high-dose inhaled corticosteroids. There was no history of witnessed foreign-body aspiration or feeding-related symptoms. She was born at term with an uneventful neonatal course. Since age 1 year, she had intermittent cough and wheeze treated as asthma; there was no family history of atopy.

On examination, growth parameters were normal. Respiratory rate was 40 breaths/minute without retractions. Oxygen saturation was 94–95% on room air, and she was afebrile. Lung auscultation revealed decreased air exchange over the left lung; the remainder of the examination was normal.

A chest radiograph showed hyperlucency of the left lung. A barium swallow study was normal, with no esophageal indentation or evidence of gastroesophageal reflux. Routine hematology and biochemistry tests were within normal limits. Virology PCR for CMV, EBV, and adenovirus was negative. Acid-fast bacilli smear, culture, and TB PCR were negative.

Flexible bronchoscopy revealed no airway foreign body but demonstrated significant external, nonpulsatile compression of the left main bronchus, with otherwise normal airway anatomy. A thoracic CT angiogram showed a soft-tissue mass in the middle mediastinum compressing the carina and proximal right and left main bronchi, more pronounced on the left. MRI of the thorax with contrast revealed a lobulated cystic mass lesion.

A 36-year-old Japanese man with a 14-month history of HIV infection (CD4 count persistently <200 cells/mm3 despite HAART) presented with a four-week history of fever, pulsating headache, lumbago, nausea, and vomiting. He had completed treatment for Pneumocystis pneumonia and was maintained on atovaquone for P. jirovecii prophylaxis because of intolerance to trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole and pentamidine. On examination, his temperature was 38.2°C and he had neck stiffness. Chest radiography and noncontrast CT of the brain were normal. Lumbar puncture revealed an elevated neutrophil count in cerebrospinal fluid, and he was treated empirically for purulent meningitis; however, his symptoms persisted despite broad-spectrum antimicrobials. CD4-positive lymphocyte count was 146 cells/μL. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay revealed no rise in IgG or IgM anti–Toxoplasma gondii antibodies. Three weeks after admission, worsening headache and lumbago prompted MRI of the brain and lumbar spine, which showed multiple small ring-enhancing nodules in the pons and cerebellum, peripheral enhancement suggesting granuloma formation, and corresponding vertebral lesions—findings suggestive of tuberculous meningitis. However, PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis in the CSF was negative.

A 54-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of progressively worsening neck pain and numbness of the left upper extremity and left face, without trauma. His symptoms fluctuated initially but gradually worsened over 2 months, prompting evaluation. Neurologic examination showed a mildly spastic gait and exaggerated deep tendon reflexes in all extremities; muscle strength and vibration sense were normal, and there was no Babinski sign. He reported mild dysuria and constipation. Laboratory tests, including peripheral blood studies, were unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was within normal limits except for a slightly elevated protein concentration (65 mg/dl; normal, 10–40 mg/dl). Unenhanced computed tomography of the cervicothoracic spine revealed diffuse dorsal epidural calcification extending from C3 to T6, appearing as a crescent-shaped mass along the dura mater with a well-defined border at the vertebral arch. Magnetic resonance imaging showed the lesion to be hypointense on T1- and T2-weighted images, with heterogeneous enhancement on post-contrast T1-weighted sequences, causing cervical spinal canal stenosis. Head imaging was normal. Based on these findings, CPPD crystal deposition of the ligamentum flavum was suspected, and a C5–6 laminectomy was planned for biopsy confirmation.

A 37-year-old African American woman with a 6-week history of persistent dry cough, intermittent low-grade fever, night sweats, fatigue, weakness, and exertional dyspnea presented for evaluation. She denied orthopnea, PND, toxic exposures, weight loss, appetite changes, or joint pain. She was a non-smoker and social drinker.  
On admission: temperature 100.2 °F; pulse 113 beats/min; respirations 18 breaths/min; BP 150/80 mm Hg; PaO₂ 60 mm Hg on room air. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies: WBC 11,600 cells/μL (82% neutrophils, 13% lymphocytes), hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, MCV 82 fL, platelets 518,000 cells/μL, ESR 117 mm/hr, CRP 7 mg/dL.  
Chest radiograph: nodular infiltrates in bilateral upper lobes and perihilar fullness. CT chest: extensive bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy with perihilar and peripheral consolidation. Pulmonary function tests: mild restrictive pattern.  
Initial differential diagnosis included atypical pneumonia, tuberculosis, fungal or other opportunistic infections, sarcoidosis, interstitial lung disease, connective tissue or autoimmune disease, lymphoma, and occult malignancy.  
She received erythromycin and ceftriaxone (later changed to moxifloxacin) without improvement. Blood and sputum cultures for bacteria, mycobacteria, and fungi were repeatedly negative. PPD and HIV tests were negative. Serologic analyses for rheumatoid factor, ANA, and ANCA were negative. CT abdomen and pelvis were unremarkable.  
A mediastinal lymph node biopsy showed only reactive anthracosis with no granulomas or malignant cells.

A 34-year-old woman with a smoking history and a past history of asthma, nasal polyps, and sinusitis presented with sudden severe chest pain followed by ventricular fibrillation. After successful resuscitation, her consciousness and vital signs were normal. Cardiac enzymes were elevated (CK-MB 7.1 ng/mL [<5.0 ng/mL]; troponin I 0.23 ng/mL [<0.028 ng/mL]). ECG showed right ventricular hypertrophy without ischaemic changes. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated preserved left ventricular function, right ventricular dilatation, tricuspid regurgitation with a peak gradient of 61 mmHg, and an RV fractional area change of 16.5%. Emergent contrast-enhanced CT excluded pulmonary embolism and aortic dissection. Urgent right heart catheterization revealed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 66 mmHg, indicating severe pulmonary hypertension. 

During hospitalization, she experienced recurrent chest pains despite therapy with benidipine, nicorandil, and nitrates; ECG during episodes showed ST-segment elevation in leads I and aVL, large T waves in V3–V6, and ST-segment depression in II, III, and aVF. She also developed severe hypoxaemia (SpO₂ 92% on 10 L/min O₂) that did not improve after two weeks of high-dose inhaled corticosteroids. 

On transfer to our center, examination revealed an accentuated second heart sound but was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed troponin T 0.244 ng/mL (<0.1 ng/mL) and marked hypereosinophilia (2.0 × 10⁹/L; 17% of leukocytes). ANCA tests and specific IgE for Aspergillus were negative on two occasions. Stool studies for parasites were negative. Chest CT demonstrated centrilobular nodular opacities. ¹⁸F-FDG-PET showed diffuse pulmonary uptake. Repeat right heart catheterization showed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mmHg and a pulmonary vascular resistance of 12 Wood units.

A 28-year-old man presented with a 24-hour history of sudden-onset odynophagia that began 3–4 hours after dinner. He reported that the pain was initially limited to solids but then progressed to include liquids. He admitted to taking his nightly isotretinoin 40 mg immediately after finishing dinner; he had been on this regimen for 5 months. He denied prior episodes of dysphagia, odynophagia, heartburn, or chest pain and had no history of gastroesophageal reflux disease, immunosuppression, or autoimmune disease. His only other medication was vitamin D 5,000 IU weekly (last dose 5 days earlier). He did not use tobacco or alcohol.

On presentation, vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed a well-appearing man in mild distress but able to handle secretions; the oropharynx was unremarkable. Complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, and electrocardiogram were all normal. Chest radiography showed no acute findings. Administration of a gastrointestinal cocktail (aluminum hydroxide and viscous lidocaine) provided no relief.

Given persistent symptoms, an urgent esophagogastroduodenoscopy was performed. Endoscopy revealed two superficial, nonbleeding ulcers in the proximal esophagus (largest 7 mm). The remainder of the esophagus appeared normal without rings, furrows, exudates, edema, stenosis, or distal erosive changes. The stomach showed patchy moderate inflammation; the duodenal bulb was normal. Biopsy specimens from the edges of an esophageal ulcer demonstrated focal mild active esophagitis with necroinflammatory exudate.

A 56-year-old Bangladeshi man presented with a 3-month history of high-grade fever and multiple nodular skin lesions. The lesions first appeared on the thigh and later involved the trunk; some enlarged, ulcerated, and discharged pus. He completed several courses of antibiotics for presumed bacterial abscesses without improvement. He reported a 6 kg weight loss over 3 months. His medical history included hypertension, ischemic heart disease, chronic kidney disease (eGFR 30 ml/min/1.73 m2), and a 2-year history of undifferentiated spondyloarthritis treated irregularly with NSAIDs and prednisolone (20 mg daily), plus one intra-articular steroid injection 6 months ago. He denied any prior tuberculosis or known exposure.

On examination, he had central obesity, facial puffiness, thinning skin, and no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Multiple warm, tender nodules of variable size and some ulceration were present on the abdomen, back (largest 4 × 3 cm), and thighs. Both knees were swollen with effusion and tenderness; range of motion was restricted. Proximal muscle bulk and power were reduced in both lower limbs; tone and reflexes were normal.

Laboratory studies showed normal blood counts, ESR 40 mm/hr, CRP 85.8 mg/L, serum creatinine 1.7 mg/dL, and eGFR 30 ml/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis was unremarkable; urine AFB smear and culture were negative. Sputum AFB smear and culture were negative. High-resolution CT of the chest, colonoscopy, and CT of the abdomen and pelvis were all normal.

A 78-year-old Hispanic man who had recently immigrated from Mexico presented with a three-day history of jaw pain and a sensation of abdominal bloating. His only medical history was untreated hypertension. He denied allergies, and the use of tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs.  
On examination, his temperature was 36.9 °C, blood pressure 165/109 mm Hg, pulse 88 beats/min, and respiratory rate 18 breaths/min. He had difficulty opening his mouth and spoke with dysphonia. There was no reproducible pain, but he was uncomfortable when his mouth was forced open. Limited oral examination revealed no caries or abscesses, and no cervical lymphadenopathy. The remainder of the ear, nose, and throat examination was unremarkable.  
The abdomen was rigid and mildly distended but non-tender. On the medial aspect of his right forearm was a healing 5 × 2 cm laceration. He reported that the wound had occurred two weeks earlier when he fell from a tractor into muddy water and had since applied a topical medication prescribed in Mexico. He denied receiving any tetanus prophylaxis for the wound or any prior vaccinations.  
Laboratory studies and computed tomography of the head and neck were within normal limits.

A 20‐year‐old man, previously healthy and not taking medications, presented with a two‐month history of swollen glands. One month before presentation, he noted multiple enlarged cervical, occipital, and right inguinal lymph nodes. He denied fever, night sweats, weight loss, or other constitutional symptoms. He was born and raised in the USA, had no recent travel or sick contacts, and had no occupational exposures. 

On examination, he was afebrile with normal vital signs. There were enlarged, non‐tender, freely movable bilateral cervical and occipital lymph nodes measuring up to 4 cm, and similarly enlarged right inguinal nodes. The left palatine tonsil was slightly erythematous and enlarged; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

A heterophile antibody (monospot) test was negative for Epstein–Barr virus infection. He was treated empirically with azithromycin for three days and, one week later, with amoxicillin–clavulanate because of persistent lymphadenopathy. Initial laboratory tests showed normal blood counts and serum electrolytes. An HIV antibody ELISA test was also negative. 

On return for re‐evaluation, the lymphadenopathy was unchanged and he remained asymptomatic aside from the enlarged nodes. Further history revealed that approximately one month earlier he had eaten raw kibbe, a traditional uncooked beef or lamb dish.

A 14-year-old boy presented in February 2020 with a 3-month history of persistent fever of unknown origin, constipation, and diffuse abdominal and lower back pain. On examination, a large abdominal mass was palpable from the right iliac fossa to the hypogastrium. Laboratory studies revealed elevated lactate dehydrogenase and a mild normocytic, normochromic anemia. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 170-mm segment of small-bowel wall thickening (maximum thickness, 53 mm) with luminal stenosis, inhomogeneous enhancement, and adjacent mesenteric lymphadenopathy. Video-laparoscopic Tru-Cut biopsies of the mass showed atypical lymphoid cells with a Ki-67 index of 100%, overexpression of c-Myc protein (>70%), t(8;14) MYC-IgG translocation, and an immunophenotype of CD45+, CD20+, PAX5+, CD79a+, CD38+, CD3−, CD5−. Bone marrow biopsy was normal. A diagnosis of stage III Burkitt lymphoma was made, and the patient received six cycles of chemotherapy according to the AIEOP LNH97 protocol. Serial ultrasound examinations revealed progressive reduction of the mass. In June 2020, an 18F-FDG PET/CT scan showed dramatic reduction of the bowel-wall thickening (17 mm) but intense focal FDG uptake in the distal ileum (SUVmax 7). In July 2020, after completion of therapy, repeat PET/CT demonstrated stable ileal wall thickening (17 mm) with increased tracer uptake (SUVmax 10.3) and no other abnormalities; the patient remained asymptomatic.

A 16-year-old previously healthy young man first presented with a 3-month history of pain and swelling in the right upper leg just below the knee. He denied fever or erythema and had received no prior antibiotics. On examination, the proximal tibia was slightly swollen and tender medially, with mildly decreased knee motion and an antalgic gait. Laboratory studies showed an ESR of 40 mm/hr, a CRP of 0.9 g/dL, and a leukocyte count of 6900 cells/μL. Plain radiographs revealed increased density and heterotopic bone formation along the medial proximal tibia concerning for chronic osteomyelitis, with tumor or subacute fracture also considered. Contrast MRI confirmed findings consistent with chronic osteomyelitis of the proximal tibial epiphysis and metaphysis, with a cloaca extending from a cortical disruption. He underwent open surgical debridement; cultures were sterile. A QuantiFERON Gold assay was non-reactive. Empiric nafcillin was administered for 6 weeks, followed by 6 months of cephalexin, with marked clinical improvement and normalization of inflammatory markers. Ten months after surgery, imaging showed a 1.3 cm leg-length discrepancy but no active disease, and he returned to sports without incident. 

Approximately 1 year after completing therapy, he noted a 7-day history of pain, redness, and swelling over the inner proximal right tibia at the prior surgical site, although his father reported symptoms for several months. He was afebrile. Examination demonstrated a firm, tender, erythematous mass along the medial proximal tibia beneath the surgical scar; knee motion was normal. ESR, CRP, and leukocyte counts were within normal limits. Radiographs showed worsening sclerotic changes and three lucent areas in the medial proximal tibia. Contrast MRI revealed abnormal signal intensity in the proximal tibial metaphysis and epiphysis with a fluid collection connected to a presumed chronic osteomyelitis nidus via a tract running inferior to the physis. He was taken to the operating room for abscess drainage and bone curettage.

A 30-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 2, presented at 34 weeks + 2 days of gestation with uterine contractions and fever. She was diagnosed as COVID-19 positive on admission. Her first two children were full term without neonatal jaundice. She had no history of hypertension, diabetes, epilepsy, or drug use, and her initial antenatal screen at 9 weeks was negative for red-cell antibodies. There were no further antenatal antibody screens.

A male infant was delivered vaginally with a birth weight of 2.67 kg and Apgar scores of 7 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes. On examination, the neonate was hypothermic (33.4 °C), had mild hepatomegaly (liver span 4.8 cm), and a cord blood pH of 7.214. An intravenous line was placed, and inotropic support was initiated.

Laboratory studies on day 1 showed hemoglobin 13.3 g/dL (reference 15.0–24.0), hematocrit 37% (44–70%), leukocyte count 8.84×10^3/mm^3 (9.1–34.0×10^3), platelets 274×10^3/mm^3 (84–478×10^3), and reticulocyte count 9.3%. Prothrombin time was 11.9 s (control 10 s). Peripheral blood smear revealed numerous spherocytes, nucleated red cells, and polychromasia.

By 16 hours of life, the infant was icteric up to the thighs (total serum bilirubin 11.3 mg/dL; normal <5.0 mg/dL). Liver enzymes were mildly elevated (ALT 113 U/L; GGT 65 U/L; albumin 20 g/L). TORCH screening and testing for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency were negative. The neonate’s blood group was A RhD-positive. A polyspecific direct antiglobulin test was strongly positive (4+), and monospecific testing identified IgG on the red cells.

A 51-year-old Middle Eastern woman presented with sudden onset of severe sharp pain over the outer aspect of her right hip, beginning one week earlier without trauma. She had tried over-the-counter NSAIDs with minimal relief. On examination, both hips had full range of motion; the right hip was warm and tender, and pain was elicited with FABER testing. A year earlier, radiographs had shown calcifications at both greater trochanters, and she had a history of calcific tendonitis in both shoulders treated with steroid injection and arthroscopic removal. 

Routine blood tests and a metabolic screen showed normal renal function, a normal bone profile, and a vitamin D level of 58 nmol/L. Repeat pelvic radiographs demonstrated patchy calcification at the insertion of the gluteus medius and trochanteric bursa on both sides. Ultrasound of the right hip revealed a large focus of hyperechoic calcification up to 2.5 cm within the gluteus medius and minimus tendons, with surrounding hypoechoic rim and excess fluid in the trochanteric bursa.

A 4-day-old male infant was brought with abdominal distension, bilious vomiting, and no passage of meconium since birth. The parents noted frequent bilious vomiting immediately after breastfeeding. He was born preterm via normal vaginal delivery to a mother with gestational diabetes mellitus managed with insulin; there was no significant family history. On examination, the abdomen was distended with hyperperistaltic bowel sounds. The anal opening was present, and a per-rectal examination revealed uniform rectal ballooning. General examination showed severe dehydration, scoliosis, and a right ectopic kidney. 

Ultrasonography of the whole abdomen demonstrated dilated large-bowel loops with collapsed small bowel, decreased peristalsis, and normal vascularity, suggestive of intestinal obstruction. A plain abdominal X-ray revealed centrally dilated bowel loops and absence of gas in the pelvis. Laboratory studies showed an elevated total leukocyte count and decreased serum sodium and potassium levels.

A 61-year-old woman with hypertension treated with amlodipine presented for neuro-ophthalmology evaluation of left eye vision loss. One month earlier, she had developed left herpes zoster ophthalmicus with skin lesions on the forehead, side, and tip of the nose and was treated with oral valacyclovir for 10 days. Three days after the onset of rash, an ophthalmologist noted 1+ anterior chamber cells and an intraocular pressure of 18 mm Hg and started prednisolone acetate 1% drops four times daily. The examination was stable one week later. Two weeks after the uveitis diagnosis, she developed left eye pain and worsening vision. Intraocular pressure was 52 mm Hg without signs of uveitis; gonioscopy showed open angles (Shaffer grade 3) with a visible trabecular meshwork 360° in both eyes. Topical prednisolone acetate was discontinued, and she was given acetazolamide and brimonidine-timolol, with prompt reduction of IOP to 16 mm Hg the next day. However, a new left relative afferent pupillary defect was noted along with optic disc edema. On neuro-ophthalmology examination, vision was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/100 in the left eye, there was a left RAPD, and Humphrey visual field testing showed a left inferior altitudinal defect. Anterior segment examination showed no active uveitis. Dilated funduscopy revealed a normal right optic nerve (cup-to-disc ratio 0.1) and diffuse optic disc edema on the left. Optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fiber layer measured 84 μm in the right eye and 182 μm in the left eye.

A previously healthy 23-month-old girl presented with a 2-day history of rhinorrhea, cough, decreased energy, sleepiness, tactile fever, and on the day before admission two episodes of nonbloody, nonbilious vomiting and several episodes of nonbloody diarrhea. She also developed generalized facial, arm, and leg swelling. She had completed a 10-day course of trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection, with the last dose 5 days earlier. On examination she was fussy but consolable, with mild bilateral conjunctival injection, dry lips, scattered bilateral crackles without tachypnea or retractions, and mild tachycardia without murmurs. Generalized edema, including periorbital and pedal edema, was noted. There was no jaundice, and her mentation was intact. Laboratory studies showed an AST of 889 IU/L, ALT of 740 IU/L, albumin 2.2 g/dL, INR 1.5, PTT 55 seconds, and normal bilirubin. Initial CBC revealed leukopenia (3.5 K/µL) and hemoglobin 10 g/dL; by hospital day 2 she had developed thrombocytopenia (platelets 77 K/µL) with a low reticulocyte count. Ferritin and lactate dehydrogenase were elevated. Acetaminophen level, urinalysis, blood and urine cultures were unremarkable. Viral hepatitis serologies and CMV PCR were negative; EBV IgG was positive with negative IgM. Celiac serologic tests were negative. Chest radiography showed mild bilateral pleural effusions, and abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated an enlarged, echogenic liver with pericholecystic fluid and gallbladder sludge.

A woman in her 50s with a history of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (diagnosed 6 months earlier and treated with siponimod for 5 months), type 2 diabetes mellitus complicated by proliferative diabetic retinopathy treated with pan-retinal photocoagulation, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, and chronic renal failure presented with a 6-day history of blurry vision in her left eye. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was count fingers at 2 ft in the right eye and 20/60 in the left eye without pinhole improvement. Intraocular pressure was 16 mm Hg bilaterally. Anterior segment examination was notable for moderate nuclear sclerotic cataracts. Fundus examination showed bilateral optic nerve head pallor (cup-to-disc ratio 0.3) and 360° photocoagulation scars; there was no prior history of macular oedema. Hemoglobin A1c one month earlier was 10.2%. Optical coherence tomography of the left eye revealed intraretinal and subretinal fluid in the fovea. Eight days later, repeat OCT demonstrated worsening bilateral cystoid macular oedema. Intravenous fluorescein angiography revealed late petaloid macular leakage and late optic disc staining.

A 48-year-old woman with no breast symptoms underwent routine screening mammography, which demonstrated a new 1.4-cm developing asymmetry in the inner quadrant of the right breast on craniocaudal and mediolateral oblique views. Targeted breast ultrasonography at the 4:00 position, 4 cm from the nipple, showed no discrete abnormality corresponding to the mammographic finding. Because the asymmetry persisted, a tomosynthesis-guided vacuum-assisted biopsy of the right inner breast was performed, yielding 12 core specimens. Histologic examination revealed marked perilobular and periductal mixed chronic inflammatory infiltrate enriched in eosinophils, with lymphocytes and plasma cells and no granulomata. The Allergy and Immunology service noted that the patient was asymptomatic, with no history of urticaria, asthma, angioedema, or pruritus except for seasonal allergic rhinitis. Peripheral blood eosinophil levels were within the normal range. Hypereosinophilic syndrome was excluded from consideration.

A 15-year-old male with known sickle cell disease (HbSS) presented with a 4-day history of persistent headache and two painful scalp swellings. The headache was constant, variable in intensity, unrelieved by simple analgesia, and without any history of trauma. He was on hydroxyurea and folic acid and had a history of multiple vaso-occlusive crises and a stroke without residual deficits. 

On examination, he appeared pale, icteric, and in pain. Temperature was 37.9°C, pulse 105 beats/min, blood pressure 105/65 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Two tender, fluctuant swellings were noted over the right parietal and left occipital regions with normal overlying skin; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL, hematocrit 26%, reticulocyte count 7.4%, white blood cell count 13.6 × 10^6/µL with 75.5% neutrophils, platelet count 415 × 10^6/µL, indirect bilirubin 2.7 mg/dL (conjugated 0.3 mg/dL), normal renal function, and a normal coagulation profile. Hemoglobin electrophoresis demonstrated HbS of 81.1%.

He was admitted and started on IV hydration, morphine, lornoxicam, and empirical amoxicillin-clavulanate. A nonenhanced head CT revealed skull bone infarction in the right parietal and left occipital regions with increased cortical bone thickness and two subgaleal fluid collections measuring 8 mm and 7 mm at their greatest dimensions, without evidence of intracranial extension. Right hemispheric atrophy and ipsilateral ventricular dilation consistent with prior ischemic insult were also noted.

A 73-year-old woman with Northern European ancestry and a 10-year history of open-angle glaucoma managed with laser trabeculoplasty, cataract surgery, and escalating topical therapy presented with markedly accelerated and asymmetric right-eye visual field loss over two years. She reported progressive peripheral vision loss but no diplopia, pain, or proptosis. Medical history included bilateral cataract extraction, acephalgic migraines, sleep apnea, hypercholesterolemia, cardiovascular disease, transient ischemic attack, and a T4B cutaneous melanoma of the left arm treated with wide excision, sentinel-node biopsy, and one month of interferon alfa-2b five years earlier. Medications were atorvastatin, acetylsalicylic acid, ramipril, and intermittent lorazepam, loperamide, sennosides, and an acetylsalicylic acid/caffeine/codeine combination. On exam, visual acuity was 20/150 OD and 20/25 OS with a right afferent pupillary defect, no ptosis or proptosis, and intraocular pressures of 26 mmHg OU. Despite maximal medical therapy, the right superior arcuate scotoma progressed to near-complete superotemporal and superonasal defects. The patient was intolerant of topical therapy side effects and declined glaucoma filtration surgery. Concern for metastatic melanoma impinging on the optic nerve prompted imaging. A CT of the head and orbits revealed a new 0.7×1.1 cm intraconal enhancing lesion at the superior medial right orbital apex with crowding of apical structures; imaging six years earlier was normal. Restaging CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 4 cm midpole renal lesion and a 0.4 cm hepatic lesion; abdominal imaging five years earlier had been normal.

A male infant was born at 34 + 6 weeks’ gestation weighing 1390 g (1st percentile) with Apgar scores of 7 and 8. He required CPAP and then BPAP for 24 hours before respiratory stability. Cranial ultrasound was normal. A grade II/VI systolic murmur prompted echocardiography, which showed a partial atrioventricular canal defect, pulmonary stenosis (80 mmHg gradient), a dysplastic pulmonary valve, and aorto-pulmonary collaterals. 

At birth, blood glucose was 35 mg/dL; a 10% glucose infusion normalized levels. Six hours later, glucose rose to 250 mg/dL. Broad-spectrum antibiotics were started for suspected sepsis, and a 5% glucose infusion continued. Continuous glucose monitoring confirmed persistent hyperglycaemia, and IV Humulin R at 0.01 U/kg/h was initiated. On day 7, insulin was withdrawn but severe hyperglycaemia recurred after 36 hours, necessitating resumption. 

The patient exhibited poor growth and steatorrhea. Abdominal ultrasound and low fecal elastase confirmed exocrine pancreatic insufficiency; pancrelipase was started. Mixed hyperbilirubinemia with hypocholic stools led to repeat galactosemia testing, which became positive; a lactose-free formula was introduced. Anemia required transfusion, and thiamine was trialled for presumed TRMA but was stopped after 7 days due to no improvement. These combined findings suggested a syndromic condition. Genetic testing was performed.

A 64-year-old man presented with swelling of the left gluteal and hip region. He had undergone five surgeries for bilateral elbow calcific masses during his first decade of life, but had no similar lesions for decades and no family history of calcinosis. Laboratory evaluation revealed mild hyperphosphatemia, normal levels of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and parathyroid hormone, and normal renal function.  
Plain radiographs showed a grossly periarticular calcified mass around the left hip joint and upper thigh. Contrast-enhanced multidetector CT demonstrated a grossly calcified lobular mass with large cystic areas and fluid-fluid levels inside (“CT sedimentation sign”) and only peripheral enhancement of cystic areas, without any pathologic solid portions. The lesion was localized to the region of the left greater trochanteric bursa, deep to the gluteal muscles, extending medially to the ischio-pubic branch and along the posterior compartment of the thigh.  
On MRI, the lesion had inhomogeneous diffuse low signal on T1-weighted sequences and alternating signal patterns on T2-weighted sequences with low-intensity areas and cystic components showing fluid-fluid levels (“MRI sedimentation sign”). After contrast administration, fibrous septa surrounding cystic and calcified areas enhanced, producing a “cobblestone” pattern. There was no nodular enhancement and no involvement of adjacent muscle, bone, vessels, or nerves.

A 4-year-old boy presented with a superficial lump on the left side of his abdominal wall for 1 month. Clinicians had considered a lipoma, an abscess, or a tuberculous abscess in the initial evaluation. On examination, the lesion measured 3.5 × 3 cm, was slightly tender, and felt soft to firm. Fine-needle aspiration was performed with a 22-gauge needle and 10 mL syringe without suction, yielding straw-colored, slightly turbid fluid. Smears were air-dried and stained with May–Grünwald–Giemsa and hematoxylin and eosin; one smear underwent a modified Ziehl–Neelsen stain to evaluate for tuberculosis. Microscopic examination showed numerous neutrophils, lymphocytes, palisading histiocytes, eosinophils, and degenerated cells. No granulomas or atypical cells were identified.

A 44-year-old woman with a history of possible inflammatory arthritis presented with abdominal fullness and early satiety. She had no family history or stigmata of connective tissue disease. Laboratory testing showed mildly elevated alanine aminotransferase (89 U/L; reference, 14–54 U/L). An abdominal ultrasound performed to evaluate possible gallbladder disease disclosed a mass in the neck of the pancreas. Contrast-enhanced CT imaging confirmed two well-circumscribed pancreatic nodules measuring approximately 1.4 cm and 0.6 cm in diameter; there was no lymphadenopathy or hepatic lesions. The patient also reported periodic diaphoresis and tremulousness; home glucose measurements during these episodes were as low as 60 mg/dL, with symptom resolution after oral glucose. Endoscopic ultrasound confirmed at least one hypoechoic pancreatic lesion, and fine-needle aspiration was nondiagnostic. The patient underwent a 72-hour supervised fast during which multiple serum glucose levels measured 40 mg/dL (reference, 70–125 mg/dL), but insulin was 9 mcIU/mL (reference, <18 mcIU/mL) and C-peptide was 0.2 ng/mL (reference, 1.0–7.6 ng/mL), findings felt to be inconsistent with an insulinoma.

A 24-year-old right‐hand–dominant man presented with a 2-year history of a slowly enlarging, “ball-like” swelling on the dorsal aspect of his right wrist. Over the past 6 months he noted intermittent, dull aching pain (3/10) over the lesion, worse with hand motion and partially relieved by analgesics. He denied trauma, constitutional symptoms, and had no pertinent medical or surgical history. On examination, there was an approximately 1-cm, well-circumscribed, soft and mobile lump over the second and third carpometacarpal (CMC) joints, surrounded by an underlying hard bony protuberance. Wrist flexion and extension were limited by 5°–10° with pain; other movements, neurovascular exam, and tendon testing were normal. Laboratory studies were within normal limits.  
Plain radiographs of the right hand and wrist showed osteophyte formation at the base of the second and third metacarpals and at the distal aspects of the capitate and trapezoid, with mild joint‐space narrowing.  
Wrist ultrasonography demonstrated a well-defined, subcutaneous cystic lesion measuring approximately 7 × 2 mm overlying the bony prominence.

A 24‐year‐old unmarried woman presented with a 2‐month history of gradually enlarging, mildly painful swelling over the right sternoclavicular joint, without any draining sinus. She also reported neck stiffness and pain with movement. Over the preceding 4 months, she had experienced cough, weight loss, severe nocturnal neck pain (“night cries”), and low‐grade fever. She denied trauma, prior tuberculosis, or known TB exposure. Multiple courses of antibiotics and analgesics had produced no improvement.

On examination, there was a 2 × 3 cm erythematous, warm, mildly tender swelling over the right sternoclavicular joint. Hemoglobin was 10.4 g/dL, white blood cell count 10.3 × 10^3/mm^3, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 34 mm/hr. HIV ELISA was negative.

Plain radiographs of the chest and clavicle showed a sclerotic, destructive lesion at the medial end of the right clavicle and diffuse pulmonary infiltrates. MRI of the thorax and cervical spine demonstrated bilateral upper‐lobe pulmonary infiltrates, arthritis of the right sternoclavicular joint with surrounding fluid collection, destruction of the atlanto‐axial junction, involvement of the D7‐8 intervertebral disc space, and a paraspinal fluid collection from D5 to D8.

A 77-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after a loss of consciousness. He had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 11/15. His vital signs were: heart rate 120 beats/minute, respiratory rate 32 breaths/minute, blood pressure 85/66 mmHg on inotropic support, and oxygen saturation 96% on 8 L of oxygen via a Venturi mask. The patient reported a history of chronic cough that had intensified over the past week and an episode of acute abdominal pain preceding presentation. He denied haematemesis or weight loss but had a 50–pack–year smoking history and chronic alcohol use disorder.  
On examination, percussion was dull bilaterally, with absent breath sounds on the left. A chest radiograph revealed a homogenous left-sided opacity suggestive of pleural effusion. Chest ultrasound confirmed bilateral pleural effusions, left greater than right, with a positive jellyfish sign. Initial blood tests were within normal limits. An electrocardiogram showed atrial fibrillation with a controlled ventricular rate. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a normal ejection fraction and no atrial thrombus.  
Diagnostic thoracentesis was performed, and 800 mL of brown fluid was drained via a left intercostal tube. Pleural fluid analysis showed an exudative effusion with: protein 2.6 g/dL (reference 1–2 g/dL), glucose 20 mg/dL (reference 90–120 mg/dL), adenosine deaminase 53.3 IU/L (<40 IU/L), lactate dehydrogenase 2636 IU/L (<50% of plasma), and amylase 7530 U/L (<40 U/L). Following drainage, the patient’s oxygen requirement decreased to 2 L.

A 25-year-old woman with a body-mass index of 40 and no prior medical history underwent a laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy. Three weeks postoperatively she had five episodes of fresh bloody vomiting and three episodes of melena, accompanied by palpitations and fatigue. She denied headache, dyspnea, and chest pain but noted mild, diffuse, dull abdominal pain. On examination, her blood pressure was normal, heart rate was elevated, she was alert, and her abdomen was soft with diffuse tenderness. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin concentration of 6.5 g/dL. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated focal extravasation of contrast from the left gastric artery.

A 53‐year‐old otherwise healthy Mexican woman reported a 40‐year history of generalized pruritus and wheal formation during bathing and while washing dishes, with lesions appearing within minutes of contact and persisting for 30–60 minutes after stopping water exposure. She denied angioedema, dyspnea, asthma, atopy, or allergies and had no affected family members. Physical examination revealed clear skin and a negative dermographism test.

To reproduce her symptoms, a room‐temperature wet compress was applied to the skin for 20 minutes without reaction. Subsequently, her right arm was immersed in room‐temperature water; after 5 minutes, multiple wheals, intense erythema, and pruritus developed over the immersed area. Cold and heat urticaria were then tested and excluded by applying an icepack and a heating pad, respectively.

A 51-year-old man with no chronic medical conditions and no recent trauma or infection received his first dose of the ChAdOx1-S COVID-19 vaccine. Within hours he developed fever, malaise, and asthenia. Four days later, he noted progressive, severe pain at the injection site and self-treated with paracetamol, NSAIDs, and pregabalin. One month after vaccination, he experienced hypoesthesia and difficulty abducting and elevating his left arm. 

Neurologic examination revealed atrophy of proximal muscles of the left upper limb and paresis of the left deltoid, biceps brachii, triceps brachii, and infraspinatus muscles. There were no changes in superficial or deep sensation and no motor deficits elsewhere. Deep-tendon reflexes were normoactive and symmetric. He was alert, oriented, and cooperative; there were no fasciculations, pathological upper motor neuron signs, or cranial nerve abnormalities.

Three months after symptom onset, electroneuromyography demonstrated signs consistent with brachial plexus neuritis, including reduced amplitude of the left axillary nerve action potential and mild to moderate peripheral neurological damage with signs of reinnervation in multiple proximal muscles.

A 54-year-old woman presented with a 6–9-month history of continuous dull aching pain in the right lower back tooth region. The pain worsened with chewing and talking and was only slightly relieved by medication. Four years earlier, she had sharp, intermittent pain in the same area; she underwent extraction of all right posterior teeth without relief. She was subsequently diagnosed with trigeminal neuralgia and treated with medications for one year, again with no benefit. Three years ago, a right mental nerve block produced relief, prompting right mental nerve avulsion under local anesthesia; pain resolved completely but recurred two months later as a dull, burning ache in the same distribution.

Her medical and dental histories were otherwise unremarkable. Vital signs and temporomandibular joint examination were normal. On extraoral exam, there was paresthesia of the right lower lip, chin, and cheek. Intraorally, a firm, tender, fibrosed scar (~0.5 cm) was noted on the alveolar mucosa above the right mandibular premolar region; it could be pinched off from underlying bone. Periodontal status was poor, and generalized enamel hypoplasia was present.

A provisional diagnosis of neuropathic pain in the right mental region was made. Given her history of mental nerve avulsion and extractions, traumatic neuroma and infected or retained root stumps were included in the differential. To assess the mandibular canal and premolar region, radiologic examination was planned.

A 76-year-old Caucasian man with hypothyroidism and recurrent urinary tract infections presented with several weeks of progressive shortness of breath, nonproductive cough, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. He also reported a 40-lb weight loss and new dysphagia but denied fevers, chills, or wheezing. His medications included levothyroxine, calcium, and nitrofurantoin, which he had taken daily for approximately 15 years for UTI prophylaxis. He was a former smoker (78 pack-year history, quit in 1986) with no history of asthma, COPD, pneumonia, interstitial lung disease, or occupational exposure to asbestos or heavy metals.

On examination, he was in moderate respiratory distress. Blood pressure was 110/65 mm Hg, heart rate 85 bpm, temperature 97.3 °F, respiratory rate 30 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. Breath sounds were diminished bilaterally with dry crackles, more pronounced on the right.

Laboratory studies showed a normal white blood cell count of 8.4 × 10^9/L and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate >140 mm/h. An antinuclear antibody screen was positive, but anti–double‐stranded DNA, rheumatoid factor, Scl‐70, anti–centromere B, anti–Jo‐1, anti–ribosomal P, anti-RNP, anti-Sm, anti–SS-A, anti–SS-B, and ACE level were all negative. Testing for HIV 1/2 and a Quantiferon TB Gold assay was negative.

Chest radiography revealed extensive basilar fibrosis, pleural thickening, and possible basilar infiltrates. Chest CT with contrast demonstrated severe fibrotic changes in both lungs with honeycombing predominantly at the bases and diffuse pleural wall thickening.

Nitrofurantoin was discontinued on admission.

A 41-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of swelling and burning pain in her left axilla. Over that period, she also experienced fevers and night sweats. One week earlier she had been treated with an NSAID without relief. She reported no radiation of pain, no erythema of the axilla, and no breast masses. Her surgical history was notable only for a cesarean section and left tibial internal fixation; her family history was unremarkable. On examination, she appeared well and in no acute distress; vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 18 200 cells/ml; other routine labs were normal. Tests for sexually transmitted infections were negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed multiple enhancing soft-tissue lesions in the left axilla, the largest measuring 4.0 × 3.5 × 4.3 cm, demonstrating internal areas of necrosis and adjacent infiltrative changes; the right axilla was unremarkable. The initial differential diagnosis included neoplastic, metastatic, infectious, or inflammatory processes. General surgery was consulted to rule out an abscess, and a plan was made for excisional biopsy of the axillary lesion.

A 91-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of deep vein thrombosis in her left common and external iliac veins and progressive worsening of left lower extremity swelling and pain. On examination, the left leg was swollen with overlying inflammation but no skin ulceration. Duplex ultrasonography of the left femoral vein demonstrated an occluded iliac segment and a high-velocity arterialized waveform within the femoral vein. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography in the arterial phase showed early opacification of the left common femoral vein, and in the venous phase revealed occlusion of the left common and external iliac veins with multiple enlarged collateral vessels.

A 35-year-old Samoan American man with congenital deafness, hypertension, and asthma presented with worsening night sweats, rash, productive cough, dyspnea, fevers, intermittent back pain, and an enlarging neck nodule. He had been diagnosed with “Valley Fever” 2 months earlier in California and treated with fluconazole 400 mg daily for 1 month. On admission he was afebrile, tachycardic (120 bpm), and had an SpO2 of 91% on room air. Examination showed scaling plaques on the right forehead; small ulcerated lesions on the right lower lip and posterior neck; coarse breath sounds in the left upper lung field; and a 3.5×3.5 cm nontender lymph node in the left anterior neck. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, elevated ESR and CRP, transaminitis, total protein 10.0 g/dL, albumin 1.7 g/dL, corrected calcium 11.0 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 167 U/L, lactic acid 2.7 mmol/L, LDH 341 U/L, ferritin 3366 ng/mL, and anemia of chronic disease. A respiratory viral panel was positive for respiratory syncytial virus. Serum coccidioides IgG ELISA was 8.3 IV (reference ≤0.9 IV) and IgM ELISA was 3.0 IV (reference ≤0.9 IV). Direct sputum microscopy revealed spherules resembling coccidioides. MRI of the spine showed numerous discrete hyperintense lesions of variable size throughout the spine, sacrum, and iliac bones, with indeterminate hyperintense lesions in the bilateral psoas muscles.

A 61-year-old woman presented with a two‐month history of a wet cough and progressive dyspnoea. Her medical history included type 1 diabetes mellitus managed with insulin. She was a current smoker (20 cigarettes daily for 41 years) and had an ibuprofen allergy. There was no history of dust exposure, arthralgia, or skin lesions. Her brother had rheumatoid arthritis; her son had neurosarcoidosis.

On examination, she was afebrile with a respiratory rate of 16 breaths per minute and an SpO2 of 94% on room air. She had digital clubbing and fine crackles at both lung bases. No peripheral lymphadenopathy, joint swelling, or skin abnormalities were noted.

High‐resolution chest computed tomography revealed diffuse bilateral interstitial shadows characterized by bronchovascular bundle thickening, interlobular septal thickening, pleural thickening, and hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Whole‐body contrast CT and MRI of the head and neck showed no abnormalities outside the lungs.

Laboratory studies showed: IgG 2436 mg/dL, IgG4 482 mg/dL, rheumatoid factor 269 IU/mL, KL-6 2900 U/mL, SP-D 314 ng/mL, sIL-2R 1372 U/mL, anti-SSA 15.8 U/mL; negative antinuclear antibody, ANCA, anti-CCP, and anti-ARS antibodies. Arterial blood gas on room air showed PaO2 67.5 Torr. Pulmonary function tests demonstrated restrictive impairment (FVC 80.6% predicted) with reduced diffusing capacity (DLCO 46.0% predicted).

She was admitted for surgical lung biopsy to establish a diagnosis.

A 14-year-old girl was referred for psychiatric assessment at Jimma University Teaching Hospital after a 2-week pediatric admission. She had a 4-month history of progressive low back pain, headaches, decreased appetite, and cultural sensations of “a moving live animal” in her abdomen. Two months before transfer, she developed intractable vomiting and frequent retching, followed by difficulty walking and marked weight loss. 

Her father reported multiple prior evaluations at regional hospitals, including CT scans and an MRI of the spinal cord, all of which were normal. At admission to the pediatric ward, her vital signs were normal. Physical examination revealed sunken eyeballs, generalized weakness, significant muscle wasting, slight abdominal tenderness, and a body mass index of 12.6 (below the 3rd percentile). With support she could sit but could not stand or walk. A nasogastric tube was placed for feeding and empiric treatment for peptic ulcer disease was initiated. 

After two weeks of investigations, including a detailed neurological examination, no organic pathology was identified. She was transferred to the psychiatric ward with a referral diagnosis of suspected early onset schizophrenia and a differential diagnosis of conversion disorder.

On psychiatric evaluation she appeared chronically ill and weak, with severe leg atrophy and incessant retching. She maintained good eye contact, followed commands, and her speech was coherent but low in volume and monotonous. She did not exhibit depressed affect, delusions, or disorganized thought. She was irritable, hyperaroused, and intermittently tearful. Her development was prepubertal.

A 70-year-old woman with a history of KRAS G12C–mutant pulmonary adenocarcinoma treated 2 years earlier with lobectomy, brain stereotactic radiotherapy, and chemotherapy–immunotherapy presented with a 4-day history of severe radiating lower back pain accompanied by nausea and vomiting. Five weeks earlier, she had begun adagrasib in a clinical trial at 600 mg twice daily, which was reduced to 400 mg twice daily after 2 weeks because of a transient grade 1 increase in creatinine. The pain was located in the thoracolumbar region, radiating toward the ventrolateral aspects of both legs. On neurologic examination, there was hypesthesia of the left upper leg, bilaterally reduced distal vibratory sensation, reduced deep tendon reflexes in the upper extremities, absent reflexes in the lower extremities with normal plantar responses, and slightly reduced strength of the ankle extensors bilaterally; other strength was intact. Vital signs were within normal limits, and there was no urinary or fecal incontinence. Laboratory studies showed elevated liver enzymes (ALT 102 U/L, AST 102 U/L, GGT 95 U/L, ALP 240 U/L) with low inflammatory markers. MRI of the entire neuraxis revealed contrast enhancement of the cauda equina without cervical involvement. Two cerebrospinal fluid analyses demonstrated mild pleocytosis (15 and 7 cells/μL), elevated protein (783 and 816 mg/L), normal glucose, negative testing for Varicella Zoster virus, Borrelia, and syphilis, and no malignant cells on cytology.

A 65-year-old woman of Indian origin, living in the UK, was referred for rheumatology evaluation with a 5-year history of mild arthralgia in her shoulders, hands, and elbows, and a 6-month history of productive cough without hemoptysis accompanied by weight loss. She denied fevers, night sweats, chest pain, or dyspnea on exertion. Physical examination was notable only for Heberden’s and Bouchard’s nodes in the hands, without synovitis; chest, cardiovascular, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 118 mm/hr, a C-reactive protein level of 18 mg/L, a rheumatoid factor of 108 IU/mL, and an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:160; tests for extractable nuclear antigens, anti-double-stranded DNA, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. Computed tomography of the chest revealed multiple pulmonary subsolid opacities—some part-solid with a ground-glass halo and others pure ground-glass nodules—distributed in all lobes, without mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy. A repeat CT after 3 months showed persistence of these lesions without growth. Bronchial washings contained squamous and respiratory epithelial cells, mixed leukocytes, and blood; “no malignant cells were seen,” and “the washings did not grow bacteria or acid-fast bacilli.”

A 27-year-old man with a Crouzon syndrome phenotype presented with multiple episodes of epistaxis over several days and several months of progressive nasal obstruction. He had no other medical history. On examination, a polypoid mass was visible in the right nostril, with facial asymmetry and prominence of the right canine fossa. Computed tomography of the paranasal sinuses revealed an inhomogeneous soft-tissue mass completely filling the right nasal cavity, maxillary sinus, and anterior and posterior ethmoidal cells. The mass caused extensive bone remodeling of the right maxillary sinus with loss of the anterior wall, erosion of the posterior wall extending into the pterygopalatine fossa, and erosion of the ipsilateral orbital floor and medial wall with intraconal extension. Despite its size, the lesion appeared well defined without obvious invasion of adjacent structures. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits, and odontogenic disease was excluded by maxillofacial consultation. A biopsy under local anesthesia demonstrated nonspecific inflammation.

A 31-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of a facial rash affecting both cheeks and the bridge of the nose. She had no personal or family history of skin disease, denied constitutional symptoms, and reported no recent trauma or cosmetic procedures. Two months after lesion onset, treatment with hydrocortisone 1% cream and an emollient produced no improvement. On examination, there were multiple yellowish superficial cysts overlying an erythematous plaque, along with scattered open comedones in a malar distribution; the rest of her skin was unaffected, and there was no oral ulceration or alopecia. Dermoscopic evaluation revealed multiple milia cysts, follicular keratotic plugs, perifollicular whitish halos, pigmentation, and telangiectasia. Routine laboratory investigations showed a normal complete blood count and negative HIV and rapid plasma reagin tests. Antinuclear antibody, anti–double-stranded DNA antibody, and anti–Sm antibody screens were all within normal limits.

A 20-year-old primigravid woman, previously healthy, had a term spontaneous vaginal delivery complicated by postpartum hemorrhage from retained placenta requiring manual extraction. She underwent dilation and curettage, with pathology suggestive of endometritis and retained products. Beginning immediately postpartum, she had cyclical high-grade fevers that persisted despite three weeks of broad-spectrum antibiotics. Fevers continued even after all antibiotics were stopped for several days.

Two weeks postpartum, she developed acute kidney injury, elevated liver enzymes (AST 380 U/L, ALT 250 U/L, ALP 920 U/L, total bilirubin 4.4 mg/dL), hepatomegaly, thrombocytopenia (platelet nadir 63,000/mm^3), and anemia (hemoglobin nadir 6.7 g/dL). Exploratory laparoscopy and a second dilation and curettage were unrevealing; the second procedure was complicated by intrauterine hemorrhage requiring emergent bilateral uterine artery embolization. She received six units of packed red blood cells, three units of fresh frozen plasma, four units of platelets, and two units of cryoprecipitate. Postoperatively she developed transfusion‐associated circulatory overload requiring brief intubation, followed by successful extubation and diuresis.

Persistent fevers prompted further evaluation. On postpartum day 24, laboratory studies revealed a serum ferritin level >20,000 ng/mL (normal 10–291 ng/mL) and triglyceride level 960 mg/dL (normal 35–160 mg/dL).

A 21-year-old woman with a known history of anorexia nervosa, binge/purge subtype, presented with mild abdominal pain following an episode of binge eating. She reported 5 days of worsening constipation and progressive abdominal distension. She could pass flatus but had been unable to vomit. She had no other medical conditions. There was no relevant family or social history. 

On examination, her vital signs were within normal limits. She appeared severely underweight with a body-mass index less than 18 and had no physical stigmata of purging. Abdominal examination revealed marked distension without tenderness or peritoneal signs; cardiopulmonary and other systems were unremarkable.

An abdominal radiograph showed a large soft‐tissue density in the upper abdomen displacing the transverse colon inferiorly; there was no pneumoperitoneum or evidence of bowel obstruction. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a massively distended stomach measuring 17 × 18 × 24 cm (approximately 4 L) containing multiple radiodense bodies. The proximal duodenum was dilated with an abrupt taper at the third portion, which appeared compressed as it crossed anterior to the aorta, with collapse of distal small-bowel loops. The mesentery was compressed posterior to the stomach. There was no free air or free fluid. The hepatobiliary and genitourinary systems were unremarkable.

A 54-year-old man with metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma of the right maxillary sinus, hypertension, hypothyroidism, and nonalcoholic steatohepatitis presented with a 1-week history of altered mental status, abdominal pain, dyspnea, and fever. He was not receiving active cancer therapy. Over the preceding 3 months he had progressive liver dysfunction with two episodes of ascites and coagulopathy. He had discontinued atorvastatin 2 months earlier for myalgias and had been using acetaminophen up to 2 g daily. On examination he was febrile, ill appearing, lethargic, and oriented only to person. He had diminished bibasilar breath sounds, tense ascites with guarding, hypoactive bowel sounds, right lower quadrant tenderness, and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies showed WBC 5.0×10^3/µL, hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL, platelets 60×10^3/µL, prothrombin time 22.5 s (INR 2.02), fibrinogen 141 mg/dL, AST 395 U/L, ALT 54 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 432 U/L, LDH 3449 U/L, ferritin 6031 ng/mL, and triglycerides 101 mg/dL. A peripheral blood smear revealed neutrophilia, monocytosis, reticulocytopenia, and marked platelet clumping without microangiopathic changes. Imaging studies demonstrated small pleural effusions, ascites, and hepatosplenomegaly without portal hypertension or splanchnic thrombosis.

A 29-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 0, presented at 23 weeks of gestation with a 7-week history of rapidly progressive bilateral breast enlargement. She reported severe breast tenderness, debilitating back pain, dyspnea, poor sleep, and difficulty with activities of daily living. The patient first noted the increase in size at 16 weeks’ gestation. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable for breast disease.

On examination, both breasts were massively enlarged (each approximately 7 kg), with marked pitting edema, prominent superficial veins, and areas of skin ulceration. No discrete masses were palpable. Vital signs were within normal limits, and there was no fever or evidence of systemic infection.

Breast ultrasonography revealed skin thickening, diffuse hypoechoic regions, and distended retroareolar ducts consistent with marked hypertrophy. Subsequent mammography was technically limited but showed no suspicious lesions. Ultrasound-guided biopsies of breast tissue and adjacent skin were performed; both specimens were negative for malignancy. Laboratory studies, including prolactin level and thyroid function tests, were within normal ranges.

A 15-year-old male presented with a 6-week history of subacute lower back pain, initially in the left costophrenic angle and ipsilateral hip and groin, associated with unintentional 6 kg weight loss and lethargy. He had no significant family history and was previously healthy; 2 years earlier he had anterior chest wall tenderness after a fall treated with NSAIDs. On examination he appeared pale and thin, limped due to pain, and had multiple acne scars. Findings included midline lumbar tenderness, a 2 cm soft non-tender left inguinal lymph node, and a palpable liver edge.  
Initial blood tests showed microcytic anemia, thrombocytosis, a CRP of 51.2 mg/L, an ESR of 101 mm/hr, elevated ferritin, low serum iron, and a mildly prolonged INR of 1.5. Renal and hepatic ultrasounds were unremarkable; blood film was normal.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed mild fat stranding around the sacroiliac joints, especially on the left, and bone-window images showed subtle erosions and joint-space widening of the left sacroiliac joint consistent with sacroiliitis.  
A three-phase bone scan demonstrated increased tracer uptake in both sacroiliac joints (left > right), the right anterior sixth rib, and the right ankle. A gallium scan was negative, and blood cultures showed no growth.  
Lumbar spine MRI and dedicated sacroiliac joint MRI showed asymmetric sacroiliitis with mild articular erosion of the left sacroiliac joint and periarticular bone marrow edema with enhancement. An ankle MRI revealed patchy marrow edema in the distal tibia, fibula, talus, navicular, and calcaneus suggesting noninfectious osteitis.

A 46-year-old woman, G2P2, presented with gradually progressive right lower–quadrant abdominal pain that was aggravated by movement and relieved by rest. Over the preceding month, she developed symmetrical abdominal distension associated with early satiety, nausea, diarrhea, and alternating constipation; she denied vomiting, jaundice, or respiratory symptoms, and had no known tuberculosis contacts. Vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, the abdomen was distended with normal contour and bowel sounds; there was tenderness in the right iliac fossa without palpable masses. Both external and internal genital examinations, including the cervix, were normal. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (14.5×10^9/L, 76% neutrophils), hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL, and an elevated CA-125 level of 52.5 U/mL; renal and liver function tests were normal, and C-reactive protein was 800 mg/L. A chest radiograph was normal. Abdominal ultrasonography showed massive ascites, a heterogeneous mass posterior to the uterus, and mesenteric lymphadenopathy. Based on these findings, a clinical diagnosis of ovarian cancer was made.

A 65-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia presented for urologic evaluation. His prostate-specific antigen level was 0.796 ng/mL. Uroflowmetry revealed reduced urine flow, prolonged micturition time, and obstructive findings. He was started on oral Alfuzosin 10 mg once daily. On day 9 of therapy, he reported loss of appetite and malaise, followed by generalized pruritus, dark urine, and jaundice. He denied use of aspirin, acetaminophen, or herbal medicines and had no history of liver disease. On examination, he was jaundiced but had no stigmata of chronic liver disease.
