Laboratory studies showed leukocyte count 5.8 K/μL, AST 175 U/L (0–40), ALT 402 U/L (0–55), alkaline phosphatase 235 U/L (15–250), γ-glutamyl transferase 327 U/L (8–61), total bilirubin 7.6 mg/dL (0.2–1.2), and direct bilirubin 5.8 mg/dL (0–0.25). Abdominal ultrasonography showed normal liver, gallbladder, common bile duct, and intrahepatic bile ducts. Serologic tests for HBsAg, anti-HBc IgM, anti-HCV, anti-HAV IgM, anti-HEV, HEV RNA, and HCV RNA were negative. Autoimmune markers (ANA, AMA, ASMA, LKM-1) were negative. Metabolic evaluations—including transferrin saturation, ferritin, alpha-1 antitrypsin, ceruloplasmin, 24-hour urinary copper, and ophthalmologic exam for Kayser–Fleischer rings—were normal. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography demonstrated a normal biliary anatomy.

A woman in her 50s with no known medical history presented with 5 days of right upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. The pain was gradual and accompanied by multiple episodes of yellow emesis and one episode of hematemesis. She denied fever, chills, night sweats, diarrhea, or constipation. She took no medications and denied tobacco, alcohol, or drug use. On examination, she was afebrile (36.7°C), with a heart rate of 87/min, blood pressure 139/77 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. The abdomen was soft, non-tender, non-distended, without guarding. Laboratory studies showed a leukocytosis of 15.0×10^9 cells/L (78% neutrophils), HbA1c 14.2%, and normal transaminases (AST 14 U/L, ALT 14 U/L), alkaline phosphatase 126 U/L, total bilirubin 1.1 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.1 mg/dL, and albumin 3.0 g/dL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and a multiphase liver protocol showed three peripherally enhancing, cystic lesions in liver segments VI (5.4×7.0×4.4 cm), VII (5.1×5.8×4.2 cm), and VIII (4.3×3.8×4.0 cm), with mass effect on the hepatic vein. A 3.2-cm arterially enhancing vascular lesion in the porta hepatis followed the blood pool on arterial, portal venous, and delayed phases, concerning for a hepatic artery aneurysm.

A 55-year-old man with untreated diabetes mellitus was diagnosed with COVID-19 at another hospital because of dyspnea. His respiratory condition worsened; he was intubated, mechanically ventilated, and transferred to our emergency department. On admission, he was febrile (40 °C), hypotensive (74/39 mmHg), tachycardic (144 bpm), tachypneic (35 breaths/min), and had an SpO2 of 95% on an FiO2 yielding a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 114 mmHg. Laboratory tests showed a blood glucose level of 642 mg/dL, hemoglobin A1c of 15.2%, and a C-reactive protein level of 47.8 mg/dL. Initial diagnoses were COVID-19 pneumonia, sepsis, hypovolemic shock, and hyperglycemic hyperosmolar syndrome. He received intravenous fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, continuous insulin infusion, and electrolyte correction. Two sets of blood cultures obtained on admission grew Candida spp., and serum β-D-glucan was 412 pg/mL (normal < 20 pg/mL). Empiric micafungin (100 mg/day) was started on hospital day 5. Chest CT on day 5 showed consolidation along the bronchovascular bundles with bronchiectatic cavity formation and centrilobular nodules. Given these imaging findings, therapy was changed to voriconazole (400 mg/day) on day 7.

A 41-year-old man presented with a 7-day history of jaundice. Seven days earlier, an abdominal CT at another hospital had shown a space-occupying lesion in the pancreatic head, and pancreaticoduodenectomy was recommended. He had no prior illnesses, no history of alcohol or tobacco use, and no relevant family history. On examination, he was afebrile, with normal vital signs except for scleral icterus and cutaneous jaundice; the abdomen was soft with no tenderness or palpable mass. Laboratory studies showed: leukocyte count 6.7×10^9/L (76% neutrophils); normal coagulation and C-reactive protein; alanine aminotransferase 440 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 107 U/L, gamma-glutamyltransferase 2734 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 435 U/L, total bilirubin 53 μmol/L, direct bilirubin 28 μmol/L; alpha-fetoprotein 9.13 ng/mL, CA19-9 108.8 U/mL, ferritin 1584.7 ng/mL. Fecal and urine tests, chest X-ray, ECG, and arterial blood gas were normal. 
Pancreatic ultrasound revealed a 4.4×3.0×2.4 cm hypoechoic round mass in the head of the pancreas with an unclear border and punctate strong echoes. Contrast-enhanced CT showed an irregular 4.0×3.0×1.7 cm medium-density mass in the pancreatic head with incremental enhancement, punctate calcifications, and upstream dilation of the pancreatic duct, extrahepatic bile duct, and intrahepatic ducts. Contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated a bulky irregular lesion in the pancreatic head that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, relatively hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed a honeycomb-like incremental enhancement pattern. Chest CT showed no pulmonary infiltrates, only scattered bullae in the upper lobes.

A 43-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of recurrent febrile attacks to >39 °C lasting 3–4 days, initially occurring every 2 weeks and then increasing in frequency. Episodes began with an urticarial rash on the trunk and legs, high fever, and progressive bilateral femoral pain; the rash and pain persisted between fevers.

On examination, temperature was 37.1 °C (10 days after her last fever), blood pressure 120/72 mmHg, pulse 92/min, and respiratory rate 24/min. She had widespread urticarial lesions over the trunk and extremities and tenderness over the left hip. Chest and abdominal examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 11 900/μl, C-reactive protein 6.18 mg/dl, and serum amyloid A 32.5 μg/ml. Autoimmune markers, including anti–nuclear and anti–neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, were negative. Serum protein immunoelectrophoresis revealed no monoclonal protein, and bone marrow aspiration was normal. Liver and renal function tests were within normal limits. Serological testing was negative for HBV, HCV, and syphilis; tests for cytomegalovirus antigenemia, EBV DNA, Parvovirus B19 DNA, an interferon-γ release assay for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and β-D-glucan were all negative.

Fluorine-18 FDG PET/CT showed diffuse uptake in the bone marrow of both femoral and pelvic bones. MRI of the femurs demonstrated diffusely abnormal signal intensity in the medullary bone on T1-, T2-, and STIR-weighted images. A skin biopsy of an urticarial lesion revealed perivascular and interstitial neutrophilic infiltrates without leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

A 25-year-old South Asian man with no past medical history presented after a seizure that began with left-sided facial and upper-limb jerking, progressed to generalized shaking, and lasted a few minutes. He reported similar episodes for the past year, the most recent occurring two months prior. He also noted mild, nonspecific headaches and right frontal scalp swelling over two months but denied fever, weight loss, night sweats, visual changes, or systemic symptoms. He had no history of trauma, bleeding disorders, medication use, or substance use. On examination, vital signs were stable, and neurologic and systemic examinations were unremarkable.

He was started on phenytoin. Initial blood tests, including CBC, coagulation profile, chemistry panel, and liver and renal function, were normal. Chest radiography showed hazy, ill-defined shadows in the right upper zone, left upper zone, and right base. Noncontrast head CT demonstrated a 13 mm right extra-axial crescentic hyperdensity along the frontoparietal convexity with adjacent sulcal effacement and a 5 mm midline shift, plus an osteolytic lesion in the right frontal bone. Contrast MRI of the head revealed a right extra-axial crescentic mass with low T2, FLAIR, and T1 signal, intense postcontrast enhancement, dural thickening (maximum 13 mm), irregularity of the inner skull table, a full-thickness right frontal bony defect with diploic and extracranial enhancing swelling, and mild compression of the right lateral ventricle with a 5 mm midline shift.

The working differential included an infective process (tuberculosis and fungal infections), neoplastic lesion (carcinomatosis, lymphoma, and leukemia), histiocytosis, and inflammatory granulomatous processes such as sarcoidosis and Wegener granulomatosis. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed multiple enhancing pulmonary nodules predominantly in both upper lung lobes. Laboratory studies revealed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 67 mm/h (reference 5–28) and C-reactive protein of 129 mg/L (reference 1–5) with a normal procalcitonin level; TB PCR from histopathology was negative. Serum and urine protein electrophoresis were unremarkable. Flow cytometry showed no definitive immunophenotypic evidence of a monotypic B-cell population. ANA and ANCA were negative.

A 58-year-old postmenopausal Middle Eastern woman with diabetes, hypertension, and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis presented with a 10-month history of painless enlargement of her right breast. She denied fever, night sweats, or weight loss. She had no personal or family history of breast or ovarian cancer, and her gynecologic history included three cesarean deliveries and 1 year of oral contraceptive use. 

On examination, the right breast was diffusely enlarged and non-tender. Multiple firm, non-fixed, non-tender lymph nodes were palpable in the right axilla. There was no skin redness, discoloration, or palpable breast mass. 

Laboratory studies showed peripheral eosinophilia (14%; normal, 1–3%) and an elevated serum IgE level (2153 UI/mL; normal, 80–120 UI/mL). 

Initial differential diagnoses included primary breast carcinoma or sarcoma, breast metastasis, primary or secondary breast lymphoma, inflammatory disorders (including non-puerperal mastitis), and superior vena cava obstruction due to thrombosis or mediastinal mass. 

Mammography of the right breast demonstrated diffuse enlargement with increased density, trabecular and dermal thickening, and right axillary lymphadenopathy but no suspicious mass lesion or microcalcifications. Ultrasound showed skin thickening, multiple hypoechoic areas consistent with fat edema, and no focal mass; ipsilateral axillary nodes had thickened cortices and preserved fatty hila with mildly increased vascularity. Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed diffuse right breast enlargement with fat stranding and dermal thickening, multiple right axillary lymphadenopathies, and no pulmonary or mediastinal mass, nodule, or lymphadenopathy. The patient declined breast MRI due to claustrophobia and concerns about gadolinium.

A 57-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and essential hypertension presented with a 4-month history of a painful ulcer on the glans penis. He reported progressive pain and necrosis but no systemic symptoms. 

On examination, there was a 2.3-cm circumferential ulcer encircling the urethra on the glans, topped by a yellow-green crust.

Over the preceding 6 years, his serum calcium, creatinine, and phosphate levels had been measured annually and remained within normal limits. 

Laboratory studies at presentation showed:  
• Parathyroid hormone–related protein, 9 pg/mL (normal, 11–20 pg/mL)  
• Parathyroid hormone, normal  
• Urine protein electrophoresis with elevated total protein but no monoclonal bands  
• Hemoglobin A1C, 9.0%  

A tangential shave biopsy of the lesion and two subsequent punch biopsies revealed ulceration with necrotizing inflammation but no evidence of malignancy. Empiric ciprofloxacin was prescribed to cover possible Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection.

One month later, the ulcer had extended proximally with increased necrosis and pain. Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis demonstrated diffuse atherosclerosis without hemodynamically significant arterial stenosis and soft-tissue calcification of the penile vessels and corpora cavernosa. Doppler ultrasound confirmed diffuse atherosclerotic changes but no significant stenosis of the cavernosal or dorsal penile arteries.

A 16-year-old girl presented with sudden-onset headache, photophobia, left lower–leg weakness, and jerking movements of both upper and lower limbs. She had no relevant past medical history. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. A chest radiograph and noncontrast head CT scan were unremarkable. A lumbar puncture was performed, and cerebrospinal fluid was collected into two tubes: the first contained 0.5 mL of clear, colorless fluid, and the second contained 0.3 mL of slightly blood-tinged fluid. Cytospin preparations from both tubes were stained with Papanicolaou and Romanowsky-based stains. Both specimens showed cellular elements, with the second specimen more cellular; they contained myeloid and erythroid precursors at various stages of maturation, together with occasional lymphocytes and monocytes. No megakaryocytes were identified.

A 48-year-old man was admitted following a crush injury to his right foot at work. He fell from a step ladder after it slipped on spilled oil, and his foot became caught in an industrial vertical fan. He immediately noted pain and swelling over the dorsum of the foot. 

On examination, there was swelling on the dorsum of the foot and tenderness at the base of the first metatarsal. Distal foot pulses were palpable, and there were no sensory or motor deficits. There was no pain on passive stretching of the foot.

Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the right foot showed an avulsion fracture of the base of the first metatarsal.

A 64-year-old woman presented with a two-year history of progressive right-sided hearing loss. She had no prior medical conditions and took no medications. Otoscopic examination of the right ear revealed a white-colored, calcified-appearing mass beneath an intact tympanic membrane, located anteriorly. Pure-tone audiometry demonstrated a right conductive hearing loss with a 50 dB air–bone gap. High-resolution CT of the right temporal bone showed a well-defined, non-erosive, nodular calcified mass in the anterior tympanic cleft, attached to the malleus handle and the anterior middle ear wall. Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI of the temporal bone revealed a hypointense mass on T1 images with homogeneous gadolinium enhancement.

A 60-year-old man with hepatitis B–related cirrhosis underwent orthotopic liver transplantation from a cadaveric donor. He was 40 days posttransplant and maintained on tacrolimus, mycophenolate, tenofovir, and folic acid. Twenty-one days after transplantation, routine hepatic ultrasonography revealed a 20 × 15 mm well-defined hyper-echogenic lesion in the inferior capsule of the right hepatic lobe of the graft. On admission, his vital signs were stable and he was afebrile; the physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed stable hematologic parameters, a creatinine of 1.4 mg/dL rising to 2.6 mg/dL during hospitalization, and an alkaline phosphatase elevated at 243 U/L. Alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase were within normal limits. Cytomegalovirus and SARS-CoV-2 PCR assays were negative. To investigate the lesion and to rule out causes such as autoimmune or viral hepatitis, a CT-guided core biopsy of the hepatic mass was performed.

A 60-year-old man without prior medical history presented with 4 hours of severe, continuous, compressive left-sided chest pain radiating to the left hand, aggravated by exertion, relieved by nitroglycerine, and accompanied by diaphoresis and nausea. He denied fever, dyspnea, palpitations, or trauma. He quit smoking 10 years ago and stopped opium 3 months ago. He arrived hypotensive (85/55 mmHg on norepinephrine), tachycardic (103 bpm), and afebrile (36.9°C), with cold lower extremities and an otherwise unremarkable chest, abdominal, heart, and lung exam.

An initial ECG showed ST depression in V5 and V6, which later resolved with T-wave inversion. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a normal-sized left ventricle with severe systolic dysfunction (LVEF 15–20%) and global hypokinesia, an enlarged right ventricle with mild dysfunction, mild mitral regurgitation, and mild to moderate tricuspid regurgitation. Coronary angiography demonstrated significant mid–left anterior descending artery stenosis, and simultaneous aortography showed no evidence of dissection; the LAD lesion was stented.

Laboratory studies showed troponin 1.5 ng/dL (normal <2), D-dimer 280 ng/mL, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 68 mg/dL, C-reactive protein 56 mg/dL, and white blood cell count 10.4×10^3/µL (92.7% neutrophils). After ruling out cardiogenic shock from acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, aortic dissection, and pericardial tamponade based on ECG, echocardiography, angiography, and basic labs, suspicion for septic shock arose. Empirical antibiotics were initiated, and further investigations including chest CT, blood cultures, liver enzymes, urine analysis, and urine culture failed to identify a source.

A 21‐year‐old woman presented with palpitations and dizziness. Her resting ECG showed bigeminal premature ventricular contractions but a normal ST segment, QT interval, and T waves. Twenty‐four‐hour ambulatory ECG monitoring recorded 34 787 ventricular ectopic beats and multiple non‐sustained runs of ventricular tachycardia. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated mitral valve prolapse with minimal mitral regurgitation and a probable abnormal location of the mitral annulus but was otherwise normal. To further evaluate potential structural causes of her arrhythmias, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was performed; it confirmed mitral valve prolapse and revealed a mitral annulus disjunction measuring up to 10 mm in the posterolateral wall, without any evidence of myocardial inflammation or scarring.

A 21-day-old boy was evaluated for poor feeding and failure to regain birth weight. Initial laboratory studies showed sodium 106 mmol/L, potassium 7.1 mmol/L, and glucose 1.8 mmol/L. Pregnancy and delivery had been uncomplicated. Neonatal course was notable for hypoglycemia on day 1 and two brief admissions for unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia treated with phototherapy. His parents noted progressive “bronzing” of the skin over three weeks.

On examination, weight was 3.1 kg (7th percentile), blood pressure was 68/33 mmHg, and the skin was diffusely hyperpigmented without dysmorphic features. Genitalia were normal with descended testes.

He underwent a high-dose ACTH stimulation test, which demonstrated markedly elevated baseline and stimulated 11-deoxycortisol levels. A 17-hydroxyprogesterone level sent by the primary pediatrician returned at 5.6 nmol/L (reference ≤ 2.9). The following day, baseline and stimulated 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels were 4.5 nmol/L (within the normal range), arguing against 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

A 77-year-old woman with a remote history of surgery for ectopic pregnancy and wound dehiscence 28 years earlier presented with intermittent abdominal pain and was diagnosed with small-bowel obstruction. Initial management with long-tube decompression relieved her symptoms, and she was referred for further evaluation. On admission she was asymptomatic. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including CEA and CA19-9, were within normal limits. Serum IgG4 was not measured. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed an enhanced, radially shaped oval mass, 3 cm in diameter with an unclear rim at the root of the distal ileal mesentery, possibly involving the adjacent ileum. Double-balloon enteroscopy and gastrografin enterography revealed no abnormalities. FDG-PET demonstrated mild uptake in the mass (SUVmax 4.4). The nature of the mass—whether malignant or inflammatory—remained uncertain.

A woman in her early 40s presented with lower abdominal pain and fever for several days. Her temperature was 37.6 °C, and she had tenderness in the right lower abdomen. Obstetric history was gravida 3, para 2 with two normal vaginal deliveries 13 and 11 years earlier; there was no history of gynecologic abnormalities, abdominal surgery, or trauma. Menstrual cycles were regular, and her last menstrual period was 2 weeks earlier. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 11 210/µL, a C-reactive protein level of 1.54 mg/dL, and normal serum levels of carcinoembryonic antigen, CA19-9, and CA125. 

Transvaginal ultrasonography revealed a 132 × 120 × 155 mm cystic lesion with an 80 × 37 mm solid component on the ventral side of a retroflexed uterus; a 43 × 34 mm posterior subserosal leiomyoma was also noted. Magnetic resonance imaging showed that the cystic lesion had high signal intensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images without fat suppression, suggesting bloody or protein-rich contents. A dorsal sediment was consistent with old clots. The cyst wall measured up to 5 mm and was isointense to normal myometrium. Diffusion-weighted images demonstrated some diffusion restriction within the cyst. The lesion appeared contiguous with the right ovary. An intramural leiomyoma was present on the dorsal cervix. No congenital uterine, renal, or urinary tract malformations were identified. 

Based on these imaging findings, an infected endometriotic cyst of the right ovary was initially diagnosed.

A 58-year-old woman with BRAF-mutated metastatic melanoma was referred for evaluation of severe oral pain persisting for 4 months after extraction of the lower right third molar. The patient had been treated by her dentist for presumed alveolar osteitis with three separate 1-week cycles of amoxicillin–clavulanic acid (2.25 + 0.75 g per day) and daily chlorhexidine 0.2% mouthwash irrigation; she also had occasional zinc oxide eugenol applications. Despite these measures, the site remained painful, and she denied any extra-oral swelling or abscess.

On intraoral examination, the socket was nonhealed, revealing visible, nonvascularized, nonsuppurative bone surrounded by swollen mucosa. A panoramic radiograph obtained 3 days earlier demonstrated a persistent nonhealed alveolus 4 months after extraction.

Her medical history was notable for cutaneous melanoma resected in 2009. In 2015, she received ipilimumab (3 mg/kg IV every 3 weeks for 4 cycles) for lung metastases, with complete remission. In 2017, hepatic progression led to dabrafenib + trametinib, which was discontinued for fever, and she was switched to vemurafenib + cobimetinib (currently 1440 mg + 60 mg per day), ongoing at the time of extraction. She had no history of smoking or head and neck radiotherapy. Among her medications, only ipilimumab has been linked to osteonecrosis of the jaw.

A 19-year-old girl with no prior menarche presents with delay in menarche and bilateral inguinal masses noted since age 16. She is sexually inactive. Medical history is unremarkable except for prior excision of an eye cyst. Two maternal aunts had primary amenorrhea and underwent bilateral inguinal surgery. On exam, she has normal female habitus and voice, BMI 27.2, Tanner stage-3 breasts, normal female external genitalia, and sparse pubic and axillary hair. Abdominal examination reveals non-distension and mildly tender bilateral inguinal masses (~3 cm each). Hormonal studies show FSH 6.5 mLU/mL, LH 23.27 mLU/mL, estradiol 28.18 pg/mL, total testosterone 4.48 ng/mL (female range 0.15–0.7), free testosterone 0.08 ng/mL (female range 0.001–0.007), and DHEAS 510.7 μg/mL (female range 70–320), with normal TSH and prolactin. Pelvic MRI demonstrates congenital absence of uterus, cervix, ovaries, and internal vagina; a 2.5 cm blind-ended vaginal remnant; and bilateral 3 cm masses at the external inguinal rings.

A 70-year-old woman presented with 24 hours of severe upper abdominal pain radiating to the back, associated with nausea and vomiting. Her medical history included essential thrombocytosis, hypertension (on amlodipine and candesartan), dyslipidemia, carotid atheromatosis, prior hysterectomy, and surgery for bowel obstruction. She was a former smoker (20 pack-years, quit 30 years ago) and consumed approximately five alcoholic units daily.

On examination, she was afebrile, conscious, and overweight. Blood pressure was 150/90 mmHg, heart rate 100 beats per minute, and heart sounds were normal without murmurs. Lung fields were clear. The abdomen was distended with spontaneous pain and guarding; within the first day a well-defined, tender supraumbilical mass developed, with diminished bowel sounds.

Laboratory studies demonstrated an inflammatory syndrome (C-reactive protein elevated), leukocytosis with neutrophilia, thrombocytosis, hyperglycemia with elevated HbA1c, elevated lactate dehydrogenase, markedly increased serum amylase and lipase, cholestasis (elevated gamma-glutamyl transferase and alkaline phosphatase), hyponatremia, hypochloremia, and low serum iron.

An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm at 96 beats per minute without ST-T changes. Chest radiograph revealed a globally enlarged heart and accentuated interstitial markings at the bases. Abdominal radiograph was unremarkable. 

Abdominal ultrasound showed an enlarged hyperechogenic pancreas with a visible main pancreatic duct, non-dilated biliary tree, a normal-sized gallbladder containing multiple mobile stones up to 8 mm, and a thin layer of fluid in Morison’s pouch.

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan demonstrated an enlarged pancreas with heterogeneous attenuation, multiple peripancreatic collections up to 14 mm consistent with necrosis, small interaortocaval and peripancreatic lymph nodes, and liver enlargement with mild steatosis and perfusion abnormalities in segment VIII. There was a 2 cm heterogeneous filling defect occupying about 50% of the superior mesenteric vein lumen and an 80% occlusive thrombus in the splenic vein; the spleen showed wedge-shaped hypodense areas suggestive of infarction. The gallbladder contained a 6 mm calculus without biliary duct obstruction. A Bosniak type I cortical cyst was seen in the left kidney. A 34 mm hiatal hernia was also noted.

An 11-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of recurrent focal seizures and right-hand weakness. He was born at term after an uneventful pregnancy and neonatal period, with normal developmental milestones and no history of trauma or childhood infections. At age 7, right shoulder abduction weakness was noted; physiotherapy produced no recovery. Four years later, he began having focal seizures several times per month, which impaired school performance. 

On examination, there was isolated weakness of right shoulder abduction; the remainder of the neurologic and general physical examination was normal. Vital signs were within normal limits.

Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, serum electrolytes, and blood glucose, were all normal. Electroencephalography showed low amplitude with slow background activity in the left cerebral hemisphere.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed that the left cerebral hemisphere was smaller than the right, with relative thickening of the left skull vault; widened extra-axial subarachnoid spaces; deepened sulci on the left; and dilation of the left lateral ventricle with an undulating ventricular wall. There was enlargement of the left frontal sinus compared to the right. Atrophy was also noted in the left basal ganglia, brainstem, and cerebellum, with loss of arborization. T2-weighted and FLAIR images showed hyperintensity in the left corona radiata and centrum semiovale without diffusion restriction. Mild thinning of the posterior corpus callosum was observed. The right cerebral hemisphere and the rest of the scan were unremarkable.

A 24-year-old healthy man presented with pain and swelling of the upper right front tooth for 1 week. He had sustained bicycle trauma 5 years earlier. On examination, tooth #11 was tender to palpation and percussion, exhibited Grade II mobility, and had negative responses to cold and electric pulp tests. An intraoral periapical radiograph showed a horizontal root fracture at the junction of the middle and apical thirds of tooth #11, with blunting and loss of lamina dura of the coronal fragment, widening of the fracture line, and substantial linear displacement of the apical segment. To assess spatial displacement, a limited-field-of-view CBCT scan was obtained, confirming the mid-root fracture and revealing a large radiolucent area (gray-scale value 89) between the fractured segments, erosion of the labial cortical plate, and approximately 8 mm of apical segment displacement compared with the contralateral incisor. There was also a periapical radiolucency around the apical segment, indicating pulp necrosis.

A late preterm female infant (36 weeks 5 days’ gestation) was referred soon after birth for respiratory arrest, decreased level of consciousness, and poor feeding. Arterial blood gas analysis showed metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation. She had been delivered by lower-segment Caesarean section for thick meconium-stained liquor and cried immediately after birth. Attempts to pass a feeding tube failed beyond 16 cm, prompting consideration of a tracheoesophageal fistula and referral for a water-soluble upper gastrointestinal contrast study.

On a lateral chest radiograph, a wide-bore tube was seen traversing the mouth and pharynx down to the distal oesophagus, consistent with a malpositioned endotracheal tube, and a longitudinal translucent streak anterior to it indicated air in the trachea. Frontal fluoroscopic oesophagography demonstrated spillage of contrast from the laryngopharynx at the level of the cricopharyngeus into the tracheobronchial tree and gastroesophageal reflux in the Trendelenburg position; otherwise, contrast passed smoothly from the oropharynx into the stomach. In the prone position, no communication was seen between the oesophagus and the tracheobronchial tree, although reflux from the gastroesophageal junction into the thoracic oesophagus persisted in Trendelenburg.

A limited noncontrast CT scan of the thorax revealed an oval air-containing structure posterior to the oesophagus, extending from the T2 vertebral level down to the renal hila. Two nasogastric tubes were placed—one tip in the stomach and one in the blind-ending structure. Instillation of diluted non-ionic contrast into the second tube opacified a lumen arising posteriorly from the oesophagus at T2, running parallel through the posterior mediastinum into a pouch-like structure at T8–T9, then terminating infra-diaphragmatically with few air foci; axial dimensions were approximately 4.5 × 2.7 mm. Three-dimensional volume-rendered images confirmed a blind-ending duplicate lumen running alongside the oesophagus. There was no pneumomediastinum and no vertebral segmentation anomalies. On oesophagoscopy, the opening of the second lumen exhibited peripheral oedema, and further exploration was deferred.

A 2-month-old full-term female with known complex congenital heart disease (single ventricle defect, double-outlet right ventricle with D-transposition of the great arteries, and an ostium secundum atrial septal defect with left superior vena cava) was admitted for evaluation of occasional cyanosis. She was in good general condition, weighed 5 kg, had an oxygen saturation of 80%, and showed no signs of respiratory distress. Her medications included furosemide and spironolactone. The team planned a pulmonary artery banding, but during the procedure the patient became hemodynamically unstable and suffered a cardiorespiratory arrest requiring cardiac massage, so the operation was aborted. To gather hemodynamic data, cardiac catheterization was performed via the left femoral artery, with the catheter tip in the single ventricle, using serial doses of nonionic iodinated contrast (Iopromide) totaling 3 mL/kg over 30 minutes. Approximately 12 hours after the procedure, the patient developed clonic movements of the left upper limb and persistent sucking motions. A noncontrast head CT obtained after this first seizure showed a slight diffuse increase in cortical density predominantly in the right frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes and, to a lesser extent, in the left parietal and occipital lobes; there was no mass effect, hemorrhage, or other intracranial abnormality.

A 24-year-old woman from rural Kazakhstan presented with a 1-year history of intermittent stabbing precordial pain, progressive dyspnea, fatigue, and generalized weakness. The symptoms had worsened over the past 3 months. She denied weight loss, fevers, travel outside Kazakhstan, or contact with known infectious patients, but reported regular exposure to household pets. Her medical history was unremarkable for hepatitis, tuberculosis, diabetes, hypertension, asthma, or prior surgeries.

On examination, blood pressure was 125/77 mmHg, pulse 96 beats/min, and temperature 36.2°C. Cardiovascular, pulmonary, abdominal, and neurologic examinations were normal. A chest radiograph was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed a positive ELISA for immunoglobulin G and mild hypoalbuminemia, slight reductions in total protein, urea, sodium, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and mean corpuscular volume, along with slight elevations in glomerular filtration rate and C-reactive protein. Other parameters were within or near normal limits.

Abdominal ultrasound showed a 10.0 × 8.0 cm cystic lesion in the left hepatic lobe and moderate bile stasis due to a bend in the gallbladder neck. Transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated no intracardiac thrombi or masses.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen revealed uniform opacification of the cardiac chambers without filling defects, but identified within the posterior-inferior myocardium of the left ventricle a 5.4 × 4.2 × 2.7 cm round-oval lesion with well-defined margins and attenuation values ranging from +12 to +44 Hounsfield units. On CT of the liver, the left-lobe lesion measured 7.8 × 7.5 cm, appeared as a round-oval formation with thickened walls, septations, and areas of calcification, and had an attenuation of up to +17 Hounsfield units.

Cardiac MRI without contrast confirmed an intramural, round-oval mass in the basal and mid segments of the left ventricle measuring approximately 6.2 × 5.8 × 5.7 cm, with a heterogeneous hyperintense signal and internal partitions. A similar multi-chamber cystic structure measuring 8.4 × 8.1 × 8.7 cm was seen in the left hepatic lobe, each with smooth, clear borders and thick capsules.

A 50-year-old man presented with a 10-year history of a pruritic, annular, vesiculopustular eruption involving his axillae, groin, postauricular area, neck, and trunk. He had been treated with dapsone (100 mg daily) for 2 years without significant improvement. 

On examination, there were multiple flaccid pustules on an erythematous base with areas of postinflammatory hyperpigmentation in the axillae, groin, postauricular region, and neck.

Punch biopsy of an abdominal lesion showed a subcorneal pustule containing neutrophils, epidermal acanthosis with neutrophilic spongiosis, and papillary dermal edema with a mixed lymphocytic, eosinophilic, and neutrophilic infiltrate.

Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin demonstrated intercellular IgA deposits on keratinocyte surfaces.

A 69-year-old man presented to the emergency department with acute onset right-sided upper abdominal pain, associated sweating and vomiting. On examination, his heart rate was 104 beats/min, temperature 36.8 °C, and oxygen saturation 91% on 4 L of oxygen. There was voluntary guarding on palpation of the epigastric region; no other abnormalities were noted. Serum amylase was elevated at 727 U/L (normal 30–110 U/L). Abdominal ultrasound revealed sludge within a thin-walled gallbladder, and a diagnosis of acute pancreatitis secondary to gallstones was made. His Glasgow severity score was 1 (for age > 55 years).

On hospital day 4, he developed pain in the left lower abdominal quadrant. Examination revealed a tender, irreducible, erythematous swelling in the left groin. Contrast CT of the abdomen showed extensive peripancreatic fluid with some infiltration of the left paracolic gutter, as well as extensive subcutaneous oedema and a small left inguinal hernia that did not contain any bowel loops. The hernia became more painful, and repeat CT scans demonstrated a marked increase in the volume of fluid surrounding the pancreas and greater fluid tracking to the anterior and posterior paranephric spaces and left paracolic gutter. A laparoscopic cholecystectomy and open hernia repair were planned.

A 32-day-old girl was admitted with fever and restlessness since the previous day. There was no history of coryza or conjunctivitis. On examination, she had left submandibular swelling with overlying erythema; palpation of the area elicited irritability. Prenatal and postnatal histories were unremarkable; parents were consanguineous. She was delivered by cesarean section for breech presentation, birth weight 3500 g; current weight 4300 g, length 52 cm, head circumference 38 cm, and she was breastfed. Vital signs: pulse 130 /min, respiratory rate 50 /min, axillary temperature 37.8 °C. The anterior fontanel was normal; eyes, ears, chest, and abdomen were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed RBC count 3.1 × 10^12/L, WBC count 12.6 × 10^9/L with 60% neutrophils, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 20 mm/L, and negative C-reactive protein. Urinalysis and urine culture were normal. Blood urea nitrogen, electrolytes, and blood glucose were normal. Serum amylase was 10 U/L. Ultrasonography of the neck demonstrated bilateral multiple reactive lymph nodes (6 × 10 mm) in the anterior cervical chain associated with the left facial swelling. Chest radiograph was normal.

A 47-year-old woman with Marfan syndrome underwent ascending aortic replacement and SVG bypass to the PDA in 2017 for Stanford type A dissection involving the RCA ostium. The SVG occluded early, but collateral flow kept her asymptomatic. Five years later, she developed enlargement of the aortic root and arch with moderate–severe aortic regurgitation and reversible ischemia in the RCA territory. She underwent aortic arch replacement, Bentall procedure, and repeat SVG to the RCA. Her post-operative course was initially unremarkable. On post-operative day 12, routine coronary CT angiography to assess graft and anastomoses showed severe stenosis of the mid–left anterior descending artery, which had been normal before surgery. She was asymptomatic.  
Vital signs: BP 101/56 mmHg, HR 98 bpm, T 36.4 °C, O₂ sat 98% on room air.  
Physical examination: regular rhythm with mechanical click, no murmur.  
Cardiac enzymes: not significantly elevated.  
Electrocardiogram: new ST-segment depression in leads V5 and V6.  
Transthoracic echocardiography: new anteroseptal wall motion abnormality without vegetations or valvular abnormalities.

A 71-year-old man with cardiomyopathy and long-standing type 2 diabetes was admitted for worsening leg edema and weight gain. He denied fever or headache but reported a chronic, foul-smelling purulent discharge from his right nostril for several years. Vital signs were: temperature 97.3°F, blood pressure 110/65 mmHg, heart rate 75 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Cardiac exam showed an irregular rhythm and a grade 2/6 systolic murmur at the apex. Lung exam revealed minimal crackles bilaterally in the lower posterior fields. Abdominal exam was notable for mild distention, and there was pitting edema of the lower extremities. Anterior rhinoscopy of the right nasal cavity revealed a hard foreign body coated with purulent secretions. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 7.7×10^3/mm^3 (74% neutrophils) and a serum creatinine of 1.7 mg/dL. A portable chest radiograph demonstrated marked cardiomegaly. A CT scan of the sinuses revealed extensive bilateral maxillary sinusitis and a calcified foreign body in the right nostril.

A 74-year-old woman with a 13-year history of gastroesophageal reflux disease (grade M), maintained on esomeprazole, underwent annual surveillance endoscopy at Tokyo Medical University Hospital. Despite seven attempts at Helicobacter pylori eradication, she remained H. pylori–positive. Her prior history included endoscopic submucosal dissection for tubular adenoma at age 61 and early-stage gastric cancer at age 71, both cured.

In 2009, white-light endoscopy revealed a 10-mm whitish, slightly depressed lesion on the lesser curvature of the gastric cardia. The surrounding mucosa showed open-type atrophic gastritis with intestinal metaplasia and diffuse redness. Physical examination, routine blood tests, and tumor markers were normal. Contrast-enhanced CT showed no mass lesion or lymphadenopathy. The patient was not taking NSAIDs, aspirin, steroids, or bisphosphonates.

Over the next 13 years, the lesion gradually increased to 15 mm on white-light imaging. Indigo carmine chromoendoscopy continued to highlight a depressed lesion. Narrow-band imaging (NBI) demonstrated a depressed whitish mucosa distinct from surrounding atrophic gastric mucosa and esophageal mucosa. Texture and color enhancement imaging (TXI) modes 1 and 2 emphasized the border of the depressed whitish area, with no abnormal vascular or structural patterns identified that would suggest neoplasia. A biopsy specimen was obtained from the lesion for histopathologic evaluation.

A 25-year-old man presented to the emergency department with involuntary, sustained upward deviation of both eyes for one day. He reported weekly marijuana use for five years and that, one day earlier, he had smoked a small amount of “angel dust” (phencyclidine) mixed with tobacco and snorted a little. He felt dizzy and slept through the night. On awakening, his eyes were involuntarily deviated upward, and subsequent attempts to bring them down by forceful effort lasted only seconds before they deviated upward again.

He denied fever, headache, light-headedness, slurred speech, weakness, diplopia, auditory or visual hallucinations. His medical history was notable only for marijuana use; he denied any prescription medication use or accidental use of antiemetics or antipsychotics. He had no family history of seizures, stroke, or cancer.

On presentation, he was hemodynamically stable and fully oriented. Pupils were equal and reactive to light. Sustained conjugate upward eye deviation was noted, with normal intraocular pressure and fundoscopic appearance. Cranial nerve functions were intact, muscle strength was 5/5 in all extremities, and there was no sensory deficit. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, serum electrolytes, and renal and liver function tests, were within normal limits. A urine drug screen was positive for phencyclidine (PCP).

A 76-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 2-week history of worsening shortness of breath on exertion and a nonproductive cough. She denied chest pain, fever, or hemoptysis. Five years earlier, she had been diagnosed clinically with asthma and used a salbutamol inhaler with minimal relief. Her medical history included diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and gout. Six months before this presentation, she was found to have iron deficiency anemia (hemoglobin, 8.0 g/dL) and underwent upper endoscopy, which revealed multiple arteriovenous malformations in the gastric fundus, antrum, and duodenum. There was no pertinent family history.

On examination, her oxygen saturation on room air was 93%. Bibasilar crackles were present, and air entry was decreased in the left lower hemithorax; mild pedal edema was noted. Electrocardiogram and cardiac enzymes were normal.

A chest radiograph demonstrated an ill-defined, tortuous opacity in the left lower lung.

A 17-year-old male presented with multiple skin lesions on the bilateral lower limbs for 7 months. The lesions began as painless vesicles with clear fluid, later drained pus, and resolved spontaneously. One month before presentation, he had 10–14 episodes per day of small-volume loose stool with mucus for 14 days, without fever, abdominal pain, or vomiting. Subsequently, he developed sharp, nonradiating pain at the tip of the left second toe progressing to dry gangrene of half the phalanx. He also noted bilateral lower limb swelling and facial puffiness that subsided by evening. He had a productive cough with streaky hemoptysis but no chest pain or dyspnea. He reported fatigue, anorexia, and significant weight loss. He denied hair loss, ear discharge, joint pain, rash, photosensitivity, mucosal ulcers, lymphadenopathy, and muscle weakness. There was no drug use.

On examination, he was pale. Pulses were absent in both dorsalis pedis and the left posterior tibial artery. Dry gangrene with a sharp line of demarcation was present on the left second toe. Patchy hair loss over both toes and multiple hyper- and hypopigmented lesions were noted on the lower limbs. Chest examination revealed diminished movement on the left side, a woody dull percussion note, and decreased breath sounds.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL; leukocyte count 28 560/mm3 with 36% eosinophils (absolute eosinophil count 10 288/mm3); ESR 73 mm/hr; hs-CRP 10 680 ng/mL; aPTT 37.7 s (control 29 s). Urinalysis revealed 1+ protein; 24-hour urine protein was 3.17 g/day. Peripheral smear showed elevated corrected reticulocyte count and LDH, with a positive direct Coombs test. ANA was positive (homogeneous pattern, 3+); ANA immunoblot was negative. Anti-dsDNA was elevated. Lupus anticoagulant was borderline elevated; anticardiolipin and anti–β2 glycoprotein I antibodies were normal. C3 and C4 levels were normal.

Contrast-enhanced chest CT and pulmonary angiography revealed multiple intermediate-walled cavitary lesions in both lower lobes; biopsy of one lesion showed necrotic tissue. Mantoux test and sputum for acid-fast bacilli were negative. Serologies for hepatitis A, B, C, HIV, and leptospirosis were negative. Repeated examinations of blood, urine, sputum, and stool for bacterial and parasitic infection were unremarkable; stool microscopy revealed no parasites.

A 57-year-old man with a history of laryngeal cancer treated by surgery, tracheotomy, and 8 weeks of adjuvant radiochemotherapy presented with a 1-week history of intermittent fever and nonproductive cough that progressed to dyspnea. He had no known HIV risk factors. SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR testing was negative on two occasions. Laboratory studies showed lymphopenia, a CD4+ T-lymphocyte count below 400 cells/mm3, and a C-reactive protein level of 60 UI. Chest CT revealed bilateral postero-basal ground-glass opacities with peribronchovascular thickening and interlobular septal thickening (“crazy paving”), a diffuse central and peripheral distribution, and multiple pulmonary cysts of variable size and wall thickness.

A 22-year-old Japanese man dislocated his right hip posteriorly while snowboarding and underwent closed reduction within three hours. He had no history of hip disease or risk factors for bone fragility. Two days after reduction, MRI showed no bony injuries or bone marrow edema around the hip joint. He was advised to avoid weight-bearing for one week, was discharged after two weeks, and remained at home using crutches for two months. Three months after the injury, he returned to work lifting heavy laundry loads and standing all day. Four months after the injury, he suddenly experienced right hip pain without new trauma. On examination, right hip range of motion was slightly limited (flexion 110°, extension 0°, external rotation 40°, internal rotation 20°). An anteroposterior radiograph showed an irregular contour along the lateral femoral head with focal bone loss. T1-weighted MRI revealed a low-intensity band convex to the articular surface above the epiphyseal scar. STIR imaging demonstrated surrounding bone marrow edema. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI showed enhancement of the band and adjacent marrow with diffuse edema. SPECT/CT with Tc-99m hydroxymethylene diphosphonate demonstrated increased uptake throughout the femoral head.

A 54-year-old man with a history of pulmonary and extrapulmonary sarcoidosis underwent a positron emission tomography scan for disease surveillance, which demonstrated focal increased uptake in the head and tail of the pancreas. A contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan was subsequently performed and did not show any pancreatic mass or dilation of the main pancreatic duct. Endoscopic ultrasound revealed several heterogeneous, infiltrative lesions with ill-defined borders involving the pancreatic head and tail. Fine-needle biopsy of these lesions was performed. Histopathology demonstrated nonnecrotizing granulomas.

An 80-year-old woman with idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura status post splenectomy presented with seven days of nighttime fevers, chills, night sweats, and weight loss. She was independent in her activities of daily living and had been asymptomatic until one week earlier. On examination, she appeared fatigued and had icterus, enlarged right cervical and left supraclavicular lymph nodes, hepatomegaly, and right upper quadrant tenderness.  

Initial laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 19.7 × 10^9/L (31% neutrophils, 58% lymphocytes, 11% monocytes), an alkaline phosphatase level of 595 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase of 281 U/L, alanine aminotransferase of 200 U/L, and total bilirubin of 2.0 mg/dL. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed multiple enlarged porta hepatis lymph nodes and findings suggestive of choledocholithiasis. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography showed no choledocholithiasis or ductal dilatation but did demonstrate prominent interaortocaval, periportal, and common hepatic lymph nodes. Computed tomography of the chest revealed enlarged bilateral axillary nodes and significant anterior and superior mediastinal lymphadenopathy suggestive of lymphoma.  

An infectious-disease evaluation, including tests for viral hepatitis, mononucleosis (monospot test), coccidioidomycosis, ehrlichiosis, rickettsia, QuantiFERON-TB Gold, histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, cytomegalovirus, and toxoplasmosis, as well as blood cultures, was negative. An excisional biopsy of a right cervical lymph node showed an atypical lymphoid proliferation. After multidisciplinary discussion, ultrasound-guided percutaneous core biopsies of liver parenchyma and periportal lymph nodes were obtained, and those specimens also revealed an atypical lymphoid infiltrate.

A 71-year-old woman presented with a 1-week history of painful vision loss and floaters in her left eye. She had no history of myopia, ocular trauma, or surgery. Visual acuity was 20/30–2 in the right eye and 20/80 in the left eye; intraocular pressure was 21 mm Hg OD and 17 mm Hg OS. The right eye was normal except for a mild nuclear sclerotic cataract and no inflammation. The left eye had rare anterior chamber cells, 1+ vitreous cells, choroidal detachments in the nasal and temporal periphery, and an overlying retinal detachment with shifting subretinal fluid; no retinal breaks were identified. Her medical history was unremarkable. Laboratory studies (CBC, basic metabolic panel, HIV, T-spot, syphilis screen, and ANCA panel) were normal. MRI of the brain and orbits showed mild posterior scleral enhancement but no intraocular mass. Fluorescein angiography showed late leakage in the temporal periphery; fundus autofluorescence was normal; optical coherence tomography revealed shallow subretinal fluid and a posterior vitreous detachment. She was started on 80 mg oral prednisone for presumed serous retinal detachment secondary to posterior scleritis. Two weeks later, the choroidal detachments had resolved but the retinal detachment persisted and appeared more corrugated; intraocular pressures remained normal and no retinal breaks were seen.

A 46-year-old man underwent orthotopic liver transplantation for hepatitis B–related cirrhosis 10 weeks earlier and was maintained on routine immunosuppression. His postoperative course was complicated by pulmonary aspergillosis, for which he underwent left lower lobe wedge resection. Three weeks after thoracic surgery, he began to experience low back pain that progressed over several weeks despite conservative therapy.  

On examination, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Neurologic examination was normal. Plain radiographs of the lumbar spine were unremarkable.  

Lumbar spine MR imaging revealed the following:  
• T1-weighted images showed band-like to diffuse hypointense signals in vertebral bodies L2 through L5.  
• T2-weighted images showed vertebral isointensity to minimal hyperintensity.  
• In the L2–3 and L4–5 intervertebral discs, intranuclear clefts were preserved and discs lacked hyperintense T2 signal; in the L3–4 disc, the intranuclear cleft was lost.  
• Endplate irregularities were seen at involved levels, with disc space narrowing at L3–4 and L4–5.  
• Postcontrast images demonstrated band-like or diffuse enhancement of involved vertebrae and an epidural fluid collection.  
• A relatively well-defined paraspinal abnormal signal was present.  

Based on these MR findings, a diagnosis of tuberculous spondylitis was favored over pyogenic spondylitis.

A 64-year-old man presented with six months of chest discomfort and exertional dyspnea. His past medical history was unremarkable. On examination, blood pressure was 124/66 mmHg and heart rate was 86 beats/min. Cardiac auscultation revealed a grade 4/6 continuous biphasic murmur along the left sternal border and a grade 3/6 systolic murmur at the apex. There were no stigmata of Marfan syndrome.

Electrocardiography showed atrial fibrillation, ventricular premature beats, left ventricular hypertrophy, and ST–T–wave abnormalities. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated:
- A dilated heart with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 42%.  
- An abnormal channel between the ascending aorta and left ventricle, visualized in the parasternal long-axis view.  
- Color Doppler imaging revealed anterograde systolic and retrograde diastolic flow between the aorta and left ventricle, with retrograde diastolic flow also seen in the apical five-chamber view.  
- On a modified parasternal long-axis view, a third orifice communicating with the right ventricle was identified; color Doppler showed a jet from the channel into the right ventricle, and a biphasic spectral profile (peak velocity 489 cm/s) was recorded.  
- The aortic valve was tricuspid, calcified, and had a small aneurysm of the noncoronary cusp.  
- The posterior mitral leaflet at P2–P3 segments showed chordal rupture with severe eccentric regurgitation.

Laboratory studies revealed an N-terminal pro–brain natriuretic peptide level of 641 pg/mL; other blood counts, electrolytes, renal and hepatic panels, coagulation tests, autoimmune and inflammatory markers were within normal limits.

A 66-year-old woman with a history of multiple myeloma was admitted for initiation of teclistamab with planned step-up dosing. Two days after her first dose, she noted a new lesion at the site of injection on her right abdomen. She was afebrile, and her vital signs were stable. Dermatologic examination revealed a single indurated, erythematous, purpuric annular plaque on the right abdominal pannus that was tender to palpation. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 7.5 g/dL, platelet count of 406 000/µL, a normal white-cell count with an absolute neutrophil count of 4300/µL, and an absolute lymphocyte count of 200/µL. A punch biopsy of the plaque demonstrated a moderately dense infiltrate of neutrophils and lymphocytes extending into the deep reticular dermis and superficial subcutis; no necrosis was seen, and the epidermis was unremarkable. Tissue cultures (gram stain, acid-fast bacilli stain and culture, periodic acid–Schiff stain, Grocott stain, and anaerobic cultures) were all negative, and there was no evidence of myeloma on histopathologic evaluation.

A 70-year-old woman from a rural village presented with a 6-month history of more than 10 watery diarrheal stools per day and an 18-kg weight loss. Laboratory studies showed normal hemoglobin; white-cell count with differential; C-reactive protein; serum albumin; immunoglobulin levels; iron studies; vitamin B12; and folate; the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 40 mm/hr. Chest radiograph was normal. Two stool examinations for occult blood, leukocytes, parasites, and bacterial pathogens were negative. Colonoscopy with biopsies was unremarkable, and duodenal biopsies showed only mild, non-diagnostic villous changes. Serologic tests for tissue transglutaminase antibodies, endomysial antibodies, chromogranin-A, and HIV were negative. A small-bowel videocapsule endoscopy demonstrated mucosal areas of denuded villi and prominent submucosal vessels in the jejunum, as well as multiple linear whitish lesions surrounded by reddish mucosa in the ileum.

A 42-year-old man who underwent gastric sleeve surgery 3 years ago (weight reduced from 153 kg to 98 kg) presented with a 1-week history of intermittent left ankle pain that worsened with walking and improved with rest, accompanied by a limping gait. Two weeks before presentation, he had jogged for 30 minutes for the first time since his surgery, with no history of trauma. On examination, there was mild dorsal hind-foot swelling, decreased range of motion, and lateral ankle tenderness; neurovascular status was intact. Laboratory studies, including an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 14 mm/h (normal, 0–15 mm/h) and a C-reactive protein level of 6.23 mg/L (normal, <10 mg/L), were within normal limits. Plain radiographs of the left ankle (AP, mortise, and lateral views) showed no abnormalities. Four weeks later, his pain had worsened, and an MRI of the left ankle demonstrated diffuse bone marrow edema of the talus body and neck.

A 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and hypertension presented with severe retrosternal chest pain and progressive shortness of breath. On examination, his oxygen saturation was 91–92% on room air, blood pressure 220/120 mm Hg, and pulse rate 120 beats/minute. Initial laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 14.7 g/dL, platelet count of 229 × 10^9 /L, troponin of 309 ng/mL, prothrombin time within normal limits, partial thromboplastin time of 32 seconds, and creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL. The 4T-score for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia was low. An electrocardiogram demonstrated ST-segment elevation in the anterolateral leads and reciprocal ST-segment depression in the inferior leads. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed an ejection fraction of 45% with hypokinesia of the left anterior descending artery territory. The patient was given aspirin, β-blockers, and intravenous nitroglycerin and then taken for coronary angiography, which showed a total thrombotic occlusion of the mid–left anterior descending artery, 30% stenosis of the left circumflex artery, and subtotal occlusion of the obtuse marginal branch. Balloon angioplasty and deployment of a drug-eluting stent were performed. During the procedure, he received intravenous unfractionated heparin and a 180 mg loading dose of ticagrelor. Six hours after the procedure, routine blood work revealed a platelet count of 70 × 10^9 /L on two separate measurements, with no signs of active bleeding. A peripheral blood smear was unremarkable, with no schistocytes. Hemoglobin and creatinine levels remained stable and comparable to baseline.

A 67-year-old man presented to the emergency department with acute central chest pain. Four months earlier, he had undergone bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement and a saphenous vein graft to the obtuse marginal artery for severe aortic stenosis. His history included hypertension, percutaneous coronary intervention to the posterior descending and obtuse marginal arteries two years earlier, and monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance. On examination he was diaphoretic, with a soft systolic murmur over the aortic area. Initial ECG showed normal sinus rhythm without ST-T changes. High-sensitivity troponin I was 185 ng/L (normal 0–34 ng/L). One hour later, during recurrent chest pain, ECG revealed ST-segment depression in the inferolateral leads. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 95 g/L, leukocyte count 11.5 × 10^9/L, and C-reactive protein 167 mg/L. Urgent coronary angiography demonstrated unchanged appearance of the left main stem, left anterior descending artery, and obtuse marginal graft, but a new severe stenosis in the proximal to mid–right coronary artery. Optical coherence tomography of the right coronary artery showed a normal trilaminar appearance without plaque rupture or intracoronary thrombosis. The stenosis improved but did not fully resolve after intracoronary nitrate administration, and no percutaneous intervention was performed.

A 77-year-old man presented with six months of worsening vision in his left eye, without significant metamorphopsia. His best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 OD and 20/200 OS. Anterior segments were unremarkable except for moderate corticonuclear cataracts; intraocular pressures were normal. He had a history of arterial hypertension (controlled) and cardiac arrhythmia and no diabetes; family history was positive for age-related macular degeneration.

Spectral-domain OCT of the right eye showed a classic epiretinal membrane only. In the left eye, OCT revealed a large atrophic lamellar macular hole with intraretinal cavitation and tissue loss affecting the inner nuclear and outer plexiform layers, thinning of the outer plexiform layer with a central foveal bump, reduced central foveal thickness, disruption of the ellipsoid zone, and extensive lamellar hole-associated epiretinal proliferation (LHEP). Within the LHEP were numerous small hyperreflective round structures, single lesions with hyporeflective lumens and hyperreflective walls, and large hyporeflective cystoid spaces.

Fundus photography of the left eye showed two red dot–like lesions temporal to the fovea without gliosis or retinal folds. Near-infrared and blue autofluorescence imaging displayed these as hyporeflective dots; blue autofluorescence also showed a hyperreflective area corresponding to the lamellar defect. Fluorescein and indocyanine green angiography demonstrated an anomalous vascular network with intraretinal and intra-LHEP exudation; the hyperfluorescent structures corresponded to dilated abnormal vessels. OCT angiography revealed that these vessels originated in the deep retinal plexus and extended to the superficial plexus, with an area of capillary rarefaction in the superficial plexus and a temporal microvascular loop in the deep plexus. No flow was detected inside the LHEP.

A 42-year-old woman with a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with a 3-month history of severe pain in the left leg, progressive muscle weakness, and difficulty climbing and descending stairs. Over this period, she also experienced a 15-kg weight loss, loss of appetite, and sleep disturbances. She was treated for a lumbar disc herniation (L4–5 midline protrusion on MRI) without improvement of her pain. Her current medications included oral antidiabetic agents and gabapentin 300 mg three times daily, with a visual analogue scale score of 9/10 for her pain. Her body-mass index was 19.0 kg/m2.

On examination, there was obvious atrophy of the deltoid and quadriceps muscles bilaterally. Upper-extremity muscle strength was normal, but lower-extremity strength was 3/5 proximally and 4/5 distally. Glove-stocking hypoesthesia was present, hip movements were painful and restricted, and the adductor, flexor, and hamstring muscle groups were shortened. Reflexes were hypoactive in the upper extremities and absent (Achilles and patellar) in the lower extremities. No pathological reflexes were noted.

Laboratory studies showed fasting blood glucose of 166 mg/dL, postprandial glucose of 266 mg/dL, and hemoglobin A1c of 7.8%. Complete blood counts, routine biochemistry, and acute-phase reactants were within normal limits. Brucella agglutination test was negative. Vitamin D and B12 levels, muscle enzymes, and thyroid function tests were normal. Her Beck Depression Inventory score was 28, indicating moderate depression. She admitted to poor glycemic control and lack of dietary adherence.

A 75-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a several-day history of constant, sharp right upper-quadrant abdominal pain and back pain that had no clear trigger and did not relate to food intake. He denied nausea, vomiting, fever, jaundice, rash, or itching. His medical history was notable for degenerative spine disease treated with multiple lumbar infiltrations and fusion surgeries. On examination, he had mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant and a negative Murphy’s sign. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies showed normal complete blood count, liver function tests, pancreatic enzymes, and no evidence of inflammation or cholestasis. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography confirmed gallstones and incidentally noted side-branch intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms of the pancreas. The emergency physician’s initial working diagnosis was symptomatic cholelithiasis. An abdominal ultrasound again demonstrated gallstones, and the patient was referred for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy while receiving scopolamine butylbromide and ibuprofen for pain control. The consulting abdominal surgeon noted that the patient’s pain was constant rather than colicky and detected bulging of the right lateral abdominal wall, hypesthesia of the overlying skin, and pain along the lower right-sided ribs.

A 17-year-old male, confirmed SARS-CoV-2–positive by RT-PCR on a nasal swab two weeks earlier, initially experienced fever, cough, headache, myalgia, and anosmia and was treated as an outpatient with penicillin, acetaminophen, and nadroparin. He now presents with severe oral pain, poor appetite, inability to eat or speak, a burning sensation in the mouth, fatigue, and occasional oral bleeding. 

On examination, the lips and adjacent oral mucosa are vermilion in color with numerous erythematous bullous and erosive lesions. There are vesiculobullous and macular lesions on the oral mucosa consistent with EM-like lesions. No pulmonary symptoms are present, but there are multiple dark red, purpuric, irregular maculopapular lesions on the abdomen, which are asymptomatic. Ruptured mucosal vesicles on the lips leave thick white or yellow exudate and ulcerations with hemorrhagic crusting. Oral hygiene is poor due to pain. The bilateral submandibular lymph nodes are enlarged and tender.

Laboratory tests reveal a mildly elevated white blood cell count (11.5 × 10^9/L), C-reactive protein 7.2 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 16/32 mm/h, and D-dimer 0.85 µg/mL FEU. Samples from the oral mucosa and tongue are negative for bacterial and fungal pathogens.

A previously healthy 4-year-old boy of Indian origin was admitted with a 2-day history of vomiting, diarrhoea, and fever, complicated by sudden disturbance of consciousness on the day of admission. He was fully vaccinated except for rotavirus vaccine, with no recent travel or animal exposure. On examination, his temperature was 39.6 °C, heart rate 155 beats/min, respiratory rate 30 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 99 % on room air, and blood pressure 92/59 mm Hg. He appeared mildly dehydrated. He was drowsy with transient agitation and had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 13; he was lethargic, unable to recognize his parents, and intermittently confused, uttering incoherent words and unable to answer questions appropriately.

Laboratory studies showed haemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, leucocyte count 11,100 cells/µL, platelet count 225,000 cells/µL, serum sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 92 mmol/L, urea 8.3 mmol/L, creatinine 54 µmol/L, alanine aminotransferase 105 U/L, ammonia 85 µmol/L, and C-reactive protein 25 mg/L. Cerebrospinal fluid examination revealed no leukocytes, protein 0.15 g/L, and glucose 3.6 mmol/L. Cranial CT scan was unremarkable. On hospital day 4 (six days after symptom onset), MRI of the brain showed a solitary hyperintense lesion in the splenium of the corpus callosum on T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted images with corresponding diffusion restriction on apparent diffusion coefficient mapping. An initial EEG on day 2 demonstrated widespread slow-wave activity, more prominent in the right hemisphere, without seizures. Rotavirus RNA was detected by PCR in a stool specimen but not in CSF; the genotype was identified as G1P8.

A 9-year-old girl presented with two weeks of right upper-quadrant abdominal pain, decreased appetite, vomiting, weight loss, malaise, and low-grade intermittent fever. She had no diarrhea, jaundice, cough, or known TB contact. On examination, she was afebrile (maximum temperature 37.8 °C) with moderate wasting (BMI 13.5 kg/m2) and a non-tender liver palpable 3 cm below the right costal margin (span ∼12 cm); there was no splenomegaly or fluid collection. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (WBC 15 500/mm3) with 50% eosinophils, 25% neutrophils, and 20% lymphocytes; hematocrit 39.1%; platelets 501 700/mm3. Liver and kidney function tests, chest radiograph, and stool examination were normal. Serologic tests for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly with an abnormal echo-pattern and cystic changes. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated multiple cystic lesions with small daughter cysts forming a communicating hypoechoic mass-like lesion in the liver. Hydatid cyst was considered, and the patient was started on albendazole; intravenous antibiotics were discontinued.

A 17-year-old female presented with a one-day history of generalized painful skin rash and extensive blistering involving the lips and eyelids. She reported a preceding five-day history of cough, sore throat, and fever for which she had been taking oral azithromycin. On the third day of antibiotic therapy, she developed a nonpruritic eruption of bumps on the trunk that rapidly spread to more than 20% of her body surface area, followed by blistering and crusting of mucosal surfaces. Examination revealed swollen eyelids and lips and detachment of approximately 20% of the epidermis. A clinical diagnosis of Stevens–Johnson syndrome–toxic epidermal necrolysis overlap with tracheobronchitis was made and azithromycin was discontinued. Two days after stopping the antibiotic, new cutaneous lesions continued to appear without clinical improvement. Laboratory evaluation showed a leukocyte count of 8000/μl with 60% lymphocytes and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 70 mm/hour; liver enzymes and serum creatinine were within normal limits. Serologic tests for syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B and C, herpes simplex virus, Epstein–Barr virus, influenza A/B, and Chlamydia pneumoniae were negative.

A 46-year-old man with a 20-year history of gout presented with nontender subcutaneous nodules on the abdomen, groin, and right thigh. The nodules had been present for two years; over the past three weeks some became erythematous and then ulcerated. Three and a half weeks before presentation, he had been admitted with congestive heart failure and acute renal failure. He had never received treatment for gout. His medical history also included type II diabetes mellitus and morbid obesity (BMI 40.6).

On examination, there were multiple whitish subcutaneous nodules and four ulcers in the lower abdomen, right groin, and right thigh. The ulcers measured 1–3 cm in diameter and were covered by fibrinous, necrotic, chalky material over poorly formed granulation tissue. The nonulcerated nodules were pale, 1.0–1.5 cm in diameter, and had focal erythema. There was also swelling of the right elbow and right-hand metacarpophalangeal joints.

Laboratory tests on recent admission showed: uric acid 14.3 mg/dL (4–7), blood glucose 255 mg/dL (70–99), BUN 47 mg/dL (5–20), creatinine 1.61 mg/dL (0.8–1.4), and eGFR 46 mL/min/1.73 m2 (≥59). At the time of surgical removal of the ulcerated nodules 3–4 weeks later, uric acid was 10.8 mg/dL and 11.2 mg/dL; BUN 38 mg/dL; creatinine 1.65 mg/dL; eGFR 45 mL/min/1.73 m2; and blood glucose 147 mg/dL.

Excisional biopsies of two abdominal lesions and one right-thigh lesion were performed over a three-week period. On gross sectioning, multiple areas were filled with white, chalky material.

A 31-year-old woman from a rural area with no significant medical history presented with a progressively enlarging mass in the medial aspect of her left upper thigh, first noted 1 year earlier. She denied fever, chills, weight loss, or trauma. On examination, there was a fixed, non-tender 7 × 4 cm subcutaneous mass without overlying skin changes or lymphadenopathy. Hip and knee motion were normal, and peripheral pulses were equal bilaterally. 

Plain radiographs of the left femur showed no bone involvement or calcification. MRI revealed a well-circumscribed cystic lesion within the adductor muscles of the left thigh that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted and fat-saturated sequences, and contained multiple smaller “daughter” cysts. After gadolinium administration, moderate peripheral enhancement was noted around the main cyst and its internal daughter cysts. 

Abdominal ultrasonography and chest radiographs showed no evidence of hepatic or pulmonary lesions. Initial laboratory tests were within normal limits, and hydatid serology was negative.

A two-month-old male was referred for evaluation of facial dysmorphias. His mother, a 19-year-old woman, had a dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy complicated by suspected acute Toxoplasma gondii infection at six weeks’ gestation (maternal anti–T. gondii IgM positive). She experienced a threatened miscarriage at 11 weeks’ gestation, and by 14 weeks only one fetus was visible on ultrasound. In the third trimester, ultrasound revealed a unilateral complete palatal defect in the surviving twin.

The infant was delivered by cesarean section at 38 weeks’ gestation with a birth weight of 2.78 kg (10th percentile), length 48 cm (10th–25th percentile), and Apgar scores of 8 and 9. On initial examination, he lacked the left eye and had an ipsilateral oblique oro-orbital cleft. On day 4, a TORCH screen showed positive IgG for T. gondii, rubella, and cytomegalovirus, with negative IgM for all three agents. A complete blood count and metabolic screen were normal. Auditory screening demonstrated bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. At two months of age, he had no psychomotor delay and normal findings in the right eye.

Cranial computed tomography revealed a left oblique oro-orbital and parasagittal cleft, absence of ipsilateral bony tissue and soft palate, left choanal atresia with a narrow vestibule, a narrowed right choanal passage, and hypoplastic left turbinates. Nasal endoscopy confirmed these findings. The left orbit contained no eyeball or optic nerve but showed hypoplastic extraocular muscles; the brain parenchyma and right facial structures were normal.

A 4-year-old boy presented with longstanding chest discomfort, mild tachypnea, and wheezing. On physical examination, he had cardiac enlargement without murmurs. Cardiac percussion confirmed an enlarged cardiac silhouette. Three years earlier, transthoracic echocardiography had suggested a dual-chamber left ventricle, and no treatment was instituted. 

In January 2022, evaluation at our hospital included the following findings:  
– Coagulation studies: prothrombin time 12.9 s (11.5–14.5), prothrombin activity 104% (80–120), INR 0.98 (0.8–1.2), activated partial thromboplastin time 45.9 s (28.5–43.5), thrombin time 17.6 s (14–21), fibrinogen 2.82 g/L (2.0–4.0), D-dimer 0.18 μg/mL (<0.5), fibrin degradation products 2.50 μg/mL (0–5).  
– N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide: 113 pg/mL (<150).  
– 24-hour Holter monitor: sinus rhythm with first-degree left bundle branch block.  
– Chest radiograph: abnormal protrusion of the left cardiac margin.  
– Transthoracic echocardiography: the left ventricle was divided into a main and an accessory chamber by abnormal muscle bundles in the mid-cavity, with only scant slit-like communications (largest orifice 4.8 mm). The accessory chamber had severely reduced systolic function with almost no blood motion, and spectral Doppler demonstrated low-velocity flow between the two chambers.

On March 1, 2018, at a university teaching pig farm in Namibia’s Khomas Region, two adult pigs (a boar and a sow) were found dead without prior signs. Nonclotting blood was dripping from their nostrils, and scrotal hyperemia was noted. To rule out anthrax, blood smears were stained with M’Fadyean stain; results were negative for Bacillus anthracis. The remaining herd of 57 pigs received intramuscular procaine benzylpenicillin and benzathine benzylpenicillin as postexposure prophylaxis.

On March 7, four additional pigs died suddenly. Two other pigs (a boar and a sow) were found ill with sternal recumbency, weakness, reluctance to move, skin hyperemia (notably scrotum), inappetence, rectal temperatures of 39.5–39.8 °C, and respiratory rates of about 10 breaths per minute. They were treated with amoxicillin–clavulanate and flunixin meglumine but died two days later.

Necropsy of these pigs revealed large patches of skin hyperemia; multifocal ecchymotic hemorrhages on the neck; copious unclotted blood in pleural and peritoneal cavities; diffuse carcass congestion; splenomegaly; pulmonary consolidation; hemorrhagic, frothy airways; hepatomegaly with congestion; congested gastric mucosa; enlarged, congested kidneys; epicardial and endocardial hemorrhages; and in one boar and one sow, a markedly enlarged, congested urinary bladder.

Tissues (spleen and gastrohepatic lymph nodes) were tested by PCR targeting the p72 gene of African swine fever virus; all samples were negative. At this stage, the differential diagnoses included African swine fever, actinobacillosis (Actinobacillus suis and Actinobacillus pleuropneumoniae), anthrax, Mycoplasma suis, septicemic salmonellosis, and swine erysipelas.

A 17-year-old previously healthy male presented with a 6-week history of dull, poorly localized abdominal discomfort. He reported evening fevers up to 101.4°F without chills or rigor but with significant diaphoresis, and an 8-kg weight loss over 6 months. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 6.2 mg/L, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 53 mm/hr, and mildly elevated liver enzymes (AST 52 U/L; ALT 62 U/L). Abdominal ultrasonography revealed multiple subcapsular hypoechoic lesions in the right hepatic lobe, the largest measuring approximately 24 × 9 mm, each with central liquefaction. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a subcentimetric hypodense lesion in segment VIII contiguous with a minimal subcapsular collection, several additional subcapsular hypodense lesions without significant enhancement, and mild thickening and enhancement of the hepatic capsule and subcapsular region.

A 19-month-old unimmunized boy presented with a five-day history of truncal ataxia. He had been healthy, met developmental milestones normally, walked at 12 months, and ran by 15 months. Three weeks before presentation, his mother noted irritability and disrupted sleep.
