Five days before admission, he developed an axillary fever of 38°C, lost the ability to sit or walk unassisted, and had a sudden slowdown in language acquisition. Initial treatment for presumed bilateral otitis media did not improve his symptoms.

In the emergency department, his temperature was 36.7°C, heart rate 116 beats/min, respiratory rate 29 breaths/min, blood pressure 101/68 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He was awake, alert, and verbal. Muscle bulk and tone were normal, antigravity strength was intact in all extremities, and deep tendon reflexes were normal. Neurologic examination revealed profound truncal ataxia; he could not sit or walk unassisted, showed a left-hand preference, but had no dysmetria. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

On hospital day 0, laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 24,000 cells/µL with 18% eosinophils and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 39 mm/hr. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis on hospital day 0 revealed 13 WBCs/mm3 with 29% eosinophils, 2 RBCs/mm3, glucose 50 mg/dL, and protein 33 mg/dL. Repeat CSF on hospital day 4 showed 31 WBCs/mm3 with 41% eosinophils, 0 RBCs/mm3, glucose 48 mg/dL, and protein 33 mg/dL.

Brain MRI demonstrated diffuse, confluent, symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the supratentorial periventricular and deep white matter and bilateral cerebellar hemispheres around the deep cerebellar nuclei. Postcontrast images showed punctiform and curvilinear enhancement predominantly in the bilateral cerebral and cerebellar periventricular white matter with a perivascular distribution. Spinal MRI was normal. Extensive CSF testing for viral, bacterial, fungal, amoebic, and mycobacterial pathogens was negative.

A 16-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes mellitus diagnosed at age 10 presented for her first routine visit to our clinic in 2006. She reported poor glycemic control and difficult adherence since diagnosis. She had been on multiple daily insulin injections (mean 0.97 U/kg/day) and was switched to insulin‐pump therapy in 2006. 

Physical examination revealed two yellow-brown, atrophic plaques with raised violaceous rims on the right lower abdomen (measuring 2 × 0.5 cm and 3.5 × 2 cm) and multiple similar plaques on both legs. The lesions were shiny and telangiectatic but nonulcerated and asymptomatic. 

After the switch to pump therapy, her insulin requirement decreased to 0.70 U/kg/day, but her mean HbA1c remained elevated at 12.9% (± 1.1). By December 2010, back on multiple daily injections, her HbA1c was 12.8% with an insulin requirement of 1.58 U/kg/day. Topical corticosteroids were applied without improvement of the skin lesions.

A 45-year-old woman with a 4-year history of seronegative rheumatoid arthritis treated with leflunomide and intermittent low-dose prednisolone presented with increasing pain and swelling of her right hand. Two weeks before evaluation, she had received prednisolone 20 mg daily for 10 days with only slight improvement. On examination, the third metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint of the right hand was swollen and tender, and prednisone was increased to 40 mg daily. Two weeks later she returned with persistent swelling over the back of the right hand and the third MCP joint; other joints were unaffected. Musculoskeletal ultrasound showed tenosynovitis of the third extensor tendon with intense power Doppler signal. Laboratory studies revealed thrombocytosis (422 × 10^3/μl), leukocytosis (15.9 × 10^3/μl), neutrophils 83.9%, and a C-reactive protein of 7.6 mg/l; other tests were normal. On cutaneous examination of the right hand there was reddish-purplish discoloration over the distal and intermediate phalanges of the third and fourth fingers with central golden scabs on papules and nodules. A single reddish-purplish erythematous nodule in a linear “sporotrichoid” distribution was noted on the proximal right forearm. No axillary lymphadenopathy was present. The patient reported regular fish-tank cleaning and recent seaside travel. A clinical diagnosis of “swimmer’s granuloma” was made, and a biopsy was obtained for microbiological analysis.

A 69-year-old Asian woman with a history of stage IVa colorectal adenocarcinoma metastatic to the lung—status post resection and chemotherapy with stable disease—underwent nonenhanced head CT as part of a preoperative evaluation. The CT scan revealed a 1.0 cm × 0.9 cm × 1.2 cm hyperdense mass in the left frontal lobe with inhomogeneous calcification. Brain MRI demonstrated an iso- to low-intensity lesion on T1-weighted imaging, low intensity on T2-weighted imaging, low intensity on diffusion-weighted imaging, low intensity on susceptibility-weighted imaging, and minimal enhancement after gadolinium administration. There was no surrounding edema or mass effect, and the patient had no neurological symptoms.

A 78-year-old man was admitted with progressive dyspnea. He had never smoked, had a 30-year history of mine work, atrial fibrillation, and congestive heart failure treated with warfarin, famotidine, and furosemide. On examination, blood pressure was 190/118 mm Hg, pulse 102 /min, temperature 36.0 °C, respiratory rate 28 /min, and oxygen saturation 96% on 3 L nasal oxygen. Breath sounds were decreased bilaterally; heart sounds were muffled. Laboratory studies showed WBC 13 900/mm3 with a left shift, LDH 942 U/L, AST 1072 U/L, ALT 1561 U/L, albumin 3.1 g/dL, CRP 6.8 mg/dL, and soluble IL-2 receptor 2760 U/mL. Serum T-SPOT, tuberculosis, and HTLV-1 tests were negative. Echocardiography revealed a moderate pericardial effusion and normal ejection fraction. Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral pleural effusions with innumerable tiny lung nodules, and CT confirmed bilateral pleural and pericardial effusions plus diffuse bilateral micronodular lung infiltration. On hospital day 2, pericardiocentesis and pleurocentesis were performed, and cytologic examination of both fluids revealed malignant lymphoma.

An 8‐year‐old female Shetland sheepdog was referred for evaluation of a progressively enlarging mass in the left parotid region. The owner first noted a subcutaneous nodule measuring <1 cm 20 months earlier. The dog, weighing 12.9 kg, was not obese and had no other lipomatous lesions. On presentation, the mass measured 9.0×7.0×1.5 cm but the dog was otherwise asymptomatic. Ultrasonography demonstrated a well‐circumscribed capsule around the lesion, and skull radiographs showed no evidence of bone invasion. A Tru‐Cut biopsy performed one week before surgery was non‐diagnostic; histopathology showed “scattered serous lobules (probably of salivary gland origin) between mature lipid cells and hemorrhagic foci.” The entire left parotid gland was surgically excised. Grossly, the gland had a flat, smooth surface without distinct fibrous encapsulation, and its lobular configuration was well maintained. In formalin, the gland floated, suggesting high fat content. On microscopic examination, individual and variably sized sheets of mature adipocytes diffusely infiltrated interlobular and intralobular spaces, occupying the greater proportion of the gland, while the remaining serous acini and ducts showed little morphological change. A thin collagen fiber capsule was intermittently present around the gland, and there was no infiltration of adipocytes into adjacent tissues.

A 70-year-old man with lymphoma treated with chemotherapy and type 2 diabetes presented with left neck swelling, sore throat, exertional dyspnea, and low-grade fever for several days. He had no history of smoking, alcohol use, respiratory infections, allergies, or medication noncompliance. Examination showed left lateral neck swelling with normal overlying skin. Flexible nasolaryngoscopy revealed swelling over the left arytenoid and false vocal cord with reduced mobility and slight reduction in respiratory airflow; the true vocal cords were normal. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 23.5×10^9/L, hemoglobin of 10.9 g/dL, and C-reactive protein of 112 mg/L; other biochemistry and coagulation profiles were normal. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the neck demonstrated a 17×13×12 mm cystic lesion with fluid collection and an enhancing wall in the supraglottic region at the level of the thyroid cartilage, extending through the thyrohyoid membrane.

A 30-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 2+0, at 35+1 weeks of gestation presented with a one-day history of per vaginal bleeding and a two-week history of absent fetal movements. Her prior pregnancies were both uncomplicated spontaneous vertex deliveries. On abdominal examination, the fundal height measured 30 cm with a cephalic-presenting fetus and no detectable fetal heart tones; there was no abdominal tenderness, and fetal parts were not easily palpable. Speculum examination revealed slight blood oozing from the cervix. An initial impression of antepartum hemorrhage—suggestive of placenta previa—with intrauterine fetal demise was made. A formal obstetric ultrasound reported fetal demise at 27+4 weeks and a low-lying placenta. The patient was admitted for induction of labor with misoprostol (five 100-µg sublingual doses), followed by placement of a Foley catheter, and then oxytocin infusion; after 48 hours, there was no cervical change. The patient was re-evaluated, and a bedside obstetric ultrasound demonstrated an empty uterus, leading to considerations of chronic uterine rupture and abdominal pregnancy. A decision was made to proceed to exploratory laparotomy.

A 30-year-old woman at 14 weeks’ gestation (gravida 2, para 1 by previous cesarean delivery) presented with a 12-hour history of diffuse abdominal pain, malaise, and a syncopal episode. Earlier that day she had seen her primary care physician for mild abdominal pain and nausea, received intravenous fluids and analgesics, and was discharged after symptom improvement. On return to the emergency department, her heart rate was 108 bpm, blood pressure 90/60 mmHg, and she appeared pale. Abdominal examination revealed moderate hypogastric tenderness, decreased bowel sounds, and a positive rebound test. The uterine fundus was palpable 2 cm above the pubic symphysis, and the fetal heart rate was 140 bpm. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 5.3 g/dL and hematocrit 16.7%. Transabdominal ultrasound demonstrated a large amount of free fluid in the abdomen, suggestive of hemoperitoneum.

A 60-year-old male farmer from central India presented with a 6-month history of a progressively enlarging palatal swelling that eventually ulcerated, accompanied by 5 months of widespread, painful, skin-colored papules and nodules. He reported 1 month of low-grade fever, weight loss, productive cough, and dyspnea. He had frequented local caves and forts but had no travel outside his region, no unprotected sexual exposures, and no history of diabetes or tuberculosis. He was a chronic alcoholic and smoker. On examination, he appeared undernourished and cachectic, with pallor, generalized lymphadenopathy, and xerosis. Cutaneous lesions were multiple 0.5–1.5 cm umbilicated papules and nodules with hemorrhagic crusts distributed over the scalp, face, neck, trunk, and extremities. There was a firm, ulcerated nodular lesion measuring approximately 2 × 2 × 0.5 cm on the hard palate. Routine hematological parameters were normal except for an ESR of 50 mm/h. A chest radiograph revealed bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. HIV ELISA was nonreactive, and the CD4 count was 720 cells/mm3.

A 36-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of pain and a mass in her right gluteal region. The pain worsened with walking and limited hip motion. On examination, there was mild erythema and a small swelling over the right gluteal area compared with the contralateral side. She had been evaluated at another center, where an abscess was suspected and needle aspiration was performed without clinical improvement. Plain radiographs of the hip showed no pathologic findings. Serologic tests, including an echinococcal indirect hemagglutination assay, were normal. Ultrasonography revealed a 52 mm × 47 mm hypoechoic intramuscular cyst with internal septations. Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis demonstrated a well-defined cystic lesion within the posterior gluteal musculature extending inferiorly without involvement of bone.

An 85-year-old Caucasian man presented on day 2 of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection with a dry cough and localized right posterolateral chest pain. His medical history included asthma, COPD, Crohn’s disease, hypertension, and obesity; he was an ex-smoker (13 pack‐years) with no prior thoracic surgery. His COVID-19 was treated with inhaled budesonide and a 5-day course of ritonavir/nirmatrelvir. He described extreme stabbing pain over the right lateral chest wall when coughing, with mild discomfort at rest, unchanged by deep inspiration or expiration. On examination, he was exquisitely tender to palpation over ribs 8–10 on the right side. Vital signs and blood tests were unremarkable. Initial chest X‐ray showed no acute changes, with long-standing hyperexpansion of the lung fields. The initial impression was musculoskeletal pain, with a differential diagnosis of hepatobiliary pathology or pneumonia. He was admitted for analgesia, but despite oral and subcutaneous opioids and an erector spinae plane nerve block, his pain remained extreme on coughing. On hospital day 4, he developed an extensive flank haematoma inferior to the site of his pain, and clinical examination demonstrated significant bulging of the chest wall on deep breathing and coughing.

A 22-year-old previously healthy man presented with a 3-day history of high fevers (up to 40.2 °C), myalgia, arthralgia, headache, dry cough with dyspnea, and vomiting. Initial laboratory tests showed neutrophilia (93.2%), lymphopenia (3.3%), and thrombocytopenia (51 × 10^9/L). He reported a mild subfebrile COVID-19 illness two weeks earlier and had received one dose of COVID-19 vaccine. On examination he was febrile (40.0 °C), tachycardic (129 bpm), normotensive (104/70 mmHg), and cardiopulmonary compensated; there was no rash, conjunctivitis, lymphadenopathy, or focal findings. Lung ultrasonography was normal. A nasopharyngeal SARS-CoV-2 PCR was positive (Ct 33.5), and influenza A/B PCR was negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed mild splenomegaly. 

Despite symptomatic care, by hospital day 2 he remained febrile, with further thrombocytopenia and rising CRP and IL-6. He developed diarrhea and abdominal pain, but stool studies were negative. Profound lymphopenia prompted HIV testing and initiation of broad anti-infective prophylaxis. 

Over the next 48 hours he continued to have fevers up to 40 °C, developed dyspnea with O2 saturation 92%, hypotension, and tachycardia. He now had a maculopapular rash on the chest, eyelid edema, and nonpurulent conjunctivitis. Repeat lung ultrasound showed confluent B-lines; ECG revealed sinus tachycardia with bigeminal ventricular extrasystoles. Laboratory tests demonstrated worsening thrombocytopenia, elevated CRP, IL-6, procalcitonin, troponin T, and NT-proBNP.

A 54-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of a rash localized to her right breast. Six months earlier, she had been diagnosed with oral pemphigus vulgaris (PV) on the basis of elevated anti-desmoglein (Dsg) 3 (150 IU/mL) and Dsg1 (100 IU/mL) IgG antibodies; she achieved remission on low-dose prednisone (7.5 mg/day). Her medications included trazodone, sertraline, lamotrigine, and duloxetine for major depressive disorder.

On examination, there was marked retraction of the right breast and nipple; the patient reported that breast retraction had been noted by her 18 months prior but was not evaluated until the rash appeared. The overlying skin of the right breast displayed multiple confluent erosions, hyperkeratotic scales, and crusts. The left breast was normal. Erythematous-scaling plaques were also present on the back. Mucosal surfaces, including the oral mucosa, conjunctivae, and genitals, were unremarkable.

A skin biopsy from an erosion showed suprabasal epidermal acantholysis. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin revealed intercellular IgG and C3 deposition in the epidermis. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay confirmed high levels of IgG autoantibodies against Dsg1 (101.3 IU/mL) and Dsg3 (148.8 IU/mL). Indirect immunofluorescence on monkey esophagus substrate was positive for intercellular IgG; on rat bladder epithelium it was negative. These findings were consistent with a relapse of pemphigus vulgaris.  

A computed tomography scan and subsequent breast biopsy confirmed an invasive triple-negative ductal carcinoma in the right breast.

A 19-year-old woman presented with sudden loss of central vision in her right eye. Her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/200 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Intraocular pressures were normal, and slit-lamp biomicroscopy of the anterior segment was unremarkable. Multicolor ophthalmoscopy of the right eye revealed a reddish-brown parafoveal lesion in the nasal macula; the left macula appeared normal. Infrared reflectance imaging showed tortuous retinal arteries in both eyes and a parafoveal hyporeflective area in the right eye.

Two weeks earlier, she had experienced flu-like symptoms; otherwise, her medical history was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a D-dimer level of 0.3 mg/L (normal <0.55 mg/L), fibrinogen 2.3 g/L (normal 1.8–3.5 g/L), and C-reactive protein 15 mg/L (normal <3 mg/L). Swept-source optical coherence tomography of the right eye demonstrated hyperreflectivity predominantly in the outer plexiform and outer nuclear layers, with extension to the photoreceptor inner segment–outer segment junction. Optical coherence tomography angiography revealed areas of reduced capillary density in the nasal parafoveal quadrant, with hyperdense projection artifacts from superficial vessels overlying a hyperreflective lesion. Fluorescein angiography showed no leakage or ischemia. There was no cilioretinal artery, and the location of the intraretinal hyperreflectivity did not correspond to any such supply area. Tortuosity of the retinal vessels was noted in both eyes.

A 46-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of progressively worsening lumbar pain localized to her left hip and buttock, with radicular symptoms radiating to her left anterior thigh. Her medical history was notable for Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, degenerative arthritis, scoliosis, a prior hysterectomy, a left hip replacement, two knee surgeries, and an appendectomy. Neurologic examination revealed no focal motor or sensory deficits but demonstrated pain in a left L4 and L5 distribution. Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine before and after contrast administration showed a multilobulated lesion with variable enhancement and possible fluid levels in the left L4 neural foramen. On the basis of these imaging characteristics, the radiologist’s differential diagnosis included a hemangioma or a nerve sheath tumor.

A 50-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of painless visual decline in the left eye. He had pulmonary silicosis with progressive fibrosis and a prior history of systemic nocardiosis (lung, cerebral, and skin abscesses) treated with sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim until December 2017. On examination, visual acuity was 10/10 in the right eye and 4/10 in the left. Anterior segments and intraocular pressures were normal bilaterally. Posterior segment examination of the left eye revealed no vitritis and a one-disk–diameter submacular white mass with fluffy borders and intraretinal hemorrhages, along with a smaller well-defined white lesion in the inferior temporal arcade. Spectral-domain OCT of the macular lesion showed a subretinal mass with disorganized retinal layers and subretinal fluid; the temporal arcade lesion appeared as a well-defined choroidal mass. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated early hypofluorescence progressing to late hyperfluorescence with leakage in the macula and hyperfluorescence without diffusion in the temporal lesion. Indocyanine green angiography showed persistent hypofluorescence in both lesions. The patient also reported fever and dry cough. Empiric therapy with oral trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole and intravenous imipenem was started. Three days later, left visual acuity declined to counting fingers; the macular lesion had enlarged with increased hemorrhages, neurosensory detachment, and a pseudohypopyon appearance. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein concentration of 84.8 mg/L and negative serologies for HIV, HCV, Toxoplasma, syphilis, CMV, EBV, and herpes viruses. Brain MRI and chest/abdomen/pelvis CT scans revealed no active infection. An anterior chamber tap was negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, herpesvirus, Toxoplasma, syphilis, and Nocardia.

A 31-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with an 18-month history of a gradually enlarging left lateral neck swelling. He denied otological or rhinological symptoms. On examination, there was an 8-cm, painless, slightly mobile, nonpulsatile, renitent mass extending from the level of the hyoid bone to the supraclavicular region. The overlying skin was unremarkable, and there was no palpable inferior margin of the mass. Examination of the oropharynx, nasopharynx, and laryngopharynx was normal.

Cervical ultrasound showed a well-defined, unilocular cystic mass deep to the left sternocleidomastoid muscle, measuring 85 mm in its longest dimension; the differential included a second branchial cleft cyst or a cystic lymphangioma. MRI of the neck demonstrated a prevascular, unilocular mass under the middle cervical fascia on the left side, measuring 11 × 51 × 73 mm, displacing the jugulocarotid vessels and the sternocleidomastoid muscle, with slight extension into the upper mediastinum.

An 80-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after an episode of syncope and dizziness; he had awakened on the floor earlier that morning. He denied headache or neck pain but reported dysphagia.  
His medical history included atrial fibrillation on sotalol (warfarin stopped 2 weeks earlier), two-vessel coronary artery bypass grafting, hyperlipidemia, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and a known 4.8-cm abdominal aortic aneurysm under surveillance.  
On examination, temperature was 97.7°F, blood pressure 160/94 mmHg, heart rate 65 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. He had a small left forehead abrasion and contusion, appeared awake and coherent, and had prominent soft tissue fullness in the anterior neck. Cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable, and coagulation studies were normal.  
Over the next 10–15 minutes, his dysphagia worsened, and the left anterior neck swelling progressed. Within 30 minutes, he developed increasing fullness on the left side of his neck and anterior chest wall without crepitus, became hoarse, and assumed a “sniff” position. Due to airway compromise, endotracheal intubation was performed without difficulty.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a large retropharyngeal hematoma posterior to the thyroid gland with active arterial extravasation thought to arise from the thyrocervical trunk. The hematoma measured 6.7 cm transversely by 3.2 cm anteroposteriorly, extended from the lower nasopharynx to the posterior mediastinum (total length, 25 cm), deviated the larynx anteriorly, and compressed the esophagus.

A 67-year-old German woman with no prior illnesses presented to ENT colleagues with an intraoral laceration in the upper left wisdom-tooth region. She felt faint and had a high fever. Laboratory testing showed a normal leukocyte count (5.88 × 10^3/μl) and an elevated C-reactive protein level (224 mg/l). She was treated with intravenous penicillin V (10 mega units once daily) and underwent extraction of the impacted upper left wisdom tooth on the same day. Despite this regimen, her condition did not improve; she developed higher fevers and progressive swelling of cervical lymph nodes. Twenty-five days after tooth extraction, her cervical lymph nodes had enlarged to approximately 30 mm in diameter, and she was hospitalized for repeat intravenous antibiotics (penicillin V 10 mega units once daily plus metronidazole 0.5 g twice daily). Sonography at that time demonstrated markedly enlarged cervical lymph nodes without clear fluid collections.

A 58-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of a right-breast lump. She had no family history of breast cancer, had been menopausal for 5 years, denied eating frogs or snakes, but recalled drinking impure water. On examination, she reported migratory discomfort and pain in the right axilla and upper-outer quadrant, and a mobile lump was palpated.  
Breast ultrasonography using a 13-MHz transducer revealed:  
- Upper-outer quadrant: a hypoechoic, tubular structure with surrounding increased echogenicity, measuring 5.0 × 1.7 × 0.7 cm (BIRADS 4b)  
- At 6 o’clock: an oval, low-echo mass with well-delineated contours, measuring 1.8 × 1.2 × 0.4 cm (BIRADS 4a) and closely abutting the pectoralis major  
- At 11–12 o’clock: two small hypoechoic masses in the fat layer, measuring 0.5 × 0.3 cm and 0.3 × 0.2 cm  
No obvious blood-flow signals were detected within any of these lesions on color Doppler flow imaging.  
What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 32-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of exertional dyspnea and a 2-week history of intermittent palpitations. Four weeks before referral, she had transient palpitations that resolved upon arrival in the emergency department. Over the next 2 weeks, her dyspnea worsened and became nearly constant. She reported chest fullness, recurrent palpitations, and edema of the ankles and face, for which she received hydrochlorothiazide. 

On referral, transthoracic echocardiography revealed an extrapericardial large cystic lesion markedly compressing the right side of the heart. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest showed a large (97 mm) heterogeneous, enhancing cystic mass in the right anterior mediastinum with peripheral linear calcifications, producing mass effect on the right atrium and ventricle.

A 46-year-old female refugee from the Dominican Republic with hypertension presented for management of presumed left axillary hidradenitis suppurativa diagnosed 4 years earlier. The lesions had remained confined to the left axilla, and she denied ever having similar lesions elsewhere. She had undergone multiple courses of antibiotics with minimal improvement and was treated with intralesional triamcinolone, topical clindamycin, and oral doxycycline. Two months after therapy initiation, the nodules had progressed, and two subcutaneous fluctuant masses developed beneath the existing nodules.

On examination, there were three tender erythematous nodules with friable granulation tissue and sinus tracts in the left axilla. Two large subcutaneous fluctuant masses were palpable in the superior-lateral quadrant of the left breast and pectoral region. A solitary left cervical lymph node was palpated. No double comedones or HS lesions were visible in other skin folds.

Routine laboratory studies were unremarkable. Surface ultrasound of the left axilla showed three heterogeneous fluid collections in the left deltopectoral groove (5 × 2 × 3 cm), left subclavian space (1.8 × 1.6 cm and 2.8 × 2.4 cm), and superolateral quadrant of the left breast (4.5 × 3.4 × 3.7 cm), all suggestive of suppurative adenitis.

A 40-year-old White British woman, dependent on a wheelchair because of neuromyelitis optica, presented with an 8-day history of a swollen, hot, and painless right forearm. She had been treated with oral antibiotics for presumed cellulitis without improvement; instead, the forearm developed visible deformity and instability. On examination, there was marked swelling and deformity but no reported pain. A forearm cast was applied, and plain radiographs revealed comminuted fractures through the midshafts of both the radius and ulna with significant soft‐tissue swelling. Laboratory studies showed normal C-reactive protein and white blood cell counts.

A 48-year-old woman with a 7-year history of dopamine-nonresponsive parkinsonism and autonomic failure (diagnosed as multiple system atrophy–parkinsonian type) was admitted for 3 months of frequent episodes of dizziness (even when supine) and transient involuntary twitching of her upper limbs. Five years earlier she had developed postural syncope due to orthostatic hypotension and decreased sweating; over the past year she lost independent ambulation and developed dysphagia from pseudobulbar palsy.  

Medical history was notable only for treated hyperthyroidism. Family history was unremarkable.  

On admission, supine blood pressure was 136/74 mmHg, falling to 82/46 mmHg at 45° head-up tilt. Neurologic examination showed mild cognitive impairment, hypophonia, severe dysphagia, rigidity and bradykinesia in all limbs, hyperreflexia, positive pathological reflexes in the lower limbs, diffuse muscle atrophy, and autonomic features (anhydrosis, orthostatic hypotension, constipation, dysuria). She had recurrent, asynchronous, arrhythmic myoclonic movements of the upper limbs and abdomen at rest, which were also stimulus-sensitive. Very mild cerebellar ataxia was present; there was no palatal tremor.  

Ophthalmologic evaluation revealed involuntary eye movements consisting of repetitive, rapid, random, multidirectional conjugate saccades of irregular amplitude and frequency, present at rest and exacerbated by attempted gaze.  

Routine blood tests and cerebrospinal fluid analysis were normal. Serologic testing for HIV, herpes simplex virus, Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, varicella-zoster virus, Japanese encephalitis A and B viruses, and JC virus was negative. Autoimmune panels—including antinuclear, anti–double-stranded DNA, antineutrophil cytoplasmic, antithyroid, and antiphospholipid antibodies—were negative. A paraneoplastic CSF panel (anti-Hu, anti-Ri, anti-Yo, anti-Ma/Ta, anti-VGKC, amphiphysin, anti-gliadin antibodies) was unrevealing.  

Electroencephalography during myoclonus showed only generalized slowing without epileptiform discharges; somatosensory evoked potentials did not demonstrate giant responses. Full-body CT showed mild right lower-lobe aspiration pneumonia but no primary or metastatic tumor. Brain MRI revealed linear T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in the putamina bilaterally and mild cerebellar and pontine atrophy. Tc-99m-ECD SPECT demonstrated hypoperfusion of the cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, and brainstem with only slight cerebellar hypoperfusion.

A 57-year-old white man of German and Nicaraguan descent presented for cataract surgery with symptoms of glare and decreased visual acuity. He works as a mechanical engineer and has no significant past medical or family history. Seven months earlier he had an episode of cold-induced dark urine and developed acrocyanosis of the fingers, nose, and feet. On examination he had acrocyanosis and modest splenomegaly; vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.0 g/dL, hematocrit 39.5%, reticulocytes 5.2%, total bilirubin 5.3 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 587 IU/L, and a cold-hemagglutinin titer of 40 960. During routine, uncomplicated cataract surgery, intermittent flow of balanced salt solution over the ocular surface induced a conspicuous change in conjunctival blood flow: small vessels near the limbus showed interrupted flow with visible red-cell clumping, whereas larger distal vessels appeared less affected. The surgery was otherwise uneventful.

An 83-year-old man with no history of bleeding diathesis or anticoagulant use was admitted after right thoracic trauma, with right hemothorax and fractures of the ipsilateral ribs VII–X. On examination, a mass in the left upper abdominal quadrant was incidentally noted. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen demonstrated a large left retroperitoneal mass of uncertain renal versus adrenal origin, displacing the spleen, pancreatic body and tail, left kidney, and stomach, with no radiologic evidence of metastatic disease. The patient reported that 10 years earlier a 2.3-cm left adrenal incidentaloma had been diagnosed; CT densitometry at that time was suggestive of a benign cortical adenoma, and he had been advised regular follow-up. Six years later, contrast CT showed growth of the lesion to 7 cm. At that time he had no signs or symptoms of hormone excess. Endocrine evaluation showed that a 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test excluded cortisol excess; urinary fractionated metanephrines excluded pheochromocytoma; and, after washout of antihypertensive agents, an aldosterone/renin ratio excluded primary aldosteronism. All other laboratory studies were normal. The patient was asymptomatic and did not return for further follow-up until the current admission.

A 28-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of edema, gross painless hematuria, and uremic symptoms. He had no history of diabetes or hypertension and smoked 2–3 cigarettes per day for 2 years. On examination, blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg; there was pallor and bilateral pitting edema. Urinalysis showed 3+ protein, numerous red blood cells, and red-cell casts. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL, white-cell count 14 830/mm3, platelets 230 000/mm3, and serum creatinine 16.5 mg/dL. Serum electrolytes and complement levels were normal; total calcium was 7.1 mg/dL. Tests for hepatitis B and C, HIV, antinuclear antibodies, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. Renal ultrasonography showed bilaterally enlarged echogenic kidneys (12.9 cm). A renal biopsy was performed. Light microscopy showed four glomeruli, each with circumferential cellular crescents, fibrinoid necrosis, and disruption of the glomerular basement membranes and Bowman’s capsules; there was severe acute tubular injury. Immunofluorescence in seven glomeruli demonstrated strong linear staining (4+) of glomerular capillary walls for IgG and kappa light chain, with negative staining for IgA, IgM, C3, C1q, and lambda. Subclass staining showed linear IgG1 (3+) along capillary walls and negative IgG2, IgG3, and IgG4. Electron microscopy revealed no electron-dense or powdery deposits.

An 11-year-old boy with unremarkable prior development and family history was hospitalized in early March for cervical lymphadenitis and received ceftriaxone. During antibiotic therapy he developed persistent epigastric pain and pruritus of the anterior chest and abdomen, which partially improved with acid suppression and antihistamines but did not fully resolve.

On April 10, he developed dysuria and urinary retention. Neurologic examination revealed reduced bilateral Achilles-tendon and knee-jerk reflexes. He was diagnosed with postinfectious inflammatory nervous system involvement and treated with intravenous immunoglobulin (2 g/kg over 4 days), dexamethasone, and pyridostigmine. 

Within days he developed altered consciousness and limb rigidity; anticonvulsants (valproate, carbamazepine) and intravenous midazolam were added, with transient relief of stiffness. His condition then progressed to tachypnea, dysphagia, and hypoesthesia below the umbilicus, with bilateral leg weakness and loss of deep tendon reflexes. He was transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit for plasmapheresis.

After three plasma exchanges his consciousness and myoclonus improved, and he received additional steroids and immunoglobulin. However, he relapsed with worsening dyskinesia characterized by head‐instability, shoulder shrugging, and neck-turning weakness. Both lower limbs were flaccid (strength 0/5) with sensory level to the base of the neck. He developed generalized myoclonus during sleep and sudden episodes of rigidity lasting tens of seconds, aggravated by emotional stress, accompanied by a shallow comatose state.

A 48-year-old African man with hypertension and a long history of well-controlled epilepsy (on valproic acid and levetiracetam) was transferred in status epilepticus after receiving diazepam and phenytoin. He had no facial asymmetry or known hemiplegia and normal cognition. On arrival he was afebrile, GCS 11 (E3V3M5), with spastic hypertonia and 3/5 strength in the left limbs. He was tachypneic (30/min), saturating 84% on 40% oxygen, BP 118/88 mmHg, pulse 98 bpm, and had bilateral chest crepitations. Labs showed mild renal impairment (urea 8.8 mmol/L, creatinine 122 µmol/L), CRP 23 mg/L, and therapeutic anticonvulsant levels. SARS-CoV-2 PCR was positive. Despite escalating anticonvulsants (20 mg diazepam, 1500 mg phenytoin, 1500 mg valproate), seizures persisted. Noncontrast CT of the head revealed marked atrophy of the right cerebral hemisphere with ipsilateral calvarial thickening, no paranasal sinus or mastoid air-cell hyperpneumatisation, and no acute hemorrhage, infarct, or mass.

A 48-year-old woman with a history of alcohol use disorder presented three days after a dog bite with joint pain, body aches, subjective fever, and fatigue. On initial evaluation her vital signs were normal; laboratory studies showed elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. She received 6 mg of dexamethasone and was discharged.

Three days later she returned with fever to 103.6 °F, polyarthralgia—particularly in the hands—worsening rash, and hypoxia requiring supplemental oxygen. Her white-cell count was 16 300 /µL. Chest radiography showed bilateral infiltrates, though she denied cough or dyspnea.

On examination she had large, well-demarcated annular and arcuate, mildly erythematous plaques with central dusky erythema or purpura on the back, trunk, and extremities; there was no mucosal involvement. Initial differential diagnoses for the rash included urticarial vasculitis, erythema marginatum, granuloma annulare, erythema annulare centrifugum, subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus, and erythema migrans.

Empiric treatment began with vancomycin and aztreonam, later changed to azithromycin for possible atypical pneumonia, and finally ceftriaxone; intravenous methylprednisolone was added. An infectious workup was negative for Lyme disease, Mycoplasma, Legionella, Streptococcus, SARS-CoV-2, hepatitis, and HIV. Bronchoscopic airway samples were negative on viral panel, Gram stain, bacterial and fungal cultures, and cytology. Blood cultures during admission showed no growth. An autoimmune workup, including antinuclear antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, cryoglobulins, rheumatoid factor, and complement studies, was negative. Despite the non-diagnostic workup, her rash and systemic symptoms improved, and she was discharged on 40 mg of oral prednisone daily.

A 41-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of gradually worsening glare, visual discomfort in sunlight, and difficulty with near work.  
His medical history was notable only for impaired glucose metabolism diagnosed 2 years earlier, managed with lifestyle modifications. He had no other relevant clinical or family history.  
On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 and near vision was N5 with effort in both eyes. Pupils were dilated to 7.5 mm bilaterally, with vermiform segmental contractions in the superior quadrants and light–near dissociation. In bright light, pupils constricted only to 7 mm.  
After instillation of 0.1% pilocarpine every 5 minutes for 45 minutes, bilateral pupillary constriction to 3 mm was observed.  
The remainder of the ocular and systemic examination was unremarkable. Extensive laboratory investigations, including HIV and syphilis serologic tests, were within normal limits.

A 40-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of chronic, dull, vague lower abdominal pain. She denied nausea, vomiting, constipation, melena, trauma, or oral contraceptive use. She reported polymenorrhagia and dysmenorrhea for 7 months. On examination, her abdomen was soft and lax with central obesity and a Pfannenstiel scar; no palpable abdominal mass was noted. Pelvic examination revealed an anteverted uterus and a minimally tender cystic mass in the pouch of Douglas. Routine laboratory tests and tumor markers (CEA 1.8 ng/ml; CA 19-9 15 U/ml; CA 125 14.6 U/ml; α-fetoprotein 1.1 IU/ml) were normal. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed a 12.4 × 10.2 × 10 cm multiloculated, thick-walled cystic mass with low internal echoes posterior and left to the uterus, separate from both ovaries and suggesting hydrosalpinx with mild hypervascularity. Pelvic MRI confirmed a large multiloculated cystic mass abutting the rectum and uterus. At diagnostic laparoscopy, a 12 × 10 cm retroperitoneal multiloculated cystic mass was noted to the left of midline, thick-walled and completely separate from the uterus; both ovaries and fallopian tubes appeared normal and were separate from the mass.

An 18-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of bilateral Achilles and posterior calf pain that was dull and aching, worsened by running, and did not occur at rest. She had undergone physical therapy, NSAIDs, and night splints with minimal benefit. On examination, she had bilateral tenderness over the superficial posterior compartment at the musculotendinous junction and muscle belly, mild swelling, and 4/5 strength on dorsiflexion; range of motion was normal. Ankle radiographs demonstrated a mild Haglund deformity bilaterally. Magnetic resonance imaging showed subtalar synovitis and an os trigonum, but these findings did not reproduce her primary posterior leg pain. She was offered pre- and postexertional compartment pressure measurement but declined further testing.

A 70-year-old woman presented with 24 h of left upper quadrant abdominal pain and vomiting but no fever or change in bowel habits. Her medical history was notable for hypertension and a prior open cholecystectomy. She was afebrile. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the left upper quadrant; the remainder of the abdomen was soft and non-tender. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 15 300/mm3 and a C-reactive protein level of 3.20 mg/dL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 5.4 cm × 5.8 cm × 4.6 cm round lesion arising from the jejunum in the left side of the abdomen, containing faecal-like material mixed with gas, with densification of the adjacent mesenteric fat and a few inflammatory lymph nodes. There was no intra-abdominal collection or pneumoperitoneum.

A 16-year-old male presented with a 2-week history of sore throat, progressive dyspnea, and spiking fevers. On arrival, his temperature was 103 °F and SpO₂ was 89% on room air; other physical findings were unremarkable. Initial laboratory tests showed a normal white cell count, normal liver function and coagulation tests, but mild anemia, mildly elevated bilirubin, and increased LDH. Notable abnormalities included a creatinine of 277 μmol/L, urea of 94 mg/dL, and D-dimers of 13 970 µg/L. A chest radiograph was initially normal. He was admitted with a working differential of sepsis-induced acute kidney injury, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, and pulmonary-renal syndrome. Over the next 48 hours, he deteriorated with worsening dyspnea, hypoxia (SpO₂ 70% despite supplemental oxygen), and a leukocytosis to 24 × 10⁹/L. Repeat chest radiography demonstrated extensive bilateral consolidation, and a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest revealed right-sided extensive consolidation with a parapneumonic effusion. An extensive diagnostic workup including ANA, anti-GBM antibodies, tests for infectious mononucleosis, pneumococcal and Legionella antigens, influenza A and B, and respiratory syncytial virus was negative. Thoracentesis yielded exudative pleural fluid; both Gram and Ziehl–Neelsen stains were negative.

A 56-year-old Japanese man was referred for persistent pain in the right buccal mucosa. He had been treated for stomatitis with topical corticosteroids without improvement. On intraoral examination, there was a pouch-shaped depression approximately 4 mm in diameter and 6 mm deep located just posterior to the right parotid papilla. To further evaluate, contrast-enhanced computed tomography was performed with contrast medium–soaked gauze in the oral cavity; images showed an enhancing area measuring 5 mm in width and 9 mm in depth, situated 20 mm posterior to the orifice of the right parotid duct and extending under the buccal mucosa. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an oval nodule measuring 7 × 3 mm and 5 mm deep in the same location, showing no signal on T1-weighted images and low signal intensity on T2-weighted images. Ultrasonography revealed a hypoechoic area about 4 × 3 mm and 3 mm deep in the right buccal mucosa with a diverticulum-like appearance; the interior of the pouch was isoechoic to hypoechoic, and color Doppler examination showed no increased blood flow signal in the lesion.

A 16-year-old Hispanic male was referred for evaluation of bilateral neck masses noted on routine exam. He first noticed firm swelling beneath his jaw 2 months earlier, with gradual enlargement and no fever, weight loss, night sweats, or pain. Treatment with antibiotics produced no improvement. On exam, firm bilateral submandibular glands measured about 4 cm in diameter; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed homogeneous enlargement of both submandibular glands without ductal dilation or stones; the parotid and lacrimal glands appeared normal, and there was no cervical lymphadenopathy. An open biopsy of the left submandibular gland revealed a dense lymphocytic infiltrate with mixed B and T cells and reactive secondary follicles, but no evidence of lymphoid neoplasia. Laboratory testing showed a C3 level of 87 mg/dL (normal ≥90 mg/dL) and total serum IgG of 1885 mg/dL (normal ≤1584 mg/dL). Quantiferon gold assay, urinalysis, renal and liver function tests, complete blood count, hepatitis B and C serologies, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (10 mm/h), and C-reactive protein (<0.5 mg/dL) were within normal limits. Autoantibodies including anti–SS-A, anti–SS-B, antinuclear antibody, and rheumatoid factor were negative.

An 8-year-old Chinese girl was referred for evaluation of a cardiac murmur. She was asymptomatic, denied dyspnea, diaphoresis, or cyanosis, but had frequent upper respiratory infections and reduced exercise tolerance. Vital signs were normal. Cardiac examination revealed a grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur at the left upper sternal border; S1 and S2 were normal. ECG showed sinus rhythm without ischemic changes. Chest radiography demonstrated cardiomegaly. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a dilated right coronary artery with aneurysmal change and a fistulous connection to the right ventricle, extensive intercoronary collateral vessels, severe mitral regurgitation, a left ventricular ejection fraction of 61%, and fractional shortening of 33%. There was no shunt across the interventricular septum.

A 10-year-old, 6.5 kg, neutered indoor domestic longhair cat presented for evaluation of severe azotemia and a 2-day history of inappetence and vomiting. Initial biochemistry showed a creatinine of 9.7 mg/dL (ref 0.8–2.4) and BUN of 113 mg/dL (ref 16–36). Abdominal radiographs revealed asymmetrically sized kidneys (left enlarged, right small). The patient was treated outpatient with antiemetics, sucralfate, aluminum hydroxide, and subcutaneous fluids; however, azotemia worsened and the cat was referred.

On presentation at the referral center the cat was bright and alert but extremely fractious, requiring sedation. Thoracic auscultation was normal; no respiratory or cardiovascular abnormalities were detected. The right kidney was palpably enlarged; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory findings included PCV 30% (25–45%), TP 7.0 g/dL (6.1–8.0), venous blood gas pH 7.12 (ref 6.5–8.0), pCO2 34.5 mmHg, BUN >100 mg/dL, creatinine >12 mg/dL. CBC was within reference intervals. Chemistry revealed BUN 203 mg/dL (18–39), creatinine 16.7 mg/dL (0.7–1.6), phosphorus 15.8 mg/dL (3.1–6.5). Urinalysis showed hyposthenuria (specific gravity 1.007).

Abdominal ultrasound showed an enlarged right kidney (5.6 cm), bilateral pyelectasia (right 5.7 mm, left 10.3 mm), proximal hydroureter, and two parenchymal nodules in the left kidney poles. Renal aspirates revealed rare mesenchymal cells. A hyperechoic focus in the left liver lobe was suspected biliary mineralization.

To screen for metastatic disease prior to planning urinary surgery, three-view thoracic radiographs were obtained. They revealed a moderate pneumothorax with intrapleural gas in the caudodorsal thorax causing retraction of the caudal lung lobes, concurrent pulmonary atelectasis with a patchy unstructured interstitial pattern in multiple lobes, and subcutaneous emphysema consistent with previous subcutaneous fluid administration.

A 41-year-old man with childhood-onset epilepsy well controlled on valproic acid, levetiracetam, and clonazepam (no recent seizures) was diagnosed with an ulcerated nodular melanoma (Clark III, Breslow 7.0 mm, pT4b N1 M0) on the right torso. Ipsilateral axillary lymphadenopathy was confirmed clinically and on PET–CT; no other metastatic disease was identified. He received nivolumab (1 mg/kg) plus ipilimumab (3 mg/kg) every 3 weeks. One week after his fourth cycle, he had an anaphylactic reaction that was treated successfully. Shortly thereafter, he noted a new right homonymous hemianopia without headache, fever, or other neurologic deficits. Examination confirmed the visual-field defect; otherwise, the neurologic exam was normal. Gadolinium-enhanced brain MRI showed focal T2 and FLAIR hyperintensity in the left occipital cortex, suggestive of an inflammatory process. Brain PET–CT revealed decreased tracer uptake in the corresponding left occipital lobe. Lumbar puncture revealed normal cell counts, glucose, protein, and negative cytology.

A 21-year-old healthy male soldier presented two weeks after sustaining multiple bites from suspected fire ants on his left arm. Shortly after the bites, he developed a local reaction with flare, wheal, and subsequent erythema, edema, and induration, followed two days later by spiking fevers treated at a local clinic. Five days after the bite, he experienced severe nausea, vomiting, and a progressive decrease in urine output. Initial treatment with intravenous fluids, acetaminophen, and metoclopramide provided no improvement, and he was transferred to our hospital.

On examination, temperature was 37.0°C, blood pressure 150/84 mmHg, pulse 75/min, and respiratory rate 20/min. He was mildly obese (BMI 28.2 kg/m2) and had pale conjunctivae; there was no edema, icterus, abdominal mass, or palpable kidney enlargement.

Laboratory values on admission were: sodium 128 mEq/L, potassium 3.9 mEq/L, BUN 153 mg/dL, creatinine 20.1 mg/dL, calcium 8.4 mg/dL, phosphorus 3.9 mg/dL, albumin 4.2 g/dL, AST 127 U/L, ALT 36 U/L, total bilirubin 2.0 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL, uric acid 19.1 mg/dL, myoglobin 422 ng/mL, LDH 3400 U/L, CK 503 U/L, CK-MB 10.1 ng/mL, troponin 0.01 μg/L, and haptoglobin <7.0 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas showed pH 7.27, PaCO2 41 mmHg, PaO2 91 mmHg, and bicarbonate 18 mEq/L.

A CBC revealed hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL, WBC 8.8×10^3/μL, platelets 57×10^3/μL, and reticulocytes 6.8%. Coagulation studies were normal. Direct and indirect Coombs tests were negative. A peripheral smear showed 2–3 schistocytes per high-power field. Immunoglobulins G, A, and M were within normal limits; IgE was 408 IU/mL. Complement C3 was 102 mg/dL and C4 was 22.6 mg/dL. Tests for ANA, VDRL, HBsAg, hepatitis C, and HIV were negative. Urinalysis revealed dark brown urine with 3+ protein, 0–3 RBCs, 3–5 WBCs per high-power field, and positive hemoglobin. Renal ultrasound demonstrated grade I increased echogenicity in both kidneys with normal sizes.

A 45-year-old woman presented with a palpable mass in the axillary tail of her left breast and left-sided chest discomfort. She reported a change in the appearance of her left breast but denied nipple discharge, fever, or trauma. Her mother had breast cancer and her father had lung cancer. She was otherwise healthy, had two children, and had undergone a hysterectomy two years earlier for benign disease; her ovaries were retained.  

On examination, two firm, non-tender nodules were palpable: a 20 mm lesion in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast (axillary tail) and a 10 mm node in the left axilla. The right breast, axilla, abdomen, and other systems were normal.  

A diagnostic mammogram of the left breast showed a smooth-outlined, soft-density lesion without microcalcifications and a few small axillary lymph nodes. Breast ultrasound demonstrated a 2 cm solid, hypoechoic lesion in the lateral left breast and a 1 cm solid axillary node; the findings were classified as BIRADS M4 U4 (suspicious abnormality).  

Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) of the axillary node was indeterminate (C3) but revealed numerous monotonous lymphocytes and lymphogranular bodies suggestive of granulomatous inflammation; no malignant cells were seen. A core needle biopsy of the breast lesion showed aggregates of epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells consistent with granulomatous inflammation and no evidence of malignancy.

An 11-year-old previously healthy Black female presented with rapidly progressive mucocutaneous blisters and pharyngitis-like symptoms over 24 hours. Her illness was preceded by four days of fever, malaise, headache, conjunctivitis, odynophagia, abdominal pain, emesis, and dysuria. She had no recent medication use or known infectious exposures.

On examination, she was febrile and tachycardic with diffuse abdominal tenderness. There were multiple well-defined, tense, clear fluid–filled vesicles and bullae (1–10 mm) on the face, trunk, proximal extremities, and labia majora, affecting approximately 20% of body surface area. The vermilion border of the lips showed skin sloughing with hemorrhagic crusting, and the oral mucosa was diffusely eroded. The genital mucosa exhibited marked erythema and erosions without anal involvement. Both Nikolsky and Asboe-Hansen signs were negative. There was nonpurulent ocular exudate with scleral conjunctival erythema but no corneal or eyelid ulcerations.

Laboratory studies revealed lymphocytopenia, elevated transaminases, and increased inflammatory markers. COVID-19 testing (including serology) and a respiratory pathogen panel were negative. Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgM was indeterminate. Chest radiography, cardiac evaluation, and autoimmune connective tissue disease workup were unremarkable.

Skin biopsy showed vacuolar interface dermatitis with a superficial dermal perivascular inflammatory infiltrate, described as consistent with erythema multiforme/Stevens–Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis. Perilesional direct immunofluorescence was negative.

Given these findings, the differential diagnoses included drug-induced Stevens–Johnson syndrome, multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children, toxic shock syndrome, and Kawasaki disease.

A 39-year-old woman presented with dysarthria and dysgraphia of the right hand. She had no significant medical history. On examination, vital signs were stable, and neurologic assessment was notable only for mild slurring of speech and difficulty writing with the right hand.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the head showed a high-intensity lesion with rim enhancement in the left corona radiata on diffusion-weighted and T2-weighted images, and a separate high-intensity lesion in the right cerebral cortex without enhancement. Cerebrospinal fluid testing revealed elevated myelin basic protein, negative anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies, and positive oligoclonal IgG bands. One criterion for multiple sclerosis was fulfilled: dissemination in time and space. Intravenous methylprednisolone (500 mg daily for 3 days, then two courses of 1000 mg for 3 days) was administered, and her symptoms improved; follow-up MRI showed persistent lesions but resolution of the ring enhancement.

Routine chest computed tomography performed before steroid administration demonstrated a 30 mm homogeneous, hypodense mass with smooth contours and heterogeneous enhancement in the anterosuperior mediastinum. Serum soluble interleukin-2 receptor, carcinoembryonic antigen, and anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody levels were within normal limits. A thymoma was suspected, and video-assisted thoracoscopic thymectomy was planned.

A 24-year-old woman at 34+2 weeks of gestation presented to the emergency department with bilateral hip pain and an inability to bear weight after feeling her legs “give way” and falling from her doorway. She had felt a click in her left hip before the fall and experienced immediate severe bilateral hip pain on impact. She sustained no other injuries; both lower limbs were neurovascularly intact. Obstetric examination was unremarkable. Earlier in the month, she had attended maternity triage twice with pelvic pain managed conservatively without imaging due to perceived fetal radiation risks.

Her obstetric history included a previous twin pregnancy delivered by lower segment caesarean section. She was otherwise healthy, with a body mass index of 32.8, no regular medications, no alcohol use, and no smoking. Family history was notable for an uncle who underwent operative management for avascular necrosis of the femoral head at age 25.

Initial radiographs of the pelvis obtained at 34+2 weeks gestation demonstrated bilateral minimally displaced subcapital neck of femur fractures.

A 70-year-old woman with coronary artery disease and a remote history of morbid obesity (preoperative BMI 52 kg/m2) presented with one month of persistent postprandial nausea, regurgitation, and mild dysphagia to solids and liquids. She had undergone laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass two years earlier, complicated by a gastro-gastric fistula and gastro-jejunal ulcer that required revision two months before presentation. She denied weight change, abdominal pain, or altered bowel habits.

On examination, vital signs were normal. The abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds; her recent surgical wound was healing well. Laboratory tests, including liver enzymes and stool studies for Clostridium difficile toxin, ova, and parasites, were unremarkable. A contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed enteric contrast within a dilated distal esophagus and was “suspicious for a mild stricture at gastroesophageal sphincter (GES),” with no peri-gastric inflammation. She was admitted for further evaluation.

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy the next day revealed large amounts of thick esophageal secretions. “The esophagus was tortuous, dilated and had a ‘sigmoid esophagus’ appearance, but no strictures, stenosis or evidence of malignancy were noted.” A barium swallow study demonstrated “persistent narrowing of the gastroesophageal junction with a moderately dilated, debris-filled esophagus proximally and some tertiary esophageal contractions. These findings were suggestive of achalasia.”

A 49-year-old Indian man with a 15-year history of alcohol abuse presented with six months of constant dull-aching epigastric pain radiating to the back and postprandial nonbilious vomiting. He denied jaundice, gastrointestinal bleeding, fever, or weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory investigations including complete blood count, electrolytes, liver function tests, serum amylase, and lipase were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed subtle hypoattenuation of the pancreatic head with effacement of the pancreatico-duodenal groove and fluid tracking; there was no arterial phase hyperenhancement. The main pancreatic duct measured 7 cm, the common bile duct measured 9 mm, and intrahepatic biliary radicles were dilated. Tumor markers CA 19-9, CEA, and serum IgG4 levels were normal. Upper endoscopy revealed edematous mucosa and narrowing of the second portion of the duodenum. Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated a bulky, heteroechoic pancreatic head with periduodenal soft tissue thickening. EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration yielded chronic inflammatory cells. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of groove pancreatitis was made, although malignancy could not be excluded, and Whipple pancreaticoduodenectomy was planned.

A 33-year-old non-smoker woman with stage III B follicular lymphoma diagnosed by lymph node biopsy and immunohistochemistry (CD10+, CD20+, Bcl-2+, Bcl-6+, Ki-67 22%) and uninvolved bone marrow received four cycles of R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisolone). Two weeks after the fourth cycle, she was admitted with three days of exertional dyspnea and dry cough without fever. On examination, she was tachypneic with bilateral basal crackles. Arterial blood gas showed hypoxemia. Complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, urine analysis, and D-dimer were normal. ECG showed sinus tachycardia. Chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral reticulonodular infiltrates. High-resolution CT of the lungs revealed bilateral patchy ground-glass opacities, predominantly in the upper lobes. Pulmonary function tests showed a restrictive pattern. 

To exclude infection, sputum Gram stain, Ziehl–Neelsen stain for acid-fast bacilli, fungal and Pneumocystis carinii stains were negative, and routine bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal cultures were sterile. Antinuclear antibody and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody tests were negative. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid cytology showed no malignant cells. Pulmonary eosinophilia was excluded clinically and by laboratory studies. There were no extrapulmonary findings of sarcoidosis (no skin, joint, or eye involvement; no bilateral hilar adenopathy; no anemia; no elevated liver enzymes; no hypercalciuria; no granulomatous lesions on imaging). Echocardiography including ventricular function was normal.

A 65-year-old Greek woman presented with a 1-month history of dry cough, fever, 5-kg weight loss, and progressive dyspnoea, which worsened over the last 2 weeks despite oral macrolide and β-lactam therapy. She was a lifetime non-smoker, had no known environmental or occupational exposures, and her medical history (osteoporosis, hyperlipidemia) was unremarkable. On examination, she was tachypneic (respiratory rate 20/min) and tachycardic (heart rate 100 bpm) but not hypoxaemic (PaO2 84 mmHg). Lung auscultation revealed crepitations and diminished breath sounds over the right lower hemithorax and inspiratory crackles posteriorly on the left. There was no clubbing, skin lesions, lymphadenopathy, or joint swelling. The ESR was 65 mm/h; white and red cell counts, liver and renal function tests, and CRP were normal. Tests for ANA, ENA, and ANCA were negative. Pulmonary-function tests were normal except for a mildly reduced DLCO (60% predicted). Chest radiography showed patchy peripheral and subpleural consolidations, predominantly in the right lung. HRCT confirmed multiple subpleural and peribronchovascular consolidations with air bronchograms and ring-like opacities with central ground-glass attenuation (“reversed halo sign”). A tuberculin skin test was negative. Flexible bronchoscopy showed no endobronchial lesions; BAL fluid was smear and culture negative for common bacteria and acid-fast bacilli and revealed 16% lymphocytes with a normal CD4/CD8 ratio. To exclude malignancy, a video-assisted thoracoscopic lung biopsy of right lower-lobe lesions was performed one week after presentation.

A 32-year-old Persian man with a 13-year history of chronic refractory immune thrombocytopenic purpura presented for evaluation of new episodic neurologic symptoms. His ITP had relapsed 20 months earlier following meningococcal vaccination and pharyngitis, with a platelet count persistently below 10,000/µL despite splenectomy and multiple immunosuppressive therapies; only transient responses occurred after intravenous immunoglobulin.

Twenty months after the ITP relapse, he developed sudden-onset hypersomnia, compulsive hyperphagia, clumsiness, and abnormal behavior. His wife reported that he slept approximately 20 hours per day during symptomatic periods, awakening only for voiding and not in response to calling. He had consumed coffee the night before onset. CT and MRI scans of the brain and spinal cord were unremarkable; symptoms resolved spontaneously.

Three months later, neurologic symptoms recurred in temporal association with a thrombocytopenic episode (platelet count, 12,000/µL). During hospitalization, two doses of IVIG and steroids produced temporary improvement. On neurologic evaluation, he was amnesic for the episodes; his wife described 18–20 hours of daily sleep, waking two to three times per day, and hyperphagia of seven to eight complete meals per day, especially sweets. He reported delayed ejaculation during intercourse. Each neurologic episode lasted 1–2 weeks.

His past medical history was notable only for childhood malaria. He denied narcolepsy, other sleep disorders, or seizures. He did not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. Family history was noncontributory.

On examination between episodes, he appeared well, with normal vital signs and unremarkable head, neck, chest, abdomen, genitalia, and extremities. He was alert and oriented to time and place but exhibited mild psychomotor slowness. Cranial nerves were intact, strength and reflexes were normal, and sensation was preserved. He had bilateral bidirectional nystagmus on Hallpike testing and a slightly slow, clumsy gait.

Laboratory studies—including complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, vitamin B12 level (mildly low), and cerebrospinal fluid analysis—were unremarkable except for thrombocytopenia (platelet count, 25,000/µL). EEG showed no epileptiform activity. A subsequent episode was less severe (12–14 hours of sleep per day, milder hyperphagia and sexual disturbance) and resolved spontaneously. Single-photon emission computed tomography of the brain performed during an episode was normal.

The differential diagnosis included episodic ataxia, mood disorders, metabolic encephalopathy (eg, urea–ammonia cycle disorders), Lyme disease, Klüver–Bucy syndrome, and Kleine–Levin syndrome.

A 57-year-old man with congenital hypothyroidism and a history of tetralogy of Fallot repair at age 17 years, not on antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy, presented to the emergency department with 3 days of retrosternal chest pain, diaphoresis, nausea, and a nonproductive cough without fever. On examination, blood pressure was 85/50 mmHg, heart rate 134 bpm, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. 

Electrocardiography showed minimal ST-segment elevation in leads V1, V2, and aVR. Urgent transthoracic echocardiography revealed normal left ventricular function, moderate enlargement of the pulmonary artery (4.5–5 cm), mild-to-moderate pericardial effusion with apparent intrapericardial clot formation causing near tamponade physiology and right ventricular strain, and no evidence of aortic dissection. 

Contrast-enhanced CT angiography of the chest demonstrated a 2-cm hyperdense pericardial collection (42 Hounsfield units) consistent with hemorrhagic pericardial effusion and confirmed the absence of aortic dissection.

A 78-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of mild chest discomfort and then sudden onset of chest pain, dyspnea, and dizziness 1 hour before admission. His medical history was significant for hypertension. On examination, his blood pressure was 80/40 mmHg, heart rate was 54 bpm and irregular, mental status was blurred, and his lungs were clear. ECG showed Wenckebach atrioventricular block, pathologic Q waves, ST‐segment elevation in leads II, III, aVF, and V7–V9 with inverted T waves (note: limb-lead reversal). Laboratory tests revealed a troponin I level of 9.94 ng/mL, CK-MB of 31.5 U/L, and D-dimer of 0.1 mg/dL.

A 20-year-old woman was referred with suspected ovarian malignancy. She reported chronic pelvic and lumbar pain and a progressively enlarging abdominal mass over 6 months, accompanied by constipation, night sweats, and a 4-kg weight loss. She denied fever, chronic cough, known tuberculosis exposure, and had not received BCG vaccination. On examination, she was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and had pale conjunctivae. Abdominal examination revealed a firm, fixed right iliac fossa mass extending to the umbilicus; there was no hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, or lymphadenopathy.  
Laboratory tests showed a leukocyte count of 14,130/μl with 12,120 neutrophils/μl and hemoglobin of 10.5 g/dl; renal function was normal. Serum CA125 was within the normal range. Pelvic ultrasonography revealed bilateral hydronephrosis attributed to pelvic obstruction. Contrast-enhanced abdomino-pelvic CT demonstrated a large complex cystic mass occupying the abdomino-pelvic cavity, compressing adjacent organs, and displacing the uterus anteriorly.

A 67-year-old woman presented with palpitations and dizziness of 2 days’ duration. She reported fatigue on minimal exertion, an 11-kg weight loss over 3 years without anorexia, and hand tremor. She denied dyspnea, orthopnea, chest pain, heat intolerance, or changes in bowel habits. Her medical history was notable for right radical mastectomy and chemotherapy for breast cancer at age 37, and total thyroidectomy at age 60 for a nontoxic multinodular goiter (preoperative TSH 3.77 μU/mL, free T4 1.53 ng/dL). She had been taking levothyroxine 100 μg daily since surgery without follow-up. She smoked 20 cigarettes per day for 50 years.

On examination, temperature was 36.7 °C, BMI 19.7 kg/m^2, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, heart rate 130 bpm, and there was a fine resting tremor. There was no proptosis or periorbital edema. Neck examination revealed no palpable thyroid tissue or lymphadenopathy; Pemberton’s sign was negative. Lung and heart sounds were unremarkable, and there was no peripheral edema.

Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, normal white blood cell and platelet counts, normal liver and renal function, albumin 32.6 g/dL, corrected calcium 9.6 mg/dL, B-type natriuretic peptide 442.2 pg/mL, and troponin I <0.010 ng/mL. Thyroid studies revealed TSH <0.000 μU/mL, free T4 3.22 ng/dL, and free T3 8.46 pg/mL. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia (117 bpm) with incomplete right bundle branch block and left anterior fascicle block. Chest radiograph was normal. She was diagnosed with presumed iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis; levothyroxine was discontinued and bisoprolol 5 mg was started.

Ten days after levothyroxine withdrawal, her heart rate remained <100 bpm, but hand tremor persisted and repeat thyroid function tests showed ongoing elevation of free T4 and free T3. Thyroglobulin was elevated at 294 mg/mL (reference 0–55). A cervical ultrasound scan revealed no thyroid remnant in the gland bed. Test results for anti–TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb) were positive at 19.7 U/L (reference <1.8), and anti–thyroid peroxidase antibodies were negative.

A 49-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 5-day history of intermittent throbbing abdominal pain that began periumbilically and localized to the right lower quadrant, associated with nausea and increased stool frequency. Her medical history was notable for laparoscopic cholecystectomy in 2009 and a supracervical hysterectomy with bilateral salpingectomy for uterine fibroids in 2012, at which time endometriosis was noted. Examination showed moderate tenderness in the right lower quadrant and a positive Rovsing sign. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed lobulated tubular soft tissue and inflammation adjacent to the terminal ileum/ileocecal valve, and the appendix was not identified, leading to a presumptive diagnosis of acute appendicitis. The patient received broad-spectrum antibiotics and underwent diagnostic laparoscopy, which showed mild inflammatory changes of the terminal ileum and adhesions but no appendix despite full mobilization of the cecum and small-bowel run; biopsy of inflamed areas demonstrated acute inflammation and foci of endometriosis. The patient improved and was discharged but returned two hours later with sharp right lower quadrant pain, nausea, and vomiting. Repeat white-cell count was 13.2×10^9/L. Repeat CT showed small-bowel obstruction at the terminal ileum, likely secondary to an adjacent pericecal soft-tissue mass. The differential diagnosis included inverted appendix versus neoplasm.

A 57-year-old man with no prior medical history or cardiovascular risk factors presented with moderate diffuse abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, and two non-bloody watery stools that began 72 hours earlier after a heavy meal. Vital signs were blood pressure 130/70 mmHg, heart rate 80 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, and temperature 36.6°C. The abdomen was slightly distended with epigastric and left middle quadrant tenderness without peritonitic signs. Laboratory tests showed an inflammatory syndrome (CRP 11.98 mg/dl, ESR 65 mm/h, fibrinogen 759.1 mg/dl), a white-cell count of 8.1×10^9/L with 92% neutrophils, hemoglobin 14 g/dl, and normal amylase, lipase, lactate, and liver function tests. A plain abdominal radiograph was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 6.6-cm jejunal segment with a 7.5-mm thickened wall, preserved peristalsis, and adjacent mesenteric lymph nodes. Color duplex sonography showed a normal SMA origin with Vmax 0.86 m/sec, no turbulent flow or dissection, a non-dilated abdominal aorta, and good vascularization of the thickened jejunal wall. These findings were initially suggestive of acute enterocolitis of infectious or inflammatory origin. Stool tests for Salmonella, Shigella, and parasites were negative, and tumoral markers (CEA, CA19-9) were within normal limits. The fecal occult blood test was positive. To exclude a neoplasia or an ischemic process, contrast-enhanced computed tomography was ordered.

A 68-year-old woman with metastatic melanoma, hypertension, prior deep-vein thrombosis, and pulmonary embolism (with an IVC filter) received her second dose of ipilimumab and nivolumab shortly before presentation. She arrived at the emergency department with altered mental status, hypotension, and fever.

Two weeks earlier, she had undergone prophylactic right femur nailing with excision of a metastatic lesion and then developed fever, hypotension, and acute tubular necrosis; she completed a course of vancomycin, aztreonam, and metronidazole for presumed sepsis, with all cultures negative, and was discharged to rehabilitation. Four days after discharge, she returned with fever and hypotension.

On arrival, temperature was 98.4 °F, blood pressure 75/40 mm Hg, heart rate 110/min, respiratory rate 24/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. She was ill‐appearing, in moderate respiratory distress, with altered mental status and bilateral lower‐extremity edema.

Laboratory studies before fluid resuscitation showed hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL, WBC 13.9 K/µL, platelets 164 K/µL, sodium 133 mEq/L, potassium 3.1 mEq/L, chloride 110 mEq/L, bicarbonate 1 mEq/L, BUN 23 mg/dL, creatinine 3.2 mg/dL, AST 737 U/L, ALT 399 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 99 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, calcium 7.3 mg/dL, magnesium 1.5 mg/dL, phosphorus 2.5 mg/dL, procalcitonin 59.11 ng/mL, lactic acid 1.7 mmol/L, INR 1.46, and a venous blood gas with pH 7.24 and PCO2 24 mm Hg.

An electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with occasional premature ventricular contractions. Chest radiograph showed no consolidation or effusion. CT of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast revealed perinephric stranding and cholestasis. CT of the head without contrast was unremarkable.

Urinalysis showed few white blood cells and red blood cells, no casts, a urine pH of 7.5, urine anion gap of 40 mEq/L, and a fractional excretion of sodium of 0.6%.

A 64-year-old man presented for routine annual follow-up after treatment for relapsing diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) from 1996 to 2006. His initial lymphoma arose in the ileocecal region and was treated with resection and CHOP chemotherapy. He relapsed in 2002 in a cervical lymph node treated with radiotherapy (40 Gy) and again in 2005 in the tonsils and inguinal nodes treated with R-EPOCH, high-dose chemotherapy, and autologous stem-cell retransfusion. He has been in complete remission since 2006.

He was asymptomatic at the 2016 visit. Routine abdominal ultrasound revealed a 7 × 7 cm mass in the right adrenal gland. FDG-PET showed an FDG-avid lesion in the right adrenal gland (SUV 8.3) and two small subpleural nodules in the right middle lobe (5 mm and 19 mm; SUV max, 3.1). No lymphadenopathy was present.

Based on imaging, the leading diagnoses were primary adrenal carcinoma or metastatic lung cancer, with relapsed DLBCL considered unlikely due to the absence of lymphadenopathy.

A 60-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 2-month history of progressive right-sided exophthalmos and visual disturbance. He reported pain over the orbit but denied diplopia. Examination revealed right proptosis with intact extraocular movements and no cranial nerve palsies; visual acuity was reduced on the right, and funduscopic examination was unremarkable. The patient was afebrile. Examination of the ears, nose, and throat was normal. 

An orbito-cerebral CT scan with contrast showed a homogeneous soft-tissue mass occupying both the intraconal and extraconal compartments of the right orbit, with mild contrast enhancement and associated enlargement of the lacrimal gland. There was nodular mucosal thickening of the right maxillary sinus with thickening of the sinus walls but no bone lysis.

Magnetic resonance imaging was not performed due to lack of financial means. A complete blood count and C-reactive protein level were within normal limits.

A previously healthy two-year-old boy presented with a history of recurrent skin lesions that first appeared after BCG and DTP vaccinations at two months of age and recurred after each hepatitis B vaccination. The lesions began as papules that evolved into vesicles with purulent exudate and then into multiple ulcers with draining sinuses at the injection sites. On admission, he had violaceous, tender 5–7 mm superficial ulcers with draining sinuses on the right forearm, left deltoid area, and right cheek. There were no constitutional symptoms. Laboratory studies showed WBC 9,220/μL (56% neutrophils), hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL, platelets 426,000/μL, ESR 24 mm/h, and CRP 0.43 mg/dL. Plain radiographs of the humerus, radius, and ulna were normal. 

Initial workup for immunodeficiency and defects in the IL-12/interferon-γ axis—including immunoglobulin levels, lymphocyte subsets, CD40/CD40L expression, complement levels, adenosine deaminase, oxidative burst (phagoburst), and receptor expression—was unremarkable. Functional and genetic studies of IL-12β1 and IFN-γ receptors were normal. Skin biopsy showed noncaseating granulomas. Acid-fast bacillus smears and cultures for bacteria and mycobacteria were negative. The patient was started empirically on isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide, with gradual improvement of skin lesions.

Five months later, ESR rose to 74 mm/h without new skin lesions. Cultures of blood and urine, peripheral and bone marrow smears, Mantoux test, serologies for Brucella and Salmonella, and abdominal ultrasound were normal. Serologic tests for HLA-B27, ANA, ANCA, and rheumatoid factor were negative.
