Genetic testing for Familial Mediterranean Fever, TRAPS, and IL-1 receptor defects was negative except for an IL-1RN intron 2 variable tandem repeat polymorphism. Ciprofloxacin was added, and ESR normalized.

After two months, he developed new purulent skin lesions on the left forearm and left medial malleolus. Bone scintigraphy showed increased uptake in the right frontoparietal bone, and plain radiograph of the distal radial metaphysis revealed osteolytic lesions. No biopsy was performed. He received three weeks of teicoplanin; cultures of abscess material remained negative.

Three months later, he presented with pain, swelling, and warmth of both ankles. Radiograph of the left distal tibia showed osteolytic lesions surrounded by reactive hyperostosis consistent with chronic osteomyelitis.

A 69-year-old woman with a 2-year history of mild memory loss presented on November 2 with sudden visual hallucinations that resolved after hours. Over the next days, she developed headache, recurrent vomiting, cognitive impairment, speech difficulty, and generalized weakness, peaking three days after hospitalization at a local hospital. She had no fever prodrome and a 10-year history of well-controlled diabetes mellitus with retinopathy.  
Initial brain MRI one week after onset showed symmetrical periventricular T2 hyperintensity, diffuse atrophy, and ventricular dilation without enhancement. CSF analysis revealed normal WBC count, elevated protein (796 mg/L) and glucose (5.9 mmol/L). Serum testing detected anti–DPPX antibody (titer 1:32), but it was negative in CSF. Pulse IV methylprednisolone was given for three days, then tapered; vomiting and muscle strength improved but cognitive disturbance persisted.  
On referral (November 22), she was afebrile with normal vital signs. Neurologic exam showed impaired attention and reaction, miosis, mixed aphasia, generalized MRC grade-4 weakness, and reduced reflexes. Routine labs were notable for elevated neutrophil percentage (88.1%), hyperglycemia (11.43 mmol/L), and HbA1c 7.4%; CK, lactate, ketones, homocysteine, immunoglobulins, sex hormones, and cortisol were normal. EEG showed diffuse slow waves and sharp waves over the left frontotemporal region. Nerve conduction studies indicated demyelinating motor polyneuropathy.  
Repeat MRI on November 23 demonstrated restricted diffusion along the left temporo-occipitoparietal juxtacortex, stenosis of M2 segments of the right MCA and bilateral PCAs, and on perfusion-weighted imaging, prominent hyperperfusion in the left occipitotemporal cortex. Retrospective review noted faint DWI hyperintensity at the corticomedullary junction and high-intensity signals in the cerebellar paravermis.

A 61‐year‐old man was referred for sudden loss of vision in his left eye for 6 days. He had a 1‐year history of non–insulin‐dependent diabetes and was found to have a blood pressure of 180/100 mm Hg on presentation, prompting initiation of antihypertensive therapy. His visual acuity was counting fingers at close range in both eyes. Intraocular pressure was 14 mm Hg in the right eye and 16 mm Hg in the left eye, and gonioscopy showed open angles bilaterally. Anterior segment examination was unremarkable in both eyes, except for a dense nuclear and posterior subcapsular cataract in the right eye; the left eye was pseudophakic. Fundus examination of the right eye was limited by cataract but showed a cup:disc ratio of 0.8:1. Examination of the left eye revealed a cup:disc ratio of 0.8:1, dilated arterioles with arteriovenous crossing changes, cotton‐wool spots, and multilayered preretinal and subretinal haemorrhage around the optic disc and macula. Fluorescein angiography of the left eye demonstrated blocked retinal and choroidal fluorescence from the overlying haemorrhage and a discrete “light‐bulb” hyperfluorescent focus at the centre of the optic nerve head in the mid and late phases.

An 18-month-old boy was admitted with fever and rash. Four days earlier he had gastroenteritis and fever; shortly afterwards he developed a skin eruption on the ears and purpuric lesions on the extremities. On admission, temperature was 38.2°C. Examination showed bright-red, circular, painful purpuric lesions around the mouth and periorbital blushing. The ears were markedly edematous and purple. Tender, bright-red, slightly infiltrated papules and nodules were scattered on the trunk and extremities; the skin was otherwise intact. Laboratory studies revealed a C-reactive protein level of 135.9 mg/L and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 38 mm/hr; leukocyte and platelet counts were normal. Lumbar puncture was performed on suspicion of meningococcal disease; cerebrospinal fluid was normal. Skin biopsy was then performed.
Histologic examination showed a well-established leukocytoclastic vasculitis with marked fibrinoid necrosis and granulocyte infiltration in the vessel wall.

A 14-year-old girl was referred for elective hospital admission because of recent weight loss, a 2-week history of intermittent epigastric abdominal pain, iron deficiency anaemia, and a palpable epigastric/left upper quadrant mass. She had lost 1 kg in the past week despite a normal appetite, reported intermittent dark stools attributed to oral iron, and denied nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, or constitutional symptoms. Exercise tolerance was slightly reduced. Her past history included congenital adrenal hyperplasia, delayed puberty, and poor growth over 3 years, and she had experienced similar episodes of abdominal pain and a palpable mass over the past year. An abdominal ultrasound in June 2017 was unremarkable apart from a small left kidney. Medications were hydrocortisone, fluticasone, and oral iron.

On admission, vital signs were normal. Examination revealed a firm, non-tender mass in the epigastric and left upper quadrant regions with mild abdominal distension; the remainder of the abdomen was soft and non-tender. There was no alopecia, mucosal ulceration, or skin changes. Height was 146 cm (1st percentile) and weight 34.6 kg.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 76 g/L, MCV 67 fL, albumin 32 g/L, ferritin < 5 µg/L, and ESR 25 mm/hr. Extensive urine, stool, and blood tests—including autoimmune, endocrine, infectious, and vitamin panels—were negative.

An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated grossly enlarged left upper quadrant lymph nodes, free fluid in the right iliac fossa, and an atrophic left kidney with lower pole cystic changes; the report concluded these findings were atypical for mesenteric adenitis and recommended CT or MRI. A chest radiograph showed no mediastinal lymphadenopathy or other pathology.

A 60-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a history of chronic gout was admitted for emergency neurological evaluation of acute-onset bilateral lower-limb weakness and numbness of 1 day’s duration, accompanied by acute urinary retention.  
On examination, temperature was 36.5 °C, heart rate 68 beats/min, respiratory rate 17 breaths/min, and blood pressure 137/78 mm Hg. He had bilateral lower-limb weakness and sensory loss, absent deep-tendon reflexes at the knees and ankles, saddle anesthesia, and a lax anal tone.  
Laboratory studies showed C-reactive protein 144 mg/L (≤ 4.9), erythrocyte sedimentation rate > 130 mm/h (1–10), white-cell count 23.02 × 10^9/L (2.00–10.00), and uric acid 526 μmol/L (202–417).  
Lumbar–spine radiographs revealed spondylosis and mild anterolisthesis of L4 on L5. MRI of the lumbar spine demonstrated facet-joint effusions at L3–4 and L4–5 and a posterior epidural collection extending from L2 to S1, causing severe canal stenosis and cauda equina compression. Within the collection were lobulated foci that were hypointense on T1-weighted images, of intermediate signal on T2-weighted images, and showed marginal enhancement after gadolinium administration.

A 63-year-old woman with a history of combined liver and kidney transplantation in 2016 for autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease was referred for iron-deficiency anemia and a persistent dry cough. One year earlier, a colonoscopy performed because of a positive fecal occult blood test had shown diverticulosis and internal hemorrhoids. Six months later, worsening anemia prompted plans for repeat colonoscopy and gastroscopy. In the weeks before presentation, she developed a nonproductive cough and a low-grade fever. 

Chest radiography revealed multiple bilateral patchy infiltrates confirmed on CT scan. On admission, she reported dry cough, fatigue, intermittent fever, night sweats, and a 3-kg weight loss over 3 months. Her temperature was 37.9 °C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and other vital signs were normal. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, C-reactive protein 32 mg/L, a normal total leukocyte count with neutrophilic predominance, and creatinine at her baseline. Her maintenance immunosuppression consisted of mycophenolate mofetil 1000 mg daily and tacrolimus 4.5 mg daily.

She was born in Suriname, moved to the Netherlands at age 7 and to Belgium at age 11, with no recent travel outside Europe. She had never smoked. Bronchoscopy was macroscopically normal; lavage fluid was sent for cultures and respiratory PCR. Colonoscopy showed a bulging mass at the ileocecal valve, from which biopsy specimens were obtained. 

An 18F-FDG PET/CT scan demonstrated multiple hypermetabolic pulmonary infiltrates, a hypermetabolic mass at the ileocecal valve and one in the descending colon, and mesenteric as well as pulmonary lymphadenopathies. During her stay, she had intermittent fevers up to 40 °C; repeated blood cultures and bronchoalveolar lavage cultures (including auramine staining and culture for acid-fast bacilli, and galactomannan) were all negative. A respiratory PCR panel detected only respiratory syncytial virus. PCR assays for cytomegalovirus and Pneumocystis jiroveci were negative. Blood testing revealed an elevated 1,3-β-d-glucan level of 90 pg/mL (reference <60, positive >80). 

Given the lack of a definitive diagnosis, she was referred for exploratory laparoscopy with excisional biopsy of an abdominal lymph node for histopathology, culture, and panfungal PCR.

A 27-year-old otherwise healthy man presented with a 1-year history of multiple, gradually enlarging dark-colored warty growths over the scrotum and buttocks. The lesions were asymptomatic. He reported unprotected heterosexual intercourse with multiple partners. He denied any history of genital ulceration or discharge.

On examination, there were multiple hyperpigmented annular plaques 1–3 cm in diameter with a verrucous surface and prominent ridge-like borders on a background of hyperpigmented, velvety skin. Lesions involved the ventral scrotum, medial thighs, and buttocks. Systemic examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory investigations were within normal limits, and viral serologies (including HIV and HPV markers) were negative.

A 13-year-old Maasai boy from rural Arusha, northern Tanzania, presented with a 2-month history of progressive dyspnea and dry cough that turned blood-streaked over the previous 2 weeks. He reported unintentional weight loss and intermittent low-grade fevers. There was no known tuberculosis contact, and a course of unspecified antibiotics at a local dispensary yielded no improvement. He lives on a farm and keeps livestock. On examination, he was moderately pale, afebrile (36.7 °C), pulse 85 beats/min, blood pressure 108/60 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Chest expansion was greater on the right side, percussion was dull, and air entry was reduced over the right hemithorax. Abdominal and neurologic examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, leukocyte count 7.39×10^9/L, platelet count 492×10^9/L, ESR 95 mm/hour, serum creatinine 42 μmol/L, urea 3.77 mmol/L, and normal electrolytes and bilirubin; urine analysis was unremarkable. A posteroanterior chest radiograph revealed a well‐circumscribed cystic mass occupying the right hemithorax with mediastinal shift to the left. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a 15 × 11 × 14 cm cystic lesion in the right upper and middle hemithorax displacing the mediastinum contralaterally and compressing adjacent lobes; the cyst had a thick rind with double membranes on its anterior and posterior walls containing clear fluid and no internal daughter cysts. GeneXpert testing for Mycobacterium tuberculosis was negative.

A 23-year-old woman, 13 weeks into an unplanned pregnancy, was followed for a mechanical aortic valve replacement (21 mm St Jude valve) performed at age 15 for Streptococcus viridans endocarditis. Six weeks before presentation, her warfarin (INR target 2.5, range 2.0–3.0) was switched to subcutaneous enoxaparin without anti-Xa monitoring. At this visit she was asymptomatic but had been compliant with enoxaparin and had declined aspirin. A factor Xa level was subtherapeutic at 0.8 IU/mL. On examination, she had a loud Grade 3/6 crescendo-decrescendo murmur, preserved S2, no thrill, and no diastolic component, loudest at the right upper sternal border. 

Transthoracic echocardiography showed a peak gradient of 87 mmHg, a mean gradient of 58 mmHg, a Doppler velocity index of 0.24, and an acceleration time of 130 ms across the mechanical aortic valve; trace expected aortic insufficiency was noted. Two years earlier her peak and mean gradients had been 24 and 15 mmHg. 

Fluoroscopy, with precautions to shield the fetus, demonstrated one completely immobile leaflet and one leaflet that was fixed in the aortic position.

A 25-year-old woman presented with a 1-week history of acute decreased vision, photophobia, and redness in her right eye. She denied trauma, prior ocular surgery, or systemic diseases such as diabetes or hypertension. Four months earlier she had experienced mild fever and right shoulder pain, and over the ensuing months had intermittent low-grade fever and shoulder discomfort. She lived rurally, consumed unpasteurized dairy, and had animal contacts. Because brucellosis is endemic in her region, Wright and 2-mercaptoethanol tests were performed and returned positive at titers of 1/80 and 1/40, respectively; her ESR was 38 mm/h and CRP was 1+. She was prescribed doxycycline and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole but reported poor adherence.

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was hand motion with projection in the right eye and 10/10 in the left. Intraocular pressures were normal bilaterally. Right-eye slit-lamp exam revealed a clear cornea, 1+ hypopyon, flare, and 4+ vitreous cells without iris nodules or posterior synechiae. Fundus examination showed optic disc swelling, diffuse retinal vasculitis, and a single retinitis patch one disc diameter below the optic nerve head. The left eye was normal.

She was admitted with a working diagnosis of vision-threatening endogenous endophthalmitis or infectious retinitis. Systemic evaluation—including blood, urine, and throat cultures, chest radiography, CBC, platelet count, BUN, creatinine, urinalysis, and cardiology consultation to exclude infective endocarditis—was unremarkable, though her Wright test remained positive. A neurology consultation showed no abnormalities. Under anesthesia, a 25-gauge pars plana vitreous tap was performed for smear, culture, and PCR (targeting Herpes Simplex virus, Varicella Zoster virus, Cytomegalovirus, and Brucella). Intravitreal vancomycin (1 mg/0.1 mL) and ceftazidime (2.25 mg/0.1 mL) were injected. Regarding the suspicion of herpetic retinitis, valacyclovir 1000 mg orally every 8 hours was initiated.

A 56-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus was admitted with severe COVID-19 pneumonia. She had not received vaccination against SARS-CoV-2. On admission, she was treated with intravenous methylprednisolone (250 mg daily) followed by dexamethasone (16 mg daily for 7 days, then 8 mg daily for 3 days), after which she was transitioned to an oral prednisolone taper. Although her acute viral pneumonia improved, she remained dependent on high-flow nasal-cannula oxygen and developed multiple nosocomial bacterial pneumonias. On day 30 of her illness, she developed hemoptysis. High-resolution CT of the thorax on day 32 demonstrated new cavitary lesions in both upper lobes containing soft-tissue attenuation. Bronchoscopy was deferred because of the risk of worsening respiratory failure.

A 39‐year‐old woman with a history of alcohol use disorder presented to the emergency department with two days of atraumatic left leg swelling and pain. She had no risk factors for deep venous thrombosis and no personal or family history of thromboembolic disease or hypercoagulability. On examination, her left lower extremity had significant swelling with a positive Homans’ sign and severe pitting edema extending from the foot to the groin; the extremity was well perfused, hyperemic, with palpable distal pulses. Doppler ultrasonography revealed a large occlusive thrombus in the left common femoral vein extending inferiorly to the great saphenous vein. Given the severity of her symptoms, lack of predisposing factors, and extensive thrombus burden, a CT venogram was obtained to evaluate for underlying structural pathology. The CT venogram showed a fully occlusive filling defect in the left common iliac and femoral veins extending into the distal inferior vena cava, with evidence of compression of the left iliac vein by the overlying artery.

A 64‐year‐old male cattle farmer presented with an asymptomatic left‐sided neck swelling of 2 years’ duration, static over the past year. He denied voice changes, dysphagia, dyspnea, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. Examination revealed a well‐defined, non‐tender nodular mass measuring 7 cm × 4 cm on the anterior left neck; it moved with swallowing but not with tongue protrusion, and the overlying skin was intact.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, normal thyroid function tests, normal renal function, an ESR of 11 mm/h, and a CRP of 0.25 mg/dL. Serologic testing by ELISA was positive for Echinococcus granulosus. Ultrasonography of the neck demonstrated a large multiloculated heterogeneous anechoic lesion measuring 8.1 cm × 4 cm × 5 cm in the left thyroid lobe (TI-RADS 3); the right lobe and cervical lymph nodes appeared normal. CT scan confirmed that the lesion was confined to the thyroid gland. Ultrasound‐guided fine‐needle aspiration yielded 18 mL of clear, watery fluid, which was sent for cytologic evaluation.

A 38-year-old man presented with a three-hour history of abdominal pain and nausea. He denied chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, cough, or hemoptysis. Two weeks earlier, he had been discharged after a 3-week hospital course for COVID-19 pneumonia requiring endotracheal intubation; a CT pulmonary angiogram at that time showed no pulmonary embolism. His history was notable for a traumatic PE at age 16 treated with 6 months of warfarin and a second PE at age 30 complicated by chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension treated with pulmonary thromboendarterectomy followed by long-term warfarin. A hypercoagulable work-up after his second PE was negative, and he reported consistent adherence to warfarin with therapeutic INRs. 

On presentation, temperature was 100.4°F, blood pressure 129/86 mm Hg, heart rate 99 bpm, and respiratory rate 16/min. Examination revealed obesity and moderate, bilateral symmetrical lower extremity edema. Laboratory studies showed WBC 12.94×10^9/L, normal basic metabolic panel, negative high-sensitivity troponin, normal platelets, INR in the therapeutic range, PT elevated at 34.7 s, and PTT 37.4 s. An abdominal CT scan was unremarkable for intra-abdominal pathology but demonstrated an incidental possible filling defect in a partially imaged dilated descending right pulmonary artery. A dedicated CT pulmonary angiogram revealed a large filling defect in the right main pulmonary artery consistent with thromboembolism. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a dilated right atrium with septal bowing, severely dilated right ventricle with reduced systolic function, diastolic and systolic septal flattening, and a dilated inferior vena cava. Lower extremity Doppler ultrasound did not demonstrate deep vein thrombosis.

A 29-year-old man with second-degree Mobitz type II atrioventricular block had a dual-chamber right ventricular pacemaker placed 5 weeks earlier. He presented with 1 week of sharp, intermittent, unprovoked left-sided chest pain over the pacemaker site.  
On arrival: pulse 78/min, blood pressure 171/99 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, temperature 98.3°F. He appeared comfortable but had reproducible chest pain over the device.  
A 12-lead ECG showed deep, symmetric T-wave inversions in multiple leads. Electrolytes and complete blood count were within normal limits, and troponin I was undetectable. He received aspirin and a heparin drip and was admitted to the coronary care unit.  
Four hours later, a repeat ECG showed a ventricular-paced rhythm. Troponin I remained undetectable on three measurements over 11 hours, and the heparin drip was discontinued. A transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated normal left ventricular size and function without wall motion abnormalities and mild concentric hypertrophy. Pacemaker interrogation revealed adequate function and battery life. Ultrasound of the left chest wall excluded a hematoma or fluid collection around the pacemaker. He was started on oral nifedipine for hypertension, remained asymptomatic, and was discharged the next morning.

A 48-year-old Sri Lankan woman presented with sudden, bilateral, painless loss of vision. Six months earlier she had noted bilateral breast lumps that slowly enlarged and ulcerated, causing intense pain. Over the past 3 months she developed painful, nonhealing ulcers on the palate. She reported a 1-year history of constitutional symptoms but denied fever or known TB exposure. Two days after admission, she developed a dry cough and moderate hemoptysis without fever. 

On examination she was afebrile, of average build, with no lymphadenopathy. Lung auscultation revealed diffuse, coarse bilateral crepitations. Ophthalmologic examination showed absent light perception bilaterally with no pupillary reflexes. Brain and orbital MRI were normal. Indirect retinoscopy demonstrated bilateral panuveitis with hemorrhagic retinal angiopathy. 

Laboratory studies showed an ESR of 135 mm/h and CRP of 96 mg/dL. Chest radiography revealed bilateral mid- and lower-zone infiltrates with cavitation and small pleural effusions, confirmed on CT. Three consecutive sputum AFB smears were negative. Pleural fluid was exudative (protein difference 15 g/L; lymphocytes 70%), LDH 600 U/L, ADA 101 IU/L, with negative cytology, Gram stain, AFB smear, PCR, and cultures. 

Breast ultrasound showed hypoechoic, ill-defined abscesses; biopsy revealed well-formed noncaseating granulomas without malignant cells. Palatal ulcer biopsy showed granulomatous inflammation with necrosis. HIV test was negative. Serum ACE was normal. Renal function and urinalysis were normal. Serum PR3-ANCA was 190.74 IU/mL (normal < 20); MPO-ANCA, ANA, and rheumatoid factor were normal.

A 57-year-old woman underwent laparoscopic total hysterectomy with bilateral adnexectomy, uterosacral ligament suspension, anterior colporrhaphy, and urethropexy for grade III cystocele and grade I uterine prolapse. Preoperative evaluations were unremarkable except for thyroid nodules on ultrasound; thyroid biopsy showed no atypical cells. On postoperative day 1, she reported left neck discomfort and limited motion. Examination revealed a soft, fluctuating 9×8 cm mass in her left lateral neck. Color Doppler ultrasonography showed widening of the left external jugular vein extending to the subclavian vein inlet, suggestive of a thrombus. On day 2, she developed progressive dyspnea. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated findings suggestive of neck cellulitis and bilateral pleural effusions. Laboratory studies showed neutrophils 81.4% (normal 50–70), lymphocytes 12.1% (20–40), D-dimer 1.85 mg/L (0–0.55), procalcitonin 0.114 ng/mL (0–0.05), potassium 3.18 mmol/L (3.5–5.3), calcium 2.03 mmol/L (2.11–2.52), albumin 25.6 g/L (40–55), and total protein 47.8 g/L (65–85). To further clarify the nature of the effusion, 3 mL of pleural fluid was extracted.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a seven-month history of generalized abdominal pain, predominantly epigastric, accompanied by nausea and vomiting. Over the past three years, she had experienced intermittent abdominal pain, recurrent nausea and vomiting, episodes of inability to pass gas, and constipation, leading to at least ten hospitalizations. Her medical history included asthma, tubal ligation, umbilical hernia repair, cholecystectomy, diagnostic laparoscopy, and appendectomy. On admission, her temperature was 37.2°C, pulse 85 beats per minute, and blood pressure 110/75 mmHg. The abdomen was mildly distended with generalized tenderness, greatest in the epigastrium and right abdomen, without rebound or guarding. Rectal examination was normal. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 9900/mm3 with 24% lymphocytes, hemoglobin 16.1 g/dL, and hematocrit 46.6%; biochemistry tests were within normal limits. Upper endoscopy showed bile reflux, erythematous gastritis, and a gastric body ulcer. Abdominal ultrasonography was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated torsion around a narrow mesenteric stalk, malposition of the duodenojejunal flexure to the right of midline, obstruction of the duodenum, and a “beak” appearance of the proximal jejunum.

A 74-year-old woman with hypertension, hypothyroidism, osteoporosis, Sjögren’s syndrome, bronchiectasis, rheumatoid arthritis, and a penicillin rash presented with persistent itching and a burning rash. She had atopic dermatitis diagnosed clinically and had been treated with tralokinumab injections for 2 months with minimal response. Her other medications included adalimumab for rheumatoid arthritis (40 mg every 2 weeks for 2 years), levothyroxine, alendronate, albuterol, benzonatate, losartan, and omeprazole.

On initial examination, she had erythematous, scaly papules and plaques over more than 25% of her body surface area, as well as lichenified papules and nodules on her lower back and sacrum. Tralokinumab was discontinued, and she received a 600 mg loading dose of dupilumab.

Three days after the dupilumab dose, she noted a burning rash on her scalp, face, chest, and upper back. On examination 10 days after the dose, there were polymorphic annular patches and plaques with some erosions, hemorrhagic crusting, and impetiginization on sun-exposed areas of the face, scalp, upper chest, and upper back. She denied fever, joint pain, or headache.

A biopsy of a perilesional, sun-protected area on the upper back showed superficial perivascular lymphocytic inflammation with exocytosis, clefting, dyskeratotic keratinocytes, and areas of full-thickness epidermal necrosis. Direct immunofluorescence showed no staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or fibrinogen, but colloid bodies were present.

A 9-year-old boy from a rural area presented with mild left flank pain for 3 months, without fever or digestive symptoms. The family reported contact with sheep. On examination, vital signs were normal and abdominal examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, white blood cell count 11,000/mm³, platelet count 443,000/mm³, and Echinococcus antibody titer 1:320 (negative). Abdominal ultrasound revealed a well-defined cystic lesion in the spleen without internal solids. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 5 × 5 cm well-defined, non-calcified cystic lesion at the splenic periphery that did not enhance with contrast.

A 47-year-old previously healthy woman presented with a 1-month history of epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting of gastric contents. She had no fever or diarrhea. Initial evaluation at a local hospital showed a blood lipase level of 216.2 U/L (normal < 60 U/L), normal amylase levels, and abdominal CT and ultrasound demonstrating inflammation and fluid collections consistent with pancreatitis and peritoneal effusion. She was diagnosed with cholecystitis and pancreatitis, treated with IV fluids, pancreatic‐rest measures, and somatostatin, which normalized pancreatic enzymes, but her epigastric pain and anorexia persisted. A repeat abdominal CT showed mild pancreatic swelling.  

Over the ensuing days, she developed peripheral edema, cough, and pain in the right upper limb; ultrasound revealed thrombosis of the right axillary and subclavian veins. Chest CT demonstrated focal pulmonary opacities and bilateral pleural effusions. Laboratory studies revealed:  
• White-cell count 2.18 × 10^9/L (3–9.5), hemoglobin 91 g/L (115–150), platelets 33 × 10^9/L (125–350)  
• Urinalysis: 1+ protein, 1+ blood; 24-h protein excretion 7.9 g  
• Bone marrow biopsy: active hyperplasia, normal megakaryocyte count with rare platelets, megaloblastic granulocytes  
• ANA titer 1:1280; anti–double-stranded DNA and anti-SSA positive; anti–Smith, anti-RNP, and anti-SSB negative  
• IgG 24.3 g/L (7–16), IgG4 0.409 g/L (0.03–2.01)  
• C3 0.56 g/L (0.9–1.8), C4 0.06 g/L (0.1–0.4)  
• ESR 82 mm/h (0–20), CRP < 10 mg/L (0–10), procalcitonin 0.066 mg/L (< 0.064)  
• Anticardiolipin antibody and lupus anticoagulant positive  
Vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, she was afebrile, blood pressure 119/71 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, pulse 86/min. Her abdomen was soft with epigastric tenderness; skin, joints, and neurologic exams were unremarkable.

A 66-year-old man presented with three episodes of substernal chest pain over 2 days and was diagnosed with unstable angina. His medical history was notable for longstanding hypertension managed with beta-blockers and a history of chronic smoking; there was no family history of coronary artery disease. On examination, vital signs were stable. An electrocardiogram demonstrated dynamic ST-T changes in the anterior precordial leads. Cardiac enzymes were within normal limits, and two-dimensional echocardiography showed normal left ventricular function without regional wall-motion abnormalities. Routine laboratory tests were unremarkable.

Because of recurrent anginal episodes during hospitalization, coronary angiography was performed. Left coronary angiography revealed a left anterior descending artery (LAD) arising from the left main coronary artery that was unusually short and terminated prematurely in the anterior interventricular sulcus (AIVS), raising suspicion for mid-LAD occlusion. This short vessel gave rise to a first diagonal branch with 80% proximal stenosis. The left circumflex artery was dominant, giving rise to the posterior descending artery. Selective right coronary angiography showed a nondominant right coronary artery and an additional vessel originating from its proximal segment; this long vessel coursed toward the left, gave off septal and diagonal branches, and then reentered the distal AIVS to reach the apex.

A 56-year-old mixed-ancestry man with end-stage kidney disease from malignant hypertension underwent a deceased-donor renal transplant in 2002. His baseline serum creatinine is 91 μmol/L (reference 64–104) with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 58 mL/min/1.73 m2. Maintenance immunosuppression includes tacrolimus 2 mg twice daily, prednisone 10 mg once daily, and mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg twice daily.

Over the past four months, he has experienced progressive functional decline, confusion, inappropriate behavior, intermittent rigors, and significant weight and appetite loss. He has no history of gardening, animal exposures, alcohol use, or smoking. Review of his records revealed treatment two years ago for articular sporotrichosis of the left wrist, for which he completed 10 months of oral itraconazole.

On examination, temperature was 36.4 °C, blood pressure 135/72 mmHg, heart rate 96 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and random blood glucose 12 mmol/L. He appeared chronically ill with bilateral temporalis wasting. His extracellular fluid compartment was contracted, and he had chronic nonpitting lower-limb edema. There was symmetrical synovial hypertrophy of the small joints of the hands without destructive changes. There were no cutaneous or lymphocutaneous lesions. His Glasgow Coma Scale was 12 (E4 M5 V3); there was no meningism, focal neurologic deficit, or papilledema.

Chest radiography showed patchy alveolar infiltrates. Computed tomography of the brain demonstrated mild global cerebral atrophy and microangiopathic changes. Given the high background prevalence of tuberculosis and his immunosuppressed state, empiric rifampicin-sparing anti-tuberculous therapy was initiated (moxifloxacin, isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, and pyridoxine). The patient’s clinical state continued to deteriorate despite more than four weeks of anti-tuberculous treatment.

A 49-year-old woman presented with a 1-week history of anorexia, asthenia, pruritus, abdominal pain, nausea, and liquid stools. She lived in poor conditions and had mild cognitive impairment and blindness since childhood. On examination, her temperature was 38.2 ºC; there was tenderness in the right upper abdominal quadrant, scratchy skin lesions on the lower limbs, short stature, and a dysmorphic face. No neurologic deficits were noted.

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL, leukocytes 11 × 10^9/L, platelets 633 × 10^9/L; blood smear showed rouleaux formation, microcytosis, hypochromia, and granulations and vacuoles in neutrophils. Inflammatory markers were elevated: sedimentation velocity 130 mm/h, C-reactive protein 28.51 mg/dL; ferritin 18 953 ng/mL; lactate dehydrogenase 750 U/L; d-dimer 18 898 ng/dL; fibrinogen 502 mg/dL; triglycerides 164 mg/dL; soluble interleukin-2 receptor 2752 pg/mL; interleukin-6 97.2 pg/L. There was hypergammaglobulinemia, mild cholestasis (AST 210 U/L, ALT 71 U/L, γGT 111 U/L, ALP 183 U/L), hypoalbuminemia (2.78 mg/dL), low HDL cholesterol (24.6 mg/dL), and 24-h urine protein 377 mg.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed bilateral axillary, cervical, mediastinal, and mesenteric lymphadenopathies; splenomegaly; and pericardial, peritoneal, and bilateral pleural effusions. A PET scan demonstrated diffusely increased bone marrow uptake, increased uptake in cervical adenopathies (SUVmax 5.64), and increased splenic uptake.

A 49-year-old obese woman (BMI 30.6) was referred after an incidental paraspinal mediastinal mass was detected on MRI during evaluation for migraine headaches and cervicalgia. She is G1P1, currently uses an intrauterine device, and took oral contraceptive pills for 15 years. Her medical history is notable for C5–C6 anterior cervical discectomy and fusion. She has a strong family history of breast cancer and is positive for a Necdin (NDN) variant; she declined prophylactic mastectomy. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the thoracic spine showed a well-circumscribed, homogeneous mass with signals compatible with a simple cyst, measuring 2.0 × 1.2 × 2.2 cm, located along the right anterolateral aspect of the T5 vertebral body. Given her genetic predisposition and family history, the patient elected robotic surgical resection for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. 

Under general anesthesia with a double-lumen endotracheal tube and left lateral decubitus positioning, the da Vinci Si robot was docked. Four ports were placed along the seventh intercostal space with CO2 insufflation. The lung was retracted anteriorly to expose a cystic lesion adherent to the paraspinal T5 level. A distinct surgical plane permitted complete excision, although the cyst wall was inadvertently ruptured, releasing serous fluid. The patient recovered well postoperatively and was discharged on postoperative day 2.

A 14-year-old previously healthy Caucasian boy was admitted with a 5-day history of fever, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. On the day of admission, he developed a diffuse skin rash and bilateral conjunctivitis. He had no personal or family history of cardiovascular disease. On examination, temperature was 38.3 °C, blood pressure was low, heart rate 112 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. 

Laboratory studies showed elevated N-terminal pro–brain natriuretic peptide, troponin, C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, D-dimer, fibrinogen, and hyponatremia. A SARS-CoV-2 nasopharyngeal swab was negative, but anti–SARS-CoV-2 IgG was positive. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated biventricular dilatation, global hypokinesia, and an ejection fraction of 30%. 

Electrocardiography in standard leads showed sinus rhythm, normal ventricular conduction, and diffuse repolarization abnormalities. Modified precordial-lead ECG revealed sinus rhythm with QRS fragmentation in lead D3 and saddleback ST-segment elevation.

A 77-year-old woman with hypertension and hyperlipidemia noted 3 months of intermittent staggering when walking and, 2 months ago, sustained a head bruise after a fall. A head CT at that time showed a hypodense area in the right parietal region. She presented with light-headedness on walking but had no subjective cognitive complaints. On examination, she had a mild ataxic gait and no other focal neurologic deficits or evidence of cognitive impairment. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral, asymmetric subcortical hyperintensity in the parietal lobes on T2-weighted and FLAIR images, with corresponding high signal on the apparent diffusion coefficient map but no restriction on diffusion-weighted imaging, consistent with vasogenic edema. T2*-weighted gradient-echo imaging revealed several subcortical microbleeds in the right parietal lobe. Post–gadolinium T1-weighted images showed no enhancement.

A 28-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with a one-week history of pleuritic chest pain, cough, low-grade fever, and shortness of breath. He denied hemoptysis or weight loss but reported difficulty swallowing solid foods. On examination, his blood pressure was 111/80 mm Hg, heart rate 105 beats per minute, respiratory rate was normal, and oxygen saturation was 96% on room air. Lung auscultation was clear bilaterally, and the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. An electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 15.6×10^3/μL with 78.8% neutrophils, a potassium level of 3.4 mmol/L, and a D-dimer of 470 ng/mL. A computed tomography angiogram of the chest ruled out pulmonary embolism but demonstrated a 7.0×4.5×3.5 cm subcarinal mass with small punctate calcifications causing mild mass effect on the right main pulmonary artery. The mass had an attenuation of 40 Hounsfield units; the calcifications measured 140 Hounsfield units. Multiple mediastinal and right hilar calcified lymph nodes were also present, along with a calcified splenic granuloma. The patient is a lifelong nonsmoker, has never traveled outside the United States, takes no medications, works as an Amazon delivery driver, and has no pets.

A 2-year-9-month-old girl with an unremarkable perinatal history and normal early development was referred to pediatric neurology for left eyelid drooping. One month earlier, she had been treated for bilateral conjunctivitis with tobramycin for 12 days. Toward the end of treatment, her mother noticed episodic left eyelid drooping (up to 30 seconds, worse in afternoon), with persistent asymmetry of the palpebral fissures. An ophthalmologist noted physiological hyperopia and left eyelid drooping. The child was then seen by ENT and neurology. The ENT specialist prescribed amoxicillin–clavulanate and intranasal mometasone for presumed sinusitis; nasal discharge improved, but ocular symptoms persisted and snoring developed. In the interim, she had chickenpox and her mother also noted tachycardia. A cardiology evaluation revealed a heart rate of 130 bpm with otherwise normal cardiac structure and function. The mother additionally reported up to five loose stools per day for months; celiac disease was excluded. 

On examination, the child was hyperactive with attention deficit. Height was at the 97th percentile and weight between the 50th and 85th percentiles. Vital signs included a heart rate of 130 bpm. Ocular exam showed a widened right palpebral fissure with proptosis, left eyelid ptosis, and lip closure weakness. Neurologic exam revealed marked weakness of the pelvic girdle muscles, decreased tone, hyperreflexia in the arms, and hypoactive reflexes in the legs. Gait was wide-based and clumsy; she used a Gowers’ maneuver to rise from the floor and could not lift her head or legs when supine. 

Laboratory studies showed:  
• TSH <0.008 μIU/mL (normal 0.67–4.16)  
• Free T3 >20 pg/mL (normal 3.3–4.8)  
• Free T4 >6.0 mg/dL (normal 0.74–1.28)  
• Creatine kinase 48 U/L (normal 58–293)  
• Hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL, HCT 32.1%, MCV 68.9 fL, microcytosis 27%

A man in his early 50s with a BMI of 29.9 kg/m2 and no history of dyslipidaemia, diabetes, or other comorbidities was treated for stage IIIC mucinous adenocarcinoma of the left colon (pT4a pN2a [5/22] cM0, MSS/pMMR). Preoperative blood tests, including a fasting triglyceride level, were within reference ranges. He underwent left hemicolectomy with R0 margins and began adjuvant FOLFOX chemotherapy (5-FU 400 mg/m2 bolus on day 1, 5-FU 2400 mg/m2 continuous infusion over 48 hours on days 1–2, leucovorin 200 mg/m2 on day 1, and oxaliplatin 85 mg/m2 on day 1) every 2 weeks. After five cycles he developed grade 1 peripheral neuropathy. On day 2 of the ninth cycle, a deep vein thrombosis of the right axillary vein was diagnosed, and low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) was started daily. Three weeks later, immediately before the tenth cycle, blood samples appeared markedly lipaemic despite fasting. Repeat sampling confirmed a milky plasma supernatant. A lipid panel revealed triglycerides of 37.1 mmol/L (3286 mg/dL), total cholesterol of 13.3 mmol/L (514 mg/dL), LDL cholesterol of 1.90 mmol/L (73 mg/dL), and HDL cholesterol of 0.50 mmol/L (19 mg/dL). There was no evidence of diabetes, thyroid dysfunction, renal impairment, pancreatitis, or cutaneous xanthomas on examination.

A 37-year-old HIV-negative woman with a history of polysubstance abuse, commercial sex work, and recently diagnosed seizure disorder presented with several months of left-sided weakness, urinary incontinence, mild photophobia, ataxia, and headache. She denied fever, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, prior childhood seizures, or vision changes. Four months earlier, she had a maculopapular rash on the soles; rapid plasma reagin was 1:32, and she received a single dose of benzathine penicillin G for presumed secondary syphilis. On admission, her rapid plasma reagin titer had fallen to 1:4, and treponemal antibody testing was positive. 

Brain MRI demonstrated extensive vasogenic edema of the frontoparietal lobes, most prominent at the vertex with downward mass effect on the corpus callosum; there was nodular enhancement of the frontoparietal lobes and along the superior sagittal sinus (approximately 5 cm) and multiple nodular dural enhancements along the right interhemispheric fissure. No hydrocephalus was present. After initiation of benzathine penicillin G, her condition worsened, and she was transferred intubated and sedated. On arrival, she was bradycardic (heart rate 36 bpm), moved her lower extremities spontaneously but did not follow commands, and had constricted but reactive pupils bilaterally.

Noncontrast head CT showed large bilateral hypoattenuated areas in the supraventricular white matter consistent with diffuse vasogenic edema, with effacement of sulci and the right lateral ventricle, and three osteolytic lesions in the right frontal bone. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI again revealed nodular enhancement along the falx cerebri, rim-enhancing lesions with dural tails at the superior frontal lobes, diffuse vasogenic edema with sulcal and ventricular effacement, and three mildly enhancing intraosseous calvarial lesions measuring up to 1.2 × 0.9 cm. A punctate focus of restricted diffusion in the superomedial right frontal lobe suggested a small vascular infarction.

On hospital day 7, CT with contrast of the thoracic spine showed age-indeterminate superior endplate compression fractures of T3 through T6 without osteopenia. Follow-up thoracic spine MRI demonstrated mild STIR hyperintensity along the superior endplates of T3–T6, linear T1 hypointensities with corresponding T2 hyperintensities consistent with superior endplate compression fractures, and no spinal cord stenosis or marrow edema.

A 50-year-old Chinese Han woman presented with a 6-day history of sudden difficulty walking, numbness on the left side of her body, and dysuria. Twelve days earlier, she had been diagnosed with incomplete Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada disease after developing blurred vision in both eyes, bilateral granulomatous iridocyclitis, retinal edema, and exudates. She received high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone followed by a tapering course of prednisone. During the steroid taper, she developed headache, tinnitus, difficulty climbing stairs, left-sided numbness, and urinary retention. She reported an upper respiratory tract infection 1 month prior but denied recent vaccinations.

On examination, vital signs were normal. There was no lymphadenopathy or mucocutaneous lesions; skin and hair examinations were unremarkable. Visual acuity was 20/200 bilaterally, and funduscopic examination revealed papilledema. Motor examination showed increased tone, diminished strength in all extremities, hyperactive deep-tendon reflexes, bilateral Babinski signs, and a slow, stiff gait. Sensory examination revealed decreased pinprick sensation on the left without a defined sensory level; proprioception was intact. Cerebellar testing showed impaired finger-to-nose performance, and Kernig’s sign was absent.

Laboratory studies demonstrated normal routine blood tests; C-reactive protein, rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies, ANCA, anti–double-stranded DNA, anti–Smith, anti–RNP, anti–SSA, and anti–SSB antibodies were negative; ESR was 39 mm/hr. CSF analysis showed 128 WBCs/mm³ (94% mononuclear) and protein of 4.83 g/L; cultures were negative. Nerve conduction studies revealed mild polyneuropathy; visual evoked potentials were normal. Chest radiography and brain MRI were unremarkable. Optical coherence tomography showed bilateral disc edema with serous retinal detachment. Spinal MRI revealed a T2 hyperintense lesion with gadolinium enhancement extending from C1 to C3.

A 68-year-old man residing in a nursing home presented with decreased consciousness, tachypnea, hypoxia, and hypotension. His medical history included long‐standing type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with dapagliflozin, bladder and bowel dysfunction after a thoracic spinal cord injury, chronic prednisolone therapy for pemphigoid, and placement of an inferior vena cava (IVC) filter 12 years earlier.

On admission, his temperature was 38.1 °C, pulse 100 beats/min, blood pressure 78/32 mm Hg, respiratory rate 42 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on a 10 L reservoir mask. He had glossoptosis and bilateral coarse crackles; the abdomen was soft without tenderness. Laboratory data showed a white blood cell count of 20 100/μL, C-reactive protein 22.3 mg/dL, and serum lactate 5.3 mmol/L. Urinalysis revealed pyuria and bacteriuria.

Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated intramural gas in the bladder wall and gas in the left renal pelvis and parenchyma. He was diagnosed with septic shock due to emphysematous cystitis and pyelonephritis and was started on intravenous norepinephrine and meropenem. Two days later, he remained hemodynamically unstable and was transferred to the intensive care unit, where meropenem was continued at an extended infusion.

Blood and urine cultures grew extended‐spectrum beta‐lactamase–producing Escherichia coli. Despite clinical improvement and no drainable abscess on repeat CT, blood cultures remained positive. A possible diagnosis of infective endocarditis was considered, but transesophageal echocardiography showed no vegetations. At this point, IVC filter infection was the remaining differential diagnosis.

A 64-year-old man was brought to the emergency department with anorexia, diarrhea, and an episode of altered consciousness. Earlier that day, a computed tomography scan had revealed a large mass in the right upper lobe of his lung, and he was admitted for evaluation of the pulmonary lesion. Shortly after admission, he developed bloody diarrhea, lower abdominal pain, and hypotension. 

His medical history included hypertension and depression; he was a heavy smoker (44-year pack history) but denied alcohol use. On examination, he was severely emaciated, normothermic, and hypotensive; his abdomen was soft with mild tenderness in the lower quadrants. Laboratory studies showed a white-blood-cell count of 15.4 × 10^3/μL (86.5% neutrophils), hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, blood urea nitrogen 69.4 mg/dL, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, prothrombin time 27.4%, and activated partial thromboplastin time 46.1 s. HIV testing was negative.

An urgent contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan demonstrated extensive intestinal ischemia, intestinal pneumatosis, free intra-abdominal gas, intussusception of a small-intestinal mass, and a small amount of ascites. Chest CT again showed a large right upper-lobe mass. 

The preoperative diagnosis was bowel necrosis and perforation with intussusception of a small intestinal tumor. Accordingly, emergency subtotal colectomy and enterectomy were undertaken.

A 32-year-old woman presented for evaluation of recurrent myalgia, muscle weakness, and dark-colored urine since infancy. Her first episode occurred at age 1 year with fever, sudden quadriparesis, cyanosis, tachypnea (respiratory rate 60/min), and sinus tachycardia (heart rate up to 180/min); she required two weeks to stand with support. Subsequent episodes at ages 18 and 20 months were associated with transient flaccid weakness; at 22 months, fever, weakness, red urine, and dyspnea prompted evaluation for hemoglobinuria. At age 4 years, urine myoglobin was detected but porphobilinogen testing was negative. Further episodes at ages 6, 9, 22, 28, and 30 years varied in severity and were temporally linked to drugs (theophylline, co-trimoxazole, mefenamic acid) or combined oral contraceptives; symptoms resolved on withdrawal. Between crises she reported exercise intolerance with calf and thigh numbness progressing to dyspnea, nausea, and vomiting on stress testing. She had a consanguineous family background; her sister died at age 2 years of a similar episode. Two years after her last crisis, while asymptomatic, her BMI was 25.7 kg/m2, pulse 110/min, blood pressure 110/60 mmHg; limb strength was grade 4/5 with normal reflexes. Past laboratory summaries showed marked elevations of serum creatine kinase and transaminases. Urine organic acids were normal; plasma amino acids showed nonspecific reductions. Abdominal ultrasound revealed grade 1 fatty liver. Bioimpedance analysis demonstrated increased fat percentage (40.2%) with normal muscle mass. A muscle biopsy revealed occasional myofiber necrosis, inflammatory infiltrates, and focal atrophy; Gomori trichrome and PAS stains showed no ragged red fibers or vacuolation; Oil Red O stain demonstrated minute lipid droplets; Sudan black stain showed occasional subsarcolemmal lipid aggregates.

A 46-year-old morbidly obese woman presented with 2–3 months of painful redness and swelling of her right medial thigh. She had no known medical history but was found to be hypertensive. An ultrasound of the right lower extremity to exclude deep vein thrombosis was negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the right thigh demonstrated skin thickening and reticular soft-tissue attenuation compatible with edema throughout the subcutaneous fat at the area of redness. The patient was treated for presumptive cellulitis with diuretics and intravenous antibiotics, then discharged on a 7-day course of oral antibiotics; a compressive stocking was recommended but not obtained. Over the next 2 years, she was admitted four times for recurrent right thigh pain, redness, and swelling; she remained afebrile with normal white-cell counts on all admissions. An ultrasound during this period showed a lobular contour of subcutaneous fat with edema but no organized abscess. Fifteen months later, she returned with 3 weeks of right thigh swelling, intermittent fevers, and a larger, more well-defined medial thigh mass. MRI showed a large exophytic mass arising from the subcutaneous fat of the medial thigh, isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on fat-suppressed fluid-sensitive sequences, minimal peripheral and dermal enhancement, and regions of interposed fat. An ultrasound-guided biopsy was nondiagnostic.

A 46-year-old woman with no significant medical history noted a firm nodule in her right medial thigh that had been present for 4 months and was slowly enlarging. She reported no pain, systemic symptoms, recent travel, or known exposures. On examination, there was a 2-cm, well-defined, elastic, non-tender, immobile, oval subcutaneous nodule. The initial clinical impression was an atheroma or epidermal cyst. Soft-tissue sonography demonstrated a 2-cm lesion directly adherent to the epidermis without deep subcutaneous fat separation. Given its progressive growth, the lesion was surgically excised, yielding a 2.2-cm encapsulated nodule.

A 64-year-old woman presented with 1 month of painful genital lesions and persistent vaginal itching.  
History of present illness:  
• 1 week before initial presentation, she developed painful genital lesions and was diagnosed at urgent care with a urinary tract infection and fungal dermatitis. She received nitrofurantoin, metronidazole, and ketoconazole 2% cream without relief.  
• Two days later, she presented to the emergency department with intractable groin pain, worsened dysuria, subjective fever, and vaginal discharge; she was diagnosed with chancroid and herpes simplex virus and treated with azithromycin and acyclovir.  
• At a follow-up 2 weeks later, lesions were nearly resolved but slight itching persisted. Two weeks after that, lesions recurred intensely, prompting her presentation to our clinic.  
She denied sexual intercourse, recent vaginal penetration, changes in detergents, trauma, or scratching.  
Vital signs were within normal limits.  
Examination of the pelvic skin and mucosa showed dark purple and white patches in a thick reticular pattern, with no edema, drainage, fluctuance, or inguinal lymphadenopathy.  
Laboratory studies revealed a normal white blood cell count, hemoglobin, and platelets; an elevated eosinophil count of 0.46 bil/L (reference range 0.03–0.39 bil/L); and negative tests for herpes simplex virus 1 and 2, HIV 1 and 2, vaginal pathogens, Pap smear/HPV, gonorrhea, and chlamydia. Urine culture grew 10,000 CFU/mL of pan-sensitive Escherichia coli; deep wound culture showed no growth.

A 63-year-old African man presented with a 6-month history of painless swelling of the penis. He denied genital trauma, urethral discharge, or urinary symptoms and had no other skin lesions. He was married with no extra-marital relationships. Examination revealed a 1×2 cm firm, non-tender nodule on the ventral aspect of the penis. Excisional biopsy showed epithelioid histiocytes palisading around necrotic collagen with mucin deposition, suggestive of granuloma annulare.

One year later, he returned with similar painless subcutaneous nodules on his right upper limb that had spread to his chest and trunk. He reported no respiratory symptoms, fever, or joint pain. He looked comfortable, with no palpable cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy. Multiple 1×2 cm firm, non-tender nodules were noted over the right arm, chest, and trunk. Chest auscultation and cardiovascular examination were normal.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, fasting glucose, and most liver-function tests except an elevated AST. Renal function tests indicated acute kidney injury (creatinine 205 µmol/L, GFR 28 mL/min/1.73 m2). Electrolytes were normal except for hypercalcemia (3.35 mmol/L) with a low parathyroid hormone level (0.4 pmol/L). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated at 37 mm/hr, C-reactive protein was <1 mg/L, and serum angiotensin-converting enzyme was elevated at 243 ACEU.

Chest radiography revealed a superior mediastinal mass and bilateral hilar enlargement. Chest CT showed multiple enlarged mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes without parenchymal infiltrates. A repeat excisional biopsy of a right arm nodule demonstrated non-caseating discrete granulomata with a thin lymphocytic cuff and no evidence of vasculitis or panniculitis.

A woman in her 70s presented 8 days after receiving the first dose of the AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine with a 1-week history of feeling generally unwell. She reported a transient right-sided weakness and a generalized headache that improved with glucose ingestion. She denied fever, urinary symptoms, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, joint pains, mouth ulcers, or back pain. She took no over-the-counter or herbal medications and had no NSAID use. 

Her medical history included type II diabetes mellitus (diagnosed 2004) with background diabetic retinopathy and hypertension, treated with alogliptin, glimepiride, metformin, olmesartan, and simvastatin. She was independent in activities of daily living, a non-smoker, and drank no alcohol.

On ambulance arrival, her blood glucose was 1.6 mmol/L. A CT scan of the head showed no acute intracranial pathology. Laboratory studies revealed stage III acute kidney injury with metabolic acidosis and hyperkalemia (serum potassium, 6.1 mmol/L). Her serum creatinine on admission was 416 μmol/L (baseline ~80 μmol/L), peaking at 618 μmol/L. She had a normocytic anemia (hemoglobin, 97 g/L); liver and bone profiles were normal. Urinalysis demonstrated hematuria and proteinuria; the urine protein–creatinine ratio was 135 mg/mmol, with no eosinophiluria. A renal vasculitis and myeloma screen was unremarkable. 

Renal ultrasound showed two normal-sized kidneys with good cortical preservation and no stones, masses, or hydronephrosis. A renal biopsy was then arranged to investigate an intrinsic cause of her acute kidney injury.

A 63-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and obesity presented with worsening chest discomfort, dizziness, and palpitations. On examination he was euvolemic, with dual heart sounds and no murmurs. The electrocardiogram showed complete atrioventricular dissociation with a sinus rate of 100 beats per minute and a ventricular escape rate of 36 beats per minute; the QRS width was 100 ms. Serum troponin was not elevated, routine blood chemistry was within normal limits, and he was biochemically euthyroid.

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a normal left ventricular ejection fraction (55–60%) and an echogenic mass measuring 3.1 × 3.0 cm on the mitral annulus extending into the basal septum, with mild mitral leaflet thickening, mild regurgitation, and no stenosis.

Transesophageal echocardiography showed a well-circumscribed circular intramyocardial mass in the basal posterior medial aspect of the left ventricle extending into the posterior mitral annulus, measuring 2.5 × 2.0 cm; the mass was echodense, without central liquefaction, mass effect, or valvular impingement. The differential diagnoses at that stage included lipomatous hypertrophy, noncaseous granuloma, and mitral annular calcification.

A 6‐year‐old girl was admitted on day 7 of a dengue fever recovery phase with new‐onset profuse, watery, mucous‐containing loose stools, vomiting, and generalized abdominal pain. She initially tested positive for dengue NS1 antigen 5 days earlier, with nadir platelet count 30 × 10^3/cumm and WBC 2.8 × 10^3/cumm; on admission her platelets were 90 × 10^3/cumm and WBC 4.5 × 10^3/cumm. Liver enzymes were mildly elevated (SGOT 145 IU/dL, SGPT 98 IU/dL), and C‐reactive protein was 12 mg/dL. Urine and blood cultures were negative. On the night of the same day, she developed the intestinal symptoms and abdominal pain. Stool cultures were pending. Repeat labs showed WBC 11 × 10^3/cumm and platelet count 92 × 10^3/cumm. On examination she was febrile (38.5 °C) with tachycardia; the abdomen was diffusely tender with demonstrable guarding and rigidity.

A 64-year-old Chinese man was admitted with chest pain and palpitations of 45 minutes’ duration that resolved on arrival. He had no history of hypertension, diabetes, or known heart disease. Physical examination was unremarkable. An electrocardiogram showed ST-segment depression greater than 1.0 mm in leads V3 through V6. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed no abnormalities. On admission, cardiac troponin I was 0.09 ng/ml (normal < 0.08 ng/ml), increased to 0.52 ng/ml on hospital day 2, and returned to the normal range by day 3. He was treated for presumed acute coronary syndrome with aspirin, clopidogrel, low-molecular-weight heparin, and atorvastatin. Coronary angiography was scheduled one week after admission.

A 37-year-old Persian man was referred to a periodontics clinic with a 1-month history of upper tooth mobility and purulent gingival discharge. Three months earlier, he had been hospitalized for severe COVID-19 with 40% lung involvement; he received remdesivir and a three-day course of dexamethasone, during which his serum glucose rose to 400 mg/dl necessitating insulin therapy, which was continued on discharge. Shortly afterward, he developed headache and maxillary pain with gum swelling and gingival abscesses. A general dentist prescribed intramuscular penicillin, oral co-amoxiclav, metronidazole for 1 week, and chlorhexidine mouth rinse without improvement. Non-contrast CT showed severe right and moderate left maxillary sinus opacification and mild right ethmoid opacification with ostiomeatal complex involvement. MRI with contrast demonstrated right maxillary sinusitis with pre-antral, retro-antral, and infratemporal soft-tissue infiltration without necrosis, bilateral nonspecific white-matter hyperintensities, and no orbital infiltration; visual acuity was normal. Diagnosed as partially treated acute sinusitis, he received broad-spectrum antibiotics. Three days later, examination showed grade III mobility of all maxillary teeth, negative vitality tests, 10–12 mm periodontal pockets, multiple apical abscesses with fistulae, and pus discharge. Laboratory tests revealed an HbA1c of 10.5% and fasting glucose of 400 mg/dl. Cone-beam CT of the maxillary area showed generalized alveolar bone rarefaction from the right tuberosity to the left edentulous area, buccal and lingual cortical defects, bilateral maxillary sinus opacification, perforations of the nasal floor and sinus walls, and sclerosis of the sinus walls; ethmoid, sphenoid, and frontal sinuses were clear. To alleviate pain, the clinician drained the abscesses; despite initial relief, pain and purulent discharge increased, and the patient was referred to a maxillofacial surgeon.

A 23-year-old man presented to a rural hospital with a single gunshot wound to the right chest, resulting in a sucking chest wound. He was managed according to Advanced Trauma Life Support protocols, including placement of an intercostal drain and closure of the bullet entry site. An initial CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no additional injuries. One hour after presentation, he developed paresthesia of the left leg and experienced a generalized tonic–clonic seizure.

After seizure control, neurologic examination showed decreased sensation in the left leg. MRI of the brain demonstrated bilateral superior cerebellar infarcts and a small infarct in the left occipital lobe. MRI of the spine revealed focal cord infarcts at anterior C2–C3 and posterolateral left T6–T7, without evidence of traumatic injury at those levels. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed no valvular pathology or intracardiac shunt. Doppler ultrasound of the lower extremities and CT pulmonary angiography showed no evidence of deep venous thrombosis or pulmonary embolism. The patient had no preexisting vascular risk factors, and a coagulation screen was unremarkable.

A 35-year-old woman (65 kg, 159 cm), G2P1, with no history of seizures or neurologic disorders, was scheduled for a repeat cesarean section under combined spinal–epidural anesthesia. Preoperative evaluation was unremarkable, and she was ASA physical status I. In the operating room, standard monitoring and bladder thermistor were applied. With the patient awake and in the left lateral decubitus position, an epidural catheter was placed at T12/L1 and a spinal tap at L2/L3. After confirming clear cerebrospinal fluid, 12.5 mg of hyperbaric 0.5% bupivacaine and 15 µg of fentanyl were injected intrathecally. The patient was then positioned supine, and a sensory block to cold up to T3 with accompanying motor block was achieved. Vasopressors (8 mg ephedrine and 0.6 mg phenylephrine) and fluids (900 ml crystalloid, 500 ml colloid) maintained blood pressure >100 mmHg. The surgery proceeded uneventfully; a live male infant and placenta were delivered at 9 and 11 minutes after incision, respectively. No sedatives were used, and the patient remained awake. One hour and ten minutes after the spinal tap, at the end of the operation, involuntary movements began in both upper extremities (left greater than right). Vital signs were stable before (105/74 mmHg, HR 87 bpm) and during (110/69 mmHg, HR 93 bpm) the movements. The sensory block had regressed to T8, and motor and sensory function in the arms was intact. The patient was fully conscious and calm, reported inability to stop the movements, but denied feeling cold. Bladder temperature was 36.8 °C, and no peripheral coldness was noted. The movements persisted without intervention for 33 minutes.

A 12-year-old girl presented with enlargement of her right breast over 2 months. She had first noticed a small nodule near the nipple that rapidly increased in size. There was no nipple discharge. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. Menarche occurred at age 11, and her menstrual cycles were normal. On physical examination, the right breast was substantially enlarged and replaced by a large lump occupying the entire breast, with diffuse tenderness and firmness on palpation. There was no skin thickening or nipple retraction. Ultrasonography of the right breast using an 8–10 MHz linear array transducer showed a heterogeneous hypoechoic mass measuring 17.3 cm in maximum diameter, with multiple cystic channels within the lesion. The right axilla contained lymph nodes with benign features. The lesion was classified as BI-RADS category 4, and ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy was advised.

A 63-year-old woman with an 11-year history of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis treated with infliximab and methotrexate presented with a 1.5-month history of fever, cough, and dyspnea. She was initially treated for community-acquired pneumonia with antibiotics and systemic steroids, with only transient improvement before recurrence of her symptoms. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.8 g/dL, platelets 51 × 10^9/L, ferritin 28 000 ng/mL, low C3 at 21 mg/dL and C4 <2 mg/dL, hypofibrinogenemia, elevated C-reactive protein, normal lipid profile, and mildly elevated liver enzymes. Chest CT revealed a subpleural opacity without parenchymal infiltrates. On examination, she had chronic limitation of the left wrist without active synovitis. Given persistent fever, cytopenias, hyperferritinemia, and failure to respond to antibiotics, secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis was suspected. Soluble IL-2 receptor was elevated at 7970 U/mL (reference 45–1105). She met five of eight HLH-2004 criteria and was started on high-dose glucocorticoids; however, fevers persisted, and bone marrow biopsy was pursued.

A 24-year-old man with a history of bronchial asthma presented with a 1-month history of recurrent left-sided epistaxis.  
Nasal endoscopy revealed persistent bloody rhinorrhea originating from the orifice of the left sphenoid sinus; other otolaryngologic findings were unremarkable. He denied trauma or other systemic disease.  
Noncontrast CT of the paranasal sinuses showed an expansive, solitary lesion in the left sphenoid sinus with minimal bone thinning and heterogeneous attenuation (–43 to 106 Hounsfield units).  
Noncontrast MRI demonstrated an internally heterogeneous high-intensity signal on both T1- and T2-weighted images, with a marked hypointense peripheral rim on T2.  
Contrast enhancement was not performed because of his asthma.  
What is your differential diagnosis?

A 34-year-old man presented with intermittent headache and hoarseness for 10 days. The headaches were intense during attacks but improved with rest. He had no dizziness, nausea, vomiting, limb weakness, limb twitching, swallowing difficulty, or choking when drinking. On examination, he was alert and slightly hoarse in speech; pupils were equal, round, 2.5 mm, and reactive to light. Limb strength was grade V with normal tone.  
Noncontrast CT of the head showed an abnormal density in the brainstem, and CT angiography showed no significant vascular abnormalities.  
Brain MRI revealed a lamellar lesion in the brainstem, measuring approximately 19 mm × 19 mm on axial images, with slightly long T1 and T2 signals. The lesion enhanced markedly after contrast administration. FLAIR imaging showed hyperintensity, and T2 images demonstrated flow‐void signals with prominent anterior and posterior vascular markings around the brainstem. MRI raised the possibility of an arteriovenous fistula affecting the brainstem.

A 37-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 3-month history of left flank pain. On initial evaluation in the emergency department, she was hemodynamically stable, and routine laboratory studies were within normal limits.  
Renal ultrasonography demonstrated a large cystic mass with multiple internal septations and lobulated margins in the lower pole of the left kidney, measuring approximately 12.3 × 8.6 cm.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a single, well-defined, thin-walled, parapelvic complex cystic lesion arising from the lower pole of the left kidney, measuring 11.9 × 9.3 × 8.8 cm (craniocaudal × transverse × anteroposterior). The lesion had thick internal septations, showed no significant post-contrast enhancement, and contained no solid nodules. There was no adjacent fat stranding, regional lymphadenopathy, or involvement of the renal veins, and the remainder of both kidneys and their vascular structures appeared normal.

An 8-year-old boy, born full term to non-consanguineous parents, with a history of mental retardation and epilepsy diagnosed at 6 months, presented with an increase in seizure frequency and a recent sensation of heaviness in his left hemibody. There was no history of meningitis, head trauma, or delayed motor milestones. On examination, vital signs were normal and the neurologic and general examinations revealed no focal deficits. An electroencephalogram was normal. Brain MRI demonstrated enlargement of the subarachnoid spaces over the right convexity and Sylvian fissure, mild dilation of the right choroidal fissure, and T2- and FLAIR-hyperintense signal in the right cortico-subcortical region without diffusion restriction or gadolinium enhancement, consistent with gliosis. Additional findings included right hemispheric cortical and subcortical atrophy, thickening of the right cranial vault, and hyperpneumatization of the right frontal sinus.

A 20-year-old man presented with bilateral lower extremity paralysis. He denied trauma or prior episodes. His medical and surgical history was unremarkable. He reported a single male sexual partner and a recent negative HIV test. Five hours before symptom onset, he insufflated heroin, ingested Xanax, and smoked marijuana, then fell asleep. He awoke around 3 AM lying on the floor next to his bed and noticed flaccid paralysis of both legs and distal arm weakness.

On examination, he was alert and oriented with normal gaze and no facial droop. Handgrip strength was 2/5 bilaterally. He was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Neurologic examination showed 1+ patellar reflexes, bilateral negative plantar responses, and tingling in the lower extremities. He denied headache, loss of consciousness, seizures, or incontinence. His social history included a 2-pack-year smoking history and 2 years of heroin insufflation without a prolonged abstinence period; he had used heroin again 24 hours earlier.

Urine toxicology was positive for opiates, benzodiazepines, and tetrahydrocannabinol. Emergent lumbar and sacral MRI, thoracic CT, and head/neck CT findings were unremarkable. Sagittal noncontrast cervical MRI showed diffuse cord enlargement from C4 to C6 with increased T2 signal in the central gray-white matter. Sagittal noncontrast T1-weighted images revealed an abnormal signal in the same region. Axial T2-weighted images confirmed central gray matter T2 hyperintensity at C5. Axial noncontrast and contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images demonstrated a T1-isointense lesion without enhancement. A lumbar puncture with cytology was nondiagnostic for multiple sclerosis and primary neoplasm. CT angiography of the neck showed no vertebral artery abnormalities.

An 11-year-old Saudi boy with no prior medical history presented with a 5-year history of a right-sided, non-painful facial mass that had progressively enlarged and recurred after multiple interventions. He had undergone prior surgical excision with recurrence, a temporary reduction after intravenous steroids followed by regrowth one year later, and embolization of the right internal maxillary artery without resolution. There were no orbital or oral symptoms, no history of facial trauma or tattooing, and no family history of tumors or hematologic disease.

On examination, a 2 × 3 cm soft, mobile, non-tender mass was noted over the right zygomatic prominence; the overlying skin was hyperpigmented. There was no cervical, axillary, or inguinal lymphadenopathy. Ophthalmologic and dental evaluations were normal.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, normal urea and electrolytes, and normal coagulation profile; serum IgE was elevated at 8977 IU/mL (normal < 200). 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the facial bones demonstrated a 2.6 × 7 × 8 cm hypo- to iso-dense soft-tissue mass in the right buccal region without bone or skin involvement. MRI of the face revealed a heterogeneously hyperintense mass on T2-weighted images and heterogeneous enhancement on postcontrast T1-weighted images, with no intraorbital extension. 

Given the non-specific imaging and persistent nature of the lesion, a transoral biopsy via a sublabial approach was performed.

An 82-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and prior coronary bypass surgery presented with one week of right ear pain and itch. He had long-standing right hearing loss with periodic otorrhea. Examination revealed a retained cotton swab in the right external auditory canal without canal inflammation. On removal under microscopy, a gush of pus emerged through a large central chronic tympanic membrane perforation. He underwent aural toilet and received topical ciprofloxacin. He missed a one-week follow-up. 

One month later, he returned with two weeks of coughing when eating—worse with solids than liquids—and persistent right ear pain. A general practitioner suspected stroke; brain MRI showed no infarct. Neurologic examination revealed deviation of the tongue to the right on protrusion (cranial nerve XII), absent right gag reflex (IX), impaired right soft-palate elevation and right vocal-cord mobility (X), and weakness of the right sternocleidomastoid muscle (XI). Nasoendoscopy showed a smooth bulge in the right postnasal space. Videofluoroscopy demonstrated moderate pharyngeal and oral dysphagia with aspiration on fluids. Chest radiograph was normal. 

Contrast MRI of the head showed a large mass with central necrosis in the right skull base, centered on the petrous bone and clivus, involving the jugular foramen, carotid canal, hypoglossal canal, and nasopharynx. The right jugular bulb and upper right internal jugular vein were not visualized, and there was opacification of the right mastoid air cells.

A 47-year-old woman with hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, seizures, and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis presented from her dialysis session with bleeding from her right upper-arm arteriovenous graft. On arrival, she was febrile to 103.0 °F, hypotensive (74/45 mm Hg), tachycardic (heart rate in the 120s beats/min), tachypneic (respiratory rate 23 breaths/min), and had altered mental status (oriented only to person). She was in septic shock, requiring a norepinephrine infusion, and received vancomycin and cefepime. An arterial catheter and two peripheral IV lines were placed, and she was admitted to the ICU.

In the ICU, she underwent hemodialysis, continued on vancomycin and cefepime, received levetiracetam for seizure prophylaxis, insulin for glycemic control, and up to 4 L/min of oxygen by nasal cannula. Vascular surgery, neurology, nephrology, and infectious disease were consulted. Ultrasound of the arteriovenous graft showed no abscess. Over the next days, her white-blood-cell count rose and her platelet count fell, prompting one platelet transfusion. Three days after collection, blood cultures grew ESBL-producing Escherichia coli in two bottles. Antibiotics were narrowed to meropenem, and daily blood cultures were obtained. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed an echodensity in the right atrium.

A 9-year-old Persian boy presented with a 3-day history of left lower-quadrant abdominal pain and one episode of nonbilious, nonbloody vomiting. He was born by cesarean section without perinatal complications and had no known chronic illnesses. He had two prior hospitalizations (11 months for pneumonia; age 5 for fever and left cervical lymphadenopathy), and chest radiographs at those times showed no diaphragmatic abnormalities.

On examination, his blood pressure was 135/75 mmHg, pulse 75/min, temperature 36.7 °C, respiratory rate 40/min, and SpO₂ 99% on room air. Lung auscultation revealed markedly decreased sounds on the left; the right lung was normal. Heart sounds were louder on the right. The abdomen was soft, nontender, and without palpable masses.

A chest radiograph showed a round lesion with clear borders and an air–fluid level in the left thorax, with rightward shift of the heart and mediastinum. Initial blood tests were unremarkable (WBC 8.8 ×10⁹/L; hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL; platelets 312 ×10⁹/L; electrolytes, renal function, coagulation profile, and inflammatory markers within normal limits).

Chest ultrasound demonstrated a dilated stomach containing echogenic material occupying the left hemithorax. Abdominopelvic ultrasound revealed only mild free fluid in the abdomen and pelvis.

A 57-year-old man presented with progressive shortness of breath over 6 months. He was an ex-smoker (30 pack-year) and had lost weight from 50 kg to 34.5 kg over 6 years. He had experienced three spontaneous pneumothoraces in the past 5 years. His body-mass index was 12.4 kg/m2. Vital signs were normal, and chest auscultation was unremarkable.
