Chest radiography showed upward displacement of the hilar structures. Chest CT demonstrated mild, subpleural, wedge-shaped airspace consolidations confined to the apices of both lungs and overinflation of the lower lobes; there was no lower-lobe fibrosis. The thoracic cage was flattened, with a flat-chest index of 0.50.

Laboratory studies revealed KL-6 214 U/mL, surfactant protein-D 80.4 ng/mL, rheumatoid factor 7 IU/mL, antinuclear antibody <1:40, anti–aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase antibody index <5.0, aldosterone 292 pg/mL, renin activity 1.1 ng/mL/h, adrenaline 9 pg/mL, noradrenaline 923 pg/mL, dopamine 26 pg/mL, TSH 1.135 μIU/mL, and free T4 1.52 ng/dL. Arterial blood gas on room air showed pH 7.350, PaO2 91 Torr, PaCO2 44 Torr, HCO3− 24.3 mmol/L.

Pulmonary function tests showed FVC 1.19 L (30.8%), FEV1 1.19 L (36.6%), FEV1/FVC 100%, FRC 3.8 L (116%), TLC 4.56 L (80.6%), RV 3.38 L (182%), RV/TLC 74.1% (199%), and DLCO 7.58 mL/min/mmHg (54.8%), indicating marked restrictive ventilatory dysfunction with an increased RV/TLC.

Because of mild extremity muscle weakness and severe emaciation, evoked electromyography was performed, showing no neurogenic changes. Myositis was excluded by laboratory data and physical examination. Endocrine causes of emaciation, including hypothyroidism, primary aldosteronism, and pheochromocytoma, were ruled out by normal thyroid function tests and imaging.

On the basis of emaciation, chronic respiratory symptoms, recurrent pneumothorax, upper-lobe–predominant fibrotic lesions, platythorax, and restrictive ventilatory dysfunction with increased RV/TLC, a clinical diagnosis was made.

A 47-year-old woman (G0) was referred with suspected uterine and ovarian tumors, presenting with sudden right lower abdominal pain and fever (38.5 °C) on a background of several years of abdominal distention, with rapid growth over the past 6 months. On examination, there was a giant, soft abdominal mass tender in the right lower quadrant and a protruding umbilicus with bluish-purple discoloration and a 3 × 4 cm subcutaneous hard, painless nodule; there was no umbilical bleeding or discharge. Menstrual history revealed irregular periods and oligomenorrhea without dysmenorrhea or menorrhagia. She had no prior medical or surgical history.

Laboratory studies showed white blood cell count 10,540/ml, hemoglobin 12.5 g/dl, C-reactive protein 4.32 mg/dl, CA125 58.28 U/ml (slightly elevated), CA19-9 12.25 U/ml, CEA 0.4 ng/ml, and LDH 206 U/l. 

Transabdominal ultrasonography demonstrated marked uterine enlargement with two solid hypoechoic tumors (14 cm and 11 cm), two cystic tumors (12 cm and 7 cm), and a large mass containing multiple variable-sized cysts surrounding these lesions; color Doppler showed poor flow. 

Magnetic resonance imaging revealed:
- An umbilical tumor with signal hypointensity on T2-weighted imaging, slight hyperintensity on fat-suppressed T1-weighted imaging, small foci of slight hyperintensity on T2-weighted imaging, hyperintensity on diffusion-weighted and fat-suppressed T1-weighted imaging, and no contrast enhancement.
- Multiple large uterine masses: solid tumors typical of leiomyoma, cystic tumors, and markedly degenerated lesions with cystic and edematous changes showing heterogeneous high signal on both T1- and T2-weighted imaging, all poorly enhanced after gadolinium.
- A 6-cm right ovarian cystic lesion without solid component, containing fluid that was hyperintense on T1 and hypointense on T2, with poor enhancement.

Computed tomography showed no lymphadenopathy or evidence of metastatic disease.

A 50-year-old male farmer presented with an 8-day history of high-grade fever and 4 days of pain in the calf and thigh muscles, followed by 1 day of pedal edema and decreased urine output. He had no rash, cough, jaundice, or urinary symptoms. He had been treated at a local health center with chloroquine, analgesics, and IV fluids for 2 days before transfer for persistent fever and hematuria. On arrival, his pulse was 90/min, blood pressure 130/80 mm Hg; he had bilateral pitting pedal edema and an eschar on the right medial shoulder. The remainder of the systemic examination was unremarkable. Urinalysis showed myoglobinuria. Laboratory studies revealed elevated creatine phosphokinase, deranged renal parameters, and normal liver function tests. Complete blood count was within normal limits with no malarial parasites on smear. ECG showed tall, tented T waves at a rate of 88/min. Chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasound were normal. Blood and urine cultures were sterile. Widal test, leptospira serology, and dengue serology were negative.

A 51-year-old woman presented with cough and shortness of breath that began in the morning after she awoke. The cough was productive of pink sputum, and she was using accessory muscles to breathe. Family members reported that she had been drowsy, confused, and unresponsive for about 30 minutes; afterward she was alert but could not recall the event. A point-of-care blood glucose measurement was 8.5 mmol/L.

Her medical history was notable for resection of a right temporal meningioma 3 years earlier and type 2 diabetes mellitus with a well-controlled HbA1c. Home medications included phenytoin 200 mg twice daily, lamotrigine 200 mg three times daily, escitalopram 10 mg once daily, and metformin/sitagliptin 1000/50 mg twice daily. She had continued to experience seizures despite these therapies.

On examination, her temperature was 37.3 °C, blood pressure 89/47 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 82% on room air. Respiratory examination revealed bilateral crackles to the mid zones. Neurologic examination was unremarkable. 

Arterial blood gas on room air showed pH 7.41, PaO2 48.8 mmHg, PaCO2 35 mmHg, HCO3– 22.5 mmol/L, and a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 232. A chest radiograph demonstrated multiple confluent and patchy air-space opacities diffusely involving both lung fields. ECG showed sinus tachycardia with premature ventricular complexes. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed good global contractility, no regional wall-motion abnormalities, normal left ventricular systolic function, and an ejection fraction of 58–60%.

A 32-year-old woman, G1P0, with a history of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia treated by loop excision and remote spontaneous wound-healing complications after breast reduction, underwent a cesarean delivery at 31 weeks’ gestation for suspected fetal distress. Postoperatively, she received intravenous amoxicillin–clavulanate; her temperature normalized and C-reactive protein (CRP) fell from 170 to 84 mg/L. 

On postpartum day 5, she developed spiking fevers; examination of her lungs, breasts, and Pfannenstiel incision was unrevealing. CRP rose to 321 mg/L, and the white-cell count (WBC) to 27.5×10^9/L. Vaginal, throat, urine, and stool cultures were negative. Serologic tests for toxoplasmosis, syphilis, rubella, cytomegalovirus, and herpes simplex virus were negative. On day 8, despite discontinuation of antibiotics and normal chest radiography and abdominal ultrasound, fevers and elevated CRP persisted.

On day 9, the Pfannenstiel wound developed purulent discharge and peri-incisional erythema. By day 11, a wound culture grew Staphylococcus aureus, and flucloxacillin was started. Although the definitive culture later proved negative and therapy was switched to oral clindamycin on day 17, the wound became more erythematous, with blue-red margins, infiltration, and gaping at the corners. At that time, CRP was 85 mg/L and WBC 17.7×10^9/L. Standard conservative wound care was instituted, and she was discharged on day 19 to home nursing.

On day 23 after delivery, she was readmitted with severe wound pain. CRP was 409 mg/L and WBC 34.1×10^9/L. Examination revealed an expanding ulcer at the Pfannenstiel incision with violaceous-colored borders. A wound biopsy showed epidermal necrosis with edema and bullae and intense granulocytic infiltration in the dermis; there were no signs of vasculitis, and immunofluorescence assay was negative for immune complex vasculitis.

A 49‐year‐old man who works in the oil fields of West Texas presented with a 1‐year history of right knee pain and swelling. His medical history included GERD, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea, obesity, and coccidioidomycosis pneumonia diagnosed 15 months earlier, which was treated with fluconazole for 12 months and then itraconazole for 3 months. His pulmonary symptoms resolved, but right knee pain and swelling persisted.

On examination, the lungs were clear. The right knee had a large effusion, with palpable soft‐tissue fullness in the lateral supra‐ and infra‐patellar regions. He walked with an antalgic gait, and knee motion elicited discomfort from full extension to 110° of flexion. No other joints were involved.

Arthrocentesis of the right knee yielded yellow, hazy fluid with a white‐cell count of 12,579 cells/mm3 (56% neutrophils, 44% monocytes). Radiographs of the right knee showed a large joint effusion without underlying osseous abnormality. MRI of the knee demonstrated a very large effusion containing debris, extensive synovial thickening and enhancement compatible with synovitis, and subcutaneous abscesses superficial to the quadriceps and patellar tendons.

A 51-year-old woman with a history of gastric adenocarcinoma—treated with neoadjuvant FLOT chemotherapy, gastrectomy, and adjuvant FLOT—was found one year later to have metastatic lesions in the liver, pancreas, left adrenal gland, para-aortic lymph nodes, and a lytic bone lesion in the left iliac bone. She received palliative radiotherapy (20 Gy in 4 fractions) to the L4 vertebra for back pain. On follow-up, she appeared ill but was hemodynamically stable (normal vital signs) with an ECOG performance status of 2. Cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable; the abdomen was soft, with a palpable liver and well-healed surgical scars. A peripheral blood smear showed scattered red blood cell fragments (schistocytes) among normal red blood cells. Direct and indirect Coombs tests were negative. Laboratory results: hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL, hematocrit 23.4%, MCV 85 fL, RBC count 2.76 × 10^6/μL, platelets 22.3 × 10^3/μL, total bilirubin 2.4 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL, indirect bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL, haptoglobin 0.0 mg/dL, LDH 1621 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 1669 U/L, PT 19 s, PTT 28.1 s, fibrinogen 208 mg/dL, INR 1.24, creatinine 0.5 mg/dL. Her PLASMIC score was 6 (high).

A 71-year-old man with a history of prediabetes and renal insufficiency presented in early 2021 with one week of blood with wiping and anal pain. He reported three loose stools per day for two weeks, beginning three days after his first dose of the Moderna mRNA-1273 COVID-19 vaccine; his bowel habits were previously normal. On examination, an anal fissure was noted; his pain resolved with topical therapy, but he continued to have occasional rectal bleeding. Eighteen days after the first dose, he received his second vaccine and subsequently developed up to 12 watery bowel movements daily, including four at night. One week later, in the gastroenterology clinic, he denied recent antibiotic use, travel, sick contacts, or other exposures; he used NSAIDs rarely and had no family history of colon cancer or inflammatory bowel disease. Laboratory tests showed a creatinine of 1.22 mg/dL (normal 0.67–1.17), a markedly elevated fecal calprotectin of 2634 mg/kg (normal <50), negative tissue transglutaminase IgA, and negative C. difficile and gastroenteritis PCR panels. Five days after that visit, an urgent colonoscopy demonstrated continuous, edematous, erythematous, granular mucosa in the sigmoid colon, with tortuosity and edema that required a smaller-diameter endoscope to reach the cecum; the terminal ileum appeared normal, and mild edema and erythema extended from the cecum to the descending colon. Biopsies were obtained throughout the colon.

A 4-year-old boy was admitted for evaluation of acute exacerbation of presumed severe asthma. He had a history of four episodes of recurrent respiratory symptoms (one at 10 months, three after age 3) characterized by cough, fever, and wheeze. On admission he reported intermittent cough, wheezing, shortness of breath, orthopnea, fatigue, pallor, and sweating, all worse at night. The parents denied any foreign-body aspiration, weight loss, or trauma. Physical examination showed tachypnea, cyanosis, suprasternal retraction, and prolonged expiratory crackles. Oxygen saturation was 91% on supplemental oxygen. Skin-prick testing was negative, and serum IgE was not elevated. Pulmonary-function testing revealed airway hyperresponsiveness: V75 and V50 were mildly reduced, peak flow was moderately reduced, and there was no reversibility with bronchodilator. Bronchodilators and systemic corticosteroids produced only partial improvement, and each outpatient episode lasted more than 20 days. After admission, flexible bronchoscopy demonstrated tracheal narrowing at the lower trachea without any internal airway lesion. A noncontrast chest CT scan showed no parenchymal lung disease.

A 17-year-old female presented with a palatal gingival mass noted for over 1 year without pain or bleeding. On examination, there was a 5 × 5 mm pedunculated, exophytic nodule located palatally between the upper left central and lateral incisors. The lesion was firm, homogenous in texture, and covered by normal, non-ulcerated mucosa. A periapical radiograph showed no root resorption or alveolar bone loss. There was no history of local trauma, the patient was in good oral hygiene, took no medications, and had no systemic disease. The clinical differential diagnosis included fibroma and peripheral ossifying fibroma, and an excisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia.

A 73-year-old man with a remote history of prostate cancer, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia presented with intermittent vision changes in his right eye. He denied any recent or past head trauma and was not taking antiplatelet or anticoagulant medications. Vital signs were within normal limits. On fundoscopic examination, there was mild bilateral papilledema; the remainder of the neurologic and physical examination was unremarkable.

An unenhanced head CT demonstrated a large, left parietal convexity, heterogeneous hyperdense extra-axial collection with local mass effect on the adjacent brain parenchyma but without midline shift. There were no calvarial fractures, scalp contusions, or subjacent parenchymal edema. The initial differential diagnosis included a chronic walled-off intracranial hemorrhage versus a hemorrhagic extra-axial lesion. Given the atypical presentation for a chronic hemorrhage and the absence of trauma or anticoagulant use, MRI was obtained for further characterization.

MRI of the brain revealed that the left parietal convexity extra-axial lesion was heterogeneous on both T1 (predominantly hyperintense) and T2 (predominantly hypointense) sequences, with minimal internal enhancement on post-contrast T1-weighted images. Susceptibility-weighted imaging showed susceptibility artifacts within the lesion. There was upliftment of the dura along the anterior and posterior margins of the lesion with subtle heterogeneous enhancement suggestive of a dural tail. Dynamic susceptibility contrast perfusion imaging indicated an increased relative cerebral blood volume, although this was considered likely artifactual due to the susceptibility artifacts. Based on these findings, the leading diagnostic consideration was a calcified meningioma; less likely possibilities included a walled-off extra-axial hemorrhage or a metastatic lesion.

A 64-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a four-week history of progressive unsteadiness and ataxia, initially diagnosed as labyrinthitis. Her only past medical history was a total thyroidectomy in 1993 for papillary carcinoma, with subsequent levothyroxine replacement and no residual disease. She had no allergies, occupational exposures, or relevant family history, and she neither smoked nor drank alcohol.

On examination, she was afebrile and disoriented, with marked gait ataxia and horizontal nystagmus; muscle strength, tone, and deep tendon reflexes were normal. Chest, abdominal, and other physical examinations were unremarkable.

Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral parenchymal edema and leptomeningeal and cortical enhancement involving the cingulate gyri and the region of the superior sagittal sinus. Lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure greater than 34 cm H₂O, reactive cytology (lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages, and occasional eosinophils) with no cells detected on automated count, and an elevated protein concentration of 742 mg/L. A staging CT of the chest identified a right upper lobe mass with a satellite nodule. Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme was within the normal range, and EEG showed no epileptiform activity.

Further history obtained from the patient revealed a two-year history of intermittent joint pains responsive to NSAIDs, two episodes of inflammatory eye disease treated with topical steroids, and occasional nosebleeds.

A 74-year-old man with no history of renal disease presented 13 days after two-vessel coronary artery bypass grafting with progressive shortness of breath and orthopnea. He required supplemental oxygen.  
Computed tomography of the chest showed a left pleural effusion, a small pericardial effusion, and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates concerning for pneumonia.  
Laboratory evaluation revealed a serum creatinine of 1.64 mg/dL (baseline 0.8 mg/dL at discharge), a C-reactive protein level of 165 mg/L, a pro–BNP of 589 pg/mL, a white blood cell count of 22 × 10^9/L, a hemoglobin level of 7.2 g/dL, and negative blood cultures.  
He was treated with intravenous furosemide and piperacillin–tazobactam but showed no clinical or laboratory improvement.  
Given the lack of response to diuresis and antibiotics, pulmonology recommended assessment for an autoimmune process.

A 9-year-old Pakistani girl was referred for recurrent pneumonia. She had global developmental delay and psychomotor regression beginning at 15 months of age. Born at term to first-degree consanguineous parents after an uncomplicated pregnancy and vaginal delivery, her early milestones were on time. At 15 months, she developed tip-toe walking and leg aching, then progressively lost the ability to walk, sit, and use her hands; language and social skills regressed thereafter. She later had prolonged seizures, resistant hypertension, gastroesophageal reflux, chronic constipation, obstructive sleep apnea, recurrent urinary and respiratory infections, diaper rash, bed sores, and skin abrasions, with multiple ICU admissions. On examination, blood pressure was elevated; neurologic evaluation showed spastic quadriplegia, increased tendon reflexes, bilateral Babinski signs, absent lower-limb sensation, and preserved pain response in the upper limbs. Other systems were unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including CBC, electrolytes, renal and liver function tests, CRP, procalcitonin, arterial blood gas, urine culture, and CSF analysis, were all within normal limits. EEG showed nonspecific findings. Brain MRI at age 9 demonstrated newly developed generalized supra- and infratentorial atrophy with ventricular dilatation, prominent cortical sulci and extra-axial spaces, T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in deep periventricular white matter, and thinning of the corpus callosum. A previous MRI at age 2½ had been normal.

A 28-year-old man presented with sudden onset of severe neck pain radiating to both shoulders and the right lower limb, associated with numbness over both upper limbs and the right lower limb. He had no history of trauma, anticoagulant use, or systemic symptoms. On initial examination, he was ambulant with localized paravertebral and shoulder tenderness but no midline spinal tenderness; strength and sensation were full in all four limbs, cranial nerve and cerebellar exams were normal, Lhermitte’s sign was positive, and Hoffmann’s sign was negative. Cervical spine radiographs were normal, and he was discharged after analgesia.

He re-presented 2 days later with recurrent neck pain (pain score 8/10), dyspnea, and chest pain, after a fall due to right-sided limb weakness that began 9 hours earlier. He remained continent and had no headache, vision changes, or speech problems. Examination revealed tenderness over the lower cervical and upper thoracic spine; strength was 5/5 in the left limbs and 4/5 in the right upper and lower limbs. A CT scan of the brain and CT aortogram showed no large ischemic stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, or aortic dissection. Seven hours into his ED stay, his neck pain resolved, right upper-limb strength improved, but right lower-limb strength worsened. Neurosurgical assessment showed right C5 and C7 power of 3/5, C6, C8, and T1 power of 4/5, and right lower-limb power of 2/5; left limbs remained 5/5, sensation and proprioception were intact, and there was subtle hyperreflexia. Pulses were normal and systemic examination was unremarkable. The neurosurgery team admitted him to the acute stroke unit with plans for MRI of the brain and whole spine.

A 45‐year‐old woman with a history of hepatic hydatid cysts, gallbladder disease, and total thyroidectomy underwent multiple biliary procedures, including an open cholecystectomy and hydatid cyst excision complicated by a bile leak managed with percutaneous drainage. Because of persistent symptoms, she underwent ERCP with sphincterotomy and biliary stent placement. About 6 hours after ERCP, she developed acute nausea and severe epigastric pain. Two hours later, she noted severe bilateral breast pain accompanied by erythema, tenderness, pitting edema, and peau d’orange changes.  
  
Laboratory studies showed markedly elevated serum amylase (3976 U/L; reference 0–100 U/L) and lipase (1820 U/L; reference 0–60 U/L), with a C‐reactive protein of 21 mg/L (reference <5 mg/L). A contrast‐enhanced CT scan of the abdomen revealed pancreatic enlargement with peripancreatic fat stranding but no necrosis or fluid collections. Given the persistent breast findings, an urgent breast ultrasound was performed, demonstrating diffuse skin thickening, increased echogenicity of the subcutaneous fat, and multiple well‐defined cystic lesions, suggestive of an inflammatory process.

A 36-year-old man from rural Tunisia presented with a 3-month history of progressive headaches and visual disturbances. He denied seizures, vomiting, or fever. On examination he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Ophthalmologic assessment revealed bilateral decreased visual acuity without papilledema; visual fields, ocular alignment, and binocular function were normal. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 11,640 cells/mm3 with a normal eosinophil count, hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, platelets 278,600 cells/mm3, and C-reactive protein 8 mg/L. Serologic testing for hydatidosis was negative. 
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated two well-defined intra-axial occipital lesions, measuring 5 × 5 × 5.5 cm on the left and 7.5 × 8 × 7.5 cm on the right, hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with no gadolinium enhancement or surrounding edema. Thoracoabdominal computed tomography revealed no cystic lesions elsewhere.

A 95-year-old woman with ischaemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 20%), prior TAVR for aortic stenosis, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, mitral regurgitation, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease presented with 2 days of progressive dyspnoea on exertion, leg swelling, orthopnoea, and weight gain. Four months earlier, a subdural haematoma had prompted discontinuation of all heart-failure medications and anticoagulation. In clinic, she was started on furosemide. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed unchanged LVEF of 20% and normally functioning prosthetic valve. ECG showed sinus rhythm with left bundle-branch block. 

On hospital admission: BP 123/87 mmHg, RR 21 breaths/min, SpO₂ 96% on room air, HR 130–160 b.p.m. (irregular), afebrile. Examination revealed bilateral pulmonary rales, jugular venous distention to the mandible at 45°, an irregularly irregular tachycardia, cool extremities, and pitting oedema to the upper thighs. ECG confirmed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. Laboratory tests showed haemoglobin 9.6 g/dL, normal thyroid function, and creatinine 1.73 mg/dL (CrCl 16 mL/min).

A 25-year-old man with known Fine-Lubinsky syndrome presented with two weeks of dyspnea on exertion and bilateral lower extremity swelling. He reported a one-month history of a dry, nonproductive cough. He denied fever, myalgias, chest pain, recent travel, or sick contacts. A prior COVID-19 test was negative. Outpatient chest radiography showed cardiomegaly, prompting referral.

On examination, he was afebrile, breathing nonlaboriously, with blood pressure 106/74 mmHg and heart rate 106 beats/min. Jugular venous distension was noted, and auscultation revealed an S3. His abdomen was distended, and he had trace pitting edema of the lower extremities.

His past medical history was notable for Fine-Lubinsky syndrome, with cranial abnormalities, early auditory problems, intellectual disability, speech impairment, and multiple intracranial fibrous dysplasia resections. Family history included hypertension in both parents and a grandfather with early myocardial infarction and heart failure. He denied smoking, illicit drug use, alcohol use, and had no history of hypertension or diabetes.

Laboratory studies revealed a brain natriuretic peptide of 2878 pg/mL, troponin <0.02 ng/mL, normal thyroid function, ferritin 62 ng/mL, white blood cell count 9.4 × 10^3 cells/cm^3, hemoglobin 15.2 g/dL, and hemoglobin A1c 5.5%. 

Chest radiography showed pulmonary vascular cephalization and cardiomegaly. Chest CT excluded pulmonary embolism but demonstrated a moderate right pleural effusion, interstitial edema, and ascites; there were no coronary calcifications. Electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia without ST-segment changes.

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed severe left ventricular dilation with an ejection fraction below 20% and global hypokinesis; the right ventricle was normal in size with severely reduced systolic function. No significant valvular abnormalities were noted.

Cardiac MRI with gadolinium showed a severely dilated left ventricle (end-diastolic volume index 166 mL/m^2) with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 11% and right ventricular ejection fraction of 22%. Left ventricular wall thickness was normal. There was no delayed enhancement to suggest scarring or infarction, no myocardial iron overload, and normal coronary arterial anatomy. A small patent foramen ovale was visualized.

A 33‐year‐old man with a history of percutaneous closure of a secundum atrial septal defect in 2008 was referred for evaluation of valvular heart disease. A transthoracic echocardiogram performed for a murmur was technically difficult because of mesocardia and revealed grossly normal left ventricular wall motion, moderate posteriorly directed eccentric mitral regurgitation, mild prolapse of the anterior mitral leaflet, mild aortic insufficiency, and an echogenic structure contiguous to the lateral aspect of the tricuspid annulus; the right atrium and ventricle were poorly visualized. The patient reported overall well‐being but experienced fatigue after walking 200–400 meters. An exercise stress test on a standard Bruce protocol lasted 12 minutes 26 seconds, achieving 14.2 METS and 96% of the age‐predicted maximal heart rate; he had no chest pain or ischemic ECG changes. A chest radiograph suggested possible right ventricle on the left side of the chest, raising concern for dextrocardia or congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries. Cardiac CT angiography showed normal origin and course of all coronary vessels without evidence of coronary artery disease. CT evaluation of cardiac structure demonstrated that the right ventricle received blood from the left atrium via the tricuspid valve and ejected into the aorta, while the left ventricle received blood from the right atrium via the mitral valve and ejected into the pulmonary artery; the right ventricle had concentric hypertrophy, with a mid‐septal wall thickness of 9.9 mm.

A 66-year-old woman with hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and migraines but no known coronary artery disease presented with sudden onset of headache and left jaw pain that progressed to central chest pressure with left arm numbness. She denied nausea or diaphoresis and had no prior similar episodes. She lived independently and had no recent infections or travel; she was a non-smoker with a negative family history of premature cardiovascular disease.  

On arrival, her temperature was 97°F, heart rate 90 bpm, blood pressure 133/81 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. The cardiovascular and pulmonary examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a D-dimer of 394 ng/mL (normal <500) and a Troponin-T of 0.33 ng/mL (normal <0.01). The initial ECG demonstrated normal sinus rhythm with 1 mm ST-segment elevations in leads V1, V2, and aVR.  

She received aspirin, high-intensity statin therapy, sublingual nitroglycerine—which relieved her chest pain—and unfractionated heparin. Despite resolution of pain, persistent ECG changes and troponin elevation prompted emergent coronary angiography, which revealed only minimal luminal irregularities and markedly tortuous coronary arteries. During an attempted ventriculogram, she experienced transient ventricular fibrillation requiring defibrillation, so further invasive imaging was deferred.  

A transthoracic echocardiogram showed an ejection fraction of 41% with regional wall motion abnormalities affecting the mid anteroseptum, mid inferoseptum, and apical septum, while basal segments were preserved.

A 15-year-old male was admitted after a motor vehicle crash with right flank impact. He reported right flank pain. On examination, he was hemodynamically stable (BP 110/60 mm Hg; HR 93 bpm), with bruises and minor abrasions on the right flank. A Foley catheter yielded no gross hematuria. Laboratory studies showed a WBC count of 20,480/mL; red-cell count, hemoglobin, hematocrit, platelets, BUN, creatinine, electrolytes, and urinalysis were within normal limits. Screening of family members was negative for kidney disease. 

Renal ultrasound demonstrated disruption of the right upper-pole structures with intraparenchymal and subcapsular hematoma. The remainder of the right kidney was heterogeneous and hypoechoic, with multiple sac-like structures having calcified walls; no fluid–fluid levels were noted. 

Unenhanced and contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a hemorrhagic contusion, subcapsular hematoma, and a laceration of the upper pole of the right kidney without collecting-system involvement. The CT also showed hypo-dense regions in the mid-kidney in all phases, suspected by the radiologist to represent segmental infarctions without active bleeding. The case was initially classified as a Grade IV right renal injury (AAST scale), but the urologist noted discordance between the CT findings and the clinical and laboratory data and requested further radiology review.

An 82-year-old woman with metastatic melanoma developed locoregional recurrence and was treated with nivolumab followed by combined nivolumab and ipilimumab. After two cycles of combination therapy, she was admitted with extreme fatigue and grade 3 diarrhea. Initial labs showed: potassium 2.0 mmol/L, bicarbonate 16 mmol/L, phosphate 0.48 mmol/L, creatinine 2.7 mg/dL (baseline 0.88 mg/dL), and CRP 114 mg/L. Urinalysis revealed potassium wasting (79 mmol/g creatinine), pH 7.1, glucosuria, and tubular proteinuria. Abdominal CT and colonoscopy confirmed diverticulitis with nonspecific grade 3 colitis. Immunotherapy was discontinued; she received IV fluids, high-dose potassium supplements, and corticosteroids, with normalization of creatinine but persistent electrolyte disturbances. Infliximab and then vedolizumab were administered for refractory colitis; diarrhea improved, but high potassium supplementation remained necessary. Three months later she was discharged on oral potassium and spironolactone. Five days later, she was readmitted with severe symptomatic hypokalemia (2.3 mmol/L) and low bicarbonate (14 mmol/L), and continued to demonstrate urinary potassium loss and metabolic acidosis.

A 62-year-old woman was evaluated for worsening breathlessness in early 2018. Her medical history included osteoarthritis, asthma, type II diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia (statin intolerance), junctional tachycardia, and multiple percutaneous coronary interventions for non-ST-elevation myocardial infarctions: a drug-eluting stent to the circumflex artery in 2011; three drug-eluting stents to the right coronary artery later in 2011; balloon angioplasty to the right coronary artery in June 2014; and a 3.0 mm × 38 mm stent to the ostial right coronary artery in September 2014. A transthoracic echocardiogram performed as an outpatient showed a new, discrete, calcified, round mass measuring approximately 0.9 × 0.7 cm arising from the right coronary sinus in the aortic root. There was no aortic stenosis and only mild central aortic regurgitation. A 12-lead ECG showed inferior Q waves unchanged from 2014. A transoesophageal echocardiogram confirmed a 1.0 × 0.7 cm calcified, fixed mass attached to the anterior wall of the aorta, arising from the right coronary sinus abutting the sinotubular junction and lying distal to the aortic valve leaflets without impairing leaflet mobility.

A 27-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after a fall from a bicycle. He has a known history of surgically corrected craniosynostosis deformities, including underdeveloped midface, widely spaced eyes, and a high forehead. He also reports a history of multiple craniofacial surgeries in childhood and scoliosis.

On examination, vital signs were normal. There were no focal neurologic deficits. The craniofacial appearance included maxillary hypoplasia with a pronounced underbite and overlapping teeth suggestive of prognathism; the hands and feet showed broad thumbs and great toes but no syndactyly.

An emergent noncontrast CT scan of the head showed:
- No acute intracranial hemorrhage or fracture.
- Absence of the coronal and sagittal sutures; faint visualization of the lambdoid sutures.
- Hypoplastic maxilla with underbite and prognathism.
- Nonvisualization of the jugular foramina.
- An anomalous venous channel extending from the left sigmoid sinus through the temporal bone near the left temporomandibular joint.
- A diminutive posterior fossa with downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils below the foramen magnum and effacement of the prepontine cistern and cisterna magna.
- Enlargement of the ventricular system consistent with mild obstructive hydrocephalus, likely at the level of the foramina of Luschka.

A 72-year-old Japanese man with a history of periodontal disease and benign prostatic hyperplasia presented with acute disturbance of consciousness. He was febrile to 38.2°C, agitated, and responded with incoherent speech. His Glasgow Coma Scale score was E4V4M6. Neurological examination showed cerebellar ataxia, sensory aphasia, and bilateral asterixis; there were no meningeal signs.

Laboratory studies revealed blood urea nitrogen 88.2 mg/dL, creatinine 2.09 mg/dL, and D-dimer 7.6 mg/L; other coagulation parameters were normal. Noncontrast head CT and brain MRI showed no hemorrhage, infarction, or focal lesions. Lumbar puncture demonstrated opening pressure of 26 cmH2O; CSF analysis revealed 88 leukocytes/mm3 (85 mononuclear), protein 105 mg/dL, and glucose 76 mg/dL (serum 132 mg/dL).

Given the acute febrile encephalopathy, sensory aphasia, and CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis, empirical intravenous acyclovir was started for presumed herpes simplex encephalitis.

A 44-year-old man with a 5-year history of diabetes mellitus was transferred to the Emergency Department with painful swelling of the upper cervical region and progressive motor weakness. He reported multiple acupuncture treatments for nuchal pain in a traditional oriental hospital.  
On arrival, his temperature was 38.3 °C. Physical examination revealed a tender, swollen upper cervical area. Neurologic examination showed paraparesis (grade 3/5 in the upper extremities and grade 2/5 in the lower extremities) and bilateral extensor plantar responses.  
Laboratory studies demonstrated a white-blood-cell count of 12 800/mL, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 46 mm/hr, and a C-reactive protein level of 19.8 mg/dL.  
Computed tomography of the cervical spine revealed complete destruction of the C2 vertebral body with multiple areas of “punched-out” bone resorption. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging showed extensive retropharyngeal and spinal epidural collections at the upper cervical level, destruction of the C2 body, and severe spinal cord compression.  
With a presumed diagnosis of cervical vertebral osteomyelitis and cord compression, the patient underwent emergency anterior and posterior surgical drainage and decompression under general anesthesia.

A 52‐year‐old man with no significant medical history presented with a 2-week history of an intensely pruritic, diffuse rash that began on his upper extremities and spread to his trunk. Over‐the‐counter topical steroids provided minimal relief, and he reported no recent use of new medications. He subsequently developed fever, malaise, and shortness of breath and was tested for COVID-19, HIV, and syphilis; results were positive for COVID-19 and negative for HIV and syphilis. 

On dermatologic examination, there were diffuse salmon-pink papules and plaques with overlying white scales on the trunk, groin, and upper and lower extremities, punctate scaly papules with erythema on the palms, and koebnerization at a prior surgical site. A 4-mm punch biopsy of the left lower abdomen showed psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia, hypogranulosis, and areas of confluent parakeratosis; no intraepidermal neutrophils or eosinophils were seen, and there was a mild perivascular mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate. A PAS silver stain was negative for fungal organisms, and no plasma cell infiltrates were observed.

A 67-year-old man with no known history of immunodeficiency presented with a wet cough. He was afebrile, had no oxygen desaturation, and physical examination revealed extensive white plaques on the oral mucosa. A chest radiograph showed a cavitary lesion in the right upper lung field. Chest computed tomography demonstrated a 40 mm cavitary lesion in the anterior segment of the right upper lobe, surrounded by nodular, granular, and ground-glass opacities. Laboratory studies revealed a CD4+ T-lymphocyte count of 5 cells/mm3 and a positive HIV screening test. Additional blood tests were negative, including an interferon-γ release assay, anti–glycopeptidolipid-core IgA antibody for Mycobacterium avium complex, (1,3)-β-D-glucan, Aspergillus galactomannan antigen, and Aspergillus IgG antibody. A bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy and bronchial lavage of the right upper lobe anterior segment was performed.

A 74-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of dry cough and dyspnea of three weeks’ duration that had persisted since late October. Two weeks before referral, she was given antibiotics by her family physician without improvement. Her medical history included hypertension and allergic rhinitis; she took antihypertensive medications, had no known drug or food allergies, and was a lifelong never-smoker. She lived in a 40-year-old wooden house and used quilts.

On examination, temperature was 36.4 °C, respirations 18/min, and oxygen saturation 88% on room air. Cardiovascular examination was unremarkable, and the lungs were clear to auscultation. Laboratory testing showed a white blood cell count of 8400/μL (61.9% neutrophils, 25.6% lymphocytes, 5.1% eosinophils), a C-reactive protein level of 8.4 mg/dL, and a Krebs-von-den-Lungen-6 (KL-6) level of 536 U/mL; surfactant protein-D was normal at 89.8 ng/mL. Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral ground-glass opacities. High-resolution CT of the chest revealed diffuse, bilateral, nonsegmental ground-glass opacities without centrilobular nodules.

Bronchoscopy performed on hospital day 4 yielded bronchoalveolar lavage fluid with 3% neutrophils, 75% lymphocytes, and 20% eosinophils; the CD4/CD8 ratio was 9.48. Over the next several days of hospitalization, her symptoms, oxygenation, and imaging findings improved spontaneously.

A 64-year-old previously healthy Asian woman presented with a 4-day history of fever, painful ankle arthralgia, a painless red eye on the left, and multiple tender red skin lesions. The lesions measured 1–3 cm in width; were irregularly shaped, palpable, non-scaly, erythematous plaques over the dorsal aspects of her knees, elbows, and shins. There was no proximal muscle weakness or periorbital purpura. Vital signs showed fever; the rest of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 117 mm at 1 hour, C-reactive protein of 168 mg/dL, white-cell count of 12.5×10^3/µL with 67% neutrophils, and a normal creatine phosphokinase of 72 U/L. A septic screen was negative. She was started empirically on intravenous co-amoxiclav and oral ciprofloxacin. Further history elicited that 12 years earlier she had a similar febrile rash treated in hospital, and 5 years earlier she had biopsy-proven erythema nodosum that resolved without sequelae.

A 37-year-old Caucasian man with known sickle cell/β+ thalassemia presented with worsening jaundice after stopping his regular exchange transfusions and declining hydroxycarbamide. He was in good general condition. On examination, he had marked scleral and skin jaundice and a non-tender liver palpable 4 cm below the costal margin; all other findings were normal. His history included splenectomy at age 13, cholecystectomy, right shin osteomyelitis, and bilateral avascular necrosis of the hips. Over the prior two years, he had two episodes of painless cholestasis when his hemoglobin S exceeded 30% during periods of nonadherence; both resolved with exchange transfusions and hydroxycarbamide. Laboratory studies showed total bilirubin 46.8 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 18.68 mg/dL, WBC 26,400/μL, hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL, reticulocytes 28.2%, HPLC with HbS 74.5%, HbF 9.4%, HbA 26.9%, AST 303 U/mL, ALT 108 U/mL, ALP 150 U/mL, LDH 830 U/mL, PT 14.9 sec (INR 1.4), APTT 38.9 sec, and ferritin 350 ng/dL. Workup for viral hepatitis, cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, biliary obstruction, autoimmune liver disease, Wilson’s disease, and Gilbert’s syndrome was negative. Abdominal MRI demonstrated intrahepatic bile duct dilatation.

A 52-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with 2 months of reduced speech and decreased verbal output, which worsened over the past month. She reported slowness in daily activities, anorexia, and an approximately 10-kg weight loss; she denied fever, headache, vomiting, seizures, visual changes, or trauma. 

On examination, she was alert and oriented (GCS 15). Cranial nerve testing revealed mild left eyelid ptosis, right upper-motor-neuron facial palsy with loss of the right nasolabial fold and facial asymmetry, and decreased sensation over the right face. Motor strength and sensation elsewhere were intact, and cerebellar testing showed slight dysdiadochokinesia of the left upper limb.

Contrast CT of the brain demonstrated ill-defined hypodensities in the right posterior parietal and left frontoparietal white matter without focal enhancement, suggestive of edema. Subsequent MRI of the brain showed multiple well-defined intra-axial lesions in the left high frontal parasagittal region, bilateral parietal regions, and right basal ganglia (including the posterior limb of the internal capsule and thalamus). The lesions were hypointense on T1, heterogeneously hyper- and hypointense on T2, not suppressed on FLAIR, and exhibited peripheral rim enhancement on post-contrast T1 with rim diffusion restriction on DWI/ADC. Several lesions contained enhancing mural nodules. 

Without a known immunocompromised state, the initial impression was multiple cerebral metastases. Differential diagnosis included multicentric glioblastoma and infection.

A 64-year-old Japanese woman with a 10-year history of generalized anxiety disorder treated intermittently with alprazolam and haloperidol presented with new-onset psychotic symptoms. In March of the 11th year after her initial visit, she experienced dizziness without neck pain, followed by the rapid emergence of the belief that others were recounting her past failures. She reported auditory hallucinations, insomnia, and persistent delusional thoughts but denied mood swings or psychomotor agitation. 

Her medical history was notable for Hashimoto’s thyroiditis diagnosed at age 48, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. At age 54 she had palpitations, sweating, anxiety, and sleep disturbance, but normal thyroid function tests (TSH 1.8 μIU/mL, fT4 1.25 ng/dL) and elevated antimicrosomal antibody titers. Over the first five years of follow-up she had five episodes of psychosis lasting 1–3 months, each treated with haloperidol; thyroid function was normal after the fifth episode.

On current evaluation, she was alert, with a palpable small goiter and blood pressure of 130/90 mmHg. Laboratory studies showed TSH 0.028 μIU/mL (normal 0.4–4.0), fT3 2.85 pg/mL (2.5–4.3), fT4 1.7 ng/dL (0.8–1.9), CRP 0.1 mg/dL (<0.3), antimicrosomal antibody titer 1600 (<100), antithyroglobulin antibody 6400 (<100), anti-Tg 40.5 U/mL (<0.3), anti-TPO 78 IU/mL (<16), and TSH receptor antibody 15.3% (<20). Under an unrestricted-iodine diet, radioactive iodine uptake was 1.8% at 1 hour and 2.2% at 1.5 hours. Ultrasonography demonstrated a diffuse goiter and a left lower parathyroid cyst. Brain CT was normal.

A 34-year-old man reported floaters and blurred vision for 3 weeks. He was initially diagnosed with uveitis and treated with topical dexamethasone followed by loteprednol. Two weeks later at our center, his best-corrected visual acuity was 0.8 in the right eye and 1.0 in the left; intraocular pressures were 13 mmHg and 18 mmHg, respectively. Examination of the right eye showed no anterior-chamber cells or flare but revealed cells and mild turbidity in the anterior vitreous. The left eye was normal. Funduscopic examination of the right eye demonstrated “snow banking” and vitreous opacities in the inferior periphery. Macular OCT images were normal. Fluorescein angiography showed optic-disc hyperfluorescence and peripheral vascular leakage in the right eye.

Possible infectious causes of intermediate uveitis (tuberculosis, Borrelia burgdorferi, Bartonella henselae, syphilis, and toxocariasis) were ruled out. Consultations in neurology, rheumatology, and chest disease excluded noninfectious systemic causes (including sarcoidosis, multiple sclerosis, inflammatory bowel disease, lymphoma, tubulointerstitial nephritis and uveitis syndrome, and Sjögren’s syndrome). With a diagnosis of pars planitis, he received three sub-Tenon injections of triamcinolone and continued topical steroids without improvement.

Systemic cyclosporine was started but discontinued due to fatigue and vomiting, and therapy was switched to subcutaneous adalimumab (80 mg loading, then 40 mg every 2 weeks). In the fifth month of adalimumab treatment, a single depigmented patch appeared on his lower jaw. On examination, visual acuity was 1.0 in both eyes; both anterior chambers were quiet, with sparse vitreous cells and minimal peripheral leakage on fluorescein angiography. Reassessment for Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada syndrome revealed no ocular or systemic findings. Complete blood count and biochemistry were within normal limits, and repeat systemic evaluations found no underlying pathology. The dermatology service recommended continuation of adalimumab and initiation of topical tacrolimus ointment. At a 3-month follow-up, the lesion had not progressed, and both therapies were continued.

A 51-year-old Japanese woman with no prior medical history and no coronary risk factors presented to the emergency department with the sudden onset of anterior chest pain while shopping. On arrival, her blood pressure was 192/100 mm Hg and her pulse was 64 beats/min and regular. A 12-lead electrocardiogram demonstrated ST-segment elevation in leads V2 through V5. Transthoracic echocardiography showed akinesis of the left ventricular apex with preserved basal contraction. Laboratory studies revealed a white-blood-cell count of 10 480 /μL and a positive troponin T assay. 

Given her presentation—a postmenopausal woman with chest pain, ST-segment elevation, and apical wall-motion abnormality—left ventricular apical ballooning syndrome was initially suspected. Emergency left ventriculography confirmed apical akinesis with basal hyperkinesis, consistent with that diagnosis. Subsequent coronary angiography showed a normal right coronary artery and left circumflex artery, but the distal portion of the left anterior descending artery appeared markedly narrowed, “like a withered branch.” To evaluate for possible vasospasm, 3 mg of isosorbide dinitrate was injected directly into the left coronary artery, but there was no change in the LAD appearance. At that time, her chest pain had nearly resolved and vital signs had stabilized, and the procedure was concluded.

A 69-year-old man was admitted with abrupt onset of bilateral lower-limb paraplegia, a clearly defined sensory level at L1, and urinary incontinence that developed over a few hours. His medical history included benign prostatic hyperplasia, hypertension treated with perindopril and indapamide, and irregular low-dose aspirin use. On examination, he was alert and oriented with normal vital signs, speech, and funduscopic findings. Motor testing revealed 0/5 strength in both lower limbs and 5/5 in the upper limbs. He had loss of all sensory modalities below L1, absent deep tendon and plantar reflexes in the lower limbs, and normal reflexes in the upper limbs. There were no cerebellar, extrapyramidal, or cranial-nerve abnormalities. 

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 26,900/μL (90.9% neutrophils), C-reactive protein of 71.3 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 60 mm/h. Liver and renal function tests, electrolytes, and urinalysis were normal. MRI of the entire spine with gadolinium demonstrated T2 hyperintense signal changes at the T10–T12 levels without any compressive lesion. He received a 5-day course of intravenous methylprednisolone without clinical improvement.

CSF analysis revealed turbid fluid with 30 WBCs/μL (95% neutrophils), 2760 RBCs, glucose 63 mg/dL, protein 67 mg/dL, IgG 5.22 mg/dL with a normal IgG index, and no malignant cells. Chest CT excluded tuberculosis, and GeneXpert PCR on CSF was negative. Immunologic testing showed negative anti-aquaporin-4 IgG and anti-myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein autoantibodies. Electrophoresis demonstrated positive oligoclonal bands consistent with systemic inflammation. The patient reported consumption of unpasteurized dairy products, so a real-time PCR for Brucella species was performed.

A 26-year-old man presented with a one-month history of gradually worsening pain and swelling in the right calf. Two months earlier, he had undergone external fixation and vascular repair of a left tibial open fracture, followed by a rotational flap; postoperative prophylaxis included rivaroxaban. Three weeks postoperatively, he had a flap debridement and resumed rivaroxaban. Two months later, he experienced mild posterior calf pain that improved with elevation and was treated for presumed cellulitis after Doppler ultrasound showed patent vessels and minimal soft-tissue edema. Two weeks after that, the pain and swelling progressed despite conventional therapy. On examination, vital signs were normal. The right calf was uniformly swollen, warm, and tender without discoloration; distal pulses were present. Laboratory studies showed normal CBC, renal and liver function, and bleeding time; activated partial thromboplastin time was prolonged at 41.6 s (reference, 23–32 s). Ultrasound of the right calf revealed a well-localized fluid collection beneath the gastrocnemius muscle; Doppler imaging showed no vascular abnormality or leak.

A 63-year-old man from urban Cali, Colombia, who underwent orthotopic liver transplantation 11 years earlier for nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, presented with a 2-month history of progressive severe myalgia, extremity weakness, persistent fatigue, and mild dyspnea. Two weeks before admission, he noted jaundice and dark urine. His medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, hyperlipidemia, and obesity. He was prescribed cyclosporine and mycophenolate but admitted poor adherence. 

On examination, he was disoriented and somnolent. Vital signs: temperature 36.3°C, blood pressure 150/100 mmHg, pulse 84 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min. Laboratory tests showed: 
• Leukocyte count 18,990/µL (86.5% neutrophils)  
• Hemoglobin 16.9 g/dL  
• Platelets 268,000/µL  
• C-reactive protein 0.64 mg/dL  
• AST 999 U/L, ALT 511 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 53 U/L  
• Creatine phosphokinase 10,302 U/L  

Abdominal ultrasonography, Doppler ultrasound, and MR cholangiography were normal. Brain MRI demonstrated nonspecific frontal subcortical white-matter hyperintensities, and lumbar puncture was unremarkable. A transjugular hepatic biopsy showed no evidence of graft rejection. Cultures were obtained, and urine and blood cultures grew Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli, both sensitive to ceftriaxone.

An 18-year-old Iranian woman presented with multiple purple nodules on her proximal lower limbs that first appeared approximately 2 years ago after trauma and fracture of her left elbow. She had not had a previous diagnosis and this was her first consultation for these lesions. 

On examination, there were mobile purple nodules measuring 0.5–1.5 cm in diameter on the proximal lower limbs, each with a positive dimple sign. Inspection revealed abnormal finger shape. The skin was hyperextensible and fragile, and wide atrophic scars were noted on the upper limbs. Joints were hypermobile, especially in the fingers, with Swan-neck deformities. Additional findings included nodules on the knee, striae alba on the legs, and piezogenic papules on the heels.

Her history was notable for onset at puberty of skin hyperextensibility, joint hypermobility, skin fragility, and easy bruising. She had xerosis and atopic dermatitis since infancy and was diagnosed with asthma 5 years ago, treated with inhaled corticosteroids for 2 years, which were discontinued 1 year before presentation. She reported no cardiovascular, ophthalmic, skeletal, or gastrointestinal disorders, and family history was noncontributory.

Transthoracic echocardiography was normal, and ophthalmologic examination revealed no abnormalities. A skin-nodule biopsy showed fibrohistiocytic proliferation, acanthotic epidermis, and elongated rete ridges, findings suggestive of dermatofibroma.

A 35-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of right-sided hemifacial flushing and sweating, occurring during exertion of more than one hour. She reported no trauma, no surgeries or invasive procedures, no smoking, and no systemic symptoms such as cough, weight loss, or appetite changes. Her past medical, family, and social histories were unremarkable.

On examination at rest, vital signs were normal. General and skin examinations were unremarkable. Neurological examination—including higher mental function, cranial nerves, motor and sensory systems, deep tendon reflexes, coordination, and pupillary responses—was entirely normal; specifically, there were no signs of Horner syndrome.

The patient then exercised for over an hour and returned immediately for re-examination. Post-exercise, she demonstrated marked right-sided facial and upper neck erythema accompanied by sweating, with no changes on the left side.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and cervicothoracic spine was normal. Computed tomography of the chest, including the thoracic sympathetic chain, was also normal.

A 15-year-old girl with a 6-month history of recurrent acute and chronic pancreatitis, most recently complicated by infected walled-off pancreatic necrosis, was treated with 14 days of broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics after admission for high-spiking fever and a C-reactive protein level of 600 mg/L. Three days after her fever resolved, she noted sudden, painless loss of vision in her left eye. She denied eye pain, floaters, or flashes and had no prior visual pathology. Visual acuity was 1/60 in the left eye and 6/6 in the right eye. An urgent ophthalmology evaluation included fundoscopy and optical coherence tomography (OCT). Findings in the left eye included blurred disc margins, macular edema with exudates, multiple retinal nerve fiber layer hemorrhages with interspersed cotton wool spots predominantly in the peripapillary and macular regions, and well-demarcated areas of retinal whitening between vessels (Purtscher flecken). OCT showed central macular thickness >700 µm with multiple exudates.

An 85-year-old man presented with 4 hours of typical, squeezing chest pain associated with diaphoresis and nausea. Over the preceding 3 days, he had high fever, dyspnea, sore throat, and fatigue. He denied diabetes or hypertension and reported contact with a relative who tested positive for SARS-CoV-2.  
On examination, blood pressure was 130/90 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, heart rate 104 bpm, temperature 39 °C, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air (increasing to 99% with 6 L/min by mask). Pulmonary auscultation revealed coarse rales bilaterally; other findings were normal.  
Initial ECG during pain showed nonspecific ST–T changes in leads V2–V5. After sublingual nitrate, chest pain resolved and ECG revealed biphasic T-wave inversions and minimal ST elevation in V2–V3. A pre-transfer, pain-free ECG demonstrated deeply inverted T waves in V2–V4.  
Laboratory studies showed leukopenia (3.88×10^3/μl) with neutrophilia (89.4%) and lymphopenia (3.6%), thrombocytopenia (102×10^3/μl), elevated AST (80.3 U/L), ALT (44.4 U/L), and CK-MB (10.4 ng/mL); renal function was normal. The GRACE score was 159 and the CRUSADE bleeding score 37.  
Chest X-ray demonstrated persistent and new consolidations in the left apical, middle, and lower zones and the right lower peripheral region. Chest CT revealed bilateral diffuse consolidation with multifocal ground-glass opacities and crazy-paving patterns. A SARS-CoV-2 rapid immunochromatographic test and an initial nasopharyngeal RT-PCR assay were both negative.

A 51-year-old man presented with acute painful visual loss in his left eye of 3 days’ duration. His best-corrected distance visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and hand motions in the left eye. Ocular movements were full bilaterally. The anterior segment examination was unremarkable in both eyes. Fundus examination of the left eye showed optic nerve head swelling, choroidal bulging, multiple patches of subretinal fluid accumulation, and retinal pigment epithelial corrugations; the right eye was normal. Optical coherence tomography of the left eye revealed mild retinal pigment epithelial and choroidal bulging, hyper-reflectivity with back shadowing, subretinal and intraretinal fluid, and mild retinal thickening. Indocyanine green angiography demonstrated a geographic area of macular hypocyanescence, and blue-autofluorescence showed a speckled autofluorescence pattern at the macula. B-scan ultrasonography revealed optic nerve enlargement. Fluorescein angiography disclosed optic nerve–head vascular leakage and a geographic patchy hypofluorescent area with speckled hyperfluorescent margins measuring approximately three disc diameters. Orbital and brain MRI with gadolinium enhancement showed a retrobulbar nodular mass at the junction of the optic nerve and sclera. An oncology consultation yielded no remarkable findings.

A 45-year-old woman from Mexico presented with icteric sclerae, headache, and confusion. One month earlier, she had acute hepatitis A in Mexico with full recovery on supportive care. On arrival, her vital signs were normal. Examination showed altered mentation, icteric sclerae, jaundice, and asterixis. Laboratory studies revealed an ALT of 2869 U/L, AST 1469 U/L, total bilirubin 15.1 mg/dL (direct 6.2 mg/dL), INR 1.6, and ammonia 55 μmol/L; her MELD score was 22. Further evaluation showed ferritin 1657 ng/mL and IgG 2580 mg/dL. ANA, antimitochondrial antibody, antismooth muscle antibody, P-ANCA, C-ANCA, and anti–liver-kidney microsomal type 1 antibody were negative. Ceruloplasmin and alpha-1 antitrypsin levels were normal. Viral serologies revealed anti-HAV IgM positive; HEV IgG and IgM were positive but HEV RNA was undetectable. She denied use of herbal or alternative medicines. Abdominal ultrasound and CT scan showed no significant abnormalities.

A 43-year-old man was evaluated for gait unsteadiness and frequent falls that had insidiously begun one year earlier and progressively worsened. His history was notable for chronic diarrhea and developmental delay resulting in intellectual disability; he had lived independently prior to the onset of these neurologic symptoms.  

On examination, he had macrocephaly, turricephaly, and multiple eyelid xanthelasmas. Musculoskeletal examination revealed bilateral pes cavus and a soft‐tissue mass at the left Achilles tendon. Neurologic examination showed an unsteady paraparetic gait; lower extremities had mild weakness (Medical Research Council grade 4/5), spasticity (Ashworth 1+/4), and bilateral hyperreflexia. There were no overt cerebellar signs.  

Brain MRI demonstrated diffuse cerebellar atrophy with fourth‐ventricle dilatation; symmetric T2‐weighted and FLAIR hyperintensity of the dentate nuclei and cerebellar white matter with adjacent calcifications; thinning and hyperintensity of the superior cerebellar peduncles; and subtle pyramidal tract hyperintensity.  

Neck Angio-CT and carotid Doppler ultrasound revealed a lipid‐rich atherosclerotic plaque at the right carotid bulb causing 65–70% stenosis by NASCET criteria (peak systolic velocity 190 cm/s, diastolic 95 cm/s).  

Ultrasound of both Achilles tendons showed marked enlargement and smooth hypoechoic intrafibrillar infiltration (anteroposterior diameters of 21 mm on the right and 30 mm on the left). MRI of the Achilles tendons confirmed fusiform thickening (craniocaudal lengths 12 cm right, 10 cm left) with diffuse low-intensity infiltration, well-defined margins, and no adjacent soft-tissue invasion.

An 82-year-old man was referred for evaluation of an anterior mediastinal mass. Eleven years earlier, he had been diagnosed with IgG4-related disease on the basis of autoimmune pancreatitis and had been maintained on oral steroids. At that time, chest CT revealed a 2.5-cm well-defined homogeneous mass in the anterior mediastinum that decreased to 2 cm after steroid therapy. On current evaluation, chest CT showed regrowth of the mass to 3 cm, and PET–CT demonstrated increased uptake (SUV max 3.6) in the lesion. Concurrent peripancreatic lymphadenopathy with FDG uptake was also noted five months prior, prompting an increase in oral steroids from 2.5 to 10 mg/day. The mediastinal mass was suspected to be an encapsulated thymoma because of its lobulated shape, degree of fluorodeoxyglucose accumulation, response to steroids, moderate enhancement on contrast CT, and gradual enlargement. The patient was asymptomatic, and physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed an elevated serum IgG4 level of 715 mg/dL and soluble interleukin-2 receptor level of 604 U/mL; C-reactive protein and anti-acetylcholine-receptor antibody were within normal limits. Given the concern for thymoma, surgical resection by video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery was planned.

A 17-year-old adolescent girl with obesity presented with 2 days of right-sided abdominal pain. Her vital signs were stable. On examination, she had right upper quadrant tenderness without peritoneal signs. Initial laboratory studies showed aspartate aminotransferase 272 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 536 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 272 U/L, total bilirubin 3.4 mg/dL (direct 2.7 mg/dL), international normalized ratio 1.0, and lipase 46 U/L. Abdominal ultrasound revealed gallstones without cholecystitis, biliary dilation, or choledocholithiasis. She received supportive treatment and underwent cholecystectomy within a week. An abnormal intraoperative cholangiogram prompted endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with clearance of obstructive material from her common bile duct. Pathology of the gallbladder showed eosinophilic cholecystitis.

One month later, she remained asymptomatic but still had elevated liver biochemistries. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated elevated liver stiffness (2.86 kPa), normal hepatic fat fraction (3.29%), and mild intrahepatic ductal irregularities without beading, stenoses, or residual filling defects. A broad serologic workup was negative, including viral hepatitis panel; antinuclear, antimitochondrial, and anti–smooth muscle antibodies; liver-kidney microsomal antibody; celiac serologies; parietal cell antibody; and soluble liver antigen antibodies. Liver biopsy showed mild-to-moderate mixed portal inflammation, normal bile ducts without ductopenia, minimal reactive changes, no steatosis, fibrosis, or interface hepatitis, and mild sinusoidal dilation.

She was lost to follow-up and returned three years later when she became pregnant. During her first pregnancy, liver‐test elevations flared, and pregnancy ended in an incomplete abortion. In her second pregnancy she again had cholestatic liver‐test elevations and was referred to hepatology in the second trimester with a working diagnosis of intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. Repeat magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography revealed two segmental areas of intrahepatic ductal dilation suspicious for strictures. Repeat liver biopsy was concerning for obstruction but could not rule out early primary sclerosing cholangitis. An ERCP showed no evidence of primary sclerosing cholangitis but revealed a persistent filling defect in a left intrahepatic duct compatible with an intrahepatic stone. The stone was located in a tortuous duct and could not be removed endoscopically. After multidisciplinary discussion, conservative management was recommended.

A 53-year-old man with a history of a small restrictive muscular ventricular septal defect, a bicuspid aortic valve (right–left coronary cusp type), and percutaneous stent placement for coarctation of the aorta in 2016 presented with several weeks of fatigue, night sweats, and chills. On examination, he was febrile (40°C), blood pressure was 153/78 mm Hg, and heart rate was 106 b.p.m.; a known systolic murmur was noted. The ECG showed sinus tachycardia with first-degree atrioventricular block. Laboratory studies revealed a leucocyte count of 11.1 × 10^9 /L, C-reactive protein of 66 mg/L, and haemoglobin of 8.2 mmol/L. Blood cultures were obtained, and intravenous ceftriaxone was started for presumed endocarditis. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no evidence of endocarditis. Transoesophageal echocardiography demonstrated that the bicuspid valve functioned well, with a peak velocity of 1.8 m/s, no regurgitation, and no vegetations. Blood cultures grew Streptococcus gordonii, and antibiotics were switched to penicillin. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed no valve vegetations, no aortic wall thickening, aneurysm, or abscess. A PET–CT scan with 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose revealed increased uptake at the distal end of the aortic stent in the descending aorta.

A 29-year-old Kurdish man presented with a 10-day history of right-sided neck pain and dyspnea, accompanied by fever, rigors, cough, and generalized body aches. Over the following 24 hours, he developed palpitations, sweating, dizziness, tremors, headache, vomiting, fatigue, and numbness; he reported a 4-kg weight loss during the preceding week. He denied eye symptoms or prior thyroid disease and had no relevant medication use or family history.

On examination, he was agitated, anxious, and diaphoretic, with a temperature of 40.0 °C, heart rate of 135 beats/min, respiratory rate of 29 breaths/min, and blood pressure of 150/75 mm Hg. Eye examination was normal. The thyroid gland was tender, especially on the right, without appreciable goiter or bruit. The skin was warm and moist, and a fine tremor was noted.

Laboratory studies showed an undetectable TSH level, free T4 of 113 nmol/L, T3 of 2.29 nmol/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 105 mm/h, and C-reactive protein (CRP) of 105 mg/L. Complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, and electrolytes were normal. ECG revealed sinus tachycardia. Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated mild enlargement of the right lobe with bilateral patchy areas of decreased echogenicity and vascularity, suggestive of subacute thyroiditis.

A 48-year-old man presented after a road traffic accident that followed a syncopal episode 15 minutes after a bee sting. He had a history of large local reactions to bee stings but no prior anaphylaxis. His medical history included avocado oral allergy and a transient ischemic attack for which he was taking aspirin. The episode resolved rapidly after intramuscular adrenaline (500 μg). Baseline serum mast cell tryptase (MCT) was elevated at 19.2 μg/L (normal <14.0 μg/L), and total IgE was 344 kU/L (normal <111 kU/L). Bee venom–specific IgE was very high at 60.5 kU/L (very high >17.5 kU/L). 

He began bee venom subcutaneous immunotherapy. Six months later, on maintenance dosing, he developed rapid-onset visual changes, malaise, light-headedness, and a sensation of impending collapse, which resolved after adrenaline. Two years into therapy, he again experienced hypotension, light-headedness, and prolonged symptoms requiring two doses of adrenaline, IV hydrocortisone, and fluids. One week later, he was admitted with persistent light-headedness and impending collapse and was started on prednisolone and antihistamines. During admission, he had a postural blood pressure drop of 40 mmHg and a transient episode of severe lower abdominal pain. Repeat MCT was 18.0 μg/L. 

Hypoglycemia, myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, and infection were excluded (normal glucose, troponin, CK, d-dimer, CRP). Tests for pheochromocytoma (serum fractionated catecholamines and metanephrines) and carcinoid syndrome (urinary 5-HIAA) were negative. Dermatological examination found no cutaneous mastocytoma. Bone marrow aspirate showed normal trilineage hematopoiesis with no increase in mast cells. Molecular testing for c-KIT D816V in marrow and serum was negative, and trephine staining for CD2 and CD117 did not demonstrate a significant mast cell population. Serum protein electrophoresis was negative for monoclonal immunoglobulins, full-body PET scan showed no abnormal uptake, and bone mineral density T score was –1.5 at the spine.

A 15-year-old boy from the Philippines, with low socioeconomic status and no significant medical history, presented with a 7-day history of a right abdominal mass, occasional dry cough, and marked asthenia. He denied fever, weight loss, or trauma. Vital signs: T 36.8°C, HR 100/min, RR 20/min, BP 107/74 mmHg, SpO₂ 97% on room air. On exam, he had two dental caries on lower molars and small bilateral cervical lymph nodes. Chest auscultation revealed decreased breath sounds in the right mid-apical area with ipsilateral basal crackles. Abdominal exam showed an 8 cm round, taut-elastic, tender mass in the right hypochondrium with slight warmth. Point-of-care lung ultrasound demonstrated a subpleural anechoic lesion in the right mid-apical chest with hyperechoic spots and a small right pleural effusion. Chest radiograph showed a semi-moon opacity in the right upper and middle lung fields with adjacent atelectasis and slight ipsilateral mediastinal shift. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 9×6 cm bilobed, fluid-filled, apparently extrahepatic mass compressing the liver. Laboratory studies: WBC 16.97×10³/µL (78% neutrophils), CRP 3.56 mg/dL, LDH 370 U/L, GGT 83 U/L, normal electrolytes and hepatic/renal function. Thoraco-abdominal contrast CT showed an extrapulmonary necrotic lesion with air bubbles extending from the apical pleura to the sixth intercostal space, a 2×1.4 cm right hilar lymph node without colliquation, and an 11.8×6×13 cm extrahepatic mass with central colliquation and peripheral rim enhancement displacing hepatic segments II, IV, and VII. Rhino-pharyngeal swabs for respiratory viruses, Mycoplasma, and Chlamydia pneumoniae were negative. Quantiferon and viral serologies were negative. Blood, sputum, urine, and stool cultures were sterile. Galactomannan antigen detection and serologic tests for Entamoeba histolytica and Echinococcus were unremarkable. Tumor markers (chromogranin A, CEA, β-hCG, AFP, metanephrines, VMA, HVA) were negative. First-level immunologic tests, including immunoglobulins, lymphocyte subsets, NBT, and DHR, were normal. A percutaneous biopsy and drain placement were performed; results are pending.

A previously healthy 6-year-old boy was transferred for evaluation of incidentally discovered hypertension and bradycardia during workup for a 1-week history of abdominal pain, cough, congestion, frontal headache, and decreased appetite. He had received a 2-day course of prednisolone 4 days earlier, which was discontinued when hypertension was noted. There was no use of over-the-counter decongestants. His perinatal course was notable only for transient tachypnea of the newborn. He had undergone multiple corrections for bilateral club feet and reportedly slept more than peers. Review of prior records showed mild hypertension and low heart rate since age 4½ years. Family history included early-onset hypertension in his father (age 29) and premature cardiac deaths on the maternal side; no renal or thyroid disease was reported.

On examination, he was alert and afebrile. Heart rate was 54 beats per minute, blood pressure was 160/91 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Height and weight were at the 8.7th and 14.5th percentiles, respectively. Cardiovascular exam revealed a grade 2/6 ejection systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border with otherwise normal heart sounds. There were scars on both feet; chest, abdominal, and neurologic examinations were normal.

Initial laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, electrolytes, renal function, and urinalysis. ECG demonstrated complete heart block with atrioventricular dissociation, junctional escape rhythm, and left axis deviation. Echocardiography revealed no structural heart disease, normal ventricular function, and mild left ventricular hypertrophy. Lyme titers were negative. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (3.44 uIU/mL) and free T4 (11.3 µg/dL) were normal. Plasma renin activity was normal. Renal ultrasound and duplex studies showed no abnormalities or stenosis.

An angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor was initiated, and the patient was observed without hypotension or other events. He was discharged with diagnoses of likely congenital complete heart block and primary hypertension and scheduled for outpatient cardiology follow-up.

A 26-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of a gradually enlarging mass on the anterior aspect of the left side of his neck. He reported that the lesion began after sustaining what he believed was a cigarette burn. He denied fever, weight loss, night sweats, or other constitutional symptoms. 

On examination, there was a 3 × 2 cm, well-circumscribed, nontender, ulcerated, pink, ovoid mass with scant serous exudate, surface crust, and a dull erythematous border. Adjacent skin showed small, skin-colored papules and a dark, healed ulcer superior to the main lesion. No oral lesions or regional lymphadenopathy were noted. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Given concerns for a cutaneous malignancy, the mass was excised under local anesthesia for microscopic evaluation.

A 15-year-old girl with mild depression presented with a 2-month history of worsening bilateral knee pain, ankle swelling, and a generalized rash, accompanied by easy bruising and fatigue. She had noticed a lower-leg rash beginning seven years earlier, which in the past two months extended to her wrists; she also reported ten months of amenorrhea. She described a highly restricted diet consisting of bread, cereal, chips, and butter. 

On examination, she was tachycardic with orthostatic changes. There was a perifollicular petechial hemorrhagic rash with corkscrew hairs extending from the ankles upward, multiple ecchymoses, and bilateral knee and ankle edema without warmth or rubor. Ankle range of motion was limited, and she had an antalgic gait. Her weight was 48.6 kg (34th percentile), height 172.7 cm (95th percentile), and BMI 16.3 (5th percentile). 

Initial laboratory evaluation revealed a normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 7.1 g/dL) and elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 30 mg/dL, ESR 43 mm/hr). On hospital day 2 she spiked a fever to 38.4 °C; blood and urine cultures were negative. She was diagnosed with avoidant restrictive food intake disorder and admitted for severe malnutrition and anemia. 

Knee radiographs showed possible osteopenia; chest radiograph revealed mild scoliosis. Ultrasound of the right knee demonstrated a complex effusion, which was deemed inconsistent with clinical septic arthritis. MRI of the ankles and knees showed patchy enhancement of the distal right metaphysis and calcaneal body with dark T1 and bright T2 signals. Radiology’s differential diagnosis included leukemia/lymphoma, chronic multifocal osteomyelitis, and Langerhans cell histiocytosis.

A 70-year-old woman with FIGO stage IVB high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma received six cycles of neoadjuvant carboplatin/paclitaxel followed by interval debulking surgery, then maintenance bevacizumab (10 cycles) and olaparib without hypertension or proteinuria. Sixteen days after her 10th bevacizumab infusion, she was admitted with urinary incontinence, grade 2 asthenia, and acute confusion. On exam her Glasgow Coma Score was 14; vital signs were normal, and the rest of the neurologic exam was unremarkable. She had no history of seizures or neurologic disease. Laboratory studies, urine and blood cultures, ECG, and chest radiograph were all normal. Noncontrast head CT showed no hemorrhage and no abnormalities in the posterior circulation. Lumbar puncture was negative for infectious, inflammatory, or neoplastic cells. Empiric ceftriaxone was started. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral high signal intensity in the cortex and subcortical white matter of the posterior parietal and occipital lobes on FLAIR images, without diffusion restriction; ADC values were increased, indicating vasogenic edema.

An 86-year-old Japanese man with a 3-month history of ulcerative colitis (on prednisolone 15 mg/day and azathioprine 75 mg/day) was referred for worsening diarrhea and anal pain.
