Endoscopic evaluation and biopsy confirmed active colitis, and metronidazole and budesonide were added; isoniazid and pyridoxal phosphate were started because intestinal tuberculosis could not be excluded. 

On hospital day 80, serum potassium, calcium, inorganic phosphorus, and magnesium began to decline. By day 95, despite oral supplementation with sodium dihydrogen phosphate and calcium l-aspartate, his serum levels were:  
– Potassium 2.3 mEq/L  
– Corrected calcium 5.5 mg/dL  
– Inorganic phosphorus 1.0 mg/dL  
– Magnesium 0.9 mg/dL  

He continued to have muddy stools. His diet provided 2220 mg K/day, 992 mg phosphorus/day, and 237 mg magnesium/day. 

Physical examination: BMI 17.5, temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 105/65 mmHg, pulse 77 bpm. 

Laboratory studies on day 95:  
– Blood gas: pH 7.511, HCO₃⁻ 35.3 mmol/L  
– Serum albumin 2.2 g/dL, BUN 14 mg/dL, creatinine 0.47 mg/dL  
– Urinalysis: protein +1, RBC 1–4/HPF  
– Urine biochemistry: FENa 0.81%, FEK 1.75%, FEMg 2.06%, FECa 0.30%, %TRP 39.1%  
– N-acetyl-β-d-glucosaminidase index 28.2 IU/gCr  
– Plasma renin activity 0.5 ng/mL/h, aldosterone 10 pg/mL, cortisol 6.81 µg/dL

An 11-year-old boy with no past medical history presented with a 3-day history of sharp right-sided flank pain radiating to the groin and intermittent hematuria. He denied fever, vomiting, or bowel changes. On examination, he had tenderness at the right costovertebral angle. Laboratory studies showed a serum creatinine of 1.2 mg/dL and microscopic hematuria. Renal ultrasonography revealed right-sided hydronephrosis with proximal ureteral dilatation. A noncontrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed right hydronephrosis but did not identify any ureteral stone.

A 63-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of horizontal diplopia when looking to the right and a severe headache. One month earlier he had developed right-sided otorrhea and headache; the otorrhea transiently improved with empirical systemic and otic antibiotics, but the headache persisted. Five days before presentation his headache worsened, accompanied by nausea and vomiting. Three days before presentation he noted binocular diplopia in primary gaze, worse on right gaze. The headache was constant, located in the right frontal and retro-orbital area, and radiated throughout the head. 

His medical history was significant only for a right radical mastoidectomy 30 years earlier; he remained lost to follow-up with persistent right ear discharge. On examination, otoscopy of the right ear showed mucoid discharge and granulation tissue in an inflamed mastoid cavity with a high facial ridge. The left ear was normal. Neurologic examination revealed an isolated right abducens nerve palsy; all other findings were normal.

Laboratory studies showed elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, elevated C-reactive protein, and leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance. Audiometry demonstrated moderate right mixed-type hearing loss. Ear swab cultures were negative for microorganisms, and a biopsy of the right external ear and mastoid cavity revealed only chronic inflammation.

A thin-slice, noncontrast CT scan of the temporal bones demonstrated partial opacification of the right middle ear and residual mastoid air cells consistent with chronic otomastoiditis, a defect in the anterolateral mastoid wall from prior surgery, and poor pneumatization of the right petrous apex filled with fatty marrow.

A 56-year-old retired civil servant was referred with an FNAC report of a benign salivary gland tumor. He had a one-year history of gradually progressive, bilateral submandibular swellings with no size change on feeding. Initially painless, he later developed a burning sensation in the head and neck. Concurrently, he noted progressive tongue enlargement that nearly filled his oral cavity and impaired speech. He denied purulent discharge, halitosis, dry mouth or eyes, eyelid swelling, weight loss, abdominal discomfort, or musculoskeletal symptoms.  

On examination, he appeared anxious, with an open-mouth posture and “hot potato” speech. The skin of the head and neck was thickened. He had massive, moist, pink macroglossia with a depapillated surface, obscuring the oropharynx. Bilateral submandibular glands measured 4×3 cm, were bosselated, firm to hard, and fixed to skin. There was no lacrimal gland swelling or slanting of the palpebral fissures.  

A provisional diagnosis of multiple myeloma with amyloidosis was made, with Mikulicz disease as a differential. Laboratory tests showed a PCV of 38%, WBC 6,400/cmm (neutrophils 42% [low], lymphocytes 46% [slightly high], monocytes 7%), and platelets 123,000/cmm. Electrolytes, urea, creatinine, and urinalysis were normal. HIV-1/2 testing was nonreactive. Neck ultrasound showed a normal thyroid gland and diffusely enlarged submandibular glands without stones, cysts, or lymphadenopathy.  

An open biopsy of the left submandibular gland provoked a torrential bleed, suggesting major arterial injury, but no discrete vessel was found; hemostasis was achieved with mass suturing. Approximately 250–500 mL of blood was lost. He was discharged after 48 hours with a clinical diagnosis of submandibular haemangioma. He rebled spontaneously on postoperative days 25 and 29. The submandibular swelling had become massive and was nearly compromising the airway, making further neck exploration hazardous.

A 30-year-old man presented with 4 months of gradually progressive dysphagia, predominantly to solids. He denied weight loss, vomiting, abdominal pain, hematemesis, melena, dyspnea on exertion, or peripheral edema. He had no significant medical history or addictions. On examination, vitals were normal, and abdominal and respiratory exams were unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including hematologic and biochemical parameters, were within normal limits. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a well-defined submucosal lesion bulging into the lumen of the distal esophagus on the right anterolateral wall just above the gastroesophageal junction; the overlying mucosa appeared normal, and there was mild luminal narrowing but the scope passed easily. Abdominal ultrasonography was unrevealing. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the thorax demonstrated a 3.5 × 2.3 × 3.0 cm well-defined homogeneous hypodense cystic lesion in the right anterolateral wall of the distal thoracic esophagus, suggesting a submucosal or intramural origin.

- A 25-year-old healthy man presented with a one-week history of a painful lesion on the right lateral border of the tongue. He reported severe pain exacerbated by food and tooth contact, leading to difficulty eating.  
- On examination, a tender, firm, and mobile lymph node was palpable in the right submandibular area. No other cervical lymphadenopathy was detected.  
- Intraoral exam revealed a solitary 20 × 20 mm lingual lesion with an infiltrated and exophytic base, elevated borders, and a fibrinous exudate covering its center. The lesion was rubbery in consistency without induration on palpation.  
- Adjacent to the lesion, the right mandibular second molar (tooth 47) was significantly decayed and fractured, presenting a sharp lingual edge on palpation.  
- Panoramic radiography of tooth 47 showed profound coronal radiolucency invading the pulp chamber and periapical radiolucency around the root apex; the tooth was deemed unrestorable.  
- The differential diagnosis included a lingual traumatic ulcer and a malignant lesion of the tongue.  
- Management plan: extraction of tooth 47, soft diet, avoidance of hot and spicy foods, stringent oral hygiene with tongue scraping, and use of antiseptic mouthwash and topical hyaluronic acid gel four times daily for one week.

A 32‐year‐old woman with a history of hypothyroidism and major depressive disorder presented with a 3‐day history of fever, chills, anorexia, myalgia, and a dry cough that later became productive. She then developed vomiting and watery secretory diarrhea, and her family reported one episode of bloody diarrhea followed by hypotension and tachycardia. On admission, she was somnolent; temperature 37°C, blood pressure 77/42 mmHg, heart rate 136 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min. Physical examination revealed severe dehydration. Initial laboratory values included a creatinine of 0.8 mg/dL, arterial pH 7.16, WBC 3300/µL, platelet count 79 000/µL, hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, CRP 152 mg/L, ESR 83 mm/h, and normal BUN. She received aggressive fluid resuscitation without hemodynamic improvement and was started on vasopressors. Echocardiography was normal. She was transferred to the ICU for refractory shock and treated with broad‐spectrum antibiotics (vancomycin, meropenem) and corticosteroids, with gradual clinical improvement allowing discontinuation of vasopressors and steroids. Due to persistent cough, a high‐resolution CT of the chest was performed, showing patchy ground‐glass opacities with interlobular septal thickening. A repeat CT one day later demonstrated consolidation in the posteromedial segments of the lower lobes.

A 40-year-old nonpregnant woman presented with severe, atraumatic right hip pain 8 weeks after undergoing a duodenal switch for morbid obesity. She localized the pain to her groin and upper thigh; it worsened with movement and weight-bearing and had progressed over 3 weeks, rendering her essentially bed bound. Outpatient evaluation included a lower‐extremity Doppler and nerve‐conduction studies, both of which were negative. She denied any recent infection, steroid use, or trauma. Her medical history was significant for hypertension, gastroesophageal reflux disease, dyspepsia, bipolar disorder, and morbid obesity (body mass index decreased from 66.2 to 54 after surgery). Preoperatively, she had vitamin D deficiency corrected to normal levels and was taking calcium citrate and vitamin D3 postoperatively. 

On consultation, anteroposterior pelvic radiographs showed no abnormalities in bone structure, joint space, or density. Laboratory studies revealed a normal white-cell count (5.9 × 10^9/L) and a normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate (18 mm/h). MRI of the pelvis demonstrated diffuse edema in the right femoral head and neck with an associated joint effusion; the radiologist noted a small, isolated area of linear low signal on T1 images and initially interpreted the findings as osteonecrosis. After orthopedic assessment, the working considerations were idiopathic transient osteoporosis of the hip versus early osteonecrosis. The patient was placed on protected touchdown weight-bearing and discharged with plans for close outpatient follow-up.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a painless swelling in her left axilla of two years’ duration. She denied fever, breast masses, or systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a firm-to-hard, mobile mass measuring 10 × 5 cm in the left axilla without skin changes or lymphadenopathy. Routine blood counts and biochemistry, including liver function tests and inflammatory markers, were within normal limits. Ultrasound of the axilla revealed a 10 × 5 cm thick-walled cystic lesion that was anechoic without internal echoes. Mammography of both breasts was normal. Abdominal ultrasound and chest radiography showed no abnormalities in the liver or lungs.

A 24-year-old male farmer was brought to the emergency department after voluntarily ingesting 100 mL of a pesticide formulation containing Novaluron 5.25% and Indoxacarb 4.5%, diluted in a soft carbonated beverage. He had undergone gastric lavage at an outside hospital prior to transfer. On arrival, his Glasgow Coma Scale score was 15/15; he was afebrile, with a pulse of 110 beats/min, a respiratory rate of 30 breaths/min, blood pressure of 130/70 mm Hg, and an oxygen saturation of 84% while receiving 14 L/min of oxygen via a non-rebreather mask. He was conscious and oriented, but tachypnoeic with intercostal retractions. Chest auscultation revealed normal vesicular breath sounds bilaterally. Bluish discoloration of the buccal mucosa was noted. Cardiac examination was unremarkable. Neurologic examination showed normal pupils, flexor plantar responses, and no fasciculations. Initial differential diagnoses included chemical pneumonitis, methemoglobinemia, and aspiration pneumonitis. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed a pH of 7.45, a pCO2 of 39 mm Hg, a pO2 of 89 mm Hg, and an sO2 of 100%. Other laboratory values were within normal limits. High‐resolution computed tomography of the chest showed minimal bilateral pleural effusions without consolidations. The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit for further evaluation, including measurement of methemoglobin levels.

A 34-year-old gravida 2 woman, conceived by IVF, was referred at 14 weeks 6 days of gestation for evaluation of fetal skeletal abnormalities. Her first pregnancy ended in spontaneous abortion; family history was unremarkable. 

Ultrasound at 14+6 weeks showed:
• Severe shortening of all long bones  
• Narrow, bell-shaped chest with short ribs  
• Bowing of the femora  
• Excess soft tissue over thighs and lower legs  
• Suspicion of retrognathia  
• Ulnar deviation of the wrists  

A poor-prognosis skeletal dysplasia was suspected, and a probable diagnosis of thanatophoric dysplasia type I was considered. Amniocentesis was performed at 15 weeks.

At a targeted ultrasound at 17 weeks:
• Temporal-lobe sulcation was normal  
• Bilateral brachydactyly of the hands  
• Mild polyhydramnios  
• Moderate pericardial effusion and small hydrothorax  
• Mild retrognathia without overt Pierre–Robin sequence  
• Severe rib shortening suggesting pulmonary hypoplasia  
• Protuberant abdomen with relative limb soft-tissue excess  
• Femur length 14.2 mm (–3 SD), fibula length 9.2 mm (>–3 SD)  
• No other anomalies were noted

A 13-year-old boy from Mauritania presented with acute urinary retention and progressive gait disturbances over several days. He reported a 1-month history of drinking unsafe water. On examination, he had urinary retention; a brisk right patellar reflex; ataxia on the right side; and an indifferent plantar response bilaterally. Routine blood tests showed a white-cell count of 4430 cells/mm3 with 450 eosinophils; other hematologic and biochemical parameters were within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine demonstrated an enhancing intramedullary mass involving the conus medullaris at the L1–L2 level, findings that suggested an arteriovenous malformation or a cavernoma.

A 35-year-old woman presented with three months of progressive exertional dyspnea and bilateral lower extremity edema. She noted a gradual increase in dyspnea to the point of being unable to climb one flight of stairs without resting. She also endorsed a nonproductive cough, pleuritic chest pain, occasional orthopnea, and a 20-lb unintentional weight loss over one month. She denied fevers, chills, night sweats, gastrointestinal symptoms, bleeding, and known risk factors for tuberculosis. She had no past medical history, denied intravenous drug use, and had no history of structural heart disease.

On examination, she was nontoxic, mildly tachycardic (109 bpm), afebrile, with normal blood pressure and respiratory rate. Lung auscultation was clear bilaterally; she spoke in 4–5-word sentences with mild tachypnea. Cardiac auscultation showed tachycardia without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. No jugular venous distention or carotid bruits were present. She had 2+ pitting edema to the midshins bilaterally. Skin examination revealed no purpura, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, splinter hemorrhages, or track marks. Abdominal and neurologic examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory testing revealed mild hyponatremia (Na 127 mEq/L), chloride 90 mEq/L, and normocytic anemia (Hb 8.5 g/dL). There was no leukocytosis, troponin was undetectable, and brain-natriuretic peptide was normal. A 12-lead ECG showed sinus tachycardia without acute injury or signs of right-heart strain. Chest radiography was interpreted by radiology as “bilateral patchy atelectasis,” but the treating physicians noted a pleural-based wedge-like consolidation in the right lower lobe consistent with Hampton’s Hump.

The initial differential diagnosis included pulmonary embolus, pneumonia, congestive heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, cardiomyopathy, and infectious endocarditis. A third set of blood cultures was obtained prior to further imaging.

A 31-year-old man was ejected from a car during a rollover collision. He lost consciousness at the scene but arrived in the emergency department fully alert. He was not intoxicated. Vital signs: blood pressure 148/92 mmHg, pulse 96 bpm, respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, Glasgow Coma Scale 15/15. Examination showed mild neck tenderness, clear chest auscultation, soft abdomen, and normal lower-limb neurologic function. Initial anteroposterior chest X-ray revealed a right clavicle fracture and mild haziness of the left lung field. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed mild left pleural effusion, fracture of the left lateral ramus of C6, fracture of the anterior rim of T10 with hematoma around the descending aorta. The patient was admitted for observation. On hospital day 2, a portable chest X-ray showed homogeneous opacification of the left hemithorax with mediastinal shift to the right. A chest tube was placed, draining 1500 mL of milky, blood-stained fluid. Pleural-fluid analysis showed 80% lymphocytes and 20% neutrophils, and bacteriological culture was negative.

A 58‐year‐old man presented to the emergency department with a 24‐hour history of right iliac fossa pain, nausea, and diarrhea. His surgical history was notable for a laparoscopic appendectomy performed 8 months earlier; he had no other significant past medical history. On examination, he was febrile, and his hemodynamic and respiratory parameters were stable. Abdominal palpation elicited pain in the right lower quadrant without peritoneal signs. Laboratory studies showed a white‐blood‐cell count of 25,000 cells/mm3 with 85% neutrophils and a C‐reactive protein level of 180 mg/dL; all other laboratory values were within normal limits. An abdominal CT scan demonstrated a swollen and thickened tubular structure measuring 36 × 27 mm at the cecal pole, with a 25‐mm pericecal collection adjacent to surgical clips.

A 10-year-old girl with Thevenards syndrome presented with a 7-month history of painless right hip swelling and progressively restricted movement. Seven months prior, she sustained a bicycle fall onto her hip. One week after the trauma, she developed functional impairment of the right lower limb. An anteroposterior pelvic radiograph showed a right hip dislocation and extensive heterotopic ossification in the soft tissues, mainly over the posterior capsule and gluteus muscles, clearly separated from bone; pelvic bones were normal without periosteal reaction. The patient was treated conservatively but was lost to follow-up.

On re-presentation, clinical examination revealed markedly reduced abduction, extension, and internal rotation of the right hip, with inability to stand or walk. A firm, well-circumscribed mass was palpable over the anterolateral aspect of the right hip.

Follow-up pelvic radiographs demonstrated persistent hip dislocation and increased ossifying masses in the soft tissues projecting over the acetabulum and right femoral head and neck; the periphery of these masses was denser than their centers. A contrast-enhanced CT scan showed an extensive area of ossification within the right iliopsoas, obturator, and gluteus muscles, extending from the pelvic inlet to the lesser trochanter. There was a clear cleavage plane between the calcified mass and the adjacent iliac bone. Multiple well-defined calcific areas suggestive of mature bone were seen at various levels. In more caudal images above the lesser trochanter, a hypodense central zone was surrounded by hyperdense zones with a focal, well-defined calcification anteriorly. No significant enhancement was noted after contrast administration.

An 18-year-old man with no significant past medical or family history presented with dysuria, lower abdominal pain, and fever. A urine culture grew Klebsiella pneumoniae, and he was treated for a urinary tract infection. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a well-defined echogenic splenic cyst measuring 10.3 cm in diameter. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a solitary multilocular splenic cyst, 10 cm in diameter, with parietal calcifications. MRI of the abdomen demonstrated a multilocular cyst in the medial spleen measuring 92 × 90 × 80 mm that was hyperintense on T1-weighted images, suggestive of lymphangioma or hamartoma. Routine hematological and biochemical tests were within normal limits, and the indirect hemagglutination test for Echinococcus granulosus was negative.

A 57-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of persistent cough and nasal discharge. Initial evaluation at an outside hospital revealed leukopenia (WBC 700/μL), and CT scanning showed mild right upper-lobe pneumonia and mild-to-moderate splenomegaly. She was referred for further hematological assessment.

On examination at our center, she was afebrile with stable vital signs and had no skin lesions. She had no medications, an unremarkable medical history except for prior pregnancies, and no family history of hematological or autoimmune disease. Laboratory studies showed:  
• WBC 710/μL (11% neutrophils, 57% lymphocytes)  
• RBC count 4.23×10^6/μL, hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, platelet count 141×10^3/μL  
• Normal serum biochemistry  
• C-reactive protein 0.5 mg/dL  
• Soluble interleukin-2 receptor 1,880 U/mL  

Serologic testing excluded hepatitis B and C, HIV, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis; Epstein–Barr virus serology indicated past, not recent, infection. FDG-PET–CT demonstrated diffuse mild uptake in the spleen and the bone marrow of the trunk and proximal extremities.

A bone marrow biopsy revealed a slightly hypercellular marrow with mild reticulin fibrosis. Smears showed a marked decrease in mature segmented neutrophils (0.4%) with a relative increase in myelocytes; there were no blasts and no morphological dysplasia. Flow cytometry disclosed no abnormal lymphoid populations, and cytogenetic analysis showed a normal karyotype.

A 70-year-old woman with hypertension presented with a 1-year history of intermittent difficulty swallowing liquids—especially with large boluses—and occasional dysphagia when eating rice. Symptoms occurred about once monthly and were associated with a mild loss of appetite. She denied odynophagia, globus sensation, weight loss, abdominal pain, hematochezia, and dyspepsia. Physical examination was unremarkable.

A lateral neck radiograph showed multilevel moderate anterior cervical spine osteophytes without displacement of the anterior prevertebral soft tissues, and no radiopaque foreign body was seen. Double-contrast barium esophagography revealed a smooth anterior compression of the lower esophageal lumen with well-defined margins that persisted during barium ingestion; no other strictures or mucosal defects were identified. Decreased primary peristalsis was also noted.

Upper endoscopy demonstrated a non-obstructive Schatzki ring 2 cm proximal to the gastroesophageal junction; the endoscope passed into the stomach without difficulty, indicating a lumen diameter greater than 12 mm. The ring produced minimal luminal narrowing and was not apparent on the esophagogram.

A contrast-enhanced chest CT scan was ordered for further evaluation of the esophageal compression.

A 62-year-old Hmong man presented with sudden-onset chest pain, dizziness, and palpitations. He appeared mildly distressed and weak. Initial vital signs: blood pressure 60–80/?, heart rate 150–220 bpm. ECG showed sinus rhythm with low-amplitude P waves and junctional beats with narrow QRS complexes, followed by ventricular ectopic beats with right bundle branch block morphology and left axis deviation, diffuse ST-segment depression, a prolonged QT interval, and ectopics on the terminal portion of the T wave.  
Laboratory results: potassium 2.9 mmol/L, pH 7.21, anion gap 17, lactate 9.7 mmol/L, troponin T <0.01 ng/mL, digoxin level 0.1 ng/mL. Intravenous saline was administered.  
Bedside echocardiography revealed hyperdynamic left ventricular function without regional wall motion abnormalities or pericardial effusion, with no evidence of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy. Urgent coronary angiography showed nonobstructive coronary atherosclerosis with slow flow; ventriculography confirmed hyperdynamic function and no wall motion defects. A diagnosis of vasodilatory shock was made.  
Despite fluids, the patient required vasopressor support and insertion of an intraaortic balloon pump, and was intubated for impending respiratory failure. Blood cultures were obtained and empiric antibiotics started.  
The patient developed progressive atrioventricular conduction delay and multiple dysrhythmias, including left bundle branch block–pattern and right bundle branch block–pattern ventricular ectopy, nonsustained and sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, and bidirectional ventricular tachycardia. Arrhythmias persisted despite intravenous amiodarone and multiple attempts at cardioversion, with little hemodynamic improvement.

A 60-year-old woman was referred to the otolaryngology clinic for presumed aggressive left glomus jugulare. She reported four months of left ear discharge, decreased hearing, and non-pulsatile tinnitus. Her medical history included chronic kidney disease on hemodialysis and a prior stroke with residual left facial palsy and hemiparesis; she denied otalgia, aural fullness, or vertigo.

On examination, the left tympanic membrane had a central wet perforation with mildly congested middle-ear mucosa. She had central left facial palsy; other cranial nerves were intact. Audiometry demonstrated left conductive hearing loss. Flexible nasopharyngoscopy revealed a bulge in the left nasopharyngeal wall without an obvious mass. After a course of oral and topical ciprofloxacin, her ear discharge resolved.

Computed tomography of the temporal bone showed a large, ill-defined, infiltrative mass of mixed cystic and solid density with extensive contrast enhancement. The lesion involved the left petrous apex and clivus, extended inferiorly into the infratemporal fossa and parapharyngeal spaces displacing the nasopharynx, infiltrated the mastoid air cells and middle ear cavity, and involved the left jugular bulb and proximal jugular vein with non-opacification. There was significant osseous destruction of the left petrous bone and occipital condyle, with dehiscence, carotid canal resorption, and jugular foramen widening.

Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a heterogeneous lesion at the left petrous apex. The cystic component was hyperintense on T2-weighted and FLAIR images; the soft-tissue component was isointense on all sequences without diffusion restriction.

A 34-year-old woman presented with a 9-year history of a pruritic, macular erythematous rash on her arms and legs, associated with headaches and angioedema of the hands, feet, lips, and eyelids. The rash first appeared 2–3 days after the birth of her second child in 2009, then recurred one to two weeks before each menses and resolved within a few days of menstrual onset. Over the following six months, cyclical urticaria progressed to include dyspnea, nausea, dizziness, and abdominal cramping, all following the same luteal-phase timing. Initial treatments—first- and second-generation H1 and H2 antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants, calcineurin inhibitors, and PUVA therapy—were ineffective. She achieved partial relief with prednisone up to 100 mg daily, but flare-ups persisted premenstrually. Three years after symptom onset, an immunologist suspected autoimmune progesterone dermatitis with possible catamenial anaphylaxis. Baseline serum tryptase was 2.8 μg/L (reference 3.8–11.4 μg/L). A progesterone skin test produced a wheal-and-flare reaction, confirming the diagnosis.

A 68-year-old woman with a 10-year history of systemic sarcoidosis presented with a 2-month history of two asymptomatic yellow-red plaques on the anterior right thigh and knee. She denied pruritus or pain, and had no prior similar skin lesions. Her sarcoidosis had been diagnosed based on hilar lymphadenopathy and restrictive pulmonary physiology; she was maintained on low-dose oral steroids. Physical examination revealed nontender yellow-red plaques with central atrophy and telangiectasia; no other lesions were seen. A punch biopsy was performed with a differential diagnosis that included annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma, cutaneous sarcoidosis, granuloma annulare, and necrobiosis lipoidica. Histopathology showed several layers of necrobiosis in the dermis and subcutis surrounded by a palisade of histiocytes and giant cells, dermal fibrosis, superficial and deep perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates with few plasma cells, and a few scattered naked sarcoid-type granulomas. Alcian-blue staining showed no dermal mucin deposition, and acid-fast staining showed no acid-fast bacilli. Laboratory evaluation revealed normal random and fasting blood sugar levels and hemoglobin A1C on two occasions, no personal or family history of diabetes, normal serum calcium, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and ESR, and an elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme level. Ophthalmologic examination was unremarkable. Chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Topical steroids were prescribed for the skin lesions, but no marked improvement was detected after several months.

A 48-year-old man presented with acute chest pain. Two weeks earlier he had an upper respiratory tract infection with sore throat; family members had acute tonsillitis. On admission he was febrile and appeared ill. Vital signs were stable; cardiac and pulmonary exams were unremarkable; no skin rash or edema.

ECG showed diffuse, saddle-shaped ST-segment elevations in anterior leads; PR interval was normal. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a hypercontractile left ventricle without wall motion abnormalities. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis (15.85×10^3/µL), elevated C-reactive protein (6.28 mg/dL), and evidence of myocardial injury (hs-Troponin T initially 589 pg/mL, rising to 1009 pg/mL; CK 410 U/L; CK-MB 15 ng/mL). Chest radiograph was normal.

Given suspicion of ST-elevation myocardial infarction, he received aspirin and heparin and underwent urgent coronary angiography, which showed normal coronary arteries. Further testing revealed negative Coxsackie A/B and echovirus IgA, negative influenza PCR, negative Borrelia burgdorferi IgG/IgM, and negative anti–cardiac muscle, myolemmal, and sarcolemmal antibodies. Anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase B titers were markedly elevated (1879 IU/mL and 2000 U/mL). Blood cultures remained negative.

He was started on ampicillin/sulbactam, with gradual resolution of ST-segment elevations and development of T-wave inversions. After a 3-day interruption of antibiotics to obtain blood cultures, he experienced recurrent chest pain and a rise in hs-Troponin T to 1000 pg/mL. A cardiovascular magnetic resonance study was planned to clarify the diagnosis.

A 24-year-old African American man presented with six months of episodic diffuse crampy abdominal pain and three months of watery diarrhea occurring three to four times daily, accompanied by anorexia and a 10-lb weight loss. He denied fever, nocturnal diarrhea, recent antibiotic use, travel, or sick contacts, and had no pulmonary, joint, skin, or urinary symptoms. His medical history was significant only for childhood Lyme disease and attention-deficit hyperactive disorder; he had no family history of IBD or GI malignancy. On examination he was malnourished with temporal wasting but had a soft, non-tender abdomen and normal vital signs. Laboratory studies including complete blood count, liver enzymes, celiac serology, and carcinoembryonic antigen were within normal limits. Stool studies for leukocytes, culture, ova and parasites, Giardia, and Cryptosporidium were negative. Colonoscopy revealed a circumferential, partially obstructing stenotic mass with granular, inflamed mucosa at the hepatic flexure; the scope could not be passed beyond the lesion. Biopsy of the mass showed focal active chronic colitis with ulceration, polypoid granulation tissue, reactive epithelial changes, and noncaseating granulomata. Special stains for tuberculosis, fungi, and other microorganisms were negative; crypt architecture was preserved, and there was no basal plasmacytosis. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy was normal on biopsy. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed circumferential thickening of the cecum and ascending colon, moderate ascites, and nodular peritoneal thickening.

A 63-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis and mixed connective tissue disease presented to the emergency department with new-onset chest pain 11 hours after receiving her third dose of the Pfizer–BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine. She denied use of immunosuppressive agents at the time of presentation. Physical examination was unremarkable, with no pericardial rub or murmurs. 

Initial electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm without ST-segment changes. Initial cardiac troponin I was 0.02 ng/mL (upper reference limit <0.03 ng/mL). The following day, she returned with persistent chest pain; the electrocardiogram remained unchanged, and troponin I had risen to 1.60 ng/mL. 

Cardiac computed tomography demonstrated normal coronary arteries, normal left ventricular function, no regional wall motion abnormalities, and a normal pericardium. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed normal cardiac structure and function without pericardial disease. 

Serial cardiac troponin I measurements were obtained to evaluate the time–concentration curve.

A 35-year-old woman presented with per rectal bleeding mixed with stool and crampy lower abdominal pain for five days. She also reported a three-month history of productive cough, night sweats, and a 10-kg weight loss. Her history included rheumatic heart disease and atrial fibrillation treated with warfarin, and she had undergone mitral valvuloplasty two years earlier. Medications were warfarin 5 mg daily, carvedilol, and furosemide. On examination, she appeared pale with bipedal edema; cardiac auscultation revealed mitral stenosis and aortic regurgitation, and the abdomen was soft without tenderness or masses. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 9.24 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin of 5.3 g/dL, platelets of 572 × 10^9/L, and an INR of 2.78; renal and hepatic tests were normal. Warfarin was withheld, and she received three units of packed red cells. Colonoscopy revealed segmental inflammation of the ascending colon with ulcerations and polyps covered by yellowish exudate, distension of the ileocecal region, and mucosal edema with an aberrant vascular pattern extending to the hepatic flexure. CT of the chest and abdomen showed right lung consolidation, focal subsegmental consolidations in the left lung, and subcentimeter lymph nodes in the small-bowel mesentery.

A 55-year-old man presented with a 30-year history of chronic stage II dyspnea and recurrent respiratory infections. He quit smoking 22 years ago after a long history of smoking. He had no history of tuberculosis, connective tissue disease, autoimmune disease, or other significant personal or family illnesses. Over the past 4 months, his dyspnea worsened to stage III, associated with a productive cough and frequent episodes of bronchial superinfection. On examination, he was febrile, with an increased anteroposterior chest diameter and snoring rales on auscultation. A thoracic CT scan demonstrated:  
• A trachea dilated to 45 mm in the transverse plane and 32 mm in the sagittal plane with an irregular wall and multiple diverticula.  
• Right and left main bronchi measuring 26 mm and 31 mm, respectively.  
• Bilateral cylindrical and cystic bronchiectasis with mucoid impactions.  
• On expiration, the tracheal anteroposterior diameter decreased to 21 mm.  
• Maximum-intensity and 3D reconstructions confirmed marked tracheobronchial dilatation and wall irregularity.

A 34-year-old man was brought to the emergency department with a gunshot wound to the chest. During transport he received 3 units of whole blood and multiple liters of intravenous fluids but became hemodynamically unstable. On admission his hemoglobin was 7.3 g/dL, hematocrit 23%, sodium 149 mEq/L, potassium 3.1 mEq/L, chloride 114 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 34 mg/dL, creatinine 1.2 mg/dL; arterial blood gases on FiO₂ 100% showed pH 6.57, PaCO₂ 28 mm Hg, PaO₂ 216 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 5 mEq/L; toxicology screen was negative. He suffered hypovolemic shock and a 10-minute cardiac arrest before an emergency thoracotomy with direct cardiac compressions restored circulation. He then underwent surgical repair and was admitted to the ICU intubated, on full mechanical ventilation, sedated with propofol, and receiving neuromuscular blockade. A non-contrasted head CT showed mild bilateral supratentorial edema, with an initial differential of early hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, positive fluid balance, or closed head trauma. He was kept normothermic (37 °C), positioned with head elevation, received mannitol, and was monitored with continuous EEG. Forty-eight hours after discontinuation of sedatives and paralytics he remained comatose, unresponsive to verbal or painful stimuli, but had intact direct and consensual pupillary responses, corneal and gag reflexes, generalized hyperreflexia (+++/++), and bilateral Babinski signs. On hospital day 5, median-nerve somatosensory evoked potentials (mSSEPs) and brainstem auditory evoked potentials (BAEPs) were obtained for prognostication.

A 43-year-old immunocompetent man of low socioeconomic status was referred for evaluation of persistent, nonhealing ulcers on the lower lip and buccal mucosa lasting 6 months. Initially painless, the ulcers became tender over the last 3 months. He denied weight loss, fever, hemoptysis, or systemic medication use. He had a remote history of occasional tobacco chewing but quit over a year ago. Previous treatments, including chlorhexidine and metronidazole gels, topical corticosteroid paste, and multiple oral antibiotics, provided no improvement.

On examination, two oval ulcers with slightly raised borders and a yellowish-gray pseudomembrane were noted: one 1.5 × 1 cm lesion on the left lower labial mucosa and another 1 × 0.8 cm lesion on the right buccal mucosa near the labial commissure. The bases were granular and mildly indurated, with mild tenderness on palpation. No cervical lymphadenopathy or other mucocutaneous lesions were present.

Considering chronic nonhealing ulcers recalcitrant to conservative management, a differential diagnosis was formulated, including aphthous ulcer, traumatic ulcer, malignant ulcer, drug reaction, and infections (bacterial, fungal, and viral).

A 60-year-old man was referred to our neurology clinic after 3.5 months of relapsing, diffuse headaches lasting several days, one episode of nausea and vomiting, a 15-minute period of diplopia, and intermittent back and shoulder pain. He denied fever but reported sporadic night sweats. His medical history was unremarkable, and neurologic examination findings were normal. 

Initial MRI showed cerebellar edema and extensive leptomeningeal enhancement. A lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 25 cm H2O, pleiocytosis (325 leukocytes/μl), and elevated protein (990 mg/L). Tests for tuberculosis (IGRA, tuberculin skin test, and CSF PCR) were negative.

He was referred with a differential of malignancy versus central nervous system infection. CT scans of the chest and abdomen, as well as a total-body PET scan, showed no evidence of malignancy. Repeat MRI demonstrated new leptomeningeal lesions with reduced cerebellar edema and focal contrast enhancement at L5–S1. A second lumbar puncture (June 2015) showed 301 cells/μl (predominantly polyclonal T-lymphocytes) and low CSF glucose (2.3 mmol/L). Serologic testing excluded HIV, Treponema pallidum, and Borrelia infection. Because his symptoms were mild and no diagnosis was reached, no empirical treatment was initiated.

At 3- and 9-month follow-up visits, he was clinically well and MRI findings had normalized. In August 2016, he returned with persistent mild headaches, disorientation, dizziness, and palpitations. Physical and neurologic examinations remained unremarkable, but MRI revealed new nodular leptomeningeal enhancement. A PET scan remained negative for focal FDG uptake, and a follow-up MRI in February 2017 showed a slight increase in meningeal contrast enhancement. In March 2017, an extended effort was made to detect malignant cells in the CSF and to further exclude infectious causes.

An 11-year-old boy from a rural area presented with a three-month history of right hip pain and intermittent claudication, with worsening over the past five days to intense pain and inability to walk. He also had a fever for two days. He had no respiratory symptoms, skin lesions, history of trauma, or known immunosuppression.  
On examination, vital signs were notable for low-grade fever; the right hip was tender with limited range of motion.  
A chest radiograph was normal. A pelvic radiograph showed an osteolytic lesion in the meta-diaphyseal region of the right femur with cortical discontinuity and increased soft-tissue density over the joint, consistent with effusion.  
CT of the right hip confirmed a meta-diaphyseal osteolytic lesion with cortical disruption and hypodense intra-articular material. MRI demonstrated T1 hypointensity and T2 hyperintensity in the same region, diffuse enhancement with contrast, periosteal reaction, joint effusion with synovitis, and adjacent muscle edema.  
The patient underwent surgical drainage of the joint and a bone biopsy; intravenous antibiotics were started.

A 28‐year‐old man presented with sudden‐onset penile pain, deformity, swelling, and bleeding from the urethral meatus beginning 45 minutes earlier during vigorous intercourse in the doggy‐style position. He felt his penis impact his partner’s buttocks, heard a “cracking” sound, then experienced extreme pain, immediate detumescence, and curvature of the penis. He had no prior medical or surgical history. On arrival, he was tachycardic (heart rate 140 bpm), hypertensive (150/100 mm Hg), and tachypneic (31 breaths/min); other vital signs were normal. Local examination revealed deviation of the penis to the right at the proximal junction, urethrorrhagia, increased volume at the root, and tenderness on manipulation. A urethral catheter was placed with difficulty and initially drained reddish urine, which then cleared. Hemoglobin was 15 g/dL; coagulation profile and Chlamydia serology were normal. Urinalysis showed 7–9 bacteria, 4–6 leukocytes, and 9–11 red blood cells per high‐power field. No imaging studies were obtained before planned surgical intervention.

A 24-year-old woman, a current smoker with one prior pregnancy and 18 months of uneventful breastfeeding, presented with a sudden, indurated, palpable mass in the upper-inner quadrant of her left breast, associated with mild erythema and local swelling. She noted that the lesion appeared 48 hours after receiving the BNT162b2 mRNA COVID-19 vaccine and progressed rapidly over the next 36 hours. She reported mild tenderness but no fever or nipple discharge.  
On examination, there was a firm, poorly defined mass approximately 5 cm in diameter with overlying mild erythema; the nipple–areolar complex was normal. Four ipsilateral axillary lymph nodes with cortical thickening were palpable.  
Bilateral breast ultrasound revealed an extensive, ill-defined heterogeneous area underlying the palpable mass, containing multiple irregular hypoechoic regions with posterior acoustic shadowing, and four enlarged axillary lymph nodes with focal cortical thickening. No fluid collections were seen.  
Breast MRI showed a broad area of heterogeneous, non-mass-like contrast enhancement in the inner quadrants of the left breast, with restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging (ADC 0.83 × 10⁻³ mm²/s), and marked adjacent parenchymal edema.

A 38-year-old man with end‐stage renal disease underwent cadaver‐donor renal transplantation in October 1999. His early posttransplant course was complicated by delayed graft function and two steroid-responsive acute rejection episodes. Maintenance immunosuppression included basiliximab induction, methylprednisolone, cyclosporine, and azathioprine, with a stable plasma creatinine concentration of approximately 2.0 mg/dL. In October 2002, azathioprine was replaced by sirolimus and cyclosporine was withdrawn. He had no further rejection or infectious episodes.

In October 2010, routine laboratory testing revealed an asymptomatic rise in plasma creatinine to 3.2 mg/dL. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a hyperechoic solid‐appearing mass enveloping the transplanted kidney. On referral, plasma creatinine had risen further to 4.2 mg/dL. The allograft was non‐tender on palpation and urine output was preserved. Repeat ultrasonography showed a 10.4 × 4.1 cm nonvascularized mass wrapping the kidney with echogenicity consistent with fat and concomitant hydronephrosis. Noncontrast CT confirmed extensive fatty proliferation around the renal pelvis; the ureter was not visualized, and no renal or ureteral calculi were identified.

A 60-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of ulcers on the left lower leg. Her medical history was notable for monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance and type 2 diabetes mellitus. She had been managed at a wound care center for presumed venous stasis ulcers and had failed treatment with silver sulfadiazine, compression wraps, and clobetasol ointment. On dermatologic examination, there was a purulent ulceration with jagged, undermined, violaceous borders and surrounding edema on the left lower leg. A bacterial culture was obtained, and she was prescribed ciprofloxacin and topical triamcinolone for presumed superinfection and inflammation, respectively, but the ulcer continued to enlarge. Intralesional steroid injections and a class I topical steroid were then administered without improvement. Tissue was sampled and sent for histologic examination and culture. Histopathology revealed ulceration with underlying acute and chronic inflammation and tissue necrosis, and cultures were negative.

A 36-year-old woman, never smoker and with no significant medical history, presented with a several-month history of persistent cough, recurrent lower respiratory tract infections, and intermittent small-volume haemoptysis. Physical examination was unremarkable. Chest radiography and high-resolution CT of the chest demonstrated a soft-tissue mass arising from the right lower lobe bronchus and abutting the middle lobe bronchus. Bronchoscopic and CT-guided biopsies revealed inflammation and granulation tissue with some evidence of squamous metaplasia but no malignant cells. An FDG-PET scan showed a 70 mm × 80 mm endobronchial mass with an SUV of 6.4 and a subcentimetre subcarinal lymph node with an SUV of 4.5. Pulmonary function tests demonstrated an FEV1 of 1.93 L (63% predicted), FVC of 2.43 L (69% predicted), TLCO of 4.72 mmol min–1 kPa–1 (52% predicted), and evidence of obstruction in the right lower lobe.

A 73-year-old woman was referred for swelling of the right maxillary premolar buccal gingiva and diffuse swelling of the right cheek. She had a 5 mm fistula 10 mm above the right oral commissure, with purulent drainage. Cone-beam CT demonstrated an apical lesion of the right upper second premolar, and probing from the skin fistula reached the periapical region. She was diagnosed with right buccal cellulitis and an orofacial external fistula secondary to apical periodontitis of the right upper second premolar. Cefcapene pivoxil (300 mg/day) was given for three days, and root canal treatment of the right upper first and second premolars was performed. 

After improvement, the external fistula was excised and apicoectomy was performed. Histologic examination of the resected tissue showed mucus deposition, mucous nodule formation, foreign-body giant cell infiltration, mild calcification, negative AE1/AE3 staining, absence of epithelium, and vimentin-positive stromal cells. The initial histopathologic impression was of a mucin-producing odontogenic tumor or mucinous adenocarcinoma. 

Two months later, swelling and fistula formation recurred at the same site. Bacterial culture of pus yielded Streptococcus anginosus. MRI of the cheeks demonstrated irregular high-signal intensity areas under the subcutaneous tissue bilaterally on T2-weighted fat-suppressed images, more extensive on the right. She denied any history of facial filler injections. Cefcapene pivoxil was administered for 28 days, with clinical improvement, but a 10×10 mm subcutaneous nodule persisted and intermittent clear effusion continued. Local minocycline ointment was injected through the fistula, and MRI six months later showed reduction of the nodule. 

One year after initial presentation, swelling with fluctuation recurred in the right cheek. Puncture aspirate grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus, and cefcapene pivoxil was reinitiated. MRI now showed ill-defined high-signal lesions on T2-weighted images and low-signal lesions on T1-weighted images in the right cheek subcutaneous tissue.

A 19-year-old man presented with a four-month history of non-productive cough and gradually progressive dyspnoea on exertion. He had no history of diabetes, immunosuppression, steroid use, or other predisposing conditions. Physical examination was unremarkable. A chest radiograph showed a small right-sided pleural effusion. Laboratory studies revealed a neutrophilic leukocytosis and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 30 mm/h; fasting blood glucose was normal. 

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a soft-tissue mass diffusely infiltrating both atria and the interatrial septum, with multiple pedunculated lesions in the left atrium extending into the ostia of the superior pulmonary veins. Color Doppler imaging showed moderate tricuspid regurgitation and severe pulmonary hypertension. 

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest revealed an extensive mediastinal soft-tissue mass encasing both main bronchi, the superior vena cava, pulmonary veins, and the arch of the aorta; the mass infiltrated the right atrium and extended through the interatrial septum into the left atrium.

At this point, the differential diagnoses included lymphoproliferative disorders or primary cardiac tumours, thrombus, invasive fungal infections, sclerosing mediastinitis (such as tuberculosis or histoplasmosis), and other neoplastic processes.

An 80‐year‐old man with end‐stage renal failure status post renal transplant 7 years ago (on tacrolimus switched to sirolimus 2 months earlier) was admitted with bilateral leg swelling and oliguria. On exam, he was afebrile, blood pressure 128/62 mm Hg rising later above 200 mm Hg systolic; pulse 93 beats/min; lungs clear; abdomen soft; pitting edema in both calves; mild arm bruising. Initial labs showed creatinine 329 μmol/L (baseline 200), hemoglobin 82 g/L (baseline 110), and platelets 43 ×10^9/L (baseline 160), later dropping to 27 ×10^9/L. Three days into admission, his wife noted he was struggling to read the clock, but he made no complaint. Ophthalmology evaluation revealed visual acuity reduced to hand movements bilaterally despite his insistence that vision was normal (anosognosia), and he pointed to a non‐existent person in a striped shirt when asked (visual confabulation). Pupillary reflexes and fundoscopy were normal.  
What is the most likely diagnosis, and what underlying process best explains his presentation?

A 25-year-old Caucasian man presented with a skull defect over the left frontotemporal region that had progressively enlarged over a 3-year period. He reported mild dull local aching headaches, short-term memory impairment for one year, occasional visual symptoms, and subjective hearing decrease. His past medical history was significant for depression and polysubstance abuse. On examination, general physical findings were unremarkable except for a clearly visible osseous depression of the left frontoparietotemporal region with mild tenderness, interspersed softness, and thinning yet firm skull. He was neurologically intact. Plain skull radiographs showed widespread loss of calvarial structure consistent with an osteolytic process. Head CT revealed patchy erosive osteolysis of the left frontoparietotemporal skull region, with patent coronal, sagittal, and lambdoid sutures. Postcontrast MRI demonstrated marginal enhancement of the calvarial defect without brain invasion or soft tissue component. A bone survey and chest radiograph showed no additional skeletal or pulmonary lesions. Metabolic and endocrine laboratory studies were within normal limits.

A 57-year-old white man presented with headache and a focal seizure that occurred one month earlier. Neurological examination was normal except for left hemianopia on visual field testing. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 5.0-cm, relatively well-defined mass in the right parietal lobe that was heterogeneously hypointense on T2-weighted images, isointense on T1-weighted images, and exhibited peripheral contrast enhancement with peri-lesional vasogenic edema, findings suggestive of a primary neoplasm. Dexamethasone therapy was initiated. Preoperative chest radiography showed multiple bilateral micronodules with emphysematous changes in the apices. The patient was referred for surgery and underwent craniotomy, during which a yellowish, hard lesion with a good cleavage plane and thick yellowish content was encountered.

An 8-year-old girl with no prior medical history presented after one hour of speech confusion following a four-day febrile illness with decreased appetite. She had no headache, dizziness, loss of consciousness, abnormal body movements, or focal deficits. On examination, she was afebrile, alert with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15, and oriented to time, place, and person. Cranial–nerve, motor, sensory, reflex, and cerebellar examinations were normal. Laboratory studies including complete blood count, serum electrolytes, and renal function tests were all within normal limits. Echocardiogram and carotid Doppler were unremarkable. Brain MRI revealed multifocal acute infarcts in the left frontoparietal watershed territories. MR angiography demonstrated diffuse narrowing of the left distal internal carotid artery, the left A1 segment of the anterior cerebral artery, and the left middle cerebral artery with attenuated distal branches.

A 67-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of a hard, painless right submandibular mass that had worsened over the preceding 10 days with new swelling and fever. On examination, the right submandibular gland was hard and tender, and palpation and massage of the submandibular duct elicited pain with no salivary flow. Ultrasonography showed enlargement of the right submandibular gland measuring 54.4 × 29.9 mm with unclear borders; diffuse low echogenicity with local anechoic areas; hardened zones with severe peripheral vascularization; surrounding free fluid; and mildly enlarged lymph nodes measuring 13.0 × 13.3 mm. Hepatomegaly and diffuse fatty liver were also noted. Her history was notable for a 4-year history of autoimmune hemolytic anemia treated with prednisolone for 3 years and ammonium glycyrrhizinate for 1 year. After a 7-day course of antibiotic therapy, pain and swelling initially improved, but she returned with fever, right submandibular pain, and firm swelling without skin erythema. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 109 × 10^9 g/L, a red blood cell count of −3.56 × 10^12/L, a lymphocyte percentage of 23.3%, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 50 mm/h. Submandibular gland extirpation by urgent indication was planned.

A female infant was born at 37 weeks’ gestation to a gravida 3 para 1 mother with no medical history and negative maternal labs. At birth, her heart rate was consistently above 200 beats per minute. APGAR scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes. Physical examination was unremarkable except for a 4 cm × 4 cm blanching hemangioma on the back. 

In the neonatal ICU, ECG showed a heart rate of 235 bpm, broad QRS tachycardia with P waves following the QRS complexes, and possible delta waves. Vagal maneuvers and escalating doses of IV adenosine failed to terminate the tachycardia, so synchronized cardioversion restored sinus rhythm. The infant was started on an IV procainamide infusion and oral propranolol; procainamide was discontinued after 24 hours. 

The ECG continued to show wide‐complex tachycardia, and the initial differential included VT versus SVT with aberrant conduction. Assuming SVT, vagal maneuvers and adenosine were repeated; adenosine produced 1:1 conduction with no AV dissociation but did not terminate the tachycardia, necessitating another cardioversion. 

On day 2, multiple recurrences of wide‐complex tachycardia at ~200 bpm occurred, all resistant to adenosine and treated with cardioversion twice more. Propranolol was increased, and IV procainamide was replaced with IV amiodarone. On day 3, ECG again showed wide QRS tachycardia at 170 bpm, which resolved spontaneously on day 9 of life. Transthoracic echocardiography during admission showed no cardiomegaly or intracardiac masses.

A 74-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with globus-type sensation. Examination of the oral cavity and upper aerodigestive tract was unremarkable. He was diagnosed with laryngopharyngeal reflux and started on omeprazole 10 mg twice daily and Gaviscon Advance 10 mL at bedtime.  
Four months later, his globus symptoms had improved, but examination revealed an ulcerative lesion on the uvula and a similar lesion in the right hypopharynx. The uvular lesion had raised clinical suspicion for squamous cell carcinoma, and an urgent laryngopharyngooesophagoscopy with excisional biopsy of the uvula lesion and biopsy of the hypopharyngeal lesion was arranged.

A 52-year-old man presented with a complaint of tightness and blurring of vision in the right eye. His blood pressure was 122/82 mmHg, and pulse rate was 72 beats/min. Visual acuity was light perception in the right eye and 6/12 in the left eye, with no improvement on pinhole testing. Intraocular pressures were 24 mmHg in the right eye and 25 mmHg in the left eye by applanation tonometry. Pupillary examination revealed sluggish reactions in both eyes. On dilated fundoscopy, the right optic disc was pale, consistent with optic atrophy and a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.3, while the left optic disc was swollen with a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.3. A relative afferent pupillary defect was present in the right eye. The patient was started on a course of oral prednisolone and referred for neuroimaging and neurology consultation.

A 25-year-old man presented with progressive swelling of the left middle finger. His family first noticed the swelling after direct trauma to the finger in early childhood. The finger was surgically excised at age four but the swelling recurred and continued to enlarge without pain or limitation of motion. He had no neurological symptoms, no family history of musculoskeletal deformities, and no constitutional complaints. On examination there was a healed scar over the dorsal aspect of the left middle finger and a soft, fatty, lobulated mass distal to the proximal interphalangeal joint, with macrodactyly of the middle finger. There was full range of motion of all finger joints, normal neurovascular status of the fingertip, no signs of inflammation, no lymphadenopathy, and no stigmata of neurofibromatosis. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. Plain radiographs of the left hand showed a heterogeneous lobulated soft-tissue mass on the volar aspect of the middle and distal phalanges without arthritic changes. Magnetic resonance imaging with intravenous contrast showed distal fatty overgrowth with striated appearance and no capsulation surrounding the middle and distal phalanges of the middle finger, most pronounced on the palmar aspect.

A 22-year-old woman fell down stairs onto her right buttock. She subsequently developed an antalgic gait and pain in the right inferior gluteal area radiating to the proximal posterior thigh, worsened by sitting and squatting. Initial MRI performed a few days after injury demonstrated an extensive hematoma involving the quadratus femoris and obturator externus muscles, consistent with a grade II strain. She was treated with NSAIDs but had no improvement.

Six months later she was referred for persistent sciatica. Examination revealed tenderness at the right ischial tuberosity, reduced strength of right hip external rotators, reproduction of symptoms on straight-leg raise at 30° with a positive Lasegue test, and pain on passive hip internal rotation with positive Freiberg and FADIR tests. Vascular and lumbar spine examinations were normal. Radiographs of the hip, pelvis, and lumbar spine were unremarkable. Laboratory studies excluded infection and coagulopathy. Based on these findings, the initial clinical impression was piriformis syndrome. 

A repeat MRI showed minimal resolution of the hematoma in the quadratus femoris and obturator internus muscles and persistent high signal at the bone-tendon junction of the quadratus femoris. A one-month course of external rotator strengthening failed to improve her symptoms, and CT-guided drainage was not possible due to absence of a discrete fluid collection. Surgical exploration was then planned.

A 73-year-old woman was evaluated for persistent right groin pain and a leg-length discrepancy since an uncemented right hemiarthroplasty performed 6 months earlier for a fragility fracture. On examination, she had tenderness in the groin and limited internal rotation of the hip. Laboratory studies showed a normal white-cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein. Fluoroscopically guided aspiration of the hip joint yielded a turbid, green, “pea-soup like” fluid. Microbiologic cultures were negative. Serum cobalt and chromium levels were 34 and 7 nanomoles per litre, respectively. Magnetic resonance imaging of the hip demonstrated periprosthetic fluid but no soft-tissue compromise or pseudotumour formation. An intra-articular injection of local anaesthetic provided temporary relief and confirmed the hip as the source of her pain.

A 39-year-old man with HIV infection presented with progressive muscle weakness and an 8 kg unintended weight loss over 2 weeks. He reported watery stools twice daily for 3 months without fever or other signs of acute infection. HIV had been diagnosed 3 months earlier with an initial viral load of 1 120 000 copies/mL and a CD4+ count of 38 cells/µL; workup at that time revealed disseminated Mycobacterium avium infection, cytomegalovirus infection (9 500 IU/mL), and AIDS-related wasting. His history also included diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (primary gastric, stage I E) treated with R-CHOP 15 months earlier, now in remission.

He was adherent to daily abacavir/lamivudine/dolutegravir and rifabutin, ethambutol, and clarithromycin. He took no thiazide diuretics or vitamin D supplements.

On examination, he appeared cachectic and hypovolemic but afebrile. Laboratory studies showed serum calcium 3.27 mmol/L, creatinine 1.77 mg/dL, C-reactive protein 3.8 mg/dL, albumin 3.0 g/dL, and normal LDH. Abdominal ultrasound excluded postrenal obstruction but revealed splenomegaly with inhomogeneous parenchyma. Intravenous fluids and furosemide were started, but serum calcium and creatinine rose further (calcium not retaken, creatinine 3.64 mg/dL). Repeat testing showed HIV RNA 170 copies/mL, CD4+ count 152 cells/µL, B-cell count 1 cell/µL, suppressed PTH, and elevated calcitriol at 118 pg/mL. An ^18FDG-PET/CT scan demonstrated cervical, mediastinal, abdominal, and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy.

A 31‐year‐old woman in labor at 36.2 weeks’ gestation (gravida 4, para 3) was admitted for delivery. Her obstetric history was notable for obstetric hemorrhage during her second delivery and an anaphylactic reaction to ketorolac after her third cesarean section. She had allergies to acetaminophen, ketorolac, and penicillin. 

An epidural anesthetic with lidocaine and adrenaline was placed uneventfully, but 5 minutes later she developed hypotension (blood pressure 60/40 mmHg), dyspnea, and desaturation (SpO₂ 84% on 7 L/min O₂). She was intubated and treated with intramuscular adrenaline 1 mg for presumed anaphylactic shock, and underwent emergency cesarean section with minimal bleeding. Persistent hypotension was managed with two 500 mL normal‐saline boluses and a noradrenaline infusion (5 μg/min). 

On arrival to the intensive care unit she was sedated on mechanical ventilation (FiO₂ 35%, SpO₂ 99%), with mean arterial pressure 70 mmHg on noradrenaline. Examination revealed normal heart sounds, no jugular venous distention, clear lungs, normal peripheral pulses, and no edema. 

Electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm, new ST‐segment depressions in leads V3–V6, II, III, and aVF, and ST‐segment elevation in lead aVR. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a normal‐sized left ventricle with basal segment dyskinesia, apical hyperkinesia, and an ejection fraction of 48%; there was no significant valvular disease and estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure was 26 mmHg. 

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 12 g/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, lactate 2.6 mmol/L, and troponin I 1276 ng/L.

A 60-year-old man with hypertension underwent open right hemicolectomy for ascending colon adenocarcinoma (pT3N0M0, high-risk stage II) 2 years earlier. Vessel ligations and a hand-sewn ileocolic anastomosis were performed using silk sutures and 3-0 Monocryl. He received adjuvant oral tegafur/uracil and was followed every 3 months without complications.  
Recent contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed a new infiltrative heterogeneous soft tissue lesion near the right mesenteric root adjacent to the ileocolic anastomosis, causing tissue traction and small-bowel adhesion. Two months later, MRI showed lesion progression with hypointensity on T2, moderate postcontrast enhancement, hyperintensity on diffusion-weighted imaging, and water restriction on the ADC map. PET/CT was not performed.  
He denied fever, abdominal pain, nausea, or other symptoms. Tumor markers were mildly elevated: CEA 2.50 ng/mL (3 months earlier 2.43 ng/mL) and CA 19-9 50.61 U/mL (3 months earlier 33.51 U/mL). Local recurrence was suspected, and the patient elected surgical resection.

A 68-year-old man with biopsy-proven prostate cancer and a prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level >250 ng/mL underwent hormonal therapy after a baseline 99Tc-MDP whole-body bone scintigram showed multiple metastatic lesions in the vertebral column, ribs, left scapula, left fronto-orbital region, pelvis, and right proximal femur. There was also faint, diffuse uptake in the left hemi-pelvis, deemed insufficient at that time for a diagnosis of active Paget’s disease. He received local radiotherapy for back and right hip pain. Post-therapy PSA returned to normal (0.31 ng/mL). One year later, he presented with new-onset left hip pain. A repeat bone scintigram demonstrated total disappearance of all previously noted metastatic lesions except for persistent, faint focal uptake in the right fourth rib, and diffuse, low-grade uptake in the left hemi-pelvis.

A 28-year-old man was admitted with a seven-month history of malaise, fever, and headache, recently accompanied by increased cough and chest pain. His past history included hepatosplenomegaly, generalized lymphadenopathy, pleural effusion, hemoptysis, pancytopenia, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and plasma cell dyscrasia; he had discontinued therapy during prior hospitalizations. On admission to the infectious diseases ward, his mental status was normal and there were no skin or ocular lesions. Laboratory studies showed WBC 1.9×10^3 cells/mm^3, RBC 3.11×10^6 cells/mm^3, platelets 86×10^3 cells/mm^3, hemoglobin 6.2 g/dL, serum procalcitonin 0.068 ng/mL, and CRP 67.8 mg/L. A nasopharyngeal RT-PCR was positive for SARS-CoV-2 and chest CT demonstrated bilateral lung involvement; chest X-ray showed a right lobar pneumonia. Brain MRI revealed multiple hyperintense lesions in white matter. During the hospitalization, he developed dizziness, vomiting, sweating, and hyponatremia. An initial lumbar puncture revealed an elevated opening pressure, CSF WBC count 50 cells/mm^3 (70% neutrophils, 30% lymphocytes), glucose 35 mg/dL, protein 71 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 64 mg/dL, adenosine deaminase 10.9 U/L, and CSF procalcitonin 0.084 ng/mL.

A 67-year-old African-American woman with lifelong severe hypercholesterolemia was evaluated for persistent corneal arcus and tendon xanthomas.  
• At age 11, she developed bilateral arcus and tendinous xanthomas; total cholesterol was >1,000 mg/dL. Rapid xanthoma growth led to resection of elbow and knee lesions at age 12. A partial ileal bypass at age 12 lowered cholesterol to 608 mg/dL, and she was placed on a low-cholesterol diet.  
• Psychosocial history included parental abuse, suicidal ideation, and becoming a ward of the state at age 13 years.  
• Family history: father had arcus, hypercholesterolemia, and fatal myocardial infarction at age 60; mother had hypercholesterolemia; three siblings presumed heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia; one daughter with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia.  
• Lipid-lowering treatments:  
  – Age 21: clofibrate and probucol (discontinued for rash and pregnancy)  
  – Age 21–26: cholestyramine (paused for hemorrhoids), restarted when LDL-C rose to the high 400s mg/dL  
  – Age 29: nicotinic acid, titrated to 1 g three times daily  
  – Age 32: lovastatin, increased to 40 mg twice daily  
• At age 33, she developed exertional chest pain. Echocardiogram showed preserved left ventricular ejection fraction; cardiac catheterization revealed 100% occlusion of the right coronary artery, 99% of the first diagonal branch of the left anterior descending artery, and 40% of the left circumflex artery.  
• Age 34–40: plasmapheresis and then lipoprotein apheresis, which acutely reduced LDL-C from ~500 to 60 mg/dL after each session.  
• Age 42: lovastatin switched to atorvastatin 80 mg daily; age 61: evolocumab 420 mg monthly added; age 62: apheresis discontinued; age 66: ezetimibe 10 mg daily initiated.  
• At age 67, physical examination was notable for bilateral corneal arcus and xanthomas over both Achilles’ and patellar tendons and interdigitally.

A 42-year-old man originally from North Africa, with a history of alcoholism and recurrent epigastric pain, presented with 3 days of severe central epigastric pain radiating to the back and worsened by lying supine, accompanied by nausea. He had no other significant medical history. On examination, there was a firm, palpable mass in the left hypochondrium and epigastrium. Laboratory studies showed a lipase level of 1500 U/L (normal, 0–70), moderate hepatic cytolysis (ALT, 241 U/L; AST, 403 U/L), a WBC count of 65.29×10^3/mm^3, a CRP level of 320 mg/L, and mildly altered renal function. At 72 hours after symptom onset, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed an enlarged, homogeneously enhancing pancreatic gland with extensive peripancreatic fat stranding and fluid collections consistent with stage E pancreatitis, and a well-defined 155×65 mm cystic mass in the pancreatic tail that communicated with the dilated main pancreatic duct and appeared to fistulize into the adjacent gastric wall.

An 88-year-old Caucasian woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension (ambulatory 145/90 mmHg), and Parkinson disease was referred for evaluation of a one-week history of an asymptomatic white area on her hard palate. During the initial four days she had a temperature as high as 38°C and noted an unintentional weight loss of 5 kg. On oral examination, the lesion was nonraised, occupied over half the hard palate, and had a well-demarcated fibrinous border corresponding to a vascular territory. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL, white blood cell count 6300 cells/μL (55% neutrophils), serum creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 107 mm/hour. Serum antigen tests for hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, and parvovirus B19 were negative. A test for anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies was also negative. Given these findings, an incisional biopsy of the peripheral margin was performed under local anesthesia.

An 18-year-old man presented with a two-week history of fever to 40°C, headaches, night sweats, and diffuse arthralgias. He had received two weeks of ampicillin/sulbactam without improvement. He lived on his parents’ farm, caring for cattle, chickens, and cats, and had traveled to Turkey three months earlier. He was currently in military service. 

On examination, he was febrile with bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy and otherwise unremarkable vital signs. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 11.41 mg/dL, a white-cell count of 9.21 G/L with lymphopenia (16%), and normal hemoglobin and platelet counts. Ampicillin/sulbactam was discontinued and serial blood cultures; serologic testing for Entamoeba, Francisella tularensis, and Brucella spp.; broad-spectrum fungal, bacterial, and viral PCRs; and a QuantiFeron-TB test were all negative. Screening for autoimmune disease including rheumatoid factor, c-ANCA, and p-ANCA was also negative.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen revealed multiple hypodense lesions in the liver and spleen (largest, 2 cm) and subchondral sclerosis with erosion of the anterior vertebral bodies of the thoracic spine, most prominently at T7. MRI of the thoracic spine confirmed a ventral base-plate fracture of T7 with 20% height loss and bone-marrow edema, findings suggestive of an infectious process.

A 25-year-old woman presented to the emergency department complaining of left-sided vaginal pain and swelling that began approximately five hours earlier and was progressively worsening. She described severe, throbbing pain that prevented comfortable sitting or walking. The patient reported five episodes of sexual intercourse over a two-hour period the day before and had applied ice afterward. She denied abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, or discharge and had no history of medical problems, including sickle cell disease or bleeding disorders. She was not on medications and had no known allergies. 

On examination, she was in mild distress from pain. Vital signs were: temperature 36.1° C; blood pressure 123/86 mm Hg; pulse 96 beats/min; respiratory rate 14 breaths/min; oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal examinations were normal. Genitourinary examination revealed marked swelling of the left labia majora and minora; the area was dark, firm, and tender to palpation. A speculum examination was deferred due to pain.

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, basic metabolic profile, coagulation studies, D-dimer, urinalysis, and urine pregnancy test, were all within normal limits. The gynecology service was consulted, and a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the pelvis was obtained.

A 27-year-old woman, one month postpartum after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery, presented to the emergency department after an episode of syncope and with a complaint of heavy vaginal bleeding. She reported a history of heavy bleeding at delivery but had been well until three days ago, when she noted light spotting. Thirty minutes before arrival, she experienced syncope and then heavy vaginal bleeding associated with mild suprapubic pain. She denied fever, foul discharge, or other symptoms. 

Her past medical and surgical history was unremarkable. On arrival, her blood pressure was 118/70 mm Hg, pulse 103 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, temperature 36.6 °C, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. She appeared anxious and pale and had a small abrasion on the bridge of her nose. Abdominal examination revealed mild suprapubic tenderness; the uterus was not palpable above the pubic symphysis. Pelvic examination showed active bleeding and clots obscuring the cervical os, which was otherwise closed after suctioning. 

Initial laboratory studies revealed a normal hemoglobin concentration and a negative serum human chorionic gonadotropin level.

A 7-year-old girl presented with a 6-month history of an asymptomatic, diffuse, bony-hard swelling of the left mandible and intermittent nausea, vomiting, and abdominal cramps. On extraoral examination, there was a painless, hard swelling from the left mandibular body to the pre-auricular area; intraorally, there was buccolingual expansion from tooth 36 to the ascending ramus with normal overlying mucosa. Baseline blood testing showed hyponatremic, hypochloremic metabolic acidosis (Na+ 134 mmol/L; Cl− 92 mmol/L; HCO₃− 14 mmol/L; anion gap 33 mmol/L), treated with fluids and antiemetics. A panoramic radiograph revealed a poorly defined, multilocular radiolucency in the left mandibular body extending to the condylar and coronoid processes, with bowing of the inferior border and inferior displacement of an unerupted tooth. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a 42×34×45 mm expansile, lytic, multilocular lesion of the left mandibular body and ramus with areas of cortical perforation. A provisional radiographic diagnosis included central giant cell granuloma, unicystic ameloblastoma, or aneurysmal bone cyst. An incisional biopsy showed mononuclear spindle to ovoid cells with numerous multinucleated osteoclastic giant cells in a loose, fibrovascular stroma, consistent with a giant cell lesion.

A 66-year-old woman (BMI 28) with highly symptomatic atrial fibrillation and atypical atrial flutters was referred for single-chamber pacemaker implantation with left-bundle branch area pacing and planned atrioventricular node ablation. Her history included two prior AF ablations, recurrent atrial arrhythmias despite cardioversions and maximal rate control, an Amplatzer closure device for secundum atrial septal defect, and amiodarone-induced hyperthyroidism. On examination 3 months after her last ablation, she was in atrial fibrillation with a heart rate of 130 bpm on bisoprolol 10 mg daily. Laboratory studies, including serum electrolytes, renal function, hemoglobin, and thyroid parameters, were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal left ventricular ejection fraction, a dilated left atrium (83 mL/m2), and moderate mitral and tricuspid regurgitation.

The patient consented to device implantation under local anaesthesia (lidocaine), intravenous nalbuphine, and midazolam. After creating the left deltopectoral pocket, an experienced operator attempted axillary venous puncture using the second rib as a fluoroscopic landmark. Despite venous blood return, neither standard nor hydrophilic guidewires could be advanced. A venogram via ipsilateral peripheral access with diluted iodixanol revealed significant spasm of the axillary vein. The operator then attempted left subclavian vein puncture; again, no blood could be aspirated. A second venogram showed progression of the calibre reduction, now affecting both the axillary and subclavian veins.
