A 70-year-old current smoker (80 pack-years) with hypertension and a history of colon cancer presented two months after a brainstem hemorrhage caused by a cavernous malformation. At that time, MRI had also shown multiple nodules suspected to be brain metastases, which resolved after medical management. On admission, vital signs were: temperature 35.9 °C, heart rate 103 bpm, blood pressure 107/71 mmHg, SpO₂ 95% on room air; the neurologic examination was normal.

Laboratory studies revealed a pro–gastrin-releasing peptide level of 541.5 pg/mL (normal <77.8 pg/mL), carcinoembryonic antigen 2.5 ng/mL, and cytokeratin fragment 21-1 at 1.7 ng/mL. Chest CT showed two nodules in the right lower lobe with hilar lymphadenopathy. A clinical diagnosis of extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer was made. He was treated with carboplatin (AUC 5), etoposide (100 mg/m²), and atezolizumab (1200 mg). Three weeks later, he underwent whole-brain irradiation (3 × 10 Gy).

Four weeks after the initiation of chemotherapy, he developed tactile and pain disturbances in the L2–L3 dermatomes. Examination revealed loss of bilateral patellar and Achilles tendon reflexes, no motor weakness, a negative Babinski sign, a positive lower limb Barre test, dysmetria on finger–nose–finger and knee–heel testing, and an ataxic gait.

Lumbar puncture showed a CSF protein of 146 mg/dL, glucose 156 mg/dL, one mononuclear cell per μL, and no malignant cells. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI demonstrated decreased size of known metastatic lesions and no new hemorrhage. Contrast-enhanced lumbar spine MRI revealed nerve root compression at the L2–L3 level without abnormal peripheral nerve enhancement. Nerve conduction studies showed absent sensory nerve action potentials in the sural nerves with preserved motor conduction.

A 21-year-old woman with a 3.5-year history of bipolar disorder was admitted for a manic episode characterized by aggression, irritability, pressured speech, decreased need for sleep, and racing thoughts without psychotic features. She had two prior hospitalizations: a depressive episode with two suicide attempts three years ago and a manic episode with psychotic features 1.5 years ago. Following the second episode, she received monthly flupentixol decanoate, most recently 1.5 months before admission, and had discontinued biperiden and lithium therapy five months prior. Family history was notable for major depressive disorder in her mother and sister. She had no medical comorbidities, no history of brain trauma, autistic disorder, or withdrawal from benzodiazepines or alcohol. Laboratory studies were within normal limits except for severe vitamin B12 deficiency attributed to vegetarianism. Brain MRI was normal. On examination, she was noncooperative, with an irritable mood and congruent affect, pressured speech, and full orientation. Vital signs were normal, and there were no tremor, rigidity, or other extrapyramidal signs. Over three weeks, she remained nonresponsive to lithium (up to 1200 mg/day, serum level 1 mg/dL), quetiapine (up to 600 mg/day), and biperiden (4 mg/day), leading to tapering and discontinuation of lithium. Bitemporal ECT was then administered every other day at 25% energy, producing seizures of 22–45 seconds under IV atropine, succinylcholine, and thiopental. After the fourth session, she exhibited some negativism; following the fifth session, she developed waxy flexibility, posturing, negativism, mutism, and echolalia. Vital signs remained normal, with no autonomic dysfunction or extrapyramidal signs.

A 43‐year‐old man with hypertension, hyperuricemia, android obesity and bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome presented with intermittent right lumbar pain. On examination, a firm epigastric mass was palpated; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. 

Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 24 × 15 × 13 cm partially cystic mass in the epigastric region, situated between the left hepatic lobe, stomach, pancreas and transverse colon. Laboratory studies showed a carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) level of 281 µg/L and a normal CA 19-9 level. 

MRI demonstrated a well‐defined cystic lesion in the epigastric region abutting the gastric antrum, pancreas, spleen and hepatic hilum, with no clear communication to the gastric lumen. 

^18F-FDG PET-CT showed moderate hypermetabolic uptake in the posterior wall of the lesion, without definitive features of benignity or malignancy. 

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed extrinsic compression of the gastric body with intact, normal‐appearing mucosa.

A 70-year-old woman was admitted with acute dyspnea and orthopnea of a few hours’ duration. She had COPD (Gold II) on home oxygen, chronic respiratory insufficiency, heart failure (NYHA III), insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, and BMI 44.1. In the emergency department, ABGs showed respiratory acidosis with hypoxemia (pH 7.349; pCO2 56.2 mmHg; pO2 65.5 mmHg; O2 sat 82%), blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, heart rate 84 bpm. Chest radiograph showed no abnormalities; blood glucose was 450 mg/dL. She was diagnosed with an acute COPD exacerbation, stabilized, and transferred to pulmonology.

Over a 16-day hospitalization, her respiratory status improved. Routine urine sediment examination revealed 25–30 leukocytes and 8–10 squamous epithelial cells per field, rare bacteria, and mobile parasitic trophozoites; urine culture was negative. Microscopy identified two distinct protozoa by morphology and motility:

• Ciliates (~40 × 20 μm) that were kidney-shaped, bore short cilia, had a cystotome cleft one-third from the anterior end, a posterior contractile vacuole, an ovoid macronucleus, and multiple food vacuoles.  
• Flagellates (~15 × 10 μm) that were egg-shaped with a pointed anterior end, a centrally located spherical nucleus, a posterior spherical inclusion, and two flagella 1.5–2 times body length.

Under 40× magnification, ~20 flagellate trophozoites per field and fewer ciliates were seen. Chronologically, the first urine sample contained both protozoa, subsequent samples contained only the flagellate, and the final pre-discharge sample showed no trophozoites. No cysts were observed in any sample.

A 31-year-old woman presented with 4 weeks of menorrhagia and 3 weeks of lethargy, palpitations, exertional dyspnea, postural dizziness, syncopal episodes, headache, and vomiting. She initially denied visual symptoms but later reported 2 weeks of pulsatile tinnitus, intermittent blurred vision, and transient visual obscurations; 3 days of neck pain and photophobia; and 2 days of mild clumsiness of the right arm and hand with numbness of the right scalp and fingertips. Her body mass index was 24, and her medical, drug, and family history were unremarkable.

On examination, she was afebrile and mildly hypotensive (87/62 mmHg). Best-corrected visual acuity was 6/9 in the right eye and 6/6 in the left eye. There was severe papilledema (Frisén grade 5) and a partial right lateral rectus palsy. Color vision, pupillary responses, intraocular pressure, anterior segment, peripheral retina, and other cranial nerves were normal. Goldmann perimetry revealed an enlarged left blind spot and concentric peripheral constriction bilaterally. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated peripapillary and macular subretinal fluid.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 74 g/L, mean cell volume 63.0 fL, platelet count 584×10^9/L, and peripheral smear with microcytic hypochromic red cells and anisopoikilocytosis. Iron studies confirmed iron deficiency (serum iron 2.2 μmol/L; total iron binding capacity 94.7 μmol/L; transferrin saturation 2.3%; ferritin 2 μg/L). Serum chemistry, liver function, renal function, thyroid function, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, clotting screen, C-reactive protein, vitamin B12, and folate were normal. Transvaginal ultrasound, infection and autoimmune screens were negative.

An urgent CT head and CT venogram showed no intracerebral lesions, bilateral focal narrowing at the transverse–sigmoid junctions (more conspicuous on the left), filling defects in the proximal right sigmoid sinus consistent with arachnoid granulations, and no evidence of venous sinus thrombosis. There was prominence of the perioptic cerebrospinal fluid spaces with minimal flattening of the sclera, especially on the left.

A 52-year-old man with a history of coronary stent placement and living-donor kidney transplantation (on prednisolone 5 mg daily and mycophenolate mofetil 360 mg twice daily) presented with a 2-week history of positional vertigo and a 3-day history of tinnitus, ear pressure, and left-ear hearing loss. He denied other neurologic complaints.  

On neurologic examination, Weber lateralized to the right, there was bilateral nasolabial-fold blunting, and truncal ataxia; other cranial nerves, motor, sensory, cerebellar testing, and otoscopic examination were unremarkable. The initial impression was multiple cranial nerve palsy.  

Brain MRI showed bilateral facial nerve enhancement (left > right) and subtle FLAIR hyperintensity with T1 hypointensity in the left temporal white matter. He was admitted with an initial diagnosis of Ramsay–Hunt syndrome and received intravenous dexamethasone, oral methylprednisolone, famciclovir, and intratympanic dexamethasone, which aggravated bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. He was then referred to neurology with the impression of encephalitis of infectious or autoimmune etiology.  

CSF examination showed 8 leukocytes/µL (75% lymphocytes), a normal protein level (39 mg/dL), and negative Gram stain, bacterial culture, and cryptococcal antigen. CSF PCR was positive for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and negative for mycobacteria, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, varicella zoster virus (VZV), and John Cunningham virus (JCV). Serum JCV PCR was positive. EBV viral capsid antigen IgG was positive, but IgM was negative.  

After 2 weeks of antiviral treatment, follow-up brain MRI demonstrated FLAIR hyperintensity and T1 hypointensity in the subcortical white matter of the left temporal lobe and dorsal pons, suggesting lymphoproliferative disease or progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. Whole-body PET revealed no abnormal hypermetabolism. An initial workup including ganglioside antibodies, antinuclear antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, angiotensin-converting enzyme level, aquaporin-4 IgG, myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein IgG, vitamin B12, and folate levels was normal.

A 35-year-old Congolese immigrant man presented with 1 week of colicky abdominal pain and progressive abdominal distension, 3 days of nonbilious vomiting, and failure to pass stool or flatus. He also reported 5 days of worsening dyspnea. He had no history of prior abdominal surgery, trauma, or chronic constipation.

On examination, he was alert and lying with knees flexed, with sunken eyes and dry mucous membranes. Blood pressure was 130/96 mmHg, pulse 97/min, temperature 37.0 °C, respiratory rate 20/min, and SpO2 86% on room air. A right chest tube had been placed on admission for presumed pneumothorax but produced no drainage or bubbling.

Cardiopulmonary exam revealed distended right external jugular vein, hyperinflation and reduced expansion of the right hemithorax, mild right-sided tenderness, leftward tracheal deviation, and an apex beat at the 6th intercostal space on the left anterior axillary line. Percussion was hyperresonant on the right with absent breath sounds; the left lung had normal vesicular sounds.

Abdominal exam showed moderate distension without respiratory movement, visible bowel loops in the left upper quadrant, tenderness and firmness without guarding or rebound, and absent bowel sounds. Rectal exam revealed an empty rectum.

Imaging studies:
– Chest X-ray: a grossly dilated bowel loop beneath an elevated right hemidiaphragm, collapse of the right lung, and mediastinal shift to the left.  
– Erect abdominal X-ray: multiple air-fluid levels.  
– Right chest point-of-care ultrasound: pleural sliding in the upper chest, dense echogenic components and fluid in the lower chest at the diaphragm level.  
– Abdominal ultrasound: grossly distended bowel loops with no free intraperitoneal fluid.

A 34-year-old Hispanic woman was admitted with a 2-week history of a painful, nonhealing infra-umbilical wound. Two weeks earlier she noted scabs in the infra-umbilical area that became pruritic and irritated; she applied plain gauze and petrolatum, but the scabs evolved into tender ulcers.  

Her medical history included end-stage renal disease secondary to amphotericin-B–induced nephrotoxicity, managed with continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis for 5 years; secondary hyperparathyroidism (intact PTH as high as 2400 pg/mL and outpatient phosphorus 10 mg/dL six months ago); gastroesophageal reflux disease; obesity; anemia of chronic kidney disease; and prior disseminated coccidioidomycosis. She reported nonadherence to phosphate binders due to financial constraints. Home medications included sevelamer carbonate. She denied tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drug use.

Her peritoneal dialysis regimen was 4 daily exchanges of 2 L 2.5% dextrose solution, with a weekly Kt/V of 2.1 and no residual renal function.  

On examination, she was morbidly obese and in mild distress from abdominal pain. Vital signs were normal. Abdominal inspection revealed multiple tender, indurated ulcers with surrounding erythema and black eschar in the lower abdomen and exposed subcutaneous tissue with granulation in the lateral walls.  

Laboratory studies showed WBC 21 000/mm3, hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL, platelets 526 000/mm3, sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 3.4 mmol/L, BUN 59 mg/dL, creatinine 13.26 mg/dL, albumin 3.3 g/dL, calcium 8.6 mg/dL, phosphorus 8.3 mg/dL, intact PTH 712 pg/mL, and CRP 129.8 mg/L. Peritoneal dialysis fluid and blood cultures were negative for infection.  

CT of the abdomen and pelvis with and without contrast revealed anterior abdominal wall subcutaneous calcification.

A 50-year-old male farmer presented with an 18-month history of a slowly enlarging, painless swelling over the dorsum of the right foot that developed multiple nodules and serosanguinous discharge. He denied any history of trauma, diabetes, or other systemic disease. Three months earlier, he was treated empirically for tuberculosis without improvement. On examination, the right foot was grossly swollen with intense erythema, numerous well-demarcated nodular lesions, and multiple discharging sinuses obstructed by dried pus. The discharge was yellowish, purulent, and foul smelling without any apparent granules. Tenderness was present; pitting edema extended to the knee. The patient had low-grade fever. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10 g/dl, WBC count 11,900/mm3 with 80% neutrophils, and an ESR of 40 mm/h. HIV serology, liver and renal function tests, and electrolytes were normal. Radiographs of the right foot revealed soft-tissue density in the interphalangeal and metatarsal spaces without bony involvement. A sample of the purulent discharge was obtained for microscopy. On Gram’s stain, thin, branching, Gram-positive filamentous bacilli were seen. On modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain (1% H2SO4 decolorizer), the filaments were weakly acid fast.

A 53-year-old Indian man with hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and chronic kidney disease presented with sudden visual impairment in both eyes followed minutes later by a brief generalized tonic–clonic seizure. He had no prior history of epilepsy or substance abuse, but a history of skin abscesses attributed to poor glycemic control. In the emergency department, he was postictal—agitated and drowsy—without focal deficits. Laboratory studies showed:  
• Random plasma glucose, 581 mg/dL; HbA1c, 11.4%; serum ketones, negative.  
• Serum sodium, 136 mEq/L; creatinine, 2.9 mg/dL.  
Lumbar puncture yielded normal cerebrospinal fluid, and noncontrast head CT was unremarkable. Intravenous phenytoin, insulin infusion, and hydration were initiated. 

After regaining consciousness, examination revealed a complete right homonymous hemianopia. Multiple brief complex partial seizures were observed, characterized by rightward head and eye deviation, right-sided nystagmus, and impaired awareness, each lasting about 60 seconds. Brain MRI demonstrated focal hypointensity in the left occipital lobe on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences. Conventional scalp EEG recorded three seizures, each beginning with high-amplitude fast activity over the left occipital region with ipsilateral and contralateral spread, followed by gradual postictal slowing.

A 21-day-old female newborn was admitted for widespread skin redness and blistering. The illness began with sore throat and conjunctivitis. Within 48 hours she developed fever and tender erythema that progressed to generalized erythematous lesions, predominantly in the axillary and groin regions, associated with large, fragile, superficial blisters that ruptured with minimal pressure and left extensive denuded skin; the Nikolsky sign was positive. 

Maternal history was notable for an otherwise uneventful pregnancy except for hemoglobin AC trait; she received Tanakan, Folifer, and Fansidar at 26 and 32 weeks and used traditional medicines from the third month until delivery. Vaginal delivery at 40 weeks under epidural anesthesia resulted in a birth weight of 3.7 kg, length of 45 cm, head circumference of 33 cm, and Apgar scores of 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes.

On admission, the newborn was afebrile (36.2 °C), with a respiratory rate of 45 breaths/min, heart rate of 120 beats/min, and normally colored integuments. Skin examination revealed peeling and widespread blisters over the lower limbs extending to the trunk, with large erythematous, eroded, oozing areas covered by epidermal flaps. Mucous membranes were intact. Genital examination showed blisters on the labia that bled on contact. Other systems were normal. The detached skin area was estimated at 31.35% of the body surface. Laboratory tests showed a marked inflammatory syndrome with a positive C-reactive protein level.  

Three differential diagnoses were evoked: (1) toxic epidermal necrolysis drug induced (Lyell syndrome), (2) Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS), and (3) Staphylococcal Shock.

A 44-year-old man presented with his first episode of a hemodynamically unstable sustained ventricular tachycardia (VT) with a cycle length of 250 ms, which required two electrical cardioversions by emergency medical services. He reported sudden palpitations, fatigue, and mild dyspnea while cycling; no chest pain. His medical history was remarkable only for a self-inflicted thoracic gunshot wound at age 16, with emergency cardiac surgery documenting a bullet perforation of the pericardium and contact with the anterolateral left ventricular surface. He had recovered fully, with no ongoing medications or illicit drug use, and maintained regular exercise. On admission, he was asymptomatic in stable sinus rhythm. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed elevated troponin I (187 pg/mL; normal <14 pg/mL) with normal creatine kinase. Electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus rhythm with flattened or inverted T waves in leads I, II, aVL, and V5–V6. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed normal biventricular function. Coronary angiography showed no coronary artery disease. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging identified a localized transmural myocardial scar with regional thinning in the mid–left ventricular free wall without any T2-weighted signal enhancement. Other differential diagnoses, including cardiac sarcoidosis, were considered but deemed unlikely based on the patient’s history and imaging findings.

A 3-month-old female infant, born at term by elective cesarean delivery to third-degree consanguineous parents, presented with pallor and dehydration following an upper respiratory infection. Psychomotor development was normal. On examination, her weight was 7 kg, length 63 cm, and head circumference 42 cm.

Laboratory studies revealed:
- Plasma glucose: 270 mg/L  
- HbA1c: 8.2%  
- Hemoglobin: 5.3 g/dL  
- White blood cell count with lymphocyte predominance; platelet count within normal limits  
- Abdominal ultrasound and echocardiography: no noteworthy findings  
- Peripheral blood smear: hypochromatic red cells with anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, histiocytes, and target cells  
- Bone marrow aspirate: normal cellularity with enhanced megaloblastic erythroblasts  
- Iron profile: low ferritin  
- Endocrine and metabolic tests: TSH 1.2 mLU/L; C-peptide 1.1 ng/mL; vitamin B9 20 ng/mL; vitamin B12 365 pg/mL (all within normal limits)  
- Auditory brainstem response testing: bilateral sensorineural hearing loss

A 25-year-old woman with known chronic rheumatic valvular heart disease presented in her third trimester with worsening exertional dyspnea, orthopnea requiring two pillows, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and lower-extremity edema. She also had a one-year history of episodic cough productive of blood-tinged sputum and recent pleuritic chest pain. Transthoracic echocardiography before intervention showed thickened and doming mitral leaflets with restricted motion, a mitral valve area of 1.2 cm2, a mean transmitral gradient of 24 mm Hg, pulmonary hypertension (systolic pressure 164 mm Hg), and preserved left ventricular systolic function; all other valves were normal. Her Wilkins score was <8. She underwent percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty using a 25 mm Mansfield balloon, with resolution of her symptoms. She delivered a healthy term infant without complications.

Forty-five days after the procedure, she developed high-grade persistent fever, easy fatigability, weight loss, headache, reddish urine, epigastric pain, and three days of postprandial crampy abdominal pain. She denied swelling, jaundice, palpitations, chills, or rigors. On examination, temperature was 38.9 °C, blood pressure 110/60 mm Hg, pulse 104 beats/min, respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. Lung fields were clear. Jugular venous pressure was not elevated. Cardiac auscultation revealed a grade II holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the left axilla. There was mild hepatomegaly and a positive splenic percussion note. Neurologic examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory tests showed WBC 10,500/mm3 (81% neutrophils), hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, platelets 162,000/mm3, ESR 42 mm/h, and normal renal and liver function. Two sets of blood cultures were negative. HIV, VDRL, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C antibody tests were nonreactive. Current transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a thickened mitral valve with restricted motion, a mitral valve area of 1.8 cm2, a mean gradient of 11 mm Hg, pulmonary hypertension (120 mm Hg), preserved left ventricular function, and structurally normal other valves.

A 40-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 0 at 21 weeks of gestation, presented with 5 days of sudden, severe frontoparietal headache, projectile non-bilious vomiting, right eyelid droop, and bilateral visual deterioration, with altered sensorium for 3 days. She denied fever, neck stiffness, trauma, abdominal pain, per-vaginal bleeding, or rash. Her antenatal course had been uneventful.

On arrival, she appeared ill but hemodynamically stable; Glasgow Coma Scale was 14 (E3V5M6). Neuro-ophthalmologic examination revealed that she could count fingers with the right eye and had vision of 1/60 in the left. Right ptosis was present, and the right pupil was 4 mm with a sluggish light reaction and a Grade I relative afferent pupillary defect; the left pupil was normal. Fundoscopy showed disc and macular edema in the right eye. Other cranial nerves were intact. Motor strength was 4+/5 in all limbs; reflexes and tone were normal, but plantar responses were upgoing bilaterally. The rest of the neurologic and systemic examinations were unremarkable. Obstetric examination confirmed a 20-week uterus with palpable fetal parts.

She was initially treated at a local center for impending eclampsia with intravenous magnesium sulfate and transferred for further care. Laboratory studies showed sodium 147 mmol/L, potassium 2.6 mmol/L, elevated uric acid, ALT 237 U/L, AST 142 U/L, and prolactin >200 ng/mL. Obstetric ultrasound demonstrated a single live intrauterine pregnancy of 19 weeks + 2 days with placenta previa.

Because MRI was not feasible, a non-contrast CT scan of the head was obtained, which showed sellar and suprasellar hyperdensity with a cystic hypodensity lesion, findings suggestive of pituitary apoplexy on a pituitary adenoma.

An 86-year-old woman with a history of hepatic hydatid cyst diagnosed in 2012 presented in November 2016 with productive cough, yellowish-green sputum, mild shortness of breath, and a loss of appetite. She denied chest pain, fever, palpitations, nausea, vomiting, or changes in bowel or urinary habits. She lived in a rural area and had been on long-term antiparasitic medication, although the indication, type, and duration were not documented.

On examination, her lungs were clear with good bilateral air entry but fine crepitations were heard. Sputum culture grew scant normal respiratory flora, and a nasal swab was positive for rhinovirus. A chest radiograph showed a mass-like opacity in the right lower zone adjacent to the cardiac silhouette and a nonhomogenous airspace opacity in the left lower zone with a small left pleural effusion.

Contrast-enhanced thoracic CT demonstrated multiple intraluminal, well-circumscribed, fluid-attenuation filling defects in the right main pulmonary artery and its lobar branches, along with one large cystic lesion in the right lower lobe and another air-containing cystic lesion in the left lower lobe; minimal bilateral pleural effusions were also seen. MRI of the thorax confirmed a lesion within the right pulmonary trunk extending into the right lower lobe that was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images with internal septations, as well as cystic lesions in both lower lobes with adjacent atelectasis and a small left pleural effusion.

A 36-year-old woman was admitted with 72 hours of diffuse abdominal pain and fever. Over the preceding 3 months, she had experienced dry cough, night sweats, diarrhea, asthenia, hyporexia, an 8-kg weight loss, and swelling/pain of wrists, knees, and elbows limiting mobility. In May she had been diagnosed with Crohn’s disease and treated with proton pump inhibitors and prednisone without improvement. She had no toxic habits or significant past history.

On examination, vital signs were notable for fever; pulmonary auscultation revealed crackles in the right upper lobe. Laboratory tests showed a C-reactive protein level of 14 mg/L; other blood counts, biochemistry, and coagulation were normal. Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral interstitial and alveolar infiltrates predominating in the right lung with cavitations in the right upper lobe. Chest CT confirmed loss of volume in the right lung and bilateral pseudonodular infiltrates, predominantly in the right lung. 

Bronchoscopy showed 90% stenosis of the right upper‐lobe segmental bronchi. Bronchoaspirate PCR, culture, and bacilloscopy identified Mycobacterium tuberculosis sensitive to first-line agents. The patient began rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, and corticosteroids. Gastrointestinal biopsy revealed granulomatous inflammation in the submucosa and serosa; culture grew M. tuberculosis, and the Crohn’s diagnosis was revised to intestinal tuberculosis. She later underwent jejunal resection for perforation, with biopsy again positive for M. tuberculosis.

Two weeks after starting antituberculous therapy, she reported persistent migratory arthralgias, particularly in the left knee; examination revealed left knee monoarthritis without definitive synovitis. Full blood count, liver function, urate, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein were normal. Autoantibodies—rheumatoid factor, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies, antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and antistreptolysin O—were all negative. Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme and calcium were normal. Synovial fluid from the left knee contained 0.1 × 10^9 leukocytes/L with lymphocyte predominance and no crystals. Synovial biopsy showed mild chronic inflammation with no features of tuberculosis. Synovial fluid and tissue cultures and acid-fast bacilli smears were all negative.

A 32-year-old man presented with fever, chills, renal colic, and urinary obstruction. Five years earlier, he was diagnosed with cystinuria and multiple bilateral kidney stones, including staghorn calculi, which rendered his right kidney atrophic. Despite seven percutaneous nephrolithotomies (PCNLs), two extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsies, and one transurethral lithotripsy, he progressed to chronic kidney disease (baseline creatinine, 3.0 mg/dL) and had multiple hospitalizations for presumed pyelonephritis treated with intravenous antibiotics, antifungals, double-J stents, and nephrostomy tubes without lasting benefit.

Thirty-five days before the current admission, PCNL drained pus from the left renal pelvis; histology showed acute inflammation without evidence of malignancy. An abdominopelvic CT scan demonstrated multiple bilateral renal calculi, an atrophic right kidney (79 mm), and severe hydronephrosis of the left kidney (143 mm).

On presentation (day 0), temperature was 38.4 °C, heart rate 87 beats/min, blood pressure 120/85 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95%. Physical examination revealed left flank tenderness. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.3 g/dL, hematocrit 33.6%, WBC count 13,900 cells/mm³, BUN 29 mg/dL, creatinine 4.9 mg/dL, and C-reactive protein 93 mg/dL. Urinalysis revealed protein 2+, blood +, leukocyte esterase +, 10–12 RBCs/hpf, and 28–30 WBCs/hpf; urine culture was sterile. Immunologic tests (C3, C4, anti-dsDNA, ANA, C-ANCA, P-ANCA, anti-GBM) were within normal limits. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. He was started on intravenous antibiotics and underwent another PCNL on day +3.

A 38-year-old white man presented with daily, high-intensity, mechanical pain on the medial plantar surface at the base of his left great toe that began insidiously in October. He reported self-limited episodes of mild local swelling without overt erythema or warmth. He was an otherwise healthy athlete, playing soccer and tennis daily, and reported a family history of gout in his father. He did not take regular medications, denied smoking, and consumed alcohol in small to moderate amounts on weekends. 

On examination, vital signs were normal. There was limited dorsiflexion of the left hallux and mild swelling over the medial sesamoid region, with tenderness on palpation. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 14.4 g/dL, leukocytes 5570/mm3, platelets 208,000/mm3, uric acid 5.6 mg/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 11 mm/h, C-reactive protein negative, antinuclear factor negative, rheumatoid factor 5.3 U/mL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, and normal glucose and lipid profile. A 24-hour urinary uric acid excretion was 639 mg. 

Foot radiographs demonstrated a bilateral bipartite medial sesamoid. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left foot revealed a bipartite medial sesamoid with diffuse marrow edema, periarticular soft-tissue edema, small joint effusion, and a suspected stress fracture line. The patient was treated with an orthopedic boot for immobilization, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, intramuscular corticosteroid, and analgesics, with only partial and transient improvement. Four months later, he developed a similar painful syndrome in the right hallux.

An 81-year-old woman was found on the floor of her home after being missing for two days. Firefighters measured 180 ppm CO in the atmosphere and 234 ppm in her exhaled air. On arrival at the emergency department, her blood pressure was 143/92 mmHg, pulse 97 beats/min, temperature 35.7 °C, and Glasgow Coma Scale score was 13 (eyes to voice, confused but able to answer questions). Her medical history included left breast carcinoma resected 30 years earlier and a known duplicate superior vena cava. She had no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism.

On examination, both temples were swollen and tender; palpation of the scalp over the left parietal bone worsened the pain. Temporal pulses were palpable, and sinus palpation was nonpainful. Cardiopulmonary and upper airway examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a carboxyhemoglobin level of 13% (normal 0.5–1.5%), arterial blood gas with PaO₂ 31.3 mmHg (35–40 mmHg), PaCO₂ 38.9 mmHg (36–44 mmHg), oxyhemoglobin 61% (68–73%), oxygen saturation 70.6% (68–73%), and lactate 2.1 mmol/L (0.6–1.4 mmol/L). White blood cell count was 14.34 ×10³/μL (3.8–9.1) with neutrophils 12.81 ×10³/μL (1.5–5.4), C-reactive protein 129 mg/L (< 5), creatine phosphokinase 968 IU/L (< 170), troponin 0.26 ng/L (< 0.10), creatinine 83 μmol/L (eGFR 57 mL/min), and NT-proBNP 13 294 ng/L (< 125). Electrocardiography showed sinus rhythm with a normal ST segment. Oxygen therapy and intravenous isotonic saline were initiated.

A 29-year-old man was referred to the emergency department by his ophthalmologist after a blood pressure measurement of 250/150 mmHg and findings of retinal hemorrhages. He reported a 2-week history of blurred vision, a 2-month history of headache, and several days of unsteady gait. Family members noted recent confusion. He denied chest pain, dyspnea, arthralgias, urinary symptoms, smoking, illicit drug use, and over-the-counter intake except occasional ibuprofen. He had previously consumed alcohol heavily but had reduced intake 2 weeks earlier. He had no significant past medical history and no features of Cushing syndrome. On examination, his blood pressure was 250/150 mmHg, and an S4 gallop was auscultated. Neurologic exam was notable only for visual disturbance.

Laboratory studies showed creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, sodium 139 mEq/L, potassium 3.2 mEq/L, bicarbonate 21 mEq/L, chloride 109 mEq/L, hemoglobin 12.0 g/dL dropping to 10.5 g/dL the next day, indirect bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL (normal <0.5 mg/dL), lactate dehydrogenase 352 U/L, and low haptoglobin. A peripheral smear was negative for schistocytes. Repeat LDH and creatinine began to improve.

Brain MRI revealed extensive bilateral supratentorial and infratentorial subcortical hyperintensities involving the splenium of the corpus callosum and pons, with sparing of subcortical U-fibers and two foci of petechial hemorrhage in the cerebellum. There was no evidence of restricted diffusion or post-contrast enhancement. MR angiography was unremarkable.

Further evaluation included a negative urine drug screen; negative serologies for antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil-cytoplasmic antibodies, rheumatoid factor, and normal complement fixation tests; an aldosterone-to-renin ratio < 20; and mildly elevated catecholamine levels in the context of clonidine therapy.

A 50-year-old man presented to the emergency department with diffuse body pain of 2 hours’ duration. He described severe (10/10) abdominal pain, worsening at his usual sites of metastasis—including the jaw, bilateral scapulae, chest wall, and left inguinal region—and unrelieved by his home analgesics. His medical history was notable for hypothyroidism and metastatic melanoma (brain, lung, liver, and bone); he had completed seven cycles of carboplatin–paclitaxel several months earlier, with recent disease progression.  

Home medications included temozolomide, esomeprazole, acetylcysteine, atorvastatin, dexamethasone, gabapentin, levetiracetam, levothyroxine, magnesium lactate–pyridoxine, metoclopramide, ondansetron, oxycodone, and sitagliptin–metformin.  

On examination, he appeared ill and in pain but was alert and oriented. Vital signs were: temperature 37.3°C, blood pressure 126/96 mmHg, heart rate 105 beats per minute, and SpO2 95% on room air. Cardiovascular and pulmonary examinations were unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed diffuse tenderness without peritoneal signs.  

Initial laboratory tests showed a WBC count of 8824/mm3 (64% neutrophils), RBC count 2.84 million/mm3, hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL (down from 12.5 g/dL one month earlier), hematocrit 25%, MCV 89.7 fl, and platelets 107,000/mm3. Peripheral blood smear demonstrated left-shifted granulocytes, polychromasia, many spherocytes, rare target cells, elliptocytes, schistocytes, and multiple dehemoglobinized “ghost cells”; the direct antiglobulin test was negative.  

Chemistry results included creatinine 1.2 mg/dL, BUN 37 mg/dL, total bilirubin 5.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 235 IU/L, AST 662 IU/L, ALT 24 IU/L, and lipase <3 U/L. Coagulation studies showed an aPTT of 42 seconds, PT 25.7 seconds, and INR 2.1. Serum lactate was 11.6 mmol/L.  

A Foley catheter yielded dark red/black urine, and venous blood samples were repeatedly grossly hemolyzed and dark in color. An arterial blood gas showed pH 7.20, PaCO2 34.8 mmHg, PaO2 87.1 mmHg, bicarbonate 13 mmol/L, SaO2 99%, carboxyhemoglobin 4.4%, methemoglobin 4.9%, hemoglobin 6.1 g/dL, and lactate 10.9 mmol/L.  

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed new metastatic hepatic lesions, peritoneal and lymph node disease, but no intraabdominal collections or hemorrhage.

A 10-month-old female, 2.5 months after an ABO-incompatible orthotopic heart transplant for idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy, was referred for evaluation of bright red blood in her diaper. Her post-transplant immunosuppression included tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisolone; she had a prior admission for nonbloody, nonbilious emesis treated as viral gastroenteritis. Over the preceding 7 weeks, her mother noted intermittent pink streaks in stool initially attributed to milk protein allergy.

On evaluation at an outside emergency department, she was afebrile with stable vital signs. Echocardiography showed normal graft function without evidence of rejection. Abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable, but a plain abdominal radiograph demonstrated linear lucencies adjacent to the cecal wall and markedly dilated, edematous bowel consistent with pneumatosis intestinalis. Her absolute neutrophil count had declined from 3090/mm3 two weeks earlier to 1550/mm3.

Upon transfer, repeat radiographs confirmed pneumatosis. On admission day, the ANC dropped to 640/mm3 and to 210/mm3 the next day, reaching a nadir of 110/mm3 in the following 10 days. Tacrolimus level was supratherapeutic at 28.8 ng/mL (therapeutic range, 8–10 ng/mL). Epstein–Barr viral load rose from 29 copies/mL 1.5 months prior to 2471 copies/mL one week into admission; the donor was EBV-positive, and the recipient was EBV-negative pretransplant. A PET-CT scan obtained for concern of posttransplant lymphoproliferative disease showed no evidence of malignancy but revealed concentric thickening of the rectosigmoid consistent with colitis. Cytomegalovirus colitis was considered but deemed unlikely given an undetectable serum CMV level.

A 26-year-old male laborer presented with sudden onset of severe chest pain, shortness of breath, and dizziness occurring 3 months after an initial cough that progressed to dyspnea. He reported these symptoms began immediately after strenuous work involving heavy lifting. He denied any past cardiac history or family history of congenital or hereditary disorders.

On examination, he was pale and diaphoretic. Temperature was 98°F, heart rate 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 148/100 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Cardiovascular examination revealed a harsh pansystolic murmur best heard at the right upper sternal border. Lung fields were clear, and the remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. Chest radiography demonstrated cardiomegaly with an increased cardiothoracic ratio. Routine laboratory studies, including complete blood count, metabolic panel, coagulation profile, lipid profile, and cardiac enzymes, were within normal limits or showed only mild nonspecific abnormalities.

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 55%, normal right ventricular systolic function (tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion 17 mm), mild aortic regurgitation, severe tricuspid regurgitation, and moderate pulmonary hypertension with pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 45 mm Hg. Other valves appeared normal in structure and function; there was no intracardiac thrombus or pericardial effusion.

A 9-year-old Persian girl presented with a 6-month history of burning epigastric pain and intermittent palpitations. The pain was nonpositional and unrelated to meals or bowel movements. She had no prior medical or surgical history, no medication use, and no known family history of liver disease; she was born via in vitro fertilization. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits, and there was a mild palpable bulge in the right upper quadrant without tenderness. Routine laboratory tests, including complete blood count and liver-function values, were within reference ranges. An abdominal ultrasonogram showed a large echogenic mass with moderate vascularity adjacent to segment VI of the liver. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a well-circumscribed 92 mm × 70 mm mass emanating from the right lobe of the liver. The lesion was hypodense before contrast, hyperenhancing in the portal phase with a central nonenhancing scar, isoattenuating in equilibrium, and demonstrated delayed enhancement of the scar. Alpha-fetoprotein and antihydatid antibody levels were both normal. Based on these findings, the leading considerations were pedunculated focal nodular hyperplasia and hepatocellular adenoma.

An 11-year-old girl with recurrent medulloblastoma underwent a second autologous stem cell transplant. As part of her conditioning regimen, she received high-dose thiotepa and carboplatin; concomitant medications included acetaminophen, diphenhydramine, mannitol, hydrocortisone, ondansetron, omeprazole, and lorazepam. Twelve days after transplantation, she developed a blistering rash, prompting dermatology consultation for concern about Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis. On examination, there were scattered, nonerythematous, tense bullae and erosions on the upper extremities, intertriginous hyperpigmented patches, and linear tense bullae on the medial thigh beneath a urinary catheter. She was afebrile, and there was no mucosal involvement. A punch biopsy of a thigh bulla showed superficial epidermal necrosis with rare dyskeratosis.

An 85-year-old woman with type II diabetes and heart failure presented with a 4-month history of a rapidly growing mass in the soft tissues of the right cheek. The lesion was painless, firm, and round, without overlying skin changes. There was no history of trauma or other associated symptoms. On examination, a 25-mm palpable lesion adherent to the fascia was noted in the right cheek. An ultrasound scan confirmed a well-circumscribed nodular mass measuring 25 mm and showed no involvement of local lymph nodes. What is your differential diagnosis?

A 21-year-old man who works as a plasterer in northwestern Iran presented with a 3-month history of pruritic, hemorrhagic nodular lesions on his face and upper lip. He reported no fever, chills, weight loss, or respiratory or urinary symptoms. He had no known allergies and was on no medications. Vital signs were within normal limits. Examination revealed multiple discrete hyperkeratotic nodules with erythematous, prominent borders on the face and upper lip; surrounding skin appeared normal, and there was no regional lymphadenopathy. Routine blood tests, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were normal. The patient had undergone multiple courses of topical therapies, oral antibiotics, and antihistamines without improvement; topical corticosteroids transiently reduced inflammation and swelling. A skin biopsy showed multiple subepithelial granulomas composed of epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, and surrounding lymphocytes.

A 51-year-old right-hand–dominant woman presented with a 2-year history of left anterolateral shoulder pain. Her baseline pain was rated at 3 on a visual analog scale (VAS) with a shoulder subjective value (SSV) of 70%. One month before presentation, she experienced an acute exacerbation with pain rated at 8 on the VAS, sleep disturbance, and severe end-range pain in forward flexion (FF), external rotation (ER), and internal rotation (IR). She had undergone anti-inflammatory medications, activity modification, and home exercises without relief.

On examination, passive range of motion in the left shoulder was 160° FF, 50° ER, and IR to T11, with pain at the end of each arc. The Neer and Hawkins impingement signs were markedly positive. Strength was 4/5 in FF and ER; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Plain radiographs of the shoulder (anteroposterior and axillary views) showed a large, well-defined calcific deposit in the supraspinatus tendon with apparent extension toward the greater tuberosity. Coronal and axial T2-weighted MRI revealed a 13-mm hypointense focus at the supraspinatus tendon insertion, with extension into the greater tuberosity footprint, associated with significant osteolysis of the greater tuberosity and intramedullary edema.

A 59-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a 2-year history of urinary frequency, dysuria, and a bulging sensation in her vagina. She had no significant medical or surgical history. There was no abnormal vaginal discharge, weight loss, or fatigue. Her last menstruation was over eight years ago, and she reported occasional dyspareunia. She had four prior vaginal deliveries. 

On examination, a soft, bulging red mass measuring approximately 32 mm × 28 mm surrounded the urethral meatus. Palpation of the anterior vaginal wall showed no extension of the mass into the urethra or bladder neck. The initial differential diagnosis included urethral caruncle, urethral mucosal prolapse, and malignancy.

Urinalysis was normal. Under local anesthesia, a biopsy of the lesion was performed without complication. Flexible urethrocystoscopy revealed no urethral stenosis or bladder abnormalities. Human papilloma virus screening was negative.

A 27-year-old woman presented with involuntary movements of her right arm and leg that began 4 weeks earlier and progressively worsened, causing difficulty holding objects and walking. She had no rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, arthralgias, Raynaud’s phenomenon, sicca symptoms, oral contraceptive use, weight loss, headache, loss of consciousness, or seizures. There was no family history of rheumatic or neurologic disease. She was a nonsmoker and nondrinker, with two prior uncomplicated pregnancies.

On examination, there were jerky, purposeless, intermittent, and irregular choreic movements of the right hand and foot. Other systems were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, blood chemistry, and liver function tests. The coagulation profile revealed a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time of 68.8 seconds (reference, 25–36.5). Antinuclear antibody titer was 1:1280; anti–double-stranded DNA was 70.5 IU (reference, <25 IU); anti–Smith antibody was positive; complement C3 was low; C4 was normal. Lupus anticoagulant was positive; anticardiolipin IgG was borderline positive at 18.5 GPL (reference, <15 GPL); anticardiolipin IgM and anti–β2-glycoprotein-1 were negative. Antistreptolysin O titer was 157 IU/mL (reference, <200 IU/mL). Thyroid function tests were normal.

Brain MRI demonstrated tiny foci of high-intensity signal on FLAIR and T2-weighted images in the bilateral basal ganglia and occipital periventricular white matter. Magnetic resonance angiography showed normal cerebral arterial caliber without stenosis, occlusion, or aneurysm.

A 42-year-old woman with uterine leiomyomata underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingectomy via a midline vertical incision. Her preoperative workup showed mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL) and a normal creatinine (0.71 mg/dL). She had no prior cross-sectional abdominal imaging.

Intraoperatively, a nonmobile 18-cm leiomyomatous uterus and extensive adhesive disease were encountered; both ureters were visualized distal to the iliac bifurcation, and left ureteral peristalsis was noted. After the hysterectomy, cystoscopy showed a normal bladder and a patent left ureteral orifice with efflux of urine; the right ureteral orifice was stenotic, difficult to visualize, and had no efflux. Urology was consulted.

Repeat cystoscopy confirmed these findings. A right retrograde pyelogram demonstrated a dilated distal ureter, extravasation of contrast proximal to the iliac vessels, and no opacification of the proximal ureter or renal pelvis; a catheter could not be advanced proximally. The left retrograde pyelogram was normal. The right ureter was then dissected up to the external iliac vessel—its tissue was of poor quality, dilated distally, thinned to obliteration in the mid ureter, and showed no peristalsis.

An intraoperative intravenous pyelogram was performed. The left collecting system opacified with normal drainage; the right collecting system and ureter showed no contrast pooling.

A 40-year-old man was admitted with a 3-day history of skin lesions and a 1-day history of fever (peak, 38.2 °C), followed by intense headaches and myalgia responsive to paracetamol. The lesions began as a single vesicle on the scalp approximately 5 days earlier, which was crusted at presentation, and then became asynchronous pustules predominantly on the face, neck, abdomen, hands, and perineal area. The pustules measured 2–4 mm, had an erythematous base, and showed central umbilication; a few painful erosions (2–3 mm) were noted in the perineal region. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy, no signs of pneumonia, and no abdominal organ involvement. He denied recent travel, known contact with infected individuals, or other risk factors. Given the ongoing monkeypox outbreak, he was managed under a protocol for emerging infectious diseases, with investigations to distinguish monkeypox from varicella zoster virus infection. Laboratory tests showed normal C-reactive protein, interleukin-6, procalcitonin, and white-cell count, with only a mild increase in interleukin-2 receptor levels. Serologic testing for VZV IgM and IgG was negative.

A 66-year-old immunocompetent woman presented with ulcerations on her right hand that ascended her arm in a lymphocutaneous distribution. She denied antecedent trauma. Her only animal exposures were a dog and a cat. She had traveled to Arizona 6 months earlier and had been exposed to floodwater in her home 5 months earlier. She was an avid daily gardener and had received a potted Haworthia fasciata plant imported from South Africa 1 month before symptom onset. On examination, there were punched-out ulcerations with yellow-white crust and minimal surrounding erythema along the lymphatic drainage of the right arm. A skin biopsy showed a dense papillary dermal lymphohistiocytic infiltrate without well-formed granulomas. Gram, Fite, and Ziehl-Neelsen stains were negative. Aerobic culture grew Candida parapsilosis. She was treated with oral cephalexin and fluconazole without clinical improvement.

A 45-year-old woman was referred to breast services with marked asymmetry of her right breast. She reported a 6-month history of dramatic enlargement of the right breast, associated with pain, heaviness, and difficulty fitting clothing. Her medical history was notable for bilateral breast augmentation in 2011. On examination, there was gross right-sided breast enlargement without skin ulceration or lymphadenopathy. 

Bilateral mammography, compared with 2014 films, demonstrated longstanding glandular asymmetry with a possible mass in the right breast; both implants appeared intact. Ultrasound of the right breast showed an intact implant and extensive ill-defined hypoechoic areas with calcifications and variable-sized cystic changes in the upper and lower midline, features described as suspicious. 

Two ultrasound-guided core biopsies were obtained: the upper-midline lesion showed pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia (PASH) and the lower inner quadrant was benign. A subsequent ultrasound-guided vacuum-assisted core biopsy of the upper-midline area again yielded PASH with fibrocystic change. A multidisciplinary team concluded that sampling was representative and no further biopsy was needed.

A 62-year-old Japanese man presented with a 4-week history of progressive dyspnea on exertion. He denied fever, anorexia, cough, or chest pain. At an outside hospital, he was found to be hypoxemic, and a chest radiograph demonstrated consolidation in the upper lung fields. Transthoracic echocardiography showed marked right ventricular dilation, interventricular septal flattening, and severe pulmonary hypertension with a transtricuspid pressure gradient of 109 mm Hg. 

His past history was notable for stage IIIA gastric cancer treated 5 years earlier with distal gastrectomy and adjuvant chemotherapy; follow-up for 2 years showed no recurrence. He was a former smoker (20 pack-years). 

On transfer, he was afebrile, normotensive, and hypoxemic with an SpO₂ of 88% on 3 L/min of oxygen by nasal cannula. Physical examination revealed purpura on the upper extremities and trunk; the remainder was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed normocytic anemia with leukoerythroblastosis, evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation, a markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase level (3205 U/L), and normal transaminases. 

Chest CT demonstrated diffuse ground-glass opacities in the upper lobes with emphysematous changes, moderate bilateral pleural effusions, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and enlargement of the right ventricle and main pulmonary artery. CT pulmonary angiography revealed no pulmonary embolism. Lung perfusion scintigraphy showed multiple segmental defects, and bone scintigraphy revealed diffuse uptake. A bone marrow biopsy demonstrated signet-ring cells confirming recurrent gastric adenocarcinoma. Bronchoscopy was deferred because of bleeding diathesis.

An 18-year-old right-handed man presented with asymptomatic, gradually increasing fusiform swelling of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint of the left middle finger over the past 5 years. He reported no pain, no functional limitation, and denied any repetitive movements or compulsive habits. His family history was noncontributory, and psychiatric evaluation excluded emotional distress. 

On examination, there was diffuse thickening of the soft tissues over the radial and ulnar aspects of the left middle-finger PIP joint, with intact overlying skin, no pigmentation, and no neurologic deficits. The range of motion was full, and there were no signs of inflammation. 

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and rheumatoid factor, were within normal limits or negative. 

Plain radiographs of the hand showed fusiform soft-tissue swelling around the PIP joint without joint-space narrowing, bony erosions, or other structural abnormalities. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated circumferential and longitudinal soft-tissue thickening that was isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously hyperintense on postcontrast fat-suppressed T1-weighted images, with no joint effusion, tenosynovial fluid, or hemorrhagic changes.

A 58-year-old woman with locally advanced basal cell carcinoma of the left eye, treated for 6 months with cemiplimab and with no prior liver disease, presented 1 month after stopping therapy with new-onset ascites. On admission, diagnostic paracentesis demonstrated a serum-ascites albumin gradient greater than 1.5. Laboratory findings were: sodium 129 mmol/L; creatinine 0.8 mg/dL; albumin 2.9 g/dL; total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL (direct 0.5 mg/dL); ALT 59 IU/L; AST 51 IU/L; alkaline phosphatase 884 IU/L; GGT 373 IU/L; INR 2.1. A viral hepatitis panel, including HAV IgM, HCV antibody with reflex to RNA, HBc antibody, and HBs antigen, was negative. Abdominal CT showed diffuse heterogeneous enhancement of the liver suggesting passive congestion. Quantitative CMV PCR was 427 IU/mL.

The patient was started on prednisone 100 mg daily for presumed checkpoint-inhibitor–mediated hepatitis, without improvement in alkaline phosphatase or clinical status, and steroids were tapered to 40 mg daily while monitoring CMV viral load.

One month later, she was transferred with recurrent ascites and worsening liver tests. Laboratory values were: WBC 11.1×10^9/L; hemoglobin 14.3 g/dL; platelets 295×10^9/L; sodium 129 mmol/L; creatinine 0.7 mg/dL; albumin 3.0 g/dL; total bilirubin 12.6 mg/dL (direct 7.3 mg/dL); ALT 220 IU/L; AST 147 IU/L; alkaline phosphatase 2025 IU/L; INR 1.6. Repeat viral hepatitis panel, ANA, AMA, and ASMA were all negative. Paracentesis cultures were negative. Quantitative CMV PCR was 330 573 IU/mL; blood cultures, COVID-19, and influenza tests were negative. ESR was 8 mm/h; CRP 1.3 mg/L; complements C3 79 mg/dL and C4 19 mg/dL were low; urinalysis was normal. Cryoglobulin, PR3-ANCA, MPO-ANCA, beta-2 glycoprotein, anticardiolipin IgG, HSV PCR, and EBV IgG/IgM were negative. CT angiography of the abdomen and lower extremities showed no evidence of large-vessel inflammation. Doppler ultrasound demonstrated slow hepatopedal flow with patent hepatic vessels.

A 12-year-old Caucasian boy was referred for orthodontic assessment.  
History of present illness: No history of trauma; poor oral hygiene; parental history of presumed dental abscesses attributed to primary tooth exfoliation without treatment.  
Examination: Moderately increased mobility of the maxillary lateral incisors and mandibular first premolars; right maxillary lateral incisor in crossbite.  
Radiography: Orthopantomogram showed permanent teeth with extremely short or absent roots, sharp conical apical constrictions, and crescent-shaped pulpal remnants parallel to the cementoenamel junction. Prior panoramic radiographs at ages 7 and 10 demonstrated similar rootless teeth in both dentitions.  
Family evaluation:  
– 10-year-old sister with no tooth mobility or crown abnormalities; prior panoramic radiograph revealed identical apical root constrictions and pulp chamber changes.  
– Father with history of early loss of permanent teeth replaced by prosthetics; panoramic radiograph displayed multiple teeth with short, pointed roots and pulpal obliteration.  
Pedigree is consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.

A 70-year-old man with diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and prostate cancer was referred for cataract evaluation of the right eye. He reported no photophobia, eye pain, discharge, contact-lens use, ocular trauma, or prior ocular procedures, and no personal or family history of metabolic disorders or corneal dystrophies. Medications included atorvastatin, chlorthalidone, clopidogrel, metformin, primidone, topiramate, tamsulosin, and propranolol. 

Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/40 in the right eye and 20/30 in the left. Pupillary reactions and intraocular pressures were normal bilaterally. Corneal pachymetry measured 549 µm centrally and 681 µm peripherally in the right eye, and 547 µm centrally and 673 µm peripherally in the left. 

Slit-lamp examination revealed symmetric bilateral circular mid-peripheral full-thickness stromal white rings (7–8 mm in diameter). Corneal sensation was intact; there was no vascularization, fibrosis, thinning, or fluorescein staining. Gonioscopy showed open angles without a thickened Schwalbe’s line or iris processes. Posterior-segment examination was unremarkable bilaterally.

Laboratory studies—including basic metabolic panel, complete blood count, lactate dehydrogenase, beta-2 microglobulin, and serum protein electrophoresis—were within normal limits. Lipid profile showed slightly reduced high-density cholesterol. Anterior-segment optical coherence tomography demonstrated highly reflective material throughout the entire corneal stroma.

A 29-year-old man presented with blurred vision and left eye pain. Three months earlier he acquired a kitten. Two months earlier he had been deer hunting, sustained multiple tick bites, and developed a transient rash. He denied fever, myalgias, headache, or nausea. Concurrently, he began treatment with an antibiotic for chlamydia. Two weeks before presentation he noted a “dark spot” in the left visual field and pain with eye movement, prompting urgent-care evaluation.

On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/70 in the left eye. Confrontation visual fields showed a superior-temporal defect in the left eye. External and slit-lamp examination was unremarkable on the right; the left eye had 2+ vitreous cells. Funduscopic examination revealed normal findings in the right eye and 2+ optic disc edema with telangiectatic vessels and macular edema in the left eye.

Laboratory evaluation demonstrated normal results for Bartonella (IgM and IgG), syphilis T.ab, T-spot, a tick-borne disease PCR panel, angiotensin-converting enzyme, and Rocky Mountain spotted fever IgM. Positive findings included Rocky Mountain spotted fever IgG at 1:64 (reference, 0–1:64), Toxoplasma IgM >160 IU/mL (≤7.9 AU/mL), and Toxoplasma IgG 57.9 IU/mL (≤7.1 IU/mL).

A 75-year-old woman with a history of mild rheumatic mitral stenosis not followed for 20 years and not on anticoagulation presented to the emergency department with near-syncope followed by acute dyspnea. Shortly after arrival, she developed haemodynamic instability with cardiogenic shock (cold and wet profile, SCAI stage C) and pulmonary oedema on chest X-ray. ECG showed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. Immediate electrical cardioversion restored sinus rhythm. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed severe metabolic acidosis (pH 7.04), lactate 16 mg/dL, and pO2 50 mmHg. Despite IV diuretics, she remained unstable and was intubated, mechanically ventilated, and started on norepinephrine (0.5 µg/kg/min) and dobutamine (0.5 µg/kg/min).

Urgent transthoracic echocardiography showed:  
• Severely reduced LVEF (15%) with diffuse hypokinesia.  
• Normal-sized right ventricle with severe systolic dysfunction, severe tricuspid regurgitation, and pulmonary systolic pressure of 50 mmHg.  
• Severely calcified, doming mitral leaflets with a mean diastolic gradient of 5 mmHg (rising to 16 mmHg with inotropes), consistent with severe rheumatic mitral stenosis.  
• A markedly dilated left atrium containing a large, rounded mass.

2D–3D transesophageal echocardiography confirmed severe mitral stenosis and biventricular dysfunction. The left atrial mass measured 40 × 40 mm, was perfectly spherical with a double-walled appearance, largely immobile, leaning against the lateral atrial wall, and showed no clear attachment. The external contour was echo-dense with a 4 mm fibrous cap, an inner thinner layer, and a friable central core, giving a “truck-tire” appearance. 3D-TEE further characterized the mass composition.

A 31-year-old woman presented with dissatisfaction regarding her facial and dental appearance and reported a year-long odyssey through multiple dental and orthodontic practices without resolution. Her medical history was notable for multiple vertebral compression fractures. On examination, she was 1.6 m tall and had lax, wrinkly skin most prominent on her hands, feet, and abdomen, with drooping cheeks giving an aged appearance disproportionate to her chronological age. Prior dentists had extracted several maxillary teeth to address crowding attributed to a hypoplastic maxilla, but occlusal normality was not achieved. Orthodontic evaluation showed a dental Class III occlusion with bilateral lateral open bite, a marked curve of Spee, and anterior head‐to‐head bite. Panoramic and cephalometric imaging revealed maxillary retrognathia, mandibular prognathism, a skeletal Class III relationship (ANB −2.2°, WITS −6.6 mm), a horizontal mandibular plane (ML-NL 11.9°), apical radiopaque halos from hypercementosis, and superimposition of dental roots on the mandibular canal.

A 36-year-old previously healthy army man presented with intermittent fever for 3 days (maximum temperature, 103°F) associated with body aches and with intermittent, nonradiating chest pain of 2 months’ duration that was unrelated to exertion or respiration. He denied respiratory symptoms, palpitations, substance use, and family history of cardiac disease; he reported occasional dizziness during strenuous training. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 14.4 g/dl, platelets 176 000/mm3, total leukocyte count 3200/mm3 (neutrophils 77%, lymphocytes 17%), total bilirubin 1.3 mg/dl, urea 32 mg/dl, creatinine 0.82 mg/dl, sodium 138 mmol/l, potassium 3.74 mmol/l. A fever tropical panel was positive for Plasmodium falciparum; chest radiography was normal. An electrocardiogram showed coved ST-segment elevation (>2 mm) followed by T-wave inversion in leads V1 and V2. Serial cardiac markers (troponin I, CK-MB) were within normal limits, and echocardiography revealed no structural abnormality or ventricular dysfunction.

A 34-year-old man with a 5-year history of heavy alcohol use (abstinent for the past year) was evaluated for recurrent postprandial epigastric pain, nonbloody vomiting, and unintentional weight loss over 6 months. Six months earlier, he had undergone duodenal stenosis bypass surgery at another institution after similar symptoms, without available details of imaging or histology. On examination, he appeared malnourished; bowel sounds were mildly decreased, and there was moderate periumbilical tenderness without rebound or guarding. 

Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 12,000/mm3, serum amylase of 780 IU/L (normal 27–102), urine amylase of 7940 U/L (normal 10–500), AST 113 U/L, ALT 102 U/L, ALP 259 U/L, γ-GT 118 U/L, and normal bilirubin. Serum CEA and CA 19-9 were within normal limits.

Abdominal ultrasound, CT, and MRI of the upper abdomen showed concentric thickening and stenosis of the second portion of the duodenum with intramural cystic foci, tissue between the duodenum and pancreatic head, longitudinal narrowing of the main pancreatic duct, mild common bile duct dilation, and multiple cystic lesions in the pancreatic head. Findings were confirmed on MRCP. 

Upper endoscopy demonstrated a prior gastroenteric anastomosis with functioning loops, severe edema and stenosis of the second portion of the duodenum, and erosive inflammation. Biopsy specimens of duodenal mucosa revealed mild nonspecific gastritis and hyperplastic Brunner gland proliferation.

A 52-year-old woman with no known comorbidities presented with 3 days of acute, burning right iliac fossa pain that became generalized and worsened over 1 day. She also had nausea and 2–3 episodes per day of non-bilious, non-bloody vomiting for 1 day and no flatus or stool passage for 3 days. There was no fever, urinary or vaginal symptoms. She had a hysterectomy 10 years earlier without complications.  
On examination she was alert and hemodynamically stable (temperature 98.8°F). The abdomen was distended, tender—particularly in the right iliac fossa—and there was guarding on deep palpation. Bowel sounds were present. Other systems were unremarkable.  
Laboratory tests—including CBC, liver and renal panels, amylase, and lipase—were within normal limits.  
An upright abdominal radiograph showed multiple air-fluid levels; the supine film showed dilated small-bowel loops with valvulae conniventes and absence of gas beyond the ascending colon—consistent with small-bowel obstruction.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed dilated distal jejunal and proximal ileal loops with air-fluid levels and a “string of pearls” sign. There was an abrupt transition in the distal ileum in the right iliac fossa, suggestive of a transition point. No clear mass or hernia was seen.  
The patient was managed conservatively with bowel rest and fluid resuscitation but had no improvement, continued obstipation, and on day 4 developed fever (100.8°F), tachypnea (RR 35/min, SpO₂ 85% on room air), and tachycardia (HR 130 bpm). Repeat labs showed leukocytosis, and repeat abdominal radiographs remained unchanged.

A 29-year-old man with no history of skin or autoimmune disease presented with a six-month history of an intermittently itchy rash. The lesions began as light-colored macules on his wrists and gradually spread up his arms. He had applied triamcinolone 0.05% cream twice daily for several weeks without improvement. He denied any other medications or supplements.

On examination, there were porcelain-white, hypopigmented, atrophic macules coalescing into patches on the bilateral volar forearms, extending onto the dorsal forearms, and a solitary patch on the sacrum. Many of the macules contained central hair follicles and keratotic plugs resembling open comedones. Dermoscopic evaluation of the forearm lesions revealed hypopigmented macules with central keratotic plugs.

The differential diagnosis included lichen sclerosus, morphea, discoid lupus erythematosus, lichen planus, and anetoderma.

A 36-year-old Caucasian Greek man presented with a two-month history of gradually progressive right shoulder weakness and limited active abduction and elevation, notably while carrying heavy objects on his shoulder. He denied any neck or shoulder pain, specific trauma, or recent infection. He had no significant medical or surgical history.

On examination, his right shoulder was depressed with noticeable asymmetry and winging of the scapula, becoming most evident during abduction and disappearing in forward elevation. He was unable to abduct the right arm above 80° in either the frontal or scapular plane, though passive range of motion was full and comparable to the left side. There was marked wasting of the right trapezius muscle with decreased shrugging. The ipsilateral sternocleidomastoid muscle appeared normal, and there were no other cranial nerve deficits or signs of brachial plexus involvement. His rotator cuff was judged to be intact.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and serum biochemistry, were all within normal limits. Initial shoulder radiographs were unremarkable. Computed tomography of the shoulder girdle demonstrated diffuse atrophy of the right trapezius muscle. Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine, right shoulder joint, and skull base showed mild atrophy of the right sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles without other pathology.

Electrophysiological testing of the right spinal accessory nerve with surface stimulation and recording from the trapezius yielded no compound muscle action potential. Needle electromyography of the right trapezius revealed active denervation (fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves), marked reduction of insertional activity, and absence of motor unit recruitment, indicating severe axonal loss. Electromyography of the right sternocleidomastoid showed mild axonal injury, while the levator scapulae, serratus anterior, and rhomboid muscles were normal.

A 35-year-old woman with obesity, substance and tobacco (22-pack-year) use, major depression, anxiety, and a diet limited to cheesesteaks, chicken, and pork chops presents with 6 months of painful lower-extremity swelling, dyspnea, gingival bleeding, poor oral intake, and ecchymoses. She had received corticosteroids for presumed vasculitis or undifferentiated connective tissue disease without improvement and required multiple transfusions for persistent anemia. On admission, HR 105 bpm; BP 115/59 mmHg; RR 24 breaths/min; SpO₂ 99% on room air. Exam shows pallor, poor dental hygiene with oral blood pooling, diffuse joint swelling with ecchymoses, perifollicular petechiae with corkscrew hairs, lower-extremity tenderness, and diminished breath sounds with mild crackles. Labs: hemoglobin 6.6 g/dL (12.0–15.3); PT-INR 1.50 (0.87–1.17); platelets 152 K/µL (140–400); BNP 2714 pg/mL (0–299); folate <2.0 ng/mL (>4.5); thiamine <7 nmol/L (8–30). Blood cultures grew Streptococcus anginosus; antibiotics were started. Bone marrow biopsy revealed dyserythropoiesis, nuclear–cytoplasmic asynchrony, and erythroid hyperplasia; smear showed anisocytosis, left-shifted neutrophils, and normal platelets. V/Q scan excluded pulmonary embolism; vasculitis and viral studies were negative. Transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 86 mmHg, a dilated inferior vena cava with right atrial pressure 15 mmHg, a severely enlarged right ventricle with D-sign, and a concentrically hypertrophic left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 70% and left ventricular outflow tract septal obstruction.

A 66-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 1-hour history of altered sensorium, bilateral upper-limb weakness, and slurred speech. She denied any seizure activity, tongue biting, or incontinence. Her medical history was notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus (metformin), hypertension (amlodipine and losartan), and primary hypothyroidism (levothyroxine), all of which she had taken for 10 years. She reported stopping her antihypertensive medications 1 week earlier. She did not smoke or drink alcohol, and her family history was noncontributory.

On examination her blood pressure was 210/110 mm Hg, pulse 115 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, SpO2 95% on room air, and Glasgow Coma Scale score 13/15. Her random blood glucose was 140 mg/dL. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. Neurologic examination revealed motor strength of 3/5 in the left upper limb and 5/5 in the right upper limb; 5/5 in the left lower limb and 4/5 in the right lower limb. No visual field deficits were noted. Fundoscopic examination showed grade 1 hypertensive retinopathy.

Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL, triglycerides 430.7 mg/dL, TSH 9.7 IU/mL, and HbA1c 9.31%. Echocardiography revealed grade 1 left ventricular diastolic dysfunction. An immediate noncontrast head CT scan was normal, and a CT pulmonary angiogram showed no pulmonary embolism. Despite the normal initial CT, ischemic stroke and cerebral venous thrombosis remained considerations.

On hospital day 2, a repeat noncontrast CT scan of the head demonstrated bilateral symmetrical white matter hypodensities in the frontal lobes.

A 25-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of pleuritic chest pain localized to the base of the left hemithorax. The pain was initially intermittent and variable in duration. She denied fever, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. Her medical history included asthma and papillary thyroid carcinoma resected 8 years earlier, with no evidence of relapse. On examination, vital signs were normal, and the only notable finding was a central neck scar.

A chest radiograph demonstrated a round opacity at the base of the left lower lobe. Thoracic computed tomography confirmed a peripheral, juxtapleural lesion in the anterior segment of the left lower lobe, measuring approximately 2.5 cm in its greatest dimension.

Given her history of thyroid cancer, a neoplastic process was suspected, and the patient underwent a thoracotomy with wedge resection of the pulmonary lesion.

A 44-year-old man with a history of gastroesophageal reflux disease presented with a 3-month history of intermittent fever, an 11-kg weight loss, abdominal fullness, poor appetite, general malaise, night sweats, and right upper-quadrant discomfort. He had been treated as an outpatient with oral antibiotics without improvement. On admission, he appeared mildly cachectic and was febrile (38.7 °C); heart rate was 91 beats/min, blood pressure 135/89 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 100 % on room air. Physical examination revealed mild right hypochondrial tenderness and hepatomegaly; there was no jaundice, lymphadenopathy, or splenomegaly.

Laboratory studies showed C-reactive protein 152 mg/L (normal < 10), mildly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, serum sodium 121 mEq/L, white-cell count 8500/mL, hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, platelets 280 000/µL, aspartate aminotransferase 18 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase 25 IU/L, total bilirubin 2.2 mg/dL, creatinine 3.2 mg/dL, and blood urea nitrogen 21 mg/dL; prothrombin time was normal. Tests for HIV, carcinoembryonic antigen, cancer antigen 19-9, α-fetoprotein, prostate-specific antigen, serologic hydatid disease, and amoebic hemagglutination were negative. Multiple blood and sputum cultures were negative for bacteria, fungi, and acid-fast bacilli.

Abdominal ultrasonography showed marked hepatomegaly and a 7-cm lesion in segment VIII that was partially hypoechoic with a hyperechoic component; there was no ascites or lymphadenopathy. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen revealed a 7-cm low-density lesion in segment VIII with heterogeneous fat densities. Chest radiography was unremarkable. A percutaneous liver biopsy was performed to exclude malignancy. Direct examination of the specimen did not reveal organisms, and histological examination showed an inflammatory pseudotumor with Langerhans giant cells and without caseous necrosis.

A 30-year-old Caucasian woman presented to the emergency department with right-sided facial and lower limb twitching. She reported a 5-day headache similar to her usual migraines and had taken a newly prescribed dose of sumatriptan approximately 6–8 hours before presentation. Shortly after the dose, she developed gradually worsening twitching of the right face and lower limb, discomfort in the right arm and leg, and difficulty with speech. She had taken only paracetamol at home and denied any other medications, including over-the-counter or herbal supplements, and denied recent alcohol or illicit drug use.

Her medical history included longstanding depression managed with fluvoxamine 100 mg daily, hemiplegic migraines, endometriosis, and paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia. She denied any changes in her fluvoxamine dose and was not taking pregabalin or tranexamic acid on the day of presentation.

On examination, her heart rate was 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 144/96 mmHg, temperature 36.5 °C, and Glasgow Coma Scale score 15. She had diaphoretic palms and a resting tremor in her right arm and leg. Pupils were bilaterally sluggish and dilated with ocular clonus. She had increased tone and hyperreflexia of both lower limbs with six to seven beats of inducible clonus at the ankles. Power and sensation were normal throughout, and the remainder of her neurological examination was unremarkable.

An electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia with a QT interval below the treatment line on the QT nomogram. Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function tests, and serum β-human chorionic gonadotropin were unremarkable. Computed tomography of the head showed no intracranial lesion and was grossly normal for age.

A 78-year-old woman with palliative pancreatic head cancer presented initially with mild fever (37.6°C), upper abdominal pain, and jaundice. She had undergone chemotherapy and had a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, deep vein thrombosis (on rivaroxaban), and chemotherapy‐induced peripheral neuropathy.
