Contrast‐enhanced CT showed a dilated common bile duct and an enlarged gallbladder with wall thickening, suggestive of cholecystitis; no pseudoaneurysms were seen. ERCP with endoscopic sphincterotomy and nasobiliary drainage was performed, and two days later a fully covered self‐expandable metal stent was placed uneventfully. Her fever and jaundice resolved, and she was discharged 7 days after stent placement.

Seven days after stent placement, she returned with two episodes of copious hematochezia accompanied by mild upper abdominal pain and fever. On examination, her temperature was 37.0°C, heart rate 87 bpm, blood pressure 137/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and SpO₂ 95% on room air. She was jaundiced but had no abdominal tenderness or Murphy’s sign. Laboratory tests demonstrated anemia, elevated inflammatory markers, and elevated liver enzymes.

A 44-year-old Indian man presented with a 1-year history of painless lesions on the medial aspects of his right upper and lower eyelid margins, associated with epiphora without discharge and occasional foreign-body sensation. He had well-controlled type II diabetes mellitus for 5 years and no history of eyelid trauma or other systemic illness. Visual acuity was 20/20 OU, and anterior and posterior segment examinations were normal. Slit-lamp examination revealed numerous pinkish-white, hard, keratinized, minimally mobile, papillomatous-appearing lesions along the posterior eyelid margins bilaterally, more prominent in the upper lids. On the right side, a 2 mm × 2 mm lesion completely covered the punctal and peripunctal regions of both upper and lower lids. Fourier-domain anterior-segment OCT showed elevated lesions covering the punctal orifices with a patent proximal vertical canaliculus. The patient underwent excision biopsy of the lesions; the underlying puncta and lacrimal drainage system appeared normal. Systemic evaluation showed normal renal function (including GFR), normal complete blood count, normal liver function tests, and unremarkable bone and joint examination. Serum calcium and parathyroid hormone levels were within normal limits; serum phosphorus was elevated, and serum vitamin D and chloride were low.

A 56-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with a 6-month history of severe nausea attacks followed by cold sweats and shivering. Initial gastrointestinal evaluation was unremarkable. Several months later she noted that during these attacks the muscles of her extremities contracted tightly, and she began experiencing shooting pain and numbness in her hands and feet on standing and sitting. Over the next few years she developed gradual loss of mobility in her arms and legs. In 2006, she reported discrete, pressure-point lumps on her fingers and soles that were worse in the evenings and associated with shooting pain and numbness. Electromyography at that time showed a diffuse neuropathy of unknown etiology, and she was diagnosed with bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome. 

Between 2007 and 2012 she was lost to follow-up, during which she lost 50 lb and developed deformities of her hands and feet. The previously intermittent lesions on her hands became persistent. Orthopedic and rheumatologic evaluations, including serum protein electrophoresis and a panel of autoimmune serologies (antinuclear antibody positive; anti-SSA, anti-SSB, anti-Smith, anti-RNP, anti-centromere, anti–Jo-1, anti–Scl-70, anti-dsDNA, and rheumatoid factor all within normal limits), yielded no diagnosis.

On dermatologic examination, her hands and feet were diffusely bluish to purplish with symmetric, moderately firm, nontender papules over the dorsal hand joints and coalescing plaques on the palms and soles. She had soft papules on both antihelices and on the nasal columella. Neurologic examination revealed loss of temperature sensation in the distal hands and feet with preserved vibration and proprioception, hypoactive reflexes, positive Phalen and Tinel signs bilaterally, weakness of grip strength with thenar atrophy, and limited motor function.

An 81-year-old woman presented with acute onset of nonradiating, sharp right upper-quadrant abdominal pain that began after eating and was associated with nausea and fever to 38.8°C. Her medical history included hypertension, allergic sinusitis, and multiple prior abdominal surgeries. On examination she was febrile but otherwise nontoxic. Laboratory studies revealed a normal white-cell count and normal liver-function test results. Contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic computed tomography showed a dilated gallbladder containing a 5.4-cm stone without signs of cholecystitis. Right-upper-quadrant ultrasonography demonstrated marked gallbladder-wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, and a positive sonographic Murphy’s sign. She was admitted for presumed acute cholecystitis and treated with intravenous antibiotics and analgesics. Shortly thereafter, she developed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response requiring cardiology consultation. A surgical consultation was obtained, and an urgent robotic-assisted cholecystectomy was scheduled.

A 15-year-old male presented with a protruding mass on the left anterior chest wall that had grown gradually over one year and then enlarged rapidly over recent weeks. He denied any history of trauma or local irritation. The lesion was asymptomatic but interfered with daily activities due to its protruding nature. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender, 4 × 3 cm subcutaneous mass immediately superior to the left clavicle. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a 4 × 3 × 3 cm inhomogeneous subcutaneous tumor without apparent invasion of underlying structures. Computed tomography confirmed no bone involvement. A core needle biopsy demonstrated fibromyxoid tissue with focal spindle cell proliferation, inflammation in a loosely myxoedematous matrix, and extravasated red blood cells. Fluorescence in situ hybridization using a USP6 dual‐color break‐apart probe revealed many USP6 rearrangements, strongly suggesting a diagnosis of nodular fasciitis. Although these histopathological and molecular findings indicated a benign process, the rapid enlargement and protruding appearance raised concern, and the patient was initially managed with observation.

A previously healthy 7-year-old boy presented with a 1-week history of fever, cough, and left earache. He had normal palatal studies on prior evaluation for hypernasal speech and no other significant history. A chest radiograph at the referring hospital suggested a diaphragmatic hernia. On arrival, a repeat chest radiograph showed a large air-filled cavity at the left lung base and smaller cystic cavities medially at the left base and in the right mid to lower zone. Contrast-enhanced thoracic CT revealed a large left-sided empyema with an air-fluid level, collapse of the left lower lobe with a multiloculated fluid collection suggestive of a necrotic lung abscess, a large thrombus in the left pulmonary vein extending into the left atrium, and a segmental left lower lobar pulmonary embolus; the left hemidiaphragm was intact and no abdominal source of sepsis was identified. On hospital day 2, he underwent left thoracotomy, which revealed a bronchopleural fistula at the left lung base; pleural debridement was performed and chest drains were placed. Over the next 7 days, chest radiographs demonstrated a persistent and increasing left pneumothorax with worsening consolidation. On postoperative day 8, he acutely deteriorated with reduced oxygen saturations, and imaging disclosed a new right-sided tension pneumothorax that required emergency drainage.

A 69-year-old right-handed Caucasian man with bipolar disorder type I presented for evaluation of a resting tremor. He had been taking aripiprazole daily for psychosis for two years. Eighteen months after starting aripiprazole, he noted a resting tremor of his right arm; the dose was then increased to 10 mg daily. Over subsequent months, the tremor became both resting and postural, impairing his ability to hold objects, though fine motor tasks such as writing remained intact. He also developed unsteadiness with a tendency to stumble but remained independent in daily activities. He denied changes in speech, cognition, or behavior.

On examination, he had mild hypomimia, hypophonia, and bradyphrenia. There was a right-greater-than-left resting and postural tremor, mild bilateral arm rigidity, dysdiadochokinesia, and reduced right arm swing during gait. He scored 2.5 on Hoehn and Yahr staging and 29/30 on the Mini-Mental Status Examination. Sensation to light touch and vibration was mildly reduced in the distal lower extremities. Brain MRI was normal except for age-appropriate volume loss.

A 37-year-old woman with depression and obesity (BMI 32) presented with one week of nausea, anorexia, fatigue, and two days of jaundice. Four days before admission, her stools lightened and then turned pale; her urine became dark. Two days before admission, she noted scleral icterus. Her only home medication was venlafaxine for several years; she denied alcohol use. On further questioning, she reported starting an herbal supplement containing Kratom two weeks before symptom onset, consuming about 3 g over three days in powder and tablet form to “boost energy.” On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs and had jaundice but was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory studies on admission showed: total bilirubin 10.3 mg/dL (normal <1.0), alkaline phosphatase 672 U/L (50–160), ALT 578 U/L (0–30), AST 455 U/L (0–40); complete blood count, metabolic panel, coagulation studies, TSH, and ANA were normal. Viral and autoimmune hepatitis panels were negative. Ceruloplasmin was normal; antimitochondrial antibody was negative. Abdominal ultrasound and CT showed diffuse hepatic steatosis without biliary duct dilation or stones; MRCP showed no ductal abnormalities.

A 52-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of a painful perianal ulcer that began as a small nodule and progressively enlarged. He reported a significant loss of appetite and weight over the past 6 months but denied diarrhea, abdominal pain, fever, cough, night sweats, joint pains, or eye symptoms. He had no comorbidities, addictions, intravenous drug use, or high-risk sexual behavior and no known history of tuberculosis or household contacts with TB.

On examination, there was an irregular perianal ulcer measuring 10 × 6 cm, extending from the 2 o’clock to the 6 o’clock position around the anal verge, with pinkish granulation tissue and areas of slough. Bilateral inguinal lymph nodes were palpable, discrete, firm, and up to 2 cm in diameter.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin of 14 g/dL, leukocyte count of 6040 cells/mm^3, platelet count of 445,000/mm^3, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 73 mm/hr, total protein 8 g/dL, albumin 3.6 g/dL, creatinine 0.3 mg/dL, and fasting glucose 102 mg/dL. HIV and syphilis serologies were negative.

A punch biopsy of the ulcer performed two months earlier revealed a noncaseating granuloma. A repeat perianal biopsy showed acanthotic squamous epithelium with a dense acute-on-chronic inflammatory infiltrate, foci of granulomas, and Langhans-type giant cells; acid-fast bacilli were not seen. Fine-needle aspiration of an inguinal lymph node demonstrated well-formed epithelioid granulomas without acid-fast bacilli. Culture and nucleic acid amplification tests of the biopsy and lymph node aspirate were negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Computed tomography enterography and colonoscopy were normal. A chest radiograph and thoracic CT scan revealed a right lung cavitary lesion with bilateral diffuse reticulonodular opacities.

A 67-year-old man was transferred from an inpatient rehabilitation facility with a 2-day history of rapidly progressing redness and irritation of his right eye, accompanied by periorbital edema. His medical history was notable for hairy cell leukemia, recent ischemic stroke of the left anterior cerebral artery, and two months of chemotherapy administered via a peripherally inserted central catheter. He had no prior ocular history or surgery. On examination, he was nonverbal with altered mental status. The right eye had only light perception, restricted extraocular motility in all directions, pronounced periorbital erythema, and marked chemosis with necrosis of the inferior conjunctiva. The left eye was unremarkable. Funduscopic examination revealed no red reflex in the right eye and peripheral cotton-wool spots in the left eye. B-scan ultrasound of the right eye showed dense vitreous debris, choroidal effusions, and a thickened sclera with a T-sign. Brain MRI demonstrated acute on subacute bilateral anterior cerebral artery infarcts and right-eye proptosis with marked edema. 

Endogenous panophthalmitis was considered the most likely diagnosis given his immunocompromised status and indwelling catheter. He underwent a vitreous tap with intravitreal injections of vancomycin (1 mg/0.1 mL), ceftazidime (2.25 mg/0.1 mL), and voriconazole (100 μg/0.1 mL), and was admitted for further evaluation. Initial cultures of vitreous fluid and blood showed no growth. Chest radiography and transthoracic echocardiography revealed no infectious source. He was started on systemic vancomycin and cefepime, along with topical prednisolone forte, atropine, and erythromycin ointment. Given minimal clinical improvement, he underwent three additional vitreous taps with intravitreal injections of vancomycin, ceftazidime, voriconazole, amphotericin B, and was started on systemic voriconazole.

A 76-year-old white man with a history of severe Parkinson’s disease with profound motor impairment and mild cognitive impairment was referred by neurology and psychiatry for progressive vision loss that interfered with his daily activities.

He reported daily visual phenomena, including seeing a little girl playing with blocks, a cat at his window, and men dismantling his neighbor’s roof, which he recognized as unreal. These experiences were distressing and impaired his ability to perform household tasks and engage with family.

Despite recent pharmacologic adjustments for presumed Parkinson’s disease–related psychosis—including titration of quetiapine to 300 mg twice daily over 3 weeks, addition of pimavanserin 34 mg daily for 3 weeks, reduction of carbidopa–levodopa dosage, and initiation of clozapine (increased to 150 mg twice daily over 3 weeks)—his visual disturbances persisted.

On ophthalmic examination, his best-corrected visual acuity was 20/200 in each eye. Slit-lamp examination showed mild corneal guttae bilaterally, well–positioned posterior chamber intraocular lenses bilaterally, and visually significant posterior capsular opacification in both eyes. The anterior and posterior segments were otherwise unremarkable.

A 66-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a 1-year history of low-grade fever and productive cough, despite two hospitalizations for pneumonia in the past year. She had a history of hypopharyngeal cancer treated with radiation 20 years earlier. She was a non-smoker with no alcohol use; her younger brother had pulmonary tuberculosis. On admission, temperature was 37.3°C, heart rate 72 bpm, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg. She appeared underweight (BMI 14.2 kg/m2). Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 1.6 mg/dL; arterial oxygen tension was 85 mmHg. On auscultation, coarse crackles were heard bilaterally in the lower lung fields. A chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral infiltrates and micronodular changes in the lower lobes. Chest CT revealed diffuse centrilobular micronodules and areas of consolidation in the left lower lobe and right middle lobe, with bronchiectasis in the right middle lobe. On hospital day 6, bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and transbronchial lung biopsy (TBLB) was performed. BAL fluid showed a total cell count of 2.1 × 10^6/mL with 90% neutrophils; cultures grew Klebsiella pneumoniae and Acinetobacter baumannii; tests for mycobacteria were negative. TBLB specimens from the right lower lobe revealed inflammatory infiltrates and giant cells within the bronchioles; there was no evidence of malignancy.

A 64-year-old man presented with six months of progressive dyspnea. He had a history of asthma but no smoking history. Cardiac evaluation, including echocardiogram and stress testing, was normal. Noncontrast CT of the chest showed bilateral mild ground-glass opacities, slightly more pronounced in the right middle and lower lobes. Laboratory studies revealed a p-ANCA titer of 1:640, a negative anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody, a myeloperoxidase level >8 units (normal <0.4), and a negative proteinase-3 level. Wedge biopsies of the right upper, middle, and lower lobes appeared red to purple grossly. Microscopic examination showed diffuse alveolar hemorrhage with numerous hemosiderin-laden macrophages but no definite vasculitis. An external expert review rendered a diagnosis of idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis and commented that (1) the findings were consistent with a diffuse alveolar hemorrhage syndrome; (2) the absence of vasculitis and capillaritis argued against granulomatosis with polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and microscopic polyangiitis; and (3) Goodpasture’s syndrome remained possible but required identification of anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies.

A 61-year-old non-smoking woman was admitted with a 2-week history of facial edema, dry cough, and dyspnea on exertion. She appeared tachypneic with moderate respiratory distress. Vital signs were: blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg, heart rate 110 beats/min, respiratory rate 28/min, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. Examination revealed facial edema and distended non-pulsatile superficial veins over the neck and chest; no peripheral lymphadenopathy was noted and the remainder of the systemic examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory test results were within normal limits. A chest radiograph showed marked widening of the mediastinum without lung parenchymal lesions. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated enlargement of the right upper paratracheal lymph node (45 mm) and both lower paratracheal lymph nodes (20 mm on the right, 23 mm on the left), compressing the superior vena cava; each node had marginal contrast enhancement with low central attenuation. Positron emission tomography showed increased FDG uptake in the upper paratracheal (SUVmax 16.1), lower paratracheal (SUVmax 14.4), and hilar (SUVmax 11.0) lymph nodes. Because of the short history and SVC obstruction by mediastinal lymph nodes, the differential diagnosis included lymphoma, tuberculosis, and bacterial infection. Initial acid-fast bacillus staining of the sputum as well as blood cultures were all negative.

A 12-month-old boy with a history of perinatal asphyxia leading to hypoxic encephalopathy with tetraparesis and epilepsy, plus dysphagia requiring home gastrostomy feeding with an amino-acid based hydrolysed formula thickened with carob seed flour, presented with one week of abdominal pain, fever, and nausea. He was referred for an acute abdomen. 

On arrival, his temperature was 42 °C, he exhibited cyanosis and epileptic seizures, and had respiratory insufficiency (arterial pO₂ < 80 %). Laboratory studies showed pH 7.23; leukocytes 28,200/μl; platelets 84,000/μl; hemoglobin 14.9 g/dl; lactate 6.6 mmol/l; and rising transaminases. 

An abdominal radiograph demonstrated dilated bowel loops with lucencies in the bowel wall. Ultrasonography revealed free air bubbles in the hepatic vessels and portal vein. Blood and cerebrospinal fluid cultures were sterile; Pseudomonas aeruginosa was isolated from a pharyngeal swab.

A 70-year-old woman presented with asymptomatic, thickened, yellowish plaques on the extensor surfaces of both forearms, present for 10 years. Fourteen years earlier, she had undergone partial thyroidectomy for goiter and was started on 100 μg of thyroxine daily without subsequent monitoring. She denied palpitations, tremor, or changes in sweating. There was no history of eye symptoms. On examination, ill-defined yellowish indurated plaques with prominent follicular openings and a peau d’orange appearance were noted on both forearms. The lower limbs, scalp hair, and eyebrows appeared normal. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a suppressed TSH level of 0.015 μIU/mL and elevated T4 (69.3 μg/dL) and T3 (39.2 ng/mL). ECG and echocardiography were normal. A skin biopsy from an affected area demonstrated unremarkable epidermis and in the dermis extensive mucin deposition with splaying of collagen bundles, empty spaces between fibers, and prominent periadnexal deposits. Alcian blue staining highlighted abundant mucin in the dermis.

A 72-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease fell while intoxicated and presented with left hip pain and decreased mobility. Radiographs revealed a left intertrochanteric femoral-neck fracture, and he underwent fixation with a dynamic hip screw without immediate complication. Postoperatively, he reported medial thigh pain; radiographs were interpreted as normal and he was discharged. Fifteen months later, he returned with persistent left thigh pain and progressive swelling. Examination showed a large, fixed mass in the left anteromedial thigh; distal pulses and sensation were intact. Pelvic radiographs demonstrated union of the fracture and a well-positioned screw but revealed scalloping of the medial femoral cortex and protrusion of screws beyond the cortex. Ultrasound was inconclusive. A magnetic resonance image, performed to exclude sarcoma, showed an asymmetric expansion of the left proximal thigh by an 11 × 11 × 12 cm heterogeneous lesion impinging on the neurovascular bundle. Differential diagnosis at this stage included vascular aneurysm formation, osteomyelitis with abscess formation, and a neoplastic process.

A 37-year-old man presented with 3 months of jaundice, pruritus, fatigue, diarrhea, and significant weight loss. His only medication was oxycodone for chronic back pain. He denied alcohol, supplement, or excessive acetaminophen use. On examination, he had scleral icterus and jaundice without encephalopathy, exophthalmos, heart murmurs, hepatosplenomegaly, or stigmata of chronic liver disease. Blood pressure was 122/82 mm Hg, heart rate 85 beats/min, and electrocardiography showed atrial fibrillation. Initial laboratory tests showed a normal platelet count, international normalized ratio, albumin, and renal function. Liver tests revealed an AST of 132 U/L, ALT of 222 U/L, and ALP of 222 U/L (R factor 2.6), with a total bilirubin of 17.3 mg/dL (direct bilirubin 9.4 mg/dL). Hepatitis A, B, and C, human immunodeficiency virus, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein–Barr virus testing was negative. Autoimmune studies showed a negative antinuclear antibody, negative antimitochondrial antibody testing, normal immunoglobulins, and an antismooth muscle antibody titer of 1:20. A magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography was normal. Serum ferritin was 2938 ng/mL, ceruloplasmin was normal, and hemochromatosis gene testing revealed heterozygosity for the H63D mutation.

A 47-year-old woman with no previous medical history was brought to the emergency department for acute‐onset confusion that began that morning. Her blood pressure was 270/220 mm Hg, heart rate 112 beats/min, and temperature 38.1 °C. On neurologic examination, she was disoriented to time, place, and person, and had bilateral positive Babinski responses; no other focal deficits were noted. 

Laboratory studies showed leukocytes 14 010/µL, blood urea nitrogen 48.7 mg/dL, creatinine 3.0 mg/dL, fasting blood sugar 282 mg/dL (HbA1c 7.3%), sodium 134 mmol/L, and C-reactive protein 0.83 mg/dL. Results of tests for ammonia, antinuclear antibody, antiphospholipid antibodies, rheumatoid factor, and lupus anticoagulant were within normal limits.

Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated vasogenic edema without enhancement involving nearly the entire pons, the left side of the midbrain, and the bilateral medial thalami; diffusion-weighted and gradient-echo sequences were unremarkable. Electroencephalography showed continuous attenuation of background activity with loss of the posterior dominant rhythm. 

A lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 21 cm H₂O, CSF protein 102.6 mg/dL, CSF albumin 64.8 mg/dL, 4 leukocytes/mm³, normal glucose (159.3 mg/dL with serum glucose 267 mg/dL), and negative oligoclonal bands. CSF polymerase chain reaction tests for herpes simplex virus types I and II, varicella-zoster virus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and Japanese encephalitis virus were all negative. Blood and urine cultures, sputum bacterial studies, and acid-fast bacilli smear and culture were negative. 

The patient received conservative management of hypertension, azotemia, and hyperglycemia.

A 33-year-old Nepalese man presented with a 1-year history of a large recurrent swelling on the dorsum of his nose. Seven years earlier, he first noted a small nasal dorsum swelling that enlarged slowly. He denied any facial trauma or surgery until 2 years ago, when he underwent open rhinoplasty with excision of the lesion; the swelling recurred 1 year later and progressively enlarged, causing cosmetic deformity but no nasal obstruction. On examination, there was a large globular, erythematous, non-tender swelling over the nasal dorsum extending bilaterally; nasal airflow was normal. Contrast MRI of the head demonstrated a multiloculated, lobulated cystic lesion on the nasal dorsum, with areas of high proteinaceous signal on T1 and T2/FLAIR, peripheral postcontrast enhancement, no diffusion restriction, and no connection to the cranial cavity. The radiologic impression was that these features were likely presenting a dermoid cyst.

A 49‐year‐old man with stage IVB lung adenocarcinoma (EGFR L858R) treated with first‐line osimertinib achieved a partial response. Seven months later, the primary lesion progressed, and transbronchial re-biopsy confirmed poorly differentiated non–small-cell lung cancer with a PD-L1 tumor proportion score of 100 %. Six days after the bronchoscopy, second-line therapy with atezolizumab, bevacizumab, carboplatin, and paclitaxel was initiated. Two days after starting chemotherapy, he presented with chills and anterior chest‐wall pain. On examination, he had a fever of 39.4 °C, crepitus in the left pectoral region, and erythema and tenderness of the left upper chest wall. Chest radiography showed a large cavitary mass with an air–fluid level in the left upper lung field and subcutaneous emphysema. Laboratory tests revealed leukocytosis (18 130 cells/mm3, 87% neutrophils) and a C-reactive protein level of 19.36 mg/dL; blood and sputum cultures were negative. Empirical meropenem and vancomycin were administered. After 9 days of therapy, fever persisted, C-reactive protein increased to 25.82 mg/dL, and the white‐cell count decreased to 1690 cells/mm3 (52.6% neutrophils). Chest CT demonstrated a 10 cm gas-containing cavitary lesion in the left upper lobe and subcutaneous emphysema of the chest wall.

A 35-year-old Ethiopian man presented with a 2-year history of a gradually enlarging lower abdominal swelling. He noted increased urinary frequency without dysuria, urgency, intermittency, or hematuria. Two months before presentation, the swelling became painful. He had no history of abdominal trauma, surgery, or tuberculosis, and denied fever, weight loss, night sweats, or gastrointestinal bleeding.

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. Abdominal inspection revealed a firm, non-tender, 20 × 13 cm abdominopelvic mass that was movable laterally but not vertically, with no overlying skin changes and no other organomegaly or ascites. Rectal examination was unremarkable. Routine blood tests, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were normal.

Abdominal ultrasonography showed a 20 × 13 × 16 cm predominantly cystic intra-abdominal mass with soft-tissue components along its superolateral margin, and moderate right hydronephrosis likely from mass effect. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 16 × 12 × 10 cm well-defined, lobulated, predominantly cystic peritoneal lesion with a thick enhancing wall, internal septations, and an 8 × 6 cm heterogeneous enhancing mural soft-tissue component. The lesion extended into the pelvis, displaced the bladder anteriorly and to the left, compressed and displaced bowel loops and major vessels posterolaterally, and caused moderate right-sided pelvicaliceal dilation without renal calculi.

A 33-year-old woman with a childhood history of hydronephrosis secondary to vesicoureteral reflux presented with a 9-year history of diffuse erythroderma. Examination showed confluent folliculocentric erythematous scaly plaques with islands of uninvolved skin, orange palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, and scattered eczematous lesions. Initial diagnostic considerations included pityriasis rubra pilaris, psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, and epidermotropic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.  
• Flow cytometric and molecular studies of skin and blood failed to demonstrate a T-cell clone.  
• Peripheral blood screening did not reveal Sézary cells or phenotypically atypical lymphocytes.  
• Whole-genome sequencing, including analysis of CARD14, did not identify a causal mutation.  
• Multiple skin biopsies demonstrated epidermal acanthosis, alternating orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, and a dermal lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with few neutrophils.

A 3-year-old male intact domestic shorthair stray cat was found emaciated with multifocal alopecic, abrasive, and ulcerated lesions on the lateral aspects of the forelimbs, right hip, both ear bases, and the bridge of the nose. The cat also had signs of upper respiratory infection, including sneezing with bloody mucous discharge. A SNAP FIV/FeLV combo test was positive for FeLV. Complete blood cell count revealed leukocytosis (32 980 cells/µL; reference range 5 500–19 500 cells/µL) and anemia (packed cell volume 27.7%; reference range 30–45%), with normal creatinine and alanine aminotransferase levels. Because of the ulcerated and crusted skin lesions, the initial differential diagnoses included deep pyoderma and deep mycotic infection. Cytologic examination of an ulcerated lesion showed numerous cigar-shaped yeasts (2–5 µm in diameter), some within macrophages, along with intracellular cocci and degenerate neutrophils.

A 42-year-old man with a history of crack-cocaine, opioids, IV heroin use, and ongoing benzodiazepine use disorder complicated by withdrawal seizures presented to the emergency department after an unwitnessed fall. He purchases etizolam and carisoprodol online and endorsed use of both at the time of the fall. On examination, he had multiple head, face, chest, abdominal, and back abrasions and ecchymoses. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 17.4×10^3/μL, sodium 122 mmol/L, potassium 5.4 mmol/L, creatinine 1.74 mg/dL (baseline 1.3), and creatine kinase 42 900 U/L. A urine drug screen was positive for benzodiazepines. 
A chest radiograph revealed patchy and nodular opacities at the right lung base. CT of the brain and face was unremarkable except for soft-tissue hematomas. Because of flank ecchymoses and frank hematuria, CT of the abdomen and pelvis was performed; the kidneys were normal, but scattered centrilobular and tree-in-bud ground-glass nodules were seen in the lung bases, more pronounced on the right than the left. These were considered likely infectious or inflammatory in origin, and a dedicated CT chest in three months was recommended. 
Nearly five months later, a noncontrast CT of the chest was obtained, showing increased gravity-dependent ground-glass opacities in a primarily centrilobular distribution, with clear central airways.

A 60-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department after two consecutive out‐of‐hospital cardiac arrests at home with immediate bystander CPR and ACLS by ambulance personnel. Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) was achieved after 27 minutes; she then had a PEA arrest en route with ROSC after 4 minutes and a third arrest in the ED for 4 minutes (total collapse to ROSC time 35 minutes). She was intubated and mechanically ventilated on arrival.  
Her history included diabetes, hypertension, heart failure, and hypothyroidism. Medications included sacubitril‐valsartan, carvedilol, ivabradine, levothyroxine, gliclazide, metformin, and dapagliflozin. Prior echocardiography showed an EF of 49% with mild hypokinesis; previous angiography showed moderate LCX and mild proximal LAD disease.  
Post‐ROSC ABG showed pH 7.18, PCO2 26 mmHg, PO2 173 mmHg, HCO3 9.6 mmol/L. ECG on admission revealed an old LBBB. Head CT demonstrated ventricular dilatation without midline shift. CT pulmonary angiography excluded PE but showed mild cardiomegaly, bilateral pleural effusions, and extensive consolidations.  
In the ICU she required high vasopressors; GCS was 3/15. AKI prompted CRRT. Day 2 CT brain was normal. Day 6 EEG showed encephalopathy. On day 8, brain MRI with DWI revealed bilateral restricted diffusion in the cortical and subcortical posterior occipital lobes, corresponding to hyperintensities on FLAIR, with no hemorrhage on SWI.

A 24-year-old man presented with sudden-onset, nontraumatic, excruciating abdominal pain. Over the preceding months, he had experienced intermittent abdominal pain, fevers, anorexia, a 10-kg weight loss, generalized weakness, myalgias, and arthralgias of the small joints. He denied any bleeding diathesis or use of anticoagulant therapy.  

On examination, his temperature was 37.4 °C, pulse 80 beats/min, and blood pressure 110/60 mmHg. He appeared uncomfortable and had left costovertebral-angle tenderness. There were no skin rashes or lesions, and his genital examination was normal.  

Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 23.9 × 10^9 cells/L (reference, 4.6–10.2), hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL (12.2–18.1), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 70 mm/hr (0–15). Renal function and other biochemical values were within normal limits. Urinalysis revealed 3+ proteinuria and 3+ hematuria. Tests for hepatitis B surface antigen, antinuclear antibody, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative.  

A contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan demonstrated multiple small, wedge-shaped, hypoenhanced areas in both kidneys, with suspicion of intrarenal hemorrhage, hemorrhagic cyst rupture, or a right perirenal hematoma.

A 24-year-old left-handed woman with no significant medical history, who smokes one pack per day, presented the day after sustaining an injury during a workout. While performing a side plank—supporting her entire body weight on her fully extended left arm—she felt a sudden “pop” in her anterior shoulder and chest. She experienced immediate pain without numbness or tingling, which persisted and began to radiate to her neck, anterior chest, and down her arm.

On examination, there was mild asymmetry of the left anterior axillary crease but no gross deformity or ecchymosis. Palpation elicited tenderness over the left biceps groove and along the pectoralis major tendon, and resisted internal rotation of the arm reproduced her pain. The brachial plexus and axilla were nontender. Active scapular protraction and retraction were painful, and the coracoid tip was tender to palpation. The remainder of the shoulder examination, including range of motion and a neurovascular assessment, was unremarkable.

Radiographs of the left shoulder showed no abnormalities.

A 43-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of chronic abdominal pain without alarming features. Her physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. 

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed a well-defined, sausage-shaped, retroperitoneal cystic lesion measuring 7.4 × 3.6 cm, adjacent to the pancreatic tail and distinct from the gastric wall. MRI and MRCP demonstrated that the lesion was separate from both the stomach and the pancreatic duct, with no evidence of communication. 

Endoscopic ultrasound revealed an anechoic cystic lesion near the pancreatic tail with no connection to the pancreatic duct or the stomach. Fine-needle aspiration of the cyst yielded fluid with a carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) level of 865 ng/mL and an amylase level of 1878 U/L; cytology showed no malignant cells.

A 72-year-old man with distal esophageal adenocarcinoma undergoing neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (completed 1 week earlier) was referred after an outpatient CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed free intraperitoneal gas. His history included emphysematous changes on CT, a left upper lobectomy for lung adenocarcinoma 10 years ago, and placement of a feeding jejunostomy 3 months ago for dysphagia. He reported 48 hours of increasing shoulder-tip pain, generalized lethargy similar to prior post-chemotherapy episodes, new non–blood-containing diarrhea, but denied worsening abdominal pain or fevers.  
On examination, he was afebrile, heart rate 94 bpm, blood pressure 129/86 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, clinically dehydrated, and mobile without distress. His abdomen was mildly distended, tender across the upper quadrants, but without peritoneal signs.  
Laboratory tests showed leukopenia (white cell count 1.5 × 10^9/L), a normal venous blood gas and electrolytes, and a C-reactive protein of 16 mg/L.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated pneumoperitoneum predominantly in the right subhepatic space, extensive mesenteric gas, and intramural gas locules within the hepatic flexure. There was no free fluid, bowel wall thickening, or hypoenhancement to suggest ischemia.

A 15-year-old Han Chinese boy presented with a 2-week history of fever, weakness, pallor, edema, dyspnea, and progressively increasing abdominal girth. He was the product of a full-term, non-consanguineous pregnancy with markedly slow growth and development, but good school performance. At age 9, he underwent splenectomy for an unexplained splenomegaly. Since then he had multiple hospital admissions for fever of unknown origin without a clear diagnosis.

On examination, his height was 135 cm and weight 30 kg, with no secondary sexual characteristics. His temperature fluctuated between 37.2 °C and 39.7 °C. He appeared pale and distressed. There was no jaundice or rash. Superficial inguinal lymph nodes were palpable. He had periorbital edema, large bilateral tonsils without pharyngeal congestion, harsh breath sounds with bilateral crackles, and a heart rate of 114 beats/min without murmur. His abdomen was distended; the liver was firm, nontender, and palpable 10 cm below the costal margin. He had shifting dullness and marked pitting edema of the lower limbs. Neurologic examination was normal.

Laboratory testing over several days showed a white blood cell count > 20 × 10^9/L, progressive anemia and thrombocytopenia, elevated lactate dehydrogenase (301 U/L), AST 45 U/L, ALP 218 U/L, total bilirubin 72.9 μmol/L, hypoalbuminemia (29 g/L), and slight prolongation of PT and APTT with an elevated D-dimer. Renal function and urinalysis were unremarkable. Other positive findings included procalcitonin ~ 0.2 ng/mL, ASO 259 IU/mL, Widal’s TH 1:160 and TO 1:320, CA-125 384 U/mL, CA724 38.8 U/mL, ferritin 550 ng/mL, hepatitis E virus IgG(+), and Legionella pneumophila IgM(±). Tests for thyroid function, ESR, CRP, CD64 index, T-lymphocyte subsets, and G6PD were normal. Coombs test; interferon-γ release assay; ANA; HAV, HBV, HCV, HIV antibodies; and HSV, CMV, and EBV DNA were negative. Blood and fungal cultures were negative. Bone marrow smear showed an infectious pattern with occasional atypical lymphocytes.

Abdominal ultrasound revealed a grossly enlarged liver (164 mm), gallbladder wall swelling, left renal calculi, and massive ascites; the portal vein and common bile duct were normal. There was slight pericardial effusion. Enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen demonstrated severe pulmonary interstitial fibrosis with infection, multiple lymph node enlargement, and an irregularly shaped enlarged liver without vascular abnormalities.

He received empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics, antiviral therapy, diuresis, liver-protective measures, human serum albumin, intravenous immunoglobulin, and blood transfusions, with gradual improvement of fever. Given the multisystem presentation and difficulty attributing all findings to a single etiology, a rare genetic metabolic disorder was suspected. To pursue a definitive diagnosis, archived splenic tissue was retrieved for pathological examination.

A 50-year-old Caucasian man with a 2-month history of persistent dysphonia, dysphagia, and odynophagia radiating to the right ear presented with recurrent aspiration of liquids and a 3-kg weight loss. He had a 40-pack-year smoking history and no alcohol abuse. Flexible laryngoscopy revealed an ulcer on the right false vocal cord extending to the epiglottis, oedema with decreased mobility of the right true cord, and diffuse swelling of both arytenoids. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy on neck ultrasound. A routine chest radiograph showed miliary nodules predominantly in the upper lung fields bilaterally. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated an enhancing mass in the right false vocal cord with obliteration of the paraglottic fat, extension into the anterior commissure, and obliteration of the right piriform sinus. Full blood count and electrolytes were normal. Direct laryngoscopy under general anaesthesia revealed a tumour covering the entire right false vocal cord and extending to the laryngeal side of the epiglottis without glottic involvement. The lesion was clinically staged as a T3N0 supraglottic laryngeal carcinoma.

A 47-year-old woman presented with a 10-day history of progressively worsening severe pain, foreign-body sensation, and decreased visual acuity in her left eye. She wore soft contact lenses with poor hygiene and routinely slept in them. She had no prior ocular or systemic disease. On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/200 in the left. The left cornea had a 2 × 2 mm fluffy white infiltrate slightly superior and to the left of the visual axis, surrounded by scattered stromal subepithelial infiltrates, 1+ corneal edema, 1+ scleral injection, and a 10 mm epithelial defect. The initial differential diagnosis included herpes simplex virus, Acanthamoeba, and bacterial infection, but because of the infiltrate’s appearance, a fungal keratitis was presumed. Topical voriconazole drops every hour and gatifloxacin drops four times daily were started, along with oral acyclovir. Corneal scrapings were taken and directly inoculated onto blood agar and Sabouraud dextrose agar. No Gram stain was performed, but scrapings evaluated in pathology showed epithelial cells and septate fungal elements. Culture plates incubated at 30 °C showed within three days compact velvety colonies that were initially white, later turning dark green on the surface and brownish orange on the reverse. Tease preparations and slide culture demonstrated numerous cylindrical microconidia in chains.

A 50-year-old man with no history of abdominal surgery or chronic illness presented with 12 hours of colicky abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and progressive distension. He reported similar but self-resolving episodes over the past year. On examination, he was afebrile; blood pressure was 120/70 mmHg, heart rate 95/min, and BMI 18 kg/m2. The abdomen was mildly distended, soft, and non-tender; rectal examination revealed an empty rectum. Laboratory evaluation showed leukocytosis and hypoalbuminemia; renal function and electrolytes were normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a markedly dilated duodenum with the “bottle gourd” sign and intraluminal feces, with abrupt collapse of the jejunum, findings interpreted as consistent with an incarcerated left paraduodenal hernia but without signs of ischemia or perforation. He was managed conservatively with intravenous fluids, nasogastric decompression, bowel rest, and parenteral nutrition. His symptoms and imaging findings resolved over 6 hours.

A 52-year-old man with diabetes presented with a central retinal vein occlusion, secondary macular edema, and neovascular glaucoma in his left eye; visual acuity was counting fingers. He underwent an in-office intravitreal injection of ranibizumab and concurrent anterior‐chamber (AC) paracentesis under aseptic technique. Postprocedure, he was prescribed topical ofloxacin and aqueous suppressants.

One day later, he returned with severe left eye pain. Examination showed an intraocular pressure of 60 mm Hg, a 1-mm hyphema, and diffuse corneal edema. An emergent slit-lamp AC paracentesis reduced the IOP to 2 mm Hg; a small leak was noted at the entry site but the AC remained deep. He was sent home on topical antibiotics and maximal anti‐glaucoma therapy.

Two days later, he was asymptomatic but vision had declined to hand motion. Findings included conjunctival injection, a 2-mm hypopyon overlying hyphema, mild fibrin in the AC, and a hazy cornea without keratic precipitates. The fundus view was limited and B-scan ultrasonography showed mild-to-moderate vitritis. A diagnosis of acute post-procedural infectious endophthalmitis was suspected.

A 48-year-old active-duty service member first presented in 2007 with progressive dyspnea on exertion. He denied recurrent sino-pulmonary infections but had a history of seasonal allergies. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory testing showed mild microcytic anemia with normal iron studies and mild hypoproteinemia. Chest radiography was normal. Spirometry demonstrated an FVC of 100% of predicted, FEV₁ of 92% of predicted, and FEV₁/FVC of 80% of predicted; methacholine challenge testing was negative. Despite these findings, he was diagnosed with asthma and treated with inhaled corticosteroids, bronchodilators, courses of azithromycin for presumed infections, and repeated oral corticosteroids—with minimal improvement.

Over the next decade, he continued to have exertional dyspnea that limited his military fitness, and allergen testing, repeat spirometry, treatment for gastroesophageal reflux, and an initial high-resolution chest CT scan were unrevealing. In 2016, chart review noted a CT scan of the abdomen done for appendicitis that showed numerous ground-glass nodules. A dedicated noncontrast CT of the chest subsequently revealed innumerable ground-glass and consolidative nodules with mediastinal, supraclavicular, and axillary lymphadenopathy. A PET–CT scan confirmed multiple hypermetabolic thoracic and abdominal lymph nodes and mild splenic uptake. Given concern for malignancy, an excisional biopsy of a right axillary lymph node was performed; pathology demonstrated reactive lymphoid hyperplasia with scattered granulomas, and “there was no evidence of malignancy on histology or flow cytometry.”

A 69-year-old woman presented with a 12-year history of progressive gait disturbance. She reported multiple episodes of vertigo and worsening ataxia. Initial brain CT showed mild cerebellar atrophy and communicating hydrocephalus, for which a ventriculoperitoneal shunt was placed without any relief of neurological symptoms. Over the subsequent four years, she developed painful weakness and sensory loss in her upper and lower limbs. She underwent bilateral carpal tunnel decompressions, but symptoms persisted. Nerve conduction studies revealed a progressive sensory neuropathy with absent sensory nerve action potentials and relative sparing of motor fibers. MRI of the brain demonstrated cerebellar degeneration predominantly affecting the vermis. Vestibular testing revealed bilateral vestibular hypofunction. There was evidence of autonomic involvement, including features suggestive of defective baroreflex function. No history of significant alcohol use, infections, metabolic or endocrine disorders, or hereditary neuropathies was identified, and relevant laboratory testing was unremarkable.

A 13-month-old child weighing 10 kg presented with a 15-day history of nasal blockage and chest congestion, a 1-week history of croupy voice and stridor, and 1 day of worsening shortness of breath. Five days earlier the child had chewed nuts. Initially, foreign body aspiration and viral croup were considered; aspiration was excluded after clinical work-up, and the child was treated for croup with epinephrine nebulization and dexamethasone and discharged. The next day, the child returned with stridor and a croupy voice, again responded to epinephrine nebulization and dexamethasone, and was sent home. On the third presentation, the child was lethargic with a croupy voice, respiratory distress, central cyanosis, and pallor. Examination showed severe inspiratory stridor, bilateral wheezes, and decreased air entry on the left. After epinephrine nebulization, cold saline nebulization, and intramuscular dexamethasone the oxygen saturation remained at 80 %, so the child was intubated emergently and transferred to the surgical ICU. Foreign body aspiration was again excluded on surgical evaluation. Contrast CT of the neck and chest showed a circumferential thickening of the airway from the level of the hyoid bone to below the thyroid cartilage, involving the supraglottis and glottis, likely due to edema. Two days later the child was extubated but required reintubation for respiratory distress. Video laryngoscopy and bronchoscopy were then performed and revealed Grade II subglottic stenosis.

A 15-year-old boy had a one-month history of intermittent fever (37.4–38.0 °C), sore throat, and fatigue unresponsive to antipyretics and cefuroxime. Two weeks before admission, he developed nausea, vomiting, anorexia, jaundice, and dark urine. He met the 2019 EULAR/ACR criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus and received intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg twice daily, which improved his fever and fatigue but only partially corrected leukopenia, anemia, elevated liver enzymes, and hyperbilirubinemia. He then had a six-minute generalized seizure with postictal unresponsiveness; EEG was normal, and levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily was started.

On admission, he had nocturnal episodes of disordered speech, disorientation, inattention, auditory and visual hallucinations, and persecutory delusions, with daytime lethargy. Olanzapine 5 mg daily was initiated. Two days later, his hallucinations and delusions abated, but he began displaying intermittent abnormal movements: repetitive buttock elevation with sustained posturing, maintenance of passive limb positions, echolalia, mutism, fixed staring, resistance to passive movement, and minimal responses to pain or verbal stimuli.

Initial labs showed leukopenia, anemia, elevated transaminases, hyperbilirubinemia, elevated C-reactive protein, hypocomplementemia (C3 and C4), ANA 1:1280, and anti-dsDNA antibodies 311 IU/mL; abdominal ultrasound revealed mild splenomegaly. During hospitalization, anti-dsDNA titers fell to 105 IU/mL, ANA to 1:160, and complement levels normalized. Tests for antiphospholipid, anti-NMDA receptor, anti-GABA, and anti-VGKC antibodies were negative. CSF examination was normal. Brain MRI showed slight widening of the sulci and fissures.

A 42-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of dry cough and a 2-month history of weight loss and anorexia. He denied fever, chest pain, or dyspnea. His medical history was notable for type II diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. He was a nonsmoker with no known exposures to tuberculosis or environmental agents. 

On examination, his vital signs were within normal limits. He had clubbing of the fingers and toes. A firm, non-tender right supraclavicular lymph node was palpable. Respiratory and other system examinations were unremarkable except for a painless right-sided scrotal swelling, which the patient had not previously noticed.

Chest radiography showed bilateral hilar prominence without parenchymal infiltrates. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated enlarged upper and lower paratracheal, subcarinal, and bilateral hilar lymph nodes; the lung windows were clear. Laboratory tests revealed a normal total lymphocyte count (6700 cells/mm3), normal liver and renal function, and a serum calcium of 10 mg/dL (reference range, 8.6–10.2 mg/dL).

Given the chronic symptoms and lymphadenopathy, tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, and lymphoma were initially considered. Sputum smear for acid-fast bacilli and CBNAAT were negative, and a tuberculin skin test showed no induration after 48 hours. A surgical excision of the cervical lymph node was planned. Meanwhile, urology evaluation of the testicular swelling led to MRI of the abdomen and pelvis, which revealed multiple enlarged paraaortic and iliac lymph nodes in addition to a right testicular mass. The radiological features favored a testicular tumor.

A 22-year-old man was admitted with a 1-week history of mild fever, diffuse abdominal pain, and loose, watery stools. Initial vital signs were within normal limits, and the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests on admission showed:  
• Platelet count 55,000 cells/μl  
• Total leukocyte count 1900 cells/μl (neutrophils 24%, lymphocytes 80%)  
• Hemoglobin 9.6 g/dl  
• Normal serum iron profile, reticulocyte count, and vitamin B12 level  
A peripheral blood smear revealed 8% atypical blast cells with normocytic normochromic anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia. Stool occult blood testing was positive. Abdominal ultrasonography was normal. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy demonstrated hypocellularity (<10%) with adipocyte replacement of marrow spaces, and parvovirus IgM positivity.  

During his hospitalization, he developed worsened abdominal pain, passage of reddish-black stool, abdominal distention, and low-grade fever (100°F), which was alleviated by antipyretics. On abdominal examination, there was guarding, tenderness, and rigidity in the right iliac fossa. Petechiae were noted on both upper and lower extremities. Initially stable, his blood pressure then fell to 80/60 mmHg, prompting fluid resuscitation and a noradrenaline infusion that raised his blood pressure to 110/80 mmHg. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was performed.

A 38-year-old Asian man with a history of chronic sinusitis presented with 6 months of gradually progressive, painless blurred vision and bilateral proptosis. He denied periocular sensory changes or trauma. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/30 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left eye. Slit-lamp and funduscopic examinations were unremarkable. Pupils reacted sluggishly without a relative afferent pupillary defect, and color vision was normal. Ocular motility was full, and exophthalmometry measured 21.5 mm in both eyes (base 112 mm). Thyroid‐stimulating hormone and free thyroxine levels were normal. Serologic studies showed an IgG4 concentration of 2650 mg/dL (normal < 135 mg/dL), IgG 2630 mg/dL (normal 751–1560 mg/dL), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 31 mm/h (normal < 15 mm/h), and total IgE 1903 IU/dL (normal < 87 IU/mL). The IgG4/IgG ratio was 100% (normal < 6%), and there was no eosinophilia. 

Postcontrast T1-weighted fat-suppressed MRI demonstrated a “doughnut” sign encircling the right optic nerve, inferior sheath enhancement of the left optic nerve, and bilateral tram-track signs along the optic nerve sheaths. Additional findings included bilateral enhancing lesions at the pterygoid plates, pterygomaxillary fissures, and sella, with involvement of both maxillary nerves and infraorbital nerves; enlargement of multiple extraocular muscles (most notably bilateral inferior rectus, right medial rectus, bilateral superior rectus, and bilateral lateral rectus); and mucosal thickening in the ethmoid, maxillary, sphenoid, and frontal sinuses.

A 45-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an abnormal chest radiograph detected during a routine check-up. She was a former smoker (2 pack-year) with no occupational exposures and denied fever, shortness of breath, and cough. She had no joint pain, muscle ache, or weakness but had dysmenorrhea treated with a hormone preparation for over a year.

On examination, she had mechanic’s hands on both fingers, Gottron’s papules on the dorsum of the knuckles, and keratotic erythema on her elbows and knees. No crackles were audible. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 6700/µL, C-reactive protein 0.00 mg/dL, creatine kinase 107 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase 233 U/L, KL-6 2990 U/mL, and SP-D 507 ng/mL. Screening for anti-aminoacyl tRNA synthetase (ARS) antibodies was positive; anti-Jo-1 and anti-MDA-5 antibodies were negative. Pulmonary function tests, including spirometry and diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide, were normal.

Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral consolidation predominantly in the lower lung fields with volume loss. Thin-section CT of the chest revealed bilateral patchy ground-glass opacifications with interlobular septal thickening and intralobular lines—referred to as a “crazy paving” appearance—predominantly in the lower lobes. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was neither bloody nor milky. Transbronchial lung biopsy specimens were non-diagnostic.

A 59-year-old Caucasian woman with stage IV lung adenocarcinoma (PD-L1 60–70%, KRAS G12V mutation) and no prior liver disease began pembrolizumab. After two cycles her tumors regressed, but after six cycles she developed asymptomatic grade 4 cholestatic liver–function–test abnormalities (GGT 1690 U/L, ALP 2696 U/L) with an accompanying grade 3 transaminitis (ALT 235 U/L, AST 252 U/L). A contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed diffuse biliary-tree wall thickening and a common bile duct dilated to 10 mm without intrahepatic biliary dilatation. Pembrolizumab was held and oral prednisone 50 mg daily was started. Four weeks later, ALT and AST normalized (35 and 33 U/L), but cholestatic enzymes remained elevated (GGT 1195 U/L, ALP 938 U/L). Pembrolizumab was resumed and 10 days later cholestatic derangement recurred (ALP 988 U/L, GGT 1363 U/L). MRCP demonstrated no choledocholithiasis but revealed subtle intrahepatic ductal irregularity, a common bile duct dilated to 9 mm with wall thickening, and heterogeneous arterial enhancement of the liver, consistent with cholangitis. Four days later, she had worsening cholestatic LFTs (GGT 2563 U/L, ALP 1783 U/L), a mild transaminitis (ALT 159 U/L, AST 105 U/L), and bilirubin of 25 μmol/L. Prednisone 50 mg daily was restarted and pembrolizumab was discontinued. An infective panel (HBV, HCV, EBV, HPV, CMV) and an autoimmune panel (ANA, AMA, SMA, anti–LKM, IgG4) were unremarkable.

An 11-month-old intact male Labrador retriever was evaluated for a four-week history of chronic perianal dermatitis. The dog lived in the southeastern United States with exposure to fields, ponds, and woods. On examination, the perianal region from 12 to 7 o’clock around the anus showed a well-demarcated, asymmetrical erythematous area of lichenification with papules, crusts, punctate ulcerations, and fistulae; the lesions measured up to 5.5 cm × 5 cm × 1 cm. Superficial and deep skin scrapings revealed no ectoparasites. Cytology of the lesion showed neutrophils and macrophages with intra- and extracellular cocci, consistent with pyogranulomatous inflammation and secondary bacterial dermatitis. During routine castration, four 6 mm full-thickness punch biopsies of the lesion were obtained. 

Histopathology revealed chronic, severe pyogranulomatous and necrotizing nodular dermatitis and panniculitis with intralesional hyphae 6–14 μm wide, with non-parallel walls, irregular non-dichotomous branching, frequent septation, and occasional bulbous terminal dilatations. Hyphae stained positively with Periodic acid–Schiff and Grocott-Gomori’s methenamine silver stains and had no immunoreactivity for Pythium sp. antigen on immunohistochemistry. Potassium hydroxide tissue digests demonstrated tissue invasion by irregular hyphae producing little to no branching. 

Aerobic culture grew methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus pseudintermedius; anaerobic culture was negative. Serum Pythium ELISA results were 7% positivity at 1:1000 dilution, 6% at 1:2000, and 1% at 1:4000, consistent with a negative result. On Day +42, thoracic and abdominal radiographs, abdominal ultrasonography, CBC, biochemistry profile, and urinalysis showed no evidence of systemic dissemination.

A 49-year-old woman presented with acute left-sided, ibuprofen-resistant neck pain localized over the left common carotid artery. The pain began 3 weeks earlier and worsened over the past 8 days; she had no focal neurologic deficits. Her medical history was notable for hypertension and dyslipidemia, and she had received her second mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccination (elasomeran, mRNA-1273) in the left arm 7 days before symptom onset. An outpatient carotid ultrasound showed wall thickening of the left common carotid artery, prompting referral.

On admission, CT angiography demonstrated a semilunar hypodense thickening of the left common carotid artery with slight luminal narrowing. MRI showed periarterial STIR-signal enhancement in the middle third of the left common carotid artery on postcontrast T1-weighted Dixon sequences, along with a membranous structure within the artery and ventrally accentuated circumjacent contrast enhancement. High-resolution ultrasound revealed a 30 mm long, medially located focal eccentric wall thickening of the middle third of the left common carotid artery with a multilayered appearance and a minor, hemodynamically irrelevant stenosis; no intraluminal thrombus or dissection membrane was seen. Initial laboratory tests showed a mildly elevated C-reactive protein (16 mg/L); vasculitis and sarcoidosis laboratory screenings were negative.

A 2-day-old male infant, born at home by spontaneous vaginal delivery at 38 weeks’ gestation and weighing 2.5 kg, was referred for abdominal distension, failure to pass meconium, and bilious vomiting since birth. According to the mother, the neonate was born with a distended abdomen and had passed white “pellets” per rectum shortly after delivery. The abdominal distension increased progressively, and each attempt at feeding was followed by bilious emesis.  

On examination, the infant appeared lethargic and in respiratory distress, with visible peristaltic waves across a distended abdomen. Vital signs showed a temperature of 100 °F, respiratory rate of 45 breaths per minute, and heart rate of 150 beats per minute. A digital rectal examination revealed multiple meconium beads.  

A preliminary diagnosis of neonatal intestinal obstruction secondary to meconium ileus was made, with distal intestinal atresia in the differential. The infant was resuscitated with intravenous fluids, given vitamin K, started on broad-spectrum antibiotics, and nasogastric decompression was instituted.  

An abdominal radiograph demonstrated markedly dilated small-bowel loops. A contrast enema with gastrografin revealed a microcolon and multiple intraluminal filling defects consistent with meconium beads. Despite enemas, the patient’s abdominal distension worsened and clinical status deteriorated, prompting decision for exploratory laparotomy.

A 25-year-old Japanese man with a 6-year history of ulcerative colitis, maintained on mesalazine and low-dose prednisolone after a flare 3 months earlier, presented with acute vision loss and pain in the right eye upon waking. Ten days before presentation, he had developed right eye redness, malaise, and fever and was treated with topical steroids for presumed uveitis. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/200 in the right eye and 20/16 in the left. The right eye showed ciliary hyperemia, 4+ anterior chamber cells and flare, 3+ vitreous opacification, and a fixed subconjunctival abscess in the inferonasal quadrant. The left eye was normal. He was febrile (38.2 °C), had a pansystolic murmur at the apex, mild left lower-quadrant tenderness, and a non-painful pustular rash on the face and trunk. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 11,700/μL with 83% neutrophils and a C-reactive protein level of 13.9 mg/dL. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated severe mitral regurgitation due to anterior leaflet perforation with an aneurysm. Contrast-enhanced CT imaging revealed multiple pulmonary nodules and abscesses in the liver, spleen, muscle, and subcutaneous tissues, with no intracranial or cervical lesions.

A 38-year-old man with known epilepsy, who had discontinued his antiepileptic drugs, was brought to the emergency department after being found in the street confused and amnestic. History was limited by bradyphrenia and amnesia; he had no psychiatric history.  
In the emergency department:  
• Physical and neurologic examinations were unremarkable.  
• Urine toxicology screen was negative.  
• Noncontrast CT of the brain and CSF analysis (cells and protein) were normal.  
• Blood tests showed a slight leukocytosis.  
• EEG revealed generalized slowing without epileptiform discharges.  

He was admitted to neurology for further evaluation. On hospital day 2, he reported having fallen during what he believed was a generalized tonic–clonic seizure and acknowledged nonadherence to his antiepileptic drugs; valproic acid was restarted at 1500 mg/day. Repeat labs showed a decreased leukocytosis, creatine kinase of 521 U/L, and C-reactive protein of 16.2 mg/L. Brain MRI was normal.  

On hospital day 4, nursing staff witnessed a generalized tonic–clonic seizure; valproic acid was increased to 2000 mg/day. EEG remained unchanged. Subsequently, the patient became bradyphrenic, spoke minimally, and maintained a fixed stare, prompting psychiatric consultation. Mental status examination showed clear consciousness, flat affect, intact orientation, normal attention, and no perceptual disturbances. Initial assessment noted insufficient DSM-5 criteria for catatonia.  

Three days later, he exhibited hand-rubbing stereotypies, grimacing, sustained posturing, and ambitendency. The Bush–Francis Catatonia Rating Scale score was 12. A repeat EEG remained without epileptiform activity.

A 61‐year‐old woman with premenstrual dysphoric disorder treated with fluoxetine and bupropion for 5 years underwent an elective coronary artery bypass graft and mitral valve replacement for multivessel coronary artery disease and a depressed left ventricular ejection fraction. Home serotonergic medications had been held for 2 days before surgery. Intraoperatively, she developed vasoplegic syndrome requiring three doses of methylene blue, and received a single dose of meperidine postoperatively. On postoperative day 1, after extubation, she became confused and agitated, with a temperature up to 39.9 °C, tachycardia, diaphoresis, generalized muscle rigidity, hyperreflexia, and horizontal clonus.

A 4-year-old girl was brought to the hospital with intermittent fever for 4 days, generalized edema and oliguria for 2 days, and an erythematous macular rash on her trunk and limbs for 1 day. She also had two episodes of vomiting. There was no history of jaundice or previous similar illness.

On examination, she was febrile, tachycardic (heart rate 134/min), and hypotensive (blood pressure 88/50 mm Hg) with poor peripheral perfusion. She had anasarca, a blanching macular erythematous rash over her trunk, hands, and legs, and multiple nontender, nonmatted cervical lymph nodes (largest 1.5 × 1.5 cm). Her lips were erythematous and cheilotic, but she had no strawberry tongue or conjunctival injection. Abdominal examination revealed tender hepatomegaly and splenomegaly.

Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, white cells 10,000/μL (72% neutrophils), platelets 430,000/μL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 4 mm in the first hour. Blood cultures were negative and peripheral smear showed no malarial parasites. Liver tests were notable for ALT 155 IU/L, total protein 4.8 g/dL, and albumin 2.0 g/dL. Tests for dengue IgM and leptospira IgM were negative. Cardiac monitoring was normal, and serum creatinine and creatine phosphokinase were within reference ranges.

She was treated empirically with intravenous ceftriaxone and saline boluses; because hypotension persisted, dopamine was started. Fever continued, and on hospital day 3 she developed red lips and a strawberry tongue, although her rash resolved over the next 2 days. Dopamine was discontinued on day 4. On day 5, repeat studies showed a platelet count of 477,000/μL and an ESR of 135 mm in the first hour.

A previously healthy 17-year-old Caucasian male, an active high school student in an intensive training program, experienced transient fatigue and general weakness during exercise one month before admission. Later that day, he noted lower-limb weakness and numbness at bedtime, which resolved by morning. He also reported intermittent sharp pain in his back and lower limbs during training sessions. The night before presentation, he had a brief episode of non-specific abdominal and chest pain.

On the day of admission, during a mixed aerobic and power-exercise session, he developed tingling and numbness in his lower limbs, back, and head. As he began to run, he felt sudden, severe stabbing pain in his lower back (8/10 on visual analog scale) and within seconds was unable to move or feel his legs. He denied recent trauma, infection, or new medications.

In the emergency department, he was hemodynamically stable. Neurologic examination showed normal mental status and cranial nerves; flaccid paralysis of both lower limbs (0/5 strength, except 1/5 at the left foot), absent deep tendon and pathological reflexes; sensory level at T10 with loss of pain and temperature but preserved proprioception and light touch; and diminished rectal tone and anal sensation. Bladder retention was noted.

Noncontrast CT of the thoracic and lumbar spine showed mild disc protrusions with minimal dural sac contact and no spinal stenosis. CT also revealed an overdistended bladder containing 1200 mL, and splenomegaly (14 cm) confirmed by ultrasound. CT angiography of the chest and abdomen was normal.

Thoracolumbar MRI demonstrated small nonenhancing T2 hyperintense lesions in the anterior cord from T4 to T8 and Schmorl’s nodes at T7–8 and T11–12. Initial laboratory studies showed protein C activity 54% (normal 70–150%), hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL with microcytic hypochromic anemia, and otherwise normal coagulation. Autoimmune tests (anti-cardiolipin, anti-MOG, anti-AQP4) were unremarkable. Lumbar puncture revealed opening pressure 28 cmH₂O, normal protein and glucose, five mononuclear cells, negative cultures, and no oligoclonal bands.

Eight days after admission, repeat MRI showed increased T2 signal hyperintensity with diffusion restriction in the anterior spinal artery territory, extending from T1–2 to T10 over 14 cm.

A 36-year-old woman, gravida 5 para 5, at 41 weeks of gestation underwent an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery of a 3720 g infant. Six hours postpartum, she developed increasing pelvic pain over the pubic symphysis radiating to the groin, which was attributed to pelvic girdle strain. She was discharged 24 hours later. Forty-eight hours after delivery, she returned with fever (38.5 °C) and was unable to stand or walk. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 12.9 × 10^9/L (84.6 % neutrophils) and a C-reactive protein level of 331 mg/L. Blood cultures were obtained, and she was started on intravenous cefazolin. Pelvic ultrasonography demonstrated an endometrial thickness of 2.3 cm with heterogeneous contents, raising the possibility of retained products of conception or blood clots. A plain anteroposterior pelvic radiograph revealed a mild pubic symphyseal diastasis of 0.8 mm. Blood cultures grew gram-positive cocci in clusters subsequently identified as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, and her regimen was changed to intravenous vancomycin.

A 29‐year‐old man with an 8-month history of elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) was managed with timolol-dorzolamide-brimonidine every 12 hours and bimatoprost once daily in both eyes. He had undergone LASIK 1 year earlier. On presentation, his best-corrected visual acuity was 0.20 LogMAR in each eye; IOP was 34 mmHg in the right eye and 38 mmHg in the left. The anterior segments were notable only for well-positioned LASIK flaps and open angles on gonioscopy. Fundus examination showed 80% glaucomatous optic disc cupping bilaterally with peripheral vascular sheathing but no hemorrhages, detachments, or other abnormalities. Automated perimetry confirmed glaucomatous field defects.

Fluorescein angiography performed to evaluate peripheral vasculopathy demonstrated dye leakage and parietal staining of peripheral vessels. Laboratory studies to rule out rheumatologic, infectious, and thromboembolic causes of retinal vasculitis were all negative. Despite maximal medical therapy, IOP remained above 30 mmHg, and the patient underwent sequential Ahmed valve implantation in both eyes.

On the first postoperative day, visual acuity was 1.00 LogMAR in the right eye and 0.50 in the left; IOP measured 0 mmHg and 3 mmHg, respectively. Slit-lamp examination showed a functioning filtering bleb, a formed anterior chamber, and patent tube openings. Pupillary responses were delayed with a slight afferent defect. Fundus examination revealed a hyperemic, blurred optic disc with peripapillary hemorrhages and multiple white-centered intraretinal hemorrhages in the posterior pole and periphery of both eyes, accompanied by macular folds in the left eye. The patient was started on prednisolone acetate 1% four times daily and atropine 1% three times daily.

One week later, repeat fluorescein angiography showed blocked hypofluorescence corresponding to the retinal hemorrhages and disc hyperfluorescence but no delay in venous filling.

An 80-year-old woman with hypothyroidism, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and hypertension presented with progressive low back pain and acute left lower-extremity numbness leading to a fall. One year earlier, she had a mechanical fall down stairs causing back pain that initially improved with conservative measures. Six months ago, intermittent low back pain developed radiating to the left buttock; she was treated briefly with tramadol. One month before presentation, bilateral lower-extremity radiculopathy emerged, and she self-medicated with aspirin and acetaminophen. On the day of admission, she experienced severe left leg numbness and fell. She denied fevers, chills, incontinence, weight loss, and other systemic symptoms.

On examination, she was afebrile (36.4 °C), blood pressure 104/65 mmHg, pulse 54 bpm, respiratory rate 16/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, BMI 32.1 kg/m2. She appeared uncomfortable but in no acute distress. Lumbar spine had mild point tenderness without overlying erythema or skin changes. Neurologic exam was intact: strength, sensation, reflexes, and rectal tone were normal. She had chronic-appearing abdominal fold and bilateral groin skin breakdown.

Laboratory studies revealed blood urea nitrogen 32 mg/dL, creatinine 1.23 mg/dL, corrected calcium 11.1 mg/dL, and white blood cell count 11.8 K/µL; other labs were within normal limits. A CT scan of the spine showed advanced degenerative joint disease with severe L4–L5 spinal stenosis. Intravenous dexamethasone was administered, and on hospital day 2 an MRI of the spine demonstrated vertebral body edema and enhancement most evident at L4–L5, with paravertebral soft-tissue thickening at L5–S1 concerning for osteomyelitis/discitis, along with severe central canal stenosis at L4–L5. Empiric intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam were initiated.

A 56-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of left middle finger edema, swelling, and severe pain, associated with a mass-like structure over the first phalanx and preceded by several days of fatigue and weakness. Her medical history was notable for a 15-year progression of deformities of the fourth and fifth fingers, previously attributed to sarcoidosis and treated with anti-inflammatories and low-dose steroids without improvement. On physical examination, there was swelling at the base of the middle finger, tenderness, and decreased range of motion. Laboratory studies were within normal limits except for elevated C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate; a purified protein derivative test was negative. Radiographs of the hand showed a lytic lesion involving the distal half of the first phalanx with poorly defined margins and deformities of the fourth and fifth fingers. Magnetic resonance imaging of the middle finger revealed a hyperintense signal in the first phalanx and subcutaneous fluid collections on both sides of the bone.

A 67-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a 3-month history of discomfort in the tongue. He had end-stage renal disease and had undergone hemodialysis for 39 years after developing chronic renal failure at age 27. His history was notable for right and left nephrectomies for renal cell carcinoma, parathyroidectomy, surgery for lumbar spinal stenosis, surgery for destructive spondyloarthropathy, right-side colon resection for ileus due to intestinal tuberculosis, surgical decompression of carpal tunnel syndrome, and an ileal biopsy suggestive of amyloidosis. Current medications included alfacalcidol, ursodeoxycholic acid, sevelamer hydrochloride, and lanthanum carbonate. His serum β₂-microglobulin level was 20.7 mg/L. 

Oral examination revealed a collection of painless, relatively hard, rugged, whitish-yellow papules on the ventral surface of the tongue tip. There was no tongue movement disorder, no dysphagia, and no difficulty eating. No other abnormalities were noted in the oral cavity or regional lymph nodes.

A 28-year-old primigravida at 8 weeks of gestation presented with 1 week of severe generalized abdominal pain and distention. Her respiratory rate was 24/min, pulse 110 beats/min, and blood pressure 110/80 mmHg; she was afebrile, and a tilt test was negative. She reported nausea without vomiting and had no prior medical history. On examination, her abdomen was distended, diffusely tender with shifting dullness, and auscultation revealed rales at the lung bases; bilateral leg edema was noted. Laboratory tests showed a hematocrit of 48% and a leukocyte count of 14 000/mL. The hCG level was 96 103 U/L; serum creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, electrolytes, estradiol, and FSH were normal. Thyroid function tests were normal. CA-125 was 86 U/mL (normal <35), while CA 15-3, CA 19-9, and CEA were within normal limits. Abdominopelvic ultrasonography revealed a single viable intrauterine pregnancy consistent with 8 weeks’ gestation and normal amniotic fluid. Both ovaries were markedly enlarged and multicystic (left ovary 120×110 mm with cysts up to 65×49 mm; right ovary 124×85 mm with cysts up to 59×60 mm), and free fluid was present in the pelvic cavity and paracolic gutters.

A 33-year-old Caucasian man presented with 2 days of fever, chills, extremity pain, sore throat, and right lower quadrant abdominal pain. He had Hodgkin’s disease treated with BEACOPP in 2015 (currently in remission) and HIV infection (stage A2) on antiretroviral therapy with undetectable viral load.
