On examination, he was tachycardic, mildly hypotensive, and febrile (39 °C). Abdominal palpation elicited tenderness in the right lower quadrant without peritoneal signs. The oropharynx showed enlarged, stippled tonsils and mildly enlarged right cervical lymph nodes. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 117 g/L [140–180 g/L], leukocyte count 1.0 × 10^9/L [4–10 × 10^9/L], absolute neutrophil count 0.0 × 10^9/L [1.4–8.0 × 10^9/L], and C-reactive protein 281 mg/L [< 8 mg/L]. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck, thorax, and abdomen demonstrated appendicitis with a phlegmonous inflammatory reaction surrounding the appendix, without abscess or appendicolith. There was no imaging evidence of recurrent Hodgkin’s disease. Serial tests for Epstein–Barr virus, coronavirus disease, and HIV viral load were negative. Prior leukocyte counts had been within normal limits.

A 24-day-old Southeast Asian infant girl was brought for evaluation of pink urine. She had no fever, jaundice, bleeding, rash, or seizures. She was exclusively breastfed. Family history was significant for an elder sibling who had seizures, pink-colored blood, and died by 3 months of age; a second sibling is healthy at 4 years. On examination, the infant appeared well with no eruptive xanthomas or dysmorphic features. The abdomen was soft with mild hepatomegaly. Vital signs were: heart rate 128/min, respiratory rate 46/min, SpO2 97% on room air, and temperature 36.6°C. Urinalysis showed pink-colored urine with numerous red blood cells. When blood was drawn for renal studies, it appeared grossly pink, viscous, and milky. Manual measurement showed a triglyceride level >4000 mg/dL. Liver-function tests were normal, blood cultures were sterile, and abdominal ultrasound was normal.

A 76-year-old man presented with a recurring swelling on the gum of the left lower front jaw for the past 3 months. The lesion had appeared gradually, was painless, and recurred twice within 2 weeks after excision at a private clinic (this was the fourth recurrence). He denied trauma to the area. His medical history was notable for well-controlled hypertension managed with aspirin; he had no recent dental visits except 20 years ago.

On extraoral examination, no submental or submandibular lymphadenopathy was noted. Intraorally, there was a sessile, smooth, sharply demarcated, bluish swelling measuring approximately 5 × 5 × 5 mm on the facial attached gingiva between the left mandibular lateral incisor (tooth 32) and canine (tooth 33), with its lower border near the mucogingival junction. On palpation, it was soft, cystic in consistency, nontender, slightly movable, and depressible, with no discharge or bleeding. Periodontal probing depths were 2 mm without bleeding; tooth 33 had Miller class I recession. Pulp vitality testing of the lateral incisor and canine was positive.

An intraoral periapical radiograph showed no osseous anomaly. On the basis of these clinical and radiographic findings, a provisional diagnosis of a cystic lesion of the gingiva was made. The differential diagnosis included lateral periodontal cyst, peripheral fibroma, parulis, odontogenic keratocyst, peripheral giant cell lesion, melanocytic nevus, angioleiomyoma, Kaposi sarcoma, and melanoma.

A 74-year-old woman presented with a 4-day history of severe headache and neck pain. Her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 15, and she had no focal neurological deficits. Brain MRI showed subarachnoid hemorrhage in the left Sylvian fissure without acute infarction. Hunt and Hess grade was II. CT angiography demonstrated a 5 mm conical-shaped outpouching at the left middle cerebral artery bifurcation and a separate 3 mm saccular aneurysm at the basilar tip. Routine blood tests, including electrolytes, blood counts, coagulation profile, and lipid panel, were normal. Neurosurgical consultation recommended surgical clipping of the presumed ruptured MCA aneurysm.

A 48-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of a painful, red rash on the bilateral malar cheeks. She experienced daily flares of intense burning pain exacerbated by heat and wind, which disrupted her work and sleep. Over the past year, flares had become associated with gastrointestinal distress, photosensitivity, body aches, depression, and anxiety. Symptoms improved moderately with cooling measures, including water spritzes, fans, and ice packs.  

She had failed to tolerate or respond to pulsed-dye laser, hydrocortisone cream, metronidazole gel, ivermectin cream, propranolol, and oral doxycycline. Dietary alterations, avoidance of cosmetics, and naturopathic remedies did not ameliorate her symptoms. Her medical history was notable for Raynaud phenomenon. She was taking combined estrogen/progesterone oral contraceptive pills.  

On examination, minimal erythema was noted on the bilateral malar cheeks, and purple-red plaques were present on both hands. Patient-supplied photographs of flares demonstrated bright red, well-circumscribed patches on the malar cheeks and white fingertips consistent with Raynaud phenomenon.  

Extensive autoantibody testing was positive only for anticardiolipin IgM. Antinuclear antibodies and antibodies to dsDNA, Ro/SS-A, La/SS-B, RNP, Smith, Scl-70, centromere, KU, EJ, OJ, PL-7, and SRP were negative.  

Because of the burning character of her facial rash, erythromelalgia was suspected, and she was started on pentoxifylline, 400 mg three times daily, and gabapentin, 300 mg nightly. Pentoxifylline was discontinued because of worsening symptoms, and she was unable to tolerate increased doses of gabapentin.  

After discontinuation of oral contraceptive pills, the frequency of her facial flares decreased from daily to once monthly, occurring one week before menses. During a flare, her serum progesterone level was 12.9 ng/mL, within the normal range for the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle.

A 16-year-old male with known sickle cell disease presented with a 3-day history of progressively worsening, maximal-intensity headache and bilateral scalp swelling. His mother noted increased fatigue and daytime somnolence. He reported photophobia and back pain but denied fever, cough, dizziness, weakness, numbness, or tingling. His medical history included multiple vaso-occlusive crises, acute chest syndrome, and avascular necrosis of the left hip with prior hip arthroplasty. Family history was notable for maternal seizures.

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. Neurologic assessment revealed no focal deficits, though he reported 10/10 head pain. Bilateral scalp swelling was noted. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (WBC 20.35 × 10⁹/L), mild anemia (hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, hematocrit 29.3 %), elevated reticulocyte count (11 %), and hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 3.7 mg/dL), consistent with hemolysis. Chest radiography was unchanged from one month earlier.

Noncontrast CT of the head demonstrated a new 2.4 × 1.6 cm extra-axial lesion with an attenuation of 50 Hounsfield units, straddling and displacing the anterior falx, with minimal bilateral frontal lobe mass effect and no midline shift. Extensive enlargement of subgaleal soft tissue was also present. MRI and MR venography were obtained for further evaluation.

A 15-year-old boy with no known exposure to tuberculosis and negative HIV status presented with a one-month history of chronic cough without fever, chest pain, dyspnea, night sweats, malaise, or weight loss. He had received BCG vaccination at birth and had no history of allergy. His weight was at the 50th percentile and vital signs were stable. Examination revealed no retractions, good air entry, and normal breath sounds.  
Initial chest radiograph showed reticulonodular infiltrates in both upper lung zones, plate-like atelectasis in the right upper zone and left perihilar region, and minimal right pleural effusion. Sputum was positive for acid-fast bacilli, and culture grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis susceptible to all first-line drugs. Complete blood count and blood chemistry were within normal limits. All household contacts had normal chest radiographs.  
He was started on isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide with good compliance and initially improved. Three weeks into treatment, he developed sudden right pleuritic chest pain without fever, and his vital signs remained stable. Follow-up chest x-ray revealed two new mass-like pleural-based opacities in the right lower lung zone, persistent upper-zone infiltrates, and minimal right pleural effusion. Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated multiple centrilobular nodules with a tree-in-bud pattern in both upper lobes, two heterogeneous enhancing pleural-based masses with central necrosis in the basal segment of the right lower lobe, and multiple enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes.

A 64-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of stabbing pain, itching, and an evolving rash on her right anterior shoulder. She had asthma but no other significant past illnesses. On initial examination, she had multiple erythematous grouped vesicles in the right C4-5 and T1 dermatomes and hypoesthesia in the right C5 distribution; muscle strength was normal. On hospital day 3, she noted acute weakness in her right upper extremity with strength graded as shoulder flexors 2–/5, shoulder extensors 3/5, shoulder abductors 2–/5, elbow flexors 2/5, elbow extensors 4/5, wrist flexors 5/5, wrist extensors 4/5, and finger flexors 5/5. Reflexes and passive range of motion were normal. Laboratory tests showed a C-reactive protein level of 1.59 mg/dL (normal 0–0.5 mg/dL) and a positive polymerase chain reaction for varicella zoster virus; complete blood count, muscle enzymes, renal function, and electrolytes were within normal limits. Computed tomography of the brain revealed no abnormalities. Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine demonstrated cervical kyphosis and spondylosis with spur formation at C4–C6 and mild intervertebral disc herniation at C4–C5 without evidence of nerve root compression.

An 8-year-old, 15.1-kg spayed female Blue Heeler was evaluated for suspected snake envenomation after momentarily running out of view and vocalizing during a hike; the owner had seen a snake in the dog’s path. The dog returned acutely ataxic and lethargic. On presentation, she was ataxic, weak, tachypneic (60 breaths/min), with pale pink mucous membranes, muffled bilateral heart sounds, and decreased lung sounds. On the left ventral neck there was marked non-painful ecchymosis with a 4 mm central indentation and devitalized tissue; a demarcation line was drawn around the lesion. Thoracic point-of-care ultrasound revealed bilateral pleural effusion and a hyperechoic structure adjacent to the heart.  
Complete blood count showed low plasma protein (5.0 g/dl; RI 5.9–8.2 g/dl) with normal hematocrit (40.4%); PT and PTT were within reference ranges; blood lactate was elevated at 4.9 mmol/L (RI <1.6 mmol/L). Chemistry revealed mild azotemia (creatinine 129.95 μmol/L; RI 61.88–114.92 μmol/L), hyperphosphatemia (1.71 mmol/L; RI 0.61–1.42 mmol/L), hypocalcemia (4.3 mmol/L; RI 4.7–5.35 mmol/L), hypoalbuminemia (23 g/L; RI 28–37 g/L), hypoproteinemia (41 g/L; RI 53–70 g/L), and low total CO₂ (16 mEq/L; RI 18–25 mEq/L). Pulse oximetry showed SpO₂ of 93%–94%; blood pressure was 84/56 mmHg, then 72/38 mmHg 30 minutes later.  
The dog received a 10 ml/kg IV bolus of lactated Ringer’s solution followed by 50 ml/hr; buprenorphine 0.01 mg/kg IV q8h was given for pain. Left-sided thoracentesis yielded 10 ml of hemorrhagic, non-clotting fluid (effusion HCT 47.3%; TP 6.2 g/L). Blood typing and crossmatching were performed. Aminocaproic acid 50 mg/kg IV q8h was administered. The patient was placed in a 40% oxygen cage and monitored with telemetry overnight.

A 47-year-old woman presented with new linear growths on both upper eyelid blepharoplasty scars. She first noticed the lesions 6 months earlier, and they had gradually increased in thickness. Her medical history was unremarkable, and she had undergone bilateral blepharoplasty about 20 years ago. On examination, there were tiny erythematous, firm papules arranged in a linear array along the upper eyelid scars. There were no palpable lymph nodes, pulmonary symptoms, ocular complaints, or other skin lesions. Under the initial impression of hypertrophic scars, a punch biopsy was performed. Histopathologic examination showed non-necrotizing, non-caseating granulomatous inflammatory structures composed of epithelioid cells and Langerhans giant cells with lymphocytic infiltration. Periodic acid-Schiff and Grocott’s methenamine silver stains were negative for microorganisms. A chest radiograph and measurement of angiotensin-converting enzyme levels were within normal limits.

An 80-year-old Caucasian man presented with dizziness, generalized weakness, fatigue, and three days of increased diarrhea. His history was notable for chronic diarrhea, shoulder, wrist, and back pain, night sweats, and an approximately 100-pound weight loss over recent years. Past medical history included prostate cancer status post prostatectomy, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, macular degeneration, gastroesophageal reflux disease, antiphospholipid syndrome, and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. He reported hives with sulfonamide antibiotics. On examination he was afebrile, tachycardic to 107 beats per minute, hypotensive to 96/61 mmHg, and had a leukocytosis of 14.5 K/μL.

Empiric ceftriaxone and metronidazole were initiated. Clostridioides difficile toxin and antigen assays and a gastrointestinal pathogen panel were negative. An abdominal CT scan showed no acute abnormalities. Two sets of blood cultures, obtained five days apart, showed no growth. HIV serology was negative. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed mild aortic valve thickening, moderate mitral annular calcifications with leaflet thickening, and mild regurgitation, without evidence of vegetations. On hospital day 2, C-reactive protein was elevated at 12.51 mg/dL.

After six days without clinical improvement, with leukocytosis rising to 21.4 K/μL and anemia progressing from hemoglobin 10.0 to 6.7 g/dL, esophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy were performed to evaluate for gastrointestinal bleeding. The EGD showed esophagitis with a white lesion and scalloping of duodenal folds. Colonoscopy identified and removed a sessile sigmoid polyp. Biopsies were obtained from the lower esophagus, stomach, duodenum, terminal ileum, cecum, and sigmoid colon.

A 79-year-old man living in a rural area was admitted for acute right upper-limb weakness and fever. Ten days earlier he had developed fever (39 °C), treated at home with acetaminophen and antibiotics. He had no trauma or recent travel. Medical history included type II diabetes, hypertension, and hypothyroidism. 

On admission: temperature 37.8 °C, respiratory rate 30/min, blood pressure 190/100 mmHg, signs of dehydration. Neurologic exam showed right upper-limb muscle strength of 2/5 in the triceps, wrist and finger extensors and flexors, and 3/5 in the biceps, arm abductors, arm flexors, and forearm; no altered mental status, pain, sensory changes, or meningeal signs. 

Laboratory tests: normal inflammatory markers; blood and urine cultures negative. Brain CT and MRI were unremarkable. Chest CT and abdominal ultrasound showed no pathology. On further history, he reported multiple mosquito bites. Serum IgM, IgG, and RT-PCR for West Nile virus were positive, meeting CDC criteria for infection. 

After spontaneous defervescence, on hospital day 4 he developed acute right upper-limb pain that worsened at night and was unchanged by rest or activity. Neurologic re-examination showed new weakness (2/5) of interossei and thenar and hypothenar muscles and 3/5 strength in the trapezius; sensory testing was not repeated. 

Shoulder ultrasound demonstrated supra- and infraspinatus tendinosis with calcifications and full-thickness rupture of the subscapularis tendon. Cervical spine MRI showed a right posterolateral C7–C8 disc protrusion. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography revealed (1) symmetric mixed sensorimotor polyneuropathy, mainly in the lower limbs; (2) cervical polyradiculopathy predominant at right C7–C8; and (3) signs of recent nerve damage at right C5–C7 with preservation of sensory nerve potentials.

A 68-year-old man with untreated hypothyroidism and hypertension and no medical care for over 10 years presented with two weeks of nausea, vomiting, and progressive lower extremity weakness. Two prior episodes of severe chest pain had prompted EMS evaluation, but he declined transfer. On the day of admission, EMS found slurred speech and a left facial droop; he was brought in for possible stroke.

On examination he was hypothermic (35.8 °C) with periorbital edema, puffy facies, macroglossia, hoarse voice, and delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes. Heart rate was in the 40s with EKG showing low-voltage QRS complexes and sinus bradycardia. Neurologic exam confirmed chronic left facial droop and dysarthria; motor strength was 5/5 in all extremities. Head CT and MRI showed no acute intracranial pathology but chronic microvascular ischemic changes and remote microhemorrhages. Lumbar MRI revealed multilevel degenerative changes and neural foraminal stenosis without central canal compromise.

Initial labs: TSH 63.4 IU/mL, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL (rose to 9.7 g/dL after 2 units RBCs), normal WBC. He was admitted for management of severe hypothyroidism and anemia evaluation. Next morning creatinine rose to 3.1 mg/dL, potassium 5.1 mMol/L, WBC 15 ×10^9/L (94% neutrophils), platelets 131 ×10^9/L, and CPK 500 IU/L. Chest radiograph showed left lower lobe consolidation; antibiotics were started. He remained anuric despite aggressive IV fluids; bladder scan yielded 48 mL urine and urine studies revealed FeNa 0.96%.

By evening, creatinine rose to 4.1 mg/dL, lactate 3.7 mMol/L, and urine output remained zero. Nephrology and endocrinology attributed his acute renal failure to hypothyroidism-induced low flow and initiated levothyroxine and liothyronine with continued fluids. On hospital day 3, creatinine climbed to 6.1 mg/dL, WBC 16.7 ×10^9/L, platelets 92 ×10^9/L, LDH 1014 IU/L. Schistocytes were absent and haptoglobin was normal.

He then developed abdominal pain and diarrhea. Abdominal CT without contrast demonstrated colitis, either infectious or ischemic, and suggested a possible aortic dissection.

A 70-year-old woman presented with a 12-day history of left-sided neck swelling and a 10-day history of pain that worsened with swallowing. She denied fever, difficulty eating, or speaking. The swelling began small and gradually increased to 4×3 cm. Her medical history was unremarkable. 

On examination, there was a well-defined, smooth, spherical swelling measuring 4×3 cm, extending from 1 cm below the mandible to the upper border of the thyroid cartilage. The overlying skin was red and shiny. The mass was tender with fluctuation, soft and rubbery in consistency, and not fixed to the skin; it was not warm to touch. Intraorally, there was a grossly carious lower left second molar, fractured crowns on the first molars, heavy calculus, and missing upper first molars bilaterally. 

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, were within normal limits. Panoramic radiography showed a carious root fracture of the lower left second molar and a periapical radiolucency at the lower left third molar. Ultrasonography revealed a lobular, ill-defined hypoechoic lesion with heterogeneous solid architecture in the left submandibular region, unchanged posterior echoes, and no calcifications. The ultrasonographic impression was an enlarged submandibular gland with a focal abscess, suggestive of either a submandibular abscess or sialadenitis.

A 13-year-old girl was referred in June 2006 for dyspnea on exertion and wheezing. She had pneumonia in infancy and asthma in early childhood, which had remitted after starting school; she had no atopy or allergies. Chest radiography and computed tomography revealed a giant bulla in the right upper lobe and marked hyperlucency of the right lower lobe with diminished vasculature due to a hypoplastic right pulmonary artery; there was no bronchiectasis. In March 2007, her exhaled nitric oxide level was 27.9 ppb (normal < 20 ppb), and sputum eosinophils were 2.5 %. Pulmonary function tests (July 2006) showed a severe obstructive pattern. Peak expiratory flow monitoring documented a diurnal variation of 19 % (210 L/min morning, 250 L/min evening). A pulmonary perfusion scan demonstrated decreased arterial flow on the right side (right:left = 1:3).

An 82-year-old man with relapsed stage IV nodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma involving abdominal lymph nodes presented with a 2-day history of fever, chills, and progressive dyspnea. Symptoms began 4 days after his first rituximab infusion (375 mg/m2) with premedication of acetaminophen and diphenhydramine. He denied recent upper respiratory infection, chest pain, blood loss, or new medications.

On examination, he was tachypneic and tachycardic. Lung auscultation revealed bibasilar inspiratory crackles. Oxygen saturation was 90% on a nonrebreather mask, and arterial blood gas showed a PaO2 of 54 mmHg on 100% FiO2. Laboratory studies revealed normal blood counts, liver and renal function tests, and D-dimer. Chest CT demonstrated bilateral diffuse patchy infiltrates involving approximately 75% of the lung fields. A two-dimensional echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 55%, stage I diastolic function, and no valvular disease; the B-type natriuretic peptide level was 95 pg/mL. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage yielded negative bacterial, viral, and fungal cultures; BAL fluid was also negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii and malignant cells.

An 8-week-old male Finnish Lapphund puppy was referred for evaluation of poor mobility and limb deformities. The puppy and one male littermate had been noted at 3 weeks of age to be significantly smaller and less mobile than four healthy littermates; both had delayed eruption of deciduous teeth but were eating well and had normal elimination. At presentation the puppies weighed 1.2 kg and 1.6 kg. Physical examination revealed mild hypodontia, retrognathism, valgus deformities of both carpi, limited range of motion at the elbows and shoulders, profound muscle atrophy of all four limbs, pain on hip extension and knee flexion, and a varus deformity with contracture of one hindlimb. Neurologic evaluation found delayed proprioception in all limbs, deemed to be pain related.  

Complete blood counts showed mild anemia (hematocrit 34%), mild reticulocytosis, and a mild mature neutrophilia. Serum biochemistry showed mild panhypoproteinemia, hyperphosphatemia (5.7 and 6.5 mg/dL; reference 2.7–5.4), alkaline phosphatase within adult reference range (86 and 88 U/L; expected to be higher in puppies), and increased creatine kinase (592 and 751 U/L) and lactate dehydrogenase (412 and 369 U/L).  

Radiographs and CT imaging revealed diffuse osteopenia with severe cortical thinning throughout the skeleton and multiple “folding” fractures of long bones with minimal callus formation.

A healthy 9-year-old Caucasian boy was referred for poor vision noted since age 4. There was no family history of eye disorders and no parental consanguinity. Cycloplegic refraction was plano/–2.50×10° in the right eye and plano/–3.50×180° in the left eye. Slit-lamp examination was unremarkable. Fundus examination revealed a blunt foveal reflex in both eyes without other retinal abnormalities. Optical coherence tomography showed absence of a foveal pit, continuous inner retinal layers across the foveal centre, and increased central macular thickness (270 μm OD and 272 μm OS versus 227 μm OD and 239 μm OS in an age-matched control). Axial length was 23.5 mm bilaterally. Fundus photographs demonstrated a poorly defined foveal zone and vascular branches crossing the anatomical fovea. Best-corrected visual acuity was 0.50 logMAR OD and 0.40 logMAR OS. Colour vision testing (Ishihara and Farnsworth-Munsell 100-Hue) was classified as “probably normal” for both eyes. Cover testing at near showed intermittent exotropia; horizontal nystagmus was present only at extreme gaze positions.

A 54-year-old man was referred for evaluation of interstitial lung disease of uncertain origin. He had several weeks of fever with chills, dry cough, and pleuritic chest pain. Chest radiography showed a right subclavicular interstitial consolidation. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen revealed: an interstitial consolidation with centrilobular branching linear structures, bronchial dilatation, and multifocal ground-glass attenuation in the right upper and middle lobes; pleural thickening at the lingula; and fibrotic lines with consolidation in the anterior segment of the left upper lobe. Bilateral mediastinal lymphadenopathy was also noted.

Laboratory studies demonstrated an ESR of 28 mm/h (normal ≤10) and CRP of 6.66 mg/dL (normal 0–5). ANA, cryoglobulins, ENAs, anti-DNA native antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, and ANCA were negative. Complement levels were normal. RF was 24 UI/mL (normal <12) and anti-CCP was 17 UA/mL (normal <5). ACE levels and Quantiferon-TB Gold were normal/negative. Serologies for Legionella, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Chlamydia were negative. Pulmonary function testing showed no restrictive defect and a normal DLCO. He had never smoked.

Flexible bronchoscopy with BAL revealed negative bacterial cultures, negative cultures/genome for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and cytology excluding monoclonality but showing increased neutrophils and eosinophils. A whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT showed increased uptake in bilateral axillary lymph nodes and in the pulmonary consolidation; these findings were thought to represent inflammatory disease such as vasculitis. Echocardiography, nailfold videocapillaroscopy, and upper abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable.

Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics at home and in the hospital led to defervescence but persistent radiologic abnormalities. A trial of systemic corticosteroids produced subjective improvement. Several weeks later, he developed painful swelling of the right knee; Doppler ultrasound excluded deep-vein thrombosis. Subsequently, he experienced synovitis of the right wrist, knee, and ankle. Point-of-care lung ultrasound at the right fifth posterior intercostal space demonstrated multiple ultrasound lung comets fanning out from the pleural surface.

A 4-year-old girl was referred with a 3-year history of ocular misalignment and a 1-year history of poor distance vision in the left eye. There was no history of head or facial trauma, diplopia, pain on eye movement, systemic symptoms, or family history of strabismus. Developmental and medical histories were unremarkable.

Unaided visual acuity was 6/24 in the right eye and counting fingers in the left eye; with refraction, acuity improved to 6/9 and 6/60, respectively, with a hypermetropic correction of +4.50 diopters in each eye. Anterior and posterior segment examinations were normal bilaterally.

Prism cover testing in primary gaze revealed a 10-prism-diopter left hypotropia without horizontal deviation or abnormal head posture. Palpebral fissures were equal in the primary position. Ocular motility testing showed marked limitation of elevation of the left eye on adduction (looking to the right), with nearly full elevation on abduction (looking to the left). Under sedation, a forced duction test demonstrated marked mechanical restriction of passive elevation of the left eye in adduction. Systemic examination was normal.

A 42-year-old woman with a history of asthma presented in winter with 1 week of worsening shortness of breath, general malaise, and diarrhea. She denied fever or chills but reported a sore throat. She was an ex-smoker and denied alcohol or recreational drug use. On arrival, she was in respiratory distress with an oxygen saturation of 50% on room air, afebrile, blood pressure 105/60 mmHg, and heart rate 65 beats per minute. Chest auscultation revealed diffuse crackles bilaterally. Cardiovascular examination showed normal heart sounds with no murmurs, rubs, gallops, jugular venous distension, or peripheral edema. 

Laboratory studies showed a normal leukogram and hemogram. A rapid influenza swab was negative. B-type natriuretic peptide was elevated at 626 pg/mL (reference <100), creatinine was 1.11 mg/dL (reference 0.42–1.06), and troponin I peaked at 0.07 ng/mL (reference 0–0.05). Electrocardiogram demonstrated normal sinus rhythm without ischemic changes. Chest radiograph revealed diffuse bilateral patchy opacities, pulmonary vascular congestion, and a mildly enlarged cardiac silhouette. Chest CT showed bilateral ground-glass opacities, more prominent in the left lung.

She was admitted to the intensive care unit and started on ceftriaxone and azithromycin for presumed community-acquired pneumonia and oseltamivir given high clinical suspicion of influenza. Legionella and pneumococcal urinary antigens and blood cultures were negative. On hospital day 5, her respiratory status deteriorated and she required endotracheal intubation. Bronchoalveolar lavage did not identify bacterial or fungal pathogens.

A 44-year-old woman, gravida 4 para 3+1, with gestational diabetes mellitus and known multiple uterine fibroids, presented throughout her pregnancy with right-sided abdominal pain. A second-trimester bedside ultrasound demonstrated rapidly enlarging fibroids with signs of degeneration. She underwent an elective term Cesarean section for a macrosomic infant; the procedure was uncomplicated, and she was discharged in good condition.

One week post-discharge, she returned with worsening abdominal pain and foul-smelling vaginal discharge but no fever. She was hemodynamically stable. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 18.3 × 10^9/L and a C-reactive protein level of 163.5 mg/L; renal function and other blood parameters were normal. On speculum examination, copious foul-smelling pus was draining from the cervix.

A bedside pelvic ultrasound revealed a complex cystic collection with intralesional moving echogenic debris. An urgent contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed:
- Two large, well-defined, wall-enhancing complex cystic collections with intralesional air locules measuring 8.7 × 11.0 × 9.8 cm (mid-abdomen) and 7.9 × 9.0 × 9.2 cm (pelvis).
- Mild hydrometra and air locules within the endometrial cavity.
- A small communication track between the larger mid-abdominal collection and the endometrial cavity.
- A suspicious tiny communication track between the pelvic collection and collections within the rectus abdominis muscles.
- Extensive mesenteric fat stranding and enlargement of pelvic, bilateral inguinal, para-aortic, and aortocaval lymph nodes.

A 33-year-old African-American man presented with a 1‐month history of bilateral eye pain, redness, and blurry vision. He had been treated for presumed conjunctivitis without improvement and now complained of throbbing pain in both eyes. He also had a pustular rash over his face, neck, and upper chest. 

On examination, visual acuity was 20/100 uncorrected (pinhole 20/70) in the right eye and 20/150 uncorrected (pinhole 20/60) in the left eye. Slit‐lamp examination revealed multiple perilimbal stromal infiltrates with vascularization and areas of thinning superiorly and inferiorly in both eyes. In the right eye, there was an inferotemporal perilimbal ulcer. In the left eye, there was an inferotemporal perilimbal corneal perforation measuring about 4.5 × 3 mm plugged with prolapsed iris and superotemporal peripheral thinning. There was no scleral involvement, but there was significant conjunctival injection and bilateral keratitic precipitates. A dilated fundus examination was unremarkable.

Review of systems was notable only for the skin rash; he denied fevers, weight loss, arthralgias, and any history of severe acne, cold sores, or travel. He admitted to unprotected sex with multiple female partners but denied genital lesions or discharge. 

Corneal scrapings were negative for herpes simplex virus by PCR, and culture of the right cornea grew Staphylococcus aureus. Vitamin A level was normal, and a urine toxicology screen was negative.

A 79-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of rapidly progressive, painful ulcers on his bilateral cheeks and upper lip. He reported onset after shaving with a razor and noted rapid enlargement following surgical debridement. On examination, there were deep ulcers with irregular, violaceous, undermined borders on both cheeks and the upper lip. He had fever and laboratory studies showed elevated inflammatory markers and leukocytosis. Atypical mycobacterial infection was initially suspected, and the patient received rifampicin, amikacin, and clindamycin for four days; however, his temperature rose to 40.2 °C and the facial lesions progressed. Serological and culture tests for viruses, bacteria, atypical mycobacteria, and deep fungi were negative. PPD and T-SPOT tests were negative. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing of lesional tissue did not detect any pathogens. During hospitalization, a papulopustule developed at an intravenous cannula site, indicating a positive pathergy phenomenon. A skin biopsy of the facial ulcer demonstrated an intense neutrophilic infiltrate with pustules and abscess formation.

A 9-year-old boy presented with palpitations during routine activities for 1 year. He had been treated with propranolol without improvement. On examination, he was clinically stable with blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg and pulse rate 130 beats/min. Lung and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia with a normal axis. A standard chest radiograph was normal. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed an echolucent space adjacent to the posterior wall of the left ventricle, causing external compression; ventricular size and function were otherwise normal, and there was no valvular disease. Contrast-enhanced chest CT showed a retrosternal, pericardial‐confined mass containing serous fluid, compressing the posterior wall of the left ventricle. Tests for inflammatory markers, blood cultures, viral antibodies, collagen vascular markers, sputum AFB, and PPD were all normal.

A 9-month-old Caucasian girl was admitted with a 3-week history of persistent erythematous skin rash and redness of the eyes. Her past history was notable for mild atopic dermatitis since 6 months of age. She had no fever before or during admission. 

On examination, she had an erythematous rash over the trunk and limbs, fissured lips, erythema of the oral mucosa, bilateral nonpurulent conjunctival injection, and enlarged laterocervical lymph nodes. Respiratory and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Cardiac examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds.

Laboratory evaluation showed a white-cell count of 8500/mm3 with a normal differential, hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL, platelet count 376 000/mm3, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 35 mm/hour, C-reactive protein 1.5 mg/dL, albumin 2.8 g/dL, alanine aminotransferase 24 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 27 U/L, γ-glutamyl transferase 59 U/L, direct bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL, IgG 589 mg/dL, and IgA 34 mg/dL. Serum-specific IgE against cow’s milk proteins was elevated at 12.5 kU/L (normal, 0–0.35 kU/L). Blood and urine cultures were sterile. Serologic tests for Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, measles, rubella, parvovirus, and adenovirus were negative. Antistreptolysin O titers were normal. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. 

Echocardiography demonstrated mild pericardial effusion and perivascular brightness of the proximal left anterior descending coronary artery.

A 52-year-old man presented with painful, coalescent, erythematous, papulo-infiltrative nodular plaques on his midface. His history was notable for uncontrolled type II diabetes mellitus and an episode of cutaneous leishmaniasis three years earlier, which began as a slowly growing papule on his nose and was confirmed by a positive smear for Leishmania amastigotes; it healed with a scar after a 20-day course of systemic meglumine antimoniate. Two years later, he experienced lesion recurrence at the scar margin; folk remedies led to severe ulceration and nasal deformity. 
On dermatologic examination, there were extensive erythematous papules and nodular plaques on the nose, upper lip, and cheeks, with telangiectasia on the cheeks and deep ulcers with scarring on the nose and upper lip; the remainder of the face was spared. There was no evidence of systemic involvement. 
Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 16.5×10^3/μl with 12.8×10^3/μl granulocytes, a blood glucose level of 340 mg/dl, a C-reactive protein level of 7.53 mg/dl, and a serum calcium level of 7.9 mg/dl; other values were within normal limits. 
A skin biopsy from a facial plaque revealed epidermal atrophy and a mixed dermal infiltrate of lymphocytes, histiocytes, plasma cells, and Langhans-type multinucleated giant cells; no Leishmania amastigotes or caseating granulomas were seen.

An 18-year-old man with neurodegenerative Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) presented with mild right eye pain, headache, and blurred vision. He was diagnosed with LCH in infancy, developed central hypothyroidism, diabetes insipidus, and ACTH deficiency from cranial involvement, and molecular testing had demonstrated a BRAF V600E mutation in his skin lesion. Given progressive neurologic decline, he was started on dabrafenib. Four weeks later, he noted mild right periorbital discomfort, holocephalic headache, and intermittent blurring of vision. On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally, with no afferent pupillary defect and normal intraocular pressure. Extraocular motility revealed a mild supraduction deficit of the right eye and a long-standing left-beating nystagmus in left gaze; confrontational visual fields and dilated funduscopy were normal. Orbital MRI with contrast demonstrated an enhancing, fusiform mass in the right lateral rectus muscle measuring 16 × 8 × 9 mm within his prior radiation field. Given concern for either recurrence of LCH or a neoplastic process, he was advised to discontinue dabrafenib.

A 40-year-old woman with newly diagnosed stage IV gallbladder adenocarcinoma metastatic to the liver received four cycles of intravenous gemcitabine and cisplatin. Ten days after the fourth cycle, she presented with convulsions and altered mental status. On admission, she was normotensive; serum electrolytes were normal, and renal function tests were deranged. On hospital day 2, she developed aphasia and bilateral lower limb weakness. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintense signal involving the gyri of both parieto-occipital lobes and the subcortical white matter of the right parietal lobe, with abnormal contrast enhancement and a glutamine peak on spectroscopy.

A 24-year-old primigravida was first noted at 8 weeks of gestation to have a 13-cm intramural posterior fundal uterine fibroid on transvaginal ultrasound. At 22 + 6 weeks, ultrasound demonstrated the original 13-cm fibroid plus two additional 7-cm fundal fibroids; the cervical length was 13.2 mm. Cultures of vaginal swab, cervical, and urine specimens were negative. Six days later, the patient had spontaneous rupture of membranes and delivered a stillborn infant. Pathologic examination of the placenta and repeat genital cultures showed no evidence of infection. Over the next nine days, she had swinging fevers and elevated inflammatory markers. Repeat pelvic ultrasonography revealed enlargement of the posterior fibroid, anterior displacement of the endometrium, and fluid-filled areas of increased echogenicity. She was diagnosed with a degenerating fibroid, treated with escalated antibiotics, became afebrile, and was discharged.  

Forty days after the miscarriage, she was readmitted with high fever and lower abdominal pain. On arrival, her temperature was 39.6 °C, heart rate 173 bpm, and blood pressure 91/63 mmHg. A bimanual examination revealed uterine enlargement to the level of the umbilicus. On speculum examination, a large foul-smelling fleshy mass was visible at the dilated cervical os but did not protrude into the vagina. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 43 mg/L; arterial blood gas analysis revealed respiratory alkalosis. Blood cultures were obtained, and empiric meropenem was initiated. Pelvic ultrasonography now demonstrated three submucosal fibroids measuring up to 17 cm, with heterogeneous echogenic areas bulging into the uterine cavity.

A 27-year-old man with no significant medical history and no history of trauma was referred for evaluation of an extensive, asymptomatic mandibular lesion discovered incidentally on a panoramic radiograph. Ten years earlier, the mandibular right first molar had received extensive amalgam restoration and an endodontic treatment of questionable quality.  
 
On examination, there was no buccal or lingual bone expansion, no lymphadenopathy, and the mucosa was intact. Both the first and second right mandibular molars were asymptomatic; the second molar responded normally to pulp-sensitivity testing.  

Panoramic imaging showed a well-defined, unilocular radiolucent lesion with sclerotic borders extending between the roots of the first and second molars, superimposed on the inferior alveolar canal, and slight displacement of the second molar. The first molar’s distal root exhibited signs of apical resorption and a poorly filled canal. A periapical radiograph confirmed these findings.  

CBCT revealed a well-circumscribed lesion causing thinning and perforation of the lingual cortical plate at the apical third of the first molar’s distal root.  

Ultrasound with color-power Doppler demonstrated a transonic (fluid-filled) cavity with a hyperechoic bony outline, peripheral vascularity, and no internal blood flow, consistent with a cystic lesion.  
 
What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 19-year-old man presented after a motorbike accident with an open mid-shaft fracture of the left tibia. On the day of injury, the wound was cleaned, sutured, and dressed under anesthesia, and an above-knee plaster cast was applied. Initial vital signs and peripheral circulation were normal. 

On the following day, during assisted mobilization, he suddenly developed severe shortness of breath. He was tachycardic (pulse 150/min), tachypneic (respiratory rate 56/min), and hypoxemic on room air. Blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg. He was conscious but drowsy, intermittently agitated, and complained of headache. Respiratory examination revealed mildly reduced air entry in the right lower lung zone. He was placed on a non-rebreather mask with 15 L/min of oxygen, improving his saturation to 92%.

Electrocardiogram showed an S1Q3T3 pattern with sinus tachycardia. Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated type 1 respiratory failure with severe hypoxemia. D-dimer levels were markedly elevated. He then developed high-grade fever without cough or other localized signs of infection. He was transferred to the intensive care unit and placed on high-flow nasal oxygen.

An urgent computed tomography pulmonary angiogram was performed to evaluate for pulmonary embolism. The angiogram was negative for pulmonary emboli but revealed a generalized ground-glass appearance with bilateral lower-zone consolidations, consistent with acute respiratory distress syndrome.

A 79-year-old man was admitted with abdominal pain and diagnosed with ileitis and a partial small-bowel obstruction. His medical history included an intraductal papillary neoplasm of the bile duct with liver and presumed lung metastases, for which he had been receiving capecitabine for 8 weeks. He also had a widespread papulovesicular rash with hemorrhagic centers on his face, chest, and back, which first appeared after initiation of capecitabine and worsened with each subsequent treatment. Hematologic studies did not suggest either a drug eruption or a viral infection. Because of concern for an adverse cutaneous reaction to capecitabine, the drug was discontinued and systemic corticosteroids were started. Dermatology was consulted, and punch biopsy specimens were obtained for histological examination and direct immunofluorescence.

A 34-year-old woman presented with a 9-month history of a progressively enlarging, painless swelling in her left breast. She noted the mass while showering; there was no nipple discharge, skin changes, or history of trauma or prior breast surgery. She had no family history of breast cancer. 

On examination, there was a 6 × 8 cm non-tender, hard mass fixed to the skin in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast; there was no erythema, ulceration, or discharge. Vital signs were normal.

Ultrasound of the breast showed an anechoic cystic mass with a double-layered wall and posterior acoustic enhancement. Fine-needle aspiration produced a crystal-clear fluid; cytologic examination revealed a few laminated, metachromatic materials without cellular atypia.

A man in his 60s presented in 2015 with a 2-month history of progressively increasing papules on his face, most notable over the nose, associated with mild pruritus. He had received a kidney transplant in July 2014 for hypertensive nephropathy and was maintained on mycophenolic acid and tacrolimus. His medical history also included osteoarthritis, gout, and IgA monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance. Other medications were amlodipine, phosphate, magnesium, pantoprazole, and aspirin.

On skin examination, there were follicular, flesh-coloured to pinkish, monomorphic papules on the central face (forehead and nose) each with a central white protruding spine. The scalp, mucous membranes, palms, and soles were uninvolved.

Given his immunosuppression, the initial differential diagnosis included infectious etiologies—molluscum contagiosum, filiform verrucae, and trichodysplasia spinulosa—and noninfectious conditions such as idiopathic follicular hyperkeratotic spicules and various adnexal lesions (sebaceous hyperplasia, trichoepithelioma, fibrofolliculoma, trichodiscoma, facial fibrous papules).

A biopsy of a papule was performed.
Histopathologic examination showed dilated follicular infundibula with keratin plugs and viral-like changes characterized by large, irregular eosinophilic and basophilic trichohyalin-like granules within inner root sheath cells.

A 50-year-old man presented with ulcerations of the lower lip for 6 months. Six months earlier, he noted an itching sensation of the lower lip followed by multiple small ulcerations. Over the past 2 months, he experienced a burning sensation and mild, dull intermittent pain in the ulcerated areas, worsened by hot or spicy foods. His medical history was unremarkable except for bidi smoking (2–3 packets/day for 20 years). He had not received any prior treatment. He denied lip biting, excessive sun exposure, and systemic symptoms. 

On examination, there was a diffuse erosive lesion of the lower lip, extending to the mucocutaneous junction and inner labial mucosa, measuring approximately 2 × 3 cm with irregular margins, surrounded by erythema, and covered with blood-tinged crusts. Greyish-white radiating striae bordered the inner aspect of the labial mucosa. On palpation, the lesion was mildly tender and nonindurated, with mild diffuse swelling of the lip. Gentle manipulation of adjacent normal mucosa did not produce new lesions (negative Nikolsky’s sign). Oral hygiene was poor, and there were no other oral, ocular, cutaneous, or genital lesions.

A 73-year-old woman with a history of myocardial infarction and arteriosclerosis obliterans was found on MR angiography, performed for recurring headaches, to have an unruptured basilar-tip aneurysm measuring 9 mm. Two weeks of aspirin (100 mg/day) and clopidogrel (75 mg/day) were given before elective coil embolization. Under general anesthesia with propofol (60 mg) and rocuronium (60 mg) and intravenous heparin (6000 units to maintain an activated clotting time of 250–300 seconds), the aneurysm was occluded using a double-catheter technique without balloon or stent assistance. Postprocedural angiography demonstrated a patent thalamoperforating artery (artery of Percheron) arising from the left posterior cerebral artery. 

Immediately after the procedure, she was alert and knew her name but was unable to recall the date, her location, the reason for admission, or the identity of her neurosurgeons, asking repeatedly, “Where am I and why am I here?” She exhibited retrograde amnesia for the 4 days between hospital admission and surgery. Examination of cranial nerves, motor strength, sensation, and cerebellar function was normal. She received argatroban and edaravone for presumed ischemia. Her anterograde amnesia resolved 12 hours after embolization. Diffusion-weighted MRI at that time revealed a focal high-intensity signal in the right mesial thalamus.

A 68-year-old man presented with 1 day of nausea, vomiting, colicky abdominal pain, and obstipation. He had a history of emphysema and a mesh repair of a chronically incarcerated right inguinal hernia 2 years earlier. He was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and in no acute distress. The abdomen was distended and tympanitic, with mild right lower quadrant tenderness on deep palpation. A small, fat-containing, reducible left inguinal hernia was noted. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 12.8 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 18.1 g/dL, blood urea nitrogen 22.2 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.1 mg/dL. An upright chest radiograph showed no free air. Abdominal CT revealed marked small-bowel dilation with a focal transition point in the distal ileum and a small amount of pelvic free fluid. Intravenous fluids and nasogastric decompression were initiated, and the patient was scheduled for exploratory laparotomy with possible bowel resection.

A 76-year-old woman was admitted after a syncopal episode. For 3 months, she had been treated with prednisone (25 mg daily) for tender cutaneous nodules on her legs. A skin biopsy had shown a neutrophilic infiltrate in lobules of subcutaneous fat with fat necrosis and reactive fibroblasts. She reported intermittent chest pain but had no prior cardiovascular disease and was taking no medications known to affect atrioventricular conduction. Her medical history included hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. On examination, her body‐mass index was 27 kg/m2, and vital signs were normal apart from occasional bradycardia.  
Electrocardiography demonstrated complete atrioventricular block with a ventricular escape rhythm at 40 beats per minute, occasionally interspersed with conducted sinus beats. Blood tests revealed normal electrolytes, mild renal impairment, a troponin level of 13.65 μg/L (reference <0.06), and an N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide level of 7894 pg/mL (reference 0–125). Transthoracic echocardiography showed moderate left ventricular hypertrophy, pseudonormal filling, and preserved systolic function without wall‐motion abnormalities, pericardial effusion, or valvular disease.  
Atropine was administered, resulting in restoration of sinus rhythm without ischemic changes, and an isoprenaline infusion was then initiated owing to intermittent block. Despite this, conduction remained unstable, prompting consideration of infiltrative cardiomyopathies such as sarcoidosis.

An 18-month-old boy presented with a 5-day history of fever up to 39.9 °C, mild cough, 1–2 episodes of vomiting and 2–3 yellowish diarrheal stools per day. On initial examination he was febrile (38.8 °C) without other abnormalities. Laboratory evaluation showed leukocytosis (26 500/μl) with 47% neutrophils, an ESR of 57 mm/1 h and a CRP of 100 mg/l. A rotavirus antigen was detected; other infection studies were negative. 

On hospital day 1 a papulonodular rash (up to 2 cm, some with central ulceration) appeared on the trunk and extremities. The patient remained febrile, new crops of similar lesions developed, and blood neutrophilia and elevated ESR/CRP persisted. On day 6 he developed restriction of movement of the left hip, but hip radiographs and ultrasound were normal. 

Empiric intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanate was started, then broadened to acyclovir, vancomycin and ceftazidime, although skin-lesion cultures remained negative. 

On hospital day 11 he was transferred. He had fever (39 °C), left hip movement restriction and multiple polymorphous skin lesions: deep ulcers on the buttocks, bullous lesions on the face and extremities, purulent ulcerations on the knees and elbows, and crusted erosions in the perianal area and oropharynx. Leukocyte count was 25 050/μl with 71% neutrophils; ESR was 100 mm/1 h and CRP 30 mg/l. Pathergy-like eruptions appeared at sites of minimal trauma. 

Initial clinical differential diagnoses included Sweet's syndrome, a superficial bullous variant of pyoderma gangrenosum, Behçet's disease and bacterial superinfection of varicella lesions. Antibiotic and antiviral therapies were continued, and serological tests, immunologic studies, Tzanck smear, microbiological cultures and a skin-lesion biopsy were obtained.

A 13-year-old immunized girl presented with a 5-month history of milky-white urine, progressive weight loss over 3 months, abdominal distension for 2 months, generalized swelling for 15 days, and diffuse abdominal pain for 10 days. There was no dysuria, urinary frequency, fever, or respiratory symptoms. Appetite was decreased. There was a history of frothy urine but no oliguria. Her grandmother had pulmonary tuberculosis 3 years earlier. There was no history of travel, surgery, substance use, or other sick contacts.

On examination, vital signs were stable. There was matted, non-tender anterior and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy (largest node 2×1 cm). BMI was 13.3 kg/m2. The abdomen was distended with moderate ascites and generalized tenderness; there was no organomegaly. Breath sounds were decreased at both lung bases. Cardiac and neurologic examinations were normal.

Initial laboratory studies showed mild anemia (hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL) with normal renal function, lipid profile, complement levels, ANA, dsDNA, serum phosphorus, amylase, and lipase. Urinalysis revealed chyle positive with urine triglyceride 121.35 mg/dL and protein 3+. Peripheral smear for microfilaria was negative, and the microfilariae antigen test (immunochromatographic test) was negative. Dengue, scrub typhus, and malarial serologies were negative.

A 75-year-old woman with treated hypertension and long-standing stable angina despite maximal medical therapy (bisoprolol 5 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, isosorbide mononitrate 40 mg twice daily) was referred for PCI of a chronic total occlusion (CTO) in the proximal right coronary artery (RCA). Baseline ECG showed sinus rhythm without Q waves, and transthoracic echocardiography revealed preserved LV systolic function with mild inferior hypokinesia. Coronary angiography confirmed a dominant RCA CTO (J-CTO score 1) and non-flow-limiting disease in the left system. 

The procedure was performed via dual access (right radial 6 Fr and right femoral 8 Fr). After crossing the occlusion with a Gaia 2nd wire and pre-dilating with a 2.5 × 15 mm balloon, extensive dissection occurred. Two overlapping drug-eluting stents (3.5 × 36 mm and 3.5 × 33 mm) were deployed, after which her blood pressure fell to 60/40 mmHg. Two additional overlapping stents were placed distally, but hypotension persisted, refractory to fluid boluses and intravenous phenylephrine boluses. The patient complained of dizziness and had elevated venous pressures. 

Pericardial tamponade was suspected; an urgent echocardiogram showed no pericardial effusion in the subcostal view. A careful review of the angiograms showed no evidence of coronary perforation or catheter-related dissection in the left system, and the ECG remained unchanged. Femoral angiography excluded access-site bleeding. Other considerations—nitrate effect, vagal reaction, and anaphylaxis—were deemed unlikely given the timing, vital signs, and lack of response to fluids, vasopressors, and antihistamines. With ongoing hypotension, an intra-aortic balloon pump was inserted, achieving a systolic pressure of 100 mmHg. Laboratory tests revealed a hemoglobin drop from 13.2 g/dL pre-procedure to 11 g/dL. To rule out a retroperitoneal bleed, an urgent CT scan was performed.

A 31‐year‐old woman with a 7‐year history of adult‐onset Still’s disease, maintained on prednisolone, cyclosporine A, and tocilizumab, presented in January 2021 with 3 days of fatigue, anorexia, and jaundice. She denied fever, arthralgia, sore throat, rash, or new medications. On examination she was afebrile and had diffuse jaundice without lymphadenopathy or rash. Laboratory evaluation showed:  
  • AST 1884 U/L, ALT 2072 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 371 U/L, γ-GTP 87 U/L  
  • Total bilirubin 6.86 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 5.41 mg/dL  
  • CRP 0.11 mg/dL, ferritin 2202 ng/mL  
  • IgG 2362 mg/dL; ANA titer 1:80; AMA negative  
  • Viral hepatitis serologies and HIV negative  
  • Other autoimmune serologies (rheumatoid factor, ANCA) negative  
Abdominal ultrasound and CT scans revealed mild hepatosplenomegaly and periportal edema, with no evidence of biliary obstruction or focal hepatic lesions.

A 31-year-old man was referred for evaluation of recurrent kidney stones. He had his first episode at age 20 while drinking parsley infusions and continued to have multiple recurrences, particularly in the right kidney, despite extracorporeal lithotripsy and surgery. His father also had urolithiasis; there was no history of significant dairy intake or other medications.

On examination, his blood pressure was 100/60 mmHg; height, 196 cm; weight, 74 kg; BMI, 19.2 kg/m2. Urine dipstick was negative for protein, blood, and glucose. There were no extrarenal abnormalities.

Analysis of a right coral-shaped stone removed at age 30 showed Weddellite (50%), carbapatite (40%), anhydrous ammonium acid urate (5%), carbonated amorphous calcium phosphate (1%), and whewellite (1%). 

A 24-hour urine collection revealed calcium 5.52 mmol/24 h (normal 2.5–7.5 mmol/24 h), phosphate 24 mmol/24 h (7–32 mmol/24 h), and low-molecular-weight proteinuria of 3 g/24 h (normal <0.3 g/24 h). Serum studies showed calcium 2.77 mmol/L (2.25–2.60 mmol/L), creatinine 200 µmol/L, albumin 53 g/L, and estimated GFR 36.4 mL/min/1.73 m2. Parathyroid hormone was 19.1 pg/mL (26.5–96 pg/mL). Autoimmune tests, protein electrophoresis, and urine cultures were normal or negative.

Renal ultrasound demonstrated a small right kidney (9.0 cm), enlarged left kidney (11.5 cm), and medullary nephrocalcinosis without vesicoureteral reflux.

A 72-year-old woman presented with two days of diffuse abdominal pain and a new mass in the left lower quadrant. She denied nausea or vomiting. On examination, she was afebrile, with a heart rate of 88 beats/min and blood pressure of 120/95 mmHg. The abdomen was distended; a firm, tender 10 × 10 cm mass was palpable in the left lower quadrant without skin changes. Bowel sounds were hyperactive. Rectal examination revealed an empty ampulla. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 10,800/mm3 with a normal differential; hemoglobin, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, amylase, and glucose were normal. Plain abdominal radiographs showed multiple air–fluid levels, indicating intestinal obstruction. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a fluid- and air-filled mass within the soft tissue of the left lower abdominal wall.

A 17-year-old Japanese girl noted a painless mass in her left calf that had gradually increased in size over seven months. She had no history of trauma, relevant medical history, or family history. On examination, there was a 3 cm × 3 cm hard, mobile, tender mass within the left soleus muscle; no Tinel-like sign was present. Blood tests, including markers of inflammation, were within normal limits. Plain radiographs of the leg were unremarkable. MRI of the calf revealed two well-demarcated lobular masses within the soleus muscle: on T1-weighted images, areas were isointense to muscle with foci of low signal intensity; on T2-weighted images, the lesions showed predominantly low signal intensity consistent with fibrous tissue; and on gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted images, the lateral lesion demonstrated homogeneous enhancement, while the medial lesion showed irregular focal enhancement. Based on these findings, the preoperative differential diagnosis included solitary fibrous tumor and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, although malignant tumors such as fibrosarcoma or synovial sarcoma could not be excluded.

A male infant was born at 39 + 2 weeks’ gestation by spontaneous vaginal delivery to a 27-year-old woman after an uneventful second pregnancy. Prenatal ultrasound at 20 + 2 weeks noted a duplex right kidney with upper-moiety dilatation (10.8 mm), which resolved by 32 + 1 weeks. There was no family history of renal disease or congenital anomalies. 

At 12 days of age, renal ultrasonography showed an uncomplicated right duplex kidney (6.1 cm) and a normal left kidney (5.2 cm), both located within their renal fossae, with normal parenchymal differentiation and no pelvic dilatation. The infant was asymptomatic, with normal blood pressure and renal function. 

At 3.5 months of age, ultrasound could not visualize the right kidney within the renal fossa but identified it in a higher position posterior to the liver. 

At 4.5 months of age, MRI demonstrated the right kidney posterior and superior to the liver, immediately below an intact diaphragm, with normal size and differentiation. There was no evidence of a duplex system or of diaphragmatic herniation. There was no history of trauma.

A 70-year-old Asian man presented with seven months of progressively worsening upper abdominal pain, accompanied by fever and chills. He denied nausea, vomiting, jaundice, or weight loss. His temperature was 38.3 °C, blood pressure 129/67 mmHg, pulse 89 beats/min, and respirations 18 breaths/min. Abdominal examination revealed localized right upper–quadrant tenderness without guarding or rebound. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 16.4 × 10^9/L (neutrophil predominance), aspartate aminotransferase 72 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase 137 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 405 IU/L, gamma glutamyl transpeptidase 155 IU/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL, and a mildly elevated CA 19-9 level of 49.1 U/mL. Ultrasound demonstrated a distended gallbladder with sludge and dilation of the intrahepatic bile ducts. ERCP showed normal filling of the right intrahepatic ducts but failure to opacify the left intrahepatic ducts at the confluence. Abdominal contrast-enhanced CT revealed dilation of the left intrahepatic bile ducts without any detectable mass or lesion.

A 48-year-old man with a history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation off long-term anticoagulation presented with a 7-day history of diarrhea, generalized fatigue, dyspnea, and cough. A rapid antigen test confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection. 

On admission, he was hypoxemic (SpO2 80% on room air, improving with face-mask oxygen), tachyarrhythmic (heart rate 160/min, atrial fibrillation on ECG), and normotensive (119/100 mm Hg). Arterial blood gas analysis showed metabolic acidosis (pH 7.126, base excess –19 mmol/L) and elevated lactate (12.6 mmol/L). Laboratory tests revealed elevated C-reactive protein, ferritin, transaminases, D-dimer, and troponin I, consistent with infection-associated multiple organ dysfunction.

A thoracic CT scan showed bilateral ground-glass opacities with consolidation in the lower lobes. Abdominal CT scan identified a diffuse hepatic lesion without vascular flow abnormalities. Despite oxygen supplementation, volume resuscitation, and antiarrhythmics, he deteriorated rapidly and was transferred to the ICU for high-flow nasal oxygen, invasive hemodynamic monitoring, remdesivir, dexamethasone, tocilizumab, and stress-ulcer prophylaxis. His APACHE II and SOFA scores on ICU admission were 18 and 9, respectively. To control refractory atrial fibrillation and prevent thrombosis, he received landiolol, enoxaparin (2 × 80 mg), and acetylsalicylic acid (300 mg).

Viscoelastic testing (ClotPro) on ICU admission demonstrated:
• Normal clot firmness  
• Prolonged clotting times on EX-test, FIB-test, IN-test, and TPA-test assays  
• Preserved fibrinolysis with a trend toward resistance on the TPA assay (lysis time 325 s, ML 95%)

After 24 hours, he developed severe hypoxemia and hemodynamic instability requiring intubation, mechanical ventilation (FiO2 1.0), and prone positioning. His inflammatory markers rose further, acute kidney injury emerged, and liver enzymes and bilirubin increased, consistent with acute liver failure. Continuous veno-venous hemodialysis with hemoadsorption was initiated. 

Repeat laboratory studies showed:
• Prolonged aPTT and elevated INR  
• Increased D-dimer  
• Severely decreased fibrinogen  

Repeat ClotPro assays revealed:
• Persistently prolonged clotting times  
• Normal clot formation time and maximal clot firmness  
• Progression to complete fibrinolysis shutdown on the TPA assay (ML 0%)

At this point, the care team suspected a macrovascular thrombotic event as the cause of his acute liver failure.

A man in his 50s was admitted with 4 months of generalized myalgia, weakness, and bilateral hand and wrist swelling. He also reported mild dysphagia, early morning headaches, nausea, and blurred vision in the left eye but denied fevers, night sweats, or weight loss. His medical history included bilateral lung transplantation 5 years earlier (for cystic fibrosis–related bronchiectasis), stage 3 chronic kidney disease, post-transplant diabetes, chronic migraines, and osteoporosis. His immunosuppressive regimen comprised tacrolimus, mycophenolate sodium, and prednisolone (recently increased to 17.5 mg daily). He lived rurally, with significant soil exposure, drank UV-filtered rainwater, and had no recent travel.

On examination: afebrile; blood pressure 150/90 mm Hg; respiratory rate 20 breaths/min; SpO2 100% on room air. There was bilateral dorsal hand swelling without synovitis; muscle compartments were soft but painful on passive stretch. No rashes, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or focal neurologic deficits were noted.

Laboratory studies showed: creatinine 426 μmol/L (baseline ~290 μmol/L 1 month earlier), eGFR 13 mL/min; corrected calcium 2.95 mmol/L; PTH 1 pmol/L; CK 578 U/L; LDH 374 U/L; CRP 138 mg/L; ESR 30 mm/hr; lymphopenia. CT of head, chest, abdomen, and pelvis was unremarkable except chronic sinusitis. On hospital day 8, fevers to 38.3°C developed; blood, urine, and mycobacterial cultures remained negative. LP and brain MRI were nondiagnostic.

MRI of limbs demonstrated diffuse myositis in intrinsic hand muscles and multifocal lower‐limb muscle edema. FDG PET/CT revealed innumerable FDG-avid intramuscular lesions throughout the body, most pronounced in the limbs, with extensive subcutaneous edema and uptake in the oropharyngeal region.

A 7-year-old girl presented with pain and delayed eruption of her mandibular molars. On examination, bilateral buccal swellings of 2–3 cm were noted in the regions of the first permanent mandibular molars; the overlying mucosa appeared slightly whitish. The right first molar was partially erupted, and the left first molar was unerupted; both areas were firm and tender to palpation. Cone-beam computed tomography showed well-defined hypodense lesions involving the crowns and roots of both first mandibular molars. There was bulging and thinning of the buccal cortical bone, tilting of the molar roots toward the lingual cortex, and evidence of basilar cortical resorption on the right side.

A 39-year-old woman with no history of oral contraceptive use and no children presented with a two-week history of pain, redness, and swelling of the left breast. She was a current smoker (5–10 cigarettes/day), had a BMI of 33.3, and three prior pregnancies. She denied fever or systemic symptoms.  
Breast ultrasound revealed multiple irregular, solid, heterogeneous hypoechoic masses in the left breast (largest diameter 16 mm) without axillary lymphadenopathy (BIRADS-4). MRI showed a 3.5 × 5 cm area of heterogeneous enhancement in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast.  
Laboratory tests demonstrated an elevated C-reactive protein level (12.4 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (37 mm/h), with normal CA 125 and CA 15-3 levels. Gram stain of drained abscess fluid showed Gram-positive cocci, but cultures remained sterile.  
Core-needle biopsy of the lesion revealed noncaseating granulomatous inflammation consistent with granulomatous mastitis. The abscess was drained, and she received oral corticosteroids (Prednol 4 mg/day and topical betamethasone) for two months along with a 10-day course of cefuroxime axetil, but there was no clinical improvement.

A 3-year-6-month-old girl of Comorian descent was evaluated for progressive neuroregression and seizures. She was the third child of second-degree consanguineous parents, born at term by cesarean delivery (birth weight 3.1 kg) after an uneventful perinatal course. From 2 weeks of age, she developed lethargy, diaphoresis, and dyspnea with feeding, as well as recurrent aspiration and lower respiratory tract infections. Cardiac examination revealed a holosystolic murmur; echocardiography demonstrated a moderate perimembranous ventricular septal defect, left atrial and ventricular dilation, trivial aortic regurgitation, and elevated pulmonary artery pressure. She was noted to have laryngomalacia.

By 3 months of age, diminished motor movements were apparent; weight gain flattened by 5 months with failure to thrive. At 6 months, there was developmental arrest followed by progressive loss of milestones. Since 8 months, she exhibited a severe startle response, and from 9 months recurrent focal seizures with secondary generalization. On examination at 3 years, she had macrocephaly, coarse facies, hyperacusis, central hypotonia with peripheral hypertonia, a positive Babinski reflex, and no organomegaly. Ophthalmologic evaluation revealed bilateral macular cherry-red spots and inability to fixate.

By 12 months, she required gastrostomy feeding for gastroesophageal reflux. She was frequently hospitalized for aspiration pneumonia. Complete blood count, electrolytes, and renal and liver function tests were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography was unremarkable. Noncontrast CT of the brain showed mild bilateral symmetric thalamic hyperdensity. EEG demonstrated delta slowing with drowsiness. Video-fluoroscopic swallow study confirmed aspiration. Brain MRI revealed extensive T2 hyperintensity in supratentorial white matter, symmetric T2 hypointensity and T1 hyperintensity in the thalami, marked delay in myelination, thinning of the corpus callosum, and mild hypoplasia of the C1 posterior arch. MR spectroscopy showed no elevated creatine, N-acetylaspartate, or lactate peaks.

A 31-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 0, at 16 weeks of gestation presented with a 2-week history of gradually worsening headaches and vision changes, more prominent in the left eye. She reported no antecedent trauma or fever. An ophthalmologic evaluation revealed bitemporal hemianopsia on visual field testing. On neurologic examination, there were no cranial-nerve deficits other than the visual field defect; motor and sensory examinations were normal.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain without contrast showed an enlarged pituitary gland measuring 1.8 × 1.3 × 1.1 cm with slight superior compression of the optic chiasm. Laboratory evaluation revealed:
• Prolactin: 467.3 ng/mL (normal range during pregnancy, 50–270 ng/mL)  
• Total thyroxine (T4): 7.3 μg/dL (normal range in second trimester, 8.9–17.4 μg/dL)  
• Thyrotropin (TSH): 0.38 μIU/mL  
• Cortisol: 26 μg/dL  
• Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1): 238 ng/mL

A 27-year-old woman, two weeks postpartum after preterm delivery of twins, presented with pruritic pink macules and papules on the bilateral legs, forearms, shoulders, and abdomen. Two weeks earlier, she had been diagnosed with a hospital-acquired pulmonary embolus and started on enoxaparin 50 mg daily; approximately 10 days after initiation she noted the lesions. She denied new foods, medications, or exposures other than enoxaparin. Review of systems was negative for fevers, chills, mucosal sores, abdominal pain, or systemic complaints. 

Laboratory studies showed negative heparin/platelet factor-4 antibodies and a normal complete blood count (WBC 3.9 × 10^3/µL; RBC 3.74 × 10^6/µL; hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL; platelets 246 × 10^3/µL). She was diagnosed with a nonspecific inflammatory papular dermatitis and started on triamcinolone ointment.

Three days later, she returned to dermatology with progression of the rash and persistent pruritus. Physical examination revealed dozens of 2–8 mm blanching pink papules with surrounding faint halos on the arms, legs, abdomen, and back. To evaluate pregnancy-related dermatoses, biopsies of an active abdominal lesion were performed for hematoxylin–eosin staining and direct immunofluorescence. Triamcinolone therapy was continued.

A 56-year-old Caucasian postmenopausal woman, gravida 2, para 2, presented for her annual gynecological examination. She reported that she first noticed a lesion in her right inguinal region and upper anterior thigh during puberty and that it enlarged gradually after her first delivery. On examination, there was a painless, smooth, soft, and mobile raised lesion located inferior to the inguinal ligament and lateral to the adjacent inguinal vessels. Close inspection revealed a skin-colored region with a hypoplastic nipple and surrounding areola. No other similar lesions were identified; her breasts and axillary regions were normal. She denied cyclic pain, enlargement, or discharge, but noted slight discomfort and oversensitivity on pressure. Her medical history included appendectomy and hyperlipidemia treated with atorvastatin; her family history was negative for similar findings. An ultrasound scan and diagnostic mammography of the lesion were unable to differentiate between lipoma and breast tissue. Bilateral mammography of the breasts showed no abnormalities. Urinalysis, hematological tests, and biochemical parameters were within normal limits.

A 50-year-old man presented with a 1-day history of worsening epigastric and left upper quadrant abdominal pain. He noted unintentional weight loss of 20 lb over 6 weeks but denied pancreatitis, trauma, surgery, fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, or bowel or urinary symptoms. His medical history included hypertension, untreated hepatitis C infection, intravenous drug use, and smoking; he denied recent alcohol use. On examination, he was afebrile, heart rate 92/min, blood pressure 150/113 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Breath sounds were diminished at the left lung base. He had tenderness in the epigastrium and left upper quadrant without peritoneal signs. 

Laboratory studies showed: WBC 18,700/mm³, hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL (baseline 14.1 g/dL), platelets 222,000/mm³, PT 14 seconds, INR 1.2; electrolytes and renal function were normal. Total bilirubin was 0.7 mg/dL; ALT 120 U/L; AST 80 U/L; ALP 71 U/L. Troponin I was 0.014 ng/mL; procalcitonin 0.11 ng/mL. Urine drug screen was positive for methamphetamine and fentanyl. Hepatitis C antibody was positive; HIV and SARS-CoV-2 were negative. 

Noncontrast CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed a high-density left pleural effusion and fluid in the deep pelvis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated wall thickening of the mid-distal esophagus and gastric cardia with a large surrounding high-density collection consistent with hematoma, a small focus of active contrast extravasation medial to the gastric cardia, and a moderate left hemothorax. Small-volume high-density fluid in the left upper quadrant tracked along the greater curvature of the stomach, most compatible with hemoperitoneum.

A corroborating history and these imaging findings raised suspicion for possible malignancy, esophageal perforation, bleeding varix, and left-sided hemothorax.

A 45-year-old woman from northern Morocco presented with a 7-month history of indurated swelling of the sole of her right foot. She initially noted a single subcutaneous nodule, with additional nodules appearing over two months on the outer edge and sole. These lesions developed sinuses that intermittently discharged yellow granules and coalesced into a cauliflower-like mass measuring 7 cm, causing foot pain and difficulty walking. She had been treated empirically with antibiotics previously without improvement. 

On examination, she was afebrile, with no erythema, warmth, or purulence. There was no lymphadenopathy. The mass was mildly tender, firm, nonfluctuant, and extended from the plantar surface to the lateral border of the foot. Multiple dry fistulae and crusted lesions were present; there was no foul odor or crepitus. Pedal pulses were palpable.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 9500 /mm3, hemoglobin 9 g/dL, platelets 250 000/mm3, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 4 mm/h, and C-reactive protein 2.05 mg/L. 

Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an extensive inflammatory edematous infiltrate in the dermo-hypodermal tissues of the lateral foot and sole, extending to contact the plantar fascia and the abductor muscle of the fifth toe, without any fluid collection or bone involvement. Standard foot radiographs revealed only soft-tissue thickening without calcifications, bone lesions, or osteolytic changes.

A 54-year-old man with a 25-pack-year smoking history and hypertension treated with candesartan and amlodipine presented with sudden severe central chest pain of one-hour duration. On arrival, a 12-lead ECG showed ST-segment elevation in leads V2–V5. He received aspirin, heparin, ondansetron, and morphine and was taken emergently to the catheterization laboratory. By the time of angiography, his chest pain and ST-segment elevations had resolved. Coronary angiography revealed diffuse epicardial atherosclerosis with dilated segments and stenoses in the distal left anterior descending artery, second diagonal branch, distal right coronary artery, and distal circumflex artery, but no occlusion and TIMI grade III flow in all vessels. Left ventriculography demonstrated normal left ventricular function with only discrete apical hypokinesia. Based on these findings and his history, intracoronary acetylcholine testing was planned to evaluate for coronary spasm.

A 48-year-old man was admitted for severe anemia. He reported 2 weeks of weakness, dizziness, and intermittent epigastric pain. He denied melena, hematemesis, or other signs of overt blood loss. His history was notable for chronic pancreatitis, long-term alcohol abuse, and smoking; he had undergone a laparotomy years earlier for a knife injury to the small bowel. On examination, he appeared pale. Vital signs were: blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg, heart rate 92 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. Abdominal examination revealed mild mid-epigastric tenderness without peritoneal signs. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin of 4.7 g/dL; white-cell count, platelets, serum amylase, lipase, and liver tests were within normal limits.
