He received 4 units of packed red blood cells, raising his hemoglobin to 8.3 g/dL. Abdominal ultrasound was inconclusive but suggested diffuse pancreatic changes and hepatic steatosis. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a large amount of fresh blood in the second portion of the duodenum and continuous oozing of blood from the major papilla. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen demonstrated features of chronic pancreatitis with multiple calcifications in the pancreatic head and a 6-mm saccular pseudoaneurysm of the splenic artery located near its origin from the celiac trunk.

A 65-year-old man was transferred for management of recurrent ICD shocks in VT storm. Fifteen years earlier, he had an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest; workup at that time showed a baseline right bundle–branch block on ECG, no obstructive coronary disease, and no cardiomyopathy on imaging. He underwent dual-chamber ICD implantation. One month later he received a shock for PVC-triggered polymorphic VT; Holter monitoring showed over 10 000 PVCs in 24 hours with a left bundle–branch block, inferior-axis morphology. Cardiac CT at that time demonstrated mild-to-moderate RV dilatation with possible fat infiltration of the RV free wall, and he was diagnosed with ARVC. During an electrophysiology study, pause-dependent PVCs with identical morphology were felt to arise from his RVOT ICD lead tip, which was then repositioned to the RV apical septum; the PVCs resolved. He was maintained on atenolol and remained stable for several years.

In the month before transfer, he developed episodes of monomorphic VT, receiving seven appropriate ICD shocks despite oral amiodarone. He was started on IV amiodarone and lidocaine and referred for invasive management. A repeat transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a moderately enlarged left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 58% and apical dyskinesis, mild RV enlargement with mildly reduced function, mild mitral valve prolapse, and a sub-mitral aneurysm along the inferolateral LV wall. Cardiac MRI showed mild patchy midmyocardial late gadolinium enhancement at the RV insertion in the mid inferoseptum, dyssynchronous RV free-wall contraction with a small focal aneurysm, and normal RV size.

A 54-year-old man, a farmer and former heavy smoker (46 pack-years), with no history of treated tuberculosis, presented with a 10-month history of productive cough with yellow sputum, occasional moderate hemoptysis, low-grade fevers, and weight loss.

On examination, his temperature was 37.8 °C, respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation was 89% on room air (96% on supplemental oxygen). There was dullness to percussion over the entire left hemithorax, poor oral hygiene, and firm, mobile, non-tender bilateral axillary lymph nodes (approximately 1 cm each).

Initial investigations included:
- Chest radiograph: dense homogeneous opacity obliterating the left pleural recesses and left cardiac border, with an air-fluid level, suggestive of a hydropneumothorax.  
- Pleural fluid analysis: chocolate-colored purulent fluid; direct Gram stain demonstrated branching filamentous gram-positive bacilli.  
- Sputum and pleural fluid testing for Mycobacterium tuberculosis with acid-fast bacilli smear and GeneXpert MTB/RIF: negative.  
- Laboratory studies: C-reactive protein 180 mg/L; hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL; white blood cell count 16,000/mm^3 (neutrophil predominance); fasting glucose 2.1 g/L; HIV serology negative.  
- Chest CT scan: a left lung cavitary lesion communicating with the left lobar bronchus; a left pyopneumothorax communicating with the abscess; and right-sided peribronchovascular micronodules with an infectious appearance.

A 69-year-old man was admitted for management of an oropharyngeal mass, with a 2-month history of progressive dysphagia. He had a history of total laryngectomy and tracheostomy with chemoradiation 15 years earlier for laryngeal carcinoma, which was considered cured. He was breathing via tracheostomy and otherwise independent. He had quit smoking 15 years prior and took no medications. On admission, he was hemodynamically stable, with difficulty swallowing due to the mass. Laboratory studies showed normocytic anemia and serum sodium 128 mEq/L. ECG revealed atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 70 bpm. An open gastrostomy was performed on hospital day 3 without immediate complications. Enteral feeding began postoperatively.

On day 8, he became intermittently confused and less responsive, though vital signs remained within normal limits. Examination showed facial puffiness and dry skin. Labs revealed TSH 15.056 mIU/L, free T4 0.04 ng/dL, undetectable free T3, and morning cortisol 19 µg/dL. Primary hypothyroidism was diagnosed, and oral levothyroxine 25 µg/day was started via gastrostomy.

Chemoradiation began on day 14. By day 19, free T4 remained 0.04 ng/dL, and confusion persisted. Sodium fell further to 125 mEq/L, and he developed hypoglycemia requiring dextrose. LT4 was given on an empty stomach with enhanced nutritional support, but his mental status did not improve.

On day 28, he was unarousable to voice. Temperature was 33.4°C, heart rate 40 bpm and irregular, blood pressure 80/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 12 bpm. Plasma glucose was 56 mg/dL, CK-MB 182 U/L, troponin T 102 ng/L. ECG showed atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 40 bpm without ischemic changes. Echocardiography demonstrated global hypokinesia without regional wall-motion abnormalities and a small pericardial effusion. Chest radiograph revealed right upper lung haziness.

A 27-year-old man presented with a 7-day history of intermittent fever with evening spikes up to 103 °F, chills, rigors, fatigue, three episodes of vomiting over 4 days, and epigastric pain. He had no known medical conditions. On examination, he was alert; blood pressure was 110/60 mmHg, pulse 107 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, axillary temperature 99.8 °F, and SpO2 96% on room air. The abdomen was soft, with no palpable hepatosplenomegaly.

A rapid test confirmed Plasmodium vivax malaria. Serologies for typhoid, dengue, scrub typhus, brucella, Leptospira, hepatitis, and HIV were negative. An initial complete blood count showed hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, leukocytes 3370/mm3, and platelets 45,000/mm3. Abdominal ultrasound noted gallbladder calculi. He received intravenous paracetamol and pantoprazole, chloroquine (600 mg daily × 2 days, then 300 mg on Day 3), and primaquine (15 mg daily for 14 days). Quantitative G6PD activity was 8.4 U/g Hb (normal range).  

On Day 1, hemoglobin was 11.7 g/dL and total bilirubin 4.3 mg/dL. On Day 2, hemoglobin fell to 9.8 g/dL, total bilirubin was 4.2 mg/dL, leukocytes rose to 17,870/mm3, and platelets increased to 197,000/mm3. The patient remained febrile but had no overt signs of sepsis.

A 28-year-old man with acute myeloid leukemia refractory to two prior allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplants was admitted for salvage chemotherapy. One year after his second transplant, he presented with recurrent pneumonia and developed watery diarrhea and a maculopapular skin rash. A CT scan on admission showed a left lower-lobe infiltrate but no intestinal edema; meropenem and vancomycin resolved his pulmonary symptoms. On hospital days 4–9, he received mitoxantrone, etoposide, and cytarabine. During chemotherapy, his diarrhea worsened and his rash spread. On day 10, abdominal CT revealed diffuse intestinal wall thickening. Laboratory studies showed white cells 20/μL, hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL, platelets 12 000/μL, lactate dehydrogenase 228 U/L, and C-reactive protein 1.24 mg/dL. Stool assays were negative for Clostridium difficile toxins A/B and glutamate dehydrogenase. Suspecting acute gut graft-versus-host disease, methylprednisolone was increased to 120 mg/day and beclomethasone dipropionate was started, but diarrhea continued to worsen. On days 13–15, he received methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3 days. Colonoscopy was deferred because of his condition.

A 9-month-old full-term unvaccinated Amish female with no prior medical history presented with fever, cough, and increased work of breathing. On exam, she was ill-appearing, in significant respiratory distress with bilateral wheezing, and did not improve after nebulized albuterol, necessitating intubation for persistent tachypnea. A chest radiograph showed normal lung volumes with bilateral infra-hilar streaky opacities. Laboratory studies revealed an unremarkable complete blood count. She received a dose of ceftriaxone, was admitted to the pediatric ICU, and was continued on piperacillin/tazobactam. 

Notably, 21 days earlier she had been hospitalized for acute hypoxic respiratory failure secondary to left lower lobe pneumonia after an unwitnessed aspiration while bottle-feeding. At that time, tracheal aspirate cultures grew Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae, and she improved with bronchodilators and a 7-day course of ceftriaxone. After discharge, she continued to have increased work of breathing, cough, and wheezing on scheduled albuterol and then developed fever and acutely worsening respiratory symptoms, prompting this admission. 

During the current stay, chest radiographs showed persistent left lower lobe atelectasis. Tracheal aspirate cultures grew H. influenzae and respiratory viral panel detected rhinovirus and enterovirus; piperacillin/tazobactam was discontinued after repeat cultures were negative. Contrast chest CT demonstrated significant left lung volume loss with complete opacification of the left lower lobe, and an irregular filling defect in the left mainstem bronchus was suspected to represent secretions, debris, and inflammation rather than a foreign body; no vascular ring or sling was identified. 

Bedside flexible bronchoscopy retrieved large amounts of mucus from the left bronchial tree, and dornase alfa was started with temporary radiographic improvement of left lung aeration. However, she later developed sepsis, was treated with vancomycin and ceftriaxone, and on return of bilateral wheezing was given inhaled fluticasone. A subsequent chest radiograph again showed left lung collapse, and she completed a 10-day course of vancomycin and cefepime without lasting improvement.

A 3-year-old boy with chronic kidney disease, secondary hypertension, and a history of left nephrectomy at age 1 for Wilms’ tumor was admitted for resection of a new right renal mass. Preoperative evaluation was otherwise unremarkable. He underwent partial right nephrectomy with complete tumor excision and primary repair of the renal pelvis. Central venous and peritoneal catheters were placed at the time of surgery. 

The procedure was uncomplicated, and initial postoperative recovery was uneventful. On postoperative day 3, he developed acute respiratory distress. Chest radiography revealed a right pleural effusion occupying approximately two thirds of the hemithorax. Clinicians considered pneumonia with a parapneumonic effusion. 

A right-sided thoracostomy tube was placed, and over the next 20 hours, 1,050 mL of yellowish fluid was drained. During this period, the patient became oliguric and febrile. Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics (meropenem and vancomycin) were initiated.

A 60-year-old man was referred for evaluation of persistent right pleural effusion. One month earlier, he had been treated for suspected pneumonia at an outside hospital, where contrast-enhanced chest CT showed a small volume of right pleural effusion with diffuse pleural enhancement despite antibiotics. Thoracentesis revealed cytologic findings suggestive of malignant cells. On admission to our hospital in January 2017, his temperature was 36.5°C, blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg, heart rate 70 beats/min, and respiratory rate 20 breaths/min. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 6.1 × 10^3/μL and a C-reactive protein level of 0.209 mg/dL. His history was notable for recurrent pneumonia and suspected diffuse panbronchiolitis with bronchiectasis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a decrease in pleural effusion and tubular and varicoid bronchiectasis with bronchial wall thickening and mucous plugging in the right middle lobe, left lingula, and both lower lobes. Additionally, there was a well-defined, round 11-mm lesion adjacent to the descending aorta at the level of the left bronchus. The lesion enhanced to a similar degree as the aorta, indicating a vascular structure, and axial images showed that it was connected to the left bronchial artery.

A 12-year-old boy presented with a 48-hour history of anterior knee pain and swelling, worsened by walking and standing. He had no fever, trauma, or prior rheumatologic history. On examination, he had an antalgic gait and point tenderness at the inferior pole of the patella, with pain on passive flexion and active extension limited to 140°-20°-0°. The extensor mechanism was intact. Initial anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the knee showed calcifications and irregular ossification of the lower pole of the patella, with thickening and heterogeneity of the proximal patellar tendon. Laboratory tests revealed a C-reactive protein level of 64 mg/L, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 15 mm/h, and a normal white-cell count. He was treated with NSAIDs and immobilization in a brace. At follow-up 24 hours later, his physical findings were unchanged, he remained afebrile, and his C-reactive protein level had risen to 96 mg/L. Given the concern for an infectious process, magnetic resonance imaging of the knee was performed, which demonstrated T2 hyperintensity within the inferior patella consistent with bone marrow edema and a fluid-filled collection within Hoffa’s fat pad with surrounding edema.

A 4-year-old girl was brought by her parents because of hypersensitivity of her teeth to heat and cold, even during normal breathing. She had never undergone a dental examination or treatment. On examination, the enamel of teeth 11, 21, 31, 41, and 36 showed hypomineralisation. The lesions on the incisors were white-yellow in color with well-defined borders and a smooth enamel surface. On tooth 36, the enamel was broken with areas of hypomineralisation on the occlusal and vestibular surfaces.

A previously healthy 2-year-old boy presented with a 1-week history of cold, cough, and runny nose. One day before presentation he developed a fever of 39.5 °C responsive to antipyretics. On the day of arrival, he had four episodes of vomiting and two episodes of loose stools and was treated elsewhere for presumed viral gastroenteritis with antiemetics and IV fluids. He was discharged but vomited again and became very drowsy en route, prompting admission to our emergency department. 

His parents denied neck pain, stiffness, rash, or photophobia. He had fluctuating levels of consciousness and fever en route. Notably, he had received no immunizations after age 4 months. There was no travel or sick contacts. 

On examination his Glasgow Coma Scale fluctuated between 10 and 11. Temperature was 38 °C, pulse 137 beats/min, blood pressure 80/50 mmHg, and capillary refill time 4 seconds. Pupils were 3 mm with slow reaction to light and accommodation. There was no neck stiffness or meningeal signs. Tonsils were mildly enlarged and erythematous. 

Laboratory results on admission showed: WBC 2.73 ×10^9/L (low), neutrophils 80.2% (high), C-reactive protein 72.9 mg/L (high), procalcitonin 95.7 ng/mL (very high), prothrombin time 19.4 s (high), partial thromboplastin time 41.2 s (high), INR 1.65 (high), lactate 3.0 mmol/L (high). 

A noncontrast head CT performed after initial resuscitation showed mild diffuse cerebral edema without evidence of raised intracranial pressure.

A 44-year-old woman with a 7-year history of Behcet’s disease, migraines, and a prior presumed stroke presented after awakening with increased right lower-extremity weakness and 3 days of worsening urinary incontinence. Eleven months earlier, she had residual slurred speech, urinary incontinence, right-sided weakness, and bilateral hyperreflexia attributed to a suspected stroke. At that time, MRI of the brain showed a chronic left pontine lacunar infarct and extensive white-matter changes. A cervical-spine MRI and lumbar puncture were recommended but not performed. 

On current presentation, she was afebrile with normal vital signs. Neurologic examination revealed mildly slurred speech; mild right pronator drift; mild right upper-extremity weakness; mild right hip-flexion weakness; diffuse bilateral hyperreflexia; right-sided hemiparetic gait with inability to heel-toe walk; and intact cranial nerves and sensation. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. Noncontrast head CT and CT angiography of the head and neck showed no acute intracranial process, early signs of stroke, or large-vessel occlusion.

Brain MRI with and without contrast demonstrated markedly abnormal brainstem findings with expansile T2 hyperintensity involving nearly the entire pons and extending into the ventral medulla, medullary pyramids, midbrain, cerebral peduncles (greater on the left), and the posterior limb of the left internal capsule, with significant progression compared to MRI performed 8 months earlier. Additional findings included a few nonspecific scattered punctate foci of T2 hyperintense signal in the cerebral white matter and a new nonacute left corona radiata lacunar infarct.

A term male newborn, first child of nonconsanguineous parents, was born by cesarean delivery at 40 weeks’ gestation after an uneventful pregnancy and discharged on exclusive breastfeeding. At 15 days of age, he developed diffuse erythroderma with desquamation; emollient therapy produced no improvement. At 24 days, he presented with fever and was admitted. On examination, he weighed 3850 g, had diffuse erythroderma, desquamation, alopecia, and absence of eyelashes and eyebrows. Abdominal examination disclosed a soft abdomen, a liver palpable 1 cm below the costal margin, and no palpable spleen. Laboratory tests showed a C-reactive protein level of 68 mg/L, leukocytosis of 28 800/mm³ with lymphocytosis (20 448/mm³) and eosinophilia (288/mm³), hemoglobin of 12 g/dL, and thrombocytopenia (88 000/mm³). Serum electrolytes were normal. Chest radiography was unremarkable, with a visible thymus. He was treated with a third-generation cephalosporin and an aminoglycoside for suspected postnatal infection. A dermatologic consultation suggested congenital ichthyosis. His condition initially improved, with resolution of fever and a decrease in C-reactive protein, but thrombocytopenia persisted.

A 61-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus (on metformin and dulaglutide), hypertension, and a total right hip arthroplasty performed over one year earlier presented with one week of lateral right hip pain, poor appetite, and several episodes of vomiting. She denied urinary symptoms, illicit drug use, and recent travel; she cares for pet animals. In the emergency department she was afebrile and normotensive. Examination revealed dehydration, distress, and tenderness over the lateral aspect of the right hip; range of motion was limited by pain, and the surgical site appeared clean. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 16,000 cells/ml with a left shift, blood glucose of 974 mg/dl, venous blood pH 7.29 with bicarbonate of 17 mEq/l and an anion gap of 20, lactic acid 4.8 mg/dl, C-reactive protein 67.8 mg/dl, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 112 mm/hour. Hemoglobin A1c was 13.9%. Chest radiograph was clear. The initial clinical suspicion was septic arthritis, and she received fluid resuscitation, insulin infusion, and empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics.

Anteroposterior radiograph of the right hip was unremarkable. Point-of-care ultrasound suggested a joint effusion. Computed tomography of the pelvis showed subcutaneous inflammatory stranding and heterogeneous attenuation of the musculature surrounding the right hip. Serum creatine kinase was elevated above 1200 U/l. Arthrocentesis yielded clear fluid; synovial fluid analysis revealed calcium pyrophosphate crystals, and cultures of the aspirate were sterile.

A female infant, the second child of healthy nonconsanguineous parents, was noted antenatally to have polyhydramnios. She was born at 37 weeks’ gestation, weighing 2500 g (Apgar scores 10 at 1, 5, and 10 min). Beginning on the day of birth, she passed 3–6 liquid stools per day and had abdominal distension despite routine antidiarrhoeal therapy and lactose-free formula. Over the first 6 months, feeding of breast milk and cow’s milk was associated with very slow weight gain; at 5 months she could raise her head, but by 7 months she could not sit unaided and weighed only 6 kg. There was no family history of protracted infantile diarrhea.

At 7 months of age, she was admitted with more than 10 watery stools per day and severe dehydration. Blood pressure was 84/45 mmHg, heart rate 162 beats/min, and respiratory rate was increased. She appeared dehydrated and malnourished, with a distended abdomen and active bowel sounds; lung fields were clear. Laboratory studies showed haemoglobin 11 g/dL, serum creatinine 17.15 µmol/L, bicarbonate 44.6 mmol/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 2.12 mmol/L, calcium 2.78 mmol/L, chloride 74 mmol/L, and arterial pH 7.53, consistent with hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, hypochloraemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Plasma aldosterone was 137.19 pg/mL (normal 10–160), angiotensin 137.67 pg/mL (25–129), and renin activity 67.17 pg/mL (4–24). Urinalysis showed pH 8.00 and 1+ protein; stool and urine electrolyte levels were not measured.

She received intravenous fluids and oral NaCl and KCl (6 mmol/kg/day), after which her acid–base status and serum electrolytes normalized, urinary pH decreased to 6.50 with resolution of proteinuria, and stool frequency decreased to 4–5 per day, although the stool remained watery.

A 34‐year‐old man is evaluated for chest pain on exertion. Two years earlier, he underwent orchiectomy and three cycles of adjuvant bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin for stage IIa seminoma. He reports no chest pain during or immediately after chemotherapy. He has no history of smoking; his only cardiovascular risk factor is dyslipidemia.

On examination: height 170 cm, weight 64 kg, blood pressure 110/75 mm Hg, heart rate 65 bpm. Cardiac auscultation is normal; there is no peripheral edema. Resting electrocardiogram shows normal sinus rhythm without ST–T changes. Chest radiograph is unremarkable. Cardiac troponin I is normal. Laboratory studies show total cholesterol 223 mg/dL, LDL cholesterol 146 mg/dL, creatinine 0.86 mg/dL (eGFR 83 mL/min/1.73 m2), and BNP 5 pg/mL. Brachial–ankle pulse‐wave velocity is approximately 1230 cm/s bilaterally.

Because of ongoing exertional chest discomfort, coronary angiography is performed and reveals no organic stenosis.

An 18-year-old man was admitted with a 3-year history of chest tightness and dyspnea that acutely worsened 1 week before presentation, when he developed orthopnea and anuria. Four years earlier in Beijing, he had been diagnosed with non-obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a small pericardial effusion, and chronic bilateral lung inflammation; he also experienced a cerebral infarction at that time.

He denied any family history of genetic disorders. On examination, blood pressure was 92/62 mmHg. He had normal development and cognition. Muscle strength initially was grade 5 in all limbs, but at this admission the right upper limb was grade 4 and the other three limbs were grade 1. There was no retinal abnormality. Resting ECG showed atrial and ventricular premature beats and ventricular blocks but no pre-excitation.

Laboratory studies showed high-sensitivity troponin T 0.187 ng/mL, NT-proBNP 6554 pg/mL, creatine kinase 936–1545 U/L, creatine kinase-MB 58–63 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase 728 U/L, alanine transaminase 206 U/L, and aspartate transaminase 273 U/L.

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy (septal thickness 20–31 mm, lateral wall thickness 26 mm) and right ventricular hypertrophy. Tissue Doppler imaging showed an E velocity of 70 cm/s, septal e′ 3 cm/s, and lateral wall e′ 4 cm/s, indicating elevated end-diastolic filling pressures.

Coronary CT angiography demonstrated patency of the coronary arteries, excluding acute coronary syndrome. Cardiac MRI showed biventricular hypertrophy, marked myocardial trabeculation, minor pericardial effusion, and extensive late gadolinium enhancement of both ventricles sparing only the mid-basal interventricular septum.

A 7-year-old girl was referred to dermatology after several visits for a suspected monkey-pox infection. Her general condition was good. She had retroauricular lymphadenopathy but was otherwise well. The mother noted a few episodes of mild cough over the prior 10 days. Skin examination revealed a diffuse, relatively monomorphic vesiculobullous eruption on the neck and face, sparing the palms and soles. Many lesions coalesced into rosette-like clusters. To reduce new lesions, pruritus, and prevent superinfection, systemic amoxicillin-clavulanate and low-dose betamethasone were started. A skin biopsy for perilesional direct immunofluorescence and serologic testing for CMV, EBV, parvovirus, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae were obtained.

A 29-year-old Hmong man with no prior medical history presented with a 6-month history of progressive abdominal pain, substantial weight loss, and weakness. His symptoms deteriorated, and he re-presented with progressive confusion. On examination, he was severely cachectic, jaundiced, and hypotensive (blood pressure 72/46 mm Hg). He had diffuse skin petechiae and palpable splenomegaly. 

Laboratory studies demonstrated multiorgan dysfunction with elevated liver enzymes, coagulopathy, acute kidney injury, and severe pancytopenia. A chest radiograph revealed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. His oxygen saturation fell to 54%, necessitating intubation and mechanical ventilation for hypoxemic respiratory failure. He received multiple vasopressors and broad-spectrum antibiotics for presumed septic shock and was started on continuous hemodialysis for refractory metabolic acidosis.

Initial infectious workup, including HIV, tuberculosis, hepatitis panels, respiratory viral PCR, and body fluid cultures, was negative, and no definitive infectious source was identified. On hospital day 4, a bone marrow biopsy was performed; the initial results showed no overt malignant infiltrates. An abdominal CT scan demonstrated splenomegaly, multiple hepatic and splenic lesions, and lymphadenopathy. The family declined further biopsy because of the patient’s clinical deterioration.

A 73-year-old African American woman with coronary artery disease, chronic venous insufficiency, hypertension, and rheumatoid arthritis presented with two weeks of oral mucositis progressing to odynophagia, epistaxis, gingival bleeding, and easy bruising that evolved into bleeding ulcerations after minimal trauma. She had no prior hematologic or oncologic disease. Home medications included aspirin, carvedilol, enalapril, folic acid, furosemide, clopidogrel, simvastatin, and methotrexate. Two months earlier her methotrexate dose was increased from 7.5 mg weekly to 2.5 mg daily, and she had received no outpatient monitoring of CBC, creatinine, or liver function since.  
On examination, pulse was 68 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, blood pressure 152/85 mm Hg, temperature 98.7 °F. Multiple petechiae were scattered over the upper body.  
Laboratory studies showed:  
• WBC 2.0 × 10^9/L (polys 23%, lymphocytes 55%, monocytes 2%, eosinophils 20%)  
• Hemoglobin 7.0 g/dL, MCV 89 fL  
• Platelet count 3 × 10^9/L  
Two months earlier: WBC 7.6, Hb 10.2, platelets 194.  
• BUN 36 mg/dL, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, AST 27 U/L, ALT 26 U/L  
Chest radiograph showed multiple scattered pulmonary infiltrates.

A 64-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on peritoneal dialysis presented with two weeks of progressive upper abdominal pain and bloating. He reported a “sloshing” sensation with movement and noted that his dialysis bag had been unusually distended with air two weeks earlier. He had one episode of vomiting several days before presentation but denied ongoing nausea, fever, or chills. He was hemodynamically stable without chest pain or shortness of breath. On examination, the abdomen was distended with diffuse tenderness but no rebound, guarding, or peritoneal signs; bowel sounds were present. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 9.3 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, platelets 167 × 10^3/µL, and a C-reactive protein of 0.6 mg/dL. A chest radiograph revealed free air under the diaphragm without pneumothorax or pleural effusion. A non-contrast CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a large volume of free intraperitoneal air.

A 79‐year‐old man with high‐risk, non–muscle‐invasive bladder cancer (T1N0M0) was receiving weekly intravesical BCG (80 mg). Three days after his sixth instillation he became acutely immobile and developed difficulty moving; he was brought to the emergency department. 

His history included transurethral resection of bladder tumor, unstable angina status–post percutaneous coronary intervention, and robot‐assisted prostatectomy for prostate cancer. He had a 50–pack‐year smoking history; baseline serum creatinine had been 1.0 mg/dL.

On admission, he was febrile (38.5 °C) and hypotensive (90/62 mmHg) with clouded consciousness. Examination showed dry mucous membranes, clear lung fields, no murmurs, a soft non‐tender abdomen, and markedly reduced skin turgor. There was no peripheral edema.

Laboratory evaluation revealed:  
• C‐reactive protein 28.3 mg/dL; WBC 7,700/µL; neutrophils 90.7%  
• Creatinine 7.97 mg/dL; eGFR 6 mL/min/1.73 m2  
• CK 26,660 U/L; AST 509 U/L; ALT 160 U/L  
• Myoglobinuria; metabolic acidosis (pH 7.31; HCO3 13.4 mmol/L)  
• Blood cultures for general bacteria: negative

A trunk CT on Day 1 showed no pulmonary lesions and normal kidney and liver morphology. He was admitted to the ICU for presumed sepsis and rhabdomyolysis‐induced AKI, started on ceftriaxone, aggressive IV fluids, and renal replacement therapy. He improved, was transferred to the ward on Day 3, and intermittent hemodialysis was discontinued on Day 7 as renal function recovered, though fever and elevated CRP persisted.

He received meropenem on Day 6, and vancomycin for MRSA catheter infection on Day 7. Fever continued; antibiotics were held on Day 11 for suspected drug fever, but CRP remained elevated. On Day 13, chest CT revealed slight bilateral infiltrates, prompting sputum cultures and initiation of ampicillin/sulbactam. Fever persisted despite antibiotic changes.

By Day 27, fine crackles were heard bilaterally, and repeat CT demonstrated diffuse interstitial shadows in both lungs, consistent with interstitial pneumonia. No bronchoscopy was performed due to frailty. All antibiotics were stopped and the patient was started on methylprednisolone pulse therapy.

A 62-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive speech disorder. On neurologic examination, she had motor aphasia. Plain computed tomography of the head showed a faint hyperdense mass lesion in the left frontal lobe. T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging revealed an isointense mass with high-intensity rims and extensive perifocal edema. Gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted MRI demonstrated ring enhancement of the lesion.

A 48-year-old woman presented with a 12-month history of progressively worsening chronic pelvic pain. She denied irregular vaginal bleeding, dyspareunia, gastrointestinal, or urinary symptoms. She had been menopausal for four years without hormone therapy. Her medical history was notable only for primary infertility. Surgical history included a laparoscopy 14 years earlier for a benign ovarian mass (no cystic formations noted at that time), hysteroscopic excision of an endometrial polyp nine years ago, and cholecystectomy at age 35.

On pelvic examination, there was a hard, non-tender, fixed mass measuring approximately 7 cm in the left pelvis. Speculum examination revealed no cervical abnormalities, but a firm, protruding 6 cm mass was palpable in the cul-de-sac of Douglas. Transvaginal ultrasonography demonstrated a well-circumscribed, round, multicystic mass measuring 6 cm in the cul-de-sac, with homogeneous cystic content, and multiple anechoic cystic formations surrounding the uterine fundus. Serum CA-125 level was within the normal range.

A 70-year-old man presented with a 10-month history of a large left thigh lesion that had rapidly increased in size and become painful over the past month. He denied trauma, fever, or weight loss. His past medical history was unremarkable; he was a chronic smoker. 

On examination, there was a diffuse, tender, warm, ill-defined swelling measuring 40 × 40 cm over the medial aspect of the left thigh. The overlying skin was stretched without discoloration or erythema. The mass was not fluctuant, not pulsatile, and had no palpable thrill or bruit. Distal neurological examination was normal. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses were palpable, and the foot was well perfused and warm. 

A clinical abscess was considered unlikely given the lesion’s chronicity and absence of infection signs, and a soft-tissue sarcoma was strongly suspected. A plain radiograph showed a soft-tissue shadow with calcified margins, without bone erosion or scalloping. An outpatient MRI was arranged.

Two weeks later, he re-presented with increased swelling, new bruising, and overlying skin necrosis of the medial thigh. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses were now impalpable, although the foot remained warm and well perfused. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin of 106 g/L and a mild acute kidney injury treated with intravenous fluids. An urgent same-day MRI scan was performed for the presumed expanding soft-tissue sarcoma.

A 56-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and severe portal hypertension (MELD score 13) and chronic portal vein thrombosis extending into the superior mesenteric vein underwent orthotopic liver transplantation with end-to-end portal vein and hepatic artery anastomoses. Intraoperative ultrasound showed good intrahepatic arterial inflow (resistance index 0.60) and no abnormal portal flow. At the end of surgery, laboratory values were notable for lactate 5.2 mEq/L, LDH 3503 mUI/L, AST 1542 U/L, ALT 1173 U/L, total bilirubin 5.78 mg/dL, INR 1.43, and fibrinogen 148 mg/dL. The patient was transferred to the ICU on vasopressors and standard immunosuppression. Over the next 48 hours, lactate, transaminases, LDH, bilirubin, and INR continued to rise (e.g., AST 2446 U/L, ALT 2481 U/L, lactate 6.3 mEq/L, total bilirubin 7.67 mg/dL, INR 2.37). Doppler ultrasound showed markedly increased portal vein flow (44 cm/s) and absent intrahepatic arterial signals. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a patent but small-caliber hepatic artery and no significant intrahepatic arterial perfusion.

A 4-year-old boy presented with severe constipation, abdominal pain, abdominal distension, and occasional vomiting. He had a history of delayed passage of meconium at birth, managed successfully with enema; since then, he was unable to pass stools without enemas. His developmental milestones, chest examination, and vital signs were normal. His height was 100.2 cm and weight was 14.5 kg; appetite and micturition were normal. Two months earlier, at a tertiary center, he was diagnosed with Hirschsprung disease and advised to undergo surgery. He was the only child; no family history of similar symptoms was reported.

On examination, he appeared anxious. Neurologic evaluation—including higher mental function, cranial nerves, motor strength, coordination, and sensation—was unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed marked distension with palpable, dilated loops of colon. On rectal examination, the rectal vault was empty, and there was forceful expulsion of fecal material upon withdrawal of the examining finger. 

Complete blood count, thyroid profile, and anti–tissue transglutaminase IgA levels were all within normal limits.

A 2-month-old full-term male infant was brought by his parents because of an “abnormally soft” skull. He was born at home via vaginal delivery to a 20-year-old primiparous mother at 39+5 weeks’ gestation. Two antenatal visits included a second-trimester ultrasound reported as normal. There was no history of maternal infection, teratogen exposure, or family history of congenital anomalies. The infant fed and voided normally and met developmental milestones appropriate for age.

On examination, vital signs were stable. Weight was 4.5 kg (85th–97th percentile), length 56 cm (97th percentile), and head circumference 37 cm (between −1 and −2 Z score). Inspection of the skull and face appeared normal, but palpation revealed absence of the bilateral parietal bones. Frontal, temporal, occipital, and facial bones were palpable beneath an intact scalp. The remainder of the physical and neurologic examination, including head control, tone, reflexes, cranial nerves, and other organ systems, was unremarkable.

A skull radiograph demonstrated absence of the parietal bones with normal frontal, temporal, occipital, and facial bones. A full infantogram was otherwise normal. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, serum calcium, phosphate, and alkaline phosphatase, were all within normal limits.

A 49-year-old Syrian man, a lifelong shepherd, presented with acute right flank pain, dark urine, and passage of stones and cream-colored, grape-skin–like structures in the urine. He had a history of a hepatic hydatid cyst treated by PAIR and albendazole years earlier but lost follow-up. He denied fever, dysuria, or other urinary symptoms. On examination he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable; abdominal examination revealed right flank tenderness without masses or peritoneal signs. Laboratory tests showed normal leukocyte count without eosinophilia, serum creatinine 1.03 mg/dL, hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL, normal electrolytes and liver function tests, and an estimated GFR of 81 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis revealed leukocytes and 6–7 RBCs per high-power field, with sterile cultures. Passed stones were  calcium oxalate and urate. Echinococcus indirect hemagglutination assay was positive at a titer of 1:2048. A KUB x-ray was unremarkable. Renal ultrasound demonstrated multiple unilocular hypoechoic cystic structures in the right kidney. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed three thick-walled exophytic cystic lesions in the mid and lower right kidney (largest 9×8×7.5 cm, Bosniak III) with heterogeneous, nonenhancing hyperdense contents, occasional border calcification, and communication with the pelvicalyceal system; these caused grade III hydronephrosis and debris-filled calyces. The left kidney appeared normal. A calcified defect in the right hepatic lobe suggested prior treated hydatid disease. Dynamic renal scintigraphy revealed negligible function (5%) of the right kidney and normal function of the left kidney. Based on his epidemiologic history, prior hepatic cyst, positive serology, pathognomonic hydatiduria, and imaging findings, a preliminary diagnosis was made.

A 41-year-old Brazilian man with a 10-year history of episodic arthritis and well-controlled hypertension (losartan 50 mg daily) was admitted for a polyarthritis flare with low-grade fever. He initially had monoarthritis of the right first metatarsophalangeal joint, progressing over 5 years to recurrent polyarthritis of large and small joints without morning stiffness.  

On examination, temperature was 37.8 °C and blood pressure 130/80 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Musculoskeletal examination showed reversible swan-neck deformities of the fingers; his ankles, knees, and elbows were swollen and warm. He had multiple painless subcutaneous nodules (0.5–1 cm) of firm consistency on the extensor surfaces of the forearms and legs.  

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL, white blood cell count 12 700 cells/mm3, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 62 mm/h, C-reactive protein 418 mg/L, and serum uric acid 6.7 mg/dL (upper normal range). Anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies were low-positive (38 U; negative <20 U); rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies, anti–double-stranded DNA, and anti–SSA/Ro antibodies were all negative.  

Plain radiographs of the hands showed no bone erosions or joint space narrowing.

A 38-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with a 3-month history of biliary colic, followed 1 week earlier by intermittent fever and vomiting containing membranes. On examination, she was febrile (38.5 °C) with mild tachycardia; abdominal evaluation revealed distension and right hypochondrial tenderness. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 240 mg/l, a white-cell count of 10,000/mm3, and normal cholestasis parameters (total bilirubin 4.2 mg/l, aspartate aminotransferase 37 IU/l, alanine aminotransferase 30 IU/l). Initial differential diagnoses included gallstone complications (acute cholecystitis, cholangitis), liver abscess, pancreatitis, pyelonephritis, subhepatic appendicitis, and right basal pneumonia. A plain abdominal radiograph demonstrated an abnormal extra-luminal gas collection in the epigastric region. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a multiloculated cystic mass adjacent to the left liver lobe and stomach, suggestive of a type III Gharbi hydatid cyst. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen identified a cystic mass in the left hepatic lobe with a thickened wall and air–fluid level compressing the stomach, an air-filled communication track with the gastric wall, mass effect on the splenic vein with collateral formation, and coeliomesenteric lymphadenopathy.

A 55-year-old right-handed woman with no history of rheumatologic disease presented with 2 days of increasing pain, swelling, and progressive numbness in the right hand involving all five fingers. She denied trauma, injections, or penetrating injury. She reported chills and night sweats without fever and no prior similar episodes. Her medical history included hepatitis C, distant intravenous heroin use (last, 25 years ago), and osteoarthritis of the knees, hips, and spine. She denied personal histories of gout, pseudogout, autoimmune disorders, or kidney stones; her family history included rheumatoid arthritis in maternal relatives.

On examination, the right hand had erythema and swelling most prominent in the hypothenar region extending into the volar wrist. The distal volar forearm, wrist, thenar, and hypothenar compartments were profoundly taut and tender. She had numbness and paresthesia in both the median and ulnar nerve distributions with diminished two-point discrimination; radial sensation was normal. Motor function was severely limited by pain but all intrinsic and extrinsic hand muscles could be weakly activated. The hand was warm, well-perfused, and pulses were intact. She was afebrile and hemodynamically stable.

Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 9,300/mm3 (reference 4,300–10,800), C-reactive protein 8.1 mg/L (reference <10 mg/L), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 29 mm/h (reference 0–30 mm/h), and serum uric acid 3.1 mg/dL (reference 2.4–6 mg/dL). Other chemistries, complete blood count differential, and liver function tests were normal. Intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam were initiated for presumed infection.

Plain radiographs of the right hand showed diffuse soft-tissue swelling without fracture or obvious calcification at the triangular fibrocartilage. A CT scan was obtained to exclude a deep space abscess; preliminary reads showed no fluid collection, and subsequent review identified a small irregular radiopaque calcified mass overlying the hook of the hamate just radial to the ulnar artery and nerve.

A 55-year-old woman was referred for several months of cervical discomfort with a voluminous, hard-consistency goiter, dyspnea, and dysphagia. She was clinically euthyroid; serum FT3 and FT4 were normal, antithyroglobulin and antithyroid peroxidase antibody titers were elevated, erythrocyte sedimentation rate was raised, and calcitonin levels were normal. Neck ultrasound showed a markedly enlarged thyroid (anteroposterior diameters 28 mm on the right and 29 mm on the left) with diffusely reduced echogenicity comparable to adjacent prethyroid muscles, poorly defined margins blending with strap muscles, inhomogeneous parenchyma with hypoechoic areas, scant vascularity, and signs of tracheal compression and vascular displacement. CT and MRI confirmed left-lobe predominance, extension into the superior mediastinum, contralateral tracheal displacement, and an inhomogeneous hypodense area in the left lobe; regional lymph nodes were enlarged but of normal density. Given the clinical suspicion for Riedel disease versus fibrous variant Hashimoto thyroiditis, a fine-needle thyroid biopsy was performed, revealing diffuse chronic lymphocytic infiltration and dense fibrous tissue with complete absence of thyroid follicles.

A 47-year-old Caucasian woman with a history of congenital long QT syndrome Type 2, for which she has a dual‐chamber implantable cardioverter‐defibrillator (ICD) and beta‐blocker therapy, presented to the emergency department after receiving an ICD shock during sleep. She arrived in an electrical storm, requiring six ICD shocks for recurrent ventricular fibrillation. Intravenous magnesium sulfate (2 g) successfully suppressed further episodes, and 10 mg of diazepam was given for anxiety. The patient denied chest pain but noted some paresthesia in both arms and the chest after the discharges. Her medical history included hypothyroidism (on levothyroxine) and depression; she smoked 25 pack‐years, had a body mass index of 26 kg/m^2, and was taking metoprolol 47.5 mg twice daily. On examination during sinus rhythm, her heart rate was 90 beats/min, blood pressure 105/66 mmHg, and cardiovascular findings were unremarkable. The initial 12‐lead ECG showed atrially triggered ventricular pacing, and despite the paced QRS complexes, there were distinct ST‐segment elevations in the inferior leads. The patient was loaded with aspirin and heparin intravenously, and primary coronary angiography was immediately performed.

A 24-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 15 weeks of a dichorionic twin pregnancy presented with weakness, repeated vomiting, and inability to tolerate oral intake. Since early pregnancy, she had severe nausea managed with doxylamine/pyridoxine and metoclopramide. On examination, she was mildly agitated with a temperature of 37.5°C, heart rate 120 bpm, blood pressure 115/80 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air; no tremors were noted. An electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia at 104 bpm, ST-segment elevation in the inferolateral leads, and a prolonged QTc interval (603 ms). Laboratory studies revealed severe hypokalemia (K+ 1.9 mmol/L) and hyponatremia (Na+ 118 mmol/L), which were corrected promptly. Cardiac enzymes were elevated (troponin T 9082 ng/L, CK-MB 420 µg/L). Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated inferior wall hypokinesia with an ejection fraction of 55%. Over the next day, she developed sustained ventricular tachycardia requiring defibrillation, persistent tachycardia, and hemodynamic support with an intra-aortic balloon pump; repeat echocardiography showed a decline in ejection fraction to 40%. She also developed massive bilateral pleural effusions leading to noninvasive and then invasive mechanical ventilation. Empirical antibiotics and steroids were initiated for suspected myocarditis, and blood cultures, cardiotropic viral studies, and autoimmunity tests were obtained.

A 30-year-old Hispanic man with no past medical history presented with a 2-day history of a severe headache that began suddenly during weightlifting and squatting. He described the pain as sharp and stabbing, starting in his neck and radiating to the back of his head, initially 13/10 in intensity, settling to 6/10 at rest but worsening to 15/10 during sexual intercourse and defecation straining. At presentation the headache was 3/10. He denied trauma, loss of consciousness, neurologic deficits, vision changes, family history of stroke or aneurysm, polycystic kidney disease, drug use, and daily medications. 

Vital signs were stable (T 36.9 °C; BP 128/85 mm Hg; HR 88 bpm; RR 18/min; SpO2 98% on room air). Physical examination was normal, with an NIH Stroke Scale score of 0. 

Non-contrast head CT showed no acute intracranial process. Lumbar puncture revealed normal CSF without blood or xanthochromia. CT angiography of the head and neck demonstrated a long segment of moderate stenosis in the mid-basilar artery, with an abrupt 50% caliber reduction over 9 mm and no other intracranial abnormalities; these findings were interpreted as typical for an acute basilar artery dissection, and there was no evidence of cerebral vasoconstriction.

28-year-old Hispanic man with no past medical history presented with three weeks of progressively worsening bloody diarrhea and diffuse myalgias localized to the bilateral lower extremities. He denied recent travel, sick contacts, or new medications; he had completed a 10-day course of amoxicillin for presumed streptococcal pharyngitis without improvement. On admission, temperature was 101.8°F, WBC 17,600/mm3, hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL (decreasing to 8.9), ESR 114 mm/hr, CRP 33.6 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 183 IU/L, AST 145 IU/L, CPK 1433 IU/L, and potassium 2.7 mmol/L. Hepatitis panel, HIV, coccidioidomycosis, gonorrhea and chlamydia PCR were negative. Stool studies were negative for enteric pathogens and C difficile. CT of the abdomen and pelvis was unremarkable. Colonoscopy revealed continuous colitis from cecum to rectum; biopsies showed crypt abscesses and mixed lamina propria inflammation consistent with ulcerative colitis. He was treated with IV fluids, mesalamine, and a prednisone taper, with resolution of symptoms and normalization of CPK; he remained in remission for one year.

One year later, he returned with worsening bilateral lower extremity pain and difficulty ambulating, without gastrointestinal symptoms and on maintenance mesalamine. He was febrile, WBC 25,300/mm3, CPK 9455 IU/L, and abnormal liver tests. MRI of the lower extremities with contrast showed numerous intramuscular abscesses and extensive muscle infiltration in the left thigh and fewer abscesses in the right thigh, without periosteal reaction. Empiric antibiotics were started but then discontinued when blood and tissue cultures were negative. Prednisone was initiated, and his symptoms improved. A muscle biopsy of the left lower leg demonstrated myonecrosis with acute inflammatory exudate. Acid-fast and Gram stains, pan cultures, immunohistochemical staining, and metabolic assays were normal. Autoimmune serologies, including a myositis panel, were negative except for an ANA titer of 1:80. He experienced two further similar hospitalizations over five months, with repeat MRI and biopsy showing consistent findings while his ulcerative colitis remained quiescent on mesalamine.

A 46-year-old immunocompetent man presented with a 6-month history of increasing left heel pain with intermittent exacerbations since childhood. He had been treated irregularly for a presumed heel spur with conservative measures and analgesics for 6 months. He then noted worsening pain and the new onset of nocturnal pain, prompting referral. There was no history of penetrating injury; examination revealed no erythema, swelling, redness, or drainage of the foot. Pain was elicited on palpation over the heel spur and along both the medial and lateral aspects of the heel.

A plain radiograph of the left calcaneus showed a localized radiolucent lesion in the calcaneal body with a narrow zone of transition, a sclerotic rim, and no endosteal scalloping or periosteal reaction. MRI with gadolinium contrast revealed a 2.5 cm unicameral cystic lesion without fluid–fluid levels, hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, surrounded by bone marrow edema and a sclerotic rim. On the basis of these benign-appearing radiologic findings, the lesion was felt to represent one of several benign entities, and conservative treatment was restarted for 10 days; however, the patient’s pain increased. Given the lesion’s benign character on imaging, the decision was made to proceed with curettage and grafting without a preceding biopsy.

A 1-year 5-month-old boy was brought for evaluation of reddish discoloration of his nappies and clothes, noted over the preceding weeks, and breath-holding spells. There was no foul odor to his skin or urine, no history of dysuria, poor urinary stream, bleeding, fever, rash, abdominal pain, constipation, or altered sensorium. The parents were first cousins; the mother had thalassemia trait. 

On examination, his weight was 8.5 kg, head circumference 44 cm, and length 81 cm. He was alert, with no jaundice or dehydration. Vital signs: SpO2 94% on room air, heart rate 146/min, respiratory rate 26/min, blood pressure 73/44 (mean 54) mm Hg. Cardiovascular and respiratory exams were unremarkable; abdomen soft, liver 1 cm below costal margin, no splenomegaly; normal reflexes, hypotonia, and no meningeal signs. 

Initial laboratory studies:  
– Urine routine examination and abdominal ultrasound were normal.  
– Hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, microcytic hypochromic anemia: hematocrit 31.9%, MCV 68 fL, MCH 21.8 pg, MCHC 32%, RDW 17.1%.  
– Serum iron studies and ferritin were within reference ranges.  
– Hb analysis by HPLC showed Hb A0 80.4% and Hb A2 6.1%, consistent with β-thalassemia trait, confirmed by DNA studies.  
– Serum electrolytes, bicarbonate, renal and liver function tests were normal.  
– Urine porphyrin levels were within normal limits.  
– Myoglobin and hemoglobin were undetected in urine.  
– EEG was normal.  

Urine was of normal color when voided but turned black over variable periods spontaneously.

An 8-year-old boy was brought by his guardian who noted that it “looked like a tooth was rising behind the front teeth.” On intraoral examination, there was an anomalous projection on the cingulum of both maxillary central incisors (elements 11 and 21). The projection measured approximately 6 mm in height and was bordered by a 1–2 mm deep groove that retained biofilm and food debris but showed no carious lesions. The projection caused occlusal interference and premature contact with the permanent lower central incisors, which exhibited first-degree mobility. A periapical radiograph revealed a “V”-shaped radiopaque structure arising from the cervical third of the crowns, overlapping the crown images; it was not possible to determine whether the projection contained pulp tissue.

A 67-year-old Middle Eastern woman with a history of Child-Pugh Class A cirrhosis (presumed NASH), mild pancytopenia, GERD, prior H. pylori infection, remote cholecystectomy, and hyperlipidemia presented with acute on chronic diffuse abdominal pain associated with nausea and vomiting. She denied fevers, night sweats, weight loss, extraintestinal symptoms, diet changes, or recent travel. Medications included metformin, domperidone, and pantoprazole. Physical examination showed mild epigastric tenderness without organomegaly, rash, or joint findings.

Laboratory studies revealed WBC 3.2×10^9/L, hemoglobin 105 g/L, platelets 88×10^9/L, AST 45 U/L, ALT 54 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 150 U/L, GGT 26 U/L, total bilirubin 12 μmol/L, albumin 24 g/L, INR 1.2. Serologies were negative for hepatitis C, HAV IgM, HIV, ANA, ANCA, anti–smooth muscle, antienterocyte, antigoblet cell, antitransglutaminase, antiparietal antibodies; antimitochondrial antibody was intermittently low-titer positive. Serum protein electrophoresis showed diffuse polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. Abdominal ultrasound revealed mild ascites without thrombosis.

Initial EGD with endoscopic ultrasound identified a polypoid, friable 0.8-cm nodule at the gastroesophageal junction and similar nodules in the gastric body. Biopsies showed active chronic gastritis without granulomas; CMV inclusions were detected on routine histology and immunohistochemistry. She received 2 weeks of oral valganciclovir.

Seven weeks later, repeat EGD for persistent symptoms showed growth of the original nodule to 1.3 cm, new fundal nodules up to 1.5 cm, and friable mucosa along the lesser curvature. Biopsies again showed severe active chronic gastritis with ulceration, no granulomas, and CMV on immunohistochemistry. CMV IgM was nonreactive, and serum CMV DNA was undetectable. Tests for H. pylori, treponemal organisms, acid-fast bacilli, dysplasia, and malignancy were negative. She was treated with 6 weeks of intravenous ganciclovir.

Subsequent EGDs demonstrated persistent inflamed polypoid lesions in the antrum and duodenum. Biopsies were negative for CMV on immunohistochemistry but revealed noncaseating granulomas with moderate-to-severe lymphoplasmacytic inflammation, lymphoid aggregates, cryptitis, and crypt abscesses.

Thoracic and abdominal CT, CT enterography, and colonoscopy showed no evidence of inflammatory bowel disease but did reveal multiple subcentimeter mediastinal, precordial, and mesenteric lymph nodes and stable splenomegaly (21 cm).

A 33-year-old man was admitted after a frontal motor-vehicle collision with airbag deployment. He had a brief loss of consciousness, a mild headache, and moderate low-back pain radiating to the left leg. On examination, he had a small forehead bruise, lumbar paraspinal tenderness, and could not lift his left leg more than 6 inches due to pain, though strength, sensation, and plantar and dorsiflexion were intact. Initial CT showed an acute traumatic pseudoaneurysm of the thoracic aorta, traumatic subluxation of L5 on S1, and a left L5 transverse-process fracture. MRI demonstrated severe spinal canal narrowing at L5–S1 with soft-tissue edema, a hematoma at the left L5 neural foramen, and nerve expansion. The aortic injury was successfully stented. On hospital day 3, he underwent posterior lumbar decompression with fusion and skin-flap reconstruction in the prone position for 5 hours. At the end of the procedure, the scrotum was noted to be trapped between the right thigh and the table, with scrotal discoloration but no necrosis or signs of infection. Emergent scrotal ultrasound with a 12-MHz transducer revealed a 3.0-cm heterogeneous mass superior to the right testis on gray-scale imaging. Color Doppler showed flow around but not within the mass; both testes had preserved blood flow, with increased capsular and centripetal flow on the right compared to the left.

A 15-year-old boy presented with crowding of his upper and lower front teeth. He had midface retrusion and a history of surgically repaired bilateral cleft lip from childhood. Examination revealed small, bilateral, paramedian lower lip pits, each 3 mm in diameter and 5 mm deep; compression of one pit expressed mucous. Intraoral findings included a collapsed V-shaped palate with severe upper anterior crowding, obliteration of the upper labial vestibule by a thick fibrous band that blanched on lip retraction, a short uvula, and ankyloglossia due to a short lingual frenum. A posterior crossbite was noted. No other systemic abnormalities were identified. Radiographs—including chest radiograph, lateral cephalograph, orthopantomograph, and maxillary occlusal view—were obtained; genetic studies were not performed.

A 14-year-old girl presented with a 1-month history of swelling in the left submandibular region accompanied by sore throat and pain on swallowing. She was afebrile, and her vital signs were within normal limits. On palpation, there was a 1.5 × 1.5 cm soft, slightly tender swelling beneath the middle third of the left submandibular area; the overlying skin was unremarkable. The swelling moved vertically on swallowing. Intraoral examination showed features of oral submucous fibrosis but was otherwise noncontributory. Intraoral periapical radiographs of teeth 34–36 were normal. Ultrasonography of the submandibular region demonstrated a well-defined cystic lesion with a thick wall measuring 1.13 × 1.27 cm; the thyroid gland was in its normal position. Aspiration yielded clear viscous fluid, and fine-needle aspiration cytology indicated a simple cystic lesion without lymphoid or malignant cells. Preoperative chest radiograph, complete blood count, urine analysis, and blood chemistry values were all within normal limits.

A 44-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of right upper quadrant abdominal pain that radiated to the back and was colicky in nature. He had no fever or weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and liver‐function tests, were within normal limits. He was initially diagnosed with biliary colic. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated multiple subcentimeter gallstones and a heterogeneous mass thought to arise from the liver. An abdominal CT scan with intravenous contrast subsequently revealed an 11 × 8 cm well-circumscribed mass located in the retro-duodenal space, immediately anterior to the right kidney. The initial differential diagnosis included a duodenal gastrointestinal stromal tumor and a retroperitoneal sarcoma.

An 85-year-old man with a history of inflammatory bowel disease treated with corticosteroids and bowel resection presented with left hip pain after a fall. Over the preceding months, he had developed iron-deficiency anemia, mild heart failure, malnutrition, frailty, and weight loss. Three months earlier, a contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis showed no malignancy.

On admission, a pelvic radiograph revealed fractures of the left superior and inferior pubic rami and the left S2 sacral arcade; the left femoral neck appeared equivocal. A subsequent CT of the pelvis confirmed those fractures but remained indeterminate for a femoral neck fracture. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 84 g/L (reference 130–180) and albumin 22 g/L (reference 34–54); kidney function, lactate, COVID-19 test, and vital signs were normal.

Two days later, an MRI of the pelvis was obtained to assess for an occult femoral neck fracture. On the T1-weighted sequence, the trabecular bone and subcutaneous adipose tissue appeared uniformly gray, and on the STIR sequence, both regions were diffusely hyperintense; the signal intensity of urine in the bladder confirmed correct sequence weightings. The radiology report and technologists suspected a technical malfunction. A repeat MRI on a different scanner the next day demonstrated identical findings.

A 68-year-old woman presented with several months of local discomfort and swelling in the right popliteal fossa that worsened with walking and climbing stairs. Her history included chronic bilateral venous insufficiency beginning after pregnancy, bilateral saphenectomy, and recurrence of varicosities about 12 years later. There was a strong family history of varicose veins. 

On examination, vital signs were normal. The right popliteal fossa showed a soft mass that was painful on deep palpation, without erythema, warmth, or bruit. There were signs of chronic venous insufficiency in both lower extremities. Chest and abdominal examinations were normal, and there were no signs of peripheral arterial disease. Chest X-ray, oxygen saturation, and electrocardiogram findings were unremarkable.

Colour Doppler ultrasonography of the right leg revealed a saccular dilatation measuring 2.3 × 1.9 × 2.4 cm in the distal popliteal vein. Spectral analysis showed an altered venous waveform during a calf-muscle squeeze test, and the lesion increased slightly in size with the Valsalva maneuver. Although blood flow within the dilatation was slow, there was no evidence of thrombosis; the lesion completely refilled with blood on compression and during the squeeze test. The right popliteal artery had a normal Doppler waveform.

A 37-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of insidious onset upper back pain and altered pain and temperature sensation over the right half of his body below the nipple. He denied motor weakness, involuntary movements, bowel or bladder dysfunction, history of trauma, fever, weight loss, or other constitutional symptoms. He had no chronic medical conditions. On examination, there was no spinal tenderness or deformity. Motor strength in both lower limbs was 5/5 throughout (L2–S1), reflexes were normal, and plantar responses were flexor. Abdominal reflexes were intact. Sensory testing revealed loss of pain and temperature below the right nipple; light touch and vibration were not described as abnormal. Bowel and bladder function were preserved.

Plain radiographs of the thoracic spine were unremarkable. MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrated tethering of the spinal cord and an anterolateral defect on the left side of the dura at the T2–T3 level. CT of the thoracic spine confirmed a focal dural defect at T2–T3.

A 9-year-old boy was referred for a six-month history of recurrent abdominal pain and vomiting, initially diagnosed as cyclic vomiting by his family physician. Two days before admission, his symptoms worsened. On admission, he had lost 2.7 kg over three months but had normal height gain. Vital signs: temperature 36.0 °C, pulse 60 beats/min, blood pressure 93/49 mmHg. He appeared slightly pale; abdominal examination revealed normal bowel sounds, no distention or guarding, and mild tenderness in the lower mid-abdomen. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 13.9 g/dL, ferritin 46 ng/mL, normal total protein and albumin, no elevated inflammatory markers, and a mildly elevated fecal human hemoglobin of 232 ng/mL. Abdominal radiograph was unremarkable. Ultrasonography demonstrated a multiple concentric ring sign and pseudokidney sign in the ileum without spontaneous reduction by peristalsis; a mass-like structure at the tip of the invagination showed marked Doppler flow. After two hours of fasting and fluids, symptoms and sonographic signs resolved. On hospital day 2, transanal double-balloon endoscopy under sedation revealed a stalked polyp-like structure approximately 90 cm proximal to the ileocecal valve.

A 17-year-old girl presented with a 1-month history of low-grade intermittent fever, fatigue, anorexia, and generalized weakness. She had no cough, abdominal pain, diarrhea, headache, or dysuria. An oral antibiotic course 2 weeks earlier did not improve her symptoms. She has normal menstruation, no drug use, and has been a strict vegetarian since birth.

On examination, temperature was 38.8 °C, pulse 104/min, respiratory rate 16/min, blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg, and BMI 20 kg/m2. She had severe pallor, mild scleral icterus, and hyperpigmentation of the knuckles. There was no lymphadenopathy, clubbing, or edema. Abdominal, respiratory, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed severe anemia and thrombocytopenia. Peripheral blood smear demonstrated anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, polychromasia, microcytosis, macrocytosis, occasional Cabot rings, Howell–Jolly bodies, schistocytes, and hypersegmented neutrophils. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 36 mm/h. Reticulocyte count was 4% (absolute count 1.7%) with a reticulocyte index of 0.7. Iron studies were within normal limits (serum iron 128 μg/dl, saturation 34.6%, TIBC 370 μg/dl, ferritin 68.6 ng/ml).

Infectious and serologic work-up revealed negative blood and urine cultures, negative malaria smears and antigen tests, negative dengue NS1, negative Widal test, negative HIV, HBsAg, anti-HCV, and VDRL tests. IgM ELISA for EBV, CMV, and parvovirus were also negative.

A 57-year-old Japanese man presented with a one-month history of back pain and fever. Computed tomography revealed an infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring 34 mm with surrounding adipose-tissue inflammation, bilateral pulmonary nodules, and left maxillary sinusitis. On admission, his temperature was 39.6 °C, blood pressure 98/69 mmHg, and pulse 84 beats/min. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 10,000/μL, C-reactive protein 29.5 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 0.66 mg/dL. Urinalysis revealed 1+ occult blood and 20 red blood cells per high-power field. Serologic testing demonstrated an anti–proteinase-3 ANCA level of 187 IU/mL; anti-MPO-ANCA was normal. The abdominal aneurysm was initially suspected to be infected, and antibiotics were started, but the patient’s condition did not improve.

A 21-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of reddish-white patches on the right buccal mucosa and hard palate, accompanied by a burning sensation. He recalled initially feeling a small, fluid-filled swelling on the palate that ruptured, after which the lesion enlarged; a similar lesion appeared on the right inner cheek around the same time. He had no significant medical, dental, or family history, maintained good oral hygiene, did not smoke or chew tobacco, but frequently ate spicy foods. Topical antifungal therapy had provided only temporary relief of burning.

On examination, the right buccal mucosa showed a single 4 × 2 cm erythematous plaque with elevated white, irregular margins and radiating white striae at the level of the occlusal plane (from tooth 45 to distal of 47). The lesion was soft and non-tender. On the hard palate, there was a single 4 × 4 cm elevated erythematous lesion interspersed with white striae and multiple minute round erythematous projections, extending from behind the incisive papilla to 1 cm above the soft palate; the palatal rugae and incisive papilla were spared. No skin or nail abnormalities were noted.

Correlating the history and clinical morphology, the provisional diagnoses included bullous lichen planus, lichen planus pemphigoides, pemphigus, pemphigoid, allergic stomatitis, erythroleukoplakia, and erythematous candidiasis. Basic hematological parameters were within normal limits. The patient was referred for an incisional biopsy of the lesion.

A 60-year-old woman of rural origin presented with a 4-day history of dull, intermittent, progressively severe right iliac–region pain associated with fever, nausea, and vomiting. She reported transient episodes of abdominal pain months earlier but denied diarrhea or hematochezia and had no recent travel to tropical areas. On examination, her temperature was 38.9 °C, and she had tenderness in the right hemiabdomen without a palpable mass. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 12 g/dL, leukocytosis (14 650/mm3), and C-reactive protein 176 mg/L. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated irregular, non-stenosing cecal wall thickening measuring 7 cm with surrounding fat stranding and hypodense areas suggestive of a perilesional abscess. An infected cecal tumor was suspected.

A 55-year-old man presented to the emergency department with worsening shortness of breath and retrosternal chest pain radiating to the left arm and jaw. He had a history of hypercholesterolaemia, prior spinal surgery after traumatic neck injury, a remote COVID-19 infection, and was an ex-smoker.

On examination, he was tachycardic (heart rate 120 b.p.m.), hypoxic (oxygen saturation 80% on room air), and tachypnoeic, with a blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg. Chest auscultation revealed normal heart sounds without murmurs and bilateral crepitations. 

The preliminary working diagnosis was a late-presenting STEMI complicated by congestive heart failure. Mechanical complications of myocardial infarction, including acute mitral regurgitation due to papillary muscle rupture and ventricular septal defect, were also considered.

An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with upsloping ST-segment elevation, Q waves, and poor R-wave progression in the anterior leads. High-sensitivity troponin I was >50 000 ng/L, and creatine kinase was 795 U/L.

A bedside transthoracic echocardiogram revealed an unruptured aneurysm of the sinus of Valsalva with mild aortic regurgitation, moderate functional mitral regurgitation, a normal-sized left ventricle with severely impaired systolic function (ejection fraction 20%), and regional wall motion abnormalities. 

A chest radiograph demonstrated cephalization of pulmonary vessels and indistinct vascular markings compatible with pulmonary oedema.

A 3-day-old male neonate (weight 2.2 kg) born at term to consanguineous parents was referred for evaluation of failure to pass meconium, progressive abdominal distension, and bilious vomiting since birth. There was a maternal history of polyhydramnios, and the infant had not tolerated feeds. On examination, he had a cleft lip and palate; otherwise, the general examination was unremarkable. The abdomen was distended with visible bowel loops. A rectal thermometer could not be advanced beyond 1.5 cm from the anal verge. Abdominal radiography showed a large gas shadow in the right abdomen and a ground-glass appearance in the left abdomen. Ultrasonography demonstrated a large gas-filled bowel loop in the right abdomen. A working differential diagnosis of rectal atresia resulting in colonic dilatation and/or associated congenital pouch colon was considered.

A 38‐year‐old woman presented with continuous acute lower abdominal pain rated 10/10. She reported several episodes of loose stools but denied hematochezia, nausea, or vomiting. The pain was central in the lower abdomen and constant. She had an irregular menstrual cycle; her last menstrual period began 10 days earlier and lasted 7 days without atypical genital bleeding. She did not report urinary symptoms or back pain. Her medical history was notable for a cesarean section and untreated uterine fibroids; she denied any current gynecologic or inflammatory bowel disease.

On arrival, her vital signs were: blood pressure 120/69 mm Hg, heart rate 100 beats/min, respiratory rate 19 breaths/min, SpO₂ 100% on room air, temperature 37.2°C, and Glasgow Coma Scale score E4V5M6. Physical examination revealed tenderness in the mid–lower abdomen without muscular guarding. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 7200/mm³. A pregnancy test was negative. Abdominal ultrasonography did not indicate pyelectasis or a mass lesion in her lower abdomen.

Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated stenosis of the sigmoid colon with proximal dilatation but no free air, significant ascites, or diverticula. A subsequent colonoscopy revealed a narrowed stenotic segment with discoloration of the mucosa. We therefore suspected mesenteric ischemia.

A 20‐year‐old woman with a 2-year history of primary Sjögren syndrome and autoimmune thyroiditis (on levothyroxine, 50 µg daily) presented with a 2-week history of muscle cramps, progressive lower-limb weakness and salt craving. The weakness had no relation to high-carbohydrate meals, diurnal variation, fatigue or other neurologic symptoms, and there was no preceding infection or gastroenteritis. She denied use of diuretics or laxatives and had no personal or family history of similar episodes.

On examination, blood pressure was 100/70 mm Hg, pulse 78 bpm, and she was not volume depleted. There was no muscle wasting or tenderness; muscle power was 3/5 in the lower limbs, and deep-tendon reflexes were diminished. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory results showed: serum sodium 135 mmol/L, potassium 2.5 mmol/L, magnesium 1.8 mg/dL, chloride 91 mmol/L, bicarbonate 28 mmol/L, arterial pH 7.50, PaCO2 43 mm Hg, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, renin activity 60.6 ng/mL/h. ECG revealed T-wave flattening and U waves. Renal imaging showed no nephrocalcinosis. Urinary studies revealed: potassium 40 mmol/L, chloride 64 mmol/L, trans-tubular potassium gradient 13, spot urine K/Cr ratio 3.1 mmol/mmol, and spot urine Ca/Cr ratio 0.01 g/g.

A 54-year-old woman presented with a 15-month history of progressively worsening dyspnea, wheezing, and occasional cough. Initially, her symptoms occurred only with strenuous exertion. She had a normal chest radiograph and a spirometry ratio (FEV1/FVC) of 0.76; she was diagnosed with asthma and treated for one year without improvement. Current spirometry showed FEV1 1.61 L, FVC 2.11 L, and negative bronchodilator reversibility. Over the past months, her dyspnea—predominantly inspiratory—worsened even with mild activities. On examination, there was a wheeze audible over both lung fields, loudest at the upper third of the trachea. Repeat spirometry demonstrated blunting of both the inspiratory and expiratory limbs of the flow–volume loop.

A 15-year-old Mexican girl with neurofibromatosis type 1 presented with a 5-month history of pain and swelling over the left mandibular body. She had intermittent fever (up to 39 °C) and tachycardia. Examination revealed a soft, tender mass in the left submental and submandibular regions (12 cm in diameter), a draining intraoral fistula with purulent discharge, and mobility of adjacent teeth. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12 g/dL, hematocrit 36.7%, and a white-blood-cell count of 6.9 × 10^3/μL with a normal differential. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head demonstrated cortical erosion and perforation of the left hemimandible. SPECT/CT with technetium-99m-ciprofloxacin showed intense uptake at the left mandible, the right elbow, and soft tissues of the right hand, suggesting a disseminated infectious process. Intraoral secretion cultures grew Streptococcus parasanguinis and high-level gentamicin- and vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium. Antibiotic‐susceptibility testing revealed resistance to ampicillin, erythromycin, vancomycin, cefazolin, gentamicin, streptomycin, levofloxacin, oxacillin, and penicillin G, with susceptibility to daptomycin, doxycycline, linezolid, moxifloxacin, nitrofurantoin, quinupristin/dalfopristin, and rifampicin.

A 48-year-old man with end-stage renal disease secondary to hypertension and interstitial nephritis was admitted for a redo deceased donor renal transplant. He had undergone a prior transplant in 2011 complicated by rejection and graft failure requiring hemodialysis. On admission, his examination and preoperative laboratory studies were unremarkable. He received thymoglobulin induction and underwent renal transplantation with ureteroneocystostomy and stent placement; the new right renal graft was placed in the left hemipelvis because of his previous right-sided graft. His postoperative course was notable for delayed graft function requiring hemodialysis for hyperkalemia. On postoperative day 7, he developed abdominal pain and distention requiring nasogastric tube decompression. Given a history of idiopathic gastroparesis, metoclopramide was started. Workup included CT imaging, esophagogastroduodenoscopy, small bowel radiography, and endoscopic ultrasound. The CT scan showed changes suggestive of ileus versus early partial small bowel obstruction with scattered small-volume pneumoperitoneum. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy was unremarkable except for a possible inverted duodenal diverticulum, and endoscopic ultrasound was normal. Small bowel radiography demonstrated persistent obstruction. Total parenteral nutrition was initiated on postoperative day 13, and his bowel function eventually returned. He was discharged in stable condition on postoperative day 15. Two days later, he was readmitted with abdominal pain and inability to tolerate oral intake. Computed tomography showed partial small bowel obstruction with a transition point in the left lower quadrant.
