A 62-year-old man with a 111 pack-year smoking history and chronic sinusitis presented with cough, wheezing, and dyspnea. He reported allergies to theophylline and levofloxacin, which caused rashes. Initial chest CT showed consolidation in the right lower lobe, bilateral emphysema, and bronchial wall thickening. He was admitted with presumed pneumonia and treated with antibiotics, inhaled fluticasone/salmeterol (500/100 μg), and tiotropium (5 μg), with transient symptom improvement followed by recurrent wheezing and dyspnea. 

On reevaluation, he was labeled as having severe asthma and COPD based on peripheral-blood eosinophilia (698 /μL), elevated serum IgE (1077 IU/mL), emphysema, and bronchial wall thickening. A short course of oral corticosteroids, high-dose budesonide/formoterol (1280/36 μg), tiotropium, and montelukast (10 mg/day) did not prevent another severe exacerbation necessitating noninvasive ventilation and systemic corticosteroids. 

On referral, physical examination revealed bilateral wheezes. Laboratory studies confirmed persistent blood eosinophilia and high IgE levels. Specific IgE was positive to Dermatophagoides species, Alternaria, Candida, and Aspergillus. Pulmonary function testing showed FEV1 1.17 L (40.6% predicted) without significant bronchodilator reversibility. FeNO was elevated at 108 ppb. Chest CT demonstrated improvement of the right lower lobe consolidation but persistent bilateral bronchial wall thickening. 

Because of refractory asthma with type 2 inflammatory features, allergic bronchopulmonary mycosis was listed as a differential diagnosis.

A 68-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes, cirrhosis (with hepatitis C), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and benign prostatic hyperplasia presented with a 2-week history of progressive dyspnea, generalized weakness, subjective fevers, and right upper–quadrant abdominal pain. On examination, he had diminished breath sounds on the left and evidence of ascites. Vital signs were notable only for mild tachypnea; he was afebrile. Laboratory studies showed: normal white-cell count and hematocrit, normal renal function and electrolytes, AST 19 IU/L, ALT 5 IU/L, albumin 2.9 g/dL, total bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL, prothrombin time 15.6 s. Tests for hepatitis B surface antigen and HIV-1/2 antibodies were negative. A chest radiograph demonstrated a large left pleural effusion. Thoracentesis revealed an exudative fluid by Light’s criteria with negative cytology. Paracentesis of the ascitic fluid showed a serum–ascites albumin gradient of <1.1, a polymorphonuclear cell count <250 cells/mm^3, and negative bacterial culture. A repeat paracentesis to evaluate for malignancy or tuberculosis again showed no malignant cells, an adenosine deaminase level of 3.4 IU/L, and negative Ziehl–Neelsen stain, Lowenstein–Jensen cultures, and PCR for mycobacteria. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan revealed diffuse peritoneal nodularity (“peritoneal carcinomatosis”) and multiple subcentimeter lesions in the liver, spleen, and adrenal glands.

A 37-year-old man presented with a four-month history of perianal discharge and ulceration. One year earlier, he had an incised and drained perianal abscess that recurred two months after healing. On admission he weighed 40 kg, appeared dehydrated, and was tachycardic (110/min). His temperature was 38.5 °C and blood pressure was 90/60 mm Hg. No lymphadenopathy was noted. Abdominal examination showed generalized tenderness. Inspection of the perianal region revealed large bilateral infected ulcerations with purulent discharge. Digital rectal examination showed slight sphincter hypotonia; anoscopy and rectosigmoidoscopy were normal. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL, white blood cell count 12,300/μL, elevated C-reactive protein, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 50 mm/h; other tests were normal. Chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral nonhomogeneous infiltrates and a cavitary lesion in the right lung. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed multiple mesenteric and retroperitoneal necrotic lymph nodes.

A 28-year-old male Gaelic football player presented with a 1-day history of sudden-onset left buttock pain that began while bending and twisting during play. He reported tenderness over the left ischial tuberosity and deep gluteal region. Passive external rotation and extension of the left hip elicited pain. The patient was referred for magnetic resonance imaging of the left femur with a suspected left common hamstring tendon avulsion. MRI demonstrated mild inflammatory changes at the left common hamstring tendon but showed no evidence of avulsion.

A 58-year-old man presented with a 4–5-year history of a slowly enlarging, painful perineal mass located dorsal to the scrotum. He noted constant weight and a body–mass index of 27.8. Pain was aggravated by bicycle riding. His only comorbidity was Parkinson’s disease, treated with a dopamine agonist, monoamine oxidase inhibitor, and selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor. He was a non-smoker, non-alcoholic, and had no relevant family history. 

On examination, vital signs were normal. There was a soft, mobile, 5 × 5 × 4 cm mass in the perineum resembling labia majora. No inguinal or intra-abdominal lymphadenopathy was palpable. Ultrasound confirmed a homogeneous, hyperechoic subcutaneous mass without lymphadenopathy. Routine hematology, liver and renal function tests, and lipid profile were all within normal limits. 

Non-contrast computed tomography of the perineum demonstrated a subcutaneous fat-density lesion without a capsular structure or definite border and no invasion into deeper tissues, findings suggestive of a benign adipose tumor.

A 62-year-old man was referred for evaluation of an asymptomatic, small swelling on the upper labial mucosa in the region of tooth positions 13 and 14. He reported that the lesion appeared intermittently over several months and spontaneously resolved within 1–2 days. There was no extraoral swelling, lymphadenopathy, or fever. He had no history of trauma or systemic illness. On intraoral inspection, there was a mild, diffuse, oval elevation measuring approximately 0.5 cm × 0.7 cm, with normal mucosal color and no signs of inflammation or discharge. On bidigital palpation, the lesion was firm to hard, nonfluctuant, and nonadherent to deeper tissues. Based on the history and clinical examination, provisional diagnoses included mucocele, epulis, and salivary duct obstruction (minute salivary duct calculi). Routine hematological tests were normal, and the patient was scheduled for surgical excision. During surgery, no minor salivary glands or ducts were identified in association with the lesion. The excised mass measured 0.5 cm × 0.6 cm, was firm and slightly compressible, dark cream-black in color, and surrounded by loose connective tissue. The specimen was sent for histopathological examination.

A 46-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of fatigue, hypersomnia, weight loss, and bifrontal headaches. Since January, he had persistent, treatment-refractory diarrhea, abdominal pain, intermittent large-joint pains, and hyperpigmented papules on his lower legs. Neurologic examination revealed smooth, continuous, slow (1–3 Hz), pendular, convergent-divergent nystagmus with concurrent masticatory-muscle contractions, supranuclear vertical gaze palsy, and occasional rhythmic limb movements. Abdominal examination showed mild epigastric tenderness. Routine blood tests and cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed mild lymphocytic pleocytosis. Brain MRI demonstrated left-predominant nodular enhancement of the hypothalamus, inferior basal ganglia, and cingulum. Abdominal CT revealed retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Upper endoscopy with duodenal biopsy showed infiltration of the lamina propria with macrophages containing periodic acid–Schiff–positive inclusions. CT scans of the chest and pelvis were unremarkable, and transesophageal echocardiography was normal.

A 55-year-old Vietnamese man with no significant past medical history presented with a 2-week history of generalized, cramping abdominal pain and progressive distention. He also reported nausea and nonbilious vomiting but denied fever, weight loss, changes in bowel habits, sick contacts, or recent raw-food ingestion. He had returned from Vietnam one year earlier, was taking no medications, and had no known allergies.

On examination, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. The abdomen was moderately distended, with active bowel sounds and diffuse tenderness without rebound; moderate ascites was noted. There was no hepatomegaly, skin rash, or peripheral edema.

Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 15,400/mm3 with 36% eosinophils. Liver function tests and other chemistries were normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed moderate ascites and circumferential thickening of the gastric antrum and proximal small bowel. 

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy demonstrated mild duodenitis; mucosal biopsies showed nonspecific, predominantly lymphocytic inflammation. Stool tests for ova and parasites were negative, and a multiplex screen for Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Isospora, and Sarcocystis was unrevealing. He improved on bowel rest and IV fluids and was discharged on empiric albendazole.

Two weeks later, he was readmitted with worsened abdominal pain and greater distention. The white-cell count had risen to 17,100/mm3 with 71% eosinophils, and serum IgE was elevated at 548 IU/mL. Repeat stool studies and serologic tests for Toxocara, Trichinella, Strongyloides, filariae, Schistosoma, Echinococcus, and Cysticercus were all negative. Repeat EGD remained nondiagnostic. Peripheral-blood flow cytometry showed no evidence of myeloid or lymphoid malignancy. Serum β2-microglobulin and LDH levels were within normal limits. 

Ultrasound-guided paracentesis yielded 6,600 WBCs/mm3 in the ascitic fluid, of which 95% were eosinophils; fluid LDH was 284 U/L, and albumin was 3.2 g/dL (concurrent serum albumin 4.1 g/dL).

A 71-year-old Japanese man with a history of primary open-angle glaucoma underwent EX-PRESS filtering surgery in the left eye, followed one month later by the right eye. Intraocular pressures were well controlled bilaterally. Seven months after the right-eye surgery, he reported redness and a foreign-body sensation in the right eye. On slit-lamp examination, there was a marginal corneal ulcer with an epithelial defect near the site of the EX-PRESS implant, accompanied by limbitis and severe scleral injection. Nylon sutures were removed, and topical 0.5% levofloxacin and 0.1% fluorometholone were initiated, resulting in slight reduction of the ulcer but no complete resolution. Topical 1% betamethasone sodium phosphate was then started, with gradual decrease in corneal ulceration, limbitis, and scleral injection.

Three months later (ten months after the left-eye surgery), a similar marginal corneal ulcer developed in the left eye near its EX-PRESS implant site. After removal of the limbal sutures, topical 0.1% betamethasone sodium phosphate was continued in both eyes. Despite ongoing topical steroids, both corneal ulcers progressed, showing stromal thinning with steep, undermined leading edges. Gram staining of corneal scrapings showed no organisms, cultures for bacteria and fungi were negative, and there was no mucopurulent eye discharge.

An early-80s man with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidemia (no smoking history) was brought in for progressive dyspnea since that morning. On arrival: BP 140/70 mmHg, SpO2 94% on humidified oxygen, bradycardia, and no fever. Electrocardiography showed ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated normal left ventricular function and no pericardial effusion. Cardiac biomarkers were elevated (CK-MB 290 ng/ml; troponin I 91.69 ng/ml), and acute inferior myocardial infarction was diagnosed. The patient received aspirin 200 mg, prasugrel 20 mg, and underwent temporary pacing for bradycardia. Coronary angiography revealed complete occlusion of the right coronary artery, which was successfully revascularized. Post-PCI medications included aspirin, prasugrel, a proton-pump inhibitor, statin, linagliptin, empagliflozin, and a continuous heparin infusion.  

That night, he developed fever and tachypnea with worsening respiratory status. The following morning, he became hypotensive (BP 62/48 mmHg) with shock and decreased consciousness. Repeat echocardiography showed a new moderate pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology. Laboratory tests revealed C-reactive protein of 30.18 mg/dL and a white blood cell count of 3600/μL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest confirmed a large pericardial effusion without evidence of aortic dissection. With concern for post-infarction cardiac rupture, the patient was taken for emergent surgical exploration.

A 54-year-old Caucasian man presented with two weeks of gradual blurred vision, decreased contrast sensitivity, and persistent floaters in his right eye. He denied recent trauma or infection. His medical history included gastroesophageal reflux disease and an allergy to diclofenac. The left eye had longstanding trauma from 40 years earlier with subsequent cataract removal, vitrectomy with silicone oil, basal iridectomy, uveitis, and secondary glaucoma leading to no light perception; posterior segment examination of the left eye was not possible.

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 0.5 in the right eye and no light perception in the left eye. Intraocular pressures were 14.6 mmHg (right) and 31.8 mmHg (left). The right anterior segment showed early lens opacities but no signs of anterior uveitis. Fundus examination of the right eye revealed multiple scattered, creamy-yellow, round chorioretinal lesions in all quadrants, 1+ vitreous cells, and optic disc edema without macular edema. B-scan ultrasound of the right eye showed posterior vitreous detachment and vitreous opacities.

Optical coherence tomography of the right macula demonstrated thickening of the outer nuclear layer, retinal pigment epithelium disorganization, and intraretinal cysts. Optic nerve OCT showed thickened retinal nerve fiber layer nasally, temporally, and inferiorly. OCT angiography revealed capillary loops and increased intercapillary spaces with reduced vessel density in both the superficial and deep plexuses, with lesions visible in each vascular layer.

Fluorescein angiography of the right eye showed an arteriovenous transit time of 27 seconds; early hypofluorescent lesions that became hyperfluorescent in later phases; a few focal leaks; blurred margins and intense optic disc hyperfluorescence from the early phases; and a spotty choroidal pattern throughout the study. Visual field testing identified a large central scotoma involving the blind spot and peripheral constriction in all quadrants.

Electroretinography of the right eye using photopic flicker revealed reduced amplitude and delayed latency, while scotopic responses showed amplitude and latency within reference ranges. Routine laboratory tests were notable only for a mild eosinopenia and slight elevation in urea; complete blood count, metabolic panel, coagulation, blood glucose, and C-reactive protein were otherwise normal. Infectious serologies, including syphilis, tuberculosis, Borrelia burgdorferi, Toxoplasma gondii, CMV, and HIV, were negative. HLA-A29 testing was negative. Chest radiography was unremarkable.

A 4½-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a painless expansile lesion of the left maxilla and delayed eruption of primary and permanent teeth in that quadrant. He was otherwise healthy. On examination, there was mild left facial asymmetry with fullness of the upper lip and cheek, ipsilateral skin erythema, increased facial hair, and a nasolabial scar. Intraorally, the left maxillary arch showed buccolingual expansion with gingival overgrowth since age 3; the primary molars were delayed in eruption, and adjacent gingiva was thickened, red, and edematous. Panoramic radiograph demonstrated left maxillary enlargement with lack of/delayed tooth eruption. Cone-beam CT showed a left alveolar expansile lesion with dystrophic-appearing, ill-defined trabeculation oriented along the y-axis, well-maintained cortical plates, missing posterior secondary teeth, expansion into the maxillary sinus with inferior displacement of the nasal fossa, and hypoplasia of the left maxillary antrum. A clinical impression of a fibro-osseous lesion such as fibrous dysplasia or juvenile active ossifying fibroma was made by the surgeon.

A 6-year-old boy presented on illness day 4 with daily fevers up to 102°F, sore throat, dysuria, dark urine, and over the preceding days developed jaundice, a maculopapular truncal rash, and an erythematous tongue with papules. He was afebrile in the ED (99.7°F) on unknown acetaminophen, pulse 115/min, blood pressure 98/64 mm Hg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO₂ 97% on room air. Examination showed a well-appearing child with an erythematous, papular tongue; icteric and injected sclerae with bulbar conjunctival injection sparing the limbus; no significant cervical lymphadenopathy; diffuse jaundice; an erythematous maculopapular rash on face and trunk sparing palms and soles; normal heart and lung exams; non-tender abdomen; and normal neurologic findings. Laboratory studies revealed WBC 16.3 K/μL (86% neutrophils), platelets 369 K/μL, total bilirubin 5.4 mg/dL with conjugated bilirubin 2.9 mg/dL, AST 59 U/L, ALT 169 U/L, ALP 425 U/L, and urinalysis with trace protein, large bilirubin, 3–5 RBCs, trace hemolysis, 3–5 WBCs. A rapid throat streptococcal test was negative.

A 49-year-old woman with ER-positive/PR-negative/HER2-negative breast cancer metastatic to bone and liver began a clinical trial on January 3, 2019 (cycle 1 day 1) of fulvestrant (500 mg IM), palbociclib (125 mg orally daily for 21 days of a 28-day cycle), and erdafitinib (8 mg orally daily). Baseline liver function tests were within normal limits.

On cycle 1 day 3, she developed increasing fatigue and nausea. On cycle 1 day 4, she had watery, pale diarrhea. On cycle 1 day 5, she experienced intense crampy right upper quadrant and mid-epigastric pain. She stopped the oral trial medications on day 7, and her symptoms largely improved, leaving only intermittent right upper quadrant discomfort.

On cycle 1 day 8, laboratory studies revealed:  
• AST 698 U/L (17.5× upper limit of normal)  
• ALT 893 U/L (16.2× upper limit of normal)  
• Alkaline phosphatase 336 U/L (2.2× upper limit of normal)  
• Total bilirubin within normal limits  

She had no fever, jaundice, altered mental status, or bleeding diathesis. She was admitted for further evaluation.  
– Hepatitis A panel, hepatitis B panel, hepatitis C IgG, hepatitis D antibody, CMV, and EBV were all negative.  
– Acetaminophen and ethanol levels were within normal limits.  
– Antinuclear antibody and F-actin IgG were negative.  
– Abdominal ultrasound showed no evidence of cholecystolithiasis or biliary obstruction.

A 38-year-old man presented with syncope preceded by chest and epigastric pain without fever or dyspnea. Over the past year he had three syncopal episodes, at rest and while standing, sometimes following intense epigastric pain, as well as presyncopal events. He was an active smoker (20 pack-years) with no other cardiovascular risk factors. Holter monitoring performed before presentation showed recurrent daytime asystolic pauses of up to 4 seconds, accompanied by chest pain and a feeling of faintness. In the emergency department, physical examination, electrocardiography, echocardiography, and laboratory tests including high-sensitivity troponin were normal, and hemodynamic parameters were stable. A lateral chest radiograph revealed a giant bulla in the left posterior mediastinum.

A 54-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of cough, dyspnea at rest, chest discomfort, and backache. Two years earlier she had undergone right hemithyroidectomy; current thyroid‐function tests were normal. A posteroanterior chest radiograph showed an opacity in the right hemithorax. Electrocardiography and echocardiography were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a 7.3×5.5×9.3-cm, well-circumscribed, subpleural rim-enhancing cystic lesion in the posterior mediastinum without daughter cysts; the radiologist’s leading diagnosis was a bronchogenic cyst. In the setting of resource limitations (no serologic testing), a provisional diagnosis of echinococcosis was considered. On the night of admission, she developed one day of worsening right chest pain, fever to 38°C, and dyspnea. Examination revealed temperature 38°C, pulse 131/min, blood pressure 93/63 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, oxygen saturation 83% on room air, right-sided dullness to percussion, and decreased breath sounds. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (11.37×10^3/μL) with 73.8% neutrophils. Intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g) was administered. During the infusion she became drowsy, developed wheezing, and had increased shortness of breath. She received nebulized ipratropium bromide, supplemental oxygen, intravenous hydrocortisone, intramuscular promethazine, and a fluid bolus. An urgent chest radiograph then demonstrated rupture of the right mediastinal cyst.

A 31-year-old man was brought to a level I trauma center after sustaining a stab wound to his left knee while intoxicated. On arrival, he was stuporous, hypothermic, and acidotic (pH 6.772; lactic acid 27 mmol/L). Computed tomography angiography showed transection of the left popliteal artery and vein. Within 3 hours of injury, he underwent surgical end-to-end anastomosis of both vessels and a prophylactic anterolateral fasciotomy. Intraoperatively, he received 14 units of packed red blood cells and 11 units of fresh frozen plasma, with systolic blood pressure maintained above 80 mmHg.

Immediately postoperatively, his blood pressure and hemoglobin were stable, but aspartate aminotransferase (AST) was 712 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 612 U/L, and prothrombin time was prolonged to 44.5%, necessitating further plasma transfusion. On postoperative day 1, hemoglobin and acid–base status normalized (pH 7.368; lactic acid 2.3 mmol/L), but thrombocytopenia persisted (platelets 68×10^3/μL), prothrombin time was 32.3%, and AST/ALT rose to 1,655/1,465 U/L. The calf remained soft and well perfused, and he was given aggressive hydration and hydrocortisone.

On postoperative day 2, laboratory studies showed AST 8,600 U/L, ALT 6,690 U/L, creatine phosphokinase 26,817 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase 7,398 U/L, interleukin-6 178 pg/mL, ferritin 41,079 ng/mL, C-reactive protein 3.55 mg/dL, D-dimer >20 μg/mL fibrinogen equivalent units, persistent thrombocytopenia, and coagulopathy.  
  
Given the rapidly worsening organ dysfunction and inflammatory markers, a decision was made to proceed with plasmapheresis.

A 56-year-old non-smoking Chinese woman presented with a 45-day history of cough, sputum production, and throat discomfort, without fever, chest pain, or congestion. Examination revealed multiple pale, dome-shaped papules on the cheeks, eyelids, axillae, and back. She first developed a right-sided pneumothorax at age 36, was treated with tube thoracostomy, and had recurrences at ages 48 and 50; at the third event, her right lung was 40% collapsed, prompting surgical resection. Intraoperatively, multiple thin-walled bullae (0.1–3.0 cm) and a >10 cm fissural bulla were resected; histology showed cysts lined by CK7-positive, TTF-1–positive pneumocytes with internal septa. 

She reported frequent illnesses during childhood. Her mother and maternal aunt both had pulmonary bullae and recurrent pneumothoraxes; her mother died of renal cancer at age 71. A 31-year-old daughter and a 69-year-old cousin had no similar findings. 

Chest CT demonstrated numerous round to oval cysts with thin, uniform walls, predominantly in the lung bases, including a dominant 8.4 × 5.1 cm cyst anterior to the heart. A new 2.8 × 2.3 cm solid lesion with irregular margins and adjacent pleural thickening was noted in the posterior basal segment of the right lower lobe. Ultrasound-guided percutaneous biopsy of this lesion revealed fibroblastic proliferation with plasma cells and lymphocytes, negative staining for CEA, IgG4, IgG, and ALK. Abdominal ultrasound showed no renal masses, and thyroid ultrasound revealed multiple nodules.

A 57-year-old woman with a history of well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus presented to the outpatient clinic in early April 2021 after awakening with left-sided facial weakness. She reported no fever, headache, or other systemic or neurological symptoms. Neurological examination confirmed an isolated left peripheral facial palsy (House–Brackmann grade 4 of 6); the remainder of the cranial nerve and neurologic examination was normal. A clinical diagnosis of Bell’s palsy was made, and she was prescribed oral prednisolone, 60 mg daily for 5 days followed by a tapering regimen. Three days later, she developed severe neuropathic pain in her left shoulder and upper arm corresponding to the C5 dermatome. No new neurologic deficits were observed, and no additional blood tests or imaging studies were performed. Over the next five days, the neuropathic pain intensified and then gradually subsided, while the facial palsy remained unchanged.

A 34-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a 2-week history of acute confusion, imbalance, headache, and dizziness. He denied fever, loss of consciousness, seizures, or sensory loss and had no history of trauma or similar prior episodes. He received two doses of the Sputnik V COVID-19 vaccine, with the second dose 3 weeks before presentation. 

On examination, he was hemodynamically stable and afebrile but confused, disoriented to person and place, able to follow only one-step commands, and occasionally provided irrelevant answers. There were no signs of skin or joint involvement. Neurologic examination revealed bilateral proptosis; cranial nerves, sensation, muscle power, and tone were otherwise normal in all four limbs. Gait was ataxic.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count. Viral PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2, adenovirus, HSV-1 and ‑2, EBV, CMV, and HIV was negative. CSF analysis demonstrated lymphocytic pleocytosis and mildly elevated protein; cultures, cytology, oligoclonal bands, antibodies to HSV, syphilis antigens, cryptococcal antigen, and VZV were all negative. Autoimmune serologies (thyroid antibodies, ANCA, rheumatoid factor, anticardiolipin) and vitamin levels were normal. SARS-CoV-2 IgG was positive. 

A brain MRI with FLAIR sequencing revealed patchy hyperintense signal along the ependymal surfaces of the lateral, third, and fourth ventricles, the periaqueductal gray matter, thalamus, corpus callosum, and optic chiasm. A cervical spine MRI was normal.

A 37-year-old man presented 24 hours after the onset of intermittent diplopia and dizziness. He had no past medical history and took no medications. On neurologic examination he was fully conscious, well oriented, and cooperative, with no motor, coordination, or sensory deficits. Neuro-ophthalmologic evaluation showed intact visual acuity, color vision, and pupillary reflexes; slit-lamp and fundus examinations were normal. Confrontation testing revealed no visual-field defects, and there was orthophoria in primary gaze. Conjugate voluntary saccades and pursuit movements of downgaze were absent bilaterally; the globes could not move below the horizontal meridian, and the patient compensated by rotating his head to look downward. The oculocephalic reflex was preserved, indicating a supranuclear downgaze palsy.

Cerebral magnetic resonance imaging on diffusion-weighted (DWI) and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences demonstrated high signal intensity in the bilateral paramedian thalami. Coronal T2-weighted and axial FLAIR sequences showed hyperintensity in the rostral midbrain. 

Large-panel laboratory studies—including complete blood count, prothrombotic workup, hepatic and renal panels, hemoglobin electrophoresis, glycosylated hemoglobin, autoantibody tests, syphilis serology, hepatitis and HIV tests—were all normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal. Electrocardiogram, Doppler ultrasonography of the cervical arteries, transesophageal echocardiography, and Holter monitoring were unremarkable.

A 14-year-old previously healthy boy presented with a 5-day history of fever and sore throat, followed 3 days later by vertigo, nausea, and vomiting. On admission, his oropharynx was hyperemic, and he had vesicles on his upper lip. He was lethargic, with gait unsteadiness, nystagmus, and absence of the vomiting reflex. He was started on acyclovir (30 mg/kg/day) and ceftriaxone (4 g/day). Over the next 2 days, he developed tetraparesis, pyramidal signs, impaired consciousness, and respiratory failure, and he required tracheal intubation. MRI of the brain with FLAIR, DWI, and ADC sequences showed symmetric hyperintense lesions on FLAIR in the inferior, middle, and superior cerebellar peduncles, with corresponding diffusion restriction on DWI and hypointensity on ADC maps. The remaining brain structures were normal. CSF analysis revealed 42 cells/mm³ (89% lymphocytes), glucose 86 mg/dL, and protein 57 mg/dL.

A 2-year-8-month-old girl was referred for persistent abdominal distension over the past 18 months. During the previous year, she was noted to have anemia and thrombocytopenia on routine blood tests, with normal liver and renal function and normal hemoglobin chain analysis. On examination, she appeared well but had massive splenomegaly extending into the low hypogastric region and hepatomegaly; growth and neurologic examination were unremarkable.

Laboratory evaluation showed hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, platelets 62 000/µL, and a normal white-cell count. Peripheral-blood smear demonstrated anisopoikilocytosis without immature forms. Immunoglobulin levels and lymphocyte immunophenotyping were within normal limits for age. Infectious studies, including hepatotropic viruses, leishmania, salmonella, brucella, and borrelia, were negative. An autoantibody panel (ANA, LKM1-2, ASMA, AMA) was unremarkable for age.Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT and MRI confirmed massive splenomegaly and revealed a solitary focal lesion in the liver.

A 40-year-old man from a rural area in Tunisia, with no prior medical history and a farming occupation, presented with 4 months of dull left upper-quadrant abdominal pain and a sensation of heaviness, without systemic symptoms. He was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Abdominal examination revealed splenomegaly. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 14.5 g/dL, platelets 280 000/mm^3, prothrombin time 12 s, C-reactive protein 3 mg/L, ALT 25 U/L, AST 30 U/L, and total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL. An indirect hemagglutination test for Echinococcus species was positive (titer >160). A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the thorax and abdomen demonstrated a solitary 10 cm cystic lesion of the spleen without other visceral involvement.

A 63-year-old man presented with 6 months of progressive blurring of vision, hearing loss, and left-sided trigeminal neuralgia. He was an agriculturist who reared sheep and cattle and had a pet dog. On examination, there was wasting of the left temporalis muscle and sensory loss in the distributions of the left V1, V2, and V3 divisions of the trigeminal nerve. No other motor or sensory deficits were noted. Routine hematological and biochemical parameters, chest radiography, and abdominal ultrasonography were normal. Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI of the brain showed a large, heterogeneously enhancing mass arising from the central skull base, predominantly at the left petro-spheno-clival junction and petrous apex, with intracranial extension and infiltration of the surrounding bone. A diagnosis of chondrosarcoma was considered, and the patient was scheduled for surgical decompression.

A 25-year-old woman with nonmetastatic round cell sarcoma of the mandible began neoadjuvant chemotherapy consisting of ifosfamide and etoposide 14 days before presentation. Two days ago, her family noted nonsensical texting and verbal outbursts, and by the following day she was refusing commands and then became unresponsive to verbal or physical stimuli. She took no other medications and had no acute substance use; her last cannabis oil exposure was months earlier.

On arrival, her vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 24 × 10^3/μL, calcium 10.2 mg/dL, creatinine 0.83 mg/dL, normal liver-function tests, and a negative urine drug screen. Neurologic examination revealed a fixed gaze without tracking, a mild tremor, and occasional grunting. A noncontrast head CT and brain MRI were unremarkable. EEG demonstrated diffuse slowing, consistent with encephalopathy.

Haloperidol, lorazepam, and scheduled olanzapine were administered without symptomatic improvement. Psychiatry and neurology were consulted; conversion disorder was excluded, and a diagnosis of encephalopathy was made. Oncology was then asked to evaluate infectious, oncologic, and medication-related causes of her encephalopathy.

A 3-year-old Caucasian girl was referred for surgical repair of an incidentally discovered large secundum atrial septal defect. She was asymptomatic, with a soft systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border and an oxygen saturation of 99% on room air. Chest radiography showed cardiomegaly and pulmonary plethora. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a 14×12 mm multi-fenestrated atrial septal defect with significant left-to-right shunting, right ventricular volume overload with normal function, no pulmonary hypertension, no valvular pathology, and no intracardiac masses.

Under median sternotomy, cardiopulmonary bypass was established (34 °C) with aortic and bicaval cannulation and vacuum-assisted venous drainage. The aorta was cross-clamped, and cold blood cardioplegia was administered. During right atriotomy, air was noted in the inferior vena cava cannula, which was repositioned before completing the pericardial patch closure of the defect. After de-airing and cross-clamp release, the heart was weaned from bypass uneventfully.

A routine post-CPB transesophageal echocardiogram revealed a new, well-defined, round heterogeneous mass (2×3 cm) arising from the left atrial wall near the anterior mitral leaflet and below the pulmonary veins, with no internal flow on color Doppler. The mass was freely mobile and pendulated toward the anterolateral commissure, without causing mitral stenosis or regurgitation.

A 48-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of a central scotoma in both eyes. Six days earlier she had been diagnosed clinically with influenza A by throat-swab antigen testing and had a fever of 38.5 °C. On presentation, her visual acuity was 20/16 bilaterally. Pupils were reactive and slit-lamp and fundus examinations were unremarkable; no inflammatory cells were seen in the anterior chambers or vitreous. Goldmann perimetry revealed a central scotoma in each eye. Fundus photography was normal, and fluorescein angiography showed no leakage in the retina or optic discs. Brain MRI showed no evidence of optic neuropathy. Spectral-domain OCT demonstrated focal disruption of the ellipsoid-zone line in the macular areas of both eyes.

A 69-year-old man with hypertension (on lisinopril and metoprolol), hyperlipidemia (on simvastatin), and treated prostate cancer presented with continuous right lower abdominal pain and signs of peritonitis. He had quit smoking six months earlier and had no allergies. On admission, the white-cell count was 16.2×10^9/L and C-reactive protein was 231 mg/L. Abdominal ultrasound and contrast CT scan showed a perforated appendix with two appendicoliths and two small abscesses; the abscesses were deemed too small for percutaneous drainage. Intravenous amoxicillin/clavulanic acid was started, and laparoscopic appendectomy confirmed purulent peritonitis. A free appendicolith was removed, the appendix was stapled off at the cecal base, and local irrigation performed. Postoperatively, leukocyte count and CRP declined slowly. On postoperative day 8, the CRP increased again and hemoglobin fell from 14.5 g/dL to 11.3 g/dL. CT angiography revealed a new right lower abdominal abscess and multiple aneurysmal dilatations arising from the medial colic artery, pancreaticoduodenal artery, several intrahepatic branches, and the splenic artery, all surrounded by a large infiltrating mass.

An 10-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of progressive developmental regression. She was born at term to first-degree-related healthy parents, with normal early milestones: sitting by 6 months, walking by 12 months, babbling by 9 months, first words by 10 months, two-word associations by 18 months, and toilet training by age 2. After age 2, her language advanced slowly; she never formed sentences, and toilet control was lost around age 5.

Upon school entry, her teacher noted poor language, impaired attention, and social withdrawal. Between ages 5 and 6, she experienced three fever-associated episodes of extreme fear followed by falls to her knees without loss of consciousness; these were treated as febrile seizures despite normal interictal EEGs. Following these episodes, she lost previously acquired language and toileting skills and developed severe agitation, restlessness, and impulsivity. Trials of methylphenidate, risperidone, and cyamemazine failed to improve her behavior.

At age 7, formal behavioral observations and assessments revealed limited speech (only a few words), inability to follow instructions or imitate, poor eye contact, lack of symbolic play, rapid shifts between low-grade repetitive activities, pica, induced vomiting, and gastro-esophageal reflux. The Childhood Autism Rating Scale score was 44.5 (severe), and on the Brunet-Lézine Scale her developmental ages ranged from 14 months (language, socialization) to 42 months (motor skills). 

Physical examination showed no dysmorphic features; growth parameters were within normal limits; auditory and visual functions were intact. EEG showed no epileptiform activity. Brain MRI at age 8 revealed thinning of the posterior corpus callosum and bilateral temporal lobe T2 hyperintensities consistent with gliosis.

An 86-year-old male farmer with transfusion-dependent myelodysplastic syndrome, coronary artery disease with coronary stents, atrial fibrillation, and presumed amiodarone-induced interstitial lung disease on 2 L/min oxygen presented with several months of intermittent nonmassive hemoptysis and one week of progressive dyspnea and fatigue. His hemoptysis persisted despite discontinuation of dual antiplatelet therapy, and his anemia required transfusions beyond expectations for his myelodysplastic syndrome.

On examination, he was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and had an oxygen saturation of 94% on 2 L/min oxygen. Breath sounds revealed fine bibasilar crackles; he had bilateral lower extremity pitting edema. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 21.1 × 10^3/µL with a left shift, hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL with microcytosis, creatinine 1.31 mg/dL, NT-proBNP 5,375 pg/mL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate >100 mm/hr, and C-reactive protein 23.2 mg/dL. CT of the chest demonstrated bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities with central predominance and a small right pleural effusion.

He was treated with diuresis for presumed volume overload and empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics but continued to deteriorate, requiring 6 L/min oxygen; arterial blood gas revealed a PaO₂ of 38 mm Hg. Further history elicited late-onset Raynaud’s phenomena, occasional arthralgias without swelling, and oral sicca symptoms; he denied photosensitivity, rashes, ulcers, or skin thickening. His sister has a history of SLE. Serologic testing showed an ANA titer 1:160 homogeneous, low C4, normal C3, anti–double-stranded DNA 194 IU/mL, anti-Ro (SSA) 6.0, anti-La (SSB) >8.0, and negative anti-Smith, anti-RNP, antichromatin, proteinase 3, myeloperoxidase, and anti–glomerular basement membrane antibodies.

An 18-year-old man with a history of Rothmund–Thomson syndrome diagnosed at age two presented with acute right mid-leg pain after cutting to kick a soccer ball. Four years earlier, he had sustained a right tibial fracture during play; radiographs then showed mild tibial deformity from the healed fracture and a mildly displaced, comminuted mid-diaphyseal tibial fracture with focal anterior cortical thickening at the fracture site. The fracture was treated with closed reduction and casting. Serial radiographs over 13 months demonstrated delayed and incomplete union of the tibial fracture. At 13-month follow-up, radiographs of the left tibia—performed for a painless bump at the mid-shin—revealed focal anterior cortical thickening of the mid-diaphysis without a fracture line or lytic lesion.

Approximately four years later, he presented with a left olecranon fracture sustained during a soccer fall 3.5 weeks earlier. Radiographs showed a mildly displaced subacute olecranon fracture with early cortical remodeling but more osteolysis than expected for the reported fracture age. A bone biopsy of the olecranon was performed and was negative for neoplasm and infection; the fracture was fixed with tension-band wiring. Two-month follow-up radiographs showed early remodeling without bridging bone formation.

Five years after the olecranon injury, he again presented with acute right mid-leg pain after an awkward landing playing soccer. Radiographs demonstrated a mildly displaced acute fracture through the previous right tibial fracture site. MRI of the right leg with and without contrast was obtained to exclude an underlying malignancy; no bone tumor was seen. Radiographs of the left tibia and fibula were also obtained for a long-standing asymptomatic bump, revealing increased focal anterior mid-tibial cortical thickening and a stress fracture through this area, along with an incidental old nonunited transverse fracture of the left lateral malleolus. The right tibial fracture was treated with closed reduction and casting; the left tibial stress fracture was managed nonoperatively.

A 58-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of severe lower right abdominal pain, fever, and diarrhoea. He denied nausea or vomiting and had maintained normal oral intake. His medical history was notable only for hypertension, and he had no prior abdominal surgeries. He consumed alcohol occasionally and was a smoker.

On physical examination, his abdomen was soft but severely tender in the right iliac fossa, with a positive Rovsing sign. Vital signs were within normal limits, including a normal body temperature. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 9.5 × 10^9/L (reference range, 3.0–10.0 × 10^9/L) and a C-reactive protein level of 31 mg/L (reference range, 0–5 mg/L).

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis in the portal venous phase revealed several markedly inflamed diverticula at the medial aspect of the appendix, surrounded by fat stranding. The appendix itself was not distended and had a normal thin wall. There was no fluid collection. Several reactive lymph nodes were noted in the draining mesentery. Mild, uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulosis was also present.

An 8-week-old male infant, born at 33 weeks’ gestation, presented with a history of gastroesophageal reflux, persistent emesis, and poor weight gain. His birth weight was 1.87 kg; on admission he weighed 1.98 kg. He was exclusively breastfed but “spit up one-third to one-half of every feed” despite reflux precautions and omeprazole started two weeks earlier. 

An outpatient abdominal ultrasound performed for suspected hypertrophic pyloric stenosis showed echogenic foci in the liver suggestive of portal venous gas. On arrival to the hospital, he was mildly hypothermic. Laboratory results revealed a total bilirubin of 3.0 mg/dL and a direct bilirubin of 0.4 mg/dL; all other labs were within normal limits. 

A repeat abdominal ultrasound showed a normal-appearing pyloric sphincter with free passage of gastric contents into the duodenum, but also demonstrated multiple echogenic foci consistent with air within the liver, portal vein branches, and the stomach wall. The patient’s physical examination was otherwise benign, and an extensive sepsis workup, including blood cultures, was negative. 

To evaluate for an upper GI structural anomaly, a fluoroscopic upper GI series was performed and revealed unobstructed contrast flow through the upper gastrointestinal tract with no evidence of malrotation. Newborn metabolic screening tests were negative.

An 18-year-old woman, 38 weeks pregnant, was referred for evaluation of oral lesions of 2 months’ duration. She reported pain on eating but deferred treatment until after delivery. Examination of the oral cavity revealed exophytic yellowish pustular lesions with an erythematous background and areas of hemorrhage in a “snail track” pattern, affecting the floor of the mouth, buccal and labial mucosa, palate, lips, gingiva, and tongue. On the skin, yellowish crusts surrounded by erythema were observed in the groin, thigh, and on a finger. Laboratory studies showed eosinophilia (10%, 834/mm3) and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 50 mm/hr. Twenty days postpartum, an incisional biopsy of a lower-lip lesion was performed. Microscopic examination demonstrated pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with widespread eosinophilic and neutrophilic infiltration, acantholysis with intraepithelial cleft formation, and intraepithelial and subepithelial pustules containing neutrophils and eosinophils.

A 40-year-old man presented with rapid onset of pain behind his left eye during sexual intercourse, followed by drooping of his left eyelid. Vital signs were normal. Physical examination was unremarkable. Neurologic examination revealed left semiptosis, enophthalmos, and miosis without facial anhidrosis. Ophthalmologic evaluation showed normal visual acuity and intact fundi bilaterally. There were no carotid bruits. He had a 20–pack-year smoking history and denied alcohol or drug use. Cranial MRI demonstrated no acute ischemic lesions on diffusion-weighted imaging. On T1-weighted fat-suppressed MRI, a hyperintense signal was noted in the cervical and petrous segments of the left internal carotid artery. MR angiography showed focal narrowing of the C1 and C2 segments of the left internal carotid artery. Routine laboratory tests and markers of vasculitis were normal.

A 66-year-old man with a history of Gleason score 8 (4 + 4) prostate adenocarcinoma treated with radiotherapy and hormonal therapy presented in September 2017 after two episodes of generalized tonic–clonic seizures followed by postictal confusion. His prostate-specific antigen level at that time was 1.53 ng/mL. He reported new memory and concentration difficulties and a progressive depressive syndrome starting after the first seizure. 

On initial examination, vital signs were stable; neurologic examination was notable for mild confusion but no focal deficits. Standard laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were unremarkable. Noncontrast head CT and brain MRI showed no acute abnormalities. 

Levetiracetam was started but soon discontinued owing to poor seizure control, and the patient was readmitted for recurrent generalized seizures. During hospitalization, he developed confusion, slurred speech, impaired comprehension, and focal seizures characterized by chewing movements, sniffing, rightward gaze deviation, and automatisms. 

An electroencephalogram demonstrated epileptiform discharges originating in the left frontotemporal region with secondary generalization. Intravenous clonazepam and levetiracetam led to clinical improvement, although interictal slow-wave foci persisted on follow-up EEG. 

Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal cell counts, glucose, and protein levels; bacterial cultures and herpes simplex virus PCR were negative. Oligoclonal immunoglobulin bands were present, and testing for anti-Hu, anti-Ri, and anti-Yo antibodies in the CSF was negative.

A 62-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes presented with 2 weeks of right shoulder pain and inability to raise her arm. She reported generalized malaise and weight loss but denied fever or trauma. On examination, the right shoulder and proximal arm were warm, tender, and had a restricted range of motion; there was no skin lesion or neurologic deficit. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 10 g/dL, a white-cell count of 9500/mm3 with 65% neutrophils and 30% lymphocytes, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 40 mm/h. Plain radiographs and MRI of the right shoulder revealed a transverse fracture of the proximal humeral shaft, 5 cm distal to the surgical neck, with no articular involvement. Given the concern for tumor or infection, a CT scan of the chest was obtained, followed by a Mantoux test and bronchoalveolar lavage. Considering the differential diagnoses, a J-needle biopsy of the lesion was performed, and tissue samples were sent for histopathological examination and AFB culture.

A 66‐year‐old Japanese woman was evaluated for a one‐year history of low‐grade fever and progressively worsening shortness of breath. She had a one‐year history of asthma treated with fluticasone/salmeterol inhalation and a tulobuterol patch. She was a non‐smoker and took no other medications. On examination, her temperature was normal, oxygen saturation was 94% on room air, and she had bilateral wheezes and coarse crackles at the right middle and left basal lung fields. Laboratory studies showed a white‐cell count of 18 840/µL with 62.3% eosinophils and an IgE level of 1791 IU/mL. Comprehensive metabolic panel and urinalysis were unremarkable. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed pH 7.432, PCO2 36.5 mmHg, PO2 60.7 mmHg, and HCO3− 23.9 mmol/L. Chest radiography demonstrated infiltrates in the right middle and left upper and lower lung zones. A chest CT scan showed bilateral homogeneous consolidation with subpleural predominance.

An man in his 80s (height 148 cm, weight 50 kg) with hypertension and a history of asymptomatic cerebral infarction (on aspirin) underwent surgical excision of extramammary Paget's disease under general anesthesia. Preoperative ECG showed complete right bundle branch block; routine labs were unremarkable. Anesthesia was induced with propofol, fentanyl, remifentanil, and rocuronium, and maintained with sevoflurane, remifentanil, and intermittent rocuronium. Intraoperative hemodynamics and oxygenation remained stable. Surgery lasted 2 h 49 min. After discontinuation of anesthetics, the patient opened his eyes at an end‐tidal sevoflurane concentration of 0.1%–0.2%, received sugammadex, and was extubated. Minutes later, his level of consciousness declined to a Glasgow Coma Scale score of E1V1M1, with stable respiratory status. Naloxone was given without improvement. Body temperature was 37.0 °C. Blood gas analysis showed normal pH and electrolytes, and blood glucose was 110 mg/dL. New right conjugate eye deviation was noted. Head CT and MRI revealed no new infarction or hemorrhage. There were no respiratory or circulatory abnormalities, and he was transferred urgently to the ICU for close observation.

A 75-year-old man with locally advanced pancreatic adenocarcinoma, deemed unresectable on CT, received two cycles of mFOLFOX (oxaliplatin, leucovorin, infusional 5-FU) followed by one cycle of FOLFIRINOX (oxaliplatin, irinotecan, leucovorin, infusional 5-FU). Several days after the second cycle, he began having episodes of hypertensive crisis (systolic 180 mm Hg, diastolic 100 mm Hg) controlled with amlodipine, irbesartan, and hydrochlorothiazide. After the third cycle, he became lethargic and disoriented to place and time.  
On examination, his blood pressure was 180/100 mm Hg, heart rate 110 bpm, and temperature 38 °C. Laboratory studies showed a normal white blood cell count (4,100/μL), elevated C-reactive protein (90 mg/L), and mild hyponatremia (129 mEq/L). He had intermittent shaking of the left upper and lower extremities, consistent with focal seizures.  
A lumbar puncture yielded cerebrospinal fluid negative for malignant cells, bacterial cultures, virological panels (including HSV, VZV, EBV, CMV, JC, BK, adenovirus, influenza), and fungal and mycobacterial studies. He was started empirically on meropenem, vancomycin, acyclovir, and anidulafungin.  
The following day, he had horizontal and vertical nystagmus and no response to painful stimuli. Brain MRI showed bilateral T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in the thalamus, hypothalamus, fibers of the reticular formation, anterior cerebellar vermis, and mild edema of the left parahippocampal gyrus, with no evidence of brain metastases.

A 32-year-old Caucasian female nurse working in a private clinic in northern Italy presented on March 13, 2020, with mild fatigue and an intensely itchy erythematous rash. The rash began as small folliculocentric papules on her hands, feet, forearms, legs, and the back of her ears, and then spread to her trunk and lower limbs, sparing her face, scalp, and abdomen. Pruritus was severe at night, disturbing sleep. She had no chronic illnesses, no history of atopy or autoimmune disease, no recent medication use, and no known exposure to new soaps or cosmetics.

Seven days later, she developed an axillary temperature of 37.5 °C and experienced three to four episodes per day of watery diarrhea. On remote telephone evaluation, her general practitioner noted her high epidemiological risk as a healthcare worker and suspected COVID-19. The patient was advised to self-isolate, maintain hydration, take paracetamol 500 mg as needed, and begin cetirizine 10 mg once daily for pruritus. Follow-up calls were scheduled every three days. Over the following week, she developed a dry cough, her fever remained intermittent (≤ 37.5 °C), her diarrhea improved, and her rash resolved after ten days of antihistamine therapy.

A 13-year-old girl with a known history of Proteus syndrome was referred to the dermatology clinic for evaluation of a new skin lesion. The patient’s Proteus syndrome had been diagnosed in infancy based on postnatal disproportionate overgrowth of the scalp and extremities, linear verrucous epidermal nevi, and port-wine stains; genetic confirmation was not available. Four months before presentation, she noted a mildly pruritic, sharply demarcated, well-defined erythematous and scaly hyperkeratotic plaque measuring 5 × 8 cm on her left upper arm, arising on a preexisting linear epidermal nevus. Initial evaluation at a local clinic in an area endemic for cutaneous leishmaniasis included a smear that was reported positive, and she received two sessions of intralesional meglumine antimoniate without improvement; subsequent cryotherapy also failed. On examination at our clinic, the plaque was nonulcerated, nonbleeding, and nontender; nails and mucosa were normal. A punch biopsy was obtained. The primary differential diagnoses included leishmaniasis, mycotic infection, and mycobacterial infection.

A 64-year-old man presented with 4 months of vague upper abdominal pain and discomfort. Fourteen years earlier, he had undergone left radical nephrectomy and splenectomy for renal cell carcinoma (pT2N0M0) and had defaulted further follow-up. His medical history included well-controlled epilepsy on levetiracetam; otherwise it was unremarkable. Family history was noncontributory. He was 168 cm tall, weighed 72 kg (BMI 25.5 kg/m2), and his examination, including abdominal examination, was normal.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen revealed a contrast-enhancing focal lesion in the region of the pancreatic tail and a smaller enhancing nodule in the anterior peripancreatic tissue. Magnetic resonance imaging of the upper abdomen showed a lobulated malpositioned pancreatic tail simulating a mass; the smaller lesion was suggested to be a lymph node or splenunculus. There was no evidence of recurrence in the left renal bed or liver metastases.

A 12‐year‐old girl presented with a 10‐day history of intermittent, crampy abdominal pain that intensified over the preceding week and was accompanied by non‐bilious vomiting the night before presentation. She denied urinary symptoms, constipation, diarrhea, fever, weight loss, or recent travel. She had previously undergone ultrasonography, CT scans, and routine blood tests at three other hospitals, all of which were reported as negative, and appendicitis was ruled out. On examination, she had a stooped posture and difficulty walking due to pain. She was afebrile with normal heart rate and blood pressure. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the right iliac fossa with a positive McBurney’s sign but no rebound tenderness or guarding; Rovsing’s, psoas, and obturator signs were negative. The rest of the examination, including genitourinary and gynecological assessments, was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 6.9 × 10^9/L and a CRP level of less than 4 mg/L; liver and kidney function tests were normal. Urinalysis was within normal limits, and pregnancy test was negative. Abdominal ultrasonography did not visualize the appendix and revealed no abnormalities. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated minimal endometrial fluid, an appendix of average caliber measuring 5.2 mm in diameter, and mild hepatomegaly, without any appendiceal wall thickening, periappendiceal fat stranding, or appendicolith.

A 32-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of a painful swelling in the anteromedial mid-third of his right arm. The swelling was insidious in onset, non-progressive, and tender, worsening with heavy lifting or twisting movements and relieved by rest and analgesics. He reported no trauma, fever, or similar swellings elsewhere; his medical history was unremarkable. He was an occasional smoker and drinker, ate meat, and had no family history of similar complaints.

On examination, there was a firm, tender swelling without overlying skin changes or increased local temperature. The lesion did not bulge with muscle contraction, and the skin was freely mobile.

Plain radiographs of the arm were normal apart from a soft-tissue shadow. Ultrasonography revealed a 7-mm cystic lesion with a central hyperechoic focus suggestive of either granuloma or cysticercosis. To exclude systemic involvement, a brain MRI, fundus examination, and stool examination were obtained and were all negative. MRI of the arm demonstrated a 7.7 × 4.8 mm lesion in the anteromedial muscle with surrounding edema, interpreted as a granuloma. In view of the patient’s severe pain and localized pathology, excision of the mass was planned, with medical therapy deferred until histopathology.

A 54-year-old woman presented with progressive severe dyspnea over several weeks. She had a history of clinical hyperthyroidism diagnosed in 2003, for which she had been prescribed tiamazole, beta-blockers, and an ACE inhibitor but had stopped all medications 2 months earlier. Since then, she developed asthenia, tremors, weight loss of 10 kg, and worsening dyspnea.

On examination, she was in semi-orthopneic posture with generalized anasarca, marked peripheral edema, ascites, and bilateral pleural effusions. Her pulse was irregular at 110 beats/min, and ECG showed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a markedly dilated, hyperkinetic right ventricle with paradoxical interventricular septal motion, tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion of 28 mm, and severe tricuspid regurgitation in the absence of elevated pulmonary artery pressures. The left ventricle contracted normally, and there was a small pericardial effusion.

Laboratory tests showed suppressed TSH (< 0.01 mU/ml), elevated free T3 (32.53 pg/ml) and free T4 (12.75 ng/dl), and a BNP of 1420 pg/ml. To exclude an intracardiac shunt, contrast transesophageal echocardiography and CT angiography were performed and were negative for interatrial defects or anomalous pulmonary venous return.

A 39-year-old man presented with acute abdominal pain, fever, and chills. Ten years earlier, he underwent a renal transplant for end-stage renal failure secondary to amyloidosis and had been maintained on prednisolone, tacrolimus, and mycophenolate sodium. Ten months ago, he was treated for presumed pneumonia after pleuritic chest pain, fever, and weight loss; TB workup (chest radiograph, chest CT, blood cultures, urinary antigen, tuberculin skin test) was inconclusive. He continued to experience night sweats and weight loss. His father had pulmonary tuberculosis treated with rifampicin seven years earlier.

On examination, he appeared septic with a temperature of 38.3°C, blood pressure 130/80 mmHg, heart rate 96/min, respiratory rate 28/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. The abdomen was diffusely rigid with rebound tenderness. Digital rectal examination revealed painful rectal ulcers. Laboratory tests showed WBC 14,900 cells/mm3, hematocrit 28.7%, BUN 78 mg/dL, creatinine 3.1 mg/dL, and C-reactive protein 168 U/dL; other results were normal. A chest X-ray demonstrated subdiaphragmatic free air. Abdominal CT revealed pericecal inflammation and bowel perforation without distal obstruction.

A 55-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of chronic rhinosinusitis that failed to improve after multiple courses of intranasal corticosteroids and antibiotics. She noted persistent bilateral nasal obstruction, purulent rhinorrhea, and anosmia. 

On anterior rhinoscopy and nasal endoscopy, there was mucosal edema of both inferior turbinates, septo-turbinal synechiae, and adherent crusts throughout the nasal cavity. The remainder of the ENT and general physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed a lymphocyte count of 5500/mm^3 (reference, 1000–4000/mm^3) and a serum calcium level of 18.5 mg/dL (reference, 8.5–10.5 mg/dL); all other routine blood tests were within normal limits.

Noncontrast CT of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated irregular mucosal hypertrophy of the nasal cavity, bilateral enlargement of the inferior turbinates, and a frame-like mucosal thickening in the right maxillary sinus.

A 29-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of ten to eleven loose, nonbloody, nonmucoid stools per day and episodes of vomiting gastric contents. Forty-eight hours into his illness he developed moderate-intensity epigastric pain. He had no fever. He drank alcohol socially, denied smoking, allergies, or recent drug exposures, and had no family history of gastrointestinal disease. His surgical history included amygdalectomy, appendectomy, renal lithotomy, and a ureteral stent placement without complications. Two weeks before presentation he had received pneumococcal and influenza vaccines.

On examination, he was hemodynamically stable. He had nontender, mobile cervical lymph nodes and mild tenderness in both lower quadrants. There was no rash or joint swelling.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 13.1 × 10^3/mm^3 with 27% eosinophils (absolute eosinophil count 3,537/mm^3). Other cell lines and a basic metabolic panel were within normal limits. Stool examination identified Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites and cysts, and metronidazole with iodoquinol was started. Given persistent eosinophilia, an abdominal ultrasound was performed, revealing free fluid in both iliac fossae and pelvis and a 6-mm calculus in the lower pole of the left kidney. Ultrasound-guided paracentesis yielded an exudative fluid (albumin 1.7 g/dL; total protein 3.3 g/dL; glucose 65 mg/dL) with 4,400 cells/mm^3 of which 70% were eosinophils; cultures were negative.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed diffuse ascites, terminal ileal wall thickening, and enlarged pelvic and inguinal lymph nodes, but no mass lesions. Upper endoscopy showed a redundant esophagus with moderate mucosal thickening and diffuse gastric inflammation; the antrum, pylorus, and duodenum appeared normal. A rapid urease test for Helicobacter pylori was negative. Colonoscopy revealed normal mucosa throughout.

Duodenal and colonic biopsies demonstrated mild chronic duodenitis with a mean of 30 eosinophils per high-power field and mild chronic colitis with a mean of 24 eosinophils per high-power field. No microorganisms or histopathological features of malabsorption were identified. Serum IgE concentration was normal.

A 12-year-old boy from Quang Binh province, Vietnam, presented with a 1-week history of dry cough, two small-volume episodes of hemoptysis at home, and right-sided chest pain but no fever. He had no significant past medical history or medication use. On examination he appeared well, was afebrile, in no respiratory distress, and had diminished breath sounds over the right lung; there was no lymphadenopathy. A chest radiograph showed an opacity in the right middle lung zone. Chest CT revealed a 22×31×28 mm consolidation with surrounding ground-glass opacity at the upper edge of the right hilum. Laboratory studies demonstrated a white blood cell count of 14,500/mm³ with 13.7% eosinophils, mildly elevated C-reactive protein, negative parasite serology tests, and normal serum IgE, LDH, and uric acid levels. A percutaneous needle biopsy of the lesion was performed, and the patient was started on ceftazidime and vancomycin pending histopathologic results.

A 20-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of painless enlargement of her left breast, associated with chronic back pain. She had no personal or family history of breast or ovarian cancer. On examination, the left breast contained a large, well-circumscribed, firm mass; the right breast harbored two small, palpable nodules. There was no nipple discharge, retraction, skin changes, or palpable lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies—including β-hCG, thyroid-stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, prolactin, and liver function tests—were within normal limits.  
  
Breast ultrasound showed a heterogeneous, hypoechoic mass with circumscribed margins and no significant internal vascularity in the lateral aspect of the left breast (assigned BI-RADS category 3), along with two well-defined, hypoechoic lesions in the right breast. Chest CT confirmed a well-circumscribed, rounded mass measuring 13 × 8 cm occupying most of the left breast and two well-defined right breast nodules (largest, 2 cm).  

A differential diagnosis of benign breast tumors, including atypical fibroadenoma and phyllodes tumor, was suspected. Given the size of the lesion, surgical excision via an inferior circumareolar incision was recommended.

A 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus (30 years) and rheumatoid arthritis complicated by infective spondylodiscitis had been admitted for three months of severe right hip and lumbosacral pain. He was managed with Ayurvedic therapies, initially including Amrutotharam Kwatha and Chiriwilwadi Kwatha on a Muhurmuhu (every-2-hour) schedule, later changed to Guggulu Tiktakam Kwatha with continued frequent dosing. On the night of November 20, 2023, he developed dysuria and a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying, which progressed to inability to void by 11:00 AM on November 21, accompanied by lower abdominal pain. He was advised to drink 1 L of water. Despite this, he remained anuric. A point-of-care abdominal ultrasound at approximately 16:00 hours showed acute urinary retention with a pre-void bladder volume of 502 mL and grade 2 prostatomegaly. His serum creatinine remained unchanged from baseline.

A 67-year-old Japanese woman presented in June 2002 with a chief complaint of swelling at the left nasal alar base. She reported no intranasal or intraoral discharge, pain, history of trauma, or signs of inflammation. Her medical history was notable for restrictive lung disease and a gastric cancer resection at age 60. There was no relevant family, social, or environmental history.

On extraoral examination, there was a diffuse, non-tender swelling of the left nasal alar base; the left nasolabial fold was less distinct and the left ala appeared elevated. Intraorally, the left upper gingivolabial sulcus was swollen, with a normal mucosal surface and fluctuant, non-tender consistency; the right sulcus was normal.

A panoramic radiograph showed apical periodontitis of the left upper central incisor but no other abnormalities. Computed tomography demonstrated a well-circumscribed oval lesion measuring approximately 19 × 14 × 12 mm inferior to the left nasal alar base, with relatively homogeneous low density compared to muscle. There was no clear maxillary or septal bone absorption. A small high-density area was also noted adjacent to the right piriform aperture, but a definitive lesion could not be confirmed.

A 34-year-old Hispanic man with no significant medical history presented with a 3–4-month history of gnawing, moderate, intermittent epigastric pain that improved with meals and was associated with reflux and early satiety. He had been noted to have “low platelets” on routine labs one year earlier. He denied gastrointestinal bleeding, bruising, epistaxis, or gingival bleeding. He took no medications or supplements, had no history of rheumatologic or bleeding disorders, and denied intravenous drug use or high-risk sexual behavior. On examination, vital signs were normal, and only epigastric tenderness was present. Laboratory testing showed a platelet count of 50×10^3/µL (previously 91×10^3/µL), a positive urea breath test, and otherwise unremarkable complete blood count, lipid profile, and urinalysis. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a trace effusion between liver and diaphragm; noncontrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed no other abnormalities.

A 4-week-old male infant was brought to the emergency department with 3 days of nonbilious, nonbloody emesis after feeds, fussiness, tachypnea, and decreased urine output. He had no fever, respiratory symptoms, diarrhea, or sick contacts. He was born full-term after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery and had been well until the current illness. On examination, weight was 3.9 kg, temperature 36.5 °C, heart rate 147 bpm, blood pressure 78/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 70 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. He had mild tachypnea, mild abdominal distention, and hepatomegaly; cardiovascular and pulmonary examinations were otherwise unremarkable. An abdominal ultrasound showed no pyloric stenosis. During an attempted oral feeding trial, he developed moderate respiratory distress. Supplemental oxygen was started, and chest radiography revealed mild cardiomegaly and pulmonary edema. Capillary blood gas showed pH 6.84, PCO2 64 mmHg, HCO3 11 mEq/L, and base deficit 24. He was intubated and given two 20 mL/kg normal saline boluses. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a structurally normal heart with severely decreased biventricular systolic function (left ventricular shortening fraction 13%, normal 28–44%) and a normal end-diastolic diameter (Z score −0.6). He was transferred to the neonatal intensive care unit for dopamine and milrinone infusions. A 12-lead ECG showed sinus rhythm at 150 bpm, a short PR interval (50 ms), and a delta wave with QRS duration 110 ms, consistent with ventricular preexcitation (Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome). Due to the absence of observed tachycardia, the possibility of tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy was raised but not confirmed. Laboratory testing for inborn errors of metabolism and viral serologies was ordered to evaluate other potential causes of acute cardiomyopathy.

A 71-year-old man was referred with a 2-week history of intermittent fever, weakness, decreased appetite, and an enlarging neck mass. Two years earlier, he had a similar febrile illness that resolved with antibiotics and anti-inflammatory therapy. His history also included cataract surgery, secondary glaucoma, and an episode of acute granulomatous uveitis treated with high-dose corticosteroids. In 2023, he was diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis based on chest CT findings of fibrosis, bronchiectasis with mosaic attenuation, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy; antituberculosis therapy was discontinued after 2 weeks because of hepatotoxicity. After a 2-month stable period, his fever and anorexia recurred late in 2023. On presentation, he was subfebrile and the neck mass was no longer palpable. Laboratory evaluation showed hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL, leukocytes 11.6 × 10^3/μL, and an angiotensin-converting enzyme level of 7 U/L (reference 9–67). Chest radiography revealed mild pulmonary fibrosis. Empiric antibiotics and antipyretics failed to resolve the fever, but intravenous corticosteroid therapy led to clinical improvement. An 18F-FDG PET-CT study demonstrated widespread hypermetabolic lesions, and an advanced malignancy was suspected. A multidisciplinary team recommended tissue sampling, including thyroid surgical biopsy and cervical lymph-node fine-needle aspiration.

A 37-year-old man presented with a 14-month history of burning, painful sensations in his hands and feet that began two weeks after an upper respiratory tract infection. The symptoms were constant but worsened with activity and stress. He also noted frequent twitching of his hands and face, regular facial flushing, and disrupted sleep. He denied memory problems or abnormal sweating. His medical history included mild renal dysfunction and ongoing antibiotic therapy for cellulitis of the left elbow. He did not smoke and drank minimal alcohol.

On examination, he had generalized myokymia and fasciculations of the face, tongue, trunk, and all limbs. Muscle strength, coordination, and reflexes were normal. Pain sensation was reduced at the ankles and wrists; other sensory modalities were intact.

Electromyography showed widespread continuous semi-rhythmic doublets and triplets at low frequency with interspersed silent periods, plus fasciculations in the right tibialis anterior and opponens pollicis and some polyphasia in the tibialis anterior. Motor and sensory nerve conduction velocities were normal. Laboratory tests revealed a mildly elevated creatine kinase (474 U/L) and serum creatinine (111 µmol/L) with an eGFR of 67 mL/min/1.73 m2. Tests for anti-voltage gated potassium channel antibodies, antinuclear antibodies, anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies, and anti-Hu, anti-Yo, and anti-Ri antibodies were all negative. A CT scan of the chest was unremarkable. He experienced no relief with gabapentin but noted improved pain and sleep on amitriptyline and some further sensory improvement on lamotrigine.

A 36-year-old woman with no significant past medical history was found in her bathtub with decreased responsiveness and profound weakness. One month before admission she developed frequent headaches and blurry vision, and her family noted that she had become socially withdrawn. 

On presentation she appeared confused and dehydrated, with multiple bruises on her extremities. Vital signs were notable for a blood pressure of 207/148 mmHg and a heart rate of 110 beats per minute. 

Laboratory studies on admission revealed:  
• White blood cell count 20.5 × 10^9/L  
• Hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL  
• Platelet count 44 000/µL  
• Creatinine 7.0 mg/dL  
• Anion-gap metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis  
• Prothrombin time 11.6 sec, activated partial thromboplastin time 21.5 sec, fibrinogen 345 mg/dL  
• Elevated troponin levels without ST-segment changes on ECG

Ophthalmology evaluation attributed visual loss and color blindness to intraretinal hemorrhages. Noncontrast CT of the head showed numerous acute hypodensities in the frontal and parietal white matter. 

Further testing demonstrated lactate dehydrogenase 3720 U/L and a reticulocyte count of 4.2%. After intravenous hydration, her hemoglobin fell to 9.6 g/dL. A peripheral blood smear showed more than five schistocytes per high-power field, thrombocytopenia with large platelets, and features of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. 

These findings were concerning for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, prompting initiation of therapeutic plasmapheresis.

A male newborn, 18 hours old, third child of healthy Nigerian parents, born at 38 weeks via cesarean delivery, was noted to have abdominal distension and dysmorphic features, including brachydactyly with hypoplasia of distal fingers and nails, small dysplastic toenails, elongated palpebral fissures, and bilateral preauricular pits. Pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated; family history was unremarkable. TORCH screening and bacterial cultures were negative.  
Abdominal ultrasonography showed markedly distended intestinal loops with thin walls, and contrast enema revealed reduced colonic distensibility. On day 3, a low ileostomy was performed; intestinal biopsies confirmed congenital aganglionic megacolon. Due to ongoing high ostomy output, feeding intolerance, and dehydration, the infant required placement of a more proximal ileostomy, gastrostomy, and total parenteral nutrition via central venous catheter.  
Laboratory studies at admission were notable only for an elevated alkaline phosphatase level (1689 U/L; normal 140–500 U/L) and hyperphosphatasia. At 1 week of age, the neonate developed persistent tremors involving limbs, eyes, and trunk with associated desaturation. Electroencephalography showed a highly immature tracing; brainstem auditory evoked potentials were absent; brain ultrasonography was unremarkable.  
On day 12, brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated bilateral symmetric diffusion restriction in the superior cerebellar peduncles, dorsal mesencephalus, dorsal cerebral peduncles, and globi pallidi, along with corpus callosum thinning and increased T2 signal in the periventricular white matter. At 35 days of life, a repeat MRI showed progression to extensive cortical and subcortical white matter T2 hyperintensity and diffusion restriction in the parietal and temporal lobes and splenium of the corpus callosum. Genetic studies were initiated.

A 64-year-old African American woman with hypertension and a known heart murmur presented with 4 days of acute onset shortness of breath, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and a non-bloody cough productive of clear sputum. She also reported 1 week of fatigue, anorexia, bilateral leg swelling, and lightheadedness. She denied fever, chest pain, recent hospitalizations, new medications, or travel.  
Her home medications included hydralazine, amlodipine, losartan, metoprolol succinate, amiodarone, aspirin, gabapentin, cetirizine, trazodone, zolpidem, cyclobenzaprine, chlorzoxazone, fluticasone, docusate sodium, pantoprazole, ferrous sulfate, ibuprofen, and pravastatin.  
On examination, she was afebrile; blood pressure 158/76 mmHg; heart rate 90/min; oxygen saturation 96% on room air. She had mild respiratory distress, pale conjunctiva, and bilateral pitting lower-extremity edema. Cardiac auscultation revealed a grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex. Pulmonary examination showed bilateral diffuse coarse rales (worse on the right). The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies revealed:  
· Hemoglobin 6.9 g/dL (baseline 12 g/dL)  
· White blood cells 5.9 × 10^9/L; platelets 267 × 10^9/L  
· Serum creatinine 4.9 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL)  
· Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 124 mm/h; C-reactive protein 169 mg/L  
· Urinalysis 3+ blood, 1+ protein
