A chest radiograph showed diffuse nodular densities bilaterally, more prominent on the right. Chest CT demonstrated bilateral irregular peripheral and pleural-based nodules, asymmetric to the right. Renal ultrasound revealed a complex right renal cyst and a simple left renal cyst without hydronephrosis or calculi. Transthoracic echocardiography showed an ejection fraction of 65–70%, mild aortic stenosis, and no vegetations.

A 75-year-old woman with no smoking history and a one-year history of chronic kidney disease (estimated GFR ~10 mL/min/1.73 m2 without dialysis) was found on routine chest radiography to have an abnormality. Further workup diagnosed lung adenocarcinoma, clinical stage IIIB (cT2aN3M0). Because of her severe CKD, she received radiation therapy to mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes. Midway through a planned 50 Gy course (after 30 Gy), she developed progressive dyspnea and was admitted.

On admission:
• Oxygen saturation 90% on room air  
• Arterial blood gas: PaO2 68.2 Torr, PaCO2 18.5 Torr (room air)  
• Laboratory data: hemoglobin low, platelets low; LDH 478 IU/L; D-dimer 31.2 μg/mL; BNP 129.5 pg/mL  
• Non–contrast chest CT: mild dilation of pulmonary arteries, patchy mosaic attenuation of lung parenchyma, and a 3-cm mass in the left lingual lobe (known primary)  
• Because of renal failure, contrast CT was not performed.  

Initial impression was acute pulmonary embolism, and anticoagulation with heparin was started. On hospital day 2, lung perfusion scintigraphy with 99mTc-MAA and ventilation with 81mKr showed multiple peripheral mismatched defects.

A 34-year-old woman, at 28 weeks of gestation, was referred for evaluation of a more than 2-year history of intermittent, disfiguring edema, erythema, and pruritus of the bilateral hands and lower legs. She was receiving oral buprenorphine for opioid dependence. Her past medical history was notable for years of heroin self-injections into the hands and lower legs, hepatitis C antibody positivity (RNA negative), bilateral hand cellulitis and tenosynovitis, and nonhealing open wounds on the legs. Physical examination revealed severe pitting and woody edema of all four limbs, nodular erythema of the dorsal hands extending to the wrists but sparing the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, and erythema underlying pitted, hyperpigmented scars on the lower legs.

A 48-year-old man presented with a five-week history of intermittent fever, chills, drenching night sweats, anorexia, and a 15-lb weight loss. He also reported several days of back pain and diarrhea, and noted a transient rash at symptom onset. He denied travel, tuberculosis exposure, respiratory symptoms, or family history of hematologic disease. 

On admission, CT of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast showed enlarged portacaval and retroperitoneal lymph nodes (up to 1.5 cm); CT of the neck and chest was unremarkable. Laboratory studies revealed a C-reactive protein of 2.04 mg/dL, elevated β2-microglobulin (4.53 mg/L), and lactate dehydrogenase of 450 U/L; serologies (hepatitis, HIV, ANA, anti-dsDNA, rheumatoid factor), blood and urine cultures, and stool studies were negative or non-diagnostic. Viral serologies showed negative CMV IgM with elevated IgG, elevated EBV IgG without IgM, and a borderline rise in coxsackievirus B4 and B6 titers. 

Empiric intravenous antibiotics produced no clinical improvement. He was found to have leukopenia with absolute neutropenia; peripheral smear showed no malignant cells. Bone marrow biopsy demonstrated normal hematopoiesis; AFB cultures were negative. PET/CT revealed mildly to moderately hypermetabolic enlarged lymph nodes in the upper abdomen and retroperitoneum (maximal size 4.2×2.5 cm, SUV 2.8; portacaval nodes 2.7×1.7 cm, SUV 3.5). 

Excisional biopsy of periportal and retroperitoneal nodes showed an atypical lymphoid proliferation with foci of necrosis, and the differential diagnosis included Hodgkin lymphoma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, or lupus lymphadenitis. Flow cytometry revealed no evidence of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and the specimen was sent for expert consultation.

A 20-year-old man with known beta-thalassemia major, diagnosed at 6 months of age and status post-splenectomy, presented with a 6-month history of mechanical low back pain that became inflammatory in character over the past month, associated with prolonged morning stiffness. He also noted bilateral lower-limb paresthesia and weakness. He denied any trauma, fever, weight loss, upper limb symptoms, or bladder or bowel dysfunction.

On examination, he was in significant pain (VAS 9/10). Neurologic assessment revealed lower-limb hypoesthesia and muscle strength of 3/5, with normal tone, symmetrical reflexes, and negative Babinski signs. Anal sphincter tone and perianal sensation were intact.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 5 g/dL, white blood cell count 20 600/mm3, platelets 558 000/mm3; peripheral smear demonstrated anisopoikilocytosis, hypochromia, and nucleated red blood cells. ESR was 55 mm/h and CRP 5 mg/L; infectious workup was negative; other biochemistry was unremarkable.

Spine radiographs revealed diffuse osteopenia with expanded medullary spaces and a lace-like trabecular pattern. MRI of the thoracolumbar spine demonstrated diffusely hypointense marrow on T1-weighted images, paraspinal and epidural masses extending from T2 to L2 causing spinal cord compression at T5–T6, and an anterior epidural mass at S1 compressing the filum terminale.

A 25-year-old G2P1 woman at 38 weeks’ gestation was referred for prolonged labor (15 hours of pain, membranes ruptured 10 hours) and had been fasting for 9 hours. Antenatal labs at a nearby health center showed blood group O+, nonrevealing urinalysis, normal CBC (WBC 9000/μL, RBC 4.1 million/μL, Hct 36%, platelets 153 000/μL), nonreactive VDRL, HBsAg, and HIV. Obstetric ultrasound indicated a singleton fetus in cephalic presentation at 39 weeks and estimated weight 3100 g.

Her past obstetric history included one normal vaginal delivery; there was no history of hypertension, diabetes, cardiac or renal disease, drug use, smoking, or alcohol. On exam, she was afebrile, BP 100/70 mmHg, PR 100 bpm, RR 18/min, with dry mucous membranes and sunken eyeballs. Cardiorespiratory and neurologic exams were normal. Abdominal exam showed a term-sized uterus, FHR 143 bpm, and active contractions. Cervical dilation was 8 cm with vertex at station 0 and grade 1 meconium-stained fluid.

With a diagnosis of cephalopelvic disproportion secondary to malposition, she was admitted and prepared for emergency cesarean delivery. Preoperatively, CBC and urinalysis remained normal; random blood glucose was not measured. In the operating room, she received 1000 mL normal saline preload. Spinal anesthesia (12.5 mg hyperbaric bupivacaine at L3–L4) was administered, and she was positioned supine with left tilt. The baby was delivered within 6 minutes; the placenta was removed by cord traction, and there was no significant bleeding.

Shortly thereafter, she became restless, drowsy, and unresponsive to verbal commands, with sweating. Her blood pressure fell and she developed bradycardia and two generalized seizures. She had no chest pain or cough. Oxygenation by face mask was initiated, but her condition worsened, culminating in apnea and sudden cardiac arrest.

A 39-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with a 2-week history of gradually worsening frontal headache, intermittent fever, nausea, vomiting, disorientation, and incoherent speech. On examination, her pupils were miotic but reactive to light, with no papilledema. Meningeal signs were positive (Kernig and Brudzinski), and the rest of the neurologic examination was normal. Laboratory studies showed normal complete blood count and liver function tests, but blood chemistry revealed hyponatremia and a low thyroid-stimulating hormone level. Brain MRI with and without gadolinium demonstrated generalized leptomeningeal enhancement—basal predominance and multinodular appearance—with evidence of hydrocephalus. A lumbar puncture yielded straw-colored CSF with polymorphonuclear-predominant leukocytosis, hypoproteinorrachia, and hypoglycorrhachia; Gram stain was negative, and cultures were obtained. 

A ventriculostomy was placed, and the patient received empiric meropenem, vancomycin, acyclovir, and prednisone. CSF cultures remained negative. During hospitalization she developed hypernatremia attributable to diabetes insipidus that did not respond to fluid restriction. She improved neurologically and was discharged on a tapering steroid regimen.

One month later she experienced a recurrence of frontal headache, intermittent fever, nausea, vomiting, disorientation, incoherent speech, polyuria, and polydipsia. Repeat lumbar puncture showed marked hyperproteinorrachia without pleocytosis. Chest radiography revealed a diffuse reticulonodular interstitial pulmonary pattern and mild mediastinal widening.

A 20-year-old Caucasian woman presented with exertional dyspnoea and recurrent dizziness. A 12-lead ECG showed complete atrioventricular (AV) block with a ventricular escape rhythm at 34 bpm. On admission, she was asymptomatic at rest. Vital signs: temperature 37.3 °C, blood pressure 135/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, oxygen saturation 100%. Physical examination was unremarkable; no peripheral lymphadenopathy, skin lesions, murmurs, or oedema. There was no personal or family history of cardiac arrhythmias.

Laboratory studies: normal blood counts, cardiac enzymes, and inflammatory markers. Electrolytes showed sodium 134 mmol/L and potassium 4.70 mmol/L on admission, which normalized on repeat testing. Renal, liver, and thyroid function tests were normal. PCR for SARS-CoV-2 was negative. Serologic testing for Lyme disease and multiple viruses was negative.

Transthoracic echocardiography: left ventricular ejection fraction 60%, mild mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, no regional wall motion abnormalities, and no ventricular wall thickness changes. Continuous ECG monitoring and 24-h Holter revealed intermittent first-, second-, and third-degree AV block with nocturnal asystolic pauses up to 6600 ms, but the patient remained haemodynamically stable.

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated late gadolinium enhancement in the basal interventricular septum. Subsequent 18 F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT revealed intense tracer uptake in the basal septal wall and in a few small mediastinal lymph nodes.

A 61-year-old man with persistent atrial fibrillation refractory to antiarrhythmic therapy underwent pulmonary vein isolation with roofline and cavotricuspid isthmus ablation. He had an uncomplicated immediate postprocedural course and was discharged on dabigatran. Approximately 3 months later, he presented with progressive dyspnea. His electrocardiogram showed low QRS voltage in the limb leads. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated preserved biventricular function and a mild circumferential pericardial effusion measuring 8 mm, without signs of hemodynamic compromise. Several examinations were performed for exclusion of phrenic nerve palsy, pulmonary vein stenosis, and anemia. Because of the possibility of effusive pericarditis, the patient was treated with colchicine and ibuprofen, and anticoagulation was continued. Over the next several months, his symptoms progressed, with clinical features of right-sided heart failure. A repeat transthoracic echocardiogram performed 9 months after the ablation revealed paradoxical interventricular septal motion and a restrictive transmitral filling pattern with an E/A ratio of 2.84, a septal e′ velocity of 0.16 m/s, and a lateral e′ velocity of 0.10 m/s.

A 54-year-old Chinese woman was referred in October 2018 for evaluation of hyperthyroidism, persistent hyperkalemia, and elevated parathyroid hormone levels. 

History of Present Illness:  
- In August 2017, she presented with palpitations, fatigue, tremor, and weight loss.  
- Diagnosed with Graves’ disease: elevated TT4, TT3, FT4, FT3; suppressed TSH; positive TRAb; thyroid ultrasound with increased blood flow.  
- Serum potassium at that time was 5.48 mmol/L, which was not addressed.  
- Thiamazole started at 15 mg daily, later reduced to 10 mg; thyroid function normalized, but serum potassium remained 5.3–5.8 mmol/L.  
- In August 2018, she developed dizziness and hypertension (167/94 mmHg); treated with metoprolol, nifedipine, and furosemide, yet blood pressure remained elevated and serum potassium persisted at 5.7–5.9 mmol/L.

October 2018 Evaluation:  
- Serum PTH: 123.6 pg/ml (reference <88).  
- Serum calcium: 2.39 mmol/L (2.20–2.65).  
- 24-hour urinary calcium: 9.52 mmol/day (5.9–6.5).  
- Serum K⁺: 6.18 mmol/L; Na⁺: 139 mmol/L; Cl⁻: 108.6 mmol/L; total CO₂: 21.2 mmol/L.  
- Blood pressure: 162/80 mmHg; BMI: 29.8 kg/m²; thyroid diffusely enlarged and soft.  
- Repeat labs: persistent hyperkalemia and elevated PTH with low-normal serum calcium.  
- Second 24-hour urinary calcium: within normal range.  
- Arterial blood gas: metabolic acidosis.  
- Bone turnover markers: elevated ALP and TRAP-5b.  
- 25-Hydroxyvitamin D: 16.04 nmol/L (75–250).  
- Serum creatinine: 57 µmol/L; eGFR: 101.2 ml/min/1.73 m².  
- Serum cortisol and ACTH: normal; plasma renin: low–normal; aldosterone: normal.  
- Abdominal ultrasound: normal pancreas and adrenal glands.

A 64-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of jaundice and general fatigue. Two days before admission she noted yellowing of her bulbar conjunctiva and low-grade fever. She had no history of alcohol use, dietary supplements, or exposure to hepatotoxins. Her body-mass index was 24. Her older sister died in her thirties of hepatic failure of unknown cause.

On examination, she was alert, afebrile, and hemodynamically stable. Abdominal examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies showed: total bilirubin 33.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 25.5 mg/dL, ammonia 143 μg/dL, prothrombin time 19% (INR 2.43), hemoglobin 6.1 g/dL, platelets 202 ×10^3/μL, AST 164 U/L, ALT 15 U/L, ALP 26 U/L, γ-GTP 371 U/L. Viral hepatitis serologies, antinuclear antibody, anti–mitochondrial M2 antibody, and other autoimmune markers were negative.

Contrast CT of the abdomen revealed hepatosplenomegaly without focal lesions or biliary dilation. She was diagnosed with acute hepatic failure and treated with fresh frozen plasma transfusions and plasma exchange under continuous hemofiltration.

Over the next 2 days, her hemoglobin and platelet counts declined further. Reticulocyte count rose to 175‰, haptoglobin was < 10 mg/dL, and both direct and indirect Coombs tests were negative. Additional testing did not reveal viral, autoimmune, or drug-induced causes. A liver biopsy could not be performed due to coagulopathy.

On hospital day 4 she developed flapping tremor and confusion consistent with grade II hepatic encephalopathy (NH₃ 168 μg/dL). On day 5, bone marrow examination demonstrated macrophages phagocytizing blood cells, fulfilling HLH-2004 criteria.  
Based on guideline definitions, she was diagnosed with fulminant hepatitis accompanied by hemophagocytic syndrome of unknown etiology.

A 62-year-old woman presented with severe right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and vomiting, worsened by fatty meals. She denied fever, jaundice, abdominal distension, or dyspnea. Her medical history was unremarkable, and she had no comorbidities. 

On examination, she was hemodynamically stable and afebrile. Vital signs: blood pressure 110/80 mmHg; heart rate 110 beats/min; respiratory rate 19 breaths/min; temperature 36.5 °C. Abdominal examination revealed mild tenderness in the right hypochondrium without guarding or rebound. 

Laboratory studies showed a total white-cell count of approximately 9000 cells/mm^3 with normal differential, and normal renal and liver function tests except for a mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase of 150 U/L (reference range, 35–130 U/L). 

Transabdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 7.3-cm calculus in the distal common bile duct causing gross proximal ductal dilation, with a separate nonobstructive 3.9-cm calculus in the proximal biliary radicals. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a hyperdense calculus measuring 6.8 × 4.7 cm in the distal common bile duct with proximal dilation (maximum diameter, 4.5 cm) and a 3.8 × 3.2-cm calculus in the common hepatic duct. There were no imaging features of cholangitis or pancreatitis.

A 35-year-old woman with a history of recurrent oral ulcers and panuveitis presented with acute loss of consciousness. Five years earlier she had been treated with azathioprine and cyclosporine for Behçet’s disease but had been lost to follow-up for one year. Two weeks before admission she developed a sore throat and low-grade fever (38 °C) treated with antibiotics; the fever then rose to 39 °C, and over the ensuing three days she developed photophobia, right-sided weakness, and gait difficulty. On arrival she was unconscious (Glasgow Coma Scale 8/15: E2 V3 M3), with bilateral vertical nystagmus, right-foot myoclonus, brisk deep-tendon reflexes, and bilateral Babinski signs. Examination of other systems was unremarkable. Laboratory studies—including complete blood count, C-reactive protein, vitamin B12 and B9 levels, thyroid function tests, serum electrolytes, and renal and hepatic panels—were normal. Noncontrast CT of the brain showed a hypodense lesion centered in the left thalamus, with no pathologic enhancement on contrast. MRI revealed bilateral asymmetric T2 and FLAIR hyperintense, T1 hypointense lesions in the corpus callosum (more pronounced on the left), internal capsules, left thalamus, meso-diencephalic junction, midbrain, and hippocampi, with heterogeneous contrast enhancement and surrounding vasogenic edema causing a 5 mm rightward midline shift; leptomeningeal enhancement was noted in the right internal temporal region. MR angiography of the head and neck showed no arterial occlusion or stenosis, arteriovenous malformation, or aneurysm. Lumbar puncture revealed elevated protein with otherwise normal cytochemistry. Fungal (cryptococcus), parasitic (toxoplasmosis), bacterial (syphilis and tuberculosis), and viral (HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C) studies were negative. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no evidence of malignancy.

A 29-year-old man with no past medical history presented with extreme lethargy and a witnessed generalized seizure. He had awoken that morning with a severe right frontotemporal headache and collapsed. Over the preceding weeks he had experienced left-sided weakness, lethargy, impulsivity, and had lost 30–45 pounds over six months. In the field he received midazolam; in the emergency department he was given naloxone and IV fluids for uncertain history. Family history was notable for Behçet’s disease, and rheumatology was consulted, but no uveitis or other classic findings were identified. Initial laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 17.1×10^9/L with a left neutrophil shift, sodium 135 mEq/L, potassium 5.3 mEq/L, chloride 95 mEq/L, and creatinine 1.26 mg/dL. The next day, his neurologic examination was normal. Noncontrast head CT revealed decreased attenuation in the right parietal deep white matter and right temporal lobe. Brain MRI without contrast demonstrated an expansile T2-hyperintense signal involving the midbrain, pons, middle cerebellar peduncles (right greater than left), right pontomedullary junction, right anterior cerebellar hemisphere, splenium of the corpus callosum, right thalamus, and posterior basal ganglia, with supratentorial edema in the right frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes and a shine-through effect on diffusion-weighted imaging without definite restricted diffusion, findings suspicious for an underlying mass. Contrast-enhanced MRI redemonstrated diffuse enlargement and abnormal T2/FLAIR hyperintense signals in the same regions. Video EEG showed 1–1.5 Hz delta waves with occasional sharp spikes in the right hemisphere. Inflammatory markers and infection studies—including CRP 7.63 mg/L, ESR 48 mm/h, HIV antigen/antibody, HSV PCR, West Nile virus, JC virus, meningitis panel, VDRL, ANA, and anti–NMDA receptor antibodies—were negative or nonreactive. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed mild pleocytosis, elevated protein, and positive major basic protein but no pathogens. MR angiography showed no evidence of vasculitis. Neurosurgery and neuro-oncology were consulted for further management.

A 29-year-old man presented to the emergency department with acute epigastric pain. He had epigastric tenderness on examination but no respiratory or cardiac symptoms. Laboratory tests showed an elevated serum lipase level. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed no signs of cholecystitis or ascites. Three days after the onset of symptoms, abdominal CT performed for stage D pancreatitis incidentally demonstrated a cystic mass in the interventricular septum with a partially calcified wall. An electrocardiogram was normal, and serologic tests for echinococcosis were negative. Further review of his medical history revealed surgical excision of liver and thyroid cysts 13 years earlier and of a soft-tissue leg cyst 3 years earlier. No other cystic lesions were identified.

A 24‐year‐old Malay woman with known hemoglobin H–Constant Spring thalassemia, managed with 3‐monthly blood transfusions and subcutaneous deferoxamine chelation, presented with a 1‐month history of fever, headache, and painful enlarged neck lymph nodes. She has a family history of Hb H disease, no parental consanguinity, and is a nonsmoker and teetotaler.

On examination, she was pale and jaundiced, with a temperature of 38 °C, no rash, and bilateral tender, rubbery cervical lymphadenopathies up to 4 × 4 cm without overlying skin changes. She had hepatosplenomegaly; other systems were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hypochromic microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 7.5 g/dL), leukopenia (2.8 × 10^9/L), normal platelets, and ferritin 3500 ng/mL. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 80 mm/h. Serologic tests for hepatitis B and C, HIV, toxoplasma, cytomegalovirus, Brucella, and antistreptolysin O titre were negative. Antinuclear antibody, c-ANCA, and p-ANCA were also negative.

Peripheral blood film demonstrated features of chronic hemolysis. Capillary electrophoresis revealed Hb A 69.1%, Hb A2 0.4%, Hb F 0%, Hb H 26.6%, Hb Barts 1.5%, and Hb Constant Spring 2.4%. DNA analysis confirmed heterozygosity for the SEA deletion and the Constant Spring termination codon mutation, consistent with Hb H–Constant Spring disease; β-globin gene analysis was normal.

Abdominal ultrasonography and transthoracic echocardiography showed no abscesses or vegetations. MRI T2* demonstrated moderate hepatic iron overload and normal myocardial iron. Whole‐body CT revealed diffuse cervical, axillary, and abdominal lymphadenopathy, with the largest node measuring 4 × 4 cm. A cervical lymph node biopsy was performed.

A 36-year-old gravida 4, para 2-0-1-2 Asian woman of Bengali descent presented for antepartum care. Her history included hypothyroidism on levothyroxine, gestational diabetes on metformin, one prior miscarriage, and two prior cesarean deliveries. Noninvasive prenatal testing was negative and indicated a female fetus. At 27 weeks 5 days, an anatomy ultrasound showed fetal weight at the 25th percentile, an enlarged heart, mild ascites, and a bladder with posterior diverticulosis; kidneys appeared normal. Fetal echocardiography confirmed hydrops with 2 mm pericardial effusion, ascites, and mild cardiomegaly. Serologic testing for parvovirus and CMV IgM was negative. At 27 weeks 6 days, fetal MRI demonstrated a midline pelvic cystic structure posterior to the bladder and anterior to the rectum, left urinary tract dilatation with a 7 mm anterior–posterior pelvic diameter, central calyceal dilatation, proximal ureteral dilatation, mild–moderate ascites, a normal-appearing rectum, and possible ambiguous genitalia. Subsequent ultrasound at 28 weeks showed persistent ascites, a 10 mm left renal pelvic diameter, mild ureteral dilation, polyhydramnios (AFI 27), and normal female external genitalia. Amniocentesis was declined, but expanded carrier genetic testing revealed that the mother was a carrier of BBS12 and the father had a variant of uncertain significance in BBS12. The patient underwent cesarean delivery at 37 weeks; the female newborn (2720 g) had abdominal ultrasound on day 1 showing an 11 cm cystic pelvic structure, poor bladder visualization, and bilateral moderate hydronephrosis with caliectasis.

A 55-year-old man with a 6-month history of abdominal pain and weight loss was referred for evaluation. He is a heavy smoker with no history of diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, peripheral or coronary artery disease; he underwent cholecystectomy in the past.  
– The pain began in the epigastrium, worsened after fatty meals, and improved with fasting; there was an 18-kg weight loss over 4 months, with intermittent watery diarrhea and bloating, but no vomiting, melena, fever, or rash.  
– Initial gastroscopy showed multiple antral healed ulcers and aphthous ulceration; biopsy revealed mild chronic inflammation and no Helicobacter pylori. He received proton pump inhibitors without improvement.  
– Colonoscopy demonstrated a grossly normal terminal ileum and colonic mucosa with active hemorrhoids; laxatives were prescribed.  
– Two contrast CT scans of the abdomen and pelvis were reportedly normal.  
– On admission he was cachectic (BMI 18), afebrile, blood pressure 125/70 mm Hg, heart rate 85 bpm. Physical examination revealed a scaphoid abdomen, diffuse tenderness in the epigastrium and lower quadrants, bilateral 1+ lower-limb edema; cardiopulmonary and neck examinations were normal.  
– Laboratory tests showed WBC 14.9 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL, platelet count 250 × 10^3/µL, albumin 2.9 g/dL, lipase 81 U/L, ESR 30 mm/h; hepatitis markers and chest radiography were unremarkable.  
Differential diagnoses included intra-abdominal malignancy (especially small-bowel or pancreatic), chronic pancreatitis, inflammatory bowel disease, chronic mesenteric ischemia, and celiac disease.

A 69-year-old woman presented with an 8-month history of progressive gait disturbance. Soon after onset, her family noted a symmetrical hand tremor, slowness of movement, and frequent falls. One month later, she described a subjective “chilling” sensation inside her body. She then developed personality changes, persecutory delusions, and unprovoked fear. Over the following months, her gait worsened, necessitating a walking aid, tremors intensified in both hands and her chin, and generalized myoclonic jerks appeared.

Her medical history was notable for breast cancer treated with lumpectomy, chemoradiotherapy, and tamoxifen two years earlier, with no evidence of recurrence.

On examination, she was awake and alert but disoriented to time and place. Her Mini-Mental State Examination score was 13/30. There was symmetrical rigidity and bradykinesia in all limbs, a resting tremor of the hands and chin, and a stooped posture with short-stepping gait and occasional freezing. Deep tendon reflexes were 1+ to 2+ symmetrically; plantar responses were flexor. Sensory examination was unremarkable, although she reported distal paresthesia in her upper limbs. Frontal release signs included a grasp reflex, utilization behavior, and a positive Myerson sign.

Laboratory studies, including electrolytes, liver and kidney function tests, vitamin B12, thyroid function tests, and anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody, were normal. Tests for systemic vasculitis were negative. Paraneoplastic and autoimmune antibodies in blood and CSF were negative. CSF analysis showed no white blood cells, a protein level of 39 mg/dL, normal glucose, and was positive for 14-3-3 protein.

Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral T2 and FLAIR hyperintensities in the caudate nuclei, putamina, and medial thalami, with corresponding diffusion restriction on DWI and ADC sequences. Cortical ribboning was noted in the parieto-occipital and medial frontal regions on DWI. EEG revealed nonspecific generalized slowing without periodic sharp waves.

A 32-year-old man presented with pain and swelling below the left eye obstructing vision for 1 month and an ulcer on the roof of the mouth for 15 days. The pain was gradual in onset, severe, throbbing, continuous, and radiated to the left temporal region. He also noted insidious, progressively enlarging swelling over the left maxillary sinus region causing nasal obstruction and periorbital edema, along with recurrent serous nasal discharge from the left nostril for 20 days. Fifteen days earlier, he developed an ulcer on the hard palate that rapidly increased in size and interfered with speech.

His medical history was notable for poorly controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus of 2 years’ duration, treated with 14 units of mixed insulin daily; he was a tobacco chewer for 15 years, and his father had type 1 diabetes. On examination, he was febrile with a blood pressure of 160/90 mmHg. Extraoral inspection revealed diffuse soft-to-firm tender swelling over the left maxillary sinus region, extending from the left supraorbital margin to a line from the left corner of the mouth to the ear, and from the nasal bridge to the ear; the overlying skin was normal, and there was left eyelid ptosis. Intraoral examination showed an approximately 3 × 4 cm ulcer on the hard palate covered by necrotic slough with exposed underlying bone, non-tender with erythematous margins.

Laboratory tests revealed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 34 mm in the first hour and a random blood glucose of 220 mg/dL; tests for HIV and hepatitis B surface antigen were negative. A Waters’ view radiograph of the facial bones demonstrated diffuse opacification of the left maxillary sinus extending into the left nasal cavity. Computed tomography of the facial bones showed opacification along the walls of the left maxillary antrum with focal bony destruction extending into the left nasal cavity and the floor of the left orbit.

A 73-year-old frail woman with rheumatic heart disease (mechanical aortic and mitral valves on warfarin), nonischemic cardiomyopathy, chronic atrial fibrillation, prior cerebral hemorrhage, type II diabetes, chronic kidney disease, congestive heart failure, and peripheral artery disease presented with a 1-month history of progressive, debilitating bilateral thigh muscle weakness (left > right) and left lower extremity pain. She also reported intermittent bilateral rest pain and claudication. She was hemodynamically stable and afebrile.

On examination, there was marked bilateral thigh and calf muscle atrophy and reproducible pain with active and passive movement of the left hip. Both calf and leg compartments were soft, with focal tenderness along the left lateral thigh and milder tenderness on the right. Sensory testing was limited by baseline diabetic neuropathy and peripheral artery disease.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count persistently near 19,000/mcL, creatinine rising from 1.1 to 1.4 mg/dL, potassium of 4.7 mEq/L, lactate of 1.9 mg/dL, creatine kinase >1000 U/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 80 mm/hr, C-reactive protein of 117 mg/L, and procalcitonin of 0.28 ng/mL.

The neurology service concluded that the clinical picture was inconsistent with a neuropathic process. Rheumatology, concerned about inflammatory myositis or vasculitis in the setting of her family history of lupus, recommended muscle biopsy. Emergency surgery was consulted to exclude lower extremity compartment syndrome, but suspicion remained low given the soft calf and leg compartments.

Contrast CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 7.6 × 3.9 cm intramuscular hematoma within the left iliacus muscle without active extravasation. There was also severe, diffuse atherosclerotic plaque in the abdominal aorta and iliac arteries, an ostial occlusion of the right superficial femoral artery, and a midsegment left superficial femoral artery occlusion. Ankle-brachial indices were 0.55 on the right and 0.53 on the left.

A 73-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of progressive leg edema and dyspnea on exertion. His medical history included spasmodic angina, midbrain infarction, and chronic renal failure. On evaluation at our hospital, blood tests were notable only for mildly decreased renal function (creatinine 1.22 mg/dL; indocyanine green 15-min retention 26.2%) with otherwise unremarkable hematology, liver tests, and coagulation studies.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen revealed multiple hepatic cysts. The largest cyst (13 cm) in segment 8 compressed the right side of the heart and right thoracic cavity. Multiple cysts in the caudal lobe lay dorsal to the inferior vena cava (IVC), causing bilateral compression. Additional cysts in the hilar region compressed the portal bifurcation, with stenosis of the right portal vein branch.

Venous angiography demonstrated marked IVC stenosis with an 11 mm Hg pressure gradient across the lesion. Superior mesenteric artery angiography showed patent antegrade portal flow and the development of a left gastric vein–left renal vein shunt. No intestinal edema was observed. These findings suggested mild portal hypertension in association with IVC compression.

A 74-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of worsening visual acuity, reporting difficulty reading small print and failure to recognize faces in photographs. Over three years, her visual acuity deteriorated from 6/7.5 to 6/10. Optical coherence tomography showed bilateral retinal nerve-fiber–layer damage, but color vision, visual fields, and pupil reactions were normal. She had bilateral cataracts and bilateral papilledema on ophthalmologic examination; ocular pressures were normal. She also described intermittent headaches for several months without identifiable triggers and no relief from simple analgesics. There were no features to suggest migraine, giant-cell arteritis, or meningism. 

Her past medical history was notable for acute myeloid leukemia treated 18 years earlier with intrathecal chemotherapy, during which she developed raised intracranial pressure requiring therapeutic lumbar punctures; she was lost to ophthalmology follow-up but was symptom‐free and without leukemia recurrence at oncology review 2 months before presentation. 

On examination, vital signs were normal. Neurologic examination was unremarkable, visual fields were full, and cranial nerves were intact. Fundoscopy again showed bilateral disc swelling. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, renal function, bone profile, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (26 mm/h), and HbA1c (38 mmol/mol), were within normal limits. 

An unenhanced CT scan of the brain revealed an enlarged, fluid-filled pituitary fossa. A neurologist arranged an urgent MRI of the brain to exclude venous sinus thrombosis.
MRI confirmed a fluid-filled sella turcica with a flattened pituitary gland and excluded any other intracranial pathology.

A 66-year-old man from Myanmar, with a 12 pack-year smoking history, presented with a 3-month history of cough, exertional dyspnea, anorexia, and weight loss. He denied hemoptysis or occupational dust exposure. Multiple courses of antibiotics for presumed respiratory infections failed to improve his symptoms. 

On referral, chest radiography showed right-sided multifocal discrete opacities and a moderate left pleural effusion. Chest CT demonstrated a 2.3×2.2-cm right upper lobe mass with intralesional calcification, two right lower lobe masses (4.3×3 cm and 4.2×2.2 cm), multiple left pleural‐based nodules, and a large left pleural effusion with collapse-consolidation of the left lower lobe. There was fibrosis and pneumonitis in the apico-posterior segment of the left upper lobe and no obvious hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy. 

Diagnostic thoracentesis yielded a clear yellow fluid with 70% polymorphonuclear cells, protein 43 g/L, glucose 6.7 mmol/L, and cytology showing neutrophils, lymphocytes, histiocytes, and reactive mesothelial cells but no malignant cells. 

He was empirically started on four-drug antituberculous therapy despite negative sputum TB studies but discontinued after 3 weeks due to side effects. At our institution, vital signs and routine blood tests were unremarkable. PET-CT confirmed FDG-avid right lung masses and left pleural and pericardial nodules, with borderline enlargement of mediastinal nodes. 

Endobronchial ultrasound–guided transbronchial needle aspiration of a right paratracheal node yielded lymphoid tissue with multinucleated cells. Transbronchial lung biopsy of a right lower lobe lesion revealed epithelioid granulomas with multinucleated giant cells, epithelioid histiocytes, and lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, without necrosis or evidence of malignancy. Ziehl–Neelsen staining was negative for acid-fast bacilli. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid grew Klebsiella pneumoniae sensitive to standard antibiotics. AFB smear, mycobacterial culture, and TB nucleic acid amplification tests were negative in sputum, BAL fluid, and biopsy specimens.

A 53-year-old woman with congestive heart failure, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and obesity status post Roux-en-Y gastric bypass revision 4 months earlier presented with sudden-onset nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. The vomiting self-resolved, but she continued to have explosive, watery, nonbloody diarrhea several times per day, often preceded by a burning sensation in the anal area and occasional incontinence. The day before symptom onset, she had eaten pork chops and ground beef at a church dinner; notably, her dog, after consuming the same ground beef, developed similar gastrointestinal symptoms. She denied fevers, chills, abdominal pain, melena, hematochezia, recent antibiotic use, or other systemic complaints. 

On examination, she was afebrile and alert. Abdominal examination revealed a soft, nontender, nondistended abdomen with hyperactive bowel sounds. Significant pitting edema was noted in the lower extremities. No focal neurologic deficits or signs of systemic infection were present. 

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 11.3×10^9/L (which peaked at 19×10^9/L during admission and subsequently trended downward), a lactic acid level of 0.6 mmol/L, a serum creatinine of 1.5 mg/dL, and a potassium of 2.8 mmol/L (replaced as needed). A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast demonstrated postgastric bypass changes, a prominent gallbladder, and a normal appendix without intestinal wall thickening. Abdominal radiographs showed no acute abnormalities. Urinalysis revealed 0–5 white cells per high-power field, 2+ leukocyte esterase, positive nitrites, and many bacteria. A Clostridium difficile antigen test was negative. HIV, rapid plasma reagin, and hepatitis C serologies were nonreactive. 

The patient was admitted and empirically started on ceftriaxone and metronidazole.

A 52-year-old Bangladeshi man was referred to ENT for a 1-week history of odynophagia and a persistent sensation of a foreign body in his throat following fish-bone impaction. He had presented to the Emergency Department with similar symptoms and was diagnosed with a right tonsillar foreign body. He denied dysphagia, dyspnea, otalgia, or weight loss. His social history was notable for moderate tobacco use and habitual betel-nut chewing.

On examination, there was no visible fish bone. Instead, a protruding lesion was observed through the right palatine tonsil; it was hard, mobile, well-delineated, nontender, and yellowish-white in color. Flexible fibreoptic nasopharyngoscopy showed no mucosal ulceration or mass elsewhere in the upper aerodigestive tract, and no cervical lymphadenopathy was palpable. A lateral neck radiograph revealed no fish bone but demonstrated a uniform, ovoid calcification overlying the right tonsillar region abutting the mandibular ramus.

A 4-month-old female with Tetralogy of Fallot and severe right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) obstruction, managed shortly after birth with an RVOT stent, presented after a 5-minute hypoxaemic event at home, with oxygen saturations of 40% on her home pulse oximeter. She had been stable at home with saturations ≥93% on room air. She was born at 36 weeks to a mother with type 1 diabetes. 

On admission: temperature was normal, blood pressure 97/53 mmHg, heart rate 129 beats/min, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, and SpO₂ 71% on room air. She was alert, in no distress, and acyanotic. Respiratory examination was normal. Cardiac examination revealed a grade III/VI holosystolic murmur at the left upper sternal border. Peripheral pulses were 2+, capillary refill 3–4 seconds. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Transthoracic echocardiography showed a widely patent RVOT stent with a peak Doppler gradient of 22 mmHg and minimal turbulence across the stent, but there was flow acceleration in all four pulmonary veins. Computed tomography angiography demonstrated severe stenosis of all pulmonary veins at their entry into the left atrium, with near atresia of the left lower, right upper, and right middle veins. Diagnostic cardiac catheterization revealed elevated pulmonary vascular resistance (12.58 iWU) and confirmation of stenosis in all pulmonary veins.

A 59-year-old Syrian woman presented with a 2-month history of intermittent, fresh gross hematuria and irritative voiding symptoms. She denied fevers, arthralgias, or rash. Eighteen years earlier, she had been diagnosed with bladder amyloidosis and treated by transurethral resection, with no subsequent follow-up.

On examination, vital signs were normal, and the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a normal CBC and normal renal, liver, and bone biochemistry. Urinalysis revealed uncountable red blood cells, a few white blood cells, granular casts, and hemoglobin positivity; urine culture was negative. 

Renal-bladder ultrasound demonstrated irregular thickening of the bladder wall up to 9 mm. Intravenous urography was unremarkable. Cystoscopy revealed multifocal yellowish lesions on the bladder mucosa. Histologic examination of biopsy specimens showed extensive amorphous deposits compatible with amyloid.

To assess for systemic involvement, an ECG and chest radiograph were obtained and showed no abnormalities. Tuberculin testing and 24-hour urinary mycobacterial studies were negative. There was no elevation in lymphocyte count or protein gap. Bone marrow biopsy and a CT scan of the abdomen were both normal.

A 35-year-old man was admitted with a 2-week history of high-grade intermittent fever associated with loss of appetite, dry cough, generalized weakness, and diffuse moderate-to-severe abdominal pain refractory to analgesics. He denied vomiting, changes in bowel habits, jaundice, urinary symptoms, headache, neck stiffness, or altered mentation.

On examination, temperature was 38.3°C, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, pulse 80 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and BMI 23.3 kg/m2. He appeared acutely ill but had no pallor, icterus, or lymphadenopathy. Cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable. The abdomen was soft, with mild lower-quadrant tenderness, mild hepatomegaly, and a tipped spleen; bowel sounds were present and there was no rebound or costovertebral angle tenderness. Neurologic examination was normal.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 5600/µl (81% neutrophils), hemoglobin 12.1 g/dl, platelets 202 000/µl, ESR 44 mm/h, ALT 74 IU/L, AST 94 IU/L, total bilirubin 0.46 mg/dl, albumin 3.4 g/dl, sodium 130 meq/L, and normal renal function. QuantiFERON-TB Gold and Widal tests were negative. Blood cultures grew Salmonella typhi. Abdominal ultrasound revealed thickening of the terminal ileum, ileocecal valve, and cecum with enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes. CT of the abdomen showed multiple enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes with surrounding fat stranding.

He was started on intravenous ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin, briefly escalated to meropenem, then completed a 10-day course of ceftriaxone. After 72 hours his fever abated. On hospital day 4, he had three episodes of painless, frank red rectal bleeding. He remained hemodynamically stable (BP 100/60 mmHg, pulse 90 bpm, temperature 37.2°C) with moist mucous membranes and unchanged abdominal findings.

Colonoscopy after bowel preparation showed multiple transverse, shallow, punched-out ulcerative lesions in the terminal ileum, ileocecal valve, and cecum with stigmata of recent bleeding. Biopsy from the cecal ulcers demonstrated multifocal active colitis with ulceration, granulation tissue, and mixed inflammatory infiltrate with focal neutrophilic cryptitis; there was no evidence of crypt architectural distortion. Mallory cells were not seen, and there was no evidence of parasites, granuloma, dysplasia, or malignancy.

A 39-year-old man was admitted with rapidly progressive left hemiparesis, evolving from motor grade III to IV over several days. He was alert and exhibited no other neurologic deficits. To exclude an acute cerebrovascular accident, a brain MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging was obtained. Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images revealed a low–signal–intensity lesion with ring enhancement in the right frontal lobe and surrounding low intensity consistent with edema. Serologic testing showed positive HIV antibody and positive Toxoplasma gondii immunoglobulin G antibody, with undetectable T. gondii immunoglobulin M antibody. Plasma HIV RNA was 209,898 copies/mL, and the CD4+ cell percentage was 1.9% (reference, 38–46%).

A 51-year-old Japanese woman was admitted for evaluation of heavy proteinuria, deteriorating renal function, and severe hypertension. Her history was notable for rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed at age 42, treated over two years with tacrolimus (2–3 mg/day) plus prednisolone, and multiple other disease-modifying agents discontinued for allergy. Twenty months after starting tacrolimus, her blood pressure rose from 120/70 mmHg to 140/80 mmHg. Proteinuria increased from a baseline of 0.3–0.5 g/g creatinine at 24 months, while serum creatinine remained ~0.8 mg/dL. Tacrolimus and tocilizumab were stopped at 27 months, and two months later proteinuria worsened, severe hypertension (190/100 mmHg) and progressive renal dysfunction developed. She was started on telmisartan/amlodipine, but creatinine rose to 2.63 mg/dL, prompting admission three months after tacrolimus discontinuation.

On examination, temperature was 36.5 °C, blood pressure 170/102 mmHg, pulse 88 beats/min. She had numbness in her hands, joint pains and swelling, and mild bilateral leg edema; there was no abdominal bruit, skin sclerosis, or evidence of vasculitis. Fundoscopy showed no exudates, hemorrhages, or papilledema.

Laboratory studies revealed:  
• Urinalysis: heavy proteinuria, microscopic hematuria, elevated urinary N-acetyl-β-D-glucosaminidase and low-molecular-weight proteins.  
• Blood: anemia, hypoalbuminemia, creatinine 2.63 mg/dL, hypocalcemia; serum complements normal; rheumatoid factor and anti-SS-A antibody positive; anti-DNA, anticardiolipin, MPO-ANCA, and PR3-ANCA negative.  
• Peripheral smear: no schistocytes or hemolysis.  
• Renin activity and aldosterone markedly elevated.  
• Imaging: normal-sized kidneys, liver hemangiomas; echocardiogram showed left ventricular hypertrophy without dysfunction.

With a clinical suspicion of secondary amyloidosis, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, or malignant nephrosclerosis, renal biopsy was performed.

A 26-year-old woman presented with 2 weeks of anal and vaginal suppuration without fever or other symptoms. She had two prior deliveries and a history of Bartholin’s gland abscess drainage during pregnancy. She denied intrauterine device use, recent travel, alcohol use, or relevant medical comorbidities.

On examination, an external fistulous orifice was noted in the posterior perineum near the left labium majus, and there was induration of the left anterior rectal wall; the gynecological exam was otherwise unremarkable. Pelvic CT showed no abscesses or masses. Under anesthesia, two fistulous tracts (one involving the vagina) were identified and setons were placed; rectal-wall biopsies and pus were obtained.

One month later, pelvic MRI demonstrated multiple complex fistulous tracts, including trans-sphincteric, suprasphincteric, and a rectovaginal fistula. Over the next 3 years, the patient underwent multiple abscess drainages, seton revisions, and empirical antibiotic courses without improvement. Extensive evaluation for inflammatory bowel disease—including upper endoscopy, colonoscopy with ileoscopy, small-bowel capsule endoscopy, CT enterography, and mucosal biopsies—was unremarkable, and anti–Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies were negative. Cytology and cultures of rectal and vaginal exudates and rectal biopsies were negative for neoplastic cells and microorganisms, including Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Serologies for Chlamydia trachomatis, HIV, and syphilis were negative.

A 47-year-old farmer presented with a 2-month history of pain and difficulty walking due to multiple ulcerated nodules on the right lower leg and diffuse swelling over the dorsum of the right foot. The lesions began as papules, progressed to nodules, and then ulcerated, discharging seropurulent fluid; there was no history of trauma, systemic symptoms, or discharge of granules. On examination, three tender ulcerated nodules (1–3 cm) were noted on the anterior and medial right leg with surrounding hyperpigmentation and diffuse pitting edema; regional lymph nodes were not enlarged. The foot swelling was tender. He was provisionally diagnosed with furunculosis, and scrofuloderma, cutaneous sporotrichosis, and erythema nodosum were considered. Routine hematological and biochemical tests, throat swab culture, anti-streptolysin O titer, chest radiograph, and abdominal ultrasonography were all normal. HIV serology was non-reactive, the Mantoux test was negative, a direct smear for tubercle bacilli was negative, and culture on Lowenstein-Jensen medium showed no growth.

A 33-year-old man presented with profuse rectal bleeding mixed with stool for 3 days and one episode of black, tarry stool, associated with easy fatigability. He denied fever, weight loss, night sweats, appetite loss, cough, chest pain, dyspnea, edema, diarrhea, or other bleeding. He had no history of tuberculosis, diabetes, hypertension, or cardiac disease and reported 15 years of heavy alcohol use without smoking.

On examination, he appeared ill, with pallor and dehydration. Vital signs: temperature 98°F, heart rate 110/min, blood pressure 80/60 mm Hg, respiratory rate 19/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Digital rectal examination revealed fresh blood; the remainder of the abdominal and cardiac examinations was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, hematocrit 31.6%, white blood cell count 11 510/mm3 (78% neutrophils), platelets 291 000/mm3, prothrombin time 14 seconds (INR 1.08), albumin 2.4 g/dL, total protein 6.1 g/dL, bilirubin 0.7/0.1 mg/dL, ALT 97 U/L, AST 114 U/L, HbA1c 7.2%, and normal renal function and electrolytes. Urinalysis showed trace glucose and ++ albumin. Fecal occult blood was positive.

Sputum acid-fast bacilli stain and chest radiograph were negative. Abdominal ultrasound and upper GI endoscopy were normal. CT of the chest and abdomen revealed asymmetric circumferential thickening of the ileocaecal region with lobulated thickened caecum, soft-tissue stranding, and necrotic mesenteric lymphadenopathy. Colonoscopy showed multiple transverse ulcers with exudates in the terminal ileum, ascending colon, and transverse colon. Histopathological examination of ileal and colonic biopsies demonstrated patchy ulcers with granulation tissue, fibrosis, deep lymphoplasmocytic inflammation, crypt regenerative changes, and fibrinoid changes in scattered capillaries and venules; these findings were deemed inconclusive.

A 35-year-old woman from the Philippines, with no known immunodeficiency and no history of tuberculosis exposure, presented to a Canadian hospital with a 1-month history of epigastric and chest pain that worsened with food ingestion. She denied dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, fever, or night sweats. Physical examination was unremarkable: no cervical lymphadenopathy and a soft, non-tender abdomen without masses.

An upper gastrointestinal contrast study showed a well-circumscribed mass in the midesophagus on the left anterolateral wall, associated with linear ulceration, and features of reflux esophagitis. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a 3-cm raised submucosal lesion with central ulceration, located 25–28 cm from the incisors. Multiple biopsies were obtained from the lesion, and gastric biopsies were taken to assess for Helicobacter pylori.

Histopathology demonstrated multiple caseating granulomata with a dense mixed inflammatory infiltrate rich in eosinophils. Gastric biopsies were negative for H. pylori. Fungal stains (Grocott methenamine silver and periodic acid–Schiff) and culture of the esophageal biopsy, Ziehl–Neelsen and Warthin–Starry stains, and immunohistochemistry for herpes simplex virus and cytomegalovirus were all negative. There was no evidence of dysplasia.

A 7-month-old previously healthy Caucasian male was referred for evaluation of a suspected right diaphragmatic hernia identified at 4 months of age during an episode of cough, cyanosis, and respiratory distress that resolved with antibiotic therapy. Since then he has been asymptomatic and thriving without recurrence of respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms. On examination, he was well-appearing with normal vital signs; abdominal and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. Complete blood count and serum biochemistry values were within normal limits. A three-dimensional contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest and abdomen showed a dilated bowel loop (hepatic flexure) interposed between the right hemidiaphragm and liver, with minimal superolateral displacement of the heart, normal liver anatomy, and no radiographic defect in the hemidiaphragm. Fluoroscopic imaging demonstrated normal diaphragmatic movement during inspiration and expiration.

A 37-year-old woman presented with 6 months of bleeding, painful oral lesions and progressive facial deformity. She reported no relevant past medical or family history. On examination, there was a firm cervical mass on the left side of the neck. Intraorally, an exophytic mass extended from the right mandibular lateral incisor to the molars, with associated tooth mobility; a second soft, tender swelling involved the palatal midline to the posterior right maxilla. Panoramic radiographs demonstrated an ill-defined osteolytic lesion of the mandible with cortical expansion, loss of the lamina dura, and root resorption. CT imaging revealed additional areas of bone rarefaction in the proximal phalanx of the third toe and ribs. Neck CT showed a large septated cystic-solid lesion posterior to the left thyroid lobe and multiple thyroid nodules. Bone densitometry demonstrated reduced bone mineral density for age. Parathyroid scintigraphy identified hyperfunctioning parathyroid tissue on the left. An incisional biopsy of the mandibular lesion showed intense hemorrhagic exudate, numerous multinucleated giant cells, and haemosiderin pigment. Laboratory studies revealed a serum calcium level of 15.7 mg/dL (reference 8.6–10.2) and a parathyroid hormone concentration of 1472 pg/mL (reference 16–87).

A previously healthy 2-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of 1 day of fever (to 103.6°F), cough, nasal congestion, and poor oral intake. His mother denied vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, respiratory distress, ear pain, or sore throat. He appeared dehydrated, was agitated but consolable, and had no external ear or nasal deformities. Ear canals were patent; tympanic membranes were intact, gray, translucent, and mobile. Nares were patent; nasal turbinates were erythematous without inflammation. Oral mucous membranes were moist and pink without lesions or exudates; no dental caries. His neck was supple, with no cervical lymphadenopathy, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.  
Initial laboratory studies showed leukocytosis with left shift (26 500 cells/µL) and elevated CRP (24.7 mg/L). A rapid influenza test was negative. On re-evaluation the next day, he had erythematous tonsils, midline uvula, and small posterior cervical nodes; hydration had improved. A urinalysis by catheterization was negative. He received an intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone and was sent home. By day 4, WBC was 20 000 cells/µL and CRP was 14.6 mg/L; he initially improved but then redeveloped high fever (103.8°F). On day 6, he returned with new left neck swelling, cervical asymmetry, and deviation of the left tonsil toward the midline.

A 20-year-old man presented to the emergency department with acute chest pain, cough, and dyspnea. He was a computer science student with no prior medical history, minimal smoking exposure (1 pack-year), no alcohol use, no medications, and no known toxin exposures. Three days before presentation, he had participated in social gatherings during which he inhaled more than 10 cannabis joints per day.

On arrival, cardiac evaluation—including electrocardiography, serum NT-proBNP, troponin levels, and transthoracic echocardiography—was normal. Chest radiography showed a bilateral interstitial pattern. Contrast‐enhanced thoracic CT revealed regular septal thickening, diffuse ground-glass opacities, and moderate bilateral pleural effusions.

Laboratory studies demonstrated a rapid rise in peripheral eosinophils over 3 days, peaking at 5559 cells/mm3 (normal <500 cells/mm3), neutrophilic leukocytosis, and an elevated C-reactive protein level of 116 mg/L (normal <5 mg/L). Given a presumptive diagnosis of intracellular germ pneumonia, the patient was started on dual antibiotic therapy. Bronchoscopy was performed and revealed diffuse inflammatory changes.

A 46-year-old woman was admitted for evaluation of a pulmonary mass of unknown origin. Four weeks earlier, she developed a dry cough, chest pain, and mild sore throat unresponsive to inhaled corticosteroids and a β2-agonist. She denied fever, weight loss, night sweats, smoking, alcohol, or illicit drug use. She was born in Thailand, had lived in Germany for 27 years, and three weeks before symptom onset had returned from a 6-month visit to rural northeastern Thailand.

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory tests showed mild thrombocytosis and a C-reactive protein level of 12.9 mg/l; complete blood count, liver and renal function, and lactate dehydrogenase were normal. Chest CT revealed a 5.3 × 4.6-cm right central soft-tissue mass with patchy-confluent opacities in the right upper lobe and a 1.2-cm circumscribed cavitation, along with coalescing adenopathy at the right hilum and infracarinal mediastinum.

Bronchoscopy demonstrated an endobronchial tumor in the right main bronchus and enlarged, hyperechoic mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes. Biopsy samples and transbronchial needle aspirations were sent for histology and microbiology. Cultures of bronchial fluid showed no bacterial growth after 48 hours. Acid-fast stains, mycobacterial cultures, and PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis on all specimens were negative. Histopathology of the endobronchial lesion showed chronic granulation tissue and fibrinous inflammation; lymph node samples contained epithelioid cells and neutrophils but no malignant cells.

Because another bacterial infection could not be ruled out, she was started on oral amoxicillin-clavulanic acid and clindamycin and discharged with outpatient follow-up arranged.

A 27-year-old gravida 2, para 2 woman at an estimated 32 weeks of gestation presented with uterine contractions. She had received no antenatal care. Her first pregnancy had ended in preterm delivery at 33 weeks without long-term sequelae. On examination, her blood pressure was 140/89 mm Hg, and a urine dipstick was negative for protein. Obstetrical examination revealed a fundal height of 26 cm, a cephalic‐presenting fetus with a regular heart rate of 140 beats per minute, and a cervix that was 2 cm dilated with partial effacement. She was admitted for threatened preterm labor and incidental gestational hypertension. Intravenous nicardipine was started for tocolysis, intramuscular betamethasone was administered for fetal lung maturation, and 2 g of intravenous ampicillin was given. During an ultrasound scan, she experienced sudden vaginal bleeding and spontaneous rupture of membranes. Given her hypertension, uterine contractions, and acute bleeding, placental abruption was suspected, and an emergency cesarean section was performed in less than 15 minutes. A male infant weighing 1340 g was delivered with an Apgar score of 1. Placental examination then revealed torn vessels running along the membranes, connecting the placenta to an aberrant cotyledon.

A 17-year-old healthy girl presented with a slowly enlarging swelling on the left side of her face, present since birth, and progressive decrease in mouth opening. She had a surgical procedure at the same site at age 1 but had no records and did not follow up. Examination revealed a tender, firm, bony-hard, nonfluctuant, noncompressible, nonpulsatile mass extending from the upper border of the zygomatic arch superiorly and medially to the body of the zygoma; lateral and inferior borders were indistinct. The patient was afebrile with no other anomalies. Axial CT scan showed a well-delineated, variably dense soft-tissue lesion in the left infratemporal and buccal spaces that enhanced heterogeneously with areas of hypodensity and peripheral enhancement. The lesion abutted the posterolateral wall of the left maxillary sinus and medial aspect of the zygoma, causing anterior and lateral displacement of the zygomatic bone, and extended posteriorly to the ramus of the mandible and between the pterygoid plates. The CT features were interpreted as consistent with a dermoid cyst.

A 54-year-old man presented to the emergency department with abrupt onset of tearing central chest pain radiating to the posterior thorax and associated respiratory distress. His blood pressure was 260/140 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and pulse 106 beats per minute. He had a history of hypertension treated with antihypertensive therapy. Initial electrocardiography and blood counts were within normal limits, but the plasma d-dimer level was elevated at 850 ng/mL (normal <500 ng/mL). A chest radiograph demonstrated a conspicuous widening of the mediastinum and a left-sided pleural effusion. On the basis of these findings, he was clinically diagnosed with acute pulmonary embolism and referred for CT examination.

A 44-year-old previously healthy man presented in June 2020 with 12 days of fever (peak 38.3°C), persistent cough, anosmia, diarrhea, myalgias, and progressive bilateral lower-limb weakness. He had unprotected contact with his SARS-CoV-2–positive brother one week before symptom onset.

On examination, temperature was 38.1°C, other vital signs were within normal limits, and oxygen saturation was 78% on room air; high-flow nasal cannula (60 L/min, FiO2 40%) improved SpO2 to 89%. Neurologic examination revealed bilateral lower-limb muscle strength of 3/5, gait ataxia, and areflexia at the knees and ankles; sensation was intact. Lung auscultation showed bilateral crackles at the bases.

Emergency electromyography of the lower limbs demonstrated delayed distal latencies with normal conduction velocities. Upper limbs were not tested; no biopsy was performed. Laboratory studies showed lymphocytopenia (0.51 × 10^9/L), elevated C-reactive protein (247 mg/L), lactate dehydrogenase (1222 U/L), D-dimer (3.6 μg/mL), ferritin (1123 ng/mL), interleukin-6 (778 pg/mL), and slight creatine kinase elevation (616 U/L); renal and hepatic function were otherwise normal. ADAMTS13 activity was reduced at 8% with normal antibody levels. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal cell count and protein. SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed by RT-PCR. Chest CT showed bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities without pulmonary embolism. Fourteen hours after presentation, he developed severe hypoxia (SpO2/FiO2 100) and septic shock, necessitating intubation and ICU transfer, where he received ARDS-net ventilation, prone positioning, antiviral agents, broad-spectrum antibiotics, vasopressors, hydrocortisone, and prophylactic anticoagulation.

A 20-year-old male student with no history of allergies or prior drug reactions was referred with a 1-month history of fever, decreased appetite, and headache, and a 4-day history of purpuric skin lesions. He had been diagnosed with tubercular meningitis and had received daily streptomycin 0.7 g intramuscularly, rifampicin 450 mg, isoniazid 300 mg, ethambutol 800 mg, and pyrazinamide 1500 mg orally for the preceding 14 days. 

On examination, he was afebrile with normal vital signs. There were multiple discrete erythematous purpuric rashes over the trunk and extremities. There was no lymphadenopathy or clubbing. 

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.0 g/dL, leukocyte count 8800/mm3 with a normal differential, normal renal and liver function tests, bleeding time 7 min, clotting time 13 min, and a platelet count of 40 000/mm3. He was seronegative for HIV and HBsAg, the Widal test was negative, and antinuclear antibodies were negative. A strongly positive Mantoux test showed 22 mm induration.

A 41-year-old White-British woman presented with intermittent swelling of the left parotid gland for 3 years, associated with tenderness and pruritus. She also reported recurrent urticarial and eczematous lesions on the trunk and limbs. Her medical history included hay fever, childhood atopic eczema, and hypothyroidism. On examination, the left parotid gland was slightly enlarged and tender; intraoral findings were normal. Urticated erythematous plaques and papules were present on the trunk and limbs. 

An external parotid biopsy showed benign lymphoid aggregates with follicular hyperplasia of intra- and peri-parotid lymph nodes. Laboratory studies, including inflammatory markers, renal function, autoimmune screen, serum ACE, protein electrophoresis, and viral serology, were unremarkable; allergen patch testing was negative. Ultrasonography of the parotid gland indicated sialadenitis, and sialography demonstrated normal unstimulated flow. Sjögren’s syndrome was excluded. The patient received a course of co-amoxiclav and metronidazole for presumed chronic sialadenitis and was started on cetirizine for presumed chronic urticaria, but her symptoms persisted after one year. 

Sialoendoscopy with corticosteroid washout provided limited benefit. A PET scan demonstrated increased uptake in the left parotid gland and bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. Biopsies of cervical lymph nodes and cutaneous lesions were non-specific, showing no obvious pathology. CT imaging revealed multifocal soft tissue abnormality in the left parotid gland with enlarged left cervical and superficial supraclavicular lymph nodes. Laboratory studies at this time showed a serum IgE level of 541 KU/L (normal 0–81) and an eosinophil count of 0.9 ×10^9/L (normal 0.0–0.4).

A 27-year-old primiparous woman at 37 weeks of gestation presented with severe right lumbar pain of 6 hours’ duration. She had no significant medical history and had been followed regularly during her pregnancy. On examination, her BMI was 29 kg/m2; she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Abdominal palpation revealed tenderness in the right lumbar region. Vaginal examination showed a long, closed, posterior cervix. Laboratory studies were normal, and a urinary culture was negative. Transabdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a single live fetus in cephalic presentation, appropriate in size, a posterior placenta without signs of detachment, no dilation of the renal collecting system, and a 7.5 cm hemorrhagic cystic structure adjacent to the right adnexa, likely of ovarian origin. Adnexal torsion was suspected.

A 1½-year-old boy presented with a 6-month history of progressive swelling over the right wrist and three discharging sinuses on the dorsal, volar, and ulnar aspects. Initial swelling developed after removal of a sacred thread from the wrist; one month later, purulent volar discharge prompted local debridement and a 1-month course of IV cefpodoxime, followed by IV linezolid for inadequate response. Two additional sinuses then appeared, and he was referred for persistent discharge.

On examination, he appeared well. There was a partially healed, indurated circumferential scar at the wrist with three subcentimetric sinuses exuding minimal seropurulent fluid and exuberant granulation tissue. The hand was swollen and erythematous. He demonstrated active finger movements but had a pointing index, suggesting median nerve palsy. Capillary refill was brisk.

Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 9500/mm3, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 32 mm/h, and a C-reactive protein level of 5.2 mg/L. Plain radiographs of the wrist were unremarkable. MRI of the wrist revealed diffuse synovial thickening and effusion in the intercarpal and wrist joints, bony erosions in these areas, and a circular, thin foreign body in the proximal wrist joint with three fistulous tracts extending to the skin.

An 84‐year‐old woman living independently was found on her bedroom floor and brought to the emergency department, complaining of mild diffuse pain (VAS 3/10). She had no recent trauma and a history only of chronic sotalol use. Initial vital signs were: blood pressure 149/61 mm Hg, pulse 60 beats/min, oxygen saturation 98%, and temperature 35.4 °C. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Neurologically, she was alert and oriented with normal speech, although communication was limited by hearing loss; she could not recall a fall. The right foot and lower leg were cold, with delayed capillary refill and absent peripheral pulses. The medial aspect of the left lower leg showed light reddish discoloration without blisters or crepitus; pulses were palpable and temperature was normal. Both hips were painful on movement, and posterior skin and spine examination revealed no abnormalities.

Initial arterial blood gases and labs (returned within 1 hour) showed hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL, lactate 2.3 mmol/L, urea 80.6 mg/dL, and creatinine 2.2 mg/dL. Arterial thrombosis of the right leg was suspected, and fluid resuscitation per contrast‐nephropathy protocol was started in preparation for imaging. Subsequent labs demonstrated elevated troponin T (0.037 ng/mL), NT‐proBNP (34 600 pg/mL), D‐dimer (> 8000 ng/mL), C‐reactive protein (205 mg/L), creatine kinase (1757 U/L), lactate dehydrogenase (365 U/L), and AST (55 U/L). At 17:15, an extended CT scan (thorax, abdomen, and limbs) was performed. On re‐evaluation, the left leg discoloration had progressed to a near‐circumferential purple hue with bullae formation. She received intravenous amoxicillin–clavulanate, and her mental status declined to GCS 14 (E4, V4, M6). CT images demonstrated a polypoid mass at the ileocecal valve; gas surrounding the right iliac vessels; gas in the retroperitoneal space most pronounced at L5–S1; gas bubbles in the right popliteal artery; and gas within muscle compartments of both lower legs.

A 22-year-old Saudi Arabian man with no known chronic illnesses presented with 12 days of pleuritic chest pain, exertional dyspnea, hemoptysis, subjective fever, and sweating. He reported no leg pain or swelling. Over the previous 4 months, he had recurrent painful oral aphthous ulcers lasting 3–5 days and recurrent painful genital ulcers on the scrotum. He also noted an 8-kg weight loss over 6 months.  
Vital signs: temperature 37.4 °C; blood pressure 126/70 mmHg; heart rate 110 bpm; respiratory rate 20/min; oxygen saturation 95% on room air; BMI 19 kg/m2.  
Examination revealed three small tender ulcers on the oral mucosa and base of tongue, and one minor tender nonpurulent ulcer on the scrotum. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies: WBC 13.7 × 10^9/L (68% neutrophils), hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, platelets 337 × 10^9/L, INR 1.1, D-dimer 0.04 mg/L, ESR 78 mm/h, CRP 10.9 mg/dL. Renal, hepatic, and electrolyte panels were normal.  
Screening tests for ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-cardiolipin antibodies, HBV, HCV, Brucella serology and culture, and HIV were negative. Tuberculin skin test was 8 mm, and three sputum specimens for AFB smear, TB PCR, and GeneXpert were negative.  
Chest radiograph and transthoracic echocardiogram were unremarkable. Fundus examination showed bilateral vitreous degeneration and acute posterior uveitis. Abdominal Doppler ultrasound demonstrated a 13-cm nonthrombosed but enlarged spleen; hepatic, portal, mesenteric, and splenic veins were patent.  
Contrast-enhanced CT pulmonary angiography revealed crescentic filling defects in the right interlobar and lower lobar segmental arteries without evidence of aneurysm. A ventilation-perfusion scan confirmed multiple perfusion defects in right middle and lower lobe segments.

A 50-year-old postmenopausal Congolese refugee woman (gravida 9, para 8) presented within 30 days of arrival in the U.S. with years of intermittent lower abdominal pain and discomfort, chronic dyspepsia, and a gurgling sensation after eating. Her pre-resettlement health records listed “Calcified Abdominal Pregnancy and Essential Hypertension,” noting fetal biometry consistent with 28 weeks’ gestation at time of demise. She reported eight prior spontaneous vaginal deliveries (three neonates died shortly after birth) and a ninth pregnancy 9 years earlier complicated by preterm fetal demise; she declined intervention and no products of conception were ever passed, resulting in a persistent abdominal mass. Her only medical history was untreated hypertension; she had no surgeries and denied medications. She had no genitourinary or constitutional symptoms; her last menstrual period was 2 years prior. Socially, she had experienced multiple years in refugee camps, spoke limited Swahili, and had low literacy. 

On examination, blood pressure was 162/83 mm Hg. A firm, mobile, non‐tender lower abdominal mass measuring approximately 15 × 20 cm was palpated. The patient recounted that after fetal demise was diagnosed in the camp, she was accused of “evil works” and refused further care.

One week later, she presented to the emergency department with nausea and intractable vomiting. Laboratory testing showed hypokalemia (potassium 3 mmol/L). Abdominal radiography revealed a fetal skeleton and mild small-bowel distention. She was admitted for observation but declined oral intake. She disclosed prior episodes of bowel obstruction treated conservatively in the refugee camp. Serum β-hCG was negative, and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 71 ml/min per 1.73 m2 (stage 2 CKD). 

Abdominopelvic CT with oral and intravenous contrast demonstrated calcified fetal bony parts in the anterior lower abdomen and upper pelvis, possibly external to the uterus, with associated dilated loops of small bowel consistent with obstruction and compression of the inferior vena cava with pelvic venous collaterals.

A 32-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of an intensely pruritic eruption on his back. He noted the onset after lying on a rock in Thailand; a stinging sensation developed immediately, progressing to severe nocturnal itching (8/10 on a numeric scale). Pimple-like lesions appeared the next day. Initial treatment with prednisolone 15 mg, oral antihistamines, and calamine lotion provided mild relief but new lesions continued to emerge. One month after onset he was examined: there were hyperpigmented patches, erythematous papules and plaques on the back, and in some areas atypical serpiginous patterns were observed. He had no significant medical history. Laboratory tests were ordered (complete blood count, ESR, IgE), and his prednisolone dose was increased to 40 mg daily with antihistamines and topical emollients. One week later he reported marked improvement in itching, but new lesions still appeared. Results showed elevated total white blood cells, eosinophils, and IgE levels.

A 25-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of dull, aching pain in the right groin that was insidious in onset, gradually progressive, nonradiating, aggravated by walking and squatting, and relieved by rest and medications. He noted an abduction gait and progressive restriction of right hip motion. There was no history of trauma. On examination, the skin over the medial right groin was unremarkable, and no sinus, scar, or swelling was present. A firm mass was palpable in the right perineal region. Active adduction of the right hip was limited to 20°, external rotation to 25°, internal rotation to 10°, and extension to 5°. Thigh muscle circumference on the right was decreased by 2 cm compared with the left. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, serum calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone, and alkaline phosphatase, were within normal limits. An anteroposterior pelvis radiograph showed a well-corticated bony protuberance arising from the right ischium and extending toward the lesser trochanter, with no evidence of joint degeneration. Computed tomography with three-dimensional reconstruction confirmed a 5.2 × 2.0 cm bone formation between the right ischial tuberosity and lesser trochanter. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated surrounding marrow edema but no cartilage cap.

A 35-year-old woman with no prior medical or psychiatric history presented with a 6-week history of intermittent severe headaches, blurred vision, and left-hand numbness. She also endorsed night sweats, fatigue, and neck and back muscle pain. One month before referral, she developed acute agitation, shouting, confusion, disorientation, and inappropriate speech. 

She first went to an emergency department, where CT of the head, brain MRI, ECG, and CBC were normal; she was diagnosed with anxiety and discharged. When her symptoms persisted, she was admitted to psychiatry for an acute confusional state; repeat CT, MRI, MR venography, and MR angiography were all unremarkable. She was treated with quetiapine, citalopram, and mirtazapine, improved temporarily, and was discharged with a diagnosis of conversion disorder, although she had amnesia for the admission period.

Ten days later, she was evaluated in a neurology clinic. She denied fever, travel, raw meat or unpasteurized dairy ingestion, and animal contact. On examination, she was afebrile, alert, and oriented with a normal neurologic examination. 

Laboratory studies showed WBC 6.4×10^3/μL, hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL (microcytic hypochromic), platelets 281×10^3/μL, CRP 4.7 mg/L. Autoimmune screening (ANA, lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin) was negative. Brain CT, MRI, and MRV were normal. 

CSF analysis revealed 27 leukocytes/μL (100% lymphocytes), protein 24 mg/dL, glucose 95 mg/dL, Gram stain negative, culture negative, cytology negative. FilmArray meningitis/encephalitis panel was negative.

A 16-year-old girl presented with severe lower abdominal pain each month since age 15, requiring school absence. Menarche was at 13 years with regular cycles. On examination, speculum inspection revealed a single cervix and no vaginal septum.
