Transvaginal ultrasonography showed two uterine hemi-bodies, each containing blood consistent with hematometra; the kidneys were normal. Pelvic MRI demonstrated two endometrial cavities divided by an asymmetrical septum, with a 5 cm hematometra in the left cavity, and an external fundal contour that was flat to slightly concave. Hysteroscopy identified the right fallopian tube ostium but no communication to the left cavity. Hysterosalpingography confirmed patency of the right tube with contrast filling only the right hemi-uterine cavity and none in the left.

A 35-year-old man presented with over 10 years of chronic rhinorrhea and sneezing, and 13 months of recurrent cough and asthma episodes. Beginning in 2006, he had morning-predominant serous nasal discharge and cough diagnosed as allergic rhinitis and treated with intranasal corticosteroids, systemic antihistamines, bilateral turbinectomies, and montelukast without improvement. In 2016, progressive cough and adventitious lung sounds led to a diagnosis of bronchial asthma treated with budesonide–formoterol, but exercise-induced bronchospasm prompted hospitalization. His history also included untreated hypertension (recorded as high as 190/110 mmHg), bilateral inferior turbinectomies (2012, 2016), and left facial neuritis in 2015 resulting in facial paralysis. He was admitted with lobular pneumonia and right middle lobe bronchiectasis.

On examination, temperature was 36.2 °C, pulse 85/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and blood pressure 145/94 mmHg. He was alert, well-nourished, and ambulated independently but had left-sided facial nerve palsy. Cardiorespiratory, abdominal, and skin examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 8.7×10^9/L with eosinophils 18.8% (1.6×10^9/L). Spirometry demonstrated FVC 3.94 L (79.7% predicted), FEV1 2.89 L (70.4% predicted), and an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.79 with a 19.9% increase in FEV1 after 400 µg salbutamol. Fractional exhaled nitric oxide was 165 ppb. Skin allergy testing was negative, but total serum IgE was elevated at 772.25 IU/mL.

During hospitalization, leukocytes were 7.4×10^9/L with eosinophils 18.7% (1.4×10^9/L). Autoantibodies (MPO, PR3, c-ANCA, p-ANCA) were negative. Serum procalcitonin, beta-D-glucan, and Aspergillus galactomannan antigen were within normal limits. Chest CT before admission showed patchy opacities in the right middle lobe; repeat CT post-admission was normal. Paranasal sinus CT revealed bilateral sinusitis and inferior turbinate hypertrophy.

Bronchoscopy revealed smooth bronchial mucosa without pathogens; mucosal biopsy showed chronic inflammation with mild eosinophilic infiltration. Cardiac emission CT demonstrated localized perfusion defects in the left ventricular apex, anterior, and inferior walls, consistent with myocarditis, with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 61%.

A 48-year-old woman underwent dual liver and kidney transplantation on day 0 for autosomal dominant polycystic kidney and liver disease. The immediate postoperative course in the ICU included resolution of a right-sided haemothorax confirmed on CT. She was extubated on day 9. That same day, a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) was placed via the left basilic vein for total parenteral nutrition (TPN); chest radiography confirmed the tip in the subclavian vein and TPN was started. Thirty-six hours later she noted mild voice changes and shortness of breath. The PICC could not be aspirated and was presumed occluded but left in place. Over the next 24 hours her voice quality further altered, she developed dysphagia, chest pain, tachypnea (18–25 breaths/min), and hypoxemia (SpO2 91–93% on Hudson mask). An urgent CT angiogram of the neck, chest, and abdomen demonstrated a mediastinal collection, mediastinal emphysema, and extensive retropharyngeal air tracking; the report noted that the PICC line was “not convincingly intravascular and appeared to be outside the great vessels.” A barium swallow was thought to show a communication between the oesophagus and trachea.

A 10-month-old boy was referred for evaluation of pustules and crusts localized to the scalp. The rash had been treated as impetigo with oral phenoxymethylpenicillin and dicloxacillin for 14 days without improvement; a bacterial swab was negative. One week after completing antibiotics, the rash recurred, and he was readmitted and given oral flucloxacillin for 10 days despite two further negative bacterial swabs. On day 10 of the second course, he experienced a flare and was switched to intravenous dicloxacillin in combination with a high-potency topical steroid. A peripheral blood sample showed an eosinophil count of 4.2 × 10^9/L (normal <0.5 × 10^9/L). After 3 days of intravenous therapy, new pustules appeared. Dermatologic examination revealed a few pustules and postinflammatory hyperpigmented areas on the scalp and several papules on the right ankle. An examination for fungi and a punch biopsy were performed.

A 74-year-old retired government official with no prior history of diabetes presented with fever, disorientation, fruity breath odor, fatigue, oliguria, and severe weakness. He was found to have diabetic ketoacidosis and treated in the emergency department; an HbA1c level was 15%. He had a history of ischemic heart disease with coronary stents placed 8 years earlier. 

On hospital day 2, he complained of right knee pain with hamstring spasm. The pain and spasm progressed, and by day 6 the knee was held at 30° of flexion with a marked inverted horseshoe–shaped effusion, warmth, tenderness along the joint line, and erythema. A complete blood count showed a total leukocyte count of 6000 per mm3 (35% lymphocytes, 64% neutrophils), and C-reactive protein was 73 mg/L.

An ultrasound-guided aspiration yielded 40 mL of deeply turbid yellow fluid with a cobweb-like coagulum. Gram stain, India ink, and acid-fast bacilli stain were negative, and aerobic, anaerobic, fungal, and BACTEC cultures showed no growth. Fluid analysis revealed marked leukocytosis with 90% polymorphonuclear cells. 

He received intravenous paracetamol and empiric linezolid but had little improvement in range of motion despite repeated aspiration, compression, ice, anti-inflammatory medications, and below-knee traction. Repeat ultrasound 2 days later showed a fibrotic synovial lining and frond-like projections, consistent with chronic synovial pathology. 

Further history revealed a 6-kg weight loss over 9 months, anorexia, exertional fatigue, and conjunctival pallor. Chest examination and radiograph were normal. A similar synovial swelling developed in the ipsilateral ankle. Cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification testing of synovial fluid was negative on two occasions, and MRI was contraindicated by his pacemaker. A planned synovial biopsy was deferred due to concerns about wound healing in the context of diabetes.

A 79-year-old Caucasian man with essential hypertension, diet-controlled type 2 diabetes, and stage 3 chronic kidney disease (baseline creatinine 1.3–1.7 mg/dL, no prior proteinuria) presented in November 2016 with new-onset nephrotic-range proteinuria and hematuria and acute kidney injury. Three weeks earlier, hydralazine had been started for blood-pressure control. On evaluation, serum creatinine rose from a baseline of 1.5 mg/dL in June 2016 to 1.9 mg/dL in October and 2.6 mg/dL in November. Twenty-four-hour urine protein was 5.24 g, and urinalysis showed hematuria. A CT urogram showed no obstruction or stones. Immunologic studies revealed a positive antihistone antibody and a highly positive anti–double-stranded DNA antibody titer of 1:2560; complement levels were normal. Tests for cytoplasmic ANCA and perinuclear ANCA, anti–glomerular basement membrane antibodies, serum protein electrophoresis, cryoglobulins, and anti–smooth muscle antibodies were negative.

A 45-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with a one-week history of generalized abdominal pain, jaundice, dark urine, and lower-extremity edema. He denied alcohol use for 20 years, intravenous drug use, or medication use other than a multivitamin. On examination he was afebrile with a pulse of 95/min, respiratory rate 16/min, and SpO2 95% on room air. He was cachectic and markedly jaundiced with scleral icterus and proptosis. His thyroid was symmetrically enlarged with an audible bruit. His cardiac rhythm was irregularly irregular; skin was warm with a fine tremor and intermittent asterixis. Abdominal examination revealed diffuse mild tenderness without ascites or organomegaly; bilateral lower-extremity edema was present.

Laboratory evaluation showed hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, platelets 115×10^3/µL, leukocytes 11.8×10^3/µL, INR 2.4, sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, creatinine 1.77 mg/dL, BUN 57 mg/dL, and glucose 159 mg/dL. Liver tests revealed total bilirubin 19.8 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 13.8 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 332 U/L, AST 86 U/L, ALT 50 U/L, and γ-glutamyltransferase 20 U/L. Iron studies and ferritin were normal; hepatitis A, B, and C serologies were negative.

Thyroid studies showed TSH 0.026 µg/mL, free T4 4.3 ng/dL, free T3 4.6 pg/mL, TSH receptor antibody >40 IU/L, and thyroid peroxidase antibody >1000 IU/mL. Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a mildly enlarged, heterogeneous, hypervascular gland without nodules. Cardiac evaluation revealed an ejection fraction of 55–60% with right ventricular dilation, valvular regurgitation, atrial enlargement, and elevated central venous and pulmonary artery pressures. Abdominal ultrasound showed increased hepatic echogenicity and trace ascites; CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated fatty liver, cardiomegaly, and diffuse irregular trabecular bone appearance. ERCP and EUS showed normal intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts without obstruction. A transjugular liver biopsy revealed cholestasis and mild ductal proliferation with focal pericholangitis but no steatosis, fibrosis, hepatocellular injury, or necrosis; glycogen content and iron stores were normal.

A 10-year-old girl presented with a 1-month history of gradually increasing swelling in the left parotid region, associated with mild pain and difficulty eating. There was no fever, cough, weight loss, trauma, or known exposure to tuberculosis. She reported no other systemic symptoms. She had lived in a hostel for the past 2 years.

On examination, she was thin, pale, and her weight was below the 2nd percentile for age. A well-defined, firm, vertically mobile, nontender mass measuring 7 cm × 6 cm was palpable at the left angle of the jaw, with a smooth overlying skin surface and no sinus. Multiple small (≈1 cm), mobile, nonmatted cervical lymph nodes were present on the left. No other lymphadenopathy was noted. The right parotid region was unremarkable.

Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, total leukocyte count 5600/mm3 (40% neutrophils, 52% lymphocytes), and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 64 mm/hr. Ultrasonography of the swelling revealed a 180 cc hypoechoic lesion with septations and debris, suggestive of an abscess. As there were no clinical signs of inflammation, a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the neck was performed, which demonstrated an abscess involving the left temporalis and masseter muscles, the left parotid and submandibular glands, and bony destruction of the anterior border of the left mandibular ramus.

A 63-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and a remote cerebrovascular accident with minimal residual weakness has been on twice-weekly maintenance hemodialysis for 2 years. He presented with a 1-month history of decreased speech output and difficulty walking, and over the preceding 2 weeks he developed progressive sensorium impairment, tiredness, drowsiness, and weakness. He had no fever, headache, or new focal neurological deficits. His last dialysis session was 2 days before admission.

On examination, he was drowsy and mute. Vital signs were: pulse 56/min, blood pressure 180/90 mm Hg, SpO₂ 99% on room air, afebrile, and he appeared anemic. Neurologic evaluation revealed mild right-sided limb weakness, asterixis, rigidity of all limbs, and bradykinesia.

Laboratory studies showed: blood urea nitrogen 19.63 mmol/L; serum creatinine 609 μmol/L; sodium 138 mmol/L; potassium 4.8 mmol/L; hemoglobin 104 g/L; WBC count 4.9 × 10³/mm³; platelets 90 × 10³/mm³; serum ammonia 25 μmol/L; bilirubin 10.26 μmol/L; ALT 0.47 μkat/L; CRP 10.48 nmol/L; alkaline phosphatase 4.01 μkat/L; viral markers negative. Venous blood gas revealed pH 7.28, HCO₃⁻ 17.9 mmol/L, PCO₂ 38 mm Hg; lactate was 7.1 mmol/L.

Noncontrast CT of the brain showed hypodensity in the bilateral basal ganglia. MRI of the brain (T2/FLAIR) demonstrated hyperintensity in the bilateral basal ganglia region, consistent with the “lentiform fork sign.” Review of his medication list revealed long-term use of metformin prescribed at his hemodialysis unit.

A 37-year-old Iraqi man presented with a 2-year history of progressive dyspnea on exertion and dry cough. He was afebrile. He reported two prior episodes (at 2 years and 1 month before admission) of severe dyspnea and hypoxemia; chest radiographs on both occasions showed a left pneumothorax, managed with tube thoracostomy. He had served in the military and worked as a carpenter. Body-mass index was 21 kg/m2; resting oxygen saturation was 97% on room air.

On examination, the thorax was flattened with decreased breath sounds on the left. Arterial blood gases showed pH 7.43, PaCO2 40 mm Hg, PaO2 84 mm Hg. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 5350/μL, neutrophils 60%, lymphocytes 30%, monocytes 5.8%, eosinophils 2.1%, hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, hematocrit 40%, creatinine 0.4 mg/dL, TSH 0.51 mIU/L, and free T4 11.53 pmol/L. A transthoracic echocardiogram was unremarkable. Tests for purified protein derivative, antinuclear antibodies, and rheumatoid factor were negative.

Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery was performed for decortication of fibrous tissue and a wedge biopsy from the right apex. Histopathological examination showed prominent interstitial fibrosis involving the subpleural and deeper lung parenchyma with only limited islands of normal tissue, dense fibroelastotic scarring without active fibroblastic foci, occasional dilated airspaces, and ectatic lymphatic spaces in the subpleural fibrotic parenchyma. No granulomatous tissue was detected.

A 50-year-old Korean man presented with a 2-month history of an enlarging nodule on his frontal scalp. He played soccer regularly and frequently struck the ball with his frontal scalp; he recalled a forceful bump a few days before the nodule appeared. His medical history was unremarkable, and a review of systems was negative.

On examination, there was a 5 × 5 cm, well-demarcated, dome-shaped, salmon-colored, waxy nodule on the frontal scalp, with overlying purpuric plaques and mild tenderness. 

Punch biopsies were obtained from both the salmon-colored and purpuric areas. Histopathologic examination showed follicular plugging, thinning and flattening of the stratum malpighii, and deposition of acellular amorphous eosinophilic material throughout the dermis. There was a mild to moderate perivascular and interstitial lymphocytic infiltrate with plasma cells, mast cells, and a few eosinophils, along with focal interstitial mucin.

Congo red staining exhibited apple-green birefringence under polarized light. Electron microscopy demonstrated uniform, long, straight filaments.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, blood chemistry, and urinalysis, were within normal limits; the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 14 mm/hr (reference, 0–9 mm/hr). A chest radiograph and electrocardiogram were unremarkable. Antinuclear and anti–SS-A/SS-B antibodies were negative. Serum and urine protein electrophoresis were normal.

A 28-year-old man presented with progressive left nasal obstruction and foul-smelling nasal discharge for 5 years, worsening over the past 3 years. He had received multiple courses of antibiotics and intranasal steroids without relief. He denied any history of inserting objects into his nose but recalled a childhood head injury in a sandy environment. On anterior rhinoscopy, there was an irregular, hard mass surrounded by thick crusts and secretions, lodged between a septal spur and the inferior turbinate in the left anterior nasal cavity; attempts at removal in the clinic caused minor bleeding. Plain radiographs and CT scanning revealed a dense, irregular, calcified-appearing mass occupying the floor of the left nasal cavity, without extension beyond the nasal cavity.

A 57-year-old man presented with a 10-year history of symmetrical papules and indurated nodules on both upper limbs accompanied by intense itching. He was initially diagnosed with “eczema” at a local hospital and treated intermittently with topical and systemic corticosteroids without improvement. Five years ago, the lesions gradually spread over the trunk and head, with the appearance of indurated erythema and infiltrative plaques, worsened pruritus, and exudation. A skin biopsy of trunk and neck lesions led to a diagnosis of atopic dermatitis (pruritic rash type). The patient denied any history of sexually transmitted disease.

On examination, there were scattered 2.0–4.0-cm reddish to dark erythematous infiltrative plaques on the head; the lesions were isolated, nonconfluent, and showed loss of central hair. The trunk and extremities exhibited numerous well-demarcated, indurated papules and nodules without coalescence. A few 1.0–2.0-cm non-tender cervical lymph nodes were palpable; there was no hepatosplenomegaly.

Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 12.8×10^9/L, absolute neutrophils 8.75×10^9/L, eosinophils 1.40×10^9/L, IgE 8988 IU/mL, rheumatoid factor 55.8 IU/mL, IgG4 5682.6 mg/L, IgG 23.39 g/L, and a positive homogeneous antinuclear antibody titer of 1:80. Tests for antinuclear antibodies, parasite antibodies, treponema pallidum antibody, HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were all negative. Other hematological, biochemical, and tumor marker tests were within normal limits.

In February 2017, a skin biopsy of the trunk showed lymphohistiocytic and eosinophilic infiltrates around blood vessels and hair follicles in the superficial dermis. In April 2021, a posterior neck nodule biopsy demonstrated focal parakeratosis, acanthosis, pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, focal edema, and sparse lymphohistiocytes and eosinophils around superficial dermal vessels, leading to a diagnosis of prurigo nodularis.

A woman in her 40s presented with a 3-day history of bilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, dizziness, and painful left head flexion. She had been seen twice in the prior 48 hours and discharged with symptomatic therapy only.  
On otolaryngological examination, there was bilateral tympanic‐membrane perforation and right eardrum hyperemia without signs of acute infection; vestibular testing was limited by neck pain but showed no spontaneous nystagmus.  
Pure‐tone audiometry revealed mixed hearing loss at low and mid frequencies and sensorineural loss at high frequencies bilaterally.  
Initial head CT and neurologic consultation were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis and elevated C-reactive protein, and she was started on oral amoxicillin/clavulanate.  
Overnight, she developed a right facial palsy (House–Brackmann grade II progressing to III). Repeat head CT ruled out vascular events. Therapy was changed to intravenous methylprednisolone, valaciclovir, and ceftriaxone, and she was admitted.  
Neck pain improved over the next 2 days, but her hearing loss and facial palsy persisted. A high-resolution ear CT showed no dehiscence of the facial‐nerve canal. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI demonstrated symmetrical, bilateral pathological enhancement of the distal intracanalicular, intralabyrinthine segments, geniculate ganglion, and tympanic tract of the facial nerves.

A 59-year-old woman with tumor-stage cutaneous T-cell lymphoma presented with fevers and new leg ulcers. Seven days earlier, she had been discharged after treatment of aseptic thrombophlebitis of the right upper extremity with vancomycin and cefepime for 7 days. Her CTCL had been diagnosed in 2000 on the basis of patches on her thighs and a positive clonal T-cell receptor gene rearrangement; treatments over the years included topical steroids, photochemotherapy, acitretin, methotrexate, bexarotene, romidepsin, denileukin diftitox, vorinostat, six cycles of EPOCH chemotherapy, total-body electron beam radiation, an autologous stem-cell transplant, and gemcitabine infusions.

On examination, there were two annular ulcerative plaques with pseudovesicular borders, each measuring 4 × 4 cm on the left medial calf, and a larger, severely painful, rapidly enlarging ulceration with pseudovesicular borders measuring 13 × 9 cm on the right medial calf. These lesions were not present at the time of her discharge 7 days before.

Two 4-mm punch biopsy specimens were obtained from the right medial calf, with half of each specimen sent for hematoxylin–eosin staining and half for tissue culture. Histologic examination showed a diffuse infiltrate of neutrophils in the dermis extending to the subcutis. Immunohistochemical stains showed no evidence of lymphoma. Stains and tissue cultures for fungi, bacteria, and mycobacteria were normal. Laboratory studies revealed a C-reactive protein level of 322 mg/L (reference range, <2.90 mg/L) and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 75 mm/h (reference range, 0–20 mm/h) as the only abnormalities.

A 32-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a persistent resting heart rate of up to 140 bpm. He reported intermittent bilateral knee pain and swelling but denied palpitations or syncope. Three months earlier he had found an engorged tick on his left knee; Lyme serology at that time was negative. One week after the tick bite he developed a bull’s-eye rash over the posterior left knee that resolved with ibuprofen.  

On presentation he was afebrile, heart rate 143 bpm, blood pressure 122/78 mm Hg. Examination revealed only a small area of hyperpigmentation at the left knee; no rash or tick was seen. Laboratory studies, including CBC, metabolic panel, toxicology screen, and thyroid function tests, were normal. Echocardiogram showed normal ventricular function and no structural disease. Chest radiograph was unremarkable.  

Telemetry and serial ECGs were obtained. Initial ECG showed a narrow-complex tachycardia with retrograde P waves and short RP intervals, consistent with AV nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT). Intravenous adenosine (2 doses), IV diltiazem, and IV metoprolol failed to terminate the tachycardia. A diltiazem infusion was also ineffective. The patient was transitioned to oral metoprolol and given one dose of flecainide, resulting in brief conversion to sinus rhythm with evidence of first- and second-degree AV block (PR intervals 240–320 ms). He was then started on propafenone and continued metoprolol, which achieved more sustained rate and rhythm control.

A 40-year-old Caucasian woman with hypertension presented with a 4-month history of constant rocking and swaying sensations that began a few hours after returning from a one-week ship cruise. She described her symptoms as worse when lying still at bedtime or upon awakening and notably improved with motion, such as driving. She denied nausea, vomiting, headache, diplopia, tinnitus, hearing loss, or vertigo. Her medical history included hypertension (on lisinopril), acid reflux, and remote cholecystectomy. She did not smoke or use alcohol or illicit drugs. On examination, vital signs were stable and the physical and neurologic evaluations were unremarkable, with no signs of depression. The patient had received empirical treatments for motion sickness (meclizine, scopolamine) and a low-dose steroid course for possible labyrinthitis without benefit. Videonystagmography (VNG) and vestibular evoked myogenic potential (VEMP) testing were normal. All laboratory studies were within normal limits. CT and MRI of the head showed no abnormalities.

A 42-year-old woman with no significant past medical or family history presented with a 5-day history of progressive neurologic symptoms that began after emotional stress. Initial symptoms included bradykinesia, motor stereotypies, ataxia, bruxism, mutism, dysphagia, and urinary incontinence. She was treated for presumed conversion disorder with benzodiazepines and promethazine but continued to deteriorate and had two generalized seizures.

On admission, she was hemodynamically stable with normal respiratory status but was disoriented and unable to follow commands (GCS score of 10: eye opening to pain, localizing painful stimuli, inappropriate words). Pupils were mid-sized, equal, and reactive. Examination revealed bilateral Babinski signs, spasticity of all limbs, and hyperactive deep tendon reflexes (4+ in the upper extremities, 3+ in the lower extremities). Formal cerebellar and sensory testing were not possible due to lack of cooperation.

Brain MRI showed multiple confluent high-signal lesions on FLAIR and T2 in the bilateral frontoparietal white matter and corpus callosum, with peripheral edema and diffusion restriction. Post-contrast images demonstrated nodular and partial ring enhancement of oval lesions arranged perpendicular to the lateral ventricles. Cervical spine MRI and CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis were unremarkable. Toxicology screening was negative except for benzodiazepines.

Laboratory studies revealed a serum magnesium level of 1.5 mg/dL (normal 1.9–2.5) and C-reactive protein 11 mg/L (normal 0–6). HIV and hepatitis B/C serologies were negative. CSF analysis showed 12 heterologous oligoclonal bands with none in serum and evidence of intrathecal IgG synthesis. CSF cell counts, chemistry, Gram stain, culture, and HSV PCR were unremarkable. Paraneoplastic and autoimmune encephalitis antibody panels in serum and CSF were negative except for a mildly elevated cardiolipin IgM antibody. EEG demonstrated generalized background slowing without epileptiform discharges or delta brushes.

A 32-year-old man with no significant medical history presented for evaluation of chronic headaches. He was afebrile, with stable vital signs, and initial laboratory studies were unremarkable. Noncontrast CT of the head showed an indeterminate lytic defect in the bony clivus with a well-demarcated, smoothly corticated margin, raising concern for an underlying malignancy. Subsequent MRI of the brain with and without contrast revealed a well-defined midline retroclival cystic lesion measuring 5 × 12 mm that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and followed cerebrospinal fluid signal on T2-FLAIR. The lesion did not restrict diffusion and did not demonstrate any abnormal contrast enhancement.

A 35-year-old woman with a 5-year history of primary infertility treated with letrozole presented at 37 days of gestation with a 10-day history of painless vaginal bleeding. Her vital signs were stable, and serum β‐hCG was 6000 IU/L. On examination, the abdomen was soft and non-tender; speculum examination revealed less bleeding than a menstrual period and a completely closed cervix; Hegar’s and Chadwick’s signs were positive. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed a gestational sac containing a yolk sac and an embryonic pole with positive fetal heart rate located near the internal os at the beginning of the cervical canal. The crown–rump length was 4 mm, endometrial thickness was normal, and most of the sac was seen in the proximal cervix. Therefore, cervical pregnancy was diagnosed, and the patient was hospitalized for further treatment.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of a painful, palpable mass in the lower quadrants of her left breast. The mass was tender to palpation, had developed a fistulous tract to the overlying skin, and there was no history of trauma. Ultrasound of the left breast revealed three lesions measuring 35 mm, 15 mm, and 8 mm in the lower quadrant, communicating with a superficial areolar abscess collection and forming a fistulous path to the skin. This ultrasound appearance was suspicious for suppurative mastitis; although, a necrotic tumor could not be ruled out. An ultrasound-guided needle biopsy demonstrated inflammatory and abscess features of the breast parenchyma without histological signs of malignancy.

A 67-year-old man with hypertension, dyslipidaemia, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, active smoking (35 pack-years), a family history of ischaemic heart disease, and prior percutaneous coronary interventions (2008, 2017, 2022) for non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction presented with Canadian Cardiovascular Society Class III angina. A recent exercise stress test induced angina at 50 W without ECG changes. On admission, he appeared anxious; the physical examination was unremarkable. A 12-lead ECG showed normal sinus rhythm, Q waves in lead III, and biphasic T waves in leads III and aVF. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 65% without regional wall-motion abnormalities. Coronary angiography demonstrated patent stents in the circumflex artery, non-significant disease in the left anterior descending artery, and significant ostial right coronary artery stenosis with in-stent restenosis in the mid-segment, which was treated with three drug-eluting stents. After transfer to the intensive care unit, he complained of worsening chest pain; ECG showed ST-segment elevation in leads V1–V3, and echocardiography remained normal. A second angiogram showed patent stents but subocclusion of the right coronary postero-lateral branch, successfully treated with balloon angioplasty, relieving his pain. Shortly thereafter, he developed recurrent sustained polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation requiring seven external shocks and 15 minutes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Post-resuscitation ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm with persistent precordial ST-segment elevation and new QTc prolongation to 500 ms. Repeat echocardiography revealed akinesia of all apical segments, later extending to mid-segments, hyperkinesia of the basal segments, and severely reduced LVEF of 35%, leading to suspicion of takotsubo syndrome.

A 36-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of palpitations and dyspnea. He had stable vital signs and an unremarkable physical examination. ECG showed sinus rhythm with frequent monomorphic ventricular extrasystoles and negative T waves in the inferior leads. High-sensitivity troponin T was mildly elevated (23–26 ng/L; normal < 13 ng/L). Chest radiography was normal. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed mild left ventricular hypertrophy, preserved ejection fraction, and no segmental wall-motion abnormalities. Continuous monitoring captured symptomatic runs of slow non-sustained ventricular tachycardia. Coronary angiography was normal. Laboratory tests showed normal electrolytes, ferritin, renal and thyroid function; N-terminal pro–brain natriuretic peptide was 55 ng/L; C-reactive protein was mildly elevated at 7.8 mg/L. Despite escalating bisoprolol, he had a hemodynamically tolerated sustained ventricular tachycardia and was started on amiodarone, which reduced the arrhythmic burden. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated moderate left ventricular hypertrophy, preserved ejection fraction, extensive non-ischaemic late gadolinium enhancement in a subepicardial and transmural pattern, and T2-weighted signs of myocardial edema; the right ventricle was non-dilated with mildly reduced function, the pericardium was normal, and subcarinal plus right perihilar adenopathies were noted. An ^18F-FDG PET-CT scan showed multiple supra- and infra-diaphragmatic hypermetabolic lymph nodes and patchy myocardial uptake. He was born in India, moved in 2013, and reported contact with a TB-positive person 2 months before symptom onset. He denied systemic symptoms. A tuberculin skin test and interferon-gamma release assay were positive. Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme was 74 U/L (normal < 60 U/L); HIV testing was negative. Endomyocardial biopsy showed inflammation without granulomas; microbiological stains and cultures, including MT-DNA, were negative. Bronchoalveolar lavage had a CD4:CD8 ratio of 1.2. Fine-needle aspiration of a subcarinal node was inconclusive.

A 75-year-old Chinese woman with hypertension and recent ray’s amputation for osteomyelitis presents asymptomatically with abnormal liver tests on routine follow-up. Two months after completing antibiotics, her labs showed: albumin 34 g/L; bilirubin 20 μmol/L; ALP 803 U/L; ALT 234 U/L; AST 145 U/L; GGT 667 U/L; total leukocyte count 7.75 × 10^9/L; eosinophils 23.1% (1.79 × 10^9/L); IgE 1064 IU/mL. Viral and autoimmune serologies and stool parasite studies were negative. Abdominal ultrasound revealed biliary sludge without gallstones, no biliary dilation (CBD 5 mm), and a prominent pancreatic duct. MRCP showed gallbladder stones without cholecystitis, a 9 mm CBD without obstructing stones or mass, borderline dilatation and strictures in subsegmental ducts with mild periportal edema. Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated a mildly thickened CBD wall that was endosonographically unremarkable and no dilatation of the biliary tree; no intervention was performed.

A 53-year-old man with a 2-year history of Crohn’s disease in clinical remission on mesalazine and azathioprine underwent routine imaging. He denied fever, cough, dyspnea, and gastrointestinal symptoms. Vital signs were normal, and the physical examination was unremarkable.

Chest CT revealed two nodules in the right lung: a 7-mm lesion in the upper lobe and a 20-mm irregular lesion in the lower lobe. PET-CT showed marked uptake in the lower nodule (elevated SUV) and physiologic uptake in the upper nodule. A CT scan 3 months earlier had shown only old inflammatory changes in the right upper lobe.

Bronchoscopy revealed no endobronchial abnormalities. Transbronchial biopsy of the right lower lobe lesion demonstrated granulomas with chronic inflammatory cells around the bronchus and non-obsolete fibrosis; no malignant cells were seen. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and lung tissue cultures were negative for bacteria, mycobacteria, and fungi.

A 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes underwent a screening colonoscopy after a positive fecal occult blood test. Three hours after the procedure he developed right upper-quadrant abdominal pain, but did not seek care until 2 days later because he lived remote from medical services. On presentation he was febrile and tachycardic. Laboratory studies showed neutrophilia, an elevated C-reactive protein level, and mild hyperbilirubinemia; hepatic transaminases were within normal limits. On examination he had focal tenderness and voluntary guarding in the right upper quadrant. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a distended gallbladder with adjacent gas locules and fat stranding around the hepatic flexure of the colon. The leading considerations were a contained microperforation at the hepatic flexure versus emphysematous cholecystitis. He was hemodynamically stable and was treated nonoperatively with intravenous ampicillin, metronidazole, and gentamicin, bowel rest, and aggressive fluid resuscitation.

A 38-year-old white man with Crohn’s disease treated with adalimumab presented with a 1-month history of scalp irritation that was intermittently tender and pruritic. One year earlier, he had an erythema multiforme–like rash with hot and cold sweats; chest radiography at that time suggested right lower-lobe pneumonia, and he received a prednisone taper with rapid symptom resolution. 

On examination, there was a 1.5- to 2-cm adherent yellow-brown crust overlying an indurated, fluctuant plaque on the vertex of the scalp without alopecia; cervical lymphadenopathy was present. A swab for bacterial and fungal cultures grew methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus, and he was treated for bacterial cellulitis with oral cefadroxil and 4% chlorhexidine gluconate shampoo. After 17 days of therapy, and despite the later addition of topical Liquor Carbonis Detergens 20%, the lesion persisted. 

At a 6-month follow-up, there was no improvement. Over the next 3 months, he received oral doxycycline, topical clindamycin lotion, intralesional triamcinolone, and clobetasol shampoo. The plaque continued to enlarge, areas of scarring alopecia developed, and tufts of hair were appreciated. A punch biopsy and tissue cultures for bacteria, atypical mycobacteria, and fungus were performed, and his immunosuppressive therapies were temporarily held.

A 36‐year‐old Iranian man presented with a 1-month history of pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, fatigue, and, over the preceding 10 days, intermittent fevers and chills. The chest pain was sharp, radiated to the left shoulder, worsened when supine, and improved when leaning forward. He described exertional dyspnea corresponding to NYHA class III–IV. He denied rash, alopecia, oral ulcers, arthralgia, or morning stiffness.  

He had no recent infections. A chest CT scan performed by a pulmonologist showed an enlarged cardiac silhouette, severe pericardial effusion, and a mild to moderate left pleural effusion.  

On examination, his temperature was 39.5°C; pulse, 82 bpm; blood pressure, 110/70 mmHg; respiratory rate, 14 breaths/min; and jugular venous pressure was elevated. Heart sounds were muffled; breath sounds were decreased at the left base. He had bilateral 1+ pitting edema of the lower legs. Pulsus paradoxus was absent.  

Electrocardiography showed generalized low QRS voltages. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a large (>4 cm) circumferential pericardial effusion with loculations and fibrin strands (“bread and butter” pattern), pericardial thickening (>1 cm), septal bounce, marked respiratory variations of mitral and tricuspid inflow velocities (>40% and >50%, respectively), annulus reversus on tissue Doppler, septal shift with respiration, and a dilated inferior vena cava without collapse. These findings were consistent with acute fibrinous pericarditis with constrictive physiology.  

Abdominal ultrasonography showed no evidence of malignancy. Laboratory studies demonstrated a leukocyte count of 14,850/µL and elevated CRP and ESR. A tuberculin skin test (PPD) and interferon‐γ release assay were negative. Viral serologies were negative, and investigations for other infectious causes, including tuberculosis, were unremarkable.  

The patient was started on oral ibuprofen 600 mg every 8 hours and colchicine 0.5 mg daily while further evaluation for an immune‐mediated etiology was planned.

A 53-year-old right-handed woman with a 25-year history of hypothyroidism (on levothyroxine), 5-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus (on glibenclamide and ertugliflozin), and 1-year history of megaloblastic anemia (on monthly cyanocobalamin and daily folic acid) presented with 3 weeks of progressive lower extremity weakness. The weakness began in her left leg and involved her right leg over 5 days. She also noted a band-like tightening sensation over her mid-torso, burning pain, tingling, and increased sensitivity to light touch, especially in the left leg. She denied bladder dysfunction, headache, trauma, speech or swallowing difficulty, behavioral changes, or memory loss.

Eighteen months earlier, she had a 3-month history of headaches and painful visual loss in her right eye. Brain MRI at that time showed right pre-chiasmatic optic nerve swelling with contrast enhancement. She was treated with high-dose methylprednisolone followed by an oral prednisone taper, with partial recovery of light perception.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Neurologic examination revealed:
- Glasgow Coma Scale 15 (E4 V4 M6); Mini-Mental Status 25/30  
- Pupils midsized and reactive; right eye visual acuity limited to light perception  
- Motor: upper limbs 5/5 bilaterally; lower limbs 1/5 bilaterally  
- Tone: normotonic in arms; hypotonic in legs  
- Reflexes: 2/4 in arms; 1/4 in legs  
- Sensory level corresponding to mid-thoracic region  

Laboratory studies:
- Complete blood count, electrolytes, renal and liver function tests within reference limits  
- Serum vitamin B12 level normal  
- ANA positive; anti-dsDNA and anti-Ro/La negative; complement levels normal  

Spinal MRI revealed an increased T2 signal extending from C7 throughout the thoracic cord to the distal cord, consistent with longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis.

A 68-year-old Caucasian woman with an 8-year history of typical motor symptoms of Parkinson’s disease presented with binocular diplopia. Her Parkinsonian features included a right-hand resting tremor, bradykinesia, and gait instability. Vascular risk factors included hypertension, insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and depression. She was taking carbidopa–levodopa 25–100 mg three times daily and clonazepam, among other medications. A brain MRI three years earlier showed mild, nonspecific periventricular white-matter changes consistent with small-vessel ischemia and no brainstem or basal-ganglia strokes. 

On examination, visual acuity with pinhole was 20/25 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left; intraocular pressures, pupils, and optic nerves were unremarkable. Retinal evaluation revealed an epiretinal membrane and macular cystic degeneration temporal to the fovea of the left eye, with mild atherosclerotic vascular changes and no diabetic or hypertensive retinopathy. Optical coherence tomography showed a normal retinal nerve fiber layer bilaterally. Neurologically, she had decreased facial expression and blink rate, no eyelid-opening apraxia, and no cognitive impairment. 

Eye-movement testing demonstrated full versions and ductions, good fixation without square-wave jerks, and no gaze-evoked nystagmus. Smooth pursuit was slightly saccadic horizontally and vertically. She was orthophoric at distance with convergence insufficiency at near. Horizontal reflexive saccades were mildly hypometric with latencies under 1 second. Optokinetic responses were present and symmetric. 

During testing, she intermittently experienced severe difficulty initiating saccades: she would be able to start reflexive saccades and then suddenly be “frozen” for about 20 seconds before resuming horizontal and vertical saccades. She verbally expressed distress that she could not perform the task. Speech became slower and more dysarthric, and blink rate decreased. Notably, she did not blink or use a head thrust to initiate eye movement. She was able to break the freezing episodes by performing smooth pursuit, after which reflexive saccades resumed but were more hypometric, slower, and had latencies of about 7 seconds.

A 56-year-old woman with metastatic vulvar melanoma involving the lungs, liver, and pelvic nodes was treated with seven cycles of nivolumab after initial combination ipilimumab–nivolumab therapy. She was due for cycle 8 when she reported one week of fatigue, nausea, vomiting, cough, and congestion. Her baseline serum creatinine had been 0.5 mg/dL; on presentation it was 4.5 mg/dL. On admission she received two liters of normal saline, but her creatinine rose further to 4.8 mg/dL. She remained non-oliguric with urine output >2 L/day. Other home medications included omeprazole, aspirin 325 mg daily, and opioid analgesics; she denied use of NSAIDs or herbal remedies. Urinalysis showed 1+ blood and 1+ leukocyte esterase, with a bland sediment and no casts; the urine protein–creatinine ratio was 331 mg/g and the microalbumin/creatinine ratio was 72 mg/g. Serologic studies, including ANA, dsDNA, and ANCA testing, were negative. Renal ultrasound revealed bilaterally increased parenchymal echogenicity without hydronephrosis or obstruction; the kidneys measured 11.8 cm (right) and 12.0 cm (left). Because she had been taking aspirin until admission, renal biopsy was not performed.

A 65-year-old man with proliferative diabetic retinopathy and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis presented with sudden vision loss of the right eye over 15 days and painless right-eye swelling for one month. On examination, vision was light perception in the right eye and 20/20 in the left. Intraocular pressures were normal. The right eye had a relative afferent pupillary defect, 3 mm proptosis with complete ptosis, chemosis, and total ophthalmoplegia. Humphrey visual field testing showed a mean deviation of −32.05 dB OD and −6.65 dB OS. Dilated fundus examination and OCT were unchanged from 6 months earlier.

Orbital MRI revealed a diffuse infiltrative, enhancing soft-tissue lesion in the right orbit, optic canal, cavernous sinus, and pterygopalatine fossa, with swelling of the extraocular muscles and encasement of the optic nerve. Laboratory studies showed mild normocytic anemia, an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and negative results for antinuclear antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, angiotensin-converting enzyme, and IgG4. Navigation-guided biopsy of the medial orbital wall and sphenoid sinus showed nonspecific inflammation with fibrosis.

The patient received intravenous methylprednisolone 250 mg four times daily for three days, then oral prednisolone, but right-eye vision declined to no light perception, despite reduction in the lesion size and improved motility. Sixty-three days after presentation, he developed vision loss in the left eye to hand motion; MRI showed extension of the right lesion and a new infiltrative lesion at the left orbital apex and cavernous sinus. High-dose steroids and IVIG were administered, but vision deteriorated to no light perception in the left eye. Until this point, idiopathic sclerosing orbital inflammatory syndrome was considered the most probable diagnosis.

A 36-year-old man presented on March 14, 2020, with a 3-day history of fever, dry cough, headache, and limb aches. He was previously healthy and had completed a half marathon one week before presentation. On arrival at a nearby hospital, he reported progressive shortness of breath and had a reduced general condition. Physical examination revealed crackles in the right upper lung field. His medical, family, and psychosocial history was unremarkable.

Because of concern for SARS-CoV-2 infection, he was admitted directly to the ICU. Initial therapy included piperacillin/tazobactam (4.5 g three times daily i.v.) and clarithromycin (500 mg twice daily i.v.). Polymerase chain–reaction tests for SARS-CoV-2, influenza virus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and Legionella species were all negative. Two days later, because of persistent fever, elevated inflammatory markers, and further respiratory deterioration, broadening antimicrobial coverage to meropenem (1 g three times daily i.v.), linezolid (600 mg twice daily i.v.), and fosfomycin (3 g i.v.) was undertaken, while the working diagnosis of COVID-19–related ARDS was maintained.

Chest imaging (X-ray and CT) demonstrated a diffuse interstitial reticular pattern, multilobular patchy ground-glass opacification, and consolidation of the right upper lobe. After one week of high-flow oxygen, the patient’s oxygenation index (PaO2/FiO2) fell to 130 mm Hg, necessitating endotracheal intubation. Despite prone positioning, he developed worsening hypercapnia, respiratory acidosis, and a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 108 mm Hg with escalating vasopressor requirements. On March 22, an ECMO team was mobilized for transfer under COVID-19 precautions. After review of ventilator settings, imaging, and laboratory data, on-site ECMO was deferred, and the patient was moved under full COVID-19 PPE protocols.

Upon arrival, bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was performed, and repeat naso- and oropharyngeal swabs for SARS-CoV-2 were obtained. A new chest X-ray showed predominantly right-sided pneumonia, felt to be “not typical for COVID-19,” and the working diagnosis was revised to an atypical pneumonia. Meropenem was continued, and clarithromycin (500 mg twice daily i.v.) was reintroduced. Laboratory studies revealed hemolysis with elevated bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase, low haptoglobin, and macrocytic hyperregenerative anemia (hemoglobin 5.3 g/dL, mixed-venous oxygen saturation 67%). A direct Coombs’ test was positive for cold agglutinins.

A previously healthy two-year-old girl presented on day 8 of an 8-day history of fever and rash. Eleven days before symptom onset, she had spent the night camping in a wooded area of Indiana; no tick bites were noted. On day 1 of fever, a maculopapular rash appeared on her chest and shoulders; by day 2 she was seen in an emergency department (ED) where she had diffuse maculopapular lesions on the trunk and legs (sparing palms, soles, and face), mild transaminase elevations (ALT 88 U/L, AST 127 U/L), and otherwise normal labs. The rash had resolved by the time of dermatology evaluation, and she was diagnosed with a viral syndrome and given ibuprofen. On day 6, she returned to a second ED with persistent fever, diffuse fine maculopapular rash, and decreased activity; a throat swab was positive for group A Streptococcus and she was prescribed amoxicillin for presumed scarlet fever. Fevers and lethargy continued. On day 8 she presented to our ED with persistent fever, increasing rash, lethargy, and inability to walk. Vital signs were: T 37.0°C, pulse 175/min, respirations 28/min, BP 93/55 mmHg, O2 sat 90% on room air. Exam showed impaired consciousness, hypotonia, periorbital edema, and a petechial, nonblanching rash on the extremities, trunk, and both palms and soles. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (24 × 10^3/μL), thrombocytopenia (38 × 10^3/μL), low fibrinogen (104 mg/dL), hyponatremia (132 mmol/L), elevated ALT (61 U/L) and AST (141 U/L). A noncontrast head CT showed no acute intracranial abnormality.

A 16-month-old pair of twin boys was admitted for persistent skin lesions that began at 12 months of age. They are the product of a non-consanguineous, full-term pregnancy and were breastfed for 7 months before weaning. The parents noted sequential onset of erythema around the mouth in each twin, followed by large areas of sharply demarcated erythema with peeling in the perianal region. Prior topical treatments had been ineffective.

On examination, both boys had normal growth parameters (9–10 kg, 78–79 cm) and no developmental delay. The skin was dry and hyperpigmented, and both appeared lethargic with weak crying; alopecia was absent. They exhibited intermittent episodes of increased irritability. Symmetrical erythematous lesions were present in the perioral region, hands, wrists, knees, feet, genital, and perianal areas.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and liver and kidney function tests. Serum zinc was 4.2 mg/L (reference range 3.7–7.3 mg/L), and alkaline phosphatase was 45 U/L (reference range 37–147 U/L), both within normal limits.

An 89-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a left-sided neck lump of six months’ duration. It began as a pea-sized nodule and grew to a smooth, fixed 3 × 4 cm mass. She reported no fever, dysphagia, weight loss, night sweats, or hoarseness. Her medical history was notable for a splenectomy; she had been taking daily penicillin prophylaxis. She described a three-year history of recurrent neck swellings that formed abscesses, discharged, and healed slowly, leaving visible scarring on either side of her neck. Previous swabs from these lesions failed to grow Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

On examination, there was a firm, non-tender left cervical mass with overlying scarring from prior abscesses, and a partially healed right neck abscess with scrofuloderma changes.

Investigations included a chest radiograph demonstrating chronic fibrotic changes without evidence of active pulmonary tuberculosis. Fine-needle aspiration of the lesion yielded necrotic debris and foam cells; acute inflammatory cells were not prominent and granulomata were not seen. Ziehl-Neelsen staining of the aspirate revealed no acid-fast bacilli. Part of the aspirate was sent for conventional and mycobacterial cultures.

The initial differential diagnosis included neoplasia, tertiary syphilis, deep fungal infection (for example, sporotrichosis, actinomycosis), and chronic granulomatous disease.

A 31-year-old multigravida at 38 weeks and 6 days of gestation presented with 2 days of diffuse abdominal pain, progressive distension, and two episodes of bilious vomiting. She had no significant past medical history and no regular medications. On examination, she had epigastric tenderness and mild abdominal distension without guarding or peritonism. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 20.0 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein of 100 mg/L, and a lactate level of 4.0 mmol/L; all other parameters were within normal limits. After resuscitation, fetal monitoring with cardiotocography was normal. Obstetrical ultrasound demonstrated a normal uterus and placenta. An erect chest radiograph showed what was thought to be gastric dilatation. A nasogastric tube was inserted, draining less than 200 mls, and symptoms persisted. An urgent oesophago-gastro-duodenoscopy was performed and detected no abnormalities. An ultrasound of the biliary tract was unremarkable.

A 7-year-old girl was brought to the emergency department after two hours of rightward eye deviation, altered consciousness, and unresponsiveness, followed by urinary incontinence and right-sided focal convulsions that became bilateral tonic-clonic but remained more intense on the right. She had no fever but complained of frontal headache and foaming at the mouth. In the ED she received IV phenytoin 15 mg/kg, which controlled the seizures after 20 minutes, and was started on maintenance phenytoin, vancomycin, and ceftazidime. 

Her history was notable for otalgia 3 weeks earlier diagnosed as acute otitis media treated with inadequate antibiotics. There was no prior surgery or congenital disease, but her parents were fourth-degree consanguineous. On arrival, vital signs were normal, Glasgow coma scale was 11/15 after 90 minutes, pupils were equal and reactive, and there were no meningeal signs. On hospital day 2 she was alert, but had upper extremity hypotonia more pronounced on the left. 

Laboratory studies showed: CRP 30 mg/dL, WBC 16,300/mm3, hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL, platelets 676 × 10^9/L, creatinine 0.37 mg/dL, and urea 18 mg/dL. Noncontrast head CT showed cerebral edema with a low-density area in the left temporal lobe. MRI demonstrated a 24 mm left temporal lobe mass with low T1 and high T2-FLAIR signal, a hyperintense rim on diffusion-weighted imaging, and smooth circumferential enhancement. Imaging also revealed left mastoiditis.

An 88-year-old Asian woman noted a mass in her right breast 1 month earlier. She had no history of trauma to the breasts. Her past medical history was notable for a left breast cancer treated surgically 12 years ago (T1N0M0, hormone-receptor–negative, no adjuvant therapy). 

On examination, there was a 20 mm, elastic-hard, less mobile mass in the lower outer quadrant of the right breast, 25 mm from the nipple; no axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy was palpable. 

Mammography showed a dense, round, microlobulated mass. Ultrasonography revealed an 18.1 × 16.2 × 14.4 mm, round, hypoechoic solid lesion with heterogeneous internal echoes, lateral shadowing, a partially broken anterior margin, and an intact posterior margin. 

A core needle biopsy demonstrated proliferating spindle cells but did not yield a definitive diagnosis of malignancy. Because imaging and needle-biopsy results could not exclude a malignant tumor, an excisional biopsy was planned.

A previously healthy 24-year-old Hispanic man presented with a 2-day history of a nonpruritic rash on his legs and feet that had ascended toward his buttocks and was evolving into fluid-filled lesions. Five days before presentation, he had fever, headache, cough, and sore throat; rapid streptococcal antigen, monospot testing, and throat culture were negative, and he received symptomatic treatment for presumed viral pharyngitis. He denied insect bites, new medications, and exposures to vegetation, seawater, chemicals, or new footwear. On examination, vital signs were normal. There were diffuse petechiae and purpura on the anterior aspects of both lower extremities and the plantar surfaces of his feet, with tense bullae on both ankles and the dorsum of both feet; no desquamation was observed. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 7.5×10^9 per liter, a platelet count of 417×10^9 per liter, and a C-reactive protein level of 159.6 mg/L. Alanine aminotransferase was 95 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 42 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 172 U/L. Serologic tests revealed Epstein–Barr virus IgM <0.91 and IgG >5.00; Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgM 1327 (normal, 0.90–1.09) and IgG 2.20 (normal, 0.90–1.09). Monospot testing, HIV screening, hepatitis panel, antinuclear antibodies, proteinase 3 antibodies, and myeloperoxidase antibodies were all negative. Blood cultures were sterile after 5 days, and urinalysis was normal. A skin biopsy from a lesion on the right medial calf showed epidermal spongiosis, subepidermal vesicles and pustules, with a neutrophilic predominance and rare eosinophils.

A 62-year-old man was brought to the psychiatric emergency service after reporting suicidal ideation, including a plan to cut his wrists. He described a three-week history of progressively depressed mood, intrusive negative thoughts, irritability, and increased sensitivity to sound. He denied psychotic symptoms and recent substance use.

Collateral history revealed two months of social isolation, despondency, and hopelessness following vision deterioration, medication changes, and a neighbour altercation. No psychiatric admissions in the past decade, though three occurred in the 1990s and in 2001. On mental status examination, he appeared younger than his age, was slow in movement, spoke softly and monotonously, had organised thought processes, and endorsed negative ruminations without perceptual disturbances. Mood was low and affect flat; cognition grossly intact.

Upon voluntary admission to inpatient psychiatry, he reported lifelong depression with no childhood or adult history of suicide attempts beyond the current crisis and denied ongoing intent. He lives with his wife and three adult children, has disability from vision loss since 1993, smokes tobacco, and uses cannabis occasionally. He has a remote history of alcohol use disorder, abstinent 20 years. Family history is positive for depression. Past psychiatric treatments since 1993 include trials of citalopram, fluoxetine, venlafaxine, reboxetine, phenelzine, tranylcypromine, mirtazapine, lamotrigine, perphenazine, diazepam, psychotherapy, and ten ECT treatments in 1995 without benefit.

He was diagnosed with ADHD as an adult before 2001, with documented concentration difficulties but no other ADHD symptoms or childhood history. He was treated with methylphenidate until dependence developed, then switched to clonidine and later atomoxetine. Past medical history includes glaucoma with legal blindness, migraines, dyslipidaemia, obstructive sleep apnoea, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and renal cell carcinoma treated in 2004. Preadmission medications were amphetamine 30 mg twice daily, lurasidone 40 mg daily, mirtazapine 60 mg nightly, perphenazine 4 mg twice daily, quetiapine 300 mg morning and 700 mg bedtime, with diazepam 10 mg as needed.

He had been tapering paroxetine and adding vortioxetine while attending group cognitive-behavioural therapy prior to admission.  
Laboratory investigations, including CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, fasting glucose, and lipid panel, were within normal limits. A urine drug screen was positive for amphetamines, benzodiazepines, and THC. A brain MRI demonstrated two 12 mm meningiomas of unclear clinical significance; a repeat MRI two months later showed stable findings.

A 55-year-old man reported a 6-month history of right upper-quadrant abdominal pain that responded to medication but recurred. Four months after onset, he developed progressive jaundice, clay-colored stools, pruritus, a 6-kg weight loss, and anorexia. He denied awareness of any abdominal mass, distension, or chronic cough. On examination, he was icteric without lymphadenopathy; the gallbladder was palpable, smooth, and firm. Laboratory studies showed a total bilirubin level of 6.93 mg/dL (direct 4.26 mg/dL), aspartate aminotransferase 175 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 153 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 1100 U/L. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed echogenic soft-tissue thickening along the gallbladder neck and proximal common bile duct with intrahepatic biliary-radical dilatation. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated enhancing thickening of the gallbladder neck (up to 5.5 mm) with periductal spread along the cystic duct and proximal common bile duct causing obstruction and upstream biliary dilatation; multiple homogeneously enhancing periportal, precaval, and interaortocaval lymph nodes were noted without compression of the biliary system. MR cholangiopancreatography showed complete block at the level of the common bile duct with bilobar intrahepatic dilation, and axial T2-weighted images depicted T2 hypointense wall thickening of the gallbladder neck that restricted diffusion. A diagnosis of gallbladder malignancy with likely periductal spread to the common bile duct was made. Preoperative image-guided biopsy was not performed because of the high risk of tumor seeding in malignancy.

A 5-year-old boy with no prior medical history was brought by his parents for evaluation of bilateral external auditory canal stenosis noted at birth. Over time, the patient developed progressive bilateral hearing loss and delayed language acquisition. On examination, there was complete bilateral stenosis of the external auditory canals without fistula or other ear malformations. Pure-tone audiometry showed a hearing threshold of 80 dB in the right ear and 90 dB in the left ear. Computed tomography of the temporal bones revealed polypoid soft-tissue filling the right external auditory canal and bulging into the middle ear. Similar findings were seen on the left, with enlargement and smoothing of the canal walls, discrete ossicular lysis, erosion of the scutum, tegmen tympani dehiscence, and bilateral fibrous stenosis of the external auditory meatus.

A 46-year-old woman presented with a 1-day history of bilateral periorbital edema, conjunctival injection, oral erosions, mild facial edema, and vulvar vesicles. Over the next several hours, she developed a pruritic, erythematous morbilliform eruption on the trunk with a positive Nikolsky sign and worsening oral erosions. She was afebrile and had no lymphadenopathy or eosinophilia. Thirty-two days earlier, she had started carbamazepine. An infectious workup was negative. Skin biopsy showed vacuolar interface dermatitis with basal cell hydropic degeneration, apoptotic keratinocytes, a mild perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, and rare eosinophils. She was diagnosed clinically as having early Stevens-Johnson syndrome with a SCORTEN score of 1 and did not meet the RegiSCAR criteria for DRESS.

A 61‐year‐old man with no significant medical history presented with 4 months of right lateral buttock pain that was inflammatory in character and partially relieved by nonsteroidal anti‐inflammatory drugs. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a C‐reactive protein level of 40 mg/L and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 45 mm/h; the complete blood count and serum protein electrophoresis were normal. 

A pelvic radiograph revealed an osteolytic lesion in the right ischiopubic ramus. Pelvic CT showed cortical bone destruction of that ramus without periosteal reaction. Pelvic MRI demonstrated a lesion that was isointense on T1‐weighted images, hyperintense on diffusion‐weighted images, and showed marked enhancement after gadolinium administration, with cortical rupture and soft‐tissue extension. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no pulmonary parenchymal lesion, no mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and no additional osseous or visceral lesions.

A 4-day-old female infant, born at 39 weeks’ gestation via uncomplicated vaginal delivery to a healthy 25-year-old mother, presented to the emergency department with a painful skin lesion on her back. Pregnancy and delivery had been uneventful; the infant’s birth weight was 3150 g, APGAR scores 9 and 10, and she was discharged on day 2 of life. On day 4, parents noted an extensive flat, firm, erythematous area with heat and edema on the back and left shoulder. There was no fever, feeding difficulties, irritability, or history of trauma. The infant was clinically well otherwise.

Laboratory studies on day 4 showed hemoglobin 11 g/dL, leukocytes 6.8 × 10^3/uL (67% neutrophils), platelets 316 × 10^3/uL, C-reactive protein 5.58 mg/dL, and procalcitonin 1.41 ng/mL. She was admitted with a presumptive diagnosis of cellulitis and started on intravenous flucloxacillin and gentamicin.

Between days 5 and 6, the skin lesions progressed to the upper limbs, thighs, and abdomen and changed in color from erythematous to purplish plaques; irritability increased, and antibiotics were escalated to gentamicin, ampicillin, and cefotaxime. On day 7, multiple erythematous subcutaneous nodules appeared on the back, upper limbs, and thighs, and a serum calcium level of 14.7 mg/dL was detected. The infant was transferred to the neonatal ICU and started on intravenous fluids, oral furosemide, and prednisolone.

A 43-year-old woman was referred for chest and abdominal computed tomography (CT) for staging of a known anterior mediastinal mass. On contrast-enhanced CT, there was a 4 × 6 × 12 cm soft-tissue mass in the upper mediastinum ventral to the heart, with broad contact to the anterior pericardium, ascending aorta, and pulmonary trunk. The mass surrounded and compressed the superior vena cava, causing focally disrupted contrast enhancement, and similarly compressed the left brachiocephalic vein. Prominent paravertebral venous collaterals were noted. In the bone window, in addition to multisegmental spondyloosteochondrosis intervertebralis, there were diffuse hyperdense lesions in the posterior regions of thoracic vertebrae T2 through T6, which were interpreted as highly suspicious for metastatic disease. A diagnosis of superior vena cava thrombosis secondary to extrinsic compression was made, and anticoagulation therapy was initiated.

A 63-year-old right-handed woman with dyslipidemia, hypertension, hypothyroidism, and obesity (BMI 33) presented with 1 month of severe, disabling pain in her left shoulder. The pain occurred spontaneously, worse in the morning and after exertion, was localized over the anterior shoulder with radiation laterally down the arm, and was not preceded by trauma. She had no constitutional symptoms. On examination, active and passive range of motion was preserved, except for painful terminal adduction and internal rotation. Palpation over the anterior proximal humerus was tender. There was no neurovascular deficit. Laboratory studies showed no inflammatory syndrome but revealed elevated parathyroid hormone levels. CT and MRI of the shoulder demonstrated a 4.2-cm calcific deposit at the humeral insertion of the pectoralis major, with adjacent cortical erosion and surrounding bone edema, but no soft-tissue mass and no muscle denervation.

A 12-year-old competitive male gymnast presented with a two-year history of left shoulder pain. His pain began at age 10 as a two- to three-month history of worsening discomfort, associated with a “tic” movement of hyperextension of the left shoulder performed multiple times per day for relief. He had no history of acute injury. Initial management with NSAIDs, rest, and focused physical therapy yielded only transient improvement; each return to gymnastics was followed by recurrence of pain and tightness. No comprehensive examinations or further imaging were performed, and he was repeatedly diagnosed with “overuse syndrome.”  

At age 12, after three months of intensive physical therapy and two weeks back in gymnastics, he experienced severe left shoulder pain, worsening tic movements, visible atrophy of the left scapular region, and vague left upper-extremity weakness. An MRI of the cervical spine showed an unusual nodular mass at the apex of the left hemithorax involving the anterolateral aspect of the left first rib, with less well-defined contiguous soft-tissue thickening of the left second and third ribs. The report stated that imaging characteristics were nonspecific and that “tumor cannot be excluded.” A chest CT was recommended for further evaluation.

An infant born at 23 + 6 weeks’ gestation weighing 680 g underwent umbilical venous and arterial catheter placement for parenteral nutrition and care in the NICU. Initial anteroposterior chest and abdominal radiograph and point-of-care ultrasound confirmed the UVC tip at the junction of the inferior vena cava and right atrium. On day of life 2, the infant developed progressive abdominal distension and increased oxygen requirements. Laboratory evaluation revealed leukocytosis, elevated serum creatinine, and metabolic acidosis. Repeat ultrasound showed that the UVC tip had migrated into the distal ductus venosus and was subsequently withdrawn. A radiograph demonstrated marked paucity of bowel gas and decreased lung field aeration. Point-of-care ultrasound of the abdomen revealed moderate to large ascites in all quadrants and bilateral pleural effusions. The loops of small bowel appeared compressed, bright, and echogenic, without substantial internal gas or fluid, and did not float freely in the ascitic fluid. Under ultrasound guidance, 29 mL of milky, yellow fluid was aspirated from the peritoneal cavity.

A 36-year-old woman at 12 weeks of gestation presented to the emergency department with intense nausea. She received 8 mg of intravenous ondansetron. Immediately after the infusion, she developed severe oppressive chest pain, headache, and a sudden rise in blood pressure. On examination, heart and lung sounds were normal, and there were no cutaneous or respiratory findings.

An electrocardiogram showed ST-segment elevation in leads aVR and V1 and ST-segment depression in the remaining leads. Serial troponin measurements at 6-hour intervals were 1.18 ng/ml, 1.67 ng/ml, and 0.40 ng/ml (reference <0.01 ng/ml).

She was treated with 200 mg of aspirin and 300 mg of clopidogrel, sublingual nitrate, and 2 mg of morphine, after which her chest pain resolved. A subsequent ECG demonstrated T-wave inversion in the precordial leads. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed basal septal hypokinesia. She was started on diltiazem 30 mg twice daily.

A 48-year-old man with a 25-year history of chronic alcoholism (increasing to 2 L/day of red wine over the past 4 months) and severe malnutrition for 1 year presented with 10 days of confusion, stupor, apathy, difficulty manipulating objects, language and balance disturbances, and urinary incontinence. On examination, he was cachectic and apathetic, with dysarthria, comprehension difficulties, astasia-abasia, spastic hypertonia with hyperreflexia in all four limbs, gestural perseveration, and a bilateral grasp reflex.  
Noncontrast head CT showed hypodensity of the splenium of the corpus callosum. Two days later, brain MRI revealed uniform T2 and FLAIR hyperintensity and T1 isosignal throughout the corpus callosum, with diffusion-weighted hyperintensity and relatively decreased ADC values in these regions; bilateral frontal cortical FLAIR hyperintensity was also noted. MR angiography was normal.  
Laboratory studies showed elevated γ-glutamyl transpeptidase, alanine aminotransferase, and aspartate aminotransferase levels, macrocytosis, and decreased serum vitamin B9.

A 43-year-old man with no significant medical history presented in December with a 4-day history of fever to 38.8 °C, shaking chills, hemoptysis, and worsening dyspnea. He reported several months of intermittent night sweats, arthralgias of the wrists and ankles, and a 10-kg weight loss. One day before admission, he noted a painful ecchymotic lesion on his left calf; over the next 24 hours, similar lesions appeared on his abdomen, back, right upper arm, and right calf. His 3-year-old son had recently had a respiratory illness. On examination, temperature was 35.3 °C, blood pressure 117/75 mmHg, pulse 112 beats/min, respiratory rate 29 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Bilateral wheezes were present, and there were multiple painful ecchymoses with hemorrhagic bullae over the trunk and extremities. Laboratory studies showed a WBC count of 9000/mm3 (87% neutrophils), hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, normal renal and liver function, lactate dehydrogenase 799 IU/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 81 mm/h, and C-reactive protein 38.5 mg/dL. Chest radiography and CT demonstrated multifocal alveolar infiltrates, and CT angiography showed no pulmonary embolism. Empiric intravenous ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin were started for presumed community-acquired pneumonia. On hospital day 2, a punch biopsy of a skin lesion revealed superficial and deep dermal thrombotic paucicellular vasculopathy involving skin appendages without significant neutrophils or leukocytoclasia. Tests for cryoglobulin, protein C, protein S, rheumatoid factor, anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies, anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies, complement levels, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and anti–glomerular basement membrane antibodies were negative. Antinuclear antibody titer was 1:160; lupus anticoagulant was prolonged at 82 seconds (reference range, 27–41); anticardiolipin IgM was 64 (reference range, 0–12); and anti–phosphatidylserine IgM was >100 (reference range, <10). Nasopharyngeal testing for influenza antigen, streptococcal antigen, and Legionella antigen was negative. A FilmArray respiratory panel was positive for respiratory syncytial virus and negative for other respiratory viruses and atypical bacteria. Epstein-Barr virus DNA PCR was positive at 8696 copies/mL; tests for HIV, cytomegalovirus, and hepatitis A, B, and C were negative.

An 18-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset, sharp right-sided pelvic pain and two episodes of vomiting. She was afebrile and hemodynamically stable except for a heart rate of 110 bpm. On examination, the abdomen was soft with localized tenderness in the right iliac fossa. Laboratory studies showed a negative beta-human chorionic gonadotropin test and no biological inflammatory syndrome. A transabdominal pelvic ultrasound revealed a normally sized uterus with secretory endometrium and a 6 cm anechoic, homogeneous, thin-walled cystic structure lateral to the right side of the uterus, without endocystic vegetations or solid components. The right ovary appeared elevated, enlarged, and congested, with peripheral follicular distribution; the left ovary was normal.

A 69-year-old man with a history of subtotal gastrectomy with Billroth II reconstruction 25 years earlier for peptic ulcer presented with sudden onset of constant right thoracic and right upper-quadrant abdominal pain (7/10) beginning after lunch, associated with nausea and mild fatigue. He denied fever, dark urine, pale stools, alcohol use, medication or supplement use, or prior liver disease. He had a remote history of angina but no current cardiac issues. On examination, he was afebrile, jaundiced, and hemodynamically stable. Cardiac evaluation including ECG and cardiology consultation excluded an acute cardiac etiology. Laboratory studies showed: WBC 9.8×10^3/µL, neutrophils 87%, hemoglobin 11.0 g/dL, platelets 241×10^3/µL, INR 0.85, albumin 4.1 g/dL; total bilirubin 3.24 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL; γGT 506 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 120 U/L, AST 213 U/L, ALT 299 U/L; lipase and amylase normal; CRP 72.5 mg/L. Abdominal ultrasound showed a 2 cm calcification in segment V of the liver, a few biliary cysts, normal intrahepatic ducts and common bile duct, and sludge in the gallbladder infundibulum. Contrast CT of the abdomen was inconclusive but excluded hepatobiliary and pancreatic malignancies. Viral markers (HBV, HCV) and tumor markers (AFP, CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA) were negative. MRCP revealed mild intrahepatic bile-duct dilation, a 6 mm common bile duct containing a 4 mm biliary stone with sludge, and a distended gallbladder with sludge.

A 74-year-old woman with well-controlled diabetes mellitus and hypertension for 10 years was evaluated preoperatively for bilateral senile cataracts. A dry-eye assessment with the Oculus Keratograph 5M revealed a tear meniscus height of 14 mm in the right eye and 27 mm in the left eye. Tear break-up times were 8 s (right) and 10 s (left). A fluorescein dye disappearance test showed partial obstruction of the left lacrimal drainage system. The patient denied conjunctivitis, epiphora, or purulent discharge. On palpation, there was a localized prominence over the left lower lacrimal canaliculus without tenderness. Ultrasonic biomicroscopy (50 MHz) demonstrated an expanded lumen of the left lower lacrimal canaliculus containing a small, nonopaque structure; there was no soft-tissue mass or edema.

A 70-year-old woman presented with a one-week history of progressive erosive stomatitis associated with hoarseness and odynophagia. She had no significant medical history and was not taking any medications. Physical examination revealed extensive painful erosions on the soft and hard palate, buccal mucosa, and tongue, as well as symmetric swelling of the larynx on laryngoscopic examination. Enlarged right cervical lymph nodes were noted. A 4-mm punch biopsy of the oral mucosa showed suprabasal acantholysis and a sparse lymphocytic infiltrate in the dermis. Direct immunofluorescence testing demonstrated deposition of complement component 3, IgG, IgA, and IgM on cytoid bodies. Microbiologic investigations for herpes simplex virus, bacteria, and fungi were negative.

A 40-year-old woman presented with a 2-day history of electric shock–like sensations in her head, exacerbated by neck flexion. She had a longstanding 10-year history of chronic oral ulcers, widespread musculoskeletal pain, fatigue, symmetric distal paresthesia, depression, and an episode of left optic neuritis in 2021 treated with methylprednisolone. Her medical history included hypothyroidism, fibromyalgia, and iron deficiency anemia treated with levothyroxine, duloxetine, and ferrous sulfate. Neurologic examination was normal. Brain, orbital, and cervical MRI performed during the optic neuritis episode showed 4–5 scattered subcortical unidentified bright objects on T2 FLAIR without active demyelination. ANA was 1:160 (fine speckled); ENA, anti-dsDNA, NMO, and MOG antibodies were negative. On follow-up, she reported worsened head sensations, increased musculoskeletal pain, forgetfulness, decreased attention, and slowed thinking; MMSE was normal. Laboratory testing revealed hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, MCV 81.2 fL, MCHC 33 g/dL, ferritin 57 ng/mL, vitamin B12 < 150 pg/mL, and TSH 1.4 mIU/L.
