A 46-year-old woman with a history of LASIK performed 4 years earlier presented 3 hours after removal of eyelash extensions and permanent eyeliner tattooing with acute bilateral eyelid swelling, redness, photophobia, and blurred vision. An experienced cosmetic technician had applied a cyanoacrylate-dissolving gel remover to the lashes while the patient’s eyes were closed, prompting an immediate burning sensation; the technician then flushed her eyes with saline. The technician proceeded with permanent eyeliner tattooing, applying several topical anesthetics (40% lidocaine/60% tetracaine followed by lidocaine with epinephrine) while instructing the patient to keep her eyes open throughout. Upon completion, the technician noted marked conjunctival redness and drove the patient to the emergency department.

In the ED, both eyes were irrigated with saline for 15–20 minutes. A provisional diagnosis of chemical conjunctivitis was made without slit-lamp examination, and the patient received a 5-day course of erythromycin ointment. Seventy-two hours later, she reported bilateral eyelid pain, photophobia, blurred vision, and tearing. Her uncorrected distance visual acuity was 20/100 in each eye. Slit-lamp examination showed bilateral eyelid edema, conjunctival injection, and a 6 × 6 mm epithelial defect overlying each LASIK flap. Topical moxifloxacin and loteprednol were started, erythromycin was discontinued, and bandage contact lenses were placed.

Two days later, the right epithelial defect had healed completely and the left was 1 × 1 mm; eyelid edema and injection had improved. Loteprednol was stopped, and combination tobramycin-dexamethasone drops were started. One week after injury, both epithelial defects had healed but there was significant superficial punctate keratopathy bilaterally. The visual acuities were 20/25 OD and 20/50 OS. She was switched to prednisolone acetate drops. Three weeks after injury, her visual acuity remained suboptimal; slit-lamp examination revealed anterior basement membrane changes with significant corneal staining, and she was referred for tertiary care.

At the initial tertiary evaluation four weeks after the injury, she complained of ocular pain, photophobia, dry eyes, and daily headaches. She denied a prior history of dry eyes. Uncorrected distance visual acuities were 20/30 OD and 20/40 OS with no improvement on refraction. Extraocular movements and visual fields were full. Slit-lamp examination revealed a healed epithelial defect over each LASIK flap, significant confluent superficial punctate keratitis (worse in the left eye), and trace corneal interface haze in both eyes. The remainder of the anterior and posterior segment examinations was normal.

A 41-year-old woman with a history of fibromyalgia and antiphospholipid antibody syndrome presented initially with several weeks of asthenia, weight loss, headache, tinnitus, and dyspnea, followed by one week of odynophagia treated with metronidazole. On admission, she was found to have severe anemia (hemoglobin 4.3 g/dL) requiring transfusion. Workup including chest, abdomen, and pelvis CT, gastroscopy, and gynecological evaluation was unrevealing. During a two-week hospitalization, she developed diffuse abdominal pain attributed to cannabis withdrawal.

One month later, she was readmitted for severe pain in her shoulders and trunk, described as shock-like and burning, present at rest and night, refractory to tramadol, and accompanied by progressive upper-extremity weakness. Examination showed reduced strength in arm abduction (3/5 right, 5/5 left), shoulder external rotation (3/5 bilaterally), and finger extension (3/5 bilaterally), with dysesthesia over the lateral shoulders and normal reflexes. Nerve conduction studies revealed mildly decreased sensory amplitudes in the superior trunk distribution. Needle electromyography demonstrated fibrillations at rest in C5–C6 innervated muscles and posterior interosseous-innervated muscles, with reduced recruitment; lower-limb studies were normal. Sudoscan testing was abnormal in both feet. A diagnosis of neuralgic amyotrophy involving the superior trunk and posterior interosseous nerve, with possible small-fiber neuropathy, was made. She improved over several months.

Fourteen months after the initial neurologic symptoms, she experienced a relapse with worsening left-hand weakness, new severe abdominal burning pain, and two weeks of constipation. Visual hallucinations occurred for two days after starting opioids. Two months into this relapse, examination confirmed severe left finger-extension weakness (2/5), and electrophysiological testing showed further deterioration of posterior interosseous-nerve function.

A 71-year-old Japanese man with hypertension and prior bilateral inguinal hernia repairs presented with 6 days of swelling and pain over his left inguinal incision. He was afebrile, and vital signs were normal. On examination, tender, elastic, hard masses were palpated in the left inguinal region without overlying skin or mucosal lesions; the genitalia and lower limbs were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 8350/µL and a C-reactive protein level of 10.19 mg/dL. Abdominal and pelvic CT demonstrated a left inguinal hernia and five to six enlarged left inguinal lymph nodes (1–4 cm) with increased surrounding soft-tissue density; no other lymphadenopathy was seen. A clinical diagnosis of left inguinal infectious lymphadenitis was made, and an excisional biopsy was performed.  
Grossly, the lymph nodes were fragile and exuded pus. Histologically, there were multifocal abscesses with central suppuration and peripheral purulent exudate. Lymphoid follicles and the capsule were inconspicuous, and dense fibrosis was absent. Numerous histiocytes formed vague granulomas, and occasional multinucleated giant cells were seen. The cortex showed marked interfollicular hyperplasia with perivascular plasma cells. Neutrophils within vessel lumina suggested endarteritis and phlebitis. The findings were interpreted as suppurative granulomatous lymphadenitis.

A 37-year-old man presented with a 4-year history of recurrent left mandibular swelling and trismus. He had no history of trauma, paresthesia, or skin lesions and no significant medical or family history. His dental history was notable for extraction of a carious left mandibular third molar after painful swelling, with complete resolution. Two months later, sudden swelling occurred in the left submandibular region with pain and restricted mouth opening; symptoms resolved with antibiotics but recurred after 2 months. Over the next year he experienced eight similar episodes, each with swelling and 2 weeks of restricted opening followed by gradual resolution. An early panoramic radiograph showed no infectious focus but mild mandibular sclerosis that was overlooked.

On examination, he was afebrile. There was facial asymmetry and a diffuse 7×5 cm firm, non‐tender swelling over the left masseter region. Interincisal opening was 5 mm. Intraoral examination revealed no focus of infection and all mandibular teeth responded to vitality testing. A provisional diagnosis of trismus secondary to chronic infection was made, and the differential included masseter hypertrophy and an atraumatic variant of myositis ossificans.

Intraoral periapical radiographs showed a coarse sclerotic trabecular pattern in the left premolar and molar region. Panoramic radiography revealed unilateral diffuse sclerosis of the left hemimandible with a ground-glass appearance extending from the left canine to the ipsilateral condyle and resorption of the condylar head. Multislice CT demonstrated extensive endosteal sclerosis of the left hemimandible, cortical thickening, mild periosteal new bone formation, and condylar head resorption with loss of cortical–medullary border demarcation. MRI showed the left hemimandible as hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and on postgadolinium images there was intramedullary enhancement along with enhancement of the overlying masticatory and floor-of-mouth muscles.

A 67‐year‐old woman presented with severe right-sided loin pain and recurrent Escherichia coli urinary tract infections. She had a history of open right pyeloplasty in 1970 and an open right nephrolithotomy in 1975. Her medical history was otherwise notable for depression and eczema. Laboratory testing showed a serum creatinine level of 61 µmol/L and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 85 mL/min/1.73 m^2.  

Noncontrast CT of the renal tract demonstrated a solid-looking lesion in the right renal pelvis, leading to a differential diagnosis of a tumour or a poorly calcified stone. A subsequent contrast CT urogram showed contrast outlining multiple radiolucent structures within the calyces and pelvicaliceal system, likely representing atypical stones; there was no opacification of the right ureter, and the right kidney exhibited extreme cortical thinning over the calyces. A DMSA scan revealed 36% function of the right kidney, and a MAG-3 renogram suggested moderate to severe right pelviureteric junction obstruction with preserved renal function.

A 76‐year‐old man presented with jaundice without abdominal pain or fever. He had undergone a laparoscopic cholecystectomy 1 year earlier. On examination, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable, with visible jaundice and a soft, non‐tender abdomen. Laboratory tests revealed a total bilirubin level of 20 mg/L (normal <10 mg/L), alkaline phosphatase 524 U/L (1.9× ULN), and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 1001 U/L (18× ULN). Abdominal ultrasonography showed dilation of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, with the common bile duct measuring 12 mm and a small hypoechoic nodule, 5 mm in diameter, at the transition zone. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography demonstrated dilation of the common hepatic duct to 9.6 mm and a main bile duct measuring 5 mm, with a small circumferential pseudomenbranous stenosis at the junction of the common hepatic and common bile ducts and no pathological enhancement.

A woman in her 40s with a more than 10-year history of well-controlled HIV infection (on efavirenz/emtricitabine/tenofovir) presented with a 3-year history of recurrent, painful oral erosions despite chronic acyclovir therapy. Physical examination revealed irregularly shaped erosions of the tongue. An initial differential diagnosis included HIV aphthae, herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection, and erythema multiforme (EM). Acyclovir was continued, and colchicine was initiated. 

A tongue biopsy showed mucosal ulceration and parakeratosis with a superficial and deep mixed inflammatory infiltrate consistent with a lichenoid hypersensitivity reaction, including both drug allergy and EM; clinicohistologic correlation supported the diagnosis of EM. Over the next 6 months, her oral erosions repeatedly flared, remitting for 2 to 3 weeks before each recurrence, and led to several hospitalizations for pain control and hydration. During severe flares, examination showed diffuse erosions of the vermillion lips, tongue, buccal mucosa, and palate; some episodes also included anogenital erosions and violaceous papules on the distal extremities.

During one flare, serologic testing revealed negative HSV1/2 IgM and positive IgG. Mycoplasma IgM titer was elevated, but IgG titer, culture, and respiratory PCR were normal, and a convalescent mycoplasma titer failed to document an increase in IgG. Despite trials of acyclovir, prednisone, dapsone, colchicine, azithromycin, niacinamide, and topical corticosteroids, her mucositis continued to worsen.

A 35-year-old woman with a history of regular narrow-complex tachycardia presented for an elective electrophysiology study. Two weeks earlier, her tachycardia had not responded to adenosine administered by paramedics and terminated spontaneously in the emergency department. The recorded tachycardia had a narrow QRS complex, a cycle length of 330 ms, and no evident retrograde P waves.

On presentation in the EP laboratory, she was in sinus rhythm. Quadripolar catheters were placed in the right ventricular apex, His position, and right atrium; a decapolar catheter was positioned in the coronary sinus. At a sinus cycle length of 820 ms, the AH and HV intervals were 83 ms and 42 ms, respectively. Ventricular pacing showed concentric and decremental retrograde conduction. During programmed atrial stimulation, dual AV nodal physiology was evident, and a nonsustained 1:1 narrow-complex tachycardia with cycle lengths of 280–350 ms was easily induced.

During tachycardia, the atrial activation was concentric with a septal VA time of 20 ms. On two occasions, tachycardia was induced after a 2-for-1 response. The tachycardia terminated spontaneously with the atrial electrogram consistently last. His‐synchronous premature ventricular contractions did not advance or delay the atrial electrogram or the tachycardia. Entrainment from the right ventricular apex at 10–20 ms shorter than the tachycardia cycle length yielded a V-A-V response with a post-pacing interval minus tachycardia cycle length of 170 ms and a stimulus‐atrial minus VA difference of 115 ms. Atrial pacing at 260 ms during tachycardia dissociated the atrium without affecting the tachycardia cycle length.

During sustained tachycardia, there were intermittent loss of atrial depolarizations and periods of Wenckebach and 2:1–3:1 VA periodicity with fixed VA intervals. Further ventricular pacing entrainment resulted in complete VA dissociation, with the ventricular rate unchanged and stable QRS morphology and HV interval. Ventricular pacing at a rate faster than the tachycardia had no effect, and intravenous adenosine (6 mg followed by 12 mg) failed to terminate the tachycardia.

A 37-year-old man presented with decreased vision in both eyes. He had no prior medical or ophthalmologic history and was taking no medications. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in each eye. The refractive error was −14.5 diopters in the right eye and −14.0 diopters in the left eye, and axial lengths were 30.8 mm OD and 30.6 mm OS. Dilated fundus examination revealed enlarged optic disk cups bilaterally but no ophthalmoscopic abnormalities in the peripheral fundus. Glaucoma was suspected, and Goldmann perimetry showed a slight reduction in sensitivity in the nasal visual field of the left eye. To further evaluate the peripheral fundus, fluorescein angiography demonstrated multiple arch-shaped, hyperfluorescent linear lesions running circumferentially in the peripheral fundus of both eyes, some of which ran parallel to each other. Fundus autofluorescence imaging showed hypoautofluorescence at the corresponding sites.

A 68-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of progressive hoarseness. His medical history included hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and asthma treated for over 10 years with inhaled corticosteroids, a long-acting β₂-agonist, and a long-acting muscarinic antagonist. He had also received mepolizumab for 8 months without improvement and was switched to omalizumab three months before symptom onset. He was a former smoker (60 cigarettes per day for 34 years, quit 15 years ago) and did not consume alcohol. Current medications included lansoprazole, torasemide, amlodipine, loratadine, montelukast, atorvastatin, dextromethorphan, fluticasone/formoterol inhaler (500 μg/day), tiotropium, and omalizumab.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Lung auscultation revealed bilateral wheezing; the rest of the physical examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory tests, including HIV and HTLV-1 antibodies, were within normal limits. Chest radiography and CT scans showed no abnormalities. Pulmonary function tests demonstrated a vital capacity of 100.8% predicted and an FEV₁/FVC ratio of 0.69 (85.1% predicted FEV₁).

Flexible laryngoscopy showed an elevated red lesion on the right true vocal fold, with a normal left fold. Bronchoscopy revealed multiple white, flat, elevated lesions extending from the trachea to the left upper lobe bronchus. Biopsies from the vocal fold, trachea, and bronchus demonstrated squamous cell metaplasia, neutrophilic inflammation, and histiocyte-like cells with foamy cytoplasm beneath the epithelium.

A 44-year-old man with well-controlled hypertension and no prior renal disease presented with fever and pharyngeal pain and received a 10-day course of antibiotics. Nineteen days later he noted facial and leg edema and was admitted. He had no family history of kidney disease. On examination, T 36.9 °C and BP 175/109 mmHg with periorbital and pedal edema.  

Laboratory studies showed:  
• Urinalysis: specific gravity 1.015; pH 5.0; protein 3+; blood 3+; 20–29 RBCs/HPF; 30–49 WBCs/HPF.  
• Serum creatinine 5.46 mg/dL; BUN 17.5 mg/dL; CRP 4.05 mg/dL.  
• Complement C3 28.8 mg/dL (low), C4 27.9 mg/dL (normal).  
• ASO titer 3440 IU/mL; ASK titer 40 960 IU/mL; IgG/IgA/IgM 2130/660/50 mg/dL.  
• ANA, anti–double-stranded DNA, MPO-ANCA, PR3-ANCA all undetectable.  
• Rapid antigen test of throat swab positive for group A Streptococcus; urinary pneumococcal antigen negative.  

A clinical diagnosis of severe poststreptococcal acute glomerulonephritis was made. Symptomatic management and ceftriaxone were begun. Renal function improved but gross hematuria persisted.  

Over the next 2 weeks, hemoglobin fell to 8.8 g/dL, platelet count to 9.2 × 10^4/μL; haptoglobin <10 mg/dL; LDH 514 IU/L; coagulation parameters minimally changed. ADAMTS-13 activity was 88%. Stool cultures and assays for Shiga-like toxin and O157 LPS antibody were negative. A direct Coombs test was positive on hospital day 11 and negative on day 21.

A 65-year-old man with atrial fibrillation status post cardioversion, coronary artery disease, and hypertension presented with one month of progressive headaches and lethargy. One month earlier, a noncontrast CT of the head had shown a 1-cm hypodense lesion in the right cerebellum. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed numerous subcentimeter cysts in the liver, a cyst in the spleen, and one in the kidney, none of which were suggestive of malignancy. A subsequent outpatient PET scan showed a tiny left adrenal nodule with mild to moderate hypermetabolic activity. He received a short course of dexamethasone with transient relief. He re-presented with worsening headache, nausea, vomiting, and poor oral intake. Laboratory studies demonstrated a white-cell count of 18,100/µL, hemoglobin of 10 g/dL, sodium of 121 mmol/L, AST of 22 U/L, and ALT of 53 U/L. During the admission, he acutely developed fevers and altered mental status requiring intubation. Neurologic examination revealed absent brainstem reflexes and anisocoria. Brain MRI showed restricted diffusion in the posterior limbs of both internal capsules (right greater than left), the right thalamus, and the pons, with mild hydrocephalus. Lumbar puncture yielded 535 nucleated cells/mm3 (89% neutrophils), protein > 200 mg/dL, and glucose 17 mg/dL. A meningitis/encephalitis BioFire panel was unremarkable, CSF fungal cultures showed no growth, and HIV testing was negative. He was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics, acyclovir, and, given concern for tuberculosis meningitis, the RIPE regimen. A decision was made to proceed with bronchoscopy and bronchoalveolar lavage for further evaluation.

A 12-year-old girl presented with 1 day of spontaneous left eye pain that worsened with horizontal movement, especially on right gaze, accompanied by photophobia and slight blurring of vision. She had no diplopia, color-vision deficit, headache, neurological symptoms, fever, or trauma. She used a nasal decongestant for 2 days and had received antibiotics for tonsillitis 1 month earlier. On examination, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. The left eyelid was mildly ptotic with periocular redness and swelling, conjunctival hyperemia, and lateral chemosis; there was no tenderness on palpation. Ophthalmoscopy and pupillary responses were normal. A provisional diagnosis of preseptal cellulitis was made. ENT evaluation, including flexible laryngoscopy, was normal. Sinus CT showed no subperiosteal abscess but revealed inflammatory changes in the left lateral rectus muscle, medial preseptal soft-tissue swelling at the left lamina papyracea, and left osteomeatal complex occlusion from slight ethmoid/sphenoid mucosal thickening. She was started on oral amoxicillin–clavulanate and discharged. Two days later, she returned with worsened left vision and desaturation of color perception. Examination showed mild tenderness, restricted abduction and adduction, impaired upward gaze, proptosis, diffuse chemosis, and temporal conjunctival hyperemia. Visual acuity was 0.63 in the left eye despite a normal fundus. Infection parameters were within normal limits. Intravenous antibiotics produced no improvement. Contrast-enhanced orbital MRI demonstrated a diffusely thickened left lateral rectus muscle along its full length, including the tendon insertion, with increased enhancement and adjacent preseptal soft-tissue and lacrimal gland inflammation.

A 3-year-old girl, second child of healthy nonconsanguineous parents, had normal prenatal history and developmental milestones until age 2. At that time, she had prolonged focal seizures involving the left side of her body that required multiple antiepileptic drugs for control. After discharge, she remained on sodium valproate and was seizure-free but developed persistent weakness of the left upper and lower limbs. She was referred for evaluation of ongoing hemiparesis and delayed psychomotor development. 

On examination, her growth parameters were appropriate for age. Neurologic examination revealed spastic left hemiparesis and delayed motor milestones; other systems were unremarkable. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed marked atrophy of the right cerebral hemisphere with ex-vacuot dilatation of the ipsilateral ventricle and hyperintense signal in the subcortical white matter on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences.

A 17-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of pain and aesthetic concerns involving his upper front teeth. His medical history was noncontributory.  
On clinical examination, the maxillary central incisors were notably broad bilaterally; there was moderate crowding elsewhere and carious lesions affecting the palatal aspects of the left central incisor. No teeth were missing on either arch. The left permanent maxillary central incisor had an accessory cusp-like projection on the palatal surface and a deep carious lesion extending toward the pulp.  
To clarify root anatomy, a cone-beam computed tomography scan was obtained. On CBCT, the right central incisor demonstrated a single enlarged pulp chamber with a single root canal, and the left central incisor showed one pulp chamber that divided into two separate root canals in the coronal two-thirds of the root.

A 20-year-old Caucasian man with no prior medical history presented with five days of intractable vomiting. In the emergency department he had multiple seizures requiring intubation. On examination he was tachycardic with dry mucous membranes. Laboratory evaluation showed metabolic alkalosis, acute kidney injury, and a positive urine drug screen for cannabis; he was treated for presumed cannabis‐induced cyclic emesis. On hospital day five he developed high-grade fevers to 39.5 °C and new bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. He was started on vancomycin and piperacillin–tazobactam. Bronchial aspirate cultures grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli, both sensitive to the prescribed antibiotics. Despite ten days of antibiotic therapy—including escalation to meropenem and addition of micafungin—his fevers persisted. His respiratory status worsened to acute respiratory distress syndrome requiring venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Review of imaging revealed hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory tests showed hypertriglyceridemia (379 mg/dL), hemoglobin 6.4 g/dL, platelets 88 × 10^3/mm^3, and ferritin 1188 ng/mL.

A 28-year-old primigravida at 32 weeks and 3 days of gestation was transferred for management of preeclampsia with severe features. She had no significant medical history, was born in Mexico, and worked on a dairy farm. On admission, she reported a mild headache and one subjective fever two weeks earlier. Vital signs were: T 36.8°C, BP 131/67 mmHg, HR 117/min, RR 16/min. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory results showed hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, platelets 288×10^3/µL, AST/ALT 78/114 U/L, LDH 264 U/L, fibrinogen 786 mg/dL, and urine protein/creatinine ratio 1111 mg/g; creatinine, total bilirubin, and haptoglobin were normal, and peripheral smear showed no hemolysis.

During triage she developed fever to 38.1°C with maternal and fetal tachycardia, prompting an uncomplicated cesarean delivery. Postpartum, she experienced quotidian fevers up to 40.5°C with chills and night sweats, interspersed with periods of wellness. Initial work-up included an unremarkable chest radiograph, CT chest negative for pulmonary embolism, RUQ ultrasound showing hepatomegaly with steatosis, and normal echocardiogram. Blood and amniotic fluid cultures were negative. Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics (ampicillin, gentamicin, clindamycin, then piperacillin-tazobactam and doxycycline) and therapeutic heparin for suspected deep septic thrombophlebitis yielded no clinical improvement.

On postpartum day 12, laboratory testing revealed Epstein–Barr virus DNA quantification 280 IU/mL with negative monospot and early antigen, CRP 104.5 mg/L, ESR 78 mm/h, serum iron 48 µg/dL (saturation 15%), TIBC 311 µg/dL, and ferritin 12 667 ng/mL.

A 27-year-old gravida 2 para 0 woman, with a history of a second-trimester termination for fetal chromosomal abnormalities, presented with mild, deep lower-abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding for several days. Based on her last menstrual period, she was estimated at 8 weeks 2 days’ gestation. For ten days she had been labeled as a pregnancy of unknown location. Serial β-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) levels measured every other day were 4113, 3904, and 4207 mIU/mL. On admission her hematocrit was 33.9%, hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, platelets 243 ×10^3/mL, white blood cells 9.90 ×10^3/mL (79.9% neutrophils); coagulation and biochemical studies were normal. Bimanual examination revealed marked cervical-motion tenderness and right adnexal tenderness. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed no gestational sac in the endometrial cavity, an inconclusive mass in the right adnexa, and blood clots in the pouch of Douglas. Given these findings and concern for impending hemodynamic instability, surgical management was planned.

A 72-year-old woman with hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes mellitus, and a history of coronary artery disease treated with multiple percutaneous coronary interventions presented with a 2-month history of angina on minimal exertion. On examination, her blood pressure was 130/70 mm Hg, heart rate 63 beats/min, and the remainder of the physical examination was normal. An electrocardiogram was unremarkable, and routine laboratory tests showed no abnormalities. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a 21 × 15 mm echo-dense, spherical, mobile, tumor-like mass in the periannular posterior region near the ventricular side of the posterior mitral leaflet; the mass had sharp, distinct borders and markedly bright echogenicity compared with adjacent myocardium. The posterior leaflet was stretched and arched over the mass, the anterior leaflet was normal, and Doppler mapping showed mild mitral regurgitation without stenosis. The left ventricle was mildly hypertrophic with normal segmental wall motion, and the left atrium was slightly enlarged. Coronary angiography showed stable coronary lesions and demonstrated a calcific mass attached to the mitral annulus. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed a hypointense mass in the posterior mitral annulus on T2 sequences, perfusion, and cine imaging, with no late gadolinium enhancement 15–20 minutes after contrast administration.

A 30-year-old man with recurrent Hodgkin’s lymphoma underwent an autologous stem-cell transplant in 2010 and recently had disease recurrence in abdominal lymph nodes confirmed by biopsy. During that hospitalization, he received two doses of ampicillin-sulbactam and limited doses of promethazine, metoclopramide, and baclofen. He reported taking a supplement, Carnivora, for about 1 year and discontinued it during the hospital stay; his creatinine at discharge was 0.94 mg/dL.

After discharge, he resumed Carnivora at a higher dose (4 capsules three times daily). Four weeks later, his creatinine was noted to be 2.78 mg/dL before starting brentuximab vedotin. A CT scan of the abdomen showed bilateral renal enlargement from 11 cm to 14 cm without hydronephrosis. He received brentuximab and was referred to nephrology several days later for progressive renal insufficiency.

On nephrology evaluation, he reported several days of fevers, nausea, and vomiting. He denied NSAID use, hematuria, dysuria, or decreased urinary frequency. Physical examination revealed dry mucous membranes; vital signs were stable. Laboratory studies showed a creatinine of 3.42 mg/dL, BUN 32 mg/dL, and a white-blood-cell count of 10.9×10^3/mm^3 with a normal eosinophil count. Serum urate, lactate dehydrogenase, and phosphorus levels were normal. Urinalysis revealed fewer than 1 eosinophil per high-power field, 4+ leukocytes, and 3+ protein; the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio was 0.76. The patient was admitted for intravenous fluids and kidney biopsy.

A 24-year-old man presented after a single generalized tonic–clonic seizure. He denied fever, sweating, weight loss, smoking, alcohol or drug use, trauma, surgery, and had no history of sinus disease. His appearance was normal; blood pressure and heart rate were stable. Neurologic examination revealed intact motor and sensory function but impaired cognition. Non-contrast head CT showed bilateral lesions in the anterior cranial fossa with multiple calcifications, erosion of the cranial vault bones, and displacement of adjacent structures. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral frontal solid-cystic masses compressing the lateral ventricles, with low signal on T1-weighted images, high signal on T2-weighted images, restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging, and heterogeneous rim enhancement with multiple septations after gadolinium administration.

A 23-year-old man was referred for evaluation of progressive left-sided facial wasting.  
History of present illness: He underwent adenotonsillectomy at age 6, and 3 months later developed numbness of the left face. Over the next 2 years he noted progressive shrinkage and weakness of the left side of his face; the process further progressed over the next decade. He underwent two autologous fat injections at ages 14 and 16, with only transient cosmetic benefit.  
Physical examination: Vital signs normal. There is marked atrophy of cutaneous and subcutaneous fat tissue on the left face, with zygomatic depression. The left ocular bulb is phthisical with corneal atrophy. The left temporal muscle is visibly smaller than the right. There is hemiglossal atrophy with widened fissuring on the left tongue. Maxillary atrophy has displaced the left upper teeth upward and backward. There are no dermal lesions, no extremity involvement, and no family history of similar findings.  
Laboratory studies: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein levels are within normal limits. Serologic testing for autoantibodies is negative.  
 Imaging: Unenhanced CT of the head shows no evidence of cortical neurodegeneration; there is decreased retroorbital fat on the left and ocular atrophy, with asymmetric temporal muscle volume loss. MR angiography reveals no abnormalities of the internal or external carotid arteries or their branches.

A 24-year-old man presented with a 15-day history of a soft, pulsating swelling on the left side of his upper lip. He reported no trauma, bleeding, or interference with speech or mastication. His medical history was unremarkable, and he did not smoke. On examination, there was a 3 mm × 3 mm sessile nodule on the left upper labial mucosa at the vermilion border. The lesion had a normal surface color, was soft, nontender, and pulsatile on palpation. The remainder of the oral mucosa was normal, and a provisional diagnosis of a peripheral angiomatous lesion was given.

Color Doppler ultrasonography from the mucosal side using a 7–15 MHz linear transducer revealed an arterial vessel with a tortuous course in the submucosa of the left upper lip. The vessel lay 0.9 mm below the mucosal surface and measured 1 mm in diameter near the periphery. Spectral analysis demonstrated a peak systolic velocity of 58.06 cm/s, end-diastolic velocity of 11.87 cm/s, a pulsatility index of 1.95, a resistivity index of 0.80, and a dicrotic notch with forward flow in both systole and diastole. There was no evidence of arteriovenous shunts, abnormal vascular communication, or calcific deposits.

A 24-year-old white man presented with an 8-month history of persistent swelling around his left eye. He had no history of significant acne vulgaris or rosacea and no visual symptoms. He had been evaluated by an allergist and an ophthalmologist and had not improved with corticosteroid ophthalmic solutions or oral antihistamines. On examination, there was non-erythematous, non-pitting edema of the left periorbital region without conjunctival inflammation. Paranasal radiography and maxillofacial CT scans showed only periorbital soft-tissue swelling. Patch testing with the North American Standard Series was negative, and a tuberculin skin test result was negative. A skin biopsy revealed numerous dermal ectatic blood vessels and lymphatics with a sparse lymphocytic infiltrate.

A 68-year-old man with pseudophakic bullous keratopathy underwent Descemet Stripping Automated Endothelial Keratoplasty (DSAEK) in the right eye. His postoperative course was initially uneventful under topical and systemic corticosteroids. He had a history of an eye infection by Thaumetopoea pityocampa (pine processionary) 9 months before DSAEK, which had resolved prior to surgery.

Two months after DSAEK, he was referred for evaluation of keratitis in the right eye. On examination:
• Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/200 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye.  
• Pupils were isocoric and isoreactive without an afferent pupillary defect.  
• There was no pain with ocular movements.  
• Slit-lamp biomicroscopy of the right eye showed brown, multilobular lesions confined to the deep corneal stroma, with no conjunctival hyperemia, no discharge, and no epithelial defect.  
• The anterior chamber was deep and clear. Intraocular pressure and fundus examination were normal. The left eye was unremarkable.

Anterior segment optical coherence tomography of the right eye revealed a central infiltrate involving all corneal layers and a peripheral infiltrate concentrated in the deep stroma.

A 40-year-old Hispanic woman with a history of obesity (BMI 32) and hypertension presented with a 3-day history of a squeezing bifrontal headache that was gradual in onset and progressively worse. The headache was accompanied by nausea, vomiting, dizziness, transient visual disturbances in the right eye, and a feeling of bilateral ear fullness. One day before presentation, she noted numbness and weakness on the right side of her face, with difficulty closing the right eye and raising the right eyebrow. She denied diplopia, persistent vision loss, photophobia, tinnitus, fever, recent illness, tick bite, or other focal neurologic symptoms. She was not taking oral contraceptives.

On examination, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Mental status and speech were normal, with no meningeal signs. Cranial nerve testing showed equal pupils reactive to light and accommodation, intact extraocular movements, and no abducens palsy. There was right-sided lower facial droop, decreased right eye closure, and impaired right forehead movement; facial sensation was intact bilaterally. Motor strength, sensation, reflexes, coordination, and gait were normal. Funduscopic examination revealed bilateral grade I–II papilledema.

A noncontrast head CT showed right pontomedullary hypodensity. Brain MRI with MR venography demonstrated stenosis of the lateral aspect of the transverse sinus, partial empty sella turcica, and mild papilledema, consistent with raised intracranial pressure. Lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 28 cm H₂O; CSF cytology and chemistry were otherwise normal, with 2 white cells (100% lymphocytes), protein 24 mg/dL, 13 red cells, and glucose 58 mg/dL.

A 35‐year‐old woman with no psychiatric or medical history presented to the emergency department with a 3-week history of diffuse malaise, weakness, dizziness, shortness of breath, chills, and headache. She left against medical advice before blood tests could be performed. Two days later, she returned with acute onset of disorganized speech and hallucinatory behavior. 

On examination, she was agitated and delirious, with urinary incontinence. Initial laboratory studies showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia; a comprehensive metabolic panel, noncontrast head CT, urine toxicology screen, and blood alcohol level were all unremarkable. Neurology and psychiatry were consulted. 

A lumbar puncture revealed lymphocytic pleocytosis: total protein 0.31 g/L, glucose 2.59 mmol/L, nucleated cells 34/mm3 (94% lymphocytes), and 343 red blood cells/mm3. Empiric intravenous acyclovir and ceftriaxone were started. Brain MRI showed subtle FLAIR hyperintensity and mild contrast enhancement of the superior fronto-parietal sulci, suggestive of meningitis. 

Over the next week, she became increasingly delirious with mixed hyperactive and hypoactive features and developed facial twitching and abnormal lip and tongue movements associated with autonomic instability. Intravenous immunoglobulin and methylprednisolone were initiated for presumed autoimmune encephalitis, and levetiracetam was added for seizure control. 

A pan-MRI to screen for malignancy was negative. Thyroid studies showed mildly elevated TSH, normal free T4, and high anti-thyroid peroxidase and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies. In the absence of infection, tumor, or stroke, a provisional diagnosis of Hashimoto’s encephalopathy was made, and levothyroxine was started.

A 61-year-old Latin-Caucasian woman presented with passage of gas and later fecal material through the vagina. Her medical history was notable for heavy tobacco use and an abdominoplasty. Two years earlier, she had undergone a vaginal hysterectomy at another hospital. Four days after that procedure, she noticed gas passage per vagina, urinary incontinence, and nocturia, followed by fecal leakage. 

Two weeks after the hysterectomy, the obstetrics–gynecology service attempted a first repair via the vagina. One month later, the fistula recurred, and she underwent a second repair with a transanal mucosal/submucosal flap and fibrin sealant, which initially closed the rectal defect. Two months after the second repair, she had a third recurrence of symptoms and reported severe sexual dysfunction and poor quality of life.

On examination, a fistulous tract was confirmed, with fibrosis 5 cm from the anterior anal verge. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. A rigid anoscopy and flexible colonoscopy confirmed a recurrent rectovaginal fistula. Differential diagnoses, including inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease), chronic infection, and local foreign body reaction, were ruled out.

A 64-year-old woman presented with one week of progressive dyspnea, nonproductive cough, and fever. She had a 40 pack-year smoking history and a longstanding morning cough that worsened over the past month. She had psoriasis in remission for 20 years. On the day of admission she was dyspneic at rest. 

Vital signs: afebrile, respiratory rate elevated, oxygen saturation 91% on room air. Lung examination revealed diffuse bilateral inspiratory crackles. 

Arterial blood gas analysis: pH 7.47, PaCO2 4.5 kPa, PaO2 7.5 kPa. Laboratory studies: leukocyte count 24×10^9/L, C-reactive protein 275.6 mg/L, procalcitonin 0.08 ng/mL. 

Chest radiograph showed diffuse bilateral reticulonodular opacities. CT pulmonary angiography excluded pulmonary embolism and revealed a diffuse ground-glass pattern with upper-lobe hyperinflation. 

Empiric therapy with ceftriaxone and clarithromycin was initiated, along with supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula.

A 35-year-old West African man with no prior psychiatric or medical history presented to clinic with a 1-week history of escalating behavioral changes. His family reported episodes of talkativeness, incoherent speech, visual and auditory hallucinations, insomnia, and grandiose and persecutory delusions. He denied head injury, substance use, or stressors and had no family history of psychiatric illness. He worked as a mechanical engineer in a mining community with potential mercury exposure and had no systemic or respiratory symptoms despite known community spread of COVID-19.

On examination he was afebrile, BP 135/80 mmHg, pulse 88 bpm, and with normal respiratory rate and oxygen saturation. General and neurologic exams were unremarkable. He appeared disheveled, restless, and agitated but was oriented to time, place, and person. Speech was loud and clear without latency. He exhibited circumstantial thought, grandiose delusions (“I am a prophet of God”), persecutory delusions, and both auditory (“gunshots”) and visual (a mob) hallucinations. Memory was intact and he had no insight.

Laboratory studies showed a normal CBC, renal function, and albumin; γ‐glutamyl transferase was elevated at 81 IU/L (normal < 55) and total bilirubin 26 μmol/L (normal 3.4–20.5). Malaria and typhoid screens were negative. Urinalysis revealed transient proteinuria and glycosuria that normalized on repeat. Head CT scan was normal. A lateral flow COVID-19 antigen test and confirmatory RT-PCR were both positive.

A 62-year-old man was referred for progressive bilateral blurred vision of long duration. He had no history of diabetes, hypertension, inflammatory disease, obstructive sleep apnea, carotid occlusion, or blood dyscrasias; he was on anticoagulation for a mitral valve replacement. Best-corrected visual acuity was 75 letters in the right eye and 80 letters in the left eye. Anterior segments were unremarkable; cataracts were not significant. 

Fundus examination revealed, in the right eye, three large perifoveal aneurysmal lesions with small hemorrhages and intraretinal hard exudates; the left eye had one similar isolated lesion. Multicolor imaging and autofluorescence showed no retinal pigment epithelium alteration. Fluorescein angiography of the peripheral retina was normal.

Macular FA and ICGA in early and late frames demonstrated only the perifoveal hyperfluorescent aneurysms, with no leakage. Optical coherence tomography showed cystoid intraretinal fluid in both eyes, with round intraretinal hyperreflective lesions with variably reflective lumina, and well-preserved outer retinal layers; there was vitreomacular adhesion. 

OCT angiography of the central 3×3 and 9×9 mm areas demonstrated flow signals corresponding to the intraretinal aneurysmal lesions, mainly within the superficial capillary plexus and involving the deep capillary complex; the choriocapillaris was preserved, and no anastomoses were seen.

A 46-year-old Caucasian man presented with five days of right-sided facial numbness in the ophthalmic (V1) and maxillary (V2) distributions, inability to close his right eye, inability to wrinkle the right side of his forehead, deviation of the mouth toward the left, and painless swelling of the upper lip and right side of the face. He had a two-year history of recurrent right lower motor neuron facial palsy treated with oral prednisone, with symptomatic improvement after each episode. He denied a family history of similar complaints, and he had no fissured tongue or history of sarcoidosis or Crohn’s disease. On examination, blood pressure was 220/120 mm Hg. He had right facial fullness, upper lip swelling, decreased sensation in the right V1 and V2 distributions, and an isolated right-sided facial nerve paralysis. 

To evaluate for possible secondary causes, chest radiography, renal duplex ultrasonography, colonoscopy, and noncontrast head CT were performed; all studies were unremarkable. An MRI of the brain with a focused nerve protocol could not be obtained because of insurance restrictions.

A 14-month-old spayed female Ragdoll cat, kept strictly indoors and adopted online a year earlier, was evaluated for a 12-month history of pruritus. Within days of acquisition, the owner noted generalized scratching, alopecia of the tail and face, and dark cerumen in both ears. A primary veterinarian diagnosed otodectic mange and administered a single 45 mg spot-on selamectin treatment, leading to resolution of ear mites and skin lesions and marked but incomplete relief of pruritus. Over the following months, the cat continued to scratch at a low intensity and had intermittent vomiting and diarrhea. At 13 months of age, the owner observed a flare of pruritus shortly after rabies vaccination. The veterinarian prescribed an exclusion diet with hypoallergenic food and two doses of dexamethasone given 3 days apart. After 1 month, only slight improvement was noted, and the cat was referred for further evaluation. On examination, there was self-induced alopecia and papulosquamous lesions on the abdomen, as well as gingivitis. Skin scrapings and Scotch-tape tests were negative. However, stereomicroscopic examination of a coat brushing sample revealed several mites.

A 29-year-old male farmer presented with a 10-day history of severe swelling on the right side of his face. He noted that it began as a small reddish raised lesion on his right upper eyelid, progressed to vesicle formation, and then to a dark ulcerative wound with swelling extending to the upper lid, lower lid, and cheek. One week before onset, he had slaughtered an ill ox in his village and eaten uncooked meat. There was no history of trauma or surgery. He self-administered oral antibiotics for one week prior to presentation. 

On examination, there was diffuse non-pitting edema of both the upper and lower right eyelids with a central ulcerated dark eschar. The lesion was non-tender and there was no abscess. He was unable to open the affected eyelids, but the cornea appeared normal. Vital signs were within normal limits, with a temperature of 36.1°C. The white blood cell count was 7,800 × 10^3 cells/mm^3.

A 14-year-old boy presented with a 2-year history of episodic bilateral ear erythema. He experienced 2–3 attacks per week, each lasting 30–45 minutes, associated with a burning sensation rated 5–6/10 on a visual analogue scale. Episodes were aggravated on awakening and occurred mainly during the summer. He denied earache, headache, visual disturbances, ear discharge or fullness, tinnitus, gait difficulty, or burning of the hands or feet. 

On examination, he was alert and oriented. The pinnae appeared normal at baseline, and otoscopic examination of both ears was unremarkable. Neurologic examination was normal. He displayed photographs on his mobile phone showing bilateral ear erythema occurring after sleep. 

He had been treated with amitriptyline and methylcobalamin for 2 years without symptom relief. Thyroid function tests and blood glucose levels were within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain was normal.

A 13-year-old girl with severe developmental delay and presumed epilepsy—on levetiracetam despite multiple normal EEGs—was admitted in a postictal state with slight dehydration. She was hemodynamically stable (HR 99 bpm, normal blood pressure, SpO2 99%).  
Laboratory studies showed marked rhabdomyolysis (CPK 6640 U/L, later rising to >42 670 U/L) with elevated troponin I (1156 ng/L) and transaminases (AST 187 U/L, ALT 65 U/L); serum electrolytes were normal. The initial ECG demonstrated a normal QTc interval.  
Levetiracetam was discontinued, and she was transferred to a pediatric center, where repeat ECG revealed QTc prolongation (570 ms), prompting initiation of oral propranolol (1 mg/kg/day). Over the next days, she developed hypotension and hydro-electrolyte disturbances and was admitted to the PICU.  
She then experienced non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (HR ~200 bpm) treated with intravenous magnesium (50 mg/kg) and lidocaine bolus followed by infusion (35 µg/kg/min). Echocardiography showed no structural or functional abnormalities.  
Upon transfer to the cardiac ICU, she was managed as presumed congenital long QT syndrome with maintenance of normal plasma potassium, calcium, and magnesium while on lidocaine. After a brief return to sinus rhythm, frequent polymorphic ventricular premature beats in short–long–short sequences triggered torsades de pointes and ventricular fibrillation requiring defibrillation.  
A temporary pacemaker was placed for ventricular pacing, and esmolol infusion (25 µg/kg/min) was added to ongoing lidocaine, resulting in transient rhythm stabilization. Despite this, two further episodes of torsades de pointes occurred, each requiring defibrillation, concurrent with worsening rhabdomyolysis and a drop in LVEF to 40%.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 1-week history of lower abdominal pain and a “feeling of pressure in the rectum” during bowel movements associated with an increased urge to defecate. She had not been sexually active for more than 10 years. On examination, she was afebrile; her lower abdomen was tender bilaterally, and cervical motion tenderness was elicited. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 12.4×10^9 per liter and a C-reactive protein level of 62 mg per liter; a pregnancy test was negative. She was diagnosed with pelvic inflammatory disease and started on intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics.  
  A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed two cystic structures in the pelvis. A transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a 5.8-cm unilocular simple cyst in the right ovary and a 3-cm left tubo-ovarian complex with associated hydrosalpinx. Ovarian tumor markers, blood cultures, vaginal swabs, and tests for sexually transmitted infections were negative.  
  The patient’s symptoms and laboratory values improved, and on hospital day 3, she was discharged on oral metronidazole and doxycycline with outpatient follow-up. Three months later, a repeat ultrasound showed a persistent 5-cm simple cyst of the right ovary and a left hydrosalpinx; she continued to have intermittent lower abdominal pain. Given the ongoing pain and imaging findings, she was scheduled for a bilateral salpingectomy and right ovarian cystectomy.

A 60-year-old man with metastatic renal cell carcinoma, treated since 2017 with four induction cycles of nivolumab (3 mg/kg) plus ipilimumab (1 mg/kg) every 2 weeks followed by maintenance nivolumab (3 mg/kg every 2 weeks), presented after his 10th cycle with progressively worsening fatigue. He denied abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or changes in fluid intake. On examination, he was afebrile; blood pressure was 110/70 mm Hg with no orthostatic changes, heart rate 78 beats/min, and he appeared fatigued but alert. Laboratory tests showed a serum sodium concentration of 117 mg/dL; renal function tests and thyroid function studies were within normal limits.

A 61-year-old woman (BMI 29.1) underwent two separate surgeries, each followed by inspiratory stridor and respiratory distress shortly after extubation. 

First surgery (cervical laminectomy for C2–C3 extradural tumor): 
– Induction with propofol and rocuronium; easy intubation with a 7.5 mm armored tube (Cormack–Lehane grade 1).  
– Maintenance: desflurane/50% O₂ for 3 h 30 min; no intraoperative events.  
– Reversal with pyridostigmine/glycopyrrolate; extubation was uneventful, with SpO₂ 99%.  
– Five minutes later in the PACU, she developed tachypnea, respiratory difficulty, and inspiratory stridor despite accessory-free lungs; SpO₂ remained 99% on 2 L/min nasal O₂.  

Second surgery (laparoscopic cholecystectomy, ten months later):  
– Preoperative ENT evaluation showed normal vocal cord structure and movement.  
– Induction with propofol/rocuronium; lidocaine given before intubation; intubated with 6.5 mm cuffed tube; dexamethasone given before extubation.  
– Maintenance: desflurane/50% O₂ plus remifentanil infusion for 50 min; uneventful.  
– Adequate neuromuscular recovery confirmed by TOF; extubation performed; shortly thereafter she developed respiratory difficulty with inspiratory stridor and maintained SpO₂ ≥ 98% with 100% O₂.  

Laboratory studies during the second event showed mild respiratory alkalosis (pH 7.48, PaCO₂ 31.6 mmHg, PaO₂ 106 mmHg).

A 21-year-old university student experienced syncope shortly after exercise. He reported no chest pain or dyspnea but had a self-limited diarrheal illness two weeks earlier. In the emergency department he was afebrile, blood pressure was 127/78 mmHg, heart rate 81 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Examination was unremarkable. His mother had idiopathic cardiomyopathy; his maternal grandmother died of sudden cardiac arrest.

On telemetry, he developed sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a cycle length of 220 ms, treated with intravenous metoprolol, amiodarone, and lidocaine. In the coronary care unit, he had polymorphic VT that degenerated into ventricular fibrillation; he was successfully defibrillated.

Serum chemistry was normal. Initial troponin I was 0.23 ng/mL (normal <0.04 ng/mL) and subsequently decreased. Pre-arrest ECG showed sinus rhythm with premature ventricular complexes of left bundle branch block, inferior axis morphology; there were no epsilon waves, precordial T-wave inversions, conduction delays, or QT prolongation. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a dilated left ventricle with ejection fraction 45% and severe basal-anterior hypokinesis with mild hypokinesis of adjacent segments. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated sub-epicardial late gadolinium enhancement in the basal-anterior and basal anterolateral segments and additional mid-inferior and mid-anteroseptal enhancement. The right ventricle was normal in size and function without late enhancement. An endomyocardial biopsy showed mild lymphocytic myocarditis, interstitial fibrosis, and myocyte hypertrophy.

A 50-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of headache and, on the day of admission, abrupt onset of dizziness, dysarthria, and aphasia while shoveling snow. Vital signs were within normal limits. Noncontrast brain CT showed a hypoattenuated lesion without enhancement in the left parietal cortex and underlying white matter. On MRI, T2-weighted images revealed a localized irregular, low-signal-intensity lesion with surrounding high T2 signal. Susceptibility-weighted imaging demonstrated dark signal intensity within the lesion. Gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted images showed a thin peripheral rim of enhancement. Diffusion-weighted images and ADC maps both showed low signal intensity in the lesion and surrounding edema, indicating a lack of diffusion restriction, though this was attributed to susceptibility artifact from blood products. Perfusion MRI revealed no increase in relative cerebral blood volume at the lesion. MR spectroscopy demonstrated an increased lactate peak, decreased N-acetyl aspartate peak, and no elevation of choline. The initial differential diagnosis was between a hemorrhagic brain tumor and a hemorrhagic non-tumorous lesion. The patient underwent excisional biopsy of the lesion; minimal active bleeding was noted intraoperatively. One week later, follow-up MRI revealed multiple new lesions in both supratentorial and infratentorial regions, each showing peripheral high T2 signal, central dark SWI signal, thin rim enhancement, surrounding edema, and low signal on DWI and ADC maps. The patient tested negative for HIV and had no history of immunodeficiency.

A 55-year-old man with a history of hyperlipidemia and metastatic lung adenocarcinoma (PD-L1 > 50 %, EGFR exon 20 insertion) presented 19 days after his third cycle of pembrolizumab (given alone after prior chemoimmunotherapy and a dexamethasone taper). He had initially responded, with regression of lung, brain, and bone metastases. He now reported fever and chills.  
On arrival, temperature 102.0 °F, blood pressure 64/44 mm Hg, heart rate 87 beats/min, respiratory rate 35 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 92 % on room air. He was lethargic with increased work of breathing.  
Laboratory studies revealed:  
• Ferritin > 40 000 ng/mL (normal 28–365)  
• LDH 3465 U/L (normal 87–241)  
• ESR 85 mm/h (normal 0–16)  
• CRP 281 mg/L (normal 0–3)  
• Acute kidney injury (creatinine 1.9 mg/dL)  
• Elevated AST 536 U/L and ALT 384 U/L  
• WBC 2200/µL with ANC 658/µL and ALC 579/µL, normal hemoglobin and platelets  
Chest radiograph showed the known right apical mass without new consolidation. He was admitted to the ICU for vasopressor support, received IV fluids and empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics.  
Differential diagnoses included COVID-19 infection, tuberculosis, bacterial pneumonia, viral hepatitis, adrenal insufficiency, and immune-related adverse events such as cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).  
Workup revealed:  
• Negative COVID-19 testing on four occasions  
• Unrevealing IFN-gamma release assay, hepatitis A/B serologies, EBV serologies, Bordatella pertussis antigen, HIV, aspergillus antigen, urine histoplasma, and multiple blood, sputum, and urine cultures  
• Negative respiratory viral panel (including influenza, adenovirus, RSV, and others)  
• CMV PCR 2902 IU/mL (interpreted as shedding)  
• Morning cortisol normal at 19.6 µg/dL  
• Soluble IL-2 receptor 23 020 U/mL (normal ≤ 1033) and IL-6 75 pg/mL (normal ≤ 5)  
Bone marrow biopsy could not be obtained due to his critical condition.

A 48‐year‐old woman with a history of asthma presented with a 2‐day history of right lower‐extremity numbness and pain that worsened despite conservative measures. She denied any low back pain. On examination, manual muscle testing of the right tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus was 3/5, and gastrocnemius and flexor hallucis longus were 4/5; deep‐tendon reflexes were normal. Straight‐leg‐raising was positive at 70 degrees; the femoral‐nerve stretch test was negative. 

Plain radiographs showed degenerative scoliosis at L5–S1. Lumbar MRI demonstrated a right‐sided disc herniation at L5–S1 without significant nerve‐root or cord compression. Initial peroneal‐nerve conduction studies revealed a motor conduction velocity of 51.5 m/s. Ankle‐brachial indices were decreased (0.78 on the right, 0.73 on the left), but lower‐extremity arteriography showed no significant vascular lesions. Based on these findings, she was diagnosed with lumbar disc herniation and treated symptomatically with Neurotropin®. 

By day 7, muscle strength nearly normalized, but lateral leg pain persisted. On day 22, pain increased, and by day 26 she developed right foot drop (tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, flexor hallucis longus, and peroneus longus 1/5; left side 4/5) with absent Achilles reflexes bilaterally. Urgent MRI showed no new nerve‐root compression. Repeat peroneal conduction studies failed to elicit an evoked myogenic potential. On day 30, she was unable to walk and was admitted for further evaluation.

A 26-year-old man presented with 2 days of nausea, recurrent bilious emesis, nonradiating epigastric pain, and upper abdominal fullness that worsened after meals. He noted mild postprandial discomfort for a week and endorsed a 12-lb weight loss over the preceding 3 weeks during Ramadan fasting. He denied prior emesis, postprandial pain, gastrointestinal bleeding, peptic ulcer disease, or NSAID use. Bowel movements were normal.  
On examination, blood pressure was 103/62 mm Hg, heart rate 94 beats/min, respiratory rate 17 cycles/min, and temperature 36.8 °C. BMI was 18.2 kg/m2. There was mild epigastric tenderness with diffuse fullness; no peritoneal signs.  
Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 10,200 cells/µL, neutrophils 75.9%, hemoglobin 14.5 g/dL, hematocrit 45.0%, platelets 201,000/µL, and lipase 200 U/L; liver function tests, lipid panel, electrolytes, BUN, and creatinine were normal.  
Noncontrast abdominal CT revealed a massively dilated stomach and proximal duodenum with a transition point around the region of the superior mesenteric artery, an estimated aortomesenteric angle of 20° and distance of 6 mm, no free intraperitoneal gas, and no features suggestive of pancreatic inflammation.  
A barium upper gastrointestinal series with small-bowel follow-through demonstrated a markedly distended stomach and proximal duodenal dilation with a sharp transition point between the second and third parts of the duodenum near the midline in the region of the SMA.  
He was started on maintenance IV fluids and underwent nasogastric decompression, yielding 800 mL of bilious contents.

A 62-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a mass over the right side of the nasal bridge associated with mild pain. There was no history of trauma, and he was otherwise asymptomatic. His medical history was notable for hypertension and chronic gout affecting both ankles, treated with allopurinol and colchicine; despite compliance, he had persistent hyperuricemia (serum urate, 0.62 mmol/L). On examination, there was a 2-cm firm, non-tender mass over the right nasal bridge, separated from the overlying skin, with mild erythema but no signs of active inflammation. Both nostrils were patent. CT of the paranasal sinuses showed a well-defined, mildly hyperdense 1.6-cm round lesion centered over the right nasal bridge with associated erosion and partial replacement of the right nasal bone; there was no intralesional calcification or cavitation and no similar lesions elsewhere.

A 27-year-old woman presented with a 10-day history of decreased vision and pain in her right eye. Visual acuity was 20/100 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left. Fundus examination of the right eye demonstrated an elevated nonpigmented mass measuring approximately 2.5×2.5 disc diameters just superior and temporal to the optic disc, with a flat retinal detachment in the macular area. Optical coherence tomography revealed an 892-µm choroidal elevated mass associated with a serous retinal detachment. Initial differential diagnoses included choroidal neoplasia (primary tumor or metastasis) and infectious or inflammatory diseases. Laboratory evaluation showed a negative angiotensin-converting enzyme titer and negative toxoplasma and HIV serologies. Given her risk factors for tuberculosis and unclear BCG vaccination history, both a QuantiFERON-TB test and purified protein derivative skin testing were performed; the former was positive and the latter revealed an induration of 13 mm. Chest radiography was normal.

A 57-year-old Japanese man presented 17 weeks after uncomplicated cataract surgery with a one-week history of right eye epiphora and photophobia. His decimal best-corrected visual acuity was 1.2 bilaterally and intraocular pressures were 19 mmHg. Examination of the right eye showed conjunctival hyperemia, fine keratic precipitates, and grade 1+ inflammatory cells in the anterior chamber; the vitreous and retina were unremarkable. He was otherwise in good health. An initial diagnosis of iritis was made, and he received topical steroids and a subconjunctival steroid injection; the symptoms improved only slightly. Three days later, he developed eye pain and recurrent hyperemia. Postoperative bacterial endophthalmitis without vitreous involvement was suspected, and an anterior chamber tap was performed. He received subconjunctival vancomycin (5 mg/0.5 ml) and ceftazidime (11.25 mg/0.5 ml), topical cefmenoxime, and oral minocycline (200 mg), but his condition worsened. The results of both culture and a multiplex PCR assay were negative. Considering a low-grade bacterial or fungal infection, a second anterior chamber tap was performed, and PCR testing targeting Actinomycetales and fungi was requested.

A 65-year-old man presented with a two-year history of an asymptomatic swelling on the lateral aspect of his left ankle. There was no history of trauma, and the size had remained stable. On examination, a 5 × 9 cm well-defined, firm-to-hard, nonmobile, nontender mass was noted over the lateral malleolus with mild discoloration of the overlying skin but no warmth or induration. Anteroposterior radiographs of the left ankle demonstrated a sessile, well-circumscribed radiopaque lesion overlying the lateral malleolus, with a homogeneously calcified matrix, no areas of lysis, no periosteal reaction, and no pressure erosions of the underlying fibula; the ankle joint itself appeared normal. Laboratory studies showed a serum calcium level of 10 mg/dL, phosphate 4 mg/dL, and alkaline phosphatase 127 U/L, all within normal limits. Initial differential diagnoses included synovial chondromatosis, tophaceous gout, calcified lipoma, myositis ossificans, and malignant tumors such as synovial sarcoma, osteosarcoma, and chondrosarcoma.

An 84-year-old man presented with two weeks of right upper-quadrant abdominal pain associated with non-projectile coffee-ground vomiting, melena, and weight loss. He denied fever, abdominal distention, or constipation. An initial ultrasound suggested an intrahepatic mass. Serologic tests for hepatitis A, B, and C and HIV were negative.

On examination, the patient was weak, emaciated, pale, and icteric, with bilateral lower-limb edema. He had a history of moderate alcohol use but no known tuberculosis exposure or prior TB infection. Vital signs were within normal limits. The abdomen was soft with tenderness in the right upper quadrant; there was no hepatosplenomegaly and normal bowel sounds.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 110 mm/h, hemoglobin 6.9 g/dL, total bilirubin 108 μmol/L (direct bilirubin 34.8 μmol/L), ALT 44 I/U, and AST 81 I/U. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed mildly dilated intrahepatic bile ducts, common hepatic duct, and common bile duct (1.3 cm) with an abrupt cutoff at the ampulla of Vater, suggestive of ampullary vs. peri-ampullary obstruction. The gallbladder was dilated with asymmetrical wall thickening and a contained anterior wall perforation; no gallstones were seen.

These findings were interpreted as mild biliary obstruction secondary to ampullary obstruction with contained perforated acalculous cholecystitis. A presumptive diagnosis of gallbladder or cholangiocarcinoma was made, and the patient was taken to surgery. Intraoperatively, the gallbladder and surrounding tissues were grossly inflamed; the fundus and body of the gallbladder appeared necrotic with marked wall edema. No mass was palpable at the pancreatic head. A subtotal cholecystectomy sparing the neck was performed, and reconstruction was via a Roux-en-Y cholecystojejunostomy. The excised gallbladder tissue was submitted for histopathological examination.

A 51-year-old man with gastroesophageal reflux disease and chronic pain managed with a spinal stimulator was diagnosed with autoimmune optic papillitis after several months of progressive vision loss. A lumbar puncture, brain MRI, and autoimmune workup excluded multiple sclerosis. He received six rounds of plasma exchange, corticosteroids, and then rituximab with improvement in vision.

After 4 years of rituximab therapy, he developed 6 months of diffuse abdominal pain, nonbloody diarrhea with nocturnal urgency, and an unintentional 60-lb weight loss. Physical examination showed diffuse periumbilical tenderness without peritoneal signs or distension; there were no oral ulcers or skin rashes. Laboratory studies revealed a C-reactive protein level of 68 mg/L (reference ≤4.9), albumin 2.8 g/dL (reference 3.6–5.1), and stool calprotectin 482 μg/g (reference ≤49). An evaluation for infectious etiologies, including stool Clostridioides difficile toxin, enteric pathogen PCR panel, cytomegalovirus DNA, and coccidioidomycosis, was negative.

Computed tomography enterography demonstrated pancolitis without small bowel involvement. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy was grossly normal. Colonoscopy revealed a normal terminal ileum, segmental ulcerations in the distal ascending and proximal transverse colon, and erythema in the distal descending and sigmoid colon. 

Pathology of colonic biopsies showed focal active colitis, cryptitis, scattered crypt abscesses, and branching crypts.

A 14-year-old boy with Loeys–Dietz syndrome and a prior valve-sparing aortic root replacement was admitted for elective mitral valve repair due to asymptomatic severe primary mitral regurgitation from bileaflet prolapse. One month before surgery, echocardiography showed an LVEF of 60% with moderate LV dilatation (diastolic diameter 65 mm, systolic diameter 43.5 mm) and severe regurgitation; preoperative CT angiography revealed no coronary lesions. Mitral valve repair was performed with a cardiopulmonary bypass time of 74 min, cross-clamp time of 59 min, and standard Del Nido cardioplegia. Intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography confirmed normal LV function and a competent repair. After weaning from bypass, the patient required norepinephrine (0.3 μg/kg/min) and epinephrine (0.1 μg/kg/min). Upon ICU arrival, he was in cardiogenic shock with cold extremities, oliguria, tachycardia, metabolic acidosis, and lactate of 15.9 mmol/L; milrinone was started and lactate improved. Forty-eight hours postoperatively, he sustained a cardiorespiratory arrest; return of spontaneous circulation was achieved after 5 min of CPR, but he remained on high-dose inotropes (epinephrine 0.8 μg/kg/min, norepinephrine 1 μg/kg/min). ECG showed inverted T waves in precordial leads. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed an LVEF of 30% with mid- to distal diffuse hypokinesia and relatively preserved basal segment contractility. Peripheral venoarterial ECMO was initiated.

A 36-year-old primiparous woman at 32 weeks of gestation presented with an extensive, intensely pruritic rash. The eruption began as erythematous papules in her abdominal striae and rapidly spread over days to involve the trunk, thighs, buttocks, calves, legs, and arms. The lesions had been unresponsive to high-potency topical corticosteroids.  

On admission, her temperature was 38 °C. She denied other symptoms or illnesses and had gained 15 kg during the first two trimesters. Obstetric ultrasound showed a 32-week fetus with normal morphology, estimated weight 2350 g (above the 90th percentile), a normal amniotic fluid index, and fetal tachycardia (fetal heart rate 180–200 bpm).  

Laboratory studies were all within normal limits, including c-ANCA, p-ANCA, circulating immune complexes, and rheumatoid factor. Infectious workup—including serologies and PCR for rubella, ECHO virus, coxsackievirus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2, HIV types 1 and 2, and Toxoplasma gondii—was negative. Procalcitonin and C-reactive protein levels were normal. Hematologic evaluation excluded leukemia and lymphoma.  

Given the location of lesions around the abdomen and the pruritic character, pemphigoid gestationis was considered. Anti–BP180 antibody ELISA returned 12 U/mL (reference <20 U/mL), and indirect immunofluorescence was negative for both BP180 and BP230 antibodies; leukocyte counts were normal. The patient declined a skin biopsy.

A 41-year-old man with a history of chronic cocaine and alcohol abuse was admitted in a stuporous state with urinary incontinence. Over the preceding 15 days he had developed dysarthria, mutism, prominent drowsiness, and psychomotor disturbances.

On examination, he was afebrile. Neurologic evaluation confirmed decreased responsiveness without focal deficits.

Laboratory tests were within normal limits, and the virological screening together with Quantiferon, HIV, and treponemal tests was negative. C‐reactive protein was mildly elevated at 1.18 mg/L. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed a high albumin level, no oligoclonal bands, and a normal immunoglobulin G index. Electroencephalography recorded low α and θ waves. Urine toxicology detected low levels of cocaine; benzodiazepines, barbiturates, oxycodone, amphetamines, methadone, and cannabinoids were negative. (Urine levamisole was not tested.)

Noncontrast head CT revealed multiple hypointense circular lesions in the bihemispheric white matter surrounded by edema. Brain MRI showed multiple well-circumscribed concentric lamellar lesions in the bihemispheric white matter, including the corpus callosum, with alternating bands of iso-/hypointensity on T1-weighted images and alternating hypo-/hyperintensity on T2‐weighted/FLAIR images. Diffusion-weighted imaging (b = 1000) demonstrated a rim of restricted diffusion, confirmed on the apparent diffusion coefficient map. After gadolinium administration, the lesions exhibited patchy “onion-like” concentric ring enhancement on T1-weighted images. Double inversion recovery sequences further delineated the lamellar structure. MR spectroscopy showed elevated choline and lactate peaks with a decreased N-acetylaspartate peak.

A 28-year-old primigravida at 39 weeks and 3 days of gestation was referred for evaluation of jaundice. She reported 5 days of yellow discoloration of her urine and sclera and 2 days of polyuria and polydipsia. Her antenatal course had been uneventful; she denied medication use, gestational hypertension, flu-like symptoms, or travel to malaria-endemic regions. HIV and hepatitis panels were negative.

On examination, she was jaundiced with moderate pallor. Temperature was 98.4°F, pulse 100/min, and blood pressure 120/80 mm Hg. Abdominal examination revealed a term-sized uterus, breech-presenting fetus with a heart rate of 140/min. Cervix was posterior, soft, uneffaced, and closed.

Laboratory studies showed:
• Random blood sugar 2.6 mmol/L (3.9–5.6)  
• Hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL; peripheral smear with microcytic hypochromic cells, target cells, spherocytes, bite cells  
• WBC 14,000/µL; platelets 163,000/µL  
• Total bilirubin 14.8 mg/dL (0.1–1.2), direct bilirubin 9.2 mg/dL (<0.3)  
• Bile acids 6.7 µmol/L (≤11.0)  
• PT 33 s (11–13.5), INR 2.75 (0.8–1.1), APTT 60 s (21–35), fibrinogen 76 mg/dL (200–400), D-dimer 2 mg/dL (<0.5)  
• AST/ALT 158/169 U/L, ALP 591 µkat/L, LDH 641 IU/L  
• Creatinine, electrolytes, and urine studies were unremarkable.

Ultrasound of the liver showed increased echogenicity and mild to moderate ascites. Obstetric ultrasound revealed a 3.4-kg fetus in breech presentation, anterior placenta, and amniotic fluid index of 15.5 cm.

Obstetric cholestasis was ruled out because of normal bile acids, and HELLP syndrome was considered unlikely in view of normotension and a normal platelet count.

A 13-year-old boy presented with a 5-day history of intermittent rectal bleeding and malaise. The stool was described as dark red. He denied abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, fever, trauma, or bleeding elsewhere. There was no personal or family history of chronic gastrointestinal disease. His prior episode of rectal bleeding in 2019 had been attributed to intestinal inflammation. 

On examination, his vital signs were stable. He had pale conjunctivae but no abdominal distension, and palpation elicited no tenderness; there was no organomegaly. Other findings were normal. 

Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, hematocrit 23.1%, erythrocyte count 2.86×10^6/µL, MCV 80.8 fL, MCHC 35.1 g/dL, platelet count 406×10^3/µL, and leukocyte count 14.66×10^3/µL. 

A noncontrast CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis (axial, coronal, and sagittal images) revealed only thickening of the intestinal mucosa.

A 14-year-old boy presented with unilateral left-sided breast enlargement for the past 12 months, accompanied by mastodynia rated 5/10 in severity that was worsened by tight-fitting shirts. He reported embarrassment and peer teasing, leading to avoidance of swimming and sports. He had been referred for liposuction but sought medical therapy to avoid surgery.

On examination, the left breast measured 3 cm in diameter with marked prominence, and a tender, firm, mobile ‘disk’ of tissue was palpable beneath the areola. His BMI was 20.2 (60th centile), and he was in Tanner Stage 3 puberty with normal secondary sexual characteristics. He denied any regular medications or illicit substance use. Family history was notable for pubertal gynaecomastia in two older brothers, one of whom underwent liposuction.

Laboratory studies revealed: testosterone 27 nmol/L (high-normal), SHBG 93 nmol/L (15–50), DHEAS 5 μmol/L (0.1–4.2), free androgen index 29%, estradiol <50 pmol/L, prolactin 305 mIU/L, β-hCG <5 IU/L, FSH 1.7 IU/L, LH 2.0 IU/L, normal full blood count and electrolytes, and a 46,XY karyotype.

An 11-year-old Croatian boy of Mediterranean origin with a history of asthma since age 6 was referred for evaluation of difficult-to-control asthma over the past six months. He reported dyspnea on exertion, multiple exacerbations (one requiring hospitalization) resistant to systemic corticosteroids, and used fluticasone-salmeterol 250 μg/50 μg twice daily, montelukast 5 mg once daily, and salbutamol four times daily as needed. His history included atopic dermatitis, cow’s milk allergy, and childhood epistaxis. His asthma had been well controlled without prophylaxis until two months before admission, when he developed poor appetite and frequent headaches. 

On examination, he appeared mildly ill and had resting hypoxemia (SaO2 92% on room air, unresponsive to supplemental oxygen), a grade 2/6 discontinuous systolic murmur along the left sternal border, decreased breath sounds over the right lung, and telangiectases on the left cheek and back; his mucous membranes were pale to cyanotic. Body plethysmography showed an FVC of 2.65 L (79% predicted), FEV1 of 2.61 L (97% predicted), an FEV1/FVC ratio of 95%, airway resistance of 0.38 L (155% predicted), residual volume of 1.57 L (156% predicted), and a total lung capacity of 4.26 L (97% predicted). Post-bronchodilator, FEV1 and FVC each increased by 5%. The DLCO was 61% predicted. 

Bronchoscopy revealed compression of the superior lingular bronchus. Chest radiography demonstrated a homogeneous soft-tissue mass measuring 20×30 mm in the left upper lobe. Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal cardiac structures with no evidence of pulmonary hypertension. CT pulmonary angiography revealed a 35-mm arteriovenous malformation in the perihilar left upper lobe and a small AVM in the apical segment of the right upper lobe.

A 66-year-old African man from a rural area presented with dull lower-back pain for three months, radiating to both thighs and aggravated by farming, relieved with rest and without accompanying numbness or urinary symptoms. Four days before presentation, he noted a mass protruding per anus during defecation, associated with severe pain and obstipation. He denied prior constipation, intermittent prolapse, changes in bowel habits, blood in stool, tenesmus, incomplete emptying, weight loss, or abdominal swelling. An attempted reduction at a district hospital failed, and he was referred for further care.
