On examination he was alert, in pain, afebrile (37 °C), dehydrated, with blood pressure 100/70 mm Hg and a weak regular pulse of 90 beats/min. There was no lymphadenopathy. The abdomen was scaphoid, non-tender, moving with respiration, tympanic to percussion, with increased bowel sounds and no palpable mass. Digital rectal examination revealed a large, foul-smelling, gangrenous sigmoid-shaped mass protruding per anus.

A provisional diagnosis of sigmoid intussusception with a differential of rectal prolapse was made. Hemoglobin was 10 g/dL. The patient received intravenous fluids and antibiotics and was prepared for emergency exploratory laparotomy.

A 24-year-old woman presented with 2 days of severe abdominal cramps and diarrhea. She denied skin rash, facial swelling, urticaria, difficulty breathing, nausea, or vomiting. She also denied recent drug use, travel, or sick contacts. Three days earlier she had a single fever to 39°C and reported a 1-week loss of appetite. Her medical history was significant for childhood angioedema affecting the face, larynx, and tongue treated with danazol, discontinued 5 years ago due to breathlessness, weakness, and amenorrhea; at age 11 she underwent emergency intubation for asphyxiation. There was no family history of similar symptoms or hereditary conditions. On examination, she was afebrile with stable vital signs. The abdomen was distended and tender with hyperactive bowel sounds; there was no rash, urticaria, or facial or tongue swelling. Laboratory evaluation showed a white-cell count of 6.2×10^9/L, C-reactive protein 4 g/L, serum ferritin 102 ng/mL; stool cultures were negative for Salmonella and Shigella; urinalysis was unremarkable. She was admitted for suspected acute abdomen, made nil per os, and received intravenous fluids, paracetamol, pantoprazole, and empiric ceftriaxone. Abdominal computed tomography revealed segmental wall thickening with submucosal edema of the ascending colon and proximal transverse colon with abrupt return to normal caliber. Endoscopy was unremarkable. A gastroenterologist initiated cetirizine for suspected histamine-mediated angioedema, but there was no response, and her symptoms resolved spontaneously, after which she was discharged.

A 21-year-old man was referred to oral and maxillofacial surgery for a draining cutaneous lesion beneath his chin, approximately 2 cm in diameter, present for 6 months. He had no tooth pain or facial trauma. Initially, a physician diagnosed a carbuncle and prescribed amoxicillin–clavulanate and clindamycin for 7 days, after which drainage and lesion size transiently decreased. However, the lesion recurred and gradually enlarged, prompting dental evaluation.

On extraoral examination, there was a well-demarcated sinus tract opening on the chin with minimal surrounding erythema. Intraorally, the mandibular anterior teeth had existing restorations, but the teeth and periodontal tissues appeared healthy, with no tenderness to palpation or percussion.

An intraoral periapical radiograph (without gutta-percha tracing) demonstrated a radiolucent lesion at the apex of the lower right central incisor, consistent with pulp inflammation and chronic apical periodontitis.

A 70-year-old nonsmoking woman with a 10-year history of severe persistent asthma and comorbid diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and ischemic heart disease was referred for uncontrolled nocturnal asthma symptoms over the preceding 4 months that worsened during sleep. Her regimen included fluticasone/salmeterol (250/50 mcg) 2 puffs twice daily, montelukast, sustained-release theophylline, procaterol, and salbutamol as needed for dyspnea. 

On examination she was obese with expiratory wheezing and audible stridor in the supine position. Chest radiography showed mild cardiomegaly, and parasinus radiography showed no sinus infection. Pulmonary function testing revealed moderate restrictive lung disease with a forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) of 59% of predicted. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a left ventricular ejection fraction of 70% with marked concentric hypertrophy. 

To further evaluate her persistent respiratory symptoms, dynamic multislice CT of the chest with virtual bronchoscopy was performed, which demonstrated collapse of the posterior tracheal wall on expiration, forming a crescent-shaped lumen without evidence of intraluminal or extraluminal mass.

A 65-year-old woman with a history of morbid obesity status post laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding nine years earlier presented with one week of progressive shortness of breath and one day of acute left pleuritic chest pain. She was afebrile but tachycardic, and her white-cell count was 20 600 per μL. Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen performed at an outside hospital demonstrated a moderate pericardial effusion, pneumopericardium, pneumoperitoneum, a filling defect in a segmental pulmonary artery consistent with pulmonary embolism, and esophageal dilation. She underwent gastric-band decompression in the emergency department, was admitted to the intensive care unit, and received broad-spectrum antibiotics. 

A single-contrast upper gastrointestinal examination showed an increased phi angle of the band concerning for gastric-band slippage but revealed no definitive leak, perforation, or fistula. Transthoracic echocardiography confirmed a pericardial effusion with signs of impending tamponade and preserved ejection fraction. She underwent pericardiocentesis, with removal of approximately 340 mL of serous fluid and placement of a pericardial drain. 

On hospital day 3, an esophagogastroduodenoscopy demonstrated erosion of the gastric band through the gastric wall just distal to the lower esophageal sphincter.

A 53-year-old male farmer with no underlying diseases presented with a 1-month history of prolonged fever and pleuritic chest pain. He denied any history of tuberculosis exposure.  
On examination, he was febrile (38.5°C) with a blood pressure of 101/47 mmHg and a pulse of 100/min. He had jugular venous engorgement and distant heart sounds; breath sounds were equal and clear.  
Electrocardiography showed sinus rhythm with low-voltage QRS complexes. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 1.4551×10^9/L with 75.85% neutrophils; renal and liver function tests were within normal limits.  
A chest radiograph demonstrated superior mediastinal widening and a soft-tissue opacity along the right paratracheal region. Contrast-enhanced CT angiography of the chest showed a normocaliber thoracic and abdominal aorta; a right paratracheal multiloculated rim-enhancing lesion with internal hypoattenuation; an enhancing pericardium; and a moderate pericardial effusion. The lung parenchyma was clear, the pleural spaces were unremarkable, and abdominal organs appeared normal.  
Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a thickened pericardium and a large circumferential hyperechoic pericardial effusion (∼2.5 cm), an ejection fraction of 62.8%, a swinging heart motion, right atrial and right ventricular diastolic collapse, inferior vena cava plethora, and more than 25% respiratory variation in mitral inflow velocity—findings compatible with cardiac tamponade.

A 71-year-old Chinese woman with a history of advanced non–small-cell lung cancer (adenocarcinoma) harboring an ALK fusion had progressive disease after initial chemotherapy. She began crizotinib (250 mg twice daily) and, after 2 months, her primary lung tumor and known metastases markedly regressed. Three months into crizotinib therapy, she was hospitalized with low-grade fever (38 °C), back pain, and fatigue. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 11.78 × 10^9/L. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated multiple cystic lesions in both kidneys and the liver. A needle biopsy of a renal cyst drained approximately 10 mL of pus-like fluid. Pathological examination revealed granulation tissue with mild lymphocytic infiltration and no malignant cells. Immunohistochemical staining of the biopsy was negative for TTF-1, AE1/AE3, CK7, PAX-8, P40, and Villin; Ki-67 was 5% positive. Treatment with moxifloxacin and imipenem–cilastatin was initiated empirically, despite negative blood cultures, but the fever and cystic lesions persisted.

A 57-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis, treated initially with methotrexate and tofacitinib and recently started on the TNF-α inhibitor golimumab after negative tuberculosis and viral hepatitis screening, was admitted with persistent fever to 39.4°C and fatigue. On examination, she was pale with splenomegaly; heart rate was 110 bpm, and other vital signs were stable. Initial laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 2.5 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL, platelet count 131 × 10^9/L, AST 505 U/L, ALT 333 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 439 U/L, total bilirubin 9.5 mg/dL, ferritin 2411 ng/mL, and triglycerides 398 mg/dL. CT of the chest and abdomen showed diffuse ground-glass opacities, new pulmonary nodules, fatty liver, and splenomegaly (14.6 cm). Over the next days, she developed acute hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring intubation (ARDS), circulatory shock on three vasopressors, and acute kidney injury requiring renal replacement therapy. Liver enzymes worsened (AST 6732 U/L, ALT 1160 U/L), and cytopenias progressed (hemoglobin 6.6 g/dL, platelets 29 × 10^9/L). Broad-spectrum antibiotics (vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam) were administered without improvement. Repeat labs showed triglycerides 398 mg/dL and fibrinogen 58 mg/dL, yielding an HScore of 267 (probability of HLH >99%).

A woman in her seventh decade presented with low back pain for 4 weeks, progressive difficulty walking and standing due to weakness, loss of sensation in both lower limbs, and bowel and bladder disturbance of the same duration. Two months earlier, she had a trivial fall at home and was managed conservatively with a brace and medications. Four weeks after the injury, she developed worsening weakness. She denied fever, night sweats, weight loss, or appetite change. 

On examination, there was diffuse dorsolumbar tenderness, localized kyphosis, and paraspinal muscle stiffness. Neurologic assessment showed bilateral lower-limb weakness, sensory loss below the nivél of the lesion, and reduced reflexes.

Plain radiographs demonstrated a compression fracture of the D12 vertebra with an intravertebral vacuum cleft. MRI of the thoracolumbar spine revealed increased signal intensity within the D12 vertebral body (intravertebral fluid), a linear area of decreased signal intensity on either side (double-line sign), and significant spinal cord compression at that level; there was no paravertebral fluid collection or mass.

Laboratory studies—including total and differential leukocyte counts, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, serum vitamin D, serum protein electrophoresis, and alkaline phosphatase—were all within normal limits. DEXA scanning confirmed osteoporosis (T score −2.7; Z score −2.2). Contrast CT of the chest and abdomen showed no masses or other abnormalities.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 9½-year-old child presented with a long history of postprandial vomiting since age 6 months, initially managed as gastroesophageal reflux with only slight improvement. Over several years, the patient developed a progressive sensation of abdominal heaviness and early satiety after minimal food intake. On examination, a palpable mass was noted in the right hypochondrium. 

Laboratory studies were unremarkable. An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a thin-walled cystic formation with purely anechoic content in the region of the left adrenal gland. To further characterize the lesion, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT was performed and showed a non-communicating retro-gastric cystic mass measuring approximately 87 × 59 mm, without evidence of connection to adjacent structures, raising the first suggestion of a gastric duplication cyst.

A woman in her late 40s was referred for evaluation of multiple abnormal findings on high-resolution CT. Ten months earlier she had begun abemaciclib, along with a gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist and fulvestrant, to prevent recurrence of hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer after surgery and chemoradiation. She had no respiratory symptoms. She was an ex-smoker (8 pack-years), worked in an office, had no pets, and took no other medications.  
On examination, her oxygen saturation was 98% on room air, and lung auscultation was normal. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 3.7×10^9/L, C-reactive protein 0.1 mg/dL, Krebs von den Lungen-6 756 U/mL, and surfactant protein-D 139.4 ng/mL. Autoantibodies for collagen vascular diseases were negative.  
Chest radiography revealed consolidation and a reticular shadow in the left lower field. HRCT showed bilateral, multiple nonsegmental ground-glass opacities and areas of consolidation with an organising-pneumonia pattern; review of prior scans demonstrated that these findings appeared and resolved in varying locations during the 10-month treatment period.  
Bronchoalveolar lavage from the left lower lobe yielded 47% lymphocytes, with no evidence of infection or malignancy.

An 82-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus treated for many years with metformin (1,000 mg/day), sitagliptin, and gliclazide was brought to the hospital with weakness and malaise. He had chronic kidney disease (baseline serum creatinine 1.7 mg/dL, eGFR 29.5 mL/min/1.73 m2), and his metformin dose had been reduced one month earlier. He was a picky eater, subsisting mainly on white rice, and had suffered heat stroke 7 days before admission, with minimal oral intake but continued his medications until one day before presentation.

On arrival, his Glasgow Coma Scale score was E3V4M4; respiratory rate 24 breaths/min; blood pressure 76/42 mmHg; pulse rate 100 beats/min; SpO2 97% on room air; temperature 36.2°C; BMI 17.9 kg/m2. He had dry mucous membranes and axillae. There were no focal neurologic deficits. 

Arterial blood gas analysis showed pH 6.58, HCO3– 1.0 mEq/L, base excess –34.6 mEq/L, and lactate 12.4 mmol/L. Laboratory tests revealed serum creatinine 7.61 mg/dL, eGFR 5.9 mL/min/1.73 m2, and potassium 6.6 mEq/L. Abdominal ultrasonography showed bilateral renal atrophy, no hydronephrosis, and a collapsed inferior vena cava. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a left ventricular ejection fraction of 65%, with no wall-motion abnormalities. 

He was diagnosed with lactic acidosis and hypovolemic shock, attributed to metformin accumulation and volume depletion. He received 2 L of crystalloid without urine output, was started on norepinephrine, and underwent continuous hemodiafiltration. His pH and lactate gradually normalized, and norepinephrine was discontinued 36 hours after admission.

On hospital day 5, his respiratory status acutely worsened. Chest radiography showed pulmonary congestion and bilateral pleural effusions, and his BNP rose to 1997 pg/mL. Echocardiography now showed diffuse hypokinesis and an LVEF of 28%. Electrocardiography revealed ST-segment depression in leads V3–V6. His systolic blood pressure remained near 100 mmHg despite worsening oxygenation.

A 59-year-old woman with a history of Guillain–Barré syndrome and a prior gastric ulcer, maintained on naproxen and omeprazole, presented with a 6-month history of intermittent abdominal pain accompanied by progressive postprandial nausea, vomiting, and unintentional weight loss. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies revealed iron deficiency anemia. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated circumferential mural thickening of the proximal duodenum. Upper endoscopy showed a clean-based antral ulcer extending into the duodenum and a severe obstructing duodenal stricture that precluded passage of an adult gastroscope. Biopsy specimens from the stricture site revealed acute on chronic duodenitis, and gastric biopsies were negative for Helicobacter pylori. Although peptic ulcer disease was initially suspected, the possibility of malignancy could not be excluded, and the patient underwent a Whipple procedure.

A 79-year-old man was admitted with acute onset of diffuse abdominal pain over several hours, associated with fatigue and altered bowel habits but no fever. His medical history included hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes mellitus, and prior cholecystectomy; there was no history of sigmoid diverticulitis.  
On examination, temperature was 37.9 °C, heart rate 105 beats/min, blood pressure 90/50 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. Abdominal examination revealed generalized tenderness with signs of peritonitis.  
Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 16,000 × 10^9/L.  
An urgent contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated thickening of the distal jejunal loop, mesenteric fat infiltration, and an isolated collection of free air within the mesentery, suggesting a possible small-bowel perforation.

A 35‐year‐old man presented in February 2021 with persistent fever and nonresolving left‐sided pneumonia. He had a PCR‐confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2 infection in October 2020, managed at home. Two weeks later he redeveloped high fevers; imaging showed left lower‐lobe consolidation treated initially with oral amoxicillin‐clavulanate. One month later, consolidation had increased in size; bronchoalveolar lavage grew Streptococcus pneumoniae and he received linezolid.

His history was notable for presumed autoimmune optic neuritis treated with 13 doses of rituximab from January 2017 to May 2019, resulting in persistent B‐cell depletion (absolute count zero) and hypogammaglobulinemia (IgM 12 mg/dl, reference 40–230). In February and March 2021, SARS‐CoV‐2 RT‐PCR and antibodies against nucleoprotein and spike receptor‐binding domain were undetectable.

Differentials including tuberculosis, organizing pneumonia, lymphoma, ANCA‐associated vasculitis, and lung malignancy were considered. Sputum Xpert‐TB‐PCR was negative. Multiple blood cultures, bone marrow biopsy, and fungal cultures were negative. Transbronchial lung biopsy revealed organizing pneumonia. He was started on high‐dose steroids and improved.

In April 2021 he was readmitted with persistent fever. Sputum culture grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa and piperacillin was initiated. A chest CT showed resolution of the previous left lower‐lobe consolidation but new bilateral ground‐glass opacities.

A 23-year-old woman with no significant medical or psychiatric history presented with convulsions, agitation, and rapidly progressive disorientation. Three weeks earlier she had a mild viral prodrome with dry cough and rhinitis. On examination her vital signs were normal; Glasgow Coma Scale was 12/15. She had fluctuating cognition, confusion, disorientation, and involuntary facial and limb movements. Initial blood tests—including a complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, thyroid function tests, and viral serologies—were unremarkable. Despite treatment with risperidone, her agitation and psychosis persisted. A lumbar puncture showed lymphocytic pleocytosis with a predominance of CD4+ T cells, elevated protein, and normal glucose. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral multifocal high T2 signal changes surrounding the ventricles and in the basal nuclei with vasogenic edema.

A 63-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 3-month history of low back pain that began after a day of hiking. The pain radiated to her left lower limb and was associated with paresthesia in the lateral aspect of the thigh. Neurological examination revealed no sensory or motor deficits. 

A lumbar spine MRI was obtained. On T1-weighted images, there was an elongated extradural space-occupying lesion in the left anterolateral epidural space and neural foramen at L2–L3, without apparent dependence on the intervertebral disc. On T2-weighted and other fluid-sensitive sequences, the lesion was hyperintense compared with adjacent muscle. 

After intravenous contrast administration, the lesion demonstrated peripheral enhancement and a central filling defect.

A 60-year-old right-hand–dominant Colombian cleaner presented with a 3-week history of pain and swelling in the tip of her right thumb. She had hypothyroidism treated with thyroxine, was a non-smoker, and functionally independent. She reported a longstanding vertical midline split of the right thumbnail and felt her symptoms began after trimming this nail. A 5-day course of oral flucloxacillin prescribed by her general practitioner yielded no improvement.

On examination, the right thumb was swollen with tenderness under the nail plate but no pulp tenderness, erythema, or fluctuant collection; there were no Kanavel signs. A small area of peeled, devitalized skin was present at the tip. The digit was neurovascularly intact.

Blood tests were unremarkable. Plain radiographs of the right thumb showed a lytic lesion involving the tuft of the distal phalanx. She was admitted for presumed infection, treated with elevation and intravenous antibiotics, and underwent emergency surgical washout and debridement. Intraoperatively, no pus was found in the pulp, but the distal phalanx bone was eroded and soft. Multiple bone specimens were sent for microscopy, bacterial culture, acid-fast bacilli (AFB) culture, and histopathology.

Citrobacter freundii was isolated from bone biopsies on enrichment culture, and AFB cultures were negative. Two weeks after biopsy, the histopathology report described “fragments of a cellular spindle cell tumour with islands of osteoid, which was suspicious for a primary bone malignancy.”

A 54-year-old man was admitted with a 20-day history of left knee swelling and deformity. He denied any trauma. The knee was mildly painful; he could flex and extend but could not bear weight. An earlier local X-ray reportedly showed a displaced fracture of the left tibial plateau.

His medical history was notable only for a positive serum Treponema pallidum antibody. He had no known diabetes or other systemic illness.

On examination, vital signs were stable. There was no spinal deformity or limitation of spinal movement. Upper limbs had normal strength and sensation. Left knee inspection showed swelling and varus deformity. There was a positive floating patella test, mild tenderness, and percussion pain. Range of motion was 120° of flexion to 20° of extension. Left lower-extremity muscle strength was graded 4/5; right was 5/5. The American Knee Society clinical score was 45; functional score, 30. There was hyperpigmentation of the left leg, shallow hypoesthesia over the lateral plantar surface, and absence of the left great toe. Distal pulses were intact; Babinski and Hoffmann signs were negative.

Laboratory studies showed normal liver and renal function, electrolytes, blood glucose, hemoglobin A1c, and tumor markers; elevated platelet count, mildly increased high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate.

Imaging of the left knee included X-rays and CT scans, which demonstrated a comminuted medial tibial plateau fracture with articular surface fragmentation, collapse, displacement with bone resorption, and surrounding soft-tissue calcification. MRI of the left knee revealed tears of the medial and lateral patellar retinacula, anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments, and medial collateral ligament; medial meniscus injury; and bone contusions.

MRI of the cervical and lumbar spine showed no evidence of syringomyelia. CT venography of the left lower extremity showed stenosis of the popliteal vein at the level of the fracture without filling defects and mild femoral vein stenosis. Electromyography revealed severe damage to the left tibial and sural nerves and mild delay in right sural nerve conduction.

A 78-year-old man with diabetes, hypertension, vascular leukoencephalopathy, and coronary heart disease was admitted for COVID-19 and treated with oxygen and steroids. On hospital day 2, he developed de novo atrial flutter, and therapeutic enoxaparin was started after myocardial infarction was excluded by ECG and absence of chest pain. On hospital day 5, he had sudden-onset right-sided hemiparesis (NIHSS score 7) with spontaneous, complete recovery within 24 hours. Cerebral MRI, including time-of-flight angiography, showed no acute lesion. He was diagnosed with a transient ischemic attack, and anticoagulation was continued. A nonconvulsive epileptic seizure was considered, and levetiracetam 2,000 mg/day was initiated; on hospital day 7, although seizure-free, the dose was increased to 3,000 mg/day.

A 44-year-old man with no history of chronic disease presented with a one-week history of diffuse abdominal pain, most pronounced in the right hypochondrium, and fever. On examination, he was tachycardic (144 beats per minute) with a blood pressure of 120/86 mm Hg. Abdominal palpation elicited generalized tenderness without peritoneal signs, and a palpable mass was noted in the right upper quadrant. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (17 000/mm^3) with 82% neutrophils, hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, platelet count 148 000/mm^3, serum creatinine 0.7 mg/dL, sodium 128 mmol/L, and albumin 1.6 g/dL. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed marked thickening of the right colon wall, a perforation at the hepatic flexure communicating with a subphrenic abscess, segmental destruction of the right hepatic lobe, and multiple peripheral hepatic abscesses.

A 33-year-old Bulgarian man was evaluated for an 18-month history of progressive attention and memory impairment, apathy, anxiety, and irritability. His brother first noted confusion and forgetfulness that interfered with his work as a construction worker. The patient had limited formal education but had been fully independent in activities of daily living until symptom onset.

On examination, he was not fully oriented to time but was relatively oriented to place. Neuropsychological testing showed mild to moderate dementia (MMSE score 16/30), severe verbal learning impairment (immediate recall 4/10 words; delayed recall 1/10; recognition 0/10), difficulty recalling personal information, mild anomia, poor categorical fluency (10 animals/min), and a severe dysexecutive syndrome (coding score 8 with two mistakes; letter fluency 1 “M”-word/min). 

Neurological examination revealed preserved pupillary light and accommodation reflexes without signs of Argyll-Robertson pupils, but pyramidal and extrapyramidal signs, dysarthria, and impaired coordination were present. Routine blood tests (CBC, electrolytes, glucose, liver and renal function, thyroid function, B12, folate) were normal.

Cerebrospinal fluid was clear, with 1×10^6/L erythrocytes, 39×10^6/L leukocytes (82% lymphocytes), protein 0.88 g/L, and positive oligoclonal bands. Serum VDRL titer was 1:128 and TPHA 1:2560; CSF VDRL was 1:64 and TPHA 1:640. HIV testing was negative.

MRI of the brain demonstrated moderate cortical atrophy and marked bilateral hippocampal atrophy on FLAIR and T1-weighted images, without focal areas of increased signal intensity.

A 65-year-old woman presented with severe abdominal pain, fever, and profuse diarrhea. She had completed a 7-day course of amoxicillin for sinusitis. On examination, temperature was 39°C, heart rate 112 beats/min, and blood pressure 99/65 mmHg. Abdominal examination revealed hyperactive bowel sounds and diffuse tenderness with rebound; there was no guarding. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 17,000/μL and a creatinine level of 1.7 mg/dL. An enzyme immunoassay was positive for toxigenic Clostridium difficile. She was resuscitated with intravenous fluids and started on oral metronidazole. 

That night, she developed sudden severe retrosternal chest pain with dyspnea. Electrocardiogram showed ST-segment elevation in leads V1–V5. Initial troponin-I was 2.16 ng/mL (peaking at 9.8 ng/mL), and B-type natriuretic peptide was 447 pg/mL. Chest radiography and hepatobiliary ultrasound were unremarkable. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated apical ballooning and global left ventricular hypokinesis with an ejection fraction of approximately 20–25%.

A 27-year-old woman with class III obesity presented with severe fatigue and generalized muscle weakness, progressive over several months, leading to multiple falls and decreased oral intake. Five months earlier, after starting a low-carbohydrate, calorie-restricted diet, she developed proximal lower-extremity weakness and severe vomiting; she stopped the diet after losing 20 lb. Initial testing showed a mildly elevated TSH (5.45 μIU/mL; reference 0.55–4.78) with positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies and an elevated CK of 588 U/L (34–145). Despite levothyroxine therapy, her TSH remained elevated and weakness worsened. Autoantibody panels for myositis, necrotizing myopathy, and myasthenia gravis were negative, and a muscular dystrophy genetic panel was unremarkable. Electromyography suggested an inflammatory, genetic, or metabolic myopathy. A vastus lateralis biopsy revealed vacuolated muscle fibers with lipid droplets. Plasma acylcarnitine profile showed elevated small-, medium-, and long-chain species. Urine organic acid analysis revealed markedly elevated orotic acid and 2-hydroxy glutaric acid. 

On hospital admission for worsening weakness and decreased intake, examination showed proximal > distal weakness of all extremities, neck weakness, and reduced lower-extremity reflexes. Imaging revealed bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli. Laboratory evaluation demonstrated a venous pH of 7.00 (7.32–7.43), beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.67 nmol/L (0.02–0.27), CK 4656 U/L, and lactate 6.0 mmol/L (<1.3). She was admitted to the ICU for management of severe ketoacidosis and rhabdomyolysis and treated with bicarbonate, fluids, thiamine, dextrose, and heparin. Empiric carnitine, riboflavin, cyanocobalamin, and coenzyme Q10 were started for a presumed riboflavin-responsive lipid storage myopathy.

A 16-year-old male was referred with a clinical diagnosis of ameloblastoma. He was asymptomatic and had no significant medical history. Panoramic radiography demonstrated a multilocular radiolucent lesion surrounding the crown of the impacted mandibular right second molar, extending from the mandibular notch to the right first premolar and displacing the mandibular canal and third molar. Intraoral examination revealed a slight, painless swelling of the buccal and lingual cortices from the lower right first molar region to the mandibular ramus. To further characterize the lesion, multislice CT was performed, showing a unilocular hypoattenuating area without septations. The attenuation values ranged from 3.9 to 22.9 Hounsfield units, suggesting a fluid-containing lesion that could be compatible with a dentigerous cyst or a unicystic ameloblastoma.

A 63-year-old African-American woman with hypertension, obesity, and prediabetes presented with 9 days of a pustular skin rash and 3 days of bilateral eye pain and redness. She had no prior ocular history. A few hours before the rash began, she received trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection. Review of systems was positive for subjective fever, headache, cough, and dry mouth.  

On examination, she was afebrile and had normal blood counts and a normal comprehensive metabolic panel. Dermatologic examination showed multiple small erythematous pustules on the trunk and extremities, sparing the face, palms, and soles.  

Ophthalmologic examination revealed visual acuity of 20/20 in both eyes, normal pupils, and intraocular pressures of 14 mm Hg OD and 12 mm Hg OS. Slit-lamp examination demonstrated bilateral sectoral conjunctival injection, inferior gelatinous limbal corneal infiltrates without overlying epithelial defects, and diffuse punctate epithelial erosions with tear‐film irregularity, more severe in the right eye. The anterior chambers were quiet, and the dilated fundus examination was unremarkable.  

The corneal infiltrates were presumed sterile due to their bilateral distribution and intact epithelium, and she was started on prednisolone acetate four times daily and erythromycin ointment three times daily in both eyes, as well as topical triamcinolone ointment twice daily for her skin.

A 63-year-old man presented with 3 days of left upper limb pain. It began with sudden-onset numbness of the left fingers that progressed to severe, sharp pain ascending to the left shoulder, left side of the neck, chest, shoulder, and back, accompanied by headache episodes. The pain worsened when lying flat, improved with walking, and was unrelieved by multiple painkillers. He denied dyspnea, chest tightness, palpitations, cough, blurry vision, or lower limb swelling. His past medical history was unremarkable except for well-controlled heartburn; he denied trauma. He is a mason who resumed weight lifting 1 month before symptom onset.

On examination, there was muscle tenderness of the left chest and arm with reduced lower-limb reflexes. Vital signs were: blood pressure 187/117 mmHg, pulse 133 bpm, respiratory rate 28/min, temperature 36.8°C, and SpO₂ 97% on room air. 

Laboratory studies showed a normal full blood count, normal serial troponins, a slightly elevated D-dimer, and an HbA₁c of 13%. Electrolytes were normal except for a mildly low calcium level. Serial ECGs showed mild ST elevation in leads V2 and V3. Chest, left shoulder, and cervical spine radiographs were normal. 

He was started empirically on treatment for peptic ulcer disease and myocardial infarction, but the MI treatment was discontinued after a coronary CT angiogram showed normal findings. Antihypertensive and antihyperglycemic therapies were initiated. Despite these measures and high-potency analgesics, his pain remained severe. Two days after admission, he developed episodes of twitching in his left hand lasting a few minutes, precipitated by holding objects such as a book.

A 55-year-old man with a history of end-stage post-traumatic osteoarthritis of the left ankle treated three years earlier with a three-component mobile-bearing total ankle arthroplasty presented with new-onset ankle pain, severe weight-bearing impairment, and limitations in daily activities despite ongoing medical and physical therapy. On examination, the skin and surgical scar appeared healthy without signs of infection, but the ankle was diffusely swollen. Pain was localized to the medial malleolar region and anterior aspect of the prosthesis. Radiographs of the ankle showed mild bone resorption at the tibial and talar interfaces with early medial and anterior component loosening, and a periarticular soft-tissue mass extending anteriorly from the tibial component with diffuse intra- and perilesional ossifications. Laboratory studies, including leukocyte count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein, were all within normal limits. A differential diagnosis of septic loosening was considered but initially ruled out due to the absence of local or systemic inflammation and normal inflammatory markers. An infectious-disease consultation supported a planned surgical approach and recommended biopsy sampling. Neoplastic degeneration was considered unlikely given the absence of a tumor history, unremarkable radiographic features for malignancy, and the close spatial and temporal relation to the prosthesis. The condition was initially interpreted as aseptic loosening. A computed tomography scan was proposed; however, the patient declined further diagnostic investigations, and because there was no evidence of severe bone loss, it was not performed.

A 17-month-old girl was referred for a second opinion regarding macular scars and poor vision. She was born at 37 weeks’ gestation via uncomplicated vaginal delivery, weighing 4 lb 7 oz. Prenatal ultrasound noted intrauterine growth retardation; the mother had first-trimester chlamydia treated with antibiotics. No systemic or genetic workup was performed after birth. 

Around 3 months of age, the mother observed abnormal eye movements, poor response to visual stimuli, and occasional generalized limb jerking. A local retinal specialist reported retinal scarring with no available intervention.

At the University of Florida pediatric ophthalmology clinic, examination under anesthesia revealed borderline microcornea (horizontal corneal diameter 10 mm), myopic astigmatism, and extensive multifocal chorioretinal pigmented scars involving the macula and peripheral retina with fibrous vitreous strands in the right eye. The left eye showed a large macular scar extending between the arcades to the periphery. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated hyperfluorescent staining centrally with hypofluorescent borders and no signs of active disease.

TORCH studies returned negative with the exception of Toxoplasma IgG positivity >400 IU/mL (normal <8.8 IU/mL). Brain MRI showed scattered supratentorial white matter calcifications, and EEG monitoring captured no seizure activity.

A 32-year-old right-handed Caucasian woman presented with a 3-week history of left shoulder pain and numbness along her left forearm and fifth finger, exacerbated by elbow extension against resistance. She was initially diagnosed with medial epicondylitis and treated with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug. The next morning she awoke to find her left arm swollen and with a purplish discoloration over the dorsal distal forearm. 

On examination, her left upper-arm circumference was 33 cm (31.5 cm on the right) and left lower-arm circumference was 23 cm (21 cm on the right). There was subtle purplish discoloration over the dorsal distal forearm. Both limbs were warm, with normal radial pulses and capillary refill. Range of motion of the shoulders, elbows, and wrists was normal bilaterally, and deep tendon reflexes were intact. She had numbness over the dorsal and ventral left forearm and the lateral palm of the left hand but normal strength. 

She was afebrile and normotensive. Her lungs were clear and heart sounds normal. She was a non-smoker, had no history of trauma, surgery, or cancer, and no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism. She engaged in regular cross-training and had a body mass index of 25.8 after losing 40 kg over three years. Her only medication was an oral contraceptive containing drospirenone. Chest, shoulder, and elbow radiographs were normal.

A 48-year-old male triathlete (height 1.82 m; weight 69 kg; body-mass index 20.8 kg/m²) presented with a 12-month history of deep pain in the left gluteal region. The pain was insidious in onset, worsened during faster running and sprinting, and was aggravated by prolonged sitting. He denied any acute trauma, prior surgery, or other comorbidities. He reported no radiating pain or neurovascular symptoms.

On physical examination, there was focal tenderness to palpation over the left ischial tuberosity and pain elicited by passive stretching of the hamstring muscles. The Puranen–Orava test, the bent-knee stretch test, and the modified bent-knee stretch test were all positive. His Victorian Institute of Sport Assessment–Hamstring (VISA-H) score was 23.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis demonstrated thickening of the proximal hamstrings complex with intrasubstance heterogeneity and evidence of partial tendon rupture, along with bone marrow edema of the ischial tuberosity.

A 6-month-old Bangladeshi girl was brought to the hospital with a 2-day history of moderate-volume watery stools (12–15 per day), fever, and 12 hours of lethargy. She had no vomiting, rash, convulsions, or blood/mucus in the stool. The mother reported that the child became excessively thirsty, and, instead of her usual diet, received five packets of rice-based ORS (each mixed in 500 mL water instead of 1100 mL) and five packets of properly diluted glucose-based ORS. The child passed urine a few hours prior to admission. 

On examination: axillary temperature 39.4 °C; pulse 134/min, normal volume; blood pressure 100/50 mmHg; respiratory rate 54/min; capillary refill 3 s. Weight 5.9 kg; length 63 cm; Z-scores for weight-for-age −1.29, weight-for-length −0.40, length-for-age −1.21. She was lethargic and irritable to touch. There were no signs of dehydration, edema, pallor, or cyanosis. Chest and heart sounds were normal; abdomen was soft, non-tender, with active bowel sounds. Bedside blood glucose was 11.9 mmol/L; oxygen saturation 99% on room air.

Initial assessment: acute watery diarrhea, lethargy with excessive thirst, and possible sepsis.  

Laboratory results on day 1: hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL; WBC 8900/mm3 (neutrophils 44.5%, lymphocytes 42.0%); total calcium 1.86 mmol/L; total magnesium 1.22 mmol/L; serum creatinine 47 μmol/L. Chest X-ray, stool RME, and urine RME were normal. Blood culture grew Enterobacter spp; rectal swab culture was negative. She was started on IV ampicillin and gentamicin for presumed sepsis.

A 10-year-old boy with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia diagnosed 3 months earlier (bone marrow: 95% precursor B-ALL; CSF without blasts) is receiving induction chemotherapy per MRC UK ALL-12 protocol (daunorubicin and vincristine on days 1, 8, 15, and 22; prednisolone days 1–28; L-asparaginase days 17–28). During the fourth week of therapy, three days after his fourth dose of vincristine, he developed rapidly progressive ascending weakness of all four limbs over 48 hours without any preceding infection. On examination, he had pure motor areflexic quadriplegia (upper-limb power grade 3, lower-limb grade 0) with intact bladder, respiratory, and bulbar functions. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (14 300/mm^3) and thrombocytopenia (98 700/mm^3). CSF analysis revealed glucose 53 mg/dL, protein 128 mg/dL, 5 lymphocytes/mm^3, and no blasts. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain and spine was normal. On day 5 of illness, electrophysiological evaluation demonstrated a pure motor axonal polyradiculoneuropathy: bilateral peroneal and tibial nerves were unexcitable; median and ulnar nerves had reduced compound muscle action potentials, prolonged latencies, and normal conduction velocities; F waves were absent in the lower limbs and prolonged in the upper limbs; sensory nerve action potentials were normal; needle electromyography showed a neurogenic pattern.

A 20-year-old man enrolled in a first‐in‐human trial of KM-819, an investigational anti-Parkinson agent, received 200 mg orally once daily for 7 days. He underwent lumbar punctures for cerebrospinal fluid sampling on Day 1 (pre-dose) and on Day 7 (1 hour after dosing) using a 22G traumatic needle. He was discharged on the morning of Day 8; one hour later he developed a severe, throbbing, grade 3 headache in the bilateral frontal regions. He also experienced nausea, vomiting, neck stiffness, and extremity numbness (grades 1–2). These symptoms worsened when he was upright and improved within minutes of lying supine. Five days later, with worsening headache, he was referred to neurology and admitted for further evaluation.  
On neurologic examination, there were no abnormal findings. Vital signs and laboratory tests were within normal limits. A noncontrast head computed tomography scan showed no abnormalities.

A 17-year-old girl presented with a 1-month history of progressive bilateral lower-limb pain, swelling, and tenderness, with limitation of movement for 1 week. She reported no fever or other systemic symptoms. Vital signs were normal (BP 120/70 mmHg; HR 72 bpm; T 98°F; RR 16/min; SpO₂ 98% on room air). Developmental history was notable for delayed milestones (neck control at 6 months, sitting at 9 months, first speech at 3 years, walking at 5 years) and frequent falls with difficulty in combing hair, dressing, and climbing stairs since age 5. Menarche occurred at age 13, with occasional irregular cycles. On examination, she had short stature (sitting height 28.7 in, arm span 25.2 in), an MMSE score of 29/30, lower-limb weakness with swelling and tenderness, and marked limitation of movement. Her hands and feet showed congenital brachydactyly, and nasal bridging was prominent.  
Laboratory tests showed Hb 9.9 g/dL, WBC 8.4×10^9/L, platelets 509×10^9/L, ESR 80 mm/h; creatine phosphokinase 592 IU/L (elevated), LDH and aldolase within normal limits; PTH 130 pg/mL (15–65), 25-OH vitamin D 65.2 nmol/L (75–100), calcium 2.35 mmol/L (2.10–2.55), phosphate 0.79 mmol/L (0.74–1.52), glucose 6.1 mmol/L (4.2–6.1).  
X-rays of the hands showed reduced metacarpal height, mild periarticular osteopenia, and decreased bone density. X-rays of the feet showed reduced height of the first and fourth metatarsals with mild osteopenia and decreased bone density—“these findings were also suggestive of pseudohypoparathyroidism as the differential diagnosis.” Muscle biopsy revealed small muscle fibers with centrally located nuclei and ring fibers; the overall impression was suggestive of myopathy.

A 60-year-old man with a 3-year history of allergic rhinitis and therapy-resistant asthma presented with severe central chest pain radiating to the back, nausea, sweating, neck pain, fatigue, and generalized weakness. He had no prior cardiac disease or cardiovascular risk factors. On examination, blood pressure was 100/60 mm Hg, heart rate 130 beats/min, heart sounds were normal, and the lungs were clear. A 12-lead ECG showed sinus tachycardia with globally flat T waves and no dynamic ST-segment changes. Laboratory tests revealed a white-cell count of 18.16 × 10^9/L with 27.3% eosinophils (5.0 × 10^9/L), C-reactive protein 92 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 22 mm/h, troponin T 1267 ng/L, and NT-proBNP 6470 ng/L. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated segmental anterior left ventricular wall-motion abnormalities, mildly reduced ejection fraction, and a small pericardial effusion. Invasive coronary angiography showed unobstructed coronary arteries. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging confirmed regional hypokinesia of the anterior and anteroseptal segments with mildly impaired systolic function, myocardial oedema on T2-weighted imaging, and subendocardial late gadolinium enhancement in a non-ischaemic distribution. In the context of the very high eosinophil count, a vasculitic process was considered as the working diagnosis.

A 46-year-old man with no past medical history presented with 6 days of fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, headache, weakness, cough, and rhinorrhea. He denied travel to malaria-endemic regions and worked as a motorcycle taxi driver transporting passengers to an international airport. On examination, temperature was 37.6 °C, blood pressure 100/65 mmHg, heart rate 126 beats/min, respiratory rate 36/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on 5 L/min nasal cannula. Physical findings included scleral icterus, acral edema, bilateral calf tenderness, and a maculopapular abdominal rash. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 15.1 g/dL, leukocytes 7800/µL, platelets 51,000/µL, sodium 120 mmol/L, potassium 2.8 mmol/L, chloride 87 mmol/L, AST 172 U/L, ALT 91 U/L, and total bilirubin 6.26 mg/dL (direct 4.90 mg/dL). Renal tests showed urea 119 mg/dL, creatinine 1.34 mg/dL, and albumin 2.7 g/dL. Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated pH 7.44, pO2 90 mmHg, pCO2 36 mmHg, and HCO3 25 mmol/L. PCR for SARS-CoV-2 and leptospira serology were negative. Chest radiography showed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates at the lung bases and a left pleural effusion. He was transferred to a high-care unit, received penicillin G and electrolyte repletion, and was intubated for worsening respiratory failure. Hepatitis B and C serologies were negative. On hospital day 4, a malaria rapid diagnostic test and peripheral-blood smear were both negative.

A 53-year-old woman was admitted with a one-month history of night sweats, fevers up to 39.5 °C, 10 kg weight loss, fatigue, weakness, abdominal discomfort, and headache. She had no relevant family, drug, surgical, or psychosocial history. On examination, she was febrile but had no peripheral lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, C-reactive protein 100.6 mg/L, and fibrinogen 6.57 g/L. Blood, throat, and urine cultures and serologic tests for Brucella spp., Chlamydia spp., Cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, Francisella tularensis, HIV, Mycoplasma spp., Toxocara spp., Treponema pallidum, and Yersinia spp. were all negative. Serology for Toxoplasma gondii showed a false-positive IgM with negative IgG and IgA, and follow-up IgM levels trended toward normalization. Antistreptolysin-O titer and rheumatoid factor were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography, transthoracic echocardiography, chest radiography, and abdominal CT scan were unremarkable. Consultation with rheumatology, cardiology, and hematology specialties revealed no abnormalities. The illness met criteria for fever of unknown origin. A PET/CT scan was then performed, revealing multiple hypermetabolic retroperitoneal lymph nodes (maximum SUV 7.4) between the inferior vena cava and the aorta from the bifurcation up to the left renal vein, with perinodal soft-tissue infiltration and thickening of the retroperitoneal fascia. Exploratory laparotomy and biopsy were planned for definitive diagnosis.

A 47-year-old Hispanic man with asthma and type 2 diabetes was referred to a uveitis specialist for several weeks of bilateral conjunctival injection, photophobia, and hazy vision. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/30 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left. Examination revealed anterior chamber cells and iris nodules in both eyes; the posterior segments were unremarkable. On physical examination, there was elevation and erythema of the skin around tattoos on his forearms. He was diagnosed with chronic bilateral alternating anterior uveitis and started on topical prednisolone acetate, atropine drops, and oral prednisone (60 mg daily with rapid taper).

Two weeks later, his vision worsened to 20/50 in the right eye and 20/30 in the left. Fundus examination showed bilateral optic disc edema and multiple hypopigmented peripapillary subretinal lesions. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated intraretinal fluid in the nasal macula of both eyes and a choroidal granuloma with adjacent retinal pigment epithelial irregularity and subretinal fluid in the right eye.

Laboratory studies revealed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 88 mm/h, C-reactive protein of 61.6 mg/L, angiotensin-converting enzyme of 110 nmol/mL/min, lysozyme of 2.13 mcg/mL, alkaline phosphatase of 180 U/L, alanine aminotransferase of 86 U/L, and aspartate aminotransferase of 36 U/L. Chest radiography showed bilateral hilar shadows, bronchial wall thickening, and a small right pleural effusion.

Given the ocular findings, tattoo-site inflammation, elevated liver enzymes, and chest radiograph abnormalities, a differential diagnosis was formulated.

A 13-year-old girl was evaluated for recurrent episodes of right-lobe pneumonia over three years. She had lost 3 kg in recent weeks but denied fever or night sweats. She was born in Israel, and between ages 6 and 8 her family lived in Panama, Mexico, and Florida. On examination she appeared well, with no respiratory distress; lung auscultation revealed decreased breath sounds over the right lung. Basic laboratory tests showed no significant elevation of inflammatory markers. A chest radiograph demonstrated consolidation in the right lower lobe, pleural thickening and effusion, and marked right lower lobe volume loss. Bronchoscopy revealed severe external compression of the right bronchus intermedius and complete obstruction of the bronchus to the right middle lobe; bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for bacteria, mycobacteria, and fungi. A contrast-enhanced chest CT scan showed a 3.6 cm subcarinal mass and a 2 cm right hilar mass with prominent calcifications, severely compressing the right bronchial tree, right pulmonary artery, and right inferior pulmonary vein, and causing complete atelectasis of the right middle lobe. In the differential diagnosis of the calcified masses were tuberculosis, fungal infection, malignancy, healed granulomas (for example, varicella pneumonia), sarcoidosis, primary pulmonary amyloidosis, pulmonary chondroma (Carney triad), calcium/phosphate metabolism abnormalities, and calcifying fibrous pseudotumor of the lung.

A 51-year-old man, 6 months after orthotopic heart transplantation for AL amyloidosis, presented with fever up to 101 °F, new back pain, and severe left lower-extremity pain. His immunosuppressive regimen included dexamethasone, bortezomib, tacrolimus, and mycophenolic acid. Medical history was notable for chronic kidney disease, lower-extremity deep-venous thrombosis, and a pacemaker for sinus-node dysfunction. On admission, he was febrile and had tenderness in the posterior left thigh without overlying rash or discharge. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 14.7 × 10^3/µL and a positive anti-streptococcal antibody level. Empiric intravenous vancomycin was initiated. Contrast-enhanced CT of the left thigh demonstrated edema and a heterogeneous density within the adductor longus muscle, with inflammatory stranding along the adductor longus and sciatic nerve, interpreted as compatible with myositis and/or cellulitis.

An 11-year-old girl was admitted with a one-month history of postprandial vomiting. Her past medical history was unremarkable, and she had no abnormal eating behaviors. Over the preceding weeks, her general condition had declined slightly. On admission, her vital signs were normal for age, and laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver function tests, and renal function tests, were within normal limits. A barium upper gastrointestinal series demonstrated narrowing at the level of the gastric outlet. Differential diagnoses included gastric outlet obstruction due to foreign body, bezoar, antral web, or diaphragm. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a normal esophagus and a stomach filled with undigested food, with severe narrowing at the pylorus through which the endoscope could not advance. No ulcers were observed, and due to the severe stenosis, endoscopic removal of the suspected membrane was not possible.

A 52-year-old woman was evaluated for a 1-year history of intermittent fever, night sweats, and myalgia. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory testing disclosed a leukocyte count of 16,000/μL (80% neutrophils, 18% lymphocytes). Blood, urine, and stool cultures were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed multiple hypodense lesions measuring 7–15 mm in the liver. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a diffuse infiltrative lesion in the right hepatic lobe. A CT-guided needle biopsy of the hepatic lesions was performed.

A 52-year-old man with treated hypertension and diabetes mellitus presented after a first generalized tonic-clonic seizure, regaining consciousness before arrival. Two weeks earlier, he sustained a minor head injury with scalp abrasion but had no deficits. The day after discharge, he had another 5–6-minute generalized seizure with loss of consciousness and was admitted. He then experienced generalized tonic-clonic seizures twice daily and persistent right calf paresthesia that sometimes progressed to generalized seizures despite antiepileptic therapy.  
On examination, there were no signs of other organ involvement; in particular, there was no glandular enlargement or orbital disease. Abdominal ultrasound showed a normal liver, gallbladder, pancreas, and kidneys. Hemogram revealed no leukocytosis, and C-reactive protein was normal. Lumbar puncture showed a normal cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) glucose relative to blood glucose, no leukocytes, and CSF cytology was negative for malignant cells.  
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated focal thickening and enhancement of the dura near the superior sagittal sinus, with adjacent skull bone effacement and loss of normal fatty marrow signal.

A 54-year-old woman with a history of anorexia nervosa–binge/purge subtype and chronic hypokalemia was admitted for medical stabilization and ongoing hemodialysis. Two months earlier, she presented elsewhere with a serum creatinine of 9.56 mg/dL and hypokalemia (K 2.7 mmol/L), prompting initiation of dialysis. Her baseline renal function was unknown, and she had never required dialysis before.  

Her medical history included over 10 years of hypokalemia, anorexia nervosa, hyponatremia, psychogenic polydipsia, osteoporosis, and hypophosphatemia. She reported two years of pruritus attributed to uremia. She denied any laxative or diuretic use beyond prescribed docusate.  

On admission, she weighed 44.2 kg (BMI 15.2 kg/m2), with blood pressure 110/66 mmHg, heart rate 71 bpm, respiratory rate 15 breaths/min, temperature 36.5 °C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Mucous membranes were dry; conjunctivae were pale. Cardiopulmonary, abdominal, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable. A tunneled dialysis catheter was in place.  

Laboratory data: sodium 133 mmol/L; potassium 2.8 mmol/L; chloride 92 mmol/L; CO2 30 mmol/L; BUN 76 mg/dL; creatinine 6.91 mg/dL; phosphorus 6.4 mg/dL; magnesium 2.3 mEq/L; hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL; prealbumin 19.6 mg/dL; TSH 0.17 µIU/mL; free T4 0.83 ng/dL.  

Urinalysis from the prior hospital showed moderate blood and protein. Renal ultrasound demonstrated small kidneys with increased cortical echogenicity and thinning, without hydronephrosis, nephrolithiasis, mass, or cysts.

A 53-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of progressive vulvar swelling and firm labial nodules, accompanied by cutaneous swelling of the groin. She denied discharge, dyspareunia, fever, urinary symptoms, weight change, gastrointestinal complaints, oral ulcers, joint symptoms, ocular inflammation, or respiratory symptoms. Her obstetric history included nine cesarean deliveries and, 5 years ago, a total abdominal hysterectomy. Two prior colonoscopies with biopsy and a barium meal over the previous 3 years had been normal. 

On examination, she appeared well, with normal vital signs. Genital inspection revealed brownish, indurated, firm, coalescing nodules encircling the vulva and skin-colored, serpiginous, firm plaques on the pubic area, suggestive of lymphatic fibrosis. There was no anal fistula, ulcer, abscess, or scarring. The remainder of her examination, including pulmonary, cardiovascular, and gastrointestinal systems, was unremarkable. 

A dermatologist described the lesion as a verrucous, skin-colored tumor encircling the labia majora with surrounding lymphatic fibrosis. Initial differential diagnoses included cutaneous Crohn’s disease, deep fungal infection, cutaneous tuberculosis, verruciform xanthoma, hidradenitis suppurativa, and verrucous carcinoma. 

Laboratory testing showed normal complete blood count, liver function, coagulation profile, urea and electrolytes (including calcium), antinuclear antibody, double-stranded DNA, angiotensin-converting enzyme, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels. A purified protein derivative skin test was negative. CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was normal. 

Vulvar biopsy demonstrated scattered dermal noncaseating epithelioid granulomas surrounded by lymphocytes, with no polarizable foreign material. Histochemical stains (Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver, periodic acid–Schiff, and Ziehl-Neelsen) showed no fungal elements or acid-fast bacilli.

A 7-year-old girl with a history of focal seizures and headaches awoke with sudden-onset blurry vision. She was referred from her pediatrician to an optometrist, who noted a new myopic refraction despite prior 20/20 distance vision. Over the same day, she developed red eyes, swollen eyelids, excessive tearing, and photophobia but denied ocular pain, discharge, or systemic symptoms. She had started topiramate 25 mg at bedtime two weeks earlier; her last dose was 20 hours before presentation.

On examination in the pediatric emergency room, uncorrected visual acuity was light perception at 20 ft, count-fingers at 14 in, and 20/20 at 3 in in both eyes. Pupils were 6 mm and minimally reactive, with no afferent defect. Confrontation visual fields were constricted 360° bilaterally. Intraocular pressures were 40 mmHg in the right eye and 41 mmHg in the left eye. External exam showed mild eyelid edema. Slit-lamp examination revealed 1+ conjunctival injection and chemosis, no corneal edema, and a diffusely shallow anterior chamber without iris bombe. The lenses were clear. Funduscopic examination showed healthy optic discs with 0.25 cup:disc ratios and otherwise unremarkable retina; no choroidal effusion was seen.

A 9-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of left scrotal swelling and pain, present for one year and progressively enlarging. He denied fever, weight loss, evening chills, or hematuria. He had applied local remedies without relief and had received antibiotics and analgesics without improvement. 

On examination, he appeared well nourished with no jaundice or pallor. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Genitourinary examination revealed a slightly tender, irreducible, cystic swelling of the left scrotum in which the upper pole could not be palpated, and a clinical impression of hydrocele was made. 

Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL and blood group B Rh+. Urine and stool microscopy revealed no ova or other abnormalities. 

The patient was taken to the operating room for a planned hydrocelectomy. Intraoperatively, a hydrocele was confirmed, but the tunica vaginalis appeared thickened and multiple small nodules were noted on the surface of the testis, raising suspicion for a testicular tumor. An orchidectomy was performed.

A 73-year-old man was referred to a sarcoma unit with an 11-week history of sudden onset, painful swelling of the right upper arm. Six months earlier, he had been diagnosed with T3bN0M0 Gleason score 4 + 5 prostatic adenocarcinoma and elected systemic therapy. Three months before presentation, he began depot injections of leuprorelin acetate 11.25 mg every 3 months; the route of injection (intramuscular versus subcutaneous) was not documented. He had no other medical history and no known infections or travel. On examination, there was a firm, approximately 5 cm mass in the distal right biceps just above the tendon. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a 5.4 cm, ill-defined heterogeneous mass within the distal biceps muscle, with peripheral enhancement and mildly increased T2/T1 signal intensity relative to skeletal muscle, findings interpreted as concerning for sarcoma. No other lesions were identified.

An 11-year-old girl was referred to pediatric endocrinology for bilateral multicystic ovarian enlargement and pituitary gland enlargement noted on imaging. She was the first child of nonconsanguineous parents, with normal development. She had two prior hospitalizations for acute abdominal pain: the first episode was simple, and five months later she returned with abdominal pain, a distended belly, pale cool skin, and hemoperitoneum after minimal trauma. At surgery, both ovaries were enlarged with multiple cysts, approximately 200 mL of blood was evacuated, and hemostatic sutures were placed on bleeding cysts. She experienced recurrent intense abdominal pain and consulted a gynecologist, who obtained hormone tests and pelvic ultrasound and provided symptomatic treatment.

Six months later at our tertiary center, pelvic ultrasound and MRI showed multicystic ovarian enlargement (right ovary 97 × 55 mm; left ovary 62 × 50 mm) with septations and contrast uptake. Ovarian tumor markers—AFP, CA-125, CA19-9, and hCG—were all within normal limits. Brain MRI revealed pituitary enlargement measuring 25 × 16 × 13 mm with homogeneous contrast enhancement and no discrete sellar mass.

On further history, she had one year of constipation, decreased activity, and weight gain; six months of excessive sleep and intermittent galactorrhea from the left breast; and no headaches, visual changes, or vomiting. Her school performance declined over six months. On examination, she was lethargic and pale with facial puffiness. Vital signs were normal. Weight was 43 kg (+1 SD), height 142 cm (−0.5 SD), BMI 21 kg/m². Tanner staging was A1 B3 P1; she had breast enlargement but no pubic or axillary hair, brittle hair, and dry, scaly skin. Abdominal examination revealed distension and tenderness in both iliac fossae; there was no organomegaly. Laboratory tests showed microcytic hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL); blood glucose, liver and renal function, and electrolytes were normal. Bone age was estimated at 9–10 years.

A 39-year-old African American woman presented with 5 days of epigastric pain, nausea, and anorexia, and 1 day without flatus or bowel movements. She had a 9-year history of moderately severe ulcerative colitis treated with prednisone and mesalamine and a history of hysterectomy 8 years earlier for endometriosis. A surveillance colonoscopy 3 months earlier was limited at the hepatic flexure. On examination, she was afebrile, heart rate 52/min, blood pressure 111/77 mm Hg, with moderate epigastric tenderness and no peritoneal signs. Laboratory studies showed WBC 6.8×10^9/L, hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, platelets 427×10^9/L, normal liver enzymes and lipase, and C-reactive protein <3.0 mg/L. Abdominal and pelvic CT with contrast demonstrated a stricture with wall thickening from the hepatic flexure into the transverse colon with upstream dilation consistent with large-bowel obstruction, and an infiltrative soft-tissue mass extending from the stricture to encase the gastroepiploic vessels near the pancreatic head (33×29 mm). Endoscopic ultrasound revealed an irregular, partially calcified, hypoechoic heterogeneous 5-cm perigastric mass.

A 49-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension presented with a 7-day history of right groin swelling and pain. He denied nausea, vomiting, constipation, fever, or dysuria. On examination, his temperature was 39.2 °C, heart rate 122 beats per minute, and blood pressure 160/80 mm Hg. The right groin and hemiscrotum were swollen and erythematous, with tenderness most pronounced along the spermatic cord and epididymis. The swelling was non-reducible, and no hernia defect was palpable.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 17 500/μL with a left shift, serum glucose 492 mg/dL, hemoglobin A1c 17%, sodium 123 mEq/L (129 mEq/L corrected), and urinalysis with 160 white cells per high-power field. Initial differential diagnoses included incarcerated inguinal hernia, scrotal abscess, and epididymo-orchitis.

Scrotal ultrasound demonstrated a heterogeneous tubular lesion with increased vascularity extending into the right hemiscrotum, findings suspected to represent a dilated vas deferens with vasitis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a tubular, fluid-filled structure in the course of the right spermatic cord, with mucosal enhancement, surrounding fluid, and inflammation; the structure was not contiguous with small bowel. CT also demonstrated rim-enhancing fluid collections consistent with right and small left perinephric abscesses in the setting of acute pyelonephritis.

A 77-year-old Italian man presented with a two-week history of melena and hematochezia. He had chronic atrial fibrillation (on rivaroxaban and digoxin) and a remote cholecystectomy. His vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, digital rectal inspection confirmed melena; nasogastric lavage returned clear. Initial laboratory testing revealed hemoglobin 5.1 g/dL. He received blood transfusions and underwent esophagogastroduodenoscopy, which showed a small hiatal hernia, bile in the stomach, and a 10 mm fibrinous duodenal ulcer. Rivaroxaban was held, and he was started on low-molecular-weight heparin and continuous pantoprazole infusion. 

Despite argon plasma coagulation of ulcer margins and H. pylori eradication, he continued to pass melena and hematochezia and required additional transfusions. Repeat EGD confirmed ulcer healing with regenerative hyperplasia on histology. Ileocolonoscopy demonstrated bright red blood in the ileum and colon without a visible source. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and aorta showed no bleeding source and only minor incidental findings.

Given ongoing bleeding after negative upper and lower endoscopy and imaging, further small-bowel evaluation was planned.

A 70-year-old man with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, diabetes mellitus, and hypertension presented with five days of dyspnea, cough, and fever. He had been taking amiodarone, 200 mg daily, for five years. On arrival, his blood pressure was 160/110 mmHg, respiratory rate 34/min, and oxygen saturation 89% on room air. ECG showed atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 110/min. Examination revealed diminished breath sounds and right basal crackles. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 13.1 × 10^3/µL (83% neutrophils), creatinine 180 mg/dL, C-reactive protein 296.4 mg/dL, gamma‐glutamyl transferase 80 mg/dL, and lactate dehydrogenase 315 mg/dL. Chest radiograph demonstrated diffuse bilateral perihilar nonhomogeneous infiltrates. He was admitted to the ICU, treated with high-flow oxygen, empirical amoxicillin–clavulanic acid plus levofloxacin, and amiodarone was discontinued. One week later, repeat radiographs showed no change; blood and urine cultures were sterile. High-resolution CT of the chest revealed diffuse interlobular septal thickening with extensive ground-glass opacities in the upper lobes, focal consolidation in the right upper lobe anterior segment, bilateral pleural effusions, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Transthoracic echocardiography showed interventricular septal hypertrophy, normal systolic function, and grade II diastolic dysfunction. Right‐sided thoracentesis yielded sterile fluid.

A 69-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a hepatic mass discovered on CT one month earlier. She had experienced intermittent abdominal distention for two months but no other symptoms. Her medical history included hypertension for 40 years and type II diabetes mellitus for 10 years; she had no history of hepatitis B or tuberculosis.  

On examination, findings were unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed normal blood counts, normal liver function (AST, ALT, bilirubin, PT), and an albumin/globulin ratio of 0.9. Antinuclear antibody testing was positive (nucleolar type, 1:640; cytoplasmic type, 1:80), and smooth muscle antibody was positive at 1:320. Other hepatopathic autoimmune antibodies were negative. Serum IgG (18.2 g/L) and IgA (4.58 g/L) were mildly elevated. Tumor markers (AFP, CA242, CEA, CA19-9) and thyroid parameters were normal.  

Dynamic CT revealed a 1.0-cm solid, well-delineated mass in segment II with slight arterial-phase enhancement and venous-phase washout. MRI showed a 9.6×8.9 mm round nodule in segment II that was slightly hyperintense on T1 and isointense on T2. No other hepatic lesions were identified. Based on the hypervascular appearance and washout, the lesion was presumed to be hepatocellular carcinoma.

A 3-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a painless left testicular mass and a left inguinal hernia. His mother had noticed a mass in the left scrotum during dressing. He was a healthy term infant who underwent bilateral orchiopexy in the first year of life for undescended testes. On examination, there was a reducible left inguinal hernia and an immobile left testicular lesion. Scrotal ultrasonography demonstrated a 10×5 mm solid, immobile lesion within the left testis and a reducible left inguinal hernia. Alpha-fetoprotein was within normal limits. Given the history of prior orchiopexy and concern for testicular malignancy, the patient underwent open left inguinal hernia repair and left orchiectomy.

A 20-year-old woman was referred to the endocrinology clinic in 1997 for progressive thinning of both wrists. She had no significant medical history in her parents; of her two brothers, one had diabetes mellitus, cataracts, and genital hypoplasia, and the other was unaffected. On examination, her height was 143 cm, and her extremities appeared thin. She had a bird-like nose and prematurely gray hair. Menarche occurred at age 13 with regular menses for 3 years, after which her periods ceased. She had bilateral cataracts on ophthalmologic evaluation. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed genital hypoplasia. A DEXA scan showed osteopenia (T-score –1.55). Serum follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone, and estradiol levels were elevated above normal ranges.

A 36-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 2, presented with a 3-day history of right breast pain and swelling. She had no history of breast trauma, tuberculosis exposure, breast cancer, or autoimmune disease. She breastfed two children for 1 year each and used combined estrogen–progestin oral contraception for 3 years. She was afebrile. Examination revealed a 5 cm tender mass in the lower inner quadrant of the right breast with overlying erythema, “orange-peel” skin changes, nipple retraction, and a central 2 cm irregular, painful area; there was no nipple discharge or axillary lymphadenopathy.  
Mammography showed localized areas of increased density in the lower inner quadrant. Breast ultrasound demonstrated two hypoechoic lesions (24 × 20 mm and 18.5 × 16 mm) and multiple peri-lesional abscesses (largest 12 × 12 mm), categorized as BI-RADS 4A.  
She received a 5-day course of amoxicillin without improvement and then underwent ultrasound-guided core biopsy and drainage of the abscess under local anesthesia. Cultures of the drained pus were sent. Intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g/day) was initiated. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 10 mg/L and a white blood cell count of 11,000/μL. Local inflammation improved but the patient continued to experience pain and purulent drainage at the incision site.

A 20-year-old woman presented with intermittent pus discharge at the base of her chin for the past 3 years. She denied any tooth pain or swelling. She reported facial trauma while playing at school 4–5 years earlier; a cutaneous draining lesion appeared on the chin about 2 years after the injury. She had received several courses of oral antibiotics and had been evaluated by a dermatologist and an otorhinolaryngologist without lasting improvement.  

On extraoral examination, there was a 1-cm-diameter sinus tract on the chin rimmed by erythema; palpation elicited purulent exudate. Intraoral inspection revealed a slightly discolored mandibular right central incisor without visible caries or swelling. Pulp-vitality testing was positive for all mandibular incisors except the lower right central incisor. A panoramic radiograph showed a well-defined, unilocular periapical radiolucency measuring approximately 2 cm × 4 cm associated with the mandibular incisors. A computed tomography scan confirmed a radiolucent lesion involving the labial cortical bone at the apex of the mandibular right central incisor.

A 31-year-old Indo-Surinamese woman with primary infertility presented with 3 months of worsening cyclical vulvar pain during menstruation. She had four prior spontaneous abortions and a diagnostic laparoscopy that showed no endometriosis. Family history was noncontributory. On examination, a 1×2 cm cyst was palpated in the right Bartholin gland. Transvaginal ultrasonography revealed normal gynecologic anatomy without abnormalities. Because of recurrent pain associated with the cyst, surgical management was planned.

A 7-year-old girl of Spanish descent was referred for evaluation of recurrent unexplained fevers and multiple bone injuries. She was born to healthy, nonconsanguineous parents. She displayed no response to painful stimuli and had evidence of self-inflicted skin lesions. Developmental assessment revealed cognitive delay. On examination, her skin was warm and dry with an absence of sweating, and there was marked thickening of the palms and soles. Lower-limb edema was noted. Skeletal radiographs demonstrated avascular necrosis, generalized osteopenia, extensive osseous destruction, and, following a midshaft fracture of the right tibia sustained four months earlier, features of hypertrophic pseudoarthrosis.

An 87-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a one-week history of no bowel movements and one episode of bilious vomiting, although she continued to pass flatus. She reported mild-to-moderate periumbilical abdominal pain without fever or chills. Her past history was notable for a hysterectomy 20 years earlier, hypertension, and a cerebrovascular accident.  
On examination, her temperature was 36.9 °C, respiratory rate 17/min, pulse 80 beats/min, and blood pressure 150/90 mm Hg. Lung and heart auscultation were normal. The abdomen was moderately distended with a midline hysterectomy scar, bowel sounds were decreased, and there was periumbilical tenderness without rebound. Digital rectal examination showed normal fecal material.  
Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 10 100/μL (80% neutrophils), hemoglobin 14 g/dL, platelets 208 000/μL; blood sugar 124 mg/dL; creatinine 1.0 mg/dL; amylase 39 U/L; sodium 140 mEq/L; potassium 3.7 mEq/L; PT 13 s; PTT 28 s; INR 1.0.  
Abdominal radiography revealed multiple distended loops of small intestine consistent with obstruction. A CT scan was not performed because of progressive tenderness on serial examinations.  
A nasogastric tube was placed, yielding one liter of fecaloid fluid, and the patient was prepared for open surgical exploration.

A 17-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of multiple radio-opaque ovoid or circular lesions noted on an ankle radiograph obtained after an ankle sprain. He was asymptomatic with no history of fractures, bone pain, or other illness. His medications history was unremarkable. Family history was notable only for paternal hypertension; no bone disease was reported.

On examination, he appeared well. Vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination was unremarkable except for a mild ocular squint; there were no skin lesions or bone tenderness.

Laboratory studies showed normal alkaline phosphatase activity, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, antinuclear antibodies, serum electrolytes, and tumor markers. The only abnormality was a mild vitamin D deficiency.

Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the right ankle showed multiple small, well-demarcated sclerotic lesions in the epiphysis and metaphysis of the tibia and fibula. Subsequent pelvis and bilateral hand radiographs confirmed numerous similar enostoses symmetrically distributed in the epiphyses and metaphyses. The pelvic film also demonstrated longitudinal bands of confluent sclerotic lesions extending from the epiphyses into the metaphyses.

A 19-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 1-day history of crampy right iliac fossa pain. She denied nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, bleeding, or weight loss. She was afebrile and appeared well. On examination, there was no distension or peritoneal signs, but gentle palpation in the right iliac fossa elicited mild tenderness and suggested a palpable mass in a thin patient. White-cell count was 7.8×10^9/L. Pelvic ultrasound revealed a 69×33×28 mm cystic mass in the right parauterine region and a distinct 41 mm ovarian cyst. Prior magnetic resonance imaging, performed nine months earlier for similar pain, had shown a 65×32×30 mm cystic lesion adjacent to the uterus and in contact with small bowel but separate from the ovary; it was presumed to be a right hydrosalpinx.
