Given the stable appearance over nine months and current presentation, a hydrosalpinx remained the leading diagnosis, though an appendiceal mucocele was also considered. The patient underwent diagnostic laparoscopy: no hydrosalpinx or mucocele was found; there was only a small benign-appearing ovarian cyst (serous fluid was aspirated), and the colon, appendix, small bowel, and mesentery appeared normal; an appendectomy was performed prophylactically. Thirteen days later, she returned with severe abdominal pain, distension, and vomiting. Temperature was 37.5 °C; white-cell count was 15.2×10^9/L. Computed tomography of the abdomen showed ileocecal intussusception.

A 106-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of generalized bone pain, low-grade fever, and progressive inability to walk; she had been ambulatory at home without assistance before this time. A general practitioner had initially diagnosed osteomalacia and prescribed vitamin D and calcium. She had a family history of rheumatoid arthritis in a relative treated with methotrexate and rituximab.

On examination, vital signs were normal. There was bilateral swelling and tenderness of the wrists, metacarpophalangeal joints, proximal interphalangeal joints, and metatarsophalangeal joints. She had been unable to stand due to pain for the past 3 months. Her medical history was notable only for well-controlled hypertension; she was a non-smoker.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10 g/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 65 mm/h, positive C-reactive protein, and positive rheumatoid factor. Serum uric acid, liver function tests, renal function tests, and thyroid function tests were all within normal ranges. Virology screening was negative. Chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasonography were normal.

Anteroposterior radiographs of the hands demonstrated bilateral osteopenia with erosions at the wrists, metacarpophalangeal joints, and proximal interphalangeal joints.

A 60-year-old Caucasian man with obesity presented with a 4-year history of facial dermatitis unresponsive to oral corticosteroids. He reported good general health and denied systemic medications. On dermatological examination, there was severe, solid erythematous edema of the forehead, glabella, and both eyelids, impairing eyelid opening; erythema and telangiectasia were noted on the nose and cheeks. General physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests and instrumental studies—including echography of the periorbital area, carotids, and thyroid; chest X-ray; electrocardiogram; echocardiogram; and abdominal ultrasound—were all within normal limits or negative. Histopathological examination of a skin biopsy showed dermal edema, perivascular and periadnexal lymphohistiocytic infiltrate, and sebaceous gland hyperplasia; no mast cells or granulomas were observed.

A 30-year-old Moroccan man with no significant past medical history presented with a 6-month history of left flank pain, urinary frequency, and gross hematuria. He also reported anorexia and a 10-kg weight loss over this period. On examination, he was fatigued. Urogenital examination revealed tenderness of the left epididymis; the prostate was normal in size but slightly firm without nodules. Laboratory studies showed a serum creatinine of 66 μmol/L, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 120 mm/h, a C-reactive protein level of 200 mg/L, and otherwise unremarkable findings. Renal and pelvic ultrasound demonstrated left hydronephrosis and hydroureter. CT urography revealed left ureterohydronephrosis in the lumbar ureter with focal ureteral wall thickening.

A 17-year-old girl presented with a one-month history of swelling and pus discharge from the left mandibular posterior region, onset approximately one month after extraction of the left first molar. Antibiotics and topical mouthwashes provided no relief. On intraoral examination, there was a vestibular sulcus swelling with a draining sinus at the extraction site; palpation revealed a fibrotic band. Oral hygiene was good, and cervical lymph nodes were not palpable. The patient was afebrile, well appearing, and denied fever, weakness, or weight loss. Her history was notable for two episodes of tuberculous lymphadenitis about two years earlier, with unclear details of antitubercular therapy; her father had completed treatment for tuberculous meningitis. An orthopantomogram showed an ill-defined radiolucency with loss of normal trabecular pattern at the extraction socket. Routine blood tests revealed a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate. With these findings, the provisional diagnoses included a chronic inflammatory lesion, residual cyst, actinomycosis, and osteomyelitis of the mandible. An excisional biopsy was planned, and pus was sent for cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification testing.

A 75‐year‐old woman with no significant past medical history was struck by lightning while standing approximately 3 meters from a tree. On initial evaluation at the scene, she was prone; her clothes and shoes were partially burned and were removed. She was hemodynamically stable (blood pressure 138/87 mmHg; heart rate 87 beats per minute) and conscious, with transient amnesia for the event. Physical examination revealed linear first‐degree and superficial second‐degree burns with blisters extending from the left ear to the left toe, involving about 6% of the total body surface area. 

In the emergency department, a total‐body CT scan showed no acute internal injuries except for an old fracture of the second thoracic vertebra. An electrocardiogram demonstrated a right bundle branch block, deep symmetrical T‐wave inversion in the precordial and lateral leads, and a prolonged QT interval of 480 ms. Serum troponin T was elevated, peaking at 403 ng/L. Other laboratory tests, including a complete blood count and electrolytes, were within normal limits, except for a serum creatinine of 89 µmol/L.

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 40% with apical akinesia and preserved basal segment contractility. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging confirmed apical hypokinesia with mild left ventricular dysfunction and showed no signs of myocarditis or myocardial infarction.

A 38-year-old man presented to the emergency department 12 hours after a road-traffic accident, reporting 4 hours of worsening abdominal pain, distension, nausea, and non-bilious vomiting. He also complained of left leg pain and difficulty walking. He had no prior abdominal surgeries or significant past medical history.

On examination, he was hypotensive (blood pressure 80/40 mmHg) and tachycardic (pulse 120/min). His abdomen was distended, with diffuse guarding, tenderness, and hypoactive bowel sounds. The left proximal leg was tender, but distal pulses were intact. Initial laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin level of 6.0 g/dL, a creatinine level of 2.6 mg/dL, and normal electrolytes.

He was diagnosed with hypovolemic shock due to intra-abdominal bleeding from blunt abdominal trauma and a left proximal tibia fracture. After resuscitation with crystalloids and whole blood, he underwent emergent laparotomy. Intraoperatively, approximately 3 L of hemoperitoneum and a grade IV splenic laceration with active bleeding were identified; a splenectomy was performed. Further exploration revealed a 3 × 3 cm, white, spherical, firm, freely mobile, extra-luminal mass on the mesenteric side of the transverse colon. The mass, with a smooth surface resembling a boiled egg, was excised and sent for histopathologic analysis.

A previously healthy five-year-old boy presented with a one-week history of intermittent abdominal pain. There was no vomiting, abdominal distension, bleeding per rectum, diarrhea, or constipation. Vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, the abdomen was soft with no palpable masses; rectal examination was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed an ileocolic intussusception. A hydrostatic reduction was attempted but only partially successful, so the patient underwent laparotomy. Intraoperatively, a 4 cm × 4 cm submucosal solid mass was identified in the cecum, associated with multiple enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes. The mass and sampled lymph nodes were resected with clear margins.

A 36-year-old white British man presented with three weeks of progressively worsening exertional central chest pain and breathlessness. He had a ten-year history of Erdheim–Chester disease, previously controlled with pegylated interferon; nine months earlier he had COVID-19 complicated by deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, for which he was taking apixaban. A recent disease flare had prompted increases in interferon and a course of prednisolone. He had no traditional cardiovascular risk factors. On admission, ECG showed sinus rhythm with <1 mm convex ST-segment elevation in V1–V6 and T-wave inversion in leads I and aVL. High-sensitivity troponin T was 51 ng/L, rising to 132 ng/L at six hours; D-dimer was 608 ng/mL. Transthoracic echocardiography was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced gated CT coronary angiography demonstrated a zero calcium score but an ostial left anterior descending (LAD) non-calcified plaque 1.5 cm in length with positive remodelling and a low-density lipid core causing severe stenosis; a small pulmonary infarct was also seen. Invasive coronary angiography confirmed an ostial filling defect in the LAD with TIMI 3 flow; the left main stem, circumflex, and right coronary arteries were normal.

A middle‐aged woman was brought to the emergency department after an episode of benzodiazepine intoxication, with central nervous system depression requiring supportive care. Her past medical history was notable for nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) cirrhosis, prolapsed lumbar intervertebral disc with chronic back pain, two episodes of gastric polypectomy in 2016 and repeat polypectomies in 2020 and 2024, dysfunctional uterine bleeding treated medically, and chronic melena over the past 2 years. She had a documented history of hypokalemia on five occasions over the last 5 years, managed with oral potassium replacement.

On admission, vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination was notable only for mild abdominal distension and pallor. Initial laboratory studies revealed:

• Serum potassium 2.1 mmol/L (reference 3.5–5.0)  
• Serum calcium 5.9 mg/dL (8.5–10.5)  
• Serum magnesium 0.40 mmol/L (0.75–1.25)  
• Metabolic alkalosis on arterial blood gas  

An initial trial of intravenous potassium and calcium supplementation produced only minimal improvement, and serum electrolytes remained labile. Given persistent electrolyte disturbances, renal tubular handling was assessed:

• Urine calcium/creatinine ratio 0.11 (normal < 0.14)  
• Urine magnesium/creatinine ratio 0.20 (normal < 0.15)  
• 24-h urine calcium 150 mg/day (100–300)  
• 24-h urine magnesium 350 mg/day (72–156)  

Her mother had died of recurrent, unexplained hypokalemia and hypocalcemia.

A 33-year-old G1P0A0 woman was referred for a routine second-trimester (20-week) ultrasound. Her first-trimester scan had shown a viable twin A with normal heart rate and crown–rump length; an adjacent abnormal structure was noted but not interpreted.  

On repeat sonography at 20 weeks 6 days by Hadlock criteria, two intrauterine fetuses shared a single placenta, sonographically monochorionic. Twin A had a two-vessel cord, all four cardiac chambers appeared normal, and M-mode fetal heart rate was 153 bpm. Estimated fetal weight was 375 g. Amniotic fluid volume measured approximately 8 cm (borderline high).  

Twin B was grossly abnormal: on grayscale imaging, no limbs were identified; the skull appeared small for gestational age with ossified calvarium but no definitive brain tissue; sagittal spine was only partially visualized; large fluid collections filled the thoracic and abdominal cavities; cine clips showed three rudimentary cardiac chambers beating synchronously; no distinct cord insertion was seen. The sonographer could not identify an intertwin membrane and initially classified the pregnancy as monochorionic-monoamniotic.  

Later that same day in the fetal assessment unit, Twin A had a middle cerebral artery velocity of 36–42 cm/sec and normal umbilical artery Doppler. Ductus venosus Doppler showed reversed “a”-wave flow. Twin B’s head measurements corresponded to a 13-week fetus; its chest and abdomen were distended with fluid and soft-tissue edema. Fetal heart rate in twin B was 110 bpm.

A 34-year-old man presented with blurred central vision and reduced visual acuity in his left eye. Three years earlier, he had been diagnosed with central serous chorioretinopathy of the left eye based on serous macular detachment on examination and OCT-confirmed subretinal fluid, and he received a single intravitreal anti-VEGF injection after 3 months of persistent fluid.

On current presentation, best-corrected visual acuity was 1.0 in the right eye and 0.5 in the left. Examination of the posterior poles showed a serous retinal detachment superior to the optic disc in the right eye and a well-defined serous macular detachment in the left eye. OCT confirmed subtle interpapillomacular subretinal fluid in the right eye and a significant inferotemporal subretinal fluid pocket in the left eye. Fundus fluorescein angiography demonstrated punctate hyperfluorescent pinpoint foci in the macula of both eyes in the early venous phase, with pooling of dye around the optic disc (OD) and superior and inferior to the fovea (OS) in the late phase. Notably, there were no typical leakage spots to guide laser photocoagulation.

Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, p-ANCA, PR3 IgG, ANA, circulating immune complexes, Borrelia antibodies, Toxoplasma antibodies, and HIV testing, were all normal or negative. The only positive result was CMV IgG, considered incidental in this immunocompetent patient.

A 54-year-old female farmer from rural Chungchung Province, South Korea, presented with a 7-day history of fever, myalgia, fatigue, and poor oral intake. Two weeks earlier, she had climbed a mountain. Initial outpatient treatment with antipyretics and fluids provided no relief. On the fifth hospital day at a local facility, she became somnolent and could not follow commands and was transferred.

On examination at our hospital: temperature 37.2 °C, blood pressure 125/81 mm Hg, pulse 105 bpm, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 92% on room air. She appeared acutely ill and was confused (Glasgow Coma Scale, 13), with normal pupils and no meningeal signs. Conjunctiva were clear; no rash, ecchymoses, eschar, or insect bite sites were noted; lymph nodes were not palpable except in both inguinal areas.

Laboratory studies revealed leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. Chemistry tests showed azotemia (creatinine 2.92 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 58 mg/dL), hyperkalemia (6.7 mmol/L), elevated liver enzymes (AST 4,944 IU/L, ALT 884 IU/L), and markedly elevated muscle enzymes (creatine kinase 5,944 IU/L, myoglobin 8,416 ng/mL, aldolase 200.6 U/L), consistent with rhabdomyolysis. Blood cultures were negative. Serologic tests on illness day 14 for Hantaan virus, Leptospira interrogans, Orientia tsutsugamushi, and Rickettsia typhi were negative. A reverse-transcriptase PCR assay for severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus was pending. Chest radiograph showed mild pulmonary congestion with bilateral pleural effusions. Abdominal CT scanning revealed no hepatobiliary or renal lesions. Brain CT and MRI were unremarkable.

A 45-year-old man with decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis (MELD-Na 36), type 2 diabetes, and active intravenous drug use presented after being found unresponsive in a car. He had a history of bacteremia with Lacticaseibacillus species 3 months earlier.  
On arrival, he was in pulseless electrical activity arrest; return of spontaneous circulation was achieved after 20 minutes of CPR. He was hypothermic (29.3 °C), heart rate 75 beats/min, respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, blood pressure 135/94 mmHg on norepinephrine infusion, and GCS 3 with endotracheal tube placement. Physical examination revealed diffuse bilateral crackles, ascites with positive fluid wave, flank dullness, and 3+ pitting edema of the lower extremities.  
Initial laboratory tests showed a metabolic acidemia with elevated lactate, marked liver function test abnormalities, thrombocytopenia, anemia, leukopenia, and coagulopathy. CT angiography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated extensive bilateral airspace opacities suggestive of multifocal pneumonia, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, and malposition of the endotracheal tube.  
In the ED, he received 1500 mL normal saline, cefepime, calcium gluconate for hyperkalemia, and norepinephrine to maintain MAP ≥ 65 mmHg. Admitted to the ICU, antibiotics were changed to meropenem and vancomycin. He did not undergo targeted temperature management due to hypothermia, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, and hemodynamic instability. Paracentesis and cultures of ascitic fluid, urine, and respiratory specimens were unrevealing. One of four blood culture bottles grew Serratia marcescens. He received albumin, red blood cells, platelets, and cryoprecipitate.  
Approximately 20 hours after presentation, hematology was consulted for new pancytopenia (WBC 1.1 K/μL), and a work-up for possible HLH was initiated, including triglycerides, ferritin, and soluble IL-2 receptor levels. Triglycerides were normal; ferritin was 2994 ng/mL. Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV every 8 hours was started.

A 65-year-old woman presented with sudden, painless bilateral vision loss and generalized weakness. She reported worsening dysphagia over several days and exertional chest tightness radiating to her left arm. Eight days earlier, she had undergone transscleral micropulse cyclophotocoagulation (mTS-CPC) in her left eye for refractory glaucoma.

Her medical history included CREST syndrome with Raynaud’s phenomenon, type 2 diabetes mellitus, asthma, chronic kidney disease stage 3, osteoporosis, anemia, hearing loss, pancreatitis, and pulmonary hypertension. Ocular history was significant for chronic angle-closure glaucoma, cataract surgery, laser peripheral iridotomy, and trabeculectomy in both eyes. Current medications included topical timolol OU, latanoprost OD, prednisolone acetate OS, moxifloxacin OS, oral prednisone, amlodipine, atorvastatin, metformin, aspirin, and others. She had allergies to clindamycin and sulfa drugs and denied tobacco, alcohol, or recreational drug use.

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/30 OD and 20/100 OS. There was no relative afferent pupillary defect. Intraocular pressures were 9 mm Hg OD and 15 mm Hg OS. Anterior segment exam showed a cystic bleb superiorly in both eyes and 1+ anterior chamber cell OD. Posterior segment exam revealed mild vitritis OD; cup-to-disc ratios of 0.8 OD and 0.9 OS; retinal pigment epithelial mottling OU; cotton-wool spots and peripapillary white membranes OD; sclerotic vessels with mild perivascular sheathing OU; and cotton-wool spots along the nasal arcade OS.

At follow-up one day later, cotton-wool spots and vasculitis were present in all quadrants OU. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated arteriovenous-phase hypofluorescence from nonperfusion and late perivascular hyperfluorescence with leakage OU. Optical coherence tomography showed macular thickening OD > OS.

Laboratory evaluation for uveitis and infectious causes was negative, including antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), rheumatoid factor (RF), human leukocyte antigen-B27 (HLA-B27), angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), lysozyme, interferon-gamma release assay, Bartonella antibodies, rapid plasma reagin (RPR), and others. Antinuclear antibody (ANA) testing was positive at a titer >1:640.

A 34-year-old woman was referred from dermatology for a chronic, discharging submental lesion. She reported recurrent submental swelling that had been treated as a sebaceous cyst with incision and drainage followed by antibiotics, without improvement. She was otherwise healthy. Dental history was notable for trauma 12 years earlier and two previous root canal treatments on mandibular incisors about 2 years ago. On examination there was a 40 mm nonfluctuant, nontender submental swelling with an overlying sinus tract and purulent discharge on palpation. A gutta-percha point was inserted into the sinus and a periapical radiograph was obtained.  
The intraoral periapical radiograph revealed that the gutta-percha traced to the apical regions of teeth 31 and 41 and there was a diffuse periapical radiolucency around the roots of these previously treated teeth.

A 20-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of generalized tonic-clonic seizures. He had experienced recurrent waxing and waning episodes of neurologic symptoms since age 8, including seizures, choreoathetosis, kinesigenic dystonia, truncal hypotonia, apraxia, and ataxia, with spontaneous improvements between episodes. Previous workups had included multiple brain MRIs showing transient bilateral basal ganglia and cortical hyperintensities, repeated lumbar punctures, extensive infectious and rheumatologic testing (all negative), and empirical treatment for presumed acute disseminated encephalomyelitis without lasting benefit. He was maintained on levetiracetam for seizure prophylaxis.

On this admission, he exhibited hyperthermia and progressive encephalopathy. A cerebral angiogram showed mild nonspecific hyperemia but no luminal irregularity or stenosis. Brain biopsy was nondiagnostic, revealing no vasculitis, acute infection, or demyelination. Large-volume lumbar punctures revealed normal white-cell counts, protein, and glucose; cultures were negative for bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal pathogens.

Brain MRI demonstrated extensive FLAIR hyperintense signal in the bilateral caudate, putamen, medial thalami, periaqueductal gray matter, multiple areas of cerebral cortex, and the cerebellum. Most of these areas showed restricted diffusion, and post-contrast images revealed sulcal leptomeningeal and basal ganglia enhancement. Findings were described as corresponding to a broad differential, including toxic, metabolic, and autoimmune etiologies.

A 21-year-old African American woman with homozygous sickle cell disease presented with three days of generalized pain, fever, fatigue, and dyspnea. She described severe bilateral thigh pain and dark urine but denied chest pain or dysuria. Five days earlier she had been hospitalized for a pain crisis, treated with IV hydration, analgesics, and one unit of packed red blood cells for a hemoglobin of 6.7 g/dL.

On examination, she was febrile (38.2 °C), tachycardic (111 beats/min), and normotensive; oxygen saturation was 97% on room air. She had conjunctival pallor, skin tenting, and tenderness of both thighs; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Blood and urine cultures were obtained, and empirical IV antibiotics were started.

Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 5.3 g/dL, hematocrit 19.7%, white blood cell count 17.2 k/µL, total bilirubin 5.2 mg/dL, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 934 U/L. Chest radiograph, ECG, and CT of the abdomen and pelvis were unremarkable. She received two units of packed red blood cells without immediate reaction, but a repeat hemoglobin measurement fell to 4.5 g/dL. Hematology consultation was requested.

Further testing revealed a negative direct antiglobulin test and negative alloantibodies. LDH rose to 4230 U/L, indirect bilirubin was 2.9 mg/dL, ferritin 4327 ng/mL, C-reactive protein 6.4 mg/dL, and reticulocyte count 0.5%. Hemoglobin electrophoresis showed 45.2% HbS and 44.8% HbA. Blood and urine cultures remained negative, and parvovirus IgG and IgM titers were negative.

A 72-year-old Caucasian man presented with progressive dyspnea over 3 months, worsening during the week before admission, and atypical chest pain. He was a heavy smoker with no known medical history; a family history of hypertension was noted. On examination, blood pressure was 155/75 mmHg, pulse 95 bpm; cardiac auscultation revealed a severe systolic murmur best heard in the aortic area, radiating to the left parasternal border and diminishing at the apex; lung fields were clear. A chest radiograph showed a normal cardiac silhouette and clear lungs. Electrocardiography revealed T-wave inversion in lateral leads and horizontal ST-segment depression in leads V4–V6. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated an oval, well-marginated tissue attached to the proximal anterior leaflet of the mitral valve, causing left ventricular outflow tract obstruction during systole, with a peak gradient of 55 mmHg; the aortic cusps were normal, left ventricular size and wall motion were normal, pulmonary artery pressure was 18 mmHg, and no other cardiac anomalies were seen.

A 69-year-old Caucasian woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus, resistant hypertension, and diastolic congestive heart failure with preserved ejection fraction presented to nephrology with acute kidney injury. Five years earlier, she had a pacemaker placed for sick sinus syndrome. Three months before presentation, she was diagnosed with recurrent atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response and was started on amiodarone and chlorthalidone.

Her baseline serum creatinine had ranged from 1.2 to 1.7 mg/dL; on presentation it was 3.88 mg/dL. She noted a new pruritic rash on her chest, arms, and legs that began three months after initiation of the two drugs. She had a prior rash with hydrochlorothiazide and reacted similarly to chlorthalidone.

Her home medications included apixaban, atorvastatin, cholecalciferol, clonidine, fexofenadine, insulin glargine, labetalol, latanoprost eye drops, nifedipine, and topical triamcinolone for the rash. Blood pressure had improved from 159/66 mmHg at drug initiation to 120–140/80 mmHg.

Laboratory evaluation showed:  
• Liver enzymes normal (ALT 22, AST 25, ALP 67, total bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL).  
• Thyroid studies: TSH 8.1 μIU/mL, free T3 283 pg/dL, free T4 1.6 ng/dL (subclinical hypothyroidism).  
• Serologies: ANA 1:160 homogeneous; anti–double-stranded DNA 874 IU/mL; anti-histone 2.0 units; anti–smooth muscle antibody 1:160; negative anti-RNP, anti-Smith, SSA, SSB, rheumatoid factor, scleroderma antibodies, Jo-1, anti-CCP, thyroid peroxidase antibodies, and ANCA; borderline anticardiolipin IgG 16 GPL.  
• Urinalysis: moderate baseline proteinuria (0.6 g protein/g creatinine, unchanged), red blood cells increased from 1 to 9 per high-power field, white blood cells increased from 4 to 13 per high-power field, no urinary or peripheral eosinophils.

A 50-year-old woman with HIV for 6 years, newly started 2 weeks ago on abacavir-lamivudine and darunavir, was admitted with 4 days of lethargy and a painful cold cyanotic right hand. Her partner found her very drowsy on the floor and summoned emergency services. Earlier that week, a general practitioner treated her arm pain as lateral epicondylitis with NSAIDs. 

On admission, her Glasgow Coma Scale was 13 (conscious but sleepy, slow speech, oriented), cranial nerves intact. She had a cyanotic right hand up to the wrist and cyanotic toes on the right foot; no pulses were palpable in any limb; no edema. Blood pressure was 140/70 mmHg, heart rate 80/min, oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Abdominal exam was unremarkable; hyperactive bowel sounds; no fever; normal urine output.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 11.5×10^9/L, CRP 24 mg/dL, CK 2285 U/L, sodium 121 mEq/L, chloride 87 mEq/L, lactate 0.7 mmol/L; troponins were negative; D-dimer was 2.2 mg/L. HIV viral load was 42 copies/mL and CD4 count 380 cells/mm^3. Toxicology, including ethanol, was negative.

Head CT showed no acute intracranial abnormality. Over the next 3 days, her consciousness worsened, and limb ischemia progressed. Platelet and coagulation disorders were excluded. On day 3, CT angiography of the aorta and lower limbs demonstrated multiple renal infarctions, narrowing of the external iliac arteries, and bilateral femoral-popliteal arteries with multiple stenoses or occlusions; radiologists noted difficulty distinguishing among thrombogenic disease, arterial spasm, hypovolemia, or congenital hypotrophic arteries.

A 45-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a swelling on the mandibular labial gingiva present for 6 months. She reported no pain or discomfort, only occasional watery discharge from the lesion. On examination, there was a 0.5 cm × 0.5 cm firm, pale-yellow swelling between the right mandibular canine and first premolar. An intraoral periapical radiograph showed no osseous involvement, and the adjacent teeth were vital. A complete oral prophylaxis was performed, and the lesion was excised for further evaluation.

A 42-year-old Chinese man with a 4-year history of gout and multiple untreated peripheral tophi presented with worsening lower back pain and left leg symptoms.  
- Two years earlier, he had an episode of sudden lower back pain radiating to the left lower limb that resolved with NSAIDs, with similar intermittent episodes over the next 18 months.  
- Two months before admission, he developed severe lower back pain radiating into the left lower limb accompanied by left lower limb weakness. He denied fever, trauma, weight loss, or incontinence.  
- He had monthly gout flares involving first MTP joints, ankles, knees, and shoulders and self-treated with NSAIDs; he had never received urate-lowering therapy.  

Physical examination  
- Multiple tophi on hands, elbows, ankles, and toes  
- Left thigh flexion/extension 3/5, left knee flexion 4/5; reduced left knee and ankle reflexes  
- Decreased sensation in left L4 and L5 dermatomes; normal anal tone and upper limbs  

Laboratory studies  
- WBC 18 × 10^3/μL; Hb 11 g/dL; platelets 526 × 10^3/μL  
- Creatinine 165 μmol/L; clearance 58 mL/min  
- Na 130 mmol/L; K 3.2 mmol/L; urea 7.6 mmol/L; uric acid 524 μmol/L; CRP 96 mg/L  

Imaging  
- Lumbosacral radiographs: irregular L4, L5, S1 endplates; reduced L4/L5 and L5/S1 disc spaces  
- MRI spine: T2WI hyperintensity within L4/L5 and L5/S1 discs; T1WI hypointense endplate erosions; heterogeneous enhancement of endplates and an epidural mass on post-contrast T1WI  

Based on these findings, the patient was presumed to have an epidural abscess with spondylodiscitis and was started on intravenous cloxacillin.

A 7-year-old Yorkshire Terrier (3.2 kg, BCS 4/9) was evaluated for vomiting, anorexia, and abdominal discomfort of several days’ duration. On exam, the dog was mildly dehydrated and had abdominal tenderness without jaundice. CBC showed mild neutrophilic leukocytosis. Serum chemistry revealed elevated ALT (5.46 μkat/l; RR 0.17–1.96), AST (1.05 μkat/l; RR 0.23–0.75), GGT (0.25 μkat/l; RR 0–0.12), total bilirubin (20.52 μmol/l; RR 1.71–10.26), cholesterol (13.78 mmol/l; RR 3.24–6.99), amylase (33.15 μkat/l; RR 3.34–20.04), lipase (38.43 μkat/l; RR 3.34–30.06) and decreased BUN (2.14 mmol/l; RR 2.50–8.92). Canine pancreas-specific lipase was 1928 μg/l (RR < 400). Abdominal ultrasound showed no gallbladder wall thickening but a small hyperechoic nodule in the gallbladder. CT demonstrated a dilated common bile duct, mineralized foci presumed to be choleliths adherent to the gallbladder wall, and heterogeneous contrast enhancement of the pancreatic body. The dog was treated for pancreatitis with fluids, protease inhibitors, antiemetics, antibiotics, and liver support. Two weeks later labs normalized.

Four years later, the dog returned with vomiting and anorexia. Exam again showed epigastric pain without jaundice. CBC showed mild neutrophilic leukocytosis. Amylase (28.79 μkat/l) and lipase (32.48 μkat/l) remained elevated and cPL was 1521 μg/l. Liver enzymes were normal. Ultrasound revealed absence of bile in the gallbladder and visualization of an atrophic hyperechoic nodule (~5 mm). CT confirmed a trace 5 mm hyperattenuated atrophic gallbladder, a normal-sized common bile duct, and no other biliary obstruction.

A 45-year-old woman from Ethiopia was referred for evaluation of a 1-year history of odorless vaginal discharge that progressed from intermittent and minimal to continuous and copious. She also reported pelvic pain and loss of appetite. She is para 5 with no history of miscarriage or abortion and has no history of diabetes, hypertension, immunosuppression, cough, or known exposure to tuberculosis. She completed HPV vaccination.

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. Respiratory and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Pelvic examination revealed odorless whitish discharge; no cervical mass was palpable.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 9.8 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, platelet count 305 × 10^9/L, ESR 65 mm/h, and normal liver and renal function. HIV and VDRL tests were negative. Chest radiograph was normal, and abdominopelvic ultrasound showed no masses.

A Papanicolaou smear demonstrated atypical glandular cells (favor benign), prompting a punch biopsy of the cervix. Grossly, the biopsy consisted of multiple gray-white to gray-brown tissue fragments measuring 2 cm in aggregate. Microscopic examination with routine H&E stain revealed subepithelial repetitive granuloma formation with Langhans-type giant cells and dusty granular necrosis. Special staining for fungus was negative.

A 31-year-old man with a history of peptic ulcer disease treated with partial gastrectomy 10 years earlier presented with a 2-year history of antibiotic-resistant purulent scalp lesions and 5 days of night sweats, weight loss, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and hematochezia. On examination, he had bilateral lower abdominal tenderness and multiple erythematous interconnecting plaques on the frontal, parietal, and occipital scalp; some plaques were boggy with dried yellow crust and scant purulent drainage. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL, platelets 365,000/mm3, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 52 mm/h, and C-reactive protein 138 mg/L. A comprehensive infectious evaluation for diarrhea was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated pancolitis. Colonoscopy revealed diffuse, severely friable mucosa with contact bleeding and extensive pseudopolyps in the descending colon, as well as discontinuous areas of nonbleeding ulcerated mucosa in the rectum.

A 77-year-old woman with severe, symptomatic aortic stenosis (aortic valve area 0.7 cm2; mean gradient 45 mmHg) and extensive leaflet calcification was referred for transcatheter aortic valve implantation. She had NYHA class III symptoms. On examination, she had a systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border. Pre-procedural CT angiography measured an aortic annulus area of 457.3 mm2. Under conscious sedation, an ACURATE neo™ 25 mm self-expandable bioprosthesis was deployed after balloon pre-dilatation. Post-deployment TTE showed moderate paravalvular regurgitation localized to the right coronary cusp. An initial post-dilatation with a 25 mm balloon did not reduce the leak. A second, more aggressive post-dilatation with a 26 mm balloon was then performed. Immediately afterward, the patient became hypotensive (diastolic pressure < 20 mmHg), and TTE revealed severe aortic regurgitation.

A 55-year-old woman with no past medical or family history presented with a 1-day history of worsening shortness of breath. She reported 6 months of exertional dyspnea, occasionally progressing to rest dyspnea. On examination, she was conscious but in severe respiratory distress; temperature was normal, oxygen saturation 70% on room air, blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg, respiratory rate 25/min, and pulse 110/min. Bilateral basal crackles and hepatomegaly were noted. Initial laboratory values were hemoglobin 10 g/dL, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4 mmol/L, urea 106 mg/dL, creatinine 3.4 mg/dL, and NT-proBNP 1500 pg/mL. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia at 115 bpm with a QTc interval of 498 ms. Chest radiography revealed cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio >0.5) and pulmonary venous congestion. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated dilation of all chambers, global left ventricular hypokinesis, moderate mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, mild aortic regurgitation, mild concentric LV hypertrophy, LV diastolic dysfunction, and an ejection fraction of 30–35%; estimated RV systolic pressure was 50 mm Hg. She was treated with oxygen and diuretics for presumed heart failure but showed no clinical improvement by hospital day 2. On that day, she developed muscle spasms, tetany, circumoral numbness, and positive Chvostek and Trousseau signs.

A 19-year-old woman presented with recurrent nonspecific upper abdominal pain of several weeks’ duration. She had no jaundice, no palpable abdominal mass, and normal laboratory studies. Ultrasonography demonstrated a hypoechogenic, nearly spherical, homogeneous formation with a smooth contour in direct contact with the underside of the liver and no intervening tissue layer, suggestive of a large hepatic cyst. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a well-demarcated, hypodense, homogeneous structure measuring 11 cm in transverse diameter, located adjacent to segment 5 of the liver, anterior to the right kidney, and posterior to the gallbladder. A second, similar-appearing hypodense structure of 3 cm was noted on a lower CT slice. Serologic testing excluded cystic echinococcosis. On the basis of these findings, both lesions were interpreted as congenital hepatic cysts. Because of persistent pain, laparoscopic fenestration of the larger cyst was recommended.

An 84-year-old Asian man was admitted with dyspnea and found to have a large recurrent right-sided pleural effusion—his third since starting empiric RIPE (rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) nine months earlier for presumed extrapulmonary tuberculosis despite negative cultures and imaging. The initial colonoscopic biopsy showed granulomas with an acid-fast stain–positive organism, but cultures were negative; subsequent biopsies and sputum cultures have remained negative and QuantiFERON-TB Gold testing was negative. 

Four weeks after starting RIPE, he developed dyspnea, cough, and weakness and was hospitalized for a large right effusion. Thoracentesis yielded an exudative, lymphocyte-predominant fluid with red color; stains and cultures were negative. He was diagnosed with a paradoxical tuberculous effusion and given systemic corticosteroids while continuing RIPE. 

Two months later, he represented with a similar effusion; repeat thoracentesis again yielded an exudative lymphocyte-predominant fluid, culture-negative. 

Two weeks later, a third re-accumulation prompted video-assisted thoracoscopic pleural biopsy. Pleural fluid showed lymphocytosis (96%), exudative protein and LDH, an adenosine deaminase of 23.8 U/L, and a low complement activity (CH50 10). Cytology was benign. Multiple pleural biopsies showed inflammation without granulomata; all cultures were negative. The pleural fluid ANA was negative. Serum testing revealed an ANA titer of 1:160 with a speckled pattern and a negative antihistone antibody assay.

A 52-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 2-hour history of progressive somnolence, disorientation, and weakness of the right side. Her medical history was notable for ischemic heart disease and essential hypertension that had been untreated for decades; she had not taken any prescribed antihypertensive or antithrombotic medications for a prolonged period. Family history was remarkable only for hypertension.

On examination, her blood pressure was 200/110 mm Hg. She was somnolent but arousable, disoriented to time and place, and had 4/5 strength in the right upper and lower extremities. No other focal neurologic deficits were noted initially.

An urgent noncontrast cranial CT scan revealed bilateral thalamic hemorrhages with extension into the lateral ventricles and a subarachnoid component over the frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes. Small hemorrhages were also seen in the pons and the fourth ventricle. CT angiography showed no active contrast extravasation and no macrovascular source of bleeding; there were no signs of sinus or deep cerebral vein thrombosis.

Laboratory studies, including INR, activated partial thromboplastin time, prothrombin time, and platelet count, were within normal limits. Electrocardiography showed sinus rhythm, and HbA1c was 5.7%.

A 22-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of epigastric pain radiating to the right and left hypochondria and to the back, associated with bilious vomiting, fever, chills, and progressive abdominal distention. Ten days earlier, she had a normal vaginal delivery and had received intramuscular diclofenac for analgesia; she took oral iron supplements for anemia. She denied smoking or alcohol use. On examination, temperature was 39.5 °C, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, heart rate 116 beats/min, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, and pain was rated 10/10. Abdominal examination revealed epigastric tenderness and shifting dullness; the remainder was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a serum amylase level of 370 U/L. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a moderate amount of ascites. Diagnostic paracentesis yielded turbid fluid with glucose 8 mg/dL, albumin 0.5 mg/dL, LDH 1846 U/L, total protein 0.7 mg/dL, and amylase 2700 U/L; cytologic examination showed budding yeasts. The ascitic white cell count was 7000 cells/μL with neutrophils >250 cells/μL. Empirical therapy with cefotaxime and metronidazole was initiated. Cultures on various media grew organisms identified as Candida by germ-tube test, and fluconazole was added.

A 40-year-old woman was admitted with a 3-month history of progressive lower abdominal pain and a 15-day history of a palpable abdominal wall mass. The pain was associated with low-grade fever and a 2-kg weight loss. She had retained an intrauterine contraceptive device for 21 years, which was removed one month before presentation. Her only other notable history was pulmonary tuberculosis in 2003, for which she completed nine months of therapy.

On examination, she appeared ill and mildly pale. Abdominal palpation revealed a tender, firm, mobile 6 × 7 cm mass located 1 cm lateral to the umbilicus; the mass was irreducible, with negative cough impulse and a negative Carnett sign. Digital rectal examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 14.2 × 10^9/L with 85.9% neutrophils, hemoglobin of 8.4 g/dL, and a normal C-reactive protein level. Blood and urine cultures, HIV screening, sputum acid-fast bacilli staining, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR were all negative. Other laboratory values were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 5.1 × 2.6 cm heterogeneously enhancing lesion in the left anterior abdominal wall involving the left rectus abdominis muscle, with adjacent fat stranding separated from the transverse colon. There was mild circumferential thickening and pericolonic fat stranding of the distal transverse colon, with several prominent adjacent lymph nodes (largest, 1.1 × 0.7 cm). Colonoscopy showed no abnormalities.

A 12-year-old boy presented with a 3-week history of right elbow pain and swelling. He denied trauma; he had fevers during the first 3 days only. There was no weight loss, anorexia, cough, or prior surgery. On examination, there was a slightly tender, fluctuant swelling over the right elbow, with normal overlying skin temperature and no wounds, scars, or sinuses. Elbow movement was painful and limited. A plain radiograph of the right elbow showed a well-defined cavitary osteolytic lesion in the distal humerus, surrounded by a rim of sclerosis, with cortical expansion and periosteal reaction. Initial considerations included tubercular abscess and eosinophilic granuloma. MRI was unavailable. A CT scan demonstrated a 1.5 × 1 cm radiolucent lesion in the distal humeral metaphysis with cortical thickening and mild joint effusion. Laboratory studies revealed a normal white-cell count, a C-reactive protein level of 15 mg/dL, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 20 mm/h.

A 40-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of painful oral lesions. Ten months earlier, she had been diagnosed with stage IVA diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and treated with R-CHOEP followed by R-CHEVP, achieving remission but complicated by dilated cardiomyopathy. Five months into treatment she developed pancytopenia with 10–13% myeloblasts (RAEB-2), which progressed to acute myeloid leukemia (40% blasts). She received three cycles of azacitidine with prophylactic ciprofloxacin, acyclovir, and fluconazole. 

On examination at the oral medicine clinic, there were 1-cm ulcerations on the vestibular mucosa above teeth 21, 22, 25, and 26; a 3-mm ulcer in the retromolar area behind tooth 46; and additional ulcers on the tongue. All ulcers were covered with thick pseudomembranes and had minimal surrounding inflammation. Tooth 46 had an implant-supported crown. Orthopantomogram and tooth vitality tests indicated non-odontogenic origin, and there was no dental plaque. 

Laboratory studies showed leukocytes 0.9 × 10^9/L, red blood cells 3.38 × 10^12/L, hemoglobin 99 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 88 fL, and platelets 29 × 10^9/L. Medications included methyldigoxin, furosemide, ramipril, spironolactone, carvedilol, pantoprazole, fluconazole, and ciprofloxacin. To manage her oral pain, she was prescribed Curasept mouthwash, lidocaine gel, Gelclair, benzydamine hydrochloride solution, and betamethasone in orabase.

A 58-year-old man presented after awakening to find his upper left second premolar spontaneously avulsed without pain or bleeding. He reported no preceding trauma or symptoms. Medical history was notable only for long-term phenytoin therapy for epilepsy. On examination, the adjacent upper left canine had grade 2 mobility and the first premolar had grade 3 mobility; the extraction socket was empty. A firm, erythematous, non-tender, non-bleeding nodule was noted on the buccal margin of the socket. The remainder of the oral examination was unremarkable.

Periapical radiography of the left maxilla (lateral incisor through second premolar) demonstrated unilateral widening of the periodontal ligament space distal to the second premolar. Because of sudden tooth loss and asymmetric periodontal ligament widening, a biopsy of the nodular lesion was performed; histopathology showed chronic diffuse inflammation.

Three weeks later, the patient reported a progressively enlarging mass at the extraction site. On repeat examination, a firm, non-tender, non-bleeding mass filled the extraction socket and caused buccopalatal expansion. Cone-beam computed tomography of the left maxilla revealed a radiolucent lesion with a moth-eaten border extending from the distal canine to the molar region, limited to the alveolar process. The sinus floor and basal bone were intact. There was asymmetric destruction of the lamina dura, persistent periodontal ligament widening, absence of root resorption, and perforation of the buccal cortical plate.

A 55-year-old man with a 20-year history of rheumatoid arthritis (not on disease-modifying therapy), hypertension, and alcohol use disorder presented with a 5-day history of purpuric rash, progressive lower-extremity edema, and abdominal distention. He denied fever, chills, or abdominal pain. On examination, temperature was 98.1°F, blood pressure 142/84 mm Hg, pulse 104 bpm; he had shifting dullness, marked pitting edema, ulnar deviation of the hands, and a purpuric rash over the lower extremities. 

On hospital day 1 he developed fever, hypotension, tachycardia, and tachypnea and was treated for presumed sepsis. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, platelets 81,000/μL, AST 1105 U/L, ALT 224 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 426 U/L, total bilirubin 4.6 mg/dL, creatine phosphokinase 30,000 U/L, and creatinine 2.3 mg/dL (baseline 0.8). Urinalysis was positive for blood without protein or leukocytes; urine myoglobin was 1,091 ng/mL. Urine sediment revealed scattered dysmorphic red cells and rare granular casts. 

Serologic studies demonstrated rheumatoid factor 1,512 IU/mL, anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody 269 U/mL, ANA 1:320, C3 46.8 mg/dL, C4 8.9 mg/dL; MPO-ANCA, PR3-ANCA, SSA, SSB, dsDNA, hepatitis B and C serologies, and cryoglobulins were negative. Serum electrophoresis showed mild IgA elevation. Chest radiograph revealed multilobar airspace opacities and small bilateral effusions. Abdominal ultrasound showed mild ascites and a hepatic echo texture consistent with cirrhosis; the kidneys appeared normal. Blood cultures grew Klebsiella oxytoca. 

Despite one week of antibiotics and supportive care, he remained oliguric and required continuous veno-venous hemodialysis. A kidney biopsy was performed.

A full-term female neonate, the first child of second-cousin parents, was delivered by cesarean section after an antenatal ultrasound at 31 weeks showed severe oligohydramnios and multiple cystic lesions in the right kidney. Maternal history was notable only for subseptate uterus and folic acid supplementation; there was no teratogen exposure. Birth weight was 1.5 kg, crown–heel length 45 cm, and head circumference 30 cm (all below the third percentile). The neonate died 35 minutes after birth despite resuscitation.

On external examination, there were low-set ears with folded lobes, a beaked nose, micrognathia, bilateral varus deformity of the feet, left claw-foot ectrodactyly with two toes and a cleft to the metatarsal head, and a right foot with five toes and varus deformity. A tuft of long hair was noted over the spine without a dimple.

Radiographs showed mandibular hypoplasia with absent ramus, left foot ectrodactyly of two metatarsals and two toes, right foot varus deformity of five metatarsals and five toes, a cystic lesion in the right lower thorax, and spinal dysraphism with broad sacral vertebrae.

At autopsy, the right kidney was uniformly enlarged and contained multiple cysts; the left kidney was normal. A 1×2 cm cyst was present in the right lower lobe of the lung. The reproductive tract showed a unicornuate uterus and a right fallopian tube distended with obliterated fimbria.

A woman in her 60s presented with a 12-hour history of sudden-onset, severe right-sided, crampy upper abdominal pain that waxed and waned, associated with nausea, bloating, and constipation. She had no significant comorbidities and no history of abdominal surgery.

On examination, her abdomen was soft with upper abdominal tenderness, a negative Murphy’s sign, and no palpable masses. Vital signs were stable. Laboratory studies and a urine dipstick test were normal.

An abdominal ultrasound showed gallstones but no features of cholecystitis. She was treated with analgesics for presumed biliary colic; however, overnight her pain worsened and became refractory to analgesia. Inflammatory markers remained normal, and a static picture of partial bowel obstruction persisted.

A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was performed. The scan showed an abnormally positioned caecum with its pole situated closer to the greater curvature of the stomach in the left gastric space without any volvulus or strangulation features. A portion of small bowel was noted within the lesser sac.

A 13-year-old boy presented with two months of fatigue and generalized edema, as well as bilateral painless submandibular masses that had been progressively enlarging over six months. He had a history of nephrotic syndrome diagnosed one year earlier by renal biopsy showing focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, for which he received corticosteroids, and a known subclinical hypothyroidism. He denied smoking, alcohol use, and had no family history of renal or autoimmune disease.

On examination, temperature was 36.9°C, pulse 81/min, blood pressure 131/82 mm Hg, respiratory rate 17/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Two non-tender, poorly mobile masses (1.5 × 1 cm on the right, 1.5 × 0.5 cm on the left) were palpated in the submandibular regions with normal overlying skin. There was 3+ pitting edema of both lower extremities. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 4200/μL (neutrophils 52.2%, lymphocytes 35.5%), hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL, platelets 472 000/μL, sodium 139 mEq/L, potassium 4.9 mEq/L, chloride 102 mEq/L, calcium 7.7 mg/dL, phosphorus 4.7 mg/dL, albumin 1.7 g/dL, LDH 715 IU/L, ESR 90 mm/h, TSH 8.28 μIU/mL with normal free T4, ALP 585 IU/L, ALT 17 IU/L, AST 34 IU/L. A 24-hour urine collection showed protein 3100 mg/day, volume 1100 mL; serum creatinine was 1.4 mg/dL. Urinalysis revealed specific gravity 1.025, 15 RBCs/μL, and 2–4 granular casts. Rheumatologic and communicable disease screening tests were negative. Thyroid ultrasound was unremarkable. Neck ultrasonography revealed multiple enlarged lymph nodes bilaterally, the largest measuring 15 × 7 mm in the right submandibular region and 12 × 5 mm along the left carotid sheath.

A 9-year-old boy presented with a 1-week history of nontraumatic leg pain, worse on the left, and progressive difficulty ambulating. Initial radiographs of the left knee showed a benign nonossifying fibroma in the proximal tibial metadiaphysis without fracture or effusion; he was advised rest and acetaminophen. Three days later, he returned unable to walk, with posterior left knee pain; ultrasound of the left popliteal fossa demonstrated an ill-defined fluid collection with overlying soft-tissue swelling but no joint effusion. He also reported vague right leg and chest-wall pain and was transferred for further evaluation.

On arrival, he was afebrile, in no acute distress, but refused to ambulate due to pain posterior to the left knee. Height was 140 cm (84th percentile) and weight 40.6 kg (95th). Laboratory studies revealed microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, MCV 72.5 fL), mild leukocytosis (WBC 12.0 × 10^9/L with left shift), and elevated C-reactive protein (16.8 mg/L); the WBC count normalized on repeat. The clinical differential diagnosis included septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, ruptured Baker’s cyst, osteoid osteoma, and malignancy. An MRI of the knees was performed using T1 and T2 fat-saturated sequences.

MRI demonstrated confluent T1 hypointense and T2 hyperintense signal in the metaphyses of the left distal femur and proximal tibia; extensive T2 hyperintense signal infiltrated the popliteal fossa, calf muscles (especially at myotendinous junctions), and subcutaneous tissues. An extended field-of-view study including the contralateral leg and proximal hips revealed symmetric metaphyseal marrow abnormalities in both distal femora and proximal tibiae, with milder changes in proximal femora. Gadolinium was not administered due to the symmetry of the marrow abnormalities indicating a systemic process rather than a focal lesion.

An 18-year-old woman presented in September 2024 with a 1-month history of low-grade intermittent fever accompanied by rigors, chills, myalgias, and arthralgias, followed 20 days later by scleral icterus that progressed to generalized jaundice with a purplish rash and dark urine. She then developed bizarre behavior, an initial mutism, and later irrelevant speech, while remaining conscious. Over the preceding 18 months, she had experienced oral ulcers, alopecia, and arthralgias of the small joints of the hands and feet without swelling or stiffness, as well as exertional dyspnea and palpitations for 1 year. There was no history of sore throat, cough, gastrointestinal bleeding, or medication use prior to these symptoms. Her parents were consanguineous; her father had a long‐standing psychiatric illness.

On examination, she was febrile (102°F), disoriented to time and place, mildly jaundiced, and pale, with facial puffiness, bilateral nontender parotid enlargement, angular cheilitis, and livedo reticularis with necrotic plaques on the skin. Neurologically, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 13, with no focal deficits, no meningeal signs, and no Kayser–Fleischer rings. The abdomen showed mild splenomegaly.  

Laboratory studies revealed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 6.6 g/dL, leukocytes 2.0 × 10^9/L, platelets 40 × 10^9/L), AST 1292 U/L, total bilirubin 11.5 mg/dL, and a reversed albumin:globulin ratio. Hepatitis B and C serologies were negative; hepatitis E IgM was positive. Ceruloplasmin was low (0.2 g/L), and 24-hour urinary copper excretion was elevated (204 µg). Autoimmune testing showed a positive ANA (coarse speckled pattern), high anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, anti-Ro, anti-La, U1-RNP, rheumatoid factor, anticardiolipin antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, a positive direct Coombs test, and low complement levels.  

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated mild hepatosplenomegaly, increased hepatic echogenicity, and a small amount of perihepatic fluid. MRI of the brain with contrast, MRA, and MRV showed dilated ventricles with minimal subependymal seepage, mucoperiosteal thickening of the sphenoid sinus, and a normal appearance of the basal ganglia; the remainder of the studies were unremarkable.

A 29-year-old man presented with epigastric and right upper quadrant pain. On examination, there was no remarkable tenderness; vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis, with other hematologic and biochemical tests normal. 

An abdominal ultrasonogram revealed a normal gallbladder containing multiple gallstones and a fusiform cystic structure adjacent to it (no biliary-tract dilatation; gallbladder wall normal in thickness and echogenicity). 

To further delineate biliary anatomy, magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography was performed, demonstrating a normal gallbladder with multiple intraluminal stones and a second adjacent gallbladder; both structures drained via a common cystic duct entering the common hepatic duct. The common hepatic duct and common bile duct were otherwise normal without intraluminal filling defects.

A 33-year-old man presented with several months of chronic right facial and nasal cavity pain. Seven months earlier, he underwent extraction of the right maxillary canine. Three months after symptom onset, a CT scan of the sinuses with contrast showed drainage occlusion in the right maxillary and sphenoid sinuses. He was treated for presumed acute bacterial sinusitis with multiple courses of penicillin, clindamycin, and amoxicillin–clavulanate, as well as nasal saline irrigations and oxymetazoline sprays, without improvement. Two months before presentation, he reported fevers, chills, headache, nasal congestion, ear pain, blurred vision, and photophobia. On examination, he was in mild distress, with right-sided facial tenderness and poor dentition. Nasal endoscopy demonstrated right septal deviation, purulent discharge, and mucosal edema. Cultures of nasal discharge grew Aspergillus flavus, which was initially attributed to environmental contamination. Six weeks later, symptoms persisted despite ongoing amoxicillin–clavulanate. Repeat endoscopy showed a right septal spur, diffuse mucosal edema, purulent discharge, crusting, and an inferior synechia. He underwent right maxillary antrostomy, anterior ethmoidectomy, debridement of necrotic tissue in the right nasal cavity, and removal of the septal spur. Surgical cultures again grew Aspergillus flavus.

A 52-year-old woman with a history of asthma since childhood and recurrent fever, arthralgia, and fatigue over the past two years presented with worsening chest pain of several weeks’ duration. Twelve months earlier, she had been diagnosed with idiopathic pericarditis associated with eosinophilia and treated with NSAIDs, with rapid symptom remission. Two weeks before admission she experienced angioedema, painful subcutaneous nodules of the arms and legs, and numbness and paresthesia of her toes and hands. 

On presentation, the chest pain was pleuritic and improved by sitting up and leaning forward. Vital signs were normal. Cardiac examination revealed a holosystolic regurgitant murmur at the apex; there were no skin rashes or focal neurologic deficits. ECG showed diffuse T-wave flattening in the inferior, lateral, and precordial leads. Laboratory studies demonstrated C-reactive protein 101 mg/L (normal <16 mg/L), eosinophils 2.14 × 10^9/L (normal <0.5 × 10^9/L), high-sensitivity troponin T 193 ng/L (normal <52 ng/L), and NT-proBNP 1153 ng/L (normal <300 ng/L). 

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed mild left ventricular dysfunction (LVEF 47%), severe mitral regurgitation due to posterior leaflet prolapse, and a small pericardial effusion without tamponade. Coronary angiography showed no obstructive lesions. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an LVEF of 47% with left ventricular dilatation, absence of late gadolinium enhancement, and normal T1 and T2 mapping values.

A 102-year-old woman with no relevant past medical history presented with rigors and dysuria. Her temperature was 38.4 °C, pulse 117 beats/min, and supine blood pressure 87/63 mm Hg. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. A 12-lead electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia. Laboratory studies revealed a hemoglobin level of 13.7 g/dL, white-cell count of 11.5×10^9/L, C-reactive protein of 100 mg/dL, and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 46 mL/min/1.73 m^2. Urinalysis was strongly positive for infection, and blood cultures grew Escherichia coli. A chest radiograph showed a well-defined hemispherical soft-tissue density projected over the right parahilar region. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated an 8 cm×5 cm low-attenuation lesion abutting the pericardium, the anterior mediastinum, and the anterior chest wall.

A male infant was born at 37 weeks’ gestation to a 19-year-old G3P1001 mother with idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura toward the end of pregnancy. Maternal serologies were negative for hepatitis B, HIV, and group B Streptococcus; rubella and VDRL status were unknown. Delivery was vaginal with spontaneous rupture of membranes 2 hours prior; Apgar scores were 9 and 9. Birth weight was 2499 g. 

On initial examination, a thin, yellow, shiny collodion membrane covered most of his skin. He was active, alert, and responsive. Findings were notable for incomplete eyelid closure, blanching of the eyelids, eclabium (inability to purse lips), and limited joint motion due to taut skin. Hearing was normal, and nails appeared normal without dystrophic changes.

On day 7, increased work of breathing occurred due to upper-airway obstruction from dried skin plugs. He was admitted to the NICU in a humidified incubator. At 6 hours of age, electrolytes were normal. Nasogastric feedings were started because he could not suck. Daily baths with gentle soap, frequent applications of Eucerin and Aquaphor, and Bacitracin zinc to skin fissures were implemented. Lacri-Lube was applied to the eyes, and ammonium lactate was added once peeling began. He received high-calorie formula via nasogastric tube for possible protein loss. A family pedigree was unremarkable.

During the second week, diffuse peeling occurred, especially on the face, and ectropion resolved as skin shed around the eyes. By day 27, skin markedly improved though lower-extremity edema persisted. On day 29, he was treated for anemia (hematocrit 22.8%, reticulocyte count 76 k/µL). He completed a 7-day course of nafcillin and gentamicin for abdominal wall cellulitis; vancomycin was briefly given for suspected coagulase-negative Staphylococcus sepsis, later deemed contamination. By day 31, his vital signs and skin status were stable, and he was discharged home.

A 65-year-old woman presented with 2 months of progressive pain and swelling over the lateral aspect of her left hip. The pain was dull, constant, worsened by weight bearing, and partially relieved by analgesics. There was no history of trauma, fever, or other constitutional symptoms, and she had no comorbidities. Thirty years earlier, she had a similar presentation with a discharging sinus over the left thigh, was diagnosed with tuberculosis of the left trochanteric bursa based on clinical and radiographic findings, and was cured after a 6-month course of antitubercular therapy.

On examination, there was an 8 × 4 cm fluctuant swelling over the left greater trochanter with a healed sinus dimple, minimal warmth, and tenderness. Hip range of motion was normal; she walked with an antalgic gait. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, WBC count 9960 cells/mm3 with a normal differential, and ESR 50 mm in the first hour. Liver and renal function tests and blood glucose were normal. Chest radiograph was normal. Pelvic radiograph revealed a lytic lesion of the left greater trochanter with sharp margins suggestive of benign tumour or infection. MRI of the pelvis demonstrated a focal osteolytic lesion with cortical destruction of the greater trochanter and an enlarged trochanteric bursa with an enhancing wall suggestive of an abscess; the collection extended laterally through a deep fascial defect into subcutaneous tissue in a dumbbell shape with multiple small loose bodies. Fine-needle aspiration cytology was inconclusive.

A 24-year-old man presented to the emergency department after a seizure following four days of fever. He reported a one-month history of productive cough with yellow sputum and gradual weight loss. Four months earlier, he had been hospitalized for inferior paraparesis and evaluation of a calvarial mass that was presumed metastatic, with a lung primary suspected.

On examination, vital signs showed fever; neurological examination confirmed lower extremity weakness. Laboratory studies were notable for C-reactive protein 263 mg/L, white blood cell count 19,300 cells/μL, and serum potassium 5.5 mmol/L.

Head imaging with enhanced CT and MRI demonstrated left parietal bone destruction with rim-enhancing soft tissue extending intracranially, causing focal parietal meningoencephalitis. Thoracolumbar MRI revealed posterior vertebral destruction of the lamina, pedicle, and transverse and spinous processes at T5–T6, with an extradural mass compressing the spinal cord and visible dural enhancement. An irregular mass was also noted in the right lung on MRI.

Subsequent enhanced and unenhanced thoracic CT showed an irregular solid mass in the right mediobasal lung segment, multiple conglomerated lymph nodes in the right parabronchial, subcarinal, and lower paratracheal regions, and bone destruction of T5–T6 and the sternum with a rim-enhancing soft tissue mass.

These findings were suggestive of a malignant solid lung mass with multiple bone metastases.

A 58-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of a right groin mass that had gradually increased from 3 cm to 10 cm in diameter. Over the past 8 months, he noted concurrent right scrotal swelling up to 12 cm. He reported that pressing on the mass prompted additional urination after spontaneous voiding, and that the mass visibly decreased in size after he voided. He also described lower abdominal discomfort, scrotal pain during micturition and coughing, and lower urinary tract symptoms including incontinence, straining, urinary frequency, and a sensation of incomplete emptying. He denied gastrointestinal or systemic symptoms. His medical history was notable for right inguinal hernia repair 6 years earlier. 

On examination, vital signs were normal. Abdominal palpation elicited mild hypogastric pain (5/10). Inspection of the right inguinal region revealed a 10 cm irreducible mass with mild tenderness that enlarged with Valsalva maneuver. Right scrotal swelling measured approximately 12 cm, was mildly tender, and had no overlying skin changes. When the mass was manually reduced, the patient experienced an urgent need to urinate.

Laboratory studies were unremarkable. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography demonstrated a widened right inguinal canal containing peritoneum and a “teardrop” lesion extending through the inguinal canal into the right scrotum. No bladder wall thickening or urinary tract stones were seen.

A 39-year-old Iranian woman presented with a six-month history of menstrual disturbance, headaches, vertigo, decreased libido, polyuria, and polydipsia. She had been infertile for two years. Her medical history was unremarkable except for a minor head injury four years earlier without skull fracture or cerebrospinal fluid leak. She denied visual changes, diplopia, signs of Cushing syndrome, or acromegaly.  

On examination, vital signs were normal. Neurological examination, including cranial nerves, was normal. Visual fields and fundoscopy were unremarkable; visual acuity was 10/10 bilaterally.  

Laboratory studies showed:  
• Prolactin: 73 ng/mL (non-pregnant reference < 25 ng/mL; diluted 52 ng/mL)  
• TSH, T4, LH, FSH, and morning cortisol were within or near reference ranges.  

Dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI of the pituitary gland demonstrated an enlarged pituitary with a thickened infundibulum and a peripherally enhancing T1-hypointense lesion.

A 38-year-old Sudanese woman presented with a 1-year history of a progressively enlarging swelling of the left upper thigh and hip. She initially sought medical advice but deferred intervention until mild discomfort prompted re-evaluation. On examination, there was a firm, non-tender, well-circumscribed mass measuring approximately 16×12 cm in the left upper thigh near the hip. The overlying skin was normal without erythema or warmth. The mass was hard, fixed to deep structures but not to the skin; there was a palpable inguinal lymph node, and hip range of motion was limited.

Routine blood tests, including complete blood count, viral screening, and renal function studies (serum phosphorus and calcium), were all within normal limits. Plain radiography of the left hip and thigh revealed a cloud-like, well-defined calcified mass abutting the hip joint, with a characteristic “chicken-wire” pattern of calcification in the surrounding soft tissue and no evidence of bony involvement, fracture, destruction, or periosteal reaction. A chest X-ray and abdominopelvic ultrasound examination were unremarkable. Local ultrasound of the thigh showed a well-circumscribed echogenic mass splaying adjacent soft-tissue planes. Regional inguinal lymph-node biopsy demonstrated reactive changes without histological evidence of malignancy or granulomatous reaction.

A 25-year-old man presented with persistent posterior heel pain 5 months after an inversion injury to his left ankle. Initially, he experienced lateral ankle and posterior heel swelling and pain, which improved laterally but remained posteriorly. On examination at 5 months, there was mild residual tenderness over the posterior aspect of the left distal tibia without soft-tissue mass. 

Radiographs of the left ankle showed a solid, smooth periosteal reaction along the posterior aspect of the distal tibia without evidence of fracture. MRI demonstrated a corresponding periosteal new bone formation without adjacent soft-tissue mass. CT of the left ankle confirmed a thick, solid periosteal reaction at the posterior distal tibia.

A 29-year-old businesswoman presented with a 4-month history of tender, palpable nodules on the palmar surfaces of both hands. The tenderness initially resolved spontaneously but recurred intermittently over the subsequent 3 months. She denied any preceding trauma or relevant family history. Physical examination revealed multiple firm, fixed nodules on the palmar aspects of both hands, several of which were tender to palpation adjacent to the metacarpophalangeal joints. Routine blood tests, including inflammatory markers, were within normal limits.

MRI of both hands was obtained on a 1.5 T scanner with a surface coil. On T2-weighted sequences, there were multiple round, nodular lesions in the subcutaneous plane of the palms, each exhibiting very high signal intensity. On T1-weighted images, the lesions were isointense to skeletal muscle. Post-gadolinium T1 images demonstrated variable enhancement: some lesions enhanced homogeneously, while others showed a linear peripheral rim of enhancement.

High-resolution ultrasound using 18 MHz and 33 MHz probes confirmed multiple well-defined hypoechoic lesions up to 4 mm in diameter within the subcutaneous tissue of the palms. The lesions showed marked posterior acoustic enhancement and lacked internal Doppler flow. Comparative ultrasound images demonstrated a significant increase in the number and size of these structures compared to a normal reference.

A 62-year-old man with an 11-year history of dialysis for chronic renal failure presented with 5–6 years of progressive pain around the second and third metatarsal heads and numbness in the second and third toes. The pain was accentuated by walking and by shoes with a tight toe box and had worsened despite intermittent local analgesic injections and other conservative measures. On presentation, he was unable to walk more than 10 minutes because of forefoot pain. On static standing examination, the second and third toes showed hammertoe deformities and did not touch the ground. Palpation elicited tenderness over the second and third MTP joints and the second intermetatarsal space. The foot squeeze test (Mulder’s sign) produced severe radiating pain without a click. The drawer test at the second and third MTP joints revealed more than 50% subluxation and reproduced intolerable radiating pain in the toes. Radiographs of the feet showed no apparent fractures or toe deviations but demonstrated slight opening of the second MTP joint space. Coronal T1-weighted MRI of the forefoot revealed an upside-down bulbous-shaped lesion with low-signal intensity between the second and third metatarsal heads.

A 24-year-old man presented with a 12-month history of a slowly enlarging mid-line neck swelling. He reported no dysphagia, dyspnoea, voice change, or other aero-digestive symptoms. He had no significant occupational or social history. On examination, there was a 6 cm diameter mid-line, soft, fluctuant, non-tender mass just above the sternal notch that did not move on swallowing. The swelling became noticeably more prominent when he performed a Valsalva manoeuvre. Flexible naso-laryngoendoscopy was unremarkable. 

Given the expansile nature of the mass, an external laryngocoele was suspected. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the neck demonstrated a well-defined 5 × 4 cm cystic lesion in the suprasternal region with no obvious communication to the larynx or trachea. Ultrasound-guided aspiration yielded mucoid fluid, and cultures showed no microbial growth.

An 11-year-old Thai girl presented with a one-month history of low-grade fever followed by ten days of high-grade fever, malaise, anorexia, throbbing headache, intermittent diplopia, and acute bilateral vision loss one day before admission. On examination, temperature was 38.3°C; other vital signs were normal. She had a discoid rash on the left ear, a painless hard-palate ulcer, hepatosplenomegaly, proximal upper-extremity weakness (grade 4), hyporeflexia in the arms, areflexia in the legs, bilateral abducens-nerve palsies with limited abduction (worse on the left), and a grade-2 relative afferent pupillary defect in the right eye. Visual acuity was hand motion with light projection in the right eye and finger counting at 2 feet in the left. Funduscopic examination showed bilateral disc edema, peripapillary hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, and subretinal fluid in the left macula. Laboratory studies revealed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL, WBC 2100/µL, platelets 81 000/µL), direct Coombs test 3+, anti–double-stranded DNA 1:80, ANA >1:5 homogeneous pattern, low C3 (0.13 g/L) and C4 (0.06 g/L), proteinuria with hematuria, negative anti-cardiolipin IgG, and positive anti-β2-glycoprotein 1 IgG/IgM/IgA.

A 24-year-old man presented to the emergency department on April 4, 2021, with a 2-week history of left calf pain following receipt of the ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccine. The pain was initially mild but gradually increased over 4 weeks to moderate intensity, was nonradiating, localized below the knee, and aggravated by movement. He denied fever, swelling, trauma to the leg, and had no prior similar episodes. He was a nonsmoker with no relevant medical history and was taking acetaminophen as needed.

On examination, temperature was normal. Pulse was 64 beats/min, blood pressure 110/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. The left calf showed no swelling or warmth, but there was tenderness on compression (negative Homans sign). The Wells score for deep-vein thrombosis was low (< 4). The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed: WBC 6,100/μL (60% neutrophils, 38% lymphocytes, 2% eosinophils), RBC 5.1×10^12/L, hemoglobin 14.5 g/dL, platelets 337,000/μL; prothrombin time 13.8 sec (control 12 sec), INR 0.98; total cholesterol 114 mg/dL, triglycerides 68 mg/dL, HDL 48 mg/dL, LDL 52 mg/dL; urea 23 mg/dL, creatinine 1 mg/dL, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.5 mmol/L; ECG showed sinus rhythm at 64 bpm; hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibody, and HIV antibody tests were nonreactive.

A 50-year-old man with metastatic renal cell carcinoma (clear‐cell histology with sarcomatoid features, pT1bN0M1) presented initially with left neck and anterior chest pain. He underwent robot‐assisted radical nephrectomy and palliative radiotherapy (20 Gy) to a painful sternal lesion. Baseline laboratory tests showed a CRP of 18.21 mg/dL, hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL, and corrected calcium 10.6 mg/dL. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 64 mm left renal mass, multiple pulmonary nodules, and a lytic sternal lesion; MRI confirmed metastatic lesions in the sternum and right ilium. He was classified as poor risk and started on nivolumab (3 mg/kg) plus ipilimumab (1 mg/kg). Five days after the first dose, NSAIDs were restarted for right thigh pain. On day 10 after the second ICI dose, he developed a fever of 38.5 °C with marked elevations in CRP and interleukin-6. Empiric broad‐spectrum antibiotics were initiated. Blood and urine cultures were negative, and chest and abdominal CT scans showed no evidence of infection. Additional tests revealed elevated ferritin and soluble IL-2 receptor levels, while endocrine and liver function tests remained normal. He remained hemodynamically stable without hypotension or respiratory compromise.

A 34-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 2-hour history of sudden, severe thoracic back pain that began as a dull ache and became sharp. He denied any trauma, drug use, or heavy exertion and had no significant past medical history. On arrival, he was alert, with normal vital signs and an unremarkable physical examination. Initial laboratory tests, including a complete blood count, chemistry panel, and coagulation studies, were within normal limits. Three hours after the onset of pain, he developed weakness and numbness in both lower limbs. On neurologic examination, muscle strength was 2/5 in thigh flexion and foot dorsiflexion bilaterally, the lower extremities were flaccid, plantar responses were extensor on both sides, sensation was decreased below the T10 dermatome with perineal anesthesia, and he had urinary retention. Emergency MRI of the thoracic spine showed an anterior epidural mass extending from T3–T4 to T8–T9, with maximal cord compression at T5–T6. The mass was isointense to the spinal cord on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images. Diffusion-weighted imaging revealed no signal abnormalities in the spinal cord.
