A 29-year-old G2P1 woman at 35 weeks 5 days of gestation presented with severe headache, nasal congestion, lower extremity swelling, and epigastric pain. She denied cough, fever, chest pain, or shortness of breath. On examination, temperature was 98.5°F, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, heart rate 110/min, and oxygen saturation 89%–91% on room air. She appeared ill, with facial flushing and cyanotic lips, and episodes of fetal tachycardia were noted. Laboratory studies showed a normal white blood cell count, aspartate aminotransferase of 42 U/L, and a urine protein/creatinine ratio of 0.31. A nasopharyngeal nucleic acid amplification test for Influenza A/B and respiratory syncytial virus was negative, and a reverse-transcriptase–polymerase-chain-reaction assay for SARS-CoV-2 was sent.

A 45-year-old Bangladeshi woman presented with severe generalized itching and skin lesions over the extremities, neck, upper back, chest, oral cavity, and genitalia for 4 years. She had seen multiple physicians and had been treated with topical and systemic antifungals and steroids without improvement; she also received a course of dapsone for suspected dermatitis herpetiformis with no significant benefit. Over the past month, she noted gradual bilateral visual loss, recurrent fever, and weight loss. Her husband, who has similar skin lesions, has lived in South Africa for 8 years. She denied tuberculosis exposure and blood transfusions; family members are healthy. 

On examination, she was emaciated and moderately anemic, with normal vital signs and no lymphadenopathy. Skin examination showed multiple excoriated, lichenified papules with exudation and crusting on the extremities, neck, and upper back; there were whitish patches on the tongue and oral mucosa and a nonhealing ulcer on the labia. Fundoscopic examination revealed disc swelling with splinter hemorrhages and exudates in the superior and inferior quadrants of the right eye, and a pale disc with exudates in the superior and inferior quadrants of the left eye. Routine investigations, including abdominal ultrasound, hematological and biochemical profiles, were unremarkable.

A 51-year-old woman presented with a several-month history of dyspepsia. Physical examination and routine laboratory studies were within normal limits. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed diffuse hyperemia and edema of the gastric mucosa; the esophagus appeared normal. Multiple biopsies were obtained from the gastric corpus. Histologic evaluation showed expansion of the lamina propria by numerous plasma cells containing intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions (Mott cells) in the background of chronic gastritis. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated that these plasma cells were positive for CD138 and negative for cytokeratin. Staining for kappa and lambda light chains revealed a polyclonal pattern. Giemsa stain was positive for Helicobacter pylori organisms.

A 70-year-old man with a 20-year history of diabetes mellitus presented with a 1-month history of a painful ulcerative lesion on the tip of his left middle finger. The lesion began as a small blister at the distal fingertip, then ruptured and became ulcerated with serous, nonfoul-smelling discharge. He had sustained a cat bite to that finger one month before the lesion appeared. He received multiple courses of broad-spectrum antibiotics, including oral amoxicillin–clavulanate, and underwent daily wound dressings for presumed diabetic ulcer care, but the lesion continued to enlarge, extending to the interphalangeal joint area, causing pain.

On examination, vital signs were normal and capillary blood glucose was 7.9 mmol/L. The left middle finger showed an approximately 2×2 cm ulcer with irregular margins, serous and bloody discharge, and tender palpation; the surrounding skin was normal without erythema. There were no palpable nodules on the dorsum of the hand or forearm and no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory evaluation revealed hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL, white-cell count 6.0×10^9/L, platelet count 165×10^9/L, normal liver and renal function tests, and hemoglobin A1c 7.9%.

A skin biopsy from the lesion showed irregular epidermal hyperplasia with hyperkeratosis and parakeratosis, inflammatory-cell infiltration within the epidermis, and marked acute and chronic inflammatory-cell infiltrates with histiocytes in the dermis.

A 73-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer on leuprolide presented with a 2-week history of a mildly pruritic rash on his chest. Two weeks before rash onset, he had initiated intravenous docetaxel (75 mg/m2). He denied heat exposure, new personal-care products, new medications other than docetaxel, or a prior history of similar rashes.

On examination, there were erythematous papules and eroded macules on the upper and medial portions of the chest without pustules or involvement of the back. A clinical differential diagnosis included miliaria rubra, folliculitis, demodicosis, and Pityrosporum folliculitis. 

A punch biopsy of a representative lesion showed hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, focal epidermal suprabasilar acantholysis, and dyskeratosis without significant spongiosis.

A 55-year-old woman with a history of smoking presented with a 4-day history of headache, fever, and progressively worsening consciousness. On examination, she was comatose (Glasgow Coma Scale score 6) with bradycardia and hypertension. She was intubated for airway protection. Urgent noncontrast CT of the head revealed an extra-axial expansile lesion in the anterior frontal region measuring 8.5 × 7 × 5 cm, with homogenous iso- to hypodense content, marked compression of the bilateral frontal lobes, thinning of the frontal bone with sclerotic margins, and rim enhancement on contrast imaging.

A 41-year-old man with a 20-year history of presumed multiple sclerosis presented for reevaluation. Twenty years earlier he experienced left-eye visual loss that did not recover; he was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis and received monthly IV methylprednisolone for several years. Seven years ago he developed sudden left-ear hearing loss. An audiogram showed total sensorineural deafness of the left ear and 20% hearing loss in the right ear. Brain MRI at that time was interpreted as consistent with a demyelinating disease.

One year ago he had sudden right-eye visual loss. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated a branch retinal artery occlusion in the right eye. Pattern-shift visual evoked potentials showed a P100 peak latency of 114 ms in the right eye (normal range, 90–120 ms) and no identifiable waveform in the left eye. He was treated with hyperbaric oxygen and aspirin, and his vision returned to near normal within 20 days.

On current examination, visual acuity was 20/100 in the left eye and 20/20 in the right eye, with no other neurologic deficits. T2-weighted brain MRI demonstrated multiple small foci of increased signal intensity. Electroencephalography showed mild diffuse slowing with low-voltage alpha rhythm (7–8 Hz) and rare frontotemporal theta activity (4–6 Hz). Brain-stem auditory evoked potentials yielded no waveform from the left ear and normal I, II, and IV waves on the right. A follow-up visual evoked potential one year after the right-eye event showed improvement of the P100 latency from 114 ms to 102 ms.

Cranial MR angiography and transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography were normal. Serologic testing showed weakly positive ANA and elevated rheumatoid factor; ferritin, vitamin B12, homocysteine, platelet count, coagulation studies, fibrinogen, D-dimer, and sedimentation rate were within normal limits. Anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein, lupus anticoagulant, and anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies were negative. Antiphospholipid antibodies, C-reactive protein, total IgA, IgM, IgE, complement C3 and C4, and a hepatitis screen were all normal. He denied any neuropsychiatric symptoms despite the EEG findings of frontotemporal slowing.

A 61-year-old man with hepatitis B–related cirrhosis, portal vein thrombosis, and prior portal-systemic encephalopathy was admitted for elective living-donor liver transplantation. His postoperative regimen included aspirin and nafamostat mesilate for thrombosis prophylaxis; prostaglandin E1 for graft perfusion; tacrolimus and prednisolone for immunosuppression; and ampicillin/sulbactam, fluconazole, and nystatin for infection prophylaxis. On postoperative day (POD) 6, the patient’s mental status deteriorated and motor strength was decreased in all extremities (upper, grade III; lower, grade I). By POD 7, lower-extremity strength improved to grade III. A neurologic consultation on POD 7 revealed a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 12 (E4, V2, M6) and equal, reactive pupils. On POD 8, he had a generalized tonic–clonic seizure lasting 2 minutes with rightward eye deviation; the seizure aborted after lorazepam. Levetiracetam (2000 mg/day) and pregabalin (150 mg/day) were started, but brief seizure episodes recurred with position change or suctioning. Laboratory tests, including arterial blood gases, complete blood count, coagulation profile, electrolytes, glucose, and liver-function parameters, were within normal limits except for mild, stable hyponatremia. A noncontrast head CT scan on POD 8 showed no acute intracranial abnormality.

A 73-year-old non-alcoholic woman presented with a 1-month history of gradually progressive abdominal distension associated with early satiety, bipedal edema, generalized weakness, fatigue, and weight loss. She denied jaundice, melena, hematemesis, pruritus, abdominal pain, vomiting, fever, or dyspnea. Her history was notable for hypertension and treated pulmonary tuberculosis over 20 years ago; she had no alcohol use or prior abdominal surgery.

On examination, she was mildly cachectic, afebrile, anicteric, and hemodynamically stable (pulse 104/min, BP 132/75 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 95% on room air). There was bipedal pitting edema to mid-shin without lymphadenopathy. Abdominal examination revealed gross distension, a positive fluid thrill, mild epigastric tenderness, and hepatosplenomegaly (liver span 5 cm, spleen 8 cm below costal margin).

Laboratory studies showed WBC 92×10^3/μl with lymphocytosis (73.8×10^3/μl), hemoglobin 10 g/dl, neutropenia (2.1%), and platelets 67×10^9/l. Peripheral smear demonstrated small mature lymphocytes with condensed chromatin and smudge cells. Uric acid was 718 μmol/l and LDH 297 IU/l; renal function and electrolytes were normal. Liver tests revealed albumin 25 g/l, AST 85 IU/l, INR 2.63, and HBsAg positivity. Ascitic fluid had a SAAG of 1.3 g/dl and no malignant cells; AFP was 10.5 ng/ml. Abdominal ultrasound showed a shrunken liver with coarse echotexture, massive ascites, and splenomegaly.

A resting ECG showed sinus tachycardia. Plain chest radiographs demonstrated air under the right hemidiaphragm with apparent haustral folds within the air, leftward tracheal deviation, and reduced left lung volume.

A 19-year-old man presented with a one‐year history of recurrent right-sided pleuritic chest pain, fever, cough, and dyspnea. One year earlier, he had a motor vehicle accident complicated by right pleural effusions treated multiple times by thoracentesis; pleural biopsy at that time showed reactive pleuritis without granulomas or malignancy. On admission, vital signs were normal. Physical examination revealed decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the right lower chest. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. Chest ultrasonography demonstrated multiple septations and a thickened parietal pleura. Chest CT confirmed a right-sided loculated pleural effusion. Analysis of pleural fluid showed an exudative effusion (protein 3.8 g/dL, serum protein 6.5 g/dL; LDH 800 IU/L, serum LDH 190 IU/L; bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL, serum bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL). Cytologic examination was unremarkable. A 28-French chest tube was placed, and a limited thoracotomy with pleural decortication was performed. During surgery, extensive adhesions and yellow plaque‐like deposits were noted on the pleural surfaces.

A 79-year-old man with a recent diagnosis of chronic myelomonocytic leukemia presented with a 1-month history of a persistent, intensely pruritic eruption on the forehead, chest, abdomen, and upper extremities; the lower extremities were spared. On examination, there were multiple excoriated follicular papules and nodules on the face, trunk, and arms. Skin biopsies demonstrated a perifollicular mixed infiltrate composed of lymphocytes and eosinophils with follicular spongiosis. Multiple‐level sections highlighted prominent exocytosis of eosinophils in the follicular epithelium and rare eosinophils in the infundibular epithelium and sebaceous lobules. The infiltrate consisted predominantly of CD3+ T cells with a CD4/CD8 ratio of approximately 4:1, and cytologic atypia was absent. Immunohistochemical stains for myeloperoxidase, CD117, and lysozyme were negative, and Alcian blue staining did not demonstrate intrafollicular mucin. A complete blood count showed 1.6% eosinophils (300/mm3) with a white blood cell count of 16,600/mm3. Serologic testing for HIV was negative.

An 82-year-old woman presented for a routine dental checkup in August 2020, reporting a slow-growing, painless swelling on her lower right gingiva that she first noticed several months earlier. She denied trauma to the area. Her dental status was poor, with tooth wear, discolorations, old resin fillings, and multiple missing teeth; periodontal exam showed slight attachment loss but no active periodontitis. Her medical history included resection of colorectal adenocarcinoma 5 years earlier, type II diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, and hypertension, all untreated. She had never used tobacco. 

On intraoral examination, there was a solitary, translucent, yellowish, firm nodule measuring 3 × 3 mm with a smooth, round surface and sessile base located on the attached gingiva between the lower right mandibular canine and first premolar. Pulp vitality testing of the adjacent teeth was normal. Panoramic and intraoral radiographs showed no osseous involvement. A provisional diagnosis of a cystic gingival lesion was made. The differential diagnosis included a fibroma, a retained foreign body, a lipoma, peripheral ameloblastoma, peripheral odontogenic keratocyst, and lateral periodontal cyst.

A 13-year-old girl was referred for persistent right periorbital and frontal headache with vomiting. One month earlier she had a mild SARS-CoV-2 infection. Two days after headache onset, she developed dizziness, right gaze diplopia, and right upper-eyelid edema without fever or other neurologic signs. Her past development was unremarkable. On day 2, neurologic examination showed limited adduction and elevation of the right eye, right ptosis, and a dilated pupil consistent with a right third-cranial-nerve palsy. Endocrine evaluation revealed weight 73.8 kg (> 97th centile), BMI 33.6 kg/m2, hepatic steatosis on abdominal ultrasound, LDL cholesterol 129 mg/dL, HDL cholesterol 31 mg/dL, and otherwise normal blood tests. Noncontrast head CT was normal. Brain MRI with TOF angiography demonstrated linear thickening of the right tentorial profile with intense contrast enhancement extending from its anterior insertion and thickening of the lateral wall of the right cavernous sinus. CT angiography confirmed abnormal vessel thickening in the same region. A comprehensive blood work-up for viral and bacterial agents, thyroid dysfunction, and antiganglioside antibodies, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis including antiganglioside antibodies, were unremarkable.

A 35-year-old man with a seven-month history of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis treated with daily oral prednisone presented with sudden bilateral loss of vision and periorbital swelling. He also reported fever and pedal edema.

On examination, visual acuity was light perception with inaccurate ray projection in both eyes. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy showed 2+ cells in the anterior chamber and pigment deposits on the anterior lens capsule bilaterally. Funduscopic examination revealed hazy media, inferotemporal retinal detachment, subretinal exudates, intraretinal hemorrhages, dilated veins, and narrowed arteries in both eyes. Intraocular pressures were 16 mmHg in each eye.

His blood pressure was 160/100 mmHg, and heart rate was slow. He was treated with systemic corticosteroids, furosemide, cefixime, and amlodipine. Two days later, he developed generalized hypotony, truncal ataxia, a staggering gait, buccal and proximal muscle weakness, and diminished plantar reflexes. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated multiple subcentimeter ring-enhancing lesions scattered throughout both cerebral hemispheres, suggestive of tuberculomas or neurocysticercosis.

A 41-year-old woman with inflammatory polyarthropathy and Crohn’s disease treated with infliximab (10 mg/kg every 8 weeks), methotrexate (15 mg weekly), and prednisone (5 mg daily) presented with a 6-month history of progressive pruritic and tender erythematous papules and pustules on the upper back. An initial punch biopsy was interpreted as suppurative granulomatous dermatitis. She received a 10-day course of clindamycin and a 7-day course of levofloxacin without improvement, and the plaques continued to expand. On evaluation at our institution, acne conglobata was suspected; she was started on isotretinoin for 1 month and her prednisone dose was increased to 40 mg daily. After 4 weeks, she developed extensive red papules coalescing into infiltrative plaques with scattered yellow crust across the upper back. A repeat punch biopsy revealed lichenoid and diffuse dermal granulomatous inflammation with numerous multinucleated giant cells; rare neutrophils but no frank abscess were seen. Special stains (Gomori methenamine silver, Fite, Ziehl-Neelsen, Giemsa, Twort Gram) and spirochete immunostaining were negative for microorganisms. Given her clinical history and histopathologic findings, a diagnosis of cutaneous Crohn’s disease was favored. She was started on oral metronidazole 500 mg three times daily, her prednisone dose was increased to 50 mg daily, and plans were made to transition from infliximab to upadacitinib.

A 21-year-old man presented with a painless nodular swelling on the left cheek of several months’ duration. The lesion measured approximately 1.5 cm in diameter and was palpable both under the skin and intraorally; it was not mobile on palpation. The overlying skin and oral mucosa appeared normal, and there was no regional lymphadenopathy. His medical history was unremarkable, and he denied any facial trauma or insect bites. Routine hematological examination revealed no abnormalities. A working differential diagnosis included an adenoma arising from minor salivary glands, a fibrosed or calcified lymph node, an inspissated submucosal abscess, and an infected sebaceous cyst. The decision was made to enucleate the lesion via an intraoral approach.

A 59‐year‐old woman presented with a single episode of acute rectal bleeding and no prior history of similar bleeding. Her medical history was notable only for essential hypertension. Surgical history included a total abdominal hysterectomy 20 years earlier for fibroids and a left oophorectomy for a large ovarian cyst. On examination, vital signs were stable and physical findings were unremarkable. A stool occult-blood test was positive.

Laboratory studies showed elevated tumor markers: CA 19-9 at 482 U/mL and CA 125 at 65 U/mL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 7 × 6 × 5 cm pelvic mass surrounding and invading the sigmoid colon. Pelvic MRI confirmed a similar‐appearing mass invading the sigmoid colon, but the site of origin (colonic vs. extra-colonic) remained uncertain.

Colonoscopy identified a 4 × 4 cm mass in the sigmoid colon with a heterogeneous contour. Multiple biopsy specimens demonstrated normal tissue with necrosis, and no conclusive origin could be determined. Given the concern for malignancy (colon cancer versus ovarian cancer), the patient underwent en bloc surgical resection. Intraoperatively, the mass was deep in the pelvis, grossly resembling ovarian tissue; an intraoperative frozen section of the mass was reported as a benign lesion of undetermined significance. A segmental sigmoidectomy with end colostomy was performed due to extensive inflammation and adhesions.

An 80-year-old woman was brought for evaluation of transient abnormal behavior. Computed tomography of the head showed a large low-density area involving the right temporal, parietal, and occipital lobes with mild midline shift. On admission, she had no focal neurologic deficits other than the prior behavioral changes. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a low-intensity area on T1-weighted images and a corresponding high-intensity area on T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery images, involving the cortex and white matter without gadolinium enhancement. T2*-weighted images revealed several low-signal intensity spots in the bilateral temporo-occipital regions, distinct from the main lesion. Initial impression was a low-grade glioma with associated vasogenic edema, and further imaging studies were planned. Over the next 6 days, the patient’s condition deteriorated to coma and left hemiplegia, and repeat MRI showed worsening edema without enhancement. She underwent emergent stereotactic-guided biopsy via a small occipital craniotomy. Intraoperative views revealed cortical swelling without obvious tumor. Rapid pathological examination showed no neoplastic cells.

A 56-year-old woman who has worked as a lettuce farmer for 36 years was admitted in May with a 2-week history of low-grade fever, worsening cough, and dyspnea on exertion. She reported similar episodes each May. A family physician treated her empirically with amikacin and azithromycin without improvement. She had no smoking history, no animal or chemical exposures aside from lettuce farming, and no history of wheezing or rhonchi.

On examination, temperature was 37.9°C and oxygen saturation was 91% on room air. There was no clubbing. Chest auscultation revealed bilateral inspiratory wheezes; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable. Arterial blood gas on room air showed pH 7.431, PaO2 65.4 mmHg, PaCO2 36.9 mmHg, and HCO3– 24.2 mmol/L. The leukocyte count was 7330/µL (eosinophils 9.8%); C-reactive protein was 3.55 mg/dL.

Chest radiography demonstrated ground-glass opacity in the right upper lobe. Computed tomography showed mild infiltrates, ground-glass opacities, and reticulo-nodular shadows in both upper lobes. Pulmonary function testing during the harvest season revealed a mixed obstructive and restrictive defect, which normalized off-season. Fractional exhaled nitric oxide was elevated at 42 ppb. Skin prick testing was positive for lettuce; specific IgE testing revealed multiple sensitivities (timothy grass, cedar pollen, cat, peanut, etc.), though lettuce-specific IgE was unavailable.

Bronchoalveolar lavage from the right upper lobe yielded 19.7×10^2 total cells/µL with 8.5% eosinophils; cultures were negative for bacteria and fungi.

A 65-year-old man from the central hill region of Sri Lanka presented on day 4 of illness with high fever, headache, arthralgia, myalgia, nausea, dry cough, chest pain, sore throat, watery diarrhea, and dark urine. He owned a small dairy farm and a pet dog. On examination, he was dehydrated; temperature 38°C; pulse 120/min; blood pressure 70/40 mmHg; few basal crepitations on the right lung; mild epigastric tenderness; no lymphadenopathy. A hematocrit was 48%. Abdominal ultrasound showed gallbladder wall edema and a small amount of free fluid. Laboratory tests on admission showed elevated liver transaminases, creatinine, and blood urea, with a neutrophil percentage above 90% and elevated CRP. ECG demonstrated T-wave inversions in leads V5 and V6 (later isolated to V5), and troponin I was elevated. Echocardiography revealed global hypokinesia with grade II aortic regurgitation and an ejection fraction of 30%; mitral and tricuspid regurgitations were also noted on re-evaluation. He was managed with intravenous fluids, dobutamine, furosemide infusions, methylprednisolone followed by prednisolone, ceftriaxone, and oseltamivir. Tests for dengue IgM and IgG and for influenza A and B viral RNA returned negative. He never developed jaundice, conjunctival suffusion was absent, and calf myalgia was minimal. Considering these findings, doxycycline was started on day 6 for suspected rickettsial infection.

A 12-year-old boy with a history of multiple fractures since age 3 months was evaluated. He was born at term, with an unremarkable family history. By 3 months of age, he had bone rickets and multiple skull and long-bone fractures, leading to a clinical diagnosis of osteogenesis imperfecta, subtype unspecified. At age 9, he underwent biopsy of a right humeral lesion. CT of the right humerus showed a medullary lesion suggestive of osteosarcoma; chest CT was negative for metastases. Whole-body bone scintigraphy revealed intense uptake in the right humerus, spine, maxilla, and sacrum, attributed to his bone disease. The right arm was amputated; histopathology of the resected lesion showed a malignant mesenchymal neoplasm composed of epithelioid cells with increased nuclear–cytoplasm ratio, anisocytosis, anisokaryosis, and prominent nucleoli, with tumor cells positive for vimentin and CD99.  

On examination at age 12, he was nonambulatory, had plagiocephaly, flat nasal bridge, gingival melanosis, and thick lips. Weight was 25.4 kg (1st percentile), height 106 cm (<1st percentile), head circumference 52 cm (11th percentile). There were no blue sclerae or hearing loss. Radiographs of the spine and extremities showed osteopenia, evidence of multiple prior fractures, diaphyseal bowing of long bones, beaded ribs, mild thoracolumbar scoliosis (Cobb angle 11°), and intramedullary rods in previously operated bones. Laboratory studies demonstrated normal serum calcium, phosphate, magnesium, parathyroid hormone, vitamin D, and lactate dehydrogenase; decreased urinary calcium; and elevated alkaline phosphatase. He receives vitamin D, intravenous zoledronic acid, growth hormone, and orthopedic care for deformity corrections.

A 59-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a progressively enlarging thoracic para-aortic mass. He had undergone noncontrast CT at an outside hospital, which revealed a 5-cm para-aortic mass in the right posterior mediastinum initially thought to be of venous origin because of its proximity to the azygos vein. The patient was asymptomatic, and the clinical examination was unremarkable.

Medical History: Hypertension, nasal skin cancer; prior Bentall procedure, resection of coronary artery ostial aneurysms, and aortoiliac bypass for aortic and bilateral iliac dissection.

The differential diagnosis of posterior mediastinal masses included neurogenic tumors, infectious spondylitis, meningocele, thoracic aortic aneurysm, aortic dissection, dilated azygos vein, esophageal varices or tumors, lymphoma, and lymphadenopathy.

Investigations: Time-resolved, cardiac MR angiography demonstrated a 5.5 × 4.5 cm, partially thrombosed mass to the right of the proximal descending thoracic aorta, connected by a narrow stalk at the level of the right bronchial artery origin. The mass exhibited arterial pulsation and, on venous-phase imaging, had no connection to the azygos vein. Cardiac-gated CTA confirmed an ectatic and tortuous right bronchial artery immediately cranial to the pseudoaneurysmal neck feeding right hilar bronchopulmonary collaterals.

A 23-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 2, presented with a severe, continuous frontal headache and neck stiffness immediately after a difficult epidural analgesia for vaginal delivery (four attempts). On postpartum day 1, an anesthesiology consultation led to an epidural blood patch despite headache lacking positional characteristics; the pain remained unchanged. Neurology evaluation the same day listed tension-type headache and post–dural puncture headache as leading differentials, and she was discharged after a modest pain reduction with conservative measures. Two days later, she was readmitted with a hypertensive emergency, severe frontal headache, and laboratory abnormalities including elevated lactate dehydrogenase, elevated uric acid, and proteinuria. She was diagnosed with postpartum preeclampsia and treated with 24 hours of magnesium sulfate. Her headache persisted despite antihypertensive therapy and multiple analgesics (Fioricet, Toradol, Compazine, Neurontin, caffeine, methylprednisolone), and neurologic examination remained intact. A noncontrast head CT showed possible sphenoid sinusitis, slight prominence of the pituitary gland, intraventricular air, and tentorial dural calcification. The headache improved after blood pressure control, and she was discharged. On postpartum day 10, she returned with worsening frontal headache, neck pain, and low-grade fever; her neurologic examination remained unchanged, and a CT venogram was requested.

A 37-year-old woman presented with 6 hours of acute hypogastric pain and nausea. She reported occasional postprandial abdominal discomfort but had no history of abdominal surgery, trauma, or chronic illness. On examination, there was localized tenderness in the right lower abdomen and hypogastrium with a positive McBurney’s sign and rebound tenderness; bowel sounds were normal and there was no distention. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 19,000/μL; other values were unremarkable. Initial differential diagnoses included acute appendicitis, gynecological disorders, and inflammatory bowel disease. An abdominal radiograph and pelvic ultrasonography were negative for gynecological pathology and were inconclusive for appendicitis. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis (axial, coronal, and sagittal reformats) demonstrated an abnormally low transverse colon and right colic flexure, with small-bowel loops clustered above and to the right. The third portion of the duodenum was not seen in its expected location. There was an abnormal superior mesenteric artery–vein relationship, with the vein coursing to the left of the artery. The clustered loops showed mesenteric congestion with prominent vessels but no signs of ischemia. The appendix appeared normal.

A 75-year-old man with a history of urothelial bladder carcinoma and stage IB cutaneous melanoma developed widespread metastatic melanoma in March 2018. He began pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks in April 2018. After 12 cycles, PET-CT showed partial remission of metastases but revealed new diffuse low-level uptake in the stomach wall, suggestive of inflammation. The patient was asymptomatic and was taking pantoprazole 20 mg/day for known GERD. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy demonstrated diffuse mucosal erythema without focal lesions. Gastric biopsies from the body and antrum showed moderate lymphoplasmacytic and neutrophilic infiltration of the lamina propria with cryptitis, crypt abscesses, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. Immunostaining revealed the infiltrate to be predominantly CD3+ T cells with CD8+ cells exceeding CD4+ cells. There was no histological or immunohistochemical evidence of Helicobacter pylori or cytomegalovirus infection.

A 32-year-old man with antiphospholipid syndrome, recurrent deep venous thromboses, and pulmonary emboli on warfarin and rituximab therapy presented with 1 day of progressive exertional dyspnea and blood-streaked sputum. He denied chest pain or purulent sputum. Three months earlier, he had elevated antiphospholipid and beta-2 glycoprotein antibodies, a positive p-ANCA, elevated ANA and ds-DNA antibodies, and was treated with rituximab, hydroxychloroquine, and warfarin. One month prior, echocardiography excluded significant cardiac disease. 

On examination, temperature was 37.1°C, heart rate 120 bpm, blood pressure 115/75 mmHg, and oxygen saturation was in the low 80s on room air, improving to the low 90s on 8 L/min oxygen. Lung auscultation revealed coarse bilateral inspiratory crackles greatest in the upper lobes; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Chest CT angiography showed right lower lobe segmental pulmonary emboli, upper-lobe–predominant diffuse ground-glass opacities, and bilateral centrilobular nodules. Laboratory studies revealed a normal CBC, electrolytes, and creatinine; INR 1.9; PaO2 69.3 mmHg on oxygen; ESR 64 mm/h; CRP 54.5 mg/L; negative ANA, ds-DNA, c-ANCA, p-ANCA, MPO, PR3, and anti-GBM antibodies; persistently elevated antiphospholipid and beta-2 glycoprotein antibodies; and urinalysis with 1+ protein but no cells or casts.

A bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage was performed, and the fluid became progressively more hemorrhagic on serial aliquots. Prussian blue staining revealed hemosiderin-laden macrophages; gram stain, culture, and viral PCR were negative.

A previously healthy 16-year-old male returned from a three-week volunteer trip to Ghana in June and July 2013 without taking malaria prophylaxis. Ten days after his return, he presented with a four-day history of fever, chills, headache, nausea, and vomiting. A blood smear was positive for malaria parasites, later identified as Plasmodium falciparum with a parasitaemia of 2.5%. A rapid diagnostic test detected P. falciparum–specific histidine-rich protein-2, while a Plasmodium genus aldolase assay was negative. On transfer to our hospital, he was hypotensive with elevated liver enzymes (ALT 134 U/L; AST 106 U/L; GGT 55 U/L) and thrombocytopenia (platelets 19 × 10^9/L). A pre‐treatment smear showed 2.4% P. falciparum parasitaemia. He received a three-day course of intravenous artesunate and oral atovaquone/proguanil. By day 5 he was afebrile, his laboratory values were improving, and repeat smears were negative, although HRP-2 remained detectable. He was discharged and was asymptomatic with a negative smear at one week follow-up.

One month later he returned with a two-day history of headache, nausea, and vomiting but no fever. A blood smear demonstrated malaria parasites at <0.1% parasitaemia; all other laboratory results were within normal limits. It was initially presumed that he had a recrudescence of P. falciparum malaria. Three consecutive daily smears were sent for species identification while he was treated with another three-day course of oral atovaquone/proguanil. His symptoms were mild and resolved quickly, and he was discharged within 48 hours.

A 61-year-old man presented with a 3-week history of cough productive of mucopurulent sputum with blood streaking and a 1-week history of intermittent low-grade fever. He denied dyspnea, chest pain, or aspiration. He had no history of diabetes, underlying lung disease, or tuberculosis exposure and no significant travel or animal exposures. Twenty months earlier, he had undergone esophagogastrectomy and adjuvant chemoradiotherapy for esophageal adenocarcinoma, with surveillance imaging at 6 months showing no recurrence. Twelve months after surgery, he developed altered sensorium; brain MRI showed multiple ring-enhancing lesions with mass effect and perilesional edema in the right frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes, presumed to be metastases. He was treated with dexamethasone, levetiracetam, and cranial irradiation.

Two weeks later, he developed fever, cough, and hemoptysis and was referred to our clinic. On examination, he was febrile, pale, emaciated, and had digital clubbing. He was confused but had no focal neurologic deficits. Chest auscultation revealed bilateral scattered wheezes. A chest radiograph showed a cavitary lesion in the left upper zone, a nodular opacity in the right midzone, and a left pleural effusion. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 9500/μL with 95% neutrophils, hemoglobin of 10 g/dL, and a C-reactive protein level of 360 mg/L. HIV testing was negative.

Sputum was sent for acid-fast bacilli smear, Gram stain and culture, Xpert MTB/RIF testing, and fungal stain. The patient was started on intravenous amoxicillin–clavulanate. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a thick-walled cavitary lesion in the left upper lobe, left pleural effusion, and multiple bilateral nodules, some cavitating—findings thought to be consistent with multiple pulmonary metastases or a second primary lung malignancy. After the sputum AFB smear was reported as negative, antibiotics were escalated to piperacillin–tazobactam and levofloxacin. In view of persistent fever in an immunocompromised patient with pulmonary and intracranial lesions, the differential diagnoses included tuberculosis, bacterial pneumonia with possible brain abscess, metastatic malignancy with secondary infection, invasive fungal infection, and other uncommon infections.

Despite broad-spectrum antibiotics, he continued to have fevers. A flexible bronchoscopy was performed, and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was sent for Gram stain, bacterial and fungal cultures, Xpert MTB/RIF testing, AFB smear and culture, and periodic acid–Schiff staining; all results were negative, and no malignant cells were identified.

A 2-year-1-month-old Japanese boy was referred after dental trauma to his maxillary primary incisors. His history included atopic dermatitis, and his siblings had congenitally missing incisors. On initial intraoral examination, the maxillary right primary central incisor was displaced palatally and the left primary central incisor was extruded, but periapical radiographs showed no fractures. The traumatized tooth was splinted for 1 month, and he was followed serially. By age 6 years 5 months, mild pulp‐chamber narrowing and external root resorption were noted, but no other abnormalities were seen. Permanent central incisors erupted by age 7 years 10 months. 

At age 8 years 10 months, panoramic radiography showed that the maxillary right lateral incisor was twisted in the alveolar bone and its eruption was delayed relative to the left. The tooth erupted spontaneously by age 9 years 6 months. At age 10 years 10 months, panoramic imaging revealed a radiolucent line on the palatal side of the erupted maxillary right lateral incisor. At 11 years 3 months, intraoral examination identified a talon‐cusp‐like calcified projection on the palatal surface. Three months later, the projection was more pronounced on periapical radiography, and further evaluation with cone‐beam computed tomography (CBCT) was undertaken for definitive diagnosis.

A 41-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a 6-month history of erosions and crusts on her lower lip accompanied by pain and a burning sensation. Despite multiple topical therapies, the lesions persisted without improvement. On examination, there were crusted erosions confined to the lower lip; no lesions were observed on the skin or other mucosal surfaces. Initial laboratory tests were unremarkable. Our initial differential diagnosis included actinic cheilitis and erosive lichen planus. A biopsy was performed to establish a definitive diagnosis.

A 54-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of diffuse intermittent colicky abdominal pain, constipation, and involuntary weight loss of 10% of her body weight. She had no prior surgeries, no known diseases, was postmenopausal, and had never used an intrauterine device. On examination, her abdomen was distended with a palpable stiff mass filling the right lower quadrant and extending to the umbilicus; there was no guarding or rebound. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 8300 per cubic millimeter, a C-reactive protein level of 3.2 mg per liter, and a hemoglobin level of 10.1 g per deciliter. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen revealed a redundant sigmoid colon extending to the level of the umbilicus, with a mass lesion invading its entire length, extension into the mesocolon and mesenteric root, and enlarged lymph nodes. Colonoscopic examination demonstrated stenosis of the sigmoid colon that prevented passage of the colonoscope, without visualization of an intraluminal lesion.

A 20-year-old man with a history of psychomotor delay and epilepsy presented with 3 days of abdominal distension, rigidity, diffuse pain, obstipation, and vomiting, beginning 3 days after a perineal perforating injury. On arrival: blood pressure 104/58 mmHg, heart rate 138/min, respiratory rate 20/min, temperature 36.2 °C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Examination showed rebound tenderness, decreased bowel sounds, diffuse abdominal pain, and a rectal ampulla filled with stool; the anal sphincter was tonically competent. He had a Frankel grade B spinal cord lesion at L2–L3. Initial labs: hemoglobin 16 g/dL, white blood cell count 3250/mm3, urea 25 mg/dL, creatinine 6.9 mg/dL, electrolytes normal. No imaging was available. The patient became hemodynamically unstable (blood pressure 90/50 mmHg, heart rate 148/min, oxygen saturation 94%) and was taken to the operating room.

A 53-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of scrotal redness, burning sensation, and pain. He had previously been diagnosed elsewhere with contact dermatitis and had used topical hydrocortisone and other unspecified creams for 2 months, which he discontinued at presentation. He denied pruritus. On examination, there was sharply demarcated, bright-red erythema confined to the scrotum without scaling, excoriations, or involvement of adjacent skin. Wood’s lamp examination was unremarkable. A potassium hydroxide preparation and fungal culture from the area were negative.

A 27-year-old man was evaluated for recurrent pulmonary infections and possible immunodeficiency. Since June 2017 he had recurrent pneumonias and a 1½-year history of productive cough with green sputum. He also reported intermittent headaches, sinus congestion, rhinorrhea, intermittent diarrhea, fatigue, and anosmia but denied fever, chills, or night sweats. At disease onset he lost 10–11 pounds. Family history was notable for a brother with thrombocytopenia who died of a brain aneurysm.

In 2017, platelet counts ranged from 91 to 108 × 10^9/L; other CBC parameters, metabolic panel, and urinalysis were normal. Over the next year, quantitative immunoglobulins were IgG 256–308 mg/dL (reference 700–1600), IgM 9–25 (40–230), and IgA 23–33 (70–400). CT of the chest and abdomen revealed mediastinal and upper abdominal lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and multiple pulmonary nodules. Pulmonary function tests showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 59% with a normal vital capacity and moderate diffusion impairment. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and endobronchial lymph node biopsies was negative for bacterial, fungal, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, and no malignancy was identified.

He was treated with inhaled fluticasone, umeclidinium, and vilanterol, improving the FEV1/FVC ratio to 85%. After a positive serum aspergillus galactomannan assay, he received isavuconazonium sulfate for 5 weeks but discontinued it due to elevated liver enzymes, nausea, and vomiting. A repeat CT in December 2018 showed progression of multifocal pulmonary nodules with persistent mediastinal lymphadenopathy. In January 2019, video-assisted thoracoscopic surgical biopsy of the right lower lobe was performed. Histologic examination showed lymphoid hyperplasia with interstitial fibrosis, patchy foci of organizing pneumonia, rare giant cells and histiocytes, acute bronchopneumonia, and occasional fibrin exudates.

A 7-year-old previously healthy boy was seen in the outpatient clinic for evaluation of a painless lump on the right side of his neck that he and his parents first noticed 3 days earlier when he coughed. There were no accompanying symptoms of fever, upper respiratory infection, dyspnea, dysphagia, dysphonia, or facial swelling. He had no history of trauma, surgery, or relevant family history.

On examination, his growth parameters were normal. A 3 × 3 cm, nontender, fusiform swelling was visible anterior to the right sternocleidomastoid muscle and extended toward the anterior triangle of the neck and clavicle, appearing only during coughing. There was no palpable thrill or audible bruit over the swelling. No cervical lymphadenopathy was present, and the oropharyngeal and systemic examinations were unremarkable.

Ultrasonography of the neck demonstrated fusiform dilatation of the lower segment of the right internal jugular vein, with a resting diameter of 2.5 cm, increasing to 3.1 cm during coughing. Doppler imaging revealed turbulence within the vein without any evidence of thrombosis. Magnetic resonance imaging of the neck confirmed fusiform dilatation of the lower segment of the right internal jugular vein, which enlarged further during Valsalva maneuver.

A 61-year-old woman presented with a rapidly worsening soft-tissue infection of her left buttock extending to her posterior thigh. She had been previously healthy with no regular medications. Two years earlier, excision of a chronic left perineal sinus had led to CT and colonoscopy findings of asymptomatic sigmoid diverticulosis. One year ago, evaluation of a left maxillary sinus mass—which radiographically suggested granulomatosis with polyangiitis—revealed only osteomyelitis on pathology. Repeat CT at that time showed new left hydronephrosis with inflammatory changes consistent with chronic sigmoid diverticulitis; colorectal carcinoma was excluded by colonoscopy, and a ureteric stent was placed. The patient elected conservative management for her diverticulitis.

Four weeks before the current presentation, she developed a blistering rash over her left buttock and gluteal fold, treated for 10 days with acyclovir for shingles with good response. Three days before presentation, she experienced a new painful induration over her left buttock, diagnosed as an early abscess and prescribed amoxicillin–clavulanate. On the day of presentation, the induration had enlarged, with 1 day of serous discharge and chills. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 22,200/mm3 and a creatinine level of 191 μmol/L. Noncontrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with free air tracking inferiorly into the left pelvis with a 5.5 × 3.3-cm abscess, and extensive gas throughout the left buttock tracking posteriorly along the hamstring muscles to the popliteal fossa.

A 58-year-old woman of North African origin with morbid obesity (BMI 37.5) and erosive seropositive rheumatoid arthritis (RA) presented with a 1-month history of polyarthritis involving the right second and third metacarpophalangeal joints, wrists, elbows, and right knee. She had been treated with methotrexate until 2015 without efficacy and maintained on leflunomide 20 mg daily since 2015 with satisfactory control. Comorbidities included sleep apnea and hypertension on perindopril and amlodipine.

On examination, she was afebrile, with 9 of 28 tender joints and 6 of 28 swollen joints. Left knee aspiration yielded 15 mL of citrine yellow inflammatory fluid; synovial fluid analysis showed 32 000 cells/µL (93% neutrophils) with no organisms on culture. Laboratory studies revealed C-reactive protein 259 mg/L, leukocytes 10 046/µL (66.1% neutrophils), and hemoglobin 8.8 g/dL. Blood cultures, COVID-19 PCR, and urine analysis were negative. Bronchoscopy was normal, and bronchoalveolar lavage was non-diagnostic. An interferon-gamma release assay was negative.

A thoracic CT scan showed three cavitary nodules measuring 13 mm, 10 mm, and 6 mm: two in the right lower lobe (one subpleural) and one in the left lower lobe. PET scanning demonstrated hypermetabolism of all nodules. CT-guided aspiration of the right middle lobe subpleural nodule was performed; direct search for bacteria and fungi was negative, aerobic and anaerobic cultures showed no growth, and cytology revealed no malignant cells.

A 61-year-old man presented with general discomfort and multiple episodes of melena over the previous 24 hours. His history included hypertension treated with amlodipine, prior major trauma with diaphragmatic laceration repaired via laparotomy, and deep venous thrombosis on warfarin. He had no prior gastrointestinal disorders. On examination, his abdomen was diffusely tender without masses or peritoneal signs. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 8.8 g/dL, hematocrit 27.2%, and INR 3.00. Anticoagulation was switched to low–molecular-weight heparin, and he received two units of packed red blood cells, raising hemoglobin to 10.5 g/dL.

Diagnostic upper endoscopy revealed a 25 mm submucosal lesion on the posterior wall of the antrum with a 4 mm superficial ulcer, and thickened gastric body folds. Biopsies of the lesion showed foveolar hyperplasia without Helicobacter pylori. Contrast-enhanced CT scan confirmed a 50 × 20 mm irregular antral lesion without metastases. Radial EUS showed a 5.0 × 2.8 cm heterogeneous submucosal mass penetrating the muscularis propria without subserosal involvement. On contrast-enhanced EUS, the lesion’s septa were hyperechoic while its cavities remained anechoic. Fine-needle biopsy with a 22-gauge needle was non-diagnostic. Despite the inconclusive biopsy, the endoscopic, radiological, and EUS findings were felt to be indicative of a gastrointestinal stromal tumor.

A 67‐year‐old man with hyperlipidemia, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and Gleason 3+4=7 prostate cancer underwent transrectal ultrasound–guided brachytherapy with 104 seeds delivering 125 Gy. One month later he developed intractable burning pain of the penis and scrotum during urination, preventing complete voiding. His International Prostate Symptom Score was 35/35, urinary bother score 6/6, and pain 10/10 at its worst; pain worsened on sitting. There were no sensory or motor deficits on examination. Cystoscopy showed a normal urethra and bladder. Trials of intrarectal diazepam, oral amitriptyline, pelvic‐floor physical therapy, tadalafil, and acupuncture were ineffective for pain control; morphine reduced his pain from 10/10 to 8.5/10, and diazepam plus amitriptyline eased urination. High‐resolution 3 Tesla magnetic resonance neurography with metal artifact reduction revealed brachytherapy seeds in close proximity to the right and left pudendal nerves, raising the possibility of radiation‐induced pudendal nerve injury.

A 75-year-old man with high myopia and primary open-angle glaucoma in the right eye presented three weeks after an uncomplicated deep sclerectomy. He had undergone pars plana vitrectomy 10 months earlier for an epiretinal membrane, achieving a visual acuity of 0.4 on the Snellen chart (5 m). Preoperative axial length was 25.86 mm and pachymetry 550 μm. The deep sclerectomy included placement of an intrascleral hydroxyethyl methacrylate implant and intraoperative mitomycin-C (0.02% for 1 minute). His preoperative IOP was 24 mm Hg on maximal medical therapy. Postoperative IOP measurements were 4 mm Hg at 24 hours, 12 mm Hg at one week, and 10 mm Hg at three weeks. At the three-week visit he reported decreased vision with visual acuity reduced to 0.15. Fundoscopic examination revealed multiple small, round intraretinal and preretinal hemorrhages in the posterior pole involving the optic disc. Optical coherence tomography confirmed macular edema. No choroidal folds, retinal striae, optic disc swelling, or retinal vessel tortuosity were observed, ruling out a retinal venous occlusion.

A 44-year-old Caucasian man noted sudden onset of a blurred central circle in his left eye while skiing at 1,800 m. He reported recent sun exposure while using a laptop on a balcony without sunglasses and denied systemic symptoms. He was otherwise healthy, with no medical or recreational drug use and no recent vaccinations. One week later, visual acuity was 85 EDTRS letters in the right eye and 45 EDTRS letters in the left. Fundus examination of the left eye showed a pale circular area surrounding the fovea. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated submacular fluid, an area of increased hyperreflectivity of the subfoveal retinal pigment epithelium corresponding to loss of the ellipsoid and interdigitation zones in the detached macula, thickening and hyperreflectivity of the detached ellipsoid, interdigitation, and outer plexiform layers, and thinning of the outer nuclear layer. The right eye was unaffected, and there were no inflammatory cells in either chamber. An initial diagnosis of central serous chorioretinopathy was made, and follow-up was arranged for four months later.

At the four-month follow-up, the patient’s symptoms and visual acuity were unchanged. Fundus examination showed a fine hypopigmented dot at the fovea. OCT revealed resolution of the submacular fluid with reduced thickness of the ellipsoid, interdigitation, and outer plexiform layers but persistent subfoveal loss of the ellipsoid and interdigitation zones and thinning of the outer nuclear layer.

A 38-year-old woman presented with a more than 10-year history of pruritic papular lesions on her face, neck, and upper trunk and more recently noted similar lesions on her genitalia. She had no relevant family history and was otherwise healthy.

Examination revealed multiple tan to brown papules on the face, neck, and upper trunk resembling seborrhoeic keratoses. On the labia majora, there were numerous small (1–5 mm), round, dark-brown macules with a smooth surface in a symmetric distribution; these were asymptomatic.

Punch biopsies were obtained from one neck papule and one labial macule. Histologic examination of the neck lesion showed acanthosis, hyperkeratosis, and papillomatosis. Histologic examination of the genital macule showed branching elongation of the rete ridges with basal hyperpigmentation and no atypical keratinocytes or melanocytes.

A 27-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of worsening breathlessness and cough. He was conscious, well oriented, with a respiratory rate of 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation of 93% on room air, corresponding to New York Heart Association class IV symptoms. Routine blood tests showed mild relative neutrophilia and polycythemia. He had a history of recurrent respiratory tract infections since childhood.

A frontal chest radiograph revealed gross cardiomegaly with prominent pulmonary vascular markings bilaterally. A 2D echocardiogram demonstrated global hypokinesia, dilated cardiac chambers, a D-shaped left ventricle, severe ventricular dysfunction (ejection fraction 30%), and a grossly enlarged main pulmonary artery. The left ventricular internal dimensions were 6.4 cm in diastole and 4.4 cm in systole; interventricular septal thickness at end-diastole was 1.43 cm.

Contrast-enhanced CT pulmonary angiography confirmed marked dilation of the main pulmonary artery (approximately 40.5 mm) and its branches, without evidence of intraluminal thrombus or embolism. An anomalous vascular connection measuring about 2.2 cm between the main pulmonary artery and the distal aortic arch was identified, with contrast shunting into the descending aorta during the arterial phase. Abdominal ultrasound and CT demonstrated absence of the right kidney with compensatory hypertrophy of the left kidney. Incidentally, CT also revealed scoliosis with multiple thoracic hemivertebrae and fusion of the right third and fourth ribs posteriorly. Evaluation for anorectal malformations, tracheoesophageal fistula, and limb anomalies showed no abnormalities.

A 58-year-old woman was referred for a 6-month history of progressive hoarseness and dysphagia, associated with a 20-lb weight loss. Over the preceding year, she had right hand and lower limb pain and weakness; she was diagnosed with carpal tunnel syndrome and C6, C7, and L5 radiculopathies. Four months before presentation, she had right middle lobe pneumonia treated with antibiotics. A thoracic CT scan at that time showed right middle lobe consolidation, atelectasis, and mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy; bronchoalveolar lavage, brush biopsies, and endobronchial biopsies were negative for malignancy, and her vocal cords were documented as normal. A follow-up CT demonstrated moderate resolution of the pneumonia.

Her history included a 40–pack-year smoking history and COPD, with no prior head or neck surgery. On examination, she appeared cachectic with audible inspiratory stridor and increased work of breathing. Flexible nasolaryngoscopy revealed bilateral vocal cord paralysis. There was no palpable neck mass, and the remainder of the cranial nerve and head and neck examinations were normal. After tracheostomy, a CT scan from the skull base to the aortic arch showed no lesion along the course of either vagus nerve. A modified barium swallow demonstrated mild oral and moderate pharyngeal dysphagia with frank aspiration, and enteral feeding was initiated.

A 48-year-old man presented with a mild swelling on the left side of his cheek. He was afebrile and in no distress. On extraoral examination, there was a mild, tender swelling at the angle of the mandible. Intraoral examination revealed buccal vestibular obliteration in the left retromolar region and a grossly decayed left mandibular third molar (tooth #38) that was tender on percussion. He was treated with a 5-day course of antibiotics, and the decayed tooth was extracted atraumatically under local anesthesia; the socket healed uneventfully. Two months later, he returned with a gradual increase in the extraoral swelling and mild trismus, with a maximum mouth opening of 23 mm. Examination showed a 2 × 3 cm solitary, firm, nonpulsatile, nonfluctuant mass extending from the midbody of the mandible to the angle and ramus, fixed to underlying structures, with mild tenderness and normal overlying skin. Contrast-enhanced CT of the left face revealed a cystic lesion in the masseteric space involving the ramus of the mandible, with lytic and sclerotic areas; an impression of osteomyelitis with a submasseteric abscess was suggested. Routine blood tests were normal except for an elevated ESR of 40 mm/hr; HIV and HBsAg tests were negative. An intraoral open incisional biopsy of the masseteric region was performed under general anesthesia, and two tissue specimens were sent for histopathological examination.

An 81-year-old Japanese woman with an 11-year history of hepatitis C virus seropositivity and known Helicobacter pylori infection (serum H. pylori IgG positive, no eradication therapy) presented with abdominal discomfort. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a flat elevated lesion measuring approximately 2 cm in diameter on the anterior wall of the mid-stomach. A single biopsy of the lesion showed numerous cells with abundant eosinophilic crystalline cytoplasm and eccentric nuclei infiltrating the lamina propria; gastric glandular structures were well preserved, and lymphoepithelial lesions were absent. Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated that the infiltrating cells expressed CD79a and faintly CD20, while the cytoplasmic crystals were positive for IgA; staining for cytokeratin AE1/AE3 was negative. In situ hybridization revealed no kappa or lambda light-chain restriction of immunoglobulin, and both the gastric epithelium and infiltrating cells were negative for EBV-encoded RNA (EBER).

A 20-year-old man presented with a gradually enlarging mass in the right parotid region of one year’s duration. He denied pain, fever, night sweats, weight loss, respiratory symptoms, or any history of tuberculosis. Examination revealed a mobile, non-tender 3-cm mass in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland without overlying skin changes or cervical lymphadenopathy. Facial nerve function was intact. Complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and biochemical studies were within normal limits. A chest radiograph showed no abnormalities. Ultrasonography demonstrated a well-defined hypoechoic solid lesion in the superficial parotid lobe. Fine-needle aspiration cytology was nondiagnostic. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 16 × 21 × 30 mm mass in the posterior superficial lobe that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed homogeneous contrast enhancement.

A 71-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with 5 months of pelvic pain without fever, trauma, or systemic symptoms. She also reported constipation and difficulty with defecation. Laboratory evaluation revealed a normal white-cell count and a negative C-reactive protein test. Pelvic radiography showed heterogeneous osteolysis of the coccyx. Pelvic CT identified an expansive, poorly defined osteolytic lesion of the sacrum extending into the right gluteus maximus and medius muscles. MRI demonstrated an aggressive sacrococcygeal mass infiltrating the right gluteus maximus. These findings suggested a primary or metastatic malignant tumour, prompting a staging work-up including thoracoabdominal CT, cervical ultrasound, mammography, cervical spine radiography, bone scan, gynecological evaluation, and tuberculosis testing, all of which were negative.

A 44-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus and disseminated tuberculosis, including tuberculous meningoencephalitis, was readmitted 80 days after initiation of anti-TB therapy and 4 weeks after her last intravenous cyclophosphamide infusion for lupus nephritis. She had a 2-week history of progressive postural instability, diplopia, inattention, vertical gaze palsy, and myoclonic jerks. Vital signs were stable. Neurologic examination confirmed vertical gaze palsy, dysmetria, and profound inattention but no focal motor weakness. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed mild hyperproteinorrachia (68 mg/dL) without pleocytosis. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed:
• A T1-hyperintense, T2/FLAIR-hypointense lesion in the left lateral sulcus at the frontotemporal junction, with perilesional vasogenic edema and ring contrast enhancement abutting the middle cerebral artery at the M1–M2 transition  
• Smaller contrast-enhancing lesions adjacent to the left cavernous sinus and in the right lateral sulcus  
• Contrast enhancement of the left oculomotor nerve in its cisternal segment  
• Bilateral thalamic ischemic lesions

A 53-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of vague, generalized abdominal pain, bloating, and several episodes of bloody-mucous rectal discharge accompanied by changes in bowel habits. Her medical history was unremarkable; she had never used an intrauterine device and was postmenopausal for 5 years. She was afebrile, and vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed mild generalized abdominal tenderness without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies showed mild normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL, MCV 82 fL), a normal C-reactive protein level, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 13 mm/hr. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography were unremarkable. Colonoscopy demonstrated a polypoid, mass-like lesion with surrounding necrotic material in the distal sigmoid colon, located 20 cm from the anal verge. Multiple biopsies were obtained for histopathological examination.

A 4-year-old African-American girl presented with a several-day history of cough, nasal congestion, intermittent fever, severe intermittent abdominal pain, and bloody stools. Her medical history included sickle cell disease, ulcerative colitis, and autoimmune hepatitis, treated with hydroxyurea, mesalamine, and azathioprine. On examination, she had clusters of 2–7 mm hemorrhagic vesicles on her palms, knees, and soles, and a tender, swollen right knee. Laboratory evaluation showed a C-reactive protein level of 31.1 mg/dL, leukocytosis (25.5 × 10^3 cells/µL), and anemia (hemoglobin 6.6 g/dL, hematocrit 18.7%). Bacterial and viral cultures of vesicle fluid were negative. Four months earlier, she had a similar episode attributed to a sickle cell crisis versus a flare of ulcerative colitis; biopsy at that time revealed a neutrophilic panniculitis. During the current admission, a repeat skin biopsy showed subcorneal and subepidermal edema and a dense acute neutrophilic infiltrate extending into adipose tissue and septa. Direct immunofluorescence of the lesion was negative.

A 35-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of an asymptomatic, grey-brown nodule on the left cheek. The lesion began as a pinpoint papule and gradually enlarged to 2.5 cm × 1.5 cm. Two years later, similar lesions appeared on the forehead, both arms, and upper back. She denied photosensitivity, fever, joint pain, or systemic symptoms. Her past medical history was unremarkable.

On examination, multiple well-defined, grey-brown, indurated plaques measuring 0.5 cm × 0.5 cm to 1.5 cm × 2.5 cm were present on the left cheek, left forehead, both arms, and upper back. The surface of the plaques showed prominent follicular openings, telangiectasia, and peri-lesional erythema. Macular amyloidosis was also noted on the upper back.

Routine hematological and biochemical investigations were within normal limits.

A 67-year-old man presented with a two-week history of debilitating low cervical and upper dorsal pain associated with fever and asthenia. He described the pain as severe, throbbing, and occurring in brief, spontaneously remitting crises with an inflammatory pattern. He had no other symptoms and no focal signs of infection. His history included morbid obesity; paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (on digoxin, a β-blocker, and warfarin); and type 2 diabetes mellitus controlled with glimepiride (blood glucose 162 mg/dL, HbA1c 6.8%). 

On examination, he was afebrile. He had cervical stiffness and pain on flexion, with exquisite tenderness over C7–T1. Neurologic and cardiac examinations were normal. Laboratory studies showed an elevated CRP of 306 mg/L (normal < 5 mg/L) and an ESR of 68 mm at 1 hour (normal < 21 mm). Complete blood count and liver and renal function tests were normal. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. 

Spinal radiographs demonstrated diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis with dorsal pseudoankylosis; no obvious disc calcification was seen. MRI of the cervical–thoracic spine revealed inflammatory changes of the C7 and T1 vertebral bodies with T2 hyperintensity, T1 hypointensity, and marked gadolinium enhancement; the C7–T1 disc showed neither T2 hypersignal nor enhancement. CT of the spine showed erosions of the anterior lower endplate of C7 and upper endplate of T1 with a calcified focus at the anterior C7–T1 disc space, as well as calcifications in adjacent dorsal disc spaces. 

Transthoracic echocardiography showed no evidence of endocarditis. Urine and blood cultures were negative, and serologies for Wright (Brucella), Bartonella, Q fever, hepatitis B and C, and HIV were negative. Three additional blood-culture sets remained negative. Radiographs of the knees, wrists, shoulders, and pelvis showed no calcium pyrophosphate deposition. A disco-vertebral biopsy was planned but delayed because of anticoagulation with warfarin.

A 15-year-old Caucasian girl experienced sudden onset of severe neck pain during class, radiating to her left arm and right upper arm. She denied trauma or recent illness. On examination, she was alert, with tenderness over both trapezius muscles (left > right). Strength was 4/5 in the left arm and 5/5 in the right arm, and movement was limited by pain. There was hypoesthesia in the left C4–C5 dermatomes and asymmetric tendon reflexes (left > right). She had no family history of vascular anomalies. Routine laboratory studies were unremarkable. MRI of the cervical and thoracolumbar spine revealed diffuse spinal cord edema from C2 to T4, with imaging characteristics suggestive of either an arteriovenous malformation or a hemangioblastoma.

A 35-year-old morbidly obese woman (BMI 45.5 kg/m2) presented with a 7-month history of umbilical bleeding that occurred in a cyclical pattern, beginning 2 days before and continuing throughout her menses. She denied umbilical pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, infertility, or any prior diagnosis of endometriosis. Her surgical history was notable for two lower-segment cesarean deliveries via Pfannenstiel incisions. Laboratory studies revealed iron-deficiency anemia (hemoglobin, 11.4 g/dL); other blood work was unremarkable. Physical examination was limited by her body habitus, making assessment of an umbilical mass or hernia challenging. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 1.9 × 1.67 mm subcutaneous umbilical nodule with an underlying umbilical hernia.

A 67‐year‐old man presented with an 18‐hour history of chest pain that was worsened by exertion. On arrival, heart rate was 70 beats/min and blood pressure was 120/80 mm Hg. The initial electrocardiogram showed ST‐segment elevation in leads V2, V3, and aVF. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated hypokinesis of the basal septal and inferior walls with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 49% and no pericardial or pleural fluid.

His history was notable only for heavy smoking. The initial differential diagnosis included acute myocardial infarction and acute aortic dissection with coronary extension. The patient underwent emergent coronary angiography, which revealed acute total occlusion of the right coronary artery (RCA) and 90% proximal stenosis of the left anterior descending artery (LAD). A 3.5 × 48‐mm drug‐eluting stent was deployed in the RCA via right radial access, restoring flow without immediate complications.

Thirty minutes postprocedure, he developed severe chest pain refractory to medical therapy; he remained hemodynamically stable and the electrocardiogram was unchanged. Repeat angiography showed contrast extravasation from the distal RCA suggestive of vessel perforation, and echocardiography revealed a small amount of pericardial fluid. Two coils were deployed to embolize the perforated branch, with an acceptable angiographic result.

One hour later, he again complained of unremitting chest pain. Potential causes considered included aortic dissection, acute branch occlusion, and in‐stent thrombosis; tamponade was excluded due to minimal pericardial fluid. On a third angiography, coil embolization was unsuccessful and Spongel was injected. Aortic angiography was normal. During repositioning of the imaging equipment, a massive left pleural effusion was noted, severely compressing the lung; the radiopacity of the pleural fluid matched that of the contrast material at the perforation site.

A 46-year-old Japanese woman with a history of endometriosis and uterine myomas presented with lower abdominal pain. Physical examination and transvaginal sonography were unremarkable, and she was treated with analgesics. One week later, her pain resolved but she developed hematochezia and was admitted. 

Lower gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a submucosal tumor–like elevation with a stricture extending from the rectum to the sigmoid colon; the scope passed with resistance. The lesion was covered by dilated short vessels without surface irregularity and showed granular, cobblestone changes in the stenotic area. These macroscopic findings suggested type 4 colorectal cancer involving three-fourths of the wall. 

The first biopsy of the granular nodules, performed without regard to the menstrual cycle, yielded a diagnosis of lymphoid cell infiltration, possibly mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue; none of three specimens showed endometriosis. Tumor markers were as follows: carcinoembryonic antigen 2.8 ng/mL, cancer antigen 19-9 undetectable, and cancer antigen 125 94.2 U/mL. 

A second colonoscopy and biopsy during the intermenstrual period demonstrated similar endoscopic findings. Six specimens were obtained; pathology showed chronic colitis without malignancy, and no endometriotic features were seen. The patient noted that her bleeding coincided with her menstrual cycle and agreed to undergo endoscopy during menstruation.

A 44-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with sudden visual impairment and left-sided weakness. On examination, her blood pressure was 25 mm Hg lower in the right arm than the left, and the right ulnar and radial pulses were absent. Non-contrast CT of the brain showed a hypodense area in the right posterior temporal and occipital lobes, consistent with posterior cerebral artery ischemia. MR angiography of the brain revealed occlusion of the basilar artery and right posterior cerebral artery; MR venography was unremarkable. Cervical MRA demonstrated lesions at the origin of the right vertebral artery. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 13,000 /µL, hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL, ESR 105 mm/h, CRP 31 mg/L, AST 153 U/L, ALT 213 U/L, total bilirubin 2.4 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 1.3 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 3696 IU/L, gamma-glutamyltransferase 1244 IU/L; ANA, anti-dsDNA, APS antibody, P-ANCA, and C-ANCA were negative.

A 33-year-old woman with a spontaneous twin pregnancy underwent an uncomplicated cesarean delivery. Two days postpartum, she developed high fever (up to 42 °C) with chills. Blood pressure was 90/50 mm Hg and pulse 110 bpm. On examination, she had right lower quadrant abdominal pain with rebound tenderness. She reported similar right lower abdominal pain at 22 weeks’ gestation, but no imaging had been performed.

She was transferred one week later with the following laboratory results: hemoglobin 8 g/dL (12–15 g/dL), lipase 128 U/L (13–60 U/L), amylase 183 U/L (20–100 U/L), platelets 150,000/mm³ (150,000–450,000/mm³), prothrombin time ratio 5.06 (0.8–1.2), partial thromboplastin time ratio 2.21 (0.8–1.2), fibrinogen 866 mg/dL (200–400 mg/dL), antithrombin III 81% (80–120%), and D-dimer 3376 µg/L (0–550 µg/L).

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen revealed a 28 mm thrombus in the right ovarian vein and an 18 mm thrombus in the left renal vein.

A 62-year-old woman presented with weakness and dizziness. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed pericardial tamponade, and pericardiocentesis of sanguineous fluid was performed. She then experienced a tonic–clonic seizure and worsening shock, necessitating intubation and initiation of epinephrine and norepinephrine infusions.

Computed tomography demonstrated a type A aortic dissection extending into the proximal transverse arch, innominate artery, right common carotid artery, right vertebral artery, and left common carotid artery. The patient was taken emergently for surgical repair, undergoing hemiarch replacement with a 30 mm Dacron Gelweave branched graft and aortic valve resuspension under deep hypothermic circulatory arrest. Cardioplegic solution was administered via both antegrade and retrograde techniques, with normal coronary sinus pressures intraoperatively.

Immediately before and after separation from cardiopulmonary bypass, transesophageal echocardiography showed a new dissection flap along the posterior lateral wall of the left atrium that expanded after bypass. The dissection measured 3 cm × 5 cm, with mean and peak pressure gradients across the narrowed left atrial space of 3 mm Hg and 6 mm Hg, respectively. TEE images demonstrated direct communication between the dissection cavity and the coronary sinus. The patient required norepinephrine (7 μg/min), epinephrine (4 μg/min), and vasopressin (0.1 units/min) but maintained blood pressures of approximately 90/60 mm Hg on these infusions. The surgical team elected to defer further intervention given hemodynamic stability, normal pulmonary artery pressures, and the challenging location of the coronary sinus injury.

A 21-year-old woman presented with symptoms of hyperviscosity syndrome accompanied by episodic angioedema, lymphadenopathy, and peripheral eosinophilia. Laboratory studies showed an eosinophil count of 10.6×10^9/L (normal <0.8), total IgG 77.4 g/L (normal <15), IgM 2.6 g/L, IgA 1.4 g/L, and IgE 912 µg/L (normal <430). Rheumatoid factor was 246 IU/mL (normal 0–15); antinuclear antibodies, extractable nuclear antigens, and ANCA were negative; complement C3 and C4 levels were normal. Serum IL-5 was 9.8 pg/mL (normal <3.5), IL-6 was 45.9 pg/mL (normal <4), and C-reactive protein was 14 mg/L. Serum viscosity measured 22.1 (normal 1.4–1.8). A bone marrow biopsy revealed plasmacytosis and eosinophilia. A right submandibular lymph node biopsy demonstrated a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with reactive follicular hyperplasia, peri-ductal fibrosis, acinar atrophy, and scattered eosinophils.

A 74-year-old man presented with a 1-day history of worsening shortness of breath and pleuritic right-sided back pain that was worse on inspiration. Over several days he had also been hoarse, which he attributed to a recent flu. He had just returned from a Middle Eastern country, where he was hospitalized for acute pulmonary edema and community-acquired pneumonia. His medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypercholesterolemia, severe triple-vessel coronary disease with ischemic cardiomyopathy, and left ventricular dysfunction. He had maintained a reasonably good functional status. On examination, he was febrile (38.6 °C) and tachycardic (100 bpm) but hemodynamically stable. Lung auscultation revealed bilateral crackles; the rest of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed elevated inflammatory markers and D-dimer, a low-grade anemia, and a stage 1 acute kidney injury. A chest radiograph demonstrated a well-defined right upper mediastinal opacity with a widened mediastinum measuring 9.7 cm in diameter. He was treated empirically for chest sepsis and isolated because of concerns about Middle East respiratory syndrome, and pulmonary embolism was also considered but anticoagulation was withheld due to concern for possible aortic dissection.

An 81-year-old woman living at home with her son, fully independent in activities of daily living, was admitted at night after an accidental fall causing right hip pain. Her history included osteoporosis with prior vertebral collapses (on calcium and vitamin D), hypertension controlled with ramipril, dyslipidemia on statin therapy, and lifelong anxious temperament without pharmacologic treatment. She had normal cognition, no allergies, and no recent weight loss. Physical examination showed a right upper cervical femur fracture; blood tests (complete blood count, electrolytes, liver and kidney function, protein electrophoresis, coagulation, blood gases) and a standard ECG were unremarkable. She was admitted to the orthogeriatric unit and scheduled for right cemented hemiarthroplasty under spinal anesthesia, performed 60 hours after admission. Ten minutes after cement injection, while haemostatic maneuvers were underway, she developed severe bradycardia progressing to cardiogenic shock and cardiac arrest. The surgical team placed her supine without breaching sterility, initiated CPR, performed endotracheal intubation, and administered atropine and epinephrine, achieving return of spontaneous circulation after 7 minutes. A post-resuscitation ECG showed ST-segment elevations in the inferior leads. The working diagnosis was bone cement implantation syndrome. She was transferred to the ICU, where dopamine (5.33→16 µg/kg/min) and norepinephrine (0.06–0.13 µg/kg/min) infusions were started, 3500 mL of crystalloid fluids were administered, and furosemide 40 mg IV was given. Because hypotension persisted (SBP 80 mmHg, MAP 50 mmHg) with sinus tachycardia, bisoprolol was added.

A 71-year-old woman with hypertension and a history of subarachnoid hemorrhage underwent hemiarch replacement for Stanford type A acute aortic dissection. Two months later, she presented with intermittent claudication of the left leg.
