Examination revealed absence of the left femoral pulse, with pain and coldness of the foot but no sensory or motor deficits. An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated normal cardiac function without intracardiac thrombus or atrial enlargement. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and lower extremities revealed occlusion extending from the left common femoral artery through the superficial, deep femoral, and popliteal arteries. A diagnosis of acute arterial occlusion of the left lower extremity was made, and emergency thrombectomy was performed. Warfarin was started (target INR, 1.8–2.5). One month later, her left leg pain recurred, and emergency thrombectomy was repeated; warfarin and aspirin were administered. One month after that, she experienced a third episode of left leg pain and underwent a third emergency thrombectomy.

A 5-month-old infant, known to have total anomalous pulmonary venous connection and ventricular septal defect, was awaiting corrective surgery when he developed fever and two generalized seizures. He required intubation during the second seizure for decreased oxygen saturation, which subsequently normalized with supportive care. A repeat COVID-19 PCR test on admission was positive. Laboratory studies revealed elevated liver enzymes (AST 60 U/L, ALT 65 U/L) without hyperammonemia or hyperbilirubinemia; other laboratories were unremarkable except for a mild electrolyte imbalance that was corrected. Eight days after seizure onset, brain MRI showed:
• On coronal T2-weighted images, confluent high-signal areas in the subcortical white matter, consistent with hypomyelination.  
• On axial T1-weighted images, multifocal cortical hemorrhages and cortical necrosis in both hemispheres.  
• Diffusion-weighted images demonstrating restricted diffusion in both thalami and the splenium of the corpus callosum.

A 13-year-old boy presented with a 2–3-month history of a slowly enlarging hole in the anterior hard palate, associated with difficulty eating and a nasal quality to his speech. On examination, there was a 1-cm perforation in the anterior hard palate; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, a leukocyte count of 11 700/mm3 (57% neutrophils, 30% lymphocytes, 13% eosinophils), and a platelet count of 294 000/mm3; other biochemical tests were within normal limits. A chest radiograph was normal, and a Mantoux test was negative. Cerebrospinal fluid examination was unremarkable. A skeletal survey showed no periosteal lesions or perichondritis. Ultrasonography of the abdomen and pelvis was normal. No Hutchinson’s teeth or other orofacial stigmata were noted, and an ophthalmic examination including fundoscopy was normal. There were no neurologic symptoms.

A 26-year-old Asian woman presented with a 6-week history of constant headache accompanied by persistent nausea, uncontrollable vomiting, and hiccups, and recent slurring of speech. On examination, she had tongue fasciculations, leftward gaze-evoked nystagmus, increased deep tendon reflexes on the left, cerebellar ataxia, and paresthesia at the base of the neck. Routine hematology, biochemistry (including C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate), and coagulation studies were all within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and spine revealed a focal hyperintense signal on T2-weighted, T2-FLAIR, ADC, and diffusion-weighted sequences affecting the area postrema region of the inferior dorsal medulla.

A 3-year-old, 3.7 kg intact female Miniature Poodle was presented with intermittent seizures, agitation, and hyperthermia. One hour before presentation, the dog may have ingested an unknown crystalline substance at a nightclub. On initial examination, heart rate was 138 beats/min, respiratory rate 62 breaths/min, and rectal temperature 42 °C. External cooling was begun. When evaluated 2.5 hours after ingestion, the dog exhibited flushed skin with extensive abdominal petechiae, watery bloody diarrhea, and had experienced three 50-second seizures en route. Physical examination showed rectal temperature 41.5 °C, heart rate 186 beats/min without arrhythmias, panting, systolic blood pressure 166 mmHg, diastolic 117 mmHg, and mean arterial pressure 137 mmHg. The dog was alert but extremely agitated, with bilaterally dilated pupils and continuous anticlockwise circling.

Complete blood count revealed leukocytosis (21,000/μL), mild anemia (hematocrit 31.2%), and thrombocytopenia (55,000/μL). Biochemistry showed mildly elevated ALT (112 U/L), ALKP (238 U/L), and mild hypoglycemia (70 mg/dL). Coagulation testing demonstrated prolonged PT (16.8 s) and aPTT (125 s). Blood gas analysis showed pH 7.20 and base deficit 17.8 mmol/L; electrolytes were normal. Abdominal radiographs demonstrated severe distension of the stomach and small intestine with air, and air-filled colon, suggestive of functional or paralytic ileus. A rapid urine immunochromatographic drug screen was performed for ketamine, methamphetamine, methadone, and morphine.
The test was positive only for methamphetamine.

A 49-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented to the plastics and burns dressing clinic 10 days after an inferior-pedicle bilateral breast reduction. She reported fevers, chills, rigors, and increasing bilateral breast tenderness and swelling. She had completed a 7-day course of co-amoxiclav postoperatively. On examination, she was febrile, and both breasts were tender with overlying erythema and edema. No imaging was performed, and laboratory results were pending. Empirical ciprofloxacin and clindamycin were initiated for a presumed infected hematoma. Twenty-four hours later, her condition worsened: dressings were soiled with purulent discharge, and patchy areas of skin necrosis with fluid-filled bullae appeared on both breasts.

A 56-year-old man with C4 tetraplegia, autonomic dysreflexia (baseline blood pressure ≈90/60 mmHg), post-traumatic epilepsy, and past alcohol abuse was readmitted with 4 days of dyspnea, fever, fatigue, and left shoulder pain after exercise. He had been treated for a presumed urinary tract infection with cefotaxime, developed urticaria, was switched to ciprofloxacin, and was discharged, but then deteriorated. Current medications included gabapentin, carbamazepine, baclofen, salbutamol, and others for his baseline conditions.

On examination he was drowsy but arousable. Blood pressure was 97/68 mmHg, heart rate 89 bpm, temperature 37.1 °C, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Cardiac exam revealed weak heart sounds, a split S2, and jugular venous distension. The abdomen was soft and non-tender.

Electrocardiogram showed slow septal R-wave progression, 1 mm ST-segment elevation in leads I, III, aVF, V3, and V5–V6, and 1.5 mm ST-segment elevation in leads II and V4, with biphasic T waves in leads III, aVL, aVF, and V3–V4. Laboratory studies revealed C-reactive protein 354 mg/L (reference <5), troponin I 63 ng/L (reference <40) rising to 75 ng/L at 6 hours, sodium 129 mmol/L, and potassium 5.1 mmol/L.

He was started on cefuroxime and gentamicin (later changed to clindamycin), then developed severe hypotension and asystolic cardiac arrest. After 1 minute of CPR, return of spontaneous circulation was achieved. A chest radiograph showed a widened mediastinum with air surrounding the cardiac silhouette, consistent with pneumopericardium. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the thorax demonstrated air within the pericardial sac, a normal remainder of the mediastinum, no pneumothorax, and no pericardial exudate or fat stranding.

A 76-year-old Chinese man was admitted with a 1-month history of exertional chest tightness associated with diaphoresis and shortness of breath but no chest pain. A resting ECG showed abnormal Q waves in leads II, III, and aVF, and cardiac troponin T was elevated; he was diagnosed with an acute coronary syndrome and discharged on aspirin, clopidogrel, metoprolol, and rosuvastatin. On admission to our hospital, his high-sensitivity troponin T was 21.58 ng/L, ECG again showed abnormal Q waves in the inferior leads, and a routine blood count was normal with a platelet count of 201×10^9/L. He denied any history of blood disorders or smoking and alcohol use. Coronary angiography revealed left main and three-vessel coronary artery disease; after an initial 2000-unit heparin bolus, he chose percutaneous intervention over bypass surgery. Four days later, multivessel PCI with drug-eluting stents and a drug-coated balloon was performed over 2 hours with 6500 units of heparin. Post-procedure, he received intravenous tirofiban at 0.15 µg/kg/min along with his usual aspirin, clopidogrel, metoprolol, rosuvastatin, and benazepril. Four hours after the procedure, a complete blood count showed a platelet count of 21×10^9/L, confirmed by manual examination of the blood film.

A 48-year-old man with a 30–pack-year smoking history was admitted for refractory hypoglycemia attributed to a suspected insulinoma. His complete blood count showed a white blood cell count of 9.9 × 10^3/µL with an absolute eosinophil count of 0.1 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, and platelets 442 × 10^3/µL. A metabolic panel revealed mild hyponatremia and a glucose level of 34 mg/dL; liver function tests were normal. Hormonal studies demonstrated an insulin level of 133 mIU/mL, proinsulin 46.5 pmol/L, C-peptide 9.3 ng/mL, and a random cortisol of 129.1 µg/dL. Vital signs were normal, and he was afebrile.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed multiple pulmonary nodules, the largest measuring 1.4 × 1.2 cm in the left lung. Serologic testing for histoplasma, aspergillus, coccidioides, and blastomyces by immunodiffusion and complement fixation was negative. An interferon-gamma release assay for tuberculosis was also negative. CT-guided core needle biopsy of the largest nodule revealed a necrotic granuloma on microscopy. Fungal and mycobacterial cultures of the biopsy specimen remained negative at 4 and 6 weeks, respectively. No sputum cultures were obtained. The patient had no fevers during hospitalization.

Further social history revealed ownership of three dogs, one of which had fatigue, weight loss, and hair loss; the patient was uncertain whether his dogs had received heartworm preventative treatment. He denied any travel history.

A 24-year-old woman was referred for endoscopic ultrasound evaluation after a contrast-enhanced CT scan showed a 3.0 × 2.9 cm round, hypervascular, hypodense mass in the tail of the pancreas. She reported 1 month of dull epigastric pain radiating to both upper quadrants and the lumbar region. Her medical history was notable for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura treated with splenectomy 5 years earlier. A second-degree relative had pancreatic cancer. Laboratory tests were within normal limits, tumor markers were negative, and the peripheral blood smear showed 1+ Howell-Jolly bodies. Endoscopic ultrasound revealed a 2.8 × 2.9 cm, well-defined, homogeneous, hypoechoic mass in the pancreatic tail without other abnormalities.

A 63-year-old man presented with a two-year history of right-sided facial discomfort, medial canthal swelling, and nasal obstruction. He denied epistaxis or visual changes but reported pain and persistent epiphora on the right. His medical history included ischemic heart disease, hypertension, and diabetes; he took regular analgesics for right frontotemporal headaches. He was a lifelong nonsmoker and had worked for 25 years as an engineer on open machines that manufacture metal pins, with daily direct contact with metal-working (Suds) oil and inhalation of its mist.

On examination, there was a firm medial canthal swelling. Flexible nasal endoscopy showed a large mass arising from the right middle meatal opening; the left nasal cavity was clear. MRI of the paranasal sinuses revealed a discrete mass originating in the right ethmoid sinus, extending into the right nasal cavity, thinning the medial orbital wall, and likely impinging on the nasolacrimal duct.

A decision was made to proceed with complete endoscopic excision. Intraoperatively, a soft, rubbery, well-encapsulated tumor was removed via a right sphenoethmoidectomy and extended frontal Draf IIc procedure with macroscopic clearance.

On initial histologic examination, the findings were inconclusive. An external head and neck pathology review noted a fibromyxoid proliferation without cytological atypia, marked variation in cellularity, or inflammatory cell infiltrate. Numerous foamy macrophages containing eosinophilic material were identified. Periodic acid–Schiff/Alcian blue staining was negative for mucin but highlighted the eosinophilic material.

A 64-year-old Chinese woman presented with two months of abdominal discomfort and nausea, without fever, cough, chest or abdominal pain, night sweats, weight loss, or anorexia. Her only surgical history was a cholecystectomy 4 years earlier. She had no history of tuberculosis or HIV infection. 

On examination, her temperature was 36.5 °C. Abdominal palpation revealed epigastric tenderness without hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies showed mild anemia (hemoglobin 100 g/L) and a platelet count of 242 × 10^9/L. Liver function tests, tumor markers, and HIV antibody testing were all within normal limits or negative. 

Chest radiography and cardiac ultrasound were unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 6.9 × 6.9 × 6.7 cm splenic hypoechoic lesion with regular margins and homogenous internal echo. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound showed a rounded lesion with a clear boundary, heterogeneous enhancement, and central irregular necrosis. A presumptive diagnosis of lymphoma was made.

Abdominal CT imaging demonstrated a 6.4 × 6.5 cm hypodense splenic lesion with an initially unclear boundary that became well defined on enhancement, heterogeneous enhancement, and central necrosis. Based on CT findings, an inflammatory pseudotumor was suspected.

A man in his early 40s presented with a 2-week history of bilateral leg pain and swelling and lower back pain. He initially experienced a 10/10 “sciatica-like” shooting pain down the left leg at rest that lasted about 30 minutes, then improved to a dull ache in the lower back radiating to both legs. Over several days, he noted progressive swelling of both calves and thighs, with tightness and significant limitation of mobility. He denied trauma or prolonged immobility but had reduced outdoor exercise in recent months. His only notable history was longstanding varicose veins for which he had intermittently worn compression stockings. He denied chest pain, dyspnoea, cough, or haemoptysis. 

On examination, there was gross bilateral pitting oedema up to the thighs, prominent superficial vessels, and tenderness along the posterior thighs. The legs were not erythematous, and there were no signs of bruising, infection, or vasculitis. The rest of the examination was unremarkable. His Wells score was 3, indicating high pretest probability for DVT. 

Initial investigations showed normocytic anaemia with iron deficiency, a mild clotting‐time derangement, elevated C-reactive protein, and elevated ferritin. Doppler ultrasound failed to demonstrate compressibility or flow in either common femoral vein, consistent with bilateral DVT. A chest radiograph was normal. 

Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated extensive thrombosis of the superficial, common femoral, and iliac veins bilaterally. The subhepatic inferior vena cava was not visualized, and venous return appeared to occur via dilated azygous veins. A solitary low‐density lesion on the liver capsule was noted, likely a simple cyst or haemangioma.

A 3-year-old girl presented to the emergency department 12 hours after arriving at 2270 m above sea level with acute onset of shortness of breath and cough. She lived at 70 m elevation and had a history of right congenital diaphragmatic hernia repaired at 6 months, resulting in right lung hypoplasia, recurrent pneumonia, and viral-induced wheezy episodes requiring emergency visits but no recent hospitalizations. She was fully immunized.

On examination, she was in acute respiratory distress: temperature normal, heart rate 190 bpm, blood pressure 100/62 mmHg, and SpO₂ 40% on room air. Her weight was 11 kg (10th percentile). Chest auscultation revealed bilateral diminished air entry with diffuse inspiratory crackles. Chest radiography showed bilateral patchy opacities. Laboratory tests were obtained and are summarized in Table 1.

Because of persistent hypoxemia and respiratory distress, she was intubated and mechanically ventilated. Empiric therapy included broad-spectrum antibiotics, intravenous methylprednisolone, and nebulized bronchodilators. On hospital day 2, transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated normal cardiac structure and function without pulmonary hypertension. Six hours later, repeat chest radiography showed marked improvement in pulmonary opacities. She was successfully extubated and off supplemental oxygen by day 4.

A 32-year-old G2P1 woman with a history of a term cesarean delivery 3 years ago presented with 2 months of persistent low-grade metrorrhagia following a spontaneous miscarriage. Initial evaluation showed a plasma β–HCG level of 13,500 mIU/mL. On referral, she was hemodynamically stable, afebrile, with no anemia. A pelvic examination revealed a normal cervix and no active endocervical or endometrial bleeding. Repeat plasma β–HCG was 7100 mIU/mL, and hemoglobin was 12.1 g/dL. Transvaginal ultrasound revealed an anteverted, anteflexed uterus of normal size, a thin regular endometrium, and a heterogeneous, richly vascularized lesion in the anterior isthmus over the cesarean scar measuring 62 × 56 × 29 mm. Color Doppler imaging showed multiple dilated vessels with venous velocities over 50 cm/s and low-resistance arteries with systolic peaks over 100 cm/s. A high-flow vascular malformation associated with retained trophoblastic tissue was suspected.

A 22-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after a motor-vehicle accident. He sustained midshaft fractures of the right radius and ulna with a puncture wound over the proximal dorsal forearm. On initial examination, he had limited active flexion and extension of all four fingers, but finger abduction was intact. Thumb motion and sensation in the median and ulnar nerve distributions were normal. The forearm compartments were soft.

On day 1 after injury, he underwent open reduction and internal fixation of the radius via a volar (Henry) approach and of the ulna via a direct ulnar approach. Intraoperatively, the flexor digitorum superficialis muscle belly was noted to be impaled by a proximal radial fragment.

On postoperative day 3, he was noted to have a drop of the medial three fingers and radial deviation of the wrist. The tests for median and ulnar nerve function remained normal. Passive tenodesis testing was unreliable, and a partial PIN neuropraxia was diagnosed. He was managed with a splint and mobilization exercises; nerve conduction studies, electromyography, and ultrasound were planned.

A 5-year-old boy, the third child of consanguineous parents, presented with a right femoral shaft fracture after a fall. His two older siblings were healthy. Since infancy, he had recurrent fevers and injurious behaviors, such as biting his nails and striking hot objects, leading to loss of three toes and one thumb. He also had anhidrosis with episodes of hyperpyrexia and areas of compensatory hyperhidrosis. 

On examination, he had multiple ulcers and dry skin lesions around the oral cavity, eyes, palms, and soles, as well as wound scars on his fingers and toes. Dental examination showed absent teeth; there was notable nasal cartilage damage. His hair was dry and sparse, with numerous healed scars on exposed sites. Neurologic testing revealed complete loss of pain and temperature sensation in the extremities, with preserved vibration and pressure sensation. Ophthalmologic evaluation showed reduced corneal sensation, dry eyes, and corneal ulcers.

Laboratory studies demonstrated a hemoglobin level of 6.2 g/dL (reference, 12.0–16.0 g/dL), a lymphocyte percentage of 45.1% (reference, 20.0–40.0%), a sodium level of 146 mEq/L (reference, 135–145 mEq/L), and normal potassium and chloride levels.

A previously healthy 13-year-old girl developed recurrent clonic movements of her right arm and leg lasting about 2 minutes without loss of consciousness, for which she was started on levetiracetam. Two weeks later she presented with right leg weakness, right hand and foot paresthesia, and acute aphasia. On admission she was febrile (38 °C), alert but inarticulate with impaired comprehension, had continuous right arm clonic movements, and exhibited right-sided motor power of 4/5 with paresthesia. Cranial nerves were intact; there was no rash, trauma, or significant past medical history.  
Laboratory studies showed a normal CBC; ANA, RF, immunoglobulins, complement levels, thyroid function, and α-fetoprotein were within normal limits. CSF analysis revealed no pleocytosis or biochemical abnormalities; bacterial and viral cultures were negative. Serum and CSF antibody titers for HSV, enterovirus, and Japanese encephalitis virus were not elevated.  
EEG demonstrated continuous slow waves in the left hemisphere with frequent left temporal spikes and multiple electroclinical seizures. Brain MRI (T2-weighted) showed multifocal high-signal intensity lesions with cortical swelling in bilateral temporal lobes, predominantly on the left, involving the limbic system.  
Empiric therapy with intravenous vancomycin, cefotaxime, acyclovir, azithromycin, dexamethasone, and antiseizure medications was initiated. On hospital day 2, IVIG (400 mg/kg/day for 5 days) was added given concern for limbic and autoimmune encephalitis based on MRI findings.

A 46-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of progressive, painless enlargement of his right maxilla. His medical history was notable for asthma, allergic rhinitis, and multiple drug allergies. He had undergone septoplasty 7 years earlier and extractions of maxillary teeth 2 years before presentation; retreatment of the right maxillary first premolar and periodontal scaling provided no relief. On examination, there was visible swelling of the right maxilla with elevation of the nasal ala. Intraoral inspection showed a firm, non-tender swelling from the right maxillary incisors through premolars, elevation of the hard palate with reddish telangiectatic areas, and no lymphadenopathy.  
Contrast CT of the region revealed a mixed hypodense lesion causing expansion and resorption of the buccal and palatal cortices, extending into the maxillary sinus, crossing the midline, contacting an impacted supernumerary tooth, and involving the apex of the endodontically treated first premolar. Under the working diagnoses of radicular cyst, dentigerous cyst, and ameloblastoma, an exploratory puncture yielded sanguineous fluid, and an incisional biopsy was undertaken, during which intense bleeding was encountered.

A 32-year-old gravida 1 para 0 woman at 38 + 1 weeks of gestation presented with a 4-week history of persistent suprapubic and pelvic pain, occasional low‐grade fevers at home (maximum temperature, 37.8 °C), abundant leukorrhea, a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying, and dysuria. She had no prior abdominal surgery or urological disease. She visited the emergency department three times over four days; obstetric evaluations showed sporadic uterine contractions that were not significant. Initial empirical outpatient antibiotics (cefixime followed by amoxicillin–clavulanate) failed to relieve her symptoms. On admission, she was afebrile; laboratory studies showed a white-blood-cell count of 16,300 cells/µL and a C-reactive protein level of 158 mg/L. Obstetric examination revealed a posterior cervix, 1–2 cm dilated and partially effaced, with a cephalic presentation at –4 station. Nine hours later, she entered active labor, received epidural analgesia, but continued to experience severe suprapubic pain. On physical examination during labor, a 5 cm soft, tender mass was palpated in the suprapubic region. A transabdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 2 × 6 × 4 cm nonhomogeneous lesion with clear margins in the anterior lower uterine segment, which was interpreted as a colliquated median anterior isthmic subserous myoma.

A 21-year-old man presented with a 1–2-year history of chronic right knee pain without any history of recent trauma or violent injury. He had no other relevant medical history. On examination, there was mild joint swelling but no restriction of movement. The posterior drawer sign and the posterior tibial sag sign were negative, making posterior cruciate ligament avulsion unlikely. Standard knee radiographs, though not available for review, were reported as normal. Knee MRI revealed two small lesions adjacent to the posterior horn of the medial meniscus; these lesions were isointense to bone marrow and were surrounded by a rim of low signal intensity.

A 25-year-old man from Ghana presented with 7 days of altered mental status, weight loss, neck pain, cough, fever, nausea, vomiting, and photophobia. He reported greenish sputum with streaks of blood and an approximately 20-lb weight loss over the past month. He denied chest pain, dyspnea, diarrhea, or skin rash. His medical history was notable only for intermittent asthma and migraines. He smoked 10 cigarettes daily, drank alcohol occasionally, and denied illicit drug use except for marijuana. He last traveled to Ghana 6 months earlier. He was sexually active with multiple partners.

On examination, he appeared cachectic and lethargic but was oriented to person, place, and time. Vital signs: temperature 98°F, heart rate 102 bpm, blood pressure 108/69 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, oxygen saturation 96% on room air. His BMI was 19.2 kg/m2. He had no lymphadenopathy, clear bilateral breath sounds, and unremarkable cardiovascular and abdominal exams. Neurologic examination revealed neck stiffness.

Laboratory testing on admission revealed HIV infection with a CD4 count <20 cells/mm3 and a high viral load. A lumbar puncture showed opening pressure 23 cm H2O, CSF white blood cell count 2 cells/mm3, red blood cell count 57 cells/mm3, protein 102 mg/dL, glucose 25 mg/dL, and negative Gram stain and bacterial antigen tests. He was treated empirically for bacterial meningitis and started on quadruple antitubercular therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide).

A chest radiograph demonstrated numerous small nodular opacities throughout both lungs, suggestive of a miliary pattern. A noncontrast chest CT scan confirmed diffuse micronodular infiltrates. Despite a negative quantiFERON-TB test, antitubercular therapy was continued. Over the next days, the patient had four negative sputum acid-fast bacilli smears and a negative M. tuberculosis PCR assay. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial biopsy was planned to obtain tissue for diagnosis.

A 56-year-old man with a 15-year history of severe chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and a 25-pack-year smoking history, developed sudden hoarseness of voice. Fiberoptic laryngoscopy revealed left vocal cord palsy, and the remainder of the otolaryngologic examination was normal. A chest radiograph, unchanged from prior films, demonstrated massive dilatation of the central pulmonary arteries and tapering of the peripheral pulmonary vessels. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and chest performed to evaluate for malignancy showed no tumor. The CT did reveal extensive central pulmonary artery dilatation with wall-adherent thrombus, abrupt narrowing of peripheral pulmonary vessels, right ventricular hypertrophy, enlargement of the right ventricle and right atrium, dilated bronchial arteries, and a mosaic pattern of lung attenuation. Measurements demonstrated progressive aneurysmal enlargement of the pulmonary trunk (from 5.2 cm to 7.0 cm over ten years) and of the right and left pulmonary arteries (from 4.7 cm and 5.6 cm to 7.0 cm and 9.0 cm, respectively).

A 54‐year‐old Black man presented with a 3‐ to 4‐year history of hundreds of asymptomatic, soft nodules on his trunk that have slowly increased in number without seasonal variation. He denied systemic symptoms. His medical history was notable only for active tobacco smoking. On examination, there were hundreds of small, flesh‐colored to hypopigmented soft nodules distributed on the back, chest, and lateral arms; the scalp and face were unaffected. A punch biopsy from the chest revealed a superficial and deep perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate with increased dermal mucin and no alteration of the dermoepidermal junction. Laboratory studies showed a positive antinuclear antibody titer of 1:320; complete blood count, metabolic panel, and urinalysis were otherwise unremarkable.

A 70-year-old man with a history of pulmonary vein isolation 5 years earlier was referred for recurrent atrial fibrillation. Under deep sedation with propofol and dexmedetomidine, isoproterenol infusion provoked atrial fibrillation at a maximum heart rate of 130 bpm. Mapping identified paroxysmal atrial contractions in the superior vena cava (SVC) triggering atrial fibrillation. During atrial fibrillation, an isolation line was placed approximately 5 mm above the earliest sinus activation site in the right atrium and SVC. After delivering two-thirds encircling ablation at 25 W, a defibrillation shock restored sinus rhythm without junctional rhythm, and the heart rate was 53 bpm. Electroanatomic mapping then showed atrial activation originating from a lower non‐sinus pacemaker. On repeat isoproterenol infusion, the maximal heart rate reached approximately 110 bpm, compared with 130 bpm before SVC isolation. Post-procedure and off isoproterenol, the patient’s resting heart rate was around 50 bpm with mild hypotension requiring temporary dopamine infusion. A short PR interval was observed immediately after ablation but normalized by the next day. Right phrenic nerve palsy was noted on the day of the procedure but fully resolved by discharge on day 3; at discharge his resting heart rate remained 50 bpm and he was asymptomatic.

A 67-year-old Caucasian woman, non-smoker, with hypertension and hypothyroidism presented with a 12-month history of exertional dyspnoea and dry cough. She denied systemic, nasal or gastrointestinal symptoms and had no history of atopy, tuberculosis exposure or occupational dust exposure. Her medications (levothyroxine, aspirin, losartan) were unchanged. Examination was unremarkable; vital signs were stable with an SpO2 of 97% on room air. Pulmonary function tests showed FEV1 57% predicted, FVC 67% predicted, FEV1/FVC 71%, TLCO 71% predicted and KCO 131% predicted. ECG and transthoracic echocardiography were normal. Chest radiography revealed blunting of both costophrenic angles and scattered peribronchial thickening in the mid and lower lung zones. High-resolution CT of the chest demonstrated bilateral hilar and central mediastinal nodal calcification without significant lymphadenopathy, perilymphatic nodularity in the upper and mid lung zones, and bilateral pleural effusions (left > right). Laboratory tests showed a mildly elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level. Ultrasound-guided thoracentesis yielded an exudative, yellow lymphocytic effusion (70% lymphocytes) with normal adenosine deaminase level and negative cultures for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

A 41-year-old man with a history of pyoderma gangrenosum, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and long-standing cocaine abuse presented with an 8-day history of worsening pain and ulceration. He noted the lesions began to worsen approximately 10 days after his most recent cocaine use. He denied fever, respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms. 

On examination, there were extensive cribriform ulcerations with irregular, undermined borders and purulent drainage covering approximately 30% of his body surface area, involving the upper back, left trunk, right arm, left shoulder, left infraorbital maxilla, and right temporal area extending behind the ear.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, metabolic panel, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, complement levels, and autoimmune profile, including negative antinuclear antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, cryoglobulins, C-ANCA, and P-ANCA. Serologic tests for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV were negative. A biopsy from an ulcer obtained one month earlier showed perivascular plasmacytosis with focal vasculitis, suggestive of pyoderma gangrenosum. The patient also tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 by PCR.

A 25-year-old woman presented with a 12-month history of recurrent syncopal episodes and subjective weakness triggered by minimal activity. Her medical history included anxiety, psychogenic seizures, and migraines. She consumed alcohol socially, denied illicit drugs, and had no family history of cardiac disease.

At an outside clinic, ECG showed sinus rhythm with first-degree atrioventricular block, an atypical right bundle branch block, and a Brugada-like pattern. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed normal left and right ventricular size and function without valvular abnormalities. An event monitor demonstrated episodes of first-degree AV block with junctional escape and right bundle branch block but no high-grade AV block. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed mild dilation of the right ventricular outflow tract without scar or delayed enhancement.

An electrophysiology study with isoproterenol induction provoked non-sustained ventricular tachycardia of left bundle-branch morphology, but mapping was inconclusive. A transvenous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator was placed. The following day, she developed lightheadedness, hypotension, and device-detected slow ventricular tachycardia, for which sotalol was initiated. Repeat echocardiography showed biventricular failure (left ventricular ejection fraction 40%, severely reduced right ventricular function) without pericardial effusion. A CT pulmonary angiogram was negative for embolism.

Despite aggressive resuscitation, she progressed to cardiogenic shock requiring pressors and intubation. On transfer, laboratory studies showed troponin I 0.10 ng/mL (reference 0.00–0.05 ng/mL), B-type natriuretic peptide 990 pg/mL (0–100 pg/mL), AST 86 U/L (7–40 U/L), ALT 77 U/L (7–56 U/L), and normal inflammatory markers. Right heart catheterization revealed elevated right-sided filling pressures and a cardiac index of 1.8 L/min/m2.

Initial differential diagnoses included autoimmune/infiltrative cardiomyopathy, arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, ischaemic disease, Lev-Lenegres disease, sodium channelopathies, and cardiomyopathy secondary to toxic/metabolic causes.

A previously healthy 2-month-old male infant, born at term (3.020 kg) to parents from Romania and Lebanon, presented with bilateral forearm fractures. A few days earlier, his mother noted that he would cry with passive movement of his arms. An orthopedic evaluation and X-rays revealed a supracondylar fracture of the left elbow, lytic areas with probable fractures and displacement of the distal radius and ulna bilaterally, mild osteopenia, and distorted end plates of the peripheral radius and ulna.

On admission, he was well-appearing, with mild hypotonia, hypertelorism, a low nasal bridge, and mild tachypnea with rhinitis; feeding was reduced. Physical examination revealed a palpable liver and spleen. Laboratory studies showed: hemoglobin 7 g/dL; WBC 14×10^3/µL; platelets 421×10^3/µL; sodium 130 mmol/L; albumin 3 g/dL; globulin 4.7 g/dL; AST 79 U/L; ALT 142 U/L; alkaline phosphatase 431 U/L; CRP 47 mg/L; and normal calcium, PTH, 25-OH vitamin D, coagulation studies, and thyroid hormones. Brain ultrasound and MRI, chest radiograph, fundoscopy, and hearing tests were all normal. Skeletal survey showed no additional fractures. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated mild hepatomegaly (7 cm) and splenomegaly (6.8 cm). 

Because of the hepatosplenomegaly and anemia, screening for congenital infections was performed: Toxoplasma, Rubella, parvovirus B19, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, and HIV serologies were all negative.

A 49-year-old woman presented with progressive right‐sided hemiparesis. Her first acute attack occurred in 2007, and she had similar relapses in 2012 and 2015, each treated with methylprednisolone pulses with partial recovery and mild residual weakness. Over the past 2 years, her right hemiparesis continued to worsen without further remissions or new relapses. She has no personal or family history of neurologic disorders and no toxic exposures.

On examination, cranial nerves were intact except for a right Babinski sign. Motor strength was 4/5 in the right upper and lower limbs, with a limping gait; the left side was normal.

Brain MRI (3D T2 FLAIR) showed no signal abnormalities. Cervical-spine MRI revealed a focal, anterocentral hyperintense lesion at C1–C2 without contrast enhancement; this lesion was unchanged in size, location, and signal intensity compared with the original studies from 2007.

CSF analysis: cell count <5 cells/μL; protein 45 mg/dL; oligoclonal bands absent; IgG index normal. Aquaporin-4 antibody and MOG antibody tests were negative. Blood tests, including complete blood count, metabolic panel, liver and kidney function, thyroid function, vitamin and mineral levels (including B12), and inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), as well as ANA, lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipin, SSA, SSB, and ANCA, were all within normal limits. CT and FDG-PET imaging excluded neoplasm. Thoracic MRI and digital subtraction angiography of the brain and spinal cord showed no abnormalities.

A 90-year-old woman presented with 3 months of generalized headaches, anorexia, and nausea. She was alert, afebrile, and hemodynamically stable, with an unremarkable neurologic examination. Her medical history was notable for resection of localized bowel cancer and skin melanoma, as well as hypertension; she had no diabetes, HIV infection, prior chemotherapy, immunomodulatory therapy, or craniofacial trauma. Medications included ramipril. Routine laboratory tests, including full blood count, serum electrolytes, and C-reactive protein, were within normal limits. A pituitary hormone panel revealed mildly elevated prolactin at 714 mU/L (normal <536), with other pituitary hormones in the normal range. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. 
Brain computed tomography showed dehiscence of the floor of the sella, mucoperiosteal thickening of the sphenoid sinus, and curvilinear calcifications. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a contrast-enhancing mass measuring 12 mm in maximal craniocaudal dimension within the superior aspect of the sphenoid sinus, communicating with the pituitary fossa through the defect in the sella floor. The pituitary gland was heterogeneous in signal intensity on both pre-contrast T1- and T2-weighted sequences and showed heterogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. The imaging findings suggested a pituitary neoplasm with a downward growth pattern, but the mucoperiosteal thickening in the sphenoid sinuses and the presence of calcification on CT raised the possibility of a mycetoma.

A previously healthy 24-month-old boy was seen by his pediatrician for a two-week history of recurring fever, cough that worsened with exertion, rhinorrhea, and intermittent bilateral conjunctivitis. On initial examination, he appeared well and alert. Vital signs were normal except for a temperature of 38.0 °C and a respiratory rate of 40 breaths per minute. Auscultation was notable for obstructive breath sounds over both lungs. Laboratory tests showed a leukocyte count of 24 × 10^9/L and a C-reactive protein level of 457 nmol/L. He was treated with bronchodilators, empirical cefaclor, and antipyretics.

Three days later, his fever had risen to 40.0 °C, and the cough persisted, but auscultation no longer revealed obstructive sounds. The pediatrician suspected pneumonia due to a resistant pathogen and referred him to the pediatric emergency department.

At the ED, his temperature was 39.3 °C, respiratory rate approximately 40/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Auscultation now showed markedly diminished breath sounds over the right lung without crackles, bronchial breath sounds, or pleural rub. Repeat labs demonstrated a leukocyte count of 25 × 10^9/L and CRP of 1333 nmol/L.

Differential diagnoses considered at that time included pneumonia due to a resistant organism, (tension-)pneumothorax, foreign-body aspiration, and infection at an extrapulmonary focus.

A 12-year-old girl with a history of mitochondriopathy (suspected POLG1 mutation), neurodevelopmental delay, epilepsy, and chronic constipation managed at home with daily transanal irrigation using 1.5 L of tap water presented with persistent hiccups for 1 day. Over the preceding few days, her parents noted that only about 1.0 L of the instilled irrigation fluid was being evacuated. On examination, she was alert and had hiccups several times per minute but was otherwise at her neurologic and cardiovascular baseline. Laboratory evaluation revealed a serum sodium concentration of 120 mmol/L, a serum osmolality of 246 mOsmol/kg, and a urine sodium concentration below 20 mmol/L.

An 82-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of shortness of breath and productive cough without haemoptysis, fever, or weight loss. Her medical history included COPD, hypothyroidism, hypertension, mitral regurgitation, and varicose veins. She had a 21–pack-year smoking history. Medications were Seretide 500 µg twice daily, levothyroxine, ramipril, bisoprolol, amlodipine, and salbutamol as needed.

On examination, she had bilateral expiratory wheezes and scattered crackles. Vital signs were: respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 95% on 28% oxygen, temperature 36.9 °C. Laboratory studies showed a WBC count of 10.9 × 10^3/µl (neutrophils 9.8 × 10^3/µl, eosinophils 0.0 × 10^3/µl) and a CRP level of 161 mg/L. Arterial blood gas on room air revealed pH 7.5, pO2 6.1 kPa, pCO2 4.8 kPa, and HCO3− 28 mmol/L. Sputum cultures were negative. Autoimmune serologies, including anti-nuclear antibodies, ANCA, and rheumatoid factor, were negative.

Chest radiography demonstrated right upper to mid-zone infiltrates. CT of the chest showed consolidation, mild volume loss, and ground-glass opacification in the right upper lobe, along with a small to moderate right anterior pneumothorax. On day 2, the serum procalcitonin level was 0.13 ng/mL (reference range 0.00–0.25).

A 20-year-old man with a 5-year history of adrenal insufficiency on hydrocortisone presented with 24 hours of sudden generalized dull abdominal pain that rapidly increased in severity. He denied nausea, vomiting, or fever. He was initially treated at another hospital with intravenous fluids, antibiotics, and analgesics for suspected appendicitis without improvement and was transferred for further evaluation.

On arrival, he was hypotensive. Abdominal examination revealed generalized tenderness—worse in the right lower quadrant—along with guarding, rigidity, and hypoactive bowel sounds; no mass was palpable. A provisional diagnosis of peritonitis with suspected bowel perforation was made.

An erect chest radiograph showed no free air under the diaphragm. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated mildly thickened distal ileal loops with minimal free fluid in the right iliac fossa and a linear area of hyperdensity in the mid-ileal loops traversing the bowel wall without adjacent extraluminal air, suggestive of a foreign body causing inflammation of the small intestine.

A 68-year-old woman was admitted with sudden onset of left leg paresthesia, spastic paraparesis, and sphincter dysfunction. She also reported a recent history of tension-type headache, confusion, nausea, and vomiting. On examination, she had a positive left Babinski sign and hyperactive deep tendon reflexes in the left lower extremity; cognition and cranial-nerve function were normal. Routine laboratory and serological tests (including rheumatologic panels) were unremarkable except for a positive antinuclear antibody. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain revealed a small cluster of cortical–subcortical hypointense foci on susceptibility-weighted imaging in the right superior temporal and angular gyri, consistent with microhemorrhages; T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences showed no abnormal signal in the surrounding white matter, and there was no contrast enhancement.

A 37-year-old man with a 1-year history of untreated HIV/AIDS presented with a 5-week history of lesions on his face, torso, groin, and buttocks. The lesions were nonpainful for the first week but became excruciatingly painful, prompting medical attention. Two days before presentation, he noted subjective fevers and chills. On examination, he had necrotic, confluent ulcerations with yellow crusting on the left side of his face and nose; ulceronecrotic nodular plaques on his torso; and ulcerative papulonodules on the digits of both hands. Laboratory studies revealed a CD4 count of 52 cells/mm3 and an HIV viral load of 242 000 copies/mL. The initial differential diagnosis included atypical mycobacterium, malignant lues, leishmaniasis, and deep fungal infection.

A 53-year-old white woman was referred to the oral and maxillofacial surgery service after a routine panoramic radiograph revealed a lesion in her anterior maxilla. She reported a painless increase in maxillary volume and numbness of the palate that did not interfere with daily activities. On examination, there was a well-defined, oval swelling of the hard palate posterior to the palatine papilla along the midline, with expansion of both buccal and palatal cortical plates. Cone-beam computed tomography showed an approximately 25 mm oval radiolucent lesion intimately related to the apices of the central incisors and the mesial aspects of the lateral incisors, with thinning of the buccal cortex and perforation of the nasal floor, but no evidence of root resorption.

A 27-year-old, 68-kg man with multiple endocrine neoplasia type IIb—manifested by metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytomas—presented for excision of a vocal cord neuroma. He had no cardiac history and reported good exercise tolerance. Surgical history included bilateral adrenalectomies five years earlier and total thyroidectomy. Medications were hydrocortisone 15 mg in the morning and 10 mg in the evening, fludrocortisone 0.05 mg daily, and levothyroxine 137 µg daily; he took his usual thyroid and steroid replacement on the morning of surgery. Preoperative vital signs showed a heart rate of 106 bpm and blood pressure of 115/68 mmHg; other vitals and laboratory results were within normal limits.

After placement of standard monitors, anesthesia was induced with propofol 120 mg, rocuronium 50 mg, and fentanyl 75 µg. A 5.5-mm laser endotracheal tube was inserted under C-MAC guidance to avoid trauma to mucosal neuromas. Dexamethasone 10 mg IV was administered for prophylaxis against airway edema and postoperative nausea. Ten minutes after incision, the patient developed persistent hypotension—systolic blood pressure < 70 mmHg and mean arterial pressure < 50 mmHg for approximately 15 minutes—despite a 500-mL bolus of 5% albumin and multiple doses of ephedrine, phenylephrine, calcium, norepinephrine, and vasopressin. The end-tidal concentration of desflurane never exceeded 4.4%. Physical examination revealed no rash or urticaria and no increase in airway pressures.

A 33-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, was referred at 12 weeks’ gestation for evaluation of an enlarged, multicystic placenta. Her prior pregnancy had been uncomplicated. She booked at 10 weeks 6 days; her BMI was 20.7, and she was a nonsmoker. A dating scan at 12 weeks 2 days showed a single viable intrauterine fetus and an enlarged, multicystic (‘grape-like’) placenta. First-trimester serum screening was low risk for trisomies 13, 18, and 21, with an hCG level of 245.64 U/L (5.08 MoM) and a PAPP-A of 5008.13 mU/L (1.75 MoM).  
At the fetal medicine unit, ultrasound confirmed placentalomegaly with a multicystic appearance. Fetal anatomy appeared appropriate for gestational age. The differential diagnosis of partial molar pregnancy versus placental mesenchymal dysplasia was discussed, and invasive testing was offered; the patient elected conservative management with interval scan.  
At 16 weeks 1 day, repeat ultrasound again demonstrated an enlarged multicystic placenta. Estimated fetal weight was below the 3rd centile by Hadlock standards. There was oligohydramnios, with a maximum vertical pool of 13.4 mm. Despite suboptimal views from oligohydramnios, fetal anatomy remained unremarkable.

A 1-year-old girl presented with fever for 3 days. Three weeks earlier she had flu-like symptoms. There were no respiratory or abdominal complaints. Vital signs were normal. Examination showed left chest asymmetry with diminished breath sounds and a palpable spleen. Laboratory studies revealed WBC 3800/μL (68% lymphocytes, 25% neutrophils), platelets 87 000/μL, MCV 76 fL, and MCH 25 pg. Arterial blood gas was unremarkable. Cytogenetic analysis was 46,XX. Bone marrow biopsy showed increased megakaryocytes without metastatic or immature cells. Chest radiograph demonstrated a left diaphragmatic hernia with rightward mediastinal shift. Ultrasonography confirmed splenomegaly (10 cm).

A 71-year-old man with atrial fibrillation and degenerative mitral valve disease presented for elective mitral valve repair and biatrial Maze procedure. Preoperative transthoracic echocardiography showed bi-leaflet prolapse with severe mitral regurgitation and a markedly dilated left atrium (volume index, 80 ml/m2); right and left ventricular function were normal. Preoperative coronary angiography demonstrated right coronary dominance without obstructive coronary artery disease or pulmonary hypertension. 

Intraoperatively, a quadrangular resection of a flail P2 segment, sliding plasty, and placement of a 38 mm posterior annuloplasty band were performed via left atriotomy. After removal of the aortic cross-clamp and during partial separation from cardiopulmonary bypass, transesophageal echocardiography revealed an expanding double density along the posterior wall of the left atrium with a jet originating at the posterior mitral annulus flowing into a suspected false lumen.

A 57‐year‐old woman with a history of HIV infection who had discontinued antiretroviral therapy 2 years earlier presented with a 2-week history of progressive dyspnoea and cough. Her oxygen saturation was 90% on room air, and her temperature was 37.6°C. A CT pulmonary angiogram showed diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities with well-demarcated peripheral sparing. Laboratory studies revealed an HIV viral load of 4.2 × 10^6 copies/mL, a CD4 count of 50 cells/mm^3, and an induced sputum PCR for Pneumocystis jirovecii of 2.8 × 10^8 copies/mL. She was treated with intravenous trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole and high-dose prednisone, with clinical recovery. After 3 weeks, she was switched to prophylactic dosing of trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, and bictegravir–emtricitabine–tenofovir alafenamide was initiated on hospital day 16. She was discharged on day 18 and prednisone was stopped after 20 days.

Twenty-one days after starting antiretroviral therapy, she returned with a 5-day history of cough and post-tussive emesis but no dyspnoea. Her temperature was 38.1°C and oxygen saturation was 96% on room air. Rigours occurred on day 2 of admission. A high-resolution CT scan revealed new bilateral consolidation in regions that had previously shown ground-glass opacities, with preservation of the previous boundaries and persistent peripheral sparing, as well as new interlobular septal thickening and bilateral pleural effusions. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid contained 9.3 × 10^5 copies/mL Pneumocystis jirovecii with a lymphocyte predominance of 23%; viral cytopathic changes and fungal hyphae were absent. Tests for cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, and other respiratory viruses were negative. Fluorescence microscopy did not reveal acid-fast bacilli, and subsequent mycobacterial and fungal cultures remained negative. Repeat HIV viral load had fallen to 43 copies/mL. A review of her medications showed no drugs associated with drug-induced pneumonitis.

A 3-year-old boy presented to the pediatric emergency department with a 3-day history of fever and shortness of breath and a 2-day history of productive cough. He had no chills or hemoptysis. His mother reported frequent colds and multiple previous pneumonic infections since infancy. There was no history of travel, sick contacts, smoking in the home, or pets. Family history was notable for a sister diagnosed incidentally with a right-sided heart; his parents were unrelated and healthy.

On arrival, he was in severe respiratory distress. Temperature was 38 °C, respiratory rate 50/min, heart rate 120/min, blood pressure 110/60 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 75% on room air. He was diaphoretic with nasal flaring and marked suprasternal, intercostal, and subcostal retractions. The cardiac apex was palpated in the right fourth intercostal space with heart sounds best heard on the right. Lung auscultation revealed diminished air entry bilaterally, diffuse wheezes, coarse crackles at both bases, and rhonchi in the upper lobes. Ear and throat examinations were unremarkable except for Grade 3 tonsillar hypertrophy without signs of acute infection.

A chest radiograph showed dextrocardia with the cardiac apex and aortic arch on the right side, right-sided gastric bubble, and otherwise clear lung fields. Chest CT confirmed dextrocardia and showed no evidence of bronchiectasis. Abdominal ultrasound and CT demonstrated the liver and gallbladder on the left and the spleen on the right, consistent with situs inversus. A CT scan of the paranasal sinuses revealed opacification of the maxillary and ethmoidal sinuses, indicating sinusitis. Electrocardiogram showed inverted P waves in lead I, right axis deviation, and progressive diminution of QRS complexes from V1 to V6. Echocardiography confirmed dextrocardia with normal cardiac chambers and situs inversus of the great vessels.

To exclude other conditions, a sweat chloride test was performed twice and was negative on both occasions. A tuberculin skin test was negative, and serum immunoglobulin levels were within normal limits.

An eight-year-old female spayed Great Dane was presented to the emergency department of a referral hospital after radiographs confirmed gastric dilatation–volvulus. The dog was weak and unwilling to walk. Emergency surgery with an incisional gastropexy was performed. For the procedure, the dog was placed in standard dorsal recumbency and secured to the operating table with four limb ties. Postoperatively, the dog was unwilling to rise and could not be walked frequently overnight due to limited staffing and reluctance to stand.

On the morning after surgery, the patient was reluctant to walk and had mild knuckling of the left hind limb. Two days after presentation, sores were noted on both elbows and a wound on the left hind foot. The dog’s paresis progressed, and she was unable to walk without assistance. 

Neurologic examination revealed:
- Ambulatory to nonambulatory tetraparesis with severe knuckling of the left hind limb  
- Hopping mildly delayed in the left forelimb and severely delayed to absent in the hind limbs  
- Withdrawal reflex decreased in the left hind leg; patellar reflexes, cutaneous trunci, and perineal reflexes were within normal limits  
- Mild caudal lumbar pain on palpation  

Deficits were localized to the left sciatic nerve and C1–C5 spinal cord segments.

A 45‐year‐old man presented with a 4-week history of increasing stridor and difficulty swallowing. He denied haemoptysis, paraesthesia, and numbness. His temperature was 36.6 °C; chest auscultation was clear, with no cutaneous eruptions or peripheral neuropathy. Neck CT showed marked swelling of the epiglottis partially obstructing the airway. Chest CT revealed bilateral multiple nodular consolidations. Laboratory tests demonstrated a white blood cell count of 8500/µL with 85.4% neutrophils, C-reactive protein of 12.1 mg/dL, normal serum creatinine at 0.5 mg/dL, and microscopic haematuria on urinalysis. Testing for PR3-ANCA, MPO-ANCA, and other autoantibodies was negative. Bronchoscopy revealed a swollen epiglottis with whitish nodular lesions; biopsy showed neutrophilic infiltration and necrosis without evidence of vasculitis or granuloma. Special stains for bacteria, acid-fast bacilli, and fungi were negative. A 3-day course of sulbactam/ampicillin did not improve his condition. Video-assisted lung biopsy of a right lower-lobe nodule demonstrated neutrophilic vasculitis; cultures and special stains remained negative, and microscopic haematuria persisted despite a normal creatinine.

A 25-year-old woman presented with a recently noticed right-sided neck mass. She had no prior medical or surgical history. On examination, there was a 4 cm × 4 cm soft, compressible, non-tender, non-pulsatile swelling in the posterior triangle of the right supraclavicular region. The mass appeared when she lay supine or exercised, enlarged with a Valsalva maneuver, and disappeared when she was upright. A Doppler ultrasound demonstrated a well-defined, compressible, cystic lesion measuring 5 cm × 2 cm in the right supraclavicular area, most likely arising from the right internal jugular vein. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed a fusiform, aneurysmal venous tributary in the right lower neck originating from the right internal jugular vein and rejoining it before its junction with the right subclavian vein, measuring 6 cm in length and 4 cm in maximum diameter. There was no compressing mass in the chest or neck, and the superior vena cava was normal.

A 64-year-old Caucasian woman was admitted for treatment of co-occurring major depression, alcohol dependence and lorazepam dependence. Daily alcohol use began ten years earlier; daily lorazepam use began one year earlier. Her medical history included hypothyroidism (on levothyroxine), menopause hormone therapy (17β-estradiol, dydrogesterone), hyperlipidemia (atorvastatin), hypertension (felodipine, metoprolol, lisinopril), aspirin for cardiac prophylaxis, and pantoprazole for gastroesophageal reflux.  

On admission, lorazepam 5–10 mg daily was started to prevent withdrawal. Antidepressant treatment began with mianserin (60 mg daily), with a partial response; venlafaxine was added (up to 450 mg daily) and then switched from mianserin to mirtazapine (up to 75 mg daily). Two months later, depressive remission was achieved on venlafaxine 150 mg and mirtazapine 60 mg daily. Lorazepam was tapered off over six weeks.  

One day after the final lorazepam dose, she developed inattention, psychomotor agitation, anxiety, tangential thoughts and dissociative features consistent with benzodiazepine withdrawal. Orientation remained intact, so delirium was not diagnosed. Lorazepam was reinstated at 3 mg daily, with symptom resolution. After one month on lorazepam 3 mg daily, lorazepam was discontinued without taper and replaced by diazepam 15 mg daily (equivalent dose).  

Within 24 hours of the switch, she became increasingly irritable and agitated, with fluctuating consciousness, impaired attention, disorientation, incomprehensible speech and memory deficits. A diagnosis of benzodiazepine withdrawal delirium was made, and she received lorazepam 4 mg plus haloperidol 4 mg. The acute delirium resolved within hours. Haloperidol was stopped after two weeks; lorazepam 4 mg daily was continued, and she was discharged one month later.

A 30-year-old woman presented with several months of unexplained weight loss. She denied fevers, night sweats, cough, dyspnea, chest pain, or hemoptysis. Her physical examination was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed a well-demarcated, 5.5 × 2.6 cm solid mass along the right paramediastinal border in the right upper lobe, with associated atelectasis. The lesion had an average attenuation of 33 HU. Traversing this segment, a large venous tributary draining into the azygous vein was identified. The thymus was noted to be separate from the mass. The leading diagnostic considerations were mediastinal lymphoma and thymic malignancy, and the radiologist was confident that the finding represented a solid mass.

A 33-year-old woman was admitted for evaluation of persistent fever.   
Twelve days earlier, she had a positive SARS-CoV-2 PCR on nasopharyngeal swab after presenting only with fever of 39°C.  Over the subsequent 10 days, her fever continued, prompting admission on Day 0.  
She had immigrated from Nepal 1 year earlier, lived with her husband, and occasionally served restaurant customers; she denied known exposures to tuberculosis.  
On admission, her temperature was 37.6°C, blood pressure 104/75 mmHg, heart rate 107 bpm, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.  Physical examination, including lung auscultation, was unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL, C-reactive protein 3.33 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 275 IU/L, D-dimer 6.1 μg/mL, with otherwise normal counts and chemistries.  SARS-CoV-2 PCR remained positive.  
A chest radiograph was normal, but computed tomography revealed multiple enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes.  
Deep venous thrombosis of the left femoral vein was identified, and anticoagulation with rivaroxaban was initiated.  Her high fever persisted; therefore, tests for chronic infections—including HIV screening and an interferon-gamma release assay—were performed.

A 40-year-old woman with a history of cutaneous lupus erythematosus, pulmonary sarcoidosis with prior CNS involvement (on methotrexate, infliximab, prednisone, poorly compliant), an unspecified seizure disorder, and recent orthopedic surgeries presented with altered mental status, slurred speech, and possible seizure. She was found soiled in urine and feces.  
On admission: blood pressure 104/66 mm Hg, pulse 97 bpm, respirations 24/min, temperature 36.7 °C. She was confused, disoriented, and had dry mucous membranes. Neurologic examination was unremarkable.  
Initial assessment attributed confusion to UTI (urinalysis positive), and she received broad-spectrum antibiotics and levetiracetam. Continuous EEG showed mild diffuse encephalopathy without epileptogenic focus. Brain MRI demonstrated improvement in prior leptomeningeal enhancement, mild residual enhancement in the posterior fossa, and new 5-mm right parietal infarction.  
Over the next five days, serum sodium rose from 138 mmol/L to 170 mmol/L despite D5W administration. Urine sodium was 48 mEq/L, urine osmolality 113 mOsm/kg, and serum osmolality 335 mOsm/kg, suggesting diabetes insipidus. However, urine output remained low (maximum ≈100 cc/hr).  
A DDAVP stimulation test showed a >100% increase in urine osmolality and >60 mOsm/h sodium excretion, confirming central diabetes insipidus. A pituitary hormone panel revealed: LH 4.8 mU/mL (1–25), FSH 6.1 mU/mL (4.7–21.5), prolactin 23.2 ng/mL (2.0–17.4), free T4 0.6 ng/dL (0.7–1.8), TSH 2.34 µU/mL (0.4–5.5), IGF-I 61 ng/mL (93–278), morning cortisol 26 µg/dL (3.4–26.9), ACTH 19 pg/mL (9–52).  
What is the most likely unifying diagnosis and mechanism for her presentation?

A 23-year-old woman (height 165 cm; weight 67 kg; BMI 24.6 kg/m2) presented with a 2-month history of progressive pelvic pain and tenderness over the symphysis pubis. There was no history of trauma or sports injury. Two weeks before presentation, she developed fever, headache, and myalgia. On examination, there was diffuse tenderness in the lower mid-abdomen and marked tenderness localized to the symphysis pubis.  
Anteroposterior and frog-leg lateral pelvic radiographs showed an ill-defined osteolytic lesion of the right pubic tubercle with preservation of the cortex and no periosteal reaction. MRI of the pelvis demonstrated a well-defined, 3.0 × 4.7 cm expansile cystic lesion abutting the right symphysis pubis, with intermediate signal on T1-weighted images and high signal on T2-weighted and fat-suppressed T2 images, accompanied by bone marrow edema of the right superior and inferior pubic rami and adjacent myositis of the right adductor muscle.  
Laboratory studies revealed a C-reactive protein level of 45.8 mg/L (normal 0–5), an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 120 mm/h (0–20), and a white-blood-cell count of 10,530/mm3 with neutrophil predominance. The patient was immunocompetent, and her lipid profile was within normal limits.

A 4-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of a swelling over his mid-upper back that his parents first noticed when he was 6 months old. The lesion was initially small and painless; 2 months before presentation, he developed a dull aching pain over the area. There was no history of trauma, fever, weight loss, tuberculosis exposure, or similar family illness.

On examination, there was a 2×1-cm firm, well-defined, rounded mass in the subcutaneous plane of the left paraspinal region at the upper thoracic level. The overlying skin was normal, and the mass was non-tender, non-fluctuant, non-reducible, and without local warmth. 

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, were within normal limits. Plain radiographs of the dorsal spine and chest were unremarkable. An ultrasound examination showed a 1.8×1.2-cm anechoic lesion without internal vascularity or calcification, located primarily in the subcutaneous plane with minor extension into the underlying muscle, “giving it an impression of a nerve sheath tumor.”

A 78-year-old woman (ASA physical status 2) with controlled hypertension and no prior anesthesia complications underwent lumbar decompression under general anesthesia. Preoperative blood urea nitrogen, serum electrolytes, and ECG were normal. Intraoperative induction included fentanyl, propofol, and rocuronium; anesthesia was maintained with desflurane per study protocol, and, near the end, she received a propofol infusion (193 mg over 29 minutes). The 140-minute surgery was uneventful. After reversal of neuromuscular blockade, she opened her eyes to commands and demonstrated purposeful movements. She was extubated and transferred to the PACU.

In the PACU she remained unresponsive to verbal and noxious stimuli despite stable vital signs: heart rate 65/min, blood pressure 122/68 mm Hg, SpO₂ 98% on 4 L/min O₂, respiratory rate 8–10/min. Neuromuscular monitoring showed a train-of-four ratio > 0.9. Pupils were equal and reactive to light, with a glassy-eyed stare; she made no resistance to eye opening. Airway, breathing, and circulation were intact. Laboratory tests for electrolytes and blood glucose were obtained. Intravenous naloxone was administered, and a CT scan was initiated. Review of the anesthetic chart and history revealed no drug interactions, renal or hepatic dysfunction, or psychiatric illness. After 90 minutes in the PACU, she gradually regained responsiveness and was transferred when considered adequately awake.

A 36-year-old Caucasian man with known HIV infection for 15 years, off antiretroviral therapy for the past 8 years, presented with a 6-week history of a disseminated skin eruption and joint pains in his hands and feet. He had constitutional symptoms including night sweats, decreased appetite, and fatigue. He denied recent travel, environmental exposures, or sexual encounters and reported a childhood penicillin allergy. 

On examination, he appeared unwell and was mildly tachycardic. Mucous membranes were pink and dry; white adherent plaques were present in the mouth. Cutaneous examination revealed annular, scaly papules and plaques—some ulcerated or crusted—distributed over the trunk, extremities, and face. There was swelling and tenderness of the wrists and ankles; the rest of the examination was noncontributory.

Laboratory studies showed mild pancytopenia (white blood cells 3.4 × 10^3/mm^3, hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, platelets 123 × 10^3/mm^3), a CD4 count of 57 cells/μL, and HIV RNA 365 000 copies/mL. Autoimmune assays (ANA, rheumatoid factor) were negative. A rapid plasma reagin test was positive at 1:64, and Treponema pallidum particle agglutination was confirmatory. Lumbar puncture yielded a negative VDRL. Blood cultures and wound swabs were negative; the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 132 mm/hr.

Punch biopsies of skin lesions showed psoriasiform lichenoid dermatitis. A modified Steiner stain demonstrated spirochetes within the epidermis. Plain radiographs revealed cortical irregularities of the hands, feet, forearms, and legs without joint erosion. Follow-up bone scintigraphy showed bilateral, extensive polyostotic uptake in the hands, feet, forearms, and tibiae/fibulae.

A 78-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of progressively worsening right cheek swelling, pain, and trismus. He denied any history of facial trauma or fever. His past medical history was notable only for prostate cancer treated with radiation therapy 2 years earlier; he was not on immunosuppressive medications and reported no exposures to birds or soil. On examination, there was marked swelling of the right zygomatic region with severe spontaneous pain and tenderness; maximal interincisal opening was approximately 2 cm. Laboratory studies revealed a C-reactive protein level of 0.45 mg/dL (reference range, 0–0.14), a white blood cell count of 6700/mm3 with 54.4% neutrophils, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 35 mm/h (reference range, 2–10). Routine chemistries, including alkaline phosphatase, calcium, phosphorous, glucose, HbA1c, and liver enzymes, were within normal limits. Serologic tests for hepatitis B and C were negative. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the face demonstrated a 30-mm lesion in the right zygomatic arch with bone destruction, surrounding contrast enhancement, and extension into the subcutaneous cheek tissue without calcification or periosteal reaction. These findings raised concern for a malignant tumor of the zygomatic bone or a focal abscess with atypical features.

A 22‐year‐old woman presented with pain in her right shoulder. Radiographs of the proximal humerus showed a poorly defined, irregular osteolytic lesion. MRI demonstrated low signal intensity on T1‐weighted images and heterogeneous low- to high-signal intensity on T2‐weighted images. An open biopsy established the diagnosis of Ewing sarcoma. Routine laboratory studies were unremarkable except for a mildly elevated C-reactive protein level of 0.83 mg/mL; serum albumin remained normal, and her weight was maintained during treatment. She underwent neoadjuvant chemotherapy with vincristine, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, and etoposide, followed by surgical resection and joint replacement. Total cumulative doses included doxorubicin 375 mg/m², cyclophosphamide 10 800 mg/m², vincristine 1.8 mg/body, ifosfamide 72 000 mg/m², and etoposide 4000 mg/m². At the completion of chemotherapy, a routine chest CT revealed a new 5-mm solitary nodule in the right upper lobe, which had not been present on initial staging CT. A follow-up CT six weeks later showed persistence of the solitary nodule. Given the high metastatic potential of Ewing sarcoma, surgical resection of the lung lesion was undertaken.

A 59-year-old man with a history of smoking and vitiligo was admitted with a 2-month history of 6-kg weight loss and persistent high fevers. He had been discharged 2 days earlier with a diagnosis of right basal bronchopneumonia after treatment with azithromycin, amoxicillin–clavulanate, and clarithromycin; at that time, his white-cell count was 15,000/mL and C-reactive protein level was 15 mg/dL. The day after discharge, he returned with recurrent high fever and right leg pain. Ultrasound studies showed a 1.9-cm hepatic cyst and inflammatory thickening of the right leg. High-resolution chest CT revealed inflammatory interstitial thickening with subpleural distribution, traction bronchiectasis in both lower lobes, and small subpleural emphysematous bullae in the upper lobes. In the emergency department, his white-cell count was 22,220/mL (89% neutrophils) and CRP was 23.1 mg/dL; piperacillin–tazobactam and levofloxacin were begun.  

On transfer to our ward, laboratory studies confirmed leukocytosis (22,220/mL, 89.4% neutrophils), CRP 22.7 mg/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 76 mm/hr, and low serum iron (17 μg/dL); liver and kidney function were normal. Fever persisted despite antibiotics. Extensive microbiologic testing — including bacterial cultures, urinary antigens, viral serologies, Quantiferon test, and PCR for respiratory viruses on bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) — was negative. BAL cytology showed no malignant cells or mycobacteria; lymphocyte phenotyping revealed a predominance of CD4+CD103+ T cells. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed no vegetations. Serum electrophoresis revealed hypogammaglobulinemia (IgG 464 mg/dL), and peripheral-blood immunophenotyping demonstrated a 1.5% monoclonal B-cell population deemed clinically insignificant. Autoimmune serologies, including ANA, ANCA, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, and C1qIgG, were all negative; complement levels were normal except for a mildly elevated C3. Pulmonary function tests were normal except for a mild reduction in DLCO (67% predicted). PET–CT showed bilateral hilar hypermetabolic foci (SUVmax 3.8 right, 4.3 left) and activity in the Barety space (SUVmax 3.4) consistent with an inflammatory or infectious process; there was reactive skeletal uptake. The patient remained febrile with elevated inflammatory markers, and antibiotics were discontinued given the lack of respiratory symptoms and negative infectious workup.

A 40-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after being struck by a vehicle while intoxicated. On arrival, he was deeply drunk and unresponsive to history; initial vital signs were within normal limits (BP 108/69 mm Hg; HR 117 beats/min; RR 30 breaths/min; T 36.0 °C; O₂ sat 94% on room air), and the physical examination revealed no deformity or tenderness. Once alert, he reported lumbar pain and exhibited paresthesia over the entire left foot with left foot drop. Motor testing of the left lower extremity showed strength of 4/5 for knee flexion, 3/5 for knee extension, 4/5 for ankle plantarflexion, and 1/5 for ankle dorsiflexion; strength was 5/5 on the right. Deep-tendon reflexes were 2+ bilaterally. Laboratory studies, including a coagulation panel (INR 0.96) and platelet count (590,000/μL), were normal. Plain radiographs demonstrated fractures of the left inferior pubic ramus, bilateral superior pubic rami, left sacral ala, and spinous processes of T2–T8. Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbosacral spine revealed a fracture with bone marrow edema involving the left sacral body and ala (S1–S2) and an abnormal collection in the spinal canal at the L5–S1 level.

A 39-year-old Caucasian woman presented with an eight-month history of nonproductive cough and progressive dyspnea. Initial chest radiography was interpreted as pneumonia and treated with cefuroxime without improvement. High-resolution CT of the chest showed focal parenchymal infiltrates with ground-glass opacities and septal thickening in a peripheral distribution, predominantly in the lower lobes. Transbronchial biopsy revealed scant bronchial fragments with adjacent alveolar collapse and a minimal focus of interstitial inflammatory infiltrate. Prednisone 20 mg daily was started.

Twelve months after symptom onset, she was evaluated for worsening dyspnea on minimal exertion and systemic symptoms including diffuse pain in arms and legs, fingertip burning, fatigue, sleep disturbance, Raynaud phenomenon, xerostomia, and xerophthalmia. She had a personal and family history of Hashimoto thyroiditis. Vital signs: blood pressure 90/60 mmHg; heart rate 96 bpm; respiratory rate 20/min. Examination showed bilateral basal crackles without skin thickening or arthritis; oroscopic examination was normal. Laboratory tests revealed elevated ESR with negative CRP, normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 9.8–13.3 g/dL), intermittent lymphopenia, negative ANA, RF, anti–Scl-70, anti–Jo-1, anti–RNP, anti–SS-A, anti–SS-B, and c-ANCA, with p-ANCA 1:20. Chlamydia pneumoniae IgG was 1:512 (IgM negative); Mycoplasma serology was negative. Salivary gland biopsy was normal. Nailfold capillaroscopy demonstrated moderate capillary ectasia and focal devascularization consistent with an early scleroderma pattern. A diagnosis of early systemic sclerosis was made, and a 1 g pulse of cyclophosphamide was planned.

Three weeks later, she developed fever to 39°C and dyspnea at rest and was admitted. On presentation she was tachypneic (RR 40/min), hypoxemic (PaO2 48.4 mmHg; SpO2 88.5%), and had bilateral basal crackles. By hospital day 3 she developed respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation. Repeat chest CT showed diffuse ground-glass opacities with peripheral consolidation and air bronchograms in both lungs, mild pleural thickening, and scattered calcified nodules; no pleural effusion. Echocardiography showed pulmonary artery pressure of 31 mmHg. Blood and urine cultures were negative, serologies for hepatitis B and C were negative, and CRP rose to 147 mg/L. The pulmonologist considered nonspecific interstitial pneumonia, Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia, and viral pneumonia (CMV, adenovirus, herpes 1 and 2). On hospital day 4 she underwent open lung biopsy (segmentectomy of the right middle and lower lobes), and tissue cultures for bacteria, mycobacteria, and fungi were all negative.

A 60-year-old Caucasian man was referred for bilateral painless visual decline over several months. He had no systemic symptoms and a history of a self-sealing penetrating wire injury to the left eye 5 years earlier. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/63 in the right eye (RE) and counting fingers at 50 cm in the left eye (LE); intraocular pressures were 13 and 20 mmHg, respectively. Examination of the RE revealed early lens sclerosis and findings consistent with chronic central serous chorioretinopathy, explaining the limited acuity. Slit-lamp examination of the LE showed two ovoid, nonpigmented structures affecting about 180° of the inferior iris circumference, displacing the iris anteriorly toward the corneal endothelium. Ultrasound biomicroscopy demonstrated that the lesion dissected the iris stroma, with a mildly to highly echogenic outer layer, central vacuolation, and a hyporeflective inner layer; the iris root and ciliary body were unremarkable, and the lens had heterogeneous content without obvious capsule breaks. Anterior-segment OCT visualized only the cornea and the anterior wall of the dilated iris structure. Orbital MRI confirmed an iris deformation in the LE measuring 9 × 7 × 3 mm, with mild contrast enhancement. Complementary blood tests and systemic imaging to evaluate for inflammatory, infectious, or metastatic disease (including sarcoidosis, syphilis, tuberculosis, chest CT, and abdominal ultrasound) were negative.
