A 36-year-old Caucasian man presented after an episode of presyncope. He had sudden dizziness in the bathroom, lay down for 15 minutes, and then improved. There was no history of seizures, incontinence, weight loss, night sweats, or high-grade fever, but he noted chills a few hours earlier.

One week earlier, he had been admitted elsewhere for chest pain; cardiac catheterization was negative, but abdominal ultrasound showed ascites, prompting referral.  

In the emergency department, vital signs showed mild tachycardia. Examination revealed a soft grade II/VI systolic ejection murmur at the left sternal border and splinter hemorrhages under the nails; the remainder of the exam, including neurologic assessment, was normal.  

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a 0.8 × 0.6 cm vegetation on the mitral valve. CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed multiple lytic bone lesions, splenic and renal infarcts, malignant-appearing ascites, and omental caking.  

He was started on intravenous penicillin G and gentamicin for presumptive bacterial endocarditis, and a hypercoagulability panel was obtained. The panel showed elevated D-dimer and LDH, heterozygosity for an MTHFR mutation, and a positive lupus anticoagulant; other tests, including anticardiolipin antibodies, antinuclear antibodies, and anti–β₂-glycoprotein antibodies, were normal.  

Tumor markers revealed elevated carcinoembryonic antigen and CA 19-9, while alpha-fetoprotein and prostate-specific antigen were within normal limits.

A 60‐year‐old carpenter presented with sudden onset of right hip pain. He had been taking oral prednisolone (maximum dose 50 mg daily; average 18 mg daily) for 10 months for dermatomyositis. He denied any trauma or alcohol abuse. Two weeks before presentation, he felt acute right hip pain while half‐sitting and lifting a 10 kg log. 

Vital signs were within normal limits. Routine laboratory tests were unremarkable. On examination, right hip motion was slightly limited (flexion 90°, abduction 30°, adduction 10°, internal rotation 0°, external rotation 40°). The Harris hip score was 75/100. 

Dual X‐ray absorptiometry showed a lumbar spine BMD of 0.786 g/cm2 (T score −1.9), right femoral head 1.697 g/cm2, right femoral neck 0.667 g/cm2, left femoral head 1.693 g/cm2, and left femoral neck 0.460 g/cm2. 

A plain radiograph of the right hip was unremarkable. On T1‐ and T2‐weighted MRI of the right hip, there was a thick, very‐low‐signal‐intensity band at the medial femoral neck and a linear low‐signal‐intensity band extending to the intertrochanteric area. T1‐weighted MRI of the left femoral head showed a deep wedge‐shaped low‐intensity band. 

Bone scintigraphy demonstrated increased uptake in the medial subcapital area of the right femur and decreased (“cold”) uptake in both femoral heads. Tomosynthesis and CT of the right hip revealed a sclerotic linear lesion in the medial subcapital region.

A 56-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of gradually worsening horizontal and vertical diplopia, pronounced photosensitivity, and intermittent headaches. She had undergone bilateral silicone breast augmentation 10 years earlier for cosmetic reasons and reported no history of facial or body filler injections. 

On examination, she had restricted extraocular motility in all directions in the right eye with normal motility in the left eye. Diplopia occurred in all gaze directions except primary position. Visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes; slit-lamp and funduscopic examinations were unremarkable. She had 2 mm of right-sided proptosis. The remainder of her general examination was normal.

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood cell count with differential, electrolytes, angiotensin-converting enzyme level, rheumatoid factor, C-reactive protein, and thyroid hormone levels, were all within normal limits.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the orbits demonstrated enlargement of the right superior and lateral rectus muscles, the right inferior oblique muscle, and the anterior portion of the right inferior rectus muscle, along with slight enlargement of the right lacrimal gland. There was also diffuse enlargement of the lacrimal gland and rectus muscles in the left orbit.

Positron emission tomography–computed tomography with ^18F-FDG showed pathological metabolic activity in both extraocular muscles and lacrimal glands, in a left retromandibular lymph node, multiple right axillary lymph nodes, along the right common and internal carotid arteries, in the right thoracic wall, the right pulmonary hilum, left pelvic lymph nodes, and the internal oblique muscle of the abdominal wall. Notably, there was prominent FDG uptake around the right silicone breast implant.

Subsequent mammography and ultrasound confirmed rupture of the right breast implant with intracapsular silicone leakage and silicone deposition in the axillary lymph nodes.

A 66-year-old Italian woman was evaluated for a two-month history of low-grade fever, malaise, fatigue, night sweats, decreased appetite, and a 4-kg weight loss. During the past month she noted painful enlargement of right lateral cervical lymph nodes. Her medical history was notable only for hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. She denied any history of tuberculosis or known exposure.

On admission, vital signs were: temperature 37.5 °C, heart rate 90 bpm, blood pressure 110/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. Physical examination revealed two fixed, painful right laterocervical lymph nodes; there was no hepatosplenomegaly or other lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory studies showed:  
• C-reactive protein 20 mg/L (normal <2.9)  
• Lactate dehydrogenase 705 U/L (normal <450)  
• Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 54 mm/h  
Thyroid function tests and tumor markers were within normal limits. Antinuclear antibody, anti–double-stranded DNA, and rheumatoid factor were negative. Serologic tests for HIV, cytomegalovirus IgM, herpesvirus IgM, Epstein–Barr virus IgM, Brucella, and Toxoplasma were all negative. A Quantiferon assay was negative. Chest radiography was unremarkable.

Ultrasonography of the neck demonstrated right-sided hypoechoic laterocervical lymph nodes (up to 1.7 cm) and a 1.0-cm submental node, each with low peripheral flow, cortical thickening, and hilar eccentricity. Contrast-enhanced total-body CT confirmed these localized cervical lymphadenopathies without other abnormalities.

Given the persistence of symptoms and nondiagnostic noninvasive studies, an excisional biopsy of the largest right laterocervical lymph node was planned.

A 7-year-old boy presented with a 6-year history of a gradually enlarging neck swelling. The mass was first noted at 6 months of age. At 3 years old, an excisional biopsy diagnosed lymphangioma, and he underwent two sessions of sclerotherapy without resolution of the mass.

On examination, there was a large, non-tender mass over the anterior and right lateral neck, extending posteriorly to cover the entire right side. The overlying skin and upper chest showed a red-purple discoloration with swelling of the right arm. The arterial pulses in the right arm were weaker than those on the left. A palpable thrill and a continuous machinery murmur were heard in the right supraclavicular area. The airway was Mallampati class III, with mildly restricted neck flexion and extension. There was no fever or signs of acute infection.

A differential diagnosis of arteriovenous malformation and enlarged lymph node was raised, and a computed tomography angiogram was planned.

An 80-year-old woman with diabetes and hypertension was brought to the emergency department by ambulance for altered mental status. Her family reported a rapid onset of worsening lethargy that began shortly after she awoke. En route, emergency medical services noted tachycardia and hypotension. On arrival, she was somnolent but arousable to voice and unable to provide a history.

Vital signs: temperature 38.4 °C; heart rate 128 beats/min; blood pressure 100/64 mm Hg; respiratory rate 32 breaths/min; oxygen saturation 97% on room air.

Physical examination of the left lower extremity revealed mottled skin with intact dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses; no crepitus or bullae; the entire extremity was tender to palpation, especially in the groin and proximal calf.

Laboratory studies: white cell count 12.2×10^9/L; venous lactate 9.8 mmol/L; serum creatinine 3.05 mg/dL (baseline 1.00); sodium 140 mmol/L; glucose 167 mg/dL; venous blood gas pH 7.21, pCO2 32 mm Hg, HCO3– 13 mmol/L. Blood cultures were obtained.

Plain radiographs of the left lower leg showed mild soft-tissue edema without gas in the tissue planes.

Point-of-care ultrasonography of the left calf demonstrated thickened subcutaneous tissue with a fluid collection >4 mm superficial to the deep fascial layer in the superficial posterior compartment. Distal to the popliteal fossa, deep to the fascial layer, there was an anechoic fluid pocket with swirling on compression. The gastrocnemius muscle exhibited abnormal sonographic architecture.

Noncontrast CT of the left lower extremity revealed soft-tissue swelling, subcutaneous fatty stranding, and mildly enlarged inguinal lymph nodes with a possible small hematoma.

A 38-year-old Filipino nurse presented with a one-year history of right-sided neck pain, right otalgia, and odynophagia. Initial examination revealed a right tonsillar cyst but no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. Neck ultrasonography showed enlarged right cervical lymph nodes. Tonsillar cyst biopsy demonstrated chronic tonsillitis with dilated crypts. 

Two weeks later, she returned with uncontrolled right facial pain. A repeat ultrasound noted a mildly enlarged right parotid gland and larger right-sided reactive cervical lymph nodes. MRI of the head and neck showed a 3.8 cm × 2.5 cm × 1.2 cm mass encasing the right internal carotid artery just below the skull base, along with smaller lymph nodes at level V. 

Fine-needle aspiration of the level V nodes revealed atypical cells, and low-grade lymphoma could not be excluded. An excisional biopsy of these nodes was planned for definitive diagnosis.

A 39-year-old Chinese woman was admitted to the intensive care unit with acute pancreatitis after presenting three hours earlier with sudden abdominal pain. Three hours after admission, she had a brief generalized convulsion lasting approximately 10 seconds that resolved spontaneously. Fifteen minutes later, she reported complete loss of vision in both eyes. An ophthalmologic examination revealed no abnormalities.

Her history was notable for two prior episodes of pancreatitis. She also had untreated hypertension and hyperlipidemia, and a history of anxiety treated intermittently with propranolol, alprazolam, and long-term venlafaxine. She denied other systemic, infectious, or psychiatric illnesses.

On examination, her blood pressure was 145/77 mmHg, and other vital signs were within normal limits. She was alert and oriented. Pupils were equal, 3 mm in diameter, and reactive to light, but she was unable to see objects or count fingers at 30 cm, although she could perceive light. Optokinetic nystagmus was absent, and fundoscopic examination was normal. Neurologic examination of cranial nerves, motor and sensory function, reflexes, and coordination was unremarkable. There were no meningeal signs.

Laboratory studies on admission showed a normal complete blood count except for a neutrophil count of 8.68×10^9/L (normal 2–7.71). Liver function tests, procalcitonin, D-dimer, immunologic and thyroid panels were normal. Hepatitis A, B, and C serologies, syphilis, and HIV tests were negative. Lipid profile revealed severe hypertriglyceridemia (78.68 mmol/L; normal 0.34–2.30) and elevated total cholesterol (10.62 mmol/L; normal 3.9–6.46). Electrolytes showed K^+ 3.03 mmol/L, Mg^2+ 0.67 mmol/L, Ca^2+ 1.76 mmol/L, and CRP 277 mg/L (normal 0–5.0). Renal function and serum amylase were normal on admission; on day 2, creatinine rose to 105.5 µmol/L (normal 41.0–73.0) and amylase to 466 U/L (normal 0–150).

Abdominal CT on admission confirmed pancreatic swelling. Given the acute cortical blindness, a noncontrast head CT and head and neck CT angiography were performed, showing no intracranial hemorrhage, arterial occlusion, or vascular malformation. After excluding hemorrhage, she received intravenous thrombolysis with recombinant tissue plasminogen activator. Three hours later, a brain MRI demonstrated no apparent abnormality.

A 59-year-old woman with a history of hypertension, tobacco abuse, coronary artery disease, and prior percutaneous coronary intervention underwent elective coronary angiography via the right radial artery. A 5-French Jacky catheter was used for the left coronary system and a 6-French Judkins Right 4 catheter for the right coronary system. The procedure was reported as uncomplicated, and the patient was transferred to recovery in stable condition.

Within minutes, she developed midsternal chest pain and odynophagia. Vital signs remained stable. A stat electrocardiogram showed no new ischemic changes, and a bedside transthoracic echocardiogram was unremarkable. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest revealed an ill-defined fluid collection in the superior mediastinum. The radiology report also noted an aberrant right subclavian artery coursing posterior to the trachea and esophagus. An esophagram was performed and showed no evidence of esophageal perforation or intrinsic esophageal lesion.

A 69-year-old man with stage IIIB follicular lymphoma, atrial fibrillation, and pulmonary sarcoidosis presented with two months of progressive dysarthria and right-sided weakness. He had completed six cycles of rituximab and bendamustine one year earlier for lymphoma. MRI of the brain showed multiple confluent T2-weighted FLAIR hyperintensities in the inferior frontal lobes and left corona radiata, and vascular imaging demonstrated no flow-limiting stenosis, occlusion, or aneurysm. Admission laboratory tests, including CBC, metabolic panel, rheumatologic markers (ANA negative; ANCA titer <1:20; complement C3 and C4 normal), inflammatory markers (CRP 0.16 mg/dL; ESR 17 mm/hr), and ACE level (27 mcg/L), were within normal limits. HIV and HCV screens were nonreactive; immunoglobulin levels were normal; syphilis and Lyme serologies were negative. Evaluation for lymphoma recurrence—including beta2-microglobulin, LDH, PET scan, and skin biopsy—revealed no evidence of disease. Lumbar puncture showed clear fluid with normal cell counts, glucose of 57 mg/dL, protein of 38 mg/dL, nonreactive VDRL, and negative JC virus PCR (<500 copies/mL). Empirical high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone yielded no improvement. A repeat MRI showed mild enlargement of nonenhancing confluent subcortical and periventricular T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in the left corona radiata and right temporal lobe with associated restricted diffusion and scattered punctate enhancement.

A 40-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of a vulvar growth characterized by multiple nodules with sinus openings and yellowish-white discharge. Culture of the discharge grew Staphylococcus, but several courses of antibiotics led to no improvement. She had an incomplete treatment course for pulmonary tuberculosis 15 years earlier. She denied any premarital or extramarital sexual relationships. Menstrual cycles were regular, and she had two living children. 

On examination, there was a hypertrophied, cauliflower-like mass covering the entire labia majora. Bilateral inguinal lymph nodes were discrete and nontender. Pelvic ultrasonography showed normal uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries. Routine blood and biochemical tests were within normal limits. 

A partial vulvectomy was performed. The specimen measured 9 × 4 × 2.5 cm, with a nodular skin surface containing sinus openings. The cut surface was pale-white, glistening, predominantly solid, with tiny blood-filled capillary-sized vascular spaces. 

Microscopic examination revealed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia of the epidermis; a loose, edematous dermis with fibrocollagenous and fibrovascular tissue and mononuclear cell infiltration; focal myxoid areas; and granulomas composed of epithelioid cells and Langhans giant cells surrounded by lymphocytes, plasma cells, and histiocytes. Ziehl–Neelsen staining for acid-fast bacilli was negative.

A 68-year-old man presented with a 6-day history of intense retrosternal pain radiating to the dorsum and left arm, accompanied by fever. His medical history was notable only for hypertension, treated with olmesartan 20 mg daily, and headaches. On admission, he was hypertensive (162/81 mmHg) and febrile (38.2°C). Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. Chest radiography and electrocardiogram were normal. Laboratory studies showed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (81 mm) and C-reactive protein (9.2 mg/dL); myocardial necrosis markers were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated mild pericardial thickening, and acute pericarditis was diagnosed; he was discharged on a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug.

He returned 2 days later with persistent symptoms and continued elevation of acute-phase reactants (ESR 82 mm, CRP 11.1 mg/dL). Myocardial necrosis markers and D-dimer levels remained normal. He was admitted for further evaluation. Serologic and virologic tests excluded a broad range of infections (including tuberculosis, syphilis, Brucella, Rickettsia, Salmonella, hepatitis B and C, HIV, influenza, parainfluenza, adenovirus, and Coxsackie A and B). Blood and urine cultures were negative. Autoantibody tests (antinuclear, anti-dsDNA, ANCA, antiphospholipid, anti-citrulline, and rheumatoid factor) were negative; angiotensin converting enzyme levels were normal. A repeat echocardiogram and abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable. Under NSAID therapy, his symptoms and inflammatory markers improved, and he was discharged.

Over the next 6 months, he experienced recurrent chest pain, lower-limb claudication, headaches, and worsening hypertension (managed with olmesartan plus hydrochlorothiazide). He then presented with a 12-day history of fever and severe headaches. Laboratory studies revealed ESR 120 mm, CRP 11.4 mg/dL, normochromic normocytic anemia (Hb 11.6 g/dL), and hypoalbuminemia (albumin 3.0 g/dL). Chest radiograph, transthoracic echocardiogram, and head CT scan were normal. A temporal artery biopsy was performed and was negative for vasculitis.

A 12-year-old boy from Yemen presented with a 6-month history of increasing mobility of his teeth. His deciduous teeth erupted normally but were exfoliated by age 3. By age 10, multiple permanent teeth had been extracted because of mobility, and he now reports mobility of his remaining permanent dentition. His parents are consanguineous, and his 11-year-old brother has had similar dental problems.

On examination, there were bilateral, well-demarcated, hyperkeratotic plaques on the palms and soles; the knees and elbows were spared. Intraoral examination showed only a subset of permanent teeth present in both the maxilla and mandible. Several of these teeth exhibited flaring and mobility, with severe gingival inflammation, thick plaque accumulation, and deep periodontal pockets. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated alveolar bone loss around the affected teeth; third-molar buds were visible in bony crypts with normal crown development and no other bony abnormalities.

A 49-year-old woman with hypertension, prior coronary bypass graft, and laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 3 years earlier presented with 3 days of intermittent abdominal pain. The pain began in the right lower quadrant, became diffuse, and radiated to her back. She noted dark, loose stools with transient relief after defecation. On the morning of presentation, her pain turned constant and was accompanied by several episodes of non-bloody, non-bilious vomiting. 

In the emergency department, she was afebrile with blood pressure 181/88 mmHg, heart rate 86, and weight loss from 108 kg (BMI 37.6) pre–bypass to 72.1 kg (BMI 24.9) now. Abdominal examination revealed poorly localized tenderness. Laboratory testing showed hemoglobin 10.1 mg/dL (baseline 11.6), leukocyte count 21 × 10^9/L, and lactate 1.0 mmol/L. She denied daily NSAID use (two ibuprofen doses this week), smoking, or prior GI bleeding. She remained on aspirin but had stopped clopidogrel over a year earlier; her last EGD and colonoscopy 3 years prior were unremarkable.

While awaiting evaluation, she had an episode of dark-red hematemesis. Gastroenterology was consulted; she was started on a pantoprazole drip and scheduled for EGD the next morning, with initial suspicion of Mallory-Weiss tear. 

A CT angiogram of the abdomen demonstrated dilated loops of small bowel with surrounding inflammatory changes and decreased wall enhancement, findings concerning for bowel ischemia secondary to intussusception versus internal hernia. There was no active contrast extravasation or free air. After surgical evaluation, the patient was taken to the operating room for exploratory laparotomy and intraoperative EGD.

A 28-year-old Indian construction worker with no prior medical or ocular history presented with a 4-day history of right-eye redness, pain, and photophobia. He denied trauma or foreign-body exposure. Systemic, travel, and contact histories were unremarkable. Visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye showed circumciliary injection, 2+ anterior chamber cells without fibrin or hypopyon, and fine keratic precipitates. There were no vitreous cells, and the posterior segment was unremarkable. No relative afferent pupillary defect was present. He was diagnosed with acute non-granulomatous anterior uveitis and started on hourly topical prednisolone acetate and twice-daily 1% atropine. 

Five days later, he returned with increased pain and redness in the right eye. Visual acuity had declined to 20/80. Examination revealed right upper-eyelid ptosis, fibrinous anterior chamber reaction, vitritis, and cystoid macular edema. Given the rapid progression on intensive topical steroids and his construction work, there was concern for occult ocular trauma with infective endophthalmitis. Anterior chamber paracentesis was performed for Gram stain and PCR, and vitreous tap was obtained for bacterial and fungal cultures. Intravitreal antibiotics were administered, and intensive topical antibiotics plus oral ciprofloxacin were started. Computed tomography of the orbits showed no intraocular foreign body but did reveal right lacrimal gland inflammation.

A 65-year-old man with a history of sigmoid diverticulosis presented to his general practitioner with mild, acute left lower quadrant abdominal pain. On examination, there was no abdominal tenderness and routine blood tests were normal. He was diagnosed with mild sigmoid diverticulitis and discharged with oral antibiotics. Twenty-four hours later, he returned to the emergency department with worsening abdominal pain, fever of 38.1°C, and nausea. He reported a history suggestive of possible intestinal malrotation. On examination, localized periumbilical and left lower quadrant tenderness was noted. Laboratory tests showed a normal white blood cell count and an elevated C-reactive protein level of 52 mg/L. Abdominal computed tomography revealed complete intestinal malrotation and an inflamed diverticulum containing a calculus in the left upper quadrant. The appendix was located in the left lower quadrant, and there were no radiological signs of acute appendicitis.

A 52-year-old man with a history of appendectomy presented with sudden-onset periumbilical cramping pain. The pain persisted despite oral medication, and one week later he was referred to the hospital. He remained on a liquid diet and had no vomiting. On examination, his pulse was 108 beats/min, blood pressure 140/80 mmHg, and temperature 37.2 °C. He had mild abdominal distention and tenderness without external hernia. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 10.2 × 10^3/µL and a C-reactive protein level of 0.12 mg/dL.  
Multidetector CT with contrast demonstrated signs of small-bowel obstruction, with two closely arranged constricted segments of ileum in the left pelvic space forming a short closed-loop sign on axial and sagittal images. The sigmoid colon was collapsed, oriented ventral to dorsal, and displaced to the right of the closed loop. Between the ascending and descending limbs of the sigmoid colon, the mesentery coursed from right to left, and proximal small bowel was dilated to the right of the sigmoid colon. Routine sagittal MPR images revealed narrow belt-shaped fluid retention at the tip of the incarcerated loop alongside the psoas muscle.

An 83-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of right knee pain and instability. Twenty years earlier he had bilateral total knee replacements; on the right side he underwent two subsequent revisions at approximately 5 and 10 years after the primary procedure (operative records unavailable). He walked with a limp, using a cane, and demonstrated clinical varus instability of the right knee. There was no erythema, warmth, drainage, or systemic symptoms. Neurovascular examination of the limb was normal. Routine laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level, were within normal limits. A preoperative radiograph of the right knee showed a long-stem revision total knee prosthesis (LINK rotating-hinge, version 01) with apparent hinge breakage and varus malalignment; the distal femur and proximal tibia appeared osteoporotic, and multiple metaphyseal screws were noted in the tibial component.

An 87-year-old right-hand-dominant woman presented with a 2-year history of right wrist pain and swelling. She denied any trauma to the wrist. Two years prior, she had been hospitalized for severe pneumonia; in the months that followed, she noted throbbing wrist discomfort with occasional sharp pains. Bracing, NSAIDs, and tramadol provided no relief.

Previous radiographs revealed chondrocalcinosis of the wrist and first carpometacarpal joint osteoarthritis. MRI showed extensor and flexor tenosynovitis with multiple rice bodies and cystic changes. Chest radiographs demonstrated a calcified granuloma at the right lung base. She had no history of immunosuppression.

On examination, there was non-tender, boggy swelling of the volar wrist measuring 8×5 cm proximal to the wrist crease and a 4×2 cm dorsal swelling over the fifth and sixth extensor compartments. ESR was 51 mm/hr and CRP 16.8 mg/L. CBC, metabolic panel, creatine phosphokinase, uric acid, and a basic rheumatoid panel were all within normal limits.

Given persistent symptoms and imaging findings, she was scheduled for radical synovectomy of both dorsal and volar wrist compartments. At the time of surgery, the working differential diagnosis was chondrocalcinosis versus an atypical bacterial infection. Synovectomy was performed and specimens were sent for fungal, aerobic, anaerobic, acid-fast bacilli staining, and Lowenstein-Jensen cultures.

A 35-year-old Russian woman presented with fatigue, chest pain, joint pain, and dyspnea. One year and ten months before her first Pfizer SARS-CoV-2 vaccination, she was hospitalized for three days with presyncope, palpitations, and a high burden of premature ventricular contractions (PVCs). Three weeks after her second vaccination, she redeveloped lightheadedness, fatigue, frequent presyncope, shortness of breath, and chest pain and was admitted with a high PVC burden. Cardiac magnetic resonance showed borderline cardiomegaly with left ventricular enlargement but no infarct, fibrosis, or amyloidosis; the ejection fraction was 62.3%. She underwent catheter ablation on two consecutive days, after which symptoms improved. Transthoracic echocardiography then showed trace mitral and tricuspid regurgitation and a small pericardial effusion. Two months later, she was treated with ibuprofen for pericarditis. Three weeks after that, she tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 and subsequently developed recurrent chest pain with movement and breathing, joint pain, and dermatitis that persisted for six months.  
Genetic analysis revealed mutations in six CVD/diabetes susceptibility loci (including APOC1 and CETP) and no variants in immune-system–related genes. Her family history was notable for diabetes, hypertension, and cardiac cirrhosis. The differential diagnosis included long COVID-19, arthritis, and systemic lupus erythematosus.  
Laboratory investigations showed an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:80 with a nuclear homogeneous pattern. A double-stranded DNA antibody test was negative. Liver enzymes (alkaline phosphatase, aspartate transaminase, alanine transaminase) were within normal limits. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (proteinase 3 and myeloperoxidase) were negative. Additional autoantibodies, including cyclic citrullinated peptide (IgG), complements C3 and C4, antiphospholipid antibodies, Sjögren syndrome antigens, and Smith/RNP antibodies, were not detected. Blood tests showed normal hormone and white-cell counts, an LDL cholesterol of 112 mg/dL, and an HDL cholesterol that declined from 79 to 65 mg/dL over the year prior to symptom exacerbation.

A 63-year-old woman presented with recurrent microhematuria. She denied flank pain, episodes of gross hematuria, hypertension, renal trauma, or prior renal instrumentation. On examination, her blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg without abdominal bruit, and the remainder of the physical examination was normal. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. Urinalysis was negative for infection but positive for erythrocytes. Renal ultrasonography revealed a discrete hypoechogenicity in the left upper renal pole. Intravenous pyelography demonstrated an irregular configuration of the upper pole collecting system, which was confirmed on retrograde ureteropyelography. Cystoscopy and ureterorenoscopy showed blood clots in the upper calyceal group but no apparent mass; biopsy of the pericalyceal tissue revealed no malignant cells on cytology or histology. A ureteral stent was placed, and the patient was discharged. Four days later, she was readmitted with hemodynamically significant gross hematuria and a hemoglobin concentration of 70 g/L, requiring transurethral clot evacuation. Duplex sonography and computed tomography angiography revealed multiple arteriovenous fistulas with erosions into the calyceal system.

A child with genetically confirmed progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type 1 underwent an ABO‐compatible living‐related liver transplantation. Pretransplant, there was cirrhosis with portal hypertension, failure to thrive, and intractable pruritus. Postoperatively, immunosuppression was basiliximab induction followed by tacrolimus monotherapy with careful blood‐level monitoring.  

On day 5 posttransplant, the patient developed biopsy‐confirmed acute cellular rejection; echo Doppler of the liver vasculature was normal. She received intravenous methylprednisolone (5 mg/kg/day for 3 days, then taper). By day 7, transaminases had normalized.  

On day 9, a colonic perforation with peritonitis required surgical resection and antibiotics. On day 12, she developed acute respiratory distress syndrome with pleural effusion requiring oxygen and drainage.  

On day 15, after a second rise in liver enzymes and a liver biopsy showing coagulative necrosis and canalicular damage, she received another methylprednisolone pulse (10 mg/kg for 3 days, then taper). Despite stable graft function thereafter, her general condition worsened with increased respiratory distress and high transfusion requirements of platelets and red cells, prompting ICU transfer.  

On day 21, laboratory studies showed:  
• Schistocytes 11.5% on peripheral smear, direct Coombs test negative  
• Hemoglobin 6.4 g/dL, platelets 20 000/mm3  
• Lactate dehydrogenase 585 U/L, haptoglobin <0.1 g/dL  
• Blood urea nitrogen 87 mg/dL  
• ADAMTS13 activity 11%

A 54-year-old man was referred after advanced gastric cancer was detected on an annual health examination. Fifteen years earlier, he had undergone splenectomy and left nephrectomy after a traffic accident. He had no abdominal symptoms. On examination, he had only a left paramedian surgical scar. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and chemistry panel, were within normal limits; hepatitis B and C serologies were negative. Carcinoembryonic antigen was 0.87 ng/mL, and CA 19-9 was 34.0 U/mL. 

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed a Borrmann type 2 lesion at the gastric angle extending into the muscularis propria. Biopsy confirmed moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma (cT2). For staging, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated gastric wall thickening in the antrum, perigastric lymphadenopathy (cN1), a gallstone, and a 3.5 × 1.5 cm mass of splenic tissue in the left subdiaphragmatic area without a vascular pedicle. There was no detectable liver lesion on CT, and PET-CT showed no abnormal uptake in the stomach or liver. 

Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a new 2.5 × 1.7 cm nodular, heterogeneous, hypoechoic lesion with clear margins in segment II of the liver. Superparamagnetic iron oxide–enhanced liver MRI identified a 2.0 × 1.5 cm nodule in segment II that was slightly hyperintense on T2-weighted imaging, hypointense on T1-weighted imaging, and remained hyperintense on the SPIO-enhanced T2-weighted sequence.

A 33-year-old man in otherwise good health presented with a subacute enlargement of a pulsatile mass in the left temporal region. He denied any history of accidental or iatrogenic head injury, headache, or cardiovascular risk factors. On examination, there was a small, nontender, elastic, pulsatile swelling over the upper lateral border of the left orbital arch with slight overlying skin inflammation. Echo–color Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated triphasic flow within the lesion, which was hypoechogenic compared with the surrounding tissue, and a partially occluding, apparently recent thrombus. Three-dimensional CT angiography of the intracranial and extracranial vessels and the aortic arch revealed an 8.4 × 5.7 mm aneurysm of a branch of the left superficial temporal artery (the zygomatic orbital artery). No cerebral aneurysms or aortic arch lesions were detected. Blood tests, including inflammatory markers and autoantibody panels, showed no evidence of systemic arteritis or autoimmune disease.

An 18-year-old boy presented with an 18-month history of persistent right flank and right upper quadrant discomfort, with acute worsening about once per month and exacerbation by large fluid intake. He denied hematuria, dysuria, fever, or urinary tract infections. His medical history was otherwise unremarkable, and there was no family history of genitourinary anomalies. On examination he was afebrile, normotensive, and in no distress; the abdomen was soft and non-tender.

Laboratory testing included a normal esophagogastroduodenoscopy and urinalysis showing calcium oxalate crystals. Renal ultrasound demonstrated cystic spaces and cortical thinning in the lower pole of the right kidney; the upper pole and contralateral kidney were normal. A Tc99m-MAG3 renogram with diuretic washout showed accumulation of tracer in a dilated pelvicalyceal system of the right lower pole with delayed flow, uptake, and excretion (post-Lasix t½ >24 minutes), and slightly delayed uptake and excretion in the upper pole; function was 38.5% right and 61.5% left, with no evidence of obstruction on the left.

Differential diagnoses included ureteropelvic junction obstruction, calyceal diverticulum, cystic kidney disease, malignancy, or other congenital anomalies. Cystoscopy with retrograde pyelogram demonstrated calyceal diverticula and infundibular stenosis in the right kidney; the anatomy was not amenable to stenting. 

To further characterize the anatomy, contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed dilated calyces and diffuse cortical thinning in the lower pole of the right kidney, with a normal right upper pole and no evidence of obstruction or duplication.

A 73-year-old previously well and independent woman was brought to the emergency department with a 2-week history of worsening confusion and new behavioral changes. Her family described vivid visual hallucinations, including seeing men around her bed and searching for her deceased sister. Two weeks prior, she experienced vertigo and a fall without head trauma. She had a history of hypertension, depression, and anxiety, and had recently restarted paroxetine. She took prochlorperazine and doxazosin, denied alcohol or illicit drug use, and had no infective symptoms.

On examination, she was alert (GCS 15), scored 9/10 on the Abbreviated Mental Test, and had blood pressure 160/63 mmHg. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal exams were normal. Neurologically, she had a wide-based gait, veered left on standing, brisk lower-limb reflexes (left>right), left-sided intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesis, and past‐pointing—consistent with a predominantly cerebellar syndrome with some upper motor neuron signs.

Initial blood tests showed CRP 9.8 mg/L (0–7.9), urea 9.0 mmol/L (2.8–7.2), and otherwise normal FBC, U&E, bone profile, LFTs, and TFTs. Urine dipstick was negative. Chest radiograph was normal. Head CT showed no acute intracranial abnormality. Brain MRI reported a few small nonspecific white matter lesions with no intracranial abnormality correlating with her symptoms; no comment was made on the thalamus or basal ganglia.

A 33-year-old previously healthy man was hospitalized for persistent fever and a new rash. Over the past month he had daily fevers up to 39°C with chills, and a nonpruritic pink-purple rash (2–3 cm) appeared on his face and neck one week before admission. He also reported nausea, vomiting, weakness, and a 20 kg weight loss over three months. On examination, temperature was 38.5°C, heart rate 88/min, and blood pressure 110/70 mmHg. No peripheral lymphadenopathy or organomegaly was noted. 

Laboratory studies showed WBC 850/µL (neutrophils 320/µL, lymphocytes 430/µL), hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, platelets 155 000/µL, ESR 48 mm/h, CRP 23 mg/L, AST 58 U/L, ALT 38 U/L, BUN 14 mg/dL, creatinine 0.6 mg/dL. ANA was slightly positive; anti-dsDNA, anti-RO, anti-LA, P-ANCA, and C-ANCA were negative. Serologies for EBV, HIV, parvovirus B19, rubella, measles, mumps, RSV, HHV-6, HHV-8, parainfluenza viruses, and Toxoplasma gondii were negative.

Chest CT revealed multiple 1 cm mediastinal lymph nodes. His neutropenia deepened to 170/µL; empirical meropenem was given without improvement. PET-CT showed multiple hypermetabolic lymph nodes (SUV max 9.7) supra- and infradiaphragmatically, notably in the right axilla and mediastinum. During hospitalization, new axillary and cervical lymph nodes became palpable. Bone marrow biopsy was normal, and he was referred to hematology for further evaluation.

A 74-year-old Caucasian man presented in late June with a 5-day history of nightly fevers, nausea, and hematuria. His medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, gout, and hypothyroidism. 

Five days earlier, he had been evaluated for hematuria and nausea; he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Labs showed creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, WBC 6.9 × 10^9/L, bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, ALT 42 U/L, AST 38 U/L, and ALP 70 U/L. He was discharged with outpatient follow-up.

He returned with persistent fevers. CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed diverticulosis, a 5-mm right lower lobe lung nodule, hiatal hernia, small umbilical hernia, and enlarged prostate. Repeat labs showed creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, ALT 84 U/L, and sodium 132 mmol/L. He was again discharged.

Outpatient labs days later demonstrated worsening renal and liver function: creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, AST 128 U/L, ALT 166 U/L, and total bilirubin 3.9 mg/dL; ESR was 58 mm/h. He was referred back to the emergency department.

On admission, he was febrile to 38.8 °C and otherwise stable. Laboratory evaluation revealed:
• Creatinine 2.2 mg/dL  
• WBC 11 × 10^9/L; hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL; platelets 96 × 10^9/L  
• ALT 186 U/L; AST 148 U/L; total bilirubin 6.6 mg/dL; γ-GT 310 U/L; ALP 298 U/L  
• Ferritin 5130 ng/mL

A 30-year-old North African man presented with two similar episodes of headache, memory dysfunction, sensory symptoms, decreased visual acuity, and seizures. During the first episode, he had left-sided paresthesia and transcortical aphasia. Brain MRI with gadolinium showed right hemispheric cortical and subcortical hyperintensity on T2-FLAIR, cortical hyperintensity on diffusion-weighted imaging with overlying leptomeningeal enhancement, and arterial spin labeling perfusion images revealed hyperperfusion in the right hemisphere. Serologic testing for HIV, syphilis, and antinuclear antibodies was negative. Body CT showed no evidence of malignancy or granulomatous disease. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal opening pressure, protein, glucose, cytology, IgG index, and no oligoclonal bands. He was treated with antiepileptic drugs, his symptoms resolved spontaneously, and a one-month follow-up MRI was normal.

Two months later, he was readmitted with seizures, memory dysfunction, and right upper limb paresis. MRI demonstrated new left temporal and occipital cortical T2-FLAIR hyperintense lesions with cortical swelling; diffusion-weighted imaging showed cortical brightness with subtle ADC reduction and overlying leptomeningeal enhancement. ASL perfusion again showed focal hyperperfusion in left occipital regions. MR spectroscopy of the lesions revealed a high choline peak with reversed Cho/Cr ratio, decreased NAA peak, and prominent lactate and lipid resonances at 1.31 ppm, consistent with an inflammatory profile.

A 24-year-old Hispanic man with a 1-year history of systemic lupus erythematosus (diagnosed on renal biopsy) and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis presented with 3 days of nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, progressive shortness of breath, and bilateral lower extremity edema. He also reported leg pain. He underwent emergent hemodialysis for hyperkalemia, uremia, and hypervolemia, but his abdominal symptoms persisted. 

On examination, he was icteric with significant right upper quadrant tenderness without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies on admission showed:  
– AST 2365 µ/L, ALT 1315 µ/L (peaking at 3594 µ/L and 1705 µ/L on hospital day 1)  
– Total bilirubin 1.5 mg/dL  
– Albumin 2.2 g/dL  
– INR 1.9 (no anticoagulation)  

Initial evaluation for acute liver failure revealed immunity to hepatitis A and B, false-positive hepatitis C serology but negative RNA titers, and a negative toxicology screen for acetaminophen. Right upper quadrant ultrasound with Doppler flow was normal, excluding venous thrombosis, cirrhosis, steatosis, or mass. There was no history of hypotension to suggest ischemic hepatitis, and no clinical evidence of metabolic liver disease. Autoimmune hepatitis markers were negative, including anti–mitochondrial and anti–smooth muscle antibodies. Complement levels were low at C3 23.6 mg/dL (normal 80–150) and C4 3.8 mg/dL (normal 15–40).

A 54-year-old man with gastric adenocarcinoma underwent gastrectomy with lymph node dissection followed by adjuvant chemotherapy. His regimen included a continuous intravenous infusion of 5-fluorouracil at 200 mg/m2 over 24 hours. Immediately after the second cycle, he developed sudden agitation, stereotypic movements, and right lower extremity weakness (muscle strength 4/5). Laboratory studies revealed no metabolic disturbances, and renal and hepatic function were normal. Brain MRI showed bilateral, symmetrical, confluent hyperintensities of the periventricular white matter on T2-weighted, FLAIR, and diffusion-weighted images, with faint bilateral enhancement and no hemorrhage.

A 33-year-old man with a 6-year history of poorly controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus presented with 4 days of severe bilateral medial thigh pain and 2 days of low-grade fever. The pain was gradual in onset, localized to the medial thighs, worsened with movement, and improved with rest. He reported associated polyuria, nausea, and vomiting but denied trauma or other muscle group involvement.  

On examination, he was tachypneic (RR 30/min), tachycardic (HR 104/min), and febrile (reported but not documented). Both medial thighs were warm, swollen, and exquisitely tender; peripheral pulses were intact, and motor and sensory examinations were normal.  

Laboratory tests on admission showed:  
• Random blood glucose 250 mg/dL; HbA1c 14%  
• WBC count 9,700/µL; CRP 200 mg/L; ESR 25 mm/hr  
• Serum creatine kinase (CK) >900 U/L  
• Urine acetone +++; serum electrolytes and liver function tests were within normal limits  

A Doppler ultrasound of the lower limbs was negative for deep venous thrombosis. He was treated for presumed diabetic ketoacidosis and possible inflammatory myositis; fluids, insulin, analgesics, and antibiotics were administered. After 6 days, DKA resolved, his CK level normalized to 25.6 U/L, and CRP decreased to 25 mg/L; he remained unable to bear weight on his legs.  

A contrast-enhanced MRI of the thighs demonstrated diffuse edema of the medial muscle groups in the upper third of both thighs, appearing as low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2- and fat-suppression sequences. There was no evidence of an enhancing abscess or free fluid collection.

A 63-year-old retired truck driver presented with a 1-week history of dysphasia, headache, and right-sided sensory symptoms. Eleven years earlier, he was diagnosed with a low-grade temporoparietal astrocytoma, treated 9 years ago with 52.2 Gy of radiotherapy over 6 weeks; recent surveillance MRI had shown radiation leukoencephalopathy and stable residual tumor. He had complex partial seizures for several years, treated with lamotrigine, with erratic compliance in the week before admission. On examination, he had a receptive dysphasia and a right inferior quadrantanopia. Noncontrast head CT and CT angiography showed no new abnormalities. He was initially diagnosed with migraine with aura.

An 87-year-old man presented with right‐sided vision loss of one and a half months’ duration. One month earlier, funduscopic examination was normal, and noncontrast CT of the head showed only right maxillary sinusitis. Brain MRI at that time demonstrated a right maxillary sinus mass with high signal intensity on T1-weighted images and low signal intensity on T2-weighted and FLAIR images; MRA showed no aneurysm. He was diagnosed with optic neuritis and treated with steroid pulse therapy, but vision did not improve, and right‐sided hearing disturbance developed.

On the day of admission to our hospital, he became unresponsive and exhibited wandering behavior. His medical history included hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia; he had not received immunosuppressive therapy. On examination, GCS was E4V4M6; he was disoriented, could follow only simple commands, and had no light reflexes in the right eye with a relative afferent pupillary defect. Motor and sensory examinations were normal, and there were no meningeal signs.

Laboratory studies showed a WBC count of 10,700/μL, CRP 4.68 mg/dL, and β-D glucan 3.259 pg/mL (normal <11.0). Autoimmune serologies were negative. CSF analysis revealed 65 cells/μL (50 mononuclear, 15 polymorphonuclear), protein 900 mg/dL, and glucose 59 mg/dL (blood glucose 136 mg/dL); blood and CSF cultures were negative, and India ink stain was normal. Brain MRI showed no parenchymal lesions; MRA revealed a 3 mm aneurysm in the right internal carotid artery siphon.

Empirical ceftriaxone and acyclovir were initiated for suspected septic meningitis or herpes encephalitis. HSV IgM and CSF HSV DNA were negative. On hospital day 6, consciousness worsened to E3V1M5, and head CT showed subarachnoid hemorrhage likely from aneurysm rupture. Because antibiotic and antiviral therapy failed to improve his condition, a fungal infection was suspected.

A 57-year-old man with a 2-month history of lepromatous leprosy treated with rifampicin, clofazimine, and dapsone presented with abdominal distension, constipation, vomiting, and a 10-kg weight loss. He was vitally stable, with peripheral lymphadenopathy and a distended abdomen with shifting dullness. Abdominal CT showed terminal ileal mural thickening, enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes, mesenteric fat stranding, and free intraperitoneal fluid, suggesting either granulomatous infection or a neoplastic process. Paracentesis revealed atypical large lymphocytes; flow cytometry showed an abnormal CD4/CD8 double-negative T-cell population (38%) with multiple aberrancies. Cervical lymph node biopsy confirmed high-grade peripheral T-cell lymphoma, and bone marrow was uninvolved. He was staged as IV and started on dexamethasone. After developing severe sepsis requiring one week in the ICU, he recovered and received six cycles of dose-adjusted EPOCH chemotherapy with intrathecal methotrexate. After four cycles, PET/CT showed complete metabolic remission, but he had multiple episodes of febrile neutropenia and bacteremia.  

During this admission, he developed progressive, generalized weakness without sensory changes or clear fatigability. Neurologic examination showed symmetric proximal and distal muscle weakness (Medical Research Council grade 3/5) with preserved sensation and reflexes. Given his ICU stay, neurotoxic drug exposure, and malignancy, the differential diagnosis included critical illness myopathy–neuropathy, toxic neuropathy, and paraneoplastic syndrome.  

Nerve conduction studies showed normal distal motor latencies, normal compound muscle action potentials, normal conduction velocities, and normal F-waves in all motor nerves. Sensory nerve studies revealed normal onset latencies, normal sensory nerve action potential amplitudes, and normal conduction velocities. Needle electromyography of proximal and distal muscles in all limbs exhibited normal insertional activity, no spontaneous activity, and normal motor unit action potentials, but with poor recruitment. Finally, repetitive nerve stimulation at 30–40 Hz elicited a marked incremental response, suggesting a presynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder.

A 28-year-old woman presented with acute onset of abdominal pain of 2 hours’ duration. The pain was localized under the umbilicus on both sides of the linea alba, was not related to eating, and worsened with walking or changes in position. The pain had started suddenly during her second session of sit-ups; she denied nausea, vomiting, urinary symptoms, vaginal discharge, or trauma. Her menstrual cycles were regular, with the last period 20 days earlier; she had stopped accutane 2 months prior. There was no personal or family history of bleeding disorders. 

On arrival, her blood pressure was 100/80 mmHg, heart rate 90/min, respiratory rate 10/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and temperature 37 °C. Abdominal examination revealed localized bilateral tenderness under the umbilicus without rebound or palpable mass; the skin was normal. Gynecologic and other systemic examinations were unremarkable. Coagulation studies, complete blood count, and urinalysis were normal; serum βHCG was negative. 

Bedside abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated two heterogenic hypoechoic regions: one measuring 9×22×23 mm (~2.5 cc) in the right rectus muscle and another measuring 4×25×45 mm (~3 cc) in the left rectus muscle, 13 mm below the skin and 10 cm below the umbilicus, findings suggestive of a rectus sheath hematoma. No ultrasonographic abnormalities were seen in the appendix, ovaries, or vagina.

A 28-year-old Hispanic woman with a history of severe Ebstein anomaly underwent staged palliative surgeries in childhood, including a fenestrated extracardiac Fontan at age 12 and fenestration closure at age 25. She presented with 5 days of chest pain, progressive dyspnea, and fatigue. She denied recent illness or travel. On arrival, her oxygen saturation was 78% on room air, improving to 88% on 4 L/min of nasal cannula. She was tachypneic but comfortable. On examination, her lungs were clear, she had a single S1 and S2, non-pulsatile jugular venous distension, and no peripheral edema. ECG showed sinus tachycardia at 117 bpm and a known right bundle branch block. Laboratory studies revealed a hemoglobin of 14.8 g/dL (normal, 11.5–16.0), hematocrit 45.3% (37–47), platelets 203 K/μL (130–400), an INR of 1.15, and normal brain natriuretic peptide and troponin levels. She had been on rivaroxaban for chronic thromboprophylaxis in the setting of Fontan physiology but had recently discontinued it following a miscarriage. A helical chest CT angiogram was interpreted as showing a submassive pulmonary embolism with no contrast filling the proximal branch pulmonary arteries. She was started on an unfractionated heparin infusion and transferred for further management.

A 43-year-old healthy man presented with recurrent melena. He had no relevant medical history. On examination, he was anemic (hemoglobin, 8.1 g/dL), and all other findings including carcinoembryonic antigen and cancer antigen 19-9 levels were within normal limits. Eighteen years earlier, esophagogastroduodenoscopy had revealed a 25-mm submucosal tumor in the posterior wall of the gastric angle, and fine-needle aspiration of that lesion had established a diagnosis of gastric heterotopic pancreas. Five years ago, the lesion measured the same size. Current esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed that the submucosal tumor had increased to 40 mm and had an erythematous, eroded mucosal surface on the posterior wall of the gastric angle. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography demonstrated a round mass with multiple cystic lesions and wall thickening along the lesser curvature of the stomach. Endoscopic ultrasonography revealed multiple cystic formations located in the third layer of the gastric wall. Endoscopic ultrasonography–guided fine-needle aspiration yielded non-atypical crypt epithelium and stroma without evidence of malignancy. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography showed a hypointense mass with hyperintense multiple cystic lesions on T2-weighted images, without any mural nodules or solid components. Although these findings did not suggest malignancy, the increase in size over five years and the bleeding raised concern for either malignant transformation or inflammatory change. Consequently, the patient underwent laparotomy for diagnosis and treatment.

A 34-year-old gravida 1, para 0 woman with no prior medical history underwent D&C at 15 weeks’ gestation for a missed abortion. Two weeks postprocedure she had minimal bleeding. Two months later she returned with significantly increased spotting, severe cramping, menorrhagia, and passage of clots. 

On examination she was hemodynamically stable without fever. Laboratory evaluation included a normal hemoglobin for her presentation and a negative β-hCG. 

Transvaginal ultrasound showed multiple small cysts and an echogenic uterine mass measuring 2.1 × 1.8 × 1.6 cm with increased Doppler flow. The primary considerations were retained products of conception versus uterine AVM. 

Pelvic MRI with contrast demonstrated a mixed signal endometrial mass with areas of solid enhancement, an indistinct endometrial–myometrial interface posteriorly, and serpiginous low T2 signal structures within the myometrium. 

To resolve the ambiguity, a pelvic CTA was performed, revealing a 2.3 × 2.1 cm cluster of vessels in the myometrium supplied by uterine arteries with early venous filling.

A 50-year-old edentulous woman presented with a one-year history of a slowly progressive swelling of the right anterior mandible that obliterated the buccal ridge. The swelling was hard in consistency, mildly tender on palpation, and associated with occasional mild pain during mastication. Head and neck examination was otherwise unremarkable. Panoramic radiography revealed a unilocular, well-defined, scalloped radiolucency extending from the right posterior mandible across the midline to the anterior section. Cone-beam computed tomography confirmed buccal ridge thinning and thinning of the alveolar crest in the region of the lesion, with no root stumps in the mandible or maxilla. Aspiration of the defect yielded amber-yellow fluid, indicating a cystic lesion. Marsupialization was initiated by creating a mucoperiosteal flap and suturing the fenestrated cyst wall to the oral mucosa to establish a window.

A 37-year-old woman presented with a 12-month history of intermittent right upper quadrant abdominal pain and left iliac fossa pain, accompanied by abdominal distension. She denied nausea or vomiting. She had no significant medical or surgical history. A farmer by occupation, she lived in overcrowded conditions with poor hygiene and had kept a dog for five years. On examination, her vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness over the right hypochondrium with a palpable mass; there was also a smooth, non-tender, palpable mass in the left iliac fossa that did not move with respiration. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurological examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a normal blood count except for an elevated eosinophil percentage of 15%. Serological testing by ELISA demonstrated an elevated IgG antibody level to Echinococcus of 19.5 U/ml. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a well-defined hypoechoic heterogeneous lesion in the right lobe of the liver and a complex multiloculated anechoic lesion in the left iliac fossa, both with internal echoes suggestive of hydatid disease. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen showed a 10 × 8 cm complex heterogeneous lesion with internal septations in segment 8 of the liver and a 7 × 6 cm lobulated lesion with septations in the left iliac fossa.

An 81-year-old man presented with sudden onset of right-sided abdominal wall bulging and sharp pain radiating in the Th11 dermatome. He denied leg pain, back pain, bladder or bowel dysfunction, or gait disturbances. Sensation was intact throughout, and there were no skin lesions. His medical history included a left middle cerebral artery stroke and hypertension. On examination, there was a visible bulge of the right abdominal wall and reproducible radicular tenderness in the Th11 distribution; the remainder of the neurologic and abdominal examinations was unremarkable. A CT scan of the abdomen was performed and showed no evidence of an abdominal wall hernia.

A 15-year-old female with congenital hypothyroidism on thyroxine presented with 15 days of gradual, colicky, intermittent periumbilical pain accompanied by nausea, non-bilious vomiting, anorexia, and alternating constipation and diarrhea. Five days before transfer, her pain intensified and she underwent an open appendectomy at a rural hospital; she had transient relief but then developed multiple episodes of bilious vomiting and intermittent obstipation. Thirty-six hours before arrival, obstipation became unresponsive to enemas. On the day of transfer, she developed sudden, constant, severe generalized abdominal pain unrelieved by analgesics. She denied fever or genitourinary symptoms. 

On examination, she was mildly tachycardic and tachypneic, with normal blood pressure and temperature. The abdomen was asymmetrically distended above the umbilicus, moved painfully with respiration, and showed a McBurney scar. There was generalized guarding and tenderness, absent bowel sounds, and no palpable masses. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis (WBC 12 000/μL) and hypokalemia (K 2.9 mmol/L); other values were normal.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated normal hepatobiliary and renal structures with no free fluid, but moderate dilation of intestinal loops with edematous walls. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed thickening of gastric and small-bowel loops, stenosis at the distal duodenum, and a classic “whirlpool sign” around the superior mesenteric artery.

A 60-year-old Japanese woman presented to the emergency department with a 1-day history of gradually worsening left flank pain. She had a history of myelodysplastic syndrome, hypertension, and prior cerebral infarction with left hemiplegia. Her medications included antihypertensive and acid-reducing drugs; she was not taking antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy. On examination, she was alert; blood pressure was 173/101 mm Hg, heart rate 110 beats/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Her abdomen was flat, with moderate tenderness in the left flank without peritoneal signs. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7 g/dL (baseline ∼8 g/dL), hematocrit 20.8%, platelets 118,000/µL, prothrombin time 13.3 seconds, activated partial thromboplastin time 31.9 seconds, and fibrinogen 209.4 mg/dL; blood chemistries were otherwise near normal. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed a 5 × 5 × 8 cm solid mass in the left middle abdomen, appearing to arise from the greater curvature of the gastric antrum. The mass was fed by a branch of the superior mesenteric artery, and there was evidence of contrast extravasation within the lesion.

A 5-year-old Caucasian boy was evaluated for mild spinal asymmetry. Parents had first noticed a slight shifting of his shoulders and pelvis at age 3. On forward-bend (Adams) testing, minimal curvature of the spinous processes was observed in the lower thoracic region. Spinal radiographs demonstrated a scoliotic curve associated with an L1 supernumerary hemivertebra. CT and MRI of the spine revealed congenital scoliosis with a left L1 supernumerary semi-segmented hemivertebra and a left L5 transverse megapophysis articulating with the sacral wing; no other spinal or visceral malformations were detected. All other biological and functional examinations were within normal limits, and the child had no physical impairment. On imaging, the left side of L1 displayed the morphology of a T12-like vertebra in its upper part and an L1-like vertebra in its lower part. The scoliotic curve measured approximately 20° by Cobb angle, with an estimated progression rate of 2.5–3° per year.  
Which is the true hemivertebra: the upper or the lower component of the L1?

A 76-year-old retired man with chronic active hepatitis C (hepatitis C antibody reactive, index >11.00), JAK2-positive myelodysplastic syndrome, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and treated prostate cancer presented with a 1-year history of recurrent skin lesions on the dorsum of both hands. He denied recent travel, chemical exposures, or animal contacts. The lesions began as small disruptions of the skin, evolved into bullae described as abscesses, and eventually ulcerated. Multiple physicians had treated him with surgical debridements and broad-spectrum antibiotics without improvement.

On examination, he appeared cachectic and sallow but was not in distress. There were violaceous papules and nodules on the dorsal surfaces of both hands, including a 1-cm edematous papule over the proximal interphalangeal joint of the left middle finger. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, platelet count 89 ×10^3/µL, neutrophil count 9.2 ×10^3/µL, eosinophil count 1.7 ×10^3/µL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 51 mm/h, and C-reactive protein 2.50 mg/dL. A biopsy of a lesion on the left third digit revealed dense neutrophilic infiltration in the dermis with leukocytoclastic debris and no evidence of vasculitis. Bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures were negative.

A 68-year-old woman with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and prior antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)–associated vasculitis in remission was evaluated for renal dysfunction. Routine laboratory tests revealed a serum creatinine level of 1.3 mg/dL (baseline approximately 0.8 mg/dL) and a urine protein–creatinine ratio of 16.2 g/g. Evaluation for monoclonal proteins was negative. Serologic studies showed negative ANCA and negative antinuclear antibody. A kidney biopsy was subsequently performed.

A 48-year-old man presented with progressive neck swelling without fever or respiratory symptoms. He denied alcohol use or metabolic disorders. His medical history was notable for β-thalassemia intermedia status post splenectomy and autoimmune hemolytic anemia requiring transfusions. On examination, he had bilateral nonpitting jugular‐venous distention most evident in the supraclavicular regions and no lymphadenopathy or peripheral edema. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory evaluation showed hemoglobin 8.8 g/dL, hematocrit 28.8 %, red‐cell count 3.65×10^6/μL, RDW 23.2 %, total bilirubin 2.5 mg/dL (direct normal), LDH 397 mU/mL, and otherwise normal thyroid, lipid, renal, and liver panels. Neurologic examination was unremarkable. ECG and echocardiography showed no cardiovascular pathology. Doppler ultrasonography revealed mild compression of the right jugular vein without jugular, axillary, or subclavian thrombosis or lymphadenopathy. Chest radiographs were normal. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the neck and chest demonstrated symmetric, nonencapsulated fat‐density tissue in the anterior and posterior subcutaneous layers of the neck with extrinsic compression of the right jugular vein. MRI confirmed superficial, well‐defined, nonencapsulated subcutaneous fat with homogeneous T1 and T2 hyperintense signals and no signs of invasion or malignancy.

A 24-year-old Sri Lankan man with a history of Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome (hemihypertrophy of the right lower limb and strawberry naevi since age 6) presented with effort intolerance (NYHA class III) and lethargy. He had episodic rectal bleeding since age 17; prior colonoscopy and mesenteric angiography showed lower gastrointestinal varices. 

On examination, he was pale and had splenomegaly (1 cm below costal margin), with no hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy or neurologic abnormalities. He had the known cutaneous and vascular findings of Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome.

Laboratory studies: hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, MCV 77.6 fL, MCH 24.7 pg, MCHC 31.8 g/dL; WBC and platelet counts normal; peripheral blood film showed mixed hypochromic microcytic and normochromic red cells and acanthocytes (>20%), reticulocyte count 4%, direct Coombs test negative. Biochemistry: LDH 360 U/L, AST 34 U/L, ALT 36 U/L, ALP 199 U/L, total bilirubin 16 μmol/L, direct bilirubin 3.1 μmol/L, creatinine 61 μmol/L. Serum iron 22 μg/dL, TIBC 256 μg/dL, transferrin saturation 8.5%. Thyroid and lipid profiles were normal. First-degree relatives had no acanthocytosis on blood film.

Colonoscopy (4 months earlier) revealed extensive hemangiomas in the transverse and descending colon and rectal varices. Abdominal ultrasound showed a 15 cm spleen with multiple cystic lesions. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated multiple nonenhancing hypodense splenic cystic lesions and a nonenhancing hypodense (–4 HU) retroperitoneal para-aortic lesion encasing mesenteric vessels, suggestive of lymphangiomas. Transthoracic echocardiography showed LVEF 60%, cardiac output 3.3 L/min, cardiac index 2.3 L/min/m2.

A 46-year-old woman with a history of hypothyroidism and mild bronchial asthma presented with 5–6 days of persistent chest and upper back pain radiating to her neck, and a 3–4 month history of dry cough. There was no fever, weight loss, anorexia, or systemic symptoms. She was overweight and taking only thyroxine and an as-needed bronchodilator. 

On examination, her temperature was 98.3°F, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, heart rate and respiratory rate were normal, and oxygen saturation was 99% on room air. Jugular venous pressure was elevated at 10 cmH2O with non-pulsatile neck veins. Cardiac examination was unremarkable. Lung auscultation revealed decreased air entry at the right lung base without wheezes. There was no lymphadenopathy, clubbing, or edema.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL, leukocyte count 13 500/mm3 (92% neutrophils), C-reactive protein 186.4 mg/L, normal renal function, corrected calcium 8.5 mg/dL, and negative antinuclear antibody. Electrocardiography and troponin-I were normal.

A chest radiograph demonstrated a widened mediastinum. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax revealed a 14×10.3×11.7 cm homogenously enhancing mediastinal mass encasing the trachea, bronchi, pulmonary vessels, esophagus, and great vessels, with infiltration into the right atrium but no lung parenchymal lesions. 

An FDG-PET scan showed an FDG-avid, ill-defined soft-tissue density mass involving the entire mediastinum with central necrosis and hyperenhancing solid components. Due to sampling concerns from prior needle biopsy, a limited thoracotomy was performed to obtain a larger tissue sample for definitive diagnosis.

An 83-year-old woman with non–insulin-dependent diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, GERD, and chronic kidney disease presented with 3 months of intermittent sharp right upper quadrant pain, rated 6/10, accompanied by nausea and occasional constipation. She denied fever, diarrhea, bloody stools, dysuria, chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, or syncope. There had been no bowel movement for 2 days. Exercise tolerance was one block, limited by dyspepsia.

On examination, blood pressure was 156/80 mm Hg, pulse 93/min, respiratory rate 16/min, temperature 36 °C. The abdomen was soft with normal bowel sounds, no distention, tenderness, or masses. The remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 20,000/μL, normal liver function tests, hemoglobin A1C of 9.4%, and C-reactive protein of 15.5 mg/L. Electrocardiogram demonstrated normal sinus rhythm with left axis deviation and nonspecific ST–T–wave abnormalities.

An RUQ ultrasound revealed a 2.0 cm stone at the gallbladder neck, common bile duct dilatation, gallbladder wall thickening, and a positive sonographic Murphy’s sign; a second 1.3 cm gallstone was noted in the gallbladder body. Abdominal CT confirmed gallbladder distention with mucosal enhancement. The patient was started on IV piperacillin and scheduled for laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

On the morning before surgery, ECG showed 2–3 mm T-wave inversions in the inferior leads in the absence of chest pain. Cardiac biomarkers were elevated: troponin 7.4 ng/mL (reference 0.01–0.05) and CK-MB 43.2 ng/mL (reference 1.3–6.3). She was referred for diagnostic coronary angiography.

A 70-year-old woman presented to her orthopedist with several weeks of left groin pain accompanied by numbness and tingling in the left medial thigh. Her medical history included hyperlipidemia, overactive bladder, chronic low back pain with occasional radicular symptoms, bilateral total hip arthroplasty (left side performed 15 years earlier), and left total knee arthroplasty. On hip examination, flexion was 100°, external rotation 25°, internal rotation 10°, and abduction 25°, with mild pain on movement that was attributed to possible radiculopathy. She was treated with a course of oral steroids, cyclobenzaprine, and physical therapy, without symptomatic relief.

She subsequently went to the emergency department. Anteroposterior radiographs of the pelvis and anteroposterior and lateral views of the left femur showed well-fixed hip components without evidence of loosening or hardware failure. A magnetic resonance imaging study of the lumbar spine revealed multilevel degenerative changes and severe canal stenosis at L3–L4; additionally, it noted inflammatory changes in the left iliacus muscle that “may represent myositis.” Her distal pulses were normal, and the examination was otherwise unremarkable. She was discharged with a presumptive diagnosis of iliacus myositis and lumbar radicular pain.

Four days later, she returned to the emergency department with persistent groin pain and thigh numbness. A noncontrast computed tomographic scan of the abdomen and pelvis was interpreted as inflammation of the left iliacus muscle, thought to be caused by a prominent acetabular screw. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 23.3 mg/L (normal <10.0) and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 26 mm/hr (normal <30). Her symptoms were again attributed to myositis, and she was discharged for outpatient follow-up.

In the outpatient setting, her pain continued despite two transforaminal epidural steroid injections at L3–4 and L4–5, which provided no relief.

A 29-year-old Western European woman was referred for evaluation of pronounced abdominal blind-ending fistulas. In early 2019, weeks after a tick bite, she developed multiple recurrent abscesses of the abdominal skin. Between January 2019 and July 2020, she underwent repeated incision of abscesses with antibiotic therapy, but the lesions never fully healed. Instead, subcutaneous abscess cavities coalesced into a network of connected fistulas, as seen on MRI enterography. 

When examined in 2020, the abdominal fistulas measured up to 2 cm in diameter, showed active inflammation, and intermittently secreted purulent fluid. On physical examination, a separate blind-ending subcutaneous fistula on the thigh also exhibited active inflammation and secretion. 

A biopsy of an abdominal fistula revealed a granulomatous infiltrate with histiocytes and multinuclear giant cells forming non-caseating granulomas, alongside lymphocytes, plasma cells, neutrophils, eosinophils, and granulomatous perivasculitis.

A 36-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of a solid, asymptomatic nodule in the left parasternal region at the level of the second sternocostal joint. The mass was firm, measured 3.0 × 2.5 cm, and showed no overlying skin changes. He denied any trauma or prior malignancy; routine blood tests were unremarkable.  
High-frequency ultrasound of the left chest wall showed a 32 × 18 × 29 mm hyperechoic nodular lesion within the sub-fascial layer of the pectoralis major muscle, with internal septa and an incomplete external capsule, without invasion of surrounding structures or regional lymphadenopathy. Color Doppler imaging revealed weak peripheral vascular signals.  
Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-circumscribed, round mass in the fatty tissue beneath the musculo-tendinous junction of the pectoralis major, displaying slight hyperintensity on T1-weighted images, inhomogeneous hyperintensity on T2-weighted and SPAIR sequences, and marked diffusion restriction on DWI, with no evidence of local invasion.  
The patient was scheduled for en-bloc surgical excision of the lesion for histopathologic evaluation.

A 21-year-old woman presented with a three-month history of a painless lump on the left lateral side of her neck. On examination, there was a 5 × 4 cm uniform, mobile, smoothly outlined mass in the left supraclavicular region without fluctuation, erythema, ecchymosis, or regional lymphadenopathy. Ultrasonography revealed a 4 × 5 × 5 cm homogenous, anechoic cyst with a slightly thick wall in the left supraclavicular area. A lateral radiograph of the neck and cervical spine showed a mass without bony involvement. Coronal T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a unilocular, well-defined, high–signal-intensity cystic lesion with a hypointense rim. Contrast-enhanced axial T1-weighted images showed a well-defined, hypointense cystic mass with peripheral enhancement. Chest and abdominal radiographs and ultrasound revealed no evidence of hepatic, pulmonary, or other organ involvement.

A 46-year-old woman was evaluated for a 2-year history of intermittent fevers (up to 38.9 °C), fatigue, and frequent urination. Episodes were accompanied by muscle weakness, joint stiffness, and severe headache lasting about 30 hours. She denied chest or abdominal pain, changes in bowel habits, or weight loss.  
Her medical history included thalassemia, dermatographism, and three early miscarriages. Surgical history was notable for a gastric sleeve and a hysterectomy complicated by a pelvic abscess treated with drainage 4 months earlier. Her family history was positive for autoimmune diseases (gout, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus).  
On examination, temperature was 36.6 °C, and the abdomen was soft with no tenderness. Laboratory studies showed a microcytic anemia with occasional schistocytes; results of a comprehensive metabolic panel, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, HIV assay, Quantiferon tuberculosis test, blood cultures, lactate dehydrogenase, antinuclear antibody, and serum protein electrophoresis were all within normal limits. Additional serologic tests (including lupus anticoagulant, viral hepatitis profile, complement levels, and multiple extractable nuclear antigens) were normal.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a misty appearance of the mesentery in the left hemiabdomen with multiple enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes, the largest measuring 1 cm in short axis, findings that were interpreted as suggestive of chronic mesenteric panniculitis.

A 3-year-old boy from a rural, Buruli ulcer–endemic area presented with a one-month history of an extensive, painless, plaque-like lesion on the right thigh. On examination, the lesion was firm, woody hard, and nonerythematous, and the patient was afebrile and in good general condition. A skin biopsy was performed. Laboratory tests on the biopsy for Buruli ulcer—including direct smear after Ziehl-Neelsen staining, culture, and IS2404 PCR—were negative. Initial histopathological examination of the biopsy showed granulomatous inflammation and was interpreted as possible Buruli ulcer.

A 66-year-old right-hand–dominant woman with no significant past medical history fell onto her outstretched left hand and presented the same day with left shoulder pain and visible upper-arm deformity. She was neurovascularly intact distally. Radiographs showed a four-part proximal humerus fracture with glenohumeral dislocation. On hospital day 3, she underwent open reduction and internal fixation via a deltopectoral approach; the cephalic vein was identified and preserved, and there were no intraoperative complications. She was discharged on postoperative day 2 on aspirin 325 mg daily for DVT prophylaxis. On postoperative day 5, she returned with increased swelling and discomfort of the left upper extremity. Physical examination revealed marked swelling with pitting edema but an intact neurovascular exam. An upper-extremity duplex ultrasound demonstrated occlusive thrombosis in the cephalic and deep brachial veins of the left forearm.

A 43-year-old non-smoking woman was referred for management of an extensive lesion affecting the maxillary right lateral incisor. She reported mild discomfort at that tooth and a history of a fall 10 years earlier, after which the tooth was asymptomatic. Several years ago, caries had been removed from its proximal surfaces, and an external cervical resorption (ECR) lesion was diagnosed at a private clinic. Discomfort gradually increased as radiographic translucency enlarged. She had no relevant medical history, no history of orthodontics or parafunctional habits, and her oral hygiene was good.  

On examination, there was no mobility of the affected or adjacent teeth, no tenderness to palpation, and slight pain on vertical percussion. Pulp sensibility tests elicited no response to cold or electrical stimulation, in contrast to adjacent teeth. Periodontal probing depths were <3 mm on the buccal side and 4 mm with bleeding and slight pus exudate on the distal palatal aspect. Root caries was ruled out as no infected dentine was detected.
