Periapical radiography demonstrated a large radiolucent defect extending from the distal to proximal surfaces without periapical pathology. Cone-beam computed tomography revealed that the lesion had reached the pulp tissue along one-third to one-half of the root in the axial plane, and horizontally involved approximately 180° of the palatal root surface. On the basis of these findings, the lesion was classified as Class III by Heithersay’s criteria and Class 2Bp by Patel’s criteria.

A 45-year-old man with morbid obesity (BMI 38), diabetes, dyslipidemia, and recovery from COVID-19 pneumonia 2 months prior presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset acute right upper quadrant pain. He denied vomiting, jaundice, fever, changes in urine or stool color, and chest pain. On examination he was afebrile (37 °C), blood pressure 140/85 mm Hg, heart rate 90 beats/min, respiratory rate 19 breaths/min, and O₂ saturation 97% on room air. Cardiac and pulmonary examinations were unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the right upper quadrant without Murphy’s sign; the remainder of the abdomen was soft and nonrigid. Laboratory testing showed a white-cell count of 8.9 × 10³/μl with 80% neutrophils; cardiac enzymes, bilirubin, amylase, liver enzymes, and albumin were within normal limits. A noncontrast CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated fine early fat stranding in the omentum anterior to the hepatic flexure of the colon and an 8 mm stone in the gallbladder with no sign of cholecystitis; all other intra-abdominal organs appeared normal with no free air or fluid collection. The admission impression was biliary colic.

A 31-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, and cirrhosis had been on prednisone and azathioprine for autoimmune hepatitis for two months. She presented with five days of fever, chills, dyspnea, dry cough, and pleuritic chest pain. She had recently visited a hunting shack in northern New York. She had no history of tuberculosis and prior PPDs were negative.  

On examination, temperature was 102°F, pulse 120/min, respiratory rate 20/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 90% on 2 L/min nasal oxygen. Lung fields were clear.  

Labs showed WBC 16,000/µL (neutrophils 14,400/µL), hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL, platelets 167,000/µL, ALT 62 U/L, AST 87 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 158 U/L, total bilirubin 13.2 mg/dL, and INR 2.9.  

Chest radiograph demonstrated a small left pleural effusion without infiltrates. Empiric vancomycin and meropenem were started. The next day, chest CT revealed multiple small bilateral cavitary nodules, and amphotericin was added for presumed fungal infection.  

On hospital day 3, CT‐guided biopsy of a pulmonary nodule was performed. On day 4, bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was done; Gram stain, fungal stain, and cultures were negative.  

On day 6, repeat chest CT showed increased size and number of cavitary nodules with surrounding ground‐glass opacities despite continuation of vancomycin, meropenem, and amphotericin.

A 4½-year-old girl of Kurdish, Iraqi, and Yemenite ancestry presented with a 3-day history of fever (39.5 °C), tender nodular erythematous lesions on both lower legs, and bilateral knee pain with swelling. She also had painful perineal ulcers.  

On ophthalmologic examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 in both eyes. The right eye was normal. The left eye showed mild anterior chamber inflammation (cells +1), mild vitritis (haze +1), and a macular star consistent with late-stage neuroretinitis.  

Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 20 000 cells/mm3 (76% neutrophils), C-reactive protein 89 mg/L (normal 0–5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 84 mm/h, normal serum chemistry, normal angiotensin-converting enzyme level, negative antinuclear antibodies, normal antistreptolysin O titer, and negative serology for Bartonella henselae.  

Abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable. Colonoscopy with biopsy showed no evidence of intestinal inflammation.

A 34-year-old Hispanic woman with a history of Langerhans cell histiocytosis of the hypothalamus, complicated by pan-hypopituitarism and central diabetes insipidus, presented with a 1-week history of painful erythematous nodules. The lesions first appeared on the distal left upper extremity and then spread to involve all four extremities. She also reported fevers, nausea, and vomiting coinciding with onset of the nodules.

Her oncologic history dated to 2015, when resection of hypothalamic lesions confirmed Langerhans cell histiocytosis with a BRAF V600E mutation. She had been treated with vemurafenib, 480 mg twice daily, for 10 months without serious adverse effects aside from a self-limited erythematous rash on the face, palms, and soles.

On examination, there were numerous tender, 2–3 cm subcutaneous nodules with overlying erythema on all extremities, sparing the trunk, head, and neck. Some lesions on the proximal left arm were confluent. She denied arthralgia but noted left-hand edema. No mucosal lesions or lymphadenopathy were observed.

A punch biopsy of a left arm nodule revealed a lobular neutrophilic panniculitis with an overlying perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate in the dermis. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 92.7 mg/L and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 130 mm/h. An infectious work-up, including bacterial, fungal, and acid-fast bacilli cultures of tissue; a QuantiFERON TB Gold assay; antistreptolysin O titer; and hepatitis A, B, and C serologies, was unremarkable. Serum lipase (87 U/L), amylase (48 U/L), and α₁-antitrypsin (284 mg/dL) levels were normal, and antinuclear antibodies were negative. White blood cell count, electrolytes, renal function, and thyroid function studies were within normal limits.

A 40-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of bilateral lower-extremity radiculopathy and neurogenic claudication with a walking distance of approximately 300 m. She reported intermittent low back pain but denied fever, weight loss, night sweats, or a history of tuberculosis.  
On examination, she was afebrile, and there was no paraspinal tenderness, muscle spasm, or local warmth. Neurologic examination was unremarkable except for mild bilateral lower-extremity paresthesias.  
Plain radiographs of the lumbar spine were normal. Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine showed hypertrophy of the ligamentum flavum and a posterior soft-tissue mass causing significant spinal-canal narrowing.  
Computed tomography of the lumbar spine demonstrated a lytic lesion in the right lamina of the second lumbar vertebra.  
Laboratory studies revealed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein.

A 70-year-old Asian woman was referred for evaluation of a right breast mass. Examination revealed a 20-mm movable hard mass in the inferolateral quadrant without skin changes. Mammography showed a spiculated mass with segmental and linear calcifications. Ultrasonography demonstrated a rough-bordered, hypoechoic mass measuring 16 × 12 × 11 mm. MRI revealed a 14 × 13 × 11 mm round mass with rim enhancement. Core needle biopsy confirmed estrogen receptor–positive, HER2-positive invasive ductal carcinoma. Fine-needle aspiration of a 12-mm right axillary lymph node revealed malignant cells. PET/CT showed FDG uptake in the right breast primary (SUVmax 11.5), right axillary node (SUVmax 2.1), and multiple lymph nodes in the right supraclavicular fossa, mediastinum, bilateral hilum, dorsal pancreatic head, abdominal aorta, right common iliac, and bilateral external iliac regions (highest SUVmax 17.0), raising concern for distant nodal metastases. Her past medical history was notable for uveitis of unknown cause 5 years earlier. Laboratory studies revealed a serum ACE of 9.9 U/mL (reference 7–25) and an elevated soluble interleukin-2 receptor level of 627 U/mL (reference 122–496).

A 56-year-old woman presented with a 1-week history of involuntary, irregular, non-rhythmic, jerky movements of the left arm, gradually progressing to the left leg and perioral area. The distal limbs were more affected than proximal, and movements worsened with action and disappeared with sleep. She reported no headache, fever, seizures, weakness, or recent infections. 

Her medical history was notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed 2 months earlier, treated with diet and metformin, but she admitted to poor adherence. She denied family neurologic disease and any use of neuroleptic, antidepressant, antihistamine, or other chorea-inducing medications.

On examination, vital signs were stable and mental status was normal. Cranial nerves and sensory testing were intact. Continuous choreiform movements were observed in the left upper and lower extremities, with decreased tone and an impersistent left hand grip. Motor and reflex testing was otherwise normal, and there was no entrainment or distraction variability.

Laboratory studies showed a random blood glucose of 412 mg/dL and HbA1c of 9.9%. Thyroid function tests, C-reactive protein, electrolytes, and vitamin B12 were within normal limits. Tests for antinuclear antibody, anti–streptolysin O antibody, and anti–NMDA receptor antibody were negative. Urinary ketones were absent. Chest radiograph and Mantoux test were unremarkable.

A noncontrast CT scan of the head revealed areas of high density in the tail of the right lenticular nucleus and right caudate nucleus, as well as hypodense regions in the right occipital lobe with encephalomalacia and multiple small lacunar infarcts in the bilateral corona radiata. MRI was not performed due to patient refusal.

A 38-year-old nonsmoking woman presented with left-sided chest pain and dyspnea for three days. She denied fever, weight loss, arthralgia, or skin rash. On examination, blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg, pulse 85 beats/min, temperature 37.5 °C, and respiratory rate 28 breaths/min. Breath sounds were decreased at the left lower lung zone; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. 

A chest radiograph showed two pulmonary nodules, basal atelectasis of the left lower lobe, and a left-sided pneumothorax. Chest CT revealed consolidation with collapse of the left lower lobe, pneumothorax, and two small cystic lesions within the collapsed segment. 

Laboratory studies demonstrated a white-cell count elevated with neutrophil predominance; erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein were elevated. The nitroblue tetrazolium test was 99% (normal). Antinuclear antibodies, C-ANCA, P-ANCA, and anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies were negative. The HIV antibody test was negative. Pulmonary function testing showed a moderate restrictive defect.

An 85-year-old man presented with one day of acute shortness of breath. His medical history included basal cell carcinoma, hypertension, and myasthenia gravis. His medications were amlodipine, losartan, pantoprazole, prednisone, and dapsone. One month earlier, he had a mechanical fall but did not seek care; since then he was less mobile due to back pain. He denied fever, cough, leg swelling, overt bleeding, or other symptoms.  
On examination: temperature 37°C; blood pressure 126/76 mmHg; pulse 78/min; respiratory rate 18/min; SpO2 95% on room air; cardiac and pulmonary exams were unremarkable.  
Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL (baseline 13.0) with MCV 108 fL; platelets and leukocytes were normal; basic metabolic panel was unremarkable. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm; chest radiograph was normal.  
CT angiography of the chest revealed new right upper and middle lobe segmental pulmonary emboli, and he was started on a heparin infusion. Over the next 2 days his hemoglobin fell to 7.0 g/dL without any overt bleeding. CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed no source of hemorrhage; vital signs remained stable.  
Further testing revealed an indirect bilirubin of 2.5 mg/dL (noted to be elevated 2 months prior), lactate dehydrogenase 460 U/L, haptoglobin <30 mg/dL, INR within normal limits, and an absolute reticulocyte count of 247 ×10^3/µL. Direct antiglobulin testing was negative. Peripheral blood smear demonstrated bite cells.

A 52-year-old man with hepatitis C–related cirrhosis and alcoholism in remission received an orthotopic liver transplant. His postoperative course was complicated by acute kidney injury requiring temporary hemodialysis on POD 1; graft function was otherwise good. Immunosuppression included tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and methylprednisolone. He had a history of bipolar disorder in remission on olanzapine, which was restarted at a lower dose on POD 1.

On POD 4, he refused to get out of bed and became noncommunicative, prompting concern for depression. By POD 6, he alternated between blank stares and seeming paranoia, sometimes holding his head to one side for seconds. He reported auditory hallucinations but would not elaborate. Speech fluctuated between whispering, long pauses, and no response. His Bush–Francis Catatonia Rating Scale score was 2. Neurologic exam showed a mild bilateral resting tremor. Blood work, including infectious studies, was unremarkable. Tacrolimus trough was 1.4 ng/mL. EEG showed no epileptiform activity or diffuse slowing.

On POD 7, he had an episode of unresponsiveness. Neurology noted nonfocal exam findings with occasional mutism and head turning; they recommended MRI to rule out intracranial pathology. Later that day he again became unresponsive and motionless. Repeat blood work and CT of the head were normal. Neurology suspected nonconvulsive seizures and administered 2 mg IV lorazepam. He initially recovered, then again became unresponsive with hypotension and hypoxia, requiring ICU transfer. Repeat EEG showed only diffuse background slowing. Serial neurologic examinations then revealed immobility, negativism, waxy flexibility, catalepsy, posturing, staring, and mutism (BFCRS score 18).

A 60-year-old man and his 55-year-old wife, married for 37 years, present with a shared history of “insects” infesting their bodies. The husband, a former alcoholic who abstained 13 years ago, reports a 2-year history of a persistent tingling sensation (“formication”) he associates with worms or bugs crawling under and emerging from his skin and orifices. He insists the parasites exit “where the poop comes out, from my eyes, my nose, and my genitals.” His mental status evaluation revealed average intelligence, intact thought process, but a fixed somatic belief of infestation without hallucinations outside of generalized cenesthetic sensations. He has no obsessions, phobias, or thought disorder. Physical examination, including detailed skin inspection, revealed no lesions or excoriations; laboratory tests were normal. No imaging or toxicology could be obtained. 

The wife initially attempted extensive household cleaning without finding any pests. Over the past year, she developed intermittent formication—“I feel invisible animals…they run all over my body, I do not see them, but I feel them”—though less intense than her husband’s symptoms. Their three adult children remain asymptomatic.

An 83-year-old man with idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy and prior CRT-D implantation presented for routine follow-up with dyspnea on exertion. At age 79, he was diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy (LVEF 27%, QRS 134 ms in ventricular escape rhythm) complicated by CHF, complete AV block, and sustained VT, and underwent CRT-D implantation (Claria MRI Quad) with the LV lead in a lateral mid-ventricular vein. One year later, he developed persistent atrial fibrillation despite catheter ablation; ventricular pacing remained at 100% in VVI 80 ppm, so AV nodal ablation was not performed. Three years after implantation, the generator was exchanged due to rising LV pacing threshold; output was set to 3.0 V/0.8 ms (LV1–3, VV delay 0 ms). Two weeks before this visit, he developed worsening dyspnea and was started on furosemide and pimobendan. On examination he had lung congestion, pretibial edema, and an NT-proBNP of 5771 pg/mL. ECG showed biventricular pacing during AF. LV threshold was 2.5 V/1.0 ms (LV1–3), impedance 304 Ω, and %Vp 100%. The LV polarity was changed to LV1–coil (threshold 2.0 V/1.0 ms, impedance 190 Ω), output 3.0 V/1 ms, and adaptive autocapture was enabled. The pacing mode was set to VVIR 80 ppm and the EffectivCRT algorithm was activated. Three months later, his CHF symptoms had improved, but the percentage of effective biventricular pacing (%EBiVp) was <30% immediately after activation of EffectivCRT despite 100% ventricular pacing and stable thresholds. Review of the unipolar LV1–RV coil electrogram when %EBiVp was ≈30% showed that each beat had a negative deflection preceding a positive deflection, consistent with effective capture, yet some beats were classified as “ineffective.” Pseudofusion, loss of capture, LV conduction latency, and anodal capture were considered as possible mechanisms.

A 68-year-old man with type II diabetes mellitus presented with a 2-week history of left-sided neck pain, especially on swallowing, and persistent low-grade fever. He had no response to nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs. Examination by otolaryngology revealed marked soft-tissue destruction of the left peritonsillar region and tonsillar fossa without active bleeding. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. 

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the neck demonstrated an extensive lesion in the left peritonsillar and pharyngeal region with a liquefied central component. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a mass in the left submandibular region, lateral to the major neck vessels, compressing the internal jugular vein. The lesion lay posterior to the submandibular gland, displacing it anteriorly, and there was a defect in the lateral oropharyngeal wall, heterogeneous thickening of the palatine tonsil, and a necrotic lymph node adjacent to the internal jugular vein. 

Differential diagnoses included abscess versus tumor. Biopsy specimens were obtained twice to exclude malignancy.

A 28-year-old man was referred to the sleep clinic for a 3-month history of snoring, witnessed apnea, poor sleep quality, and excessive daytime sleepiness. He also reported a 4-year history of occipital headache, present most of the day and worst on awakening, aggravated by Valsalva maneuvers and neck flexion, without photophobia, phonophobia, visual scotoma, nausea, vomiting, or Lhermitte’s sign. He had no history of smoking, alcohol use, or substance abuse and lived at 1189 m above sea level. 

On examination, his BMI was 29.4 kg/m2, neck circumference 40 cm, and he had a short neck. STOP-BANG score was 5 and Epworth Sleepiness Scale score was 15. Mallampati score and tonsil grade were both 2. Neurologic examination showed normal mental status, cranial nerves, fundoscopic exam, motor strength, plantar responses, and sensory, cerebellar, and gait testing. Deep tendon reflexes were increased, with a positive Hoffman sign and non-sustained clonus.

Overnight polysomnography (AASM 2015) showed a total sleep time of 440 min, sleep efficiency 95.7%, and apnea-hypopnea index of 82.4/h, with 423 central apneas, 26 obstructive apneas, 88 mixed apneas, 68 obstructive hypopneas, and no central or mixed hypopneas. Mean oxygen saturation during sleep was 89.1%, with a nadir of 73%.

He was diagnosed with central sleep apnea. Cardiac evaluation revealed a normal ejection fraction of 65%. Fasting blood glucose, thyroid function, and renal function tests were all normal. Arterial blood gas analysis showed pH 7.44, PCO2 34 mmHg, and HCO3– 23.1 mEq/L. According to his neurologic signs, brain and cervical MRI was performed.

A 42-year-old man presented with a one-month history of slowly enlarging, painless masses over the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints of both hands, most notably affecting the 4th and 5th fingers of the left hand. He reported progressive restriction of extension in those fingers, with extension deficits of 20° and 30°, respectively. Neurovascular examination was intact. On inspection, multiple firm, non-tender nodules were palpable over the extensor aspects of all MCP joints bilaterally. The patient also had bilateral arcus corneae. His family history was notable for early deaths from myocardial infarction, and laboratory testing revealed elevated serum cholesterol levels. Plain radiographs of the hands were unremarkable. Superficial ultrasonography demonstrated multiple solid masses intimately engaged with the extensor tendons, most prominently at the 4th and 5th MCP joints.

A 62-year-old woman with Philadelphia-chromosome–positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia diagnosed 3 months earlier underwent induction with hyper-CVAD and intrathecal methotrexate, then switched to dasatinib after acute kidney injury. She presented with a 2-day history of sudden, severe (10/10) headache, worse than prior post–intrathecal therapy headaches; neck pain radiating down her back (now resolved); low-grade fever; progressive generalized weakness; difficulty ambulating; and new-onset confusion. Her last intrathecal methotrexate dose was 4 days before presentation. In the emergency department, she was febrile to 101.5°F, tachycardic, normotensive, increasingly diaphoretic, lethargic, and noted to have neck stiffness. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 6.9 g/dL (down from 8.8), white blood cell count 6.8 K/µL. CT of the head revealed no acute process; MRI was contraindicated by a spinal stimulator. Neurology recommended empiric cefepime, vancomycin, and ampicillin before lumbar puncture. She was also on prophylactic fluconazole and acyclovir (escalated to treatment dosing). An initial LP attempt was unsuccessful due to patient confusion; she then deteriorated, requiring rapid‐sequence intubation. A fluoroscopic‐guided LP yielded cerebrospinal fluid with 24% granulocytes, 60% lymphocytes, and 3% macrophages; cultures showed no growth, and PCR was negative for herpes simplex virus, varicella-zoster virus; Lyme disease; and West Nile virus IgG and IgM. Respiratory and viral panels, including influenza and SARS-CoV-2 PCR, were also negative.

A 75-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis and type 2 diabetes presented with 4 months of intractable nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, associated with a 30-lb weight loss. She denied fever, abdominal pain, melena, hematochezia, or loss of appetite. Her symptoms were not triggered by specific foods and did not improve with a strict gluten-free or low-residue diet. She had taken methotrexate for RA until 2016 but no other immunosuppressants.  

At a community hospital, stool studies for enteric pathogens were negative, and celiac serologies (anti–tissue transglutaminase IgA) were normal. Initial esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed nonspecific inflammation of the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum; biopsies were negative for cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, and Helicobacter pylori. Duodenal biopsies demonstrated acute and chronic inflammation without villous blunting. Colonoscopic examination appeared normal, and no colon biopsies were obtained. She was diagnosed with viral gastroenteritis and irritable bowel syndrome and treated with rifaximin and ondansetron, but her symptoms continued to worsen, prompting admission.  

On examination, she was emaciated with stable vital signs and a benign abdominal examination. Laboratory studies showed albumin 1.7 g/dL and magnesium 1.3 mg/dL; C-reactive protein, liver and thyroid function tests, antinuclear antibody, HIV, immunoglobulin levels, and QuantiFERON‐Gold were normal or negative. Contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT was unremarkable.  

Repeat esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed scalloping and friability of the duodenal mucosa. Colonoscopy to the terminal ileum was normal. Duodenal and terminal ileal biopsies revealed glandular destruction, epithelial apoptosis, goblet cell depletion, and villous blunting without significant intraepithelial lymphocytosis. Periodic acid–Schiff staining was negative for Whipple disease, random colon biopsies were normal without microscopic colitis, and antienterocyte antibodies were negative.

A 13-year-old boy with a history of atopic dermatitis presented with a 2-week history of an itchy, vesicular rash in crops over his body, most pronounced on the distal extremities, accompanied by low-grade fever and intermittent headache. He had no animal exposures, travel history, or similar contacts. On examination, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. His skin showed clusters of centrally umbilicated pustules on an erythematous, edematous base over the hands, and well-demarcated eroded plaques with haemoserous crusts on the trunk and lower extremities. Complete blood count, chemistry panel, liver and renal function tests were within normal limits. He was admitted for diagnostic work-up, which included a punch biopsy of the pustules for histopathology, bacterial culture, and monkeypox PCR testing. Empiric therapy with intravenous ceftriaxone and clindamycin was initiated.

A 24-year-old man with no medical history presented with a 3-week history of fevers and nonproductive cough after returning from the Bahamas. He had completed a course of amoxicillin-clavulanate and a short steroid taper, but his fevers persisted. On admission, his temperature was 39.3 °C. Physical examination revealed palpable bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, right upper-quadrant abdominal tenderness, and a painless chancre on the glans penis; he reported recent unprotected sexual activity with one female partner.

Initial laboratory studies showed:  
• Aspartate aminotransferase 1,749 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase 1,928 IU/L  
• Ferritin 53,386 μg/L  
• Triglycerides 295 mg/dL  
• Sodium 128 mmol/L, creatinine 1.27 mg/dL  
• Platelets 105 × 10³/μL; other blood counts and coagulation tests were within normal limits  

An extensive workup for acute liver injury revealed negative acetaminophen, salicylate, and alcohol levels; negative viral hepatitis and autoimmune hepatitis serologies; and unremarkable right upper-quadrant ultrasonography and liver magnetic resonance imaging.

A 74-year-old Japanese man was referred in October 2018 for a painless swelling in the right maxillary region at the junction of the free gingiva of the canine–premolar area and the buccal mucosa. On inspection, the overlying mucosa was intact and of normal color; palpation revealed a movable, soft-to-rubbery, nontender lesion measuring approximately 18 × 8 mm, with no induration. Submandibular lymph nodes were not palpable. Dental records showed maintenance care with fair periodontal status; pocket depths around the involved teeth were 3–4 mm. His history was notable for endoscopic submucosal dissection for esophageal cancer in 2016 and gastric cancer in 2017. A periapical radiograph showed no maxillary bone changes except cervical bone resorption near the central incisors, canine, and first premolar. MRI demonstrated a well-defined lesion with low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted and STIR images, suggesting a fluid-filled lesion; mild thickening of the adjacent maxillary sinus mucosa was also noted. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a non-enhancing mass of low attenuation without bone resorption, but “the possibility of a neoplastic lesion could not be denied.” Light microscopy of a biopsy specimen showed a mucoid matrix and fibrous connective tissue, and “a myxoid tumor including odontogenic myxoma was suspected.”

A 54-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of pain and progressive multiple swellings on the right hand and wrist. He denied trauma, weight loss, night sweats, or known tuberculosis exposure. On examination, there was a 5×4×2 cm fluctuant swelling on the dorsum of the hand and two 2×1×1 cm swellings over the dorsolateral wrist. Active palmar flexion was 0–60° (painless) and 60–70° (painful with 10° restriction), and dorsiflexion was 0–60° (painless) and 60–70° (painful with 20° restriction); radial deviation was 0–10° and ulnar deviation 0–20°. There was no lymphadenopathy or neurovascular deficit. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and metabolic panel, but ESR and CRP were elevated. Wrist radiographs revealed no bony abnormalities. Ultrasound demonstrated extensor tendon‐sheath effusion with synovial hypertrophy, consistent with tenosynovitis.

A 69-year-old African Caribbean woman presented with a bilateral upper visual field defect and long-standing peri-orbital skin lesions. She had a history of kidney transplantation for end‐stage polycystic kidney disease and denied any periocular trauma or inflammation. The cutaneous lesions first appeared around age 35 and had progressively extended; they were described as keratotic, hyperpigmented papules. On ophthalmologic examination, there was bilateral ptosis (interpalpebral fissure 2 mm on the left and 4 mm on the right) and ectropion of the lower eyelids. Slit-lamp examination revealed bilateral punctate superficial keratitis and an inferior corneal pannus. Pupils were equal and reactive without an afferent pupillary defect, extraocular movements were full, and upper-eyelid levator function measured 12 mm. A full review of systems was otherwise unremarkable.

A 65-year-old woman with no significant medical history was found to have an abnormal chest shadow on screening. She had no respiratory symptoms, normal vital signs, and an unremarkable physical examination, including no clubbing or cyanosis. Routine blood tests, including tumor markers, and pulmonary function tests were normal. High-resolution CT of the chest revealed a 1.5 cm ground-glass nodule in the right lower lobe (segment 6). A transbronchial lung biopsy showed atypical cells without overt malignancy. Three months later, surveillance CT demonstrated a slight increase in the size of the nodule. For definitive diagnosis, video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery was performed. Histologic examination of the resected tissue revealed diffuse lymphoid follicular hyperplasia, infiltration of the alveolar septum by small lymphocytes and plasma cells, follicular bronchiolitis, and macrophage and lymphocyte exudation in alveolar spaces. Immunohistochemical staining showed CD20 positivity in follicles, CD3 positivity in alveolar septal lymphocytes, and no monoclonal growth of κ or λ positive cells.

A 16-year-old obese (BMI 34.7) virgin girl presented to the emergency department in hypovolemic shock. She reported a one-month history of new-onset dysmenorrhea superimposed on previously irregular, heavy menstrual bleeding for which she was taking ferrous sulfate. She had menarche at age 12, no previous surgeries, and no use of contraceptives or hormonal agents. On examination, her abdomen was distended and diffusely tender without a palpable mass. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 6.0 g/dL, LDH 1476 U/L, CA-125 1063 U/mL, CA19-9 1347 U/mL, and a negative serum hCG. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 13 × 12.5 × 10 cm heterogeneously enhancing mass in the uterine corpus, and chest CT showed enhancing nodules in the right (3.5 cm) and left (1.5 cm) lower lobes, all suggestive of a uterine malignancy with metastatic disease.

A 31-year-old primigravida with an uncomplicated IVF-conceived pregnancy presented in spontaneous full-term labor. Her past history was notable only for a recovered eating disorder and secondary amenorrhea; there was no family history of thrombosis. After an assisted forceps vaginal delivery of a healthy daughter, she developed hemorrhagic shock from a retained placenta. She received 5 L intravenous fluids, six units of packed red cells, two units of fresh frozen plasma, one pool of platelets, 2 g of tranexamic acid, intramuscular ergometrine, and intrauterine carboprost. As she became increasingly unstable (arterial lactate 8 mmol/L, hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL), she was intubated and taken to the operating room.  

In the ICU, she was diagnosed with disseminated intravascular coagulation: platelets 59 × 10^9/L, fibrinogen 1.3 g/L, prothrombin time 17.2 s, aPTT 117 s, and D-dimer 35 mg/L. Two days later, after extubation, she had difficulty following commands; the stroke team diagnosed speech apraxia. Brain MRI showed extensive acute ischemia in both cerebral hemispheres (large cortical infarcts with subcortical sparing) and cerebellum, raising concern for a reversible vasoconstriction syndrome.  

Her ECG then demonstrated diffuse T-wave inversions. A high-sensitivity troponin-I was 37,000 ng/L. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed severe left ventricular systolic impairment, apical akinesia, and mobile echogenicity suggestive of thrombus.

A 75-year-old woman presented with a 4-week history of right-sided scalp dysaesthesia and formication and a 2-week history of right ptosis. Visual acuity was 20/25 bilaterally, intraocular pressures were normal, and there was no evidence of uveitis. Examination revealed a smooth, painless mass palpable in the right superior and inferior orbit, with 4 mm of proptosis and 2 mm of globe dystopia. Right upper-lid ptosis was almost complete with no levator function. Extraocular motility was full, and optic nerve function was intact.

Laboratory studies showed an unremarkable inflammatory and vasculitic screen, including C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, antinuclear antibody, proteinase 3, and myeloperoxidase antibodies. Angiotensin-converting enzyme was normal at 52 U/L, and serum IgG4 levels were within normal limits.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the orbits demonstrated a right supraorbital mass centred in the lacrimal gland with extension into the superior and lateral orbit. The lesion exhibited homogeneous contrast enhancement and restricted diffusion. The right frontal nerve was noted to be enlarged and enhancing.

An orbital biopsy via a superior lid crease approach revealed non-caseating granulomatous inflammation composed of tight collections of epithelioid histiocytes without evidence of vasculitis. No acid-fast bacilli or fungal elements were seen on staining, and PCR testing for tuberculosis was negative. Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no signs of systemic disease.

A 56-year-old man with a 21-year history of Waldenström’s macroglobulinaemia, previously treated with fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and plasma exchange, was enrolled in a trial and received zanubrutinib 160 mg twice daily for relapsed disease. He also took aciclovir and co-trimoxazole prophylaxis. He had a history of mild psoriasis, a BMI of 30, weekly alcohol intake of 300 g, and a 10 pack-year smoking history. He had no other regular medications and no recent new drug exposures.

After 28 months of zanubrutinib, routine labs showed an asymptomatic rise in transaminases and total bilirubin. Eight weeks later he developed pale stools, dark urine, pruritus, and jaundice and was admitted. On examination, he was jaundiced but had no signs of liver failure. Admission labs were: ALT 2474 IU/L (ULN 45), AST 1257 IU/L (ULN 35), ALP 114 IU/L (ULN 130), total bilirubin 141 µmol/L (ULN 21), and prothrombin time 14 s (ULN 12). 

Ultrasound of the liver showed a normal biliary tree and an echogenic liver consistent with fatty changes. A comprehensive serologic liver screen—including viral hepatitis markers and autoimmune liver antibodies—was entirely negative.

A 56-year-old Caucasian woman with no comorbidities first noted severe, generalized fatigue and myalgias predominantly in her calves and thighs; she was diagnosed with fibromyalgia and treated supportively without improvement. One year later, she developed bilateral hip and knee arthralgias with prolonged morning stiffness, intermittent fevers up to 38.9 °C—initially nocturnal, later constant—and a nonpruritic rash that began on the chest wall and became diffuse. She also reported intermittent bluish discoloration of her fingernails and diarrhea; workup for Raynaud phenomenon and celiac disease was negative. Due to progressive bilateral lower-extremity pain and weakness, an MRI of the spine to evaluate for lumbar stenosis was performed and was unrevealing. An autoimmune panel—including ANA, rheumatoid factor, p-ANCA, c-ANCA, SSA/SSB, SM-Ab IgG, and RNP IgG—was unrevealing. Inflammatory markers were elevated (CRP 30 mg/L [< 0.5]; ESR 37 mm/h [0–25]). Evaluation for Lyme disease was negative. Serum protein electrophoresis revealed a monoclonal gammopathy of 0.3 g/dL. A punch biopsy of the skin showed dermal neutrophilic and eosinophilic infiltrates consistent with chronic urticaria. The rash persisted despite antihistamines; she had an initial response to steroids with rapid relapse upon taper. A 6-month course of celecoxib and hydroxychloroquine provided no benefit and was discontinued. She underwent right and then left hip arthroplasties for worsening pain; synovial and bone pathology showed acute and chronic synovitis with reactive changes. With ongoing fevers, arthralgias, nonpruritic urticaria, elevated inflammatory markers, and IgM kappa monoclonal gammopathy, she was started on high-dose steroids with a provisional diagnosis of adult-onset Still’s disease and referred to hematology for further evaluation of her monoclonal gammopathy.

A 12-year-old Korean girl presented with a 9-year history of multiple asymptomatic hypopigmented papules on the trunk and extremities. The lesions first appeared at age 3 and have slowly increased in number. Each papule measured several millimeters, was slightly indurated, and was distributed asymmetrically. There was no history of trauma or preceding inflammation at the involved sites, and there was no family history of similar skin conditions. A biopsy of a papule on her arm showed a hyperkeratotic epidermis with a perivascular lymphoid infiltrate in the superficial dermis. Hematoxylin-eosin staining revealed an increased thickness of finely woven collagen fibers in the upper dermis, and elastic tissue staining demonstrated primarily decreased and some fragmented elastic fibers in the same layer. The lesions persisted without treatment over a two-year follow-up period.

A 26-year-old woman with a 6-year history of end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis presented with 10 days of mid–thoracic back pain, progressive weakness of both lower extremities, and gait disturbance. On neurologic examination, she had spastic paraparesis, symmetrically hyperactive lower-extremity reflexes, bilateral Achilles clonus, and hypoesthesia below the T10 dermatome. Physical examination also revealed a swelling on the left side of the jaw. Magnetic resonance imaging of the thoracic spine showed an extradural, heterogeneous T2-weighted mass lesion causing cord compression at the T8 level. Computed tomography of the thoracic spine demonstrated an expansile, lytic lesion with collapse of the T8 vertebral body. A CT scan of the mandible revealed a similar expansile lytic lesion on the left mandibular ramus. Laboratory studies showed a parathyroid hormone level of 1289 pg/mL (reference, 30–70), a serum calcium level of 9.8 mg/dL (8.4–10.2), and a serum phosphorus level of 3.8 mmol/L (2.7–4.5). Ultrasound examination revealed enlargement of the parathyroid glands.

A 5-year-old girl was brought by her mother for evaluation of her discolored and rapidly wearing primary teeth. The mother’s chief concern was impending school entry and potential peer harassment due to her daughter’s dental appearance. The child was born full-term, achieved normal developmental milestones, and had no history of unusual bone brittleness, drug use, or any systemic illness. Oral hygiene was fair, with limited intake of sugary foods. Family history was notable for the mother’s diagnosis of dentinogenesis imperfecta type II and two affected siblings.

Extraoral examination showed marked loss of vertical dimension of occlusion with an edentulous–like appearance, decreased lower facial height, a prognathic profile, and reduced lip support. Intraoral examination revealed severe attrition of all primary teeth down to the gingival level, with teeth exhibiting a yellow–brown, translucent appearance.

Panoramic and periapical radiographs demonstrated severe enamel loss with marked occlusal attrition. Several primary molars had pulpal involvement and periapical radiolucencies. Developing permanent tooth buds were visible, showing thin enamel, enlarged pulp chambers, and mild cervical constriction of the crowns. The child’s dental age matched her chronological age.

A 20-year-old man presented with a 2½-year history of intermittent scleral icterus. His total bilirubin measurements ranged from 1.8 to 7.2 mg/dL, with an isolated elevation of the indirect fraction. He denied abdominal pain, swelling, bleeding, fever, chills, neurologic symptoms, or any precipitating factors. He took no medications or supplements, used no tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs, and had no significant birth or neonatal history.

On examination, vital signs were normal, and there was no jaundice beyond mild scleral icterus. Abdominal and systemic examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed normal ceruloplasmin, peripheral blood smear, lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin, acetaminophen level, and thyroid-stimulating hormone. Acute viral hepatitis serologies were negative for hepatitis A IgM, hepatitis B core IgM, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C antibody. An abdominal ultrasound revealed a liver of normal size and echogenicity without intrahepatic biliary dilatation; the gallbladder was normal without stones or pericholecystic fluid.

Given the patient’s asymptomatic indirect hyperbilirubinemia, the differential diagnosis included Crigler–Najjar syndrome type 2 versus Gilbert syndrome, and targeted mutation analysis of the UGT1A1 gene was sent.

A 79-year-old Japanese woman with a history of hypertension and arrhythmia suddenly developed left-sided weakness and drowsiness and was admitted to the emergency department. On examination, she was mildly obtunded, had conjugate gaze deviation to the right, mild dysarthria, left unilateral spatial neglect, left facial weakness, left arm and leg weakness, and left sensory loss. 

Laboratory studies on admission showed hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL, hematocrit 39.8%, serum sodium 142 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 16 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.69 mg/dL. Electrocardiography revealed atrial fibrillation. Brain MRI demonstrated a large diffusion-weighted hyperintense lesion in the right middle- and posterior-cerebral artery territories, and MRA showed occlusion of the right internal carotid artery. Noncontrast CT showed no hemorrhage, and she was started on anti-edema therapy and a continuous heparin infusion.

Her neurological status remained stable, and follow-up CT showed improving edema. On day 14, MRA revealed recanalization of the right internal carotid artery, but new hemorrhage appeared in the right middle-cerebral-artery infarct, prompting discontinuation of heparin. On day 15, CT showed expansion of hemorrhage and edema, and her level of consciousness worsened. Concurrently, she developed marked polyuria and hyponatremia, with clinical signs of dehydration, including reduced skin turgor, collapse of the inferior vena cava, and a 4.6% loss in body weight. Despite aggressive fluid replacement (input 3410 mL vs. urine output 3710 mL on day 20), she remained in negative fluid balance.

On day 28, a water-deprivation antidiuretic hormone stimulation test was performed by administering 10 µg of intranasal desmopressin, but her urine volume did not decrease.

A 24-year-old man presented with 4 days of moderate left-sided chest pain radiating to his back, worse on deep inspiration. He denied fever, chills, cough, hemoptysis, night sweats, weight loss, or recent travel. His history was notable for three episodes of left lower lobe pneumonia over the past 6 months, treated with various antibiotics; he currently took meloxicam as needed for chest pain. He had a remote right inguinal hernia repair but no family history of cancer or cardiac disease. He had immigrated from Guatemala 4 years earlier; he denied high-risk sexual behaviors, drug use, and had no smoking history.

On examination he was tachycardic (101 bpm) and tachypneic (22 breaths/min); the remainder of the physical and respiratory examination was normal. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 14×10^9/L (75% neutrophils); basic metabolic panel and liver function tests were normal. Urine Legionella antigen and HIV antibodies were negative. Tuberculin skin test demonstrated 18 mm of induration at 72 hours; interferon-gamma release assay was negative. Blood cultures showed no growth after 5 days. A chest radiograph demonstrated a left lower lobe opacity.

CT angiography of the thorax revealed a 9 cm well-defined area of low attenuation in the left lower lobe with internal infiltrates. A dedicated pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein arose from the hilar region and entered the lesion. No systemic arterial supply, pleural involvement, or abnormal lymphadenopathy was identified.

A 13-year-old boy presented with a 3-week history of blistering rash on the hands and arms accompanied by abdominal cramps and diarrhea. He had recently re-introduced gluten into his diet. The gastrointestinal symptoms resolved, but the rash spread to his back and thighs. At urgent care, he was diagnosed with erythema multiforme and treated with topical hydrocortisone 1% cream and cetirizine. Ten days later, on dermatology evaluation, examination revealed a polymorphous eruption of tense vesicles on the hands and feet, smooth pink papules on the trunk and extremities, tense vesicles on the vermilion lips extending into the mucosa, and deep red atypical targetoid macules on both hands. He was presumed to have herpes simplex virus–induced erythema multiforme and received valacyclovir 2 g daily for 5 days plus a 14-day prednisone taper (40 mg daily for 1 week, then 20 mg daily). Two weeks later, although the eruption had improved, new blisters developed in areas of trauma on the hands, feet, and lips; prior blisters healed with atrophic scars. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and metabolic panel. No herpes virus antibodies were detected, and anti-Mycoplasma IgG was elevated while IgM was absent.

A 24-year-old man presented with an 8-year history of insidious onset, gradually progressive thinning and weakness of his right lower limb, leading to toe walking and difficulty squatting on that side. Three years ago, he noted progressive muscle thinning and deformity of the right half of his face and chest. He denied fever, headache, fasciculations, sensory changes, vision or hearing loss, seizures, trauma, chronic infections, drug abuse, hypertension, or diabetes. Family history was unremarkable.

On examination, there was marked atrophy of the right lower-limb muscles with a 2.5 cm difference in thigh and leg circumference compared with the left, and foot deformity with contracture. Facial asymmetry was evident from atrophy of the right cheek, chin, and lips, with a hyperpigmented patch and “coup de sabre” scar on the right frontal and mandibular regions. The right mandible, maxillary, zygomatic, and frontal bones appeared depressed. Intraoral examination showed atrophy and fissuring of the right side of the tongue. The right hemithorax was depressed due to wasting of subcutaneous tissue and thoracic muscles. Higher mental functions and funduscopic examination were normal. Muscle strength (MRC scale) was 4/5 proximally and distally in the right lower limb and 5/5 elsewhere. Deep tendon reflexes, plantar responses, sensory examination, and cerebellar testing were normal.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, serum biochemistry (including thyroid function and vitamin B12), and abdominal ultrasonography without organomegaly or free fluid. Serologies for HIV, HBsAg, and HCV were negative. Antinuclear antibodies, anti–double-stranded DNA, anti-histone, rheumatoid factor, and anti-centromere antibodies were negative. Electrocardiography and echocardiography were normal. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography of the face and limbs were normal. Radiographs demonstrated disparity in the lengths of the right and left femur and tibia. MRI of the lower limbs confirmed thinning of the right leg and thigh musculature. Facial CT with three-dimensional reconstruction showed atrophy of the right mandibular, maxillary, zygomatic, and frontal bones. MRI of the brain and spine was normal.

A 35-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of recurrent spontaneous pneumothoraces. Five years earlier, she developed sudden left-sided chest pain and dyspnea after air travel. Emergency imaging showed a large left pneumothorax with midline shift, and she underwent video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) with apical bleb excision and mechanical pleurodesis. Surgical biopsy revealed subpleural fibrosis with reactive changes. Three months later, she presented with sudden dyspnea and chest pain; imaging showed a small right apical pneumothorax, which resolved with supplemental oxygen. Pulmonary function tests demonstrated a mild obstructive defect (FEV1/FVC 68%, FEV1 85%). Transthoracic echocardiography was normal. Genetic analysis for α1-antitrypsin was negative, and cystic fibrosis screening was unremarkable. Six months before the pulmonary consultation, she again presented with right-sided pneumothorax and was found on CT to have multiple bilateral parenchymal lung cysts; she underwent right VATS and pleurodesis. On examination, she had bilateral follicular papules on her cheeks, and she reported multiple family members with spontaneous pneumothoraces.  
What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 37-year-old Caucasian man was referred for chronic low back pain without radicular radiation and known disc prolapse at T10–T11. His history was notable for:
• A 1993 gunshot injury to the right lung, requiring resection of ribs 1–3 and right lower lobectomy  
• A second gunshot in 1996 causing a skull fracture behind the right ear and traumatic lesions of the facial, statoacoustic, and trigeminal nerves, resulting in persistent right-sided anacusis, tinnitus, peripheral facial palsy, and hemihypesthesia  
• Pulmonary tuberculosis in 1998 treated with a single drug for three years, followed by chronic bronchitis  
• Occasional panic attacks, holocranial or occipital headache, and no prior episodes of pressure palsies  
• No family history of neuromuscular disorders  

Neurologic examination revealed:
• Anacusis on the right, hypoacusis on the left, right peripheral facial palsy, and right facial hemihypesthesia  
• Neck-muscle soreness  
• Mild distal limb weakness (e.g., finger spreading M4 / M5−, hand flexion M4+, foot extension M5− / M4+, foot flexion M4+)  
• Discrete diffuse wasting and generally reduced tendon reflexes  
• Sensory hypoesthesia of the left ulnar hand border and digits 4–5, and a right stocking-type distribution  
• Positive Romberg with a tendency to fall backward to the left  

Laboratory and imaging studies showed:
• Positive anti–hepatitis C antibodies, HCV‐RNA titer 4.5 × 10^6, ANA 1:1280  
• ECG with incomplete right bundle‐branch block  
• Pulmonary function tests with basal air‐trapping; bronchoscopy negative for active tuberculosis  
• CSF protein 76.7 mg/dL (normal <43)  
• MRI with disc prolapses at C6–C7 and T11–T12  
• Nerve conduction studies demonstrating generally prolonged distal latencies, severely reduced conduction velocities, conduction blocks at sites predisposed to compression, and absence of denervation in the right anterior tibial muscle  
• Transcranial magnetic stimulation with normal central conduction times but prolonged peripheral latencies to the abductor digiti minimi, arguing against a myelopathic cause of weakness

A 49-year-old woman presented with a 12-hour history of sudden-onset, progressively worsening right hip pain, with fever developing 2 hours after pain onset. She rated the pain as 8/10 when bending the hip and was unable to bear weight. She had no history of trauma or comorbidities. On arrival, her temperature was 37.8°C, pulse 93/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and blood pressure 128/80 mmHg. Physical examination showed tenderness of the right medial thigh and painful limitation of movement, especially internal rotation. Laboratory tests revealed a white blood cell count of 14,200/μL with 87.6% neutrophils, hemoglobin 13.3 g/dL, and platelet count 295,000/μL. Plain radiographs of the hips showed only mild degenerative changes. Ultrasonography revealed diffuse swelling of the right hip joint. Under ultrasound guidance, 12 mL of yellow, cloudy, moderately viscous fluid was aspirated, and the patient’s pain improved to 4/10; she was able to walk. Joint fluid was sent for analysis, Gram staining, and culture. Four days later, on follow-up, her WBC count was 6,229/μL (67.5% neutrophils), joint fluid WBC count was 8,979/mm³ (78% neutrophils) with 1,000 RBCs/mm³, and Gram staining showed gram-negative bacilli.

An 81‐year‐old Caucasian woman presented with a 10-month history of a right groin bulge and mild exertional pain. She had no systemic disease and no prior episodes of acute cholecystitis. Surgical history included urinary incontinence surgery 12 years earlier and a left Lichtenstein hernioplasty 10 years earlier without recurrence. She had known thoracic and abdominal aortic aneurysms planned for endovascular repair and a cystocele.

On examination, there was a firm, nonreducible bulge in the right inguinal region that did not increase with coughing; palpation elicited pain.

Ultrasound of the groin revealed an elongated tubular structure containing multiple calculi, originating from the right hypochondrium and projecting into the femoral canal.

A 30-year-old man presented with recurrent seizures. His first episode occurred 4 months earlier, with a left-sided headache followed by inability to speak, preserved awareness without vocalization, right-sided facial twitching, and maintained consciousness for about 3 minutes. He did not seek immediate care. Two months before presentation, he had two similar episodes, each lasting about 2 minutes, prompting evaluation. 

He denied hypertension, diabetes, prior neurologic events, or significant family history. He smoked one pack of cigarettes per week and drank alcohol occasionally but had stopped. He took no regular medications. On exam, he was alert and oriented; vital signs were normal. Neurologic evaluation revealed no focal deficits, intact cranial nerves, normal strength and sensation, and no meningeal signs.

A noncontrast head CT demonstrated a hyperdense lesion in the left parietal lobe with surrounding hypodense perifocal edema, raising a differential diagnosis of arteriovenous malformation versus brain tumor. Subsequent brain MRI showed multiple flow‐voids within the lesion, evidence of ischemic components, and a left frontal lobe hemorrhage.

A 58-year-old man was admitted with 1 month of left iliac fossa pain, worsening constipation, rectal bleeding, and weight loss; he recently developed fever. His history included bronchial asthma, chronic hepatitis B, quadriplegia from spinal surgery, and the use of homemade enemas with tap water. On examination, he was febrile (38.3 °C), pulse 93/min, blood pressure 122/61 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min, and oxygen saturation 98%. The abdomen was diffusely tender with a tender mass in the left iliac fossa; external hemorrhoids were noted, and the remainder of the exam was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed WBC 5.7 × 10^9/L, eosinophils 0.8 × 10^9/L, platelets 703 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL, C-reactive protein 141 mg/L, creatinine 43 µmol/L, albumin 25 g/L, and normal liver enzymes; HIV test was negative. An initial CT scan showed a mass and perforated descending colon with pericolic fluid collection, suggesting colon carcinoma. Emergency laparotomy identified a mass extending from the sigmoid to the splenic flexure; a Hartmann procedure was performed. Grossly, there was an 11 × 5 cm hard mesenteric mass with a yellowish necrotic cut surface encasing the bowel. Histopathology revealed severe chronic granulomatous inflammation with necrosis, extensive fungal elements with marked necrosis, and multiple foci of angioinvasion.

A 72-year-old woman with osteoarthritis underwent an elective right total knee replacement under combined spinal–epidural anesthesia. A pneumatic thigh tourniquet was inflated to 300 mmHg for 90 minutes. Prophylactic enoxaparin was administered postoperatively. On the first postoperative day, she developed severe right lower leg pain that was exacerbated by any passive movement of the toes. She reported a sensation of tension across her entire calf and noted paraesthesia. On examination, distal pulses were palpable but weak. A handheld manometer (Stryker Intra-Compartmental Pressure Monitor) revealed compartment pressures of 26 mmHg (anterior), 32 mmHg (lateral), and 42 mmHg (posterior).

A 7-year-old boy was referred for chest pain and fever. He had sustained a blunt injury to the right chest during martial-arts training several days earlier. He denied cough, dyspnea, hemoptysis, night sweats, weight loss, or appetite changes. His history included allergic rhinitis and treated episodes of bronchitis. Family history was noncontributory.

On admission, temperature was 38.6 °C; he appeared anxious with tachypnea, shallow respirations, dyspnea, and intercostal retractions. Examination disclosed submandibular and cervical lymphadenopathy; purulent secretions on an erythematous posterior pharynx; chronic tonsillitis; and diminished breath sounds over the right lower lobe.

A chest radiograph showed a round right lower-lobe lesion suggestive of parenchymal infiltration; ultrasound revealed hypoechogenic areas. He received intravenous cefotaxime and clarithromycin for presumed pneumonia; his general condition improved but the right-lung consolidation persisted.

Chest CT demonstrated a solid, well-defined mass in the right lower lobe with calcifications, surrounded by ground-glass haze and contiguous with the posterior chest wall, diaphragm, and hilum. Video-assisted thoracoscopic lung biopsy revealed an inflammatory pseudotumor.

Laboratory studies showed a white blood count of 10.61 G/l with lymphocytic predominance and CRP of 2.46 mg/dl. Serologies for Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Toxoplasma gondii, HBV, HCV, and CMV were negative; EBV-DNA was 1400 copies/ml. Galactomannan and QuantiFERON-TB were negative. Sputum culture grew MSSA. Serum AFP, CEA, and β-HCG were within reference ranges; 24-hour urinary catecholamines were normal. Total IgE was elevated at 660 kU/l with low-level specific IgE (class 1) to airborne and food allergens. ANA and ANCA panels were negative.

A 54-year-old man with well-controlled HIV on Truvada and raltegravir and a history of treated syphilis presented with 4 weeks of progressive left leg weakness, bowel and bladder changes, and 1 week of dysesthesia. He denied infective symptoms, weight loss, TB exposure, recent travel, or new sexual contacts. On examination, reflexes were brisk in all limbs; left leg power was 0/5 (MRC scale); and there was sensory dissociation below T5, consistent with an incomplete Brown–Séquard syndrome. MRI of the spine showed two peripherally enhancing cavitating lesions at T4–T5 with associated meningeal thickening and cord oedema. Empiric anti-TB therapy was initiated. CSF analysis revealed a protein level of 3.07 g/L and a white-cell count of 7 × 10^9/L; CSF cryptococcal antigen, TB molecular testing, microscopy and culture, and viral PCR were all negative. Serial sputum AFB smears, blood cultures, and interferon-γ release assays were negative.

A 31-year-old Japanese man with no significant past medical history other than sinusitis presented with a 2-week history of low-grade fever and progressively worsening mild headache. He was alert, with no focal neurologic deficits. Fundoscopy showed no papilledema. There were no respiratory findings. Complete blood count and routine chemistry were normal. C-reactive protein was negative; erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 14 mm/h (normal, 1–9 mm/h). Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme was 10.7 U/L (normal, 8.3–21.4 U/L), and the CD4/CD8 ratio was mildly elevated at 3.27 (normal, 0.9–3.1). Tumor markers and tuberculin reaction were negative. 
Chest radiography revealed bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lung fields. Chest CT confirmed extensive mediastinal, hilar, and paratracheal lymphadenopathy. Noncontrast head CT demonstrated marked hydrocephalus with dilation of all ventricles, most pronounced in the fourth ventricle. MR imaging excluded Chiari type I malformation; cine MR showed patency of the aqueduct with absent CSF flow in the cisterna magna. Gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted MR imaging revealed millet seed–like leptomeningeal enhancement, multiple small enhancing lesions along the Virchow–Robin spaces, and enhancement around the fourth ventricular outlet. Gallium scintigraphy supported a diagnosis of sarcoidosis. 
Lumbar puncture yielded an opening pressure of 14 cm H₂O; the CSF was clear, with mild lymphocytic pleocytosis and a total protein level of 213 mg/dL. CT cisternography showed sparse backflow of contrast into the fourth ventricle, suggesting incomplete obstruction at the fourth ventricular outlet. A ventriculoperitoneal shunt was placed, and intracranial CSF pressure measured 20 cm H₂O intraoperatively. Open biopsies of the arachnoid membrane and frontal cortex revealed a nonspecific scar‐like lesion that was not characteristic of sarcoidosis but did not exclude it.

A 41-year-old woman with a 3-year history of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis presented with the sudden onset of visual disturbances. At the time of her SSc diagnosis, she had skin sclerosis of the fingers, hands, forearms, and face, Raynaud’s phenomenon with digital ulcers, multiple facial telangiectasias, esophageal reflux, and interstitial lung disease. Nail-fold capillaroscopy showed capillary loss with dilatation and microhemorrhages. A forearm skin biopsy demonstrated increased dermal collagen and superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltration. Laboratory studies revealed a positive antinuclear antibody titer (>1:320) with a nucleolar pattern, negative anti-centromere antibody, and negative anti-Scl-70 antibody. She was treated with bosentan and aspirin, with stable pulmonary findings over two years.

Seven days before transfer, she was admitted elsewhere for fever over 38°C and headache. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed protein 161.6 mg/dL, glucose 39 mg/dL, red blood cells 0 /mm3, and white blood cells 459 /mm3 (88% polymorphonuclear cells). Serum C-reactive protein was 10.6 mg/dL and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 82 mm/h. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated T2 hyperintense lesions in the frontal, left parietal, and left occipital lobes with leptomeningeal enhancement. Empirical ceftriaxone and vancomycin were initiated. After four days, she developed visual disturbances; repeat MRI showed increased size and number of multifocal T2 hyperintense lesions along both cerebral hemispheres and midbrain, including a 4.5-cm lesion in the right posterior lobe. Tests of CSF—including Gram stain and culture, PCR for herpes simplex virus and enteroviruses, cryptococcal antigen, and fungal cultures—were negative. She was then referred to our hospital.

On arrival, she could only count fingers at close range and also reported headache, dizziness, fever, myalgia, polyarthralgia, and bilateral foot tingling. Blood pressure was 192/103 mmHg, heart rate 48 beats/min, and temperature 37.3°C. Electrocardiogram showed sinus bradycardia. Neurologic examination revealed drowsiness, neck stiffness, symmetrical proximal and distal weakness (muscle strength 4/5), paresthesia in both feet, brisk biceps reflexes, absent patellar reflexes, and bilaterally positive Babinski signs. A 4 × 5 cm ulcer was noted over the right lateral malleolus; there was no synovitis. The white-cell count was 14,090 /mm3, C-reactive protein was 3.09 mg/dL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 56 mm/h. She continued antibiotics, and intravenous acyclovir, nicardipine, mannitol, and dexamethasone were added. Blood pressure stabilized within six hours, but her visual impairment worsened, and she developed left-sided weakness and new Raynaud’s phenomenon in her fingers. Emergent cerebral angiography revealed diffuse stenosis and a beaded pattern of the anterior and middle cerebral arteries and their branches, along with diffuse luminal narrowing and dysplastic changes in the right distal vertebral artery and basilar trunk, consistent with cerebral angiitis.

A 32-year-old woman with a 9-month history of primary hyperthyroidism due to diffuse toxic goitre presented 30 minutes after multiple bee stings with severe dyspnea, wheezing, pruritus, facial swelling, generalized urticarial rash, angioedema, nasal congestion, tachypnea, a rapid thready pulse, and hypotension (96/66 mm Hg). She was diagnosed with anaphylactic shock and treated with high-flow oxygen, levosalbutamol nebulization, and intravenous crystalloids. After 1 hour without relief and with no epinephrine available, she received 100 mg intravenous hydrocortisone. Her respiratory distress and hypotension resolved. Eight hours after admission, she developed rapidly progressive, symmetrical flaccid weakness—first in proximal lower limbs, then proximal upper limbs over 1 hour—with muscle strength graded 2/5, depressed deep tendon reflexes, intact sensation, and normal cranial nerves. She denied pain, paresthesia, dark urine, recent infections, trauma, or vaccination. Vital signs were blood pressure 124/64 mm Hg and pulse 112/min (collapsing). Cardiac examination revealed a hyperdynamic circulation and diffuse thyroid enlargement. Laboratory studies showed serum potassium 2.3 mEq/L; sodium, chloride, calcium, phosphate, and magnesium were normal; other biochemistry was normal. ECG demonstrated prominent U waves and QTc interval 0.32 s. EMG and nerve conduction studies, performed within 1 hour of weakness onset, were normal. Urine sodium and potassium, serum aldosterone, and renin levels were normal; urine potassium/creatinine ratio was 1.4 and transtubular potassium gradient was 2.6, indicating no renal potassium loss. MRI of the brainstem and cervical spinal cord showed no demyelination, vascular lesion, or features of transverse myelitis.

A 74-year-old man presented with a two-month history of progressive dysphagia, abdominal pain, jaundice, anemia, pale stools, dark urine, diarrhea, weight loss, and fatigue. His history included hypertension, prostatic hypertrophy, longstanding myopathy, type 2 diabetes, a 55-year, 20-cigarette/day smoking history, moderate alcohol intake, and prior removal of malignant melanoma and basal cell carcinoma. Recent esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed esophageal candidiasis treated with nystatin. On examination he was jaundiced; an abdominal ultrasound revealed gallbladder sludge, a hypoechoic pancreas, and a dilated common bile duct (8.7 mm). Contrast-enhanced CT showed a common bile duct diameter of 11 mm, intrahepatic cholestasis with stenosis at the hepatic-duct bifurcation, a liver cyst, pancreatic calcifications, and a benign-appearing pancreatic-neck cyst. Laboratory tests revealed CRP 79 mg/L (normalized after treatment of Escherichia coli urosepsis), hemoglobin 6.6 mmol/L (7.4 mmol/L after antibiotics), ALT 164 U/L, bilirubin 252 µmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 500 U/L, normal amylase, and serum CA 19-9 of 3003 kU/L (dropped to 165 kU/L after stenting). MRCP demonstrated a normal main pancreatic duct, intrahepatic cholestasis, and biliary changes suspicious for a Bismuth-Corlette type IV bile duct carcinoma. ERCP revealed multiple strictures of the small intrahepatic bile ducts, common bile duct dilation (12 mm), and a bifurcation stenosis; stenting improved liver tests. Serology showed IgG4 12.9 g/L, total IgG 25.69 g/L, negative ANCA panels, positive rheumatoid factor, and negative viral hepatitis and autoimmune liver–kidney microsome, smooth-muscle, antimitochondrial, and other autoantibodies. Hereafter, bile duct carcinoma or primary sclerosing cholangitis was suspected.

A 2-year-old boy was seen for progressive inability to fully extend his right elbow over several weeks without any preceding trauma. On examination, there was no swelling, erythema, or warmth. Flexion, pronation, and supination were preserved, but active extension was limited to –30 degrees. A firm, palpable mass was noted over the posterior distal aspect of the elbow. Radiographs showed an ossified mass arising from the proximal ulna. A Tc-99 bone scan demonstrated mildly increased uptake in the right elbow. MRI of the elbow revealed an ossified mass with surrounding edema extending from the proximal ulna into the triceps muscle. There was no medullary continuity between the mass and the ulna.

A 69-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of low-grade fever, a 9-kg weight loss, anorexia, and generalized weakness. He denied cough, dyspnea, night sweats, gastrointestinal symptoms, and recent travel. His history included poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 9.9 %) and hypertension. On exam, he was cachectic, temperature 101 °F, blood pressure 140/80 mmHg supine and 130/70 mmHg standing, pulse 84 bpm, and normal respiratory rate; there was no lymphadenopathy. Labs showed hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, sodium 129.7 mmol/L, and ESR 65 mm/h; urinalysis revealed glycosuria without ketonuria. Abdominal ultrasound and CT demonstrated bilateral adrenal masses (right 4.2 × 2.4 cm; left 3.8 × 2.5 cm). A 9 a.m. cortisol was 19.8 μg/dL and ACTH 10.6 pg/mL. A presumptive diagnosis of adrenal tuberculosis was made, and empiric antitubercular therapy was started. Over the next 2 months, symptoms worsened and he developed recurrent vomiting, confusion (GCS E4M6V2), hypotension (systolic 74 mmHg), hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia. Repeat cortisol was 19.9 μg/dL with ACTH 124 pg/mL. He was treated with IV fluids and hydrocortisone. After stabilization, a CT-guided biopsy of the adrenal mass was planned.

A 68-year-old man with pancreatic cysts previously identified in the tail and monitored as presumed branch-duct IPMNs was referred when contrast-enhanced CT suggested a new mass in the pancreatic body. He reported no abdominal pain or jaundice. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed normal CA19-9 and CEA levels, a normal serum IgG4 level of 46.5 mg/dL, and elevated pancreatic enzymes (amylase 181 U/mL, lipase 384.8 U/mL).

Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 3 cm pancreatic body mass with low density in the early phase and homogeneous delayed enhancement in the portal and late phases. MRI showed the lesion to be hypointense on T1- and T2-weighted images and hyperintense on diffusion-weighted imaging. MR cholangiopancreatography revealed stenosis of the main pancreatic duct in the body, upstream dilation to 3 mm, and multiple branch-duct cysts up to 3 cm in the body and tail. Endoscopic ultrasound confirmed a 3 cm low-echoic mass with heterogeneous internal echoes in the pancreatic body, and separate 30 mm multilocular cysts without mural nodules in the tail. Endoscopic retrograde pancreatography showed obstruction of the main pancreatic duct in the body with no upstream visualization.

Although invasive carcinoma derived from IPMN or pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma was suspected, localized autoimmune pancreatitis could not be excluded given the imaging characteristics; thus, endoscopic ultrasound–guided fine-needle aspiration was performed to obtain tissue for diagnosis.

A 42-year-old Thai woman presented with a 3-year history of multiple asymptomatic dark spots on her face, the dorsa of both hands and feet, wrists, and legs. The lesions appeared approximately 2 months after about 20 acupuncture sessions for bilateral tinnitus. She denied any prior systemic treatment, use of tattoo dye, or application of topical formulations before the procedure. Her only medical history was allergic rhinitis. On examination, there were bilateral, symmetric, round, faint, blue-gray macules measuring 1 to 3 mm in diameter over the preauricular regions, nasolabial folds, dorsa of the hands, wrists, legs, and dorsa of the feet. No lesions were noted elsewhere on the skin or mucous membranes. An incisional biopsy of a lesion on the right leg was performed. Histopathologic examination showed a normal epidermis and numerous clumps of black globoid particles of various sizes within the walls of the superficial and deep vascular plexus. Dark-field microscopy revealed numerous refractile granules predominantly around the eccrine glands and vascular structures.

A 36-year-old man presented with 2 years of progressive blurred vision in his right eye. He had undergone bilateral LASIK 10 years earlier. One month before presentation, he had been treated with topical prednisolone acetate 1% every 3 hours. On examination, uncorrected distance visual acuity was 20/400 in the right eye (improving to 20/80 with pinhole) and 20/20 in the left eye. Intraocular pressure by Goldmann applanation was 26 mmHg in the right eye and 17 mmHg in the left eye. Refraction in the right eye was +3.00 −2.00 ×30. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy of the right eye showed a large temporal patch of epithelial ingrowth reaching the visual axis, subepithelial edema with microbullae, and fluid accumulation between the LASIK flap and stromal bed; the flap was intact with a superior hinge. Anterior segment OCT demonstrated interface opacities and fluid collection. Central corneal thickness was 579 μm on pachymetry. Fundoscopic examination was normal in both eyes.

A 38-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and past tuberculosis underwent an elective left total hip arthroplasty via a posterior approach for advanced degenerative hip disease. Her body-mass index was normal, and she was not on antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy. The surgery was uncomplicated, and on postoperative day 1 she reported appropriate pain control and denied any weakness, numbness, or tingling. Her hemoglobin decreased from 10.7 g/dL preoperatively to 8.7 g/dL, and she ambulated 100 feet with therapy. She was discharged on aspirin 325 mg twice daily with home healthcare. On postoperative day 11, she noted increased swelling over the lateral hip and four days of numbness and tingling from her knee to her foot. In the emergency department, she was found to have a left foot drop and paresthesias in the L5 and S1 distributions. On postoperative day 15, musculoskeletal ultrasound demonstrated a fluid collection along the posterolateral hip that appeared to be compressing the sciatic nerve.

A 42-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of abdominal pain localized to the right iliac fossa and hypogastrium. He denied fever, vomiting, constipation, or diarrhea. His history was notable for bilateral orchidectomy at age 13 for cryptorchidism, with chronic hormone-replacement therapy, and ten days earlier he had received antibiotics for suspected gonorrhea (urethral discharge), which had subsequently resolved. On examination, palpation of the right iliac fossa and hypogastrium elicited pain without guarding or peritoneal signs. A small, painful, irreducible mass was noted in the right groin; it did not change with Valsalva maneuvers and was thought to be an adenopathy. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis and elevated C-reactive protein. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a noncompressible, aperistaltic tubular structure arising from the abdominal cavity into an inguinal hernia sac and was painful when pressed but could not be fully characterized. A subsequent CT scan was interpreted as showing “an inflamed appendix with its tip inside a right inguinal hernia.”

A female neonate, the second twin of a cesarean delivery at 37 weeks, was born to a healthy mother without a family history of malformations. Birth weight was 2705 g; Apgar scores were 9 and 10. Blood type was B positive in both mother and infant.

On examination, there was a large mass extending from both gluteal regions to the perineum, with a tiny central orifice draining urine. No external genitalia or anal opening were identified. A sacral dimple was noted a few centimeters below the iliac crest, and palpation revealed a bony protuberance. Limb movements were normal.

Investigations included:
- Karyotype: 46 XX
- Echocardiogram: patent foramen ovale and persistent left superior vena cava
- Spine ultrasound: low-lying conus with rhombus termination, no intramedullary masses
- Abdominal ultrasound: anteriorly rotated left kidney, no bladder or uterus visualized
- Spine radiograph: pubic diastasis, sacrococcygeal eversion with upward‐oriented bony protrusion
- Abdominal MRI (day 2): incomplete rotation of the left kidney with mild pyelocaliceal distension; distal ureters joined an amorphous pelvic structure leaking urine; bladder and uterus not characterized; small intestine protruded through a pubic diastasis into the perineal region, causing marked distension

A 22-year-old man with cystic fibrosis and exocrine pancreatic insufficiency treated with pancreatic enzymes presented with one day of sharp periumbilical pain that worsened and localized to the right lower quadrant. He reported three days of nausea and anorexia; his last bowel movement was two days before admission. He had no prior history of constipation or chronic abdominal discomfort. Medications included inhaled albuterol and dornase alfa, aztreonam lysine nebulization, azithromycin three times weekly, lansoprazole, lumacaftor-ivacaftor twice daily, pancreatic enzyme capsules three times daily, and a daily multivitamin.  
On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. Abdominal examination revealed diminished bowel sounds and right lower quadrant tenderness with equivocal rebound. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis (WBC 13.0 × 10^3/mm^3; neutrophils 62%) and normal electrolytes.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated thickening and edema of the terminal ileum, inflammatory changes in the adjacent colon, free fluid in the right paracolic gutter by the cecum, an appendix measuring 5.3 × 4.6 mm, and reactive lymphadenopathy.

A 62-year-old woman on maintenance dialysis for 27 years (chronic renal failure secondary to malignant hypertension) presented with 2 weeks of chest discomfort that worsened with deep inspiration; she noted palpitations for a few hours before arrival. On presentation, blood pressure was 85/54 mmHg, pulse 150 bpm, SpO2 95% on room air. ECG showed atrial fibrillation, which spontaneously converted to sinus rhythm within 1 hour; the ECG then demonstrated slight ST elevation in broad leads, especially I, II, and aVF. 

Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal left ventricular wall motion, thickness, and size; no valvular dysfunction; and diffuse mild pericardial fluid (maximum thickness 6 mm anterior to the right ventricle) without chamber collapse. 

Laboratory tests revealed normal creatine kinase and CK-MB levels, elevated C-reactive protein (5.2 mg/dL), and elevated high-sensitivity troponin I (86 ng/mL). Plain and contrast-enhanced chest CT showed diffuse pericardial effusion with CT values of 35–74 HU (suggestive of bloody effusion) but no evidence of aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, or contrast leakage into the pericardium.

A diagnosis of pericarditis was made, and she was admitted for observation.
