Over the first several days, her inflammatory markers normalized, the ST changes resolved, and she became asymptomatic on no medications. Blood pressure stabilized at 120–140/80–90 mmHg. On hospital Day 9, the pericardial effusion increased to 12 mm anterior to the right ventricle, causing mild diastolic right atrial collapse, but her hemodynamics remained stable. By Day 11, the effusion had decreased to 5 mm anterior to the right ventricle.

A 14-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes since age 4 (hemoglobin A1c 7.5%) was referred for slowly progressive finger joint contractures. At age 12 he developed puffy hands and Raynaud phenomenon. Over 2 years he noted mild pain, reduced range of motion of all finger joints, and tight skin on the dorsum of the fingers. 

On examination, he had sclerodactyly, periungual erythema, pachydactyly, and tapered fingertips of the 1st and 2nd digits bilaterally; no digital ulcers or muscle weakness. Metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints were held in flexion (40°–45°), with contractures at the wrists and elbows and trigger fingers of the 1st and 5th digits. The “prayer sign” and “tabletop test” were positive. No clinical respiratory or cardiovascular signs were present.

Laboratory studies showed a normal blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, muscle enzymes, pro-BNP, and urinalysis. Antinuclear antibodies were 1:640 (fine‐speckled); anti-Mi-2b and anti-Ro52 were positive; anti-Scl-70, anti-centromere, and anti-U1RNP were negative. 

Ultrasound revealed thickening of flexor tendon sheaths, especially at the 3rd and 4th fingers bilaterally; hand x‐rays and MRI were unremarkable. Nailfold capillaroscopy demonstrated disorganization of the microvasculature, megacapillaries, branching capillaries, microhemorrhages, and avascular areas. Cold‐challenge infrared thermography at 10 minutes showed an abnormal temperature gradient >1°C in all fingers. 

Pulmonary function tests revealed a restrictive pattern with mildly reduced DLCO (72%). Chest HRCT showed bilateral interstitial lung thickening with perihilar distribution and a fibrotic area in the apex. Echocardiogram revealed mildly reduced global longitudinal strain (−17.5%) without pulmonary hypertension; cardiac MRI showed no myocardial fibrosis.

A 36-year-old woman was found unconscious with generalized stiffening and urinary incontinence but reported no chest pain. Three weeks earlier, she had a brief gastroenteritis after eating shellfish in Vietnam. She had no family history of seizure or liver disease (including Wilson’s), no acetaminophen or excessive alcohol use, and no recreational drugs.  
On examination: BP 99/75 mmHg, HR 117 bpm, RR 17/min, no respiratory distress, JVP not elevated, no jaundice or Kayser–Fleischer rings, and a hepatic flap was present. Abdominal exam revealed mild epigastric tenderness without organomegaly. Heart sounds were regular, no murmur; lungs clear; no edema. Neurologic exam: pupils equal and reactive, cranial nerves II–XII intact, full strength and sensation in all limbs.  
Initial labs showed ALT 388 U/L and AST 378 U/L with normal bilirubin, ALP, INR, and PT. Abdominal ultrasound excluded cirrhosis or biliary obstruction. Viral hepatitis serologies (A, B, C, E; EBV; CMV) and autoimmune screen were negative. CT of the brain excluded intracranial bleeding or mass.  
Chest radiograph showed a possible soft-tissue opacity over the right upper mediastinum. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without significant ST-segment changes. Bedside echocardiography revealed preserved function without significant valvular pathology but a moderate-sized pericardial effusion without tamponade.  
Within 12 hours, she developed acute liver failure (ALT 3430 U/L, AST 3000 U/L, PT 14.9 s), became hypotensive with oliguric KDIGO stage 3 AKI, metabolic acidosis, and hyperkalaemia requiring treatment. Intravenous acetylcysteine was administered. Her serum troponin rose from 89 to 1089 to 1217 ng/L, and the widened mediastinum prompted an urgent CT aortogram.

A 43-year-old woman presented with progressively worsening right-sided neck pain for 3 days that did not respond to paracetamol. She had no recent upper respiratory infection or trauma. On examination, there was focal tenderness over the right side of the neck and mild right cervical lymphadenopathy without masses or bruits. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 6.35×10^9/L (neutrophils 57.1%, lymphocytes 29.6%, eosinophils 4.4%), platelet count of 134×10^9/L, C-reactive protein of 3.6 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 20 mm/hr. Initial ultrasound of the neck demonstrated a few prominent reactive lymph nodes at Level II but otherwise normal neck anatomy. She was treated empirically with oral co-amoxiclav and metronidazole for a presumed dental infection and given celecoxib for pain. After 4 days, the pain persisted, and on reassessment a focal tender point was noted over the right carotid pulse at the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage. A focused second-look ultrasound with a 7.5-MHz transducer showed increased echogenicity of the anterior and lateral perivascular tissues surrounding the distal right common carotid artery, carotid bulb, and proximal external carotid artery with obliteration of normal fat planes; no carotid wall thickening, plaques, luminal stenosis, or abnormal Doppler flow was seen. The left carotid region was normal.

A 32-year-old woman presented with a two-year history of progressive abdominal swelling. The swelling began in the left side of her abdomen and gradually involved the entire abdomen, becoming particularly prominent over the past year. She also noted a dull, aching pain in the left flank but denied hematuria, dysuria, or other urinary symptoms.

Her vital signs were within normal limits: temperature 37.0 °C, pulse 83 beats/min, blood pressure 100/80 mmHg, and respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. On examination, the abdomen was markedly distended, especially on the left, with a palpable, cystic mass that was not fixed to underlying structures. There was no tenderness beyond the flank discomfort; bowel sounds were normal.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, serum electrolytes, renal function tests, and urinalysis, were all within reference ranges.

Renal ultrasonography revealed a massive left-sided hydronephrosis extending across the midline and occupying most of the abdominal cavity. A noncontrast CT scan of the abdomen demonstrated massive left kidney pelvicalyceal dilatation with a thinned cortical rim measuring approximately 3 mm. The dilated collecting system spanned seven vertebral bodies in length, with its inferior border reaching into the pelvis. The left ureter and renal artery were not visualized, and there was significant mass effect on adjacent abdominal organs.

A 4-year-old girl with autism spectrum disorder was hospitalized for evaluation of fever and progressively poor oral intake. Her height was 91.5 cm, weight 14.5 kg, and she was nonverbal with limited social interaction. Three months earlier, she had been diagnosed with right corneal ulceration, left chalazion, and night blindness due to vitamin A deficiency, and was using cephem-type antimicrobial and hyaluronic acid eye drops. On admission, her temperature was 38.7 °C, blood pressure 100/77 mmHg, heart rate 100 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Laboratory testing showed a leukocyte count of 21,600 cells/µL, hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL, and C-reactive protein 6.57 mg/dL. Urinalysis revealed cloudy urine with bacteria, and she was started on piperacillin for a presumed urinary tract infection.

On hospital day 9, she developed swelling of both labia majora, more pronounced on the left side. Pelvic ultrasonography demonstrated a subcutaneous fluid collection in the labia majora. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography showed bilateral labial fluid accumulation with peripheral enhancement.

A 53-year-old woman presented with acute right lower quadrant abdominal pain. On examination, she had right lower quadrant tenderness with guarding and rigidity. Laboratory studies showed a leukocytosis with neutrophilia, and urinalysis was negative. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a right adnexal mass. 

Her history was notable for splenectomy at age 18 after trauma and four prior cesarean deliveries. She denied urinary or pelvic infections. The patient underwent bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. Intraoperatively, there were dense adhesions in the upper abdomen and pelvis, hydrosalpinx of the right fallopian tube, and multiple cysts on both ovaries.

Histologic examination of the right fallopian tube confirmed hydrosalpinx and adhesions. Both ovaries contained follicular and inclusion cysts. Additionally, the left ovarian serosa harbored a 5.0 mm well-defined nodule. Microscopic sections of this nodule revealed lymphoid aggregates with eccentric arterioles (white pulp) surrounded by vascular venous sinuses (red pulp). No true capsule was identified, though short trabeculae were present.

A 49-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of pain, swelling, and a discharging sinus over the proximal phalanx of the right third finger. The swelling was insidious in onset and gradually progressive; the sinus developed 1 year ago. He denied trauma, cough, weight loss, or decreased appetite and had no known risk factors for infection. He had previously undergone incision and drainage and courses of antibiotics elsewhere with no lasting improvement.

On examination, there was a firm, globular swelling at the base of the third digit with a single discharging sinus over the proximal phalanx. There were no signs of acute inflammation. Movement of the finger was painful and restricted.

Plain radiographs of the hand showed increased bone density, mild periosteal reaction, and an osteolytic lesion of the proximal phalanx of the third finger. A chest radiograph was normal. Local ultrasonography revealed a heterogeneous collection measuring approximately 1.25 × 1.37 × 1.30 cm. Laboratory studies showed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein; other laboratory parameters, including white-cell count, were within normal limits.

A 23-month-old boy presented with a 7-day history of fever (intermittent, to 102°F, two to three spikes daily) and a 5-day history of nonproductive cough and progressive shortness of breath. Similar episodes had occurred twice before in the past four months, each requiring hospitalization with a working diagnosis of pneumonia. His birth and developmental histories were unremarkable; immunizations were up to date.

On examination, he was tachypneic (respiratory rate 32/min) with subcostal and intercostal retractions and required 2 L of supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 of 94%. Heart rate was 112/min and blood pressure 96/60 mmHg. Auscultation revealed reduced air entry over the right posterior, infra-axillary, and inframammary regions, with bilateral wheezes and crackles. The remainder of the physical examination was normal.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL, white blood cell count 13,000/mm3 (neutrophils 28%, lymphocytes 51%, monocytes 6.8%, eosinophils 13.5%), platelets 380,000/mm3, ESR 6 mm/h, CRP 0.7 mg/L. Blood cultures grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus; tuberculosis workup was negative. Chest radiograph showed consolidation and collapse of the right lower lobe.

Because of recurrent lobar collapse and consolidation, an HRCT scan was obtained, demonstrating volume loss with consolidation and air bronchograms in the lateral segment of the right middle lobe and the entire right lower lobe, with distal bronchiectasis or collapse.

A 59-year-old man presented with 3 days of abdominal cramps and watery diarrhea up to 10 times daily. Nine months earlier, he had a 3-week history of similar but less severe symptoms; colonoscopy at that time showed a granular laterally spreading lesion in the ascending colon with a depressed area suspicious for invasive adenocarcinoma, and he underwent right colectomy with resolution of symptoms. He had a history of sinusitis with resected nasal polyps 7 months earlier. Two months ago he developed dysphagia; upper endoscopy showed reflux esophagitis (Los Angeles grade A), and his dysphagia improved on esomeprazole. He had no known drug or food allergies and no other atopic history. His medications included amlodipine, losartan, nebivolol, and atorvastatin. Physical examination was unremarkable. He received a 7-day course of ciprofloxacin and metronidazole for presumed acute gastroenteritis without improvement. Laboratory studies showed intermittent peripheral eosinophilia and an elevated serum IgE of 315.6 IU/mL (normal <130 IU/mL). Stool ova and parasite examinations and serologic tests for toxocara, Strongyloides stercoralis, and Schistosoma mansoni were negative. Abdominal CT showed ileal wall thickening (>4 mm) and mild ascites. Endoscopic evaluation revealed white papules in the esophagus, erosions in the duodenum, and erythema of the ileum. Biopsies from the esophagus and duodenum demonstrated 76 and 64 eosinophils per high-power field, respectively; the initial ileal biopsy was negative for eosinophils, but repeat ileal biopsy eight days later showed 249 eosinophils per high-power field. Review of the archived right colon specimen revealed a tubular adenoma with high-grade dysplasia and marked eosinophilic infiltration of the mucosa, submucosa, muscularis propria, and serosa. A QuantiFERON-TB Gold test was positive; sputum studies were negative, but imaging suggested mediastinal lymph node tuberculosis. He was anti–hepatitis B core–antibody positive and hepatitis B surface–antigen negative.

A 32-year-old nulligravida Hispanic woman presented with several days of worsening malaise, progressive abdominal distension, anorexia, diffuse abdominal pain, and dyspnea. She had a history of endometriosis diagnosed at exploratory laparotomy for hemorrhagic ascites two years earlier; she had discontinued hormonal therapy to attempt conception. On examination, her abdomen was distended and diffusely tender. Pelvic ultrasonography and CT scanning demonstrated a large volume of free intraperitoneal fluid without discrete mass lesions. Paracentesis yielded 5 L of thick bloody fluid with an erythrocyte count > 50,000/µL and negative bacterial cultures and cytology. Eight days later, she returned with recurrence of symptoms; repeat ultrasound and pelvic MRI again showed massive ascites. She underwent diagnostic laparoscopy, during which 10 L of hemoperitoneum was evacuated and extensive “frozen” pelvic adhesions with obliterated surgical planes were noted.

A 29-year-old primigravida woman at 15 weeks and 4 days of gestation presented with progressively worsening, 10/10 cramping right flank pain for 5 days. Four days earlier, she had been diagnosed clinically with a urinary tract infection and started on cephalexin; despite therapy she developed flank pain, chills, dysuria, hematuria, nausea, vomiting, and difficulty walking, and pain was refractory to acetaminophen. 

On admission, a renal ultrasound revealed a complex, hypovascular lesion in the interpolar region of the right kidney measuring 6.9 × 6.8 × 3.7 cm, with mild dilation of the upper pole calyces and no dilation of the renal pelvis. The patient was started on piperacillin–tazobactam. By hospital day 4, repeat ultrasound showed enlargement of the lesion to 8.0 × 7.5 × 6.1 cm, and on day 5 she had a fever of 100.9 °F.

An abdominal and pelvic MRI demonstrated moderate bilateral hydroureteronephrosis and an 8 cm complex cyst in the right kidney with a branch-shaped internal morphology that appeared to connect with the mid-pole collecting system; the lesion contained material hypointense to urine. To characterize the lesion without ionizing radiation exposure, ultrasound-guided percutaneous drainage of the inferior pole fluid collection was performed, yielding approximately 100 mL of purulent fluid. Cultures of that fluid grew Streptococcus anginosus and Prevotella bivia.

A 63‐year‐old woman with no recent infections or vaccinations developed headache, followed the next day by lightheadedness, nausea, diplopia, and bilateral upper‐limb ataxia. On day 3, brain MRI showed T2 hyperintense lesions around the dentate nuclei, cerebellar peduncles, right ventral medulla, and tegmentum. By day 5, she had mild impaired consciousness and left upper‐limb weakness, and MRI revealed a new right temporal lobe lesion. On day 6, she was transferred for further evaluation. 

On admission: temperature 36.8 °C, pulse 63/min, blood pressure 146/88 mmHg, respirations 17/min. Neurologically, GCS score was E4V4M6; there was left hemiparesis (MMT 3), extremity ataxia, and neck stiffness. 

Laboratory studies: WBC 11,100/µL, CRP 1.26 mg/dL; normal liver, renal, electrolyte, and coagulation panels. Autoimmune and vasculitic markers—including RF, ANA, SS‐A/SS‐B, MPO‐ANCA, PR3‐ANCA—were negative. Anti‐AQP4 and anti‐MOG antibodies were negative on both ELISA and cell‐based assay. 

CSF analysis: opening pressure 11 cm H2O; 50 mononuclear cells/µL; protein 96 mg/dL; β2‐microglobulin 1.71 µg/mL; IgG 10.7 mg/dL; MBP 33,000 pg/mL; IgG index 0.64; IL‐6 1410 pg/mL; no atypical cells. 

Repeat brain MRI showed extensive T2 hyperintense lesions involving bilateral cerebellar hemispheres, brainstem, bilateral thalami, right basal ganglia, right posterior limb of the internal capsule, and subcortical hemispheres, with extension via the corpus callosum to the left cingulate gyrus. A mass effect with right ventricular deformation and leftward midline shift was present. No spinal cord lesions were identified.

A 53-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of annular plaques on her forehead, cheeks, shoulders, and back. Her medical history included inactive pulmonary sarcoidosis, hyperlipidemia, thalassemia minor, and hypothyroidism. She had stable chest radiographs since 2015 and normal electrocardiogram and echocardiogram findings, and she had never required therapy for sarcoidosis. Skin treatments over the preceding years included hydroxychloroquine; methotrexate (discontinued for nausea); leflunomide (discontinued for alopecia and diarrhea); adalimumab (partial improvement); and tofacitinib (improvement but discontinued for muscle cramping). On referral, she was taking hydroxychloroquine and adalimumab. Examination revealed annular plaques with raised erythematous borders and hypopigmented centers in sun-exposed areas. The differential diagnosis included cutaneous sarcoidosis, annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma, and granuloma annulare. A 4-mm punch biopsy of a shoulder lesion showed an interstitial and nodular infiltrate of mono- and multinucleated histiocytes containing degenerated elastic fibers, histiocytes palisading around mucin, an admixed perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, and no evidence of microorganisms. Hemoglobin A1c was 5.6%.

A 42-year-old previously healthy man presented with a 1-week history of progressive jaundice, abdominal distention, and fluctuating fatigue. He denied abdominal pain, pruritus, hematemesis, fever, pale stools, use of homeopathic or allopathic medications or supplements, IV drug use, needle-stick injuries, and any family history of liver disease. On examination, he had deep jaundice, grade 2 pedal edema, and tense ascites without abdominal tenderness; vital signs were within normal limits.  

Laboratory studies showed: AST 35 U/L, ALT 58.3 U/L, ALP 268 U/L, total bilirubin 31.6 mg/dL (direct 22.9 mg/dL), albumin 2.69 g/dL, prothrombin time 16 s, creatinine 2.17 mg/dL. Serum iron and ferritin were normal. Alpha-fetoprotein, ceruloplasmin, and urine copper were within normal ranges. Viral serologies (HBsAg, anti-HCV, HIV) were negative. Autoantibodies (ANA, ASMA, AMA, anti-LKM) were negative.  

Abdominal ultrasound showed a normal-sized liver with mild coarse echotexture, pleural effusion, patent portal and biliary tracts, and no organomegaly. Contrast CT of the abdomen demonstrated irregular nodular hepatic margins, caudate-lobe hypertrophy, ascites, patent portal vein and branches, no focal hepatic lesions, and perigastric and perisplenic collaterals.  

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed grade 2 esophageal varices. Diagnostic paracentesis yielded a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 2.1 g/dL, total protein 0.9 g/dL, and 639 nucleated cells (80% neutrophils); culture grew Escherichia coli.

A 48-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a lesion at the medial aspect of the right upper eyelid. It began as a small white pustular lesion that gradually enlarged, became erythematous, and discharged purulent material. Topical fusidic acid and chloramphenicol ointments had no effect, and the lesion enlarged dramatically after incision and curettage elsewhere. He denied fever, weight loss, arthralgia, haemoptysis, rash, or urinary symptoms.

On examination, the right eyelid was erythematous and edematous with a palpable mass superomedially in the right orbit. Visual acuity was 6/9 in the right eye and 6/6 in the left; elevation of the right eye was limited. C-reactive protein was 36 mg/L (normal <7), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 25 mm/hr (normal 0–20). Serum IgG4, rheumatoid factor, p-ANCA, c-ANCA, ANA, ENA, and Quantiferon gamma were negative. Complement levels, thyroid function, and angiotensin-converting enzyme were normal. Cultures from discharge yielded no organisms.

MRI of the orbits showed a soft-tissue enhancing mass in the medial anterosuperior aspect of the right orbit, with mild globe displacement. A biopsy via an upper eyelid skin-crease incision revealed friable, necrotic tissue. Histopathology demonstrated sclerotic connective tissue and fat containing dense mixed inflammatory infiltrates of neutrophils, lymphocytes, macrophages, and plasma cells with neutrophilic microabscesses. The IgG4:IgG plasma-cell ratio was 30%, with up to 45 IgG4+ cells per high-power field. There was no geographical necrosis, clear vasculitis, or well-formed granulomas. Immunohistochemistry showed a mixed, predominantly T-cell infiltrate, and molecular studies revealed a polyclonal arrangement. The findings were deemed consistent with a reactive inflammatory process.

A 46-year-old obese woman presented to the emergency department 2 weeks after twin delivery (first vaginal, second by cesarean section via a Pfannenstiel incision) with significant lower abdominal pain and two episodes of vomiting. Her postoperative recovery had been uneventful. On examination, she was afebrile, with a mildly distended lower abdomen and regular bowel sounds; a single vomiting episode occurred in the ED. Gynecologic examination was normal, and routine laboratory studies were within normal limits. Clinically, an incisional hernia through the Pfannenstiel scar was suspected. An abdominal computed tomography scan showed herniation of small-bowel loops through the transversalis fascia and the rectus sheath without radiologic signs of strangulation and suggested a visceral hernial defect at the level of the Pfannenstiel incision. Surgical exploration was planned.

An 80-year-old man presented in March 2015 with recurrent fever, fatigue and bloody diarrhoea. He appeared septic, with hypotension (86/64 mmHg), tachycardia (115 /min), and fever of 38.6 °C. Examination revealed bibasal crepitations and hepatosplenomegaly; weight was 76 kg. Laboratory tests showed leukopenia (3.1 G/l), normal hemoglobin and platelets, elevated liver enzymes (ASAT 60 U/l; ALAT 71 U/l), and impaired renal function (creatinine 183 µmol/l; GFR 29 ml/min). 

Since 2009, he had non-specific granulomatous inflammation on liver biopsy, treated empirically with corticosteroids, azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil without improvement. A kidney biopsy in 2013 showed similar granulomas; immunosuppression was continued. His history included hypertension, type II diabetes, abdominal aneurysm repair, and treated Q-fever in 1984. Born in Holland, he lived in Switzerland and, as an engineer, had prolonged stays until 1995 in Sudan, Bangladesh, Suriname and Indonesia, and short trips to Indonesia and India in 2000. Since 2000 he traveled only to Sardinia. Serologies for HIV, histoplasmosis and Coxiella were non-reactive (Coxiella IgG positive, IgM negative).

Because of his bloody diarrhoea, a colonoscopy was performed, revealing extensive colitis. Biopsy specimens were sent for histopathological and microbiologic evaluation.

A 22-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks of gestation presented in preterm labour. She had no prior history of allergies. For Group B streptococcal prophylaxis, a penicillin skin sensitivity test was negative and she received 1.5 g intravenous crystalline penicillin. Five minutes later she developed acute shortness of breath. On examination, she was alert, tachycardic at 116 beats/min, hypotensive at 70/30 mm Hg, respiratory rate 30 breaths/min, and SpO2 97% on room air. Anaphylactic shock was diagnosed, and she received three intramuscular doses of adrenaline, supplemental oxygen, crystalloid boluses, left uterine displacement, and leg elevation. Fifteen minutes after symptom onset, her blood pressure stabilized at 121/72 mm Hg. Continuous fetal monitoring remained reassuring. She was transferred to the ICU, penicillin was switched to clindamycin, and steroids and antihistamine were administered.

Twenty-four hours later, she returned to the ward. Six hours thereafter, a pathological cardiotocograph with late decelerations prompted an emergency cesarean section under spinal anesthesia. A healthy neonate was delivered with Apgar scores of 9 and 10. Over the next 12 hours, the mother developed increasing oxygen dependence and bibasal fine crepitations without wheeze or stridor; she remained hemodynamically stable. Cardiac evaluation with ECG, 2D echocardiogram, and troponin I was normal. Clinical assessment, including IVC collapsibility, suggested euvolemia and urine output was adequate. Arterial blood gas analysis showed a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 180. Lung ultrasound revealed increased B lines. Chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral diffuse coalescent opacifications. The remainder of inflammatory markers, routine cultures, and COVID-19 PCR were unremarkable.

A 32-year-old woman with lifelong cognitive impairment presented with progressive gait instability and painless swellings over the right malar eminence and the posterior aspects of both ankles. She had undergone bilateral cataract surgery at age 22. On examination, she was alert but had a broad-based ataxic gait and bilaterally enlarged, soft, non-tender swellings over the Achilles tendons and a similar swelling over the right malar area. Laboratory studies showed total cholesterol 306 mg/dL (LDL 205, VLDL 46, HDL 55), triglycerides 526 mg/dL, and otherwise normal routine blood chemistries. Radiographs of both ankles showed soft-tissue radio-opacities posterior to the calcanei in the region of the Achilles tendons. MRI of the ankles demonstrated fusiform enlargement of both Achilles tendons with signal intensity similar to muscle and a speckled appearance on axial images. MRI of the brain revealed bilateral T2-weighted and FLAIR hyperintensity of the dentate nuclei, deep cerebellar white matter, and posterior limbs of the internal capsules, with corresponding T1 hypointensity.

A 65-year-old man with a history of tuberculous cardiac tamponade (2018) treated with pericardiocentesis and antituberculous therapy, and HIV infection on antiretroviral medication, presented with 6 months of progressive dyspnea on exertion, easy fatigability, and bilateral lower-extremity swelling. On examination, jugular venous pressure was 6 cm above the sternal angle, the cardiac apex was in the fifth left intercostal space at the midclavicular line, and a pericardial knock was audible. Two-dimensional echocardiography revealed a localized pericardial effusion compressing the right ventricle, with septal bounce and an exaggerated E/A ratio of 3.5. Left ventricular systolic function was normal. A chest radiograph showed an enlarged cardiac silhouette with irregular margins, a soft-tissue mass overlying the cardiac silhouette, and blunting of the right costophrenic angle. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a large thin-walled, well-defined (15.6 × 14.9 × 20.0 cm) homogenous cystic lesion in the anterior and middle mediastinum, compressing the right atrium and ventricle without solid components, calcifications, septations, or abnormal enhancement. The intrathoracic inferior vena cava was dilated, and there was a small right pleural effusion.

A 33-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of intermittent mid-epigastric pain and a 4-kg weight loss. She denied fever, cough, or jaundice and had no history of tuberculosis, BCG vaccination, or TB exposure. On examination, she had moderate splenomegaly, no hepatomegaly, and no ascites. Laboratory tests showed normal hemoglobin, leukocyte, and platelet counts; elevated serum amylase and lipase; an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and lactate dehydrogenase; normal bilirubin and carcinoembryonic antigen levels; and negative tests for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV. A chest radiograph was normal. Noncontrast abdominal CT revealed multiple solid-cystic masses in the pancreas and spleen with peripancreatic lymphadenopathy. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated an inhomogeneous cystic mass with peripheral rim enhancement in the body and tail of the pancreas, periportal lymphadenopathy with central low attenuation, and an enlarged spleen containing multiple 1–3 cm hypodense lesions showing mild enhancement after contrast.

A 29-year-old previously healthy African-American woman presented with a one-year history of bilateral progressive breast enlargement, persistent palpable nodules, left breast tenderness, left upper-extremity pain, and back pain. Antibiotics had provided no relief. On examination, she had bilateral macromastia with left-greater-than-right asymmetry and multiple palpable breast nodules.

At an outside hospital, diagnostic mammograms showed diffuse skin thickening and edema throughout the left breast. Ultrasound of the left breast revealed retroareolar ductal prominence with multiple cysts. A skin biopsy was noncontributory. Breast MRI demonstrated innumerable homogeneously enhancing masses throughout both breasts, more pronounced on the left, the largest measuring 3.0 × 2.0 cm, with no axillary or internal mammary lymphadenopathy. Differential diagnoses included inflammatory breast cancer, severe mastitis, severe fibrocystic changes, and, less likely, phyllodes tumor.

Two excisional biopsies of the left breast were interpreted as fibroadenoma and lymphangiectasia with mild lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate. She was referred for further evaluation. Ultrasound-guided biopsies of right breast nodules revealed fibrosis, duct ectasia, and apocrine metaplasia with no evidence of malignancy. Repeat MRI confirmed worsening asymmetry and macromastia. Antihormonal therapy with tamoxifen was recommended, but the patient declined.

A 71-year-old man with a 7-year history of stage III–IV B-cell chronic lymphocytic leukemia treated with fludarabine (last dose 1 month prior) presented with progressive dyspnea over several months. He denied chest pain, hemoptysis, and cough. Vital signs were temperature 36.8 °C, heart rate 88 bpm, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 88% on room air. On examination, breath sounds were absent at the right lung base. 

Chest radiography showed a homogeneous opacity in the right lower zone. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest confirmed a moderate right pleural effusion without mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies revealed WBC 5.2 ×10^3/µL (neutrophils 55%, lymphocytes 32%), hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, and platelets 135 ×10^3/µL. 

Diagnostic thoracentesis yielded white, milky fluid. Pleural fluid analysis showed: LDH 363 U/L, protein 5.2 g/dL, triglycerides 575 mg/dL, and cholesterol 62 mg/dL. Simultaneous serum values were LDH 504 U/L, protein 7.1 g/dL, triglycerides 32 mg/dL, and cholesterol 110 mg/dL. The pleural fluid met criteria for an exudate, and the elevated triglyceride level confirmed chylothorax. 

The patient was made nil per os, received central venous total parenteral nutrition, and had an intercostal chest tube placed for drainage.

A 35-year-old male refugee from Eritrea, with no chronic illnesses, presented at a routine clinic visit one year after arriving in Switzerland with a soft, slightly painful swelling on the right buttock at the site of a prior surgical scar. He reported multiple surgeries in 2001 for recurrent abscesses in that area. Physical examination revealed a 20 cm linear scar on the lateral right buttock and, medially, deep indurated exophytic nodules with visible openings and spontaneous serosanguinous drainage. He was afebrile and had no lymphadenopathy. A punch biopsy of a nodule produced sanguinolent discharge containing conglomerates of small, firm blackish pellets, suggestive of eumycetoma. Histologic evaluation showed chronic suppurative inflammation with fungal elements. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis demonstrated a pseudotumoral infiltration of cutaneous and subcutaneous tissues extending into the gluteal musculature without bone involvement.

A 35-year-old woman presented with acute pulmonary edema. Two weeks earlier, she had an episode of gastroenteritis treated by her general practitioner. Afterwards she developed pronounced fatigability, syncope, and dyspnea on exertion. On arrival she was pale, cold, and clammy; pulse 110 beats/min (regular, low volume); blood pressure 92/66 mmHg. Bibasilar fine crepitations were present; an S3 gallop was heard without murmurs. She was placed in a sitting position and given high-flow oxygen, IV furosemide, digoxin, and low-dose dopamine. ECG showed sinus tachycardia with diffuse nonspecific ST-T changes; chest radiograph revealed cardiomegaly and pulmonary edema. Hemoglobin was 9.5 g/dL; liver and renal function tests were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed mitral regurgitation with normal cusps and severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction (EF 25%). A diagnosis of dilated cardiomyopathy with LV failure was made and treated accordingly.

Despite resolution of pulmonary edema, her systolic blood pressure remained around 90 mmHg, and she continued to experience fatigue, light-headedness, apathy, anorexia, and nausea. Psychomotor slowing and hoarseness of voice were noted. Further history revealed profuse bleeding during her first delivery 11 years earlier, with large-volume IV fluids and 2–3 units of blood given. She recovered, but thereafter had episodes of syncope, salt and water cravings, and cold intolerance. She went on to have two more uncomplicated pregnancies over the next 5 years, but with lactation failure each time. She continues to have normal menstrual cycles and normal axillary and pubic hair.

A 78-year-old Ukrainian woman living in Switzerland for 6 months presented with a three-week history of sudden, relatively painless swelling in the lower right orbit. She had no improvement after courses of corticosteroids and antibiotics. Because of a recent diagnosis of breast cancer, she was referred with suspicion of an orbital tumor or metastasis. She lived with family dogs but recalled no mosquito bites or recent travel. Visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally; intraocular pressures and funduscopic examination were normal. There was no conjunctival injection or hemorrhage. On palpation, there was a round, hard, subcutaneous mass that was not very mobile in the region of the lower lid/anterior orbit. Computed tomography of the orbits showed a well-defined, round mass in the lower left orbit. An excision of the mass was performed under local anesthesia.

A 50-year-old Southeast Asian woman presented with a history of angina beginning at age 30, when she was found to have severe three-vessel coronary artery disease treated with bypass grafting. Three years later, she had a non–ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction managed with vein-graft intervention, followed by redo bypass surgery six years later for graft failure. She has no diabetes or renal disease and is a lifelong nonsmoker. Her mother and two brothers died of premature myocardial infarctions; her father and two other brothers underwent bypass surgery in their 70s and 50s. Her parents were first cousins.

On atorvastatin 80 mg daily in 2010, her total cholesterol was 316 mg/dl, LDL-C 273 mg/dl, triglycerides 86 mg/dl, and HDL-C 26 mg/dl. After discontinuation of statin therapy in 2016 for myalgias, evolocumab and niacin were begun. She was referred to the lipid clinic in late 2017.

Physical examination revealed a BMI of 31 kg/m2, a left Achilles tendon xanthoma, bilateral corneal arcus, xanthelasma, and multiple tendon xanthomas on her hands. Her past medical history included peripheral arterial disease with claudication, bilateral carotid endarterectomies, mild aortic stenosis, renal and iliac artery stenoses, and well-controlled hypertension.

A man in his 50s presented with lifelong left-flank burning abdominal pain that intensified over the past decade. He rated the pain 8–9/10, which worsened with trunk muscle contraction. He had undergone multiple interventions—including infra-umbilical nerve resection and subcutaneous neurostimulation—without benefit. He had a history of left hip osteoid osteoma resection with prosthesis in 2010; no leg-length measurements were recorded then.

On examination, his pelvis was tilted, with compensatory right trunk rotation and visible 4 cm left lower-limb shortening (anterior superior iliac spine to medial malleolus measurement and block testing). Gait analysis showed asymmetric stance and swing phases linked to limb-length difference. Palpation of the left flank elicited pain without guarding, and muscle contracture was palpable. Active trunk flexion and right rotation increased his pain. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies, abdominal ultrasonography, CT, spine X-rays, and lumbar MRI showed no visceral, fibrotic, or vascular pathology. A teleroentgenogram confirmed a 3.8 cm left lower-limb discrepancy. Ultrasound of the left external oblique muscle revealed thickening, and electromyography demonstrated abnormal muscle overactivity. Ultrasound of the rectus abdominis showed no significant asymmetry.

A healthy 50-year-old man underwent his first screening colonoscopy. He had no significant medical history and reported normal bowel habits. Endoscopic inspection of the transverse colon revealed a pedunculated lesion with a 2.0-cm stalk and a 0.9-cm polypoid head. On gentle probing, the head felt firm rather than soft. A few small diverticula were scattered throughout the colon. No other abnormalities were seen.

A 52-year-old African Caribbean man with a 10-year history of hypertension presented to the emergency department with multiple episodes of nonbloody, watery diarrhea beginning 5 days after returning from Haiti. He appeared severely dehydrated, with dry oral mucosa, decreased skin turgor, blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg, and pulse 110 /min. Admission laboratory values were: hemoglobin 16 g/dL, blood urea nitrogen 87 mg/dL, serum creatinine 9.8 mg/dL, serum bicarbonate 6 meq/L, an anion gap 15 meq/L, and serum albumin 4.6 g/dL. An indwelling urethral catheter was placed and yielded 15 mL of urine over the first 24 hours. Urinalysis showed a specific gravity of 1.025 and urine sodium of 5 meq/L. The initial clinical diagnosis was acute kidney injury secondary to dehydration from profuse diarrhea, later confirmed to be due to cholera infection. Despite two days of aggressive intravenous normal saline, the patient remained anuric and his serum creatinine rose to 10.4 mg/dL. On hospital day 3, the bladder was noted to be grossly distended on abdominal examination.

A 69-year-old man presented with progressive asthenia of eye-opening and bilateral ptosis for more than one year. He denied itching, swelling, pain, or other periocular discomfort and had no visible lesions on the eyelids or face. He underwent neuroelectromyography, neostigmine test, myasthenia gravis antibody assays, thyroid-function tests, and brain imaging; all results were normal, and neurogenic and myogenic causes were excluded. He was initially diagnosed with senile blepharoptosis but declined surgery and returned when his ptosis worsened.

His medical history was notable only for well-controlled diabetes and hypertension. He denied dermatoses (rosacea, acne, erysipelas, contact dermatitis, angioedema, lupus), trauma, surgery, or periocular rash, and had no known allergen exposures. His father had a similar progressive ptosis.

On examination, moderate bilateral blepharoptosis was seen without overt edema, erythema, papules, or masses. Careful palpation revealed subtle skin infiltration and shallow glabellar wrinkles. Seven days after skin biopsy of the upper eyelid and forehead, faint erythema appeared at the biopsy sites.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver and kidney function, electrolytes, antinuclear antibody, anti‐DNA, anti‐ENA, muscle enzymes, and IgE, were all normal or negative. Repeat neuroelectromyography, neostigmine test, myasthenia gravis antibodies, and thyroid function remained normal.

Histopathological examination of eyelid and forehead skin showed dermal edema, lymphatic hyperplasia and dilatation, perivascular lymphocytic infiltration, and an increased number of mast cells (>5 per high‐power field). Craniocerebral imaging was unremarkable.

A 33-year-old woman with no prior medical or surgical history presented with a 6-month history of a dragging sensation in her left upper abdomen. She was hemodynamically stable: temperature 37 °C, blood pressure 120/60 mm Hg, pulse 70 beats/min, and respiratory rate 18 breaths/min. On examination, there was tenderness in the left upper quadrant and splenomegaly. She had no known exposure to pet dogs or sheep. Routine laboratory tests were unremarkable.  
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a splenic cyst with a clear wall and multivesicular contents measuring 12 cm by 9 cm. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a large cystic lesion in an enlarged spleen without involvement of the liver or other organs. Indirect hemagglutination was positive for Echinococcus. The patient originated from an endemic area for hydatid disease and reported consuming undercooked meats.

A 50-year-old man with a 25 pack-year smoking history and prior myocardial infarction presented with acute right hemiparesis (arm, leg, and face) and a right homonymous hemianopia. Initial noncontrast head CT and MRI demonstrated a left parieto-occipital infarction in the posterior cortical watershed territory. Carotid duplex ultrasonography and MR angiography revealed complete occlusion of the left internal carotid artery; carotid dissection was suspected but no intramural hematoma was seen on neck MRI. He recovered well over 12 days and was discharged on aspirin, dipyridamole, and simvastatin.

Two months later, he was readmitted with a primary focal seizure with secondary generalization and mild postictal right-sided weakness. Routine blood tests, renal function, glucose, ESR, chest radiograph, 12-lead ECG, echocardiogram, and 24-hour Holter monitoring were unremarkable. Repeat MRI showed a new right anterior cortical watershed infarct. He regained independent mobility within a week and was started on sodium valproate for presumed post-stroke epilepsy.

Over the ensuing year, he experienced numerous episodes of collapse characterized by right-sided weakness and jerking movements followed by loss of consciousness, with good recovery of motor function each time but evidence of subtle cognitive decline on serial Mini-Mental State Examinations. Despite therapeutic valproate levels, he continued to present with recurrent seizures. A follow-up MRI revealed multiple new deep watershed infarcts in addition to the prior cortical infarcts and persistent occlusion of the left internal carotid artery.

A 36-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of generalized epileptic seizures and altered perception. He had no significant past medical history. Neurological examination showed bilateral Babinski signs. Cranial MRI revealed multiple dural-based, contrast-enhancing lesions with surrounding cerebral edema. Chest radiographs were normal, and cerebrospinal fluid examination was unremarkable and clear.

An 85-year-old man presented with left buttock pain radiating to his left leg, left foot drop, and gait disturbance of 4 weeks’ duration. Two months earlier, he had undergone a left posterior iliac bone marrow biopsy for evaluation of a suspected nasopharyngeal plasmacytoma. Immediately after the biopsy, he experienced severe left buttock pain radiating to the leg, treated with oral analgesics. Four weeks later, he noted onset of left foot drop and worsened gait disturbance without improvement on gabapentinoids, oral steroids, NSAIDs, or painkillers. 

His medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, COPD, type II diabetes mellitus, and coronary artery disease for which he was taking aspirin. On examination, he was afebrile with normal infection markers and a hemoglobin level of 12.3 g/dL. There was mild swelling and tenderness over the left buttock; the straight-leg-raising test was positive at 30°. He had hypesthesia in the sciatic distribution and severe weakness (0/5) of the left tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, and peroneal muscles. 

Given the concern for either an intraspinal or extraspinal cause of sciatic palsy, an MRI of the lumbar spine and pelvis with intravenous contrast was obtained. Spine MRI showed a moderate left L3–L4 intraforaminal disc herniation, which seemed unlikely to account for the patient’s presentation. Pelvic MRI revealed a 4.5 × 3.2 × 3.0 cm soft-tissue mass adjacent to the left piriformis muscle, compressing the sciatic nerve, which was felt to represent either a hematoma or a pseudoaneurysm in the context of the recent biopsy.

A 58-year-old woman with HIV (on ART for 2 months, good adherence) presented with a 3-day history of headache, fever, vomiting, confusion, and a 1-day history of loss of consciousness; she denied seizures. On admission she was afebrile, had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14, marked neck stiffness, and no focal neurologic deficits. Her CD4 count was 26 cells/μL and serum glucose 6.1 mmol/L. CSF opening pressure was 23 cmH2O; cryptococcal antigen was positive; WBC count 0 cells/mm3; RBC count 160 cells/mm3; protein 3.01 g/L; glucose 2.2 mmol/L; quantitative cryptococcal culture showed 910 CFU/mL. She received high-dose fluconazole and flucytosine. She improved clinically, required daily lumbar punctures for raised intracranial pressure, and by day 14 had normalized pressure and sterile CSF culture. She was switched to fluconazole consolidation and discharged.

Twenty-eight days after initial presentation, she returned with headache, confusion, neck pain, and a new right-sided upper motor neuron facial palsy. Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 28 cmH2O; serum glucose 5.2 mmol/L; CSF WBC 0 cells/mm3; RBC 130 cells/mm3; protein 2.61 g/L; glucose 2.2 mmol/L; cryptococcal antigen remained positive; quantitative culture grew 700 CFU/mL; CD4 count was 49 cells/μL. Brain MRI revealed a 6 × 5 × 6 cm multicystic mass in the left temporal lobe with surrounding edema, early hydrocephalus, and a 1 cm midline shift.

A 53-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of dull, aching pain in both hips and difficulty walking. The pain was aggravated by activity, relieved by rest, and associated with low backache and significant weight loss. On examination, there was tenderness over the left greater trochanter and lower back, and a 4×3-cm swelling on the anterior neck that moved with deglutition. Laboratory tests showed serum calcium 15.2 mg/dL (normal 8.4–10.7 mg/dL), serum albumin 4.3 g/dL (3.4–4.8), and vitamin D₃ 32 pg/mL (25–45). Pelvic radiographs revealed multiple lytic expansile lesions involving the left ischial tuberosity, bilateral iliac bones, both iliac crests, the neck and intertrochanteric region of the left femur, and the head of the right femur, with cortical breach and thickening of the left femoral neck. CT of the chest and abdomen showed multiple well-defined lytic expansile lesions in the left glenoid and the posterior aspects of the right ninth and twelfth ribs. A skull radiograph was normal.

A 66-year-old woman presented 3.5 hours after undergoing varicose vein sclerosing therapy with headache, blurred vision, and syncope. In the emergency department, she was haemodynamically stable. Neurologic examination showed a flaccid left upper extremity, increased tone in the left lower extremity, and left-sided hemi-neglect. Cardiovascular examination revealed a regular rhythm at 81 b.p.m. without murmurs. An electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with occasional premature ventricular contractions.

Her medical history included thyroid cancer and osteoporosis, and her only home medication was levothyroxine. She was a non-smoker and consumed alcohol twice weekly.

The initial differential diagnosis included acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic cerebrovascular accident, atypical migraine, hypertensive encephalopathy, hypoglycaemia, and electrolyte abnormalities. Laboratory studies revealed a normal comprehensive metabolic panel, complete blood count, coagulation studies, and a high-sensitivity troponin of 10 ng/L (normal <14 ng/L). 

Computed tomography angiography of the head and neck demonstrated an occlusion of the right distal M1 middle cerebral artery with limited flow in the M2 superior division; the occlusive material was thought to consist of air and thrombus. She underwent urgent endovascular thrombectomy. Final pathology of the retrieved clot revealed laminated blood consistent with a thromboembolus and amorphous material composed of an exogenous agent. As part of her stroke evaluation, a transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a patent foramen ovale.

A 3‐year‐old, male intact Persian cat was referred for a 2‐month history of chronic skin lesions. The cat was thin with dry skin; it was kept entirely indoors, and the owner and two housemate cats had no lesions. Initial oral itraconazole (5 mg/kg for 1 month) gave partial improvement but was discontinued 1 month before referral.

On day 0, physical examination revealed an emaciated cat with generalized alopecia, hyperpigmentation, and scaling. Multiple ulcerated nodules were present, including three large nodules at the chin, left submandibular, and left inguinal areas; the chin nodules had draining tracts with bloody discharge. Differential diagnoses included deep bacterial infections, deep fungal infections, and cutaneous neoplasia.

Cytological examination of a draining chin nodule revealed coccoid bacteria, numerous neutrophils and macrophages, and branching septate fungal hyphae. Skin biopsy of the chin nodule was performed for histopathology, with specimens fixed in formalin and stained with H&E and PAS. Chest and abdominal radiographs and abdominal ultrasound were within normal limits. Tests for feline leukemia and immunodeficiency viruses were negative. CBC, liver enzymes (ALT, ALP), and renal panel (BUN, creatinine) were normal. The cat was started on amoxicillin–clavulanic acid (20 mg/kg orally twice daily) and topical chlorhexidine–climbazole pending biopsy results.

A 37-year-old pregnant woman (gravida 2, para 1), with no systemic disease, was referred at 25 + 5 weeks of gestation for evaluation of a persistent and enlarging left adnexal mass. At 7 weeks’ gestation, routine ultrasound had demonstrated a left ovarian cyst measuring 3.4 × 2.5 cm. Follow-up sonography revealed gradually increasing moderate echogenic protrusions within the cyst. On presentation, transvaginal and transabdominal ultrasound showed an 8.4 × 5.8 cm multilocular cystic mass in the left ovary, with abundant blood-flow signals in papillary projections from the capsule wall and inner wall. Serum CA-125 was 44.9 U/mL (normal, 0–35 U/mL), and CA19-9 was 41.4 U/mL (normal, 0–34 U/mL). After multidisciplinary discussion, concern for ovarian malignancy led to recommendation for laparoscopic left salpingo-oophorectomy at 26 + 1 weeks’ gestation.

A man in his late 40s with hypertension and a mildly symptomatic COVID-19 infection one month earlier presented after a gunshot wound to his left arm. He reported a transient episode of left-sided weakness and facial droop about 10 days before admission, for which he did not seek medical attention. He denied tobacco, alcohol, or intravenous drug use and was unvaccinated against COVID-19; his sister had died from a pulmonary embolism in the setting of COVID-19. 

On examination, he was tachycardic but otherwise afebrile and normotensive, with no audible murmurs, no neurological deficits, and no skin or nail lesions. Two days into hospitalization, he developed chest pain, fever, and tachycardia. A CT scan of the chest showed multiple acute subsegmental pulmonary emboli in the right middle and lower lobes. Cardiac troponin was 1.85 ng/mL, and coronary angiography for a non–ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction revealed a 100% occlusion of the proximal right coronary artery with left-to-right collaterals, 50% stenosis of the mid–distal left anterior descending artery, and 60% stenosis of the distal left circumflex artery in a patient with minimal coronary calcification.

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated normal biventricular function and a small vegetation on the ventricular aspect of the non-coronary cusp of the aortic valve. Transesophageal echocardiography confirmed a 6 × 1 mm mobile linear mass on the ventricular aspect of the non-coronary cusp of a trileaflet aortic valve without regurgitation or stenosis. Brain MRI revealed restricted diffusion in the occipital/parietal region and an older infarct in the right frontal lobe.  

Blood and fungal cultures, as well as serologies for Brucella, Bartonella, and Q fever, were all negative. Antinuclear antibody testing was negative.

A 66-year-old man was transferred with intense abdominal pain and acute renal failure (blood urea nitrogen 178 mg/dL, creatinine 7.92 mg/dL) after receiving an estimated 3 mg/kg of amphotericin B deoxycholate for a biopsy-confirmed diagnosis of nasal leishmaniasis. He had been HIV-positive for more than 10 years but was nonadherent to antiretroviral therapy; his most recent viral load was 92 494 copies/mL and CD4 count was 5 cells/mm3 (CD4/CD8 ratio 0.08). His only other history was gastroesophageal reflux disease; he was a former smoker. On admission, he was pancytopenic (hemoglobin 6.0 g/dL, leukocytes 1620 cells/µL, lymphocytes 142 cells/µL, platelets 64 000 cells/µL). He was afebrile but emaciated, with a severe ulcer in the hard palate and an extensive necrotic lesion of the left nasal ala and septum; his voice was dysphonic. Chest CT showed bilateral pulmonary consolidation and small pleural effusions. Hemodialysis was initiated because of worsening renal failure. He received amphotericin B deoxycholate 5 mg/kg/day for 3 days, then liposomal amphotericin B 4 mg/kg/day for a total of 16 days. On day +16, he developed acute respiratory distress due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa sepsis, melena, and worsening blood dyscrasia, and was admitted to the ICU. A right scrotal ultrasound revealed a 3.2 × 2.5 cm thick-walled, multiseptate fluid collection contiguous with the epididymis. A diagnostic orchiectomy showed a swollen testicle with necrotic areas and fluid accumulation. He had an unfavorable clinical course and died a few days later.

A 25-year-old woman presented in 1994 with sustained episodes of flashes in both eyes and transient visual-acuity drops that normalized over days. She was morbidly obese (140 kg) and a smoker. She also reported monthly right-sided headaches with photophobia lasting less than 24 hours, episodes of blurred vision, and paresthesias in the left jaw, arm, and leg. Examination, including optic discs and neurologic assessment, was normal. Multiple sclerosis was considered but deemed unlikely, and she was diagnosed with complicated migraine.

In 1998, she re-presented with intermittent tingling bilaterally, a sensation of imbalance, and short-lasting visual obscurations. Neurologic examination remained normal. An MRI could not be performed due to body habitus.

In 2002, she developed bilateral granulomatous uveitis and multifocal retinal periphlebitis; the optic discs were healthy, with no cystoid macular oedema. Laboratory tests showed a normal ANA, antiphospholipid screen, full blood count, an ESR of 28 mm/hour, and an atypical ANCA. A brain MRI demonstrated lesions involving the deep white matter. Visual evoked potentials were normal; lumbar puncture was not performed.

Between 2002 and 2004, she experienced episodes of vitritis, hypopyon, and macular oedema requiring high-dose oral prednisolone. There was debate about a demyelinating process versus vasculitis, and she received six cycles of intravenous cyclophosphamide followed by mycophenolate mofetil. 

In 2005, despite treatment, she had a posterior circulation transient ischaemic attack and retinal haemorrhage. Repeat MRI showed progression of white matter lesions with multifocal deep grey matter and brain stem involvement. She was treated with aspirin, a β-blocker, and a statin. 

From 2004 to 2010, she continued to have uveitis and retinal bleeds treated with high-dose prednisolone. A follow-up MRI demonstrated progressive, multifocal small-vessel disease. The unusual distribution of the lesions and ongoing clinical progression sparked the search for alternative diagnoses.

A 47-year-old man with a 5-year history of untreated type 2 diabetes mellitus (hemoglobin A1c 13% on admission) presented with a 4-day history of fever and dyspnea. Two days before admission, he tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 by RT-PCR. He denied known contact with COVID-19 cases. On admission, temperature was 38.3°C, heart rate 90/min, blood pressure 132/83 mm Hg, respiratory rate 24/min, and SpO2 93% on room air. Chest CT showed bilateral ground-glass opacities and patchy shadows consistent with COVID-19 pneumonia. On hospital day 2, his respiratory status worsened, and he was intubated and transferred to the ICU. From hospital days 6 to 8, he had remittent fevers of 37.5°C to 40.4°C. On day 9, the patient developed sustained fever of 40°C to 41°C unresponsive to acetaminophen, accompanied by marked disturbance of consciousness and hypotension with systolic pressures <70 mm Hg, consistent with warm shock. His PaO2/FiO2 ratio declined from 202 to 140 mm Hg. He received large-volume fluid resuscitation, vasopressors (norepinephrine, vasopressin, and epinephrine), hydrocortisone, and was started on venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) on the night of day 9. Laboratory testing revealed lactic acidosis, acute kidney injury, disseminated intravascular coagulation, hepatic dysfunction, and profound rhabdomyolysis (creatine kinase peaking at 255 870 U/L). After VA-ECMO initiation, his sustained fever rapidly abated and multiorgan failure began to improve.

A man in his early 30s was referred for evaluation of progressive spasticity and intellectual disability. He was born at term (40 weeks, 3.3 kg) with no perinatal complications. He achieved independent sitting at 1 year and walking at 3 years. An equinus gait pattern emerged at age 7, and spasticity of both lower extremities developed around age 12. Convulsions began at age 3, and he started anticonvulsant therapy; because seizures increased to five to six per day, a vagus nerve stimulator was implanted at age 30. Orthopedic surgeries included bilateral heel cord and hamstring lengthening at 18 and bilateral femur extension with supramalleolar derotational osteotomy at 20, followed by multidisciplinary rehabilitation.

On examination, upper-extremity strength was grade 4 and lower-extremity strength grade 3. Hyperactive patellar and ankle reflexes, bilateral Babinski signs, and ankle clonus were present. He could stand unaided for 10–15 seconds and ambulate indoors. He required repetitive cues for simple self-care tasks. On the modified Ashworth scale, tone was G1 in the upper limbs and G2 in the lower limbs; his Functional Independence Measure score was 49. Neuropsychometric testing (Korean Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale–IV) yielded an IQ below 45. Brain MRI showed focal volume loss in the splenium of the corpus callosum and several nonspecific T2 hyperintense white-matter lesions.

Family history was notable for a younger brother born at term (2.8 kg) with neonatal jaundice, severe developmental delay, and a progressive decline in motor and cognitive function. He began walking with two-hand support at age 5, required a wheelchair by age 19, had refractory seizures managed with a vagus nerve stimulator, underwent tracheostomy and gastrostomy for airway and swallowing issues, and died at age 24 of sudden cardiac arrest. Both brothers had initially been diagnosed with cerebral palsy.

A 39-year-old woman with a history of Noonan syndrome—characterized by short stature, webbed neck, low-set ears, ocular hypertelorism, ptosis, and developmental delay—and childhood repair of tetralogy of Fallot was known to have Chiari I malformation with hydrocephalus and a large syringomyelia extending from C1 to the conus. In 2003 she underwent foramen magnum decompression and placement of a cervical syrinx-subarachnoid shunt, but a sizable syrinx persisted. 

In 2010 she presented with acute onset of progressive gait disturbance, dysesthesia in both legs and the perineal area, and complete urinary retention—consistent with a conus medullaris syndrome. Routine hematological, serological, and coagulation tests were all normal. Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine showed the known large syringomyelic cavity with a new heterogeneous mass at its caudal end. The lesion demonstrated mixed intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images and partial gadolinium enhancement in its center.

A 75-year-old man with a history of congestive heart failure, coronary artery disease, and atrial fibrillation presented with 4 months of progressively worsening, watery diarrhea and a 30-pound weight loss. He reported 30 watery bowel movements daily (total stool output 8 L per 24 hours), including nocturnal movements. He had multiple emergency visits for dehydration, hypotension, hypokalemia, and renal insufficiency. On admission, vital signs were normal. Stool electrolytes were K 53 mmol/L and Na 58 mmol/L (stool osmotic gap 68 mOsm/kg). Laboratory tests showed Na 137 mmol/L, K 4.1 mmol/L, Cl 109 mmol/L, bicarbonate 17 mmol/L, Mg 1.5 mg/dL, lipase 14 U/L, albumin 2.5 g/dL, total protein 5.5 g/dL, C-reactive protein 6.7 mg/L, and white blood cell count 9.3 K/μL with a normal differential.  
Tests that were normal included celiac serology; stool culture with ova and parasite screen; stool Clostridium difficile toxin assay; serum gastrin, vasoactive intestinal peptide, somatostatin, and calcitonin levels; thyroid-stimulating hormone; morning cortisol; chromogranin A; 24-hour urine metanephrine, normetanephrine, and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid. Cranial, thoracic, abdominal, and pelvic CT scans and an octreoscan were unremarkable. Medication review showed no known enteropathy-causing drugs (eg, olmesartan, high-dose colchicine, mycophenolate mofetil, methotrexate, azathioprine). Total parenteral nutrition led to almost complete resolution of diarrhea within 3 days.  
Push enteroscopy revealed macroscopic villous atrophy in the duodenum and jejunum. Biopsies showed villous atrophy with marked reduction of goblet and Paneth cells, increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, and crypt apoptoses. The patient’s serum was negative for antienterocyte and antigoblet cell antibodies on indirect immunofluorescence.

A 68-year-old Hispanic man with end-stage renal disease treated by thrice-weekly hemodialysis presented with a 4-day history of progressive confusion, agitation, dysarthria, and auditory hallucinations. Four days earlier, he had developed a painful vesicular rash in the right T9 dermatome and was prescribed oral acyclovir 800 mg five times daily. His other medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, anemia of chronic kidney disease, and secondary hyperparathyroidism. Home medications were amlodipine, metoprolol, aspirin, insulin, and oral acyclovir; no other recent medication changes.

On arrival, he was agitated and oriented only to self. Temperature was 37.3 °C, blood pressure 177/90 mmHg, heart rate 100 bpm, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 93% on 2 L nasal cannula. Neurologic examination showed dysarthric speech, spontaneous movements of all extremities with withdrawal to pain, and diffuse 3+ reflexes without clonus. Skin examination demonstrated erythematous papules and vesicles distributed along the right T9 dermatome.

Laboratory studies revealed serum sodium 133 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 43 mg/dL, creatinine 5.9 mg/dL, white blood cell count 6.8 × 10^9 cells/L, and glucose 170 mg/dL. MRI of the brain showed no infarct or vasculopathy. EEG demonstrated diffuse slowing without epileptiform activity. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed protein 85 mg/dL, glucose 76 mg/dL, zero red blood cells, zero white blood cells, and no organisms on Gram stain. CSF PCR returned positive for VZV and negative for other common viral or bacterial pathogens.

Based on the clinical presentation and positive CSF PCR result, he was started on intravenous acyclovir, dosed at 5 mg/kg per hemodialysis protocol, and admitted to the medicine service.

A 42-year-old woman presented with 2 months of localized, sporadic, colicky abdominal pain responsive to analgesia. She reported a 10-kg weight loss but denied changes in bowel habits, bleeding, or chronic diseases. There was no personal or family history of inflammatory bowel disease; her father died of colon cancer at age 80. Physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies were within normal limits: WBC 7.28 × 10^9/L; hemoglobin 11 g/L; CEA <1.7 mg/mL; CA19-9 14 U/mL; CA125 19 kU/L; CA15-3 16.8 U/mL; CRP 8 mg/L. 

Abdominal CT showed a soft-tissue mass in the distal transverse colon extending along the gastrocolic ligament and invading the greater curvature of the stomach, with regional lymphadenopathy and peritoneal nodules, but no obstruction or perforation. Colonoscopy revealed circumferential wall thickening and an obstructing left colonic mass 65 cm from the anal verge; biopsies showed colonic mucosa with crypt distortion but were “negative for granuloma, viral cytopathic effects, dysplasia and malignancy.” 

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy demonstrated a thickened gastric fold; biopsy showed chronic gastritis with Helicobacter-shaped bacilli and was “negative for intestinal metaplasia, dysplasia and malignancy.” Repeat colonoscopy yielded similar findings; MRI confirmed a locally infiltrative distal transverse colon mass with lymphovascular invasion to the stomach and peritoneal nodules. 

After multidisciplinary review, surgical resection was recommended given the patient’s symptoms and high suspicion for malignancy.

A 64-year-old man with hypertension presented for evaluation of a 6-month history of intermittent cough, mild dyspnoea on exertion, and episodic hoarseness. Chest radiography showed a 10-mm rightward deviation of the trachea. On neck examination, the thyroid gland was enlarged, predominantly involving the left lobe. Thyroid‐function tests were within normal limits.

Neck ultrasonography demonstrated:
• Right lobe: 20 × 21 × 49 mm, normal echotexture.  
• Left lobe: 80 × 70 × 55 mm, hypoechogenic, lobulated, markedly hypervascular, extending retrosternally, with several cystic areas and a vascular plexus in the lower portion (arterial diameters up to 12 mm).  
• No cervical lymphadenopathy.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a retrosternal left-lobe mass deforming and compressing the trachea, with a large inferior-pole nodule displacing the aortic-arch vessels and associated multiple venous plexuses up to 20 mm in width; cervical lymph nodes appeared benign. On auscultation over the left lobe, a bruit was audible. Given the complex vascular anatomy and high risk of bleeding, the patient was referred for further preoperative planning.

A 64-year-old woman with a 4-year history of pulmonary and cutaneous sarcoidosis, diagnosed by transbronchial lung biopsy and treated with prednisone, had been in remission off medication for 2 years. Over the preceding 9 months, she experienced intermittent abdominal pain, bloating, and unintentional weight loss. Four months earlier, she developed diarrhea that alternated with obstinate constipation. 

On examination, she had tenderness in the right lower quadrant and a poorly defined deep mass; pelvic, pulmonary, and cutaneous examinations were otherwise normal. Total colonoscopy revealed a stenotic lesion in the ascending colon. Biopsy specimens showed no evidence of neoplasia but did demonstrate an inflammatory infiltration of the submucosa rich in eosinophils. 

Contrast enema demonstrated a long, irregular stenotic segment of the ascending colon. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a 4 × 5 cm hypoechoic mass in the ascending colon without evidence of distant metastases. Computed tomography of the abdomen revealed an 8-cm stenotic tumor in the ascending colon with adjacent fat infiltration and multiple satellite lymph nodes, but no metastatic lesions. 

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 10,200 per mm3, hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL, normal liver function tests and serum electrolytes, and a carcinoembryonic antigen level of 3.6 ng/mL.

A one‐year‐old boy was referred with a 4-day history of cough and rhinorrhea and a 2-day history of low-grade fever and hemorrhagic skin eruption. The rash began on both knees, then involved the upper extremities, feet, face, ears, and oral mucosa, and was followed by swelling of the knees, hands, feet, and scrotum. There was no vomiting, urinary complaint, or recent immunization. 

On examination, he was well appearing and afebrile. He had multiple rounded, palpable purpuric patches over the upper and lower limbs, face, oral mucosa, and ears, with sparing of the trunk. There was non‐tender edema of the knees, hands, and feet and erythema with edema of the scrotum. Joint range of motion was unimpaired, and there was no abdominal tenderness.

Scrotal ultrasonography showed marked bilateral scrotal skin thickening, small bilateral hydroceles, and normal testicular blood flow. Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood count, an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (47 mm in the first hour) and C‐reactive protein (100 mg/dL), with normal urinalysis, coagulation tests, and a normal random protein‐to‐creatinine ratio.

A 33-year-old man from Nepal, who immigrated to the United States 3 years earlier, presented with 10 days of pain and redness in his right mid-arm. He reported no fever, weight loss, or systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a red, swollen, and tender area over the mid-arm, and palpation revealed enlarged ipsilateral axillary lymph nodes. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right arm demonstrated an enhancing soft-tissue mass with infiltrative features that partially encased the brachial vessels, as well as axillary lymphadenopathy. Foci of low signal intensity were noted on both T1- and T2-weighted images.

A 40-year-old gravida 1 woman at 11 weeks+2 days’ gestation presented for noninvasive prenatal testing because of advanced maternal age. Whole-genome sequencing of cell-free fetal DNA detected no aneuploidies of chromosomes 13, 18, or 21, but reported two X chromosomes and a partial Y chromosome, a pattern not fully consistent with Klinefelter syndrome. At 14 weeks+3 days, repeat testing confirmed these findings. At a routine 18-week fetal anatomy scan, no structural anomalies were noted and the external genitalia appeared male. Because of the discordance between the NIPT sex genotype and the ultrasound phenotype, further prenatal cytogenetic evaluation was recommended.

A 72-year-old woman with morbid obesity (BMI 42) presented with fatigue, nosebleeds, and easy bruising.  
Initial laboratory evaluation showed:  
• WBC 5.34 K/μL, hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, platelets 13 K/μL  
• Peripheral smear with 19% promyelocytes, 9% granulated blasts, and Auer rods  
• Coagulation studies: PT/INR 18.3 s/1.5, PTT 30.2 s, D-dimer 8115 ng/mL, fibrinogen 77 ng/mL  
Renal function was at baseline (creatinine 0.8 mg/dL). Cytogenetics revealed t(15;17) and trisomy 8, with PCR confirming a PML-RARA fusion, establishing acute promyelocytic leukemia.  

She began induction therapy with oral all-trans retinoic acid 45 mg/m2 twice daily on admission and intravenous arsenic trioxide 0.15 mg/kg daily starting on day 5. On day 8, she developed dyspnea, headache, and edema consistent with differentiation syndrome, which resolved with dexamethasone.  

Between days 19 and 30, she experienced intermittent loose stools progressing to fever (102°F) on day 30. Broad-spectrum antibiotics were administered briefly; blood cultures, SARS-CoV-2 PCR, and stool studies for bacterial pathogens, Clostridioides difficile, ova and parasites, adenovirus, rotavirus, and norovirus were all negative.  

By day 32, she developed nonbloody, rice-water diarrhea producing 3–6 L/day unaltered by fasting, accompanied by crampy abdominal pain. CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed diffuse ileus without focal colonic lesions. On day 34, colonoscopy revealed grossly normal mucosa; random biopsies demonstrated atrophic crypts and scattered neutrophilic crypt microabscesses, with negative CMV staining.  

Concurrently, she reported epigastric pain and nausea; serum lipase was 428 U/L (ULN 60 U/L), and abdominal CT showed acute edematous pancreatitis.

A 76-year-old man was referred with 20 days of progressive dyspnea and generalized edema. He was hemodynamically stable (heart rate 72 beats/min, sinus rhythm), well perfused, with jugular venous distension, bibasilar crackles, a systolic murmur at the tricuspid area, voluminous ascites, and marked peripheral edema. His BMI was 27.8 kg/m2. On admission, transthoracic echocardiography showed right ventricular systolic dysfunction (fractional area change 33%), severe tricuspid regurgitation (vena contracta 14 mm), preserved left ventricular function, a normally functioning aortic bioprosthesis, and a cardiac index of 8.0 L/min/m2. A TTE 9 months earlier had been normal. His history included hypertension, hypothyroidism, chronic alcoholism, low meat intake with weight loss over 6 months, aortic valve bioprosthesis, and coronary bypass grafting. 

Investigations included 3D transesophageal echocardiography, which confirmed severe tricuspid regurgitation (effective regurgitant orifice area 0.94 cm2, regurgitant volume 59 mL) and tricuspid annular dilation (44 mm) with hepatic vein flow reversal. Pulmonary scintigraphy was performed; cardiac magnetic resonance excluded myocarditis and myocardial ischemia by showing an unspecific nonischemic delayed enhancement pattern. Right and left heart catheterization demonstrated grafts with normal flow, no obstructive lesions, pulmonary artery pressure 55/13 mm Hg (mean 27), and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure 13 mm Hg. Laboratory tests revealed acute kidney injury (KDIGO stage 2), lactate 1.0 mmol/L, normal thyroid function, serum thiamine 34.2 μg/L (reference 32–82 μg/L), and ascitic fluid with a serum–ascites albumin gradient ≥1.1.

A 21-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with retrosternal chest pain, cough, globus sensation in the throat, and dysphonia that had progressed over several hours. Symptoms began during an endurance training session on her racing bicycle, when she noted episodes of tachycardia and a decline in performance. She denied trauma, vomiting, or recent respiratory infection. Her medical history was unremarkable; she did not smoke and took no medications.

On examination, she was in no acute distress. Vital signs were within normal limits and she was afebrile. There was right-sided cervicothoracic swelling with palpable crepitus. Cardiac examination revealed a normal rate and regular rhythm without murmurs or friction rub. Breath sounds were equal bilaterally without wheezes or crackles.

An electrocardiogram was normal. A chest radiograph demonstrated mild pneumomediastinum, pneumopericardium, and subcutaneous emphysema without pneumothorax. She was observed and treated conservatively; her symptoms resolved and follow-up radiograph 8 days later showed near-complete resolution of the air.

Two years later, she returned with similar chest tightness occurring after a cycling workout. Physical examination again showed mild tachycardia but was otherwise unremarkable; there was no subcutaneous emphysema this time. Laboratory studies revealed mild leukocytosis. A low-dose chest CT confirmed recurrent pneumomediastinum and pneumopericardium without other abnormalities. Flexible bronchoscopy and esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed no evidence of tracheal or esophageal injury.

A 10-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of extensive dental caries. He was born at term to healthy, nonconsanguineous parents after an uncomplicated pregnancy; there is no family history of craniofacial disorders, and he has two unaffected siblings. At age 2, a diagnosis of a branchial-arch malformation syndrome was made when facial and limb anomalies became evident. 

Physical examination showed hemifacial atrophy, severe maxillomandibular hypoplasia with micrognathia, malar hypoplasia, a flat nasal bridge, cleft palate with uvular atresia, and atresia of the left ear canal with absence of internal and external ear structures. He has marked restriction of jaw opening. He also has feeding difficulties, speech impairment, and uses a nasopharyngeal airway during sleep. Limb examination revealed a short forearm with limited elbow extension and absence of some digits. His intelligence was reported as normal.

Intraoral and radiographic examination revealed poor oral hygiene, numerous carious teeth, hypomineralization of several molars, severe micrognathia with restricted mouth opening, and crowding in both dental arches.

A 63-year-old man presented with 12 hours of constant right iliac fossa pain, vomiting, and fever (38 °C). Examination showed marked tenderness in the right iliac fossa with a positive McBurney’s sign. Laboratory tests revealed a C-reactive protein level of 49.9 mg/L and a neutrophilic leukocytosis of 10.29 × 10^3/μL. Blood cultures were drawn. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT was interpreted as uncomplicated acute appendicitis. 

Laparoscopic exploration revealed a necrotic-hemorrhagic vermiform appendix twisted 360° in an anti-clockwise direction 0.5 cm from its base; an appendectomy was performed, and intravenous amoxicillin–clavulanic acid was started. 

On postoperative day 1, admission blood cultures grew multi-sensitive Escherichia coli and Enterococcus faecalis in all samples. 

By postoperative day 3, despite treatment, the patient had persistent fever (> 38 °C) and right iliac fossa pain. A contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan identified thrombosis of the ileocolic vein with significant peripheral fat inflammation.
