A 78-year-old man with a history of idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus treated 8 years earlier with a lumboperitoneal shunt presented with progressive difficulty walking due to pain in the lower back and right thigh. He had no motor weakness, pathological reflexes, or urinary dysfunction. A sagittal CT scan of the lumbar spine showed that the lumbar catheter ran through the spinal canal from L3/4 to L2 without coiling or snaking. Lumbar MRI revealed an extradural fluid-containing mass at the L3/4 level compressing the spinal dural sac anteriorly and impinging on the cauda equina.

A 75-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of a painful, pruritic, erythematous plaque on his left arm. One week before lesion onset, he had sustained a minor abrasion while repairing a clogged clay sewage pipe, despite wearing protective clothing. The lesion began as a 2×2 cm hyperemic patch and gradually progressed to involve the entire length of the left upper limb. He reported burning pain and itching, but no systemic symptoms. 

On examination, there was an ill-defined, infiltrative, erythematous plaque extending from the shoulder to the wrist, with mild scaling but no frank ulceration or vesicles. 

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and basic metabolic panel, were unremarkable. HIV serology was negative. 

After evaluation by a dermatologist, the lesion was diagnosed clinically as dermatophytosis, and oral terbinafine (250 mg once daily) was prescribed. Over the next four weeks, the lesion continued to spread, and discomfort increased markedly. 

Because of the progressive worsening despite antifungal therapy, a skin biopsy was performed for histopathological and microbiological analysis.

A 19-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of intermittent swelling of her left deltoid, with four episodes each lasting about 2 months. Each episode was associated with pain and tenderness. She denied any trauma to the region and had no systemic illnesses, significant family history, or medications. On examination, she had full range of motion of the shoulder and neck, and her neurological and vascular findings were normal. Plain radiographs of the shoulder were unremarkable. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the left shoulder showed diffuse oedematous signal changes within the deltoid muscle on proton density–weighted sequences; there was no evidence of plexiform neurofibroma. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography revealed an axillary nerve M-wave amplitude of 14.1 mV and normal motor action potentials in the deltoid, confirming the absence of an axillary nerve lesion. 

During symptomatic periods, her erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated at 26–73 mm/h and C-reactive protein was 12 mg/L; both returned to normal when symptoms subsided. She was screened for connective tissue disorders with antinuclear, antineutrophil cytoplasmic, and extractable nuclear antigen antibodies, and for diabetes; all tests were negative. Creatine kinase and lactate dehydrogenase levels during the acute phase were within normal limits. 

A sequential MRI performed after symptom resolution showed a reduction in the oedematous signal within the deltoid muscle.

A 65-year-old man with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis presented with a 6-month history of a pruritic rash and a painful oral sore. The rash appeared within weeks after he began nintedanib (150 mg twice daily) for his pulmonary fibrosis. He was initially treated in urgent care with permethrin 5% cream, without improvement, and later with triamcinolone 0.1% ointment for one week, with only transient relief. He also reported mild nausea and gastrointestinal upset on nintedanib. His other medications included omeprazole (for 2½ years) and atorvastatin (for 1 year, with a dose increase 2 months before presentation). His medical history was notable for gastroesophageal reflux disease, coronary artery disease, prior herpes simplex virus infection, and a remote history of smoking.

On dermatologic examination, there were a few intact vesicles and pustules on the forehead and numerous scattered 1–2 mm crusted papules with erythematous bases on the forehead, scalp, face, upper chest, and both knees. Examination of the oral mucosa revealed a linear ulcer. Vital signs were within normal limits, and no other abnormalities were noted.

A 30-year-old G2P1 woman was referred at 34 weeks’ gestation for evaluation of fetal intestinal dilatation. At 34 weeks, ultrasound showed a single segment of intestinal dilation (24 mm) without polyhydramnios. At 36 weeks 5 days, repeat ultrasound demonstrated worsening intestinal dilation (26 mm) with poor peristalsis. Cardiotocography revealed loss of baseline variability and recurrent late decelerations. An emergency cesarean section was performed for fetal distress.

A male infant weighing 2652 g was delivered with Apgar scores of 5 and 7 at 1 and 5 minutes. A nasogastric tube was placed, and bilious output was noted. Examination revealed marked abdominal distension with diminished bowel sounds, generalized edema, and bluish-white discoloration of the abdominal wall. The infant passed meconium immediately after birth. Vital signs were notable for a heart rate of 170 beats/min and respiratory rate of 42 breaths/min; blood pressure was 42/18 mmHg. Respiratory distress was severe due to abdominal distension, necessitating intubation and mechanical ventilation.

Laboratory studies: WBC 12.3 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, platelets 258 × 10^9/L. Blood gas: pH 7.31, PaO2 27.9 mmHg, PaCO2 45.7 mmHg, HCO3– 22.3 mmol/L, lactate 3.0 mmol/L. Abdominal radiograph showed gastric bubbles without intestinal gas and elevated diaphragm. Ultrasound revealed segmental small-bowel dilation with wall thickening; meconium was visualized from the sigmoid colon to the rectum, and no ascites was present.

A clinical diagnosis of abdominal compartment syndrome secondary to bowel dilatation was made.

A 33-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 5-day history of abdominal pain that began in the epigastrium and later localized to the right lower quadrant, where it intensified. She reported associated constipation and poor flatus passage but denied any relation of her symptoms to menstrual cycles. Her medical history was unremarkable, with no prior surgeries or pregnancies.  
On examination, her pulse was 65 beats per minute, blood pressure 140/90 mm Hg, and temperature 36.5 °C. Physical examination revealed rebound tenderness, guarding, and a palpable mass in the right lower quadrant.  
Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 12×10^9/L (75% neutrophils), C-reactive protein 8 mg/dL, and hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL. Serum β-hCG, CA 19-9, and carcinoembryonic antigen were within normal limits.  
Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a heterogeneous 10×8×5 cm mass composed of a conglomerate of intestinal loops in the ascending colon. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis confirmed an ileocolic intussusception associated with a tumoral mass in the cecum.  
Given the suspicion of a cecal neoplasm causing intussusception, a decision was made to proceed with surgical resection.

A male infant was born at 38 weeks’ gestation by Cesarean delivery, birthweight 3.4 kg, to parents whose fetal echocardiogram had suggested d-transposition of the great arteries (D-TGA) with a small perimembranous ventricular septal defect and possible coarctation. An unrestrictive atrial septal defect had been noted, and no other vascular anomalies were reported. Apgar scores were 9, 9, and 9. 

On initial examination, there was marked differential cyanosis: the right arm and right anterior chest appeared pink with an oxygen saturation of 100% in the right arm, whereas the rest of the body was cyanotic with a saturation of 75%. Peripheral pulses were palpable and symmetric in all four limbs. Noninvasive blood pressures showed similar systolic values of approximately 80 mmHg in each extremity; diastolic pressure was 35 mmHg in the right arm versus 41–44 mmHg elsewhere.

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated atrioventricular concordance, ventriculoarterial discordance, and parallel great vessels consistent with D-TGA and a left-sided aortic arch. A 4 mm atrial septal defect was present. A patent ductus arteriosus showed predominantly left-to-right shunting with intermittent right-to-left flow during systole. Detailed imaging excluded coarctation of the aorta and a ventricular septal defect. Notably, no abnormal branching of the first head-and-neck vessel or origin of the right subclavian artery distal to the left subclavian artery was visualized.

A 30-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 3-day fever followed 6 days later by fluent but non-meaningful speech, word-finding difficulty, comprehension deficits, and impaired repetition consistent with Wernicke’s aphasia. She remained fully conscious, with no focal motor or sensory deficits. Vital signs were normal except for a temperature of 38.5°C. Routine blood tests, inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), an extensive autoimmune screen (including ANA, extractable nuclear antigens, dsDNA, ANCA), and serum ACE were all within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed mild diffusion restriction at the periphery of lesions on FLAIR and T2-weighted sequences and, after gadolinium administration, no enhancement. Gradient echo and susceptibility-weighted sequences were not performed. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a protein level of 54 mg/dL, glucose of 50 mg/dL, 60 cells/mm3 (60% polymorphonuclear, 40% lymphocytes), and six oligoclonal bands in CSF with none in serum; no organisms were seen. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy demonstrated normal levels of N-acetyl aspartate, creatine, choline, and lactate in the affected regions.

A 53-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a left cranial nerve VI palsy and an enlarged pituitary on MRI. For 3 months, she had daily headaches, sinus pressure, and bilateral eye redness treated empirically as allergies without improvement. Two weeks earlier, she developed acute diplopia, lightheadedness, and vertigo; covering her left eye improved the diplopia. On examination, she had isolated left abducens palsy, periorbital edema, bilateral conjunctival injection with chemosis, and a delayed relaxation phase of the biceps reflex. Her blood pressure was 137/67 mmHg, pulse 65/min, and there were no postural changes. Laboratory results showed sodium 142 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, undetectable random cortisol, and ACTH 5.5 pmol/L. A 250-μg cosyntropin test yielded a basal cortisol of 27.6 nmol/L, rising to 405 nmol/L at 30 minutes and 488 nmol/L at 60 minutes. TSH was 2.21 mIU/L, free T4 9.78 pmol/L, and prolactin 1.7 nmol/L. Other pituitary hormones were normal for age. Noncontrast head MRI demonstrated an enlarged anterior pituitary gland with upward convexity into the suprasellar cistern; there was no cavernous sinus invasion but bilateral low-signal foci were noted within the cavernous sinuses, raising the question of aneurysms or abnormal venous flow.

A 37-year-old Caucasian woman with a 14-year history of Graves disease was referred in March 2016 for recurrent thyrotoxicosis. She was first diagnosed in 2002 with hyperthyroidism manifesting as fatigue and heat intolerance and was treated with carbimazole for 2 years, achieving remission. In 2007 she became spontaneously hypothyroid and was started on thyroid hormone replacement (thyroxine plus thyroid extract), with normal TFTs thereafter. In May 2015 she developed palpitations, tremor, anxiety, increased appetite, and heat intolerance. Her replacement regimen was changed in July 2015 from thyroid extract plus alternating doses of thyroxine to T3 alone, and subsequently all hormone was withdrawn when symptoms persisted. She began carbimazole 10 mg twice daily in December 2015. 

On examination in March 2016, her hands were warm and moist with fine tremor; the thyroid was not enlarged and there was no bruit or ophthalmopathy. Cardiovascular and neurological examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory results showed:  
• Free T4 16 pmol/L (10–20)  
• Free T3 7.0 pmol/L (2.5–6.8)  
• TSH < 0.05 mU/L (0.4–4.0)  
• TSH-receptor antibody (TRAb) 7.3 IU/L (< 1.0)

A 35-year-old woman presented with three weeks of progressive abdominal distension and a single episode of self-limited diarrhea. She reported recent dietary increases in nuts and green tea use. Her medical history was notable only for recurrent allergic bronchitis.

On examination, vital signs were normal. There was moderate, doughy abdominal distension without pallor, icterus, or peripheral edema. 

Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated moderate ascites without signs of portal hypertension or liver or renal disease. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed free peritoneal fluid and diffuse, circumferential thickening of small-bowel loops as well as the distal stomach and esophagus.

Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 22,900/mm3 with 52% eosinophils and no immature myeloid precursors. C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and IgE levels were within normal limits. Tumor marker CA-125 was normal. Skin-prick testing for food allergens and stool studies for bacteria, ova, and parasites were negative.

Diagnostic paracentesis yielded moderately cellular fluid composed entirely of eosinophils; cultures were sterile and no malignant cells were identified. 

Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy showed only mild erythema of the gastric antrum; the esophagus, duodenum, terminal ileum, and colon appeared normal. Histologic examination of gastric and duodenal mucosal biopsies revealed a mild inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and scattered eosinophils in the lamina propria.

A 16-year-old previously healthy female presented with acute left lower quadrant abdominal pain that had intensified over the past few hours, on a background of two years of intermittent abdominal pain, alternating constipation and diarrhea, and a prior diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome. Her current pain was severe and associated with non-bloody, non-bilious vomiting. On admission, she was afebrile, diaphoretic, and tachycardic (heart rate 150 bpm), with fluid resuscitation improving her vital signs. Abdominal examination revealed a soft but diffusely tender abdomen with voluntary guarding on the left and hypoactive bowel sounds. A rectal examination showed good tone and no stool in the vault. Initial laboratory studies, including urinalysis, complete blood count, and basic metabolic panel, were unremarkable.

An abdominal CT scan demonstrated a stool burden through the distal left colon to the mid-sigmoid with a collapsed distal sigmoid and rectum, for which Hirschsprung’s disease was suggested as a differential diagnosis. There was also fat stranding around the sigmoid, raising concern for inflammatory bowel disease. She was started on intravenous hydration and broad-spectrum antibiotics for a possible infectious process. On hospital day 2, she developed fever and right shoulder pain; an abdominal X-ray then revealed pneumoperitoneum. She was taken for emergent exploratory laparotomy, which revealed a large necrotic perforation in the sigmoid, fecal peritonitis, and friable mesentery and surrounding tissue. The sigmoid colon was resected to grossly healthy tissue, and a colostomy was created. The patient recovered uneventfully from surgery.

A 48-year-old African-American woman with a 2-year history of waxing and waning crusted lesions of the lower lip presented for evaluation. She has a longstanding history of ulcerative colitis that has been refractory to mesalamine and adalimumab, and her lip flares coincide with worsening of her bowel disease. Examination showed a fissured, thickened plaque with yellow-brown hemorrhagic crust covering most of her enlarged, depigmented lower lip. The remainder of the skin and mucous membranes was unremarkable. She had previously received topical corticosteroids for presumed cheilitis with minimal improvement. 

Punch biopsy of the lip demonstrated a dense, diffuse inflammatory infiltrate composed predominantly of plasma cells (CD138+), with admixed histiocytes (CD68+), T cells (CD3+), B cells (CD20+), and rare CD30+ cells. There were no granulomas, keratinocyte atypia, or solar elastosis. Immunohistochemical studies showed plasma cells positive for κ and λ light chains and IgG4. Tissue PCR testing for varicella-zoster virus and herpes simplex virus was negative.

A 35-year-old woman, gravida 5 para 2022 at 36 weeks 2 days of gestation, presented with new-onset vaginal bleeding and a five-day history of fever, headache, neck stiffness, and altered mental status beginning three days after a dog bite to her index finger. Her prenatal course was notable for intrauterine growth restriction diagnosed at 32 weeks 5 days. Medical history included splenectomy after a motor vehicle accident, a seizure disorder, and prior cesarean deliveries.

Before presentation, she had fevers up to 102.7°F, tremulous chills, gait instability, slurred speech, significant fatigue, headache, and transient phenomena of spotting across bilateral visual fields; she subsequently developed bright-red vaginal bleeding. On arrival, the bite wound appeared well-healing without erythema or tenderness. Fetal monitoring revealed a category-2 tracing, prompting an emergent repeat low-transverse cesarean section; the neonate required brief intubation for respiratory failure.

Admission laboratory studies showed a platelet count of 8 × 10^9/L; after two units of platelet transfusion it rose to 55 × 10^9/L but fell to 16 × 10^9/L postoperatively (baseline 400 × 10^9/L). Initial considerations included immune thrombocytopenia and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, but hematologic evaluation revealed no schistocytes on peripheral smear and a normal ADAMTS13 level. Coagulation studies, including fibrinogen, prothrombin time, and partial thromboplastin time, were normal. The patient was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics—clindamycin, gentamicin, and metronidazole—later changed to meropenem and doxycycline based on exposure history. A lumbar puncture was deferred due to thrombocytopenia and encephalopathy. MRI of the brain with contrast showed no evidence of encephalitis or acute intracranial processes.

A 59-year-old woman presented with a palpable, longstanding (>10 years) mass in the periphery of her left breast that had become painful over the past 8 months. She had no history of breast trauma, hormone replacement therapy, or family history of malignancy. On examination, there was a nonfixed, smooth-bordered mass in the peripheral left breast; the overlying skin, nipple, areola, and axillary lymph nodes were normal. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. Mammography (craniocaudal and mediolateral oblique views) showed a dense, lobulated mass at the 9 o’clock position in the left breast, without microcalcifications or macrocalcifications.

A 6-year-old girl was admitted with a 1-week history of pelvic pain and vaginal bleeding. Her mother believed the child had been raped by a 10-year-old boy. On admission, the child’s weight was 19 kg and height 107 cm (normal for age). She appeared asthenic; her temperature was 36.8 °C, heart rate 112 bpm, respiratory rate 24 per min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Capillary refill was < 2 s, and extremities were warm. She had conjunctival and palmar pallor. There were no lymphadenopathies, hepatosplenomegaly, petechiae, bruises, or vulvar lacerations. The remainder of the exam was unremarkable. She was treated with intravenous ampicillin for 3 days and discharged. Two days later she was readmitted with profuse vaginal bleeding. Vitamin K (5 mg IM) was administered, but bleeding continued. On re-examination her temperature was 37.4 °C, pulse 104 bpm, oxygen saturation 92%, and conjunctivae remained pale. On vaginal examination by a general practitioner, a foreign body was seen attached to the vaginal wall.

A 78-year-old man was admitted with progressive bilateral lower extremity swelling that was severe enough to prevent him from wearing his usual shoes. He also noted swelling of his face and upper extremities. His history was notable for vasospastic angina diagnosed two months earlier (with transient ST-segment elevation relieved by sublingual nitroglycerin and catheter-cine coronary angiography demonstrating reversible left anterior descending stenosis). He had chronic kidney disease and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. His medications included nifedipine 80 mg daily, diltiazem 200 mg daily, and a nitroglycerin patch.

On admission, blood pressure was 126/62 mmHg, pulse 83 beats/min, and body weight had increased by 10 kg from his baseline. Physical examination showed pitting edema of both lower extremities; jugular veins were not distended. Laboratory tests revealed creatinine 1.25 mg/dL and B-type natriuretic peptide 128 pg/mL, both unchanged from his usual values. Serum albumin, liver function tests, and thyroid hormone levels were within normal limits. ECG showed atrial fibrillation without new ST-segment changes. Chest radiography demonstrated a cardiothoracic ratio of 48% with blunting of both costophrenic angles. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60%, normal chamber dimensions, mild tricuspid regurgitation, and otherwise preserved valvular function.

A 9-year-old girl with no significant medical history presented with progressive lumbar back pain that began after minor trauma. The pain worsened over time and was exacerbated by movement and flexion. Initial management included NSAIDs and a Jewett brace for thoracic and lumbar support.

On examination, her BMI was 22.8 kg/m^2 (overweight). In the sitting position, her torso appeared shortened, and the left lower extremity was asymmetrically shorter than the right. Pathological thoracic kyphosis and shoulder asymmetry were noted.

Laboratory studies showed normal blood counts, renal and liver function tests, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, lactate dehydrogenase, and serum electrolytes. Total serum IgG and total serum protein were elevated. Calcium–phosphate metabolism markers and alkaline phosphatase were within reference ranges. Blood cultures for aerobic bacteria were negative. A QuantiFERON assay was negative. Autoantibodies associated with rheumatic diseases were absent.

Magnetic resonance imaging and computed tomography of the thoracic and lumbar spine revealed compression fractures of the T8, T12, and L1 vertebral bodies, with abnormal trabecular structure, marginal ridges, vertebra plana at T8, and multifocal lesions from T7 to T12.

Two bone biopsies yielded negative bacterial cultures. Histopathological examination demonstrated a nonspecific inflammatory process without neoplastic cells. Immunohistochemical staining of bone marrow was negative for CD1 and S100 expression.

Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry of the lumbar spine (L1–L4) and total body (less head) showed significantly decreased bone density (z-scores of –2.9). A technetium-99m MDP bone scan demonstrated increased radiotracer uptake at multiple foci in T8–T12, with peak intensity at T10.

A 57-year-old postmenopausal woman was referred with 4 months of progressive lower abdominal pain, mild offensive vaginal discharge, significant weight loss (19 kg over 1 month), anorexia, dysuria, and constipation. Her medical history included bipolar disorder, hypothyroidism, and hypertension. She had used a copper intrauterine device for 9 years. On examination, she was afebrile. Abdomen: mild generalized tenderness and a palpable mass between the umbilicus and pubis. Pelvic exam: uterus enlarged to 20-week size and a fixed, solid abdominopelvic mass; no cervical motion tenderness. Laboratory tests: hemoglobin 9 g/dL, WCC 27 × 10^3/µL, CRP 118 mg/L. Pelvic ultrasound: bilateral complex predominantly cystic pelvic masses inseparable from each other. CT abdomen and pelvis: inseparable bilateral ovarian masses, a 60 × 25 × 60 mm soft tissue mass in the anterior abdominal wall below the umbilicus involving the right rectus abdominis muscle, small fluid in the right paracolic gutter, generalized peritoneal disease, and sigmoid involvement—“The overall picture was suggestive of malignant ovarian disease.” Tumor markers: CA-125 39 U/mL; CEA and CA 19-9 normal.

A 56-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a painless papule at the right labial commissure. The lesion had a white-yellow color, measured approximately 3 mm in diameter, and was firm to palpation. She reported a history of trauma to the area one year earlier, with initial swelling that diminished and then slowly increased in size over the past year. Her medical history was unremarkable. No imaging studies were obtained. On examination, the papule was submucosal and noncompressible, without evidence of pulsation or tenderness. The clinical diagnostic hypotheses were neurofibroma and pleomorphic adenoma. An excisional biopsy was performed for definitive diagnosis.

A 56-year-old woman with a history of pulmonary Mycobacterium avium complex and hypertension, and no history of smoking or alcohol use, was treated for high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma. After multiple lines of chemotherapy and interval debulking surgery, she received pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (PLD) for 22 months (total dose 1140 mg/m2) with partial response. Two months after completion of PLD treatment, she was noted to have a white lesion on the left side of her tongue. The lesion did not rub off with friction. She had no ill-fitting dentures, sharp teeth, chronic cheek biting, syphilitic glossitis, or evidence of candida infection. On this basis, the lesion was clinically diagnosed as leukoplakia and attributed to prior PLD exposure.

An 81-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of a painful, nonhealing ulcer on the left hard palate. She had no history of trauma, and removal of her upper denture did not improve the lesion. Her medical history was notable only for diet-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus; she was not on immunosuppressive therapy and had no other known immunodeficiency. She was a nonsmoker and did not consume alcohol. She denied systemic symptoms.

On examination, there was a 3.5 × 3.5 cm, round, well-circumscribed, deep ulcer on the posterior left hard palate, extending from the midline laterally to the alveolar ridge and from hard–soft palate junction anteriorly. The ulcer had a slightly raised indurated border and a tan-white granular base. No extraoral lesions, lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly were present. Initial clinical differential diagnoses included necrotizing sialometaplasia, squamous cell carcinoma, malignant salivary gland tumor, and lymphoma.

An incisional biopsy showed large areas of necrosis with scattered viable tissue composed of small blood vessels with fibrin deposits, surrounded by a polymorphous infiltrate that included atypical lymphoid cells. These atypical cells had large vesicular nuclei with one to two prominent nucleoli and were positive for CD20, CD30, and LMP1. In situ hybridization for Epstein–Barr virus–encoded RNA (EBER) revealed scattered positive cells comprising 1–2% of the cellular infiltrate, especially at the interface between necrotic areas and inflamed mucosa.

Six weeks later, the ulcer had extended posteriorly to involve the soft palate; the anterior aspect had healed but exhibited a slightly raised, irregular mucosal surface. A second biopsy of the ulcer again showed extensive necrosis and a similar atypical lymphoid infiltrate. A biopsy of the healed, thickened mucosa revealed only mild focal inflammation without atypical lymphoid cells.

A 73-year-old man with a history of sigmoid adenocarcinoma treated by sigmoidectomy one year earlier and subsequent bilateral pulmonary metastases resected via video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery and two posterolateral thoracotomies presented three months after his last thoracotomy with progressively worsening localized right-sided thoracotomy site pain rated 4–5 on the visual analogue scale, unresponsive to oral analgesics. A chest radiograph showed a new, round opacity in the right middle lung zone.

A 4-year-old boy was admitted with a 4-day history of high fever (maximum, 40 °C) and severe left lower abdominal pain. He had no diarrhea or vomiting, and a course of oral antibiotics had been ineffective.

On examination, he was febrile but otherwise stable. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 23,000/μL with 67% neutrophils, a platelet count of 396,000/μL, and a C-reactive protein level of 11.7 mg/dL; other laboratory tests were within normal limits. Stool cultures grew only nonpathogenic Escherichia coli.

An abdominal radiograph demonstrated distended bowel loops containing fecal material. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed segmental thickening of the sigmoid-colon wall to 6 mm, predominantly in the submucosal layer, inflammatory changes in the surrounding fat, and slightly decreased blood-flow signals on color Doppler.

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT confirmed localized wall thickening of the sigmoid colon without evidence of arterial or venous occlusion in the mesenteric vessels.

Colonoscopy showed a 7-cm segment of severe, circumferential wall thickening with slight mucosal redness and luminal narrowing in the sigmoid colon, but no bleeding, exudate, ulceration, aphthous ulcers, or cobblestoning; the remaining colon appeared normal. Biopsy specimens from the sigmoid colon demonstrated nonspecific colitis with lymphocytes, histiocytes, neutrophils, and eosinophils in the lamina propria; there were no crypt abscesses, basal plasma-cell infiltration, crypt distortion, or granulomas.

After two days of intravenous antibiotics, the patient’s fever and abdominal pain persisted.

A 13-year-old multiparous Quarter Horse mare at day 332 of gestation was referred for dystocia. Approximately 24 hours before referral, she exhibited intermittent mild colic signs without progression to Stage II labor. The following morning, she was found in lateral recumbency and unwilling to rise. On presentation, the mare was anxious with moderate colic signs, a heart rate of 60 beats/min, respiratory rate elevated, and temperature 38.6 °C. Mucous membranes were hyperemic with a capillary refill time of <1 s. Packed cell volume was 42% and total solids 7.0 g/dL. CBC showed mild leukocytosis (10,000 WBC/µL). Serum chemistry revealed mild hypernatremia (143 mmol/L), hyperchloremia (103 mmol/L), hyperalbuminemia (4.0 g/dL), hyperglycemia (138 mg/dL), mildly elevated GGT (23 U/L), and mild indirect hyperbilirubinemia (1.7 mg/dL). Venous blood gas showed pH 7.42, bicarbonate 18.1 mmol/L, mild hyperlactatemia (1.8 mmol/L), hypocalcemia (5.8 mg/dL), and hypomagnesemia (0.9 mg/dL).  
Abdominal palpation per rectum revealed broad ligaments without tension and a firm uterine body; no fetal heartbeat was detected on ultrasound. Vaginal examination showed a 4 cm cervical dilation with serosanguineous malodorous exudate. Digital examination revealed a nonviable fetus in a transverse, head-back position. Given inadequate cervical dilation and malpresentation, controlled vaginal delivery was not viable, and cesarean section was recommended.

A 48-year-old woman presented to the emergency department in March 2023 with a several-day history of progressive abdominal pain, distension, and features of intestinal obstruction. She was afebrile and had no significant past medical history. 

Abdominopelvic CT scan revealed an enlarged right adnexa containing multiple fluid-filled cysts; thickening of the left uterine wall contiguous with the left bladder wall; colonic wall thickening with hyperemia; and heterogeneous peritoneal fluid collections. 

On physical examination, the abdomen was distended and tender. Bimanual pelvic examination demonstrated indeterminate solid tissue and firm adnexal adhesions. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a thin, linear endometrium; an enlarged right ovary; and the left ovary densely adherent to the sigmoid colon.

Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (white blood cell count 15.02 × 10^3/µL) and elevated C-reactive protein (40.49 mg/L). 

Given the high suspicion for a gynecologic malignancy based on clinical and imaging findings, the patient underwent a laparotomic hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, sigmoid resection with ileostomy, omentectomy, appendectomy, and peritoneal biopsies.

An 84-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation, remote colorectal cancer treated with partial colectomy and colostomy, and prior small-bowel resections presented with a 3-week history of six to eight voluminous, watery, nonbloody bowel movements per day and mild, diffuse, crampy abdominal pain that worsened with eating. She denied fever, chills, nausea, or vomiting.  
On examination, T 36.8°C, BP 132/68 mm Hg, pulse 72 irregularly irregular, RR 18, O₂ sat 99% on room air; she appeared nontoxic. Cardiovascular exam revealed an irregular rhythm; lungs were clear. The abdomen was soft with mild diffuse tenderness to deep palpation without rebound or guarding. Loose brown stool and gas were evident in her colostomy bag.  
Laboratory studies showed a normal white-cell count and a normal serum lactate level. A non–contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen demonstrated gas within the wall of the pelvic cecum and remaining rectum without bowel-wall thickening, a nonobstructive gas pattern, and no free intraperitoneal air.

A 75-year-old woman was referred after repeated episodes of hematemesis and melena. One week earlier, she had started treatment for herpes zoster. Her medical history included thyroidectomy for adenomas, hypertension, and a prior cerebral hemorrhage; she had no abdominal surgeries. On arrival, blood pressure was 116/69 mmHg, heart rate 78/min, and oxygen saturation 96%. Laboratory tests showed anemia (hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL) with otherwise normal blood counts, coagulation, and tumor markers. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed thickening of the gastric antrum wall without lymphadenopathy; incidental pulmonary nodules and gallstones were also noted. A positive T-SPOT test prompted isolation until tuberculosis was excluded. Urgent upper endoscopy demonstrated a submucosal ridge on the anterior antral wall with a central ulcer and active bleeding; hemostasis with electrocoagulation was only temporarily successful. After persistent melena and worsening anemia despite transfusion, surgery was planned. Imaging had suggested a small submucosal tumor, such as a gastrointestinal stromal tumor, and to avoid postoperative deformity, laparoscopic distal gastrectomy with Roux-en-Y reconstruction and cholecystectomy was chosen.

A 33-year-old woman with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (euthyroid on levothyroxine) underwent elective total thyroidectomy for mild compressive symptoms. Preoperative CT showed a 4×5 cm gland without retrosternal extension. Flexible laryngoscopy before surgery was normal. General anesthesia was induced with midazolam, propofol, fentanyl, and rocuronium, and a size 7.0 mm endotracheal tube was placed on the first attempt. Anesthesia was maintained on desflurane; intraoperative medications included paracetamol, diclofenac, dexamethasone, and granisetron. Surgery lasted 2 hours, during which both recurrent laryngeal nerves were identified and preserved, and hemostasis was secured. After closure, the subcutaneous wound was infiltrated with 5 mL of 0.25% bupivacaine; morphine was given intravenously. The patient was extubated awake with normal vocal cord motion and transferred to the PACU with stable vital signs and normal voice. Thirty minutes later, she developed progressive dyspnea, dysphonia, and inspiratory stridor, with SpO₂ decreasing from 99% to 92%, managed with CPAP. Flexible laryngoscopy showed bilateral adducted vocal cords without edema. Serum calcium was 1.9 mmol/L (normal 2.09–2.54). She was re-intubated and ventilated; after 12 hours in the ICU, extubation was successful, and laryngoscopy showed normal vocal cord motion.

A 16-month-old boy was referred for evaluation of precocious puberty. His parents first noted pubic hair at six months of age and subsequently observed rapid linear growth. There was no exposure to exogenous androgens, and no family history of early puberty or short stature. 

On examination, his height was above the 99th percentile (midparental target 50th percentile). He had pubic hair at Tanner stage 2 and stretched penile length of 11 cm, with prepubertal testes. A bone-age radiograph obtained at 12 months of age was assessed as 12–18 months; by 21 months bone age was 6 years, and by 26 months bone age was 8 years.

Laboratory studies showed:  
• Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone, androstenedione, and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate within normal limits.  
• Basal luteinizing hormone 0.7 mIU/mL (prepubertal <0.3 mIU/mL).  
• Serum testosterone 289 ng/dL (prepubertal <5 ng/dL).

An adrenocorticotropic hormone stimulation test ruled out congenital adrenal hyperplasia. A leuprolide stimulation test ruled out central precocious puberty. Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen and pelvis was normal. Scrotal ultrasound revealed prepubertal testes with bilateral testicular microlithiasis and no masses. An initial α-fetoprotein level was elevated but normalized on repeat testing; β-hCG, insulin-like growth factor-1, and thyroid function were normal.

At 26 months of age, the leading diagnostic considerations were familial male-limited precocious puberty and McCune-Albright syndrome.

An 8-year-old boy presented with a 2-year history of oral ulcers and difficulty eating. Parents first noticed small ulcerations on the tongue and buccal mucosa 2 years ago. For the past 8 months, he reported a burning sensation exacerbated by spicy and hot foods. Previous local treatments had been ineffective, and no records were available. His medical and family histories were unremarkable, and there was no history of vesicular or bullous skin eruptions.

Physical examination revealed no cutaneous, genital, scalp, or nail lesions. Oral inspection showed white interlacing striae extending from the commissures to the retromolar areas bilaterally at the occlusal plane. On the left buccal mucosa, there was a 2 cm × 3 cm erosive lesion in the retromolar region; the right buccal mucosa exhibited slender radiating white striae. The dorsum of the tongue had depapillated areas interspersed with white striae and melanin pigmentation. Lesions were flat, non-tender, non-indurated, and non-scrapable. Oral hygiene was fair; deeply carious first molars were noted bilaterally without any restorations. 

Routine hematological investigations were unremarkable.

A previously healthy 20-year-old Caucasian man presented after two episodes of loss of consciousness at rest over a fortnight. A witness described collapse followed by shaking of all four limbs but no other epileptiform activity; he recovered spontaneously after a few minutes. He denied alcohol or drug use and had no personal or family history of blackout, collapse, or sudden death. Examination was entirely normal; he was haemodynamically stable.  
Electrocardiography showed sinus rhythm with a corrected QT interval of 588 ms (normal <450 ms); the PR interval and QRS duration were within normal limits.  
Admission blood tests revealed a corrected calcium level of <1.25 mmol/L (normal 2.2–2.5), phosphate 2.88 mmol/L (0.8–1.4), and alkaline phosphatase 172 μ/L (35–135). Magnesium, potassium, and renal function were normal. Endocrine studies showed a parathyroid hormone level of <3 ng/mL (14–72), vitamin D 24.1 nmol/L (25–50), and normal thyroid function tests.  
Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated no structural abnormalities and preserved ventricular function. Noncontrast head CT was unremarkable.

A 54-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department for progressive lethargy and poor verbalization. Eight days earlier she had developed headache and facial tenderness, along with drowsiness but no fever. Over the preceding year she had intermittent headaches with nausea, vomiting, and a 15 kg weight loss. On examination she was oriented to person and place but lethargic, with slurred speech, poor eye contact, and decreased psychomotor activity. Pupils were 3 mm and reactive bilaterally; neurologic examination was nonfocal except for brisk reflexes in the right upper extremity. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 6.5 × 10^3/μL, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 67 mm/hr, and a C-reactive protein level of 7.74 mg/dL; urine toxicology was negative. Noncontrast CT of the head revealed an 8.3 cm hypodense lesion in the left temporal lobe with areas of hemorrhage in the mesial temporal region. A lumbar puncture was deferred because of concern for herniation. MRI of the brain demonstrated a large lesion of the left temporal lobe extending into the frontal lobe and separate ill-defined lesions in the right temporal lobe. MR spectroscopy showed an increased choline peak at the medial left temporal lobe, and MR perfusion revealed patchy hyperperfusion in the left perisylvian region and left anterior temporal lobe.

A 67-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an abnormal mediastinal shadow discovered on a routine chest radiograph. Seven years prior, her radiograph was normal, but over the past four years serial films demonstrated progressive protrusion of the left third aortic arch. A CT scan performed two years ago revealed a 4-cm mass in the left mediastinum, although it was not reported at the time. She denied chest pain, dyspnea, or other cardiovascular symptoms and had no relevant medical history. On current contrast-enhanced CT, the mass measured approximately 5 cm abutting the left pulmonary artery and was initially considered to represent lymphoma, neurogenic tumour, or germ cell tumour. PET-CT showed no uptake of 18F-FDG. Arterial-phase images demonstrated internal contrast enhancement equivalent to that of a blood vessel and areas of thrombus. The patient was referred to cardiology for further assessment.

A 45-year-old man with opioid use disorder, major depressive disorder, and fibromyalgia was brought to the ED after several falls and with altered mental status of 3 days’ duration. On arrival, he was hemodynamically stable but lethargic. CT of the head, cervical spine, chest, abdomen, and pelvis without contrast showed only bibasilar atelectasis. EEG revealed no epileptiform discharges. CBC showed a WBC count of 14,500/µL; CMP was normal. Initial blood, urine, and sputum cultures were obtained, and he was started on IV ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin. As his mental status declined, he was intubated with IV fentanyl (2 mcg/kg) and propofol (3 mg/kg) and sedated with fentanyl infusion (0.7–1 mcg/kg/h) and propofol infusion (1–3 mg/kg/h). Four hours after ICU admission, he developed fevers of 38.1–39.5 °C, tachycardia, and diaphoresis. Antibiotic therapy was escalated for presumed infection; repeat blood, sputum, and urine cultures and CSF analysis remained negative. On ICU day 3, neurologic examination revealed deep tendon hyperreflexia and inducible muscle clonus, in addition to persistent hyperthermia (38.1 °C), tachycardia, flushed skin, agitation, and diaphoresis.

A 72-year-old non–English-speaking man with hypertension and hyperlipidaemia underwent a right lower lobectomy for stage IIIA lung adenocarcinoma. Prior to surgery, he was functionally independent, walked 2 km without limitation, and had normal pulmonary function tests. Six weeks after lobectomy, he developed subacute, progressive dyspnoea and on admission could walk less than 10 m. He was taking rosuvastatin, perindopril, and metoprolol. Two hospital admissions in the preceding 6 weeks led to empirical treatment for pneumonia with antibiotics and for heart failure with diuretics, but his dyspnoea continued to worsen. 

On this admission, a complete blood count, urea and electrolytes, and C-reactive protein were within normal limits. A CT scan of the chest showed non-specific, left-predominant, bilateral ground-glass changes. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage revealed a normal cell count and differential; no pathogens were isolated on standard cultures or acid-fast and fungal media; and PCR assays for Pneumocystis jiroveci, herpes simplex viruses, varicella zoster virus, cytomegalovirus, influenza A/B, enterovirus/rhinovirus, picornavirus, parainfluenza 1–3, adenovirus, human metapneumovirus, Bordetella pertussis, and respiratory syncytial virus were negative. Serologic testing, including antinuclear antibody, double-stranded DNA, extractable nuclear antigens (Sm, RNP, SSA/Ro, SSB/La, Scl-70, Jo-1, PCNA, ribosomal P, Pm-Scl, centromere protein B), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, anti–glomerular basement membrane antibody, creatine kinase, and a myositis antibody panel, was negative.

Despite intravenous ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and diuresis with IV furosemide, his dyspnoea worsened and he developed platypnea—dyspnoea on assuming an upright position. On pulse oximetry, his oxygen saturation fell from 93% on room air while supine to 86% while upright. Arterial blood gases confirmed a drop in PaO2 from 75 mmHg supine to 56 mmHg after 5 minutes upright (on FiO2 0.21).

A 41-year-old man presented with a 6-year history of chronic redness, irritation, and tearing of the left eye. He had undergone multiple slit-lamp examinations at various clinics, and each time any visible lash was epilated, only to recur within weeks. He noted that longer lash regrowth reduced the irritating sensation and tearing.  
His visual acuity and intraocular pressures were normal bilaterally. He had no history or clinical features of atopic eczema, allergic dermatitis, or preseptal cellulitis. On slit-lamp examination, eversion of the left lower eyelid revealed a single hair follicle on the palpebral conjunctiva, associated with mild conjunctival hyperemia and focal punctate keratopathy of the inferior cornea. There was no palpable mass or pigmented lesion, and the remainder of the anterior and posterior segments was within normal limits.

A 12-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of a 3-year history of slowly progressive, painless, bilateral posterior jaw swelling. She had undergone multiple courses of antibiotics without improvement. 

On examination, both parotid glands were symmetrically enlarged, firm, non-tender, non-pulsatile, and fixed, with unremarkable overlying skin. Intraoral findings included multiple cervical caries, large restorations on permanent molars, and retained food debris. A chair-side unstimulated salivary flow (spitting test) yielded 0.2 mL in 15 minutes. 

Her parents denied fever, weight loss, respiratory symptoms, or gastrointestinal complaints. She reported eye dryness and had been using ophthalmic lubricating drops. At age 8, she had a single episode of bilateral knee swelling and pain treated with aspiration and analgesics.

Laboratory studies showed hypochromic microcytic anemia, elevated serum GOT and GPT, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 30 mm/h, and a negative C-reactive protein. Rheumatoid factor (IgG and IgM) was negative. 

Neck ultrasonography demonstrated enlarged parotid glands with multiple inflammatory cervical lymph nodes; abdominal ultrasound was normal. Two years earlier, neck ultrasound had shown diffuse microcalcifications within enlarged salivary glands, and fine-needle aspiration cytology had revealed lymphoepithelial islands with lymphocytic infiltration consistent with autoimmune sialadenitis. Serologic tests, including creatinine, urea, antinuclear antibodies, complement C3 and C5 levels, and thyroid function tests, were within normal limits.

A 25-year-old woman presented with three months of episodic fever and headaches. Initially, she had low-grade fever managed with NSAIDs as an outpatient. Routine blood counts, urine and blood cultures, chest radiograph, and abdominal ultrasound were normal, and no lymphadenopathy was noted; her fever resolved over four days.

Three weeks later, she developed small nodular swellings in the neck and high-grade fever with headache. On admission, her temperature was elevated, and examination showed four firm, discrete lymph nodes in the posterior triangle of the neck without meningeal signs. Laboratory studies revealed leukopenia (TLC 3200/μL). Urine and blood cultures, contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen, lumbar puncture, and CSF examination were noncontributory. She received supportive care; her fever and lymphadenopathy regressed, and she was discharged after two weeks.

Two weeks later, she was re-hospitalized with high-grade fever and headache. Examination showed multiple firm cervical and axillary lymph nodes ~2 cm in size. Laboratory testing revealed mild anemia, leukopenia, and an elevated ESR of 70 mm in the first hour. Immunological tests, including ANA and RF, were within normal limits. Repeat contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen again demonstrated enlarged cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy. Excision biopsy of a cervical lymph node was then performed for definitive diagnosis.

A 10-year-old boy presented with pain when chewing on the left side. He had no facial asymmetry. Intraoral examination revealed absence of the permanent left second premolar, retention of the left second primary molar with a large amalgam restoration, and a firm, non-tender swelling in the left mandibular body obliterating the buccal sulcus; the overlying mucosa was normal. A panoramic radiograph showed a well-defined, unilocular radiolucent lesion with a radiopaque halo encompassing the crown of the unerupted left second premolar. The lesion measured 3.3 cm × 2.7 cm, extended from the periapical region of the left first premolar to the mesial root of the left first molar, and the tooth was displaced with 14 mm depth of inclusion.

A 5-year-old boy presented with a 2-week history of a painful mass on his left upper eyelid. He had been treated with a course of oral amoxicillin by a general practitioner without improvement. There were no similar lesions noted on his body or among family members. His past medical, surgical, nutritional, social, and family histories were unremarkable, and his growth and development were within normal limits. On ocular examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes; the conjunctiva was quiet, the cornea was clear, the anterior chamber was deep and quiet, the lens was clear, and the red reflex and fundus were normal. Examination of the left upper eyelid revealed a single, tender, mobile mass with a focal abscess and a 1-cm-diameter opening with granulation tissue at the margin; there was no overlying skin. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. The patient was admitted, and the decision was made to perform surgical excision and curettage of the mass with closure using absorbable suture.

A 38-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of continuous vomiting that had worsened over the previous 4 hours. He reported intermittent fever, with a maximum temperature of 38.9°C, and had experienced a small amount of hematemesis but denied abdominal pain. His medical history was unremarkable, with no prior abdominal surgery or trauma. 

On examination, his abdomen was soft and non-tender, with no rebound. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 13.4×10^9/L (neutrophils 91%), hemoglobin 69 g/L, procalcitonin 19.5 μg/L, C-reactive protein 262 mg/L, lactate 1.8 mmol/L, arterial pH 7.22, PO2 82.2 mm Hg, PCO2 40.5 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 95%. A nasogastric tube returned large volumes of gastric fluid with blood.

An upright abdominal radiograph showed clustered dilated loops of small bowel with air–fluid levels. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated partial mesenteric volvulus, poor perfusion of a segment of small intestine, and fluid of high density in the peritoneal cavity. Three-dimensional CT reconstruction localized the obstruction, confirmed ischemic changes, and showed fluid around the small intestine. 

To characterize the peritoneal fluid, an ultrasound-guided abdominal paracentesis was performed, yielding bloody ascites.

A 19-year-old woman was found unconscious at home by her parents after reportedly ingesting twenty 25-mg tablets of baclofen in a suicide attempt. She has a history of posttraumatic stress disorder and depression, treated with venlafaxine and clomipramine. On arrival, she was afebrile, oxygen saturation was 70% on room air, and her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 4. She was intubated emergently and transferred to the intensive care unit.

On examination, jugular venous distention was noted, bilateral crackles were present, and breath sounds were decreased at the left lung base. Pupils were reactive without anisocoria. There was no evidence of subcutaneous emphysema, trauma, or deformity of the neck or chest wall.

Chest radiography and computed tomography revealed pneumomediastinum, atelectasis of the left lower lobe, and leftward mediastinal shift. Electrocardiography was unremarkable, and echocardiography could not visualize the heart due to extensive mediastinal air. A brain CT and MRI showed no intracranial abnormalities.

A left-sided chest tube was placed, immediately releasing air, and it was removed on hospital day 4 without recurrent air leak.

A 38-year-old man with end-stage renal disease secondary to type 1 diabetes had been on continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis for 18 months and automated peritoneal dialysis for 40 months. He had no prior episodes of PD-related peritonitis. He presented with a 2-day history of emesis, diarrhea, cloudy peritoneal dialysate, and upper abdominal pain. On admission he was afebrile, blood pressure 125/85 mmHg, pulse 143 beats per minute. There was no abdominal tenderness, and the peritoneal catheter exit site was clean. Electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia without ischemia. Laboratory studies revealed: white-cell count 14.6×10^9/L with 83% neutrophils, hematocrit 33%, platelets 313×10^9/L; C-reactive protein 138 mg/L; procalcitonin 1.1 ng/mL. The first dialysate leukocyte count was 1055/µL with 93% neutrophils. Gram stain of the effluent was negative. Empiric intraperitoneal cefazolin and ceftazidime were initiated. Three days later, repeat dialysate Gram stain and cultures, exit-site culture, and stool culture were all negative. Abdominal X-ray and ultrasound were unrevealing. Despite antibiotic therapy, he remained symptomatic, developed epigastric and right-upper-quadrant tenderness, inappetence, and anuria. He was switched to hemodialysis. On hospital day 6 he reported left arm pain; ECG remained nonischemic, but troponin T was mildly elevated. On hospital day 7, with persistent pain and a rising dialysate leukocyte count of 4385/µL (99% neutrophils), a decision was made to remove the peritoneal catheter.

An 18-year-old woman presented with 2 days of fever and vomiting followed by 1 day of weakness in all four limbs and speech difficulty. Her temperature was 101.4 °F; other vital signs were normal. She was fully conscious (GCS 15). Fundoscopic examination was normal. Neurologically, she had bilateral horizontal gaze palsy with impaired oculocephalic reflexes, bulbar dysarthria, and quadriplegia with bilateral extensor plantar responses; there were no signs of meningeal irritation. Chest, cardiac, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory evaluation showed anemia, reduced packed cell volume, and thrombocytopenia. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a normal total cell count (all lymphocytes) and mildly elevated protein. Serum dengue NS1 antigen was positive; anti-dengue IgM and IgG were not detected. MRI of the brain demonstrated T1 hypointensity and T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the bilateral thalami, pons, medulla, and left cerebellum, with intense diffusion restriction on DWI and central blooming on GRE sequences, producing a “double-doughnut” appearance; there was also an acute infarct in right frontal white matter.

A 27-year-old woman presented to the infertility clinic with one year of secondary infertility. Her BMI was 32. She had two prior vaginal deliveries, most recent five years ago, after which she underwent hysteroscopy, insertion of a levonorgestrel intrauterine system, tension-free vaginal tape, and posterior repair in one session for heavy menses and stress incontinence. Six weeks after IUS insertion, her general practitioner could not visualize the strings on examination; a transvaginal ultrasound did not locate the device and it was presumed expelled, with no further evaluation. Eighteen months later, she discontinued an Implanon implant and attempted conception. She reported irregular cycles of 4–8 weeks without intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding. Cervical cytology was normal; she had a history of CIN3 treated nine years earlier, and treated chlamydia and herpes infections. She has long QT syndrome managed with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator. She is a nonsmoker, drinks 18 units of alcohol weekly, and her partner is healthy and has previously fathered a child. Physical examination of both partners was unremarkable. Laboratory evaluation revealed a normal follicular-phase profile, normal serum prolactin, and a luteal-phase serum progesterone level of 28.9 nmol/L, suggesting borderline ovulation. Semen analysis was normal. A hysterosalpingogram demonstrated normal tubal patency and revealed an intra-abdominally located IUS.

A 26-year-old primigravida at 26 weeks’ gestation was referred for fetal echocardiography after ultrasound documented fetal tachycardia. On echocardiography, there was a large aneurysmal pouch arising from the region immediately beneath the posterior mitral leaflet. The sac protruded predominantly into the right atrium (measuring 8 × 7 mm) and to a lesser extent into the left atrium. The aneurysm enlarged during ventricular systole and collapsed during ventricular diastole. Doppler assessment showed normal tricuspid and mitral valve inflow velocities without evidence of inflow obstruction or mitral regurgitation. No other intracardiac abnormalities were seen. Transient episodes of fetal tachycardia were noted, with heart rates up to 210 beats per minute and a PR interval of 70 msec with 1:1 atrioventricular conduction; at other times, the rate varied between 140 and 160 beats per minute. Ventricular function was normal, and there was no pericardial effusion.

A 61-year-old man with a remote history of subarachnoid hemorrhage presented with sudden onset of high fever, severe occipital headache, and neck stiffness. He was afebrile before this episode. On admission, his temperature was 39.3 °C. He had no focal neurologic deficits and a negative Kernig’s sign.

Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 12 270/μL and a C-reactive protein level of 23.29 mg/dL. Serum uric acid was 5.2 mg/dL. Serologic tests for connective tissue disease and vasculitis—including rheumatoid factor, cytoplasmic and perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, anti-nuclear antibody, and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody—were negative.

Blood cultures were negative, and serum procalcitonin was not elevated. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed 1 white cell/μL and a protein level of 47 mg/dL; cultures and viral antibody tests for herpes simplex and varicella-zoster virus were negative.

Brain MRI demonstrated slight residual subdural hematoma without gadolinium enhancement but was otherwise unremarkable. A plain cervical CT scan and three-dimensional reconstruction revealed a prominent crown-like calcification encircling the odontoid process. Cervical MRI showed hyperintense soft-tissue surrounding the odontoid on T2-weighted fat-suppressed images without gadolinium enhancement. Knee radiography and CT identified calcium deposits within the articular cartilage.

A 25-year-old man presented with 7 days of numbness and paralysis of both lower limbs. Initial spine MRI at the local hospital showed hyperintensity in the spinal cord, and acute transverse myelitis was diagnosed; after 3 days of dehydration and neurotrophic treatment, his strength and sensation normalized. Five days later, he developed recurrent lower-limb numbness and paralysis accompanied by chest and back pain and was admitted to our hospital. He had no significant medical or traumatic history except an upper respiratory infection 1 month earlier.

On admission, temperature was 36.6 °C, pulse 70 bpm, and blood pressure 132/88 mmHg. Thoracic and lumbar spine lateral pressure elicited significant pain. Muscle tone was mildly increased in both lower limbs. Neurologic examination showed paresthesia and weakness (left lower extremity MMT 4/5; right 3/5), with positive Babinski and Oppenheim signs on the right. Other examinations were unremarkable.

Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a protein count of 1305 mg/L (normal 200–400 mg/L), a white blood cell count of 2 × 10^6/L, and normal glucose and other parameters. Initial MRI of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine performed 36 h after admission demonstrated a T1–T2 fusiform mass at the T1–T2 level, isodense on the sagittal T1-weighted image with central hyperintensity, and hyperintense on T2, causing dorsal spinal cord compression and narrowing of the local subarachnoid space. Seven days after admission, his lower-limb strength worsened further to MMT 1/5 with urinary dysfunction. Contrast-enhanced MRI showed a fusiform epidural mass from C7 to T2 with significant but uneven enhancement, an obvious strip-band enhanced lesion with a clear outline, anterior displacement of the compressed dorsal cord, and a narrowed subarachnoid space at T1–T2.

An 85-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 2½-month history of a gradually enlarging mass on the vertex of her scalp. She initially noted a nontender plaque with occasional clear drainage and was treated by her primary care physician with griseofulvin (500 mg daily for 30 days) and cephalexin (500 mg three times daily for 10 days) without improvement. A noncontrast head CT showed a homogeneous area of soft-tissue thickening in the scalp without bone erosion or dural involvement. She denied recent travel, trauma, medication changes, or a history of skin cancer and had no fever, chills, or weight loss.

On examination, there were multiple violaceous, indurated, nontender papules coalescing into a plaque with clustered nodules and central crusting on the occipital scalp. A punch biopsy demonstrated dense dermal inflammation composed predominantly of eosinophils with focal neutrophils, reactive fibroblast/fibrohistiocytic changes, and vascular ectasias but no evidence of vasculitis. Periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott methenamine silver, Gram, and acid-fast stains were all negative, and there were no histologic features of malignancy.

Two weeks later, a new indurated, tender nodule had developed adjacent to the initial lesion. Repeat punch biopsies of the left vertex and midline scalp again showed a diffuse, focally dense eosinophilic inflammatory infiltrate with associated neutrophils, focal eosinophilic degranulation, and scattered reactive vessels lined by CD31-positive endothelial cells. Tissue cultures were negative for bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial organisms. A complete blood count revealed leukocytosis (WBC 12.9 × 10^3/µL) with transient eosinophilia (7.6 × 10^3/µL).

A 70-year-old man presented with a one-month history of multiple asymptomatic, red, raised lesions on his back. He had lepromatous leprosy and was receiving multidrug therapy for multibacillary Hansen’s disease for six months. One year earlier, he had begun allopurinol for hyperuricemia; six months ago, similar lesions had appeared and resolved one month after stopping allopurinol. Four months before presentation, he had resumed allopurinol on his own. He denied other medications or systemic symptoms.

On examination, there were multiple grouped but discrete, annular, firm, non-tender, smooth-surfaced, skin-colored papules 0.5–1 cm in diameter over the back. There was diffuse loss of touch and temperature sensation over the dorsal aspects of both hands and feet, with thickening of the bilateral ulnar and common peroneal nerves, bilateral ulnar clawing, and a blister on the right index finger.

Routine blood counts, liver and renal function tests, thyroid function tests, and random blood sugar were within normal limits. Chest radiograph was normal. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for HIV 1 and 2 was nonreactive.

A 68-year-old African-American man was admitted for atrial flutter and started on anticoagulation. On hospital day 4, he had hematemesis and was transferred to the ICU. His medical history was notable for a packed red-cell transfusion in 2002. On admission, his hemoglobin was 13.6 g/dL, platelet count 265 × 10^9/L, prothrombin time 17.6 seconds, and aPTT 30.4 seconds. In the ICU he completed antibiotic courses for pneumonia and C. difficile colitis, and received six units of PRBC and two units of plasma on day 4, six units of PRBC on day 5, and additional plasma on days 13 and 14. He improved and was transferred to the ward on day 21.

On day 25, his platelet count began to fall. By day 29, it was 51 × 10^9/L and he developed hematuria; he was afebrile and without signs of infection. On day 30, the platelet count was 31 × 10^9/L, coagulation studies were normal, and a peripheral smear showed large platelets with decreased overall numbers. The differential diagnosis included drug-related thrombocytopenia, post-transfusion purpura, and immune thrombocytopenic purpura. Several medications were discontinued. Despite this, his platelet count continued to decline, reaching a nadir of 7 × 10^9/L on day 32.

A 50-year-old man of Pakistani origin was referred for a new-onset pruritic bullous eruption. His medical history was notable for past hepatitis B infection and chronic pruritic plaques on his legs treated intermittently with topical corticosteroids. He was taking no medications or supplements, and review of systems was negative, including for weight loss or constitutional symptoms. 

On examination, tense bullae and vesicles clustered in an annular “string-of-pearls” arrangement on an erythematous base were noted on both forearms. Lichenified erythematous plaques with overlying vesicles and some bullae were present on the dorsal hands and feet. Mucous membranes were normal. 

Given the patient’s age and the annular configuration of lesions, linear IgA bullous dermatosis and pemphigus herpetiformis were initially suspected. A skin biopsy and direct immunofluorescence study were obtained, and the patient was started on prednisone 20 mg daily. 

Laboratory studies showed an eosinophil count of 1.0 × 10^9 g/L; the remainder of the complete blood count and metabolic panel were within normal limits.

A 38-year-old previously healthy woman from the northern coast of Peru was diagnosed with dengue without alarm signs by positive IgM ELISA and received outpatient symptomatic treatment. Four weeks later, she noted intense pain in the anterior cervical region radiating to the mandible and auricular area, associated with neck swelling, general malaise, odynophagia, dysphagia, palpitations, and tremor of the limbs. On ultrasonography, the thyroid gland was heterogeneously echogenic; in the left lobe there was a 27×15 mm solid, hypoechogenic nodule with irregular margins and no calcifications (ACR-TIRADS 4). Multiple enlarged cervical lymph nodes (groups II, III, and VI and bilateral suprasternal) were rounded, with well-defined contours, preserved hyperechogenic hila, and increased vascular flow. Thyroid function tests showed a TSH of 0.043 µIU/mL, elevated free T4 and free T3, negative antithyroperoxidase and antithyroglobulin antibodies, and a thyroglobulin level of 118.6 ng/mL. Thyroid scintigraphy with Technetium-99m demonstrated absence of radionuclide uptake in the thyroid bed. An ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the nodule yielded Bethesda II cytology.

An 11-year-old boy presented with 3 months of worsening fatigue, intermittent crampy abdominal pain, occasional nausea, and pallor. Laboratory studies showed microcytic iron‐deficiency anemia (hemoglobin 4.1 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 62 fL, absolute reticulocyte count 74.8 × 10^3/μL, ferritin 1.9 ng/mL). The initial differential included hematologic malignancy, inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, Helicobacter pylori infection, and excessive milk intake. Initial evaluation revealed normal fecal calprotectin, thyroid-stimulating hormone, urinalysis, fecal occult blood test, C-reactive protein, chest radiograph, and metabolic panel. Initial celiac testing showed borderline antiendomysial antibodies and normal tissue transglutaminase antibody, with repeat celiac testing normal. He received packed red blood cells and 3 months of oral iron and was advised to reduce milk intake. After stopping iron supplementation, his anemia recurred, and an esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) was visually normal; gastric biopsies showed only mild chronic active gastritis without evidence of celiac disease or H. pylori. Two months later, recurrent anemia prompted repeat upper and lower endoscopy, which showed marked gastric nodularity. Gastric biopsies revealed a patchy increase in lamina propria eosinophils (up to 40 per high-power field) with focal eosinophilic microabscesses and mild chronic inflammation with lymphoid follicles; terminal ileum and colon biopsies were normal. Stool studies were negative for ova and parasites. He was offered prednisone; because a food allergy–driven process was considered, he eliminated wheat for 3 months and underwent a third EGD.

A 15-year-old girl with a history of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) diagnosed at age 9 presented with a 2-day history of agitation, grandiose beliefs, and distractibility. Over the preceding 4 months, both she and her parents noted worsening irritability. She reported no need for sleep during the 2 days, spent nights planning unrealistic projects, and was unable to attend school or care for her hygiene. There were no identifiable recent stressors.

Her preschool years were marked by family financial instability, frequent relocations, and periods of physical and emotional abuse by her parents—events the parents described as “rarely occurred” or “insignificant.” She had no other psychiatric history, no physical illnesses, and no prior substance, alcohol, or medication use. Her maternal aunt had recurrent bipolar disorder since adolescence.

On mental status examination, she was unable to remain seated, was excessively active, and exhibited logorrhea, accelerated speech, flight of ideas, grandiose beliefs, and irritability. She denied hallucinations or suicidal ideation. Vital signs and general physical examination were within normal limits.

Baseline laboratory tests, including complete blood count, electrolytes, thyroid function tests, and urinalysis, were normal. Electroencephalogram and brain magnetic resonance imaging findings were also normal.

A 55-year-old man was admitted with a 15-day history of persistent distending pain in the right upper quadrant, without fever, acid reflux, or diarrhea. He had no notable past medical history. On examination, vital signs were stable and the abdominal exam revealed tenderness in the right upper quadrant without guarding or rebound. Laboratory tests showed a marked eosinophilia (eosinophil count 2.68 × 10^9/l; reference range 0.02–0.52 × 10^9/l); other routine hematologic and biochemical tests were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a localized fluid collection beneath the right hepatic capsule with uneven density and no enhancement, multiple patchy space-occupying lesions in the right lobe of the liver with low density on delayed imaging, and inhomogeneous enhancement in the arterial phase. Following consideration of the patient’s imaging findings and medical history, the working diagnosis was hepatocellular carcinoma with rupture and hemorrhage.

A 21-year-old woman was referred for evaluation before initiating contraception. She had menarche at 13, regular menstrual cycles, and no prior pelvic complaints. On speculum examination, her cervix appeared normal, and there was a painless, soft, cystic lesion on the right vaginal wall measuring approximately 2 × 2 cm, with translucent content. Transvaginal ultrasound confirmed a cystic lesion in the same location. She denied urinary symptoms, infection, pelvic pain, or vaginal discharge.

A 23-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of peripheral facial palsy, treated with oral prednisone with initial improvement but followed by development of right-sided hearing loss and decreased visual acuity when the dose was tapered. On examination, he had mild left facial palsy with lagophthalmos, severe impairment of right-sided hearing, and multiple papulovesicular lesions on the face and back. Ophthalmic examination showed best-corrected visual acuity of 20/32 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye; the anterior segments were normal, and intraocular pressures were 13 mmHg bilaterally. Funduscopy revealed mild hyperemia and blurred borders of both optic discs without vitreous or retinal inflammation. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 27 mm/h and a C-reactive protein level of 33.25 mg/L. An infectious and immunologic panel was notable only for a positive Weil-Felix reaction. Brain MRI demonstrated right-sided cranial multineuritis involving cranial nerves II, III, V, VII, and VIII. Lumbar puncture revealed normal opening pressure and negative microbiologic and serologic studies. Visual evoked potentials were normal. Audiometry showed complete right-sided hearing loss and a normal left ear.  
He was presumed to have rickettsial infection and treated with doxycycline and corticosteroids for 10 days, resulting in resolution of facial palsy and optic disc hyperemia; visual acuity improved to 20/20 bilaterally. Two weeks later, while on prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day, he noted decreased visual acuity in the left eye (20/30), and mild left optic disc edema recurred. Repeat laboratory testing and full-body PET scan were unrevealing, with only the Weil-Felix reaction remaining positive but Rickettsia conorii IgM and IgG both negative. He received intravenous methylprednisolone followed by an oral taper, resulting in normalization of left visual acuity and resolution of disc edema.  
Two weeks later, while on prednisone 0.75 mg/kg/day, he complained of decreased hearing in the left ear, and audiometry confirmed a sensorineural loss of 5–10 dB at 4000 Hz.

A 26‐year‐old woman presented with a 1‐year history of pruritic plaques on her lower extremities that did not improve with topical corticosteroids. On examination, there were well‐defined hyperpigmented, hyperkeratotic plaques with thick adherent scales and a peripheral rim of erythema distributed symmetrically over the dorsum of both feet and around the knees. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, negative hepatitis C and B serologies, and normal levels of aspartate and alanine aminotransferases. Plasma zinc was at the lower end of normal (72 μg/dL; reference range 70–120 μg/dL), and thyroid‐stimulating hormone was elevated at 16.6 mIU/L (reference range 0.5–5 mIU/L). A 4‐mm punch biopsy of a lesion revealed hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, focal subcorneal clefting with keratinocyte necrosis, slight intracellular edema, and a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate.

A 4-day-old male neonate, born at term to a para-IV mother after an uncomplicated pregnancy, presented with intermittent reddish discoloration of urine and occasional frank blood per urethra. Delivery was by spontaneous vaginal delivery after 9 hours of labor complicated by shoulder dystocia; APGAR scores were 7 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively, and birth weight was 5000 g. Vitamin K was not administered after birth. 

On examination: heart rate 112 /min, respiratory rate 42 /min, temperature 36.7 °C, oxygen saturation 96%; weight 4600 g, head circumference 35.5 cm. Abdomen was soft with no masses or organomegaly; bright red blood was noted on the diaper. There was no pallor, bruising, or petechiae, and reflexes were intact. 

Laboratory studies showed WBC 11,190/µL, hematocrit 69%, platelets 244,000/µL; urinalysis with trace blood and 3–7 RBCs per high-power field; creatinine 0.84 mg/dL and BUN 20.4 mg/dL. 

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated bilateral suprarenal echo-complex masses (right 4.3×2.2 cm; left 4.0×2.0 cm). Abdominal CT scan revealed bilateral hypo-dense non-enhancing fluid-attenuated suprarenal gland masses (right 4.3×2.5 cm; left 3.9×2.4 cm) with a final conclusion of bilateral suprarenal gland collection likely hemorrhage.

A 42-year-old office worker with known atopic asthma presented with increasing cough, sputum production, and exertional dyspnea of over 1 year’s duration, with the cough noted as problematic for up to 13 years but worsened in the prior 12 months despite multiple steroid courses for presumed asthma. He was a lifelong non-smoker taking budesonide/formoterol inhaler. Skin testing showed sensitization to house dust mite, grass pollen, horse and dog dander, but negative to feathers, cats, tree pollen, and mould spores. He kept two cats, used feather bedding, and worked in an air-conditioned office. 

On examination, crackles were heard at both lung bases. Chest radiograph showed cardiomegaly without overt congestion and increased markings in the lower lobes. Spirometry demonstrated a restrictive pattern: FEV₁ 43% predicted, FVC 40% predicted, FEV₁/FVC 89%. Exhaled nitric oxide was 19 ppb (normal <25), and methacholine PC₁₉₀ >32 mg/ml. Laboratory lung-function tests showed FVC 38%, TLC 46%, RV 69%, DLCO 46%, VA 52%, KCO 93%. Resting oxygen saturation on room air was 92%, with desaturation to 78% on light exertion. Arterial blood gas showed type 1 respiratory failure (PaO₂ 9.1 kPa). Overnight oximetry revealed mean saturations of 83% with nadir 75%. A shuttle walk distance was 670 m with desaturation to 69%.

Echocardiogram was normal. High-resolution CT of the chest revealed bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities with mosaic perfusion predominantly in the lower lobes, no reticular change or UIP pattern, and small paraseptal emphysematous areas in the upper lobes. 

Routine blood tests, immune panels, autoantibodies, and HIV screening were negative. Avian precipitins were positive to budgerigar IgG at 22.5 mg/L (normal <10 mg/L) and negative to pigeon. On further history, he reported a past weekend job cleaning parrot and macaw aviaries for 7 years during adolescence. 

Bronchoscopy showed inflamed airways; BAL fluid was negative for bacterial, fungal, Pneumocystis, and atypical pathogens and contained no malignant cells. BAL differential cell count showed CD3+ lymphocytosis with CD8+ T cells 47% (normal 10–39%) and CD4+ T cells 51% (normal 28–57%).

A 52-year-old man presented with 4 days of sore throat, odynophagia, and a productive cough with clear-white, blood-tinged sputum. He reported a 10-lb unintentional weight loss over 3 months, but denied fever, night sweats, or prior pulmonary disease. He also noted nausea, vomiting, polydipsia, and polyuria for several days after discontinuing his long-acting insulin. His primary care physician had obtained a chest radiograph the day before, noted abnormalities, and started cephalexin for presumed community-acquired pneumonia.
