Medical history was notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin and insulin. He immigrated from Central America 40 years ago and had not traveled since. He was a former smoker (10 pack-years, quit 20 years ago) and worked as a short-haul truck driver.

In the emergency department, his temperature was 97.8°F, blood pressure 123/90 mmHg, heart rate 134 bpm, respiratory rate 40 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He appeared cachectic and mildly dyspneic but had no nasal flaring or retractions. Examination revealed dry mucous membranes, a hoarse voice, diffuse bilateral crackles on lung auscultation, and tachycardia with a regular rhythm. No hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy was noted.

Laboratory studies showed: blood glucose 532 mg/dL, anion gap 35 mEq/L, β-hydroxybutyrate 8.09 mmol/L, WBC count 13 000/µL with no eosinophils, venous pH 7.13, pCO2 32 mmHg, and lactate 5.46 mmol/L. Urinalysis revealed 4+ glucose and 3+ acetone. HIV antigen/antibody was negative; CD4 count was 343 cells/µL.

Chest radiograph demonstrated diffuse bilateral reticulonodular opacities and air-space disease with a possible cavitary lesion in the lingula. Noncontrast chest CT confirmed numerous bilateral tiny nodules—most prominent in the upper lobes—and a cavitary lesion in the lingula, with a few mildly enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes.

He received IV vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam, insulin infusion, and aggressive fluid resuscitation. He was admitted to the ICU on airborne precautions with an initial differential diagnosis of coccidioidomycosis, tuberculosis, and lymphangitic carcinomatosis, complicated by diabetic ketoacidosis.

A woman in her 50s presented with a 1-month history of abdominal fullness. Examination revealed thrombocytopenia and splenomegaly. Initial investigations showed urinary protein excretion of 0.37 g/g creatinine, serum creatinine of 1.03 mg/dL, and urine β2-microglobulin (B2M) of 11,831 μg/L. Kidney function gradually declined over 3½ years, with serum creatinine rising to 1.29 mg/dL, urinary protein to 0.84 g/g creatinine, and urine B2M to 48,279 μg/L. Two months later, on admission, physical examination was notable for a spleen palpable 2 finger-breadths below the left costal margin. Urinary protein excretion was 0.8 g/d, urine N-acetyl-β-D-glucosaminidase was 16.6 U/L, and urine B2M was 174,875 μg/mL; Bence-Jones protein was negative. Blood tests showed leukocytes 4,370/μL (lymphocytes 60%), serum total protein 8.5 g/dL, creatinine 1.32 mg/dL (eGFR 33.3 mL/min), and C-reactive protein 0.6 mg/dL. She had hypouricemia (uric acid 2.1 mg/dL) with increased fractional excretion of uric acid (37.4%) and clearance of uric acid (14.9 mL/min); there was no renal glycosuria. Immunoassay revealed IgG 2,126 mg/dL, IgM 671 mg/dL, IgG4 136 mg/dL, free κ light chains 243 mg/L with κ:λ ratio of 7.81, and IgMκ-type M-protein on serum immunoelectrophoresis. Bone marrow examination showed 1.0% plasma cells and 44.6% small lymphoid cells that were CD20-positive and weakly CD5- and CD23-positive, leading to a diagnosis of low-grade B-cell lymphoma.

A 21-year-old man presented with acute, persistent chest pain that began the previous evening. His only cardiovascular risk factor was a 1.5 pack-year smoking history. His medical history included bronchial asthma, coeliac disease, depression treated intermittently with citalopram 10 mg daily for 2 years, and ADHD diagnosed 6 years earlier. Three days before presentation, methylphenidate 20 mg daily was started for worsening attention deficits.

On examination: blood pressure 117/63 mmHg, heart rate 53 bpm, temperature 36.9 °C; physical findings were unremarkable. ECG showed ST-segment elevations of 0.1 mV in leads II, III, aVF and 0.2 mV in leads V4–V6. A bedside troponin test was positive. Serum assays confirmed troponin 990 pg/mL and CK 1068 U/L (CK-MB 89 U/L).

He received morphine, aspirin, and heparin, and was transferred for coronary angiography. Angiography revealed a vasospasm in segment 1 of the right coronary artery, with otherwise normal coronary arteries. Echocardiography demonstrated a mildly reduced left ventricular ejection fraction of 49%. Over the next 4 days, CK peaked at 1800 U/L and troponin fluctuated around 900 pg/mL before declining; the ECG normalized within 48 hours. 

Urine toxicology was positive for tetrahydrocannabinol, and the patient admitted sporadic cannabis use 2 days before admission.

A 1-month-old corrected-age male infant (birth weight 1,070 g at 32 + 1 weeks, small for gestational age) was transferred for respiratory insufficiency. He had a 50-day neonatal admission with pneumonia requiring O₂ for 4 days; chest imaging then excluded hyaline membrane disease or bronchopulmonary dysplasia. On examination, breath sounds were bronchial with rhonchi; cardiac examination revealed regular rate and rhythm with a grade 2 systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border.

Echocardiography showed a secundum atrial septal defect (7 × 12 mm), right-sided volume overload, tricuspid regurgitation with a peak gradient of 55–60 mmHg, a dilated main pulmonary artery (19 mm), branch pulmonary arteries (11–12 mm), and estimated pulmonary artery pressure of 58–65 mmHg. 

At first admission, he required intubation and mechanical ventilation for progressive respiratory distress. Chest radiographs demonstrated severe collapse of both lungs. CT at 1 month revealed collapse of the dependent right lung and total collapse of the left lower lobe, with narrowing of the main bronchus and right intermediate bronchus; “intrinsic cause like bronchomalasia was suspected.” Viral cultures (RSV, adenovirus, influenza A) were negative.

After two weeks of ventilator support, he was weaned and discharged on digoxin, furosemide, spironolactone, and lung physiotherapy. Up to 4 months corrected age, he had three additional admissions for recurrent respiratory infections; on the fourth admission, he required 40 days of mechanical ventilation. Follow-up echocardiography showed persistent pulmonary hypertension (tricuspid regurgitant gradient 60 mmHg). 

After extubation at 8 months corrected age, repeat CT demonstrated a dilated pulmonary artery compressing the left main bronchus and right intermediate bronchus, with improvement of lung consolidation and mild improvement of right bronchial stenosis.

A 9-year-old previously healthy girl was admitted to a closed psychiatric ward for acute behavioral problems. Two months earlier, she had mild somatic complaints—including abdominal pain, headache, and eye discomfort—followed a week later by abrupt-onset cessation of verbal expression, strange vocalizations, severe irritability, agitation, and sleep disturbance. She also showed mild bilateral upper-extremity stiffness but had no prior neurological history or family history of psychiatric or neurologic disorders.

In the emergency department, vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood count and metabolic panel, were unremarkable. Noncontrast head CT showed no abnormalities. She was diagnosed provisionally with psychotic disorder not otherwise specified and started on risperidone, paroxetine, and benztropine, but symptoms worsened, with auditory and visual hallucinations.

Five days later, she was admitted to a child psychiatry unit for presumptive early-onset schizophrenia. Risperidone and then olanzapine were titrated, improving irritability and sleep only slightly; bizarre behaviors and disorientation in time and place persisted. Neurology was consulted. Ten days after admission, brain MRI revealed no parenchymal or cerebrospinal fluid–space abnormalities. Electroencephalography and lumbar puncture were planned but could not be performed because of the patient’s agitation. Given her young age, rapid progression, and poor response to antipsychotics, autoimmune encephalitis was suggested as a possible diagnosis.

A 79-year-old woman reported several months of near-syncope when turning her head to the left. Within seconds of leftward rotation, she experienced lightheadedness, tinnitus, and darkening of vision, all of which resolved immediately when she returned her head to neutral. She denied weakness, numbness, speech changes, or other visual disturbances. Her medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and osteoporosis. She had no relevant surgical history, was a never-smoker, and drank alcohol socially. On examination, vital signs were stable. Neurologic and cranial nerve exams were normal, but cervical spine evaluation reproduced her lightheadedness and visual darkening with leftward head turning; no nystagmus was seen. A carotid ultrasound showed 16%–49% stenoses in both carotid arteries and antegrade Doppler flow in the bilateral vertebral arteries. CT angiography of the head and neck revealed a hypoplastic right vertebral artery (V4 segment) and a dominant left vertebral artery approximately three times larger in caliber. Dynamic cerebral angiography demonstrated nearly 100% stenosis of the left vertebral artery at C4–C5 when her head was turned to the left, with full patency in neutral position.

A 21-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of progressive left-sided facial thinning. Four years earlier she first noted asymmetry of her left cheek and temple region. Over time the soft-tissue loss slowly advanced, accompanied by mild left-eyelid drooping and frequent, throbbing left-sided headaches. She denied facial trauma, infection, or prior injections in the area. Her medical history was otherwise unremarkable, and she took no regular medications.

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. Inspection revealed marked wasting of subcutaneous tissue over the left cheek, temple, and periorbital area, with mild ptosis of the left upper eyelid. The overlying skin was intact, without induration or discoloration. Neurologic examination was notable only for tenderness over the left trigeminal distribution; motor strength, sensation, and reflexes were otherwise normal. Ophthalmologic examination revealed no enophthalmos or uveitis, and visual acuity was preserved.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the head showed no intracranial abnormalities but confirmed soft-tissue loss of the left facial region with slight deviation of pharyngeal structures toward the atrophic side.

A 37-year-old man presented with high fever, severe frontal headache, left retrobulbar and hemifacial pain, and nasal obstruction. He had no history of facial trauma, dental treatment, sinus surgery, or chronic illness. On examination, he had diplopia and absence of motility on left lateral gaze, consistent with an abducens nerve palsy; other cranial nerves were intact, and visual acuity and pupillary reflexes were normal. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis (22.6 × 10^3/µL) and a C-reactive protein level of 14.06 mg/dL. Nasal endoscopy demonstrated polypoid neoformations occupying both nasal cavities. Maxillofacial CT revealed a voluminous expansile lesion in the left parasellar region involving the ipsilateral cavernous sinus and all paranasal sinuses, with osteostructural rearrangement of the posterolateral wall of the left sphenoid sinus lacking a well-defined bony outline. MRI of the brain, orbits, and paranasal sinuses confirmed a large expansile process in the left sphenoid sinus extending into the infratemporal fossa and pterygoid muscles, compressing the temporal lobe and involving the cavernous sinus but without evidence of thrombosis of the internal carotid artery. Because the radiological features were nonspecific, a neoplasm could not be excluded. The patient was therefore submitted to endoscopic sinus surgery with the goal of reducing mechanical compression on the cavernous sinus and obtaining a definitive histopathological diagnosis.

A 40-year-old man with no prior medical history was found unresponsive about 1 hour after arriving home from work at an industrial cabinet factory. Emergency medical services noted pink, frothy secretions on intubation. Initial vital signs and labs at an outside hospital revealed:  
• WBC 15,800/mm³, Hgb 17.4 g/dL, platelets 252,000/μL  
• BUN 15 mg/dL, Cr 1.8 mg/dL, bicarbonate 16.8 mmol/L, glucose 371 mg/dL  
• ABG on FiO₂ 100%, PEEP 10 cm H₂O: pH 6.99, PaCO₂ 68 mmHg, PaO₂ 63 mmHg  
Chest CT angiography showed no pulmonary embolism but bilateral dependent airspace opacities. Toxicology was positive only for tetrahydrocannabinol.  
Transferred to our ICU, he remained hypotensive and hypoxemic. Repeat labs showed WBC 11,900/mm³, Hgb 18.4 g/dL, platelets 244,000/μL, BUN 13 mg/dL, Cr 1.23 mg/dL, lactate 4.0 mmol/L (later 2.5 mmol/L). ABG on FiO₂ 100%, PEEP 15 cm H₂O: pH 7.20, PaCO₂ 52 mmHg, PaO₂ 53 mmHg.  
Urinalysis revealed >50 RBCs/hpf and 1+ protein without active sediment. Liver and coagulation panels were normal. The patient could not safely undergo bronchoscopy due to oxygenation and PEEP requirements.  
Infectious workup (endotracheal aspirate, blood, urine cultures; Legionella antigen; cryptococcal antigen) was negative, and he remained afebrile. Echocardiography showed normal biventricular function without shunt and suggested elevated right atrial pressure. He received broad-spectrum antibiotics.  
Given acute hypoxemic respiratory failure with frothy pulmonary secretions despite normal cardiac function and microscopic hematuria, a vasculitic pulmonary–renal syndrome was considered. Testing for HIV, ANA, ANCA (PR3 and MPO), and hypercoagulability (antiphospholipid antibodies, anticardiolipin, Russell Viper Venom test) was negative. His microscopic hematuria resolved with hydration. C-reactive protein was 8.4 mg/dL and ESR 105 mm/hr.  
At this point, diagnostic uncertainty persisted.

A 35-year-old man with a history of left-sided biphasic malignant pleural mesothelioma presented in April 2018 with a symptomatic pleural effusion. He had no known asbestos exposure or BAP1 syndrome. He underwent extra-pleural pneumonectomy in June 2018, followed by palliative radiotherapy for spinal involvement in autumn 2018. He received multiple lines of chemotherapy until October 2019 and then entered a trial of nivolumab for relapsed disease, which was discontinued after three months for progression. After further radiotherapy in March 2020, he began combination immunotherapy with ipilimumab (1 mg/kg every 6 weeks) and pembrolizumab (2 mg/kg every 3 weeks). 

Four weeks after starting combination immune checkpoint blockade, he noticed subtle, symmetric livedoid skin changes on all four limbs. After six weeks, these changes became more extensive, with a prominent purpuric lesion on the left hallux. He had no history of autoimmune disease, dermatologic conditions, myalgia, or arthralgia. He was hospitalized to exclude acute limb ischaemia.

Findings on admission:
• CT imaging: patent left subclavian artery despite external compression by tumour.  
• Duplex Doppler ultrasonography: normal arterial supply to lower limbs, no evidence of embolic or thrombotic occlusion.  
• Transthoracic echocardiogram: no vegetations or significant valvular abnormalities.  
• Laboratory studies: speckled ANA positive at 1:640; extractable nuclear antigens positive for Ro 60 and weakly positive for La; rheumatoid factor, anticardiolipin antibodies, cryoglobulins, ANCA, and double-stranded DNA were negative; HIV serology negative; complement levels normal.  
• The patient declined a skin biopsy, limiting histopathologic confirmation.

A 31-year-old woman on thrice-weekly hemodialysis for 7 years presented with a 9-month history of an enlarging palatal swelling that had become painful and was associated with moderate eating difficulties and slight weight loss. She had no history of bone fractures. On examination, there was a firm, homogeneous swelling of the palate covered by normal mucosa, deforming the upper dental arch; no other bony deformities were noted. A head and neck CT scan showed well-defined, expanding osteolytic lesions in the palate, clivus, mandible, and odontoid process, along with diffusely decreased bone density. Laboratory studies revealed a normal serum calcium level of 2.52 mmol/L (reference 2.25–2.6), hyperphosphatemia of 1.83 mmol/L (0.74–1.52), elevated total alkaline phosphatase of 1550 U/L (40–150), and a parathyroid hormone level of 2580 pg/mL (26.5–96.5).

A 60-year-old woman with obstructive sleep apnea, seasonal allergies, and osteoarthritis presented with 4 weeks of weakness and numbness in all four extremities. She initially noted burning pain at the tips of her fingers and toes that progressed to paresthesia, accompanied by low-grade fever, bowel and bladder incontinence, and dull neck pain. Five months earlier, she had undergone decompressive laminectomy for a C1–C5 dorsal epidural cervical mass, which was reported as an inflammatory lesion with collagenized stroma and mixed lymphoid and plasmacytoid cells.

On examination, she was alert, afebrile, and hemodynamically stable. The neck was supple with tenderness but no lymphadenopathy. Cranial nerves were intact. Strength was 3/5 in the upper extremities with 2+ reflexes and 2/5 in the lower extremities with 3+ reflexes; sensation was intact. Laboratory studies, including CBC and serum electrolytes, were normal. MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrated a T2-hyperintense, enhancing extradural soft-tissue mass causing marked spinal canal stenosis at T4–T5. Whole-body PET scan showed no evidence of malignancy but revealed mildly increased uptake in bilateral jugular nodes (SUV 2.6 on the right, 2.3 on the left). Lumbar puncture yielded cerebrospinal fluid with mature lymphocytes and monocytes and no malignant cells. Flow cytometry of the CSF showed no immunophenotypic evidence of non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma. A T2–T6 laminectomy with excisional biopsy of the epidural mass was performed.

A 53-year-old woman with pale skin presented for prosthetic rehabilitation. During routine oral examination, a 0.5-cm nodular lesion was found on the right ventral surface of the tongue. The lesion was yellowish, submucosal, with a smooth surface, a sessile base, and well-defined borders. The patient reported that the “bubble” had been present for about 1 year without pain, history of trauma, discharge, or change in size. On review of systems she denied any other symptoms. With a working diagnosis of an oral lymphoepithelial cyst, an excisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia. The specimen was fixed in 10% formaldehyde and submitted for histopathological examination.

A 53-year-old woman presented with a three-month history of a painful mass on the left lateral aspect of her neck. She denied fever or weight loss. On examination, there was a hard, fluctuant, tender 10×7 cm mass in the left supraclavicular region with overlying skin inflammation and no palpable lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 40 mm/h. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. Computed tomography of the neck demonstrated a 14×10 cm binocular cystic mass in the left supraclavicular region containing numerous thin-walled cystic formations. From these clinical and radiographic findings, a pyogenic abscess or tuberculosis was suspected, and excision or drainage was planned.

An 8‐year‐old castrated male American Bulldog (48 kg) was examined for a 10‐day history of polyuria and polydipsia. Rectal temperature was 38°C. CBC was unremarkable; serum chemistry showed hyperglobulinemia (4.3 g/dl; RR, 2.4–4.0). Urine specific gravity was 1.006 with negative dipstick and inactive sediment. One week later, intermittent left forelimb lameness and left cubital pain were noted; radiographs were unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound identified small hypoechoic nodules in the liver and spleen. A 4Dx SNAP test for Borrelia burgdorferi, Ehrlichia spp., Anaplasma spp., and Dirofilaria immitis was negative. The dog was treated with gabapentin and tramadol. Five days later, non‐ambulatory hind‐limb paraparesis developed. Spinal radiographs were normal, and serum protein electrophoresis revealed a polyclonal gammopathy. Splenic aspirates showed lymphoid hyperplasia. Referral evaluation revealed bilateral cubital joint effusion; arthrocentesis documented neutrophilic inflammation with occasional large basophilic synovial cells. Bartonella henselae indirect immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) titer was 1:64 (B. koehlerae and B. vinsonii subsp. berkhoffii <1:16). Doxycycline and prednisone were prescribed. Six weeks later, relapse of hind‐limb paraparesis occurred, and left cubital swelling persisted. Compared with prior radiographs, there was new osteolysis and irregular osteoproliferation of the medial epicondyle of the left humerus with moderate soft tissue swelling.

A 36-year-old Chinese man with no chronic illnesses presented with acute generalized weakness of 5 hours’ duration upon awakening. The previous day he had felt febrile and consumed a large evening meal; he denied recent strenuous exercise, alcohol use, or diuretic therapy. He reported no palpitations, tremor, abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, or sensory changes, and had no prior episodes.  
Vital signs were blood pressure 121/63 mmHg, temperature 36.6 °C, pulse 102 beats/min, and respiratory rate 18 breaths/min. On neurologic examination, muscle strength was reduced in the lower extremities (proximal 2/5, distal 4/5) and mildly reduced in the upper extremities (proximal 4/5, distal 5/5); reflexes were present, and sensation was intact. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies showed serum potassium 2.2 mmol/L and magnesium 1.8 mg/dL. A spot urine sample revealed a transtubular potassium gradient of 7.02 and a fractional excretion of potassium of 7.12, indicating renal potassium wasting. Following infusion of 19.2 mEq of potassium chloride over 4 hours, his serum potassium rose to 3.8 mmol/L.  
Thyroid function tests demonstrated a suppressed TSH (< 0.0025 uIU/mL), elevated free T4 (1.8 ng/dL), and normal T3 (1.4 ng/mL), consistent with hyperthyroidism.

A 30-year-old man presented with abnormal movements of his left foot that began in 2016. He described visible movements of his toes with associated pulsation and twitching in the lower medial and posterior leg at the level of the Achilles tendon. The movements were constant, present at rest, and diminished with ambulation; they caused mild discomfort and occasional difficulty falling asleep but did not awaken him at night. His past medical history was significant for a left ankle sprain and Achilles tendinopathy in 2016, treated surgically with scar tissue debridement and gastrocnemius resection, without improvement; the abnormal movements developed shortly afterward.

On neurologic examination, there was a very slow, repetitive, rhythmic flexion–extension oscillation of toes 2–4 on the left foot with occasional abduction; these movements were distractible, suppressible briefly, and decreased in amplitude with active motion. There was near-constant involuntary twitching in the medial inframalleolar area. Strength, sensation, coordination, and gait were normal, with no upper or lower motor neuron signs.

Needle electromyography of selected left lower-extremity muscles showed a rhythmic slow 2–3 Hz discharge isolated to the flexor digitorum brevis muscle. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left ankle revealed noninsertional Achilles tendinosis and a posterior tibialis tendon sheath effusion. Brain MRI was unremarkable, and cervical and thoracic spine MRI showed only mild foraminal stenosis at C3–C6 and small disk protrusions at T6–T7 and T7–T8.

A 60-year-old man with chronic schizophrenia was found on the floor, unable to rise or walk. On examination he had an asymmetrical smile and apparent paresis of his left leg; he was hospitalized with a working diagnosis of stroke. His psychiatric history dated from age 40, with treatment on olanzapine (7.5–15 mg daily) and risperidone previously, and his medical history included type 2 diabetes (diagnosed at 55) and osteoporosis (diagnosed 2–3 months earlier). Family reported 4–5 years of progressive swallowing difficulty, dysarthria, unsteady gait, recent weight loss (4–5 kg), hypersomnia (10–12 h/night), fatigue, and stair-descent by sliding. He was a heavy smoker and modest alcohol user. 

On admission he was alert, oriented, afebrile, with BP 136/83 mmHg, pulse 82 bpm, SaO₂ 97%, and weak inspiratory effort. Neurologic exam showed impaired rapid tongue movements, dysarthria, symmetrically reduced upper-extremity strength (5–/4+), reduced strength in the left leg, and asymmetrical plantar reflexes (right downgoing, left indifferent). CBC was normal. Chemistry showed glucose 10.0 mmol/L, HbA1c 7.5%, ALT 94 U/L, ALP 130 U/L. MRI of the brain was normal and facial asymmetry resolved; stroke was discarded when a left hip fracture was found and surgically repaired. Postoperatively he developed bilateral pulmonary emboli, suspected sepsis (culture-negative), aspiration pneumonia, clouding of consciousness with agitation, and persistent anxiety responsive to diazepam. Neurologic considerations included motor neuron disease, diabetic neuropathy, and antipsychotic extrapyramidal effects; EMG showed lower-extremity sensorimotor polyneuropathy but normal upper-extremity studies, “not compatible with motor neuron disease or acute polyneuropathy.” 

On day 23 after admission, during psychiatric re-evaluation, he was noted to clutch the bed rails with both hands. When asked to extend his four ulnar fingers he could barely release his hold. Subsequently both hands lay on the duvet with wrists in palmar flexion (left > right), the four ulnar fingers fully flexed, and thumbs partially extendable with resistance. Passive extension of wrist and finger joints was limited, with resistance increasing proportionally to applied force (“elastic feel”). There was non-pitting swelling on the dorsum of the left hand and forearm but no visible or palpable Dupuytren’s contracture or other trauma. He had no pain in his hands and could not explain the clenching.

A 40-year-old woman (G1P1) presented with recurrent vomiting, abdominal pain, and progressive drowsiness over several days. Over the past five months she has noted weight loss and generalized weakness; she stopped eating normally 20 days ago. She denied any hospitalizations except for her only delivery 11 years ago, which she recalled as uncomplicated with minimal blood loss. Since that time she has had secondary amenorrhea and was unable to lactate. 

On examination she was hypotensive (60/30 mm Hg), bradycardic (60 beats/min), and had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 11. Findings included generalized pallor, anasarca, asthenia, axillary and pubic hair loss, and widespread skin depigmentation. Initial laboratory studies revealed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL, leukocytes 4000/µL, platelets 110 000/µL) and hyponatremia (serum sodium 118.1 mmol/L) with inappropriately concentrated urine (high urine osmolality and sodium) and low serum osmolality. Further endocrine evaluation demonstrated low free thyroxine and inappropriately normal thyroid-stimulating hormone, along with low serum cortisol and adrenocorticotropic hormone levels, consistent with central hypothyroidism and secondary adrenal insufficiency.

A term male infant was born at home to a 29-year-old primigravida after an uncomplicated pregnancy. Apgar scores were 4, 5, and 8 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes; intermittent positive-pressure ventilation was required for 3 minutes. Birth weight was 3760 g (57th percentile), length 54 cm (88th percentile), head circumference 38.2 cm (98th percentile). 

At 18 hours of age, the infant was mottled with subcostal and intercostal recession. Pre-ductal oxygen saturation was 88% on room air; respiratory rate was 70 breaths/min. He was afebrile and normotensive, with a normal cardiovascular examination and clear breath sounds. The abdomen was soft, tone was normal, and he was not encephalopathic. 

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, electrolytes, and inflammatory markers. Capillary blood gas revealed metabolic acidosis (pH 7.24, pCO₂ 40 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 16.1 mmol/L, base excess −10.3, lactate 3.4 mmol/L). A chest radiograph showed cardiomegaly without collapse or consolidation. Echocardiography demonstrated normal cardiac anatomy, a 2.9 mm patent ductus arteriosus with bidirectional flow, and mild suprasystemic pulmonary hypertension. 

Initial differential diagnoses included sepsis, perinatal asphyxia, respiratory distress syndrome, and transient tachypnoea of the newborn. Management comprised CPAP with supplemental oxygen to maintain pre-ductal SpO₂ ≥ 95%, intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin, and maintenance fluids. The oxygen requirement resolved within 48 hours, but work of breathing persisted and metabolic acidosis remained. He developed coagulopathy (INR 3.3, APTT 66 s, PT 37 s), renal impairment (urea 6.8 mmol/L, creatinine 99 µmol/L), hyponatraemia (Na 126 mmol/L), oliguria, and oedema. Blood cultures were negative; an umbilical swab grew Group B streptococcus. He received intravenous vitamin K, fresh frozen plasma, and hypertonic saline. The working diagnosis was perinatal asphyxia. 

On day 5, he acutely deteriorated with severe respiratory distress, poor perfusion, minimal responsiveness, oliguria, and hyponatraemia (Na 117 mmol/L). Examination now demonstrated worsening generalized oedema, ascites, and hepatomegaly. A repeat chest radiograph showed increased cardiomegaly. He was intubated and ventilated, fluid restricted, and treated with furosemide, bicarbonate correction, and cefotaxime.

A 10-year-old girl with eczema presented with 1 week of right hip and thigh pain and intermittent high fevers, beginning about one week after minor trauma with bruising of the right lower extremity. Temperature was 39 °C. On examination, she had tenderness of the right hip and thigh, pain with internal rotation of the hip, no erythema or decreased range of motion, and no neurovascular deficits. She was unable to fully bear weight and had a limp. Laboratory studies demonstrated a WBC count of 14.98×10^9/L with an absolute neutrophil count of 12×10^9/L; ESR rose from 60 to 121 mm/hour and CRP from 145.79 to 150.95 mg/L over 1 day. Blood and urine cultures were sterile. Pelvic radiographs showed bilateral focal lucency and expansion of the ischiopubic synchondroses, more pronounced on the right, with a subtle crescent-shaped bone fragment along the superior aspect of the right synchondrosis; the remainder of the pelvis and hip joints appeared normal. Hip ultrasound revealed a trace right hip effusion. MRI of the pelvis demonstrated abnormal signal intensity in the inferior pubic and ischial rami with involvement of the right ischiopubic synchondrosis and breach of the outer cortex; there was connected intramedullary contrast enhancement and a large multiloculated intramuscular collection in the right quadratus femoris and adductor magnus muscles extending through the obturator foramen to involve the obturator internus, with reactive myositis of adjacent muscles and a small hip effusion.

An 11-month-old intact male Irish Setter weighing 29 kg presented with acute onset of vestibular ataxia and a head tilt. The referring veterinarian had administered cephalexin, carprofen, and meclizine without improvement. On admission, the dog was quiet but alert and responsive, with a right head tilt, vestibular ataxia, and changing nystagmus (resting rotary fast phase to the left switching to vertical in dorsal recumbency). Proprioception was normal in all limbs, segmental reflexes were increased in the pelvic limbs, and fundic examination was normal. Localization was to the central vestibular system (caudal fossa). Hematology and serum biochemistry panels were within normal limits. Serologic testing for Rickettsia rickettsii, Neospora caninum (IgM and IgG), Toxoplasma gondii (IgM and IgG), and a SNAP 4DX test for Dirofilaria immitis, Ehrlichia canis, E. ewingii, Anaplasma phagocytophilum, A. platys, and Borrelia burgdorferi were all negative. MRI of the brain (1.5 T) demonstrated diffuse contrast enhancement of the leptomeninges. Differential diagnoses included fungal meningitis, round cell neoplasia, and immune-mediated or other infectious meningitis. A CSF sample was then collected from the cerebellomedullary cistern for cytologic analysis.

A 28-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of progressive scoliosis. She reported a history of short stature and delayed dental development with multiple retained deciduous teeth and malocclusion. There was a positive family history of similar skeletal anomalies in her father and grandmother. On examination, she had a wide, protruding forehead, facial hypoplasia of the mid-face, and an open anterior fontanelle. Both shoulders were markedly mobile and chest palpation suggested hypoplastic clavicles. She also had bilateral genu valgum and complained of lower-extremity discomfort. Pelvic examination noted a slightly widened pubic symphysis and shortened femoral necks suggestive of coxa vara.

Radiographs of the chest confirmed bilateral pseudoarthrosis of the clavicles. Cranial radiographs showed persistence of the open anterior fontanelle. Pelvic films revealed small iliac wings, a widened pubic symphysis, and coxa vara. Long-leg alignment films demonstrated bilateral genu valgum. Spine radiographs showed a right-convex thoracolumbar scoliosis measuring 45 degrees without vertebral fractures or lesions.

A 32-year-old man with ileocolonic Crohn’s disease status post ileocecectomy with perianal involvement, Type 1 arthropathy affecting both knees, hypertension, recurrent cellulitis, and obesity presented for ustekinumab infusion. He reported a 3-day history of right knee pain and swelling similar to prior arthropathy flares, accompanied by intermittent fevers and chills. During the infusion, he experienced sudden worsening of knee pain radiating into the right calf, ankle, and foot, with tightness and tenderness of the posterior calf. He denied cough, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, headache, lightheadedness, or dizziness. On arrival to the emergency department, he was tachycardic to 136 beats/min and febrile to 38 °C. Laboratory evaluation showed a white‐cell count of 14.4×10^3/μL, potassium 3.3 mEq/L, creatinine 0.63 mg/dL, and creatine kinase 21 units/L. Blood cultures and knee‐joint aspiration cultures were negative. Empiric antibiotics were initiated, and orthopedics was consulted for concern for compartment syndrome; distal pulses remained intact on Doppler. Radiographs of the lower extremity were unremarkable. A venous duplex ultrasound was performed to evaluate for deep vein thrombosis; it was negative for DVT but revealed soft‐tissue swelling of the posterior calf and an incidental 6.8×4.0 cm Baker’s cyst in the medial calf, along with a small joint effusion.

A 47-year-old woman was found collapsed in a plaza; the duration of unconsciousness was unknown. She lives alone, has a long history of amphetamine addiction, and is on multiple psychotropic medications (lithium, alprazolam, brotizolam, eszopiclone, levomepromazine, chlorpromazine). On arrival, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 14 (E4V4M6) and vital signs were normal after initial hypotension corrected with leg elevation. Physical examination was notable only for a caesarean-section scar. She admitted to consuming an excessive amount of her prescribed medications, but a urine drug screen was positive for amphetamines and opioids and negative for other prescribed agents.  
Laboratory studies showed dehydration (hematocrit 47.5%), renal failure (creatinine 4.10 mg/dL), normal vitamin B1, B12, and folate levels, and a low blood lithium concentration of 0.04 mEq/L (therapeutic 0.6–1.2). Chest radiography and whole-body CT scans were unremarkable.  
Over the next days, her GCS declined to E4V2M4 with fixed gaze, facial twitching, restlessness, and myoclonic limb movements. EEG showed mixed theta and alpha background activity without spike or slow-wave complexes. Haloperidol was started for suspected encephalopathy or psychogenic seizures. On day 5, she developed fever to 39°C, and a urinary tract infection was treated with ceftriaxone. By day 7, her level of consciousness remained unchanged, and brain MRI demonstrated a focal signal change in the splenium of the corpus callosum.

A 35-year-old woman presented with a 4-week history of right upper quadrant pain, low-grade fever, fatigue, and anorexia. One month before symptom onset, she had traveled to the Gilan Province of Iran. On examination, her temperature was 37.8 °C; blood pressure 122/78 mmHg; pulse 75 beats/min; respiratory rate 14 breaths/min. Mild right upper quadrant tenderness was noted; liver span was normal. 

Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 9300/mm3 with eosinophilia (15%), AST 76 IU/L, ALT 80 IU/L, LDH 295 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 223 IU/L, CRP 12 mg/L; bilirubin and renal function were normal. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated clusters of focal, ill-defined hypodense lesions in the right hepatic lobe and subcapsular regions with peripheral contrast enhancement, forming tunnel-like tracts from the Glisson capsule into the deeper parenchyma. No biliary duct dilatation, wall thickening, or high-density intraductal foci were seen. 

On MRI, multiple ill-defined lesions were hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images in the right lobe, extending from the capsule toward the periportal regions. Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images showed round, clustered hypointense subcapsular/parenchymal lesions with mild peripheral enhancement. No bile duct dilatation or intraductal filling defects were present.

A 40-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks of gestation presented with two days of diffuse abdominal pain, sharpest in the left iliac fossa, unresponsive to analgesia. She also had nausea, vomiting, and one day of constipation. Her antenatal course had been uneventful. On examination, blood pressure was 117/67 mmHg, pulse 93 bpm, and she was afebrile. The abdomen was distended and tender without uterine contractions or signs of fetal distress. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 21,300/mL with 88% neutrophils and a C-reactive protein level of 19.1 mg/dL. An abdominal ultrasound was normal. A computed tomography scan of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated densification of pericolic fat tissue suggesting an inflammatory process of indeterminate nature and no other alterations. Corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation and empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics were started, with temporary clinical improvement. On the following day, the patient experienced intense pain with abdominal guarding and rebound, and her inflammatory markers rose further. A second abdominal ultrasound was nonconclusive. Differential diagnosis included appendicitis, bowel obstruction, perforated ulcer, inflammatory bowel disease, and diverticulitis. Obstetrical and gynecological causes were not excluded but were less plausible.

A 16-year-old male presented with a 2-month history of neck pain and progressive bilateral lower-limb weakness. The pain had a sudden onset, was dull and aching, and radiated to both shoulders and the occipital region. He also reported difficulty walking, episodes of giddiness, and numbness in his fingertips. There was no history of trauma, bowel or bladder dysfunction, or constitutional symptoms.

On examination, he had a low hairline, a short neck, and restricted neck movement. Cranial nerve function was normal. Upper-limb motor strength was MRC grade 5 bilaterally; lower-limb strength was MRC grade 4 in hip flexors, knee extensors, extensor hallucis longus, and flexor hallucis longus. Deep tendon reflexes were exaggerated in all limbs, with patellar and ankle clonus and a positive Babinski sign. Sensation was intact.

Plain cervical spine radiographs (AP and lateral) were falsely suggestive of absence of the atlas. Sagittal T2-weighted MRI showed the tip of the odontoid process projecting 13–14 mm above Chamberlain’s line, consistent with basilar invagination, and the foramen magnum was narrowed to approximately 7.5 mm. Axial imaging demonstrated posterior displacement of the odontoid compressing the cervicomedullary junction.

A 43‐year‐old woman presented to the bariatric surgery clinic for evaluation of intermittent umbilical bleeding. She reported that the bleeding occurred in direct correspondence with her menstrual cycles. She had no prior diagnosis of endometriosis but recalled heavy menses in her youth. Her surgical history was notable for a laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass in 2018 and two cesarean sections in 2003 and 2005. She initially lost weight after her bypass but later regained weight and was lost to follow-up.

On examination, there was a small, non‐tender mass deep to the umbilicus without overlying skin changes. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 2.5 × 1.4 × 1.4 cm complex solid and cystic mass located beneath the umbilicus, without internal vascular flow.

A 53-year-old man, asymptomatic from a respiratory standpoint, underwent a routine chest computed tomography (CT) 8 months earlier, which revealed multiple bilateral ground-glass opacities. Because of the high prevalence of tuberculosis in the region, he received isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 6 months without radiologic improvement. Bronchoscopy showed only left upper lobe bronchial mucosal congestion. Subsequent therapy with roxithromycin for 1 month likewise yielded no change. 

His medical history was significant only for hypertension; he had no family history of illness. He worked in a woolen mill with dust exposure. Physical examination findings were unremarkable. 

Positron emission tomography–CT demonstrated:
• Multiple subependymal calcified nodules in bilateral cerebral ventricles  
• Diffuse ground-glass nodules throughout both lungs, most numerous in the middle and upper lobes, without significant FDG uptake  
• Multiple low-density, fat-containing liver lesions, without increased FDG uptake  
• Multiple sclerotic bone lesions with mildly increased FDG uptake  
• Multiple cysts in both kidneys  

The radiology team interpreted these findings as multiple-organ involvement consistent with tuberous sclerosis complex, noting that the bilateral lung nodules had imaging features suggestive of multifocal micronodular pneumocyte hyperplasia.

A 60-year-old woman with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus (last HbA1c, 10.9%) presented with a 3-day history of acute visual loss in the right eye. She was taking oral hypoglycemic agents. Visual acuity was 6/360 in the right eye and intraocular pressures were 15 mmHg bilaterally. She was phakic and had a normal anterior examination with no afferent pupillary defect. Fundus examination of the right eye revealed a swollen optic disc with peripapillary hemorrhages; fundus autofluorescence showed diffuse peripapillary hypoautofluorescence. The left eye had moderate nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy. Fundus fluorescein angiography demonstrated dye leakage from the optic disc. Spectral-domain OCT of the right eye showed increased retinal nerve fiber layer thickness and macular edema. MRI of the brain and laboratory evaluation—including inflammatory and infectious panels and ESR—were all normal.

A 25‐year‐old man with no prior medical history fell onto his outstretched right hand and presented with severe right wrist pain, marked swelling, and restricted range of motion. Vital signs were normal. Radiographs of the wrist showed a dorsally displaced, intra‐articular distal radius fracture; the distal metaphysis was nearly replaced by a cyst‐like lesion containing free bony fragments (the “fallen fragment sign”). CT confirmed an AO type 23-C2 pathologic fracture through a bone cyst. The lesion measured 3.8 × 2.3 × 1.7 cm, was surrounded by a sclerotic rim, had a cyst index of 3.77, and an intra-cavity density of 40–55 Hounsfield Units.

A 53-year-old man presented with progressive dyspnea and a 3-kg weight loss over 4 months. He had emphysema, a seizure disorder treated with phenytoin, and hepatitis C. He smoked 35 pack-years and had injected heroin intravenously for 10 years, ending 30 years ago. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, were normal, and HIV serology was negative. A chest radiograph showed an ill-defined density near the right heart border. CT of the chest demonstrated a 4.5 × 2.2 cm opacity in the medial right middle lobe, emphysematous changes, and additional spiculated opacities in both lungs that were concerning for malignant spread. CT of the abdomen and pelvis was unremarkable. Autofluorescence bronchoscopy revealed patent airways without lesions. Endobronchial ultrasound–guided transbronchial needle aspiration biopsies were obtained from the right hilar echodensity and from four other echodense areas in both lungs.

A 42-year-old Sri Lankan man presented with a one-year history of right knee swelling and pain. The knee symptoms occurred in the context of longstanding inflammatory arthritis affecting both small and large joints of the limbs, accompanied by intermittent fever and progressive weight loss over the same period. His medical history was notable for seronegative rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed 3 years earlier (2010 EULAR/ACR score of 7) and non-specific interstitial lung disease, managed with methotrexate, sulfasalazine, leflunomide, mycophenolate mofetil, and intermittent oral prednisolone. Despite good adherence, his disease activity remained high (DAS28 > 5), and biologic therapy was unavailable.

On examination, the right knee was swollen, tender, and effused with limited range of motion. Multiple proximal interphalangeal, metacarpophalangeal, wrist, elbow, and shoulder joints were symmetrically tender, with no other abnormalities. Laboratory studies showed an ESR persistently above 50 mm/hr, CRP 14 mg/L, WBC 6600/mm^3 (72% neutrophils), platelet count 480 000/mm^3, hemoglobin 12.0 g/dL, and serum uric acid 6 mg/dL.

Plain radiographs of the right knee showed only soft-tissue swelling. Ultrasonography confirmed effusion and marked synovial thickening. Over the past year, the knee was aspirated repeatedly for symptomatic relief. One month prior, synovial fluid analysis revealed 18 240 polymorphonuclear cells/mm^3 and 60 320 lymphocytes/mm^3, with no red cells. Routine bacterial cultures were repeatedly negative, and no uric acid crystals or malignant cells were identified. Eight months earlier, empirical intravenous antibiotics were administered for suspected septic arthritis, followed by two intra-articular steroid injections, without lasting improvement.

A 41‐year‐old man, lifelong non‐smoker with no significant medical history, presented with a two‐week history of worsening shortness of breath and dry cough. He had been treated empirically in the community with amoxicillin and clarithromycin for presumed atypical pneumonia. He reported no gastrointestinal symptoms. The family history was notable only for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in his father. He worked as a long‐distance lorry driver with no relevant exposures.

On examination he was hemodynamically stable, afebrile, and had an oxygen saturation of 91% on room air. Lung auscultation revealed fine crepitations throughout; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed: hemoglobin 158 g/L, white blood cell count 10 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 328 × 10⁹/L, and C‐reactive protein 22.3 mg/L. Liver and renal function were normal. Coagulation studies: prothrombin time 12.1 s, APTT 27.2 s, fibrinogen 4.08 g/L, D‐dimer 13 units. Arterial blood gas revealed type I respiratory failure (pO₂ 7.68 kPa).

Chest radiograph demonstrated widespread patchy consolidation and reticulonodular interstitial changes. He was started on IV piperacillin–tazobactam, IV clarithromycin, oral steroids, regular nebulizers, and supplemental oxygen.

Microbiologic and serologic tests were negative for Legionella and pneumococcal antigens, HIV, CMV, ANCA, anti-GBM antibodies, and rheumatoid factor. Immunoglobulin levels including IgG subclasses and ACE level were normal. Extrinsic allergic alveolitis screen, Aspergillus IgG, and total IgE were normal. Respiratory syncytial virus was detected in sputum; PCR for influenza A/B, Pneumocystis jiroveci, Bordetella pertussis, and Chlamydia psittaci was negative.

High‐resolution CT of the chest showed reticular nodular interstitial change with alveolar infiltrates, thickening of secondary pulmonary lobules, and a small pericardial effusion; there was no lymphadenopathy. Although he initially improved, he remained hypoxic. 

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a right ventricular systolic pressure of 75 mmHg, mild right atrial and ventricular enlargement, and septal flattening consistent with right ventricular pressure overload; left ventricular function was normal.

Bronchoscopy showed thick, orange, jelly‐like secretions but no mucosal abnormality. Cytology revealed a mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate, degenerate bronchial epithelial cells, and occasional atypical cells thought to be reactive pneumocytes. Bronchial cultures grew Escherichia coli sensitive to meropenem.

Despite antibiotic adjustment, on day 19 he developed acute unilateral visual loss; ophthalmology diagnosed a retinal vein thrombosis attributed to steroid therapy. Over the next two days he became more dyspneic, and his white blood cell and platelet counts began to fall. On day 24 he developed frank hemoptysis, acute respiratory distress, and type I respiratory failure requiring intubation.

At ICU admission he was pancytopenic with hemoglobin 114 g/L, white blood cell count 3 × 10⁹/L (neutrophils 35%), platelet count 30 × 10⁹/L, prothrombin time 15.8 s, APTT 31.7 s, fibrinogen 1.04 g/L, and D‐dimer 47.3 units. A repeat CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed increased bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, no thoracic lymphadenopathy, no intra-thoracic or intra-abdominal mass, no pulmonary embolus, and one 1.5 cm celiac axis lymph node.

A 19-month-old boy was referred for evaluation of a poor urinary stream. His history was significant for recurrent urinary tract infections. On examination, there was a fluctuant, soft, cystic swelling on the ventral aspect of the penile urethra that collapsed completely with manual pressure while urine was expelled per urethra. Vital signs were normal. Urinalysis, complete blood count, and serum creatinine were all within normal limits. Renal ultrasonography showed kidneys of normal size and shape and a normal bladder without hydronephrosis.

The patient was the second child of a consanguineous couple, born at term by cesarean section (birth weight 3400 g) after an uncomplicated pregnancy. Beginning at 4 months of age, he developed chronic diarrhea that led to failure to thrive by 8 months despite cessation of breastfeeding and nutritional interventions. Neurodevelopment was otherwise age-appropriate.

On examination, hepatomegaly was noted. Laboratory studies showed:

• Total cholesterol 428 mg/dL; LDL 374 mg/dL; HDL 16 mg/dL; triglycerides 190 mg/dL  
• AST 87 U/L (3× ULN); ALT 144 U/L (4× ULN); GGT 59 U/L (2× ULN); ALP 1014 U/L (4× ULN)  
• Albumin, coagulation tests, glycemia, and CBC within normal limits  

A percutaneous liver biopsy revealed enlarged portal tracts with mild fibrosis and septa, microvesicular steatosis, and macrophages with cytoplasmic microvacuoles. Leukocyte enzyme assays showed low acid sphingomyelinase activity (53.9 nmol/h/mg; normal 86–173) and elevated acid phosphatase (37.1 U/L; normal 0.5–11). Electron microscopy of liver tissue did not demonstrate cholesterol crystals in hepatocytes or histiocytes.

Over childhood, the patient experienced recurrent bronchospasms and asthma, progressive splenomegaly, and signs of portal hypertension. Upper endoscopy revealed esophageal varices, duodenal polyps, and mucosal irregularities suggestive of deposits. Duodenal biopsy showed thickened villi with numerous xanthomatous histiocytes in the lamina propria and submucosa. Stool studies were unremarkable.

Chest CT demonstrated interstitial lung changes consistent with a storage process; spirometry indicated a restrictive pattern. Contrast echocardiography was positive for intrapulmonary shunting. Arterial blood gas analysis showed PaO2 68.7 mmHg and O2 saturation 93.6%, supporting hepatopulmonary syndrome. Recurrent ascites and worsening respiratory status led to a MELD score of 17. At 18 years of age, he underwent orthotopic liver transplantation from a deceased donor.

A 66-year-old man with no prior gastrointestinal disease presented with sudden-onset left lower quadrant cramping, fevers, night sweats, and mucoid diarrhea that progressed to hematochezia. He was initially diagnosed with diverticulitis based on physical examination and CT scan and treated with oral ciprofloxacin and metronidazole, but his symptoms persisted despite compliance. After a 4-day course of IV antibiotics and a second course of oral antibiotics with no improvement, he was referred to our tertiary center 2 weeks after symptom onset.

His temperature was normal, heart rate 92 bpm, blood pressure 127/91 mm Hg, and BMI 30.4. He had lost 30 pounds over 4 weeks. The abdomen was soft with mild tenderness in the lower quadrants; no organomegaly or lymphadenopathy was noted. Rectal examination revealed an empty vault without masses.

Laboratory studies showed normal serum and liver chemistries, mild microcytic anemia, CRP 0.76 mg/dL (ref ≤0.60), ESR 71 mm/hr (ref <20), and a normal fecal calprotectin (21 µg/g). Stool cultures, leukocytes, and parasite studies were negative; C. difficile toxin was not detected.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed circumferential wall thickening, edema, and adjacent inflammatory changes from the rectum through the distal descending colon, with areas of decreased enhancement suggestive of possible superimposed ischemia. Prominent, tortuous submucosal vessels and superior rectal vasculature were present; the remainder of the colon, appendix, and small intestine were normal.

Flexible sigmoidoscopy revealed diffuse, continuously congested, erythematous, and friable mucosa from the rectum to the mid-descending colon; the proximal descending colon and transverse colon appeared normal, and no diverticula were seen. Cold-forceps biopsies of the affected segment were obtained.

Histopathologic examination demonstrated superficial mucosal necrosis and lamina propria fibrosis with dilated, thick-walled capillaries containing fibrin thrombi, suggestive of ischemia, and pathologists raised specific concern for idiopathic myointimal hyperplasia of the mesenteric veins.

A 37-year-old married man presented with a 5-year history of severe pain, burning, and tingling in both lower limbs (up to the knees) and both hands, with worsening over the past 6 months. He described persistent, progressive symptoms that disrupted sleep. His medical history was unremarkable, with no known comorbidities or family history of neurologic disease. He adhered to a vegan diet but had poor appetite, low food and water intake, and occasional constipation. He was a chronic tobacco chewer and did not exercise regularly.

On examination, he was lean (BMI 20 kg/m2) with normal vital signs. Neurologic evaluation showed preserved pain, touch, and temperature sensation and no signs of large‐fibre involvement; orthostatic hypotension was absent. His Visual Analogue Scale score for pain was 10, and Neuropathic Pain Scale score was 39.

Laboratory studies, including hematological tests and biochemical profiles, were within normal limits. Bence Jones protein and thyroid function tests were normal. Antinuclear antibody (ANA) and anti‐neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) tests were negative. Serum protein electrophoresis showed no monoclonal band; vitamin B12 levels were normal. Nerve conduction studies and Doppler ultrasound of the lower limbs were normal. MRI of the lumbar spine revealed a posterior disc bulge at L4–L5 without compressive elements.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 71-year-old woman presented with diffuse bone pain involving both shoulders and multiple ribs. She had a history of bilateral lung transplantation for emphysema six years earlier; her post-transplant course was complicated by severe Scedosporium apiospermum sepsis, and she has since been on chronic oral voriconazole prophylaxis. On examination, strength was slightly reduced in both upper extremities, range of motion in both shoulders was full but painful, and there was diffuse tenderness over both shoulders and several left-sided ribs. 

Laboratory evaluation revealed an elevated serum alkaline phosphatase level of 220 U/L (reference range, 30–130 U/L). 

Radiographs of the chest and shoulders showed new areas of sclerosis and juxtacortical mineralization at the left proximal humerus and clavicle compared with prior post-transplant imaging. A subsequent whole-body radionuclide bone scan demonstrated multifocal radiotracer uptake confined to the periosteum of both clavicles, both humeral heads (more pronounced on the left), the left scapula, and the left third through fifth ribs. SPECT CT confirmed periosteal new bone formation at these sites.

A 9-year-old boy of Iranian descent was referred for evaluation of severe intellectual disability and developmental delay. He has never walked or spoken and cannot hold his head up. He has had generalized seizures since age 4, managed with phenobarbital. His growth is cachectic. On examination, he has bilateral nystagmus, microcephaly, spastic quadriplegia, and macroorchidism. Family history is notable for an affected older brother and a maternal uncle with similar neurologic impairment. Prior evaluations included a normal chromosomal study and normal molecular testing for fragile X syndrome. Brain MRI was reported as showing cerebral atrophy.

A previously healthy 5-year-old girl presented with a 15-day history of progressive weakness in both lower limbs. This began 15 days after receiving her fifth dose of combined diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis vaccine (intramuscular) and sixth oral poliomyelitis vaccine as part of routine immunization.  

On examination, she was febrile (38 °C), with paraparesis of the lower limbs, increased deep tendon reflexes, bilateral Babinski signs, and neck stiffness. Sensory examination was normal; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.  

Laboratory studies revealed neutrophilic leukocytosis and mild thrombocytosis. Lumbar puncture showed clear cerebrospinal fluid with elevated protein (0.73 g/L) and lymphocytic pleocytosis (53 cells/mm3). A noncontrast head CT was normal.  

Brain and spinal MRI demonstrated multifocal, bilateral, asymmetrical T1-hypointense, T2- and FLAIR-hyperintense white-matter lesions—most >1 cm in diameter—located supra- and infratentorially, sparing U-fibers and periventricular regions, without diffusion restriction or contrast enhancement. In the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar cord, there were longitudinally extensive (>3 vertebral bodies) T2-hyperintense lesions.

A 31-year-old woman presented with epigastric pain accompanied by nausea and vomiting. She had a history of multiple prior episodes of acute pancreatitis with no known etiology and no cyclical pain pattern. She had no prior surgeries and no family history of pancreatic disease or neoplasms. 

On examination, her vital signs were normal. Lung auscultation was clear. The abdomen was soft with mild epigastric tenderness. Serum pancreatic enzyme levels were elevated, confirming acute pancreatitis. She was admitted for management and further evaluation.

On day 2, contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed no peripancreatic stranding or calcifications but identified a unilocular cystic lesion in the pancreatic tail measuring 3.6 × 3.3 cm, with slight atrophy of the distal tail beyond the cyst. No lymphadenopathy or vascular involvement was noted.

Subsequent MRI showed the cyst to be hypointense on T1-weighted fat-saturated sequences, hyperintense on T2 HASTE images, and without diffusion restriction. Post-contrast images demonstrated minimal cyst‐wall enhancement without septations or internal solid components.

Based on her history of recurrent pancreatitis and imaging, a pancreatic pseudocyst was initially suspected, but a mucinous cystic neoplasm was also considered. Endoscopic ultrasound–guided fine-needle aspiration of the cyst fluid yielded a CEA level of 370 µg/L and an amylase level of 621 U/L; cytology was negative for malignant cells.

A 42-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 1-week history of lethargy and intermittent dizziness but no syncope. He had no prior medical history or medications. His father had dilated cardiomyopathy and a CRT-D and died at age 75. The patient was a non-smoker with a physically demanding job and no athletic training. 

On examination he was hemodynamically stable; cardiovascular and other systems were unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed normal renal function and normal troponin levels. A chest radiograph was normal, with no hilar lymphadenopathy. 

Electrocardiogram revealed Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) atrioventricular block at 40 b.p.m., with a narrow QRS complex and normal QT interval. He was admitted to the coronary care unit for monitoring. 

Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal LV size, wall thickness, and systolic function (EF 55–65%), with biatrial dilatation. Overnight telemetry captured multiple episodes of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, though he remained asymptomatic. 

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a mildly dilated LV (EDV 213 mL; normal 117–200 mL) with preserved systolic function (EF 59%), moderate left atrial dilatation, and normal right ventricular function. Late gadolinium enhancement revealed a single mid-myocardial focus of high signal at the distal right ventricular insertion point and a linear high-signal area over the basal septum, findings described as non-specific but consistent with dilated cardiomyopathy.

A 23-year-old woman at 31 weeks’ gestation with no prior medical history was admitted for an urgent cesarean section because of preeclampsia (blood pressure 180/100 mm Hg, nephrotic-range proteinuria 7 g/24 hr, and edema). Five days after delivery, she developed tonicoclonic seizures, a hypertensive crisis, and laboratory evidence of thrombotic microangiopathy: hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal impairment. On peripheral blood smear, schistocytes were present. Laboratory values included lactate dehydrogenase 3254 IU/L (normal, 208–408), total bilirubin 4.2 mg/dL (normal, 0.3–1.2), serum creatinine 4.9 mg/dL (normal, 0.67–1.17), and platelet count 40×10^9/L (normal, 150–480×10^9/L). Intensive plasma exchange was begun twice daily for 22 days in parallel with dialysis, resulting in transient improvement (creatinine 2.8 mg/dL; LDH 605 IU/L; platelets 141×10^9/L). Four months later, her renal function deteriorated (creatinine 8 mg/dL) and hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia recurred (platelets 80×10^9/L). A direct Coombs test was negative. ADAMTS13 activity was detectable, excluding TTP, and stool samples did not detect Escherichia coli O157:H7/O104:H4 or Shiga toxin, excluding STEC-HUS.

A 28-year-old woman presented with an 8-month history of left lower abdominal and pelvic pain accompanied by intermittent low-grade fever. She had three prior vaginal deliveries, no surgical history, no menstrual irregularities, and no remarkable medical history. She took over-the-counter antibiotics and analgesics intermittently. On examination, the left lower quadrant was slightly distended, and a regular, mobile, soft mass with mild tenderness was palpated. Bowel sounds were normal. Vital signs: temperature 37.2 °C, blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg, heart rate 83/min, respiratory rate 16/min. An erect abdominal radiograph was unremarkable. Transabdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 9.2 × 7.3 cm left adnexal cystic mass with internal septations and echoes; the lesion was well defined and regular. The liver, spleen, kidneys, right adnexa, and uterus appeared normal. Complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, and chest radiography were within normal limits.

A 93-year-old Middle Eastern man with hypothyroidism, hypertension, and dyslipidemia was admitted for fatigue and intractable hiccups of 2 weeks’ duration. He reported a 2-year history of intermittent hiccups that persisted despite trials of proton-pump inhibitors, chlorpromazine, and baclofen. His home medications were levothyroxine, amlodipine, and rosuvastatin. He denied dysphagia, odynophagia, food impaction, heartburn, vomiting, or weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 9000 per mL with 18% eosinophils. Stool studies were negative for parasitic infection. Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen was unremarkable. Upper endoscopy revealed a normal-appearing esophagus. Biopsies from the mid and distal esophagus showed 15 eosinophils per high-power field.

An 89-year-old man with a DDD pacemaker implanted 8 years earlier for sick sinus syndrome and atrioventricular block presented with chest pain and presyncopal episodes. He described sudden-onset chest pain while gardening 2 weeks prior. A 12-lead ECG showed severe bradycardia at 20–40 bpm with intermittent ventricular pacing failure. Pacemaker interrogation revealed a ventricular pacing threshold of 4.25 V at 0.4 ms, lead impedance of 425 Ω, and inability to measure R-wave sensing due to a slow intrinsic rate. His history included hypertension, COPD, and regular device checks every 6 months, during which ventricular impedance had gradually declined over the past 3 years but other parameters were unchanged. On examination, blood pressure was 128/97 mm Hg, pulse 40 bpm, and SpO2 98% on room air. Chest radiograph demonstrated that the ventricular lead tip had advanced to the distal cardiac silhouette. Pacing failure occurred frequently during inspiration. Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal LV wall motion, no pericardial effusion, and suggested that the RV lead tip had penetrated the RV free wall.

A 52-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of intermittent, nonspecific pain at the angle of his left mandible, radiating to the vertex, occiput, and the left shoulder. He also noted difficulty with head rotation and ipsilateral eye and ear pain. His medical history was notable for recently diagnosed Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, irritable bowel syndrome, and depression; his brother and sister also have Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome. Surveillance chest CT had shown multiple thin-walled cysts in the lung bases. 

On examination, there was a well-defined, superficial lump on the left side of the face, immediately below the skin and anterior to the parotid gland. Ultrasound of the left parotid region revealed a well-defined, hypoechoic subcutaneous lesion. Ultrasound also incidentally identified a well-defined hypoechoic area deep to the left submandibular gland, suggestive of a tongue-base lesion. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the parotid region confirmed a solitary, well-defined superficial subcutaneous lesion measuring 18×12×10 mm. Three separate enhancing lesions were also identified along the left tongue: the largest measured 23×12 mm, was T1 hypointense and T2 hyperintense, and lay along the inferolateral aspect of the tongue deep to the hyoglossus, with no infiltration of adjacent extrinsic tongue muscles. 

A PET-CT scan was performed because a sinister tongue lesion could not be excluded. The subcutaneous parotid‐region lesion showed no significant FDG uptake. In contrast, high FDG activity was noted in the left glossotonsillar sulcus and inferolateral tongue lesions (SUV max 9.3), with additional hypermetabolic foci anteromedially in the other two lesions.

A 19-year-old primigravida at 40 weeks and one day gestation was admitted for elective induction of labor. Her pregnancy had been uncomplicated. Labor was induced with misoprostol and oxytocin. At 3 cm cervical dilation, an epidural analgesia was requested. Placement at L4–L5 in the sitting position was noted to be technically difficult, with transient tachycardia that resolved spontaneously. Analgesia with fentanyl was effective.

Eight hours after epidural catheter placement, she developed a severe frontal headache and neck pain rated 10/10, pounding in nature, nonradiating, and worsened by head movement and upright positioning. She denied visual disturbances, photophobia, nausea, vomiting, or limb weakness. Vital signs remained normal, and neurologic examination was unremarkable. The epidural infusion continued for labor analgesia.

Labor failed to progress, and she underwent an uncomplicated Cesarean section. Postoperatively, she continued to complain of persistent positional headache with waxing and waning intensity. On postoperative day 1, because of ongoing headaches, a noncontrast CT scan of the head and neck was obtained.

A 42-year-old woman with severe intellectual disability was brought by her sister because over the past few months she had developed difficulty moving and was frequently bumping into surrounding objects. Two years earlier, an ophthalmologist had found visual acuity of light perception bilaterally, bilateral corneal edema, and intraocular pressures of 69 mmHg in the right eye and 70 mmHg in the left eye; she underwent two sessions of 270-degree laser diode transscleral cyclophotocoagulation 6 months apart and was treated with topical dorzolamide/timolol and latanoprost, but her vision and mobility worsened. On examination, her height was 140 cm (<3rd percentile). She was gentle, with a coarse face, thick eyebrows, narrow and short palpebral fissures, a broad nasal bridge and tip, anteverted nares, thickened and everted vermilion lips, and down-turned corners of the mouth. Both hands and feet were small; there was hypoplasia of the distal phalanges of the fifth fingers and small nails on the second to fifth digits of hands and feet. A comprehensive ocular examination was limited by her disability. She was tentatively diagnosed with Weill-Marchesani syndrome and secondary angle-closure glaucoma. Because both lenses were noted to be small and spherical, she underwent intraoperative phacoemulsification and intraocular lens implantation. Ocular biometry immediately before surgery showed axial lengths of 33.0 mm (right) and 34.3 mm (left); anterior chamber depths of 3.20 mm and 3.14 mm; keratometry values of 42.75/43.75 D (right) and 40.0/44.0 D (left); intraocular lens powers of –3.0 D and –4.0 D (A-constant 118.3); and central corneal thicknesses of 660 μm and 667 μm. Postoperatively, intraocular pressure was controlled with medications, but vision did not recover due to chronic elevated pressures and severe glaucomatous optic nerve damage.

An 18-month-old Egyptian boy was referred for evaluation of generalized hyperpigmentation associated with weakness, vomiting, and recurrent convulsions. He was born to consanguineous parents after an uneventful pregnancy. One sibling had died at nine months with similar hyperpigmentation and convulsions, while other siblings are healthy. The parents noted hyperpigmentation in the first weeks of life, darker than his siblings. At 10 and 11 months, he had two brief febrile generalized tonic-clonic convulsions; no evaluation was performed at that time.

On examination, he spoke only a few words and walked with support. Weight was at the 5th percentile; length and head circumference at the 50th percentile. Blood pressure was 90/60 mmHg. He had generalized symmetric deep hyperpigmentation, especially of the elbows, knees, hands, feet, and buccal mucosa, and hypotonia. No dysmorphic features. External genitalia were normal, with bilaterally palpable testes. There were no signs of alacrima or achalasia. Other findings were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed:
• Glucose 48 mg/dL  
• Sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4 mmol/L, chloride 109 mmol/L  
• ALT 28 IU/mL, AST 30 IU/mL  
• Complete blood count normal  
• Cortisol 0.6 μg/dL (normal 2.8–23)  
• ACTH 708 pg/mL (normal 6–48)  
• No rise in cortisol after ACTH stimulation  
• 17-OH progesterone 0.01 ng/mL (normal 0.03–0.9)  
• Androstenedione 0.01 ng/mL (normal 0.1–0.17)  
• DHEA 3 ng/mL (normal 50–480)  
• Plasma renin activity 57 ng/mL/hour (normal 2.35–37)  
• Aldosterone 801 pg/mL (normal 50–900)

Bone age by left hand radiograph was two years (chronologic age 18 months). Adrenal ultrasonography showed small adrenal glands (6 × 8 mm on the left, 7 × 8 mm on the right). Brain CT was normal.

A 67-year-old Hispanic woman underwent extraction of teeth 32, 33, 42, and 43, alveoloplasty, and placement of two implants under local anesthesia. A full-thickness flap was raised from the distal of tooth 33 to the distal of tooth 43. Teeth were extracted uneventfully, and bone reduction was performed with an air-driven high-speed surgical handpiece. During drilling, slight swelling was noted in the left floor of the mouth, which was attributed to flap retraction. At procedure end she was asymptomatic, and vital signs were stable. 

The next day, she returned for denture insertion complaining of severe pain and swelling beneath her tongue on the left side. Her temperature was 98.5°F, and blood pressure was 145/80 mm Hg. The pain began the afternoon of the procedure immediately after the local anesthesia wore off and was described as a sensation of the tongue “sitting on something.” On examination, there was marked edema of the left floor of the mouth in the lateral incisor/canine region, extending from the initial surgical site and causing the lingual mucosa to cover the left alveolar ridge. A pathological consultation was obtained, and a differential diagnosis of emphysema or mucocele was made.

A 14-year-old boy presented with progressive enlargement of the second through fifth toes of the right foot, noted since birth and worsening over time. At age 7, he developed inability to wear shoes; one month before presentation he began to experience forefoot pain and difficulty walking. He had no other anomalies, no family history of similar conditions, and an uneventful past medical history. On examination, vital signs were normal. The right foot showed enlarged second through fifth toes without tenderness; the neurovascular examination was intact. Laboratory studies were unremarkable, with hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL, hematocrit 33.1%, MCV 78 fL, potassium 3.96 mmol/L, sodium 138.3 mmol/L. Plain radiographs of the right foot demonstrated enlargement of the phalanges—especially the distal phalanges—with soft-tissue overgrowth, “no fracture, sclerotic or osteolytic changes,” no bone erosion, and preserved joint spaces and ankle alignment, “features suggestive of macrodactyly.”

A 21-year-old man presented with a 9-year history of progressive deformity of the right side of his face. He first noted at age 12 a gradual thinning of the soft tissues on the right cheek. He denied any history of trauma, fever, or systemic symptoms.  

On examination, there was marked asymmetry of the face with hypoplasia and hyperpigmentation of the skin on the right. The right eyebrow showed hair loss, and the vermilion border of the upper lip was deviated toward the right. A linear, indented, hyperpigmented demarcation (“coup de sabre”) extended from the right forehead to the mandibular menton.  

Intraorally, the right soft palate and faucial region were atrophic, and the right buccal mucosa felt firm on palpation. On general inspection, the entire right half of the body appeared more atrophic than the left.  

Cone-beam computed tomography with three-dimensional reconstruction demonstrated a decreased vertical height of the right mandibular body compared with the left.

An 8-year-old boy presented with a 1-month history of pain and swelling in his right knee following a minor sprain. Initial knee arthrotomy with joint-fluid cultures showed no bacterial growth. Over the next two weeks, his symptoms progressed to migratory arthritis involving both knees, both wrists, and the metacarpophalangeal joints. He developed intermittent fevers and noted blue discoloration of the second and fifth fingertips of his right hand.

On transfer to our center, he appeared ill and febrile (39.5°C), with a heart rate of 112 bpm and blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg. He had pallor and severe arthralgias. There was no Raynaud’s phenomenon, livedo, or skin ulcers. Musculoskeletal examination revealed flexion contractures of both knees and active arthritis of the wrists and metacarpophalangeal joints. There were ischemic changes of the right second and fifth fingertips and several painful subcutaneous nodules on his forearm.

Laboratory studies revealed WBC 25,500/mm3, platelet count 507,000/mm3, hemoglobin 7.0 g/dL, ESR 95 mm/h, CRP 57 mg/L, ferritin 291 ng/mL, IL-6 462 pg/mL, and an ASO titer of 2850 IU/mL. Serologic tests including ANA, ANCA, RF, and anti-CCP were negative. Blood cultures were negative. Bone marrow aspiration and a thoracoabdominal CT scan showed no evidence of malignancy.

A 14-year-old girl, previously healthy, had measles diagnosed on the basis of fever and maculopapular rash three months prior; her immunization was incomplete and she recovered within 10 days. Six weeks after recovery, she developed recurrent tonic-clonic seizures affecting the left face and body, followed by progressive left hemiparesis. Over the next month the focal seizures became continuous (epilepsia partialis continua), accompanied by dull holocranial headache, and ten days before admission she developed progressive right hemiparesis. She remained alert, with age-appropriate cognition. 

On examination, vital signs were normal. She had generalized wasting, oral thrush, and an MMSE score of 27. Deep tendon reflexes were present in the upper limbs and absent in the lower limbs. There was an upper motor neuron–type right facial palsy, left-sided epilepsia partialis continua, and quadriparesis.

Laboratory studies revealed pancytopenia (Hb 10.1 g/dL, WBC 2400/µL, platelets 100 000/µL). Serum electrolytes, liver, renal, and thyroid function tests, anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies, chest radiograph, and abdominal ultrasound were normal. HIV-1 serology was positive, with a CD4 count of 97 cells/µL; her mother was also HIV positive. 

CSF analysis was unremarkable. An autoimmune encephalitis panel and ANA profile were negative. CSF culture, PCR for JC virus and EBV, and TORCH serologies were negative. EEG showed focal epileptiform discharges. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral, asymmetrical long-TR hyperintensities in juxtacortical white matter of both parietal lobes, left temporal lobe, and left basal ganglia, without contrast enhancement or diffusion restriction.

A 62-year-old right-handed man presented with sudden onset of mixed dysphasia and reported a poorly localized headache for 2 weeks prior. He had type 2 diabetes managed with metformin and no other significant history. On examination, he was hyperreflexic with upgoing plantar responses, but had normal power and sensation.

Initial non-contrast CT of the brain was unremarkable.
