Brain MRI showed multifocal regions of diffusion restriction almost exclusively in the left parietal and temporal lobes, with prominent areas of cortical fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensity and cortical thickening. Magnetic resonance angiography of the circle of Willis was normal.

One week later, repeat MRI revealed multiple new ischemic lesions in the left hemisphere, extensive leptomeningeal enhancement confined to the left temporal region, subcortical microhaemorrhages, and minor convexity subarachnoid blood not seen on the initial scan.

Laboratory studies revealed a normal full blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and angiotensin-converting enzyme. Antinuclear antibodies were positive at a low titre (1:80, nucleolar pattern), but extractable nuclear antigens were negative. Serum antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, rheumatoid factor, anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide, double-stranded DNA antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, lupus inhibitor, dilute Russell’s viper venom time, and cryoglobulins were all negative or normal. Tumour markers (CA 125, CA 153, CA 199, and CEA) and serologies for HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and syphilis were negative.

Initial cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed albuminocytological dissociation (protein 0.94 g/L; 2 mononuclear cells). Two weeks later, CSF demonstrated a lymphocytic pleocytosis (32 cells, some atypical), protein 1.75 g/L, and xanthochromia. CSF PCR for herpes simplex virus, enterovirus, varicella zoster virus, and Epstein–Barr virus was negative; cryptococcal antigen and oligoclonal bands were absent.

A 76-year-old woman underwent a pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure) for a malignant ampulloma. On the fifth postoperative day, she developed acute epigastric pain with nausea, vomiting, and fever (maximum temperature, 38.6°C). A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen showed nonspecific inflammatory stranding surrounding mildly enlarged adrenal glands, which had appeared normal on a preoperative CT scan. No anastomotic leak or other surgical complications were identified. The leukocyte count was within the normal range, but systemic infection was suspected and empiric antibiotic therapy was initiated. 

Despite antibiotics, the patient’s epigastric pain persisted, and on the 13th postoperative day she presented with a drop in hemoglobin (120 g/dL), hypotension, signs of hypovolemia, and tachycardia (130 bpm). Laboratory studies revealed sodium 126 mmol/L, potassium 6.9 mmol/L, a low serum cortisol level (5 mcg/dL), and an elevated plasma ACTH level (>300 ng/L), findings suggestive of adrenal crisis.

A 47-year-old woman of Chinese ancestry with a 12-year history of polycythemia vera presented for evaluation of a newly detected carotid bruit. In the waiting room, she developed sudden lightheadedness that did not improve with sitting; her blood pressure was 211/72 mm Hg in the right arm and 125/75 mm Hg in the left arm. She reported feeling sweaty and clammy in her right hand and numbness in her left hand. The lightheadedness resolved after ten minutes of supplemental oxygen. She had no prior episodes of lightheadedness. 

Her polycythemia vera had been diagnosed by bone marrow biopsy, and she had been managed intermittently with phlebotomy; she had been noncompliant with hydroxyurea and aspirin. 

Initial CT angiography of the chest and neck showed complete occlusion of the left subclavian artery proximal to the vertebral artery origin, a patent distal subclavian artery and left vertebral artery, severe stenosis at the origin of the right vertebral artery, and marked stenoocclusive disease of the bilateral supraclinoid internal carotid arteries with multiple small collaterals reconstituting the proximal middle and anterior cerebral arteries. MR angiography confirmed these findings, and brain MRI revealed multiple chronic watershed infarcts. Conventional cerebral angiography demonstrated bilateral supraclinoid internal carotid occlusions with prominent moyamoya-type collaterals, high-grade (70%) right vertebral artery stenosis, and left subclavian artery occlusion. 

MR angiography of the chest and abdomen revealed mild wall thickening of the aortic arch and abdominal aorta, bilateral (50%) renal artery stenoses, superior mesenteric artery stenosis, and right common iliac artery stenosis. 

Laboratory studies showed a normal white-cell count, hemoglobin of 15.9 g/dL, and platelets of 660 K/μL. Testing for antiphospholipid antibodies was negative. Inflammatory markers and autoimmune serologies, including C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, anti–double-stranded DNA, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, were all within normal limits. Further testing confirmed the presence of a JAK2 V617F mutation.

A previously healthy 19-year-old Chinese man presented with progressive weakness of his right limbs over six months. Initially, he had right lower limb weakness with a normal ankle radiograph and no treatment. Two months before presentation, he developed right upper limb weakness and worsening right lower limb strength, accompanied by fever up to 39.5°C, blurred vision in his left eye, and mild episodic headaches lasting several minutes; there was no nausea or vomiting. Computed tomography at an outside hospital revealed numerous well-circumscribed low-density cysts rimmed by high-density calcifications scattered throughout both cerebral hemispheres. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated extensive white matter hyperintensity consistent with leukoencephalopathy and multiple cysts of varying sizes in the hemispheres, thalamus, basal ganglia, and left ventricle; the cyst walls enhanced with gadolinium, and the contents were heterogeneously hyperintense on T1-weighted and FLAIR images. On examination, visual acuity was 0.15 in the left eye and 0.5 in the right; motor strength was grade 4/5 in the right limbs with a positive Babinski sign on the right. Initial differential diagnoses included parasitic infection, glioma, and leukoencephalopathy.

A 32-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of fevers up to 39.5°C, symmetric arthritis of the knees, ankles, and shoulders, a nonpruritic papular rash involving the neck and upper abdomen, myalgias, and weight loss. Laboratory studies showed an ESR of 110 mm/hr, LDH of 1975 IU/L, and normal liver-function tests; the rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibodies were negative. Blood cultures were negative. On examination, there were several non-tender, immobile, rubbery right anterior cervical lymph nodes (2 × 3 cm) and left posterior auricular lymph nodes (0.5 × 1 cm), bilateral knee and ankle swelling, and papular skin lesions on the neck and upper abdomen; there was no hepatosplenomegaly. A chest radiograph showed a left lower-lobe pleural effusion. CT of the abdomen and pelvis was normal. An excisional cervical lymph-node biopsy and a bone-marrow biopsy were negative for malignancy. A celiac angiogram performed to rule out vasculitis was negative.

A 29-year-old pregnant woman presented with subacute abdominal pain, weakness, and nausea. Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin concentration of 4.5 g/dL, a mean corpuscular volume of 68 fL, and a ferritin level of 1.6 ng/mL. She had no history of menorrhagia or overt gastrointestinal bleeding and was thought to have chronic iron loss from prior vaginal bleeding exacerbated by physiologic anemia of pregnancy. Her anemia responded to oral and intravenous iron supplementation and stabilized at a hemoglobin concentration of 11.8 g/dL. 

Sixteen months after an uncomplicated delivery, she returned with symptomatic anemia. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy was unremarkable, with normal gastric and duodenal biopsies. Colonoscopy, including visualization of the terminal ileum, showed old blood throughout the colon. She was lost to follow-up for 8 months, then presented again with a hemoglobin concentration of 5.8 g/dL and melena. Capsule endoscopy revealed old blood in the distal small bowel without identifying a source. 

Abdominal computed tomography showed multifocal fluid-filled lesions within the ileal mesentery with thin, faintly enhancing walls; some lesions involved the ileal wall and appeared to extend to the lumen without perceptible overlying mucosa.

A 73-year-old Japanese woman with no smoking history and a 15-year history of presumed interstitial pneumonia was referred in January 2018 for progressive dyspnea. She had undergone uncomplicated coronary artery bypass grafting in her 50s. On presentation, her respiratory rate was 20 breaths/min, pulse 86 beats/min, blood pressure 102/60 mmHg, temperature 36.3 °C; SpO2 was 93% on room air at rest and 88% during ambulation. Chest auscultation revealed inspiratory fine crackles bilaterally, most prominent in the lower lung fields. There was no Raynaud phenomenon, skin rash, joint swelling, dry eyes or mouth, or digital clubbing.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 5400/μL without abnormal cells, LDH 306 IU/L, C-reactive protein 1.17 mg/dL (normal ≤0.14), soluble IL-2 receptor 1077 U/mL (normal 157–474), KL-6 1297 U/mL (normal <500), surfactant protein D 215 ng/mL (normal <110), and surfactant protein A 74.7 ng/mL (normal <43.8). 

Chest radiography demonstrated diffuse micronodules and ground-glass opacities in both lungs. Thin-section CT revealed numerous well-defined, uniform 1–3 mm micronodules distributed diversely (centrilobular, peribronchovascular, and perilobular), with interlobular septal thickening, ground-glass attenuation, and traction bronchiectasis/bronchiolectasis predominantly in the lower lobes. Air trapping in the lower lobes created a mosaic attenuation pattern. 

At this point, the team considered diseases causing lymphatic tract abnormalities—lymphoproliferative disorders, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, HTLV-1–associated bronchioloalveolar disorder, collagen vascular disease, and drug-induced lung injury—as well as fibrotic chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis. A surgical lung biopsy was planned for definitive diagnosis.

A 69-year-old man was admitted for evaluation of chronic respiratory insufficiency. Two years earlier, at age 67, he had developed exertional dyspnea while farming. He was found to have atrial fibrillation without cardiomyopathy and underwent successful catheter ablation. At age 68, he experienced daytime somnolence. At age 69, he developed palpitations and fatigue and was diagnosed with heart failure with low cardiac output due to atrial flutter. High-flow oxygen was administered, after which his consciousness declined; he developed hypercapnic respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation and tracheotomy. After stabilization, he was referred for neurologic evaluation of a suspected restrictive pulmonary disorder.

On examination, he had mild weakness of the neck flexor muscles but full strength in the upper and lower extremities. His gait was normal. The serum creatine kinase level was normal. Chest expansion was reduced, and pulmonary function testing showed a forced vital capacity of 61% of predicted. An electromyographic examination of the right semitendinosus muscle demonstrated myopathic changes, and nerve conduction studies were normal. Muscle CT revealed thinning of the diaphragm and fatty replacement of the bilateral semitendinosus muscles, with preservation of the tibialis posterior muscles. A biopsy of the left biceps brachii muscle showed variation in fiber size on hematoxylin and eosin staining and cytoplasmic bodies on modified Gomori trichrome staining.

A 55-year-old man presented with one week of neck stiffness and dysphagia. He denied trauma or fever and reported only occasional alcohol use. On examination, he had limited neck movement and tachypnoea; lung auscultation was normal. His abdomen was soft, non-tender, and without palpable masses. 

A radiograph of the neck (anteroposterior and lateral views) showed thickening of the prevertebral soft tissues with anterior displacement of the airway; cervical vertebrae showed only degenerative changes and no evidence of discitis or osteomyelitis. A concurrent frontal chest radiograph revealed a homogeneous opacity displacing the right paratracheal stripe and thickening of the paravertebral stripe, as well as a near-homogeneous retrocardiac opacity silhouetting the left hemidiaphragm. 

Given these findings and the clinical scenario, a retropharyngeal abscess with mediastinal extension was initially suspected.

A 32-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks 3 days of gestation presented with acute left lower abdominal pain and vomiting. She denied vaginal bleeding, urinary symptoms, constipation, or changes in bowel habits. Her observations were stable, and she appeared clinically well. On examination, there was slight tenderness in the left abdomen without guarding; the uterus was soft and relaxed. Foetal movements and monitoring were normal.

Her antenatal course had been uneventful except for a 70 × 60 × 60 mm left ovarian cyst first noted at 5 weeks and thought to be endometriotic. Follow-up scans at 32 weeks showed the cyst measured 63 × 33 × 69 mm with internal echoes and an avascular solid component. Tumour markers (CEA, CA-19-9, CA-125) were within normal limits, and an MDT review deemed the cyst benign and recommended surveillance.

On admission, Hb was 121 g/L, WCC 10.0 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 9.1 × 10^9/L, platelets 270 × 10^9/L, and CRP 30 mg/L. Over three days, CRP rose to 209 mg/L while WCC remained stable. Repeated transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasounds by an experienced sonographer showed the left adnexal cyst unchanged in size and appearance with no whirlpool sign, stromal oedema, absent Doppler flow, or free pelvic fluid. MRI was considered but not performed due to the rapid clinical change.

At 37 weeks 1 day, her pain worsened with vomiting, and abdominal exam revealed generalized tenderness with guarding in the left iliac fossa. Given the acute abdomen, rising inflammatory markers, and concern for ovarian torsion, the decision was made to proceed with a caesarean section followed by surgical management of the adnexa.

A 39-year-old woman with no prior medical history was brought to the emergency department for progressive lethargy. Family members reported a 3-week history of fatigue and forgetfulness, followed by difficulty keeping her eyes open during conversation. Eventually, she fell asleep during meals and became bedbound.

On examination, she was somnolent with bilateral ptosis and impaired extraocular movements: adduction was absent and movement in all other directions was markedly restricted bilaterally. 

An MRI of the brain and orbits with and without contrast demonstrated extensive nonenhancing T2 hyperintensities involving the periaqueductal gray matter, medial thalami, mammillary bodies, the region surrounding the third ventricle, and the area postrema; the optic nerves were spared.

Given concern for Wernicke’s encephalopathy, whole blood thiamine levels were drawn, and high‐dose IV thiamine was administered. The patient’s family denied any history of alcohol use disorder or bariatric surgery and stated that she consumed regular, unrestricted meals. The differential diagnosis was broadened to include arboviral infection and demyelinating disease; serum aquaporin-4 and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibodies were collected.

Empiric IV acyclovir was started, and a lumbar puncture was performed. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed 50 nucleated cells with 95% lymphocytes, protein 83 mg/dL, normal glucose, and a negative HSV PCR; acyclovir was discontinued.

Despite thiamine supplementation, her condition deteriorated over the next 6 days: ophthalmoplegia progressed to complete paralysis, she developed recurrent hiccuping, her somnolence worsened, and she required transfer to the Neurocritical Care Unit for respiratory support. Serum and CSF testing revealed positive West Nile virus IgG antibodies and negative IgM antibodies. A repeat whole blood thiamine level was elevated at 191 nanomoles per liter.

A 37-year-old man presented with a first episode of hemoptysis and stabbing right hemithoracic pain. He is a current heavy smoker (29 pack-years) and works in a fiberglass-boat factory. His medical history is notable for easy bruising and capillary fragility but no prior pulmonary disease.  
On examination, vital signs were stable. Chest radiography showed a large, distended cystic bulla in the right upper lobe, compressing adjacent lung. CT of the chest confirmed multiple emphysematous bullae in the right middle and upper lobes, and paraseptal and panlobular emphysema in the left upper and lingular lobes.  
Arterial blood gas analysis on room air was normal. Laboratory tests showed mild elevations of CRP, ESR, and fibrinogen; coagulation studies were normal. Bronchoscopy localized bleeding to the right upper lobe. Pulmonary-function testing revealed normal lung volumes, a moderate reduction in diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO, 54% predicted), and a marked difference between slow vital capacity (6.24 L) and forced vital capacity (4.84 L).  
Family history elicited a monozygotic twin brother, also a heavy smoker, who was found on screening chest radiograph to have bullous emphysema. α₁-Antitrypsin levels were normal in both brothers. Physical examination revealed thin, translucent skin and slight hyperextensibility of the small joints of the extremities. An Ehlers–Danlos syndrome was suspected.

A 73‐year‐old woman with end‐stage renal disease on hemodialysis, chronic anemia, diabetes mellitus, and hypertension presented with a 1‐day history of dark, tarry stools and abdominal cramping. She also noted new‐onset mild dyspnea on exertion and significant fatigue over the same period. She had multiple prior admissions for similar melena requiring transfusion, most recently 2 months earlier. She denied abdominal pain, changes in bowel habits, NSAID use, fevers, weight loss, or bleeding elsewhere.

On examination, temperature was 98 °F, respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, heart rate 100/min, and blood pressure 90/60 mm Hg. She appeared pale with cold extremities and weak peripheral pulses. A left upper‐extremity arteriovenous fistula was present. Cardiac auscultation revealed a crescendo‐decrescendo systolic murmur at the right sternal border radiating to the carotids. The abdomen was soft, nontender, and nondistended.

Laboratory results showed hemoglobin 5.2 g/dL, hematocrit 15.9%, white blood cell count 10.1 × 10^9/L, platelets 266 × 10^9/L, and reticulocyte count 4.4%. The peripheral smear showed polychromasia and schistocytes. BUN was 53 mg/dL, creatinine 6.3 mg/dL (baseline 3 mg/dL), and BNP 1880 pg/mL. Coagulation studies and electrolytes were normal. Troponin was mildly elevated at 0.089 ng/mL; serial EKGs were unremarkable.

Two units of packed red blood cells raised her hemoglobin to 8.9 g/dL. An echocardiogram revealed an ejection fraction of 50–55%, grade 1 diastolic dysfunction, and severe aortic stenosis with an aortic valve area of 0.8 cm^2. Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy showed no active bleeding, though angiodysplasia was suspected. Her primary care provider reported that a capsule endoscopy performed one year earlier had demonstrated angiodysplasias throughout her gastrointestinal tract.

A 32-year-old man presented with 2 weeks of swelling in the right cheek. He had chewed tobacco for 3 years. On examination, there was an oval, firm, 2.5 × 2 cm swelling located 2 cm above and medial to the right angle of the mandible. The oral cavity examination was normal.  
An ultrasonogram of the cheek showed an anechoic cystic swelling in the bucco-masseteric region with perilesional edema. MRI of the face and neck demonstrated a hyperintense cystic lesion with perilesional edema in the bucco-masseteric region on T2-weighted images.  
Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the lesion revealed chronic inflammatory infiltrate, and no evidence of malignancy was seen.  
What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 65-year-old man with hypertension and hyperlipidemia on aspirin suffered a mechanical fall with head trauma and was found to have a left subdural hematoma. He underwent craniotomy and hematoma evacuation on September 18 and was transferred for postoperative care on September 21. His postoperative course was uneventful: he was afebrile, CBC and liver enzymes remained normal, and he did not require blood transfusion. Metformin was started for new diabetes and levetiracetam for seizure prophylaxis; he continued losartan, metoprolol, and atorvastatin. He was discharged home on September 24.

He returned to the ED on October 1 with a 4-day history of fever, malaise, and dark urine. On presentation, temperature was 100.8 °F, pulse 92/min, blood pressure 98/62 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. He was alert and oriented, with an unremarkable exam; the craniotomy incision was clean and dry and there were no rashes or lesions. Laboratory studies showed elevated lactate and liver enzymes, mild hyponatremia, and thrombocytopenia; white-cell count and hemoglobin were normal, with no eosinophilia. CT of the head, chest, abdomen, and pelvis and MRI of the brain revealed no acute abnormalities. He received IV fluids, antipyretics, vancomycin, and piperacillin–tazobactam. Neurosurgery found no evidence of meningitis, abscess, cerebral edema, or surgical-site infection, and the subdural hematoma had improved.

Over the next 24 hours, he developed high fevers (up to 104 °F), progressive anemia, thrombocytopenia, and rising bilirubin. Hematology reviewed a peripheral blood smear and noted numerous ring-form intraerythrocytic organisms, concerning for babesiosis versus malaria.

A 48-year-old white man with a history of intravenous drug use presented with a 5-year history of left thigh pain, progressive loss of hip range of motion, and decreasing ability to walk without support. He denied any history of trauma. On examination, there was tenderness over the left trochanteric region and pain with passive internal and external rotation of the left hip. Active flexion of the left hip was limited to 30°, internal rotation to 10–15°, and external rotation to 15–20°. His Harris Hip Score was 36.65. 

Weight-bearing pelvic radiographs showed apparent bone necrosis of the left femoral head and neck. CT of the left hip demonstrated complete reabsorption of the left femoral head and neck. MRI of the left hip revealed complete bone resorption of the proximal femur, a vascular-appearing mass in the joint space, and invasion of the acetabular fossa, the upper acetabular wall, and the ipsilateral iliac wing. Bone scintigraphy showed destruction of the left coxofemoral joint with late radiopharmaceutical fixation.

A 35-year-old woman presented with a 15-month history of vaginal bleeding and intermittent sensation of a mass in the vagina. She described bleeding with clots every 1–2 weeks lasting 2–5 days without a separate menstrual cycle; between bleeding episodes she had a watery, nonfoul-smelling vaginal discharge and occasional postcoital bleeding. She denied dyspnea, palpitations, or bleeding from other sites. Her obstetric history included three home vaginal deliveries; she underwent minilaparotomy sterilization 11 years prior and tubal recanalization 5 years ago. Prior evaluations—including coagulation studies, pelvic ultrasonography, and empiric therapy with progesterone, tranexamic acid, and antibiotics—had not alleviated her symptoms.

On examination she appeared pale but hemodynamically stable. Abdominal exam was unremarkable. On bimanual pelvic examination there was a firm, globular 6×4 cm mass within the vaginal canal; a separate cervical os could not be identified and the uterine fundus was not palpable. Active vaginal bleeding was noted. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 5.3 g/dL with normal platelet count and PT/INR. Pelvic ultrasonography—performed multiple times, including in the preoperative area—was reported as normal and was unable to clarify the origin of the mass. Magnetic resonance imaging was not available. After resuscitation with intravenous fluids and two units of whole blood, she was scheduled for emergency surgical management.

A farm in Romania acquired five Texel sheep (one male and four pregnant ewes) one month before presentation. The animals were housed together, with free access to water and fed good-quality hay and a commercial compound feed intended for pigs that contained copper bilysinate at 14.22 mg/kg. No molybdenum was added to the feed. Six weeks after starting this diet, a three-year-old pregnant ewe developed anorexia, weakness, and apathy. On examination she was icteric, had hemoglobinuria, abdominal pain, rumen stasis, and a normal temperature. She preferred sternal recumbency but could rise. She died two days after onset. One week later, a three-year-old ram developed similar signs and died. The high-copper feed was then withdrawn, but three weeks later a second ewe died with the same presentation. The two remaining pregnant ewes had mild anorexia and apathy, recovered, and delivered healthy lambs. A blood smear revealed oxidative hemolytic anemia with erythrocyte ghosts and Heinz bodies.

A 40-year-old man presented with two months of painless gross hematuria. He denied dysuria, urinary frequency, flank pain, fevers, night sweats, weight loss, joint pains, or history of tuberculosis. Physical examination was unremarkable: vital signs were normal, there was no abdominal or pelvic tenderness, no palpable masses, and no inguinal lymphadenopathy. Digital rectal examination showed no prostatic enlargement. Laboratory testing revealed hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL, white blood cell count 6,000/µL, and platelets 250,000/µL. Urinalysis demonstrated numerous red blood cells; urine culture was sterile. Urine cytology showed red blood cells and a few degenerate atypical-appearing cells. Serum creatinine and liver-function tests were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography showed no abnormalities. Pelvic ultrasonography revealed a cauliflower-like mass, measuring 3.1 × 2.9 × 1.9 cm, arising from the right lateral wall of the bladder. Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis confirmed a well-defined, hyperdense, enhancing lesion 19 mm in thickness on the right lateral bladder wall, with no calcification, extravesical extension, or lymphadenopathy. Cystoscopy demonstrated a 3 cm solid, erythematous lesion on the right lateral bladder wall. Transurethral biopsy specimens included mucosa and submucosa. Histologic examination showed squamous metaplasia of the urothelial lining and subepithelial interstitial deposits of homogenous eosinophilic material accompanied by foreign‐body giant cells and chronic mononuclear inflammation. Congo-red staining revealed orange-red deposits, and polarized microscopy demonstrated apple-green birefringence.

A 13-year-old boy born to first-degree–consanguineous parents presented with a 1-year history of recurrent episodes of fever and annular vesiculobullous eruptions clinically diagnosed as erythema multiforme minor. He also reported numbness, tingling, and hypoesthesia over the right lower leg (mononeuritis multiplex) and, more recently, left-sided facial pain with diminished hearing. On examination, he had silvery-white hair over the scalp, eyebrows, and body; phototanning with freckles on sun-exposed areas; and target lesions on the face and upper trunk. Neurologic examination confirmed decreased sensation in the right common peroneal nerve distribution. Pure-tone audiometry demonstrated 95% sensorineural hearing loss in the left ear. 

Peripheral blood smears on six occasions showed no leukocyte abnormalities or giant granules. Light microscopy of hair shafts revealed evenly distributed melanin granules of regular diameter that were larger than those in normal hair. Under polarized light, hair shafts appeared uniformly bright with variegated individual colors. Ophthalmic examination showed mild photophobia with normal visual acuity and fundi. Abdominal ultrasonography was unremarkable without organomegaly.

A patient presented with intermittent right axillary pain for 1 month and noted a lump under the axilla. On examination, a firm, approximately 7 cm mass was palpable on the medial aspect of the upper right arm. Routine laboratory tests were normal. MRI of the right axillary region showed a well-demarcated lesion measuring 62 × 58 × 44 mm encircling the humerus with localized thinning of the humeral cortex, high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, and close relation to the radial artery.

A 33-year-old woman with alopecia areata and recurrent herpes zoster presented with one month of vague bilateral thigh pain, worse on the right, initially treated as piriformis syndrome. Her left thigh pain resolved, but right-sided pain progressed until weight-bearing was barely tolerable. She then experienced an audible crack in the right leg with immediate pain and collapse during ambulation. She reported a 5-lb unintentional weight loss over the prior month but denied fevers, night sweats, fatigue, numbness, or recent dental procedures.

On examination, the right lower extremity was shortened, internally rotated, and tender, with erythema and swelling of the right midthigh; distal neurovascular status was intact. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (11.5×10^3/µL) with neutrophilia (9.03×10^3/µL), monocytosis (1.0×10^3/µL), alkaline phosphatase 151 U/L, ESR 54 mm/hr, CRP 158.4 mg/L, and negative HIV test. She was started on vancomycin and ceftriaxone for presumed sepsis.

Plain radiographs demonstrated a pathologic fracture of the right femoral shaft at a site of permeative bone destruction with both organized and nonorganized periosteal new bone formation. Noncontrast CT 3 days later confirmed aggressive bone destruction with indolent periosteal reaction, and contrast CT showed a hypodense collection in the vastus muscles surrounding the fracture. 

CT-guided biopsy of the bone around the fracture was performed.

A 36-year-old woman presented in January with a 2-month history of a burning, minimally pruritic rash in her axillae and inframammary folds. She had no fevers, systemic symptoms, or oral lesions. Her medical history was notable for obesity (BMI 36.5 kg/m2) and nephrolithiasis. Medications included multivitamins, fish oil, and a levonorgestrel intrauterine device (unchanged for >1 year) and compounded semaglutide, initiated weekly in late October. She denied new skincare products or detergents. 

Prior treatments—topical clotrimazole-betamethasone, ketoconazole, hydrocortisone, and oral fluconazole—provided minimal relief. On examination, there were ill-defined erythematous patches with fine scale in the axillary and inframammary folds, without vesicles, pustules, satellite lesions, lymphadenopathy, or mucosal involvement. A KOH preparation was deferred. Initial differential diagnoses included contact dermatitis, symmetrical drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema, and erythema annulare centrifugum. She was treated with topical hydrocortisone and a prednisone taper, but the rash progressed.

After missing two doses of semaglutide, she noted partial improvement; however, the rash recurred rapidly three days after her most recent injection. Examination now showed annular erythematous patches with prominent trailing scale in the axillary and inframammary folds. A punch biopsy from the left axilla revealed subcorneal pustular dermatosis with parakeratosis, mild acanthosis, mild spongiosis, and a superficial lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltrate; periodic acid–Schiff staining was negative.

A 13-year-old boy was admitted to the emergency department with acute onset of severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and 6–7 episodes of fresh bloody diarrhea over two hours. He had been taking amoxicillin–clavulanate and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for three days for acute otitis media. His vital signs were normal. On examination, there was periumbilical tenderness without guarding or rebound.  
Laboratory tests showed: WBC 17,300/µL (79% neutrophils), hemoglobin 14.8 g/dL, platelets 288,000/µL, and C-reactive protein 0.34 mg/dL; renal and liver chemistries, coagulation studies, and electrolytes were normal.  
Abdominal CT demonstrated edematous wall thickening from the ascending colon to the splenic flexure consistent with colitis. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed only minimal reflux esophagitis and bile reflux gastritis. Colonoscopy showed severe mucosal hemorrhage, erythema, and granular erosions with edema from the ascending to the transverse colon, most pronounced at the hepatic flexure.  
Histopathologic examination of colonic biopsies revealed acute hemorrhagic colitis with fibrinoid change of superficial mucosal red blood cells without distortion of the glands or cryptitis.

A 35-year-old woman was referred to an endocrine surgery clinic for evaluation of presumed recurrent primary hyperparathyroidism after subtotal parathyroidectomy. Six months earlier, she had presented with fatigue and was found to have a serum calcium level of 11.4 mg/dL (RR, 8.5–10.5) on routine screening. She denied symptoms of hypercalcemia. Her family history was notable for hypercalcemia in her mother, maternal uncle, and maternal aunt; her mother had undergone parathyroidectomy over 20 years earlier with persistent postoperative hypercalcemia.  

Initial evaluation included:  
- Vitamin D 25(OH): 40 ng/mL (RR, 30–85)  
- Intact PTH: 31 pg/mL (RR, 10–65)  
- 24-hour urine calcium: 117 mg/day (RR, 50–300)  
- Bone densitometry showing lumbar spine Z-score –1.1 and femoral neck Z-score –1.1  

Neck ultrasound had shown a hypoechoic structure at the left inferior pole, interpreted as “possible parathyroid adenoma versus lymph node,” and a technetium-99m sestamibi scan was nonlocalizing. The patient underwent subtotal parathyroidectomy with intraoperative PTH decreasing from 87 pg/mL to 34 pg/mL. Pathology described mildly enlarged glands.  

Postoperatively, her fatigue persisted. At referral, physical examination was unremarkable. Point-of-care neck ultrasound showed no residual parathyroid gland enlargement. Repeat laboratory testing revealed:  
- Serum calcium: 10.2 mg/dL (RR, 8.5–10.5)  
- Ionized calcium: 5.79 mg/dL (RR, 4.52–5.28)  
- Intact PTH: 39 pg/mL (RR, 10–65)  
- Undetectable 24-hour urine calcium  
- Normal phosphorus, magnesium, PTH-related protein, and serum protein electrophoresis  

Abdominal CT performed for flank pain showed small nonobstructing renal calculi. Given her young age, family history of hypercalcemia, and marked hypocalciuria, she was referred for genetic counseling and underwent germline testing for endocrine and cancer-susceptibility genes associated with hypercalcemia.

An 18-year-old male presents with a 4-year history of a nonhealing, painful ulcer over the medial malleolus of the left leg. Over the past 8 months he has experienced pain and swelling of bilateral wrists, elbows, and knees with morning stiffness, and during the past 3 months he has had weight loss and yellowish discoloration of the eyes and urine. He reports intermittent fevers for 1 month. He denies rash, oral ulcers, photosensitivity, or bleeding from other sites. Two years ago he received blood transfusions and previously had a similar ulcer on the right leg that healed after repeated dressings.

On examination he is pale, icteric, and cachectic with a Marfanoid habitus and generalized lymphadenopathy; vital signs are stable. A single large ulcer with well-defined indurated margins and surrounding hyperpigmentation is present over the left medial malleolus, with lipodermatosclerotic change of adjacent skin. Multiple joints are swollen with a flexion deformity of the left knee, resulting in a painful gait. Hepatomegaly and splenomegaly are noted; peripheral pulses are intact and there is no sensory or motor deficit.

Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 50 g/L, total bilirubin 78.7 μmol/L (indirect 65 μmol/L), total protein 82 g/L, albumin 35 g/L, positive ANA, anticardiolipin antibody (36 arbitrary units), and lupus anticoagulant on two occasions 12 weeks apart; rheumatoid factor is negative, C-reactive protein is 44.6 mg/L, HIV and hepatitis B and C serologies are negative, reticulocyte count is 0.4%, Coombs tests are negative, and hemoglobin electrophoresis indicates β-thalassemia trait. Fine-needle aspiration of an axillary lymph node shows reactive hyperplasia. Radiographs show juxta-articular osteopenia of the wrists and bilateral sacroiliitis. Synovial fluid is inflammatory (5318 cells/μL, 90% neutrophils) with negative culture.

Based on this profile, an initial diagnosis of a venous ulcer and a differential diagnosis of a vasculitic ulcer were made; however, color Doppler ultrasonography of the lower limbs and abdomen is normal with no evidence of arteriovenous fistula or venous insufficiency.

A 57-year-old man with follicular non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, localized below the diaphragm with lumbar spine involvement, presented 4 days after his third cycle of R-CHOP with headache, malaise, and fevers up to 102 °F. Four days earlier, a chest CT at an outside hospital showed a right upper lobe opacity concerning for pneumonia; he was treated with 11 days of vancomycin, cefepime, and doxycycline, then discharged on levofloxacin and doxycycline, but continued to feel unwell. He was readmitted with malaise and tachycardia. He had not traveled outside New England and denied animal exposures. On admission, his temperature was 100.5 °F, blood pressure 130/90 mm Hg, heart rate 130 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Examination was unremarkable without lymphadenopathy or skin lesions. Laboratory studies showed lymphopenia (absolute lymphocyte count 250 cells/μL) and hyponatremia (125 mEq/L). Blood, urine, and sputum cultures were negative. A PET/CT performed to evaluate for lymphoma progression showed enlarged, FDG-avid mediastinal lymphadenopathy, new from 3 months earlier, with a maximum SUV of 7, suggestive of active lymphoma. A bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration of a mediastinal lymph node was performed.

A 31-year-old woman, gravida 5 para 4, at 18 weeks’ gestation presented with a 4-month history of progressive bilateral breast swelling associated with erythema and pain. Her baseline breast size was B-cup, and she denied similar changes in prior pregnancies. She was treated with dicloxacillin for presumed mastitis without improvement.  
Bilateral breast ultrasound scans showed no fluid collections or masses. Breast magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated symmetrical skin thickening of both breasts without discrete masses, findings suggestive of mastitis. To exclude inflammatory breast carcinoma, bilateral incisional biopsies were performed; pathology revealed chronic dermal inflammation without evidence of malignancy.  
Laboratory studies, including C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, serum calcium, liver-function tests, and prolactin level, were within normal limits. A repeat biopsy of the right breast demonstrated lymphedema, and tissue cultures were negative.  
The patient was admitted for worsening breast pain. Hormonal studies showed normal prolactin, estradiol, progesterone, and thyrotropin levels. An autoimmune panel revealed a low-titer antinuclear antibody of 1:40, considered nonspecific.  
What is the most likely diagnosis?

48-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with fever and left chest pain. One day prior, after drinking alcohol, he had two episodes of non-bloody vomiting. Immediately after the second, he developed severe left-sided chest pain radiating to his interscapular area, followed by fever and chills. He was initially diagnosed with pneumonia and respiratory failure at a rural hospital and received one dose of ceftriaxone and gentamicin before transfer.

On arrival: blood pressure 100/60 mmHg; pulse 106/min; temperature 37 °C; respiratory rate 26/min; SpO2 96% on 3 L/min nasal oxygen. Examination revealed dullness to percussion, decreased breath sounds, and decreased tactile fremitus over the left lower hemithorax. White blood cell count 11 100/mm3 with 88.7% neutrophils; other blood tests normal.

A chest radiograph at 22:00 showed left hydropneumothorax. He was diagnosed with left lung abscess and acute respiratory failure and started on intravenous antibiotics. Over the next 22 hours, his condition worsened: SpO2 fell to 80% on 6 L/min oxygen, blood pressure dropped to 80/50 mmHg, and he became agitated. A second chest radiograph at 20:00 the next day showed a large left pleural effusion with rightward tracheal deviation. He then underwent fluid resuscitation, diagnostic thoracentesis, and insertion of a left chest tube.

A 45-year-old Ashkenazi Jewish woman presented with a two-month history of mild sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy. She was afebrile, and examination revealed splenomegaly. Laboratory tests showed mild, nonprogressive pancytopenia (platelets 72×10^9/L, lymphocytes 1.7×10^9/L, neutrophils 0.6×10^9/L, hemoglobin 98 g/L), a ferritin level of 111 µg/L, and mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase (159 U/L) and γ-glutamyl transferase (54 U/L) with normal ALT and bilirubin. 

Bone marrow biopsy demonstrated a moderately hypercellular marrow with reduced trilineage hematopoiesis and interstitial aggregates of small, mature CD3+ T cells without hemophagocytosis. Flow cytometry showed no clonal B-cell or abnormal T-cell population (mature T cells 93%; CD4/CD8 ratio 2.4; no aberrant markers; CD30–; ALK–). A subtle monoclonal TCR gene rearrangement peak accounted for about 5% of T cells. PET-CT revealed diffuse marrow uptake and hepatosplenomegaly without lymphadenopathy. 

A presumptive diagnosis of T-cell lymphoma was made. The patient received two cycles of CHOP chemotherapy, with reduced marrow infiltrate but increased splenomegaly. Etoposide was added for four more cycles, each supplemented with G-CSF on days 6, 8, 10, and 12. Post-treatment marrow biopsy showed persistent but reduced T-cell burden, and autologous stem cell transplant was planned. Stem cells were mobilized with daily G-CSF for 10 days. 

Fourteen days after G-CSF completion, laboratory tests revealed worsening pancytopenia. Thirty-four days after G-CSF, she was readmitted with high-grade fevers and increasing splenomegaly. Investigations showed hemoglobin 91 g/L, WBC 0.9×10^9/L, platelets 8×10^9/L; ALT 735 U/L, bilirubin 198 µmol/L, GGT 685 U/L, ALP 785 U/L; ferritin 16 634 µg/L; soluble CD25 > 60 000 pg/mL; fibrinogen 0.9 g/L; normal triglycerides. Serologic and PCR-based tests for hepatitis A–E, CMV, EBV, HIV, HSV, adenovirus, HTLV-1/2 and bacterial/fungal cultures were all negative. 

Repeat bone marrow biopsy showed marked increase in T-cell infiltration without overt hemophagocytosis. Liver core biopsy revealed a dense portal polymorphous lymphoid infiltrate with hepatocellular necrosis; immunohistochemistry showed a mixed, activated T-cell population without abnormal phenotype. A targeted lymphoid NGS panel on liver tissue did not demonstrate hotspot mutations associated with T-cell malignancy. Repeat TCR gene rearrangement on marrow and liver tissue demonstrated a polyclonal pattern.

A 65-year-old Japanese woman with FLT3-ITD–positive acute myeloid leukemia underwent umbilical cord blood transplantation after failing induction chemotherapy and gilteritinib. Thirty-five days after transplantation, she developed dysgeusia and was found to have a serum zinc level of 66 µg/dL (reference range, 80–130 µg/dL). Zinc acetate dihydrate tablets were started that day. On the same day, she experienced vomiting and anorexia and was referred for gastrointestinal evaluation. 

Her medications included amlodipine, lansoprazole, ursodeoxycholic acid, ambroxol, brotizolam, acyclovir, letermovir, Clostridium butyricum preparation, mycophenolate mofetil, and zinc acetate dihydrate. On day 41 after transplantation, esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed multiple reddish spots in the gastric body and shallow ulcers with white coat adhesion in the gastric fornix. Zinc acetate dihydrate was discontinued due to suspected association with the gastric lesions. As a hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipient under immunosuppression, involvement of graft-versus-host disease, transplant-associated microangiopathy, and cytomegalovirus infection were also considered as differential diagnoses of gastric mucosal damage.

A 69-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of progressive lower abdominal pain, nonbloody diarrhea, and vomiting. She denied fever, cough, or dyspnea. Her surgical history was notable for an uncomplicated open cholecystectomy 30 years earlier. She recalled nearly identical symptoms beginning the day after her cholecystectomy and recurring intermittently, managed conservatively on one prior hospitalization without an identified cause. On this admission, her symptoms were more severe than ever.

On examination, she appeared distressed but was afebrile and without jaundice. The abdomen was soft, non-distended, with normoactive bowel sounds and no palpable masses; there was tenderness in the lower abdomen. Laboratory tests showed no pancreatitis, leukocytosis, anemia, or electrolyte abnormalities. Abdominal plain films revealed distended loops of small bowel. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a small-bowel obstruction at the mid-jejunum and a concentric intraluminal ring suggestive of intussusception.

A 43-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with one day of severe shortness of breath, diffuse neck swelling, and neck pain. Six months earlier, she underwent bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for Stage III ovarian immature teratoma followed by six cycles of bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin. Over the preceding four months she had progressive dyspnea; one week before admission she developed fever and severe cough treated at a local hospital. 

On examination, she was in respiratory distress with a respiratory rate of 32/min, SpO2 82% on room air, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, and heart rate 110/min. Subcutaneous emphysema was palpable over the neck and chest wall. Lung auscultation revealed bilateral fine basal crepitations; heart sounds were muffled. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance, a normal metabolic panel, and arterial blood gas with pH 7.42, PaCO2 34 mmHg, and PaO2 65 mmHg. 

Chest radiography demonstrated subcutaneous and mediastinal emphysema with bilateral lower-zone haziness and alveolar opacities. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax revealed bilateral ground-glass opacities, peripheral consolidation, and mediastinal emphysema.

An 8-year-old boy presented with a 3-month history of erythema, scaling, sticky yellow discharge, and patchy hair loss on his frontal scalp. His symptoms worsened despite brief courses of cephalexin, terbinafine, and betamethasone, and he developed pain and swelling of the left tragus and ipsilateral cervical lymph nodes. He had no animal exposures, sports participation, immunodeficiency, or topical steroid use. On examination, he was afebrile and well-appearing. Vital signs were stable. Dermatologic examination revealed a 3 × 4 cm erythematous, scaly plaque on the frontal scalp with yellow, paste-like crusting and relative alopecia, and a tender, swollen left parotid region. Laboratory evaluation showed a hemoglobin of 13.2 g/dL, white-blood-cell count of 13,700/mm3 with 70% neutrophils, an ESR of 25 mm/h, and a mildly elevated CRP. Urinalysis and cultures were negative. A potassium hydroxide preparation of hair and scalp scrapings was performed, and fungal culture was requested for definitive identification.

A 22-year-old woman with ileal and jejunal Crohn’s disease, complicated by rectovulvar fistulae and treated with prednisolone, azathioprine, mesalazine, and infliximab, underwent ileal resection and right hemicolectomy for a pelvic abscess in September. After tapering steroids, she presented in December with six weeks of fever, intense swelling, stiffness, and impaired range of motion of both knees. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (17,000/mm3 with 89% neutrophils) and an elevated ESR (28 mm/h). Bilateral arthrocentesis yielded purulent fluid that grew Streptococcus pneumoniae. She was treated with antibiotics and bilateral arthrotomy; histology confirmed acute septic arthritis. After immobilization and rehabilitation, inflammatory signs resolved, but she developed persistent bilateral knee pain exacerbated by movement, especially on stair climbing. Plain radiographs of the knees demonstrated multiple bilateral hypotransparent areas in the distal femurs, proximal tibiae, and patellas, without subchondral collapse. CT confirmed multiple lacunar areas in the same locations.

A 64-year-old woman with early-stage breast cancer presented with 2 days of weakness, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, and watery nonbloody diarrhea following a restaurant meal. In the emergency department, temperature was 37.4°C, heart rate 156 beats/min, and blood pressure 95/63 mm Hg; she was alert and oriented. Laboratory studies showed WBC 21 430/μL, hemoglobin 14.8 g/dL, platelets 227 000/μL, potassium 3.5 mEq/L, lactate 8.68 mg/dL, creatinine 2.2 mg/dL, BUN 37 mg/dL, and creatine kinase 10 846 U/L. She was diagnosed with hypovolemic shock and acute kidney injury secondary to rhabdomyolysis, received aggressive IV fluids and empiric antibiotics, and was admitted to the ICU.

Over the next five days, she became anuric and transitioned from continuous renal replacement therapy to hemodialysis. She developed severe thrombocytopenia (nadir 50 ×10^3/μL) and anemia (hemoglobin nadir 5.0 g/dL). A peripheral blood smear showed numerous schistocytes and reticulocytosis, and laboratory tests confirmed hemolysis. Cold agglutinin, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria markers, antinuclear antibody, and direct antiglobulin tests were negative. Fecal pathogen PCR was positive for enteropathogenic Escherichia coli. ADAMTS13 activity was 32% (normal > 67%) with a PLASMIC score of 2 (low risk for TTP). Complement levels were low in the acute setting. An atypical HUS genetic panel was negative, and CH50 and C1 esterase inhibitor levels were normal. Other etiologies—including DIC, HELLP syndrome, severe hypertension, medication interactions, autoimmune disease, vitamin B12 deficiency, dialysis-related mechanical hemolysis, and occult malignancy—were ruled out. Urinalysis revealed 3+ hemoglobin without myoglobin, 15 RBCs/HPF, and nephrotic-range proteinuria (2 g/day).

A 67-year-old woman with well-controlled asthma, hypertension, and severe osteoporosis (on denosumab every 6 months for 3 years) was admitted for 3 days of nonmassive hemoptysis and progressive dyspnea. She denied fever, chest pain, orthopnea, edema, or new environmental exposures; she was on no other new medications and had no history of vasculitis or renal disease. On examination, she was in respiratory distress: T 37 °C, BP 167/84 mmHg, HR 98 beats/min, RR 48 breaths/min, SpO2 84% on room air; she had pale conjunctivae, bilateral bronchial breath sounds, and crackles in both lower lung fields. She rapidly progressed to require intubation for hypoxemic respiratory failure. 

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 5.7 g/dL (baseline ~11.6 g/dL), WBC 17,490/µL with 91% neutrophils, platelets 635,000/µL, normal renal and liver function, ESR 119 mm/hr, CRP 141 mg/L, and normal coagulation studies. Urinalysis revealed no hematuria or proteinuria. Arterial blood gas on FiO2 0.6 showed pH 7.37, PaO2 79 mmHg, PaCO2 42 mmHg (PaO2/FiO2 = 131). 

Chest radiography showed new extensive bilateral alveolar opacities, more pronounced at the bases. Chest CT demonstrated diffuse peribronchovascular ground-glass opacities and consolidations in both lower lobes. Echocardiography was normal.

Bronchoscopy revealed minimal blood in basal bronchi; sequential BAL aliquots became progressively bloodier. BAL fluid had 313,000 RBCs/µL and 1,265 WBCs/µL (82% neutrophils), with no organisms on Gram, AFB, or fungal stains. Transbronchial biopsy showed organizing diffuse alveolar damage without evidence of vasculitis or granuloma. Anti–GBM antibodies, ANA, antiphospholipid antibodies, rheumatoid factor, complement levels, MPO-ANCA, and PR3-ANCA were sent.

A 37-week–gestation male neonate was born to a 24-year-old primigravida by uncomplicated vaginal delivery. The birth weight was 2640 g, and anthropometric measurements were normal. No resuscitation was required. On day 1, a small blister was noted over the ring finger of the left hand. Over the next 2 days, additional blisters appeared over the medial malleoli, dorsal feet, knuckles, flexural wrists, neck, and perioral region—sites corresponding to mechanical trauma. The blisters were well defined, some eroded spontaneously. There was no involvement of mucous membranes, scalp, nails, oral cavity, palms, or soles, and the infant remained hemodynamically stable without systemic signs.  
The mother had lifelong blistering of lesser severity over trauma-prone sites, followed by hyperpigmented scarring and itching, along with nail deformities of the hands and feet. No other family members were affected.  
Ultrasonography of the abdomen, echocardiography, and neurosonogram were normal.

A 35-year-old man of Asian Indian descent with no prior neurologic disease presented on day 1 with frontal and binocular ocular pain and a rapid decline in visual acuity. He had normal brain CT and retinal fluorescein angiography. Routine blood tests, renal and hepatic panels, fasting glucose, complete blood count, inflammatory markers, serum proteins, iron studies, vitamin B12, folate, urinalysis, and toxicology (blood lead, trichloroethanol; urine methanol, trichloroacetic acid, lead) were all within normal limits or undetectable. Tests for systemic infection were negative. Visual-evoked potentials showed delayed P100 latency bilaterally. He was diagnosed with bilateral optic neuritis and received IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days without improvement in vision.

On day 5, he developed rapidly worsening paraparesis with bladder dysfunction. Brain and total spinal cord MRI revealed an 8 mm T2-hyperintense, noncontrast-enhancing lesion in the left parietal subcortical white matter, additional small nonspecific T2-hyperintense subcortical lesions, and three thoracic spinal cord lesions (<3 vertebral segments) that were T2-hyperintense, T1-isointense, and contrast-enhancing.

On day 20, neurologic examination showed paraparetic gait (right > left), lower-limb weakness with mild right spasticity, hyperreflexia with right ankle clonus, bilateral Babinski signs, and visual acuity reduced to hand motion in both eyes. Cognition and upper-limb function were intact. CSF analysis revealed protein 71 mg/dL, 4 cells/mm^3, and absence of oligoclonal bands. CNS infectious workup was negative. Serum screening for autoimmune diseases (ANA, ENA panel, ANCA, AMA, ASMA, APCA, anticardiolipin, anti-TPO, anti-TG, ACE) was negative, and serum neoplastic markers were normal. Both serum myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein IgG and aquaporin-4 IgG, tested by cell-based assays and repeated in a second laboratory, were negative. A second course of IV methylprednisolone was administered, yielding partial improvement in paraparesis but no change in visual deficit.

A 33-year-old G2P2 woman from Vietnam presented with a 2-week history of acute abdominal pain, diarrhea, infrequent melena, nausea, and headache. She had been taking ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily for 10 days for abdominal pain. She denied pet contact, raw meat ingestion, or geophagia in her family. Vital signs were normal. On examination she was in moderate distress with a distended abdomen consistent with ascites and diffuse abdominal tenderness.  
Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 27.4 cells/mm³, with 11.6 K/μL eosinophils and 11 K/μL neutrophils; other routine serum studies were normal. Empiric intravenous ceftriaxone and metronidazole were started for presumed intra-abdominal infection. Ultrasound-guided paracentesis yielded 1,040 mL of cloudy amber fluid. Fluid analysis showed 15 RBCs/mm³ and 6.1 nucleated cells/mm³, of which 93% (5,704) were eosinophils; cultures for aerobic and acid-fast bacilli showed no growth.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated extensive circumferential wall thickening from the distal esophagus through the small bowel and a large volume of proteinaceous ascites; the colon was spared. Liver Doppler ultrasound was unremarkable. Serologic tests for hepatitis, complement C4, C1-esterase inhibitor, tuberculosis, HIV, gonorrhea, chlamydia, stool pathogens, and urinalysis were all negative or normal.  
Upper endoscopy was grossly normal except for nonbleeding erosive gastropathy. Biopsy specimens from the midesophagus, distal esophagus, gastric antrum, and duodenum showed marked intraepithelial eosinophilia (32 eosinophils per high-power field in the midesophagus, 50 per HPF in the distal esophagus, and similar findings in the stomach and duodenum). Intravenous methylprednisolone was initiated.

A 27-year-old woman, gravida 1 at 17 weeks’ gestation, presented with one month of left-sided neck pain that began at 12 weeks, radiated to the jaw, and intensified over the last five days to the point of disrupting sleep. She denied chills, fever, palpitations, tremor, or sweating. She had no personal or family history of thyroid disease and a normal menstrual history. On examination, temperature was 37.4 °C, heart rate 98 beats/min, and blood pressure 110/70 mmHg. The thyroid gland was bilaterally enlarged, firm, and tender to palpation. Laboratory results at 12 weeks showed: TT4 122.2 ng/mL (50–130), TT3 1.481 ng/mL (0.8–1.9), FT4 9.444 pmol/L (9.1–24.8), FT3 4.321 pmol/L (3.3–9.15), TSH 0.149 µIU/mL (0.27–4.2), anti-thyroglobulin antibody <6% (<30%), TPO antibody <5% (<34%), TRAb 4.3 U/L (<12), and ESR 31 mm/h (0–20). At 14 weeks: TT4 222.1 ng/mL, TT3 3.07 ng/mL, TSH 0.058 µIU/mL. At 17 weeks: TT4 255.4 ng/mL, TT3 3.18 ng/mL, TSH 0.005 µIU/mL. Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a solid hypoechoic area in the left lobe, suggestive of an inflammatory thyroid process.

A 63-year-old male farmer presented with a 10-day history of a painless ulcer in the oral cavity and 3 days of bilateral earache and throat pain. He had no fever, weight loss, or systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a single 1.8 cm ulcer on the left alveolar mucosa involving the premolar and molar region, with an irregular, friable margin and bleeding on touch; it extended laterally into the gingivolabial sulcus and medially toward the soft palate. The incisors, canine, and first premolar teeth on that side were intact. The oropharynx was congested. Vital signs were normal.

Routine hematological and biochemical investigations were unremarkable. A chest radiograph showed no abnormalities, and there was no radiographic evidence of underlying bone involvement. Serological tests for syphilis and HIV were negative.

A 73-year-old man from California presented with a 2-month history of cough and a right lung mass, along with mild intermittent headache. Two months earlier, he had received a 5-day course of oral levofloxacin for presumed pneumonia; symptoms recurred one week after finishing therapy. He had no significant past medical or surgical history, denied medications, and reported a 30 pack-year smoking history. He had traveled to Alaska and Argentina six months earlier for hunting and fishing, and denied animal exposures, tick bites, or sick contacts.

On examination, temperature was 99.2 °F, blood pressure 130/70 mm Hg, pulse 80 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. Respiratory examination revealed decreased breath sounds over the right middle lobe. The remainder of his cardiovascular, neurologic, abdominal, and skin examinations was unremarkable.

Initial laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. Tests for tuberculosis and fungal infection were negative: interferon gamma release assay, serum β-d-glucan, serum Aspergillus galactomannan antigen, serum Coccidioides antibodies, and urine Histoplasma antigen all were negative.

Chest CT showed a 3.6 cm mass in the right middle lobe. The patient underwent excisional biopsy of the lung lesion, and Gram staining revealed branching gram-positive rods consistent with Nocardia species. Contrast CT of the head was unremarkable; however, brain MRI demonstrated a 0.8 cm ring-enhancing lesion in the left frontal cortex and a 0.6 cm ring-enhancing lesion in the left temporal lobe.

On hospital day 6, he developed posterior right knee pain with a palpable lump. MRI of the right knee showed a 2.5 × 2.4 cm ill-defined mass in the distal gastrocnemius muscle. Fine-needle aspiration of the knee lesion revealed granulation tissue with plasma cells, macrophages, and neutrophils, but cultures yielded no growth. HIV testing was negative, and CD4 count was within the normal range.

A 19-month-old boy was brought to the emergency department after an episode of reduced consciousness while bathing. His parents reported that when lukewarm water was poured over his chest, he turned blue around the lips and began gasping for air. During this time, his eyes “rolled back,” and he did not interact with his parents. There were no clonic movements, and he did not respond to physical stimulation. He subsequently fell asleep for approximately 1 hour and was brought to the ED.

On arrival, he was alert and appeared well. There were no focal findings on examination, his development was appropriate, and laboratory studies—including a blood glucose level of 5.5 mmol/L—were normal. His parents reported similar, less profound episodes during bathing over the previous 2 weeks, in which his head would go back, his eyes would roll upward, and he would become floppy and limp for 2–3 minutes, followed by sleepiness. These episodes occurred only during bathing; contact with water in other settings did not provoke symptoms. He had normal developmental milestones and no significant past medical or family history.

An electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus rhythm with a normal QT interval. Bathing in lukewarm water while his vital signs were monitored provoked hypotonia, tachycardia, and brief apnea with associated desaturation. He stared straight ahead and made mouthing movements; he was removed from the bath, given high-flow oxygen, and again slept for about 1 hour. A further similar episode occurred later while he was sleeping, without any provocation. The first interictal EEG was normal using the standard 10–20 system. Because he was clinically well between episodes and there was an avoidable trigger, he was discharged with plans for follow-up investigations, including a brain MRI, a bathing EEG, and outpatient review.

A 76-year-old woman presented with acute paresthesia of the left hand and face. Examination revealed left-sided hemiparesis with hypoesthesia and hypoalgesia, accompanied by neuropsychological symptoms. Noncontrast head CT showed no acute ischemia or hemorrhage. Initial brain MRI demonstrated a subcortical lesion in the right hemisphere, interpreted as a lacunar infarct. Despite standard treatment for cerebral ischemia, her hemiparesis progressed, and she was transferred to a neurology unit. Repeat MRI showed new T2-weighted hyperintense lesions in the right thalamus and left subcortical regions, while other periventricular and subcortical white-matter lesions remained unchanged. Diffusion-weighted imaging revealed abnormal diffusion in the right thalamus. On T1-weighted postgadolinium imaging, many lesions—both old and new—showed patchy, faint enhancement not present on the initial study. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed mild pleocytosis and elevated protein. CSF studies excluded bacterial meningoencephalitis, Lyme disease, tick-borne encephalitis, Herpes-simplex virus types 1 and 2, and Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease.

A previously healthy male infant, born at term after an uneventful pregnancy to first-cousin parents, presented at 9 months of age when his parents noted he could not sit unsupported. By 12 months, he developed sudden jerky movements of his extremities, trunk, and eyes, diagnosed as myoclonus, and exhibited psychomotor regression with loss of sitting, crawling, babbling, and social engagement. Examination showed dysmorphic facial features (low-set ears, up-slanted palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, depressed nasal bridge), generalized hypotonia, brisk reflexes, and no organomegaly or skin lesions. Initial laboratory tests—including complete blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes, thyroid function, and plasma lactate—were within normal limits. Noncontrast CT and brain MRI were normal. EEG demonstrated generalized slowing with spikes and slow waves without photic sensitivity. 

At 18 months, he had his first generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Neurologic exam revealed worsening hypotonia and developmental regression. He lost the ability to sit, track objects, and recognize familiar faces, and developed a frequent laugh. Ophthalmologic evaluation showed a hypopigmented fundus with slight temporal disc pallor. Repeat MRI showed mild generalized brain atrophy and white matter disease. Follow-up EEG revealed generalized high-amplitude sharply contoured delta slowing intermixed with theta and alpha activity, with disorganized spikes and sharp waves; photic stimulation was not performed. Despite phenobarbital, levetiracetam, valproate, and clonazepam, generalized seizures and action myoclonus increased in frequency. The clinical presentation suggested neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis among other possibilities, and whole-exome sequencing was requested.

A 17-year-old female with a history of depression, anxiety, chronic abdominal pain, and heavy painful menses managed with oral contraceptives presented with a two-week history of worsening constant dull pelvic pain accompanied by nausea, bilious emesis, and mild chest pain. Four days earlier, she had been prescribed hyoscyamine with minimal relief. She admitted to smoking 5–7 cigarettes daily and denied alcohol or drug use. 

On examination, she was tachycardic and hypertensive; cardiac auscultation was normal without murmurs. Abdominal examination revealed diffuse lower-quadrant and pelvic tenderness without distention; cervical motion tenderness and white vaginal discharge were noted. A wet preparation was negative for trichomonas, yeast, and clue cells. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 30 850/mm3 with 52.4% eosinophils. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated duodenal and proximal jejunal wall thickening with edema, upper abdominal ascites, and a collapsed hemorrhagic cyst in the left adnexa.

She received intravenous doxycycline, cefotetan, and analgesics; gynecology recommended medical management for a presumed ruptured ovarian cyst and possible culture-negative pelvic inflammatory disease. On hospital day 2, she developed bilious emesis, severe hypotension, and hypoxemia and was transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit for suspected septic shock, where she was intubated and started on inotropic support. An exploratory laparotomy revealed edematous, thickened proximal jejunum with full-thickness enteritis, serosal erosion with omental adherence, and pale bowel with lymphadenopathy; a diverting jejunostomy was performed. Despite maximal ventilatory support, she progressed to multiorgan dysfunction and was placed on venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated severe mitral regurgitation from a nonfunctioning valve and moderate left atrial enlargement.

A 35-year-old man with no past medical history presented with a 1-month history of jaundice and generalized pruritus. He is nonalcoholic, monogamous, and has taken an unspecified homeopathic remedy every other day for 6 months for musculoskeletal pain. On examination, he appeared pale and jaundiced, with a heart rate of 110 bpm, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, and temperature 100°F. He had widespread excoriations, bilateral scleral icterus, and mild hepatomegaly; the rest of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 9.5 g/dl, leukocytes 7000/mm3 (78% neutrophils), and normocytic normochromic anemia. Liver tests showed total bilirubin 26.5 mg/dl, AST 140 U/l, ALT 639 U/l, ALP 350 U/l, GGT 40 U/l, and total protein 5.5 g/dl. Inflammatory markers were elevated (ESR 50 mm/h, ferritin >1500 ng/ml, normal transferrin saturation), and viral serologies for hepatitis A, B, C, E, and HIV were negative. Malaria and dengue tests were negative. Renal function, urinalysis, and blood/urine cultures were normal.

Chest radiograph was normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed mild hepatomegaly with normal biliary anatomy. Upper endoscopy revealed mild gastric ulceration without varices. Slit‐lamp examination and 24-hour urinary copper excretion were normal.

A 78-year-old woman presented with nausea, diffuse sharp abdominal pain, and fatigue for three to four days. The pain was nonremitting and not related to food intake. She denied fever, vomiting, or changes in bowel habits. One week earlier, she had received an intra-articular cortisone injection into her left wrist for carpal tunnel syndrome and had received a similar injection into her right shoulder two months before presentation. Her medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, insomnia, and gastroesophageal reflux disease; medications were gabapentin, insulin, and mirtazapine.

On admission, blood pressure was 115/69 mm Hg without orthostasis, heart rate 68 beats/min, and BMI 21.0 kg/m2. Physical examination showed mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without guarding or rigidity. Laboratory studies revealed serum sodium 122 mmol/L (126 mmol/L corrected for hyperglycemia), chloride 87 mmol/L, potassium 5.2 mmol/L, glucose 275 mg/dL, creatinine 0.7 mg/dL, serum osmolality 277 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 240 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 55 mmol/L, and urine potassium 9 mmol/L; these findings were consistent with euvolemic hypotonic hyponatremia. A morning cortisol level at 6:18 AM was <0.5 μg/dL. A high-dose (250 μg) cosyntropin stimulation test revealed a subnormal cortisol response with a relatively low ACTH. Further testing showed ACTH 8.7 pg/mL, aldosterone <1 ng/dL, plasma renin activity 1.13 ng/mL/h, and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate 15.1 μg/dL. Prolactin, follicle-stimulating hormone, and luteinizing hormone were within postmenopausal ranges. Pituitary MRI identified a 3–4 mm lesion consistent with a microadenoma; endocrinology deemed it unlikely to explain the adrenal suppression. She was diagnosed with secondary adrenal insufficiency.

A 74-year-old man with a history of myelodysplastic syndrome underwent open cholecystectomy via a right subcostal incision after difficulty removing an impacted stone laparoscopically. Four days after surgery, the surgical wound became erythematous. The wound was opened, cleansed with sterile saline, and treated with moist dressings for presumed surgical-site infection. Despite these measures, inflammation spread with erosion. On postoperative day 10, intra–wound continuous negative-pressure and irrigation therapy was initiated, yet the wound continued to enlarge with a purulent coating and was accompanied by edema extending from the lower back to the lower extremities. Systemic antibiotics and local irrigation failed to improve the condition. Bacteriological examination detected Enterococcus faecalis and Pseudomonas aeruginosa in low counts. Given the lack of response to standard treatments, a biopsy of the skin surrounding the wound was performed to analyze the pathological condition.

A 44-year-old African American man with end-stage renal disease due to hypertensive nephrosclerosis underwent a four–antigen–mismatch, flow–crossmatch–negative deceased donor kidney transplant. He received basiliximab induction and maintenance immunosuppression with tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone. Donor CMV status was positive and recipient negative; he received trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and valganciclovir prophylaxis.

Postoperatively, he had slow graft function, with a serum creatinine level >3.0 mg/dL on day 5 without dialysis. By day 19, the creatinine fell to 2.33 mg/dL (eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73 m^2). On day 22, the creatinine rose to 2.81 mg/dL (eGFR 30) and urinalysis showed 10–100 RBCs/μL and a few atypical epithelial cells but no decoy cells. Tacrolimus trough levels were 8–10 ng/mL, and volume status was adequate. On day 24, renal ultrasound showed increased parenchymal echogenicity with poor corticomedullary differentiation and normal perfusion and resistive indices.

A renal allograft biopsy revealed diffuse severe interstitial inflammation with macrophages, neutrophils, lymphocytes, and noncaseating granulomas; extensive necrosis; and basophilic, hyperchromatic, smudgy intranuclear inclusion bodies in tubular epithelial cells. There was widespread tubular basement membrane disruption, minimal tubulitis, and no glomerular inflammation or vasculitis. Immunostains for polyoma (BK virus) and CMV were negative. Immunofluorescence for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q, fibrinogen, κ, λ, and C4d were negative. Periodic acid–Schiff and Jones stains were negative for bacteria or fungi. Blood and urine cultures, routine viral cultures, and PCR assays for Epstein–Barr virus, CMV, and BK virus were all negative. Electron microscopy demonstrated viral particles of varying densities in the nuclei of tubular epithelial cells.

A 36-year-old man with no past medical history received his first dose of the inactivated COVID-19 vaccine BIBP (Sinopharm). Twenty-four hours later, he noted numbness in his left arm and leg accompanied by headache. On the next day, he developed facial asymmetry and worsening consciousness. On admission, he was afebrile, with stable vital signs, Glasgow Coma Scale score of 13, and agitation. Neurologic examination revealed left hemiplegia with hypotonia of the left hemibody and left facial paralysis; deep tendon reflexes and plantar responses were bilaterally present, and proprioception and vibration sensation were intact.  
Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 6.26 mg/L; white blood cell count 8830/mm3; procalcitonin 0.02 ng/mL; lactate dehydrogenase 256 UI/L; ferritin 41 ng/L; D-dimer 250 µg/L; fibrinogen 3.1 g/L; normal platelet and lymphocyte counts; normal coagulation profile and renal function. A noncontrast brain CT scan demonstrated a right deep parietal ischemic infarct. Cerebral MRI confirmed extensive superficial and deep right parietal ischemia with early hemorrhagic change; MR angiography of the supra-aortic vessels was normal.

A 50-year-old man presented with 20 days of persistent, involuntary movements of the right arm and leg that ceased only during sleep and severely impaired his daily activities. One month earlier, he had developed polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss and was diagnosed with diabetes mellitus, for which he was prescribed metformin and glimepiride but proved poorly compliant.

On examination, he was alert and cooperative but undernourished. He had nonrhythmic, jerky, flailing movements of the right upper and lower limbs consistent with hemichorea with a ballistic component. Vital signs were: pulse 90 /min regular, blood pressure 120/80 mm Hg, random capillary glucose 18 mmol/L. Higher functions and cranial nerves were normal. There was no tremor, rigidity, cerebellar signs, or sensory deficits. Muscle strength and reflexes were normal; gait was unstable. Other systemic examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin A1C 15.1% (141.5 mmol/mol), fasting glucose 14.2 mmol/L, postprandial glucose 19.1 mmol/L, hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, ESR 21 mm/h, normal leukocyte and platelet counts. Urinalysis demonstrated sugar (++), no albumin, and no ketones. Serum creatinine and electrolytes were within normal limits.

Noncontrast CT of the head was unremarkable. Brain MRI demonstrated a T1 hyperintense lesion in the left caudate and lentiform nuclei that was iso- to hyperintense on T2/FLAIR, with no diffusion restriction and no enhancement after contrast administration.

A 40-year-old man presented with a 15-day history of anorexia, chronic abdominal pain, and progressive obstructive jaundice. He had no significant medical history. On examination, he was icteric with scleral icterus but had no stigmata of chronic liver disease. Laboratory studies showed a cholestatic pattern of liver function tests.  
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed homogeneous hepatomegaly, dilation of the extrahepatic bile duct (15 mm), dilated intrahepatic bile radicles, and mild ascites without an obvious obstructing lesion.  
Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated narrowing of the distal common bile duct with a thick, hyperenhancing wall in the portal phase; upstream dilation of the gallbladder and biliary tree; hepatomegaly; splenomegaly; mild peritoneal effusion; and enlarged perisplenic, mesenteric, and porta hepatis lymph nodes with central necrosis compressing the portal vein and collateral venous circulation. Thoracic CT was unremarkable.  
Abdominal MRI showed an 18 mm long, asymmetric distal common bile duct stricture with luminal irregularity and 4 mm wall thickening that hyperenhanced relative to liver parenchyma during the portal phase, resulting in upstream biliary and gallbladder dilation, with additional signs of proximal cholangitis and portal hypertension. These imaging findings were consistent with a malignant biliary stricture.

A 57-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with 2 days of diffuse abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. He was tachycardic and hypotensive on arrival, and developed monomorphic ventricular tachycardia requiring synchronized cardioversion. Laboratory studies showed ketonuria, hyperglycemia (470 mg/dL), metabolic acidosis (pH 7.27, bicarbonate 15 mEq/L), AST 2356 U/L, ALT 2438 U/L, thrombocytopenia (9380 platelets/µL), and rising total bilirubin (1.59 mg/dL). Viral hepatitis and flavivirus serologies were negative. Physical examination revealed mild right upper-quadrant tenderness without fever; other vital signs were stable. On day 2, abdominal ultrasound with Doppler showed multiple heterogeneous nodular lesions in both hepatic lobes without portal vein or hepatic artery thrombosis. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated multiple hypoattenuating, heterogeneous liver lesions with slight peripheral enhancement and a wedge-shaped transition between affected and normal peripheral parenchyma. A repeat CT on day 10 was unchanged but incidentally revealed a right subsegmental pulmonary embolism. MRI on day 16 confirmed multiple irregular nodular lesions with slight peripheral gadolinium enhancement. Because of persistent cholestasis and uncertainty regarding these lesions, an ultrasound-guided liver biopsy was planned.

A 41-year-old nulliparous woman presented with four months of lower abdominal pain following a midline cesarean delivery at 22 weeks’ gestation for fetal demise complicated by chorioamnionitis. One month after surgery, diagnostic hysteroscopy revealed a posterior uterine myoma without intrauterine adhesions.
