Thereafter, she experienced persistent abdominal pain and intermittent metrorrhagia, prompting multiple gynecologic evaluations. In December, she received seven days of oral metronidazole and amoxicillin–clavulanate “for suspicion of endometritis,” but her symptoms did not improve. In early February, she noted a tender, erythematous lesion in the right iliac fossa, worsening abdominal pain, metrorrhagia, purulent vaginal discharge, anorexia, and an 8-kg weight loss over two months. She was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 13.7×10^9/L, C-reactive protein of 244 mg/L, and hemoglobin of 87 g/L. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 7.5×7.5×11 cm fluid collection extending from the right antero-lateral uterine fundus to the anterior abdominal wall.

A 63-year-old man with a history of hypertension and hypercholesterolemia presented with a 2-week history of nonbloody, nonmucoid, watery diarrhea occurring more than 20 times daily, intermittent abdominal pain, nausea, and an 8-kg weight loss. He had been taking atorvastatin (20 mg daily) and olmesartan (20 mg daily) since 2019. He had no prior surgeries. Initial empirical treatment with nitazoxanide (3 days) and ciprofloxacin (500 mg twice daily for 7 days) yielded no improvement. There was no fever, and physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory evaluation revealed a white-cell count of 7420 cells/µL, hemoglobin of 14.4 g/dL, platelets of 174 × 10^3/µL, sodium 138 meq/L, potassium 3.8 meq/L, blood urea nitrogen 26 mg/dL, creatinine 1.05 mg/dL, ALT 65 U/L, and AST 51 U/L. Stool studies including culture, Clostridium difficile assay, leukocytes, ova and parasites, and fecal calprotectin were negative; fecal occult blood was initially positive. Serologic tests including tissue transglutaminase IgA, perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, and anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies were normal; TSH, C-reactive protein, and COVID-19 serologies were unremarkable. Colonoscopy with serial biopsies was normal. Abdominal ultrasonography showed gallbladder wall thickening, echogenic bile, hydrops, acalculous cholecystitis, and mild steatohepatitis. Gastroscopy demonstrated a small hiatal hernia, erythematous gastritis with mucosal erosions, and in the second part of the duodenum mucosal atrophy with loss of folds. Biopsies of the second portion of the duodenum revealed a severe atrophic mucosa with complete loss of villi and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes.

A man in his 60s with HIV on antiretroviral therapy and a history of pacemaker implantation for complete heart block (3 years earlier) and subsequent ICD upgrade for ventricular tachycardia presented with 4 months of exertional dyspnea without palpitations. Echocardiography, CT angiography, endomyocardial biopsy, and gallium scintigraphy were unremarkable. A 12‐lead ECG showed atrial flutter with sawtooth waves in the inferior leads and a tachycardia cycle length of 330 ms. During electrophysiological study under sedation, catheters were placed in the coronary sinus, right atrial septum, and tricuspid annulus. Intracardiac electrograms showed craniocaudal activation in the lateral right atrium, caudocranial activation in the septal right atrium, and proximal-to-distal activation in the coronary sinus. Entrainment pacing from the high and low lateral right atrium and the ostial coronary sinus yielded post-pacing intervals matching the tachycardia cycle length, whereas pacing from the distal coronary sinus did not. Because the cycle length was relatively long for typical flutter, high-resolution activation and voltage mapping of the right atrium was performed. The activation map accounted for only 60% of the cycle length, and the voltage map revealed extensive transverse low-voltage scar in the septal-posterior right atrium.

A 22-year-old woman with no comorbidities was diagnosed with infiltrating ductal carcinoma of the right breast during lactation; receptor status was ER 5%, PR 70%, HER2 negative, Ki-67 95%. Staging PET revealed a right breast lesion with right axillary and internal mammary lymphadenopathy and a 16×12 mm right lower lobe pulmonary nodule. She began a TAC chemotherapy regimen (docetaxel 75 mg/m², doxorubicin 50 mg/m², cyclophosphamide 600 mg/m²) with pegfilgrastim support. On day 7 after chemotherapy she developed an 8/10 right‐sided abdominal pain, obstinate constipation since the day of therapy, and fever. Examination showed abdominal tenderness. Laboratory tests revealed a neutrophil count of 500/mm³. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated circumferential thickening of the ascending colon, cecum, and proximal transverse colon measuring 15 mm, with diffuse mucosal hyperemia and marked submucosal hypodensity.

A 21-year-old previously healthy woman presented with a 2-month history of recurrent, dull upper abdominal pain lasting 1–2 days approximately twice weekly, often accompanied by fever and, on a few occasions, nausea and vomiting. The symptoms began after a 1-week episode of gastroenteritis on return from a backpacking holiday in Southeast Asia; she had no further diarrhea and no weight loss. She denied urinary or bowel changes and had no known aggravating or relieving factors.

On examination, she had localized tenderness in the right lower quadrant without palpable masses. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 7.9×10^9/L (normal 3.5–8.8×10^9/L), C-reactive protein 37 mg/L (normal <10 mg/L), normal hemoglobin and liver enzymes, negative urine pregnancy test, and fecal calprotectin <30×10^−6 (normal <50×10^−6). Extensive microbiological investigations—including malaria testing (×3), blood cultures, stool cultures and PCR for bacteria, viruses, and parasites, and serologies for HIV, hepatitis A–C, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein–Barr virus—were all negative.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 10 mm thickened, hypoechoic, hyperemic appendix with moderate periappendicular edema and no abscess or perforation.

A 35-year-old European woman, gravida 1 para 0, with an unplanned pregnancy presented for antenatal care at 35 weeks’ gestation. Her medical history included asthma managed with a salbutamol inhaler. At presentation, her weight was 147 kg (BMI 54 kg/m2). An oral glucose tolerance test was normal, and throughout antenatal visits she remained normotensive with no proteinuria. She reported dyspnoea on exertion, bilateral leg swelling, and marked weight gain, which were attributed to her pregnancy.

At 40 weeks + 3 days, she developed bilateral leg erythema, oedema, and tenderness; Doppler ultrasound excluded deep venous thrombosis, and she received antibiotics and physiotherapy. A fetal ultrasound estimated the weight at 4755 g and noted polyhydramnios. At 41 weeks + 1 day, after prelabour rupture of membranes and 6 hours of unsuccessful oxytocin induction, an emergency caesarean section was performed. Intraoperatively, subcutaneous abdominal oedema and ascites were noted. A healthy male infant weighing 4750 g was delivered without complications. She was started on prophylactic antibiotics and low-molecular-weight heparin postoperatively.

On postpartum day 4, she complained of chest tightness and dyspnoea. Examination showed tachycardia (heart rate elevated), normotension, and no fever. Oxygen saturation was 97% on room air; arterial blood gas analysis was normal. Lung auscultation revealed bilateral wheezes; cardiac examination noted an S3 gallop. Electrocardiography demonstrated normal sinus rhythm. A computed tomography scan of the chest showed mild inflammatory changes and ruled out pulmonary embolism. She was commenced on antibiotics, nebulisers, and intravenous hydrocortisone for presumed asthma exacerbation secondary to chest infection.

A 52-year-old woman was referred for left-eye corneal ulceration and pain 8 days after intravitreal ranibizumab injection for diabetic macular edema. Her left-eye visual acuity was count-fingers. Slit-lamp examination revealed a 5 × 5 mm ring-shaped stromal infiltrate with a 3 × 3 mm central epithelial defect staining with fluorescein, surrounded by chemosis and corneal edema. Corneal smears and cultures, including those for atypical pathogens, were obtained. In vivo confocal microscopy showed possible double-walled cysts in two images from one sequence. She was started on fortified vancomycin and tobramycin drops, topical chlorhexidine, and oral valacyclovir. All smears and cultures remained negative. After 2 weeks, fortified antibiotics were discontinued and ofloxacin 0.3% four times daily plus polymyxin/bacitracin ointment nightly were initiated. At 3 and 5 weeks, repeat smears, cultures, and confocal microscopy remained negative. At 6 weeks, chlorhexidine was discontinued and the ring infiltrate was unchanged.

A 55-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with sudden onset of severe abdominal pain. On arrival, his blood pressure was 95/56 mmHg and heart rate was 55 beats/minute. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed high-density fluid localized in the left greater omentum, consistent with hemorrhagic ascites, and the left omental artery showed focal dilatation and stenosis with adjacent hematoma, compatible with a sentinel clot sign. There was no evidence of arterial calcification or other signs of atherosclerosis on imaging. Laboratory studies, including inflammatory markers and a vasculitis screen, were within normal limits, and there were no clinical features to suggest systemic vasculitis. Segmental arterial mediolysis of the left omental artery was suspected as the source of bleeding, and transarterial embolization was planned after obtaining informed consent.

A 26-year-old man returned to the UK after three months of travel through Southeast Asia, including Thailand, Nepal, and India, with a non-healing ulcer on his left lower leg. He recalled an insect bite just above the lateral malleolus in Thailand that became erythematous, then enlarged and ulcerated. Despite surgical debridement in Nepal and India and multiple courses of oral antibiotics, the lesion failed to heal, and two new adjacent ulcers appeared. He remained systemically well without fever, lymphadenopathy, or organ dysfunction.

On examination, there were three undermined ulcers on the distal left leg with violaceous edges; there was no surrounding cellulitis. Laboratory tests showed a normal complete blood count, urea, electrolytes, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein. Serologic studies for HIV, Schistosoma, Strongyloides, Mycoplasma, and Leishmania were negative. Antinuclear antibody was weakly positive (1:80, nucleolar), and double-stranded DNA was negative. MRI of the left leg revealed no tendinopathy or osteomyelitis.

An incisional skin biopsy demonstrated ulceration with overlying acanthotic epithelium and a deep dermal infiltrate of neutrophils, lymphocytes, histiocytes, and plasma cells; there was no granuloma, vasculitis, malignancy, or viral inclusions. Special stains (Gram, DPAS, Grocott, Giemsa, Ziehl-Neelsen, and Wade-Fite) were negative. Tissue bacterial and fungal cultures produced no significant growth, and Leishmania PCR was negative.

A 47-year-old man with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidaemia presented to his general practitioner with the sudden onset of lower back pain that began during sexual intercourse and radiated down his right leg. He was initially diagnosed with acute disc prolapse and referred for neurosurgical evaluation. An MRI scan showed no evidence of spinal cord pathology, and he was advised that the pain was probably musculoskeletal and would settle. Over the next six weeks, the pain persisted and increased in severity, and he noted claudication-type pain in his right leg after walking approximately 100 metres. He returned to his general practitioner. On examination, the heart rate was 68 beats per minute and regular. Blood pressure was 160/80 mmHg in the left arm and 130/70 mmHg in the right arm. Cardiac examination was normal, and there was no palpable abdominal aortic aneurysm. Examination of the right lower limb revealed absent pulses, whereas left lower limb pulses were present and of good volume.

A 70-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of continuous, severe, frontoparietal headache rated 10/10 on a visual analogue scale. The pounding pain was constant, disrupted his sleep, and was provoked by movement. He also reported right-sided otalgia for 9 months. He denied nausea, vomiting, or autonomic features but had photophobia and scalp tenderness when combing his hair; there was no jaw claudication.  

His medical history was significant for diabetes, hypertension, deep vein thrombosis, and atrial fibrillation treated with oral anticoagulation. He had no prior history of headaches. Neurological examination was normal except for tenderness over the skull; there was no papilledema. Vital signs, including blood pressure and temperature, were normal.  

Noncontrast CT of the head, performed 7 days after presentation, showed a lytic lesion of the skull base, largest beneath the occiput and right petrous bone. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 7.3 mmol/L (normal 8.0–10.5), leukocyte count 10.5×10^9/L (normal 3–10), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 42 mm/h, and C-reactive protein 89 mg/L (<8 mg/L). Serum protein electrophoresis showed an M‐protein of 4 g/L (IgG kappa) with free kappa light chains elevated at 35.3 mg/L (normal 3.3–19.4 mg/L).  

18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated a metabolically active skull base lesion suspicious for malignancy but revealed no other sites of disease. MRI of the brain revealed a large destructive lesion centered at the right petrous apex, extending to the clivus, across to the contralateral side of C1, eroding into the right sphenoidal sinus, mastoid, middle ear, and adjacent soft tissues, with areas suggestive of necrosis or abscess formation.  

The differential diagnosis included multiple myeloma, skull base osteomyelitis, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, metastasis, and inflammatory diseases.

A previously healthy 5-year-old girl of Middle Eastern heritage presented with spontaneous bruising and well-demarcated purpura on her face, extremities, and trunk, sparing the mucous membranes. She had progressive periorbital edema and swelling of her upper arms and thighs over 2 days; the purpuric areas were warm and painful to touch. Two days before presentation, she had a prodrome of mild cough and coryza without fever; low-grade temperatures (up to 37.5°C) were recorded in hospital. She was born at term without complications, had normal growth and development, no surgical history, and no personal or family history of bleeding; her parents are first cousins. There was no history of drug ingestion or toxin exposure. On examination, she was afebrile, normotensive, hemodynamically stable, and euvolemic. Urinalysis was normal; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Full blood examination was within normal limits; electrolytes, renal and liver function tests were normal; C-reactive protein was 26 mg/L. Coagulation studies showed an INR of 5.7, PT 57.1 seconds, and aPTT of 95 seconds. Mixing studies with normal plasma corrected both PT and aPTT. Fibrinogen level was 3.2 g/L (normal range 1.5–4.0), largely excluding disseminated intravascular coagulation.

A 54-year-old right-handed Caucasian woman presented with a sudden onset of the “worst headache of her life.” She had been taking two tablets of butalbital-acetaminophen-caffeine every 6 hours for three days for headaches. On arrival, her blood pressure was 178/87 mm Hg, heart rate 76/min, respiratory rate 18/min, and temperature 98.2°F. She described a sharp, pounding unilateral headache involving the left periorbital area and left occipital-temporal scalp, with associated sensory changes in the left arm and gait instability. She denied photophobia, nausea, vomiting, neck stiffness, or vision changes.

The day before, she had undergone a non-contrast head CT and lumbar puncture at another hospital, both of which were nondiagnostic. She was diagnosed with complex migraine and discharged with butalbital-acetaminophen-caffeine, metoclopramide, and ibuprofen.

Her medical history included hypertension (on losartan/hydrochlorothiazide), hyperlipidemia, anxiety (on duloxetine), and neuropathic leg pain (on gabapentin). She had no history of smoking, alcohol, illicit drugs, seizures, or stroke.

On examination, she was in acute distress from headache but oriented. She had a left monocular visual field deficit; pupils were equal and reactive; extraocular movements intact. Cerebellar testing was abnormal on finger-nose and heel-shin maneuvers, and gait was unstable. She also demonstrated sensory changes in the left upper extremity and cognitive impairment in memory and concentration. In the ED, she had focal seizure-like activity involving her left arm without loss of consciousness.

A brain MRI and MRA were obtained. The MRA was normal. The MRI demonstrated edema in the subcortical white matter of the right occipital lobe, right parietal lobe, and left occipital lobe.

A 57-year-old man with no past medical history presented with a 3-month history of right upper-quadrant pain and unintentional weight loss of 20 kg. Three months after initial evaluation, the pain radiated to his back and worsened with ambulation. He was found to have new-onset, untreated diabetes mellitus with poor glycemic control. On referral, his temperature was 38.7 °C, blood pressure 133/90 mm Hg, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, pulse 98 beats/min, and Glasgow Coma Scale score was 15. Neurological examination was nonfocal. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 9.7 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 11.69 mg/dL, hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, hematocrit 36.5%, and hemoglobin A1c 6.7%. Tumor markers were not elevated, HIV testing was negative, and three sputum acid-fast bacilli smears were negative.

Chest computed tomography revealed an invasive intrathoracic mass initially measuring 72 × 30 mm in the right lower mediastinum, compressing the lower right lung lobe, and partially infiltrating the T7–T8 vertebral bodies with osteolysis. Four weeks later, contrast-enhanced CT showed that the mass had enlarged to 85 × 67 mm, with bone infiltration and a compression fracture of the thoracic vertebrae. A low-density area within the mass was interpreted as necrosis from either malignancy or abscess formation. On diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging, there was no high signal intensity typical of an abscess.

A 66-year-old man with a history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension presented with acute onset of left-sided hemiplegia. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated diffusion-restricted lesions in the right parietooccipital and left occipital lobes with an embolic pattern. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed moderate-to-severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction (ejection fraction, 30%), global hypokinesia, mild left ventricular hypertrophy, mild mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, normal pulmonary artery pressure, and normal right ventricular function. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis, an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and an elevated C-reactive protein level. One blood culture grew Escherichia coli, and broad-spectrum antibiotics were initiated. To identify the source of sepsis, a noncontrast chest CT scan was performed and showed a soft-tissue density surrounded by gas in the posterior mediastinum.

A 42-year-old woman, G1P0 at 34 2/7 weeks of gestation, was admitted with preeclampsia with severe features (blood pressure 205/112 mmHg and 3+ proteinuria). She was initially asymptomatic, with normal fetal movement and no signs of distress. She received magnesium sulfate and corticosteroids. After 24 hours, induction was unsuccessful due to multiple uterine fibroids, and cesarean delivery was performed under spinal anesthesia (hyperbaric bupivacaine 0.75% 15 mg, fentanyl 15 mcg, preservative-free morphine 0.2 mg), achieving a T6 sensory level. The low transverse incision revealed clear amniotic fluid, and external uterine pressure was used to facilitate vacuum suction delivery. During delayed cord clamping, the patient became unresponsive, hypoxic, and hypotensive (noninvasive blood pressure 48/25 mmHg) and was promptly intubated. She then decompensated into pulseless electrical activity arrest. Advanced cardiac life support was initiated, and after multiple rounds of CPR and epinephrine, return of spontaneous circulation was achieved. Central venous and arterial lines were placed, and infusions of norepinephrine and vasopressin were started to maintain organ perfusion. Intraoperative transthoracic echocardiography showed right ventricular dilation with a large pericardial effusion.

A 31-year-old Japanese man presented with a 3-week history of fever and headache. Three weeks earlier, he noted fever (37–38°C) and headache and received antibiotics and NSAIDs without improvement; his temperature then rose to 39°C. His only past medical history was aseptic meningitis accompanied by axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy 5 months before, which resolved with NSAIDs. On examination, he was alert and oriented; temperature 38.5°C, blood pressure 128/60 mmHg, pulse 72/min, respiratory rate 20/min. Neurologic findings, including meningeal signs, were unremarkable. Multiple tender bilateral cervical lymph nodes were palpated. Laboratory studies showed WBC 3,200/µL, AST 22 U/L, ALT 15 U/L, CRP 1.77 mg/dL, and ANA negative. CSF analysis revealed 57 cells/µL (96% mononuclear), protein 96 mg/dL, and glucose 38 mg/dL (serum glucose 99 mg/dL; CSF/serum glucose ratio 0.38). CSF cultures for bacteria, mycobacteria, and fungus were negative. PCR assays for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, HSV-1/2, HHV-6, EBV, CMV, and VZV were all negative. No Mollaret cells were detected in the CSF. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed multiple bilateral cervical lymphadenopathies and splenomegaly.

A 34-year-old man from Punjab, India, presented with a 7-year history of gradual bilateral intention tremor initially diagnosed as spinocerebellar ataxia. Over the past 2 years, he developed progressive psychiatric symptoms including severe depression, anxiety, and mood lability managed with mood stabilizers, antidepressants, and antipsychotics with limited benefit. After emigrating to Canada, he experienced rapid functional decline over one year, with gait instability, rigidity, scanning speech, dysphagia, choking episodes, restlessness, sexual disinhibition, aggression, and social inappropriateness. By summer 2011, he was nonambulatory and had an acute in-hospital episode of dystonia, prompting admission. 

Family history was notable only for the patient’s maternal grandfather, who developed rapidly progressive gait disturbance and cognitive impairment at age 62 and died ~8 months later; there was no known consanguinity. The patient’s parents and sister had normal neurologic examinations except for a mild intention tremor in the mother.

On examination, vital signs were normal. He was agitated with labile mood. Neurologic findings included scanning dysarthria, severe rigidity in all extremities, hyperreflexia, appendicular dystonia, dysdiadochokinesia, and truncal ataxia. Ophthalmologic examination by fundoscopy showed no Kayser–Fleischer rings; slit-lamp exam was not possible due to rigidity. Cardiac, respiratory, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable with no hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, stigmata of liver disease, or asterixis.

Brain MRI revealed generalized atrophy and a “giant panda sign” in the midbrain. Abdominal ultrasound showed coarse liver echogenicity, irregular contours, and a hepatic span of 10.2 cm, suggestive of cirrhosis. Liver biopsy showed grade 2–3 fibrosis with bridging; Orcein stain was negative for copper. A complete biochemical and pathologic workup was negative for viral hepatitis, alpha-1 antitrypsin disease, hemochromatosis, and autoimmune hepatitis. Routine blood counts, electrolytes, renal function, liver enzymes, and synthetic liver function tests were all normal. Serum ceruloplasmin was 0.05 g/L (normal >0.21), serum copper 3.4 μmol/L (normal >11), and 24-hour urinary copper 1.8 μmol (normal <0.6).

A 75-year-old woman with a history of squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix was followed for bilateral uretero-hydronephrosis complicated by impaired renal function. She underwent urgent bilateral nephrostomy and systemic rehydration, leading to improvement in renal function. As part of tumor staging, an abdominopelvic MRI demonstrated bilateral perirenal masses measuring 4 × 2.5 cm on the right and 5 × 3 cm on the left. These masses showed diffusion hypersignal, low ADC values, and a thin peripheral enhancement after gadolinium administration. Notably, an ultrasound performed before the nephrostomy had shown the perirenal spaces to be free of lesions. This discrepancy prompted further evaluation.

A 38-year-old woman with pronounced dental phobia but no needle phobia was scheduled for extraction of her left mandibular third molar under intravenous sedation. She reported occasional brief fainting episodes in daily life that resolved within seconds when lying supine; these events were never evaluated with central nervous system or cardiac studies. She had no personal or family history of cardiovascular disease or sudden cardiac death, and routine physical examinations and physician consultations were unremarkable.

Preoperative laboratory studies, including blood biochemistry, were normal. A screening ECG showed normal sinus rhythm at 69 bpm. After topical application of 18 mg lidocaine patch for 30 minutes, an intravenous line was placed with minimal pain under noninvasive blood pressure monitoring (118/76 mmHg) and lead II ECG (73 bpm). The patient showed no signs of hypovolemia or dehydration but received lactated Ringer’s solution.

Immediately after cannulation, she complained of discomfort and nausea. The ECG tracing revealed a progression from severe sinus bradycardia (<30 bpm) to transient asystole lasting 18 seconds, accompanied by loss of consciousness and a brief convulsion. Preparations for resuscitation were in place, but within seconds of administering oxygen, additional fluid loading, and positioning supine with elevation of the lower extremities, her rhythm recovered to an atrioventricular junctional rhythm, and she regained consciousness (blood pressure 111/67 mmHg; heart rate 75 bpm).

A 48-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with severe chest pain. Her electrocardiogram was normal, but high-sensitivity troponin I rose from 45 to 1133 pg/mL (upper reference, 38). She had mild dyslipidaemia, diet-controlled glucose intolerance, and smoked 10 cigarettes per day. Her medical history was unremarkable, and she took no regular medications; she reported allergies to ceftriaxone and betamethasone. 

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. There were no signs of heart failure, breath sounds were normal, jugular venous pressure was not elevated, and the neurologic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a normal haemogram and creatinine of 0.95 mg/dL (reference range, 0.55–1.02). A chest radiograph was unremarkable. Bedside echocardiography revealed mild lateral and apical left ventricular hypokinesia with an ejection fraction of 55%, without pericardial effusion or right ventricular overload.

She received aspirin and high-intensity statin therapy. Because of recurrent angina, invasive coronary angiography performed via the right radial approach showed non-obstructive coronary artery disease with left coronary dominance and no evidence of dissection or plaque disruption. 

On hospital day 2, echocardiography again demonstrated normal biventricular dimensions, mild inferior-lateral mid-apical hypokinesia, and an ejection fraction of 54%. On day 3, cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging using T2‐weighted and late gadolinium enhancement sequences demonstrated high signal intensity in the inferior segment on T2‐weighted images with subendocardial late gadolinium enhancement in the mid-apical posterolateral region.

A 14-year-old child with a history of neurofibromatosis type 1 and end-stage chronic renal failure on hemodialysis presented with a 6-month history of progressively enlarging left mandibular swelling. On examination, the patient had scoliosis, multiple café-au-lait spots, lower-limb deformities, and a generally diminished health status.

A CT scan of the face revealed:
- A well-circumscribed, multilocular osteolytic lesion of the left mandibular body, with regular contours, cortical expansion without cortical lysis or periosteal reaction, and displacement of adjacent dental roots.
- A second lesion with identical characteristics in the left upper alveolar process.
- Diffuse thickening of the cranial vault and facial bones with a “salt and pepper” appearance.
- Multiple lacunar osteolytic foci involving the cranial vault, the spinous processes of the cervical spine, and the left clavicle.

A 55-year-old woman with gastroesophageal reflux disease treated with famotidine (20 mg twice daily for 2 years) was admitted with 15 days of lethargy, confusion, and painful muscle cramps in her hands and legs, resulting in multiple falls. She denied nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and urinary incontinence, and her oral intake was good. Her vital signs were stable. On examination, she was alert and oriented to person and place but not time; her skin was dry, and she had positive Chvostek’s and Trousseau’s signs.

Laboratory studies revealed:
• Sodium 141 mmol/L, BUN 13 mg/dL, creatinine 0.7 mg/dL  
• Calcium 5.7 mg/dL (albumin 3.9 g/dL), magnesium 0.55 mg/dL, phosphorus 3.4 mg/dL  
• AST 17 U/L, ALT 12 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 60 U/L, bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, INR 0.8  

She received multiple doses of IV magnesium sulfate (2 g) and calcium gluconate (1 g), after which her calcium rose to 9.5 mg/dL and magnesium to 2.1 mg/dL. Further evaluation showed low parathyroid hormone (PTH) and normal PTH-related peptide, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels. She was discharged on oral calcium and magnesium supplements.

Two weeks later, she returned with recurrent lethargy and muscle cramps. Repeat labs showed calcium 6.8 mg/dL and magnesium 0.9 mg/dL. She denied missing her supplements and again reported no gastrointestinal losses. A 24-hour urine collection for calcium and magnesium was unremarkable.

An 11-month-old girl of Pakistani descent was referred for evaluation of severe hypercalcemia. She was born full term, with appropriate growth through 9 months, and was fed mixed Similac® formula, oatmeal, and pureed vegetables and fruits. At 10 months of age, she developed intermittent nonbloody, nonbilious emesis, irritability, and decreased oral intake, tolerating only formula and refusing previously accepted solids. Over the ensuing 3 weeks, she lost 283 g. 

On examination, she was fussy but consolable and tachycardic, with otherwise age-appropriate vital signs. Growth parameters remained at the 66th percentile for length without notable dysmorphic features or signs of metabolic bone disease. The abdomen was soft with no masses; neurologic exam was normal. 

Initial laboratory studies revealed: serum calcium >15 mg/dL; ionized calcium 6.84 mg/dL; intact PTH <5 pg/mL; normal phosphate, magnesium, alkaline phosphatase, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and serum creatinine; and an elevated urine calcium-to-creatinine ratio of 0.86 mg/mg. White blood cell count was 18.8 k/µL, platelet count 574 k/µL, and inflammatory markers were within normal limits. Thyroid and liver function tests were normal. 

Renal ultrasound demonstrated bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis. Chest radiography, serum uric acid, lactate dehydrogenase, and PTH-related peptide levels were normal. The initial laboratory tests confirmed hypercalcemia and did not reveal an underlying etiology.

A 32-year-old woman was admitted with a 1-week history of moderate haemoptysis associated with vague chest pain and chest tightness. She denied fever, weight loss, anorexia, and dyspnoea. Her history was notable only for a thyroidectomy, and she had never had a chest radiograph before this admission. On examination, air entry was decreased at the left lung base and oxygen saturation was 97% on room air. Initial blood tests showed a marginally elevated white-cell count with neutrophilia and a mildly increased C-reactive protein level. A chest radiograph demonstrated a heterogeneous opacity in the left lower zone. An abdominal and pelvic ultrasound was normal. She was diagnosed with community-acquired pneumonia and started on empirical antibiotics. Despite treatment, she continued to have intermittent mild haemoptysis, and her haemoglobin fell from 129 g/L to 103 g/L. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest revealed a multiloculated cystic solid mass with low-density lesions in the left lower lung.

A 51-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of bleeding gums and ulceration of the mouth, causing difficulty in chewing and swallowing. He reported a febrile illness with lymphadenopathy one month earlier. He worked as a driver and had a 5-year history of tobacco chewing and smoking. 

On examination, there were no scars or lesions on the skin of the face, trunk, or extremities, and he denied any prior cutaneous lesions. Intraoral findings included multiple tender, diffuse ulcerated nodules (<1 cm) on the hard and soft palate with surface hoarseness. The maxillary labial gingiva displayed a cobblestone appearance with marked erythema, granular inflammation, and bled on probing. Oral hygiene was poor. Neck examination revealed bilaterally enlarged, tender submandibular lymph nodes. 

Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis. Serologic tests for HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C virus were nonreactive. Biopsy specimens were obtained from the maxillary labial gingiva and the ulcer margin on the palate for histologic examination.

A 70-year-old man was admitted with a 3-day history of fevers up to 39 °C and 24 hours of confusion and disorientation. His history included benign prostatic hyperplasia, β-thalassemia trait, and cholecystectomy; he had traveled to Madagascar 8 months earlier. Over the preceding 8 weeks, he had multiple hospital admissions for fevers of 38–39 °C, temporal headaches, and transient ischemic attacks manifesting as hemiparesis, dysarthria, facial droop, and right upper-limb numbness, all resolving within hours. Blood cultures were repeatedly negative, and empirical antibiotics had no effect. Inflammatory markers were markedly elevated (ESR 65 mm/h; CRP 102 mg/L). Magnetic resonance angiography was interpreted as showing possible inflammatory stenoses of the right vertebral and left common carotid arteries. A temporal artery biopsy was negative. Intravenous corticosteroids produced clinical and biochemical improvement (ESR 25 mm/h; CRP 3.7 mg/L). Tests for ANA (1:80), ds-DNA, p-ANCA, c-ANCA, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP antibodies, immunoglobulins, and complement levels were nondiagnostic. Two weeks after discharge, he returned on prednisolone 60 mg daily, methotrexate 20 mg/week, and clopidogrel. On examination, his vital signs were stable, temperature 37.5 °C, and he was disoriented without focal findings. Noncontrast CT of the brain showed only mild frontal subarachnoid space asymmetry. Laboratory tests revealed WBC 13.5 × 10^3/μL (88% neutrophils), CRP 80 mg/dL, and ESR 45 mm/h. Differential diagnosis included CNS infection and treatment-resistant autoimmune disease.

A 37-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of fever, headache, and myalgia, along with epigastric pain, nausea, and diarrhoea. Three days before symptom onset, he sustained a dog bite on his right hand. His only past medical history was active smoking; he had no splenic disorders, alcohol excess, or immunocompromise. He denied any chest pain. On admission, temperature was 38.2 °C, heart rate 130 b.p.m., blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Examination was notable only for a bite wound on the right hand without cellulitis or necrosis. Laboratory tests showed CRP 417 mg/L, white blood cell count 9.45 G/L (91% neutrophils), procalcitonin 8.42 μg/L, platelets 29 G/L, creatinine 189 μmol/L (×3 baseline), AST 2× upper limit, ALT 3× upper limit; high‐sensitivity troponin T peaked at 1129 ng/L (upper limit 50 ng/L) and NT‐proBNP was 1127 pg/mL (upper limit 500 pg/mL). A 12-lead ECG demonstrated mild diffuse ST-segment elevation with micro-Q waves in inferior and lateral leads. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed mild global left ventricular hypokinesia with an ejection fraction of 42% and preserved right ventricular function; there was no pericardial effusion. Empirical intravenous cefotaxime was started, and blood cultures were drawn.

A 68-year-old woman from North India with a 5-year history of diet-controlled diabetes mellitus and 3-year history of cryptogenic chronic liver disease presented with a one-month history of dry cough, generalized weakness, and significant weight loss. On examination she was thin, pale, afebrile, and haemodynamically stable; systemic examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.2 g/dl, total leukocyte count 12 × 10^9 cells/l, platelet count 150 × 10^9/l, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 59 mm/h. The leukocyte differential was 41% neutrophils, 27% lymphocytes, and 32% eosinophils (absolute eosinophil count 4 × 10^9/l). Liver function tests were normal except for hypoalbuminemia (2.78 g/dl); renal function was normal. HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and anti-hepatitis C antibody tests were negative. The tuberculin skin test reaction was less than 10 mm. Chest radiography revealed increased bronchovascular markings with right hilar prominence. Two stool examinations showed no ova or parasites. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a coarse hepatic echotexture. The patient received albendazole and diethylcarbamazine, but repeat blood counts showed persistent eosinophilia. Echinococcus serology and anti-filarial antibodies were negative. Tests for anti-nuclear and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. Transthoracic echocardiography was normal, with no vegetations. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax and abdomen revealed enlarged non-necrotic mediastinal lymph nodes and features of chronic liver disease. Microscopic examination of a needle-aspirated bone marrow specimen showed increased eosinophilic precursors with no abnormal cells.  
What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 34-year-old woman with no medical or surgical history presented with a 6-month history of hoarseness, chronic cough, and frequent throat clearing. She denied heartburn. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. Vital signs were normal, and cervical lymph nodes were not palpable. Laryngeal videostroboscopy demonstrated bilateral intrachordal lesions with mild edema, erythema, and arytenoid hypertrophy. Vocal-cord mobility was normal bilaterally, and the right lesion appeared larger than the left.

A 68-year-old man presented with an enlarging, erythematous, non-healing lesion on the left dorsal forearm of several months’ duration. His medical history included chronic kidney disease, congestive heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and non-melanoma skin cancer. On examination, there was a tender, brightly erythematous, dome-shaped papule measuring 1.8 cm in diameter. The initial differential diagnosis included keratoacanthoma, squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, and metastatic carcinoma. The patient did not recall any trauma to the area but reported a hobby of gardening and raising farm animals. A shave biopsy was performed. Histopathologic examination showed epidermal acantholysis overlying a large nodule composed of a granulomatous infiltrate surrounding multiple cysts. Round, thick-walled bodies were present within the cystic microabscesses. Periodic acid–Schiff staining highlighted pigmented fungal cells with appropriately reactive controls, suggestive of a deep fungal infection. A fungal culture was not performed.

A 64-year-old man presented with a 6-day history of cough and worsening dyspnea. His cough was intermittently productive of white sputum. He denied fever, chest pain, palpitations, gastrointestinal or neurologic symptoms. 

His medical history included rheumatic heart disease with a mechanical aortic valve, nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy, atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia. Eleven months earlier he had a ventricular tachycardia treated with oral amiodarone (200 mg twice daily). He was a former heavy smoker (≈ 40 pack-years) and drank 20 standard alcoholic drinks per week. His medications included sacubitril–valsartan, bisoprolol, dapagliflozin, furosemide, thyroxine, warfarin, budesonide–formoterol, and amiodarone.

On examination, he was afebrile, blood pressure 85/63 mm Hg (lying) and 92/66 mm Hg (standing), heart rate 55 beats/min, respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 90% on room air. He appeared thin and mildly cachectic with resting dyspnea. Jugular venous pressure was 5 cm. Heart sounds were dual with a mechanical click. Crackles were heard bilaterally throughout both lung fields and did not clear with coughing. There was no peripheral edema.

An electrocardiogram showed ventricular pacing at 55 beats/min. Respiratory viral testing, including SARS-CoV-2 PCR, was negative. Laboratory tests revealed leukocytosis (17 × 10^9/L), neutrophilia, mildly low hemoglobin, an INR of 6, elevated liver enzymes, and a B-type natriuretic peptide of 3998 ng/L. Thyroid function and an autoimmune screen were within normal limits or negative. Echocardiography showed severely dilated ventricles, an ejection fraction of 19%, and a right ventricular systolic pressure of 78 mm Hg.

A chest radiograph demonstrated diffuse bilateral fine reticular interstitial densities, peribronchial thickening, cardiomegaly, and no discrete consolidation. High-resolution CT of the chest revealed diffuse ground-glass opacities with basal predominance, interstitial thickening, traction bronchiectasis, minimal patchy lobular sparing, upper-lobe emphysematous changes, and no honeycombing or consolidation.

His initial diagnostic impression was decompensated heart failure with fluid overload.

A 29-year-old Thai woman presented to the emergency department with acute onset of itching in her palms and soles, nasal congestion, eyelid swelling, ocular redness, rhinorrhea, chest tightness, and difficulty breathing. One hour before symptom onset, she had eaten 10 pieces of fried coconut rice cake prepared with a mixed cooking flour. Sixty minutes after eating, she began her usual jogging routine; 20 minutes into exercise, she noted the above symptoms and immediately sought medical attention. Her medical history was significant for moderate to severe perennial allergic rhinitis since childhood, controlled with intranasal corticosteroids. She denied any food or drug allergies and reported tolerating ibuprofen and diclofenac without adverse reactions. She also noted that one week earlier she had eaten 15 pieces of the same coconut rice cake made with the same bag of flour without exercising and had no reaction. In the emergency department, her blood pressure was 94/62 mmHg, heart rate 110 beats/min, respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Examination revealed angioedema of the eyelids and widespread urticarial wheals; the lungs were clear. She received intramuscular epinephrine with symptomatic improvement.

A 10-year-old boy with a history of prematurity and a sister who died in infancy from presumed vitamin K–related intracranial bleeding was referred for sudden onset of a scalp mass and fever. There was no history of head trauma, although he had massaged his scalp the day before admission. On examination, his temperature was 38.8°C and he was clinically stable. A 5×5-cm soft, non‐tender mass was noted over the right temporal scalp without signs of inflammation. Petechial rashes were present on the oral mucosa, trunk, and limbs, and new petechiae appeared readily at the site of tourniquet compression. Laboratory studies showed a normal platelet count and normal prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, and fibrinogen level; a white-cell count of 2900/mm3 with relative lymphocytosis; and a C-reactive protein level of 3.26 mg/dl. Head computed tomography revealed subcutaneous hemorrhage without skull fracture or intracranial bleeding. The presumptive diagnosis was Henoch–Schönlein purpura, although the rashes were non‐palpable and had an atypical distribution. Further testing, including bleeding time, protein C and S levels, and screening for collagen‐vascular diseases, was unremarkable. No additional bleeding occurred, and his symptoms resolved spontaneously over several days; he was discharged on hospital day 6.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of a left-sided groin mass. The mass was occasionally painful and became more prominent when standing or straining. She denied abdominal or pelvic pain, gastrointestinal or urinary symptoms, and vaginal discharge. Her medical history included treated cervical intraepithelial neoplasia; she had two prior cesarean deliveries. 

On examination, a 2 cm mobile, fluctuant, irreducible mass was noted lateral to the left pubic tubercle. The mass enlarged on standing but displayed no cough impulse. The overlying skin was unremarkable, with no lymphadenopathy. Abdominal and pelvic examinations were normal.

Groin ultrasound showed a 59 × 25 × 13 mm anechoic thin-walled cystic structure within the left inguinal canal.

A 7-year-old Middle Eastern girl presented with 2 days of vomiting and upper abdominal pain that began after she fell from her bed, and 2 weeks of left-sided chest pain radiating to her left shoulder, worse with deep breathing and relieved by propping herself on two pillows; she also noted gradual weight loss. Two siblings had pneumonia in the past month. 

On examination, she was tachypneic and in respiratory distress with an oxygen saturation of 90% on room air; air entry and chest movement were markedly reduced on the left side, and a small bruise was present over the left chest. The abdomen was soft, nontender, and without masses. 

An anteroposterior chest radiograph revealed an air–fluid level occupying the entire left hemithorax. A chest tube was placed on suspicion of hydropneumothorax. A subsequent chest radiograph showed the tube lying between the chest wall and the air collection and failing to drain any fluid, raising further diagnostic uncertainty.

A 68-year-old man with a 5-year history of Parkinson’s disease was evaluated at home for a routine frailty assessment. He reported no bowel movement for five days, with abdominal discomfort, bloating, and mild nausea for the past two days. He denied fever, vomiting beyond mild nausea, hematochezia, or changes in medications, diet, or activity.

He used Bisacodyl intermittently and takes 1–2 sachets of macrogol twice daily, with adequate fiber, hydration, and exercise. He and his partner noted that he often has constipation episodes up to five days long that resolve with these measures, and they were not concerned.

On examination, he appeared well-hydrated but slightly pale. Parkinsonian rigidity and tremor were present. Vital signs were within normal limits. Abdominal examination showed mild, diffuse tenderness most pronounced around the umbilical region without guarding or rebound; bowel sounds were present.

Given persistence beyond his usual pattern and lack of response to usual laxatives, he was transferred by ambulance to the emergency department. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 11.4 × 10^9/L (neutrophils 9.6 × 10^9/L) and a lactate level of 3.8 mmol/L. An erect chest radiograph was normal. A plain abdominal radiograph demonstrated dilated small-bowel loops.

A 45-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with acute-onset swelling and mild pain of her right upper extremity during a high-intensity exercise routine. After initial resolution over 48 hours with rest and ice, she returned to exercise but 15 days later developed a second episode, this time with severe pain. On examination in the emergency department, her right arm was cyanotic and swollen with paresthesia and muscle weakness (4/5) of all muscle groups; the left arm was normal. After 48 hours, the swelling improved but the weakness persisted. Wright’s hyperabduction test reproduced cyanosis and abolished the right radial pulse. Sensation and deep tendon reflexes were otherwise normal. A color Doppler sonogram failed to visualize the entire subclavian vein. Contrast venography of the right upper limb showed near-complete obstruction of the subclavian vein, venous stenosis, and thrombosis from the axillary to the subclavian vein. A computed tomography scan, electromyogram, and nerve conduction study were performed to evaluate for neurogenic involvement but showed no abnormalities.

A 12-month-old girl presented with a 12-hour history of progressive difficulty breathing. On examination she was febrile and tachycardic. A chest radiograph showed a large soft-tissue–density mass occupying the left upper and mid hemithorax, silhouetting the mediastinal margins and causing rightward mediastinal shift. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, with injection in the left antecubital fossa, demonstrated a multicystic mass with variable attenuation of cystic components and ill-defined serpiginous high-attenuation structures that converged into a vessel joining an ectatic peripheral left brachiocephalic vein draining into the superior vena cava. Focal areas of contrast reflux and pooling within these serpiginous vessels mimicked calcifications. The mass infiltrated and encased adjacent vascular structures without luminal narrowing, and there were adjacent ground-glass and consolidative opacities in the lung. Laboratory studies revealed elevated white-cell count, platelet count, and lactate dehydrogenase. The patient was treated with antibiotics and her symptoms resolved.

A 3-month-old infant presented with recurrent high-grade fevers, diffuse urticarial skin eruption, and polyarthritis. Laboratory evaluation showed anemia, leukocytosis, and elevated inflammatory markers; evaluations for infection, hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, and malignancy were negative. Whole-body MRI confirmed extensive polyarthritis. An autoinflammatory gene panel revealed a heterozygous Met694Val mutation in MEFV, but the early presentation was atypical. Higher-coverage sequencing demonstrated 5% mosaicism for NLRP3 p.Asp305Glu, supporting a diagnosis of neonatal-onset multisystem inflammatory disease (NOMID). The patient began subcutaneous anakinra, initially dosed at 2 mg/kg. Three months after starting anakinra—and following a dose increase to 4 mg/kg—the patient developed intermittent pruritic, erythematous, linear “scratch-mark” patches over the back, upper arms, and thighs.

A 16-year-old girl presented with a 3-month history of intermittent, bilateral bloody tearing. Her menarche began at age 13, with regular menstrual cycles and no correlation between episodes of bloody tearing and menses. She had no history of trauma, bleeding diathesis, or hematologic disorders, and there was no relevant family history.

On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. Findings on slit-lamp examination, intraocular pressures, and funduscopy were normal. Pupils were equal and reactive. There were no foreign bodies, vascular lesions, or lacerations on the eyelids, conjunctiva, cornea, or in the punctal region. The lacrimal glands were neither enlarged nor tender, and compression of the nasolacrimal ducts did not produce a blood-stained discharge. Nasolacrimal passages were patent.

Dacryocystography and gradient-echo magnetic resonance imaging of the nasolacrimal canals showed no abnormalities. Intranasal endoscopic evaluation was normal.

Two samples of the bloody tears were sent for pathological examination; analysis revealed numerous squamous cells and dysplastic cells but no endometrial tissue. Hematologic workup, including platelet count, prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, bleeding time, and a full coagulation panel, was within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a 1–2 cm ovarian cyst. Further investigations for systemic or ocular causes were unrevealing.

A male Iranian infant was born at 32 weeks’ gestation to a healthy 28-year-old primigravida mother after 19 hours of preterm premature rupture of membranes. Vaginal delivery was uncomplicated with Apgar scores of 9 and 10. Birth weight was 2180 g, length 42 cm, and head circumference 30 cm. On delivery, the umbilical cord appeared markedly thickened (diameter ~6 cm; length ~50 cm) with clear mucoid fluid and bulky, fluctuating Wharton’s jelly permitting easy visualization of three vessels. The umbilical ring measured 11 mm. Examination of all other organ systems was normal, and there was no family history of umbilical or urinary anomalies.

A 53-year-old man presented with a 1-day history of multiple pruritic, burning, blanching erythematous macules on his trunk and bilateral upper extremities. He had a history of hypertension and a left-sided ischemic stroke 7 days earlier, after which he was discharged on aspirin 75 mg once daily, enalapril 10 mg once daily, atorvastatin 20 mg once daily, and omeprazole 20 mg twice daily. He denied any new foods, environmental exposures, pet contacts, or family history of allergic skin disease. He had no angioedema, respiratory symptoms, or prior allergic reactions. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 12,000 cells/mm3 with an eosinophil count of 550 cells/mL; other blood counts and chemistry panels were unremarkable. Because angiotensin‐converting enzyme inhibitors can cause drug rashes, enalapril was replaced with amlodipine 5 mg once daily, and he was started on an H1-antihistamine for symptomatic relief, but the rash and pruritus did not improve.

A 62-year-old man from Seoul presented to a Chilean hospital with fever, rash, and severe malaise. Two days earlier, after his arrival in Chile, he reported worsening flu-like symptoms—including chills, headache, and myalgia—that had begun five days before presentation. He had recently visited a farm south of Seoul. On examination, his temperature was 38.8 °C, heart rate 108 bpm, and he appeared acutely ill. He had a generalized, nonpruritic maculopapular rash predominantly on his trunk, sparing his palms, soles, and mucous membranes. On the left posterior thigh there was a painless, necrotic lesion approximately 6 mm in diameter with a surrounding erythematous halo.  
Laboratory studies revealed a platelet count of 91,000/μL, hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL, normal leukocyte count with 20% bands, toxic granulation, and atypical lymphocytes. Inflammatory markers were elevated (ESR 32 mm/h; CRP 3.6 mg/dL). Serum sodium was 134 mEq/L. Liver enzymes were raised (AST 180 U/L; ALT 161 U/L; GGT 327 U/L; ALP 208 U/L) and LDH was 718 U/L. A molecular respiratory viral panel and IgM serologies for EBV, CMV, and parvovirus B19 were negative.

A 12-year-old boy was evaluated for bilateral ear deformities and hearing loss present since early childhood. He had normal developmental milestones and no family history of similar anomalies; there was no maternal exposure to known teratogens. Physical examination revealed:
• Bilateral microtia with external auditory canal atresia  
• Dolichocephalic skull, antimongoloid slanting palpebral fissures, and sparse eyelashes  
• Normal heart sounds  
• Normal speech and cognitive performance

Audiometry demonstrated bilateral severe conductive hearing loss. A computed tomography scan of the face and temporal bones showed:
• Absence of both bony and cartilaginous portions of the external auditory canals and malformed pinnae  
• Hypoplastic middle ear cavities with absent ossicles; hypoplastic, poorly pneumatized mastoids; grossly normal inner ears  
• Downward slant of superior orbital walls; hypoplastic facial bones and bilateral zygoma with poorly formed zygomatic arches  
• Dental crowding in both arches; normal condylar and coronoid processes of the mandible  
• Retrognathia, micrognathia with an obtuse mandibular angle, and a small posterior hard-palate cleft with normal choanae  
• Leftward deviation of the nasal septum with a bony spur; otherwise normal paranasal sinuses

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 16-year-old woman, 24 hours postpartum, presented with headache, vomiting, and two generalized seizures. She reported mild weakness in the right upper limb but had no history of hypertension or proteinuria. Initial noncontrast head CT revealed an expansive, ring-enhancing lesion in the left parietal lobe with surrounding vasogenic edema and slight midline shift. Brain MRI showed a T2-hypointense intraparenchymal mass with heterogeneous ring enhancement on T1 postcontrast images, prominent vasogenic edema on FLAIR, no areas of markedly increased relative cerebral blood volume in the enhancing rim on perfusion imaging, and spectroscopy demonstrated an elevated choline peak, decreased N-acetylaspartate, and a lipid–lactate peak. Chest and abdominal imaging were unremarkable, and routine laboratory studies, including complete blood count and basic metabolic panel, showed no abnormalities. Given persistent diagnostic uncertainty, a stereotactic biopsy was performed.

A 7-day-old term male infant was brought for evaluation of progressively enlarging lumps on his back. He was born at 39 weeks’ gestation after an uneventful pregnancy; Apgar scores were 7 and 7 at 1 and 5 minutes, and his initial newborn examination noted subcutaneous nodules in the thoracolumbar region. At 2 hours of life he developed tachypnea, grunting, and fever, was treated with antibiotics in the NICU, and was discharged on day 5. His mother observed that the back nodules continued to grow. On day 7, examination revealed multiple, firm, nontender, erythematous nodules on the upper back. Vital signs were temperature 37.4°C, heart rate 132/min, and respiratory rate 56/min. Laboratory studies showed WBC 21,900/mm3 with 41% neutrophils and left-shifted forms, platelets 436,000/mm3, D-dimer 4.36 mg/L, and normal coagulation indices; blood cultures were obtained.  
Ultrasound of the back demonstrated an 18 cm × 18 cm × 5 cm hypervascular, bilobed, predominantly solid mass with several small cystic areas. Head and abdominal ultrasound were normal. MRI of the back revealed a lobulated, heterogeneously enhancing soft-tissue mass in the subcutaneous posterior thoracic region without spinal canal extension; a limited gadolinium-enhanced MR angiogram showed no obvious arterial feeder. Given the discrepancy between the apparent vascular imaging and the firm, noncompressible nature of the mass on examination, plans were made for biopsy.

A 65-year-old man with dyslipidaemia and psoriatic arthritis presented with angina. ECG showed ST-segment elevations in the inferolateral leads consistent with an inferolateral STEMI. Physical examination was unremarkable. He received 250 mg IV aspirin and underwent urgent coronary angiography, which revealed a subtotal occlusion of the mid left anterior descending artery (LAD) with a large thrombus burden and thrombotic apposition in a recurrent apical branch supplying the inferior and inferior-septal walls, consistent with distal embolization. A drug-eluting stent was implanted in the mid-LAD and balloon angioplasty performed in the distal segment. During the procedure, he received unfractionated heparin (100 IU/kg) and a 60 mg loading dose of prasugrel.

Six days later, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (1.5 T) showed mild systolic left ventricular dysfunction with akinesis of the inferior and lateral apical walls. Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) demonstrated a transmural pattern (>75% wall thickness) in the inferior and lateral medium-distal walls and an intramyocardial pattern in the mid inferior-septal wall. Both LGE regions corresponded to areas of increased signal on T2‐weighted images and elevated T2 times (average 70 ms; normal <50 ms), T1 times (average 1200 ms; normal 950–1050 ms), and extracellular volume (average 50%; normal 25–33%), consistent with acute myocardial edema.

A 72-year-old nonsmoking woman of African origin with idiopathic nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy (LVEF ≈25–28%) had a two-chamber ICD with the HeartLogic feature enabled since 2018. She had been stable in NYHA class II for >6 months on spironolactone, bumetanide, bisoprolol, and sacubitril–valsartan. For >6 months her HeartLogic index remained <16.  

Seven days before presentation, her HeartLogic index rose steeply from 9 to 63. Contributing trends included decreased heart-rate variability; a strongly increased third heart sound; a rapid fall then steep rise in the first heart sound; increased thoracic impedance; increased respiratory rate; increased nightly heart rate; a lower activity level; fewer apneas; and an overall higher average heart rate.

She presented to the emergency department with severe dyspnea beginning 36 hours earlier and a dry cough for several days. She denied fever; temperature was 36.2 °C. She had not traveled to high-risk regions but a close neighbor had confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection.

On examination, she had a known mitral insufficiency murmur, clear lung fields without wheezes or rhonchi, a respiratory rate of 25–30/min, blood pressure 137/80 mmHg, pulse 70 bpm, and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. ECG showed sinus rhythm at 70 bpm with left ventricular hypertrophy and a QRS duration of 110 ms, unchanged from prior studies.

Laboratory tests revealed mild leukopenia with an absolute lymphocyte count of 930 µL⁻¹, D-dimer 4701 ng/L, LDH 301 IU/L, C-reactive protein 70 mg/L, and an acute-on-chronic renal insufficiency (eGFR 50 mL/min; baseline 70 mL/min).

A 49-year-old man presented with fatigue and progressive dyspnea. He had worked as a plasterer for 30 years and was initially diagnosed with silicosis at another center. He was referred for clinical deterioration and confirmation of the diagnosis. An occupational hygienist confirmed exposure to construction dust, including crystalline and amorphous silica. High-resolution computed tomography of the chest showed mediastinal and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, subpleural nodules, consolidations, bronchiectasis, and fibrotic lesions.

A 22-year-old woman from Eastern Nepal presented with a 2-day history of fever (103 °F), agitation, earache, severe headache, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, and neck pain. She denied pulmonary or systemic TB symptoms. She had no comorbidities.  
On examination: T 103 °F; BP 130/80 mm Hg; HR 96 bpm; RR 22 breaths/min; SpO₂ 99% on room air. She appeared ill and irritable, with neck stiffness and positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs; there was no lymphadenopathy or other focal findings.  
Laboratory studies: Hb 10.2 g/dL; WBC 23,500/mm³ (90% neutrophils, 7% lymphocytes); ESR 58 mm/h; Na 133 mmol/L; Ca 8.0 mg/dL; Mg 1.2 mg/dL; HIV, HBsAg, HCV, and VDRL/RPR nonreactive; dengue serology negative; sputum AFB negative. Noncontrast head CT and chest radiograph were normal.  
She received empiric IV ampicillin, ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and acyclovir. Lumbar puncture yielded clear, light-yellow CSF with cobweb coagulum. CSF analysis showed: total nucleated cell count 195/µL (90% lymphocytes, 10% neutrophils); glucose 23 mg/dL; protein (albumin) 200 mg/dL; ADA 12 IU/L; GeneXpert MTB/RIF negative; serum CRP positive; anti-JE IgM in serum and CSF negative.

A 43-year-old man presented with an 8-day history of persistent non-bloody, non-bilious vomiting and occasional sharp, burning epigastric pain. He had a history of gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, and alcohol use disorder and reported binge drinking immediately prior to symptom onset. He denied prior episodes of pancreatitis. At symptom onset, he tested positive for COVID-19 by home test; he remained asymptomatic from a respiratory standpoint. He reported a 10-kg weight loss since symptom onset.

On examination, he was well-nourished with dry mucous membranes and epigastric tenderness without a palpable mass. Laboratory studies showed hypokalemia (K 2.6 mEq/L), metabolic alkalosis (HCO₃ 50 mEq/L), acute kidney injury (creatinine 3.13 mg/dL; baseline 0.7 mg/dL), lipase 76 U/L, CEA 1.1 ng/mL, and CA19-9 <3 U/mL. 

An abdominal radiograph showed mild gastric distension. Ultrasound revealed a 4.3 cm cystic structure near the pylorus. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a moderately distended stomach with a cystic lesion at the gastric antrum near the porta hepatis, without evidence of metastatic disease. EGD with endoscopic ultrasound revealed a 4.8 cm × 3.5 cm walled-off extramural cystic lesion compressing the gastric antrum; the pancreatic parenchyma and ducts appeared normal. Fine-needle aspiration of the lesion yielded fluid with a CEA level of 1247 ng/mL, amylase 35,850 U/L, and culture grew Candida glabrata. MRCP confirmed a partially cystic, hemorrhagic/proteinaceous mass at the pylorus/antrum with no distant spread.

A 39‐year‐old man presented with a single scalp nodule of 12 months’ duration. He denied any pain or itching. On examination, there was a 15 mm, dome‐shaped, skin-colored alopecic nodule located in the occipital region; the surrounding scalp appeared normal. The lesion was soft, mobile, and, when punctured, released a sterile citrine-colored fluid. A scalp biopsy revealed a circumscribed perifollicular inflammatory infiltrate in the deep dermis composed of neutrophils, plasma cells, and lymphocytes, with focal granuloma formation. Special stains and cultures for bacteria and fungi were negative.

A 42-year-old man presented with 3 months of persistent pain and tingling in the posterior aspect of his right thigh. The symptoms began after a mountain-climbing hike during which he walked backward with flexed knees for 1.5 hours; that evening he noted discomfort in the upper posterior thigh, which he initially attributed to muscle soreness. The pain and tingling persisted and worsened, particularly at night and during prolonged sitting, but did not occur with walking or running. He had no history of low back pain, tobacco or alcohol use, systemic illnesses, or medication use.

On examination, gait and posture were normal. There was no ecchymosis, edema, or acute atrophy. Skin color and hair growth on the affected side were normal. A scar on the anterior right knee was attributed to ACL reconstruction 5 years earlier. Hip range of motion was full and painless. Isometric testing of the semitendinosus muscle showed mild strength reduction without pain. Lumbar spine, sacroiliac joint, and piriformis involvement were assessed and ruled out by negative straight-leg–raise, slump, distraction, compression, FABER, Gaenslen’s, thigh thrust, active piriformis stretch, Freiberg’s, and FAIR tests.

One month earlier, MRI of the posterior thigh had demonstrated absence of the distal semitendinosus muscle on the right, interpreted as a high-grade tear of the semitendinosus. The patient underwent five sessions of physiotherapy including ultrasound, TENS, low-level laser, and hamstring exercises, without improvement.

During the current assessment, sustained pressure for 30 seconds using thumbs over the course of the PFCN between the sacrotuberous ligament and the semitendinosus muscle stump reproduced his pain and tingling in the posterior thigh. Pressure applied along the PFCN in the thigh did not reproduce symptoms.

A 32-year-old woman presented with 3 weeks of progressive abdominal distension accompanied by shortness of breath, cough, fatigue, and loss of appetite. She denied fever, weight loss, or night sweats. Three days before symptom onset, she had undergone a medical termination of pregnancy. Her medical history was otherwise unremarkable.

On examination, blood pressure was 100/70 mmHg, pulse 72/min, respiratory rate 28/min, temperature 36.6°C, and oxygen saturation 85% on room air. Chest auscultation revealed dullness and decreased air entry over the lower thirds of both posterior lung fields. Abdominal examination showed marked distension with positive shifting dullness and a fluid thrill. The skin was coarse and dry on trunk and extremities; there was no palpable thyroid enlargement.

Laboratory studies showed moderate anemia, normal liver enzymes and creatinine, a thyroid-stimulating hormone level of 49 μIU/mL, free T3 of 1.1 pg/mL, and free T4 of 0.3 ng/mL. Tests for antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and HIV were negative. Analysis of pleural fluid revealed 1 200 cells/μL (93.3% lymphocytes), protein 5.6 g/dL, LDH 704 U/L, and glucose 47 mg/dL, consistent with an exudative effusion. Echocardiography showed mild pericardial effusion, and abdominal ultrasound confirmed ascites. Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral pleural effusions. Thyroid ultrasound revealed heterogeneous echogenicity of both lobes measuring 0.4 mL, suggesting atrophy.

A 54‐year‐old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with acute coronary syndrome and underwent elective percutaneous coronary intervention via femoral access, with stent placement in the left anterior descending and an obtuse marginal artery. A total of 150 mL of iodinated contrast was used. His blood pressure remained between 132/84 mmHg at admission and up to 140/92 mmHg during the procedure. Baseline electrocardiography showed normal sinus rhythm, and echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 45% without valvular dysfunction. Two hours after the procedure, he reported new‐onset horizontal diplopia. He had no prior history of ocular or neurologic disease. Emergency noncontrast head CT and MRI of the brain showed no acute abnormalities. Neuro‐ophthalmologic examination revealed isolated paresis of the left lateral rectus muscle; there was no ptosis, pupillary light reflexes were normal, and no other neurologic deficits were identified.

A 57-year-old man was evaluated for left renal colic and consideration of definitive treatment for nephrolithiasis. His medical history included chronic hepatitis B, hypertension, left bundle-branch block, prostate enlargement, and a splenectomy performed in childhood after a motor-vehicle accident. He reported no other symptoms. On examination, his vital signs were within normal limits and the abdominal examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, showed no abnormalities. CT-urography demonstrated a 9 mm calculus in the lower calyx of the left kidney and multiple nodular lesions up to 3 cm in size along the left and right iliac axes, within pelvic peritoneal fat, and along the intestinal serosa, particularly adjacent to the sigmoid colon and cecum, findings suggestive of pathologic lymphadenopathy.

A 48-year-old man presented with three days of generalized abdominal pain, obstipation, and nausea. He denied fever, chest pain, dyspnea, loss of consciousness, seizures, bleeding disorders, or anticoagulant use. One year earlier, he had experienced a playful punch to the abdomen, followed by transient severe pain that resolved within a day. On examination, he was alert (GCS 15), with stable vital signs and no pallor, jaundice, lymphadenopathy, edema, or signs of dehydration. Abdominal examination revealed generalized tenderness without organomegaly. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, WBC 6100/mm3, platelets 118 000/mm3, mild elevations in AST, ALT, and GGT, and normal bleeding time, clotting time, PT, and INR. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen demonstrated marked proximal dilatation of jejunal loops, collapse distally, and an intramural soft-tissue density in the jejunum consistent with a mass lesion causing small-bowel obstruction.

A 12-year-old boy with a known diagnosis of galactosialidosis (late infantile form) presented with relapsing episodes of progressive swelling in the patellar region of both knees. He is the first child of consanguineous, healthy parents of Turkish descent. His GS diagnosis was made at 17 months of age after identification of hepatomegaly, vertebral deformity, coarse facial features, and biochemical confirmation of deficient PPCA, GLB1, and NEU1 activities. Since then, he has exhibited short stature, kyphosis, joint dysplasia, contractures, mild valvular regurgitation, and macular cherry-red spots.

At age 8, he developed mild right knee swelling. Whole-leg X-rays showed progression of valgus malalignment bilaterally but no joint space narrowing, osteophyte formation, or arthrosis. Knee ultrasound and contrast-enhanced MRI revealed severe effusion and extensive thickening of the enhancing synovial membrane throughout the joint.

At age 12, he reported 3 months of progressive right knee swelling with mild activity-related pain but no morning stiffness, nocturnal pain, fever, trauma, or preceding infection. He had no other joint symptoms. Physical examination showed warmth and severe swelling of the right knee only. Height was 111 cm (<−3 SD) and weight 19 kg (−0.5 SD for age). Family history was negative for autoimmune disease.

Laboratory tests: leukocyte count 4.7 × 10^9/L (4–14 × 10^9/L); C-reactive protein 1.1 mg/L (0–5 mg/L); antistreptolysin titer negative; Borrelia serology negative; HLA-B27 negative; ANA negative; IgM rheumatoid factor 18.0 kU/L (0–49 kU/L); anti-CCP 9 kAU/L (0–25 kAU/L).

Initial differential diagnoses included juvenile idiopathic arthritis, infectious arthritis, reactive arthritis, and malignancy. Four months later, diagnostic arthroscopy of the right knee demonstrated severe synovitis. Synovial fluid analysis showed high cellularity with mononuclear cell infiltration and a predominance of macrophages; it was negative for bacterial pathogens (including Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Borrelia), not suspicious for malignancy, and showed no crystals. Microscopic examination of the synovial tissue revealed numerous foamy macrophages with extensive vacuolization, consistent with the previous diagnosis of GS.

A 70‐year‐old woman with an undifferentiated connective tissue disorder and rheumatoid arthritis was treated with hydroxychloroquine in 2010, after which she developed a severe generalized bullous and pustular rash that resolved over three months following drug discontinuation and corticosteroid therapy. In 2022, hydroxychloroquine was restarted for her rheumatoid arthritis. Three days after restarting the drug, she was admitted with widespread erythema, desquamation, and pustulation. She denied any history of psoriasis. Laboratory studies revealed marked leukocytosis, hyperglycemia, hypoproteinemia, transaminitis, and an elevated C‐reactive protein level. Skin biopsies from the back demonstrated separation of the stratum corneum with multifocal subcorneal collections of neutrophils, underlying spongiotic epidermis with neutrophilic exocytosis, papillary dermal edema, and a superficial perivascular and interstitial infiltrate composed of lymphocytes, histiocytes, neutrophils, and rare eosinophils.

A 47-year-old man with chronic cognitive impairment from a remote motor vehicle–related head injury lived in a nursing home. He required tracheostomy and was fed via a PEG tube with an Isosource® HN formula (1800 kcal/day). At baseline, he spoke in simple sentences and was oriented but unable to perform ADLs. Over several days, he became increasingly agitated, confused, and drowsy, with a reversed sleep cycle. 

He was on chronic phenytoin therapy; an initial level was supratherapeutic at 143 μmol/L (therapeutic 40–80 μmol/L), and the dose was reduced to achieve levels of 63 μmol/L and later 14 μmol/L without any improvement in mental status. He remained oriented only to person. 

Laboratory evaluation showed normal hematologic profile, electrolytes, renal function, glucose of 6.6 mmol/L, normal liver biochemistry, an International Normalized Ratio within normal limits, total bilirubin 8 μmol/L (normal <18 μmol/L), and albumin 29 g/L. Multiple measurements of serum ammonia were elevated at 75–100 μmol/L (normal <35 μmol/L). He was not taking any medications other than phenytoin that are associated with hyperammonemia.

• A 74-year-old man was referred after an antero-septal STEMI treated with primary PCI and stenting from the left main to the LAD.  
• Past history: dyslipidemia, overweight (BMI 25.8 kg/m²), active smoker, surgically repaired infra-renal abdominal aortic aneurysm.  
• Physical exam: unremarkable cardiovascular and respiratory findings.  
• Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE): mild LV dilation (EDD 57 mm), LVEF 46% due to anterior/mid-septal and apical akinesia; grade II diastolic dysfunction; severe LA enlargement; sclerotic aortic and mitral leaflets with mild AR and moderate MR; normal RV size and function; mild TR (PASP 52 mmHg); normal IVC; no pericardial effusion; mild ascending aorta dilation.  
• TTE also identified a ~9 mm round, hyperechoic mass adherent to the ventricular surface of the anterior tricuspid leaflet, moving toward the RA in systole.  
• Transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) confirmed a 6×8 mm non-solid structure on the ventricular aspect of the anterior tricuspid leaflet with a “finger-in-glove” blind-ended protrusion, internally empty with filamentous adherent elements (“garland-like”), echogenicity matching adjacent tissue, bulging in systole and relaxing in diastole.  
• The patient remained asymptomatic. Contrast-enhanced chest CT excluded pulmonary embolism, and blood cultures were negative.

A 40-year-old man presented with subacute, progressive sensory and motor deficits. One week after endovenous laser ablation therapy of varicose veins in the right leg, he noted numbness in that leg. Over the next week, sensory loss spread to the left leg and ascended to the T6 dermatomal level. Seven weeks after symptom onset, he developed impaired balance, bilateral leg weakness, and erectile dysfunction.  

His medical history included Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, prior shoulder surgery, and a remote history of heavy alcohol use (in recovery for 5 years). Physical examination revealed hyperreflexia, sensory ataxia, and loss of deep sensation below T6, with inability to perceive crude touch, vibration, and proprioception in the upper limbs.  

Laboratory studies showed macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin 11 g/dL) and a serum vitamin B12 level <150 pg/mL; antiparietal cell antibodies were present. Electromyography demonstrated symmetric sensory polyneuropathy.  

MRI of the brain revealed multiple nonconfluent T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions in the frontoparietal white matter. Spinal MRI showed a longitudinally extensive T2-hyperintense lesion confined to the dorsal columns from the area postrema through the lower thoracic cord, with an axial “inverted V-sign”; there was no cord expansion or atrophy, and T1-weighted images were normal.

A 65-year-old woman with a history of non-Hodgkin lymphoma treated with chemotherapy, an autologous transplant in 2006, and a subsequent allogeneic transplant for relapse presented two months after her last cycle of bendamustine and rituximab with progressive weakness. She had received two cycles of bendamustine (90 mg/m2 on days 2 and 3) and rituximab (375 mg/m2), achieving remission; the third cycle was held due to delayed blood count recovery.
