She initially noted lower extremity weakness that advanced to generalized weakness over weeks, resulting in multiple falls and bed confinement. On examination, strength was 4/5 in both upper extremities and 3/5 in both lower extremities; deep-tendon reflexes were 2 to 3 of 4, and sensation was intact.  

Magnetic resonance imaging of the head revealed generalized atrophy, small-vessel ischemic changes, and an old right occipital infarct, without any acute intracranial process. MRI of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine demonstrated no lesions to explain her symptoms.  

Laboratory studies showed normal serum levels of vitamin B12, copper, methylmalonic acid, and homocysteine. A lumbar puncture produced cerebrospinal fluid with glucose 70 mg/dL, protein 61 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 23 IU/L, and no oligoclonal bands, malignant cells, or cryptococcus. Molecular tests on CSF were negative for JC virus, Epstein–Barr virus, human herpesvirus 6, and cytomegalovirus.

A previously healthy 5‐year‐old girl was referred with six days of fever, non‐productive cough, and general malaise despite two days of amoxicillin. She also reported diffuse lower‐extremity pain. On examination she had slight wheezing but no rash, arthritis, or other abnormalities. Initial laboratory tests showed elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 326 mg/L, leukocytes 16.4×10^9/L, neutrophils 14.0×10^9/L) and a lung radiograph suggested possible consolidation. She was treated empirically for bacterial pneumonia and started on azithromycin after Mycoplasma serology was sent.

Two days later, fever and pain persisted and CRP increased to 437 mg/L; Mycoplasma serology was negative. Physical examination remained unremarkable and she was admitted for intravenous antibiotics as a fever of unknown origin. Over the next days she had quotidian fever spikes with intervening normal periods. Repeat labs showed persistently elevated CRP (232→177→122 mg/L), ESR 111 mm/h, and rising ferritin (3501 µg/L on day 2, 1891 µg/L on day 5). Criteria for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis were not met. Extensive screening for infectious, oncologic, autoimmune, and immunodeficiency disorders was negative. In consultation with a tertiary centre, an FDG‐PET/CT scan was planned to further evaluate the cause of her systemic inflammation.

A 9-year-old girl of eastern Indian origin with no past medical history presented with a 3-day history of fever, abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She had completed a 2-dose Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccination series 31 days earlier and had an asymptomatic positive SARS–CoV-2 PCR test 16 days before presentation; a subsequent home antigen test was negative. After travel to the US Virgin Islands without illness, she returned and developed persistent fever, emesis, and abdominal pain. A respiratory viral panel was negative, and she received a dose of oseltamivir. 

On day 3 of illness, in the emergency department, her temperature was as high as 40.0 °C, heart rate 124–133 bpm, respiratory rate 20–30 breaths/min, blood pressure 94–102/44–54 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 96–100% on room air. Examination showed mild conjunctival injection and epigastric tenderness; no rash was noted.

Initial laboratory studies revealed mild hyponatremia, leukopenia (2,580 cells/µL), thrombocytopenia (68,000/µL), lymphopenia (absolute lymphocyte count 0.24×10^3/µL), elevated C-reactive protein (15.87 mg/dL), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (37 mm/hr), ferritin (1,028 ng/mL), procalcitonin (2.45 ng/mL), D-dimer (10.86 µg/mL FEU), lactate dehydrogenase (409 unit/L), BNP (253 pg/mL), and normal troponin T. SARS–CoV-2 PCR and rapid streptococcal antigen were negative. Urinalysis showed trace protein, small leukocyte esterase, and WBCs 10–19/hpf.

She received 2 g/kg IVIG and empiric ceftriaxone and doxycycline; antibiotics were discontinued after 72 hours when cultures remained negative. Approximately 5 hours after IVIG, she developed a macular, nonpruritic, nonpetechial rash on the neck and hands, and bilateral conjunctival injection without discharge appeared on hospital day 1. She became afebrile 24 hours after completing IVIG and was started on prednisone (2 mg/kg/day). She experienced intermittent confusion and agitation. Low-molecular-weight heparin was given for DVT prophylaxis and later stopped; echocardiography was unremarkable.

Despite decreasing inflammatory markers, pancytopenia persisted with nadirs of hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL, platelets 30,000/µL, white-cell count 2,580 cells/µL, and absolute lymphocyte count 240 cells/µL, while BNP peaked at 4,114 pg/mL on hospital day 3. Complement levels were normal; ANA was positive at 1:320 with negative anti-dsDNA and Smith antibodies. Proinflammatory markers were elevated (IL-6 284 pg/mL; CXCL-9 13,122 pg/mL). Direct antiglobulin test was negative, and peripheral smears before and during steroids showed no blasts. Bone marrow aspiration was considered but deferred. Thrombocytopenia began to improve on hospital day 7, with a platelet count of 104,000/µL at discharge.

A 70-year-old woman was referred for a tender, red, and painful swelling with purulent secretions in the left medial canthus, just below the lower punctum lacrimale. She first noted mild tenderness in this area 2 years earlier, which progressed to recurrent purulent discharge. Treatments with steroid and antibiotic eye drops yielded only temporary relief, and the lesion was labeled as a recurrent chalazion. 

On examination, visual acuity was normal. There was an inflamed, firm, nodular swelling at the medial canthus. Digital pressure over the lesion produced purulent discharge through a pouting lower punctum, and a second exit of purulence was noted along the palpebral conjunctiva below the lacrimal caruncle. 

The patient underwent an incision via the inner palpebral approach, using a standard chalazion-surgery technique. Under pressure, a gray mass was expressed and sent for histopathological evaluation; the cavity was drained.

A 32-year-old woman with a history of two first-trimester miscarriages was referred at 15 weeks of gestation for routine obstetric ultrasound. She had no vaginal bleeding or pain. First-trimester ultrasound showed a normally developing fetus (crown–rump length, 64.6 mm) without anomalies. Maternal serum β-hCG was 0.773 MoM and PAPP-A was 2.323 MoM. Given her obstetrical history and a calculated 1:180 risk of preeclampsia, she received low-molecular-weight heparin, aspirin, and low-dose prednisone.

At 16 weeks, ultrasound showed early-onset fetal growth restriction, a hyperechogenic fetal bowel, and a hypertrophic, anterior placenta with multiple anechoic cysts (maximum thickness, 4 cm). At 19 weeks, repeat ultrasound revealed a voluminous placental mass with a bumpy surface, severe oligohydramnios, and symmetric growth restriction (estimated fetal size 3 weeks behind gestational age). Continuous monitoring noted frequent fetal bradycardia episodes over 30 minutes. Doppler studies of the umbilical artery, uterine artery, and ductus venosus were normal. Serologic tests for parvovirus B19 and Listeria monocytogenes were negative. Amniocentesis was deferred because of oligohydramnios. A multidisciplinary team recommended a medically induced abortion due to the high risk of intrauterine fetal demise. 

At dilation and evacuation, the placenta was noted to be highly adhesive with a spongy appearance. A 400 g fragmented specimen of the fetus and placenta was submitted for histopathological evaluation.

A 50-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after being found minimally responsive at home. He had a history of mitral valve endocarditis, intravenous heroin use, tobacco use, and atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation. Ten days earlier, he had been hospitalized elsewhere for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia with documented mitral valve vegetations but left against medical advice.

On arrival, he appeared ill and in acute distress. His Glasgow Coma Scale score was 8 (E2, V2, M4). He was afebrile; heart rate, 140 beats/min with an irregular rhythm; blood pressure, 131/78 mm Hg; respiratory rate, 30 breaths/min; and oxygen saturation, 100% on a non-rebreather mask. Blood glucose was 167 mg/dL. He occasionally groaned but did not follow commands. Cardiac examination showed tachycardia with an irregular rhythm. Pupils were 3 mm, equal, sluggishly reactive; there was a right conjugate gaze deviation. He withdrew from pain in his right arm and leg but did not localize, and he had left-sided hemiparesis. His NIH Stroke Scale score was 26. Skin examination revealed pallor and multiple track marks on the upper extremities.

Point-of-care transthoracic echocardiography revealed a large mitral valve vegetation. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 30,900/mm^3 with neutrophilic predominance, lactate 7.3 mmol/L, and creatinine 3.48 mg/dL. Noncontrast CT of the head and CT angiography of the head and neck demonstrated a right internal carotid artery terminus occlusion with poor leptomeningeal collateral flow to the right cerebral hemisphere and small areas of hemorrhagic transformation in both hemispheres, right greater than left.

A 45-year-old Arab man presented with a 3-cm mass at the peno-scrotal junction. He had paraplegia from a traffic accident 10 years earlier and total urinary incontinence managed by iterative prolonged urethral catheterizations. He reported recurrent urinary tract infections and had been voiding by manual scrotal compression for several months. On examination, there was a firm mass at the peno-scrotal junction, and compression of the mass caused urine to leak from the urethral meatus. Urine culture showed no bacterial growth. A retrograde urethrogram demonstrated an anterior outpouching of the urethra at the peno-scrotal junction that filled with contrast.

A 77-year-old woman was referred with a 3-year history of constant, progressive left temporomandibular‐joint (TMJ) pain. Her medical history included ischaemic heart disease, multinodular-goitre thyroidectomy, asthma, chronic kidney disease (eGFR 21 mL/min/1.73 m2), irritable bowel syndrome, atrial fibrillation, and anxiety. She took amiodarone, metoprolol, mebeverine, frusemide, thyroxine, venlafaxine, sodium valproate, quetiapine, and theophylline. 

On examination there was a tender swelling over the left TMJ without neurological deficits or limitation of mouth opening. She was fully edentulous and had no cervical lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory studies showed a CRP of 77.2 mg/L (normal <3.0) and low eGFR consistent with her renal impairment. Other routine blood tests were unremarkable; serum urate was not measured.

Noncontrast CT and MRI of the skull base revealed destructive arthropathy of the left TMJ with well-defined articular and juxtaarticular erosions, through-and-through defect of the skull base, and surrounding dense lobulated soft-tissue thickening. The adjacent brain parenchyma was normal.

Initially, malignancy was suspected because of the degree of joint destruction and skull base erosion; however, a head and neck radiologist noted that “the imaging findings were centred in and around the joint and involving either side of the joint relatively equally,” pointing instead to an inflammatory arthropathy. Given the absence of soft-tissue calcifications, pseudogout was deemed less likely (“Gout was considered instead of pseudogout because of the lack of soft tissue calcifications…”). A CT-guided biopsy of the periarticular soft tissue and aspiration of synovial fluid was performed.

A 58-year-old man presented with severe swelling of both the upper and lower lips. Six months earlier, he had a one-week episode of lip swelling that resolved spontaneously; three weeks later, swelling recurred and progressively increased over six months. He denied prior surgical, dental, or cosmetic procedures, and reported no dyspnea, throat obstruction, or urticaria. He had no fever, gastrointestinal symptoms, fatigue, weight loss, or known allergies, and was not taking antihistamines or steroids.

Medical history included uncontrolled diabetes with retinopathy, hypertension, obesity, hyperlipidemia, and ischemic heart disease. Medications were rosuvastatin, bisoprolol, aspirin, fenofibrate, amlodipine/valsartan/hydrochlorothiazide, and insulin.

Examination showed indurated, firm, non-tender, diffuse swelling of the lower lip (more pronounced than the upper lip) and left buccal area, with scaling and dryness. The tongue was normal, facial nerve function intact, and no lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory studies: normal CBC, ESR 16 mm/h, CRP 5.1 mg/L, ALT 57 U/L, AST 49 U/L, normal electrolytes, normal urinalysis. Skin prick tests for airborne and food allergens were negative, as were epidermal prick tests. Tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, and HBV and HCV infections were excluded. Abdominal ultrasound showed grade II fatty liver; chest radiograph was normal. Rheumatology consult ruled out connective tissue disease (ANA 1:80). Laryngology exam was unremarkable; neurology confirmed no facial palsy.

Dental evaluation revealed no fissured tongue, mild gingival overgrowth, normal TMJ and masticatory muscles, and no stomatitis. Orthopantomogram showed bone loss around tooth 16 and mild lateral bone loss in both jaws; periapical radiographs of incisors were normal and all tested teeth were vital. No odontogenic infections were identified.

A 54-year-old previously healthy man presented 1 hour after being struck on the head against a concrete wall with a  headache and diplopia. He denied loss of consciousness or vomiting. He was a nonsmoker with no history of coagulopathy, anticoagulant use, alcoholism, or prior head injury. On examination he was fully alert and oriented. Neurologic examination revealed a dilated right pupil, right eyelid ptosis, and a right oculomotor nerve palsy manifest as impaired adduction, elevation, and depression of the right eye with intorsion. Sensation in the face was intact, and there were no other cranial-nerve or motor deficits. A noncontrast head CT was obtained.
CT of the head showed a right tentorial subdural collection measuring 0.9 cm in thickness without evidence of mass effect on the cerebral hemisphere.

A 50-year-old man presented with gross hematuria. Six months earlier, he had an ischemic stroke treated with fondaparinux and clopidogrel and, after an episode of melena, underwent endoscopy showing erosive gastritis with discrete eosinophilic infiltrate. He denied any allergies, asthma, or respiratory disease. On examination, he had dark macules in the interdigital spaces of his hands. 
An ultrasound revealed a mass on the posterior bladder wall. Cystoscopy confirmed the lesion and he underwent endoscopic resection; histology showed polypoid cystitis. He required multiple blood transfusions and hemostatic transurethral resections for persistent hematuria and anemia. Subsequent cystoscopy demonstrated mucosal inflammation and an ulcerated pseudopolypoid lesion; biopsy revealed a rich eosinophilic–giant cell lympho‐granulocyte infiltrate with granulomatous features and focal necrosis, without peripheral eosinophilia. A further biopsy again showed intense chronic inflammation with abundant eosinophilic granulocytes and no microorganisms. 
Uro-CT demonstrated diffuse bladder wall thickening with low capacity, small lumen, and enlarged regional and para-aortic lymph nodes. Testing for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Quantiferon and urine), Schistosoma eggs, and fungal pathogens was negative. A coagulation-factor study and thromboelastogram (TEG) were performed to evaluate a bleeding diathesis and were normal.

A 57-year-old Japanese man was referred after an abnormal chest radiograph discovered at a routine checkup. He was asymptomatic. He delivered newspapers and had smoked 40 cigarettes daily for 40 years. He had no significant environmental exposures or family history. Vital signs were normal. Examination was unremarkable, with clear lung fields and no rash or joint abnormalities. His modified Medical Research Council dyspnea score was zero. A 6-minute walk distance was 520 m without desaturation. Pulmonary function testing showed VC 3.70 L (102.5% predicted), FEV1 3.12 L (105% predicted), FEV1/FVC 84%, and DLCO 13.01 mmol/min/kPa (66.2% predicted). Arterial blood gas on room air was PaO2 87.5 mmHg. Laboratory tests revealed KL-6 825 U/mL and MPO-ANCA 31.7 RU/mL (normal <20 RU/mL); PR3-ANCA was <2.0 RU/mL. Urinalysis was negative for blood and protein. Chest radiography showed bilateral hyperlucency and coarse reticular opacities in the lower lung zones. High-resolution CT demonstrated centrilobular and paraseptal emphysema in the upper lobes and bilateral subpleural reticular and ground-glass opacities surrounding emphysematous cysts in the lower lobes, without honeycombing. Bronchoalveolar lavage yielded 1.75×10^5 cells/mL (72% lymphocytes; CD4/CD8 ratio 1.24). Rheumatology evaluation found no evidence of systemic vasculitis.

A 41-year-old woman with Fitzpatrick skin type 5 noted a painless, non-pruritic papulosquamous rash on her back that had been present for 1 week. The lesions measured 5–8 mm in diameter, were well-circumscribed, red, raised, and scaly. She presented to the emergency department, where a diagnosis of varicella was made and valacyclovir was prescribed. Over the next month, the rash continued to spread to her face, scalp, palms, and soles. She saw her family physician, who prescribed cephalexin, but there was no improvement. Two months after the initial presentation, she developed fever and her lesions became painful with bleeding and crusting. She returned to the emergency department, and skin biopsies of the right arm and right inner leg were obtained.

A 25-year-old white woman was referred for routine removal of a semi-impacted left lower third molar. In May 1999, under local anesthesia, the tooth was surgically extracted without complication and the postoperative course was uneventful. No cystic lesion was noted at that time.

On October 6, 2003, during a routine dental evaluation, a panoramic radiograph revealed a well-circumscribed unilocular radiolucent area in the left mandibular ramus measuring approximately 3 × 2.5 cm. The margin was slightly irregular—partly well-defined with a radiopaque border and partly ill-defined. The patient was asymptomatic, with no pain, swelling, or paresthesia. Clinical examination showed no expansion of the buccal or lingual cortices and no palpable lymphadenopathy. Her medical history was noncontributory.

A computed tomography scan confirmed a cyst-like low-density area confined to the left ramus of the mandible.

A 63-year-old woman with HIV/AIDS (on dolutegravir, emtricitabine, tenofovir), hepatitis B, and a history of pulmonary tuberculosis presented with two days of pain and acute vision loss in the left eye. She had a TB relapse seven months earlier and had been on rifabutin 450 mg, isoniazid, and pyridoxine daily; her body weight was 62.3 kg. Three weeks before presentation, her CD4 count was 166 cells/mm3 and HIV viral load was <20 copies/mL.

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and light perception in the left; intraocular pressures were 9 mm Hg OD and 8 mm Hg OS. The right eye was normal. Slit-lamp examination of the left eye showed a fibrinous anterior chamber reaction with 4+ cell and flare, a pupillary membrane, and a 1 mm hypopyon. B-scan ultrasonography of the left eye revealed vitritis.

Concerned about endogenous endophthalmitis, she received intravenous vancomycin and cefepime, oral trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and valacyclovir, intravitreal vancomycin, ceftazidime, voriconazole, and ganciclovir, and topical prednisolone acetate and atropine. An aqueous sample was sent for bacterial and fungal cultures and viral and toxoplasmosis PCR testing.

Over three days, the hypopyon resolved and visual acuity in the left eye improved to 20/30 with residual 1+ vitreous cell and haze. Repeat labs showed a CD4 count of 199 cells/mm3, controlled viral load, mildly elevated AST at 49 U/L, and normal ALT. Chest imaging showed improvement of pulmonary disease. Aqueous sampling and systemic workup were unrevealing for other infection.

Two weeks later, she returned with a nearly identical presentation in the right eye. Visual acuity was light perception OD and 20/30 OS. The right anterior chamber had a fibrinous reaction with 4+ cell and flare, a pupillary membrane, and a 1.5 mm hypopyon; ultrasonography again showed vitritis. The left eye had improving vitreous consolidation, a cotton-wool spot, and cystoid macular edema on OCT.

She received the same intravitreal and topical treatments in the right eye. Once the inflammation subsided, fundus examination of the right eye revealed diffuse white plaques along the retinal arteries in all quadrants. Fluorescein angiography showed early hypofluorescence of the lesions with normal arterial filling and late progressive staining without non-perfusion or vascular leakage. Late petaloid leakage consistent with CME was seen on FA and OCT.

A 79-year-old man with a history of unstable angina treated with coronary stent, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted for evaluation of bicytopenia. Two months of facial and hand flushing had preceded admission. Medications included aspirin, a beta-blocker, a calcium-channel blocker, and prednisolone. On admission, vital signs were stable. He was alert and oriented. Examination showed purpura on the lower legs and pale conjunctiva. Heart sounds were regular without murmur. Breath sounds were clear without wheezing or crackles. Initial laboratory results included hemoglobin 7.1 g/dL, platelet count 7.0×10^9/L, white-cell count 4.0×10^9/L with 8% blasts, blood urea nitrogen 15.9 mg/dL, creatinine 1.2 mg/dL, prothrombin time 12 sec (INR 1.07), aPTT 36.2 sec, and lactate dehydrogenase 397 U/L. Acute leukemia was suspected, and because of severe thrombocytopenia and purpura, six units of platelet concentrates were transfused. Approximately 30 minutes after the transfusion, he suddenly developed dyspnea, diaphoresis, and stupor. Arterial oxygen saturation fell to 45% despite 100% mask oxygen, and systolic blood pressure dropped to 80 mmHg. He was intubated and transferred to the intensive care unit. Repeat chest radiography, which had been clear 6 hours earlier, now showed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. A central venous catheter was placed, revealing a low central venous pressure, making cardiogenic pulmonary edema unlikely.

A 20-year-old Caucasian woman was transferred to the ICU in septic shock with multiorgan dysfunction. Her history included allergic asthma and Basedow’s disease managed by partial thyroidectomy. Four weeks prior, she was treated with cefuroxime for a retroareolar inflammation; persistent fever and diarrhea prompted sequential changes to metronidazole and then vancomycin. Stool studies, blood, and urine cultures repeatedly showed no pathogens and C. difficile toxin was negative. A colonoscopy demonstrated multiple small ulcerations throughout the colon, most pronounced in the ileum, cecum, and sigmoid colon. A necrotic lesion of the right breast grew Staphylococcus aureus, Actinomyces turicensis, and Peptostreptococcus species; surgical exploration excluded an abscess. Despite broad-spectrum antibiotics (imipenem–cilastatin, moxifloxacin, fluconazole) and vasopressor support, she remained anuric (creatinine 5.0 mg/dL), with elevated bilirubin (2.9 mg/dL), AST 2572 U/L, ALT 608 U/L, WBC 27.0 G/L, CRP >230 mg/L, and procalcitonin 9.3 μg/L. A repeat colonoscopy again showed multiple mucosal ulcerations. Because of refractory septic shock and risk of perforation, a subtotal colectomy was planned.

A 41-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, gastroesophageal reflux disease, depression, and posttraumatic stress disorder presented with a 2-month history of severe, diffuse joint pain and a 50-lb weight loss over 6 months. His medications included losartan, metformin, alogliptin, and glipizide. He had previously been a heavy user of alcohol, tobacco, and cannabis but had abstained for 6 months. His mother died of breast cancer.

On examination, he had tender, bony nodules throughout his extremities, diffuse rib tenderness, and severely restricted shoulder and lumbar spine motion due to pain. Two months earlier, radiographs had shown multiple fractures and periosteal reactions in the ribs, radius, ulna, and humerus. At that time, his alkaline phosphatase level was 1018 IU/L (reference range, 48–121), with normal bilirubin, alanine aminotransferase, and aspartate aminotransferase levels.

A whole-body nuclear bone scan revealed numerous foci of abnormal uptake in the skull, long bones, ribs, pelvis, and spine, concerning for metastatic osseous disease. Further evaluations included serum protein electrophoresis (negative for multiple myeloma), prostate-specific antigen (within normal limits), bone marrow biopsy (no evidence of malignancy), and bone biopsy of a scapular lesion (no metastatic disease). Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis suggested a possible pancreatic or gastric mass, but endoscopic ultrasound showed no pancreatic or gastric malignancy and instead revealed Barrett’s esophagus and a gastric bezoar.

Upon admission for pain control, laboratory tests again showed an elevated alkaline phosphatase level, a vitamin D level of 31 ng/mL (reference range, 30–100), a calcium level of 8.9 mg/dL (reference range, 8.4–10.6), and a phosphorus level of 3.2 mg/dL (reference range, 2.5–4.5). Positron emission tomography/computed tomography demonstrated increased uptake in the sigmoid colon but no uptake in any osseous lesions.

A 47-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with 3 days of intermittent epigastric and central abdominal pain radiating to the back, worse after eating, associated with one episode of vomiting. She appeared well, alert, and oriented; vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination showed a non-distended, soft abdomen with mild epigastric tenderness. Initial laboratory tests revealed white cells 16.7×10^9/L, C-reactive protein 2 mg/L, hemoglobin 132 g/L, international normalized ratio 1.0, amylase 62 IU/L, and platelets 139×10^9/L (baseline 175×10^9/L). Lactate peaked at 7 mmol/L but normalized with fluids. She had no prior thromboembolism or heparin exposure and no family history of clotting disorders; she did report five previous spontaneous pregnancy losses that were not further investigated.  
Urgent CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed equivocal duodenitis and minimal peripancreatic fat stranding. Empirical IV piperacillin–tazobactam, gentamicin, omeprazole, and analgesics were started. On hospital day 1, oesophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed mild duodenitis in D1; duodenal biopsies were normal. Over the next 5 days, the platelet count fell to 11×10^9/L. Fibrinogen was 4.2 g/L, and there was no splenomegaly on imaging. It then emerged that she had received the ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccine 8 days before presentation; her D-dimer was 24,000 mcg/L.

A 72-year-old Asian man presented with severe pain and decreased vision in his left eye beginning on postoperative day 5 following uncomplicated cataract surgery performed 6 weeks earlier. Postoperatively, vision was good until day 5, when severe pain and visual loss prompted a working diagnosis of surgically induced necrotizing scleritis (SINS) and initiation of systemic and topical corticosteroids by his primary ophthalmologist. When symptoms persisted and vision continued to decline, topical natamycin was added hourly and topical ciprofloxacin every 2 hours while corticosteroids continued. At presentation, visual acuity was counting fingers at 1 meter in the right eye and at 2.5 meters in the left eye; the right eye had a grade 3 nuclear cataract but was otherwise normal. Slit-lamp examination of the left eye showed a well-demarcated area of scleral necrosis predominantly posterior to the posterior lip of the scleral incision, involvement of the anterior lip, surrounding scleral congestion, a clear cornea, and 2+ anterior chamber cells. The posterior segment appeared normal on limited examination. A presumptive diagnosis of SINS was made.

A 43-year-old male fisherman with a history of metabolic syndrome (post bariatric surgery in 2011), gout since 2000 without regular control, and recurrent right‐side dacryocystitis presented with severe left low back pain radiating to the lateral thigh and anterior leg for more than 7 days. He had received analgesics at a local hospital without relief. 

On admission he was afebrile. Physical examination showed clear consciousness, multiple tophi over bilateral elbows and ankles, generalized decreased deep tendon reflexes, and an antalgic gait due to pain; sensory and motor function of the lower limbs and sphincter function were normal. 

Laboratory studies revealed a C-reactive protein level of 18.55 mg/dL and a serum uric acid level of 8.7 mg/dL; other laboratory values were within normal limits. 

Plain radiographs of the lumbar spine were unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine showed a lobulated posterior epidural lesion measuring approximately 2.5 × 0.8 × 0.4 cm at the L4–L5 level, compressing the dural sac and nerve roots. The lesion demonstrated non-specific low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, heterogeneous high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, and marginal enhancement after gadolinium administration.

A 33‐year‐old Gx patient was referred at 21 weeks for monochorionic twin pregnancy complicated by twin‐to‐twin transfusion syndrome. Her obstetric history included HELLP syndrome, intrauterine growth restriction, and a cesarean delivery at 31+2 weeks.  

At 21+5 weeks, she became anxious and hypotensive (BP 60/30 mm Hg; pulse 105 beats/min). On palpation, the uterus was tense without signs of contractions. Ultrasonography showed two viable fetuses with a normally implanted adjacent placenta and free intraperitoneal fluid. Vaginal examination revealed no bleeding and 1 cm cervical dilation. She received 2 L of crystalloid. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL (previously 9.1), prothrombin time 16.1 s, and fibrinogen 3.3 g/L. The initial differential diagnosis included threatening labor, uterine rupture, and placental abruption.

After placement of an epidural, cervical dilation progressed to 2 cm, but she remained hemodynamically compromised (BP 100/60 mm Hg; pulse 120 beats/min) despite a total of 4.5 L of fluids; GCS was 15. She then developed fever (38.1 °C) and was started on antibiotics. The differential diagnosis broadened to include uterine rupture, infected hematoma, and intrauterine infection. A CT scan of the abdomen was planned.

A healthy 4-year-old girl (18 kg, ASA I) of Northern European descent presented for laser tonsillotomy, adenoidectomy, and tympanocentesis. Premedication included oral midazolam (0.1 mg/kg) and ibuprofen (10 mg/kg). Standard monitors were applied. Anesthesia was induced with fentanyl 20 µg, propofol 70 mg, and mivacurium 6 mg. Dexamethasone 2.5 mg and ondansetron 2 mg were given for PONV prophylaxis. Anesthesia was maintained with remifentanil (0.5 µg/kg/min) and propofol (10 mg/kg/h) under processed EEG monitoring (Narcotrend target 40–60).

Five minutes before the end of surgery, anesthetics were discontinued. The Narcotrend index rose to B1–B2 (80–89), indicating light residual sedation. Over the next 25 minutes, the patient remained apneic without spontaneous ventilation. The index then decreased to C1–C2 (70–79) before sharply increasing to A (94), despite sustained apnea. Sedation was resumed with remifentanil (0.2 µg/kg/min) and propofol (4 mg/kg/h). Train-of-four testing (2 Hz) elicited no twitches (TOF 0/4), indicating residual neuromuscular blockade.

A 30-year-old Japanese man presented with a 3-month history of fatigue, palpitations, weight loss, tremor, and heat intolerance. On examination, temperature was 36.3 °C, blood pressure 110/50 mmHg, pulse 70 beats/min, and the thyroid gland was slightly enlarged, non-tender, and softly elastic without exophthalmos. Laboratory tests showed elevated free T3 and free T4 with undetectable TSH. Anti-TSH–receptor, anti–thyroid peroxidase, and anti–thyroglobulin antibodies were positive. Thyroid ultrasonography revealed diffuse enlargement without nodules. A diagnosis of Graves’ disease was made, and methimazole was started. Over the next 6 months, his symptoms resolved and thyroid function normalized on methimazole 10 mg/day. He remained on maintenance therapy at a local hospital, with periodic testing showing elevated free T3 and free T4 but normal or slightly elevated TSH.

Eighteen years later, at age 48, he was referred for further evaluation. He was asymptomatic, with a heart rate of 80 beats/min and no stigmata of thyrotoxicosis. On methimazole 10 mg/day, laboratory evaluation revealed free T3 5.4 pg/mL (2.4–4.3), free T4 1.7 ng/dL (0.9–1.8), and TSH 4.77 μIU/mL (0.35–4.94), consistent with inappropriate secretion of TSH despite elevated thyroid hormones.

A 73-year-old man (ASA II; height 156 cm; weight 51 kg) with benign prostatic enlargement was scheduled for transurethral resection of the prostate under spinal anesthesia. His medical history was notable only for ureterorenoscopic stone manipulation one month earlier under spinal anesthesia, without complications or hypersensitivity reactions to bupivacaine, midazolam, or cefazolin. He had no history of cardiovascular disease or thromboembolism. 

Preoperatively, his blood pressure was 155/98 mmHg, heart rate 66 beats/min, respiratory rate 12 breaths/min. Physical examination revealed no leg swelling or tenderness. ECG, chest radiograph, and coagulation tests were unremarkable. Spinal anesthesia was established with 12 mg of 0.5% hyperbaric bupivacaine, achieving a sensory block to T6, and 400 mL of crystalloid was infused without hemodynamic instability. Cefazolin was administered, and 100% O₂ at 6 L/min was delivered by mask. 

Before surgery, compression stockings were applied and the patient was positioned in lithotomy using knee-crutch leg holders. Approximately 15 minutes after leg manipulation, he complained of severe chest tightness and shortness of breath. On examination, breath sounds were clear bilaterally; blood pressure was 132/85 mmHg, heart rate 62 beats/min, and SpO₂ 89% on oxygen. There were no signs of skin flushing, urticaria, or angioedema. The spinal block level remained at T5–T6.

An acute myocardial infarction was initially suspected, and 3 mg of morphine was given. A 12-lead ECG showed no ischemic changes. Cardiac enzymes were sent. The patient became agitated, his heart rate increased to 110 beats/min, blood pressure dropped to 98/60 mmHg, and oxygen saturation fell to 89%. He was intubated after induction with midazolam, propofol, fentanyl, and rocuronium, and mechanically ventilated. End-tidal CO₂ was 0–19 mmHg. Arterial blood gas on FiO₂ 1.0 showed pH 7.49, PaO₂ 82.6 mmHg, PaCO₂ 35.3 mmHg, yielding a PaCO₂–EtCO₂ gradient of 16 mmHg. 

Transesophageal echocardiography did not show visible thrombi in the ventricles or right ventricular dysfunction, but pulmonary embolism was suspected.

A one-year-old boy was brought to the emergency department for acute-onset respiratory distress during sleep, perioral cyanosis, and severe cough. His mother reported that she works at a farmers’ market selling beans and vegetables, including unprocessed seeds of Lupinus mutabilis (“chocho”), and that she had seen her son place a chocho seed in his mouth about three hours before presentation. 

On examination, the child had inspiratory stridor. Flexible bronchoscopy was performed but revealed no foreign body in the airway. Upper endoscopy showed grains of chocho in the gastric cardia and stomach. Six hours after arrival, he became irritable with altered consciousness and shallow breathing. Examination then showed dilated, sluggishly reactive pupils; dry mucous membranes; and a distended, tympanic abdomen. His heart rate was 100 beats per minute, respiratory rate 26 per minute, and oxygen saturation 98% on 30% FiO2 by nasal cannula. 

An arterial blood gas showed pH 7.50, PCO2 23 mm Hg, PO2 135 mm Hg, and HCO3– 18.4 mEq/L. Laboratory values were: sodium 144 mEq/L, potassium 3.4 mEq/L, WBC count 8,800/mm3, hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, platelets 316,000/mm3, glucose 107 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, and negative C-reactive protein. Because of his altered mental status, he was admitted to the intensive care unit and started empirically on intravenous fluids, ceftriaxone, and mannitol. 

Computed tomography of the head was normal, and lumbar puncture showed normal cerebrospinal fluid. All empiric medications were then discontinued, and he remained in the ICU for monitoring and supportive care.

A man in his late 60s presented with progressive dysphagia. He had no fever. Laboratory studies showed mild leukocytosis (WBC 13.9×10^9/L) with neutrophilia, normal eosinophil and platelet counts, mildly elevated C-reactive protein (18.3 mg/L) and D-dimer (3.62 mg/L), and a normocytic anemia consistent with anemia of chronic disease. Other blood tests, including renal, liver, electrolyte panels, and immunological markers (SSA, SSB, MPO-ANCA, PR3-ANCA, dsDNA, RNP, Sm, cryoglobulins, TPO, Tg), were unremarkable.  
   
Upper endoscopy revealed narrowing of the mediodistal thoracic esophagus with dense fibrin deposition that barely allowed passage of the scope. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed an extensive, irregular, partly necrotic, infiltrative mass involving the distal esophagus, paraesophageal fat, mediastinal pleura, pericardium, and adjacent aortic wall. No other mediastinal or abdominal pathology was identified. These imaging features were interpreted as consistent with a locally advanced esophageal carcinoma.

A woman in her 50s presented with acute urinary retention and paresis of the right lower limb. Over the preceding 3 days, she noted abdominal distension, anorexia, and nausea. Two weeks earlier, she had a 12-hour episode of urinary retention that resolved spontaneously when she lay supine, followed by polyuria and pollakiuria. Since then, she could only empty her bladder completely in dorsal decubitus and required diapers when seated. At presentation, she had been anuric for 3 hours. A Foley catheter yielded 1.5 liters of clear urine. She had regular menses and no prior deliveries.  

On neurologic examination, right lower-limb strength was decreased. A gynaecological examination showed that the cervix was not visible on speculum inspection; on bimanual exam the cervix was displaced anteriorly and the cul-de-sac was obliterated by a painful, non-mobile pelvic mass.  

Laboratory studies showed a negative β-hCG, hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL, C-reactive protein 13.3 mg/dL, CA 19-9 94.5 U/mL (normal <37), and CA 125 817 U/mL (normal <35). Renal function, electrolytes, and urinalysis were normal.  

Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed no infection, glucose 67 mg/dL, and protein 30.1 mg/dL. Brain and spine MRI were normal. Electromyography indicated a subacute right L5 radicular lesion.  

Abdominopelvic CT showed an enlarged uterus and right uretero-hydronephrosis. Pelvic MRI demonstrated significant hypertrophy of the posterior uterine wall suggestive of adenomyosis, right anterolateral displacement of the bladder, and an elongated, anteriorly displaced cervix compressing the urethra and bladder neck. The ovaries appeared normal. The diagnosis of uterine incarceration was hypothesised.

A 4-year-old boy was evaluated for recurrent falls that began 2 years earlier after a left-sided simple focal seizure. He has had two additional similar seizures. He was born after an uneventful antenatal course; postnatally he required phototherapy for neonatal jaundice. Developmental milestones were mildly delayed: head control at 5 months, standing with support at 18 months, walking without support at 2 years; speech of small sentences by 1.5 years. At presentation, he could climb stairs one at a time and copy a circle. Parents are third-degree relatives; there is a similar developmental history in an older sibling.

On examination he was alert, active, and afebrile, with enlarged head (circumference 51.5 cm, 85th–97th centile), height 94.5 cm, and weight 10 kg (<1st centile). Neurologic exam showed decreased muscle tone and a wide-based, swaying gait. Routine blood tests were normal. EEG demonstrated epileptiform discharges from the right central region.

Brain MRI revealed marked megalencephaly, bilateral anterior temporal subcortical cysts with CSF‐like signal intensity, diffusion facilitation in the affected anterior temporal lobes, involvement of subcortical U fibers, and relative sparing of the deep and cerebellar white matter. MR spectroscopy of affected white matter showed a marked reduction in the N‐acetyl aspartate peak.

A 69-year-old man with a history of unicentric Castleman’s disease (plasma cell type) resected in 2010 and in remission through 2013 presented in June 2016 with a one-week history of nausea, vomiting, diffuse abdominal discomfort, and edema of the distal extremities. He had no history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, smoking, or alcohol use. 

On physical examination, he was pale, with conjunctival pallor and pitting edema of both legs; there was no hepatosplenomegaly or peripheral lymphadenopathy. 

Laboratory studies showed:  
• Hematocrit 25.7%, hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL, MCV 87 fL  
• Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 80 mm/h, C-reactive protein 76 mg/L  
• Blood urea nitrogen 75 mg/dL, creatinine 6.2 mg/dL  
• Total protein 5.9 g/dL, albumin 2.4 g/dL, intact PTH 151 pg/mL  
• Other electrolytes and liver enzymes within reference ranges  

Urinalysis revealed 3+ protein without erythrocyte or leukocyte casts; the 24-hour urine protein was 10 g. Serologic tests including ANA, anti–double-stranded DNA, anti–GBM, and ANCA were all negative. 

Renal ultrasonography demonstrated normal-sized kidneys with grade 2 cortical echogenicity. PET-CT showed only multiple millimetric paraaortic lymph nodes without fluorodeoxyglucose uptake.

A 78-year-old woman with a history of essential tremors underwent an abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan for neurologic screening, which incidentally revealed multiple hepatic nodules. She reported no abdominal pain, weight loss, fever, or other systemic symptoms. Her medical history was unremarkable except for tremors; she denied alcohol use and had no known liver disease or prior malignancy.

Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 6940/mm3, hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, and platelet count 208 × 10^3/mm3. Liver function tests were within normal limits: aspartate aminotransferase 21 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase 19 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 204 IU/L, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 37 IU/L, and total bilirubin 1.0 mg/dL. Serum tumor markers—including α-fetoprotein, PIVKA-II, carcinoembryonic antigen, carbohydrate antigen 19-9, and soluble interleukin-2 receptor—were all within normal ranges. Viral hepatitis B and C serologies were negative. Serum immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM, and IgG4) and autoantibodies (antinuclear, anti–double-stranded DNA, and anti–smooth muscle) were unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced ultrasonography demonstrated low-echoic lesions in segments 2 and 3 measuring 13 mm and 8 mm, respectively, with arterial-phase enhancement, portal-phase washout, and defects in the Kupffer phase. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed nodules in segments 2, 3, 4, and 8 showing ring enhancement in the arterial phase and washout in the portal phase; CT arterial portography revealed perfusion defects, and CT hepatic arteriography showed strong early enhancement with ring enhancement in the late phase. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated low T1 signal, slightly high T2 signal, and diffusion-weighted hyperintensity; on Gd-EOB-DTPA–enhanced dynamic MRI, the nodules exhibited arterial-phase ring enhancement and defects in the hepatocyte phase. Whole-body positron emission tomography–CT showed uptake in the hepatic lesions with maximum standardized uptake values of 4.6 and no other abnormal foci.

Because of atypical imaging findings in a patient without cirrhosis or tumor-marker elevation, the differential diagnosis included hepatocellular carcinoma, metastatic liver tumor (unknown primary origin), malignant lymphoma, inflammatory pseudotumor, and pseudolymphoma.

A 55-year-old woman with a 4-month history of chemotherapy for hairy cell leukemia presented with 3 months of intermittent left flank pain, nausea, anorexia, and weight loss. Her family history was unremarkable. On examination, she was cachectic (height 140 cm; weight 35 kg; BMI 17.85) with massive splenomegaly; vital signs were normal. Laboratory testing revealed hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL; urinalysis was normal. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a heterogeneous splenic parenchyma and a spleen span of 210 mm. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed massive splenomegaly with areas of infarction, a markedly enlarged splenic vein measuring 19 mm in diameter, and prominent bilateral gonadal and pelvic veins. The angle and distance between the abdominal aorta and the superior mesenteric artery were within normal limits, and there was no retroperitoneal mass lesion. Both kidneys appeared normal. Mild ascites, mild hepatomegaly, and signs of secondary portal hypertension were also noted.

A 76-year-old Taiwanese man presented with a 3-month history of a left lower back bulge. He had no systemic diseases, abdominal trauma, or prior surgery. On examination, there was a 10 cm × 6 cm reducible, soft, non-tender, non-numb mass in the left flank. Abdominal computed tomography revealed retroperitoneal fat protruding through the superior lumbar triangle bounded by the 12th rib, quadratus lumborum, and internal oblique muscles.

A 61-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of dull pain and mobility of her lower front teeth, triggered by biting and relieved upon release. She denied trauma or infection in the jaw. Her medical history included hypertension and osteoarthritis; there were no allergies. Examination showed a symmetrical face, normal temporomandibular joint function, and no facial numbness. The maxilla was firm. The dentoalveolar segment from tooth 34 to 44 moved as a unit against a firm mandibular border; there was no bone expansion, mucosal change, periodontal pockets, or caries. The affected teeth were vital. Panoramic radiograph revealed an ill-defined radiolucency localized to teeth 34–44, widening of the periodontal ligament space at teeth 33 and 34, and a “floating teeth” appearance. Cone-beam computed tomography confirmed localized alveolar bone destruction in the anterior mandible.

A 55‐year‐old man was admitted after an unwitnessed collapse. Over the prior six months he had progressive memory difficulties. He was a smoker with no chronic illnesses and took no medications. On examination, vital signs were normal. His score on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment was 24/30, with deficits in delayed recall, language fluency, and orientation. Laboratory hematological and biochemical tests and cardiovascular studies were normal. Electroencephalography showed nonspecific irregular slowing without epileptiform discharges. Noncontrast head CT demonstrated right frontal gliosis, likely old trauma. Brain MRI on hospital day 2 showed high T2 signal and atrophy in the right frontal area consistent with gliosis, plus bilateral mesial temporal T2 hyperintensity. Lumbar puncture revealed 16 white blood cells/μL (100% mononuclear), protein 77 mg/dL, normal glucose, and a negative Gram stain. Brain 18F‐FDG PET demonstrated a focus of intensely increased uptake limited to the head of the right hippocampus on a background of globally reduced cortical uptake.

An 80-year-old woman was referred for infectious-disease consultation because of diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, and fever of 1 week’s duration during rehabilitation after spinal stenosis surgery. Three weeks earlier, she had undergone spinal stenosis surgery and then received methylprednisolone (250 mg daily for 1 week) for postoperative lower-extremity paralysis. Prior to consultation, she had been treated with piperacillin/tazobactam for 7 days and cefixime for 4 days for a urinary tract infection.

One week before referral, she developed diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, and fever. A stool PCR test was positive for C. difficile toxin B. Abdominal and pelvic CT showed diffuse rectal wall thickening with mild perirectal fat infiltration in the upstream colon. She was treated with oral vancomycin (250 mg every 6 hours) for 10 days, after which her fever and diarrhea improved for 10 days. Subsequently, her symptoms recurred with bloody diarrhea and fever.

Her medical history included hypertension and diabetes. She had no family history of gastrointestinal disease. On examination, her temperature was 37.8 °C, blood pressure was 110/60 mmHg, pulse 84 beats/min, and respiration 18 breaths/min. She was alert (GCS 15), had hyperactive bowel sounds, and no abdominal tenderness, rebound, or distension.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL, C-reactive protein 7.3 mg/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 61 mm/h, and white-cell count 9730 cells/mm3 (80% neutrophils, 15% lymphocytes). Stool cultures for Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, and E. coli O157:H7 were negative. Routine stool examination revealed no helminths or protozoa and 1–5 white blood cells per high-power field.

An 85-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of right groin pain and swelling that had appeared 1 week earlier and was initially painless. He reported nausea but denied fever, vomiting, or diarrhea. His past history was notable for a right inguinal herniorrhaphy 25 years earlier.  
On examination, temperature was 36.1 °C, pulse 78 beats/min, blood pressure 102/78 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 14 breaths/min. A 4 × 4 cm tender, nonreducible, nonfluctuant mass with overlying erythema was palpable below and lateral to the pubic tubercle in the right groin. The abdomen was soft, nondistended, nontender, with normal bowel sounds and no signs of obstruction.  
Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 7 × 10^3/μL (reference range, 6–10 × 10^3/μL) and normal electrolytes.  
Transabdominal pelvic ultrasonography demonstrated a 2.4 × 2.6 cm tubular structure in the right femoral region with minimal surrounding fluid. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 3.7 × 4.2 × 3.6 cm dilated tubular structure arising from the base of the cecum and protruding through a widened right femoral ring; the appendiceal wall showed mild homogeneous enhancement and a focal defect near the tip, with a small adjacent fluid collection containing air.

A 40-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of a gradually enlarging swelling on the plantar aspect of his left foot. Examination revealed a firm, 7.5 × 8 cm, non-tender mass without overlying ulceration, nodules, sinus tracts, or regional lymphadenopathy. He denied fever, pain, trauma, or barefoot walking. Routine blood tests, including leukocyte count, differential, ESR, and alkaline phosphatase, were all within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging of the foot showed a soft-tissue mass of presumed fibrous or muscular origin. On the basis of these findings, a working diagnosis of soft-tissue malignancy was made, and an excisional biopsy was planned.

A six-month-old girl, born to second-degree consanguineous parents, was brought for evaluation of scant scalp hair growth over the past three months. At birth, only a few tufts of scalp hair were present; eyebrows and eyelashes were completely absent from birth. There was no family history of hypertension, atopy, hair loss, or autoimmune disorders. The infant had been otherwise healthy, with normal developmental milestones, up-to-date vaccinations, and normal sweating and body temperature regulation. There was no history of seizures, and her two-year-old sibling was healthy.

On examination, there was complete loss of hair on the occipital and bilateral temporal scalp regions, with only sparse terminal hairs on the frontal and parietal regions. Superciliary and ciliary hairs were absent, and no hair was noted on the rest of the body. The hair‐pull test was negative. There were no signs of follicular inflammation or hypopigmented streaks. Mucous membranes and nails were normal. An asymptomatic erythematous-to-pink, blanchable patch with a well-defined border (3 × 4 cm) was noted on the occipital scalp.

Trichoscopy demonstrated remaining terminal hairs of moderate thickness with patent follicular openings and no perifollicular pigmentation or inflammation. Microscopic examination of the hair shaft and bulb was normal. Laboratory studies showed normal levels of vitamin D3, serum calcium, and immunoglobulin E. A scalp biopsy was not performed due to lack of parental consent.

A woman in her 50s presented with a 1-week history of worsening right-sided abdominal pain.  
Her medical history included chronic back pain managed with methadone and hepatitis C treated 9 years earlier; she had no known vascular disease. She reported longstanding abdominal discomfort, bloating, and frequent flatulence and was taking lactulose 50 mL once daily for constipation related to methadone use. She was an ex-smoker and former IV drug user.  
On examination, she appeared in some distress, vital signs were normal, and abdominal examination revealed localized peritonism in the right abdomen.  
Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 6.2 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 2.8 × 10^9/L, and a C-reactive protein level of 6 mg/L.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated multiple subserosal and submucosal gas locules in the caecum and ascending colon and a small volume of free intraperitoneal air; there was no free fluid, no evidence of ischaemia, and no diverticulosis.

A 69-year-old woman was referred with a 1-month history of appetite loss, general fatigue, and low-grade fever. She has rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed at age 60 and had been treated sequentially with salazosulfapyridine, low-dose corticosteroids, adalimumab, etanercept, and, for the past 6 years, certolizumab pegol, with good control of her polyarthritis. She never smoked and had no history of tuberculosis; a baseline IFN-γ release assay before adalimumab was negative.

On admission, her temperature was 37.4 °C. Examination revealed ulnar deviation of both hands without superficial lymphadenopathy or skin lesions; chest auscultation was clear. Laboratory studies showed an elevated rheumatoid factor (40 IU/mL) but normal C-reactive protein, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, and angiotensin-converting enzyme levels. Arterial blood gas analysis was normal. Pulmonary function tests showed a vital capacity of 1.64 L (76% predicted), FEV1 of 1.30 L (87% predicted), and a DLCO of 8.42 mL/min/mmHg (68% predicted). Electrocardiogram and echocardiogram were unremarkable.

Although she had no ocular complaints, slit-lamp examination revealed granulomatous uveitis with mutton-fat keratic precipitates and snowball vitreous opacities bilaterally. Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Chest CT confirmed bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy and multiple micronodules predominantly in the upper lobes; there were no signs of old tuberculosis. Gallium scintigraphy showed increased uptake in bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes.

Bronchoalveolar lavage yielded 2.43 × 10^5 cells/mL (68% macrophages, 25% lymphocytes, 1% neutrophils) with a CD4/CD8 ratio of 99. No microorganisms, including Mycobacteria and Propionibacterium acnes, grew on BAL fluid cultures. A transbronchial lung biopsy from the right upper lobe showed no significant findings.

A 58-year-old Middle Eastern woman presented with 4 months of progressive abdominal distension. Her medical history was unremarkable. On examination, shifting dullness was noted. Abdominal ultrasound showed a single asymptomatic gallstone and approximately 500 mL of ascitic fluid; other intra-abdominal structures appeared normal. Laboratory tests were notable only for an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 75 mm/h and C-reactive protein of 65 mg/L. To rule out malignancy, a diagnostic laparoscopy was performed, revealing diffuse miliary lesions throughout the peritoneum. Ascitic fluid and omental/peritoneal biopsies were obtained. Chest radiography was normal, and a Ziehl–Neelsen stain of bronchial lavage was negative. The patient was started on isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. 

Four months later, she developed moderate upper back pain and chest paresthesia. A computed tomography scan demonstrated destruction of the fifth thoracic vertebra with adjacent soft-tissue formation, and incidentally revealed a nodular formation in the left breast. Clinical breast examination identified a firm, ill-defined 3 × 2 cm mass without overlying skin changes or nipple discharge.

A 20-year-old woman presented with a two-year history of an asymptomatic white patch on her gums. The lesion had gradually increased in size over the first year and then stabilized. She was otherwise healthy, on no medications, and had no history of alcohol, tobacco, or areca nut use. There was no family history of similar lesions or local trauma. On examination, she was moderately built with Fitzpatrick skin type IV and had no extraoral abnormalities. Intraorally, a diffuse white patch measuring approximately 1.5 cm × 1 cm involved the maxillary gingiva from the mid-right central incisor to the distal canine, extending from the attached gingiva to the mucogingival junction. A less pronounced patch (1 cm × 0.5 cm) was present on the left maxillary gingiva extending from the distal central incisor to the canine, and a 0.5 cm × 0.5 cm patch was noted on the attached gingiva of the right mandibular central incisor. No other mucocutaneous abnormalities were found.

A 33-year-old primigravid woman at 31 weeks of a twin pregnancy conceived by in vitro fertilization presented with intermittent chest tightness for 12 weeks, which worsened over the prior week, and acute poststernal colic chest pain lasting 4 hours accompanied by sweating and nausea. She had no history of cardiovascular disease, hypertension, diabetes, smoking, or family history of coronary artery disease. Medications included nifedipine, dexamethasone, progestin, and prophylactic enoxaparin. On examination, temperature was 36.0 °C, pulse 95 bpm, blood pressure 119/73 mmHg, and respiratory rate 20/min; she appeared ill but had no murmurs or pulmonary findings. Laboratory tests showed elevated CK (2924 U/L), CK-MB (21.5 ng/mL), troponin I (47.7 ng/mL), LDH (558 U/L), and myoglobin (1442.7 ng/mL). Initial ECG demonstrated ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, aVF, V3R–V5R, and V7–V9. Echocardiography revealed akinesis of the inferior left ventricular wall and hypokinesis of the basal posterior wall. Given ongoing chest pain, she was treated with antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy. On hospital day 7, simultaneous coronary angiography demonstrated severe proximal stenosis (90%) of the right coronary artery with a thrombus shadow and TIMI flow grade 3; the left coronary circulation was angiographically normal.

A 61-year-old man with nonischemic idiopathic cardiomyopathy and recurrent ventricular tachycardia refractory to multiple endocardial ablations was admitted for acute decompensated heart failure. Given his intractable arrhythmias and advanced heart failure, a multidisciplinary team elected to perform simultaneous surgical arrhythmia ablation and left ventricular assist device (LVAD) implantation. 

Intraoperative course:
• Surgical epicardial cryoablation was performed on cardiopulmonary bypass, targeting inducible VT substrates in the basal lateral and inferior left ventricle.  
• A HeartWare HVAD was implanted; the patient was successfully weaned from bypass at 2700 rpm with flows of 3.0 L/min.  
• Intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) at the end of the procedure demonstrated low-normal left ventricular size and normal wall thickness.  

Postoperative course in the cardiothoracic ICU:
• Initially stable, the patient subsequently developed persistently low VAD flows (<2.0 L/min) with minimal flow variability.  
• Pericardial tamponade was excluded.  
• Lactate dehydrogenase, LVAD power, and bilirubin were normal, thus excluding acute LVAD thrombosis.  
• Adjustments to LVAD speed and inotropic support did not improve flows.  
The decision was made to return to the operating room to assess for acute outflow graft obstruction.

A 47-year-old woman presented with chronic low back pain and right L5 radiculopathy. MRI of the lumbar spine (T1 and T2 weighted) showed multiple mass-like lesions in the right paraspinal soft tissues, including one at the right L5–S1 neuroforamen; all lesions had low signal intensity on both T1 and T2 sequences, and one posterior paravertebral muscle lesion demonstrated a fluid–fluid level. Noncontrast CT of the lumbar spine confirmed calcified mass-like paraspinal lesions without contrast enhancement. Incidental images of the lung bases suggested interstitial lung disease, and a dedicated chest CT showed bilateral pulmonary fibrosis with a craniocaudal gradient and oesophageal dilatation with an air–fluid level. The patient also reported dyspnea, generalized weakness, arthralgia, and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.

6-year-old boy with 2-week history of high-grade intermittent fever, erythematous facial rash, anorexia, and weight loss. Treated empirically for lower respiratory tract infection without improvement. No history of intravenous cannulation, instrumentation, or blood transfusion. On arrival: febrile (104 °F), pulse 140/min, BP 100/60 mm Hg, RR 30/min. He was conscious, dyspneic, pale, irritable, with generalized lymphadenopathy, mild abdominal distension, pedal edema, and a 4-cm soft, non-tender hepatomegaly. Lung exam suggested left-sided collapse consolidation. Cardiovascular and neurological exams, including fundus, were initially unremarkable. Initial working diagnoses were prolonged fever due to left-sided pneumonia with anemia and congestive cardiac failure; typhoid fever and malaria were also considered. Blood, urine, and sputum cultures were obtained, and broad-spectrum antibiotics, supportive care, and diuretics were started. Laboratory tests showed normocytic hypochromic anemia, neutrophilia, moderate thrombocytopenia, and mild left shift; malarial parasites were absent; Widal test was negative. Urine microscopy and cultures were normal. ECG was normal. Chest radiograph revealed a left lower lobe pneumonic patch with mild left pleural effusion. Despite intravenous antibiotics, fever spikes continued. On hospital day 2, repeat cardiovascular examination revealed a faint systolic murmur with a diastolic “tumor plop.”

A 24-year-old Bangladeshi woman with a 2-month history of polyarthralgia, photosensitive rash, intermittent fever, oral ulcers, and alopecia presented with sudden, progressive, painless vision loss in both eyes and progressive weakness of both lower limbs over 48 hours. She denied headaches, seizures, bowel or bladder dysfunction, Raynaud’s phenomenon, or trauma. 

On examination, her vital signs were normal. She had a malar rash, oral ulceration, alopecia, and swollen tender wrist joints. Visual acuity was reduced to hand movements bilaterally; light projection was intact, the direct pupillary reflex was sluggish, and the consensual reflex was normal. Intraocular pressure was 15 mmHg in both eyes. Fundoscopy showed bilateral pale, swollen optic discs with a superotemporal flame-shaped hemorrhage in the right optic disc. 

Neurologic examination revealed bilateral upper motor neuron–type weakness in the lower limbs (muscle power reduced with brisk knee and ankle reflexes and extensor plantar responses) and sensory loss to pain, temperature, and joint position up to the T8 level. Other systemic findings were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed normocytic normochromic anemia, strongly positive ANA (homogeneous), high-titer anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies, low complement levels (C3, C4), and positive anti–aquaporin-4 IgG antibody. Cerebrospinal fluid was normal, with absent oligoclonal bands. 

MRI of the spine with contrast revealed multiple enhancing T2-weighted hyperintense lesions in the cervical and dorsal cord extending over more than three vertebral segments with diffuse cord edema; MRI of the brain and orbits was unremarkable.

An 81-year-old man presented with 3 months of progressive pain and swelling of his right knee after a ground-level fall. He had already undergone four knee aspirations at another facility without symptom resolution. On examination, there was anterior swelling of the right knee with reduced range of motion and an antalgic gait. He rated his pain as 7/10 on a visual analog scale. There were no signs of erythema or warmth. Radiographs showed early degenerative changes but were otherwise unremarkable. A diagnosis of hematoma was made, and the patient underwent irrigation and debridement. Intraoperatively, an organized hematoma was evacuated from the subcutaneous tissue, cultures were taken, and a wound vacuum was applied. Postoperatively, cultures were negative. On postoperative day 2, edema returned to approximately 75% of its original size, and the swelling progressively worsened on day 3. There was no indication of underlying infection.

A 57-year-old African-American woman was seen for a 4-year history of right eye proptosis associated with excessive tearing. She also reported generalized headaches diagnosed as migraine, without improvement on topiramate. On review of systems, she noted pain triggered by chewing, speaking, and brushing her teeth, along with numbness, burning, and tingling in the V1 and V2 distributions of the right trigeminal nerve. She described intermittent right-sided facial muscle spasms and hyperesthesia to external stimuli. She denied any periorbital lesions, herpetic keratitis, head trauma, or infection. Her medical history was negative for diabetes, thyroid disease, cancer, oral herpes, recent infection, or head trauma; her family history was noncontributory.

On examination, pupils were equal, round, and reactive; extraocular movements were intact; and funduscopic exam was normal. The right eye was actively tearing and proptotic, with a Hertel measurement of 25 mm on the right versus 21 mm on the left. There was mild right upper-eyelid ptosis and right eyelid closure weakness. No other neurologic or systemic abnormalities were noted.

Screening tests for diabetes and thyroid disease were within normal limits, and HIV testing was negative. MRI of the orbits, face, and neck with and without contrast demonstrated enlargement and enhancement of the right trigeminal nerve from the cavernous sinus through the superior orbital fissure, foramen rotundum, and foramen ovale, with a 17 × 16 mm well-circumscribed solid and cystic mass arising from the V2 division in the right pterygopalatine space, causing anterior displacement of the globe. Nasal endoscopy revealed only a left mid-septal deviation without other abnormalities.

A 60-year-old retired Ethiopian high-school teacher presented with a 6-year history of anterior neck swelling that had enlarged over the past 3 months. She had taken unspecified antibiotics at a local health center without improvement. She reported low-grade intermittent fever, unquantified weight loss, and night sweats but denied cough, anorexia, pressure symptoms, or other systemic complaints. She had no significant past medical or surgical history and no known exposure to malignancy or thyroid disease in her family. 

On examination, she was afebrile. There was a soft to firm, multinodular mass in the anterior neck, the largest nodule measuring 2 × 3 cm in the left thyroid lobe; there was no cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 4000 µL (54% granulocytes, 42% lymphocytes), hemoglobin 14.5 g/dL, platelet count 350 000 µL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 75 mm/hr. Renal and liver function tests were within normal limits. HIV testing was nonreactive. Thyroid-stimulating hormone was 3 µIU/mL, total T4 7 µg/dL, and total T3 1.5 ng/mL. 

Neck ultrasound showed multiple thyroid nodules with fluid collections suggestive of abscess formation in the left lobe against a background of multinodular goiter. Chest radiography demonstrated normal lung parenchyma and confirmed the presence of a thyroid mass. Abdominopelvic ultrasound was normal.

A 46-year-old Japanese woman presented with a 2-year history of right hemifacial spasm. She had normal development, no history of malignancy, severe head injury, or family neurological disease. Physical and neurologic examinations were unremarkable except for right hemifacial spasm with synkinesis. A non-contrast head CT revealed a 6 mm intraosseous defect in the right occipital bone. Heavily T2-weighted MR cisternography showed a 6 mm isointense mass outside the right cerebellar hemisphere, corresponding to the bone defect. A rim of high-intensity signal consistent with cerebrospinal fluid surrounded the mass and was continuous with the intracranial subarachnoid space.

A 40-year-old Pakistani man was brought to the emergency department with agitation, decreased level of consciousness, and delirium. He had a generalized tonic–clonic seizure that was aborted with intravenous diazepam. This was his first neurologic event, and he had no relevant past medical history. On examination he was afebrile, without neck rigidity, meningeal signs, or rash. Neurologic examination was otherwise unremarkable.

Noncontrast cranial CT was normal. Laboratory studies were negative for HIV antibodies, TB-PCR, hepatitis B and C serologies, and Brucella; blood cultures showed no growth. Lumbar puncture yielded clear CSF with an acellular smear; no acid-fast bacilli were seen, latex agglutination was negative, and culture showed no growth. CSF analysis revealed a protein concentration of 108.4 mg/dL, no cells, lactate dehydrogenase 38 U/L, and glucose 4.9 mmol/L.

Brain MRI demonstrated multiple asymmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions in the supratentorial cortical and subcortical white matter of the parieto-occipital regions (predominantly right temporo-occipital), juxtacortical U fibers in the superior frontal areas bilaterally, bilateral cerebellar hemispheres, and a small focus in the right thalamus. None of the lesions showed mass effect, diffusion restriction, hemorrhage, or enhancement after gadolinium; there was no meningeal enhancement.

He was admitted to the intensive care unit, mechanically ventilated for five days, then transferred to the medical ward for nine more days. Empiric treatment with intravenous ceftriaxone, vancomycin, aciclovir, and dexamethasone was initiated. The initial clinical impression was meningoencephalitis.

A 48-year-old woman presented with intermittent palpitations but no chest pain, syncope, or dyspnea. She was afebrile, blood pressure was 116/70 mm Hg, and pulse 66 beats/min. Cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable. Her medical history was notable only for migraines with aura and occasional palpitations; she had no history of thyroid disease, myocardial infarction, or congenital heart disease. A 12-lead electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a moderately enlarged left ventricle with elevated filling pressure and a mildly enlarged right ventricle; right ventricular systolic pressure was 55 mm Hg. Color Doppler imaging demonstrated a patent foramen ovale with bidirectional shunting, with significant right-to-left flow after Valsalva maneuver.  Coronary computed tomography angiography showed a dominant right coronary artery, enlarged proximally, giving rise to a sizable tortuous vessel coursing posterior to the right atrium near the crista terminalis and entering the superior vena cava.

An 11-year-old previously healthy Caucasian boy was referred for an 11-month history of recurrent low-grade fevers (99–100 °F), anorexia, a 7-lb weight loss, and progressive fatigue. He had night sweats and muscle aches for 4 weeks and developed facial perioral vitiligo. He denied muscle weakness, rash, joint pain or swelling, eye complaints, oral ulcers, and Raynaud’s phenomenon. Family history was negative for autoimmune or rheumatologic disease. On examination, he was thin and fatigued with perioral vitiligo and tachycardia. Carotid auscultation revealed the left carotid pulse to be fainter than the right; no bruits were heard and four-extremity blood pressures were normal. Laboratory studies showed albumin 3.2 g/dL, total protein 8.8 g/dL, microcytic normochromic anemia, ESR 91 mm/h, CRP 7.41 mg/dL, elevated IgG/IgA/IgM, and negative fecal calprotectin. A chest radiograph was unremarkable, and ECG showed normal sinus rhythm without ventricular hypertrophy. A whole-body bone scan showed no focal uptake. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated concentric thickening of the aortic arch with approximately 70% stenosis and diffuse intimal thickening of the left common carotid artery; renal and abdominal vessels were uninvolved. These findings were consistent with arteritis.

A 6-year-old boy presented with a 5-month history of left ankle swelling and progressive pain on walking, with inability to bear full weight. He had a history of atrial septal defect but no trauma. On examination, there was marked swelling on the anteromedial and posteromedial aspects of the left ankle, with palpable bony prominences just medial to the tibialis anterior tendon and on the medial aspect of the Achilles tendon distal to the joint line; these sites were tender. Range of motion was 0° of dorsiflexion and 15° of plantar flexion. Neurovascular examination was normal. 
Plain radiographs (anteroposterior and lateral) showed irregularity of the talar articular surface with exuberant calcifications in the anterior joint compartment and on the posterior aspect of the talus. MRI demonstrated bone marrow edema adjacent to the bony protuberances, synovitis around the lesions, and some joint effusion. CT defined the exact size and location of bony masses in the anterior and posterior ankle compartments. The preoperative American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society hindfoot score was 68/100.

A 16-year-old female with a family history of celiac disease presented with a six-month history of difficulty swallowing solid foods, describing food as “stuck” in her throat and chest, accompanied by mild dizziness and fatigue. She denied weight loss, fever, joint pain, or diarrhea. Her weight was 44.7 kg (BMI consistent with underweight), and her height was 166 cm. Examination revealed no tonsillar enlargement, no thyroid enlargement, and no palpable neck nodules. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 66 g/L, ferritin 1.6 μg/L, vitamin D 34.4 ng/mL, and an RBC count of 4.15 × 10^12/L. Thyroid ultrasound was unremarkable. She was diagnosed with chronic iron-deficiency anemia and received a one-week course of 1 g IV iron, with reported improvement in her swallowing. A standard barium swallow study performed by a radiologist showed aspiration into the trachea on lateral view but no reflux, no abnormal mucosal outline, and no filling defects or narrowing. She was referred to a swallowing clinic. Fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES) revealed a delayed swallow trigger at the vallecula with thin and thick liquids, vallecular residue with all consistencies, and silent aspiration with liquids; she was diagnosed with moderate (level 3) pharyngeal dysphagia. A subsequent videofluoroscopic swallow study (VFSS) confirmed delayed airway closure with aspiration of thin and thick liquids, residues in the vallecula and pyriform sinuses, and additionally demonstrated a circumferential, thin, linear radiolucent defect (approximately 0.2 cm) in the upper third of the esophagus at C5, protruding from the anterior wall with a jet-phenomenon of contrast passage, consistent with an esophageal web.

A 51-year-old man with non-valvular atrial fibrillation (CHADsVASc score 1 for hypertension) presented with intermittent dysgraphia and brief episodes of receptive dysphasia over the preceding week. On the morning of presentation, he awoke at 06:30 with a diffuse headache and at 10:30 developed a 2-minute right superior visual field disturbance characterized by colourful pixelation; the same symptoms recurred at 16:30 with full resolution. His history included rapid atrial flutter treated with direct current cardioversion in 2015 (on sotalol and apixaban), flutter ablation in 2016, recurrent AF treated with cardioversion and sotalol, and a switch from apixaban to dabigatran 150 mg twice daily in October 2018. Other medications were digoxin, fenofibrate, atorvastatin, allopurinol, fluvoxamine, and metoprolol. He used a pharmacy-packed medication box.

On examination, his heart rate was 81 bpm (irregular), blood pressure 127/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air; he was afebrile and cardiovascular and neurological examinations were unremarkable. Initial blood tests showed an eGFR of 36 mL/min/1.73 m2 (previously ≥60) and creatinine 182 µmol/L; other results were normal. ECG demonstrated atrial fibrillation. CT angiography of the brain, carotids, and circle of Willis and brain MRI showed no acute or recent infarction. Provisional diagnosis was a transient ischaemic attack despite therapeutic dabigatran. Admission coagulation studies revealed an APTT of 38 s (25–37 s) and a thrombin time of 83.7 s (14–20 s), suggestive of subtherapeutic dabigatran. After four further supervised doses of dabigatran 150 mg twice daily, peak plasma levels were undetectable (<40 ng/mL).

A 25-year-old man with no past medical history presented to the emergency department with chest pain, shortness of breath, and throat tightness. Six days earlier, he had had similar symptoms, a normal chest radiograph and laboratory tests, and was discharged with symptomatic treatment for a presumed viral syndrome. He returned with persistent chest pain and shortness of breath, now accompanied by acute visual loss in the right eye and weakness in the legs. On examination, his blood pressure was normal; auscultation revealed a loud, holosystolic murmur; and both radial and femoral pulses were diminished. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable. A ventilation–perfusion scan demonstrated homogeneously decreased perfusion throughout the entire left lung, which was interpreted as high probability for pulmonary embolism.

A 62-year-old Caucasian man with a history of heavy alcohol use and a necrotizing pancreatitis 3 years earlier presented with 3–4 weeks of progressive, migrating joint and bone pain. He first noted involvement of both elbows, then ankles, wrists, and metacarpal and interphalangeal joints. He also had a painful, erythematous swelling of his left wrist. Nine months earlier he had had a similar episode of joint pain. He had been treated with doxycycline and 20 mg prednisone daily for presumed reactive arthritis after positive Chlamydia pneumoniae serologies, which normalized his lipase and CRP levels but only partially relieved his joint pain.
