On readmission, he had severe left knee pain with swelling and erythema; lesser pain affected his shoulders, wrists, elbows, and ankles. He denied abdominal pain or current alcohol use. Physical examination showed “sausage toes” of the left fifth toe and two right toes. The abdomen was soft and non-tender. Laboratory studies revealed lipase 232 000 U/L (normal 73–383), amylase 11 920 U/L (normal 25–115), and C-reactive protein 147 mg/L (normal 0–5). Serologies for RF, ACPA, ANCA, ANA, immunoglobulins, complement levels, HIV, hepatitis B and C were all negative. A pretibial fluid collection yielded sterile, bloody material.

Two-phase bone scintigraphy showed symmetric increased uptake in the proximal tibiae, patellae, elbows, wrists, ankles, metatarsals, calcanei, and all interphalangeal joints, with an intense central gap in the left proximal tibia. MRI demonstrated multiple circumscribed T1-hypointense, T2-hyperintense lesions with marginal enhancement in the proximal tibiae and patellae, and similar lesions in the distal tibiae, calcanei, talus, and all tarsal bones; there was an enhancing effusion in the left knee.

Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI of the abdomen revealed a 1.3 cm cystic lesion in the pancreatic head and partial thrombosis of the adjacent superior mesenteric vein.

A 38-year-old woman with no prior comorbidities presented with a 3-week history of holocranial headache, weight loss, and anorexia, followed over 1 week by fluctuating alertness and a single episode of nonbilious, non–blood-stained projectile vomiting. She denied fever, photophobia, blurred vision, or seizures. One week before transfer she was diagnosed with HIV-1 infection at another hospital and started on tenofovir, lamivudine, and efavirenz. 

On examination, her pulse was 136 beats/min, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, and respiratory rate 24/min. She was drowsy but arousable and afebrile. Neurologic findings included bilateral papilledema, restriction of upward gaze, bilateral gaze-evoked nystagmus, and neck stiffness. The remainder of her physical examination was unremarkable.

Initial laboratory studies showed anemia (hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL), leukopenia (total WBC count 2 × 10^9/L), thrombocytopenia (platelets 95 × 10^9/L), and a CD4+ T-cell count of 46 cells/μL. 

Noncontrast CT of the head revealed communicating hydrocephalus with periventricular hypodensities suggestive of transependymal CSF seepage. An external ventricular drain was placed, and CSF analysis showed 80 WBC/mm^3 (lymphocytic predominance), protein 108 mg/dL, glucose 2.72 mmol/L (simultaneous blood glucose 6.22 mmol/L), negative Gram stain and India ink, negative CSF Xpert® MTB/RIF, negative bacterial and fungal cultures, negative cryptococcal antigen in serum and CSF, negative toxoplasma IgM and IgG, and no abnormal cells on cytospin. CSF PCR was positive for CMV DNA.

After removal of the external drain, a ventriculoperitoneal shunt was placed. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI demonstrated resolution of hydrocephalus and numerous periventricular high T2-signal regions with restriction on diffusion-weighted imaging, as well as faint enhancement lining the ependymal surfaces of the lateral ventricles.

A 24-year-old woman at 13 weeks’ gestation presented with 2 weeks of severe right leg pain and fevers up to 39.4 °C. She subsequently developed bilateral calf and left upper-quadrant pain, generalized weakness, fatigue, and inability to bear weight on her right leg. Her medical history included hyperemesis gravidarum with weight loss and mandibular fracture 9 months earlier treated with internal fixation hardware. She owned a rescued wild bird, a cat (with prior bites and scratches), and four pet rats that she allowed to nibble on her fingers; she also noted exposed mandibular hardware. She denied injection drug use and reported a penicillin-induced rash in the past but used marijuana for nausea. 

On examination, she appeared pale and febrile (38.4 °C); right pedal and tibial pulses were diminished. Cardiac auscultation revealed a 2/6 high-pitched holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla. She had left upper-quadrant tenderness and a palpable spleen; there were no rashes or lymphadenopathy. A metal plate was visible below the lower right teeth. The right calf was tender, and a clean, healing bite wound was noted on her finger.

Laboratory studies showed iron deficiency anemia, normal renal and hepatic function, and a normal leukocyte count. Doppler ultrasound demonstrated a right popliteal artery thrombus. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed a 2.0 × 0.7 cm vegetation on the atrial side of the posterior mitral valve leaflet, and angiography showed multiple splenic and bilateral renal infarcts. A right popliteal thrombectomy was performed, and blood and thrombus cultures remained sterile.

A 75-year-old woman with stage IVB lung adenocarcinoma (PD-L1 TPS 90%) and known brain metastases treated by radiotherapy and steroids presented with 5 days of lightheadedness and gait instability. Three days after her second pembrolizumab infusion, she became drowsy with short-term memory loss. Laboratory studies, including leukocyte count and C-reactive protein, were normal. Brain MRI showed stable metastatic lesions without new enhancement, but diffusion-weighted imaging revealed a new high-intensity focus in the right frontal lobe. She received anticoagulation for presumed infarction, yet her mental status declined. On hospital day 12, CSF analysis showed glucose 57 mg/dl, protein 123 mg/dl, 51 cells/μl (94% monocytes), and no malignant cells; CMV IgG and IgM were positive in serum and CSF, while all other viral studies were negative. EEG demonstrated diffuse 4–6 Hz slow waves without epileptiform activity. Repeat MRI was unchanged, and repeat CSF showed protein 79 mg/dl and 24 cells/μl. Her consciousness continued to worsen.

A 5-day-old male neonate, full-term by cesarean section, presented with bilious vomiting since birth and a palpable epigastric mass noted by his parents. The pregnancy was poorly monitored externally, with no maternal medication use reported and no family history of tumors. On examination, he was in good general condition with scleral jaundice, normal vital signs, and no cyanosis. Abdominal examination revealed a distended, soft abdomen with an easily palpable, mobile mass in the epigastrium. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 15.8 g/dL, white blood cell count 12,000/mm³, platelet count 623,000/mm³, and normal tumor markers (CEA, CA 125, CA 19-9, AFP, β-HCG). Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 4.5×3.8 cm non-adherent cystic lesion extending from the epigastrium to the umbilicus with an undetermined origin. Contrast-enhanced CT scan revealed a 5×5 cm cystic mass with attenuating contents located between the liver and right kidney, abutting the posterior renal parenchyma. Differential diagnosis included a duplication cyst and a mesenteric cyst.

A 37-year-old woman with no medical history underwent general anesthesia for laparoscopic appendectomy. Anesthesia was induced with lidocaine 80 mg, propofol 100 mg, and rocuronium 40 mg, and maintained with remifentanil and desflurane. Twenty minutes before the end of surgery, a drip infusion of nefopam 20 mg in 100 mL saline was started for postoperative analgesia. At the end of the procedure, glycopyrrolate 0.2 mg and pyridostigmine 10 mg were given to reverse neuromuscular blockade. The operation lasted 80 minutes with stable vital signs. The patient was extubated after demonstrating adequate spontaneous ventilation and alertness and transferred to the recovery room.

Upon arrival, she reported pain of 8/10 and received fentanyl 100 µg IV. Three minutes later, she developed intense, uncontrolled myoclonus of both arms (3–4 Hz), rigidity of both legs, agitation, aphasia, periocular swelling, facial flushing, and neck swelling. Pupils were 3–4 mm with normal light reflex. Vital signs were blood pressure 100/42 mmHg, heart rate 90/min, respiratory rate 30/min, temperature 36.7 °C, and oxygen saturation 98% on 10 L/min by face mask with reservoir. 

Suspecting opioid-induced myoclonus and rigidity, naloxone 40 µg IV was given; one minute later the myoclonus, rigidity, aphasia, and agitation persisted. Dexamethasone 5 mg IV was administered for swelling. The bispectral index was 80–85. A Doll’s eyes examination was normal. Arterial blood gas analysis and serum electrolytes were within normal limits. Midazolam 2 mg IV produced slight improvement in agitation and gradual resolution of facial swelling. A neurologic examination revealed no evidence of organic brain abnormality, hypoxic injury, or seizure activity.

A 10-year-old boy presented with a 6-year history of recurrent upper respiratory tract infections, occurring 2–3 times per month, characterized by cough, nasal congestion, fever, and difficulty swallowing. He also had snoring, mouth breathing, and a preference for sleeping in the prone position. There was no significant past medical or family history. He had received multiple courses of antibiotics without lasting improvement.

On examination, he was well nourished and in no acute distress. Bilateral level IIIb cervical lymph nodes were palpable. Oral examination revealed markedly enlarged (grade III), congested tonsils bilaterally, and a clear posterior pharyngeal wall. Chest auscultation was normal.

Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin of 13 g/dL, total leukocyte count of 5800/mm3, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 6 mm. Liver and renal function tests were within normal limits. A Mantoux test demonstrated 18 × 20 mm of induration. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. HIV serology was negative.

Fine‐needle aspiration of a cervical lymph node revealed reactive hyperplasia, and staining for acid‐fast bacilli was negative.

A 36-year-old woman, 5 weeks postpartum, presented with 48 hours of nausea and vomiting, plus 2 days of malaise and worsening dyspnea. She denied chest pain, palpitations, diarrhea, headaches, alcohol use, or illicit substances. To lose weight postpartum, she had been eating only small, high-protein, carbohydrate-free meals and had lost 30 lb since delivery. Initial vital signs were temperature 37 °C, blood pressure 140/63 mmHg, heart rate 84 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min; weight was 59.8 kg. She appeared unkempt and lethargic. Examination was otherwise benign except for blunted mentation. Her only medication was percocet for post–cesarean pain; her past history was notable for a cesarean section complicated by bladder injury, now resolved. 

Laboratory results showed: sodium 144 mEq/L, potassium 4.8 mEq/L, chloride 104 mEq/L, bicarbonate <5 mEq/L, BUN 3 mg/dL, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, glucose 133 mg/dL, lactate 2.1 mmol/L, phosphate 1.0 mg/dL, magnesium 1.6 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas on room air: pH 6.9, PCO2 19 mmHg, PO2 137 mmHg, O2 saturation 100%. White blood cell count was 17 600/mm3, hemoglobin 13.7 g/dL, hematocrit 43.1%, platelets 340 000/mm3. Urinalysis revealed a pH of 5.5 and ketones <80 mg/dL. The serum osmolar gap was 7. A comprehensive drug screen, including salicylates and acetaminophen, was negative. Chest radiograph was normal, and blood and urine cultures were negative. The patient was volume-depleted with an anion gap of 35 and a severe metabolic acidosis.

A 6-year-old boy, previously healthy and visiting from Russia, presented on day 4 of illness with fever, right-sided hip and thigh pain, and diffuse lower abdominal pain. The fever had reached 39.1°C and was associated with increasing difficulty bearing weight on the right leg and a noticeable limp. He had been seen twice as an outpatient and received paracetamol and ibuprofen without improvement. On examination he appeared acutely ill and in pain. Vital signs were: temperature 39.1°C, heart rate 110 beats/min, blood pressure 92/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. The lower abdomen was tender with guarding. The right hip was held flexed and externally rotated, with restricted movement in all directions. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 5500/mm3 (85% neutrophils), hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, platelets 184,000/mm3, and a C-reactive protein level of 110.8 mg/L. Blood and urine cultures were repeatedly negative. Ultrasound examination of the hip and abdomen showed no echogenic debris in the hip joint and no appendicular pathology. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen, pelvis, and proximal thighs revealed focal fluid collections measuring 1.3 × 2.0 × 1.4 cm in the right obturator externus muscle and 1.0 × 1.9 × 1.2 cm in the right obturator internus muscle, interconnected at the level of the right ischiopubic ramus, consistent with abscess formation.

A 55-year-old man with a history of acquired copper deficiency (Human Swayback), atrial fibrillation, and cryptogenic cirrhosis was transferred for inpatient liver transplant evaluation for acute on chronic liver failure (MELD-Na 29). Ten years earlier, he had developed lightheadedness, gait instability, cognitive changes, lower extremity weakness, tremors, hallucinations, and headaches. Evaluation at that time showed a serum ceruloplasmin of 14.4 mg/dL (normal 15–30 mg/dL), serum copper < 5 mcg/L (normal 15–60 mcg/L), and negative 24-h urine copper, leading to a diagnosis of Swayback disease. He was started on copper supplementation at 2 mg/day but was lost to follow-up and self-escalated to 8 mg/day. Three years after starting supplementation, he developed severe diffuse abdominal pain requiring multiple ED visits, hernia repair, and exploratory laparotomy, during which cirrhotic liver morphology was noted. Postoperatively, he developed refractory ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, and hepatorenal syndrome, prompting transfer. On admission, laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 6.6 g/dL (baseline 13 g/dL), MCV 108.7 fL, haptoglobin < 14 mg/dL, LDH 239 U/L, total bilirubin 6.3 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 3.8 mg/dL, ALT 51 U/L, AST 190 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 68 U/L, creatinine 1.45 mg/dL, cystatin C 1.35 mg/L, ceruloplasmin 10.9 mg/dL, serum copper 1.73 mcg/mL, and urine copper > 6210 mcg/24 h. Examination revealed scleral icterus, no Kayser–Fleischer rings, abdominal distention with fluid wave, and diffuse tenderness. He denied alcohol use. Serological evaluation for other causes of liver disease was negative, including testing of the ATP7B gene for Wilson disease.

A 16-year-old Caucasian male with ulcerative colitis treated with mesalazine and adalimumab presented with a few minutes of resting chest pain not radiating, accompanied by nausea and sweating. He reported a recent fever that triggered a flare of his inflammatory bowel disease. On examination he was asymptomatic, normotensive, afebrile, and eupnoeic, with marked pallor of the skin and mucous membranes; cardiopulmonary examination was normal. ECG showed ST-segment depression in leads V4–V6 and negative T waves in V1–V3 and aVL. Initial troponin I was 350 ng/L (normal 0–46 ng/L) rising to 13 489 ng/L. He was admitted with a preliminary diagnosis of acute myocarditis. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed inferoseptal hypokinesia, an LVEF of 52%, and a 10×7 mm mobile pedunculated mass on the right coronary aortic valve leaflet without dysfunction; transesophageal echo confirmed this. Three sets of blood cultures drawn on days 1 and 5 were negative. Given his underlying predisposition, marantic endocarditis was suspected, and enoxaparin was started. A thrombophilia workup was negative. Other differential diagnoses considered included infective endocarditis and papillary fibroelastoma.

A 16-month-old girl, born to distantly consanguineous parents, was referred for evaluation of persistent neutropenia noted over the past year. She presented with a low-grade fever and vomiting. Developmentally, she had delayed motor milestones (holding head at 2 months, sitting at 6 months, walking not yet achieved) and speech delay requiring therapy. She had one prior urinary tract infection with normal renal sonography. Her mother had two prior stillbirths; otherwise there was no family history of disease.

On examination, temperature was 37.9 °C; other vital signs were normal. Growth parameters were within normal limits. Her gums showed a few sores; pharyngeal tonsils were normal; and there was no organomegaly. Facial features included thick forehead hair, prominent upper central incisors, and thick, long eyelashes. She had abdominal obesity with slender limbs, a cheerful affect, hypermobile joints, and tiny, nonpruritic petechiae on her lower limbs. Ophthalmologic and nephrologic examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies over 16 months showed persistently low absolute neutrophil counts (ranging from 0.30 to 2.16 ×10^3/μl, most recently 0.30 ×10^3/μl). Hemoglobin and platelet counts were within or near normal limits. Immunoglobulin levels, lymphocyte subsets, nitroblue tetrazolium test, flow cytometry, bone marrow aspiration, and abdominal sonography were normal.

A 30-year-old Asian man presented with 10 days of gradual-onset right hypochondrial and epigastric pain, vomiting, intermittent fever with chills, and progressive weakness. He had been treated 3 months earlier for a right-lobe liver abscess diagnosed as amoebic on the basis of positive serology. He had no history of tuberculosis or known TB contacts. 

On examination, he appeared ill, dehydrated, and anemic. Vital signs were: temperature 38.5 °C, pulse 92/min, blood pressure 106/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min. There was no jaundice or lymphadenopathy. Abdominal examination showed tenderness and guarding in the right upper quadrant and hepatomegaly (liver span 16 cm); there was no splenomegaly, ascites, or other masses. The cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were unremarkable.

A chest radiograph showed elevation of the right hemidiaphragm and blunting of the right costophrenic angle, without focal pulmonary lesions. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 5.6×6.8×8.8 cm ill-defined, heterogeneous hypo-echoic lesion with cystic areas in the right lobe of the liver, consistent with an abscess; the liver was enlarged (span 16.6 cm), with no perihepatic fluid or other focal lesions.

Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL; white-cell count 22 600/mm³ (76% neutrophils); platelets 376 000/mm³; erythrocyte sedimentation rate 52 mm/h; blood urea 28 mg/dL; total bilirubin 1 mg/dL; alkaline phosphatase 7 IU/L; AST 29 IU/L; ALT 39 IU/L; serum protein 6.6 g/dL; albumin 4.0 g/dL; and prothrombin time 15 s (control 10.1 s).

Under local anesthesia, pigtail catheter drainage yielded 150 mL of cream-colored pus, which was sent for Ziehl–Neelsen staining, mycobacterial culture, PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and routine bacterial, fungal, and parasitic studies.

A 14-year-old girl from eastern Nepal presented with a one-year history of massive, gradually progressive enlargement of both breasts, causing chest discomfort, pressure sores in the inframammary folds, and grooving of the shoulders from bra straps. She felt embarrassed and limited her school attendance and social activities. On examination, both breasts were markedly pendulous and firm, without discrete masses or tenderness; the areolae were widened, and there were areas of pressure necrosis. Axillary lymph nodes were not enlarged. Her BMI was 23.15 kg/m2. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, C-reactive protein, thyroid function tests, follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone, estradiol, progesterone, and prolactin, were all within normal limits.

A 19-year-old Caucasian woman is referred for evaluation of suspected demyelinating disease. Since age 10, she has had five episodes of idiopathic bilateral optic neuritis, each treated with intravenous methylprednisolone followed by an oral prednisone taper, with full recovery of visual acuity and fields between episodes. She had no recurrences after age 15 despite several negative evaluations for multiple sclerosis.

She now reports 2–3 weeks of progressive paraesthesia in her left upper and lower extremities. On hospitalization:

• MRI of the cervical spine (1.5 T) shows a longitudinal T2-hyperintense lesion extending from C3 to C6–C7; brain MRI is normal.  
• Chest radiograph is normal.  
• Lumbar puncture, performed off steroids for 2 months, reveals normal leukocytes, protein, and glucose; no oligoclonal bands; normal IgG index; and negative tests for Borrelia and herpes viruses.  
• Serum studies—including CBC, electrolytes, liver function tests, glucose, coagulation panel, TSH, folate, 25-hydroxy vitamin D, cobalamin, immunoglobulins, ANA, ANCA, rheumatoid factor, SS-B, and ACE—are all within normal limits.  
• Serologic testing is negative for aquaporin-4 IgG and weakly positive for myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein IgG by cell-based assay (standard 1:10 dilution; semiquantitative scale).  

She is treated with a 5-day course of IV methylprednisolone (1000 mg/day). Two months later:

• Pattern-reversal and multifocal visual evoked potentials show normal latencies and amplitudes bilaterally.  
• Best-corrected visual acuity is 1.2 in each eye, visual fields are normal, and there is no afferent pupillary defect.  
• Optical coherence tomography reveals bilateral thinning of the peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer (69 μm OD, 54 μm OS) and ganglion cell layer (70 μm OD, 64 μm OS).  
• Repeat myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein IgG testing by the same assay is strongly positive.  
• Follow-up cervical-spine T2 signal is decreased.

A 53-year-old man presented with an 8-month history of tenderness and burning of the lower lip. He first noted mild tingling and minute ulcerations without vesicle formation on the lower lip. Over the last 3–4 months he experienced burning, especially with hot or spicy foods, and mild tenderness. His medical and dental histories were unremarkable; there was no history of lip biting or excessive sun exposure.

On examination, there was a diffuse, erosive, crusted lesion on the lower lip measuring 3×1 cm with irregular margins, bordered by peripheral lacy grey-white striae. The lesion extended approximately 1.5 cm from the mucocutaneous junction onto the labial mucosa, and mesiodistally from the right canine to the left lateral incisor. Palpation revealed mild tenderness without induration, and Nikolsky’s sign was negative. Examination of the remaining oral, cutaneous, ocular, scalp, and genital mucosae was unremarkable.

On the basis of the chronic course without vesicle formation and the typical clinical appearance, a provisional diagnosis of isolated lichen planus of the lower lip was made. Erythema multiforme, discoid lupus erythematosus, actinic cheilitis, pemphigus vulgaris, and oral lichenoid reaction were included in the clinical differential diagnosis.

An 11-year-old boy noted a “fuzzy Dorito-shaped” spot obstructing his central vision in the right eye for 3 days and began intermittently seeing new shapes in the left eye the previous evening. He denied systemic symptoms at presentation but reported a mild cough 2–3 weeks earlier. His medical history was notable only for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder treated with methylphenidate; there was no ocular or systemic family history.

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was counting fingers at 5 feet in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye. Intraocular pressures were 11 mmHg OD and 13 mmHg OS. Pupils, confrontational fields, and the anterior segment were normal bilaterally. Slit-lamp exam revealed rare vitreous cells in the right eye. Funduscopy showed a central macular lesion with pigmentary changes OD and mild retinal pigment epithelium changes OS.

Fluorescein angiography demonstrated early ring-like hyperfluorescence with central hypofluorescence and late staining OD, and temporal foveal pinpoint hyperfluorescence OS. Optical coherence tomography revealed an elevated, irregular RPE with overlying subretinal fluid at the fovea OD and trace ellipsoid zone changes temporal to the fovea OS. Indocyanine green angiography showed central hypofluorescence OD and late temporal hyperfluorescence OS. OCT angiography revealed no choroidal neovascularization.

Laboratory evaluation, including CBC, CMP, syphilis serology, Quantiferon-TB Gold, toxoplasmosis serologies, angiotensin-converting enzyme, lysozyme, ESR, and ANA, was unremarkable except for an elevated ESR of 24 mm/hr. The patient was started on oral prednisone 40 mg daily with a taper. One week later, visual acuity remained count fingers at 5 feet OS, and he drew the shapes of his scotomas. Repeat OCT showed additional subfoveal hyperreflective material OU.

He was admitted for MRI of the brain and orbits with contrast, which was normal, and received intravenous steroids. Coxsackie B3 antibody titers were 1:20, with all other coxsackie serotypes negative. His vision subjectively improved with corticosteroids, and he noted that his “Doritos” were shrinking in size.

A 32-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of progressive numbness, tingling, and weakness in his legs. He first noted sudden vibrations in his left lower extremity that gradually increased in frequency and became bilateral. These sensations were intermittent at onset but later persisted, and he developed numbness and tingling in both toes as well as electric shock–like sensations in the posterior neck on movement. Over 2 months, he experienced increasing difficulty walking, ultimately requiring a wheelchair. He denied trauma, surgery, preceding illness, visual disturbances, bowel or bladder symptoms, fevers, or rash. His diet consisted mainly of injera with legumes, with occasional meat, dairy, and fruits.

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. He was alert and oriented with intact cranial nerves. Strength in all lower extremity muscle groups was 3/5; deep tendon reflexes were brisk with clonus at the ankles and patellae; Babinski sign was bilaterally positive. Vibration and position sense were absent in the toes but intact elsewhere, while pinprick and temperature sensation were preserved. Upper extremities and general physical examination were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, blood chemistries, CRP, and ESR. Organ‐ and thyroid‐function tests were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis (cell count, protein, VDRL, aquaporin-4 antibody), viral markers (hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV), and antinuclear antibody testing were within normal limits. Serum vitamin B12 was 416 pg/mL (reference range, 200–900 pg/mL). Brain and spinal cord MRI scans were unremarkable. A nerve conduction test was performed, and the results were unremarkable. Electrophysiological studies were not available at our institution. Malabsorption evaluations, including serum tissue transglutaminase antibody, colonoscopy with biopsy, and fecal calprotectin, were all negative.

A 68-year-old man presented with a progressive, painless swelling of his left leg. Forty years earlier, he had sustained ipsilateral tibial and fibular fractures treated with open reduction and internal fixation, followed by a postoperative left common peroneal nerve deficit. Two years ago, after a minor muscle strain to the same leg, he noted a palpable, painless mass that had enlarged substantially over the past five months. On examination, there was a nonadherent, extra-osseous mass at the anterior aspect of the left leg that was tender but not painful to palpation; the overlying skin was dry and without erythema. Dorsiflexion of the left foot was weak, consistent with his known peroneal nerve deficit. Radiographs of the left leg showed extensive calcification within the soft tissues of both the anterior and posterior compartments. A computed tomography scan demonstrated a fusiform soft-tissue mass with peripheral, plaque-like calcification oriented linearly through the muscles of the anterior and posterior compartments and extending through the interosseous membrane. Laboratory studies were within normal limits.

A 6-day-old male newborn was referred with a 3-day history of progressive abdominal distension and non-projectile bilious vomiting. His first and only spontaneous meconium passage occurred 3 days before admission after an enema, with no subsequent spontaneous stools. He had been kept NPO with orogastric and rectal tubes yielding ~10 mL of bilious gastric contents and minimal feces. The infant was born at 38–39 weeks’ gestation via cesarean delivery to a COVID-19–positive mother, birth weight 2800 g; APGAR scores were 7 and 8. On examination, he was alert, normothermic, with HR 140/min, RR 40/min, SpO2 98%, and normal breathing and perfusion. Abdominal examination revealed distension with prominent veins, weak bowel sounds, tympany to percussion, and minimal stool on rectal exam. Laboratory studies showed progressive anemia, an increasing leukocyte count with neutrophilia, initial thrombocytopenia, persistently elevated C-reactive protein, prolonged PT and APTT, normal electrolytes, and reactive SARS-CoV-2 IgG and IgM with two negative RT-PCR tests. Plain abdominal radiographs (AP babygram) demonstrated right-sided abdominal opacities suggesting free peritoneal fluid, limited gas in the stomach and small bowel, absent distal bowel gas, and no visible colon. Left lateral decubitus film showed an air-fluid level indicating pneumoperitoneum but no pneumatosis intestinalis.

A 51-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with sudden-onset right-sided weakness and altered level of consciousness. He denied alcohol, tobacco, or illicit-drug use. On arrival, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Noncontrast CT of the head showed no hemorrhage or acute infarct, and he was outside the window for thrombolysis. Laboratory studies on admission revealed hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, white-cell count 8,490/µL, platelets 264,000/µL, glucose 102 mg/dL, urea 183 mg/dL, creatinine 3.12 mg/dL, sodium 150 mmol/L, potassium 3.68 mmol/L, and normal liver-function tests. Blood, urine, and tracheal cultures were negative.

By hospital day 3, he had become anuric, tetraparetic, and his creatinine had risen to 3.9 mg/dL. Repeat head CT remained normal. He underwent lumbar puncture and brain MRI, both of which were normal. Serologic tests for herpesviruses, Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, syphilis, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR were all negative. Electromyography was unremarkable. A urinalysis revealed more than 1 million leukocytes, 60,000 red cells, hyaline and granular casts, and proteinuria of 944 mg/dL; empirical ceftriaxone was initiated for presumed urinary infection, although cultures remained negative. Over the first week, he underwent four sessions of hemodialysis for volume overload, after which his neurologic deficits improved markedly. Renal ultrasound showed no obstruction.

A 38-year-old woman with a known diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis presented with a 4-month history of progressive, frequent episodes of amaurosis fugax in her left eye. Vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, bilateral carotid bruits were noted, more pronounced on the left; peripheral pulses were normal and blood pressures were equal in the upper and lower extremities. Visual acuity and the remainder of the neurologic examination were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein level within normal limits. Computed tomography angiography of the head and neck demonstrated focal stenotic segments in the right common carotid artery and internal carotid artery, with near-occlusion of the proximal left common carotid artery.

An 8-year-old girl was brought with a 2-week history of right ear purulent discharge and right postauricular swelling, intermittent high-grade fevers, and 3 days of altered mental status. She had a 2-year history of recurrent right ear discharge diagnosed as chronic otitis media and was treated with a 7-day course of amoxicillin two weeks before presentation. There was no history of trauma or other medical illness. On examination, she was confused with a temperature of 38.5 °C, heart rate 114 bpm, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, blood pressure 100/70 mm Hg, and SpO₂ 94%. The right ear showed foul-smelling purulent discharge. There was a 3 × 4 cm erythematous postauricular swelling with a 0.5 × 0.4 cm opening draining serosanguinous fluid. Neurologic examination revealed a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 13, intact cranial nerves, symmetric normal strength and reflexes, positive nuchal rigidity, and negative Kernig’s and Brudziński’s signs. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 6 g/dL and WBC count 22.3 × 10³/μL with 80.8% neutrophils. A lumbar puncture performed before antibiotics showed clear CSF with no cells or organisms, glucose 65 mg/dL, and protein 0.2 g/L. Cultures of ear and abscess pus showed no growth. Empiric intravenous metronidazole and ceftriaxone were started.

An 83-year-old man with no significant medical history was referred for home medical care (HMC) 70 days after an intensive care admission for airway obstruction and respiratory compromise. After discharge, he required assistance for daily activities; he could eat soft meals, use the toilet independently, but could no longer climb stairs. On initial HMC evaluation, vital signs were blood pressure 102/55 mmHg, heart rate 63 bpm, respiratory rate 20/min, temperature 35.3°C, and oxygen saturation 98%. Physical examination was unremarkable. An enteral nutritional supplement was prescribed, but adherence was poor.

Five days later, his family noted behavioral changes including tearing clothing and scratching furniture, initially attributed to relocation stress. At a follow-up visit 28 days after HMC initiation, he was restless and disoriented, unable to answer “Where are we?” Vital signs were blood pressure 126/55 mmHg, heart rate 65 bpm, respiratory rate 16/min, temperature 35.4°C, and oxygen saturation 98%. Examination revealed a dry tongue and skin. He ambulated with handrails due to lower extremity weakness. His clinical picture fulfilled DSM-5 criteria for delirium. 

“We considered dehydration due to poor oral intake, electrolyte abnormalities, side effects of drugs, chronic subdural hematoma, etc.,” and blood studies were obtained. “VB1 deficiency was also taken into consideration as the cause of delirium based on the fact that a family member had reported that his oral intake had decreased to 30% of normal.”

A 29-year-old man who works on a farm presented with a 3-month history of a slowly enlarging swelling of the right genian (cheek) region. He reported no pain, sensory changes in the infraorbital nerve distribution, functional impairment, facial trauma, or recent travel. His medical history was unremarkable.

On examination, the overlying skin was normal. There was a firm–elastic, oval, mobile, painless mass measuring 18 × 15 × 10 mm in the right cheek. No cervical or generalized lymphadenopathy was noted. Vital signs were normal.

Laboratory studies showed a complete blood count with only mild thrombocytopenia and otherwise within normal limits.

High-resolution ultrasound of the right cheek revealed a well-defined, round, hypoechoic lesion measuring approximately 18 mm in diameter that contained a tubular, filamentous structure approximately 10 mm long and 1 mm wide, which demonstrated active movement within the lesion.

A 33-year-old Caucasian woman of Mediterranean descent presented with asymptomatic left cervical lymphadenopathy of two months’ duration and no fever, night sweats, or weight loss. An excisional biopsy of a supraclavicular node showed classical nodular-sclerosing Hodgkin’s lymphoma with CD30+ and CD15+ Reed-Sternberg cells. A pretreatment 18F-FDG PET/CT scan confirmed metabolically active lymphadenopathy confined to the left lower cervical and supraclavicular regions, with no other sites of disease; bone marrow biopsy was negative. She received two cycles of ABVD chemotherapy followed by involved-field radiotherapy (30 Gy). Two months after completing radiotherapy, a restaging 18F-FDG PET/CT scan showed resolution of the original cervical and supraclavicular uptake but new, widespread bilateral FDG-avid mediastinal and pulmonary hilar lymphadenopathy, raising concern for progressive Hodgkin’s disease.

A 39-year-old man presented in 2017 with recurrent episodes of dry, painful swelling of the right eye. CT imaging showed enlargement of the right lacrimal gland and increased size of the right lateral rectus muscle. He underwent right orbitotomy, posterior lateral rectus muscle biopsy, dacryoadenectomy, and temporal tarsorrhaphy. Grossly, the lacrimal gland was firm. Histopathology demonstrated intraglandular follicular lymphoid hyperplasia and intramuscular follicular lymphoid hyperplasia, with no phenotypically abnormal lymphocytes on flow cytometric analysis. 

His medical history included eosinophilic esophagitis and malignant hypertension managed with multiple antihypertensive agents. He denied weight loss, night sweats, or fevers. Over the subsequent two years, he received multiple courses of oral steroids of varying doses and durations, which were poorly tolerated due to his hypertension. 

In 2019, he experienced worsening flares with 10/10 ocular pain, new-onset diplopia, and severe palpebral edema (“so bad I can’t open my eye”). Examination revealed mild right proptosis, right ptosis, evoked diplopia with inability to fully medialize the right globe, and incomplete conjugate gaze at extreme fields; visual acuity remained normal. Repeat CT did not show new findings. Blood tests were negative for EBV, HIV, and CMV, and quantitative immunoglobulins (G, M, A) were within normal limits. 

Given this constellation of findings and history, a request was made for IgG4 immunostaining of the previous orbital biopsy specimens.

A previously healthy 12-month-old boy was brought with a 4-day history of fever (maximum 39°C, axillary) and rash. On day 2 of illness, parents noted erythematous maculopapular, erythema multiforme–like targetoid lesions beginning on the soles, ascending symmetrically to the trunk and face; the rash was nonpruritic and slightly edematous. There was no history of drug or food allergy; vaccinations were up to date. The child received a single dose of azithromycin at home. Both parents, who are nurses, had symptomatic COVID-19 20 days earlier and had close contact.

On arrival: temperature 38.2°C, blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg, heart rate 98 bpm, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min; oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Skin exam: targetoid erythematous maculopapular lesions on trunk and extremities, erythematous facial patches, mild edema; palms and soles involved, mucous membranes spared. Oropharynx and tonsils were erythematous; right conjunctival mucopurulent discharge. No lymphadenopathy. No initial respiratory distress.

He was admitted for suspected COVID-19. Ceftriaxone (40 mg/kg IV every 12 h) and supportive care were started. First-day laboratory results: WBC 8200/µL (65% neutrophils, 29% lymphocytes), hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, platelets 189,000/µL, C-reactive protein 96 mg/L, ESR 54 mm/h, albumin 3.4 g/dL, BUN 5 mg/dL, creatinine 0.7 mg/dL; blood culture (BACTEC) showed no growth. Chest radiograph and high-resolution CT scan showed no typical findings of SARS-CoV-2 infection.

An 89-year-old woman with no prior pulmonary disease and never a smoker presented with a 1-week history of dry cough that became productive, and progressive shortness of breath. A nasopharyngeal swab was positive for SARS-CoV-2 RNA. 

On admission:
• Respiratory rate 26/min; SpO₂ 85% on room air  
• Physical exam: decreased breath sounds, diffuse systolic murmur, time-space disorientation  
• Hematobiochemical tests unremarkable  
• ABG on 7 L/min low-flow O₂: PaO₂/FiO₂ = 250  
• Patient repeatedly removed nasal cannula; SpO₂ fell, so Venturi mask FiO₂ 60% was applied → PaO₂/FiO₂ = 153  
• Chest X-ray: diffuse interstitial thickening  

Therapies started: methylprednisolone, hydroxychloroquine, azithromycin, enoxaparin, and N-acetylcysteine.  

Hospital day 4:
• PaO₂/FiO₂ = 85.5 → high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) FiO₂ 72%, flow 40 L/min → SpO₂ 96%  
• High-resolution CT: widespread ground-glass opacities, diffuse interstitial thickening, crazy paving  
• Under HFNC: PaO₂/FiO₂ 126  

Day 14:
• Chest X-ray: slight improvement  
• HFNC titrated to FiO₂ 36%, flow 45 L/min → SpO₂ 97%  

Day 21:
• New dyspnea and left-sided chest pain worsened by respiration, radiating to the neck  
• ECG: no evidence of myocardial infarction  
• Cardiac enzymes: normal  
• Exam: decreased breath sounds, hyper-resonant percussion, no coarse crackles  
• PCR, procalcitonin, WBC: negative; no signs of bacterial pneumonia  
• SpO₂ improved; HFNC weaned to FiO₂ 21%, flow 45 L/min  
• D-dimer elevated at 1.02 mg/L (normal 0–0.55)  
• Concern for pulmonary embolism → CT scan including pulmonary arteries was performed

A 20-year-old man with a history of arterial hypertension, morbid obesity, and schizophrenia was working in a field for 4 hours in 30°C heat. His medications included risperidone, biperiden, and enalapril. At 4 pm, he experienced dizziness and headache, became highly agitated, and suddenly collapsed. He remained in direct sunlight for approximately 2 hours until emergency services arrived.

On arrival, he was moaning and unresponsive (Glasgow Coma Scale score of 7), with eye deviation and labored breathing. His skin was very hot and dry. Vital signs showed blood pressure 80/25 mmHg, pulse rate 176 bpm, and axillary temperature 39.6°C. He received intravenous fluids, was intubated, rapidly cooled, and transported to the ICU 50 minutes later.

In the ICU, he was deeply sedated and hypotensive (50/20 mmHg); rectal temperature was 41.8°C. Electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia with diffuse subendocardial ST changes, and myocardial markers were markedly elevated. Echocardiography revealed diffuse hypokinesis. Chest radiography was compatible with early pulmonary edema. A cerebral CT scan revealed no abnormalities. To exclude an infectious cause, lumbar puncture yielded normal cerebrospinal fluid.

Laboratory results were notable for severe mixed acidosis (pH 7.11, PCO2 70 mmHg, HCO3 17 mmol/L), elevated creatinine (2.6 mg/dL) and BUN (30 mg/dL), sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L, chloride 115 mmol/L, platelet count 41 000/mm3, prothrombin time 13%, partial thromboplastin time >200 sec, INR 7.37, fibrinogen 70 mg/dL, hematocrit 52.9%, hemoglobin 18.9 g/dL, and leukocyte count 28 400/mm3 (58% neutrophils, 12% bands).

A 58‐year‐old man with a history of polysubstance abuse and HIV infection on antiretroviral therapy presented with a 2‐day history of shortness of breath and cough. He also described a vague pain in the left chest and upper abdomen aggravated by deep inspiration. Although he initially denied recent drug use, he later admitted to smoking crack cocaine 2 days earlier.

On examination, his temperature was 37.8°C, heart rate 115/min, respiratory rate 22/min, and blood pressure 115/66 mm Hg. Chest auscultation revealed equal breath sounds. Abdominal examination showed vague tenderness in the epigastrium and left upper quadrant without guarding or rigidity.

Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 16,200/mm³ with 88% neutrophils, hemoglobin 13.9 g/dL, creatinine 4.1 mg/dL, lactate 2.2 mmol/L, and creatine kinase 41,000 U/L. Urine toxicology was positive for cocaine metabolites. Chest radiography showed bilateral basal opacities suspicious for early consolidation. He was diagnosed with pneumonia‐associated sepsis and acute kidney injury from rhabdomyolysis, treated with broad‐spectrum antibiotics and aggressive intravenous hydration, and transferred to the step‐down unit.

Several hours later, his left upper‐quadrant pain acutely worsened and radiated to his back. On repeat examination, the abdomen was diffusely tender with guarding and rigidity. He remained tachycardic, and his blood pressure fell to 86/62 mm Hg despite a fluid bolus. Repeat laboratories showed a drop in hemoglobin to 10.7 g/dL, a rise in the leukocyte count to 25,400/mm³, and an increase in lactate to 7.8 mmol/L. His clinical condition continued to deteriorate with worsening hypotension unresponsive to fluids, irregular respirations, escalating abdominal pain, and confusion. Concern for intra‐abdominal bleeding arose; he was intubated for poor respiratory effort and received additional fluid boluses.

A 31‐year‐old woman noted a painless, barely palpable swelling over the right mid‐anterior thigh. She had no chronic illnesses or known exposures. On examination, there was subtle skin discoloration over the lesion; vital signs were normal and there was no inguinal lymphadenopathy. Laboratory testing revealed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, elevated C‐reactive protein, and an increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate; tests for HIV and viral hepatitis were negative. Chest and thoracolumbar spine radiographs were normal. A pelvic radiograph showed irregular osteolytic areas with well‐defined sclerotic rims in the superolateral and superomedial right acetabular region, with possible penetration of the articular surface. Ultrasound of the right thigh demonstrated a large oblong, thick‐walled cystic lesion (195 × 60 × 24 mm) in the subcutaneous and intermuscular planes, continuous with a similar 115 × 47 × 24 mm collection in the right iliopsoas compartment. Both collections contained turbid fluid. Abdominal ultrasound showed no renal or perinephric collections and no intestinal masses; pelvic ultrasound showed no tubo‐ovarian pathology. Pelvic and thigh MRI with contrast revealed an oblong, rim‐enhancing cystic lesion extending from the right iliac fossa through the iliopsoas muscle to the mid‐thigh, along with distal right iliac bone and acetabular roof cystic areas (26 × 26 × 15 mm) with rim enhancement, likely breaching into the hip joint. Noncontrast CT of the pelvis confirmed lower right iliac bone osteolytic lesions with cortical defect and fragmentation, without calcifications or regional lymphadenopathy.

A 12-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of sparse scalp hair, eyebrows and eyelashes, and trauma-induced blistering that was first noted at age 3 months. He was born to non-consanguineous parents after an uncomplicated pregnancy and had normal developmental milestones. At age 3 years, his parents observed progressive nail deformities; palms and soles also became rough with mild thickening. He reported decreased sweating over much of his body but noted hyperhidrosis of the palms, soles, nasal tip and right cheek.

On examination, the scalp hair was lusterless, short and sparse; eyebrows were absent and eyelashes were sparse. He had frontal bossing, retraction of the ala nasi, and an erythematous plaque over the right infra-orbital area with prominent sweating at the nasal tip. Multiple crusted erosions and hyperpigmented macules were present on the trunk, groins, thighs and dorsal hands and feet. A tense bulla was seen over the left ankle and a ruptured bulla on the left thigh. Palms and soles showed hyperhidrosis and mild keratoderma. Dental examination revealed hypodontia of lower incisors, abnormal canines and delayed loss of deciduous teeth. Nails exhibited koilonychia, anonychia and dystrophy. Nikolsky’s sign was negative. 

Routine laboratory tests, electrocardiogram and chest radiography were normal. Skin biopsy showed a blister within the stratum spinosum with occasional acantholytic cells. Direct immunostaining for IgG and IgA was negative.

A 46-year-old Asian man presented with a 5-day history of absolute constipation, vomiting, and central abdominal pain. He reported similar, milder episodes of partial bowel obstruction over the previous 6–8 months that had been managed conservatively. Four months earlier, abdominal CT had shown ileal thickening, and he had received a 3-month empirical course of antituberculosis therapy without symptom relief. He had no other comorbidities.

On examination, he was dehydrated, with a pulse of 104 beats/minute and a blood pressure of 130/70 mmHg. His abdomen was distended, tender centrally, and had hyperactive bowel sounds; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Blood urea nitrogen was 32 mg/dL, and creatinine was 1.2 mg/dL.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated mildly dilated and thickened jejunal and ileal loops that were encased in a thick fibrocollagenous membrane and displaced toward the center of the abdominal cavity, with collapsed large-bowel loops peripherally. He was managed with intravenous fluids and nasogastric decompression, with partial symptom relief. Given the regional prevalence of tuberculosis and his prior therapy, colonoscopy was performed and revealed a normal terminal ileum, colon, and rectum. The case was then discussed by a multidisciplinary team, and the decision was made to proceed with diagnostic laparoscopy.

A 68-year-old man was admitted with a 2-day history of diffuse abdominal pain and hematochezia and a 4-day history of palpable purpura that began on the lower legs and spread to involve his torso. Nine days earlier he had completed mediastinal radiation after partial response of limited-stage small cell lung cancer to four cycles of etoposide and cisplatin. On admission he appeared ill, complained of vague abdominal pain, and was afebrile with stable vital signs.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 8,520/mm³ (72.7% neutrophils, 18.0% lymphocytes), hemoglobin 15 g/dL, and platelets 179,000/mm³. Total protein was 6.9 g/dL and albumin 3.2 g/dL; renal and liver function tests, lipid profile, and coagulation studies were normal. Direct and indirect Coombs’ tests were negative. Urinalysis showed 3+ hematuria and 2+ proteinuria; a 24-hour collection revealed protein excretion of 3.005 g/day. Complement levels were C3 68 mg/dL and C4 10.6 mg/dL (both low). Rheumatoid factor was 105.5 IU/mL. Tests for ANCA, anti-MPO, cryoglobulin, and ANA were negative; immunoglobulin levels and serologic tests for hepatitis B antigen, parvovirus, and HIV were normal or negative. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. Abdominal CT showed diffuse edematous thickening of the duodenum to proximal jejunum with prominent mucosal enhancement.

A 43-year-old Jewish man presented for evaluation of multiple pigmented skin lesions. He reported that brown macules first appeared at age 3 and had gradually increased in number. He was otherwise healthy, with unremarkable birth and developmental history and no family history of similar skin lesions.   
On examination, there were numerous flat brown-to-black macules on the face, neck, torso, back, and limbs. Facial features included ocular hypertelorism, a broad nasal root, and low-set ears. There was pectus excavatum and winging of the scapulae.  
A punch biopsy of a representative lesion showed mild epidermal acanthosis, increased melanocytes without atypia in the basal layer, and basal hyperpigmentation, consistent with lentigo simplex.  
Audiometry revealed bilateral sensorineural hearing loss at frequencies above 2000 Hz. Holter monitoring demonstrated a Mobitz type I AV block. A standard electrocardiogram and echocardiogram were otherwise normal, with no evidence of pulmonary stenosis.

A 33-year-old woman, gravida 4 para 0, with three prior ectopic pregnancies (left partial salpingectomy in 2004; methotrexate–treated right tubal pregnancy in 2006; right salpingectomy in 2009) underwent in vitro fertilization in November 2010, receiving two frozen-thawed embryos. Fourteen days after transfer, her serum β-hCG was 205 IU/mL, rising to 732 IU/mL on day 16 and 1633 IU/mL on day 19. On day 22 post–embryo transfer, she presented with lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. Vital signs were stable; examination showed diffuse lower abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs. Hemoglobin was 11.8 mg/dL. Transvaginal ultrasound revealed no intrauterine gestational sac and a small amount of fluid in the pouch of Douglas; β-hCG was 1518 IU/mL. She was admitted for observation. The next day, ultrasound demonstrated 8.2 × 2.9 cm of fluid in the cul-de-sac with no intrauterine sac. Serial β-hCG values plateaued between 2065 and 2173 IU/mL from days 24 to 29. One month after transfer, transvaginal ultrasound showed a 25 mm mass in the left tubal angle, apparently outside the myometrium, with approximately 100 mL of fluid in the cul-de-sac.

A 59-year-old man undergoing hemodialysis for chronic renal failure presented with progressive anemia over 2 months despite increased erythropoietin doses. He was asymptomatic and had undergone laparoscopic distal gastrectomy one year earlier for stage IIB gastric cancer. He had also taken zinc supplements for eczema for one year. On examination, he was pale without lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies showed white blood cells 2100/µL, hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, platelets 104 000/µL, serum iron 95 µg/dL, ferritin 751 ng/mL, folate 5 ng/mL, vitamin B12 126 pg/mL, zinc 74 µg/dL, and C-reactive protein 1.05 mg/dL. Tumor markers were within normal limits (CEA 5.9 ng/mL, CA19-9 28 U/mL). An 18F-FDG PET/CT scan demonstrated diffuse bone marrow uptake.

A 62-year-old Asian woman presented with a 5-year history of a swollen left upper eyelid and repeated episodes of epistaxis. Initial computed tomography showed an osteoclastic mass with calcification in the left maxillary sinus and a swollen left eyelid. She underwent surgical resection of the sinus mass and an eyelid biopsy; histology showed dense fibro-inflammatory cells without malignancy, and IgG4-positive plasma cell infiltration with elevated serum IgG4 levels led to a diagnosis of IgG4-related disease. Treatment with oral prednisolone (15 mg/day) resulted in symptom resolution. Five years later, after tapering prednisolone to 7.5 mg/day, she experienced recurrent eyelid swelling. The dose was increased to 12.5 mg/day without improvement, and she was referred for further evaluation.

On admission, she had bilateral eyelid swelling without salivary gland enlargement. Laboratory studies showed: white blood cell count 9.0×10⁹/L, neutrophils 7.2×10⁹/L, lymphocytes 1.2×10⁹/L, eosinophils 9.9×10⁷/L, hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL, platelet count 2.47×10¹¹/L, lactate dehydrogenase 222 U/L, C-reactive protein 1.28 mg/dL, serum IgG 1072 mg/dL, CH50 >60 U/mL, serum IgG4 147 mg/dL (normal <121), and soluble interleukin-2 receptor 296 U/mL. Antinuclear antibody, anti-SS-A antibody, and ANCA were negative.

CT revealed a bone-destructive mass with calcification in the left maxillary sinus and soft-tissue swelling of the left upper eyelid. MRI of the orbit showed a swollen left medial rectus muscle with low intensity on T1-weighted imaging and high intensity on diffusion-weighted imaging. There was no evidence of disease in other organs.

A 48-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease on maintenance hemodialysis twice weekly for 6 months and hypertension underwent elective robotic-assisted laparoscopic renal transplantation from a living donor. She had no history of diabetes mellitus: fasting and postprandial glucose levels and HbA1c were repeatedly normal preoperatively. Preoperative dialysis was performed 24 hours before surgery.

Anesthesia was induced at 10:00 AM under standard monitoring. Baseline vital signs were: heart rate 94/min, mean arterial pressure 103 mm Hg, SpO2 100%, central venous pressure 12 cm H2O, and core temperature 98.6°F. An initial arterial blood gas (ABG) after induction showed pH 7.38 and lactate 1.9 mM/L. Ventilation was adjusted to maintain end-tidal CO2 between 35 and 40 mm Hg.

Three hours later, heart rate rose to 122/min, mean arterial pressure fell to 72 mm Hg, and central venous pressure increased to 16 cm H2O. Repeat ABG showed metabolic acidosis with an elevated lactate level, hyperglycemia, an increased anion gap, and a drop in hemoglobin. Ketone bodies were negative and were re-checked every 4 hours to rule out diabetic ketoacidosis. Intravenous fluids and two units of packed red blood cells were administered for presumed occult bleeding. During vascular anastomosis, a noradrenaline infusion was started to maintain a mean arterial pressure of 90 mm Hg. Sodium bicarbonate and an insulin infusion were initiated for acidosis and hyperglycemia, respectively. The allograft was reperfused after 25 minutes, and urine output was established.

Seven hours after induction, the patient was transferred to the intensive care unit on noradrenaline (0.12 μg/kg/min) for elective ventilation and possible continuous renal replacement therapy. ICU ABG analysis revealed progressive lactic acidosis with persistent hyperglycemia despite bicarbonate and insulin therapy; urine output remained approximately 300 mL/h. A procalcitonin level was 14.6 ng/mL.

A 41-year-old woman presented with 4 days of progressive dyspnea, worsening to minimal exertion in the last 24 hours, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. She also noted mild asthenia over 2 months without prior evaluation. On arrival, arterial oxygen saturation was 90%, blood pressure 153/88 mm Hg, and heart rate 90 beats/min. Examination revealed a new panfocal, holosystolic, high-intensity heart murmur and bilateral lung crackles; no other abnormalities were noted.

Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia and asymmetrical T-wave inversion in the anterolateral leads. Labs revealed NT-proBNP 4,925 ng/L (normal < 300), CRP 70 mg/L (normal < 5), and mild microcytic, hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin 110 g/L). White blood cells, platelets, renal, and hepatic function were normal. Chest radiography displayed bilateral infiltrates and pleural effusions, left-sided predominance.

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated moderate systolic left ventricular impairment and significant nondegenerative thickening of the aortic valve with severe stenosis (mean gradient 55 mm Hg, peak velocity 4.4 m/s) and mild regurgitation.  

Her history included hypertension, dyslipidemia, and diabetes, all treated medically. A routine echocardiogram one year earlier was normal. She had undergone two dental procedures in the past 3 months with antibiotic prophylaxis, the most recent 1 week before symptom onset.

A large-for-gestational-age (4184 g) female neonate was born at 38 weeks 2 days to a mother with insulin-treated gestational diabetes. Apgar scores were 8 and 9. On day 2, she developed rhythmic multifocal jerking of the extremities with associated desaturations, and phenobarbital was initiated after a septic workup. At 49 hours of life, duplex power Doppler echoencephalography showed normal brain anatomy with lenticulostriate vasculopathy. Transcranial Doppler through the left temporal window demonstrated anteroposterior flow in both posterior communicating arteries and retrograde flow in the P1 segments of both posterior cerebral arteries, with anterograde flow in the P2/P3 segments. Through the anterior fontanelle, power Doppler and color Doppler revealed continuous retrograde flow in the basilar artery and left vertebral artery, while the right vertebral artery flow remained anterograde. Lower-extremity blood pressure was 50/30 mmHg (MAP 37 mmHg); right arm pressure was unobtainable. An echocardiogram was recommended to evaluate the aortic arch.

A 27-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a draining sinus tract on the right side of her neck that had been present for six years. Her medical history was unremarkable. Initially, she consulted an ENT specialist, who prescribed chlorhexidine mouthwash for two weeks without improvement. She then saw an infectious disease specialist and took doxycycline (100 mg daily) for six months, yet pus discharge continued. Surgical excision by a general surgeon temporarily resolved symptoms, but the sinus recurred one year later. Subsequent evaluation led to a presumed diagnosis of tuberculosis; polymerase chain reaction and culture for Mycobacterium tuberculosis were negative. A second surgical excision was performed for a suspected branchial cyst; pathology revealed only an “infected wall of a sinus tract,” and the lesion recurred again. The patient declined further surgery and used herbal remedies without benefit before referral to dental school.

On examination, a fistulous opening was noted in the right submandibular region with intermittent seropurulent discharge. Teeth #30 and #31 (right mandibular first and second molars) were asymptomatic on percussion but elicited no response to pulp‐vitality testing. Periapical radiographs showed severe bone destruction around the apex of tooth #31 and widening of the periodontal ligament space around tooth #30. Cone-beam computed tomography confirmed extensive bone loss in the body of the right mandible.

A 66-year-old man with uncontrolled type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity, chronic kidney failure, and chronic heart failure presented with a 14-day history of painful swelling in the perianal region. He delayed seeking care because of the Covid-19 pandemic. On arrival, his temperature was 38.5 °C, blood pressure 175/75 mm Hg, and pulse 112 beats/min. Examination revealed a large area of necrosis extending laterally from the roots of the thighs, upward onto the scrotum, and downward onto the buttocks, encircling the last 3–4 cm of the rectal circumference and involving the levator ani plane. Laboratory evaluation showed anemia, leukocytosis, hyperglycemia, elevated serum creatinine, azotemia, hypoalbuminemia, and decreased bicarbonate, potassium, sodium, and calcium levels. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 6 × 4 cm perianal/perirectal abscess with irregular, poorly defined contours, contralateral displacement of the distal rectum, hydroaerial levels, extension of the abscess to the levator ani muscles, marked subcutaneous fat thickening with multiple gas bubbles in the perianal and mesorectal regions, and small locoregional lymphadenopathy.

A 32-year-old woman, two weeks postpartum after cesarean delivery for intrauterine fetal demise at 7 months’ gestation, presented with a 5-day history of progressive dyspnea, fever, productive cough with blood-tinged sputum, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. She denied weight loss, appetite change, joint symptoms, rash, or tuberculosis exposure. On examination she was febrile to 38.6 °C, tachycardic at 120 bpm, respiratory rate 24/min, blood pressure 120/75 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Chest auscultation revealed right infrascapular dullness and diminished breath sounds. Hemoglobin was 9.4 g/dL, leukocyte count 9.6×10^6/mL, platelets 635×10^3/mL, CRP 1.6 mg/L, ESR 63 mm/hr, and arterial blood gas showed respiratory alkalosis. Initial chest radiograph demonstrated right costophrenic angle obliteration with underlying consolidation. She was treated for health-care-associated pneumonia with piperacillin/tazobactam and levofloxacin. On hospital day 2 her dyspnea worsened; echocardiography was normal, Doppler ultrasonography showed no deep venous thrombosis, and CT pulmonary angiography revealed a right segmental pulmonary embolism with right pleural effusion and consolidation. Therapeutic enoxaparin was initiated and autoimmune studies, including antiphospholipid antibodies, were negative. By hospital day 5 she remained febrile with progressive cough; blood, sputum, and urine cultures were negative, as were sputum acid-fast bacilli smears, Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR and culture. Pelvic ultrasound was unremarkable. Repeat chest radiograph was unchanged. Ultrasound-guided thoracentesis yielded turbid, lymphocyte-predominant exudate (pH 7.4, protein 4.9 g/dL, LDH 316 IU/L), with negative Gram stain, Ziehl-Neelsen stain, bacterial culture, MTB-PCR, and cytology showing no malignant cells. Fiber-optic bronchoscopy and bronchoalveolar lavage were negative for bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial pathogens. Video-assisted thoracoscopic pleural biopsy was performed, revealing grossly healthy pleura with focal inflammation.

A 19-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with an 8-month history of progressive bilateral leg weakness and paresthesias following a mechanical fall onto her lower back while dancing. Her Oswestry Disability Index score was 68%. On neurologic examination, lower extremity strength was graded 3/5 bilaterally, with leg apraxia, paresthesias below the T7 dermatome, and symmetric hyperreflexia in the lower extremities. 

An initial thoracic spine MRI demonstrated multiple flow voids at the midthoracic level, most prominent at T8, concerning for dural arteriovenous fistula, but a subsequent spinal angiogram was negative. Two additional spinal MRIs and a CT myelogram were interpreted as normal. On retrospective review of the most recent MRI, the thoracic spinal cord was displaced ventrally, with evidence of thoracic stenosis and turbulent adjacent cerebrospinal fluid flow, but without extrinsic cord compression, neural foraminal narrowing, syrinx formation, or the scalpel sign. Retrospectively, similar flow abnormalities were noted on the prior MRIs and serpiginous CSF filling defects were seen on CT myelogram, all of which had been deemed artifactual initially.

In the setting of her long-term symptoms and radiographic evidence of spinal cord stenosis with surrounding flow abnormalities, surgical exploration was planned.

A 42-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of a gradually enlarging right breast swelling. She had no history of tuberculosis or tuberculous contact and no family history of cancer. She had five children and had been using a contraceptive device for 5 years. On examination, there was a tender swelling in the outer half of the right breast with overlying warmth, erythema, and nipple retraction. A mobile ipsilateral axillary lymph node measured 2.5 cm. There was no nipple discharge. An infectious workup, including inflammatory markers and cultures, was strictly normal. Ultrasonography and mammography showed an ACR-4 lesion in the supero-external quadrant of the right breast, and empirical fluoroquinolone was started. After 7 days, a skin fistula developed with pus extruding and an “orange peel” appearance of the overlying skin. Breast MRI revealed multiple oval and rounded lesions with irregular thick walls throughout the gland, extending to the skin, with peripheral enhancement.

A 48-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with progressive fatigue. Initial outpatient laboratory tests showed anemia and leukopenia, and he was directed to the emergency department. On arrival he was hemodynamically stable. Review of systems was notable for bilateral hand paresthesia previously attributed to cervical spondylosis. He reported decreased exercise tolerance, having gone from eight miles of bicycling per day to difficulty carrying groceries. Six months earlier he had recovered from COVID-19 infection; he denied other recent infections, family history of malignancy or autoimmune disease, and new medications, but endorsed taking multiple over-the-counter supplements of unknown composition.

Initial studies revealed a macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin, 6.7 g/dL; mean corpuscular volume, 107 fL), leukopenia (white blood cell count, 1.4 × 10^3/μL; absolute neutrophil count, 490/μL), and thrombocytosis (platelets, 459 × 10^3/μL). Iron studies showed low serum iron (22 μg/dL), normal iron-binding capacity (318 μg/dL), and elevated ferritin (1,160 ng/mL). Serum folate and vitamin B12 levels were normal. Viral serologies for hepatitis B and C, cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, and HIV were negative. Peripheral blood smear demonstrated macrocytosis, target cells, dacrocytes, and atypical immature white blood cells concerning for blasts.

He was transferred for further evaluation. On examination, findings were unremarkable. A bone marrow biopsy was performed and showed hypercellular marrow (80–90%) with dysplastic erythroid changes, cytoplasmic vacuoles in erythroid and myeloid precursors, and rare erythroid nuclear budding. Iron staining revealed 14% ring sideroblasts.

A 73-year-old cachectic Iranian man presented with a general feeling of being unwell, acute loss of vision in his left eye, and severe headache. He denied pain elsewhere. He had a history of painless, dry, mobile skin nodules on his buttocks, back, and arms. On brain magnetic resonance imaging, multiple contrast-enhancing masses with surrounding edema were noted. Chest computed tomography showed a few cavitary lesions in the upper lobes. Abdominal imaging, including computed tomography and ultrasonography, was unremarkable. A lumbar puncture was negative for tuberculosis by direct smear, polymerase chain reaction, culture, and cytologic examination. Serum tumor markers (PSA, CA125, CA19-9, AFP) were within normal limits. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 70 mm/hr and a highly reactive C-reactive protein level. Fine-needle aspiration of the skin lesions revealed bacterial infection but no Mycobacterium tuberculosis. A purified protein derivative skin test yielded 20-mm induration. A technetium-99m methylene diphosphonate bone scan demonstrated multiple foci of intense uptake throughout the axial and appendicular skeleton—including regions of the skull, clavicle, sternum, ribs, humerus, forearm, wrists, hands, femur, tibia, ankle, and first metatarsophalangeal joint—findings suggestive of metastatic bone disease.

A 44-year-old woman was referred after a six-month history of progressively worsening dyspnoea, orthopnoea, and increased dependence on non-invasive ventilation (from 10 to 23 hours per day), becoming profoundly dyspnoeic when NIV was withdrawn for meals. She denied infective symptoms, headaches, nausea, vomiting, or altered consciousness. Her medical history included cerebral palsy, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and a prior pulmonary embolism. She used NIV for chronic ventilatory failure due to central and obstructive sleep apnea, kyphoscoliosis, and chronic right hemidiaphragm elevation from paralysis. Spirometry four years earlier showed severe restriction: FEV₁ 0.43 L (17% predicted), FVC 0.44 L (15% predicted), FER 84%. Neurosurgical history included a ventriculo-atrial shunt at age 2, revised to a ventriculo-peritoneal shunt at age 14, and converted to a ventriculo-pleural shunt at age 26. Examination revealed oxygen saturation 100% on room air while on NIV (IPAP 22 cm H₂O, EPAP 7 cm H₂O), stable hemodynamics without features of tension, absent breath sounds over the right lung field, and euvolemia. A chest radiograph demonstrated complete opacification of the right hemithorax. Chest CT confirmed a large, simple-appearing right pleural effusion with mediastinal shift. There was no clinical or radiologic evidence of shunt obstruction, and CT of the brain showed no new ventricular enlargement. Laboratory studies showed a WBC count of 10.4×10⁹/L, CRP 15.2 mg/L, BNP 69 ng/L, albumin 37 g/L, and creatinine 28 μmol/L. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed normal systolic function with mildly elevated pulmonary artery pressure (34 mmHg).

A 43-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of progressive weakness, bilateral lower-leg swelling, a 10% unintentional weight loss, and recurrent upper respiratory infections. She had no significant past medical history. On examination, her blood pressure was 130/80 mm Hg, pulse 64 beats/min; she appeared weak and had 2+ pretibial edema. Cardiac and pulmonary examinations were normal; abdominal examination showed no distension, hepatosplenomegaly, or ascites, with normoactive bowel sounds.  

Laboratory tests revealed lymphopenia (250 cells/mm3) and hypoalbuminemia (2.1 g/dL); renal and hepatic function tests, urinalysis, fecal occult-blood testing, tumor markers (CEA, CA 19-9), celiac serologies, and autoimmune panels were all within normal limits. Upper endoscopy showed only erythematous antral gastritis; colonoscopy was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated multiple anechoic cystic nodularities in the intestinal wall protruding into the fluid-filled lumen. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed increased wall thickness of a 40-cm segment of the ileum and low-attenuation mesenteric root expansion. Capsule endoscopy identified a 40–50 cm segment in the mid-distal jejunum with polypoid, infiltrative mucosal lesions.  

Given the lymphopenia, a bone marrow biopsy was performed, showing normocellular marrow, and flow cytometry detected no abnormal immunophenotype. FDG PET-CT revealed only diffuse ileal wall thickening without hypermetabolic lesions.

A 15-year-old female presented with a 2-day history of bilateral blurred vision and headache. She initially declined hospitalization but returned with recurrent generalized seizures, decreased level of consciousness, worsening headache, and persistent blurred vision. She had no past medical or medication history. Two weeks earlier, a rapid COVID-19 test was positive and lung HRCT demonstrated bilateral multilobar ground-glass and consolidation opacities in the peripheral lung fields. On examination, her vital signs were normal, with no fever and no hypertension. Glasgow Coma Scale was 10. Neurologic examination revealed mid-sized reactive pupils, grade I–II bilateral papilledema, and decreased visual acuity; other findings were unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies showed normal electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, and creatinine; C-reactive protein was 50 mg/dL; white blood cell count was 12 000/μL; and oxygen saturation was approximately 92%. She was admitted to the ICU for three days due to seizures, restlessness, and altered consciousness, then transferred to neurology. A noncontrast head CT scan was normal. Brain MRI without contrast showed bilateral parieto-occipital hyperintensities on T2-weighted images and no diffusion restriction on DWI.

A 50-year-old man with chronic hepatitis C presented with a several-year history of a progressive, mildly pruritic eruption on his ears, face, and bilateral upper extremities. He attributed the lesions to repeated occupational exposures as a janitor. On examination, there were scaly erythematous to violaceous thin plaques, some with hyperpigmented rims, most prominently on the extensor surfaces of the arms, nasal ala, bilateral concha bowls, and palmar surfaces of the hands. A 5-mm punch biopsy demonstrated epidermal and follicular interface dermatitis, basement-zone thickening, and mucin deposition. Antinuclear antibodies were positive at a titer of 1:320. Direct immunofluorescence revealed thick granular deposition of IgM and C3 along the epidermal basement membrane.

A 32-year-old woman presented with progressive generalized abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She had recently completed a 6-month course of antituberculous therapy for intestinal tuberculosis diagnosed by endoscopy in India. On examination she appeared severely ill, with abdominal distension and generalized tenderness without guarding. Her heart rate was 127 beats per minute, blood pressure was 102/54 mm Hg, and temperature was 37.6 °C. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 23.1 × 10^9/L (reference range, 4.0–10.0 × 10^9/L) and a C-reactive protein level of 210 mg/L (reference range, 0–8 mg/L). Ultrasound imaging revealed free and multiloculated ascites. Ultrasound-guided aspiration yielded cloudy yellowish fluid that was sent for cytopathologic and microbiologic analysis. A chest radiograph showed no signs of pulmonary tuberculosis. Contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography demonstrated ascites, diffuse small-bowel wall thickening with enhancement, peritoneal thickening, and free air in the peritoneal cavity adjacent to the terminal ileum. In the context of her history and clinical presentation, a working diagnosis of tuberculous peritonitis with small-bowel perforation was made, and emergency laparotomy was planned.

A 71-year-old man with a history of cecal cancer with lymph node metastasis presented with progressive oedema 2 weeks after initiation of ramucirumab. Five years earlier, he had undergone ileocecal resection followed by chemotherapy and remained stable until imaging showed recurrent disease. He was restarted on folinic acid, fluorouracil, irinotecan, and bevacizumab. During bevacizumab treatment, he developed 3+ proteinuria on dipstick but was monitored without renal insufficiency. One year later, because of progressive disease, bevacizumab was replaced with ramucirumab. Two weeks after the first dose, he was admitted for worsening oedema.  
On examination, blood pressure was 172/83 mm Hg (baseline 150/80 mm Hg on an angiotensin II receptor blocker and a calcium-channel blocker), and his weight had increased from 61 kg to 68 kg. He had pitting oedema in the lower extremities.  
Laboratory studies showed:  
• Serum creatinine rise from 1.08 mg/dL to 2.56 mg/dL  
• Nephrotic-range proteinuria of 12.1 g/gCr (selectivity index 0.39)  
• Serum albumin decrease from 3.9 g/dL to 3.2 g/dL  
• Urinary red blood cells 5–9/HPF  
• Urinary β2-microglobulin 6777 µg/L  
Renal ultrasound showed normal-sized kidneys (108×56 mm right, 117×56 mm left).  
A percutaneous kidney biopsy was performed.

A 30-year-old woman presented with fever (101 °F) and a painful right inguinal swelling for 7 days following minor blunt trauma to the area. She had noticed a small, painless swelling 2 years earlier, which gradually enlarged over the last 4–5 months to 3 cm by 2 cm. On examination, the swelling lay below the inguinal ligament, inferolateral to the right pubic tubercle; it was oval, fixed to deeper tissues, tense-cystic, poorly transilluminant, non-pulsatile, and irreducible, without an expansile cough impulse or bowel sounds. A single small right superficial inguinal lymph node was palpable. She had no prior abdominal surgery or chronic cough. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis (10 000/mm3) with neutrophilia; urine analysis was normal. Ultrasonography of the right inguino-labial region demonstrated a mildly echogenic cystic swelling measuring 2.8 cm × 1.35 cm below the inguinal ligament and medial to the femoral vessels, with no intra-abdominal communication or ascites. Color Doppler imaging showed no vascular flow in the lesion.

A 22-year-old primigravida underwent routine first-trimester aneuploidy screening at 12 weeks 3 days of gestation. Transabdominal sonography demonstrated a live fetus with a large intact omphalocele containing intestines. Measurement of crown–rump length and nuchal translucency was not possible because of a cystic hygroma and vertebral deformity. Subsequent transvaginal scanning revealed severe lumbosacral scoliosis and a midline supraumbilical abdominal wall defect with herniated liver and ectopia cordis, alongside the large omphalocele. The abdominal aorta could not be visualized.

A 71-year-old white man with a history of irritable bowel syndrome, diabetes mellitus, and atrial fibrillation on warfarin presented with several months of worsening abdominal pain and alternating constipation and diarrhea. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) and colonoscopy at that time showed antral erythema and two diminutive colonic polyps. Pathology revealed inactive chronic gastritis and two tubular adenomatous polyps, with no evidence of microscopic colitis or Helicobacter pylori. Over the next nine months, his abdominal symptoms progressed and he experienced an unintentional 15-lb weight loss. On examination, he had alopecia and onychodystrophy.
