Laboratory studies showed low ferritin, low hemoglobin, low total protein, and hypoalbuminemia; stool guaiac testing was positive. Repeat EGD and colonoscopy one year after the initial endoscopic evaluation demonstrated innumerable polyps throughout the gastric antrum, ileum, and colon. Biopsies of both polypoid and intervening mucosa revealed foveolar hyperplasia with chronic gastritis in the stomach and lamina propria inflammation with cystically dilated crypts and glands in the colon.

A 45-year-old man with diabetes mellitus and hypertension presented with three months of intermittent left-sided abdominal pain, occasional vomiting 2 hours after meals, and weight loss. He had no abdominal tenderness or palpable masses on examination. 

Initial considerations included intussusception in adults, duodenal gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST), biliary colic, and duodenal malignancy. 

An abdominal ultrasound revealed gallbladder polyps with cholelithiasis and fatty liver but no obvious mass. A contrast-enhanced CT scan showed a small soft-tissue lesion on the posterior wall of the fourth part of the duodenum. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy were normal. Push enteroscopy to the proximal jejunum showed no luminal lesions, narrowing, or stricture. 

A PET CT scan demonstrated a persistent duodenal lesion that was not metabolically active. A repeat CT scan in the prone position, performed to dislodge any suspected foreign body at the posterior duodenal wall, again showed a persistent intramural lesion at the posterior wall of D4. 

Blood parameters and tumor markers were within normal limits.

A 2-year-old neutered female outdoor domestic shorthair cat was evaluated for a 4-month history of progressive respiratory signs. Initially, the cat had snoring, dysphonia and an unproductive cough that later became productive. Empirical treatment with corticosteroids, nebulisation and multiple antibiotics (marbofloxacin, doxycycline, cefovecine) yielded no improvement. The cat was not regularly vaccinated but had undergone recent deworming with praziquantel and pyrantel. It lived in a multi-cat rescue household with free outdoor access near a forest; no other cats were symptomatic.

On presentation, the cat was febrile (40.0°C), tachypneic (80 breaths/min) and tachycardic (>200 beats/min). Thoracic auscultation revealed severe bilateral wheezing and crackles, increased tracheal sounds and tracheal hypersensitivity. Thoracic radiographs were unremarkable. Bronchoscopy showed laryngeal oedema, tracheal inflammation and abundant mucoid-to-mucopurulent secretions. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid cytology demonstrated moderate cellularity with >90% degenerative neutrophils and intracellular coccobacilli, consistent with suppurative bronchitis.

An in-clinic ELISA for feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV) and feline leukaemia virus was performed, revealing FIV infection. Complete blood count showed leukocytosis (27.3×10^9 cells/L), mature neutrophilia (23.6×10^9 cells/L) and mild monocytosis (0.8×10^9 cells/L).

A 47-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of abdominal distention. Physical examination revealed a large palpable mass in the lower abdomen. Laboratory studies showed an elevated carcinoembryonic antigen level of 335.2 ng/mL (normal <5 ng/mL) and a CA125 level of 219 U/mL (normal <45 U/mL), with a normal CA19-9. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 15-cm round pelvic mass without ascites or pleural effusion. Colonoscopy revealed an elevated stenotic lesion in the sigmoid colon, and biopsy confirmed moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma. Two weeks later, she developed acute dyspnea and generalized edema. A repeat CT scan showed massive bilateral pleural effusion with atelectasis and new-onset ascites. She underwent thoracic drainage and emergent laparotomy. Intraoperatively, the sigmoid colon tumor was found to invade the serosa, and a right ovarian mass and several small peritoneal nodules were noted. A total of 3800 mL of serous ascitic fluid was drained, and cytologic examination of both ascites and pleural effusion fluid revealed no tumor cells.

A 48-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a rapidly enlarging goiter causing dysphagia and dyspnea. Two years earlier she had been diagnosed with primary hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. Initial ultrasound had shown a heterogeneous multinodular goiter with right and left lobar nodules measuring 22 mm and 18 mm, respectively. She reported no history of neck irradiation, no family history of thyroid cancer, and no symptoms of hypocalcemia.

On examination, her BMI was 44.8 kg/m2, temperature 37.2°C, blood pressure 125/80 mmHg, and heart rate 90 beats/min. The thyroid gland was markedly enlarged, multinodular, painless, firm to hard, and nonmobile, with nonpalpable lower poles.

Laboratory studies showed:
• Total serum calcium 1.87 mmol/L (normal 2.14–2.54); albumin-corrected calcium 1.95 mmol/L  
• Intact PTH 12 ng/L (normal 15–68)  
• Serum phosphorus 1.25 mmol/L  
• C-reactive protein 15.6 mg/L (normal 3–5)  
• TSH 0.39 mIU/L, FT4 1.2 ng/dL  
• Antithyroid peroxidase antibodies negative  

Chest radiograph demonstrated a plunging, compressive goiter. Thyroid ultrasound revealed enlarged lobes (right 53×20×27 mm; left 59×29×36 mm) with three isoechoic nodules (17, 18, and 23 mm) containing macrocalcifications. Cervicothoracic CT scan confirmed a heterogeneous goiter with the left lobe plunging into the mediastinum, compressing the left internal jugular vein, esophagus, and trachea, without cervical or mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

A total thyroidectomy was planned.

A 4-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of recurrent chest infections and wheezing. He had eight hospital admissions for pneumonia in the first 2 years of life, beginning at age 2 weeks; each episode presented with cough, tachypnea, and wheezing and responded to antibiotics and bronchodilators. Between episodes he was well, with no choking events. He was born at term after an uneventful pregnancy and had normal developmental milestones. 

On examination, he was playful and in no respiratory distress; oxygen saturation was 94%–96% on room air. He weighed 14 kg and measured 106 cm in height (all anthropometric indices > –2 SD except weight-for-height between –2 and –3 SD). Chest examination showed rightward tracheal deviation, decreased air entry over the right lung, and relative dullness on percussion of the right hemithorax. Cardiac auscultation was normal. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits and HIV testing was negative. 

Chest radiograph revealed hyperinflation of the left lung, reduced volume of the right lung with decreased vascular markings, and rightward mediastinal shift.

A 67-year-old Japanese woman with no significant past medical history was admitted for one week of anorexia, rigidity, and symmetrical arthralgia in the extremities. On hospital day 2, brain MRI demonstrated a hyperintense lesion in the right caudate nucleus on diffusion-weighted imaging and bilateral basal ganglia hyperintensity on FLAIR and T2-weighted imaging; CT and T2*-weighted MRI showed right basal ganglia calcification without hemorrhage. On day 5, ^18F-FDG PET-CT revealed increased uptake in bilateral basal ganglia with no abnormal trunk uptake. By day 38, DAT-SPECT showed reduced radiotracer uptake in the basal ganglia. On day 41, ^123I-MIBG myocardial scintigraphy was normal, and Parkinson’s disease was discarded. The patient developed prolonged fever, worsening somnolence progressing to coma, and severe parkinsonism despite treatment with prednisolone and L-dopa. She was transferred to a tertiary center on day 66. On admission, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 5 (E2V1M2); she exhibited persistent rigidity and akinesia. White blood cell count was 9.6 × 10^3/μL and CRP was 0.3 mg/dL. Serologic testing for antinuclear, thyroid peroxidase, thyroglobulin, glutamic acid decarboxylase, aquaporin-4, and D2R antibodies was negative; screening for neuronal surface autoantibodies (including NMDAR, AMPAR, GABA_AR, GABA_BR, mGluRs 1, 2, 5, DPPX, IgLON5, LGI1, CASPR2) was negative in both serum and CSF. CSF analysis showed lymphocytic pleocytosis (30 cells/μL) with normal protein and IgG index; CSF culture and HSV-PCR were negative. Spinal MRI was unremarkable on day 68, and EEG on day 70 exhibited generalized slow waves.

A 24-year-old man with a history of Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease diagnosed at age 13 and a recent dural venous sinus thrombosis on apixaban presented after an episode of syncope. He reported 1 week of nonbloody vomiting, diarrhea, and blood in stools, accompanied by mild lower abdominal pain, loss of appetite, and recurrent oral ulcers. On examination, he was febrile, tachycardic, and tender in the lower abdominal quadrant. Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 5.7 g/dL (later dropping to 4.8 g/dL despite transfusion), platelets 334,000/μL, white blood cell count 19,000/μL with an elevated band count, elevated international normalized ratio, and mildly increased AST and ALT levels. An abdominal and pelvic CT scan revealed multifocal high-density areas throughout the small and large bowel, suggesting acute hemorrhage, and a 3.7 cm incidental liver lesion. The patient received multiple blood transfusions and was admitted to the ICU. Upper endoscopy showed a clean ulcer on the tongue but no bleeding sources; colonoscopy revealed numerous discrete small to large round ulcers throughout the colon and terminal ileum without active bleeding. Biopsies of the terminal ileum were unremarkable; biopsies from the ileocecal valve and colon showed focal ulceration, cryptitis, and lymphoid aggregates without granulomas. The pathology report noted that ulcers such as these may be indicative of Behçet’s disease.

An 11-year-old boy with no prior medical history was admitted for atraumatic right knee pain, fever, and limping. The temperature was 38.6 °C. On examination, there was tenderness, swelling, and limited range of motion of the right knee, with a palpable inflammatory swelling adjacent to the proximal tibiofibular region and a generalized petechiae-like rash. Blood cultures were negative. Plain radiographs of the knee were unremarkable. Ultrasound demonstrated a 40 × 10 mm mass near the fibular head. MRI of the right knee revealed a 30 mm × 4 mm fusiform collection adjacent to the neck of the fibula, in contact with the common peroneal nerve and the proximal tibiofibular joint, with no intraosseous signal abnormalities.

A 72-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of gallbladder polyp-like lesions and bile duct wall thickening found incidentally on screening abdominal ultrasonography. She was asymptomatic. Her medical history included hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and diabetes mellitus; she had no family history of malignancy. Laboratory studies showed mildly elevated aspartate aminotransferase (32 U/L) and alanine aminotransferase (26 U/L) levels; carcinoembryonic antigen and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels were within normal limits; and serum IgG4 was normal. 

Abdominal ultrasonography revealed polyp-like lesions in the neck of the gallbladder and relatively uniform wall thickening of the common bile duct, with continuity of the thickening into the cystic duct. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated diffuse wall thickening of the gallbladder and the perihilar bile duct. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography did not clearly detect the lesion. 

Endoscopic ultrasonography showed diffuse irregular wall thickening and polyp-like lesions up to 5 mm in diameter in the gallbladder and diffuse wall thickening of approximately 2 mm in the perihilar to distal bile duct. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiography revealed mild irregularities of the distal to perihilar bile duct wall without stricture and round translucencies corresponding to the gallbladder polypoid lesions. Intraductal ultrasonography confirmed diffuse irregular wall thickening from the perihilar to the distal bile duct.

A 62-year-old man presented with mild discomfort and slight swelling of the lower left face. One month earlier, he had undergone extraction of a mobile lower left molar. Medical and family history were unremarkable. On examination, there was mild diffuse swelling of the left mandibular region; the overlying skin was intact. Intraoral inspection revealed a partially edentulous left mandible corresponding to the extracted molars. A panoramic radiograph showed an extensive, ill-defined radiolucent (osteolytic) lesion of the left mandibular body, extending from the region of tooth 37 through the angle and up the ramus. Initial laboratory studies, including serum calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, and parathyroid hormone levels, were within normal limits. A provisional diagnosis of intraosseous malignant neoplasm was made, with differential considerations of metastatic tumor, metabolic bone disease, and osteomyelitis. The patient underwent curettage of the lesion, during which the bone was found to be virtually absent under the mucosa. Histopathological examination of the curetted tissue revealed fibrous connective tissue containing numerous thin-walled vascular channels and only minimal chronic inflammatory cells; no cellular atypia was observed.

A 38-year-old woman underwent a routine medical check-up. She had no weight loss, anorexia, or weakness. Twenty years earlier, she had undergone splenectomy for traumatic splenic rupture. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, liver function, and alpha-fetoprotein, were within normal limits. An unenhanced abdominal CT scan showed no spleen and revealed a homogeneous mass at the splenic fossa. On arterial-phase CT, the mass enhanced heterogeneously; on venous-phase CT, the enhancement was homogeneous. There was no surrounding fat stranding. Coronal reconstructions demonstrated that the mass compressed the left kidney and received blood supply from branches of the splenic artery. Subsequent MRI confirmed a well-circumscribed, round mass at the expected splenic site. It was hypointense to liver on T1-weighted images without signal loss on opposed-phase, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and exhibited restricted diffusion. In the arterial phase, the mass enhanced markedly and inhomogeneously; in the venous phase, the enhancement was homogeneous. The normal left adrenal gland was clearly visualized. The mass was reported to be contiguous with the tail of the pancreas. The preoperative diagnosis was a tumor of the pancreas tail.

A 36-year-old man who is an avid weightlifter with a history of anabolic steroid use presented with a 2-hour history of sudden-onset pain in the fourth and fifth fingers of his left hand. He felt a “popping” sensation in his palm while performing heavy squeezing wrist exercises and immediately noted pain. Within minutes, the affected fingers became numb, cold, and turned progressively blue. 

On examination, ulnar artery pulsations were absent, and there was profound cyanosis with early signs of ischemia in the fourth and fifth fingers. The distal left palm was tender, and the affected fingers were cool. No carotid or subclavian bruits were detected. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable. 

Laboratory tests, including a complete blood count, metabolic panel, coagulation assays, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein, were all within normal limits. An electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with no evidence of atrial fibrillation. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed no cardiac source of emboli or valvular stenosis. Radiographs of the left hand were normal. 

Given the suspicion of vascular injury, emergent computed tomography angiography of the left hand was performed. Imaging demonstrated thrombosis of the ulnar artery directly overlying the hook of the hamate and a corkscrew-like tortuosity of the ulnar artery, with embolic occlusion extending into the proper digital arteries of the fourth and fifth fingers.

A 62-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes mellitus presented with weakness, jaundice, pruritus, and weight loss that began three days after his second dose of the inactivated Sinopharm COVID-19 vaccine. He had no symptoms after the first dose and denied recent fever, cough, sore throat, or dyspnea. His medications included metformin, glibenclamide, and losartan. He had no history of alcohol use or immunodeficiency.

On examination, he was alert with yellow-tinged skin and scleral icterus. The abdomen was soft and nontender, with a normal liver span (10 cm) and no hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, or lymphadenopathy. Vital signs were: RR 30/min, HR 85/min, BP 140/90 mmHg, T 36.8 °C.

Abdominal ultrasonography showed mild hepatic parenchymal coarseness and wall thickening of the common bile duct; endoscopic ultrasonography and MRCP were normal. Laboratory tests revealed ALT 722 U/L, AST 435 U/L, ALP 512 U/L, total bilirubin 8.0 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL, negative ANA, ASMA, and anti–LKM-1, and negative viral hepatitis markers.

A sonoguided core needle liver biopsy demonstrated severe portal (3/4) and lobular (4/4) infiltration by lymphocytes, eosinophils, and neutrophils, prominent interface hepatitis (4/4), feathery change, and ductular reaction, with no confluent necrosis (0/6). The modified Ishak hepatitis activity index was 11/18 with staging 1/6.

A 30-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with sudden onset of palpitations, lightheadedness, chest tightness, and nausea immediately following a large meal. He reported a similar episode nine months earlier during a febrile illness, which was attributed to a viral infection. In the emergency department, his temperature was 37.2 °C, heart rate 108 beats/min, blood pressure 125/78 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Physical examination was unremarkable. Electrocardiogram showed mild T-wave inversions in the precordial leads. Complete metabolic panel, complete blood count, and high-sensitivity troponin were all within normal limits. He was discharged but returned the next morning with recurrent palpitations, now accompanied by fever to 38.0 °C, a pounding headache, and vertigo. Repeat vital signs showed a heart rate of 110 beats/min; repeat laboratory studies remained normal. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest and abdomen, performed to evaluate for pulmonary embolism, was negative for emboli but revealed a 7 cm right suprarenal mass with a fluid attenuation of approximately 25 Hounsfield units. A dedicated triple-phase CT of the abdomen confirmed a 7.0 × 5.3 × 6.5 cm right adrenal lesion of fluid density (22 HU), without solid enhancing components.

A 68-year-old woman presented to her general practitioner with a unilateral left-sided facial rash that had appeared the previous night. Her medical history included dyslipidemia, hypertension, and a diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica made 9 months earlier; she had been on oral prednisolone with a current dose of 5 mg daily after gradual tapering. She had a prior varicella zoster virus infection. Current medications included ezetimibe-simvastatin and telmisartan/hydrochlorothiazide; she did not smoke or drink alcohol.

On examination, there were multiple confluent erythematous blisters over the left cheek, with similar lesions on the ipsilateral buccal mucosa and the left half of the tongue; the external auditory meatus and eyes were normal, and there was no involvement of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve. In addition, there were numerous bilateral tender points over the neck, chest, shoulder girdle, upper and lower back, hips, and upper legs. 

Previous laboratory results, obtained at the time of her polymyalgia rheumatica diagnosis, showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 32 mm/h (typical values in PMR are >50 mm/h) and a hematocrit of 39%. The patient also reported three years of nonrestorative sleep and persistent widespread pain despite treatment with prednisolone 20 mg daily.

A 38-year-old Caucasian woman presented with painful skin lesions on her bilateral upper and lower extremities and joint pain in her knees, wrists, and ankles. Two weeks earlier, she had an upper respiratory illness with sore throat, cough, congestion, and body aches that improved over 2–3 days with over-the-counter medications. She then traveled to Europe for 10 days; towards the end of that trip she developed joint pain. Two days prior to presentation, she noted the first skin lesion on her right wrist. 

She had no significant past medical history, was in generally good health, and had a negative tuberculin skin test one month earlier. She denied recent antibiotic use or birth control pills. Family history was notable for maternal hypothyroidism. She did not smoke and drank alcohol socially.

On examination, vital signs were stable. The posterior pharynx showed cobblestoning without cervical lymphadenopathy. Dermatologic exam revealed multiple raised, erythematous, tender nodules on the palms, forearms, anterior lower legs, and dorsal feet. There was decreased range of motion of the wrists and ankles due to pain; strength was 5/5 and reflexes were 2+ throughout.

Erythema nodosum was suspected. She was started on amoxicillin 875 mg twice daily for 10 days and ibuprofen 800 mg every 8 hours for pain. A CBC with differential, CMP, TSH, ASO titer, ESR, and chest radiograph were ordered, and she was instructed to return in one week.

A 41-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease secondary to long-standing hypertension has been on maintenance hemodialysis via a left brachiocephalic arteriovenous fistula (AVF) for 6 months. She presented with 6 hours of dizziness, 1 day of shortness of breath, and 2 weeks of chest pain with orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. She last dialyzed 2 days earlier. There was no trauma to the AVF.

On examination, temperature was normal. Heart rate was 46/min, blood pressure 60/40 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16/min, and oxygen saturation 86% on room air. She was drowsy but oriented. Jugular venous distension was present; heart sounds were muffled. There was no bruit over the AVF.

Initial investigations showed ECG with a prolonged PR interval and tall T waves. Serum potassium was 6.6 mmol/L and creatinine 10.2 mg/dL. Cardiac enzymes were not elevated. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed moderate pericardial effusion without tamponade, dilated inferior vena cava, normal left ventricular systolic function, mild concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, and grade II diastolic dysfunction. D-dimer was elevated at 5 mcg/mL (baseline 0.9 mcg/mL).

She underwent emergency continuous veno-venous hemodialysis for refractory hyperkalemia and hemodynamic instability, with gradual improvement over 48 hours. Two days later, vascular surgeons attempted AVF salvage by venous incision and manual milking; a 0.5 × 0.5 cm thrombus was removed and a thrill returned. Immediately after the procedure, she developed acute shortness of breath, cough, and a drop in oxygen saturation. Oxygen support escalated, and she was intubated for worsening respiratory distress.

In the ICU, she had sinus tachycardia at 130/min, blood pressure 90/60 mm Hg on noradrenaline, and SpO₂ 89% on 70% FiO₂. The working diagnoses included an acute coronary event and pulmonary embolism. ECG showed sinus tachycardia; echocardiography revealed no regional wall motion abnormalities and no pericardial tamponade. Troponin I was elevated. A CT pulmonary angiography was done.

A 36-year-old woman was referred to the emergency department for markedly elevated creatine kinase levels. Three days earlier, her general practitioner obtained a serum CK of 25 000 IU/L. She reported the sudden onset of painful swelling in both upper arms for 3 days, with difficulty in moving her arms and painful extension of the forearms. She denied nausea, vomiting, fever, or other systemic symptoms.

On examination, both upper arms were warm, firm, and enlarged (left 28.5 cm, right 29.5 cm in circumference), with a hematoma on the left. Neurological examination was normal.

A color-Doppler ultrasound of both arms showed patent axillary and brachiocephalic veins, moderate edematous infiltration of the muscle bellies—most pronounced in the triceps—and associated subcutaneous edema.

Further history elicited that the patient, otherwise healthy and regularly athletic, had completed a boot-camp session heavy in push-ups one week earlier. She denied recent trauma, drug use, or systemic illness.

A 5-year-old boy presented with a 3-month history of progressive holocranial headache, irritability, and occasional vomiting, followed by 3 days of altered sensorium. On examination, his Glasgow Coma Scale score was E3 V4 M6. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated a large, fluid-filled cystic lesion within the right frontal horn of the lateral ventricle. The lesion contained an irregular, free-floating membrane within its cavity and obstructed the foramen of Monro, resulting in marked hydrocephalus.

A 93-year-old woman with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, and known situs inversus totalis presented with four days of severe, diffuse, persistent, nonradiating abdominal pain. She also reported nausea, vomiting, decreased appetite, and 3–4 days of constipation, although she continued to pass flatus. She denied fevers, chills, or recent trauma. Her heart rate was 110 beats/min, blood pressure 119/58 mm Hg, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and temperature 98.7 °F. On examination, she had diffuse abdominal tenderness, distension, and voluntary guarding without rebound tenderness or rigidity. Cardiac auscultation revealed an irregular rhythm best heard on the right side of the chest. Laboratory studies showed an INR of 1.65, lactic acid 2.0 mEq/L, creatinine 1.67 mg/dL, and a white-cell count of 6.2 K/µL. A noncontrast CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed multiple small foci of free intraperitoneal air, predominantly anteriorly and more pronounced on the right, a few borderline dilated small-bowel loops, a left-sided liver, and a right-sided stomach.

A 42-year-old woman with a history of Barrett’s esophagus, erosive gastritis, and prior gastric sleeve surgery presented with a one-year history of progressive bilateral lower-extremity distal weakness and burning, which had advanced proximally to the knees and, more recently, was affecting her hands. On examination, she had reduced light touch, pinprick, proprioception, and vibration sensation in all four extremities, more pronounced distally, without sensory ataxia. Distal lower-extremity strength was 4/5 bilaterally, and deep tendon reflexes were 1+/4 symmetrically in both upper and lower extremities. 

As part of the neuropathy evaluation, a lumbar puncture was performed; cerebrospinal fluid showed a normal cell count, normal protein level, and a negative meningitis panel. Six hours after the procedure, she developed a positional headache and neck pain, without fever or meningeal signs. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine with and without contrast revealed a 76 mm long and 8 mm thick ventral enhancing process extending from the odontoid process to the inferior C5 level, which was described as suspicious for an epidural abscess versus hematoma. Brain MRI showed diffuse pachymeningeal enhancement suggestive of intracranial hypotension.

A 44-year-old Asian woman with symptomatic myasthenia gravis presented for elective thymectomy. She reported right eyelid drooping, facial weakness, difficulty holding her head up, chewing problems, dysarthria, and fatigable limb weakness. A myasthenia panel was positive for acetylcholine receptor binding antibody (7.81 nmol/L; normal <0.02). Preoperative chest CT showed a 3.5 × 2 cm anterior mediastinal mass along the right heart border and phrenic nerve, suspicious for Masaoka Stage III thymoma. She was managed on mycophenolate mofetil without prior myasthenic crises or preoperative IVIG.  

Under general anesthesia with left-sided double-lumen intubation, she was positioned supine with a right chest bump and right arm padded and dependent. Three 8 mm robotic ports were placed in the right 2nd, 4th, and 6th intercostal spaces, and CO2 insufflation was maintained at 12 mmHg. Intraoperatively, a 3 × 3 cm mass invading the right phrenic nerve and pericardium was identified. A complete thymectomy was performed en bloc, including resection of the right phrenic nerve and a 4 × 4 cm portion of pericardium over the right atrium and ventricle. A 28-Fr chest drain was placed, hemostasis achieved, and the robot undocked. As the port sites were closed and insufflation ceased, the patient became acutely hypotensive (lowest recorded blood pressure 43/31 mmHg).

A 35-year-old man of Indian origin, employed sorting vegetables in London, presented with a two-month history of a painless lump over the dorsum of his right hand. There was no history of trauma or systemic symptoms. He underwent an excision biopsy but was lost to follow-up. Eight months later, he returned with recurrence of the hand swelling and a new painless soft-tissue swelling over the dorsum of his right ankle. Both lesions were non-tender and without systemic features. Examination showed, on the right ankle, an 8 × 5 cm firm, nonfluctuant, tethered mass adherent to hyperpigmented overlying skin without lymphadenopathy. On the right hand, there was a 6 × 5 cm soft, fluctuant nodular mass adjacent to a well-healed midline dorsal scar, tethered at deep and superficial levels, also without lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies revealed a normal white-cell count, immunoglobulin levels, and CD4 and CD8 counts; HIV test and C-reactive protein were negative. Plain radiographs of both sites showed no bony abnormality or periosteal reaction. T1-weighted MRI of the ankle demonstrated a 6 × 2 cm heterogeneous soft-tissue lesion with scattered cystic areas, prominent vasculature, and surrounding edema, findings described as “suspicious of either a vascular malformation or a neoplasm.”

• 73-year-old retired accountant with bipolar I disorder (remote manic episodes 12 years prior; one episode of lithium toxicity in 2006).  
• Medications on presentation: lamotrigine 100 mg morning, 200 mg nightly; lithium 600 mg nightly; quetiapine 75 mg nightly (plus PRN); gabapentin; levothyroxine; propranolol (self‐discontinued); perindopril; amlodipine; furosemide.  
• Presented December 9, 2012, with increasing confusion, tremor, rigidity; admitted under neurology for presumed lithium toxicity; lithium held—level 0.75 mmol/L.  
• Serum alcohol and urine toxicology negative; empiric amoxicillin for mixed‐bacteria urinary culture.  
• Psychiatry consulted: initial differential included delirium due to anticholinergic effects or prodrome of bipolar relapse; possible dementia; MMSE 18/30.  
• Transferred December 18 to psychiatric unit; lithium reduced to 150 mg nightly—but florid confusion persisted.  
• Mental status: disorientation to place/time, wandering, disorganized behavior; fluctuating cognition with occasional lucid intervals showing normal speech and occasional racing thoughts; irregular sleep with episodes of lying on floor, mumbling.  
• Workup: CBC, glucose, electrolytes, B12, folate all normal; EEG negative for seizure; chest X-ray, blood and urine cultures negative; no focal neurological or systemic signs—lumbar puncture deemed unnecessary.  
• Brain imaging: CT revealed pituitary mass; MRI confirmed 1.5 cm microadenoma without optic compression; pituitary hormones (cortisol, FSH, LH, prolactin) normal.  
• Thyroid function tests normal (TSH 0.97 mIU/L, free T3 5.1 pmol/L, free T4 16 pmol/L).  
• Medication adjustments: lamotrigine reduced; quetiapine stopped for deliriogenic potential; risperidone 0.25–0.5 mg PRN; brief trial of levodopa/carbidopa for parkinsonism without improvement.  
• Collateral history: baseline high functioning at home with only minor short-term memory issues—dementia ruled out.  
• Four weeks into admission, severe disorientation, agitation, drowsiness persisted despite withdrawal of psychotropics (lithium discontinued January 9; lamotrigine tapered off by January 29).  
• During lucid intervals, observed occasional racing thoughts, slight expansiveness, and mood lability.

A 66-year-old Somali woman with history of Helicobacter pylori infection, gastroesophageal reflux disease, hyperlipidemia, and type 2 diabetes mellitus was admitted for excision of a large pelvic sarcoma. Preoperative airway evaluation showed Mallampati class II, full cervical, atlanto-axial, and atlanto-occipital mobility, mouth opening of three fingerbreadths, a somewhat hypoplastic mandible, and a thyromental distance of less than three fingerbreadths. 

Premedication included midazolam. Induction was with fentanyl, lidocaine, propofol, and rocuronium. Mask ventilation was easy and direct laryngoscopy with a Miller 2 blade provided a Grade 1 view; intubation was atraumatic. A nasogastric tube was placed without difficulty. The surgery lasted 11 hours, during which bilateral ureteral stents were placed and the sarcoma was removed. 

At the end of the procedure, spontaneous respirations returned but she was slow to follow commands. She was extubated in the PACU, transferred to the SICU on supplemental oxygen, and remained somnolent overnight. A nurse noted that she was unable to close her mouth and appeared to be in severe pain. Examination by the on-call surgery resident led to a diagnosis of muscle spasm, and hydromorphone PCA was initiated. 

The following morning, the primary surgical and SICU teams re-evaluated her; she still could not close her mouth despite analgesia, and muscle spasm remained the presumed etiology.

A 47-year-old man from Colombia presented with a 6-month history of intermittent abdominal pain, fatigue, and a 25-lb unintentional weight loss. He denied bleeding, melena, or diarrhea. His past medical history was notable for vitiligo and chronic anemia. He emigrated 6 years earlier and had no recent travel. There was no personal or family history of colorectal polyps, cancer, celiac disease, or inflammatory bowel disease. On examination, he had pallor and vitiligo. 

Laboratory evaluation showed hemoglobin 3.1 g/dL, microcytosis, eosinophils 26.4%, iron and vitamin B12 deficiencies, a positive intrinsic-factor–blocking antibody, albumin 3.0 g/dL, and a positive fecal occult blood test. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein were normal. After transfusion of 5 units of packed red blood cells, he underwent upper and lower endoscopy. 

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed chronic inflammation of the gastric antral mucosa, suggestive of autoimmune atrophic gastritis, and a grossly normal duodenum. Colonoscopy revealed friable, matted mucosa with loss of vascular markings from the cecum to the sigmoid, with sparing of the ileum, distal colon, and rectum. In the ascending colon there was a 3-cm ulcerated mass. 

Histologic examination of colonic biopsies from the inflamed areas showed mild crypt distortion with lymphoplasmacytic and eosinophilic infiltrates in the lamina propria. Biopsy of the mass demonstrated invasive low-grade adenocarcinoma without surrounding mucosal dysplasia.

A 36-year-old woman was evaluated before knee surgery after 3 months of palpitations and dyspnea. Vital signs were normal. Cardiac auscultation revealed arrhythmic heart sounds. Initial ECG showed sinus rhythm without abnormalities, and transthoracic echocardiography was reported as normal. A 24-hour Holter monitor demonstrated frequent PVCs with a 35% arrhythmic burden, and β-blocker therapy was initiated. To investigate etiology, ischemic heart disease was excluded with a dobutamine stress echocardiogram; testing for Chagas disease and serum electrolyte measurements were unremarkable. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging revealed prominent trabeculae and deep recesses in the left ventricular apex and anterior, inferior, and lateral walls. The right ventricle had normal myocardial morphology and function.

A 26-year-old primigravida with an unremarkable medical and family history underwent a routine obstetrical ultrasound at 21 weeks’ gestation that revealed a 1.0 cm cystic structure at the floor of the fetal mouth. At 25 weeks’ gestation, a targeted ultrasound demonstrated a 1.4 cm × 1.4 cm cystic lesion located posterior and inferior to the tongue; the fetal lips, nose, mandible, palate, and facial profile appeared normal. The initial differential diagnosis included a thyroglossal duct cyst and a branchial duct cyst. At 26 weeks, fetal magnetic resonance imaging showed a 1.4 cm × 2.0 cm × 1.9 cm midline cystic lesion at the base of the tongue/floor of the mouth, prompting expansion of the differential to include epidermoid cyst and lymphangioma.

A 20-year-old woman presented with a nine-month history of a painless white lesion at the back of her mouth. She reported that it began as a pinhead and gradually enlarged. She denied trauma, surgery, medications, systemic symptoms (including fever, fatigue, sore throat, headache, earache, neck stiffness, cough, sneezing, dysphagia, halitosis, lymphadenopathy, weight loss), and her medical, dental, family, and social histories were unremarkable.

On extraoral examination, findings were normal. Routine blood tests were within normal limits. Intraoral inspection showed a 0.5 cm, light yellow-white, smooth, raised, soft, movable, well-circumscribed, unilateral submucosal nodule without exudate arising from the normal-sized left palatine tonsil. An orthopantomograph demonstrated normal anatomy and no radiopacities in the region.

The differential diagnosis included tonsillar cyst, tonsilloliths, tonsillitis, papilloma, lipoma, streptococcal pharyngitis, infectious mononucleosis, oropharyngeal candidiasis, and peritonsillar abscess.

A 56-year-old African American woman with no significant past medical history presented with a six-day history of progressive swelling of the left labia, which ruptured and began draining serosanguinous fluid two days before admission. On arrival, her temperature was 36.8 °C, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg despite intravenous fluid resuscitation, pulse 96‒100 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 17.4 × 10^9/L. Empiric intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam were initiated, and a surgical consultation was obtained. Pelvic CT imaging demonstrated an ulceration of the left labia with air in the subcutaneous fat of the left groin and lower abdominal wall, as well as inflammatory fat stranding along the left lateral abdominal wall. The Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis (LRINEC) score was calculated as 3, with the potential to rise to 7 pending C-reactive protein results. Despite non-definitive laboratory and imaging findings, concerns for sepsis, subcutaneous gas on CT, and the LRINEC score led to the decision to proceed with immediate exploratory surgery.

A 57-year-old man was admitted with a 1-month history of high fever, night sweats, and progressive back pain. He reported touching an unpasteurized sheep stomach with an injured hand about 1 month earlier. Initial outpatient therapy with oral cefprozil provided no lasting benefit. On admission, he had no fever but complained of worsening back pain and malaise.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 7170/mm3 with 80% neutrophils, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 35 mm/hour, a C-reactive protein level of 3.19 mg/dL, and a procalcitonin level of 0.21 ng/mL. A serological test for tuberculosis was negative. He was started on intravenous sulbactam–cefoperazone. On hospital day 6, blood cultures grew a Gram-negative bacillus. That same day, he developed weakness and numbness in both legs and difficulty with urination. Neurologic examination revealed grade 3/5 strength in the right lower limb, grade 4/5 in the left, hypertonia of both lower extremities, and tenderness on percussion and palpation of the T9 and T10 spinous processes.

Contrast-enhanced thoracic magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an inflammatory lesion of the T9 lamina and a posterior epidural abscess compressing the spinal cord at T9–T10. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography showed osteolytic destruction of the neural arch of T9. He was transferred to the Department of Orthopedics for surgical management.

A 55-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a nontender swelling on the right side of her neck, first noticed several weeks earlier. On examination, there was a firm, 20 mm, mobile subcutaneous nodule in the left occipital triangle (level V), without overlying skin changes, and palpably enlarged middle jugular lymph nodes (level III) on the right. Ultrasonography of the neck showed an 11 mm hypoechoic lymph node and two smaller nodes (5 mm and 6 mm) in the left occipital triangle, and an 8 mm lymph node in the right submandibular triangle. No other cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. An incidental 13×14 mm oval thyroid nodule was seen in the left thyroid remnant, consistent with an adenoma. Laboratory tests revealed a leukocyte count of 10.2×10^9/L with 25% eosinophils (normal 1–5%), total protein 8.3 g/dL (normal 6.2–8.2), potassium 5.04 mmol/L (normal 3.6–5), and elevated cholesterol and triglycerides.

A 23-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus since age 12, poorly controlled, was transferred for evaluation of 2 months of progressive generalized swelling. She had no arthritis, arthralgia, hair loss, or family history of edema. Her weight increased from 70 kg to 140 kg. Examination showed massive anasarca of all extremities, abdominal wall, and back. Chest imaging revealed bilateral pleural effusions; echocardiography demonstrated a large pericardial effusion with impending tamponade and a normal left ventricular ejection fraction (> 55%). Admission laboratory studies: hemoglobin 13.7 g/dL; normal white-cell and platelet counts; normal renal and liver function; serum albumin 3.1 g/dL; urinalysis with no proteinuria; random urine sodium 8 mmol/L; B-type natriuretic peptide 18 pg/mL. Thyroid function showed TSH 5.18 μIU/mL, free T4 0.93 ng/dL, free T3 1.62 pg/mL. Inflammatory markers were low (C-reactive protein 0.8 mg/dL, ESR 8 mm/hr). Autoimmune testing: ANA positive 1:80 speckled; anti-dsDNA and ENA negative; complements normal. Infectious serologies (HBV, HCV, HIV) were negative. Serum protein electrophoresis revealed total protein 4.9 g/dL, albumin 2.2 g/dL, and a small monoclonal IgG κ on immunofixation; κ/λ light-chain ratio 3.08. IgG subclasses showed low IgG2 and undetectable IgG4. C1 esterase inhibitor level was 33 mg/dL. Total vitamin D was 5.0 ng/mL. Abdominal fat biopsy was negative for amyloid on Congo red stain.

A 52-year-old woman with a childhood diagnosis of biopsy-confirmed pityriasis rubra pilaris presented with poorly controlled, psoriasiform plaques on her upper and lower extremities. She had failed multiple systemic immunomodulators (isotretinoin, methotrexate, cyclosporine, adalimumab, secukinumab, ustekinumab). She denied muscle pain, weakness, dysphonia, or dyspnea. On examination, she had well-demarcated, salmon-colored plaques over the bilateral extensor forearms, elbows, and thighs. She also had subtle violaceous discoloration of the eyelids (heliotrope sign), erythema of the upper chest in a V-distribution, and erythema over the knuckles. Laboratory studies revealed an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:320, positive anti-signal recognition particle and anti-PM/Scl-100 antibodies, a low-titer anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, and normal creatine kinase and aldolase levels. Skin biopsy showed psoriasiform dermatitis with confluent parakeratosis and orthokeratosis in a checkerboard pattern without epidermal atrophy or interface change. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated intravascular deposition of C3 and C5b-9, while direct immunofluorescence was negative for IgA, IgG, and IgM.

A 10-year-old girl presented with intermittent throat pain and globus sensation, predominantly on the left side, for 3 years. Her past surgical history was significant for adenotonsillectomy at age 7 for obstructive sleep apnea. Since that surgery, she has had recurrent throat pain episodes, all with negative streptococcal tests. She denied cough or congestion. On examination, vital signs were normal. Oropharyngeal inspection was unremarkable, but palpation of the left tonsillar fossa elicited tenderness. A noncontrast computed tomography scan of the neck was obtained, revealing bilateral elongated styloid processes measuring 24 mm on the right and 25 mm on the left.

A 26-year-old man presented with malaligned and missing upper front teeth, difficulty chewing, and facial deformity. He reported congenital abnormalities of his hands and feet and had undergone orthognathic surgery with extraction of a maxillary incisor 4 years earlier. He was the first child of nonconsanguineous parents; prenatal course and delivery were uneventful, though the mother had taken abortion pills early in pregnancy. His developmental milestones were delayed (walking at age 3 years; delayed eruption of both dentitions). His brother and sister each had fused toes.

On examination, his head was dolichocephalic (head circumference, 58 cm) with a leptoprosopic face. He had midface deficiency, a depressed nasal bridge with septal deviation (“parrot’s nose”), mild facial flattening, hypertelorism, exotropia, downward-slanting palpebral fissures, and slight mandibular prognathism. Cutaneous syndactyly was present between the right forefinger and middle finger and between the left thumb and forefinger. Preaxial polydactyly was noted in the right foot.

Intraoral examination showed poor oral hygiene, periodontal involvement, retained deciduous teeth (52, 53, 55, 63, and 65), and a missing right central incisor (extracted). A panoramic radiograph revealed elongation of the right styloid process, multiple mini-plates in the maxilla and mandible, retained deciduous teeth with missing permanent successors (12, 13, 15, 22, 24, and 25). A lateral cephalogram showed a concave facial outline, midface hypoplasia leading to mandibular prognathism, and an enlarged frontal bone with a flat posterior skull. A hand radiograph confirmed soft-tissue syndactyly of the left thumb and forefinger.

A 51‐year‐old never‐smoker dentist presented with 15 days of left chest pain, mild exertional dyspnea, dry cough, evening fevers up to 38.5 °C, and 5 days of diffuse arthralgias. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. On admission she was febrile (39.2 °C) and tachypneic (25 breaths/min). Chest examination revealed decreased expansion, dullness to percussion, and reduced vesicular sounds at both lung bases. Arterial blood gas showed pH 7.44, PaO₂ 67 mmHg, PaCO₂ 29 mmHg. Laboratory studies: WBC 12 000/µL, hemoglobin 12.7 g/dL, ESR 33 mm/h. Chest radiograph demonstrated a left pleural effusion, and empiric ampicillin–sulbactam with azithromycin was started. Thoracentesis yielded 5000 WBC/mm³ (38% neutrophils, 30% lymphocytes, 20% eosinophils). Blood, urine, and sputum cultures, stains and cultures of bronchial wash, and tuberculin skin testing were all negative. CT of the chest and abdomen, abdominal ultrasound, mammography, and fiberoptic bronchoscopy ruled out malignancy. CT pulmonary angiography showed no pulmonary embolism but revealed a small right‐sided effusion. Rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies, ANCA, and anti-CCP antibodies were negative. She denied chest trauma, travel, parasitic symptoms, and use of any drugs known to cause EPE. On hospital day 5, fevers recurred to 39.4 °C with worsening dyspnea; chest radiograph showed an increased right pleural effusion, and 1 L of exudative fluid (22% eosinophils) was removed via chest tube (stains, cultures, and cytology negative). She continued to report arthralgias, and exam revealed arthritis of the small joints of the hands and feet and the knees, with no evidence of connective‐tissue disease, systemic vasculitis, or other chronic inflammatory disease.

A 65-year-old man presented with 12 hours of sudden, severe, crampy peri-umbilical abdominal pain, mild abdominal distention, and failure to pass stool or flatus. He reported chronic intermittent constipation and distention but no hematochezia or vomiting. He was on amlodipine for hypertension but admitted poor compliance; he had no prior abdominal surgery. Vital signs: BP 215/109 mm Hg, HR 60 bpm, RR 24 bpm, T 36 °C, SpO2 99% on room air. Physical examination showed a mildly distended abdomen with hyperactive bowel sounds and voluntary guarding in the upper abdomen but no tenderness, rigidity, or peritoneal signs. Digital rectal examination revealed an empty rectum. Laboratory studies, including CBC, liver and renal function tests, troponin, and pancreatic enzymes, were within normal limits. An ECG was normal.  
An erect chest and abdominal radiograph demonstrated a lucency beneath the right hemidiaphragm containing both haustral markings and valvulae conniventes, as well as centrally located multiple air-fluid levels. These findings were initially reported as pneumoperitoneum with generalized peritonitis; however, the clinical examination lacked peritoneal signs, and the lucency exhibited bowel patterning suggestive of intraluminal rather than free air. A contrast-enhanced CT scan was obtained to clarify the diagnosis.

A 63-year-old Chinese farmer presented with a 1-month history of papules and pustules on his nose. He reported prior trauma to his nasal skin during farm work. He denied fever, cough, joint pain, or other systemic symptoms. His medical history was unremarkable for hypertension, diabetes, or immunosuppression. Examination revealed multiple papules and pustules on an erythematous base over the nasal dorsum, some with superficial ulceration and yellow crusting. There was no palpable cervical, axillary, or facial lymphadenopathy. He had been treated with systemic and topical antibiotics at a local hospital without improvement.

A 51-year-old woman presented with a 15-day history of sudden onset of reduced tone and texture of her voice. Her voice was feeble but understandable, improving with morning rest and worsening through the day to near-inaudibility. She denied choking, coughing, aspiration, or throat discomfort. She had a long-standing history of constipation but was otherwise healthy, with no tobacco or alcohol use and no family history of chronic illness.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Systemic and neurologic examinations were unremarkable: muscle strength 15/15 on the Medical Research Council scale, normal gait and tandem walking, intact gag reflex and cranial nerves, and normal deep-tendon reflexes. Speech articulation was intact with no scanning, normal tone and resonance, but low intensity and slow rate. An ENT evaluation found no laryngeal pathology, and initial treatment there had no effect.

MRI of the brain and spine was normal. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, infectious disease panel, and myopathy panel with creatine kinase, were within normal limits. At this point, other causes having been excluded, clinicians suspected myasthenia gravis.

A 33-year-old woman with a five-year history of essential thrombocythemia presented after detection of a palpable mass in her left flank. She reported no weight loss, fever, or abdominal pain. On examination, the liver and spleen were both enlarged and palpable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 14.7 g/dL, platelet count 73 × 10^3/µL, and leukocyte count 24 010/µL. Serum α-fetoprotein was <3 ng/mL, and serologic tests for hepatitis B, C, and A were negative. A recent bone marrow biopsy demonstrated transformation of essential thrombocythemia into idiopathic myelofibrosis.

Noncontrast CT of the abdomen revealed a 2-cm, well-defined, homogeneously low-attenuation mass in segment VI of the liver, with diffuse hepatosplenomegaly. On portal-venous-phase contrast-enhanced CT, the lesion showed intense homogeneous enhancement; no other focal lesions were identified. On MRI, the mass was homogeneously hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on fat-saturated T2-weighted images, with no signal change on in- and opposed-phase T1 sequences. After administration of gadolinium contrast, the lesion enhanced homogeneously and intensely in the arterial phase and remained enhanced at five minutes. Ten minutes after intravenous superparamagnetic iron oxide (SPIO) administration, there was no signal drop in the lesion on T2*-weighted images.

Considering her history of anabolic steroid use for thrombocythemia and the appearance of a well-defined hypervascular lesion, the leading radiologic diagnosis was hepatocellular adenoma. Differential considerations also included focal nodular hyperplasia, hepatocellular carcinoma, angiomyolipoma, and a solitary hypervascular metastasis.

A 34-year-old professional ballerina presented with a 10-month history of bilateral medial knee pain that impaired her performance and daily activities. Eight years earlier, she had undergone a partial meniscectomy of the right knee at another institution. She had no other medical, personal, or family history of knee disorders.

On examination, her BMI was 23.0. There was pain and tenderness over the medial joint line of both knees. Medial McMurray and Appley tests were positive. There was full range of motion without laxity. No laboratory studies were performed.

Magnetic resonance imaging of both knees demonstrated a homogeneous, low-signal-intensity linear structure on T1- and T2-weighted images, coursing anterior to the anterior cruciate ligament and connecting the medial portion of the anterior horn of the medial meniscus to the posterolateral intercondylar notch. There was also a tear of the posterior horn of the medial meniscus in each knee; the right knee additionally showed surgical changes from the prior partial meniscectomy. Plain radiographs of the knees and lower limbs showed no bony abnormalities or malalignment.

A 52-year-old woman with no past medical history presented with two days of bilateral hand swelling and pain. Four days earlier, she had strained her left shoulder while helping cut down a tree with a rope and was diagnosed with a rotator cuff tear at an outside hospital, where she received IV morphine in her left arm and then developed left hand swelling. On returning to that hospital, she received IV morphine in her right arm and subsequently developed right hand swelling. She denied any direct trauma to her hands; the pain was relieved only by placing her hands in cold water. She also noted atraumatic left knee swelling. She smoked marijuana and had a remote history of methamphetamine use but denied current tobacco, alcohol, or IV drug use.

On arrival, she was afebrile (36.6°C), tachycardic (110 bpm), and had a blood pressure of 142/106 mmHg. Examination revealed puffy edema on the dorsal aspects of both hands extending to the wrists with mild erythema but no induration or fluctuance. Range of motion at the wrists and fingers was intact but limited by swelling, and there was no pain with micromotion. Sensation was intact, radial pulses were strong, capillary refill was brisk, and compartments were soft. The left knee showed mild erythema, edema, and warmth with full range of motion but pain at the extremes. Distal pulses and compartments in the lower extremity were normal.

Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 20,000/mm3 with 22% bands, a C-reactive protein level of 631.2 mg/L, and a rheumatoid factor of 45 IU/mL. Radiographs of both hands and wrists revealed diffuse soft tissue swelling without fracture or dislocation. Point-of-care ultrasound demonstrated bilateral wrist effusions and fluid surrounding the extensor tendon sheaths.

A 6-year-old spayed female Ragdoll cat was referred for evaluation of a 4-day history of acute onset retching and anorexia. The day after administration of oral alendronate for idiopathic hypercalcaemia, the owner noted intermittent vomiting, followed by persistent retching and inappetence. On presentation, the cat was bright, alert and responsive and was observed to cough with a terminal retch. Due to aggression, sedation with intramuscular tiletamine-zolazepam was used to perform a physical examination, which was unremarkable.

Laboratory tests showed a mild neutropenia (2.27 ×10^9/L; RI 2.3–10.29 ×10^9/L) and hypophosphatemia (0.69 mmol/L; RI 1–2.42 mmol/L); serum ionized calcium was normal. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a focal fluid-dilated segment of small intestine. Thoracic radiographs demonstrated an alveolar pattern in the right cranial ventral lung lobes and tracheal narrowing at the thoracic inlet. An echocardiogram was normal.

Given the history of vomiting, cough and right cranial ventral alveolar pattern, aspiration pneumonia was suspected. The cat was hospitalized and treated with intravenous amoxicillin (22 mg/kg q8h). Cough resolved but hyporexia persisted, and buprenorphine was added for presumed esophageal discomfort. After 3 days, the cat was discharged with a single subcutaneous cefovecin injection.

Four days later, the cat re-presented with progressive coughing, persistent anorexia and intermittent neck extension with open-mouth breathing. Repeat physical examination under sedation was unremarkable.

An 8-year-old boy was brought by his parents with concern about an unusually large and unattractive upper lip that had become progressively more prominent over the preceding 3 to 4 years. The patient had no difficulty with speech or eating but was self-conscious about the appearance. There was no history of trauma, oral habits, infection, or prior surgery involving the lip, and no family history of similar lip abnormalities. His medical history was unremarkable.

On examination, at rest the upper lip appeared normal, but when the patient smiled or spoke, there was a bilateral fold of excess mucosal tissue with a central constriction, giving a cupid’s bow appearance. The mucosal surface was intact without ulceration or induration. There were no other oral or facial anomalies, and eyelid appearance was normal. Vital signs were within normal limits.

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and metabolic panel, were normal. Ultrasonography of the neck showed no thyroid enlargement.

A provisional diagnosis was made.

A 10-year-old, spayed female Australian Shepherd was evaluated for intermittent urinary incontinence of 2 weeks’ duration, noted when the dog lay down or rose from a bed. The dog otherwise appeared normal.  
Previous medical history included a treated Escherichia coli urinary tract infection 4 months earlier.  
On initial examination, the vulva appeared enlarged and swollen, and a possible mass was palpated at the ventral commissure.  
Complete blood count and serum chemistry were within reference limits.  
Urinalysis showed a specific gravity of 1.026, pH 8.0, and 4–10 struvite crystals per high-powered field; sediment examination and microscopy were otherwise unremarkable. A cystocentesis urine culture was negative.  
Abdominal radiographs were unremarkable.  
On referral, a firm, hairless, 3.0 cm diameter mass was noted protruding from the ventral commissure of the vulva. Fine-needle aspiration yielded clear viscous fluid with specific gravity 1.008. Cytology revealed a cystic lesion with chronic lymphoplasmacytic inflammation, with no neoplastic cells or infectious agents identified.  
Contrast-enhanced thoracoabdominal CT demonstrated a pedunculated, thin-walled, fluid-attenuating cystic mass (approximately 4.4 × 2.6 cm) arising from the ventral commissure of the vulva in the region of the clitoral fossa and clitoris, with a nest of tortuous, strongly enhancing vessels dorsal to the mass.

A 38-year-old Greek woman presented with a 1-week history of left-sided abdominal pain without other symptoms. She had no prior episodes, and her medical history was unremarkable. On examination, she had focal tenderness in the left abdomen; vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed an anechoic lesion in the upper left quadrant. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen demonstrated a well-defined, hypodense cystic mass measuring 7.08 × 6.05 cm in the left upper abdomen, with mild peripheral enhancement.

A previously healthy nine-year-old boy was referred for surgical evaluation of a suspected congenital pulmonary airway malformation. He had a one-month history of recurrent fever, cough, and sputum production. Initial chest radiography demonstrated left lower lobe pneumonia, and he received oral antibiotics for one week with minimal symptomatic improvement. On October 18, contrast-enhanced chest CT showed a thick-walled multiloculated lesion with a smooth inner border and homogeneous central low density in the left lower lobe. No prior imaging was available. He was treated with three weeks of intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, after which infection appeared controlled, and he was referred for lobectomy to prevent recurrent infection.

On presentation to our institution, he had a persistent dry cough without fever. Temperature was 36.8 °C, blood pressure 110/75 mmHg, heart rate 100 beats/min, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Examination was unremarkable except for decreased breath sounds over the left lower lobe. Routine laboratory tests, including hematological and blood chemistry panels and ECG, were within normal limits. He had no history of night sweats, weight loss, chest pain, hemoptysis, trauma, or witnessed choking. To assess the residual lesion prior to surgery, a repeat contrast CT on November 14 revealed an irregular patchy shadow in the lateral segment of the left lower lobe without any septa or multicystic cavities, and the lesion appeared smaller than on the initial scan. Considering this change in morphology and extent, diagnostic bronchoscopy was arranged for further evaluation.

A 64-year-old woman, gravida 3, with menopausal onset at age 59, was referred for evaluation of virilization. Her medical history included hypothyroidism and osteoarthritis. Examination revealed central obesity (BMI 30 kg/m2; waist circumference 97 cm). Laboratory tests demonstrated impaired fasting glucose (100 mg/dL) and hypercholesterolemia.

She reported a 10-year history of progressive alopecia, hirsutism, clitoromegaly, deepening of the voice, increased muscle mass, and muscle pain, with marked worsening over the past 2 years. She denied use of exogenous androgens.

Transvaginal ultrasonography showed a large, well-circumscribed cystic mass in the left pelvic cavity (volume 1,230 mL), possibly ovarian, and an irregular hyperechoic focus with acoustic shadowing (3 × 3.5 × 3 mm) in the right ovary. Serum hormone measurements revealed severe hyperandrogenism (testosterone 483.4 ng/dL) with a normal dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate level (35.3 μg/dL). Repeat ultrasonography confirmed a left ovarian anechoic cyst (volume 1,214 mL) and a right ovary of normal volume with posterior acoustic shadowing.

A 59-year-old Turkish man presented with fatigue, loss of energy, and dark-colored urine. He reported that over the past year he had developed hyperpigmentation of the hands and face after sun exposure; these areas sometimes blistered and healed with scarring. He had transitioned from social alcohol use to daily consumption over the past year. He worked as a butcher and ate more than 300 g of meat most days, noting that his symptoms worsened after large meat meals. His medical and family histories were unremarkable.

On examination, brown pigmented lesions were noted on the dorsal surfaces of both hands, along with erosions, scars, and 1-mm firm white papules consistent with milia. The facial skin was diffusely darker than previously reported. His body‐mass index was 38 kg/m2.

Laboratory testing revealed: AST 125 U/L (normal 0–50), ALT 89 U/L (0–50), GGT 1190 U/L (0–55), LDH 268 U/L (0–248), CK 174 U/L (0–171), ALP 123 U/L (30–120), ferritin 503 ng/mL (23–336), and vitamin B12 1275 pg/mL (145–914). Tests for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, and autoimmune markers were negative. Urine was noted to be turbid.

Twenty-four–hour urine studies showed porphyrin excretion of 832 μg (normal ≤ 100) and porphobilinogen excretion of 1.65 mg (normal ≤ 1.65).

A 37-year-old man was referred for evaluation of flashes and photopsias, predominantly in the right eye. He had been diagnosed with presumed bilateral posterior uveitis in 2016. Initial laboratory tests in 2016, including CBC, CMP, hemoglobin A₁c, and iron studies, were within normal limits. Tests for infectious causes—QuantiFERON-TB Gold, RPR, and FTA-ABS—were negative. MRI of the brain was unremarkable. He received topical corticosteroids, intravitreal bevacizumab OD, and oral prednisone 60 mg daily. In December 2016, cyclosporine and methotrexate were started but discontinued in 2017 for lack of efficacy. Adalimumab was then given with symptomatic improvement but stopped in early 2019 for reduced serum iron. In October 2019 he received a fluocinolone acetonide intravitreal implant OD without improvement.

On examination in January 2020, he reported moderate ocular discomfort (OD > OS), hazy vision (OD > OS), and floaters OU. Visual acuity was 20/20 OU. Intraocular pressures were 13 mm Hg OD and 12 mm Hg OS. Anterior segment showed 1+ flare OU and a mild posterior subcapsular cataract OD. Dilated fundus examination revealed optic disc edema (OD > OS) and peripapillary and peripheral ovoid hypopigmented chorioretinal lesions OU. OD also demonstrated temporal peripapillary atrophy, 1+ vitreous cells, macular RPE pigmentary changes, and a small superotemporal peripheral retinal hemorrhage. Spectral-domain OCT showed peripapillary intraretinal fluid and mild epiretinal membrane OD > OS. Fluorescein angiography revealed disc leakage and peripapillary staining OD and diffuse disc leakage with mild segmental venular staining OS; several lesions were hyperfluorescent without leakage OU. Two weeks later, full-field ERG showed mild-to-moderate global dysfunction with delayed 30 Hz flicker implicit times (OS > OD). Visual evoked potentials showed symmetric delay for small and large stimuli. Goldmann and Humphrey visual fields revealed blind-spot enlargement OD and normal fields OS.

Laboratory evaluation was notable only for HLA-A29 positivity; ACE, lysozyme, and repeat QuantiFERON-TB Gold were within normal limits.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive visual loss in her left eye and erythematous lesions on both thighs. She had no significant past medical or lifestyle history. On funduscopic examination, vitreous opacities and phlebitis in the left eye led to a diagnosis of uveitis. Chest radiography revealed bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed an elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level of 33.4 IU/L (normal 8.3–21.4 IU/L), serum lysozyme 12.9 μg/mL (normal 5.0–10.2 μg/mL), and soluble interleukin-2 receptor 1442 U/mL (normal 121–613 U/mL), raising suspicion for sarcoidosis. Topical steroids led to improvement of the ocular and cutaneous lesions.

Three weeks later, she developed numbness over the anterior aspect of her left thigh, which progressed to involve her left cheek, both upper limbs (predominant on the right), her left back, and both feet. She also noted difficulty with fine motor tasks in her right hand and left-sided facial weakness. MR neurography (3D spin echo T2-weighted imaging with fat suppression) demonstrated asymmetric enlargement of the dorsal root ganglia at right C7 and C8, left L3, and right L5. Gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted MRI showed contrast enhancement in the same ganglia. FDG-PET/CT revealed increased uptake in those dorsal root ganglia and in the left T11 dorsal root ganglion. Chest CT showed enlarged supraclavicular, mediastinal, and hilar lymph nodes.

A stray kitten was acquired by a shelter along with its dam and sibling. At the time of adoption, the kitten had a few alopecic nodules at the base of one ear and on the nasal bridge. Facial dermatitis progressed rapidly after adoption, prompting veterinary examination. Apart from dermatologic findings, clinical examination was unremarkable. A complete blood count showed a normal leukocyte count. Tests for anti–feline immunodeficiency virus antibodies, feline leukemia virus antigen, and qPCR from a conjunctival swab for Chlamydophila felis, feline calicivirus, feline herpesvirus, and Mycoplasma felis were all negative. Abdominal ultrasound and total thyroxin were within reference ranges, and a bacterial culture from a skin lesion swab yielded no growth. Initial treatment with methylprednisolone acetate and amoxicillin–clavulanate failed to halt progression; a subsequent trial of doxycycline led to only slight, temporary improvement. Ten days after the initial examination, the kitten was referred to a veterinary dermatologist. The kitten was thin but alert. Dermatologic examination revealed marked, firm, symmetrical, alopecic swelling of the bridge of the nose, cheeks, and eyelids, obscuring the eyes and distorting facial anatomy. The edges of the pinnae were thickened with firm alopecic nodules and confluent yellow crusts. Multifocal alopecic nodules were present on the limbs, and the distal third of the tail was swollen and alopecic. Two wedge biopsies and cytologic and bacteriologic samples were obtained from pinnal lesions. Cytology showed pyogranulomatous inflammation dominated by macrophages filled with numerous pleomorphic intracellular organisms, ranging from tiny ovoid basophilic structures to large foamy spherules and distinct banana-shaped tachyzoites. Histopathology of the skin demonstrated severe, diffuse interstitial macrophage-rich inflammation effacing the dermal architecture; basophilic protozoal organisms representing multiple apicomplexan developmental stages were abundant within macrophages and epidermal and follicular epithelial cells, with the most plentiful stage being unsporulated oocysts forming capsulated aggregates of foamy basophilic material.

A previously healthy 4-year-old girl was brought to the pediatric clinic with a 2-day history of painless, progressively drooping and swollen right upper eyelid. Visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. Ophthalmologic examination revealed right-sided upper eyelid ptosis, proptosis, and ophthalmoplegia, with otherwise normal funduscopic and slit-lamp findings. She was also unable to use her left arm and left leg at presentation. 

Given the acute motor deficit, noncontrast cranial CT was obtained to exclude intracranial hemorrhage or mass; the study was normal. Complete blood count, electrolyte levels, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were within normal limits, and peripheral blood smear showed no atypical cells.

Orbital MRI with fat-saturated, postgadolinium T1-weighted sequences demonstrated marked contrast enhancement of the right medial and inferior rectus muscles. Additional imaging showed enlargement of the superior, inferior, and medial rectus muscles and their tendons on fat-saturated T2-weighted images, with minimal hyperintensity.

A 23-year-old woman with an 8-year history of systemic lupus erythematosus and lupus nephritis presented after four generalized tonic-clonic seizures accompanied by severe headaches, visual disturbances, and altered mental status. Two days before her first seizure, she had developed moderate occipital headaches, and 6 hours before the seizures she noted declining vision. She received her first dose of rituximab 5 days earlier for refractory lupus nephritis and a second dose before hospital discharge; visual blurring and retro-orbital pain began acutely after the second dose. On examination she was listless, confused, and intermittently seizing; neurological examination showed bilateral cortical blindness and hyperreflexia. Glasgow Coma Scale scores fluctuated between 5 and 9. Vital signs were within normal limits. Complete blood count, electrolytes, and renal function tests were unremarkable. 

Emergency brain MRI revealed multifocal, asymmetrical hypointensities on T1-weighted images and corresponding hyperintensities on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences involving subcortical U-fibers and deep white and gray matter in bilateral frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes (predominant in occipital lobes), bilateral thalami, gangliocapsular regions, corona radiata, centrum semiovale, hemipons, middle cerebellar peduncles, and cerebellar hemispheres, with mild vasogenic edema and effacement of adjacent sulci. DWI showed few areas of patchy reduced diffusivity; SWI demonstrated no susceptibility artifacts.

A 12-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a facial angioma. MRI of the brain showed no leptomeningeal vascular malformations. Examination revealed bilateral naevus flammeus along the ophthalmic and maxillary divisions of the trigeminal nerve, more extensive on the right. Visual acuity was 20/20 in each eye. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye showed iris heterochromia with diffuse hyperpigmentation and evenly distributed micronodular elevations on the iris surface. Intraocular pressure measured by Icare tonometry was 22 mm Hg in the right eye and 12 mm Hg in the left. Gonioscopy demonstrated open angles bilaterally with diffuse trabecular hyperpigmentation in the right eye. Anterior-segment OCT revealed increased reflectance of the iris surface in the right eye. Funduscopic examination showed increased retinal vessel tortuosity and a diffusely darker fundus in the right eye. B-scan ultrasonography measured choroidal thickness of 2.2 mm in the right eye versus 1.4 mm in the left. Macular spectral-domain OCT confirmed a thicker choroid in the right eye. Standard automated perimetry detected early visual-field defects in the right eye, and peripapillary OCT showed borderline retinal nerve-fibre-layer thickness on the right. Topical latanoprost was initiated in the right eye, reducing intraocular pressure to 17 mm Hg.

A 76-year-old man with coronary artery disease (status post bypass), mitral regurgitation, left ventricular hypertrophy, and atrial fibrillation presented with insidious atraumatic right shoulder pain beginning at 0300 on the day of presentation. He reported body aches and chills but remained afebrile. The pain initially resolved then returned, prompting an ED visit. He had played 18 holes of golf the previous day, with no other precipitant. 

Medications included aspirin, Norvasc, Flomax, topical diclofenac, and Norco as needed. He had allergies to cephalexin and latex (rash). He was a former half-pack-per-day smoker; denied alcohol or drug use. 

On examination, he was afebrile; vital signs were normal. Inspection of the right shoulder showed no erythema, swelling, fluctuance, or lesions. There was minimal tenderness to palpation over the glenohumeral joint. Active range of motion was limited by pain. Passive flexion and abduction reached 100°, internal and external rotation 45°, with pain at extremes. Axial loading of the shoulder elicited pain.

Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 33,100 c/µL (normal 4,800–10,800) and C-reactive protein of 11 mg/dL (normal 0–0.8). Plain radiographs of the right shoulder were unremarkable aside from acromioclavicular joint degenerative changes. MRI of the right shoulder demonstrated a supraspinatus tear, a moderate glenohumeral effusion, and a thickened capsule.

A 14-year-old male baseball catcher with no prior medical history presented with left knee pain of several weeks’ duration without any inciting injury. Initial anteroposterior and lateral plain radiographs were unremarkable, and he was treated conservatively for overuse without relief. One month later, he continued to have medial knee pain. Physical examination showed mild swelling and point tenderness over the medial proximal tibia without erythema or increased temperature and full range of motion. Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 3800/µL and a C-reactive protein level of 0.86 mg/dL. Repeat anteroposterior plain radiography of the left knee demonstrated a well-defined osteolytic lesion at the medial edge of the proximal tibial metaphysis. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left knee showed that on T1-weighted images the central portion of the lesion was low in signal intensity, surrounded by a thin isointense layer and an outer low-signal rim, while fat-suppressed T2-weighted images revealed high signal intensity centrally.

A 34-year-old man was referred for a several‐year history of hematochezia accompanied by abdominal discomfort, tenesmus, and urgency. He denied nocturnal stooling, weight loss, infectious or extraintestinal symptoms. Family and social histories were noncontributory.

Outpatient MRI of the abdomen showed diffuse mural thickening and mucosal hyperenhancement of the distal colon and rectum. Laboratory studies revealed a mild normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL) and mild thrombocytopenia (platelets 140×10^9/L); electrolytes, creatinine, ferritin, liver enzymes, celiac serologies, and C‐reactive protein were normal.

On examination, there was a discrepancy in limb size, ectatic veins on the arms, and port‐wine skin lesions. The abdomen was soft and nontender without organomegaly; digital rectal examination was normal.

Two years earlier, a geneticist had confirmed a diagnosis of CLOVES syndrome based on limb overgrowth, port‐wine stains, superficial vascular malformations, macrodactyly, and imaging that demonstrated congenital absence of several deep veins with extensive venous varices.

Diagnostic colonoscopy revealed, in the rectum, sigmoid, and descending colon, diffusely raised nodular mucosa overlying bluish dilated vessels resembling varices, without signs of inflammation or ischemia. In the transverse and ascending colon, numerous arteriovenous malformations were seen on otherwise normal mucosa; the terminal ileum appeared normal, and there was no active or recent bleeding.

Contrast CT angiography of the abdomen demonstrated dysplastic venous drainage with absence of a normal inferior mesenteric vein and multiple pericolic and intramural phleboliths, correlating with the areas of wall thickening seen on MRI.

An 87-year-old woman presented with 1 week of dyspnoea and fatigue. Two weeks earlier, she underwent revision of her right atrial pacemaker lead for loss of sensing and capture. She has a history of Ebstein’s anomaly with prior tricuspid valve surgery, sinus-node dysfunction, paroxysmal atrial tachycardia, and atrial flutter, and 3 years ago was upgraded to a dual-chamber pacemaker programmed to DDDR with automatic mode switching to VDIR for atrial rates >170 b.p.m. Her medications included nebivolol, warfarin, and amiodarone (held for 2 months).

On examination, blood pressure was 128/78 mmHg, heart rate 70 b.p.m., respiratory rate 16 per minute, temperature 98.2 °F, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. There was a grade 3/6 pansystolic murmur at the left parasternal border and fine crackles at both lung bases; there was no jugular venous distension or peripheral oedema. Laboratory tests showed a B-type natriuretic peptide level of 925 pg/mL and normal troponin I. Chest radiography revealed bilateral lower lung interstitial infiltrates.
