Electrocardiography demonstrated a ventricular-paced rhythm at 70 b.p.m. with retrograde P waves. Transthoracic echocardiography showed an ejection fraction of 65%, a dilated right ventricle with reduced systolic function, moderate tricuspid regurgitation, and no significant pericardial effusion.

The chief differential diagnosis was congestive heart failure. Given her recent device revision, procedural complications such as pericardial effusion, pacemaker malfunction, and pacemaker syndrome were also considered. Pacemaker interrogation was performed.

A 45-year-old woman from rural Kashmir, married with four children, presented with two episodes of generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Over the past 3 years she had three to four similar admissions for generalized seizures. On each admission her serum sodium level was low (110–121 mEq/L), and on the current admission it was 115 mEq/L. Hemogram, liver and kidney function tests, blood glucose, urinalysis, calcium, potassium, chloride, protein and lipid levels were all within normal limits. Brain magnetic resonance imaging and abdominal ultrasonography were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid examination was unremarkable. One of three electroencephalograms showed nonspecific epileptic discharges. Initially, her seizures were attributed to thiazide-induced hyponatremia, and thiazides were discontinued, but hyponatremia and seizures recurred on subsequent admissions. She had been receiving phenytoin sodium, 300 mg daily, since her first seizure without any significant improvement.

A 35-year-old right-hand-dominant woman presented with a 2-day history of spontaneous onset of swelling and tenderness of the left middle-finger metacarpophalangeal joint. She recalled no trauma, is a smoker, and had a laparoscopic cholecystectomy years earlier. Two weeks before, she experienced a similar episode at the same joint that resolved within 24 hours without intervention.  
On examination, the joint was swollen, exquisitely painful on passive movement, erythematous, and warm.  
Laboratory studies showed normal serum calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone, vitamin D, and thyroid-function levels.  
Plain radiography demonstrated a 12 mm × 4 mm prominent area of soft-tissue calcification projected dorsolateral to the head of the middle-finger metacarpal bone.  
Ultrasound-guided biopsy could not aspirate any material due to the relative solidity of the lesion.

A 27-year-old woman presented with seven weeks of amenorrhea and a markedly elevated serum hCG (>200 000 IU/L). She had regular menses, no dysmenorrhea, and no prior gynecologic issues. Transvaginal and abdominal ultrasound showed a right unicornuate uterus with endometrial thickness of 1.7 cm and an empty uterine cavity. Between the left ovary and the uterine corpus lay a 3.5 × 3.0 cm gestational sac containing a 1 cm fetal bud with cardiac activity. Abundant circumferential blood flow surrounded the sac, and a 0.5 cm thick muscular wall encased the sac, connecting it to the right myometrium. Pelvic MRI confirmed a right unicornuate uterus and demonstrated the gestational sac in a left adnexal horn surrounded by myometrium; renal anatomy was normal.

A 53-year-old South Asian man presented with more than 24 hours of chest pain and left-arm numbness that began while driving but resolved upon arrival. He had no abnormal findings on examination (heart rate 65 bpm; blood pressure 108/76 mmHg; respiratory rate 16 breaths/min; O₂ saturation 98% on room air). His history included type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, and hepatitis B. He had two prior admissions for cTnT-positive chest pain (2002 and 2015), each with unobstructed coronaries and a working diagnosis of myocarditis.

An admission ECG showed no ischaemic changes. Initial cTnT was 1588 ng/L (normal <15 ng/L) and 1842 ng/L on repeat. Renal function was normal (creatinine 102 μmol/L) and hemoglobin was 137 g/L. Serial troponins remained above 1600 ng/L. Creatine kinase was borderline elevated at 338 U/L (normal 40–320 U/L). Transthoracic echocardiography revealed no regional wall motion abnormalities and an LVEF of 60–65%. A CT aortagram excluded aortic dissection and, within its limits, ruled out pulmonary embolus. Coronary angiography demonstrated only mild right coronary disease and otherwise unobstructed vessels. Cardiac MRI with gadolinium showed preserved biventricular function with no scar, fibrosis, or edema. He remained on telemetry for 7 days without documented arrhythmia. After extensive investigations had excluded myocardial damage and any other clinical condition as a likely cause of the troponin elevation, the biochemistry laboratory was contacted for assistance.

An 18-year-old man with no personal or family history presented in 2021 with chest pain. Physical examination was unremarkable. ECG showed an incomplete right bundle-branch block and negative T waves in the inferolateral leads. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed apical akinesia of the left ventricle with a preserved ejection fraction of 55%. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with late gadolinium enhancement demonstrated subepicardial contrast uptake in the apex and apical segments of the anterolateral and inferior LV walls; the right ventricle appeared normal. A diagnosis of myocarditis was made on the basis of myocardial fibrosis, and the patient was prescribed a β-blocker, with poor compliance.

One year later, during a football match, he experienced exertional syncope. ECG now showed repolarization abnormalities. Troponin and brain natriuretic peptide levels were elevated. Repeat cardiac MRI revealed akinesia of the LV apex extending to the apical and mid segments of adjacent walls, with a mildly reduced LV ejection fraction of 45%, and akinesia of the inferior RV wall. Late gadolinium enhancement was transmural in the apex and in the apical and mid segments of the inferior, anterior, septal, and lateral LV walls, with enhancement of the inferior and lateral RV walls. Two diagnoses were considered: necrotic sequela versus arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy. To rule out ischemic necrosis, coronary angiography was performed and found to be normal.

A 31-year-old man from Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, employed in an animal-feed industry, presented with a seven-month history of cough, asthenia, progressive dyspnea, fever, and papular skin lesions on the trunk. He denied travel, exposure to decaying wood, or illicit drug use but noted that two coworkers had been diagnosed with “pigeon disease.” On initial examination he was tachypneic, had papules on the trunk, and oral candidiasis; there were no neurological signs or symptoms.

Laboratory studies on day 0 revealed a rapid HIV-positive test with a CD4 count of 50 cells/mm³, arterial hypoxemia (pO₂ 63 mm Hg), and a chest radiograph showing diffuse bilateral reticular infiltrates. A serum lateral flow assay (LFA) for cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) was positive. Lumbar puncture showed normal glucose (50 mg/dL), protein (49.1 mg/dL), 2 cells (100% mononuclear), with negative CSF CrAg LFA and India ink staining. Induced sputum was negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis by molecular testing and for acid-fast bacilli.

Treatment was initiated with trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole for presumed Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and fluconazole 800 mg daily for preemptive management of isolated cryptococcal antigenemia. By day 4, the patient’s dyspnea and skin lesions had improved, but he began to complain of headache. Blood cultures remained negative, double immunodiffusion for histoplasmosis was nonreactive, and double immunodiffusion for Paracoccidioides brasiliensis (PCM) was reactive at a titer of 1:16.

A 44-year-old man presented with a one-week history of left-sided abdominal and flank pain that had spread to his left thigh. He also reported a preceding febrile illness with diarrhea. His medical history was significant only for mild asthma managed with inhaled steroids and bronchodilators and allergic rhinitis. 

On examination, he was initially afebrile but later developed a fever. Abdominal examination showed tenderness in the left iliac fossa and left flank; straight-leg raising on the left exacerbated his pain. Neurologic examination at presentation was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed a leukocytosis and a C-reactive protein level greater than 100 mg/L; renal and hepatic function tests were normal. Chest and abdominal radiographs demonstrated loss of the left psoas shadow without free air or bowel obstruction. He was treated empirically with intravenous fluids, analgesia, co-amoxiclav, and gentamicin for presumed acute diverticulitis with a psoas abscess.

The next day, his left thigh pain worsened and new weakness of the left quadriceps was noted. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed diffuse inflammation of the left peritoneum, pelvis, left psoas muscle, and retroperitoneum, with no fluid collection. On hospital day three, he developed numbness in an L1/L2 distribution and bilateral quadriceps weakness. MRI of the thoracolumbar and sacral spine showed no significant abnormalities of the spine or nerve roots and confirmed inflammation of the left psoas and retroperitoneum.

Repeat blood tests at this time revealed an eosinophil count of 4.52 × 10^9/L (reference 0–0.5 × 10^9/L). Colonoscopy was performed to evaluate for inflammatory bowel disease; the colon was macroscopically normal and random biopsies were microscopically normal. Tests for ANA, p-ANCA, c-ANCA, cryoglobulins, complement levels, hepatitis serologies, and serum protein electrophoresis were all within normal limits.

A 56-year-old woman presented with a 4-year history of a slowly enlarging lesion on her lower lip. She had no significant medical history, was a non-smoker, and denied weight loss. On examination, there was a painless, firm, indurated, crusted area measuring 4 cm with central ulceration, giving the lip a “bitten-off” appearance. The surrounding skin and oral mucosa were normal. There were no palpable lymph nodes, and ultrasonography confirmed the absence of lymphadenopathy. Complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and routine serum chemistries were all within normal limits. An incisional biopsy including normal mucosa and skin showed a non-specific ulcer with inflammation and granulation tissue and revealed no cellular atypia suggestive of malignancy.

A woman in her late seventies presented with an 8-month history of a progressive rash, accompanied by a 6-kg weight loss and difficulty swallowing. The rash began as red, keratinized patches on the ears, fingers, and toes. She was diagnosed with psoriasis and treated for 6 months with oral methotrexate, topical calcipotriol, and ultraviolet A therapy, without significant improvement. The lesions subsequently spread symmetrically to the face, hands, feet, forearms, calves, buttocks, and neck. She denied itching or pain.

Physical examination revealed multiple erythematous, scaly plaques and patches on both ears, cheeks, buttocks, legs, and the dorsum of the hands and feet. Pronounced palmoplantar hyperkeratosis with central sparing was noted, along with roughening, thickening, and discoloration of both great toenails; fingernails were unaffected.

A skin biopsy from the gluteal region showed hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, acanthosis, and perivascular lymphocyte infiltration in the superficial dermis. Mycological analysis of toenail samples was negative for fungal infection.

An 81-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department after a fall down a flight of stairs. Paramedics noted approximately 500 mL of blood loss from a scalp wound that had been bandaged before arrival. On assessment, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 15, but she appeared pale and reported retrograde amnesia and dizziness; she had no recollection of why she had climbed the stairs. On removal of the head bandage, there was no active bleeding, and the scalp lesion resembled a large haematoma.

Her medical history included mild vascular dementia, asthma, angina, hypothyroidism, and congestive heart failure. She lived with her daughter, slept on the ground floor because of mobility issues, was a non-smoker, and did not consume alcohol.

Initial investigations showed a white-cell count of 16.03 × 10^9/L with neutrophils of 14.17 × 10^9/L. Urinalysis was positive for nitrites, and urine cultures grew Escherichia coli. The initial haemoglobin concentration was 99 g/L. 

Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen revealed multiple undisplaced right rib fractures and fractures of the T8 vertebra and the left lateral process of L3. Cranial CT showed a large posterior subcutaneous haematoma over the parietal bones with no skull fractures or intracranial abnormalities. A log roll was contraindicated because of the T8 fracture, limiting further examination. Plain radiographs as part of the secondary survey showed no additional injuries.

Over the next 48 hours, her haemoglobin level fell to 75 g/L, and she required a blood transfusion. The cause of this normocytic anaemia remained undetermined.

A 57-year-old Caucasian man with hypertension and sick sinus syndrome had a pacemaker placed 8 months ago. One month later, he developed recurrent atrial fibrillation and was started on amiodarone 400 mg daily, metoprolol, and oral anticoagulation. After maintaining sinus rhythm for 6 months, amiodarone was discontinued. Three weeks later, he presented with a 2-day history of right lateral sharp chest pain and worsening shortness of breath. He denied fever, chills, weight loss, palpitations, or leg swelling and had a remote tobacco history. 

On examination, he appeared ill and tachypneic (respiratory rate 28 breaths/min), afebrile, blood pressure 115/74 mmHg, heart rate 60 bpm, and oxygen saturation 86% on room air. Cardiac auscultation was normal. Breath sounds were diminished at both lung bases. The abdomen was soft, and the legs showed no edema or tenderness. There was no rash, clubbing, or lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia and elevated inflammatory markers, an INR of 3.1, and an unremarkable cardiac peptide. Arterial blood gas revealed significant hypoxemia. A chest X-ray showed bilateral lower lobe consolidations with stable pacer-lead position. Electrocardiography demonstrated a paced rhythm with first-degree AV block and a prolonged QT interval. 

A contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed focal high-attenuation areas of multiple conglomerate consolidations in both lung bases with no evidence of pulmonary embolism.

A 55-year-old man with a 2–pack-year smoking history and a history of left-sided thoracotomy 40 years earlier was first evaluated two years ago for chronic dry cough and intermittent hemoptysis. Initial CT of the chest revealed a 15-mm solitary nodule in the left lower lobe. Bronchoscopy showed no endoluminal lesions or active bleeding, and bronchial washings and brushings were negative for malignant cells; microbiological cultures yielded no pathogens. Given the patient’s minimal tobacco exposure and prior thoracic surgery, follow-up imaging was planned.

He presented again after an acute lower respiratory tract infection, reporting recurrent dry cough, hemoptysis, and occasional chest pain for two months. He denied fever, night sweats, weight loss, or dyspnea. CT now showed an irregular 28-mm nodule in the left lower lobe without mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy. Lung function tests revealed mild restrictive physiology (FEV1 73% predicted; TLC 74% predicted). Routine blood tests, including white-cell count and C-reactive protein, were normal. A whole-body PET-CT demonstrated intense FDG uptake in the left lower-lobe nodule, with no other areas of abnormal uptake.

A 72-year-old man presented with a 15-day history of fever, productive cough with purulent sputum, breathlessness, an evening rise of temperature, and weight loss. On examination, he had digital clubbing and crepitations over the right lower lobe. His erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated. Sputum smears and cultures for acid-fast bacilli were negative. Chest radiography showed a right lower lung opacity. Ultrasound of the chest revealed a loculated right pleural effusion. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest confirmed consolidation in the right posterior basal segment with associated effusion. He was treated empirically with intravenous piperacillin–tazobactam and clindamycin, and pleural fluid was aspirated; fluid analysis showed lymphocytosis and no malignant cells. Empirical anti-tubercular therapy was then initiated, and bronchoscopy with bronchial aspirate and bronchoalveolar lavage was performed. The aspirates were negative for acid-fast bacilli on staining and GeneXpert, and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid appeared turbid.

A 13-year-old celibate girl was referred for evaluation of a 2-month history of intermittent, spasmodic right lumbar and right iliac–region abdominal pain radiating to the right leg. Five days before presentation, the pain was accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and fever. Menarche occurred at age 11 with regular cycles complicated by dysmenorrhea, clot passage, and heavy bleeding; she also reported burning micturition during menses. She had noted a gradually enlarging abdominal mass on self‐examination. She had no relevant medical or trauma history. 

On examination, she was alert and oriented, with pallor and a palpable, tender suprapubic mass in the right lower quadrant. The remainder of the abdominal and pelvic examination was unremarkable. An ECG showed sinus tachycardia. Pelvic ultrasonography revealed a well‐defined anechoic cystic lesion measuring 10.9 × 10.0 × 11.1 cm (volume 641 cc) adjacent to the right ovary, with only a few eccentric cystic areas and no internal septations or debris; the right fallopian tube appeared edematous, deformed, and filled with free fluid medial to the lesion. A preoperative diagnosis of paraovarian cyst was made, and exploratory laparotomy was planned.

A 26-year-old man presented with a 24-hour history of palpable crepitus in the face and neck. He also reported mild chest pain on deep inspiration and throat pain. Two days earlier, all four third molars had been extracted under general anesthesia without incident and without the use of an air turbine. He smokes three cigarettes per day and has no other medical history. Postoperative instructions included ibuprofen, paracetamol, amoxicillin, and chlorhexidine mouthwash.

On examination, temperature was 37.1°C, blood pressure 120/70 mmHg, heart rate 60/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Cardiopulmonary auscultation was normal. Palpable subcutaneous crepitus was noted bilaterally over the frontal, temporal, retroauricular, jugal, and subclavicular regions; palpation was non-tender, and there was no swelling, erythema, or warmth. Submucosal crepitus was present at the site of the lower left third molar extraction, without dehiscence or signs of infection. Blood tests, including inflammatory markers, were within normal limits. The patient denied sneezing, coughing, nose blowing, or other Valsalva maneuvers since the extraction, except for a bout of anger during which he “might have performed a Valsalva maneuver” while arguing.

A 6-year-6-month–old girl was referred for a routine dental examination. Her height and weight were below the fifth percentile, with a notably short neck and mild scaphocephaly. She walked with an abnormal gait but had normal speech and no neurologic deficits. Four years earlier, laboratory evaluation had shown elevated urinary keratan sulfate levels and markedly reduced N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfate sulfatase activity in leukocyte cultures; no genetic tests were performed, and she has not received enzyme therapy. Family history was unremarkable. Dietary history revealed low daily carbohydrate intake.

On examination, she had pectus carinatum, stubby hands, kyphosis, and mild rotation of the lower extremities. Craniofacially, she had brachycephaly, a convex and biprotusive facial profile, a flat nasal bridge, a closed nasolabial angle, an apparently large mouth, and broad lips.

Intraoral findings included mixed dentition with deep caries in all primary molars, ovoid dental arches, an anterior crossbite, a mild anterior open bite, macroglossia with tongue thrusting, generalized moderate gingivitis, and a high labial frenum. Oral hygiene was poor. She exhibited thumb-sucking and mouth-breathing habits. Both temporomandibular joints were normal on clinical examination. She was anxious and had difficulty maintaining a supine position.

A 72-year-old Caucasian woman was referred for evaluation of 6 months of exertional dyspnea and a history of annual winter chest infections. She had no childhood respiratory disease, had smoked (30 pack-years) until age 47, and worked as a nursing auxiliary. She took 1 mg of prednisolone daily for polymyalgia rheumatica, with no other regular medications. She reported good exercise tolerance. Vital signs were normal, with an oxygen saturation of 95% on room air. Pulmonary function tests revealed an obstructive pattern (FEV1 1.14 L [55% predicted], FVC 2.09 L [83%], FEV1/FVC 54%).A chest radiograph obtained 2 years earlier showed increased radiolucency of the left lung. Two recent radiographs demonstrated a persistently hyperlucent left hemithorax with progressive peripheral opacification and volume loss of the right middle and lower zones. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest was obtained to evaluate persistent infections and radiographic changes. It showed a hypoplastic left pulmonary artery and attenuated peripheral pulmonary artery branches on the left, with hyperinflation, air trapping, and cystic bronchiectasis in the lingula and left lower lobe. The right lung was reduced in size and demonstrated subpleural reticulation, traction bronchiectasis, and ground-glass opacification.

A 26-year-old man with homozygous sickle cell anemia, maintained on routine follow-up and medications, presented with a 2-week history of oliguria and frothy urine, preceded by leg and facial swelling for 1 week. He reported anorexia, generalized weakness, early satiety, abdominal fullness, and nausea, without fever, vomiting, jaundice, or change in bowel habits. He noted dyspnea, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. He had a history of infrequent vaso-occlusive crises treated supportively and had received blood transfusions twice in the current illness.

On examination, he was dyspneic, afebrile, and had anasarca and pallor without cyanosis. Pulse was 108/min, regular; blood pressure was 160/90 mm Hg. Jugular venous pressure was elevated. Cardiovascular examination revealed a hyperdynamic precordium, a displaced heaving apex, an S3 gallop, and a pansystolic murmur at the apex. Pulmonary examination showed bilateral basal fine crepitations. The abdomen was distended with firm, smooth hepatomegaly and shifting dullness.

Initial laboratory studies showed urinalysis with 3+ proteinuria and no red-cell casts. Packed-cell volume was 14%; peripheral smear demonstrated hypochromia, polychromasia, anisocytosis, and fragmented cells. Serum creatinine was 645 μmol/L, urea 35 mmol/L, bicarbonate 13 mmol/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, and potassium 4.1 mmol/L. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed bilaterally shrunken kidneys, hepatomegaly, and ascites. Chest radiography showed marked cardiomegaly and pulmonary edema. Echocardiography demonstrated four-chamber dilatation and biventricular systolic dysfunction.

An 80‐year‐old man underwent ultrasound‐guided fine‐needle aspiration (FNA) of a 1.8×2.2 cm well‐defined, cystic thyroid nodule in the right lobe. Two passes were made without immediate complications. Three hours later he noted anterior neck swelling and progressive pain. Four hours after FNA he presented to the emergency department with severe respiratory distress and underwent emergency intubation. He was hemodynamically stable. His medication history was notable for long‐term anticoagulation for cardiovascular disease. Laboratory studies showed a normal platelet count and liver function, with an international normalized ratio of 1.35 (reference range, 0.85–1.15). Axial neck CT revealed a large retropharyngeal hematoma causing anterior tracheal deviation. Sagittal CT images demonstrated contrast extravasation within the hematoma, suggesting active bleeding.

A 52-year-old South Asian man presented with a 3-month history of a gradually enlarging swelling of the left cheek. On examination, there was a diffuse, firm, non-tender mass measuring about 4 × 5 cm that extended from the infraorbital region superiorly to the lip commissure inferiorly, medially obliterating the nasal ala, and laterally approaching the preauricular area. Intraoral examination revealed a well-defined vestibular swelling measuring 4 × 3 cm, extending from the distal aspect of the left canine to the second molar. Routine hematologic parameters were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck showed a mildly homogeneously enhancing soft-tissue density lesion in the left premaxillary region with adjacent bony destruction of the maxillary alveolus. Based on the clinical findings, a provisional diagnosis of malignancy of the left maxilla was made, and the differential diagnosis included benign tumor, sarcoma, lymphoma, and melanoma. An incisional biopsy suggested myositis with lymphoid hyperplasia.

A 70-year-old non-smoking Japanese woman with advanced ALK-positive lung adenocarcinoma had been receiving crizotinib (500 mg twice daily) for 60 days. She presented in mid-September 2012 with progressive dyspnea, fever, and coughing. Her temperature was 38.6 °C; blood pressure, 128/66 mm Hg; pulse rate, 92 beats/min; and respiratory rate, 23 breaths/min. Fine crackles were heard in both lower lung fields without peripheral edema. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air showed a PaO2 of 54.2 torr, PaCO2 of 35.0 torr, and pH of 7.44. Chest radiography revealed a bilateral diffuse interstitial shadow, and chest CT showed diffuse ground-glass opacities in both lungs. She produced only a small amount of mucinous sputum. Bacterial, mycological, and mycobacterial cultures of respiratory specimens were negative. The white blood cell count was 8200/μL (73% neutrophils), hemoglobin was 8.7 g/dL, and liver enzymes were within normal limits. Serum LDH was 316 IU/L; CRP, 3.76 mg/dL; KL-6, 1439 U/mL; and surfactant protein D, 225.0 ng/mL. Most autoantibodies for collagen diseases were negative, except for an ANA titer of 1:160 with a PCNA pattern. Tests for galactomannan antigen, candida antigen, influenza antigen, mycoplasma antibody, and cytomegalovirus antibody were all negative. Electrocardiography and echocardiography showed no abnormalities.

A 54-year-old man presented with a 10-day history of diffuse, dull, nonradiating abdominal pain, high-grade fever, and three to four daily episodes of bloody diarrhea. He had traveled to Pakistan and over the preceding three months noted looser, more frequent stools but no prior history of diarrhea. His medical history was notable only for hypertension; he denied diabetes, tuberculosis, smoking, or alcohol use. HIV and hepatitis B surface antigen tests were negative. 

On examination he was tachypneic (respiratory rate 35/min) with SpO2 88% on room air. The abdomen was mildly tender without a palpable mass. Hepatomegaly was noted (liver span 17 cm), and digital rectal examination revealed blood and mucus. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 24.6×10^9/L with neutrophilic predominance and mildly elevated liver-function tests. He developed acute renal impairment requiring dialysis and was transferred to the ICU for BiPAP support. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed diffuse irregular circumferential thickening of the cecum and ascending colon, significant luminal narrowing, focal air pockets along the right colonic wall suggesting a sealed perforation, collapsed distal colon, dilated small-bowel loops with multiple air-fluid levels, prominent fat stranding in the right iliac fossa, enlarged heterogeneous soft-tissue nodules in the greater omentum, and an enlarged liver (18 cm) containing two hypodense nonenhancing lesions (largest 4.6×4.4×5 cm).

A 62-year-old African American man with a history of prostate cancer presented to the emergency department after being found down in his apartment with altered mental status. One week earlier, he was in his usual state of health but had noted difficulty stepping into a car. Over the prior two months, he had complained of shoulder pain, weakness, and difficulty with dressing and bathing. Four years earlier, he had received radiation and hormone therapy for prostate cancer; his last known prostate-specific antigen level was not elevated.

On arrival, temperature was 37.1 °C, heart rate 138 bpm, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, blood pressure 151/96 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. He was oriented to person only, agitated, with a Glasgow Coma Scale of E4V5M6. Examination revealed diffuse tenderness to touch, dry mucous membranes, decreased skin turgor, ulcerated lesions on lips and tongue, a diffuse scaly macular rash, and bilateral wrist swelling with pitting edema. He was unable to lift his upper or lower extremities and had generalized proximal muscle atrophy.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 86 mm/h, C-reactive protein of 8.34 mg/dL, serum sodium 156 mmol/L, potassium 5.2 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 47 mg/dL, creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, and normal creatine phosphokinase. Rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, antinuclear antibody, and rapid plasma reagin were negative. Brain MRI was negative for acute infarction. A skin biopsy of the rash demonstrated epidermal spongiosis with eosinophilia. His mental status improved significantly with intravenous fluids. Synovial fluid aspiration from the left wrist showed leukocytosis without crystals, consistent with inflammatory arthritis.

A 4-year-5-month-old girl presented for evaluation of her bite. She had no caries lesions and normal oral soft tissues, with a full complement of deciduous teeth. On inspection, there was a unilateral posterior crossbite on the left side. When the mandible was guided into a centric position, premature occlusal contacts were noted, and the median lines met, indicating a functional shift. The maxillary arch appeared constricted transversely, resulting in end-to-end contact of the canines and occasional posterior involvement. To avoid discomfort, she habitually shifted her mandible laterally until finding a more comfortable occlusion. Evidence of dental trauma from occlusal interferences was observed on the contacting teeth. Selective occlusal wear was performed with a high-speed diamond bur under irrigation. However, these adjustments were insufficient to achieve midline centralization or eliminate the crossbite.

A 13-year-old boy with an unremarkable past medical history presented with several months of severe fatigue. Four days before admission he became progressively sleepy and developed a sudden, severe frontal stabbing headache accompanied by vomiting and phonophobia. On examination he was febrile (38 °C) with a normal level of consciousness and no focal neurologic deficits. He had no visual disturbances, and extraocular movements were intact. Linear growth and pubertal development were normal (height SDS 0.0; BMI 20 kg/m2 [+1.0 SDS]; Tanner stage G3P3A2). 

Initial laboratory studies showed a normal white blood cell count (9.2×10^9/L; 54% neutrophils), elevated C-reactive protein (201 mg/L), and hypoglycemia (2.8 mmol/L). Empirical intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics were started. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated a 2.5×2.0 cm sellar mass with suprasellar extension and slight optic chiasm compression. The lesion was heterogeneously hyperintense on T1-weighted images, hypointense to isointense on T2-weighted images, and showed rim enhancement after gadolinium; sphenoid sinus mucosal thickening was also noted. 

Endocrine testing revealed central hypothyroidism, hypocortisolism, hypogonadism, and low serum IGF-I and IGFBP-3 levels consistent with growth hormone deficiency. Stress-dose hydrocortisone was administered, followed by hydrocortisone and levothyroxine replacement. One day later, the fever resolved and C-reactive protein declined to 48 mg/L by day 4 and normalized after 2 weeks. Surgery was deferred in view of rapid clinical improvement, marked sella enlargement (unusual for abscess), and the sphenoid sinus findings. Three days after admission, diabetes insipidus developed, and oral vasopressin was initiated. The patient was discharged after five days on oral antibiotics, hydrocortisone, levothyroxine, and vasopressin.

A 25-year-old man was referred for evaluation of dark-colored urine and leg swelling. Three weeks earlier, he had presented with nausea, fatigue, anorexia, malaise, jaundice, and right upper–quadrant discomfort. At that time, his temperature was 100 °F, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, pulse 95 beats/min, and respiratory rate 16/min. Examination showed scleral icterus, dry mucous membranes, flat jugular venous pressure, decreased skin turgor, mild right upper–quadrant tenderness, and a palpable liver edge without splenomegaly; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory tests revealed total bilirubin 8 mg/dL, AST 1,020 U/L, ALT 1,750 U/L, normal alkaline phosphatase and γ-glutamyl transferase levels, and normal serum albumin. LDL cholesterol was 146 mg/dL, triglycerides 312 mg/dL, uric acid 7.8 mg/dL, and total cholesterol 190 mg/dL. Serum creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL. An anti–hepatitis E virus IgM and IgG assay was positive, and urinalysis showed specific gravity 1.030 and 1+ proteinuria. He was diagnosed with acute hepatitis E and treated supportively, with discharge after 3 days.

Two and a half weeks later, he noted bilateral lower-extremity edema and dark urine and was seen in nephrology. His blood pressure was 145/90 mmHg, pulse 70 beats/min, respiratory rate 12/min, and he was afebrile. Examination revealed 2+ pitting edema of both legs; chest, cardiac, abdominal, neurologic, and skin examinations were otherwise normal. Laboratory studies now showed serum creatinine 1.7 mg/dL, albumin 3.2 g/dL, and total cholesterol 320 mg/dL. Urinalysis revealed 15–20 RBCs per high-power field, and urine protein-to-creatinine ratio was 4.7 g/day. Tests for antinuclear antibody, antistreptolysin O, complement C3 and C4, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, and hepatitis A were negative. A real-time ultrasound-guided core kidney biopsy was performed.

A 58-year-old man was referred in February 2011 with a 6-month history of severe femoral and tibial pain (9/10), night sweats, an unexplained 6-kg weight loss, and pruritic urticarial lesions on the trunk and extremities. He had a 13-year history of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory–treated chronic ostealgia diagnosed as chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis after a bone biopsy in 1998. On referral, laboratory studies showed a CRP of 6.98 mg/dL, leukocyte count of 11.4 G/L, IL-6 of 30.6 pg/mL, and an IgM level of 596 mg/dL. Abdominal CT revealed marginal enlargement of intra-abdominal and inguinal lymph nodes. MRI of the femora, tibiae, clavicles, sacrum, pelvis, and fibulae demonstrated diffuse low-to-intermediate T1 and high STIR signal bone-marrow infiltration with cortical thickening and periosteal apposition, without adjacent soft-tissue reaction. A radiograph of the left femur showed subtle periosteal reaction along the distal lateral metaphysis. Bone biopsy of the left distal femur revealed sclerotic marrow with plasma cells, mast cells, scattered granulocytes, and histiocytes, without evidence of malignancy. Skin biopsy showed a superficial dermal and perivascular neutrophilic infiltrate.

A 78-year-old woman presented with one day of altered mental status characterized by irrelevant speech, increased talkativeness, and inability to recognize family members. She reported a two-week history of daily evening high-grade fevers associated with malaise, myalgia, and anorexia. She denied cough, abdominal pain, jaundice, diarrhea, dysuria, or rash. Her medical history included hypertension, bilateral knee osteoarthritis, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; her medications were losartan, furosemide–spironolactone, and as-needed salbutamol. She was a social drinker, non-smoker, used firewood for cooking, and had no recent travel.

On examination, her temperature was 98°F, blood pressure 140/90 mm Hg, pulse 108 beats/min, SpO2 92% on room air, and Glasgow Coma Scale score was 15/15. Neurologic examination was normal without meningeal signs. Laboratory tests showed anemia, neutrophilic leukocytosis, and elevated C-reactive protein; electrolytes were normal. A head CT scan was normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed elevated protein, normal glucose, and lymphocyte-predominant leukocytosis. CSF PCR assays for Japanese encephalitis virus, herpes simplex virus, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis were negative. Brain MRI showed chronic infarcts in the left caudate and lentiform nuclei.

She was treated empirically for subacute meningitis with intravenous ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and acyclovir. Because of persistent fever and worsening laboratory parameters, tubercular meningitis was suspected, and antitubercular therapy with adjunctive corticosteroids was initiated. The patient became afebrile the next day, and her white-cell count and C-reactive protein levels improved. She was discharged after 12 days on antitubercular therapy and a tapering course of prednisolone.

Twenty-five days later, she returned with fever of 104°F and an erythematous macular rash on her limbs and trunk. Blood tests showed anemia, neutrophilic leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, and elevated liver enzymes. She was managed symptomatically and sent home. After another month, she was readmitted with altered mentation and fever following three months of antitubercular therapy. Antitubercular therapy was held because of rising liver enzyme levels.

A 58‐year‐old man presented with a 25‐year history of postprandial epigastric pain that had been managed as peptic ulcer disease. Over the past few weeks, he developed intermittent jaundice, right upper‐quadrant abdominal pain, fever, nausea, and vomiting. He had unremarkable prior abdominal ultrasounds and no significant past medical history except remote chemical‐weapon exposure.

On examination, vital signs were stable. The epigastrium was mildly distended, and an ill‐defined mass was palpable; the remainder of the examination was normal.

Laboratory studies (24‐hour interval) showed:
• SGOT: 135 → 148 U/L  
• SGPT: 187 → 173 U/L  
• Alkaline phosphatase: 564 → 520 U/L  
• Total bilirubin: 7.8 → 7.9 mg/dL  
• Direct bilirubin: 3.4 → 3.8 mg/dL  

Plain abdominal radiographs were normal. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 5-cm ovoid cystic mass arising from the gastric lesser curvature near the antrum, extending toward the portal vein. Color Doppler sonography of the hepatic arteries and portal vein, performed to assess for cholangiocarcinoma or pancreatic adenocarcinoma, showed reduced arterial flow without evidence of any intraluminal lesion. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a 70×30×35 mm fluid‐density mass with thin wall calcifications posterior to the gastric antrum and pylorus; the pancreas and other adjacent organs appeared normal.

A 41-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of insidious, progressive uncoordinated walking and, over the past year, intermittent occipital headache and effortful, unclear speech. He had no history of smoking, alcohol use, toxin exposure, significant past illness, or medication use. He reported that two of his siblings had similar gait problems, whereas his parents and his sister’s children were unaffected.

On examination, he was alert and oriented, with normal vital signs. There was no pallor, icterus, cyanosis, clubbing, lymphadenopathy, or edema. Neurologic examination showed hypotonic limbs with full strength, normal sensation, and intact cranial nerves. Cerebellar signs included scanning speech, horizontal nystagmus, dysmetria on finger-nose testing, dyssynergia on heel-knee testing, dysdiadochokinesia, positive rebound, broad-based gait, and impaired tandem walking. Deep-tendon reflexes were diminished to 1+ in the upper limbs and 2+ in the lower limbs, with pendular responses.

Noncontrast CT of the brain demonstrated marked cerebellar atrophy with prominent folia and widened surrounding cerebrospinal fluid spaces.

A 59-year-old white man with a history of depression and alcohol abuse was found unconscious in the woods and brought to the emergency department intubated for altered mentation. He lived alone in a cabin. Home medications included dexlansoprazole, venlafaxine, amitriptyline, hydroxyzine, sulfasalazine, and topical triamcinolone; no allergies were known. On arrival his temperature was 103.5 °F, heart rate 101 beats/min, and blood pressure 97/66 mmHg. An electrocardiogram showed a QRS duration of 104 ms. Urine toxicology was positive for amitriptyline, venlafaxine, and ketamine; serum alcohol, acetaminophen, and salicylate levels were undetectable. Laboratory studies revealed WBC count 3.6 × 10^3/µl, platelet count 71 × 10^3/µl, INR 4.6, AST 85 U/l, and ALT 42 U/l. CT scans of the head, abdomen, and pelvis were unremarkable; CT of the chest showed basilar consolidations. A lumbar puncture demonstrated CSF WBC count 28 × 10^3/µl, glucose 60 mg/dl, and protein > 600 mg/dl.

A previously healthy 3-year-old Caucasian boy presented with a 4-month history of intensely pruritic erythematous papules and plaques on the upper and central trunk and upper extremities. The lesions failed to clear after a 3-month course of topical corticosteroids. A clinical diagnosis of scabies was made 3 weeks earlier, and symptoms worsened after application of permethrin cream 5%, suggesting a hypersensitivity reaction. The rash did not improve with topical pimecrolimus cream 1%. On examination, there were erythematous papules and plaques in a V-shaped distribution on the chest and back, with papular eruptions on the upper arms and thighs, sparing the palms, axillae, soles, and lower extremities. A skin biopsy from the back showed a neutrophilic infiltrate within and surrounding the eccrine ducts, with sparing of the coiled secretory glands.

A 57-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of sharp, burning right heel pain that radiated laterally, worsened with walking, and improved with rest. There was no relevant medical or family history. She had undergone shoe and activity modification, stretching, physiotherapy, and NSAIDs without relief. On examination, the skin over the heel was normal; foot arches and alignment were normal, and range of motion was painless. Palpation revealed tenderness in the middle of the heel that radiated laterally. The Achilles tendon was intact and non-tender. Plain radiographs were inconclusive. 

MRI of the right ankle was performed. Imaging showed a prominent plantar calcaneal enthesophyte with a mildly thickened and hyperintense plantar fascia measuring approximately 5 mm adjacent to the calcaneal spur, and significant heel fat-pad edema. There was marked atrophy with near-complete fatty replacement of the abductor digiti minimi muscle on axial T1 and PD-fat-saturated sequences. A partial tear of the Achilles tendon was noted approximately 5 cm proximal to its insertion, with multiple intra-tendinous osseous bodies.

A 63-year-old man presented with acute onset of severe right shoulder pain, stiffness, localized warmth, and erythema around his arthroscopic portal scars. Nine months earlier, he had sustained a fall on his right shoulder, and magnetic resonance arthrography at that time showed full-thickness tears of the subscapularis (Lafosse stage 3), supraspinatus (Patte stage 2), and anterior infraspinatus (Patte stage 2), with biceps-long-head dislocation and acromioclavicular osteoarthritis. In June 2021, he underwent arthroscopic rotator cuff repair (triple-row technique for the supraspinatus and infraspinatus, single-row for the subscapularis), biceps tenodesis, synovectomy, subacromial decompression, acromioplasty, and distal clavicle resection. Seven bioresorbable PLGA/β-TCP anchors were placed. His postoperative course was unremarkable: at six weeks he was pain free, and by six months he had restored full range of motion and excellent strength.

In January 2022, he developed SARS-CoV-2 infection. Concurrently, he noted painful erythematous patches on his right hand, foot, and leg, and acute shoulder discomfort. On examination in March 2022, his shoulder showed decreased range of motion, warmth, and erythema around the arthroscopic portals, with painful rotator cuff testing but preserved strength compared to prior exams. Laboratory tests revealed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 69 mm/hr, C-reactive protein of 13 mg/L, and a white-cell count of 10.26×10^9/L without a left shift. He was treated with NSAIDs, but three weeks later the pain persisted, and repeat labs showed a CRP of 41 mg/L and a white-cell count of 9.4×10^9/L. An arthro-MRI demonstrated intact rotator cuff repairs, marked intra-articular synovitis, subacromial bursitis, and humeral osteitis.

A 49-year-old Japanese woman with a 6-year history of Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada disease (VKHD), previously treated with high-dose corticosteroids and topical drops, presented with new sensory disturbances. One month earlier, she underwent dental treatment of her left lower molar, after which she developed a persistent dysesthesia around her left cheek that spread to the left half of her face. Similar dysesthesia appeared in her left ring and little fingers, later extending to the ulnar side of her forearm. Her ophthalmic findings remained stable, and she was referred for further evaluation.

Her past medical history was notable only for VKHD. There was no family history of collagen disease or neuropathy. On examination, blood pressure was 107/65 mm Hg, heart rate 76 bpm, and temperature 36.0 °C. Multiple small subcutaneous nodules were palpated on her trunk and extremities. Neurologically, her right eye was blind, and best corrected visual acuity in the left eye was 0.08. Dysesthesia and decreased sensation were present on the left face (trigeminal distribution), the ulnar side of the left forearm (medial antebrachial cutaneous distribution), and the ulnar aspects of the left ring and little fingers. Motor strength, cerebellar function, and autonomic examination were normal.

Laboratory tests showed serum calcium 9.4 mg/dL (normal 9–11), angiotensin-converting enzyme 43.7 U/L (normal 8.3–21.4), lysozyme 25.4 µg/mL (normal 5–10.2), and soluble interleukin-2 receptor 4380 U/mL (normal 145–519). Anti-DNA, rheumatoid factor, anti-Ro/SSA, anti-La/SSB, anti-thyroglobulin, anti-thyroid peroxidase, myeloperoxidase-ANCA, and proteinase 3-ANCA were all negative. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed 3 cells/3 µL (100% mononuclear), protein 35 mg/dL, and glucose 51 mg/dL. HLA typing: B46, B48, DR8, DR15. Nerve conduction studies were unremarkable. Chest radiography showed no obvious hilar lymphadenopathy, but chest CT demonstrated enlargement of mediastinal lymph nodes. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the head and cervical spine showed no inflammatory lesions. A biopsy of a subcutaneous nodule on the right arm was performed.

A 29-year-old woman, with no significant past medical history, was referred for evaluation of multiple intra-abdominal cystic lesions. She reported no acute abdominal pain, weight loss, or fever. On examination her abdomen was soft, with an epigastric fluctuant area; otherwise the physical and systemic examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed mildly abnormal liver function tests and “a strongly positive hydatid serology.” Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated “a hydatid cyst of segment III of the liver fistulized in the subcutaneous soft tissues measuring 4.19 × 1.98 cm and continued with another formation measuring 3 × 2 cm.” Contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT revealed “multiple hepatic, splenic and peritoneal cystic formations, of which one of the hepatic lesions is fistulized to the wall, the most voluminous being pelvic (40 × 43 mm), and a cystic umbilical formation (13 × 10 mm), with the main biliary tract containing dense material with upstream dilatation of 10 mm of hydatid origin, with the presence of aerobilia suggestive of a bilio-digestive fistula.”

A 1-year-old girl was brought with sudden onset of hematemesis; the vomitus resembled coffee grounds. She was born full-term, had no significant medical or family history, no allergies, and no medication use, including NSAIDs. On arrival she was lethargic; temperature 36.8 °C, heart rate 160 bpm, respiratory rate 24 bpm, blood pressure 83/35 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 100% on 2 L nasal oxygen. Physical examination showed pallor but was otherwise unremarkable. A nasogastric tube aspirated a small amount of blood. Laboratory tests revealed WBC 9,500/μL; hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL; platelets 220×10^3/μL; CRP 0.55 mg/dL; normal liver function tests; prothrombin time 13.2 s (INR 1.01); aPTT 31.7 s; normal factor XIII and plasma gastrin levels; ESR 2 mm/h. Serologies for cytomegalovirus-IgM, EBV-VCA-IgM, and H. pylori-IgG were negative, and stool antigen testing excluded H. pylori. Blood cultures and stool parasite testing were negative. Abdominal radiography and ultrasonography were normal, and contrast-enhanced CT showed no active bleeding. She received two units of packed red blood cells and famotidine, yet her hemoglobin remained low. Thus, on hospital day 2, early upper endoscopy was planned to identify the bleeding source.

A male infant was born at 40 weeks’ gestation to a 22-year-old primiparous mother after an uneventful pregnancy, except for relatively reduced abdominal enlargement and fewer perceived fetal movements. The parents are first cousins. Delivery was by spontaneous vaginal birth. Birth weight was 2.2 kg, length 46 cm, and head circumference 32 cm (all < third percentile). 

On examination, the neonate had:
· Prominent forehead with dilated scalp veins  
· Widely spaced eyes with downslanting palpebral fissures  
· Broad flat nasal bridge and a pronounced philtrum  
· Bilateral large, low-set ears each with a preauricular pit  
· High-arched palate and micrognathia  
· A small penis (1.5 cm) with both testes fully descended  

Echocardiography showed a moderately large subaortic ventricular septal defect. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed absence of the right kidney. Hearing assessment demonstrated mild sensorineural hearing loss. Ophthalmologic examination was unremarkable.

A 58-year-old Middle Eastern woman presented with progressive left radicular pain extending to the hip, the lateral posterior thigh, leg, and lateral toes, accompanied by lumbar back pain rated 10/10 for 1 month. She had difficulty walking and denied trauma. Her history was notable for two prior episodes of right-sided lumbar radicular pain in 2018 and 2020, each lasting about 3 months and resolving with painkillers; both prior lumbar MRIs were reported as normal.

On examination, lower-limb strength, tone, and tendon reflexes were normal, and the Lasègue test was highly positive on the left. Lumbar magnetic resonance imaging revealed an extradural cystic lesion in the L5–S1 spinal canal adjacent to the left facet joint, hypointense on T1-weighted images and slightly hyperintense on T2-weighted images.

A 55-year-old woman with hypertension and a history of smoking presented with chest pain and was found to have an anterior wall ST-elevation myocardial infarction. She underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention 1 hour 45 minutes after symptom onset, with successful recanalization of the mid–left anterior descending artery. Initial transthoracic echocardiography showed an LVEF of 30%, akinesia of the anterior, septal, and apical walls, and a small pericardial effusion. She was treated for heart failure (Killip class II) and epistenocardiac pericarditis and discharged on aspirin, ticagrelor, ramipril, bisoprolol, ivabradine, furosemide, spironolactone, and statin/ezetimibe.

Two days after discharge, she was readmitted with worsening heart failure symptoms and pleuritic chest pain. Echocardiography revealed an apical thrombus, a small circumferential pericardial effusion, and worsening LV dilation and dysfunction (LVEF 28%). She was started on warfarin plus dual antiplatelet therapy. Seventeen days later, repeat TTE showed further LV dilation (indexed volume 85 ml/m^2), LVEF 28%, an apical aneurysm with organized thrombus, and a small pericardial effusion. One week later as an outpatient, she remained in NYHA class III.

A subsequent TTE demonstrated a significant increase in LV indexed volume to 102 ml/m^2, LVEF 21%, a small pericardial effusion, and apical dyskinesia with a very thin wall. In the apical 4-chamber view, a 42×5 mm linear structure was attached to the endocardial border of the apical segments, raising concern for aneurysm versus pseudoaneurysm.  
Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed extensive anterior myocardial necrosis, severely depressed LV function (LVEF 25%), and findings interpreted as rupture at the mid-distal interventricular septum without a visible communication to the right ventricle, “compatible with a large apical pseudoaneurysm.”

A 50-year-old man with a 2-year history of altered stool form, previously labeled as irritable bowel syndrome, presented with recent dull upper and mid–abdominal pain, occasional hiccups, and sour regurgitation. On examination, he had epigastric tenderness on palpation. A C14 breath test was positive for Helicobacter pylori. Gastroscopy showed congested, oedematous mucosa in the gastric antrum with predominantly white, punctate erosions, and a 5×10 mm ulcer in the duodenal bulb surrounded by congestion, oedema, and smudgy exudate. Biopsy of the whitish gastric antral mucosa was performed. 

Histopathology revealed chronic inflammatory infiltrates in the lamina propria and numerous cytoplasm-rich, nucleus-displaced, signet ring–like cells (5–13 μm) containing a basophilic, mucus-like substance, distributed in focal or lamellar clusters. H. pylori organisms were seen as short thin rods in superficial pits. 

Immunohistochemical studies on the signet ring–like cells showed:  
• Cytokeratin (CK): negative  
• PAS and D-PAS: negative  
• Leukocyte common antigen (LCA), MUM1: strongly positive  
• CD79a: strongly positive  
• CD138: positive  
• Kappa light chain: strongly positive  
• Lambda light chain: positive  
• CD20, Bcl-2, Bcl-6, CD163, CDX2, CEA, CK20, CK7, CD5, ALK, CD3, CD56, cyclin D1, SOX-11: negative  
• Ki-67 proliferation index: approximately 1%

A 61-year-old man (weight, 50 kg) with a history of chronic alcoholism and 50 h of abstinence was scheduled for open reduction and internal fixation of a left intertrochanteric femur fracture under regional anesthesia. Physical examination was unremarkable; laboratory studies showed mild elevation of liver enzymes. He received aspiration prophylaxis, prophylactic intravenous multivitamins, and oral lorazepam (2 mg at bedtime and 2 h before surgery). In the block room, standard monitors were applied and a left fascia iliaca compartmental block was performed with 30 mL of 0.25% bupivacaine via landmark technique. Thirty minutes later, spinal anesthesia was administered with 2.5 mL of 0.5% hyperbaric bupivacaine and fentanyl (20 µg). After positioning on the operating table, midazolam (2 mg IV) was given. Twenty minutes after the surgical incision, he became agitated, was talking irrelevantly, and was noted to be confused and disoriented; he developed tachycardia, hypertension, and tremors. Airway patency was maintained, and oxygen was administered by face mask. Boluses of midazolam (total, 10 mg) were given, and an esmolol infusion was started for hypertension and tachycardia. Because of persistent agitation, propofol infusion was initiated and maintained at 50 µg/kg/min, after which the patient became sedated with stable vital signs, and the surgery was continued.

A 3-day-old female Asian neonate was referred for absence of the right eyelid. She was born at term via cesarean delivery to a 23-year-old primigravida; there was no consanguinity. Pregnancy was notable for mild oligohydramnios, maternal hyperglycemia at 6–7 months, and a single cord loop at 33 weeks; there were no infections, teratogen exposures, or family history of ocular anomalies. Birth weight was 3416 g; the neonate cried at birth but required 2 days in the NICU for respiratory support.

On examination, the right eye lacked the eyelid, eyebrow, and eyelashes; the left eye was normal. Head circumference, anterior fontanelle, nasal bridge, and systemic examination were unremarkable. B-scan ultrasonography of the right eye showed absence of a posterior chamber and membranous lens, a shallow anterior chamber, and posterior staphyloma; the left eye had normal anterior and posterior chambers. Chest radiography was normal. Renal ultrasonography revealed mild right hydronephrosis and irregular bladder walls.

A 12-year-old girl presented with bilateral ankle pain and recurrent ankle sprains. She reported right ankle pain on both the medial and lateral sides for more than three years and difficulty walking on uneven ground. On examination, there was tenderness over the medial and lateral aspects of both ankle joints, and anterior drawer as well as inversion and eversion stress tests were limited by pain. Standing anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the feet showed bilateral multiple tarsal coalitions, including talonavicular and talocalcaneal coalitions. The American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society (AOFAS) score was 61, and the Oxford Ankle Foot Questionnaire for Children (OxAFQ-C) score was 26. The talonavicular coalition was a synostosis on the right and a synchondrosis or syndesmosis on the left. A C-sign suggestive of talocalcaneal coalition was evident on both sides, although the patient denied pain in the talonavicular regions and there was no tenderness over those joints. Magnetic resonance imaging, performed to evaluate for ligament injury, demonstrated intact anterior talofibular and calcaneofibular ligaments and fibrocartilaginous talocalcaneal coalitions bilaterally. With a provisional diagnosis of talocalcaneal coalition, conservative treatment with activity modification, anti-inflammatory medication, and physical therapy was undertaken for three months. However, the conservative treatment failed.

A 72-year-old Japanese woman was admitted with palpitations and dyspnea of 1 month’s duration and diarrhea for 1 week. Her history was notable for Sjögren syndrome; she had no known endocrine or hepatobiliary disease, allergies, or significant alcohol use. On examination she was tachypneic with orthopnea and diaphoresis; she had a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland, an irregular cardiac rhythm, and bilateral pitting edema of the lower limbs. Laboratory studies showed thyrotropin <0.003 µIU/mL, free triiodothyronine 13.5 pg/mL, free thyroxine 4.17 ng/dL, TSH-receptor antibody 27.9 U/L, thyroglobulin antibody 85.0 IU/mL, thyroperoxidase antibody >600 IU/mL, and brain natriuretic peptide 617.4 pg/mL. Thyroid ultrasonography showed diffuse enlargement with increased blood flow. Chest radiography revealed bilateral pleural effusions. Electrocardiography demonstrated paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and echocardiography showed impaired left ventricular systolic function.

She was diagnosed with Graves’ disease and started on methimazole (15 mg daily) and potassium iodide (50 mg daily), with concurrent treatment for atrial fibrillation and heart failure. Her thyroid hormone levels gradually declined.

On hospital day 12, she developed fever to 38.3 °C, acute periumbilical abdominal pain, nausea, and diarrhea. Initial labs showed C-reactive protein 0.98 mg/dL and a normal serum amylase (76 U/L). Abdominal plain CT demonstrated a relatively high-density area in fat tissues adjacent to an ascending colonic diverticulum; therefore, diverticulitis was suspected. Empirical cefmetazole did not ameliorate her fever or pain, and blood cultures were negative. On hospital day 16, serum amylase rose to 212 U/L, lipase to 923 U/L, elastase-1 to 1537 ng/dL, and CRP to 9.97 mg/dL, although contrast-enhanced CT showed no pancreatic abnormalities. Her BISAP score was 1.

Further evaluation revealed no history of alcohol abuse (triglycerides 68 mg/dL), normocalcemia (corrected calcium 9.8 mg/dL), and an immunoglobulin G4 level of 114 mg/dL (below the threshold for autoimmune pancreatitis). Abdominal imaging and normal hepatic enzymes, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin levels excluded cholelithiasis, biliary sludge, biliary dilatation, and choledocholithiasis.

A 47-year-old man with chronic pancreatitis secondary to alcohol excess and multiple pancreatic pseudocysts presented with acute epigastric abdominal pain. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a 3.8 cm expansile lesion at the pancreatic tail with peripheral low density and a centrally enhancing component of 1.3 cm; this component was slightly hypodense to the splenic artery in the arterial phase and slightly hyperdense on delayed phase images, raising the suspicion of a splenic artery pseudoaneurysm. He was transferred for angiography, which demonstrated no evidence of pseudoaneurysm or active hemorrhage. The patient was discharged with plans for repeat imaging in one month. On re-admission, triple-phase CT showed that the lesion had increased to 5.3 cm with the central component now measuring 2.6 cm; it remained hypodense relative to the splenic artery on arterial phase images and isodense to the portal vein on delayed phase images. Given the prior negative angiography, this finding created diagnostic uncertainty: the venous-phase enhancement suggested either a splenic vein aneurysm or a narrow-necked splenic artery pseudoaneurysm with delayed filling.

A 44-year-old Hispanic man with no significant medical history presented with progressive pain, a sensation of heaviness, and difficulty walking due to swelling of his left thigh. At age 19, he had sustained blunt trauma in a four-track vehicle accident and had been diagnosed with a left-thigh hematoma, which had been drained at that time. Twenty-five years later, he noted gradual onset of left-thigh swelling. On ultrasound, there was a lobulated hypoechoic fluid collection without internal vascularity in the left lateral thigh. MRI demonstrated a well-defined lesion between the fascia and subcutaneous fat of the left lateral thigh, with centrally hyperintense signal suggestive of proteinaceous fluid, heterogeneous nodular components, and a hypointense peripheral rim. He underwent open biopsy and drainage; the specimen contained pleomorphic eosinophilic material with inflammatory cells and proteinaceous debris, and both Gram stain and cultures were negative. One month later, he developed erythema, swelling, and pain at the surgical site and underwent a second surgical drainage for what was thought to be an infected seroma, followed by a 10-day course of intravenous antibiotics. Two months after that intervention, he continued to experience left-thigh pain and recurrent swelling. On referral to the plastic surgery clinic, examination revealed a round, soft, tender, yellowish mass projecting from the left lateral thigh with serous drainage.

A 26-year-old woman, gravida 5 at 27 weeks of gestation, presented with a two-week history of widespread pustular skin lesions. She had a two-year history of psoriasis vulgaris managed with topical steroids and no other medical conditions or relevant family history. She reported fever and fatigue; on examination, her temperature was elevated, pulse was 110 beats per minute, and blood pressure was normal. Dermatologic examination revealed numerous pustules on erythematous plaques clustering on the back, arms, and legs; the oral mucosa was uninvolved, and there was no arthralgia.

A punch biopsy of a lesion showed neutrophilic subcorneal pustules consistent with spongiform pustules. Serological tests for hepatitis B and C and HIV were negative. Gram staining and bacterial cultures of pustules, blood, and urine were all negative. Obstetric ultrasonography demonstrated a single fetus with no structural abnormalities and normal amniotic fluid volume. Routine laboratory studies revealed anemia, mild leukocytosis, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 55 mm/h (reference range 20 mm/h), and a C-reactive protein level of 20.8 mg/L (reference range ≤6 mg/L).

A 60-year-old Caucasian woman with stage 5 chronic kidney disease presented with a 7-day history of heaviness and pain in the medial aspect of her left thigh. She denied fever, chills, or rigors. Her medical history included coronary artery disease, hypertension, well-controlled type II diabetes mellitus (HbA1C 5.6% six months earlier), and chronic kidney disease stage 5 (GFR 12 mL/min/1.73 m²). Medications were pioglitazone, furosemide, atenolol, lovastatin, lisinopril, isosorbide mononitrate, and metolazone. On examination, there was tenderness of the left thigh without edema or erythema; peripheral pulses were palpable bilaterally. A Doppler ultrasound of the lower extremities was negative for deep vein thrombosis. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 13.1×10³/mm³, hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL, BUN 52 mmol/L, creatinine 4.7 mmol/L (baseline ∼5.0 mmol/L), calcium 10.4 mg/dL, albumin 2.2 g/dL, phosphorus 8.0 mg/dL, and PTH 2138 pg/mL (1381 pg/mL six months earlier). On hospital day 5, she developed peridermal necrotic areas with erythema and tenderness on the thigh. She was started on vancomycin for presumed cellulitis. However, the absence of fever and the markedly elevated PTH level prompted consideration of other causes. An x-ray of the thigh demonstrated extensive vascular calcifications.

A 45-year-old woman was admitted with decompensated heart failure. Her history included:
• Postnatal cardiomegaly and a ventricular septal defect with a 40% left-to-right shunt.  
• At age 13, psychomotor developmental delay; at age 19, hypergonadotropic hypogonadism treated with oestradiol and norethisterone.  
• At age 31, despite exertional fatigue, myalgias, arthralgias, and a positive Sokolow index on ECG, transthoracic echocardiography was normal.  
• No family history of cardiac or other relevant disease; parents are unrelated.  

Current symptoms developed over weeks and included thoracic tightness, dyspnoea on exertion, orthopnoea, rapid fatigability, ankle and eyelid oedema, and unproductive cough. Examination:
• Blood pressure 106/79 mmHg; pulse 90/min regular with frequent extrasystoles.  
• 2/6 band-shaped systolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla.  
• Signs of decompensation: jugular venous distension, ankle oedema, cool extremities; breath sounds diminished at bases without crackles.  
• Respiratory rate 24/min; SpO2 86% on room air.  
• Weight 49.3 kg; height 167 cm; BMI 17.6 kg/m2.  
• Slight blepharoptosis, right convex thoracic scoliosis, hyperkyphosis; absent breast tissue; sparse axillary and pubic hair.  
• Montreal Cognitive Assessment score 22/30, with language and memory impairment.

Laboratory findings:
• High-sensitivity troponin I 57.4 ng/L (normal <19).  
• NT-proBNP 5406 pg/mL (normal <450).

Echocardiography:
• Dilated left ventricle (LVEDD 6.3 cm; LV mass index 102 g/m2; relative wall thickness 0.16).  
• Severely reduced LVEF 25% (Simpson biplane); global longitudinal strain –7%.  
• Normal right ventricle size and function; enlarged left atrium (LAVI 41 mL/m2).  
• Moderate to severe secondary mitral regurgitation; severe pulmonary hypertension (RV–RA gradient 50 mmHg; estimated RA pressure ~15 mmHg).

Electrocardiogram:
• Complete left bundle branch block with low-voltage QRS complexes; no voltage criteria for LV hypertrophy.

Pelvic ultrasound:
• Antivertic uterus; ovaries not visualized.

Thus, she presented with a triad of:
1. Severe dilated cardiomyopathy (unknown aetiology)  
2. Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism on hormone substitution  
3. Intellectual disability

A 19‐year‐old man with a 2‐month history of ulcerative colitis maintained on mesalamine presents with 2 weeks of bloody stools, fatigue, and unintentional weight loss. He denies fever, chills, chest pain, shortness of breath, cough, abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting. On admission he is hemodynamically stable. Physical examination reveals conjunctival pallor; the remainder of the exam is unremarkable.

Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin level of 9.3 g/dL (baseline), a white‐cell count of 10 600/μL, and normal serum lipase, AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin levels. Stool studies are negative for common diarrheal pathogens. Abdominal CT demonstrates diffuse thickening of the colon; incidentally, multiple ill‐defined nodules are noted at the lung bases. He receives intravenous fluids and broad‐spectrum antibiotics.

Flexible sigmoidoscopy the following day confirms pancolitis. Dedicated thoracic CT reveals bilateral cavitating pulmonary nodules ranging from 0.2 to 1.6 cm. An infectious workup, including blood cultures, an interferon‐gamma release assay for tuberculosis, urine histoplasma antigen, serum cryptococcal antigen, blastomyces antibody, coccidioides antibody, and HIV testing, is negative. Rheumatologic studies are notable for a homogeneous‐pattern ANA titer of 1:250, positive Scl‐70 antibodies, anticentromere antibodies, and ANCA; however, he does not fulfill criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus or scleroderma, and these markers are attributed to his ulcerative colitis flare.

A 58-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of a progressive, expanding erythematous plaque on the central chest with mild pruritus. Her medical history was notable for invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast treated with lumpectomy, trastuzumab-based chemotherapy, and radiation (completed 2015) and for autoimmune thyroiditis on levothyroxine. She denied nipple pain or discharge, joint pain, fevers, or other systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a single well-demarcated erythematous plaque on the chest; there were no palpable masses or lymphadenopathy. She resides in a Lyme disease–endemic region. A 4-mm punch biopsy was performed, and serologic studies for Lyme disease were ordered. Histologic sections showed a diffuse interstitial granulomatous infiltrate predominantly composed of histiocytes throughout the dermis and superficial subcutis, an associated perivascular lymphoplasmacytic component with rare eosinophils, and increased CD68-positive histiocytes.

A previously healthy 5-year-old boy had a flu-like illness two months before presentation. After three weeks of worsening headache and nausea, he underwent evaluation at a local hospital. Routine blood tests, a neurologic examination, and an ophthalmologic examination were normal. Brain MRI showed distension of both perioptic nerve sheaths, mild posterior scleral flattening, and slight intraocular protrusion of the optic nerves. Lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 39 cm H₂O and a cerebrospinal fluid white cell count of 10 cells/mm³ (2 polymorphonuclear cells, 8 mononuclear cells). He was diagnosed with idiopathic intracranial hypertension without papilledema and started on acetazolamide at 25 mg/kg/day.

One month later, he deteriorated acutely over 24 hours, becoming encephalopathic with worsening headache, nausea, and impaired vision. Visual acuity was 0.1 in the right eye and light perception only in the left eye, with stage 5 papilledema bilaterally. Repeat lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure >50 cm H₂O. A head CT scan demonstrated signs of increased intracranial pressure. He was transferred to a tertiary pediatric center, where brain MRI revealed multiple bilateral subcortical hyperintense lesions on FLAIR images, predominantly in the parietal and occipital lobes; incomplete ring or nodular enhancement of several lesions on T1 post-gadolinium images; and bilateral optic nerve head protrusion into the globes with diffuse contrast enhancement.

A 35-year-old Caucasian woman with a history of atopic diathesis including bronchial asthma and relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis presented for evaluation of chronic respiratory discomfort and recurrent coughing that worsened in autumn. She reported poor asthma control despite inhaled corticosteroids combined with a long-acting β2-agonist, short-acting β2-agonist nebulization as needed, and a recent course of prednisolone; her asthma control test score was 8 points (target ≥19), indicating poorly controlled disease. Spirometry showed stable static and dynamic flow values with slight obstruction, and there were no signs of acute infection. Her multiple sclerosis—managed with dimethyl fumarate and glatiramer acetate—had caused two relapses over 9 years, leaving mild hypoesthesia, gait disturbance, and chronic fatigue. On examination, she was in good condition (BMI 21 kg/m2), with vesicular breath sounds, no rales, no cardiac murmurs, and no digital clubbing. Laboratory testing revealed a hypereosinophilia (0.27 G/L) and persistent hypoxemia (PaO2 67 mmHg on room air, 72 mmHg on 3 L O2) that did not correct with rest or exertion; B-type natriuretic peptide levels were normal. Given the unexplained hypoxemia, further diagnostic evaluation was undertaken.

A 17-year-old girl was admitted with recurrent abdominal cramps, nausea, and vomiting. She had several prior hospitalizations and two diagnostic laparoscopies for similar symptoms. Her medical history included allergic rhinitis and neurodermatitis, without known food allergies. Initial laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 13,300/μL with 58% eosinophils and a C-reactive protein level of 5.2 mg/L. Laparoscopy had revealed large‐volume ascites and enlarged intraabdominal lymph nodes, and a single PCR assay of ascitic fluid was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA, leading to initiation of rifampin, isoniazid, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide. After six months of antitubercular therapy, her symptoms persisted.

On readmission (while still taking rifampin and isoniazid), her temperature was 37.8 °C, and physical examination showed diffuse abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 13,100/μL with 53% eosinophils, total IgE of 1870 kU/L, and CRP of 32 mg/L. Autoimmune serologies were negative. Abdominal ultrasound and CT scanning demonstrated moderate ascites and circumferential thickening of the lower esophagus, stomach, and small and large bowel walls. She developed severe abdominal pain requiring opioid analgesia. An iliac-crest bone marrow biopsy showed greater than 40% eosinophils without dysplasia or leukemia. Analysis of ascitic fluid again revealed a high eosinophil count. Blood tests, stool cultures, and ova and parasite examinations were negative. Upper- and lower-gastrointestinal endoscopy showed grossly normal mucosa.

A 26-year-old Caucasian woman was referred for evaluation of recurrent broad complex extrasystoles and nonsustained wide-complex tachycardia. She first experienced palpitations at age 12 and had an exercise-related syncope while jumping on a trampoline. Initial transthoracic echocardiography revealed a structurally normal heart; resting ECG showed polymorphic wide complex extrasystoles. She was started on beta-blockers, which were later discontinued because of persistent palpitations. At age 20, she had another syncope while standing, without further workup.

In February 2022, outpatient evaluation for reduced exercise tolerance following symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection again revealed wide complex extrasystoles and nonsustained wide complex tachycardia with varying QRS axes, prompting referral. Family history was negative for sudden or unexplained death. Physical examination was normal aside from frequent extra beats; vital signs and body habitus were within normal limits.

Surface ECG showed sinus rhythm with left posterior fascicular block and frequent supraventricular extrasystoles characterized by monophasic negative P-waves in leads II, III, and aVF and monophasic positive P-waves in lead V1. During treadmill testing, narrow and wide complex extrasystoles increased at 50 W, and at 100 W (heart rate 153 bpm) testing was halted due to recurrent polymorphic wide complex extrasystoles and couplets displaying both left bundle branch block and right bundle branch block morphologies.

A 24-hour Holter monitoring demonstrated marked rhythm instability with frequent narrow and wide complex extrasystoles; the predominant wide complexes again had either left bundle branch block or right bundle branch block morphology, and there were ten nonsustained wide complex tachycardias (maximum heart rate 185 bpm, duration up to nine beats). Transthoracic echocardiography and cardiac MRI excluded structural heart disease and myocarditis. Beta-blocker therapy was resumed, and exercise was temporarily restricted. 

To further evaluate for catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, beta-blockers were withheld and an intravenous epinephrine infusion was administered, after which there was an increase in both supraventricular extrasystoles and polymorphic wide complex extrasystoles/couplets with left or right bundle branch block morphologies; some ectopic complexes with right bundle branch block morphology exhibited atypical fascicular block.

A 24-year-old virgin Persian woman presented with a labial mass that had appeared at age 12 and grown gradually in size but remained painless until recent discomfort with standing and sitting. She had no underlying disease, regular menstrual cycles since menarche at age 11, and no family history of breast or gynecologic cancer. On examination, there was a pedunculated 75 × 44 mm mass on the upper left labium major resembling a penis; its texture was soft, skin temperature normal, and it had clear boundaries without ulceration. There was no relation of lesion growth to her menstrual cycle, and no lymphadenopathy was noted. Vital signs were normal. Ultrasonography of the lesion showed a hyperechoic mass with clearly defined margins, internal echoes, and fibroglandular tissue measuring 70 × 40 mm. Pelvic ultrasound demonstrated a normal uterus and ovaries. Blood, urine, and serologic tests were unremarkable.

A 45-year-old woman with a history of iron deficiency anemia and schizophrenia presented after sudden loss of consciousness while walking. She sustained a 1-inch full-thickness occipital laceration and was witnessed to have a tonic-clonic seizure of unknown duration. She was not on any medications at the time of the event and denied prior seizures, dizziness, or visual changes. On arrival, her blood pressure was 139/80 mmHg, pulse 80/min, respiratory rate 17/min, and SpO₂ 98% on room air. There was no tongue biting or fecal or urinary incontinence. Neurologic examination revealed an alert, fully oriented patient with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15, intact sensation, normal motor strength and reflexes, and no gait or coordination deficits.
