Initial laboratory studies showed: serum calcium 5.0 mg/dL, ionized calcium 3.1 mg/dL, intact parathyroid hormone 9.4 pg/mL, phosphorus 6 mg/dL, vitamin D 25-OH 17.7 ng/mL; hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, ferritin 9 ng/mL, serum iron 13 μg/dL, total iron-binding capacity 292 μg/dL, transferrin saturation 4%. Toxicology screen was positive for cannabinoids only. Electroencephalography was unremarkable. Cervical spine CT was normal. Chest and pelvic radiographs showed no acute osseous abnormalities. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated an ejection fraction of 55–60% with normal left ventricular systolic function, and ECG showed diffuse T-wave inversions without acute events on telemetry. The patient was admitted for management of hypocalcemia and anemia.

A 53-year-old woman presented with several months of increasing swelling and pain in her right breast. She had no other symptoms and an unremarkable medical history. On examination, the right breast was enlarged, tender over the upper outer quadrant, with erythematous skin thickening and peau d’orange changes; there was no nipple retraction or arm lymphedema. A 5 × 6 cm hard, fixed mass in the right axilla suggested pathologic lymphadenopathy. Initial blood tests, including complete blood count, inflammatory markers, and hormone levels (TSH, FSH, LH, testosterone, 17β-estradiol), were all within normal limits, with no peripheral eosinophilia. Mammography showed edema-type changes in the right breast, trabecular coarsening, and skin thickening without discrete masses. Breast ultrasound confirmed diffuse edema and skin thickening but no focal lesion; axillary ultrasound revealed a large vascularized hypoechoic mass. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated a poorly defined soft-tissue mass in the right axilla without distant metastases and an ill-defined soft-tissue mass in the left thyroid lobe. The patient underwent ultrasound-guided core biopsies of both the axillary and thyroid lesions.

An 82-year-old man was admitted with fever, seizure, and altered consciousness. His history included subarachnoid hemorrhage with secondary epilepsy treated with phenytoin, gastrectomy, and eight years of being bedridden in a nursing home with minimal sunlight exposure. Two weeks before admission, he developed an acute seizure followed by poor oral intake; three days before admission he became febrile (>38°C) and developed respiratory failure. 

On examination, he was hypotensive (84/52 mmHg), febrile (40.0°C), tachypneic on supplemental oxygen (8 L/min), and had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of E1V2M5. Coarse crackles were present at the left lung base, and both Chvostek and Trousseau signs were positive.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 10 390/μL; albumin 3.1 g/dL; BUN 13.8 mg/dL; creatinine 0.44 mg/dL (eGFR 134.5 mL/min/1.73 m^2); phosphate 1.6 mg/dL; total calcium 3.7 mg/dL (corrected 4.6 mg/dL); ionized calcium 0.55 mmol/L; magnesium 2.97 mg/dL; intact PTH 386.8 pg/mL; and CRP 1.67 mg/dL. ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm with a prolonged QT interval. Chest CT revealed left lower lobe consolidation and pleural effusion; head CT showed chronic frontal lobe atrophy without acute lesions. A diagnosis of bacterial pneumonia with sepsis was made, and meningitis was clinically excluded.

Given the low ionized calcium and elevated PTH, true hypocalcemia was confirmed and further evaluated. CKD was excluded by normal renal function; severe hypomagnesemia was not present; pancreatitis was ruled out by normal amylase, lipase, and imaging; and sepsis‐related urinary calcium losses were unlikely given a fractional excretion of calcium of 0.13%. An additional mechanism for the severe hypocalcemia was considered.

A 16-year-old boy collapsed with cardiopulmonary arrest while playing soccer. He had experienced exertional chest pain since age 12; at that time, transthoracic echocardiography showed a normal ejection fraction of 57% and a trabeculation at the left ventricular apex suggestive of non-compaction, and a treadmill exercise test was negative. During the current event, he was defibrillated three times by an automated external defibrillator and achieved return of spontaneous circulation. On admission, he was comatose and underwent therapeutic hypothermia. Laboratory studies revealed a B-type natriuretic peptide level of 103.2 pg/mL (normal <18.4) and a troponin I level of 0.09 ng/mL (normal 0.00–0.03). Arterial blood gas analysis showed pH 7.233, pCO2 39.0 mmHg, pO2 101.0 mmHg, and lactate 93.0 mg/dL. Chest radiography demonstrated cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio 58%) and pulmonary edema. A 12-lead electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with 2-mm ST-segment depression in the anterolateral leads and a QTc of 441 ms. Repeat transthoracic echocardiography revealed diffuse left ventricular hypokinesis with an ejection fraction of 34% and persistent trabeculation at the left ventricular apex.

A 35-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of bilateral frontal, episodic headaches and secondary amenorrhea. Six months before referral, evaluation revealed a prolactin level of 125 ng/mL (reference, 4.8–23.3 ng/mL) and a pituitary MRI reported as a 13×10×12 mm macroadenoma. Cabergoline 0.5 mg twice weekly was started, but after 6 months her amenorrhea persisted and gonadotropin levels remained low. She had no personal or family history of autoimmune disease. On examination, vital signs were normal and visual fields were full. Laboratory testing demonstrated panhypopituitarism. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the sella showed a 13×11×12 mm lesion with heterogeneous intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images, diffuse enhancement extending toward the infundibulum and dura, and no optic-chiasm compression. These findings were interpreted as suggestive of a complicated cyst, cystic adenoma, hemorrhage, or hypophysitis. Hydrocortisone and levothyroxine were initiated, and transsphenoidal surgery was planned for tissue diagnosis and decompression.

A 49-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of progressive left hip pain that limited daily activities. He lived in an urban area and had no relevant medical history, no fever, chills, weight loss, prior trauma, tuberculosis history, or animal contact. He ambulated with crutches and had a limp. On examination, there was tenderness over the left gluteal region and painful, reduced range of motion of the left hip; the skin was unremarkable. Routine blood tests showed normal leukocyte count, no eosinophilia, and normal C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate.  
Plain radiographs of the pelvis showed expansive bone destruction of the left ischium, ilium, acetabulum, femoral head, and trochanteric region without periosteal reaction. Hip ultrasound revealed an intra-articular effusion without collection. MRI demonstrated multiple cystic lesions extending from the ischium and ilium to the trochanteric region with cortical bone destruction, associated with a multiloculated cystic mass in the gluteal soft tissues. The cysts had intermediate to low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted images in both bone and soft tissue.

A 41-year-old man with no known comorbidities presented with three months of unintentional weight loss and a hard, non-tender mass in the left supraclavicular area.  
Laboratory studies showed:  
- Complete blood count within normal limits (neutrophils 5.72 × 10^6/mm^3, lymphocytes 3.69 × 10^6/mm^3, monocytes 0.55 × 10^6/mm^3, eosinophils 0.07 × 10^6/mm^3).  
- C-reactive protein elevated at 151.1 mg/L (reference < 5.0 mg/L); lactate dehydrogenase normal at 191 mg/L (reference 135–225 mg/L).  
- T-cell immunophenotyping, B and NK cell analysis, and interferon-γ receptor expression all within normal limits.  
- Viral serologies for HIV, hepatitis viruses, and HTLV were negative.  
- Acid-fast bacilli stain (BAAR) of peripheral samples was negative.  
Chest radiography and computed tomography revealed enlarged mediastinal and left supraclavicular lymph node conglomerates without focal pulmonary parenchymal lesions. Ultrasonography confirmed multiple enlarged nodes in the left supraclavicular region.  
The leading diagnostic considerations were lymphoproliferative disorders (such as lymphoma) and granulomatous infections (notably tuberculosis).  
A fine-needle aspiration of the left supraclavicular lymph node was performed.

A 53-year-old woman with well-controlled hypothyroidism and a recently diagnosed anal fissure presented with a 2-day history of fever and diffuse swelling of the right thigh, associated with severe pain that made her unable to walk. On examination, she was febrile (40 °C) with a mildly altered general state. The right thigh was markedly swollen, erythematous, and firm to palpation; the remainder of the examination, including cardiac auscultation, was unremarkable. Initial laboratories showed a leukocyte count of 12 000/mm³ with neutrophil predominance and a C-reactive protein level of 443 mg/L; muscle enzymes and other routine parameters were normal. Urinalysis was negative, and viral serologies for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV were negative. Antinuclear antibodies were negative. Chest radiography, transthoracic echocardiography, and abdominal ultrasonography were normal. A soft-tissue ultrasound of the thigh demonstrated heterogeneous thickening of the vastus lateralis muscle with edematous subaponeurotic infiltration consistent with acute myositis. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right thigh showed diffuse inflammatory involvement of the vastus lateralis muscle and subcutaneous fat edema of the anterior thigh. Muscle-biopsy specimens revealed marked variation in fiber size, foci of necrosis and regeneration, significant connective-tissue edema with septal fragmentation, autophagic vacuoles, and an intraparenchymal and perivascular inflammatory infiltrate; there was normal fiber-type distribution and no mitochondrial, glycogenic, or lipid accumulation. These histologic findings were described as “suggestive of severe inflammatory myopathy evoking pyomyositis or dermatomyositis.” No muscle-tissue culture was performed at the time of biopsy, and myositis-specific autoantibodies were negative.

A 9-month-old previously healthy girl was brought to the pediatric emergency department for sudden onset dyspnea. She had a 2-day history of rhinorrhea and cough.  
On examination:  
• Pulse 180/min (normal 80–160/min), blood pressure 70/40 mmHg  
• Respiratory rate 48/min with chest indrawing (normal 30–40/min)  
• Temperature 38.9 °C  

The initial 12-lead ECG showed ventricular tachycardia, which spontaneously reverted to a regular rhythm with frequent extrasystoles. Orotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation were initiated.  

A chest x-ray demonstrated cardiomegaly with bilateral pulmonary congestion. Laboratory studies revealed:  
• Serum potassium 5.6 mmol/L (normal)  
• Lactate dehydrogenase 1234 U/L (reference 230–460)  
• Creatine phosphokinase (CPK) normal  
• Troponin I 0.81 ng/mL (reference <0.25)  

Three hours later, a follow-up ECG showed ST-segment elevation in leads V3–V6 and ST-segment depression in V1–V2. Repeat cardiac biomarkers disclosed CPK 2066 U/L (reference 95–195) and troponin I 1.92 ng/mL.  

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed diffuse hypocontractility and dilation of the left ventricle without focal wall motion abnormalities.

28-year-old Chinese woman admitted for fever and severe, intermittent abdominal pain over 5 days. Three days before admission she had nausea and vomiting. She had undergone cesarean section 3 months earlier. On admission, BP 122/70 mm Hg, pulse 80/min; physical exam showed slight tenderness below the xiphoid process without rebound or rash. Family history unremarkable. On night of admission and on day 3 she had two generalized tonic–clonic seizures treated with diazepam. On hospital day 2, brain MRI revealed symmetric T1 hypointense, T2 and FLAIR hyperintense lesions in frontal, parietal, occipital lobes and cerebellar hemispheres; DWI was isointense or slightly hypointense. MRA showed right vertebral artery tortuosity and aneurysmal dilation of the left vertebral artery. On day 3, transferred to neurology; BP 160/128 mm Hg, pulse 140/min; urine became dark. Neurologic exam showed mild consciousness disturbance, quadriparesis, depressed deep-tendon reflexes. ECG initially showed sinus tachycardia and right ventricular hypertrophy, then developed Q waves in II, III, aVF and ST-T changes. Troponin I elevated at 3.013 ng/mL. Echocardiography indicated segmental dyskinesia, left ventricular dysfunction (EF 44%). Labs on day 4: WBC 16.10×10^9/L, RBC 6.40×10^12/L, Hb 167 g/L, platelets 387×10^9/L, AST 52 U/L, ALT 49 U/L, CK 245 U/L, CK-MB 26 IU/L, LDH 286 U/L, HBDH 208 IU/L, lactate 8.37 mmol/L, sodium 131.5 mmol/L, potassium 3.28 mmol/L. Urinalysis: epithelial cells 80/μL, occult blood +–, urine bilirubin ++, ketone ++, dark discoloration. Cerebrospinal fluid normal. EEG showed generalized slowing without epileptiform discharges. Nerve conduction studies were normal except low F-wave incidence in median nerves.

A 54-year-old woman with obstructive sleep apnea presented with fever, nausea, and right lower quadrant abdominal pain. She was clinically diagnosed with acute appendicitis, but CT imaging showed a normal appendix without other acute findings. Diagnostic laparoscopy revealed extensive inflammatory adhesions in the right lower quadrant and an appendix that appeared acutely inflamed with surrounding phlegmon; an appendectomy was performed and a Jackson–Pratt drain was left in place. Postoperatively, the patient initially improved and was discharged on postoperative day 2. Surgical pathology demonstrated acute appendiceal serositis with a small focus of mucosal inflammation and no perforation. 

A few days after discharge, the patient’s JP drainage increased in volume and became feculent. Her nausea, fever, chills, abdominal pain, and constipation recurred, and she was transferred for further care. On arrival she was slightly febrile and hypertensive, with a white-cell count of 21,500 cells/mm3 and a lactate level of 1.0 mmol/L. Examination revealed morbid obesity (BMI 51), marked lower-quadrant tenderness, and cellulitic changes around the drain site with dark, feculent fluid. A diagnosis of appendiceal stump dehiscence vs bowel perforation was made, and the patient was taken for exploratory laparotomy.

A 59-year-old Ghanaian woman presented with a 2-month history of recurrent right cheek swelling with an acute exacerbation over the past week. She denied trismus or toothache. Her medical history was unremarkable. On examination, there was a 4 × 3 cm swelling over the right posterolateral mandible with normal overlying skin; the mass was soft, mildly tender, nonfluctuant, and slightly warm. Ultrasonography of the right cheek showed an ovoid nodular lesion in the masseter region measuring 1.14 cm with eccentric calcification suggestive of sialolithiasis. A CT scan demonstrated three well-circumscribed hyperdense lesions, the largest measuring 5.6 × 5.2 mm, with reactive inflammation around the right masseteric region. The calculi were isolated from all major salivary glands, and the ipsilateral parotid gland and its duct were free of lithiasis and inflammation. Routine hematological investigations were normal.

An 80-year-old woman with a history of rectal cancer treated in 2008 by liver metastasectomy followed by Hartmann’s procedure with intraoperative radiotherapy (5×5 Gy) and adjuvant capecitabine, oxaliplatin, and bevacizumab presented in January 2011 with intermittent gross hematuria. Since December 2009 she had bilateral JJ stents for ureteral strictures, replaced regularly. In November 2010 she required drainage of a pelvic abscess after stent occlusion complicated by Candida glabrata infection. Her medical history also included type 2 diabetes mellitus and angina pectoris.

On presentation, her hemoglobin was 7.2 mmol/L and creatinine was 370 μmol/L. Renal ultrasound showed bilateral hydronephrosis. Because of persistent hematuria and suspected stent occlusion, cystoscopy and ureteral stent exchange were performed: removal of the right double-J catheter revealed pulsatile arterial bleeding from the right ureteral orifice. The stent was changed, bleeding subsided, and she received four units of packed red cells intraoperatively. Open surgery was considered too high risk.

A CT angiogram demonstrated active hemorrhage at the right renal pelvis with clots in the collecting system. The patient was hemodynamically stable and managed expectantly, but that night she had recurrent gross hematuria. Embolisation of the right renal artery with coils was performed. During subsequent left stent repositioning, retrograde ureterography revealed a ureteroileal fistula, and a new ureteral catheter was placed; conservative management was advised. Within 24 hours, massive hematuria recurred and her hemoglobin continued to fall despite further transfusion.

A 53-year-old man was admitted with non-exertional chest pain and a positive exercise stress test. Coronary angiography revealed total occlusion of the right coronary artery, and percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty with placement of drug-eluting and bare-metal stents was performed. After the procedure, he became hypotensive. Transthoracic echocardiography was obtained to exclude pericardial effusion and revealed a 6.5 × 4 cm mass in the left atrium, left atrial dilatation, and an estimated systolic pulmonary artery pressure of 43 mmHg; the left ventricular ejection fraction was 60%. He was referred for surgical excision with a presumptive diagnosis of left atrial myxoma.

A 42-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with acute, diffuse abdominal pain. Three days earlier she had fever and right upper quadrant pain treated at a local clinic. She had no significant medical history. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (11.2×10^3 cells/µL), elevated C-reactive protein, markedly elevated liver enzymes, and hemoglobin of 7.8 g/dL requiring transfusion.  
Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a large, heterogeneous subcapsular lesion in the right hepatic lobe and a perihepatic fluid collection. The initial differential diagnosis included a subcapsular hepatic abscess or a mass such as a cavernous hemangioma.  
Triphasic multidetector CT revealed an approximately 9-cm, low-density, irregular lesion in the right hepatic dome that was largely nonenhancing; however, multiple irregular, linear, septa-like densities were isoattenuating to adjacent liver on all phases. Adjacent to this was a heterogeneous hyperdense subcapsular collection, consistent with acute hematoma. On arterial, portal venous, and delayed phases, most of the lesion remained nonenhancing, except for multiple small foci that gradually enlarged and became isodense to liver parenchyma; the interface with normal liver was shaggy and irregular. A separate 1-cm lesion in the right lobe was low attenuation on the arterial phase, showed peripheral isodense enhancement on the portal venous phase, and became isodense or slightly hyperdense on the delayed phase.  
Hepatic angiography performed for presumed rupture of a hepatic tumor revealed a large hypovascular area corresponding to the subcapsular hematoma and an irregular parenchymal defect in the dome, with no feeding vessels, contrast accumulations, or vascular malformations.

A 4-year-old Malay boy was brought by his mother with a 3-day history of fever, nasal congestion, and decreased appetite, followed by left eyelid redness. On the day of initial symptoms, a nasopharyngeal swab for SARS-CoV-2 was negative. The next day he developed mild left eye redness and was started by a general practitioner on oral antibiotics and topical chloramphenicol. Despite treatment, the left eyelids became increasingly swollen, erythematous, and painful, extending to the cheek region; he was unable to open the left eye. The mother denied any history of sinusitis, facial trauma, or insect bite. 

On examination, the patient was febrile and mildly dehydrated. There was marked tender, warm periorbital and facial edema on the left, involving the nasal bridge and maxilla, with contralateral nasal tip deviation. He could not voluntarily open the left eye; there was mild ophthalmoplegia with proptosis. The remainder of the external ocular examination was unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 17.11 mg/dL and a white blood cell count of 17.9 × 10^9/L (78.9% neutrophils). Computed tomography of the head, orbits, and sinuses demonstrated left proptosis; opacification of the left maxillary and ethmoidal sinuses; a left subperiosteal collection; and thickening with enhancement of the left extraconal superior, medial, and inferior spaces extending into the periorbital region, cheek, and mandible. 

Empirical intravenous antibiotics were initiated, but the ocular findings remained unchanged after 48 hours.

A 38-year-old woman was admitted with a 2-day history of chills, fevers up to 39.5 °C, nausea, and two episodes of vomiting, followed by 1 day of severe, diffuse, treatment-refractory abdominal pain and a sensation of abdominal fullness. Her medical history included gestational diabetes mellitus; surgical history included two cesarean deliveries, cholecystectomy 4 years earlier, and ventral hernia repair with mesh 4 years earlier.  
On examination, she was alert but appeared acutely ill and was in severe pain. Temperature was 38.9 °C; other vital signs were stable. There was mild scleral icterus, right upper quadrant tenderness, abdominal rigidity, and guarding; the liver and spleen were not palpable.  
Laboratory studies showed:  
• Leukocytosis 54.9 ×10^9/L with 88.3% neutrophils  
• Hematocrit 26.1%, hemoglobin 8.3 g/dL, platelets 280 ×10^3/mL  
• C-reactive protein 49.33 mg/L  
• Blood urea nitrogen 53 mg/dL, creatinine 0.66 mg/dL  
• AST 434 U/L, ALT 296 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 133 U/L, γ-GT 29 U/L  
• Total bilirubin 4.28 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 1.89 mg/dL  
• PT 15.44 sec (INR 1.29), PTT 39.49 sec  
• Glucose 281 mg/dL, total protein 6 g/dL, albumin 3.4 g/dL  
A chest radiograph was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a mixed collection containing air and debris measuring 8 × 7 × 5.5 cm in the posterior left hepatic lobe (segments II and III), limited laterally by the left portal vein and extending medially toward the lesser curvature of the stomach, associated with moderate intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary dilation; emphysematous alveolarization of the adjacent hepatic parenchyma was also noted.

A 72-year-old man with recalcitrant psoriasis vulgaris and psoriatic arthritis had been treated with adalimumab for 1 year, achieving rapid improvement. Twelve months after starting adalimumab, he reported a several-month history of nocturnal cough and occasional hemoptysis without fever. Ear, nose, and throat and pulmonary evaluations were noncontributory. At dermatology follow-up, he had new-onset, asymptomatic, ill-defined reddish plaques and nodules covered by serum crusts on his back and on the dorsum of the right hand and right middle finger. Routine blood counts, liver and renal function tests, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were all within normal limits. Annual HIV and QuantiFERON-TB Gold tests were negative. He denied high-risk exposures apart from home gardening. A skin biopsy of a back lesion showed micropustular formations within the epidermis and a dense lymphohistiocytic dermal infiltrate. Periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott, Ziehl–Neelsen, and Alcian blue stains were negative for microorganisms. Skin swab cultures grew no organisms.

A 33-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department after a syncopal episode at work. She reported a 2-week history of fever and cough and a 2-month history of anorexia and weight loss. On arrival, she was tachypneic and dyspneic. Examination revealed palpable cervical lymph nodes, generalized coarse crackles, and bilateral pitting edema of the lower limbs. Vital signs were: blood pressure 100/40 mm Hg, heart rate 110 beats/min, respiratory rate 30 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 92% on room air.

An electrocardiogram showed sinus bradycardia with nonspecific T-wave inversion in the precordial leads and intermittent complete right bundle branch block. Chest radiography revealed diffuse bilateral miliary changes. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated severely reduced global left ventricular systolic function (ejection fraction, 15%), an apical mural thrombus, and a small pericardial effusion. High-sensitivity troponin I was elevated at 85 pg/mL, and C-reactive protein was 9.85 mg/dL. Tests for COVID-19 and HIV were negative.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis showed disseminated disease involving the lungs, intestines, and bones, with possible tuberculomas in the liver and spleen. The scan also confirmed the presence of a left ventricular apical thrombus.

A 51-year-old primipara postmenopausal woman presented with abnormal vaginal discharge and vulvar itching. She had no significant medical or surgical history. At a local gynecology clinic, she underwent vaginal examination, cytocervical sampling, and transvaginal ultrasound. The next day, she developed fever, diarrhea, and vomiting and was diagnosed with gastroenteritis. Despite outpatient care, her symptoms persisted, and she experienced weakness and difficulty walking. Seven days after the procedure, she was transported to our hospital.

On arrival, blood pressure was 69/49 mmHg, heart rate 62 beats per minute, respiratory rate 25 breaths per minute, temperature 37.7°C, and oxygen saturation 93% on ambient air; she was alert with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Abdominal examination revealed marked tenderness in the lower quadrants with guarding. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 12,100 per µL and a C-reactive protein level of 31.4 mg/dL. Transabdominal ultrasound and computed tomography of the abdomen demonstrated intestinal edema, bowel dilatation, and a large volume of ascites. Intravenous fluids raised her blood pressure to 92/74 mmHg, and she was admitted with an initial diagnosis of gastroenteritis and dehydration.

Nine hours after admission, she lost consciousness and became hypotensive. Necrotizing enterocolitis and septic shock were suspected, and she underwent an exploratory laparotomy. The procedure yielded over 2000 mL of milky-white purulent ascites without evidence of intestinal necrosis or other intraabdominal infection sources; a diagnosis of primary peritonitis was made. She was transferred to the intensive care unit for ongoing resuscitation and broad-spectrum antibiotics.

A 27-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a suspected food allergy. He had a 3-year history of seasonal rhinitis and ocular itching each spring. In January 2018, he experienced lip swelling 5 minutes after eating two kiwifruits, which he had consumed immediately after a gym workout (isometric training then treadmill). He then noted itchy scalp and facial edema; about 60 minutes later he developed generalized urticaria, weakness, and ear “rumbling.” His symptoms improved within 25 minutes of antihistamines, although facial swelling persisted for 24 hours. He had previously eaten kiwifruit without difficulty and denied alcohol use, NSAIDs, or other cofactors. He was a non-smoker, occasional drinker, and had no chronic medications; his grandfather had asthma.

Physical examination was unremarkable. Skin-prick tests were negative for multiple foods (rye, wheat, banana, egg, milk, meats, fish) but positive for grass, rye, weed, Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus, and fresh kiwi. A bronchial histamine challenge was normal. Total IgE was 92.6 kU/L; specific IgE levels (ImmunoCap) were 43.45 kU/L to early grass, 17.68 kU/L to late grass, 0.94 kU/L to kiwi, and 1.71 kU/L to shrimp; other inhalant and food sIgE were <0.35 kU/L. 

Based on history and tests, allergic rhinitis to timothy grass was diagnosed. The positive kiwi test appeared inconsistent with his tolerance of kiwifruit at rest, and the shrimp sIgE had no clinical correlate. Considering these discrepancies, a decision was made to perform oral and exercise provocation testing.

A 65-year-old Japanese woman was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus at age 53 and noted bilateral sensorineural hearing difficulties from age 56. Her mother, maternal grandmother, and mother’s sister had short stature and diabetes. The patient was of short stature and low weight. From age 57, she had progressive gait disturbance and dysarthria. Since age 62, she experienced partial seizures of the right arm and foot once monthly that evolved to generalized convulsions despite sodium valproate 400 mg/day; during seizures, her serum glucose was normal and valproate levels were >50 μg/mL. 

On neurologic examination, she had bilateral gaze-evoked horizontal nystagmus, left-dominant sensorineural hearing loss, limb coordination deficits, a cerebellar ataxic gait, and mild slurred speech; there was no ophthalmoplegia. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies showed normal creatine kinase and renal function and elevated lactate and pyruvate levels in blood and cerebrospinal fluid. Brain MRI revealed moderate atrophy of the cerebellar vermis and hemispheres, a normal-volume brainstem, and mild cerebral atrophy without abnormal high-intensity lesions. EEG showed occasional theta slowing in the left frontal, central, and parietal leads.

A 24-year-old woman with a history of cholecystectomy and relapsed acute promyelocytic leukemia presented with a 2-day history of nausea, vomiting, and epigastric pain. One year after induction with cytarabine, daunorubicin, and ATRA, she began arsenic trioxide (17 mg IV daily, 5 days/week). On day 11 of therapy, she developed her current symptoms. Examination showed epigastric tenderness. Laboratory studies revealed an amylase of 405 U/L (normal 30–110), lipase of 4960 U/L (normal 6–75), AST 43 U/L (normal 14–36), and hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL (normal 12.3–15.3). CT of the abdomen/pelvis showed post-cholecystectomy changes. Right upper quadrant ultrasound demonstrated a normal pancreas, a common bile duct of 3.5 mm without intrahepatic ductal dilation, and no gallbladder. MRI/MRCP showed normal pancreatic morphology with no evidence of pancreas divisum. Bile aspirate was negative for microcrystalline disease. Triglycerides, antinuclear antibodies, and IgG4 levels were within normal limits. Arsenic therapy was held; she improved with intravenous fluids, pain control, and antiemetics, and her enzymes normalized by hospital day 8. One week later, arsenic was resumed at 0.1 mg/kg/day. On day 14 of therapy, she developed mental-status changes, respiratory distress, hypotension, and recurrent epigastric pain. Amylase and lipase were again elevated. CT showed pancreatic heterogeneity consistent with pancreatitis. Arsenic was held, succimer chelation was initiated, and blood and urine arsenic levels were found to be significantly elevated 25 days after cessation. EEG revealed generalized slowing consistent with toxic metabolic encephalopathy. She ultimately required tracheostomy and percutaneous gastrojejunostomy and was transferred to a long-term care facility.

A 55-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a several-month history of right-eye photophobia, which worsened when moving from a dark to light environment. Her past ocular history was notable for a presumed diffuse multifocal iris/ciliary body melanoma in the right eye, for which an iris biopsy performed one month later yielded inconclusive results.

On presentation two months after biopsy, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20– in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye; intraocular pressures were 13 mmHg and 15 mmHg, respectively. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye revealed full-thickness iris defects at 2:00, 3:30, and 6:30 o’clock, as well as a 0.7 × 0.8 mm hyperpigmented iris lesion at 8 o’clock. Ultrasound biomicroscopy demonstrated an iris lesion at 7 o’clock measuring 0.7 × 0.8 × 1.3 mm, without evidence of extraocular extension, spontaneous vascular pulsations, or intraocular extension.

At this point, there were no overt signs of definitive malignancy, and given the inconclusive biopsy results, the assumption of an atypical iris nevus prevailed as the working diagnosis.

A 16-year-old female presented with a 12-hour history of intermittent upper and central abdominal cramps and progressive distension. The pain became persistent and agonizing, followed by vomiting of ingested matter and obstipation. She denied fever, chills, vaginal discharge, or bleeding; her last menstrual period was 1 week earlier. She had no prior surgeries and no alcohol or tobacco use.

On examination she appeared acutely ill and in pain. Temperature was 37.1°C, pulse 110/min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min. The abdomen was grossly distended centrally with hyperactive bowel sounds and mild upper abdominal tenderness; digital rectal examination revealed an empty rectum.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 11.9×10^3/μL, hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, platelets 248×10^3/μL; urine β-hCG was negative and other blood chemistries were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated a markedly dilated sigmoid colon measuring 8.9 cm with air-fluid levels and twisting and wrapping of ileal loops around the sigmoid base, with a characteristic whirlpool sign of the mesenteric vessels.

A 54-year-old woman awoke from a nap with sudden onset of sharp, pricking pain in her upper back. Over the next hour the pain spread to her lower back, and she developed numbness followed by weakness in both lower limbs, resulting in paraplegia and urinary retention. Her medical history was notable for hypertension and coronary stenosis treated with clopidogrel for 5 years; she had no other comorbidities. 

On arrival in the emergency department, MRI of the entire spine was obtained within 30 minutes. T1- and T2-weighted images demonstrated an acute anterior epidural collection extending from C7 to T9, with maximal thickness and spinal cord compression at T2–T5 and T2 hyperintensity at the T4–T5 level suggestive of cord edema or contusion. Postcontrast imaging showed no abnormal enhancement to suggest vascular malformation.

An 18-year-old male from a rural area presented with a 5-month history of back pain, low-grade fever, progressive lower-limb weakness, and difficulty voiding. The pain was localized to the lumbar spine, tender to palpation, and radiated to both legs. Neurologic examination showed slight left lower-limb weakness (MRC 3+/5) without sensory loss or reflex changes; mild urinary retention was noted. Lumbar MRI demonstrated increased T2 signal in the L4 vertebral body and disc consistent with inflammatory spondylodiscitis, along with a linear T2 hyperintensity at the conus medullaris indicative of inflammatory myelopathy. There was no contrast enhancement or evidence of epidural abscess, disc herniation, or spondylolithiasis. Brucella serology was positive, with a standard tube agglutination titer of 1:64 and a positive Rose Bengal test.

A 70-year-old man was referred for surgery for an aortic arch aneurysm. He reported slight hoarseness. His medical history included dyslipidemia and hypertension. Preoperative contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed multiple lesions of varying size in the anterior and superior mediastinum with slight contrast enhancement, low-density areas equivalent to fat, and spotty calcification. Laboratory studies showed elevated LDL-cholesterol (216 mg/dL), triglycerides (170 mg/dL), and soluble IL-2 receptor (496 U/mL); carcinoembryonic antigen, alpha-fetoprotein, and human chorionic gonadotropin levels were normal. He had no history of trauma and was not on anticoagulants. Coronary angiography demonstrated coronary artery stenosis, and brain MRI revealed an asymptomatic old cerebral infarction.

A 77-year-old man with metastatic Merkel cell carcinoma involving iliac, inguinal lymph nodes and bone presented for evaluation. His medical history was notable for sarcoidosis diagnosed 10 years earlier by mediastinal biopsy after an episode of hypercalcemia; remission was achieved with glucocorticoids, although calcified mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy persisted. 

He completed six cycles of carboplatin and etoposide over six months, with a partial response: most inguinal lymphadenopathy resolved, and existing pulmonary, hilar, and calcified mediastinal nodes remained unchanged. He was then started on avelumab.

After three doses of avelumab, routine labs revealed a serum calcium concentration of 2.81 mmol/L and a creatinine clearance of 0.70 mL/s/m^2. The hypercalcemia was presumed to be malignancy-related and managed with intravenous zoledronic acid and fluids; avelumab was continued. Two weeks later, his serum calcium rose to 3.07 mmol/L, and creatinine clearance fell to 0.52 mL/s/m^2, prompting hospital admission for additional intravenous fluids and a second dose of zoledronic acid.

Further laboratory evaluation showed:  
• Serum parathyroid hormone level, 5 ng/L (reference range, 15–68)  
• Serum 25-hydroxy-vitamin D, 66 nmol/L (RR, 50–140)  
• Serum 1,25-dihydroxy-vitamin D, 280 pmol/L (RR, 60–210)  
• Urinary calcium excretion, 8.1 mmol/day (RR, 2.5–7.2)  
• Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level, 2,200 nkat/L (RR, 483–1,866)

Restaging investigations showed no progression of Merkel cell carcinoma compared to pre–avelumab studies.

A 57-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of an itchy skin eruption that began on her left thigh and progressively extended. Her medical history was notable for mitral valve prolapse repaired in 2018; she had no history of cutaneous disease, asthma, or nasal polyps. Current medications included aspirin, bupropion, citalopram, and zopiclone. She worked in an office, had not traveled recently, and her cancer screenings were up to date.

On examination, she had large annular and arcuate erythematous and edematous plaques over the trunk and extremities, sparing the palms, soles, genitalia, and face. Plaques on the legs were more purpuric and annular. Vesicles were seen at the periphery of plaques on the arms. The eruption was fixed, and she reported fatigue, anorexia, and peripheral edema. She was afebrile; there was no lymphadenopathy, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

A 4-mm punch biopsy showed spongiotic dermatitis with intraepidermal vesicles and abundant eosinophils without flame figures or vasculitis. Perilesional direct immunofluorescence was negative. Laboratory studies revealed an absolute eosinophil count of 2.7×10^9/L, a slightly elevated C-reactive protein level of 12.8 mg/L, and a normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Hemoglobin, platelets, renal and liver function tests, thyroid function, hemoglobin A1c, complement levels, and urinalysis were all normal. Indirect immunofluorescence for cutaneous basement membrane antibodies was negative.

She was treated with oral prednisone (50 mg daily for 5 days, then tapered by 5 mg every 5 days) and topical betamethasone. One week after starting prednisone, her eosinophil count rose to 5.3×10^9/L without lymphocytosis. A hematologic work-up was performed: serum immunoglobulins, vitamin B12, and tryptase were normal; hepatitis B and C serologies were negative; serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation showed no monoclonal spike; molecular genetic studies were all negative, including FIP1L1-PDGFRA and BCR-ABL fusion genes, JAK2 V617F and KIT D816V mutations, PDGFRB, and T-cell receptor gene rearrangements; flow cytometry revealed no monoclonal lymphocytic population; interleukin-5 level was 2.4 pg/mL; and abdominal ultrasound showed no hepatosplenomegaly.

A 37-year-old man with a history of Silver-Russell syndrome presented with progressive, constant anterior shoulder pain, worse on the left than the right, persisting despite NSAIDs, intra-articular steroid injections, and physical therapy. The pain was aggravated by movement, lifting, and activities such as driving and typing. He also reported mild bilateral shoulder weakness and decreased range of motion. He denied any prior trauma to the shoulders or previous shoulder surgery. 

On physical examination, the arms appeared normal without any deformity or signs suggestive of long head of the biceps tendon injury. His relevant medical history included bicuspid aortic valve, hypogonadism with azoospermia, cryptorchidism (right orchiectomy), an atrophic left testicle, kyphoscoliosis, and congenital failure of segmentation of the T4–T6 vertebral bodies.

Bilateral shoulder MR arthrography demonstrated absence of the long head of the biceps tendon on both sides along with smooth, shallow intertubercular grooves. The short head of the biceps tendon was normally developed, arising from the coracoid processes bilaterally.

A 28-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of cough, chest pain, runny nose, and sore throat. He had systemic hypertension diagnosed 13 years earlier and was taking amlodipine 10 mg once daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg once daily, and enalapril 10 mg twice daily. Vital signs showed an upper extremity blood pressure of 150/100 mm Hg. A complete blood count revealed lymphocytosis. A chest radiograph demonstrated normal lung fields and no consolidation, but multiple subtle irregularities along the bilateral inferior ribs suggestive of rib notching. Reexamination revealed a lower extremity blood pressure of 90/65 mm Hg, and the popliteal and dorsalis pedis pulses were markedly reduced compared with strong radial pulses.

A 75-year-old man was admitted on December 20, 2020, after left pleural effusion was detected on examination two weeks earlier. He had no facial edema or muscle pain and a history of hypertension. Vital signs were normal. On exam, breath sounds were diminished at the left lung base. CT of the chest showed moderate left pleural effusion with partial collapse of the left lung and scattered solid nodules in the right lung. Laboratory studies revealed an absolute eosinophil count of 0.30×10^9/L, creatine kinase 48 U/L, serum protein 55.1 g/L, and LDH 141 U/L. Other serum tests were normal. Thoracentesis yielded red, turbid fluid with clots. Pleural fluid analysis: specific gravity 1.022, Rivalta test positive; nucleated cells 3180/µL (98.9% mononuclear, 1.1% multinuclear); glucose 5.52 mmol/L, protein 36.5 g/L, albumin 22.2 g/L, chloride 111.3 mmol/L, LDH 220 U/L, ADA 9 U/L. Cardiac and abdominal ultrasounds were unremarkable. Chest ultrasound confirmed a large left pleural effusion (maximum depth 7.6 cm). PET/CT showed no muscle involvement or malignant lesions.  
He received cefotaxime–sulbactam for 1 week with no decrease in effusion. Pleural fluid cytology showed a few lymphocytes and mesothelial cells and no atypical epithelial cells. On hospital day 11, he was treated empirically for tuberculosis (rifampicin, isoniazid, moxifloxacin) for 25 days; repeat imaging showed no fluid reduction, and anti-tuberculosis therapy was discontinued.

A 36-year-old woman presented with painless vision decline and a dark shadow over her left eye for 10 days. She had no history of ocular trauma, surgery, systemic disease, or medication use. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/30 in the right eye and 20/100 in the left. Slit-lamp examination revealed no inflammatory signs in the anterior chambers or vitreous of either eye. Dilated fundus examination showed white-yellow subretinal exudates in the posterior pole of both eyes and an inferior corrugated bullous retinal detachment in the left eye with shifting subretinal fluid; no retinal break was identified. Routine blood tests, infectious disease screening, blood biochemistry, tumor markers, chest CT, and ECG were all normal. B-scan ultrasonography confirmed a bullous retinal detachment in the left eye; the right eye was normal. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated a discontinuous retinal pigment epithelium band in the right eye and a neurosensory detachment with hyperreflective material in the left eye. Fundus fluorescein angiography revealed multifocal patchy leakage, low fluorescence damage, and retinal vascular leakage in the detached area; the optic disc leaked slightly late. Indocyanine green angiography showed multifocal mid-stage hyperfluorescent flakes and late-stage hypofluorescence in the detached area of the left eye; the fellow eye exhibited analogous findings.

A 43-year-old Asian woman presented with a 3-day history of worsening chest pain that intensified over the past day. She also reported lethargy, anorexia, nausea, fever, and intermittent headaches; paracetamol had transiently reduced her fever. She had no chronic medical conditions. Her residence was in an area endemic for leptospirosis and dengue fever.

On admission, she was alert but appeared weak. Vital signs were: blood pressure 81/43 mmHg, heart rate 41 bpm, respiratory rate 20/min, and temperature 38.2 °C. Physical examination revealed pale conjunctiva, scleral icterus, and jaundice. Lung auscultation detected crackles. Abdominal examination showed hepatosplenomegaly and right upper quadrant tenderness.

An electrocardiogram showed total atrioventricular block with a junctional escape rhythm at 45 bpm and no signs of myocardial infarction. A chest radiograph demonstrated cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio 0.52) with increased bronchovascular markings.

Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis, hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL, platelets 98×10^9/L, blood urea nitrogen 92 mg/dL, creatinine 4.1 mg/dL, AST 102 IU/L, ALT 65 IU/L, C-reactive protein 9 mg/dL, and high-sensitivity troponin I 361 ng/dL.

A 35-year-old Caucasian woman with a history of asthma (on salmeterol/fluticasone), allergic rhinitis and a prior provoked pulmonary embolism presented with left-sided pleuritic chest pain, dry cough, dyspnea and subjective fevers. She worked as a nurse in a rural setting in Northern Territory, Australia, with no notable environmental exposures, smoking or drug use. 

On admission, computed tomography pulmonary angiography showed multifocal bilateral rounded pulmonary consolidations and small bilateral pleural effusions. Laboratory tests revealed a white-cell count of 11.3 × 10^9/L with an eosinophil count of 1.5 × 10^9/L and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 73 mm/h. Urinalysis was normal, and multiple blood cultures were negative. Serologic studies demonstrated an elevated Legionella longbeachae indirect fluorescent antibody titre and a positive Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgM with negative IgG. Anti–neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative.

She received oral amoxicillin, doxycycline and dexamethasone for 7 days, with initial symptomatic improvement, but she subsequently relapsed. A large right pleural effusion developed; pleurocentesis yielded an exudate by Light’s criteria, but the fluid was clotted and cultures (bacterial and mycobacterial) remained sterile; adenosine deaminase was not elevated and cytology showed an inflammatory exudate.

A fluorodeoxyglucose PET scan revealed uptake confined to the pulmonary lesions. Bronchoscopy with cultures and nucleic acid amplification testing was non-revealing. CT-guided transthoracic biopsy of a peripheral consolidation showed scattered non-necrotizing granulomas, abundant histiocytes and focal eosinophilia; a diagnosis of hypersensitivity pneumonitis was initially raised.

A 16-month-old boy was referred for evaluation of esotropia and a white pupil in the right eye first noticed at 12 months of age. On examination, he was esotropic in the right eye. Slit-lamp evaluation of the anterior segment was normal in both eyes, but ophthalmoscopy revealed a total retinal detachment in the right eye, with the detachment close to the lens preventing visualization of the peripheral retina. B-mode ultrasonography showed a diffuse, high-echo area in the right vitreous cavity with no apparent sign of calcification. A computed tomography scan performed one month earlier also showed no evidence of calcification in the right eye. Magnetic resonance imaging at one hospital demonstrated high-intensity signals in T1-weighted images and low-intensity signals in T2-weighted images in the vitreous body of the right eye, and a repeat MRI three months later showed high-intensity signals in T2-weighted images in the same region. No evidence of a mass lesion was seen in either eye on the MRI studies.

A 40-year-old woman presented with a several-month history of intermittent right iliac fossa pain and loose motions. She also reported longstanding dysmenorrhoea and menorrhagia but denied other gastrointestinal or systemic symptoms. There was no significant past medical history or family history of endometriosis. On examination, including a full gynecologic evaluation, no abnormalities were detected. Laboratory studies revealed iron deficiency anemia (hemoglobin, 11.1 g/dL; mean corpuscular volume, 71 fL; ferritin, 8.4 ng/mL). A colonoscopy identified a sessile 1-cm lesion in the cecum; biopsy showed a metaplastic polyp. An initial attempt at polypectomy was unsuccessful. At a tertiary center, repeat colonoscopy demonstrated that the lesion appeared to arise from an inverted appendix, and submucosal nodules were noted in the sigmoid colon, thought to be endometrial in origin given her gynecologic history. A preoperative CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis did not reveal any definitive evidence of endometriosis and showed only small ovarian cysts.

A 79-year-old woman with hypertension presented with acute onset of severe posterior neck pain, occipital headache, fever, neck stiffness, vertigo, and vomiting. Two weeks earlier she had mild, activity-related neck pain, but then developed continuous, severe pain radiating into the occipital region, worse at night, with progressive restriction of neck motion. She denied weight loss, myalgia, arthralgia, morning stiffness, jaw claudication, or visual symptoms, and had no history of trauma. She reported only mild knee pain with walking.

On examination she was alert, temperature 37.8 °C, with no lymphadenopathy or skin changes. Temporal arteries were normal. Neurologic evaluation was intact, and Kernig’s sign was negative. The cervical spine had severe rigidity, diffuse paraspinal tenderness (most marked in the nape), and muscle spasm; passive rotation and lateral flexion were limited to 10°, flexion and extension to 20°, with pain at end range. Knees showed medial joint line tenderness, crepitus, and mild painful limitation of motion. 

Laboratory studies showed C-reactive protein 5.28 mg/dL (normal 0.0–0.5), white cells 13,600/mm3 (86% neutrophils), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 21 mm/hour; liver, kidney, thyroid tests, electrolytes, glucose, uric acid, and urinalysis were unremarkable. Blood cultures were negative. Cervical spine radiographs two weeks earlier showed spondylosis and loss of lordosis; knee radiographs showed advanced osteoarthritis without chondrocalcinosis.

Based on these clinical features, pyogenic spondylodiscitis was highly suspected and cervical magnetic resonance imaging was ordered, which revealed soft tissue thickening posterior to the dens with low-intermediate signal on T1 and low signal on T2 images, advanced multilevel degenerative changes, and spinal cord compression.

A 66-year-old woman presented with isolated uterine bleeding for 6 months. Examination revealed a cervical tumor, confirmed by biopsy as well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. As part of staging, a thoraco-abdomino-pelvic CT scan showed a large right‐sided retroperitoneal abdominal-pelvic cystic mass that displaced the right kidney anteriorly. The mass had well-defined, regular contours with a thin wall, multiple thin septa, and dense fluid content that enhanced faintly after contrast administration. Delayed CT acquisitions at 15 minutes and 2 hours demonstrated slow, progressive, and partial filling of the mass by contrast medium. Ultrasonography revealed an anechoic cystic mass with multiple fine septa in a fishnet pattern, displacing the kidney anteriorly. In addition, there was bilateral ureterohydronephrosis, with a 17-mm pelvicalyceal dilation on the left and a 51-mm dilation on the right. Laboratory tests showed elevated urea and creatinine, an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 11 mL/min, mild hyperkalemia without ECG changes, and leukocytosis.

A 70-year-old woman presented two weeks after sustaining a knife injury to the dorsum of her left hand while cutting lamb. One week after the injury, she noted a rapidly expanding asymptomatic erythematous and bullous plaque at the injury site, which did not improve with flucloxacillin and betadine. On dermatologic examination, there was a 30 mm desquamating erythematous bullous plaque on the dorsum of the left hand, extending to the bases of the index and middle fingers. 

Her medical history was notable for scleroderma diagnosed at age 50, manifest as symmetrical skin thickening of the hands and secondary Raynaud’s syndrome; she had no systemic organ involvement. Medications included diltiazem and a statin. She reported no constitutional symptoms but had itching, redness, and swelling of the hand without pain. Skin assessment also revealed slight thickening and hardening of her hands consistent with her scleroderma.

A biopsy of the blister was performed for microbiologic studies (fungi, atypical mycobacteria, Nocardia) and for histologic examination. Microscopic findings showed atypical dermal squamous proliferation consistent with pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia.

A 71-year-old woman with hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and a history of transient ischemic attack underwent an upper endoscopy for reflux disease. She awoke with a brief episode of bilateral upper extremity weakness, marked clumsiness of her left hand, left extremity numbness, and word-finding difficulty; all symptoms resolved within 20 minutes. She reported mild recurrent headaches over the past few years and firm nodules on her scalp that had been under observation. She denied vision or hearing changes, nausea, vomiting, or seizure activity. She had a 7-pack-year smoking history and a history of alcohol abuse. 

A head and neck CT angiogram showed no vascular stenosis, occlusion, aneurysm, or acute infarction. Non–contrast head CT demonstrated a 6-mm isodense extra-axial collection along the right convexity, with slight mass effect but no midline shift. The bone windows revealed sclerosis of the calvarium with focal inner-table erosions and periosteal reaction, along with overlying scalp soft-tissue swelling. These findings were initially interpreted as compatible with a chronic subdural hematoma, with a differential that included primary or secondary neoplasm.

A 44-year-old Caucasian woman with a 6-month history of asthma treated with inhaled corticosteroid and β-agonist presented with sudden onset central crushing chest pain, shortness of breath, and collapse. An ECG showed anterior ST elevation in leads V2–V5. She had no conventional risk factors for ischemic heart disease. On examination, cardiovascular findings were unremarkable; respiratory examination revealed bi-basal crepitations, more prominent on the left. Troponin-T was 772 ng/L (normal <14 ng/L). A chest radiograph showed extensive left-sided consolidation. Urgent coronary angiography demonstrated unobstructed coronary arteries, with diffuse coronary spasm that resolved with intracoronary nitrate. A working diagnosis of myopericarditis secondary to pneumonia was made, and the patient received intravenous co-amoxiclav with supportive care. Viral swabs and urinary antigens for atypical pneumonia were negative, and serological viral and autoimmune screens for myocarditis were negative; the patient did not improve despite antibiotic treatment. Peripheral white-cell count was 17.34 × 10^9/L with an eosinophil count of 7.23 × 10^9/L. A CT pulmonary angiogram confirmed left-sided consolidation and showed multiple small pulmonary emboli. Bronchoalveolar lavage revealed acute inflammation without organisms or eosinophilic damage. Serum troponin-T remained elevated at 1131 ng/L. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed extensive myocardial oedema on native T1 and T2 mapping, patchy subendocardial late gadolinium enhancement in the apical segments and right ventricle, and a circumferential pericardial effusion.

A 25-year-old man presented with progressive shortness of breath of 1 year’s duration. He had a history of IgA nephropathy diagnosed by renal biopsy at age 19. His parents were non-consanguineous with no relevant family history. On examination, he had cyanosis of the lips and clubbing of the fingers and toes. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air showed a PaO2 of 51 mmHg. A computed tomography pulmonary angiogram demonstrated diffuse centrilobular ground‐glass shadows and nodular shadows, a dilated pulmonary artery, and right ventricular enlargement. Pulmonary function testing revealed a severe decrease in diffusing capacity. Transthoracic echocardiography indicated an intermediate probability of pulmonary hypertension, which was confirmed by right heart catheterization showing a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 34 mmHg, a pulmonary artery wedge pressure of 10 mmHg, and a pulmonary vascular resistance of 5.8 Wood units. Autoimmune screening was negative. Therefore, pulmonary veno-occlusive disease or pulmonary capillary haemangiomatosis was highly suspected, and a genetic test for EIF2AK4 mutations was performed; the result was negative. Five months later, he developed nausea, vomiting, an elevated NT-proBNP of 3000 pg/mL, and an increased echocardiography-estimated pulmonary arterial systolic pressure of 74 mmHg. Laboratory studies revealed macrocytic anaemia (haemoglobin 84 g/L), elevated total bilirubin (42 µmol/L), and direct bilirubin (17 µmol/L). A direct Coombs test was positive, vitamin B12 and folate levels were normal, and bone marrow aspiration showed megaloblastic changes. A diagnosis of haemolytic anaemia-associated pulmonary hypertension was considered, and he was treated with steroids, ambrisentan, and sildenafil. His dyspnoea improved, and NT-proBNP and pulmonary arterial systolic pressure decreased over the next 6 months; however, his hypoxaemia persisted.

A 48-year-old Sinhalese man with a 2-year history of acetylcholine receptor–positive myasthenia gravis presented for an upper gastrointestinal contrast study to evaluate 3 months of progressive dysphagia to solids and then liquids. He underwent thymectomy in 2016 and had two prior myasthenic crises precipitated by respiratory infections, both requiring mechanical ventilation. His maintenance medications included pyridostigmine 50 mg every 6 hours, mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg twice daily, and daily prednisolone; he was functionally independent with 5/5 limb power and normal respiratory parameters on admission.

Under fluoroscopic guidance, 10 mL of iohexol was administered orally, but the contrast entered his right main bronchus, and the study was aborted. He was transferred to the emergency unit on high-flow oxygen with SpO₂ above 90%, but 45 minutes later his respiratory rate fell to 10 breaths per minute and his work of breathing declined. Nebulized salbutamol and a single 500 mg dose of IV metronidazole were given without improvement, and he required endotracheal intubation using IV midazolam and atracurium. A chest radiograph showed only right apical segment collapse. He was then transferred to the intensive care unit with a working diagnosis of respiratory distress due to contrast aspiration.

A 42-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of hematochezia requiring 5 units of packed red blood cells. On examination, he was pale, and his hemoglobin level was 7.0 g/dL. Colonoscopy revealed bluish red, elevated vascular lesions occupying the entire circumference of the anorectum up to 14 cm from the anal verge. A contrast-enhanced CT scan showed diffuse thickening of the anorectal wall with intravascular calcifications (phleboliths). Pelvic T2-weighted MRI demonstrated diffuse anorectal wall thickening, increased vascularity of the mesorectal fat planes, and additional vascular lesions in the urinary bladder wall.

A 57-year-old woman with a 4-year history of monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance presented with several weeks of dry mouth, polydipsia, and episodes of confusion. Her primary care physician noted a serum calcium level of 14.4 mg/dL and referred her to the emergency department. On examination, she had dry mucous membranes; other findings were unremarkable. Initial laboratory values were: calcium 14.4 mg/dL, albumin 5.0 g/dL, parathyroid hormone 7 pg/mL, creatinine 1.94 mg/dL. Complete blood count showed mild pancytopenia (WBC 3.5 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL, platelets 145 × 10^3/µL). She received intravenous saline and was admitted; her calcium normalized to 10 mg/dL, and calcium supplements were discontinued for presumed milk-alkali syndrome. Given concern for progression to multiple myeloma, a bone marrow biopsy was performed, revealing non-necrotizing granulomas and no evidence of plasma cell dyscrasia or other malignancy. Two weeks later, her calcium rose to 12.7 mg/dL despite adequate hydration, prompting readmission. An extensive hypercalcemia workup was pursued: repeat serum and urine electrophoreses and free light chains were unchanged; parathyroid hormone–related peptide was undetectable; PET–CT showed no FDG-avid lesions; and infectious studies for granulomatous disease were negative.

A 30-year-old Japanese man with a 7-year history of schizophrenia and longstanding water-drinking behavior (≈10 L/day) presented with 6 days of progressive nausea. Two days before admission he developed mild disorientation and speech disturbance.  
On transfer to the regional emergency hospital his Glasgow Coma Scale was E4V1M5. Physical examination showed no signs of volume overload or depletion and no focal neurologic deficits. Chest radiography was unremarkable.  
His outpatient regimen included over 10 oral psychotropic agents, all of which were discontinued on admission.  
Laboratory tests revealed: serum sodium 96 mEq/L, potassium 1.9 mEq/L, plasma osmolality 195 mOsm/kg; urine sodium 53 mEq/L, urine osmolality 332 mOsm/kg; urine-specific gravity 1.011; normal adrenal and thyroid studies; fractional excretion of sodium 0.45 %; negative free water clearance.  
An echocardiogram showed normal left ventricular size and systolic function. Renin–aldosterone activity was not elevated. Extracellular fluid volume was judged to be normal.  
He was fluid-restricted (≤500 mL/day) and received hypertonic (3%) saline and isotonic extracellular-like fluid, with serum sodium monitored every 4 h. Twelve hours after initiation, sodium had risen by 12 mEq/L and hypertonic saline was stopped. On day 3, serum sodium was 121 mEq/L and mental status improved to GCS E4V4M6.  
On hospital day 2 (after transfer), consciousness again deteriorated to GCS E4V1M4 without focal weakness. Brain MRI on day 3 showed bilateral high-intensity signals in the ventral posterolateral nucleus on T2-weighted images.

A 30-year-old man with HIV infection (diagnosed at age 28) on efavirenz, emtricitabine, tenofovir, and trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole presented with a 3-week history of fever, cough, and weight loss. He had a prior episode of Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia. On admission, his CD4 count was 724 cells/mm3 (up from 160 before HAART) and his viral load was 1350 copies/mL (down from 292 000). Chest radiography showed multiple well-defined cavitary lesions in the right upper lobe. Sputum smears were positive for acid-fast bacilli; no cultures were sent. A presumptive diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis was made, and he was started on isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide. After rifampicin-induced hepatotoxicity, rifampicin was replaced with moxifloxacin, and the patient’s respiratory symptoms improved.

Twelve weeks after initiation of antituberculosis therapy, he developed a large, tender, erythematous swelling on the right side of his neck without fever or weight loss. Ultrasound revealed necrotic lymph nodes with abscess formation. A paradoxical inflammatory syndrome was suspected; antituberculosis therapy was continued and a tapering course of corticosteroids was started, resulting in marked reduction of the neck swelling over 2 months. Two weeks after completing steroids, the swelling recurred to its prior size, again without systemic symptoms. Sixty milliliters of purulent material were aspirated and sent for mycobacterial culture, and corticosteroids were reinstated along with continuation of the same antituberculosis regimen.

A male neonate was delivered at 38 weeks’ gestation to a mother with well-controlled Graves’ disease on propylthiouracil. His birth weight was 2910 g. Two days after birth, he developed tachycardia (sleeping heart rate 150–160 beats per minute), frequent bowel movements, and marked irritability. Laboratory evaluation revealed elevated free T4 and free T3 levels with an inappropriately normal TSH. Antibodies associated with thyroid disease (thyroglobulin antibody, thyroid peroxidase antibody, TSH-receptor antibody, and thyroid-stimulating antibody) were within normal ranges. Electrocardiography showed a regular sinus rhythm with persistent tachycardia. Thyroid ultrasonography demonstrated a normal-sized gland without nodules. A TSH-secreting adenoma was excluded by magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary gland, and serum human chorionic gonadotropin β levels were normal.

A 22-year-old Somali woman presented with 1 week of acute visual loss, worse in the right eye. She reported eye pain with movement, and the right eye had no light perception; the left eye retained approximately 70% light perception. Examination revealed a right relative afferent pupillary defect, normal anterior segments, and normal-appearing optic discs in both eyes. Extraocular movements were full. She also noted joint discomfort, muscle weakness, headaches, and fatigue. She appeared ill but was alert and cooperative. 

Her temperature was 35.0 °C, blood pressure 115/80 mm Hg, pulse 70 bpm, and respiratory rate 18 breaths/min. Her past medical and family histories were unremarkable. Brain MRI with contrast showed no parenchymal abnormalities. 

Laboratory studies revealed a TSH level of 115.6 mIU/L (reference 0.35–5.1), T3 0.01 nmol/L (1.8–3.9), and T4 0.01 ng/dL (0.5–1.8). Anti–thyroid peroxidase and anti–thyroglobulin antibody titers were markedly elevated. Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated an enlarged gland with a hypoechoic, diffusely heterogeneous echotexture and no nodules.

A 23-year-old woman fell from a height of 5 m and presented with severe low back and right foot pain. She had no head trauma and a Glasgow Coma Score of 15. On examination, she had left L5 root paresis (1/5 long toe extension) with diminished light touch and pinprick sensation, perianal hypoesthesia, and urinary retention; anal sphincter function was impaired. Radiographs and CT showed A3/AO fractures of L2, B1/AO fractures of L5, and a comminuted Sanders type 4 right calcaneal fracture. Thirty hours after admission, she underwent posterior minimally invasive stabilization from L1 to S2 with L5 decompression and Ilizarov fixation of the calcaneus; both procedures were done prone under one anesthetic, lasting 4.5 hours. Immediately postoperatively, the anesthesiologist noted that the left pupil was larger than the right with a slower, incomplete reaction to light, while visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally and the right pupil reacted normally.

A 21-year-old Syrian woman presented with a swelling of the right mandible and numbness of the lower lip. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. Intraoral examination showed an intraosseous mass expanding both the buccal and lingual cortical plates of the right mandible. Panoramic radiography revealed a unilocular radiolucent lesion extending from the right first premolar to the right first molar. Cone-beam computed tomography confirmed the exact extent and well-defined borders of the lesion. Based on these images, the radiologic differential diagnosis included odontogenic keratocyst, unicystic ameloblastoma, and central giant cell granuloma. A biopsy was obtained and sent for histologic evaluation.

A 21-year-old G2P2 woman presented with profuse per vaginal bleeding. She denied any prior surgical procedures, dilatation and curettage, or use of pharmacologic contraceptives. On examination, she appeared pale with a hemoglobin concentration of 3.2 g/dL; she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Transabdominal ultrasound revealed an enlarged uterus with an anechoic mass in the posterior lower uterine segment; the endometrial lining was thin, and there were no signs of intra- or extra-uterine gestation. Color Doppler imaging showed a hypervascular mass with a yin-yang flow pattern, color aliasing, and flow reversal. Spectral Doppler interrogation demonstrated a peak systolic velocity of 71.5 cm/s and a resistive index of 0.42. A contrast-enhanced CT angiogram of the pelvis showed a complex cystic lesion with vivid central enhancement within the posterior myometrium, multiple dilated tortuous arterial feeders from bilateral uterine and gonadal arteries, and early venous drainage into the bilateral internal iliac and gonadal veins.

A 76-year-old man with metastatic sarcomatoid carcinoma of pulmonary origin was treated with carboplatin, paclitaxel, and combination nivolumab and ipilimumab, with partial response. Six months after starting therapy and 6 days after his last nivolumab dose, he was admitted with 7 days of increasing lethargy, diminished appetite, mild abdominal discomfort, and one episode of confusion with disorientation. He had intermittent fevers up to 39°C and fluctuating attention. Examination showed splenomegaly 3 cm below the costal margin without rash or abdominal tenderness. Initial laboratory studies revealed:  
• Hemoglobin 76 g/L, platelets 52 ×10^9/L, WBC 2.7 ×10^9/L, reticulocytes 8 (normal 10–100), haptoglobin <0.1 g/L  
• INR 1.4, PTT 77 s, fibrinogen 2.5 g/L  
• Peripheral smear: pancytopenia without schistocytes  
• Creatinine 70 μmol/L, AST 126 U/L, albumin 27 g/L, sodium 125 mmol/L, bilirubin normal, LDH 1,897 U/L  
• Ferritin >200,000 μg/L, triglycerides 1.42 mmol/L  
Blood and urine cultures showed no bacterial growth after 5 days. As thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura was considered, ADAMTS13 activity was sent and was normal.

A 61-year-old woman who did not smoke or drink alcohol was referred for evaluation of recurrent bilateral lower-limb skin lesions. Over the preceding 2 months, she had been admitted three times with presumed lower-limb cellulitis and treated with oral and intravenous antibiotics without improvement. She had a history of schizophrenia treated with risperidone. On examination, there were multiple tender, erythematous, non-suppurative nodules on both lower limbs extending to the thighs. A skin biopsy showed striking fat necrosis in the dermis and subcutis with focal neutrophilic infiltrate; ghost outlines of fat cells were seen with focal basophilia, raising the possibility of pancreatic fat necrosis. Her serum amylase was 148 IU/L (reference range, 0–100 IU/L).

A 13-year-old girl presented with a three-month history of dorsal spine pain. On initial evaluation, she had arthritis of the left knee without skin lesions. Laboratory studies showed an ESR of 33 mm/h, a CRP level of 9 mg/L, and an antinuclear antibody titer of 1 : 160; all other tests, including a bone marrow aspiration smear, were normal. MRI of the spine revealed multiple osteolytic and sclerotic lesions in thoracic vertebrae. 

Over the next six months, her back pain and knee symptoms worsened despite courses of amoxicillin/clavulanate, ceftriaxone, and cefuroxime. Arthroscopy of the left knee and open vertebral biopsy showed only nonspecific chronic inflammation; cultures and universal PCR for bacterial and mycobacterial DNA were negative. 

By December, she was febrile (39.5 °C) and could barely stand. Examination revealed severe thigh muscle atrophy, slight right-convex dorsal scoliosis, and increased swelling of both knees. ESR was 68 mm/h, CRP was 134 mg/L, leukocyte count was 7.41×10^9/L, anti-TPO antibodies were 90 IU/mL, and HLA-B27 was negative. Ultrasound and MRI of the knees showed synovitis and effusion but no metaphyseal bone lesions. A bone scan demonstrated increased uptake in both knees, T5 and T6 vertebrae, the left hip, and the sternum. A repeat MRI of the entire spine showed multiple unchanged vertebral lesions that did not cross intervertebral discs.

A 34-year-old woman at 31 4/7 weeks gestation presented with a 2-day history of frontal headache partially relieved by acetaminophen, nonpruritic erythematous maculopapular rash on her trunk and arms, and fever to 103.1 °F. She worked as a veterinary technician and was initially discharged with acetaminophen. She returned after 24 hours with malaise, fever, and arthralgia; laboratory evaluation revealed elevated aminotransferases and thrombocytopenia, and she was diagnosed with a nonspecific viral syndrome and discharged. On day 3, she re-presented with fever to 103.4 °F; blood tests showed elevated liver enzymes, proteinuria, thrombocytopenia, and leukopenia. She was transferred to the ICU and started on vancomycin, piperacillin–tazobactam, and azithromycin. Fetal ultrasound was normal. Blood and urine cultures, a respiratory PCR panel for RSV, adenovirus, influenza A/B, and parainfluenza virus, and serologies for viral hepatitis, syphilis, HIV, CMV, HSV, EBV, coccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis, and parvovirus were obtained.

A 29-year-old woman at 13 1/7 weeks gestation presented with a 2-day history of fever to 102.7 °F and headache. She denied sick contacts but reported household pets recently treated for fleas. Group A Streptococcus PCR and throat culture and a respiratory PCR panel were negative. Two days later she returned with subjective fever, headache, and cough; urinalysis suggested a urinary tract infection, and she received nitrofurantoin. She re-presented 24 hours later with fever to 102.9 °F, dyspnea, elevated aminotransferases, and leukocytosis with left shift. Fetal ultrasound remained normal; chest imaging showed bibasilar infiltrates, and right upper-quadrant ultrasound showed hepatomegaly. She was started on vancomycin, meropenem, and azithromycin. Repeat blood, urine, and stool cultures and the same serologic panel were all negative except for EBV IgG, consistent with past infection.

A 49-year-old Caucasian woman with Fuchs endothelial dystrophy and narrow angles status post bilateral peripheral iridotomies underwent combined extracapsular cataract extraction, intraocular lens implantation, and Descemet’s membrane endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK) in the right eye. The inferior peripheral iridotomy was enlarged to ~500 μm 12 days preoperatively. Surgery was uncomplicated. Postoperative medications included topical moxifloxacin, ketorolac, and prednisolone acetate. At 4 weeks, she reported intermittent flashing lights and two central dark shapes in the right eye. Visual acuity was 20/20. Fundus exam showed hypo-pigmented deep retinal/choroidal lesions along the superior and inferior temporal arcades. Fluorescein angiography revealed early autofluorescence, late blocking of the lesions, and surrounding retinal pigment epithelium staining. Optical coherence tomography showed placoid subretinal deposits, RPE attenuation with outer retinal distortion, and overlying vitritis.

Three months later, she underwent uncomplicated combined cataract extraction and DMEK in the left eye, with an inferior peripheral iridotomy performed 5 days prior. One week postoperatively, visual acuity was 20/20. Ten days postoperatively, she noted patchy central scotomas in the left eye. Visual acuity was 20/40. Exam showed a triangular hypo-pigmented choroidal lesion along the superotemporal arcade. Fluorescein angiography and OCT demonstrated a placoid chorioretinal lesion with subretinal fluid and a subfoveal serous pigment epithelial detachment.

A comprehensive laboratory investigation, including CBC, RPR, FTA-ABS, QuantiFERON Gold, ACE level, lysozyme, Lyme serologies, blood cultures, and chest radiography, was unremarkable. Systemic prednisone (40 mg daily) was initiated.

A 35-year-old man with a 5-year history of heavy alcohol use (1–2 pints of vodka, 5–6 times per week) who had stopped drinking 3 weeks earlier was evaluated for 3 weeks of fatigue, bilateral lower-extremity swelling, and orange-colored urine. Physical examination showed hepatosplenomegaly and pitting edema of both legs. Initial laboratory studies revealed aspartate aminotransferase 295 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 230 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 505 U/L, total bilirubin 3.4 mg/dL, ferritin 12 799 ng/mL, and iron saturation 68%. On admission, the patient had pancytopenia (normocytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, lymphopenia), worsening hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 15.3 mg/dL), elevated lactate dehydrogenase (477 U/L), prolonged INR (1.5), and hypoalbuminemia (1.4 g/dL). Positron emission tomography showed hypermetabolic splenomegaly, mediastinal and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, and marrow abnormalities. Endoscopic ultrasound again demonstrated widespread enlarged lymph nodes from the supraclavicular area to the liver. Liver, spleen, and lymph-node biopsies were normal. Bone marrow biopsy showed normocellular marrow with mild erythroid hyperplasia. Serologic testing revealed positive CMV IgM and IgG, positive EBV IgG, and positive EBV nuclear antibody; tests for hepatitis viruses, HIV, parvovirus, Histoplasma, and β-D glucan were negative. Autoimmune markers (ANA, AMA, anti–smooth-muscle antibody) were negative.

A 53-year-old woman with acute myeloid leukemia underwent allogeneic peripheral blood stem cell transplantation from her HLA-matched sister 42 days earlier after a reduced-intensity conditioning regimen. Graft-versus-host prophylaxis included cyclosporine and mycophenolate mofetil. Pre-transplant, she had a neutropenic fever treated with meropenem and vancomycin and received a 15-day course of methylprednisolone for possible engraftment fever.

She presented with fever, new-onset headache, confusion, and neck stiffness. Examination was limited by her altered mental status. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral thalamic and basal ganglia lesions that were hyperintense on T2-weighted images with peripheral contrast enhancement.

Empirically, meropenem was increased to 6 g/day and ampicillin to 8 g/day for suspected opportunistic infection, and methylprednisolone was replaced with dexamethasone for presumed raised intracranial pressure. Her neurologic status deteriorated, requiring intubation and transfer to the ICU.

Lumbar puncture revealed a protein of 375 mg/dL with normal glucose and white-cell count. CSF studies showed negative PCR assays for cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2, negative Mycobacterium PCR, and sterile fungal cultures.

A 7-year-old boy presented with left hip pain and inability to bear weight after a trivial fall one day earlier. He reported mild left hip pain for 3 weeks prior, worsened by the fall. There was no fever or other joint involvement.
