Examination showed decreased flexion (0–80°), internal rotation (0–20°), and external rotation (0–35°) of the left hip, inability to perform a straight-leg raise due to pain, a positive Patrick test, no swelling or erythema, and intact neurovascular status. Laboratory tests were unremarkable (C-reactive protein 5.8 mg/L; WBC count 7.5×10^9/L). 

Plain radiographs of the pelvis demonstrated a small lytic lesion with surrounding sclerosis at the inferomedial aspect of the left femoral neck on anteroposterior and lateral views. 

Computed tomography of the hips revealed well-defined bilateral lesions in the inferomedial aspects of the femoral necks, measuring 7×3 mm on the left and 2×1 mm on the right, each with a sclerotic border, small cortical defect, and fat density. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis showed minimal left hip joint effusion and loculated fluid in the trochanteric bursa, the largest measuring 0.9×1.5 cm.

A 68-year-old Japanese man with systemic AL amyloidosis, diagnosed in 1999 by kidney and bone marrow biopsy and treated with intermittent melphalan-prednisone for seven years, presented with fatigue, exertional dyspnea, and bilateral lower-extremity edema. Two months before admission, dyspnea on exertion began; one month before, chest radiographs showed bilateral pleural effusions, worse on the right. Weekly thoracentesis removed 1 L of yellow serous fluid from the right hemithorax; fluid analysis showed a nucleated cell count of 2600/mm³ (24% neutrophils, 71% lymphocytes), total protein 0.4 g/dl (pleural-to-serum ratio 0.11), LDH 26 IU/l (ratio 0.12), cholesterol 11 mg/dl, glucose 118 mg/dl—consistent with a transudate. Pleural cytology was negative for malignancy; cultures for bacteria, fungi, and mycobacteria were negative. Diuretics failed to reduce the effusion, which rapidly reaccumulated within one week of drainage, so he was admitted for refractory pleural effusion.

On admission, he was comfortable at rest. Temperature was 36.5 °C, blood pressure 124/69 mm Hg, pulse 84 beats/min. Examination revealed diminished breath sounds over the right lower lung field, slight coarse crackles at the left base, and lower-extremity edema. Laboratory studies showed BUN 31 mg/dl, creatinine 1.3 mg/dl, creatinine clearance 39 ml/min/1.73 m², 24-hour proteinuria 3.5 g, total protein 4.6 g/dl, and serum albumin 1.6 g/dl—findings consistent with nephritic syndrome and renal insufficiency, but unchanged from one year earlier. Serum protein electrophoresis was negative for a monoclonal spike, immunoglobulin levels were normal, and troponin T and CRP were normal. Echocardiography showed symmetric LV wall thickening (interventricular septum 14 mm; posterior wall 15 mm) with slightly increased echogenicity and preserved function (fractional shortening 40%; ejection fraction 0.71), suggesting infiltrative cardiomyopathy without acute heart failure. Chest radiograph demonstrated moderate right and slight left pleural effusions; chest CT confirmed moderate right effusion with right lower-lobe atelectasis.

A 43-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with fever up to 41°C, vomiting, diarrhea, and severe pain in the distal parts of her fingers and toes. She had undergone splenectomy at age 18 for immune thrombocytopenic purpura; pneumococcal vaccination had lapsed more than 5 years earlier. On examination, temperature was 36.3°C, heart rate 94/min, blood pressure 111/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Both fingers and toes were symmetrically cyanotic and extremely tender.

Laboratory studies showed: CRP 291 mg/L; hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL; white blood cell count 17.8×10^3/μL; platelet count 63×10^3/μL; INR 1.99; fibrinogen 82 mg/dL; D-dimer >35 000 ng/mL; von Willebrand factor antigen 200%; ADAMTS13 activity 17%; serum creatinine 2.55 mg/dL; LDH 783 IU/L; total bilirubin 1.1 mg/dL; schistocytes <1%; direct Coombs test negative; haptoglobin 1.76 g/L; complement C3 0.92 g/L; C4 0.32 g/L; ANCA, anticardiolipin antibodies, and cryoglobulins negative. Urinalysis revealed 5 RBCs/hpf, 8 WBCs/hpf, proteinuria of 0.83 g/g creatinine, and albuminuria of 316 mg/g creatinine.

Blood cultures drawn on admission grew Streptococcus pneumoniae (serogroup 24) after 9 hours of incubation.

A 56-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of bitemporal hemianopia and left labial numbness. On examination, he had visual impairment, bitemporal hemianopia, and right abducens nerve palsy. Laboratory studies showed: TSH 0.658 μU/mL, free thyroxine 0.41 ng/dL, growth hormone 0.62 ng/mL, LH < 0.2 mIU/mL, FSH < 1.0 mIU/mL, prolactin 19.7 ng/mL, cortisol 0.5 μg/dL, ACTH 16.4 pg/mL, testosterone < 5.0 ng/dL, and IGF-1 119 ng/mL (−0.73 SD), consistent with hypopituitarism. Dynamic pituitary stimulation tests confirmed gonadotropin, thyroid, and adrenal axis deficiencies and severe GH deficiency. Serum IgG4 was elevated at 319 mg/dL (normal 4.8–105), with a normal total IgG of 1284 mg/dL (IgG4/IgG ratio 0.25).  
Pituitary MRI demonstrated diffuse swelling of the pituitary body and stalk, a 7-mm poorly enhancing mass in the right anterior lobe, loss of the posterior pituitary bright spot on T1-weighted images, and thickening of the sphenoid sinus mucosa. Chest CT revealed a nodular lesion in the left lung field, raising suspicion for systemic IgG4-related disease. No other organ involvement was identified on systemic imaging.  
Given the combination of hypopituitarism, elevated IgG4 levels, and imaging findings, the patient underwent endoscopic transnasal surgery of the pituitary gland for definitive diagnosis.

A 70-year-old man with hypertension and a remote stroke presented with a 3-month history of an unpleasant burning sensation of the distal upper and lower extremities and scalp. He denied weakness or autonomic symptoms. Over the preceding 4 years, he had episodic exertional dyspnea, initially stable but with gradual progression in the months before presentation, coinciding with the onset of dysesthesia. He also noted nonprogressive bilateral lower limb swelling for 6 months. He had no cough, wheeze, fever, weight loss, or known tuberculosis exposure.

Initial high-resolution CT of the chest revealed reticular opacities in bilateral upper and lower lobes and two irregular soft-tissue nodules, suggestive of old healed granulomatous infection. Two years later, repeat HRCT and contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) showed multiple reticular nodular opacities, horizontal fissure thickening, and pretracheal, right paratracheal, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. At three years, CECT of the chest demonstrated bilateral centrilobular “tree-in-bud” opacities with fibrotic changes; concurrent CECT of the abdomen revealed bilateral cortical hypodense renal lesions (3–5 cm each) without arterial phase enhancement. Mantoux tests, sputum GeneXpert, BAL GeneXpert (four samples over 4 years), and EBUS-guided lymph node biopsy were all negative for tuberculosis.

On examination, BMI was 23 kg/m2, he was pale with bilateral pitting ankle edema, and no lymphadenopathy. Neurologically, he had a right-sided hemisensory deficit from his prior stroke and subjective dysesthesia but no objective peripheral neuropathy. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL with macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils, persistently elevated ESR (> 100 mm/h over 4 years), and normal renal function. Nerve conduction studies demonstrated mononeuritis multiplex. Given the bilateral renal cortical lesions, a renal biopsy was performed.

A 73-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of trismus and then sudden respiratory distress with cyanosis. She had no relevant past medical history and took only macrogol, escitalopram, mometasone, indapamide, and lorazepam; she had no history of antipsychotic or antiemetic use. Vaccination history was unknown, and she had no substance abuse. On examination she was alert, with trismus and mild neck rigidity but normal motor strength, sensation, and reflexes; the remainder of the physical exam was unremarkable. Laboratory tests, brain and neck CT, and CSF analysis were all normal; cultures were sterile. Empiric treatment for tetanus was initiated with antitoxin, vaccination, and metronidazole. Over the first 12 hours her condition remained stable with persistent trismus. Twenty-four hours after admission she experienced sudden respiratory collapse with a 2-minute hypoxic cardiac arrest. After sedation was discontinued she continued to require ventilatory support for persistent trismus but had no new focal deficits.

A 34-year-old man presented with a history of trivial trauma and a painful, deformed right leg. He reported longstanding stiffness and deformities of multiple joints. He was of short stature with bilateral fixed flexion deformities of the elbows and grossly restricted movements at the shoulders, elbows, and wrists. He had a short trunk without spinal deformity, bilateral coxa vara of the hips, and fixed flexion deformities of both knees. Examination of the right leg revealed clinical signs consistent with a proximal tibial fracture. Laboratory studies showed a vitamin D3 level of 5 ng/mL (reference range, 25–80 ng/mL), normal serum calcium and phosphate levels, normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein levels, normal parathyroid hormone level, and a negative rheumatoid factor. Radiographs demonstrated decreased bone stock, cortical thinning, multiple intra-articular loose bodies around the knees, significant joint-space narrowing, dysplastic femoral condyles, platyspondyly of the cervical and dorsolumbar spine, bilateral coxa vara with dysplastic proximal femora, and dysplastic radial heads and distal humeri at the elbows.

A 58-year-old white man with a history of hemophilia A (baseline factor VIII activity 12%), type 2 diabetes mellitus, and prior testicular cancer presented with bright red blood per rectum. During evaluation, abdominal CT revealed an incidental 18 × 17 × 16 cm heterogeneous, hemorrhagic mass in the left suprarenal fossa exerting mass effect on the stomach, pancreatic tail, and left kidney. Physical examination was notable only for a large, firm, nonpulsatile, nontender mass in the left upper quadrant. He was normotensive, not tachycardic, normokalemic, and had no cushingoid features or gynecomastia. He received recombinant factor VIII to maintain activity between 80% and 100%. Comprehensive biochemical evaluation for a functional adrenal lesion—including plasma metanephrine (<0.20 nmol/L), normetanephrine (0.22 nmol/L), 17-hydroxyprogesterone (74.6 ng/dl), estradiol (30 pg/ml), dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (43 μg/dl), dexamethasone suppression tests, adrenocorticotropic hormone (27 pg/ml), aldosterone (3 ng/dl), renin activity (8.5 ng/ml/h), and androstenedione (0.215 ng/ml)—showed no evidence of hormone overproduction. On further questioning, he recalled a minor fall weeks earlier, suggested as a possible cause of hemorrhage. A repeat CT at 4 weeks showed no change in size; at 7 weeks, he reported early satiety and left upper-quadrant discomfort but imaging remained unchanged. Given the persistence of the mass and new symptoms, surgical resection was planned.

A 17-year-old Caucasian woman was admitted with seven days of malaise, fevers (to 39°C), chills, anorexia, vomiting, and scleral jaundice. Two days earlier she had discontinued norethisterone for polycystic ovaries. She lived in Athens, did not consume alcohol or illicit drugs, and reported no exposure to rat excrement.

On examination, temperature was 38.8°C. She had mild epigastric tenderness without hepatosplenomegaly or stigmata of chronic liver disease, and mild slurring of speech; the remainder of the exam was normal.

Laboratory studies revealed:
• White-cell count 16,770/mm3 (80% neutrophils)  
• Hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, hematocrit 28.3%, reticulocytes 6%  
• Platelets 240,000/mm3; ESR 36 mm/h; peripheral smear normal  
• INR 2.76, aPTT 72.11 s  
• Glucose 49 mg/dL; creatinine 0.79 mg/dL; albumin 2.8 g/dL  
• Alkaline phosphatase 32 IU/L, ALT 33 IU/L, AST 140 IU/L  
• Total bilirubin 27.79 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 16.44 mg/dL; GGT 184 IU/L

Serologic tests for hepatitis A, B, and C viruses; cytomegalovirus; and HIV types 1 and 2 were negative, as were tests for ANA and AMA. A serum acetaminophen level was undetectable, and blood cultures were negative. A serologic test for Leptospira interrogans was positive (IgM > 1:80), and treatment with penicillin G was initiated.

Although she became afebrile, her mental status deteriorated with drowsiness and flapping tremor. Repeat labs showed total bilirubin 66.7 mg/dL, INR 7.7, ammonia 95.7 μmol/L, and hematocrit 17.6% from hemolysis; a Coombs’ test was negative. She received lactulose, neomycin, packed red blood cells, fresh frozen plasma, glucose, and vitamin K without correction of the coagulopathy. Her Nazer score was 8, consistent with fulminant hepatic failure, and she was referred for emergency liver transplantation.

A 9-month-old Sudanese boy was referred for evaluation of hypercalcemia. He was born at term to healthy first-degree–related parents after an uncomplicated pregnancy, with low birth weight. Since age 2 weeks he had irritability on handling, painful pigmented swellings over the knuckles, and progressive deformities of the elbows, wrists, hips, knees, and ankles. Over the next 6 months he developed recurrent infections, oral thrush, diarrhea, constipation, vomiting, poor feeding, and failure to gain weight, with delayed gross and fine motor milestones; there were no polyuria, seizures, or fractures. He had been diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis and treated with corticosteroids for 6 months without improvement. Routine tests at that time showed serum calcium 18 mg/dl, alkaline phosphatase 93 U/l, and PTH 69.1 pg/ml (normal 10–65 pg/ml). 

On examination he was a hypotonic, nondysmorphic infant with gingival hypertrophy, an umbilical hernia, and no organomegaly. He had tender, hyperpigmented nodules over the elbows, wrists, fingers, knees, and ankles, with limited joint movement, and a diffuse tender erythematous swelling in the lumbosacral region. Weight was 4.7 kg (–4 SD), length 60 cm (–3 SD), head circumference 42.2 cm (3rd percentile), with a wide anterior fontanel, consistent with severe malnutrition. 

Laboratory studies revealed serum calcium 18 mg/dl, phosphate 2.5 mg/dl, PTH 166 pg/ml (15–65 pg/ml), 25-hydroxy vitamin D 8.61 ng/ml, and a urinary calcium-creatinine ratio of 0.062. ESR was 10 mm/h, CRP 1.9 mg/dl; urine culture grew Escherichia coli; hemoglobin 8.7 g/dl; white cells 14 800/mm3 (56% neutrophils); platelets 960 000/mm3; renal function was normal except for hyponatremia and hypokalemia. 

Radiographs of the long bones showed osteopenia. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated chronic renal parenchymal changes, medullary nephrocalcinosis, and multiple nonobstructing renal stones. Neck ultrasound revealed small lower cervical lesions suggestive of a thyroid nodule, parathyroid adenoma, or lymph node.

A 30-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of pain and swelling in both lateral lower legs. He reported recurrent aphthous ulcers since his early twenties, a single painful scrotal ulcer, and intermittent papulopustular skin lesions on the neck, upper back, and lower extremities. Five years earlier, he had a right calf episode of pain and erythematous swelling diagnosed as cellulitis and myositis; MRI had shown a 1 cm T1-low/T2-high lesion in the right gastrocnemius with muscle and subcutaneous edema, but tissue cultures were negative. Similar unilateral or bilateral leg myalgias recurred every few months, sometimes with fever and overlying erythema, resolving in 4–7 days with NSAIDs. One month prior to presentation, he was treated elsewhere for fever and left calf pain; MRI again showed an abscess-like lesion in the left gastrocnemius with muscle, fascia, and subcutaneous edema, and he received antibiotics plus low-dose prednisone. Sixteen days after discontinuing medications, he developed severe bilateral distal leg pain and swelling. On examination, he had tenderness of the lower extremities and a few folliculitis lesions. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 9.44×10^9/L (72.6% neutrophils), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 47 mm/h, C-reactive protein 3.31 mg/dL, and HLA-B51 positivity; renal and liver function, serum creatine kinase, and electrolytes were normal. Ultrasonography demonstrated diffuse swelling with heterogeneous echogenicity in the peroneus longus muscle.

An 8-year-old boy from southern Saudi Arabia presented with a 3-month history of perianal pain, constipation, and gluteal swelling associated with intermittent low-grade fever. He underwent incision of a presumed gluteal abscess and received antibiotics without improvement. On referral, he reported episodic fever, decreased oral intake, dysuria with urinary frequency and scant output, and back pain partially relieved by acetaminophen. On examination, he was febrile and underweight, with a firm erythematous gluteal mass extending to the perianal region and bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL, hematocrit 0.353 L/L, MCV 59 fL, WBC 16.74 × 10^9/L with 2.3 × 10^9/L eosinophils, ESR 88 mm/h, CRP 205 mg/dL, and creatinine 44 mg/dL; blood and urine cultures were negative. Ultrasound, CT, MRI, and PET/CT demonstrated a hypermetabolic mass arising from the bladder base/prostate with intravesical extension, involvement of the left pelvic sidewall and obturator internus muscle, a large left gluteal subcutaneous mass, bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy, and left hydroureteronephrosis. An initial diagnosis of bladder-base rhabdomyosarcoma with obstructive uropathy was made. Cystoscopy-guided biopsies of the bladder neck and posterior urethra showed benign urothelium with polypoid cystitis and acute and chronic inflammation, findings deemed inconsistent with rhabdomyosarcoma. A bone marrow biopsy showed normocellular marrow without evidence of leukemia, lymphoma, or nonhematopoietic malignancy.

A 30-year-old man presented with a history of absence of the right testis in the scrotum since birth. At age 15, he noticed a right-sided perineal swelling that grew progressively in size. The swelling was initially painless but over the past year became painful on sitting; there was no history of pain or increase in size on standing, fevers, nausea, or vomiting. He denied urinary or sexual dysfunction, prior surgeries, regular medications, or a family history of similar problems.

On examination, the right hemiscrotum was hypoplastic, and the left testis in the scrotum was normal in size, shape, and consistency. On the right perineum there was a 1 × 1 cm well-circumscribed, oval, firm, freely mobile, non-tender mass with normal, pinchable overlying skin. 

A provisional diagnosis of perineal ectopic testis was made, with a differential of lipoma, sebaceous cyst, dermoid cyst, and abscess. Ultrasonography of the perineal mass revealed a homogeneous, well vascularized, testicular-like structure with a volume of 6.5 cc; the left intrascrotal testis measured 7.6 cc with normal echotexture.

A female infant was born at 40 + 3 weeks’ gestation (birth weight 3117 g) by vacuum-assisted delivery for fetal decelerations and failure to progress. Apgar scores were 7 and 8 at 1 and 5 minutes. Over the first 18 hours, she had mild hypoglycemia and temperature instability, prompting admission to the NICU. She then developed moderate respiratory distress and regurgitation of feeds. At 19 hours of life, arterial blood gas analysis showed: pH 7.26, pCO2 12 mmHg, pO2 131 mmHg, bicarbonate 5 mmol/L; serum lactate was 19.8 mmol/L (reference < 2.2 mmol/L). Liver tests were abnormal (AST 243 U/L, ALT 54 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 333 U/L). At 24 hours, thiamine (100 mg every 12 h) and biotin (8 mg every 12 h) were started and continued for 4 days. Over the next 24 hours, lactate levels, blood glucose, and respiratory status improved. Echocardiography and creatine kinase were normal. At 21 hours of life, metabolic studies showed: plasma amino acids with elevated alanine, proline, glutamine, and tyrosine; urine organic acids with increased lactic acid and tyrosine metabolites; and an acylcarnitine profile revealing increased glutarylcarnitine and multiple long-chain species.

A 34-year-old gravida 3 para 2 woman with a spontaneous monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy was referred at 20 weeks for suspected growth restriction in one twin. Twin 1 had an estimated fetal weight of 335 g, normal amniotic fluid, normal structural survey, unremarkable umbilical artery and ductus venosus Doppler studies, and a middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity of 19 cm/s (0.74 MoM), suggestive of polycythemia. Twin 2 had severe growth restriction (EFW 118 g; 65% discordance), anhydramnios, an empty bladder, a pericardial effusion, absent end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery, a reversed a-wave in the ductus venosus, and a middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity of 52 cm/s (2 MoM), suggestive of anemia. The placental region of twin 2 appeared thickened (7 cm) with multiple cysts. The working diagnosis was severe early-onset discordant growth related to diandric triploidy or partial mole in one twin with associated twin anemia polycythemia sequence. Parents were offered amniocentesis of twin 1 and chorionic villus sampling of twin 2 but declined invasive testing.

A 19-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with a 2-week history of sudden left-sided chest pain, dyspnea, and fever. Physical examination was unremarkable. Pulmonary function testing, electrocardiography, bronchoscopy, and coronary angiography showed no abnormalities. A posteroanterior and lateral chest radiograph revealed a well-demarcated, homogeneous 6-cm mass in the left parahilar region. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a large, cystic anterior mediastinal mass lateralized to the left side without signs of local invasion, findings that “evok[ed] a cystic teratoma or a cystic thymoma.” Serum α-fetoprotein and β-human chorionic gonadotropin levels were within normal limits.

A 59-year-old man with a history of diabetes mellitus presented with one day of left-sided weakness, left facial paresis, difficulty speaking, and drowsiness. His NIH Stroke Scale score on admission was 10. He denied recent head trauma or family history of stroke or thrombosis. He was a non-smoker but used opiates.  

On examination, he was confused and could not follow commands. Temperature was 37.4 °C, blood pressure 150/90 mm Hg, heart rate 73 bpm, respiratory rate 16/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. There was no pallor, jaundice, petechiae, or organomegaly. Cranial-nerve exam was normal except for left facial paresis. Motor testing showed left hemiparesis (3/5 in the arm, 4/5 in the leg) with decreased pain response on the left and an upgoing plantar response on that side.  

An ECG showed normal sinus rhythm. A noncontrast head CT performed >24 h after symptom onset revealed an acute right MCA territory infarct in the right parietotemporal lobe. Twenty-four hours later, because of worsening consciousness, a repeat CT showed a new infarct in the left frontal lobe (left MCA territory).  

Initial laboratory results included a platelet count of 77 × 10^3/μL and hemoglobin 15 g/dL. Over the next several days, the platelet count declined to 21 × 10^3/μL, and hemoglobin fell to 11.8 g/dL. Reticulocytes were 2.6%, LDH was 1148 U/L, total bilirubin rose from 1.9 mg/dL to 4.4 mg/dL (indirect bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL), and acute-phase reactants (ESR, CRP, ferritin, fibrinogen, D-dimer) were elevated. Coagulation studies, troponin, liver function tests, lipid profile, and electrolytes were within normal limits. Peripheral blood smear showed occasional schistocytes. Direct and indirect Coombs tests were negative.

A 45-year-old man with a history of confluent erythematous and violaceous patches and plaques on the scalp—initially diagnosed as photodermatitis—presented with a new skin lesion on the left upper chest. The chest lesion was a sharply demarcated plaque with raised dusky, violaceous, and erythematous borders, central clearing, and an overlying scaly crust. Similar erythematous plaques were noted behind both ears. The lesions were nonpainful, nonpruritic, and there was no sensory loss. He denied systemic symptoms and reported prior improvement with oral steroids. There was no family history of autoimmune disease. On examination, there was no cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy, and hair and nail examinations were unremarkable.

A 47-year-old woman with iron deficiency anemia presented with acute left neck and upper chest swelling and a pressure sensation. The swelling began suddenly on the left side of her neck, increased in size over a few hours, and extended into the left upper chest. She denied fever, cough, chills, shortness of breath, discharge, insect bites, trauma, or recent medications; she had no known allergies.

On examination, she was alert and oriented. Vital signs were: blood pressure 126/86 mm Hg, heart rate 92 beats/min, respiratory rate 19 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 94% on room air, and temperature 37 °C. There was a left-sided neck swelling extending from the upper border of Zone 1 to below the left clavicle, which had expanded over 2 hours, with a clear line of demarcation. The trachea was deviated to the right, and carotid pulses were intact bilaterally.

Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 11.9 g/dl, hematocrit 36.4%, mean corpuscular volume 77.3 fl, mean corpuscular hemoglobin 25.3 pg, C-reactive protein within the reference range, INR 1.14, and a random blood sugar of 153 mg/dl.

A posteroanterior chest radiograph demonstrated rightward tracheal deviation, normal lung fields and cardiac silhouette, and visible left neck soft-tissue prominence. A contrast-enhanced CT scan revealed soft-tissue and subcutaneous edema involving the left neck region, extending to the left infraclavicular and mediastinal regions, without frank extravasation; a few prominent cervical lymph nodes were noted.

A 43-year-old man presented with progressive abdominal distention. He had a history of heavy weekend alcohol use but had quit. He recalled a severe upper respiratory infection before symptoms began. Initial labs showed an alkaline phosphatase level of 407 U/L and bilirubin 2.5 mg/dL; transaminases were normal. Abdominal CT revealed ascites and hepatosplenomegaly. Upper endoscopy demonstrated portal hypertensive gastropathy. An evaluation for chronic liver disease—including viral markers, transaminases, antinuclear, anti–smooth muscle, anti–mitochondrial antibodies, alpha-1 antitrypsin, and iron studies—was normal. His INR was 1.4 and platelet count 157,000/μL. He was treated for presumed alcoholic cirrhosis with diuretics and underwent liver MRI, which showed sequelae of portal hypertension but no steatosis or cirrhosis. Despite dietary sodium restriction and diuretics, he required frequent large-volume paracenteses. A transjugular liver biopsy revealed marked sinusoidal dilatation without fibrosis, steatosis, or granulomas. Hepatic venous pressure measurements showed a portosystemic gradient of 1 mm Hg, with right atrial and inferior vena cava pressures of 25 mm Hg. Ascitic fluid analysis demonstrated a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 1.6 g/dL, fluid albumin 2.7 g/dL, and total protein 4.4 g/dL; cytology was negative. Based on these findings, a cardiac cause of his ascites was suspected. Repeat examination revealed a jugular venous pressure of 14–16 cm H₂O and a paradoxical rise on inspiration (Kussmaul's sign).

A 49-year-old woman with a 10-year history of end-stage renal disease secondary to systemic lupus erythematosus and prior methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) bacteremia presented with prolonged, recurrent fevers. Four years earlier, she had an infected left upper–extremity hemodialysis graft. One month before this admission, she was hospitalized for MSSA bacteremia attributed to mastitis and was discharged on outpatient intravenous antibiotics. Despite compliance, she continued to have fevers up to 38.3 °C.

On readmission, laboratory studies showed a normal white-cell count, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 101 mm/h (reference range, 0–20), a C-reactive protein level of 10.7 mg/dL (reference range, 0.0–1.0), and persistent positive blood cultures for MSSA. Extensive clinical evaluation and conventional imaging failed to localize a source. She also reported left arm pain, prompting concern for infection of her abandoned left upper–arm vascular graft.

An 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron-emission tomography/computed tomography (18F-FDG PET/CT) study was obtained. It revealed a lobulated soft-tissue mass adjacent to the aortic arch with intense FDG uptake. There were also enlarged paratracheal mediastinal and bilateral axillary lymph nodes with mild FDG uptake. Neither the abandoned left upper-arm vascular graft nor a new right thigh hemodialysis graft showed abnormal FDG activity.

A 46-year-old woman presented with a long-standing history of low back pain radiating to the anterior aspect of the left thigh that was unresponsive to conservative therapy. She reported progressive difficulty with left hip flexion and numbness over the anterior left thigh. On examination, left hip flexion strength was 4−/5, and sensation was diminished in the L3 and L4 dermatomes of the left thigh. The left patellar reflex was absent, and sphincter function was normal. Laboratory studies, including inflammatory markers, were within normal limits.  
Lumbar MRI with T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and STIR sequences demonstrated a large mass at the L2–L3 level that had migrated from the anterior to the posterior epidural space, encasing the thecal sac and causing severe compression of the traversing nerve roots.

A 46-year-old woman with HIV on stable ART (tenofovir, lamivudine, dolutegravir) for 14 years and hypertension controlled by diet presented with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. On arrival: blood pressure 210/130 mmHg, pulse 96 bpm, respiratory rate 20/min, temperature 37.1 °C. Examination was notable only for elevated blood pressure; there was no abdominal tenderness and other findings were unremarkable. She received intravenous cimetidine 400 mg, followed 5 minutes later by oral nifedipine 30 mg. One hour later, she developed carpopedal spasm of the fingers, rigid plantar flexion of the feet, and could not stand. She also experienced severe retrosternal chest pain, shivering, chills, and shortness of breath. Blood pressure was 160/110 mmHg; there was no rash. She was administered intranasal oxygen, morphine 5 mg IV, and calcium gluconate 1 g IV over 30 minutes. The spasms resolved over the hour of calcium infusion, but chest pain persisted without ECG evidence of ischemia. Twelve hours later, chest pain diminished and she remained stable except for mild epigastric discomfort. Laboratory evaluation before calcium showed total serum calcium 7.1 mg/dL; two days later it was 8.8 mg/dL. Serum albumin was 5 g/L; sodium, potassium, and chloride were normal. CD4 count was 573 cells/mm³; complete blood count, renal and liver function tests were all normal. A brain CT scan showed no intracranial lesion. Tests for ionized calcium, parathyroid hormone, vitamin D, and phosphate were unavailable.

A 76-year-old woman with common variable immunodeficiency (diagnosed at age 60 and on weekly immunoglobulin infusions) was referred for evaluation of a four‐year history of worsening diarrhea and abdominal pain. She had a confirmed diagnosis of cytomegalovirus colitis by colonoscopic biopsy 4 years earlier and was treated sequentially with ganciclovir, foscarnet, and cidofovir, along with weekly IgG infusions. Despite these interventions, her symptoms persisted, and serial CMV viral loads continued to rise. Resistance testing detected a D843D/V mutation in the UL54 gene. Over the ensuing years, she received multiple therapies, including interferon alpha, valganciclovir, letermovir, leflunomide, and interleukin-2 injections, without clinical improvement. CT scans of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated progressive thickening of the colon, which initially involved only the ascending colon and cecum but later extended to the entire colon. A repeat colonoscopy revealed pan colitis with ulcerations and severe inflammation on biopsy.

A 14-year-old girl presented to the emergency department with left lower extremity bruising, swelling, and pain. Two months earlier, during a softball game, she collided with another player’s cleat and was diagnosed that day with a hairline fracture of the left tibial diaphysis with an overlying hematoma. She followed up with orthopedics, completed physical therapy, and was cleared to resume sports six weeks before this presentation. Six days prior, she played two softball games, denying any significant trauma or sliding events during these games. Five days before presentation, she awoke with pain and bruising of her left lateral shin and treated her pain with ibuprofen—the first NSAID she had taken in two months. Over the next days, her pain and bruising worsened, and she noted edema of the left calf. 

On re-presentation, she required morphine for pain. Vital signs showed mild hypertension; all other vitals were normal. Examination revealed extensive bruising, edema, and pain with light palpation or weight-bearing of the left calf; no erythema, abrasions, or skin tightness; distal dorsalis pedis pulses were 2/4 and symmetric; Homan sign was negative. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, complete metabolic panel, prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time, creatine kinase, C-reactive protein, lactate dehydrogenase, and uric acid, were within normal limits for age. 

Frontal and lateral radiographs of the left leg demonstrated anterior, medial, and lateral subcutaneous soft-tissue edema of the proximal and mid leg. An ultrasound showed a complex fluid collection in the lateral subcutaneous soft tissues, prompting further evaluation with MRI.

A 29-year-old Caucasian man with a history of hepatitis C, posttraumatic stress disorder, polysubstance abuse, and tobacco use was brought to the emergency department after being found agitated and erratically wandering the streets and then unresponsive with multiple skin abrasions. He reported ingestion and insufflation of “bath salts,” a history later confirmed by his family. He denied other medications or supplements and had no known drug allergies.

On examination, temperature was 107°F, blood pressure 91/52 mm Hg, and pulse 93/min. He was confused and intermittently agitated, with pupils 3 mm and equal. Cardiovascular exam showed weak peripheral pulses without jugular venous distention or murmurs; lungs were clear; abdomen was soft; no focal neurologic deficits.

Laboratory studies on admission showed features of severe rhabdomyolysis. Serologic testing confirmed chronic hepatitis C but was otherwise unremarkable. Serum toxicology tests were negative for ethanol, acetaminophen, and salicylates. Urine toxicology detected only lorazepam and cotinine but was negative for over 80 other substances, including cannabinoids, cocaine, ecstasy, ephedrine, lysergide, methamphetamine, methylphenidate, oxycodone, and phencyclidine.

Noncontrast CT of the head, MRI of the cervical spine, EEG, and chest and abdominal radiographs were normal. Right upper-quadrant ultrasonography revealed gallbladder calculi, a normal pancreatic duct, and an echogenic right kidney with prominent corticomedullary differentiation.

He received aggressive IV fluids, a norepinephrine infusion, and a bolus of amiodarone. Hyperkalemia was treated with sodium polystyrene sulfonate, calcium gluconate, insulin with glucose, and IV bicarbonate. For severe hyperthermia, he was given dantrolene and placed on cooling blankets. He was sedated, intubated, and mechanically ventilated, and received rasburicase for hyperuricemia. Urine output was 4200 mL over the first 24 hours, then declined to 825 mL and 150 mL over subsequent 24-hour periods. He was started on daily hemodialysis for volume control and solute clearance.

A 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension was brought to the emergency department with a decreased level of consciousness of unknown duration. He was last seen awake at 6 p.m. the previous evening after dinner and his usual medications, and was found unconscious at home at 2 a.m. Two recent falls were reported, one two days earlier and another the same morning. There was no history of fever, convulsions, chest pain, cough, rash, decreased urine output, or substance use.

On arrival, he was unresponsive with a snoring airway. Vital signs were: temperature 97 °F, blood pressure 140/70 mmHg, pulse rate 68 bpm, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Neurologic examination revealed a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 7 (E1V2M4); pupils were 2 mm bilaterally with sluggish reaction to light; deep tendon reflexes were hypoactive, and plantar responses were extensor bilaterally.

A point-of-care glucose measurement was 19 mg/dL. After administration of 50 mL of 50% dextrose, his blood glucose normalized to 110 mg/dL, but his Glasgow Coma Scale remained at E1V1M4. Arterial blood gas analysis showed compensated metabolic acidosis. A noncontrast CT scan of the head revealed no evidence of ischemic changes, intracranial hemorrhage, or space-occupying lesions. 

Subsequent brain MRI demonstrated signal changes with restricted diffusion in the bilateral cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, and caudate nuclei, findings suggestive of ischemia with cortical necrosis likely due to hypoxic–ischemic injury.

A 68-year-old retired man with no prior medical history presented with two months of dorsal spine pain and gradually progressive motor weakness of the left lower extremity. One week before admission, his weakness acutely worsened, rendering him unable to stand or walk without assistance; there was no history of trauma.  

On neurologic examination, he had spastic paraparesis with weakness of the quadriceps, hamstrings, ankle dorsiflexors, and toe extensors on the left. Patellar and ankle jerks were increased, with sustained clonus at the left ankle and bilateral Babinski signs. Superficial hypoesthesia was present below the T7 level, and bladder and bowel function were preserved.  

Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervico-thoracic spine revealed a well-circumscribed, extra-axial mass posterolateral to the right side of the spinal cord at C7–T1, causing marked canal stenosis and cord deformation. The lesion was intermediate in signal intensity on T1-weighted images and homogeneously low in signal on T2-weighted images. On fat-saturated postcontrast T1-weighted images, it demonstrated a thin rim of enhancement with no internal enhancement.

A 49-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an incidental low-density area on liver CT, initially suspected to represent peliosis hepatis. Her history included an acute myocardial infarction treated with percutaneous coronary intervention at age 49 and treatment of a large left internal carotid aneurysm and right middle cerebral artery aneurysm at age 45. Laboratory studies showed a normal blood count and no elevation in liver enzymes. Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI of the liver revealed an early and persistently enhancing hypervascular nodule in segment 7, multiple small enhancing lesions consistent with telangiectases, and early opacification of the portal and hepatic veins, indicating arterioportal and arteriovenous shunts. There were no signs of portal hypertension, although the portal vein was dilated. Follow-up ultrasound showed stability of the nodule.  

One year later, she presented with anemia (hemoglobin, 6.0 g/dL). Gastrointestinal endoscopy was negative, but capsule endoscopy identified multiple angiodysplasias in the small intestine. Two years later, anemia recurred (hemoglobin, 8.9 g/dL), and gastric angiodysplasias were treated with argon plasma coagulation. Several years afterward, a chest CT incidentally revealed a small pulmonary arteriovenous fistula. Detailed history taking uncovered recurrent spontaneous epistaxis beginning in her teens. She had no visible cutaneous telangiectasia and no known family history of similar symptoms; her mother had died suddenly at age 29, and her two adult children had no history of epistaxis.

A 79-year-old Hispanic woman presented with a one-week history of a painful rash on her palms and soles. She reported no recent viral illness, travel, previous rashes, joint pains, or new lotion, soap, or fabric exposures. Her history was notable for metastatic colon cancer treated with radiation and hemicolectomy three years earlier; she was in the second week of capecitabine therapy (1250 mg/m2 twice daily). She had no other medications. On examination, she was afebrile, normotensive, and appeared chronically ill. Her palms and soles were tender, erythematous, and diffusely edematous, with desquamation over the fingertips and toes. Laboratory studies, including a complete metabolic panel and complete blood count, were within normal limits.

A 3-year-old girl of Greek descent was evaluated for gait disturbance and undiagnosed skin lesions. She had delayed motor milestones, standing at 13 months and walking at 16 months, and spoke 8–10 words by 16 months. There was no history of seizures. She was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy to a consanguineous couple.

On examination, she had extensive hyperkeratosis and scaling of the skin, especially on the palms and soles, and hyperpigmented flexures. Neurologic examination revealed spastic diplegia of the lower extremities, mild generalized hypertonia, brisk deep tendon reflexes in the legs, and bilateral Babinski signs. Growth parameters and head circumference were within normal limits. Cognitive testing showed an IQ of 95.

Electroencephalography, otoacoustic emissions testing, abdominal and renal ultrasound, and chest and hip radiographs were normal. Brain MRI disclosed diffuse symmetrical high-intensity lesions in the deep white matter of the centrum semiovale and frontal lobes and milder lesions in the posterior parietal lobes and corpus callosum. Brain MRS demonstrated increased lipid and myoinositol levels, with normal N-acetylaspartate, choline, and creatine peaks.

Ophthalmologic evaluation, including fundoscopy and optical coherence tomography, showed no retinal pathology. Cycloplegic refraction revealed high myopic error, and visual acuity with correction was attributed to refractive amblyopia.

Skin biopsy specimens demonstrated orthokeratotic hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and papillomatosis of the stratum spinosum.

A 24-year-old heterosexual man with a recent diagnosis of HIV infection presented for his first HIV clinic visit. He reported a nonpruritic, nonpainful rash on the upper arms for 2 months that had progressed to involve the face, bilateral upper thighs, and scrotum. A biopsy of the rash performed at an outside institution revealed non-necrotizing granulomatous inflammation, and he was treated with steroids for 1 week without improvement.

On examination, he had indurated papules with a rubbery texture across the lower legs, upper thighs, arms, back, scrotum, soles of the feet, and perioral area. Occasional lesions were annular or macular with intermittent fine scales. As part of the routine evaluation of a new HIV-infected patient, a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test was performed and showed a titer of 1:512. A complete chemistry and metabolic panel were within normal limits other than elevated protein in the urine.

A 67-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia (BMI 32 kg/m²) underwent elective dynamic hip screw fixation for an intertrochanteric fracture. She received opioids for postoperative pain control for three days. On postoperative day 2, she reported gradual abdominal distention with gas and stool retention. Examination revealed a soft, tympanitic abdomen with normal bowel sounds. Vital signs were: BP 140/70 mmHg, HR 95 beats/min, SaO₂ 97%, and temperature 38.0 °C. Laboratory tests showed WBC 11.1×10⁹/L, hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL, urea 86 mg/dL, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, potassium 3.77 mmol/L, glucose 263 mg/dL, and CRP 0.5 mg/dL. Digital rectal examination yielded a small amount of stool, and enemas released minimal gas and mucus. She remained under observation. On postoperative day 9, the abdomen was grossly distended, severely tympanitic, diffusely tender, and bowel sounds were diminished. An abdominal CT scan (no plain films were possible) demonstrated massive colonic dilatation, with the cecal diameter measuring 92.4 mm.

A 12-year-old Syrian boy was brought to the pediatric emergency department with fatigue, dizziness, and palpitations. He had a history of recurrent seizures diagnosed as epilepsy based on EEG showing centro-parietal theta rhythmic activity with 2–3 Hz generalized waves and spikes, and he had been taking sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily. On examination, he was alert; blood pressure was 90/60 mm Hg, and the pulse was rapid and feeble. ECG showed sustained wide QRS tachycardia mimicking a left bundle branch block morphology in the superior axis. Intravenous amiodarone up to 15 mg/kg was ineffective, and synchronized DC cardioversion restored sinus rhythm. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, electrolytes (K⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, Na⁺), creatinine, and TSH, were all within normal limits. A 12-lead ECG in sinus rhythm demonstrated right bundle branch block, T-wave inversion, and ε waves in leads V1 to V5. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed right ventricular structural alteration with blood stagnation; the parasternal short-axis RV outflow tract measured 35 mm, and there was regional right ventricular dyskinesia.

A 62‐year‐old man with end‐stage diabetic nephropathy has been on hemodialysis for two years. Two years earlier he underwent transmetatarsal amputation of the right foot and amputation of two toes of the left foot. His medications include insulin and lanthanum carbonate; he is not taking vitamin K antagonists. He has chronic ulcerated wounds on his lower limbs. He first noted painful, whitish macules on the glans penis, surrounded by erythema and mild pruritus. Candidiasis was diagnosed clinically and treated with topical antifungal agents without improvement. A biopsy of the balanic mucosa led to a diagnosis of lichen planus, and topical steroids were prescribed. 

Three months later, he returned with a diffuse whitish “cardboard” appearance of the balanic mucosa that was subjectively painless and an area of necrosis around the urinary meatus. On examination, the distal phalanges of the right hand also showed early digital necrosis. Laboratory studies showed a serum phosphorus level of 0.71 mmol/L, a calcium level of 2.20 mmol/L, and an intact parathyroid hormone level of 181 pg/mL. Computed tomography angiography of the trunk and right upper limb revealed calcification of the aorta and of the radial and ulnar arteries. Doppler ultrasound of the right upper limb showed arterial wall calcification at the antebrachial bifurcation with absent flow in the interosseous artery.

An 80-year-old woman was admitted to psychiatry for adjustment of her therapy. Three months earlier, she had complained of anxiety, anhedonia, loneliness, fatigue, and fear of living alone after the death of her only son. She was initially diagnosed with adjustment disorder with depressed mood. Despite trials of several antidepressants, she developed apathy, loosely structured delusions (guilt, hypochondriac, and nihilistic), reduced speech output, psychomotor retardation, and pseudocatatonic postures. She was then diagnosed with a major depressive episode with catatonia, and eight bilateral electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) sessions were administered over 25 days without any clinical improvement.

During and after the ECT course, she became progressively disoriented, inattentive, and perseverative; her speech became hypophonic, monotonous, and sparse, with naming difficulty and impaired comprehension of complex commands. She developed rigidity, postural tremor, bradykinesia, and gait disturbances and became wheelchair bound. There was no myoclonus, ataxia, or pyramidal tract signs. 

Given the lack of response to ECT and the new neurological signs, a neurologic consultation was requested. Blood and cerebrospinal fluid studies, electroencephalography (EEG) before and after treatment with levetiracetam, and brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were performed. MRI diffusion-weighted imaging showed bilateral parieto-occipital cortical hyperintensities with reduced apparent diffusion coefficient; minimal changes were seen on FLAIR sequences. EEG demonstrated diffuse periodic sharp-wave complexes predominantly in the left hemisphere that did not change with antiepileptic treatment. CSF analysis was positive for 14-3-3 protein. At that point, a diagnosis of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease was suggested.

An 11-year-old boy with no personal or family history of epilepsy began at age 6 with brief (seconds to 2 minutes) stereotyped episodes of seeing colorful objects in the left visual field, accompanied by pallor, headache, and hypersomnolence. Valproic acid was initiated, and these events remained isolated for one year. At age 7, he had a left hemibody tonic-clonic seizure with postictal weakness, leading to the addition of levetiracetam. By age 9, he developed weekly episodes characterized by visual hallucinations followed by impaired awareness, oral and manual automatisms, left hemibody dystonia, and occasional secondary generalization, accompanied by psychomotor regression and declining school performance. A brain MRI at that time was normal, and clobazam was added. Over the next two years, seizures continued twice weekly despite therapy with carbamazepine, levetiracetam, and clobazam. 

On examination in November 2023, he was alert and interactive. Neurological evaluation revealed mild left hemiparesis and asymmetry of muscle tone, without sensory deficits or reflex asymmetry. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed 1 WBC/mm3 and normal glucose, protein, and lactate. Thyroid function tests, antinuclear antibody screening, complement levels, viral serologies for VZV, CMV, hepatitis B and C, and onconeural markers were all within normal limits or negative. 

Interictal EEG demonstrated repetitive slow-wave discharges originating in the right occipital region and spreading ipsilaterally. Perictal EEG showed occipital background slowing with diffuse delta activity progressing centrally, followed by rhythmic acceleration. A repeat brain MRI revealed marked right hemispheric atrophy. FDG-PET demonstrated diffuse hypometabolism throughout the right frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes and ipsilateral basal ganglia.

A 69-year-old woman with a history of hypertension presented with upper abdominal pain. She was found to be hepatitis C virus–RNA positive. On admission, her white-cell count was 5200/mm3 and C-reactive protein was 0.64 mg/dL. Liver tests showed AST 42 IU/L, ALT 27 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 479 IU/L, leucine aminopeptidase 93 IU/L, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 55 IU/L, and albumin 3.9 g/dL. Tumor markers revealed PIVKA-II of 181 mAU/mL and AFP of 7 ng/mL. Enhanced CT demonstrated an 81×65 mm lesion in segment 3 of the liver with rim enhancement and central hypoattenuating nodules. Gd-EOB-DTPA–enhanced MRI showed an additional 17×12 mm lesion in segment 5; both lesions exhibited arterial hyperenhancement and delayed washout. A 13 mm lymph node in the hepatoduodenal ligament was enlarged, with enhancement and high signal on diffusion-weighted MRI similar to the liver lesions. No other lymphadenopathy was noted. Her Child–Pugh score was A, and all lesions appeared resectable. She subsequently underwent left lateral segmentectomy, partial segment 5 resection, and dissection of the enlarged lymph node in the hepatoduodenal ligament.

A 60-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 2-day history of blurry vision and photophobia in his left eye. He had undergone penetrating keratoplasty (PK) in that eye 45 years earlier and, at a visit 6 months prior, had a visual acuity of 6/9 with rigid gas-permeable contact lenses, a mild localized sectoral subepithelial edema temporally and inferiorly, and a central corneal thickness (CCT) of 621 µm that had been stable for 2 years. Examination on presentation showed a visual acuity of hand motion in the left eye, mild conjunctival injection, and severe stromal and epithelial edema of the graft in the inferotemporal quadrant extending superonasally into the visual axis. The CCT was 1077 µm. There were no endothelial precipitates or anterior chamber cells or flare. Fundus examination was within normal limits.

A 37-year-old previously healthy woman presented with 10 days of right-breast pain and skin retraction. On examination, there was a palpable, subcutaneous, cord-like fibrous lesion extending from the upper lateral quadrant to the lower lateral quadrant adjacent to the areola, with overlying skin retraction. The remainder of the breast and general physical examination was unremarkable. Vital signs were within normal limits. Ultrasonography of the right breast demonstrated a 7-mm-wide, long, superficial, beaded, tubular, anechogenic structure in the subcutaneous tissue. Doppler imaging showed no blood flow within this structure, with flow only in the surrounding fibroglandular tissue in its proximal portion.

A 55-year-old nulliparous woman presented with a three-month history of progressively worsening left lower-quadrant abdominal pain and occasional low-grade fever, and six months of abnormal vaginal bleeding despite multiple courses of oral hormonal therapy. Her menopause occurred five years ago. On examination, she had tenderness with mild guarding in the left lower abdomen; the uterus was slightly enlarged and firm, and there was white vaginal discharge. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL, serum iron 23 μg/dL, leukocyte count 12.3×10^9/L, C-reactive protein 28.9 mg/dL, and urine with 10–15 pus cells per high-power field. Transvaginal ultrasound revealed a left adnexal tubo-ovarian mass measuring 5.5×4 cm, an abnormally sized uterus, and free fluid in the cul-de-sac. Given the fever, elevated inflammatory markers, leukocytosis, and vaginal discharge, pelvic inflammatory disease was initially diagnosed, and oral antibiotics were started. The patient did not improve and was switched to intravenous antibiotics. Persisting symptoms and concerning ultrasound findings led to consideration of malignancy. Given the acute presentation and risk of worsening infection, a decision was made to perform a laparotomy for definitive diagnosis and treatment.

A 5-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of short stature. She measured 96 cm in height and weighed 13 kg. Her developmental milestones were delayed. On examination, she had stubby fingers, a coarse face with facial hirsutism, bushy eyebrows, telecanthus, a flat nasal bridge, a long philtrum, low-set ears, and a short neck. Her medical history was notable for jerking seizures treated with phenobarbital and phenytoin, and a patent ductus arteriosus managed with digoxin.

Spine radiographs revealed mild kyphoscoliosis, reduced vertebral body height, and low bone density. A left hand radiograph showed mild acroosteolysis of the distal phalanges. Head and neck radiographs demonstrated an elongated sella turcica and an elevated palate. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry of the lumbar spine showed a Z-score of −4.8 (BMD 0.232). Routine laboratory studies and a karyotype were normal.

Osteogenesis imperfecta was initially suspected based on the osteoporosis, but the clinical and facial features suggested mucopolysaccharide disorders. Screening for lysosomal MPS enzymes returned normal results.

A 78-year-old Caucasian man was referred for evaluation of acute kidney injury. Twenty-five years earlier he had been diagnosed with acromegaly, initially treated with radiotherapy and for the past 10 years maintained on octreotide (10 mg every six weeks) with good control of IGF-1 levels. Over the preceding four months he had lost 15 kg without fever, dysuria, diarrhea, or other symptoms. Several months before admission, he received sulfamethoxazole–trimethoprim and ciprofloxacin for a urinary tract infection; his serum creatinine rose and then partially improved, and was attributed to immuno-allergic nephritis, with an estimated GFR of 50 ml/min/1.73 m2. In the weeks before admission, multiple courses of penicillin and two cephalosporins over five weeks for a multiresistant Enterobacteria were followed by a further rise in creatinine.

On admission he was afebrile, blood pressure 120/70 mmHg, pulse 72 beats/min, and examination was unremarkable without rash or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests showed serum creatinine 4.9 mg/dL (stage F by RIFLE), bicarbonate 18.9 mmol/L, phosphorus 6.59 mg/dL, calcium 8.8 mg/dL, and mild anemia; leukocyte count was normal without eosinophilia. Urine dipstick showed traces of protein and hemoglobin; microscopy revealed 4 red cells and 123 white cells per high-power field, with 3% eosinophils. Urine culture grew penicillin-resistant Citrobacter koseri. Immunologic tests and viral serologies were unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound showed multiple cortical cysts in the left kidney, no hydronephrosis, and multiple gallstones.

A renal biopsy demonstrated normal glomeruli, diffuse tubular atrophy with epithelial cell necrosis, and numerous intratubular and intracytoplasmic birefringent crystals; immunofluorescence was negative. Infrared analysis identified whewellite (monohydrated calcium oxalate). When reinterviewed, he denied vitamin C supplementation, excessive oxalate intake, urinary stones, or a family history of renal disease. A 24-hour urinary collection revealed oxalate excretion of 1150 μmol/24 h (normal 78–89) and low citrate; urinary glycolate and l-glyceric acid levels were negative.

A 15-year-old previously healthy male presented with 2.5 months of progressive unsteady gait, initially noticed as difficulty kicking a soccer ball, advancing to frequent tripping. He also reported bilateral tinnitus and urinary hesitancy.  
On arrival: T 37 °C, BP 132/71 mm Hg, HR 94 beats/min, RR 19 breaths/min, SpO₂ 94% on room air.  
Neurologic examination revealed dysmetria and intention tremor greater on the right, hyperreflexia of the patellar reflexes, bilateral ankle clonus, decreased sensation in the right lower extremity, and a wide-based gait veering to the right.  
Laboratory studies showed WBC 5.5 × 10⁹/L, Hb 14.7 g/dL, platelets 185 × 10⁹/L, ferritin 18.9 ng/mL (low), triglycerides 172 mg/dL (high), fibrinogen 179 mg/dL (low), and normal AST, ALT, CRP, and ESR.  
Brain and whole-spine MRI with contrast demonstrated multifocal enhancing hemorrhagic lesions in the cerebral white matter, brainstem (largest in the left pons), cerebellum, and spinal cord.  
A noncontrast MRA of the head revealed no vessel narrowing or aneurysm.  
CSF studies were unrevealing for infection or malignancy.  
Given concern for a demyelinating or vasculitic process, he was treated with methylprednisolone 60 mg daily.

A 34-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of acute, painless vision loss in the left eye. Best-corrected visual acuity was 10/10 in the right eye and 3/10 in the left. Ocular motility and anterior segments were normal bilaterally without inflammation. Dilated fundus examination of the left eye revealed a geographic, pale lesion measuring approximately one disc area at the papillomacular bundle, including the nasal foveal region; the right fundus was unremarkable. Near-infrared reflectance imaging showed a geographic hyperreflective lesion at the left macula. Optical coherence tomography angiography demonstrated ellipsoid-zone discontinuity and a wedge-shaped choriocapillaris flow void in the affected area. Systemic evaluation, including purified protein derivative skin testing and infectious disease consultation, was unremarkable.

A 2-month-old male infant was brought by his mother because of a white nodule on his penis. He voided normally and was breastfeeding well. There were no similar lesions elsewhere, and maternal screening for HIV, hepatitis B and C, and syphilis was negative. The infant was born full-term via spontaneous vaginal delivery, with a birth weight of 3.5 kg. On examination, his general and systemic findings were unremarkable. External genital examination revealed a single, round, yellowish-white nodule measuring 0.5 × 0.5 cm over the penile foreskin. The lesion was soft and non-tender, and there was no evidence of trauma or infection.

A 57-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of progressively worsening pain in the right groin radiating down the medial thigh to the anterior knee and medial lower leg and foot. The pain was aggravated by stair climbing and walking and was not relieved by nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs. Over the preceding 2 months, she became unable to climb stairs or walk long distances because of paresthesias and hypoesthesia of the medial side of the right lower leg and foot. 

On examination, there was tenderness over the anterior right hip without palpable mass or muscle atrophy. Neurologic examination revealed altered sensation to light touch over the medial right lower leg and foot. Internal rotation, external rotation, and extension of the right hip were painful and markedly limited. Vascular examination of the right lower limb was intact, and the straight-leg-raising test was negative. 

Laboratory studies, including blood sugar, serum electrolytes, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, complete blood count with differential, rheumatoid factor, and antinuclear antibodies, were all within normal limits. Radiographs of the hip and lumbar spine were normal. 

Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging of the right hip region demonstrated a 2.6 × 1.4 cm cystic lesion of high signal intensity on T2-weighted and low signal intensity on T1-weighted images arising from the anteromedial aspect of the acetabulum and displacing the femoral nerve, artery, and vein. Color duplex Doppler ultrasonography excluded an aneurysmal lesion. Electromyography revealed evidence of muscle denervation in the affected limb.

A 34‐year‐old African American man with hemophilia A, HIV‐1 infection, and hepatitis C virus infection presented with a 3‐month history of intermittent fever, unintentional weight loss, and progressive lip swelling with painful ulcerations. Six months earlier he had resumed antiretroviral therapy, with his CD4 count rising from 94 to 160 cells/mm3; the lip lesions developed approximately two months after the CD4 count began to improve. He had received multiple courses of antibiotics and systemic corticosteroids without benefit. He was taking acyclovir for herpes simplex prophylaxis and dapsone for Pneumocystis jiroveci prophylaxis. 

On examination, his lips were markedly edematous, with multiple superficial ulcers having heaped‐up margins. There was no hepatosplenomegaly. The initial differential diagnosis included herpetic ulcers, bacterial infection, fungal infection, and angioedema. 

Diagnostic studies showed an undetectable HIV viral load and undetectable hepatitis C viral load. A polymerase‐chain‐reaction assay for herpes simplex virus from an ulcer base was negative. Complement C1 esterase inhibitor levels were within normal limits. Gram stain, acid‐fast stain, and mucicarmine stain of lesion samples were negative. Fungal blood cultures and both urine and serum Histoplasma antigen tests were negative.

An 18-year-old primigravid woman at 16 weeks’ gestation presented with a 1-month history of worsening nausea, vomiting, generalized weakness, fatigue, tremor, and a 15-lb weight loss, along with a 1-day history of dark urine, lower-extremity edema, blurred vision, difficulty walking, and altered mental status. She was afebrile (36.6 °C) and reported taking no medications or supplements. Her personal and family histories were negative for autoimmune disease. On examination, her heart rate was 125/min with a regular rhythm, she had a fine hand tremor and mild thyromegaly without a bruit. Laboratory tests showed hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypochloremia, metabolic alkalosis, and leukocytosis. Liver and renal tests were abnormal: AST 128 U/L, ALT 212 U/L, total bilirubin 4.1 mg/dL, creatinine 4.2 mg/dL. Thyroid testing revealed an undetectable TSH, free T4 >6.99 ng/dL, and T3 238 ng/dL. The Burch-Wartofsky score was 50, consistent with thyroid storm.

A 51‐year‐old Spanish‐speaking man with hypertension and diabetes mellitus complicated by end‐stage kidney disease on twice‐weekly hemodialysis via a tunneled catheter presented for routine dialysis with 1 month of subacute abdominal swelling and discomfort. He reported 6 months of intermittent diarrhea and constipation, night sweats, and a 10‐lb weight loss, but denied cough, shortness of breath, bruising, and vomiting. He emigrated from Mexico 24 years earlier, had no prison exposure, and was uninsured.

Five months earlier, outpatient evaluation for bilateral pleural effusions, chronic hypoxic respiratory failure on home oxygen, and cervical lymphadenopathy had been nondiagnostic: pleural fluid was exudative and lymphocytic with negative AFB cultures and cytology, and fine‐needle aspiration of a lymph node showed granulomatous inflammation with negative cytology and flow cytometry. One month before admission, new ascites was drained and attributed to “nephrogenic ascites” from underdialysis.

On admission, blood pressure was 160/60 mmHg and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Examination showed temporal wasting, anicteric sclerae, a moderately distended abdomen with shifting dullness, painless mobile cervical lymphadenopathy, and decreased basilar breath sounds. Laboratory studies revealed BUN 84 mg/dL, creatinine 10.2 mg/dL, hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL, alkaline phosphatase 585 U/L, calcium 13.0 mg/dL (previously 8.7 mg/dL), parathyroid hormone 12 pg/mL, and vitamin D 1,25‐hydroxylase 100 ng/mL. Admission chest radiograph confirmed bilateral pleural effusions; echocardiogram 4 months earlier had shown normal systolic function and no pericardial effusion.

Chest CT demonstrated multistation mediastinal lymphadenopathy, bilateral upper lobe–predominant perilymphatic lung nodules, and pleural thickening, which was described as “suggestive of pulmonary sarcoidosis with a differential of atypical mycobacterial infections.” Abdominal CT revealed anasarca, large‐volume ascites, peritoneal thickening, and nodularity of the omentum. MRI with contrast showed enhancing soft‐tissue thickening throughout the greater omentum, “suggesting the possibility of malignancy with peritoneal carcinomatosis with recommendation for tissue sampling.” 

For diagnostic and therapeutic purposes, paracentesis was performed, and the ascitic fluid analysis revealed a serum‐ascites albumin gradient of less than 1.1 g/dL.

A 70-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of vertigo, nausea, and bilious vomiting and 2 days of bloody diarrhea and diffuse, crampy abdominal pain. She reported 12 episodes of diarrhea, associated fevers, chills, fatigue, poor oral intake, and weight loss. She denied recent travel, sick contacts, antibiotic use, hematemesis, or tenesmus. Her medical history included hyperlipidemia, lactose intolerance, and irritable bowel syndrome; a colonoscopy 3 years earlier was normal.

On admission, temperature was 37.1 °C, pulse 117 beats/min, respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, and blood pressure 171/96 mm Hg. Examination showed sinus tachycardia, mild abdominal distention, diffuse tenderness, and decreased bowel sounds; there was no peripheral edema.

Initial laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 18 700/μL, hemoglobin 15.9 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 91.3 fL, platelet count 206 000/μL, indirect bilirubin 1.5 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 75 U/L, and lactate dehydrogenase 961 IU/L; creatinine, coagulation studies, lactic acid, and lipase were normal. A CT scan demonstrated acute colitis in the ascending and partial transverse colon. She was started on ciprofloxacin and metronidazole.

On hospital day 2, colonoscopy revealed mucosal edema, friability, and ulceration from the transverse colon to the sigmoid colon; biopsies were consistent with ischemic colitis. CT angiography showed no evidence of mesenteric arterial insufficiency, with improvement in wall thickening in the right and transverse colon compared with the admission CT. Serologic studies (ASCA, ANA, MPO) and stool studies for E. coli O157:H7, Clostridium difficile, Salmonella, Yersinia, and Campylobacter were negative. Her bloody diarrhea resolved.

On hospital day 3, the platelet count was 76 000/μL and hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL. By hospital day 7, the platelet count had fallen to 39 000/μL and hemoglobin to 7.8 g/dL; the neurologic examination remained unremarkable. Hematology consultation was obtained. Laboratory evaluation revealed a decreased haptoglobin, elevated D dimer, elevated lactate dehydrogenase, normal PT/PTT, elevated thrombin time, and increased CRP and reticulocyte count. Schistocytes were observed on the peripheral blood smear and bone marrow biopsy.

A 50-year-old African-American woman with hypertension presented with a two-week history of blurred vision associated with facial discomfort and a generalized headache. She denied fever, speech or swallowing problems, weakness, numbness, gait disturbance, preceding infection, or recent vaccination.

On examination, there was swelling of the left upper eyelid. Extraocular movements revealed that the right eye failed to move in the horizontal plane, and the left eye had impaired adduction with normal abduction, consistent with a pseudo 1 and ½ syndrome. The left upper eyelid was ptotic, and on upgaze the left eye failed to elevate fully. A Cogan lid twitch was positive. Visual acuity, fundoscopic examination, and the remainder of her neurologic examination were normal. The patient declined the ice pack test.

Investigations to rule out central etiologies—including CT of the orbits, MRI of the brain, MRA, MRV, and routine blood tests—were unremarkable.

A 4-day-old female newborn was noted to have a midline mass over the nasal bridge at birth. She was born at term by cesarean section to a hypothyroid mother after an uncomplicated perinatal course. Her birth weight was 3.180 kg, and Apgar scores were 9 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. On examination, there was an extranasal mass over the nasion, protruding slightly to the left, measuring 1.5 × 2 cm. It was firm in consistency, had a small purplish hue on its surface but no telangiectatic vessels, and was non-pulsatile and non-expandable with crying or straining. There was no intranasal component. Magnetic resonance imaging showed an extranasal lesion isointense to brain tissue on T1-weighted images, and T2-weighted images revealed no fibrous stalk or intracranial communication. Echocardiography and abdominopelvic ultrasonography were unremarkable.

A 56-year-old man with hypertension presented with palpitations that had gradually increased in frequency over 6 months, particularly during physical activity, but without impact on his daily life. On examination, his pulse intermittently rose to 105 beats per minute with occasional pauses, findings corroborated by cardiovascular auscultation. A resting 12-lead ECG showed a junctional rhythm. A 24-hour Holter monitor demonstrated predominantly sinus rhythm with runs of junctional rhythm and episodes in which some sinus P waves failed to conduct to the ventricles. During treadmill exercise testing, in the fourth minute of exertion, two consecutive sinus P waves were nonconducted to the ventricles, with the PR interval before and after these nonconducted beats remaining unchanged at 160 ms, thereby mimicking a Mobitz II second-degree atrioventricular block.

A 12-year-old boy was admitted with a 7-day history of fever, abdominal pain, headache, and weight loss. He had been treated empirically with ceftriaxone and clindamycin. An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated multiple hypoechoic lesions in the liver, and he was transferred on hospital day 11 with ongoing fever, abdominal pain, and an 8-kg weight loss. He reported playing with a kitten but denied any scratches or skin lesions. On examination, he was febrile and had bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy; there were no rash or papules on the skin. He had no history of immunodeficiency. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 10,400/mm³, hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, platelets 385,000/mm³, C-reactive protein 10.1 mg/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 57 mm/h, aspartate aminotransferase 168 U/L, and alanine aminotransferase 67 U/L. Blood and urine cultures and HIV serology were negative. Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging showed multiple hepatic lesions, and cranial and thoracic imaging were unremarkable.

A 46-year-old woman with a history of right breast invasive ductal carcinoma (cT2N1M0, ER-positive, HER2-positive) underwent neoadjuvant anthracycline- and taxane-based chemotherapy with anti-HER2 therapy followed by surgery, achieving a pathological complete response. She was planned to receive 10 years of tamoxifen and 1 year of trastuzumab. She had no prior cardiac disease and had achieved a sustained virologic response after treatment of hepatitis C two years earlier.

Two months after starting tamoxifen and resuming trastuzumab, she presented to her general physician with fever and dyspnea and was referred to the emergency department for suspected drug-induced liver injury. On arrival, she was alert; temperature 36.6 °C; blood pressure 110/70 mmHg; heart rate 80 bpm; respiratory rate 20 breaths/min; SpO2 99% on room air. Laboratory studies showed:  
• AST 636 U/L (normal 5–37)  
• ALT 80 U/L (6–43)  
• ALP 446 U/L (38–113)  
• LDH 801 U/L (124–222)  
• Platelets 59,000/µL (153,000–346,000)  
• PT-INR 1.43 (0.90–1.10)  
• Marked metabolic acidosis  

She was placed on bed rest and given intravenous fluids while awaiting admission for presumed fulminant hepatitis due to tamoxifen.

A 23-year-old man with childhood asthma presented with a 2-day history of subjective fever, chills, dry cough, dyspnea, and myalgia. He denied gastrointestinal symptoms, sputum production, known COVID-19 contacts, and recent travel. He had taken NSAIDs without relief. On arrival, temperature was 39.0°C, blood pressure 135/65 mmHg, pulse 134 bpm, respiratory rate 22/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. He was febrile, tachycardic, alert, in no respiratory distress, and had clear lung fields without wheezes or rales.

Laboratory results showed WBC 15.3×10^3/μL (neutrophils 86.8%, lymphocytes 7.9%), hemoglobin 13.3 g/dL, platelets 290×10^3/μL, albumin 2.8 g/dL, ALT 69 U/L, AST 66 U/L, ferritin 375.6 ng/mL, CRP 27.7 mg/dL, and procalcitonin 1.43 ng/mL. Urinalysis was unremarkable. A respiratory pathogen panel and SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR on a nasopharyngeal swab were both negative. Chest radiography revealed bilateral interstitial infiltrates. He received empiric ceftriaxone, doxycycline, intravenous fluids, and acetaminophen and was placed in respiratory isolation.

On hospital day 2, he developed diarrhea, persistent high fever (39.1°C), and oxygen desaturation into the 80s with ambulation, requiring 2 L nasal cannula. A second SARS-CoV-2 test was negative. Liver enzymes, D-dimer, and WBC count began to improve, and LDH was 275 U/L. Blood and urine cultures remained negative. CT of the chest with contrast showed no pulmonary embolism. Toxicology was positive for marijuana and opioids. Further history revealed he had vaped marijuana three times weekly for two years.

On hospital day 3, a third SARS-CoV-2 test on an endotracheal specimen was negative; HIV antigen was nonreactive; and urinary Streptococcus pneumoniae antigen was not detected.

A 48-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and obesity (BMI 32) presented with several days of fever, cough, nausea, and dyspnoea. She tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 and was initially discharged to self-quarantine. Three days later, she returned with worsening dyspnoea on minimal exertion. On examination, she was tachycardic, tachypnoeic, and hypoxic (oxygen saturation 79% on room air, improving to 93% with 4 L nasal cannula). Lung auscultation revealed no significant crackles, and there was no cardiac murmur. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 11 700/mL, D-dimer 432 ng/mL, and an eGFR of 106 mL/min. Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral patchy airspace opacities. She was admitted for presumed COVID-19 pneumonia, developed progressive respiratory failure, and was intubated for acute respiratory distress syndrome. Her course was complicated by non-oliguric acute renal failure. On ICU day 6, she became hypotensive requiring norepinephrine and developed worsening hypoxia despite 100% FiO₂ and PEEP of 12 mmHg. Telemetry showed ST changes.  
An electrocardiogram revealed sinus tachycardia with new, prominent ST elevations in leads V2–V5 and an S₁Q₃T₃ pattern. High-sensitivity troponin T was 138 ng/L. Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal left ventricular function with no wall motion abnormalities; the right ventricle was dilated (mid-diameter 5.1 cm) with severe hypokinesis of the base and mid segments but preserved apical motion, consistent with McConnell’s sign. Estimated right ventricular systolic pressure was 45 mmHg, and there was no atrial septal defect.

A 14-year-old previously healthy girl was referred for a 2-week history of unexplained hair loss on the left side of her forehead. She had no other initial sites of hair loss. Over the preceding 2 months, she experienced poor sleep and intermittent episodes of rapid breathing. Her parents were elderly, overprotective, and limited her social interactions; she missed her school friends due to COVID-19 closures. 

On examination, she was well-nourished, active, and normotensive. Cutaneous examination revealed an oval patch of hair loss on the left forehead without erythema, tenderness, ulcers, or scarring; the remainder of her examination was normal. Dermoscopic evaluation showed a uniform loss of hair with all follicular openings filled with intact black hair shafts. A hair-pull test was negative.

A 56-year-old man presented to the ENT clinic with a 3-month history of a foreign-body sensation in the neck and intermittent painful swallowing. He denied any history of neck trauma. His medical history was notable for hypertension and angina; he was a heavy smoker, reported increased alcohol consumption, and appeared malnourished. 

On examination, routine ENT evaluation and flexible laryngoscopy were unremarkable. A barium swallow study showed no abnormalities. The patient underwent examination under anesthesia with direct hypopharyngoscopy, microlaryngoscopy, and esophagoscopy. The esophagus and larynx appeared normal, but there was a smooth bulge of the left posterior hypopharyngeal wall protruding into the left piriform sinus. On palpation, the lesion felt firm, with bony or cartilaginous consistency, and showed no features of malignancy. It was suggested that the thyroid cornu might underlie this finding, and a CT scan of the neck was ordered.
