A 72-year-old man presented with a tender plaque on his right knee. He reported that 20 years earlier, while wading in Chesapeake Bay, he scraped his knee on a rock; the wound required two incision and drainage procedures over the ensuing years and healed to a scaly plaque approximately 4 cm in diameter. The plaque remained stable in size but became tender, prompting dermatologic evaluation. One dermatologist diagnosed psoriasis and prescribed topical and systemic anti-inflammatory therapies, but the lesion worsened over three years.

On presentation at our institution, vital signs were normal. Examination revealed a tender, indurated, violaceous, ulcerated plaque with irregular borders, approximately 10 cm in diameter, over the right medial knee and thigh. Our differential diagnoses included infection (bacterial and fungal), leishmaniasis, and granulomatous mycosis fungoides. The patient was started empirically on doxycycline, and punch biopsies were obtained from the ulcer border for bacterial, fungal, and acid-fast bacilli culture as well as microbial polymerase chain reaction testing.

A 70-year-old woman with no prior medical history and no smoking history presented with a one-week history of cough, dyspnea, anorexia, and fever. She was diagnosed with COVID-19 by PCR from a nasopharyngeal swab and admitted for treatment.  
On admission: temperature 37.9 °C; blood pressure 136/67 mmHg; heart rate 88 beats/min; respiratory rate 29 breaths/min; SpO₂ 95% on 5 L/min oxygen via mask.  
Laboratory studies showed elevated C-reactive protein, lactate dehydrogenase, and ferritin; normal procalcitonin, D-dimer, KL-6, and SP-D; and lymphopenia with eosinopenia.  
Chest CT on admission demonstrated bilateral ground-glass opacities with superimposed intralobular reticulations in a crazy-paving pattern. There were no findings of pulmonary embolism, purulent sputum, infiltrative shadows, or signs of bacterial infection, and no clinical evidence of heart failure (no lower leg edema).  
She was treated with favipiravir, ciclesonide, and nafamostat. Her fever, cough, dyspnea, and CRP improved, and by hospital Day 8 her SpO₂ was 95% on 2 L/min oxygen via nasal cannula.  
On hospital Day 10, she developed rapidly progressive respiratory failure: SpO₂ fell to 94% on 10 L/min oxygen via reservoir mask. Repeat CT showed progression from ground-glass opacities to dense bilateral consolidations without new ground-glass areas. Her serum SP-D level was higher than on admission.

A 36-year-old Greek man was hospitalized in March 2019 for three months of persistent fever, non-productive cough, dyspnea, weight loss, and fatigue. He is a man who has sex with men, with no prior HIV testing, denies smoking or substance use, and has a history of a single hospitalization for bacterial pneumonia.

On examination, his temperature was elevated, respiratory rate was increased, oxygen saturation was 96% on room air, and breath sounds were reduced bilaterally. He had generalized lymphadenopathy, oral candidiasis, and a moderately enlarged liver. Laboratory tests revealed pancytopenia. A chest X-ray was normal.

HIV infection was confirmed by Western blot, with a CD4 count < 50 cells/mm3 and an HIV RNA level of 300 000 copies/mL. He was negative for hepatitis B and C, syphilis, and had a 0 mm tuberculin skin test. CMV and Parvovirus B19 IgG were positive, IgM antibodies were negative.

Bronchoscopy was grossly normal. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) cultures were negative for Pneumocystis jiroveci, Aspergillus, Cryptococcus (India ink), and Mycobacterium avium complex, but grew MRSA and Candida albicans. A brain CT was unremarkable.

He began prophylaxis with atovaquone for Pneumocystis jiroveci and azithromycin for MAC. Despite normal resting and six-minute walk oxygen saturations, his dyspnea and non-productive cough persisted. 

High-resolution CT of the chest showed multiple areas of ground-glass opacity at the right lower lobe base, centrilobular nodules with a linear branching (“tree-in-bud”) pattern, multiple bronchial cysts, and diffuse interstitial infiltration across all lobes.

A 15-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of developmental delay and sensorineural hearing impairment. She was born at term to consanguineous parents and had sparse medical follow-up until age 5, when bilateral hearing aids were fitted. Parents reported frequent balance loss in toddlerhood. By age 7, she had toe-walking with tight, almost spastic Achilles tendons; brain MRI showed a central lesion in the mesencephalon extending from the red nucleus dorsocaudally to the cerebellar peduncles. At age 12 she developed bilateral peroneal muscle weakness and absent peripheral reflexes; electrodiagnostic studies demonstrated sensorimotor polyneuropathy and chronic neurogenic changes in leg muscles. Repeat brain MRI was unchanged. At age 13, cognitive delay, impaired gross and fine motor skills, and tremor prompted consideration of a neurometabolic disorder. By age 15 there was generalized muscle weakness, hyperflexible fingers, planovalgus feet, poor balance, delayed growth (skeletal age 10.7 at chronologic 14), primary ovarian failure, and absence of pubertal signs. No retinal or optic-nerve abnormalities were noted.  
Laboratory studies at age 13 showed: moderately elevated plasma C26:0 with increased C26:0/C22:0 ratio, borderline C24:0/C22:0 ratio, markedly elevated phytanic and pristanic acids, and normal erythrocyte plasmalogen levels.  
Fibroblast studies revealed normal VLCFA concentrations and normal dihydroxyacetonephosphate-acyltransferase activity. Immunofluorescence microscopy for catalase showed normal peroxisomal staining in most cells at 37 °C but a markedly reduced number of peroxisomes in some cells. After 2 weeks at 40 °C, catalase staining became completely cytosolic, indicating a temperature-sensitive defect in peroxisome import.  
Given these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?

A 14-year-old previously healthy boy presented with 5 days of fever, headache, generalized body aches, and retro-orbital pain. On day 3 of illness, dengue NS1 antigen was positive; a complete blood count showed a platelet count of 170 × 10^3/µL and a white blood cell count of 5.7 × 10^3/µL. He received outpatient supportive care with oral fluids. On day 5, his platelet count fell to 98 × 10^3/µL and white blood cell count to 4.2 × 10^3/µL, and he was admitted for observation. Admission vital signs: pulse 140/min, blood pressure 100/70 mmHg, capillary refill <2 s; hematocrit rose from a baseline of 36% to 42%. Over 24 h, he developed vomiting and abdominal pain without bleeding. Exam showed generalized flushing, right hypochondrial tenderness, and 3 cm hepatomegaly; bedside ultrasound revealed a mild pleural effusion and gallbladder wall thickening. Lab tests demonstrated leukopenia (2.2 × 10^3/µL), thrombocytopenia (68 × 10^3/µL), and mild transaminitis (ALT 88 U/L, AST 124 U/L). He was managed in a high‐dependency unit for dengue hemorrhagic fever; platelets nadired at 6 × 10^3/µL on day 7, and dengue IgM and IgG were positive. He clinically recovered by day 11; at discharge, white blood cells were 7.5 × 10^3/µL and platelets 52 × 10^3/µL. Follow-up at 2 weeks showed platelets of 47 × 10^3/µL and at 1 month 100 × 10^3/µL. He then defaulted from follow-up, and over the next year his platelets ranged from 30 to 45 × 10^3/µL. One year after discharge, he re-presented with a one-week history of multiple purpuric lesions and documented persistent thrombocytopenia.

A 35-year-old woman presented with right groin pain of gradual onset. Four years earlier, she had undergone total hip arthroplasty for osteonecrosis of the femoral head that developed following pregnancy. She denied fever or trauma. She reported receiving high-dose corticosteroids after a recent COVID-19 infection. On examination, passive right hip motion was near full range but painful at extremes, and she walked with an antalgic gait. Neurologic examination was normal.

Plain radiographs of the right hip showed severe acetabular sclerosis and a radiolucent line around the acetabular component. Laboratory studies revealed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 14 mm/h and a C-reactive protein level of 16 mg/L. A 99mTc bone scan demonstrated mild hyperflow in angiographic and blood-pool phases and intense uptake in the delayed phase. Magnetic resonance imaging with metal-artifact reduction was unavailable. Aspiration of the hip joint yielded no organisms. Given concern for prosthetic failure, removal of the acetabular component and placement of a cement spacer were performed, and a postoperative CT scan confirmed acetabular sclerosis.

An 11-year-old girl was referred for orthodontic evaluation of non-erupted maxillary permanent canines. Her father had been diagnosed with dentin dysplasia type I.

Extraoral examination showed a convex facial profile, mildly reduced lower facial height, and an increased labionasal angle. Intraoral examination revealed a mixed dentition with a Class II molar relationship, an overjet of 2 mm, an overbite of 10%, and good oral hygiene.

A panoramic radiograph demonstrated that most teeth had short, blunt roots; pulp chambers were obliterated; and there were periapical radiolucencies in the absence of periodontal disease or caries. Several teeth showed horizontal crescent-shaped lines at the cementoenamel junction. On the basis of these radiographic features, the patient was classified as having DD-Ic. Both permanent maxillary canines were impacted: the right canine was labially positioned and the left palatally positioned; each was located above and in close proximity to the roots of the adjacent lateral and central incisors on cone-beam computed tomography. There was no sclerosis of the maxilla, mandible, or skeleton.

Cephalometric analysis showed an upper-to-lower facial height ratio (UFH/TFH) of 47%/53%, a Z-angle of 67°, an incisor mandibular plane angle (IMPA) of 98°, and a labionasal angle of 119°.

A 77-year-old white woman presented with 3 months of a pruritic rash accompanied by progressive fatigue, proximal muscle weakness, and dyspnea on exertion. She had recently been diagnosed with dermatomyositis based on clinical features, laboratory studies, and skin biopsy. Her rash and muscle weakness had improved with prednisone and azathioprine but recurred during prednisone tapering. Her medical history was notable for breast cancer treated with lumpectomy and radiation, with no evidence of recurrence; malignancy screening was otherwise negative.

On examination, she had:
• Erythematous plaques on the forehead, central face, upper chest and back, and the lateral arms and thighs  
• Pink, flat-topped papules overlying the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints (Gottron papules), cuticular dystrophy, and nail-fold capillary dropout  
• Edematous, pseudovesicular pink to violaceous papules and plaques with central scalloped erosions and ulcerations on the bilateral buttocks  

Laboratory studies showed an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:160, a positive anti–transcriptional intermediary factor 1-γ antibody, aspartate aminotransferase 52 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 53 U/L, and a normal serum creatine phosphokinase level.

A 36-year-old Japanese man with biopsy-proven sarcoidosis was referred for ocular evaluation in July 2017. Two days earlier, he had begun oral prednisolone (70 mg daily) for thrombocytopenic purpura (platelet count, 4000/μL) attributed to sarcoidosis-related splenomegaly. His history included cervical lymph node, subcutaneous nodule, and transbronchial lung biopsies (2015–2016), all showing noncaseating granulomas. Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme was 8.4–16.4 IU/L (normal); serum lysozyme was elevated. Tests for toxoplasma, tuberculosis, and other infections were negative; serum calcium, eosinophil count, and ESR were normal.

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 and intraocular pressures were normal in both eyes. There were no signs of intraocular inflammation. Fundus examination of the left eye revealed an asymptomatic, white, round choroidal mass (1.5 disc diameters) superior-temporal to the macula. B-scan ultrasonography showed an intrachoroidal lesion without calcification. Enhanced depth imaging–OCT demonstrated a dome-shaped choroidal elevation with effacement of choroidal vessels and overlying subretinal fluid. Fluorescein angiography showed early hypofluorescence with late leakage; indocyanine green angiography showed persistent hypofluorescence. Brain/orbit MRI and CT scans showed no orbital mass or neurosarcoidosis; whole-body PET-CT found no evidence of malignancy.

A 24-year-old para 1 woman of African descent presented 5 months after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery with a painful growth at the site of a left mediolateral episiotomy. She reported dyspareunia and had applied topical povidone-iodine ointment with no improvement. She had no history of puerperal sepsis, allergies, or poor wound healing. On examination, her vital signs were within normal limits. Inspection of the introitus revealed an exuberant, sessile lesion arising from the episiotomy scar at the 5 o’clock position, extending superiorly into the lower third of the vagina, inferiorly into the upper thigh, and involving the fourchette from the 5 to 7 o’clock positions. No other risk factors for abnormal wound healing were identified.

A 21-year-old woman with no known illnesses was incidentally found to have hypercalcaemia (2.84 mmol/L; reference 2.15–2.50) on routine pre-operative blood tests. She denied symptoms of hypercalcaemia, including polyuria, constipation, abdominal pain, bone pain, and had no history of nephrolithiasis. There was no significant family history. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed phosphate 0.71 mmol/L (0.78–1.42), and PTH 10.3 pmol/L (2.0–8.5), with normal renal function. Twenty-five-OH vitamin D was deficient, ruling out vitamin D toxicity. A 24-hour urine collection performed twice demonstrated a fractional excretion of calcium of 0.01 on both occasions. Parathyroid scintigraphy revealed an ill-defined focus of uptake above the left thyroid lobe. Skeletal survey and renal ultrasound showed no bone lesions or calculi.

A 50-year-old man presented in 2011 with a 2-year history of right wrist volar pain, swelling, and erythema. He had no significant medical history. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 18 mg/L, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 24 mm/h, and a white-cell count of 6460×10^3/mm^3. He was diagnosed with seronegative arthritis and treated with prednisone (4 mg daily) and sulfasalazine (500 mg daily). Pain improved, but swelling and redness persisted.

In 2013, a wrist radiograph demonstrated increased soft-tissue density, soft-tissue swelling, and periarticular osteoporosis. Magnetic resonance imaging of the wrist showed millimetric, nodular lesions along the flexor tendon sheath on T2-weighted images and diffuse synovitis.

On March 19, 2013, he underwent right wrist synovectomy and flexor retinaculum release. Intraoperatively, multiple rice bodies were noted around the flexor tendons. Specimens sent for aerobic and anaerobic cultures and liquid media remained sterile. His symptoms regressed after surgery.

Six months postoperatively, he again developed volar wrist pain, swelling, and redness. Laboratory studies and MRI findings were consistent with recurrent synovitis.

A 58-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, and coronary artery disease presented with a  few weeks of malaise, weakness, and skin lesions. She had PCR-confirmed COVID-19 60 days earlier, with fever, cough, malaise, anosmia, and ageusia treated at home. Forty-five days after COVID-19, she noted periorbital erythema and edema and an intensely pruritic erythematous rash on her malar areas, which over days spread to her hands, neck, and buttocks. She then developed profound fatigue limiting daily activities.

Her medications included losartan, aspirin, metformin, levothyroxine, and doxepin. On examination, temperature was 38.5°C, pulse 90/min, blood pressure 100/70 mm Hg, respiratory rate 26/min, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. Cutaneous findings included pink-violet papules on the knuckles, ragged cuticles, midface erythema involving the nasolabial folds, an erythematous plaque on the upper back, and multiple vesicles with erythematous bases on the upper extremities. There was no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Neurologic examination showed proximal muscle weakness (2/5) at the shoulders and hips.

Laboratory studies showed AST 67 U/L, ALT 66 U/L (normal 5–40), aldolase 12.4 U/L (normal 1–7), creatine phosphokinase 2611 U/L (upper limit 195), LDH 517 U/L, and ESR 57 mm/h. Complete blood count and thyroid function were normal. Serologies for ANA, anti–dsDNA, anti–Smith, and a panel of myositis-specific antibodies were negative. SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative; SARS-CoV-2 IgG was positive.

Electromyography demonstrated early inflammatory myopathy of proximal upper and lower limbs. Endoscopy, colonoscopy, mammography, CT of the paranasal sinuses, and ophthalmologic examination were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography showed left ventricular, septal, and anterior wall hypokinesia, mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, and an ejection fraction of 45%. Chest CT revealed bilateral multifocal patchy consolidations with a reverse-halo sign, suggestive of the chronic phase of organizing COVID-19 pneumonia.

A 35-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of jaundice, fever, and right upper abdominal pain. On examination, he had scleral icterus and right upper quadrant tenderness without a positive Murphy’s sign. Initial laboratory tests showed total bilirubin 6.2 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 5.3 mg/dL, lipase 1029 U/L, ALT 328 U/L, and AST 221 U/L. By hospital day 3, total bilirubin rose to 14.6 mg/dL and direct bilirubin to 13.4 mg/dL; lipase decreased to 33 U/L, and ALT and AST remained elevated.

Abdominal ultrasound revealed thin gallbladder walls without stones and an oval proximal biliary duct dilation measuring 12 mm. Contrast-enhanced CT showed nondilated intrahepatic bile ducts and a 16 mm cystic dilation of the proximal common bile duct (CBD) without distal CBD dilatation; no calculi were seen. MRCP demonstrated a 2.1 × 1.9 × 2.3 cm cystic lesion at the hepatic hilum separated by a thin septum from the CBD and no pancreaticobiliary maljunction.

ERCP was performed to delineate the anatomy and place a stent. Contrary to prior imaging, ERCP revealed a proximal fusiform dilation of the CBD receiving the right and left hepatic ducts; both hepatic ducts and the distal CBD were of normal caliber, and cannulation of those ducts was unsuccessful.

A 31-year-old woman with no prior psychiatric history was evaluated for a 21-month progression of neuropsychiatric symptoms. Initially she had a 2-week period of mood swings and compulsive behavior. Two months later, she had a first generalized seizure, affective lability, cognitive deficits, and aggression. CSF analysis showed WBC 23/µl and protein 487 mg/l; MRI of the brain was normal. She was treated empirically with ceftriaxone, aciclovir, clobazam, and valproate without clinical improvement. Over the next month she developed disorganized agitation, partial amnesia, disinhibition, delusions, and delirium, for which antipsychotics and benzodiazepines were used. At 3 months, she became catatonic with waxy flexibility and unresponsiveness to pain, and was diagnosed with catatonic schizophrenia. By 5 months, her catatonia resolved but she remained apathetic and slow. Nearly one year after onset she entered rehabilitation with persistent concentration problems and social withdrawal. Repeat CSF showed WBC 20/µl and protein 550 mg/l. Long-term EEG revealed left temporal and right hemispheric dysfunction without epileptiform discharges. Brain MRI showed right temporo-occipital signal changes. Antimicrobial therapy with aciclovir and piperacillin again failed. Antiepileptics were adjusted but poorly tolerated, and her condition worsened with enuresis and inability to care for herself. Twenty months after onset she was admitted to our psychiatry service. On exam she was tired but oriented; she had memory loss, impaired speech, intermittent mutism, echolalia, palilalia, right-hand fidgeting, left ocular muscle contractions, lip smacking, stereotypies, and waxy flexibility. CSF now showed protein 561 mg/l with an elevated albumin quotient, normal cell count, and no intrathecal Ig synthesis. EEG showed intermittent right-central delta foci and frontotemporal delta and theta components on independent component analysis. MRI revealed only moderate perisylvian/temporal atrophy. FDG-PET demonstrated global cortical hypometabolism of the left hemisphere, milder temporal hypometabolism on the right, and right cerebellar hypometabolism. Single-voxel 1H-MRS in the prefrontal cortices showed markedly reduced glutamate+glutamine concentrations and Glx/Cr ratios on the left compared with the right.

A 73-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with a 4-month history of progressive dyspnoea (NYHA class III) and leg and facial oedema without cough, fever, or night sweats. Symptoms did not improve with diuretic therapy, prompting referral to cardiology. On examination, he had markedly engorged neck veins. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed subtotal compression of the right side of the heart by an external mass. Laboratory studies showed creatinine 3.5 mg/dL (GFR 18 mL/min), NT-proBNP 2543 pg/mL, and D-dimer 1393 µg/L. Contrast-enhanced thoracic CT demonstrated a large (89 × 58 mm) intrapericardial thick-walled mass with fluid accumulation, homogeneous enhancement of the cyst wall, maximal pericardial thickness of 2 mm, and compression of the right atrium and ventricle. Multiple supracarinal pretracheal lymph nodes measured up to 19.7 × 12.3 mm. The imaging diagnosis was a large pericardial cyst with signs of concomitant infection. The patient was referred for surgical management.

A 50-year-old man was admitted with 5 days of progressive right-sided hemiparesis and aphasia. He had a 1-year history of painful ophthalmoplegia, initially involving cranial nerves III, IV, and VI on the left and III and IV on the right, with decreased visual acuity (6/60 left, 6/36 right) and sensory loss in the left V2 distribution. Initial MRI showed bilateral cavernous-sinus enhancement with sphenoid-sinus mucosal thickening; sphenoid-sinus biopsy revealed inflammatory tissue with lymphoid aggregates. He received a 5-day course of oral prednisolone with improvement but was lost to follow-up.

Eight months later, he re-presented with right-eye chemosis, proptosis, and diplopia; exam showed partial III and VI palsies on the right. MRI demonstrated enlargement and contrast enhancement of the right superior and lateral rectus muscles extending through the superior orbital fissure into the cavernous sinus, and mild involvement of the left medial rectus. He again improved with a 1-week course of oral prednisolone.

Four months later, he developed progressive right hemiparesis, aphasia, and headache, without ocular symptoms. MRI showed an intensely enhancing extra-axial mass in the left cavernous region compressing and invading the anterior temporal lobe, with peripheral hemorrhage, marked edema, and midline shift. Orbital structures were normal. Laboratory studies demonstrated a normal hemogram, ESR, metabolic panel, and thyroid and cortisol levels. VDRL, HIV, HBsAg, and HCV antibody tests were negative. Immunological tests (rheumatoid factor, ANA, cANCA, pANCA, SSA, SSB antibodies, and angiotensin-converting enzyme) were within normal limits. CSF analysis revealed 4 lymphocytes, a glucose of 56 mg/dL, protein of 35 mg/dL, and a negative PCR for tuberculosis.

A 40-year-old man presented to the emergency department after an episode of syncope that occurred at work. He had no history of cardiac disease. On physical examination, vital signs were within normal limits, and the cardiovascular and neurologic examinations were unremarkable. A 12-lead ECG showed regular sinus rhythm at 70 beats per minute, a complete right bundle branch block, posterior left hemiblock, and a PR interval of 120 ms. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed normal chamber dimensions, normal left ventricular systolic function, and no structural abnormalities.

A 66-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes, and intermittent sinusitis was transferred for progressive encephalopathy. Three weeks earlier he received levofloxacin, steroids, and clarithromycin for presumed sinusitis. Two days before presentation he developed headache, sinus pressure, epigastric pain, and dry heaving, followed by confusion. He had no fever. At an outside hospital he became obtunded and was intubated. Empiric vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and acyclovir were started. CSF showed protein 53 mg/dL, glucose 160 mg/dL (serum 240), 1 WBC/mm³, and negative VDRL, West Nile IgM/IgG, cryptococcal antigen, and cultures. EEG revealed no seizures but diffuse slowing; phenytoin then levetiracetam were started. Brain MRI showed chronic mild periventricular white-matter changes without acute lesions. 

On transfer (hospital day 3), he was comatose with intact brainstem reflexes and extensor posturing. Labs showed normal liver function tests, serum ammonia 120 μg/dL (65–107), respiratory alkalosis, and negative hepatitis panel. Repeat CSF showed 3 WBC/mm³, protein 28.5 mg/dL, lactic acid 2.6 meq/L, and negative HSV PCR and enterovirus panel; acyclovir was stopped. Lactulose was begun, but ammonia rose to 494 μg/dL within hours. Rifaximin, L-carnitine, and emergent hemodialysis were initiated. MRI showed symmetric restricted diffusion and FLAIR hyperintensities in bilateral temporal, insular, frontal, and parietal cortices without enhancement. Continuous EEG showed generalized low-voltage slowing; intermittent facial twitching lacked electrographic correlate. Abdominal CT with venogram showed no portosystemic shunt. An amino acid panel to evaluate inborn errors of metabolism was sent.

A 70-year-old left-handed man presented with abnormal movements of his left arm, left visual field loss, and unsteadiness. Two months earlier, he had a sudden episode of left arm numbness and weakness that resolved within seven hours and was treated as a transient ischemic attack with aspirin, antihypertensive, and lipid-lowering therapy, which he stopped after one month. On examination, he had a mild left visual field deficit and distal choreiform movements of the left upper limb. He was normotensive and had an unremarkable cardiovascular examination. Brain MRI showed multiple acute infarcts in the right cerebellar hemisphere, right occipital and parietal cortices, and corpus callosum, suggesting an embolic source. CT angiography revealed a 3.5 cm aneurysmal dilatation at the origin of the brachiocephalic trunk with a large ulcerated soft plaque and complete occlusion of the right internal carotid artery with distal reconstitution.

A 4-year-old girl was evaluated for a 2-month history of dull, aching pain over the left midfoot, with mild swelling. Weight bearing became painful 15 days before presentation. There was no history of trauma, fever, or weight loss. On examination, there was diffuse tenderness over the midfoot. Ankle movements were full but limited by pain. Local skin temperature was mildly elevated; there were no sinuses or induration.

Plain radiographs of the ankle showed an osteolytic, cystic lesion of the navicular bone, with osteopenia, intact cortices, and no periosteal reaction. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 11,200 per mm3 with 23% lymphocytes, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 58 mm at one hour, and a nonreactive C-reactive protein.

A 41-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with intermittent right upper–quadrant pain for 20 days, associated with decreased appetite and lassitude. She denied fever, cough, weight loss, night sweats, or known tuberculosis exposure. Vital signs were normal. Physical examination revealed mild anemia (hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL), a slightly distended abdomen, and a palpable lump in the right upper quadrant; there was no lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 23,000 cells/mm3; liver and renal function tests were normal. Tumor markers were elevated: CEA 7.3 ng/mL (normal 0–2.9) and CA19-9 41 IU/mL (normal <37). 

Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a distended, moderately thickened gallbladder containing a 37 mm calculus and two smaller stones; adjacent to the fundus was a 3.0×4.2×3.8 cm heterogeneous collection extending into the abdominal wall. The common bile duct was dilated to 14 mm proximally. 

Contrast-enhanced CT showed a distended gallbladder with a 5.1 mm thickened wall and multiple stones (largest 14 mm), a focal breach in the fundus, and an adjacent 3.5×5.7×4.3 cm peripherally enhancing collection reaching the subcutaneous plane. A large, irregular peripancreatic lymph node (8×1.1 cm) and hepatosplenomegaly were also noted. 

Given concern for neoplastic versus inflammatory etiologies, a laparoscopic cholecystectomy was planned.

A 30-year-old man of African descent presented with progressively worsening, severe swelling of both lips that began in 2006, initially affecting the upper lip and later the lower lip. He had no significant medical or family history. He reported functional limitation, reduced local sensation, and marked social embarrassment. Prior treatments included intralesional triamcinolone injections and systemic prednisolone, both of which were followed by progression of the edema, and off-label infliximab therapy, which stabilized the disease.

Chest high-resolution computed tomography, colonoscopy, and intestinal biopsy excluded tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, and Crohn’s disease. Neurologic examination showed no peripheral facial nerve palsy. Local examination revealed severe, firm, elastic swelling of both lips; the superficial mucosa was translucent, dry, with paramedian brownish dots and fissuring. Intraoral exam showed no tissue abnormalities and no fissured tongue. An incisional biopsy of the upper lip was performed.

A 7-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of an asymptomatic left scrotal mass found on routine examination. He had no significant medical or surgical history and was developing normally. Vital signs were within normal limits.

On physical examination, the right testicle and epididymis were normal in size and consistency, with a palpable vas deferens and no inguinal hernia or varicocele. On the left side, there was a grade IV varicocele, an atrophic testicle and epididymis, and a more prominent left vas deferens. A medial paratesticular mass on the left was palpated; it was similar in size and consistency to the atrophic left testis.

Serum tumor markers for testicular cancer (alpha-fetoprotein, human chorionic gonadotropin, and lactate dehydrogenase) were within normal ranges.

Scrotal ultrasound showed an echogenic, oval mass measuring 0.9 × 0.6 × 0.7 cm, located between the left epididymis and testicle. The mass was separate from the left testis and demonstrated slight intralesional Doppler flow with posterior acoustic reinforcement.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the scrotum demonstrated a normal right testis (15.2 × 12 × 10.2 mm) and, on the left side, two oval structures (9.5 × 7.5 × 7.5 mm each) with hypointense signal on diffusion, isointense signal on T1, and hyperintense signal on T2 compared with the right testis. These left structures were surrounded by dilated veins. Only one epididymis was identified on the left, and a single spermatic cord draining both structures was noted; this cord measured 10 mm in diameter, compared with 4 mm on the right.

A 22-year-old, 48-kg woman with a 6-month history of temporomandibular joint pain was scheduled for bilateral temporomandibular meniscopexy. Her previous anesthesia included an uneventful appendectomy at age 10. On arrival, HR was 92 bpm, RR 16/min, BP 128/78 mmHg, and SpO₂ 91% on room air. Anesthesia was induced with midazolam 2 mg IV, remifentanil infusion, propofol 140 mg IV, and rocuronium 35 mg IV. Following topical vasoconstrictor and local anesthetic, nasotracheal intubation was confirmed uneventfully.

Shortly after securing the airway, the patient developed sinus bradycardia with ST changes that rapidly progressed to supraventricular tachycardia (HR 168 bpm), hypotension, desaturation, piloerection, and persistent ST changes. Airway pressures rose with rhonchi, and bronchospasm was suspected; she received four puffs of salbutamol and 100 mg IV hydrocortisone. Bloody fluid then appeared in the endotracheal tube, and chest radiography showed severe bilateral pulmonary edema.

An intraoperative transesophageal echocardiogram demonstrated severe left ventricular dysfunction with akinesia of the apical and mid anterolateral and septal segments, hypokinesia of the anterior and anteroseptal walls, and preserved basal segments; the right ventricle was moderately dilated with mild dysfunction and moderate tricuspid regurgitation. Cardiac output was 1.8 L/min. Norepinephrine infusion was started, with gradual hemodynamic improvement, and the surgery was canceled. 

In the ICU, a pulmonary artery catheter revealed a cardiac index of 1.63 L/min/m², a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 20 mmHg, and normal resistances. Transthoracic echocardiography confirmed severe biventricular dysfunction with hypokinesia of the distal third of the anterior and inferior septum, and milrinone 0.5 µg/kg/min IV was initiated. Troponin I was 3.7 ng/mL on day 1 and 0.7 ng/mL on day 2.

A 12-year-old girl presented with a sudden visual scotoma in her right eye. She had no past ocular history or recent flu-like illness but had been taking combined oral contraceptive pills for 5 months. Visual acuity was 20/20 (-1.0 D) bilaterally; anterior segments and pupillary responses were normal, and intraocular pressures were 14 mm Hg in both eyes. Fundus examination revealed a subtle abnormal retinal reflex in the macula of the right eye.  
Color fundus photography showed slight macular alteration more apparent on infrared retinography. Red-free imaging was normal, and fundus autofluorescence demonstrated a subtle hypo-autofluorescent signal in the right macula. Fluorescein angiography showed normal filling in all phases without hyper- or hypofluorescent areas.  
Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the right eye demonstrated focal hyperreflective lesions in the deep retinal layers corresponding to the infrared retinography findings. Initial OCT angiography (OCT-A) of the right eye showed normal flow in the superficial and deep retinal plexuses, choriocapillaris, and choroid.

A 56-year-old man was admitted with acute gout of the right knee on a background of 6 months of lethargy, easy bruising, epistaxis, and recent episodes of visible hematuria. He denied fever, night sweats, or weight loss. His medical history included gout, daily alcohol consumption (10 drinks per day), gastroesophageal reflux disease, and prior gastric fundoplication; he took no regular medications. He smoked 20 pack-years and denied illicit drug use. 

On examination, his blood pressure was 140/80 mmHg, with a normal mental status, no focal neurologic deficits, mild hepatomegaly, subcutaneous bruises, spider naevi, and frank hematuria on voiding. 

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 73 g/L, white cells 5.8×10^9/L, platelets 35×10^9/L, creatinine 260 μmol/L (baseline ~113–100 μmol/L over the preceding months), urea 17.6 mmol/L, and normal coagulation studies (INR 1.2, aPTT 27 s). Blood film confirmed thrombocytopenia without schistocytes. Retrospective review showed thrombocytopenia (platelets 60×10^9/L) eight months earlier. 

Serologic testing was negative for ANA, ENA, ANCA, anti-GBM, and anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies; serum electrophoresis showed no paraprotein; viral serologies were negative. Serum IgA was elevated at 6.7 g/L; C3 was 0.56 g/L and C4 0.10 g/L. Blood cultures remained sterile. 

Urinalysis of a midstream sample revealed >999×10^6 erythrocytes/L, 10×10^6 leukocytes/L; microscopy showed dysmorphic erythrocytes and erythrocyte casts. A 24-hour urine collection demonstrated protein excretion of 1.8 g. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed mild hepatomegaly with steatosis; each kidney measured ~11 cm with no hydronephrosis. 

Acute glomerulonephritis was suspected. He received intravenous methylprednisolone, platelet transfusion to 102×10^9/L, and an urgent renal biopsy was scheduled alongside a bone marrow biopsy.

A 40-year-old woman presented with a soft, nodular, mobile swelling measuring 3.0 cm by 2.0 cm on the right forearm near the wrist joint. She reported no systemic symptoms. A radiograph of the forearm showed a soft-tissue swelling without bone involvement. Clinically, the lesion was suspected to be a ganglion or, alternatively, a soft-tissue tumor. Fine-needle aspiration yielded thick mucoid material. Leishman-stained cytologic smears showed numerous neutrophils, foamy macrophages, occasional multinucleated giant cells, and macrophages containing coarse dark granular pigment within the cytoplasm, along with many degenerated cells and lymphocytes. On further history taking, the patient recalled an injury to the area with a wooden splinter several weeks earlier.

A 42-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of asthenia. She denied fever or lymphadenopathy. On examination, she had hepatosplenomegaly without other abnormalities. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 16 g/dL, platelets 480 000/µL, AST 55 U/L, ALT 60 U/L, total bilirubin 2 mg/dL, and LDH 300 U/L; serum electrolytes were normal. A bone marrow biopsy revealed a myeloproliferative disorder. An abdominal ultrasound showed hepatosplenomegaly and portal vein thrombosis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a mass encircling the common bile duct and compressing it, with enhancement only during the portal venous phase; hepatosplenomegaly, a portosystemic shunt, and a hepatic perfusion defect were also noted. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography revealed a sleeve of tissue around the common bile duct at the hepatic pedicle with intermediate T2 signal, no arterial enhancement, and intense, homogeneous portal-phase enhancement causing compression of the duct.

A 25-year-old man presented 13 days after his first dose of an mRNA SARS-CoV-2 vaccine with progressive fatigue, exertional dyspnea, headache, nausea, and a diffuse petechial rash. He had no significant past medical history, denied other medications, illicit drugs, or family history of hematologic or autoimmune disease. On examination, he was afebrile, normotensive, and had petechiae on both legs. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 999 U/L, haptoglobin <0.1 g/L, schistocytes 2.1%, platelet count 29/nL, and creatinine 1.5 mg/dL (eGFR 64 mL/min/1.73 m2). A PLASMIC score was 6, indicating high risk for severe ADAMTS-13 deficiency. Neurological examination and head CT were normal. He underwent cranial MRI/MRA, which showed no cerebral thrombosis. Routine tests for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia were negative, and assays for PF4-dependent platelet activation were pending.

A 29-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1 at 24 weeks’ gestation, presented with a 1-week history of gradually worsening, generalized crampy abdominal pain, constipation, and nonbilious vomiting of food material. She denied fever, trauma, or vaginal discharge but noted decreased fetal movements. Her obstetric history was notable for a prior cesarean delivery via Pfannenstiel incision for preeclampsia; current pregnancy was otherwise uncomplicated. 

On examination, she appeared ill, was mildly pale and dehydrated, and had a temperature of 38.0 °C, pulse 136 beats/min, and blood pressure 112/81 mmHg. A nasogastric tube drained fecal material. The abdomen was symmetrically distended, tense, and diffusely tender with hyper-tympany on percussion and absent bowel sounds. Rectal and pelvic examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 9.17 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, platelet count 441 × 10^9/L, and serum potassium 2.52 mmol/L (corrected with IV potassium). Obstetric ultrasound revealed a viable 24-week fetus and extensive gaseous distension of the maternal bowel. A supine abdominal radiograph demonstrated multiple high air–fluid levels and a distended gastric bubble, findings consistent with intestinal obstruction and raising the possibility of a perforated hollow viscus. She was kept nil per os, received IV fluids and electrolyte correction, and was consented for emergency laparotomy.

A 3-year-old boy, fully immunized and previously well, presented with a 3-month history of a painless swelling at the outer corner of his right eye, along with two painful bony swellings: one over the right shin for 2 months and one on the forehead for 15 days. He had no fever, weight loss, cough, visual changes, trauma, bleeding, or known TB exposure. On examination, there was a 3×3 cm soft, erythematous, fluctuant swelling at the right outer canthus, a pea-sized firm swelling on the forehead without inflammation, and an ill-defined, tender, firm bony swelling on the mid-shaft of the right tibia. There was a visible BCG scar and no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and normal liver and renal function tests. A Mantoux test was positive at 14 mm. Noncontrast CT of the head revealed a small lytic lesion in the frontal bone and a hypodense, focal lytic lesion with periosteal reaction in the right zygoma extending into the right infratemporal fossa, with extra-conal soft-tissue thickening in the inferolateral orbit. Orbital ultrasound confirmed an intra-orbital, extra-conal lesion with internal echoes. X-rays of the right tibia showed an ill-defined lytic defect in the medulla of the mid-diaphysis with thick periosteal reaction and surrounding soft-tissue thickening. 

Ultrasound-guided aspiration of the orbital lesion yielded 7 mL of purulent fluid. Gram stain showed only pus cells; bacterial and fungal cultures were sterile. Cytopathology revealed acute inflammatory exudate and necrosis, the acid-fast bacilli stain was negative, and no malignant cells were seen.

An 18-year-old man presented with a one-year history of right foot pain and swelling. He had no history of significant trauma, systemic symptoms, respiratory complaints, or known tuberculosis exposure. The pain was dull, persistent, worsened with activity, and partially improved with rest. On examination, there was tenderness over the first tarsometatarsal joint and dorsal swelling with warmth but no erythema; the range of motion of the ankle and other foot joints was normal. Vital signs were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a normal C-reactive protein level (0.16 mg/dL), an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (20 mm/h), and a negative HIV test. Plain radiographs of the right foot revealed a lucent lesion and bony destruction at the base of the first metatarsal and the medial cuneiform. Chest radiography was normal. MRI of the midfoot demonstrated prominent bone marrow edema, destruction of the first metatarsal base and medial cuneiform, degenerative changes in the first tarsometatarsal joint, and a dorsal fluid collection with localized tenosynovitis of the anterior tibialis tendon. The general appearance was suggestive of septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, or a bone tumor.

A 35-year-old man was referred for a two-month history of nonproductive cough, chills, fever, and significant weight loss despite several courses of oral antibiotics. He denied chest pain, dyspnea, or dysphagia. On examination, his oral temperature was 38.5 °C, and bilateral inspiratory crackles were audible in the mid lung fields. A chest radiograph showed mid-zone consolidation of the right lung. Computed tomography of the chest revealed bilateral patchy alveolar consolidation and a dilated esophagus containing food. Laboratory studies revealed a hemoglobin concentration of 11.8 g/dL, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 50 mm/h, normal white-cell counts without neutrophilia or eosinophilia, and negative rheumatologic testing. Transthoracic fine-needle aspiration of the lung lesions showed granulation tissue in bronchiolar lumens and alveolar ducts with interstitial infiltration by mononuclear cells and foamy macrophages. Upper endoscopy demonstrated a dilated esophagus filled with food; barium esophagography confirmed achalasia.

A 28-year-old man was admitted with a 2-day history of intermittent, sharp, central chest pain with diaphoresis. The pain was pleuritic and worsened when he sat forward. He denied recent viral symptoms and had not received a COVID-19 booster. His medical history was significant for ulcerative colitis diagnosed 3 weeks earlier, for which he started mesalazine; his bowel symptoms had improved. He took no other medications and had no allergies. He smoked 3–4 cigarettes daily and denied alcohol or drug use. There was no family history of cardiovascular disease.

On examination he was hemodynamically stable; the only abnormal finding was stage 2 finger clubbing. ECG showed sinus rhythm with benign early repolarization in the anterior leads. Chest radiography was unremarkable. Laboratory tests revealed a hemoglobin concentration of 132 g/L (120–170), a low mean corpuscular volume of 75 fL (80–97), and a high-sensitivity troponin T of 275 ng/L (<14) peaking at 632 ng/L on hospital day 2. C-reactive protein was 59 mg/L (<5) rising to 173 mg/L. Serum viral and autoantibody screens were negative.

Transthoracic echocardiography showed a normal left ventricular size, borderline low systolic function (LVEF 50–55%) with dyssynchronous septal motion, and a normal right ventricle without pericardial effusion. Given his atypical pain, young age, and troponin rise, an invasive coronary angiogram was considered but deferred in favor of cardiac magnetic resonance imaging.

On hospital day 3, CMR demonstrated a normal-sized left ventricle with mild systolic dysfunction (LVEF 59%) and hypokinesia of the anterolateral and inferolateral segments. The basal lateral wall was thickened to 14 mm. The right ventricle was small with normal function. There was extensive patchy late gadolinium enhancement in a mid-wall to epicardial distribution, particularly in the basal and mid lateral wall. T2-weighted imaging suggested myocardial edema despite suboptimal image quality. There was no pericardial enhancement or effusion. These findings were consistent with an extensive inflammatory myocardial process.

A 72-year-old woman with primary open-angle glaucoma presented with progressive worsening of left peripheral vision over several months, accompanied by left-sided eyelid swelling, redness, and intermittent tearing. Her family noted decreased attention to objects in her left visual field.  
Her medical history included dry eye syndrome, remote left vitreous hemorrhage from retinal detachment, bilateral ptosis repair, and a Baerveldt glaucoma drainage device in the left eye. Current ocular medications were preservative-free dorzolamide/timolol twice daily in both eyes, preservative-free tafluprost nightly in both eyes, and netarsudil nightly in the left eye; she had used netarsudil for nearly two years. Systemic medications included atenolol, gabapentin, sumatriptan, and various supplements. She had a history of atopy and drug-related allergic conjunctivitis.  
On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/25 with pinhole in the left eye; intraocular pressures were 8 mmHg (right) and 7 mmHg (left). Slit-lamp biomicroscopy of the left eye showed 2–3 mm ptosis, superficial punctate epithelial erosions, and two sharply demarcated, branching, needle-like crystalline deposits located inferotemporally and superonasally, each overlying superficial punctate keratopathy. The deposits appeared superficial to a white, hazy corneal opacity. The right eye was unaffected. There was no anterior chamber cell or flare.

A 54‐year‐old man was diagnosed with high‐grade urothelial carcinoma of the bladder, clinical stage T3N2M0, after hematuria workup. Positron emission tomography showed FDG uptake in right paratracheal lymph nodes and a right upper lung nodule. He underwent EBUS‐TBNA of stations 2R, 4R, and 11L; bronchoscopic inspection revealed anthracotic, calcified lymph nodes, and biopsy showed anthracofibrosis. After neoadjuvant chemotherapy, planning for radical cystectomy, a follow‐up chest CT scan demonstrated a new protruding mass at the upper trachea at the previous EBUS‐TBNA site. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy revealed a round, irregular, friable mass partially obstructing the tracheal lumen approximately 7 cm above the carina.

A 14-year-old boy underwent LeFort I osteotomy with an 8 mm vertical maxillary ostectomy and mandibular advancement with bone grafting from the maxilla for Class II retrognathia and microgenia. There were no immediate complications. Several years before 2008, he developed progressive anterior mandibular pain; an “anterior mandibular cyst” was biopsied elsewhere, which relieved his pain.  
In early 2008, he presented with acute swelling, pain, and purulent discharge from what appeared to be an anterior mandibular vestibular abscess. The mandibular incisors were stable but had cervical restorations, and oral hygiene was poor because of pain. Pulp testing showed some nonvital teeth.  
A panoramic radiograph revealed a well-circumscribed radiolucent lesion from right to left canine, with a lobulated sclerotic border, apical to the incisors. CT scans showed a marrow-space lucency with perforation of both buccal and lingual cortices.  
An incisional biopsy with incision and drainage of infection was performed. After infection control, prophylactic endodontic therapy was completed on all six mandibular incisors prior to planned enucleation and peripheral ostectomy.

A 64-year-old man was hospitalized with a one-month history of mildly pruritic skin lesions on the abdomen and lower extremities. Physical examination revealed numerous erythematous, red-brown papulovesicles. He had undergone orthotopic heart transplantation 22 years earlier for dilated cardiomyopathy and was maintained on cyclosporine A and low-dose prednisone. Eleven years after transplantation, he developed an EBV-negative diffuse large B-cell lymphoma treated with six cycles of CHOP chemotherapy; azathioprine was discontinued and cyclosporine A doses were reduced by half, resulting in complete remission. 

On admission, his immunosuppression consisted of cyclosporine A (trough level 70 µg/L) and prednisone 2.5 mg daily. Laboratory studies showed creatinine 2.67 mg/dL; tests for autoimmunity, cryoglobulins, and PCR for EBV, CMV, HHV-8, HCV, and Parvovirus B19 were negative. Punch biopsies of two representative skin lesions were performed. Histopathological examination demonstrated focal hypergranulosis and suprabasal clefts containing acantholytic and dyskeratotic keratinocytes in the epidermis, with a loose perivascular lymphoid infiltrate in the superficial dermis. Direct immunofluorescence was negative.

A 38-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of hypertension first noted at age 24 during pregnancy and again at age 38 after a basal ganglia hemorrhage. She had been diagnosed with splenomegaly of unknown cause at age 21; her younger brother had a similar finding. During her admission for hemorrhage, she underwent a decompressive craniectomy and was noted to have:  
- Normochromic microcytic anemia and thrombocytopenia on full blood examination; other laboratory tests, including thyroid function, cortisol, aldosterone–renin ratio, urinary metanephrines, and renal function, were unremarkable.  
- Lipid profile showed low HDL and elevated triglycerides.  
- Renal Doppler ultrasound excluded renal artery stenosis but revealed incidental bilateral adrenal lesions and hepatosplenomegaly.  
- Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed bilateral adrenal lesions (32 HU noncontrast; absolute washout 76.5%, relative washout 39%) that were unchanged after 8 months, and gross hepatosplenomegaly with dilated portal and splenic veins.  
She had no symptoms of adrenal hormone excess, and her blood pressure was controlled on a single antihypertensive agent.

A 21-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of moderate-intensity pulsatile tinnitus in her left ear. She described the tinnitus as a deep tone synchronous with her heartbeat that increased with moderate exercise and diminished when she pressed on her neck or turned her head to the left. It was constant, unaffected by external noise, and interfered with her sleep and daily activities. She denied headache, vertigo, cervical pain, hearing loss, noise exposure, otalgia, otorrhea, head trauma, use of ototoxic medications, prior ear surgery, and recent infections. On examination, vital signs were normal and otolaryngologic and neurologic evaluations were unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including thyroid function tests, were within normal limits. Pure-tone audiometry and speech discrimination testing were normal. Cardiac Doppler ultrasound was performed to assess for internal jugular vein reflux, and transthoracic echocardiography was done to evaluate for valvular insufficiency; both studies showed no abnormalities.

A 66-year-old woman with hypertension, dyslipidemia, epilepsy, and a prior cerebrovascular accident presented after a 45-minute generalized tonic–clonic seizure, currently in the postictal phase. Blood glucose was 3 g/L. She was hemodynamically stable with an oxygen saturation of 95% on 6 L of oxygen. Laboratory tests showed a peak troponin I level of 1.5 ng/mL (normal <0.04 ng/mL). An ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm with T-wave inversions in the inferior leads. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a nonhypertrophied, nondilated left ventricle with severe hypokinesia of the basal segments, hyperkinesia of the apical segments, and an ejection fraction of 30%–35%; right ventricular function was normal. She was admitted to the cardiac care unit. Because of her altered sensorium, inability to report chest pain, and persistently elevated troponin levels, coronary angiography was performed, which showed no significant coronary artery lesions.

A 19-year-old Somali primigravida at 28 +1 weeks of gestation presented with a 12-month history of progressive right-sided weakness, double vision, a drooping left eyelid, occasional vertigo, and confusion. On examination, she had a right-sided sensomotoric hemisyndrome with facial palsy and left oculomotor nerve paresis. Cranial MRI revealed an 18 × 12 × 18 mm solitary ring-enhancing lesion in the left brainstem with perifocal edema and mild ventricular compression. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed a normal cell count and protein, slightly elevated lactate (2.1 mmol/L) and glucose (5.0 mmol/L), a normal lactate/glucose ratio (0.5), negative cytology for malignant cells, and no microbial growth (including cryptococci, mycobacteria, fungi, Nocardia, aerobe or anaerobe bacteria). A TORCH panel was unremarkable. Obstetric ultrasound confirmed a singleton with consistent growth at the 3rd percentile. Abdominal ultrasound was normal. Chest radiograph demonstrated right-sided hilar lymphadenopathy.

A 72-year-old man with no notable medical history presented in January 2016 to an emergency center for tropical diseases a few days after returning from a 2-week vacation in Cuba. He reported nonpruritic skin lesions, fever, and diffuse myalgia. Examination revealed a diffuse papular rash on the arms, legs, and trunk and two ulcerated lesions on the oropharynx. Given the recent travel and absence of sexual risk factors, a tropical infection—particularly Zika—was considered. He was tested for Zika, dengue, and rickettsiosis and received a 10-day course of doxycycline. The rash resolved completely within 2 weeks, but all tests were negative.

In March 2016, he presented to the ophthalmic emergency department with a rapidly evolving, painless, bilateral loss of vision over a few days. Visual acuity had dropped to 0.1 in the right eye and 0.05 in the left eye. He had no ocular pain, headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, proximal myalgia, arthralgia, fatigue, or other neurological symptoms, and denied recent exposure to toxins, drugs, or vaccines. Fundoscopic examination showed bilateral papillary edema with “thunder hemorrhages” in the right eye. Goldmann visual fields demonstrated an altitudinal superior deficit in the right eye and a large central scotoma in the left eye with a small preserved inferior temporal island. He was hospitalized and started on high-dose corticosteroids and aspirin. 

Fluorescein angiography of the retina excluded arterial leakage or obstruction. Orbital magnetic resonance imaging revealed increased signal of the right optic nerve and a hypersignal of the left on STIR sequences, with spiculated, irregular contrast enhancement of the intraconal fat around both optic nerve sheaths, confirming the clinical suspicion of optic neuritis.

A 62-year-old woman with a 3-year history of idiopathic Parkinson’s disease presented with 4 months of recurrent, unpredictable episodes of jitteriness, perioral and acral formications, palpitations, thoracic tightness, transient hypertension, and a dark red flush of the scalp and neck. She denied fever or altered sensorium. Three months earlier she had been evaluated in an emergency department for chest pain and dyspnea; ECG, echocardiography, and blood work were normal, and she was diagnosed with arterial hypertension and started on ranolazine. Symptoms recurred despite ranolazine; a β-blocker was initiated but discontinued by the patient due to lack of benefit. She had no history of asthma or acute respiratory illness. Her medical history was notable for obstructive sleep apnea on CPAP and chronic hypothyroidism on levothyroxine.  
Her medications at admission were moclobemide 450 mg/day, agomelatine 50 mg/day, pramipexole 0.525 mg/day, rasagiline 1 mg/day, levodopa/benserazide retard 200/50 mg/day, ranolazine 375 mg/day, and levothyroxine 100 μg/day. The moclobemide dose had been raised from 150 mg to 450 mg about 1 year earlier.  
On examination she was alert, oriented, and calm. Neurologic exam showed moderate right upper-extremity rigidity and adiadochokinesia; gait was normal with no tremor. Cardiovascular and respiratory exams were unremarkable. There was severe insomnia and daytime fatigue; mood was intermittently depressed. Vital signs: BP 140/80 mmHg, HR 84 beats/min, T 36.4°C.  
Differential diagnoses considered at admission for the paroxysmal psychovegetative episodes included panic disorder, somatoform autonomic disorder, arterial hypertension with hypertensive exacerbations, iatrogenic hyperthyroidism, asthmatic disorder, and drug-induced serotonin toxicity.

A 27-year-old woman presented with recrudescent, cramp-like pelvic pain localized to the left uterine horn and a desire for a second pregnancy. At age 19, she had hysteroscopy and laparoscopy for pelvic pain refractory to step-3 analgesics; hysteroscopy showed a normal uterine cavity, and laparoscopy revealed a left anterolateral fundal nodule that yielded chocolate-brown fluid when drained. At age 23, persistent pain led to MRI, which showed a left lateral fundal mass measuring 28 mm in outer diameter with a 10 mm central lumen and no evidence of adenomyosis elsewhere. Multiple medical therapies (various hormonal contraceptives, a levonorgestrel intrauterine device, dienogest, and analgesics) provided no relief. At age 27, pelvic ultrasound confirmed a 28 mm × 10 mm mass in the left uterine horn, separate from the endometrial cavity. Diagnostic hysteroscopy again showed a normal uterine cavity with no communication to the mass.

A 78-year-old man underwent laparoscopic totally extraperitoneal repair of a left inguinal hernia (type M2) with mesh fixation. His postoperative course was uneventful, and he was discharged on day 2. Two weeks later, he noted an asymptomatic bulge in the left groin. His vital signs were normal. Examination revealed a non-tender, fluctuant swelling in the left inguinal region without erythema. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count and coagulation studies, were unremarkable. Plain computed tomography showed a 5.0 × 4.0 cm fluid collection with a well-defined capsule in the preperitoneal space and “no hernia recurrence.” Ultrasound demonstrated a mosaic internal echo pattern without detectable blood flow. Because a postoperative seroma was suspected, the decision was made to observe the patient for one month.

A 34-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1 (previous cesarean section), presented at 4 weeks 5 days of amenorrhea with a 1-day history of epigastric pain radiating to the lower abdomen. She denied fever, nausea, vomiting, or vaginal bleeding. On examination, she was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and had epigastric tenderness without rebound or guarding; Murphy’s and McBurney’s signs were negative. Laboratory testing showed a white blood cell count of 13.54×10^9/L and a β-hCG level of 523 IU/L; C-reactive protein was not performed. Transvaginal ultrasound revealed an empty uterus with normal endometrial thickness, a 1.2 cm left adnexal structure with minimal vascularity posterior to the left ovary, and a small amount of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Given the short duration of amenorrhea, absence of vaginal bleeding, β-hCG level below the discriminatory zone, and an empty uterine cavity on ultrasound, a diagnostic laparoscopy was offered to evaluate for a possible ectopic pregnancy.

A 33-year-old woman, 36 weeks pregnant, presented with a 2-week history of worsening peri-alar dermatitis that initially responded to topical hydrocortisone 2.5% cream. Despite continued hydrocortisone use, she developed papules and pustules localized to the perioral area, without comedones, leading to a diagnosis of perioral dermatitis. Topical steroids were discontinued, and sequential therapies with a calcineurin inhibitor, ketoconazole, azelaic acid, and metronidazole were instituted, but her eruption continued to worsen. Tetracycline antibiotics were avoided because of pregnancy. 

At a follow-up visit 2 weeks later, several days after the delivery of a healthy full-term infant, she had perioral and lip erythema, swelling, confluent pustules, and scaling, accompanied by pronounced pruritus and burning. The rest of her face and neck were spared. Vitals were within normal limits, and she had no history of new cosmetic products or habitual lip licking.

An 85-year-old woman was referred with nausea, vomiting, and right lower abdominal pain. Two months earlier she had been hospitalized for infectious enteritis and since discharge had recurrent episodes of diarrhea and constipation. Her history included appendicitis, collagenous colitis, myocardial infarction, hypertension, and asthma. Regular medications were aspirin, antihypertensives, and acid-suppressive therapy; she took no herbal medicines.

On examination, temperature was 38.5 °C with chills, and there was right abdominal tenderness. White blood cell count was 20,480/μL; other labs, including C-reactive protein, were normal.

Abdominal CT showed wall thickening and stricture of the ileum near the terminal ileum, surrounding fat stranding, and proximal small-bowel dilation with fluid; bowel-wall enhancement was preserved.

She was diagnosed with recurrent infectious enteritis and ileus, treated conservatively, and initially improved but relapsed on hospital day 9. Colonoscopy revealed circumferential stenosis of the ileum 20 cm from the ileocecal valve with edematous mucosa but no epithelial lesion. Contrast enterography showed a 2 cm stenotic segment.

Suspecting a neoplastic lesion or postinflammatory scar, laparoscopic partial small-bowel resection was performed. Intraoperatively, a depressed segment of ileum corresponded to the stricture; no other lesions or ascites were seen. The stenotic segment lay 30 cm from the ileocecal valve, which was preserved.

Grossly, the resected ileal segment showed deep ulceration penetrating the mesentery, focal stenosis, and proximal bowel dilation.

A 25-year-old healthy Caucasian woman presented with a three-week history of a lump on the right side of her hard palate. The lesion was non-tender on examination, although she reported a stabbing pain radiating to the temporomandibular joint region during the previous week. As a dentist, she initially suspected an abscess. On intraoral examination, a 2.5 cm submucosal nodule with normal overlying mucosal color was noted on the hard palate, and a fluctuant area was palpated posteriorly. Occlusal radiography showed no abnormalities. The leading clinical hypothesis was a malignant salivary gland tumor, most likely mucoepidermoid carcinoma. An incisional biopsy was performed.

A 9-year-old boy with no past medical history presented with severe right knee pain for 1 day after a fall. He reported progressive discomfort in the same knee over several months, aggravated by the recent trauma, and associated with intermittent fevers up to 38.5 °C, weight loss, night sweats, malaise, and fatigue. There was no personal or family history of tuberculosis. On examination, the right knee was swollen and tender without erythema or warmth; range of motion was preserved, and he could bear weight. 

Initial investigations revealed hemoglobin 12 g/dL, WBC 8500/µL (57% neutrophils), ESR 60 mm/h, and CRP 17.2 mg/L. A chest radiograph was normal. Knee radiographs showed an osseous lesion in the distal metaphysis of the femur. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the knee demonstrated an osseous lesion in the distal femoral metaphysis with physis and epiphyseal involvement, cortical breach, fistula formation, and joint effusion.

A 62-year-old woman was referred to neuropsychiatry with a 3-year history of gradually progressive dysphonia, difficulty keeping her eyes open, and falls. Her medical history included COPD, type 2 diabetes, ischaemic heart disease, hypertension, stage 3b chronic kidney disease, and anaemia. One year after symptom onset, otorhinolaryngology evaluation showed slowed hypopharyngeal and laryngeal movements on laryngoscopy, with normal orofacial muscle function but effortful and delayed vocal production; communication was often supplemented with hand gestures. Neurological examination at that time was reportedly normal apart from variable vocal output, and a brain MRI was unremarkable. A diagnosis of functional voice disorder was made, and she underwent inpatient rehabilitation for FND.

Three years after symptom onset, she reported increasing falls and withdrawal from cooking and outdoor activities, without mood symptoms. The Montreal Cognitive Assessment score was 22/30. Neurological examination demonstrated aphonia, eyelid apraxia, blepharospasm, near-constant use of sunglasses indoors, and frequent touching of the corner of her eyes (a sensory geste). A repeat MRI with susceptibility-weighted imaging showed hypointense signal in the substantia nigra, red nuclei, and globus pallidus, suggestive of iron deposition. A CT scan of the head showed no intracerebral calcification. The diagnosis was then revised to an atypical akinetic rigid syndrome.

A 12-year-old girl in northern Cambodia presented with a two-year history of a white rash extending from her forehead down her nasal bridge. The rash was described as pitted, nonpruritic, and progressively extending toward the nasal tip. She denied pain, tenderness, or preceding trauma in the area. There was no family history of rheumatic disease, and she had no functional limitations such as facial asymmetry, expression-related tightness, vision changes, or headaches. She also denied joint pain, stiffness, or swelling in her extremities.

Her past medical history was notable for bilateral exotropia treated at age 2 with spectacles and surgery. She reported no photosensitivity or vision changes since treatment.

On examination, there was a shiny, depressed, white, linear plaque over the frontal scalp extending to the nasal tip, with associated skin atrophy and localized alopecia. The oral mucosa, gums, lips, tongue, and surrounding facial and bony structures were normal.

Laboratory studies including complete blood count with differential, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, renal function, liver enzymes, rheumatoid factor, and lupus antibody latex test were all within normal limits. Skin biopsy and antinuclear antibody testing were not performed due to laboratory limitations. A chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasound were normal.

A 33-year-old woman presented with a two-month history of recurrent right upper quadrant abdominal pain radiating to the back and right shoulder, worsened by fatty meals. She had no history of smoking, alcohol use, prior surgery, or drug allergies. On examination, she was afebrile, with tenderness in the right upper quadrant and a positive Murphy’s sign. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, WBC 5.1×10^3/mm^3, serum amylase 74 U/L (reference 40–140), blood glucose 85 mg/dL, and normal liver and renal function tests. Abdominal ultrasound revealed gallbladder wall thickening and multiple gallstones, the largest measuring 4.7 mm. The patient underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy for presumed chronic calculous cholecystitis. 

On gross examination, the gallbladder measured 7 cm in length with a wall thickness of approximately 0.5 cm. A firm, well-circumscribed, yellow, lobulated nodule measuring 1.2 cm surrounded the cystic duct; a second similar nodule, 0.5 cm in diameter, was present in the serosa of the gallbladder neck. The mucosa was intact and unremarkable.

A 16-year-old African American female with obesity, depression, and a history of presumed idiopathic rhabdomyolysis presented with a one-week history of diffuse myalgia and muscle weakness in her bilateral upper arms, thighs, and buttocks, accompanied by dark urine since the morning of presentation. She denied recent strenuous exercise or systemic symptoms. She had received her second dose of the BNT162b2 mRNA COVID-19 vaccine one week earlier, with only expected local and systemic post-vaccination symptoms.

On arrival she was hemodynamically stable. Physical examination revealed diffuse myalgias and pain with passive movement but no focal neurologic deficits; strength was 4/5 in all extremities, improving to 5/5 by discharge. Laboratory evaluation showed a serum creatine kinase level of 153,000 IU/L, urinalysis positive for “blood” and protein, normal electrolytes, and calcium 7.2 mg/dL (ionized calcium 4.4 mg/dL). Electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia with a QTc of 443 ms. 

Two years earlier, she was hospitalized for febrile Group A streptococcal pharyngitis complicated by rhabdomyolysis (CK 984,800 IU/L) requiring dialysis. After her first HPV vaccination in 2014, she had similar myalgias and weakness without hospitalization. 

During the current hospitalization she did not require dialysis. Extensive metabolic testing (plasma amino acids, urine organic acids, pyruvate, acylcarnitine, total and free carnitines) was normal. Whole-exome sequencing was sent, and rheumatologic, endocrine, toxicology, and infectious evaluations were unrevealing.

A 63-year-old woman presented with a long history of recalcitrant groin plaques. She had hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine and a maternal history of a similar dermatosis. Since age 35, she experienced recurrent episodes of friable plaques and painful erosions localized to the inguinal folds; other intertriginous areas and the genital mucosa were spared. Lesions worsened with heat and sweating. On examination, there were bilateral macerated erythematous plaques with superficial erosions in the inguinal regions extending onto the lateral labia majora. Initial differential diagnoses included Darier’s disease, intertriginous candidiasis, tinea cruris, and pemphigus vegetans. A skin biopsy was performed for diagnostic clarification.
Histologic evaluation showed acantholysis at multiple levels in the epidermis, resembling a “dilapidated brick wall,” with few dyskeratotic cells and parakeratosis.

A 9-month-old girl from the Adamawa Region of Cameroon was brought to clinic for a reddish, “snake-like” rash on her abdomen that appeared 3 days earlier. Her mother noted that the lesions seemed pruritic because the child was irritable and restless during sleep. She estimated that the lesions lengthened by about 2 cm per day. The child had no fever, cough, or other systemic symptoms. There were no pet dogs or cats at home, but stray dogs frequented the courtyard. The mother did not allow her children to play in the dirt but dried their clothes on the grass in the courtyard. The patient’s twin sister had no symptoms.

On examination, the infant was alert, calm, and in no distress. Temperature was 37.4 °C, pulse 92 beats/min, respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, and weight 9 kg. Skin inspection revealed multiple erythematous, raised, thin serpiginous lesions of varying lengths over the trunk and proximal arms. The lesions did not extend further during the examination.

A 27-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with 4 days of progressive scrotal and penile edema, erythema, and pain. He reported an arthropod bite near the glans penis during a camping trip with river swimming in southern Missouri. He is monogamous with a single male partner and at symptom onset noted a single papular lesion on the right coronal sulcus. He denied dysuria, hematuria, dyschezia, and hematochezia. Two days before admission, he received cephalexin for presumed scrotal cellulitis but had worsening edema, myalgias, chills, and fevers. On inpatient evaluation by urology, there were no signs warranting surgical intervention or concern for necrotizing infection, and he was started on cefepime and vancomycin. Dermatology was consulted on hospital day 6 for persistent, tender induration over the scrotum, penile shaft, pubis, and perineum with mild erythema and without crepitus or fluctuance; a yellow-crusted papule was noted at the right coronal sulcus. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (13.7 × 10^9 cells/L), thrombocytopenia (143 × 10^3/μL), lactic acidosis (3.14 mmol/L), C-reactive protein 18.5 mg/dL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 24 mm/h. Blood cultures, skin bacterial cultures, urinalysis, HIV, HSV-1 and ‑2, VZV, Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhea, Treponema pallidum, and hepatitis C testing were negative. Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis and scrotal ultrasound showed bilateral hydroceles and inguinal adenopathy.

An 18-year-old student presented with 2 days of vaginal bleeding with passage of clots. She denied abdominal pain, trauma, instrumentation, or sexual activity. Her menarche was at 14 years, with regular 26–28-day cycles lasting 3 days; her last period was 10 days ago and normal.  
On examination, she appeared well, afebrile with a temperature of 36.8°C, pulse 100/min, respiratory rate 18/min, and blood pressure 120/80 mmHg. Abdominal examination was unremarkable. Pelvic examination showed an intact hymen. There was a polypoid, bright-red, hyperemic mass protruding from the urethral meatus, with a central dimple and active bleeding with adherent clots. The surrounding vaginal and periurethral mucosa appeared normal.

A 27-year-old man underwent a preemployment medical screening in which a loud systolic murmur was detected. He had been healthy and asymptomatic, with no history of cardiac symptoms. On examination, his heart rate was 60 beats per minute and blood pressure was 131/77 mmHg. There was a prominent right ventricular heave and a grade 5/6 harsh systolic murmur best heard at the left parasternal border, which increased in intensity with the Valsalva maneuver. No lymphadenopathy or testicular masses were noted. 

An electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a 4.0 × 2.5 cm mass with a broad base attached to the right ventricular outflow tract, with an estimated right ventricular systolic pressure of 64–69 mmHg. A contrast-enhanced chest CT scan confirmed a large soft-tissue mass seemingly arising from the interventricular septum and extending toward the aortic root.

A 41-year-old woman was diagnosed with SARS-CoV-2 infection after two positive PCR tests (November 5 and 20, 2020) and a negative test on November 30. During the acute illness, she had low‐grade fever (maximum 37.2 °C) and severe leg pain but no cough, dyspnea, or loss of smell or taste. She received no treatment and did not undergo chest imaging. She returned to work in early December, and one week later she began having severe, brief episodes of circular dizziness when getting out of bed or turning to the right. These attacks, which lasted seconds at a time, continued for six days and were accompanied by nausea and vomiting. She also had severe occipital headaches radiating to the neck during the first few days. 

On initial evaluation by her general practitioner and subsequent neurologic consultation, her dizziness had lessened. Laboratory studies were notable only for a serum potassium level of 3.7 mmol/L. She was afebrile, normotensive, independently mobile, and breathing comfortably. Her neurologic examination was normal. She was referred to otolaryngology. She had no hearing complaints and denied tinnitus but continued to have a moderate occipital headache. 

On neurotological assessment, there was no spontaneous nystagmus, and head-impulse and skew-deviation tests were negative. The Romberg test (eyes open and closed) and the Fukuda stepping test revealed no lateralization. During the Dix–Hallpike maneuver on the right, after a latency of approximately 10 seconds she experienced dizziness and nausea, and a small vertical-torsional geotropic positional nystagmus was observed for about 5 seconds. On returning to the seated position, her vertigo and nystagmus intensified.

A 75-year-old Asian man with a history of cholangiocarcinoma, early gastric cancer, emphysema, and hypertension, who was taking low-dose aspirin after thoracic aortic aneurysm repair, presented with a 3-week history of dizziness and lightheadedness that progressively worsened. One week before admission, a noncontrast head CT at a local hospital showed two cerebellar lesions, measuring 31 mm on the right and 34 mm on the left, with mixed high- and low-density mottled areas. He was admitted with presumed intracranial hemorrhagic space-occupying lesions and managed conservatively. On transfer to our center, he had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of E3V3M5 and unstable respiration. Repeat noncontrast CT showed no change in lesion size but a change in internal density and increased perifocal edema causing posterior fossa crowding and brainstem compression. Contrast-enhanced CT and 3D-CTA revealed no abnormal blood vessels or mass lesions. Laboratory studies on admission showed a platelet count of 314 × 10^3/µL, an APTT of 28.8 seconds, a PT-INR of 1.26, and an ARU of 536 on VerifyNow™ analysis.

A 32-year-old man with a history of chronic alcoholism and smoking presented with 2 weeks of colicky left lower quadrant abdominal pain and a 30-kg weight loss over 2 months. Two months earlier, he had been hospitalized for alcohol-induced necrotizing acute pancreatitis treated conservatively.
