He denied nausea, vomiting, gastrointestinal bleeding, fever, or other systemic symptoms. On examination, he was afebrile, normotensive, heart rate 92 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. The abdomen was soft with mild tenderness in the left iliac fossa and lumbar region without peritoneal signs. Laboratory studies and abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable. Colonoscopy revealed an ulcerated partial stricture of the descending colon 30 cm from the anal verge; the scope could not be advanced beyond the lesion, and balloon dilatation was unsuccessful. A tuberculosis workup—including sputum acid-fast bacillus smear, chest radiograph, purified protein derivative test, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and biopsy—was negative. Colonic biopsy showed active focal colitis with ulceration but no granulomas. Barium enema demonstrated a benign-appearing stricture without malignancy, and CT colonography showed a 6-cm stricture in the descending colon. Serologic testing revealed an ASCA IgG level of 22.2 U/mL (normal <10 U/mL), and sulfasalazine was initiated for presumed Crohn’s disease.

A 65-year-old woman was transferred to our emergency department with decreased level of consciousness. She had a history of hypertension, 10 years of diabetes mellitus, recurrent cystitis, and degenerative arthritis treated with daily dexamethasone for approximately five years. Three weeks before transfer, she was hospitalized elsewhere for drowsiness associated with fever (38.8°C) and dyspnea and treated for presumed community-acquired pneumonia with ceftriaxone and azithromycin for 14 days. After improvement, she complained of persistent left lower quadrant abdominal pain, and an abdominal CT scan revealed a mass-like lesion in the left renal area suspected to represent an abscess. While receiving ciprofloxacin, she again developed decreased consciousness.

On admission, her temperature was 36.4°C, blood pressure 134/71 mm Hg, pulse 95/min, and respiratory rate 18/min. She was drowsy but without focal neurologic deficits. Cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable, and there was no abdominal tenderness or edema. Laboratory studies showed sodium 112 mmol/L, potassium 3.4 mmol/L, chloride 77 mmol/L, total CO2 21 mmol/L, serum osmolality 240 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 315 mOsm/kg, morning cortisol 7.1 µg/dL, and a normal thyroid profile. Urinalysis demonstrated 3–5 white cells per high-power field and yeast-like organisms. MRI of the brain and angiography were normal, and chest x-ray was unremarkable. Hyponatremia was managed with sodium replacement, and secondary adrenal insufficiency due to chronic steroid use was confirmed by a low-dose cosyntropin stimulation test. Hydrocortisone was initiated, and her prednisolone was tapered to 7.5 mg daily.

On the third hospital day, her mental status and serum sodium normalized, but she developed myalgia and leukocytosis (white blood cell count 13,650/µL with 84.9% neutrophils). A second abdominal CT scan showed an ill-defined inflammatory lesion with multifocal abscess pockets in the left perirenal space extending to the descending colon, which was suspected to be actinomycosis. Urinalysis continued to show pyuria and yeast, and urine cultures yielded yeast. Intravenous ampicillin was started for presumed actinomycosis. Colonoscopy showed no specific lesion.

A 52-year-old man presented with 10 days of worsening right temporomandibular joint pain, acute malocclusion with a posterior open bite on the right, deviation of the lower dental midline to the left, and limited mouth opening. He had been diagnosed at another clinic with temporomandibular disorder and treated with a muscle relaxant and analgesics for 7 days without improvement. He had no systemic predisposing factors. On examination, maximum mouth opening was 25 mm, there was a posterior open bite on the right side, and preauricular swelling was present. Plain radiography showed widening of the joint space in the right TMJ. Laboratory testing revealed a normal serum leukocyte count and an elevated C-reactive protein level. Suspecting an infectious process of the TMJ, a provisional diagnosis of septic arthritis of the right TMJ was made, and arthrocentesis under local anesthesia was performed. Joint fluid was obtained and was observed to be turbid with whitish debris.

A 32-year-old previously healthy man presented with 3 weeks of gradually worsening periumbilical abdominal pain that began approximately 2 weeks after starting Brazilian jiu-jitsu. He attributed the pain to contusion from the opponent’s “knee on stomach” technique. The pain was constant (5–7/10), relieved by lying still, and exacerbated by movement. He reported nausea without vomiting, no fevers or chills, and reduced bowel movement frequency without blood or mucus. He denied medications, abdominal surgery, family history of liver disease or thrombosis, and risk factors such as alcohol abuse or illicit drug use.

On examination, he was afebrile with normal vital signs. Abdominal palpation elicited periumbilical and right upper quadrant tenderness without rebound; there was no hepatosplenomegaly or ascites. Laboratory studies showed AST 77 U/L and ALT 44 U/L, with normal bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, amylase, lipase, complete blood count, coagulation studies, electrolytes, and renal function. A comprehensive hypercoagulability work-up—including protein C, protein S, antithrombin, antiphospholipid antibodies, JAK2 V617F, Factor V Leiden mutation, and PNH flow cytometry—was negative; hepatitis serologies and autoimmune liver antibodies were also negative.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated partial thrombosis of the main portal vein extending into the left branch, partial thrombosis of the superior mesenteric vein with marked distention and surrounding infiltrative changes, collateral vessels at the porta hepatis, and proximal jejunal edema; there was no pneumatosis, ascites, or abdominal mass.

A 24-year-old woman with a history of antiphospholipid syndrome presented with a few days of progressive shortness of breath and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Six days earlier, she had developed a deep-vein thrombosis of the right profunda femoris vein and was receiving therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin. 

On arrival to the emergency department, a computed tomography pulmonary angiogram revealed new pulmonary emboli in the right lower lung, and electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia. She was admitted, and anticoagulation was changed to a heparin infusion. 

Five days into hospitalization, she developed worsening hypoxemia and high-grade fever; chest radiography demonstrated pulmonary edema. An infectious workup, including a respiratory virus panel, blood cultures, urine culture, and sputum culture, was negative. She was transferred to the medical intensive care unit for acute hypoxic respiratory failure.

On the first day in the intensive care unit, repeat pulmonary angiography ruled out new emboli. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 40–45%, global hypokinesia, and McConnell’s sign. She received tissue plasminogen activator. Shortly thereafter, her troponin concentration rose from 103 to 4100 ng/L. Electrocardiography continued to show sinus tachycardia with an indeterminate axis and low-voltage QRS complexes in the precordial leads. Emergent coronary angiography demonstrated non-obstructive coronary artery disease.

On the second day, she developed acute kidney injury (creatinine rising from 0.7 to 4.8 mg/dL), metabolic acidosis (pH 7.1), and refractory hyperkalemia requiring continuous renal replacement therapy. She became hypotensive, required vasopressors, and developed discoloration of the feet. Liver enzymes acutely rose (alanine aminotransferase >2000 IU/L, aspartate aminotransferase >8000 IU/L), consistent with a shock pattern. Her respiratory status deteriorated further, and she required endotracheal intubation.

Laboratory studies showed elevated white-cell count, prolonged prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time, rising troponin, and severe transaminitis. Blood cultures remained negative. Liver ultrasonography revealed patent hepatic vasculature. A peripheral blood smear showed no schistocytes, and fibrinogen levels were within the normal range.

A 25-year-old man was brought to the emergency department with confusion, episodes of syncope, and a fruity breath odor. He was acutely dehydrated, with a blood glucose level of 648 mg/dL and an arterial pH of 6.9. On examination, he was obnubilated, normoweight (BMI 22.3 kg/m2), with dehydrated skin, polypnea, tachycardia, hypotension, and a weak pulse. A diagnosis of diabetic ketoacidosis was made, and treatment was initiated.

His medical history began at age 19, when, under peer pressure, he began massive intravenous AAS cycles: daily alternating doses of 2500 mg testosterone isocaproate, 400 mg testosterone enanthate, 500 mg Stanozolol, 1000 mg Trenbolone, and 500 mg Nadrolone. Within six months, his weight rose from 80 to 157 kg. Days before completing the cycle, he developed severe chest pain after an injection. ECG showed extensive anterior STEMI, and troponin I was elevated; he declined coronarography but remained hospitalized. At discharge, ECG showed QS waves in V1–V4 and Q waves in DI and aVL; echocardiography revealed severe LV systolic dysfunction with apical hypokinesia and dilation. He was also diagnosed with dyslipidemia and started on chronic cardiovascular therapy.

At age 23, he was diagnosed with diabetes mellitus based on elevated glucose levels and symptoms. He was prescribed a basal-bolus insulin regimen (30 IU rapid-acting before each meal and 30 IU basal), but he was noncompliant due to hypoglycemic episodes and received no treatment for two years. 

In December 2020, he presented as above and was started on a revised insulin regimen: rapid-acting insulin 10 IU before breakfast, 8 IU before lunch and dinner, and long-acting insulin 34 IU at night. He was also referred for psychological support.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of generalised abdominal pain that had localised to the right iliac fossa. She reported nausea and constipation, but her bowels had opened on the day of presentation. She had no urinary symptoms, significant medical history, or regular medications. On examination, she was haemodynamically stable and apyrexial. The abdomen was soft and non-distended, with localized tenderness in the right iliac fossa but no signs of peritonitis. Laboratory studies showed a mild leukocytosis (11.2 × 10^9/L); the remainder of the complete blood count and serum biochemistry were within normal limits. She was discharged home but returned the following day with persistent symptoms and was referred to the surgical team. Abdominal ultrasonography was normal, with no appendix mass identified. After two more days of observation with non-resolving pain, the decision was made to perform a diagnostic laparoscopy for suspected appendicitis.

A 20-year-old man presented with right knee pain for 3 months without trauma or overuse. Examination revealed joint effusion and a limited range of motion; there was no locking or palpable mass. He had no significant medical history and had not received prior treatment. An MRI of the right knee showed an intra‐articular lesion around the posterior cruciate ligament that was iso- or hypointense relative to muscle on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images. The preoperative differential diagnosis included synovial chondromatosis, pigmented villonodular synovitis, and malignant soft‐tissue tumor. Arthroscopy revealed synovial hyperplasia with inflammation and a well-circumscribed mass anterior to the posterior cruciate ligament. The lesion was completely excised, and a partial synovectomy was performed. Macroscopically, the specimen was a 2.5 cm × 2 cm × 1 cm fragment of grey-red tissue.

A 49-year-old homeless woman with a 35–pack-year smoking history and no known medical problems presented with painful oral ulcerations on her gums and palate for at least 6 months. She denied fevers, weight loss, lymphadenopathy, or immunosuppressive exposures. On examination, she had hypertrophic gingiva, a 1-cm ulcer adjacent to the right upper incisor, and a palatal ulcer near the left upper molars. There was no palpable lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, rash, or joint findings.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and differential except for mild lymphopenia (950 cells/μL), normal metabolic panel, liver function tests, and lactate dehydrogenase. Autoimmune serologies (ANA, ANCA) and serologies for HIV and viral hepatitis were negative. EBV PCR in serum was negative.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed bilateral diffuse cervical lymphadenopathy (largest node 2.4 cm) but no mediastinal, axillary, abdominal, retroperitoneal, pelvic, or inguinal adenopathy. The spleen was normal in size; other viscera were unremarkable.

Biopsies of the right perimolar and left palatal lesions showed extensive mucosal ulceration with a dense infiltrate of small lymphocytes and scattered large atypical lymphocytes, including rare Hodgkin and Reed–Sternberg–like forms. These large cells were strongly CD30 positive, uniformly PAX5 positive, variably CD20 positive, uniformly EBER positive, and negative for CD3, CD15, and CD79a. Molecular studies demonstrated a clonal immunoglobulin gene rearrangement. The overall findings were consistent with a clonal EBV-driven B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder.  

Diagnostic considerations at this stage included EBV-positive mucocutaneous ulcer and other EBV-positive B-cell lymphomas, such as EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

A 24-year-old man was referred for bilateral swelling and spontaneous gingival bleeding in the posterior mandible. His medical history was noncontributory, and he had no pain, tenderness, or discharge; skin color and temperature were normal. Intraoral examination showed pericoronitis and bleeding from the periodontal pocket of the right mandibular second molar, and firm swelling in both retromolar regions. Panoramic radiographs revealed bilateral poorly demarcated radiolucent lesions measuring 4×3×3 cm on the right and 2.5×1.5×1.5 cm on the left. Family history disclosed that his father had received treatment for a parathyroid gland disorder. Laboratory tests showed a parathyroid hormone level of 714 pg/mL (normal 15–65), serum calcium 12.8 mg/dL, and alkaline phosphatase 220 U/L.

A 46-year-old woman with hypertension, obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and nicotine use was referred for evaluation of large, map-like areas of necrosis involving the mons pubis and right medial thigh. Initial laboratory evaluation revealed a leukocyte count of 12.8 × 10^3/μl and a C-reactive protein level of 183.5 mg/l. She was febrile and in poor general condition. Necrotizing fasciitis was suspected, and she was transferred for urgent surgical assessment. On admission, she was in septic shock and had skin necroses with surrounding erythema and local hyperthermia.

An 87-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of binocular diplopia, progressive left-sided ptosis, and left-sided scalp tenderness. Her symptoms began days after a fall from a stepladder, when she sustained a minor head injury without loss of consciousness; a head CT at that time showed only a left subgaleal hematoma. She was discharged without specific treatment. Two weeks later, she noted gradual onset of left-sided ptosis and lateral gaze deviation and was referred to neurology. On further questioning, she endorsed new-onset jaw claudication and scalp tenderness around the area of her injury. She denied constitutional symptoms.

On examination, she had complete left ptosis and a pupil-involving left third cranial nerve palsy, as well as restricted left eye abduction consistent with a sixth cranial nerve palsy. Visual acuity was normal, and fundoscopic examination showed a normal optic disc without anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. The remainder of the cranial nerve, motor, sensory, coordination, and gait examinations was unremarkable. Temporal artery pulsations and peripheral pulses were normal, with no bruits. There was no proximal muscle weakness.

Laboratory studies revealed a C-reactive protein level of 10.4 mg/L (upper limit of normal <6 mg/L) and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 30 mm/h (within normal range for her age). MRI and angiography of the brain and orbits were normal except for an incidental 1.3 mm middle cerebral artery aneurysm.

A 60-year-old man with hypertension, dyslipidemia, and a family history of heart disease presented with 6 hours of moderate chest pain. He had a history of episodes of brief dull left shoulder pain over the preceding month and was blind from hereditary retinopathy. On arrival, blood pressure was 150/100 mmHg. Cardiac auscultation and respiratory examination were unremarkable. ECG showed sinus rhythm at 80 beats/min, 3 mm ST-segment elevation, and formed Q waves in the anterior and lateral leads. High-sensitivity troponin was markedly elevated. The patient received 300 mg aspirin and 180 mg ticagrelor and was taken for urgent catheterization. Coronary angiography revealed occlusion of the proximal left anterior descending artery; two drug-eluting stents were placed with restoration of TIMI 3 flow and no visible complications. A 70% stenosis in the mid right coronary artery was left untreated. He remained symptom-free on dual antiplatelet therapy, a proton-pump inhibitor, and a high-intensity statin.

On the following day, transthoracic echocardiography showed a spindle-shaped mass measuring approximately 35 mm within the hypokinetic interventricular septum, with central echo-lucency. The differential diagnosis included an intraventricular thrombus, myocardial tumor, and septal hematoma. Because a soft-tip guidewire was used and no contrast extravasation was seen during or after PCI, coronary perforation was considered unlikely.

Same-day multislice cardiac CT confirmed a hyperdense spindle-shaped septal mass on non-contrast images and no enhancement on post-contrast images. Coronary CT angiography demonstrated no in-stent stenosis but significant narrowing of the LAD distal to the stents, suggestive of spasm. Despite imaging, the nature of the septal mass remained uncertain.

A 38-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of pain and swelling of the left mandible after being slightly punched in the face. He had noted some paresthesia in the area for an unspecified duration. His medical history was noncontributory. On examination, there was slight facial asymmetry and palpable crepitation along the inferior border of the left mandible. Intraorally, the lower left second premolar was absent, and there was a firm swelling with mild erythema in the left posterior mandible. A panoramic radiograph revealed a well-defined unilocular radiolucent lesion extending from the first premolar region to the second molar area, destroying bone from the alveolar crest to the inferior mandibular border. A small ill-defined area was seen at the anterior margin of the lesion, which was associated with an obvious fracture through the inferior mandibular border. The radiolucency had displaced the impacted lower left second premolar to the inferior border of the mandible.

A 17-year-old young adult underwent a splenectomy after a motor-vehicle collision, with an uneventful 1-week postoperative course on phenytoin for seizure prophylaxis. Four weeks after splenectomy and 3 weeks after discharge, he presented with high fever, generalized body pain, and severe sore throat. He was treated for presumed postsplenectomy sepsis with IV vancomycin and ceftriaxone for 4 days, then discharged on clindamycin and ciprofloxacin, with only transient improvement. Within 36 hours, he again developed fever (39.5 °C), malaise, myalgia, sore throat, generalized maculopapular erythrodermic rash, oral lesions, swollen neck, and painful lymphadenopathy. On examination, heart rate was 128 bpm, blood pressure 110/90 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 bpm. Findings included diffuse maculopapular rash with distal extremity scaling, severe nonexudative conjunctivitis with periorbital edema, inflamed lips with cracking, and multiple tender cervical and axillary lymph nodes (up to 17 mm). Cardiac, pulmonary, and abdominal examinations were otherwise unremarkable. Blood cultures were negative. Chest radiograph showed no pathology. Ultrasonography revealed bilateral neck and axillary lymphadenopathy and mild ascites; echocardiography demonstrated trace pericardial fluid, normal valves, and an ejection fraction of 70%.

A 44-year-old man with no prior medical history presented after 1 week of progressive weakness, dyspnea, nonproductive cough, fever (38.9 °C), vomiting, and diarrhea. He was admitted to the ICU with community-acquired pneumonia and respiratory failure. On admission he was febrile (38 °C), tachycardic (110 beats/min), blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, tachypneic (28 breaths/min), and had an oxygen saturation of 88% on 50% Ventimask. Lung auscultation revealed bilateral crackles; heart sounds were normal with no murmurs; there was no peripheral edema.

Empiric antibiotics and oseltamivir were started, and influenza A(H1N1) pneumonia was confirmed by PCR. He required mechanical ventilation and remained hemodynamically stable until day 12, when he developed sudden severe hypotension (systolic blood pressure < 80 mmHg), tachycardia (> 140 beats/min), and worsening respiratory status. Arterial blood gas on FiO2 60% showed pH 7.39, PaCO2 26.7 mmHg, PaO2 55.9 mmHg, bicarbonate 15.9 mmol/L, base excess − 8.1, lactate 0.9 mmol/L, and O2 saturation 91.2%.

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL, leukocytes 14.8 × 10^3/mm^3, INR 1.29, D-dimer > 10,000 ng/mL, and C-reactive protein > 90 mg/L; troponin I was 0.022 ng/dL. Cultures and urinary antigens were negative. Chest radiograph showed a right basal infiltrate.

Transthoracic echocardiography yielded poor images. Transesophageal echocardiography showed a small hyperdynamic left ventricle and a severely dilated, dysfunctional right ventricle with an RV/LV end-diastolic area ratio of 1.7, an RV/LV diameter ratio of 1.4, McConnell’s sign, and systolic flattening of the interventricular septum, consistent with acute RV pressure overload.

A 12-lead electrocardiogram demonstrated T-wave inversion in leads V1 to V4 and an S1Q3T3 pattern without ST-segment abnormalities.

A 28-year-old woman underwent a first-trimester ultrasound that revealed a septated fetal cystic hygroma, which had resolved by 20 weeks. Placental villous sampling showed a normal male karyotype (46, XY), and tests for congenital viral infections were negative. At 20 weeks, Doppler interrogation of the ductus venosus demonstrated a reversed a-wave during atrial contraction; this normalized later in gestation. 

The infant was born at 39+4 weeks’ gestation, weighing 4385 g, with a head circumference +3.4 SD above the mean. He required supplemental oxygen for several hours after delivery, then remained clinically stable. Physical examination revealed no dysmorphic features or cardiac murmurs. Electrocardiography and chest radiography were unremarkable.

Because of the prenatal hygroma, transthoracic echocardiography was performed on day 5 of life. Cardiac structure and function were normal except that neither the right nor left superior vena cava was visualized. Instead, a venous structure coursed posterior to the heart and drained into a markedly dilated inferior vena cava, which connected normally to the right atrium. Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen confirmed absence of both superior vena cavae, with head and upper-limb venous return via a plexus draining into the inferior vena cava.

Since 1 month of age, the infant experienced persistent wheezing, worsening with respiratory infections. At 8 months, magnetic resonance angiography of the chest and abdomen reconfirmed total absence of the superior vena cava: the right arm and right head drained into the azygos vein, the left side drained into the hemiazygos vein, which joined the azygos below the carina and formed a loop beneath the diaphragm to the inferior vena cava. No vascular structures compressed the trachea. 

At 1 year, abdominal ultrasonography showed no portal hypertension. Genetic testing for CATCH 22 syndrome, Sotos syndrome, and Prader-Willi syndrome was negative.

A 32-year-old man with no prior medical history underwent a tracheostomy for management of a traumatic head injury. One month after decannulation, he presented with progressive exertional dyspnea and difficulty breathing. He also reported a persistent foreign-body sensation in his throat and an inability to expectorate secretions. 
On examination, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable but had audible stridor. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 13,400 cells/mm3. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. 
Because of ongoing respiratory symptoms, a CT scan of the neck was obtained; it demonstrated a well-defined, homogenous, curvilinear soft-tissue density within the hypopharynx, larynx, and upper trachea, causing mild to moderate luminal narrowing. 
The patient then underwent fiberoptic bronchoscopy. A greyish strand of thick, glistening inspissated material was seen projecting across the vocal cords at the anterior commissure. The scope was advanced distally, revealing that this band-like structure was adherent to the anterior tracheal wall at the tracheostomy site. The vocal cords appeared normal, with no granulation tissue or narrowing at the stoma. A full inspection of the tracheobronchial tree and toileting were performed, and on reevaluation, the initial band-like structure was no longer visualized. Assuming it was a mucus strand that the patient had dislodged, the bronchoscope was withdrawn.

A 59-year-old man with a history of heavy smoking presented with 5 hours of left lower leg pain. Vital signs were notable for sinus tachycardia on ECG without ST–T–wave changes; heart sounds were normal and lungs were clear. Examination of the left leg revealed it to be cold and pale, with a weak femoral artery pulse and absence of popliteal, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses; neurologic function was intact. Duplex ultrasonography showed thrombotic occlusion of the proximal left common femoral artery (80%) and of three arteries below the knee (100%). Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated left ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVEF, 30%–35%), apical akinesia, and a mobile thrombus measuring 21 × 15 mm in the left ventricular apex. He was diagnosed with embolism-induced acute left lower leg ischemia and received intravenous unfractionated heparin (100 U/kg) followed by catheter-directed thrombolysis with recombinant tissue-type plasminogen activator (1 mg/h) and heparin (200–500 U/h). Twelve hours after initiation of therapy, the leg ischemia improved, but he developed abrupt onset of bilateral, nonradiating, sharp, constant flank pain without hematuria. His temperature was 36.3 °C, blood pressure 140/90 mm Hg, heart rate 75 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation was 98% on room air. Physical examination revealed no guarding, rebound tenderness, or hematoma.

A 33-year-old previously healthy man came to the emergency department with intense left-sided abdominal pain radiating to the left inguinal area, rated 10/10. He denied trauma, drug use, and had no significant medical history apart from an appendectomy. On examination his abdomen was soft without guarding, peripheral pulses were palpable, and there was no costovertebral or testicular tenderness. He received IV oxycodone with pain relief. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 13.4 × 10^9/L and a normal C-reactive protein level; other values, including renal function and liver enzymes, were within reference ranges. A noncontrast helical CT scan showed no urolithiasis and normal kidneys. The next morning he was pain-free, his WBC count had decreased to 10.0 × 10^9/L, and he was discharged with instructions to return if pain recurred.

He returned the following evening with rapid-onset, intense pain in the lower left quadrant radiating to the left testicle. A urologist assessed him for testicular torsion, but clinical findings did not support this diagnosis, and urolithiasis remained the provisional diagnosis. Exploratory surgery was planned, and before proceeding, a contrast-enhanced abdominal CT was ordered.

A 54-year-old man presented with severe bilateral lower-extremity swelling, redness, and pain beginning a few hours after completing a 100-mile trail ultramarathon in February (ambient 44–76 °F). He ran continuously for over 30 hours, denied any injury, fever, changes in urine color, focal pain, or neurologic symptoms, and had no prior history of similar findings. His medical and surgical histories were unremarkable.

On examination (3 days after the race), vital signs were normal. Both legs from the knees to the toes had 4+ pitting edema, moderate diffuse erythema, and warmth, without purpura. The knees, ankles, and feet were nontender; there was mild tenderness over the lower-leg muscle compartments and mild pain on passive ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion. Ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion strength was 4+/5 bilaterally. The neurovascular examination was otherwise normal.

Laboratory studies showed a serum creatine kinase level of 5800 U/L; urinalysis revealed protein 30 mg/dL, negative hemoglobin, and rare red blood cells. A basic metabolic panel and complete blood count were within normal limits. Bilateral tibia/fibula radiographs were normal. Lower-leg ultrasound demonstrated widespread subdermal adipose thickening with streaky anechoic signals among hypoechoic fat lobules and mild anechoic tenosynovial effusions around the ankle tendons; muscle architecture was normal throughout.

A 7-year-old girl from a rural area presented with two weeks of vague periumbilical abdominal pain and nausea without constipation, diarrhea, or urinary symptoms. She had no history of animal contact and no significant family history. On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs. The abdomen was soft with mild inguinal tenderness but no peritoneal signs or palpable masses. Genital examination was normal without vaginal obstruction. A digital rectal examination revealed a palpable mass above the pubis. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 12.8 g/dL, a white-cell count of 11,000/mm3, and normal platelet counts. All tumor markers, including CEA, CA 125, CA 19-9, AFP, and β-hCG, were within normal ranges. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a 4×7 cm pelvic cyst with a thickened wall and multiple septa, but its organ of origin was not identified. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis confirmed an 8×7 cm right pelvic cystic mass with thick walls and internal septations, compressing and displacing the bladder to the left. No other abnormal lesions were seen elsewhere in the body.

A 78-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of diffuse abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. He denied fever or gastrointestinal bleeding, and reported decreased appetite without weight loss. His medical, family, and psychosocial histories were unremarkable; he took no medications and had no prior abdominal surgeries or colonoscopy. On examination, a non-tender, periumbilical mass extending toward the right lower quadrant was palpable; there were no signs of peritonitis. Laboratory studies showed mildly elevated inflammatory markers and negative tumour markers. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated pronounced invagination of the small intestine into the colon, with a classic “sausage-shaped mass” on coronal images and a “bulls-eye” appearance on axial images, consistent with an ileo-colic intussusception.

A 50-year-old man with no prior significant illness presented with a 2-month history of fever and holocranial headache, one episode of a left-sided focal seizure with secondary generalization, and 15 days of decreased sensation to touch in the right half of his body. He had no known HIV risk factors and no history of immunosuppressive therapy.

On examination, he was well nourished with normal vital signs and no lymphadenopathy. Neurologic findings included bilateral papilledema; increased deep-tendon reflexes in the right upper and lower limbs with flexor plantar responses; and decreased pain and temperature sensation in the right body, sparing the face. The remainder of the examination was normal.

Brain MRI showed a T2 hyperintense lesion in the left thalamus extending into the left corona radiata, without meningeal enhancement. CSF analysis revealed no cells, a glucose level of 17 mg/dL (blood glucose 80 mg/dL), protein 125 mg/dL, a positive cryptococcal antigen titer of 1:8192, and a culture growing Cryptococcus neoformans. CSF was negative for Toxoplasma antigens. HIV-1 and HIV-2 serologies were negative.

He was treated with intravenous amphotericin B (0.5–1.0 mg/kg, cumulative dose 4 g). After 8 weeks, his cryptococcal titer decreased to 1:1024, cultures were negative, and papilledema resolved. He was discharged on oral fluconazole 400 mg daily.

Two weeks later, he was readmitted with severe holocranial headache and vomiting. Funduscopic examination again showed papilledema; no new focal neurologic deficits were noted. CT of the head demonstrated hydrocephalus. Repeat CSF analysis showed glucose 26 mg/dL, protein 100 mg/dL, cryptococcal antigen titer 1:2048, and a culture growing fluconazole-resistant C. neoformans. CSF cytology and repeat HIV serology were negative. CT scans of the chest and abdomen were normal. He was restarted on intravenous amphotericin B.

A 9-year-old boy from Northern Tanzania with no prior medical history presented with a 3–4-month history of progressive confusion, difficulty walking, episodic aggression and hyperactivity fluctuating over days (worse at night), and new urinary and fecal incontinence. He had normal developmental milestones but was consistently below the third percentile for height (110 cm) and fifth percentile for weight (24 kg). On examination, he was partially aware of his environment, had preserved cranial nerves, normal fundoscopy, moderate spasticity with exaggerated deep tendon reflexes, bilateral upgoing plantar responses, slightly decreased proximal leg bulk, and required assistance to walk with a broad-based, high-stepping gait. Over the same period, he developed fatigue, generalized lassitude, cold intolerance, anorexia, and slate-grey hyperpigmentation around the nose, mouth, tongue, palms, and old scars. Laboratory studies revealed hyponatremia (116 mmol/L) and hyperkalemia; HIV test was negative. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed normal cell count, protein, and glucose. Noncontrast CT of the brain demonstrated posterior white matter hypodensities with volume loss; MRI confirmed extensive posterior white matter abnormalities with contrast enhancement.

A 27-year-old woman presented with headache and worsening visual disturbance. Ten years earlier, she had tuberculous meningitis treated with a 12-month course of first-line anti-tuberculosis therapy and adjunctive corticosteroids; she attained bacteriological remission but was left with bilateral counting-finger vision and had a ventriculoperitoneal shunt placed for hydrocephalus. Since treatment completion, she had been asymptomatic but had remnant tuberculomas in the bilateral ambient cistern on CT.

On admission, she was afebrile and alert. Neurologically, her vision had deteriorated from counting fingers to light perception; there was no meningeal irritation. Blood tests showed a CRP of 0.37 mg/dL; an interferon-γ release assay was positive. Chest radiography was unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed protein 570 mg/dL, 6 cells/µL, glucose 60 mg/dL, and opening pressure 130 mm H₂O. CSF and serum tests for Cryptococcus, Toxoplasma, Aspergillus antigens, and Taenia solium antibody were negative; CSF soluble interleukin-2 receptor and angiotensin-converting enzyme levels were normal.

Head CT demonstrated new tuberculomas in the left sylvian fissure with a low-density area in the left temporal lobe. Brain MRI showed contrast-enhancing tuberculomas with surrounding hypointensity on T1-weighted images and a hyperintense rim on FLAIR, consistent with edema. Repeated CSF mycobacterial cultures and real-time PCR were negative. Over two weeks of observation without specific therapy, her symptoms remained stable.

A 53-year-old woman with no known chronic illnesses presented with intermittent fever, rigors, and chills for 15 days, right upper-abdominal pain for 10 days, and progressive abdominal distention for 3 days. On examination, she was febrile but hemodynamically stable; the abdomen was soft, bowel sounds were normal, and there was no tenderness, guarding, or rigidity. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 5.8 g/dL, white blood cells 20 500/mm3, platelets 1.8 × 106/mm3, prothrombin time 17.7 s (INR 1.26), normal serum urea and creatinine, bilirubin 1.0 mg/dL, AST 176 IU/L, ALT 200 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 1263 IU/L, albumin 2.3 g/dL, blood glucose 148 mg/dL, and HbA1c 7.1%. Urinalysis revealed no ketones, and arterial pH was 7.36. An erect abdominal X-ray showed gas under the right hemidiaphragm. Given the absence of peritoneal signs, a contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen was performed and revealed free gas under the right hemidiaphragm and two large hypodense lesions in liver segments 8, 2, and 3; these lesions contained homogenous fluid collections with specks of air and air-fluid levels.

A 60-year-old woman presented with intermittent pleuritic chest pain in the mid–chest radiating to the back and exertional dyspnea. Her medical history included non-ischemic cardiomyopathy with an ejection fraction of 20%–25%, hypertension, type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease, a remote ischemic stroke with residual right-sided weakness, and stage IVB grade 2 endometrial adenocarcinoma with omental metastasis (post hysterectomy and salpingo-oophorectomy). Three months earlier, nuclear perfusion imaging had shown no ischemia or infarction. She was compliant with furosemide and metoprolol and had received adjuvant chemotherapy one month before presentation.  
On arrival, her systolic blood pressure was 90 mmHg; the remainder of her vital signs was unremarkable. Physical examination revealed no murmurs, rubs, or gallops, no lower-extremity edema, and clear lung fields. Laboratory studies showed a troponin I level of 0.158 ng/mL (normal, 0.02–0.03), an absolute neutrophil count of 0, a white blood cell count of 0.05 K/μL (normal, 3.70–10.40), hemoglobin of 9.2 g/dL, and a B-type natriuretic peptide level of 681 pg/mL (normal, 5–100). A chest radiograph demonstrated cardiomegaly. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia, a left bundle branch block, and left ventricular hypertrophy, findings unchanged from prior tracings.  
To evaluate for pulmonary embolism, a computed tomography pulmonary angiogram was performed and revealed filling defects at the apices of both the right and left ventricles, concerning for biventricular thrombi; no pulmonary embolism was identified.

A 41-year-old woman with a 3-year history of primary immune thrombocytopenic purpura, maintained on low-dose methylprednisolone, was admitted after 3 weeks of fever (up to 40°C), chills, headache, dry cough, and a painful skin eruption on the chest and back. One month after the onset of fever, she developed painful enlargement of both breasts. She had no nipple discharge, axillary lymphadenopathy, or changes in breast skin texture. Oxygen supplementation was required for worsening dyspnea.

On examination, her temperature was 40°C. Multiple tiny erythematous papules with central necrosis and brown crusts were scattered over her face, chest, abdomen, and back. Breast masses were bilaterally mobile, firm, and large without overlying skin changes.

Lung CT showed a poorly marginated consolidation with air-bronchogram and cavitation in the right upper lobe, scattered small nodules elsewhere in both lungs, and bilateral pleural effusions. Brain MRI was normal.

Breast ultrasound revealed diffuse, hypoechoic, homogeneous, well-defined lesions predominantly in the left breast with surrounding edema and fat infiltration. The lesions were soft on elastography and showed vascular flow (BI-RADS U4). Mammography demonstrated global asymmetry in the left breast and a focal asymmetry in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast without suspicious calcifications or architectural distortion (BI-RADS 3).

Laboratory studies showed a white-blood-cell count of 16.2×10^9/L and a platelet count of 85×10^9/L.

A 76-year-old man with dyslipidemia and no allergies or history of smoking or alcohol use underwent elective arthroscopic rotator cuff repair under general anesthesia for a 3-month history of left shoulder pain. Preoperative laboratory studies were within normal limits. After induction with propofol and fentanyl, endotracheal intubation and maintenance with sevoflurane were uneventful. The patient was positioned in the right lateral decubitus position with the left arm in 30° abduction and 20° flexion under approximately 10 pounds of traction. The 110-minute procedure was completed without complications, and the patient was extubated and transferred to the ward.

The next morning, he noted painless swelling of the left cheek in the region of the parotid gland. On examination, there was non-tender swelling without erythema, crepitus, or fluctuance. He was afebrile. There was no history of prior neck mass or salivary stones. An ear–nose–throat consult was obtained. Enhanced computed tomography of the neck revealed enlargement of the left parotid gland and adjacent subcutaneous tissue without salivary calculus or ductal dilation; level II lymphadenopathy was present. Flexible laryngoscopy showed no redness or swelling of the nasopharynx, oropharynx, laryngopharynx, or epiglottis, and there was no airway obstruction. Laboratory tests demonstrated a white-cell count of 12.9×10^3/µL, C-reactive protein of 5.46 mg/dL, and serum amylase of 2433 U/L.

A 35-year-old woman, gravida 9, para 8, presented on postpartum day 13 with a 5-day history of right-sided weakness and generalized tonic–clonic seizures. Her family history was notable for sudden deaths of two brothers and one sister, all with similar neurologic symptoms. Five days before presentation, she developed an abrupt, severe headache with blurred vision and visual field deficits, followed by rapid mood fluctuations. Initial treatment at a local clinic with unspecified oral medication yielded no improvement. She denied known use of herbal remedies.

She had an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery at home, no prior thromboembolic events, and no chronic medical conditions. On admission she received haloperidol and diazepam, after which her consciousness declined. 

On examination, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 9/15. She was restless and agitated, normocephalic, with neck stiffness but no facial asymmetry. Vital signs: blood pressure 130/90 mmHg; heart rate 100 bpm; respiratory rate 20/min; oxygen saturation 96% on room air; temperature 36.9°C. Neurologic exam showed vigorous movements of the left limbs, hypotonia on the right, and equivocal plantar responses.

Initial investigations showed:  
• CBC: WBC 11,100/µL (neutrophils 9500/µL), hemoglobin 7.5 g/dL, MCV 61.2%, platelets 455,000/µL  
• Renal function: BUN 17 mg/dL, creatinine 0.6 mg/dL  
• Liver function: AST 17 IU/L, ALT 21 IU/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL  
• Urinalysis: pH 5, protein 2+, WBCs 1–5/hpf  

Based on this presentation, initial differential diagnoses were considered before proceeding to neuroimaging.

A 35-year-old man presented with an 8-year history of episodic hypersomnia lasting 15–20 days, occurring every 2–3 months. During episodes he slept about 20 hours a day, remained somnolent and inactive, and had to be woken forcefully to eat or use the bathroom. He also reported increased sexual desire. Between episodes he was asymptomatic. There was no history of seizure, altered sensorium, hyperphagia, aggressive behavior, impulsivity, or similar illness in family members. On examination he had generalized pallor; the neurologic examination was otherwise unremarkable. Prior records showed microcytic-hypochromic iron deficiency anemia (hemoglobin 6.8–8.5 g/dl) managed with carbamazepine and oral iron but with poor compliance. Six months earlier, during a similar admission, his hemoglobin was 6.3 g/dl; MCV was 65 fl, MCHC 18 g/dl; serum iron 32 µg/dl, ferritin 6 ng/ml, TIBC 360 µg/dl; bone marrow aspiration confirmed iron-deficient erythropoiesis; stool studies, endoscopies, and abdominal ultrasonography showed no blood loss or parasitic infection. Thyroid function tests and vitamin B12 levels were normal. Gadolinium-enhanced brain MRI and electroencephalography were normal. The Epworth Sleepiness Scale score was 20 during an episode and 6 when asymptomatic. Polysomnography during the asymptomatic period was normal. During a hypersomnolent episode (after blood transfusion), PSG revealed a sleep onset latency of 9.5 minutes and mean sleep latency of multiple sleep latency testing of 8 minutes, with normal sleep architecture and no evidence of breathing dysfunction, narcolepsy, obstructive sleep apnea, or periodic limb movements; the patient could not be easily aroused from sleep.

A 68‐year‐old man presented with six months of slowly progressive exertional dyspnoea and productive cough. His medical history included ischaemic heart disease, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and prior community‐acquired pneumonias. He was a former smoker (22 pack‐years), with no relevant environmental or occupational exposures and no family history of pulmonary, connective tissue, or haematological disease.  
On examination, respiratory findings were unremarkable and oxygen saturation was 97% on room air.  
Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 151 g/L, white cell count 7.8 × 10^9/L, platelets 199 × 10^9/L, eosinophils 0.1 × 10^9/L, creatinine 74 μmol/L, calcium 2.48 mmol/L, normal liver function, coagulation, C‐reactive protein, and viral serologies. Antinuclear antibody was mildly elevated at 1:160 (homogeneous), while rheumatoid factor, extractable nuclear antigens, anti–double‐stranded DNA, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and angiotensin‐converting enzyme were within normal limits. Immunoglobulin levels, including IgE and IgD, were normal.  
Sputum cultures for bacteria and mycobacteria were negative.  
Chest imaging revealed bilateral interstitial infiltrates on radiograph and diffuse ground‐glass and nodular pulmonary infiltrates with patchy consolidations and mild mediastinal, hilar, and axillary lymphadenopathy on CT. These findings remained stable over three months despite a course of oral antibiotics.  
Pulmonary function tests showed a mild obstructive defect (FEV1 71%, FVC 81%, FEV1/FVC 64%) with normal DLCO (72%).  
Bronchoalveolar lavage yielded 73% macrophages, 25% lymphocytes, and 2% neutrophils, without malignant cells or pathogens. EBUS TBNA of an enlarged right paratracheal node and transbronchial biopsies from the left upper lobe were non‐diagnostic.  
Given the persistent, unexplained interstitial lung disease, the patient was referred for surgical lung biopsy.

A 69-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with four days of constant right-sided abdominal pain described as mild to moderate, associated with constipation and dark urine. He denied fever, chills, nausea, weight loss, or recent abdominal trauma. On examination, he was jaundiced with abdominal distension but without tenderness. Laboratory studies showed aspartate aminotransferase 196 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 664 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 193 U/L, γ-glutamyl transferase 186 U/L, total bilirubin 10.02 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 6.81 mg/dL, and no leukocytosis or elevated C-reactive protein. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a distended gallbladder with wall thickening, sludge and microlithiasis, and a common bile duct measuring 9.6 mm, with no clear obstructing stone and no free intraperitoneal fluid. On day 4, contrast-enhanced CT showed a fluid collection anterior to the right psoas muscle, perirenal fat densification, and urothelial thickening. By day 12, the patient’s right upper quadrant tenderness worsened and inflammatory markers rose, and a repeat CT demonstrated expansion of the retroperitoneal fluid collection. On day 18, MRCP confirmed multiple filling defects in the distal common bile duct consistent with choledocholithiasis but did not identify a site of biliary leak.

A 47‐year‐old man presented with new urinary symptoms (polyuria, nocturia), episodes of mild abdominal pain, and known gastroesophageal reflux. Urological evaluation revealed benign prostatic enlargement without obstruction. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated ascites; no other abnormalities were described. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed ascites, showed a focal calcification between small‐bowel loops in the right lower quadrant, and revealed an atypically straight, slightly fluid‐distended proximal jejunal loop with swirling mesenteric vessels suspicious for an internal hernia; there were no signs of small‐bowel obstruction. Physical examination was unremarkable: no tenderness, masses, or peritonitis. Laboratory studies and a colonoscopy performed one year earlier were normal. The patient had no history of abdominal surgery, medication use, or significant past medical conditions. Due to the unclear imaging findings, the potential internal hernia, and the possibility of pseudomyxoma peritonei as the source of the calcification and ascites, surgery was planned.

An 18-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of diffuse abdominal discomfort—worst in the right lower quadrant—accompanied by vomiting and fresh blood in his stools, passing bloody stools five times in the last 36 hours. On examination, blood was noted on rectal examination. Vital signs were: blood pressure 110/70 mmHg; pulse, 92/min; respiratory rate, 16/min; temperature, 37.1°C. Laboratory results showed WBC 7.53 K/µL (56.2% neutrophils), hemoglobin 11.3 g/dL, hematocrit 29.3%, platelets 239 K/µL, CRP 0.1 mg/dL, ESR 1 mm/h; renal and liver function tests were normal.

He had a 6-year history of intermittent mild right lower quadrant pain radiating to his back without bleeding. Three years earlier, abdominal ultrasound suggested ileitis; contrast CT showed terminal ileal wall thickening and pelvic fluid, raising concern for inflammatory bowel disease. Colonoscopy with biopsies showed no macroscopic abnormalities but “histological findings were compatible with Crohn’s disease,” and mesalazine was started. His symptoms persisted; video capsule endoscopy, CT enteroclysis, and abdominal MRI all showed no abnormalities. An exploratory laparoscopy was then performed, revealing no explanatory lesions; an incidental appendectomy was done.

He was referred for further evaluation.

A 45-year-old man with Binet stage B chronic lymphocytic leukemia treated previously with fludarabine and cyclophosphamide presented with a 2-week history of fever, painful bullous skin lesions that ruptured into erosions with hemorrhagic crusts, and painful oral and lip mucosal ulcers causing difficulty eating. He had received penicillin 3 weeks earlier for an unrelated infection. He also reported small amounts of anal bleeding. On examination, there were painful erosions of the ocular, oral, and urogenital mucosae; hemorrhagic crusts on the lips; and polymorphic cutaneous lesions including bullous erosions, ulcerations, and hemorrhagic crusts on the chest, scalp, back, and palms. Nikolsky’s sign was positive. Laboratory tests and chest imaging were unremarkable. He was admitted to the intensive care unit, treated with intravenous immunoglobulin, daily wound care, meropenem, and fluconazole for presumed Stevens–Johnson syndrome. Despite this therapy, the skin and mucosal lesions progressively worsened, and he required supplemental oxygen. Given the unsatisfactory evolution, biopsies of the skin lesions were performed.

A previously healthy 10-year-old girl presented with a 5-day history of intermittent fever up to 39 °C and a dry cough. She denied sputum production, hemoptysis, or rhinorrhea, and reported malaise and decreased appetite. There was no history of sick contacts, and her immunizations were up to date. On examination, temperature was 38.5 °C, pulse 98 beats/min, blood pressure 102/58 mmHg, and respiratory rate 24 breaths/min. She appeared mildly distressed; the throat was mildly injected, and she had small, soft bilateral submandibular lymph nodes. Lung auscultation revealed decreased air entry with bronchial breathing over the right lower zone. A two-view chest radiograph demonstrated two well-demarcated, homogeneous, round opacities in the right upper and lower lobes. Laboratory tests showed a normal peripheral blood count, serum electrolytes, glucose, lactate dehydrogenase, uric acid, and renal and liver function. Serum anti–Mycoplasma pneumoniae antibodies were nonreactive, a rapid urinary antigen test for Streptococcus pneumoniae was positive, blood cultures were negative, and a tuberculin test was negative.

A 16-year-old male with recently diagnosed B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia was undergoing induction chemotherapy (vincristine, pirarubicin, prednisone, and pegaspargase followed by cyclophosphamide, cytarabine, and mercaptopurine). Four days after resuming chemotherapy—during which he had a mild COVID-19 infection managed conservatively—he presented to the emergency department with a 1-day history of fever to 39°C, left facial swelling, severe headache, purulent rhinorrhea, and a foreign-body sensation in the left nostril. On examination the following day, there was erythema and edema of the left eyelid with limitation of ocular opening and necrotic crusts visible in both nostrils. Ophthalmology and otorhinolaryngology consultations raised concern for bacterial or fungal infection, and empiric therapy with fluconazole and cefepime was initiated. Despite this treatment, his condition deteriorated rapidly, necessitating transfer to the intensive care unit and initiation of inotropic and vasopressor support.

A 75-year-old man presented with a 3-week history of progressive lower-extremity edema and a 4-kg weight gain. He had a 40–pack-year smoking history and a performance status of 1. On examination, there was pitting edema of both lower legs. Laboratory studies showed proteinuria of 7.1 g/day, serum albumin 2.2 g/dL, total protein 5.1 g/dL, and total cholesterol 372 mg/dL. A diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome was made. Imaging revealed a mass in the right lower lung field, and biopsy confirmed stage IV squamous cell lung cancer (cT3N2M1b); the squamous cell carcinoma antigen was elevated at 17.0 ng/mL (normal < 1.5 ng/mL). A renal biopsy was performed. Light microscopy demonstrated mild thickening of glomerular walls with spikes on silver stain, and immunofluorescence revealed granular deposition of IgG along the glomerular basement membrane.

A 12-year-old Black female (weight 130.5 kg; BMI 47.4 kg/m^2) with well-controlled asthma, obstructive sleep apnea, and genu valgum underwent elective distal femoral and proximal tibial osteotomies with internal fixation under general anesthesia. She received midazolam 2 mg IV premedication; anesthesia was induced with propofol 200 mg, lidocaine 100 mg, and succinylcholine 200 mg, followed by endotracheal intubation. A lumbar plexus block and popliteal block were placed on the operative limb. Anesthesia was maintained with sevoflurane in O_2/air (expired concentration 2.1–2.5%) without EEG bispectral monitoring. Two tourniquets were applied sequentially on the operative leg; use of compression devices on the nonoperative limb was not documented.

After the second tourniquet deflation (approximately 4 hours into the case), pulse oximetry fell to 60%, end-tidal CO_2 decreased to 10–15 mmHg, and heart rate rose to 120–140 bpm. The patient was ventilated with 100% O_2 and sevoflurane was discontinued, but hypoxemia and hypotension persisted. The expired sevoflurane concentration abruptly fell from 2% to 0.2% over 4 minutes and remained negligible. Endotracheal suctioning yielded clear secretions. Given ongoing unresponsiveness and negligible anesthetic, flumazenil was administered.

Arterial blood gas on FiO_2 1.0 showed pH 7.22, lactate elevated, PaO_2 84 mmHg, and PaCO_2 51 mmHg (EtCO_2 14 mmHg). SpO_2 remained 60–93% for 30 minutes despite vasopressor support (phenylephrine infusion). Transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated moderately decreased right ventricular function, mild right ventricular dilation, and no intracardiac thrombus or shunt. CT of the head was inconclusive for infarct. CT of the chest revealed branching hypoattenuations in the perihilar pulmonary arteries, though image quality was suboptimal and filling defects were not definitively identified.

The patient was transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit. Over the next 3 hours—during which only 300 mg of additional propofol was administered—she began to open her eyes and follow commands. She was extubated shortly after arrival in the PICU, and prophylactic enoxaparin (40 mg twice daily) was initiated.

A 27-year-old man presented with a three-month history of daily fevers (up to 39 °C), rigors, and right lower quadrant abdominal pain. He had leukocytosis (25,000/mm3 with 80% neutrophils) and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate >100 mm/h. He had no hepatosplenomegaly or peripheral lymphadenopathy. Initial treatment with ciprofloxacin and metronidazole led to transient improvement but fevers recurred. 

On admission, vital signs were notable for temperature 39 °C, heart rate 90 bpm, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Physical examination was significant only for right lower quadrant tenderness without rebound. Laboratory studies showed WBC 22.3×109/L (80% neutrophils), hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, platelets 51×109/L, C-reactive protein 17.3 mg/dL, ESR 80 mm/h, fibrinogen 851 mg/dL, and ferritin 663 mg/dL. Liver and renal function tests, serum ACE, protein electrophoresis, thyroid function, and 24-hour urine calcium and protein were normal. Autoimmune serologies (ANA, RF, dsDNA, ANCA, and others) were negative. Genetic testing for familial Mediterranean fever mutations was negative.

Abdominal CT scan demonstrated mesenteric lymphadenopathy (up to 2.7 cm) with hypodense centers; no bowel inflammation or organomegaly was seen. Blood, urine, stool, and lymph node cultures (including mycobacteria and fungi), broad viral and bacterial serologies, PCR assays, and stool ova and parasite examinations were all negative. Upper and lower endoscopies, enteroclysis, capsule endoscopy, and intestinal biopsies were unremarkable. 

Laparotomy with excision of a mesenteric lymph node revealed granulomatous lymphadenitis with central suppuration; Gram, Giemsa, Ziehl–Neelsen, and fungal stains were negative, and immunohistochemical studies and PCR for pathogens were unrevealing.

A 72-year-old man with a body-mass index of 28.4 presented with a 2-week history of chest tightness and nausea. He had no history of thoracic or abdominal trauma. A chest radiograph showed a double contour along the right hemidiaphragm. Chest computed tomography revealed a well-circumscribed mass in the right posterior thoracic cavity measuring 28 cm × 9 cm × 10 cm that compressed the right lower lobe. The mass consisted predominantly of fatty tissue, contained no intestinal loops or other organs, and appeared to be continuous with retroperitoneal fat. Routine blood chemistry, including tumor markers, was within normal limits.

Differential diagnoses included lipoma, liposarcoma, and diaphragmatic hernia.

A 35-year-old woman, 30 days post–neurosurgical decompression for a cerebellar hemorrhage and cesarean delivery, was in a neurorehabilitation unit. She was on enoxaparin prophylaxis, antihypertensive therapy, anti-seizure drugs, and proton-pump inhibitors. After emerging from a minimally conscious state, she participated in passive and then active mobilization, including therapist-assisted bed-to-wheelchair transfers.

During one assisted transfer, she experienced acute severe right leg pain radiating to the mid-thigh, rated 10/10 on the numerical scale with both active and passive movement. Examination showed symmetric legs with normal skin and temperature, preserved peripheral arterial pulses, and reduced reflexes; passive hip extension was possible but elicited intense pain. Tenderness was noted in the right lower abdomen. Vital signs were normal (BP 120/80 mmHg, HR 90 bpm, SpO2 98%, T 36.5 °C). Laboratory studies revealed an acute drop in hemoglobin from 12.5 to 10.5 g/dL, platelets 39,500/mm³, WBC 12,650/mm³ with neutrophil predominance, C-reactive protein 20.35 mg/dL, creatinine 0.49 mg/dL, INR 1.3, aPTT 1.14, and normal transaminases and CPK. 

A right hip X-ray showed no abnormalities. Abdominal ultrasound excluded peritoneal effusion but was limited by bowel gas. Contrast-free CT demonstrated enlargement and inhomogeneity of the right iliacus muscle without overt bleeding and excluded other causes of leg pain. MRI revealed enlargement of the right iliacus muscle with areas of hypo- and hyperintensity on T2 and STIR sequences, partially extending into the gluteal muscles, consistent with lesions at different stages.

A 60-year-old postmenopausal woman presented for a routine 6-month follow-up  after partial mastectomy and sentinel lymph node biopsy for T1N0M0 left breast cancer. Histopathology showed invasive ductal carcinoma (10×8 mm, nuclear grade 1), ER+/PR+, HER2–, Ki-67 5%, negative margins. She received adjuvant external beam irradiation (50 Gy/25 Fr) and letrozole.

One year postoperatively, her cancer antigen 15-3 (CA15-3) level rose gradually to 40 U/mL; carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) remained normal. Computed tomography and bone scintigraphy showed no evidence of recurrence. At 2 years and 6 months postoperatively, her CA15-3 level increased to 80 U/mL, and routine labs revealed asymptomatic anemia. She was referred to hematology and hospitalized for further evaluation. 

Positron emission tomography–computed tomography and bone marrow biopsy showed no metastatic lesions. Laboratory testing demonstrated pancytopenia with an elevated mean corpuscular volume.

A 20-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of primary amenorrhea. She reported normal pubertal development and had fully developed secondary sexual characteristics. Physical examination revealed normal external genitalia without abnormal masses in the groin. 

A transabdominal pelvic ultrasound showed:
• Complete non-visualization of the uterus, cervix, and vagina.  
• Both ovaries were not seen in their normal pelvic locations; on extensive search they were localized within bilateral inguinal canals with multiple follicles and no evidence of vascular compromise on Doppler imaging.  
• Incidentally, bilateral ureteroceles were noted at the vesicoureteric junctions.

Given these findings, cross-sectional imaging was recommended for further evaluation of urogenital anatomy.

An 18-year-old man presented with insidious onset of weakness in his right hand and forearm, progressing over the past year, and difficulty with fine tasks such as writing and buttoning. He denied neck pain, paresthesias, gait disturbance, dysphagia, or bowel/bladder dysfunction, and had no history of trauma or other medical conditions. On examination, neck movement was painless. There was marked wasting of right hand muscles with weakness of handgrip, and finger abduction and adduction were reduced. Wrist flexion was Medical Research Council grade 3 on the right; strength was grade 5 elsewhere in the upper limbs and in both lower limbs. No involuntary movements, sensory deficits, cerebellar signs, or cranial-nerve abnormalities were noted; bowel and bladder function were intact. Routine blood tests were unremarkable. Cervical spine radiographs showed loss of cervical lordosis. MRI in the neutral position demonstrated a subtle intramedullary T2-weighted hyperintensity in the lower cervical cord. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography revealed chronic motor axon denervation with likely localization to the anterior horn cells.

A 19-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of skin lesions on her hands, elbows, and knees. She had a 10-year history of systemic lupus erythematosus, currently well controlled on hydroxychloroquine.

On examination, there were multiple erythematous papules with central umbilication and crusting over the extensor surfaces of the upper and lower limbs, as well as a few pustules on the palmar aspects of the fingers.

Simultaneously, she developed a 5-cm cervical lymph node conglomerate. Fine-needle aspiration showed chronic granulomatous lymphadenitis with caseous necrosis. Ziehl–Neelsen staining and mycobacterial cultures were negative. A tuberculin skin test produced a 28-mm induration with bullae, necrosis, and a residual atrophic scar.

Based on the cutaneous lesions in the setting of presumed lymph node tuberculosis, the initial clinical diagnosis was papulonecrotic tuberculid. She was started on standard antituberculous polychemotherapy with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol.

A 45-year-old Japanese man was referred after routine urinalysis revealed microscopic hematuria and proteinuria. He had a history of recurrent intensely pruritic blistering eruptions on the trunk and extremities since age 25; a skin biopsy at that time led to a diagnosis of dermatitis herpetiformis, and he responded well to dapsone. On examination, blood pressure was 138/76 mm Hg, pulse 66 beats per minute, and the skin was tanned and free of vesicles. Urinalysis showed 2+ protein and 1+ blood on dipstick, 10–19 red blood cells per high-power field, and a urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio of 1.2 g/gCr. Serum creatinine was 0.68 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 12.1 mg/dL, and estimated GFR 99.2 mL/min/1.73 m2. Hematologic, liver-function, and cholesterol levels were normal. Serologic tests were negative for syphilis, hepatitis B and C viruses, ANA, anti–double-stranded DNA, PR3-ANCA, MPO-ANCA, and anti-GBM antibodies. Complement C3 and C4 levels were within normal ranges. Chest and abdominal imaging showed no evidence of malignancy.

Ultrasound-guided renal biopsy yielded three cores. Light microscopy showed 30 glomeruli, three globally sclerosed, with moderate mesangial widening, capillary-wall thickening, lobular accentuation, segmental nodular formation, and double contours. Immunofluorescence revealed strong granular deposits of IgG, C3, and C1q along capillary walls and mesangium; IgA, IgM, and fibrinogen were weak or negative. Electron microscopy demonstrated effaced podocyte foot processes and massive electron-dense deposits in mesangial, subendothelial, subepithelial, and basement-membrane locations with segmental GBM duplication. These findings were consistent with the Burkholder variant of MPGN type 3. Staining for IgG subclasses was positive for IgG1 and IgG2 and negative for IgG3 and IgG4. Immunohistochemistry showed both κ and λ light chains in glomerular deposits, indicating polyclonal IgG deposition.

A 61‐year‐old man with no relevant family history was referred for evaluation of a 1‐month history of progressively worsening involuntary contractions of his respiratory and abdominal muscles, associated with a sensation of respiratory restriction and epigastric pain that significantly impaired his quality of life. 

On neurologic examination, there was clonic twitching of the diaphragm followed by co‐contraction of the abdominal muscles with variable frequency and amplitude; no audible sounds accompanied the contractions. Routine laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits.

To investigate a possible spinal cause, magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical and thoracic spinal cord was performed and showed no focal lesions. Electroencephalography demonstrated normal brain activity without epileptiform discharges. Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was unremarkable, and there was no evidence of compression of the phrenic nerves along their course.

A 34-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, stage 2 chronic kidney disease, and a history of bilateral embolic middle cerebral artery infarcts presented with recurrent transient right leg weakness and right hand shaking. These episodes occurred several times daily while walking, lasted about 30 seconds, and resolved on sitting. Examination revealed recovering dysphasia and mild right-sided pyramidal weakness requiring a walking stick. In March 2019, she had slurred speech, left-sided weakness, and visual neglect; MRI confirmed multiterritory acute infarcts, and CT angiography plus digital subtraction angiogram (DSA) showed severe intracranial atherosclerotic disease with bilateral supraclinoid internal carotid artery occlusion but no features of moyamoya disease. She had negative thrombophilia and no cardioembolic source and was treated with aggressive risk-factor control, dual antiplatelet therapy, and antihypertensives. In March 2020, she presented with diabetic ketoacidosis, hypotension (70/40 mmHg), and new right-sided weakness; MRI showed new left MCA territory embolic infarcts. During neurorehabilitation, concerns arose for poststroke focal motor seizures, and levetiracetam was started. However, the brief events spared the face, lacked a Jacksonian march, and were precipitated by position changes and dehydration. When reviewed in the stroke clinic, cerebral hypoperfusion syndrome was suspected, and cerebral perfusion imaging with acetazolamide challenge was planned.

A 40-year-old Afghan woman was referred for a persistent cutaneous lesion on the right cheek lasting more than one year, unresponsive to dermatologic and otolaryngologic treatment. She underwent root canal therapy of tooth #16 in two sessions, with calcium hydroxide dressing and an amalgam restoration. One month later, she returned with a persistent sinus tract and purulent discharge from the cutaneous lesion. On examination, tooth #16 had normal probing depths and mobility; adjacent alveolar mucosa was non-tender. Her medical history was noncontributory. A periapical radiograph showed a radiolucency around the roots of tooth #16 despite a well-obturated root canal filling. Periapical surgery was planned. Under local anesthesia, a full-thickness mucoperiosteal flap from teeth #14 to #17 was reflected, revealing a periapical lesion around all three roots of tooth #16. Granulation tissue was excised and sent for histopathologic evaluation. Apicoectomies of the mesiobuccal, distobuccal, and palatal roots were performed, and retropreparations were filled with mineral trioxide aggregate.

A 19-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of a mass protruding from her genital region associated with urinary retention. The mass spontaneously retracted when she lay supine but increasingly required manual reduction. It protruded during urination or straining, causing pain and difficulty voiding.

On examination, vital signs were normal. A 5 × 5 cm solid, elastic, nontender mass arose from the upper vulva and appeared to originate from the urethral meatus; the hymen was intact. A prior gynecologic procedure had repositioned the mass into the urethra and placed a urinary catheter, with discharge during reduction appearing to be urine.

Abdominal ultrasound showed heterogeneous echogenic lesions on the posteroinferior bladder wall without hydronephrosis in either kidney. CT intravenous urogram demonstrated a 4.1 × 3.4 cm distal ureteral dilation with a 0.3 cm wall thickness, fluid density, and contrast filling in the delayed phase, as well as a 0.9 × 0.6 cm stone at the left vesicoureteral junction that did not cause obstruction.

A 40-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of dry cough and exertional dyspnea. She had no history of tuberculosis, smoking, chemical or organic dust exposure, regular medications, or prior surgery. On examination, she was afebrile with stable vital signs. Chest auscultation revealed reduced breath sounds on the right side, accompanied by wheeze and occasional crackles; cardiac pulsations were palpable on the right chest. A frontal chest radiograph showed volume loss of the right lung, ipsilateral tracheal and mediastinal shift, cardiac dextroposition, and tenting of the right hemidiaphragm. Based on these findings, a provisional diagnosis of right lung collapse was made. The differential diagnoses for the etiology included: (a) post-tubercular sequelae (common in this part of the world), (b) neoplastic processes, and (c) mucus plugging or a forgotten foreign body.

A 66-year-old woman presented in December 2012 with a 10-day history of explosive, watery diarrhea accompanied initially by fever and chills for two days, crampy abdominal pain, nausea, and anorexia; there was no rectal bleeding. She had lost 8 kg over the preceding four months. She had no recent travel or known infectious contacts but made weekly visits to a nursing home. Four months earlier she had received amoxicillin for a dental infection. She had two prior one-week episodes of diarrhea, 14 months and nine months before. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. Medications included atorvastatin and diclofenac/misoprostol. 

On examination she appeared thin; vital signs were normal and she was afebrile. Abdominal examination revealed generalized tenderness, worse in the left lower quadrant; the remainder of the physical examination was normal. 

Laboratory studies showed normal results for complete blood count, electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate, glucose, and liver-function tests. Stool specimens were sent for culture, sensitivity, and C. difficile toxin testing. 

Empiric ciprofloxacin and metronidazole were initiated. The following day, flexible sigmoidoscopy was normal, and C. difficile toxin testing was positive; ciprofloxacin was discontinued and metronidazole was continued for 10 days with probiotics. Three days after completing therapy, severe diarrhea recurred. 

Oral vancomycin was given, but symptoms returned. Repeat blood tests remained normal except for a serum calcium level of 2.7 mmol/L (reference, 2.10–2.55 mmol/L). Repeat C. difficile toxin test remained positive. Fidaxomicin (200 mg twice daily for 10 days) was administered, but once again symptoms recurred. Vancomycin was restarted while options for further management were explored.

A 50-year-old man with erectile dysfunction treated with a penile prosthetic implant and a history of urothelial bladder cancer treated by radical prostatectomy with neobladder creation was referred for evaluation of a cecal subepithelial mass. Four weeks earlier, screening colonoscopy had revealed a smooth, round lesion in the cecum with normal overlying mucosa; mucosal biopsies showed normal cecal mucosa. He denied weight loss, hematochezia, melena, or changes in bowel habits. Laboratory studies were notable for a hemoglobin of 13.1 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 88.0 fL, mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration 3.2 g/dL, and platelet count 172 ×10^3/μL. Review of prior abdominal CT showed a spherical, smooth fluid-filled device in the right lower quadrant without overt bowel compression or new intraabdominal findings. On repeat colonoscopy, a 3–4 cm round, firm, smooth structure with normal overlying mucosa was seen in the cecum adjacent to the appendiceal orifice. A 12 MHz mini-probe ultrasound passed through the colonoscope demonstrated a 4.0 × 3.5 cm, anechoic, fluid-filled round structure with a thin, regular wall abutting the cecal wall.

A 2-month-old girl was referred for evaluation of noisy breathing. She was born at term, with an uncomplicated delivery and birth weight of 2.8 kg. She has been fed by both breast and bottle. Over the prior 15 days, her noisy breathing worsened during feeding. She weighed 3.5 kg at presentation (below the 3rd percentile) but was afebrile with normal vital signs and maintained an oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. Examination revealed inspiratory stridor with suprasternal and intercostal retraction. Flexible upper endoscopy demonstrated a 1 cm cystic lesion in the vallecula pushing the epiglottis backward and partially compromising the airway. A same-day CT scan of the neck showed a well-defined, rounded, nonenhancing hypodense cystic lesion measuring 9 mm, projecting into the oropharynx, with no soft tissue component. A provisional differential diagnosis of thyroglossal or retention cyst was suggested. Thyroid function tests were normal.

A 10-year-old boy from the Indian subcontinent presented with persistent jaundice, intermittent pruritus, and clay-colored stools since 10 days of age. He had a gradually enlarging upper abdominal lump for 7 years. Over the past 6 years he experienced intermittent productive cough with sneezing and throat soreness, mostly in cold and rainy seasons. For 4 years he had intermittent epistaxis, post‐traumatic violaceous-red patches at injury sites, and fractures of the upper limbs after mild trauma. For 3 years he reported difficulty with night vision. There was no history of altered sensorium, hematemesis, or melena. The patient was born two weeks post–term with low birth weight (2.1 kg), delayed cry, delayed developmental milestones, and poor weight gain. There was no family history of liver disease or consanguinity.

On examination, height was 113 cm (z < –3), weight 13 kg (z < –3), BMI 10.2 kg/m2. He had mild pallor, icterus, clubbing, multiple café au lait spots, and scratch marks. Facial features included triangular face, broad forehead, deep-set eyes, hypertelorism, prominent ears, small pointed chin, and saddle nose with bulbous tip. Abdomen exam revealed an enlarged firm nodular liver (span 9 cm at the right midclavicular line) and spleen palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin. Ophthalmologic exam showed posterior embryotoxon, iris strands, and increased intraocular pressure. Respiratory and neurologic exams were normal.

Laboratory studies showed elevated total bilirubin (4.1 mg/dL), direct bilirubin (3.4 mg/dL), AST (292 IU/L), ALT (121 IU/L), alkaline phosphatase (978 IU/L); low albumin (2.4 g/dL), low platelets (1.3 × 10^5/mm^3), and INR 1.3. Viral hepatitis serologies were negative. Wrist X-ray showed osteopenia; chest X-ray revealed cardiomegaly; echocardiography demonstrated pulmonary hypertension and tricuspid regurgitation. Gastroduodenoscopy found no varices. Abdominal ultrasound showed a shrunken right hepatic lobe with coarse parenchyma, enlarged left lobe, mild splenomegaly, and poorly visualized hepatic and portal veins. Liver biopsy revealed ten portal tracts with a conspicuous absence of interlobular bile ducts, mild portal inflammation, fibrosis, occasional nodules, and feathery hepatocytes without inflammation.

A 35-year-old woman presented with awareness of a mass in her left breast. She underwent ultrasonography-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy twice, with benign findings both times.
