Four months later, ultrasonography-guided core needle biopsy was performed; “phyllodes tumor and a spindle cell carcinoma, among other entities, were included in the differential diagnosis, but there was no definitive diagnosis.” She was referred for further evaluation.

On examination, there was a well-defined, 13 mm hard mass in the upper inner quadrant of the left breast without axillary lymphadenopathy. There was no history of trauma. Her medical and family histories were negative for malignancy.

Mammography showed a dense breast without a discrete mass. Ultrasonography revealed a hypoechoic lesion with an irregular margin and no acoustic shadow, extending from the anterior border of the mammary gland. Magnetic resonance imaging (T1-weighted, fat suppression) demonstrated enhancement of the lesion.

Because malignancy could not be excluded on imaging, an excisional biopsy with adequate margins was planned.

A 27-year-old man presented to the emergency department with persistent left hypochondrial pain of three days’ duration. He was hemodynamically stable (blood pressure 100/60 mmHg; pulse rate 88 /min). Laboratory examinations, including peripheral blood counts and tumor markers (CEA and CA125), were within normal limits. A post-contrast CT scan of the abdomen demonstrated the spleen in its normal position, with homogeneous density and smooth outlines, and a second cystic heterogeneous lesion of similar density to the spleen at its lower pole. The lesion compressed the left kidney, without evidence of infiltration or invasion of surrounding structures, and was interpreted on imaging as most consistent with a splenic lymphangioma.

A 6-day-old girl was brought with vomiting, lethargy, and severe dehydration. She was born full-term (3.0 kg) to consanguineous Pakistani parents; the pregnancy was complicated only by insulin-treated gestational diabetes. On examination she was ill appearing with pale skin, poor perfusion, and sunken eyes; genitalia were normal without clitoromegaly, and there was no abdominal mass. Laboratory studies showed Na+ 124 mEq/L, K+ 10 mEq/L, HCO3− 10 mEq/L, and urine Na+ 150 mEq/L. Serum aldosterone was 8.97 nmol/L (0–6 nmol/L), plasma renin activity 13.39 ng/mL/hr (2–35 ng/mL/hr), cortisol 634.8 nmol/L (>500 nmol/L), and 17-hydroxyprogesterone 0.7 nmol/L (0.2–2.3 nmol/L). A sweat chloride was 34 mEq/L (0–29 mEq/L), and renal ultrasound was normal. The patient received two normal-saline boluses, oxygen, oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate, sodium bicarbonate, and an insulin–glucose infusion; serum sodium and potassium normalized within 2 days.

A 90-year-old woman presented with epigastric pain and coffee-ground emesis. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed a tortuous, dilated esophagus with large amounts of retained undigested food. A barium swallow demonstrated markedly decreased lower-esophageal peristalsis with a characteristic bird’s-beak appearance, consistent with achalasia. Manometry was not performed. She underwent endoscopic injection of 80 units of botulinum toxin around the lower esophageal sphincter without intraprocedural complications. The patient initially noted symptomatic improvement and tolerated a diet. Within hours, however, she developed profound neuromuscular weakness of her upper extremities. Neurologic examination revealed 0/5 deltoid strength, 3/5 biceps, 2/5 triceps, 4/5 wrist extension, and 4/5 intrinsic hand muscle strength bilaterally, with decreased tone and absent reflexes in the upper extremities. Sensation was intact. Lower extremity and cranial nerve examinations were unremarkable, and the patient remained alert and conversant.

A 62-year-old man with alcohol use disorder and chronic hepatitis C–related cirrhosis underwent liver transplantation 5 years ago for hepatocellular carcinoma. He was cured of hepatitis C, maintained on tacrolimus monotherapy, and had stable graft function. One year after transplant, he developed pulmonary and abdominal wall metastases of poorly differentiated non–small-cell carcinoma, treated sequentially with sorafenib, carboplatin/gemcitabine, and FOLFOX without response. Two months before presentation, he began palliative nivolumab and radiation therapy.

He now presents with mild abdominal pain and severe jaundice but no fever, chills, nausea, or vomiting. Laboratory testing shows alkaline phosphatase 813 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase 1,265 IU/L, aspartate aminotransferase 696 IU/L, and total bilirubin 8.3 mg/dL. He is hemodynamically stable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis shows no new hepatic or intra-abdominal masses but reveals mild ascites. Given concern for nivolumab-induced liver injury, high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (2 mg/kg daily) is initiated.

A 74-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis status–post colectomy and hypertension initially presented with fatigue, myalgia, and confusion. Her temperature was 100°F, blood pressure 108/60 mmHg, heart rate 106 bpm, and respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute. She was disoriented but had normal heart sounds and decreased breath sounds at the lung bases without crackles. Laboratory tests showed hyponatremia (sodium 128 mEq/L), creatinine 1.21 mg/dL, lactate 3.0 mEq/L, and a urinalysis suggestive of urinary tract infection. CBC revealed WBC 8.8 k/cmm, hemoglobin 15.1 g/dL, and platelets 131 k/cmm. CT of the brain and chest radiograph were unremarkable. She received IV fluids and ceftriaxone, improved, and was discharged after 3 days.

Two days later she returned with fever (103°F), heart rate 115 bpm, blood pressure 90/65 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and normal mentation. Labs showed WBC 3.31 k/cmm, hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, platelets 60 k/cmm, lactic acid 5.4 mEq/L, AST 237 U/L, ALT 189 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 146 U/L. Chest radiograph showed right middle lobe infiltrates; she received vancomycin and piperacillin–tazobactam. Four days into admission she developed worsening respiratory failure requiring noninvasive ventilation and was transferred to the ICU. CT of the chest revealed bilateral pleural effusions; thoracentesis yielded 750 mL of exudative fluid. She progressed to bilateral interstitial infiltrates consistent with ARDS and was intubated. 

Despite broad-spectrum antibiotics, her fever persisted. Blood, sputum, urine, and stool cultures were negative for bacterial, fungal, mycobacterial, and parasitic organisms. Repeat labs showed WBC 1.4 k/cmm, hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL, platelets 45 k/cmm, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, BUN 65 mg/dL, AST and ALT in the thousands, worsening jaundice, and INR 8.0 with normal factor V and VIII activities. Abdominal ultrasound and MRI of the liver and pancreas were unremarkable. Laboratory investigations showed elevated LDH (1367 U/L), elevated triglycerides (808 mg/dL), fibrinogen of 240 mg/dL, and ferritin of 40,000 ng/mL.

A 25-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of acute urinary retention and a 10-day history of bilateral lower-limb numbness and weakness. He also reported a 2-month history of productive cough, unintentional weight loss, and decreased appetite. Two years earlier, he had household exposure to a brother with tuberculosis. 

Laboratory evaluation showed a normal complete blood count and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Sputum testing for acid-fast bacilli was positive on two occasions. 

Multiplanar thoracolumbar MRI performed before and after gadolinium administration demonstrated a 12 × 16 mm intradural, extramedullary lesion at the L2 level. The lesion was isointense on T1-weighted images, isointense to hypointense on T2-weighted and STIR images, and contained a small focus of central hyperintensity on long-TR sequences. Postcontrast images showed homogeneous enhancement with a small central nonenhancing focus.

A 41-year-old woman with a history of stage IV endometriosis presented for evaluation of cyclic rectal bleeding and pain. One year earlier, she had undergone total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingectomy and left oophorectomy for endometriosis. Over the past 6–8 months, she reported 1 week of dark-red, mixed-with-stool rectal bleeding each month in the same pattern as her prior menses, accompanied by sharp lower abdominal pain. She denied bleeding or pain during the intervening 3 weeks. Her prior colonoscopy, performed before hysterectomy, showed no transmural implants. Oral contraceptives had been ineffective for symptom control. 

Medical history was notable for hypertension managed with metoprolol. She had never smoked and drank alcohol occasionally. Surgical history included multiple gynecologic procedures for endometriosis and a cesarean delivery. Family history was noncontributory for endometriosis.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Abdominal and cardiopulmonary exams were unremarkable. Rectal examination showed no external hemorrhoids, and stool guaiac was negative. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, platelet count 196 000/mm3, white blood cell count 10 000/mm3, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, BUN 13 mg/dL, and albumin 4.1 g/dL.

Pelvic MRI with and without contrast demonstrated findings consistent with invasive endometriosis, with possible invasion into the sigmoid colon. Colonoscopy revealed a stricture in the rectosigmoid colon with multiple erythematous mucosal implants suspicious for extrinsic infiltrating endometriosis involving the submucosa and mucosa. Biopsy samples were obtained from these areas.

A 5.5-year-old girl from a stockbreeding family presented with a 6-day history of fever up to 38.5 °C with afternoon spikes, accompanied by pain in the right wrist and right elbow. She had consumed homemade dairy products. Three days before transfer, initial laboratory tests showed:  
• White blood cells 7.2 × 10^9/L  
• Platelets 180 × 10^9/L  
• Hemoglobin 131 g/L  
• ESR 19 mm/h, CRP 10 mg/L  
• AST 62 U/L  
• Monotest negative, Rose Bengal negative  
• Wright agglutination reaction positive at 1/1280  
On that basis, she was started on oral trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (10 mg/kg/day) and rifampicin (15 mg/kg/day).  
On the third day of treatment, she developed generalized purpuric lesions and was found to have severe thrombocytopenia (platelets 3 × 10^9/L). On arrival, her temperature was 38.8 °C. Examination revealed diffuse petechiae, purpura, bruising, wet purpura on the palate, gingival bleeding, and hepatosplenomegaly (liver and spleen palpable 2 cm below the costal margins). Joint and neurologic examinations were otherwise unremarkable.  
Repeat laboratory values were:  
• WBC 7.5 × 10^9/L (neutrophils 45%, lymphocytes 52%, monocytes 3%)  
• Platelets 1 × 10^9/L  
• Hemoglobin 120 g/L  
• ESR 15 mm/h, CRP 7 mg/L  
• AST 64 U/L, urea 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 92 μmol/L, total bilirubin 12 μmol/L  
• Wright agglutination reaction positive at 1/1280  
• Brucella melitensis–specific IgM and IgA positive; IgG negative  
• Blood cultures sterile  
Based on these findings, what is your differential diagnosis for her acute severe thrombocytopenia?

A 71-year-old man was referred after a routine chest radiograph showed abnormal shadows. He was asymptomatic and had no significant medical history. Vital signs were within normal limits, and the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies revealed slight elevations in angiotensin-converting enzyme (21.7 U/L), KL-6 (778 U/mL), and soluble interleukin-2 receptor (743 U/mL); lysozyme was normal. Urinalysis showed mildly increased N-acetyl-β-glucosaminidase and β2-microglobulin without hypercalcemia or pyuria. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated multiple low-density lesions of variable sizes in the spleen. Chest CT revealed patchy consolidations in the right upper lobe and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial lung biopsy yielded no specific diagnostic findings.

A 25-year-old woman (gravida 2, para 0, abortus 1) presented with a 12-hour history of diffuse pelvic pain and abnormal uterine bleeding. She reported six weeks of amenorrhea and a positive qualitative β-hCG test. One year earlier, she had undergone evacuation of a partial molar pregnancy, with an uneventful follow-up.

On examination, she was hemodynamically stable. Pelvic examination revealed dark vaginal bleeding with a closed cervix. Laboratory tests showed a quantitative β-hCG of 15,000 mIU/mL, hemoglobin of 13 g/dL, and a normal coagulation profile. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed a gestational sac with a yolk sac and a crown–rump length of 5 mm without cardiac activity, and a 12 mm area of trophoblastic detachment. The right adnexa contained a corpus luteum. She was discharged with plans for follow-up ultrasound.

She returned 24 hours later with heavy vaginal bleeding. Bedside ultrasonography suggested an ongoing hemorrhagic abortion and showed abnormal Doppler flow. A quantitative β-hCG level had risen to 25,000 mIU/mL. She underwent endometrial aspiration; the product appeared normal macroscopically. Five days after the procedure, she had moderate vaginal bleeding, a β-hCG level of 10,000 mIU/mL, and remained hemodynamically stable. Transvaginal Doppler ultrasonography revealed no retained products of conception but demonstrated a focal area of hypervascularity in the anterior myometrium with a mosaic pattern of multidirectional high-velocity flow (peak systolic velocity, 55 cm/s) and an empty endometrial cavity.

A 7-year-old boy was brought to the pediatric emergency department with sudden inability to speak (anarthria), a mildly open and stiff mouth, and lethargy associated with low-grade fever. Two weeks earlier he had viral tonsillitis; there was no recent vaccination. He had normal psychomotor development and no relevant family history. 

On examination, temperature was 37.9°C; heart rate, respiratory rate, and blood pressure were normal. He was conscious and followed commands but could not articulate speech. Neck stiffness was present, with negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs. There were no sensory or limb motor deficits; muscle strength was 5/5. Masseter rigidity prevented jaw movement. Deep tendon reflexes were brisk, and plantar responses were normal. Cranial nerves other than the trigeminal nerve were intact. Coordination, gait, and all other systemic exams were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and C-reactive protein, were normal. Noncontrast head CT was unremarkable. A lumbar puncture showed 5 white blood cells/µL, glucose 28 mg/dL, and protein 79 mg/dL. Empiric ceftriaxone and acyclovir were started; antibiotics were discontinued when CSF showed no infection, and acyclovir was continued.

On hospital day 2, his speech impairment persisted; he became obtunded, developed rigidity in all four limbs, and quadriparesis (muscle strength 3/5), with preservation of only ocular movements. Brain MRI revealed asymmetrical supratentorial lesions: ovoid, poorly marginated areas of increased signal on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences involving bilateral central white matter, cortical gray matter, and basal ganglia, with no enhancement on pre- or post-contrast T1-weighted images.

A 39-year-old white woman was referred for conjunctival hyperemia and tearing in her right eye. She had undergone vitreoretinal surgery for retinal detachment a few months earlier. On examination, her right-eye visual acuity was hand motion, and intraocular pressure was 14 mmHg. There was mild ptosis, ocular inflammation, and a dense cataract that precluded visualization of the posterior segment. In the upper nasal quadrant of the bulbar conjunctiva, there was a dome-shaped lesion. The initial differential diagnosis included scleral-buckle extrusion, tumor, dermoid, ocular cysticercosis, and abscess. A clinical diagnosis of suspected scleral-buckle extrusion was made, but, because of the lens opacity, an echographic examination was ordered to assess the integrity of the posterior pole.

A 43-year-old woman presented with a 6-week history of right upper-extremity pain, swelling, and mild purplish discoloration. She denied trauma, central venous access, smoking, alcohol use, and a personal or family history of thrombotic disorders. Initial laboratory studies—including a complete blood count, metabolic panel, liver and kidney function tests, coagulation studies, and D-dimer (282 ng/mL)—were within normal limits. She was treated with analgesics and discharged. Two days later, she returned with increased arm swelling and difficulty moving her fingers; the D-dimer was 560 ng/mL. A Doppler ultrasonography was requested. Four weeks later, on transfer to a regional center, she again had persistent discoloration and edema; the D-dimer was 1100 ng/mL. CT venography of the right upper limb revealed thrombosis of the subclavian, axillary, and brachial veins, with thrombophlebitis of the basilic vein. A diagnosis of atypical upper-extremity deep vein thrombosis was made.

A 55-year-old man with essential hypertension presented with a 2-week history of speech disturbance and a right-sided spastic hemiparesis. On admission, his blood pressure was 190/100 mmHg. Brain MRI demonstrated diffuse vasogenic cerebral edema and multiple focal microbleeds on T2*-weighted imaging. He received antihypertensive (urapidil, enalapril, amlodipine) and anti-edematous (mannitol) therapy with slight clinical improvement. 

One month later, he acutely developed somnolence (GCS 12), spatiotemporal disorientation, a mild nonpulsing headache, persistent right hemiparesis, and ataxic gait over 24 hours. Blood pressure was 180/120 mmHg; the rest of the physical examination was unremarkable. Routine blood and urine studies were normal. Immuno-serologic tests (ANA, ANCA, ENA, CIC, C3, C4, VDRL) were normal. Infectious work-up revealed chronic hepatitis B infection; all other viral studies (HIV, HBsAg, HCV, HSV 1/2, CMV, VZV, EBV, JCV) were negative. Tests for neuronal surface and antineuronal antibodies were negative. Chest X-ray and abdominal and transthoracic cardiac ultrasounds were normal.

Repeat brain MRI showed confluent asymmetric white-matter hyperintensities in bilateral frontal, temporal, and parietooccipital regions, cerebral microbleeds, multiple chronic microvascular ischemic lesions, and periventricular leukoencephalopathy. Lumbar puncture revealed elevated CSF protein (1.25 g/L) with normal glucose and cell count; oligoclonal bands were present in both CSF and serum. CSF β-amyloid and tau proteins were normal; microbiologic and immunologic CSF studies were negative. Genetic testing for ApoE and NOTCH3 was negative.

A 50-year-old man presented with ongoing chest pain. Eleven years earlier, he had undergone mechanical aortic valve replacement for a bicuspid valve; preoperative angiography had shown normal coronaries. His history included treated hypercholesterolaemia and current smoking. He had no known atrial fibrillation, ventricular dysfunction, coagulation disorders, or recent cancer. On arrival, blood pressure was 95/65 mmHg, heart rate 79 b.p.m., temperature 36.2°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable. The ECG showed anterior ST-segment elevation. Emergent coronary angiography revealed total occlusion of the proximal left anterior descending artery with a large thrombus burden. Thrombus aspiration restored flow, and a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor was administered. Aside from distal embolization to the apical LAD and a filling defect in the first diagonal branch, flow was fully re-established without evidence of stenosis or atherosclerosis. Optical coherence tomography of the LAD showed a normal vessel wall without significant plaque, rupture, erosion, or intramural hematoma. Transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a 3.5 mm floating structure in the left ventricular outflow tract.

A 7-year-old boy presented with a 2-week history of bilateral decline in visual acuity. He had no prior ocular history and no significant refractive error. On examination, cycloplegic refraction was +0.25 D in the right eye and +0.50 D in the left eye. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/60 in both eyes. Anterior segments were normal and intraocular pressures were 15 mmHg bilaterally. Dilated fundus examination was unremarkable. Short-wavelength autofluorescence showed a normal pattern. Structural OCT revealed a normal retinal profile but increased choroidal thickness for age, with large hyporeflective areas bounded by irregular hyperreflective borders (pachyvessels) and numerous small, well-defined, optically void spaces predominantly in the Sattler layer. OCT angiography demonstrated absence of flow signal within these void spaces. Computerized perimetry showed scattered absolute and relative defects but was deemed unreliable due to high false-positive and false-negative rates. Full-field electroretinography revealed normal scotopic and photopic responses.

A 30-year-old woman with homozygous sickle cell disease was transferred to the ICU for respiratory failure and new neurologic deterioration during an acute vaso-occlusive pain crisis. She had fever and lower-extremity pain similar to prior episodes. On admission she was lethargic; temperature 38 °C and heart rate 140 bpm. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 8.3 g/dL, haptoglobin 17 mg/dL, white-cell count 23.1 × 10^3/µL (neutrophils 18.7 × 10^3/µL), CRP 215 mg/L, AST 121 U/L, ALT 64 U/L, ALP 450 U/L, LDH 3861 U/L, total bilirubin 3.9 mg/dL; renal function was normal. Arterial PO2 was 80%. A chest CT angiogram excluded pulmonary embolism and showed bilateral pulmonary consolidations. Unenhanced brain CT and CT angiography were unremarkable. SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR and serology were negative. Brain MRI showed a few punctate foci of restricted diffusion with corresponding T2 FLAIR hyperintensities and numerous punctate low-signal foci on susceptibility-weighted images in both supra- and infratentorial regions.

A 59-year-old woman with a 2-year history of rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate (10 mg weekly) and tacrolimus (2 mg daily) was referred in mid-June for evaluation of bilateral lung opacities. Routine chest X-ray showed diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities, and serum KL-6 was elevated to 1097 U/mL (normal < 500 U/mL). She was a lifelong nonsmoker. On environmental review, mildew was noted in her bathroom and washing machine, and other rooms were cluttered and dirty. Chest computed tomography confirmed diffuse ground-glass opacities. Her resting percutaneous oxygen saturation was 96% on room air, and she was afebrile. Fine crackles were not audible at that time.  
   
Differential diagnoses included Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, cytomegalovirus infection, drug‐induced pneumonia, and acute interstitial pneumonia associated with RA. Because of stable joint disease and concern for infection or drug toxicity, methotrexate and tacrolimus were discontinued. Seven days later, she developed acute dyspnea and was admitted with resting and ambulatory oxygen saturations of 91% and 78%, respectively. Fine crackles were now audible at both lung bases. Repeat chest CT showed progression of ground-glass opacities and new areas of consolidation.

A 31-year-old G3P2 woman at 22 weeks’ gestation with two prior cesarean deliveries and three live births was brought by ambulance to the emergency department with severe dyspnea and a brief syncopal episode. According to her husband, she had a short-lived crampy abdominal pain just before the syncope. She denied ongoing abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, fever, or other symptoms.

On examination, she appeared pale and cool. Vital signs: pulse 72 beats/min, blood pressure 110/80 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 97% on room air, temperature 37.0 °C. She had intermittent drowsiness and restlessness. The gravid uterus was palpated just above the umbilicus without tenderness. A speculum exam showed no vaginal bleeding.

Despite normal blood pressure, her cool extremities and altered mental status suggested compensated shock. Initial labs (not yet available during resuscitation) later demonstrated leukocytosis (24.4 × 10^3/mm^3), hemoglobin fall from 9.8 g/dL to 7.9 g/dL, venous pH 7.295, and lactate 4 mmol/L.

A point-of-care ultrasound revealed a large amount of free fluid in the abdominal cavity and fetal bradycardia. Uncrossmatched O– negative blood was started, and obstetrics was consulted. Repeat bedside ultrasound confirmed intra-abdominal hemorrhage and absence of fetal cardiac activity but did not localize a uterine defect. The patient was taken for emergent surgical exploration.

A 32-year-old man with a history of circumscribed scleroderma (morphoea) on his left lower limb and recurrent lower-limb ulcers—previously attributed to microtrauma—presented with left groin pain and fevers up to 39 °C with shivering. He denied recent travel, known insect or tick bites, or trauma. He had regular contact with his cat and dog. He was a carpenter and took no regular medications.

On initial presentation, blood tests showed leukocytosis (14 ×10^9/L) and normal C-reactive protein. Inguinal ultrasonography demonstrated subcutaneous edema and multiple benign reactive enlarged lymph nodes. Chest and pelvic radiographs were unremarkable except for findings thought compatible with trochanteric insertional tendinopathy, and he was discharged with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory therapy.

He returned the next day with worsening groin pain and persistent fever. Vital signs: temperature 39.2 °C, blood pressure 106/46 mmHg, heart rate 116 bpm, oxygen saturation normal. Examination of the left leg revealed a 12×6 mm superficial pretibial ulcer with a fibrinous bed overlying the healed morphoea lesion, surrounded by ill-defined erythema extending to the thigh. He was admitted, and intravenous amoxicillin/clavulanic acid (2.2 g three times daily) was initiated for presumed erysipelas.

Over the next several days, fever and localized edema worsened; C reactive protein peaked at 329 mg/L (day 5) and leukocytosis at 15 ×10^9/L (day 7). An antistreptolysin O titer was elevated at 508 U/L. Antibiotics were escalated to imipenem/cilastatin (500 mg/500 mg four times daily), with slight improvement in edema but persistent fever. Dermatology consultation noted four pairs of blood cultures taken during febrile peaks were negative; ulcer swabs and HIV serology were negative; venous duplex ultrasound excluded deep-venous thrombosis; soft-tissue ultrasound showed reactive lymphadenopathy without abscess; ankle radiographs showed no osteomyelitis.

Infectious diseases consultation was obtained. Serologic tests for Francisella tularensis (IgM and IgG ELISA) and Bartonella henselae and Bartonella quintana (IFA IgM and IgG) were ordered. At the same time, doxycycline therapy was added to the imipenem/cilastatin regimen.

A 34‐year‐old man presented with 6 weeks of fever, cough, and chest pain. He reported high fevers up to 103 °F with chills, anorexia, vomiting, weight loss, generalized body aches, and a spontaneous swelling below his left lateral malleolus, which was incised and drained as an abscess. He was newly diagnosed with diabetes mellitus (random blood sugar 35.8 mmol/L) and treated with insulin. Chest radiograph showed a cavitary lesion in the left lower lobe, and an initial CT scan suggested an aspergilloma. On transfer, he was tachypneic (RR 26/min), tachycardic (PR 110/min), hypotensive (BP 70/50 mmHg), febrile (102 °F), and anemic (Hb 7.6 g%). Examination revealed decreased air entry and crepitations over the left chest and tenderness in the right hypochondrium without organomegaly. Laboratory tests showed a WBC count of 12,700/mm3 (neutrophil predominant), random blood sugar 6.8 mmol/L, urea 8.9 mmol/L, creatinine 202 µmol/L, sodium 119.4 mEq/L, and potassium 3.2 mEq/L. Abdominal ultrasound revealed multiple small hypoechoic cystic lesions in the right hepatic lobe with minimal ascites. He was started empirically on voriconazole, metronidazole, and piperacillin-tazobactam. Sputum cultures grew Klebsiella pneumoniae, but urine, blood, and wound cultures were sterile. Sputum specimens were negative for acid-fast bacilli and fungal elements on KOH. After nine days of treatment without improvement, meropenem was initiated. A high-resolution CT scan showed multiple thick-walled cavities in the left upper and lower lobes with fibrotic changes in the right upper lobe, and antitubercular therapy was added while meropenem was continued. An ultrasound-guided aspiration of the liver abscess yielded frank pus, which was sent for microbiological evaluation.

A 69-year-old man was readmitted 9 months after discharge from severe COVID-19 with a 2-week history of fever, fatigue, dysuria, urinary urgency, and hypogastric pain. His medical history was notable for diabetes mellitus, benign prostatic hyperplasia, ischemic heart disease, spinal tuberculosis, renal stones, and a recent episode of COVID-19–associated pulmonary aspergillosis (CAPA) treated with amphotericin B followed by prolonged voriconazole, which was discontinued 3 months prior to this presentation.

On examination, temperature was 38.8 °C; he had left costovertebral angle tenderness and hypogastric tenderness. No rash, lymphadenopathy, or other abnormalities were noted.

Laboratory studies on admission:
- Hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL (12–16)
- White blood cell count 12.4 × 10^3/µL (4.5–11) with neutrophilia
- Platelets 256 × 10^3/µL (130–400)
- ESR 115 mm/h (0–22)
- CRP 73 mg/dL (≤6)
- Creatinine 1.1 mg/dL (0.5–1.0)
- Urea 40 mg/dL (7–20)
- Urinalysis: WBC 16–18/hpf, RBC 0–1/hpf
- Urine and blood cultures: negative

Abdominal ultrasound revealed two new hypoechoic masses in the right kidney (37 × 39 mm in the midpole and 50 × 45 mm in the upper pole) alongside two simple cortical cysts. A contrast-enhanced CT scan confirmed two well-defined hypodense masses in the right kidney without evidence of hydronephrosis or vascular invasion.

A 50-year-old housewife presented with a 4-month history of bilateral anterior groin pain (left greater than right), progressive limp, and difficulty sitting cross-legged or squatting. Twenty days before this presentation, she became unable to bear weight on the left side. She had no history of trauma, excessive activity, or prior fragility fractures, and no comorbidities or medications; she was two years postmenopausal. On exam, there was bilateral hip tenderness (left > right), external rotation deformity and 1 cm shortening of the left lower limb, severely limited left hip motion, and pain at extremes of right hip motion. Straight leg raise was intact on the right but not possible on the left; neurovascular exam was normal.  
An anteroposterior pelvis radiograph obtained 20 days earlier showed bilateral inferomedial femoral-neck sclerosis with cortical breach on the right and an undisplaced complete fracture line on the left; the neck-shaft angles were 130° on the right and 114° on the left. On repeat plain films at presentation, the left femoral-neck fracture was now displaced and collapsed in varus, with persistent inferomedial sclerosis and cortical breach on the right. A CT scan confirmed these findings. Blood tests revealed normal calcium, vitamin D, and parathyroid hormone levels. DEXA scanning showed normal T- and Z-scores in the hip and spine, and whole-spine radiographs were unremarkable.

A 52-year-old Japanese man was referred for evaluation of a thyroid mass discovered incidentally 4 years earlier and originally deemed benign. His history included hypertension (on an angiotensin receptor blocker and calcium-channel blocker) and diabetes (on a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor). He reported only neck discomfort. On examination, the right thyroid lobe was enlarged without palpable lymphadenopathy. 

Thyroid ultrasonography showed a 6 × 5 cm relatively homogeneous hypoechoic mass with irregular borders in the right lobe. Contrast CT confirmed a hypodense thyroid mass and revealed an anterior mediastinal mass measuring 6.6 × 2.4 × 2.2 cm. MRI of the mediastinal lesion demonstrated isodense areas intermingled with high-density regions on both T1- and T2-weighted images, suggesting adipose tissue. FDG PET/CT was performed to exclude malignancy and showed weak uptake in the mediastinal mass. 

Laboratory studies revealed elevated serum thyroglobulin (833 ng/ml) with normal free T3, free T4, and TSH; anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies were negative. 

The patient underwent right hemithyroidectomy. Pathology revealed a follicular tumor of uncertain malignant potential. Postoperatively, thyroglobulin fell to 7.64 ng/ml, but the anterior mediastinal mass remained unchanged in size.

A 59-year-old man presented with a 10-year history of electric-shock sensations in the right lower extremity accompanied by progressive, significant swelling of the right knee. He denied pain, fever, or constitutional symptoms. He had no history of diabetes or known neurologic disease. 

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. The right knee was markedly swollen, firm, and non-tender, with full range of motion. Osteotendinous reflexes were absent in the lower extremities; the left knee was normal. 

Laboratory studies showed a normal C-reactive protein level, a normal complete blood count, normal fasting glucose, and normal glycated hemoglobin. An immune profile and infectious workup were unremarkable.

A CT scan of the right knee demonstrated: destruction of the lateral femoral condyle and ipsilateral tibial plateau with subchondral osteosclerosis; thickening and irregularity of the femoral and tibial cortices; disorganized periosteal reaction with cortical erosions; abundant marginal proliferative osteophytes; multiple intra-articular cystic areas communicating with the synovium, containing scattered calcified loose bodies giving a “bag of bones” appearance; and posterolateral tibiofemoral dislocation.

A 40-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of chronic abdominal pain, postprandial pain, loss of appetite, weight loss, and intermittent nausea and vomiting that persisted despite dietary modifications. She had no significant medical history, was not taking medications, and denied tobacco or heavy alcohol use. On examination, her BMI was 17.7 kg/m2, and the physical examination was unremarkable. Abdominal x-ray and duplex ultrasonography showed no significant findings. Upper endoscopy revealed a small hiatal hernia and a negative Helicobacter pylori test. Colonoscopy showed no abnormalities. Computed tomography angiography of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated 50% stenosis of the celiac artery with a characteristic hooked appearance and thickening of the median arcuate ligament.

A 50-year-old man presents with a 2-year history of bilateral hand and wrist pain involving the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints. The pain sometimes awoke him at night, was not relieved by rest, and had gradually increased in intensity. He also reports asthenia, anorexia, and weight loss. His past medical history is notable for repeated pulmonary infections. On examination, there is reducible deformity of both hands with ulnar deviation of the fingers and flexion at the MCP and PIP joints, without joint swelling or skin nodules. A painless macroglossia with lateral indentations is noted, causing moderate dysphagia. Laboratory studies show an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 66 mm/h, C-reactive protein of 59 mg/L, normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 9 g/dL), and corrected serum calcium of 3.1 mmol/L. Total protein is 69 g/L and serum creatinine is 82 μmol/L. Serum protein electrophoresis reveals hypogammaglobulinemia (6.35 g/L) without a monoclonal peak, and immunofixation identifies a kappa light chain monoclonal band in both serum and urine. Twenty-four–hour urine collection shows proteinuria of 7 g with abundant Bence Jones proteins. Serologic tests for antinuclear antibodies, anti–double-stranded DNA, anti-ENA, antifilaggrin, anticitrullinated peptide antibodies, and rheumatoid factor are all negative. Radiographs of the hands and pelvis demonstrate diffuse bone demineralization without erosions or joint-space narrowing.

A 54-year-old man with a one-year history of asymptomatic skin lesions presented for evaluation. The lesions began on his upper limbs and gradually increased in number and size. He is a house builder who works outdoors without a shirt and has a history of diabetes mellitus, with glycemic control unchanged during the course of the rash. There is no family history of similar skin changes.

On dermatological examination, there were multiple asymmetric erythematous papules and atrophic plaques with slightly elevated borders arranged in annular configurations on the neck, trunk, arms, and forearms. No mucosal or nail abnormalities were noted.

Initial differential diagnoses included granuloma annulare and leprosy. Direct mycological examination and anti-HIV tests were negative. A punch biopsy from a forearm lesion revealed fragmentation of elastic fibers in multinucleated giant cells and the superficial dermis, along with granulomas centered by necrobiosis and multinucleated giant cells with apparent palisading.

A 39-year-old white female healthcare worker with a history of diverticulosis presented with acute abdominal pain and a 10-week history of severe night sweats, progressive weight loss, and fever. On examination, she was febrile and cachectic, with no palpable lymphadenopathy. A chest radiograph was normal. CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed dilated small-bowel loops with gas–fluid levels, distal small-bowel circumferential wall thickening, extensive mesenteric fat edema, a large volume of pelvic free fluid, and a 5.0×3.6 cm low-density right adnexal lesion with a thick enhancing rim. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 16,500 cells/mm3 with 58% bands, hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, CA-125 39 U/mL, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 3.4 mmol/L, chloride 93 mmol/L, CO2 26 mmol/L, and creatinine 0.93 mg/dL. Pelvic inflammatory disease leading to a tubo-ovarian abscess was suspected, and gynecology performed a diagnostic laparoscopy followed by laparotomy. Findings included an enlarged right ovary with multiple small mucinous-appearing cysts, approximately 50 mL of pus drained from a right pyosalpinx, a normal left ovary, and extensive peritonitis with granulomas on the left upper abdominal wall. Biopsy showed chronic inflammation without malignancy. Cultures of the pyosalpinx fluid were negative for aerobes and anaerobes; acid-fast staining and cytology were not performed. The patient was discharged with postoperative diagnoses of right pyosalpinx and clinical tuberculous peritonitis.  

Ten days later, she returned with pleuritic chest pain. CT of the chest revealed a calcified granuloma in the right lower lobe and nonspecific pleural thickening. Electrocardiogram and cardiac enzymes were normal. A QuantiFERON-TB Gold assay was equivocal. Disseminated tuberculosis was suspected, and a second diagnostic laparoscopy revealed extensive granulomatous lesions throughout the peritoneum. Biopsies were obtained, and cultures for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Actinomyces, and fungi were sent and returned negative.

A 36-year-old woman with no known history of hypertension suddenly lost vision in both eyes and, a few hours later, became unconscious. On arrival, her blood pressure was 210/132 mm Hg, pulse 98 beats/min, respiratory rate 13 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation was normal. Glasgow Coma Score was 3 of 15. Noncontrast head CT revealed a well-defined hyperdense area of acute blood attenuation in the left basal ganglia with perilesional edema, compression of the third ventricle, extension into the third and anterior horn of the left lateral ventricle, acute obstructive hydrocephalus, and a midline shift. Additionally, there were bilateral focal hyperdense lentiform collections on the surface of the retinas of both globes.

A 59-year-old man with a 30-year history of pathologically confirmed Crohn’s disease presented with persistent bloating, abdominal pain, and alternating constipation and diarrhea with occasional incontinence despite infliximab and azathioprine therapy. He had undergone three prior small-bowel resections at the ileocecal junction for obstruction, most recently 15 years earlier; earlier pathology had shown transmural inflammation and inflammatory pseudopolyps. A recent colonoscopy demonstrated patchy mild inflammation from the rectum to the descending colon, but strictures and adhesions prevented passage of the scope proximal to 50 cm; mucosal biopsies at 10-cm intervals showed no active disease or dysplasia. CT imaging revealed diffuse mucosal thickening and pericolic fat edema from the rectum to the descending colon. MR enterography confirmed minimally active inflammatory disease in the rectosigmoid to descending colon, with no neoterminal ileum involvement or complications. Because his symptoms persisted, he underwent an open subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy and Hartmann’s pouch. Grossly, the resection included an ileal segment anastomosed to a markedly dilated colon with extensive fat wrapping and dense indurated mesenteric adipose tissue, especially in the mid and distal colon. The ileal and colonic walls were thickened and edematous, but the mucosal surface was unremarkable, with no strictures, ulcerations, fissures, fistulas, pseudopolyps, or perforations. Gross examination was also notable for soft submucosal nodules scattered throughout the colon.

A 91-year-old man was referred for evaluation of two enlarging lesions on the dorsal aspect of his right forearm and wrist that had been present for many years. His medical history included nonmelanoma skin cancer and decades of farm work without known immunodeficiency; he denied any trauma or inoculation of plant material. A community dermatologist’s biopsy of the right wrist lesion showed suppurative granulomatous dermatitis and scar. Periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott methenamine silver, Fite, and Ziehl–Neelsen stains were negative for microorganisms. Concerned about squamous cell carcinoma, keratoacanthoma type, he was referred for Mohs micrographic surgery consultation. On examination, there were two erythematous, cribriform, verrucous plaques with crust, pustules, and scant purulent drainage on the right lateral forearm (2.8 × 2.6 cm) and dorsal wrist (6.3 × 3.0 cm). The lesions appeared more consistent with an infectious process than a neoplasm. An excisional biopsy of the forearm plaque was performed, along with three punch biopsies for tissue culture and a wound culture of the purulent drainage.

A 31-year-old woman presented with a gradually progressive, painless lump in the left axillary tail of Spence of two years’ duration. There was no history of trauma, no nipple discharge, and no family history of breast cancer. On examination, the mass was firm, non-mobile, and measured 5 cm × 5 cm; the remainder of the breast and nipple were unremarkable. Ultrasonography of the breast revealed a thick-walled cystic lesion with floating membranes and internal echoes in the region of the lump. Chest X-ray and ultrasonography of the abdomen were unremarkable.

A previously healthy, fully vaccinated 2-year-old boy presented with 2½ weeks of daily fevers and 1 day of right leg pain and limp. He was initially treated with intramuscular penicillin G benzathine for a positive Group A streptococcal PCR (without pharyngitis) followed by a 7-day course of oral cefdinir, without improvement. There was no significant past medical or family history. Social history included a mice infestation at home and a trip to Guatemala 6 months earlier without malaria prophylaxis.

On examination, his temperature was 38.6 °C. He had a right-sided limp and pain with hip extension but otherwise full range of motion. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (WBC 14.4×10^9/L), anemia (hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL), an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (80 mm/h), an elevated C-reactive protein (3.2 mg/dL), and negative blood cultures.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the right hip demonstrated an intraosseous abscess within the right ischium with adjacent myositis and no joint involvement. Intravenous cefazolin was started to cover Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, and Kingella kingae. Although the limp resolved, daily fevers persisted.

On hospital day 8, MRI with STIR sequences revealed innumerable T2 hyperintense lesions throughout the liver in addition to the known pelvic osteomyelitis. A dedicated abdominal MRI confirmed innumerable small hepatic ring-enhancing lesions and pelvic fluid collections.

A 4-year-old girl was brought with heavy, fresh red vaginal bleeding over several days, without trauma or sexual assault. On examination she had short stature, short blunt hands, delayed dentition, bradycardia, and other stigmata of hypothyroidism; the thyroid gland was nonpalpable. Laboratory studies showed macrocytic anemia, a normal coagulation profile, markedly elevated TSH at 699 IU/mL (normal 0.35–4.9), low T3 (<1 pg/mL; normal 2.6–4.8), low T4 (<0.4 ng/dL), and thyroid peroxidase antibody 2152 U/mL (normal 0–60). Basal FSH was elevated, while LH and prolactin were within normal limits. Pelvic ultrasound revealed a 6.3×1.3 cm uterus with a tri-layered endometrium, a 5.7×3.7 cm septated cystic lesion in the right adnexa without internal vascularity, and a bulky left ovary with a dominant follicle. Neck ultrasound demonstrated bilaterally hypoplastic thyroid lobes with an absent isthmus. A skeletal survey showed delayed bone age (ossification of hamate and capitate consistent with 3–4 months; distal radial epiphysis consistent with 1 year; no triquetral or lunate ossification), multiple Wormian bones, an enlarged sella, and cortical thickening of the proximal femoral diaphyses. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the pituitary gland revealed homogeneous enlargement of the anterior pituitary compatible with hyperplasia; the posterior pituitary bright spot was preserved.

A 7-year-old boy with relapsed high-risk pre-B acute lymphoblastic leukemia presented with a 6-month history of a widespread follicular keratotic eruption. The eruption began as flesh-colored pinpoint papules on his cheeks during his first round of chemotherapy with vincristine, mercaptopurine, and methotrexate. Over time, similar papules appeared on the rest of the face, nape of the neck, trunk, buttocks, and all extremities, including the dorsal hands and feet. The lesions were only mildly pruritic. Previous treatments with topical hydrocortisone and a brief course of oral prednisone yielded no improvement. On skin examination, there was a diffuse keratosis pilaris–like eruption with prominent follicular spicules on the nasal tip and eyebrows, reminiscent of ulerythema ophryogenes.

A 50-year-old man with a remote history of treated Lyme disease, and no hypertension, hyperlipidemia, or diabetes, presented after four episodes of syncope over 24 hours. Six weeks earlier, he had a syncope while exercising; initial workup was unrevealing. Outpatient ECG then showed a new left bundle branch block. Exercise stress testing provoked presyncope with a brief burst of atrial tachycardia. A pharmacological nuclear stress test demonstrated an LVEF of 42% with a moderate-size area of inferior wall ischaemia and scar, but he had no chest pain or heart failure symptoms.

On current presentation, vital signs were blood pressure 140/66 mmHg, heart rate 54 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, temperature 36.2°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Physical examination was unremarkable. A 12-lead ECG showed sinus rhythm at 57 bpm, first-degree AV block, and a prolonged QTc. He had a brief burst of atrial tachycardia that resolved with IV metoprolol. Cardiac enzymes, thyroid function tests, serum calcium, and ACE levels were normal. Lyme antibody testing was negative. Chest radiograph was normal. Transthoracic echocardiography showed an LVEF of 45–50% with no regional wall motion abnormalities. Telemetry captured intermittent high-grade AV block with ventricular escape beats, prompting placement of a temporary transvenous pacemaker.

Coronary angiography revealed normal coronary arteries, and left ventriculography showed an LVEF of 35–40%. A permanent dual-chamber pacemaker was implanted, and he was discharged on guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure.

Outpatient cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an LVEF of 31%, RV ejection fraction of 23%, and mid-myocardial late gadolinium enhancement in the basal anteroseptal wall. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest showed mediastinal and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.

A 3-year-old girl was referred with widespread vesiculobullous lesions. One month earlier she had pruritic, red, scaly patches on her feet that were treated as eczema with emollients and topical steroids without improvement. The rash progressed to her abdomen and upper extremities, and a trial of permethrin for presumed scabies was ineffective. An unknown herbal remedy was applied for one week, after which new vesiculobullous and erosive lesions appeared.

On examination, she had generalized erythematous patches, plaques, flaccid bullae filled with clear fluid, and erosions over more than 90% of her body surface. Nikolsky’s sign was positive. Mucosal findings included buccal erosions and mild vaginal erythema; the ocular mucosa was normal. There was no family history of dermatosis.

Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (WBC 17 900/µL with 12 800 neutrophils), thrombocytosis (686 000/µL), elevated C-reactive protein (67 mg/L), negative antinuclear antibodies, and normal immunoglobulin levels. Smears and cultures from intact bullae were negative, while blood cultures grew Staphylococcus aureus.

Based on the extensive flaccid bullae, positive Nikolsky’s sign, and mucosal involvement, toxic epidermal necrolysis was initially suspected. However, the absence of systemic drug exposure, subacute onset, mild mucosal findings, and less severe oral lesions raised doubt. Other differential diagnoses considered were staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, pemphigus vulgaris, bullous pemphigoid, and bullous impetigo. A 4 mm punch biopsy of a new lesion and perilesional skin was obtained for histopathologic examination and direct immunofluorescence.

A 22-month-old girl with a history of failure to thrive presented with fever and a single generalized tonic-clonic seizure. She was found to have prerenal acute renal insufficiency, transaminitis, and anemia. A lumbar puncture was performed without difficulty after subcutaneous lidocaine infiltration. One day later, a retiform purpuric patch developed over the lumbosacral area at the puncture site. A workup, including biopsy and tissue culture, was performed to rule out other causes of large plaque retiform purpura, such as calciphylaxis, warfarin necrosis, and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia syndrome. Laboratory studies showed a creatinine level of 2.76 mg/dL, an aspartate aminotransferase level of 293 U/L, an alanine aminotransferase level of 111 U/L, a hemoglobin value of 6.4 g/dL, and a hematocrit value of 19.3%; values for platelet count, coagulation studies, antiphospholipid panel, protein C and S, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were within normal limits. The tissue culture had no growth.

A 49-year-old man with a 20-year history of gastroesophageal reflux disease presented with epigastric burning and heartburn. He had been treated intermittently with esomeprazole 40 mg once daily, with irregular adherence. An endoscopic study four years earlier had been normal. On current esophagogastroduodenoscopy, multiple whitish punctate lesions measuring 0.2 to 0.5 cm were seen predominantly in the middle third of the esophagus. The endoscopic impression was nonerosive reflux disease.

24‐year‐old man with 2‐year history of right lateral knee snapping and recurrent discomfort. Snapping was elicited on active extension and reproducible with direct pressure over the posterolateral knee; there was no history of trauma. He retained full active range of motion; an audible and palpable snap occurred when moving from flexion to extension, but passive motion was not consistently provocative. Cabot sign was positive; other special tests were negative. Plain radiographs showed a round osseous structure in the posterolateral joint. CT and MRI revealed an ovoid bone posterior and superior to the musculo‐tendinous junction of the popliteus muscle, articulating non-cartilaginously with the lateral femoral condyle; the popliteus tendon appeared inflamed. A steroid injection at the snapping point provided no relief.

A 44-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus status post mechanical mitral valve replacement presented with two days of diffuse abdominal pain and black stools. Her outpatient SLE regimen—mycophenolate mofetil, prednisone, and azathioprine—had been reduced to azathioprine alone due to insurance issues. On arrival, vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination was notable for mild abdominal tenderness without rebound or guarding; there was no rash or focal neurologic deficit.

Laboratory studies revealed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL, platelets 67,000/µL, white blood cells 2,300/µL) and acute renal failure (serum creatinine 3.0 mg/dL). A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated gallbladder wall thickening without pericholecystic fluid. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed only small gastric erosions. Serologic evaluation revealed elevated anti–double‐stranded DNA titers and hypocomplementemia (C3 18 mg/dL, C4 2 mg/dL), consistent with an SLE flare. She received intravenous methylprednisolone for three days, after which her platelet count rose transiently but her creatinine continued to climb. Renal biopsy showed class IV lupus nephritis with crescentic glomerulonephritis and 20–30% interstitial fibrosis but no evidence of thrombotic microangiopathy.

Her warfarin was held for biopsy and a heparin infusion was started. Over the next 48 hours, her platelet count fell to 11,000/µL and she developed acute encephalopathy; head CT was normal. Repeat labs demonstrated a negative direct Coombs test, haptoglobin <6 mg/dL, LDH 322 IU/L, ferritin 438 ng/mL, iron saturation 76%, normal fibrinogen (423 mg/dL), mildly elevated D-dimer (0.77 µg/mL), INR 2.0, and PTT 51 seconds. Antiphospholipid antibodies were positive, but Doppler ultrasound showed no thrombosis. HIT assay was negative. ADAMTS13 activity was 52%, and peripheral smear revealed few to moderate schistocytes and burr cells. Rheumatology and hematology considered TTP, complement-mediated HUS, SLE‐associated ITP, HIT, and drug-induced thrombocytopenia. She was treated with rituximab and another course of IV steroids for presumed ITP, and hemodialysis was initiated for worsening azotemia. Despite platelet transfusions, her count remained critically low.

An 8-year-old girl presented with a 2-day history of fever and a 5-day history of pain and erythema in the left inguinal region. She had no history of trauma or insect bites. On admission, she was febrile. Examination revealed left inguinal lymphadenitis with adjacent cellulitis; slight pharyngeal injection; clear lung fields; and no murmurs. Chest radiograph was normal. Initial laboratories showed Hb 13.7 g/dL, WBC 16.0 × 10^9/L, platelets 264 × 10^9/L, CRP 11.01 mg/dL, sodium 129.5 mEq/L, AST 55 IU/L, ALT 32 IU/L. She was started on intravenous ampicillin/sulbactam; the next day clindamycin was added for persistent fever and worsening erythema, and two days later antibiotics were escalated to meropenem for possible resistant bacteria—but fever and cellulitis persisted. Two days after admission, a polymorphous trunk rash appeared. Bilateral bulbar conjunctival injection without exudate and erythematous lips developed, followed by erythematous changes on her palms. Enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed enlarged and dense left inguinal lymph nodes, densification and thickening of the subcutaneous tissues without abscess or necrosis. Blood cultures remained negative.

A 7-year-old boy with no prior medical history presented with a painless right-sided cervical mass of 6 months’ duration. He underwent several puncture drainages at a local clinic, but persistent pus exudation from the site prompted referral. On examination, there was a small opening discharging pus located on the caudal side of the thyroid cartilage, slightly to the right of the midline, with mild induration of the surrounding skin. Ultrasonography showed a continuous cord-like echogenic image extending from the skin opening to the inferior aspect of the hyoid bone. On T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging, there was a contiguous high-signal tract from the external opening to the hyoid bone.

• A 62-year-old housewife presented with a four-month history of breathlessness on exertion. She denied drug or environmental inhalational exposures, chest pain, palpitations, ankle swelling, syncope, gastrointestinal symptoms, smoking, or alcohol use.  
• Past medical records revealed no previous clubbing or major illness. Menopause at age 45; two full-term vaginal deliveries; no family history of clubbing.  
• On examination: pulse 80/min, regular; respiratory rate 15/min; blood pressure 130/80 mm Hg; afebrile; SpO₂ 98–100% on room air. Bulbous enlargement of all toes bilaterally; fingernails unaffected. No swelling or skin changes at wrists or ankles. Chest auscultation disclosed bilateral fine end-inspiratory crepitations at the lung bases.  
• Laboratory tests: hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL; WBC 9400/mm³ (61% neutrophils); ESR 12 mm/h; normal serum chemistries; thyroid and liver function normal; ANA and rheumatoid factor negative; HIV negative.  
• Microbiology: sputum AFB smear negative; blood and sputum cultures sterile.  
• Pulmonary function testing: restrictive pattern.  
• Chest radiograph showed basal haziness. HRCT demonstrated basal interstitial thickening and honeycombing. Contrast CT of chest and abdomen showed no thoracic or abdominal aortic aneurysm.  
• Additional studies: abdominal ultrasound, fiberoptic bronchoscopy, and ECG were unremarkable; transthoracic and contrast echocardiography revealed no intracardiac shunt or pulmonary arteriovenous fistula.  
• Examination of her children and siblings revealed no clubbing.

A 72-year-old man with hypertension and stable coronary artery disease underwent right total hip arthroplasty for severe osteoarthritis. His medications included valsartan, indapamide, clopidogrel (aspirin allergy), a statin, and subcutaneous dalteparin. Sixteen days postoperatively, during rehabilitation, he felt a “click” in the operative hip and developed a wound hematoma. He underwent revision of the mobile joint components; intraoperative cultures grew Staphylococcus capitis, and he received IV ampicillin/sulbactam then IV flucloxacillin adjusted for renal function. Fourteen days later, persistent hematoma and wound drainage prompted a second revision with local vancomycin powder and replacement of mobile parts. Only one of six intraoperative cultures grew S. capitis (deemed contaminant), so flucloxacillin continued for two weeks, then oral levofloxacin and rifampicin for ten weeks. Clopidogrel was resumed after wound healing.

Following the second revision, his serum creatinine rose to 8.22 mg/dL, and hemodialysis was initiated five days after surgery. Nephrology evaluation showed proteinuria up to 500 mg/g with elevated alpha-1-microglobulin, no hematuria, and urine cultures positive for Proteus mirabilis and Escherichia coli. Autoimmune panels excluded collagenosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, ANCA-associated vasculitis, and rheumatoid arthritis. Soluble interleukin-2 receptor was elevated at 1100 U/mL (normal 158–623 U/mL); angiotensin-converting enzyme was normal. Hantavirus serology was negative; monoclonal gammopathy was excluded; and HbA1c was 4.1%.

A 69-year-old Caucasian woman with hypertension, hypothyroidism, and a history of stage IA breast cancer in remission presented with a 3-month history of daily high fevers up to 39.5 °C, severe fatigue, arthralgias of the hips and knees, a diffuse erythematous rash on the chest and upper extremities, episodic pharyngitis, and impaired vision. A chest radiograph showed diffuse airspace disease. Initial laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL, platelet count 329 × 10^3/mcL, white blood cell count 11.1 × 10^3/mcL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 102 mm/h, C-reactive protein 15 mg/dL, ferritin 1608 ng/mL, and negative antinuclear and rheumatoid factor titers. Extensive infectious and autoimmune serologies—including anti–double-stranded DNA, anti-Smith, anti-Ro, anti-La, anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide, ANCA panel, Lyme ELISA/Western blot, creatine kinase, anti-Jo-1, and anti–scl-70—were unremarkable. Her symptoms initially improved with a short course of glucocorticoids as an outpatient.

One month later, she was brought to the emergency department after a witnessed generalized seizure, worsening bilateral vision loss, digital ischemia of the toes, and recurrent high-grade fevers. Head CT was normal, and she was started on levetiracetam. Laboratory values on admission included blood urea nitrogen 73 mg/dL, creatinine 4.64 mg/dL (baseline 0.68 mg/dL), white blood cell count 23.5 × 10^3/mcL, hemoglobin 7.5 g/dL, platelet count 71 × 10^3/mcL, and complement C3 level 71 mg/dL (reference 85–193 mg/dL). She had new-onset atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response that reverted to sinus rhythm with diltiazem. Transthoracic echocardiography showed new left ventricular systolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction of 30–35%. She was admitted to the ICU with multiorgan dysfunction and started on intravenous dexamethasone.

Further studies demonstrated nonimmune hemolysis with lactate dehydrogenase 969 U/L, haptoglobin < 10 mg/dL, and 5–8 schistocytes per high-power field. A DIC panel was unremarkable, and Shiga toxin/EHEC studies were negative. Given the combination of neurologic findings, acute kidney injury, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia, a thrombotic microangiopathy was diagnosed. She underwent emergent hemodialysis and plasma exchange.

A 76-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated), hypertension, COPD, and obstructive sleep apnea presented to the ED with intermittent left-sided jaw and lower face pain that began that morning. She described the pain as “sharp and lightning-like,” waking her from sleep. She denied recent dental procedures and any other symptoms. Examination findings on first visit: temperature 36.4 °C, heart rate 105 bpm, respirations 18/min, blood pressure 151/101 mm Hg, SpO2 96% on room air. Neurologic examination was normal. There was mild tenderness over the left mandible; jaw opening and closing occurred without palpable clicking or grinding. Initial investigations: noncontrast CT of the head and facial bones was grossly normal; ECG showed rate-controlled atrial fibrillation without acute ischemic changes; chest radiograph was clear; laboratory studies revealed an ESR of 34 mm/hr (reference 0–30 mm/hr) with otherwise unremarkable CBC, CMP, TSH, troponin-I, urinalysis, and magnesium. She was restarted on apixaban, neurology recommended no changes in medication but suggested outpatient dental and neurology follow-up, and she was discharged home. 

Two days later, she returned with similar left lower face and jaw pain that was now moderate to severe despite outpatient recommendations. Early neurology consultation recommended IV methylprednisolone 250 mg and ketorolac for analgesia. Pain remained refractory, and IV fentanyl was administered. Given the persistence and severity of symptoms despite treatment, other diagnoses were considered, and a CTA of the head and neck was obtained.

A 42-year-old woman from India presented with a 1-year history of disseminated, clear fluid–filled bullous lesions primarily on her palms and soles. These lesions intermittently worsened, were pruritic, and produced a burning sensation; they ruptured on manipulation to form crusts and healed spontaneously. Exacerbations were accompanied by low-grade fever and diffuse myalgia. She self-treated flare-ups with oral antibiotics, topical steroids, and emollients. There was no history of drug ingestion known to trigger severe allergic reactions. Over the past 2 years she also experienced paresthesias in her palms and soles, slight tremors in both upper limbs, and polyarthritis involving multiple joints. She had no relevant past medical or family history.

On examination, discrete crusted erosions and a few vesiculobullous lesions of varying sizes were noted on both dorsal and palmar aspects of the hands. Multiple crusted erosions and a few intact bullae were seen on both soles, more pronounced medially. The oral mucosa, ophthalmologic and genital examinations were unremarkable. Nikolsky sign was negative. Sensation was reduced over both palms and soles, and bilateral supraclavicular nerves were tender.

Routine blood tests were within normal limits except for a mildly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. A nerve conduction study demonstrated bilateral sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy involving the tibial, peroneal, and ulnar nerves. A Tzanck smear did not yield any significant findings.

A 15-year-old previously healthy girl presented with two days of fever, malaise, pleuritic chest pain, cough, dyspnea, and new bruising lesions. One week earlier she had a self-resolved right forearm abscess. On arrival she was in marked respiratory distress and tachycardic. Examination revealed tenderness over the left lower chest, decreased breath sounds at the left base, an audible systolic murmur in all areas, and mild lower-limb edema. She rapidly required invasive mechanical ventilation, inotropic and vasoactive support.

Laboratory studies showed: negative SARS-CoV-2 antigen, positive SARS-CoV-2 IgG, negative IgM; C-reactive protein 135.2 mg/L (0–0.5 mg/dL); D-dimer elevated; troponin 1060 ng/L (0–20.3); white cells 25,580 × 10^3/µL with neutrophilia; hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL; platelets 170 × 10^3/µL; blood culture grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

An initial transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated a hyperdynamic left ventricle with preserved systolic and mild diastolic dysfunction, moderate to severe mitral regurgitation with hemodynamic repercussion, mild left atrial dilation, and pulmonary hypertension. She received pentaglobulin and broad-spectrum antibiotics. A repeat echocardiogram showed a suspected rupture of the left Valsalva sinus with a shunt into the left atrium, severe aortic insufficiency, moderate to severe mitral regurgitation, and severe left atrial dilation. She was referred urgently for emergent cardiothoracic evaluation.

A 56-year-old Japanese woman with a 55.5 pack-year smoking history was evaluated for intermittent bloody sputum and a right lower lobe shadow on chest radiograph and CT scan. Bronchoscopic biopsy confirmed squamous cell carcinoma of the right intermediate bronchus with low PD-L1 expression (tumor proportion score 30–40%). Contrast-enhanced CT and FDG-PET showed a 36×28 mm right lower lobe mass (SUVmax 6.3) and ipsilateral mediastinal lymphadenopathy (SUVmax 8.8), leading to a diagnosis of cT1cN2M0 (stage IIIA) NSCLC. She received two cycles of cisplatin and vinorelbine with concurrent thoracic radiotherapy (2 Gy × 33 fractions), followed by up to 12 months of durvalumab (10 mg/kg every 2 weeks). Five months after starting durvalumab, she developed persistent fever and altered behavior and was diagnosed with isolated ACTH deficiency, which responded to hydrocortisone. One year and again 1.5 years after completing durvalumab, follow-up CT scans showed growth of a right S6 lesion with loss of air bronchograms. PET–CT at 1.5 years demonstrated FDG uptake in this lesion (SUVmax 4.7) without new mediastinal or distant disease. Based on these findings, loco-regional recurrence of lung cancer was suspected, and biopsy was deferred due to the risk posed by surrounding vessels.

A 40-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of abdominal pain and vomiting. She reported no passage of gas or stool during this period and denied fever. Four years earlier, she underwent a hysterectomy via a Pfannenstiel incision and had experienced intermittent abdominal discomfort since. On examination, her vital signs were stable. Abdominal palpation revealed an 8-cm mass in the epigastric region. Laboratory studies demonstrated leukocytosis; other values were within normal limits. A plain abdominal radiograph showed air–fluid levels in several small-bowel loops and multiple opaque linear densities in the midline. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 107 × 60 mm mass among small-bowel loops at the L2–L4 level, closely related to the anterior abdominal wall, with peripheral contrast enhancement and linear metallic hypodense artifacts within its right aspect.

A 50-year-old premenopausal woman with hormone receptor–positive, HER2-negative invasive ductal breast carcinoma underwent right mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection followed by adjuvant chemotherapy and 5 years of tamoxifen. Fourteen years later, she developed a recurrence in the right pectoralis major and lung nodules. She was started on letrozole and ribociclib. Approximately 6 weeks after initiating ribociclib, she noted a burning, pruritic rash on both hands. On examination, there were erythematous, pink-to-violaceous, tender, annular papules with dusky centers and bullae on the palms bilaterally. The oral mucosa was uninvolved. She denied new medications other than ribociclib and letrozole. Ribociclib was permanently discontinued, and the rash gradually resolved while she continued letrozole alone. One month later, palbociclib was added to her regimen. After the first cycle of palbociclib, she developed grade 3 neutropenia and a recurrence of the rash, with tender, annular papules with dusky centers and bulls-eye bullae on her hands. A single aphthous lesion was noted on the hard palate. A punch biopsy of a hand lesion was obtained.

A 48-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of progressive clumsiness of her right hand, dysarthria, dysphagia (especially for liquids), and an unsteady gait. Her past medical history was unremarkable. On examination, she had multiple abdominal and dorsal lipomas; a slightly ataxic gait with difficulty in tandem walking; left inferior facial paresis; hyperreflexia in both upper and lower limbs; slurred speech; and mild dysmetria on finger-to-nose, heel-to-shin, and rapid alternating movements. Primitive reflexes were present. 

Brain MRI without contrast showed symmetric T2 hyperintensity of both cerebellar peduncles and dentate nuclei, with associated calcifications. Hematological, biochemical, autoimmune, neoplastic, and paraneoplastic screening tests were all normal. Tests of hypothalamic–pituitary hormones and plasma cholestanol levels were within normal limits, and genetic testing for CYP27A1 mutations was negative.

A subsequent brain MRI with gadolinium showed enlargement of the T2/FLAIR lesions in the cerebellar peduncles and dentate nuclei bilaterally, with intense, homogeneous contrast enhancement. Two symmetrical, slightly hyperintense periorbital lesions were also noted on T2-weighted images. Given suspicion for histiocytosis, transthoracic echocardiography and contrast-enhanced thoracoabdominal CT were performed; both showed no evidence of cardiac, aortic, perirenal, or retroperitoneal involvement.

A 28-year-old man with no past medical history presented with a 2-day history of severe bifrontal, throbbing headache associated with blurred vision, diplopia, photophobia, nausea and vomiting. Symptoms worsened with coughing, bending forward and straining, and did not respond to over-the-counter analgesics. He had received the Ad26.COV2.S vaccine 10 days before onset. He reported no prior headaches and no personal or family history of clotting disorders (maternal grandmother had an intracranial aneurysm at age 50). On examination, vital signs were normal; funduscopy revealed papilledema, and the remainder of the neurologic examination was unremarkable. 

Magnetic resonance venography of the brain showed filling defects in the superior sagittal sinus and the right transverse sinus extending into the right jugular vein, consistent with cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Initial laboratory studies revealed a platelet count of 63 000/μL, an international normalized ratio of 1.5, a partial thromboplastin time of 36.3 seconds, and a D-dimer level of 22 546 ng/mL. Computed tomography angiography of the chest and abdomen demonstrated multiple segmental and subsegmental pulmonary emboli in the right lung and an occluded right hepatic vein with wedge-shaped hypodensity in the corresponding liver segment. Venous duplex ultrasonography of the lower extremities was normal. An extensive workup for hypercoagulability was performed.

An 8-year-old girl was brought to the emergency department by her parents because of a 2-week history of head tilt. Two weeks earlier she had been treated for streptococcal pharyngitis with antibiotics. There was no history of trauma. On examination, she held her head tilted to the right with a fixed cervical posture and had a markedly reduced range of motion of the neck. She was afebrile, and neurologic examination was normal. Initial management included muscle relaxants, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, physiotherapy, and continued antibiotics; no otolaryngology consultation or radiologic studies were obtained. One month later, persistence of torticollis prompted computed tomography of the cervical spine, which showed rotatory C1–C2 atlantoaxial subluxation.

A 33-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of acute onset of sensory loss and weakness in both lower extremities. He had no history of trauma, bleeding disorder, hypertension, or recent infection. On examination, he was afebrile. Neurologic examination revealed paraplegia of both lower extremities, positive bilateral Babinski signs, and hypoesthesia below the T10 dermatome with saddle anesthesia. Anal sphincter tone and bilateral deep tendon reflexes were reduced. Complete blood count and metabolic panel were within normal limits, and coagulation studies including INR and APTT were normal. Emergent MRI of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine demonstrated a lesion compressing the spinal cord, showing a hyperintense signal on T1-weighted images and an isointense signal on T2-weighted images localized to the posterior epidural space.

An 18‐year‐old Indonesian woman presented with a 5‐year history of a painful lesion on the right palm that began after a traumatic injury. The lesion was described as a well‐defined, reddish, edematous, scaly plaque with contractures of the middle finger and purulent discharge. She had no history of fever, weight loss, or known tuberculosis exposure. Physical examination revealed an erythematous, scaly plaque on the right palm without regional lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count and inflammatory markers, were unremarkable. A chest radiograph showed no pulmonary abnormalities. Radiographs of the right hand showed soft‐tissue swelling without bone destruction. A tuberculin skin test was positive.

A 42-year-old woman with a history of biopsy-proven class IV lupus nephritis in 2011 (in remission off medications), psoriasis, and a 1-year history of a persistent left periorbital rash presented after three episodes of transient left eye blindness over 2 days (each lasting 1–10 minutes, resolving spontaneously). She had no oral ulcers, alopecia, arthralgias, chest pain, dyspnea, muscle weakness, or hematuria.  

A contrast‐enhanced CT of the face showed increased soft‐tissue edema around the left eye. MRI of the face and orbits with and without contrast demonstrated enhancement of the left optic nerve sheath and findings consistent with posterior scleritis. MR angiography of the head and neck was normal. Neurologic and ophthalmologic examinations were unremarkable. Echocardiography and outpatient cardiac telemetry to evaluate vascular causes of amaurosis fugax were unrevealing.  

Dermatology evaluation of the left periorbital rash—initially an erythematous papule that spread over the upper and lower eyelids—revealed no pruritus or pain, only a pins-and-needles sensation. Patch testing was negative, and she reported no new medications; previous treatments with topical hydrocortisone and tacrolimus had worsened the rash. Physical examination showed a well-demarcated, scaly, edematous purple-gray plaque on the left upper and lower eyelids.  

Punch biopsy of the lesion showed interface dermatitis of the epidermis and follicular epithelium with dyskeratotic keratinocytes, follicular plugging, pigment incontinence, and perivascular chronic inflammation. A PAS-diastase stain demonstrated focal basement membrane zone thickening, and a CD123 immunostain highlighted plasmacytoid dendritic cell aggregates.  

Laboratory studies revealed an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:160 and positive anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies. Complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, complement levels, lupus anticoagulant, and urinalysis were within normal limits. Tests for anti-Smith, anti-U1RNP, anti-Ro/SSA, anti-La/SSB, anticardiolipin, and anti–β-2-glycoprotein antibodies were negative.

An 18-year-old woman (gravida 0) presented to the emergency department with acute onset of lower abdominal pain that began several hours earlier during strenuous sports practice. She described the pain as cramp-like, similar to menstrual cramps and reminiscent of an appendicitis episode 3 years prior. The pain worsened with vomiting and urination, improved when crouching, and did not respond to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. She also experienced nausea and one episode of emesis. 

Her medical history was notable only for an uncomplicated appendectomy. Menarche occurred at age 12, with regular 60-day cycles that were not painful; her last menstrual period was 7 months earlier. She had been using depot medroxyprogesterone acetate for contraception for 3 years and had no history of sexually transmitted infections. She was afebrile, with stable vital signs. On examination, there was severe tenderness in both lower abdominal quadrants on light and deep palpation, without rigidity, rebound tenderness, or palpable masses. A pelvic examination was deferred. 

Laboratory studies showed a white-blood-cell count of 16.4×10^3/µL without a left shift, and a urine pregnancy test was negative. Transabdominal and transvaginal pelvic ultrasound demonstrated a uterus measuring 7.1×4.6×5.4 cm with a distended endometrial cavity containing homogeneous echogenic fluid; no discrete mass or congenital anomaly was identified. Both ovaries appeared normal in size, echotexture, and blood flow. 

Subsequent magnetic resonance imaging revealed a fluid-filled endometrial cavity and endocervical canal; the cervical canal measured 1 to 2 mm in diameter without dilation.

A 40-year-old man with no chronic medical or surgical history presented with a 3-day history of generalized abdominal pain. He denied fever or vomiting. On examination, he was alert; blood pressure was 118/68 mmHg, pulse 98 beats/min, temperature 37.1 °C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. His abdominal examination showed generalized tenderness with guarding, maximal in the epigastric region; there was no organomegaly or pulsatile mass, and bowel sounds were normal.
