Cardiovascular, neurologic, and musculoskeletal examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed a hemoglobin level of 12 g/dL, a white-cell count of 9.9 × 10^3/μL, a platelet count of 350 × 10^3/μL, and a serum creatine kinase (CK) level of 787 U/L (reference range, 38–308 U/L). Renal and liver profiles and serum amylase were within normal limits. A chest and abdominal radiograph showed no free air under the diaphragm or dilated bowel loops, and a bedside abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable. Computed tomography of the abdomen with intravenous contrast showed no abnormalities.

He was admitted with a presumed acute abdomen and received intravenous opioids, fluids, and supplemental oxygen. On hospital day 2, he developed marked generalized abdominal muscle wall rigidity and persistent severe pain; urgent endoscopy showed Forrest IIC gastric ulcers, and repeat chest radiography again showed no pneumoperitoneum. On hospital day 3, he developed arching of the back with persistent abdominal rigidity, and his serum CK level had risen to 10,860 U/L.

A 76-year-old man with stage IIIA squamous cell carcinoma of the lung (cT2aN2M0) completed chemoradiotherapy (2 Gy × 33 fractions with weekly carboplatin and paclitaxel). Nine days after radiation, he developed fever (38.6 °C) and a CT showed a new ground-glass opacity in the irradiation field; he was treated with oral prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day) tapered over 6 months and then discontinued. Forty-one days after radiotherapy, when the prednisolone dose had fallen to 10 mg/day, he began biweekly durvalumab (10 mg/kg). After 11 cycles and 3 weeks off prednisolone, he developed dyspnea and malaise. On admission: T 37.3 °C, HR 75 bpm, BP 111/81 mm Hg, SpO₂ 96% on room air. Chest CT showed new ground-glass opacities in both lower lobes extending beyond the irradiated areas. Laboratory studies revealed a C-reactive protein level of 8.24 mg/dL and a KL-6 level of 515 U/mL. On hospital day 2, bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) from the right B8 became progressively bloody and contained 13.4 × 10⁵ cells/mL (70% neutrophils, 10.5% lymphocytes, 11% eosinophils, 8.5% macrophages). Bacterial cultures of BAL fluid were negative. Myeloperoxidase-ANCA, proteinase-3 ANCA, and anti–glomerular basement membrane antibodies were all negative.

A 41-year-old woman with treatment-resistant schizophrenia had been stable on clozapine 600 mg daily for 14 years without prior neutropenia. Routine monitoring 12 days ago revealed an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) of less than 0.5 × 10^9/L (“red light”), and clozapine was discontinued. Five days after stopping clozapine, she manifested worsening paranoia, guarded behavior, anxiety, and pressured speech, similar to prior relapses.  
On admission, physical examination was unremarkable apart from psychiatric findings. Repeat blood tests confirmed persistent neutropenia (ANC < 0.5 × 10^9/L). Full viral and autoimmune screens were negative, and there was no history suggestive of cyclic or inherited neutropenia. A bone marrow aspirate obtained via trephine biopsy showed mild reactive changes.

A 63-year-old Indian man with no prior medical history presented with 7 days of fever and dry cough and 1 day of mild dyspnea. He was started empirically on azithromycin, cetirizine, and paracetamol and had a positive SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR test. He was admitted to the ICU when his respiratory rate rose to 34–36 breaths per minute and SpO₂ fell to 84% on room air; he remained hemodynamically stable. Initial laboratory studies showed normal hemogram, renal and liver function, and procalcitonin; C-reactive protein was 45 ng/ml, ferritin 611 ng/ml, D-dimer 2.8 µg/ml, and fibrinogen 575 mg/dl. Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral patchy infiltrates. He required noninvasive ventilation for moderate ARDS and received remdesivir, tocilizumab, methylprednisolone, enoxaparin, and empiric cefoperazone–sulbactam.  

In week 5 of illness, after testing negative for SARS-CoV-2, he was transferred to a non–COVID ICU and remained on NIV. Labs showed mild azotemia, sodium 132 mEq/l, potassium 3.3 mmol/l, HbA1c 8.3%, and SOFA score 5. High-resolution CT of the chest revealed extensive bilateral fibrotic changes. Over the next 3 weeks his steroids were tapered, antibiotics deescalated, and oxygen support weaned to 0.3 FiO₂ via Venturi mask.  

In week 9, he developed worsening hypoxemia and hypercapnia (PaCO₂ up to 108 mmHg), became drowsy, and was intubated for invasive mechanical ventilation. Repeat bacterial and fungal blood and tracheal cultures were negative. Serum galactomannan was 1.3 ODI, prompting voriconazole and cefoperazone–sulbactam. In week 10 he developed circulatory shock requiring vasopressors and hydrocortisone, with further oxygenation decline despite prone ventilation and escalation to meropenem and teicoplanin.  
Computed tomography pulmonary angiography excluded pulmonary embolism, and cardiac evaluation ruled out an acute cardiac event. Tracheal aspirate bacterial and fungal cultures remained negative, and one blood culture grew coagulase-negative staphylococcus.

A 57-year-old Chinese woman was referred for evaluation of right pre-auricular pain and a hard swelling present for over 5 years. She had consulted multiple physicians without a diagnosis and received no prior treatment. Her past medical history included left breast fibroadenoma excision, recurrent urinary tract infections, stress urinary incontinence, and infective colitis. She was also under ENT follow-up for hoarseness. She denied trauma to the jaw and had no relevant family history. 

On examination, there was a 15 × 20 mm tender, bony hard mass over the right pre-auricular region. The mass did not move with mandibular condylar translation on mouth opening; maximal mouth opening and TMJ function were normal. Overlying skin was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies, including liver and renal function tests and complete blood count, were within normal limits. A dental panoramic tomogram showed no lesions at the right TMJ. Subsequent unenhanced CT imaging revealed a sharply defined hyperdense ovoid mass measuring 10 × 13 × 20 mm within the subcutaneous layer over the right pre-auricular region, closely associated with the lateral aspect of the right TMJ. There was no bony erosion of the condyle, and the joint capsule appeared preserved.

A 30-year-old man presented with 8 hours of insidious, nonradiating periumbilical pain accompanied by nausea and two episodes of vomiting. He had no significant past medical or surgical history, did not smoke, and drank alcohol socially. Bowel and bladder habits were unchanged. On examination, there was periumbilical tenderness with guarding and rigidity. Laboratory tests showed mild leukocytosis; serum amylase and lipase were normal. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a hypoechoic lesion beneath the umbilicus. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a tubular structure measuring approximately 6–7 cm in length, arising from the antimesenteric border of the distal ileum and extending to the umbilicus, with wall enhancement, surrounding fat stranding, a small amount of free fluid, and several enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes (largest, 12 × 8 mm).

A 78-year-old retired schoolteacher with a 1-month history of behavioral changes was brought for evaluation. He had no history of substance abuse or significant medical illness aside from bilateral osteoarthritis of the knees. Over the preceding month, he exhibited excessive psychomotor activity, emotional lability, increased self-confidence, pressured speech, decreased need for sleep, and elevated energy. On several occasions, he misidentified his daughter as his late wife, who had died 6 months earlier.

On examination, he was obese (weight 92 kg, BMI >27), with stable vital signs and no focal neurologic deficits. Mental status examination revealed irritability, increased psychomotor activity, grandiosity, distractibility, and impaired judgment; there were no delusions or hallucinations. His Mini–Mental State Examination score was 28/30.

Laboratory investigations, including HIV serology, VDRL, vitamin B12, thyroid function tests, routine blood counts, serum electrolytes, blood urea, and creatinine, were all within normal limits. Electrocardiography showed a prolonged corrected QT interval of 486 msec. Noncontrast CT of the brain demonstrated cortical atrophy—most pronounced in the frontal and temporal lobes—mild frontal periventricular hypodensities consistent with small-vessel ischemic changes, bilateral basal ganglia calcifications, and no evidence of infarction. He did not fulfill international consensus criteria for behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia.

A 48-year-old woman with a history of poorly controlled diabetes mellitus presented with a 3-day history of swelling of the right side of her face, nasal bleeding, fever with rigors, headache, facial pain, difficulty opening her mouth, and maggots emerging from her right nostril. Two years earlier, she had facial swelling diagnosed as an endodontic abscess that resolved after extraction of the offending teeth; she also reported multiple other maxillary tooth extractions in the past without details.

On examination, there was right-sided facial asymmetry and tenderness. Intraorally, she had fetid breath, a completely exposed and necrotic maxillary alveolus and right hard palate, and several nonhealed maxillary extraction sockets. Nasal endoscopy revealed crusted, dried mucosa with exposed nasal septum and right lateral wall.

A CT scan of the head and neck showed mucosal thickening of the bilateral ethmoid, sphenoid, maxillary, and frontal sinuses with air specks and some enhancement, along with erosion and destruction of the right frontal bone, nasal septum, right lamina papyracea, and hard palate. There was no intracranial hemorrhage or mass effect. Several cervical lymph nodes measured up to 7.8 mm in the left level II.

Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 17.4 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, hematocrit 32%, glycated hemoglobin 9.5%, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 99 mm/hr, C-reactive protein 19.82 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 35 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.8 mg/dL. A right nasal swab culture grew moderate colonies of cloxacillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and was negative for fungi. She was started on intravenous vancomycin and insulin therapy. An otolaryngologist and maxillofacial surgeon were consulted for debridement of the necrotic maxilla and nasal cavities, and a biopsy specimen was obtained.

An 81-year-old man with hypertension presented with 4 days of fever and rapid visual deterioration of his left eye. Two days before admission he had noted left-eye pain and worsening eyesight, followed by fever and fatigue. On examination at admission, temperature was 38.7°C, blood pressure 132/49 mmHg, pulse 60 beats/min regular, respirations 20/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Cardiovascular examination revealed a grade 2 aortic diastolic murmur. Funduscopic examination showed a Roth spot in the left eye. White blood cell count was 17 720 cells/mm3, and procalcitonin was 14.08 ng/mL. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated mild mitral regurgitation, moderate aortic regurgitation with a pressure half-time of 347 ms, no holodiastolic flow reversal in the abdominal aorta, a left ventricular ejection fraction of 53% with diffuse global hypokinesis, and mild LV dilation (diastolic dimension 55 mm; systolic dimension 38 mm). Transesophageal echocardiography revealed an 8-mm thickening and perforation of the right coronary cusp causing moderate aortic regurgitation, with no evidence of aortic root abscess or abnormal mitral apparatus. Vitreous and blood cultures grew penicillin-sensitive Group G Streptococci. A diagnosis of aortic valve endocarditis with endogenous endophthalmitis was made. Intravenous penicillin G was started. By Day 5, blood cultures were negative, white blood cell count and procalcitonin had decreased to 10 100 cells/mm3 and 1.80 ng/mL, respectively; the patient had no heart failure symptoms, and repeat TTE was unchanged.

An 18-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of slightly painful, pruritic vesicles and bullae involving the face, oral mucosa, abdomen, thighs, and back. Over the preceding 2 months, she had experienced weight loss, migratory polyarthralgias with morning stiffness lasting >30 minutes, myalgias, fatigue, fever, alopecia, and a malar rash with photosensitivity. Her only medication was medroxyprogesterone acetate, administered every 3 months. She had been pregnant at age 17; venereal disease testing had shown a low‐titer reactive VDRL and a negative treponemal assay.

On examination, she appeared pale and fatigued but had normal vital signs. Skin examination revealed a malar rash and multiple tense vesicles and bullae (1 mm to 6 cm) on erythematous macules and plaques involving the eyelids, arms, abdomen, back, thighs, and vermilion border of the lips, with extension to the oral mucosa. There was no lymphadenopathy, no synovitis, and otherwise unremarkable findings.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.0 g/dL, leukocyte count 2,880 /mm3, and platelet count 105,000 /mm3. The direct Coombs test was positive, with normal lactate dehydrogenase and bilirubin levels. Urinalysis demonstrated proteinuria, hematuria, and leukocyturia without casts; the urine protein–creatinine ratio was 856 mg/g. Renal function was preserved (creatinine 0.63 mg/dL, urea 15 mg/dL). Complement levels were low (C3 < 21 mg/dL, C4 7 mg/dL). Antinuclear antibody was positive at a titer of 1:640 with a homogeneous pattern, and anti–double‐stranded DNA and anti‐histone antibodies were also positive.

An 18-year-old male presented with a six-month history of lower back pain without lower limb symptoms. The pain began spontaneously after a trivial fall, was worse with activity, and was relieved by rest and analgesics; there was no diurnal or postural variation. On examination, there was paraspinal muscle spasm and reduced range of motion of the lumbar spine; no neurological deficits, visible deformity, or swelling were noted. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein, were within normal limits. A lumbosacral spine radiograph showed irregularity of the superior end plate of L3 and decreased lumbar lordosis. Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbosacral spine revealed anterior wedging of the L3 vertebral body, erosion of the superior end plate at L3, narrowing of the L3–L4 intervertebral disk space, and Schmorl nodes in L3.

A 5-year-old boy was born at term to non-consanguineous parents after an uneventful pregnancy. Birth weight was 2900 g and length 50 cm. At age 3 days, jaundice was noted and attributed to physiologic neonatal hyperbilirubinemia. He was discharged but readmitted several days later for persistent jaundice and mild hepatosplenomegaly (liver 2.5 cm and spleen 1 cm below costal margin). Laboratory studies showed elevated total and conjugated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, cholesterol, ALT, and AST; hematology and urinalysis were normal. Neurologic examination revealed only heightened reflex irritability. Viral PCR tests for CMV, HSV, toxoplasmosis, and Chlamydia were negative. Blood galactose was 12 ng/ml (normal ≤ 7.1 ng/ml) and rose to 20 ng/ml on repeat testing; a galactose-free, lactose-free diet was instituted. By age 2 months, blood galactose normalized but cholestasis and hepatosplenomegaly persisted. On examination at 2 months 1 week, weight was 4100 g (5th–10th percentile), height 57 cm (25th percentile), and spleen 6.5 cm below the costal margin without portal hypertension. Synthetic liver function and standard metabolic parameters were normal; plasma chitotriosidase was mildly elevated (251.5 nmol/mg/hour; normal 4.5–198). Galactose-1-phosphate-uridyl transferase activity and genetic testing ruled out galactosemia. An extensive workup excluded biliary atresia, Gaucher disease type 1, α1-antitrypsin deficiency, tyrosinemia, citrullinemia type 2, progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type 3, mitochondrial disorders, and Alagille syndrome. A percutaneous liver biopsy was performed next.

A 43-year-old woman presented with gradual onset of binocular horizontal diplopia for one year. She was healthy, with a history of bilateral pterygium excision 10 years earlier. Visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. Orthoptic evaluation demonstrated a 55-prism-diopter esotropia at distance and near; forced duction testing was negative. Slit-lamp examination showed diffuse nasal bulbar conjunctival scarring in both eyes. Baseline intraocular pressures were 15 mmHg bilaterally. Cycloplegic refraction was plano in the right eye and –0.25 diopters in the left eye. Workup for acquired strabismus, including MRI of the brain and orbits and laboratory studies for acetylcholine receptor antibodies and thyroid function, was unremarkable.

She underwent left and right medial rectus recessions (6 mm each) and right lateral rectus resection (6 mm) under general anesthesia. Extensive conjunctival scarring required more cauterization than usual. On postoperative day 1, suture adjustment was performed without complication; she was orthotropic. The conjunctiva was mildly injected in both eyes, with mild chemosis in the right eye. No intraocular pressure measurement was obtained. No anterior-chamber inflammation was noted. She was started on tobramycin–dexamethasone suspension four times daily and preservative-free artificial tears hourly.

On postoperative day 3, she reported mild discomfort in the right eye. Visual acuity was 20/32 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was 30 mmHg in the right eye and 12 mmHg in the left eye. Examination revealed marked temporal conjunctival chemosis in the right eye without hematoma or dilated episcleral vessels and no proptosis. Gonioscopic examination of the right eye showed an open angle with blood in Schlemm’s canal at the temporal quadrant. The left eye was unremarkable; cup-to-disc ratios were 0.4 in both eyes.

A woman in her 70s with a history of osteopenia presented with bilateral depressions of the frontal scalp and forehead that had progressed over 3 years and were mildly pruritic without neurologic symptoms. She had undergone a coronal brow lift more than 20 years earlier and denied any more recent local procedures, trauma, or bisphosphonate use.

On examination, there was a symmetric arcuate depression along the frontal hairline and central forehead, with a subtle ivory-white change of the overlying skin without induration and hair thinning of the frontal scalp. The eyes, oral structures, and other facial features were symmetric and uninvolved, and facial muscle strength was normal bilaterally.

Radiographs, computed tomography, and magnetic resonance imaging revealed concave deformities of the calvarium with associated atrophy of scalp soft tissue and severe thinning of the frontal bone, without underlying brain pathology or evidence of malignancy, infection, or metabolic bone disease. A nuclear medicine scan showed no significant increase in bone turnover.

Skin biopsy findings demonstrated nonspecific features, including thinning of the dermis, subtle sclerosis of the reticular dermis, and a sparse inflammatory infiltrate; overall, these findings were considered potentially consistent with, though not significant enough to be diagnostic of, morphea. Additional inflammatory, metabolic, endocrine, and bone turnover studies were unremarkable, and infectious work-ups, including tuberculosis and coccidioidomycosis testing, were negative.

Given concern for an unusual presentation of en coup de sabre, the patient was treated with mycophenolate mofetil up to 1500 mg twice daily for 1 year. Despite therapy, there was no improvement and the depressions continued to progress in a horizontal configuration. Repeat radiographic studies showed stability of the bilateral frontal bone depressions without involvement of the brain.

A 26-year-old woman with a history of ataxia–telangiectasia, insulin-resistant diabetes mellitus, polycystic ovarian syndrome, osteopenia, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, spastic paresis, and frequent pulmonary infections underwent hepatic ultrasound for evaluation of her liver disease. The ultrasound revealed an incidental 5.5-cm hypoechoic mass with internal vascularity in the left perirenal space. Subsequent gadolinium-enhanced MRI showed a 4.9×2.9×5.1-cm enhancing retroperitoneal mass with T2 hyperintensity, heterogeneous enhancement, restricted diffusion, and apparent invasion into Gerota’s fascia, all concerning for malignancy. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis confirmed an extra-renal mass abutting the left kidney without clear parenchymal invasion or distant metastases. 

An image-guided core needle biopsy demonstrated abundant myxoid stroma with a paucicellular proliferation of spindle to stellate cells, rare larger atypical cells with hyperchromatic nuclei, and background chronic inflammation. Immunohistochemical stains for MDM2, CDK4, keratin, desmin, SOX10, CD34, and MUC4 were negative, and FISH for MDM2 amplification was negative, yielding a classification of a morphologically low-grade spindle cell neoplasm. Given the patient’s comorbidities and high surgical risk, active surveillance was elected. Three months later, repeat MRI demonstrated interval enlargement of the mass, more irregular enhancement, thickening of Gerota’s fascia, and new mass effect on the abdominal wall, prompting referral for surgical excision.

A 46-year-old woman with no significant past medical history initially saw her primary care physician multiple times over one week for sore throat. She was treated symptomatically for presumed viral pharyngitis. One week later, her condition acutely worsened with sore throat, odynophagia, chills, dyspnea, fever, and marked weakness. She presented to a smaller hospital’s emergency department in septic shock: temperature elevated, heart rate 120/min, respiratory rate >22/min, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, requiring 4 L of oxygen. Lab studies showed serum bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL, platelets 30,000/µL. Broad-spectrum piperacillin/tazobactam was started, and she was stabilized in the ICU. 

A chest radiograph demonstrated a round 3 × 3 × 2 cm density in the right upper lung field. Two weeks after symptom onset, on transfer to a tertiary care center, a chest CT showed multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules, some cavitary and some with a reversed-halo sign, predominantly subpleural, with early liquefaction of one lesion, bronchograms, probable atelectatic consolidations in the lower lobes, bilateral pleural effusions, and borderline mediastinal lymphadenopathy. The radiology report noted features “characteristic of septic emboli.”

Serologic testing revealed elevated total IgE and anti-Aspergillus IgG, with undetectable galactomannan and β-D-glucan. Blood cultures and routine microbial workup were negative. Antibiotic therapy was de-escalated to ampicillin/sulbactam under stewardship principles, and the patient showed clinical and laboratory improvement. An extensive serologic panel for autoimmune disease (including ANA, ANCA, complement levels, and specific autoantibodies) and HIV testing were negative. Quantitative immunoglobulins (including IgG subclasses) and serum protein electrophoresis were unremarkable except for elevated IgE.

A 25-year-old man with bilateral keratoconus underwent deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty (DALK) of the left eye using the “big bubble” technique. On post-operative day 1, he presented with left periocular pain, headache, and nausea. His visual acuity was hand motion in the left eye and intraocular pressure was 38 mmHg. The left pupil was mid-dilated and poorly reactive to light. Anterior segment examination revealed ciliary flush and a diffusely hazy, edematous corneal graft. The anterior chamber was deep centrally but very shallow peripherally at 360°, and the iris appeared to have a concave configuration. The fundus could not be visualized. Anterior segment OCT showed the corneal graft resting on a residual posterior stromal bed, a deep central anterior chamber with complete peripheral angle closure, and a thin membrane overlapping the pupil.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of occipital headache and severe neck, shoulder, and back pain. She also reported sleep disturbances with nonrestorative sleep, fatigue, intermittent abdominal pain with constipation, and depression related to domestic stress. She had no prior surgeries, systemic disease, or family history of neurologic or mental illness. Initial laboratory tests, including rheumatologic and metabolic panels and a complete blood count, were normal. Physical examination revealed a forward head and rounded-shoulder posture, widespread tenderness in 13 of 18 predefined tender points over the neck, upper chest, shoulder, upper back, buttock, and hip, and palpable hypertonicity of bilateral sternocleidomastoid, pectoralis, trapezius, supraspinatus, levator scapulae, rhomboid, quadratus lumborum, and gluteal muscles. Intervertebral restriction was noted at C5–C7, C7–T1, and L4–L5. Cervical rotation and extension were limited to 10° bilaterally by pain. Back pain intensity was 6 of 10 on a numeric rating scale. Manual muscle testing revealed 4/5 strength in left shoulder abduction, elbow extension, and knee extension. Standing radiographs showed diffuse degenerative spondylosis with reverse cervical lordosis, lumbar hypolordosis, and mild lumbar levoconvexity. Surface electromyography demonstrated elevated paraspinal muscle tension across cervical and all spinal segments.

A 52-year-old woman underwent routine screening mammography and was recalled for a new small, circumscribed opacity in the left breast at approximately the 9 o’clock position, 10 cm from the nipple. She was asymptomatic, with no palpable lesions and an unremarkable breast, axillary, and neck examination. Her medical history included Graves’ disease and hypertension; she was postmenopausal for 2 years, had no history of breast or ovarian cancer, and had never used exogenous hormones.

Diagnostic mammograms confirmed the new lesion; ultrasound showed a small, solid, avascular, hypoechoic nodule with tiny internal hyperechogenic foci and no suspicious features. An ultrasound-guided core biopsy yielded only three small fragmented linear tissues, demonstrating scattered stromal cells with chronic inflammatory cells; low‐molecular cytokeratin (LMCK) staining was negative, but the sample was too small for definitive diagnosis. 

Given her age and the abnormal imaging, she elected to undergo an open biopsy with hook‐wire localization. The excised lesion measured 7 mm in diameter, was well‐circumscribed and tan, and on hematoxylin–eosin staining appeared sparsely cellular with aggregates of lymphoid follicles and plasma cells. Immunohistochemical staining for IgG4 was performed. 

Laboratory tests showed normal full blood count, serum creatinine, and thyroid function. Serum immunology revealed an elevated total IgG level (70.1 g/L; reference 5.76–15.36 g/L) and a normal IgG4 level (1.31 g/L; reference 0.03–2.00 g/L).

A 2-year-old girl was brought by her mother for evaluation of painless bilateral groin swellings noted over the past 6 months. There were no symptoms of abdominal pain, distension, or vomiting. On examination, there were well-defined, pear-shaped, irreducible, fluctuant swellings in the bilateral inguino-labial regions. The overlying skin was normal, the swellings were non-tender, and there were no expansile impulses on coughing. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Complete blood count and urinalysis were within normal limits. Based on these findings, a working diagnosis of inguinal hernia versus hydrocele was made, and elective surgical exploration was planned.

A 21-year-old man presented to the emergency department a few hours after sustaining blunt neck trauma from strangulation lasting 1–2 minutes. He had no significant past medical history. He complained of dysphonia and odynophagia but denied respiratory distress.

On examination, he was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and breathing comfortably on room air with normal oxygen saturation. He had hoarseness and multiple ecchymoses on the neck, along with palpable subcutaneous emphysema in the cervical region. Palpation revealed preserved laryngeal contours and normal laryngotracheal mobility. Auscultation showed decreased breath sounds on the right side and normal sounds on the left.

Flexible nasofibroscopy demonstrated a mobile larynx without edema or vocal cord immobility. A cervicothoracic CT scan showed intact hyoid bone, thyroid and cricoid cartilages, and no cricoarytenoid dislocation. The CT also confirmed extensive subcutaneous cervical emphysema and a large pneumomediastinum. No discontinuity of the tracheobronchial or esophageal walls was identified.

A 35-year-old woman (G10P3) of African origin at 31 weeks’ gestation was referred for fever (38.7 °C), tinnitus, and emesis. Her history included chronic hypertension treated with nicardipine and labetalol, morbid obesity (BMI 41.9 kg/m2), and prior appendectomy. Initial labs showed hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, leukocytes 12 ×10^9/L, platelets 83 ×10^9/L, CRP 243 mg/L, fibrinogen >7 g/L, haptoglobin <10 mg/dL, proteinuria 3.89 g/L (P/C ratio 1.16 g/g), AST 53 IU/L, ALT 25 IU/L, bilirubin 34 µmol/L, creatinine 40 µmol/L, Na 135 mmol/L, K 3 mmol/L. Exam showed lower‐limb edema without headache or visual changes.

Peripheral smear confirmed Plasmodium falciparum (20% parasitemia); artesunate was started. Because of intense proteinuria, superimposed preeclampsia was presumed; magnesium sulfate and one unit of platelets were administered. Neurological decline (GCS 13) led to emergency Caesarean section; a 1700 g male infant was delivered.

Postoperatively, fever peaked at 38.6 °C and the abdomen became distended and painful. CT of the abdomen was read as “postoperative ileus and uterine hyperemia,” and metronidazole with meropenem was started. Over the next hours, oliguria developed and serum creatinine rose to 210 µmol/L despite saline infusion, while abdominal distension and pain persisted.

A 35-year-old man with a 5-year history of recurrent mucocutaneous blisters presented with intermittent flares characterized by blisters progressing to ulcers on the tongue, scrotum, elbow, and dorsal fingers. Previous workup, including multiple punch biopsies, showed subepidermal vesiculation, interface dermatitis, and mixed inflammatory infiltrates with negative direct immunofluorescence (DIF) studies. Serologic studies revealed mildly elevated bullous pemphigoid antibodies (BP180 and BP230). The differential diagnosis included erythema multiforme, fixed drug eruption, and atypical bullous pemphigoid. He failed to improve on dapsone and valacyclovir for presumed erythema multiforme and after two infusions of rituximab for presumed bullous pemphigoid. His disease was controlled on high-dose oral prednisone, but this was unsustainable long term. His maintenance regimen of mycophenolate mofetil, doxycycline, and niacinamide had been interrupted due to severe pain from tongue ulcers. He reported intermittent cigarette use and had smoked one pack one week before presentation. He was afebrile with stable vital signs. Examination revealed numerous ulcers on the tongue, scrotum, glans penis, elbow, and bilateral dorsal fingers without ocular or nasal mucosal involvement. Laboratory tests showed no leukocytosis. He was admitted for pain control and wound care and started on topical clobetasol, viscous oral lidocaine, valacyclovir, and intravenous methylprednisolone 48 mg daily. Blood and urine cultures, a respiratory viral panel, and HIV testing were negative. A shave biopsy of the right third finger showed interface dermatitis with prominent dyskeratosis and subepidermal vesiculation; DIF was negative. The biopsy also demonstrated a lichenoid interface dermatitis with prominent necrosis, full-thickness epidermal dyskeratosis, and an inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes, histiocytes, and neutrophils without significant eosinophils.

A 54-year-old man presented with 2 days of generalized abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting without any history of trauma. His past medical history was notable for diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and mechanical mitral valve replacement with aortic valve repair and coronary artery bypass grafting 3 years earlier. His medications included warfarin, oral cardiovascular agents, and diabetes medications. 

On examination, he was alert and oriented, with stable vital signs. He had mild abdominal distension and generalized tenderness without signs of peritonitis. An electrocardiogram showed atrial fibrillation without ST-segment changes. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed an ejection fraction of 30%, moderate diastolic dysfunction, no para-valvular leak, moderate-severe tricuspid regurgitation, and pulmonary artery pressure of 35 mm Hg. 

Laboratory studies showed a normal leukocyte count and hemoglobin level, lactate dehydrogenase of 370 IU/L, serum potassium of 6.1 mEq/L, neutrophils 90%, negative blood cultures, and an international normalized ratio (INR) of 10.99. He received fluid resuscitation, intravenous vitamin K, and two units of fresh frozen plasma. 

Bedside abdominal ultrasound demonstrated gallbladder stones and a 12 mm stone in the lower calyx of the right kidney. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed circumferential wall thickening of the descending colon with luminal stenosis and no mucosal breakdown, and minimal free fluid in the pelvis and abdomen.

A 30-year-old man with no prior medical or psychiatric history presented with sudden onset of painless bilateral loss of vision immediately after falling approximately 3 meters from a pickup truck, resulting in a concussion and a superficial scalp laceration. One hour after injury, he was alert and oriented (Glasgow Coma Scale score 15) and had visual acuity of counting fingers bilaterally. Systemic and neurologic examinations were otherwise unremarkable. The following day, visual acuity was no light perception in both eyes. Anterior and posterior segment examinations, relative afferent pupillary defect testing, fogging test, and menace reflex were all normal. Noncontrast computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed no abnormalities. Visual evoked potentials were normal, and electroretinography indicated no pathologic process. In view of these inconclusive findings, the patient was referred for psychiatric evaluation to rule out conversion disorder.

A 25-year-old primigravid Thai woman at approximately 25 weeks’ gestation, with no known underlying disease and no prenatal care, underwent a traditional Thai leg and foot massage at a commercial facility. About 5–10 minutes into the massage, she experienced sudden onset of dyspnea, altered consciousness, a brief convulsion, and collapse. Two nurses on site initiated basic life support, and emergency medical services arrived 20 minutes later to find her pulseless. She was intubated and received continuous CPR en route to the hospital, arriving approximately 25 minutes after CPR began.

On arrival, electrocardiography showed pulseless electrical activity. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL, hematocrit 36.0%, white blood cell count 12 850 cells/mm³, platelets 159 000 cells/mm³, prothrombin time 10.5 s (INR 0.95), activated partial thromboplastin time 29.7 s (ratio 0.93), fibrinogen 100 mg/dL, and lactate 3.14 mmol/L. Urinalysis was normal. Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated severe metabolic acidosis. Advanced cardiovascular life support achieved return of spontaneous circulation, but the patient remained comatose on mechanical ventilation.

Bedside ultrasound after resuscitation showed no intra-abdominal free fluid, no pericardial or pleural effusion, and no aortic dissection flap. Cardiac evaluation revealed a normal left ventricular ejection fraction with a hyperdynamic left ventricle, right ventricular dilation with poor systolic function, and interventricular septal shift to the left, consistent with acute right heart overload. Due to the temporal association with leg massage, sudden dyspnea, cardiovascular collapse, and evidence of right ventricular dysfunction, pulmonary embolism was highly suspected.

A previously healthy 7-year-old girl presented with sudden-onset swelling of the floor of her mouth and submental region that had appeared only a few hours earlier. She denied prior episodes, trauma, oral surgery, infections, or changes in size with eating. She reported discomfort on swallowing and speaking but no dyspnea. On examination, there was a large bluish, fluctuant, non-tender mass bilaterally on the floor of the mouth, elevating the tongue and partially obscuring the oropharynx. There was a right-predominant, midline-crossing, fluctuant, non-tender submental and submandibular swelling; the overlying skin was intact. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a 60×17×35 mm, well-defined cystic lesion in the right sublingual space without enhancement. The lesion extended posteriorly and laterally into the submandibular space, passed between the mylohyoid muscle laterally and the geniohyoid/genioglossus muscles medially, displaced the ipsilateral digastric muscle inferiorly, and extended into the contralateral sublingual space, with no invasion of adjacent structures.

A 39-year-old African American woman presented with a 3-year history of a tender, palpable right lower-quadrant abdominal wall mass. She described a burning pain that increased with menses. Her surgical history included an appendectomy and four Caesarean sections. Six weeks earlier, she had undergone a total laparoscopic hysterectomy with bilateral salpingectomy for presumed uterine fibroids; pathology showed multiple myometrial leiomyomas and benign fallopian tube segments. Since that surgery, she noted a sudden increase in the size of the abdominal wall lesion and acute worsening of pain. Review of systems was notable only for mild constipation. On examination, there was a 7 × 4 cm swelling in the right lower quadrant that was exquisitely tender to palpation and exacerbated by movement. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed a high-density soft-tissue opacity measuring 5.8 × 4.4 cm in the subcutaneous tissue of the right lower quadrant abutting the anterior abdominal wall, with moderate surrounding subcutaneous soft-tissue stranding.

A 66-year-old man presented with 2 weeks of right eye pain, redness, and a nasal visual field defect. His past ocular history was notable only for cataract surgery in the left eye; he denied trauma and was systemically healthy. On examination, visual acuity was 20/400 in the right eye. There was ciliary flush and iris heterochromia, with the right iris appearing green compared with the blue left iris. Posterior synechiae were present 360° in the right eye. Intraocular pressure was 6 mm Hg in the right eye and 17 mm Hg in the left eye. Gonioscopy and slit-lamp examination showed a markedly deep right anterior chamber with inferior posterior synechiae, 2+ flare, and no cells. Ultrasound biomicroscopy demonstrated posterior bowing of the iris and diffuse deepening of the anterior chamber. Fundus examination revealed a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment with choroidal detachment in the right eye; the left fundus was normal.

A 13-day-old term male neonate presented with bilateral breast enlargement noted since birth and a milky nipple discharge for the past 4 days. The mother reported progressive enlargement and had been squeezing the breasts to reduce their size. There was no history of breast redness, fever, trauma, or drug intake other than maternal iron and calcium supplements. He was born at 41 weeks’ gestation by emergency cesarean section for failed induction, with a birth weight of 2800 g and Apgar scores of 7, 8, and 9 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes. Examination findings were: temperature normal; heart rate 144 beats/min; respiratory rate 50 breaths/min; capillary refill <3 s; oxygen saturation 98% on room air; and no systemic abnormalities. Chest examination showed bilateral breast swellings that were soft, non-fluctuant, non-tender, and non-erythematous, measuring approximately 3.6×3.8 cm on the right and 3.2×3.4 cm on the left, with no nipple or skin changes and no active discharge. Laboratory tests showed a normal white blood cell count and normal C-reactive protein level; culture of nipple discharge yielded no growth. Ultrasonography revealed well-defined hypoechoic masses measuring 3.4×3.7 cm on the right and 3.0×3.3 cm on the left, without loculated fluid collections or significant vascularization. Based on these findings, breast abscess and other inflammatory conditions were ruled out.

A 77-year-old woman with a 45-year history of smoking and alcohol use presented with progressive jaundice over several days, tea-colored urine, clay-colored stools, upper abdominal discomfort, fever, chills, and fatigue. In the emergency department, her temperature was 39°C and heart rate 105/min. Physical examination revealed marked jaundice, a non-distended abdomen with mild right upper quadrant tenderness, and no hepatomegaly or palpable gallbladder. Laboratory studies showed alkaline phosphatase 458 U/L, γ-glutamyl transferase 1289 U/L, total bilirubin 169 mg/dL, AST 107 U/L, ALT 158 U/L, CRP 250 mg/L, and a white blood cell count of 16 545/mm³. Blood cultures grew Escherichia coli, and she was treated with ceftriaxone and metronidazole with improvement. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a dilated common bile duct without biliary lithiasis. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography revealed intra- and extrahepatic biliary dilation at the ampulla, gallbladder dilation, and three periampullary duodenal diverticula containing fluid and air. Subsequent gastroduodenoscopy confirmed three large diverticula in the second portion of the duodenum.

A 56-year-old man presents with intermittent right upper quadrant abdominal pain for 1 week. The pain is colicky, associated with fatty food intake, and similar episodes occurred twice in the past year, resolving with conservative management. He denies fever or jaundice. His medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with oral hypoglycemic agents, a 15 pack-year smoking history, and alcohol use. On examination, he is afebrile and his abdomen is soft, non-tender, with no masses, hernias, or signs of jaundice. Laboratory tests, including liver function tests, are within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography shows a large gallbladder without wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, or gallstones. The differential diagnosis included a double gallbladder or a gallbladder with a larger floppy fundus.

A 22‐day‐old boy, the first child of nonconsanguineous parents, was referred with a 1‐day history of respiratory distress. The pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated. He was born at term, weighing 2800 g, with a length of 54 cm and head circumference of 36 cm. On admission, he was lethargic, with a respiratory rate of 70 breaths per minute and intercostal retractions. The pulse rate was 160 beats per minute; peripheral pulses were equal, synchronous, and heart sounds normal. Chest examination revealed decreased breath sounds over the right hemithorax with impaired air entry. Abdominal and genital examinations were unremarkable, and a nasogastric tube passed easily into the stomach. A chest radiograph showed a homogeneous opacity in the right middle and lower zones with leftward deviation of the esophagus; no vertebral anomalies were seen. Contrast‐enhanced computed tomography of the chest demonstrated a well‐defined cystic mass in the posterior mediastinum measuring approximately 5.1 × 4.9 cm. Hematologic studies and serum chemistry were within normal limits.

A 90-year-old woman with hypertension presented with drowsiness, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, fever, tachycardia, and hypotension (BP 88/62 mmHg). Physical examination was notable only for drowsiness; there were no focal neurologic or meningeal signs. Laboratory studies showed thrombocytopenia (85,000/µL), leukocytosis (16,860/µL; neutrophils 15,800/µL), elevated C-reactive protein (18.1 mg/dL), blood urea nitrogen (93 mg/dL), creatinine (2.8 mg/dL), hyperlactacidemia (38 mg/dL), and metabolic acidosis (HCO3– 19.8 mmol/L). Urinalysis revealed leukocyturia (>500 leukocytes/µL). Chest radiography and ECG were unremarkable; renal ultrasound showed right pyelocaliceal dilation with perirenal fluid. A diagnosis of acute pyelonephritis with septic shock and acute kidney injury was made. Blood and urine cultures grew Escherichia coli. Broad-spectrum antibiotics, fluid resuscitation, and hemodynamic support led to rapid normalization of vital signs, inflammatory markers, and mental status.

On hospital day 5, she acutely deteriorated into coma without fever, meningeal signs, or focal deficits. Metabolic causes (hypoglycemia, dysnatremia, uremia, hyperammonemia) and pharmacologic agents were excluded. Noncontrast head CT showed a right frontal cortical and subcortical hypodense area but no hemorrhage or mass effect. EEG demonstrated slow bilateral frontal and temporal activity with periodic 1–2 Hz discharges, without evidence of status epilepticus. A neurologic consultation recommended valproic acid, which produced no clinical improvement.

A 49-year-old woman with metastatic pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma (ACC) under treatment with gemcitabine and paclitaxel was referred for evaluation of persistent, painful subcutaneous nodules on both lower legs. One week after starting her current chemotherapy regimen, she noted small red nodules on her right shin, which enlarged and became painful; similar lesions then appeared on her left shin. She denied fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, or other systemic symptoms. Initial management by her primary care provider included cephalexin for presumed bug bites, followed by trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, then inpatient clindamycin, vancomycin, and cefepime, and finally outpatient doxycycline; none led to improvement. On dermatologic examination, there were multiple tender, 2- to 3-cm subcutaneous nodules with overlying erythema, confluent on the right shin into a pink, poorly demarcated plaque. Laboratory studies revealed an elevated serum lipase level of 810 U/L (reference range, 13–51 U/L).

A 22-month-old previously healthy female (twin A) presented with seizures. Two weeks earlier she had rhinorrhea and diarrhea. On the morning of presentation, she became lethargic and then had several episodes of body stiffening and shaking. At the referring hospital she was unresponsive, required supplemental oxygen for hypoxia, and received a dextrose bolus for a blood glucose of 38 mg/dL (2.1 mmol/L). Her sodium was 133 mEq/L and potassium 3.4 mEq/L. She was transferred to a tertiary care children’s hospital, where she was febrile with a glucose of 100 mg/dL and tested positive for rhino/enterovirus.

History revealed a full-term twin gestation. One week after twin A’s discharge, twin B presented with new-onset congestion and a seizure. Her blood glucose was 113 mg/dL, sodium 127 mEq/L, and potassium 3.4 mEq/L; after hydrocortisone and fluid resuscitation and transfer, her sodium normalized to 144 mEq/L, potassium to 3.5 mEq/L, and glucose was 151 mg/dL.

On examination, twin A had diffuse hyperpigmentation of the skin and oral mucosa and normal external female genitalia. Later that day she had another seizure; her sodium was 124 mEq/L and potassium 4.1 mEq/L. A 250-µg ACTH stimulation test showed baseline and 30- and 60-minute cortisol levels all <0.5 µg/dL (reference ≥18 µg/dL), and baseline plasma ACTH was elevated at 1395 pg/mL (reference 7.2–63.3 pg/mL). Her 17-hydroxyprogesterone was <10 ng/dL (reference ≤148 ng/dL). Electroencephalogram and brain MRI were unremarkable. Renin and aldosterone were not measured before treatment.

Twin B also had diffuse hyperpigmentation and normal genitalia. Abdominal MRI showed normal-sized adrenal glands. Her plasma renin activity was low at 0.5 ng/mL/h (reference 1.7–11.2 ng/mL/h) and aldosterone was 5.4 ng/dL (reference 7–93 ng/dL).

At the top of the differential was Addison disease. Other considerations included congenital adrenal hyperplasia, infections, infiltrative disease, lipoid adrenal hyperplasia, familial glucocorticoid deficiency, and autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1.

A 24-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of persistent palpitations and dyspnea. He reported intermittent palpitations for 1 year, increasing in frequency over the past 2 months, and new exertional dyspnea. He had no prior medical history; he had used cannabis, alcohol, and cocaine but had discontinued all substances 2 months earlier. Family history was unremarkable.

On examination, he was hemodynamically stable (blood pressure 128/80 mmHg) with an irregular tachycardia and bilateral crackles. ECG showed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response and non-specific intraventricular conduction disturbance. Chest radiography confirmed pulmonary congestion. Laboratory tests, including a thyroid profile, were normal.

He received intravenous furosemide and deslanoside with clinical improvement. The next day, transthoracic echocardiography revealed:
• Severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction (ejection fraction 17%)  
• Elevated filling pressures (E/e′ ratio 15)  
• Mild mitral regurgitation and severe left atrial dilation (indexed volume 63.4 mL/m2)  
• Right ventricular dysfunction (TAPSE 10 mm)  
• Both papillary muscles originating from a flattened left ventricular apex  
• A spherical (“orange-shaped”) left ventricle with a deficient apex  
• An elongated right ventricle wrapping around the deficient LV apex (“banana-shaped”)

A 26-year-old man with a known history of congenital adrenal hyperplasia diagnosed at age 2 was referred for evaluation of asthenia, poor biochemical control, and severe drug-resistant hypertension despite triple antihypertensive therapy. He was initially misdiagnosed with 21-hydroxylase deficiency and treated with hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone until fludrocortisone was withdrawn after renin measurements. After puberty, he switched from hydrocortisone to dexamethasone 0.25 mg nightly due to reluctance to take multiple daily doses. He also has Hashimoto’s thyroiditis and drug-resistant multifocal partial epilepsy managed with carbamazepine, valproic acid, and perampanel.  
On exam, BP was 170/110 mmHg on ramipril 10 mg, lercanidipine 20 mg, and canrenone 50 mg daily. Height was 1.72 m, weight 77 kg (BMI 26 kg/m2), with normal male genitalia.  
Laboratory studies showed potassium 3.3 mmol/L, plasma renin < 2.0 mUI/L, aldosterone 11 pmol/L, ACTH 1063 ng/L, 17-hydroxyprogesterone 45.8 nmol/L, and androstenedione 111 nmol/L.  
Abdominal CT revealed bilaterally enlarged adrenal glands with nodules (15 × 18 mm on left; 13 × 18 mm on right). Testicular ultrasound showed bilateral hypoechoic pseudonodular lesions (~2 cm) consistent with testicular adrenal rest tumors.

A 10-year-old boy was referred for cardiac screening after being diagnosed with Becker muscular dystrophy. He initially presented to the neuromuscular clinic with exercise-induced muscular pain and markedly elevated serum creatine kinase levels (2495 U/L). Neuromuscular examination showed bilateral calf hypertrophy, decreased ankle joint range of motion, and very mild weakness of hip abduction and adduction (Medical Research Council grade 4), with preserved strength elsewhere. Genetic testing confirmed an in-frame deletion of exons 45–48 of the dystrophin gene.

The patient was asymptomatic from a cardiovascular standpoint, and cardiovascular examination findings were unremarkable. A 12-lead electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with normal PR interval and QRS axis, voltage criteria for biventricular hypertrophy, and pathological Q waves in the inferolateral leads. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed asymmetric septal hypertrophy, predominantly of the anteroseptal wall extending toward the apex, with a maximal mid-septal wall thickness of 18 mm. The left ventricular cavity was small and globally hyperdynamic, with normal diastolic performance, normal left atrial size, and no systolic anterior motion or resting outflow tract obstruction.

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging confirmed asymmetric hypertrophy of the basal and mid interventricular septum (maximal wall thickness, 18 mm) without outflow tract obstruction and demonstrated patchy late gadolinium enhancement within the hypertrophied myocardium.

A 25-year-old woman was admitted with a 6-month history of recurrent bilious vomiting and epigastric pain following a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. She had lost significant weight and developed weakness, fatigue, peripheral neuropathic sensations, and bilateral lower-limb edema.  
On admission:  
• Vital signs stable; physical examination unremarkable except for bilateral lower-limb edema.  
• Laboratory studies: hypokalemia, acute kidney injury, hypoalbuminemia, elevated liver enzymes, mild coagulopathy, mild microcytic anemia, and metabolic acidosis.  
• CT of the abdomen and pelvis: no intestinal obstruction or thrombosis.  
• Abdominal ultrasound: steatohepatitis.  
• Esophagogastroduodenoscopy: postanastomotic ulcer and gastritis.  
She was treated with IV proton-pump inhibitors, electrolyte repletion, and total parenteral nutrition, but developed refeeding syndrome and persistent vomiting. On hospital day 14, she received 3.75 mg of zopiclone at 11 pm for insomnia.  
At 2:00 am the next morning, nurses noted bradycardia (44–51 bpm); she was drowsy but arousable, with oxygen saturation 95% on 2 L/min nasal cannula. At 2:15 am her Glasgow Coma Scale score fell to 3, and a code blue was called.  
BLS and ACLS were performed:  
• Initial rhythm: asystole, followed by refractory ventricular fibrillation, pulseless ventricular tachycardia, and pulseless electrical activity.  
• Interventions over 73 minutes included 23 doses of IV epinephrine, IV amiodarone, lidocaine, sodium bicarbonate, magnesium sulfate, calcium gluconate, three DC shocks, and two 50 mg pushes of IV alteplase for suspected massive pulmonary embolism.  
• Bedside Doppler ultrasound and echocardiography during CPR showed no ventricular contractions or valve opening; pupils were fully dilated and nonreactive.  
At 3:28 am, resuscitative efforts were discontinued; the monitor displayed PEA, there was no pulse, and death was pronounced. Family was informed, and no monitoring was in place after pronouncement.

A 72-year-old Asian man presented with mild right wrist pain, moderate low back pain, and right lower-leg numbness of 12 months’ duration. The back pain began as a constant ache 2 years ago and progressed over the past year to episodic right leg numbness. Over the last 2 months, symptoms suddenly worsened, and he required a cane to walk more than 15 minutes; he also awakened frequently at night due to pain. He had a history of percutaneous coronary angioplasty and gout 10 years earlier, with no recent trauma. His back pain was rated 9/10. He was initially treated for presumed sciatica with NSAIDs and celecoxib, with only temporary relief, and then sought chiropractic care.

On examination, tophus formations were noted in both hands. Lumbar scoliosis and paraspinal muscle spasm were present. Pain was provoked by trunk extension, right bending, and right ankle inversion and eversion. Sensation to light touch was diminished in the right ankle and foot. Intervertebral restriction was identified at L4–L5 and the right sacroiliac joint. Lumbar range of motion was limited by muscle spasm. The straight-leg-raise test was positive at 30° on the right side.

Weight-bearing lumbar radiographs showed moderate spondylosis at L2–L5, moderate lumbar scoliosis, and a significantly calcified aorta from the L2–L5 region. Increased soft-tissue opacity over the volar aspect of the right wrist was consistent with gouty tophi. With a differential diagnosis of gout, abdominal aortic aneurysm, and lumbar disc herniation, the patient was referred for a lumbar MRI and an abdominal CT aortogram.

A 52-year-old man presented with 2 months of severe sudden-onset back pain radiating to the right lower extremity. He worked as a farmer and raised cows. His medical history included partial gastrectomy for gastric adenocarcinoma 3 years earlier and recently diagnosed type 2 diabetes managed with oral medication. He denied hypertension, tuberculosis, hepatitis, recent travel, or consumption of raw meat; family history was noncontributory.

On examination, manual muscle testing and deep tendon reflexes were normal in all extremities. Sensory testing revealed hypesthesia in the right L5 dermatome. Lumbar flexion, extension, lateral flexion, and rotation were limited by pain. Tenderness was noted over the L4 and L5 spinous processes, and his pain score was 9/10 on the visual analogue scale.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 56 mm/hr and a C-reactive protein level of 1.2 mg/dL; other biochemical tests were normal, and blood cultures were negative. Needle electromyography, nerve conduction studies, and sensory evoked potentials were normal.

Plain radiographs of the lumbosacral spine demonstrated erosive changes of the anterior portions of L4 and L5. A whole-body bone scan revealed increased isotope uptake in L5. Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbosacral spine showed low T1 and heterogeneous high T2 signals in the L4, L5, and S1 vertebral bodies, endplate injury in the anterior L4 and L5 vertebral bodies, contrast enhancement of adjacent soft tissues, and L3–4 and L4–5 disc herniations.

A 32-year-old woman presented with 12 hours of nausea, vomiting, dizziness, and epigastric pain. Earlier that day, after an argument, she took eight Tylenol tablets (total 2.6 g of acetaminophen). She denied alcohol use, gallbladder stones, other drug ingestion, trauma, autoimmune disease, and diabetes. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. The upper abdomen was soft with mild tenderness; there was no jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, or Murphy’s sign. Initial laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, white cells 5.5 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 65%, platelets 169 × 10^9/L; AST 13 U/L (7–40), ALT 13 U/L (13–35), albumin 3.3 g/dL; serum amylase 990 U/L (0–96), lipase 49.5 U/L (13–60), triglycerides 0.6 mmol/L (0.34–1.70). Two days later, aminotransferases remained normal, amylase 433 U/L, lipase 136.6 U/L, triglycerides 0.6 mmol/L, creatinine 53 μmol/L (45–84). Viral hepatitis markers (A, B, C, D, E), antinuclear antibody, p-ANCA, c-ANCA, and IgG4 were all within normal limits or negative. Abdominal ultrasonography was unremarkable. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography showed a bulky pancreas without peripancreatic exudation. The patient received standard pancreatitis care and N-acetylcysteine.

A 32‐year‐old woman from Pokhara, Nepal, first presented in December with high‐grade fevers, chills, rigors, headache, generalized body aches, and joint pains. Laboratory tests showed a white‐cell count of 9800/mm3 (77% neutrophils, 20% lymphocytes), a platelet count of 250 000/mm3, and normal liver and renal function studies; urinalysis was unremarkable. A Widal test was positive, and she received injectable ceftriaxone without clinical improvement. Tests for malaria were negative. A positive Brucella antibody test prompted doxycycline–rifampicin therapy, after which her fever resolved but she continued to experience severe fatigue, joint pains, neck stiffness, tingling sensations, and headache. Six months after her initial presentation, she sought further evaluation in India, where she was suspected of having a tick‐borne illness. She underwent ELISA, Western blot, and PCR testing for Borrelia burgdorferi, Bartonella species, Ehrlichia species, and Babesia species and was treated empirically with a 3-week course of doxycycline.

A 50-year-old man was referred for evaluation of an abnormal chest radiograph obtained during a medical check-up. He was asymptomatic, and similar radiographic findings had been noted two years earlier. He had a 20-pack-year smoking history. At age 30, he experienced chronic nephritis requiring three years of hemodialysis, followed by a living-donor kidney transplantation at age 33, with stable renal function thereafter. Current medications were prednisolone (5 mg daily), cyclosporine (25 μg daily), mizoribine (1 mg daily), losartan (25 mg daily), allopurinol (50 mg daily), and nifedipine (10 mg daily). He had no known parathyroid dysfunction and took no calcium supplements. On examination, vital signs were normal, and oxygen saturation was 98% on room air. Respiratory sounds were normal without crackles or wheezes. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count; serum calcium 9.9 mg/dL; liver enzymes and autoantibodies within normal limits; C-reactive protein 0.3 mg/dL; and serum creatinine 1.37 mg/dL. Pulmonary function tests were normal. High-resolution computed tomography of the chest demonstrated diffuse, irregular nodules in both lungs. A diagnostic transbronchial lung biopsy was performed.

A 15-year-old boy with no significant medical history presented to the emergency department with sudden onset of generalized muscle weakness. The weakness began one and a half hours after his first intense one-and-a-half-hour gym session and involved both proximal and distal muscles of his upper and lower limbs without pain. He denied respiratory difficulty, dysphagia, sensory symptoms, chest pain, palpitations, diarrhea, or recent weight change.

On examination, he appeared well, with stable vital signs. Neurologic examination revealed flaccid paralysis of all extremities (muscle strength 1/5) and diminished deep-tendon reflexes (2/4) with intact sensation. Cranial nerves were normal. Cardiac, respiratory, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed:  
• Serum potassium, 2.2 mEq/L (reference 3.5–5.5 mEq/L)  
• Serum sodium, 145 mEq/L; chloride, 113 mmol/L; bicarbonate, 18.5 mEq/L  
• Serum calcium, 7.6 mg/dL; magnesium, 2.1 mEq/L  
• Normal complete blood count, renal function, liver enzymes, creatine phosphokinase, and thyroid-function tests  
Urinalysis revealed no myoglobin, white cells, or red-cell casts. ECG demonstrated flattened T waves and small U waves.

A 78-year-old woman with osseous and pulmonary metastatic endometrial carcinoma receiving pembrolizumab (200 mg every 3 weeks; three cycles completed, last dose 12 days before admission) presented with 10 days of bilateral but left-predominant ptosis, new dysphagia, dysarthria, and head drop due to inability to sustain neck extension. She denied fever, chest pain, dyspnea, syncope, or dizziness. Her medical history was notable for cataract surgery months earlier and a transient ischemic stroke one year before. Home medications included aspirin 100 mg and atorvastatin 20 mg.

On admission, ECG showed alternating third-degree atrioventricular block and Mobitz II second-degree block with ventricular rates of 35–55 bpm. Laboratory tests revealed TSH 12.40 μIU/mL with normal T3 and T4, creatine kinase 910 U/L, CK-MB 81.5 ng/mL, and troponin T 1.24 ng/mL. Inflammatory markers were normal; creatinine was 0.96 mg/dL (eGFR 55.9 mL/min). A panel of autoantibodies (anti-AChR, anti-SOX1, anti-LRP4, anti-VGCC) was negative.

Transthoracic echocardiography performed one day after pacemaker implantation showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 41% with apical akinesia and apical-septal, apical-inferior, and anterior hypokinesia; mild mitral regurgitation and moderate tricuspid regurgitation were also noted.

A 41-year-old obese man with chronic alcoholic hepatopathy and uncontrolled diabetes mellitus was admitted in a comatose state with diabetic ketoacidosis. He had a 7-day history of fever and progressive difficulty walking without pain or trauma. Chest CT showed left basal-lobe pneumonia with pleural effusion; empirical levofloxacin and ceftriaxone were started. Head CT was normal. Over the next 24 hours, he developed acute paraplegia and mild bilateral arm weakness. Neurologic examination revealed weakness and hypoesthesia of the upper limbs and flaccid paralysis with anesthesia of the lower extremities.

Spine CT demonstrated emphysematous lesions in the spinal canal and intraosseous gas collections involving L4, L5 (including the interposed disc), and the first sacral vertebra, with no evidence of vertebral fractures. MRI of the spine confirmed high T2 and low T1 signal in the adjacent vertebral bodies at L4–L5 and the disc, suggestive of bone marrow edema, and foci of low signal in all sequences corresponding to intraosseous gas. There was no epidural or soft-tissue abscess.

Laboratory studies showed anemia, thrombocytopenia, neutrophilia, hypoalbuminemia, elevated C-reactive protein, hyperglycemia, and increased glycated hemoglobin.

A 64-year-old Asian man presented with gradual left scrotal swelling for 2 years. His medical history was notable for hypertension treated with felodipine and perindopril, type 2 diabetes treated with glimepiride, and chronic hepatitis B on nucleos(t)ide analogs. He denied any history of renal trauma, biopsy, or surgery. He did not smoke or drink alcohol.

On admission, blood pressure was 141/92 mm Hg, heart rate 85 beats/min, temperature 37.1 °C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Physical examination showed a grade 3 left varicocele; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed normal blood counts and chemistries; urinalysis showed 2+ glucose with normal white and red blood cell counts. Scrotal ultrasound confirmed a grade 3 left varicocele. Renal ultrasound demonstrated a 3.7 × 4.2 cm low-echogenic mass with abundant blood flow in the upper pole of the left kidney.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 3.6 × 4.3 cm irregular lesion in the upper pole of the left kidney, with dilated tortuous vessels and an early-enhanced, dilated left renal vein showing ostial stenosis, as well as an unusually dilated lumbar vein. CT also showed left-sided varicocele. T2-weighted MRI of the left kidney demonstrated large, early flow voids within the mass, suggesting a vascular lesion.

A 57-year-old woman with cT3N1 invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast and no distant metastatic disease completed neoadjuvant chemotherapy and subsequently underwent right skin-sparing mastectomy, sentinel lymph node biopsy, level I and II axillary lymph node dissection, and immediate tissue expander reconstruction. Intraoperatively, one of three sentinel nodes was positive on frozen section; multiple bulky but soft nodes were removed. No lymphatic leakage was observed intraoperatively. Three closed suction drains were placed: one in the axilla and two in the breast pocket. 

On postoperative day 1, all three drains had serosanguinous output at 12 hours. At approximately 18 hours, the axillary drain collected 100 mL of cloudy, milky fluid. A sample was sent for triglyceride measurement.

A 63-year-old Caucasian woman presented with severe dyspnea of 1 month’ duration, which had been progressively worsening over 2 years. She had a 102–pack-year smoking history and was treated irregularly for hypertension. During the prior 2 years she made five ED visits for dyspnea, each attributed to decompensated COPD from respiratory infection.  
Eighteen months earlier, chest CT demonstrated marked pulmonary hypertension—enlarged pulmonary trunk and branches, right-heart chamber dilation, moderate pericardial effusion. Pulmonary windows showed ground-glass opacities in the lung bases with subpleural sparing, thin reticulation, and traction bronchiectasis but no honeycomb cysts, consistent with non-specific interstitial pneumonia; paraseptal emphysema was noted in the upper lobes. Mild splenomegaly was also seen.  
Transthoracic echocardiography revealed normal left ventricular systolic function and an estimated pulmonary artery pressure of 100 mmHg, confirmed by right-heart catheterization. Stool examinations (three samples) and rectal biopsy were negative for Schistosoma mansoni eggs. Pulmonary angiography showed no thromboembolism, and laboratory evaluation for connective-tissue disease was negative. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed severe hypoxemia without hypercapnia.  
Over the next 18 months, she developed recurrent respiratory‐failure exacerbations with progressive hypercapnia and bicarbonate retention, signs of right-sided heart failure, and anasarca, becoming bedbound. At her sixth ED presentation, she was drowsy, disoriented, cyanotic, and icteric without fever. Blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg, pulse 84/min, SpO₂ 79% on 3 L/min O₂, and glucose 88 mg/dL. Physical examination showed symmetric lower‐limb edema (left leg skin hyperemia), jugular venous distension, a systolic murmur at the tricuspid area, crackles at the left lung base, and large ascites.  
Laboratory tests revealed normal hemoglobin, mild leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, prolonged prothrombin time, mild renal dysfunction, hyponatremia, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, and elevated C-reactive protein; blood and urine cultures were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed average liver size, dilation of the portal vein (16 mm), inferior vena cava, and suprahepatic veins, slight splenomegaly, and large ascites. Echocardiography demonstrated severe right‐chamber dilation with preserved right ventricular function, reduced left‐ventricular volume, a dilated tricuspid annulus with severe regurgitation, an estimated systolic pulmonary artery pressure of 76 mmHg plus central venous pressure, an inferior vena cava diameter of 26 mm with < 50% respiratory variation, and a nonrestrictive pericardial effusion. Electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm, diffuse low-voltage complexes, and an anteriorly deviated QRS axis.

A 65-year-old man presented with a 10-year history of a rash on the buttocks and lower extremities, with less involvement of the upper extremities. He described cyclical eruptions with blistering and subsequent flaking that “moved around” in an advancing pattern, accompanied by itching and occasional pain. His medications included metoprolol, lisinopril, pravastatin, metformin, fluoxetine, and alprazolam. He smoked half a pack of cigarettes daily and consumed three alcoholic drinks daily. On examination, the lower legs showed large, confluent, annular, pink-red erythematous patches and thin plaques with fine scale at the advancing edges; red-brown patches represented previous sites of involvement. Two punch biopsies stained with hematoxylin and eosin revealed serum crust, hyperkeratosis, irregular epidermal hyperplasia, mild spongiosis, and a superficial tight perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate. Direct immunofluorescence was negative.

A 62-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with chest pain, nausea, and vomiting. Her medical history was notable for Nail–Patella syndrome diagnosed at age 12 and end-stage renal disease managed with peritoneal dialysis for the past year. Home medications included carvedilol, simvastatin, calcitriol, and sodium bicarbonate. She had a remote history of cigarette smoking and no known allergies. On examination she was diaphoretic with stable vital signs. 
An electrocardiogram showed an inferior ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction with posterior extension. Initial troponin I was 2679.9 ng/L and brain natriuretic peptide was 7595 pg/dL. A STEMI alert was activated, and she was taken emergently to the catheterization laboratory. 
Coronary angiography revealed a 100% occlusion of the proximal right coronary artery, an anomalous left circumflex artery arising from the right coronary ostium, and diffuse aneurysmal dilatations of the right coronary artery, the mid–left anterior descending artery, the proximal circumflex branch arising from the right coronary artery, and the right obtuse marginal branch of the anomalous circumflex artery.

A man in his 70s was admitted after routine laboratory tests showed a serum creatinine level of 4.0 mg/dL, elevated from a baseline of 1.3–1.5 mg/dL one year earlier. His history included 4 years of microscopic hematuria and a 3-year history of stage 3 chronic kidney disease with trace proteinuria. Prior urologic evaluation with multiple cystoscopies was unremarkable. One year earlier, a nephrologist deferred kidney biopsy for minimal proteinuria.  

On admission, he was asymptomatic, took only occasional ibuprofen, and had trace bilateral lower-extremity edema. Urinalysis revealed microscopic hematuria, a urinary protein–creatinine ratio of 7.07 g/g creatinine, and dysmorphic red blood cells on phase-contrast microscopy. Laboratory studies showed a serum potassium level of 5.2 mEq/L and hemoglobin of 10.8 g/dL.  

Given concern for rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, he received a 3-day course of pulse-dose steroids, and an urgent kidney biopsy was planned. A full serologic and urine workup was obtained:  
• ANA titer, speckled 1:80  
• Complement C3 100 mg/dL (75–170), C4 27 mg/dL (10–40)  
• Cytoplasmic ANCA <1:40; perinuclear ANCA <1:40  
• Anti–GBM IgG <1.0 (reference <1.0)  
• Rheumatoid factor <10 IU/mL; hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, syphilis, and cryoglobulin negative  
• Serum protein electrophoresis: no restricted bands in the γ region; immunofixation: possible monoclonal free λ light chain  
• Random urinary protein electrophoresis: total protein 353 mg/dL, albumin 223.5 mg/dL; immunofixation: monoclonal free λ light chain  
• Serum free light chains: κ 3.47 mg/dL (0.33–1.94), λ 17.1 mg/dL (0.57–2.63), κ:λ ratio 0.20 (0.26–1.65)

A 27-year-old Hispanic man with no past medical history presented with a 5-day history of painful lateral cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, chills, night sweats, and rhinorrhea. He denied cough, weight loss, sick contacts, recent travel, or occupational exposures. He was afebrile on admission and in no acute distress. Skin examination showed a macular, erythematous, desquamative rash on bilateral shoulders and anterior chest. Oropharyngeal examination was unremarkable. He had bilateral cervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy, left more than right; the largest node in the left posterior cervical chain was approximately 2 cm, rubbery, tender, non-erythematous, and nonadherent. There were also mildly enlarged left axillary and bilateral inguinal lymph nodes. No hepatosplenomegaly was noted. 

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 4 500/µL (46% neutrophils, 28% lymphocytes, 14% mononuclear cells) and mildly elevated lactate dehydrogenase. Rapid streptococcal test was negative. Chest radiograph was normal. HIV, Monospot, rapid plasma reagin, anti-nuclear antibody, and rheumatoid factor tests were all negative. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis confirmed lymphadenopathy only in the cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions previously identified on physical examination.

A 58-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of progressive proximal muscle weakness, difficulty swallowing, and a right periorbital erythematous eruption. She denied fever or dyspnea. On examination, there was a well-demarcated, erythematous, edematous plaque with slight scaling on the right upper eyelid. She also had erythematous, scaly papules over the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints bilaterally and three firm, subcutaneous nodules on the left hip and right thigh. Muscle strength was 2/5 in the proximal upper and lower extremities. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, normal renal and thyroid function, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 42 mm/hour, a C-reactive protein level of 0.5 mg/dl, creatine kinase 2821 U/L (normal <180 U/L), aldolase 17 IU/L (normal <7 IU/L), aspartate aminotransferase 453 IU/L (normal <34 IU/L), and alanine aminotransferase 129 IU/L (normal <49 IU/L). Antinuclear antibody was borderline positive at 1:80 with a speckled pattern; extractable nuclear antigen testing was negative. A myomarker panel was positive for anti-NXP2 antibody and negative for anti-MDA5 antibody. Computed tomography of the orbits demonstrated asymmetric contrast enhancement and soft tissue swelling of the preseptal right orbit, with normal globes, extraocular muscles, and retro-ocular fat. A four-millimeter punch biopsy of the right upper eyelid revealed vacuolar interface dermatitis with a thickened basement membrane, epidermal atrophy, and parakeratosis.

A 53-year-old man with untreated gallbladder stones presented with progressively worsening right-sided hemiparesis and difficulty speaking. He had no fever, chest pain, or dyspnea. On examination, his temperature was normal, pulse 82/min, blood pressure 130/80 mmHg. He had mild jaundice, a grade 3 systolic murmur best heard at the cardiac apex, and hepatomegaly. Neurologic evaluation showed motor dysphasia and right hemiparesis (muscle strength 3/5). Brain MRI revealed a left periventricular infarction with hemorrhagic transformation in the left temporal lobe. Routine transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a 10.7 × 13.8 mm homogenous, slightly hypoechoic mass attached to the edge of the right coronary and noncoronary cusps of the aortic valve, with mild aortic regurgitation; an 11 × 4.4 mm mass on the atrial side of the posterior mitral leaflet with mild mitral regurgitation; and a 43 × 11 mm right ventricular mobile lesion of similar echogenicity. Transesophageal and 3D echocardiography confirmed additional masses on the left coronary cusp and better characterized their motion. Cardiac MSCT showed homogenous, non–contrast-enhancing lesions on all three aortic valve leaflets with minimal motion. Free-breathing cardiac MRI demonstrated the right ventricular lesion as a band-shaped hypointense signal without gadolinium enhancement. Three sets of blood cultures and PCR for typical bacterial and fungal pathogens were negative. Protein C, protein S, and antithrombin III levels were normal; D-dimer was elevated at >7.65 mg/L; PT was 21.8 s and APTT 42.5 s. Anti–double-stranded DNA and ANA antibodies were negative.

A 17-year-old previously healthy Caucasian female presented with 20 days of left pleuritic chest pain. She reported fever to 38 °C at symptom onset but denied weight loss, night sweats, cough, or other systemic symptoms. She was treated sequentially with clarithromycin plus levofloxacin and then amoxicillin–clavulanate; fever resolved but pain persisted. 

On admission, she appeared well and was afebrile. Vital signs were normal. Examination revealed decreased breath sounds at the left base and percussion dullness in Traube’s space; there was no lymphadenopathy, edema, or palpable organomegaly. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits; HIV and hepatitis B and C serologies were negative. 

Chest radiography showed a well-circumscribed homogeneous round opacity with a broad pleural base in the left lower lobe. Thoracic CT confirmed a heterogeneous-attenuation nodular lesion in the left lower lobe and also demonstrated splenomegaly. Bronchoscopy was unremarkable, and bronchoalveolar lavage did not demonstrate acid-fast bacilli, fungi, or bacteria.
