A 41-year-old man who has worked as a gas-station attendant for 14 years presented with a 1-year history of dry cough and nonspecific pain in the lower third of the left hemithorax, progressively worsening. He denied fevers or weight loss. He reported frequently siphoning gasoline while filling motorcycles. He was hospitalized for 15 days and treated for community-acquired pneumonia without improvement, then received empirical antitubercular therapy without response. He was referred for persistent symptoms and new dyspnea on exertion. He had no history of smoking or prior lung disease. On examination, he was afebrile with crackles at both lung bases and digital clubbing. Hemogram and blood chemistries were normal, and a purified protein derivative test was negative. Chest radiography showed consolidations in the lung bases. High-resolution computed tomography of the chest revealed extensive nonhomogeneous consolidations in the posterior segments of both lower lobes, ground-glass opacities, and areas of fibrosis with bronchiectasis. Spirometry demonstrated a moderate restrictive ventilatory defect, and a 6-minute walk distance was 420 m (range, 455–608 m). Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid showed pleocytosis with 57% lymphocytes, negative microbiologic and cytopathologic studies, and weakly positive oil red O staining.

A 22-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of intermittent colicky right hypochondrial pain refractory to proton pump inhibitors. She had no other symptoms and an unremarkable medical and family history. Physical examination and routine laboratory studies were normal.

Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a globular swelling in the medial wall of the second part of the duodenum, with the ampulla at the summit of the lesion.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen with oral contrast demonstrated dilation of the intramural portion of the common bile duct and a 2.4 × 2.3 cm cystic lesion in the second part of the duodenum. MRI confirmed a 2.4 × 2.3 cm cyst in the ampullary region and dilation of the distal intramural common bile duct.

Endoscopic therapy was attempted but the ampullary orifice could not be cannulated. Abdominal ultrasound then showed a thick-walled 4.6 × 2.6 cm cystic structure between the second part of the duodenum and the head of the pancreas, with a gut signature in the wall, active peristalsis around the lesion, and the common bile duct opening just distal to the cyst.

A male newborn was referred at 1 day of age for cyanosis; oxygen saturation (SaO2) was 80% in room air. Laboratory findings showed a hematocrit of 47.8% and a platelet count of 103 000/mm3; other values were normal and there were no signs of infection. Echocardiography revealed pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect and a patent ductus arteriosus. A prostaglandin infusion was started, raising SaO2 to 90–95%. On day 11, he underwent a systemic‐to‐pulmonary shunt operation with graft placement and PDA division. Preoperative values on day 10 were hematocrit 38.9%, platelet count 173 000/mm3, and SaO2 95% on prostaglandin. Postoperatively, hematocrit was 52.1% and platelet count was 58 000/mm3; platelet count then increased without transfusion. By postoperative day 6, he was extubated with SaO2 80–85%, hematocrit 41.1%, and platelet count 123 000/mm3. He was discharged on postoperative day 13 with SaO2 85–87%, hematocrit 33.4%, and platelet count 225 000/mm3.

At 10 months of age, he was admitted for a Rastelli operation. His SaO2 was 80%; hematocrit was 49.1% and platelet count was 68 000/mm3. He had no bleeding history or medications. Prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, and INR were normal; peripheral smear was unremarkable. Antiplatelet antibodies and platelet‐associated immunoglobulins were negative; antinuclear and anti–double‐stranded DNA antibodies were normal. Platelet aggregation time was 127 s (reference, 61–110 s). Viral and bacterial studies were insignificant. The pediatrician made a provisional diagnosis of immune thrombocytopenia and administered intravenous immunoglobulins (2 g/kg) the day before surgery. On the day of operation, hematocrit was 42.6% and platelet count was 77 000/mm3.

A 23-month-old girl presented with a 12-month history of moderate, nonbloody diarrhea (6–7 episodes per day) and progressive peripheral and facial edema beginning at 11 months of age. She had no fever, vomiting, abdominal pain, or rash. She was born at 40 weeks’ gestation by uncomplicated vaginal delivery (birth weight 1800 g), with no family history of genetic disorders. Immunizations were up to date.

On examination, weight was 10 kg (−1.5 SD), length 83 cm, blood pressure 90/55 mm Hg, pulse 120/min, temperature 37 °C. There was bilateral, pitting, non-tender edema of the lower limbs and eyelids. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL, WBC 7900/mm3 (54% neutrophils, 30% lymphocytes), platelets 452 000/mm3, and normal C-reactive protein. Serum cholesterol was 100 mg/dL, triglycerides 70 mg/dL; total protein 4.5 g/dL, albumin 2.4 g/dL. Liver and renal function tests and electrolytes were normal. Thyroid-stimulating hormone and free thyroxine were normal. Peripheral blood smear was normal. Urinalysis and culture were negative. A 24-hour urine protein was normal. Stool examination showed WBCs ++, RBCs +, starch granules +, fat granules +, fungi +, and occult blood +. Serum protein electrophoresis demonstrated decreases in all protein fractions.

Abdominal ultrasonography and echocardiography were normal. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a normal esophagus and gastric mucosa and moderate chronic duodenitis.

An 11-year-old boy, weighing 30 kg and 132 cm (both below the 3rd centile), presented with progressive generalized body swelling, pallor, and rapid breathing over 5 days. Fifteen days earlier, he had fever and diarrhea treated briefly with metronidazole. He had a similar, self-limited episode of diarrhea and mild edema at age 3. On examination, he had generalized pitting edema, grade 1 clubbing, hepatomegaly (liver span 14 cm), splenomegaly (3 cm below the costal margin), and ascites; there was no jaundice or chronic diarrhea.

Initial laboratory tests showed pancytopenia (hemoglobin, 5.2 g/dL; total leukocyte count, 2.8 × 10^3/μL; absolute neutrophil count, 1200/μL; platelet count, 86 × 10^3/μL) with eosinophilia (13%) and a reticulocyte count of 0.2%. Serum albumin was 1.2 g/dL, and vitamin B12 was 153 pg/mL. Cultures for infections and tests for malaria and dengue were negative. Urine analysis revealed proteinuria (+3) and positive nitrites; stool microscopy showed Entamoeba histolytica. Tests for hemolytic uremic syndrome and autoimmune disorders—including direct Coombs test, antinuclear antibody, and anti–double-stranded DNA—were negative except for hypocomplementemia (C3 level, 0.6 g/L). After treatment of a urinary tract infection, proteinuria decreased to trace amounts. Pediatric nephrology consultation excluded renal pathology without a renal biopsy. Initial malabsorption studies (stool globules and calprotectin) were normal except for reducing sugars, which normalized after treatment. Alpha-1 antitrypsin levels were normal. Serologic screening for celiac disease (IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase) was negative, but HLA-DQ2 typing was positive. Consent for gastrointestinal biopsy was declined.

A 56-year-old man with no prior liver disease presented with 6 weeks of progressive jaundice, followed by 4 weeks of abdominal distension and lower-limb swelling. He reported fatigue and mild generalized pruritus. On examination, he was deeply icteric, had bilateral pitting edema, a left-sided pleural effusion, a short apical systolic murmur, and a flapping tremor; his abdomen revealed massive hepatosplenomegaly and moderate ascites. Laboratory testing showed:  
• Total bilirubin 22 mg/dL; albumin 24 g/L; INR 3.2  
• Alkaline phosphatase 1,496 IU/L; γ-glutamyltransferase 136 IU/L; ALT 128 IU/L; AST 170 IU/L  
• Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL; blood urea nitrogen 45 mg/dL  
• Normal immunoglobulins; normal serum protein electrophoresis and β2 microglobulin; negative Bence-Jones proteinuria  
• Alpha-fetoprotein normal; C-reactive protein elevated  
• Hepatitis serologies unremarkable; autoimmune markers (ANA, anti–smooth muscle, anti–DNA) negative  
• 24-hour urinary protein 0.068 g/L  
Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatosplenomegaly without focal lesions and normal bile ducts. CT of the abdomen confirmed an enlarged, lobulated liver with mild portal vein dilation and thin collaterals, consistent with portal hypertension and no lymphadenopathy. Echocardiography was unremarkable except for diastolic dysfunction.  
Ascitic fluid analysis: 500 cells (90% lymphocytes), SAAG 2.1, low protein (2.4 g/L), low adenosine deaminase; PCR for tuberculosis negative; no malignant cells. These findings were consistent with portal hypertension.

A 78-year-old Caucasian woman with bilateral geographic atrophy threatening the fovea presented for evaluation. Ocular history was notable for cataract surgery OS two years earlier. Medical history included Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, vertigo, and a COVID-19 infection three months prior; she was taking levothyroxine. She had no history of anti-VEGF treatments or recent ocular infections (CMV, herpes simplex, toxoplasmosis) and no autoimmune disease or malignancy.

In March 2023, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/80 OU. Autofluorescence imaging showed progressive geographic atrophy over six years, and treatment with intravitreal pegcetacoplan was initiated in the left eye. On the day of injection, visual acuity decreased to 20/200 OS. Eleven days later, she presented to the emergency department with left eyelid edema, ocular discomfort, conjunctival injection, headache, and vision loss; topical moxifloxacin was prescribed.

Thirteen days after injection, ophthalmologic examination revealed visual acuity 20/400 OS, 1+ conjunctival injection, 1+ lid edema, minimal anterior chamber reaction, and intraocular pressure 33 mm Hg OS. Funduscopic examination showed diffuse intraretinal hemorrhages with vascular cuffing and macular edema. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated macular staining of the geographic atrophy with cystoid changes, blockage from hemorrhages, optic nerve and retinal vascular leakage, and peripheral nonperfusion without delayed filling time. Topical prednisolone acetate 1% drops were added, along with glaucoma medications.

Fourteen days after injection, visual acuity remained 20/400 OS, and intraocular pressure was 6 mm Hg OS. Examination revealed increased macular thickening and edema compared to the prior visit, confirmed on optical coherence tomography.

A 67-year-old Middle Eastern man presented with progressive bilateral lower extremity muscle weakness and myalgia. Fifteen days earlier, he had fever, rhinorrhea, and mild shortness of breath, tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 by nasal PCR, and recovered as an outpatient over 15 days. One week after resolution of respiratory symptoms, he developed myalgia and proximal weakness in both lower extremities, which progressed to involve his upper extremities, prompting hospital admission.

On examination, proximal muscle strength was graded 3/5 in the hips and thighs and 4/5 in the shoulders and arms. Muscle tone and deep-tendon reflexes were normal. There were no skin rashes, no muscle tenderness, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Initial laboratory studies showed:  
• CPK 12,000 U/L (normal 38–174)  
• LDH 757 U/L (normal 130–240)  
• Aldolase 11 U/L (normal ≤8.5)  
• White blood cell count 8.8×10^3/µL  
• ESR 9 mm/h (normal <20)  
• CRP <2 mg/L (normal ≤6)  
• Normal renal function, electrolytes, liver enzymes, and 25-hydroxy vitamin D

Bilateral thigh MRI (T1, T2, STIR) demonstrated diffuse edema within all muscle compartments with intra- and perimuscular fluid, suggestive of myositis. Electromyography and nerve conduction studies showed findings consistent with an irritable proximal myopathy in the rectus femoris, iliopsoas, and deltoid muscles.

A 4-year-old girl was admitted with fever and acute respiratory failure. She had no known SARS-CoV-2 infection. Chest imaging revealed bilateral ground-glass opacities, patchy consolidations in the lower lobes, pneumomediastinum, and bilateral cervical subcutaneous emphysema. Bronchoalveolar lavage grew Pneumocystis jiroveci and was galactomannan positive; SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative. She was intubated and ventilated.

Her history included recurrent respiratory infections since age 3, an ocular HSV infection, and oral thrush. Immunologic evaluation showed severe CD4 lymphopenia (6 cells/µL), and HIV infection was confirmed with a viral load of 83 429 copies/mL (CDC stage 3). She started ART (lamivudine, zidovudine, lopinavir/ritonavir) with trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, caspofungin, and liposomal amphotericin B. Testing also revealed CMV (31 446 copies/mL), EBV (8542 copies/mL), and oral HSV lesions; acyclovir and ganciclovir were added.

On day 51 of ART, she developed persistent fever despite broad-spectrum antibiotics and negative cultures. Labs showed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL; neutrophils 690/µL; platelets 14 000/µL), elevated C-reactive protein (4.28 mg/dL), hyponatremia (129 mEq/L), hypoalbuminemia (3.1 g/dL), hypofibrinogenemia (76 mg/dL), mild hypertriglyceridemia (160 mg/dL), ferritin > 12 000 ng/mL, high-sensitivity troponin 40.9 pg/mL, and proBNP 1548 pg/mL. HIV viral load was undetectable and CD4 count had risen to 35/µL. Immunophenotyping showed CD4+ T cells without HLA-DR or CD38 expression, whereas CD8+ T cells expressed both activation markers.

A 4-year-old girl with no prior medical history presented with 1 day of right hip pain and inability to bear weight. She denied trauma. Five weeks earlier, she had fever, upper respiratory symptoms, and a positive SARS-CoV-2 PCR; those symptoms had resolved weeks before hip pain onset. On arrival she was afebrile. Examination showed the right hip held in flexion, external rotation, and abduction, with pain on passive motion. Laboratory studies revealed a peripheral WBC count of 12.08 × 10^9/L with 72% neutrophils, a C-reactive protein level of 6.5 mg/dL, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 14 mm/h. Radiographs of the right hip and femur showed no osseous abnormalities. Ultrasound demonstrated a 6 mm right hip effusion. Because she met three modified Kocher criteria (inability to bear weight, WBC > 12 × 10^9/L, CRP > 1 mg/dL), ultrasound-guided hip aspiration was performed, yielding 4 mL of straw-colored fluid. Synovial analysis showed 8,375 WBCs (86% segmented neutrophils) and 18,500 red blood cells; gram stain was negative, and aerobic, anaerobic, and fungal cultures showed no growth. She was admitted for observation and treated with NSAIDs alone. By hospital day 1 she was walking without pain. Given exclusion of septic arthritis, fracture, and slipped-capital-femoral epiphysis, no antibiotics were given and she was discharged with NSAIDs and close follow-up. Two-week follow-up showed complete resolution of symptoms.

An 18-year-old man presented with acute onset of painless obstructive jaundice, nausea, fatigue, loss of appetite, and icterus without fever or prior similar episodes. Laboratory evaluation showed white blood cells 5270/mm3, hemoglobin 14.5 g/dL, platelets 295 000/mm3, AST 214 IU/L, ALT 314 IU/L, ALP 2367 IU/L, total bilirubin 8.1 mg/dL with direct bilirubin 6.0 mg/dL. Serum CEA, CA 19-9, IgG4 (40 mg/dL; normal 4–108 mg/dL), and IgG were within normal limits; urine bilirubin was 3+. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated abnormal thickening of the gallbladder wall appearing to invade the adjacent liver, and a 30 mm infiltrative low-density mass involving the gallbladder neck, upper biliary tract, and hilar bile duct with intrahepatic bile duct dilatation. The pancreas was not enlarged. MRI/MRCP confirmed an infiltrative mass of high signal on diffusion-weighted imaging with a sharp-beaked stenosis of the hilar bile duct and upstream biliary dilatation; the main pancreatic duct was normal. ERCP showed a hilar bile duct stricture and intrahepatic duct dilation, and a plastic stent was placed. Endoscopic ultrasound revealed a heterogeneous hypoechoic lesion (9.3 × 7.3 mm) in the gallbladder region with vascularity and apparent direct hepatic invasion. Exfoliative bile duct cytology revealed inflammatory cells without atypia. As a malignancy could not be ruled out, surgical resection was proposed, and extended cholecystectomy with intrahepatic cholangiojejunostomy including resection of the common bile duct was performed due to extensive inflammation.

A 62-year-old woman presented with gradual onset of severe left-sided headache and constant pulsatile tinnitus. Vital signs were stable. Neurologic examination was unremarkable. 

Noncontrast head CT showed a hyperattenuating pituitary gland with a convex superior margin. Subsequent pituitary-protocol MRI demonstrated an enlarged anterior pituitary that approached but did not compress the optic chiasm; there was regional heterogeneous enhancement without a discrete hypoenhancing lesion, and the infundibulum appeared normal. The patient was referred for endocrinologic evaluation; hormone laboratory studies were unrevealing.

One month later, she developed right-sided ptosis, diplopia, and acute right-sided headache. A repeat noncontrast head CT and CT angiogram revealed further enlargement of the pituitary gland, enlargement of the left superior and inferior ophthalmic veins, and bulging with early enhancement of the cavernous sinuses. The CT angiogram of the neck showed a beaded appearance of both cervical internal carotid arteries. MRI of the brain confirmed progressive enlargement of the anterior pituitary gland now contacting the undersurface of the optic chiasm, with a changed pattern of enhancement but still no discrete lesion.

A 46-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of progressive dyspnea accompanied by night sweats, fever, and weight loss. He was an electrician with no history of dust inhalation, drug use, or exposure to pet birds. He had smoked 20 cigarettes daily from age 20 until 3 months earlier, when he switched to an e-cig pen, which he used until the day before presentation.  
On examination, he appeared pale; temperature was 37.1°C. Chest auscultation revealed mild fine crackles bilaterally; heart sounds were normal.  
Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 15,200/mm3 (77.5% neutrophils, 11.5% lymphocytes, 4.0% eosinophils) and a C-reactive protein level of 11.81 mg/dL. Krebs von den Lungen-6 was elevated at 1841 U/mL. Arterial blood gas on room air revealed pH 7.504, PaCO2 29.0 Torr, PaO2 52.6 Torr, and HCO3– 22.7 mmol/L.  
Pulmonary function testing demonstrated a restrictive pattern with a vital capacity of 50.6% of predicted.  
Chest radiography showed extensive ground-glass opacities in the bilateral upper lung fields, predominantly in the lateral segments. Chest CT revealed ground-glass opacities with traction bronchiectasis throughout both upper lobes and nonsegmental ground-glass opacities with curvilinear shadows in the middle lobe, lingula, and lower lobes.

A 24-year-old man, a fitness instructor and football player, presented with a 3-day history of pain in his groin and buttocks that began after strenuous exercise and jogging the previous day. Two weeks earlier, he had undergone extraction of a wisdom tooth. He initially attributed his discomfort to a muscle strain.

On arrival he appeared anxious, was febrile (38.6 °C), with blood pressure 127/77 mm Hg and pulse 73 beats/min. He was unable to stand without assistance. Examination of the lower limbs revealed painful restriction of hip flexion and extension with full strength, and no erythema or tenderness over the hip joints. Neurologic, cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, spinal, and genital examinations were otherwise unremarkable, although there was mild lower abdominal tenderness without guarding or rebound.

Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 15.2 g/dL, white-cell count 8.7×10^9/L (neutrophils 6.8×10^9/L), platelets 412×10^9/L, and a C-reactive protein level of 142 mg/L. Renal function and electrolytes were normal. An urgent CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed no psoas or pelvic abscess. Serum creatine kinase was 40 U/L, and other muscle enzymes were within normal limits.

On the second hospital day, he developed swinging fevers up to 39 °C with rigors, and his pain worsened, limiting even turning in bed. Repeat examination disclosed marked tenderness over the pubic symphysis, especially on the left. Blood cultures were obtained and yielded heavy growth of Streptococcus viridans.

A 2-year-old girl was brought for evaluation of three painless vesicles on her lower lip, first noted 3 weeks earlier. The lesions had varied in size over time. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable, and there was no history of trauma. On examination, she was afebrile, and her food intake was normal. Inspection of the lower lip revealed three well‐circumscribed, round, bluish nodules, each approximately 5 mm in diameter; they were fluctuant and covered by normal-appearing mucosa. There was no pain, congestion, or overlying skin change. The facial appearance was symmetric without rashes, and no submandibular or cervical lymphadenopathy was present.

A 57-year-old woman with a 3-year history of refractory, biopsy-confirmed mucocutaneous pemphigus vulgaris presented with 2 weeks of a severe burning sensation on dry patches of her skin. The burning gradually progressed and was primarily localized to hyperpigmented, scaly patches scattered on her trunk and extremities at sites of prior pemphigus flares. She denied pruritus, oral lesions, genital or eye involvement, fever, night sweats, weight loss, and any topical medication use. 

Her pemphigus had been refractory to prednisolone and azathioprine; 6 months earlier, azathioprine was replaced with mycophenolate mofetil plus prednisolone. Three months ago, she developed a flare and was treated with rituximab (500 mg weekly for 4 weeks) and daily prednisolone 20 mg, leading to complete resolution of pemphigus in 2 weeks. Her current medications also include vitamin D, calcium, and alendronate.

On examination, there was diffuse, fine white scale over the trunk and extremities, most prominent on multiple dusky erythematous plaques with coarse scale (postinflammatory hyperpigmentation sites) and scattered scaly, velvety plaques in the axillae and on the thighs. There were no mucosal lesions, vesicles, or erosions.

A punch biopsy of a new hyperkeratotic, velvety plaque on the left lateral chest was performed. Histologic examination showed hyperkeratosis and parakeratosis of the epidermis with mild spongiosis, and a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with eosinophilia in the superficial dermis.

A 7-year-old girl initially presented with bright-red rectal bleeding for 26 days. Colonoscopy showed erythematous rectal mucosa with a few erosions; biopsies revealed nodular lymphoid hyperplasia and apoptotic colonopathy. She was treated with stool softeners and a topical agent.

Ten days later, she was involved in a car accident. An abdominal CT scan performed for trauma evaluation demonstrated a massive amount of fluid in the abdominal cavity; she was discharged after 3 days.

Fourteen days after discharge, she returned with progressively increasing abdominal distention. Vital signs were: blood pressure 100/75 mmHg, heart rate 110/min, respiratory rate 22/min. Weight 18 kg, height 111 cm (BMI 14.6 kg/m2). Abdominal examination revealed moderate distension; the remainder of the examination was normal.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 13.7 g/dL, white blood cell count 5000/mm3 (55.1% neutrophils, 37.4% lymphocytes). Biochemical tests: triglycerides 59 mg/dL, cholesterol 125 mg/dL, albumin 4.6 g/L, amylase 110 U/L, lipase 25 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase 479 U/L. Renal function and urinalysis were normal.

Abdominal ultrasound confirmed moderate free fluid. Under ultrasound guidance, paracentesis yielded turbid, milky fluid. Fluid analysis showed total cell count 16,750/mm3 (WBC 925/mm3 with 85% neutrophils, 15% lymphocytes; RBC 15,825/mm3), glucose 174 mg/dL, LDH 318 IU/L, albumin 4.4 g/L, triglycerides 3600 mg/dL, cholesterol 95 mg/dL, amylase 78 U/L, and adenosine deaminase negative. A follow-up abdominopelvic CT scan again demonstrated extensive free fluid.

A 34-year-old Ukrainian man (156 cm, 46 kg) with HLA-B27–positive seronegative polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) since age 4 presented with progressive right hip pain. His comorbidities included multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, marasmus, normocytic normochromic anemia, and chronic renal insufficiency. His JIA was managed with etanercept, prednisolone, sulfasalazine, and switched to tofacitinib 2 years earlier; baseline CRP was 60 mg/L. 

He was scheduled for elective total hip arthroplasty for femoral head necrosis (ARCO 4), deformity, and arthritic changes. Before the operation, he fell on his right hip; imaging showed a Garden-4 medial femoral neck fracture, and he underwent closed reduction with three cannulated screws. 

One week later, he developed severe wrist and ankle pain, diffuse myalgias, arthralgias, and a CRP of 200 mg/L; a perioperative pause of tofacitinib was felt to have precipitated a JIA flare, and he improved with a corticosteroid boost (100 mg/day). Two months later, he returned after a stumble and was treated conservatively. 

Four months after the initial fixation, he presented with atraumatic, immobilizing right hip pain; radiographs demonstrated a periosteosynthetic femoral shaft fracture. He underwent hardware removal, subtrochanteric osteotomy, cerclage, spongiosaplasty, and cementless total hip arthroplasty. Intraoperative cultures of explanted screws grew Staphylococcus aureus, and he received meropenem, rifampicin, and Spaphylex. 

In the following days, his hip pain worsened and inflammatory markers rose, prompting open joint lavage, debridement with vancomycin insertion. Intraoperative specimens were negative. Subsequent CRP rose to 454 mg/L and procalcitonin to 1.94 μg/L.

A 24-year-old G2P1011 woman was referred for management of a painful, progressive swelling on the right side of her vulva. Three days earlier, five hours after consensual coitus, she noted gradual onset of a tender mass. She denied sexual assault, instrumentation, or bleeding diathesis. She had one prior term vaginal delivery without perineal tears. On arrival, her blood pressure was 126/78 mmHg, heart rate 90 bpm, respiratory rate 18 bpm, and temperature 36.5 °C. She had mild pallor; the abdomen was soft without tenderness or rebound. Perineal examination revealed a 7 × 6 cm tense, tender, necrotic swelling of the right labia majora; a vaginal exam was not possible. A transabdominal pelvic ultrasound showed pelvic organs in normal position and a hematoma without uterine prolapse. A complete blood count revealed a normocytic, normochromic anemia with a hemoglobin level of 9 g/dL and normal platelets.

A 55-year-old man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes, and a 34-pack-year smoking history (quit 1 year ago), underwent repair of a right inguinal hernia without complications. One month later, he developed swelling of the right lower extremity, lower abdomen, and scrotum. Abdominal CT, contrast-enhanced CT to detect venous thrombus, blood tests, and urologic evaluation were unrevealing. Lymphoscintigraphy demonstrated lymphatic leakage from the scrotum to the right lateral thigh and impaired lymphatic drainage of both lower extremities. He was diagnosed with postoperative lymphedema.

One month later, he presented with mild dyspnea on exertion. Chest radiography showed mild bilateral middle and lower lung-field infiltrates. High-resolution CT revealed thickening of the broncho-vascular bundles, a tree-in-bud pattern, and interlobular septal thickening. Interstitial pneumonia, including hypersensitivity pneumonia and sarcoidosis, was suspected; however, blood tests were unremarkable and bronchoalveolar lavage with transbronchial lung biopsy yielded normal results.

Six days after bronchoscopy, he was admitted emergently after transient loss of consciousness accompanied by palpitations and chest tightness during urination. He required 1 L/min of nasal oxygen. Transthoracic echocardiography showed right ventricular pressure overload. Contrast-enhanced CT again showed no pulmonary embolism. Electrocardiography demonstrated an S₁Q₃T₃ pattern and T-wave inversions in V₁–V₄, consistent with pulmonary hypertension. He was treated as group 3 pulmonary hypertension secondary to lung disease. A gallium scan was normal. High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (1000 mg/day for 3 days) followed by oral prednisolone (60 mg/day) produced no clinical or radiographic improvement.

On hospital day 8, his respiratory status acutely worsened after urination. Repeat CT remained non-diagnostic, but echocardiography showed worsened pulmonary hypertension (tricuspid regurgitant pressure gradient 56 mmHg, tricuspid regurgitant velocity 3.6 m/sec, and a D-shaped left ventricle). Anticoagulation was deferred in the absence of visible thrombosis. Intravenous furosemide was initiated. The next morning, he awoke with severe dyspnea, progressed to cardiopulmonary arrest, and died despite resuscitation.

A 5-month-old girl was admitted with a 4-week history of fever unresponsive to antibiotics, weight loss, and pallor. She was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and had normal growth until symptom onset. On transfer after 4 weeks of fever, laboratory studies showed anemia (hemoglobin 8 g/dL), neutropenia (white-cell count 1650/µL), thrombocytopenia (platelets 100 000/µL), elevated ferritin (13 362 ng/mL), hypertriglyceridemia (674 mg/dL), hypofibrinogenemia (fibrinogen 100 mg/dL), and an increased soluble interleukin-2 receptor (>7500 U/mL). Microscopic examination of a bone marrow aspirate demonstrated hemophagocytosis features without visible amastigotes. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed marked splenomegaly with diffuse multifocal hypoechoic nodules, most smaller than 1 cm.

A 13-year-old boy with global developmental delay and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome presented with a 3-week history of progressive lower-limb bruising, pain, swelling, poor feeding, irritability, and recent loss of ambulation. Three weeks earlier, an intraoral mass on the right mandible had been noted. He had a similar presentation a year before, with bilateral lower-limb purpura, arthritis, severe anemia (hemoglobin 5.9 g/dL), normal platelet count, elevated C-reactive protein (80 mg/L), and elevated serum IgA; at that time he was diagnosed with IgA vasculitis. A second episode occurred one year later with purpura, arthritis, moderate anemia, raised acute-phase reactants, and proteinuria; he was again treated presumptively for IgA vasculitis. His medical history included epilepsy managed with phenobarbitone, valproic acid, risperidone, and lamotrigine. He was nonverbal, required full assistance for feeding, and ate mainly porridge, noodles, cabbage, and bananas. On admission, he was underweight (below the 5th percentile), irritable, and lying flexed. Blood pressure was 103/70 mmHg and heart rate 110 bpm. Examination revealed a fungating right mandibular intraoral mass without active bleeding, petechiae and ecchymoses on the extremities, pitting edema of the lower limbs, and painful, limited motion of ankles, knees, and the right wrist. Laboratory studies showed severe anemia (hemoglobin 4.0 g/dL), leukopenia (1.8 ×10^9/L), elevated CRP (89 mg/L), elevated ESR (42 mm/hr), and a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio that had normalized. Autoantibodies (ANA, PR3-ANCA, MPO-ANCA) were negative; complement levels were normal. A noncontrast CT scan of the mandible demonstrated an inflammatory mass or abscess without bony destruction. During surgical consultation, gingival friability with hypertrophy, bleeding, deep periodontal pockets, and loose maxillary and mandibular teeth were noted. All deciduous teeth were extracted, gingival tissue was debrided, and biopsies were obtained from the intraoral lesion and from skin on the upper and lower limbs.

A 55-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus (HBA1C 11.2%), hypertension, peripheral arterial disease, and a history of right above-ankle amputation presented with a 2-day history of two episodes of hematemesis (each 300–400 mL) accompanied by postprandial abdominal pain, melena, polyuria, polyphagia, and fatigue. He denied odynophagia, hematochezia, syncope, palpitations, NSAID use, alcohol use, or chronic liver disease. He had not been taking his insulin regularly.  
On arrival he was tachycardic (110 bpm) with blood pressure 141/77 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 bpm, temperature 36.6 °C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. The abdominal, chest, and cardiac examinations were unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 15.4 g/dL, hematocrit 46%, white blood cell count 6.43 × 10^9/L, platelets 304 × 10^9/L, INR 1.6, serum glucose 316 mg/dL, blood urea 41 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 3.9 mmol/L, serum amylase 19 U/L, arterial blood pH 7.34, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, and anion gap 12 mmol/L. Viral serologies (HBsAg, anti-HCV, HIV I & II) were negative.  
Abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable. He was resuscitated with IV fluids and insulin, after which a gastroenterology consultation was obtained for endoscopic evaluation of his hematemesis and melena.  
Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed diffuse, circumferential patchy necrotizing esophagitis with black discoloration and ulcerations affecting the middle and distal thirds of the esophagus beginning 25 cm from the incisors; the severity increased distally and abruptly ended at the gastroesophageal junction. Biopsies were not taken due to the risk of perforation.

A 31‐year‐old woman was referred for evaluation of persistent epigastric pain. She had been diagnosed at age 6 with Bloom syndrome based on short stature, café‐au‐lait spots, and hypogammaglobulinemia. At age 23 she underwent ileal resection and chemotherapy for primary peripheral T‐cell lymphoma, stage I, with no recurrence. 

At age 29 she developed epigastric pain; upper endoscopy showed Stage A1 duodenal ulcers and superficial gastritis without malignancy. Oral proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy relieved her symptoms, but months later the pain recurred. Repeat endoscopy revealed multiple ulcers in the stomach and duodenum. Lower endoscopy showed no mucosal abnormalities. Trials of PPI and potassium‐competitive acid blocker failed to improve her pain.

Laboratory tests showed a serum gastrin level of 1341 pg/mL (reference, 42–200 pg/mL). FDG‐PET demonstrated intense uptake throughout the gastroduodenal wall, whereas somatostatin receptor scintigraphy showed no uptake. Multiple gastroduodenal biopsies were negative for malignancy, including gastrinoma. A calcium infusion test did not increase serum gastrin by >20%. Serologic tests for Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and herpes simplex virus were negative, and histopathologic stains were negative for Helicobacter pylori. Despite ongoing medical therapy, her epigastric pain persisted and her weight progressively declined.

A 49-year-old man presented with a 7-day history of bilateral eye pain and redness that worsened with eye movement and touch. One month earlier, he had been diagnosed with chikungunya and was under rheumatology care. He had no other comorbidities or a family history of eye disease.

On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy revealed bulbar conjunctival hyperemia graded 3+/4+ with 360° ciliary injection and no other anterior segment abnormalities. Intraocular pressures were 13 mmHg and 14 mmHg. A 1% phenylephrine test produced no blanching of the vessels after 10 minutes, suggesting scleritis rather than episcleritis.

One week later, the patient returned with worsening eye pain. Hyperemia increased to 4+/4+, and examination showed medial scleral elevation, more pronounced in the right eye. Intraocular pressures were 16 mmHg and 15 mmHg. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated an edematous space between layers of the sclera in both eyes.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 15.1 g/dL, leukocytes 10,120/mm³, platelets 318,000/mm³, C-reactive protein 10.63 mg/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 25 mm/h, AST 35 U/L, ALT 105 U/L, urea 35 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.8 mg/dL. Serologic tests were negative for HIV-1/2, HTLV-1/2, hepatitis B and C, and toxoplasmosis; VDRL and FTA-ABS were negative. A PPD test measured 5 mm (BCG vaccinated), and RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 was negative. Dengue serology showed IgG positive, IgM negative; chikungunya serology showed both IgG and IgM positive. Rheumatologic screening (rheumatoid factor, ANA, anti-CCP, anti-DNA, anti-Sm, anti-Ro, anti-La, ANCA, HLA-B27) and complement components C3 and C4 were within normal limits.

A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes was referred after an incidental abdominal CT revealed a cystic lesion. He was asymptomatic. Examination revealed severe obesity (BMI 40) but no abdominal tenderness or palpable mass. Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin A1c of 7% and a serum CA 19-9 level that had normalized to 16.9 U/mL. Ultrasound demonstrated a unilocular, hypoechoic cystic mass without septations or calcifications in the lower right retroperitoneum, adjacent to the ileum and appendix, containing debris-like hyperechoic material and no internal blood flow. Enhanced CT confirmed an 8 cm unilocular cystic mass ventral to the appendix and medial to the right gonadal vessel. Review of nonenhanced CT scans over the preceding 3.5 years showed gradual enlargement from 5 cm to 10 cm, with internal density decreasing from 101 HU to 20 HU. Based on these findings and its location, retroperitoneal lymphangioma, dermoid cyst, and mucinous cystadenoma of the appendix were considered.

A 2.5-month-old male infant was brought with a 1-week history of severe pallor, hematemesis, and melena. The vomiting of blood occurred up to four times daily, always after breastfeeding; weight gain remained normal. There was progressive pallor, and laboratory testing before transfusion revealed a hemoglobin level of 3 g/dL, prompting blood transfusion. The infant weighed 5.5 kg, measured 58 cm in length, and had a head circumference of 38 cm. His mother had recovered from COVID-19 one month earlier and, during breastfeeding, had taken aspirin and unspecified NSAIDs for approximately one month without medical supervision. On examination, the infant was pale, with a pulse of 140 bpm and capillary refill of less than 3 seconds; other findings were normal. Post-transfusion laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 6.3 g/dL, a white-cell count of 11,600/µL with 76% neutrophils, platelets of 437,000/µL, an INR of 1.0, and normal liver, kidney, and electrolyte tests. Stool testing demonstrated white and red blood cells, and stool culture was negative. An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a bleeding gastric ulcer on the greater curvature.

A 7-year-old boy presented with a 2-month history of pain and swelling over the right scapula. He had no history of trauma, fever, weight loss, or known contact with tuberculosis. On examination, there was a mildly tender swelling in the right suprascapular area; shoulder joint movements were full and painless. A radiograph of the right shoulder and a chest radiograph showed clear lung fields, a normal humerus, and multiple osteolytic lesions of the right scapula. Laboratory studies revealed a hemoglobin concentration of 11.3 g/dL, a white blood cell count of 9700/mm3 (41% neutrophils, 57% lymphocytes, 6% monocytes, and 6% eosinophils), platelets of 2.97 × 105/mm3, a negative Mantoux test, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 21 mm at 1 hour. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right shoulder demonstrated extensive hyperintense erosions of the scapula with necrotic ipsilateral axillary lymph nodes.

An 80-year-old man with hypertension, dyslipidemia, and poorly controlled diabetes mellitus presented with a 1-hour history of right-sided, nonradiating, 10/10 chest pain accompanied by nausea and two episodes of maroon-colored emesis. He denied toxic ingestions or prior similar episodes. On arrival, he was afebrile; blood pressure 109/45 mm Hg; heart rate 75 beats/min; respiratory rate 18 breaths/min; SpO₂ 98% on room air. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed sodium 125 mEq/L, potassium 5.1 mEq/L, chloride 91 mEq/L, bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 145.7 mg/dL, creatinine 2.95 mg/dL, blood glucose 492 mg/dL, WBC 13.5 × 10³/mm³, hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, platelets 242 000/mm³, BNP 154 pg/mL, and troponin 0.062 ng/mL. ECG revealed normal sinus rhythm at 94 beats/min without ST-segment or T-wave abnormalities. The patient received morphine and nitroglycerin without relief. Given persistent chest pain and risk factors for ischemic heart disease, he was started on heparin and antiplatelet therapy. Cardiac catheterization showed no critical stenosis and an ejection fraction of 55%. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast was unremarkable, and gastroenterology was consulted for ongoing nausea, vomiting, and hematemesis.

A 58-year-old homeless man with hypertension, type II diabetes, and a history of prior venous thromboembolism presented with 1 week of progressive weakness and fatigue. His only medications were atenolol, lisinopril, and metformin; he was not on anticoagulants. He denied hemoptysis, dyspnea, chest pain, headache, nausea, or vomiting. In the emergency department, his heart rate was 113 bpm and the remainder of his physical examination was unremarkable. He had an infrarenal inferior vena cava (IVC) filter placed 15 years earlier and was unaware of the indication. While in the ED, he suddenly became unresponsive; ACLS was initiated for 11 minutes, after which he was intubated and transferred to the ICU. Serial hemoglobin measurements revealed a drop from 12.3 gm/dL to 6.8 gm/dL. Given concern for acute blood loss, a noncontrast CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was obtained, showing a large left-sided retroperitoneal hematoma contiguous with the aorta and IVC, mass effect on the bladder, and an expansile appearance of the IVC below the filter. A subsequent CT angiogram with arterial and venous phases excluded an arterial source of bleeding and demonstrated nonocclusive thrombi in the IVC and bilateral common iliac veins extending slightly above the IVC filter. CT angiography of the chest revealed multiple subsegmental pulmonary emboli in the right lower lobe.

A 39-year-old man with severe atopic dermatitis since childhood had been treated with dupilumab (600 mg loading dose, then 300 mg every 2 weeks) with significant improvement of his chronic eczema. After 11 weeks of therapy, he reported worsening redness, scaling, itch, and pain of the face that did not respond to topical corticosteroids. Physical examination showed erythematous, scaly plaques exclusively affecting the head and neck. Clinically, head-neck dermatitis was suspected, and because of the painful appearance, atypical rosacea was also considered. 

A skin biopsy from the affected facial skin showed marked parakeratosis with numerous neutrophilic granulocytes, acanthosis, and spongiosis. In the upper dermis, there was a dense infiltrate of lymphocytes, neutrophils, and eosinophils. The histopathologic findings did not correspond with rosacea.

A 55-year-old woman presented with two weeks of progressively worsening dyspnea and one episode of hemoptysis on the day of admission. Her past medical history was notable for severe chronic sinusitis treated with multiple antibiotic courses over the previous four months; she had no history of smoking, alcohol use, or illicit drug use.

On examination, she was tachycardic (120/min) and tachypneic (26/min), with an oxygen saturation of 92% on room air and a blood pressure of 130/75 mmHg. Chest auscultation revealed bilateral inspiratory and expiratory crackles; there was moderate to severe pitting edema of the lower extremities. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Initial laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 16 × 10^3/μL, hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, platelet count 318 × 10^3/μL, creatinine 5.2 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 68 mg/dL, and potassium 7.0 mmol/L. Chest radiography demonstrated diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities. Noncontrast chest CT confirmed diffuse airspace disease across the upper and lower lung fields, sparing the lung periphery.

The combination of acute respiratory failure, diffuse pulmonary infiltrates, and renal failure suggested a pulmonary-renal syndrome.

An 80-year-old woman with a history of colon and ovarian cancer presented with painless obstructive jaundice. Serum CA19-9 was elevated. Endoscopic evaluation suggested a periampullary mass, but biopsy showed no malignancy. She underwent transhepatic biliary drainage and placement of a common bile duct stent. One month later, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed multiple small hypodense lesions in the liver, the largest measuring 2 cm, concerning for metastases. Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood count, normal hepatic transaminases, and an elevated alkaline phosphatase level.

A 66‐year‐old man with a 10‐year history of diabetes mellitus and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease presented with persistent fever and worsening dyspnea. He tested positive for SARS‐CoV‐2, developed ARDS, and required endotracheal intubation on day 3 of admission and tracheotomy on day 15. After gradual weaning from mechanical ventilation, he was transferred to the rehabilitation unit with the tracheotomy tube in place and a fenestrated inner cannula with a decannulation plug. 

Initial nursing and speech‐language pathology (SLP) screenings for dysphagia were negative, and the patient was placed on a pureed diet. However, during supervised meals, nursing staff and the SLP observed traces of food in the tracheal tube without reflex coughing and a drop in oxygen saturation from 99% to 94% during dinner. The patient’s voice quality became wet after plug placement. Oral feeding was halted, and parenteral nutrition was initiated. 

On June 1, gastroscopy revealed no notable alterations. On June 3, fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES) demonstrated complete paresis of the right hemilarynx and partial paresis of the left hemilarynx without mucosal lesions; vallecular and retrocricoid salivary stagnation; reduced laryngeal sensibility; and a late, weak cough reflex. 

On June 5, a head and neck CT scan showed structural inhomogeneity just above the cricoarytenoid joints with sclerosis of the upper cricoid and both arytenoids. The radiologist interpreted these changes as more consistent with a chronic inflammatory process than with neoplasia.

A 61-year-old man with a recent right femur fracture was referred for evaluation of painless discharge from the right preauricular region for 3 days. He reported a fall 5 days earlier but did not recall any facial injury. His major concern remained his fractured leg. On examination, there was a 5 mm opening anterior to the right tragus with pustular discharge and surrounding crust. Minimal swelling was present; the skin was not warm. The area was mildly tender and firm, and pressure over the parotid region expressed pus from the opening. The ipsilateral Stensen’s duct orifice appeared normal without discharge. There were no palpable cervical lymph nodes. Facial nerve motor function was intact. Ear, nose, and intraoral examinations were unremarkable, and there was no trismus. Contrast-enhanced CT of the right parotid region revealed a 5.2 cm linear hypodense structure traversing the anterior part of the superficial lobe and reaching the masseter muscle, with minimal adjacent collection.

A 51-year-old African-American man presented with a six-day history of fever, chills, myalgia, progressive shortness of breath, and one day of dark brown urine. He had no significant past medical or family history and took only over-the-counter vitamin supplements.  
On arrival: temperature 99°F, blood pressure 135/75 mm Hg, heart rate 82 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 85% on room air, which normalized with 100% FiO₂ via a non-rebreather mask. Physical examination was unremarkable.  
Initial laboratory studies showed:  
• WBC 14.3 × 10³/µl (83% neutrophils, 7% lymphocytes)  
• Hemoglobin 11.2 g/dl; hematocrit 36.4%; MCV 89.4 fl; platelets 200 × 10³/µl; nucleated RBCs 1.7%  
• Total bilirubin 3.8 mg/dl (direct 0.3 mg/dl), haptoglobin < 8 mg/dl  
• AST 92 U/L; lipase 1066 U/L; CK 480 U/L  
• PT 10.2 s; INR 0.96; LDH 997 U/L  
• Ferritin 3527 ng/ml; D-dimer 3.94 mg/L FEU  
• SARS-CoV-2 PCR positive; influenza A/B PCR and urinary antigens for Legionella and Streptococcus pneumoniae negative  
Urinalysis revealed 2+ protein, 3+ blood, positive leukocytes, 9 WBC/HPF, and 100 RBC/HPF.  
Chest imaging showed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on X-ray; CT angiogram of the chest revealed no pulmonary embolism.  
On hospital day 2, his hemoglobin fell to 7.2 g/dl with a reticulocyte percentage of 6.57% (absolute count 0.1774 × 10⁶ cells/µl), while LDH rose to 1652 U/L, AST to 111 U/L, and lipase to 1593 U/L.

A 78-year-old Caucasian man with coronary artery disease (post–multivessel CABG), paroxysmal atrial fibrillation on apixaban, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (∼37%), chronic kidney disease stage III, and remote abdominal aortic aneurysm repair was admitted for gallstone pancreatitis and possible cholangitis.  
On hospital day 2, he had 50 mL of coffee-ground emesis and a transient hypotensive episode (70/50 mm Hg) responsive to 1 L IV fluids; he was treated empirically for aspiration pneumosepsis.  
MRI showed a filling defect in the common bile duct without dilation. ERCP revealed a duodenal diverticulum and erosive duodenitis, and a CBD stent was placed.  
On hospital day 4, repeat ERCP showed no CBD filling defect and persistent duodenitis.  
On hospital day 7, he complained of acute chest pain and had 200 mL of bright red emesis. Apixaban had been restarted the night before; INR was 2.5. He remained hemodynamically stable. Hemoglobin was 9.1 g/dL, hematocrit 27.4%, and WBC rose from 11 000 to 18 000/mm3.  
Esophagogastroduodenoscopy demonstrated circumferential black discoloration of the esophageal mucosa from proximal to distal, old blood in the gastric cavity, no active bleeding, linear ulcers, and a sharp demarcation at the gastroesophageal junction; there was no history of toxin ingestion.

A 4-year-old Afghan refugee girl was admitted with 3 days of intermittent periumbilical and hypogastric abdominal pain occurring every 60 minutes and lasting 20 minutes, accompanied by two episodes of bilious vomiting (last night and 1 hour before admission) and one episode of currant-jelly stool without hematochezia. Self-treatment with anticholinergics and antiemetics provided temporary relief. She had no prior medical or surgical history. 

On examination, she appeared ill, with abdominal distention and a palpable, tender mass in the periumbilical area. 

Laboratory tests showed a leukocyte count of 15,600 cells/µL (neutrophils 12,948 cells/µL) and a C-reactive protein level of 4.4 mg/dL. Urinalysis revealed 4+ ketones, 4–6 WBCs/hpf, 0–1 epithelial cells/hpf, and a few bacteria. 

Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated an ileoileal invagination with a “doughnut” sign, obstructive features, free abdominopelvic fluid, and absent vascular flow in the invaginated loop on Doppler imaging.

A 20-year-old woman was brought by her parents for evaluation of progressive forward placement of her lower jaw relative to her upper jaw. The patient’s mother first noted an enlarged head circumference at 9 months of age, with gradual worsening thereafter. The patient had no relevant medical history and no family history of congenital anomalies.

On examination, she was of short stature. Her facial features included a wide nasal bridge, hypertelorism, and bilateral exophthalmos. Intraoral examination showed a high-arched palate, hypoplastic maxilla resulting in mandibular prognathism, and a class III malocclusion. Ophthalmologic evaluation revealed papilledema, suggestive of increased intracranial pressure.

Radiographic studies were performed. A lateral skull radiograph demonstrated retrusion of the maxilla, prominent mandibular prognathism, and a copper-beaten appearance of the cranial vault. An anteroposterior cervical spine radiograph showed decreased intervertebral space between C5 and C6 vertebrae. Radiographs of the metacarpals and phalanges were unremarkable. A paranasal sinus view showed obliterated cranial sutures, small paranasal sinuses, and prominent inner-table markings. Three-dimensional computed tomography of the skull revealed increased skull circumference, and axial CT images showed moderate hydrocephalus with diffuse indentation of the inner table of the skull.

An 18-year-old woman with a history of allergic rhinitis and bronchial asthma since early childhood was referred for evaluation of an abnormal chest radiograph. She denied orthopnea, palpitations, chest pain, or weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable.  

A chest radiograph showed reduction of right lung volume with ipsilateral mediastinal shift and elevation of the right hemidiaphragm. Contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography demonstrated bilobed lungs on both sides with two hyparterial bronchi and an elevated right hemidiaphragm; the right main pulmonary artery was smaller in caliber than the left. Three-dimensional reconstruction disclosed the right hyparterial bronchus and absence of the right upper lobe bronchus and pulmonary artery.  

An abdominal ultrasonogram showed no significant anomaly in the liver, spleen, kidneys, or other abdominal organs. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed only a bicuspid aortic valve. Pulmonary function tests were within normal limits.

A 74-year-old Caucasian woman with no significant past medical history presented with left shoulder pain that began shortly after receiving an influenza vaccine 14 days before evaluation. She described subdeltoid pain and difficulty lifting her arm above her head and behind her back. She denied any other trauma or antecedent shoulder pain or surgeries. Symptoms persisted for 2 weeks despite NSAIDs.

On examination, she appeared well and in no acute distress. The skin overlying the left shoulder was intact. Cervical spine motion was full, and there were no signs of radiculopathy. The left shoulder had full passive and active range of motion but was painful with active abduction, forward flexion, and external rotation. She was nontender to palpation but had discomfort with Neer and Hawkins impingement maneuvers. Sensory and motor function in the left upper extremity were intact, and the radial pulse was palpable.

Plain radiographs of the left shoulder showed no fracture, degenerative changes, or bony lesion. The presentation was felt to be consistent with subacromial bursitis, and she received a subacromial corticosteroid injection (1 cc Kenalog 40 mg with 9 cc 1% lidocaine). NSAIDs and physical therapy were recommended.

One month later, she reported 50% improvement but persistent pain with impingement maneuvers. A noncontrast MRI of the shoulder was obtained. Imaging demonstrated marked edema throughout the infraspinatus muscle, a 3 cm full-thickness supraspinatus tendon tear, and an effusion in the glenohumeral joint.

A 26-year-old woman presented two weeks after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery with a five-day history of worsening epigastric pain and nausea. On examination she was afebrile with a pulse of 85 beats/min, blood pressure of 123/83 mmHg, normal bowel sounds, and supraumbilical tenderness; a small (< 1 cm), non-incarcerated umbilical hernia was noted. She appeared pale, clammy, and adynamic (ASA score 2–3). Laboratory studies showed a white-blood-cell count of 14.7/nL and a C-reactive protein level of 120 mg/dL; coagulation studies were normal. Abdominal ultrasound was unrevealing. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen was interpreted by the radiologist as showing an incarcerated umbilical hernia. Given the acute-abdomen presentation and elevated inflammatory markers, consent was obtained for an exploratory laparotomy.

A 54-year-old woman with insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (noncompliant) and recurrent urinary tract infections presented with a 3-day history of right lower-quadrant and right flank dull abdominal pain, fever, and dysuria. She had been lethargic, prompting ED evaluation. She denied medications or allergies, reported a 30-pack-year smoking history, and no alcohol or drug use.  

On arrival, she was minimally responsive and obtunded, requiring intubation. Initial vital signs: blood pressure 89/55 mmHg, temperature 97.8 °F, heart rate 107 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 89% on room air. Physical exam showed an intubated, minimally responsive woman with equal, reactive pupils.  

Laboratory studies revealed WBC 18.48 ×10^3/μL, BUN 73 mg/dL, creatinine 3.36 mg/dL. Blood and urine cultures were later positive for Escherichia coli. A noncontrast CT of the abdomen/pelvis showed mild right hydroureter and hydronephrosis without obstruction, plus perinephric inflammatory changes. She met criteria for septic shock: she received IV antibiotics, fluid bolus without BP improvement, and was started on norepinephrine.  

Cardiac studies: initial troponin I was negative but trended to 0.02 ng/mL, then 1.46 ng/mL, and 19.8 ng/mL. The first ECG showed sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. With the second troponin rise, ECG showed minimal ST elevations in leads I and aVL. With the third troponin rise, ECG showed ST elevations in leads I and aVL with reciprocal ST depressions in II, III, and aVF. Central venous oxygen saturation was 75%.  

Given the ST-segment elevations and rising troponins, the patient was taken for emergent coronary angiography for suspected STEMI.

A 52-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis, Raynaud disease, Hashimoto thyroiditis, and osteoarthritis underwent a right middle finger distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint arthrodesis for severe arthritis. The procedure and early healing were uneventful, with radiographs at 6 and 12 weeks demonstrating near-complete and complete union. One year later, she noted a progressively enlarging, firm, tender, 3 mm–raised linear mass aligned with the dorsal surgical scar of the right middle finger. There was no fluctuance or joint instability. Office fluoroscopy confirmed a solid fusion without lucency or ectopic calcification. A 4 mm punch biopsy of skin and subcutaneous tissue over the lesion showed chronic inflammation with associated foreign material and no evidence of malignancy; microscopic analysis revealed dermal collagen, mild fibrosis, and extensive small lymphocytic infiltrates.

An 18-year-old man with no past medical history and no tobacco use presented with 4 days of fever, dyspnea, and anorexia. Four days before presentation, he had begun continuous use of a nicotine- and tar-free vaping device purchased online. He denied use of other medications or supplements and had no history of asthma.

On arrival, he was alert. Vital signs were: temperature 39.0°C, blood pressure 114/61 mmHg, heart rate 138/min, respiratory rate 16/min, and oxygen saturation 94% on 2 L/min of supplemental oxygen. Lung examination revealed coarse bilateral crackles; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 18,370/μL with 90.9% neutrophils and 0.4% eosinophils, and a C-reactive protein level of 6.28 mg/dL. Tests for Krebs von den Lungen-6, antinuclear antibodies, and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were within normal limits. SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative.

Chest radiography and CT imaging demonstrated thickening of bronchovascular bundles and interlobular septa in both lungs. In the right upper lobe, there were peripheral granular shadows, nodules, and ground-glass opacity. A small right pleural effusion was noted; there was no cardiomegaly.

Empiric treatment with ceftriaxone (2 g/day) and azithromycin (500 mg/day) was initiated, but the patient’s oxygen requirement increased to 4 L/min.

A 45-year-old woman presented with severe mid-thoracic back pain of 1-week duration. On admission, neurologic examination showed impaired sensation to light touch, pain, and vibration in the left lower limb up to the T4 dermatome. MRI of the thoracic spine revealed a T2-hyperintense intramedullary lesion extending from T1 to T7, with contrast enhancement between T1 and T3. Brain MRI and visual evoked potentials were normal.  
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis demonstrated acellularity, normal protein, and negative oligoclonal bands. Serologic testing for HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, CMV, EBV, HBV, HCV, and HIV in both serum and CSF was unremarkable; PCR for HSV-1 and HSV-2 in CSF was negative. Serum sarcoidosis markers and tumor markers were within normal limits. Immunologic studies showed an ANA titer of 1:320, with negative anti-ENA, anti-dsDNA, anticardiolipin, anti-β2 glycoprotein I antibodies, lupus cells, and cryoglobulins.  
The patient improved after 5 days of intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g daily) followed by an oral corticosteroid taper. Twenty days after completing the taper, she developed chest pain, paraparesis, hyperreflexia, spasticity of both legs, symmetric sensory loss below T4, and urinary retention. Examination revealed bilateral Babinski signs, left lower-extremity strength of MRC grade 1/5, and right strength of grade 2/5. Repeat thoracic MRI showed lesion extension from T1 to T8, and chest CT demonstrated bilateral pleural effusions consistent with serositis.  
Two weeks later, while still on oral corticosteroids, she experienced a second relapse of thoracic myelitis; MRI revealed extension of the lesion to T12. Laboratory tests at that time showed leukopenia, an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and urinary protein excretion of 400 mg over 24 hours.

A 31-year-old single, nulligravida woman presented with a 4-month history of progressive abdominal swelling accompanied by worsening dysmenorrhea, menorrhagia, early satiety, weight loss, and abdominal pain. She reported regular 5-day menstrual cycles every 28 days since menarche at age 11 and was sexually inactive. Her sister had undergone exploratory laparotomy for an ovarian tumour 5 years earlier; details of the diagnosis were unavailable. 

On examination, there was no pallor, jaundice, or lymphadenopathy. Abdominal examination revealed gross distention with ascites; pelvic examination was deferred, and digital rectal examination was normal. Vital signs were within normal limits. 

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, serum electrolytes, renal and liver function tests, clotting profile, urinalysis, and viral markers, were all within normal ranges. Chest radiograph showed no pleural effusion. 

Transabdominal ultrasound demonstrated massive ascites, a bulky uterus with multiple fibroid nodules, and a right adnexal uniformly cystic mass measuring 5.0 × 4.8 cm. Abdominopelvic CT scan confirmed massive ascites and identified a lobulated, solid complex right adnexal mass measuring 5.0 × 4.3 cm; no lymphadenopathy or other intra-abdominal abnormalities were noted. 

The working differential diagnosis was a malignant right ovarian tumour on a background of uterine fibroids, with consideration of leiomyosarcoma. The patient was counselled for exploratory laparotomy for staging and possible total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.

A 51-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of recurrent airway infections and otitis media. She had been diagnosed with asthma at a primary care clinic and treated with bronchodilators, antibiotics, and oral glucocorticoids; she had also received pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine without reduction in wheezing episodes. She had no past medical history, no smoking history, and no allergies; her family history was noncontributory. She worked as a child minder. 

On pulmonary function testing, there was no reversibility of FEV1 with salbutamol, but the V50/V25 ratio was elevated at 4.55, suggesting peripheral airway obstruction. Chest CT showed moderate bronchial wall thickening and bronchiectasis. She was started on inhaled budesonide and formoterol. 

Two weeks later she was admitted with fever (39 °C), wet cough, and wheezing with coarse crackles on auscultation. White blood cell count was 12,350/μL (neutrophils 83.1%); CRP was 1.77 mg/dL. Chest CT revealed an infiltrative shadow in the right lower lobe, centrilobular nodules in the left upper lobe, bronchial wall thickening, bronchiectasis, and splenomegaly. A positive urine pneumococcal antigen assay led to a diagnosis of pneumococcal pneumonia, and ceftriaxone was administered, with prompt symptomatic improvement. 

Exhaled nitric oxide was low (13 ppb), and there was no eosinophilia in blood or sputum; inhaled corticosteroids were discontinued. One month after discharge, she again presented with pneumonia and wheezing, prompting consideration of an underlying immunodeficiency.

A 20-year-old athletic man with no prior medical history began his military service 2 weeks before presentation. He received a first dose of the Moderna mRNA COVID-19 vaccine on Day 0, with exemption from activity for 2 days. On Day 2, he noted muscle pain in the proximal arms and perceived swelling of his forearms. On Day 3, he performed 1 hour of personal training (pull-ups and push-ups) but subsequently experienced persistent weakness, inability to carry loads, and incomplete forearm extension. He took ibuprofen and diclofenac with minimal relief and presented to the emergency department on Day 5. He denied toxins, recreational drugs, or anabolic steroids; he took only omega-3 and magnesium. He reported no systemic, cutaneous, articular, or pulmonary symptoms and had no family or personal history of autoimmune or metabolic muscle disease.

On examination, vital signs were stable. Proximal arm strength was M4+, sensation was intact, and there was mild swelling of both elbows and forearms without skin changes or arthritis. 

Laboratory studies showed: potassium 4 mmol/L, sodium 141 mmol/L, calcium 2.5 mmol/L, phosphate 0.91 mmol/L, creatinine 72 μmol/L, CO2 25 mmol/L, BUN 2 mmol/L, CRP 7 mg/L, CK >145 000 U/L, aldolase 2.7 U/L, ALT 687 U/L, AST 1930 U/L, LDH 1850 U/L, TSH 1.87 mU/L, HbA1c 5.2%, and a normal lipid profile. Dermatomyositis panel, endocrine, metabolic, and autoimmune tests were all within normal limits. Infectious serologies for hepatitis, HIV, CMV, EBV, tuberculosis, and SARS-CoV-2 (PCR and antibodies) were negative. Anti-HMGCR antibody was negative. Free and total carnitine, acyl-carnitine, and their ratio were normal. Genetic sequencing excluded CPT II deficiency. Urine dipstick was positive for blood without red blood cells on microscopy. Arm ultrasound showed hyperechogenic patches in biceps brachii and wrist flexors without effusion. Electroneuromyography was normal. Electrocardiogram showed no abnormalities.

A 51-year-old man with end-stage renal disease of unclear etiology underwent a deceased-donor renal transplant and, one year later, was treated for acute cellular and humoral rejection. Two weeks after receiving methylprednisolone (500 mg IV × 3), plasmapheresis (× 4), IVIG (1 g/kg × 2), Rituximab (375 mg/m2 × 1), and Thymoglobulin (1.5 mg/kg × 5), he presented with fever and polyarthralgia. 

He reported that joint pain began in the right knee and then involved the left shoulder and left wrist. On examination, temperature was 38.4 °C, the left wrist was swollen, and the right knee was tender with an effusion; the remainder of the vital signs and physical examination were unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies showed WBC 7.9 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL, platelets 157 × 10^3/µL, BUN 41 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.8 mg/dL (baseline 1.7), total protein 6.7 g/dL, albumin 2.2 g/dL, AST 27 U/L, ALT 71 U/L, CK 119 U/L, and uric acid 5 mg/dL. Inflammatory markers revealed an elevated ESR and CRP, and complements C3 and C4 were low. 

Wrist radiography was normal; knee radiography showed a mild effusion. Arthrocentesis of the right knee yielded 830 nucleated cells/mm^3 (62% neutrophils, 38% monocytes), and no crystals were identified on polarized microscopy. Given his hemodynamic stability, empiric antibiotics were withheld pending further evaluation. Viral serologies for EBV, CMV, BK virus, and parvovirus B19 were all negative.

A 26-year-old woman presented with sudden-onset weakness in all four limbs and right proximal thigh pain. Five years earlier, she sustained a left proximal femoral shaft fracture after a ground-level fall that was treated with intramedullary nailing. She denied recent trauma, fever, medication use, or chronic illness. On examination, vital signs were normal. She had motor weakness in all four limbs, diminished deep tendon reflexes, downgoing plantar responses, absent clonus, and intact sensory and cranial-nerve function. Laboratory studies revealed:  
• Normal thyroid profile, blood counts, glucose levels, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, renal and liver function tests, and urine analysis  
• Normal antinuclear antibody test and normal parathyroid hormone level (23.4 pg/ml)  
• Vitamin D insufficiency (24.9 ng/ml)  
• Serum electrolytes normal except for hypokalemia (2.31 mg/dl)  
• Normal acid–base balance and urinary potassium excretion  
Plain radiographs of the right femur showed a transverse, incomplete diaphyseal fracture in the proximal third of the shaft with lateral cortical sclerosis and increased anterolateral bowing. The left femur showed a healed proximal diaphyseal fracture with an intramedullary nail in situ.

An 84-year-old man with a history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, irritable bowel syndrome, transient ischemic attack, lung cancer with bone metastases, and bilateral knee osteoarthritis presented for evaluation of right knee pain and increased back pain. He had been treated for brucellosis 5 years earlier. On examination, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. There was a 5 × 10 cm soft, fluctuant, non-tender mass in the posterior aspect of the right knee without erythema, warmth, or discharge. Knee range of motion was full, and distal neurovascular status was intact. Laboratory studies showed a low white-cell count and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Ultrasonography of the right knee demonstrated a moderate to large joint effusion without definite synovial thickening. On August 22, ultrasound-guided aspiration of the posterior knee swelling yielded 80 mL of fluid, which was sent for culture and cell‐count analysis.

A 41-year-old woman was admitted in December 2019 for thick crusts and a nonpruritic erythematous rash on her face, scalp, neck, trunk, and extremities, which began 3 months earlier on her trunk and arms and then spread. Initial treatment with oral azithromycin and topical antibiotics was given after a presumptive diagnosis of impetigo. A bacterial skin swab and a native mycological examination were both negative. A biopsy for histopathology and atypical mycobacterial culture was advised but not performed.

Over the ensuing weeks, she developed malaise, anorexia, abdominal pain, vomiting, hair loss, and chills and was briefly hospitalized. Laboratory evaluation showed elevated liver enzymes and carbohydrate-deficient transferrin; abdominal ultrasound revealed diffuse parenchymal liver damage, leading to a diagnosis of chronic alcoholic hepatitis. Her medical history was notable only for left lung lobectomy for a benign lesion, an appendectomy at 13, occasional alcohol use, and marijuana smoking; she denied immunosuppressive illness or medications. She reported unconfirmed penicillin allergy. Family history was positive for psoriasis and hypertension; she had two male sexual partners in the past year.

On examination, she was malnourished and afebrile but later developed fevers up to 38.5 °C with odynophagia. There were infiltrated plaques with crusts and erosions on the nose, cheeks, neck, scalp, trunk, and extremities. Small, nontender, freely movable supraclavicular and inguinal lymph nodes were palpable. Ultrasound of peripheral lymph nodes showed reactive lymphadenitis. MRI angiography of the aorta, echocardiography, chest radiograph, and CT of the head and paranasal sinuses were normal; abdominal ultrasound reiterated chronic parenchymal liver damage.

A 72-year-old Caucasian man presented with a one-year history of worsening dyspnea on exertion and bilateral leg edema. He reported paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea and orthopnea requiring him to sleep in a reclining chair and was limited to walking only a few steps before severe shortness of breath developed. He denied chest pain, and repeated measurements of cardiac enzymes were negative. An echocardiogram performed eight months earlier showed mild dilation and hypokinesis of the right ventricle. Trials of therapy for presumed obstructive lung disease and courses of antibiotics for erythema and leg edema had been ineffective, and evaluations excluded deep venous thrombosis and obstructive disease of the lungs, abdomen, or pelvis.
On examination, temperature was 37°C, blood pressure 126/75 mm Hg, heart rate 95 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91% on room air; ambulation reduced saturation to 87%, and he appeared cyanotic. Electrocardiography showed left atrial enlargement and nonspecific T-wave abnormalities. A chest CT scan revealed nodular thickening of the pericardium and bilateral pleura. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated severe dilation of the inferior vena cava with a central venous pressure of 30 mm Hg and intrahepatic venous dilation, marked interventricular septal shift with respiration and right ventricular compression, restrictive movement of the lateral ventricular walls with a septal bounce, and decreased mitral inflow during inspiration.

A 35-year-old man presented with fever for two weeks, severe diffuse headache and vomiting for one week, and right-eye swelling with vision loss for two days. The fever was high-grade and intermittent with chills and rigors and did not respond to diclofenac. After one week of fever, he developed headache and nonprojectile vomiting and was admitted locally and started on piperacillin–tazobactam. Two days later, he noted right-eye pain, swelling, and vision loss and was referred to our center. He had no history of trauma, smoking, alcohol use, or prior medical illness.

On examination, temperature was 100.4°F, blood pressure 101/67 mm Hg. He was alert and oriented with no nuchal rigidity or focal neurologic deficits. Ophthalmologic exam of the right eye revealed decreased extraocular movements, a relative afferent pupillary defect, and funduscopic evidence of central retinal artery occlusion. Nasal examination showed thick mucopurulent discharge in both middle meatuses.

Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 11,500/mm3 with mild neutrophilia. HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C tests were negative. Urinalysis revealed proteinuria and glycosuria, random blood sugar was 238 mg/dL, and hemoglobin A1C was 14.2%. A mucosal biopsy from the right middle meatus was sent for fungal examination. On KOH wet mount, irregularly branched septate fungal hyphae were seen.

Contrast-enhanced MRI of the head demonstrated ethmoidal sinusitis with intracranial extension across the lamina papyracea, causing right orbital cellulitis and ischemic optic neuropathy.

A 40-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 2-month history of headache, memory problems, weight loss, chronic diarrhea, and arthralgias, and new-onset significant left-sided weakness impairing his activities of daily living. His medical history included recurrent sinus infections and otitis media; there was no family history of central nervous system or immunologic disease. 

Initial noncontrast CT of the head showed an ill-defined mass in the right gangliocapsular region extending into the midbrain with approximately 10 mm of leftward subfalcine herniation. Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed a 4.4 × 2.4 × 4.5 cm right basal ganglia lesion with midbrain extension, peripheral ring enhancement, extensive surrounding edema, and a 7 mm midline shift.

CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated bilateral lower‐lobe reticulonodular infiltrates, splenomegaly, and mesenteric lymphadenopathy. A CT-guided retroperitoneal lymph node biopsy showed no malignancy. Small bowel push enteroscopy revealed acute duodenitis and mild villous blunting. An oncologist initiated steroids for presumed lymphoma or unspecified malignancy, and infectious‐disease studies for acid‐fast bacilli and fungi were ordered.

On transfer, examination showed 0/5 strength in the left upper extremity, left facial droop, midline palatal elevation, midline tongue protrusion, and right ptosis. Laboratory studies revealed a leukocytosis of 24.5 × 10^9/L; other routine blood tests were within normal limits. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis demonstrated low glucose and low protein and was negative for Cryptococcus and Streptococcus species. Serum testing showed reactive Toxoplasma IgM and IgG (17.4 IU/mL); tests for HIV antibody, rapid plasma reagin, Treponema pallidum particle agglutination, cytomegalovirus IgM, Rickettsia, Brucella, and Bartonella antibodies, antinuclear antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, urine Legionella antigen, and pneumococcal antigens were all negative.

A stereotactic brain biopsy was performed; four specimens obtained at 90° angles and an additional four deeper specimens revealed a histiocyte-predominant neuroinflammatory process on pathology.

A 27-year-old man with a history of heavy alcohol consumption presented with 4 days of hematochezia. His initial hemoglobin level was 8.5 g/dL. On admission, irrigation through a nasogastric (Levin) tube produced old blood clots, and digital rectal examination revealed melena. He received two units of packed red blood cells. Emergent esophagogastroduodenoscopy and flexible sigmoidoscopy did not identify a bleeding source. Capsule endoscopy demonstrated bleeding in the small intestine but failed to visualize a lesion due to poor video quality. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen revealed small-bowel intussusception at the distal ileum with a possible 2-cm low-density intraluminal mass.

A 29-year-old woman and nursing school graduate first presented with vertigo, ataxia, and left-sided weakness. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed oligoclonal bands, and MRI showed multiple T2 hyperintense white-matter lesions in the subcortical, periventricular, and deep white matter of both cerebral hemispheres, with involvement of the genu of the corpus callosum and the left middle cerebellar peduncle, as well as some cerebellar atrophy. She was diagnosed with relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis and received methylprednisolone and other disease-modifying therapies over subsequent years.
